Early bird travellers and residents simply curious to see how the new system worked were the first to pass through the facility when it opened at 6.30am, with some calling the clearance process “light speed”. Many travellers said they approved of the new approach, by which travellers heading in either direction need only show one identification document. Others also said they were impressed with the architecture of the building, which took six years to construct. But others found the facility mazelike and simply too huge to cross quickly, which undercut the appeal of the new clearance process. Speaking to the press after inspecting the new 24-hour checkpoint’s operation on Monday, No 2 city official Eric Chan Kwok-ki said he was pleased with the “smooth” operation. “There’s a reason we chose [Monday] to open. The National Day ‘golden week’ holiday has just ended,” he said. “We believe there will be fewer visitors. So everyone has time to get familiar with the operations. “We hope our colleagues will quickly familiarise themselves with the operation over the next few days so they can handle the bigger challenges during the peak on Saturday and Sunday when there will be more people,” the chief secretary said. Chan also said that if the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance” model worked well, the government would consider extending it to other checkpoints. Officials said clearance at Huanggang could be cut to five minutes, from about 30 minutes needed at the previous facility. Hong Kong residents who hold a valid mainland travel permit can use their Hong Kong ID cards interchangeably at the joint clearance channel for both outbound and inbound trips. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said a joint command centre had been set up with Shenzhen authorities to ensure operations went smoothly on both sides of the border. “It will be in operation as long as necessary, especially during peak times, like weekends or during the Apec conference,” Tang said. Shenzhen is hosting the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in mid-November, while the bloc’s finance ministers will gather in Hong Kong later this month. Traffic at the crossing is expected to surge on the coming long weekend, as Monday is a public holiday following the Chung Yeung Festival on Sunday. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said contingency plans were in place to ensure sufficient public transport for the anticipated rush. “We will not underestimate the challenge to be brought about in the coming long weekend,” Chan said. According to the Security Bureau, the new control point had handled 20,201 incoming and 22,011 departing travellers by 5pm. The 42,212 passenger trips recorded represented a 181 per cent increase compared with average Monday traffic last month at the previous control point. The new port also handled 2,713 incoming and 2,995 outgoing vehicles. The number of vehicle trips was 12 per cent more than the average recorded on Mondays last month. Among the first travellers using the new facility was a Shenzhen resident, surnamed Liao, who crossed into Hong Kong at around 6.30am and returned to the mainland shortly before 7am. “The clearance was done in a minute,” he said, adding praise for the architecture of the building, which he likened to a modern airport. Another mainland visitor, surnamed Wen, also praised the speed of the clearance process. “It was light speed,” Wen said. Dey Wu, a Shenzhen resident who holds an American passport, agreed the clearance was efficient. “The process took less than a minute,” she said, adding that officials told her she was the first foreigner to cross. “I used to come [to Hong Kong] once a month. Now, I would be happy to come twice a week.” But on the Shenzhen side, a 70-year-old Hong Kong traveller who uses a cane to walk, Helen Ho, said the building was too big. “I did not feel it was actually much faster as the building is so big and I had to take many lifts, and I had not been guided enough along my way,” Ho said. A Tung Chung resident also said a technical glitch prevented him from using facial recognition clearance although he had registered for the option in advance. He ended up using his Hong Kong ID card to pass the gate. Cheerful members of a mainland tour group held up signs with slogans such as “New Huanggang, first in line” as they arrived. One traveller, 52, and 11 of her family members spent five hours taking a high-speed train from Hunan province to Shenzhen. “It is great. It is modernised and service is great,” said the woman, surnamed Kuang, adding they would continue their journey to Hong Kong. Hong Kong authorities said 30 tour groups used the crossing to head south into the city. Timothy Chui Ting-pong, executive director of the Hong Kong Tourism Association, said he expected more local travel agencies to launch tours themed around the crossing in the near future. He added that some visiting mainland tour groups had already switched to the facility for their departure. Visitors also drove to cross the border, but some said the time they spent waiting for their turn was more than double compared with the previous checkpoint as drivers were not familiar with the new procedures. But celebrity feng shui master Mak Ling-ling, who also drove across, said it took her one minute for clearance. “The facility is new, it is quite natural drivers may take some time to familiarise themselves with the new procedures,” she said. “Overall, the new port has more lanes so the process was in general faster.” The crossing is expected to be able to handle up to 300,000 travellers a day. The Immigration Department said it expected about 100,000 people to use Huanggang Port daily during initial operations. It can also handle 15,000 vehicles a day. The previous facility began 24-hour clearance in 2003, becoming the country’s first land crossing to provide round-the-clock clearance for both travellers and cargo. It handled an average of 40,000 visitors a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people. On average, 9,000 vehicles used the crossing. Additional reporting by Kristen Cheung

title: Why China is likely to be cautious about recent Trump-Putin diesel deal
description: The US may still try to target major buyers of Russian energy despite the deal aimed at cutting American fuel prices, analysts warn.
content: China is likely to view the latest US dealings with Russia as “transactional”, according to observers, who said Beijing was likely to wait and see what the longer-term impact would be given the possibility that Donald Trump might abruptly change course again. The US president announced that under a deal with Vladimir Putin, Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets. He wrote on social media that another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, with a further 1 million tonnes “within a short period of time”. “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump added. Analysts said it was too soon to say if this was a temporary fix driven by domestic political concerns or the first step in a wider push to dismantle Western sanctions. The agreement marked a sharp reversal from the United States, coming just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which allows him to penalise major buyers of Russian energy. It was also struck less than a month before the midterm elections on November 3, where soaring fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ hold on Congress. The Kremlin said the deal was made during a “very substantive and friendly” call focused on the war in Ukraine. On Sunday, Trump also said both sides had agreed an “energy ceasefire” “effective immediately” but Ukraine said it knew nothing about it and Russia continued to strike power plants. Asked about the diesel deal on Monday, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China’s position on Ukraine was clear and consistent, and that it believed dialogue was the only way to resolve the crisis. Cui Hongjian, head of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said China would watch how the deal developed. He said Ukraine and Europe were hoping it would be an emergency “stopgap” rather than a “first step that sets off a domino effect” on sanctions. He added that China’s view would be shaped by whether Russia used the deal as a springboard to “pry loose the West’s entire set of energy sanctions against it”. “So China’s approach right now, in my view, will still be to wait and see which direction things develop in,” Cui said. He also said it was likely to have little impact on China’s energy trade with Russia, as Moscow still needed to sell to its largest buyer. “The question is to what extent will [the deal] actually affect China’s energy security or whether China can protect its interests in the overall energy market,” he said. “I don’t think China will be too concerned at the moment about what major direct impact this might have. It still requires a period of observation and assessment.” Zhang Chi, a senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said the diesel deal was “self-contradictory” and reflected the “selective” nature of the US approach. But he said the Graham Act could be used as a bargaining chip in talks with Russia, China and India. “Even as the US pursues Russian energy for its own benefit, the secondary tariff or secondary sanctions mechanism under the Graham Act could still be triggered to target other major importers,” Zhang said. Beijing would also need to closely monitor the sunset provisions of the Graham Act and how the resolution of the Russia-Ukraine war might affect its implementation, Zhang added. Ma Bo, an associate professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Trump was hoping the deal would help limit Republican losses in next month’s elections. “Therefore, I think this is a very transactional matter, perhaps a one-time offer, and it may be adjusted after the midterm elections,” he said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticised the deal, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia without a lasting de-escalation agreement was “an obvious weakness”. Ukraine, which Trump asked to stop “knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”, continued to target Russian refineries after the diesel deal was announced, prompting the US leader to call on Saturday for Zelensky to be replaced. Ma said Beijing would have to wait and see if these latest developments had any impact, and that China and other Asian importers should not take Trump’s deal with Putin as “a clear indicator of future tariff decisions or cooperation with Russia”. “If countries adjust their strategic planning or expect a permanent US policy shift [on secondary sanctions], that could backfire when the midterm election results are in,” he added. Zhang said the diesel deal would be a fresh test case for the evolving US-China relationship. “How the US uses and adjusts its sanctions system based on the new strategic positioning of US-China ties is a new observation point to verify the progress of improvement in US-China relations,” he said.

title: Hackers heat fridges at major French supermarkets, spoiling food
description: Authorities launch probe after chillers were cranked to 50 degrees Celsius, causing tens of millions of euros in losses.
content: Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) overnight, causing fires and spoiling food. The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday that a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”, leading to food losses and fires. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office said. France was coordinating with European ‌counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk. Felix Aime, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected. Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said all affected food had been discarded to eliminate health risks. Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarche in central Paris throwing cartfuls of defrosted frozen foods ⁠into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street. Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket group had also been targeted. “Targeting equipment essential to ‌the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X. There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV ‌the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”. Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said: “This incident underlines ⁠the importance of resilience across the entire supply ⁠chain”. Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source close to Lecornu said ‌ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems ‌updated ‌with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”. On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software ‌updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August ⁠that led to food losses after fridges were affected. In a statement, French retail association Federation du Commerce et de la Distribution called for “full transparency” from Danfoss about the incident. It said supermarkets aimed ⁠to protect consumers and return to normal operations as soon as possible. The FCD said some impacted stores were already back up and running. Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a “security issue” on its network and had taken several ‌systems offline as a precaution. A message on the retailer’s ‌smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a “cybersecurity incident”. Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders. Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets. Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying “site temporarily down”. It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

title: Selfies, queues and confusion, but Huanggang Port’s wow factor shines through
description: Motorists using checkpoint said border clearance took longer than expected, while building’s spaciousness and design impressed travellers.
content: The much-anticipated opening of the revamped Huanggang Port border crossing between Hong Kong and Shenzhen on Monday was marked by excitement, eagerness and confusion. At around 8am, 1½ hours after the control point opened, many private vehicles were neatly lining up for immigration clearance. The use of new technology, a new location and a new facility meant that extra time and patience were needed. Visitors, mostly tourists and retirees travelling on foot, had a wow moment inside the modern facility, prompting plenty of selfies. Vehicles queued at a temporary traffic buffer zone on San Sham Road in the morning before making their way to the new facility, where police cordoned off roads and directed traffic towards the building. Driver Ho Shun-ping, in his sixties, waited 25 minutes in the buffer zone and another 30 minutes at the “integrated information collection device” before finally crossing the border into mainland China by car. “It actually took a long time because many drivers were using the device from the car for the first time,” he said. “They parked a bit far from the device and had to jump out of the car to check. The staff inside the booth then had to help manually one by one.” Ho said the process had reversed the usual pattern at the old crossing: cars used to wait for passengers crossing on foot, but on Monday it was the other way round. “The overall process took longer than expected compared with my usual experience at the old crossing,” he said, adding that he used to spend only 10 to 20 minutes crossing at the old checkpoint, “even waiting for five to 10 minutes would have been long enough in the past”. The opening of the facility marked the end of the 37-year run of the Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang control point, which began operating in 1989. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Sunday called the revamped port “a critical milestone” for connectivity in the Greater Bay Area, saying the landmark project would allow the city to better integrate into and serve the overall development of the country. He described it as the most important 24-hour passenger land boundary checkpoint, with a designed daily capacity of 200,000 passenger trips. The border crossing has introduced a new “collaborative inspection and joint clearance” model, which is designed to cut clearance time from about 30 minutes to around five. Eligible passengers can complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates. Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, urged Shenzhen authorities to update electronic maps and road signs. He said unclear signs had caused confusion among Hong Kong motorists. “Some drivers spent at least 10 minutes around the Shenzhen side of the border and could not tell the road signs for the new or old border [crossing],” Lee said. Three retirees – a couple surnamed Liu and their friend surnamed Lam – set off from Sheung Shui to visit the crossing as a tourist attraction. They spent almost 30 minutes crossing the border. That included a bathroom break, photo-taking at every opportunity, connecting to the free Wi-fi, and asking an immigration officer how to register for the “joint clearance” channel. The actual time they spent crossing through the “joint clearance” channel was less than a minute. The spaciousness and the fluid design of the checkpoint building made it a popular photo spot for travellers. The Liu couple took photos on the escalators leading to the departure hall on level 5, while Lam stopped to photograph a vast glass wall overlooking Shenzhen as he passed the arrival hall on level 4. “It has high ceilings. The environment’s great, the air quality’s great. It’s very comfortable,” Mr Liu, 80, said. Shortly after 1pm, queues of about 20 people had formed at each of the “joint clearance” lanes in operation. The three retirees had waited for 12 minutes. Five minutes into the wait, Lam said he wished authorities would open all the clearance lanes. While most of the automated lanes were in use, about five were cordoned off at the first gate. “They should open all the lanes so we don’t have to queue. If they had expected many people to come, then they should open up more lanes,” Lam said. All three retirees said they preferred the Heung Yuen Wai checkpoint, which they could reach with a HK$2 fare from their homes in Sheung Shui. The fare to the revamped Huanggang checkpoint was HK$4.10 as they first had to take a minibus to the San Tin interchange before switching to a bus. “We have already retired, so we like to save every penny we can,” Lam said. “I’d come here if I needed to, but not for the sake of it again.”

title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 may lead to robotics breakthrough  as soon as next year: Unitree founder
description: Wang Xingxing says OpenAI’s latest advances have accelerated prospects for a ‘ChatGPT moment’ in embodied intelligence.
content: US start-up OpenAI’s latest advances in artificial intelligence may be a tipping point that leads to a breakthrough for the robotics industry as soon as next year, according to the founder of Chinese giant Unitree Robotics. Wang Xingxing, also the CEO of the Hangzhou-based company, said on Monday that OpenAI’s recently released GPT-6 model prompted expectations that a breakthrough could happen “within one or two years”. “It’s possible that, say, a GPT-7 model released next year could directly crack the problems of embodied intelligence,” he said at an industry event in Shanghai. In August, before GPT-6’s release, Wang said the industry could take two to three years at its fastest pace, or as long as a decade, to reach its “ChatGPT moment” – a critical threshold of technological maturity. He defined that moment as robots being able to complete around 80 per cent of tasks in 80 per cent of unfamiliar environments using voice or text commands. Wang’s latest comments came after OpenAI unveiled its flagship GPT-6 Astra model in September, demonstrating powerful capabilities in robotic manipulation. Unitree had also tested the new model on its own robots and got “good results”, he said. “The whole embodied intelligence industry has been shaken up after the release of GPT-6,” he said on the opening day of the 26th China International Industry Fair in Shanghai. “The biggest mistake I’ve made over the past decade or so is that I didn’t believe in AI enough.” As head of China’s leading humanoid robot maker, Wang’s public remarks are closely watched by investors and analysts as a bellwether of the state of the domestic robotics industry. He had previously sought to temper growing investor frenzy over China’s humanoid robot sector, warning that hardware development was progressing faster than the software needed to make robots genuinely “intelligent” and useful in real-world settings. While the physical capabilities of China’s humanoid robots have continued to impress – including the setting of several speed records at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing in August – their limited autonomy and “intelligence” have continued to raise questions about their commercialisation prospects. Previously focused on hardware, Unitree is also increasing investment in developing the “brains” of its robots. The company earlier said it planned to allocate around half of the proceeds from its recent initial public offering to research and development on robotic models. Wang said on Monday that Unitree was carrying out trials in factories, although the efficiency and ability of its robots still needed “further improvement”.

title: Review | Opera Hong Kong’s Cavalleria Rusticana and Pagliacci double bill lights up the stage
description: Cav/Pag captivates with vibrant staging and stellar performances, showcasing verismo pairing’s raw emotion, gripping tales.
content: Opera Hong Kong’s first fully staged production of Pietro Mascagni’s 1890 Cavalleria Rusticana and Ruggero Leoncavallo’s 1892 Pagliacci does justice to the classic double bill. Familiarly known as Cav/Pag, the production features lively staging, strong performances in the leading roles and splendid work by the Opera Hong Kong Chorus. Since 1893, the two operas have often been performed together for obvious reasons. Both are set in the rural Italian south and both explore themes of jealousy, betrayal and revenge that culminate in violent death. They are also outstanding examples of the verismo school of opera: gritty, realistic stories about ordinary people, abandoning traditional recitative for sung dialogue, and stripping ornamentation from the singing to focus on melody and the direct expression of emotion. Cavalleria Rusticana, or Rustic Chivalry, takes place in a Sicilian village at Easter. Turiddu returns from army service to find his sweetheart, Lola, married to the carter, Alfio. Attempting to forget her, he seduces the innocent Santuzza. However, this only rekindles Lola’s interest, and the two embark on an affair. Humiliated and distraught when Turiddu refuses to leave Lola, Santuzza reveals the betrayal to Alfio. Intent on vengeance, Alfio challenges Turiddu to a fight to the death. Pagliacci is set in Calabria and the clowns of the title are a travelling troupe performing commedia dell’arte, the ancient form of improvised theatre. The troupe’s leader, Canio, is jealously possessive of his young wife, Nedda. Becoming afraid of him, she agrees to run away with her secret lover, Silvio. One of the actors, Tonio, who had been cruelly rejected by Nedda, discovers her plan and tells Canio. As they perform the roles of a cuckolded husband and unfaithful wife on stage that night, Canio’s rage overcomes him – he stabs Nedda to death and when Silvio tries to save her, kills him, too. Director and designer Enrico Castiglione sets both operas in the same Sicilian square and prefaces them with video projections of lava flowing from Sicily’s volcano, Etna, as a metaphor for the way the burning passions of the characters erupt. Cavalleria Rusticana comes off best, not least because it is in many ways the better opera. The story is told with stark power and simplicity and momentum builds inexorably to the tragic denouement. It is also packed with gorgeous music, from Turiddu’s plaintive opening serenade to Lola – neatly presented with the singer in the auditorium, through two rousing, rollicking set pieces, Alfio’s “Il cavallo scalpita” (“The horse paws the ground”) and Turiddu’s “Viva, il vino spumeggiante” (“Hail to the sparkling wine”) to the varied, exquisite choruses. Pagliacci is more problematic, with an unwieldy structure, some longueurs in the music and characters with whom it is hard to sympathise. Where Mascagni and his librettists focus on driving the story forward, Leoncavallo (who was librettist as well as composer) combines a similarly melodramatic tale with more sophisticated elements – the play within a play, the idea that actors are human beings with real emotions – which can distract from the narrative flow. An excellent beginning has Tonio’s prologue performed in the auditorium with the singer walking around communicating directly with the audience and it was a good choice to have the most famous last line in all opera, “La commedia è finita!” (“The comedy is over!”) delivered by Tonio, as Leoncavallo originally intended, rather than Canio. This bookends the prologue and reflects Tonio’s role as the manipulator of events – the show’s director, in fact. However, overall Castiglione does not manage to achieve the pace and focus that he does in Cavalleria Rusticana. While the addition of a large group of clowns adds movement and colour, it is hard to believe that they would be part of such a small, down-at-heel commedia dell’arte troupe. In keeping with tradition, the roles of Turiddu and Canio, Alfio and Tonio are performed by the same tenor and baritone, here giving two exceptional artists the chance to showcase their dramatic range and fine singing. Leonardo Capalbo’s forceful, dark-toned tenor is perfectly suited to this style of music, he moves extremely well and his acting has both the realism and the emotional intensity these roles demand. He was outstanding as Turiddu, making the character’s changing moods and dilemmas convincingly real and brought plenty of passion to Canio, although there were moments when a little less might have been more. Alberto Gazale was superb in both operas – blessed with an elegant, ringing baritone, his confident, virile Alfio was skilfully contrasted with the devious Tonio, whose hunchback Gazale cleverly suggested through his posture, and he held the audience spellbound in the prologue. On the women’s side, Kate Jackman took the vocal honours – Santuzza can easily become strident, something Jackman’s warm, full mezzo smoothly avoided and she gave a heartfelt performance. Bing Bing Wang’s ultra-sexy Nedda made it easy to see why three men were all enamoured of her. Her singing suffered a few lapses but her acting was excellent, not holding back on the character’s mean side and neatly managing the physical elements required by the staging, including stylised moves and expressions when Nedda plays Colombina. Two local singers shone in supporting roles – Dominique Chan was believable and moving as Turiddu’s mother while Chen Yong was a lively Peppe in Pagliacci with an appealing rendition of Arlecchino’s charming serenade to Colombina. A special word for the Opera Hong Kong Chorus, whose singing brought out the full beauty and complexity of the music – especially impressive in Cavalleria Rusticana, which makes huge demands on the chorus, with music that ranges from lyrical to holy to upbeat. Equally impressive was their detailed acting and assured movement on stage. All the members are part-timers who must fit their commitment to Opera Hong Kong into busy lives, yet their performance was of truly professional calibre. Much praise goes to the chorus members and to chorus director Alex Tam for the passion and dedication that have enabled them to reach such a high level – it has been a pleasure to watch them evolve over the years. Roberto Gianola’s authoritative conducting brought out the best in the score and the Hong Kong Philharmonic. “Opera Hong Kong: Cavalleria Rusticana & Pagliacci”, Hong Kong Cultural Centre Grand Theatre. Reviewed: October 9.

title: Financial, mental health issues pushing women footballers towards early retirement
description: Extensive review by players’ trade union highlights the gulf between the sport’s rapid growth and conditions for most players.
content: Almost half of women’s footballers are considering leaving the game early, with financial pressures and mental health struggles the main reasons, according to a Fifpro report highlighting the gulf between the sport’s rapid growth and conditions for most players. The 2026 Fifpro Global Employment Report “Working Conditions in Women’s Football”, billed by the global players’ union as the most extensive review of working conditions in the women’s game in a decade, interviewed 800 players worldwide and found stark disparities. Some 49 per cent of players ‌surveyed said they were considering leaving football earlier than planned. Of those, 59 per cent cited their financial situation as a reason and 46 per cent pointed to psychological stress. “The women’s football industry has come a long way,” Fifpro director of women’s football Alex Culvin said. “[But] for 95 per cent [of players], the rest of the industry, there is a hell of a long way to go.” While inflation-adjusted average monthly club wages have tripled since Fifpro’s previous global study in 2017 to US$2,601, the median is substantially lower at US$1,669, illustrating what the report describes as “uneven and fragmented” growth. In 10 Eastern European countries analysed, average salaries remain below the national minimum wage. Even in western Europe and Asia/Oceania, which include some of the game’s bigger markets, ⁠average pay is not significantly higher than national minimum wages, according to Fifpro. “The professionalisation of women’s football is accelerating in some parts of the world and revenues are increasing; however, the progress ‌and benefits are not evenly distributed among players across the world,” Culvin said. The report found only 56 per cent of players have an employment contract, while 13 per cent receive a club pension and 47 per cent said their clubs do not have sufficient staff. Average contract length has risen from 12 months in 2017 to ‌19 months, while the proportion of players with agents has climbed sharply from 14 per cent to 41 per cent. “Whether a player has a written contract, a pension, medical cover ⁠or parental leave often depends less on her ⁠ability” than the country she lives in and the club she plays for, according to the report. Conditions have improved at the top Culvin said conditions have improved dramatically for a small group of about 5 per cent at the top, but many ‌players are being asked to meet professional demands without being given professional environments in which to work. “There is a recurring theme of precarity and fragile conditions,” she said. “Not only in terms of treatment and fair remuneration, but also just generally the expectations ‌that are ‌put on these players – professional expectations that don’t operate in professional circumstances because the conditions that are provided to them are suboptimal.” Mental health emerged as another significant concern, with 57 per cent of ‌players saying they had struggled with their mental health. Half of those players had not been provided with support by their clubs. Fifpro is calling for enforceable minimum standards covering areas including pay, facilities, ⁠staffing and healthcare to be written into employment agreements at the national level. Only eight of the 30 national women’s leagues analysed have a collective agreement with players through their unions. Fifpro wants psychological ⁠support to be mandatory. It pointed to the National Women’s Soccer League in the US, where mental health practitioners work alongside club staff and players have a right to six months of mental health leave. One area in which the global union said regulation had produced clear progress was maternity protection. Since Fifa introduced global minimum maternity ‌standards in 2021, the proportion of players considering leaving ‌football to have a family has fallen to 19 per cent, compared with 47 per cent in 2017. Culvin said women’s football had reached a point where rapid commercial expansion should be matched by greater protection for the players driving that growth. “There doesn’t need to be a choice for us between commercial growth and player protection,” she said. “Those two things need to go hand in hand and work in tandem.” For players with relatively short careers, she added, ambition cannot come solely from those on the pitch. “It can’t just be the player’s ambition,” she said. “It has to be matched by the club’s ambition, and not only ambition, resources to that ambition.”

title: Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress for Xi visit sparks interest in Chinese haute couture
description: Guo, one of China’s best-known couturiers, has also designed outfits for celebrities including pop star Rihanna.
content: Ivanka Trump’s appearance in a blue embroidered couture outfit during the welcome ceremony for President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month has drawn attention to its designer and the growing international profile of Chinese bespoke fashion. The outfit was designed by Guo Pei, one of China’s best-known couturiers, who also created the spectacular yellow embroidered cape with a long train and fur trim worn by pop star Rihanna at the 2015 Met Gala. Guo told the South China Morning Post that Trump’s outfit was not created specifically for the diplomatic occasion, but its design and colour were carefully considered. She said blue was chosen to convey calm and a shared aspiration for peace. The outfit was originally intended for a trip to China that US President Donald Trump’s eldest daughter had expected to make with her father. Guo said she and Ivanka Trump discussed its design and colour at the beginning of the year. Ultimately, Ivanka Trump did not make the journey to Beijing in May. But she had a front-row seat at the White House welcome ceremony for Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on September 24 at the start of a state visit aimed at stabilising a relationship tested by trade, technology and national security disputes. “Green is often associated with peace, but I felt blue could convey a more natural sense of calm,” Guo said. “I recommended blue, and Ivanka liked it too. She called the shade robin’s-egg blue.” Guo said she believed the colour had a serene quality that could express a shared desire for world peace. Bespoke clothing offers a level of fit and perfection that ready-to-wear simply cannot match Guo Pei, fashion designer The jacket featured silver-thread embroidery in a scrolling vine pattern, which Guo said “symbolised cultural common ground” because similar motifs appear in both Eastern and Western artistic traditions. Its wide, flared sleeves were designed to symbolise openness and acceptance, while the fitted inner dress was made longer than a normal day dress to convey the formality and respect befitting an occasion attended by national leaders, she said. Chinese-inspired clothing featured prominently throughout Xi’s visit. Xi wore a black Mao suit, a style with folded collars popularised by revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen, while senior Chinese officials also donned dark Chinese-style attire to the White House state dinner. Peng, meanwhile, showcased four looks: a dove-grey, loose-fitting dress; a navy dress incorporating qipao elements; a red, floor-length V-neck gown for the state dinner; and a purple midi dress with a Hanfu-style collar. Guo said she believed Peng’s clothing had been tailor-made. As China’s first lady, her clothes “do not rely on complicated details; instead, they highlight her poise and the formality appropriate to her position”, Guo said. Chinese bespoke fashion has gained popularity both at home and abroad, despite weak domestic consumption and the high prices of custom-made luxury clothing. China’s haute couture market was valued at US$13.42 billion last year and is projected to reach US$31.86 billion by 2034, according to HTF Market Intelligence. The market research firm said “rising disposable incomes among affluent consumers, increasing demand for exclusivity, growing luxury consumption, and expanding influence of international fashion trends” would drive the growth. Guo, a guest member of the Federation de la Haute Couture et de la Mode, French high-end fashion’s governing body, said more than 60 per cent of her brand’s pieces were priced above €20,000 (US$22,406), with demand coming primarily from international markets. While overall demand had remained “relatively stable”, Guo said she had noticed more younger clients turning to haute couture for special occasions, such as weddings and high-end events. “Bespoke clothing offers a level of fit and perfection that ready-to-wear simply cannot match,” she said. Guo said she was optimistic about the market’s prospects in China, where consumers increasingly valued aesthetics, quality and craftsmanship over simply meeting basic needs. “People are increasingly choosing things for their beauty and fine craftsmanship, and because they genuinely love them,” she said. “I believe this trend will bode well for the market.”

title: India’s opposition marches on Supreme Court as ‘cockroach’ protests gain ground
description: India’s opposition alliance is harnessing the youth-led protests, testing whether their anger can build real political momentum against Modi.
content: Indian opposition leaders and student activists marched on the Supreme Court on Monday to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter roll manipulation, as authorities erected heavy barricades and shut six metro stations across New Delhi. The rally went ahead after the Chief Justice of India turned down a meeting request from an opposition delegation, urging them instead to file a formal petition. Mainstream opposition parties have sought to harness a groundswell of public anger generated by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has spearheaded weeks of protests against alleged electoral roll manipulation. Tensions boiled over during the weekend when Delhi police detained dozens of student activists and blocked planned rallies, handing the opposition fresh political momentum for Monday’s march. Among those held was CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was picked up by police on Saturday ahead of a demonstration that authorities said lacked official clearance due to law-and-order concerns. Dipke was released the following day alongside other activists. The CJP was founded in May after India’s chief justice Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to people with fake or bogus degrees as “cockroaches”, remarks widely interpreted as a swipe at young Indians facing problems with education and employment. Embracing the slight, Dipke launched the group as a satirical online platform that quickly morphed into a formidable street-level movement. Although Dipke has repeatedly said the CJP is not a registered political party – describing it as a Gen Z-led pressure movement aimed at strengthening democracy – its growing momentum has led observers to speculate it could eventually enter electoral politics. Opposition parties and student supporters have taken to the streets almost daily this month, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a recent electoral roll update known as the Special Intensive Revision. Critics and opposition leaders say the process led to the deletion of around 130 million names from draft rolls, alleging that millions of genuine voters were wrongly removed to benefit the ruling party. The Election Commission has strongly denied the allegations, defending the removals as a routine clean-up of deceased, relocated and duplicate registrations. In response to the weekend crackdown, the Supreme Court ruled on Sunday that peaceful, unarmed protesters in Delhi could not be detained except in accordance with legal procedures. The court also directed authorities to ensure metro and railway services operated normally – a directive swiftly tested on Monday when police closed six stations citing security concerns ahead of the march. Local media reports said Rahul Gandhi, leader of the multiparty INDIA opposition alliance, had filed a petition in the Supreme Court against Kumar over alleged “vote theft”. Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an independent political commentator, said clamping down on the protests could prove counterproductive for the Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) federal coalition government. “It seems the government has not been able to come up with any counterstrategy,” Mukhopadhyay said. “They are creating a certain public mood. There is a strong possibility that the CJP could take to the electoral path.” Parallel demonstrations have broken out in major cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru and Kolkata, alongside reports of police detentions across Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and West Bengal. “The movement is escalating and becoming far more widespread than initially thought,” said Kingshuk Nag, an author and political commentator. “It is led by students and their line of thinking is unconventional. Now, opposition parties have jumped into the fray.” Nag added that while the BJP was adept at countering the main opposition Congress party, it would need a new playbook to handle student leaders. He drew comparisons to Arvind Kejriwal, founder of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), who launched his political career following a major 2011 anti-corruption movement. Nag said the CJP could potentially become a comparable – or even larger – political force. However, other analysts urge caution regarding the movement’s long-term impact. Praveen Rai, a political analyst at the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, pointed out that Congress previously ran a campaign centred on allegations of vote theft during state elections in West Bengal without gaining traction. “The ongoing street protest by Congress is a manifestation of deep political frustration arising out of several electoral defeats,” Rai said, adding that the demand for the election chief’s resignation was “politically immature” and lacked credible evidence. Nonetheless, Rai said the youth movement had galvanised the opposition to demand administrative accountability. “CJP can play an important role as a stakeholder. Elected governments tend to lose momentum and start taking things for granted if there are no active opposition parties or pressure groups.” While India’s history has seen youth-led protests capable of toppling governments – such as the 1990 student movement over caste reservations that destabilised the VP Singh administration – Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government does not appear to be in immediate danger. The next general election is not due until 2029. However, elections in key states including Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Punjab will offer an early test of whether this youth-driven momentum can pose a genuine threat to the BJP’s dominance.

title: Hong Kong electronics fairs to showcase 120 robots as firms aim to expand AI use
description: Hong Kong Electronics Fair and electronicAsia will bring together more than 3,200 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions.
content: More than 120 robots, including humanoid machines designed for factory work and elderly care, will be showcased at two major Hong Kong electronics fairs, as mainland Chinese manufacturers seek to expand the commercial applications of AI and tap overseas markets. The Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition) and electronicAsia will open on Tuesday at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, bringing together more than 3,200 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions for four days. Leo Yang, Asia-Pacific director of mainland Chinese firm Booster Robotics, said that the company was developing affordable robots capable of competing with leading American manufacturers, which he acknowledged had an edge in technology. “China and the US are the top two in this industry,” Yang said at a media preview on Monday. “The top ones [in the US] are the best ones in terms of hardware and software. But pricing is an issue, a problem. So what we are doing is developing practical, affordable and reliable robotics to compete in the market.” The company is showcasing its latest humanoid robot, the Booster T2, which was launched in August and is making its Hong Kong debut. Equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) chips and a maximum dual-arm payload of 10kg, the robot is designed to perform tasks such as grasping objects, transporting goods and sorting materials. Yang said the robot had computing power of 2,000 trillion operations per second and supported open development tools, allowing researchers and businesses to customise its functions. While its current applications largely focus on education and research, the company plans to introduce more commercial uses from late this year into 2027. These include deploying robots as security guards, factory workers and assistants capable of caring for children and the elderly. Another mainland exhibitor, Neucity, is showcasing a multifunctional service robot designed for use in hotels, hospitals and retail outlets. It can handle tasks ranging from guest reception and guided tours to delivering medicine and monitoring patients. Zhang Tao, a research and development engineer at the company, said one of its robots was already working as a lobby manager at a hotel in Guangzhou. In hospitals, the robot can deliver medication, conduct remote ward inspections and use facial recognition to verify patients’ identities before releasing medicine, while nurses can monitor its activities through smartwatches or computers. “If a nurse needs to deliver medicine to a patient in bed 30, the robot will first verify whether it is the correct patient,” Zhang said. “Only then will it open the compartment and allow the patient to collect the medicine.” Zhang said the company hoped to expand overseas, arguing that its technology offered an advantage over robots designed for a single purpose. “Many robots on the market only perform one function, such as simple deliveries,” he said. “Ours combines multiple functions with AI capabilities.” Beyond robotics, exhibitors are also developing AI-powered consumer products tailored to different overseas markets. Shenzhen-based L’Atitude 52°N is introducing its Departure Collection smart sunglasses, which offer AI-powered travel guides, real-time translation and voice-activated assistance. Hardware product manager Robin Wang said the glasses, launched in August, were already being sold in Europe and North America but were not available in mainland China. He attributed the decision to differences in consumer habits, noting that mainland consumers often preferred umbrellas for sun protection, while sunglasses were more widely worn overseas. “We noticed significant differences in consumer behaviour between the domestic and overseas markets,” Wang said. “We believe there are greater opportunities in overseas markets for outdoor travel products, so we decided to start there.” The company expects to sell several thousand pairs this year and is exploring partnerships with overseas telecoms operators and distributors. Wang said Hong Kong provided opportunities to connect with international businesses and technology suppliers as the company pursued further expansion into markets including Japan, Taiwan and Australia. The two fairs, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, will also feature a new Future Industries Zone and dedicated showcases for smart wellness and entertainment technologies, alongside business-matching activities aimed at helping mainland enterprises expand overseas.

title: Opinion | Manchester City scandal a test of Britain’s commitment to rule of law
description: After backlash to Burnham’s response, unravelling the tangled web of this sorry affair is no longer just a question of sporting integrity.
content: The visit by star-studded Manchester City, the most successful English football team of recent times, was a highlight of Hong Kong’s football festival this summer. Supporters, sporting the club’s colours, flocked to Kai Tak Stadium, turning it into a sea of blue. Now, the club has plumbed the depths, found guilty by an independent tribunal of systematic breaches of the English Premier League’s financial rules over almost a decade. The affair has, with justification, been described as one of the biggest sporting scandals ever. But it transcends football. The controversy has diplomatic and economic implications for the United Kingdom – and has become a problem for Prime Minister Andy Burnham. City are appealing against the decision and strenuously deny any wrongdoing. The club has been majority owned, since 2008, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, an Emirati royal and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates. The UAE is an important economic partner and ally of the UK. There have been reports that UAE officials, in response to the proceedings against City, have threatened to withdraw billions of pounds in investment from the UK and warned of damage to the bilateral relationship. Concerns have been raised that there will be political interference in the disciplinary process. The stakes are high. City were found guilty by the Premier League’s disciplinary commission of 114 charges involving sweeping breaches of financial rules and failures to cooperate with the investigation. “Sham” contracts were used as part of a disguised funding scheme that inflated revenue and understated costs by more than £900 million (US$1.19 billion), the panel found. This gave the club a huge advantage over its rivals, allowing it to spend more on players. It has, effectively, been found to have built its success by cheating. The offences are so serious a heavy penalty is expected, should the club’s appeal fail. It could even be expelled from the Premier League. A confidential hearing spanned 12 weeks in 2024. The tribunal’s scathing ruling, when published last month, prompted widespread public condemnation of City. But the initial response from Burnham, in a BBC interview, struck a different tone. He began by suggesting the club might have been unfairly treated and went on to say he would be concerned if its Abu Dhabi owners sold it. The prime minister, while promising not to intervene in the process, spoke of the valuable contribution the owners had made to the redevelopment of Manchester during his time as the city’s mayor. His comments sparked an instant backlash and a swift climbdown. He had, uncharacteristically, misjudged the public mood. Burnham’s remarks have also prompted scrutiny of his relationship with the owners. This is not surprising. The regeneration of Manchester has been a driving force for Burnham’s political career, helping propel him to 10 Downing Street. As mayor of the city, he joined a delegation from the club visiting Shenzhen in September 2018, welcoming the opening of its second mainland office there. This, Burnham said, showed City’s commitment to China. “I can’t help but be impressed by how football in the country is undergoing a revolution,” he added, declaring that the club’s ambition “matches that of the football authorities in China – it’s a perfect partnership”. Three months later, the Premier League investigation began. There is a need for the disciplinary process, which has already taken far too long, to be swiftly concluded, to provide clarity and certainty. Only then will the Premier League be able to move on. The league is arguably Britain’s biggest cultural export and its integrity and reputation are at stake. It is difficult, in light of the guilty verdicts, to imagine City being presented with the Premier League trophy at the end of the season, although this remains a possibility. Many believe the process will drag on. The club’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who among many other roles acts as the UAE’s special envoy to China, said in a defiant open letter to supporters that it still has a long way to run. The best outcome would be for the club to admit to wrongdoing, take the punishment and start to rebuild its reputation, perhaps in the unfamiliar setting of the lower leagues. At least it could then look ahead with a clear conscience. There is not the slightest indication that will happen. The game has moved into extra time. And City, at least, believe there is still much to play for. However long it takes, justice must be done and be seen to be done. Unravelling the tangled web woven by this sorry affair is not just a question of sporting integrity, it is a test of Britain’s commitment to the rule of law.

title: Saudi Arabia faces more drone, missile attacks after Houthi’s fatal airport strikes
description: A Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis says it has intercepted weapons including in areas where there are key oil and gas facilities.
content: Saudi Arabia said it was dealing with new drone and cruise missile attacks on Monday, posing fresh security threats to the kingdom following the weekend’s deadly strikes on Riyadh airport. “We have detected and are monitoring a threat involving drones and cruise missiles against the kingdom and the threat is being dealt with,” the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported. It cited Defence Ministry spokesman Turki al-Maliki on behalf of a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis. The coalition said earlier it had intercepted missiles and drones aimed at the kingdom overnight, including areas that are home to some of Saudi Arabia’s key oil and gas facilities. Saudi authorities on Monday extended a suspension of operations at the King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, where two separate attacks over the weekend killed at least 14 people and wounded more than 300, many critically. King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was targeted separately. Meanwhile, air strikes on two districts in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa killed one person and wounded 12 others, according to the Houthis. Their media centre blamed Saudi Arabia for the strikes. The weekend’s events mark the deadliest strikes for Saudi Arabia since the Iran war began and come a week after Saudi-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake areas held by Houthi militia, including the Bab el-Mandeb strait and “eliminate” the group. As the violence stretched into Monday, the coalition vowed a “decisive” response. There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Against that backdrop, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, one of the most senior Saudi officials to speak publicly in the wake of the strikes, sought to project resilience, telling oil industry executives that the kingdom remained committed to providing energy security. “There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix. We come out of the ashes all the time and every time,” Prince Abdulaziz said at an energy event on Sunday. At the World Petroleum Congress (WPC) on Monday, he called for a serious response to events of recent weeks, while noting the country should remain focused on economic diversification and investment. The WPC gathering has been disrupted by the hostilities, with some executives who had been scheduled to attend, including the chief executives of BP Plc and Shell Plc, withdrawing. Riyadh has been in conflict with Houthi militants ever since they took control over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government backed by Saudi Arabia to resign the following year. US President Donald Trump said over the weekend he was considering joining in the fight against the Iran-backed militant group. “The attack last night is very emblematic. A very advanced, sophisticated ballistic missile, very accurate, targeting a commercial airport and now a number of civilian casualties,” former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk told Bloomberg Television. “It’s an act of terrorism. I think there has to be a response.” A senior United Arab Emirates official, meanwhile, urged a revival of regional security arrangements. “It has become evident that we are all targets and that our security is indivisible,” Anwar Gargash, senior adviser to the UAE president, said on X. Brent crude extended gains to above US$105 a barrel on Monday following the weekend strikes. Traders weighed resilient Middle East flows against rising regional tensions and a US claim that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a so-called energy ceasefire. The Saudi civil aviation authority said one person died and 11 were injured after an unknown projectile hit the main airport in Riyadh on Sunday. That followed a strike on King Khalid airport on Saturday. The attacks brought travel at the Riyadh airport to a near-standstill. They also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work and schools to do remote learning. The FAA on Sunday issued a warning to all US airlines to exercise caution flying to or over parts of Saudi Arabia “at all altitudes”. Authorities have indicated the 25th World Petroleum Congress and associated events, scheduled to run until Wednesday, will continue. Riyadh is also scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative (FII), its flagship investor gathering, later this month. The two events draw industry heavyweights and thousands of delegates. “Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh’s airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants’ transportation and movements,” the FII’s Chief Executive Officer, Maha Al Saud, said in a statement.
