title: ‘Inconvenient truth’: Man City case spotlights realities of UK-UAE ties
description: Analysts point to a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi.
content: When Liverpool fans greeted Manchester City at Anfield on Sunday with jeers and banners demanding the Abu Dhabi-owned football club be relegated, they took aim at what critics have long dubbed “sportswashing” – the practice of using high-profile sports investments to launder a tarnished international reputation. Focusing solely on public relations, however, obscures a much deeper network of high-stakes diplomacy and geopolitical economics between London and Abu Dhabi. The reality behind the United Arab Emirates’ acquisition of the club is an “inconvenient truth” rather than a mere branding exercise, according to Simon Chadwick, a leading sports business expert and co-editor of The Geopolitical Economy of Football: Where Power Meets Politics and Business. Rather than buying influence through sport, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s 2008 takeover was the result of “intense diplomacy” that subsequently helped London navigate the global financial crisis that struck later that year, Chadwick said. An emergency £7 billion bailout of Barclays Bank organised by Sheikh Mansour, involving Emirati and Qatari sovereign wealth funds, spared cash-strapped British taxpayers from footing the bill. However, it later transpired that Barclays misled shareholders about the mechanism of the UAE’s £3.25 billion share of the bailout. They were given the impression that Sheikh Mansour had invested in his personal capacity, rather than through Abu Dhabi’s International Petroleum Investment Company, triggering a lengthy legal battle with British firm PCP Capital Group. It ended in 2021 with a British court finding Barclays guilty of “serious deceit”. Nevertheless, the City acquisition remained “part of a diplomatic landscape that saw Britain and the UAE drawing closer together”, said Chadwick, a professor of Afro-Eurasian Sport at the Emlyon Business School in France. This was evident during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Britain in 2015. Rather than touring Anfield or Old Trafford, home of Manchester United, Xi went to City, where he was prominently photographed alongside then British prime minister David Cameron and Chancellor of the Exchequer George Osborne. Chadwick, himself a generational fan of Championship team Middlesbrough, said it was “inappropriate” to describe the City case as sportswashing. “This is not sportswashing, it’s sport diplomacy,” he said. “The British government was part of this and now, of course, through this diplomatic activity, we’ve got a level of interconnectedness between the UAE and Britain the realities of which are proving to be unpalatable to a lot of people.” These realities are reflected by the £30 billion of investments in Britain made by UAE sovereign wealth funds and state-owned enterprises over the last five years. Alongside the much-vaunted urban renewal of Manchester as part of Sheikh Mansour’s strategic investment in the Blues, these injections into Britain’s defence, technology, life sciences and connectivity infrastructure have been a welcome boost after the Covid pandemic wreaked economic havoc – much like the Barclays bailout in 2008. As mayor of Manchester during the Emirati-funded renewal of Britain’s second biggest city, Prime Minister Andy Burnham now finds himself trying to pull off a diplomatic rescue act to avert retaliation by the UAE. Downing Street has made no secret of its worries that action by independent football regulators against City’s Emirati owners could have serious economic consequences. Burnham, therefore, appears prepared to weather the domestic political storm, telling the BBC in an October 1 interview that he would be “really concerned to lose them” given that the UAE had been “such a huge partner” in building modern Manchester and turning City into a global force. The prime minister’s initial response to the independent commission’s verdicts – which found the club’s leadership deliberately obstructive and evasive – was thus “tone deaf”, according to Guy Burton, a Brussels-based international relations researcher and co-host of The FootPol Podcast, a sports show focusing on the intersection of football and politics. British newspapers have also noted that the Prime Minister’s Office, when approached for comment, has not disputed their reports that the UAE could freeze its investments in the country if independent regulators deem Sheikh Mansour’s ownership of City not “fit and proper”. Shortly after taking office in July, Burnham called four Gulf leaders, including Mansour’s elder brother UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, to reiterate British support for their defence against Iranian air strikes being carried out in response to attacks by the US and Israel. Their discussion further included ideas to “step up collaboration on technology and AI”, a Downing Street spokesman said in a statement. The UAE is investing tens of billions of dollars in data centres, AI and other collaborations with US and European firms as part of a strategic drive to become a global leader in the field. In addition to Burnham’s experience as Manchester mayor, his expectations of further UAE investment were fuelled by the free-trade pact Britain agreed with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states – the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman – in May. London hopes the deal, the first free-trade agreement between the GCC and a G7 country, could boost the UK economy by an estimated £3.7 billion (US$4.9 billion) a year and increase wages by £1.9 billion annually in the long run. The UAE is Britain’s biggest economic partner in the GCC, accounting for £25 billion of the £53 billion in bilateral trade in 2025. It is home to about two-thirds of the roughly 300,000 British nationals living in the Gulf monarchies, with most clustered in Dubai, the country’s commercial centre, and more than 5,000 British-owned businesses. With City’s appeal against the verdicts and further deliberations pending, any Premier League sanctions are unlikely to be unveiled until after the end of the season in May. Burton also predicted additional fallout from other clubs “who feel they missed out on financial opportunities because of City’s financial doping”, much of which would play out during and after May, and “for years to come”. “There are a lot of twists and turns still to come in this story, much as there are in the wider instability in the region,” Burton said. With so much at stake, Burnham’s vow not to politically interfere in the case may ultimately prove to be hollow. City’s case, the governance and application of rules within the Premier League, and the thriving relationship between Britain and the UAE “are embedded within a very dense network of interconnections between the two countries”, Chadwick said. That means “it is an inconvenient truth for many people” that the City case might not result in the strict application and enforcement of rules through a “set of draconian sanctions”. Instead, the outcome could be a “negotiated diplomatic settlement”, Chadwick said. “But it’s not sportswashing,” he added.

title: China’s top diplomat to visit Azerbaijan, Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria to boost ties
description: Wang Yi’s four-nation tour comes amid Beijing’s push to shore up its trade corridors and geopolitical influence.
content: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi will visit Azerbaijan and three Balkan countries amid Beijing’s push to shore up its trade corridors and geopolitical influence in the regions. Wang will attend the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Thursday “as special representative of President Xi Jinping”, according to China’s foreign ministry. Aside from Azerbaijan, Beijing’s top diplomat will visit Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria, it said, for a four-nation trip running from October 14 to 20. This will mark Wang’s first visit to Azerbaijan in seven years. His trip to Montenegro will be the first-ever official visit by a Chinese foreign minister since the country gained independence 20 years ago. Wang last visited Bulgaria as foreign minister in 2015. According to foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning, China hopes to engage in full dialogue with all parties at the CICA summit, uphold multilateralism and work to improve governance in Asia. “As the current international and regional landscape is becoming more complex and volatile, Asian countries have a stronger wish to safeguard peace and tranquillity and promote economic growth,” she said at a press conference on Monday. Mao added that Wang on his trip would meet with the countries’ foreign ministers and hold in-depth exchanges with their leaders. His itinerary spans important logistics hubs and Balkan infrastructure partners along the Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. This transport link connects China to European markets by passing through Kazakhstan, crossing the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, continuing through Georgia and Turkey, and bypassing Russia. The countries Wang will visit have also engaged with Beijing through the Belt and Road Initiative, a China-centred global trade and infrastructure scheme. Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria are important partners for Beijing in southeastern Europe, Mao said, adding that China has had significant cooperation with the countries in trade, investment, tourism and infrastructure. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Montenegro, and the two countries have jointly delivered flagship cooperation projects, including Montenegro’s North-South highway, she added. Mao said the Peljesac Bridge in Croatia, built by a Chinese company, had become a symbol of China-Croatia and China-Europe cooperation. China hoped Wang’s visit would “strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Croatia, expand practical cooperation, and ensure that bilateral relations enjoy steady and sustained growth”, the spokeswoman added. Bulgaria became one of the early European members of the Belt and Road Initiative when it signed a memorandum of understanding in 2015. It has cooperated with China in science and technology innovation, finance, green initiatives, environmental protection, agriculture, energy, forestry and health.

title: US turns to low-cost Blackbeard hypersonic missiles to overwhelm Chinese defences
description: At US$385,000 per unit, the carrier-launched weapons are being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production.
content: The US Navy aims to field a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile on its carrier-based fighters, a weapon that could pose a new challenge to the air defences protecting Chinese warships and coastal military installations, experts said. California-based defence company Castelion’s Blackbeard is designed to fly at more than five times the speed of sound and strike ships and land targets. Unlike more expensive hypersonic weapons, it is being developed with an emphasis on affordability and mass production. In May, the Pentagon sought congressional authorisation and funding to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles for deployment across the armed services over five years. US Navy projections put the average gross unit cost at about US$385,000 in the financial years 2028-31. In contrast, the cost of Lockheed Martin’s larger Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) is estimated in US Air Force budget figures for the 2024 financial year to be about US$3.25 million. The price difference could allow US forces to build much larger stockpiles and launch repeated attacks against Chinese warships, forcing them to expend defensive interceptors and potentially making it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles to hit their targets, experts say. The Blackbeard could also threaten Chinese coastal anti-ship missile batteries and air-defence systems, although experts differed over whether American carrier-based aircraft could get close enough to strike such targets. According to the US Naval Institute (USNI), the navy ordered 50 pre-production missiles in June and a further 444 in September and is seeking early operational capability this year – though budget projections and a Castelion announcement in April pointed to 2027. USNI News reported that an F/A-18E/F Super Hornet showed in September that it could carry two Blackbeard missiles. The US Navy is planning to equip each Super Hornet to carry up to four missiles, it said. The push for larger inventories reflects concerns about how quickly American forces could run short of long-range precision weapons in a conflict involving Taiwan, a continuing point of friction between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In war games published in 2023, the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that US forces exhausted their simulated LRASM stocks within the first week in every iteration of a hypothetical attack on the island. Meanwhile, Chinese military researchers have examined the various ways they could counter potential large-scale US precision strikes, according to Christopher Sharman, director of the US Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute (CMSI). Sharman pointed to a 2023 article published by the People’s Liberation Army journal Air Force Military Studies that examined more than a dozen conflicts involving US and allied long-range strikes. CMSI published an English translation in August. The PLA authors recommended attacking US forces before they launched their weapons, jamming satellite navigation signals and coordinating drones, fighters and air-defence systems, Sharman said. However, publicly available information did not establish whether the PLA had adopted those recommendations, he added. The bigger question was not just “whether individual warships can intercept incoming missiles”, but whether the Chinese navy could “maintain an effective, integrated defence across the fleet” during a coordinated attack. Sharman stressed that he was speaking in a personal capacity and his comments did not necessarily reflect the views of the US government, Defence Department or the Naval War College. Peter Jones, a retired Australian vice-admiral and adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra, said hypersonic missiles forced defending forces to “detect, track, assign weapons about five or more times quicker” than against conventional subsonic anti-ship missiles. A “layered defence” that would draw on the networked capabilities of ships and aircraft in a task group offered the best chance of countering such attacks, according to Jones. “Whether the latest Chinese destroyers can engage these missiles is unclear,” he noted. Much would depend on the Blackbeard’s flight path and radar signature, as well as the effectiveness of Chinese radars, defensive weapons and electronic warfare systems, Jones said. Another uncertainty is how much damage a Blackbeard strike could cause. The US Navy’s requirements specified a desired payload of about 34kg (75lb), although the missile’s actual warhead weight remains unconfirmed. Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, said Blackbeard could be useful for “striking sensors such as radars that support anti-air missiles”. Damaging those radars could make it easier for larger, more powerful anti-ship missiles used alongside Blackbeard to hit their targets, he suggested. While Heath emphasises the missile’s supporting role, Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia Programme at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, sees greater potential for Blackbeard to disable a warship on its own. Calling it “a significant leap in US Navy capability”, Goldstein argued that the force of a high-speed impact could be “just as or more important than the warhead”. Even one strike could cause “mission kill”, leaving a ship unable to fight and forcing it to return for repairs, he said. Goldstein also argued that combining lighter and heavier missiles with long-range attack drones could make defending warships “especially challenging”. Yet both Goldstein and Heath identified a major obstacle to employing the Blackbeard near Taiwan: the vulnerability of US carriers and carrier-based aircraft. “The main limitation is the launch platform,” Heath said, noting that manned carrier-based strike aircraft were “expensive and vulnerable”. Beijing’s attacks could force US carriers farther from Taiwan, potentially beyond the missile’s effective range, he added. Goldstein was more cautious, expecting US carriers to “operate on the margins of any conflict in the western Pacific”, potentially putting mainland Chinese targets beyond the reach of the Blackbeard. But he predicted a possible role for the missile against PLA Navy warships operating farther into the Pacific Ocean and potentially threatening American logistics around Guam. In contrast, Heath saw greater potential for attacks on Chinese coastal missile and air-defence systems, arguing that launching Blackbeard from carrier-based aircraft would “dramatically expand the flexibility and range with which the missile can be used”. The Blackbeard’s effective range and ability to strike moving warships have yet to be publicly shown.

title: Kimi Antonelli dares to dream of historic Formula 1 title after Singapore GP podium
description: Mercedes driver could become the youngest-ever champion at next race in Texas after finishing third behind Max Verstappen in city state.
content: Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli said he was allowing himself to dream about a historic ⁠world title, which is within reach ⁠at the next race in Austin, Texas, after the ⁠20-year-old sealed his 14th podium finish of the season at Sunday’s Singapore Grand Prix. The title would make Antonelli Formula 1’s youngest-ever champion and Italy’s first since 1953. Antonelli’s third place in a Singapore GP that was controlled from start to finish by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen was scrappy, as he flirted with a penalty for testing ‌the track’s limits. But it was enough to extend his lead over teammate George Russell to 102 points and when asked if he dared to dream of clinching the title in Austin later this month on the long journey home he said: “For sure. “But at the same time, I know it’s very close, I know it’s there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can. The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win. “I think this ⁠weekend I haven’t particularly driven that well … but I feel confident that, [with] a week to reset, I’m really looking forward to being ‌back in Austin. “If I don’t do my job well, then the result won’t come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform at 100 per cent.” Sooner or later Antonelli could mathematically win the championship in ‌Austin on the assumption that there were still five races to come, with the fate of the Grands Prix ⁠in Qatar and Abu Dhabi ⁠in the air because of the conflict in the Middle East. However, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff was refusing to tempt fate. “I remind myself that this is motor racing ‌and crazy things have happened,” Wolff said. “It probably needs the other two [contenders], George and Lewis [Hamilton], to retire and him winning. So this is not a likely scenario,” he added, while ‌recognising that ‌the title was within reach and maybe inevitable. “It’s going to come towards him, whether that’s in Mexico or Brazil, or far down ‌the line.” Verstappen finally conquers Singapore Verstappen’s victory came ‌in the 250th Grand Prix start for the 29-year-old Dutchman. It was his 73rd career victory and ‌first at Singapore in 10 attempts. Verstappen, who also won the sprint race on Saturday, ⁠has now won ⁠every race that appears on the 2026 schedule except the Spanish Grand Prix at ‌The Madring in Madrid, which ran its inaugural event this year. “It’s taken a ‌while, but ‌I think this race was very good,” Verstappen said after ‌the victory. “It worked out, so of course I’m very happy ⁠to win here.” Russell, who worked his way up from the back of the starting grid due to engine penalties, finished a respectable ninth ⁠at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where overtaking is notoriously tricky. Wolff said both drivers would probably be running in Austin on an upgraded ⁠car as some, but not all, of its teething problems had been ironed out in Singapore. “I think that this new car needs a very different set-up philosophy than the previous car,” he said. “Does it have the performance that we were ‌hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t ‌think so yet, but it was a step in the right direction.” Antonelli narrowly avoided a five-second penalty, hitting the maximum limit of breaches of the track boundaries. However, Wolff praised his driving and joked about how he could boost the diminutive driver higher for a better view of the track edges. “I have a good strategy. I’m going to put a pillow from the hotel under his a***, so he can actually see the road.”

title: China, EU take a breath after surprise deal brings temporary halt to trade tussle
description: Agreement, praised on both sides, features controls on Chinese EV shipments and tariff reductions, helping to cool tensions – for now.
content: Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods. The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war – a cooldown augmented by Beijing’s subsequent reduction of value-added tax (VAT) export rebates on certain goods, which could help curb outbound shipments further. China’s Ministry of Commerce described the deal as an “upward arrangement” based on the country’s outbound shipments of hybrid cars in 2025, adding the agreement would ensure further room for the “stable growth” of Chinese companies’ exports. French President Emmanuel Macron hailed the agreement during a visit to the Paris Motor Show on Monday, saying that it would help Europe better protect its market from “disloyal competition”. Under the terms of the deal, Brussels will cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026. After the bloc’s 27 member states consent to the arrangement, the bloc will use a technical safeguard instrument to moderate the import of Chinese hybrid cars, likely to be in place from December 1. Once 350,000 units have been imported, others will be turned away at EU ports. “No measure will specifically target Chinese products, still less treat Chinese companies in a discriminatory manner. The quota China receives will be no lower than that of any other source of EU imports,” the commerce ministry said in a statement on Monday. [The deal] is like a band-tightening spell on Chinese firms ... We would of course prefer to not have it, but we have to take one for the team Chinese executive, Europe The agreement, which will be in place for a four-year period, aims to halve China’s share of the EU hybrid market from the current 12 per cent. Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the EU almost tripled from 2024 to 2025, rising from around 107,000 to around 302,000, according to the ministry, which cited the European Commission’s statistical office. “[The deal] is like a band-tightening spell on Chinese firms,” said a Chinese executive in Europe who requested anonymity to speak freely. “We would of course prefer to not have it, but we have to take one for the team.” Brussels’ goal was to push Chinese firms to bring their production chains to Europe, the executive said, estimating the move would increase production costs by 30 to 50 per cent. Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.” A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, referenced the saying when discussing the deal. “In business, there is a saying that the customer is always right. So, as a customer, we have made the point very clearly that we are hurting, and that we will remain a customer. But the volumes and the surge that we have seen are unsustainable.” The agreement would comply with World Trade Organization rules, the Chinese commerce ministry said, adding Beijing reserved all its rights under the WTO framework, including “recourse to dispute settlement and seeking trade compensation”. With petrol prices high due in large part to the US-Israel war on Iran, European customers have been making the switch to electric vehicles in greater numbers. Hybrid and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) made up 46.6 per cent of the European car market during the first eight months of this year, according to data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA). PHEV demand is booming in some of Europe’s biggest markets, with registrations in the first eight months of the year up 77.6 per cent in Italy, 33.9 per cent in Spain and 15.6 per cent in Germany, according to the ACEA. The European Union market grew by 30,720 vehicles in August, per ACEA data – a year-on-year increase of 4.5 per cent – with Chinese carmakers BYD, Chery, Leapmotor and SAIC accounting for about 92 per cent of the growth. Chinese brands are expected to have an outsize presence at the auto show in Paris, which opened on Monday. According to a report from Allianz Trade, the country’s carmakers will take up a 50 per cent share of exhibitors, as the share of European marques drops to 40 per cent. Separately, in a bid to address growing concerns from the West over trade imbalances, Beijing will cut the VAT export rebate rate for new energy vehicles from 13 per cent to 9 per cent from April 1, according to a notice issued jointly on Monday by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration. Tax rebates on e-cigarette exports will also be cancelled, per the notice.

title: Hong Kong steps up Russia arrival checks after Siberian lab worker’s death
description: Health officials order expanded surveillance at airport after researcher at anti-plague institute in Siberia dies from pneumonia of unknown origin.
content: Hong Kong will step up health surveillance measures for arrivals after a laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in Russia died from pneumonia, but authorities have stressed the risk to residents remains low. According to World Health Organization (WHO) information provided by Russian authorities, there was no evidence of ongoing transmission, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Monday. Russian authorities previously stated ‌that the worker at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute in Siberia had died from pneumonia, but that the origin of the infection ⁠had yet to ⁠be determined. The centre said it had not received any reports of residents or travellers arriving in Hong Kong from Russia with cases of pneumonia of unknown origin in recent months. “The CHP assesses that the immediate public health impact to Hong Kong is low. For the sake of prudence, the CHP has implemented a series of control and prevention measures to guard against imported cases,” a spokesman said. These included arranging for Port Health Division officers to conduct temperature checks for passengers arriving on flights from Russia, as well as conducting health assessments for arrivals exhibiting symptoms and transferring them to public hospitals for further testing. The department will also display signage and broadcast announcements in the airport arrival area and through airlines to urge passengers who have visited Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia within the past 14 days to declare their travel history. It will also provide the Airport Authority and airlines with the latest information regarding the case, and urge airlines to remind their flight crews to strictly enforce established prevention and control measures if they identify suspected cases on their flights. The centre will also send letters to all doctors and hospitals in Hong Kong, reminding them to remain highly vigilant and to strengthen surveillance. Any patient who has visited the area within 14 days before the onset of symptoms and has developed pneumonia of an undetermined origin must immediately report to the centre for further testing. “The CHP will continue to closely monitor the latest developments, respond swiftly and strictly guard against imported cases to safeguard public health,” the spokesman said. Russian media reported earlier this month that the 28-year-old laboratory technician working for the institute had died of pneumonic plague that could have come from a broken test tube. But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease. Pneumonic plague, which spreads between people and causes severe lung infections, is highly treatable if detected early. The centre said that according to the latest information from the WHO, citing data provided by Russian authorities, no plague cases had been recorded recently in Irkutsk Oblast, testing of the deceased’s contacts found no high-threat pathogens, and there were no further cases of severe pneumonia linked to this case. The Russian authorities reported that no biosecurity incidents had occurred at the laboratory, and quarantine measures were instituted in hospital where the patient was treated, according to the centre.

content: A man has died after falling from a building while trying to flee a Hong Kong police raid on a suspected drug den in Yau Ma Tei. The 42-year-old man, surnamed Kwong, was found unconscious outside 385-387 Reclamation Street at about 9.28pm on Sunday. He was rushed to Kwong Wah Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said on Monday. At 9.21pm, officers from the Organised Crime and Triad Bureau launched an operation at the building, breaking into a flat suspected of operating as a drug den. “As officers forced their way through the front door, several suspected patrons were seen fleeing through the back door and heading up the stairs towards the rooftop,” a police source said. An initial examination of the deceased found no suspicious injuries, while CCTV footage from nearby buildings showed he had fallen from height. Police said Kwong was suspected of having fallen from the rooftop while trying to evade arrest. Twenty-one Hong Kong residents – 11 men and 10 women aged between 28 and 70 – were arrested during the operation on suspicion of keeping a drug den, drug trafficking and consuming dangerous drugs. They remained in custody. Officers seized suspected drugs worth about HK$83,000 (US$10,580), including 52.3 grams of suspected cocaine, 11.4 grams of suspected methamphetamine, also known as “ice”, 32.3 grams of suspected heroin, 29 suspected midazolam tablets and drug-taking paraphernalia. Under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, drug trafficking carries a maximum penalty of a HK$5 million fine and life imprisonment upon conviction. Keeping or operating a drug den carries a maximum fine of HK$5 million and 15 years’ imprisonment, while possession or consumption of dangerous drugs carries a maximum fine of HK$1 million and seven years’ imprisonment. Police urged members of the public not to break the law.

content: A 26-year-old warehouse worker has been injured in Hong Kong after being chased by three dogs and bitten by one of them on his way to work. A source said police received a report at around 8am on Monday from the victim, surnamed Leung, saying one of the dogs pounced on him as he was walking towards his workplace at a logistics company in Yuen Long’s Kam Pok Road. Paramedics arrived at the scene and found the victim with minor wounds. He was sent to Pok Oi Hospital for treatment. The source said the man had been bitten on the left shin by a six-year-old, 1.2-metre-long (4-foot) female mongrel. The dog was captured by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for inspection. The incident is the latest in a series of reported dog attacks in recent months. Last month, a pack of dogs was suspected to have attacked a 27-year-old woman, who was found unconscious beside a bicycle in Yuen Long and later died. Surveillance footage showed she had been chased by three canines. In August, a large unleashed mastiff-type dog fatally mauled two smaller pets in Yuen Long, leading to the arrest of its owner. A few days later, a 33-year-old woman who operated a canine training centre in Ta Kwu Ling, North district, was attacked by a dog at the facility and later found dead nearby.

content: An AI-generated Chinese rap song featuring some of the country’s most well-known historical figures has taken social media by storm. Titled “The One Who’s Been There” (Guo Lai Ren), the track crossed 100 million views across platforms in less than two weeks as it tapped into the anxieties of modern life. The song brings together 10 iconic figures from Chinese history and mythology – from revered poets and statesmen to the legendary Monkey King. Rather than reciting classical verses or lecturing audiences, they rap about their own historical hardships to offer empathy, solace and encouragement to today’s burnt-out world. The track opens with Du Fu, one of the Tang dynasty’s greatest poets, best known for his classic line wishing for millions of houses to shelter those in need. In the song, Du laments still having to rent in the capital Changan in his forties, at the mercy of landlords constantly putting up the rent. He then turns directly to the listener: “You’re going through the same thing, aren’t you?” – striking a raw nerve with a modern audience grappling with mortgages and bills. Later in the track, Song dynasty literary giant Su Shi – whose political career was derailed by repeated demotions and exile – addresses the relentless pressures of the workplace. His verses touch upon the infamous “curse of 35”, an unspoken age ceiling in China where workers over 35 face widespread hiring bias and heightened job insecurity, as well as “optimisation”, a ubiquitous corporate euphemism for lay-offs. Behind the viral hit is Wang Kunzhe, a veteran visual creator with more than a decade of experience, who turned to AI-assisted production earlier this year. While Wang had previously posted several videos featuring historical figures in rap battles, those earlier efforts remained largely playful and historical, never striking a chord with the audience like The One Who’s Been There. On Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, the video had amassed more than 3 million likes and 97,000 comments by Sunday morning. The comments section has effectively evolved into an emotional outlet, with users unburdening themselves of career setbacks, mortgage strain and the loss of loved ones, while pondering the broader purpose of life. “This is hands down the best piece I’ve seen capturing the gritty reality of middle-aged struggle,” read one comment. According to Chinese news outlet The Paper, Wang said producing the track took just three to four days and cost a few thousand yuan in artificial intelligence (AI) subscriptions and computing power – a fraction of the budget typically required for traditional music video shoots. Wang laid the groundwork himself, deciding on the musical genre, structure, tempo and preliminary lyrics, while deploying AI tools to experiment with arrangements and trial-and-error iterations, Saturday’s report said. While the rise of generative AI has sparked anxiety and disruption across the traditional film and television industry, Wang views the technology as an equalising force rather than a threat. He described it as a “democratisation of technology” that placed creators on the same starting line. When generating baseline-quality works becomes relatively easy, producers’ taste, judgment, and emotional nuance matter more than ever, according to Wang. “AI can mass-produce content, but it cannot mass-produce resonance and empathy,” Wang said. He said the song was never meant to be a catalogue of misery, but rather a reminder that hardship was universal. The core message, echoed in a recurring refrain throughout the track, is simple: “You are not alone.” Encouraged by the reception, Wang plans to explore new musical styles and storytelling formats using AI, and hopes to one day direct an AI-generated feature-length film as the technology matures. Efforts to produce AI-generated films are already under way, but bringing them to the big screen remains an uphill battle. On Friday, Sanxingdui: Future Past – the first Chinese AI-produced film to receive a screening permit – hit cinemas. However, the audience response was lukewarm. The 100-minute film, which cost over 10 million yuan to make, had taken in just 914,000 yuan (US$128,000) by Sunday morning, with total box office takings only projected to reach about 2.5 million yuan.

title: Hong Kong arbitration body eyes Mideast, Africa prospects amid global tensions
description: An international arbitration body in Hong Kong is exploring business opportunities in the Middle East and Africa, citing the city’s neutrality and predictability as key draws for new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions. Domitille Baizeau, co-chairwoman of the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, said the city had benefited from an overall shift in global business growth from Europe to Asia, with overseas businesses increasingly choosing Hong Kong to arbitrate disputes. The...
content: An international arbitration body in Hong Kong is exploring business opportunities in the Middle East and Africa, citing the city’s neutrality and predictability as key draws for new markets amid rising geopolitical tensions. Domitille Baizeau, co-chairwoman of the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, said the city had benefited from an overall shift in global business growth from Europe to Asia, with overseas businesses increasingly choosing Hong Kong to arbitrate disputes. The international commercial arbitration specialist was speaking on the sidelines of the ADR in Asia Conference, an event organised by the centre last week. The conference brought together legal practitioners to discuss the latest developments in alternative dispute resolution and the use of artificial intelligence in the field. The event was part of the annual Hong Kong Arbitration Week, with more than 1,200 professionals from 53 jurisdictions registered to attend. Victor Dawes SC, co-chairman of the centre, also said the scope of growth for arbitration cases using the city was enormous, with growing offshore investment in emerging economies. He said Hong Kong’s dispute resolution strength extended beyond its proximity to mainland China. “It is the predictability and the certainty of Hong Kong’s jurisdiction that is holding its development in arbitration,” Dawes said. Dawes added that the arbitration body was exploring opportunities in the Middle East, while Africa had become another avenue of growth, with burgeoning Chinese offshore investment into the continent. “Some of those disputes are still being handled in Europe because the counterparty, a lot of them, are more familiar with London … but they are getting to know dispute resolution centres in Asia, and there will be a shift,” he said. Of the 388 arbitration cases received by the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre last year, 85 per cent of them involved at least one non-local party. Parties that used the arbitration body’s services in 2025 hailed from 61 jurisdictions, while the organisation handled cases involving 17 different governing laws. Users of the Hong Kong arbitration centre included parties from the United Arab Emirates (ranked 7th last year) and Russia (10th), as well as emerging markets such as Indonesia (8th), Brazil (9th) and South Africa.” Baizeau said Hong Kong had been able to absorb cases involving Russian parties amid heightened geopolitical tensions between the country and European powers. “A lot of corporate disputes are being heard here that may not directly involve companies headquartered here, but there’s a choice of Hong Kong as a neutral, independent, predictable framework,” she said. In addition to its established strength in private capital disputes, the city is seeing a rise in arbitrations involving digital assets and investment treaties, according to the lawyers. The key for Hong Kong to ensure its competitive edge over other global arbitration hubs amid growing geopolitical tensions was to maintain an independent and efficient judiciary that was familiar with the alternative dispute resolution process, they added. In an arbitration, the award is deemed final, enforceable and not subject to appeal. However, courts have the power to intervene in a narrow set of circumstances laid out in the city’s Arbitration Ordinance, such as one party being unable to present its case. “A competitive seat is to have a very strong court system in support of arbitration, not too interventionist,” Baizeau said. This advantage would keep Hong Kong attractive to international businesses beyond its proximity to the mainland, Dawes added. “The factors we mention that make us successful – it is independent, the quality of the institution, the quality of the panel – they are all there whether the China factor is there or not,” Dawes said.

content: Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to ⁠users following waves ⁠of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet ⁠services and raised concerns about economic stability. GMO Internet said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorised access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive 5,000 yen (US$32) ‌as “an initial gesture of good faith”, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday. The move comes after Japan said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organisations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP ⁠programming language that underpins much of the internet. Shares of GMO, which had a market value of US$2.6 billion as of Friday’s close, slumped 11 per cent in Tokyo on Monday morning, compared to flat trading in the benchmark index. Japanese ‌companies are being roiled by attacks, with experts saying AI is helping ⁠automate tasks from ⁠scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns – making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. Government and ‌company websites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the ‌PHP ‌programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts. GMO Internet has made a request to ‌the Japanese government to apply cyber defence measures in response to the cyberattack. The company ⁠said it had received a demand for money from a party believed to be ⁠behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply. GMO Internet said it would not ‌comply with the ‌demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. Separately, Park24, which operates the Times car-sharing service, said on Friday it would make 3,000 yen payments to customers following a personal data breach.

title: Chinese neighbours go viral over 200-year land dispute dating back to Qianlong era
description: A Chinese court recently heard a land dispute between neighbours who have been fighting over the same issue for two centuries and across multiple generations, stunning social media users. The court in Yanta district, Xian, in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, recently presided over a case concerning a land boundary between two neighbouring families, surnamed Du and Zhang. For the past two decades, the neighbours have repeatedly disputed the boundary. When the Dus tried to renovate their...
content: A Chinese court recently heard a land dispute between neighbours who have been fighting over the same issue for two centuries and across multiple generations, stunning social media users. The court in Yanta district, Xian, in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, recently presided over a case concerning a land boundary between two neighbouring families, surnamed Du and Zhang. For the past two decades, the neighbours have repeatedly disputed the boundary. When the Dus tried to renovate their kitchen and raise a wall, the Zhangs repeatedly objected, citing concerns about light and drainage. The disagreement led to frequent verbal and physical clashes. The police and the village committee tried to mediate dozens of times, but the deadlock remained unresolved. During one mediation session, the Zhangs presented a piece of evidence that astonished everyone: a land deed dating back to the 46th year of the Qianlong Emperor’s reign (1735–1796), during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912). On the yellowed, torn page, the well-preserved handwritten ink was still clearly legible. Zhang said it was an agreement between the families that set the boundary between their homes, marked by a persimmon tree in the courtyard. The Zhangs also believed the agreement should be honoured by future generations. The authorities then realised that the neighbours’ dispute had been going on for more than 200 years. Over the past two centuries, successive generations of the families had repeatedly clashed over the boundary, including once shortly after the People’s Republic of China was founded in 1949. But the court did not determine the boundary between the two households solely on the basis of the 1781 deed. Instead, it drew on a verse from another Qing dynasty document: a letter from politician and scholar Zhang Ying, who urged his family to yield in a land dispute with a neighbour. In the letter, Zhang wrote: “A letter from afar just for a wall, why not give up three feet? The Great Wall still stands today, but Qin Shi Huang is nowhere to be seen.” According to the story, Zhang’s family was moved by the letter and voluntarily moved their wall back three feet. Their neighbour followed suit, also moving their wall back by three feet. The two walls then formed a six-foot-wide lane, which is now a tourist attraction in Tongcheng, in central China’s Anhui province. The authorities also took repeated measurements at the homes to develop a renovation plan that would satisfy both families. Eventually, the Dus successfully renovated their kitchen, and the Zhangs accepted the outcome peacefully. “Love cannot last for 200 years, but lawsuits can,” one online observer remarked. “The land they occupy must have very good feng shui, allowing them to survive all the vicissitudes and still have the money and energy to fight,” another quipped.

title: Weapon or armour? The contentious debate over China’s open-weight AI
description: Are China’s increasingly powerful open-weight AI models a cybersecurity threat, or could restricting them ultimately make the internet less secure? The dilemma has become a growing concern as Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – continue to challenge their American rivals by releasing models that anyone can download, modify and deploy. The growing impact of advanced AI on global cybersecurity has also forced governments...
content: Are China’s increasingly powerful open-weight AI models a cybersecurity threat, or could restricting them ultimately make the internet less secure? The dilemma has become a growing concern as Chinese developers including DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – continue to challenge their American rivals by releasing models that anyone can download, modify and deploy. The growing impact of advanced AI on global cybersecurity has also forced governments and cybersecurity agencies across the world to scramble to shore up their digital defences, with this week’s uncovering of critical vulnerabilities in the internet programming language PHP just the latest example. Critics warn that open-weight models allow malicious actors to easily strip away safety protections and use advanced AI to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. But other researchers argue that the same technology could help proliferate the cyber defence capabilities of AI systems more widely to counter emerging threats. The debate has intensified following a report by US artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic that found Z.ai’s open-weight GLM-5.3 model had crossed critical thresholds for conducting sophisticated cyberattacks, similar to its own Claude models, while lacking the very safeguards that are possible due to Claude models being closed-source. Yet researchers remain divided over whether the technical risks associated with open-weight AI translate into greater real-world harm, and whether the distinction between open and closed models is the right way to assess their dangers. “Open models present different governance challenges than closed models, but that does not necessarily make them more dangerous,” said Kristy Loke, a fellow at MATS Research focusing on China’s AI innovation and governance strategies. Open-weight models inherently have a larger attack surface for misuse Edward Yee, AI safety researcher The risks of openness At the heart of the debate is a fundamental difference in how developers control their technology. Closed models are typically accessed through application programming interfaces, or APIs, allowing developers to monitor suspicious activity, restrict requests and revoke access when necessary. Open-weight models, by contrast, allow users to download the underlying parameters and run the systems independently, but they also mean malicious actors can remove safeguards designed to prevent harmful activities. Edward Yee, researcher and chief growth officer at US-based AI safety organisation Far.AI, said open-weight structures create a significant security disadvantage. “Open-weight models inherently have a larger attack surface for misuse,” Yee said. While closed models can rely on multiple layers of protection such as external monitoring systems, open-weight models depend primarily on safeguards embedded in the models themselves, which can often be removed through techniques such as “abliteration” – a technique that involves editing a model’s internal weight matrices to bypass its refusal mechanisms. As open-weight models are widely released, their model weights cannot effectively be recalled, even if developers subsequently discover dangerous capabilities. Attackers could therefore gain unrestricted access to models without the protections their original developers deployed, Yee said. The implications could become more serious as open-weight models approach the capabilities of the most advanced closed systems. While evidence of widespread harm remains limited, Yee said the lack of comprehensive data should not be mistaken for proof of safety, particularly because open models can be deployed on private servers, without knowledge of the authorities or the model developers themselves, making them difficult to monitor. The most serious concerns relate to misuse of AI systems by non-state actors, with both Washington and Beijing expressing willingness to jointly combat such risks in recent weeks. On Thursday, Tech Against Terrorism – a counterterrorism non-profit organisation backed by the United Nations – released its latest findings showing that closed models “do far better” than open models at refusing to help terrorists with planning an attack, while “abliterated” open models comply easily. Where is the evidence? Still, the ability to remove safeguards in open-weight models on paper does not necessarily translate into greater real-world harm, researchers cautioned. “Real-world harm is no longer theoretical, but so far the evidence doesn’t show that releasing the weights is what makes the difference,” said Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI. Galeev said attackers tend to use whichever AI systems best suit their needs, turning to proprietary models for their capabilities and open-weight alternatives when they are cheaper or less restrictive. “Attackers tend to shop around. They don’t care much about the theoretical distinction between closed and open-weight,” he said. Even when open-weight models are used in cyberattacks, malicious actors may access them through commercial AI platforms without downloading their weights or removing safeguards. This makes it difficult to establish whether the availability of model weights contributed to an attack, Galeev added. “For now, open and closed models fail in different ways, so neither is safe by default,” Galeev said. “The right question is not whether a model is open or closed, but what extra risk a specific model release adds,” he added. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher and author of the AI 2027 forecasting project, said a model’s capabilities mattered more than whether its weights were publicly available. “I would not say that open-weights models are inherently more dangerous,” he said. “All models are dangerous in proportion to how capable they are.” Loke warned that closed models could pose greater risks as frontier AI developers pursued techniques such as recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems progressively improve their own capabilities, making human oversight more difficult. A weapon for attackers – and defenders Complicating the debate is the dual-use nature of AI’s cybersecurity capabilities. The same technology that helps attackers discover software vulnerabilities can also help security researchers identify and fix weaknesses before they are exploited. Open-weight models offer defenders several advantages. They can be deployed on local servers, adapted to specialised tasks and used to analyse sensitive systems without sending confidential information to external providers. Clement Neo, founder of NEO Research, a Singapore-based frontier AI safety evaluation group, warned that banning open-weight models could backfire on safety. Blanket restrictions on open models would likely hurt defenders more than attackers Clement Neo, founder of NEO Research “Open-weight models are a major asset for cybersecurity,” he said. “Blanket restrictions on open models would likely hurt defenders more than attackers.” In a high-profile cyber hacking incident in July involving OpenAI’s GPT models, researchers at the affected company Hugging Face turned to a Chinese open-weight model – Z.ai’s GLM 5.2 – to investigate the breach after safeguards on closed US models refused to assist due to the companies’ built-in safeguards. Researchers cited the incident as an example of how open models could benefit defenders when proprietary systems struggle to distinguish legitimate security research from malicious activity. Open-weight models could also be particularly valuable to smaller organisations that lack the resources to purchase expensive proprietary tools or develop their own AI systems, according to Joshua Saxe, co-founder of US start-up Abundant Security and former tech lead in AI security at Facebook owner Meta Platforms. Such models could allow companies to deploy affordable defensive systems across their software and infrastructure, identifying vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. “There’s also an institutional asymmetry: criminals don’t have procurement departments, compliance committees, or lengthy AI governance processes. Defenders do,” Saxe said. “We’re in an adoption race as much as a capability race. Restrictions that slow defenders more than attackers could leave us less secure,” he added. Kokotajlo, the former OpenAI researcher, said the benefits of open-weight AI models had so far outweighed their costs. Open-weight’s transparency made it harder for developers to embed hidden agendas in the technology than in proprietary systems, whose inner workings were less accessible to outside scrutiny, he said. While open-weight models provide “real benefits” to defenders, Yee said the benefits should still be weighed against the risks. For some developers in China, running open-weight models locally has proven essential for security investigations. When investigating suspicious application server activity, Shenzhen-based independent AI engineer Wen Sheng found cloud-based AI services accessed via an API unhelpful. “The hosted model refused to analyse logs containing attack commands,” Wen said, without specifying which model. Switching to Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 model on his own server allowed his team to “reconstruct the sequence of events without uploading logs or internal credentials”, making it a boost for privacy as well. While running the open-weight model on his own server required managing hardware, permissions and updates internally, Wen noted the added control made the effort worthwhile. “Using a closed model is like renting a house: the provider holds the keys, sets the price and can lock you out,” said Shawn Lin, who leads a data annotation team at a major Chinese technology company in Shenzhen. “When we run an open-weight model on our own infrastructure, we can keep sensitive data in-house and decide how the system is used,” Lin said. “The practical question is who can access our data, what gets logged and whether we can keep using a model version that works for our workflow.” Beyond the open-versus-closed divide The debate carries particular significance for the China-US AI race, where China’s open-weight releases have become a central strategy for competing with better-funded American rivals. Contrary to suggestions that China’s open-weight approach comes at the expense of safety, Chinese researchers and developers have been taking steps to address its risks, researchers said. China’s national information security standardisation body, TC260, has begun drafting a security standard for open-weight AI models, recognising that safeguards can be removed once models are released. Chinese AI companies are also developing their own approaches to managing these risks. Z.ai has worked with Concordia AI on a safety framework addressing the specific challenges of open-weight releases. The framework distinguishes between dangerous capabilities that warrant restrictions regardless of whether a model is open or closed, and additional risks arising specifically from making model weights publicly available. “While critics of open models are afraid of the democratisation of advanced cyber capabilities, many in China believe that this democratisation is precisely what is needed,” said Concordia’s Galeev. China supports open models precisely because it recognises that they empower cybersecurity defence, he added. The challenge is finding ways to preserve those benefits as open-weight models become increasingly capable, researchers said. Galeev said models should be evaluated after their safeguards have been removed, rather than relying solely on safety tests conducted under normal operating conditions. Developers could also consider staged releases, initially providing access through controlled interfaces or to trusted researchers before making the weights more widely available. Yee of FAR.AI questioned whether the defensive benefits actually require unrestricted public release, or if providing access to trusted researchers and defenders under controlled conditions would suffice. Open-weight models currently take an extreme approach – offering “near-zero safeguards” and “maximum access for both defensive use but also offensive abuse,” he said. Saxe, the former AI security tech lead at Meta, said the industry should focus more on restricting malicious users than the models themselves. Stronger coordination among AI service providers to identify abusive users, share intelligence and terminate accounts, alongside measures to monitor access to advanced computing infrastructure, could help curb misuse without limiting legitimate access, he said. “The goal should be to restrict attackers, not models, wherever possible,” Saxe said. “AI gives us an extraordinary opportunity to find and repair vulnerabilities across the world’s enormous software infrastructure. We should be hardening as much of it as possible, as quickly as possible.” Additional reporting by Minxiao Chang

title: Tibetan river hosting world’s biggest dam is facing increasing flood risk: study
description: Chinese researchers have found that the Yarlung Tsangpo River – soon to host the largest mega dam in the world – may face increased run-off and flood risks over this century. Using tree-ring width chronologies in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, the team reconstructed the river’s run-off history from 1325 to 2020. Along with climate data, this was used to create a model that projected river run-off would increase under future climate scenarios, along with a possible increase in high-run-off...
content: Chinese researchers have found that the Yarlung Tsangpo River – soon to host the largest mega dam in the world – may face increased run-off and flood risks over this century. Using tree-ring width chronologies in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, the team reconstructed the river’s run-off history from 1325 to 2020. Along with climate data, this was used to create a model that projected river run-off would increase under future climate scenarios, along with a possible increase in high-run-off events such as floods. “These results provide a long-term perspective on hydroclimatic variability in the Yarlung Tsangpo River and a scientific basis for assessing future water-resource risks,” the team said in a paper published in the Chinese-language journal China Science Bulletin on October 8. The researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Yunnan University said future run-off should be considered in planning “water resource development and storage infrastructure” and in assessing transboundary water risks in the region. The Yarlung Tsangpo River originates near a glacier in the western Tibet Uygur autonomous region and eventually turns south into India, where it is known as the Brahmaputra. The river is the site of the world’s largest planned hydropower project, which is expected to have a total installed capacity of more than 60,000 megawatts upon completion – three times that of China’s Three Gorges Dam, the largest operating in the world. The mega dam is being built in Medog, also known as Motuo in Chinese, a border county in southeastern Tibet close to the disputed border with India. The project has drawn ire from India and Bangladesh downstream – where the river is an important source of water for millions of people – including concerns over water supply and the environment. The Tibetan Plateau has been warming at about twice the rate of the global average over the past century, which has impacted the region’s ice cover and hydrological cycle, according to the Chinese team. Among the rivers in the plateau, the Yarlung Tsangpo experiences the most run-off – or the movement of excess water or snow over land that eventually finds its way to bodies of water or drainage systems. They emphasised that changes in the river not only reflect the hydrological system within the plateau but also impact drought and flood patterns in South Asia. “In recent years, with the ongoing warming of the climate, the hydrological regime of the Yarlung Tsangpo River basin has been undergoing significant changes,” they said. Rising temperatures have accelerated glacial melting, increased permafrost degradation and shortened the duration of snow cover. Rain distribution has also become more unstable, with a rise in extreme rain events and anomalous run-off. Research has indicated that the region will trend towards a wetter climate, putting the Yarlung Tsangpo more at risk of both water scarcity and flooding. “However, our understanding of these hydrological changes remains severely constrained by data availability,” the team said. “Due to complex terrain, high-altitude environments and historical observational limitations, systematic and continuous hydrometeorological records for the basin generally only date back to the mid to late 20th century.” To reconstruct the river’s hydrological history, the team turned to tree rings as a climate proxy. Each ring signifies about a year of a tree’s life. The structure of the rings can show what kind of conditions they were formed under. Wider rings can mean more water during the growing season, and narrower rings less. These patterns can be used to form a climate history that can cover hundreds of years, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The Chinese team said the width and density of rings could be sensitive to moisture conditions during the growing season. Samples were collected between 2008 and 2020 from 11 sites of high-altitude, moisture-sensitive cypress and spruce trees using borers. Along with available data from the Nuxia Hydrological Station, these samples were used to reconstruct water-year run-off from 1325 to 2020. Located in Milin county-level city near Medog, the station is a key monitoring node on the lower reaches of the river. They found that run-off had exhibited inter- and multidecadal variability over the last 700 years, with 14 wet periods and 14 dry periods. The run-off that occurred within the period for which there have been instrumental records at the Nuxia station remains within the range of historical natural variability. The team then incorporated climate data to create a model of monthly run-off at the station from 2030 to 2100. This projected an increase in run-off in the Yarlung Tsangpo River during the 21st century, which was “accompanied by a possible increase in the occurrence probability of high-run-off events”. Under the middle-of-the-road and high-emissions climate scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, run-off was estimated to increase by about 20 per cent and 29 per cent respectively compared to the reconstructed historical period. “Overall, future annual run-off levels are expected to exceed those observed during both the reconstructed and instrumental record periods,” the team said. Projections of the distribution of run-off also suggest that there will not only be an increase in mean run-off but also a higher probability of extreme high-run-off events. The researchers said that for future management, it was “necessary to pay attention to both water resource increase potential and flood risk”. “Consequently, future basin management must holistically address the interplay between water resource utilisation, flood risk mitigation and the maintenance of ecological water requirements within the context of long-term hydrological change.” This latest study is not the only recent indication that the region will require careful management in the process of building what will be the world’s largest dam. In June, Chinese geologists said they had found that an active fault line directly beneath the planned project could pose a threat to its integrity and urged engineers to implement measures to mitigate the risk of collapses and landslides.

title: Singapore’s toxic haze probe expands to 10 palm oil, forestry firms
description: Singapore has expanded its investigation into haze-creating fires in Indonesia that have blanketed the city state in smog, requesting information from 10 locally registered companies. The National Environment Agency (NEA) sent notices seeking documents and details of land concessions in Indonesia owned by the firms, their firefighting and blaze prevention measures, and their relationship to other relevant companies, according to a Friday statement. All 10 Singapore-registered companies were...
content: Singapore has expanded its investigation into haze-creating fires in Indonesia that have blanketed the city state in smog, requesting information from 10 locally registered companies. The National Environment Agency (NEA) sent notices seeking documents and details of land concessions in Indonesia owned by the firms, their firefighting and blaze prevention measures, and their relationship to other relevant companies, according to a Friday statement. All 10 Singapore-registered companies were involved in the palm oil or forestry sectors and included Wilmar International, Golden Agri International and First Resources, the agency said. Singapore, Malaysia and other parts of Southeast Asia have experienced some of the worst pollution since 2015 as a result of haze generated by blazes in Indonesia. While fires are typical every year, the issue has been exacerbated in recent months as drought conditions have been worsened by a record El Nino. Wilmar, the world’s biggest palm oil refiner, said in a statement that “work is in progress to comply” with the NEA notice. First Resources was “reviewing the notice and will provide the requested documents and information”, it said on Saturday. Golden Agri, which operates oil palm assets across Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua, has received the request and will cooperate with the agency to provide information, according to a stock exchange filing late on Saturday. The producer said earlier this month that it was not aware of information indicating its operations had contributed to the haze, and that it had stepped up fire-prevention measures ahead of the El Nino-driven drought. The NEA earlier issued requests for information to 10 Indonesia-registered companies in connection with the haze. Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has pledged to investigate companies behind the region-wide smog and to take legal action under the Transboundary Haze Act. The law gives Singapore the ability to fine companies up to S$100,000 (US$78,000) per day of pollution. However, the city state has yet to issue any penalties under the legislation. A panel of experts including law firms, auditors and investigative companies with expertise in cross-border inquiries would support the government’s efforts, the law ministry said in a statement on Friday. “The conduct of local and foreign companies, their corporate relationships and supply chains will be examined to establish whether they have been involved in causing or condoning the fires that caused or contributed to the haze,” the ministry said. Some palm oil producers have previously denied that their operations in Indonesia have caused or contributed to the pollution, pointing to strict zero-burning policies. Air quality in Singapore improved on Sunday, with the city state’s preferred gauge – the 24-hour PSI – ranging from 102 to 135 as of 9am, levels considered to be “unhealthy”. Readings of 201 or more are considered “very unhealthy” and levels above 301 are regarded as “hazardous” and can trigger school closures.

title: Head of Hong Kong’s new drug regulator pledges to build trust, push innovation

Dr Li Zili, controller of the Hong Kong Centre for Medical Products Regulation (CMPR), said that while many other places in Asia, such as mainland China, Singapore and Japan, had established regulatory agencies long ago, Hong Kong had a distinctive...
content: The head of Hong Kong’s new drug regulatory body has pledged to build a fully capable and globally trusted agency that will become a catalyst for medical innovation rather than merely acting as a “miniature version” of existing overseas models. Dr Li Zili, controller of the Hong Kong Centre for Medical Products Regulation (CMPR), said that while many other places in Asia, such as mainland China, Singapore and Japan, had established regulatory agencies long ago, Hong Kong had a distinctive competitive edge. “We are not going to be a mini-FDA, nor a miniature version of any regulatory body in the world,” he said, referring to the United States Food and Drug Administration. Li said Hong Kong had two competitive advantages: the “one country, two systems” governing principle and the strong pharmaceutical industry on the mainland. “The US regulatory body is strong because of its pharmaceutical industry, with both sides pushing each other forward,” he said, noting that the mainland industry could have a similar symbiotic relationship with the Hong Kong regulator. “With 34 per cent of global innovative drug [pipelines] coming from mainland China now, it’s pretty clear where Hong Kong’s advantages really lie.” Educated at Beijing Union Medical College and Johns Hopkins University, Li has 30 years of drug development and regulatory experience, having served at the FDA and several multinational drug companies. He was selected after a global recruitment exercise that attracted more than 20 applicants. Li said the order in the global pharmaceutical industry was changing, noting that many multinational drug makers had limitations in responding to clinical needs because their patent-protected medicines were unaffordable to many. Meanwhile, in 2025 alone, the overseas licensing deals of Chinese innovative drugs surpassed US$130 billion, with the mainland accounting for about a third of the global active innovative drug pipeline. Li said that China was developing safe, effective and affordable medications that functioned similarly to other patented drugs, which could benefit patients around the world. As a city with trusted high standards, Hong Kong could play an important role in helping those drugs go global through its own evaluation mechanism, he said. “It’s not enough to just be a superconnector between mainland China and the rest of the world,” he stressed. “We need to leverage the strategic strengths of Hong Kong to become a catalyst for health reform and medical innovation globally.” As part of efforts to make Hong Kong an international health and medical innovation hub, the authorities set up the CMPR under the Department of Health and tasked it with implementing “primary evaluation” by 2030, assessing and approving drugs and medical devices independently without relying on foreign approvals. To facilitate that process, authorities launched the “1+” mechanism in November 2023, allowing drug makers to seek registration in Hong Kong for products supported by local clinical data and one foreign regulatory approval instead of two. Li said the primary drug approval mechanism would ensure high quality, transparency and predictability. “Drug development is a long process that can easily take 10 years … My honest opinion is that approving a drug 10 days faster or slower doesn’t make a huge difference on paper,” he noted. “What drug makers care the most about is predictability, that by following our steps it would finally lead to somewhere.” Assistant Director of Health Frank Chan Ling-fung said the duration for primary evaluation would vary by product type and the amount of clinical data, but the CMPR would benchmark its timeline against international practices. He added that the regulator working the fastest took about 200 days to complete an evaluation. Li said a major performance measure for the CMPR would be its ability to conduct independent assessments and make scientifically sound regulatory decisions. He stressed that the CMPR would seek to complement, not replace, the current framework, noting that health authorities had brought in many new drugs to meet clinical needs in Hong Kong and the rest of the Greater Bay Area in the past few decades. His office would increase the efficiency, transparency and robustness of the existing mechanism, he pledged. The body’s two other aims were to earn international trust and become “strategically distinctive”, Li explained. To achieve those aims, the CMPR would form a multidisciplinary team centred on clinical evaluation, while building meaningful international partnerships that went beyond signing memorandums of understanding, he said. Li said his office would identify unmet medical needs in Hong Kong and other places by working with partner regulators to guide resource allocation and talent development. The agency would also explore “unresolved areas” where the international community had not reached a consensus on regulatory standards. “International regulators are most uncertain about rare diseases … they have issued their own guidance, but the approaches are different, which means there is space, and there is opportunity, and more could be done here,” he said. Another potential area of focus was advanced therapies, as regulators were still discussing how standards should be established to match the rapid development of such therapies, Li explained. “We can’t expect Hong Kong to be a world leader in every aspect, but it’s possible for us to gain global recognition as quickly as possible in fields that we choose to focus on,” he said. “Our ultimate goal is to serve the people of Hong Kong and beyond.”

title: Hong Kong’s pursuit of top university rankings comes at a cost
description: The latest rankings confirm what many in Hong Kong already know: the city’s universities are exceptional.
