content: The latest rankings confirm what many in Hong Kong already know: the city’s universities are exceptional. Five institutions continue to sit among the world’s top 100, reflecting decades of investment, academic ambition and hard work. Yet behind the rankings triumph lies a question that receives far less attention: what happens to the people responsible for that success? As universities compete ever harder for rankings, grants and prestige, academics face growing pressure to produce results on ever-shorter timelines. If Hong Kong wants to sustain its success, it must look beyond rankings and ask if the risks and rewards of academic achievement are being shared fairly. Academic excellence is a collective accomplishment. Outstanding teaching emerges from interactions between professors and students. Research breakthroughs depend not only on scholars, but also on research teams, university support, funding agencies, community partners and society at large. When a university rises in the rankings, it is the product of an entire ecosystem. Yet higher education is increasingly governed by the logic of performance management. As competition intensifies, university leaders understandably seek tools that promise measurable gains. The problem is that many of these tools shift risk onto individual academics while concentrating rewards at the institutional level. Becoming an academic is already an exercise in uncertainty. Years are spent earning advanced degrees, completing postdoctoral appointments and navigating highly competitive job markets. Even after securing a position, scholars commit to research programmes, pursue funding, supervise students and undertake projects whose value may not become clear for years. Throughout, they are expected to excel in research, teaching and service. Universities face risks too. They invest in salaries, infrastructure and institutional support while deciding how performance should be evaluated and resources allocated. But this raises a fundamental question: what exactly counts as academic performance? Is it publication numbers, grant income, citations, student evaluations or social impact? How should universities compare a groundbreaking humanities monograph with a commercially valuable patent? How should teaching quality be assessed when student learning depends on factors that extend far beyond the classroom? The answers are neither obvious nor objective. Every metric captures part of the picture while obscuring another. Historically, tenure emerged as a response to this uncertainty. Universities made long-term commitments to scholars whose future contributions they believed justified institutional investment. In return, academics gained the security needed to pursue ambitious ideas. The arrangement was never perfect, but it aligned incentives around long-term excellence rather than short-term output. Today, that balance is increasingly under pressure. Across higher education systems worldwide, annual reviews, metric-based assessments and ranking-driven management play a growing role. When salary adjustments, contract renewals and promotions become tightly linked to annual indicators, universities gain more immediate control over performance and may improve the metrics that feed international rankings. Yet there is an important difference between what can be measured annually and what creates lasting academic and social value. Many influential books take years to write. Groundbreaking discoveries often emerge only after years of failed experiments. Transformational teaching and community partnerships produce benefits that may not become visible until long after students graduate. Institutions that become too focused on short-term indicators risk encouraging behaviours that boost measurable outputs while weakening the deeper foundations of scholarship and education. They may also discourage intellectual risk-taking. Research on scientists’ workplace experiences suggests satisfaction depends not only on funding or resources, but also on professional autonomy, institutional trust, supportive colleagues and confidence about career prospects. These are conditions that enable creativity, collaboration and sustained scholarly achievement. Research is inherently uncertain. The more careers are tied to short-term performance targets, the greater the incentive to prioritise safe, predictable projects. What appears efficient in the short term may ultimately reduce the very innovation universities seek to promote. This matters because universities compete not only for rankings, grants and students, but also for talent. The world’s strongest research systems increasingly recognise that attracting and retaining outstanding scholars requires more than financial investment. Researchers are more likely to thrive in environments that offer stability, supportive academic communities, meaningful participation in governance and the freedom to pursue important questions. Academic well-being is a strategic asset. The debate resembles the broader controversy surrounding rankings. Rankings provide useful information and enhance international visibility. But few would argue that a university’s true value can be reduced to its position in a table. The same principle applies to academic performance. Most importantly, discussions about institutional success often leave students out of the picture. If policies are designed primarily to improve organisational metrics, who ensures that student learning, intellectual development and well-being remain at the centre of university life? The ultimate test of a university is whether it advances knowledge, cultivates thoughtful citizens and contributes to society. For Hong Kong, the challenge is not whether universities should pursue excellence. They must. The question is whether the incentives shaping academic life remain aligned with that goal. That requires funding systems that support long-term scholarship, governance structures that give academics and students meaningful voices, and leadership that recognises the limits of metrics. It requires balancing competition with collegiality, performance with well-being, and institutional ambition with educational purpose. Hong Kong’s universities have shown they can climb the rankings. The harder task is creating the conditions under which talented scholars will continue to produce path-breaking research, inspiring teaching and meaningful public engagement. The universities that succeed in the decades ahead will not necessarily be those that measure the most. They will be those that share risks fairly, reward contributions wisely and create environments in which people can do their best work.

title: Hong Kong to tighten burgeoning premium financing market as red flags, risks emerge
description: Hong Kong’s insurance watchdog is tightening oversight of the city’s booming premium financing market, as the once-niche lending arrangement spreads to lower-tier insurance buyers, while also reviewing regulations, particularly on how insurers evaluate clients’ affordability, according to Insurance Authority executives. Premium financing allows policyholders to borrow money from financial institutions to pay upfront premiums on large life insurance policies, which are commonly used as a wealth...
content: Hong Kong’s insurance watchdog is tightening oversight of the city’s booming premium financing market, as the once-niche lending arrangement spreads to lower-tier insurance buyers, while also reviewing regulations, particularly on how insurers evaluate clients’ affordability, according to Insurance Authority executives. Premium financing allows policyholders to borrow money from financial institutions to pay upfront premiums on large life insurance policies, which are commonly used as a wealth management tool for high-net-worth clients. “Some insurers have promoted it too aggressively by lowering threshold requirements and using high leverage to attract middle-class buyers without fully ensuring that buyers fully understand the underlying risks,” said Marty Lui, the Insurance Authority’s executive director of long term business, at a media briefing on Friday. He said premium financing was absolutely unsuitable for the general public. “If interest rates rise or currency exchange rates fluctuate, borrowers’ interest costs can jump sharply. They may face margin calls or be forced to surrender their policies early at a substantial loss.” The authority highlighted severe risks in strategies combining “participating policies, premium financing and cross-currency arbitrage”. It discovered that over the past year, some policyholders borrowed low-interest Swiss francs from offshore or online banks to purchase US dollar-denominated policies. “Premium financing activity moves inversely with interest rates. Once rates reverse, the risks will surface all at once,” Lui said. “If the Swiss franc appreciates against the US dollar, buyers will face huge currency losses when converting currency to repay debt.” Additionally, disputes involving offshore banks cannot be resolved within Hong Kong’s legal jurisdiction, creating immense legal hurdles for consumers, he added. Lui warned that a further 0.5 percentage point increase in market interest rates could push some floating-rate participating policies into a negative carry – where borrowing costs exceed the policy’s actual return. Alan Wu, acting head of conduct supervision at the Insurance Authority, said at the same briefing that a new joint inspection with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) uncovered three regulatory red flags, including certain insurers evaluating client assets while ignoring existing liabilities like home mortgages, artificially inflating financial resilience. The second was that some intermediaries offered financing advice without proper training or authorisation, while insurers failed to follow up. Thirdly, insurers approved applications where borrowing interest rates exceeded expected policy returns without intervening. The Insurance Authority expected to complete the inspection by late 2026 and will discuss appropriate regulatory measures with the HKMA based on the findings. “The authority has no intention of imposing a one-size-fits-all or overly tight regime as it could trigger a fire sale and cause unnecessary shock to the market,” Wu said. Premium financing now drives significant growth for some insurers. Life insurance sales in Hong Kong rose 58 per cent in the first half of this year to another record high, with premium financing accounting for 36 per cent of new business premiums by value – up from 12 per cent in 2024 and 19 per cent in 2025, according to data from the Insurance Authority. Wu said complaints related to premium financing so far were not significant, mainly because those contracts typically ran for three or five years. “Policyholders usually discover problems only when the financing matures or rates turn, so complaints are likely to rise as rates shift.”

title: Why North Korean leader Kim Jong-un toured a Chinese bus factory in Dandong

content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s tour of a commercial vehicle factory during a surprise visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday points to Pyongyang’s drive to modernise its buses and expand industrial ties with Beijing. In a symbolic move, Kim crossed into China via the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge on Saturday and also returned to North Korea via the bridge later in the day. It was Kim’s first trip to China since he attended a military parade in Beijing last September. His visit took place on the eve of the 76th anniversary marking the entry of Chinese troops into the Korean war in 1950, when they passed through Dandong and crossed the Yalu River into North Korea. While Kim’s main focus on Saturday was commemorating the wartime alliance between Pyongyang and Beijing, his afternoon visit to an automotive plant has also drawn attention. Kim toured Dandong Huanghai Automobile, which was founded in 1951 to carry out repairs for the logistics unit of the Chinese People’s Volunteer Army during the Korean war. The factory now specialises in buses, special-purpose and new-energy vehicles. In May, the company delivered a fleet of bespoke compressed natural gas buses to Colombia. The visit appears to align closely with Kim’s push to electrify and upgrade North Korea’s bus system. An 18-minute video released by state-run Korean Central Television on Sunday shows Kim inspecting assembly lines, opening the doors of several vehicles and taking a look inside, and boarding one of the buses. China – along with other United Nations member states – is prohibited from supplying, selling or transferring industrial machinery, transport vehicles, iron, steel and other metals to North Korea under a UN Security Council resolution passed in 2017. The resolution strengthened sanctions against Pyongyang after it conducted an intercontinental ballistic missile test. The 42-year-old North Korean leader brought an entourage of top officials with him to Dandong. They included Jo Yong-won, secretary of the Central Committee of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea, and Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui. His powerful younger sister Kim Yo-jong, who is director of the WPK Central Committee, was also on the tour. Others included party secretaries Ri Il-hwan and Kim Song-nam, who also heads the WPK’s International Department, and Kim Tok-hun, the first vice-premier of the cabinet who oversees economic and industrial initiatives. Beijing sent its own delegation of top officials to meet the North Korean visitors, led by Wang Huning, the fourth-ranking member of the Chinese Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee and chairman of its political advisory body. Wang was joined by Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the party’s International Department chief Liu Haixing, as well as Ma Zhaoxu, the foreign executive vice-minister, Liaoning provincial party chief Xu Kunlin, Dandong party secretary Jiang Bing, and China’s ambassador to North Korea Wang Yajun. The visit came just weeks before China is due to host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. US President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin are both expected to attend and have voiced interest in holding trilateral talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Trump has also said he wants to meet Kim again. The pair met three times during Trump’s first term but failed to achieve any breakthrough. The South China Morning Post reported last month that Beijing is willing to help broker a fourth Trump-Kim encounter as it seeks a more active role in Korean peninsula diplomacy.

title: North Korea tells UN South ‘fabricated’ border landmine blast
description: North Korea sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, its state media reported Monday. Tensions between the two Koreas have soared since the South last month blamed the blast inside the heavily fortified demilitarised zone that separates the countries on landmines laid by the North, an accusation it has fiercely rejected. The North Korean permanent representative to the UN sent a letter on...
content: North Korea sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, its state media reported Monday. Tensions between the two Koreas have soared since the South last month blamed the blast inside the heavily fortified demilitarised zone that separates the countries on landmines laid by the North, an accusation it has fiercely rejected. The North Korean permanent representative to the UN sent a letter on Sunday to the UN Security Council regarding the “provocation the ROK committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”. The letter said that the landmine incident “fabricated by the ROK, is a sinister obstructive move to brand as a ‘military invasion’, delay and impede the DPRK’s fortification of its southern border”, using the acronyms for both countries’ official names. The incident was a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”, it added. It went on to say its ongoing border fortification efforts were “a legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty going in strict conformity with the UN Charter”, while blasting South Korea for firing warning shots at soldiers involved in the work. “This is a wanton violation of Article 2 (4) of the UN Charter which stresses the need to refrain from the use of force or threat against territorial integrity of any country in international relations,” said the official Korea Central News Agency. South Korea’s foreign ministry sent its own letter to the president of the UN Security Council last week, again blaming the explosion on a North Korean landmine and calling it a “clear violation of the armistice agreement”. The statement comes days after South Korea proposed military talks with North Korea to “mutually confirm the precise location” of their border and discuss restoring communication channels. The proposal was announced after Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, announced that Pyongyang had moved new troop units into “firing position” along the border.

title: Lula pulls off Brazil’s first-ever run-off comeback to beat Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro
description: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won re-election on Sunday in a dramatic comeback after trailing in the first round, extending the rule of a government that has overseen record Chinese investment. content: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won re-election on Sunday in a dramatic comeback after trailing in the first round, extending the rule of a government that has overseen record Chinese investment. The Superior Electoral Court said Lula had 51.79 per cent of valid votes against 48.21 per cent for right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, with 99.99 per cent votes counted. No candidate who trailed after the first round had won a run-off since Brazil adopted the system in 1989. Addressing reporters and allies at a hotel in Sao Paulo, Lula said: “this election was one in which we had to defeat interference coming from outside, through digital platforms, and we are going to have to regulate them”. “This country does not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he added. He also vowed to lead an energy and AI revolution in South America’s biggest economy. “We have to take advantage of the energy potential of a country that perhaps has the greatest renewable energy capacity, to bring here the data centres needed to keep our data in Brazil as well,” Lula promised. But the outcome could still be contested after a Supreme Court justice ordered polls to stay open for two more hours, minutes after voting officially ended at 5pm. No court had extended voting in Brazil before. The order came from Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was Lula’s lawyer before joining the court in 2023. He acted on a complaint from Lula’s campaign that cities in Bahia state run by allies of Flavio Bolsonaro had kept buses in depots and that poorer voters could not reach the polls. Flavio Bolsonaro’s lawyers had separately asked the electoral court to extend voting in 17 flooded municipalities in three states. Many stations had already shut their machines when Zanin’s order arrived, and the system does not allow a closed machine to be reopened. The electoral court then told regional courts that only stations still open should keep receiving voters until 7pm, and Zanin narrowed his order to match. Flavio Bolsonaro refused to acknowledge defeat in a speech to reporters at his campaign headquarters in Brasilia on Sunday night, about 90 minutes after the result was confirmed. “It is impossible to recognise the results of the elections in the context in which these things happened. We are going to use our legal team, we are going to ask for these elections to be annulled,” he said. Some voters were sent home at 5pm while others cast ballots until 7pm, and either campaign could cite that to seek an annulment. Any such request would go to the electoral court, chaired by Kassio Nunes Marques, Jair Bolsonaro’s first appointee to the Supreme Court. The result keeps Latin America’s largest economy – and Beijing’s biggest destination for Chinese capital – out of the group of Trump-aligned governments that now includes Argentina, Chile and Colombia, frustrating Washington’s bid to curb Beijing’s presence in the hemisphere. Talks with the US over tariffs and critical minerals will resume with a government that has offered American companies access to its rare earths but without preferential treatment. Lula’s programme also commits Brazil to a regional strategy for mapping and processing critical minerals, and to pressing ahead with a Brics agenda that Trump has threatened to punish with extra tariffs. Brics is a grouping of Global South economies formed to increase global economic cooperation and counter Western dominance. Lula, who at 80 is Brazil’s oldest-ever sitting president, will begin his fourth term in January, more than two decades after he first took office. He governed from 2003 to 2010 and returned in 2023 after narrowly beating the senator’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting to overturn that defeat. Flavio Bolsonaro built a campaign around ties to the Trump administration, which received him in the Oval Office in May. Flavio Bolsonaro pledged to join a US-led security alliance in the Americas and offered Brazil’s rare earths to Washington as an alternative to Chinese supply. For most of this year, Lula had looked like the favourite, and pollster Quaest gave him a seven-point lead over the senator in a run-off in January. Six of the seven pollsters that published surveys on the eve of the first round still had him ahead, yet he finished 2.2 million votes behind. Most run-off polls showed Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly ahead or tied within the margin of error. Lula’s team tried to deepen voters’ resistance to his rival and to bring first-round abstainers back to the polls. Lula’s political attacks focused on Jair Bolsonaro’s handling of the Covid-19 pandemic and on Flavio Bolsonaro’s dealings with Daniel Vorcaro, a banker who is now in jail. The senator had asked that banker for US$24 million to fund a biopic of his father, months before the central bank shut down the financial institution for suspected fraud. Flavio Bolsonaro responded by raising a police investigation into Lula’s son Fabio Luis. A Supreme Court justice authorised the inquiry in July to examine whether he lobbied officials for a company linked to a scheme that allegedly skimmed money from pensioners’ benefits, and Lula said in a televised debate this month that the fraud had begun under Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Sovereignty and Washington Lula had tried to keep a working relationship with Trump, whom he met at the White House in May for about three hours as Brazil sought to head off a new round of tariffs. Washington imposed duties of up to 50 per cent on Brazilian goods last year in protest at Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. During the meeting, Lula told the US president that Brazil’s critical minerals were open to any country willing to process them locally. “Americans, Chinese, Germans, Japanese, French, whoever wants to participate with us to help us mine, separate and produce the wealth that these rare earths offer us, they are invited,” he said afterwards. The talks did not stop Washington from imposing a 25 per cent tariff on most Brazilian goods in July, and Lula blamed the Bolsonaro family. The senator’s brother Eduardo had spent last year lobbying Washington for sanctions against Brazilian officials over their father’s trial. Lula made sovereignty the centre of his campaign, and in a television broadcast in September he said those willing to hand Brazil’s rare earth reserves to other countries were “the real traitors of the homeland”. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China. “There are people abroad keeping an eye on them and people here ready to hand everything over on a platter,” Lula said. “This time we will not export rocks only to buy back technology.” Two weeks later, he signed a law creating a national policy for critical minerals, including rare earths. In the final week of the campaign, he accused the US government of meddling on Flavio Bolsonaro’s behalf, and his campaign asked the electoral court to disqualify the senator over claims that Meta Platforms had boosted him online. Ties with Beijing Lula travelled to Beijing in April 2023 on a trip his government described as an effort to restart ties that had cooled under Jair Bolsonaro. In Shanghai, he toured Huawei Technologies’ research centre and called for an alternative to the US dollar in trade between the two countries. Xi Jinping returned the visit with a state trip to Brasilia in November 2024, when the two governments signed 37 agreements and raised their relationship to a “community with a shared future”. Brazil stopped short of joining the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s global infrastructure strategy, and chose instead to link it to its own investment programmes. Lula was back in Beijing in May last year for a summit with Latin American leaders and came home with 27 billion reais (US$4.7 billion) in investment pledges from companies such as Great Wall Motor and Meituan. Chinese companies put more money into Brazil than into any other country last year, with a record US$6.1 billion spread across 52 projects, according to the Brazil-China Business Council. Bilateral trade then hit a record US$143 billion in the first nine months of this year as oil sales surged after the war in Iran disrupted Gulf supply, and Brazil’s treasury is now preparing to issue its first yuan bonds in China with a view to borrowing there regularly. China takes over the chair of Brics next year, and Lula’s government programme promises closer ties with the bloc of emerging economies. Flavio Bolsonaro has said he might pull Brazil out of the grouping, which Washington has worked to undermine. Less than two weeks after Washington announced its tariffs, Xi told Lula in a phone call that China supported Brazil in “safeguarding sovereignty and independence, opposing external interference”. The hour-long call was their second this year, and the two leaders agreed to speed up talks on a trade deal between China and the South American trade bloc Mercosur without providing details.

title: Interpol’s Hong Kong meeting to consider ‘silver notice’ targeting criminal assets
description: Interpol will seek approval at its general assembly in Hong Kong next month for a new “silver notice” system to target criminals’ assets and speed up financial investigations into transnational crime. Hong Kong’s police chief also pledged to make financial investigations and scams a top priority in discussions with overseas counterparts during Interpol’s annual meeting, which the city is hosting for the first time. content: Interpol will seek approval at its general assembly in Hong Kong next month for a new “silver notice” system to target criminals’ assets and speed up financial investigations into transnational crime. Hong Kong’s police chief also pledged to make financial investigations and scams a top priority in discussions with overseas counterparts during Interpol’s annual meeting, which the city is hosting for the first time. Interpol secretary general Valdecy Urquiza said in an interview in Hong Kong that the global law enforcement organisation would strive to keep technical channels for data exchange open among member states despite growing geopolitical tensions worldwide. “Transnational crime has become the standard. Criminal activities, they necessarily relate to more than one country, you see criminal organisations in one part of the world targeting communities in a different part of the world,” Urquiza said. “The answer to that is international policing cooperation.” Interpol’s annual general assembly will be held from November 30 to December 3, with more than 2,000 representatives from its 196 member states expected to attend. The assembly, Interpol’s supreme governing body, adopts resolutions on major policies, resources, working methods and financial matters. Urquiza said the organisation aimed to pass a resolution on the silver notice system at the assembly. The system, which has been tested for two years, aims to identify and seize financial assets belonging to criminals. The notice could help prevent criminals from reorganising their enterprises and recruiting new members while law enforcement agencies were conducting investigations and arrests, he explained. Urquiza said the relevant jurisdictions would then use existing legal means to seize and seek the return of the assets in question from other jurisdictions, and that the silver notice could speed up financial investigations. “We give a powerful tool for police officials that will be able to send analysis to the entire law enforcement community about that specific [criminal] group and the specific assets that they are trying to locate,” he said. The silver notice will supplement Interpol’s colour-coded notice system, which covers international requests for cooperation, arrests and information. The red notice, which is an international request for law enforcement agencies to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition or surrender, is part of the system. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming said he hoped, as host, to build a platform for attending police forces to discuss how to combat transnational crime, while focusing on building new partnerships beyond Asia. He said financial investigations and scams would be priority areas for discussion with overseas partners. “The problem is very serious and also very imminent; that’s why it must be the priority of things,” Chow said. He noted that scams accounted for half of Hong Kong’s reported crimes last month, whereas no robbery cases were recorded. Chow said most of the force’s established partnerships for operations and intelligence exchange were with Asean members and other Asian countries. “We will try to make good use of this general assembly to build rapport and also to have more bilateral meetings, so that other than establishing contact, [we can] at least build up some mutual understanding,” Chow said. Hong Kong would also look to African states to foster mutual exchanges, he added. Urquiza also underscored the severity of global fraud trends, saying Interpol had recorded a 55 per cent increase in the number of cases reported across the world last year. “This is the sort of increase that we didn’t see before in any other type of cases,” he said. Urquiza said it was important for Interpol to ensure member countries had technical channels to exchange information regardless of diplomatic ties, as criminal activity became ever more borderless in an increasingly tense geopolitical environment. “We are an organisation that serves as a technical platform for enforcement agencies, a neutral platform,” Urquiza said. He added that if diplomatic tensions caused countries to stop communicating or sharing information, a gap could open for criminal activity to fester. Interpol’s mission would be to keep “technical channels” open for police cooperation regardless of countries’ diplomatic relations. Among its tools are databases accessible to law enforcement agencies containing more than 150 million records on wanted people, stolen property, forged documents, threats related to terrorism and cybercrime. Non-governmental organisations have accused some authoritarian states of abusing Interpol’s notice system and databases for political persecution. Urquiza said the body had robust mechanisms to prevent misuse, including an independent body that had the final say on whether information submitted was compliant with Interpol’s constitution. Every piece of information submitted for publication on Interpol’s databases is assessed by a separate group of police officials and lawyers for compliance with the organisation’s constitution, which prohibits activities of a political, military, religious or racial character. With the force establishing the Hong Kong International Academy of Policing next month, ahead of the general assembly, Chow said he hoped the institution would collaborate with Interpol to provide training programmes for members. “We would like to work closely with Interpol, just like before, and in the future,” he said.

title: South Korean CEO’s 4-year jail term over plant fire that killed 23 spurs anger
description: “How can South Korea’s law be this weak? Twenty-three people died!” Those were the words of Chinese mother Li Shun-ji after South Korea’s Supreme Court upheld a reduced four-year prison sentence for Aricell CEO Park Soon-kwan last Tuesday over a 2024 factory fire that killed 23 workers, including Li’s then-24-year-old daughter, Yan Jing-jing. content: “How can South Korea’s law be this weak? Twenty-three people died!” Those were the words of Chinese mother Li Shun-ji after South Korea’s Supreme Court upheld a reduced four-year prison sentence for Aricell CEO Park Soon-kwan last Tuesday over a 2024 factory fire that killed 23 workers, including Li’s then-24-year-old daughter, Yan Jing-jing. The blaze at the lithium battery manufacturer’s factory in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi province, killed 17 Chinese nationals, one Laotian national and five South Koreans, and injured nine others. About 35,000 lithium batteries reportedly exploded in a chain reaction, with defective products and rushed operations to meet military supply deadlines contributing to the disaster. “Are you making this decision because we are foreigners?” Li, 56, said through tears after the ruling. Under South Korea’s Serious Accidents Punishment Act (SAPA), introduced in 2022 to strengthen corporate accountability for fatal workplace accidents, Aricell was found to have sent 53 unskilled workers to work on the batteries, neglected safety training and failed to secure evacuation routes. Last year, a district court sentenced Park and his son, the factory’s managing director, to 15 years in prison each, the harshest sentences ever handed down to company executives under the law. The appeal court later cleared both men of a key charge related to the failure to install an emergency exit on the factory’s second floor and reduced the jail term to four years for Park and seven years for his son. The Supreme Court also upheld the jail sentence for Park’s son. Aricell was also fined 800 million won (US$604,000). In its ruling, the appeal court said safety regulations did not require exits on every floor and were applicable on a building-by-building basis. It also considered Aricell’s settlements with bereaved families. The Supreme Court’s judgment has drawn criticism from the victims’ relatives and labour activists, who say it reflects a judicial system that is too lenient towards corporations for offences committed by them. ‘Is this real?’ “When the court ruling ended in just 10 seconds, my heart started pounding so hard that my mind went completely blank,” Li said, referring to the time between the court convening and announcing its verdict. “I kept asking the person next to me, ‘Is this real? Is this really happening?’” Yan had worked at Aricell for only two months. She had studied to become a teacher in China but left everything behind in the summer of 2024 to join her family, who were planning to apply for permanent residency in South Korea. She took a job at the factory to help support them and received a pay rise after just two months. “She was happily telling me that her managers seemed to have a good impression of her,” Li said. “But not long afterwards, the accident happened.” Li arrived in South Korea in 2002 and later opened a Chinese restaurant in Siheung with her husband, but after the pandemic forced its closure, she joined an insurance company and he returned to factory work. The ruling has prompted criticism from civic groups, including the National Council of Churches in Korea, while legislators have highlighted shortcomings in government workplace inspections. Li has also faced online abuse, including comments telling her family to return to China. “If it were up to me, I wouldn’t want to continue living here,” she said. “After living here for more than 20 years, I have only just realised how much discrimination there is against foreigners like us.” More than 70 per cent of South Koreans in their twenties and thirties held unfavourable views of China, according to a survey by the Seoul-based think tank East Asia Institute released last year. Li, however, has decided to stay in South Korea for her 17-year-old younger daughter, who arrived as a toddler and speaks only Korean. She attends high school in Siheung. “After seeing how worried she was about me, I decided I couldn’t go on living like a dead person,” Li said, recalling the two years of her anguish following Yan’s death. “I started going out into the streets to protest and fight for justice.” Persistent workplace dangers South Korea has reported a series of deadly industrial accidents in recent months. In June, five people died in an explosion at Hanwha Aerospace’s factory in Daejeon. A special inspection by the Ministry of Employment and Labour found 473 violations, 189 of which were referred for legal action. In March, 14 people died in a fire at an auto parts factory operated by Anjeon Industrial, also in Daejeon. The company’s CEO was among 13 people referred to prosecutors on charges including professional negligence resulting in death and injury. Workplace deaths have declined in South Korea, but fatalities in manufacturing have risen. The labour ministry recorded 366 deaths in accidents at the workplace subject to official investigation between January and September, down 20 per cent from 457 in the same period last year, while manufacturing deaths increased to 132 from 119. Jeon Soo-kyong, a coordinator at the labour rights group Solidarity for Worker’s Health, said unsafe conditions disproportionately affected workers in vulnerable employment positions. “Many of the workers dying in industrial accidents in South Korea today are migrant workers, as in the Aricell case, or Korean workers on non-regular contracts,” she said. “There are subtle forms of discrimination in the workplace. A non-regular worker may be left to work alone without adequate safety measures, while a permanent employee has a colleague to help with the same task.” Jeon said such practices reflected entrenched management cultures that prioritised cost-cutting. She also pointed to South Korea’s history of treating labour activism as a threat during its rapid industrialisation in past decades. “Campaigns by workers to address industrial accidents have also been stigmatised by society, particularly by the prosecution and the government,” she said. Cases under the SAPA labour safety law have led to greater scrutiny of corporate accountability in recent years. In 2022, a district court acquitted Sampyo Group and its chairman after three workers died in a landslide at a quarry operated by Sampyo Industry in Yangju, prompting outrage among South Koreans over the verdict. Choi Cheong-hak, a law professor at the Korea National Open University, attributed the hesitancy to impose severe punishments on companies or business executives to “a widely shared belief that these people play an important role in society”. He noted that despite SAPA’s wide implementation in the country, the regulation still needed more teeth: of the 167 first-instance verdicts handed down, only three corporate executives received final prison sentences. “This is an extremely small rate.” Vow to keep fighting Shin Ha-na, the lawyer representing Aricell’s bereaved families, said she would challenge Tuesday’s ruling, arguing that it effectively gave the company a free pass. “Labour safety laws are not being properly enforced in practice, and rulings like this narrow what those laws are meant to achieve,” she said. “Our priority is to ensure that existing laws are properly implemented and enforced.” Her team is preparing to file a complaint over the ruling with the Constitutional Court within the 30-day deadline. For Li, the fight is not over as she is seeking to recover her daughter’s remains. Of the 23 people killed in the fire, only one body was found to be intact. The bereaved families hope to hold a joint funeral once the remaining remains have been recovered. Hwaseong city officials have discussed plans for a memorial park. “All the families want this case to end,” Li said. “But what we want most of all is for our loved ones to finally have a proper resting place.”

title: Standard Chartered-led Anchorpoint plans retail stablecoin as HSBC RedCoin launches
description: After HSBC RedCoin launched on Friday, Anchorpoint – the stablecoin-issuing joint venture led by Standard Chartered – said it plans to launch a retail product on a public blockchain, even as it takes a “prudent approach”. “Our next major milestone is to [help] bring regulated digital money into everyday payments and commercial applications, while connecting traditional payment infrastructure with this emerging digital finance,” said Dominic Maffei, CEO of Anchorpoint. “This is a public...
content: After HSBC RedCoin launched on Friday, Anchorpoint – the stablecoin-issuing joint venture led by Standard Chartered – said it plans to launch a retail product on a public blockchain, even as it takes a “prudent approach”. “Our next major milestone is to [help] bring regulated digital money into everyday payments and commercial applications, while connecting traditional payment infrastructure with this emerging digital finance,” said Dominic Maffei, CEO of Anchorpoint. “This is a public blockchain stablecoin, so applying this to retail, a lot of considerations need to be made.” Anchorpoint’s commitment to serving its retail customers comes as HSBC just launched its Hong Kong dollar-backed HSBC RedCoin for the 3.3 million users of its PayMe app. After releasing its institutional product in August, Anchorpoint previously said its retail product could arrive as early as the end of 2026, but did not confirm a launch date at a press conference on Friday. “We believe it’s important to build the market out in a long-term, sustainable manner,” Maffei said, adding that “rushing something or doing something the wrong way does not make sense”. Under its business-to-business-to-consumer model, Maffei said Anchorpoint was “building this open and inclusive ecosystem” in which “partners across the value chain” could work together. “Market education is key,” Maffei added. Anchorpoint launched the Tokenised Money Adoption Programme last month “to support education, research and dialogue around tokenised money”, he said. Highlighting stablecoins’ advantages, Maffei noted that “it’s 24/7, it’s instantaneous, it’s a reduction in cost, it’s programmability, interoperability, scalability.” He identified cross-border payments as a “key use case” for stablecoins in the payment ecosystem. “The goal is to connect Hong Kong to other corridors,” Maffei said. Anchorpoint had previously worked in the United Arab Emirates and would share updates on other corridors as they came live, he added. Stablecoins are digital tokens issued on a blockchain that can be transferred between parties within seconds, bypassing traditional clearing procedures. Unlike other cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin, stablecoins are pegged to a traditional currency like the Hong Kong dollar or US dollar. Tokenised financial products, including stablecoins, are expected to be a central topic at next month’s FinTech Week x StartmeupHK, co-hosted by multiple Hong Kong government authorities.

title: Trump escalates attacks on Michigan Senate hopeful El-Sayed with 9/11 comparison
description: US President President Donald Trump at a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States. “I’m here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” the president told a receptive audience in Port Huron, which is in a Michigan area where 66 per cent of the vote went to Trump...
content: US President President Donald Trump at a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States. “I’m here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” the president told a receptive audience in Port Huron, which is in a Michigan area where 66 per cent of the vote went to Trump ‌in the 2024 presidential election. If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, 2001, attacks. Michigan has one of the nation’s most competitive US Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, with former US congressman Mike Rogers, a Republican, and El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide control of the chamber. The president on Sunday compared voting against El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers. “Twenty-five years later, Michigan ⁠needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol,” said Trump. If El-Sayed wins, “he would be the only senator that will have to go through a ‌metal detector before he’s allowed to go in the Senate,” Trump said. El-Sayed has dismissed the accusations against him, and at a Sunday night event, he suggested that Trump’s frequent emphasis of El-Sayed’s name contains a measure of hypocrisy. “I get that the president of the United States takes personal offence to my first ‌name,” El-Sayed told an audience in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity, doesn’t ⁠seem to mind as much when it’s ⁠the Qataris who are giving him a US$400 million private jet.” Affinity Partners, Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner’s investment fund, has reportedly received billions from a Saudi Government entity. Qatar gifted Trump a Boeing 747 jet. The mostly White crowd at ‌Sunday’s rally cheered Trump’s comments on El-Sayed. Some attendees yelled “traitor” and others yelled “deport”, although El-Sayed was born in Michigan. Terrance Camburn, a 52-year-old disabled US Army veteran from Sandusky, Michigan, said he supported Trump’s criticism because of El-Sayed’s “political beliefs”. “I’ve been down to Dearborn and I’ve seen ‌many of ‌the things he agrees with,” Camburn said when asked about Trump’s 9/11 comments. Dearborn, Michigan, has the highest per-capita concentration of Muslims of any US city. As he left the venue after the rally, Rogers did ‌not respond to Reuters’ questions about Trump’s invocation of 9/11. But earlier on Sunday, he said on NBC’s Meet the Press that he did not agree with the notion that El-Sayed is a violent terrorist. “I’ve ⁠never called him a terrorist,” Rogers told NBC. Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups. El-Sayed has denied ⁠affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood, saying it is “shameful” for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States. Rogers told Meet the Press that El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations. “He’s a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don’t like America,” he said. Trump’s speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after ‌former president Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the ‌state, underscoring its importance in next week’s elections. At a Saturday rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed’s opponents as an attempt to make him look “less American than they are”. The former president compared them to his own experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya. “This stuff didn’t work on me,” Obama said. “Not in Michigan. It’s not going to work on Abdul.” Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans’ narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

title: Why cloud computing pioneer Wang Jian thinks space is the next AI frontier
description: Long before artificial intelligence became the next big thing in the tech industry, Wang Jian was crafting the foundational infrastructure that would eventually power it.
