content: Long before artificial intelligence became the next big thing in the tech industry, Wang Jian was crafting the foundational infrastructure that would eventually power it. In 2008, he joined Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – as chief architect and founded Alibaba Cloud in 2009, convincing the company’s leadership to invest heavily in building a cloud computing infrastructure from scratch. Today, Wang’s purview has expanded considerably. As an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the director of Zhejiang Lab, a research institution backed by the Zhejiang provincial government, his focus has turned to a new frontier: space computing. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. The current excitement over AI models is not the first wave of enthusiasm you’ve observed. How has this been different? The pace of this wave of AI development has clearly exceeded my expectations. AI has been developing for nearly 40 years, if we start from the 1980s, and I have lived through more than one developmental cycle. In the 1980s, Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer Systems initiative. People thought it would bring sweeping changes, but it ultimately fell short of expectations. Over the past decade, China has had its own wave of enthusiasm around the “four AI tigers”: SenseTime, Megvii, CloudWalk and Yitu, with their focus on computer vision technology. That, too, did not deliver what many had expected. The current wave is different. Its progress has exceeded expectations, and its impact extends far beyond AI itself. AI is no longer just an industry; it is a variable that will affect almost everything, as we are already seeing in how it assists mathematics research. To understand this wave, we need to look at how the roles of data, models and computing power have changed over time. We often discuss all three together without making it clear that their importance shifts in different phases of AI development. The AlexNet model in the 2012 ImageNet competition showed the importance of data. The introduction of the Transformer architecture in 2017 showed the importance of model design. And Nvidia’s rise over the past few years reflects the significant role that computing power has played more recently. My view is that data will become more important again over the next three to five years, perhaps longer. Internet text is depleting fast for AI training, while vast amounts of scientific data remain under-explored. I also think we need to reconsider what we mean by “artificial intelligence”. Much of the discussion today treats it as artificial human intelligence. I think that is the wrong way to frame it. I think when we talk about AI, we’re actually talking about machine intelligence. Machine intelligence and human intelligence have overlapping capabilities, but they need not develop along the same path. If we constantly measure machines against human intelligence, we risk starting from a mistaken premise. Changing that perspective could change how we think about many questions in AI. I use AI tools intensively, but I still create all my own presentation decks You predicted that 90 per cent of AI applications and technologies will disappear within the next decade. Which AI tools are truly useful, and which ones are just there to address “pseudo-demands”? I made that prediction against a very specific backdrop. At that time, everyone was just building extensions on top of ChatGPT and other GPTs. Even OpenAI wants to turn ChatGPT into a platform for developers to build applications on top of it. If you look at it today, a chat tool itself is a very small application. If you view AI so narrowly that you only derive applications from a chat platform, you are only capturing a very small fraction of what AI can do for the world. If we calculate by token volume today, the vast majority are already being used elsewhere; they are not on those initial ChatGPT-based applications. I believe AI will be able to do lots of things for us. As its capabilities expand, applications built around a chatbot platform to perform a few limited functions may struggle to be sustained. In AI applications, at least two areas deserve particular attention. The first is coding. I prefer to describe it as “coding” rather than “writing software”. Coding used to be seen as a specialised skill belonging to software engineers. Now, anyone with an idea could turn that idea into something tangible with the help of AI coding tools. This explains why I believe AI coding opens up a wide range of use scenarios and will create value far beyond the traditional software industry. The second area is scientific research. Computers were widely used in research from their earliest days, and AI could now further change research practices. In the past, people might ask how much training someone needed to become a scientist, or whether someone who had not attended a leading institution such as MIT was qualified to conduct research. AI could lower these barriers and unlock potential that previously went unrecognised. That is what I consider a seismic change: people who cannot code may be able to build software, and people without traditional research training may be able to contribute to scientific discoveries. Journalists also have to confront these changes. I do not believe good journalists will be easily replaced by AI, but repetitive work that lacks independent thinking or creativity could certainly be replaced. I use AI tools intensively, but I still create all my own presentation decks. The AI race between the United States and China has intensified, with a tendency towards decoupling at both the model and computing levels. How do you picture the future of China’s AI industry against this backdrop? I am very optimistic about China’s AI development over the long term, while recognising that there are challenges in the short term. Unlike many other technologies, AI will affect all of society and is difficult to confine to one place. It is inherently global. I agree with China’s view that AI should be a global public good. It is already too late to “decouple” China and the US in AI models and compute. For one thing, China’s open models are approaching the capabilities of leading US proprietary models in certain areas. Disruptive breakthroughs may still emerge, and it is difficult at this stage to say who has an absolute lead. For another, China’s domestically developed computing chips have already reached a certain level of capability. In an open market, Chinese computing hardware would struggle to compete with US products on price-performance and technological sophistication. But the US has disrupted that open market. Under the current conditions, China’s computing hardware has to be sufficient for itself, and it is basically sufficient. US restrictions may therefore not be a catastrophic problem; instead, the restrictions helped accelerate the development of China’s chip capabilities. China’s leading AI companies have been sticking to open-source or open-weight models, while closed-source remains the dominant format in the US. Why has there been such a divergence, and which approach will win? We cannot simply apply the experience of traditional software – open-source versus closed-source – when it comes to AI. Traditional open-source software offers an alternative in a market where commercial software has been relatively mature. AI is different: open and closed approaches have emerged side by side while the industry itself is still taking shape. There is also a worldwide debate over whether some models described as “open-source” actually qualify, since they release only their weights. Applying the traditional software definition of “open-source” may not accurately describe what a model “opens”. I prefer the term “open-resource” to describe model openness. Training each model requires substantial resources, including computing power and electricity. Some countries, even if they have the money, may not have access to sufficient electricity, computing capacity or talent. Making a model open shares the benefits of those resources, allowing people who cannot afford to make the same investment themselves to use the resulting capabilities. Open and closed models are not in a zero-sum contest, nor must one eliminate the other. Competition between them can help both advance. A company that operates efficiently and has a viable business model can also grow while making its models openly available. Valuation considerations and business conditions may differ between China and the US, so openness may affect their companies’ valuations differently. DeepSeek, for example, has maintained a high valuation despite making its models openly available. AI tokenises data. Are token prices low enough to maintain market demand while covering the computing cost? Will they drop further as technology develops? How will the token industry appear in the US and China given the gap in resource costs? A key step in AI advancement is whether token prices can fall further. This is closely tied to the importance of data represented as tokens. As I have said before, we should think about data in terms of tokens, and share and use data through tokens. The cost of tokens reflects several factors: computing power, electricity, models and crucially, the value of the underlying data. It should not be understood simply as how much electricity or computing capacity has been consumed to generate the tokens. Over time, electricity and computing expenses should account for a smaller share of token costs, while the value attributed to data should account for a larger share. I believe tokens will become increasingly affordable while still commanding a reasonable price that reflects the value of the data behind them. China and the US may gradually diverge in their approach to tokens and their underlying business ecosystems. If we look only at electricity and computing costs, their understanding of token value is likely to converge. Although these costs vary between locations, industrial production and circulation tend to keep them within a certain comparable range over time. I am reluctant to call China’s electricity abundance an ‘advantage’. Having the wiggle room is one thing, whether it could be put to good use is another The real difference lies in the value of data. One important contribution of this wave of AI development is that it has shown us how significant data is as a factor of production. Tokens should be cheap, but they are not yet cheap enough. Model training is generally expensive, and those costs must, in principle, eventually be spread across each token. Token prices in China are relatively low for several reasons. The average cost of computing resources used to train models is lower. China’s electricity supply and renewable energy development also provide wiggle room, particularly when it comes to supporting concentrated model training. Compared with the US, China has less reason to worry about electricity constraints. I am reluctant to call China’s electricity abundance an “advantage”. Having the wiggle room is one thing, whether it could be put to good use is another. When it comes to AI and computing, semiconductors are always a focus. As the US retains tight control over chip exports to China, especially the most advanced units, home-made hardware has achieved breakthroughs in recent years. How do you evaluate the actual progress of the domestic chip sector? We should not view China’s domestically developed chips narrowly as a response to the US refusing to sell advanced chips to China. Instead, we should also ask how chips made in China can serve users around the world. I believe Nvidia deserves tribute. Without Nvidia, we might all still be exploring in the dark. It initially developed chips for gaming rather than AI. But through its sustained investment in computing power, it was well positioned when the AI industry emerged and helped explore a path for the entire industry. Today, once we know the chips are serving AI, the difficulty actually drops a lot. AI chips can be categorised into two types of demand: training and inference. We know that chips need to support model training and inference, and we can design and optimise them around clearly defined requirements. Their design requirements differ, allowing developers to make more targeted trade-offs between performance, efficiency and application needs. New entrants no longer have to begin by figuring out what their chips could be used for. Nvidia undertook that exploration for the industry, lowering the barriers for those that followed. Chinese chip developers know which requirements they are designing for and understand how training and inference work. That allows them to optimise chips effectively for tasks such as inference. I am fully confident in China’s ability to develop inference chips. It is difficult to say what chips will look like in 10 or 20 years, because we do not know what AI will look like then. We must all continue to innovate and face the next set of challenges together. I do not believe the concept of “overtaking on a bend” actually exists. Today, the US and China can jointly solve the challenges we are facing as humanity. You founded Alibaba Cloud in 2009, when most people considered cloud computing an unattainable concept. What prompted you to stick to this decision? Looking back at the industrial revolutions, it was the steam engine that set change in motion, and electricity that amplified its impact. The information technology revolution followed a similar pattern. If computing had remained confined to mainframes, it would have been like the industrial revolution stopping at the steam engine: its impact would never have become so widespread. Cloud computing is a revolution in how computing power is delivered, much like the transition from steam power to electricity. Once you truly believe in that direction, you have the motivation to persevere. I once thought that if I didn’t finish the work myself, others could have carried it forward. I was fortunate enough to see the cloud computing sector thrive. The mobile internet’s explosive growth gave us tremendous support. Without it, cloud computing might have faltered. Then AI emerged, making the cloud’s importance even clearer. Nvidia’s massive chip sales to cloud providers are one example. I have always believed that cloud computing is an enduring business, not something ephemeral. Building cloud computing, like developing AI, requires wholehearted conviction. If there is even the slightest weakness in that conviction – something that may not yet amount to doubt – difficulties can overwhelm you. It is like a crack in an aircraft’s surface that gradually widens under pressure. An employee once told me that he worked hard, frequently stayed late and was willing to be “the last to leave” the company. My response was that being “the last to leave” is completely different from being “the last man standing”. The former ultimately leaves; the latter remains through the hardest times. Another colleague who later left to start an AI company described the feeling perfectly. He said he felt like a group of us were holding hands trying to hug a massive tree, but we had no idea how thick the tree actually was, or when our hands would finally meet. The uncertainty was beyond imagination. US hyperscalers have long maintained higher margins than their Chinese peers. Does this mean China’s cloud industry is smaller? How can China’s cloud computing market become bigger? China’s cloud computing market is no smaller than that of the US, and it has technological capabilities, but the industry as a whole remains underdeveloped. The US has Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as Oracle, which is increasingly focused on its cloud business. China has relatively fewer companies with comparable scale and cloud capabilities, with Alibaba Cloud being the most prominent. I would like to see two more companies similar to Alibaba Cloud emerge, giving China at least three significant cloud providers operating at scale. That would help the industry flourish, strengthen economies of scale and create fuller competition. Alibaba Cloud has played a leading role, but one company cannot drive innovation across the entire market alone. Competition does not have to mean suppliers continually undercutting one another on price. There are two kinds of competition. Destructive competition can ruin a market. Healthy competition encourages companies to improve their operations and efficiency, giving customers better prices and services while allowing providers to earn reasonable profits. Low prices don’t necessarily come at the expense of suppliers’ profitability. Fuller competition can also spur creativity across companies. When others continually push you to improve, efficiency, service quality and profit margins can rise together. Furthermore, in Chinese Premier [Li Qiang]’s government work report this year, the term “public cloud” was heavily emphasised. This was the first time it was used in such a report. In China, we used to constantly debate “public cloud” versus “private cloud”, which is not really helpful to industry development. It is a matter of public service versus proprietary networks. Computing must become a public service. No public service can exist if costs remain high, so it must scale to become cost-effective. You have served as the director of Zhejiang Lab since 2023. The research institute focuses on AI and computing, including space computing. What drove you to pivot towards space computing? The rationale is very simple: the problems facing Earth – climate change, extreme weather, geological disasters like landslides – can no longer be solved by only looking at them from the ground. You have to go to space to see the whole picture. Going into space is not just about exploring space itself, it is also about solving problems on Earth. Short-term weather forecasting for aviation, for example, requires observations made by satellites in space to see the full picture. When observations are made and data is collected in space, we also need to consider where the computing should take place. If a satellite collects data, sends it back to Earth for processing and then delivers the results to those who need them, that can delay time-sensitive work. It is like having to bring surgical instruments from a distant location when an operation is already needed. Putting computing power in space would allow data generated there to be processed promptly. AI has made this need more urgent: there is already an abundance of data in space, but what once was missing was the ability to analyse and use it in the right place. Now with AI, we are able to process all this data, hence the urgency to build space computing facilities. There is a substantial gap between satellite observations and the use of the resulting data. AI could help process and use more of it. Cameras and other observation payloads on some remote-sensing satellites sit idle roughly 90 per cent of the time because they cannot continuously collect and transmit everything. Meanwhile, roughly 90 per cent of data collected in space is lost because bandwidth is insufficient to transmit it back to Earth. Cloud computing mainly addresses computing needs on Earth. Space computing has its own requirements and development logic. It should not be understood simply as moving terrestrial data centres into orbit or finding another location to address electricity constraints on Earth. We have to be very clear about how our approach differs from Elon Musk’s. Space computing is not simply moving ground-based data centres up to space. If Musk says he wants to put a data centre in space, today he is the only one who can do it because he is the only one with that kind of launch capacity. We are not doing that. We are solving the fundamental issue of processing space-native data directly in space. The first questions are how data generated in space should be processed and how it can be turned into timely, usable results. I have also discussed this in Geneva. “Putting computing power in space” and “sending data centres into space” may sound similar, but the approach is different. Sending data centres into space may seem like a daunting task. But space computing involves much more than that, because processing space data requires an entire value chain, with opportunities for a wide range of participants.

title: Peak lighting outcry spotlights the trouble with fast-track governance
description: It’s common knowledge that Hong Kong has a spectacular skyline, especially at night. And given our current obsession with boosting tourism and other value-adding objectives, it shouldn’t come as a surprise that our tourism authorities are actively adding more light to our night skyline. The Tourism Board tried holding monthly firework and drone shows in 2024, but had to scale back after a budget cut – and amid questions of whether more frequent displays, costing the public HK$1 million...
content: It’s common knowledge that Hong Kong has a spectacular skyline, especially at night. And given our current obsession with boosting tourism and other value-adding objectives, it shouldn’t come as a surprise that our tourism authorities are actively adding more light to our night skyline. The Tourism Board tried holding monthly firework and drone shows in 2024, but had to scale back after a budget cut – and amid questions of whether more frequent displays, costing the public HK$1 million (US$127,537) a pop, were really making a bigger impression on visitors. They weren’t. Regular firework shows diminished the novelty factor of the experience and heightened the likelihood of disappointment; effectively, public money was being thrown at unimpressed visitors. And this is not to mention the environmental costs associated with all that smoke and fire. Yet, the tourism authorities seem not to have learned, or remembered, the lesson that less is more. This year, they tried to roll out a lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak, and have succeeded in causing quite the outrage. Going by the images shared online, it is not difficult to see why the lighting installations along the narrow Lugard Road and Harlech Road trail encircling The Peak have drawn such a negative response from residents. The Peak is one of Hong Kong’s treasures – providing us with access to nature, fantastic views of our city, and a window on our history. It’s an easy hike for residents of all ages. It is beloved by tourists and part of an experience that includes rides up and down on the Peak Tram. Planting metal structures along a nature trail and cutting down trees and flowers to make room for electric lighting installations do not add value to The Peak. Sure, some of us enjoy taking in the city lights at night from The Peak, but we don’t necessarily need to see more lights along the walk. Promoting tourism and the night economy shouldn’t be contentious. It only becomes so when the government fails to see the value residents see, as with the controversy triggered by the trail lighting project. Residents, and I would argue confidently, tourists too, are attracted to a dose of nature in the middle of our concrete jungle. Would light fixtures add to the appeal? Maybe, but at what cost? A novelty that disturbs the tranquillity offered by natural scenery would, well, naturally be met with frustration. But this is more than a miscalculation of the public response or a value mismatch when it comes to how the government and the public perceive environmental impact. The public outcry over the lighting project should raise a red flag for the current administration where it concerns consulting stakeholders in policymaking. In its defence, the Tourism Board said it had communicated with “residents near Lugard Road and Harlech Road” and “relevant District Council members”, and sought advice from various government departments and tree experts. But that clearly wasn’t enough, seeing as the board has now pressed pause on the project. The Peak doesn’t just belong to the handful of surrounding households, so the scope of the communication was problematic. Consulting the local district council should have done the job, in theory. But a lawmaker has said a local district councillor had not, in fact, been involved in the initial consultation. This should set multiple alarm bells ringing because it raises the question of whether the government’s district governance is impactful. Such questions go much deeper than a single lighting project. The embarrassing bus seat belt law … was passed using this exact same method Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui was quick to respond, and that’s good news. She said the Tourism Board and the Tourism Commission were gathering public feedback and would visit the relevant sites with district councillors. At least the government acknowledged having insufficiently communicated with stakeholders, though not exactly in those words. “We are still listening to opinions and may make modifications” is enough of an admission of error. We have seen the government operating like this elsewhere, by using negative vetting to push through legislation before the Legislative Council can debate it. The latest instance is how it is moving to restrict media access to land records through negative vetting, after limiting access to the vehicle and the company registries. This has been met with pushback, even as the government maintains that it is committed to transparency. Let’s hope it has not forgotten the embarrassing bus seat belt law that was passed using this exact same method. Scrutiny, feedback and oversight are not red tape to be torn down in the name of efficiency.

title: Brazil’s election left hanging as judge extends vote after polls close, sparking chaos
description: A Supreme Court justice in Brazil ordered polls in the presidential run-off to stay open for two more hours on Sunday, minutes after voting had officially ended at 5pm Brasilia time (4am on Monday in Hong Kong). The order left election officials across China’s biggest trading partner in Latin America unsure whether to reopen polling stations or send their machines to be counted. Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s lawyer before joining the court in 2023, acted...
content: A Supreme Court justice in Brazil ordered polls in the presidential run-off to stay open for two more hours on Sunday, minutes after voting had officially ended at 5pm Brasilia time (4am on Monday in Hong Kong). The order left election officials across China’s biggest trading partner in Latin America unsure whether to reopen polling stations or send their machines to be counted. Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s lawyer before joining the court in 2023, acted on a complaint from Lula’s campaign about bus shortages in cities run by allies of his rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. About an hour later he limited the order to stations whose machines had not yet been shut, so that some voters could cast ballots until 7pm while others were sent home. The confusion struck an election in which Flavio Bolsonaro is standing in for his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. The elder Bolsonaro is barred from office and was convicted by the Supreme Court last year of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022. A week after Lula took office in January 2023, thousands of Jair Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed Congress, the presidential palace and the Supreme Court in Brasilia. The Superior Electoral Court, which organises Brazilian elections, stopped publishing results at 5.20pm with 0.25 per cent of machines counted. No court had ever prolonged voting in Brazil before. Voting is compulsory in Brazil, but millions skip it and pay a small fine. Lula built his run-off strategy around getting poorer voters who depend on buses to the polls. He finished second in the first round this month with 45.16 per cent of valid votes against 47.03 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, and no runner-up has ever won a presidential run-off in Brazil. The race has also turned on Brazil’s ties with Beijing. Lula has courted Chinese investors and backed a trade deal between the Mercosur bloc and China. A memo carrying Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign branding proposed an anti-China rare earths partnership with the United States, the South China Morning Post reported in September. Flavio Bolsonaro later said he would work with both powers. Buses kept in depots The trouble started on Saturday afternoon, when Sao Paulo’s regional electoral court told the city to put its entire bus fleet on the streets for the vote. The municipal transport company said it received the order with less than 12 hours’ notice. Voters in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, complained from early morning of long waits and packed buses. Before lunchtime the head of Bahia’s electoral court had ordered the Federal Police to arrest the city’s mobility secretary, writing that the instruction to cut the fleet had come from his department. He set a fine of 1 million reais (US$197,000) for every hour the order went unmet. City officials said the secretary was in Paris on an official visit and would return on Monday. The administration, whose mayor supports Flavio Bolsonaro, blamed the delays on buses covered in campaign stickers, which electoral law forbids. By the afternoon, inspectors from Bahia’s consumer protection agency had counted 544 buses fit to run sitting in five depots. Sao Paulo, where 9.14 million people are registered to vote and whose mayor also backs Flavio Bolsonaro, had 71.7 per cent of its buses running at 1.20pm according to municipal figures. The Workers’ Party put the figure at 60 per cent. The courts rejected the party’s request to arrest the city’s transport secretary. Speaking to reporters outside his home in Sao Paulo in the afternoon, Lula called the shortages inexplicable. “We will not allow robbery, banditry and bandit mayors,” he said. Flavio Bolsonaro’s lawyers filed their own request after heavy rain, asking for voting to run until 7pm in 17 flooded municipalities in three states. Electoral court gave 30-minute deadline Lula’s Workers’ Party and its allies first asked the electoral court to extend voting in Salvador and two neighbouring cities in the early afternoon. At 3.42pm they filed a second petition naming nine more states. The court’s president Kassio Nunes Marques signed an order at 4.07pm giving Bahia’s electoral court and the electoral prosecution service half an hour to respond. The deadline expired 23 minutes before polls were due to shut. In the same order he noted that the court had refused to extend voting in the 2022 run-off because the problems reported then had not stopped people from voting. The prosecutors’ reply, which opposed any change to the legal voting hours, arrived at 5.01pm, after voting had ended. Nunes Marques reached the Supreme Court in 2020 as Jair Bolsonaro’s first appointee and has chaired the electoral court since May. The electoral court has seven judges, three of them from the Supreme Court, and is always chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Sunday’s dispute therefore pitted two members of the same court against each other. Nunes Marques has been under pressure for two months over his links to a Banco Master scandal. The central bank shut the lender down last year, and its former owner has been in custody since March. Files the Federal Police sent to the Supreme Court in September included a contract under which the bank would pay up to 427 million reais (US$84 million) in success fees to a law firm run by the wife of a federal appeals judge. Messages on the banker’s phone placed the judge in a group they referred to by the justice’s initials, KN. Other messages leaked that month showed the banker authorising monthly payments of 500,000 reais to the Nunes Marques’ son, a lawyer. In October the local magazine piaui reported that the banker had organised and paid for a party with sex workers for Nunes Marques at his Sao Paulo flat in February last year. The magazine cited messages from the banker’s phone obtained by the Federal Police. Nunes Marques has denied wrongdoing through his office, adding that he had never voted in the banker’s favour. Polls already closed when order arrived By the time the electoral court’s deadline ran out, Lula’s lawyers had already gone to the Supreme Court. They used a type of complaint that lets parties bypass lower courts when authorities are accused of defying the Supreme Court’s rulings. Lodged at 4.22pm, their filing accused mayorships of Salvador, Feira de Santana and Lauro de Freitas of breaching a precedent that obliges cities to run free buses at weekday frequency on election days. It asked for voting to be extended nationwide so that all voters would be treated equally. Zanin, to whom the case was assigned by lot, wrote that the facts had reached the court at 4.32pm. He extended voting by two hours in every polling station in Brazil and left the electoral court to enforce the order, which was issued at about 5.02pm. Machines had already started transmitting results by then, and at 5.06pm the electoral court published returns from 1,225 polling stations. Poll workers told local newspaper Folha they had received no instructions. Some had already sent their machines back to regional courts, and the system does not allow a closed machine to be reopened. Nunes Marques told regional courts in a circular at 5.49pm that only stations still open should keep receiving voters until 7pm. That ruled out reopening closed stations or using paper ballots. The electoral court in Brasilia said it had not had time to apply the extension at all. Zanin issued a clarification at about 6pm that brought his order into line with the circular. Votes in closed machines would be counted, he wrote, without prejudice to later investigations. He said he had acted on complaints from both campaigns, although Flavio Bolsonaro’s request had gone to the electoral court and was never before him. Clash between courts Members of the electoral court complained privately that the Supreme Court had trespassed on their jurisdiction, Folha also reported. A month earlier, Nunes Marques had written to the Supreme Court’s president to object to what he called an improper overlap of powers. The extension was applied unevenly, with some voters turned away at 5pm and others admitted until 7pm. That could give either campaign grounds to challenge the result, and any request to annul the vote would go to the court Nunes Marques chairs. Rogerio Marinho, Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, said he hoped “any judicial coup or administrative chicanery” would not prosper “for the good of democracy”. Flavio Bolsonaro said he would address the nation once the result was declared. Before the dispute, Nunes Marques had said the winner would probably be known between 8.30pm and 9pm.

title: Bulgaria presidential vote heads to run-off between incumbent and pro-West rival
description: The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a run-off, according to election officials. A record low turnout, attributed by observers to a general mistrust in politicians resulting in voter apathy, will pit two contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on November 1. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-Western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the...
content: The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a run-off, according to election officials. A record low turnout, attributed by observers to a general mistrust in politicians resulting in voter apathy, will pit two contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarised contest on November 1. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-Western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist President Iliana Yotova, setting clear lines of division regarding the country’s future relationships with other nations. Bulgarians voted against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The vote is the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev after its triumph in parliamentary elections in April. Despite a record number of candidates, the race had been expected to be decided in a run-off between incumbent Yotova, backed by Radev’s party, and former caretaker Prime Minister Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties. The campaign focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and Nato member country. The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict and prompted the government to ask Bulgaria’s partners for help to strengthen its maritime security. Candidates also sought to address public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet. The election had been expected to go to a run-off as none of the 27 candidates was expected to win outright. Turnout must be above 50 per cent of 6.6 million registered voters and the winner needs a majority of votes. Yotova, a 62-year-old journalist and former member of the European Parliament, is the country’s incumbent president and a front-runner in the race. She previously served as vice-president under Radev, during his two terms as head of state. She took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now seeking her own mandate. She is running as an independent but also has the official backing of Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party, where her career began. If she wins, Yotova will become Bulgaria’s first elected female president. Analysts expect her to continue Radev’s policy to keep Bulgaria on its European path but at the same time call for improved relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine. Addressing supporters at a rally this week, Yotova said she “advocated for peace through negotiations, rather than force”. Observers say that Yotova’s victory would keep the presidency in the hands of the ruling majority, and such concentration of power could prevent institutions maintaining effective checks and balances on policy decisions. Yotova’s main challenger is economist Andrei Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister who led the country in the early months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition. Gyurov, who has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership. “I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable Nato ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position,” he told supporters this week. Exit poll results show Yotova with 3 per cent to 4 per cent ahead of Gyurov. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. While the post is primarily ceremonial, the direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

title: Machado makes a dramatic return to Venezuela after a year in exile
description: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned home on Sunday after nearly a year away, ⁠following several failed attempts to return that strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. “I’m here. With you all,” the Nobel Peace Prize winner wrote on X. She appeared at a church in western Lara state, according to images shared by her press team, and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness...
content: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned home on Sunday after nearly a year away, ⁠following several failed attempts to return that strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. “I’m here. With you all,” the Nobel Peace Prize winner wrote on X. She appeared at a church in western Lara state, according to images shared by her press team, and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said. Throughout the day on Sunday, she travelled towards Caracas by road as supporters gathered along her route to cheer her on. Her return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed ‌directly on Machado’s movements and plans, who added that Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it. At the White House on Sunday, however, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado’s return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez. “She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.” Machado’s efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she has sought to cultivate as an ally since before it removed former president Nicolas Maduro from power in January. Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it ⁠was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela. US officials have asked Machado at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details ‌of how she returned. Machado travelled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her movements told Reuters. The person briefed directly on her movements said the flight took place late last week and she was guarded by US security contractors during her journey. Rodriguez and the country’s authorities were warned by the US not ‌to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday: “The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela are the ⁠direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already ⁠seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile. “We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.” A faction of the opposition ‌and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement. The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for ‌comment on ‌Machado’s return. As Machado travelled towards the capital on Sunday, thousands of people thronged to the side of the highway, many shouting: “Maria, we love you”, “welcome” and “freedom”. Machado planned to ⁠meet with victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, said. “She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections,” he added. International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and ‌US Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Machado has said that only ‌a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors. She had been barred by Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding. Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement debuted an app on Saturday to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls. Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela.

title: US attorney general denies Trump meddling with Alaska Senate race lawsuit
description: US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Trump administration’s lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race and argued that the legal challenge was a necessary step to avoid confusing voters in the closely watched midterm race. US President Donald Trump, who said on Friday that he was “the one that said do it”, is not trying to overturn state election results “in any way, shape or form” on the cusp of the November 3...
content: US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Trump administration’s lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race and argued that the legal challenge was a necessary step to avoid confusing voters in the closely watched midterm race. US President Donald Trump, who said on Friday that he was “the one that said do it”, is not trying to overturn state election results “in any way, shape or form” on the cusp of the November 3 election, Blanche told CNN’s State of the Union. “We wish that we didn’t have to do this. We hope for a resolution that works,” Blanche said. Republicans fear that a second candidate on the ballot who is named Dan Sullivan – a retired teacher and school administrator from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg – could siphon away votes from the senator and tip the outcome in favour of Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. A day after the lawsuit was filed on Thursday, Peltola called it “just flagrant, flagrant corruption in my opinion” and a diversion tactic by Republicans. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski, also criticised the lawsuit in a social media post. Trump told reporters on Sunday that he believed the ballot was illegal because it was unfair and that Senator Sullivan should be identified to voters as the sitting senator. “At least let him use the name Senator Dan Sullivan as opposed to incumbent, because a lot of people don’t know what incumbent means,” Trump said. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jnr” will not have a party affiliation. Blanche represented Trump as a personal lawyer before the Republican president appointed him to lead the Justice Department, which filed the lawsuit in Alaska. Blanche defended Trump in his election interference case before voters elected Trump to a second White House term, effectively ending the criminal prosecution. Blanche told CNN host Dana Bash that it was “crazy” for her to ask him if Trump was trying to lay the groundwork for the same sort of election challenges that took place before a mob of his supporters stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. “We are not doing anything improper. We’re not doing anything we’re not allowed to do. And we have to let the process play out,” Blanche said. “But I do think it’s important for the American people to understand that we are not – [and] President Trump is not – trying to take over a state election in any way shape or form.” The lawsuit, he told CBS’ Face the Nation, is meant to “put guardrails in place” to preserve possible evidence of voter confusion at the polls. “It’s not saying, ‘Don’t certify.’ It’s saying, ‘If a court ultimately determines that it was decided because of confusion and not the will of the voters, then we do not think the states should certify.’ And that’s consistent with federal law and consistent with even Alaskan law, if that happens,” he said. Peltola, meanwhile, was involved in a car crash on Saturday night, forcing her campaign to delay rallies planned for Sunday and Monday. “Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement. “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail.” The car carrying Peltola and her family was hit by another vehicle, according to the statement. A campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about the other driver or any political motivation. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Le Pen launches presidential bid amid French unrest, vows to ‘restore rule of law’

Le Pen – the front runner in the polls – seems to be benefiting from the convulsions France has been going through for weeks, which have seen violence flare on the sidelines of mass cost-of-living rallies. “We are going to restore the rule of law,” she said, after looting and arson erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations...
content: Marine Le Pen, France’s far-right candidate to succeed President Emmanuel Macron, kicked off her campaign Sunday vowing to “restore the rule of law” if elected next year. Le Pen – the front runner in the polls – seems to be benefiting from the convulsions France has been going through for weeks, which have seen violence flare on the sidelines of mass cost-of-living rallies. “We are going to restore the rule of law,” she said, after looting and arson erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last weekend. She was addressing 8,500 supporters of her nationalist, anti-immigration party in the city of Orleans, where Joan of Arc – revered by the far-right as a symbol of national resistance – lifted an English siege in 1429. “We are proposing for the country not a return to the past, but the dawn of a new era,” the 58-year-old told the crowd, which broke into chants of “We’re going to win, we’re going to win.” Le Pen vowed to preserve France’s cultural identity, from its language and traditions to its values and way of life, drawing thunderous cheers from supporters waving French flags. “We want France to regain its strength,” she added. Supporter Charlene Malingre, wearing a scarf emblazoned with the words “Marine President”, said she was increasingly concerned about insecurity in France. “I think Marine Le Pen could save France from the state it’s in today … particularly when it comes to the economy, security and maintaining law and order,” the 23-year-old said. More than 400,000 people marched in major French cities on Saturday to protest against the rising cost of living. Clashes erupted after groups of masked protesters broke away from the demonstrations. Police made more than 1,300 arrests and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez blamed much of the violence on “ultra-left” extremists. Similar nationwide protests a week earlier also descended into unrest, following four weeks of student demonstrations over the poor state of France’s schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will hold talks with high school student organisations on Monday, a leader of one of the groups said. “We hope the prime minister will satify our demands,” said Louis Letoublon, a leader of Les Lyceens!. The unions and Yellow Vest protesters have vowed to keep up their street marches in the weeks ahead. Le Pen addressed supporters of her far-right party after deciding to run in elections beginning in April, despite an appeals court upholding a corruption conviction against her. She has accused Macron’s centrist government of being soft on violent protesters and lacking authority. “Who can claim that there is a rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?” she said. The anti-immigration party’s veteran candidate, who has run for the presidency three times already, also promised tougher immigration laws. “We will restore our borders, and even establish double borders, both French and European,” she said. “French nationality will once again become a privilege that is either inherited or earned,” she said. Her deputy, Jordan Bardella, received a standing ovation as he took to the stage ahead of Le Pen, pledging a crackdown on the “ultra-left”, lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 and the deportation of “delinquents and criminals”. The 31-year-old’s speech was briefly interrupted by members of a Jewish student union who unfurled a banner referencing a French media report alleging he had deleted antisemitic messages from an old Facebook account. On Sunday, police were filtering traffic going into Orleans, after thousands of counterprotesters opposed to Le Pen and her anti-immigration, nationalist RN marched in the city on Saturday chanting anti-fascist slogans. “If the far-right comes to power, we fear things will become much worse,” 35-year-old yoga teacher Antonine Rochet said on Saturday. If Le Pen wins the two-stage presidential elections in April and May, she has vowed to cut the cost of living through capped household energy bills, reduced taxes and trimming France’s contribution to the European Union. She is also critical of Nato and of France’s support of Ukraine against Russia’s invasion. French voters, angry over Macron’s perceived detachment over his two terms and his recent orders to curb the protests, are turning to more extremist politics, polling suggests. An Ipsos survey published Saturday suggested Le Pen would win 32-34 per cent of first-round votes. The poll also found widespread anger over the unrest, with a majority believing that the government bears responsibility. Whoever wins the presidency will face limited room for additional spending, with France’s debt and budget deficit already above EU limits and Macron’s government struggling to push through a cost-cutting budget.

title: Netanyahu warns Iran may try to disrupt Israel election: ‘don’t test us’
description: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday’s Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts. The remarks came as Israel’s Channel 12 reported, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the prime minister denied. Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he...
content: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday’s Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts. The remarks came as Israel’s Channel 12 reported, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the prime minister denied. Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he launched against Iran in February alongside the United States and suggesting that he alone can see it through. “We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections,” Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday. “Don’t test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows,” he added, noting the military was ready for both defensive and offensive operations. In its report on the purported confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir, Channel 12 said the latter had “demanded an in-depth discussion before carrying out the directive he had received, as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political echelon”. It did not offer details of the directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain. In a television appearance later in the day, Netanyahu dismissed the report as “nothing but rubbish”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid referenced the report in a post on X, accusing Netanyahu of seeking to put off the vote. “Tonight it was published that he wants to set off an escalation and a confrontation with Iran, just to postpone the elections,” he said. “This man has lost his grip. We absolutely must send him home.” Earlier on Sunday, the premier posted an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud engulfing Tel Aviv, alongside text attributed to a right-wing political commentator calling Iran an existential threat and arguing that all the other issues discussed this election season were trivial in comparison. תקראו את הדברים החשובים של יובל בלומברג: מדינת ישראל נמצאת בסכנה קיומית אמיתית ומוחשית. אם האיראנים ישיגו גרעין, שום דבר כבר לא ישנה יותר. הכל כל כך טפל אל מול הסכנה הקיומית של איראן והציר השיעי. הסערות המבוימות והמומצאות חדשות לבקרים נועדו להסיט את תשומת הלב מהדבר האחד שהוא החשוב ביותר: סיום העבודה באיראן. זה נוגע בקיום הפיזי של כל אדם ואדם כאן. יש לנו עוד שנתיים של טראמפ לסיים את העבודה באיראן, ואין לדעת מה יהיה לאחר מכן, אם זו תהיה קמאלה האריס, או תואם מאמדני כלשהו. זה חלון הזמן שנותר לנו כדי להשלים את העבודה הנדרשת כדי להבטיח את הקיום הפיזי שלנו לשנים הבאות. כל משאבי המדינה הנדרשים, צריכים להיות מושקעים במשימה הזו. קטאר, חרדים, אוריך, גיוס, התראות. הכל מסך עשן ענקי כדי להסתיר את הנושא היחיד שניצב מעל כולם בפער. אם יפלו במרכז הארץ שתי פצצות אטום, את מי יעניינו כל סערות הסרק האלה? הדורות הבאים לא יסלחו לנו אם נפספס את חלון ההזדמנויות ההיסטורי שמאפשר לנו לנסות ולהשלים את המשימה הקריטית ביותר שעומדת בפני הדור שלנו. זה לא יקרה עם ראש ממשלה שמוחזק בצווארו על ידי האחים המוסלמים וסייעני הטרור. זה לא יקרה עם ראש ממשלה שלא מסוגל להרים את הטלפון ולנהל שיחה אינטימית רציפה עם טראמפ. זה לא יקרה עם ראש ממשלה שלא מסוגל לעמוד בלחץ של ראיון טלויזיה. השינאה לנתניהו, ככל שהיא עולם ומלואו עבור מחנה שלם, לא תעזור מול הגרעין האיראני. כל אחד שדואג לקיום הפיזי שלו, של משפחתו, ושל אהוביו, ידו צריכה לרעוד לפני שהוא בוחר במישהו שלא יהיה מסוגל להשלים את המשימה, ובכך לדון את עצמו ואת משפחתו לסכנה של שואה שניה, בגלל השינאה הפוליטית שלו או בגלל סערת דמה מטופשת וחסרת חשיבות. — Benjamin Netanyahu - בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) October 25, 2026 On Wednesday, Netanyahu said he had sent a directive to Israel’s security forces to topple Iran’s clerical state. A day earlier, he posted a video of himself in front of a fighter jet speaking to US President Donald Trump by phone saying they would “finish the job” together. Trump on Sunday called on Israelis to cast their ballots for Netanyahu, citing the US-Israel war against Iran as an example of “winning together”. “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname. Meanwhile, Trump said it was “getting to be decision time” on whether he will make a deal with Tehran or resume attacks as Iranian and Houthi threats against Americans in the Middle East continue to grow. “I have a decision to make: do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That’s all,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures. “We don’t play games.” Trump has suggested that US strikes on Iran could resume after the November 3 midterm elections, and has sent additional forces, including a third aircraft carrier strike group, towards the Persian Gulf. The US is reducing diplomatic and military staffing in parts of the Middle East amid growing threats from Iran and the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. Houthis have been repeatedly striking the Riyadh airport, which reopened Sunday for commercial flights. Iran is now bracing for a fresh US bombing campaign around the midterms and is preparing to retaliate across the Middle East, including against Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with Tehran’s thinking. title: Storms batter northern Europe, grounding flights and cutting power

content: Storms battered northern Europe Sunday, killing a man, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes and disrupting travel and phone networks. A man died when a tree fell on him in southwestern Scotland, while a runner in a marathon in northern France was injured when a tree was felled by strong winds during the race. More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen within 24 hours of each other, authorities in the countries said. In the Argyll and Bute region of western Scotland, winds of up to 135km/h were recorded. Trees and power cables brought down by the storm blocked roads and rail lines across Scotland and northern England. Britain’s Energy Networks Association said more than 400,000 homes had lost power at some stage during the storms. Part of the pier at Brighton on the southern England coast, unused since a fire in 2003, blew away in Storm Austen on Friday. The powerful winds also battered northern France across the Channel as Europe battled its first big autumn storms of the year. Experts have warned of more extreme weather events because of global warming. Authorities warned of flood risk in regions in Scotland and England. A runner was lightly injured in the northern French city of Lille near the start of the city’s marathon, which was being staged for the first time in 31 years. French energy company Enedis said that at the peak of storm Austen on Saturday, some 288,000 homes had no electricity. Some 59,000 remained without power at midday Sunday, mainly in Normandy and Brittany. It said 2,600 Enedis technicians and contractors were working to re-establish power. In Germany, Austen cut power to 10,000 homes in and around the southwestern town of Freiburg-Brisgau on Sunday. The town’s main hospital said it had had to limit service to emergency cases because of the blackout that also cut the mobile phone network. Two people were seriously hurt Saturday by scaffolding blown away by storm Austen’s winds during an autumn market in the town of Nastatten, German police said. Germany’s DWD weather agency predicted more powerful winds of up to 100km/h on the northern coast on Sunday. The storms also hit the Netherlands and Belgium, where falling trees injured four people in Brussels on Saturday. Hundreds of flights were cancelled or diverted because of the storms across northern Europe. Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport, one of Europe’s busiest hubs, cancelled dozens of flights Sunday. Agence France-Presse counted some 90 flights cancelled on the airport website, mainly to European cities including Paris, Rome and Dublin. Dozens of flights due to land at the airport were also cancelled. Flights in northern England and Scotland were also hit by the storms.

content: Philippine police are investigating a laptop found alongside images of child abuse at the former home of Meghan Markle’s estranged father, with “full results” expected in a week, the country’s interior minister told reporters. Thomas Markle, whose daughter is married to Britain’s Prince Harry, had been living in Cebu in the Philippines until reportedly returning to the US earlier this year. Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla said the country planned to take “appropriate legal actions” against Markle – who has denied all claims of alleged offending – if sufficient evidence was found. “The Philippine National Police (PNP), upon the reports of the Sun, inspected the former home of a certain Mr. Thomas Markle,” Remulla said in a text message sent late on Saturday. “Found were a trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop.” “The laptop is currently going under forensic investigation and we will have the full results in one week,” Remulla said. “The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr. Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him.” British tabloid the Sun first reported last week that Markle’s son, Thomas Markle junior, had discovered the child abuse images while going through boxes found in his father’s former home. On Friday, Meghan Markle said she was “deeply distressed” by accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse, adding she had blocked contact between him and her children over previous “troubling and disturbing” allegations. After the reports, Meghan said that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London’s Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection making similar accusations. “It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” she said in a statement. London’s Metropolitan police said it had passed on the information to the royal couple but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. The Sun reported on Sunday that Meghan had written a final letter to her father last year, telling him she knows he is an abuser and that he will never meet his grandchildren. Meghan and Prince Harry left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud. They made an unexpected return with their children to live in the United Kingdom in August.

content: A traveller was injured after a power bank overheated and emitted smoke aboard an HK Express flight from Hong Kong to South Korea on Sunday, prompting crew members to deploy emergency safety measures before the aircraft landed safely. The incident occurred on flight UO676 to Jeju, which was carrying 236 passengers and seven crew, prompting an apology from HK Express. The budget airline, a subsidiary of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, said the power bank was stored in a bag under a passenger’s seat and began overheating as the aircraft approached Jeju International Airport. Crew members immediately followed standard safety protocols, placing the device in a heat-resistant fire containment bag and submerging it in water to bring the situation under control, it said. A woman in her fifties suffered a burn to her left thumb while removing the device from her bag. South Korean media reported that the injured passenger was a Hong Kong resident and that the power bank was locally made. Korean media added that the woman declined ambulance transport to hospital, stating she would seek medical treatment independently. The airline said the flight landed safely on Jeju at around 6am local time as scheduled, adding that the injured passenger was examined by paramedics after disembarking and received further treatment on site. No other injuries were reported. “The safety of our passengers and crew remains our utmost priority. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience caused and thank our passengers for their patience and understanding,” the airline said. According to HK Express regulations on spare batteries, passengers are strictly prohibited from using in-seat power to charge power banks or using them to charge electronic devices during the flight. Power banks are also banned from overhead storage bins. All batteries must be kept in cabin baggage stowed under the seat in front or in designated storage areas, such as seatback pockets.

title: Eye on China: Japan reopens taboo debate over nuclear-powered submarines
description: With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet. “We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14. Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition. The...
content: With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet. “We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14. Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition. The Japan Innovation Party – the junior coalition partner – wants nuclear propulsion introduced quickly, while some lawmakers from Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party are asking whether the military benefits justify the high costs and legal hurdles. At issue is whether Japan needs nuclear-powered submarines when it already operates an advanced conventional submarine fleet and is developing uncrewed maritime capabilities. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told parliament last December that Japan’s pacifist constitution did not prohibit nuclear propulsion for military vessels. But the country’s Atomic Energy Basic Act restricts nuclear energy to peaceful purposes. Successive governments have interpreted this as ruling out military nuclear propulsion, a position Takaichi’s cabinet reaffirmed later that month. Beijing has criticised the controversial proposal, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning on October 16 accusing Tokyo of seeking to gradually loosen its nuclear restrictions and linking the proposal to the wider debate over Japan’s nuclear policies. Such moves threatened regional peace and stability, Mao warned. The debate comes amid growing concern in Tokyo about the People’s Liberation Army’s expanding operations in the western Pacific. On October 16, Koizumi said China’s military operations were expanding while Japan’s Pacific intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities remained limited, making stronger defences urgent. The defences include underwater assets. Japan’s conventional submarines are particularly well-suited to defending the maritime chokepoints around its southwestern islands, where operating quietly at low speeds makes them effective in ambushes. Nuclear-powered submarines could also defend these chokepoints, but their advantage lies in speed and range. Conventional submarines can only travel at high speeds underwater for a limited time before their batteries need recharging. Nuclear-powered boats can sustain high underwater speeds over much longer distances. That could help Japan reach Chinese naval forces in the western Pacific with greater speed, shift between patrol areas or interception points as they change course, and retreat more quickly from dangerous waters after an attack. Such mobility and endurance would be costly. Eric Heginbotham, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology security scholar, told The Japan Times in January that nuclear-powered submarines could cost roughly two to three times as much to buy and four times as much to operate as conventional boats, depending on design. A June study by Hudson Institute researcher Masashi Murano and four colleagues estimated that, for similar expenditure, Japan could acquire and maintain six nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSNs) or 10 large conventional missile submarines, supplementing a baseline fleet of 22 conventional boats. The researchers also estimated that an average of one or two nuclear-powered boats would be deployed at any given time, compared with three of the large conventional missile submarines. They concluded that conventional missile submarines combined with underwater drones would be likely to offer Japan better value for conventional warfare. In an interview, Murano said: “Nuclear propulsion extends a submarine’s reach, but a single boat on station cannot search blindly for Chinese SSNs across the vast Pacific.” While nuclear propulsion becomes more valuable further from home, he questioned whether Japan should prioritise such missions, noting that “distant open-ocean operations are where the US Navy is strongest”. Despite its sophisticated submarine-building industry and civilian nuclear expertise, Japan would need entirely new military infrastructure for nuclear-powered submarines. Defence Minister Koizumi highlighted the financial and technical demands of nuclear propulsion on October 9, noting that nuclear reactors were expensive, required larger submarine hulls and demanded specialist expertise for their operation and maintenance. He said nuclear-powered submarines were generally considered noisier than conventional boats, although their acoustic performance was improving. Another pivotal question is how Japan would obtain naval reactor technology. Tokyo would have to develop its own propulsion system or get help from countries such as the United States or France, with the choice affecting submarine design, construction costs and long-term dependence on foreign suppliers. American nuclear-powered submarines use highly enriched uranium, which Japan cannot currently produce, while French designs use low-enriched uranium that is closer to the fuel used in civilian reactors. Japan would also need specialised shipyards, maintenance facilities, nuclear-safety systems and trained naval reactor personnel. A US Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarine requires about 140 crew members – roughly twice the complement of a Taigei-class boat. Additional personnel would be needed for maintenance, technical support and nuclear safety, placing further pressure on Japan’s already overstretched military. The transition would take considerable time as well. Murano estimated that even if development began now, Japan would need “a decade or more” to field its first nuclear-powered submarine – “realistically not before the late 2030s and more likely the 2040s”. Establishing a sustainable operational fleet would therefore take even longer. That raises an immediate question for Tokyo: whether investing billions in nuclear-powered submarines would deliver greater military value than expanding its existing conventional submarine force and further developing its uncrewed maritime capabilities. Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, questioned whether countering the PLA Navy was necessarily the “prime function” of Japan’s interest in nuclear-powered submarines. Tokyo might instead be seeking a more survivable conventional counterstrike capability, he suggested. But this would not necessarily require nuclear propulsion. Japan is studying how to integrate vertical missile-launch systems into future submarines. Jeffrey Hornung, Japan lead for the think tank Rand Corporation, said that if he were a Japanese lawmaker, he would seek an assessment of whether nuclear-powered submarines would close “an important gap” in Japan’s capabilities. If conventional submarines, underwater drones and advanced mines could meet those needs, that should give policymakers “reason for pause” before rushing into acquisition, he said.

content: Hong Kong’s No 2 official has pledged to open extra clearance counters and vehicle lanes at the recently revamped Huanggang Port control point ahead of peak hours, after Halloween crowds and concertgoers created heavy cross-border congestion. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, who inspected the Shenzhen Bay and Huanggang ports on Sunday, said he had instructed the Security Bureau to step up advance assessments and passenger flow forecasting. He added that he had directed the Transport and Logistics Bureau to work with bus and rail operators to keep sufficient vehicles and manpower in reserve for flexible deployment based on demand. “Major events bring energy to Hong Kong while reshaping cross-border travel patterns. I urge travellers to plan ahead and stagger their trips, and to consider staying overnight after the events to experience the city’s culture and festive vibe at leisure,” he said in a social media post. The Tourism Board’s inaugural “Hong Kong Halloween Month” brought thousands to Central’s streets, including Lan Kwai Fong, triggering congestion at Huanggang Port from Saturday night into the early hours of Sunday. Canadian singer The Weeknd’s concerts at the 50,000-seat Kai Tak Stadium added to the influx. The shows were held on Saturday and Sunday, with further dates on October 30 and 31. The revamped crossing, which opened this month, is the city’s only crossing to mainland China offering 24-hour passenger clearance. Online video clips showed mainland tourists queuing late into the night for express coaches to cross the border from Mong Kok, while the San Tin Highway towards Huanggang Port was gridlocked with cars, taxis and buses. Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung, a member of the Legislative Council’s transport panel, told the South China Morning Post that this year’s Halloween events across several districts plus the Kai Tak concerts had scattered visitors to areas without coach services, with many turning to unlicensed cross-border cars, causing congestion. “Police should crack down on these illegal cross-border hired cars,” he said. “The government should also designate dedicated roads for buses and coaches, which carry far more passengers than private cars.” He also called for clearer signage inside the building to keep private cars and public transport on separate lanes, with officers deployed before drivers went the wrong way. The government said the Security Bureau had set up a forward command post at Huanggang Port before the weekend, coordinating responses with the disciplined services and the Transport Department in real time. In the two hours from midnight Saturday to 2am Sunday, 14,760 travellers crossed north, 212 per cent more than usual. In the same period, 1,200 vehicles crossed north at the checkpoint. Police opened a buffer zone, with waits peaking at 45 to 50 minutes, but by 2am, vehicles were moving smoothly again. The government noted that the Transport Department had directed bus operators to run more frequent services, although some passengers faced longer waits as coaches took longer to turn around. Extra staff and buses will be deployed at Kai Tak Sports Park on Sunday night to speed up boarding.
