content: The debate over ethnic identity in Xinjiang has triggered an online clash between Chinese and Turkish social media users. The row began earlier this month when a Turkish social media user recalled an encounter with a Uygur from Xinjiang, the region in China that is home to nearly 12 million mainly Muslim Turkic speakers. The user wrote that the woman did not look Chinese, but when asked whether she considered herself Turkic, the woman responded: “No, I’m Chinese.” The user also called on her to “return to your roots”. The post had gained over 2 million views by Friday afternoon before the account was apparently deleted. The row quickly escalated into an online debate over identity, history and statehood that was amplified by artificial intelligence translation tools used by internet users on both sides to overcome the language barrier. Tens of thousands of Uygurs are estimated to live in Turkey, making it their largest diaspora community outside Central Asia. Xinjiang has become one of the most sensitive issues in the relationship between China and Turkey as Ankara pushed to bolster its influence among Turkic-speaking peoples, including the Uygurs. Turkey has also been one of the most vocal critics of China’s alleged human rights abuses against minority groups in Xinjiang. Beijing has defended its policies in the region, saying they were designed to combat religious extremism, separatism and terrorism. The row has been further inflamed by new Turkish textbooks that replace the term “Central Asia” with “Turkestan”, which covers parts of Xinjiang and the neighbouring provinces of Gansu and Qinghai. On Friday, the semi-official China News Service republished a commentary that criticised this as a “distortion” of Chinese sovereignty. The commentary was first published by social media account Little Compasses, or Xiao Yuan Gui, whose posts are often reposted by the United Front Work Department, the Communist Party body that oversees religious and ethnic affairs related to Xinjiang and Tibet. Published under the headline “Turkestan? Pure Fantasy!”, the article rejected the idea that there were “historical origins, territorial affiliations or cultural connections” between Xinjiang and “fictitious ‘Turkestan’”. It argued that linguistic connections should not be equated with territorial belonging and historical lineage. It also said that Turkestan had never been a unified state or sovereign entity, but was rather an umbrella term used to describe areas inhabited by nomadic Turkic tribes. It said the change to the school textbooks was part of Ankara’s push to rewrite Eurasian history and export its pan-Turkic ambitions. “The new Turkish textbooks’ forcible inclusion of China’s northwestern territory into a fake ‘Turkestan’ map is a crude distortion of China’s historical sovereignty and a deliberate rupture of the history of Eurasian cultural integration,” the article argued. “In essence, it uses education to export geopolitical ambitions and engineer regional confrontation.” Ties between Beijing and Ankara have improved in recent years as Turkey, which has grappled with some of the world’s highest inflation levels, has sought to bolster business and investment ties with China. Beijing has repeatedly called for the two sides to consolidate mutual political trust and support each other’s core interests In 2024, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Xinjiang, where the two sides pledged to strengthen cooperation on counterterrorism. This call was echoed by Chinese President Xi Jinping when he met his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year.

title: Louie Shum’s death: heart disease in Hong Kong and what to do in an emergency

content: The death of veteran Hong Kong stock market commentator Louie Shum Chun-ying has drawn public attention to heart disease, after a police source revealed he had a history of the condition as well as diabetes. Heart disease was one of the leading causes of death in Hong Kong, with more than 6,500 fatalities recorded in 2024, according to the Department of Health. While residents at risk should monitor their health and seek timely medical care, a local cardiologist stressed that bystanders could also render aid when someone fell ill or collapsed, before an ambulance arrived. The South China Morning Post examines heart disease trends in the city and how to respond in an emergency. What happened to Louie Shum? The commentator, known as “Master Shum”, worked in the financial and securities industry for more than three decades. He remained active on internet radio shows after retiring as chief executive of stock brokerage Sincere Securities two years ago. An insider said Shum suddenly collapsed on Saturday night as he walked to a taxi rank in Wan Chai after visiting a friend’s home. A passer-by called emergency services. Shum was unconscious when taken to Ruttonjee Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at around 9pm. He was 66. Police did not consider the case suspicious, and the exact cause of death was subject to autopsy results, according to the source. The insider added that Shum had been diagnosed with heart disease and diabetes, and regularly received treatment at St Teresa’s Hospital in Kowloon City. How common is heart disease in Hong Kong? According to the Department of Health, heart disease was the third-most common cause of death in the city in 2024, accounting for 6,594 deaths, or 12.6 per cent of all registered fatalities. Coronary heart disease made up 52.9 per cent of those deaths. Coronary heart disease occurs when cholesterol layers deposit on the inner wall of coronary arteries, narrowing the lumens of the arteries, reducing blood supply to cardiac muscle and causing chest pain during exertion. The department also cited the 2020-22 population health survey, which found that 1.6 per cent of people aged 15 or above reported doctor-diagnosed coronary heart disease. The survey showed the prevalence of coronary heart disease was higher in men than in women, and also increased with age. What are the symptoms? People with coronary heart disease often experience crushing chest pain after physical effort, which may radiate to the arms, shoulders, neck or jaw. Rest typically helps relieve this pain. During a heart attack, however, the pain becomes severe and prolonged, accompanied by symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness, sweating, nausea and general weakness. Heart failure can also cause breathlessness and swelling in both legs. While a heart attack can strike suddenly, cardiologist Dr Duncan Ho Hung-kwong noted that some people experienced warning signs days in advance, including chest discomfort, indigestion or breathing difficulty. “The symptoms may ease after a while, but anyone experiencing severe discomfort should seek immediate medical attention,” Ho said. What should you do during a heart attack? In the event of a heart attack, people should immediately alert anyone nearby and call 999. Ho advised that individuals trained in first aid should place the person in the recovery position – on their side – to keep the airway clear. He added that members of the public should use an automated external defibrillator, or AED, if available. The device analyses the heart rhythm and delivers electric shocks if needed to restore a normal heartbeat. According to the government, cardiopulmonary resuscitation coupled with the use of an AED is the most effective way to save a person suffering cardiac arrest. How can heart disease be prevented? To prevent heart disease, Ho advised maintaining a balanced diet, exercising regularly, avoiding smoking and managing mental stress, which can trigger acute cardiac events. He warned that viral infections such as the flu could cause systemic inflammation, raising the risk of a heart attack. A history of stroke, high blood pressure, elevated glucose and cholesterol levels were also risk factors, he stressed. Ho also urged adults aged 30 or above to undergo regular health check-ups to detect and treat underlying conditions early.

content: In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play. Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants. A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.” As I follow the unrest unfolding in Europe, I find it uncanny how closely it parallels the 2019 anti-government riots in Hong Kong. Such mass disturbances almost always have many causes, including underlying social malaise and long-standing grievances. There is no single causal factor, only, perhaps, a single trigger. In Hong Kong, the trigger was a proposed extradition bill. The protests then broadened into demands for immediate democratic transition. I, and many others, have extensively documented foreign government and semi-government involvement. The players included the US Congress, the US National Endowment for Democracy, the National Democratic Institute for International Affairs, the US Agency for Global Media and the Open Technology Fund. In fact, we didn’t have to dig much. They were rather proud of their handiwork, with some testifying in Congress that they could not continue because of funding cuts by the first Trump administration. To this day, many Western media outlets still claim it was all a fight for democracy, later suppressed by the national security law. I don’t deny that democratic demands played a significant role in the 2019 riots. But they were not the sole or even the underlying cause, just as poor facilities alone cannot explain the social breakdown we are witnessing in France, even though they first led high school students into the streets. Yet mainstream Western media instinctively reach for mono-causal explanations, usually a struggle for democracy, however they define it, when mass unrest breaks out in non-Western countries. Only when similar breakdowns happen in allied or friendly countries do they allow for nuance and deeper social analysis. One reason is, of course, simple ignorance of those other societies. “Democracy” is the one-size-fits-all explanation when you need to write a column about an unfriendly country you know nothing about. I recently watched an amusing French TV news programme in which the moderator asked professional pundits to name two other living Chinese persons besides Xi Jinping, and they all had difficulty doing so. It was reminiscent of George W. Bush, while running for president, being embarrassingly unable to identify foreign leaders. Ukraine was similar to Hong Kong in this respect. The so-called Maidan revolution of 2014 is seen in the West, especially now, as a democratic revolution. Never mind that the governments that followed were as corrupt as the pro-Moscow one before. The rest of the world mostly sees it as a coup, or is at least neutral about it. At the very least, it triggered the Russian aggression that has continued ever since. Many Ukrainians may now be rethinking the wisdom of poking the bear and – for heaven’s sake – of trying to join Nato. A recorded telephone conversation between Victoria Nuland, then US assistant secretary of state, and Geoffrey Pyatt, then US ambassador to Ukraine, was leaked in February 2014. They discussed political strategy, which leaders to support and the composition of a post-Yanukovych government amid the Euromaidan protests. In the leak, she famously said, “F*** the EU”, signalling a readiness to act unilaterally. Indeed, American scholars such as John Mearsheimer and Jeffrey Sachs have argued that the 2014 uprising was a coup. Of course, everyone knows there were many causes. But everyone has an ideological axe to grind. I, for one, would argue that the world would be more peaceful today without the 2014 coup. But to each their own. While ignorance and strategic opportunism helped explain how social unrest is portrayed differently in mainstream Western media, the biggest motivation is probably ideological. What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left Between 2010 and 2020, data-tracking projects recorded nearly 7,000 protests across 153 countries, at least 900 of them major, each involving more than 10,000 participants. Naturally, Western pundits and politicians, especially those in Washington, would focus on those affecting antagonistic China and Russia. Exploiting internal opposition and unrest in unfriendly countries has long been Washington’s default playbook, followed sometimes, but not always, by its Western counterparts. But it is short-sighted. An unstable Hong Kong or China would be terrible for the world economy and, by extension, for the US. A successor state to the current Putin regime – should it collapse from losing the war in Ukraine – would probably be neither pro-Western nor democratic, but even more bent on revanchism. What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left. Several Western governments bought into their own propaganda and, from 2020, offered them exits, as if they were fleeing persecution like Ukrainians and Yemenis. Many have had difficulty adjusting to their new lives; some have returned to Hong Kong. Those same Western countries are now beset by anti-migrant populism, resulting in a brutal migrant crackdown, as in the US, or the rollback of easy access in the migrant application process, as in Canada and Australia. Meanwhile, some Hong Kong and mainland officials remain under US sanctions. Perhaps Beijing should sanction some top officials in Washington and Paris for their own brutal domestic police and military crackdowns. Of course, China has never been so petty and ridiculous.

title: China’s Liaoning carrier and USS Theodore Roosevelt may be in Philippine Sea at same time
description: China’s Liaoning aircraft carrier strike group sailed beyond the first island chain last week to reach the southernmost waters of the Philippines, suggesting an intent to position itself closer to ongoing US-Japan joint exercises. Philippine news channel BNC reported that the carrier group reached about 25 nautical miles (46km) east-southeast of Balut Island, the southernmost point of the Philippines, before sailing northeast on Friday. content: China’s Liaoning aircraft carrier strike group sailed beyond the first island chain last week to reach the southernmost waters of the Philippines, suggesting an intent to position itself closer to ongoing US-Japan joint exercises. Philippine news channel BNC reported that the carrier group reached about 25 nautical miles (46km) east-southeast of Balut Island, the southernmost point of the Philippines, before sailing northeast on Friday. That positioned the warships past the first island chain, a US-led strategic arc of maritime chokepoints running from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines. The four-strong Liaoning strike group includes the Type 055 large guided-missile destroyers Wuxi and Anshan, and the Type 052D guided-missile destroyer Huainan. If the carrier group holds its northeastward course, it could eventually enter the Philippine Sea, where American and Japanese forces are conducting their biennial Keen Sword exercise. The US Navy’s 7th fleet said in a social media post on Thursday that the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt was operating in the Philippine Sea alongside allied warships from Japan, Australia, Canada and France as part of a multilateral force taking part in the Keen Sword drills. This year’s exercise runs from October 19 to 29, taking place at sites across Japan and its surrounding waters. The Liaoning carrier group is carrying out its second round of drills in the western Pacific this year. Launched on October 14, the deployment is expected to last several weeks and overlaps with the Keen Sword exercises. BNC’s report on Saturday said the strike group transited the Basilan Strait on Thursday after being spotted off the southwestern coast of the Philippines, where it was shadowed by Philippine Navy vessels. The Japanese defence ministry reported that the warships first sailed southeast through the Miyako Strait to enter the Pacific on October 14 and turned towards the South China Sea the following day before making their way to the southern Philippines. The route suggests the group is sailing anticlockwise around the Philippines – from its northern to its western coast – reversing the course taken during drills in October 2024. Japan’s defence ministry noted that while the Liaoning was operating in waters between Okinawa and Miyako Island earlier this month, Chinese aerial surveillance assets – including a Y-9 electronic reconnaissance aircraft and a WZ-7 high-altitude drone – were also detected in the area. It remains unclear whether they accompanied the carrier group south. In a report on Saturday, China’s state broadcaster CCTV said that Japanese ships and aircraft had repeatedly shadowed the carrier group at close range during its far-sea training in June, engaging in what Beijing described as harassment and provocation. The Type 054B frigate Luohe, deployed on the group’s outer perimeter, warned off Japanese vessels from a distance, while carrier-borne J-15 fighter jets from the Liaoning intercepted and saw off Japanese P-3C maritime patrol aircraft, the report said.

title: US Marine indictment in Okinawa murder trial renews anti-base movement
description: Prosecutors indicted a 20-year-old US Marine on Sunday on suspicion of robbing and murdering a woman in Okinawa earlier this month as the case renews anti-base sentiment among locals burdened with hosting the bulk of US military installations in Japan. Devin Ballard, who is stationed at Futenma Air Base, is charged with killing the woman by wrapping a phone cord around her neck at a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southern island prefecture, and taking her backpack containing a wallet on...
content: Prosecutors indicted a 20-year-old US Marine on Sunday on suspicion of robbing and murdering a woman in Okinawa earlier this month as the case renews anti-base sentiment among locals burdened with hosting the bulk of US military installations in Japan. Devin Ballard, who is stationed at Futenma Air Base, is charged with killing the woman by wrapping a phone cord around her neck at a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southern island prefecture, and taking her backpack containing a wallet on October 3, according to the indictment. The cause of death was suffocation, it said. The local police said they found Ballard walking alone in the city of Okinawa in the late hours of October 3 and arrested him the following day on suspicion of robbery and murder. Hiroya Ishii, deputy chief of the Naha District Public Prosecutors Office, said in a statement, “In the trial, we want to do our best to make accurate arguments and prove the case based on the law and evidence.” Following the incident, Okinawa Governor Genta Koja has stepped up calls on the central government to take preventive measures, with locals already angered by past crimes committed by American service members, including those against women and girls, in addition to noise and pollution issues. The Japanese government has lodged a strong protest with the United States and urged it to fully cooperate with the investigation and enforce strict discipline among its military personnel. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the latest case a “heinous crime.” Following the arrest of Ballard, the US military in Okinawa on October 9 imposed a 30-day curfew from midnight to 5am. Japan-US talks on preventive steps have also been launched to review the effectiveness of the US military’s “liberty policy” that governs off-base conduct in Japan and joint patrols by US forces and Japanese police, according to Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.

title: ‘Really terrified’: how a blood test could spare cancer patients an agonising wait

content: In the second of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Fiona Sun looks into how a new PCR system can detect cancer, infections and birth defects within hours, and what it will take to bring such laboratory breakthroughs to patients. Part one can be found here. It began with a pimple-like lump on Audrey Kwan’s neck. Within a month, it had swollen to the size of a table tennis ball. But it took blood tests, a biopsy and CAT scans before the Hongkonger, then aged 20, was diagnosed with stage two lymphoma six years ago. Kwan recalled waiting days for her biopsy results at a public hospital, until the growing tumour caused such severe pain that she was rushed to the emergency department. Only then, she said, were the results expedited, arriving the following day. “My family and I were really terrified as we had no idea what was going on. The test results and various other procedures all took time,” she said. “In the end, I couldn’t help but wonder: if we had found out earlier, would it not have progressed to stage two? Could it have been stage one instead?” Now 26 and recovered, Kwan said she believed faster, easier and more affordable ways to detect cancer could spare patients some of that uncertainty and distress. In one or two years, however, Hong Kong patients may be able to take a screening test that detects cancer within three to four hours – for a few thousand Hong Kong dollars. The Advanced Biomedical Instrumentation Centre at the city’s Science Park is conducting clinical trials of its newly developed fourth-generation polymerase chain reaction (PCR) system, which it says can detect cancer, infectious diseases and birth defects. Sigrid Chen Sijie, the centre’s head of business development, said the system could offer a faster and more affordable alternative to some existing diagnostic tools. While CT scans might miss very small tumours, genomic sequencing could take more than a week and cost tens of thousands of Hong Kong dollars, she said. “PCR is a well-known technology that has always been a pioneer in molecular, DNA or genetic testing, appearing in our daily lives. Our fourth-generation PCR primarily focuses on increasing the amount of information it can read,” Chen said. “We are applying a fast, affordable and, most importantly, accessible technology to a more complex medical decision-making process,” she said. ‘Fishing’ in smaller ponds PCR is a laboratory technique used to rapidly produce millions to billions of copies of a specific segment of DNA, allowing it to be studied in greater detail. The process uses short synthetic DNA fragments called primers to select a segment of the genome for amplification, and then uses multiple rounds of DNA synthesis to copy it. The method became widely known during the coronavirus pandemic, when it was adopted as one of the most effective ways to detect the virus in the body. But conventional PCR has limitations in speed, sensitivity and multiplexing – the ability to test for multiple targets at once. The project to develop the new system began in 2021 at the centre, led by the University of Hong Kong in partnership with Harvard University. Chen said the centre was established to turn cutting-edge scientific research into practical tools that could help doctors better assess patients’ health. “PCR is a widely adopted technology, and everyone knows its key limitation lies in its multiplexity. That naturally has become one of the major challenges researchers in the field have been trying to tackle,” she said. The new system combines molecular bar coding with droplet microfluidics to simultaneously detect millions of target locations in a single test. Microfluidics is the technology of moving tiny amounts of fluid through narrow channels. Compared with conventional methods, it can enable faster reactions and analysis, as well as greater precision. In the new procedure, DNA information was first extracted from a patient’s blood sample before being dispersed into millions of droplets using microfluidic chips, Chen said. “We disperse samples from a large pool into individual droplets and photograph each one. This allows us to observe the processes within every droplet close up, enabling more precise target detection and enhancing sensitivity,” she said. Chen used a fishing analogy to explain the concept. “Suppose I know there are 10 fish in a pool and I want to catch all 10 of them. If the pool is huge, it might take five or six days without catching those 10 fish,” she said. “However, if I divide it into individual cups of water, you can easily see which cup contains a fish.” The heightened sensitivity, she added, was crucial to detecting diseases such as cancer at an early stage. A race against time The test could produce a report within three to four hours of a blood sample being taken, Chen said. It is expected to be affordable, costing from a few hundred to several thousand Hong Kong dollars. Faster results, she said, could help doctors make treatment decisions more quickly – a difference that could be critical for seriously ill patients. “Taking sepsis as an example, the main reason our instrument is needed is its time efficiency and control,” she said. “For every hour treatment is delayed, the risk of death increases by 8 per cent.” Current diagnosis of sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to an infection damages its own tissues and organs, often relies on a blood culture – a laboratory test that identifies bacteria, fungi or other micro-organisms in the bloodstream. “Because someone in my close family actually experienced sepsis, I know first-hand how agonising it is for a family to wait for blood culture results,” Chen said. “Blood culture means taking blood from the patient and incubating it in an environment suitable for bacterial growth. After about two to three days, once the bacteria have been cultured, a drug test is then conducted to determine which antibiotics work. “But the patient may not be able to wait several days for a result.” The new PCR system mainly targets three categories of diseases: cancers, infectious diseases and birth defects. Chen said more types of illness would be added later. From prototype to patient A ready-to-use prototype was completed in February last year. The instrument is undergoing clinical trials in Hong Kong, as well as in mainland China, the United States, Singapore and Thailand, among other places. “As we are actually dealing with genetic information, there are slight variations across different ethnicities,” Chen explained. She acknowledged that building the technology was only part of the challenge. The centre also had to bring together specialists from fields as varied as microfluidics, mechanics, electronics and biology, along with people experienced in turning laboratory research into market-ready products. “The challenge now is how to get doctors to endorse this useful tool as quickly as possible, pass a series of evaluation tests and ensure patients can benefit from it at the earliest opportunity,” she said. To build that confidence, the centre would work with its clinical partners and run the system on a larger volume of samples to demonstrate its potential. The ultimate goal, Chen said, was to integrate the technology into the medical system and everyday treatment decisions. She expected the testing method to be available to patients in laboratory settings within one to two years, before being introduced in hospitals. “Hong Kong will definitely be our first pilot location, but we believe the commercial value of this technology will not be limited to Hong Kong, and we will further extend it to the rest of the world,” she said. Turning research into remedies Established under the government’s Health@InnoHK initiative and based at the Science Park, the centre aims to bridge the gap between academic research and healthcare by turning biomedical innovations into clinical applications. Chen said Hong Kong’s innovation and technology sector had grown in recent years, buoyed by government support as the city sought to establish itself as an international hub for health and medical innovation. “I graduated with a STEM background myself, and I remember that my senior schoolmates were not as fortunate when they graduated,” she said. “Back then, if they wanted to stay in the field, there were only two paths: pursue a PhD and become a professor or join a company and sell products to hospitals.” Now, with more start-ups emerging, there was a new route for researchers to turn innovative ideas into real products, Chen added. “We have seen that, throughout our centre’s development over the past few years, we have attracted much overseas talent to Hong Kong to collaborate on turning local scientific research into real-world products we see in our daily lives,” she said. To further develop the sector and support budding start-ups, Chen called on the government to play a bigger role in connecting firms with doctors, so that companies could better understand clinical needs and refine their technologies accordingly. “We believe our platform holds infinite potential,” she said. “This includes areas such as water pollution and food safety, where reading multiple layers of information is essential and our technology is needed.”

title: Hong Kong seeks bigger role for yuan in regional trade, treasury chief says
description: Hong Kong officials held discussions with finance ministers and representatives from economies such as Brunei during last week’s Apec meeting on reducing reliance on the US dollar and expanding the use of local currencies and the yuan for bilateral trade settlement, the city’s treasury chief has said. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu on Sunday also shared lighthearted but telling anecdotes about the intangible gains made by the city from hosting the...
content: Hong Kong officials held discussions with finance ministers and representatives from economies such as Brunei during last week’s Apec meeting on reducing reliance on the US dollar and expanding the use of local currencies and the yuan for bilateral trade settlement, the city’s treasury chief has said. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu on Sunday also shared lighthearted but telling anecdotes about the intangible gains made by the city from hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Finance Ministers’ Meeting, noting how impressed delegates had been. “They directly hope that through this meeting, not only to communicate at the government level, but also to communicate with our business sector on the internationalisation of the renminbi, especially regarding the use of local currencies,” Hui told the media. “Because at the Asian level, trade between us has increased a great deal since the [Covid] pandemic,” he added. He noted that Asean has been Hong Kong’s second largest trading partner after mainland China, so their trade within Asia “does not necessarily need to use US dollar”. “We can use local currencies or even the renminbi more for trade settlement,” Hui said, referring to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which comprises Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and East Timor. Hong Kong hosted the finance ministers’ meeting on October 20 and 21 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Hui said the event allowed delegates to connect directly with local financial institutions to explore how Hong Kong’s broader financial ecosystem could support their specific needs, including issuing offshore yuan “dim sum” bonds or accessing other investment products in the currency. Strengthening Hong Kong’s role in the internationalisation of the yuan is a high priority in the city’s first five-year plan to 2030, unveiled in September. Reflecting on the event’s intangible outcomes, Hui said some delegates told him they were getting married soon and planned to return to Hong Kong for their honeymoons. He also said organisers offered Muslim guests halal food alongside local street snacks such as egg waffles and fish siu mai to showcase the city’s unique culture and hospitality. Hui framed the city’s role at Apec as a “facilitator of regional cooperation”, complementing mainland China’s role as a “stabiliser” in a complex geopolitical and economic environment. Beyond strengthening regional currency ties, Hong Kong was positioning itself as a safe haven for physical assets as it pushes to become a global bullion hub, Hui said, explaining why companies were increasingly looking to store gold in the city. Amid shifting geopolitics and logistics disruptions, institutions have come to realise that “many things are much safer kept close by”, he said, highlighting the importance of Hong Kong’s comprehensive supply-chain ecosystem. To attract players such as international gold refineries and storage providers, the government has created a “Gold Hotline” regulatory fast track, Hui said. His bureau acted as a one-stop shop to coordinate and expedite regulatory approvals across different government bureaus, making it significantly easier for foreign firms, such as two gold refiners – one from the mainland and the other from Switzerland – to enter Hong Kong. Asked about the feasibility of expanding the city’s gold storage infrastructure, Hui pointed to a recent, rapid success in a related sector, noting that in just over a year, Hong Kong had successfully secured nearly 20 warehouses storing over 60,000 tonnes of non-ferrous metals. Hui added that international metal refiners were entering Hong Kong via two distinct models: some, such as the Swiss firm, were partnering with established local enterprises, while others were setting up completely new, independent operations in the city.

title: DR Congo begins pivotal Ebola vaccine trial as outbreak kills nearly 4,700
description: A pivotal trial of vaccines against the strain of Ebola that is driving a deadly outbreak across parts of Africa has begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the epidemic originated and the vast majority of cases and deaths have occurred. The first participant was vaccinated on Friday in Bunia, eastern DR Congo, with Merck & Co’s Ervebo shot, which has been approved to guard against a different Ebola species. An experimental alternative developed specifically against Bundibugyo by...
content: A pivotal trial of vaccines against the strain of Ebola that is driving a deadly outbreak across parts of Africa has begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the epidemic originated and the vast majority of cases and deaths have occurred. The first participant was vaccinated on Friday in Bunia, eastern DR Congo, with Merck & Co’s Ervebo shot, which has been approved to guard against a different Ebola species. An experimental alternative developed specifically against Bundibugyo by Moderna Inc and another by the University of Oxford and Serum Institute of India could also be tested in the study within weeks. “I’m pretty confident that we have the window because the outbreak is not being brought under control,” Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations Chief Executive Officer Richard Hatchett said in an interview. DR Congo recorded 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of October 20, according to the World Health Organization, and is the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country, irrespective of virus species. Infections linked to the outbreak have also been detected beyond its borders. Hatchett said the outbreak has become deeply embedded across a wide area, making it unlikely that traditional control measures will suppress it before researchers can determine whether the vaccines work. Conducting the trial will still be difficult, with armed groups and decades of instability complicating efforts to enrol and follow participants. The WHO said only about 80 per cent of more than 30,000 contacts under follow-up in DR Congo were reached in the latest 24-hour period, below its 95 per cent target. Ervebo was developed to protect against Zaire Ebola, but animal studies suggest it may reduce Bundibugyo infections and significantly lower mortality, Hatchett said. Researchers will need at least several months to determine its efficacy, depending largely on how quickly the trial can enrol enough people exposed to confirmed cases. If successful, the purpose-built vaccines could be produced at scale. Serum manufactured more than 600,000 dose equivalents of the Oxford vaccine’s drug substance within nine days of receiving the material needed to begin production, Hatchett said. “We could quickly move to having millions of doses of that vaccine,” he said. That could allow health authorities to shift from vaccinating contacts around known cases to broader campaigns in heavily affected areas. Bundibugyo virus was first identified almost two decades ago, but limited resources were concentrated on more frequently occurring Ebola species, according to Hatchett. In a better-prepared world, vaccines against known threats would be developed in advance and held ready for outbreaks, he said. “We’re not there yet.”

title: 5-hour battle to bring hill fire near residential area in Tuen Mun under control
description: Hong Kong firefighters battled for five hours to bring a hill fire near a residential area in Tuen Mun under control on Sunday, with a government helicopter sent to help bring the flames under control. No injuries were reported, but the flames spread along the hillside near Shan King Estate, not far from two secondary schools, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing into the air. The blaze, reported at about 1.30pm, broke out in a patch of grass measuring about 10 metres by 20 metres (33 feet by...
content: Hong Kong firefighters battled for five hours to bring a hill fire near a residential area in Tuen Mun under control on Sunday, with a government helicopter sent to help bring the flames under control. No injuries were reported, but the flames spread along the hillside near Shan King Estate, not far from two secondary schools, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing into the air. The blaze, reported at about 1.30pm, broke out in a patch of grass measuring about 10 metres by 20 metres (33 feet by 66 feet) on Por Lo Shan near a freshwater service reservoir off Wong Yin Street. Authorities also deployed a Government Flying Service helicopter to drop water on the fire. They confirmed that no evacuations were required and no injuries were reported. The flames were brought under control by about 6.30pm, and the cause of the fire was under investigation. Sunday’s weather remained dry and windy under the influence of a dry northeast monsoon. Relative humidity hovered at about 60 per cent in the afternoon, with the yellow fire danger warning in effect. The warning means the risk of a fire in the countryside is high, according to the Observatory. Explaining what residents should do if they found themselves at risk during a hill fire, veteran mountaineer Chung Kin-man said moving down the slope was crucial as flames naturally spread upwards. Chung also advised hikers to discard any heavy belongings such as backpacks so they could move more quickly. Covering oneself with a wet towel could also help protect against burns, he said.

title: How China’s regional leadership changes offer clues to the future of the Communist Party
description: China’s five-year leadership cycle is getting under way at a provincial level, with new teams being installed in a process that offers important clues to the future of the Communist Party at a national level. Last week, four provinces – Anhui, Henan, Shanxi and Xinjiang – wrapped up their respective party congresses and appointed new standing committees for the next five years. The meetings were held a week before a key party gathering in Beijing – known as the fifth plenum – that runs from...
content: China’s five-year leadership cycle is getting under way at a provincial level, with new teams being installed in a process that offers important clues to the future of the Communist Party at a national level. Last week, four provinces – Anhui, Henan, Shanxi and Xinjiang – wrapped up their respective party congresses and appointed new standing committees for the next five years. The meetings were held a week before a key party gathering in Beijing – known as the fifth plenum – that runs from Monday to Thursday, where the Central Committee will discuss measures to strengthen party governance and discipline. The plenum will also offer an opportunity to prepare for a major overhaul of the national leadership, which will take place at the party congress next year and will be key to the country’s goals of becoming an economic and military superpower by the middle of the century. All of China’s provinces will hold their own party congresses in the run-up to the main event. As well as setting out their development plans for the next five years, these events will also determine which officials will remain in office, retire or be promoted. The process is expected to be completed by June, with 14 provinces holding their congresses by the end of the year. New party chiefs and governors have already been appointed in 10 of these provinces. Next year, the remaining local congresses will include the four municipalities under the direct jurisdiction of the central government – Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin and Chongqing – whose party secretaries generally also serve as members of the Politburo. These events will provide important clues about personnel arrangements for the national party congress, including the selection of full and alternate members of the 21st Central Committee. The provincial party chiefs and governors appointed in the coming months are almost certain to secure full membership of the committee. The third-ranking official in each province is also likely to secure alternate membership, with many taking up their seats on the body for the first time. For example, in Anhui, one of the provinces that has already installed a new leadership team, Industry Minister Li Lecheng, who was already a member of the Central Committee, was named as the new party secretary last month. Wang Dongwei, born in 1969, was installed as the acting governor and is set to join the committee next year, while the province’s third-ranked official, Shan Xiangqian, born in 1972, is likely to become an alternate member. Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region also held its party congress recently, with Chen Xiaojiang remaining as party chief and Erkin Tuniyaz staying on as chairman of the regional government. Both Chen and Tuniyaz are already members of the Central Committee, but convention suggests that the region’s party secretary will also be given a seat on the Politburo. The region’s No 3, He Zhongyou, deputy secretary of the regional party committee, born in 1965, is likely to become an alternate member of the Central Committee. As provincial party standing committees also face substantial overhauls, one source familiar with personnel work within the party said an important age threshold was in play. The source said the customary age threshold for the top two provincial leaders was 63, while the age limit for entering or remaining on a provincial party standing committee was 58 and officials would find it hard to stay in office once they had passed these cut-offs. For example, Anhui’s former party chief, Liang Yanshun, 64, and governor Wang Qingxian, 63, stepped down last month after reaching retirement age. However, some officials have been able to stay in office despite exceeding the customary age threshold, a possible sign of their continued importance to the party. Shi Taifeng, then 65, remained as party secretary of Inner Mongolia following its regional party congress in December 2021. He joined the Politburo the following year and although he has since handed over the reins at a regional level, he remains a member of the key decision-making body.

title: How ancient Chinese night watchmen patrolled streets, used ‘dripping buckets’ to tell time

content: In ancient China, before the advent of mechanical clocks and digital devices, people relied mainly on night watchmen to keep time, prevent fires and maintain their daily routines. But how did the watchmen tell the time? Chinese night watchmen mainly used two methods: clepsydras and incense sticks. A clepsydra, also known as a water clock, measures time through the regulated flow of water from a vessel. The ancient Chinese divided the night into five gengs. Each geng lasted around two hours, though the exact duration varied by season. The first geng usually ran from 7pm to 9pm, while the fifth and final geng ended around 5am. The float-arrow clepsydra is said to have been the main timekeeping device used by Chinese night watchmen. The float-arrow clepsydra is believed to have first appeared during the Han dynasty (202 BC–220). It worked through buoyancy: as the water level dropped, more of the floating arrow became visible above the water. The watchman could read the time from the marks on the arrow. During the Tang and Song dynasties (618–1279), a more complicated version was developed, consisting of three dripping buckets. A single bucket might not provide an accurate measurement, because the arrow descended more slowly as the water level fell. In the three-bucket system, the middle bucket remained full, making the flow of water from the bottom bucket more consistent. Clepsydras were also made from different materials in ancient times. Those used in the royal palace were made of gold, silver and jade. Many people were specially assigned to manage timekeeping in the royal court. According to the Old Book of Tang, a classic historical work about the Tang dynasty, nearly 400 people in the imperial city tended the elaborate dripping buckets. Their duties included replenishing the buckets, observing the time shown on the arrow and reporting it to the night watchmen. The watchmen would then strike a wooden clapper or gong as they patrolled the streets, announcing the time to residents in the neighbourhood. Alongside the clepsydra, night watchmen also used another traditional timekeeping method: burning incense sticks. Incense-based timekeeping began during the Northern and Southern dynasties (386–589). Time measured by incense was less accurate than time measured by dripping buckets, because how long an incense stick took to burn depended on its material and the surrounding environment. Thus, although “the time it took to burn an incense stick” was a commonly used unit of time, much like today’s hour or minute, it was not standardised across all incense sticks. A stick could burn for anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour. According to Chen’s Incense Manual, in 1073, when a severe drought struck the region south of the Yangtze River and prevented clepsydras from working, an official named Shen Li invented a set of timekeeping tools called the five geng incense counter.

title: Upgrade or eyesore? Why Hong Kong’s Peak light display has hit a snag
description: A controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak is in doubt following mounting complaints that the installations damage Hong Kong’s natural beauty. The South China Morning Post looks at what has gone wrong with the project. What is the project? The Tourism Board planned small light installations for selected points along the...
content: A controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak is in doubt following mounting complaints that the installations damage Hong Kong’s natural beauty. Designed as one of several new attractions meant to replace a retired light show, the initiative has been criticised by local residents and visitors. The South China Morning Post looks at what has gone wrong with the project. What is the project? The Tourism Board planned small light installations for selected points along the walking trail near Lugard Road and Harlech Road to add an attraction to The Peak. The installations feature a soft, low-glare lighting design and were scheduled to operate from 7pm to 10pm on a 12-month trial basis, according to the board. “The initiative aims to further enhance the appeal of Hong Kong’s nighttime tourism and showcase the city’s unique charm as an international metropolis,” the board said last week. Why did it trigger controversy? Many residents accused the board of removing trees and vegetation to make way for the installations and adding to light pollution. Critics labelled the installations an eyesore that ruined the area’s natural ambience, pointing out that the walkway was set to feature at least 276 spotlights and 52 trees bound with cables. One social media user said: “The LED lights are so strong that they could affect local wildlife. Cables were strung along the railings, creating a risk of electrical leakage.” Jim Chi-yung, a research chair professor of geography and environmental science at the Education University of Hong Kong, widely known as the “Tree Doctor”, said installing a lighting project in a natural setting was “incongruous” and “a mismatch”. The board said on Sunday that it took public concerns about the trees at The Peak very seriously. The body stressed it and its contractor had not felled any trees, as the project did not require it. The board said it had sought and followed professional advice from other authorities and registered arborists on tree protection and the installation of the light fittings. “All key aspects of the project are subject to endorsement by registered arborists, including the selection of trees, the method of hanging the light fittings, tree protection measures, load-bearing arrangements and installation methods,” it said. “Arborists are also required to inspect the light fittings after installation and monitor them regularly to safeguard the health of the trees.” How did the project originate? Led by the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau, the project was launched as one of several initiatives intended to replace Hong Kong’s long-running “A Symphony of Lights” display. The nightly synchronised light, laser and music show, which had illuminated Victoria Harbour since 2004, was retired on September 9. The show was named the world’s “largest permanent light and sound show” by Guinness World Records in 2005 with lights spanning more than 40 buildings on both sides of the harbour. The replacement initiative followed Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po’s budget announcement in February, which stated that the board would launch a series of new shows at various locations and times throughout the year. At a Legislative Council Finance Committee meeting in April, Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said the board would allocate about HK$200 million (US$25.49 million) to launch a new light and shadow parade, which includes The Peak light show. The show was meant to form part of a new light display set to premiere alongside the coming Hong Kong WinterFest mega-event. What does the future hold for the new light display? The project’s future remains uncertain following the public outcry. The board stated it would review the project, while security guards told the SCMP that related work has been suspended. Law noted on Wednesday that the board and the Tourism Commission were currently gathering public feedback, adding that a final decision on whether to include the installations in the Christmas display would come later.

content: The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government. It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years. High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country. Serbia’s 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students’ List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105. “The Students’ List has won,” Vucic told supporters at his party’s election night event, though he blamed Serbia’s independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an “American deep state” for the loss. Vucic said his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared with the Students’ List, which he said took around 2.2 million. Supporters of the Students’ List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting: “Aleksandar is gone,” referring to Vucic. The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day. Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic’s loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city. Vucic was seeking to become Serbia’s prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign. Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a railway station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant corruption during renovation work at the station. Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia’s voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties – the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media. While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia’s fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office. The newly formed Students’ List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists. This approach was meant to counter Vucic’s one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students’ message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy. The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas – Vucic’s traditional strongholds. The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orban after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests. Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70 per cent, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time. Recent Serbian elections were marred by irregularities and the European Union was closely watching the conduct of Sunday’s vote in a candidate nation for the bloc’s membership. Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying. Both international and local election monitors expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists. Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

title: East Asia’s cultural economies are bridging politics-driven divides
description: The appearance of K-pop singer G-Dragon on electronic billboards in major Chinese cities despite Beijing’s K-pop ban points at a contrast between political shadows clouding international relations and actual commercial linkages in East Asia. Amid tensions over Seoul’s military alliance with the United States and other issues, G-Dragon featured in eight McDonald’s products across more than 8,000 outlets in mainland China. content: The appearance of K-pop singer G-Dragon on electronic billboards in major Chinese cities despite Beijing’s K-pop ban points at a contrast between political shadows clouding international relations and actual commercial linkages in East Asia. Amid tensions over Seoul’s military alliance with the United States and other issues, G-Dragon featured in eight McDonald’s products across more than 8,000 outlets in mainland China. The penetration and appeal of Korean cultural icons show how transnational consumer demand for cultural products and figureheads creates openings beyond traditional diplomacy. While cultural ties between states are often confined to state-backed image-building programmes and soft-power diplomacy, East Asian states are witnessing rising consumer demand for cross-border television content, films, games, cuisine and tourist attractions. In addition to creating profits, jobs and business-to-business linkages, these help bridge divides through culture-driven consumerism – an important ecosystem. These trends are particularly evident in Japan and South Korea. Despite prolonged tensions over historical and territorial disputes, the Japanese animated film Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island dominated South Korea’s box office, generating 42.7 per cent of ticket revenue and more than 1.8 million admissions in the first three weeks of its screening. Further evidence of Japanese anime being an integral node in its cultural economy is visible in the series Jujutsu Kaisen being the top anime title in seven of eight tracked Asian markets in the first half of this year, according to a recent report. Anime drew a larger monthly audience than any other genre on Asian streaming platforms between July 2025 and August 2026, and viewing on Netflix grew nine times faster than the service overall. South Korea welcomed more than 15 million international visitors between January and August this year, including a 29 per cent rise in arrivals from China. These arrivals play an important part in the country’s retail sector as Chinese visitors account for the largest share of spending among foreign tourists. Aware of their potential, duty-free shops offered perks and discounts to visitors for China’s National Day “golden week” holiday, during which South Korea was the top destination for Chinese overseas travellers. Increased familiarity between East Asian consumers who are in touch with Korean phrases, Japanese neighbourhoods or Chinese content purchased online or through physical visits makes societies feel less distant and more connected as human-centric dimensions made possible through thriving cultural economies. Increased cultural consumerism in East Asia also has a positive impact on digital e-commerce, which in turn has a trickle-down effect on the telecommunications, retail and logistics sectors. This is true for China. About 90 per cent of Chinese retail leaders have expressed optimism about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on commercial operations amid businesses adopting AI pricing, business promotions and forecasting. The rising popularity of Chinese cultural products, including cosmetic brands such as Flower Nose in South Korea, allows Beijing to further build on measures to ease access for consumers and cater to rising demand by promoting AI shopping assistants, virtual shopping experiences and applications in tourism. Localised financial returns also include prospective revenues from hosting performing artists on tour and retail stores showcasing cultural artefacts, which can further boost domestic economies. These trends of culture-driven consumerism in East Asia do not indicate resolution of long-standing political disputes, and neither are they traditional pillars of national economies generating maximum export revenue. However, they do indicate that boosting consumer demand, increasing business confidence and prompting investments to support a people-centric economic ecosystem anchored in cultural exchanges is possible amid political tensions. Official boycotts amid the deterioration of bilateral relations could stymie progress witnessed. Even so, governments adopting pragmatic approaches that view these industries as integral components of the region’s social and economic infrastructure can preserve these critical economic ecosystems and promote local prosperity. This is an important policy question as East Asian cultural economies benefit local consumers, retailers and sellers amid oil price volatility and supply chain disruptions from the crisis in the Middle East. In light of this, governments should consider undertaking state-backed investments in production houses, preserving cultural artefacts and easing tourism restrictions. Development planning models with official support for licensing agreements, protection of intellectual property rights of cultural products and greater accessibility for incoming travellers will allow the East Asian cultural economy to remain resilient and benefit from multiple distribution channels and audiences to multiply. It is evident that projection of soft power is not being confined to image-building exercises in East Asia. Local economies are benefiting from consumerism, serving as key conduits for neighbouring societies and businesses to interact and generate revenue for economic prosperity. To the region’s credit, political frictions have not prevented the thriving of human-centred accounts and economic relations.

title: Beijing pledges to back Taiwan’s pro-unification ‘patriots’ as it marks key anniversary

October 25 was formally established by Beijing last year as an official memorial date known as “Taiwan Restoration Day”. content: Beijing pledged to support pro-unification forces in Taiwan as it mounted a concerted publicity campaign on Sunday to mark the 81st anniversary of the end of Japanese colonial rule over the island. October 25 was formally established by Beijing last year as an official memorial date known as “Taiwan Restoration Day”. Speaking at an event in Fuzhou, the capital of Fujian province, on Sunday, Song Tao, the head of Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said the memorial day highlighted Beijing’s “firm confidence in defending national sovereignty and territorial integrity”. Song said the Chinese nation had an “indivisible cross-strait history” rooted in shared bloodlines. “Compatriots on both sides of the strait must jointly inherit the great spirit of the War of Resistance and the national spirit, and resolutely oppose Taiwan independence separatism and external interference,” Song told the audience, according to state news agency Xinhua. He added that Beijing had rolled out 10 policy measures this year to foster cross-strait exchanges and deepen integration. “We firmly support patriotic pro-unification forces on the island and will steadily advance the reunification of the motherland,” Song said. To mark the date, state broadcaster CCTV released a 42-second video clip featuring aerial views of Taiwan captured by the commercial Jilin-1 satellite constellation, overlaid with the caption: “This is the Taiwan province of China”. The video zoomed in on major landmarks, such as the Taipei Dome, the Port of Taipei, the National Palace Museum and the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall. It also showcased well-known natural features including Mount Jade, Sun Moon Lake, the Tamsui River, Hualien’s Qingshui Cliff and coastal wetlands in Tainan and Chiayi. “Every [Taiwanese] street is clearly visible” from orbit, CCTV said, and closed with a message that read: “The yearning to return remains unchanged; reunion will come in time.” Meanwhile, Xinhua published an article headlined “The Treasure Island Regains Light” that included President Xi Jinping’s previous comments on cross-strait relations and the historical context of the 1945 handover from Japanese colonial rule. Xi said the return was the result of the broader Chinese resistance to Japan and the Allied victory in World War II. “[The] historical and legal facts that Taiwan is part of China and both sides belong to one China cannot be changed”, he said, before concluding: “The motherland must be reunited, and will inevitably be reunified”. People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s mouthpiece, used its social media accounts to call for greater cultural and national alignment across the Taiwan Strait. It urged people to “firmly strengthen their identification with the Chinese nation, Chinese culture and the great motherland”, while honouring those who fought against the Japanese. Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army Eastern Theatre Command, which oversees the Taiwan Strait, published a graphic on social media that read: “Return home”. As well as a call to “defend territorial integrity”, it said the 1945 handover was an “irrefutable link in the chain of historical and legal facts” confirming Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan. Japan took control of the island in 1895 and remained in charge until October 25, 1945. In recent years, Beijing has increasingly used that anniversary to reinforce its legal claim over Taiwan. Meanwhile, the ways in which Taipei has marked the event have varied over time and governments. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including its main international partner the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with weapons. This year’s anniversary comes weeks before Taiwan’s local elections, where the island’s history has emerged as a dividing line between its rival political camps. The ruling, independence-leaning Democratic Progressive Party has traditionally downplayed the significance of the October 25 anniversary, while the opposition Kuomintang and other members of the mainland-friendly camp – known as the pan-blue coalition – attach more importance to it. Nowhere is the political temperature higher than in the marquee race for the Taipei mayoralty. Incumbent KMT mayor Chiang Wan-an – widely seen as a potential future presidential contender – faces a fiercely contested re-election bid against DPP challenger Puma Shen Pao-yang. The race has tightened considerably in recent weeks with polls indicating that Shen, who is best known for his work on civil defence and countering Beijing’s “cognitive warfare”, has closed the gap on the incumbent. Veteran Taiwan politician James Soong Chu-yu marked the occasion by calling for peaceful resolutions to cross-strait issues and warning people not to repeat the mistakes of the past. Soong, the chairman of the pan-blue People First Party, noted that China sacrificed more than 20 million lives to defeat Japan and recover lost territories, including Taiwan. However, he also acknowledged that during the post-1945 transition, the KMT government mishandled its relationship with Taiwanese residents. True restoration, Soong argued, required self-reliance and the protection of core values, ensuring that the people lived in a society that was “free, democratic, and prosperous”. Meanwhile, former KMT chairwoman Hung Hsiu-chu wrote on social media that the return of the island must go hand in hand with safeguarding peace. She called on both sides of the strait to adhere to the “1992 consensus” – an informal agreement that there is only one China, but the two sides may disagree about what that means – oppose Taiwanese independence and restart dialogue. Hung strongly criticised the DPP, accusing it of governing under the name of the Republic of China while severing its historical links with the mainland. “Without the joint resistance of the entire Chinese military and people, there would be no restoration of Taiwan,” Hung said, adding that the shared historical memory of resisting Japanese rule should not be divided simply because the two sides were not yet unified.

content: Veteran Hong Kong stock commentator Louie Shum Chun-ying has died aged 66, with a police source revealing he had a history of heart disease and diabetes. His twin sister confirmed on Sunday that he died on Saturday night at Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai, sharing the news in a post on his social media page. Shum, also known as “Master Shum”, was chief executive of stock brokerage Sincere Securities until his retirement two years ago. He remained active on internet radio shows over the past two years to share market information and investment tips. “My brother dedicated his life to Hong Kong’s financial and securities industry, mentoring generations of students throughout his investment courses. We know deeply how much he was loved and respected by all of you. We are truly grateful for the care and companionship his students have shown him over the years,” she wrote. “Our family is currently making the funeral arrangements. Details regarding the funeral service and memorial gathering will be announced once finalised.” According to an insider, Shum felt unwell around 7.49pm on Saturday as he walked to a taxi rank on Lockhart Road in Wan Chai after visiting a friend’s home. He suddenly collapsed, and a passer-by called an ambulance, the source said. Shum was unconscious when taken to Ruttonjee Hospital and died around 9pm. Police later inspected the scene and found no signs of theft or a struggle, according to the source. “The case is not considered suspicious. The deceased’s exact cause of death is subject to confirmation by an autopsy,” the source said. The case was classified as “dead on arrival”, the insider added. According to the source, Shum was diagnosed with heart disease and diabetes, and he regularly visited St Teresa’s Hospital in Kowloon City for medical treatment. The source noted that he had a normal diet, no mobility issues, was not experiencing financial hardship, and had no known disputes with others. Shum had appeared on two finance news shows on Raga Finance, an internet radio station, on Friday, according to a search by the South China Morning Post on YouTube. Shum, who worked in the finance and securities industry for more than 30 years, reportedly said he was facing immense pressure at work and had planned to retire after experiencing a minor stroke. Cardiologist Dr Duncan Ho Hung-kwong said Shum was likely to have experienced a heart attack. “The cholesterol plaque in the vessel wall ruptured through the innermost layer of the blood vessel,” he said. “The cholesterol went into the bloodstream and triggered blood clot formation. The bloodstream will be blocked within minutes and the heart may stop beating in the worst case.” He added that coronary heart disease was the most common heart disease, while a history of stroke, high blood pressure, glucose and cholesterol were risk factors. Ho urged residents aged 30 and above to conduct regular body checks, maintain a healthy diet and positive mindset, exercise regularly and avoid smoking.
