content: Canadian singer The Weeknd surprised concertgoers in Hong Kong on Saturday with a new song inspired by the city, evoking nostalgia among local music fans. Abel Tesfaye – the Canadian singer, songwriter, record producer and actor known professionally as The Weeknd – performed “Hong Kong” to tens of thousands of fans at Kai Tak Stadium on Saturday night. It was his first of four concerts in the city as part of the “After Hours Til Dawn Tour” world tour. The crowd reacted with awe and cheers. “Hong Kong” sampled heavily from the Cantopop song titled “Seasonal Wind” or “Monsoon” in English, a melancholic ballad released by Faye Wong in 1993. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Abel (@theweeknd) The Weeknd had previously noted the influence of Hong Kong culture in his music, while expressing an appreciation for Wong’s music. He sang the new song against the backdrop of a video showcasing Hong Kong’s landmarks and familiar sights, from the skyline of Victoria Harbour, a red-sailed traditional junk boat, bustling alleys and red taxis. The montage also featured roasted chestnut hawkers, classic neon signs in Mong Kok, the circular footbridge in Causeway Bay, dim sum restaurants, the waterfront in Tsim Sha Tsui and the Peninsula hotel. “Full of elements of Hong Kong! Cantopop city vibes, retro look, HK film elements! Must be from a team that truly admires and loves the essence of Hong Kong culture!” wrote Instagram user cheng.mars in a comment. Another user, bo_queen, said: “You remind me how much I love my home HK. I’m crying because this song and the cinematography are so beautiful, the crowd’s screams give me chills. “But also because this prime Hong Kong lives on only in our memories, a place we can never go back.” Since the recording from the concert was uploaded in the early hours of Sunday, it has drawn about 9.3 million views, 600,000 likes and 5,600 comments. The Weeknd’s series of shows continues on Sunday night, with additional dates scheduled for October 30 and 31.

title: AIIB keen to fund Northern Metropolis, with loans viewed as key endorsement
description: The China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) has expressed interest in financing projects in the Northern Metropolis mega development, Hong Kong’s finance chief has said. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also told the media on Sunday that global finance leaders had set aside their political differences during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Finance Ministers’ Meeting held in Hong Kong last week and reached a consensus on promoting digital infrastructure, employment...
content: The China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) has expressed interest in financing projects in the Northern Metropolis mega development, Hong Kong’s finance chief has said. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also told the media on Sunday that global finance leaders had set aside their political differences during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Finance Ministers’ Meeting held in Hong Kong last week and reached a consensus on promoting digital infrastructure, employment and youth exchanges. “Speaking of the AIIB, it is very interested in infrastructure development in the Northern Metropolis, as this is its own expertise,” Chan said on a radio show, referring to the government’s plan to turn 30,000 hectares (74,130 acres) of land bordering mainland China into a technology and housing hub. “They told us that … if there are any Northern Metropolis projects open for co-investment, [they will be] very interested. When there are any specific projects, we will explore ways for cooperation.” The Beijing-headquartered bank is expanding its presence in Hong Kong, with plans to open a local office by the end of the year, its second outside the mainland after the launch of its Abu Dhabi operational hub in 2023. AIIB president Zou Jiayi led a delegation to the finance ministers’ meeting on October 20 and 21. Before the meeting, Zou met with Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu at Government House in Central to exchange views. Established in 2016, the AIIB is a multilateral development bank with 111 members worldwide. It finances sustainable infrastructure, prioritising carbon neutrality, green economic transformation and technology-driven projects. The bank has become more active in the city in recent years by issuing Hong Kong dollar bonds. Billy Mak Sui-choi, an associate professor at Baptist University’s department of accountancy, economics and finance, said the AIIB could provide low-interest, long-term loans for Northern Metropolis projects, as infrastructure developments took a relatively long time to generate returns. “If the loan is approved, it means an international institution endorses the Northern Metropolis – confirming that the projects are not only financially viable with repayment ability, but also beneficial to the broader regional economy,” Mak said. Given that the city generally maintained smooth relations around the world and the bank’s founding members were largely friendly with China, securing financing would not be difficult, provided they met loan requirements and demonstrated regional economic benefits, he added. Addressing Apec, minister Chan said it had been difficult to reach a consensus among member economies because of their political differences and different stages of development. “Our main ideas remain neutrality, communication, commitment and mutual respect, trying to identify common ground for collaboration,” he said. Besides infrastructure development, financial leaders also discussed the digital economy and corresponding services and financing tools, as well as employment and youth exchanges. “Whether it was at the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, or this time, employment issues are nearly always placed as the first priority,” he said. Finance ministers of the 21 Apec member economies signed a joint statement stating public organisations in the region would foster an environment that catalyses financing for digital infrastructure and also encourages the private sector to commit investments. Development banks such as the AIIB were also urged to become involved in digital infrastructure projects, especially by offering financing options. Chan said many regional economies were keen on improving their infrastructure, and Hong Kong was ready to provide support as a destination for listing and securitising their assets. The finance chief also touched on the work of Hong Kong’s Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES), which announced on Thursday a new batch of 18 enterprises planning to increase their presence in Hong Kong, bringing the total number of firms helped by the office to 142. The government estimated the companies would bring in HK$84 billion (US$10.7 billion) worth of investment and create some 26,700 jobs. Chan noted that some of the companies had established a footprint in Hong Kong before ramping up their operations with the help of OASES. “We hope these companies will not only conduct retail businesses but also establish their research and development (R&D) hubs and regional headquarters here,” he said. “We will cooperate from the perspective of [providing a] policy package and could hopefully improve local employment.” In his weekly blog, also published on Sunday, Chan revealed that among the 142 companies supported by OASES, nearly 90 per cent would establish R&D centres in Hong Kong and 70 per cent of them planned to set up their regional headquarters in the city. “They bring not only funds and employment opportunities but also functions including decision making, R&D and business coordination,” he wrote. “The conglomeration of these high value-added rings is the key to converting enterprise investment into Hong Kong’s long-term competitiveness.”

content: About 1 million employees in Hong Kong will be allowed to move their entire Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) savings to a different provider once a year, starting December 21. The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority, which regulates the mandatory pension plans, said on Sunday that the “full portability” arrangement would be carried out in two phases to ensure a smooth implementation. In a blog post, authority chairwoman Ayesha Macpherson Lau said the arrangement would allow eligible members to transfer both the employer and employee contribution portions to their preferred MPF scheme once per calendar year. Currently, under the “semi-portability” arrangement, only the employee’s portion can be moved. “This further enhances scheme members’ control over their MPF and encourages working individuals to manage their retirement savings more actively,” she said. The first phase, effective from December 21, will cover about 1 million employees who joined the workforce or changed jobs on or after May 1, 2025. As more graduates entered the workforce and employees became eligible after changing jobs, the number of employees eligible for the first phase would continue to grow, Lau said. The second phase will involve employees who started their current employment before May 1, last year. As their MPF derived from employer mandatory contributions might still be used to “offset” long service payments or severance payments for years of service before 1 May 2025, additional legislative amendments were required, Lau said. She said the government would submit an amendment bill to the Legislative Council in mid-2027 to implement the second phase of “full portability”, as mentioned in the policy address in September. Lau said the eMPF platform, which became fully operational in April, had updated its system functions to support the implementation of full portability. Employees who decide to make a transfer can complete the procedure via the eMPF platform. They can handle their 2026 transfer between December 21 and December 31 or process their 2027 transfer starting on January 1. Lau reminded members to avoid “switching for the sake of switching” and refrain from transferring funds too frequently, as the MPF was a long-term investment. Before taking advantage of full portability, scheme members should weigh various factors, carefully compare the fund choices, performance and fee levels of different MPF schemes, and make prudent decisions based on their life stage, investment goals and risk tolerance, she said. Only employers could choose the MPF provider until 2012, when the Employee Choice Arrangement was introduced. Commonly known as semi-portability, this allows employees to transfer their own contributions – but not those made by their employers – to a new provider once a year. Employees conducted about 1.1 million transactions involving HK$59 billion (US$7.5 billion) under the semi-portability regime from its launch up to September this year, Lau said. From 2021 to 2025, an average of HK$4.5 billion in MPF contributions was transferred annually to employee-selected schemes under the semi-portability arrangement, a 7 per cent increase compared with the annual average of HK$4.2 billion from 2016 to 2020, according to Lau. As of September 30, there were 359,600 employers, 2.65 million employees and 221,900 self-employed people enrolled in MPF schemes, according to official statistics.

title: What’s next for Hong Kong developers in mainland China?
description: Hong Kong’s major property developers are shifting investment in mainland China from residential projects to commercial assets, including hospitality, as weak home sales and fewer attractive investment opportunities prompt them to focus on existing properties, recurring income and debt reduction. “In recent years, after we recycled the capital from our projects, we haven’t really found many good opportunities on the mainland,” Stephen Ng, chairman and managing director of Wharf Holdings, said at...
content: Hong Kong’s major property developers are shifting investment in mainland China from residential projects to commercial assets, including hospitality, as weak home sales and fewer attractive investment opportunities prompt them to focus on existing properties, recurring income and debt reduction. “In recent years, after we recycled the capital from our projects, we haven’t really found many good opportunities on the mainland,” Stephen Ng, chairman and managing director of Wharf Holdings, said at its interim results press conference in August. Wharf’s experience reflects a broader change in how Hong Kong developers are approaching assets in the world’s second-largest economy. Once an important growth market for Hong Kong’s major developers, mainland China offers opportunities to expand beyond their home market through residential projects and established local connections. But as China’s housing downturn deepens and attractive land deals become harder to find, the contribution of mainland sales has fallen sharply. Mainland China’s contribution to property sales revenue has plunged at Hong Kong’s four major developers in their latest results, with the share falling to just 2 per cent at CK Asset Holdings and 4 per cent at Henderson Land, from 52 per cent and 25 per cent a year earlier, respectively. Sun Hung Kai Properties’ share dropped to 19 per cent from 24 per cent, while New World Development’s fell to 53 per cent from 82 per cent. All four major developers have stopped acquiring residential development land through public tenders since 2023, while their existing mainland land banks have shrunk. The retreat has been building since China’s property debt crisis erupted in 2021. The shift did not mean Hong Kong developers have left mainland China’s housing market altogether; most still held residential projects acquired before 2022, mainly in stronger-tier cities, said Rebecca Tang, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. Henderson Land’s attributable mainland development land bank fell from 35.7 million square feet at the end of 2021 to 7.5 million square feet at the end of 2025. But the prolonged downturn has changed their appetite for new projects. “Most of them do not plan to acquire new residential projects in the near- to medium-term,” she said. For Kerry Properties, mainland contracted sales plunged 88 per cent in the first half to HK$1.3 billion, with management attributing the decline to projects in second- and third-tier cities taking longer than expected to sell. The group remained selective, however, paying about 2.7 billion yuan (US$404.6 million) in July for a commercial site in Shanghai’s Pudong district, citing its location, surrounding population and retail catchment. Developers are increasingly looking to shopping malls, hotels and mixed-use developments to generate rental and operating income. “Mainland commercial [and] hospitality investments will bring about long-term stable recurring income versus one-off income from residential or Hong Kong acquisitions,” Tang said. Hong Kong developers also have an advantage in luxury retail properties because of their high-quality assets and established tenant networks, she added. Hang Lung Properties opened a 105-room hotel under Hilton’s Curio Collection in September at its Centre 66 development in Wuxi, Jiangsu province. The complex also includes a shopping centre, offices and flats. “There is no direct correlation between the residential property and hospitality trends,” said Herman Chui, Hang Lung’s senior director of office, hotel and residence. “Growth in domestic and inbound tourism on the Chinese mainland, alongside demand for experience-based travel, gives us confidence in our hospitality business.” The economics of commercial development remain challenging because of development expenses and the time it takes to generate returns; investment properties typically delivered annual returns of only low to mid-single digits relative to the capital invested, said Jeff Zhang, an equity analyst at Morningstar. Hang Lung’s asset-light projects, which involve less upfront capital because the company takes on a smaller share of the investment burden, could deliver higher returns, Zhang said. Partnerships with state-owned enterprises also help manage risk. While Hang Lung’s partnerships in Shanghai and Wuxi may be required by local governments, Zhang noted, such arrangements remain relevant as a way to reduce risk. Hongkong Land has opened the second phase of its US$8 billion Westbund Central mixed-use development in Shanghai. Lan Kwai Fong Group plans to act as an asset manager for a mixed-use project near Shenzhen’s cruise port, with China Merchants Shekou and Shenzhen YaTong Holding Group. The shift is also changing how developers manage their capital. Rather than relying solely on selling homes to fund new projects, companies are selling commercial properties, reducing debt and exploring ways to release capital from completed assets. “We view New World Development’s C-REIT application as an ongoing capital recycling mechanism, but it’s unclear if other Hong Kong developers will follow suit,” Zhang said. New World has also sold commercial properties in Shanghai and Hangzhou, while developers are exploring other ways to replenish liquidity. Allan Zeman, chairman of Lan Kwai Fong Group, said falling property prices had prompted mainland consumers to save more and travel less, although he saw opportunities in cities attracting talent through artificial intelligence and other emerging industries to boost consumption sentiment. “It takes longer, but we’re seeing daylight,” Zeman said in an interview with the SCMP in mid October.

content: Hong Kong’s regulator for in vitro fertilisation (IVF) has referred a case to law enforcement agencies after a mainland Chinese influencer was suspected of offering to bring non-local surrogate mothers of LGBTQ parents to give birth in the city. Tan Zubiao, who goes by the name of “berlinsun” on Instagram, had set up a company in the city and advertised commercial surrogacy services for LGBTQ couples on social media, according to local media reports. Tan and his foreign husband, who have two children through surrogacy, were deported from Kaohsiung in Taiwan last Thursday after being fined NT$200,000 (HK$48,109) for breaching Taiwan’s Medical Care Act by offering assisted-reproductive services. In a written reply to the South China Morning Post on Sunday morning, Hong Kong’s Council on Human Reproductive Technology said commercial surrogacy arrangements and the distribution of related advertisements were prohibited under the city’s Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance. “The Department of Health has referred the case to the council. After seeking legal advice, the council has referred the case to law enforcement agencies for follow-up action,” it said. The SCMP has reached out to Hong Kong police for comment. According to screenshots of Tan’s Instagram posts published by local media, Tan had since August claimed to have helped LGBTQ clients obtain Hong Kong permanent residency and Hong Kong passports for their children, with photos showing newborn babies, Hong Kong identity cards, birth certificates and passports. “We solve a key pain point for global Chinese LGBTQ+ families: a Hong Kong passport can be held alongside other national passports. Gifting your child a lifelong travel document is one of the greatest gifts parents can give,” one of his posts read. In another screenshot from an Instagram story titled “IVF Angel Plan”, Tan wrote that he found satisfaction in helping “milk daddies” – a term used to refer to gay fathers – with the birth of their children. “Every time helping milk daddies give birth in Hong Kong, seeing the smile of the whole family, is the driving force and sense of achievement of my job,” he wrote, with the post showing two male clients and an infant. Tan has since turned his Instagram and Threads accounts private, while his company’s website, Babysun Fertility Center, is no longer available. The company has also deleted all content from its Instagram page.

title: Will AI-powered open-door vending machines reshape Hong Kong’s retail landscape?

content: Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan in Hong Kong. The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the bulk of the time is spent deciding what to buy. The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it. “I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.” Over the decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels. These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain uncommon in Hong Kong. Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage. IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing about 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post. Hong Kong had an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said. “It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said. Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck. Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said. While the new open-door models generated 20 to 30 per cent more revenue in closed environments such as offices, traditional machines still outperformed them by 30 per cent in transient public spaces like bus stops, Lui explained. “On the streets, some consumers might find the new machines are too slow, whereas with an Octopus card on a traditional machine, the product drops in a second after a purchase is made,” he said. While nearly 90 per cent of new vending machines deployed on the mainland were AI open-door models, Hong Kong’s adoption remained significantly slower due to distinct local economic factors, said Rex Leung, general manager of IVM Technology. The offline nature of the Octopus card contactless payment system presented a significant hurdle for AI machines, which required post-purchase settlement after the door was closed, Leung said. “The physical Octopus card is an offline payment method where users tap and leave immediately, which is incompatible with this machine that charges users only after they finish shopping,” Leung added. To resolve this issue, Octopus Cards was expected to launch an integration allowing users to scan a quick response (QR) code and settle payments online via the Octopus application, Lui said. Leung added the company aimed to evolve into a platform that allowed a wider range of organisations to sell goods in their machines. FreshUp, another local vending machine operator with a network of more than 5,000 machines, had set up more than 500 smart coolers that allowed customers to open the door, take products and be charged automatically through visual recognition technology, said David Lam, the group’s founder and CEO. The smart models were generating 10 to 20 per cent more revenue per transaction than traditional push-button machines because the open-door design encouraged consumers to buy multiple items at once, Lam explained. “People might have pressed buttons for individual items in the past, but now, since they have already opened the fridge to buy a drink, they might take chocolate or potato chips if they find them interesting, increasing the overall basket value or unit items per transaction,” Lam said. The AI models required an upfront hardware cost of HK$20,000 to HK$30,000, which was similar to the price of traditional machines, he added. While the local smart retail sector was projected to grow steadily at an annual rate of 5 to 10 per cent, operators had to pay a recurring fixed back-end computing fee to software providers for data processing every time the cabinet door was opened, Lam said. Beyond commercial retail, the elimination of mechanical coils and rigid size restrictions has allowed open-door cabinets to serve as low-cost “micro-retail platforms” for non-governmental organisations and local brands seeking physical exposure without traditional overheads. The new technology provided a low-cost retail alternative for charities such as the Po Leung Kuk, which sold products made by people with disabilities, said Choi Kai-yin, a social worker and service manager at the organisation. Listing items in physical retail stores incurred high rental and administrative costs, making it difficult for charities to generate sufficient revenue to support their disabled creators, Choi said. “Renting a shop is [costly], as we are selling bottled drinks for about HK$10 each, and it is hard to calculate how many bottles we need to sell to cover the rent,” Choi added. By selling bottled tea at HK$12 through vending machines, the Po Leung Kuk hoped to create a reasonable profit margin, which would directly benefit individuals with disabilities in recognition of their contributions and participation in vocational training, Choi said. Swire Coca-Cola has been rolling out smart vending coolers on the mainland in recent years, as retail formats incorporating digital payments increase in popularity following the pandemic. Its Hong Kong bottling business has now begun introducing these coolers, which allow customers to open the door and select drinks, adapting technology and operating processes proven on the mainland. print cut begins The coolers are easy to operate: shoppers select a payment method before opening the door, choose their products and close the door. When the door is closed, the bill is settled. “Consumers today expect to see it, want it and get it almost instantly, and Hong Kong is no exception. People want a cold drink close to where they live, work, study and play, and they want paying for it to be quick and simple,” said Hunter Jin, Greater China CEO of Swire Coca-Cola. “Smart vending coolers meet that expectation by combining cashless payment with product-recognition technology, so the whole purchase feels seamless.” Swire Coca-Cola has set up more than 150 coolers across sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings to reach locations unsuitable for conventional machines. The new coolers would not completely replace the company’s network of about 6,000 conventional vending machines in Hong Kong, but would serve as a smart alternative offering a seamless digital experience, Swire Coca-Cola said. “As Hong Kong continues to welcome major events and visitors, vending can do more than sell drinks,” Jin said. “We are exploring Hong Kong-themed vending and digital experiences at venues, transport hubs and tourist destinations that showcase local culture and add to the city’s vibrancy.”

title: Hong Kong needs a civil service fit for a changed world
description: Hong Kong’s civil service has long enjoyed a reputation for efficiency, professionalism and probity. It has also been a pillar of stability, particularly during the transition from British to Chinese rule. Outside the general and administrative grades, many civil servants spend much of their careers in relatively specialised areas of responsibility. This allows them to develop deep expertise and makes them dependable regulators and administrators. However, it can also make it harder to adapt...
content: Hong Kong’s civil service has long enjoyed a reputation for efficiency, professionalism and probity. It has also been a pillar of stability, particularly during the transition from British to Chinese rule. Outside the general and administrative grades, many civil servants spend much of their careers in relatively specialised areas of responsibility. This allows them to develop deep expertise and makes them dependable regulators and administrators. However, it can also make it harder to adapt when new challenges cut across established departmental boundaries. Recent events have put this model under scrutiny. The fire that engulfed Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, claiming 168 lives and destroying more than a thousand homes, raised grave questions about building safety and regulatory oversight. Subsequent construction scandals involving luxury homes and public housing estates, together with concerns over lift installations at a major public hospital and in numerous other buildings, have further tested public confidence in the government. Hong Kong was once a British outpost built on trade. Government played a relatively limited role in economic development, while free trade, market forces and the city’s strategic position at the crossroads of East and West helped it prosper. The city continues to be recognised internationally for its economic freedom. That said, the experience since 1997 has shown that free markets cannot address every economic and social challenge. Following the handover, the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis and the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome dealt severe blows to the economy. Then-chief executive Tung Chee-hwa sought to revive growth through initiatives including Hong Kong Disneyland and the development of a cruise terminal. A substantial relaxation of travel arrangements for mainland residents subsequently helped tourism and the wider economy recover. The lesson is not that government should replace market forces, but that it must be capable of responding decisively when circumstances change. Today, the civil service must contend with changes unseen in a century. China has become the world’s second-largest economy and a major technological power. Hong Kong’s comparatively small economy is increasingly intertwined with a mainland economy undergoing rapid technological transformation. China’s strategic competition with the United States is likely to shape the global economic and technological landscape for years to come. Beijing has made the development of “new quality productive forces” a key national priority. For Hong Kong, the implications are substantial. The need to harness technology, develop new industries and improve productivity features prominently in the national development agenda and the city’s own planning priorities. The challenge is to translate these ambitions into effective policies, an enabling regulatory environment and tangible economic gains. Civil servants have already had to navigate a growing range of emerging technologies and business models. These include mobile payments, ride-hailing, autonomous driving, the low-altitude economy, green maritime fuel, sustainable aviation fuel and hydrogen as an alternative energy source. Each presents regulatory questions that existing rules might not adequately address. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents perhaps the greatest test. The government has committed substantial resources to AI research and development, including support for universities and the expansion of computing infrastructure. A proposed data centre in the Northern Metropolis is expected to increase Hong Kong’s computing capacity substantially. Investment in infrastructure is only part of the equation. Hong Kong also needs a coherent strategy for AI adoption and governance across government and the wider economy. This should address issues such as data protection, cybersecurity, accountability, workforce disruption and the responsible use of AI in public services. The organisation of government itself deserves attention. The Digital Policy Office, established in July 2024 through the merger of the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer and the Efficiency Office, provides an institutional base for advancing digital government. However, structural changes and new titles alone cannot deliver transformation. What matters is whether the government can develop the expertise, leadership and clear lines of responsibility needed to turn digital ambitions into results. Meeting these challenges will require the civil service to look beyond established routines. Recruiting specialist talent from outside government, including people with experience in technology and emerging industries, can help broaden its capabilities. There are encouraging signs of a more outward-looking and entrepreneurial approach. For example, officials have travelled to Switzerland to explore opportunities to attract gold refineries to Hong Kong. Such initiatives suggest a willingness to engage directly with businesses and pursue opportunities beyond the traditional confines of departmental administration. Geopolitical change calls for a similar adjustment. As economic influence becomes more widely distributed and countries in the Global South play a growing role in international affairs, Hong Kong needs to diversify its external connections. Officials have been working to build links with countries in the Middle East and Central Asia, in line with the broader direction of the mainland’s international engagement. The government’s leadership has also recognised the need to make the civil service more responsive to public expectations. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has introduced measures to strengthen the accountability of senior officials, while a performance appraisal enhancement scheme launched earlier this month is intended to link annual salary increments more closely to performance and address underperformance among staff. Ultimately, Hong Kong’s civil service does not need to discard the qualities that have served it well. Professionalism, integrity, institutional knowledge and administrative continuity remain essential, but these strengths must be matched by technological literacy, strategic thinking, cross-departmental cooperation and a greater readiness to adapt. The choice is not between stability and change. It is whether Hong Kong can preserve the best of its administrative tradition while equipping its civil service for a world in which yesterday’s experience is no longer sufficient to meet tomorrow’s demands.

title: School bullying cases in Hong Kong rise 32% to nearly 500 a year
description: Hong Kong schools handled an average of 496 bullying cases each academic year from 2022 to 2025 – a 32 per cent jump compared with the previous three years, according to the Education Bureau. According to the bureau, public primary and secondary schools recorded an average of 496 bullying cases each year between 2022 and...
content: Hong Kong schools handled an average of 496 bullying cases each academic year from 2022 to 2025 – a 32 per cent jump compared with the previous three years, according to the Education Bureau. A youth group attributed the increase to greater reporting driven by heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish playful jokes from bullying. According to the bureau, public primary and secondary schools recorded an average of 496 bullying cases each year between 2022 and 2025, up 32 per cent from the 377 recorded annually from 2019 to 2022. The bureau told the Legislative Council in 2023 that the number of cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, from the 2019-20 to 2021-22 school years was 411, 306 and 413 respectively. The average number for these three school years was 377. The figures were based on information contained in the bureau’s annual questionnaire surveys on guidance and discipline cases in schools. The bureau did not provide any annual breakdown for the years between 2022 and 2025. It said the data for the current school year was still being compiled. “The number of student cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, handled by schools averaged 496 per year between the 2022-23 and 2024-25 school years, with the annual figures remaining generally stable,” a bureau spokesman said. But he said comparing the two sets of figures for 2019-22 and 2022-25 might not be appropriate, as the first triennium was marked by the Covid pandemic, during which students attended some classes online. Last month, the Programme for International Student Assessment, a worldwide study of 15-year-olds’ learning and education by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), revealed that 22.2 per cent of students in Hong Kong aged 15 reported experiencing some form of bullying at least a few times a month. The city’s overall figure was higher than the OECD average of 19.6 per cent. Hong Kong ranked 32nd among the 86 surveyed countries and cities, including ones that were not members of the organisation. The Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups has been commissioned by the bureau to provide advice and counselling services on peer conflict management to students and parents at all primary and secondary schools this academic year. The group also has social workers stationed in 59 primary and secondary schools. Andy Chan Ying-kit, head of service at the youth group, partly attributed the rise in bullying cases to greater public concern driven by increased awareness of student mental health. “Some research indicates mental health issues related to bullying cases lead to emotional distress and social withdrawal,” he said. Chan added that younger generations often struggled to distinguish playful joking from bullying, such as creating altered images targeting victims or repeatedly kicking classmates out of chat groups. He said resolving cases had become significantly more difficult with some students airing their grievances on social media and drawing comments from other online users. “The victim faces severe public scrutiny and media pressure, making mediated resolutions far harder to achieve,” he said. Chan noted that some cases became more complicated because victims might turn into bullies themselves when seeking revenge, making it harder for teachers and social workers to determine fault or mediate effectively. He said parents were also paying much closer attention to their children’s well-being, and their dissatisfaction with how schools handled cases often led to confrontation with administrators. Parents should prioritise their children’s emotional well-being instead of prematurely escalating the situation, he advised. “Focus first on comforting your child, listening to their feelings and addressing their mental health,” he said. “While seeking justice or investigating what happened is important, demanding immediate consequences will not resolve your child’s emotional distress.” Schools should assign different staff members or social workers to handle various tasks, with some managing students’ emotions and others supporting and reassuring parents, Chan said. He noted that junior secondary school students recorded higher rates of bullying as they needed to rebuild their social circles during the transition and were more prone to interpersonal conflicts and misunderstandings. A bureau spokesman said it maintained a “zero-tolerance” policy towards school bullying. “The Education Bureau provides clear guidelines for schools detailing the principles, procedures, methods and follow-up work required when handling bullying incidents, and mandates that schools handle every single case with utmost seriousness,” he said.

content: Police have arrested a 34-year-old man who allegedly mixed rat poison into food left for stray cats in a Kowloon park and was found in possession of a knife. The force said it received a report at around 3.30am on Saturday that a man was suspected of putting poison in cat food that animal welfare volunteers had placed near tennis courts in Shek Kip Mei Park. Officers arrived at the scene and seized a packet of suspected rat poison and a fruit knife measuring around 14cm (5.5 inches) in length from the man. “Following a preliminary investigation, the man was arrested on suspicion of cruelty to animals and possession of an offensive weapon and is currently being detained for further investigation,” police said. The Sham Shui Po district crime squad is handling the investigation. Animal welfare volunteers said they first discovered someone appearing to poison food and water left for stray cats last month. A social media user said he installed a surveillance camera on a tree in the park and realised the suspect poisoned food and water at around 3am every Saturday. However, the camera did not capture his face. The social media user, pangxc15, saw someone resembling the suspect while passing through the area one night and decided to try to catch him in the act. “Previously, we had failed attempts because he did not show up,” the user said. “Today we tried again and started waiting from 1am until we finally caught him at around 3.10am. He was loitering for around 25 minutes and setting poison in the area.” The user posted photos of bowls of tainted water and food, and a video of the suspect walking around an area of vegetation with a flashlight. Police said no cats were injured in the case

title: 2 projector stands removed from controversial Peak lighting project after outcry
description: Parts of two installations in a controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak have been removed, days after Hong Kong’s tourism authorities pledged to balance the community’s needs and said the scheme was not “set in stone”. The removals came hours after Commissioner for Tourism Ann Chan Wai-yan inspected the site on Saturday morning with a lawmaker and a district councillor, following an outcry from residents who accused the Hong Kong Tourism Board of removing trees and...
content: Parts of two installations in a controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak have been removed, days after Hong Kong’s tourism authorities pledged to balance the community’s needs and said the scheme was not “set in stone”. The removals came hours after Commissioner for Tourism Ann Chan Wai-yan inspected the site on Saturday morning with a lawmaker and a district councillor, following an outcry from residents who accused the Hong Kong Tourism Board of removing trees and flowers to make way for the installations. When the South China Morning Post visited The Peak late on Saturday afternoon, two large metal stands that had held industrial-grade projectors had been removed, leaving only their grey foundational blocks and some bolts, which were not cordoned off. A security guard near the park on the Harlech Road and Lugard Road circular walk confirmed that the two structures had been removed that afternoon. But a smaller metal stand with a projector remained cordoned off near a pavilion. The guard said it had been tested but was not yet fully operational. While some installations were already in place, they would not be switched on yet because of the ongoing controversy, he added. Around a dozen smaller projectors remained attached to railings along Harlech Road, leading to the Peak Galleria, and light installations at a workout area remained fenced off, with security guards stationed nearby. The installations were planned for selected locations along the walking trail as part of a new light show for the coming Hong Kong WinterFest. Residents have shared photos online of the installations being tested, with neon-coloured lights directed at trees and kaleidoscopic patterns projected onto the trail. When asked about the removal work and for an update on the project, the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau referred the SCMP to a social media post and said it had nothing to add. The bureau said in the post that Ann Chan and representatives from the Tourism Board had inspected lighting installations with lawmaker Judy Chan Kapui and Central and Western district councillor Jeremy Young Chit-on along Lugard Road and Harlech Road on Saturday. “We will continue to arrange field visits to The Peak by different lawmakers and hear more opinions. We will also quickly deal with some improvements that can be done immediately on people’s suggestions and continue to relieve people’s concerns with practical actions,” it said. “We will strive to balance as much as possible the benefits of tourism, the actual situation in the district, the perception of residents and the ecological environment.” Judy Chan said she had not been told about the removal of parts of the installation during the morning inspection. She noted the lighting installations’ impact on the environment and traffic, as well as the safety risks they posed. She said that if the project attracted large crowds, the surrounding transport infrastructure and pedestrian pathways would come under significant strain, causing congestion and safety risks. “Even with technical adjustments, concealing wiring and changing the number and placement of light fixtures, it remains difficult to fully eliminate the impact of artificial installations on the visual character of natural trails and the surrounding ecosystem,” she said. She urged the government to conduct a thorough and prudent assessment after considering the environmental impact and public views. “In light of the project’s practical feasibility and actual effectiveness on The Peak, authorities should reconsider whether it is necessary to proceed, to ensure the optimal use of resources and allow the natural landscape to be restored,” she said. The SCMP learned earlier this week that related works had been suspended amid mounting complaints that the installations were damaging the environment. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said earlier that the Tourism Board and the Tourism Commission were gathering public feedback and would visit the relevant sites with district councillors. “As the project is still under way, nothing is set in stone yet,” Law said. “It is still too early to talk about advancing the project. We are still listening to opinions and may make modifications.”

title: How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change
description: Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong. For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity. “Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed...
content: Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong. For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity. “Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed money. Now, after successful pilot schemes, the initiatives have been replicated,” Chow, former senior manager of the programme, said. The drive was established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988. But the drive was preceded by early fundraising campaigns from the public broadcaster in the 1960s that featured quirky stunts to attract donations. Tony Baynes, former head of Radio 3 at RTHK and a co-founder of OSC, recalled that Captain Hamish McNinch of the British Army Air Corps dropped from a helicopter onto a Star Ferry building dressed as Santa Claus in 1981. “Santa stepped out onto ... [the] Star Ferry building on the Hong Kong side and came down to meet a horde of children who’d gathered especially for the occasion,” Baynes said. Funds raised from the event went to the Duchess of Kent Children’s Hospital at Sandy Bay. Since its inception in 1988, OSC has raised more than HK$415 million, supporting 382 charitable projects and helping over 100,000 people. Each year, OSC identifies several themes and chooses NGOs to fund while connecting corporate donors with the organisations. Recent fundraising activities included rooftop farming, corporate volunteers making mochi alongside children with special needs and a charity “hash” run mixing exercise and treasure hunting in Santa Claus costumes. This year, the scheme will support groups tackling poverty, improving health and well-being and promoting inclusivity. Chow recalled making her pitch for an NGO to OSC. “[OSC was] really concerned during the pitching process as to whether I could share human stories [of beneficiaries] with the selection panel,” she said. “Because of this, when I arrived here as a staff member, I also placed much emphasis on this aspect. This is because this is one of the niches in OSC’s charity legacy too.” She also explained how the drive had evolved over the years, saying: “To me, OSC is like a citywide engine to unlock a spirit of giving across the city. Like an engine, it will keep on moving and keep on unlocking everyone’s generosity.” Some past recipients had also become partners of the scheme, she noted. Among them is Pia Wong, founder and CEO of NGO consultancy Purpose Impact Action. She first worked with OSC as a beneficiary in 2014 when she was an executive director at Bring Me A Book Hong Kong, which promotes literacy. She later returned as a strategic impact partner to help OSC develop a new framework to evaluate the effects of the philanthropy. Wong said she hoped to turn the long list of beneficiaries into a community that could pool their insights and help each other. She is developing a “theory of change” model for OSC, where goals are mapped out to reverse-engineer step-by-step outcomes needed to achieve the aims. Wong said the model would lead to a better understanding of NGOs’ needs and how OSC could support them. “Back in 2014 it was very much “we’re kind of helping as a funder and you were the beneficiary”, whereas now it is “let’s see how we can work together’,” she said.

title: Halloween comes early to Hong Kong as festivities draw crowds, lift bar business
description: Halloween has arrived early in Hong Kong, with costumed revellers and families thronging the city’s streets a week early and some establishments seeing business increase by up to 20 per cent. The streets of Central were packed on Saturday as visitors and locals alike joined events held under the Tourism Board’s inaugural “Hong Kong Halloween Month”. content: Halloween has arrived early in Hong Kong, with costumed revellers and families thronging the city’s streets a week early and some establishments seeing business increase by up to 20 per cent. The streets of Central were packed on Saturday as visitors and locals alike joined events held under the Tourism Board’s inaugural “Hong Kong Halloween Month”. The campaign, which started last Saturday, involves street celebrations in Central, including Lan Kwai Fong, Kai Tak, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays, culminating on Halloween night. Hundreds of people of all ages filled Chater Road as part of “Halloween in Central”, which featured a large eyeball installation at Statue Square, as well as ghoulish face painting and themed food and drink options, including cake pops shaped like eyeballs. Among those taking part in the celebrations was 40-year-old Hongkonger Stephen Poon, whose daughters Gisele, five, and Gabryel, three, were dressed as Slinky from Pixar’s Toy Story films. “I think they are doing a really good job,” Poon, who works in accounting, said of the Tourism Board’s event. He said there had not been much for families to do in the city since the Covid-19 pandemic, and was glad he could bring his daughters out for some family fun. Poon added that the event had “definitely increased” his spending, with the family planning to buy about HK$500 (US$64) worth of food and other items throughout the day. “It’s just such a vibe,” he said. Phil Murphy, founder and managing director of Pyjama, the firm in charge of food and drink at the event, said that given it was the first year, he would be happy just to break even. Nonetheless, he said business seemed to be “doing quite well” given the foot traffic in the area. “I think next weekend is going to be brilliant,” he said. “This is the practice run.” Nearby, Lan Kwai Fong was also bustling as the sun set on Saturday, with dozens of costumed revellers enjoying themselves in the popular nightlife district. By 9pm, the district was packed with thousands of people slowly snaking their way through its streets, while a Halloween-themed DJ performance across Victoria Harbour in East Tsim Sha Tsui also drew large crowds. Allan Zeman, chairman of Lan Kwai Fong Group, said business at some of the bars in the area was up by 10 to 20 per cent so far this month. “Last Saturday was crazy,” he said. “There were so many people, people dancing in costumes. “Tonight will be similar – really, really busy. The whole city has really come alive this Halloween.” He added that Halloween created a “really great atmosphere” in the city and also attracted many visitors from mainland China. The month-long campaign forms part of a tourism strategy outlined in February’s budget to place greater emphasis on festivals that are less prominent on the mainland, including Halloween, to draw more visitors to the city. Kiki Weng Qi, a 21-year-old university student visiting from Shenzhen, was among the mainland visitors in the area on Saturday night. While Weng, who was dressed as video game character Mario, said she had visited Hong Kong before, she was marking her first Halloween there with her friend, 19-year-old Xie Man Si, who was dressed as a pumpkin. “The Halloween celebrations in Hong Kong are particularly great,” she said. “There are similar activities in Shenzhen but there are not so many people.” The day trippers said they planned to spend HK$2,000 between them on souvenirs and other shopping before returning to Shenzhen later on Saturday. Despite the early celebrations, some bars in the area were still taking a cautious approach to the festivities. Many people passing through Lan Kwai Fong were keen to just walk around and take photos of the Halloween decorations, rather than stop for a drink. “We don’t have a crystal ball,” said a bar employee who declined to be named. “Of course, we want it to be busier than last year. If sales are as good as last year, it will be considered a good thing.”

title: 33 held in crackdown on credit card theft ring targeting Hongkongers in Shenzhen
description: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese police have arrested 33 people in a joint crackdown on a syndicate that allegedly stole credit cards from residents who had travelled north to Shenzhen, with losses exceeding HK$1.8 million (US$229,500). Superintendent Tsang Chun-kit of the Crime Kowloon East Regional Headquarters said on Saturday that “card carriers” then immediately crossed the border to buy mobile phones and resell them for cash, all before the victims could realise what had happened. “All the...
content: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese police have arrested 33 people in a joint crackdown on a syndicate that allegedly stole credit cards from residents who had travelled north to Shenzhen, with losses exceeding HK$1.8 million (US$229,500). Superintendent Tsang Chun-kit of the Crime Kowloon East Regional Headquarters said on Saturday that “card carriers” then immediately crossed the border to buy mobile phones and resell them for cash, all before the victims could realise what had happened. “All the victims had been to tourist hotspots in Shenzhen for leisure before the crime happened,” Tsang said. “They didn’t check their personal belongings after the trip until banks notified them of abnormally large transaction records.” The Kowloon East regional technology and financial crime unit shared intelligence with Shenzhen’s Public Security Bureau and carried out an in-depth investigation before separate enforcement action was taken, he explained. Between August and October, Hong Kong police arrested 11 men and five women, aged between 17 and 45, on suspicion of handling stolen goods, conspiracy to defraud and obtaining property by deception. They included two alleged core members of the syndicate, 13 runners and an employee of a second-hand electronic device shop. They were suspected of being tied to at least 60 reports involving stolen credit cards and more than HK$1.8 million in losses. The most lost in a single case was HK$110,000. Shenzhen authorities, meanwhile, arrested 11 men and six women, aged between 36 and 56, on suspicion of theft and handling or hiding criminal proceeds. Chief Inspector Fung Chi-tat of the Kowloon East technology and financial crime unit laid out how the syndicate operated. Recruited card carriers gathered at guest houses near border checkpoints in Shenzhen, while hired thieves stole the credit cards. “Supervisors” monitored the handover of the cards. The supervisors would also travel between Hong Kong and the mainland to deliver stolen credit cards to carriers and monitor their purchases. The carriers then bought expensive mobile phones to resell for cash. The card carriers had also been instructed to sell mobile phones at a designated second-hand electronic device shop, Fung said. Senior Inspector Chow Ka-yun from the technology and financial crime unit said officers arrested suspects in Hong Kong between August and October. Police intercepted suspects outside MTR stations where supervised deliveries of stolen credit cards took place, shops where card carriers tried to make purchases and the designated second-hand electronic device shop where the phones were sold. Officers also confiscated 13 phones purchases with the stolen credit cards, nine stolen cards and multiple receipts of relevant purchases.

title: Hong Kong urged to revive growth, drive reforms with government’s ‘visible hand’
description: Hong Kong authorities should act as a “visible hand” to break down barriers erected by vested interests and revive growth momentum through reform under its maiden five-year plan, a former Beijing official overseeing the city’s affairs has said. Deng Zhonghua, former deputy director of the State Council’s Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, also said the city had to adopt a reform-oriented approach to empower emerging industries through deregulation. Hong Kong also needed to address “deep-rooted...
content: Hong Kong authorities should act as a “visible hand” to break down barriers erected by vested interests and revive growth momentum through reform under its maiden five-year plan, a former Beijing official overseeing the city’s affairs has said. Deng Zhonghua, former deputy director of the State Council’s Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, also said the city had to adopt a reform-oriented approach to empower emerging industries through deregulation. Hong Kong also needed to address “deep-rooted conflicts”, including uneven benefits from development, through improving mechanisms for sharing the fruits of growth in housing, healthcare, elderly care and education. “[The five-year plan] marks a shift from a free market adopting a positive non-interventionist approach to an organic combination of an efficient market and a capable government,” Deng, who is now president of the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said on Saturday. “[This entails] performing the role of the ‘visible hand’ of the government to effectively regulate and guide in areas where the market fails and reinforce the leading role.” Speaking at a seminar in Shenzhen, titled “Five-year plans of Hong Kong and Macau and their integration into and service to overall national development”, Deng pointed to long-standing challenges in both cities, including a narrow economic structure, insufficient growth momentum, entrenched vested interests and an uneven distribution of development benefits among residents. Deng said the five-year plans of both cities sought to tackle these issues through reform. Macau released its third five-year plan in August. “The key to overcoming these challenges lies in breaking down blockades of vested interests, fostering and expanding new growth drivers and new tracks,” Deng said. “We can only achieve breakthroughs in economic and social development and break down blockades of vested interests through reform. We can only generate new growth momentum and unleash the vitality through innovation.” Highlighting reform measures in Hong Kong’s five-year plan, including developing an international innovation and technology centre and a high-calibre talent hub, Deng urged the government to maintain a reform mindset throughout implementation, particularly in supporting emerging industries and improving residents’ livelihoods. “The implementation of the five-year plan relies on innovation,” he said. “It is not only about implementing the reform and innovative measures well, but also about further breaking free from fixed mindsets and path dependence in actual work.” Deng urged officials to pursue institutional innovation to deregulate and empower the development of emerging industries, establish a fault-tolerant and error-correction mechanism through bold reform and innovation within the legal framework. He also said the five-year plan marked a shift in Hong Kong’s approach to governance and would improve its effectiveness, but it had to be upheld to turn the blueprint into practice. He noted that the blueprints enabled Hong Kong and Macau to shift from passive responses and short-term measures to proactive, comprehensive and long-term planning for future development. They preserved core advantages such as free-port status, low tax rates, marketisation and the rule of law, while strengthening development guidance through policy incentives and government funding, Deng added. Wang Zhenmin, dean of the Institute for Governance Studies at Tsinghua University, also stressed at the seminar that Hong Kong’s five-year plan aimed to tackle deep-rooted problems the market economy had failed to resolve, particularly the wealth gap and a narrow economic structure. He rejected criticism that the document would turn the city into a mainland China-style socialist system. Noting that 1.65 million Hongkongers were living in poverty in 2020 and that many families still lived in notorious subdivided flats, Wang said fundamental problems remained unresolved despite some improvement. He added that the five-year plan sought to guide market forces to address these “pain points”. “Relying solely on the market will only intensify the conflicts and aggravate the situation. This is Hong Kong’s greatest shortcoming,” Wang said. “If this shortcoming is not addressed, not only will economic and social development be difficult to sustain, but it will also be hard to maintain social stability.” Stephen Wong Yuen-shan, head of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit, said the administration had studied the national 15th five-year plan and identified the key areas where Hong Kong’s strengths matched the country’s needs, citing the government’s efforts to build a commodity trading ecosystem and support mainland Chinese businesses in going global. Wong added that the government had been working with the mainland to deepen research on smart ports and green shipping, and to study pathways for Hong Kong to participate in China’s carbon market and support its internationalisation. Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a prominent Beijing-based state research institute and think tank, said at the seminar that the five-year blueprint served as a key instrument of executive-led governance. He noted that Hong Kong’s five-year plan set out more than 100 indicators that would allow the outcomes of governance to be examined. “Under the framework of the five-year plan, executive-led governance becomes an operable, verifiable and accountable institutional arrangement,” Gao added. Tam Yiu-chung, formerly the city’s sole member of Beijing’s top legislative body, proposed establishing a third-party assessment mechanism to enable independent and continuous monitoring of the plan’s implementation. He suggested the academy could lead the mechanism, working with local academic institutions and think tanks, to support midterm adjustments to the blueprint. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu had earlier played down the idea, saying Hong Kong did not need to follow the mainland practice of commissioning third-party organisations to evaluate policy implementation. Speaking on the sidelines of the seminar, Italian economist Pompeo Della Posta, a professor at the Belt and Road School of Beijing Normal University, said that some European businesses remained sceptical about the mainland market, and Hong Kong could leverage its financial and legal systems to help them mitigate risks. “Europeans still keep deep in their mind about the appropriateness of the Chinese system and the risks and the dangers,” Posta said. “Passing through Hong Kong and setting their activities in Hong Kong and establishing contracts and relationships in Hong Kong might induce them to feel a bit safer.”

title: Abby Choi trial so far: ex-father-in-law lied to rent village flat, bought mincer
description: The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung rented a village house flat under false pretences and bought a meat mincer and multiple saws as he allegedly prepared for the model’s killing, a court has heard. More evidence emerged regarding how three of Choi’s former in-laws allegedly planned her murder and the disposal of her body as the High Court trial entered its fourth week. content: The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung rented a village house flat under false pretences and bought a meat mincer and multiple saws as he allegedly prepared for the model’s killing, a court has heard. More evidence emerged regarding how three of Choi’s former in-laws allegedly planned her murder and the disposal of her body as the High Court trial entered its fourth week. Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial for allegedly murdering the 28-year-old influencer on February 21, 2023. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial began last month. Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were discovered at a 600 square foot rental flat on the ground floor of a three-storey house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village on February 24 that year. Hui Yan-yan, the landlady at the time, said Kwong Kau told her that he wanted a place to spend time with his wife after retiring. He also allegedly claimed that his son, daughter-in-law and their children were returning from Australia and would be living at his Mong Kok home. There was no evidence that either of Kwong’s two sons was living overseas just before their father rented the flat. Hui said Kwong gave her the contact details of his supposed wife, but she subsequently learned from the news that the woman was his mistress. The presiding judge rejected that part of her evidence as hearsay. She also noted that Kwong Kau had specifically asked whether there were surveillance cameras installed inside the flat when he signed the agreement on February 5, 2023. Kwong earlier admitted that he visited a kitchenware supplier in Yau Ma Tei and bought a commercial meat mincer, a 14-by-14-inch soup pot, a wooden chopping board and a frying sieve for HK$8,700 (US$1,110) on February 8. A saleswoman at the shop said he also asked about the price of an industrial-grade bone grinder after buying the mincer, but decided against the purchase upon learning that it cost HK$35,000. Cho Chin-to, who lived at the flat above at the time of the incident, said the flat’s windows were completely sealed between February 15 and 18, and that people outside the premises could not see what happened inside. Cho said he noticed the sound of heavy objects being carried into the flat at around 3pm on February 21, before he heard electric saws and noise that appeared to come from renovation work. He added that a “very nice aroma” resembling a typical radish and carrot soup came out of the ground-floor flat at around 7pm and lingered for a long time that night. The court heard Choi’s head was found in a large soup pot that also contained pieces of cooked carrot and radish, while her two legs and part of her pelvis and spine were found inside a refrigerator. Senior government chemist Dr Tam Cheok-ning said he found a cut mark on the spine that was consistent with the blade of one of two electric saws found in the flat. Tam also opined that the two boxes found inside the premises were the same ones the defendants allegedly used to carry Choi’s body. Prosecutors said the alleged murder arose from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so that he could keep it for himself. The trial heard Choi covered the entirety of the flat’s HK$60 million purchase price when Kwong bought the flat on her behalf in 2019. Property agent Marco Wong Tak-sing said Kwong pocketed HK$6.97 million in cash rebate and paid HK$3.09 million in stamp duty for the purchase, but he was unsure whether he settled the sum using his own money. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, previously alleged that the Kwong family had been living off her family’s wealth in the lead-up to her daughter’s killing. But Choi’s former chauffeur, Chin Kei-shun, said Anthony Kwong appeared to have given HK$600,000 to Choi when she was having financial difficulties in 2022. Chan Leong-hang, an employee of Aristo Watch & Jewellery in Tsim Sha Tsui, also said Alex Kwong had asked for part of his proceeds from selling luxury watches to the shop to go to his former partner. Tam, the forensic scientist, is expected to continue his oral testimony when the trial resumes next week.

title: 16,000 sign up for exam to drive taxis or ride-hailing cars in Hong Kong

Speaking on a radio programme on Saturday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the allocation arrangement for the 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits would be announced in November, with the government considering increasing the odds for certain drivers in the lottery draw. “We are pleased to see the enthusiastic response to the joint examination....
content: About 16,000 Hong Kong residents have signed up for a joint exam to drive taxis or ride-hailing cars, the transport chief has said. Speaking on a radio programme on Saturday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the allocation arrangement for the 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits would be announced in November, with the government considering increasing the odds for certain drivers in the lottery draw. “We are pleased to see the enthusiastic response to the joint examination. We’ve been considering how to make the best use of the quota of 10,000 permits to ensure they can be given to those who are genuinely dedicated and capable of providing ride-hailing services,” she said. “Making early preparations, such as signing up for or completing the examination, reflects their genuine commitment to taking part early in providing point-to-point services … We hope that within the lottery system, these individuals can be given higher odds of being selected.” The minister said the government was also considering giving higher odds to those who had owned a private vehicle for a certain period, such as a year. Many young people were providing ride-hailing services as a part-time job and the system would not exclude them, she added. Hong Kong recently passed legislation to regulate local ride-hailing services, capping the total number of vehicle permits at 10,000. The new rules require residents to first pass an assessment to apply for either a taxi-driving licence or a ride-hailing permit, while existing cab drivers can apply for the permit directly without taking the test. Ride-hailing platform operators are also required to obtain dedicated licenses, with applications to close on October 30. Chan said the pass rate of the exam was more than 60 per cent, which showed that the prospective drivers were taking the test seriously. She said the government expected to announce the first batch of licensed operators by the end of November at the earliest. “Through this exercise, we hope to attract capable, experienced platform operators to set up and run their businesses in Hong Kong,” she said. “Most importantly, they must be committed to establishing a local presence with their own dedicated teams, while aligning with the government’s policy of enabling ride-hailing services and taxis to coexist and complement one another. “We will also evaluate the passenger experience, such as waiting times and the mechanism of assigning vehicles … to select what best meets the needs of the public, while offering diverse options to foster healthy competition. Separately, Chan said the Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme, which was launched Friday last week had received 32 registrations so far. The first batch of five yachts that sailed to Hong Kong on October 16 stayed in the city for three to four days, docking at either yacht clubs or designated government berthing areas, she added. The five vessels included a superyacht about 100 feet long, Chan said. The minister said some visitors chose to remain on the yachts, but others stayed in hotels and went ashore to sightsee and shop, visiting Stanley, Central and theme parks. “I believe the scheme opens up a new travel model for our tourism and retail economy,” she said. More than 300 mainland Chinese yacht masters had qualified to navigate Hong Kong waters, she noted. To enable more yacht masters to participate, the Marine Department would commission local training institutions to open online courses, the minister said.

title: Hong Kong customs seizes 600 million illicit cigarettes in first 9 months of 2026
description: Hong Kong customs officers seized 600 million illicit cigarette sticks in the first three quarters of this year, the department chief has said, as he revealed plans to roll out more advanced contraband detection equipment. Commissioner of Customs and Excise Chan Tsz-tat told a radio programme on Saturday that the seizures in the first nine months this year nearly matched the 2025 total. He said that of the 600 million sticks seized, 200 million were destined for other locations but were...
content: Hong Kong customs officers seized 600 million illicit cigarette sticks in the first three quarters of this year, the department chief has said, as he revealed plans to roll out more advanced contraband detection equipment. Commissioner of Customs and Excise Chan Tsz-tat told a radio programme on Saturday that the seizures in the first nine months this year nearly matched the 2025 total. He said that of the 600 million sticks seized, 200 million were destined for other locations but were intercepted in Hong Kong after customs received intelligence. “We have around 16,000 cases of illicit cigarette seizures that involved passengers who did not declare they were carrying over 19 sticks of cigarettes,” Chan said. The cases were among 18,000 involving illicit cigarettes that customs detected from January to September. No serious drug offences occurred at the revamped Huanggang Port since it opened last Monday, the commissioner added. When asked whether customs operations at the border crossing were smooth following long queues amid crowd surges over the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend, the customs chief said both passenger and cargo clearances were steady. “The bottleneck was not at customs checks. Customs clearance hall operations were quite smooth,” Chan said. At the revamped checkpoint, vehicle clearance is handled through a “joint one-stop” lane. Drivers first pass through a customs front kiosk before supplying their identity and biometric data at a machine that shares the information with five government departments, including customs. Should customs checks be deemed necessary, drivers are notified at the customs front kiosk to drive to a separate clearance hall for checks. The department has reassigned workers from other border checkpoints, cancelled employee leave and hired a small number of retired staff to help man the newly opened land boundary checkpoint. “As more people cross the border, our workload will only increase. Adding manpower may not be the only way to cope,” Chan said. The customs chief said the department would turn to technology to introduce more advanced equipment to alleviate manpower pressure. This would include introducing active millimetre wave detectors, a device to scan for contraband items hidden on a person’s body, at more land checkpoints in the future. The detector uses a wave that is not invasive to the body and may reduce the need for body searches on passengers, according to Chan. With the unprecedented “joint clearance” system, officials earlier said processing time at the revamped Huanggang crossing could be cut to five minutes from about 30 minutes. Hong Kong residents who hold a valid mainland Chinese travel permit can use their Hong Kong ID cards interchangeably at the joint clearance channel for both outbound and inbound trips. The crossing is expected to be able to handle up to 300,000 travellers a day. The Immigration Department said it expected about 100,000 people to use Huanggang Port daily during initial operations. It can also handle 15,000 vehicles a day.
