content: A cryptocurrency trading platform on Hong Kong and Canadian regulators’ alert lists has opened an office in the city, prompting experts to urge closer scrutiny of how such firms promote themselves without undermining an open business environment. Experts told the South China Morning Post that inclusion on a regulator’s alert list did not necessarily mean a company had broken the law. But they urged authorities to step up oversight of how such firms marketed regulated financial products. Polar Tensor, a cryptocurrency investment platform that said it held company registrations in seven jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, Panama and the US states of Montana and Wyoming, opened an office at One Hysan Avenue in Causeway Bay in August. A source told the SCMP that the platform was being monitored by authorities. The firm has been on the alert list of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) since early August. It also appears on investment caution lists issued by regulators in the Canadian provinces of British Columbia, Quebec and Alberta. The SFC has classified Polar Tensor as a suspicious virtual asset trading platform, saying the firm and its associated websites were not licensed to conduct regulated activities in the city. An SFC spokesman declined to comment beyond the information published on the regulator’s website. The regulator said on its website that its alert list included entities that were unlicensed in Hong Kong and believed to be targeting local investors or claiming an association with the city. Hong Kong has a licensing regime for stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency pegged to assets such as the United States dollar. Investing through a cryptocurrency platform that is not licensed in the city is not itself illegal. However, it is illegal to offer unlicensed stablecoins to retail investors in Hong Kong or actively market them to the public. The SCMP visited Polar Tensor’s office twice in August, including for its opening event, and spoke to people who said they worked with the organisation. Posts on Polar Tensor’s Telegram channel showed that the platform organised three days of events in Hong Kong in August. These included a seminar and gala dinner at a five-star hotel, followed by an office opening party, another dinner and a junk party. At the office opening, a staff member said the premises were for “appointments” but declined to explain what these involved. He described those attending as “members” of the platform rather than clients. The office was sparsely furnished, with rows of tables set up for the opening party. It was closed when the SCMP visited again later in August. Polar Tensor describes itself on its website as an “advanced AI-powered trading platform”. Documents seen by the SCMP showed that a German citizen established a company called Polar Tensor LAB in Hong Kong last year, with a registered address in Sheung Wan. During the SCMP’s visit to Polar Tensor’s Causeway Bay office in October, the doors were locked with no one answering. A security guard at One Hysan Avenue said that she had not seen anyone at the office for the past two months. Polar Tensor’s registered entity in Hong Kong remains active as of October, the SCMP has learned. Lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong said inclusion on a regulator’s alert list did not mean a platform had broken the law. But he urged authorities to do more to develop regulations governing how firms selling regulated financial products, such as cryptocurrencies, could promote themselves. “Setting up an office in Hong Kong itself does not offend the law, but opening an office in Hong Kong to sell these products, they would need to register with the Securities and Futures Commission,” he said. Ng, who is also a technology entrepreneur, urged law enforcement agencies to go beyond issuing alerts about suspicious platforms and firms. He also called on authorities to consider whether social media platforms should bear some responsibility for the content promoted on their services. Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung said inclusion on an alert list was not in itself grounds for arrest, but suspicions about a platform’s operations or business should prompt proactive investigations. Li, who is also an investor, said common legal violations involving firms offering unlicensed financial products included actively promoting them to the public or soliciting money from users. But he said public promotion could be difficult to define, as organisations holding invitation-only events could argue they were not promoting themselves to the wider public. Acknowledging the difficulty of balancing an open business environment with crime prevention, Li said authorities could strengthen due diligence to prevent suspicious businesses from gaining access to the public or appearing to have official endorsement. “For example, I think rentals of major convention venues or advertisements in MTR stations need to be checked,” he said. Responding to a SCMP inquiry, a police spokesman said the force had received no reports concerning Polar Tensor. “If we discover criminal elements, we will follow up solemnly and in accordance with the law,” he said.

title: Why Hong Kong should rethink premiums for private recreation clubs
description: Private recreation leases have a long and contentious history in Hong Kong. Complaints about the inequity of granting land leases to private clubs at a nominal premium for the exclusive enjoyment of a small number of members have been raised many times. This issue is increasingly pressing. Twenty-seven sites are involved and almost all the leases for these sites are set for renewal next year. In response to this perceived inequality, the government reviewed its policy for clubs with private...
content: Private recreation leases have a long and contentious history in Hong Kong. Complaints about the inequity of granting land leases to private clubs at a nominal premium for the exclusive enjoyment of a small number of members have been raised many times. This issue is increasingly pressing. Twenty-seven sites are involved and almost all the leases for these sites are set for renewal next year. In response to this perceived inequality, the government reviewed its policy for clubs with private recreation leases in 2018. The public consultation found general support for the clubs, citing their contributions to sports development and promotion, ethnic harmony, attracting foreign talent, encouraging economic development and more. The review ultimately agreed and recommended retaining the clubs. National sports associations (NSAs) said during the consultation that they were frequent users of sports clubs’ facilities for squad training, league competitions and major international events. They also said club facilities helped bridge the gap between public facilities provided by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department and the top training facilities of the Hong Kong Sports Institute. A reform policy based on opening up clubs to use by non-members was eventually accepted as the way forward. Changes required the clubs to provide greater public access to their facilities. A minimum of 30 per cent of sports facility capacity must be allocated for use by eligible outside bodies such as schools. Clubs must also partner with NSAs to organise sports programmes with a minimum of 240 programme hours per month being for individual members of the public. Several sports clubs in the city have existed for more than a hundred years, and part of their legacy is the development of a sports culture in Hong Kong society. Many players, coaches and administrators have learned through sports promoted by these clubs. The problem is that the private recreation lease conditions are restrictive. Only not-for-profit organisations can hold a lease, and sale of the site is prohibited. All income generated must be used for developing and operating their sports activities and facilities, and sites can only be used for specified sports and recreational purposes. The only significant income for clubs is generated from the use of facilities, members’ monthly fees and joining fees. Also limiting is the short lease renewal term of 15 years. Such leases have long been extended on payment of a nominal premium of about HK$1,000 (US$127). However, private land holders have paid a commercial premium based on the full market value of the site for leases covering residential, commercial or industrial use. The new policy, in an attempt to be more equitable, requires private recreation lease lots to pay a concessionary premium of one-third of the site’s full market value. A fundamental technical problem is that the constraints imposed in the lease mean there is no commercial value for a private recreation lease. The requirement to open facilities to non-members while being unable to generate a profit further constrains the value of the lot. In professional valuation terms, it is doubtful there will be a positive full market value, so a one-third premium cannot be calculated. The 2018 review provided a rough estimate of premiums. A site with a private recreation lease of about 1 to 2 hectares could have to pay between HK$100 million and HK$200 million for each renewal. In the public consultation, 91 per cent of respondents did not support the premium proposal, saying it would drive up membership fees and make private sports clubs even more exclusive. It appears that the government will charge the premium despite these problems. However, there is a major change which must be considered. In July 2024, the Extension of Government Leases Ordinance came into effect. All existing general-purpose leases will now be automatically extended for 50 years with no additional premium payment. About 2,400 lots which expire up to June 29, 2047, involving from around 150 to 12,500 owners in any particular year, will not pay a premium. On June 30 of that year, leases of around 300,000 lots will all expire, involving more than 1.5 million owners. All will be extended for 50 years without paying a premium. The implications are massive. A fundamental point made in the 2018 consultation was a developer would be granted a land lease of 50 years upon paying a premium at full market value. Under the proposed concessionary premium policy, with a private sports club renewing its lease every 15 years, the total premium paid would amount to 111 per cent of full market value over 50 years. Now, only the 27 sites with private recreation leases will pay a premium and deal with 15-year extensions loaded with conditions. All other leases are being extended for 50 years without a premium. An equitable situation under the new lease extension regime requires private recreation lease lots be treated the same as general-purpose lots and extended for 50 years without paying a premium. The administration should review the need for a premium and at least extend the term for these leases to the same as for community organisations. To be equitable, clubs with private recreation leases should be offered an extension without the payment of a premium.

title: Hong Kong private secondary sector expands as local universities’ reputation grows
description: The number of private secondary schools in Hong Kong has risen by more than half in five years as demand for alternative curricula grows and new operators seek to attract families drawn by the city’s highly ranked universities, education authorities and principals have said. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, the number of private secondary institutions increased from 16 to 25, a jump of 56.3 per cent, Education Bureau figures show. Leaders at schools offering alternative curriculum pathways said that...
content: The number of private secondary schools in Hong Kong has risen by more than half in five years as demand for alternative curricula grows and new operators seek to attract families drawn by the city’s highly ranked universities, education authorities and principals have said. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, the number of private secondary institutions increased from 16 to 25, a jump of 56.3 per cent, Education Bureau figures show. Leaders at schools offering alternative curriculum pathways said that more mainland Chinese and overseas students were considering Hong Kong universities due to the institutions’ rising global reputation amid geopolitical concerns. Over the same period, the number of private primary schools also rose from 62 to 65, up 4.8 per cent. Private schools offering a non-local curriculum, which charge between HK$100,000 and HK$300,000 (US$12,800 and US$38,260) a year in tuition fees, do not receive government land grants and have no caps on their ratio of local to non-local students. International schools and private independent schools receive land grants by paying a nominal land premium. International schools typically operate under fixed ratios of non-local students, while private institutions that target local families and offer non local curriculum must enrol at least 70 per cent local students. The Education Bureau pointed to a stronger economy and shifting parental preferences as factors behind the rising number of private schools. “Driven by overall economic growth and a growing demand for diverse educational choices that cater to varying parental preferences for education, the sectors of international schools and other private schools offering a formal curriculum have been steadily expanding,” it said. St Bees (Anchors) Sixth Form College is one new private school entering the sector. It is set to open in West Kowloon’s Coronation Circle for the 2027–28 academic year. David Cardwell, founding co-chair of St Bees and former pro-vice-chancellor at the University of Cambridge, said Hong Kong’s established international curricula give families diverse pathways to maximise their children’s university prospects. “Hong Kong is the perfect place to study – a city of just 7 million people with five universities in the global top 100. It is unprecedented,” he said. St Bees will offer A-level and International General Certificate of Secondary Education programmes. Its registration application is being reviewed by the bureau, with fees to be confirmed upon approval. Cardwell said its graduates were expected to pursue higher education globally, whether at Hong Kong universities, in the United Kingdom or in the United States. The school is targeting 150 students for its first year of operation, with a long-term capacity of 500. “We would like to get 30 to 50 per cent international, if possible, but again we do not want to have a cap,” Cardwell added. School co-chair Danny Wang Tak-chi said it aimed to keep its main cohort local while recruiting internationally, although geopolitical and economic factors would shape its composition in coming years. Wang said recent adjustments to the visa policy for the dependants of arriving talent – including a two-year residency rule before they could apply for subsidised places at local universities – were designed to ensure recipients contribute to society, not to discourage arrivals. “The trend of people coming to Hong Kong will just keep growing and growing, as Hong Kong becomes a hub for education in Asia,” he said. Among the recent graduate cohort at Kellett School, more students, including non-local ones, aspired to enter university in Hong Kong. The international school said 34 of its 85 graduates this year submitted a total of 112 applications to Hong Kong universities, the most in recent years. “One of the reasons for the growth in applicants is that five of the world’s top 100 universities are here in Hong Kong, so the city has a very strong reputation for university education,” school principal and CEO Paul Tough said. “With the government’s intention to develop the university town, the growth is only going to get stronger.” He added the soaring costs of university education in the US and the UK, combined with a geopolitical climate that had parents wanting their children closer to home, were driving more families towards Hong Kong institutions. The school, which was established in 1976, opened its Sixth Form Centre at the Bay Hub, a commercial building in Kowloon Bay in August. The centre can accommodate 240 students, with 225 currently enrolled. The annual tuition fee for Sixth Form is HK$279,100. As an international school offering the A-level curriculum, Kellett maintains a 70:30 ratio of non-local to local students.

title: URA tells owners to avoid hiring lift company at centre of fire safety probe
description: Hong Kong’s Urban Renewal Authority has advised property owners under a subsidy scheme against hiring a contractor that failed to install fire safety components in lifts at hundreds of buildings, saying it had “lost confidence” in the company. The move came a day after the government suspended the performance rating for Taizoom Elevator, which was found to have failed to install required fire-resistant door frame components at 338 buildings as inspections of its work across the city are carried...
content: Hong Kong’s Urban Renewal Authority has advised property owners under a subsidy scheme against hiring a contractor that failed to install fire safety components in lifts at hundreds of buildings, saying it had “lost confidence” in the company. The move came a day after the government suspended the performance rating for Taizoom Elevator, which was found to have failed to install required fire-resistant door frame components at 338 buildings as inspections of its work across the city are carried out. Industry professionals have urged the government to step up routine inspections of lifts and called on authorities to assist the management of buildings that had signed contracts with the company and had been waiting for work to begin. “In view of the serious failures involved when Taizoom Elevator replaced lifts for multiple housing estates and buildings, the Urban Renewal Authority (URA) has lost confidence in its services,” a spokesman said in a reply to the South China Morning Post on Friday. “Therefore [the URA] does not recommend that property owners select Taizoom as the engineering contractor for the Lift Modernisation Subsidy Scheme.” The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department launched its inspections on October 15 after it was discovered the contractor had installed fire-resistant doors without the required frame components at two estates. The components prevent flames and smoke from entering the lift shaft in the event of a fire. The department has also ordered lift companies to check their installations going back a decade and submit reports. The department said on Thursday that it had suspended the regular rating of the company’s performance due to “serious failures” of its lift installation works. Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan called on the government to set up a statutory body to oversee building repairs and step up routine inspections. “The authority could act as an independent third party to monitor building maintenance and conduct spot checks to assist property owners,” Fong said. Former lawmaker Doreen Kong Yuk-foon, a lawyer by training, said in a social media post on Thursday that she had noted concerns from property owners who had signed contracts with Taizoom but were still waiting for the work to begin. Kong added that owners had lost confidence in the company and were questioning whether the URA and authorities would offer help. Police arrested a Taizoom director and two registered lift engineers last Friday, a source said. Hong Kong had 73,393 lifts as of February, according to official information.

title: Hong Kong Legco to review tighter rules on access to land records amid concerns
description: Hong Kong’s legislature will set up a subcommittee to examine proposed restrictions on access to land records following widespread public concern. At a Legislative Council House Committee meeting on Friday, lawmakers endorsed establishing the subcommittee to study proposed requirements and procedures under the Land Titles Regulation. The move came after some legislators and the Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary...
content: Hong Kong’s legislature will set up a subcommittee to examine proposed restrictions on access to land records following widespread public concern. At a Legislative Council House Committee meeting on Friday, lawmakers endorsed establishing the subcommittee to study proposed requirements and procedures under the Land Titles Regulation. The move came after some legislators and the Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation – including the Land Titles Regulation covering land record search arrangements – at Legco for negative vetting. Under negative vetting, subsidiary legislation is first gazetted and then scrutinised by lawmakers later. Most of the provisions, including the tightened search arrangements, are scheduled to take effect in the first half of next year. On Friday, Legco legal adviser Timothy Tso recommended setting up a subcommittee on subsidiary legislation, noting that his team was still examining the details of the changes. At least five legislators raised their hands in support, including Election Committee constituency members Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan, Andrew Lam Siu-lo and Thomas So Shiu-tsung, alongside Christine Fong Kwok-shan and Mark Chong Ho-fung. “I also have concerns over whether referencing specific cases during legislative questioning could inadvertently breach the law [if my team has conducted land searches],” Roundtable lawmaker Chong told the South China Morning Post. He added that when lawmakers conducted research or gathered real-life cases to address policy issues or assist enforcement – such as targeting public housing tenants who illegally own private property – there were fears of unwittingly crossing legal boundaries. He noted that while the public previously relied on the media to investigate such matters, uncertainty remained over how individuals or lawmakers should proceed if they performed searches themselves. He also said that no timeline has been set for when the subcommittee would meet, though the Legco secretariat was expected to issue a notice inviting interested lawmakers to join. The new search arrangements represent the government’s latest step to tighten public access to information, following similar restrictions imposed on the vehicle and companies registries. The government has maintained that the city currently does not restrict who can access land records and argued that the new arrangements aim to protect privacy while maintaining system transparency and efficiency. Under the proposed regime, applicants must select from nine specified purposes to obtain essential property information, such as the names of current and former owners, purchase prices, registration dates, encumbrances, application forms and supporting documents for active entries. These specific purposes include property valuation, due diligence for transactions, building management, legal proceedings, conducting academic and market research and conducting inspections in the public interest. Applications filed on public interest grounds will be assessed individually by the registrar, who will consider whether the societal benefit outweighs privacy rights and whether the documents might be misused. Meanwhile, access to historical records – such as past property transfers or complied building orders – will be restricted to 15 categories of applicants. While the list does not explicitly include journalists, it permits applications from individuals declaring a public interest purpose, current or former property owners, and professionals. Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan said she backed forming a subcommittee because many details remained unresolved, adding that the government needed to clarify the criteria and definition used to approve applications. The Hong Kong Journalists Association previously criticised the proposals, saying authorities had failed to justify the changes or consult the public, while warning that the restrictions would undermine society’s ability to monitor the property market. Additional reporting by Ng Kang-chung

title: Hong Kong sauce maker to close after 90 years, making way for Northern Metropolis

We will close permanently after selling through all...
content: One of Hong Kong’s last traditional sauce makers is to cease operations, ending its 90-year legacy, after authorities cleared land at its Kwu Tung factory on Friday. Established in 1936, Kui Lee Sauce and Preserved Fruit confirmed to the South China Morning Post that it would close down once its remaining inventory at its shop in Wan Chai was sold. “Our factory in Kwu Tung has halted production, and all remaining stock is at our retail shop. We will close permanently after selling through all inventory,” an employee of Kui Lee Sauce told an SCMP reporter, who posed as a customer. As a time-honoured Hong Kong brand, Kui Lee has been passed down through three generations and is known for being “100 per cent made in Hong Kong”. Having moved from Kowloon City to Kwu Tung in the 1960s, the factory has insisted on making soy sauce and vinegar using traditional sun-drying methods. Its soy sauce has long been renowned in Hong Kong and has been exported to other markets in recent years, including Taiwan. On Friday morning, more than 30 security guards and police officers were deployed to the Kui Lee sauce factory and Tong Kok Village in Kwu Tung to execute eviction notices. The area is subject to a land resumption operation under the government’s Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into a technology hub and serve as an economic engine. People wearing vests marked “NDA” – short for the New Development Areas under the Northern Metropolis strategy – were seen entering the sauce factory and spoke with the owner in a room for more than 30 minutes. More than 12 security guards stood outside, while another dozen cordoned off the entrance and locked the steel gate. Most of the guards left the factory at around 12.10pm after a notice was posted on the gate stating that the site had been taken over by the government. November 6 will be the final date for water and electricity supply and clearing items at the site. Three security guards still stationed at the entrance were allowing workers temporary access to the factory through the gate. The factory representatives declined to comment on the clearance. The Lands Department’s clearance operation faced pushback from villagers on the site, many of whom had lived there for half a century. A handful of residents were packing up the last of their belongings in homes they had lived in for decades, among them the Chan family. “After all, we’ve lived here for more than 50 years. I feel reluctant to leave,” said Chan, a retiree in her seventies, standing in front of her house and wiping away tears with a towel. “This is half a century of memories.” Her son, in his forties and born and raised in the house, was wrapping up a final batch of daily necessities with his wife. “We were told the exact date of the land clearance not long ago, and our electricity was cut two days ago,” Chan’s daughter-in-law said. “I was washing clothes when the power went off, and we could only use a flashlight to pack our things at night.” She added that the water pipes had been destroyed by someone in recent days. “We used to have a big family living here together for a whole life. Now we’re all separated,” she said. Nearby, dozens of security guards and lands officials had surrounded another resident’s home and were preparing to lock it up, but a dispute broke out when the owner said they had not finished packing. Staff prevented people from filming or getting closer to the site, citing “security concerns”.

content: Hong Kong recorded its highest-ever temperature for the traditional Chinese calendar’s “Frost” solar term on Friday, with the weather forecaster warning of a very dry weekend ahead. The Hong Kong Observatory said the temperature at its headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui reached 32.3 degrees Celsius by 3.30pm, the highest of the day. Frost, the 18th of the Chinese lunisolar calendar’s 24 solar terms, began on October 23. The terms mark natural phenomena and seasonal changes. Temperatures in the city have topped 30 degrees over the past few weeks, partly because of the effects of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming. The forecaster warned the public to prepare for a “fine and very dry” weekend, with a considerable difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures. Humidity fell to 39 per cent on Friday and was forecast to drop further to 35 per cent on Saturday. Earth science expert Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen earlier explained that a “super” El Nino would make the city hotter, bringing more heat and increased evaporation. Tai expected temperatures to fall gradually as winter approached but said the city would remain warm because of the lingering effects of the “super” El Nino.

title: Hong Kong constable paralysed in 2005 knife attack laid to rest with full honours
description: Hong Kong’s top government officials and police officers paid their final respects on Friday to a former constable who died 21 years after being left paralysed in an attack while on duty. Jacky Chu Chun-kwok, who died last month aged 52, was laid to rest following a service at the Universal Funeral Parlour in Hung Hom at 10.30am, which was attended by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung. The mood was sombre as family members, friends, colleagues and...
content: Hong Kong’s top government officials and police officers paid their final respects on Friday to a former constable who died 21 years after being left paralysed in an attack while on duty. Jacky Chu Chun-kwok, who died last month aged 52, was laid to rest following a service at the Universal Funeral Parlour in Hung Hom at 10.30am, which was attended by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung. The mood was sombre as family members, friends, colleagues and senior officials bid farewell to Chu. Holding Chu’s portrait, his wife, Chu Choi Yin-ping, wept alongside their daughter, Michelle, as they stepped out of the funeral parlour. Outside, uniformed officers saluted the late constable, while members of the public lined the streets to mourn him. Other senior government officials paying homage included Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming, Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan and former police chief Dick Lee Ming-kwai. Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king and Executive Council convenor Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee were also present. After the service, dozens of officers provided an honour guard escort as the cortege travelled to Cheung Sha Wan Police Station for a farewell ceremony at about 11am. Chu’s coffin, draped with the Hong Kong flag, was carried by officers and placed in a black police van converted into a hearse. At the police station, several officers bowed three times before the hearse. Shortly after noon, the hearse left for Gallant Garden at Wo Hop Shek Cemetery, where Chu was laid to rest. The dedicated memorial and burial ground within the cemetery is reserved for civil servants who have died in the line of duty. Chu died last month after spending 21 years paralysed and bedridden. On the morning of July 19, 2005, he was critically injured while on solo patrol when a man stabbed him in the neck with a 15cm-long (six-inch) knife. The attacker, Liu Chi-yung, had been carrying the knife with the intention of robbing pedestrians when Chu stopped him for an identity check outside the Po On Road Municipal Services Building in Cheung Sha Wan. When the then 30-year-old constable grew suspicious and confronted him, Liu pulled out the knife, stabbed Chu in the neck and fled. Chu pursued the attacker but eventually collapsed from excessive blood loss. Oxygen deprivation to the brain left him completely paralysed and in a vegetative state. He was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) in 2006.

title: Typhoon Champi disrupts more than 70 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan
description: More than 70 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan have been cancelled as Typhoon Champi approaches the island ahead of a possible landfall later on Friday. As of noon on Friday, more than 30 flights between the city and Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport had been cancelled, according to a South China Morning Post check of the Hong Kong airport’s website. Nine outbound flights to Kaohsiung International Airport and Taichung International Airport were also cancelled. The affected services were...
content: More than 70 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan have been cancelled as Typhoon Champi approaches the island ahead of a possible landfall later on Friday. As of noon on Friday, more than 30 flights between the city and Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport had been cancelled, according to a South China Morning Post check of the Hong Kong airport’s website. Nine outbound flights to Kaohsiung International Airport and Taichung International Airport were also cancelled. The affected services were operated by Cathay Pacific Airways and its low-cost arm, HK Express, as well as Hong Kong Airlines, Starlux Airlines, China Airlines and Eva Air. More than 30 inbound flights from Taiwan were also cancelled as Champi’s rainbands swept across the island. Torrential downpours and fierce gusts have been forecast. Greater Bay Airlines also announced flight adjustments on Friday night. Departure for flight HB710 from Hong Kong to Taipei was rescheduled from 11.55pm on Friday to 6.05am on Saturday, while the return flight, HB711, would depart Taipei at 9am on Saturday instead of 2.55am. In addition, flight HB336 from Hong Kong to Okinawa was delayed from 8.15am to 11.45am on Saturday, with the return flight, HB337, pushed back from 12.50pm to 4.20pm. Despite the severe weather, a Greater Bay Airlines flight to Taipei and an HK Express flight to Kaohsiung took off on Friday morning. Both flights landed safely in Taiwan, though passengers described the landings as tumultuous, adding that travellers applauded and marvelled at the pilots’ skill. “Greater Bay Airline pilots are so solid, we almost couldn’t land and almost had to abort and return to Hong Kong,” wrote Threads user momok_2777. In a video posted to the platform, visibility outside the cabin window appeared extremely low as rain pelted against the glass and strong gusts caused the aircraft to sway. Another video showing the HK Express landing in Kaohsiung captured the plane swaying from side to side during its approach before touching down safely. “This is the only flight that Hong Kong Express did not cancel today,” wrote Threads user plli.0811, who was on board. “They live up to the reputation of being ‘fighter jets’.” A Greater Bay Airline flight bound for Taipei Friday night was delayed to Saturday morning, while HK Express flights to Kaohsiung and Taichung on Friday evening were pushed back to Saturday morning. Cathay Pacific, HK Express and Hong Kong Airlines said they would waive ticket change fees for affected passengers. At noon, Champi – whose name means frangipani in Khmer – was centred about 290km (180 miles) southeast of Taipei. The storm has already caused one death. The Hong Kong Observatory has forecast it to move north-northwest at about 15 km/h over the seas east of Taiwan. Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said the storm’s 320km radius would cover most of the island on Friday. Its peak impact was expected to last through the night before it moved away towards southern Japan late on Saturday. Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan’s 22 counties and cities on Friday, and Taiwan’s stock exchange, one of the largest in the world, was also closed.

title: 2 women arrested over alleged child abuse after girl, 11, posts plea for help
description: Two women have been arrested on suspicion of child abuse in Hong Kong after an 11-year-old girl posted videos on social media pleading for help. Police arrested the girl’s 61-year-old grandmother and a 43-year-old domestic helper in Wong Tai Sin on Friday on suspicion of ill-treatment or neglect by those in charge of a child or young person. The girl, found with red and swollen limbs, was sent to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei on Thursday and later transferred to the Hong Kong Children’s...
content: Two women have been arrested on suspicion of child abuse in Hong Kong after an 11-year-old girl posted videos on social media pleading for help. Police arrested the girl’s 61-year-old grandmother and a 43-year-old domestic helper in Wong Tai Sin on Friday on suspicion of ill-treatment or neglect by those in charge of a child or young person. The girl, found with red and swollen limbs, was sent to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei on Thursday and later transferred to the Hong Kong Children’s Hospital in Kowloon Bay, according to police. The arrests followed the circulation of two video clips recorded by the child at home. In the first clip, filmed covertly, a man is heard aggressively shouting and insulting a sobbing child in a flat, hurling profanities and abusive phrases such as “even a kindergarten kid is smarter than you” and “you are just like your terrible mother”. In the second video clip, the terrified girl is seen seeking refuge inside a room, pleading to the camera: “I need some help, my family is going crazy.” She is interrupted by a woman aggressively pounding on the door and screaming at her to shut up, leaving the girl trembling and weeping. Police said they received a referral from the Social Welfare Department about suspected ill-treatment of a child by family members. The offence carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment under the Offences Against the Person Ordinance. The suspects are in police custody as the investigation continues. In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, the Social Welfare Department said that social workers were following up on the case. The department said it immediately contacted the girl’s family and arranged a medical assessment for her. “The social workers will maintain contact with the family and conduct case conferences with professionals to comprehensively assess the family’s situation and the child’s welfare needs,” it said. The department added that support would be provided based on factors such as the child’s safety, physical and mental development, the carer’s capabilities and the family situation. The SCMP has reached out to the Education Bureau for comment. Our Lady’s College in Wong Tai Sin said the girl was one of its students and acknowledged the widespread attention the clips had attracted, promising to take the matter “very seriously”. The school said it learned of the situation earlier and was ensuring the girl’s privacy was being protected. “In handling all student incidents, the school will process and follow up in accordance with established mechanisms and regulations as quickly as possible to protect students’ safety and interests, and to ensure healthy growth,” it said. Additional reporting by Lo Hoi-ying and Ambrose Li

title: Hong Kong security chief vows accountability, reforms ahead of Tai Po fire report
description: Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department will bear “ultimate responsibility” for following up on fire safety complaints across the city, the security chief has said, as an independent committee report is expected to identify the department as among those responsible for last year’s deadly Tai Po blaze. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung made the pledge on Friday, a day after the judge-led committee submitted its final report to the government. The minister said a series of legal reforms...
content: Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department will bear “ultimate responsibility” for following up on fire safety complaints across the city, the security chief has said, as an independent committee report is expected to identify the department as among those responsible for last year’s deadly Tai Po blaze. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung made the pledge on Friday, a day after the judge-led committee submitted its final report to the government. The minister said a series of legal reforms would be rolled out alongside administrative measures to address fire safety shortcomings. A source earlier said the report had identified failings by the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit that contributed to the blaze. During rounds of public evidential hearings, counsel for the committee criticised the Fire Services Department for failing to detect that the fire alarm system at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po had been deactivated and for avoiding its statutory duties. Tang said the government had taken steps to address the shortcomings and would hold those responsible fully accountable. “Over the past year, we have implemented many administrative measures on [handling] large-scale fires and fire alarm device malfunctions. A series of legal reforms will also be rolled out,” he told a radio programme. “The Fire Services Department has admitted its ‘ultimate responsibility’, which means when anyone files a complaint about fire [safety] to the department, even if it’s not directly under our purview, we will follow up until another department takes over.” Fire services falls under the Security Bureau. Following the blaze, the department stepped up inspections of fire services installations and proposed legislative amendments to strengthen regulation. Asked whether he or his colleagues were psychologically prepared to be held accountable for the fire, Tang cited Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s pledge that “anyone found to be responsible will be held accountable”. The fire on November 26 last year killed 168 people and displaced about 5,000 others. The South China Morning Post earlier learned that a redacted version of the report could be made public as early as next week. Legislator Chan Hok-fung, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s security panel, agreed that the department should be able to take on the additional responsibility. “The ‘ultimate responsibility’ move in a sense is not to ask the fire services to do the work of other departments as well,” Chan said. “The aim is to close any possible loopholes that may not be fully covered under the present system.” Operationally, the move will require fire officers to actively investigate and track every complaint about fire safety received by the department, even if the issue falls outside its direct jurisdiction, to ensure the matter is monitored. “This might put some pressure on the resources of the fire services. But it is an important step in the right direction,” said Chan, of the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong. However, a former fire services officer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in line with government policy, expressed concern that the “ultimate responsibility” arrangement could overload the department. “When they talk about ultimate responsibility, how much more resources and power are they going to give the Fire Services Department to do it properly?” he said. The department revealed earlier this month that none of the 3,600 old buildings of six storeys or under had completed the installation of smart fire alarm systems they were authorised to install since late April, partly because landlords failed to reach a consensus on how to carry out the work. The former officer said this showed the department needed more resources. “And it is flatly unfair to ask the fire services to do the work that is under the jurisdiction of another department,” he said. Citing rooftop huts as an example, he added: “Many are illegal structures, but the Buildings Department does not take action to clear them. They pose fire hazards. So, what should the fire services do? Should it prosecute the Buildings Department to press it to take action?” Separately, Tang addressed the chaos at the revamped Huanggang Port during the Chung Yeung Festival holiday, with passengers saying they queued for hours in the immigration hall. The minister attributed the situation to the high passenger volume and many people failing to register for the e-channel service. “Although over 300,000 registered for e-channel service, most passengers using the port did not sign up for it, which means those who registered were not using the checkpoint,” he said. Tang added that the situation eventually eased due to improved crowd management strategies and the provision of on-site help for e-channel registration. He added that Hong Kong would remain vigilant ahead of the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in mid-November, as visits by political leaders would inevitably pose security risks to the city. Authorities were preparing for potential attempts to enter mainland China via Hong Kong to carry out dangerous and illegal activities, as well as drone flights from the city aimed at disrupting the summit, he added. They were also preparing for possible visits to Hong Kong by leaders or dignitaries, he said, adding he expected any impact on the public to be limited. Drawing comparisons with social unrest in France, Tang said Hong Kong was capable of managing similar situations, but he urged the public to remain vigilant even in peaceful times and think critically to avoid being incited, given potential national security risks.

content: The annual Hong Kong Wine and Dine Festival later this month promises more booths and longer hours to help attract over 168,000 visitors. The South China Morning Post unpacks what is on offer so you can enjoy the event to the fullest. 1. What is the festival and when is it open? Organised by the Tourism Board under the theme “Taste the World’s Best,” the festival will be held from October 29 to November 1 at the Central Harbourfront, opening at 7.30pm on the first day and 1pm on the following three days. For the first time, on October 30 and 31, the event will extend its opening hours until 1am. 2. What’s new at the Wine and Dine Festival this year? The four-day festival will be larger than last year’s, with more than 340 booths, an increase of over 10 per cent. The festival footprint will also be extended to Tamar Park. The event will feature guided wine walks for the first time, where participants can experience more than 20 masterclasses led by experts who will guide them through wine tastings and share professional insights. The Tourism Board will subsequently launch “Hong Kong Gourmet Month” in November, featuring limited-edition dishes and dining discounts throughout the month. Visitors to the Wine and Dine Festival can present their ticket stubs to enjoy exclusive offers at selected restaurants, retailers and business associations. 3. What are the culinary highlights and special tasting events? Highlights include the Grand Wine Pavilion, a designated area for premium wine, the Tasting Room restaurant featuring five renowned chefs, and the Hotel Boulevard showcasing signature dishes from 26 hotels. The Grand Wine Pavilion will bring together fine wines and delicacies from around 31 countries and regions, including Australia, Canada and South Korea. It will also feature wine selections from top Bordeaux chateaux, including renowned bottles such as Mouton Rothschild Pauillac 1er Cru 1982, a prized wine from one of Bordeaux’s “first growth” estates and the legendary 1982 vintage. At the Tasting Room restaurant, diners can enjoy dishes made by famous chefs including Edward Lee, the Korean-American who made his name in Netflix’s cooking survival show Culinary Class Wars, and Michelin-starred masters including Yoda Chen Zhiping and Thierry Marx who will create a collaborative banquet alongside three other chefs. The event will also feature local “Only in Hong Kong” flavours, including innovative combinations such as black sesame soy milk pudding tart. The Hotel Boulevard will gather chefs from 26 prestigious hotels at the Central Harbourfront, each serving up signature dishes, including Hong Kong-style satay beef bun from Kowloon Shangri-La and 3 Signature Pandan Cake with Coconut Ice Cream from The Fullerton Ocean Park Hotel Hong Kong. 4. What special benefits or exclusive offers are available? Tickets for the festival are HK$40 (US$5.13) per person and HK$20 each for children aged three to 11. Each tasting token costs HK$25. Locals and visitors can purchase a Grand Wine Pass or Tasting Pass via Trip.com at a special discounted price, with complimentary admission included. Grand Wine Pass packages start from just HK$558 (valued at HK$900) and allow visitors to enjoy a wide range of signature activities at the Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival. American Express card members enjoy exclusive benefits, including a special presale price on the Premium Wine Pass and 20 per cent off when adding consumption tokens at the festival.

title: Hong Kong elderly urged to stay indoors as air pollution spikes to serious levels
description: Severe haze in Hong Kong over the past two days has prompted a government warning of serious health risks, with experts urging the elderly and vulnerable to stay indoors until sunset. content: Severe haze in Hong Kong over the past two days has prompted a government warning of serious health risks, with experts urging the elderly and vulnerable to stay indoors until sunset. Air quality health risk levels at some of Hong Kong’s roadside monitoring stations rose on Wednesday and Thursday, with experts attributing the surge to elevated ozone levels caused by sunlight and high temperatures and warning that conditions were likely to persist over the next few days. On Wednesday afternoon, the Air Quality Health Index issued by the Environmental Protection Department reached a “serious” health risk level at its Tuen Mun station, where it remained for two hourly readings. The pollution persisted on Thursday, with Central/Western, Southern, Tsuen Wan, Tuen Mun and Sha Tin stations recording “high” health risk levels at 4pm. An hour later, the Southern station reached a “very high” level. The readings at general and roadside stations fell to low to moderate levels on Friday morning. Ho Kin-fai, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Jockey Club School of Public Health and Primary Care, said light winds had brought pollutants to the city, which, combined with high temperatures and sunlight this week, intensified photochemical smog activity – the major factor leading to the formation of ozone. “Ozone remains the primary reason for the high health risk readings in the past two days, although it has occurred in different locations,” Ho said. “The situation may likely persist over the next few days.” He said elderly and vulnerable people should remain mindful of air quality when the index is at the “high” health risk level. Launched in 2013, the index tells residents of the short-term health risks posed by air pollution. It analyses three-hour average concentrations of four major pollutants, namely ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, and fine particulate matter – PM2.5 and PM10 – on a scale from 1 to 10, as well as 10+. When the health risk level is “high”, the department advises children, the elderly and people with existing heart or respiratory conditions to reduce outdoor physical activity, especially in areas with heavy traffic. They should stay indoors when the index reaches the “serious” level. For healthy adults who want to exercise outdoors, Ho suggested shortening workout durations or running later at night, as ozone levels gradually declined after sunset. Air quality was usually worse in winter compared with other seasons due to meteorological conditions, said Leung Wing-mo, a former assistant director at the Hong Kong Observatory. During winter, the northeast monsoon could bring air pollutants from mainland China over to Hong Kong, Leung said, though he added that air quality in the Pearl River Delta region had improved over the past two decades. Wind speed also played a role, he noted, as stronger winds created turbulence that lifted ground-level pollutants high into the atmosphere. Cold spells influenced by the northeast monsoon also tend to last a few days at a time, meaning conditions may ease periodically, according to Leung. Cooler temperatures were another factor, he said. As cool air near the surface settles in, the denser, cooler air beneath the warmer air leads to a higher probability of “temperature inversion”, slowing the dispersion of pollutants and causing them to accumulate near the ground. Leung said it was challenging to determine whether Tropical Cyclone Champi had affected Hong Kong’s air quality, given the presence of other competing factors. However, he noted that because Champi was a “big and intense typhoon”, its potential effect on Hong Kong through subsiding air could not be ruled out. According to the city’s forecaster, Champi will move towards the seas east of Taiwan on Friday, before it is likely to steer northwards towards Japan and Korea. Under the influence of its subsiding air, weather along the Guangdong coast would remain very hot through the latter half of the week, the forecaster added.

title: How Hong Kong can go from passive trade hub to regional control tower
description: This year has opened a rare window of relative calm in global commerce. On October 8, the World Trade Organization doubled its forecast for global goods trade growth, from 1.9 to 3.9 per cent. The easing of US-China and Europe-China tensions has given open economies some breathing space. Hong Kong has seized the moment. Its exports rose 42.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, with figures from August alone up 53 per cent, driven largely by AI-related equipment and...
content: This year has opened a rare window of relative calm in global commerce. On October 8, the World Trade Organization doubled its forecast for global goods trade growth, from 1.9 to 3.9 per cent. The easing of US-China and Europe-China tensions has given open economies some breathing space. Hong Kong has seized the moment. Its exports rose 42.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, with figures from August alone up 53 per cent, driven largely by AI-related equipment and high-value electronic components. A deeper transformation lurks beneath the headline numbers. Hong Kong is no longer merely a passive trade hub. For decades, its role in global commerce was defined by its position as a buffer in geopolitical cross-currents. The traditional model of “Made in China, shipped via Hong Kong, consumed in the West” made the city a passage point rather than a decision point. The question now is whether Hong Kong can reposition itself as a regional supply-chain management hub linking diverse Asian production networks with Western markets. Three structural shifts are creating this opportunity. First, Hong Kong’s trade is concentrating in high‑value goods. Nearly 68 per cent of exports to the United States through to August were telecoms equipment, computer parts and semiconductors, while re‑exports to mainland China are increasingly dominated by high‑end chips and AI servers. These compact, high‑value products demand fast, secure logistics, an area where Hong Kong’s air freight capacity gives it a distinct edge. Second, Hong Kong’s sourcing base is diversifying across Asia. The share of mainland-origin goods in Hong Kong’s re-exports to the US has fallen from 72.9 per cent in 2020 to 23.8 per cent in the first eight months of 2026. Vietnam has emerged as the largest source, accounting for 42.9 per cent, with India, South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia close behind. Hong Kong is upgrading from a “China window” to a core node in Asia’s production network. Third, offshore trade is rising. Offshore trade now exceeds HK$5 trillion (US$637.1 billion) annually, surpassing traditional re-exports. Increasingly, goods do not physically pass through Hong Kong, yet transactions such as orders, financing, settlement and risk management are completed in the city. The value added is shifting from logistics to finance and compliance. Hong Kong is becoming a hub for “transactional transit”, managing flows of capital and contracts rather than containers. Together, these trends create the basis for Hong Kong to evolve from a conduit for China-centred manufacturing into a control tower for a multi-node, multi-rule supply chain network. The test of that role is most evident in its relationship with the US. It is one of the few economies where the US consistently runs a goods trade surplus, reaching US$28.5 billion in 2025, up 30.2 per cent from the previous year. However, Hong Kong has yet to institutionalise its role as a true control tower. Decisions on order routing, inventory allocation, trade finance, compliance sign-off, currency hedging and contract arbitration remain fragmented. On this test, Hong Kong has assets but not yet an architecture. The policy task is to convert emerging trade patterns into institutionalised decision-making functions. Four pillars define how Hong Kong can turn this into a durable role. First, Hong Kong’s offshore wealth management sector is now the largest in the world, but supply-chain finance – receivables financing, trade settlement, currency hedging – is not yet anchored here at scale. Embedding capital-market capacity into trade finance would move Hong Kong from a transit point to a decision node. The gap is not in capital; it is the trade-finance product architecture that turns capital into working-capital solutions for Asian suppliers. Second, compliance and law. Common law and arbitration give Hong Kong a neutral forum where contracts shaped by both US and Chinese rules can be enforced. Mutual recognition is aspirational, not operational; the task is to build the case law and enforcement practice that make Hong Kong the default venue for cross-regime disputes. Third, digital and logistics. Electronic bills of lading and real-time tracking let Hong Kong manage supply chains even when goods bypass its ports. A data framework accepted by both China and the US remains a long-term goal; meanwhile, Hong Kong can build trusted digital trade infrastructure and pilot data sandboxes with major partners. Fourth, regional headquarters. About 200 US-parented companies maintain regional headquarters in Hong Kong, with another 480 running regional offices. However, presence is not mandate: a firm can keep its office and still route orders, hold inventory and sign off compliance elsewhere. The test of the four pillars is whether those mandates are exercised here. That is the outcome the other three pillars must deliver. As the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit in Shenzhen approaches, Hong Kong must act. This window of calm is a chance to lock in its role as Asia’s supply‑chain control tower. Compliance and law should be the foundation, finance the driver, digital the infrastructure and regional headquarters the visible outcome. If Hong Kong embeds these functions into a coherent strategy, it will move from a passive beneficiary of global trade to an active architect of its future.

title: Hong Kong degree holders’ pay advantage over non-graduates narrows to HK$2,500

content: Fresh Hong Kong graduates are increasingly feeling the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) as they enter the workforce, human resources experts have said, after a survey found the gap between starting salaries for degree holders and sub-degree graduates had narrowed. The results of the latest annual survey by Baptist University showed the gap had narrowed by 17 per cent, or HK$500 (US$63.70), from HK$3,000 in 2025 to HK$2,500 this year. The experts urged the government to adjust its education strategies to account for AI’s effects on the job market while also encouraging students not to treat the technology as a threat. “AI may be one reason behind the narrowing salary gap between degree levels, as some companies are unwilling to pay more for people with higher degrees when AI can help employees handle the same work,” Alexa Chow Yee-ping, managing director of human resources consultancy ACTS Consulting, said. The survey covered more than 270,000 employees at 78 companies in Hong Kong, 38 in Macau and 105 in nine Guangdong province cities. Together with Hong Kong and Macau, those cities form the Greater Bay Area. It also found Hong Kong workers received smaller pay rises this year, at 2.3 per cent compared with 2.5 per cent in 2025, while starting salaries of university graduates showed no clear upward trend. “We expected the results from this period to look better as it covers most of this year’s pay adjustments in January, April and July,” Chow said. “And in the first half of last year, Hong Kong’s performance in GDP growth was relatively strong.” Hong Kong raised its full-year growth forecast for 2026 to between 3.5 and 4.5 per cent from between 2.5 and 3.5 per cent previously after better-than-expected performance in the first half of this year. Chow explained that while starting salaries for bachelor’s degree and sub-degree graduates had drawn closer, the situation varied by sector. “In professional sectors such as healthcare and technology, where demand remains, the threshold will not easily be lowered,” she said. Chow advised students to weigh their interests with practical considerations, in particular, whether the roles they were eyeing were susceptible to AI automation. Labour sector lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, said the government should adjust its education policies in light of the shift. “Hong Kong now has universities of applied sciences. I hope more can be scaled up to train young people for AI-related industries or emerging sectors, so that they can work in the emerging industries in the Northern Metropolis in the future and reduce human resources mismatch,” he said. The Northern Metropolis project, announced in 2021, aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into an engine for economic growth and a housing hub. A separate survey by the non-government Hong Kong Institute of Human Resource Management, released in September, found that local employees received an average pay rise of 2.8 per cent this year. After inflation, the real increase was 1.1 per cent, the lowest since the Covid-19 pandemic that roiled the city from 2020 to 2023. Institute president Ian Choy Jing-man said fresh graduates were likely to feel the impact of slower pay growth most acutely. “Fresh graduates mostly start at the general or supporting staff level, so their salary increments are likely to be on par with that group, which is growing more slowly than some of the other categories we surveyed,” he said. Choy urged young jobseekers to treat AI as a tool rather than a threat. “Learn how to collaborate with it. It’s not your competition. And it’s definitely not stopping you from getting into the job market,” he said. “But if you are equipped with the necessary AI skills, then you will come out on top of the competition.”

title: Hong Kong, Beijing slam UK report’s ‘smears’ over national security law
description: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese authorities have condemned a UK report that said the city’s national security law had further eroded the openness underpinning its success as a financial hub. In a statement issued early on Friday, the Hong Kong government said it had to “refute the untruthful remarks, slanders and smears” about the city in London’s report and reject what it described as an attempt to interfere in its governance through “despicable political manoeuvres”. “The UK government smeared...
content: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese authorities have condemned a UK report that said the city’s national security law had further eroded the openness underpinning its success as a financial hub. In a statement issued early on Friday, the Hong Kong government said it had to “refute the untruthful remarks, slanders and smears” about the city in London’s report and reject what it described as an attempt to interfere in its governance through “despicable political manoeuvres”. “The UK government smeared the Hong Kong national security law, which targets only a very small number of criminals endangering national security … and continued to unscrupulously distort the facts to criticise,” a spokesman said. “This clearly exposes its hypocritical double standards, which are utterly ugly and despicable.” In the United Kingdom’s latest six-month monitoring report on Hong Kong, released on Thursday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was “deeply concerned and disturbed” by the continued imprisonment of former media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying, who was jailed for 20 years over national security offences. “We continue to call for his immediate release and will raise his case consistently as part of our frank and constructive engagement with the Chinese and Hong Kong authorities,” he said. In the report’s foreword, Miliband said Lai’s case, alongside recent developments in the trial of former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung, had reinforced concerns about the “increasingly broad application” of national security legislation. “Since 2020, the Beijing-imposed national security law has restricted rights and freedoms, stifled debate and further diminished the openness that underpinned Hong Kong’s success,” he wrote. Miliband also reaffirmed Britain’s commitment to the British National (Overseas) pathway for Hongkongers. Under the scheme, rolled out after the enactment of the national security law, more than 187,000 people had been issued BN(O) visas since 2021. A spokesman for the Chinese embassy in London hit out at the “irresponsible remarks on Hong Kong affairs” by the UK, which constituted “gross interference” in its internal affairs. “China firmly opposes this and has made solemn representations to the UK,” he said. The spokesman said security and the rule of law were being effectively upheld in the city, while governance efficiency and the business environment had improved. “China urges the UK to abandon its colonial mentality, respect China’s sovereignty and Hong Kong’s rule of law, stop issuing the so-called six-monthly report, and stop interfering in China’s internal affairs and Hong Kong affairs in any way,” he said.

title: Filipinos split on Marcos’ South China Sea handling amid row over Jing Quan’s remarks
description: Filipinos are almost evenly divided over the Marcos administration’s handling of the maritime dispute with China, even as nearly three in four favour diplomacy over confrontation, according to a new survey. That preference has taken on added significance after recent remarks by China’s ambassador to Manila sparked a diplomatic row ahead of November’s Asean summit. The feud underscored the challenge of managing tensions with Beijing, and increasingly hostile rhetoric could make the diplomatic...
content: Filipinos are almost evenly divided over the Marcos administration’s handling of the maritime dispute with China, even as nearly three in four favour diplomacy over confrontation, according to a new survey. That preference has taken on added significance after recent remarks by China’s ambassador to Manila sparked a diplomatic row ahead of November’s Asean summit. The feud underscored the challenge of managing tensions with Beijing, and increasingly hostile rhetoric could make the diplomatic path backed by most Filipinos harder to sustain, analysts say. A nationwide poll of 1,487 Filipino adults, conducted from August 18 to 23 and released on October 20 by Momentum Research, found that 45.2 per cent considered President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration effective in handling tensions in the South China Sea, while 45 per cent disagreed, with the remainder undecided or declining to answer. “Nearly three in four prefer diplomacy over show of strength,” Momentum said. Retired rear admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, a spokesman for the military’s operations in the West Philippine Sea – the eastern parts of the South China Sea that are within Manila’s territorial waters – said the findings reflected the public’s preference for peace. He said the military’s activities were not a “show of strength for aggression”, but part of its constitutional mandate. Retired Supreme Court associate justice Antonio Carpio said “the great majority of Filipinos have always been for a peaceful settlement of the dispute with China and the same is true for all cabinet officials, past and present [and] for the armed forces”. Anna Dominique “Nikki” Coseteng, a former senator and president of Diliman College, which sponsored the South China Sea forum, attributed Filipinos’ preference for peace to cultural ties between Manila and Beijing. “The people want peace. It does not matter whether against China, against America, against Russia, against whoever else. We don’t want war,” she said. Dr Carlos Tabunda Jnr, dean of the School of International Relations at New Era University, said the survey’s result reflected the belief among some Filipinos that their country would lose to China in a military conflict. “There are realistic Filipinos who believe that we can’t [fight on our own],” he said, adding that Manila could not simply assume Washington would come to its aid. Beijing claims most of the South China Sea, rejecting rival claims from other countries, including the Philippines, and a 2016 international ruling that its assertion over the waterway has no legal basis. Calling the judgment “null and void”, China has maintained that the dispute should be resolved through bilateral negotiations. Turning down the temperature While most Filipinos supported diplomacy in the survey, Chinese envoy Jing Quan’s remarks have raised concerns that an escalating war of words could narrow the space for a peaceful resolution of the maritime discord. On October 14, Philippine defence chief Gilberto Teodoro Jnr called China the region’s “real troublemaker”. Asked to respond the following day, Jing said the Philippines should feel fortunate to have China as a neighbour, adding: “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose to use force. And we love peace.” The comments saw Manila summon Jing on Monday, saying they could be interpreted as a threat while lawmakers sought to declare him persona non grata. China accused the Philippines of taking them out of context. Nearly 100 student organisations also “banned” Jing from their campuses, vowing to resist what they described as China’s threats and false narratives. Beyond the wrangling, analysts said the challenge for Manila was how to defend its maritime interests without allowing a verbal duel to undermine diplomacy. Marcos’ former national security adviser and political scientist Dr Clarita Carlos said Jing should have been “more prudent” in his remarks to the media, though she understood his perspective. As a seasoned diplomat who had served in Washington, he was accustomed to Americans’ blunt style, she said, but should have recognised that Filipinos were “more sensitive”. Tabunda criticised Jing’s choice of words, saying the ambassador should have expressed himself more carefully, even though he agreed with the substance of his remarks. “This word war and social media hostilities should not be fought and cannot be won,” said Dr Lucio Blanco Pitlo, a Filipino geopolitics and security analyst who had served as president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies. “There is no shortage of zealous nationalists on both sides that can sustain this unhealthy dynamic that may affect diplomatic space if left unchecked,” Pitlo said. Retired rear admiral Rommel Jude Ong, who started the navy’s South China Sea operations, said Jing’s statement was a “threat directed at our moral centre and unbecoming for a diplomat, but it revealed the true position of Beijing”. “They attack our sense of nation and the legitimacy of our sovereign rights, [instilling] fear among our people and indecision in our political leadership. Their desired end state for us is capitulation.”

content: The tanker detained by Indonesian authorities that was used in an attempt to smuggle 1.16 tonnes of ketamine is owned by a Malaysian-registered company. Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department director Hussein Omar Khan said the two directors of the company that owns the MT Global 168 are Malaysians. He said the company’s office is located in Johor Bahru, Malaysia’s Johor state. According to Hussein, the tanker had previously applied for registration under the Malaysian flag but had yet to be registered. It is currently sailing under the Mongolian flag. “The vessel is registered under the names of two Malaysian directors. Neither has a previous criminal record and we will call them in,” he told reporters. Earlier, Hussein said police would obtain information from their Indonesian counterparts over the seizure of 1.16 tonnes of ketamine hydrochloride worth nearly 60 million ringgit (US$14 million) from a tanker. The vessel made unusual movements between October 14 and 18 before it was detained in waters off Tanjung Balai Asahan, Indonesia, on Tuesday. It was believed to have departed from an anchorage in Pasir Gudang, Johor and stopped at Port Klang to refuel before heading towards the Andaman Sea. To evade the authorities, the vessel’s crew allegedly switched off its automatic identification system for three days. Eight crew members, comprising seven Indonesians and a Chinese national, were arrested. Indonesian police chief General Suyudi Ario Seto said authorities had been tracking the vessel’s movements since August after receiving intelligence on suspicious activities. This story was first published by The Star
