content: Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over. One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong. For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book. “Who knows, it might be the start of a new habit,” he said. Thang, 53, is spending a year travelling across Vietnam in a truck with his “Books To Every Home” project, also known as “Roaming Turtle”. In neighbouring Thailand, a similar book truck named “Somelee” (Cotton) is pursuing an equally ambitious mission: visiting all 77 provinces to take literature beyond Bangkok and the country’s other urban centres. Their goal goes beyond selling books. By taking their trucks beyond the big cities, the two projects hope to spark curiosity, build connections through storytelling and turn chance roadside encounters into lasting reading habits for people who might otherwise never enter a bookshop. But bringing books to the provinces comes at a cost – from fuel and accommodation to staff wages – and neither truck can guarantee a crowd at every stop. ‘Come with me for a year’ Thang’s decision to start Roaming Turtle followed the closure of the last branch of his Ca Chep bookshop chain on Ho Chi Minh City’s Vo Van Tan Street in June. Customers were increasingly buying online, he said, and he no longer had the time or focus to run the store. As its closure approached, a former employee offered to help him sell books. “Then come with me for a year,” Thang recalled replying. With no advance plan, the truck set off on July 15 from Ho Chi Minh City on a journey scheduled to last until July 2027. By mid-October, Thang said the Roaming Turtle had reached its 27th stop – Nam Dinh in the Red River Delta – with Thai Binh next on the itinerary. “The Ca Chep Bookstore may have closed its fixed location, but we don’t want the story of Ca Chep to end there,” he said, noting that Ca Chep means carp in Vietnamese. “Ca Chep only temporarily paused, but never stopped swimming.” Growing up in mountainous Hoa Binh province, Thang loved reading and drawing. After graduating from the University of Industrial Fine Arts in 1995, he designed book covers at a state-owned publisher before establishing Dong A, his own book company. On the road, those skills come together. Together with a driver and a sales assistant, Thang introduces readers to Dong A’s titles and hand-draws book covers upon request. Bystanders even help unload boxes, arrange displays and manage sales. His autobiography has become a particular attraction. He initially brought five copies to sell at each stop, illustrating every cover differently. When those sold out, readers began ordering copies online and bringing them to his truck to be illustrated. In Da Nang, he hand-illustrated 22 covers. “Each book cover is a unique illustration, connected to a person and a memory from my journey,” he said. Other encounters have triggered deeper personal memories. In Quy Nhon, he met an unemployed mother who used her limited savings to buy books for her child – a scene that reminded him of his own childhood and mother. Beyond the capital In Thailand, the team behind the Somelee book truck began with a similar problem of access. Bookshops and literary fairs were concentrated in Bangkok and other major urban centres, according to Yasawath Chuthivisitrathikul, a project manager at P.S. Publishing. The publisher was previously affiliated with Somewhere Bookshop and Home Cafe in Bangkok’s Yai district, which closed its doors last Sunday. “We saw this as an opportunity to reach everyone – both readers and people who have never read books before,” Yasawath said. Founded by Borisat Pongwat, or “Turk”, Somelee aims to reach regular readers and non-readers alike. So far, the five-person Somelee team, including Yasawath and Borisat, has visited about 25 venues and plans to cover all 77 Thai provinces within two years. Jarungdach Phosri, or “Ton”, who drives the truck, said journeys had grown rapidly, from three cafe visits in Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat) to a single tour covering 15 provinces over nearly three months. Somelee’s inventory initially focused on Thai novels, short stories and poetry, before expanding into children’s literature. However, the team discovered reading preferences varied widely by region. Jarungdach said some stops showed strong demand for translated literature, while others preferred short stories or Thai works. Unfulfilled reader requests are logged as feedback to guide future stock selection. “What makes it worthwhile, beyond selling books, is meeting readers,” Jarungdach said. “Some are people we have only spoken to through a keyboard. We get to meet and exchange ideas.” One reader travelled three hours on a motorcycle from another province just to visit the truck, Yasawath recalled. At Natit Coffee and Crafts in Nong Khai province, proprietor Raviya Wongsathitana said the cafe connected with Somelee through a local community page on social media while taking part in the first Nongkhai Reading Week. The cafe hosted activities alongside the truck, including a workshop on making simple handmade books or zines. Most visitors were existing customers, Raviya said, although the event also attracted wider local interest. “I see Somelee as a living mobile bookstore,” she said. “They share stories of their travels and tell people who they’ll meet and where, allowing visitors to be part of an experience beyond simply buying books.” Keeping things moving Behind these encounters is a complex mobile supply chain. To keep inventory stocked, Somelee posts book shipments ahead to hotels along their route, while local cafe owners offer travel tips and help arrange accommodation. Nevertheless, operational costs are a constant burden. Fuel, lodgings and equipment add up quickly, while turnout at remote stops can be unpredictable. Unfavourable weather, particularly heavy rain, can easily disrupt operations for days. “We want to promote a reading culture, so we started driving out to meet people in the provinces, far from Bangkok,” Yasawath said. “Both readers and people who have never read books before are welcome, and we continue to stay in touch with them online.” In Vietnam, Thang financed his truck with a bank loan of around 1.2 billion dong (US$46,360). Sales cover everyday living and operating expenses on the road, while Dong A handles staff salaries and vehicle loan repayments. Both projects sometimes lower prices to keep books accessible. Somelee offers reductions of 15 to 30 per cent – sometimes exceeding 50 per cent for students – while Thang focuses sales in cities so he can give books away for free at schools in more remote locations. For Thang, a year on the road has sharpened his approach to publishing. “Making good, beautiful books remains important, but prices must allow them to reach people with different means,” he said. “People who truly want to read should not have to give up a book they love just because they lack money.”

title: Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut
description: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports. Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests. Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to...
content: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports. Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests. Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand. About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia. “The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said. Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply. However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added. This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said. “Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said. “But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.” From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy. Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme. Wong said: “Dealing with today’s concerns is only part of our job. We must also prepare Singapore for tomorrow – that means looking ahead, anticipating problems and acting before they become more difficult to solve. “Consider the economy of the future. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.” In his speech, Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added. “We remain a trusted partner and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” the prime minister said. In addition, Singapore is proactively strengthening partnerships across different regions of the world, with office-holders travelling more frequently to build relationships and deepen cooperation. In the past week, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam made a state visit to Sweden, while Wong recently returned from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. “These countries are in different parts of the world, but they all see value in working closely with Singapore,” Wong said. “That reflects the trust and goodwill we have built over many years.” Singapore is known as a reliable partner, a trusted hub and a country that delivers on its commitment, Wong said. “This reputation is a vital asset, especially in today’s fragmented and troubled world. It helps us attract high-quality investments,” he added. “And the investments support growth, create jobs and enable incomes to rise.” Some challenges are harder to tackle as they cross national borders – these include online scams or haze. Singapore is grappling with its worst haze episode since 2015. It has sent notices to 10 Singapore-based firms and 10 Indonesian firms under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. “We cannot solve these problems through our own efforts alone. We need cooperation from other countries,” Wong said. “But that does not mean we stand by and do nothing. We are doing everything we can within our power to protect Singaporeans, strengthen our own response and work with partners to tackle these problems at source.” Touching on governance, Wong said that the Singapore we want cannot simply be delivered by the government to Singaporeans, and has to be “built with Singaporeans”. “That is the partnership we strive for: a PAP government that listens, acts and delivers. A people who step forward and contribute and a society where everyone looks out for one another.” While Singaporeans have given the PAP a strong mandate to govern for another term, this mandate is not an “entitlement”, Wong said. “It is a responsibility to deliver what we promised, tackle the difficult issues facing our country and prepare Singapore for what lies ahead. That is why we must never take the trust of Singaporeans for granted. After all, no political party has a permanent claim on that trust,” Wong said. “Every generation of PAP leaders and activists must earn it afresh. We know what is expected of us. We must listen and deliver. We must hold ourselves to high standards and we must always put Singapore and Singaporeans first.” Wong noted that while some sectors of Singapore’s economy are doing well, others are facing pressures. Some workers are benefiting from new opportunities, but others are struggling to keep up. Lower-wage workers worry about keeping pace with rising costs, while Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s who lose their jobs worry about finding work again. “We understand these concerns and we will respond to them. Our task is not just to keep the economy growing. It is to make sure that growth translates into better lives for all Singaporeans,” he said. The government is also doing more to ease the burdens on parents and give families greater assurance, as seen by measures introduced at this year’s National Day Rally, he added. Wong acknowledged that the government has a “full agenda”, such as continuing to tackle the cost-of-living pressures and helping Singapore secure better jobs. Ultimately, the government will do its part, but everybody has a part to play too, the prime minister said. “We will create opportunities and support workers through change, but workers must be prepared to learn and adapt,” Wong said. “We will reduce the emphasis on exams and broaden education pathways, but parents must give their children space to grow at their own pace. “We will strengthen support for families and seniors, but all of us must also look out for one another.” This story was first published by CNA

title: Why more Japanese women are choosing ‘silver divorce’ after decades of marriage
description: Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. content: Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. Her two daughters have grown up and left home, and her husband of more than two decades moved out nearly a year ago as they finalise a divorce. For the 62-year-old Kawasaki resident, who spoke on condition that her surname be withheld, this was not how she envisioned her later years. “He worked very long hours, including on weekends, and I was always busy taking care of the house and raising the children,” Ayumi said. “I think we worked well as a team at the beginning, but somewhere along the way, we just stopped talking like we had before.” The marriage had its fair share of ups and downs – financial stress during their daughters’ university years and the deaths of their respective parents. But the final break came when the girls left home. “It felt like we were almost strangers with nothing in common,” she said. “Before, we had always put our children first. But suddenly they had their own lives, and we both realised there was not much holding us together any more.” Ayumi’s experience reflects a growing trend across Japan. While total divorces nationwide have steadily declined since peaking in the early 2000s, separations among couples married for 20 years or longer – commonly called “silver divorce” – continue to rise. Data from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare released in September showed that such late-life break-ups reached a record 24.2 per cent in 2025, rising 0.4 percentage points from the previous year. The total number of divorces in 2025, however, fell to 179,073, down 6,831 from 185,904 in 2024. Financial independence Several changes have caused older women to re-evaluate unhappy or distant marriages later in life. Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, said an “empty nest” frequently exposed deep emotional divides built up over decades. “Many find that they had grown a long way apart during the years of raising their children,” Kawakami said. This has been exacerbated by more women entering employment, earning a wage that gives a degree of self-sufficiency previous generations lacked. A key turning point was Japan’s 2007 pension system reform, which allowed divorced spouses to claim up to 50 per cent of the Employees’ Pension Insurance contributions accumulated by their partner during the marriage. “For women earning less than 1.3 million yen [US$8,217] a year, this was significant,” Kawakami said, as it provided a financial safety net upon retirement that previously did not exist. Married, but living apart Japan’s demanding corporate culture also plays a key role long before divorce papers are filed. Under the common practice of tanshin funin (solo work transfers), companies can relocate married male employees to distant domestic or overseas offices for years at a time. Wives often stay behind so children do not have to change schools. “These situations can go on for decades,” Kawakami said. “One of my friends never actually lived in the house he bought for his family; his wife and children live there and he visits when he can. So it is not at all surprising that when the husband reaches retirement age he has nothing in common any more with his wife.” The price of silence Beyond the legal and financial costs, late-life separation can carry a distinct psychological burden. Bill Cleary, clinical director of the Tokyo-based TELL counselling service, frequently works with older couples struggling to readjust once children leave home. “They have time on their hands suddenly, find themselves face-to-face and do not know what to do,” Cleary said. “Late-age divorce has become a significant problem, even when the narrative so often is that people do not want to be alone. Humans are wired for connection, and many of us do not do well in isolation, but still people are wanting to separate.” Cleary agreed that societal stigma around both divorce and mental health support often prevented couples from seeking professional help early enough. “If your car has a mechanical problem, you take it to a garage,” Cleary said. “The same level of support should be available to care for our hearts and our thoughts. Too many people are not seeking help before it is too late and they do not know what to do, so the only thing they can think of is to get out of the marriage.” For Ayumi, who works three part-time jobs and has regular contact with her daughters, the decision has brought a mix of pragmatism and self-reliance. “I do not know what the future holds, but for now, I am confident that I can stand on my own two feet.”

title: Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency
description: Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces. Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies...
content: Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces. Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure. The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13. “We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.” Anthropic’s Claude is among the models Singapore is exploring as it seeks to strengthen its cyber defences. The US technology firm signed an agreement with Singapore on the sidelines of the summit, setting out areas of AI cooperation, including safety, security, responsible adoption and research into the impact of adoption. “Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Anthropic co-founder Benjamin Mann at the signing on October 13, a day before the firm opened its fifth Asia-Pacific office in the city state. Anthropic already has offices in Japan, India, South Korea and Australia. “With this [memorandum of understanding], we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world,” Mann said. Safety and transparency concerns The partnerships offer governments access to emerging technologies and technical expertise, but also make transparency and oversight increasingly important as AI systems become more capable and autonomous. On the sidelines of the event, Shanmugam told the media that Singapore had sought greater transparency from major technology companies, following meetings with firms including Anthropic, Google, Amazon and OpenAI. “They need to notify us early on when something happens, taking a leaf from the experience in Australia and what happened there,” he said. “Generally, the companies have expressed an attitude of cooperation. But I would say it’s work in progress. It’s something that we are talking to them about.” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticised OpenAI in September over what he called an “unacceptable” breach involving an AI agent that infiltrated a government health website and accessed public and non-public files in June. Albanese accused the firm of taking “way too long” to tell Canberra about the incident. The San Francisco-headquartered company, which said it learned of the breach in August, apologised and acknowledged that its handling of the incident was “not enough”. In July, open-source AI platform Hugging Face said it had been hacked by autonomous AI agents. Less than a week later, OpenAI revealed that the “unprecedented cyber incident” was driven by a combination of its models after it lost control of them during a security test. Singapore had yet to encounter another attack like those attributed to cyberthreat group UNC3886, Shanmugam said. Last year, he revealed that the group had been targeting the city state’s critical infrastructure. “We haven’t come across another attack like what we have heard from other countries,” he said. “But, you know, also, we don’t know what we don’t know.” Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said closer cooperation with technology companies did not necessarily increase the risk of such breaches and could help mitigate threats through information-sharing and technical evaluation. He warned, however, that expanding AI use in governance could create new vulnerabilities that existing cybersecurity arrangements might not address. “AI agents could inadvertently access unauthorised systems, expose sensitive information or be manipulated through malicious inputs,” he said, urging the establishment of clear boundaries on AI autonomy and the use of controlled environments during deployment. The partnerships could also make it harder to determine who was responsible when disruptions or breaches occurred, Gatra said. “If an AI system makes a mistake that disrupts government services, who is accountable? The government agency deploying it, the company developing it, or the officials who authorised its use?” Asean cooperation Other Southeast Asian nations have also begun drawing on resources from major technology companies to strengthen their cyber defences, but industry experts warn that a widening digital divide could leave smaller states behind. The Philippines and Google announced the expansion of a multi-year partnership in June aimed at strengthening Manila’s cybersecurity and subsea cable systems to ensure resilient digital connectivity. The country’s cyber-monitoring hub has also deployed Google Cloud’s security framework, which provides AI-driven cyber defence. Last year, Thailand announced plans to adopt the Google framework, with the aim of enabling its cyberdefence centre to coordinate responses more effectively to online threats targeting government bodies and infrastructure. But less developed states might lack the technical resources or negotiating leverage to secure timely disclosures from major technology firms through bilateral arrangements, said Gatra, who urged greater cooperation among members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “Singapore could work with Asean partners to develop common expectations around incident notification and cross-border information-sharing,” he said. The city state has said it wants to strengthen the bloc’s collective cyber resilience by deepening practical cooperation and capacity building when it assumes the Asean chairmanship next year. Shanmugam told the media that Asean already had a framework for dealing with cyberthreats but acknowledged that it remained a “work in progress”. The Asean cybersecurity cooperation strategy outlines five pillars, including strengthening readiness, advancing regional policy coordination and building capacity. “We are all catching up on this issue of AI, and each country is focused on its own issues,” he said. “Asean collectively has some work to do in trying to deal with it together too. So, these are discussions that have to carry on.”

title: How to share AI wealth? Neither the US nor Asia has the answer
description: On October 18, Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) laboratory preparing one of the largest listings in history, committed 5 per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund. The next day, Elon Musk promised one SpaceX share, next year, for “every kid in America” – about US$10.6 billion for some 73 million children. The offers differ in who holds the shares. Anthropic’s will sit in an entity the company owns, spent on the public’s behalf; Musk’s would land, by a route he has not explained,...
content: On October 18, Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) laboratory preparing one of the largest listings in history, committed 5 per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund. The next day, Elon Musk promised one SpaceX share, next year, for “every kid in America” – about US$10.6 billion for some 73 million children. The offers differ in who holds the shares. Anthropic’s will sit in an entity the company owns, spent on the public’s behalf; Musk’s would land, by a route he has not explained, in a child’s name. Should the public own the companies AI makes rich? Silicon Valley has begun answering yes, on its own terms. This came a week after International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva described AI as a “slow-moving tsunami”, shifting income from labour to capital, that could augment, downgrade or eliminate 40 per cent of jobs worldwide. She spoke in Bangkok; Asia is where economic growth has long depended on creating jobs. America shares growth through wages too, but 62 per cent of adults also own shares. For six decades, Asia’s growth reached households chiefly through the pay packet. Japan’s shunto, the annual wage negotiations between unions and employers, carried prime minister Hayato Ikeda’s 1960 pledge to double national income in a decade; the economy did it in seven years. South Korea’s factories provided wages, and the 1987 strikes gave workers a bigger share. Beijing smashed the iron rice bowl and let private factories absorb the laid-off. Singapore took another route: the state turned wages into housing wealth through compulsory savings and public housing, and during the 2001 slump handed citizens economic-growth-linked New Singapore Shares. Then pay stopped keeping pace. Since the mid-1990s, Japan’s labour ministry calculates, a 1 per cent rise in productivity has lifted wages by about 0.4 per cent, against roughly 1 per cent in America: higher productivity without higher pay, decades before AI. Past automation replaced hands on the factory floor while adding jobs above them. AI now threatens the route where it is weakest. Stanford economists using American payroll data find that employment of those aged 22-25 in the most AI-exposed occupations has fallen by 19 per cent behind the trajectory of less exposed peers, up from 15 per cent a year earlier. Causation is contested and total employment has not fallen. But the pressure is falling first on the young. The newest round of the old bargain was fought this year in Icheon, in South Korea’s Gyeonggi province. SK Hynix, riding on demand for AI chips, agreed last year to hand staff 10 per cent of its operating profit: about 700 million won (US$527,500) a head if this year’s 250 trillion won profit forecast holds. This August, union members voted down a tentative deal to take 60 per cent in shares, wary of a volatile stock and the tax bill. Last month, they settled on half cash, half shares, with the option of more stock. Even the workers closest to the AI boom haggled over how much of their dividend should be in payroll. They are the lucky ones. Last year, 450,000 young Koreans said they wanted no job at all, up from 287,000 in 2019, according to Bank of Korea. Beijing meets a record 12.7 million graduates this year with an “employment first” plan, though a China Daily commentary concedes AI may hit the young first. The dividend reached Icheon by negotiation. It has no route to the graduate who was never hired. Asia’s routes share a blind spot: they assume a job. Wage talks bargain for the employed. Singapore’s new Tripartite Jobs Council and graduate traineeships help people onto the next payroll; neither gives citizens a claim on what AI earns. A system that drafts a junior analyst’s work turns part of a salary into a software fee and the rest into margin: much of the fee flows to model-makers in California or Hangzhou, then to shareholders and a small share to customers. Retraining decides who gets the next job, not who keeps the margin. Silicon Valley’s answer is incomplete. Anthropic’s pledge awaits shareholder approval; SpaceX has shed about a third of its share price since its peak. The difference between Icheon and Silicon Valley is not cash vs shares. It is who decides. SK Hynix workers negotiated their formula and voted down the payment terms they disliked. American children hold a promise, revocable by those who made it. The workers voted. The children will not. Asia has shared growth in many ways. It has never had to do so when growth needs fewer new workers. Somewhere in Shenzhen or Pangyo, a finance director is about to sign an AI contract that removes a line from next year’s salary budget. Whose dividend is the saving?

title: Chasing Gothic Lolita demand, Japanese businesses expand to Europe
description: A Japanese fashion style inspired by historical European clothing is finding a growing following in Europe, where enthusiasts are embracing its elaborate designs and forming communities around their shared passion for lace, frills and intricate outfits. Gothic Lolita, often shortened to “Goth-Loli,” blends elements of European clothing styles with Japanese fashion sensibilities. Japanese brands are now looking to expand their presence in Europe, bringing the style back to the continent that...
content: A Japanese fashion style inspired by historical European clothing is finding a growing following in Europe, where enthusiasts are embracing its elaborate designs and forming communities around their shared passion for lace, frills and intricate outfits. Gothic Lolita, often shortened to “Goth-Loli,” blends elements of European clothing styles with Japanese fashion sensibilities. Japanese brands are now looking to expand their presence in Europe, bringing the style back to the continent that helped inspire it. In August, around 70 enthusiasts gathered at a restaurant in central Berlin for a “tea party” organised by Japanese fashion brand Atelier Pierrot, its first such event in the German capital. Dressed in elaborate outfits featuring lace, ruffles and other decorative details, participants enjoyed cakes and sweets, posed for photographs and exchanged fashion tips. Some had travelled from Belgium, Ireland and Poland to attend the gathering. Henriette, 37, who lives in Dresden in eastern Germany, has been a fan of Gothic Lolita fashion for nearly 20 years. “It’s beautiful,” she said of the clothing. “And the Japanese people, when they do something, they do it 100 per cent.” She said German enthusiasts regularly organise gatherings every month or two, sometimes drawing participants from other European countries. For Henriette, however, the biggest attraction goes beyond the clothes themselves. “The beauty is nice,” she said. “Getting to know each other, that’s the best.” Another long-time enthusiast, a 39-year-old accountant, said her interest in Japanese culture began with anime and music before expanding to fashion. She welcomed the exchange of influences between Japan and Europe, describing it as “a nice way of being inspired by each other and not seeing it as stealing.” The growing enthusiasm is also translating into increased sales for Japanese brands seeking a stronger foothold in Europe. According to Atelier Pierrot, its online sales to Europe jumped about 77 per cent in 2025 from the previous year. Sales to Germany rose around 2.3-fold, while those to France increased about 83 per cent. Connie, a model and overseas ambassador for Atelier Pierrot, attributed the growth partly to efforts to organise events, improve English-language communications and offer a wider range of clothing sizes. She said interest has increased since the COVID-19 pandemic, while in-person events have helped newcomers discover a fashion style that could otherwise seem difficult to approach. “Lolita is not a cheap fashion,” she said, explaining that potential customers can be hesitant to spend money without first seeing or trying on the clothes. She said the opportunity to examine the quality and check sizes in person could help overcome those concerns. Social media has also helped introduce the style to younger European fans. Nadine Ehrenberg, 29, a Berlin resident, said Japanese fashion was attracting more attention, particularly among teenagers and people in their twenties. “I think because of social media and everything, it gains more popularity and more people come to it,” she said. Connie said she had encountered children as young as 11 or 12, and sometimes younger, showing an interest in wearing Lolita fashion. “Sometimes you hear people saying Lolita is dying out, but I feel more than ever Lolita fashion is spreading and evolving,” she said. Encouraged by the turnout in Berlin, Connie hopes to organise more events in Germany and elsewhere in Europe, bringing together fans of a fashion culture shaped by influences from both continents.

content: Indonesia cut exports of natural gas to Singapore on Saturday to prioritise domestic demand, an official said, with the two countries at loggerheads over regional air pollution emanating from wildfires on the vast archipelago. The head of SKK Migas, a state agency supervising the oil and gas sector, said Indonesia would cut a total of 31 million standard cubic feet per day from its supply to Singapore. Fifteen million standard cubic feet per day was being cut from Natuna in Indonesia’s Riau island, and 16 million from Sumatra, SKK Migas chief Djoko Siswanto said in a statement. He said the move was “to maintain the reliability of domestic gas supply for electricity”. “We will continue to monitor developments on a daily basis,” he added. Only Singapore is affected for now. Indonesia is one of Singapore’s main sources of natural gas, providing it with 145.3 billion cubic feet in 2024, according to data from the US Energy Information Administration. The cut represents about eight per cent of that total. The Singapore government has not commented on the development. The move comes amid a diplomatic spat between Indonesia and countries in the region over haze from wildfires on Borneo and Sumatra islands choking cities in neighbouring states. On Thursday, Indonesian energy minister Bahlil Lahadalia said he was mulling curbing gas exports to prioritise domestic consumption, while warning Jakarta would act against countries that “do not respect” Indonesia. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Wednesday berated “countries that like to insult” his nation over the haze crisis. He did not name specific countries. The Southeast Asian giant has for months struggled to contain fires that deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas said have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September. The haze has sent air pollution levels surging to dangerous levels not only in Indonesia, but also in Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor, prompting Asean to call a meeting over the crisis. Singapore has promised legal action against companies responsible for the fires.

title: Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners

Barely a year on, the facade has crumbled. Last month, US President Donald Trump announced a US$200 billion tranche of the deal with no South Korean official present. content: The anxiety gripping Seoul is palpable. Under US pressure, South Korea signed a US$350 billion investment deal last November for a 10-percentage-point tariff reduction, billing it as a strategic alliance. Barely a year on, the facade has crumbled. Last month, US President Donald Trump announced a US$200 billion tranche of the deal with no South Korean official present. Blindsided, Seoul restated its “commercial viability” clause. Trump’s response was blunt. “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more,” he told reporters. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up.” For South Korea, the numbers are sobering: US$350 billion represents 18 per cent of its annual gross domestic product. Even if much of it is channelled through loans, guarantees and corporate outlays, it risks upward pressure on the won, crowding out domestic investment and political exposure if projects underperform. The episode offers three lessons for every trade-reliant economy tempted to placate Washington. The first is that appeasement is no strategy – it only invites more exploitation. Seoul’s pledge includes a clause requiring that the investments be “commercially reasonable”. The Alaska liquefied natural gas project in Trump’s announcement was abandoned by private investors in 2016, yet it is now presented as a done deal with Korean funding. This pattern extends beyond South Korea. Trump has extracted an estimated US$5 trillion in investment pledges globally. Earlier this month, he threatened up to 300 per cent tariffs on nations reneging on their US investment pledges. Crucially, many US threats appear to be bluffs. After threatening Brazil with Section 301 tariffs, Washington declared in July a 25 per cent levy, but two-thirds of goods from Brazil are exempted. The 100 per cent tariff on pharmaceutical products announced this year is phased and riddled with carve-outs for 20 jurisdictions including India. Why? Because extreme rates threaten US consumer prices, supply chains and a political blowback. A panicked response can be costly. If US trading partners had chosen serious negotiations over hasty deals, and if talks had dragged on until the Supreme Court’s February strike-down of Trump’s “reciprocal tariffs”, would they still have handed over such egregious concessions? Lesson two is that dependence itself is a point of failure. South Korea’s predicament stems from a dual lock: the US military umbrella and market access. This gives the United States leverage. The European Union caved in largely because of defence abandonment fears. Brussels locked in massive investment and energy commitments despite the Supreme Court ruling, ignoring a legal escape hatch in favour of Nato cover and car sales. Japan bowed to avoid hefty auto tariffs because the US is its largest export market. Gulf states traded oil access for security – only to find that the US umbrella came with holes. In reality, every dollar nations scramble to hand to Washington tightens their noose. If Trump succeeds in pocketing this massive forced capital transfer, it will only deepen his victims’ dependence, making them more vulnerable. The way out is to pivot away from US dependency and diversify markets. This strategy is not about confrontation; it means reducing economic and security ties to Washington, stripping it of the leverage to dictate terms. The pain of the pivot is real, yet it is the only sustainable exit. Canada stands out as an example. Despite over two-thirds of its exports going to the US, Ottawa hit back with counter-tariffs, expanded trade outreach to Indo-Pacific markets and joined the EU defence procurement mechanism. Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Beijing in January – the first by a Canadian prime minister since 2017 – to cut the US economic leverage. Lesson three is that collective action is indispensable in countering Washington’s extortion. Trump’s tariffs work because his targets negotiate individually, each hoping to be spared the worst. His playbook – bilateral deals, tariff snapbacks, calibrated threats – is designed to keep countries divided. Nations must stand together and safeguard the World Trade Organization’s most-favoured-nation principle, which Trump’s administration chips away at. Collective action is also needed in complementary areas: coordinated legal challenges at the WTO, aligned counter-tariffs, responses to secondary sanctions, emergency swap lines and a commitment not to turn against one another. A 300 per cent tariff threat loses its potency when major economies call its bluff. The US still matters – its market, capital and security guarantees carry real weight. But it has less power when facing a coordinated bloc. South Korean leaders may now be lying awake at night calculating the price of a signature. Other US trading partners would be well advised to do their sums. Rather than facing US pressure alone or seeking watered-down bilateral bargains, targeted collective action will be what holds the line and finally forces an overreaching Washington to meet its match.

title: 4 pilots killed in mid-air collision of Philippine military planes

content: Two Philippine air force planes collided during a training flight and crashed at an airbase south of Manila, killing all four pilots on board, Philippine officials said on Saturday. The two SF-260 aircraft collided while flying at a low altitude on Friday afternoon then crashed at Fernando Air Base in Lipa city in the coastal province of Batangas south of the capital. There were no injuries on the ground, the officials said. The air force did not provide details of what it called an accidental crash. Two Philippine officials with knowledge of what happened said the two planes collided in mid-air. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter. One of the two-seater aircraft went down near the barracks of military personnel in the airbase, a witness said. The air force said it has temporarily grounded all its remaining SF-260s, which were acquired from Italy, as an investigation takes place. It did not say how many SF-260s were left in the air force. In May, a Philippine air force SF-260 plane also crashed in the northern mountain province of Benguet during a navigation training flight with several other SF-260 aircraft, killing the two pilots. In 2023, another SF-260 plane of the air force crashed in a rice field in Bataan province northwest of Manila during a training flight and killed two crewmen, according to the air force. Friday’s accident was the latest setback to the underfunded Philippine military. It has long struggled to modernise its air force, navy and army due to financial constraints while dealing with decades-long communist and Muslim insurgencies and increasingly hostile territorial disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea.

title: Kim Jong-un urges North Korean military to become ‘strongest armed forces in the world’

content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un urged his military to train to become the strongest in the world at a two-day meeting of company commanders in Pyongyang, state media said on Saturday. Kim’s call for what he dubbed a “Korean-style military revolution” came the same week Seoul’s military proposed talks to clarify the border after an explosion inside the heavily fortified demilitarised zone (DMZ) further strained inter-Korean ties. Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the 1950-53 Korean war ended in a truce, not a peace treaty. The Pyongyang event, held on Thursday and Friday, was aimed at developing a plan “to train the strongest armed forces in the world”, Kim said, according to the official Korea Central News Agency (KCNA). He also called for “all the companies” of the North’s army to be “turned into a strong elite unit in military and technical aspects and consolidated into perfect combat forces”. KCNA said it was the first gathering of “the entire army” since a February party congress where Kim had called for stronger conventional forces and reaffirmed plans to develop nuclear weapons and missiles. North Korea has also tested a slew of weapons recently, including a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to use AI technology. Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible. The North has also become a key Russian ally since it launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology. South Korea proposed on Friday military talks with the North to clarify their border and restore communication channels, after Seoul blamed the DMZ blast that injured South Korean soldiers on North Korean landmines, a claim Pyongyang strongly rejected. Pyongyang, which also previously rejected Seoul’s demand for an apology over the explosion, has not responded to Friday’s proposal.

title: Overseas Filipinos feel heartache over missing parcels for loved ones, demand answers

content: At this time of year, Fatima Ramos would normally be preparing her balikbayan boxes. Overseas Filipinos typically fill these boxes with gifts, clothes, food and household items to send to their loved ones back home in the Philippines for Christmas. Ramos has previously sent the tax-exempt parcels to her family and Philippine charity organisations from Abu Dhabi, where she is a domestic worker. Now back in the Philippines, Ramos is seeking answers about the parcels she sent last year, some of which arrived severely damaged while others remain missing. “I got one of my boxes, and it was completely soaked. The clothes were faded and mouldy. The items and the box were all crushed. It was heartbreaking. The food, such as the chocolates, had melted because it got wet,” Ramos told This Week in Asia. Ric, an engineer in Saudi Arabia who asked to be identified only by his first name, has suffered a similar experience with a balikbayan – a compound word in Tagalog meaning return to a country – box. According to him, he sent a balikbayan box from Jeddah in June, and a delivery company’s representative told him in July that the parcel was still awaiting shipment. When he followed up in September, his emails and calls went unanswered. For many overseas Filipinos, balikbayan boxes often represent weeks or months of careful selection of items paid for with their hard-earned savings, and an expression of their love from afar. Their tax-exempt status reflects the Philippine government’s recognition of the role overseas Filipinos play in supporting their families. But thousands of these boxes have been left in limbo as the Christmas season approaches, with some abandoned in shipping containers at Philippine ports and others stranded in their countries of origin amid problems involving cargo forwarding companies. The boxes sent by Ramos and Ric were handled by Makati Express Cargo, a forwarding company serving customers in the United States and the Middle East. The Philippines’ Bureau of Customs (BOC) revoked the company’s licence in January and filed criminal complaints against it in May over nearly 40,000 boxes left unclaimed at ports, involving more than 30 million pesos (US$1.6 million) in unpaid duties. Ramos sent eight boxes between January and March before returning to the Philippines for good because of a heart condition that she said had worsened following Iran’s attacks on the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi. She found out about the mounting complaints against the forwarding company only after she returned home. “At first, I didn’t want to believe it. But then I started following up with my package online and through the company’s website in March. By April, I still couldn’t get an answer to verify whether my boxes had already arrived. They should have been in the Philippines by now,” she said. This Week in Asia has reached out to Makati Express Cargo for comment. On Sunday, the BOC said it had discovered 29 abandoned shipping containers holding at least 10,000 of the boxes at various ports in the Philippines, some of which had arrived in May. In June, the BOC had earlier filed complaints against five cargo forwarding companies over 3,176 abandoned boxes. Some of the boxes had already been opened, rummaged through and “slaughtered”, Ramos claimed. This Week in Asia has also reached out to the BOC for comment. Ramos, who has been gathering complaints from at least 300 overseas Filipinos in the Middle East over their unclaimed boxes, said she had spoken to officials from the BOC and the Department of Migrant Workers to help resolve the matter. Labour of love For migrant Filipinos, the unaccounted balikbayan boxes are a sore point as they symbolise their love and sacrifice, according to analysts. Over 2 million Filipinos work as overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), part of a larger global diaspora of between 10 million and 15 million. “Some Filipino families who decided to migrate to other countries may consider sending balikbayan boxes as a means of extending love and care to relatives in the Philippines. A balikbayan box could be viewed as a sustenance of relational closeness or to communicate thoughtfulness,” said Lenis Aislinn Separa, an intercultural communication researcher based in New Zealand. “Each item they buy that fills a space in a balikbayan box has a backstory of how they struggled in prioritising between what they need to survive living abroad and providing what they believe their family needs back home.” Hannah Nario-Lopez, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s sociology department, said each box was a labour of love from migrant workers, who would curate items carefully over weeks or months. “This simple, small, menial act converts the physical distance and the time spent abroad into tangible care, allowing the worker to remain present in the everyday life of their household,” she said. The box also complements regular cash remittances from OFWs by offering items for household needs such as groceries, toiletries, school supplies, bags and shoes. For some, its loss could disrupt daily routines, such as health supplements for family members who were elderly or ill, Nario-Lopez said. As such, the loss of the box would become a source of trauma for a family, according to Nario-Lopez. “The non-arrival of a box feels like a broken promise, leading to guilt for the sender, and disappointment or a feeling of abandonment for the family,” she said. Ramos said in one meeting with the Bureau of Customs, an OFW shared that she had sent a balikbayan box containing medicines for a family member, who later died. The box was lost along the way. “The medicine never made it. The commissioner [of the bureau] was moved, because he had not realised how severe the impact had been,” she said. Nario-Lopez said every loss of a balikbayan box would erode trust in Philippine institutions involved in its safe delivery, citing cases of looting at warehouses that stored such parcels. “We have to remember that the balikbayan box is actually a grant to Filipinos working overseas. It’s tax-free because they’re sustaining the country through their remittances. So because of this, it becomes a manifestation of distrust in our logistics and governance,” Nario-Lopez said. She warned that OFWs also faced unscrupulous scammers looking to exploit them. “OFWs searching for cheap shipping alternatives become valuable targets for predatory forwarders. It seems like it gives an opening to people with bad intentions,” she added. Nario-Lopez urged Philippine authorities to tighten regulations and online tracking of box movements to protect OFWs and their families. “We could pressure the state through social media, for example, to have a more systematic or universal database to actively track container ships, expose fraudulent consolidators and [praise] lobby officials or leaders who would genuinely advocate for OFWs,” she said.

title: Revised law to maintain Japan’s imperial family size takes effect
description: A revised Imperial House Law took effect on Saturday to address Japan’s shrinking imperial family while retaining the traditional male-only succession system despite public support for female emperors. The revised law also allows female members to retain their...
content: A revised Imperial House Law took effect on Saturday to address Japan’s shrinking imperial family while retaining the traditional male-only succession system despite public support for female emperors. The legislation, enacted in July in the first major revision of the 1947 law, allows the imperial family to adopt males aged 15 or older from 11 former imperial branch families who are descended from emperors through the male line. The revised law also allows female members to retain their imperial status after marrying commoners, reversing a requirement that they leave the imperial family upon marriage. While adopted members themselves are barred from becoming emperor, their male descendants are eligible to ascend the Chrysanthemum Throne. The revised law, however, does not address the possibility of female emperors or succession through the maternal line. Only males descended from emperors through the paternal line remain eligible to ascend the throne, a tradition conservatives such as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are determined to preserve despite the declining number of eligible successors and imperial family members. The revised imperial system will be reviewed every 30 years if necessary. The revision bill was drafted based on a proposal compiled by the speakers and vice-speakers of both houses of parliament after consulting all 13 parliamentary parties and groups. Although the cross-party talks focused on maintaining the size of the imperial family, the bill introduced provisions not included in the original proposal, including succession rights for male descendants of adoptees, prompting criticism from some opposition parties. Revising the Imperial House Law was part of the coalition agreement signed in October last year by the Liberal Democratic Party, led by Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, and its junior partner, the Japan Innovation Party. Opposition parties also criticised the conservative ruling bloc for holding only about eight hours of parliamentary deliberations on the revision. Imperial succession remains a pressing but divisive issue, with Japan having only three male heirs to the throne – Emperor Naruhito’s younger brother Crown Prince Fumihito, 60, Fumihito’s son Prince Hisahito, 20, and the emperor’s uncle Prince Hitachi, 90. Emperor Naruhito, 66, and Empress Masako, 62, have only one child, Princess Aiko, 24, who is ineligible for the throne despite her popularity. Japan’s hereditary monarchy is said to date back more than 2,600 years, although the existence of some early emperors is disputed. Several women have occupied the throne, but succession has traditionally followed the male line.

title: French cooking schools fuel fine-dining dreams of India’s young chefs
description: Fiercely proud of its culinary traditions, India is increasingly open to foreign influences, with French cooking schools attracting students eager to make their mark on the country’s growing fine-dining sector. “Ten or 15 years ago, there were far fewer young people dreaming of becoming chefs,” said Aabhas Jain, director of bakery and pastry training at Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school also operating in India. “But with the rise of social media … today’s students have greater ambitions in...
content: Fiercely proud of its culinary traditions, India is increasingly open to foreign influences, with French cooking schools attracting students eager to make their mark on the country’s growing fine-dining sector. “Ten or 15 years ago, there were far fewer young people dreaming of becoming chefs,” said Aabhas Jain, director of bakery and pastry training at Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school also operating in India. “But with the rise of social media … today’s students have greater ambitions in this profession,” added Jain, 36, who is also part of the Indian School of Hospitality in Gurugram, just outside New Delhi. In the world’s most populous country, the need for high-end hospitality workers is immense, fuelled by economic growth and the rise of a middle class that travels more and increasingly eats at plush establishments. “There are plenty of job opportunities,” said Saurav Chhabra, head of French hotel school Vatel’s Indian campus, which has been based in Gurugram since 2015 in partnership with Sushant University. “Employers’ expectations are very high, particularly in five-star hotel chains.” Culinary and pastry courses, once relatively rare in India, have proliferated over the past decade, with foreign private schools helping drive its high-end hospitality sector. Such is the enthusiasm that France is considering opening vocational schools, notably in Puducherry, the former French colonial port in India’s southeast. Ecole Ducasse has more than 600 students, most from affluent backgrounds. Indian chefs who have worked at prestigious restaurants, including overseas, teach their respective specialities: Indian, European, Mediterranean and Asian cuisine, as well as bakery and pastry-making. Siddhant Marwah, a final-year student, joined the school to acquire “French techniques that represent the quintessence of culinary expertise”. As he puts the finishing touches to a gratin dauphinois – a dish of sliced potatoes baked in cream – he explains that French and Indian cuisines share techniques such as “braising, blanching, and slow cooking in stews”. While France boasts its beef bourguignon, India is not to be outdone with goat nihari, a meat dish cooked for hours in a spicy broth. Drawn by the opportunities for travel and meeting people that a career as a chef offers, Marwah already dreams of opening his own restaurant in India. Nearby, Amitabh Sukhwal has just enrolled at Vatel, whose tuition fees are considerably lower than those at Ecole Ducasse. The school has around 120 students, many from modest backgrounds. Sukhwal, 18, who calls himself a “lover of the French language”, plans to go to France in four years to pursue a master’s degree, gain experience abroad and then draw on it to open his own hotel in India. He learned French through interactions with guests at the small hotel run by his parents in Chittorgarh, Rajasthan and is now honing his skills at his new school, where French-language classes are compulsory. A majority of the students interviewed by Agence France-Presse at the two schools plan to remain in India. After working for many years in India’s luxury hotels, chef Shikha Gupta, who teaches bakery and pastry-making at Vatel, is pleased to see her classes have “as many men as women”. “Over the past 10 to 12 years, attitudes have changed and many women have chosen to enter the culinary profession,” said Ecole Ducasse’s Jain. “We now see near parity, or even a ratio of 60 per cent women to 40 per cent men.” Anusha Nagia, who joined Ecole Ducasse in 2024, hopes to open a restaurant in India and one day earn a Michelin star, perhaps by betting on fusion cuisine, which is “very much in vogue”. While chicken chasseur is one of her favourite French dishes, she fondly recalls a galantine – a French preparation of stuffed meat – in which she and her classmates incorporated the spicy flavours of chicken tikka.

title: Danger, death and devotion: Japan’s festivals face crisis after fatal accidents
description: Japan’s centuries-old festivals are facing renewed scrutiny after a series of fatal accidents in recent weeks, raising questions over how communities can preserve their cultural traditions without putting lives at risk. Three people have been killed and more than a dozen injured in accidents at autumn festivals across the country in recent weeks. Meanwhile, organisers of another major festival, where two men died in February, have cancelled next year’s event, citing public safety concerns. The...
content: Japan’s centuries-old festivals are facing renewed scrutiny after a series of fatal accidents in recent weeks, raising questions over how communities can preserve their cultural traditions without putting lives at risk. Three people have been killed and more than a dozen injured in accidents at autumn festivals across the country in recent weeks. Meanwhile, organisers of another major festival, where two men died in February, have cancelled next year’s event, citing public safety concerns. The fatalities have fuelled calls for some festivals to be scrapped, even as experts warn that abandoning them would erase an important part of local identity and cultural heritage. On October 10, a danjiri (wooden festival float) toppled over while rounding a bend in Izumisano, near Osaka, killing a 51-year-old man who was helping balance the vehicle. On the same day, a 48-year-old man died after being trapped beneath a float in nearby Izumiotsu. The following Saturday, Akihiro Nabae, 62, the deputy mayor of Saijo in Ehime prefecture, was crushed to death beneath a three-tonne float carrying a large Japanese taiko drum. The festivals are highlights of many local communities, but footage of the accidents circulated on social media, triggering demands for dangerous events to be shut down. Toru Hashimoto, former governor of Osaka prefecture, echoed those concerns on a Kansai TV broadcast. He recalled that when he was in office, he issued notices to host communities, warning that if an accident led to a criminal investigation, he would order the event halted immediately. “Tradition is important, but I absolutely do not think it is right to preserve the tradition of a festival at the expense of the lives of babies or children,” Hashimoto said. “Safety should be the absolute priority in these cases, not tradition, and I told organisers to avoid events becoming criminal cases.” Some communities are trying to adapt rather than face cancellation. On October 19, the 200-year-old Katsuyama Fighting Danjiri festival in Okayama prefecture resumed after a two-year suspension caused by a previous participant’s death. The festival involves rival teams ramming two-tonne wooden floats into one another. Organisers reported no injuries this year following the introduction of new safety precautions. But other festivals are pulling back. Organisers of the 500-year-old Saidaiji Festival – more commonly known as the “Naked Man Festival”, in which loincloth-clad men wrestle to capture blessed wooden sticks – said that next February’s event was cancelled. Three participants were knocked unconscious during the festival earlier this year; two later died. “We take the loss of two people very seriously,” Minoru Omori, chairman of the festival committee, told TV Asahi. “It is extremely difficult to hold the festival with safety as the top priority. If we can ensure that safety measures to prevent a recurrence are fully implemented, we will do our best to allow you to attend the 519th festival [in two years].” Hiromichi Kubota, of the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, said that festivals were integral to community identities, emphasising that only a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of annual events across Japan ended in injury or death. “Some festivals certainly involve potentially dangerous activities, but it is precisely because of these risks that the people who organise and participate in them approach them with extraordinary seriousness and discipline, making every effort to prevent accidents,” Kubota said. “For them, an accident that prevents a festival from being carried out properly is deeply regrettable and distressing.” Kubota agreed, however, that safety risks had escalated in recent years due to several contributing factors. “Because of the coronavirus pandemic, festivals throughout Japan were suspended for several years,” he said. “As a result, the practical skills and knowledge necessary to conduct festivals safely were not always passed down adequately. “A few years ago, for example, a festival resumed after a long interruption, but one of its floats went out of control, causing casualties,” Kubota said. “The accident occurred because the techniques required to control the float had not been sufficiently maintained or shared.” Another important factor was the declining birth rate and the ageing of local communities, he pointed out. “In some cases, the shortage of younger people means that physically demanding tasks must be undertaken by older participants, which may create additional risks,” Kubota said, emphasising that participants were not recklessly disregarding safety. Kubota also drew parallels to athletics, pointing out that while serious injuries and deaths occur in sports, few demand that sports be banned entirely. “The real question we need to discuss is how we can prevent the loss of human life while allowing these activities to continue.” Takashi Minamoto, of the non-profit Japan Festival Network, agreed that these traditional events – which often began as religious rituals praying for bountiful harvests, abundant fishing catches or protection from epidemics – continued to provide spiritual support for local communities. “Many festivals do not involve any danger, and I believe that the level of danger associated with some festivals has not changed significantly over the years,” Minamoto said. “While I consider ensuring safety to be the top priority, I do think there is an aspect where the sense of achievement and exhilaration felt when successfully manoeuvring large floats, for example, goes hand in hand with danger.” With more than 300,000 festivals across Japan each year, Minamoto said local community organisers were the best equipped to determine appropriate safety precautions, warning against bureaucratic overreach. Kubota agreed: “When it comes to the safety of the people actually taking part in festivals, such as the danjiri festivals, I believe specific safety measures should primarily be determined by the participants themselves.” “The participants themselves are the people who most strongly wish to prevent accidents,” Kubota said. “And what makes these traditions so important to the people who preserve them is not whether they involve danger, but the fact that they are precious cultural practices handed down through generations.”
