content: When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable. Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives. Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision. “I thought he would turn things around. Now I feel cheated and disappointed,” Ika said. Her disillusionment reflects a broader loss of confidence in the 75-year-old former special forces commander – a sharp reversal from the position of strength he enjoyed after finally winning the presidency on his third attempt. Taking office with virtually no parliamentary opposition after bringing former rival parties into a sprawling governing coalition, Prabowo rode a post-inauguration honeymoon that saw his public approval rating hit 79 per cent at the start of his term as he began implementing his blueprint to transform Southeast Asia’s largest economy and elevate its global standing. At home, he staked his legacy on eradicating child malnutrition through his universal free nutritious meals programme – initially projected to cost 450 trillion rupiah (US$25 billion) a year at full scale – and reviving rural economies through Red and White Village Cooperatives, a state-backed network of retail and logistics hubs. For investors, his pitch was that these and other state-led initiatives would create millions of jobs and propel annual GDP growth to 8 per cent, with sovereign wealth fund Danantara central to his plan to put state assets to work in strategic industries and accelerate development. Abroad, he championed Global South diplomacy in the Brics bloc alongside a pledge to remain a stabilising anchor in Southeast Asia. Yet as Prabowo marked his first 24 months in the top job on Tuesday, those lofty ambitions have collided with harsh realities on all three fronts. An October survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) found that Prabowo’s approval rating had fallen to 44.5 per cent, below the 50 per cent mark for the first time. A separate survey by the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios) found that 75 per cent of respondents felt stressed by government policies, with high prices for basic necessities and a lack of job opportunities among their chief concerns. Simultaneously, a looming global index downgrade has triggered a bruising stock market rout, while raging forest fires have blanketed the region in toxic smog, choking neighbours Malaysia and Singapore. In the face of those challenges, analysts say Prabowo has oscillated between reactive damage control and stubborn resolve. Rather than fundamentally rethink his agenda, he has made adjustments, such as slashing the budget for the free meals programme but refusing to abandon it, and repeatedly reshuffling his cabinet. His government has also sent confusing signals abroad, approving foreign firefighting help to battle the haze before subsequently putting the offers on hold. While ruling party allies defend his adjustments as “dynamic moves” to protect fiscal stability, observers argue they merely paper over the deeper structural flaws of his administration. The question now is whether Prabowo can genuinely change course or whether the setbacks of his second year will define the rest of his term. Prabowo himself remains publicly defiant. Brushing off economic pessimism at a nickel-processing project launch on October 8, he pointed to robust state-backed investments as proof that his administration was succeeding. “Every month, they predict that we will collapse. But today, I have come here and I see a bright future for Indonesia,” he declared. Fraying mandate At the heart of the public mood shift is the troubled roll-out of the signature welfare schemes that once anchored Prabowo’s popularity. The SMRC survey showed that 61 per cent of citizens familiar with the free meals initiative were unhappy with its execution, while 71 per cent doubted the village cooperatives plan would succeed. Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at SMRC, said the poll exposed a broad defection of supporters across all demographic groups, pinpointing mismanagement of the president’s flagship initiatives as the main cause of public censure. Both the free meals initiative and village cooperatives plan “were significant factors”, Saidiman said. Those missteps are glaring to voters like Lugas Limojoyo, 31, a resident of Purwokerto in Central Java who backed Prabowo in 2024 among the three presidential tickets. Lugas, a former hotel chef, described the free meals programme and the cooperatives as Prabowo’s “main red flags”. Pointing to recurring mass food-poisoning cases, he noted a lack of basic food safety protocols – an observation echoed by Indonesia’s food and drug agency, which has repeatedly cited poor sanitation and untrained staff as the primary causes behind thousands of students falling ill. Lugas saw a similar lack of coordination in the village cooperatives initiative, noting that many state-funded warehouses “have already been built but aren’t operational, sitting there like empty husks”. Reuters has also reported concerns from analysts about the scheme’s top-down approach, the commercial viability of some locations and whether the cooperatives can respond to local needs. Still, the programmes retain pockets of support. Anissa Fadhilah, a 29-year-old greengrocer in Surabaya, said she remained satisfied with Prabowo’s performance and would vote for him again in 2029 after her daughter received school meals and her business landed supply commissions from the scheme. “I think [the free meals initiative] has the desired effect of lifting ordinary people economically, so I’m for it,” Anissa said. Officials also defended the administration’s two-year track record. Jasmine Herawan, a spokeswoman for Indonesia’s Government Communications Agency, said the administration had expanded the social safety net, with its free meals programme reaching 57 million recipients, while nearly 1.5 million people had been lifted out of extreme poverty within a year. She also cited gains in food security, saying Indonesia produced 34.71 million tonnes of rice in 2025 without importing any that year. On the extractive sector, Jasmine said: “We’ve also affirmed our mineral sovereignty by setting up a single-door export system for our key commodities.” The system is intended to give the government greater oversight of mineral exports and make it harder for companies to understate the value of what they sell overseas, potentially depriving the state of tax revenue. Market reckoning Costly spending commitments, however, have raised broader concerns about fiscal sustainability. Earlier this year, the government cut 67 trillion rupiah from the free meals programme before imposing further spending curbs across ministries in the final quarter to help keep the budget deficit within its legal ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP. But fiscal tightening did little to reassure investors. On October 16, index provider MSCI warned that Indonesia could be downgraded from “emerging” to “stand-alone” market status over concerns about opaque corporate ownership and trading manipulation, triggering a bruising sell-off in Indonesian assets. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent and the rupiah fell to 18,050 per US dollar. Despite emergency regulatory fines against market manipulators and bourse officials pledging swift governance reforms during a meeting with MSCI on Monday, the benchmark index hit a six-year low this week, as investors continued to digest the warning and the risk of billions of dollars in passive capital outflows. Siwage Dharma Negara, co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said regional investors continued to view Prabowo’s economic policy as unpredictable. “He will not give up his populist programmes, like the free meals and rural cooperatives, but it is not clear what the economic benefit for the country will be,” Siwage said. Siwage noted that the recent fiscal correction was too small to satisfy investors, many of whom viewed the free meals as a waste of state resources that should be redirected towards education, health or struggling regional governments. “Prabowo fundamentally does not trust anyone else to advise him on economic direction,” Siwage said, warning that such moves were creating a poor investment climate. “If we want to restore market confidence, the most urgent fix is reducing this state intervention in the economy.” Inside Prabowo’s ruling Gerindra party, lawmakers reject assertions that the administration’s economic agenda is faltering. Gerindra spokesman Sugiat Santoso dismissed Celios’ two-year study as “over the top” and “deliberately dramatised” to create mass panic. Defending the village cooperatives as a path to financial independence for disadvantaged communities and the free meals as an ongoing investment in future generations, Sugiat added, “The president is definitely not here to please analysts, but to bring about real changes for the welfare of the people.” Musical chairs Unwilling to abandon his core populist pledges, Prabowo has instead turned to frequent personnel changes to tighten his grip on the bureaucracy – reshuffling his cabinet or installing new officials three times in the first two weeks of October alone, bringing his total number of cabinet shake-ups to eight in two years. Arya Fernandes, head of politics and social change at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia, said these shake-ups stemmed from the president’s underlying political vulnerability – specifically Gerindra’s lack of parliamentary dominance and the lingering influence of his predecessor, Joko Widodo. This has forced Prabowo to consolidate power by accommodating a wide political spectrum, Arya noted. But the high cost of maintaining that stability – through an oversized cabinet and increased military budgets – has driven up fiscal pressure and forced the central government to slash local funding. “In sum, Prabowo has secured elite support and lost mass support,” he said. Yoes C. Kenawas, a researcher at Lembaga Survei Indonesia, said this dynamic reflected a leader whose authoritarian instincts make him insecure about elite loyalty. “He remains deeply paranoid about elite betrayal and being backstabbed by coalition partners,” Yoes said. “Even with an 80 per cent parliamentary majority, he does not feel secure.” Siwage said swapping out officials would not solve the administration’s deeper flaws: “We have seen many cabinet reshuffles so far, and he will likely continue shuffling officials, thinking a new person will fix the problem. But the real issue is that the entire system of governance is currently ineffective at implementing sound economic policy.” Fanning flames Nowhere has that administrative strain spilled beyond Indonesia’s borders more visibly than in the transboundary haze crisis. Since August, severe forest and peatland fires across Sumatra and Kalimantan have sent thick smoke across the region, forcing school closures in Malaysia, prompting diplomatic protests and leading Singapore’s prime minister to warn of action against errant companies. Siwage linked the resurgence of the fires directly to Prabowo’s domestic fiscal squeeze, which he said left local governments “without enough operational funds to fight the fires”. For months, Jakarta resisted regional offers of firefighting help, while public remarks by officials only inflamed tensions – most notably when the newly appointed communications agency head suggested neighbours should remember Indonesia’s forests “send oxygen” when there is no haze. Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in West Sumatra, says the episode highlights a stark contrast: while Prabowo frequently travels globally, “Asean does not seem to be a priority”. Pointing to the president’s failure to apologise or engage with regional counterparts over the pollution, Rifki said it suggested the bloc “might not be among Prabowo’s interests”. He attributed Jakarta’s reluctance to accept outside help to Prabowo’s suspicion of foreign involvement and repeated rhetoric blaming “foreign agents”. A diplomatic thaw seemingly arrived on October 15 when Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir announced Prabowo had approved regional firefighting help. But the administration later abruptly backtracked when security chief Dudung Abdurachman put the offers on hold, declaring Indonesia was “still capable” of managing the blazes. Prabowo then railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over the wildfires, amid growing public anger and calls for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said on Wednesday. ⁠⁠Prabowo also told his cabinet ‌on Wednesday that MSCI was trying ⁠to “scare us”, adding ‌that Indonesia was “not afraid” ‌and would not ⁠buckle, Reuters reported. Despite plunging approval ratings, a market sell-off and diplomatic fires, Yoes warned Prabowo might not feel compelled to change course because the pain of his second-year slump had not hit his immediate political centre. “The crisis is fragmented,” Yoes said. “The toxic haze chokes Sumatra and Kalimantan, but it does not blanket Jakarta or Java.” Because the distress was clustered outside the capital, it looked manageable on paper, he added, “but underneath the surface, this is a crisis in the making”. Defiance or adaptation Analysts say moving beyond short-term diplomatic firefighting to rebuild his popular mandate and calm financial markets over the remaining three years of his term could depend on Prabowo’s willingness to look outside his inner circle. So far, however, the president has framed mounting resistance not as a symptom of policy missteps but as a manufactured campaign by entrenched elites bankrolling paid protesters and online influencers – known locally as “buzzers”. “We have no doubts. Even if they have hundreds of trillions of rupiah, they pay buzzers, they pay for algorithms, they attack us on social media, and they finance demonstrations, we are not afraid. We stand with the people, we are ready to die for the people,” Prabowo said during a fiery speech on October 6. That defiant posture worries observers who believe Prabowo must adapt his approach to meet the challenges he is facing. SMRC’s Saidiman argued that reversing the polling slide would require structural reform – starting with shrinking the cabinet, pulling back from the ongoing militarisation of the civilian sphere and conducting a “radical review of the administration’s costly yet ineffective populist programmes”. “The president needs to step up and enact fundamental changes to how he governs the nation,” Saidiman said, adding Prabowo “should let opposition forces fulfil their function as a democracy should”. Siwage warned that without an effective parliamentary opposition to check the president’s instincts, financial market tremors could eventually spiral into a wider political reckoning. “Prabowo currently controls most of the government coalition and the parliament. With essentially no opposition, why would he change course when nobody dares to oppose his policies?” he said. Outside Jakarta’s corridors of power, voters who helped put Prabowo in the presidential palace say he still has a window to turn things around – if he starts listening to ordinary Indonesians. In Central Java, Lugas urged the president to break out of his palace echo chamber. “My suggestion for Prabowo is to cross-check the reports he gets from those closest to him, because obviously he is only being fed information on the good things,” he said. And in Bekasi, despite feeling let down by rising living costs, Ika said she was not ready to give up on Prabowo’s presidency just yet. “Maybe these are growing pains for us,” she said. “I’m still optimistic about Prabowo’s leadership and I pray he won’t prove me wrong.”

content: In late September, Singapore’s Reddit community erupted over the government’s new dating platform, FirstDate. Curious to get an insider’s perspective, I visited the site, connected to my Singpass account and watched as my name, age and marital status auto-populated the fields on the page. I entered my Gmail address and hit submit. The email field turned red: “Please sign up with your official work email. Personal email addresses will not be accepted.” I resubmitted the form with my work email, only to be told my agency was not included in the pilot. “We appreciate your interest,” the screen said. With that, I gave up. FirstDate is the Singapore government’s latest attempt to help its people find love, with one eye on the growing number of singles and the other on the declining birth rate. The platform uses an algorithm based on Nobel Prize-winning research and offers users one curated match per cycle. Its website promises “swipe fatigue ends here”. Singapore has tried this before. In 1984, Lee Kuan Yew’s government set up the Social Development Unit to match graduates in the civil service. Apart from a brief rise in the late 1980s, fertility has fallen steadily since. Singapore is not alone in turning matchmaking into a public-policy project. Tokyo’s metropolitan government has introduced an AI matchmaking app. Seoul runs its city-led “Seoulting 2.0” matchmaking programme, while Taipei’s city government organises “Taipei Love Academy” singles events, citing a declining birth rate as a “security crisis”. Across much of Asia, governments are treating singlehood as an ailment to alleviate. The underlying assumption is that love is a search problem: the right people are out there and simply haven’t found each other. If dating is seen as a first step towards marriage and parenthood, the outlook leaves little room for optimism. Fertility rates across much of the region remain well below the replacement level of 2.1 births per woman. Matchmaking services and government-run introductions can help people find each other, but they are insufficient on their own. Governments are trying to fix a shortage of free evenings with a surplus of matches. A late end to the working day leaves little room for people to date. South Korea has some of the longest working hours among advanced economies, Japan has taken some small steps to ease its notorious workaholic culture and the 996 work culture – working from 9am to 9pm, six days a week – is entrenched across much of China. In many workplaces, staying late is seen as commitment and a reply at midnight as diligence. Young people are doing what the system rewards. It’s hard to put relationships at the centre of their lives when the entire culture of work is built around marathon hours. Granted, more free time will not resolve every barrier to relationships. Housing concerns, financial anxiety and expectations about a partner’s earning potential will remain. Even so, time is a necessary starting point: without it, even people who want relationships have fewer opportunities to build them. The same work-centred culture that consumes people’s evenings can also shape what they look for in a partner. When professional achievement sets the terms of success, dating becomes priced by credentials. Going on a date can feel like a job interview. With little time to get to know someone, each encounter can begin to feel like a high-stakes assessment. Occupation and income act as proxies for stability, while credentials offer a short cut for judging compatibility. These can be useful signals, but they can also narrow the field of people we are willing to consider. In Shanghai, the xiangqin, or matchmaking, corner of People’s Park displays prospective partners’ degrees, incomes and flat sizes. In Hong Kong, getting on the property ladder is often treated as a prerequisite for settling down. Singapore’s “5Cs” – cash, car, credit card, condominium and country club – serve as a shorthand for a similar fixation on material success. None of these are inherently unreasonable. Financial stability matters when people are considering building a life together. The problem arises when credentials become the first filter, displacing interest in the person behind them. Changing how we date requires more than individual resolve. People make choices within environments shaped by employers, societal norms and public policy. If we want to make room for relationships, governments should examine the incentives that govern how we work. One change could begin with resetting workplace culture and expectations. Paul Yip Siu-fai of the University of Hong Kong’s Faculty of Social Sciences has proposed that governments support family-friendly workplaces through flexible hours and arrangements. The public sector matters as it sets norms for what supportive workplaces and work-life balance can look like. Predictable hours, protected time off and firm limits on overtime could be the default rather than the exception in the civil service. Governments could then encourage the private sector to take a similar approach through measures such as tripartite guidelines and tax incentives. Tokyo’s metropolitan government, for example, has offered staff the option of a four-day week alongside its matchmaking initiative. Governments could go further by running a protected-hours pilot alongside matchmaking schemes like FirstDate, then comparing which moves more people towards a relationship. FirstDate’s website ends with a shrug: “Where it goes from there is up to you.” No government can mandate a spark, but it can stop workplaces from crowding out relationships. If the state wants young people to fall in love, it should start by giving them something a matchmaking algorithm cannot: the time and space to make it happen.

content: Authorities in the Philippines are investigating Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, the ⁠wife of Britain’s Prince ⁠Harry, the Philippine justice undersecretary said ⁠on Friday, after allegations he possessed child sexual abuse images. “Our Anti-Trafficking and Anti-OSAEC (online sexual abuse and exploitation of children) task force in Cebu is currently investigating the matter,” Nicholas Ty, Philippine justice undersecretary, said. Thomas Markle could not be immediately reached for comment but he ‌was quoted by the Daily Mail newspaper in Britain as saying the allegations against him were untrue and “sick lies”. Meghan, who married King Charles’ younger son and whose royal title is the Duchess of Sussex, said she was “deeply distressed” over the allegations, first published in Britain’s The Sun newspaper on Friday. According to The Sun, Meghan’s half-brother reported his father to police in the city of ⁠Cebu in the Philippines where Thomas Markle had been living, after finding a huge collection of child sexual ‌abuse images in his father’s house. Meghan said in a statement she had known about the allegations against her father, 82, since 2018 and had prevented him ‌having contact with her children Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five to protect them. She has been ⁠out of contact ⁠with her father since the run-up to her 2018 wedding. Days before the event, Thomas Markle said he would not attend due ‌to ill health after he earlier admitted posing for paparazzi pictures. Philippine Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla said it was Markle’s son, Meghan’s ⁠half-brother, who is also called Thomas, ⁠who provided police with evidence of the allegations, including a laptop, confirming details in The Sun newspaper. Meghan’s father, who had lived in Cebu in the Philippines for ‌some time, was now believed to be back in the US, Remulla added. Meghan said she was shown a letter which had been sent ‌to British police ‌in 2018 with “troubling and disturbing” allegations about her father, adding that she was told they were being ‌investigated. British police said they were aware of “media reports ‌that officers from the Met’s Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018”. “We are ⁠undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this,” a spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said. “I am deeply distressed at the news ⁠that has come to light in the last 24 hours and my thoughts are with any children ⁠who may have been harmed,” Meghan said. “My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” she added. The Sun ‌also said Thomas Markle’s ‌son had contacted the FBI in the United States over the allegations. The Federal Bureau of Investigation did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Harry, Meghan and their children relocated to England in August after living in California for six years.

title: France unrest sparks travel jitters for Southeast Asian tourists
description: Fatimah Zainal had already paid for her flights and accommodation when videos of the unrest in France made her jittery about the Paris leg of her European holiday. “The videos definitely made me panic,” said Fatimah, who plans to visit the French capital solo from October 31 to November 3 after travelling through Belgium. content: Fatimah Zainal had already paid for her flights and accommodation when videos of the unrest in France made her jittery about the Paris leg of her European holiday. “The videos definitely made me panic,” said Fatimah, who plans to visit the French capital solo from October 31 to November 3 after travelling through Belgium. The press officer for an international organisation said the Malaysian government’s travel advisory gave her second thoughts, and changing her flight would cost up to an additional 1,200 ringgit (US$293). Friends living in Paris encouraged her not to cancel, but she has told her travel agency she may need to change her plans if conditions do not improve. Nationwide protests against rising living costs last week descended into chaos and riots in major French cities, prompting multiple Asian governments to issue safety warnings. The travel alerts come as inbound tourism from Southeast Asia to France is experiencing an uneven recovery. Tracked air-passenger numbers from six countries in the region totalled 196,091 in 2025, almost unchanged from the previous year’s 196,824, and 22 per cent below 2019, data from France’s national tourism development agency, Atout France, showed. Malaysia recorded the strongest growth among the six markets, rising 55.4 per cent year on year from 14,938 to 23,219 last year. Vietnam increased 15 per cent to 27,403, while the Philippines rose 6.4 per cent to 20,351. In terms of volume, Singapore remained the largest market with 63,726 passengers, down 14.9 per cent from 74,859 in 2024. Indonesia and Thailand also saw smaller declines at 3.5 and 4.7 per cent, respectively. While the Asia market outside China accounts for a small share of tourism arrivals to the European nation, French tourism authorities are seeking to cultivate this long-haul segment for its high-end travel potential. China’s embassy and consulates in France, meanwhile, renewed their warning ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations, urging Chinese visitors to stay away from protest areas, heed police instructions and leave promptly if trouble arises. Malaysia’s foreign ministry last week said citizens should consider postponing non-essential trips until conditions improved, although travel to France remained unrestricted. Indonesia, Thailand and Japan have also cautioned their citizens against unnecessary travel to France and other affected European countries, resulting in some itinerary changes. Singapore’s Dynasty Travel told broadcaster CNA that fewer than 10 France trips had been amended over concerns about the protests, with no outright cancellations. The agency added it was prepared to reschedule evening activities, change transport arrangements or move travellers away from affected areas. Another Singaporean agency, Chan Brothers Travel, also said it had no protest-related cancellations, noting that its November and December tour groups were proceeding as planned, subject to adjustments if conditions changed. In Vietnam, some prospective customers were delaying booking European tours while searching for more information, travel agency Hoang Viet Travel’s deputy director Luu Thi Thu told local media. She said October tours were proceeding and a France-Switzerland-Italy group arrived home safely on Monday. Atout France told This Week in Asia that travel figures from non-China Asia segments were indicators rather than comprehensive visitor counts. The numbers also did not factor land route entries or flight bookings, which, according to travel analytics firm ForwardKeys, constituted a single trip between France and the visitor’s country of origin. “Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand appear to have reached their post-pandemic peak in 2023, driven by pent-up travel demand following the Covid-19 pandemic. Since then, passenger numbers seem to have begun to stabilise,” Atout France said. “Malaysia and the Philippines, by contrast, have continued to show steady growth, which may be partly attributed to the introduction of new direct flights operated by Malaysia Airlines and Air France.” Atout France said Southeast Asian visitors were significant to the country’s upscale hospitality sector as they mostly favour hotels rated four stars and above. Figures on how much Southeast Asian travellers spend in France were not immediately available. However, Japanese visitors spent €618 million (US$691.8 million) in 2024 and their Chinese counterparts about €3.46 billion (US$3.87 billion) in 2019. France recorded €77.5 billion in international tourism receipts in 2025. French reassurances A spokesman for the French embassy in Malaysia said there was no reason for travellers to reconsider their trips as the situation was under control. The representative said measures, including curfews and additional security forces, were deployed to protect people and businesses. The embassy said the government “will not allow violence and looting to take hold. Restoring order is the top priority, without infringing on civil liberties”. The spokesman added that “a very clear distinction must be made between rioters and protesters”, calling the latter’s demands and concerns “legitimate”. But for Malaysian national Fatimah, the decision will come closer to departure. “I will play it by ear and see nearer the date whether the situation is OK or otherwise,” she said. “It still looks unstable, but it’s OK lah I will keep monitoring.”

title: What Indonesia’s warnings of energy cuts mean for Asean
description: Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources. On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia. “Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in...
content: Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources. On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia. “Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” said Bahlil at the launch of a gas facility, as reported by local media. A day earlier, he told reporters that Indonesia was considering not renewing natural gas export contracts with neighbouring countries to prioritise domestic energy needs. Bahlil, who is also the minister of energy and mineral resources, did not name any countries on either occasion. Mirza Huda, a senior research fellow at the climate and sustainability programme at think tank ODI Global, said Indonesia’s remarks were likely to put neighbouring countries who imported natural gas from Jakarta – such as Singapore, Thailand and the Philippines – on notice. Among member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Singapore was the largest importer of natural gas from Jakarta last year at 3.22 million tonnes, according to statistics agency BPS. Thailand and the Philippines imported 291,000 tonnes and 138,000 tonnes respectively. Victor Nian, founding co-chairman of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources, cites Singapore as arguably the most exposed to potential non-renewal of natural gas contracts, given that its deal with Indonesia is set to expire at the end of 2028. But the city state had diversified supplies through liquefied natural gas imports for global markets, and losing the Jakarta pipeline was likely to risk higher energy costs rather than a supply crisis, he said. Dinita Setyawati, senior Asia energy analyst at Ember, pointed out that breaching gas contracts before expiry would lead to losses for Indonesia. The warnings underscored the vulnerability of being dependent on imported gas, she said, urging investments in renewable energy and relevant technologies to serve as buffers. “Fossil fuels are molecules that cannot be reproduced.” Resource nationalism Bahlil’s remarks come as Indonesia grapples with a stock-market rout and its worst haze episode in over a decade. Jakarta has responded to the crises with public shows of nationalism. President Prabowo Subianto this week called out global index MSCI, which warned that Indonesia’s economy could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status. “MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!” During a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prabowo also slammed countries he said liked to snub his nation over intensifying wildfires. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” he said. Jakarta has reportedly held off accepting offers of help from Singapore and Malaysia to tackle the fires, which have plagued many countries in the region. Melinda Martinus, a fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s Asean Studies Centre, noted that the current transboundary haze situation might lead to the perception that Indonesia was targeting Singapore with its latest warnings. She said resource nationalism was not new in Indonesia, citing recent moves such as the establishment of Danantara Sumber Daya Indonesia by the Indonesian government to supervise commodity exports. The mineral-rich country has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy. Jakarta has also restricted palm oil exports on several occasions to safeguard domestic supply and prevent excessive price rises. “This form of resource nationalism is often framed by politicians as a means of helping Indonesia achieve its ambition of becoming a high-income country,” she said. Jakarta’s warnings reflected a broader and intensifying trend towards resource sovereignty among commodity producers, said Kaho Yu, head of energy and resources research at Verisk Maplecroft. “Southeast Asian countries reliant on Indonesian gas will need to strengthen supplier engagement and diversify their energy sources,” he said, urging states to vary suppliers and start early negotiations for long-term contracts. Nian cautioned that Bahlil’s remarks risked setting the precedent of attaching prerequisites to energy exports. On Thursday, the minister said Indonesia remained open to signing energy export agreements with countries that treated it as an equal, even if they did not have existing contracts with Jakarta. “Indonesia has every right to prioritise domestic energy security and maximise the economic benefits of its natural resources,” Nian said. “But making energy exports conditional on political ‘respect’ goes beyond legitimate resource nationalism and raises the troubling prospect of weaponising strategic resources.” Impact on Asean cooperation Observers say while Indonesia’s warnings are unlikely to hinder progress on regional frameworks such as the Asean Power Grid, they highlight the need for stronger dispute resolution mechanisms. The regional grid, first conceptualised in 1997, aims to connect the electricity networks of all 11 member states through overland and undersea links. It is expected to boost the economy of exporters while strengthening the energy security of those who receive the supply. “The fundamental premise of the power grid remains strong,” Martinus said. “Under such arrangements, everyone should benefit.” But Nian said Jakarta’s warnings risked impeding the advancement of the regional grid, which required substantial investment and mutual confidence in the long term. “The prospect of politically motivated supply disruptions could increase investment risks, financing costs and hesitation over deeper regional energy integration.” Mirza said the incident highlighted the need for long-term agreements, continued dialogue and a regional dispute resolution mechanism to address potential disagreements over electricity trade. The grid has seen gradual progress – only eight of 18 planned interconnection projects were operational in 2024, according to the Asean Power Centre – but leaders of member states seem to be pushing it up the agenda list. The Asean summit in May set out a new target of full operationalisation across all member states by 2045. Dinita was confident that discussions on the power grid would continue as usual. “As long as Indonesia stands to benefit, be it from electricity exports or toll rates for transmission lines, negotiations will continue,” she said.

title: Economic fears fuel protests in India, France as ‘social contract’ breaks down
description: Recent youth-led protests in New Delhi and other cities in India have fuelled allegations that they are connected to unrest in France and elsewhere in Europe, with an influential Hindu nationalist organisation warning of foreign forces seeking to destabilise societies. While analysts caution against concluding that foreign interference played a role in demonstrations in India, they say protesters in Europe and India share similar concerns, reflecting their mounting anger that education and hard...
content: Recent youth-led protests in New Delhi and other cities in India have fuelled allegations that they are connected to unrest in France and elsewhere in Europe, with an influential Hindu nationalist organisation warning of foreign forces seeking to destabilise societies. While analysts caution against concluding that foreign interference played a role in demonstrations in India, they say protesters in Europe and India share similar concerns, reflecting their mounting anger that education and hard work no longer guarantee them economic security or social mobility. In an address to mark the Hindu festival of Vijayadashami on Tuesday, Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, said: “A storm has swept in from the West, driven by a demonic resolve to destroy and devastate all that is decent, auspicious and rooted in cultural and human values, both in Bharat [India] and across the world.” He cited protests in France, Albania, Nepal and Bangladesh as examples of attempts to bring about a change in government without offering solutions to societal problems. Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged the Indian people in his own Vijayadashami address on the same day to unite against “the enemies of Mother India” that attacked the country’s dignity, divide society or harbour hatred towards its culture. He did not refer to the unrest in Europe in his comments. Modi later praised Bhagwat’s address as “very motivating”. A Fox News Digital investigation has alleged links between the protests in France and India, describing what it called a “red-green protest ecosystem”. It said it had identified 101 organisations involved in coordinating, organising or amplifying protests, citing groups it said had unified the same protest messages in the two countries. In India, students protested in Delhi in June and July, calling for an overhaul of the education system to improve transparency and accountability. Earlier this month, thousands of young Indians and opposition supporters in Delhi and Mumbai protested against alleged irregularities over revisions to electoral rolls, saying such a move would disenfranchise eligible voters. They demanded the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who defended the move and said it would remove duplicate and ineligible entries. Some of the protests were spearheaded by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), whose name was sparked by remarks by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who reportedly referred to people with fake or bogus degrees as “cockroaches”. The comments were widely interpreted as a swipe at young Indians struggling with education and employment, two key issues that the CJP has championed. In France, hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations over cost of living, public services and school conditions, beginning last month. The interior ministry estimated that about 550,000 people joined 110 marches on October 17, when the protests were at their height, while organisers put the turnout at 800,000. Cedomir Nestorovic, a Singapore-based professor of geopolitics at ESSEC Business School, said the protests in France and India pointed to a breakdown of the “social contract” linking education to upward social mobility. Citing challenges in the education system as a spark, Nestorovic said: “In both nations, the younger generation senses that the traditional promise – that working hard within the educational system guarantees economic security and middle-class stability – is breaking down.” Nestorovic said that while economic pressures were a trigger for the demonstrations in the two countries, the protesters in India were also demanding democratic accountability. “In France, the movement fundamentally defends the traditional public welfare state against government austerity, centring on protecting public resources, capping class sizes and resisting budget cuts,” he said. “In India, the primary demand centres on systemic fairness and administrative integrity,” he added. Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, cautioned against drawing too many parallels between the protests. “The French protests have a much stronger political element, including not just students but also opportunists from the French left, as well as more unsavoury elements of society taking advantage of the chaos to loot and pillage,” he said. Praveen Rai, academic secretary of the India-based Centre for the Study of Developing Societies, argued that the demonstrations in India were being driven more by opposition parties than by young people. “Frequent street protests and anti-statism disrupt routine government functioning, cause hardships to common people and degrade economic growth,” he said. Rai said left-wing and socialist forces, along with civil society groups opposed to right-wing and centrist politics, were capitalising on economic grievances to mobilise opposition against the government. “Unemployment, higher cost of living and growing economic divide are major problems but movements against these issues are restricted to some urban areas and are not pan-Indian,” he added. Christopher Blackburn, a London-based independent political commentator, said that while concerns about potential external influence were legitimate, allegations of its link to the protests would require evidence. He said the appropriate response was for authorities to respect the right to peaceful demonstrations and facilitate dialogue to address the protesters’ grievances. “India’s electoral and federal institutions provide resilience, but leaders should not take that for granted,” Blackburn said. Shawn Balakrishnan, a partner for Asia at Penta Group, said a major risk for the governments in India and France was an erosion of trust in institutions due to dissatisfaction with specific policies. “For India, sustained youth discontent could undermine the government’s narrative of economic progress, particularly if growth fails to deliver jobs and upward mobility,” he said. The challenge could be more immediate in France, where student mobilisation could converge with wider labour and public-sector grievances, increasing political pressure ahead of the 2027 presidential election, Balakrishnan said. Tiziano Marino, a Rome-based adviser to the Observatory on India, said the impact of the protests in India was likely to emerge over the medium to long term. “In France, by contrast, the protests are already playing a central role in electoral debate, and their political repercussions are likely to be felt in the short term, shaping the outcome of the presidential election,” he said.

title: Philippines offers US$786,000 bounty for ‘dangerous’ senator wanted by ICC
description: The Philippine government put a bounty on Friday on the head of the top enforcer of ex-president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody anti-drug crackdown, nearly a year after the International Criminal Court (ICC) ordered his arrest.
