The bounty comes just over a month before...
content: The Philippine government put a bounty on Friday on the head of the top enforcer of ex-president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody anti-drug crackdown, nearly a year after the International Criminal Court (ICC) ordered his arrest. Former Philippine police chief and sitting Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa had mostly been in hiding for months before The Hague-based tribunal unsealed the November 2025 arrest warrant against him in May and put him into flight. The bounty comes just over a month before Duterte is to stand trial on November 30 for the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder. “As of today, Senator Bato will be considered armed and dangerous. We are placing a bounty of 50 million pesos (US$786,000) for his capture,” Interior Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla told a Friday news conference. Remulla said Dela Rosa “has shown nothing but cowardice by going into and remaining in hiding”, adding: “It’s time for the gloves to come off. It’s time to bring justice to his victims.” Dela Rosa emerged from months of hiding on May 11 to take refuge inside the Senate building, but slipped out days later following a stand-off between security guards and investigators attempting to arrest him, in which shots were fired. Former president Duterte was arrested in Manila on March 11 last year and handed over the following day to the ICC. He has been in detention in The Hague ever since. Dela Rosa was named as among eight “co-perpetrators” in the drug crackdown that took place during the Duterte presidency from 2016 as well as during his earlier stint as mayor of a southern city. Philippine police have said they killed more than 6,000 drug suspects in self-defence during his presidency, which ended in 2022. Among the other co-perpetrators named by the ICC is sitting Senator Christopher Lawrence Go, though there is no known ICC arrest warrant against him. Philippine police chief Jose Melencio Nartatez said on Friday that Dela Rosa was possibly being protected “by an armed group or group of supporters”, warning that those shielding him would “face the consequences”. He said a dedicated task force had been formed to track him down and hand him over to the ICC. Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, with prosecutors alleging his involvement in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018. The true number of killings during his campaign in the Philippines is thought to be in the thousands and lawyers for the victims have argued that a full trial could encourage more families to come forward.

title: Paper straws worse for the environment than plastic, South Korea study finds
description: Paper straws, widely promoted as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic, may actually have a greater environmental impact than conventional plastic straws, according to a South Korean government-commissioned study that has renewed debate over whether switching materials truly reduces waste. The Comprehensive Study on Single-Use Straws, commissioned by South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, was disclosed on Wednesday by opposition People Power Party lawmaker Kim Wi-sang, The...
content: Paper straws, widely promoted as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic, may actually have a greater environmental impact than conventional plastic straws, according to a South Korean government-commissioned study that has renewed debate over whether switching materials truly reduces waste. The Comprehensive Study on Single-Use Straws, commissioned by South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, was disclosed on Wednesday by opposition People Power Party lawmaker Kim Wi-sang, The Korea Herald reported. The study found that paper straws had 6.33 times the carcinogenic impact of conventional plastic straws. That figure measures the potential cancer risk from emissions across a product’s entire life cycle – from raw material production to disposal – rather than health risks from direct use. Paper straws were also found to have 2.04 times the acidification impact, a metric assessing emissions’ potential to increase environmental acidity and harm ecosystems. Researchers evaluated four types of straws: conventional plastic, paper, biodegradable plastic and bio-based polythene. The life-cycle assessment covered 16 categories, including greenhouse gas emissions, human toxicity, particulate matter and acidification. Biodegradable plastic straws carried 3.34 times higher carcinogenic risk and 1.98 times the acidification impact compared with conventional plastic straws. Bio-based polystyrene – a material derived from renewable plant sources that remains chemically identical to conventional plastic and is non-biodegradable – performed the worst overall. It carried 16.18 times the risk of cancer development, 5.9 times the acidification impact and registered the highest impact in 10 of the 16 evaluation categories. In contrast, conventional plastic straws recorded the lowest environmental impact in 10 categories, including climate change, human toxicity, particulate matter and acidification. The study also found that recycling straws was virtually impossible regardless of material, local outlet SBS News reported. The assessment’s findings reflect national waste statistics showing that 73.6 per cent of discarded straws in South Korea are incinerated, while 26.4 per cent go to landfills. Kim urged the South Korean government to scrap “meaningless” regulations that merely swapped materials, calling instead for practical policies aimed at reducing single-use consumption at the source. The findings come as South Korea continues to struggle to implement a consistent policy on single-use items. Seoul first announced a ban on plastic straws in 2021 before delaying its implementation in 2022 and postponing enforcement indefinitely in 2023, according to The Korea Times. In 2025, the government decided that plastic and paper straws would only be provided upon customer request, local daily JoongAng Ilbo reported. Governments across Asia and Europe have taken varying approaches to curbing plastic straw waste. Taiwan banned single-use plastic straws in 2019, according to its environment ministry. Japan passed legislation in 2022 requiring convenience stores and restaurants to come up with plans to cut plastic consumption, The Japan News reported. In Hong Kong, a ban took effect in 2024 prohibiting restaurants from providing plastic straws to customers in favour of non-plastic alternatives, such as paper. The European Union banned single-use plastic straws across its member states in 2021, encouraging consumers to switch to reusable, paper or compostable alternatives. Despite their widespread adoption as part of global efforts to reduce plastic use, paper straws have drawn increasing backlash from consumers over their durability and questionable environmental benefits. The debate has reached high-level politics; in 2025, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order promoting plastic straws, saying paper alternatives “don’t work” and reversing anti-plastic policies introduced under his predecessor, Joe Biden, Reuters reported.

title: How the Philippines’ energy crisis is opening doors for deeper US military ties
description: The Philippines is turning to the United States to build its oil stockpile amid the global energy crunch, with observers saying the move could also serve Washington’s military interests and deepen strategic ties. A bilateral deal could deliver more immediate benefits than a broader Asean stockpile, which would entail coordination hurdles, analysts said, but questions remain over how quickly Manila could establish such a reserve and whether it would meaningfully reduce long-term dependence on...
content: The Philippines is turning to the United States to build its oil stockpile amid the global energy crunch, with observers saying the move could also serve Washington’s military interests and deepen strategic ties. A bilateral deal could deliver more immediate benefits than a broader Asean stockpile, which would entail coordination hurdles, analysts said, but questions remain over how quickly Manila could establish such a reserve and whether it would meaningfully reduce long-term dependence on imported fossil fuels. The Philippines’ Department of Energy Secretary Sharon Garin met her US counterpart, Chris Wright, in Washington on October 15 to discuss cooperation. Her department said in a statement the talks intended “to explore expanded bilateral cooperation aimed at strengthening the Philippines’ energy security, diversifying energy supply and advancing the development of indigenous resources”. As a net oil importer, the Philippines is among the Southeast Asian nations hardest hit by the global energy crisis. Over 95 per cent of its crude oil is imported from the Middle East, according to government data. Garin said Manila’s priority was to ensure “a secure, reliable and affordable energy supply for Filipino families and businesses”. The Philippines currently has no government-owned strategic petroleum reserve and plans to build one by 2027 or 2028. John Paul Flaminiano, a Manila-based economist and research consultant, said a successful agreement would offer “hedging against severe oil price fluctuations and maritime disruptions”. “The US is the largest producer of crude oil and has significant influence in the global oil market. The Philippines already has deep bilateral ties with the US, even more so than some of its Asean neighbours,” Flaminiano said, referring to the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “So although regional cooperation is ideal, the mechanisms to yield near-term benefits that can immediately address supply shocks are still being established.” Such a deal would reinforce bilateral ties between the Philippines and the US, while “positive spillover effects can also be expected from improved, shared technical expertise”, he added. Bilateral convenience The American presence in the Philippines would also be strengthened by a fuel stockpile deal, said Santiago Castillo, a Manila-based defence and security analyst at FACTS Asia. The US could help construct and set up reliable fuel storage and distribution facilities, as well as help with fuel refining, Castillo said. This arrangement was likely to yield significant benefits for both sides, he added. “For the Philippines, additional stocks of petroleum can lessen the shocks of fuel supply imported from the Middle East due to ongoing conflicts there. For the US, additional available fuel supplies improve the sustainment capacity for its forces that are stationed or operating in the country.” A petroleum stockpile deal with the US would require less consultation and coordination due to the bilateral nature of the relationship, Castillo said. “Their formal alliance mechanisms further justify deeper strategic and economic partnerships for their mutual benefit. In addition, the US has a surplus of fuel stocks that it keeps for strategic purposes,” he added. A bilateral stockpiling arrangement was also bound to fare better than efforts to establish a regional mechanism among other Asean members, observers noted. “For Asean, it would be more complicated in addressing fuel stockpiles since not all Asean member states produce enough – or are even unable to produce – petroleum to provide among themselves,” Castillo said, adding that while Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei and Thailand were the region’s main producers, their main focus was on local consumption. Castillo added that part of the support Washington was willing to provide Manila hinged on urging its partner to help shore up economic security, while signalling that Washington remained a reliable partner. “Nevertheless, this also comes with a background of unease as the world watches how US President Trump conducts himself in a manner that tests the resolve of both allies and adversaries,” he said. Chester Cabalza, president and CEO of the Manila-based think tank International Development and Security Cooperation, pointed to the Philippines’ strategic location as a key advantage for closer cooperation with Washington. “The battle of geoeconomic survival lies in strategic petroleum reserves. The crash course lesson in the Strait of Hormuz redefined the naval and tonal movements of major powers as Washington initiates a clearer grand strategy in the Indo-Pacific,” Cabalza said, adding that the country had untapped energy sources from Palawan to Sulu that could offer bright promise for national energy security. But how quickly Manila could benefit from a US-backed stockpile remained uncertain, given that the country only had a single refinery, Castillo said. “In the short term, the Philippines could harness its rich deposits of liquefied natural gas to provide for the energy needs of local consumers on certain products and services while trying to mitigate the consumption of petroleum,” Castillo said. In the long run, he added, there should be a strong push and incentives for alternative and renewable energy use to lessen household dependence on fossil fuels. It should also spur the exploration of emerging technologies, such as microgrids, which could provide much-needed energy security to off-grid or remote areas across the Philippines, he added. Flaminiano shared similar views, adding that any stockpiling effort should work towards gradually decreasing dependence on fossil fuels while transitioning towards more sustainable sources of energy. “This can be achieved by increasing investment, addressing structural and regulatory bottlenecks and strengthening technical capabilities through partnerships,” he said.

title: Malaysia’s oil-rich Sarawak heads to polls, forcing Anwar into yet another federal test
description: Malaysia’s oil-rich Sarawak state will dissolve its assembly on Monday in a test of political strength for a powerful regional coalition whose support has become crucial to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government. Anwar is facing growing pressure following electoral setbacks for his own coalition in Peninsular Malaysia, while over in Borneo, ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) continues to press for greater autonomy and control over the state’s vast oil and gas resources. Sarawak Premier Abang...
content: Malaysia’s oil-rich Sarawak state will dissolve its assembly on Monday in a test of political strength for a powerful regional coalition whose support has become crucial to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government. Anwar is facing growing pressure following electoral setbacks for his own coalition in Peninsular Malaysia, while over in Borneo, ruling Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) continues to press for greater autonomy and control over the state’s vast oil and gas resources. Sarawak Premier Abang Johari Openg announced on Friday that state governor Wan Junaidi Tuanku Jaafar had consented to dissolve the state assembly with effect from Monday, triggering an election that must be held within 60 days. “As we approach the completion of this term, it is only appropriate that a new mandate from the people is obtained,” Abang Johari told a press conference in Kuching. “The people of Sarawak must have the opportunity to exercise their democratic right to choose and elect a new government with a fresh mandate to continue the development agenda of Sarawak.” He said the state government would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until the election, with public services continuing as usual. The Election Commission will determine the nomination and polling dates. GPS, which controls 80 of the 82 seats in the outgoing assembly, has governed Sarawak since 2018, when it broke away from the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition following the latter’s historic defeat in the general election. The coalition won 76 seats in the December 2021 state election before expanding its dominance through defections and political realignments. The opposition Democratic Action Party (DAP), a component of Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, holds the remaining two seats. Sarawak first The election carries significance beyond Sarawak, where GPS has emerged as one of Malaysia’s most influential political blocs despite remaining largely outside the partisan battles of Peninsular Malaysia. Its parliamentary support helped Anwar form his government after the inconclusive 2022 general election, giving Sarawak considerable influence in federal politics and strengthening its hand in long-standing negotiations over the state’s rights. Under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63) – which established the federation with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore joining Malaya – the Borneo states were granted special safeguards and powers. Sarawak has increasingly sought to reclaim rights it argues have been eroded over the decades. At the centre of those demands is control over the state’s lucrative petroleum industry, with Sarawak’s state-owned Petros pushing for a greater role alongside national energy giant Petronas. The dispute has become a sensitive issue for Anwar, whose government must balance Sarawak’s demands with the interests of Petronas, a major contributor to federal revenue. During Malaysia Day celebrations in Sarawak capital Kuching last month, Anwar called for commercial arrangements between the two companies to be finalised. The federal government has also agreed in principle to increase parliamentary representation for Sabah and Sarawak – subject to further discussions and constitutional procedures. A decisive victory would further strengthen GPS’ bargaining position, according to political analyst James Chin, pointing to the coalition’s increasingly secure grip on the state assembly. “They’re very [confident] … Now they’re talking about losing just two or three,” the professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania said. “The stronger they are at the state level, the easier it is for them to negotiate at the federal level.” Sarawak-born Chin said GPS preferred working with Anwar’s government for now, but its allegiance could shift depending on the outcome of the next general election. “They don’t owe loyalties to any side. Whoever wins the vote in Peninsula Malaysia or cobbles together the coalition in Peninsula Malaysia, they’ll jump into the coalition,” he said. “Their No 1 priority is Sarawak. In other words, they must be part of any federal government in order to negotiate for MA63 and other concessions.” Barriers to entry Azmi Hassan, a political analyst at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said GPS had made a strong case to voters that Sarawak was better off governed by local parties, leaving little room for opposition parties from the mainland. “The main theme of its campaign ... is that GPS has done very well in terms of not only managing their wealth, but also [forcing] the federal government into giving their rights, especially those in the MA63 agreement,” he said. The bigger question, Azmi added, would be whether opposition parties, particularly Anwar’s ally DAP, could make any headway against GPS. Malaysian politics is going through an unsettled period. Anwar’s PH coalition has lost ground in successive state contests even as its federal partners have consolidated their own positions. In July, BN swept 48 of Johor’s 56 assembly seats, leaving PH with just eight. The following month, PH lost six seats in Negeri Sembilan, where BN emerged as the largest bloc. The setbacks followed last November’s election in neighbouring Sabah, where Anwar’s PH suffered a crushing defeat, winning just one of the 22 seats it contested, while the regional Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) coalition retained power under Chief Minister Hajiji Noor. Anwar’s next political test comes on November 14, when Melaka heads to the polls. BN and the Islamist Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party have explored cooperation in the Peninsular Malaysian state despite belonging to rival political camps at the federal level.

title: Indonesian wildfires threaten world’s oldest cave paintings in Sulawesi
description: The world’s oldest cave paintings on the Indonesian island ⁠of Sulawesi are under threat ⁠as heat and smoke from the ⁠country’s worst wildfires in more than a decade risk accelerating the deterioration of the more than 67,000-year-old works of art, according to researchers. Indonesia is battling its most intense forest and land fires since 2015 as a severe El Nino drives up temperatures and reduces ‌rainfall, leaving its forest and peatland vulnerable to fire. While the islands of Sumatra and...
content: The world’s oldest cave paintings on the Indonesian island ⁠of Sulawesi are under threat ⁠as heat and smoke from the ⁠country’s worst wildfires in more than a decade risk accelerating the deterioration of the more than 67,000-year-old works of art, according to researchers. Indonesia is battling its most intense forest and land fires since 2015 as a severe El Nino drives up temperatures and reduces ‌rainfall, leaving its forest and peatland vulnerable to fire. While the islands of Sumatra and Borneo are the worst affected by the disaster, fires have also spread on the island of Sulawesi, including in South Sulawesi where limestone caves house the world’s oldest prehistoric art. In a cave in South Sulawesi’s Maros-Pangkep, an artwork depicting human-like figures interacting with a pig was dated ⁠by researchers from Australia’s Griffith University to be at least 51,200 years old. In a cave on Muna island, ‌off Sulawesi, a reddish-coloured hand stencil was dated to at least 67,800 years. Near the Maros-Pangkep cave, firefighters worked to put out fires as smoke drifted over the ‌dramatic karst landscape that is a defining feature of the national park and Unesco ⁠Global Geopark surrounding the ⁠cave. Firefighter Muhammad Ikfar said fires burned near the site for more than a week earlier this month and came within ‌800 metres (2,600 feet) of the cave. More than 270 hectares (670 acres) of the national park burned between September 30 and October 18, Ikfar ‌said. “The first ‌and most destructive effect is the heat. Even without direct fire touching the paintings, it ‌could ruin them because it changes the temperature around the paintings and accelerates the process of corrosion,” said ⁠Griffith University archaeologist Basran Burhan. The smoke also creates soot. “They create soot on the paintings and cover ⁠them, so that the paintings will become blurred and difficult to identify,” he said. On Thursday and Friday, firefighters were working to put out fires in other parts of the park, Ikfar said, adding that the ‌conditions were dry with no rain yet. “If we don’t do something about this quick, if there isn’t any tactical mitigation efforts for this incident, we will lose one of the most amazing evidence of human history in Maros-Pangkep,” Burhan said. “And that is a great shame.”

title: North Korean silence signals Trump-Kim summit unlikely: US, South Korean officials
description: US and South Korean officials see the chances fading of ⁠a meeting between President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this year, according to five people with knowledge of the situation. Trump, the only US president to have met a North Korean leader, has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but Pyongyang has shown little interest in diplomacy aimed at containing its nuclear programme. The US has received no response from North Korea on holding a Trump-Kim meeting, and...
content: US and South Korean officials see the chances fading of ⁠a meeting between President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this year, according to five people with knowledge of the situation. Trump, the only US president to have met a North Korean leader, has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but Pyongyang has shown little interest in diplomacy aimed at containing its nuclear programme. The US has received no response from North Korea on holding a Trump-Kim meeting, and there is little time left before a regional summit in China next month when ‌it might occur, according to the five people – four of them briefed by senior officials from the US and South Korea, as well as a South Korean official. North Korean state media has said Pyongyang would put tough conditions on agreeing to a bilateral summit, potentially including sanctions relief, even as Kim’s powerful sister said the two leaders had an “excellent” relationship. In August, the Republican president said he planned to meet Kim later this year and that the North Korean leader had responded to his outreach. South Korea’s intelligence agency told lawmakers late last month that there was a 50 per cent chance of Trump and Kim meeting on the sidelines of the November 18-19 summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) group in Shenzhen, China. But ⁠on Monday, Trump, who met Kim three times in his first term, downplayed the prospects of such a meeting happening during the Apec meeting or a regional summit in the Philippines, also in November. “I get ‌along with him very well, and I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting,” Trump told reporters at the White House. Another South Korean official familiar with the matter said Pyongyang had made no move indicating it was preparing for a meeting with Trump. All of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to ‌relay private conversations. South Korea’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last week, Seoul’s ambassador to Washington, Kang Kyung-wha, said no concrete progress had ⁠been made towards a Trump-Kim summit. North Korea’s permanent ⁠mission to the UN did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “President Trump in his first term held three historic summits with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that stabilised the Korean peninsula,” a White House official said on condition of anonymity. “US policy ‌on North Korea has not changed. President Trump remains open to talking with Kim Jong-un, without any preconditions. No meetings to announce at this time. The leaders will meet at the appropriate time.” Last month, a senior US official told reporters that Trump was “ready” to speak ‌with ‌Kim and that “the ball is very much in North Korea’s court”. Short notice Ankit Panda, a senior fellow in the nuclear policy programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said ‌there was less than a 10 per cent chance of a meeting between Trump and Kim at the Apec summit. “If Trump wants a meeting with Kim, I think the North Koreans are looking for a costly public signal,” ⁠Panda said, arguing that a recent US decision to scale back exercises with South Korea had not been sufficient. Washington has occasionally sought the help of China, which has maintained close ties with Kim, in ⁠brokering talks with North Korea. But cordial talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, set to continue at Apec, have not produced breakthroughs with Pyongyang. The two Koreas remain technically at war under a truce that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean war. The US stations about 28,500 troops and military hardware in South Korea in combined defence against North Korea, which has ‌pursued nuclear arms and ballistic-missile development. South Korean officials, citing private ‌research group estimates, have said North Korea possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads. Trump’s meetings with Kim in 2018 and 2019, while historic, yielded no concrete results. “I don’t know when they’re going to meet,” US Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel told an event in Seoul organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea on Wednesday. If they could arrange a meeting, she said, it would likely be announced abruptly. “If it happens, then it’s going to happen the next day or within a couple of days’ notice.”

title: No bots: Japan drafts rules for social media platforms ahead of local elections
description: Japan’s communications ministry on Friday unveiled draft guidelines outlining measures for 13 major social media operators to help reduce the impact of misinformation and disinformation that could undermine fairness during elections. The guidelines also include measures such as requiring operators to establish eligibility requirements and strict screening procedures for users of monetisation features, suspend monetisation when content that harms the fairness of elections is posted, and add...
content: Japan’s communications ministry on Friday unveiled draft guidelines outlining measures for 13 major social media operators to help reduce the impact of misinformation and disinformation that could undermine fairness during elections. The guidelines also include measures such as requiring operators to establish eligibility requirements and strict screening procedures for users of monetisation features, suspend monetisation when content that harms the fairness of elections is posted, and add warning labels to harmful images and videos generated by artificial intelligence. The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications will solicit public comments starting on Saturday before formally adopting the guidelines. In July, the parliament enacted a revised law on information distribution platforms requiring operators to mitigate harmful impacts and the ministry to issue detailed implementation guidelines. The revised law will take effect March 1, 2027, and apply to unified local elections in the spring, expected to be the next major event on Japan’s political calendar. “We will work to raise awareness broadly so that effective measures can be implemented,” Internal Affairs and Communications Minister Hisayuki Fujii told a news conference on Friday, adding that the guidelines could be formally adopted as early as year-end. Bot accounts, which automatically make posts, and accounts linked to programmes used for mass dissemination will also be shut down under the new guidelines. To prioritise information from reliable sources such as public institutions and candidates, the guidelines call for functionality to make their posts more visible and the implementation of features indicating when candidates’ accounts have been verified. The guidelines will be applied during official election campaigning periods as well as before and afterwards, while the specific measures to be implemented will be left to individual operators. To minimise any infringement of individual freedom of expression, the guidelines do not call for the removal of users’ posts and stress that measures should not lead to excessive restrictions on creative activities. The revised law requires operators to publicly disclose the status of their measures once a year, to ensure the guidelines remain effective. X and Google are among the 13 operators designated by the ministry under the draft guidelines.

title: ‘I am not resigning’: embattled leader digs in as Malaysia royal crisis deepens
description: Embattled Negeri Sembilan chief minister Ismail Lasim has denied claims that he has resigned, as a constitutional crisis in the Malaysian state spiralled further following a move by his executive council to challenge their sacking by the state’s ruler in court. The state has been all but paralysed by a dispute that began in April over who has the right to sit on Negeri Sembilan’s throne, bringing down a state government aligned with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH)...
content: Embattled Negeri Sembilan chief minister Ismail Lasim has denied claims that he has resigned, as a constitutional crisis in the Malaysian state spiralled further following a move by his executive council to challenge their sacking by the state’s ruler in court. The state has been all but paralysed by a dispute that began in April over who has the right to sit on Negeri Sembilan’s throne, bringing down a state government aligned with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition and leaving Ismail with no administrative support. Ismail’s standing came under further question after he was publicly rebuked last week by state ruler Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, who was caught on camera telling the chief minister to “go away” and drop his claim that the monarch no longer held the throne. The chief minister, however, dismissed reports of his resignation as “political games” being played by certain parties. “It is not true. I am not resigning,” he was quoted as saying by local English daily New Straits Times on Friday, following an earlier news report claiming that he was stepping down to make way for a replacement. Reports that Ismail had quit surfaced on Thursday, further complicating a crisis centred on an attempt to replace Muhriz with his cousin, Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar. The state’s four territorial chiefs, known as the Undangs – who are empowered to elect the state’s ruler – issued a proclamation in April stating that Muhriz was to vacate the throne for allegedly breaching his royal duties. Federal legal authorities, however, said the claim failed to meet constitutional requirements due to a lack of evidence. Leaders from Ismail’s Umno party later withdrew support for the then PH-led state government, accusing it of disrespecting the royal mandate by failing to implement the Undangs’ proclamation. The move triggered a state election, which Umno won. Ismail, who was sworn into office before Muhriz in August, has since given conflicting accounts of his role. On September 9, he said he had signed the proclamation under duress, lodged a police report and maintained that the document was invalid. Eight days later, he confirmed that his executive council had unanimously backed the decision and instructed the state secretary to proceed with its formal publication. He reportedly wrote to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal on September 17 to tell the country’s nine royal houses that Muhriz was to be replaced by Nadzaruddin. In retaliation, Muhriz decreed on September 20 that all 10 members of Ismail’s executive council were sacked with immediate effect for failing to uphold their oath of office, which requires them to remain loyal to the ruler and the royal institution. The councillors filed a legal challenge with the country’s apex court on October 14, seeking to overturn their dismissal. They are asking the court to determine whether their sacking was constitutional, failing which the ruler’s decision should be declared null and void. Their case adds to a growing legal quandary tied to the royal tussle. In July, the Seremban High Court instructed the four Undangs and two others to answer contempt allegations raised by the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) – the state’s highest customary council. On October 15, the DKU filed a fresh application for contempt proceedings against 17 individuals, including Ismail and his 10 state executive councillors.

title: Australia sanctions 2 over North Korean fake IT workers scheme for nuclear funds

content: Australia said on Friday it had sanctioned two North Korean individuals and companies over the use of “fraudulent” IT workers and cybercrime to earn cash for the isolated nuclear-armed state. The two men are alleged to be key operators in Pyongyang’s cybercriminal activities overseas, estimated by analysts to bring in billions for the country’s weapons programme. “The North Korean entities and individuals sanctioned today facilitate North Korea’s use of fraudulent IT workers to raise revenue for the regime’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes,” the office of Australia’s foreign minister Penny Wong said. North Korea faces a slew of international sanctions over its weapons and nuclear programmes. It stands accused of seeking to skirt those sanctions by employing thousands of IT workers impersonating nationals of other countries to obtain work and income on online platforms and remit the money to government agencies. North Korea has furiously denied those allegations, deriding them as efforts to “tarnish” its image. The United States and allies warned in July that North Korean workers were using AI tools to further obscure their true identities. And last month, New Zealand’s cybersecurity agency revealed a North Korean IT worker had used a fake identity to obtain remote work with a company in that country and then threatened to release sensitive information when exposed. The two men sanctioned by Australia on Friday – Yu Pu-ung and Sim Hyon-sop – have already been named by the US government. In 2024, the US Treasury described the China-based Yu as a “linchpin” of North Korea’s illicit moneymaking activities and warned he was “skilled at employing various schemes to avoid detection”. Sim – reportedly a top “shadow banker” for the regime – is wanted by the FBI, with a US$5 million reward for information leading to the arrest for his role in helping transfer funds in and out of North Korea.

title: Rare Suu Kyi phone call to son signals shift in Myanmar junta strategy

content: The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said she sounded “fairly healthy” after speaking to the detained ex-democratic leader on Thursday for the first time in more than five years. Suu Kyi, 81, is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup. “She was sounding fairly healthy,” Kim Aris, who lives in the UK, said after the telephone conversation. It was the first time he had spoken to his mother in more than five years, he said. “She was able to say she was in good health, but being 81, things aren’t getting any better.” News of the conversation was the second rare update on Suu Kyi this week, after Myanmar authorities on Monday published pictures of her receiving a package sent by Britain’s King Charles III. Analysts say Myanmar’s rulers are increasingly advertising Suu Kyi’s well-being and her contacts with the outside world, as they bid to shake off their post-coup pariah status abroad. “Essentially we just discussed family matters,” Aris said, adding: “We knew the phone call would be recorded, so we didn’t talk about anything sensitive.” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman released photographs of Suu Kyi and Aris speaking into telephones, the detained Nobel Peace Prize laureate sitting under a calendar marked with Thursday’s date. A statement said the pair had a “consular telephone conversation” for 20 minutes starting at 2.30pm, and that Aris had taken the call from Myanmar’s embassy in London. “She was most concerned about my health and the rest of the family: that was her first question, if I was well,” Aris said. “I remain very concerned about her well-being.” Posting about the call on social media, Aris wrote: “Hearing her voice again means more than words can express.” He said Suu Kyi had been “unjustly detained,” and urged her supporters to “keep speaking up until she is free”. “My mother and all political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally. Freedom is not negotiable,” he wrote. Kim is one of two sons whom Suu Kyi had with her late husband, British academic Michael Aris. Seeking legitimacy Myanmar’s military held Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities say they have loosened her detention and have published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”. Analysts say Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing – who as military chief ousted Suu Kyi in February 2021 – is seeking international legitimacy after being installed as the country’s civilian president in April. Despite criticism from democracy watchdogs that the election putting him in office was a charade, he has made significant headway into being welcomed onto the world stage. He has been invited on numerous diplomatic trips including to members from the Asean bloc – where Suu Kyi’s status has long been a sticking point. Morgan Michaels, a research fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said authorities were “using” Suu Kyi “to extract concessions from members of the international community”. “But many within Asean and beyond want to see her release. These types of gestures are likely to be very well received even if they are insincere or tactical in nature.” One Yangon office worker, speaking anonymously for security reasons, said she still feared for Suu Kyi. “She is getting older, and I just hope she can be free, healthy and with her family,” the 30-year-old said. “But these new contacts give me some hope.” The coup ousting Suu Kyi also triggered a civil war in Myanmar, where she won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for her non-violent campaign for democracy. Analysts have said reintroducing the pacifist Suu Kyi into politics may be a canny way to peel off support for pro-democracy rebels who rose up to challenge the military after the putsch. A former senior member of Suu Kyi’s now-dissolved National League for Democracy party said she was “not a hardliner” and would likely engage with Min Aung Hlaing if released. “We have only one way and that is dialogue,” the member said on condition of anonymity for security reasons. “For the sake of the people and the country, they have to meet.” Myanmar authorities said Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative. On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace declined to comment on the announcement about the package. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Nepal set to receive first-ever US$20 million payout from UN climate damage fund
description: The United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund moved to provide US$20 million in aid sought by flood-stricken Nepal – the first time it has set aside money for any country – in a key test of the body’s credibility. In an extraordinary meeting on Thursday, the fund’s board agreed to earmark the modest sum for the Himalayan country, which was hit in August by tsunami-like floods triggered by a climate-induced ice and rock avalanche that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000...
content: The United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund moved to provide US$20 million in aid sought by flood-stricken Nepal – the first time it has set aside money for any country – in a key test of the body’s credibility. In an extraordinary meeting on Thursday, the fund’s board agreed to earmark the modest sum for the Himalayan country, which was hit in August by tsunami-like floods triggered by a climate-induced ice and rock avalanche that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing. Camila Minerva Rodriguez Tavarez, the Dominican co-chair of the board, called the outcome “truly historic” and thanked members for “allowing us to act promptly and have a response to Nepal”. Reacting to the news, Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said: “The fact that they could convene this emergency meeting in response to our letter and commit US$20 million of grant money is very welcome.” The decision does not, however, mean that Nepal will immediately receive the funding, which amounts to less than 0.5 per cent of the government’s US$4.78 billion estimate for reconstruction. The amount is the maximum countries can request in a single application. Nepal will first have to present a proposal for the board’s approval, with no firm timeline for the process. The creation of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage was hard-won at the UN climate conferences of 2022 and 2023 by developing countries, many of them among the least responsible for climate change yet most vulnerable to its impacts. Test case The fund grew out of calls for “climate reparations” from historically major emitters, which ultimately did not materialise. But since it became operational, critics have faulted both meagre pledges from rich nations – US$822 million to date – and the fact no money has been disbursed so far. Wagle said that Nepal was a test case for “how serious the world is in helping developing and fragile countries to respond to the loss and damage associated with climate change”. During the meeting, some developed countries stressed the Nepal decision should be seen as exceptional, not as a template for the fund’s long-term future. “This is not a precedent on one hand, but on the other it provides a learning for the development of the long-term model of the fund,” the European Union’s Jan Dusik said. Developing countries hit back. “I heard Jan saying that we are open for learning, but not in setting precedent. Please do not define the boundaries for learning,” said Pakistan’s Ali Tauqeer Sheikh, in comments endorsed by others. Last year, after part of Jamaica was destroyed by the worst hurricane in its history, the fund’s French co-chair at the time said that it was not meant to “provide a humanitarian response” but was aimed at “the next stage”. That wait-and-see approach became untenable after the disaster in Nepal. Developing countries, which hold a majority of the fund’s board, demanded a response to Nepal’s request. “It’s a landmark first step. At the same time, it’s also a proof of how far the fund still has to go,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation and global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, which has been pressuring the fund. The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a US$49.6 million emergency appeal after the Nepal disaster, and the United States announced US$31 million in new flood recovery support in September. But as courts increasingly rule on states’ climate obligations, developing countries and legal experts argue that such aid should be an obligation of rich countries, not voluntary. Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy programme at the Centre for International Environmental Law, said she hoped the Nepal decision “will really be a springboard” for demands that the fund and responses to escalating climate impacts be “grounded in legal obligations”.

title: Vietnam partners with Denmark to propel its wind energy ambition
description: A wind energy partnership between Vietnam and Denmark has fuelled expectations of the Southeast Asian country boosting its competitiveness in renewable electricity to serve overseas and domestic markets. Vietnam is well placed to grow its renewable electricity sector by tapping its large pool of engineering talent and abundant wind resources with help from Denmark, a global leader in wind energy, according to analysts. On Tuesday, the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership...
content: A wind energy partnership between Vietnam and Denmark has fuelled expectations of the Southeast Asian country boosting its competitiveness in renewable electricity to serve overseas and domestic markets. Vietnam is well placed to grow its renewable electricity sector by tapping its large pool of engineering talent and abundant wind resources with help from Denmark, a global leader in wind energy, according to analysts. On Tuesday, the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership during the three-day state visit by Vietnamese President To Lam to Denmark. As part of the cooperation, Vietnamese state-owned energy group Petrovietnam signed an agreement with the Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) to build the South Central Region 1 offshore wind project, a 1,000-megawatt development that forms a part of Vietnam’s electricity generation plan. Offshore wind refers to the generation of electricity using wind farms located in waters such as seas and oceans. The deal builds on Petrovietnam’s growing role in the global offshore wind supply market. In September, the company began shipping offshore substations to Poland’s Baltica 2 wind farm, which is expected to power 2.4 million Polish households in late 2027. Nam Nguyen, a Hanoi-based energy policy analyst, said Vietnam had acquired considerable expertise in the wind sector through years of developing its domestic offshore oil and gas industry, which shared many technical and infrastructure requirements with offshore wind projects, such as deploying service vessels and offshore foundations. This has allowed Petrovietnam to win multiple contracts to supply offshore wind equipment and facilities in overseas markets, according to Nam. He said Denmark had supported Vietnam’s efforts to grow its wind and other renewable energy sectors through initiatives such as the Danish-Vietnamese Energy Partnership Programme, while CIP had invested in the country for years. Manh Tri Dao, director for the Centre for Environmental Economics and Climate Change Studies, noted the synergy between the two sides by combining Vietnam’s offshore engineering capabilities with Denmark’s large-scale wind development experience and financing. Referring to the South Central Region 1 project, Dao said: “If successfully implemented, these collaborations could provide a valuable example for future projects beyond this partnership, showing Vietnam’s capacity to co-develop offshore wind with international partners.” Lam Pham, an Asia energy analyst for Ember Energy, said the partnership could boost downstream sectors within Vietnam, such as manufacturing and maintenance, leading to more skilled jobs created, citing the country’s existing partnership with Vestas, a Danish wind turbine maker. Earlier this month, Vestas announced it had secured contracts to supply 16 wind turbines to two wind farms in central Vietnam. While Vietnam is growing its overseas offshore wind markets, it is still falling short in generating electricity from nearshore wind locally, according to Pham. Nearshore wind refers to the generation of electricity using wind turbines installed in waters close to the shoreline, typically up to 15km (9.3 miles). Referring to Vietnam’s current capacity of 0.8 gigawatts of nearshore wind, Pham said: “The priority now is to build on its manufacturing strengths by establishing a clear, predictable domestic market, enabling Vietnam to benefit not only from supplying global offshore wind projects but also from developing its own wind resources.” Among the barriers that Vietnam’s domestic wind industry faced, Pham said, were uncertainties over project approvals, area planning and marine surveys, as well as financing risks. Nam said that Vietnam should also develop its supporting infrastructure to grow the industry. Citing the fragmented port infrastructure across coastal provinces, he added that such risks could limit the opportunity for companies to invest in large-scale offshore wind projects. Analysts call for Hanoi to streamline its industrial policies to boost the development of related industries and renewable electricity supply and help reduce project costs. Dao said this was crucial given that energy consumption by businesses in Vietnam would likely surge in tandem with growing demand for tech facilities. “Continued improvements to renewable power procurement rules can help Vietnamese industries and international manufacturers access clean electricity, including for emerging, energy-intensive demand such as data centres,” he added. Nam said another area that Vietnamese policymakers could do to support the growth of the wind sector was to allow for more competition. “The country would still need to accelerate the development of a more competitive electricity market and establish more stable and predictable support policies for emerging technologies such as offshore wind and other renewable energy sources,” he added. Vietnam is aiming to achieve net-zero emissions and phase out coal use by 2050 by increasing electricity generation from renewable sources such as wind and solar. It currently only generates wind power from onshore and nearshore facilities but aims to achieve 6,000MW capacity of offshore wind by 2030. Pham said: “With the right policy, financing and grid conditions, offshore wind could strengthen both Vietnam’s energy security and the long-term competitiveness of its industries.”

title: Inflation-squeezed Japanese flock to claw machines dangling everyday items
description: With one eye on her baby in a stroller, Minae Kamata operates an arcade machine in a Tokyo suburb, manipulating a claw to grab not a stuffed toy but a pack of toilet paper. content: With one eye on her baby in a stroller, Minae Kamata operates an arcade machine in a Tokyo suburb, manipulating a claw to grab not a stuffed toy but a pack of toilet paper. As inflation weighs on Japanese households, huge arcades on the outskirts of major cities are installing claw machines filled with eggs, rice, laundry detergent and other necessities. The “shop-and-play destinations” merge essential buying with entertainment so that families do not feel a choice between bringing home the basics and treating themselves to a day out. Kamata, a 25-year-old housewife, said she won her prize after only two tries, at 100 yen (US$0.64) per attempt. “If you’re a bit lucky, it’s the same as buying at a discount,” she said. Experts say the trend is a response to Japan’s prolonged wave of inflation, with prices having outpaced wage growth for years. “Spending on food and everyday products has been continuously declining for five years because these have become targets for budget cuts,” said Naoko Kuga, a consumer behaviour specialist at the NLI Research Institute. So “retailers are trying to make purchasing fun to encourage buying” and ease a sense of guilt, she added. Claw machines were already booming in Japan before the inflation wave. The “prize game” market more than doubled in 10 years to reach 417.7 billion yen (US$2.7 billion) in 2024, and now accounts for nearly 70 per cent of arcade revenues, according to the Japan Amusement Industry Association. In recent years, families in search of everyday items have become a larger part of their clientele. In Kawasaki, on the southern outskirts of Tokyo, hundreds of machines at a venue operated by the specialist chain Benex are filled with bottles of soda, bags of sweets and detergent. “When a family spends 10,000 yen on a day of karaoke or bowling, they have fun and that’s it. But at Benex, you go home with toilet paper, bottles, and toys,” said Teruaki Tsuchiya, an executive at Tisco, which operates Benex. “With inflation, parents are choosing the most cost-effective entertainment option.” The company, which has five locations in Greater Tokyo and claims more than 1 million visitors a year, scrapped its video games and token machines last year to refocus on claw machines. It says revenue through household product sales has increased 2.6-fold in two years. Tsuchiya said the model is similar to chains like Costco or Ikea: large stores on the outskirts of cities, where land is cheaper and loyal customers come by car and spend relatively more. Japan’s inflation rate has hovered near the central bank’s 2 per cent target in recent months, a modest figure for many developed economies but a shock for a country used to decades of stagnant or falling prices. After “two or three hours” on the machines, Chiaki Sugai, a 56-year-old sushi restaurant employee, pushed a huge cart filled with trophies which cost her nearly 8,000 yen. “Before, I used to buy a lot of snacks at convenience stores, but now I grab them here,” she said. Forty-nine-year-old Sachiko Iyokawa also appeared satisfied with her winnings: two boxes of premium eggs, cheaper than in supermarkets. “Normally I’m careful, but here I treat myself a little,” she said. Large retailers are jumping on the bandwagon. Aeon Fantasy, an amusements subsidiary of the sprawling Aeon Group, opened its first area dedicated to food and household prizes targeting mothers in October 2025. It now has seven such spaces and plans to open around 60 by 2030. “At a time when consumers are highly sensitive to cost, we offer an experience that combines fun with the thrill of getting a good deal,” Yuya Shiozawa, a manager at Aeon Fantasy, said. “We see, for example, customers who, after winning vegetables, go to the supermarket next door to buy ingredients to complete their dinner.” According to Kuga, the trend should outlast the current period of inflation, as bricks-and-mortar retailers seek new reasons to attract customers who are increasingly buying household products via Amazon subscriptions. She predicted that “stores will multiply initiatives to bring customers in, whether with claw machines or in other forms”.

title: Singapore pushes for quick action on PHP security flaws as hackers prowl
description: Organisations in Singapore have been urged to immediately fix two critical security flaws in a widely used programming language amid reports of widespread attempts by hackers to exploit the vulnerabilities. The flaws in PHP, which powers many websites and online services, could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data or disrupt services without needing login credentials, Singapore’s Commissioner of Cybersecurity Gwenda Fong said on Thursday. “The threat is immediate,” Fong,...
content: Organisations in Singapore have been urged to immediately fix two critical security flaws in a widely used programming language amid reports of widespread attempts by hackers to exploit the vulnerabilities. The flaws in PHP, which powers many websites and online services, could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data or disrupt services without needing login credentials, Singapore’s Commissioner of Cybersecurity Gwenda Fong said on Thursday. “The threat is immediate,” Fong, who is also CEO of the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), said in a social media post. Working exploits have already been demonstrated and security patches were released on Wednesday, she added. The vulnerabilities, collectively known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), affect all versions of PHP, according to a CSA security alert issued on Wednesday. The agency said there had been reports of widespread exploitation attempts, as well as the development of multiple proof-of-concept exploits. Cloud services firm Cloudflare recorded millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities following their public disclosure, its CEO Matthew Prince said in a social media post late on Wednesday. The flaws have also prompted website operators around the world to take precautionary measures, with government websites in Europe and elsewhere going offline on Wednesday. PHP developers released urgent security fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had gone undetected for years before being uncovered using artificial intelligence, urging users to update immediately. Fong warned that many organisations, particularly small- and medium-sized enterprises that rely on external IT vendors or hosting providers, may not realise their systems are vulnerable. PHP is widely used in websites, including those built on platforms such as WordPress, Drupal and Joomla. “My message to every organisation in Singapore is simple: do not wait,” she said. Organisations operating websites or online services should check whether their systems use affected versions of PHP, including those managed by third-party vendors. They should apply security patches immediately, prioritising systems accessible from the internet and investigate whether their systems may already have been compromised, Fong added. Those unsure whether they are affected should contact their IT teams, website developers or hosting providers. CSA said it was working urgently with government agencies, critical information infrastructure owners, major enterprises and industry partners to accelerate patching. It is also reaching out through business associations, cybersecurity service providers and technology partners to help smaller organisations address the vulnerabilities. “The priority now is to identify and patch vulnerable systems before attackers can exploit them,” Fong said. “Cybersecurity is a shared responsibility. Acting quickly now can prevent a vulnerability from becoming a serious incident.” This story was first published by CNA

title: Will China’s 4 peace principles for tackling African conflicts work?
description: Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined Beijing’s formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues during a meeting this month with visiting Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, framing it around four principles linking peace to development. The principles focus on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and...
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined Beijing’s formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues during a meeting this month with visiting Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, framing it around four principles linking peace to development. The principles focus on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development. Asked last week whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and the heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa. Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace and development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned. Beijing has financed major infrastructure projects in the region under the Belt and Road Initiative, its China-centred trade and investment scheme. These include the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Standard Gauge Railway, as well as oil, fishing and maritime interests across Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti. Yet, Beijing remains reluctant to intervene directly, opting instead to support African-led diplomacy to preserve its long-standing doctrine of state non-interference. As conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, China seeks to strike a delicate diplomatic balance, advocating for peaceful, African-led solutions that align with Xi’s conflict-resolution principles. The idea is to safeguard China’s billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while carefully maintaining its core foreign policy pledge of non-interference. But experts said lasting peace would ultimately depend on regional actors addressing internal factionalism, respecting state sovereignty and fostering inclusive dialogue alongside broader international peace efforts. Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, a Washington-based think tank, said Beijing’s response reflected concern about what renewed fighting could mean for its interests in the Horn of Africa. “I think it first and foremost points out China’s concern and aversion to instability,” Sun said. “War and conflicts fundamentally undermine China’s interests on the ground.” China also faced a diplomatic constraint, she added, saying it sought to influence how conflicts were resolved without abandoning its stated principle of non-interference in other countries’ affairs. Rather than lead a peace process itself, Beijing tends to support approaches led by countries in the region and their regional organisations. “The balance they strike is through siding [with] and supporting [a] regional approach and the involvement of regional organisations,” Sun said. “That confers legitimacy and credibility to the Chinese approach.” Ethiopian federal forces and fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) are battling again in northern Ethiopia, putting a 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement under severe strain. Ethiopian federal forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, in early October after advancing on the city and prompting TPLF fighters to withdraw. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government has announced a six-month caretaker administration in the Tigray region to restore services, return displaced people and prepare for elections. The conflict has also escalated Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the TPLF and occupying its territory. Eritrea rejects the claims and accuses Addis Ababa of threatening its territorial integrity to secure Red Sea access, which landlocked Ethiopia desperately seeks to reduce its dependence on Djiboutian ports. According to Seifudein Adem, a visiting professor at Doshisha University in Kyoto, Ethiopia must address its internal divisions if it is to resist outside intervention. “President Xi Jinping is correct to suggest that Ethiopia should put its house in order by resolving internal disagreements through dialogue because disorder is the ultimate justification for external intervention in Africa,” he said. Adem argued that the obstacle was not an inability to resolve disagreements peacefully. “Rather, these disagreements often take the form of militarised factionalism,” he said. “This, in turn, is because the Ethiopian state does not enjoy a monopoly over the means of violence in the society.” “The problem is that some of these neighbouring countries seem to view their interference as a kind of African solution to African disorder, consistent with an ‘African-led’ solution,” Adem added. Xi’s emphasis on sovereignty shifted the focus from Africa as a whole to the rights of individual states, he said. According to Costantinos Berhutesfa Costantinos, a public policy expert at Addis Ababa University and former United Nations policy adviser, China has a clear stake in containing the conflict but must use its influence carefully. “China is a friend and major trade partner and investor in the Horn,” Costantinos said, citing Beijing-backed roads, power-generation and transmission projects, and industrial estates in Ethiopia. Those investments could not deliver their intended economic benefits without peace, he added. Costantinos said China’s diplomatic initiative, together with its influence through the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, had raised expectations that Beijing would engage with countries in the region to help resolve their long-standing conflicts. China appointed Xue Bing as its first special envoy for the Horn of Africa in 2022 and convened a conference on peace, governance and development in Addis Ababa that year. Hu Changchun, who succeeded Xue last year, has continued to promote Beijing’s regional initiative. Costantinos said governments in the Horn of Africa should put Xi’s principles into practice through diplomacy to reduce tensions, protect trade routes and secure local ceasefires. “No conflict can be considered resolved if any group whose interests are affected has been left out of the negotiation or mediation,” he added, noting that the parties would not enter talks with equal influence. China should work alongside existing peace efforts, Costantinos said. “China will only add to the praiseworthy efforts by the [African Union], UN, US and [European Union],” he said. “Its initiative will in no way gainsay the work of these venerable institutions and countries.”

title: Fandom vs flag: why young Chinese embrace Japanese pop culture but reject war-era symbols

content: Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism. That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday. Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today. The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army. “A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA. Among those condemning the student were people who enjoyed Japanese pop culture, including Lucy Huang, 24. An anime fan since primary school, she has watched more than 200 anime series and read widely across manga – Japanese comic books and graphic novels. “Japan in anime cannot really be called Japan but is an idealised utopia,” Huang said, adding that she drew a clear distinction between Japan in reality and the country as depicted in anime. She said it was “unforgivable” for a Chinese person to wear the rising sun flag. Japanese anime began appearing on Chinese television in the 1980s and gradually gained a larger audience over the following decades. According to a 2018 report by Chinese consultancy iResearch, China had more than 200 million online anime users in 2018, with nearly 80 per cent of 803 surveyed anime consumers expressing a preference for Japanese animation. Yet, for many young Chinese like Huang, an interest in Japanese pop culture does not mean an embrace of Japan as a whole. Lillian Liu, a final-year university student in China’s Fujian province, echoed Huang’s anger over symbols associated with Japan’s wartime aggression against China. Liu boycotted a September collaboration between WEGO – a popular Japanese fashion brand known for its anime merchandise and clothes – and Japanese anime series My Hero Academia. Chinese platforms dropped the anime in 2020 after a character linked to Japan’s Unit 731, which conducted human experiments during World War II, appeared in the series. “I really like Japanese anime and manga, but as Chinese people, we cannot allow our country’s political stance to be violated,” said Liu, who began watching Japanese anime in kindergarten. In a September commentary, Beijing Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party’s Beijing Municipal Committee, described the collaboration as “an act of support for Japanese militarism”. “This is shameful. I won’t buy anything from the store again,” said Liu, who estimated spending up to 20,000 yuan (US$2,995) a year on Japanese pop culture merchandise and had bought three transparent bags showing anime merchandise from WEGO before the incident. WEGO Harajuku, the brand’s China subsidiary, later issued an apology, saying its Japanese parent company had cancelled the collaboration and removed related promotional posts. But Yuki, 24, an anime fan who gave only her first name, said she had noticed a shift in how young people around her viewed Japan. “The spread of anime has, to some extent, helped young people today avoid viewing all Japanese people as bad,” Yuki said. Once a fan of My Hero Academia, Yuki stopped following the series after the 2020 controversy. “Culture itself is also a form of politics. After the incident, I no longer engage with [My Hero Academia],” said Yuki, who regularly attends anime conventions where fans dress up as characters from animation and manga. She has also seen how political tensions can affect the anime scene. “The popularity of Japanese anime seems to rise and fall with China-Japan relations and political tensions,” she said, observing that a convention organiser had removed booths related to Japan after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s contentious remarks on Taiwan. In November last year, Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a Taiwan contingency could trigger the deployment of the Self-Defence Forces, eliciting heavy criticism from mainland Chinese officials and state media. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. China and Japan have long had a complex and evolving relationship, shaped by more than 1,000 years of exchanges in writing, religion, art and technology. During several dynasties including the Tang, Japan sent envoys to China to study its political system, Buddhism, written culture and urban planning. The island country drew heavily on Chinese civilisation in shaping its own institutions and culture. But Japan’s industrialisation and military expansion in the late 19th century led to war with China. Japan defeated the Qing dynasty in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95, forcing it to cede lands including Taiwan. After Japan’s 1945 surrender at the end of World War II, China and Japan moved towards diplomatic relations, normalising them in 1972. Since then, ties have improved at times, only to be repeatedly strained by historical and territorial disputes. Orna Naftali, an associate professor in the Department of Asian Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said both recent geopolitical tensions and historical factors had contributed to hostility towards Japan in China. “Every now and then, there is some kind of geopolitical tension about different issues, which is because of reasons including history,” Naftali said. As for popular culture, she thought it did not necessarily lead people to “develop more positive attitudes” towards a country’s government or its policies. Naftali said young people’s views of Japan were shaped by domestic influences and interactions with the country’s people and family members. “What to think of a certain country [is shaped] not just through textbooks but also different rituals and ceremonies and whatever the teacher says,” she added. Naftali observed that relatives’ memories of the war, whether young people had in-depth conversations with Japanese people, and their socioeconomic background also played an important role in shaping their understanding of the country. Although “there is a constant sort of animosity towards Japan in terms of the nationalist rhetoric”, young people’s views were more complex, she said, adding that some held more favourable attitudes towards Japan, while even those with negative views had nuanced perspectives. Shin Kawashima, professor in the University of Tokyo’s Department of International Relations, said young people in both China and Japan had shown considerable interest in one another’s cultures. “In that sense, in the distant future, as the current younger generations come into contact with one another, Japan-China relations may take on a form different from what they are today,” he said. However, Kawashima voiced pessimism about the prospects for building stable, positive ties between Chinese and Japanese societies through youth exchanges, noting that the “Chinese government has currently suspended most official exchanges with Japan”. “At present, the influence of the political sphere on the economy and society is increasing, and such possibilities are not expected to expand,” he said.

title: China’s next generation of leaders waiting in the wings for more senior roles
description: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed.
