content: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed. When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress. At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory. Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies, said the party was looking for cadres who had “absolute political loyalty, integrity, fighting spirit, technological or ‘hard science’ expertise, grass-roots experience and hardship resilience”. “Just like their predecessors, they must demonstrate unquestioned loyalty and integrity. But given China’s technological advancement into uncharted areas, the new leaders will have to know emerging technology and hard science as China can no longer copy from others.” However, recent patterns within the party suggest that Beijing is giving age less weight when it comes to promotions, while the far-reaching anti-corruption campaign is hitting this generation as hard as any other. The 7G Regardless of whether Xi Jinping, now 73, chooses to stay in charge beyond the 2032 party congress, he will still need a deep bench of loyal and talented younger officials to carry out his policies. In recent decades, candidates for Politburo seats have usually been identified many years ahead. Most candidates for membership of the key decision-making body in 2032 will currently be members of the party’s Central Committee or will be selected as alternate members at next year’s party congress. Traditionally, most Central Committee members, who have a ministerial-level rank, are required to step down at the age of 65. Meanwhile, Politburo members observe an informal rule known as “seven up, eight down”, in which those under the age of 67 may serve another five-year term, while those aged 68 or older must retire. Xi broke these precedents for some key figures in 2022, including top diplomat Wang Yi, then aged 69, who was seen as indispensable for managing China’s foreign relations amid escalating competition with the United States. He also kept the country’s top general Zhang Youxia, then aged 72, in place to manage the country’s military modernisation programme, but Zhang later fell from favour and was detained earlier this year on suspicion of corruption. Roughly two-thirds of the current Central Committee will have reached the statutory retirement age by the time of the party congress in October next year. Consequently, the seventh generation, currently about 8 per cent of the party’s central leadership body, is expected to become the biggest cohort. Only 7G officials who are already members of the Central Committee or those who have been newly appointed as ministers and provincial leaders – who will get their Central Committee seat in 2027 – are likely candidates for leadership roles beyond 2032. The leading candidates Some of these contenders have already taken over top regional and ministerial roles this year. They include Zhu Zhongming, born in April 1972, who was appointed as mayor of Shanghai late last month, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next party chief. Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he worked under Premier Li Qiang while he was governor. Other regional government chiefs of a similar age include Zhejiang governor Liu Jie, Jiangsu governor Liu Xiaotao, and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region’s government chairman Wei Tao – all born in 1970 – as well as Shanxi governor Lu Dongliang, who was born in 1973. Other leading candidates, including Beijing mayor Yin Yong and Hubei party secretary Guan Zhiou – who outranks the regional government chiefs – are just a few months older and also considered leading candidates to take on senior national roles. Other contenders from that generation hold central government and party roles, including A Dong, who leads the Communist Youth League Central Committee, Zhang Chengzhong, the Minister of Emergency Management, and Cheng Fubo, the director of the state-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission. Most of these 7G officials are full or alternate members of the Central Committee. Shanghai mayor Zhu and emergency management minister Zhang, both appointed only recently, are expected to be made full members of the Central Committee at next year’s party congress. Xie from Tsinghua said “resilient officials”, who had cut their teeth in difficult, under-resourced environments – mirroring Xi’s own formative years – or demonstrated versatile and effective problem-solving skills would be put on a faster track to promotion, as they will have to manage more emergencies caused by extreme weather. “The preferred style for next-generation leaders is quiet, efficient execution of central mandates rather than high-profile self-promotion or experimental local diverging policies. They must also show the ability to integrate economic development with security considerations, ensuring that local industrial policies adhere to broader central directives regarding supply-chain resilience and social stability,” Xie added. Chinese born in the late 1960s and 1970s have often been described as “the luckiest age cohort” on social media because they were too young to experience the political turmoil of the Cultural Revolution or the physical hardship experienced by “sent-down youths” who worked as farmers in rural areas. They also avoided the starvation endured by previous generations and grew up as the country’s economy started to boom. An analysis published by Li Cheng, director of Hong Kong University’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said half of the leading 7G cadres had doctorates – making them the most highly educated cohort in party history – and often had experienced life outside the party system, including overseas study. Li found that around one-third of them were trained in engineering, while economics and finance represented their other primary fields of study. There was also a significant proportion that had experience of managing state assets, financial institutions or complex industrial projects, reflecting Beijing’s demand for officials capable of navigating economic headwinds and technological competition. Yin, the mayor of Beijing, is a prominent example. He holds a master’s degree in public administration from Harvard University and previously served as vice-governor of the People’s Bank of China. Another example is 1970-born Guo Ningning one of the few high-ranking female contenders for higher office. She was appointed party chief of Fujian’s provincial government on Saturday, paving the way for her appointment as governor. She spent more than a decade leading operations for state banks in Hong Kong and Singapore before entering provincial governance. Meanwhile, Hubei’s deputy party chief Zhuge Yujie, born in 1971, was named as the new party secretary of the Qinghai government, also putting him in line to become the province’s next governor. No more fast track However, these officials have climbed the ladder more slowly than some previous generations. For example, the 2002 party congress saw dozens of officials in their late 30s or early 40s being given vice-ministerial posts, some of whom achieved full ministerial rank three years later, including Sun Zhengcai, who became agriculture minister at the age of 42, or Hu Chunhua, who became head of the Communist Youth League aged 43. At the time, these promotions were seen as filling a skills gap caused by a lack of administrative skills and economic experience among older officials. But since Xi came to power in 2012, fewer younger cadres have been given senior posts as the leadership prioritised performance and experience. The youngest members of the Central Committee were in their mid to late 40s when they were appointed and the average age of new members of the last two Politburos – around 62 – was much higher than in the previous three, where it was well below 60. Xi and other senior leaders have warned that fast-tracked young bureaucrats sometimes lack real-world experience. As early as 2011, the Central Organisation Department explicitly warned of the problem caused by “three-door cadres” – a term used to mock young civil servants who moved directly from their family’s doorstep to university and then into government offices. Xi has also introduced the concept of “letting seedlings develop firm roots”, dunmiao in Chinese, mandating that up and coming cadres spend extended periods in complex, frontline postings – such as poverty alleviation, disaster response and industrial restructuring – before being eligible for senior command. Those who crashed out An additional challenge for the 7G cadres is the country’s ongoing anti-corruption drive, which has already led to the downfall of some high-profile figures. The latest case involves Beijing’s executive vice-mayor Xia Linmao, who was placed under investigation last week. Born in 1970, Xia, who has a doctorate from Tsinghua University and held a variety of top-tier technocratic postings in the capital’s urban planning and government operations, epitomised the demographic cohort that rose swiftly through the sub-provincial ranks. His downfall is just the latest warning that rising cadres face intense and constant scrutiny and will be judged strictly on political compliance and administrative conduct rather than their potential. Other once-promising 7G officials who have fallen foul of the anti-corruption drive include former Urumqi party boss Yang Fasen, who was jailed for life last October for accepting more than 147 million yuan (US$20.7 million) in bribes, and Fei Gaoyun, who held a similar role in Hefei and was placed under investigation in May. Li Yunze, the former head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, who was celebrated as the first official born in 1970 to achieve full ministerial rank, provides another cautionary tale. He was abruptly demoted and stripped of his seat in the national legislative body in May over disciplinary violations, underscoring that a temporary lead in the political marathon provides no immunity against tightened scrutiny.

title: China’s J-20 stealth jet designers plan to put powerful radar into aircraft wing

content: Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage. Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment. Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage. The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems. “Wing-mounted early-warning radar is a new type of mission payload designed to meet the early-warning needs of distributed air combat,” researcher Ren Yunsong and his team wrote, describing the concept as “a new pathway” to developing systems with strong detection capabilities. Ren and his team are affiliated with AVIC Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, which developed China’s J-20 stealth fighter and was identified by the country’s defence ministry as the designer of the two-seat J-20S, a variant intended to operate alongside unmanned aircraft. The concept builds on distributed air combat, a strategic idea first proposed by the US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency or Darpa in 2014 to explore future air warfare. The researchers argued that this approach could not rely solely on conventional early-warning aircraft, which use large radar arrays and high-power systems, but would instead require numerous smaller, lower-cost unmanned aircraft to work together to provide surveillance. This creates a technical challenge: achieving large-scale detection capabilities with relatively small individual platforms. The proposed design integrates the antenna array, control components and associated systems within the wing structure, with the radiating surface facing downwards and a protective cover following the aircraft’s outer contours, increasing the available antenna aperture without requiring a large external radar dome. To direct the radar towards different sectors, the researchers propose changing the aircraft’s flight attitude. In the proposed side-flying mode, an unmanned aircraft rolls at an angle of more than 45 degrees, tilting the wing-mounted array from a downward-facing position towards the side. “By adjusting the drone’s flight attitude, the radar beam can be dynamically controlled, expanding the airspace covered by early warning,” Ren wrote. The design is intended to support distributed airborne early-warning operations, in which multiple smaller unmanned aircraft share surveillance duties rather than relying on a single large platform. “The research provides a reusable and verifiable design paradigm for the engineering implementation of wing warning radars and has a promising application prospect and promotion value,” Ren’s team wrote. The paper proposes four operating modes, including all-direction and multi-direction detection, as well as coordinated operations in which aircraft provide wide-area coverage, concentrate on specific targets or work together to counter electronic interference. “Cooperative detection by multiple aircraft is a core enabling technology for the operational concept of ‘small platforms, big capabilities’,” it said. The researchers said the approach could provide early-warning capabilities approaching or exceeding those of conventional early-warning aircraft without relying on large platforms. Ren said the design would provide a solid information-sensing foundation for distributed air combat involving next-generation aircraft. The concept could potentially be considered for future Chinese combat aircraft, including the J-20 and next-generation designs known as the J-36 or J-50, although the paper did not confirm that the proposed radar was being developed for any of these aircraft. The researchers also identified four core operational scenarios for the wing-mounted system: take-off, flight-attitude control, target detection and early warning, and ground testing and maintenance. Their design framework maps interactions among the radar, aircraft systems, ground stations, command centres and operators to guide future system integration. “The process links operational-scenario analysis to operating-mode design and then to system design, further advancing the engineering application of wing-mounted radar,” the team wrote.

content: A prominent Chinese economist’s social media channel has been restricted as Beijing steps up regulatory scrutiny of financial market influencers. Chinese internet users on Saturday noticed that the WeChat account of Ren Zeping, known for his outspoken comments on investments and policies, had been stopped from gaining new followers and a member of his team said posting had been suspended. Clicking the follow button generated a message saying “this account cannot be followed due to its violation of rules” and it did not appear when the name was searched for. New rules aimed at curbing unapproved financial marketing have driven numerous financial influencers offline. However, it was unclear why Ren’s social media account had been restricted. A member of his team said that due to “technical adjustments” by the platform, some content on their channel did not meet the eligibility requirements under “new regulations” and this had “resulted in a 15-day suspension of posting”. They added that the team was working to make the necessary changes. The account was still publishing posts on Friday, including one note arguing that China’s stock market had “basically bottomed out” and a rebound was “unfolding”. It also published a report on China’s demographics, where Ren urged the authorities to “fully” lift all restrictions on family sizes to encourage people to have more children. It also advertised a forum Ren was due to attend in Shenzhen on Saturday and a speaking engagement in December. Ren’s official account on Weibo, another major Chinese social media platform, remained open to new followers. The government’s latest restrictions on the online marketing of financial products, which were widely seen as an effort to contain financial risks, came into force at the end of last month. The rules said that only financial institutions and third-party internet platforms may conduct online marketing for financial products. All other entities and individuals are forbidden from doing so, “including in any disguised form”. Over the past three weeks, they have prompted an intensive regulatory crackdown, with numerous financial influencers’ accounts disappearing or being permanently banned. Ren previously worked at the Development Research Centre of the State Council, China’s cabinet. He later served as managing director of the research institute at Guotai Junan Securities before becoming chief economist at China Evergrande Group, where he reportedly earned an annual salary of 15 million yuan (US$2.3 million) that made him the country’s best-paid strategist. He has also worked for Soochow Securities and Zhongyuan Bank and set up Zeping Hongguan, a popular financial commentary and research platform, that offers investment advice. However, his career has repeatedly been dogged by controversy and he has faced criticism for making market forecasts that proved to be incorrect. Months after he left Evergrande in March 2021, the property developer’s debt crisis erupted, prompting questions over the advice he had given the company. It is not the first time one of his social media accounts has been subject to restrictions. Ren’s Weibo account was briefly muted in 2022 after his article calling on China to print an extra 2 trillion yuan to boost childbirth sparked fierce debate.

title: Clashes flare at Paris protests as more than 400,000 march across France
description: Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell. The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend. The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years. A total of 249 protests took place in...
content: Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell. The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend. The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years. A total of 249 protests took place in France on Saturday, just over half of the 430 protests that were recorded on October 17, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who added that police had detained close to 1,000 people by about 7.30pm on Saturday, with that number expected to go up. “The marches unfolded well” despite the presence of certain “radical groups”, Nunez said. In Paris, around 110,000 people took part in Saturday’s protest, according to Paris Police Prefecture, which said the situation across the city remained mostly “calm”. The march started in the afternoon in a festive but uneasy mood at the southern edge of the city. Towards Porte de Vincennes, the end point of the route, police clashed with groups of masked protesters dressed in black, an identity-hiding tactic known as the black bloc, firing tear gas and water cannon as the demonstrators set off fireworks and threw projectiles at officers. Police also fired tear gas in Lyon and Nice, where demonstrations had been banned, and in Lille and Marseille, where a single march had been authorised in each city. For many young students who gathered in Paris on Saturday, the main message was for the government to understand their struggle, their demand for better education and the general population’s suffering amid the rising cost of living. Many of the protesters shared similar sentiments: they condemned the violence from looting and rioting, but also expressed anger at police conduct. “Obviously I don’t support any kind of violence,” said Manon, a student. “But we shouldn’t blame everything on the troublemakers who came from an underprivileged background and who probably suffer from more invisible forms of violence in their everyday life.” Three friends had told Manon to be careful – not of the troublemakers, but of the police. “It’s easy to see things burning, but people too have been burning on the inside,” she said. Tensions surrounding Saturday’s demonstrations, already high, escalated further following a shooting of a “racist nature” in the western Paris suburbs of Trappes and La Verriere on Friday, which left one person dead and five injured. The Paris police prefecture cited the attack as a primary reason for altering the authorised protest route late Friday afternoon, ordering the march shifted away from Place de la Bastille in central Paris to Porte d’Italie on the city’s outskirts. Trade unions accepted the change after a failed legal challenge, but criticised the government for attempting to divide the movement and create chaos. Police began clearing Place de la Bastille around noon, directing demonstrators towards Porte d’Italie, where some local residents learned only from journalists on the scene that their neighbourhood was now along the march route. The abrupt re-routing deepened anxiety among local officials and businesses bracing for renewed unrest, with one official telling the South China Morning Post that the protest risked being “all over the place” and turning into “a mess”. With 70,000 police and gendarmes deployed nationwide and soldiers also mobilised to protect public buildings and infrastructure, the government faced intense pressure to prevent a recurrence of the widespread violence and looting seen the previous weekend. “A fiasco like this, two weekends in a row, I don’t know what explanation we could give the French. We really cannot afford to get this wrong,” an adviser to Interior Minister Nunez told broadcaster BFMTV on Saturday. Across France, authorities moved to ban most demonstrations following French President Emmanuel Macron’s intervention on Thursday, in which he stated that “the general recommendation is to hold no demonstrations in the coming days”. Protests were prohibited outright in regional cities including Bordeaux, Lyon and Nice, with only a single demonstration approved for each of Paris, Lille and Marseille. In Paris, local businesses took aggressive security precautions. Along Rue Beaurepaire and surrounding streets, storefronts were closed behind thick sheets of plywood. Burn marks on the road and paper signs reading “Fermeture pour cause de sinistre” (Closed due to unforeseen circumstances) remained visible reminders of the previous Saturday’s riots, during which a bar was torched and multiple retail outlets were ransacked. The few cafes and shops that chose to open planned to close by early afternoon. Even luxury boutiques in the west of the French capital, located far from the designated protest route, boarded up display windows and reinforced entryways against potential roving bands of vandals. Major cultural landmarks including the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay were also closed. Sweeping restrictions have intensified national debate over civil liberties and the constitutionally protected right to protest as the French government tries to maintain social order. “I want the interior minister to carry out his primary mission: guaranteeing the exercise of individual freedoms and the right to protest, and protecting people first and property second,” the green party mayor of Paris’ 11th arrondissement David Belliard told the SCMP. “That is simple and basic in a great democratic country.” Belliard’s district encompasses both Place de la Bastille and Place de la Republique – covering some areas hardest hit by last Saturday’s riots and the exact corridor where organisers had originally planned to march. France is the most prominent flashpoint in a wider wave of demonstrations over the cost of living, housing and government spending rippling across Europe this weekend, with rallies planned in Italy, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Albania. In Italy, a coalition called the “October 17 Movement” called protests across eight cities on Saturday. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reinforced police and military deployments in Milan, one week after violent clashes and looting hit the country’s financial and fashion capital.

content: Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations. The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons. Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems. “The lesson from this incident is that we cannot become overly dependent on satellite navigation services provided by a single company,” said Shu Hsiao-huang, a senior analyst at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research. SpaceX this month imposed new speed restrictions on terminals in Ukraine connected to its Starlink satellite internet service, disrupting some Ukrainian drone combat operations. The restrictions cut a terminal’s link to the internet when it travels faster than 160km/h (100mph), a speed often exceeded by Ukrainian drones equipped with Starshield, the military version of Starlink. The restrictions forced some drones to fly more slowly, making them easier for Russian forces to target or evade and prompting Kyiv to seek changes to the limits. Conflicting accounts have emerged over who was responsible for the restrictions and why they were introduced. Musk suggested that US President Donald Trump had decided to implement the limits because the US government owns and controls Starshield. Trump denied this, but said he doubted Musk was responsible, while the Pentagon also denied it was involved. Regardless of who made the decision, the episode showed the dangers of depending on a system ultimately controlled by an external provider, according to Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei. “Even the military-grade Starshield system funded or heavily supported by the US government could still potentially be disconnected or have its speed restricted at a critical moment because of political considerations or commercial interests,” Wang said. He said the risks could be more complicated for Taiwan because Musk has substantial commercial interests on the Chinese mainland, including Tesla’s Shanghai factory. While Taiwan’s military does not currently use Starlink, its legislature has eased rules that previously restricted foreign satellite communications companies from entering the local market, although detailed implementation arrangements have yet to be announced. Taipei has already struck deals with providers willing to work within its restrictions, including Eutelsat OneWeb, while pursuing indigenous low-Earth-orbit satellite capabilities. But analysts warned that replacing dependence on terrestrial and submarine networks with a single satellite constellation would merely exchange one vulnerability for another. Wang called for a “multi-orbit, multi-provider” strategy combining indigenous satellites with commercial constellations from different international suppliers. Taiwan should accelerate development of what he described as a “Taiwanese version of Starlink” to retain a communications channel beyond the control of foreign companies, while expanding cooperation with alternative operators such as OneWeb and Luxembourg-based SES. He said the approach could also support Taiwan’s defence industry by encouraging the development of unmanned systems that did not rely on the US government-operated GPS as well as communications links less dependent on satellites. Shu said redundancy would become increasingly important as Taiwan incorporated more unmanned systems into its armed forces. Satellite systems support positioning, navigation and timing – or PNT – which are essential to operations ranging from unmanned aircraft and precision weapons to telecommunications and electricity networks. Taiwan therefore needed alternatives to GPS as well as backup communication networks, Shu said. The options include inertial navigation systems that can calculate an object’s position without external signals and AI-based visual navigation and terrain matching. “The essence of satellite navigation redundancy is not putting all your eggs in the GPS basket,” Shu said, adding that weapons and critical infrastructure needed to remain functional during periods of “digital darkness”. Developing unmanned systems capable of navigating without GPS would further reduce Taiwan’s dependence on satellite services, he added. James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based international relations and strategic studies scholar, said Taiwan’s situation differed from Ukraine’s because Taipei had “chosen not to depend on Starlink or Starshield because of its concerns about Musk’s close business ties with China”. But that did not eliminate its reliance on foreign technology. Much of Taiwan’s advanced military equipment comes from the United States, meaning Taipei still needed to consider the possibility that externally supplied capabilities could be restricted during a conflict, he said. Another challenge was whether “Taiwan’s own satellites could eventually provide sufficient connectivity and withstand electronic warfare and jamming by the People’s Liberation Army”, Chen added. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Analysts also cautioned against treating Ukraine as a direct template for a Taiwan Strait conflict. Wang said Taiwan’s potential battlefield would be much smaller, while drones operating across the strait would face different geographical and weather conditions. Many Taiwanese drones would probably operate around the island or in coastal areas, where microwave links and other terrestrial communications could provide alternatives if satellite connections failed, he said. The controversy also raised a broader question about the reliability of US support, according to Huang Huei-hua, director of the Taiwan Global Talk think tank. “If Taiwan found itself in Ukraine’s predicament during a cross-strait conflict, it could end up the biggest loser,” she said. “Like Ukraine, Taiwan could face the risk of being abandoned.” Huang said relying too heavily on any single foreign partner, including the United States, carried considerable risks. “Taiwan needs to prepare a range of contingency plans, or it risks becoming expendable when the interests of larger powers change,” she said. “The crisis of trust between Ukraine and the United States should serve as a wake-up call: there is no permanent comfort zone, even between allies.”

title: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un pays unexpected visit to Chinese border city of Dandong
description: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, with both sides underlining their traditional friendship and calling to boost cooperation. content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, with both sides underlining their traditional friendship and calling to boost cooperation. The trip, Kim’s first visit to China in more than a year, comes ahead of next month’s Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Donald Trump and other world leaders are expected to gather. He was welcomed and accompanied on his trip by Wang Huning, China’s fourth-ranked official, according to state news agency Xinhua. Wang called on the two countries to expand people-to-people exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, as well as “strengthen strategic communication and coordination, and foster a peaceful and stable external environment”, so as to safeguard their “respective sovereignty, security and development interests”. Kim’s one-day visit, which had not been announced in advance, took place on the eve of the official anniversary marking the entry of Chinese troops into the Korean war in 1950. Dandong served as the primary gateway for Chinese forces as they crossed the Yalu River into North Korea during the war. Wang welcomed Kim at the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, where the North Korean leader laid a floral tribute. Kim then inspected some of the wartime artefacts on display at the memorial hall, which commemorates how the two allies fought side by side. Wang conveyed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s greetings and best wishes to Kim, Xinhua said. During their meeting, Wang noted that Kim’s special visit to Dandong – marking the 76th anniversary of the Chinese People’s Volunteer Army entering the war – underscored the great value North Korea placed on bilateral friendship. “It fully reflects the importance that the North Korean party and government attach to the blood-forged friendship between China and North Korea. It not only continues the traditional friendship between China and North Korea [and] consolidates friendly public opinion, but also deepens political mutual trust and seeks common cooperation and development, which is of great significance,” Wang was quoted as saying by Xinhua. Wang also accompanied Kim on a visit to a Dandong car factory in the afternoon. China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended all of Saturday’s events, according to Xinhua. Later in the day, both Wang Huning and Wang Yi accompanied Kim as he left Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge, Xinhua said. At the bridge’s opening ceremony last week, Chinese Premier Li Qiang reaffirmed Beijing’s support for Pyongyang and said both countries should improve connectivity. The 3km (1.8-mile) bridge was intended to increase trade and connectivity between China and North Korea, and was completed in 2014. However, it remained closed for more than a decade because North Korea delayed work on its approach roads and facilities. The four-lane bridge connects Dandong in the northeastern province of Liaoning with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju. Kim’s brief visit came just days ahead of the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee in Beijing next week, a key political meeting ahead of the leadership reshuffle next autumn. Kim expressed his wishes for the success of the fifth plenum during his meeting with Wang Huning, adding that his country was willing to work with China to “expand practical cooperation”, according to Xinhua. The North Korean media has not released any statement on Kim’s visit. The timing of the visit is significant, coming just weeks ahead of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Both Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin are expected to attend and each has voiced interest in holding three-way talks with China. Trump has indicated he is open to talks focused on nuclear weapons and denuclearisation, while Putin has floated the idea of using such a gathering to discuss the war in Ukraine. Trump has also said he wants to meet Kim again. The pair met three times during Trump’s first term but failed to achieve any breakthrough. The South China Morning Post reported last month that China was willing to help facilitate a fourth Trump-Kim encounter, as Beijing seeks a more active role in Korean peninsula diplomacy after years of being sidelined. Kim’s last trip to China was in September last year, when he and Putin visited Beijing for a parade to mark the 80th anniversary of the victory over Japan in World War II. Chinese President Xi Jinping paid a two-day visit to North Korea in June, his first in seven years. During the trip, both leaders pledged to strengthen strategic cooperation and defend each other’s sovereignty, vowing to “open a new chapter” in relations and expand political, economic and cultural exchanges.

title: Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern

content: When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”. His remarks quickly drew online criticism as well as accusations that he was using outdated figures from 2020 while ignoring differences in purchasing power. Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China. However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure. A report issued by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) last month documented a sharp decline in congressional delegations to China between 2010 and 2026, a period marked by persistent bilateral tensions. A separate analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) later in September highlighted a parallel downturn in American students studying in China and the erosion of programmes designed to train future China specialists. Observers warn that the loss of direct, on-the-ground exposure could threaten America’s ability to assess and engage its primary rival, particularly as China’s strategic importance to US foreign policy continues to grow. A broad retreat According to the CSIS report, visits by congressional delegations to mainland China and Hong Kong have fallen since the late 2010s as bilateral relations deteriorated. Tensions deepened during US President Donald Trump’s first term from 2017 to 2021, marked by a full-blown trade war, intensifying technological rivalry and recurring military stand-offs in the contested South China Sea. The report showed that visits plunged at the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic and had yet to return to earlier levels. Congressional travel to Taiwan has also dropped since 2022. The report attributed the decline to lingering fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taipei – which triggered major People’s Liberation Army drills – and subsequent caution in Washington around such delegations to avoid further provoking Beijing. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation Sun Chenghao, Chinese academic CSIS found that only 32 per cent of the 535 sitting US lawmakers had travelled to mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan, based on its tracking of congressional delegations between 2010 and 2026. The report expected that share to shrink further as veteran members left office and newer lawmakers arrived without that first-hand experience. US Senator Steve Daines is among the few lawmakers who still make such trips. He concluded his most recent visit to China in late August, just weeks ahead of President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington from September 23 to 25. After Daines visited artificial intelligence and space firms in China’s tech hub Hangzhou and the southern city of Guangzhou, he told Bloomberg the US risked underestimating “both the quality and the scale of the tech innovation ecosystem in China”. Isabella McCallum, co-author of the CSIS report, noted that the small 32 per cent share – the 172 current lawmakers who have visited mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan – suggested on-the-ground engagement was becoming less common among the people responsible for shaping US policy towards China. “With less direct experience of China, Congress will become more reliant on second-hand information for one of the country’s most consequential relationships,” McCallum said in an interview. Meanwhile, lawmakers continued to introduce legislation concerning Beijing, creating a growing gap between how much Congress acted on China and how well its members knew the country, she added. To Beijing, the concern is not simply that US lawmakers may hold unfavourable views of China. It is that their assessments may be made without enough contact with the people, businesses and institutions affected by their decisions. Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said limited direct experience could make American policymakers more likely to rely on political labels and a narrow security-focused view of China. “This could lead them to overestimate certain threats while overlooking opportunities for cooperation,” Sun said. The decline in congressional visits is part of a wider retreat in exchanges between the two countries. According to the CSIS report, fewer than 2,000 Americans are estimated to be studying in China, compared with a peak of about 11,000 in 2019. Likewise, the number of Chinese students enrolled at US universities had continued to fall from its 2019 peak of 372,532 amid tightening visa restrictions and curbs on research exchange, the report said, without stating current figures. According to the Institute of International Education’s most recent annual survey, nearly 266,000 Chinese students were in the US in 2024. The drop in academic exchange was also underscored in an analysis released by CFR on September 23. It highlighted the suspension in China of US government-backed exchange projects, including the Fulbright programme and the Critical Language Scholarship. The author, political scientist Rush Doshi, noted that these programmes had helped to cultivate generations of specialists equipped to study China through its language, society and political institutions. Meanwhile, some study-abroad programmes at US universities have been halted following a Pentagon directive in August instructing institutions to review relationships with foreign counterparts over national security concerns. The loss of these opportunities could have consequences beyond universities. Doshi noted that American government agencies and businesses largely relied on China expertise to interpret China’s actions, from geopolitics and security to trade and supply chains. “A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, track policy implementation on the ground, is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable,” he wrote. Sun said the decline in China expertise could also hurt Beijing, depriving the country of interlocutors who could accurately interpret its intentions. “In the long run, the ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation and narrowing the scope for cooperation,” he said. Rebuilding channels The CSIS report called for renewed congressional travel, arguing that visits could help lawmakers understand how China’s policies and economic decisions affected their constituents. McCallum said such trips could give Congress members a better understanding of issues they raised with Chinese officials, connecting foreign policy with practical concerns at home. She cited Daines, whose home state of Montana is a major beef producer. Daines has used his visits to press for restored Chinese market access for American beef producers. But visits must go beyond carefully arranged itineraries showcasing economic development, the CSIS report noted. McCallum said Beijing should allow visitors to have greater access to China’s economy and society, and make room for frank conversations with a range of counterparts. She also identified Chinese sanctions against US officials as a possible deterrent to congressional travel. “Sanctions on even a limited number of members can discourage others from travelling,” McCallum said, adding that expanding congressional travel took effort from both sides. Sun similarly argued that Beijing should ease visits by lawmakers from both parties and chambers of Congress, including their staff. “Exchanges should directly address constituency concerns, including agriculture, jobs and trade, while establishing follow-up mechanisms to turn single visits into sustained dialogue, preventing communication from snapping whenever the political climate cools,” he said. The need for sustained, first-hand engagement with China extends beyond Congress to education and academia. The CFR analysis called for Washington to rebuild funding and institutional support for China studies, while clarifying federal rules so that non-sensitive academic activities, such as language learning, could continue. The report also urged Washington and Beijing to protect educational programmes from the wider tensions in their relationship. Diao Daming, a professor in international studies at Renmin University of China, said efforts to strengthen Americans’ first-hand understanding of China would also benefit Beijing. “They would help both sides develop a clearer, more objective and accurate understanding of each other, deepen their appreciation of the vital importance of stable China-US relations to both countries and the wider world, and ultimately contribute to greater stability in bilateral ties,” he said. There have been signs of renewed interest in exchanges, but the larger question is whether these efforts can help rebuild American expertise on China. At his summit with Trump in September, Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange or study programmes in the coming five years. The initiative doubles an earlier target announced in 2023 – to bring 50,000 young Americans to China by 2028. Chinese authorities said that target had been reached ahead of schedule. Diao said the 2023 initiative’s early completion showed strong demand for youth and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries. “These efforts incrementally build goodwill in a subtle, quiet way,” Diao said. “They lay a solid foundation for people-to-people ties and play a crucial role in stabilising the broader bilateral relationship.” Sun, while echoing Diao’s view, cautioned that short-term visits alone could not reverse the decline in American expertise on China. Developing specialists required sustained engagement with the country, rather than brief exposure through organised exchange programmes, Sun noted. He said visits should be connected to longer-term opportunities, including Chinese-language courses, semester exchanges, graduate study and field research. Sun added that credit recognition, scholarships and academic supervision could help participants continue their studies after returning home.

title: ‘Systematically dismantled’: Hegseth’s new offensive against China’s Confucius Institutes
description: Just weeks before Donald Trump’s second trip to China this year and his third meeting with President Xi Jinping, whom he has called a “truly great” friend, his administration is intensifying its crackdown on Confucius Institutes – Beijing-backed centres that promote Chinese language and culture at universities abroad. content: Just weeks before Donald Trump’s second trip to China this year and his third meeting with President Xi Jinping, whom he has called a “truly great” friend, his administration is intensifying its crackdown on Confucius Institutes – Beijing-backed centres that promote Chinese language and culture at universities abroad. Long viewed by critics as instruments of Beijing’s soft power and cultural diplomacy, the institutes are back in the crosshairs of US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who says the Pentagon has “systematically dismantled” organisations that resurfaced under new names. Hegseth announced on Friday that the Pentagon had added what he described as Chinese government-backed organisations operating on American campuses to its list of institutions deemed threats to national security. “Eighty new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” Hegseth said in a video posted to his official “Secretary of War” social media account. The department had spent the previous two months dissolving the organisations and had “systematically dismantled every single one”, he said. Hegseth called the action a “lesson to any country trying to steal our hard-earned inventions or turn our young people against their own country”. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Launched by Beijing in 2004, Confucius Institutes promote Chinese language and culture abroad as part of China’s soft-power push. Their model is loosely comparable to institutions such as the British Council, Alliance Francaise and Goethe-Institut. But critics have increasingly accused the institutes of serving the Communist Party of China’s United Front and influence operations, raising concerns over academic freedom, transparency and potential political interference. By the late 2010s, Chinese official figures put the global network at roughly 500 to 550 institutes and more than 1,000 of the smaller Confucius Classrooms across over 140 countries. After the first US institute opened at the University of Maryland in 2005, the network eventually expanded to over 100 institutes across American college campuses, alongside numerous Confucius Classrooms in primary and secondary schools. US scrutiny intensified in the mid-2010s, with congressional restrictions on Defence Department funding to universities hosting the institutes, including measures in the 2019 and 2021 National Defence Authorisation Acts, adding to the pressure. Most US institutes closed or rebranded between 2019 and 2022. “Thankfully, Congress banned them a few years ago, these Confucius Institutes, but they came back disguised in new forms,” Hegseth said, accusing the organisations of attempting to evade restrictions by adopting different names and charters. The latest crackdown comes as Washington and Beijing continue to explore areas for cooperation alongside their strategic rivalry. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Friday called for the two countries to work together on artificial intelligence (AI) development and governance, saying they “have both the capacity and the responsibility to work together” to ensure the technology “remains under human control and benefits people”. Wang made the remarks during a meeting with John L. Thornton, co-chair of the Asia Society’s board of trustees, and New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman, who were visiting China to attend the Global Governance Forum near Beijing. According to a Chinese foreign ministry readout, Thornton and Friedman said the malicious use of AI posed the greatest risk to building a constructive US-China relationship of strategic stability and expressed hope that the two global powers would strengthen cooperation. AI is expected to feature prominently when Trump and Xi meet in China in November, the South China Morning Post reported earlier this month. Meanwhile, critics in the US welcomed Hegseth’s move as a long-overdue step against Chinese influence operations, whereas others who have worked closely with these institutes called it a strategic own goal. Peter Mattis, president of the Jamestown Foundation, a Washington-based defence policy think tank, replied to Hegseth’s post directly, saying “the Confucius Institutes are part of a political apparatus the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] uses to ‘break and shatter the enemy’”. “Keeping the pressure on the United Front system’s efforts to evade US countermeasures is an unequivocal good”, added Mattis, a former staff director of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Denis Simon, former executive vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, who was involved with three Confucius Institutes – at Pennsylvania State University, the University of Oregon and Arizona State University – argued that Washington had “sacrificed an important instrument of engagement with China”. A 2023 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine review, he said, found no unclassified evidence linking US Confucius Institutes to espionage or intellectual property theft. Simon served as a consultant to that committee. The review acknowledged risks to academic freedom, university governance, curriculums and research security, but distinguished these from allegations of espionage and theft. It recommended safeguards and waivers rather than blanket closures, Simon said. Instead, Washington “confused a legitimate influence concern with an overriding national security threat”, he argued. Closures, driven largely by the threat of losing Defence Department funding, have curtailed Chinese-language learning and China expertise just as strategic competition in technology and AI intensifies. “A United States that knows less about China is not necessarily a more secure United States. It is a strategically weaker one,” he cautioned.

title: Thousands evacuated and flights grounded as Typhoon Champi hits eastern China
description: Typhoon Champi continued to batter China’s eastern coast on Saturday, grounding over a hundred flights and prompting the authorities to relocate tens of thousands of people, while weakening as it moved towards Japan. Flights from airports in Shanghai as well as Fujian and Zhejiang provinces were grounded. content: Typhoon Champi continued to batter China’s eastern coast on Saturday, grounding over a hundred flights and prompting the authorities to relocate tens of thousands of people, while weakening as it moved towards Japan. Flights from airports in Shanghai as well as Fujian and Zhejiang provinces were grounded. China Eastern Airlines said it had cancelled 39 domestic flights to and from Shanghai’s two main airports while flights to and from the cities of Fuzhou and Wenzhou were also affected. The cities of Ningbo and Wenzhou in Zhejiang also announced the cancellation of 37 and 44 flights respectively on Saturday. The railway authorities suspended some high-speed rail services passing through Zhejiang on Saturday and imposed temporary speed restrictions on other routes in the province on Friday and Saturday. Meanwhile, the Shanghai authorities evacuated some 62,400 people ahead of the storm’s arrival on Friday, according to state broadcaster CCTV. China’s National Meteorological Centre kept a blue typhoon warning – the lowest level in the country’s four-tier system – in place on Saturday morning for the fifth straight day. The storm was expected to turn to the northeast while moving along the waters off Zhejiang and head towards southwestern Japan, although it may remain close to mainland China’s east coast on Sunday. “Typhoon Champi will continue to affect China’s eastern waters and coastal areas of east China,” the meteorological centre added. It also urged offshore workers and ships to return to port and warned people in coastal areas to stay away from beaches, mountains and river valleys. China’s State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters and the Ministry of Emergency Management also activated a level-four emergency response, the lowest of four levels, for flood and typhoon control in the province of Jiangsu on Friday. “Under the combined influence of cold air and the typhoon, strong winds will persist over the southeastern waters and along the coast of eastern China from October 23 to 26, with heavy to torrential rain in parts of Jiangsu, Shanghai and Zhejiang,” the authorities said. Champi brushed past the northeastern coast of Taiwan in the early hours of Saturday without making landfall. The island’s disaster response agency said on Saturday that the storm had killed one person and injured 527. It also recorded 6,550 incidents such as fallen trees and damage to buildings and signs. Taoyuan International Airport in Taipei said flights would gradually resume on Saturday as Champi moved away from the island. The airport cancelled 563 flights on Friday. Champi has been the strongest storm in the world by wind speed this year, with maximum sustained winds near its centre reaching 245km/h (152mph) at 8am on Wednesday, before weakening on Thursday. The National Meteorological Centre said that maximum wind speeds near the storm’s centre had dropped to 35 metres per second, or 126 km/h, on Saturday compared with 45 metres per second (162km/h) on Friday,

title: How competition between Chinese and Indian firms could reshape African drug markets

content: China is challenging India’s long-held dominance of the African market for antimalarial drugs in 12 of the continent’s hardest-hit countries, according to a new study. Last year, Chinese exports of antimalarial drugs reached US$89.3 million, nearly matching India’s US$89.6 million, according to Indian market research company Sol Gravitas. The gap has closed significantly since 2021, when Indian exports stood at US$121 million compared with US$62.6 million for China. Separately, the study examined Global Fund purchases for the same 12 countries plus Kenya between 2021 and 2025. The fund, a major international backer of malaria programmes, bought injectable artesunate for severe malaria and blister packs for seasonal prevention, most of which were made in Chinese factories. The shift could help reshape supply security for countries with some of the world’s highest rates of malaria by offering a greater choice of providers, while more competition may help bring down prices. But it might also raise questions about product dependence and the future of local antimalarial research and development as Chinese and Indian firms compete on price. China’s growing share of Africa’s antimalarial market reflects its pharmaceutical manufacturing strength, competitive prices and increasing ability to make medicines that meet international standards, according to Shenglan Tang, a professor of Global Health and Medicine at Duke University. He also said China had a particular advantage in medicines based on artemisinin, a plant-based drug that was discovered by Chinese scientists. Tang also pointed to the country’s investment in its pharmaceutical industry, saying companies had gone beyond producing active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) – the substances that produce a medicine’s therapeutic effect – to making the finished product. That had strengthened their ability to compete for contracts from major global health buyers, including the Global Fund and Unicef, he said. But Tang cautioned against reading China’s gains as a sign that it was overtaking India in the broader market for affordable medicines. He said the latter was still a major supplier of generic medicines and vaccines, with established manufacturing capacity, international regulatory experience and extensive distribution networks. Looking beyond the US dollar value of the drugs exported, India was still ahead when it came to cargo weight shipped last year, according to the Sol Gravitas analysis, accounting for 54.5 per cent of the combined weight shipped to the 12 markets. Last year, China exported more antimalarial medicines by value to Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. Meanwhile, India led in Ethiopia, Mozambique, Angola, Tanzania, Ivory Coast and Madagascar. But the analysis identified where the Global Fund medicines were made rather than where they were shipped from, and the importing countries’ customs records showed a smaller shift than the exporters’ records. In eight countries with complete import records for 2022-2025, India’s share of imports from the two suppliers fell from 71.5 per cent to 64.2 per cent. Of the US$442.7 million in deliveries examined, 45.6 per cent by value was made in China – all by Guilin Pharmaceutical, which its parent company Fosun Pharma describes as China’s largest producer of artemisinin-based antimalarials. The analysis also found that Chinese factories made most of the SPAQ co-blisters used for seasonal malaria prevention, most of the injectable artesunate used to treat severe malaria and all of the dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine. However, Indian factories made at least half of the artemether-lumefantrine purchased – a drug used to treat acute malaria and the largest category of medicines covered by the study. Prashant Yadav, a senior fellow for global health at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the study only covered Global Fund-financed purchases, not medicines bought by governments, other donors or private patients. “Where a particular medicine is supplied by one company or country, it may appear in aggregate that competition in antimalarials is increasing, but in reality it may be just dominance in specific products,” Yadav added. Yanzhong Huang, a professor and director of global health studies at Seton Hall University’s School of Diplomacy and International Relations, said stronger competition could affect both prices and supply. “I think stronger India-China competition is likely to lower prices for quality-assured antimalarials, improving affordability in Africa,” Huang said. Buying from both countries could also make supplies more reliable, he added, although reliance on a small number of pre-qualified manufacturers remained a risk. But he also warned that India’s dependence on Chinese artemisinin APIs could limit the supply-security benefit of buying finished medicines from both countries. Chinese pharmaceutical firms are also expanding production in Africa. Fosun Pharma is building a plant in Ivory Coast to make antimalarials and antibiotics, while Jiangsu Aidea Pharma and PharmaBlock Sciences (Nanjing) are working with Nigerian drug maker Fidson Healthcare to build an antiretroviral plant. Tang said China and India should invest in African production, technology transfer, workforce development and regulatory capacity, while African governments and international procurement organisations should help local manufacturers to meet quality standards and become commercially viable. Huang said newer African manufacturers still needed imported ingredients, skilled workers and financing. “Overall gains depend on quality safeguards and support for regional capacity,” he said. African companies are also beginning to produce antimalarials, but Yadav said they might be hurt in the price competition between China and India. “In this market, with Indian and Chinese firms dominating, who will undertake R&D for future antimalarials?” he said.

title: China carries out in-depth investigation of Turkey’s largest rare earth deposit
description: Chinese researchers have mapped the complex geological evolution of Turkey’s Kizilcaoren deposit, offering fresh insights into the country’s most significant known rare earth reserve while dampening expectations over its commercial potential.
