content: Chinese researchers have mapped the complex geological evolution of Turkey’s Kizilcaoren deposit, offering fresh insights into the country’s most significant known rare earth reserve while dampening expectations over its commercial potential. Although the findings shed light on how rare earth elements accumulate in carbonatite-related formations, the researchers concluded that the site was unlikely to emerge as a major global alternative to existing producers any time soon. Lead scientist Professor Yang Xiaoyong noted that the deposit’s mineralisation was “small in scale” and “still far from reaching the large scale of rare earth deposits”. The findings point to the steep geological and economic barriers nations face as they attempt to diversify their sources of critical minerals. “So far, there is no evidence that Turkey or other countries in the Middle East have substantial rare earth deposits,” Yang, a professor at the University of Science and Technology of China and Hebei GEO University, said in an interview with the South China Morning Post. “Globally, rare earth resources are concentrated mainly in China, Greenland, Australia, Canada and Southeast Asia,” he added. The peer-reviewed study, published online in Acta Geologica Sinica on October 9, was co-authored by Ren Yisu of the China University of Mining and Technology alongside researchers from the University of Science and Technology of China, Hebei Geo University, Istanbul University-Cerrahpaşa, Shanxi Energy Institute and the Xian Centre of the China Geological Survey. To reconstruct how the deposit formed, the team synthesised whole-rock geochemistry, mineralogical analysis, trace-element measurements of fluorite and strontium isotope data, tracing the site’s history from initial magma emplacement to later hydrothermal mineralisation. They identified a three-stage process: first, carbonatite magma intruded into surrounding rocks, creating the initial conditions for mineralisation; second, magma evolution triggered liquid-phase separation, generating hydrothermal fluids enriched in rare earth elements, fluorine and sulphate that transported and concentrated the metals. Finally, meteoric rainwater entered the system, altering host rocks and precipitating fluorite, barite and rare earth minerals. Yet deciphering how a deposit formed was fundamentally different from proving it could be mined economically. An earlier estimate cited in the paper put Kizilcaoren’s rare earth ore at around 4.67 million tonnes with an average grade of 2.78 per cent. Crucially, this figure reflected gross ore tonnage rather than processed rare earth oxides. That scale appears modest when benchmarked against the world’s premier deposits. Yang noted that while Kizilcaoren belonged to the same broad class of magmatic carbonatites as the Maoniuping deposit in China’s Sichuan province, it differed markedly from the massive Bayan Obo deposit in Inner Mongolia. “Our study shows that Kizilcaoren is different from Bayan Obo, but belongs to the same category as typical magmatic carbonatite deposits such as Maoniuping,” Yang said. “The scale of mineralisation is very small.” By comparison, Bayan Obo – the world’s largest rare earth deposit – holds over 57.4 million tonnes of rare earth-bearing reserves at an average grade of about 6 per cent rare earth oxides. Maoniuping ranks as the world’s second-largest producing light rare earth deposit. While divergent reporting standards preclude a direct comparison, the numbers underscore a vast discrepancy in commercial scale. The assessment follows observations by geologist Li Yang of Peking University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who noted on August 17 that Kizilcaoren and Bayan Obo shared core geological traits: “Both are igneous carbonatites, and the basic rules of mineralisation are the same.” The two views are not contradictory. Shared formation mechanisms do not imply identical grades, compositions or economic viability, and Yang’s assessment places greater weight on the deposit’s specific mineralisation scale. These geological realities reflect broader industrial bottlenecks. According to the US Geological Survey’s “Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026”, China held an estimated 44 million tonnes of rare earth reserves in 2025, followed by Brazil with 21 million and Australia with 6.3 million, with substantial reserves also in Russia, Vietnam, the United States and Greenland. Even where mining projects operate outside China – such as Mountain Pass in California and Mount Weld in Australia – extraction represents only the first step in the supply chain. Raw ore must be chemically processed and separated into individual elements before it can be manufactured into high-performance permanent magnets. A March report by the US Congressional Research Service estimated that China accounted for about 60 per cent of global mining, 90 per cent of processing and separation and 94 per cent of magnet production. Extraction is further complicated by technical and environmental factors. At Kizilcaoren, select samples contained more than 1,000 parts per million of thorium. Although that figure represents sampled rock rather than a deposit-wide average, it illustrates the radioactive hazards common to rare earth systems. “Almost all rare earth deposits have high levels of radioactive elements,” Yang said. “Sometimes these elements are themselves by-products that can be recovered.” Nonetheless, he added: “There is an environmental cost to mining.” Yang stressed that the study was purely academic rather than an operational project aimed at developing Turkey’s resources or restructuring global trade flows. “Scientific research has no borders,” he said. “This is collaborative research and free exploration.” Yang also cautioned against viewing academic discoveries as immediate commercial solutions: “A single academic paper cannot change a supply chain,” he added.

title: US-China strategic competition to keep escalating as world watches on, Rudd says
description: Kevin Rudd, president of the Asia Society and a former Australian prime minister, described US-China strategic competition as full-on and multidimensional at a Harvard Kennedy School Institute of Politics event on Friday. “There is a full-blown strategic competition under way in every dimension of national political power and influence, militarily, economically, trade and investment and technology, in foreign policy, in ideology,” said Rudd, a noted China scholar. “It’s across the world,...
content: Kevin Rudd, president of the Asia Society and a former Australian prime minister, described US-China strategic competition as full-on and multidimensional at a Harvard Kennedy School Institute of Politics event on Friday. “There is a full-blown strategic competition under way in every dimension of national political power and influence, militarily, economically, trade and investment and technology, in foreign policy, in ideology,” said Rudd, a noted China scholar. “It’s across the world, everything, everywhere, all at once.” His comments come a month after Chinese President Xi Jinping visited US President Donald Trump in Washington for a three-day state visit packed with pomp and pageantry, but with modest deliverables. Trump emphasised his personal friendship with Xi during the mid-September visit, hailing the pair’s “great friendship” and downplaying the two countries’ current rivalry, while Xi called for unity, saying “together, let us write a new chapter in our friendly relations”. Titled “Meeting the China Challenge”, Friday’s discussion on the future of US-China relations featured Rudd and Graham Allison, the founding dean of Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government. “The conventional wisdom, that I believe is correct, is that the rise of China and its impact on the international order will be the defining international issue for the lifetime of students here,” Allison said. Rudd has published two books on China: On Xi Jinping: How Xi’s Marxist Nationalism is Shaping China and the World and The Avoidable War: The Dangers of a Catastrophic Conflict between the US and Xi Jinping’s China. Allison is known for popularising the Thucydides Trap – the theory that when a rising power threatens to displace an established one, it often results in war. He also served as an assistant secretary of defence in the Clinton administration. Xi referenced the Thucydides Trap in September during his visit with his American counterpart. “Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention. The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi said. The summit outcome last month saw the pair address some areas of competition. They included plans for targeted tariff reductions and an extension of the one-year Busan trade truce aimed at reducing tension between the two giants. The truce was extended from November 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027, after an unscheduled meeting between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent shortly before Xi landed in Washington. Additionally, the presidents pledged government-to-government dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI), with China stating that the two countries should “maintain dialogue and strengthen cooperation” on the rapidly advancing technology. “China and the United States currently engage in a massive competition about who wins the AI race,” Rudd said at Friday’s event. “Let it unfold.” Speaking at an Asia Society event in September, Rudd said Beijing seeks presidential diplomacy to ensure a “minimal number of surprises coming out of the United States between now and the end of next year” as the ruling Communist Party’s 21st Party Congress approaches. Xi and Trump are due to meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and at the Group of 20 economic gathering in Miami in December, marking an unprecedented four face-to-face meetings in a single year.

title: US, allies and China vie for influence through Pacific security deals
description: Strategic competition between China and the US and its allies is intensifying across the Pacific islands, with both sides pursuing a growing range of security agreements to expand their influence, according to an interactive mapping tool released this week by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington think tank. The tool details 56 security arrangements among 14 Pacific island countries and the US, Australia, New Zealand, mainland China and Taiwan in a bid to map...
content: Strategic competition between China and the US and its allies is intensifying across the Pacific islands, with both sides pursuing a growing range of security agreements to expand their influence, according to an interactive mapping tool released this week by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington think tank. The tool details 56 security arrangements among 14 Pacific island countries and the US, Australia, New Zealand, mainland China and Taiwan in a bid to map out linkages in a region that has long seen Beijing and Washington spar for influence, particularly under the administration of former president Joe Biden. The matrix assigns different weights to treaty-level defence commitments, status of forces agreements, maritime surveillance arrangements, policing cooperation and memorandums of understanding. The mapping tool classifies them into three categories based on the level and nature of the security ties: “defence treaty ally”, “formal security agreement” without defence guarantees and “non-binding cooperation only”. The 14 island countries span three subregions: Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Nauru in Micronesia; the Cook Islands, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu and Niue in Polynesia; and the Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji in Melanesia. The findings show that China’s security engagement in the Pacific has centred on policing arrangements, law enforcement training, port infrastructure projects and disaster relief, while the US, Australia and New Zealand have focused more on military cooperation and defence treaties. Although Beijing has sought to strengthen its strategic ties with the region, it has signed only one formal security pact, with the Solomon Islands in April 2022. The US maintains a significant presence in the northern Pacific through Compacts of Free Association, granting Washington responsibility for the defence of Palau, the Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia. Washington concluded a defence cooperation agreement with Papua New Guinea in 2023 and has joint maritime patrol arrangements with 13 Pacific island countries, adding the Solomon Islands to the deal in July 2026. Australia and New Zealand, long-standing security partners in the Pacific due to their proximity, have also expanded their network of agreements in recent years. Canberra concluded a mutual defence treaty with Papua New Guinea in October 2025, followed by a security agreement with Vanuatu in June and another mutual defence treaty with Fiji in July. New Zealand reaffirmed its role as the Cook Islands’ primary security partner in a defence and security declaration in April, which followed the island nation’s comprehensive strategic partnership with China in February 2025. With the region’s security ties favouring the US and its allies, Beijing’s activities in the Pacific have drawn criticism. In July, China’s launch of a ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into international waters in the South Pacific prompted concerns over the short notice and lack of transparency surrounding the test. “Whether it was a message to the United States, to Australia, or to the entire region, the intent is clear. Beijing sees the ability to extend its military might far into the Pacific as its right,” said Charles Edel, senior adviser at the Australia Chair at CSIS. “It’s also clear that the United States, China, New Zealand, Australia and others are vying for influence across the Pacific.” However, China maintains that its relations with the Pacific islands are not part of a geopolitical competition. “China’s engagement with Pacific island countries is a form of South-South cooperation based on mutual assistance and support,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said earlier this month, following a meeting in Beijing with a delegation of politicians from the region. However, Beijing seeks to persuade Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies in the region – Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu – to switch formal recognition from Taipei to mainland China as part of a long-standing campaign to narrow the island’s international profile. Nauru, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands have all severed formal ties with Taipei and established diplomatic relations with Beijing. Taiwan has no defence pact with a Pacific island country. Its only formal agreement is the Kaitasi Treaty with Tuvalu, signed in November 2025 to formalise cooperation in areas including economic development, food security, health and education. However, it continues to engage with Pacific partners through development projects and cooperation in areas including infrastructure, renewable energy, trade and investment. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: What will China’s fifth plenum mean for the root-and-branch corruption drive?
description: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future. When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and...
content: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future. When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and its never-ending fight against corruption. The fifth plenum of the party’s 20th Central Committee will also serve as an important venue for the political momentum of next year’s quinquennial leadership transition and ratify disciplinary verdicts against dozens of fallen cadres. The four-day closed-door meeting comes roughly one year ahead of the 21st National Party Congress in late 2027 and is poised to formalise one of the most extensive turnovers of senior party, state and military personnel in modern Chinese political history. According to a tally by the South China Morning Post, 20 full and seven alternate members are facing corruption investigations and await formal expulsion from the Central Committee. The SCMP’s research also shows that about 35 full and alternate members who did not appear at last year’s plenum have made no public appearances in the current cycle, indicating potential trouble for their political careers. The fifth plenum, from October 26 to 29, is also set to endorse a key document outlining a long list of measures by the party to maintain internal discipline, ensure political loyalty and fight corruption. Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies at Tsinghua University, noted that this focus on the party’s governance came seven years after a similar document that zeroed in on modernising the nation’s governing capacity. “In 2019, the focus was on how to run the government and manage society better. Now, the focus is on the party ruling China,” Xie said. “The reason is simple: China’s overall governance starts from the ruling party. The party’s successful and effective self-governance is a prerequisite for China’s long-term governance.” Cutting down sick trees As the countdown to 2027 begins, the fifth plenum is set to see a fresh push to cement better party governance control and ensure uncompromised loyalty ahead of the next party congress. Beijing issued a series of blunt warnings via the script of a January speech by President Xi Jinping, published in the party’s top theoretical journal Qiushi on October 15. It was the first time some of the details had been made public. In the speech, Xi argued that internal regulations had long been too vague. He demanded systemic reforms to prevent “using a cattle pen to confine a cat” – a traditional idiom for lax rules that fail to restrain misbehaviour. Emphasising that corruption remained widespread and prone to recurring within the party, Xi pledged to uproot or cut down “sick trees” wherever necessary. The metaphor, from ancient Chinese poetry, suggests that new life will flourish beyond decaying trees, with the new replacing the old. Fighting corruption is also a major focus of “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new addition to the paramount leader’s expanding theoretical canon that was made public just months ahead of the plenum. Officially introduced to the party in June, the political doctrine is aimed at building a “Marxist party with long-term governance”. Besides the relentless drive to ensure officials “do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”, the doctrine calls for the party’s centralised leadership to avoid divisions that will weaken the party. It insists on comprehensive and rigorous self-governance to enforce discipline and continuous self-reform across all levels, as well as solid political and theoretical bases to enhance loyalty and avoid weakening the party’s ideological foundations. The doctrine also demands a robust organisational system to train and select high-calibre officials who strictly follow party directives. According to Xie from Tsinghua, strict and comprehensive party governance is a “key pillar” of Xi’s party building thought, especially at the juncture of the transition period for leading officials. “With the party’s self-governance system in place, the next batch of leading cadres will have a unified code of conduct and they can have a cleaner start,” he said. A Nanjing-based analyst said that while Xi’s sustained, hard-hitting efforts may address the symptoms, the plenum’s agenda suggested he was willing to go deeper and wider to address the causes of China’s chronic corruption problems, but in his own way. The political analyst, who asked not to be named as his school required him to seek approval when speaking to media, detailed some of the opportunities for corruption that the country still faced. “In China, areas like promotion of officials, public projects, military equipment acquisition and natural resources development remain highly lucrative black boxes in which one or a few key persons can dictate the decisions involving billions of dollars, despite the relentless anti-corruption fight,” he said. “While Western analysts would suggest the scrutiny of the public and the media to be part of the equation, it will not be the party’s priority as Xi firmly believes strengthening the party’s self-governance is sufficient.” Expected absences At the 20th party congress in October 2022, 205 full Central Committee members were appointed, along with 171 alternate members. Four years later, the number of empty seats at next week’s conclave could highlight an extraordinary level of attrition. The anti-corruption campaign has taken a heavy toll on the committee, with 35 of its full members either under investigation or stripped of their seats in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature. The precedent for mass adjustments was set during last year’s fourth plenum, which confirmed the expulsion of 14 full and alternate members – including former senior generals He Weidong and Miao Hua – and elevated 11 alternates to full membership. The party is set to appoint a cascade of replacements to the vacant or compromised seats as it deals with the large backlog of the remaining 21 full members and seven alternate members who are facing investigation but are yet to be expelled from the committee. The vacancies reflect a sprawling anti-corruption and political disciplinary campaign that is cutting across both party and government systems as well as the People’s Liberation Army. The SCMP’s tally shows that Xi’s anti-corruption machinery clearly accelerated after 2020, when 19 “tigers” or senior officials were caught. The number of top officials facing investigation has been on a rising trend, reaching a new high of 65 last year. Most officials in the group, supervised directly by the party’s top anti-graft body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), belonged to a pool of officials known as “centrally managed cadres”, meaning they typically ranked at deputy ministerial level or above. A smaller number held slightly lower ranks but occupied sensitive positions in important sectors. Unlike their subordinates, who are managed and supervised by local branches of the party’s organisation and disciplinary agency, senior officials are under the direct management of the Central Organisation Department, its top personnel body. The Central Committee has yet to confirm the expulsion of a slew of prominent former ministerial and regional chiefs occupying full member seats who were snared in corruption investigations over the past few months or are facing legal procedures. Among them are Jiangxi’s former party chief Yi Lianhong and provincial governor Ye Jianchun, former Inner Mongolia party secretary Sun Shaocheng and government chief Wang Lixia. They include Hu Henghua, who was mayor of Chongqing, Lan Tianli, former Guangxi government chairman, Yi Huiman, who chaired China’s securities regulator, and emergency management minister Wang Xiangxi. Several lower-ranked alternate members are facing investigations but have yet to be formally removed: ex-mayor of Shenzhen Qin Weizhong, as well as the former Xian and Hefei party bosses Fang Hongwei and Fei Gaoyun, respectively, and ex-railway chief Fei Dongbin. And with just a week to go before the plenum, Xia Maolin, vice mayor of Beijing and an alternate member of the Central Committee, has come under investigation. Bijie party secretary Wu Shenghua, who was expelled from the party and dismissed from public duties in January, became a target of name-and-shame campaigns in September when Beijing made him an exemplary case of failing to address local government debts incurred by predecessors. Missing generals There was even more turbulence in the PLA, where the anti-corruption and political rectification campaign has reached the pinnacle of its command structure, the Central Military Commission (CMC). The CMC’s former deputy chairman Zhang Youxia and member Liu Zhenli were both accused of severe political disloyalty and factionalism. A broad swathe of CMC, theatre-command and service-branch chiefs holding Central Committee seats were also implicated. Many were expelled from the national legislature before their term ended, usually a sign of serious career setback. They included Wang Peng, who was director of the CMC’s training department, its political and legal affairs committee chief, Wang Renhua, as well as the head of equipment development, Xu Xueqiang. Logistics Support Department chief Zhang Lin, General Office director Zhong Shaojun and Ju Qiansheng, who commanded the PLA’s Strategic Support Force, were also removed from their positions. Other senior expulsions included ground forces commander Li Qiaoming and four political commissars: Li Wei, from the information support force, Western Theatre Command’s Li Fengbiao, Zhang Hongbing from the armed police and the air force’s Guo Puxiao. Wang Kangping, the former commander of the Joint Logistics Support Force who was removed from the national legislature in June, is the only uniformed alternate member waiting for the Central Committee’s decision. The vanished ones There are also civilian officials who have disappeared from the public eye without explanation, which could suggest some career hiccups or that they have quietly stepped down from their positions. Among the most prominent abrupt departures was ex-agriculture minister Han Jun, who was unexpectedly removed from his position in April. Also noteworthy was the sudden exit of former international liaison department head Liu Jianchao, who vanished from public view following an overseas trip last summer. He was subsequently replaced by Liu Haixing. Two critical positions bridging Beijing’s military-civilian fusion statecraft were left vacant with the departure of Jin Zhuanglong, former industry and information technology minister, and Lei Fanpei, who chaired state-owned conglomerate China State Shipbuilding Corporation. Beijing has made no announcements about their status. The replacement dynamic Under party statutes, vacancies on the Central Committee are filled by alternate members, who are ranked based on votes received at the previous congress. However, recent sessions indicate that promotions are no longer strictly aligned with the ranking of alternate members and could even become the latest indicator of further downfall. During last year’s fourth plenum, as alternate members were promoted to fill vacancies, several were bypassed – including Wang Jiayi, Shi Yugang and Fang Hongwei, with the latter subsequently expelled from the party. Any candidate skipped in the line-up at this year’s event is likely to face intense scrutiny regarding their political standing. The round of replacements in the previous plenum did not strictly follow the established ranking of alternate members. Instead, four military and three civilian alternate members were “skipped over”. The military alternates were Wang Liyan, then-deputy commander of PLA Rocket Force, Wang Kangping, who commanded the Joint Logistics Support Force, Fang Yongxiang, ex-head of the CMC’s General Office, and Shi Zhenglu from Northern Theatre Command. The skipped-over civilian officials were the then deputy education minister Wang Jiayi, former Xian party secretary Fang Hongwei and Shi Yugang, deputy chief of the provincial political advisory body in Yunnan. Several of the skipped alternate members were later officially confirmed to be facing disciplinary investigations. Wang Kangping was stripped of his seat in the national legislative body while Xian’s Fang Hongwei was detained by the CCDI just days after the fourth plenum and expelled from the party and public office in July.

title: Zelensky hopes Beijing can use ‘influence’ over Moscow to help stop Ukraine war
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that Beijing has “influence” over Moscow it should use to stop the war in Ukraine, and that a proposed summit meeting of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders must not lead to the division of his war-torn country. Speaking virtually at an event hosted by Washington-based Hudson Institute think tank, Zelensky said he did not know what would be discussed at the potential meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and...
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that Beijing has “influence” over Moscow it should use to stop the war in Ukraine, and that a proposed summit meeting of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders must not lead to the division of his war-torn country. Speaking virtually at an event hosted by Washington-based Hudson Institute think tank, Zelensky said he did not know what would be discussed at the potential meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, Zelensky described China as a “strong” country with “influence” over Russia, one of its largest trade partners. The meeting was proposed to be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China on November 18-19. No details about the meeting have been made public. “We always supported the multilateral meetings,” Zelensky said, but addressed the possibility that the three might try to decide the nation’s fate without Kyiv being at the table. “Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” he added, referring to any peace deal to settle the four-and-a-half-year war. “[I] hope nobody will divide Ukraine, because it’s not simple for us. We need friends – not Russian friends.” “We always said that [it’s] great if we can have [a] meeting with Russia, with mediation of the United States, with the support of Europe, and if China really wants to help, they can.” The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that Putin floated the idea of three-way negotiations to end the Ukraine war at the Apec gathering during a phone call with the US president earlier this month, citing sources. Trump responded on Monday that he was willing to meet with Putin and Xi but that his focus was on denuclearisation efforts between the three nuclear-armed states, not on ending the war in Ukraine. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha also rejected the idea of peace negotiations that did not include Kyiv in a social media post on Monday, saying it would “encourage Putin to continue his war” and that only a Ukraine-US-Russia trilateral meeting would end the war “sooner”. Kyiv has refused to cede any of its pre-war territory and has demanded security guarantees as a condition for ending the war. Moscow, meanwhile, asserts that Ukraine must cede the eastern flank of its country, part of what is known as the Donbas region, which is currently split between Russia and Ukraine. The Russian military has occupied much of it since the beginning of the war and has ruled out any short-term ceasefire without a final security framework. During Friday’s event, Zelensky said that he had again spoken to US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner right before his remarks at the Hudson Institute, following their meeting in Oslo on Tuesday. Witkoff and Kushner agreed to hold trilateral talks between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow at a “team level” in the first half of November “as soon as possible”, Zelensky added, suggesting Abu Dhabi as a potential venue and adding that European nations can also be part of the conversation. According to Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov, after the meeting between the Russian president and Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Moscow had “in principle” agreed to resume trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kyiv after November 10 on ending the war in Ukraine. In an interview with a Russian television station on Thursday, Putin also confirmed that he is ready to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month. But Russia remained intent on ending the conflict rather than a short-lived ceasefire, he added, to “⁠ensure the security of Ukraine and Russia”. The US, Ukraine and Russia have held three rounds of trilateral negotiations this year, meeting twice in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by further talks in Geneva in February. But no apparent progress has been made, with Russian and Ukrainian militaries deadlocked on the battlefield. Zelensky also confirmed he was open to freezing the front lines in Ukraine. That would be a “real way” to bring about a ceasefire in the long-running conflict, he added during an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, while highlighting the need to secure security guarantees from Washington and European allies.

title: Rocket debris hitting US homeland is ‘embarrassing’ for China, says astronomer
description: A scorched hunk of metal that turned up in a US farmer’s cornfield may have handed China an awkward moment and technically an “international incident”, according to a British astronomer who has tracked rocket launches for more than 30 years. The farmer found the bowl-shaped object, measuring about 3.35 metres (11 feet) across, while harvesting corn in west-central Minnesota on October 14. Online, some residents joked that aliens had landed, while Chinese internet users said it looked like a...
content: A scorched hunk of metal that turned up in a US farmer’s cornfield may have handed China an awkward moment and technically an “international incident”, according to a British astronomer who has tracked rocket launches for more than 30 years. The farmer found the bowl-shaped object, measuring about 3.35 metres (11 feet) across, while harvesting corn in west-central Minnesota on October 14. Online, some residents joked that aliens had landed, while Chinese internet users said it looked like a giant hotpot. However, space observers said it most likely came from a Chinese rocket launched on September 15. The dome appears to be the blackened end cap of a fuel tank, and it is exactly as wide as the Zhuque-2E rocket built by Beijing-based LandSpace, which had declared the mission a success. Shortly after lift-off, residents of Kansas and Minnesota posted videos of fiery debris streaking across the sky. “It’s embarrassing for China,” Jonathan McDowell, a former Harvard astrophysicist based near London, said on Thursday. “This sort of thing should not happen.” Rocket makers usually steer returning projectiles towards remote ocean, so that any fragments that survive the plunge through the atmosphere after re-entry land safely in the water. The LandSpace rocket released 10 satellites for China’s Qianfan internet network – similar to SpaceX’s Starlink – before firing its engine again as it began its descent back to Earth. McDowell said he suspected the engine was a bit stronger than expected and fired a little too long. Instead of dropping into a lower orbit and circling Earth for a few days before falling, as LandSpace probably planned, the rocket part came straight down, he said. “It seems very unlikely that they would have targeted America,” he added, while pointing out that it was not unusual for such a sizeable fragment to survive the trip down. Large, thin parts such as the ends of fuel tanks slow down quickly high in the atmosphere, before they get hot enough to burn away. In 1997, a 250kg (550lbs) steel fuel tank from a US Delta II rocket landed nearly intact in Texas. Stevens county sheriff Jason Dingman said he could not yet answer questions about the object, including its location, but expected more details to be released soon. LandSpace did not respond to a request to confirm whether the object found in the cornfield came from its rocket or if US authorities had contacted the company. The Minnesota debris is the latest in a string of problems for the Zhuque-2E. On the rocket’s previous flight in June, its upper stage broke apart in orbit, leaving dozens of fragments, US media reported. “Restarting rocket engines in orbit is always hard,” McDowell said. “But it’s been done for a long time, and it’s meant to be a solved problem. Clearly, they’ve got some wrinkles to iron out.” The debris could also make the cornfield a matter of international law between Washington and Beijing, he said. The 1972 UN Space Liability Convention holds the country that launches a space object fully liable for any damage it causes on the ground. LandSpace needed the Chinese government’s permission to launch and in return Beijing took responsibility for the rocket, McDowell said. “It’s always about the country. It all has to go through country to country. So it’s automatically an international incident.” McDowell explained that if the farmer’s land was damaged, he would have to complain to the US government, which would then be responsible for taking the claim to Beijing, which could then settle the matter with LandSpace. Such cases were rare, so the rules had not been well tested, he said, adding that while any single falling rocket part was unlikely to hurt someone, the odds increased as more came down. “We really need to stop doing this, because eventually someone will get hurt.” Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: China warns against space arms race, urges equal rights for all in outer space
description: China has unveiled a position paper on outer space governance, prioritising the prevention of space weaponisation while calling for a global framework to protect all nations’ legitimate rights beyond Earth. Addressing the inaugural Global Governance Forum near Beijing on Friday evening, Foreign Minister Wang Yi framed the document as one of eight key actions under Beijing’s Global Governance Initiative (GGI) – an overarching vision introduced by President Xi Jinping in September last year. “We...
content: China has unveiled a position paper on outer space governance, prioritising the prevention of space weaponisation while calling for a global framework to protect all nations’ legitimate rights beyond Earth. Addressing the inaugural Global Governance Forum near Beijing on Friday evening, Foreign Minister Wang Yi framed the document as one of eight key actions under Beijing’s Global Governance Initiative (GGI) – an overarching vision introduced by President Xi Jinping in September last year. “We would like to see that the rules of outer space governance keep pace with exploration, reflect broad participation and benefit all countries,” Wang told an audience of nearly 400 representing more than 90 nations. The paper, titled “China’s Stance on Enhancing Outer Space Governance”, was released by state news agency Xinhua shortly afterwards. The release of the paper comes weeks after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – the civilian head of the department that oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force – acknowledged for the first time that the Pentagon had deployed weapons in space. Beijing has consistently classified the deep sea, polar regions, cyberspace and outer space as “new frontiers” where regulatory frameworks are falling behind human activity, calling for urgent global rule-making. Pointing to uneven space development among nations, the position paper highlighted the need to safeguard the space rights of all countries and uphold the international rule of law in outer space. “The risk of an arms race and the growing trend towards weaponisation have become the greatest threats and challenges facing outer space security. Strengthening outer space global governance is an urgent task for humanity and a shared responsibility for all nations,” it said. The paper also emphasised Beijing’s strong opposition to space activities that compromise other nations’ sovereignty, security or development interests, calling for mutual respect regarding every state’s space assets, missions and personnel. Without explicitly naming the US, the paper expressed strong opposition to “unilateral sanctions” imposed on other nations’ space activities. “[We] must adhere to the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes, and oppose the weaponisation of outer space and its transformation into a battlefield. [We] oppose any single country misusing its domestic laws to create obstacles for – or impose unilateral sanctions on – the space activities of other nations.” The US has banned Nasa-China cooperation and blacklisted several Chinese aerospace and satellite firms. Beijing views these measures as discriminatory barriers designed to curb its growing space programme and isolate its commercial sector from global supply chains. On security and legal fronts, the paper reiterated China’s resistance to turning outer space into a battlefield and to its weaponisation. To head off military conflict, the document called for a ban on offensive space doctrines and called for maximum efforts to avert an arms race. Addressing commercial space regulation, the paper called for stringent oversight of private ventures. Companies must strictly comply with domestic and international law without encroaching on the rights of other nations, it stressed, specifically warning against their illegal involvement in other countries’ armed conflicts or internal affairs. Wang’s announcement and the position paper release come days after China launched a sharp critique of US space strategy at the United Nations. Addressing a UN General Assembly meeting on Tuesday, China’s ambassador for disarmament affairs, Li Chijiang, warned that preventing an arms race in space and the weaponisation of outer space has become the “most urgent task” in space security governance. Li criticised the United States for treating space as a “war-fighting domain”, accusing Washington of seeking “hegemony in outer space” with the deployment of “space control weapons”. Outlining Beijing’s proposals, Li urged the international community to speed up negotiations on an outer space arms control treaty, emphasising that space rules must be crafted collectively by all nations rather than dictated by “exclusive cliques”. Li also highlighted emerging security risks, calling for deeper analysis of the legal disputes and practical hazards associated with commercial space assets. First proposed by Xi in 2025 as a pillar of China’s foreign policy framework alongside earlier initiatives on development, security and global civilisation, GGI advocates for a UN-centric international order and greater representation for the Global South. Chinese officials say the initiative – which Beijing says has won support from over 160 countries – is intended to address mounting “governance deficits” as traditional multilateral mechanisms face growing strain.

title: ‘Opportunistic’: experts weigh Manila’s minilateral agenda ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
description: The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”. Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and...
content: The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”. Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region. They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez indicated that the Squad could meet on the sidelines of next month’s Asean summit in Manila. If realised, the talks would come just days before US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the Apec forum sidelines, in what would be their third summit meeting this year. In the interview, Romualdez also expressed hope that Asean could one day take greater responsibility for its own security, much like Nato. Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has confirmed that the Quad will hold its first summit in more than two years during the Manila gathering. Characterised as a “diplomatic partnership” by the US, the informal bloc with Japan, Australia and India – aimed at “fostering a free and open Indo-Pacific” – has not held a summit since Trump returned to power in 2025. As reported by the SCMP, Trump refused to travel to India for a Quad meet last year after the two sides failed to strike a trade deal to his liking. The timing of the meetings has led analysts to question whether the US and its allies were seizing an opportune window to highlight minilateral security cooperation and how this push might affect Asean unity and regional flexibility towards Beijing. Arrizal Jaknanihan, a researcher with the Asean Studies Programme at The Habibie Centre in Jakarta, said the prospect of Squad meetings signalled “the Philippines’ long-standing pursuit of expanding and deepening its network of security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific”. Given the recurring maritime clashes with rival claimant Beijing in the South China Sea and limited guarantees from other Asean members, “it is only natural that leaders in Manila eye the US, Japan and Australia as trusted partners”, he added. Hosting the meetings while chairing Asean, Jaknanihan contended, offered “a strategic opportunity to show its commitment to both deepening security partnership with extra-Asean countries, while remaining committed to the regional grouping in Southeast Asia”. Maritime tensions between China and the Philippines have escalated under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, who has been more assertive regarding Philippine claims compared with his predecessor. Beijing claims most of the islands and rocks in the South China Sea and rights over their adjacent waters, with rival claimants including Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei, in addition to the Philippines. Manila also asserts sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone, a position upheld by a 2016 international arbitral ruling that China rejects. Chinese coastguard and militia vessels have repeatedly used water cannons and blocking manoeuvres against Philippine resupply missions to Second Thomas Shoal and around other disputed features, resulting in a series of collisions and injuries. Manila has responded by expanding US military access under the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement, while increasing joint patrols with Squad members. He Xianqing of the Haikou-based National Institute for South China Sea Studies described the proposed Squad meetings as “both opportunistic and deliberate”. “It’s simply convenient to hold this gathering on the sidelines of the Asean summit, with so many key officials already in town,” he said. “But it also shows Manila clearly favours a smaller, tighter group built on formal US alliances, different from the Quad.” The format of the Squad grouping was “far more military-focused and centred on deterrence”, He said, noting that the Philippines, Japan and Australia were all formal US treaty allies. He added that scheduling the talks just before the Trump-Xi meeting in southern China allowed Manila to “show it stands with US security support” without looking “like a troublemaker ahead of the crucial bilateral summit”. Jennifer Kavanagh of Defence Priorities, a think tank in Washington, questioned the actual geopolitical weight of the Squad. “Despite reports of a meeting of the Squad on the sidelines of Asean, I see no evidence the Trump administration has prioritised or is investing in this vehicle,” she said. “It is not mentioned in any US strategic documents issued in recent years,” Kavanagh added, cautioning that without sustained joint training and institutional work, “the Squad will remain most irrelevant to Asian security, as it has been since it was announced under the [Joe] Biden administration”. Pointing to Trump’s preference for bilateral engagement, she said: “A meeting of regional powers without the US would send a stronger signal to Beijing than a formulaic meeting of the Squad at this point.” Commenting on the Quad meeting confirmed by Rubio, Ken Moriyasu of the Hudson Institute said: “If the leaders of the US, Japan, India and Australia were in the same venue and they didn’t hold a Quad, that would send quite the negative signal.” But he cautioned against reading too much into a meeting alone, urging observers to focus instead on “the length and substance of the discussion, including the wording used in the joint statement”. On the Squad, he said a gathering of US treaty allies “would provide an important opportunity for the Trump administration to demonstrate to the world that America’s alliance network in Asia remains ironclad”. Ambassador Romualdez’s suggestion that Asean could evolve towards a Nato-style security alliance drew the sharpest scepticism from analysts. Jaknanihan called the idea “both unrealistic and unnecessary”, as members held “differing perceptions regarding what they consider as a security threat, including China”. An alliance built around a single threat “will be the complete opposite of Asean’s approach for decades”, he noted. He of the National Institute for South China Sea Studies said an Asean Nato was “simply not realistic strategically”, pointing to the Asian group’s diverse political systems, non-aligned tradition and resistance to binding collective defence. Manila is trying to walk a very fine line ... but right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down He Xianqing, National Institute for South China Sea Studies Kavanagh was more blunt in her assessment. “Asean will never function like Nato,” she said, noting that Nato was a US-led collective defence alliance organised around blocs, while Asean operated on consensus and had no collective defence role. On Asean centrality, Jaknanihan said the grouping had long accommodated differing external alignments as long as it did not “directly harm the security interest of other Asean members”. Provided the Philippines continued to engage Asean-led processes during its chairmanship, deeper minilateral ties “will not substantially undercut Asean centrality”, he contended. But He took the opposite view, saying that concurrent Quad and Squad activity alongside talk of an Asean Nato “looks like US-led small group diplomacy [is] taking over regional security” and this “weakens Asean’s central role”. From Beijing’s perspective, Jaknanihan said that given the proximity of the Trump-Xi summit, it would be less likely to “express frontal opposition or punitive measures in response to the potential Squad meeting to avoid escalating tension, but China will definitely signal displeasure towards the development”. According to Kavanagh, Beijing “sees the Philippines as a US puppet and will interpret the ambassador’s comments as either directed by Washington or motivated by a desire to tell Washington what it wants to hear”. Looking ahead to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen and potential talks on the sidelines between Marcos and Xi, analysts expect a familiar Philippine hedging posture complicated by the surrounding optics. Jaknanihan said the meetings “offer an opportunity to find the pathway towards a more stable relationship, while still maintaining a mitigation through deeper security partnerships with Indo-Pacific partners”. He in Haikou called the dual approach “exactly the Philippines’ hedging style”, but cautioned that if Squad coordination dominated the narrative, “the Marcos-Xi meeting will end up being nothing more than a symbolic photo opportunity, with little chance for real tension reduction”. “Manila is trying to walk a very fine line: it wants both military deterrence and diplomatic dialogue with China,” He said. “But right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down.”

title: Europe considers new quotas and tariffs to stem Chinese imports
description: The European Union may hit more Chinese industries with quotas or tariffs before further negotiations with Beijing, the bloc’s trade chief said on Friday, naming plastics as a sector in which investigations are advanced. Maros Sefcovic said that when the bloc needs to move quickly to protect its industries, it will consider safeguards, which allow emergency measures to curb surges in imports, instead of engaging in longer negotiations. “We clearly will have to put it in order, prioritise, and...
content: The European Union may hit more Chinese industries with quotas or tariffs before further negotiations with Beijing, the bloc’s trade chief said on Friday, naming plastics as a sector in which investigations are advanced. Maros Sefcovic said that when the bloc needs to move quickly to protect its industries, it will consider safeguards, which allow emergency measures to curb surges in imports, instead of engaging in longer negotiations. “We clearly will have to put it in order, prioritise, and always look at what would be the most efficient tool to use. In some cases it will for sure be further negotiations with our Chinese counterparts. For others, what would be more appropriate and faster would be safeguard measures,” the trade official told reporters at a press conference in Dublin. Sefcovic explained that the European Commission is currently gathering feedback from EU members on which areas to prioritise for protectionist measures, “when they feel that this particular sector is under a lot of stress”. “But currently, what I think is the closest is the plastics sector, and there we are working with [the directorate of] trade and looking into it,” he said, adding that the bloc needed to ensure it had a “very solid case, not only from economic but also from [a] legal point of view”. Sefcovic spoke on Friday after a meeting of EU trade ministers in Dublin. During a debate on China, attendees outlined the industries they are most concerned about. Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee, who chaired the meeting, named chemicals, machinery and some agri-food sectors as among those raised. Earlier in the day, the French minister said he was confident that his country’s push with Germany for a tougher EU China policy propelled Beijing to moderate its hybrid car exports, despite warnings from the Chinese capital that the pressure did not work. “I’m certain that it played a role, and it’s very important that the German and French engine, which is very essential to the future of Europe, starts again – and I think that’s going to be the case,” French Trade Minister Nicolas Forissier said as he arrived at the ministerial meeting in Dublin on Friday. Earlier this month, Berlin made a dramatic U-turn on its China policy, joining Paris – which has for years backed a more protectionist policy to counter distortions caused by Beijing’s model – in calling for tariffs, quotas and muscular new trade weapons. That same week, China agreed not to retaliate against a European Union move to cap the import of its hybrid cars at 350,000 per year from December 1. Across Europe, the shift was seen as a Rubicon moment for the bloc’s external policies. Beijing, however, pushed back at that suggestion. The EU should “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”, the Ministry of Commerce said. For years, Germany blocked Brussels’ efforts to steer trade strategy in a more hawkish direction. With the two biggest economies on board, however, progress is likely to move faster. The European Commission, which manages trade policy for the EU’s 27 members, is set to propose three new instruments by Christmas. DiversifyEU, a European Commission policy proposal to address strategic economic dependencies on single non-EU countries for critical goods and inputs, will compel companies in key sectors to broaden their pool of suppliers in an effort to stop the weaponisation of key inputs. A “solidarity mechanism” will compensate companies hit by retaliation from trade rivals, which is seen as a way of ensuring that EU member states do not block trade actions against China. A “kill switch”, meanwhile, will give the bloc the power to kick Chinese companies out of the EU market with near-immediate effect. Asked by the South China Morning Post whether the “kill switch” would be a new instrument or a modification of the existing anti-coercion instrument, which was never used, Sefcovic appeared undecided. In such a “turbulent world”, Sefcovic said, the commission is “looking at what would be the best parameters and best legislative procedure, which would guarantee that we would have this instrument in our hands as soon as possible”. Forissier, meanwhile, urged the bloc to stay the course, despite China warning that it would retaliate. “Chinese authorities understand when you’re clear, when you speak frankly, when you’re firm on your positions; this is necessary. We have not done that for a long time. This has to be done not only country by country but also in an EU way,” he said, adding that Europe must “be able to say no” to China. Arriving at the same meeting, Polish deputy economic development minister Michal Baranowski said Warsaw supported the new approach and welcomed the deal on hybrid cars. “It is a good beginning. But let’s acknowledge that this is just a beginning. It is a movement in the right direction because we have not seen changes in the Chinese understanding of the imbalances until now, and that’s a real movement,” Baranowski said. Baranowski added that member states would use the meeting in Dublin to identify sectors where there was concern about the impact of China’s export wave. The commission has said it will move quickly with more safeguards, which allow the quick imposition of import quotas – as with hybrid cars and before that steel – and sometimes tariffs. “A number of countries will identify their sectors as well. I think the key here is where we go next. So that’s mostly for the negotiations,” Baranowski said. “What I would emphasise is the need for us to keep building good, effective, and quick tools … to make sure that we have a credible response if things get worse.”

title: Why jaw-jaw is the best route EU leaders can take right now
description: Beijing has told Brussels not to “fantasise” that pressure will extract concessions. This came after China made a goodwill gesture in the recent hybrid-car trade deal. The European Union responded by doubling down on a proposed trade “kill switch”. The instrument follows a Franco-German proposal. It would let the bloc swiftly restrict single-market access in response to economic coercion. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen says all 27 leaders back it. Chemicals and machinery are priority sectors....
content: Beijing has told Brussels not to “fantasise” that pressure will extract concessions. This came after China made a goodwill gesture in the recent hybrid-car trade deal. The European Union responded by doubling down on a proposed trade “kill switch”. The instrument follows a Franco-German proposal. It would let the bloc swiftly restrict single-market access in response to economic coercion. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen says all 27 leaders back it. Chemicals and machinery are priority sectors. French President Emmanuel Macron wants to add plastics and ferroalloys. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and others want a tougher, unified line on Chinese trade practices, currency depreciation and critical dependencies. The formal proposal is expected in December. Unanimity among 27 leaders is itself a rare thing. It is usually reserved for communiques about how much everyone values unanimity. At a time when a proxy war with Russia, a likely trade war with China and acrimony with the United States are pushing the cost of living and livelihoods of ordinary Europeans to the brink, this is starting to look like a case of collective madness, a communal death drive. But China is the least of its problems. The union faces what may be its most precarious moment. Its leaders are deeply unpopular, and its economy is sluggish. No wonder angry Europeans are hitting the streets. I have read a description of a “European Autumn”, with citizens turning on their rulers in one capital after another, much like the Arab Spring. Could Europeans become as fed up with incompetent and arrogant leaders as Arabs did? But when in trouble, von der Leyen and foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas do what they always do: escalate on every front. In this context, it’s instructive to turn to an address last week by American economist Jeffrey Sachs at the European Parliament, where he summed up the madness. Its title was “How to Make Peace in a Crazy World”. It was, of course, duly ignored. Sachs called the war rhetoric now dominating Europe “shocking and extremely dangerous”. He said the US is in a deep political crisis, and he described his president in terms not exactly suitable for polite society. His message to Members of the European Parliament was that Europe is on its own, but its leaders are not helping by picking fights everywhere, most of all with China. His big picture started with Asia. In 1820, he said, it produced about 60 per cent of world output. By 1950, after a century-and-a-half of imperial plunder, war and chaos, that share had sunk to 20 per cent. Today it is back to about 50 per cent. Sachs, who has worked in China and India for decades, called this one of the great achievements of the past half-century. Four billion people are better off. Washington and much of Europe’s political class see only a threat in that. His explanation was that China committed the crime of refusing to stay poor. He argued that Russia committed a similar offence. He cited the historian John Howes Gleason’s study of how Britain went from ally to enemy of Russia within about 25 years after Napoleon’s defeat, apparently because Russia had grown large enough to frighten London. He called today’s Ukraine war a “second Crimean War” and “our war,” not simply Putin’s. It is an old argument, but still true. Nato expanded despite Western assurances in 1990. Washington quit the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in 2002. The 2008 Bucharest summit promised Ukraine and Georgia eventual membership over Angela Merkel’s private objections, and he said Merkel’s own memoir describes how Moscow interpreted that. Sachs called 2014 a coup in Kyiv, described the Minsk II agreement as sabotaged, and recalled telling Joe Biden’s security adviser Jake Sullivan in December 2021 to treat Moscow’s draft security proposals as an off-ramp. Sullivan, he said, cited Nato’s open-door policy. Europe continues to defer to Washington. Was it silent when the US and Israel attacked Iran? Sachs said he watched European ambassadors at the UN Security Council condemn Iran’s response but say nothing about the strike that provoked it. He proposed a straightforward ending, though it is unlikely to be heeded in European capitals. Nato should declare that it will not expand to Ukraine or Georgia, and then negotiate an armistice line in Ukraine. Merz should simply pick up the phone and call Moscow. The German leader, of course, has just called for escalation. Sachs praised former German leaders Willy Brandt, Helmut Schmidt and Helmut Kohl, who talked to adversaries, because that was what diplomacy is. Sadly, their successors prefer war-war to jaw-jaw, to paraphrase Winston Churchill.

title: Xi Jinping leads early Politburo meeting to signal anti-corruption drive ahead of plenum
description: China’s Communist Party convened an early monthly Politburo meeting on Friday to review a key internal inspection report, doubling down on its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign ahead of a major party conclave next week. Chaired by President Xi Jinping, the now 21-member Politburo met on Friday – earlier than its traditional end-of-month schedule – to discuss a comprehensive report on the seventh round of inspections by the 20th Central Committee. The latest inspection is a major internal...
content: China’s Communist Party convened an early monthly Politburo meeting on Friday to review a key internal inspection report, doubling down on its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign ahead of a major party conclave next week. Chaired by President Xi Jinping, the now 21-member Politburo met on Friday – earlier than its traditional end-of-month schedule – to discuss a comprehensive report on the seventh round of inspections by the 20th Central Committee. The latest inspection is a major internal anti-corruption sweep focused specifically on top-level central party and government organs. Launched in April, 15 central inspection teams carried out routine inspections across 36 vital central state institutions, including core political, legal and government ministries. The meeting on Friday called for the “stern rectification” of problems uncovered within central government and state organs, demanding a sustained high-pressure posture against corruption and an unyielding commitment to strict party governance, according to state news agency Xinhua. The central authorities should “strictly fulfil the political responsibility for managing and governing the party, implement all tasks of full and rigorous self-governance of the party with higher standards and more concrete measures, maintain a high-pressure stance against corruption, strictly adhere to a rigorous tone through to the end, and build politically sound agencies with a clean and healthy atmosphere,” the report said. The early gathering comes ahead of the fifth plenum of the 20th Central Committee, set for October 26-29 in Beijing. Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major milestones on the country’s political calendar. This month’s session is attracting global attention as the world’s second-largest economy navigates complex external tensions and seeks an increasingly prominent role in global affairs. The high-stakes political gathering is widely expected to focus on tightening party governance, reinforcing internal discipline and demanding absolute political loyalty. Central and state agencies were urged during Friday’s meeting to serve as the “first phalanx” in upholding the authority of the Central Committee and enhancing their political judgment and execution while taking on greater responsibility to manage risks and balance development with security, according to Xinhua. The anti-corruption drive comes against the backdrop of unprecedented scrutiny targeting the party’s elite. Of the present 205 full Central Committee members, 35 have either been placed under investigation or stripped of their legislative seats in China’s top legislature, according to calculations by the South China Morning Post. Many of those targeted have been cited for political disloyalty to the central leadership. Work is under way on a power reshuffle that will be finalised during the party congress in autumn 2027, when a new Central Committee will be formed and major leadership changes announced. In keeping with previous party conventions, preparations for next year’s party congress are expected to already be advancing, including multiple rounds of screening hundreds of officials, a process that will last until summer.

title: What Beijing’s 2-to-1 shipbuilding lead means for the US in war over Taiwan
description: Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan. Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial...
content: Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan. Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted. The Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed. The survey, compiled by maritime intelligence publication Flottes de Combat and the French Naval Industry Association, found China accounted for more than 43 per cent of global naval production tonnage in the two years, compared with just over 18 per cent for the US. Chinese yards delivered 84 vessels, up from 31 in 2022 and 2023, while American deliveries rose from 32 to 38, said the report, which was presented in Paris on Tuesday ahead of next month’s Euronaval defence exhibition. While the US Navy’s combat fleet remains more than double the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) by tonnage, China is catching up. But analysts have questioned whether total tonnage alone would prove decisive in a war fought near China’s coast. China has had the world’s largest navy by number of ships since at least 2020, according to the Pentagon, with the new survey counting 418 PLA Navy combat vessels on January 1. But at 1.44 million tonnes, they displaced less than half the 3.11 million tonnes of the US Navy’s 283 ships. The US had 11 aircraft carriers to China’s three. Still, China is rapidly renewing its fleet. More than 40 per cent of the PLA Navy’s combat ships have entered service since 2018. Chinese yards delivered 10 destroyers in 2024 and 2025 to America’s four, while the PLA Navy commissioned 26 combat vessels against the US Navy’s nine. Retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral Peter Jones attributed that pace to consistent shipbuilding practices. Designs appeared to be developed through Chinese naval research bodies and state-owned shipbuilder CSSC, avoiding repeated commercial tenders, he said. Chinese destroyers and frigates followed a process of “incremental development”, with “modest upgrades between batches” reducing production risks, Jones said. A “steady drumbeat of work” at five specialised shipyards helped build workforce expertise. By contrast, the US had “only some elements of this”, he added. Its Arleigh Burke destroyer programme was a success, but other projects suffered from “turbulence in decision-making”. Washington, he said, “just needs to return to the proven approach to shipbuilding across the fleet’s programmes”. China’s commercial shipyards reinforce that advantage. Brian Hart, deputy director of the China Power Project at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said builders had “intentionally blurred the boundaries” between naval and commercial production. Because the same yards built cargo ships and tankers, Beijing could “ramp up production of naval vessels in a protracted war”, he noted. Chinese civilian ships that are not currently counted in combat-fleet totals could serve as military transports – since 2015, national standards have required certain cargo ships to be able to meet military needs. Hart cited “dual-use barges and ferries” that could boost amphibious transport capabilities, along with unmanned systems outside traditional counts. Vessel types could distort shorter-term comparisons, said Bradley Martin, a senior policy researcher at the Rand Corporation and retired US Navy captain. American warships were often “large and complicated ships” that took years to build, so the delivery of a single carrier, such as China’s Fujian in 2025, could skew the figures. China is also catching up in firepower. Hart pointed out it “has been rapidly closing the gap” in vertical launch system cells, which fire missiles from warships and submarines. Still, Hart said, the US had nuclear-powered carriers, unlike China. It also has more capable submarines and, crucially, experience gained through decades of global operations and combat. Yet China is trying to close the undersea gap. The survey estimates that expanded facilities at Huludao – a coastal city in northeast China’s Liaoning province – can produce three nuclear-powered attack submarines annually, exceeding current US output. Martin argued that nuclear submarine warfare was not an area where “quantity can reasonably overcome quality”, though more Chinese boats could increase demands on anti-submarine forces. A war over Taiwan, however, would be fought close to mainland China’s shores, where Martin said US warships would face land-based strike forces, so ship-to-ship engagements “might not be the most relevant consideration”. The longer a conflict lasted, the more Beijing’s industrial depth would matter, particularly its ability to keep producing “landing craft and logistics support forces”. Lyle Goldstein, Asia programme director at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, called China’s shipbuilding lead “not an anomaly, but rather a persistent trend”. The western Pacific naval balance, he argued, “has been tilting decidedly in Beijing’s favour for some time”. In a mid-Pacific encounter, the US would “almost certainly prevail”, he said, but fighting around Taiwan or in the South China Sea “would radically favour China”. In waters close to the Chinese mainland, such as the Taiwan Strait, “size can actually be a disadvantage”, making smaller diesel submarines preferable to nuclear-powered ones. To keep pace, Washington would likely need allies. Martin said partners could supply smaller warships and auxiliaries and undertake “battle damage repair”. But Goldstein warned that air and missile strikes could make western Pacific yards unusable, urging stronger rear-area defences across the second and third island chains. Losses could be severe. Given the lethality of modern anti-ship weapons, “many ships and even whole fleets would be sunk or badly damaged” in a high-intensity naval war, Goldstein said. In such a conflict, starting fleets could matter less than how quickly they were replaced – and as the survey’s figures show, China is building faster.

title: Good to see you after all this time. Chinese scientists put a face to the Denisovans
description: Chinese scientists have finally put a face to the Denisovans, a mysterious species of ancient humans who were previously known only through the evidence of their DNA and fossil fragments.
