content: Chinese scientists have finally put a face to the Denisovans, a mysterious species of ancient humans who were previously known only through the evidence of their DNA and fossil fragments. The hominids were thought to have lived in parts of Siberia and East and Southeast Asia thousands of years ago. The work of reconstructing their face was based on fossils excavated from Xujiayao, a major archaeological site in northern China’s Nihewan Basin, between 1976 and 1979. Scientists also confirmed that the collection of ancient human remains belonged to the Denisovan lineage, allowing them to reconstruct what they looked like. The remains, dated between 138,000 and 199,000 years old, included skull bones and teeth that had long puzzled palaeontologists trying to classify where they fit on the ancient human family tree. Without any complete skulls to work with, the team, led by Fu Qiaomei, a palaeontologist at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, had to reconstruct their features from fragments. They concluded that their skulls were low and wide, with fairly thick bones. The sides of the braincase were relatively flat rather than rounded, while the back section of the lower jaw was quite wide, according to the official newspaper Science and Technology Daily. “This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama),” the scientists wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on Wednesday. The researchers were also able to confirm that the fossils were Denisovans through the discovery of a key protein marker that was not found in Neanderthals and modern humans. While the extraction of ancient DNA is almost impossible, proteins can survive longer than DNA without fully degrading. “The palaeoproteomic results revealed Xujiayao hominins as Denisovans,” the researchers said, adding that their “similarities with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong) indicate that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage”. The study also showed that “Denisovans could have lived in East Asia from at least [300,000 to 45,000 years ago], paralleling the temporal range of Siberian Denisovans”. “[It was] a broadly distributed homo lineage that adapted to diverse ecological zones, including the high-altitude plateau, subtropical forest and insular environments, across Siberia, East Asia and Southeast Asia.”

title: Japan’s university defence bids surge as post-war taboo fades amid China concerns
description: Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defences. The increase is the clearest sign yet that academia’s decades-long resistance to military-linked work is easing. The bids accounted for more than half the record 560 applications received by the ministry this year, up from 340 last year, with the rest coming from public...
content: Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defences. The increase is the clearest sign yet that academia’s decades-long resistance to military-linked work is easing. The bids accounted for more than half the record 560 applications received by the ministry this year, up from 340 last year, with the rest coming from public research institutes and companies. Of the 47 projects selected for funding under the 12.9 billion yen (US$82 million) programme, 30 will be led by university researchers, with 11 universities – including Osaka, Nagoya and Keio – winning grants for the first time. Speaking on Tuesday, Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi welcomed the figures, saying the attitude of universities had “clearly changed”. He said civilian and defence technologies could no longer be clearly separated, making closer cooperation with universities “essential to protecting Japanese lives”. The shift could have important implications for Tokyo’s efforts to counter Beijing’s growing military capabilities, potentially opening up a wider pool of civilian scientific expertise for the development of advanced sensors, communications systems, drones and other defence technologies. Beijing has long drawn on universities and civilian research institutions to support military modernisation through its military-civil fusion strategy. However, in Japan, whose post-war constitution renounces war, concerns rooted in the country’s militarist past have traditionally limited cooperation between academia and the defence establishment. In 1950, the Science Council of Japan pledged to never conduct research for war, reaffirming that position in 1967. In 2017, it again opposed military-linked research, citing concerns about academic freedom and the potential military use of scientific findings. University applications fell from 58 in the programme’s first year in 2015 to just nine in 2019. Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, said the recent surge reflected a broader erosion of “antimilitarist norms” as well as institutional changes encouraging military-related research. He pointed to a younger generation of scholars with different perceptions of Japan’s security environment, alongside growing competition for civilian research grants. For cash-strapped universities, the defence ministry’s research grants offer an increasingly attractive alternative. The programme’s annual budget, boosted sharply in 2017, has risen from 10.4 billion yen in 2024 to 11.4 billion yen last year and 12.9 billion yen this year, more than 40 times its initial allocation of about 300 million yen in 2015. Still, military research “remains a key controversy” at many national universities, Maslow said, particularly given the role of academia during World War II. Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, also cautioned against viewing the increase as a “sudden embrace of military research”. Rather, she said, the “institutional, financial and normative barriers” to seeking defence grants had weakened because of three “mutually reinforcing” factors: university funding pressures, the science council’s more nuanced stance on dual-use technologies since 2022 and the ministry’s campus outreach. While China’s military build-up provided “an important strategic context”, Matsuoka added, changing security perceptions were not necessarily the main explanation. The shift comes as Tokyo prepares to revise its main security policy documents by year-end. Japan’s most recent defence white paper presented China as its “greatest strategic challenge”. Although the defence ministry’s grant programme supports basic research rather than weapons development, several projects selected this year could eventually help to strengthen Tokyo’s ability to counter Beijing’s growing military capabilities. Hokkaido University, for instance, received funding for research combining infrared and visible-light imagery using artificial intelligence, which Matsuoka said could contribute to “surveillance and situational awareness”. At Nagoya University, researchers secured support for advanced millimetre-wave transistors, which Koizumi said could eventually contribute to ultra-high-speed communications. Gifu University will study lightweight carbon fibres for drones, while Osaka University is developing high-output batteries for uncrewed aircraft. Other funded projects relate to quantum communications, heat-resistant aerospace materials, satellite tracking and space debris observation, as well as rare earth-free materials that could help reduce Japan’s dependence on Chinese-dominated supply chains. Although none of the projects identifies China or any other country as its intended target, the research illustrates the growing role of universities in Japan’s defence sector. Maslow said closer cooperation between universities, companies and government pointed to a “new dynamic ecosystem” for defence innovation, even as opposition within academia persisted. Matsuoka cautioned, however, that translating successful university research into deployable military capabilities could take five to 10 years, or longer. The key question, she said, was whether Japan could “translate that research into practical capabilities” while maintaining the “institutional autonomy and openness” of its civilian research sector.

title: Typhoon Champi grounds hundreds of Taiwan flights, threatens Shanghai and Japan
description: Flight disruptions and cancellations surged across East Asia as Typhoon Champi approached Taiwan on Friday, prompting emergency precautions in eastern mainland China, including Shanghai, and in Japan during a large-scale joint military drill with the US. Taiwan’s transport ministry said 262 local flights and 715 international and cross-strait flights had been cancelled as of 10am on Friday. The island’s largest airports – Taiwan Taoyuan, Taipei Songshan, Kaohsiung and Taichung – faced widespread...
content: Flight disruptions and cancellations surged across East Asia as Typhoon Champi approached Taiwan on Friday, prompting emergency precautions in eastern mainland China, including Shanghai, and in Japan during a large-scale joint military drill with the US. Taiwan’s transport ministry said 262 local flights and 715 international and cross-strait flights had been cancelled as of 10am on Friday. The island’s largest airports – Taiwan Taoyuan, Taipei Songshan, Kaohsiung and Taichung – faced widespread flight cancellations as of Friday, according to the flight-tracking platform DAST. Meanwhile, 14 airports across eastern mainland China were expected to be affected in the coming days, including nine in Zhejiang province, a major manufacturing and tech hub, and one in Fujian province. They include Shanghai Pudong, Shanghai Hongqiao, Hangzhou Xiaoshan, Ningbo Lishe and Wenzhou Longwan. Authorities in Shanghai ordered the evacuation and relocation of residents in high-risk zones including Pudong, Jinshan and Chongming by 6pm on Friday. Mainland media reported that a total of 540 flood shelters and 7,992 temporary emergency stations had been fully prepared to house displaced residents in China’s commercial and financial capital. In addition, 188 offshore fishing vessels have returned to ports for shelter, while safety inspections and reinforcements have been carried out on tower cranes, outdoor signboards and roadside trees. All outdoor high-altitude operations have been completely suspended, with multiple emergency response teams placed on standby. In Jinshan, which borders Hangzhou Bay and Zhejiang, workers at a kiwi orchard rushed against the clock to harvest ripe fruit before the typhoon arrived. Across Shanghai, flood-control authorities lowered water levels in rivers and lakes across the city to expand storage capacity and protect residential areas. And maritime officials in Jinshan on Thursday instructed vessels to move to safer waters. Mainland airlines have also taken action in anticipation of travel disruptions. To accommodate stranded travellers, Air China, China Eastern Airlines, China Southern Airlines and other carriers have offered free rebooking or full refunds for passengers flying to and from the affected Taiwan airports. After peaking on Wednesday as a super typhoon and one of the year’s strongest storms, Typhoon Champi weakened to a severe typhoon on Thursday. The storm has since maintained its intensity, packing winds that reach up to 162km/h (101mph) near its centre, according to mainland China’s National Meteorological Centre. Between Friday night and Saturday morning, Champi is expected to weaken as it approaches Taiwan’s northeastern coast, possibly brushing past the island. The typhoon is then forecast to move north along Zhejiang’s eastern coast on Sunday, possibly skimming the mainland province, before turning northeast towards Japan. The national forecaster has issued a blue typhoon warning for Champi, the lowest level in China’s four-tier system. Champi is set to bring heavy rain and strong winds to eastern China. Mainland state news agency Xinhua reported that heavy rainfall was forecast to swell the Jiaoxi River in Fujian and several coastal waterways in Zhejiang, including the Feiyun and Oujiang rivers, as well as Taihu Lake, a major freshwater lake in eastern China, and its surrounding river network. Some smaller rivers in Zhejiang could exceed warning levels, with a heightened risk of flash floods in hilly areas. On Thursday, mainland authorities activated emergency responses for Shanghai, Zhejiang and Fujian, urging agencies to step up weather monitoring, forecasting and early-warning measures. Owing to strong gales, 56 coastal ferry routes, 130 passenger ferries and 111 maritime construction projects across Fujian were suspended as of Thursday, according to local media reports. Among the halted routes are four ferry services connecting Fujian and the outlying Taiwan-controlled islands of Quemoy, also called Kinmen, and Matsu. The routes serve as vital corridors for direct trade, travel and postal transit. Ahead of Champi’s predicted path to Japan, the island nation is bracing for the storm as well. Major Japanese carriers All Nippon Airways (ANA), Japan Airlines, Peach Aviation, Skymark Airlines and Solaseed Air cancelled more than 170 flights between Friday and Saturday, disrupting travel for nearly 16,000 passengers, according to local media reports. Japan Airlines on Friday said it had cancelled flights to Taipei Songshan and Taiwan Taoyuan. Champi is also disrupting “Keen Sword”, a massive military drill between Japan and the United States taking place around Japanese islands near Taiwan, according to Reuters. The exercise is conducted every two years, rehearsing Japan’s defence through coordinated land, sea and air operations, including missile drills and amphibious landings. Starting this past Monday and running through next Thursday, the exercise reportedly involves about 45,000 Japanese Self-Defence Forces personnel and 12,000 US troops, making it one of the largest joint drills ever held by the two allies. “Training activities are being adjusted on a day-to-day basis to ensure the safety of all participants,” the American military was quoted by Reuters as saying. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: China’s head transplant advocate Ren Xiaoping completes landmark spinal surgery in Russia
description: Ren Xiaoping, who once vowed to perform the world’s first human head transplant, has operated on a patient’s severed spinal cord in a 12-hour landmark operation in Moscow, according to the Chinese surgeon and Russian state sources. Ren said the procedure was carried out at the Sklifosovsky Research Institute for Emergency Medicine in Russia last week. “It was our Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine Second Affiliated Hospital and the Russian team working together,” Ren told the South China...
content: Ren Xiaoping, who once vowed to perform the world’s first human head transplant, has operated on a patient’s severed spinal cord in a 12-hour landmark operation in Moscow, according to the Chinese surgeon and Russian state sources. Ren said the procedure was carried out at the Sklifosovsky Research Institute for Emergency Medicine in Russia last week. “It was our Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine Second Affiliated Hospital and the Russian team working together,” Ren told the South China Morning Post on Thursday. According to an article quoting Ren and published in the New Scientist on Wednesday, the team removed a segment of spinal cord that had been severed by trauma three years earlier and replaced it with a segment from a brain-dead donor, using microsurgery and polyethylene glycol, a substance that helps fuse cell membranes for the “world’s first spinal cord transplant”. “The surgery was completed on October 14-15, lasting 12 hours. The patient’s condition is currently stable,” he said. Ren did not answer when asked if the surgery was a “world first” but said he had performed a series of Russia’s first transplant surgeries at the centre. Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin posted on Telegram on October 16 that “a patient who was originally at risk of complete paralysis has been given a chance to recover. Now, he is feeling well.” Russia’s Tass state news agency made a similar statement the evening, saying Chinese doctors had been involved and medical technology was shared. There has been no further update on the surgery or the patient. Further, no peer-reviewed paper or clinical data on the surgery has been published. The Sklifosovsky Research Institute for Emergency Medicine is one of the oldest in Russia and the largest multidisciplinary medical practice centre in Moscow. In China, Ren is well known as a surgical and transplant specialist. In 1999, while studying in the United States, he took part in the world’s first hand transplant surgery. After returning to China, Ren was director of the Hand and Microsurgery Centre at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University. In 2015, he announced he would cooperate with Italian neurosurgeon Sergio Canavero to complete the world’s first human head-transplant surgery within two years. But the surgery did not go ahead because of medical community concerns about ethics and backlash from the public. Ren said he had done head transplant experiments on monkeys in 2016, and the following year said he and Canavero had created a surgical model for human head transplant surgery on two cadavers. In 2019, he joined the Second Affiliated Hospital, Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine, the institution that last week collaborated with the Russian Medical Centre. According to an announcement on the Russian hospital’s website, the recent spinal cord transplant surgery continued an ongoing joint upper limb transplant project between China and Russia. Guangxi University of Chinese Medicine’s website said Ren had led teams to Russia for clinical cooperation multiple times. In April last year, he and the Russian National Emergency Medical Centre performed Russia’s first allogeneic, or donor-derived, hand transplant, according to the Chinese hospital’s website. Since the first case, Ren has completed six difficult allogeneic hand transplant surgeries in Russia. At the 17th Congress of Russian Surgeons in Moscow on October 12, Ren was awarded the “Mission Award” for outstanding Russian doctor. The certificate in Russian, signed by Deputy Prime Minister Tatiana Golikova, said: “You successfully performed a groundbreaking surgery, saving the patient’s life.”

title: What do the protests in France look like from China? Internet users weigh in
description: Internet users in China are watching the protests in France with a mix of geopolitical cynicism, domestic pride and sadness at the damage to French landmarks. The protests started in September, when students and teachers in southeastern Paris rallied against deteriorating school conditions. Those specific grievances quickly escalated into nationwide protests at the rising cost of living and declining public services. What began as peaceful marches has since dissolved into violence, with rioters...
content: Internet users in China are watching the protests in France with a mix of geopolitical cynicism, domestic pride and sadness at the damage to French landmarks. The protests started in September, when students and teachers in southeastern Paris rallied against deteriorating school conditions. Those specific grievances quickly escalated into nationwide protests at the rising cost of living and declining public services. What began as peaceful marches has since dissolved into violence, with rioters looting hundreds of shops and setting fire to vehicles and historic landmarks, including the 143-year-old town hall in the city of Limoges. Multiple public buildings across cities including Paris, Marseilles and Bordeaux were also targeted. The comment sections on various online news reports about the unrest were flooded with the remark “a beautiful sight” – a reference to former US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s description of the massive anti-extradition bill demonstrations in Hong Kong in 2019 as “a beautiful sight to behold”. Chinese internet users have used those words before to mock civil unrest in the United States, such as the 2021 attack on the US Capitol and 2025 Los Angeles demonstrations against immigration policies. Other sarcastic comments on France’s chaotic scenes included “such a developed country” and “France is so free and democratic”. These collective responses echo official criticism of Western politicians’ “double standards” on China’s domestic affairs. It seeks to counter the Western view of China as a strict surveillance and authoritarian state by contrasting it with turbulence under Western-style democracy. Some social media users have also linked the Paris chaos to France’s foreign policy, framing the unrest as a self-inflicted consequence of its support for Ukraine against Russia. “Keep helping Ukraine so the fire in their own backyard burns even brighter,” one commentator wrote. Another comment read: “[French] President Macron should focus more on the livelihood of his own citizens rather than pouring money into the war in Ukraine.” China has consistently described itself as neutral in the Ukraine war, calling for dialogue while refraining from condemning the Russian invasion and denying Western allegations that it has given Moscow military support. Other Chinese internet users praised the stability and safety of China. “China is so much better; it’s pure chaos abroad,” one popular comment noted. Others echoed the sentiment. “China is the safest place to be, and we should cherish the peace we have.” Yet, there was also a wave of dismay at the destruction of French cultural heritage. “A century-old historic landmark lost to fire, such irreplaceable heritage gone forever – it’s truly heartbreaking,” a comment read, amassing nearly 20,000 likes. For some, footage of the burning Limoges Town Hall prompted parallels with the destruction of Beijing’s Old Summer Palace, which was looted and burned by Anglo-French forces in 1860. In addition, commenters voiced concern for Chinese students and workers living in France. In response to the deteriorating security situation, China’s foreign ministry and its embassy in Paris have issued safety advisories, warning Chinese citizens in the country to remain vigilant and stay clear of demonstration zones.

title: Chinese state media takes aim at Japanese firm KDDI over Mongolia wildfire
description: Chinese state media has called for a Japanese telecoms firm to apologise to China over a huge wildfire in neighbouring Mongolia, as diplomatic tensions run high between Beijing and Tokyo. The grassland fire broke out on October 8 and burned about 80 per cent of a nature reserve on the Mongolia-China border. According to Japanese media reports, the company, KDDI, has acknowledged that the fire was linked to activities involving its majority-owned subsidiary MobiCom – the largest mobile network...
content: Chinese state media has called for a Japanese telecoms firm to apologise to China over a huge wildfire in neighbouring Mongolia, as diplomatic tensions run high between Beijing and Tokyo. The grassland fire broke out on October 8 and burned about 80 per cent of a nature reserve on the Mongolia-China border. According to Japanese media reports, the company, KDDI, has acknowledged that the fire was linked to activities involving its majority-owned subsidiary MobiCom – the largest mobile network operator in Mongolia. Mongolian media reported that a vehicle used by MobiCom executives had caught fire, igniting dry grass and causing the large-scale blaze, with the company potentially facing compensation claims. “We take extremely seriously the fact that a fire occurred in connection with the activities of MobiCom, a company within our corporate group, causing a significant impact on Mongolia’s natural environment,” KDDI said in a statement on Tuesday. It said the blaze started after a MobiCom vehicle caught fire during an on-site survey. “We sincerely apologise to the people of Mongolia, our customers, and all relevant parties for the tremendous trouble and concerns this situation has caused,” the statement said. That followed an apology on October 14 from MobiCom’s Japanese chief executive Yasuhiro Ochi, who said in an interview: “We deeply regret the damage we have caused to the environment and sincerely apologise to the people of Mongolia.” But a number of Chinese state-run news outlets took aim at the Japanese company on Wednesday and Thursday this week, saying that KDDI – which owns 98.85 per cent of MobiCom – had yet to make a formal statement on the impact of the fire in China. Official tabloid Global Times said China had taken on an “enormous cost” to prevent the fire from spreading across the border, deploying more than 3,400 emergency personnel who worked day and night for nearly a week. “The Japanese company involved in the incident and the individuals bearing responsibility ought to apologise to China,” the editorial said. “This is a fundamental baseline for clarifying their liability and addressing the legitimate concerns of the Chinese public, with absolutely no room for evasion.” In its commentary, Changanjie Zhishi, a social media outlet run by Beijing Daily, said that while the fire had been successfully contained on the Mongolian side of the border, the Chinese side – the Inner Mongolia autonomous region – still had to contend with smoke and dust pollution, as well as the impact on its grassland ecosystem. The KDDI statement on Tuesday confirmed that Ochi and two other executives were visiting the area on the day the fire broke out. It said they were there to “conduct 4G network communication tests” and had official permission to do so. In its commentary, Changanjie Zhishi accused the company of “concealing the true purpose of the trip”, citing Mongolian media claims that the MobiCom executives had travelled to the protected nature reserve to fish for the critically endangered taimen. “Starting with lies and offering only a selective apology after being exposed – where is the genuine remorse?” reads the commentary. The state media accusations come amid rising tensions between Beijing and Tokyo over issues including Taiwan and security. Both outlets also suggested there was a lack of coverage by Japanese media during the early stages of the incident. They claimed Japanese far-right groups could seek to shift blame onto China by portraying its response as an example of the “cognitive warfare” used by Beijing. The wildfire started in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Mongolia’s eastern province of Dornod, which neighbours China’s Inner Mongolia region. Thousands of Chinese emergency personnel were mobilised to patrol along the 330km border, widen firebreaks, clear vegetation and extinguish flames. It took until October 16 to extinguish the blaze, which was contained over the border with no casualties reported on the Chinese side, according to Xinhua.

title: China’s Xi Jinping orders urgent relief after Tibet earthquake leaves 16 dead
description: All efforts need to be focused on search and rescue for survivors and treating the injured, President Xi Jinping instructed on Friday morning, after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake killed 16 and injured 65 in China’s Tibet autonomous region overnight. “The disaster-hit area is located in a high-altitude region with cold weather. It is imperative to closely monitor seismic activity and weather changes and implement rescue operations accordingly, while preventing secondary disasters,” he said,...
content: All efforts need to be focused on search and rescue for survivors and treating the injured, President Xi Jinping instructed on Friday morning, after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake killed 16 and injured 65 in China’s Tibet autonomous region overnight. “The disaster-hit area is located in a high-altitude region with cold weather. It is imperative to closely monitor seismic activity and weather changes and implement rescue operations accordingly, while preventing secondary disasters,” he said, according to state news agency Xinhua. Xi added that emergency rescue supplies needed to be allocated and those affected in the disaster should be settled properly, while damaged infrastructure should be repaired as soon as possible. The weather in the region is minus 5 degrees Celsius (23 Fahrenheit), with a small chance of snow. Premier Li Qiang also instructed the Ministry of Emergency Management and the China Earthquake Administration to continue monitoring the region for any aftershocks. An emergency team has been sent to the scene, while the local government has organised relief efforts and settled those affected. More than 300 soldiers and more than 20 vehicles from the Tibet Military Command and the armed police were mobilised to the affected area during the night, state broadcaster CCTV reported. The earthquake hit Baqing county, a mountainous area about 400km (250 miles) northeast of the capital Lhasa, at around 10.33pm on Thursday, according to Xinhua. More than 300 houses collapsed and around 20 livestock sheds were damaged. A CCTV reporter said that after driving eight hours to the disaster area, he saw rocks across the highways, 20cm-wide (7 inch) cracks in rock walls and houses entirely destroyed. As he headed to the village, he also saw trucks delivering disaster relief supplies. One survivor told CCTV he felt a “strong tremble, almost like hundreds of yaks running together”. After being shaken awake, he heard wardrobes and timber pillars squeak in the room and realised it was an earthquake. He immediately grabbed his 80-year-old father and ran out the door, he said. A level-2 emergency response was activated in the area immediately after the earthquake, while the first batch of relief supplies – including 1,000 prefabricated houses, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds, 200 stoves and four generators – arrived on Friday morning, Xinhua said. The report said 12,489 people had been evacuated, while grid-based searches, emergency rescue operations and disaster assessment were carried out. The finance and emergency management ministries have jointly allocated 50 million yuan (US$7.49 million) to the disaster-hit region, according to CCTV. A team of 10 from the Tibet division of Sichuan’s West China Hospital has arrived with a mobile CT scanner, ambulances and emergency medicines. The China Earthquake Networks Centre (CENC) said that as of Friday morning, it had recorded 413 aftershocks in the region, with the biggest measuring magnitude 4.3. By the afternoon, local authorities had launched round-the-clock monitoring and emergency repairs at key sites, including mountains, reservoirs, power stations, rivers, old buildings and telecommunications stations, the Nagqu city government said. Electricity and communications facilities in the disaster-hit areas were being gradually restored, while monitoring stations had been issuing timely aftershock and weather warnings, a spokesman said. He also said that public security and transport authorities had inspected 12 roads covering more than 1,700km as well as 201 bridges, identifying potential hazards and clearing rocks at intersections. The earthquake was the result of pressure on the Tibetan plateau caused by the continuing collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, a CENC analyst told People’s Daily. Six earthquakes of magnitude 7.0 or above have been reported since 1900 in the Qiangtang block, which includes Baqing county. The most recent one took place in 2021 in Biru county, about 103km from Baqing, the report said. Based on historical seismicity levels and regional geographical structure, earthquakes might still happen in the region and its vicinity in the coming days, it added. Bao Xuewei, a researcher at the school of Earth sciences at Zhejiang University, told Zhejiang Daily that the hypocentre – or starting point in the Earth’s crust – of this earthquake was only 10km deep, classifying it as a typical shallow-focus earthquake. Such quakes generate stronger surface waves, which cause buildings to sway from side to side, raising the risk of damage.

title: Chinese astronomers find real 3-body system. It is not what Liu Cixin thinks
description: In author and computer engineer Liu Cixin’s science fiction hit The Three-Body Problem, three suns throw a doomed world into chaos. Using FAST, the world’s biggest single-dish radio telescope in southwestern China, the researchers found two dead stars and a “living” one locked in a steady cosmic dance about 7,000 light years from Earth. One of the dead stars is a pulsar that spins more than 300 times a...
content: In author and computer engineer Liu Cixin’s science fiction hit The Three-Body Problem, three suns throw a doomed world into chaos. Chinese astronomers say they have found a real three-star system that is far better behaved. Using FAST, the world’s biggest single-dish radio telescope in southwestern China, the researchers found two dead stars and a “living” one locked in a steady cosmic dance about 7,000 light years from Earth. One of the dead stars is a pulsar that spins more than 300 times a second, about as fast as the blades of a kitchen blender. It whirls around its partner, a white dwarf – the dim, burnt-out core of a smaller star – every eight days. Meanwhile, a star much like the sun circles the pair from afar, taking 73½ years to complete each lap. The team, led by Han Jinlin from the National Astronomical Observatories in Beijing, reported the finding in The Astrophysical Journal Letters earlier this month. It is only the second such system known, after one found by a US-led team in 2014 in which all three stars were already dead. “The detailed evolution of triple-star systems is complicated and poorly known,” the researchers wrote in their paper. The newly identified system, they added, was “unique” for studying how such star families changed over time. Triple-star systems are fairly common, but those containing a millisecond pulsar – the fast-spinning core left behind when a massive star explodes at the end of its life – are “extremely rare”, according to the team, because the star’s explosion can easily tear the system apart. Such systems give astronomers a rare chance to test theories of gravity. For instance, this one could help check a key idea in Einstein’s theory of gravity, known as the strong equivalence principle: that everything falls the same way, whether it is a feather or a city-sized dead star heavier than the sun. Pulsars are some of the most reliable clocks in the universe. As they spin, they sweep beams of radio waves across space like a lighthouse and the pulses reach Earth so regularly they can rival atomic clocks. So astronomers were puzzled when this one, first spotted by FAST in 2020, seemed to be running slow. Five years of monitoring by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory showed its spin was losing speed about 100 times faster than other pulsars of its kind. In a paper published in Nature Astronomy in April, the Xinjiang team said the finding challenged a standard theory of how such pulsars formed. They also noted hints that something else might be lurking in the system. The researchers behind the new study went looking. Combining FAST data with observations from other telescopes, including 18 years of gamma-ray data from Nasa’s Fermi space telescope, they found the culprit: a sun-like star hiding in plain sight. As the star slowly circles the pair, its gravity tugs the pulsar back and forth, making it look as if the pulsar’s spin is slowing down. The three stars were likely born together from the same cloud of gas, like triplets, the team said. Because they started out with very different masses, the siblings have aged at very different speeds. The biggest, about 20 times the mass of the sun, burned out first and exploded, leaving behind the pulsar, while the second faded into the white dwarf. The smallest, about the mass of the sun, sits far enough away to survive its siblings’ deaths and is still shining. Eventually it too will burn out, according to the researchers, leaving behind a pulsar and two white dwarfs, much like the system found in 2014. A European team, with scientists from Germany, the Netherlands, France and Britain, independently reached the same conclusion in a paper posted online in July. Both teams found that the sun-like star will swing closest to the pair in 2036. As it does, its pull on the pulsar will change quickly, allowing scientists to measure the system much more precisely.

title: Asia Society announces new permanent home in historic Washington building
description: The Asia Society announced on Thursday that it had marked out territory on the Washington policy landscape with the purchase of a US$17.5 million building that will give it a permanent spot alongside other US capital think tanks dating back more than a century, striving for influence. Rockefeller, has focused more on public policy in recent years, in addition to its traditional focus on arts, culture and education, under...
content: The Asia Society announced on Thursday that it had marked out territory on the Washington policy landscape with the purchase of a US$17.5 million building that will give it a permanent spot alongside other US capital think tanks dating back more than a century, striving for influence. The 70-year-old institution, founded by the grandson of oil mogul John D. Rockefeller, has focused more on public policy in recent years, in addition to its traditional focus on arts, culture and education, under former Australian prime minister and Asia Society President Kevin Rudd. “The Blaine Mansion is the ideal Washington location for our Policy Institute and its China Centre,” Rudd said in a statement. Thursday’s announcement came a day after it closed on the historic 15,000-square-foot James G. Blaine Mansion, which will house offices, state-of-the-art conference facilities and meeting spaces. The Guilded Age building, listed at US$29.95 million in 2023, then reduced to US$19.99 million in 2025, also has a private pool as part of its 7,000-square-foot penthouse, plus three levels of underground parking and an attached restaurant space and office annex. A quick search suggests the think tank is currently the only one in Washington with a pool, although the Asia Society is reportedly looking into renovating the rooftop area. The purchase was made possible by Stephen Schwarzman, a society trustee and the chairman, chief executive and co-founder of Blackstone, the world’s largest asset management firm, who was the lead donor, in addition to contributions by other trustees and supporters. The financier, listed by Forbes as the world’s 46th richest person with a net worth of US$41.7 billion, has long supported US-China ties. In 2023, he gave US$100 million to launch the Schwarzman Scholars programme at Schwarzman College on Beijing’s Tsinghua University campus. Earlier this month, the House Select Committee on China called on the Trump administration to sanction several Chinese institutions, including Tsinghua. “The relationships between the United States and countries in Asia will shape much of this century, and policymakers need a trusted, independent forum for candid dialogue and the sharing of expertise,” Schwarzman said in a statement. The Gilded Age mansion is located in Washington’s DuPont Circle neighbourhood, sometimes dubbed “think tank row”. Blaine is within a few blocks of the nation’s oldest, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, founded in 1910. And it is in company with the others, shuttling lawmakers, academics, foreign leaders and journalists in and out of lunch meetings, seminars and Track 1.5 and 2 “unofficial” negotiation sessions. Within a few blocks of Blaine are the Brookings Institution, the Peterson Institute for International Economics, the American Enterprise Institute, the Centre for Strategic and International Studies and the German Marshall Fund of the United States, among others. In a bid to shake their reputation as too bookish and at arm’s length from the pointy end of policy, some think tanks started rebranding themselves after the 1980s as “do tanks”. Others have at times referred to the neighbourhood as “universities without students”, the “C-Span echo chamber” and part of the “Washington is Hollywood for ugly people” characterisation attributed to Democrat strategist Paul Begala in the early 1990s. Blaine Mansion has had a storied history. Lawyer and former diplomat John Phillips and his wife, Linda Douglass, most recently sold it. Phillips, a former ambassador to Italy and San Marino from 2013-2017, practised public interest law, which would not, on the face of it, seem hugely lucrative. But he was a pioneer in the US Government’s 1980s whistle-blower reward programme meant to encourage citizens to report fraud. This saw his firm take on numerous major fraud cases that recovered over US$13 billion for state and federal governments over several decades. These were pursued under a contingency fee model – under which a law firm only gets paid if it wins – that saw his Phillips & Cohen LLP earn hundreds of millions of US dollars. The building was completed in 1882 for James G. Blaine, a Maine politician who served as US Secretary of State. Among its past lives, Blaine Mansion was the home of inventor George Westinghouse, the Japanese Embassy from 1921 to 1925, the Rural Electrification Administration during the Great Depression and the offices of the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation. Phillips and former journalist Douglass embarked on a multi-year US$20 million renovation after buying it in 2006 for US$6.2 million. “We are proud that the Asia Society Policy Institute will make this distinguished heritage building its permanent home in Washington,” said Rudd.

title: ‘Saved my mum’s life’: Chinese cancer drug on sale in US after Americans travel to buy it
description: Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca on Thursday said it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China. In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than...
content: Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca on Thursday said it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China. In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease. “I’m very thankful to all the development that companies in China have done because it saved my mum’s life,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, told the South China Morning Post. Developed by China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical, sunvozertinib is a targeted lung cancer drug designed to treat adults with an advanced form of the illness, offering another treatment option for patients. “Being in China physically, when I was there, I felt a very strong presence of connection between two very foreign, two very different places,” Doppelt said. “We are all human beings, and health transcends it all. There are no political biases or sides when it comes to health.” He added that he knew of at least 30 other Americans who had made the same trip. Doppelt said he decided to travel to Shanghai to obtain the drug after his mother’s lung cancer spread to her brain in January 2025, when she had about 10 tumours. At a lung cancer conference, a doctor told him that if his mother “happened to have lived in China, she could just get it”, as the country had approved the drug in 2023. “I became pretty obsessed over it because my first reaction was, well, why don’t we go to China?” However, at the time, he grew increasingly concerned about the escalating trade war between Washington and Beijing, marked by tit-for-tat tariffs and export controls. “I was reading that in the news every day. So my main concern was: in six months, will there still be an avenue and a route for my mum to get this medicine?” Despite the geopolitical tensions, he flew to China and returned home with 26 boxes of the China-made drug. The Washington Post first reported the story on Tuesday. AstraZeneca said on Thursday that sunvozertinib would be commercially available in the United States under the brand name Zegfrovy, after securing worldwide rights to develop and sell the drug from China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical. While the FDA granted an “accelerated approval” to the drug in July 2025, AstraZeneca announced its “exclusive license agreement” with China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical in July of this year. “AstraZeneca will acquire worldwide rights to develop and commercialise Zegfrovy,” the company said in a press release. The deal included a US$600 million upfront payment to Dizal, with a further US$900 million potentially payable upon meeting specific regulatory clearances, as well as tiered royalties on global sales of Zegfrovy. “The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory clearances,” the statement added. In an email response to the SCMP, an AstraZeneca spokesperson said the global licensing agreement was “completed” only on September 1, 2026, and that the firm “has been working to make Zegfrovy available to patients in the US as quickly as possible”. “By making Zegfrovy available in the US, we are bringing an oral, mutation-specific treatment option to a distinct patient population with substantial unmet need,” the spokesperson added. Doppelt said he initially chose not to speak publicly but became “increasingly frustrated” that the drug remained unavailable in the US despite an FDA approval. “Every single quarter, we have been told as a community, of all the lung cancer patients who have this mutation, that it’s going to be ready next quarter. It’s going to be next quarter.” However, Doppelt said he would not blame the drug maker for the 15-month delay. “Without AstraZeneca, we wouldn’t even have the drug today.” Kyle Concannon, a doctor-scientist at the University of Colorado, said Washington needed to change its approach to developing and adopting new treatments. “If the US wants to remain competitive and ensure patients don’t have to travel across the world for treatments, we need to both accept greater risk, recognising that for many patients the alternative is no treatment,” he wrote on social media. Anne Wojcicki, CEO and founder of the 23andMe Research Institute, noted that China had transformed from a country known for producing raw materials into a global force in drug discovery, contrasting its position with that of the US in the early 2000s. “The world has flipped. It’s remarkable how China has become a powerhouse in drug discovery and is now leading,” she said on social media. She added that artificial intelligence would bring another shift in the industry, with large-scale data initiatives and “nimble regulatory oversight” key to driving progress. China has rapidly expanded its pharmaceutical sector, taking the lead in clinical trial registrations between January 2024 and June 2025 with 24 per cent of the world total, according to World Health Organization data compiled by the British Medical Journal. China’s share of global early-stage drug-development programmes rose from 8 per cent in 2015 to 32 per cent in 2024, closing the gap with the US, whose share fell from 48 per cent to 37 per cent over the same period, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in March 2026. Doppelt called for FDA reforms, including greater transparency around clinical trials and data reporting, as well as greater openness to testing new cures. He also pointed to China’s approach to cellular therapy research, saying the US could adopt some of its practices. “In China, I think we could learn something from them because there are dozens of cellular therapy trials that are spun up all the time.”

title: EU mulls sanctions reprieve for Chinese fabric-maker accused of aiding Russia
description: Diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states were pressured this week to lift sanctions on Yusha Group, a Chinese textiles manufacturer accused of selling sensitive European technology to Russian buyers. In exchange, Beijing has pledged that the company will refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers. It will also remove German company Sindlhauser Materials from its own export controls list, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair. The unusual quid pro quo –...
content: Diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states were pressured this week to lift sanctions on Yusha Group, a Chinese textiles manufacturer accused of selling sensitive European technology to Russian buyers. In exchange, Beijing has pledged that the company will refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers. It will also remove German company Sindlhauser Materials from its own export controls list, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair. The unusual quid pro quo – the product of high-wire negotiations at the top level of EU and Chinese politics – is designed to protect the supply chain of Europe’s most valuable technology company, Dutch-based ASML, of which Sindlhauser is a reported supplier. Yusha Group was blacklisted by the European Union in February 2025, three years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Hubei-based company, whose primary business is textile manufacturing, was then named in an Irish Times investigation for shipping Irish-made antennae to Quasar, a Russian company that has been sanctioned by the United States for its role in the Russian invasion. Now, should EU diplomats agree to de-list it, Yusha could be free to buy and sell sensitive goods in the European market again, showing the negotiating leverage China’s grip on the global minerals market affords it. During talks in the Chinese capital this month, top-level EU trade officials led by commissioner Maros Sefcovic were presented with the proposal, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair. Sindlhauser, which was listed by Beijing in July in a dramatic response to another raft of EU sanctions, is reported to be part of the supply chain of ASML, which has cornered the market for the precision lithography machines that are essential to the global supply chain for semiconductors. Beijing’s sanctions cut Sindlhauser, which makes specialist materials used in precision coatings for the semiconductor industry, off from rare earths and other critical minerals that are essential to its manufacturing processes. Earlier this month, Bloomberg – which first reported the exchange regarding Sindlhauser but did not name Yusha – said the German manufacturer was at “risk of going out of business in the coming months” after being choked from its Chinese supplies. The European Commission declined to comment on the situation, while the Chinese Mission to the EU, Sindlhauser Materials and Yusha Group did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The dynamic shows the fraught nature of Europe’s new-found appetite for geoeconomic manoeuvres. It is heavily dependent on suppliers from China and the United States, meaning its every offensive move risks a counterpunch that can hurt its own struggling industries. Nor is it the first time the bloc has backtracked on its listing of Chinese firms. In June, EU ministers paused restrictions on Chinese chipmaker Yangzhou Yangjie Electronics, which had been sanctioned in an earlier round of measures targeting Russia’s war machine. The move allowed European carmakers reliant on the firm’s supplies to complete existing orders. During Wednesday’s debate at the Coreper II grouping of EU ambassadors, sources said some capitals had reservations about delisting a company that has been implicated in assisting Russia’s war effort. No final decision was made and the debate is expected now to move next week to the Working Party of Foreign Relations Counsellors, a committee that deals with legal, financial and institutional issues related to EU foreign policy. On Wednesday, during a speech at the European Parliament, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed the success of recent talks between her trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. While the headline deliverable was a 350,000 cap on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc, the German official talked of “the removal of certain EU companies from Chinese control lists” – an oblique reference to Sindlhauser, sources confirmed. It is unclear at this stage whether the controls have been fully lifted from Sindlhauser, but the expectation in Brussels is that Beijing will stick to its side of the deal if the EU delists Yusha. In an effort to unpick these sorts of dependencies and to restrict their impact, the commission is set to make a trio of proposals in December. DiversifyEU, an initiative aimed at reducing the bloc’s dependence on critical foreign supplies, will compel companies in key sectors to broaden their pool of suppliers in an effort to stop the weaponisation of key inputs. A “solidarity mechanism” will compensate companies subject to retaliation from trade rivals, which is seen as a way of ensuring the EU’s member states do not block trade actions against China. A “kill switch”, meanwhile, will give the bloc the power to kick Chinese companies out of the EU market with near-immediate effect. The latter is seen as a second strike weapon – usable in an instance where China weaponises its critical mineral dominance should the sides descend further into a trade war. The instruments are being developed in tandem with intense negotiations with China’s commerce ministry about rebalancing the bilateral trade relationship, talks which yielded the breakthroughs on hybrid cars and export controls. Beijing has, in recent days, repeatedly warned the EU not to believe it has landed on a “dual track” formula for extracting concessions from the Chinese government. “The EU should not fantasise about gaining benefits through pressure, nor should it underestimate China’s determination and ability to safeguard its own interests,” read a Ministry of Commerce statement last Friday.

title: 16 killed, 32 hurt after magnitude 7 earthquake strikes China’s Tibet
description: At least 16 people were killed and 32 more injured when a strong 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s western Tibet autonomous region late on Thursday, state news agency Xinhua said, citing local authorities. More than 300 houses collapsed in the earthquake, which struck on Thursday at 10.33pm. Officials were still evaluating the damage, and disaster relief work was ongoing, Xinhua said. The epicentre of the quake was located in a mountainous area about 190km (120 miles) east-northeast of...
content: At least 16 people were killed and 32 more injured when a strong 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s western Tibet autonomous region late on Thursday, state news agency Xinhua said, citing local authorities. More than 300 houses collapsed in the earthquake, which struck on Thursday at 10.33pm. Officials were still evaluating the damage, and disaster relief work was ongoing, Xinhua said. The epicentre of the quake was located in a mountainous area about 190km (120 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km northeast of the regional capital Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said. It struck at a shallow depth of 10km (6 miles) in Maru township in Baqen county. A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, Xinhua said earlier. Maru township deputy head Lhawang Dagpo said the quake was clearly felt at the township office, which sustained cracks in the walls, according to Xinhua. Power and telecoms services were disrupted in the county seat, the agency said. Earthquakes in China are relatively common, but Thursday’s quake is reportedly the strongest to hit mainland China since January 2024. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in a magnitude 6.8 earthquake in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

title: Quad confirmed, Manila envoy signals likely ‘Squad’ talks before Trump-Xi summit
description: The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks. An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US...
content: The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks. An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US and three of its treaty allies: the Philippines, Australia and Japan. The Quad, by contrast, includes India in place of the Philippines and is not a formal military alliance. Speaking exclusively with the South China Morning Post in a recent interview, Jose Manuel Romualdez also voiced hope that Asean would evolve into a Nato-like alliance capable of handling its own security. The “Squad” and Quad meetings are expected to take place in the Philippines just days before US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month. “This type of meetings regularly happen, and if it’s an opportunity that is there, I’m sure that they will do it,” Romualdez said when asked about a possible “Squad” defence ministers’ meeting. On whether the grouping would be raised to the leaders’ level, Romualdez – who is also President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s second cousin – said it would depend on “what kind of an agreement” or meetings that officials “will have on the sidelines of the Asean summit”. A source familiar with the discussions said the probability of the “Squad” meetings was “very high” and added that since many US allies and partners would be in the Philippines, the “pretence” of US diplomatic commitment could be “cheaply done”. Before the leaders’ summit from November 16 to 18 in Manila, the Philippine Department of National Defence will host the defence ministers’ meeting and related engagements on October 28 and 29 in Cebu. Manila’s ambassador to Washington stressed that Marcos had consistently pursued a “multilateral approach” to the Asia-Pacific region, backed by a network of defence agreements with other countries. “We’re counting now about seven or eight of them, but more importantly, between Japan, Australia, the United States and the Philippines,” he said. Romualdez confirmed, however, that Marcos would attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen, expressing hope that he could at least have a “possible good conversation” with Xi even if no formal meeting took place. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on Tuesday that the Quad leaders would meet in the Philippine capital next month, marking the group’s first summit in more than two years. “It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the Asean conference,” Rubio said in an interview with Indian news channel CNN-News18. “We don’t have the specific date yet, but that’s going to happen, and we’re very enthusiastic about it.” The Squad and the Quad were part of the previous Joe Biden administration’s strategy of building a “latticework” of coalitions to counter China’s clout. The first meeting of “Squad” defence ministers took place on the sidelines of the Shangri-La security dialogue in Singapore in June 2023, followed by a series of interactions. The Trump administration has continued the dialogue, with the most recent engagement between defence chiefs taking place on the sidelines of the Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, last November. Military officials of four countries also convened for a defence cooperation council meeting in May in Singapore. Beyond deepening security ties with regional powers, the Philippine envoy to Washington also floated the idea of an “Asean Nato”, reviving a proposal rejected by the country’s defence secretary, Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, in 2024. “I’m even hoping that Asean will become like a Nato, that it can take care of its own security,” Romualdez told the SCMP. He added that “having an integrated security” is more efficient as the Asean countries are “all together” and “live in the same neighbourhood”. “Then we can make agreements with countries like China as a whole, agreements with the United States,” he said. “I hope that one day we will be able to have not only our economies integrated, but even our defence and military.” Teodoro in November 2024 had dismissed the prospect, saying that Asean’s complex “dichotomies and divergence in country interests” would make it challenging to set up a unified military alliance. The ambassador’s statements come as the Trump administration recalibrates its priorities in the Asia-Pacific, prompting concerns among regional partners over the durability of US security commitments and Washington’s strategy for competing with China. In June, the US renamed the Indo-Pacific Command as Pacific Command, reversing a change made in 2018. In August, Trump ordered the annual US-South Korean military exercise be cut from 11 days to five. Washington has redeployed the Japan-based USS George Washington to the Middle East for operations against Iran, leaving no US aircraft carrier permanently stationed in the Indo-Pacific. The Trump administration has also pressed regional allies and partners to shoulder more of their own defence costs. Romualdez argued that he saw no sign of US commitments weakening for now, but stressed that Manila had to be “ready for any kind of eventuality”. “We remain focused on strengthening our armed forces to where we want it to be, so that we would be able to defend ourselves.” He also ruled out any possible involvement in a Taiwan crisis, saying the Philippines was not part of any security arrangements related to the island and that his country adhered to the one-China policy. “The only role that Philippines right now has in Taiwan is the fact that we have 250,000 workers. We obviously are concerned about that,” he added, referring to Filipino migrant workers living on the island. The ambassador’s stance is in sharp contrast to that of defence chief Teodoro, who has rejected Beijing’s warnings over Manila’s engagement with Taiwan. “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them,” Teodoro said in September. Under an expanded defence pact, the Philippines has granted the US military rotational access to strategic sites in northern Luzon, including bases in Cagayan province near Taiwan. The two countries have also expanded joint military exercises in the northernmost Batanes islands, where Manila is strengthening its own military infrastructure. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the island’s main international partner, the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force and is legally bound to supply it with weapons to defend itself.

title: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
description: Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first. In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions. Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed...
content: Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first. In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions. Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris. It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January. “I can tell you that the French-German paper you refer to was clearly seen from China as ‘OK, now it’s becoming serious’. For the first time, France and Germany agreed on this,” Pascal Canfin, the ranking member on China in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told reporters on Wednesday. Canfin was referring to a now-famous joint paper between the EU’s biggest powers, which proposed a kill switch that could kick Chinese companies out of the EU market overnight, which has now become an official policy to be proposed in December. His comments reflected a new-found confidence in Europe on how to conduct relations with China. “If you just negotiate without the credible possibility to do something differently, then negotiation is not credible at all. If we have the two legs and one voice, I think we are much stronger than we thought, because China is also dependent on the access to our market,” said Canfin, who will join a delegation of trade MEPs visiting China next week. In Berlin on Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was “surprised” at the “unanimous support” from EU members at the summit, even as he said Germany did not want a trade war with China. “The first indication that this could really have an effect on our relations is that obviously the government in Beijing is willing to accept a limited number of car imports to the European Union, which was not the case in the last couple of weeks and months. So we are making progress,” Merz said. In the run-up to last week’s summit of EU leaders, more than a dozen diplomatic and official sources suggested the bloc had landed on a “two-track” formula of intense dialogue, backed by hard trade action. The suggestion has been met with fury in Beijing, where official organs have been pushing back strongly against the idea that China could be managed in such a way. “China’s willingness to make a strategic compromise should not be confused with a willingness to accept an endless series of concessions. Mistaking the former for the latter could turn Beijing’s goodwill into the next source of confrontation,” fumed Brussels Tea House, a newsletter written by Xinhua journalists in the Belgian capital, on Wednesday. The comments echoed an official commerce ministry statement on Friday, which warned the bloc not to “fantasise” that its pressure had worked. The EU should “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”, the ministry said. On Wednesday, however, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen doubled down on the strategy, promising further trade restrictions and new instruments to defend European industries against Chinese competition. “We see jobs lost in our industrial heartlands. So last week, at the European Council, we agreed a clear approach. First, dialogue where it delivers. Second, action where needed. And third, stronger tools to defend our interests,” von der Leyen said, adding that the commission was “already working closely with our chemicals and machinery sectors”, where further quotas were expected. The deal will cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 per year from December 1. The South China Morning Post has been told that quotas will also be applied to South Korea, Japan, Turkey, Britain and Morocco, calculated using last year’s volume of exports plus an additional 15 per cent. The commission would, sources said, be examining these flows for evidence of circumvention by Chinese companies looking to fill out quotas elsewhere. In her address to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen spoke of “the removal of certain EU companies from Chinese control lists”. The SCMP understands this refers to the German company Sindlhauser, an important supplier to ASML which was added to a Chinese blacklist in July and removed in a tit-for-tat delisting. Bloomberg previously reported that, unable to access Chinese inputs, the company was at risk of going bust. Some are hoping that the Beijing agreement can be the bedrock of something more substantive. Bernd Lange, who will lead the European Parliament delegation to China next week, called for further agreements “quite soon”, adding that “negotiations forever make no sense”. “I remember the negotiation on the so-called CAI, the investment agreement, which is deep in the freezer,” Lange told reporters, referring to the Comprehensive Agreement on Investment, frozen by the parliament after a row over human rights sanctions in 2021. Lange suggested revisiting the investment provisions of the frozen agreement, including whether Brussels and Beijing could ease restrictions on each other’s investors. Behind the scenes, however, the triumphalism was less apparent. A well-placed official worried that public remarks last week overhyped what negotiators see as a first step, potentially harming the next rounds of negotiations. Some also wonder if the shift came too late. A deal to cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars is a “pyrrhic victory”, said one senior diplomat, noting that it covered a minute portion of overall trade. “Look at what is going on in France, [far-right leader Marine] Le Pen could be in next year – I am not sure any of this China hawkishness outlasts [President Emmanuel] Macron in Paris,” they said, with an eye on presidential elections in April 2027, likening the mood in Brussels to a football team celebrating a consolation goal when they are already 6-0 down.

title: China urges opening Bab al-Mandeb in first joint statement with regional nation
description: In its first formal statement with a Red Sea nation on the fallout from the US-Iran war, China said in a joint communique with Djibouti that it backs “constructive efforts” to ensure international shipping lanes are safe and open. The statement on Thursday was released a day after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart Abdoulkader Houssein Omar met in Beijing. “The two sides emphasised the importance of safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab...
content: In its first formal statement with a Red Sea nation on the fallout from the US-Iran war, China said in a joint communique with Djibouti that it backs “constructive efforts” to ensure international shipping lanes are safe and open. The statement on Thursday was released a day after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart Abdoulkader Houssein Omar met in Beijing. “The two sides emphasised the importance of safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and stressed that the navigation rights exercised by merchant vessels of all countries in accordance with international law should be respected,” the communique said. “China supports Red Sea coastal states in constructively safeguarding the unobstructed and secure operation of international shipping lanes and protecting the region’s common interests.” Chinese analysts said the situation in the Red Sea had not yet escalated to a level that warranted direct naval escorts, though Beijing would closely monitor the region and might take action if the country’s shipping came under threat. Djibouti occupies a critical strategic position just across the narrow Bab al-Mandeb Strait from Yemen. The strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is a chokepoint in trade between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean. Both sides expressed a shared desire to prevent regional tensions from further spilling over into the Red Sea, according to the communique. Djibouti has hosted a Chinese overseas military support base since 2017, which is designed to facilitate naval escorts conducting anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden. It also hosts US, French, Italian and Japanese bases. Tensions between Yemen’s Houthi movement and Saudi Arabia have worsened in recent months. While the conflict between the two has been simmering since 2014, the militant movement declared a “maritime embargo” on shipping from the kingdom passing through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait after a Saudi-backed Yemeni coalition attacked the Houthi-controlled Sanaa airport in July. “China has long championed freedom of navigation. Issuing such a joint communique with Djibouti, a nation positioned at the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and host to Beijing’s sole overseas military support base, carries far more symbolic weight than routine diplomatic statements issued under normal circumstances,” said Li Weijian, a researcher at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies. The situation did not yet require Chinese naval escort operations, as no Chinese vessels had been threatened or attacked, Li said. Beijing remained committed to seeking a peaceful and lasting solution through diplomatic channels, Li said, though if the situation changed then China’s reaction could also change. “Whether further action will be taken depends on how the situation develops. If it continues to escalate and poses a threat to Chinese shipping safety or the lives and property of Chinese citizens, I believe China will certainly take further measures,” he said. Niu Xinchun, director of the China-Arab research institute at Ningxia University, noted that the immediate threat to Chinese vessels was limited, as the Houthis had explicitly said they were targeting Saudi Arabia only. Meanwhile, the recent recovery in Middle East oil exports had eased supply pressures, further reducing any immediate need for naval escorts, Niu said. Oil exports from Middle East producers excluding Iran averaged 24.6 million barrels per day in the week to October 18, higher than a pre-war average of 23.3 million, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing data from commodities data provider Kpler. Analysts attributed the recovery in oil shipments to high profits and growing operational experience, which have kept tankers navigating the Strait of Hormuz despite lingering dangers. Beyond calling for freedom of navigation, the joint communique also addressed the role of external powers in the conflict and warned that the “flames of war” should not spread from the Middle East to the Horn of Africa. “The international community, particularly major powers from outside the region, should abandon double standards, respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of regional countries, and refrain from resorting to force or imposing unilateral sanctions,” the joint communique added. While Saudi Arabia has sought US support against the Houthis, Washington’s stance has fluctuated. Last month, US President Donald Trump called off planned air strikes against Houthi targets at the last minute, caught between defending a key ally and avoiding expanding the war with Iran. As Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia intensify, including attacks causing civilian casualties, the US on Wednesday ordered the departure of non-emergency government personnel and their families from the kingdom.

title: Luxury hotels hit the high seas with Ritz-Carlton, Four Seasons and Aman leading the way
description: Between a cruise liner and a private yacht charter lies the luxury hotel at sea, offering five-star service and intimate, experience-led voyages.
content: There are plenty of ways to travel in luxury by sea. A cruise liner cares for every practical detail, but its scale means strict schedules, crowds and little room for unique experiences. A private yacht charter, by contrast, can feel thrillingly free and discreet, but usually comes with eye-watering costs, logistical difficulties and a relative lack of fancy facilities like spa treatments and on-board entertainment. The latest launches and expansions from respected names in hospitality occupy the slim stretch of water between them: the luxury hotel at sea. This promises the calm of a design-led resort and the intuitive service of a trusted hotel brand, while retaining enough small-ship agility to make an itinerary feel personal rather than mass market. A ritzy experience The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection was early in making a convincing case for this category. The company was announced in 2017 and its first yacht, Evrima, made its maiden voyage in October 2022. Since then, it has grown from an intriguing one-ship experiment to a three-vessel fleet: its second vessel, Ilma, arrived in 2024, and Luminara followed in 2025. The idea, says Ernesto Fara, president and chief executive of The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, was to meet the needs of luxury travellers who wanted to explore by sea but did not identify with conventional cruising. “They wanted something intimate, experience-led and rooted in the standards of luxury hospitality they already knew and valued,” he says. This is the differentiator. Evrima features 149 suites, each with a private terrace, and accommodates up to 298 guests. Ilma features 224 suites and accommodates up to 448 guests.
