Luminara features 226 suites and accommodates up to 452 guests. “A private yacht offers extraordinary intimacy and access but generally cannot provide the range of restaurants, wellness, public spaces and programming available aboard The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection,” Fara says. “A luxury cruise ship provides breadth, but generally at a greater scale.” These yachts aim to offer the social and sensory range of a resort without its crowds. Guests can dine in several restaurants, spend a morning in the spa, join a cultural talk or retreat to a suite, all without chartering a boat. The company’s smaller scale also lets it pair Tokyo and Osaka with Japanese ports including Ishigaki, Otaru and Akita, rather than circling only the heavily trafficked cruise terminals. Sailing with the Four Seasons The Ritz-Carlton is not the only five-star hotel brand in the game. Four Seasons I began its maiden Mediterranean voyage on March 20 this year, on the 65th anniversary of the brand’s first hotel. Its 95-suite yacht has no interior cabins, a one-to-one guest-to-staff ratio and a chef-in-residence programme that brings in talent from Michelin-starred Four Seasons restaurants, including Guillaume Galliot of Caprice in Hong Kong. Its dedicated Experiences team tailors shore and sea days rather than selling fixed excursions, reinforcing the hotel-style proposition. Four Seasons II is scheduled to enter service in early 2028, while a third yacht is due in late 2031. The brand also operates the Four Seasons Explorer, a catamaran that can host 22 guests. Adding a yacht to the Aman world Next comes Aman, a brand that has long made privacy its signature sign of luxury. Amangati is due to launch in May 2027 and will be the brand’s first foray into the space, with just 47 suites for 94 guests, each with a private terrace. The yacht will also carry a two-to-one staff-to-guest ratio, a spa spread across two decks and two helipads. For Vlad Doronin, Aman Group’s owner, chairman and chief executive, the premise is more radical than simply adding another ultra-luxury vessel to the Mediterranean. “Today, nothing truly exists between traditional cruising and a superyacht charter,” he says. “We saw an opportunity to create something genuinely private, where guests feel as though they are on their own yacht, not a cruise.” Aman shares the same belief as The Ritz-Carlton and Four Seasons that hotel-grade food, wellness, service and cultural access can pair with a yacht’s more intimate rhythm. There will be Mediterranean, Japanese and grill dining; lounges and bars; and a spa with ocean-facing treatment suites, hammam, banya and a Japanese Zen garden. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aman at Sea (@amanatsea) Late departures, overnight calls and a preference for anchorages over berths are designed to loosen the schedule further. Its inaugural Mediterranean itineraries are expected to include smaller ports such as Beaulieu-sur-Mer in France, plus sailing timed around the Cannes Film Festival and Monaco Grand Prix. Amangati’s size will let it enter ports larger ships cannot, and its passage through Venice’s Grand Canal will be connected to Aman Venice, with flexible arrivals and departures from one of the vessel’s two helipads. The hotel and the yacht are not meant to be separate chapters of a trip, but part of one continuous Aman world. That continuity is aimed squarely at the brand’s famously devoted regulars. “We have been speaking to our long-standing Aman guests; they call themselves ‘Amanjunkies’, and they follow the brand wherever it goes,” Doronin says, adding that interest has also come from people who have never considered a conventional cruise. The challenge will be to give those Amanjunkies the personal escape they expect, while sharing the yacht with other guests. “Our goal has not been to create a cruise ship, but to create an Aman on the water, delivering the same sense of space, privacy, design and intuitive service that defines every Aman destination,” Doronin says.

title: China’s bearish stock market faces more pressure from weak earnings growth forecast
description: Earnings growth probably slowed in third quarter, dragged by industries ranging from consumer goods to green energy, brokerage says.
content: Corporate earnings are becoming another factor holding back Chinese stocks, with industries ranging from consumer goods to real estate and green energy under pressure because of weak demand or excessive capacity. Profit growth through the first nine months for mainland Chinese listed companies slowed compared with the pace in the first half, according to Shenwan Hongyuan Group. The Shanghai-based brokerage based its forecast on government data on industrial profits, which it said had a high historical correlation with listed companies’ earnings. Profit for Chinese industrial companies rose 15.7 per cent from a year ago in the first eight months, decelerating from an 18.7 per cent increase in the first half, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. “Our judgment is that third-quarter reports will post a slight drop in profit growth compared with the interim ones,” said Lin Limei, an analyst at Shenwan, without giving a specific number. Listed companies must disclose third-quarter reports by the end of the month. They logged 19.5 per cent profit growth year on year in the first six months, the fastest pace since 2022. An earnings slowdown would put more strain on Chinese stocks, after the benchmark CSI 300 Index slid into a bear market last week on disappointment over Beijing’s underwhelming stimulus measures and the fallout of the unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade in the US. State-backed funds may have intervened to buy into the most valuable exchange-traded funds tied to key indexes, but that stopped short of restoring investor confidence. The biggest drag on third-quarter earnings may come from property, consumer goods, household appliances and parts of the new-energy sector, according to Shenwan. The agricultural industry was also likely to be under strain because of a loss in the pig-farming segment, it said. Disappointing results from some bellwether companies have already set a cautious tone. Shares of Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) tumbled 14 per cent last week in Shenzhen after profit growth for the world’s biggest maker of lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles more than halved in the third quarter from the previous three-month period. On the positive side, the technology sector’s resilience probably extended into the third quarter, driven by strong demand for compute power and domestic substitution for imported products, according to Ping An Securities. Makers of optical transceivers, printed circuit boards and semiconductor equipment would be the key beneficiaries of China’s tech self-reliance and the global AI boom, while energy and commodity producers were also expected to benefit from rising prices, it said. While recent sell-offs in technology stocks drove a rotation to defensive plays such as consumer companies for hedging, the pattern may not last amid the earnings outlook, according to investment banks including BNP Paribas. Earnings forecasts for technology, industrial and material companies in the next 12 months had been boosted by nearly 5 per cent over the past three months, while those for consumer names had been cut by 2 per cent, according to the French bank. For 2027, the tech sector is the only one that has seen a lift in projected earnings, BNP said. “We maintain our sectoral preference for the production sectors over their consumption peers and believe that it remains too early to consider a more aggressive tilt towards consumption, especially given the macro trends and earnings momentum,” said William Bratton, an analyst at the bank.

title: Letters | Northern Metropolis is a chance to rethink educational spaces
description: Readers discuss why universities should look beyond classrooms and laboratories, street hygiene, and riots in France.
content: The report, “Could Northern Metropolis draw educational leasing from Hong Kong’s Grade A office sector?” (October 2), highlights growing education sector demand for commercial space and the potential of the Northern Metropolis. As educational institutions think about where to expand, I think we should also ask: what should these new spaces actually be used for? Not every valuable learning experience happens inside a classroom or laboratory. Students also need spaces where they can meet, lead projects, practise communication and learn from each other. These skills are hard to develop through lectures alone. Sometimes, simply having a meeting room or multipurpose space gives students an opportunity to turn an idea into something real and take responsibility for their own projects. I have seen this through Sea Dragons Gavel Club, a student-led youth organisation affiliated with Toastmasters International that I founded in Huizhou. We regularly hold in-person meetings where students practise public speaking and take on leadership roles. We also organise online sessions and speech contests so students outside our local community can participate. More importantly, we encourage students to apply the skills they learn in our club in community service projects. A space itself does not automatically build confidence, but it can create an environment where students feel comfortable trying, making mistakes and improving. As universities consider expanding into the Northern Metropolis, they should look beyond classrooms, laboratories and offices. Spaces for student organisations, workshops, discussions, competitions and community activities should also be part of the plan. They allow students to turn what they learn into experience they can actually use. The Northern Metropolis gives Hong Kong an opportunity to rethink what an educational space can be. There should be room not only for students to study, but also for them to speak, lead, collaborate and put what they learn into practice. Runfeng Bruce Yu, Shenzhen Invest in cleaner streets in Hong Kong I am writing to express serious concern over deteriorating street hygiene in Hong Kong. Overflowing bins, uncollected refuse, rodent activity and dirty back alleys are common sights in many districts, particularly in older neighbourhoods and areas near wet markets. A significant part of the problem lies in the apparent inefficiency of government departments in maintaining street cleanliness. Despite repeated complaints, cleaning schedules often appear inadequate and response times to reported issues remain slow. Hong Kong urgently needs greater investment in street cleaning. In particular, the government should consider procuring modern vacuum-cleaning vehicles from mainland China, which have proven effective in improving urban cleanliness. These vehicles can efficiently remove dust, litter and debris from roads and pavements, reducing the burden on manual cleaners and improving overall hygiene. Investing in such equipment, combined with better management, stricter enforcement against illegal dumping and more frequent waste collection, would send a clear signal that the government takes public hygiene seriously. A clean city is not a luxury; it is a basic expectation of residents and an essential part of Hong Kong’s image as an international financial centre. I urge the relevant authorities to act decisively, modernise street cleaning operations and hold the responsible departments accountable for their performance. Leo Arjun, Tung Chung Remember the advice from France in 2019? The riots in France have certainly been hitting the headlines in the past few days, as images of tear gas, smashed shop windows and burning buildings fill the news. And there has been no shortage of draconian responses from the French government, with thousands of arrests, nighttime curfews and condemnation of “unbridled violence”. Now at 77, I do suffer from lapses of memory, but I have no difficulty remembering that during the 2019 riots here in Hong Kong, the French government – then foreign minister Jean-Yves Le Drian – wasted no time in calling on the Hong Kong government to “renew the thread of dialogue”, “end the escalation of violence” and “find a peaceful solution”. In doing so, he was pouring fuel on the extremely violent situation. Furthermore, we had to suffer similar unsolicited advice from the folks at the European Union and others around the world. To those countries that wasted no time in criticising the Hong Kong government at the time, I say: what goes round comes around. People in glass houses should not throw rocks. Bob Rogers, Sai Kung

title: Stand-up comedian Jordan Leung on moving to the US and Hong Kong show backlash
description: ‘I don’t know how much longer I can do this,’ says the 33-year-old comic, fresh off three sold-out Hong Kong shows. Is he joking?
content: “I think about quitting all the time,” says Jordan Leung, known to his Instagram followers as @69ranch. As one of Hong Kong’s most prominent stand-up comedians to emerge in recent years, Leung’s pessimism is surprising. “I don’t wanna make social media content,” the 33-year-old admits. “Now I’m just fixated on likes and stuff … I don’t know how much longer I can do this.” Sitting directly across the table from him, it is not always easy to tell when Leung is being sincere or performing his deadpan jesting – yet, at this moment, his exhaustion sounds genuine. Leung recently returned to Hong Kong from his base in New York, taking a couple of weeks to spend time with family and recover from jet lag ahead of his “Back to Work” tour shows in Whampoa in October. Originally planning to perform one show each in English and Cantonese on October 17 and 18, the comedian added an extra Cantonese show on the final day thanks to overwhelming demand. At his English-language performance, Leung was his usual understated character: clad in black and sporting his signature thick moustache, delivering monotone observations on the bizarre experiences of his daily life. His set included stories of being hit on by a billionaire’s daughter after a gig, childhood memories of realising his uncle is gay and the challenges of touring Japan. He also touched on his life as a full-time stand-up comedian, joking that his mother would have sought an abortion if she had known this was his career choice. Ironically, during our interview, Leung reveals that since finding success in comedy, his parents insist he cannot quit. “‘You’ve spent too much time on this,’” he quotes them. A comedy career pivot Leung grew up in Hong Kong before moving to the United States at 15, then returned to the city in 2020 after getting laid off from a tech job. He has toyed with stand-up comedy since he was 23, taking classes at New York’s renowned Comedy Cellar and performing bar gigs as early as 2017. He always knew he would quit tech and pursue something more creative once he saved enough money anyway. “I knew there was a comedy scene here [in Hong Kong], and I knew I would be able to produce some shows, but I just never imagined the scale that it would eventually become,” Leung says. “But that was probably one of the most important things I did in my career.” He built a significant following through viral Instagram videos making jokes about Hong Kong life using bawdy humour, often amassing hundreds of thousands of views. Eventually, he even held shows at MacPherson Stadium in Mong Kok in 2024. Then, in 2025, Leung returned to the US. His live sets often feature jokes that lean into Asia diaspora experiences, such as learning Hong Kong slang words for intimate body parts. At his recent English live show, Leung delivered several jokes about female genitalia seemingly aimed at a much younger audience than the crowd of 30- and 40-year-olds present – but the crowd guffawed, nonetheless. The response was mixed for a particular joke deriding Shenzhen, with roaring laughter and booing from the audience alike. The gag was in vein with much of his set: “edgy” but not countercultural. Some of the funniest moments came when he switched to Cantonese to make small quips and quick jabs. However, his crowd work segment – which lasted only a few minutes – hit an unfortunate lull when audience members seemed reluctant to engage, and the interactions quickly devolved into an awkward back-and-forth. Suffering backlash Leung’s penchant for gags has brought its own fallout. Following his Cantonese show on October 18, controversy erupted over his opening act, Taiwanese-Hong Kong comedian Shen Jong, whose set included an offensive joke about the benefits of sleeping with female cancer patients. Shen, and Leung by association, have since been widely criticised on various social media platforms for making fun of terminal illness and promoting misogynistic tropes. In a follow-up interview after the backlash, he agrees he had “some responsibility” for overseeing the jokes to create a safe, comfortable environment for all. He was, however, shocked by the uproar towards him over an opening act. It’s hard to determine what’s politically correct in Hong Kong Jordan Leung Regarding stand-up comedy in general, he adds, “I will never blame someone for feeling offended because I feel like there must be a reason why you’re offended. And I know that comedy is a matter of taste. “At the end of the day, I feel like [stand-up comedy] is just a little performance,” he adds. “I feel like people take it so seriously. Maybe if you care about that issue so much, there are other ways to contribute [to] making that issue better.” Stuck between East and West Leung says he has always been careful about the jokes he shares in Hong Kong versus the US, since the same punchline can land very differently. During his show on October 18, for example, he said “there are only two genders – back then”, when speaking about a psychic who correctly guessed his gender as an unborn child. Leung says he wrote the joke as “an observation of the times”. A New York audience might giggle at how far society has come; however, he felt that the Hong Kong crowd that night cheered and applauded as if in support of returning to that era. “I [felt] uncomfortable performing my own joke because I don’t think it was the right reaction that I wanted,” he reflects after the show. “It’s hard to determine what’s politically correct in Hong Kong [and] I don’t think it’s fair to use the Western standard in Hong Kong.” Leung’s anonymity in the West is, in a way, his advantage. He believes his star status in Hong Kong hinders creative freedom as he has to be wary of brand deals and public opinion. “That’s kind of the reason why I wanted to move. I think some people will be very content to reach where I am and just kind of be a celebrity, but I think this was never my goal when I started doing stand-up,” he says. He adds that the relatively small comedy scene and the lack of infrastructure for creatives were further reasons to leave Hong Kong. Because Leung is famed for his Hong Kong-specific jokes, and the culture is so deeply embedded in his identity, he does not see himself abandoning the jokes any time soon. But he also wants to expand beyond that, and has found that his content unrelated to Hong Kong life is often under-recognised. “So I’m almost kind of stuck in this in-between,” he says. Even when he tours, most of his audience is from Hong Kong, and he worries about being pigeonholed as a “regional comedian”. After his Hong Kong gigs, he will perform a couple of shows in Australia in November. But his current goal is to tour more in the US and build his North American following. Apart from ruffling a few feathers, the comedian seems to have a good thing going, so why does he think about quitting? “I don’t feel the same joy I used to do,” Leung admits. Film interests him more. He references the career of Brett Goldstein, one of the writers of the American comedy television series Ted Lasso (2020-), as his ideal: writing scripts, starring on screen and doing stand-up on the side. For now, it is hard to envision Leung stepping down from the stage. The crowd thunderously applauded him at the end of his gig, and he even managed to add an extra show the next night. By the end of the night, it was reassuring to see live comedy succeed in the city, even if the jokes may need a little more calibration.

title: Exoskeletons, anyone? China showcases next-gen technology at annual trade fair
description: From rescue drone gear to mobility exoskeletons, Chinese firms are rapidly bringing frontier tech to market as they plough funds into R&D.
content: From drone lasers to lightweight exoskeletons, Chinese manufacturers used the country’s biggest trade fair to showcase a new wave of hi-tech, and sometimes quirky, hardware to global buyers this week. The vast range of next-generation devices – often on offer at surprisingly affordable prices – is the product of a relentless innovation drive under way in China, as firms plough funds into research and development to cope with intense competition at home and rising trade barriers overseas. The R&D wave is helping Chinese exporters expand their global sales even amid an era of higher tariffs. As of Monday last week, a whopping 189,000 buyers from 214 countries and regions had attended the October Canton Fair in Guangzhou, up 13.3 per cent from the previous edition of the trade expo in April. Many exporters at the fair’s 52-hectare (128.5-acre) advanced manufacturing exhibition said they had upped their research spending to accelerate new product iteration – sometimes investing half their income on R&D. Lingdu Intel-tech, a Guangzhou-based maker of cleaning robots, is reinvesting roughly 40 per cent of its annual revenue in developing new products, including specialised adhesive materials jointly produced with the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The company already sells sanitation robots in more than 20 countries, and it is now offering window-cleaning robots for US$70,000 that are designed to work on high-rise towers in extremely hot countries in the Middle East. “Our product engineering continuously evolves to adapt to increasingly extreme climate shifts, such as in the Middle East, where glass surface temperatures can exceed 70 degrees Celsius,” said Huang Jian, the company’s sales director. The window-cleaning robot uses computer-vision algorithms and multi-modal sensors to detect obstacles, identify glass cracks and ageing rubber seals – allowing it to quickly change its washing pressure and prevent leaks, according to Huang. Exoskeleton maker Hangzhou Taixi showcased the speed of its engineering by unveiling a revamped mobility exoskeleton at the fair just six months after releasing its predecessor. The new exoskeleton, which is designed to be worn by people with mobility issues, weighs just 1.85 kilograms – 550 grams lighter than the previous model – after the company swapped out aluminium for custom carbon-fibre materials in its linkage joints. The company spent the equivalent of millions of US dollars on developing the new model, which is on sale for just over US$1,000, according to Han Xu, a senior executive at the firm. Overall R&D spending now accounts for 30 to 50 per cent of company revenue. Hangzhou Taixi has already received sample orders from more than 80 countries for the exoskeleton, while it works with regulators on certification. Its booth at the fair was packed with foreign buyers, many paying cash on the spot for demo units. Elsewhere in the pavilion, Zhejiang Era Solar Technology was promoting a newly launched 800-watt solar power system – a plug-and-play set-up combining lightweight solar panels, microinverters and energy storage batteries that is designed to be used in regions with unstable power grids. The new system is up to 20 per cent more cost-efficient than previous models, according to the firm. It plans to sell the device in parts of Africa, Southeast Asia and Europe, with one client from Ghana placing a trial order for 200 units before a prototype was even released. Zhejiang Era set a target of iterating new products every six to eight months to maintain its “market edge”, said Xu Leiping, the company’s deputy sales general manager. CZI Intelligent Machinery, which makes rescue gear for drones, also said it invested more than 30 per cent of its annual revenue in R&D. The company recently adapted its aerial thermal imaging and laser technology for ground-based rescue equipment, which has helped the firm expand its sales into Eastern Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, according to CZI co-founder Zhang Kai. Foreign procurement managers at the fair said Chinese companies’ strategy of combining technical upgrades with competitive pricing had allowed them to resist global trade shocks. “Chinese pricing remains highly competitive against more expensive countries like Japan and Germany,” said Joerg Sageder, an Austrian buyer who is sourcing commercial robots and automation equipment. “As quality improves year by year, we can charge a mark-up in our own [European] markets.”

title: Jordan FA chief accuses Fifa head Infantino of turning AFC Congress into a political stage
description: Vocal critic Prince Ali bin Hussein denies ‘that Asia has a united position when it comes to electing the ‌next Fifa president’.
content: Jordan Football Association president Prince Ali bin Hussein accused Fifa leader ⁠Gianni Infantino on Sunday ⁠of hijacking the Asian Football ⁠Confederation Congress for political purposes ahead of his re-election bid for a fourth term. At the AFC’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, its president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, endorsed Infantino’s bid for re-election as Fifa president. Months after the confederation ‌accused Infantino of a “fundamental breach of trust” over the abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, Sheikh Salman told the congress that Asia was now united behind Infantino. But Prince Ali, who has been a vocal critic of Fifa’s leadership, painted a starkly different picture of events in Tokyo. “Having come back from Tokyo where the AFC Congress took place, the first ⁠two days were about football, which we all serve. The last day was pure politics at ‌the behest of Gianni Infantino,” Prince Ali wrote on X. When it comes to fida elections, confederation presidents have no say: the vote is by each and every member association. So any claims that have recently emerged that confederation or FIFA council members have a part in the vote, is not relevant. Having come back from Tokyo where the AFC Congress took place, the first two days were about football, which we all serve. The last day was pure politics at the behest of Gianni Infantino. There were reports that Asia has a united position when it comes to electing the next FIFA President. In fact, nobody was allowed to speak, question, debate or talk with the media. Lack of transparency leads to lack of accountability. No amount of coercion, threats or bribes should be allowed. — Ali Al Hussein (@AliBinAlHussein) October 25, 2026 “There were reports that Asia has a united position when it comes to electing the ‌next Fifa president. In fact, nobody was allowed to speak, question, debate or talk ⁠with the media. “Lack ⁠of transparency leads to lack of accountability. No amount of coercion, threats or bribes should be allowed.” Prince Ali did not ‌elaborate on his statement. Fifa and AFC have been contacted for comment. Infantino also addressed the AFC Congress, giving Sheikh Salman ‌his backing ‌for another term. In August, Prince Ali launched a public attack on Infantino, accusing him of “blackmail” ‌and saying Fifa had offered to help solve the kingdom’s problems in exchange for his endorsement. Two ⁠days later, Prince Ali confirmed Jordan’s players and staff had received outstanding reward money for their ⁠participation in the 2025 Arab Cup. The association had been waiting since December for prize money for reaching the Arab Cup final in Qatar. On Saturday, Infantino laughed off questions ‌about whether he had ‌considered resigning in the wake of the failed FFE proposal, pointing to what he described as overwhelming support from member associations around the globe. The Swiss-Italian administrator’s re-election prospects were strengthened significantly after the AFC endorsement, leaving Europe increasingly isolated and exposing the lack of a challenger.

title: Style Edit: 45R’s new knits spotlight texture and Japanese craftsmanship
description: From Jamieson’s Shetland wool to Magee 1866 Donegal tweed, the materials in 45R’s latest knit collection showcase vintage knitting techniques and rich textures.
content: The appeal of a good knit is often immediate, from the softness against the skin to the reassuring volume and warmth. At 45R, those qualities begin well before a garment takes shape. The Japanese label’s latest selection puts the making process in focus, bringing together airy merino, characterful Shetland wool and the flecked textures of Donegal tweed. Founded in Tokyo in 1977, 45R approaches clothing through monozukuri, or the “art of making”, a philosophy centred on respect for craft and attention to detail. Comfort and durability are central to that approach, as is a willingness to preserve the subtle irregularities of natural fibres rather than smooth them into anonymity. This natural approach is even reflected in the brand’s new Ginza flagship store, which foregrounds traditional materials and techniques. When it comes to this season’s knits, brown, khaki and yellow lend the collection an autumnal warmth without distracting from the materials themselves. Many knitted pieces are produced at the label’s dedicated SDL workshop, where vintage knitting machines create fabrics with distinctive variations. The material is washed in-house, then carefully cut and sewn, with particular attention paid to smooth seams. Knitting, washing and construction each contribute to the finished garment’s feel, where comfort is engineered through a succession of small but important decisions. The merino-based Float Boiled fabric offers a revealing example. Soft, light and voluminous, it requires a careful approach well before knitting begins, as the fabric may shrink by approximately 30 to 40 per cent during processing, with different areas responding differently. At the same time, pressure and friction encourage wool fibres to intertwine, softly blending selected colours. Proportions, patterns and finish must therefore be considered in anticipation of that transformation. Shetland wool brings another kind of character. Loosely knitted and then felted, it is treated to evoke the texture of a sweater shaped by years of wear and exposure to rain. The wool-jacquard patchwork collection combines several wool types with diamond checks, Fair Isle motifs, reindeer and snowflakes, giving familiar winter imagery a richly layered surface. Alongside the knits, a Donegal tweed jacket broadens the material story. Through its collaboration with Irish mill Magee 1866, 45R brings coloured flecks, salt-and-pepper patterns and substantial wool textures into refined Japanese proportions. This season’s finer, lighter yarn retains the fabric’s rugged character. In short, the pleasure of 45R’s latest knit collection is revealed upon close inspection. The interest is in the texture, the construction and the gradual softening of wool, making these clothes that are designed to become more familiar with time.

title: China’s tech giants are paying 1 million yuan for a new kind of AI engineer
description: Firms are offering lucrative annual salaries to fill the engineering roles in a race to commercialise AI applications.
content: Chinese technology giants are dangling annual pay packages approaching 1 million yuan (US$149,739) to attract artificial intelligence engineers who can turn AI models into commercial applications. Companies including ByteDance, Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding are stepping up recruitment and training of the so-called forward-deployed engineers (FDEs), who work directly with customers to develop and integrate AI applications into business operations. Demand for such professionals has been soaring. Job postings for FDEs in China surged 1,523 per cent in the first seven months from the same period in 2025, according to data from domestic professional networking platform Maimai, making it the fastest-growing AI technical role covered by the report. This demand for talent has been reflected in lucrative hiring posts. ByteDance has advertised FDE positions in its AI business offering between 35,000 yuan and 65,000 yuan a month, with 15 months of annual pay, putting potential yearly compensation at as much as 975,000 yuan, according to job postings on Chinese recruitment platform Boss Zhipin. For comparison, the annual disposable income in China was only 43,377 yuan on average in 2025, official data showed. Ant Digital Technologies, the technology arm of Ant Group, has offered between 40,000 yuan and 60,000 yuan a month for business-facing FDEs, according to Boss Zhipin posts. Ant is a fintech affiliate of Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post. “With growing interest in AI, many businesses are seeking guidance on tailored, practical implementation,” said an Alibaba Cloud spokesperson. “This is driving steady demand for forward-deployed engineers to help translate AI strategies into real-world results.” Other listings have put Tencent FDE-related positions at between 30,000 yuan and 60,000 yuan per month, while Alibaba Cloud deployment engineering roles have advertised salaries of up to 50,000 yuan per month. US AI companies are making a similar push. Earlier this month, Anthropic announced a US$100 million initiative to train 10,000 FDEs by the end of 2027. But the eye-catching pay packages do not necessarily reflect what most FDEs earn, according to George Wang, a senior human resources professional at a leading AI company in Beijing. “The high salaries advertised for some of these jobs represent only a small part of the market. Most positions do not pay that much,” Wang said. He said demand was nevertheless strong for “AI-native full-stack developers with experience building AI agents”, as companies reorganised their operations around the technology. The scramble for talent is also prompting Chinese companies to develop their own FDE workforce. Tencent Cloud earlier this year introduced what it described as the industry’s first FDE certification, targeting partner engineers and developers working with its Agent Development Platform. ByteDance’s Volcano Engine said its FDE service was among the first to receive an “advanced” rating in an assessment by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. “Our FDE team works alongside clients to break down business needs, plan the stages of implementation and develop applications from prototype to production,” the company said in a post on its official WeChat account. Beijing has thrown its support behind the profession. In late August, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology issued a notice encouraging firms to build FDE teams embedded at customer sites to help implement AI applications, while calling on universities to cultivate relevant talent. A Beijing-based engineer who goes by Su said the role had become increasingly valuable as businesses sought talent capable of bridging technical development and commercial needs. “We look for people who can quickly understand the needs of clients in different industries, choose suitable AI tools and take a solution through to implementation,” said Su, who previously led an internal FDE team at a major Chinese internet company. ByteDance and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Why we need to be careful and responsible when learning to use AI tools
description: Artificial intelligence is like a racing car – drivers need training to make safe and smart decisions with such a powerful vehicle.
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is like a super-powered computer brain that can learn and do amazing things, but we need to be careful with this power.
Think of AI like a racing car, which is incredibly fast and powerful. It can zoom past ordinary cars in seconds.
But because these vehicles are so powerful, racing car drivers need special training to know all the controls and make smart split-second decisions to stay safe. One wrong move could cause them to crash.
AI tools are similar. They are incredibly powerful, but we must learn how to use them safely.
For example, AI systems can use a camera and headphones to help blind people “see” by describing what is in front of them. They can also help doctors spot sicknesses early and can even translate languages in real-time.
But since AI is so powerful, we have to be extra cautious when we use it, just like a driver needs to be careful with a racing car.
An AI’s algorithm learns from the information humans give it, but if that data has mistakes or biases, the AI will learn them too. AI tools might make harmful or wrong decisions based on their training.
AI chatbots also do not truly understand emotions or morals. They just follow patterns, and they don’t have empathy or consideration for the impact of their recommendations.
That’s why AI can never replace humans: it can’t give you a real hug, understand how you’re feeling or be a true friend. It does not have a heart, a sense of humour or a conscience .
So, when we use AI, we must use wisdom and good judgment. We are the drivers, and AI is our racing car. We decide where to go and how quickly it should operate. We check its work, ask deeper questions and never let it make important decisions alone.
And just like a racing car, it also takes a lot of energy to run the data centres that power AI. Avoid using AI tools for things that are not necessary – especially because your developing brain needs to practise what it learns without the short cuts given by AI.
AI is a brilliant helper, but it’s not the boss. Wise, careful and kind humans should be the boss, driving responsibly into the future.

title: Chef Mel Ng is cooking her way through Hong Kong’s restaurants
description: Coming from a background in French cuisine, Ng takes shifts at the city’s eateries to learn their techniques and showcase their heritage.
content:
In the early hours of the morning, former chef Mel Ng was tasked with rolling out dumpling wrappers and mixing the next day’s fillings before surviving the chaotic lunch rush at Ah Chun Shandong Dumpling.
As she “staged” for the day at the restaurant – which has a three-decade legacy in Hong Kong – Ng tried to learn as much as she could. The practice of “staging” in the culinary world is when a cook takes a temporary unpaid shift in a restaurant to learn its techniques.
Ng has staged at more than 20 restaurants since last year, including the beloved Kamcentre Roast Goose, viral Vietnamese eatery Banh Mi Nem and the Indian restaurant Leela.
“They’ve all been very interesting to me because I’ve tried out many different kitchens, like Indian cuisine [and] Japanese ... things that I never would have tried before,” said the 36-year-old, who also works as a consultant in the food and beverage industry.
“The ones that I enjoy the most are the ones that are related more to Hong Kong local heritage, just because these are the things I grew up eating.”
Ng calls herself a “culinary wanderer”. Having staged in restaurants across Asia, she considers traditional Chinese cuisine her toughest challenge yet, largely because these kitchens rely on intuition rather than written recipes.
“A lot of the techniques were ... new to me. Working in a Cantonese kitchen meant using a wok, which I’d never done before,” she said.
For many older Hong Kong eateries, Ng noticed that staffing was a recurring obstacle, and it was even harder to find young people who wanted to learn the craft.
“Since Covid, we’ve seen a lot of restaurant closures. Even brands that have been around for 20 [or] 30 years closed down,” she said.
Her mission to stage in different restaurants is not just about honing her craft but also about using her business acumen to help struggling eateries survive.
“A chef might have a great recipe, but if the concept isn’t spot on [or] doesn’t fit the neighbourhood or ignores current trends, the business will struggle,” she said.
Ng posts videos of her staging experiences on Instagram to showcase Hong Kong’s rich culinary traditions.
Ng’s daily mantra is “ mise en place ”, a French term meaning “everything in its place”.
“In the kitchen, it means having all your ingredients and tools ready before you start,” she said.
“Whether I’m doing consulting work for a client or working a shift in the kitchen, I always have a plan in my head, thinking about the end goal and mapping out every step to get there.”

title: Why indie developers are making a horror game inspired by Hong Kong culture
description: Makers of ‘Block 13’ say they aimed to create a video game set in an old public housing estate that would connect with people in the city.
content:
Imagine being trapped in an old public housing estate in Hong Kong. As you wander dim hallways in search of an exit, you come across strange surprises.
This is the haunting concept of Block 13 , a first-person horror game built by 29-year-old developer Kennedy Liu. The Hongkonger carefully modelled the game’s layout after Fuk Loi Estate in Tsuen Wan.
Liu has been working on this project since May 2025. Next year, he plans to release it on the gaming platform Steam.
Block 13 is inspired by Hong Kong public housing estates built in the 1970s and 1980s. Liu views them as key parts of Hong Kong culture.
“When … foreigners think of Hong Kong, they instantly picture neon signs or the Kowloon Walled City,” Liu said.
“But to me, public housing is the place that nurtured multiple generations from the 50s, 60s and 70s up to today. If I had to pick something authentic that truly represents Hongkongers, nothing fits better.”
Each floor of the game has a special theme expressed through strange events that the players must face. This is inspired by the concept of the 18 levels of hell in Chinese mythology. To survive and escape, players must burn incense or perform other rituals.
Liu said he included details in the game that would be familiar to people who grew up in Hong Kong.
“I incorporated a lot of elements from local culture and Chinese traditions, including superstitious concepts or social issues revolving around work and studying,” he said.
Three people worked together to build Block 13 . Liu does the main programming and game design. One of his friends is a researcher and 2D artist. Another friend helps with programming.
The game was born out of the team’s love for Hong Kong and a lack of job opportunities.
After Liu spent six years working in the gaming industry, he was jobless.
“Because I was unemployed, I purely wanted to sharpen my skills,” he recalled.
He spent years creating cartoon parts in games for past employers, so he wanted to try making a realistic game environment.
“Since I didn’t get the chance to join a company doing that, I used my period of unemployment to upskill my game development abilities,” said Liu, who is using his savings to fund his game.
When choosing a topic, Liu realised that few games had authentic Hong Kong settings.
He thought to himself: “Since I’m capable of doing it, why not just make it about Hong Kong?”
To learn how to use complex systems to build the game, Liu leaned on artificial intelligence (AI) for help. He used it to help him break down programming logic and solve problems.
Despite how tough it has been to find a job, Liu sees this era as a golden opportunity for independent creators. He advises others who want to create their own games to take initiative.
“Creating things on your own is actually the best option right now,” Liu said.
You don’t need to study game development at a university or wait for a studio to approve your idea. Instead, he encourages creators to take advantage of modern tools and learn by doing.
“If you want to do it, you basically don’t need to ask for anyone’s permission or advice any more. If you want to build a taxi simulator , just build it,” he said.
“Don’t overthink it or feel like you need to take tons of formal classes because AI can teach you a lot if you take the time to read through things.”

title: Letters from readers about Mid-Autumn Festival, Nepal floods and a trip to Zhuhai Chimelong
description: This week, readers write about beautiful lanterns at Victoria Park, urge us to stop climate change and share a memorable trip to a marine theme park.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
My family and I went to Victoria Park to celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival. We went to admire the lanterns. What a wonderful sight!
The weather felt as hot as an oven. When the lights turned on, everyone picked up their cameras and cheered for the breathtaking beauty.
The walkway was full of lanterns from different countries. We moved quickly because it was very crowded. I liked the Vietnamese silk lanterns the most. They were shaped like teardrops.
We also found a robot sleeping on a chair. It was waiting to perform!
Recently, there was a disaster in Nepal that was caused by glaciers from the high mountains plunging into the Lhende Khola River.
It also caused a landslide and floods that destroyed everything in their way.
Scientists discovered it was not an earthquake but warming, mainly because of climate change. Global warming is melting glaciers. Rising sea levels will cause more floods.
We, humans, caused climate change. We need to help the world. We should recycle, reuse, reduce and refuse. If everyone makes a little change, the world will become a better place.
I went to Zhuhai Chimelong Ocean Kingdom this summer and enjoyed my time there a lot! The marine-themed resort has amusement rides, a water park and even a circus show!
I saw many animals, including penguins, belugas, polar bears, killer whales and Chinese white dolphins. It was a lot of fun. My family and I did not have enough time to do and see everything.

title: Feature of the Week: Jaylen Choy’s short story ‘The Silk Road’
description: The eight-year-old from German Swiss International School shares an adventure tale that follows a silk merchant and his horse on a journey from China.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
A long time ago, a silk maker in China named Bo overheard two villagers talking about all of the wonderful things “the West” had.
That night, he dreamed of going on an adventure to the West. The next morning, that’s exactly what he did.
Bo packed all his silk and set off. As he walked, he saw a small horse with a gash on its leg. Bo led the horse to a lake, fed it and nursed its wound.
The horse’s leg healed and they set off together.
The Chinese and the Huns were fighting for control of the ancient Silk Road. Sometimes, the Huns would capture merchants and take their goods. One spotted Bo and chained him up for days.
Then, one day, Bo felt the floor rumble. “Earthquake!” he shouted. But then he realised it was his horse stomping. It reared up onto its hind legs and smashed the lock!
“Thank you,” Bo said. “I’m going to call you Fei.”
Bo and Fei trotted along happily. They reached a town. Bo took his silk to the market and set up a stall. A huge crowd appeared.
“Wow! So soft and glossy. What is it? I’ll trade you anything I have for it,” one person said.
“One by one,” Bo shouted over the crowd.
He traded all of his silk for gold, silver and diamonds. Then it was time to go home.
But as the pair travelled, a real earthquake struck.
Fei shook his head. “NEIGH! NEIGH!” He bolted across fields, dashed through forest and past grassland and soared over lakes and rivers.
At last, the two caught up with a group of heavenly horses. Fei’s friends! Together, they galloped back to China.
Bo took the horses to the Emperor. “What speedy, agile horses. Nothing like the ones we have here in China,” he said.
The Emperor wanted to buy all the horses. But Bo said, “I would like to keep one and live in the palace stable together.”
Bo and Fei moved into the palace and lived a happy life.

title: John Catlin basks in ‘truly special’ win as he joins greats on Hong Kong Open winners list
description: American’s five-shot victory lands him his sixth national open on a day Matthew Cheung delivered the best result by a Hong Kong player.
content: The list of Link Hong Kong Open winners has always read like an honour roll of golf’s great and good; on Sunday John Catlin added his name to that illustrious grouping and it might be that’s what finally broke through his steely exterior. Sitting with the trophy long after the crowds had gone home, Catlin read off the names of Greg Norman, Tom Watson, Rory McIlroy, Miguel Angel Jimenez and the rest, with the kind of dawning realisation that follows any major achievement. And while Tom McKibbin’s seven-shot triumph last year may have raised the bar beyond all reason when it comes to margins of victory, Catlin’s 20-under-par total was five better than Hong Kong’s Matthew Cheung and Finland’s Kalle Samooja, who tied for second. In the relative safety of the media centre after a whirlwind of handshakes, photo ops and questions over what earning a spot at next year’s Masters and Open Championship meant, the American took time to reflect on the tournament’s “storied history”. “I could sit here for the next 10 minutes and read all the names off. It’s pretty, pretty special to join them,” Catlin said, adding that he thought the road approaching Hong Kong Golf Club should be “called Miguel Angel Jimenez Avenue” in honour of the Spaniard who won four times between 2004 and 2013. Catlin might have just claimed his first at Fanling, but he is making a habit of winning national opens, or in this instance, an event with the same status. Hong Kong is the sixth in a collection that also includes victories in Ireland, Austria, England, Thailand and Saudi Arabia. “If you’d told me that 10 years ago, I probably would have laughed at you,” Catlin said. “So, it’s truly special.” Those words could happily serve as an apt description of the 35-year-old’s final round, not that he would necessarily recognise that. It was not until Catlin reached the 18th green that he became aware of the strength of his own position. Even then, the overriding emotion was not one of relief, but of being determined to finish with the single-minded focus that brought five birdies on the back nine, and a 15ft putt for par at the last to seal the deal. “Someone could have shot six under on the back nine and that [the trophy] is theirs,” Catlin said. “When I saw the five-shot lead, my first thought was ‘I don’t have to be as aggressive on my first putt [on 18]’. “The only way I could have lost the tournament was to putt the ball into the water. You can’t start getting ahead of yourself, and, you know, you do something silly.” In truth, Catlin was largely free and clear once Cheung had dropped a shot at 11. That gave the champion a three-stroke lead and while the Hongkonger did his best, the gap proved insurmountable. Of the three players who started the day at the top of the leaderboard on 14 under, only Catlin managed to go below par in the final round. Thomas Pieters and Caleb Surratt briefly hinted at a challenge, and then posted matching two-over 72s. Anirban Lahiri should have been among that group, but was harshly penalised one shot for the almost imperceptible movement of his ball - only visible through a television camera’s close attentions - as he addressed it before chipping on to the 18th green on Saturday. Lahiri learned of his punishment before teeing off for the final round, and any energy generated by a sense of injustice was lost in a double-bogey at the first. A four-over 74 left him in an eight-way tie for 17th on nine under. Cheung’s performance was the best a local player has ever managed since the first Open in 1959, finally ending Dominic Boulet’s three-decade run since finishing fourth in 1996. His closing three-under 67 raised thoughts of what might have been had Saturday turned into something other than a struggle. Approaching the 18th green in the group ahead of Catlin, Cheung was applauded long and loud and said he felt “a chill going down my spine” as he walked towards his ball. “The whole week has meant a lot,” Cheung said. “People never thought that Hong Kong could produce good players, but we’ve done it, and it’s really cool to see. “Growing up in Australia, I never got the opportunity to go to such big events like this, and it’s really cool that I can play in front of so many small kids and maybe they can see that they can do it as well.” The result, which was the best of Cheung’s career, has more than secured his status for 2027. Up next is the first stage of Korn Ferry Tour Q-school and then the Asian Tour’s season finale, the Philippine Open. “I know I have the game to compete with the best in the world,” Cheung said. “I just need to continue to get better and keep going up from here.” Catlin, meanwhile, now has the sort of headache that only success can bring. He is already exempt from next week’s Rolex Grand Final, the season-ending event on Europe’s Challenge Tour, where there are 20 DP World Tour (DPWT) cards up for grabs. Earning himself one of those could mean an early Christmas break; not doing so brings in the final stage of DPWT Q-school into play. However, victory at Fanling propelled Catlin to fourth on the Asian Tour order of merit, and first place come November means a DPWT card. “If I do the final stage of Q-school I can’t do the Philippines, because that [Q-school] ends on November 11 and Philippines starts on the 12th. There’s an argument to be made for both, so something I have to think about.” Two dates he does not need to think about are April 8, when he will tee off at the Masters for the first time, and July 11, when a second visit to St Andrews and the Open Championship is in the offing.

title: Goldman Sachs steps up Asia hiring as wealthy clients eye US assets for diversification
description: Wall Street investment bank’s global co-head of wealth management says it is ‘very committed to hiring more advisers in the region’.
content: Goldman Sachs is accelerating the hiring of wealth management advisers across Asia as the region’s wealthy families increasingly seek to diversify into US assets after years of strong market gains, while the AI boom is creating a new generation of millionaires with growing financial planning needs. The Wall Street bank is expanding its advisory teams in Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia, alongside specialists in areas such as trading and lending, according to Nishi Somaiya, its global co-head of wealth management. “We are very proactively growing our adviser footprint here,” Somaiya said recently during her first visit to Hong Kong since being appointed to her current role this year. “We’re very committed to hiring more advisers in the region.” Goldman had seen its Asian wealth management business record double-digit growth over the past several years, and the bank aimed to maintain that pace by attracting new clients and expanding its relationships with existing ones, she said. The bank did not disclose specific hiring targets in the region. Asia’s importance in the global wealth management industry has been growing. Hong Kong overtook Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth booking centre last year, with US$2.95 trillion in assets, according to Boston Consulting Group. Meanwhile, Asia’s growing ranks of wealthy families are increasingly looking for diversification beyond their home markets, with Goldman saying United States assets were particularly attractive after years of strong returns led by technology stocks. The wealth creation through AI has been remarkable Nishi Somaiya, Goldman Sachs The S&P 500 Index has gained about 13 per cent this year, driven largely by a group of AI-related and semiconductor companies, although recent market volatility has raised concerns about the sustainability of the gains. “Many clients want to diversify their wealth … and often for Asia clients, the form that takes is investing into US assets,” Somaiya said. Many wealthy Asian families owned substantial operating businesses in their home markets and sought reinvest proceeds from share sales in US equities and private-market opportunities, she added. Somaiya said the trend was being reinforced by generational wealth transfers, as younger family members, many educated overseas, became more familiar with US markets and increasingly involved in managing family fortunes as the AI boom reshaped the wealth landscape. “The wealth creation through AI has been remarkable,” she said, adding that soaring valuations had enabled some technology workers to accumulate tens of millions of dollars in their twenties, often before they had developed mature financial knowledge to manage the wealth. In Asia, Beijing and Shenzhen rank among the world’s top 15 cities for billionaires, as AI-driven wealth accumulation has helped reshape the region’s billionaire landscape, according to a recent report by data company Altrata. Somaiya said such newly wealthy individuals increasingly needed advice on monetising company shares, managing concentrated stock holdings, diversifying investments and tax planning. Separately, tighter scrutiny of offshore wealth by mainland China tax authorities had prompted more conversations among wealthy clients about their financial arrangements. “It’s really prompted clients to think about aspects of their wealth planning,” she said, adding that clients were reviewing their governance structures, long-term objectives and diversification strategies.

title: Suit linings: the link between the NFL draft and London’s Savile Row
description: Giants and Cardinals draftees have underlined what the likes of Hackett London and Gieves & Hawkes have always known: what’s inside your suit counts.
content: Back in April, suit jackets lined with interesting graphics and prints emerged as one of the more unusual fashion trends at the 2026 NFL draft in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the annual event where professional American football teams pick out the best young players looking to enter the league. Colton Hood, then a Tennessee cornerback, now on the New York Giants’ roster, rocked up in a cobalt-blue jacket that, when opened, revealed a swathe of family photographs across the lining, chronicling his journey to the NFL and moments with relatives who joined him on the red carpet. Then-Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love, now with the Arizona Cardinals, lined his custom suit with original manga-inspired artwork depicting “Jeremonstar”, a superhero alter ego developed with his father and artist Ryan Odagawa. Meanwhile, linebacker Arvell Reese, formerly of Ohio State and now also with the Giants, decorated the lining of his tuxedo-style jacket with Reese’s branding in a nod to both his surname and ongoing partnership with the confectionery company. For the tailors of Savile Row, London’s historic centre of bespoke tailoring, using a suit lining to say something personal is nothing new. “The lining is the one part of a suit that belongs entirely to the wearer,” says Richard Anderson, co-founder and head cutter of his eponymous Savile Row house. “Nobody else sees it, and that is precisely the point. A man might commission the most sober charcoal worsted for the boardroom, but inside there could be a flash of shocking pink or a print that means something only to him. It is a secret between the customer and his tailor.” Anderson began training at Huntsman aged 17 before opening his own house at 13 Savile Row in 2001. He remembers a time when linings were generally chosen to pair subtly with the outer cloth, but says his own approach has always been more adventurous. “A bespoke suit is a deeply personal object, and the lining is where a customer can express something the outside of the garment cannot,” he adds. The lining is chosen surprisingly early in the bespoke process. At Gieves & Hawkes, one of Savile Row’s oldest tailoring houses, it’s discussed alongside the cloth and measurements. “Choosing the lining happens at the very beginning of the bespoke process as it is integral to the overall design of any garment,” says Davide Taub, head cutter at Gieves & Hawkes. “Although the lining might seem like the most discreet part of the garment, it’s also a way of showing that every element of a garment has been considered and that nothing is an afterthought.” A lining has a practical job, helping a jacket slip easily over the clothing beneath it and providing a neat finish over its internal construction. But in bespoke tailoring, where a garment is made from scratch to an individual client’s measurements and specifications, a lining’s colour, weight, texture and material are considered as carefully as what appears on the outside of the jacket. Most clients, says Taub, decide whether they want their lining to harmonise with or contrast the main cloth. “Customers might feel bolder to make a statement because they know it might not be noticed by most people,” he says. That freedom has led to some unconventional choices. Taub has previously worked with vintage mid-20th century military silk maps, silk and ramie kimono fabrics, printed Irish upholstery linen and Indian undyed cotton broderie anglaise. For Taub, those decisions are part of what makes bespoke tailoring such a special process. “As a bespoke designer you should include elements of the customer’s character, lifestyle, culture, profession, climate, purpose and longevity,” he says. “This naturally creates unique pieces that could not be designed by committee or a computer.” Sentimentality often comes into it, too. Jeremy Hackett, the British menswear designer who founded Hackett London and later JP Hackett on Savile Row, recalls creating an exclusive tweed in honour of his Sussex spaniel, Harry, then commissioning a silk lining patterned with the dog’s head. “Although one rarely sees it, it is enough that you have created something that is exclusive and special to you,” he says. Clients sometimes bring in their own fabric because it has a meaningful connection, or even because it complements a bride’s dress for a wedding. Hackett also suggests turning any leftover lining silk into a matching pocket square. Fashion designers have long understood the appeal of putting something unexpected on the inside, too. Paul Smith has frequently used colourful and patterned linings to bring an extra element of personality to his tailoring, while Thom Browne’s jackets often reveal linings in the label’s signature tricolour stripe. Tory Burch encountered the idea early on, too, through her father, Buddy Robinson, who was known for lining his suit jackets with Hermès silk scarves. The same appetite for unexpected suit linings extends into women’s tailoring. Daisy Knatchbull, founder and CEO of Knatchbull on Savile Row, says clients often use the inside of a jacket to introduce details they would never put on the outside. “We’ve created linings for our clients featuring everything from favourite pieces of art and photographs of their children, to good luck symbols, favourite animals or a design that holds a special meaning for them,” she says. Knatchbull offers thousands of options, from Liberty prints and silks, to novelty designs and more traditional plains. “One of my favourite things is when a client chooses a classic, conservative suit and pairs it with a more unexpected lining,” she adds. “It becomes their own little secret, or a wonderful reveal when they open or take off their jacket.” For Anderson, one of the most memorable examples came from much closer to home. His wife, Fran, is an artist, and the tailor recently transformed a painting she made in the late 1980s into silk for the inside of a jacket. “There is something rather wonderful about cutting a suit and knowing that stitched inside is a piece of her work,” he says. “That is exactly what a lining should be: something with meaning that you carry close, whether or not anyone else ever sees it.” And when it comes to choosing your own lining, Anderson has some words of advice. “Be as adventurous on the inside as you dare,” he says.

title: Jonathan the tortoise: a 194-year-old marvel of longevity
description: Studying the animal revealed unique genes linked to ageing and cancer resilience.
content:
The oldest-known land animal in the world is an Aldabra giant tortoise named Jonathan. He is believed to be 194 years old.
Scientists think that his amazing long life might be because of a mix of special genes and his ability to keep important systems in his cells working as they do in younger animals.
Members of this species are known to live more than 100 years, but Jonathan has far exceeded that. Scientists have studied Jonathan to explore the secrets of the animal’s longevity.
The researchers identified 287 genes with variants unique to Jonathan, including some linked to tumour suppression and ‌DNA repair. The tortoise also carries extra copies of a gene that encodes a protein that hunts down ageing and cancerous cells.

title: Greek island’s last school faces closure amid declining student numbers
description: The sole teacher at the only school on Kalamos has just two sixth graders this year.
content:
Chryssa Ntalaka’s classroom has become an object lesson in subtraction.
The sole teacher in the last school on the peaceful Greek island of Kalamos has a shorter list of students every autumn. This year, there are just two.
Last month, the sixth graders sat at Ntalaka’s table beneath the whiteboard, in front of rows of unused desks and benches.
When they head to middle school on Greece’s mainland next year, her school will be closed.
Toys and picture books still sit on shelves in the nearby kindergarten, which closed three years ago.
Falling enrolment across Greece this year prompted authorities to close 75 schools and to suspend or extend suspensions at over 400 others.
It is a situation playing out across Europe and beyond. The region has 16 of the world’s top 20 oldest nations, particularly in southern Europe, according to the independent World Population Review.

title: Why indie developers are making a horror game set in an old Hong Kong estate
description: Three-person team behind ‘Block 13’ hopes their video game can reflect authentic aspects of local culture while mixing in spooky elements.
content:
Trapped in a weathered public housing estate in Hong Kong that feels more like purgatory than home, players encounter uncanny anomalies as they wander dim hallways in search of an exit.
This is the haunting premise of Block 13 , a first-person indie horror game built by 29-year-old developer Kennedy Liu. The Hongkonger painstakingly modelled the game’s claustrophobic layout after the iconic L-shaped blocks of Fuk Loi Estate in Tsuen Wan.
Liu has been working on this project since May 2025, and he plans to release it next year on the gaming platform Steam.
Drawing heavily from Hong Kong public housing estates built in the 1970s and 1980s, Block 13 leverages local architecture and collective memories to build natural suspense.
While some might see these estates as ordinary residential blocks, Liu views them as cornerstones of Hong Kong culture.
“When people – especially foreigners – think of Hong Kong, they instantly picture neon signs or the Kowloon Walled City,” Liu explained. “But to me, public housing is the place that nurtured multiple generations from the 50s, 60s and 70s up to today. If I had to pick something authentic that truly represents Hongkongers, nothing fits better.”
Inspired by the concept of the 18 levels of hell in Chinese mythology, each floor of Block 13 introduces a distinct narrative theme – such as labour or betrayal – expressed through supernatural anomalies. To survive and escape the building, players must resolve these anomalies by burning incense or performing other rituals.
Liu noted that he included details that would resonate with people who grew up in Hong Kong.
“I hope that besides exploring the environment, players will notice the references and hidden Easter eggs,” he said. “I incorporated a lot of elements from local culture and Chinese traditions, including superstitious concepts or social issues revolving around work and studying.”
Behind Block 13 is a tight-knit, three-person operation. Liu manages the core programming, game design and 3D environment art. Two of his secondary school friends – one is a researcher and 2D artist, while the other is also a programmer – also help bring the project to life.
The game was born out of the team’s love for Hong Kong – and a lack of job opportunities.
After Liu spent six years working in the gaming industry, he found himself jobless.
“Because I was unemployed, I purely wanted to sharpen my skills – for instance, making shaders, game visual effects or gameplay logic,” he shared.
Having spent years creating stylised, cartoon assets for past employers, he seized his downtime to pivot towards photorealism.
“I had always wanted to create realistic game environments,” Liu said. “Since I didn’t get the chance to join a company doing that, I used my period of unemployment to upskill my game development abilities.”
When considering the subject for his project, Liu realised how few video games featured authentic Hong Kong settings.
He recalled thinking: “Since I’m capable of doing it, why not just make it about Hong Kong?”
Creating a game about his home meant that every design choice held deeper meaning for him.
“I realised that even if I built a lot of mechanics or technical features, if the game lacked content and a soul, it was meaningless,” said Liu, who is using his savings to fund his game.
But designing an environment set in a public housing estate meant overcoming the risk of visual monotony .
“If the whole game is just walking around identical public housing corridors, the scope for variation is tiny,” Liu noted.
That was why he incorporated the levels of hell into his design, giving each floor a distinct theme. This cultural perspective also shaped the game’s interactive elements.
“My original concept came from observing how people pray to deities whenever something happens – mostly out of personal desire, like praying for love,” Liu said.
“So burning incense when encountering anomalies in the game serves as a fun [mechanism].”
Block 13 is built entirely in Unreal Engine, a software designed for developing 3D computer game graphics. Liu used Blueprints – a programming language that allows users to construct the game by manipulating visual elements, rather than writing raw lines of code.
To navigate these complex systems, he also leaned on artificial intelligence (AI) to help him break down programming logic and troubleshoot concepts.
Despite AI’s growing presence in game creation, Liu emphasised that the heavy lifting of game development still relied on human hands. People are needed for 3D environment design, atmospheric lighting and optimising a game’s quality so that it runs seamlessly across systems.
Still, he shared that landing a job at a major gaming studio had become increasingly difficult worldwide.
“Investors … think, ‘If AI can do this, why pay so much to hire professionals?’” Liu noted.“The problem with AI isn’t direct replacement; it’s that it makes everyone feel like everything is easy now.”
According to Liu, even experienced developers, artists, programmers or designers who have worked at top-tier game studios are struggling to find work.
“I saw a senior artist whom I gave a job reference to last year – he used to work at major studios like Ubisoft … and his latest update is that he joined the government,” he said.
Despite the tough job market, Liu sees this era as a golden opportunity for independent creators. His advice to aspiring video game artists or developers is straightforward: take initiative and start building.
“Creating things on your own is actually the best option right now,” Liu said.
Rather than getting bogged down by traditional credentials or waiting for studio approval, he encourages creators to leverage modern tools and learn by doing.
“If you want to do it, you basically don’t need to ask for anyone’s permission or advice any more. If you want to build a taxi simulator, just build it,” he said.
“Don’t overthink it or feel like you need to take tons of formal classes because AI can teach you a lot if you take the time to read through things.”

title: How a 14th-century mural unites US and China in cultural collaboration
description: Artists and scholars have carefully created a copy of the Chinese Buddhist “Medicine Buddha” mural in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art.
content:
In the Chinese art area at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in the United States, one artwork grabs visitors’ attention right away.
When you enter the gallery with Chinese Buddhist art, you see a large wall filled with images of a Buddhist gathering.
Here is the Medicine Buddha, a mural from the 14th century. It comes from the Yuan dynasty, which lasted from 1279 to 1368.
Zhang Jian, the director of the Meticulous Painting Institute at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, was very impressed by the work. For three years, Zhang worked with Chinese artists and scholars to carefully study every crack, line and mark to create a full-size copy. Making a copy is much easier than bringing the artefact back to China.
In 1928, the 700-year-old relic left China after being sold by impoverished monks.
In a time when the relationship between the US and China faces difficulties, people from both countries still work together on cultural projects.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong must ensure mainland yachts are welcome
description: To make the southbound scheme a success, berthing capacity and related facilities must be expanded and the ecological impact monitored.
content: First came the cars; now come the yachts. When five Guangdong-registered vessels sailed into Hong Kong waters recently to mark the launch of the southbound yacht travel scheme, they completed a two-way maritime link that began with the northbound arrangement for Hong Kong yachts in June. The southbound scheme deserves a warm welcome. It opens a promising channel of high-value visits as the city searches for fresh sources of growth. Each widening of the door to the rest of the Greater Bay Area puts a larger share of the pie within reach, and Hong Kong must ensure its facilities are ready to serve the guests it invites. The precedent on land is instructive. The Southbound Travel for Guangdong Vehicles scheme, implemented at the end of last year, began cautiously with a daily quota of 100 cars entering the urban area. By the end of May, about 8,400 applications had been approved and some 6,700 trips booked, and bookings during the mainland’s Labour Day golden week were oversubscribed by two to three times. The quota was doubled to 200 a day in July, and the scheme extended to all nine mainland cities of the bay area. The two sides aim to cover all 21 cities of Guangdong by the first quarter of next year. Demand, in short, has outpaced expectations, and officials have been obliged to scramble to catch up. The yacht scheme starts from a similarly modest base. The Marine Department says at least 23 individuals or groups have registered through its Electronic Business System, and about 300 mainland yacht masters have qualified to navigate local waters after certification, training and examination. Visiting vessels may berth at yacht clubs or five designated areas: Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung. Together these offer 115 berths, which Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat considers sufficient, so no quota will be imposed. The economic logic is sound. Yacht owners are among the highest-spending visitors any destination can hope to attract. Their outlay extends well beyond the vessel itself, to fine dining, hotels, retail, provisioning, maintenance and crew services. Acting Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun noted at the launch ceremony that the global yacht market was projected to reach about HK$350 billion (US$44.64 billion) by 2032. He noted that there were about 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong. With its long coastline, scores of islands and sheltered bays, the city is naturally endowed to capture a share. Marine leisure is still a relatively new form of consumption in the city and across the bay area, and a reciprocal regime, reinforced by the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme approved by Beijing in June, can help it mature into a genuine regional industry. Yet the infrastructure gap is real. The five designated areas provide neither water nor electricity; visitors must rely on water-selling kiosks, bunkering points and marine service providers on the same terms as local boats. That may suffice for a handful of maiden voyages. More needs to be offered if the yacht scheme follows the trajectory of the car scheme. Hong Kong’s marina capacity has long been tight. If the 115 berths fill up on peak weekends, we must ensure we can meet demand. Environmental concerns also deserve a serious hearing. The marine chief notes that the five areas recorded about 10,000 vessel activities in the first five months of this year, more than 6,000 of them at Tai O, which suggests the additional traffic is marginal. Green groups, however, are right to point out that Tai O lies close to the habitat of the vulnerable Chinese white dolphin. Stepped-up patrols, fixed penalties for littering and referral of offenders to the mainland authorities are welcome, but they must be enforced visibly and consistently. The scheme is a sound step that deserves to succeed. To make sure it does, the government may need to expand berthing capacity, add shore-side utilities and pump-out facilities, publish data on usage and spending, and monitor the ecological impact. The pie is growing bigger. Hong Kong must ready itself to serve it well.

title: O3’s Luca Yang hated studying. So he built 24/7 study cafes to motivate people like him
description: After leaving finance and giving up a successful online tutoring business, Luca Yang set out to create a more welcoming place to learn.
content: At 22, Luca Yang was running a small teaching company in New Zealand after quitting a six-figure finance job that he hated. It had humble beginnings, where he tutored English online for A$25 (US$17.55) per hour just to get by. When one of his students got into Oxford, word spread: one student became 50, then 500. By most measures, he had already won the start-up lottery. “It was producing a lot of money, but it wasn’t something I actually loved doing,” he says. “I was having this mini existential crisis about it.” What pulled him out was a cheap coffee machine he placed outside one of his classrooms.
