Students loved it, and within weeks, a crowd would form around “the garbage machine” in the hallway practically every day. “That got me really excited for some reason, and I realised that, you know, the thing motivating them to study was the environment,” he says. “I didn’t even need to teach them any more.” Yang, who is now 27, dug into that untapped potential and, eventually, came up with O3 – a space that blends coffee, community and technology into what Yang calls “his Disneyland”. O3 operates on a “freemium” model, where anyone can walk in and use the space for three hours a week for free. Beyond that, members pay A$10 a week for unlimited 24/7 access. The goal is to make all the locations – currently Auckland, Sydney and two in Melbourne, with New York in the pipeline – 24/7 operations. The space is centralised around a single app that serves as both entry pass and social platform. Users can find study buddies, share files and collect digital creatures that unlock discounts – gamification borrowed from the world of Pokemon. Everything else about the space is whimsical, too, with the design of the interior drawing heavily on Yang’s childhood: Harry Potter, Narnia and Studio Ghibli. He describes the philosophy as “magical realism” – solving a functional problem, which in this case is the need for a productive workspace, while offering something transcendent. These are ‘worlds you escape into’ “Those are worlds you escape into,” Yang says. “By coming here every day, collecting a stupid little creature on your phone, it reminds everyone how to be a kid again, and how to be hopeful again. “Even in the absence of motivation or purpose, the environment makes you actually want to learn from building a habit and positive associations. “It keeps you moving, keeps you going. When you have a beautiful solution to a problem, it elevates your life.” If you want to create something cool, you have to be a kind of crazy Luca Yang While O3 exists to inspire learning, its founder almost dropped out of school entirely. “I used to hate studying,” he says. That changed during a trip to Beijing, a city bursting with the kind of third spaces that Auckland, by contrast, sorely lacks. Stumbling into a dimly lit coffee shop tucked inside a hutong, the atmosphere struck him immediately – it was calm, welcoming and strangely inspiring. For the first time, Yang found himself genuinely enjoying a space outside home or school. That simple experience became a turning point. He started exploring more cafes, using them as his study haunts, and found that the environment motivated him to focus. His grades improved, and his new-found discipline carried him all the way to the London School of Economics and eventually Harvard. The journey since has been far from straightforward, to say the least. Yang takes home a modest salary, has less time for old friendships and admits the stress has taken its toll – he feels like he has “aged 10 years in two”. Yet he considers these trade-offs a fair price for the fulfilment the work brings. “There’s genuinely some kind of enlightenment from putting your all into something and creating something wonderful,” he says. “You grow through changes, and you see yourself becoming this genuinely insane kind of person who can [do anything] – the normal struggles of everyday humans just don’t reach you any more.” The people behind the scenes The company is run by a lean team of six, including an engineer who handles the entire tech stack. Everything is built in-house: the app, the design and the furniture. Recently, they even put together an indoor pond at their new Melbourne branch by hand. “The more middlemen you have, the harder it is,” he says. The trade-off is brutal – long hours, constant change and zero work-life balance – but the team has bonded over years of friendship and a shared obsession with getting every detail right. When it comes to choosing the locations, rather than competing for expensive, turnkey retail shopfronts or corporate office space, Yang deliberately targets the cavernous, idiosyncratic properties that traditional retailers overlook. In Melbourne’s Brunswick, O3 leased a former industrial warehouse, and in Sydney’s Newtown, it took over the premises of the historic Gould’s Book Arcade, inheriting a vast floor plan complete with built-in character and shelving. Landlords sitting on large, difficult-to-lease properties are often willing to negotiate flexible, lower rates with a tenant who can bring consistent foot traffic – a low-budget and resourceful arrangement that works perfectly for Yang. But building beautiful spaces comes at a cost – and not just financial. For a young founder in his late twenties, navigating the bricks-and-mortar world means confronting a system designed to slow innovation down. “When you’re dealing with bricks and mortar, the reason innovation is very slow is because of all these laws that were made years ago, which they keep adding and building on,” Yang says. He describes dealing with “very old-fashioned” regulators, certifiers and engineers who are “at least 20 to 30 years older” and see him as a kid. “If you want to make money, run a marketing agency,” he says to anyone who wants to follow in step. “If you want to create something cool, you have to be a kind of crazy. “You’re giving up a big part of your life to chase something super uncertain. I wouldn’t encourage everyone to try. But if someone has an innate passion for a problem they want to solve, regardless of the money – that’s a pretty good starting point.” A motto hangs in every O3 space: “The world is your oyster.” For Yang, it’s not just branding – it is a reminder of the hope he nearly lost, and the hope he wants to give back. “I’m a very ordinary person from a very ordinary family,” he says. “But I happened to be in the right environment. I think great environments can motivate ordinary people to do extraordinary things. That’s close to my heart.”

title: Heep Hong Society seeks more support for Hong Kong ethnic minority SEN children
description: The NGO says that government-funded centres for preschool-aged kids with special educational needs can be inaccessible for many families.
content:
A non-profit group in Hong Kong is asking officials to increase support services for ethnic minority children. A pilot project showed that more than 95 per cent of participants made progress with support services.
Heep Hong Society said ethnic minority families face many problems when finding help for kids who have special educational needs (SEN). These include language difficulties and not having enough money. They may also have beliefs that make it hard to ask for help.
Government-funded centres help preschool-aged children with special needs. But these kids must have a diagnosis. Government assessments take time; private ones are costly.
The Social Welfare Department said the number of non-Chinese-speaking children getting help for special needs at preschool centres increased to 968 in the 2025-26 school year. This is up from 741 children in the 2023-24 school year.
Heep Hong Society ran a programme called Project Embrace from 2023 to 2025. It helped ethnic minority kids aged six and below through SEN assessments and support services. Oxfam Hong Kong’s study found that 95.7 per cent of programme participants improved in many ways.

title: Spark Deep Dive: Hong Kong must protect its vulnerable residents from the heat
description: Amid record-breaking temperatures, a systemic heat-health action plan to protect groups including the elderly and outdoor workers is essential.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
New research finds extreme heat may have contributed to 3,238 excess deaths in the city over a decade
The lack of a heat-health action plan puts most vulnerable residents at risk, experts warn
Neither Hong Kong’s first five-year plan nor its latest policy address included a systemic heat-health action plan.
The omission is worrying environmentalists and academics. They warned that “common sense” is not enough to protect vulnerable residents. Their comments came as new research found that extreme heat might have contributed to 3,238 excess deaths in the city over 10 years.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu delivered the five-year blueprint and the annual policy address in September. Despite rising temperatures, neither included a comprehensive plan to address urban heat.
The policy address did propose a new management system driven by artificial intelligence. It is called the “ AI city brain ”. It aims to improve collaboration between departments in extreme weather or similar incidents.
The World Health Organization outlines what is needed in a heat-health action plan. It includes management, early warning systems, surveillance and outreach.
“Including a heat action plan in the policy address or the five-year plan … could ensure heat adaptation and resilience as a citywide priority,” Prudence Yeung said. She is a Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner.
“[It would] provide a foundation for investment in heat resilience infrastructure, research and public awareness,” she added.
A Greenpeace survey from August found that nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people in Hong Kong report some form of distress during extreme heat.
Professor David Bishai is the director of the school of public health at the University of Hong Kong (HKU). In a study currently under peer review, Bishai and other researchers revised figures from 2024.
Previously, heatwaves were thought to have contributed to 1,677 excess deaths in Hong Kong between 2014 and 2023. The new estimate put that figure between 1,455 and 3,238. Bishai said the preventable excess deaths had largely gone unrecognised, as the people who died had underlying illnesses. The numbers focused on heatstroke, which is rare.
“An action plan in the face of extreme heat can be helpful in reducing death rates,” Bishai said. “We know just leaving it to common sense is not working, because we are still seeing these excess deaths during heatwaves.”
The Labour Department does issue heat-stress alerts for outdoor workers. The system was recently reworked following criticism.
The Department of Health provides public health advice.
Ren Chao is an HKU professor who specialises in climate-responsive design. She said heat-risk mapping was necessary to visualise areas experiencing hot days and nights.
1. According to the information in the news, which of the following statements is false? (1) New research showed extreme heat may have caused more than 3,000 excess deaths in Hong Kong over a decade. (2) The annual policy address delivered in September by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu included a comprehensive heat-health action plan. (3) The proposed “AI city brain” system aims to enhance collaboration between departments during extreme weather events. (4) Nearly 80 per cent of all high-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported some form of distress during extreme heat.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (3) only C. (2), (4) only D. (3), (4) only
2. Name ONE positive outcome of including a heat action plan in the policy address or the five-year plan.
3. Why did David Bishai say “leaving it to common sense is not working”? Explain using the news and your own knowledge.
1. Use the news and glossary to explain what heat stress is and how it affects labourers who work outdoors.
2. Which groups of people would benefit most if Hong Kong created a systemic action plan that tackles heat? Explain using the news, glossary and your own knowledge.
AI city brain: a system powered by artificial intelligence that links urban data, such as landslide monitoring, traffic flow, weather and public complaints, to manage emergencies and improve services
heatwaves: prolonged periods of excessively high temperatures, often with severe consequences for human health, ecosystems and infrastructure. In Hong Kong, temperatures during heatwaves typically exceed 33 degrees Celsius.
heat stress: the physical strain on the body caused by severe heat, which occurs when the body absorbs more heat than it can dissipate
heat-risk mapping: visually identifying and mapping areas that experience high temperatures across different districts to communicate heat risks to the public and guide relief efforts
It would help prevent heat-related mortality and other excess deaths, for example through proactive welfare checks on vulnerable groups. / It provides a clear policy framework for interdepartmental coordination instead of relying on reactive, common-sense measures. (accept all reasonable answers)
Professor David Bishai said this because relying on common sense has not prevented deaths during heatwaves, with new research showing that extreme heat may have caused up to 3,238 excess deaths in Hong Kong over ten years. Many of these deaths are unrecognised because heat worsens existing chronic illnesses like heart or lung conditions rather than showing up as simple heatstroke. Without a clear government action plan, such as early warning systems, cooling shelters and targeted outreach, vulnerable people like the low-income elderly cannot protect themselves using common sense alone. (accept all reasonable answers)
Heat stress is the physical strain on the body caused by severe heat, which occurs when the body absorbs more heat than it can get rid of. Outdoor labourers are strongly affected because they work directly in hot, sun-exposed environments with factors that worsen thermal strain, such as having no designated shade, poor ventilation, wearing non-breathable protective clothing and working near heat-generating equipment without heat shielding.
The groups that would benefit most are outdoor workers, low-income elderly residents and people with chronic illnesses. Outdoor workers need proper rest schedules and protected workplaces to avoid severe physical strain from continuous heat exposure. Low-income elderly residents often live in poorly ventilated homes without affordable air conditioning or nearby green spaces, making them vulnerable to physical and mental distress during heatwaves. Finally, people with chronic conditions like heart or lung diseases face a higher risk because extreme heat worsens their underlying health problems, leading to thousands of unrecognised excess deaths. A clear government action plan would protect these vulnerable groups through shelters and health outreach.

title: Learn about AI’s biases by exploring the fears and tastes that make us special
description: Artificial intelligence tools are trained on the sources they are given, so there are limits to the information they can tell us.
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is trained on information from the internet and other sources. If its sources have a bias, the AI chatbot might also show that bias.
For example, if you have only ever seen and eaten chocolate ice cream, you might think it is strange when someone offers you strawberry ice cream. You might prefer the chocolate flavour because that is what you have tried before. But that doesn’t mean there is something wrong with the strawberry ice cream.
In the same way, AI chatbots might have been trained to see things in one way. But that doesn’t always mean it is the truth.
Use the activities below to explore how you can think critically about what AI tools tell you.
Draw four monsters. Use different colours and features for each one. Try to make them as scary as possible. Then, give each monster a name.
Bring your monsters to different people, and ask them to pick the monster that they think is the scariest. Keep count of their votes in a separate notebook.
After asking at least 10 people, which monster is the scariest? Did everyone pick the same monster?
Reflect on how this shows us AI’s limits. What is “scary” can depend on each person’s fears. If AI is trained to find one monster to be scary, that doesn’t mean everyone will be afraid of it. Why should we be careful with information from AI tools?
These days, some people rely on AI for recipes and food recommendations. But just like we learned in the previous activity about what makes a “scary” monster, food and taste are also special to each person, family and community.
Ask three people in your neighbourhood about their favourite place to eat nearby. Why is this their top spot?
Next, ask an AI chatbot to suggest three places to eat in your area.
What is special about the suggestions from real people? How are they different from AI’s recommendations?

Hong Kong projected to have 101 heatwaves every year by the 2040s, a jump from an annual average of 14 hot days in the 2010s
Experts urge additional cooling shelters, greenery, shaded walkways and surfaces that counter urban heat
Hong Kong recorded a scorching 36.9 degrees Celsius at the city’s weather forecaster headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui on August 9, the highest since records began in 1884.
The extreme heat is disrupting health and sleep cycles, underlining questions about the city’s climate resilience. Areas surrounding the Pearl River Delta, including Hong Kong, will face more frequent, prolonged heatwaves by 2040, according to a study published in Weather and Climate Extremes scientific journal in May.
Jimmy Fung Chi-hung is chair professor of the environment and sustainability division at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Citing his study, Fung said Hong Kong’s already hot and humid climate was projected to worsen and intensify heat stress.
He said the number of days in a year repeatedly affected by heatwaves would jump from an annual average of 14 days in the 2010s to 101 in the 2040s.
Urban climate expert Professor Ren Chao of the University of Hong Kong (HKU) urged the government to study the potential challenges that residents in each district may face under climate change. She called for corresponding solutions and strategies to mitigate the risks, adding that pop-up cooling community centres or heat shelters were essential.
The city currently runs 19 temporary heat shelters, converted from community halls, when the very hot weather warning is in force. There are also eight community centres that open for heat refuge.
The 19 heat shelters run overnight if the warning is still in force at 4.30pm. Between August 5 and 13, the warning was issued for more than 204 hours, and the 19 shelters served between 160 and 250 residents each day.
While 70 per cent of Hong Kong is covered by green spaces, only 35 per cent of residents have greenery within 500 metres of their home on average, according to data collected in 2020 for an HKU-led study.
Bin Chen, an assistant professor at HKU’s division of landscape architecture who led the research, said the city must focus on smaller, more distributed greenery , such as street trees and shaded routes between homes and facilities.
But according to Anthony Cheung, vice-president of the Hong Kong Institute of Urban Design, the city’s existing rules and approval procedures do not facilitate building more canopies, covered walkways and footbridges.
Under the Buildings Ordinance, balconies and canopies cannot extend beyond three metres or 10 per cent of the street width, whichever is shorter. Cheung said building designs under the rule could not provide sufficient shade for pedestrians to seek shelter from the sun and rain.
Cheung acknowledged the government’s attempts to incentivise private developers to build sheltered pedestrian links, including footbridges, by waiving land premiums under certain conditions. However, he noted that approval for the scheme, launched in 2017, was a “very long process” and proposals were subject to different tests to assess their public benefit.
Theresa Yeung, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Planners, said the city should replace concrete structures with permeable materials to ease increased flooding caused by more frequent rainstorms driven by global warming.
She suggested the government mandate climate-resilient designs in relevant residential projects and eventually expand the scope to commercial buildings.
“Climate-resilient designs not only help the government but also residents by protecting their properties and assets,” she said.
The Development Bureau has said the government requires public works projects to incorporate greening elements in their planning and development stages.
1. According to Issue, what is the condition for the 19 temporary heat shelters to run overnight?
2. Explain TWO obstacles that hinder the construction of covered walkways and footbridges.
3. How can street greenery and urban design adjustments help Hong Kong adapt to extreme heat? Explain using Issue, Glossary and your own knowledge.
1. When there is a red warning, how many minutes of rest per hour are recommended for workers carrying out “heavy” labour compared with “light”?
2. Use your own knowledge to explain TWO major challenges employers might face implementing these rest schedules. What is ONE policy the government could enforce to ensure compliance?
AI city brain: an artificial intelligence-powered system that links urban data, such as landslide monitoring, traffic flow, weather and public complaints, to manage emergencies and improve services
heatwaves: prolonged periods of excessively high temperatures, often with severe consequences for human health, ecosystems and infrastructure. In Hong Kong, temperatures during heatwaves typically exceed 33 degrees Celsius.
heat stress: the physical strain on the body caused by severe heat, which occurs when the body absorbs more heat than it can dissipate
heat-risk mapping: visually identifying and mapping areas that experience high temperatures across different districts to communicate heat risks to the public and guide relief efforts
greenery: trees and flora that provide shade and lower the temperature of urban spaces
It would help prevent heat-related mortality and other excess deaths, for example through proactive welfare checks on vulnerable groups. / It provides a clear policy framework for interdepartmental coordination instead of relying on reactive, common-sense measures. (accept all reasonable answers)
Professor David Bishai said this because relying on common sense has not prevented deaths during heatwaves, with new research showing that extreme heat may have caused up to 3,238 excess deaths in Hong Kong over ten years. Many of these deaths are unrecognised because heat worsens existing chronic illnesses like heart or lung conditions rather than showing up as simple heatstroke. Without a clear government action plan, such as early warning systems, cooling shelters and targeted outreach, vulnerable people like the low-income elderly cannot protect themselves using common sense alone.
Heat stress is the physical strain on the body caused by severe heat, which occurs when the body absorbs more heat than it can get rid of. Outdoor labourers are strongly affected because they work directly in hot, sun-exposed environments with factors that worsen thermal strain, such as having no designated shade, poor ventilation, wearing non-breathable protective clothing and working near heat-generating equipment without heat shielding.
The groups that would benefit most are outdoor workers, low-income elderly residents and people with chronic illnesses. Outdoor workers need proper rest schedules and protected workplaces to avoid severe physical strain from continuous heat exposure. Low-income elderly residents often live in poorly ventilated homes without affordable air conditioning or nearby green spaces, making them vulnerable to physical and mental distress during heatwaves. Finally, people with chronic conditions like heart or lung diseases face a higher risk because extreme heat worsens their underlying health problems, leading to thousands of unrecognised excess deaths. A clear government action plan would protect these vulnerable groups through shelters and health outreach.
The 19 temporary heat shelters run overnight if the Very Hot Weather Warning remains in force at 4.30pm.
Strict regulations under the Buildings Ordinance state that balconies and canopies cannot extend beyond three metres or 10 per cent of the street width, limiting the amount of shade they can provide. The government approval process for schemes that incentivise private developers to build covered pedestrian links is very long, as proposals must go through multiple tests to prove their public benefit.
Street greenery, such as trees and plants, provides natural shade and helps lower temperatures in urban areas where concrete buildings trap heat. Urban design adjustments, such as building covered walkways and using permeable materials, protect pedestrians from direct sunlight and reduce urban heat retention. Together, these measures cool street-level environments, lowering thermal strain on pedestrians and making the city more resilient to rising temperatures.
Under a red heat stress warning, workers carrying out heavy labour are recommended to take 45 minutes of rest per hour, whereas workers performing light labour are recommended to take 15 minutes of rest per hour.
Employers may face financial and operational challenges because frequent 45-minute rest breaks can lead to project delays and lower daily productivity, and because managing worker schedules at dynamic job sites makes it difficult to track fluctuating warning levels in real time. To ensure compliance, the government could introduce legally binding safety regulations under the Occupational Safety and Health Ordinance, enforcing mandatory break periods with strict fines or penalty points for non-compliant employers. (accept all reasonable answers)

title: Scientists discover first new wildcat in 100 years
description: Tilcayo tiger cat was found in Bolivia; only two members of the species have been identified so far.
content:
Scientists have discovered a new species of wildcat. It is the first time in more than a century.
The tilcayo tiger cat is a small feline. It has a spotted coat like a leopard. It was found in the Yungas region of Bolivia.
Locals saw the creature. They thought it was an ordinary house cat, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz.
She is a biologist and National Geographic explorer. She was part of the research team that studied the cat.
The nickname “tilcayo” was given to the animal by locals. It inspired its new scientific name: Leopardus tilcayo .
Nogales-Ascarrunz called the discovery “a remarkable event.” This is because a new wildcat species hasn’t been described in 100 years.
The cat is the first new feline discovered since 1923. That is when scientists spotted the pampas cat in Uruguay.
The tilcayo is slightly smaller than a domestic cat. It measures around 45 centimetres. It also has rounded ears (see graphic).
A pair of tilcayos have undergone genetic testing, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. They are the only tilcayo cats discovered so far.
A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas. It was handed over by a family who had taken him in. A female was rescued and released into the wild. She had been attacked by locals.
Scientists began studying the animals in 2021. Research on the species was published last month in the journal Current Biology.
“So far, [the tilcayo] has only been detected in Bolivia,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. It has not been seen anywhere else on the planet.
She said tilcayo cats are classified as “vulnerable to extinction”. Their small numbers mean they could soon be considered “at much greater risk” of dying out.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): Thanks to El Nino, a desert is blooming in Chile
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] Spring has arrived in Chile, and even the desert is blossoming. A massive portion of the Atacama Desert, the driest nonpolar desert on Earth, has been covered in flowers after the El Nino weather pattern brought heavy rains to the region earlier this year. The unusually large amount of water allowed millions of seeds and bulbs to sprout and bloom, many of them after remaining dormant for decades.
[2] “It is a unique phenomenon; there are more than 200 plant species,” said Jorge Carabantes, head of the Protected Areas Department at the National Forest Corporation (CONAF). “This is a flowering event that is obviously extraordinary and unusual, very different from other blooms that occur elsewhere on the globe.”
[3] The Atacama lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes Mountains, stretching some 1,600km all the way down the northern coast of Chile. Flowering is common during the transition from winter to spring, but this year, the rocky, brownish dunes that make up the desert’s traditional landscape have turned into a vibrant, colourful carpet of wildflowers during a historic Desierto Florido, or “flowering desert”.
[4] Between July and August, Chile recorded record rainfall in several regions, with some levels never seen since records began in the 1950s. The heavy precipitation was driven by a “super El Nino”, a climate phenomenon that causes sharp rises in global temperatures and is becoming increasingly strong. “Since rainfall records began, these are the most significant figures in terms of volume,” explained biologist Cesar Pizarro, head of the Biodiversity Conservation Section at CONAF Atacama. “What has happened now has an origin, and it is called ‘super El Nino’.”
[5] The storms have caused flooding, havoc and devastation in several parts of Chile. In the north, they have also enabled the historic desert bloom, with an estimated coverage of some 17,000 sq km this year. This area is similar in size to the country’s largest and most populous area, the Santiago Metropolitan Region.
[6] According to CONAF projections, this is expected to be the most intense and extensive Desierto Florido since 1997. That is because, Pizarro said, the heavy rainfall activated the desert’s biological material, known as germ plasma. This includes seeds, bulbs and tubers, as well as the eggs of various invertebrates and reptiles.
[7] The result is a true visual spectacle featuring more than 200 species of plants and flowers. Red and yellow nanucas , purple rock purslane, white suspiros , orange terciopelos and the native garra de leon – one of the desert’s most iconic species – have transformed the hills, plains and ravines of the Atacama. “There are hills and mountain ranges where no greenery or flowers had been seen for more than 30 or 40 years,” Pizarro added. “This desert germ plasma can remain [dormant] for many years, even decades. The hills this year are the best example of that.”

title: Listen Up: Iraq’s once-vibrant film industry sees slow revival
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Joshua Dummer and Nick Dearman.
Voice 1: In the heart of old Baghdad, legendary cinema halls stand abandoned and shrouded in dust, bearing witness to Iraq’s once-vibrant cultural scene. A few kilometres away, director Ali al-Bayati oversees his camera operators as they adjust their lenses for a scene in his coming horror film, which he hopes to showcase internationally.
Voice 2: Bayati is part of a new generation of Iraqi filmmakers driving an industry comeback. Momentum is building, bolstered by recent international recognition for the Iraqi film The President’s Cake , which captures life under crippling international sanctions during Saddam Hussein’s rule. Reviving the cinema sector in Iraq is not easy, but it is not impossible either, Bayati said.
Voice 1: Film production in Iraq began in the 1940s – notably with titles co-produced with Egypt – reaching its peak in the 1950s. Among the most celebrated productions of that era was Kameran Hosni’s film Said Effendi (1956), a work recently restored as part of the Iraqi Cinematheque project supported by France and screened at the Cannes Film Festival in 2025.
Voice 2: But Saddam Hussein rose to power in the 1970s, and this was followed by decades of war, sanctions, sectarian strife and fundamentalist religious insurgency – especially with the 2003 United States-led invasion that toppled Hussein, displaced millions of Iraqis and killed at least 200,000 civilians. Ultimately, the golden age of Iraqi cinema was snuffed out.
Voice 1: Baghdad’s old cinemas that once drew film enthusiasts are now barely standing, with their faded walls, old doors and broken signs. Dilapidated shops crowd the entrance to the Granada Cinema, with clothes hanging directly on the street. Other cinemas have been repurposed as warehouses, with a few old film posters still clinging to their walls.
Voice 2: In recent years, a fragile stability has begun to revive Iraqis’ appetite for entertainment and returned focus to Baghdad’s cultural scene. Authorities seized the opportunity last year, launching an initiative to support 58 film projects. But the funding pool is just US$4 million, which is about HK$31.36 million, an amount that would fund only a single project in other countries, said Wareth Kwaish of the government-led initiative.
Voice 1: Authorities are also working to recover Iraq’s historic cinema archive in the country and abroad. And Baghdad has signed cinematic cooperation agreements with France to support its film industry. Still, the industry remains short on funding and support, making every production a gamble.
Voice 2: Filmmakers would often rely on small grants, Bayati said. He hopes to market his movie in the United States and in European countries, and is among those who benefited from government funding. The key for him is gaining the trust of Iraqi audiences, he said. Most Iraqi film-goers today frequent multi-screen cinemas in shopping malls where Hollywood and Egyptian films dominate the screens, rather than the classic venues.
Voice 1: Syrian filmmaker Abdulhadi al-Rakeb, who made a documentary about Iraq’s old cinemas, said their closure led to the disappearance of a culture of watching films in cinemas and, as a result, a decline in the very idea of filmmaking.
Voice 2: Last year, the Iraqi film The President’s Cake won a prize at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival. This year, it finally started screening in Iraq. The movie follows the story of a young girl selected to bake a cake for Hussein’s birthday at a time when sanctions made it almost impossible to find the ingredients.
Voice 1: Although the film was shot in Iraq, the production faced many challenges. Director Hasan Hadi said a shortage of experienced Iraqi film crews forced him to bring in European professionals. The local crew were not aware of international standards, and the foreign crew were unfamiliar with the local cultural context, which created more problems for us, he said.
Voice 2: According to Hadi, the lack of local crews is one of several reasons Iraqi filmmakers have been unable to work in their own country. There are more people who want to tell their stories and make films, but not enough resources. He believes the sector needs workshops to develop local talent, increased funding and better overall organisation. Hadi said he was cautiously optimistic.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): Guangzhou train station sets record with 1 million trips in a day
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
[1] A railway station in Guangzhou has set a national record in China for trips in a single day. It has also drawn attention for the frequency of bullet train departures. This happened during this month’s holiday period, the Guangdong provincial government said.
[2] Guangzhou South Railway Station handled 1,252 train services on October 1. It also handled just over 1 million trips. It was the start of the seven-day National Day holiday across mainland China. The publicity department of the province’s Communist Party committee announced the figures on its WeChat account.
[3] Crossing the 1 million-trip milestone was a first for China. At peak periods that day, trains departed every 40 seconds. It was an interval the publicity department said was “faster than people could scroll through short videos”. By comparison, combined shinkansen departures at Tokyo Station reach up to 24 trains per hour during peak periods. This averages out to one bullet train leaving every 2.5 minutes.
[4] Guangzhou South was designed to handle high traffic volumes, said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform. It is a think tank associated with the provincial government. The station is one of five major railway hubs in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong. The city has a population of 18.7 million and the station has 15 platforms and 28 tracks. Guangzhou moved early to integrate its subway system, intercity railways and high-speed railways. The city wanted to make travel relatively “seamless”, Peng added.
[5] Guangzhou South also operated 202 overnight high-speed services for the October holiday. This accounted for about one-sixth of all trains departing the station on a single day. China State Railway Group had projected a record 284 million passenger trips during a 16-day period. The number covered the National Day break and the Mid-Autumn Festival in late September.
[6] To prepare for the holiday rush, Guangzhou South expanded transfer areas and departure lanes. It also improved passenger information services and added train services based on wait-list data. The additional services strengthened links with major cities including Shenzhen, Changsha, Nanning and Zhuhai.
[7] Guangzhou South connects with a total of 196 cities, including Beijing and Hong Kong. “When you add all this together, it’s not rocket science to see why Guangzhou South is as busy as it gets,” said David Feng. He is an independent railway specialist.
Source: South China Morning Post, October 5

title: Meet Barbera Thornhill, Trump’s anti-trafficking ambassador, going viral for her ‘Maga face’
description: Following Susan Dell’s White House visit that sparked online derision over her looks, a new Trump hire is getting flak for the same reason. So who is she?
content: After Katie Zacharia was sacked as the White House press secretary amid questions about her legal qualifications, another newly appointed Trump official is going viral. Barbera Thornhill is US President Donald Trump’s new Ambassador-at-Large to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons. State Department official Riley Barnes shared the 78-year-old’s portrait on X to celebrate her appointment, but the post gained traction for all the wrong reasons. Social media users tore into Thornhill’s appearance, comparing her features to the infamous “Mar-a-Lago face”, suggesting that she may have undergone extensive cosmetic surgery. Earlier this month, philanthropist Susan Dell, who visited the White House with her billionaire husband, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, to discuss their contribution to the “Trump Accounts” initiative, was also accused of getting a “Maga makeover”. So, who is Barbera Thornhill? Read on to find out. What is Barbera Thornhill’s background? According to Thornhill’s testimony before the US Senate in June, she hails from North Carolina, where she was raised by Dr Patricia Sills Thornhill, a paediatrician, and Dr Edwin Hale Thornhill, an ENT doctor. She said her mother was one of the first women to attend the Duke University School of Medicine, and her father invented a surgical procedure called stapedectomy. However, according to Shea Clinic’s website, Dr John Shea Jr is often credited with inventing the procedure. What are Barbera Thornhill’s qualifications? According to the American Presidency Project’s website, Thornhill attended the University of California, Los Angeles. She also studied at George Washington University and North Carolina State University in Raleigh. Professionally, she served as president of the Los Angeles-based interior design firm Impact Design. Thornhill is also involved in philanthropy and has worked with several charities in Los Angeles, per BuzzFeed. During her Senate hearing, she also claimed to have worked with Mother Teresa in Kolkata, India, in 1994. In 2019, Trump nominated Thornhill to be the US ambassador to Singapore, but her nomination was withdrawn after Joe Biden became president of the United States in 2021. She is also a notable Republican donor who reportedly contributed US$98,527 to the Trump-Vance Inaugural Committee in 2024. The non-profit organisation PACT (Protect All Children from Trafficking) previously questioned Thornhill’s nomination for the TIP Office, claiming she lacked experience in federal anti-trafficking policy. Is Barbera Thornhill married? According to Hollywood Life, Thornhill was previously married to businessman Gary L. Wilson. She has a son, Hale Thornhill-Wilson, whom she introduced during her Senate testimony alongside his fiancée, Emma Evans. She also acknowledged her cousins, Fred and Fabian Thornhill, during her opening remarks.

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): Helena Law Lan, Hong Kong cinema’s grand dame of horror
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Few figures are as synonymous with Hong Kong horror films as Helena Law Lan, who has been a household name for over half a century. Unlike typical “scream queens” who gain popularity playing damsels in distress, 91-year-old Law has been the city’s on-screen spirit medium for over three decades. For years, she has served as the Halloween ambassador for Hong Kong’s Ocean Park.
[2] Law, whose real name is Lo Yin-ying, was born in Hong Kong on November 13, 1934. Her career began in 1950, when she was 15, during a visit to a film set. A crew member asked her to play an unnamed factory worker in The Kid , with a nine-year-old Bruce Lee in his first leading role.
[3] Over time, Law’s strong, well-defined facial features led her to be cast in villain roles. She was also given the stage name “Law Lan” to evoke a glamorous “bad woman” image. In a 2020 interview with Hong Kong news outlet HK01, she said: “I’d never thought I’d be the lead.”
[4] In 1971, when she was in her mid-thirties, Law signed with TVB. The 1970s saw Law become a daily fixture in local living rooms as she took on numerous supporting roles in television dramas. A bigger TV role came in 1983 when she played the facially deformed villain Kau Chin-chak in The Return of the Condor Heroes , starring Andy Lau Tak-wah and Idy Chan Yuk-lin as lovelorn martial artists – a role Law reprised in the 1995 remake.
[5] While many of Law’s contemporary female entertainers were concerned with maintaining a conventionally beautiful appearance, Law embraced her unconventional casting. “My look was quite terrifying, but many viewers remembered it,” she told HK01 in 2018. “As an actor, my job is to do justice to the script.”
[6] In 1993, Law played her most iconic role to date: supernatural medium Lung Po (or “Dragon Granny”) in Thou Shalt Not Swear , a horror comedy about the Hungry Ghost Festival. Law’s performance bagged her a best supporting actress nomination at the 13th Hong Kong Film Awards. Her turn in the 1996 sequel July 13th , which focused more on her character, earned her another nod in the same category.
[7] Gradually, Law became a pop culture icon. She went on to play the same creepy, spiritual old lady with a piercing gaze and unnerving coldness in numerous films, such as the Troublesome Night series (1997-2003), Big Fortune Hotel (2015) and I Love You, You’re Perfect, Now Change! (2019). Law had a career high when she won best actress at the 19th Hong Kong Film Awards in 2000 for her role in the crime drama Bullets Over Summer . At 65, she became the oldest actress to receive that honour. In 2002, she won a Life Achievement Award at the TVB Anniversary Awards.
[8] From 2010 to 2019, Law served as Ocean Park Hong Kong’s official Halloween Fest ambassador, playing a series of eerie characters in the theme park’s annual promotional videos. She resumed the collaboration earlier this month for a special Halloween meet-and-greet event.
Source: South China Morning Post, September 25

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): No-bake Monster Eyeball Truffles are a delicious Halloween treat
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Want to make something cute and fun for Halloween? Try these easy no-bake Monster Truffles. They are essentially bite-sized Oreo cheesecake balls decorated with candy eyes and sprinkles. They are quick to prepare. You could make your little monsters any colour you want if green doesn’t suit you. You could even do batches in different Halloween shades. They’re almost as fun to make as they are to eat!
227 grams of block cream cheese, softened
2 tablespoons of coconut or vegetable oil
[3] Directions In a food processor, pulse the Oreos until they become fine crumbs. Dump the Oreo crumbs into a medium bowl and stir in the cream cheese until it is well combined. Stir in the Snickers and Reese’s until they are well combined.
[4] Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Using a small cookie scoop, form the mixture into small balls. Place them on a prepared baking sheet and freeze until slightly hardened, about 30 minutes.
[5] In a medium microwave-safe bowl, combine the white chocolate and oil. Microwave until just melted and stir until smooth, about 2 minutes. Stir 10 drops of green gel colouring into the melted white chocolate. Add more drops until the desired colour is achieved.
[6] Dip a frozen ball into the melted green chocolate until it is coated. Remove it using a fork, letting the excess melted chocolate drip back into the bowl. Arrange the balls on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Press an eyeball onto the top of a coated truffle and sprinkle the top with sprinkles. Repeat with the remaining frozen balls and melted white chocolate. Freeze until the chocolate hardens, about 15 minutes.

title: Pickleball gets into Hong Kong mainstream as world’s top players, fans old and new gather
description: City emerging as a key regional hub for the sport in Asia, shown by Kai Tak Arena hosting region’s largest professional pickleball.
content: Loud cheers, thumping bass lines, flashing court lights, and the crisp pop of plastic paddles filled Kai Tak Arena on Sunday as Asia’s largest professional pickleball tournament reached a festive climax. Moving beyond the quiet formality of traditional court sports, finals day at the Hang Seng Bank Hong Kong Slam 2026, which drew a crowd of more than 2,000 spectators, felt more like a block party than a high-stakes championship, bringing fans within arm’s reach of the world’s elite players. The HK$8.58 million (US$1.1 million) event assembled 895 players from 22 countries and regions, spanning ages nine to 71 across professional and amateur divisions, with the world’s top-six-ranked players competing here. Feng Huanhuan, CEO of event organiser F-Sports Promotions Limited, said they were deeply honoured to bring the tournament to Hong Kong for the first time. “Over the past week, we witnessed world-class players showcasing their exceptional skill, Hong Kong athletes putting up outstanding performances with fierce determination, and countess fans filling the venue with relentless energy and cheers,” Feng said. “This truly highlights the rapid growth and overwhelming appeal of pickleball.” For 29-year-old Vince Chan, attending the finals with a group of 10 friends was a reflection of how rapidly the sport had embedded itself in Hong Kong’s recreational culture. “It allows you to meet a lot of friends, and it’s much easier for beginners to pick up compared with tennis,” said Chan, who also attended Thursday’s preliminary rounds. “The atmosphere for the finals was noticeably better than earlier in the week. You can feel that more and more people in Hong Kong are playing pickleball every year.” That growing grass roots demand has also spawned a burgeoning local industry. Among Chan’s group were local indoor venue founder Alex Fung and pickleball paddle brand founder Doug Choy. While Fung acknowledged that operating large indoor courts in Hong Kong remained commercially challenging because of high venue costs, he stressed that major international tournaments were crucial for expanding the sport’s footprint. Meanwhile, Choy was not just watching; he also competed in the amateur division, taking home a silver medal in the mixed-doubles event. “Everyone here is connected by a passion for the sport,” Fung said. “Some of us run venues, others manufacture paddles and many compete. Events like these definitely give the whole ecosystem in Hong Kong a major push.” The sport’s accessible nature has also made it a hit with families. Dick Cheung brought his five-year-old daughter to the venue after a sports injury forced him to step away from high-intensity tennis. “I used to play tennis, but after suffering an injury, I couldn’t sustain that level of physical strain any more,” Cheung said. “Pickleball allows people of different ages and skill levels, whether beginners or advanced players, to share the court together.” Cheung added that the design of the Kai Tak venue brought spectators unusually close to the action. “The distance is very close. You can clearly hear the distinct sound of the paddles hitting the ball, which creates a really immersive experience.” That proximity left a mark on the younger generation. Inspired by the world’s top-ranked player, Anna Leigh Waters, Cheung’s five-year-old daughter said she liked running and hoped to emulate the star on court in the future. A similar sentiment was shared by Bryan Rennie, a former professional rugby union player from South Africa who has lived in Hong Kong for 12 years. Attending the finals with his wife and two young daughters, Rennie admitted he was caught off guard by the scale of the event. “I was quite surprised at how many fans were here,” the former tennis player who now plays pickleball casually said, admitting he had not expected such a strong turnout. “It’s a great atmosphere: good music and a nice crowd,” Rennie said. His six-year-old daughter said watching the matches up close made her eager to give pickleball a try. The tournament’s draw extended far beyond local residents, attracting hardcore enthusiasts from mainland China. Liu Wei, 49, flew in specifically from Xian, Shaanxi province, to attend both the semi-finals and finals. Liu, who operates a pickleball club in Xian, spent more than HK$4,000 to HK$5,000 on flights and hotel accommodation, far exceeding his HK$1,800 tournament ticket, but said the experience was worth every cent given the presence of the world’s top-ranked players. Having previously attended tournaments in Beijing and Hangzhou, Liu noted a striking difference in Hong Kong’s audience demographics. “In northern mainland China, pickleball crowds often skew middle-aged or consist mainly of existing club members,” Liu said. “But here in Hong Kong, I saw so many young couples, teenagers and families in the stands. It proves that the sport is achieving true mainstream popularity here rather than remaining a niche interest.” Liu added that Hong Kong and the wider Greater Bay Area were rapidly emerging as key regional hubs for pickleball in Asia, second only to established markets such as Vietnam. “The current set-up partitioning the arena worked very well, but I believe Hong Kong has the potential to fill two-thirds or more of a full-scale stadium in the future,” Liu said. On the court, world No 1 Anna Leigh Waters and No 2 Anna Bright captured gold in the women’s doubles, overcoming world No 3 Hurricane Tyra Black and No 4 Jorja Johnson. Australia’s Andie Dikosavljevic claimed the women’s singles title against Spain’s Judit Castillo, while an all-American men’s singles final saw Hunter Johnson defeat compatriot Tama Shimabukuro for top honours. In the men’s doubles, Federico Staksrud and Hayden Patriquin pulled off an impressive victory to take gold over top-ranked duo Ben Johns (world No 1) and Gabriel Tardio (No 2). Wrapping up the tournament, Waters and Johns teamed up in the mixed doubles to defeat Bright and Patriquin, securing the final gold medal of the championship.

title: The Belgian musician fusing Western, Chinese instruments for ‘something totally different’
description: Piano and yangqin player Johan Famaey shares his musical philosophy and journey from Belgium to China and back ahead of his Hong Kong debut.
content: Johan Famaey is considered the only professional yangqin player in Belgium. When he returned to Belgium from Qingdao, China, in 2009, most people in his home country had never heard of the instrument and knew little about Chinese culture. The 47-year-old musician, who is primarily a pianist, performs with a yangqin in Belgium and beyond, showcasing both Western and Eastern music traditions in his compositions. “Whether it’s a piano, whether it’s a yangqin, we all have this in common that we try to move the people, to touch their hearts with the instruments that we play,” he says. Famaey will perform on the piano at PMQ in Hong Kong on November 14, as part of the 2026 Belgian Chocolate Festival. It will be his first visit to the city, and after that, he will perform in Macau. The concerts are part of the “Belgian Days” programme organised by the Consulate General of Belgium in Hong Kong. A cultural awakening in Qingdao Famaey’s interest in music began when he was two years old and continued through childhood. He studied the organ at an academy in the Belgian city of Lokeren, then studied piano, organ and composition during his master’s degree, which he earned from the Lemmens Institute in Leuven in 2002. In 2005, he moved to Qingdao, in Shandong province. “I wanted to do something totally different,” he says. “And I was thinking about learning Arabic or Chinese.” He met his wife – a native of Wuhan, in China’s Hubei province – while still in Belgium and moved to mainland China with her, studying Chinese at Qingdao University. He got in touch with the university’s music department to learn the yangqin and began combining Western influences with Chinese instruments. “It was like the first instrument that I thought was talking with me,” he says about his first experiences with the yangqin. The piano and the yangqin are “drastically different”, he says. “In the piano, higher keys are in your right hand, the lower part of the piano is in your left hand, and for your yangqin, it’s the opposite. So it’s really like an inversion … they’re actually total opposites in that way.” Famaey also taught chamber music at the Qingdao University School of Music and the Qingdao University of Science and Technology, and performed as an organist with the Qingdao Symphony Orchestra. Musical cross-pollination Famaey also plays the salterio, an instrument popular in Italy, Spain and Portugal during the Renaissance that he says was largely forgotten by history and only rediscovered in the last couple of decades. “The salterio is like the Italian version of the yangqin, but smaller,” he says, laughing. Both instruments’ strings are played with beaters. Since moving back to Belgium in 2009, Famaey has continued composing music with strong Chinese influences. In 2011, he composed his “Chinese Memories” series, combining Song and Tang dynasty poems with opera and film music. He created the melodies of some of the 10 songs in the series while living in Qingdao but rearranged them for strings, yangqin, organ, percussion and singers. He says most of his inspiration comes from stories: “My music is never, in a way, abstract … it always needs to somehow carry forward a story, something really deeply human from us, from our cultures.” The yangqin evolved into a chromatic instrument, which made it easier for contemporary musicians – such as Famaey – to marry it with Western instruments and feature Chinese-style pentatonic melodies and harmonies. Famaey’s advice for fusion music is to “not force it”, to avoid coming off as insincere and cliché. But his Chinese influences are undeniable; he visits his wife’s home country every year. Bridging East and West Famaey sees music as a unifying force for international relations. Tapping into traditional musical instruments also means looking back at a country’s history. By merging Eastern and Western traditions, he hopes to open dialogue between cultures. As with his coming Hong Kong performance, Famaey often performs on behalf of Belgian embassies as part of cultural or diplomatic celebrations. In 2025, he composed his piece Together through Time to celebrate the 50th anniversary of China-EU diplomatic relations. “Despite all the difficulties and economic difficulties and trade wars and so on, this [was] still an important anniversary,” he says. “We’ve been talking to each other for 50 years; let’s talk for the next 50 years, too.” Over the decades, Famaey has seen a clear evolution in how Chinese culture and music are received in Belgium. “Five years ago, it would still have been a risk to programme Chinese-style music, and especially for a whole concert,” he says. “Nowadays, if they programme a concert of Chinese New Year music, the halls will be full.” He adds that a unifying theme is usually still needed to draw crowds to concerts featuring Chinese instruments. But as a professional, internationally touring musician and a teacher at a Belgian music academy, Famaey remains steadfast on his mission to share the joy across the two musical traditions. Famaey will be performing as part of the 2026 Belgian Chocolate Festival at PMQ, 35 Aberdeen Street, Central, Hong Kong, on November 14 and 15. Admission is free. For more details, click here.

title: Asian Tour: John Catlin claims Hong Kong Open title on historic day for golf in city
description: American wins by five shots in Fanling, while Matthew Cheung produces the best finish ever by a local player in the tournament.
content: In the end there was no Sunday shoot-out at the Link Hong Kong Open, just John Catlin cruising to a five-shot victory on a historic day for golf in the city. The American’s six-under-par 64 took him to 20 under overall, and the only blip on an otherwise perfect day was a bogey at the par-3 5th. Not that it mattered. Catlin had no need to outgun his rivals, with Hongkonger Matthew Cheung and Finland’s Kalle Samooja at 15 under the closest the field got to depriving him of the places at next year’s Masters and Open Championship that came with his triumph. “‘It’s like a dream come true,” Catlin said. “I remember when I was five, 7, 10 years old, practising, hitting putts to win the Masters; it’s been a long time coming, a lot of hard work, a lot of times when I wasn’t sure what was coming, but you just kind of held the faith. To finally be at the Masters, speechless.” Catlin is making a habit of winning national opens: Hong Kong was the sixth in a collection that also includes victories in Ireland, Austria, England, Thailand and Saudi Arabia. “Anytime you can win a national open, I think it just adds a little bit of extra prestige,” Catlin said. “It’s amazing for this to be my sixth. If you’d told me that 10 years ago, I probably would have laughed at you. So, it’s truly special.” Cheung, meanwhile, finished in a tie for second because Samooja bogeyed the last, although none would deny that his career-best finish had come from his career-best performance. While the 31-year-old may yet look back on his struggles in the third round and wonder what might have been, his three under 67 produce a finish that is the best a local player has ever managed in the tournament. His walk to the 18th green in the group ahead of Catlin would have been worthy of a winner, and Cheung said it sent “a chill down my spine”. “I played really good today; unfortunately, John [Catlin] played really well as well,” Cheung said. “But I’m really happy overall.” Cheung had started the day two shots back of Catlin, Thomas Pieters and Caleb Surratt. The group at 14 under should have included Anirban Lahiri, but the India golfer was harshly penalised one shot for the almost imperceptible movement of his ball as he addressed before chipping on to the 18th green on Saturday. Lahiri learned of his punishment before teeing off for the final round, and any energy generated by a sense of injustices was lost in a double-bogey at the first. A four over 74 left him a tie for 17 on nine under. Pieters briefly flirted with a challenge, as did Surratt, but both dropped away and finished with matching 72s.

title: Luxury brands destroy unsold stock to preserve exclusivity. That may soon change
description: European laws will soon force labels to report how much stock they have destroyed amid efforts to reduce the industry’s environmental impact.
content: Earlier this month, shoppers on Yoox could snap up suede Brunello Cucinelli trainers for €617 (US$700), around half the price on the brand’s official website. If they felt like pairing them with a beige Gucci miniskirt, that was available for €800, close to 50 per cent off as well. A Burberry T-shirt? The e-commerce website sold one for less than €200, or 60 per cent off its original price. Overall, some 2,500 products from the three labels were available, heavily discounted. It is a sign of the challenges that the luxury market faces, as even wealthy customers cut back on spending. High-end fashion and leather goods makers try to avoid slashing prices or selling excess stock because it damages the aura of exclusivity that they build around their products. That is why at times, they have preferred to burn or shred their unsold goods: a controversial policy that is now banned in the European Union, home to some of the industry’s largest brands. There are loopholes that may allow brands to continue to destroy goods. Nevertheless, the EU’s drive for greater sustainability in the fashion industry is about to create a serious challenge for luxury companies. From next March, they will be required to report how many unsold products they have destroyed and why. That not only risks a backlash from customers and civil society, but could also give competitors’ commercially sensitive information about how particular ranges are selling. The new rules risk a “double penalty”, says Julie El Ghouzzi, a luxury goods consultant. “When you do something that could be understood as reprehensible, then you have a huge risk of reputation, and reputation in luxury means desirability.” The volume of high-end goods being junked in the luxury business was thrust into the spotlight by a trial in Hong Kong this year. In August, four former workers in a Chanel warehouse in the city were sentenced to between four and seven years in prison for conspiring in 2016 and 2017 to steal about HK$8.77 million (US$1.12 million) worth of stock that was destined for the shredder. The group was intercepted and more than 700 items were seized by police. “Chanel would destroy about 10,000 to 20,000 items of their fashion products once every three to six months, using their shredding machine,” the judge wrote in sentencing remarks. One of the defendants explained that Chanel’s unsold goods would typically be discounted first by 25 per cent after six months of being on the market and by 50 per cent after a year, with the possibility for staff to buy the items at 20 per cent of their retail value. Eventually, if the goods did not sell, they would end up in the shredder. In a statement, Chanel said that the figures mentioned in the trial do not reflect the company’s current practices, “which have evolved in line with its sustainability commitments”. The company said that it now only produces collections after receiving orders through its stores, and that products that cannot be sold are “redirected towards reuse, recycling or other circularity solutions”. By 2020, between 264,000 and 594,000 tons of textiles were destroyed before use in Europe annually, according to figures from the European Environment Agency – equivalent to between 4 per cent and 9 per cent of all products on the market, and accounting for a maximum of 5.6 million tons of CO2 equivalent, roughly the annual emission of a million petrol cars. In 2022, France, home to some of the luxury industry’s biggest names, adopted a circular economy law that obliges fashion companies to reuse, repurpose or recycle unsold products. Separately, the EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation – modelled on the French law – came into force for large companies this July. The UK government is also expected to be announcing circular economy measures. Although the laws ban the destruction of textile and fashion products, the regulations have loopholes. In France, companies can recycle products by shredding or pulping fabric into lower-grade materials to turn into insulation or carpet fibre, which is the industry’s “get out of jail card”, says Christina Dean, founder of The R Collective, which upcycles goods from luxury houses that would otherwise be destroyed. “You put gold in and you get crap out.” The EU requirements look stricter than in France, but there are still exemptions that will let big fashion houses continue to destroy unsold products, according to legal experts. The law excludes leather goods, including handbags – which are the mainstay of the luxury fashion business, with higher profit margins than most other items – and some limited-edition products. Garments with a logo or trademark that cannot be removed without damaging them are also exempt. “It’s a bit of a perverse stimulant to actually make it more difficult to remove them in the first place,” says Sara Matthieu, a Belgian member of the European Parliament, who was involved in drafting the law as the Green bloc’s shadow rapporteur. Companies can destroy a garment if repairing or refurbishing it would cost more than destroying and replacing it. They can also destroy something if they tried to resell it – either by themselves or through a charity – and it was not sold within eight weeks. Many of the exemptions were added late in the process, leading environmental groups to suspect that the industry was able to influence the legislation. Viola Wohlgemuth, a senior expert on textiles and the circular economy at Deutsche Umwelthilfe, a German environmental NGO, describes it as an “absolutely perfect example of lobbying”. Unlike the French rules, the EU law classifies recycling as a form of destruction, which has divided people in the business. The Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode (FHCM) – the industry body that organises Paris Fashion Week and represents high-end fashion labels – fought for the EU law to allow “high-quality recycling” and hopes to add it during the review period, which ends in 2031. A spokesperson for the FHCM says that the group “supports the ambition” of the EU regulations. Others, such as Simone Cimadomo, project and policy officer at Rreuse, a circular economy social enterprise, say that cutting up clothes to recycle the fabric is still destruction, and the fabric is not necessarily reused. “It makes sense that recycling is included because, if you really look at what’s going on mechanically to the product, it is getting destroyed,” Cimadomo says. “It is getting processed into a secondary material. “That secondary material should be used. But it is not always used, because it depends on demand for recycled fibres or recycled polyester in another product.”

title: BYD to build new factories in Europe to combat strict trade barriers targeting Chinese EVs
description: The world’s largest EV maker said it would not let EU tariff hikes and quotas on hybrid imports from China impact customers’ vehicle choices.
content: China’s BYD will build new factories in Europe for a bigger market share, as the world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) maker faces fiscal support pullback at home and rising trade barriers overseas, according to an executive. “Europe is a very important regional market for BYD. We will not let tariff increases affect local consumers’ choice of BYD,” said Liu Xueliang, vice-president at the Shenzhen-based carmaker, in a recent interview. Liu also reaffirmed that BYD was actively expanding its local footprint, with new plants in Europe set to be launched “soon”. It aligned with a plan revealed by BYD’s overseas CEO Stella Li earlier this month that a plant in Hungary will kick off mass production in the last quarter of the year. The commitment to BYD’s local production in the world’s third-largest regional car market came after the European Union said in mid-October it would impose a quota on the hybrid cars imported from China, two years after hiking the tariffs on Chinese-made all-electric vehicles to as high as 45.3 per cent. On October 12, China announced that the value-added tax rebate rate on exports of new energy vehicles will be lowered from 13 per cent to 9 per cent starting April 1, 2027. Together with the resumed battery consumption tax, China’s EV industry might see its profitability worsen “faster than expected”, JPMorgan said in a note on Tuesday. Thanks to the established factories in Southeast Asia, BYD’s Liu expected the export tax rebate reduction to have limited impact on sales in the market. In addition to the growing demand for EVs amid the global oil shock, BYD will continue to increase its overseas capacity, he added. However, Liu noted that BYD had not yet decided whether to increase selling prices in overseas markets to pass on the tax costs, as competition over price points was also intensifying. BYD’s planned capacities outside mainland China totalled 1 million EVs as of October, with only 30 per cent in Europe, according to a note by Morgan Stanley on October 13. BYD’s share in the EU’s new car market surged to 2.4 per cent in the first nine months of the year from 1 per cent one year ago, after new car registrations swelled 154.4 per cent to 206,002 units over the same period, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association showed. Even though BYD stepped up its efforts in exports to Europe, the shrinking demand at home dragged the first-half net profit to slump over 20 per cent year on year to 12.3 billion yuan (US$1.84 billion). To improve profitability, BYD accelerated the overseas launch of its premium model Denza Z9GT this year. After a global debut in Europe in April, the carmaker unveiled the Z9GT model in Hong Kong on Friday with a starting price of HK$998,000 (US$127,260), over 200 per cent higher than that of 269,800 yuan in mainland China. But Liu also admitted that BYD faced “many challenges” in overseas markets as it worked towards the goal of surpassing Japan’s Toyota and becoming the world’s top carmaker by 2030, which was announced by the chairman Wang Chuanfu at an annual meeting with shareholders in June. Instead, the reduced reliance on fossil fuels supported by the massive global EV scale was far more meaningful than reaching the No 1 spot, Liu added.

title: ‘Hairy crab freedom’: Chinese delicacy’s price tag drops amid high output, weakened demand
description: A growing supply of hairy crabs has produced a 35 per cent year on year price reduction as China’s appetite for the bristly crustaceans wanes.
content: For Guangzhou resident Claire Kou, this autumn brought a welcome surprise: “hairy crab freedom”, the ability to enjoy the beloved Chinese delicacy without worrying about its traditionally high price tag. During the National Day holiday earlier this month, Kou ordered four female hairy crabs, each weighing about 100 grams (3.5 ounces), via an online grocery platform for just 70 yuan (US$10.5). Female crabs are often considered desirable because they carry a lot of bright reddish-orange roe, reputed for its rich flavour. A check of her digital receipt from the same period last year showed a similar order cost 107 yuan, an around 35 per cent year on year drop. Following right on the heels of the Mid-Autumn Festival, this year’s National Day break created a 13-day holiday period widely seen as a barometer for Chinese consumer spending. Hairy crabs have long offered a window into this festive market. Though historically prized and sold at steep premiums during peak holidays, their prices have been sliding for the past two years as domestic demand weakens. Surging output from emerging farming regions is pushing China’s hairy crab harvest towards a record 1 million tonnes. Combined with weak demand and smaller budgets for corporate gifts, this growing supply has erased the crab’s high price, driving down both retail and farm prices. Wang Chenghui, a professor at Shanghai Ocean University, was quoted by state-backed news outlet Jiefang Daily as saying that national hairy crab production had grown steadily, reaching 939,000 tonnes in 2025 and closing in on a record 1 million tonnes in 2026. Cited by Tide News, which is affiliated with Zhejiang Daily Press Group, Zhou Yingtao, a crab farmer in Jiangsu province, described this year as the lowest and most volatile market he had ever worked through. Even more significant than the rise in production is the rapid erosion of the crab’s status as a luxury gift. Hairy crabs’ prized status has eroded, squeezing out their high price premium, according to Zhou Chunyong, head of the Anfeng Town Aquatic Industry Association, as quoted by Tide News. He noted that even for the most premium crabs, prices have fallen 10 to 20 per cent this year. Looking back to 2020, prepaid “crab vouchers” were a major driver of e-commerce sales, with gift cards often selling for thousands of yuan. In the early 2010s, a voucher for 10 premium Yangcheng Lake crabs fetched as much as 3,698 yuan, making a single crab worth about the same as a gram of gold. Today’s deep discounts mark a dramatic shift in how Chinese consumers spend. This year, corporate procurement budgets have continued to tighten amid sluggish domestic demand. “In the past, we would receive many gifts like hairy crab vouchers and baijiu from our suppliers,” said Zhu Lei, a manufacturing business owner in eastern China. “This year, almost everyone stopped sending them, opting for simple mooncake gift boxes instead.” The sustained price pressure on hairy crabs mirrors broader strains on Chinese household consumption. Data from the National Bureau of Statistics shows that consumer price growth remained subdued, with the consumer price index, a crucial gauge of inflation, rising 0.9 per cent year on year last month.

title: Max Verstappen’s advice to Kimi Antonelli at US Grand Prix: enjoy the ride and celebrate
description: Mercedes driver, who qualified in pole position, could seal title if he wins and results go his way; Verstappen chasing third ⁠straight win.
content: Max Verstappen advised Kimi Antonelli to enjoy the ride and get ready to celebrate as the Italian stands on the brink of becoming Formula 1’s youngest-ever champion. The 20-year-old Mercedes driver qualified on pole position for Sunday’s US Grand Prix and could clinch the title with five rounds ‌to spare, according to the current calendar that includes races in the Middle East, at Austin’s Circuit of the Americas if he wins and other results go his way. Red Bull’s Verstappen, a four-time champion, will be alongside on the front row and fighting for his third successive victory after Malaysia and Singapore. The Dutch driver will not be making it easy for Antonelli but he also recognised that the main battle was over. “He knows what he’s doing, ⁠so he just needs to try and win the race. If it [the title] doesn’t happen here, it will happen next ‌weekend. If it doesn’t happen next weekend, it will happen the weekend after,” he said, sitting alongside Antonelli in a post-qualifying press conference. “I think it’s just been an incredible season, so you have ‌to also just try and enjoy this kind of ride of the past few months that you’ve ⁠been in. “At one point, ⁠of course, it’s official, and then you can celebrate probably a little bit.” Verstappen said Antonelli, who is 102 points clear of teammate and closest rival George ‌Russell, deserved all the success he was having. “He’s very consistent, he’s putting the performances in when it matters, and once it’s finally official that he is world ‌champion, he’s ‌definitely a deserving winner,” he said. Antonelli said the weekend did feel different, with his first “match point” in the championship, ‌but the goal remained the same. “We still have to do the race tomorrow, still have to try and win, and then, ⁠of course, we’ll see what happens. But yeah, I feel like I can enjoy it a bit more because obviously I’m ⁠in a very good position,” he said. The Italian added that his biggest immediate achievement, on a gusty day with a tailwind blowing, had been to keep his car within the track limits. The Italian has regularly fallen ‌foul of stewards and irritated team ‌boss Toto Wolff with his breaches of the limits this season. “One of the keys was not doing any track limits. That was very good for me because I’ve had a couple of races where I’ve done track limits in crucial moments, and that kind of put myself in a bad position and under more pressure. So that hasn’t been ideal,” he told Sky Sports television.

title: Israel widens West Bank crackdown, displacing Hebron families after attack
description: Israel will close all West Bank land crossings for election day, vowing harsher anti-Hamas action after two soldiers died in an ambush.
content: Israel said on Sunday all land crossings with the West Bank will be closed on the day of next week’s election, as it pledged a harder line on militancy after Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers in the territory. The announcement came a day after Israeli forces pushed into the occupied West Bank city of Hebron and displaced around 2,000 residents, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying, “they will not be allowed to return … until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron”. Hamas, while not claiming credit, hailed Friday’s killings at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city, in which attackers shot dead two Israeli soldiers and wounded three more. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to exact a heavy price for the attack just days before the polls and said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967. The Israeli army said that, from Sunday, Palestinians would “not be permitted to enter Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley for work”, using terms many in Israel use to refer to the West Bank. The army also said it would enforce “a ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout election day” on October 27, it added. Israel’s longest-serving prime minister Netanyahu is facing a tight race for a new term in Tuesday’s polls, with his security-first reputation all but shattered by Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack.
