The Palestinian Authority, the semi-autonomous body that governs parts of the West Bank in cooperation with Israel, called for international pressure on Israel to protect residents affected by the military operation. The Israeli army said that over Friday and Saturday, it operated in 40 areas throughout the territory, with locals reporting that soldiers announced evacuations over loudspeakers late at night. Israeli forces said they “apprehended approximately 40 suspects, including terrorists affiliated with the Hamas and Islamic Jihad terrorist organisations”. In the Hebron neighbourhood of Ein Deir Baha, nestled between two hills, vacated buildings were marked by X’s and the streets were deserted, save a pair of Israeli military vehicles. Israeli flags were draped on a house on the slope apparently taken over by troops. Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper who plays a leadership role in the neighbourhood, said he was awakened at 1am by soldiers and a senior officer who said he had to leave. “I asked them how long the evacuation would last. They said: ‘Until further notice.’” He said he had only a short time to pack, adding that for some residents, getting out of the neighbourhood was an ordeal. “For example, my wife’s mother, who is 90 years old and lives in the area, had to be carried out because she is ill,” he said. Right-wing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position in the defence ministry overseeing civilian affairs in the West Bank, said he personally ordered “the immediate demolition of a row of illegal structures” following Friday’s shooting. “Anyone who messes with us will quickly understand that he will pay a painful price,” he said in a social media post. To Tamimi, the West Bank operation is only happening because Netanyahu wants to win the election on “the blood of the Palestinian people”. He said people were not going anywhere. “I have lived through all the stages of the occupation, and I will die here.” But Tamimi’s brother, Khaled Shawer al-Tamimi, 68, said he and his son left after the evacuation order rang out. “The army was announcing through loudspeakers: ‘Leave the area.’ So we left.” He said he was surprised to hear Friday’s assailants came from the neighbourhood, which he described as middle-class and law-abiding. “We have never seen or even heard a single gunshot being fired,” he said from his son’s sitting room as children flitted about. The Israeli military said the operation would last several days, but Netanyahu suggested bigger action was coming.

title: Heritage Fiesta encourages students to experience culture
description: Event aims to help students appreciate the history of the area and includes two sites that played a role in resistance against the Japanese occupation during WW
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
A plaque hangs above the main entrance of a school in Yuen Long. It reads “ bai nian shu ren ”. This means it takes a century to train people, and that good education takes time.
The phrase was written by Shum Kwong-yuet. He was a Qing scholar and calligrapher. The plaque bears witness to the site’s history of nurturing Hong Kong students.
The story begins before World War II. Back then, students in Yuen Long had limited options for secondary education. There were plans to establish a school. However, these were set aside because of the war.
Yuen Long Public Middle School first opened at Pok Oi Hospital in 1946. The school moved to a permanent campus in Au Tau in 1950. It was the first government school in the New Territories.
From 1994, the site housed TWGHs C.Y. Ma Charity Fund Practical School. It was renamed TWGHs C.Y. Ma Memorial College in 2001.
This historic building was one of 12 sites selected for the Heritage Fiesta 2026. The event was organised by the Commissioner for Heritage’s Office of the Development Bureau.
“It gives us an opportunity to let the public see our campus, which has such deep cultural heritage,” said Leung Yuk-lan. She is the school’s vice principal.
She added that the public could see “what the tradition was like and how we have revitalised it today”.
The theme of this year’s Heritage Fiesta is “Traversing Northern Metropolis”. The event runs from October to December. It will spotlight declared monuments and graded historic buildings across the Yuen Long and North districts.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu spoke about heritage conservation in his latest policy address. He said cultural promotion and urban renewal were linked to tourism and development.
There are 12 sites in the Heritage Fiesta. They fall into three categories. They are the clan culture and traditional character of the New Territories, the reuse of historic buildings and the founding spirit of schools.
Two sites from the Ping Shan Heritage Trail are highlighted. They were linked to the resistance against Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945.
Tat Tak Communal Hall took in homeless children. They had come south from the mainland to Hong Kong. The Ching Shu Hin building provided food and accommodation for people returning to the mainland. They wanted to escape the occupation.
“You can see that the residents of the two places share a very deep historical connection ... a relationship of blood being thicker than water,” David Leung said. He is Hong Kong’s commissioner for heritage.
This is the first time TWGHs C.Y. Ma Memorial College has participated in the Heritage Fiesta. The school will open to the public for guided tours by students on November 21 and 28. Tours will be held in Cantonese, English and Mandarin.
The bureau is keen to show how development and conservation can go hand in hand .
“We hope to let the public feel it for themselves, to let them experience it personally,” Commissioner Leung said.
This year’s programme includes interactive elements aimed at children and teenagers. One activity is historic building colouring workshops. These will be held at 14 public libraries from October to December.
On designated weekends, there will also be an open-top bus heritage tour.
“We hope to take this opportunity to make heritage conservation and historic buildings no longer just a matter for experts,” the commissioner said.
Details of the Heritage Fiesta schedule are available on the “HK Heritage Live” Instagram and Facebook pages.

title: Hong Kong’s Heritage Fiesta highlights cultural spots in the Northern Metropolis
description: Tour includes a government middle school, two sites on Ping Shan Heritage Trail that played a role in resisting Japanese occupation in WWII.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Above an entrance of a school building with over 75 years of history in Yuen Long hangs a plaque that reads “ bai nian shu ren ” – meaning it takes a century to train people and that good education takes time.
Written by Shum Kwong-yuet, a renowned Qing scholar and calligrapher, the plaque bears witness to the site’s history of nurturing Hong Kong students and passing the torch from generation to generation.
The story begins before World War II, when students in Yuen Long had limited options for secondary education. Plans to establish a school were set aside because of the war.
Yuen Long Public Middle School first opened at Pok Oi Hospital in 1946 before moving to a permanent campus in Au Tau in 1950. It was the first government school in the New Territories.
From 1994, the site housed TWGHs C.Y. Ma Charity Fund Practical School, which was renamed TWGHs C.Y. Ma Memorial College in 2001.
This historic building was one of 12 sites selected for the Heritage Fiesta 2026, organised by the Commissioner for Heritage’s Office of the Development Bureau.
“It gives us an opportunity to let the public see our campus, which has such deep cultural heritage – what the tradition was like and how we have revitalised it today, thereby continuing to carry forward our educational spirit,” said Leung Yuk-lan, the school’s vice principal.
Under the theme “Traversing Northern Metropolis”, the Heritage Fiesta runs from October to December and spotlights declared monuments and graded historic buildings across the Yuen Long and North districts.
In his latest policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu linked heritage conservation, cultural promotion and urban renewal to tourism and the development of the Northern Metropolis.
The area is also one of the most historically rich in Hong Kong, with 31 declared monuments, 341 graded historic buildings and Hong Kong’s first heritage trail, the Ping Shan Heritage Trail.
“Of course we need development, but as for the district’s natural and human resources, we will do our best to conserve, revitalise and protect them,” said Commissioner for Heritage David Leung.
“We hope to link up some heritage sites and historic buildings so that the public has a chance to step inside [them] in person. These historic buildings are all in use; they are living places.”
The 12 sites in the Heritage Fiesta fall into three main categories: clan culture and the traditional character of the New Territories; adaptive reuse of historic buildings and the founding spirit of schools.
Two sites from the Ping Shan Heritage Trail are highlighted for their links to the resistance against Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945. Tat Tak Communal Hall once took in homeless children who had come south from the mainland to Hong Kong. Meanwhile, the Ching Shu Hin building provided basic accommodation and food for those who sought to return to the mainland to escape the occupation in Hong Kong.
“You can see that the residents of the two places share a very deep historical connection, a spirit of mutual help, a relationship of blood being thicker than water,” Leung said.
This is the first time TWGHs C.Y. Ma Memorial College has participated in the Heritage Fiesta.
The school will open to the public for guided tours by students in Cantonese, English and Mandarin on November 21 and 28.
Vice-principal Leung explained that the campus has played many roles in the district’s development.
“It was a gathering place for local gentry, as well as a place for cultural [and commercial] exchange,” she said. “We want children here, within a traditional building, to feel the ideals of those who ran schools before them and to strive and set their own resolve.”
The bureau is keen to show how development and conservation can go hand in hand.
“We hope to let the public feel it for themselves, to let them experience it personally – what it is actually all about,” said Commissioner for Heritage Leung. “There are some tangible activities they can take part in, some actual routes they can walk.”
This year’s programme includes interactive elements aimed at children and teenagers, including historic building colouring workshops, which will be held at 14 public libraries from October to December.
Themed public lectures will be held at the Hong Kong Heritage Discovery Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui.
On designated weekends, there will be an open-top bus heritage tour.
Leung said he aims for the tours and events to encourage young people to promote Hong Kong history: “We hope to take this opportunity to make heritage conservation and historic buildings no longer just a matter for experts,” he said.
Details of the Heritage Fiesta 2026 schedule are available on the “HK Heritage Live” Instagram and Facebook pages.

title: Review | Japan’s Zentis Osaka offers a restful stay in the bustling Umeda district
description: The city hotel, opened in 2020, is a short walk from Osaka Station and major department stores like Hankyu and Daimaru.
content: Osaka, the third largest city in Japan, lacks the charm of Tokyo or the historic appeal of nearby Kyoto. Home to Kansai International Airport, Osaka is often a jumping-off point for more popular nearby destinations such as Kyoto, Nara and Kanazawa, all a short train ride away. While Osaka is not the typical tourist town with must-visit attractions like temples, shrines and museums, it’s still a great place to hang out and spend a couple of days to enjoy local specialities such as okonomiyaki and takoyaki, and check out its many shopping areas. The city has a very well-established hotel scene. Pretty much all the big names are represented, from Four Seasons to Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis and the likes. Zentis Osaka, which opened in 2020, is not a competitor to those five-star properties. Low-key and laid-back, the hotel is a short walk from Osaka Station in the bustling Umeda district, where big department stores like Hankyu and Daimaru are also located. While it’s fairly busy with office workers and locals at all hours of the day, Umeda is much quieter and less touristy than the entertainment districts of Dotonbori and Namba, which makes Zentis Osaka a great choice for those who want to be not far from the action, but also be able to take a break from the hustle and bustle. Zentis Osaka is part of the same company behind one of Japan’s most celebrated properties, Palace Hotel Tokyo, known for its authentic Japanese service that eschews the cookie-cutter approach of many international chains. The 212-key hotel is housed in a high rise with expansive views of the city’s urban jungle and futuristic skyline. Designed by the UK’s Tara Bernerd & Partners, the interiors are the definition of functional and no-nonsense. The colour palette sticks to natural hues like beige and sand while nods to Japanese crafts include bedside tables made in the kilns of Shiga and wallpaper painted with motifs evoking Japanese calligraphy. The airy lobby, decorated with artworks by local artists and plenty of coffee-table books, is home to a lively lounge with communal tables and comfy loungers where guests can enjoy free coffee and tea while working or relaxing before or after heading out. A serene garden terrace is planted with beautiful Japanese maples, which turn bright orange and red during foliage season in autumn. Upstairz, named in reference to the marble staircase that takes pride of place on the ground floor, is the hotel’s only dining venue. Located on the second floor, the bar and restaurant offers Japanese-inspired Western dishes such as roasted Japanese Wagyu rump with red port wine sauce and squid ink risotto with burrata cheese. Also on the second floor, a small gym is on hand for those who want to fit a workout in. Next door, a multipurpose lounge features a fragrance bar and a library with books about Osaka and Japan. Without too many bells and whistles and just impeccable service in a relaxed atmosphere – not to mention a very convenient location – Zentis Osaka is a great city hotel from a home-grown company that has come to define luxury hospitality in Japan and beyond. The author stayed as a guest of Zentis Osaka

title: Trump hails tariffs for new US$4.2 billion Audi plant in Georgia
description: ‘Without tariffs, they wouldn’t be coming in,’ the president told a midterm election rally in the state.
content: President Donald Trump defended his decision to wield tariffs during a campaign rally in Georgia, saying they have made the US richer, as he announced that Volkswagen agreed to build a new US$4.2 billion Audi plant in the state. “Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That’s incredible,” Trump told a crowd in the city of Perry. “This will be the single largest investment in US auto industry history, modern history.” Later, he added, “Without tariffs, they wouldn’t be coming in.” Trump was speaking as Republicans are trying to flip a Senate seat held by Democrat Jon Ossoff in the midterm election, despite trailing in the polls. The campaign stop marked Trump’s second in the state in as many weeks, an indication of the importance of the Senate contest in Georgia. With less than two weeks until election day on November 3, though, Representative Mike Collins, the Republican candidate, faces an uphill battle in a state that was once a Republican stronghold. The RealClearPolitics average of polls has Ossoff leading by more than eight percentage points, while the non-partisan Cook Political Report has forecast the race as “likely Democrat”. That dynamic is indicative of a broader political climate that has soured for Republican candidates. Trump is at historic low approval ratings and his efforts to tout manufacturing investment promises have failed to resonate with voters who are more concerned with high costs of living and wage growth. The war in Iran has also spiked energy prices, adding further strain to household budgets. The Audi announcement marks a political win for Trump, who has been on the defensive about the domestic effects of his tariffs, particularly on inflation, in a number of battleground Senate races. Volkswagen plans to manufacture the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models at the Georgia plant, according to a US official involved in the talks. Volkswagen will also expand its Scout Motors plant under construction in Blythewood, South Carolina, adding 25,000 units per year of capacity for a model yet to be determined, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail the plans. Audi said in a news release that the US$4 billion plant would create some 4,500 jobs with an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles. Construction will begin next year, with the aim of beginning vehicle production in the early 2030s. “We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Audi chairman of the board of management Gernot Dollner said at the rally, standing near Trump. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.” Richard Motes, 61, a Perry resident who used to work at an aircraft manufacturer, praised the Audi plant announcement. “That’s awesome, I want jobs to come to Georgia,” Motes said. “I’m dead red,” he added. “If they let me push a button to vote all Republican, I’d push the button.” Trump has been travelling nearly daily in the run-up to the midterms, seeking to help boost Republicans in competitive races across the country. Polls indicate Democrats are likely to regain control of the House, but the Senate is still in play with Republicans on the defensive in unexpected states such as Texas and Ohio. Another rally attendee, Chris Capp, 55, a former Army National Guard employee, said he is 50-50 on whether Trump is still an asset to Republican candidates in Georgia, given his falling popularity. “I love Trump to death, but sometimes he should keep his mouth shut,” he said. Georgia is also home to a competitive governor’s race between Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, which the Cook report has rated a toss-up. Former president Barack Obama is expected to campaign in Georgia with Ossoff and Bottoms on Wednesday. While Ossoff has pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if reelected, he has been seen as a potential Democratic 2028 contender. Trump won Georgia in 2024 and 2016, but lost to former president Joe Biden in 2020, prompting the president to promote unfounded theories of fraud in that election. Trump pressured Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find” the votes he needed to win the state. Trump and allies were indicted to face allegations of carrying out election interference, but those charges were eventually dropped. The president has repeatedly promoted false claims that he won the 2020 election and questioned the integrity of Georgia’s vote counting. Raffensperger earlier this month said that he expected the state’s election results by midnight on election day, downplaying the president’s remarks.

title: Gulf economies accelerate diversification as recession looms over Iran war
description: Even as the region’s economic downturn is expected to worsen, Gulf states are slated to spend tens of billions of dollars on infrastructure.
content: Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world. Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years. Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes. Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members. Such a shift towards long-term economic stability is important in maintaining the political legitimacy of the Gulf monarchies in the eyes of their burgeoning young populations, especially amid mounting public anger at the carnage in Gaza, according to analysts. The GCC states, as well as other Muslim-majority governments such as Pakistan and Turkey, eventually persuaded US President Donald Trump to end the Gaza war in October 2025, renewing optimism about the Gulf economies. However, everything changed soon after the Gaza ceasefire, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu managed to convince Trump to go to war against Iran. Rather than just retaliating against Israel, Iran has also vented its fury against the GCC states, attacking energy infrastructure, airports and ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. With Trump weighing his options, including both another military escalation and a politically inconclusive end to the war with Iran after midterm congressional elections on November 5, uncertainty reigns in the Gulf region. The eruption of war between Saudi Arabia and Tehran’s Houthi rebel allies in Yemen last month has exacerbated these anxieties. Driven by necessity, GCC governments have unveiled plans to stabilise their economies. The two largest in the bloc – Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are on the verge of a potential technical recession caused by the Iran war, while Qatar is already in a recession. In the second quarter of this year, Saudi Arabia’s economy – the largest in the GCC – fell by 4.8 per cent from 3 per cent growth in the first quarter. The UAE’s economy – the Gulf’s logistical hub – decreased by 2.1 per cent from an expansion of 3 per cent over the same period. Qatar’s economic outlook worsened, with its GDP declining by 15.7 per cent in the second quarter, accelerating from a drop of 7 per cent in the first quarter. According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) projections published on October 13, the UAE is expected to record a 3.9 per cent drop in its GDP in 2026 from a pre-war forecast of 3.1 per cent growth, while Saudi Arabia is projected to fall by 3.3 per cent this year from an earlier predicted 4.6 per cent growth. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are set to record double-digit GDP contractions in 2026. Like the IMF, the World Bank has forecast the GCC economies to rebound in 2027 if hostilities end this year and unhindered passage through the Strait of Hormuz is restored by next March. Tim Callen, a former chief of the IMF’s GCC division, expected the Gulf states to step up their economic diversification plans. The development of new industries would move ahead with some adjustments, including “a new focus on diversifying and better protecting energy and transport infrastructure”, Callen said. Karen Young, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Centre on Global Energy Policy in New York, said Gulf governments would continue to prioritise investments in natural gas production and its export in liquefied form, as well as the acquisition of such assets overseas. They would also focus on other “essential” areas such as more localised defence manufacturing, AI and other technologies. Young said the diversification of the power sector in the GCC to include nuclear and renewables would be crucial to reviving its economies, while other sectors like tourism could continue to come under pressure. Sovereign wealth funds like Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the UAE’s L’imad and the Oman Investment Authority would provide much of the funding and impetus needed to get the Gulf economies back on track, according to analysts. “Those funds have already demonstrated a propensity to play a greater domestic role. But these funds can’t do it all alone,” said Robert Mogielnicki, founder of Paris-based Polisphere Advisory. The involvement of foreign partners would be critical because of the considerable investments that would be needed to revive and grow the GCC economies, Mogielnicki said. Analysts predict GCC members will spend hundreds of billions of dollars to expand infrastructure across major sectors in the coming years as part of their economic transformation. One such initiative is a planned cross-GCC oil pipeline bypassing the Strait of Hormuz to be co-funded by all six members, which a report published by Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy estimated earlier this year to cost US$55 billion. HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, recently projected the value of ongoing infrastructure projects in the UAE at US$190 billion. The government of Dubai – one of the country’s seven emirates and its business centre – announced a US$572 billion pipeline of projects on October 13, including a massive new suburb and the construction of the world’s biggest airport. Mognielicki said the GCC’s ambitious infrastructure roll-out was both expensive and complex. “For the moment, most Gulf governments see a compelling justification for paying the price.” Callen said that despite these undertakings, it was far from certain whether the confidence of foreign investors in the GCC economies could rebound any time soon. Investors would be assessing the post-war demand for both energy and non-oil goods and services from the Gulf states, as well as the outlook of their tourism, conference, logistics and aviation sectors, according to Callen. “This is a very complex strategic project both because diversifying away from oil is anyway extremely difficult and to add to that now is the regional uncertainty,” he said.

title: Letters | Hardware and software both matter in a ‘car-lite’ city
description: Readers discuss agreed norms and shared civic habits on mass transit, a gold-backed route to yuan internationalisation, and the prospect of humans losing control to AI.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to “Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving” (October 3). Singapore has shown that with investment in transport hardware, people will choose public transport when it is fast, reliable and convenient. According to recent figures, 70 per cent of households are already within a 10-minute walk of an MRT or LRT station. Rail expansion, cycling paths and the development of regional hubs such as Jurong East, Paya Lebar and Woodlands have brought jobs and services closer to where people live. People are more willing to leave their cars at home when public transport offers convenience. A journey that involves short walks, dependable trains and seamless transfers feels vastly different from multiple changes, long waits or crowded interchanges. However, good hardware is only half the story. A successful public transport system also depends on software: agreed norms that make shared spaces pleasant. Courtesy campaigns, announcements and fines send a clear message about how people are expected to behave. Such measures are sometimes dismissed as paternalistic but they are needed. In dense cities, a small act of consideration can improve the experience of many others. Allowing passengers to alight before boarding, keeping noise levels low and refraining from blocking walkways help crowded systems function smoothly during peak hours. This becomes even more important in global cities such as Singapore and Hong Kong, where residents, newcomers and tourists share the same public spaces. Social norms should be visible, widely understood and consistently reinforced. Public campaigns can help, but so can active citizenship. People should be empowered to offer a polite reminder when someone behaves inconsiderately. Equally important, they should feel that fellow commuters will support them if they encounter aggressive behaviour. Many of us spend our journeys staring at our phones, withdrawing from those around us. That is understandable, but cities also need shared civic habits that encourage awareness of others. Building a car-lite future therefore requires more than trains, buses and cycle paths. It requires a culture of mutual respect. The hardware moves people efficiently. The software makes the journey worth taking. Ian Tan Yuk Hong, Singapore All that glitters Having read the op-ed, “HK gold bridge fulfils China’s yuan ambition” (October 6), I wish to offer my concerns. China has been successful in forming connections through the Belt and Road Initiative and Brics and strengthening its soft power. Its diplomatic initiatives give it bargaining power and more ease in putting forward measures. But with yuan internationalisation, I wonder if nations are not just paying lip service. After all, many have to maintain amiable relations with the United States, at least for the time being. The mechanism of “gold convertibility” also sounds less than ideal. It allows trading partners like Russia to sell oil for huge sums of renminbi, which can be immediately converted into physical gold. But wouldn’t this steadily eat into China’s gold reserves? With a gold-backed currency, China would also have to honour the promise of letting holders exchange notes for gold. We have to meticulously design a mechanism that will make China great again. But seemingly friendly nations shouldn’t be cashing in on our endeavour to achieve the ultimate goal of ending American monetary hegemony. Lo Wai-kong, Yuen Long Musk says humans won’t be in control. What then? According to Elon Musk, humans will no longer be in control in 10 years’ time. As of today, how far is it true? The very name of artificial intelligence suggests it is antagonistic towards humans. In companies all over the city, AI has become a money-saving tool detrimental to their survival. To me, there are many facets of human experience that cannot be replaced. The natural appreciation of people for a good speech, sermon or book; the joy of parents when a baby is born; the feelings of love, anger, jealousy, frustration. All these are from the bottom of human hearts and worth pages in the book of human history. What can humans do to slow down the staggering progress of AI? Not even Musk has an answer. All we can do, it seems, is live out the rest of our destiny. Jacqueline Kwan, Sai Ying Pun

title: Hongkonger Chan linked with vacant China women’s football head coach role
description: With officials looking to replace Ante Milicic quickly, fans have been discussing who could be next to lead the Steel Roses.
content: China football bosses have given themselves less than a week to find a new coach for the senior women’s team, and fans are already starting to suggest potential candidates, among them Hongkonger Chan Yuen-ting. The 38-year-old, who made history when she led Eastern to the Hong Kong Premier League title in 2016, has seen her profile rise among fans in mainland China in the past few years. Chan guided Jiangsu women to National Games gold last November, leads the team in the Chinese Women’s Super League, and has recently also been working with the Suzhou team in the local league. She is no stranger to the national set-up either, having taken charge of the China women’s under-16 side between 2019 and 2021. Still, anyone interested replacing Ante Milicic will need to act quickly, and being under the age of 55 will help too, maybe. According to the CFA’s job advert, the next head coach should be “under 55 years old, regardless of their nationality”, although that was then contradicted by the notice saying the age requirement “could be relaxed for those with outstanding coaching achievements and extensive experience in major competitions”. Milicic left on Friday, little more than eight months before the Steel Roses play in next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, and with the qualifying process for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics still to take place. The team, ranked eighth in the world, also failed to defend their Asian Cup title in Australia earlier this year, and returned home from the Asian Games in Japan empty-handed. Discussion on social media over who might get the role also centred on former player Ma Xiaoxu, who now coaches the Chinese women’s under-17 side. However, while the former forward has put together some outstanding results since taking the helm in January, her focus has been on youth training, meaning she has relatively little experience in senior competitions. But with the team having gone through 16 head coaches in the past 25 years, and few surviving more than two years in the job, fans were keen to not only find a “good coach, but also one who can commit long-term”.

title: In China’s tough job market, anxious students spend thousands on internships
description: Facing high youth unemployment and fierce competition for entry-level roles, some students are going all out to secure internships.
content: Accounting undergraduate student Wang Guilin faces a choice in her search for a winter internship: compete with thousands of applicants through standard recruitment channels or fork out thousands of yuan for a guaranteed placement. Wang considers her academic record average and, to improve her employment prospects after graduation, the second-year student hopes to add experience at a well-known company to her résumé. Yet even internships have become difficult to secure in China’s crowded graduate labour market, forcing many students to turn to brokers to land a spot at the country’s leading firms. “These positions usually go to third- or fourth-year students from top-tier universities or those with strong internship records,” Wang said. “Someone in my position would consider paying for referrals to secure a place.” The services available on the market vary widely. Some agencies offer career coaching, including résumé revisions and interview preparation, while others literally sell guaranteed back-door placements. They do share one thing in common, though: hefty fees. Wang has been quoted between 6,000 yuan (about US$900) and 12,000 yuan for a winter internship at a major accounting firm, although she said this was cheaper than the cost of a longer summer placement. Students online have reported fees running as high as 30,000 yuan for a placement – several times the typical monthly starting salary of a fresh graduate. In 2025, undergraduates earned an average of 6,435 yuan a month six months after finishing their studies, according to Beijing-based education research consultancy MyCOS. But many students are still forking out the money on solid internship experience, believing it could strengthen their applications for white-collar jobs. China’s youth unemployment rate remained elevated at 18 per cent in September after a record 12.7 million university students were estimated to have left university over the summer. Entry-level roles have been particularly squeezed, leaving some degree holders to turn to food delivery and other gig work or find work on factory floors. “In a situation with a tightening labour market – [with the risks of] artificial intelligence, plus slower overall growth, plus a growing number of young people entering the graduate labour market – there obviously is a huge amount of anxiety,” said Stuart Gietel-Basten, a professor of social science and public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST). “The worst organisations will exploit that anxiety,” he said. Some agencies offering internship experience have also turned out to be scams. In July, state-run People’s Daily reported that a Guangzhou-based firm had impersonated employees of prominent domestic and international companies and assigned tasks to students remotely. Once the work was completed, the company issued fake internship certificates and recommendation letters with forged electronic seals. In other cases, employees of major companies had illegally contracted interns to work remotely without registering them on the company’s human resource systems, according to the report. Wang, the accounting student, said she would only consider paying for an on-site internship, citing concerns about the reputation of remote placements. For now, however, she has decided to continue applying independently and hopes to gain some experience at a smaller company before targeting placements at major firms in her third year. “The cost is indeed quite high,” Wang said. “If I’m still in the same situation next year, then I might consider a paid internship again.” Meanwhile, Gietel-Basten of HKUST said the heightened competition over internships and additional qualifications risked deepening inequalities across an already-competitive education system and labour market. “My big fear is that this … would lead jobs to go not necessarily to the very best young people, but to those who have the resources and can afford to take unpaid internships or engage private sector companies to support their job search,” he said.

title: Should all Hong Kong school canteens be required to offer vegetarian options?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
For reasons of inclusivity, educational opportunities and students' health, schools should offer vegetarian meals.
A key advantage of including vegetarian meals is the increased inclusiveness of different cultures. As a global city, Hong Kong has a diverse population with different cultures and eating habits.
Plant-based eating is deeply rooted in Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism. There is also the Ital plant-based diet followed by Rastafarians in Jamaica. Hong Kong students could learn about the aforementioned cultures through their lunches by exploring food from other countries. As a result, this scheme exercises inclusiveness and equity.
Second, vegetarian meals can be educational amid a landscape of easily accessible junk food in Hong Kong. There is no doubt that eating healthy food has been ingrained in our mindset from a young age. But as fast food with high oil and sugar content is on the rise, it would be hard for most students to resist the temptation.
Vegetarian meals could serve as a reminder about our health. Schools can create curricula with the science sector to educate pupils; a hands-on experience that would leave a lifelong impression on them.
For example, a 2020 Baptist University study implemented a 10-month health education programme at a secondary school in Hong Kong’s most economically deprived district, where many students skipped breakfast and mainly consumed food at the school.
The students were allowed to make their own food choices for lunch. Most reported some change in their dietary practices.
Some worry that vegetarian meals are too unfamiliar for many students, who may reject the “unappealing” foods. This is a common misconception. A 2025 Singaporean study published in Appetite scientific journal found that nearly 80 per cent of children aged nine to 15 were willing to try plant-based meat. This shows that younger generations will eat or at least try vegetarian meals.
Additionally, as more students are exposed to these types of food, it is certain that more will grow to welcome them. Not only would plant-based meals be beneficial from an inclusive and educational standpoint, but it would also be an optimistic step towards a future with healthier eating habits.
Choices are important, but forcing a strict mandate on Hong Kong school canteens is a recipe for disaster. The impractical measure completely overlooks the structural limitations of local campuses, compromises the operational efficiency of food suppliers and degrades nutrition.
The primary obstacle is structural. Most local schools in Hong Kong suffer from space constraints, leaving minimal storage and kitchen space. To safely deliver vegetarian meals without cross-contamination, caterers would have to establish and dedicate separate preparation areas, cooking appliances and units for vegetarian meal production and storage. It could be physically impossible for older campuses.
Compounding this is the economic reality.
A Green Queen demographic survey revealed that 58 per cent of Hong Kong residents view maintaining a plant-based diet as costly. Canteen providers are already under tight budgets to keep lunchbox prices accessible. If forced to comply with this mandate, they will jeopardise the nutritional value in lunches as they inevitably rely on mass-produced, cheap dietary substitutes to maintain their margins.
The Department of Health heavily promotes the “3:2:1 Rule”, a strict ratio of grains, vegetables and meat for crucial developmental nutrition. To make vegetarian meals palatable without exceeding budgets, canteen providers would rely on ultra-processed, deep-fried mock meats doused in high-sodium sauces.
A 2023 cross-sectional study of plant-based meat in the Hong Kong market, published in Nutrients scientific journal, found that over 91 per cent of plant-based products are classified as medium to high-fat.
Forcing the inclusion of artificial, lipid-dense alternatives directly exacerbates Hong Kong’s childhood obesity crisis, where recent Department of Health data for the 2024-25 school year found that overweight and obesity rates among local students were at a staggering 17.5 per cent – around one in five children.
This mandate would also be detrimental to the environment. If canteens are mandated to cook a fixed quota of hot vegetarian meals daily, unpurchased surplus would end up in the trash, adding to the city’s waste problem. Rather than a strict regulation, schools should implement pre-order, demand-driven systems to include students who require vegetarian meals.

title: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care
description: Xuan feeds Xu liquid food spoonful by spoonful, taking an hour per meal, and turns her over 10 times daily to prevent bedsores.
content: A woman in eastern China has been devotedly caring for her daughter-in-law for 17 years, ever since she fell into a vegetative state, moving social media users. The younger woman, surnamed Xu, fell into a vegetative state in 2009 after being struck by a truck in her village in Qingyun county, Shandong province. The accident happened just one month after she got married, Shandian News reported. Since then, her mother-in-law, Xuan Fengying, has cared for her around the clock. “She married my son, so she’s my child. How could I abandon her?” the 68-year-old Xuan was quoted as saying. Xuan fed Xu liquid food one spoonful at a time, and each meal took an hour. She also helped Xu turn over more than 10 times a day to prevent bedsores. Other caregiving tasks included washing Xu after she became incontinent and regularly massaging her muscles. Xuan also talked to Xu about news from the family and their village, played her favourite songs, and repeatedly called her name. Several years ago, Xu miraculously emerged from the vegetative state. Her mother-in-law continued to care for her, as severe brain damage from the accident had left Xu with the cognitive abilities of a four-year-old. Xuan helped Xu learn to walk and take part in other rehabilitation exercises. Xu can now speak a few words and even cook simple meals on her own. “Mum, good,” Xu was filmed saying to her mother-in-law. “I have no other wish than for her to keep getting better. I feel a little relieved that she can cook. That way, after I pass away, she’ll still have something to eat,” Xuan said. “I told my son that if I pass away, he should keep caring for his wife,” Xuan added. She said her legs had ached for years and that she had high blood pressure. Xuan recalled that when Xu once fell to the ground, she had to ask a neighbour to help her get Xu back up. “Of course I envy other people’s leisurely lives. They can go dancing in the squares. But my responsibility is to care for my daughter-in-law,” Xuan said. A flood of comments followed, with many people moved by Xuan’s extraordinary devotion. “Such great maternal love! Salute to this mother-in-law,” one social media user wrote. Another commented: “Wishing this elderly woman good health and a long life.” Stories of people devoting many years to caring for family members often make headlines in China. Earlier this year, a husband in central China’s Henan province won widespread praise online for caring for his severely paraplegic wife for 25 years.

title: Jonathan, a 194-year-old Aldabra giant tortoise, reveals secrets to long life
description: The animal’s unique genes are linked to DNA repair, cancer resistance and cellular longevity.
content:
The oldest-known land animal in the world is an Aldabra giant tortoise named Jonathan. He is believed to be 194 years old.
Scientists have a couple of ideas about why he has lived for so long. They think he has special genes and can keep important systems in his cells working as they do in younger animals.
Members of this species are known to live more than 100 years. But Jonathan has lived much longer than that. Scientists have studied Jonathan to explore the secrets of his long life.
They found 287 genes with types special to Jonathan. Some are linked to repairing DNA and stopping tumours. The tortoise also has extra copies of a gene that creates a protein that hunts down ageing and cancerous cells.

title: Sri Lanka’s property boom gives Chinese developers hope. But familiar risks linger
description: Colombo’s luxury property rally is drawing fresh interest from Chinese-backed developments, but analysts warn against speculative excess.
content: A Chinese developer behind one of Sri Lanka’s biggest projects has reason to celebrate as a luxury property boom lifts sentiment in the South Asian nation and fuels optimism about the market’s prospects. Analysts, however, cautioned that a string of disappointing Chinese overseas property investments over the past decade underlined the risks of speculative excess that could lead to a boom-to-bust scenario, particularly in a country where regulation remained uneven. “Chinese developers, having already learned a hard lesson from the property market [slump in China], need to stay cautious,” said Wang Feng, chairman of Shanghai-based financial services group Ye Lang Capital. “I bet they won’t get carried away by the recent price surge in Sri Lanka because of their high risk-awareness.” Three new luxury residential projects in Colombo Port City – a landmark development built on reclaimed land by China Harbour Engineering Co (Chec) and the Sri Lankan government – had drawn strong interest from local buyers attracted by projections of substantial investment returns, according to a report by online magazine The Diplomat. The three developments, built by Sri Lanka’s top real estate firms, represent a combined investment of US$650 million. Developers had marketed the developments with projected returns of up to 100 per cent over four years, according to the report. Colombo Port City itself is a US$1.4 billion development being built by Chec, a unit of Chinese multinational engineering and construction company China Communications Construction. Construction began in September 2014 and it was described by China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission as the largest foreign direct investment-backed infrastructure project in Sri Lanka at the time. The reclaimed land was envisioned to create a new central business district focused on tourism, financial services and logistics, eventually attracting 280,000 residents and workers, according to the state-assets regulator. In May, Chec held a topping-out ceremony for an affordable public housing project in Colombo that is expected to deliver an initial 112 homes for low-income residents, with a further 1,884 units planned. A survey by Sri Lanka’s central bank found that more than 20 per cent of flats were bought for investment purposes in the first quarter of 2026, while developers continued to shift to higher-end projects to capitalise on rising demand. About 52 per cent of home sales in the three months ended March were priced above 50 million rupees (US$150,600), up from 33 per cent a year earlier, according to the survey. Sri Lanka is among the countries participating in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013 to strengthen trade and infrastructure links across Asia, Africa, Europe and beyond. Despite the optimism, questions remain about market oversight. According to The Diplomat, Sri Lanka’s Condominium Management Authority oversees the country’s luxury homes. But its main responsibility lies in monitoring and supervising completed buildings, and it has limited ability to regulate the fast-moving presale home market, where speculative capital has poured into projects. Chinese developers’ go-global drive over the past decade has also produced mixed results, particularly after Beijing tightened controls on capital outflows and China’s domestic property crisis undermined financing conditions. One of the highest-profile examples was developer Country Garden’s US$100 billion Forest City project in Johor, Malaysia, which was launched in 2016 to house 700,000 people in a sprawling development of condominium complexes, office towers, hotels, malls and schools. Yet by 2020, the project was home to only about 9,000 people, despite the sale of 28,000 units during its first phase. The challenges facing some Chinese investments in Sri Lanka have also persisted. On October 15, China Merchants Port Holdings announced it would pull out from a US$280 million logistics hub project in Colombo. The South Asia Commercial and Logistics Hub, a joint venture established in 2023 in which China Merchants Port held a 70 per cent stake, was planned as a bonded warehouse and container yard complex. The company said in a Hong Kong stock exchange filing that terminating the project was in the best interests of all parties involved.

title: Hong Kong Open readies for Sunday shoot-out as Fanling finally bares its teeth
description: Tricky greens and difficult rough hint at testing times to come as battle for major places and prestigious title goes down to the wire.
content: Fanling has finally bared its teeth and there will be an 18-hole shoot-out on Sunday that hopefully proves worthy of the rich rewards awaiting the Link Hong Kong Open champion. It should be a five-star affair as well, with a leaderboard heavy on LIV Golf talent and the strong possibility of a home golfer winning for the first time. Tied at the top on 14-under-par sit John Catlin, Thomas Pieters, Anirban Lahiri and Caleb Surratt, while Kalle Samooja, once of Cleeks GC and owner of a third-round 63, and Hongkonger Matthew Cheung are two shots back. Even the likes of Nick Voke, on 11 under, and the trio of Chase Koepka, Sampson Zheng and MJ Viljoen at 10 under will fancy their chances of claiming a spot at the Masters and the 155th Open Championship alongside a healthy winner’s cheque, even if there is every indication of a sterner test than in days gone by. Whether lessons have been learned, or the unseasonably hot weather has forced the issue is debatable, but Saturday’s third round suggests last year’s toothless set-up that allowed Tom McKibbin to reach 27-under-par and win by seven strokes has gone. Much of that difference lay in the greens, which Pieters called “crusty”, and in rough the former 4Aces GC member said had been “really soft and I would say easy” during the LIV event at Fanling in March. “Now it doesn’t play quite as easy,” Pieters, who carded a five under 65, added. “You miss a fairway, you’re instantly thinking, how am I going to make par?” Even Lahiri, who is no stranger to the course and said earlier in the week he liked it firm and fast, was caught out by the changes from the first two days at Hong Kong Golf Club. For the Crushers GC golfer, there was early evidence of the tricky greens that were to follow. A birdie putt on the first from a sidehill lie did far more than expected. “Today was one of those days where I just hit a lot of greens, gave myself a lot of looks, but ended up on the wrong side of the hole,” Lahiri, who came home with a four under 66, said. “I had too many downhill sidehill putts, and when the greens get like this, you’d rather be 25ft uphill than 12ft downhill sidehill, because you’re almost trying not to hit it 4ft by.” Lahiri made the early running this week, and led after the first round having shot a 62. What it will take to win given the course “will not get any easier” is not something he wanted to commit to. “I would have thought I had to get closer to 18 or 19 [under par] today, if the course played the way it did the first two days,” he added. “But today the golf course played completely different, and tomorrow will probably be a tougher version of what we saw today.” Catlin’s reaction to getting up and down from the front bunker on 18 to save par said much about the battle to come. The American, who has won multiple times on the Asian Tour, gave a little fist pump after knocking in the putt for par that sealed his round of 65. “This is one of those courses where it can be difficult to like really, really distance yourself,” Catlin said. “I think this is my fourth or fifth Hong Kong Open, and every one I’ve been a part of has been pretty close. “It’s one of those courses where you gotta just battle it out, and you know it’s probably going to come down to those last few holes.” Eighteen has been the scene of plenty of drama down the years, from Rory McIlroy holing out from the same greenside bunker Catlin found himself in to win in 2011, to Ben Campbell’s 15ft birdie putt three years ago. Fortunes, of course, can change earlier in a round, for good or bad, and on Saturday it was the 17th that influenced proceedings, although how much remains to be seen. Surratt was on 15 under when he came unstuck at the 406-yard par-4, the third and final blemish in a round of 67. In contrast, the same hole was the only bright spot in Cheung’s round of 72. The Hongkonger began the day three shots clear of the field on 14 under, and was three shots back at one stage as his game began to unravel. A birdie changed the narrative on the day, although the 31-year-old was quick to point out that he would have “been ecstatic” to be offered that position at the start of the week. “I didn’t have the best day out there but I grinded it out, got a good birdie on the 17th to keep myself in it,” Cheung said. “It is definitely a bit of pressure but also motivation to play with the guys who were in my group. They are some of the best players in the world, and comparing myself to them, I know I will get there.”

title: Scotland’s wild wellness boom, from Gleneagles to Loch Lomond
description: The rugged beauty of the Scottish Highlands has always held an undeniable, if chilly, allure, and now the wider wellness community is taking notice.
content: For a while, the blueprint for a serious wellness trip looked pretty much the same everywhere. A flight to somewhere warm, a resort with a view of jungle or terraced rice paddies, a treatment menu borrowing names from ancient traditions, and enough linen to last a lifetime. Scotland was never really part of that picture. It was the place people went for whisky, castles and rain, not the place they went to reset. Then this summer, Scotland’s men’s football team appeared at their first World Cup in 28 years, and the Tartan Army followed them across the Atlantic, sweeping through Boston and Miami with kilts and bagpipes and leaving an impression that had nothing to do with any scoreline. So much so, that VisitScotland’s chair, Stephen Leckie, is already calling it a long-term win for tourism, and the wellness scene – quietly building in the country for years – stands to benefit most. What began as a handful of sauna huts on loch shores has expanded into a nationwide network of cold-plunge experiences, wild swimming gatherings and contrast therapy sessions set against some of the most dramatic landscapes in Europe. The country has been pretty much designed for this with its thousands of lochs, rivers that run clear and cold year-round out of the Highlands, and a tangled coastline that goes on for thousands of kilometres. But the geography is only half of it, as Scotland has been doing some version of this for longer than “wild sauna” has existed as a phrase. Long before anyone called it wellness, doctors were prescribing cold and hot water baths as medicine, and Scotland built entire institutions around it. Craiglockhart Hydropathic, now part of Edinburgh Napier University, was a water-cure hospital during the Victorian era, before being turned into a hospital for officers suffering from shell-shock during World War I. That history is exactly why the current wave doesn’t feel like a gimmick, and why the hotels building around it have gone for the real thing rather than a spa-menu version of it. They’re spread across the country, distinct enough from each other that choosing where to go is really choosing what kind of wild you’re after. Gleneagles, the famous luxury hotel and golf course in Perthshire, for example, launched Frandy Water in May 2026, and it’s already become one of the most talked-about additions to Scotland’s wellness scene. The experience begins at the hotel’s front steps, where a Land Rover Defender collects guests and drives them 10 minutes into the hills to a private upland reservoir, wholly off-grid, where a shingle-covered wood-fired sauna sits right at the water’s edge. The sauna holds six, opens onto a private jetty for cold plunging, and comes with a bothy-style building for gathering afterwards. Gleneagles has its own railway station less than two minutes from the hotel with complimentary transfers, which makes it one of the easier luxury stays in Scotland to reach without a car. On the western side of the country, Cameron House on Loch Lomond points guests towards specific wild swimming spots within a few minutes of the grounds – from the sandy stretch at Duck Bay to Luss Beach and Milarrochy Bay further up the eastern shore – each with its own character and its own view of Ben Lomond across the water. For anyone who’d rather move through the water than sit in it, there’s stand-up paddleboarding and kayaking straight off the loch, with a safety boat trailing the paddleboard sessions, or a cruise out to the islands aboard the resort’s own motor launch. Back on land, the water keeps going: with an 18-metre pool and family splash zone at the main hotel, and a separate rooftop infinity pool, hydrotherapy pool and 20-metre relaxation pool up at Cameron Spa. Moving north to Loch Tay, Taymouth Marina resort’s houseboats sit right in the marina, each with a rooftop terrace, an outdoor dining porch and a swim ladder built straight into the deck for a direct dip into the loch. Every stay comes with complimentary daily access to the HotBox, Scotland’s first floating wood-fired sauna. There you can step straight out onto a diving board, jumping into the loch before climbing back in to warm up again. For those who want to keep moving rather than stay put, there’s also a separate sauna cruise with a skipper at the helm, drifting past views of Ben Lawers and Glen Lyon before ending in a wild swim straight off the boat. And with a watersports centre on site for canoe and kayak hire, you barely need to leave the marina to fill a day entirely on the water. Further north, the Fife Arms in Braemar works with Wild Braemar, a local guiding outfit, to run wild swims at the Wilderness Sauna. Set where the River Clunie meets the River Ey, guests are led down to the water amid a Cairngorms National Park landscape that was ranked joint second in the world for cold-water swimming back in May, alongside Canada’s Banff National Park. Braemar may take a little more effort to reach than most, but it puts guests deeper into the Cairngorms than anywhere else on this list, and the swims and saunas feel wilder for it. Whether the summertime momentum of the Tartan Army turns into an actual surge of visitors to bonnie Scotland is an open question, but the country’s wellness scene doesn’t need the tourism boost to prove itself. It was already there, cold water and all – it just took a little time for the rest of the world to notice. What to pack Barrie scarf Arch4 sweater Brunello Cucinelli trousers Burberry boots

title: Obama blasts Trump’s ‘chaos and cruelty’ while campaigning for Democrats
description: The former US president slammed his successor’s ‘corruption and incompetence’ and blamed his ‘bad decisions’ for the rising cost of living.
content: Former US president Barack Obama delivered a scathing critique of his successor, Donald Trump, at a rally in Ohio on Saturday to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,’” Obama declared in Cleveland. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.” The 65-year-old Democrat blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices. “The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for.” He noted that instead of lowering costs, the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,” Obama said. “He should be on HGTV.” He went on: “There’s gold everywhere. He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” Obama also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in this northern industrial state. “Don’t procrastinate, don’t equivocate,” Obama said. The former president retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party’s candidates in the crucial coming elections that will decide control of Congress. In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024. Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close. Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate. After Cleveland, Obama will head north to Michigan this evening for a rally in Detroit alongside Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate. While both of Michigan’s Senate seats are currently held by Democrats, El-Sayed, from the party’s left wing, is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Editorial | Hong Kong must urgently tackle its elderly isolation problem
description: Multiple cases of lonely deaths highlight a growing crisis: the city’s support network remains dangerously fragmented.
content: Tragedies involving vulnerable elderly people continue to make headlines in Hong Kong. Sadly, in a rapidly ageing society where many live alone or with an elderly partner, this seems unlikely to change any time soon. There is an urgent need to close gaps in support services. The authorities have initiated several measures, including a plan to import trained domestic carers, but that is only a start on addressing a growing problem. About a week ago, a man, 72, and his 69-year-old partner died in a suspected suicide pact after she received a diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease. A tray of burnt charcoal and a note were found in their Tuen Mun flat. This came after a man, 81, was found dead in a flat in Cheung Sha Wan, while his wife, 73, was found semi-conscious. Only weeks before, two double tragedies involved socially withdrawn brothers in their 50s and a couple in their 70s, all found dead. These cases reflect the problem of isolation. An inadequate social safety network, especially for a growing elderly population living alone or with an elderly spouse, makes more of such cases inevitable unless action is taken to counter isolation. Population ageing is common in advanced societies amid lower birth rates and increased longevity. Hong Kong is no exception. It is predicted that one in four residents will be 65 or older by 2028. That proportion could reach one in three by the 2040s. Without strong family networks, these elderly people can face isolation and loneliness, which affects their physical and mental welfare. Initiatives and pilot schemes address the problem piecemeal. The support network remains fragmented. The government can use public housing as a platform to make a difference and set a benchmark for all residential flat developments. It is good that it is putting on trial measures such as sensors that detect an abrupt halt of activity in vulnerable aged or isolated households. In the case of the two brothers found dead, said to have been financially supported by their elderly parents, investigators estimated that one had died within the previous week, while the other had died several weeks before. Police found no suspicious circumstances. Three days earlier, the authorities found the bodies of a 72-year-old man and his 74-year-old wife in the living room of their Ma On Shan home. They were believed to have suffered from a range of health problems. A forensic examiner estimated the time of death to be about three to four days earlier. Experts say a database for isolated elderly residents, and better use of technology to monitor them, could make a difference because district-level community care teams usually lack information on where they live. The city’s housing authorities announced earlier this year that they would expand the use of smart technologies, such as door sensors, in-home fall detectors and stair climbers, to enhance safety and convenience for elderly residents in public housing estates. Should these devices prove useful, it could be well worthwhile to expand their use. Of course, any concerns about privacy – apart from recording the opening of doors and any change in the pattern of use – must be addressed. When the data signals an emergency, speed could be key to an effective response, and timely medical intervention could make a life-or-death difference. The aim should be to achieve a wide acceptance of technology that enhances the ability of support services and responders to reach out to the elderly and disadvantaged in urgent need. In his latest policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced some welcome increments to aged care services. There is also room for new initiatives. It is therefore good that the government plans a pilot programme next year to bring in trained and experienced foreign domestic carers, as distinct from helpers, to support elderly residents living at home. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han has said the carers would first need to complete a 150-hour course in their home country. Details including higher minimum pay need to be worked out. Meanwhile, an improved database on isolated residents to guide district care teams and enable better use of technology remains a way forward.

title: Do you have empty nest syndrome? 5 signs – and expert ways to cope
description: Watching your children leave home triggers a wave of mixed emotions. An expert shares how to process the shift and move forward.
content: If you feel lost or overwhelmed now your children have left the nest, you are far from alone. Many parents experience empty nest syndrome at this time of the year. “Empty nest syndrome isn’t a mental health condition, but a set of feelings or symptoms that parents might feel when all their children have left home,” says Dr Elizabeth Wakeland, consultant, clinical and forensic psychologist at Cygnet Health Care in the UK. “It’s a period of significant life change where parents are trying to figure out who they are and what their life looks like now their children are no longer in the home.” Empty nest symptoms Here are five signs of empty nest syndrome to look out for and advice about how to navigate this period. 1. Sense of grief “Some parents might experience emotions around grief, loss and sadness,” Wakeland says. “Although their children haven’t passed away, there’s still a loss of presence and a change in relationship.” 2. Anxiety “There might also be some feelings of anxiety,” Wakeland says. “Children living outside the home might increase your anxiety because they are no longer with you all the time and you might be worried about their safety.” That anxiety might manifest itself in constant communication. “This anxiety might present in behaviours that are directly related, such as calling or sending messages constantly to check in on your children,” she says. “This is when our involvement, or what people sometimes refer to as ‘helicopter parenting’, might come into play.” 3. Mood changes “As well as these low feelings and a sense of emptiness, there might also be some positive feelings,” Wakeland says. “For example, you might have some excitement about your child moving on and progressing, or some pride in what they are going on to do. “So, it might feel a bit up and down for a while, and a mixture of positive and negative emotions might play out.” This can trigger guilt: “A parent might feel guilt around how they should or shouldn’t feel, or what they should or shouldn’t be doing now that their children have moved out.” 4. Identity crisis “When you become a parent you have to adapt and mould yourself and your life around your children,” Wakeland says. “Children take up a lot of time, energy and thinking, and it becomes a big part of your identity. Therefore, many parents experience a bit of an identity crisis when their children leave home. “It can provoke questions such as, ‘Who am I? What should I do with my time now?’ It’s a big shift.” 5. Loneliness “It’s wonderful to see children moving on and progressing, but it can make parents feel left behind or feel like they are not part of their child’s new world,” she says. “As their child steps into their new social life and immerses themselves into university life, parents are forced to take a back seat.” This can be particularly challenging for single parents. “If you are going through this alone as a single parent, those feelings of loneliness and loss can feel even more heightened because now it’s just you left in the house,” Wakeland says. Helpful tips If you are struggling to navigate this transition, here are some tips that could help. Be kind to yourself “It’s really normal to feel like this and it’s OK to feel happy and sad at the prospect of your children moving on,” Wakeland says. “The emotions will change and fluctuate, so don’t be too hard on yourself about it. Just allow yourself to feel those emotions and try to be kind and compassionate towards yourself and accept that this is a difficult time.” Pursue new or revisit old interests “Think about what you want your identity to look like now,” Wakeland says. “For example, are there things that you sacrificed before that you could perhaps do now? Is there something that you have always wanted to do but have never had the time or opportunity to look into? “Think about how you want to spend this extra time and if there are any hobbies or interests that you could now pursue.” Establish healthy routines “It’s important to prioritise looking after yourself,” Wakeland says. “Think about some healthy routines and habits that you could get into now that you have more time.” Stay connected “The home can feel quite quiet when children move out, so it’s really important to maintain connection with people outside the home,” Wakeland says. “It can be a great opportunity to rekindle old friendships, so reach out to people.” Establish some ground rules and boundaries around communication with your offspring. “Be open with your child about how this is affecting you and about the feelings you’ve got about this transition,” Wakeland says. “Talk to them about how you can both stay connected and communicate, and try to find something that is mutually agreeable for both parties.” Seek professional help if feelings persist “Although empty nest syndrome is a very common and typical experience, if something becomes persistent for several weeks – such as a persistent low mood or anxiety that becomes overwhelming and unmanageable – that is a sign to consider looking into professional help,” Wakeland says. “Additionally, if it starts impacting other areas of your life or if you start going out of your way to avoid social contact, then don’t be afraid to seek professional help.”

title: Write to Win: Who is the kindest stranger that you still remember? (Round 7)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form . The deadline for voting is 12pm on Tuesday, October 27.
We have prepared some exciting prizes for our top three contestants:
Winner: Kindle, City’super voucher and a YP certificate
First runner-up: Instax camera and a YP certificate
Second runner-up: City’super voucher and a YP certificate
Bonus prize: Every winner will also walk away with 2 tickets to Hong Kong Disneyland !
Jupiter: When I was eight years old, it was exam week at school, and I was determined to do my best. My father would drop me off at school on his way to work, and every morning, I tried to arrive early so that I could squeeze in a few extra minutes of revision before our exams began. One morning, while hurrying through the MTR station, I started taking the escalator steps two at a time, convinced that those few minutes would change my grade. Unfortunately, I tripped and fell onto the metal teeth of the escalator, leaving a deep bruise on my knee. My father treated the wound with his handkerchief and boarded the train, planning to get a bandage at the next station. On the train, a father and child noticed our situation and, without hesitation, handed us a cleaning solution and a bandage. That simple act of kindness has stayed with me ever since, teaching me one of humanity’s finest qualities. A stranger took the time to help us without expecting anything in return. At school, we were often encouraged to carry a first aid kit in case of emergencies, but after that experience, I began carrying one not only for myself but also for anyone who might need help.
Mars: When I was in Primary Two, my sister and I flew from Hong Kong to Singapore by ourselves. Our parents were busy with work, so we travelled alone to visit our grandparents for the holidays. The airport provided a check-in service for us, but there was no official supervision once we boarded the plane. After finding our seats and buckling in, we felt incredibly small and vulnerable. A male stranger occupied the third seat in our row, and I worried he might be annoyed to sit next to two young kids. Fortunately, instead of ignoring us, he turned out to be really kind. As soon as he noticed our matching solo-traveller badges, his face lit up with a warm smile. He spent the entire flight chatting and playing games with us, asking about our school and listening to our excitement about seeing our grandmother. He even ordered us extra snacks and helped open our meals until we reached the ground staff waiting for us at the airport. Right before the plane landed in Singapore, he took a selfie of the three of us. His genuine kindness transformed an anxious journey into a fun adventure. Even though a long time has passed, the memory remains incredibly vivid. I never saw him again, and I cannot remember his name today, but I will always cherish this unique flight that made two little kids feel completely safe and happy up in the sky.
Neptune: There are 8 billion people in the world, and most of them remain strangers to us. This phenomenon is especially common nowadays, and I believe it is largely due to our reliance on mobile phones and our own excuses. We often think that social media connects us and helps us become more informed global citizens. However, we become so absorbed in this digital world that we forget to pay attention to what is right in front of us. When I was in London, my mum and I walked through a mall. As we looked ahead, we noticed a blond-haired man smiling at us while holding the door open. We were surprised because he was about 10 metres away from us. We hurried over to say thank you. He held the door open for us again at another entrance. This kind of interaction would likely never happen in Hong Kong, where most people are too focused on their phones to notice anyone else. Even if someone did look up, it is unlikely they would hold the door open for that long, waiting for someone to pass through. This stranger’s act of kindness left a lasting impression on me. He could have easily walked away without holding the door, and I wouldn’t have given it much thought, but he chose to stay. Small acts of kindness are so rare these days, yet when they do happen, they inspire us to be better versions of ourselves. Even though I may never meet him again, I remember and honour him each time I perform a small act of kindness. So, never stop being kind to others; you never know the impact it may have.

title: This week in PostMag: how we preserve, protect and honour heritage in an ever-changing world
description: Discover how ‘super oysters’, free-play playgrounds, archipelagic festivals and zero-waste kitchens redefine heritage preservation in Hong Kong.
content: Heritage, on paper, is simple enough to define – legacies one receives from the past and passes on to the next generation – but the topic becomes more complicated and hotly debated when the question of ownership and involvement enters the picture. As a shared, experienced ecosystem, who decides who “owns” culture, and who can participate? At the same time, how do you safeguard a heritage you did not inherit, or live through? Hong Kong’s tradition of oyster aquaculture can be traced back more than seven centuries, but the fate of these bivalves has hung in the balance for many years, exacerbated by climate change, poor harvests, an ageing workforce and an overcrowding crisis.
