Out in Deep Bay, the local trade’s long-established cultivation grounds, Hei Kiu Au discovers how an Indian marine biologist – undeterred by scepticism, language barriers and a lack of consumer confidence – is using science and a resilient, lab-grown strain of “super oysters” to turn the tide for this sunset industry, preserve an intangible cultural heritage and convince Hong Kong’s last oyster farmers to carry forward their knowledge and craft. For readers keen on more nostalgic glimpses, PostMag’s photo editor, Alexander Mak, sifts through the South China Morning Post archives to present a pictorial tribute to the historical oyster-farming communities of Lau Fau Shan, in the New Territories. What creates a “home” is more than just a roof over our heads and four walls. Well-designed collective spaces influence how we live and thrive, but when planning housing for a swelling population, building suitable play areas that engage and encourage children to step outside their comfort zones is rarely a high-priority item on the list. Joyce Yip heads to some of Hong Kong’s more unconventional playgrounds to see how advocates championing “free play” as a powerful driver of cognitive development are bringing about change. “Home” is also the one you find and nurture, be it in the heart of the city or as far from it as practicality allows. Jianne Soriano journeys between a scattering of Hong Kong’s outlying islands for a preview of the next edition of the Inter-Island Festival, running throughout November. Conceived as a celebration of archipelagic lifestyles and encounters, the curator-organisers talk mission, motivation and collaboration across the water. For Hong Kong Olympian Yvette Kong Man-yi, being underwater had been her entire world. Now retired from the competitive-swimming circuit, she tells Jing Zhang about finding self-worth beyond the pool and looking ahead to new paths and passions. Elsewhere, Nicole Hurip chews the fat with JW Marriott Hotel Hong Kong’s sustainability-minded executive chef, Tony Wong Chi-chuen, on how zero-waste cooking doesn’t stop at reducing what gets discarded, and being enterprising with leftovers. Exploration – of an adventurous, Indiana Jones-like nature – is also on the cards for Charukesi Ramadurai, whose wanderings have taken her to the ancient cave-temple complexes of India’s Maharashtra state. Hewn out of basalt and superhuman determination – or extraterrestrial technology, if that’s more your conspiracy-theory flavour; archaeologists and historians remain puzzled by these architectural achievements – the giant structures, of which the Ellora and Ajanta caves are the most impressive, transport us back in time. Enjoy the read.

title: Trump, a critic of early voting, votes early in Florida
description: The US president has reversed course on the practice, hoping to mobilise his base to help Republicans keep control of Congress.
content: US President Donald Trump cast his ballot for the midterm elections in Palm Beach on Saturday, opting to vote early in his adopted home state of Florida. At rallies ahead of Election Day on November 3, Trump has been urging Republicans to cast their ballots early, reversing course on a practice he has long decried in a bid to mobilise the party’s base in an election that threatens to end their control of Congress. Asked by reporters if he voted for the party line, he said: “Very much so.” The president has regularly questioned the security of early voting methods, claiming without evidence that mail-in ballots, drop boxes and other practices during the 2020 presidential election – which he lost – were used to rig the vote. He has also called for one-day, in-person voting on Election Day. “The US attorney found potentially hundreds of thousands of illicit votes,” Trump told reporters. Earlier this month, the US Justice Department sued California for allegedly failing to join an effort to verify the status of 20,000 suspected non-citizens to prevent any fraudulent ballots from being counted. California asked a judge to deny the request to set aside those 20,000 mail-in ballots, calling the US allegations “a reckless political stunt”. Trump has long amplified false claims of widespread voter fraud in the 2020 election and since his return to the White House last year has taken steps to increase federal control of US elections. The administration has pushed to curb mail-in voting, a method Trump has used in the past. And he has pressured lawmakers to pass legislation that would require voters to have government-issued ID or other proof of citizenship to cast ballots. Senate Republican leaders have said the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) America Act lacks the support to pass. Trump has spent the better part of October criss-crossing the country to boost Republican candidates as the party faces the challenging task of retaining both the House and Senate in a midterm year. During Florida’s August 2026 primary, Trump cast a ballot by mail. He also said he voted by mail earlier this year in a Florida special election. As a presidential candidate in 2024, he voted in person on Election Day.

title: Musk admits he throttled Ukraine’s Starlink speeds, as access is restored
description: The SpaceX CEO says Kyiv’s forces had used the civilian commercial service for deadly offensive drone strikes.
content: Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia. Musk’s admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week. Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks. “The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky said on social media, adding that restoration began overnight and was sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a social media post on Saturday, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk said. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.” But he maintained that the US government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine’s defences since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country’s military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localised ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region. The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by US President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. Ukraine’s Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited “direct dialogue” and Zelensky’s diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications”. Trump has maintained that he did not make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. US Vice-President J.D. Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement. Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, local officials said on Saturday. Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts on Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks. Ukraine’s General Staff said on Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city. Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday’s attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000km (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Governor Vitaly Khotsenko said drones “reached a northern industrial hub”. Online retailer Ozon said on Saturday that its logistics centre in Omsk was attacked by a drone but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

title: Meet Tom Rhys Harries, star of DC’s body-horror Clayface
description: The White Lines actor, seemingly in a relationship with singer-songwriter Amy Allen, dreamed of a rugby career but was advised to audition for drama school.
content: With Clayface, DC trades its usual cape-donning heroes for a chilling entry into body-horror cinema. Starring Tom Rhys Harries, the film follows Matt Hagen (played by Harries), a Hollywood star from Gotham whose run-in with a crime boss leaves his face severely disfigured. Desperate to restore himself, Hagen turns to Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), whose experimental treatment makes matters worse. So Hagen finds himself on a path from Hollywood’s charming leading man to a Gotham City villain. Starring Harries, Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan, the film premiered on October 23 in North America, with its previews already bringing in US$3.5 million at the box office. Here’s everything you need to know about DC’s latest supervillain, Tom Rhys Harries. What is Tom Rhys Harries’ background? Harries was born in October 1990 in Cardiff, Wales, and is one of the few native Welsh speakers of which there are fewer than a million worldwide. He was raised in a creative household with a father who played in a band and a scriptwriter mother. Harries also credits his Welsh upbringing for nurturing his love for the arts. “The Welsh-speaking community is, by nature, very creative and quite performative,” Harries told Hunger magazine in an interview. “We have a cultural competition called the Eisteddfod every year; you’ll have five-year-olds doing recitals on a stage in front of three hundred people. So none of this ever felt alien to my family.” Falling in love with acting Despite having grown up surrounded by the arts, Harries told Fucking Young! magazine that he had never considered acting, and instead grew up dreaming of becoming a rugby player. “I honestly hadn’t considered acting as a job until I was told to audition for drama school by someone who saw me play guitar at a bar in Cardiff,” he said. Harries heeded the advice and, as it turns out, he was a natural. He attended the Royal Welsh College of Music and Drama from 2009 to 2012 and landed his debut on-screen role in the 2011 musical drama film, Hunky Dory. Since then, Harries has steadily built his career and featured in films such as The Gentlemen (2019). He also starred in Netflix’s 2020 series, White Lines. Who is Tom Rhys Harries dating? Harries is seemingly in a relationship with singer-songwriter Amy Allen, based on her Instagram posts. Although neither has publicly confirmed their relationship, Allen has shared several snaps of herself and Harries on her Instagram profile. Harries was previously linked to his White Lines co-star Laura Haddock.

title: German man detained after fire wrecks Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat
description: Firefighters battled to put out flames at the former guest house for top Nazi officials, high up in the Bavarian Alps.
content: Firefighters battled on Saturday to put out flames that tore through Adolf Hitler’s “Eagle’s Nest” mountain retreat while police detained a suspect who investigators said may have psychiatric problems. The alarm was raised late on Friday at the former guest house for top Nazi officials, 1,834 metres (6,000 feet) high in the Bavarian Alps. As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames at dawn on Saturday, and fire chief Michael Brandl told a press conference the last elements of the inferno were being put out during the afternoon. No one has entered the building because of fears it could collapse, Brandl added. “We are very lucky that there are no injuries,” Brandl said. Some 200 firefighters were mobilised for the operation at the Kehlsteinhaus residence on a summit above Obersalzberg in southern Germany that draws some 350,000 visitors a year, according to Bavarian state authorities. Authorities said access had been difficult after the fire alarm went off at 9.50pm. Heavy rain was followed by a snowstorm and then violent winds hit the mountains. Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said the firefighters had needed breathing apparatus to get near. Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said. Bavarian state interior minister Joachim Herrmann said the fire appeared to be “a malicious act” and police said that a suspect was detained at the scene. Firefighters and police heading to the Eagle’s Nest saw “a rider on a red motorcycle with no licence plate” and stopped him, Robert Holzinger, a Bavarian police official, told a press conference. The suspect is a 33-year-old German who has ties to the area but does not live there, Rainer Vietze, a public prosecutor’s spokesman, was quoted as saying by the local PNP newspaper. Possible political motives were being examined but investigators believed there was a “potential mental illness”, the spokesman added. Police blocked access to the retreat on Saturday. Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews, Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists during the Holocaust. It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator himself seldom visited the complex that was heavily guarded. Hitler had another country residence nearby at Berghof. Built of stone and granite, the Eagle’s Nest offers an exceptional view of the Alpine landscape and was designed to impress foreign diplomats. Hitler used it as a backdrop for his propaganda films. It survived World War II undamaged and later gained notoriety through post-war Hollywood films that recreated the residence. Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant. The website says the Eagle’s Nest “stands for the insanity of the regime and the world on the Obersalzberg, where plans for war and mass murder were formed”. The Bavarian interior minister said the retreat “will under no circumstances be left in a state of ruin”. “This house – the entire site and its surroundings – is linked to a specific history. It is important that we continue our work of remembrance,” Herrmann said.

title: Spanish coaches dominate Ballon d’Or, have become football’s hottest commodity
description: Country’s growing influence on world game will be on full display at glittering awards ceremony in London.
content: Spain’s growing influence on world football will be on full display at Monday’s Ballon d’Or gala, when the sport’s top performers will be honoured at a glittering ceremony in London. Four of the five nominees for the Johan Cruyff Trophy for men’s coach of the year are Spanish, as are two of the candidates for the women’s trophy. The shortlists reflect how the country, after years of winning men’s and women’s titles, has turned into a major exporter of coaching expertise. After decades in the shadow of Italian, English and German counterparts, Spanish coaches are now in high demand as both clubs and national teams seek to tap into the philosophy credited for Spain’s success on the world stage. Celebrated coaches such as Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique have brought Spain’s possession-based style of play to Europe’s top clubs, with some adjustments. Hong Kong turned to Roberto Losada to take charge of the city’s representative team after dispensing with the services of Englishman Ashley Westwood, while Inigo Calderon is presently masterminding Kitchee’s return to the top of the local game. “The cornerstone to the high esteem that Spanish coaches are enjoying now is their training and, above all, their ability to adapt to different contexts in European and global soccer,” Ivan Cancela, who heads the Spanish football federation’s coaching academy, said. Both Guardiola and Luis Enrique are among the academy’s graduates. The latter won last year’s Cruyff award – named after the Dutch great – and is a top candidate again after winning a second consecutive Champions League title with Paris Saint-Germain. Luis de la Fuente is another top contender after winning the World Cup with Spain this summer. He led Spain’s Under-19 and Under-21 teams before taking over the senior side and has also taught courses for future managers organised by the Spanish federation. “We are pioneers in coaching coaches for a long time now,” De la Fuente said last month. “We are an example to follow when it comes to coaching coaches, it is the root cause of why our coaches stand out.” It was relatively unusual for Spanish coaches to work abroad until Rafael Benitez made the leap to Liverpool from Valencia in 2004. Many have followed in his footsteps. Spaniards now make up the largest nationality group among Premier League coaches, with five teams managed by Spaniards. Two of them are candidates for the men’s Cruyff Award: Mikel Arteta at defending champions Arsenal and Unai Emery, who won the Europa League with Aston Villa last season. Spain had 107 coaches employed abroad in first-and-second-division clubs last season, up from 99 the previous season, according to Uefa. Portugal was second last season with 88. Spaniards also are being recruited by other countries’ national teams. More than a dozen national teams currently have Spanish coaches, including Qatar, Czech Republic, South Korea and the Netherlands, which recently hired former Barcelona star Xavi Hernandez. The Spanish player isn’t the fastest, they aren’t the strongest, or the tallest. But … the Spanish player is the one that best interprets the game and is the most talented Ivan Cancela, head of Spanish football federation’s coaching academy In a way, Xavi’s move to the Netherlands is a full-circle moment because Spain traces its style of play back to Cruyff – who played for Barcelona in the 1970s and returned as coach in 1988. Cruyff established a new playing philosophy in Spain based on maintaining possession and moving the ball with short passes between players constantly re-positioning themselves. That style of play impacted how Spanish coaches spotted and developed talent. “The Spanish player isn’t the fastest, they aren’t the strongest, or the tallest,” Cancela said. “But in my opinion, and I say this without wanting to sound boastful, but I believe that the Spanish player is the one that best interprets the game and is the most talented.” Luis Aragones, Spain coach from 2004 to 2008, made the possession-based approach a national trademark with a team built around midfield maestros Xavi and Andres Iniesta. The so-called tiki-taka style lifted Spain to new heights with back-to-back European Championship titles in 2008 and 2012 and the country’s first World Cup triumph in 2010. They eventually hit a wall as Xavi and Iniesta retired, and Spain failed to translate possession into goals. De la Fuente, who took over as head coach after Spain’s quarter-final exit at the 2022 World Cup, modernised the system with faster attacking transitions, using one-on-one wingers such as Lamine Yamal and Nico Williams to challenge defences from out wide. You used to see lots of drills in training that were not using the ball, but in Spain the drills are all based on situations you can see in a real game Javier Cano, president of EFA Pro Meanwhile, Spain rose to become world No 1 in the women’s game with a team built around the likes of Aitana Bonmati and Alexia Putellas. Barcelona coach Pere Romeu is among the five nominees for the coaching award for women’s football along with fellow Spaniard and former Barcelona coach Jonatan Giráldez of OL Lyonnes. They faced off in May in the Women’s Champions League final, which Barcelona won 4-0. One thing that stands out with how Spanish coaches have been training their teams is the emphasis on drills involving the ball. “You used to see lots of drills in training that were not using the ball, but in Spain the drills are all based on situations you can see in a real game,” said Javier Cano, president of EFA Pro, an association of professional Spanish coaches. “That is the great advantage that Spain has had for the past two decades.” A good example is the Spanish “rondo,” or piggy-in-the-middle drill, that Cruyff made central to training in Barcelona. The drill, whereby a small group of players must pass the ball between them in a compact area while one or two teammates try to intercept it, enhanced the basic skills of using one touch to execute – as well as open slight angles to receive – short passes under pressure, again and again. That clockwork efficiency in keeping the ball has been evident in Spain’s World Cup victories for both men and women. One of the quirks of this generation of elite Spanish coaches is how many of them come from northern Spain, specifically the Basque Country. De la Fuente has family roots in the Basque Country, the home region of Emery and other coaches like Julen Lopetegui – who led Real Madrid and Spain – and José Mendilibar. Arteta, Chelsea coach Xabi Alonso and Andoni Iraola of Liverpool played together as youngsters at Antiguoko, an amateur club in the Basque city of San Sebastian. Antiguoko vice-president Roberto Montiel perfectly recalled the trio of young boys. Even though he noticed their talent, he barely could have imagined they would all reach such heights as coaches. “It’s down to a little bit of everything,” Montiel said. “We were lucky that these three great people and players coincided at our club. Then there is the DNA of Antiguoko and the Basque society that means we are all super competitive and share the passion for football.”

title: China dad handed 3-year race ban after dragging rope-tied son around marathon
description: Viral video shows man pulling nine-year-old around Zhengzhou Marathon, with pair reportedly hitting 8-minute mile pace at times.
content: A marathon runner in China who dragged a nine-year-old boy around a half-marathon using a rope has been handed a three-year ban and had his result erased. Video clips of the child with a rope around his waist struggling to keep up as the pair competed in the Zhengzhou Marathon in Henan province have gone viral, and sparked intense debate online. While some social media users expressed surprise at the boy’s endurance, most condemned the incident, which is believed to have involved a father and son, as a dangerous breach of safety rules. According to official competition regulations, runners must be at least 20 years old for a full marathon and 18 for a half-marathon. Organisers note in the competition rules that marathons are “high-intensity, high-risk events” requiring good physical health and regular running preparation, advising runners to select suitable events based on their physical condition. On Friday, an official from the Zhengzhou Marathon organising committee announced the ban and the removal of the man’s result. Multiple runners claimed online to have passed the pair during the race, with several estimating the duo had averaged around eight minutes per mile. This is not the first time underage individuals have been illegally entered into long-distance races. At last month’s Taiyuan Marathon, an entrant, surnamed Yuan, put his bib on a minor and brought the child onto the track. Organisers issued a similar punishment, although the ban was only for two years. Earlier this year, during the Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon, a man was seen running while holding a baby in one arm and a phone in his other hand. The Hong Kong Association of Athletics Affiliates later confirmed the violation, stating race staff intercepted the runner mid-course and escorted him and the infant off the track. Medical experts have previously warned of the health risks associated with minors running marathons. Guo Jianjun, a professor at the Capital University of Physical Education and Sports’ Centre for Sports and Medicine Integration Innovation, said because minors were not fully developed physically, running long distances carried the risk of fracturing and cracking still growing bones. Chen Xueli, the head of rehabilitation medicine at Beijing Shijitan Hospital, added that elevated body temperatures during marathons posed severe risks to children because of their poor thermoregulation and undeveloped cardiac systems. “Moreover, in mass events like marathons where emergencies easily arise, children with lower social maturity also lack the ability to handle such issues,” Chen said.

title: Saudi strikes kill 11 in Yemen as Houthi missiles target Saudi cities
description: Houthi media reported a series of ‘Saudi enemy air strikes’ targeting Sanaa, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two missiles.
content: Houthi media reported that Saudi strikes killed 11 people in Yemeni capital Sanaa on Saturday, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of “Saudi enemy air strikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others. A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said. Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region. The strikes in Yemen came after the Saudi-led coalition announced it had intercepted two missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and Yanbu, in the kingdom’s west. Earlier, Riyadh’s civil defence agency broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest city, and Yanbu. The alerts were all rescinded minutes later. Residents were instructed to “proceed to the nearest safe place” by the agency. It also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to “countering missiles and drones”. Diplomats evacuated The Gulf kingdom has come under repeated attack from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis in recent weeks as part of the latter country’s revived civil war. The group has targeted the kingdom’s oil infrastructure as well as its airports. Yanbu is a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast that has allowed Riyadh to bypass Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz for much of its crude exports. An attack on Riyadh airport earlier this month killed 13 people and wounded dozens more, while this week the US ordered non-essential embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing the Houthi threat. Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in the conflict, which has devastated Yemen and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, in 2015. The dramatic escalation in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets. Egypt has suggested sending troops to help defend Saudi Arabia, while Britain and France have offered their forces to protect the Gulf kingdom.

title: Profile | Who is Kim Jae-young, imposing star of K-dramas Make Me Tingle and The Judge from Hell?
description: In another life, Kim Jae-young, who debuted in 2013, might have been a chef. He is now an award-winning actor on both the big and small screen.
content: Korean actor Kim Jae-young and his signature locks are back on screen in the currently airing romcom Make Me Tingle, where he takes on the daring role of a sex toy entrepreneur. Since his 2013 acting debut, Kim has played a variety of brooding characters that take advantage of the lithe, imposing frame that helped him start in entertainment as a model. However, Kim was not initially aiming for a career in front of the camera. Rather, he harboured an ambition to be a chef and has said in interviews that it is the career he would likely have pursued had he not become an actor. Before beginning his military service in his early twenties, Kim did not have the lean physique he is known for today. During and after his time in the army, he gradually lost 30kg (66lbs). As he grappled with uncertainty about his future after his service, his father recommended he take up modelling. Why we love him Kim’s body transformation is a testament to his tenacity and commitment, but it was not the only challenge he overcame before becoming a recognisable name. He debuted as a model in 2010 and, during those early days, became friends with other models who later entered the acting industry, such as Byeon Woo-seok and Joo Woo-jae. His first film was the competitive diving feature No Breathing (2013), in which he appeared alongside Lee Jong-suk and Seo In-guk. Yet after leaving his agency Esteem – where he trained as a model – Kim faced an 18-month drought without work. This was when he decided to pursue acting more seriously, eventually landing his first K-drama role through an audition when he was cast in the 2014 KBS series Blade Man opposite Lee Dong-wook and Shin Se-kyung. Work came steadily after that, and as Kim rose through the ranks over the years, he has never looked back. The star-making roles After a range of supporting roles, Kim scored his first main cast appearance in 2018’s hit series 100 Days My Prince, a period romcom led by Doh Kyung-soo and Kim’s current Make Me Tingle co-star Nam Ji-hyun. He played tortured mercenary Seok-ha, the elder brother of Nam’s character. Kim’s first leading role came opposite Go Hyun-jung and Shin Hyun-been in 2021’s artful mystery-melodrama Reflection of You. He plays the brooding sculptor Woo-jae, who has a history with both Go and Shin’s characters. To capture Woo-jae’s backstory, Kim shot part of the series in the Irish countryside. Next, Kim starred alongside Park Min-young and Go Kyung-pyo in the high-concept romantic comedy Love in Contract (2022). He plays Hae-jin, a corporate heir and a client of Sang-eun (Park), who specialises in an unusual profession: she poses as the perfect wife for single men. The iconic parts Kim’s next lead role cemented his status as one of K-drama’s most promising leading men. In 2024, he starred alongside Park Shin-hye in the hit legal fantasy drama The Judge from Hell. Kim plays Han Da-on, a violent crimes detective who investigates a series of bizarre cases connected to Park’s judge Kang Bit-na, whom he does not realise is a demon from hell wreaking havoc from the bench. As he learns more about her identity, he fearlessly stands up to her. At the SBS Drama Awards, Kim earned the Top Excellence Award for an Actor in a Miniseries for his performance and also shared the Best Couple Award with Park. In late 2025, Kim put his striking looks and pensive persona to use opposite Girls’ Generation’s Choi Soo-young in the K-pop-themed legal drama Idol I. He plays beloved K-pop idol Do Ra-ik, who is put on trial for the murder of his bandmate. Choi plays his superfan Se-na, a top lawyer who defends him in court. The unheralded performances Kim’s acting debut was on the big screen and, though he is now primarily known as a K-drama performer, he continues to dip his toes into cinema to expand his range. In 2016, he appeared in the gritty low-budget crime drama Derailed, which premiered at the Busan International Film Festival and featured an early leading role from future action star Ma Dong-seok (aka Don Lee). In this tale of runaway youths who fall foul of a dangerous criminal, Kim plays Sung-hoon, a wealthy young man who has recently been paroled after serving time for murder. Three years later, Kim featured in the hit financial thriller Money starring Ryu Jun-yeol, playing a cocky rookie stockbroker. Tomorrow’s turns Kim will reunite with Ma Dong-seok on the big screen in The Roundup 5, the next instalment in the hugely popular action-crime series. He is set to play the film’s main villain, with the movie due in theatres next year. Kim is also expected to return as detective Han Da-on in the second season of The Judge from Hell, which is currently scheduled to air in September 2027.

title: Hong Kong end Asian Para Games on high note, with boccia gold, fencing silver
description: Leung Yuk-wing, Cheung Yuen take title in mixed pairs, while women’s sabre team add silver to city’s haul of 41 medals.
content: Hong Kong boccia pair Leung Yuk-wing and Cheung Yuen ensured the city’s delegation ended the Asian Para Games in Japan on a high note with mixed pairs (BC4) gold on Saturday. Coupled with two more bronze medals from their teammates, as well as a pair of medals — a silver and a bronze - from the city’s fencers, Hong Kong concluded the fifth edition of the regional para games in Aichi-Nagoya with 41 medals, bringing home three gold, 14 silver and 24 bronze medals across five sports. After each claimed a silver medal in the men’s and women’s individual (BC4) events earlier, Leung and Cheung faced no trouble in the final at the Nagoya General Gymnasium, where they thrashed China’s Zheng Yuansen and Lin Ximei 9-0. It was the third Asian Para Games gold medal for Leung, with the first two coming in Incheon in 2014, while Cheung, who took mixed pairs silver with Leung in Hangzhou in 2023 and at the Paralympic Games in Paris a year later, tasted victory for the first time. Having upgraded her medal from three years ago, Cheung said she was happy with the improvement. “I didn’t do too well in the individual final, but I am happy that I played to my standard today,” the 27-year-old said. “Our performance in the competition improved with each match, and we were able to perform what we practised today, so I am very satisfied with our performance.” Leung reiterated his pre-match focus on the pairs event, and said he was happy to achieve his goal. “We played to our potential today, which may have intimidated our opponents, so we capitalised on that momentum and pushed forward,” said the 41-year-old veteran, who had competed in six Paralympics since 2004. “Overall speaking, it was quite good this time, with the only regret that I didn’t do well enough technically in the individual final, but I’m still satisfied with the results.” In other events, John Loung partnered with Yeung Hiu-lam and Chan Pak-lun to take the mixed team (BC1/BC2) bronze after beating South Korea 7-5 in the medals play-off match. Tse Tak-wah and Chan Ho-yan also combined to secure another bronze medal for Hong Kong in the mixed pairs (BC3) event, edging past the Thai pair 3-2. In para fencing, there was yet another medal for veteran Yu Chui-yee, who teamed up with Lam Ka-man, Tong Nga-ting and Chung Yuen-ping to take silver in the women’s sabre team event. Having dispatched Uzbekistan 30-12 in the semi-finals, Hong Kong then lost 30-16 China in the battle to be No 1. Tong and Lam then went on to compete in the sabre mixed team event alongside Sean Glass and Kwong Yuen-hing. Hong Kong beat Uzbekistan in the quarter-finals before losing to South Korea in the last four, but a 20-17 win over China earned the quartet a bronze medal for the first time. The week-long event concluded with the 80-strong Hong Kong delegation winning 41 medals from five sports - boccia, para badminton, para fencing, para swimming and para table tennis. While the 24 bronze medals matched the historic high from Hangzhou a few years ago, Hong Kong came away down five gold and one silver. The overall medal count was also the fewest since Hong Kong won 28 medals on the city’s debut in Guangzhou in 2010. Nevertheless, the Jockey Club Athlete Incentive Awards Scheme means a total of HK$5,562,500 (US$709,290) will be paid out to the medallists.

title: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
description: New research, facilitated by cutting-edge techniques, led to one of the first examples of physical proof for ancient ritual animal slaughter.
content: Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival. The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice. To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial arrangement of valuable artefacts. The team then used a cutting-edge protein analysis technique to find biomolecular evidence that the Sanxingdui people sacrificed bovines in ceremonies that also featured bronze, jade and ivory artefacts. The pit dates to the Shang dynasty (1600 BC–1046 BC), whose territory lay farther north than Sanxingdui. During this period, complex cultural practices, including animal sacrifice, emerged in Chinese history. “Animal sacrifice was certainly a common practice among many of the regional cultures in Bronze Age China,” said David Sena, from the Bard High School Early College in Manhattan, who was not involved in the study and previously taught Chinese history at Harvard, in a comment to the SCMP. The biomolecular analysis is significant because much of our knowledge of the period comes from early written records, such as oracle bones, while direct physical evidence of animal sacrifice is elusive. To reach their conclusion, the scientists extracted lipids and proteins to distinguish human from animal remains, as well as modern from ancient samples. They found that much of the residue on valuable items such as bronze, jade and ivory came from ancient animals, specifically bovines. “This work exemplifies how molecular archaeology can decode intangible aspects of ancient behaviour, offering a direct molecular window onto the detailed sequence of ancient ceremonies,” wrote the authors. Although the Sanxingdui excavation site is famous for being uniquely strange compared with those of its contemporaries, systematic animal sacrifice represents a cultural similarity between the Sanxingdui people and their contemporaries. Specifically, the use of bovines follows a timeline similar to the Shang-era transition from pigs to cows, hinting at the possibility of cultural exchange between the people of the Central Plains and the Sanxingdui people. “Our molecular evidence extends previous archaeological observations of cultural exchange, revealing that connections between Sanxingdui and 420 other Bronze Age centres extended into the less tangible realm of ritual performance,” wrote the authors. The discovery was facilitated by the pristine condition of the Sanxingdui excavation site, which is changing how archaeologists work at sites they could otherwise contaminate. Scientists wear protective suits as they enter sealed cabins and follow strict protocols when entering and leaving. The team said this culture has created “unprecedented opportunities for biomolecular investigation.” This careful approach, along with the remarkable preservation of the proteins analysed – likely due to historical luck – helped enable a major discovery and demonstrated the value of a new research technique. The biomolecular investigation yielded impressive results, not only showing that an ancient civilisation practised animal sacrifice, but also painting a clearer picture of how it fit into the world around it.

title: Populist Czech government pushes through media funding changes
description: The proposal drew criticism from broadcasters, international journalism groups and institutions including universities and ‌the Catholic Church.
content: In a rare overnight vote, the Czech ruling coalition pushed public media funding changes through a first parliamentary hurdle despite criticism that they could weaken broadcaster independence. The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, ‌has frequently criticised public and private media coverage of its policies and accused some outlets of bias. Opposition parties have compared the proposed changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media. The government says it is scrapping the 205 crown (US$9.45) monthly household broadcasting fee to ease costs for consumers. Funding would instead come from ⁠the state budget. The proposal was brought to the floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Friday. ‌Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled the vote for 4.36am on Saturday. The coalition’s majority then voted to send the bill ‌to committees for further discussion. Sunday protest planned Hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament, with some remaining ⁠overnight. Local media reported ⁠that several people unsuccessfully tried to enter the building. Critics say the changes would weaken the broadcasters and make them more vulnerable ‌to political pressure. Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups, while public media are among the most trusted news ‌sources in ‌the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey. The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television ‌and Czech Radio by about 15 per cent, possibly as early as next year, and keep nominal funding unchanged ⁠for several years. “There is no war for independent media,” Babis said on social media late on Friday. “There is ⁠no fight for democracy and no nationalisation of media is being prepared.” The proposal and its fast track treatment drew criticism from the broadcasters, international journalism groups and institutions including universities and ‌the Catholic Church. “The bill goes ‌against the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which requires adequate, stable and predictable funding for public service media,” the European Federation of Journalists said in a statement. Journalists and other employees at the broadcasters announced a strike for November 3, while a civic group called a public protest for Sunday.

title: Composer Huang Ruo on why opera is ‘the last dance of humanity’, and his Hong Kong show
description: Chinese-American composer discusses the threat of AI in music and using tech to unite in City of Floating Sounds, coming to Hong Kong in 2027.
content: “Nowadays, we have people listening to AI pop singers,” Chinese-American composer Huang Ruo says during a talk on music and culture in Hong Kong. “They sing so beautifully, but it’s not real. So I do believe theatre and opera are the last dance of humanity.” The 50-year-old New York-based conductor and pianist behind acclaimed cross-cultural operatic projects M. Butterfly (2022) and The Monkey King (2025) made further impassioned statements about performing arts in the modern world. “Seriously, you want to feel real?” Huang asks. “Come to see a live theatre, live opera.” But this does not mean he is against digital technology. His talk at the Asia Society Hong Kong Centre (ASHK) on October 12 was just a few days after the WestK Performing Arts Centre announced that Huang’s work will feature in their debut season in summer 2027. Described as an immersive “theatre for the city” and an “open-air musical”, City of Floating Sounds is a production that premiered in 2024. The Hong Kong iteration will feature a mobile app with proximity heatmaps and clips of orchestral music as listeners move through Hong Kong. It will eventually culminate in a full orchestral performance at one of the city’s central concert venues. From Hainan to the world stage Art and community have always mattered to Huang. He was born in Hainan, China, and describes his childhood in a village as one immersed in art and poetry. “We [would] all bring our chairs, our food, and sit under the stars to watch Chinese opera, which lasts for hours,” he says. At age 12, Huang enrolled at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music, before moving to the United States, where he earned a bachelor’s in music at Oberlin Conservatory of Music in Ohio in 2000. He then attended The Juilliard School in New York, earning his master’s in music in 2002 and his doctorate in musical arts for composition in 2008. Early in his career, Huang hunkered down, composing concertos and symphonies, then tapped into another side of his musical skill set when he turned 30. “When I was 30, this was after I even got my doctor’s degree, I thought to myself maybe I should write opera – which of course is the hardest art form,” he says on stage at ASHK. “But if I made it, I could play next to great opera composers like Verdi or Puccini.” He accordingly wrote his first opera, Dr Sun Yat-sen, over the course of four years, premiering it in Hong Kong in 2011. It was originally commissioned by Opera Hong Kong and the government’s Leisure and Cultural Services Department. The craft of ‘dimensionalism’ In a separate interview with the South China Morning Post, Huang shares more details about his creative process of fusing Western with Eastern music – which he describes as a craft of “dimensionalism”. For Huang, “dimensionalism means merging various cultures, but they are not just in fixed positions; they go in and out closer and further, and they integrate, and they recreate, reinvent themselves.” Huang disagrees with the idea that fusing various musical traditions together compromises their integrity. “Merging culture to create something new doesn’t mean it’s lesser,” he says. For example, his opera The Monkey King – which premiered in San Francisco – is based on the Ming dynasty classic Journey to the West and blends Western orchestration with Chinese folk instruments, Peking opera traditions, rock, jazz and puppetry. Librettist David Henry Hwang worked on the show, which features singing in both English and Mandarin. The production was recently nominated for the 2026 International Opera Awards in the World Premiere category. Huang has also been named the inaugural composer-in-residence for the Seattle Opera. His three-year residency will begin in the 2027–28 season and will feature the Seattle premiere of his opera M. Butterfly. Towards the end of the residency, the orchestra plans to premiere Huang’s The Wedding Banquet, adapted from Ang Lee’s 1993 film of the same name. As part of his residency, Huang will mentor young artists and help with community outreach. “Opera needs support,” he says. “This is a very expensive art form. But [we want] to let people know we are not just telling stories of Shakespeare and kings or queens from the old days. We are telling modern-day stories that are relevant to everyone.” We crave to interact with one another. We crave human connection Huang Ruo Opera diplomacy and human connection For an artist straddling the musical worlds of China and America, Huang naturally has to navigate geopolitical realities. “In the old days, there was something called ping-pong diplomacy. So to me, today we have opera diplomacy – or music diplomacy. Art could serve a very positive function,” he says. “As an artist, I also feel I’m in a unique position in that I could create art that could be performed and be appreciated by audiences in different parts of the world.” Huang connects music to major technological changes. He and technologist Josh Kopecek wanted to include mobile apps in City of Floating Sounds to turn the pandemic of addiction and isolation into a tool for human connection. Huang plans to spend a lot of time in Hong Kong in 2027, overseeing the entire production of his WestK show, including formatting and lighting. “Interactiveness is something built into our human DNA,” he says when asked about the future of theatre, adding that he believes it will increasingly integrate audience participation and site-specific theatre. “We crave to interact with one another. We crave human connection, and that is something that will keep humans alive.” The reckonings of the modern world are always on Huang’s mind, but he maintains an optimistic attitude and is determined to forge ahead: “Maybe we [will] just gather in the theatre when the end of the world comes.”

title: Chinese students in Paris hunker down as city braces for more mass protests
description: Most students say the violence has not put them off living in France, though they worry the unrest could boost the far-right.
content: France is bracing for another day of mass protests on Saturday, with the government promising that 70,000 police and gendarmes will be deployed across the country amid fears that last weekend’s scenes of violence and looting could repeat themselves. For many Chinese students living in Paris, the events last Saturday were their first taste of a major French protest turned violent. While most said the experience had not put them off staying in France, many said they worried about the country’s broader social, economic and political trajectory – and how the unrest might further boost the far-right. “I was not really shocked by the scenes of violence,” said Hannah Zhang, who moved to France for graduate school in 2024. “It was more like, ‘Ah, here they go again’.” The high school student protests for better education funding, which inspired the wider demonstrations last Saturday, have affected her studies at Paris’ elite Sciences Po university for weeks, with students barricading the campus in solidarity. While the events last weekend were the most extreme she had seen in terms of intensity, after two years in Paris Zhang has had her fair share of experiences with French public gatherings and the chaos they can bring. She recalled the night Paris Saint-Germain won the Uefa Champions League in May, when some fans celebrating “went crazy” and launched fireworks in every direction. “I knew some troublemakers would take advantage of the protest to create chaos… so I already told myself to avoid those areas,” Zhang said. Some also felt that Chinese-language reports about the protests – especially those from clickbait accounts on social media – had exaggerated the situation. Bob Bo, like many other Chinese students in France, received messages from his parents, relatives and friends checking in on him following the riot. “I told them that actually things are all right and did not impact my everyday life,” he said. Tony Zhuang, who also previously studied in the United States, said he felt safer during the recent unrest in France than he had during similar episodes in the US. Nevertheless, while the protests themselves are not a major source of concern for most students, many expressed concern that the unrest could strengthen far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen ahead of France’s presidential election next spring. “The riot will not impact my decision to stay in France but its political implications might make it more difficult for me to stay here if the far-right wins,” said Zhuang, who moved to France with his wife a year ago to start a new life and escape the competitive work environment back in China. A poll conducted by Ifop between October 17 and 19 showed Marine Le Pen widening her lead, with 36 per cent of respondents saying they would vote for her in the first round of the election, up 2 percentage points from a week earlier. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon came second with 16.5 per cent, followed by centre-left candidate Raphael Glucksmann with 13.5 per cent. With further protests planned for this Saturday and the next, plus a general strike called for November 5 by CGT, one of the country’s largest unions, many students are preparing for the prospect of prolonged unrest. “This is honestly a real first for me, and I really can’t imagine how far it will go,” Zhang said.

title: Israel launches major operation in West Bank after soldiers killed
description: The operation is expected to continue for several days and will include searches and building demolitions, the Israeli military says.
content: Israel’s military launched an operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday it said would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after gunmen killed two soldiers days ahead of Israeli elections featuring security as a key focus. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday’s vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe, and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the attack to pledge an even harder line on West Bank militancy. Security forces were searching targets and questioning suspects to “locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure” in the Hebron area from which they said the attackers had emerged, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and Shin Bet domestic security agency. Forces were also “demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter”, they said, adding that “counterterrorism operations” were under way at dozens of locations. The operation “is expected to continue for several days”, said the statement released late on Friday. Militant group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday’s fatal attack on two Israeli soldiers as a “heroic operation” and called on supporters to carry out more. A Hebron-based Agence France-Presse photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle. Israeli forces eventually shot dead the attackers. Netanyahu credited the soldiers with having “prevented what could have been a major attack” and ordered a lockdown in the West Bank. Visiting Hebron, the prime minister said he and defence chief Israel Katz were “considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since” the 1967 war. The first step would see Israeli forces “enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure”, he said. The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the United Nations said forcibly displaced thousands. Israeli rights group B’Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres through a spokesman voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides. Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”. He said authorities were “sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: if you mess with the Jews, you will pay a very painful price”. National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based “Palestinian Authority must be dismantled”. “It is impossible for there to be an authority within Judea and Samaria that incites murder, calls for murder, and works for murder,” he told reporters. No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority – which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank – was connected to Friday’s attack. Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal champions of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government but are illegal under international law. Netanyahu vowed to “pursue Hamas terrorists” everywhere, adding: “You have no place to hide.” Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the October 7, 2023 attack that resulted in 1,221 deaths, according to an Agence France-Presse tally from official Israeli figures, in what was the deadliest day in the country’s history. Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the coming vote, said he was praying for soldiers wounded in Friday’s shooting. The operation comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters. According to an Agence France-Presse tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023. Israeli figures show at least 51 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

title: In besieged Yemeni city, drinking water supplies hit crisis levels
description: The siege of Taiz by Houthi rebels has also resulted in shortages of food and fuel, making it difficult to maintain basic services.
content: Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen’s third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces. The needs of Taiz’s more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city. Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 litres (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days. “We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily,” al-Shahid said in a phone interview. Families like al-Shahid’s are paying as much as 75 per cent more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit. The siege of Taiz – a strategic gateway to southern Yemen – is not only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks. Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to “the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster”. Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents’ access to wells Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country’s north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognised government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since. War-related damage to Taiz’s ageing water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative – until recently. By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130km (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea. As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents’ access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined. The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey. As Taiz’s fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity. Shortages of fuel and food Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting – an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations’ migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz’s limited supply of water and other necessities. Some displaced families were now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesman for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid. Fuel for cooking and transport has also become scarce – and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organisation CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard. These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down. “The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises,” Laerke said. The health risks were exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said. Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50 per cent more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find. Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by. “We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food,” he said in a phone interview. Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritise their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and five-year-old son now ate mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said. Why Taiz matters to the Houthis While the Yemeni government still controls the centre of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city. Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south towards Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that will not be easy. “Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controlled roughly 80 per cent of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighbourhoods inside the city. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to brief the media, but Yemen’s foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group’s tightening grip on the city. The Houthis’ fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials say. Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians. Abdel Gaber said he could hear loud explosions every day from fighting that was happening roughly 5km away. The family is not returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety. Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive. “Staying in our home is inevitable – whether it be a matter of life or death,” al-Shahid said.

title: HSBC to open new wealth centre in Abu Dhabi despite regional conflict
description: HSBC survey found that 97 per cent of global investors rated the UAE as an attractive destination for infrastructure projects.
content: HSBC, the biggest lender in Hong Kong and Europe, will open a new wealth management centre in Abu Dhabi in December, as the lender has not found the conflicts in the Middle East have dampened demand for its wealth business in the region, according to a senior executive. Mohamed Al Marzooqi, CEO of HSBC in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), said the new project formed part of the lender’s largest investment in the Middle East in two decades, after the opening of a wealth management centre in Dubai last year – the bank’s first wealth hub in the region. “We continue to see strong growth of our new high-net-worth and wealthy customers in the region despite the uncertain global and regional geopolitical environment,” Al Marzooqi said in an online interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. Even after the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February, HSBC has continued to acquire many new high-net-worth clients in the UAE in the first half of this year, he said. “While many Middle East investors continue to diversify their portfolios geographically through Singapore, Hong Kong, London and Geneva, a growing number are also choosing to invest more of their wealth onshore in the UAE in recent years,” Al Marzooqi said. “We continue to invest heavily in technology and platforms and enhance our service and products for clients in the UAE.” Al Marzooqi was speaking with the SCMP from Dubai, where the lender held its 10th annual Future Forum and its first Wealth Investment Summit from Tuesday to Thursday. HSBC on Tuesday also released the results of a survey of more than 1,600 senior business leaders and 800 global institutional investors across 16 markets, including the US and mainland China. Conducted in September and October, the survey showed global investors expect the Middle East, North Africa and Turkey to play a strengthened role in infrastructure investment and capital flows over the rest of the decade. The report showed there were 4,500 infrastructure projects under way in the Middle East, North Africa and Turkey estimated to be worth a combined US$872 billion. “Our survey found that investors continue to have high interest in investing in the UAE, with 99 per cent of Asia-based investors and 97 per cent of global investors rating the UAE as an attractive destination for infrastructure investment over the next four years,” Al Marzooqi said. Asian and Chinese investors had high interest in these projects because they were related to sectors they were familiar with, such as artificial intelligence, renewable energy, data centres and logistics, he said. Jo Miyake, head of banking for Asia and the Middle East at HSBC, said that while the survey showed geopolitical instability remained a key concern to business leaders, they still wanted to expand in the region. Some 88 per cent of business leaders planned to expand in the Middle East within the next four years, while 14 per cent of respondents said they would increase their exposure in the region by more than 25 per cent, Miyake said. “The conflicts may lead some businesses to pace their investment, but they are not retreating,” Miyake said. “While there is uncertainty, people are more cautious, but there is still optimism in the long-term opportunities in the region, and the strategic rationale of our clients has therefore not changed.” HSBC last week announced the relocation of a senior executive from Hong Kong to run the wealth business in the region, appointing Sami Abouzahr as head of international wealth and premier banking for the UAE and the Middle East. Before this appointment, Abouzahr was based in Hong Kong, where he had served as head of investments and managed solutions, wealth and premier solutions since July 2025. HSBC launched 10 onshore funds in January, while it also introduced tokenised deposits in June to facilitate round-the-clock multicurrency movement, according to Al Marzooqi. The lender also launched the region’s first digital bond on the Abu Dhabi Exchange. “We are very proud of what we have achieved over the past 80 years in the UAE, which has been a journey of building trust with our client base,” Al Marzooqi said. “Our strategy is also aligned with the UAE government’s agile approach to economic repositioning.” He said Hong Kong and Dubai could work together to promote two-way capital flows through HSBC. “While Hong Kong and Dubai are competing in certain aspects, the two financial hubs could coexist by serving internationally minded clients who like to invest their wealth across multiple booking locations to diversify their investments,” he said. “The UAE remains a strategically important wealth and capital hub, supported by its role as a gateway between Asia, the Middle East and the global markets.”

title: Credit card defaults surge across China as older borrowers struggle to repay debt
description: China’s banks are facing a spike in delinquencies among middle-aged borrowers with secure public-sector jobs.
content: China is facing a surge in credit card delinquencies from a seemingly unlikely source: middle-aged borrowers who otherwise look like model citizens, with university educations and secure public-sector jobs. Chinese banks once rushed to lend to this group, confident they would easily be able to pay their bills. But defaults are now rising so quickly amid an economic slowdown that lenders are ramping up efforts to dispose of their non-performing loan portfolios. The past quarter saw a roughly 50 per cent jump in the value of non-performing loans registered on the Banking Credit Assets Registration and Circulation Centre – China’s official platform where banks and consumer finance firms list and trade non-performing debt portfolios. The value of newly registered bad-loan portfolios reached 148.1 billion yuan (US$22.2 billion) in the third quarter of 2026, including principal and interest. Credit card arrears accounted for 35.2 per cent of that volume, making it the largest single category. In October alone, 82 new portfolios had been listed on the platform as of Thursday. Most lenders said the average age of the delinquent cardholders was between 40 and 50. Others, such as Ping An Bank, simply described the borrowers as “middle-aged”. Analysts and banking industry insiders say the figures are part of a growing trend, with middle-aged cardholders carrying the highest credit risks. The situation stands in stark contrast to the United States, where credit card defaults have long been associated with young people. According to a February report by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, borrowers aged 20 to 39 continued to show higher serious delinquency transition rates than older cohorts in the final quarter of 2025. Key drivers included higher credit usage and thinner cash buffers. When residents face risks to their incomes or jobs, default rates are naturally bound to climb Liao Zhiming, Huayuan Securities Dong Zheng, an independent analyst with decades of experience in China’s credit card sector, says the China-US divergence is partly driven by a simple demographic reality: middle-aged people form the core base of credit card users in China, while younger borrowers now tend to favour online lending services. “And when economic momentum fades, those in their 40s become one of the vulnerable groups,” he said. “They typically carry housing mortgages and face obligations to support their families and raise children.” According to a manager overseeing credit card operations at the Shanghai branch of a Chinese state-owned bank, most delinquent cardholders pointed to steep salary cuts or lay-offs during debt collection. “When that happens, they want to hold onto their homes,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to comment publicly. “So they prioritise mortgage repayments and family expenses. Overdue credit card bills only hurt their credit profiles, with little tangible immediate impact.” The profile of the debtors is often a surprise, the person added. “We are seeing a growing number of delinquent cardholders who hold what look like stable, even decent jobs from an outside perspective – for example, at Shanghai government-owned enterprises or government departments,” he said. The details disclosed in several lenders’ bad-loan portfolios paint a similar picture. In August, Beijing-based China Everbright Bank listed a non-performing loan portfolio worth more than 10 billion yuan, noting that it had “a high share of borrowers holding college diplomas or above”. Jiangsu Lishui Rural Commercial Bank, another lender from eastern China, described the debtors in its portfolio as having “strong professional capabilities”, which meant their repayment potential was “relatively high”. Dong, the independent analyst, said many of the industry’s current issues stemmed from China’s boom in credit card usage in the mid-2010s. Back then, lenders set very low application thresholds to rapidly grow their customer bases, especially for applicants working at government agencies or state-owned enterprises, according to Dong. The banking industry source echoed this view. “Banks have an inherent trust in these borrowers and treat them as high-quality clients,” he said. “With far laxer background checks, the risks were sown years ago.” Against this backdrop, Chinese lenders are now racing to offload non-performing loans. In the first nine months of this year, portfolios worth a total of 322.2 billion yuan were registered on the Banking Credit Assets Registration and Circulation Centre, up 26.4 per cent year on year. Looking ahead, observers expect credit card bad-loan ratios to stay elevated. Analyst Liao Zhiming at Wuhan-based Huayuan Securities noted that mounting bad loans paired with tougher regulatory requirements had prompted more Chinese lenders to tighten new credit card issuance. “Even so, the ratio will remain high because of lenient approval standards in earlier years,” Liao said. “At its core, this is a social issue now. When residents face risks to their incomes or jobs, default rates are naturally bound to climb.”

title: Garment and toy exhibit shows common threads of Hong Kong childhood textiles
description: Get in touch with the city’s heritage through handmade garments and mass-produced toys at the Centre for Heritage, Arts and Textile.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
When you were younger, you probably had a teddy bear you loved even when it started looking worn out. Maybe you also had a treasured blanket you slept with every night. Over time, objects like these become old, stained or even ripped. But these signs of use are proof of the love we gave them.
An art centre in Hong Kong is giving these objects their place in the sun. The “Snuggle and Stitch” exhibit at the Centre for Heritage, Arts and Textile (CHAT) showcases local childhood textiles from the 1930s to the modern day. Items include home-made clothes and dolls, as well as ready-made fashion and mass-produced toys.
Bruce Li, an associate curator at CHAT, put together the exhibit. He said the items on display represent how people showed care for one another. They highlight the ways that Hongkongers have adapted to tough times.
“People were very resourceful . Problem-solving was like a day-to-day exercise,” said the curator, who is in his 30s. “For kids, when they couldn’t afford a proper soft toy or doll, they just used a simple piece of string … maybe poked through a tin can or a bottle cap, and it became a spinning [toy].”
The exhibit displays garments that were part of families’ everyday lives. For example, a simple fabric with sturdy straps could be tied to safely hold a baby on a caregiver’s back. Children’s clothes and blankets were often repeatedly repaired by hand because it would be too expensive to buy new ones.
Textile and garment manufacturing played a major role in Hong Kong’s economic development, especially from the 1960s to 1980s.
CHAT is part of The Mills, a heritage conservation project. It is housed on the site of a textiles factory that closed in 2008.
“The textile industry in Hong Kong is a thing of the very recent past. Surrounding our community are all the retired workers or stakeholders of the industry,” Li explained.
He hopes the exhibit will inspire former garment workers to share their stories.
“It’s a thing to be proud of. For me, making exhibitions has this effect to catalyse the conversations between the generations,” he said.
At the exhibit, visitors can also try old children’s games. One common playground activity, cat’s cradle, requires just a string and at least two players, who take turns creating different patterns with their fingers. Games like this show the importance of physical connection.
As life becomes increasingly digital, textiles help people stay connected to the real world, Li said.
“When you see [a textile], you want to touch it,” he said. “It’s a medium that makes you very empathetic. When you touch something … it is just an alternative way of learning about the world. You can … be brought back to a lot of history that you forgot.”
Li explained that this interaction was key to learning more about the world.
“Once you touch something, you will be connected. And once you learn more about it, you’ve been connected to a maker … We become more appreciative of the material and more empathetic,” he said.
“I think that’s the beauty of textiles in the age of AI [artificial intelligence].”
“Snuggle and Stitch: Childhood Textiles of Hong Kong” runs until February 21, 2027. Find it in the D.H. Chen Foundation Gallery at The Mills in Tsuen Wan. Admission is free.

title: Asian Angle | Vietnam’s 2045 vision faces a reality check as capital squeeze tests growth ambitions
description: Vietnam must choose whether to align its growth targets with the capital it can raise, or accept considerably greater economic risks.
