content: Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, a National Assembly resolution in April set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with infrastructure building expected to serve as a major growth engine. However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at a reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks. The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost US$67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts, are expected to cost at least US$22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require about US$297 billion annually, or 40 per cent of nominal GDP. Domestic banks carry most of this burden. Bank lending accounts for about 83 per cent of Vietnam’s financing mix, compared with 13 per cent for bonds and 4 per cent for equity. By late June, outstanding credit reached 19,970 trillion Vietnamese dong (US$760 billion), up 18.1 per cent year on year. Credit expanded by 7.41 per cent in the first half, while deposits grew by only 5.02 per cent, pushing the loan-to-deposit ratio to about 112 per cent. Banks have responded by competing more aggressively for funding. Posted six- to 12-month deposit rates are generally 5.0 per cent to 6.5 per cent, in line with the State Bank of Vietnam’s efforts to keep rates low. In practice, however, depositors are reportedly offered effective yields of 8.5 per cent to 11.0 per cent through private negotiations. Scarce credit is also distributed unevenly. In June, 18 major projects requiring 752 trillion dong were exempted from standard credit-growth limits. Developers include large and well-connected conglomerates like Vingroup, Sun Group and Masterise. By contrast, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for 98 per cent of Vietnamese firms, receive only about 20 per cent of bank credit. They face lending rates of 10 per cent to 12 per cent, while 93.5 per cent of loans require collateral. Yet SMEs account for most employment and household incomes. The strain is already visible: new business registrations fell 13.9 per cent year on year in July, while completed dissolutions rose by 270 per cent. This writer’s recent field trip to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City revealed that many SMEs are struggling because they cannot access the credit needed to sustain or expand operations. This is happening despite stellar headline GDP growth of 9 per cent in the first nine months of 2026. High interest rates have brought the property market close to a standstill. Average home-loan rates have reached 14 per cent to 16 per cent, while the number of residential property transactions nationwide fell by 36 per cent year on year in the first half. This has cooled speculation and reduced the risk of a property bubble. However, the high rates have also created new vulnerabilities. Developers depend heavily on property sales for cash flow, while their average bond issuance rate has risen to 11.4 per cent, and their debt-to-equity ratio has climbed to 74 per cent, against an average of 54 per cent during 2022 to 2025. Disrupted cash flows increase the risk that repayment difficulties will translate into higher bank bad debt. As China’s experience illustrates, a prolonged property slowdown can also weigh on household confidence, consumption, public finance and economic performance. The logical response is to look abroad, but external options remain limited. The international financial centres in Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City, launched in January and February, have issued certificates to only a few dozen investors, while credit-rating requirements exclude some major foreign banks. Sovereign bond issuance is constrained by Vietnam’s credit rating, which is one notch below investment grade from S&P and Fitch and two from Moody’s. The government aims to achieve investment-grade status by 2030, which analysts estimate could cut borrowing costs by as much as 1.5 percentage points. But that benefit would come too late for many projects beginning now. International capital markets are also becoming less welcoming to Vietnamese firms and banks. The US 10-year Treasury yield is about 5 per cent, while the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent in September. Surging global demand for capital, particularly to finance AI and related technologies, is intensifying competition for funding. Meanwhile, geopolitical pressures, including the US-led war against Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, are pushing up the risk premium that emerging markets like Vietnam must pay. Looking ahead There are three key implications here. First, Vietnam may need to align its growth ambitions with what it can finance at a reasonable cost, to ease funding pressures and put expansion on a more sustainable footing. Second, if Hanoi maintains its targets while domestic interest rates remain high, the wider economy will bear the strain, with SMEs likely to feel it first. High borrowing costs could produce more closures and discourage private investment, leaving the economy more fragile even as infrastructure spending sustains headline GDP growth. Third, Vietnam will increasingly need international funding, creating opportunities for foreign banks and other credit institutions. But greater reliance on debt carries risks. Much public infrastructure does not generate direct returns sufficient to service the borrowing used to fund it. In an environment of prolonged high interest rates, excessive debt-financed investment could weaken the repayment capacity of both the government and Vietnamese enterprises. Vietnam can still build the roads, railways, airports and energy infrastructure it needs, but not necessarily at the pace envisaged. Ambition must be matched by affordable capital, and the two are increasingly moving apart. A more calibrated growth target would reduce financing pressures and the risk of a costlier debt adjustment later. Le Hong Hiep is a Senior Fellow and Coordinator of the Vietnam Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

title: Why do some celebrity perfumes – think Ariana Grande, Britney Spears – stay popular?
description: Memorable scents, packaging and affordable prices make fragrances by the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Ariana Grande and Britney Spears a success.
content: There is a particular kind of deja vu that comes from a stranger’s perfume, when a scent – sugary-sweet in a lift, soft and creamy on a person’s jumper, flowery from a hug – drifts past and you know it long before you can name it. Chances are, a few of them come with a celebrity’s name. Famous names have long sold perfumes, intentionally or not. When Marilyn Monroe said in 1952 that Chanel No 5 was all she wore to bed, she did more for that bottle than any advertisement could, despite never having starred in a Chanel ad during her lifetime. Before they began marketing beauty brands, supplements and tequila, celebrities bottled their names. By the early 2000s, it felt like every pop star, actress and reality television name had a perfume of their own. Jennifer Lopez opened the floodgates with Glow in 2002, a soft, musky citrus in a frosted hourglass bottle. Soon after came Sarah Jessica Parker’s Lovely in 2005 and Mariah Carey’s butterfly-topped bottles in 2007. If you were a teenager at the time, there is a good chance at least one of these was gifted to you on Christmas Day. Part of the appeal was that a celebrity perfume felt like a piece of someone’s world at a price most people could manage. With stars all over magazines, television and radio, there was no shortage of faces to choose from, and the launches kept coming well into the 2010s. Beyonce’s Heat broke sales records at Macy’s in 2010, Katy Perry’s Purr arrived in a cat-shaped bottle that same year and Lady Gaga’s Fame went on sale in 2012 as a black liquid that sprayed clear. Many of those launches had their moment before quietly making room for the next big thing, but a handful have stuck around for years. Steve Mormoris is the CEO of Scent Beauty, a company that has developed fragrances for stars such as Sabrina Carpenter and Kylie Minogue. For Mormoris, scents such as Elizabeth Taylor’s White Diamonds (1991), Lopez’s Glow, David Beckham’s Instinct (2005), Britney Spears’ Fantasy (2005) and Ariana Grande’s Cloud (2018) are good examples of perfumes that have stood the test of time. The oldest of the lot, White Diamonds’ sparkling white florals gave it old Hollywood glamour, back when a film star launching a perfume was a novel idea. More than three decades on, a bottle reportedly still sells every minute. Britney Spears’ Fantasy arrived 14 years later, and for plenty of mid-2000s teenagers, it is still the closest thing to bottling that era. It put a cupcake-sweet scent inside a bright pink bottle, and fans have never really let it go. The Y2K revival has introduced it to a new generation, and with more than 20 versions released since the original, anyone who fancies a change has plenty to choose from. Both Taylor and Spears have had Elizabeth Arden in their corner since day one, and for Mormoris, that kind of backing is key. A lasting celebrity scent, he says, needs “a licensing partner who invests capital, and rigorously manages the celebrity brand as a business with media investment and retailer engagement”. Ariana Grande’s Cloud, a mix of lavender, pear, coconut and creamy woods, belongs to a newer generation of staples. Her fans took to it as soon as it launched and, within two years, so did TikTok after scent lovers noticed it smelled a lot like Baccarat Rouge 540, the cult Maison Francis Kurkdjian perfume. Cloud became the dupe everyone wanted at a fraction of the price, and a new crowd came for the smell first and the singer second. It also showed how much the way people find perfume had changed. Recommendations that once came from magazines or a department store counter were now coming from strangers online, and a celebrity scent could find its audience long after the launch campaign wrapped up. Sabrina Carpenter’s Sweet Tooth launched into that world in 2022, in a chocolate bar-shaped bottle. The follow-ups have stuck to the dessert menu, with Cherry Baby (2024), Me Espresso (2024) and Lemon Pie (2025). Four years in, Sweet Tooth still outsells the rest of the line, and the collection keeps reaching new countries. Newer names are pitching themselves right next to designer perfume, too. Rihanna’s Fenty Eau de Parfum (2021), made with LVMH master perfumer Jacques Cavallier Belletrud, mixes magnolia, rose and blueberry and sells at a designer price, while Billie Eilish, who launched her first perfume in 2021, has a whole range at Sephora. Getting onto the shelf is only the beginning, and for Mormoris, much depends on what happens after the launch. “The celebrity fragrances that become iconic brands in the fragrance category are driven by the continued involvement of the celebrity herself, who continues to innovate, narrate and show her love for the fragrance she created as part of her everyday life,” he says. Look past the famous faces, and the scents that have made it don’t have that much in common on paper: different decades, smells and stars. But they all land on the same few things: an instantly recognisable scent, a dresser-worthy bottle, a reasonable price point and new versions to keep things interesting.

title: Israeli election campaign turns ugly with jibes, attacks against candidates
description: Helped by AI-generated content, candidates and activists seek to portray their opponents as weak, untrustworthy or damaging for the country.
content: Days ahead of close-fought Israeli elections, campaigns have gone into overdrive with poor-taste jibes and inflammatory attacks against candidates, sometimes crossing red lines. Fuelled in part by a boom in AI-generated images flooding social media, candidates and activists are seeking to portray their opponents as weak, untrustworthy or damaging for the country as they play on stereotypes and fears to sway public opinion. The electioneering has at times turned personal, with some candidates who lost loved ones in the wars following Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack even having their bereavement dragged into the campaign. Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc neck and neck with that of his main centre-right rival Gadi Eisenkot. נתניהו, רק בריאות והצלחה באזרחות. https://t.co/iGuyupumBS — Gadi Eisenkot - גדי איזנקוט (@gadi_eisenkot) October 21, 2026 On Wednesday, Eisenkot posted a video on social media wishing Netanyahu a happy 77th birthday that featured a slate of AI-generated characters including a Hamas member speaking from a tunnel. “What can we wish for the person who has been protecting us for 20 years?” the militant says, evoking theories that the prime minister has deliberately helped the Islamist movement stay in power in Gaza, charges vehemently denied by Netanyahu. Soon after, an AI depiction of Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei pops up, telling Netanyahu: “One more round without victory and I’ll make you a bomb as a present.” Netanyahu has also liberally weaponised AI-generated content against his rival. In July, he posted a video depicting Eisenkot rejecting a hug from a young man wearing a T-shirt with the slogan “Israel unity” and instead embracing Arab-Israeli candidate Mansour Abbas. The clip sparked widespread outrage over claims the young man had been made to resemble Eisenkot’s son who was killed fighting in Gaza in 2023, something Netanyahu’s party denied. In an interview broadcast by Channel 13, Eisenkot said he had felt “deep contempt for Netanyahu and his entourage” after watching the video. Netanyahu’s camp has used AI throughout the campaign to stoke fears over a possible opposition coalition including Arab-Israeli parties. Clips have ranged from Jewish opposition politicians taking off masks to reveal Arab-Israeli candidates underneath, to Arabs looming over what appears to be a crumbling parliament building. Billboards for Netanyahu’s Likud party with the phrase “The Right or Palestine” alongside the faces of Arab-Israeli politicians have also sprung up across the country. “It’s incitement, especially from Prime Minister Netanyahu’s camp,” said Thair Abu Ras, head of the Forum for Regional Thinking at the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute. “This whole notion of having an Arab party in the coalition is illegitimate in the eyes of the right-wing and they’re trying to enforce that kind of way of thinking on the Eisenkot coalition as well,” he said. Apparently racialised comments have been levelled at Eisenkot, the son of Moroccan Jews. This month, a senior commentator on the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 television station described him as “a monkey”. While the term is not necessarily a racial slur in Hebrew, the remark drew widespread condemnation from opposition politicians and from Netanyahu himself. The election is the first since Hamas’s October 2023 attack. A number of candidates are people whose lives were transformed that day or in the wars that followed, but trauma or bereavement has not spared them from personal attacks. Laly Derai, whose son was killed fighting in Gaza in 2024, is running for the new far-right Amcha Israel party, which advocates universal conscription into the Israeli military – an increasingly contentious issue due to exemptions for religious students. She says she has faced a coordinated smear campaign against her, which has at times invoked her son’s death and accusations that she is betraying his memory. Posters calling for her to withdraw her candidacy so as not to “put the country in danger” have sprung up in the area around the settlement where she lives in the occupied West Bank. “They’re trying to break me but, paradoxically or not, this campaign has reinforced my decision to enter politics precisely to put an end to this hate-filled rhetoric,” she said. Speaking to public broadcaster KAN, she said she had received “phone calls at all hours of the day and night, disgusting comments on social media, signs posted in our towns, including near our children’s school buses – all of this just because we dared to propose something new”. Relatives of hostages formerly held by Hamas have also been caught in the crosshairs. On an unofficial Facebook page for supporters of Netanyahu’s Likud party, an image was posted on Tuesday pitting one mother of a former hostage against another. One mother, Likud candidate Talik Gvili, looks calm against the backdrop of an Israeli flag, while Einav Zangauker – a vocal critic of Netanyahu – looks frenzied around protesters tinted in red. “It is us or them,” the caption reads.

title: Some Parisians buy pepper spray, tear gas for self-defence during protests
description: A weapons shop owner says he has seen a big increase in the sale of non-lethal weapons: ‘people have been physically traumatised’.
content: Parisians are buying tear-gas canisters and pepper sprays to defend themselves and their property during protests, which are expected to continue over the weekend, the owner of a weapons shop in the French capital has said. France was hit by its worst social unrest in years last weekend as nationwide protests over high prices and declining public services erupted into riots. A town hall was torched, shops pillaged ‌and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. Police have authorised only a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday, rejecting requests for rallies lodged by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the anti-establishment Yellow Vest movement. At the Armurerie de la Bourse weapons shop in central Paris, owner Yves Gollety said he has seen a big increase in the sale of non-lethal weapons since the weekend. Shops just 30 metres (33 yards) away had been looted, with their shutters torn off, he said. “It’s the first time that we’ve seen such an increase, and with all segments of the population,” Gollety ⁠said, adding that his customers included shopkeepers, restaurant owners and individuals. “People have been physically traumatised and are afraid,” he said. The top-selling products were pepper sprays and tear-gas canisters, which Gollety ‌said could only be used in self-defence. Gollety, who is also president of the national association of gunsmiths, told French newspaper Le Parisien that orders had increased tenfold. Members of the public were only allowed to buy small canisters under 100 millilitres in size, Gollety ‌said. Reuters found no evidence that people in Paris were buying other types of weapons in response to the protests. Alain Di Crescenzo, president ⁠of France’s chamber of commerce, urged shopkeepers ⁠to refrain from using weapons to defend their businesses. Speaking on the radio station Europe 1 on Friday, he said he had personally seen shopkeepers arming themselves with baseball bats, crowbars and shotguns. Reuters was not ‌able to independently verify this. “It’s extremely worrying,” he said. “It’s not their job to do that … It would add suffering onto suffering.” “The police must be left to do their jobs and I recommend the utmost caution,” he ‌added. A shopkeeper who sells motorbikes and scooters in Paris’ 15th arrondissement said he bought three large tear-gas canisters, plus another small one, to protect ‌his shop. “You can be taken by surprise, with people arriving without any prior warning. So you have to be prepared,” said the shopkeeper, who asked not to be ⁠identified. France’s government has pledged tougher security and will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, but the increase in people considering how to defend themselves ⁠illustrates Parisians’ fears as the weekend approaches. One man visiting Gollety’s shop, a 58-year-old finance worker who did not want to be identified, said he had researched self-defence options, although he had ultimately not bought anything on this occasion. “Given what happened last week and the risk it happens again next weekend, I would ‌prefer to be sensible and protect myself,” he ‌said, adding he had had a long-standing feeling of being unsafe. “I’ve been thinking about this for a long time and I think I’m going to take some steps,” he said. Elsewhere in Paris, Yvan Weiss, who owns a finance consulting firm, said he was taking steps to avoid his shop’s windows being broken. Asked if he considered getting pepper spray or other defensive gear, he said he had thought about it but in the end decided to get mechanical metal shutters for his shopfront instead.

title: Letters | Philippines, Hong Kong can contribute together to a more productive Asia
description: Readers discuss a stronger economic relationship between the Philippines and Hong Kong, Singapore’s balancing act, the Lugard Road lighting project, and MTR rules.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. At a time of regional and global change, the Philippines is entering a period of significant economic opportunity. Its expanding consumer market, established role in regional supply chains, infrastructure needs and transition towards cleaner and more advanced industries are opening new avenues for growth. The Philippines has a young workforce, a growing consumer base, abundant natural resources and a strategic position within Asean. As a centre for finance and trade, Hong Kong provides access to international markets and commercial expertise. This brings combined opportunities such as building regional supply chains and expanding higher-value production and investment in infrastructure and industries that will support the region’s continued development. Over the past two years, the Philippine government has taken significant steps to strengthen the conditions for this partnership to grow. Its reforms are providing investors with greater predictability, reducing the time and cost of doing business and channelling capital towards productive capacity, employment and national development. The Create More Act provides up to 40 years of incentives for priority industries, supporting the longer investment horizons required for manufacturing and advanced industries. The Public-Private Partnership Code offers a clearer framework for private participation in infrastructure, while lease terms of up to 99 years can support long-term commitments. Green Lanes, right-of-way reforms, lower stock transaction taxes and longer importer accreditation are also reducing practical barriers to establishing and expanding operations. The response from investors suggests that this direction is gaining traction. Investment approvals have reached 1.9 trillion pesos (HK$240 billion) for two consecutive years. The Philippines has also achieved upper-middle-income status and continues to hold investment-grade ratings from credit rating agencies. This combination of market fundamentals and a more supportive investment framework is especially relevant in sectors where Hong Kong financing and commercial networks can complement Philippine capabilities. In semiconductors and electronics, decades of experience and a skilled workforce provide a platform for higher-value activities. Nickel and copper resources can support renewable energy, electric vehicles and other emerging industries. The basis for a stronger economic relationship is already taking shape. With capital, capable institutions and partnerships focused on long-term value, Hong Kong and the Philippines can play mutually reinforcing roles in the region’s development. By combining their strengths, both can contribute to a more connected, productive and resilient Asian economy. Frederick D. Go, secretary of finance, Republic of the Philippines Singapore needs to rethink its balancing act In November 2025, Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong suggested China should put history aside, while endorsing a larger security role for Japan in Southeast Asia. During the Cold War, Singapore thrived as a low-risk intermediary. China wanted to learn from its urban governance and industrial model; the West saw it as proof that capitalism and order could coexist. But in an age of United States-China decoupling, hedging is no longer a strategy. At the Beijing Xiangshan Forum last month, Singapore’s Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing quoted Mencius, urging great powers to win hearts with virtue, not force: elegant counsel, as Singapore continues to acquire US patrol aircraft under American security arrangements. Culturally, the Teochew-dialect film Dear You moved audiences across the Chinese diaspora, yet a Singaporean commentary described it as a “highly successful piece of United Front work”. Rather than abandon its balancing act, Singapore could evolve into a translator with a standpoint. It should recognise that Beijing, at its civilisational core, values harmony. The question is whether Singapore’s leaders will rewrite the playbook before it stops working. Fion Yip, Guangzhou Natural beauty shouldn’t be spoiled Who in their right minds decided to spoil the natural beauty of the Lugard Road trail? The Tourism Board should be held accountable for not seriously considering the impact of their ridiculous idea of a lighting project. Alison Barlow, The Peak Rules needed for public safety on mass transit I refer to the letter, “Rethink rules regarding bikes on trains” (October 16). Social media feeds have highlighted criticisms of cyclists on trains, which could increase resentment between cyclists and regular commuters. We cannot assume every resident needs to understand the inconvenience cyclists face. That’s why we need rules to ensure all have a pleasant train ride. If detaching a front wheel increases the risk of dropped equipment on escalators and in lifts, that is not the responsibility of the MTR Corporation. The cyclist could use a bag. Proper equipment management is the user’s responsibility, not a reason to lower public safety standards on mass transit. Frank Lam Wai-hin, Tuen Mun

title: Your Voice: Giving the youth a voice, superfood benefits, protecting consumers
description: This week, students write about community workshops, natto and prepaid contracts in the beauty and fitness industries.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Kaitlyn Yu , Choate Rosemary Hall (United States)
Primary school English was, at best, the bane of my classmates’ existence.
Everyone had to learn about active and passive voice, how to use “nevertheless” as a conjunction and how to punctuate lengthy passages. While we memorised the correct vocabulary to fill in the blanks, we rarely used those words outside assignments.
But in 2020, our world changed dramatically. Schools closed, and if kids weren’t doing more than memorising English words before, they certainly weren’t going to start then.
My sister and I grew up surrounded by a healthy mix of Chinese and English at home. With an abundance of free time, we turned to creative writing.
I thought about all the other students in Hong Kong, particularly those who lacked the resources to read, write or speak English with confidence. They had never used English to tell stories, daydream or explore what they could create with their words. My hope was to share with them the joy of storytelling and the limitless potential that comes with it.
What started as a small idea grew into six-plus hours a week dedicated to research and curriculum design, ultimately evolving into English story reading and creative writing workshops for primary school students.
In each session, one volunteer helped each child write a short story. Over five weeks, I witnessed their confidence and English proficiency soar, culminating in an anthology of their creative writing titled The Lab Book . Two editions later, book sales exceeded HK$21,000, and we returned the proceeds to the participants as book vouchers.
Project Co|Lab was three years old when I left for school in the United States.
In the US, media literacy education is not federally mandated, and only half of the states have policies regarding it. As a result, two-thirds of American high school students struggle to distinguish between a news story and an advertisement.
The situation is even more concerning globally. A Unesco report from 2025 found that media literacy is integrated into national curricula in only about one-third of countries in Asia and the Pacific.
Project Co|Lab’s chapter in the US focuses on four key skills: understanding current events, recognising bias and disinformation, critically evaluating information and developing personal perspectives.
It has been transformative to see kids participate in activities designed to help them spot fake news, articulate opinions on current events and share their insights in discussions.
In the summer of 2026, we reintroduced Project Co|Lab in Hong Kong, with workshops aimed at Primary Four to Six students.
By August, over 100 participants and more than 120 volunteers had been involved in over 40 workshops.
I started Project Co|Lab at the age of 12, and now, at 17, my work still feels unfinished. However, I am determined to bring creativity, media literacy and critical thinking skills to students around the world.
Ella Tung Lok-ching, St Catharine’s School for Girls
Natto is a traditional Japanese food made from whole soybeans that are fermented with beneficial bacteria. It is widely recognised as a healthy superfood. How does natto taste? Natto is known for its strong, pungent aroma and its distinct slimy, sticky texture, which becomes frothy and stringy when stirred vigorously.
When you eat it, you will notice a slippery outer layer, but it’s soft and chewy on the inside. This unique texture can make trying natto an enjoyable experience.
For those who may not know, superfoods are nutrient-rich foods that offer maximum nutritional benefits. Generally, they are foods rich in vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre, antioxidants and healthy fats.
So, what makes natto a superfood? Natto is rich in plant protein, which is broken down into amino acids and peptides during fermentation, making it easier for our bodies to absorb.
Natto is an excellent source of vitamins K, B, E and C. It is also rich in minerals such as calcium, iron, potassium, magnesium and zinc.
Additionally, natto contains high levels of dietary fibre. A unique feature of natto is nattokinase – a special enzyme found in the slimy strings when stirred. Moreover, natto is rich in probiotics, which are beneficial live bacteria produced during fermentation.
After learning about all the nutritional values of natto, you might be wondering what benefits it offers. One major benefit is that natto helps prevent cardiovascular diseases. The enzyme nattokinase breaks down fibrin, acting as a natural blood thinner and helping prevent blood clots, thereby significantly reducing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Furthermore, vitamin K, calcium and magnesium contribute to improved bone density, helping children avoid rickets while combating osteoporosis in adults and the elderly. Natto is beneficial for all ages.
Lastly, dietary fibre and probiotics help balance the microbiome, support gut health, prevent constipation and boost our immune system.
Interestingly, natto is associated with the longevity of the Japanese people. Their well-balanced, nutritious diets, which include traditional foods like natto, contribute to the world’s lowest obesity rates.
Among Japanese people, natto is commonly consumed for breakfast. It is often served with rice and seasoned with a dash of soy sauce, a sprinkle of sesame seeds or spring onions, and sometimes topped with a raw egg yolk.
From the description, I can already tell that this dish is nourishing. So, would you give it a shot? The benefits truly outweigh the drawbacks.
I am writing to express my strong support for a ban on prepaid contracts in Hong Kong’s beauty and fitness industries. As a secondary school student, I often observe how aggressive sales practices and sudden business closures negatively affect everyday citizens in our community.
The Hong Kong government is considering a bill that would require prepaid beauty and fitness services to offer customers a cooling-off period by the first half of 2027.
While introducing a cooling-off period is a positive step, it does not eliminate the risks involved. If long-term prepaid contracts were banned altogether, consumers would no longer fall victim to manipulative sales tactics or unfair lock-in periods.
Prepaid contracts leave consumers vulnerable to high-pressure sales tactics. Sales representatives frequently manipulate customers into signing long-term agreements before they can evaluate the risks.
Furthermore, paying large sums upfront carries significant financial risks when businesses fail. When a fitness centre or beauty salon closes unexpectedly, customers rarely recover their unspent money.
Although supporters of prepaid models argue that upfront fees provide businesses with steady cash flow and offer consumers discounted rates, the burden on buyers is far too high.
Leo Chim Kwan-ho, Po Leung Kuk Wu Chung College
I am writing in response to the government’s five-year plan that proposes building a “youth development city” in the Northern Metropolis. This policy has the potential to create more opportunities for young people. However, the project needs concrete targets and accountability mechanisms.
Housing affordability for young adults plays a key role in this development. If the Northern Metropolis does not have affordable housing, this does not address the real issues that youth are facing.
To tackle this, I recommend that the government allow young families to withdraw a portion of their Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) to use as a down payment for their first home.
Unemployment among fresh graduates is also a pressing concern. The recent dispute between the nurses’ union and the government highlights the plight of many nursing graduates who face underemployment despite being encouraged to pursue nursing careers. If the government cannot address the grievances of the nurses’ union, how can it credibly promise a “youth development city”?
If the Northern Metropolis is truly to become a youth development city, it must start focusing on what young people genuinely need.

title: Pet custody disputes draw increasing attention in China, where pets are treated as property
description: Public sentiment argues pets are living beings with feelings, not inanimate objects like sofas or TVs, and should not be treated as mere property.
content: Pets in China have become deeply woven into people’s lives and romantic relationships, especially those of younger couples. When romance sours, deciding “who gets custody” is becoming a painful legal grey area for many couples. According to pet industry data, China’s urban dog and cat population reached 126 million in 2025, driven largely by Gen Z and millennial. Many young couples treat their pets like children, calling each other the “Mum” and “Dad” of their fur babies. “While love may fade, human-animal bonds rarely do,” one online user aptly wrote. In recent years, posts pleading for help with post-break-up pet custody have flooded mainland Chinese social media. Desperate owners often ask how to legally retrieve a cat from an ex-partner or whether dog custody can be included in divorce agreements. A legal vacuum complicates these disputes. Chinese pet law has historically focused on administrative management, while gradually placing greater emphasis on animal welfare. However, under current law, pets are still classified strictly as personal property; there are no provisions for custody or visitation rights comparable to those for minor children. Courts typically rely on purchase receipts, adoption records, microchip registrations and veterinary bills to determine ownership, but an owner’s emotional attachment is difficult to quantify legally. In 2024, Shenzhen’s Futian District Court highlighted this divide when resolving a dispute over a dog nicknamed Kele, as reported by the Shenzhen Special Zone Daily. A woman known as Xiaojia bought and raised Kele before temporarily leaving the dog with her boyfriend, Xiaohua, while she went abroad. After they broke up, Xiaohua refused to return the dog, claiming that the time and money he had invested gave him the right to keep Kele. The court disagreed, ruling that Xiaojia was the legal owner. Xiaohua’s expenses were deemed voluntary gifts between lovers, while temporarily caring for the dog did not transfer ownership. Some pet custody battles have had more extreme consequences. In Qingdao, northern China, a dispute between a couple over their two cats ended in tragedy, according to mainland media outlet Jizhou Studio. During a heated argument, both partners tried to snatch the other’s cat. A woman then stabbed her boyfriend in the abdomen with a fallen knife. She was later sentenced to three years in prison for intentional injury. In the chaos, one cat fled in terror and disappeared, while the other suffered severe stress. For China’s younger generation, pets are no longer mere property; they are emotional anchors. This shift has helped fuel a sprawling pet economy projected to reach 405 billion yuan (US$60 billion) by 2028. From Shanghai’s viral “pet kindergarten,” which charges 98 to 138 yuan a day for fitness courses and daytime socialisation, to traditional Chinese medicine treatments such as acupuncture and tui na massage for pets, owners spare no expense. Pet grief services, including cremations and personalised memorial ceremonies, are also booming. As pet culture evolves faster than the legal framework, some online observers are urging couples to plan ahead. “Pets are not a sofa or a TV; they are living beings with memories and feelings,” one social media commentator noted. “Couples should agree on custody upfront to protect these animals from unnecessary pain.” For others, informal co-parenting remains an option. As one pet owner shared online: “My ex-boyfriend comes over every weekend to visit our dog, Wangzai, who gets so happy to see his dad. Just like humans, Wangzai is simply a child who can’t speak.”

title: Newest Chinese swimming sensation is already turning heads, and he’s only 12 years old
description: Hu Rundong emerges as stand-out junior performer at Jiangsu Provincial Games, winning five golds and four silver in 10 races.
content: China may have unearthed another swimming sensation in 12-year-old Hu Rundong, who turned heads by winning gold, setting records and meeting first-class standards at a provincial event this week. Hu emerged as the stand-out performer in the junior swimming division at the 21st Jiangsu Provincial Games, winning five gold and four silver medals across 10 events. Competing in the boys’ 12-year-old category, the Suzhou native competed in breaststroke, butterfly, freestyle and individual medley across short, middle and long distances. His performances and times are already drawing comparisons with world breaststroke champion Qin Haiyang, whose junior times were slower than the ones Hu laid down this week. Hu took gold in five events: the 100m breaststroke, 100m butterfly, 100m freestyle, 200m butterfly and 200m breaststroke. His time of two minutes, 25.39 seconds in the preliminary heats for the last of those distances was almost 10 seconds faster than the 2:35.00 benchmark required for China’s National First-Class Athlete status in a 50m pool. It was still some way short of the fastest time this year, however. Japan’s Shin Ohashi set a world record of 2:04.83 last month at the Asian Games. The tweenager also topped the 100m breaststroke heat in 1:10.07 to hit another first-class standard. By comparison, Qin clocked around 1:15.00 over the same distance when transitioning to the stroke at a similar age. Hu reached national first-class standards in several other events, winning the 100m butterfly heat in 59.27 seconds, the 200m butterfly final in 2:10.85, the 200m breaststroke final in 2:28.29 and the 200m individual medley all-around heat in 2:12.87. He also met first-class marks in freestyle events, taking silver in the 400m final in 4:11.74 and finishing second in the 100m freestyle heat in 57.01 seconds. In the 800m freestyle final, Hu secured silver in 8:42.71, narrowly missing gold but erasing the previous meet record of 8:42.57. Alongside record-breaking performances in the 100m all-around events in breaststroke, butterfly and freestyle, Hu also shattered four meet records during the Games. He also placed fourth in the 100m backstroke all-around fast heat in 1:08.27. Born to parents who were both swimmers, the 5ft 9in (1.77m) tall Hu has large hands and long feet, according to coach Zheng Liang. However, Zheng emphasised that physical gifts alone do not account for his success. “Being thoughtful, willing to study, and highly self-disciplined are this child’s most precious traits,” Zheng said. Hu was discovered by Zheng while representing a club in an amateur league as a third-grader. Impressed by his feel for the water and physical attributes, Zheng invited him for a trial at the Suzhou Children’s Amateur Sports School, where Hu subsequently began systematic training, but was a relatively late starter compared with his peers. Hu balances his sport with a regular school routine, attending academic classes during the day before starting two-and-a-half hours of intensive training at 4pm, after which he returns home to finish his school homework. While Hu excels across multiple disciplines, breaststroke remains his strongest event. Looking ahead, Hu expressed ambitious goals following his dominant showcase. “I hope I can perform better and win more gold medals at the next Provincial Games,” he said. “My target is the National Games [in 2029].”

title: ‘Not a G2 world’: Apec chief on how the forum has changed through the years
description: Eduardo Pedrosa says China is a key focus of forum, but insists smaller economies still hold important roles.
content: China is becoming more confident and ambitious, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) executive director said, as the forum returns to the country for the third time in a quarter-century. Eduardo Pedrosa, the executive director of the Apec Secretariat, told the SCMP on Thursday that the forum would crucially bring together people and businesses from across the globe, though he noted that the limelight on meetings between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. “There seems to be momentum building up,” he said. “Compared to last year, when the two presidents only met once at Apec, this year they will have met four times. That gives them a personal dynamic; they get to understand each other in a better, more personal way. “I hope we’ll see some stability and a better understanding of the approaches [that each country] would take,” he added. Pedrosa was in Hong Kong this week for the Apec finance ministers’ meeting and addressed a forum hosted by the HKU Jockey Club Enterprise Sustainability Global Research Institute. The Apec chief also said change had been “remarkable” since the first time China hosted Apec in Shanghai in 2001. “The agenda [back then] was about the World Trade Organization, because China had just joined it. It was more of a general opening up. Then we get to the 2014 Apec in Beijing, where we discussed connectivity and infrastructure to ensure the benefits from free trade would flow. “Now, with China hosting this year, we’re looking at those issues and how to move forward with the connectivity, trade and technology agenda,” Pedrosa said. Describing China’s shifting role as the world’s second-largest economy, Pedrosa highlighted an evolving dynamic between its national ambitions and global engagement. “[China] is ambitious, given its weight in the global economy and how advanced it is in its technological development. Leaders of other nations and of businesses can look at that and ask what it’s done right and what can they learn from China?” Pedrosa pointed to China’s other perceived strengths. “When China wants to do something, it gets it done. It will happen. Shenzhen, of course, is a centre of technology and people.” He also said China’s ministerial meetings so far this year had seen success. “Apec [trade officials] came together in Suzhou and came to a consensus on trade [in May]. It shows Apec members are willing to make compromises.” As the world anticipated the high-stakes talks between Chinese President Xi and US President Trump on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, Pedrosa stressed that there would be other discussions taking place. “There are people focused on the US and China, but we don’t live in a G2 world. Because of the modality of Apec, everyone has a voice. You can have smaller economies challenge, discuss and put forward their own ideas.” He also said a key focus of Apec was on easing cross-border transactions and fostering environments conducive to trade and investment. “What do businesspeople want to do, and what makes them invest? A predictable regulatory environment. Apec has a work programme on this – the ease of doing business,” Pedrosa said. Pedrosa added that the forum has other working groups on the digital economy, AI, health and other realms, and that participation and input from stakeholders had been strong. “The reason why it’s useful is we want to hear from the businesses what problems they face if they’re going to invest more and how do we make it easier for them.” Pedrosa said significant risks to supply chains remained, though he said that progress had been made, and Apec could continue to play an important role. “There are trade frictions. There’s no denying it. The Apec agenda is forward-looking to address contemporary issues, and one of the major issues we are confronting is how to make supply chains more resilient. “At the moment, the biggest issue is rising oil prices. The cost of food is also going up. That’s why resilience matters and why trade matters. If we’re able to trade, we’re able to smooth out price volatility,” he said. “We live in a global economy. We cannot rely on just one.”

title: Greek island’s last school faces closure as student numbers decline
description: A wider European trend of falling enrolment and ageing populations is hitting educational institutions.
content:
Chryssa Ntalaka is the only teacher in the last school on the Greek island of Kalamos. She has a shorter list of students every autumn.
This year, there are just two. Last month, the sixth graders sat at Ntalaka’s table beneath the whiteboard, in front of rows of unused desks and benches. When they head to middle school on Greece’s mainland next year, the school will be closed.
Toys and picture books still sit in the nearby kindergarten, which closed three years ago.
Falling enrolment across Greece this year prompted authorities to close 75 schools. They suspended or extended suspensions at over 400 others. This is happening across Europe and beyond. The region has 16 of the world’s top 20 oldest nations, according to the independent World Population Review.

title: China’s AI compute surge heavily reliant on US chips, offshore cloud access: report
description: China’s remote access alone is expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year.
content: China’s access to artificial intelligence computing power will double next year, but US-designed chips will account for about 65 per cent of that capacity, an indication of its continued reliance on foreign hardware, according to new research. Total compute available to Chinese entities was expected to expand in 2027 from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million “H100-equivalents” – a metric benchmarked against Nvidia’s data-centre graphics processing units, according to a report by the Washington-based Institute for Progress (IFP). To project these figures, IFP said it tallied domestic chips, legal imports, smuggled processors and compute accessed remotely via overseas cloud networks. Remote access alone was expected to swell to 2.8 million H100-equivalents by the end of 2027, up from roughly 1 million this year, according to the report published this week. While the US maintains a roughly 16-fold advantage in AI training compute over China, leading Chinese models lag their American rivals by only 6.5 months, the report said. IFP pointed to distillation – where developers train systems on the outputs of superior AI models – as a key factor helping China close the gap. China has previously rejected US allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation by domestic developers as groundless. In light of the findings, the institute urged US policymakers to impose stricter controls on overseas cloud access, chip smuggling and legal exports. A separate report published on Tuesday by the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy stated that US-designed compute power remained legally available for rent to foreign entities otherwise barred from buying the hardware. The Washington-based policy group called on the US Bureau of Industry and Security to restrict Chinese access to cloud capacity large enough for training frontier AI models or running them at scale, while advocating for stronger checks on customer identity and ownership. While chip exports are subject to licensing restrictions, Washington moved in January to allow case-by-case export reviews for Nvidia’s H200, Advanced Micro Devices’ MI325X and comparable processors under security conditions. American exporters must show that sales would not divert supply from US customers, while Chinese buyers must adopt formal export compliance procedures and submit chips for independent testing within the US. Meanwhile, Chinese tech giants are scrambling to bolster domestic alternatives. Huawei Technologies last month said its Ascend 960DT chip, designed for AI model training, would become available in the first quarter of 2027 – three quarters ahead of its original schedule. The Shenzhen-based firm revealed that more than 1,000 of its Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoDs had already been deployed, while its Atlas 950 system had entered large-scale commercial use. These cluster architectures link thousands of individual processors to handle demanding AI workloads. However, scaling domestic hardware production remains a challenge. In an updated report last month, San Francisco-based research group Epoch AI identified high-bandwidth memory – a crucial component for feeding data to AI chips – as the main constraint on Huawei’s output. Epoch AI estimated that Huawei’s chip output this year would deliver less than 4 per cent of the computing power of Nvidia’s global shipments.

title: Reflections | How Confucius’ teachings about morality still apply today and what we can learn from them
description: Confucius died in 479BC, but the Analects, the foundational text of his teachings, offers wisdom that remains strikingly relevant today.
content: We recently hosted visitors from Malaysia at our place in the Czech Republic, happily guiding them around Prague and several places beyond the capital, including a few that were new to us, too. There was much conviviality as the six of us explored beautiful Czech cities and towns, sampled hearty local cuisine and slipped effortlessly into the distinctive Malaysian-Singaporean patois – a lively hybrid of English, Chinese, Malay and some Indian vocabulary and syntax – that comes naturally to many of us back home. It was a lovely 10 days, and it brought to mind a famous Chinese rhetorical question: “Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?” The line comes from the Analects, the foundational collection of teachings by Kongzi (551-479BC), better known in the West as Confucius. The Analects is a collection of sayings and conversations attributed to Kongzi and his disciples, compiled by his students and later followers. Its 20 chapters span politics, ethics, education and philosophy. For anyone wishing to understand Kongzi, it is among the most direct and important surviving sources. That famous line about friends from afar opens “Xue Er”, the first chapter of the Analects. The full passage, translated by Scottish linguist James Legge (1815-1897), reads: “The Master [referring to Kongzi] said, ‘Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?’” In many ways, “Xue Er” is a compact guide to living a moral life. It considers not only learning and friendship but also filial duty, humility, self-discipline, integrity, the proper conduct of a gentleman and the relationship between material circumstances and moral character. The chapter comprises 16 short passages, presented as separate observations rather than a continuous argument. Together they sketch a coherent vision of self-cultivation. When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them Confucius Kongzi stresses respect for parents and elders, diligence in work, restraint in speech and the importance of correcting one’s faults. He also warns against being preoccupied with whether others recognise one’s worth: the greater concern, he suggests, is whether we ourselves understand and appreciate others. The emphasis is on character expressed through everyday conduct rather than abstract ideals. Several of the observations in this chapter remain strikingly relevant. “Filial piety and fraternal submission – are they not the root of all benevolent actions?” Kongzi asks, placing family relationships as the foundation of moral character. “He who aims to be a man of complete virtue … is earnest in what he is doing, and careful in his speech” could almost serve as modern workplace advice: take your responsibilities seriously and watch what you say to whom. And then there is the practical injunction: “When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.” In an age obsessed with appearing flawless, being honest about one’s mistakes and letting them go remains remarkably liberating advice. Kongzi also considers attitudes towards wealth and poverty. It is commendable, he says, to remain neither servile in poverty nor arrogant in prosperity. But when his disciple Zigong asks whether there is something higher still, Kongzi points to a more demanding ideal: to remain joyful despite poverty and courteous despite wealth. Circumstances may change, but character need not. That, perhaps, is the enduring charm of “Xue Er” and the Analects as a whole. It speaks less like a remote philosophical treatise than like a wise and patient teacher, concerned with the small choices through which a life is shaped. More than 2,000 years later, its wisdom can still feel remarkably intimate – and, after 10 happy days with friends from afar, particularly apt.

title: Wales, Australia, managing David Silva all part of Sha Tin coach’s rich tapestry
description: Tom Ballantyne’s journey through the world of football has not been a normal one, which is why Hong Kong move ‘felt like stars aligning’.
content: Tom Ballantyne was playing a pre-season friendly for Welsh club Monmouth Town when he “got clattered” and sustained a tibia plateau fracture. “I broke my knee joint, essentially,” Ballantyne said. “I never played again”. So began a life investment in coaching that would see Ballantyne stacking supermarket shelves overnight, then spending long days on the grass. He has been employed by Cardiff City and Aston Villa, and managed in three of Australia’s six states. The Englishman was the man Jim Wong Chi-chuen, the lateral-thinking Supreme Sha Tin owner, chose from a mountain of candidates this month to replace Kenneth Kwok Kar-lok as manager. Accepting that at first glance Ballantyne’s CV did not stand up against some of the other applicants, Wong said: “I love him – he has a great character and philosophy.” Head coach at Devonport City in Tasmania for the past five years, the 41-year-old Ballantyne was not concerned about joining a club where his predecessor lasted just four games. “It’s football; if you don’t do well, you get fired,” he said. “If you do well, you’re safe in your job. “I’ve just left a club where we were expected to win every game. If we drew, there’d be meetings about it. I’m lucky, I’ve been in full-time football for 15 years and never been sacked.” Undergoing a crash course in Supreme, Ballantyne quickly discovered that Wong would be part of his squad. “I just thought, ‘OK, the chairman plays’ … there are different things to deal with wherever you are,” Ballantyne said. “Back in 1992, Alex Ferguson had his son [Darren] in the Manchester United team.” From the market town of Ross-on-Wye, Ballantyne played for Ross Town, and “dabbled with Hereford United”. “Not having the traditional background of an elite player, I knew I would have to forge my own coaching route,” he said. Instead of going to university, he “worked nights in a supermarket, so I could coach during the day”, meaning he often survived on just two hours’ sleep. “I also watched as many sessions as I could,” he added. “I’d go wherever I could be part of training, or pick up someone’s cones.” Backpacking around Australia at 21, Ballantyne grew “intrigued with the coaching process” in the country. “It was tactically driven from very young,” he said. “I arrived expecting them to be behind [the UK], but, coaching wise, they were ahead. It’s why you see so many Australians coaching around the world.” After returning home, Ballantyne immediately began collecting his coaching badges and “it took off from there”. During one course, Dennis Mortimer, Aston Villa’s 1982 European Cup-winning captain, invited Ballantyne to work as a development and community coach at the club. Concurrently, he held coaching posts with Cardiff, Cheltenham Town and the Herefordshire Football Association. “I spent lots of time on the road, but I had to keep saying yes to things,” Ballantyne said. “The sheer number of sessions I coached over a short period of time, covering real amateurs to elite kids, and everything in between, meant I had to learn very fast. You had to adapt, sometimes on the fly, and it gave me a fantastic foundation.” In 2012, Ballantyne chose an offer to become Adelaide United’s head academy coach over one from the English FA to coach in disability football at Chelsea’s Cobham training headquarters. “I probably rushed my decision,” he said. “My wife’s from Australia and we jumped at it … it was a good experience, but I had to set up [the academy]. Bits were in place, but it wasn’t what I thought I was getting into.” Nonetheless, the role led to Ballantyne also coaching Sturt Marion Women’s Soccer Club, a post he held for almost 5½ years. With Devonport, he managed both the men’s and women’s teams. Ballantyne said that in “walking between the two worlds” he heeded the words of two-time World Cup winner Mia Hamm, who said she wanted to be “coached like a man, and treated like a woman”. “Coaching women, you have to explain why we’re going to do something,” Ballantyne said. “With the men, you tell them what to do, then go from there.” Adelaide club, The Cove, gave a 28-year-old Ballantyne his first senior head coach job, although that came with the daunting prospect of “trying to sell a vision to a bunch of people who’d already had a coach that season”. After six years in South Australia, and another two managing Magpie Crusaders United in Queensland, Ballantyne moved to Tasmania for his hugely decorated Devonport stint. “Each state plays very different football, so it’s been good for my learning,” he said. “In South Australia, it’s a slow, tactical, Italian-style game. Queensland’s very transitional football, and in Tasmania it’s very English: the ball’s in the air a lot, and it’s about first and second contacts.” Ballantyne’s “very understanding” wife has been a “football widow since we met”, but even her patience was tested when her husband was given 90 minutes notice for his Supreme interview. “We were watching my son play football,” he said. “We were 70 minutes from home. I took the car, and told my wife she’d have to find her own way back.” Ballantyne was attracted by the “really exciting project” Wong had in mind, and with a similar football ethos said “it felt like the stars were aligning”. Supreme recently made a splash when they tempted former Manchester City and Spain forward David Silva out of retirement to play for the club, albeit in a single encounter against BC Rangers on November 7. On the prospect of coaching a man who counts Pep Guardiola, Unai Emery and Roberto Mancini as former bosses, Ballantyne said: “I think other people are more worried about it than I am. “As far as I’m concerned, he’s a football player who I have to manage and have conversations with. It’s a great opportunity for everybody here, and I’m looking forward to it.” With pop-star ambassadors in local girl group Collar and live music at home games, newly promoted Supreme are averaging four-figure attendances. They attracted 3,329 and 4,592 for games at Mong Kok Stadium against Eastern and Lee Man, respectively, and hope for more when Silva runs out for them at 5,000-seat Kai Tak Youth Sports Ground. “Fair play to Jim for being brave enough to do it,” Ballantyne said. “It brings numbers, which increases revenue and introduces better players. That’s what needs to happen for Hong Kong football.” A 2-2 draw against Football Club in his first match last weekend arrested a run of three straight league defeats. “We want to quickly improve our level, then sign players over the next couple of transfer windows who raise our ceiling,” Ballantyne said. “We have some young players who excite us, and this is a long-term project. It’s all I’m focused on. I’ll only think about what’s next when it runs its natural course, whether that’s me being fired or another opportunity coming along.”

title: Our cheat sheet for the best things to do in Hong Kong, October 24-November 8
description: Reimagine the world through centuries of Asian fantasy at M+’s “Myth and Monsters” exhibition, indulge in an Argentinian feast at Buenos Aires Polo Club’s Polo Brunch, sample the “Taste of Gin-dulgence” experience at K11 Musea and K11 Art Mall and up your costume game for Ocean Park Halloween Fest 2026.
content: SEE THIS Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia Enter a realm of legends, folklore and storytelling at “Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia”, the latest special exhibition at M+. Running until April 4, 2027, the show examines how fantasy, mythology and the supernatural have shaped Asian art, cinema and popular culture. Curated into four sections – “Spirits Among Us”, delving into premodern beliefs and ancient tales; “Strange Realities”, exploring surreal perspectives and human imagination; “From Godzilla to Ghost in the Shell”, highlighting cinematic creations and sci-fi tropes; and “New Mythologies”, reflecting contemporary responses to anime and manga – there are more than 400 works on display, spanning visual art, architecture, fashion, video games and moving images. M+, 38 Museum Drive, West Kowloon Cultural District. For tickets, click here EAT THIS Buenos Aires Polo Club If you’re up for a grand weekend feast, Buenos Aires Polo Club’s Polo Brunch is an opulent option to put on your list. Black Sheep Restaurants’ Argentinian steakhouse experience, inspired by 20th century equestrian clubs, is available on Saturdays and features an indulgent menu that begins with a buffet of appetisers, a raw-seafood bar, a build-your-own salad counter and an eggs-your-way station, where omelettes and the like are made to order. It’s the asado-style Black Angus rib-eye carving table you want to save space for, though. Messina gelato and a selection of cakes await at the end. 7/F, 33 Wyndham Street, Central DRINK THIS Taste of Gin-dulgence Gourmands can embark on a curated journey of “cuisine meets cocktails” with “Taste of Gin-dulgence” at K11 Musea and K11 Art Mall, in celebration of Hong Kong’s first handcrafted-gin distillery, Two Moons. Across 12 dining destinations, dishes are paired with bespoke tipples made with various Two Moons releases, including concoctions such as the ginger-yuzu-driven Moonlit, alongside Unagi Yondaime Kikukawa’s signature grilled eel; the Salisbury Jade, with notes of calamansi, lime and watercress honey, served with deep-fried shrimp balls at Yung’s Bistro; and the smoky, bittersweet Dandy Butcher, to complement Glasshouse Greenery’s barbecue Peking duck pizza. Victoria Dockside, 18 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui; 18 Hanoi Road, Tsim Sha Tsui DO THIS Ocean Park Halloween Fest 2026 Ocean Park has transformed into the place for ghouls and gals to be this Halloween. With a themed party running until November 1, one of this year’s highlights is the debut of K-pop star Jackson Wang Ka-yee’s “Under the Castle”, a “haunted experience” featuring a neon-lit masquerade that fractures into a disorienting mirror labyrinth. Guests can also race alongside spooky characters in “Dark Ride: Bumper Blaster”, step into fan-favourite attractions such as the “Voodoo Boo Terror Park”, catch performances by underworld boy band Demoon King and encounter over 120 roaming spirits in the “Hong Kong Paranormal Barrier”. title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s taxi reform progresses but has far to go
description: While the demerit system has produced results, enforcement alone cannot improve an industry facing wider structural problems.
content: From ageing fleets and drivers to the likes of Uber making inroads, taxi services around the world face an array of challenges. In Hong Kong, drivers complain about unfair competition and regulatory reform pressure. At the same time, they continue to be the target of complaints in relation to refusing rides, rude service, overcharging and taking circuitous routes. In response, the government has taken steps to regulate ride-hailing platforms and introduce premium taxi fleets to enhance service quality, along with compulsory training and disqualification from driving cabs under a demerit point system. Two years into enforcement, the Taxi-Driver-Offence Points system has produced some results. As of October 2, a total of 229 taxi drivers had incurred demerit points, with 125 cases, or 55 per cent, involving a refusal to accept a hire. Three drivers were disqualified for three months after incurring 15 points or more, according to data submitted to the Legislative Council. Introduced in September 2024, the system aims to strengthen the deterrent effect on driver malpractice, thereby enhancing service quality and the overall image of the trade. Taxi drivers will receive three, five or 10 demerit points for each of the 11 types of misconduct and can be disqualified from driving a taxi for three months upon accumulating 15 points or more within two years. Repeat offenders face a six-month suspension. Of the 229 cases, 158, or about 70 per cent, have accumulated 10 to 14 points; while five have reached 15 points or more. Thirteen drivers have three points while 53 have accumulated five to nine points. Those with 10 points or more are required to take a taxi service improvement course at their own expense. The offences include overcharging, refusing hires, driving to a destination other than by the most direct practicable route, soliciting, refusing or neglecting to issue a receipt, not setting the taxi meter properly, and deceiving or refusing to inform a passenger or intending passenger as to the proper fare and route to any place. The figures are not surprising. Yet the volume of complaints indicates enforcement and service-culture reform still need to keep pace. Between the scheme’s introduction and August this year, the Transport Department received 5,944 complaints against taxi drivers, of which 605 involved refusal of hire. But when 125 drivers have been penalised for refusal of hire and only three have been disqualified, the mechanism may be perceived as lacking teeth. With the average daily taxi patronage near 1 million, the number of drivers caught under the demerit system may seem modest. Arguably, it would be unfair to treat the misconduct of individual drivers as the collective failure of the industry. But the thousands of complaints lodged over the past two years show service standards still leave a lot to be desired. Whether more drivers will eventually be suspended remains to be seen. The demerit system is well intentioned in that it distinguishes between an early warning, a mid-stage remedial education mandate and eventual removal from the road. It is also a progressive approach that gives drivers an incentive to correct conduct before the ultimate sanction applies. Separately, a new journey recording system, comprising the functions of a dash camera, an in-vehicle recording system and a global navigation satellite system, will be gradually installed in taxi compartments starting from this year to deter malpractice. But enforcement alone cannot improve the trade. Hong Kong’s taxi industry faces wider structural problems: an ageing fleet and workforce, pressure to keep up with technological applications, growing competition from ride-hailing platforms, uneven service quality and an overly protective licensing system. The demerit system is just part of a wider revamp that has been long overdue. A new premium taxi scheme has been up and running for more than a year, along with the ongoing efforts to legalise personalised point-to-point transport services provided by ride-hailing platforms. Belated as they are, the reforms are important steps to improve accountability, vehicle standards and passenger choice.

title: How procrastination can harm your physical and mental health, and practical tips to stop it
description: Experts say procrastination has serious health and financial consequences. Manage your emotions, not time, to break the cycle.
content: “Have you made that doctor’s appointment about the lump on your back yet?” your spouse asks. You sheepishly mumble that you have not. Walking past a packed wardrobe – a daily reminder of a decluttering project put off for months – you settle onto the sofa to finish binge-watching that new Netflix series. Sound familiar? Procrastination is no big deal; everyone puts off tasks they don’t want to do, right? Wrong, according to Fuschia Sirois, a professor of social and health psychology at Durham University in the UK. Sirois has spent more than 25 years studying procrastination and, while research shows about one in four people procrastinates fairly regularly, she warns the behaviour carries serious, far-reaching consequences. “The harms of procrastination can range from poor career progression and reduced earnings to poor mental health, including higher rates of anxiety, stress and depression, even poor physical health,” Sirois says. Although most of us view procrastination as a minor personal quirk, its physical toll can be severe. Unchecked, chronic delay can compromise immune function, leaving people vulnerable to flus and colds. It also fuels stress-related ailments such as insomnia, headaches and more serious conditions, including hypertension and cardiovascular disease. As Sirois summarises: “In short, procrastination increases risk for poor financial, physical and mental health.” What is procrastination? Part of the issue is that popular culture misunderstands procrastination. Most self-help guides treat it as a time management problem, offering scheduling systems and organisation hacks. But Sirois says this misses the point: procrastination is not putting things off because we are running out of hours in the day; we do it to dodge uncomfortable emotions. We are not avoiding the work itself but the negative feelings it triggers. Preparing tax filings, for instance, evokes anxiety or misery over personal finances. We put off sending a simple email not because writing it is difficult, but because we fear a recipient’s angry reaction. “Back in 2013, we reframed the underlying causes of procrastination as being due to difficulties with emotion regulation,” Sirois says. “Simply put, emotions are ground zero for procrastination. When a task gives rise to uncomfortable emotions that we feel ill-equipped to manage internally, we instead manage these externally by putting the task aside and procrastinating, which affords us immediate relief from those difficult and negative emotions.” To understand why this happens, researchers distinguish between simple delay and true procrastination. In her 2022 book Procrastination: What It Is, Why It’s a Problem, and What You Can Do About It, Sirois explains that procrastination is an unnecessary, voluntary delay of an important task, done despite knowing that the delay will likely cause problems down the line. Postponing a task to prioritise a more urgent one is smart scheduling, not procrastination. Delays caused by factors outside your control, like the sudden need to visit a loved one in hospital, don’t count either. What makes procrastination so quietly destructive is self-awareness: you know that delaying will hurt your future self, yet you do it anyway. “In procrastination, you delay the task despite knowing on some level that this delay will cause harm for yourself and/or others,” Sirois says. “The key point here is that procrastination is a form of harmful delay.” The roots of procrastination This self-defeating impulse is rooted in human neuroscience. When a task triggers negative emotions or feels threatening, the brain’s threat centre – the amygdala – activates. This survival mechanism forces our attention onto immediate mood repair, making it difficult to weigh the downstream consequences of our choices. This short-term focus shows up in familiar ways. For example, we swap a daunting assignment for immediate moments of happiness, whether that means watching funny cat videos, suddenly feeling an urge to clean the kitchen or meticulously reorganising a desk from top to bottom. Crucially, this is an automatic emotional defence mechanism, not a deliberate, calculated choice. “People often blame the task for their procrastination,” Sirois says. “While we know from the research that tasks that are complex or ambiguous or lack structure are more likely to be procrastinated, even tasks that objectively do not appear difficult or that have those qualities can be procrastinated. This means that it has more to do with how we interact with the task and the difficult emotions that the task evokes in us than the nature of the task itself.” This emotional short cut relies on a psychological disconnect from our future selves. Research shows that students are notorious procrastinators; many delay studying until the last minute, setting themselves up for sleep deprivation, extreme stress and academic failure. Despite clear warnings from educators, they repeat the pattern because the human brain tends to view the future self as almost a stranger or separate person. Pushing a stressful burden onto tomorrow feels like passing it off to someone else. “It’s this disconnection from the future self that makes it easier for people prone to procrastination to see the future self more like a stranger than a temporal extension of the present self,” Sirois says. “This is why we don’t feel more compassionate to our future self and end up making that future self our beast of burden.” We falsely convince ourselves that our future self will somehow be better able or more motivated to handle the task, even though that is usually not the case. How do we stop procrastinating? Breaking this habit requires shifting our focus from time management to mood management. “The main thing is to find healthier ways to manage difficult or uncomfortable emotions rather than defaulting to procrastination as a way to gain relief from these emotions,” Sirois says. To break the emotional loop, Sirois recommends targeted strategies centred on self-compassion and emotional awareness: Practise self-compassion: Beating yourself up for putting things off adds another layer of guilt and stress, which triggers further task avoidance – leading to an “emotional spiral”. Treating yourself with grace lowers emotional tension and enables you to focus on what needs to be done more quickly. Cultivate mindfulness: Simple mindfulness exercises help you notice and sit with uncomfortable feelings – such as self-doubt, boredom or confusion – without reflexively running away from them. This helps keep emotions in balance. Find meaning in work: Identifying a deeper purpose or personal value in a tedious task helps build tolerance for the temporary discomfort it causes. Develop future self-empathy: Before putting a project off, visualise how taking action today directly helps the version of you waking up tomorrow or next week, treating that future version of yourself with empathy rather than neglect. For more help, Sirois has developed the free online toolkit Tempo, for Taming Emotions to Manage Procrastination Openheartedly. It offers science-based practical exercises to manage the emotional triggers behind delays, providing a structured guide to help you stop putting things off. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Inside NBA star Trae Young’s US$700,000 watch collection, from Rolex to Hublot
description: The Washington Wizards point guard went from collecting G-Shocks when he was 10 to owning custom timepieces from Rolex, Pristine Jewellers and more.
content: Four-time NBA All-Star Trae Young has a watch collection as impressive as his basketball career. The 28-year-old, who signed a four-year US$212 million deal with the Washington Wizards in June this year, sat down with Robertino Altieri, CEO and founder of second-hand luxury watch dealers, WatchGuys, in an exclusive episode of Altieri’s video series, My Collection, to talk about his stunning watch rotation valued at around US$700,000. Young’s love for timepieces started when he was only 10, years before he made his NBA millions. “I was into G-Shocks early on ... We had a Best Buy in Oklahoma, and they had watches there. All the malls in Norman where I grew up. That was kind of like the most affordable watch for kids, and, and people were kind of starting to like and watch it,” Young said during the interview. “That was like what was really cool to me at the time. So I knew I was always into watches at that point.” Since then, the basketball star, known by his nickname “Ice Trae” given by rapper Quavo in reference to his 2017 track “Ice Tray”, has traded up his G-Shock for heavy hitters from Rolex, Audemars Piguet and more. Here’s a breakdown of some of his stand-out pieces. Rolex Datejust (custom turquoise dial) A Rolex Datejust, averaging at US$10,000, is typically considered an “entry-level” piece for watch enthusiasts.
