Signed by FIE secretary general Gulnora Saidova, the statement also pointed to the federation’s statutes that forbid fencers from competing in unofficial events, with international bans among the punishments available to the governing body. Saidova’s letter could set her on a collision course with some of the most influential people in the sport, with FIE vice-president Donald Anthony Jnr, and Hong Kong fencing chief Antonio Lam Hin-chung both backing the league, which held its inaugural event in Los Angeles. The brainchild of Miles Chamley-Watson, April’s US event attracted 12 fencers from eight countries and regions, including Hong Kong’s Ryan Choi Chun-yin, plus a host of A-list celebrities. Speaking to the South China Morning Post during the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong in July, Anthony Jnr said the WFL probably hoped it would “be able to continue to move forward”. “I think the FIE is going to move forward as fast,” he added. “I see this growing the sport and working together to build fencing to be the best sport you could possibly be.” The American official said the existence of private leagues could be a good thing for the sport, depending on “how it’s done”. “If it’s done in the right way, then it’s a great thing you do, because we need as much visibility as possible,” he said. “It’s like those organisations that have professionals, and they work together, and they work under the International Olympic Committee, FIE, and they’re all working together. They’re very successful. “Look at Fifa. Look at Fiba with the NBA. That is a working model when you’ve seen it work. So if it’s done correctly, it’s good for the whole sport. And they can coexist. “They should be able to coexist as long as they do the right thing. I don’t see any professional sports not existing when they’re done correctly.” Hong Kong fencing bosses, meanwhile, said while they had no official role in next year’s competition, they also had no objections to it taking place. “From our perspective, this kind of event is going to help promote the sport of fencing, so we welcome it, as long as it is nicely and neatly organised,” said Lam, the general secretary of the Fencing Association of Hong Kong, China, said. That feeling was echoed by the city’s foil head coach Greg Koenig, who earlier this year called the league a “positive move” for the sport. As part of the move to drum up interest in the WFL, two-time Olympic champion Cheung Ka-long, compatriot Kaylin Hsieh Sin-yan, WFL founder and decorated American foilist Chamley-Watson, and French sabreist Sebastien Patrice are expected to take part in an exclusive invitational exhibition in Hong Kong in January. Zhen Renteo, the league’s CEO, said Los Angeles had proved there was a demand for “fencing presented this way”, while starting the new season in Hong Kong was “a statement about where the future of fencing is heading”. “Seeing Ryan Choi win in LA in front of that crowd told us exactly where we needed to go next,” Chamley-Watson added. “We’re not creating a moment, we’re creating a legacy and Hong Kong is the next chapter.” It is not the first time a commercial league has clashed with a sport’s world governing body. In 2018, the International Swimming League (ISL) claimed Fina, now World Aquatics, had led a boycott of its event, forcing its cancellation. Earlier this year, the ISL was awarded a US$1 settlement in a US lawsuit over anti-trust issues, having claimed anti-competitive behaviour by the global governing body damaged its business interests. It had been asking for US$41 million in damages. The ISL is expected to return in December, with an all-star exhibition event at the London Aquatics Centre.

title: Girl arrested after taking US$111 from Russia to poison Ukrainian troops
description: Two soldiers died from poisoning after consuming ‘free drugs’ containing a lethal dose of methadone sent by the teen suspect.
content: Ukrainian police said on Friday they had detained a 17-year-old girl suspected of helping Russia’s security services to poison Ukrainian soldiers and that two had died. Ukraine and Russia have throughout their war since 2022 accused each other of recruiting minors for sabotage acts including poisoning. The girl, who was not named, is suspected of having packaged deadly drugs and sending them to Ukrainian soldiers she contacted by Telegram, a police statement said. She was arrested by police in Zhytomyr, west of Kyiv, after allegedly following instructions from a Russian handler in exchange for at least 5,000 hryvnias (US$111), they said. After receiving packages with “free drugs”, the soldiers were “instructed to take them on camera”, the statement said. “The recipients did not know that the capsules contained a lethal dose of methadone,” it said, adding that “two soldiers died from poisoning in the Zhytomyr region”. Police said they had identified other recipients of the packages, which “prevented four more murders” across the country. “The young woman was notified that she is suspected of aiding and abetting the premeditated murder of two people as part of a prior conspiracy,” the police statement said. She was also suspected of “shipping drugs and psychotropic substances for the purpose of distribution”, it said, adding that she faced up to 15 years in jail if found guilty. Police cautioned that Russia aims “to kill our people and destabilise the situation within the country”. “Do not accept medication or other substances, as well as food or drinks of dubious origin, from people you do not know well,” police said. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian authorities say they have opened thousands of investigations into collaboration with the enemy and frequently arrest individuals accused of working for Moscow. In 2023, Ukraine accused Russia of poisoning the wife of Kyrylo Budanov, who was then head of Ukraine’s military intelligence and is now a presidential adviser.

title: Former HSBC insurance veteran Edward Moncreiffe joins AIA in latest senior talent move
description: Appointment follows Mark Tucker’s return to AIA last year, as insurers compete for affluent clients seeking wealth and succession solutions.
content: Former HSBC Holdings global insurance head Edward Moncreiffe will join rival AIA Group as regional CEO from November 2, following a path taken by former HSBC Group chairman Mark Tucker, who returned to the Asia-Pacific region’s largest insurer as non-executive chairman last year. Moncreiffe will oversee AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand, while serving on the group’s executive committee, according to a company statement issued on Friday. He will report to group CEO and president Lee Yuan Siong. After 20 years at HSBC, Moncreiffe resigned as global insurance CEO in August. During his tenure, the lender’s insurance business became Hong Kong’s market leader in new life insurance premiums for four consecutive years and sold a record-breaking US$250 million life insurance policy in February 2024. He is the second high-profile executive to move from HSBC to AIA. Tucker became AIA’s non-executive chairman in October last year after serving as the insurer’s group CEO and president between 2010 and 2017. The appointment highlights intensifying competition for senior talent in the insurance and wealth management sector in Hong Kong and Asia, as growing numbers of wealthy customers use insurance products for wealth preservation and succession planning. “I am delighted to be joining AIA, a company distinguished by its exceptional franchise, clear purpose and long-term commitment to Asia,” Moncreiffe said. “AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand each have distinct strengths, priorities and opportunities,” he said, adding that he would work with his new team to deliver long-term value for customers, partners and shareholders. Moncreiffe holds a bachelor’s degree from Durham University and a master of business administration from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. He is also a chartered insurer. Lee said Moncreiffe’s “extensive international experience and strong track record of growing businesses and strengthening market positions” would help accelerate AIA’s next phase of growth. Kenrick Chung Kin-keung, CEO of Hong Kong-based insurance broker Equator Asset Protection, said AIA and other local insurance companies were looking to expand their top teams to take advantage of robust growth in demand. “Hong Kong has seen strong growth in life insurance sales over the past few years as wealthy mainlanders and other high-net-worth customers are coming to the city to buy policies for high investment return and succession planning,” Chung said. Life insurance sales in Hong Kong rose 58 per cent to reach a record HK$275.16 billion (US$35.3 billion) in the first half of 2026, according to data from the Insurance Authority on Friday. This was the fourth consecutive year in which first-half sales hit a record high. But the industry is also facing challenges as Beijing tightens controls on cross-border investment, with financial firms now requiring investment ­clients to declare if their source of funding is from outside the mainland. In August, several major mainland cities, including Shanghai, started collecting a 20 per cent levy on gains from offshore insurance policies. Chung, however, said that as long as the industry could provide products that offered good returns after tax, Hong Kong insurance sales should continue to grow.

title: Netanyahu orders West Bank closure after attack on Israelis ends in gun battle
description: Netanyahu warned of a major military operation in the territory after two Palestinian assailants killed two Israeli soldiers near Hebron.
content: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened a military operation in the occupied West Bank on a scale unseen in decades after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers on Friday in an attack near Hebron days before the national election. A first step would see residents displaced, homes searched and “terrorist infrastructure” destroyed, said Netanyahu, who is in the midst of a tight race for a new term in Tuesday’s vote. Militant group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised the attack as a “heroic operation” and called on supporters to carry out more. A gun battle broke out on Friday morning at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near the West Bank city of Hebron between soldiers and two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle. Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers, with the gunmen’s bodies lying on the ground next to a petrol station as troops patrolled all around. The army later said two of its soldiers “fell in combat in the Judea Junction” area near Hebron, with three others wounded. Rescuers had previously said five people were wounded, two of them seriously. Netanyahu lauded the soldiers’ response, crediting them with having “prevented what could have been a major attack” and ordered a lockdown in the West Bank. He added that troops were “carrying out stepped-up operations to thwart terrorist activities and are conducting large-scale waves of arrests”. Visiting Hebron later in the day, Netanyahu said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were “considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since” the 1967 Arab-Israeli war, in which Israel first occupied the Palestinian territory. “The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way,” he added. A first operation would see Israeli forces “enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure”. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the UN said forcibly displaced thousands. With the clock counting down to election day, Netanyahu ordered all Likud party political events to be cancelled on Friday. The military said it had “launched offensive counterterrorism operations in the Hebron area”, adding that troops were raiding homes of the suspects and others. Before Netanyahu’s announcement, far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich had called for a fresh military offensive in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”. “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists,” said Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry. “In the next government, this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.” He later said he had “ordered the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”. National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir also called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be “dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely”. No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian government in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was connected to Friday’s attack. Hamas, which carried out the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war, hailed Friday’s shooting and mourned the dead assailants. The Gaza-based group, a rival of the Palestinian Authority’s ruling Fatah faction, called the shooting a “natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people”. It called on supporters to “mobilise fully and turn the land into a fire beneath the feet of the invaders”. Netanyahu vowed to “pursue Hamas terrorists” everywhere, adding: “You have no place to hide.” Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, also praised the response by troops and said he was praying “for the complete and quick recovery of the injured”. The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters. According to an Agence France-Presse tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023. Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

title: Citigroup gets Beijing’s approval for wholly owned securities firm in China
description: Long-awaited move to make Citi seventh foreign securities firm owner in mainland China, where stock markets are worth US$15.6 trillion.
content: US bank Citigroup has received approval to set up a wholly foreign-owned securities firm in mainland China, allowing the lender to pursue more opportunities in one of the world’s largest capital markets. The long-awaited green light was given by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) on Friday, and ahead of an expected meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen next month. The nod also follows Visa winning approval for a wholly foreign-owned clearing organisation in China last week. Citigroup would be the seventh foreign player with a wholly owned securities firm in the country. Mainland China has 240 million investors, and the combined market capitalisation of its exchanges is US$15.6 trillion. The bank’s global CEO Jane Fraser said the new licence would provide the lender greater capacity to serve mainland customers. “Citi has been serving clients in China for nearly 125 years, and we appreciate the support from regulators to expand our offering in this important market,” Fraser said in a statement on Friday. “By adding onshore capabilities to our global platform, we will be able to do more for clients in China’s domestic capital markets, including helping them raise capital, access investors and trade locally, while connecting them to opportunities around the world.” Called Citigroup Securities (China), the Shanghai-headquartered firm will offer a wide range of services to both domestic and foreign clients, including underwriting capital market deals, equities brokering, providing direct access to China stock exchanges and other financial products, according to a statement from Citigroup. Citi has helped its Chinese clients raise more than US$40 billion this year in global capital markets, the lender said. This is likely to build up good momentum for the upcoming meeting between the two leaders Wilson Chan Fung-cheung, City University The firm will also offer securities research, investment advisory and trading of shares, bonds, funds and other financial instruments listed onshore, Citigroup said. “Citi will complete all statutory and regulatory procedures required to establish the securities company and prepare for the commencement of operations,” the US lender said. The CSRC said Citigroup Securities (China) will be registered in Shanghai, with registered capital at 1.2 billion yuan (US$180 million). “The wholly owned securities licence shows China’s commitment to continue to open up its market to foreign players,” said Wilson Chan Fung-cheung, an adjunct professor at City University. “The approval came just ahead of the meeting of the two presidents, and right after Hong Kong has successfully hosted the two-day Apec finance ministers’ meeting this week. This is likely to build up good momentum for the upcoming meeting between the two leaders,” Chan said. Fraser joined Trump’s high-powered delegation of business executives in May for the US president’s first visit to China in nearly a decade. During that visit, Wu Qing, chairman of the CSRC, met with Fraser in Beijing, where they exchanged views on the global economic and financial landscape and the opening up of China’s capital markets, the commission said on its official website. Citigroup has been seeking a license to establish a wholly owned securities firm in China for several years, since the country relaxed its regulations. The CSRC scrapped a cap on foreign investors in mainland-based securities firms from December 1, 2020, paving the way for foreign institutions to set up wholly owned units to trade securities. Before that, foreign firms could only set up joint ventures with local partners. “Since Citigroup is a big US player, the new licence would be a positive move for the mainland capital market as Citigroup may help bring in more US investors,” said Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary ­president of the Institute of Securities Dealers. Citigroup will join US players JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs, as well as the UK’s Standard Chartered, France’s BNP Paribas, Swiss lender UBS and Japan’s Mizuho Financial Group as the only international companies with wholly owned securities firms on the mainland, according to data from the CSRC. A new securities firm would represent an expansion for Citigroup in China after it recently exited certain businesses as part of a restructuring plan. Citigroup sold its onshore consumer wealth portfolio to HSBC in October 2023, and sold its 20 per cent stake in Chinese lender China Guangfa Bank for about 19.7 billion yuan (US$3 billion) to China Life Insurance Company in 2016. Citi China CEO Zhang Wenjie said the securities company will be an important part of the lender’s strategy in in the country. “It will enrich and enhance our capabilities to serve clients. We will be focusing on building a high-calibre local team and leveraging our global network to support domestic capital market development,” Zhang said.

title: Hong Kong life insurance sales up 58% in first half but tax crackdown threatens momentum
description: Beijing’s enforcement of taxes on overseas insurance gains will lead some mainland customers to ‘think twice’ before buying, says broker.
content: Life insurance sales in Hong Kong rose 58 per cent in the first half of this year to another record high as affluent mainland and overseas customers continued to buy policies in the city for wealth transfer, protection and medical needs. It was the fourth consecutive year in which first half sales hit a record high. The industry wrote HK$275.16 billion (US$35.3 billion) worth of new life insurance policies in the first half, compared with HK$173.7 billion a year earlier, according to data from the Insurance Authority released on Friday. In May, the Chinese government began tightening cross-border investments, which has triggered a sharp drop in offshore spending. To block capital flight, Beijing is now enforcing a strict 20 per cent personal income tax on mainland residents’ offshore trusts and overseas investment gains. This aggressive tax push is backed by a sweeping 34-article Regulation on Outbound Investment and updated rules from the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) designed to stop unapproved money leaving the country. By cracking down on unlicensed online brokerages and making it much harder for mainlanders to open Hong Kong bank accounts, authorities have effectively choked off the outflow of unauthorised private wealth. Additionally, Beijing is aggressively taxing offshore trusts and residents’ overseas income. Kenrick Chung Kin-keung, CEO of Equator Asset Protection, a Hong Kong based insurance broker, said local sales may face headwinds in the second half. “Beijing’s enforcement of taxes on overseas insurance gains would definitely lead some mainland visitors to think twice before buying the products” because it would reduce their returns, Chung said. “But some may still like to buy policies in Hong Kong as they provide better returns than mainland insurance policies even after the tax.” Wilton Kee Wing-tao, CEO of Manulife Hong Kong and Macau, said Hong Kong’s insurance market has continued to grow as a result of the city’s strength as an international insurance and wealth management hub. “Customers have diverse needs across protection, health, retirement and wealth planning,” Kee said. “As these needs become increasingly interconnected, insurers have an even greater role to play in helping customers build financial resilience, safeguard their health and plan confidently for different stages of life.” Kee said Manulife has expanded its medical specialist network sixfold to more than 1,200 experts, while it recently entered into an agreement with Ant Health for a new partnership to develop healthcare and wellness services. HSBC Life remained the top player in the life insurance market in terms of new sales in the first half, with a market share of 24 per cent, according to Insurance Authority data. The insurance unit of HSBC Holdings has taken the lead for the past four years as a whole. Daisy Tsang, CEO of HSBC Life Hong Kong and Macau, said the continued strong growth in insurance sales was driven by demand from both locals and visitors. HSBC Life issued new policies to policyholders in more than 50 markets, mostly in Asia. “This reinforces Hong Kong’s position as a leading international insurance and wealth-management centre,” she said. “We expect offshore customers to become an increasingly important source of growth in the years ahead, supported by Asia’s structural demographic trends, including rising wealth and an ageing population.” Tsang said the industry has seen an increasing number of partnerships with family offices and brokers to help drive wealthy customers to purchase policies in Hong Kong. “High-net-worth customers remain a core segment, with insurance increasingly recognised as an important solution for wealth preservation and legacy planning,” Tsang said. The Insurance Authority has not disclosed data for mainland visitors since last year, citing a review of how to define and identify them alongside other overseas buyers. But industry players said mainland visitors remained a driving force for the insurance market in the city. The number of visitors to Hong Kong rose 13 per cent to 26.7 million in the first half, with 77 per cent coming from mainland China, according to data from the Hong Kong Tourism Board. Many visitors bought insurance and wealth products while in the city, according to industry insiders.

title: Charlie Chaplin’s City Lights gets a ballet spin in Tokyo as classical dance meets comedy
description: In bringing Charlie Chaplin’s 1931 masterpiece to the stage, the National Ballet of Japan challenges perceptions of classical dance.
content: British choreographer Alastair Marriott never expected to turn his childhood love of Charlie Chaplin films into a full-scale production in Tokyo with the National Ballet of Japan. Ballet is often seen as high art: formal and reserved. Chaplin, by contrast, built his comedy on slapstick and mime. During the pandemic, Marriott, who was developing a new production at the time, decided to revisit City Lights, Chaplin’s 1931 masterpiece. In the film, Chaplin’s character, Little Tramp, falls in love with a blind flower seller and exhausts every effort to secure her rent and fund a sight-restoring surgery. “City Lights seemed perfect because there are no words,” Marriott says. “It resonated with what the world went through during the pandemic, when there were all these thoughts from all around the world of people helping each other. It lent itself to a smaller person doing touching things to help their neighbours, family and friends.” Marriott was equally struck by Chaplin’s musical compositions for his films. “He saw his scenes in his films as dances, and they’re very musical and precise,” the London-based choreographer says. “If we go a little bit further, it will make a ballet naturally.” Marriott’s ballet adaptation remains largely faithful to the film, with minor adjustments made for practical purposes, such as omitting the scene where the tramp mistakes a piece of confetti for pasta. New characters include a formidable maid who complements the butler, alongside expanded background narrative explaining how the flower seller falls ill. The choreography combines classical ballet vocabulary with Chaplin’s signature movement style. “Classical ballet is the language that we feel most comfortable with,” Marriott says. “We tell the story in that language, rather than inventing a completely new language. But that doesn’t stop you from bending the rules.” It was hard for classically trained dancers to break out of their training to do [clown-like] gestures Alastair Marriott, choreographer Incorporating English pantomime gestures presented a challenge, as many of the dancers, though aware of who Chaplin was, were unfamiliar with the film. “It’s the way Chaplin held the cane and his acting that made him the Little Tramp,” Marriott explains, referencing the vagrant persona recognisable by his bowler hat, bamboo cane, oversized trousers, toothbrush moustache and flat-footed waddle. “Without those specific nuances, it could just be any homeless person. But it was hard for classically trained dancers to break out of their training to do [clown-like] gestures.” The dancers spent months analysing Chaplin’s physical mannerisms, while Marriott collaborated with Miyako Yoshida, artistic director of the National Ballet of Japan, to refine the choreography. Yoshida, former principal dancer with the Royal Ballet in London from 1995 to 2010 following her career with Sadler’s Wells Royal Ballet (now Birmingham Royal Ballet), is a long-time collaborator of Marriott. The duo collaborated on a highly successful Giselle for the National Ballet of Japan, which won the Stef Stefanou Award for Outstanding Company at the UK’s National Dance Awards 2025, marking the first time a Japanese ballet troupe received the honour. “Miyako sees things that I don’t, and has ideas that you just think, ‘I never thought of that.’ She knows ballerina tricks and how to bourrée a set,” Marriott says with a laugh. “And if I [ask a dancer to] go over there, she’ll be like, ‘She can’t!’” “With narrative ballets, you have to be really natural [like you would act in real life] on stage,” Yoshida says. “But Japanese dancers aren’t used to that. So we keep telling them, ‘Relax and be normal.’” To spur artistic growth, Yoshida is committed to presenting both classical masterworks and contemporary repertoire, even though modern productions can be more challenging to market. The company’s repertoire spans box office staples such as Swan Lake alongside contemporary creations by Nacho Duato and William Forsythe. Yoshida also aims to elevate Japanese companies on the global stage. She feels accessible narrative productions such as City Lights provide a welcoming gateway for audiences. Looking ahead, Marriott and Yoshida plan to develop contemporary ballets inspired by Japanese culture, ranging from local adaptations of classical works to crossover productions combining ballet with kabuki or original narrative ballets based on Japanese folklore. “A dancer’s career is brief,” she says. “I want them to experience as many types of ballet as possible, and I want them to enjoy being a dancer.” City Lights runs from October 23 to November 1, 2026, at Opera Palace, New National Theatre, Tokyo. For more information, visit nntt.jac.go.jp.

title: Indian para swimmer sent home from Japan over misconduct allegations, could face life ban
description: Ex-world No 1 Mohammad Shams Aalam Shaikh accused of molesting a female hotel employee and was detained by Japanese police.
content: Former world No 1 Indian para swimmer Mohammad Shams Aalam Shaikh has been sent home from Japan after being accused of molesting a female hotel employee during the Asian Para Games, and faces a potential lifetime ban. According to local media reports as well as The Times of India, the 40-year-old athlete was detained by Japanese police and released after submitting a written apology, before being sent back to India on Tuesday. Official sources said the incident occurred on Monday at the Four Points by Sheraton hotel, where the Indian para swimming team are staying. The female employee was reportedly carrying out housekeeping duties inside the athlete’s room at the time. A senior Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) official who travelled with the delegation to Nagoya and who helped handle the matter confirmed the incident to local media. “When we reached the hotel, the police and senior hotel managers were already there. “We were told that the athlete had inappropriately touched the female housekeeping staff member, made sexually coloured gestures, attempted to grope her and made sexual advances. She rushed out and informed her superiors. This is what we were told by the police and hotel staff,” the source said. After being taken to a local police station in Nagoya, Shaikh was released, moved to another hotel, and placed on the earliest flight back to India after the delegation issued a written apology to the victim and Games organisers intervened to avert formal arrest proceedings. “Aalam is staring at no less than a lifetime ban for bringing disrepute to the entire Indian delegation participating at the Asian Para Games and for embarrassing the country on the world stage,” the official said. Describing the alleged conduct as “reprehensible and intolerable”, the official added that there was “no justification” for an athlete representing their country in an international event to behave in such a manner. The official noted that the ordeal diverted senior officials’ attention away from the Games themselves. “Instead of focusing on the Games and our athletes’ performances, we spent several hours at the police station and later at the hotel premises convincing the authorities. We were embarrassed in front of everyone,” the official said. He added that the female employee appeared deeply shaken when the delegation returned to the hotel. Hotel management and local organisers demanded to know what action India would take, warning that formal legal proceedings could be initiated if they were not satisfied with the response. The official said the PCI had notified government authorities in New Delhi of its intended measures. PCI officials, para swimming administrators and delegation members will discuss the matter after the Games conclude and recommend stern penalties to India’s Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and the Sports Authority of India. “The [Chef de Mission’s] office has already recommended a lifetime ban. A formal decision will be taken at a meeting in Delhi after we return,” the official said. According to local reports, Shaikh became paraplegic after overcoming a tumour. World Para Swimming records show he was previously ranked world No 1 in both the men’s 100m butterfly S5 and 50m breaststroke SB4 events. He represented India at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, winning gold medals in the men’s 200m and 50m breaststroke events. At the Reykjavik International Games in 2025, he secured gold in the 200m breaststroke while setting national and Asian records.

title: China’s humanoid robots hunt for work in South Korea as Seoul bets on physical AI
description: Chinese firms test humanoid robots in South Korean factories and cafes as the country races to build a physical AI ecosystem.
content: This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post. Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence. A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year. “China’s new generation of robot companies has global DNA and naturally looks overseas, and South Korea is one of the most important markets in the Asia-Pacific region,” said Ethan Qi, an associate director covering robotics at Counterpoint Research. The lack of locally built humanoid robots available at scale had created an opening for Chinese suppliers, he added. Commercial foothold Representatives of Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue in Seoul, agreed to buy UBTech’s lifelike U1 model after seeing its debut in Shenzhen in June, according to Sean Qin, overseas head of the company’s commercial robots division. The robot, designed with a female appearance and standing 1.68 metres tall, cost around 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) and was delivered to the park last month, Qin said. UBTech entered the South Korean market as early as 2019 and had since sold more than 10,000 robots to dozens of corporate and government customers, he added. In July, UBTech, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, also announced plans to trial humanoid robots on a South Korean automotive parts production line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker Ajin Industrial. Several UBTech models were undergoing on-site operational tests in the country, Qin said, without providing details. “As a manufacturing powerhouse, South Korea already makes extensive use of robotic arms, autonomous mobile robots and other conventional systems,” he said. “The next step is to help workers become more productive in tasks that demand greater flexibility. That makes Korea a key market for UBTech and for humanoids more broadly.” Zhang Yufeng, founder and CEO of Anyverse Dynamics, who previously worked with SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, said South Korea was “one of our most important overseas markets”. The Beijing-based start-up teamed up with South Korean coffee chain Hollys at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August to test robots that serve drinks, clear tables and reset seats. The robots were currently undergoing trial operations at a cafe in Beijing, Zhang said. South Korea ranked as China’s third-largest export market by value for “intelligent bionic robots” in the first nine months of 2026, behind the United States and Japan, according to Chinese customs data. Exports to South Korea totalled US$19.99 million, or 9.7 per cent of the US$206.95 million China shipped globally. China exported 16,559 robots to 108 countries and regions under the customs category, introduced this year, which covers humanoids and robot dogs. Eight of China’s 10 top-selling humanoid robot makers had been testing the waters in South Korea through product certification, trademark filings and sales channels, according to a report by industry research platform Labsdeep that was cited by Electronic Times this month. “We plan to begin trials in Korean cafes and other commercial service settings in the fourth quarter, before expanding into manufacturing,” Zhang said, noting that the company had been working on product certification for the market. Seoul’s stringent Korea Certification requirements prompted UBTech to adapt its communications modules and radio frequency settings for local use, Qin said. Factories as main testing ground China’s robotics boom has spawned a wave of unicorn firms over the past two years, some of which have already begun shipping products at scale, backed by an extensive supply chain at home. Their push to find commercial applications to justify the investment and hype surrounding humanoid robots coincides with South Korea’s drive to deploy physical AI across its industrial base. Seoul is prioritising the technology to strengthen manufacturing as its working-age population shrinks and potential economic growth slows. The government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (US$2.3 billion) in physical AI funding for 2027, more than triple this year’s level. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources’ Manufacturing AI Transformation programme, dubbed M.AX, supports AI adoption and factory trials involving robots, including humanoids, with a target of 500 AI factories by 2030. The ministry has budgeted 1.1 trillion won for AI transformation this year. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said in August that the government would support factories operated by AI and robots, helping South Korea become “a global leader in manufacturing AI transformation by 2030”. South Korea’s industrial heavyweights are also moving quickly. LG Electronics is building its Data Factory in Seoul to train robots for industrial and household applications, while testing robots on its own production lines. Samsung Electronics established its Robotics eXperience division in July, targeting manufacturing before expanding into homes and retail. A bipedal robot designed to operate round the clock in manufacturing and logistics could debut at the CES annual consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas in January 2027, JoongAng Ilbo reported on Tuesday. Hyundai Motor Group has begun training Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoids at its factory campus in the US state of Georgia, ahead of a planned 2028 deployment in manufacturing. Doosan Robotics has unveiled AI-powered sanding and palletising systems and is developing robot-control software, with support from Nvidia. South Korea’s start-up ecosystem is also drawing fresh capital. AI and robotics accounted for 45 per cent of third-quarter investments tracked by The VC, a local start-up and venture capital investment database platform. Within physical AI, funding is flowing to robot makers as well as start-ups developing foundational models for robots and supplying training data. The country offered a broad range of potential deployment sites in carmaking, shipbuilding and semiconductor manufacturing, Counterpoint’s Qi said. But gaining access was difficult for Chinese suppliers because they needed local customers willing to participate in proof-of-concept trials. Partners and rivals The growing presence of Chinese firms has stirred political debate. At a parliamentary audit on October 6, lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea brought robots from China’s Unitree and AgiBot to challenge the government over South Korea’s competitiveness in physical AI. Lawmaker Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party questioned whether the robots had undergone security checks and accused the National Assembly of providing a stage for Chinese technology. Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who is also the Science and Information and Communications Technology minister, urged South Korea to ramp up physical AI investment and development, pointing to China’s growing deployment of humanoids. “China is also deploying more humanoid robots in the field and collecting data,” he said during a Physical AI Tech Week round table in Seoul on October 13, according to news outlet MoneyToday. Bae questioned whether Korea’s plans were bold enough and called for higher targets to avoid regretting insufficient investment in the future. Companies also needed to shoulder greater responsibility because the government could not support every initiative, he said. Park Young-hoon, head of the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency’s Shenzhen office, said he also saw room for cooperation. “Companies need to explore new business opportunities using Shenzhen’s local supply chains and innovation capabilities while competing with Chinese technology companies,” he told local media outlet Newspim in October. Anyverse Dynamics’ Zhang said he saw the two countries’ industrial strengths as “highly complementary”. South Korea combined global leadership in advanced manufacturing with a capacity for AI innovation, while China offered a comprehensive supply chain, a deep pool of engineering and AI talent, and rapid product iteration, he said. For UBTech’s Qin, policies favouring domestic companies have not deterred Korean customers from considering Chinese suppliers. “The Korean customers we have dealt with are open to working with Chinese robot makers,” he said.

title: Style Edit: Hermès brings its history to the stage in Hong Kong’s West Kowloon
description: Hermèstories, set on Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, tells the story of the maison’s two centuries of crafting luxury wear and accessories.
content: The world of Hermès contains multitudes. Now, there’s a chance for the brand’s fans in Hong Kong to acquaint themselves with its products and its history and philosophy, thanks to a highly original theatrical performance. The spirit of Hermès has grown over nearly two centuries of storied history. From its beginnings in Paris in 1837 as a company making the finest harnesses, saddles and other equipment for horse riders, it has since expanded into luggage and clothing – even pioneering the use of zips there – and, for more than a century now, into the handbags that are perhaps its most iconic items. These days, Hermès also offers everything from watchmaking to textiles, perfumes to furniture, all of it infused with a unique creativity and savoir faire. All this history and all these products are brought to life in a dazzlingly fresh way from October 24 to November 8 at Freespace in the West Kowloon Cultural District. Written by acclaimed actor, writer and director Pauline Bayle, and directed by immersive theatre expert Joe Hufton, Hermèstories is an exploration of the maison’s spirit and the most coveted items it makes, presented as a surrealistic journey into the imagination. The star of the show is a groom, known as Lad, who takes care of a stable of horses, playing into Hermès’ equestrian heritage. Portrayed by a woman, the character goes for a stroll along Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, where Hermès has its headquarters. There, he meets several other characters, and their various imaginings lead the audience through the history of Hermès and its most coveted products via an adventure filled with entertaining dialogue and songs. Ingenious props and practical sound effects bring key Hermès milestones to life, while landmark products from silk scarves to a zip and a Bolide bag get their moment in the sun. Unlike so many other luxury brands, Hermès remains a family-owned company, still run by descendants of the founder, Thierry Hermès. The new production and accompanying exhibition embody the same values the brand has had since the 19th century, all part of the work of the Fondation d’entreprise Hermès, which is dedicated to promoting creativity and passing on the skills that characterise the maison’s artisans. To see those skills and the products they result in transformed into a delightful journey of theatrical discovery, head down to Freespace.

title: Market sell-off, tax scrutiny and growth: key figures shaping investor sentiment
description: A stock market slump, Beijing’s tax enforcement drive and fresh GDP data are among the developments drawing investors’ attention this week.
content: As regional equities tumbled and hopes for investor stimulus faded, the Hang Seng Index fell to a seven-month low. Attention also remained focused on Beijing’s intensified scrutiny of offshore wealth and tax compliance. Macroeconomic data pointed to steady, if uneven, domestic momentum. Here are the core figures capturing market attention this week. Hong Kong stocks suffer steepest drop in 7 months The Hang Seng Index sank 3.03 per cent in a single session to 22,934.68 points, its worst performance since March, as slowing profit growth among major tech firms and reduced expectations for stimulus weighed on sentiment. Investors were also concerned about potential share sales ahead of Beijing’s Thursday deadline for offshore trust gains. Shares of Chinese toymaker Bloks Group plunged after its chairman sold a 1.6 per cent stake for HK$250 million (US$31.9 million), a move that some market watchers linked to liquidity needs arising from the new tax regime. China’s tax workforce recruitment drive accelerates China’s 2027 national civil service recruitment plan includes 24,013 tax-related positions, accounting for more than 67 per cent of all vacancies, up from over 65 per cent a year earlier. The expansion of the tax workforce is drawing attention from businesses and wealthy families as compliance climbs higher on the policy agenda and authorities intensify enforcement efforts. Treasury yields slip below 5 per cent threshold The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note dropped below 5 per cent on Thursday for the first time in a month. The benchmark fell as low as 4.95 per cent in intraday trading, while yields on 30-year and five-year bonds also declined. China’s economy grows 4.6 per cent China’s economy expanded 4.6 per cent year on year in the first three quarters, meeting the lower end of official full-year targets while highlighting a persistent divide between strong exports and weak domestic demand. Hong Kong secures strategic investment pledges Hong Kong on Thursday attracted its seventh batch of 18 strategic enterprises, including Solana and Johnson & Johnson, which pledged more than HK$10 billion in investment and 1,600 high-end jobs to bolster the city’s tech and financial sectors. US banks pile into dim sum bonds According to a Bank of America report, US lenders helped drive a 68 per cent surge in issuance of offshore yuan-denominated bonds – known as dim sum bonds – lifting total fundraising to 774 billion yuan (US$116 billion). The surge comes as Wall Street increasingly taps Chinese capital markets even as the yield premium over dollar funding continues to narrow.

title: WHO warns Africa faces ‘complex’ Ebola outbreak as virus reaches Nigeria
description: Deadly strain spreads to West Africa for the first time in the current wave as Abuja isolates contacts of an infected diplomat’s wife.
content: The World Health Organization has warned that Africa faced a “complex” Ebola outbreak after the virus crossed from east Africa to Nigeria, marking the first case in the west of the continent. Nigeria on Tuesday had announced an imported case of the Bundibugyo strain, currently causing a major Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was detected in the wife of a diplomat who had travelled from Uganda to the Nigerian capital Abuja. Health minister Muhammad Ali Pate said Thursday the woman’s contacts had been tracked down since her arrival in Nigeria earlier this month, and that an undisclosed number of “high risk” individuals “have been quarantined, fully, in a facility”. Nigeria, the continent’s most populous nation, is the fourth African country affected by the outbreak. Kenya, in the east, has reported nine cases since October 6. The outbreak began in DR Congo and has become the deadliest in the country’s history, killing more than 4,000 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since mid-May, according to health authorities. It is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment. “We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape,” Mohamed Janabi, regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing. The patient in Nigeria arrived in the capital Abuja on October 3 after being in Uganda since September 16, the WHO representative in Nigeria Pavel Ursu said. She flew to Abuja on an Ethiopian Airlines flight and transited through Addis Ababa, an emergency meeting of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) heard on Wednesday. The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya said on Thursday. He also said she did not go to DR Congo, as suggested earlier by Ugandan authorities, who have pushed back against new cases being linked to their country after being declared Ebola-free earlier this year. Kaseya said officials were trying to piece together her travel history to establish where she could have been exposed – including the possibility that there might have been contact at the airport with Kenya’s first victim, who also left Uganda on October 3. The Nigerian case has reignited memories of a widespread west African outbreak that struck several countries and killed more than 11,000 people between late 2013 and 2016. Nigeria successfully held back that outbreak within its borders, resulting in only 19 infections and seven deaths – raising confidence the densely packed nation of 240 million can respond effectively to new public health threats. “It is contained, so far, the imported case. We have no evidence it has gone into the communities,” Pate told a news conference in Abuja. “So our focus is on the contact tracing and ensuring that we know exactly where those contacts are.” Ebola, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids and can cause severe internal and external bleeding and organ failure, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the last 50 years. In August, Uganda was declared officially Ebola-free by the WHO after recording 20 cases – almost all of them in people who had travelled from neighbouring DR Congo. Uganda has pushed back against suggestions the patient in Nigeria might have contracted the virus in the country. “It’s preposterous to suggest that just because someone was holidaying in Uganda, which by the way has no cases of Ebola, is reason enough to drag us into a conversation about Ebola in Nigeria,” Ugandan government spokesman Alan Kasujja said.

title: DeepSeek, MiniMax secure open-source licences days after new China export rules: state media
description: CCTV says the proposed measures are intended to establish clearer regulatory boundaries rather than shut the door on Chinese AI tech exports.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence model developers DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed export registration procedures and proceeded with open-source releases and overseas licensing activities, according to Chinese state media, days after Beijing moved to tighten oversight on AI tech transfers. Yuyuan Tantian, an influential social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, reported on Thursday evening that the two AI companies had completed the required registrations after Beijing proposed adding export control restrictions and prohibitions to 23 AI-related technologies last week, covering large language models, AI agents and computing clusters. The draft proposal released by the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology, which also included provisions that came into immediate effect requiring official registration for the covered technologies, raised questions about whether Beijing was restricting Chinese AI companies from expanding overseas, particularly as the country’s open-weight models have gained international adoption. However, the Yuyuan Tantian post said the proposed measures were intended to establish clearer regulatory boundaries rather than shut the door on Chinese AI technology exports. “Simply put, AI companies can continue with their commercialisation efforts as usual. Once the relevant measures are officially implemented, the vast majority of artificial intelligence technologies will still be freely exportable,” Yuyuan Tantian said. The CCTV-affiliated post acknowledged the overseas speculation over whether Beijing was shifting its stance on open-source AI, which it has championed as a superior alternative to the closed-source approach of the US AI industry. However, it highlighted the approvals for DeepSeek and MiniMax as indicative of China’s continued stance of “encouraging openness,” urging businesses to “remain calm in the face of the new regulations”. Both companies have open-sourced major updates in recent days, with Hangzhou-based DeepSeek upgrading its V4.1 Flash model and open-sourcing its in-house inference framework, while Shanghai-based MiniMax open-sourced its M3.1 model on Friday. The registration requirements covered transfers of technology ownership, overseas licensing arrangements and changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities. Companies are required to register relevant transactions with MOFCOM before proceeding. According to Yuyuan Tantian, authorities began preparing the proposed rules in the first half of the year, consulting research institutions, industry associations and leading companies before publishing the draft document. It noted that Beijing was seeking to distinguish between the transfer of underlying AI technology abroad – which it would clamp down on for national security reasons – and providing commercial AI services overseas, which it would continue to encourage. The assessment echoes remarks from a MOFCOM spokesperson last week, who said that overseas access to Chinese AI models through application programming interfaces, official websites and mobile applications would not be covered by the proposed export controls. For the open-sourcing of AI technologies, the spokesperson said that expedited “automatic licensing” measures would be applied, as quickly as “immediate reporting and export”. Beijing’s bolstering of its tech export control regime comes as the US mulls further restrictions on Chinese access to cutting-edge US technologies, including major congressional bills that would further clamp down on exports of advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment. The US Department of Homeland Security on Tuesday also ordered all US federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek and third-party tools built on it, a move that Beijing criticised as being discriminatory. In its post, Yuyuan Tantian drew a line between the US and Chinese approach to export controls, claiming that China “is not taking the path” set by the US of using such measures to isolate competitors and maintain its global technological leadership. “Our revision is a routine process carried out in accordance with laws and regulations,” it said, while noting that it would also help China gain greater influence in global technological competition.

title: One-third of the world population has been exposed to harmful air this year – so far
description: EU report finds 34 per cent of global population breathed extremely high levels of ozone pollution in first eight months of 2026.
content:
One third of the world’s population was exposed to extremely high levels of ozone pollution this year, a European Union report said last month. This was due to a combination of heatwaves, wildfires and human-caused emissions.
The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) is the European Union’s Earth observation programme. It analysed the first eight months of 2026. The report highlighted the relationship between climate change and air pollution.
Record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires contributed to this year’s ozone pollution.
Heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry. This creates ground-level ozone pollution (see graphic).
The pollution damages lung tissue, causes breathing problems and triggers asthma attacks. It also leads to other health issues.
El Nino could cause even more fires in Southeast Asia. For months, Indonesia has had major blazes. They have brought toxic haze to the country, as well as Malaysia, Singapore and parts of the Philippines for weeks.
“Air pollution does not stop at borders,” said Laurence Rouilin in the Atmosphere Watch report. She is the director of CAMS. “It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans.”
The report studied air quality from January 1 to September 15, 2026. It found that 34 per cent of the global population had been exposed to “extremely poor” air. This means the concentrations of ozone were well above World Health Organization guidelines.
Another 17 per cent of the world breathed “very poor” air. Five per cent was exposed to “good” levels of ozone.
Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution. Around 53 per cent of the continent breathes “extremely poor” air. Another 22 per cent were exposed to “very poor” ozone. New Delhi in India, Dhaka in Bangladesh, Chongqing in China, and Lahore in Pakistan were among Asian cities with “extremely poor” ozone levels.
Two thirds of North America’s population were exposed to “poor” or “very poor” air quality. In Europe, 45 per cent breathed “poor” or “very poor” air. The report said the EU had effectively reduced emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone.
In Africa, forest fires and crop burning have contributed to air pollution. Saharan dust travels as far as Europe. Eight per cent of Africa’s population breathed “extremely poor” air this year. Another 19 per cent were exposed to “very poor” or “poor” air.
Ozone levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro. But the air quality was “good” or “fair” for 81 per cent of South America’s population.
One bright spot was Oceania, which includes Australia and New Zealand. At least 66 per cent of the population enjoyed “good” ozone levels.

title: The psychology behind reading horror and mental resilience
description: Aside from thrills, reading the genre gives teenagers a safe space to process messy emotions and topics.
content:
Horror films and their spine-chilling, creepy visuals easily scare us. But nothing truly matches the human imagination. While a film displays frightening images on screen, a book comes to life entirely inside a reader’s head.
According to clinical psychologist Avis Ngan, reading horror is more than a cheap thrill. The genre also helps teenagers process intense feelings and themes, which strengthens their mental resilience.
“Stephen King once wrote, ‘Fiction is the truth inside the lie,’” Ngan said. “That’s the heart of it. [These] stories provide a safe space for teens to confront emotions and subjects too messy or taboo for normal life.”
Reading is different from watching a film or playing a video game. When we read horror stories, our brain is the one that generates the images, sounds and atmosphere. In that way, the reader is the director, camera operator and audience – all at the same time.
Ngan is also the founder of Mindsight, a mental health clinic based in Hong Kong.
“Here’s the cool part,” he said. “Your imagination tends to self-regulate. Your mind will unconsciously calibrate the scares to the level that’s intense for you without completely overwhelming you. There’s a built-in sense of control. You set the pace. You can slow down, re-read [and] pause between chapters. You’re in charge of the experience.”
On the other hand, jump scares in films are carefully timed, and the soundtrack is engineered to manipulate the audience’s feelings. This makes watching a film a far more passive event.
For young people, the horror genre not only provides excitement and stimulation but also allows them to experience powerful feelings safely. Reading frightening stories can help a teenager test their personal limits and whether they can handle fear.
“There’s real brain science behind this too,” Ngan added. “During adolescence, the prefrontal cortex, which is the part involved in abstract thinking, moral reasoning and hypothetical ‘What if?’ analysis, is actively being built and rewired.”
For the first time, teenagers begin to think deeply about serious life topics, such as death, morality, justice and parts of existence that cannot be fully explained.
“These inexplicable parts are what I’d call metaphysical experiences, and horror is one of the oldest literary traditions for exploring exactly these themes,” he explained. “By tackling themes like mortality, evil, loss of control and human nature, the horror genre serves as ground for them beginning to grapple with life’s heaviest questions.”
Reading scary stories also helps build cognitive resilience. As a person reads through terrifying scenes, they build distress tolerance and the ability to handle uncomfortable feelings without being overwhelmed. With time, this teaches the brain that fear and dread can pass safely.
This resilience is reinforced by “affect labelling” or the practice of translating raw emotions into words.
The mental health expert added that simply naming what you feel can help dial down the emotional intensity of a particular scene in the book.
“Reading naturally strengthens this habit. Literature gives us the exact vocabulary we need to identify and calm complex feelings that might otherwise seem vague and overwhelming,” he said.
But even when we work on understanding our feelings through reading, a genuinely terrifying book can still make it hard to fall asleep.
Ngan suggested resetting the mind before bed by spending 10 to 15 minutes on a lighthearted activity such as watching something funny or chatting with a friend.
“When a scary story sticks with you, it’s often because your nervous system hasn’t fully got the memo that the threat isn’t real,” he explained.
One way to calm down is to slow your breathing: inhale for four counts, hold for four and exhale for six. This helps signal to the body that danger has passed.
Another trick is to rewrite the creepy parts of the book and make it amusing. You could make the ghost trip and fall over or have a villain be scolded by a family member. It sounds silly, but it is effective.
“What you’re doing is taking back authorship and shifting your brain from a reactive, fearful mode into a creative one,” Ngan said. “That’s the gift of scary fiction. It takes the stuff we’re told not to think about too much and says: let’s think about it. Let’s feel it. Let’s see what we discover.”

title: France braces for more unrest as police face scrutiny over weapons and tactics
description: Authorities deploy reinforcements ahead of Saturday rallies while defending the use of ‘intermediate-force’ weapons.
content: Police across France are under pressure to maintain security during further protests expected in some cities, while facing scrutiny over their riot-control tactics used during previous unrest that left some teenagers seriously injured. Officers appeared outnumbered and overwhelmed during last weekend’s protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. In response, France’s Interior Ministry said it would deploy 20 per cent more police this Saturday than last weekend, even as regional authorities imposed blanket bans on demonstrations in several major cities, including Lyon and Marseille, following widespread looting and unrest. On top of the reinforced police presence, special-intervention forces normally reserved for counter-terrorism missions would be deployed if necessary, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Soldiers would help guard sensitive buildings, while helicopters, water cannons and heavy armoured vehicles known as Centaurs would also be available. In Paris, police restricted Saturday’s planned march to the eastern fringes of the capital and barred access to the city centre, prompting the precautionary closure of major cultural landmarks, including the Louvre and Musee d’Orsay. Activist groups have warned they would defy the orders. Underpinning the anger are severe injuries suffered by young demonstrators. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye while taking part in a protest in Mulhouse last Saturday, while a 17-year-old boy lost a hand in Saint-Etienne. Other teenagers have suffered disabling injuries during weeks of high school blockades and street demonstrations. French police forces are equipped with batons, tear gas, sound grenades and foam-round launchers, as well as riot shields equipped with powerful strobe lights designed to disorient protesters. Electric stun guns are prohibited in crowd-control operations. “Intermediate-force weapons are defensive response tools that allow law enforcement officers to respond to a threat in a graduated and proportionate manner,” French National Police said in a statement to Associated Press. But critics, including families of injured teenagers, say the police have been too heavy-handed. Some have called for bans on foam-round launchers, tear gas and stun grenades, echoing demands made by human rights groups since the violent 2018 “yellow vest” protests. Earlier this month, Amnesty International called for a permanent ban on all stun grenades, saying they are designed to shock, disorient and sow panic, and that some can cause permanent hearing loss and life-changing injuries from blasts and shrapnel. United Nations guidance on what it calls “less-lethal weapons” says kinetic impact projectiles should be used only against an imminent threat, targeting the abdomen and never the head, face or neck. Firing from elevated positions or at close range, or bouncing rounds off the ground, can increase the risk of serious injury. Foam-round launchers, though considered safer than rubber-bullet shotguns, “in certain circumstances, can kill,” said Neil Corney, an arms researcher at the UK-based Omega Research Foundation who helped draft the UN guidance. Proper training and guidelines can reduce injuries, he said, pointing to Spain, where authorities replaced criticised rubber-bullet shotguns with foam-round launchers following a violent police crackdown on Catalonia’s 2017 independence referendum. Injuries have declined there, he said. Foam-round launchers were initially developed for military training and later adapted for “high-risk, hostage-type situations” and anti-terrorism operations, said Patrick Wilckin, an arms researcher at Amnesty International. “They were never really meant for policing of protests,” he said. Accountability is another concern. Unlike bullets, foam rounds generally leave no traceable evidence. Activists have proposed stamping identification numbers on the rounds to help identify officers involved in incidents that cause serious injuries. Corney said the measure would greatly improve accountability at little cost. The use of such weapons reflects a broader shift in French policing towards keeping officers at a distance from protesters, said Jean-Marie Godard, an author specialising in France’s internal security. In the early 2000s, France’s conservative government moved away from community policing, which emphasised foot patrols and engagement with residents, towards specialised riot-control units. People across France’s political spectrum regret abandoning the community policing model, Godard said. French policing today differs from that in many other European countries, according to Laura Keesmann, a sociologist at the University of Antwerp who led a wide-ranging comparative study of policing methods in France, the UK, the Netherlands and Sweden. In the other countries studied, police often engage directly with demonstrators, sometimes mingling with crowds to defuse tensions, she said. “That is just really, really not the case in France,” she said. “There’s much more of an authoritarian way of policing.” Keesmann stressed, however, that French police face unusually militant and sometimes violent protesters. On the eve of last Saturday’s protests, Nunez said his instructions were “very clear: the police and gendarmes should be able to use the entirety of the intermediate weapons at their disposal”. France has more than 250,000 national police officers and gendarmes. Police generally operate in cities, while gendarmes usually cover rural areas and smaller towns. Both forces fall under the Interior Ministry, which said 997 officers and gendarmes were injured during Saturday’s unrest, seven of them seriously. Police said more than 100 protesters and residents were injured in Paris on Saturday. Authorities have not released a nationwide injury tally. About 2,400 people were arrested across France that day. Godard said protest movements have become increasingly decentralised as labour unions have lost influence over demonstrations, drawing a wider range of participants, including radical groups. French authorities have blamed much of the recent violence on far-left radicals, accusing them of orchestrating clashes with police and targeting public buildings. Others took advantage of the unrest to loot businesses, authorities said. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Bloomberg

title: Asian Football Confederation endorses Gianni Infantino for another term as Fifa president
description: Several key AFC members, including Saudi Arabia and Qatar, had publicly declared their support earlier for the Swiss’ re-election bid.
content: The head of the Asian Football Confederation said ⁠on Friday the regional body would support Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as Fifa president. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president, had previously backed opposition to Infantino’s failed plan to sell ‌off the commercial rights to Fifa tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors. He had joined with the presidents of Uefa and Concacaf to pen an open letter calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan formulated by Infantino ⁠a “fundamental breach of trust”. Infantino apologised at this month’s Fifa Council ‌and told attendees to submit any questions they had about his governance in writing so he ‌could answer them at the next meeting. In Sheikh Salman’s ⁠opening remarks ⁠at the AFC’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo, the Bahraini said the region supported ‌Infantino. “I think that we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you ‌and your ‌leadership as you seek a new mandate as a ‌Fifa president,” he said in comments directed at the Swiss, ⁠who was present at the meeting. “I think you’ve visited a lot ⁠of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. “I know your feeling. And ‌I think your ‌commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear.” Several key AFC members, including Saudi Arabia and Qatar, had publicly declared their support for Infantino, and while Sheikh Salman acknowledged he had not seen eye to eye with the Fifa president on ‌certain issues, he said it was important to look to the future. “I want to make it clear: yes, ⁠we had some issues ⁠we spoke about in the past but let’s not relate the two things together,” Sheikh Salman, who is also seeking a fourth term in office next ‌year, said. “I think the last few days we met in Zurich. You made it clear that there was a true, a clear understanding between us. We need to move ‌forward. And ‌we believe football is strongest when we work together with a shared vision and a common purpose. “As one Asian family ‌we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni. I just want to make that clear today.” Infantino also gave Sheikh ⁠Salman his backing in his address to delegates. “You’ve been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my ⁠dear Salman,” he said. “You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been ‌doing in the last years.” Asked later ‌about Sheikh Salman’s comments, Infantino said: “I feel great about the AFC’s support.” While Africa has also backed Infantino’s re-election, he continues to face opposition from European football’s governing body. The AFC has 47 member confederations and, even if all the members do not follow the direction of Sheikh Salman, those votes could be key to guaranteeing another mandate for Infantino. The Fifa president is up for re-election in March as he seeks a fourth term until 2031. The deadline for candidates to file against Infantino is November 18. So far no one has filed.

title: Beijing tightens rules on outbound capital to better shield Chinese assets
description: China says the new rules for outbound investment are to protect overseas financing and assets.
content: China has unveiled a revised rule for regulating outbound investment, requiring investors to report major adverse developments more diligently, including foreign demands to hand over technology or dispose of stakes. The new rule, announced by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) on Thursday, aimed to better prevent and mitigate rising overseas risks and protect Chinese interests, according to the economic planner. “In recent years, a small number of countries and regions have adopted discriminatory measures, with some demanding that Chinese investors hand over technology or data, or dispose of equity stakes and assets, undermining Chinese interests,” the NDRC said in a statement on Thursday. The commission said that some Chinese investors had underestimated overseas risks and responded inadequately to political instability and volatile policies, suffering losses. The NDRC said the new rule refined the reporting system for major adverse circumstances and also established an annual reporting framework for outbound investment information. It would also work to optimise the reporting requirements for reinvestment made through offshore entities and introduce early-stage reporting obligations for some large projects, or those that could affect China’s diplomatic relations with other countries. “By keeping regulatory authorities informed of such developments, investors can help foster joint efforts to guard against and manage overseas risks.” The 76-article regulation, which takes effect on December 1 and replaces the version introduced in 2017, comes as the growing scale and complexity of China’s overseas investments prompt Beijing to strengthen its regulatory framework. The changes come as Chinese companies face mounting scrutiny of their investments abroad. In recent years, US authorities have pushed TikTok’s Chinese parent ByteDance to relinquish control of its American operations, while Dutch authorities and courts have intervened in the governance of Chinese-owned chipmaker Nexperia. China’s annual outbound investment flows rose from US$158.3 billion in 2017 to US$213.6 billion in 2025, while its stock of overseas investments nearly doubled from US$1.8 trillion to US$3.4 trillion, according to the NDRC. China has ranked among the world’s top three sources of outbound investment for nine consecutive years, officials from the Ministry of Commerce said during a press conference on Thursday, adding that the country’s outbound direct investment reached US$128.62 billion in the first nine months of 2026. The revised rules also expanded the definition of investors beyond domestic companies and organisations to include individuals. It would continue to allow investors to deploy capital in overseas financial markets through existing channels, including the Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor scheme, Stock Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect scheme, without being subject to the new approval, filing and reporting requirements in most cases. According to an analysis by Chinese law firm King & Wood, extending the regulatory framework to individual residents could provide a clearer legal pathway for Chinese citizens seeking to invest overseas. The law firm said outbound investment by Chinese individuals had long been governed primarily by foreign exchange regulations, which applied to a relatively limited range of activities.

title: The history of Chinese incense, from ancient rituals to fragrance, as craft enjoys revival
description: An expert shares how incense went from the preserve of Chinese nobles to modern office workers, and how making and burning it have changed.
content: “Many people, when they first smell Chinese incense, describe it as smelling like Chinese medicine,” says Shanghai-based incense master Sun Na. “And it’s true, the classic Chinese incense we’re talking about is primarily medicinal in character.” She points to a spherical censer, a vessel designed to burn incense. “In winter, you could put it under the blankets to scent and warm the bedding,” she says. “If you had trouble sleeping, calming herbs could be added. This is what we call zhi wei bing – treating illness before it arises.” We are sitting in the Tang Xiang Cultural Space on Xikang Road in Shanghai’s Jingan district, surrounded by centuries-old incense burners. Most are from the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties, but some date back to the Western Han period (206BC-AD9). According to Sun, early Chinese incense served practical purposes. Ancient Chinese text The Rites of Zhou records the practice of burning mangcao, or Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum), to kill insects, and in southern China, the use of mugwort to keep pests away during the rainy season. During major epidemics, communities burned large quantities of herbs in collective rituals lasting three to four hours. But Sun believes this was done for practical rather than superstitious reasons. “The tribe or clan leader would gather everyone to pray to heaven and earth for protection,” Sun says. “But the herbs they were burning had anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties. The ignorant believed the ritual itself had divine power, but it was science.” Blending science and superstition Sitting at the table with tools laid out before us, Sun demonstrates an ancient Chinese incense ritual called xiang zhuan (incense seal). A pair of incense chopsticks (xiang kuai) are used to loosen ash (xiang hui), which is held in a ceramic jade-green censer (xiang lu). The surface of the ash is made level using a copper incense spade (xiang chan) before a flat-edged tool called a ce ya is used to press the ash smooth. Then, a feather brush (yu sao) is used to sweep away stray powder. The seal mould (xiang zhuan) is gently placed on the ash, and aromatic powder is sifted into the pattern before the mould is carefully lifted away. Finally, the powder is lit, and smoke curls upwards and disappears.
