View this post on Instagram A post shared by mei_mei_0946 (@mei_mei_0946) A fragrant history The history of incense reflects the trajectory of social mobility in Chinese society. In the beginning, fragrance was believed to belong to the gods; bundles of aromatic herbs were burned to communicate with ancestors. By the Han dynasty (206BC-AD220), incense had become an instrument of imperial power and was widely enjoyed by the upper class. During the Han dynasty, elaborate, mountain-shaped boshanlu censers were designed to evoke the mythical isles of the immortals, filling palace chambers with scented smoke. During the cosmopolitan Tang dynasty (618-907), Silk Road trade transformed Chinese incense. Resinous materials such as agarwood, sandalwood, frankincense and myrrh arrived from Southeast Asia and the Middle East, introducing a new principle: fragrances could be composed. Incense had reached its golden age by the Song dynasty (960-1279), when it permeated every level of society, from the literati to merchants and commoners. Incense was sold in markets, burned in teahouses, offered in temples and enjoyed at home. “Professional incense workers emerged to serve the urban market,” Sun says. “Entrepreneurs ran incense seal businesses, and a service existed where workers would visit a client’s shop each day to press fresh incense designs.” Hexiang blended incense, which combined ingredients according to principles borrowed from traditional Chinese medicine, began to emerge after the Tang dynasty. Raw materials would undergo paozhi (processing) by being steamed, roasted or soaked in wine or honey in a way similar to traditional pharmacology. Sun says that the person processing the incense has to be in harmony between heaven and Earth. She adds that humid climates, such as Shanghai’s, can cause incense tablets to mould more easily. Sun says the craft is inseparable from the artisan’s inner state. “My teacher told me he could look at an incense tablet and see the maker’s state of mind,” she says. “At that time, I thought it was nonsense. But after 10 years of practice, I know you simply can’t hide from the material.” Like wine or tea, incense has terroir, vintage and hierarchy Sun’s path to mastery began with Western perfumes and essential oils before the subtle, inward character of traditional Chinese censers drew her in. “Unlike Western perfumes, Chinese incense does not announce itself,” she says. “It’s inward-facing and creates a space for you to enter.” For much of the 20th century, Chinese incense culture survived only in fragments – memory, text and objects. “Incense doesn’t feed you, doesn’t clothe you,” Sun says. “It’s the first thing to go when times are hard. There was a gap and a break in the transmission. We lost the knowledge.” A modern lifestyle revival Over the past decade, economic growth and a generation raised on Western consumer culture have begun to explore Chinese traditions, not as heritage, but as living practices that meet the demands of urban life. Sun points out that even as recently as five years ago, incense was only used on special occasions by a small group of enthusiasts. “Now, I have white-collar students who burn a stick in the morning before work, another before sleep and when they feel stressed in the office,” she says. The Alila Shanghai hotel has positioned itself at the centre of this revival, partnering with the Tang Xiang Cultural Space to offer guests 90-minute Chinese incense blending workshops, led by Sun. “We integrate incense because it offers a complete knowledge system of materials, craft and history,” says Jtawen Yap, the hotel’s general manager. “Guests can genuinely learn through hands-on practice, rather than passive observation. “An incense session invites the mind to slow down in a state of flow – hands moving slowly, breath settling, attention returning to one thing,” he says. “They leave lighter, calmer and more connected to a side of Chinese culture they had only seen from the outside: refined, quiet and deeply human.” Like wine or tea, incense has terroir, vintage and hierarchy. As Sun says: “We have a saying: one tree, 10 scents. Or even one tree, 100 scents.” The best agarwood, chenxiang, is formed when Aquilaria trees become infected by a specific mould and slowly produce a fragrant resin. It is rarer than gold. This unpredictability gave rise to a unique cultural institution: the xianghui, or incense gatherings, where literati burned fragrant woods and competed to decipher their ingredients and provenance. Now anyone can play this game once restricted to the upper echelons of society. “People are using everyday materials like mugwort, orchid or dried orange peel,” Sun says. “They’re adapting, making it their own. That’s how culture survives.” It is a return to the original spirit of Chinese incense, before it became a luxury of the few.

title: El Salvador deploys special forces to Haiti after soldiers seized by gangs
description: President Bukele warns Haitian gangs ‘we can finish with you too’ as commandos hunt for four captive technicians.
content: El Salvador deployed 100 special forces soldiers to Haiti on Thursday to help rescue four missing soldiers from the Central American country who recently came under attack by gangs, two officials told Associated Press. The special forces arrived a day after Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele announced a military operation to rescue the four aviation technicians, issuing an ultimatum directly to Haitian gang leaders in Creole. “We have a single objective: to bring our four compatriots back home alive, without any harm,” Bukele wrote Wednesday on X. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.” Bukele said the four hostages – part of the United Nations-backed gang suppression force – were ambushed and abducted on Sunday after going shopping for food. An official with El Salvador’s government not authorised to speak on the matter said an additional 100 soldiers were going to be deployed to Haiti on Thursday night. The official said Salvadorean authorities were operating under the assumption that the four missing Salvadoreans were still alive. The Miami Herald first reported the deployment. The gang suppression force issued a brief statement late Thursday saying that “a contingent” from El Salvador had arrived “to support ongoing search and security operations” where the attack occurred. Haiti’s government said Wednesday evening that the four missing soldiers were abducted, marking its first comments since the attack that occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets. Authorities have said the soldiers were travelling in an armoured vehicle that came under fire from gangs that also used explosives. It was the first major attack since the international gang suppression force began operations, replacing a Kenyan-led force that struggled to help Haitian police quell gang violence given a lack of resources and funds. Diego Da Rin, an analyst with the International Crisis Group, said he believes that finding the Salvadoreans would be like finding a needle in a haystack. “It will be almost impossible to find them … unless the gangs agree to hand them over,” he said. Da Rin said the Salvadoreans were apparently not travelling with the type of security detail needed so deep in gang-held territory. The attack occurred in territory controlled by the Chen Mechan gang, with the 400 Mawozo gang operating just west of that area, a gang that is much more powerful and has far greater firepower. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack, and neither gang has posted about it on social media. Authorities have been fighting armed men in the area ever since the attack occurred, with the Haitian National Police task force, which includes Vectus Global – the private security firm founded by former US Navy Seal and Blackwater founder Erik Prince – working with the gang suppression force as part of a joint operation. As the heavy fighting in deep, gang-controlled territory continues, residents have been warned to remain indoors. The attack occurred as the gang suppression force numbered only a little over 2,000 of the 5,500 personnel envisioned. On Wednesday night, a gang leader known as Krisla who controls an area that is not located near the site of the attack, posted a video in which he mentioned Bukele and the ongoing gun battle. “They have bigger weapons and more technology than we do, but we’ll fight to the end,” he said. “We didn’t ask Bukele to come here, we didn’t ask Bukele to send soldiers here. Bukele has come here to protect his money at his soldiers’ expense.” Some of the contractors working with Prince’s Vectus Global are from El Salvador, Da Rin noted. El Salvador’s presidential office did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Letters | Education is the key to equitable digital transformation
description: Readers discuss how to close AI gaps, AI risk management, and what AI models should focus on.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. As China hosts Apec 2026 under the theme “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, the focus is on three pillars: openness, innovation and cooperation. Cutting across these priorities is the transformative force of artificial intelligence (AI), and the urgent question of how to harness it to close divides in learning, information and economic opportunities. Chinese President Xi Jinping advocates equitable global AI governance and has unveiled a new cooperation body underpinned by the principles of openness, win-win and boosting innovation-driven development. While governments play a critical role in narrowing this gap through policies and infrastructure investment, academia, technology and business must also collaborate to dismantle barriers to accessibility and promote responsible, ethical adoption. Only then can AI drive productivity, innovation and human development across societies. Education is central to this mission. Hong Kong, as a city where East meets West, combines the strengths of world-class universities, national support, global investment and high-calibre talent. Backed by the Chinese mainland and closely connected to Southeast Asia and belt and road countries, it serves as a vital bridge in advancing equitable digital transformation. Ranked within the top seven globally in education by QS and other major league tables, The Education University of Hong Kong exemplifies this role. Through its leadership in teacher education, lifelong learning and digital transformation, the university promotes regional capacity-building. Since serving as a consultant for World Bank education initiatives in Vietnam in 2017, the university has continued to foster academic exchange, talent development and policy dialogue in places like Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates to help learners and institutions adapt to the digital era. In recent years, the university has embedded AI across its education majors, faculties and curricula to cultivate critical thinking, problem-solving and ethical decision-making. Through joint research partnerships, academic exchanges and thought leadership, the university has shared these practices and the principles behind them with the Middle East, Southeast Asia and other belt and road countries, including Brunei, Cambodia and Indonesia. These efforts have inspired new approaches and broadened opportunities for future generations. Just as the internet did a generation ago, AI presents a dual reality of immense opportunity and systemic risk. To achieve a truly equitable global society, hardware deployment and talent development must be paired with international educational diplomacy based on multilateralism and mutual cultural respect. By fostering an open, cooperative framework for knowledge transfer and mutual learning, global leaders can ensure that the next technological wave benefits every community, fulfilling the promise of a prosperous and inclusive Asia-Pacific. Professor John Lee Chi-kin, president, Education University of Hong Kong AI risks must be robustly managed As artificial intelligence is embedded deeper into commercial operations, urban management and everyday life globally, a concerning trend has emerged. AI models have been found deviating from user prompts and bypassing preset operational limits to execute unauthorised actions. These technical anomalies pose tangible risks that compel renewed scrutiny of AI governance. A common perception is that AI only passively performs instructed tasks within fixed boundaries. But international testing of modern AI tells a different story. Equipped with sophisticated self-learning capabilities, AI can identify loopholes, permission gaps and security vulnerabilities. It may circumvent safety protocols, adjust internal operational logic and carry out unapproved functions. Such irregularities stem from two structural flaws in current AI frameworks. Ultra-fast computational progression makes full traceability impossible, resulting in unanticipated outputs. Existing safety mechanisms only supervise explicit commands, failing to capture covert algorithmic activity and leaving regulatory blind spots. To address these emerging threats, standardised defence protocols are being established in Hong Kong. Risks posed by AI are not inherent, but stem from insufficient supervision and excessive reliance. Maintaining human agency, tiered monitoring and manual validation of all AI-generated content remains essential. Robust governance ensures AI continues to serve urban development and public interests in a safe, controlled manner. P.L. Yuen, past president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers Set AI on cancer I have been concerned about the advances of AI and the need to slow it down. As it is obvious this is not going to happen, let’s try a different tack. How about these models eradicate cancer? Duncan Hancock, Lamma Island

title: From The Diplomat’s burgers to Argo’s egg waffles, Hong Kong bars are raising the bar on food
description: The city’s bars are elevating their food menus, transforming from casual drinking spots into gastronomic destinations with stand-out dishes.
content: The queue outside Bar Leone isn’t just for its acclaimed cocktails. More than a few guests are making a pilgrimage for Leone’s signature smoked olives – cheekily called “the world’s best olives (maybe)” – and its mortadella sandwich, with layers of thinly sliced mortadella, creamy whipped ricotta and tangy pickled chillies sandwiched between crispy focaccia. Up the road at sister bar Montana, the pulled-pork sliders have their own following. Not long ago, bar food in Hong Kong usually meant a bowl of peanuts, pretzels or prawn crackers to go with your drink – regardless of whether you were having beer, wine or cocktails. Now the city’s best bars are treating food as part of the main event. Not as a garnish for drinks, but a reason to come, stay and return. So pronounced is this trend that at some establishments, the kitchen is threatening to overshadow the bar. At The Diplomat, the burger – a simple yet satisfying quarter-pound Wagyu beef patty cooked medium-rare, topped with melted Cheddar cheese and house-made aioli on a toasted sesame seed bun – was named fourth-best in the world and No 1 in Asia on The World’s 101 Best Burger Places list. Owner John Nugent insists there was no campaign behind this. “It came out of nowhere. We didn’t know they had visited or rated us,” he says. “It just kind of happened, and we obviously got a lot of love from that.” On the menu since day one six years ago, the burger is now capped at 50 a day. Is it a problem when the food becomes more famous than the drinks? Nugent doesn’t think so. “We welcome people that don’t drink, drink a lot, or anything in between,” he says. “And if they just want a glass of water with a burger, a Cubano or some nuggets? Yeah, absolutely … have at it.” Lorenzo Antinori, co-founder and owner of Bar Leone and Montana, goes further. “If guests come in specifically for the mortadella sandwich and stay for a filthy martini, that’s a win,” he says. For him, strong food helps turn a bar into “a neighbourhood hub rather than just a late-night drinking venue”. This shift reflects how people are going out in Hong Kong now. Rather than committing to one long restaurant dinner, many prefer to graze – hopping between bars, sharing plates, and letting the evening unfold in stages. Gokan captures that in-between appetite perfectly. Its menu features izakaya-inspired cuisine and Japanese homestyle dishes, with a late-night bar menu that includes the bestselling Napolitan pasta and ikura potato salad. A local take on the izakaya staple, its version is made with Sichuan golden century egg, Chinese-style zha cai, and topped with soy egg and ikura. It’s light, refined, and pairs beautifully with their clean, clarified cocktails. “Cocktails aren’t the only way to attract people and let them stay,” says bar manager Morris Chang. “It’s the atmosphere and the food you provide as well.” Wine bars are also seeing this change. “When we first opened Silène Wine Bar, not many wine bars were selling food – it was mostly cheese and cold cuts, or something basic like breadsticks,” recalls Aurélien Guédès. That’s why he enlisted chef Benoit Prost (formerly of Louise) to design a small but elevated food menu that changes with the seasons. The supersized croque monsieur is a mainstay (as demanded by Silène’s regulars) but the beef tartare and juicy Spanish-style mussels with chorizo are further evidence that the plates served up from the kitchen are not there merely to keep wine glasses company. When it comes to rounding off the night, a sweet dessert is becoming the new nightcap. Argo has a Hong Kong egg waffle with pistachio ice cream, soy caramel and chocolate sauce. The Diplomat has a hot fudge sundae with home-made vanilla ice cream, while its sister bar Sugar King has its famous flan (limited to 15-20 a night). Silène offers a gluten-free chocolate cake, and Gokan serves its famous kakigori three ways: Shirokuma, Coconut Mango Yogurt, and The Macallan Crème Brûlée. So what makes good bar food anyway? According to Remus Isopel, F&B director at Four Seasons Hong Kong, “The best bar food opens the palate. It has enough character to be memorable, but it should also feel effortless.” Aled Burt, bar manager at Bourke’s – known for its moreish liver parfait toast and chicken Parmesan – adds: “Good bar food is approachable. It’s something that you can order and enjoy easily. But it’s also high quality, and there’s a story behind it.” For Antinori, it’s all about creating culinary nostalgia. “Good bar food is crave-worthy, unpretentious and punchy. It should hit high notes of salt, acid and fat and make you instinctively reach for your glass.” Nugent has watched the shift happen across the city. “We can’t just be serving nuts and something out of a fryer,” he says. “These days, the food is very much part of the programme and taken very, very seriously.” Judging by the queues – and the caps on burgers and flans – Hong Kong agrees.

title: ‘Either blood or blown’: graphic details of botched US execution revealed
description: Court filing details how Tennessee executioners struggled with 10 needles and bent equipment as Christa Pike survived two lethal injection doses.
content: Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike’s arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or “blown”, before she was injected with the lethal drug, her lawyer wrote in a court document filed Thursday. The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, lawyer Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote. Pike, 50, was hospitalised after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on September 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death. State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first does not result in death, but it does not spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection. After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her lawyers did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged. The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state’s death row are challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures. “Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true – and will continue to come true – without substantial change,” Kit Thomas, a lawyer representing people on death row in the case, said. Nearly an hour of IV attempts The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee’s execution protocols at 6.34pm, Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein. They managed to set an IV in Pike’s right arm within about 6 minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm. Pike was “wincing and grimacing” as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles. One team member said a vein “might be blowing” at 6.57pm while examining an IV in Pike’s left arm, but two others said they could not tell, Spivey wrote. “One of them said something like, ‘it’s either blood or blown, I need to know’,” Spivey wrote. The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the lawyer said. “I think it’s blown,” the lawyer recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7.07pm. After more attempts, the team decided at 7.13pm that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike’s left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor. Pike complained of burning arm pain A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later. Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines – a process that happens in an adjoining room – were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike’s left arm. It’s not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7.34pm, Pike said her arm was hurting. “I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns,” she said, according to her lawyer. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an “agitated snoring sound,” Spivey wrote. Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room. Spivey called fellow lawyers at 8.22pm and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn’t authorised under the state’s protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care. Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8.50pm, and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9.14pm.

title: Chinese stocks bounce back from bear market on suspected state support
description: CSI 300 wipes out losses of as much as 2 per cent as key ETF trading volumes surge, indicating possible state-backed buying.
content: Chinese stocks rebounded on Friday after a sell-off drove the benchmark index into a bear market, as surging trading volumes in the nation’s biggest exchange-traded funds (ETFs) pointed to possible state buying and major companies at the centre of the artificial intelligence trade sought to soothe investors. The CSI 300 Index rose 1.7 per cent to 4,105.33 at the close, reversing an earlier decline of as much as 2 per cent. Turnover in several key ETFs tracking the gauge surged, suggesting that Central Huijin Investment and other state-backed funds might have intervened to stem further losses. Among them, the CSI 300 ETF run by E Fund Management recorded 19.5 billion yuan (US$2.9 billion) in turnover, its busiest trading day since October 9, 2024. The benchmark technically entered bear-market territory a day earlier after sliding 20 per cent from its June peak. Technology stocks led the rebound. The ChiNext 50 index rallied 4.3 per cent after Zhongji Innolight and two other leading makers of optical transceivers used in AI data centres reassured investors that operations remained normal, while one unveiled a share buy-back plan. The Star Market 50 index, which tracks some of the nation’s biggest chipmakers, including Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp and Cambricon Technologies, surged 3 per cent. The dramatic turn indicated that government intervention still wielded substantial influence on China’s stock market, which Beijing views as a key funding source for its tech self-reliance strategy. The China Securities Regulatory Commission signalled earlier this month that more supportive measures could be introduced if stocks came under further pressure. Wu Qing, chairman of the regulator, also pledged this week to attract more long-term capital by further opening the onshore market to foreign investors and broadening the range of ETF products. “Investors should watch closely whether the inflows of state-backed funds can be sustained, and ETF flows are an important leading indicator,” said Jiang Lingbo, an analyst at Nanjing Securities. “If we can see persistent big inflows into equity ETFs, there’s a chance that the market could bottom out by the end of October.” Zhongji Innolight surged 3.8 per cent to 612.63 yuan in Shenzhen, while rivals Eoptolink Technology added 1.2 per cent to 261 yuan and Suzhou TFC Optical Communication rose 1.9 per cent to 200.81 yuan. In separate exchange filings at midday, the three makers of optical transceivers said demand for their products remained strong and capacity was fully utilised. Eoptolink also said that it would spend up to 1 billion yuan repurchasing its shares. Chinese stocks had come under pressure throughout the week as concerns mounted over the country’s growth outlook after Beijing refrained from introducing fresh stimulus measures and the crowded AI trade continued to unravel in the US. Global investment banks from UBS Group to Nomura Holdings said this week that China would likely stick to its current policy approach through the rest of the year after third-quarter data indicated the economy remained on track to meet its annual growth target of between 4.5 and 5 per cent. “Stronger exports and faster fiscal execution have reduced the urgency for further policy easing, with subdued domestic demand and household deleveraging continuing to constrain broader earnings growth,” said Laura Wang, a strategist at Morgan Stanley, in a note on Thursday. “Meanwhile, elevated US Treasury yields and renewed expectations of US Federal Reserve tightening remain headwinds for global liquidity and offshore equity valuations.” Investors also remained wary of the fallout from new taxes on offshore trusts held by wealthy Chinese families. The recent market weakness could partly be attributed to selling by major shareholders seeking to raise funds for tax payments ahead of the 90-day grace period that expired on Thursday, according to Hua An Securities.

title: Asia-Pacific AI agent market to surge 14-fold to US$11.2 billion by 2030, Omdia says
description: In the period to 2030, the agentic share of the region’s AI software revenue is projected to rise to 12.3 per cent from 1.7 per cent.
content: The artificial intelligence agent software market across Asia, Australia and New Zealand is set to expand more than 14-fold by 2030, according to research firm Omdia, as Chinese tech companies increasingly deploy automated tools across office and industrial operations. During its annual event in Beijing on Thursday, Omdia forecast that regional market revenue, which included mainland China and Hong Kong, would reach US$11.2 billion in 2030, up from an estimated US$782 million this year. Over the same period, the agentic share of the region’s AI software revenue was projected to rise to 12.3 per cent from 1.7 per cent. AI agents use models to autonomously plan and carry out multi-step tasks – such as data analysis, report writing and software operations – allowing users to delegate work that would otherwise require repeated instructions. China’s State Council has set targets for the penetration of next-generation intelligent devices and agents to exceed 70 per cent by 2027 and 90 per cent by 2030 under its “AI Plus” initiative. Major Chinese tech companies are accelerating deployment to capture growing adoption in their own market. Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, unveiled AgentCore last month. The enterprise platform is designed to help businesses build, run and manage AI agents, including monitoring their performance and connecting them to existing business systems. Tencent Holdings is also expanding its WorkBuddy agent workspace, which the company said can edit Word documents, Excel spreadsheets and PowerPoint presentations directly, and connect to services including Notion and GitHub to retrieve information and carry out tasks. In an August report, Moody’s Ratings expected the combined capital spending of Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance, to more than double to about US$140 billion this year from US$65 billion in 2025. Cloud services remain the main channel for monetising AI, Moody’s said, with lower-cost open-source models accelerating enterprise adoption in China. However, intense price competition and the smaller scale of Chinese cloud businesses left them less able than their US peers to fund further AI infrastructure expansion from cloud cash flow, it said. Maximising return on investment remains a priority for enterprises adopting AI. “Using more tokens does not mean producing more value,” Omdia chief analyst Su Lian Jye said, referring to the units of data processed by AI models and a common basis for charging customers. Su said businesses needed to assess the value of AI’s output and improve efficiency by matching tasks with appropriate models. Chinese companies were also using open-source models to attract developers and users, although deploying them still required substantial engineering expertise, he said. The push into AI agents is also opening a new front in competition among cloud providers. Integrating models, software and computing infrastructure could make customers harder to win away, as moving an agent-based application to another cloud could require transferring both the model and the optimisations behind it, making migration more complicated, Su said.

title: US police officer accused of taking over dead man’s home after finding body
description: Florida officer claimed he took possession of property to ‘prevent squatters from taking control of it’.
content: A Florida police officer who found a man dead during a welfare check in 2022 is accused of taking possession of the man’s home and impersonating him for years while fixing up the place, authorities said. The officer said he took possession of the property weeks after discovering the homeowner’s body to “prevent squatters from taking control of it,” according to a court document he filed. Investigators in South Florida have accused Lauderhill police officer Brian Sguros of carrying out a “complex scheme” to take control of the US$400,000 home. They say he made it appear the man was still alive by using his identification to pay taxes on the property and obtain permits to make repairs. Sguros was arrested this week and charged with five felonies, including official misconduct and criminal use of deceased personal identification. He appeared in court at a brief hearing on Wednesday and then dashed away from reporters outside. Messages seeking comment were left Thursday with one of his lawyers and Sguros, who has been suspended from his job. Court documents in a related civil case show that the officer’s attempt to take possession of the two-storey house in a tidy neighbourhood just outside Fort Lauderdale became known after a real estate group bought the house from the man’s relatives in 2025. Sguros said in an affidavit that in August 2022 – less than a month after he found Dennis West dead inside the Lauderhill home – he took possession of the property and spent the next 2½ years making repairs, spending more than US$200,000 of his own money. He said the house had been filled with trash, that its roof was partially collapsed and that the structure was unstable. Sguros said in another court document that he took over the property “believing that by cleaning, securing, and restoring a dangerous and abandoned residence he was acting lawfully and responsibly to protect the surrounding community”. He argued that he made no attempts to hide what he was doing. But investigators with Broward County Sheriff’s Office said the deception began when the officer told the county medical examiner that he was friends with West, who had died of natural causes, and that the man had no family, which was not true. Sguros paid taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name, and forged his signature to get permits for work at the home, the sheriff’s office said. Investigators said Sguros also used his access to law enforcement databases to find information about West. The officer in February 2025 filed paperwork with the county appraiser stating his possession of the home. But after the real estate group later acquired deeds to the property, he filed a civil case against the company seeking to be reimbursed for the money he spent on repairs.

title: China cancer patient who inspired hit film hopes to stop treatment after 35,000 pills over 2 decades
description: Driven by the cinematic impact of ‘Dying to Survive’, Chinese health authorities fast-tracked critical healthcare reforms for cancer patients.
content: Lu Yong, who has a slow-growing blood and bone marrow cancer and inspired the 2018 blockbuster Dying to Survive, has begun reducing his medication and hopes to stop taking it completely within three months. The acclaimed film is based on Lu’s experience. He has chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and helped patients across China obtain affordable, life-saving generic drugs from India, but was prosecuted by Chinese authorities for selling “fake drugs”. Before his diagnosis, 58-year-old Lu was a textiles trader in Jiangsu province in eastern China. Diagnosed with CML in 2002, he took Gleevec, a patented drug made by Novartis, for the first few years. Lu said Gleevec was the most effective treatment for him, but it cost 23,500 yuan (US$3,500) per packet – an expense of 800 yuan a day. In 2004, Lu contacted an Indian pharmaceutical company to buy generic drugs that had been approved for use by Indian regulators. The drugs saved him a significant amount of money. Lu then began acting as an intermediary, helping other patients who could not speak English obtain the drugs from Indian companies. He negotiated substantial price cuts to meet the high volume of demand. However, the drugs did not have a licence for import into China and were therefore considered fake there. “I built an online chat group among us patients. Every week we heard some patients pass away. This is the motivation that prompted me to continue to source these drugs,” Lu told Jimu News. He was detained in 2013 and charged with selling counterfeit drugs the following year. More than 1,000 patients signed a joint letter appealing on his behalf, drawing significant attention across the country. In January 2015, prosecutors dropped the charge against Lu. In early October, Lu visited the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After assessing his condition, doctors suggested that he try halving his medication. He is scheduled to take a gene test three months later. If the result is still negative, he will no longer need to take medication, doctors said. Over the past 24 years, Lu has taken more than 35,000 pills. “I aspire to be an ordinary person. It is a good thing to stop taking drugs, even for half a year or a year,” Lu said. “Not needing to take medicine will make me feel like a normal person. It will be a rebirth for me.” After Dying to Survive brought the plight of cancer patients into the spotlight, Chinese health authorities accelerated healthcare reforms. In 2019, the authorities decided that smuggled generic drugs would no longer be considered fake drugs under the law. In recent years, the public health insurance scheme has expanded significantly to cover a range of imported drugs, easing patients’ heavy financial burdens. While many people credited Lu with helping to bring down the prices of those imported drugs, he replied: “I am only an ordinary patient. Those who pushed forward the medical reform are legislative committee members, doctors and countless patients’ appeals.”

title: Harmful air pollution affected one-third of world population in 2026: report
description: Reports find 34 per cent of world’s population exposed to extremely high levels of ozone pollution this year, mainly linked to heatwaves, wildfires and human ac
content:
Heatwaves, wildfires and human-caused emissions combined this year to expose one third of the world’s population to extremely high levels of ozone pollution, a European Union report said last month.
In an analysis covering the first eight months of 2026, the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) – the European Union’s Earth observation programme – highlighted the close relationship between climate change and air pollution. When heat and sunlight react with airborne emissions from wildfires, vehicles and industry, they create ground-level ozone pollution (see graphic).
This damages lung tissue, causes breathing problems, triggers asthma attacks and leads to other health issues.
Despite progress in cutting the most harmful air pollutants in recent decades, ozone pollution has proved more difficult to tackle as climate change fuels the conditions that favour its formation.
This year’s ozone pollution was driven in part by record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires. These included ones that seared Europe and North America, sending smoke well beyond their borders, and more recent major blazes in Indonesia.
The warming El Nino weather pattern – which started in June and is due to peak later this year – could also contribute to more fires in Southeast Asia, according to the analysis.
“Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source,” CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report.
CAMS uses satellite data and computer models to track air pollution and wildfires.
The report found that 34 per cent of the global population was exposed to “extremely poor” air quality between January 1 and September 15, meaning concentrations of ozone were well above the World Health Organization’s exposure guidance. Another 17 per cent of the world breathed “very poor” air.
Asia has the highest rate of exposure to ozone pollution, with 53 per cent of its population breathing “extremely poor” air. Another 22 per cent were exposed to “very poor” ozone.
The continent’s widespread emissions are driven by industrialisation, economic development and transport, as well as wildfires and the burning of agricultural residue.
New Delhi in India, Dhaka in Bangladesh, Chongqing in China and Lahore in Pakistan were among the Asian cities with “extremely poor” ozone.
Two thirds of the population in North America and 45 per cent in Europe were exposed to “poor” or “very poor” air quality. EU regulation has effectively reduced emissions from air pollutants, except for ozone, the report said.
Ozone pollution is linked to 60,000 premature deaths per year in Europe, Ian Marnane, an official at the European Environment Agency, told a media briefing.
Smoke from forest fires, crop burning and cooking are significant contributors to Africa’s air pollution, while Saharan dust travels as far as Europe. Eight per cent of Africa’s population endured “extremely poor” air quality this year. It was “very poor” or “poor” for 19 per cent.
Ozone pollution levels were very high in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo and extremely elevated in Rio de Janeiro. Still, the air quality was “good” or “fair” for 81 per cent of South America’s population.
One bright spot was Oceania – including Australia and New Zealand – where 66 per cent of the population enjoyed “good” ozone levels and 34 per cent lived under “fair” conditions.
Air quality tells us how clean or polluted the air outside is. It is tracked using the Air Quality Index (AQI). The AQI has a range of values between 0 and 500 and uses six colour-coded categories.
Green and yellow (0-100): Air quality is acceptable and safe for most people.
Orange (101-150): Air quality is unhealthy for sensitive individuals, including children, older adults and people with heart or lung conditions.
Red and purple (151-300): Air quality is unhealthy to very unhealthy for everyone, including vulnerable groups.
Maroon (301-500): Air quality reaches hazardous emergency levels, posing serious health risks to the entire population.

title: Replica of 14th century Yuan dynasty masterpiece in New York’s Met museum
description: Chinese artists and scholars have carefully recreated the ‘Medicine Buddha’ mural, fostering cultural exchange despite US-China tensions.
content:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in the United States has an area with Chinese Buddhist art. There, one artwork grabs visitors’ attention right away.
It is a large wall filled with images of a Buddhist gathering. This is the Medicine Buddha, a mural from the 14th century. It comes from the Yuan dynasty, which lasted from 1279 to 1368. In 1928, the 700-year-old relic left China after being sold by poor monks.
Zhang Jian is the director of the Meticulous Painting Institute at the Chinese National Academy of Arts. He was very impressed by the work. For three years, Zhang worked with Chinese artists and scholars to carefully study every crack, line and mark to create a full-size copy. Making a copy is much easier than bringing the relic back to China.
In a time when the relationship between the US and China faces difficulties, people from both countries still work together on cultural projects.

title: Even as Beijing boosts oversight, Chinese investors continue pivot to offshore assets
description: Property values and low bank deposit rates in China are fuelling demand for wealth management alternatives, Moody’s says.
content: Chinese households are increasingly shifting assets from real estate and bank deposits into more lucrative investments at home and abroad, despite growing oversight, Moody’s Ratings said. A multi-year downturn in the Chinese property market and low interest rates are fuelling the demand for alternative investments, the ratings agency said in a report published this week. Chinese investors are looking for investments that “offer higher returns than deposits while maintaining relatively low risk,” the authors wrote. China has increased oversight of citizens’ offshore investments over the past year by stepping up efforts to enforce a 20 per cent capital gains tax on offshore investments. Growth in offshore investments by Chinese households could “moderate” in the near term as financial institutions onboard customers through more stringent procedures, Moody’s said. Yet, the ratings agency said these policies were unlikely to dim demand. “Offshore investments continue to offer a significant yield advantage over domestic alternatives,” the agency wrote. China has been cutting its benchmark one-year loan prime rate since 2020 to combat slowing economic growth, a downturn in the property sector and disruptions due to the Covid-19 pandemic that have weighed on everything from employment to consumption. Lower property values reduced the appeal of homeownership, and Moody’s said falling interest rates had prompted domestic banks to cut deposit rates. At the end of 2022, property accounted for 47 per cent of Chinese household assets and bank deposits stood at 25 per cent, according to the report. Both holdings have trended down since then, it added. The outstanding balance of mainland Chinese financial products increased by 13.9 per cent in 2024 and 15.5 per cent in 2025, according to a Moody’s estimate, while retail bank deposits rose just 10.4 per cent in 2024 and 9.7 per cent last year. Bank wealth management products, mutual funds and insurance policies have grown “rapidly” as investment tools, Moody’s added. The Moody’s report called out Hong Kong as a source of “strong interest” for Chinese investors. Special schemes such as the Hong Kong-mainland China Stock Connect and Wealth Management Connect offer “regulated channels” for Chinese investors to buy and sell equities and exchange-traded funds in Hong Kong. Southbound Stock Connect average daily turnover - meaning transactions from the mainland - reached HK$121.1 billion (US$15.4 billion) in 2025, more than double the HK$48.2 billion of 2024, stock market operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing said. Sales of non-exchange-traded investment products such as pooled investment funds grew by 40 per cent in 2024 and 63 per cent in 2025, according to a survey by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and Securities and Futures Commission. High-net-worth investors in Asia-Pacific, including mainland China, were behind the surge in Hong Kong’s asset and wealth management market, the monetary authority said in 2025. “Demand for offshore assets has materially increased,” the report said.

title: Local pair’s brush with Hong Kong Open history a sign the sport is flourishing
description: For a time on Thursday, Isaac Lam and Matthew Cheung topped the tournament leaderboard, offering a glimpse of what might be.
content: There was a moment on Thursday when history looked like being made at the Link Hong Kong Open, and while forgiving greens and some generous pins meant normal service was later restored, the glimpse on offer was of a local game in rude health. For the first time since the tournament began in 1959, two Hongkongers – Isaac Lam and Matthew Cheung – briefly sat at the top of the leaderboard at six-under-par. By the end of the day they were far from alone and further down the field than they might have hoped, with Kim Min-kyu and Yosuke Asaji also carding 64s to create a four-way tie for fifth. Above them, Anirban Lahiri and Kevin Yuan shared top spot at eight under, while Thailand pair Jazz Janewattananond and Poosit Supupramai both came home in 63. In the Open’s history, Dominic Boulet still holds the record for the best finish by a Hongkonger, with his tie for fourth in 1996. Taichi Kho came closest to challenging that two years ago, finishing sixth the year Patrick Reed shot a third-round 59 and won at a canter. And while a fine start does not necessarily mean success at the end, the opening salvoes, coupled with the fact that a host of Cheung’s and Lam’s compatriots sit close behind, is evidence that golf in Hong Kong is in the ascendancy. There have been wins on the Asian Tour, for Taichi Kho, the China Tour, for Jason Hak Shun-yat and Lam, and historic amateur team success so far this year, with the men winning the Nomura Cup and Putra Cup for the first time in a matter of weeks last month. On Sunday, the city will send a record seven men to the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship in New Zealand, a tournament where even the host country has only six representatives. “It’s cool to see,” Cheung said. “All the Hong Kong players have been playing a lot of good golf all over the world. You know, Isaac [Lam] won at the [China Tour] Fanling Classic this year, Taichi [Kho] has won in [International Series] Morocco. “We’ve had a lot of amateur wins as well. So it’s really cool to see the Hong Kong guys playing well everywhere, and especially at home and at the Hong Kong Open.” In all, there are 11 local players in the field this week, and walking, or more accurately stalking, the course as putts dropped and sporadic cheers erupted from a respectably first-day crowd was head coach Tim Tang. Amateur Jeffrey Shen Wang-ngai got much of the attention as he put together a four-under 66, and while professionals Kho, Hak and Leon D’Silva toiled away, another four amateurs – Ethan Tian, Markus Lam, Kim Joon-ho and William Tang – competed across the composite course with varying degrees of success. Isaac Lam called the sight of so many local amateurs in the field “incredible”, adding that it was “great to see how much development there has been in Hong Kong”. “When I was playing, when I was an amateur, we didn’t have that many amateur guys that were as top level as the kids are now,” he said. “Guys playing in colleges, playing professional tournaments with us, and playing well as well. It’s really good, it’s really nice to see.” Following his players and jealously guarding their fortunes is what Tang has been doing for much of the past decade, firstly with the Golf Association of Hong Kong, China, and latterly as part of the Hong Kong Sports Institute set-up. He knows more than most the journey the sport has taken in those intervening years, and before. Now the coach, he played in his home Open, and was part of the city squad that won silver at the National Games in 2013, when the approach was not necessarily as professional as it is now. “I think this [golf’s growth] is a combination of the committee getting serious about elite performance, and of bringing in Danny [Lai Yee-june, the CEO] and bringing in me,” said Tang, who joined in 2017 the year after his boss’s appointment. Any recreational ethos was jettisoned as a result, and “just beating Singapore” was replaced with “why can’t we win”. That approach has spawned a new generation in women’s golf too, where the likes of Arianna Lau, Sophie Han and Sabrina Wong have more than made their mark at an amateur level. Professionally, meanwhile, Ginnie Ding had her best finish on the Ladies European Tour at the Aramco Korea Championship earlier this month, with third place also securing her full card for next season. “We need to encourage serious golfers to be serious,” Tang said. “There are so many s*** golfers who want to cruise, they want to drag you down.” Kho’s gold at the Asian Games in 2023, and Lau’s Junior World Championship triumph the following year, lifted the association into the top tier of sport in Hong Kong. The place at the HKSI brings with it “more ammunition” for Tang to support his players and build the culture essential to further success. “I have to keep golf in Tier A, that’s my job; if I don’t do that, I get fired,” Tang said. “I need to look at who is going to get results in the next three to four years and support them. If someone doesn’t want it, I can’t force them.” As with all Olympic sports, Tang’s next major focus is the Los Angeles Games in 2028, when he would like to have the maximum four players qualified for the tournament. First though is the trip to Te Arai Links outside Auckland, and an event Tang believes in 2021 was the catalyst for the success Hong Kong is seeing on the course. “I think the biggest shift for me is when Taichi almost won in Dubai,” he said. “That tournament showed everyone in the world ‘hey, we’re not just here to make the cut, we can actually compete and finish good’.”

title: Wall Street piles into Hong Kong’s dim sum bonds despite fading yuan funding edge: BofA
description: Offshore yuan issuance jumps 68 per cent as US banks tap Chinese capital, making it their third-largest funding currency, report says.
content: Hong Kong’s offshore yuan bond market is becoming an increasingly important funding source for global banks, with US lenders driving a surge in issuance even as the currency’s traditional funding advantage over the dollar narrows. The shift offers a glimpse of how financial ties between Wall Street and China are evolving despite geopolitical tensions. For US banks, the attraction increasingly lies in access to Chinese capital rather than lower borrowing costs. Offshore yuan-denominated bonds, known as dim sum bonds, reached 774 billion yuan (US$116 billion) in issuance as of October 20, up 68 per cent from a year earlier, according to a Bank of America (BofA) Global Research report on Wednesday. Financial institutions accounted for 57 per cent of total supply, with issuance from the sector rising 139 per cent year on year. Foreign financial institutions issued 333 billion yuan of bonds, up 169 per cent from a year earlier and more than double their average annual issuance between 2022 and 2025. US banks led the surge, raising 167 billion yuan, an increase of 130 billion yuan from a year earlier. US global systemically important banks have raised the equivalent of US$22 billion through offshore yuan bonds this year, making the yuan their third-largest funding currency after the US dollar and euro, overtaking the sterling, BofA said. The surge has continued despite a fading cost advantage. At the end of September, yields on three-year yuan government bonds, after currency hedging, were only about 0.1 percentage points below comparable US Treasury yields, the bank said. The rise of offshore Chinese capital had “fundamentally changed the rationale” for yuan issuance, it added. The question is no longer whether the offshore yuan market will continue to grow, but rather how quickly regulators will allow offshore yuan capital pools to expand BofA Global Research The market was also expanding as China’s offshore US dollar bond market shrunk, having contracted to about US$400 billion from its 2021 peak, amid a collapse in property-sector issuance and corporate deleveraging, according to the report. The outstanding dim sum bond market reached 1.9 trillion yuan, or about US$284 billion, nearly quadrupling from the end of 2021 and growing to about 70 per cent of the size of the offshore dollar market, the bank said. Demand from mainland Chinese investors is supporting the expansion. Holdings through the southbound Bond Connect scheme – which allows mainland investors to access Hong Kong’s offshore bond market – reached 1 trillion yuan at the end of August, up 85 per cent year on year, after authorities broadened participation by institutional investors, BofA said. Nearly 30 per cent of dim sum bonds issued this year had an average life exceeding seven years. Chinese technology companies are also tapping the market to finance investment in artificial intelligence. Their offshore yuan issuance rose to 57 billion yuan this year, broadly matching their US dollar bond issuance. BofA estimated that China would need to invest US$1.5 trillion in AI-related capital expenditure between 2026 and 2030, including about US$900 billion by major internet platforms. More than 75 per cent of technology-sector yuan bonds issued this year had maturities of more than seven years, the report said. Future growth will depend partly on Beijing’s willingness to expand channels for mainland money to flow offshore. Authorities have raised the annual southbound Bond Connect quota to 800 billion yuan from 500 billion yuan after the previous limit was nearly exhausted. The new quota was equivalent to more than 40 per cent of the existing dim sum bond market, BofA said, making policy decisions a key determinant on future growth. “The question is no longer whether the [offshore yuan] market will continue to grow, but rather how quickly regulators will allow offshore yuan capital pools to expand,” the report added.

title: Q&A | Brunello Cucinelli on director Giuseppe Tornatore’s documentary about his life
description: The ‘king of cashmere’ talks about why he picked the Oscar-winning director of Cinema Paradiso to tell his life story, and why young people need hope over fear.
content: When designer and entrepreneur Brunello Cucinelli announced that he would be releasing a documentary about his life directed by Oscar winner Giuseppe Tornatore, it caught many by surprise. Titled Brunello, Il Visionario Garbato (Brunello: The Gracious Visionary), the film combines interviews and real-life footage with re-enactments to show Cucinelli’s childhood and his early days as a striving entrepreneur and designer, long before he became known as the “king of cashmere”. Works of this type are normally done posthumously. Still very much alive and thriving at 73, Cucinelli felt that working on this documentary while he was still around would make more sense than letting someone else look back at his life once he was gone, as he explained in a recent interview during Milan Fashion Week. Here, Cucinelli tells us what to expect from the film, which is set to be released in Greater China next month. Where did the decision to make this film come from? I wanted to do this film because normally documentaries like this one are made after the subject is dead, but once one dies it’s not easy to tell the truth about the subject and everyone only has nice things to say. I’ve seen a lot of documentaries that didn’t represent human beings that I knew as they really were but since I’m still alive you hear my real voice, so I think it’s more truthful. After someone dies, people say that a wonderful person passed away but we should say instead, “a human being passed away” and perhaps this human being wasn’t such a great person after all. Why did you decide to mix real life with reenacted scenes? I wanted to show what life in the Italian countryside in the 60s was like and preserve it for the future. We didn’t have electricity or water at home so I wanted to show that, as recently as 60 years ago, many people in the countryside still lived like that in Italy; very differently from the way they lived in cities. I approached Tornatore because he had a similar life in Sicily. He did Cinema Paradiso (1988) to represent his own experience. It was his life as a child. I only did the movie because Tornatore directed the movie and Nicola Piovani was in charge of the soundtrack. It would have been impossible to hire a younger director who didn’t know that reality and that life. How involved were you in the post-production? I only saw 10-12 per cent of all the scenes we shot. I was also lucky enough to buy the home where I was born, which stayed pretty much the same, near Solomeo; it was like a farm. I went there and saw Tornatore with all the non-professional actors and the table was the same and the fireplace was the same. He wanted me to see first-hand all the scenes as the movie was being shot. I did 60 hours of interviews with him and my wife did 10 hours and then just 40 seconds of her in the film [were used]. He spent 14 months editing the film; it’s all his work. I refused to see the movie as it was being done and I only saw it a month before it was ready. He said to look at it with a poetic mindset. I couldn’t sleep after watching the movie and he gave me a notepad to make notes but I told him not to touch it because it was perfect and really represented my life. I trusted him because he lived like me and I had seen Cinema Paradiso about him going to the movies in the little town where he grew up. What message do you want to send to the world with this film? The first message is aimed at young people: listen to your parents but not to everything they say. When you’re a teenager, parents often plan your life and tell you that you have to do this and that. I believe that children should be able to dream and to fail. My dad only once asked me, “How is school going?” He trusted me and wanted me to dream and if something didn’t go well, then things would get better eventually. I did the same thing with my daughters. Back then the fear was that if you didn’t study, you couldn’t find work and now the fear is about AI taking your job. They instilled fear in those who didn’t study for a typical job but I wanted to substitute that fear with hope. Life without hope has no meaning. This is the message for young people. Listen to your parents when they talk about big ideas, but then go on and dream and find your path. When my daughters were in school, one said she wanted to work with me and the other one that she wanted to join a circus and become a street performer and I said, “Please go ahead, I know many street performers.” When you’re in your 20s you always change your mind and you have to find your path so you have to keep dreaming and look up at the sky. When my children were young, I would help them skip class sometimes and even keep it from my wife. This makes you approach life in a different way. There is an intelligence based on traditional studying but also an intelligence based on enriching your soul. My dad always used to say that as long as you’re a good person, it’s not really about the money or anything like that, you just have to be an honest person. What did you discover while working on the movie? In 60 hours of interviews, I told Tornatore so many things, like when I used to climb an oak tree and look at the stars and my parents were looking for me and asked what I was doing and I would just say, “I’m looking at the sky and the stars.” I spent two years going through my childhood in detail with him and it was all recorded on video. I even considered being a priest when I was little because I liked spending time on my own. Now that I’m 73 years old I want to spend even more time contemplating eternity. This morning I spent time contemplating things while reading about friendship; it’s a ritual that gives me tremendous joy. We are custodians for a limited time frame on this planet so you need to nourish the soul just like you feed your body. How has the feedback been so far? I get emails from all over the world. Many young people who didn’t have the chance to live that life want to experience that; they tell me all the time. Life in the countryside without TV and with animals is fascinating to young people these days. This means that human beings need time to be themselves without preconceived notions. I don’t have any preconceptions about any human beings because everyone is different, inside and out. Are you looking forward to bringing the movie to Asia? When I go to China or Mongolia, where we source our fibres, I tell the suppliers that I couldn’t exist without them. I’ve been going for 40 years and that’s why I started studying Chinese history and philosophy. If you come to [my hometown] Solomeo you will see a bust of Plato looking at a bust of Confucius in mid-conversation and we have the same sculptures in our boutique in Shanghai. I love these discussions about big topics. This life I have came from nothing. My dad was a farmer and I began to make sweaters and now I’m here. Where there is humanity there is always something special. Three new fashion documentaries to check out Be Brave Diesel founder Renzo Rosso is the subject of this documentary, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in September. Director Francesco Carrozzini used AI to re-create scenes from Rosso’s childhood and his early years. The film also features contributions from figures such as Anna Wintour and John Galliano. Twiggy Directed by Sadie Frost, Twiggy looks at the life of British supermodel Twiggy, hailed as “the face of the 60s” by British media. Known for her gamine looks and as a symbol of the Swinging 60s, Twiggy got her nickname because of her slim frame. The film features contributions from celebrities such as Paul McCartney. Avedon Oscar-winning director Ron Howard is behind Avedon, about the life and work of legendary photographer Richard Avedon. His black-and-white photos of legendary figures such as Marilyn Monroe and Andy Warhol have come to define the second half of the 20th century. Acquired by Netflix, the documentary is set to hit screens this autumn.

title: Video shows fatal shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley by US police officer
description: Sergeant Hunter Foster, who fired his gun into a moving car while responding to a shoplifting call, has been cleared of criminal wrongdoing.
content: Mississippi released video on Thursday showing the fatal shooting of a one-year-old boy by a police officer whom state authorities have cleared of criminal wrongdoing. Kohen Wiley was killed in June when Senatobia police officer Sergeant Hunter Foster fired his gun into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call. Kohen’s family says footage of the fatal encounter shows the shooting was not justified. The Mississippi Attorney General’s office said this week its month-long probe found that Foster’s use of force was appropriate. Foster’s lawyer, Martin Zummach, has said his client had “no choice” but to shoot at the vehicle because it was going to hit him. Ben Crump, a civil rights lawyer representing Kohen’s family, said Foster was not in danger when he fired the shot that killed the one-year-old. Crump said the video shows Foster fired that shot from the passenger side of the car. Kohen’s close relatives watched the footage shot during the June 14 encounter in a Walmart car park in Senatobia, about 65km (40 miles) south of Memphis, Tennessee. The video included footage from the camera worn by the officer who shot and killed Kohen. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday in early November, Crump said during a news conference on Thursday. “The word ‘justified’ has haunted me,” Kohen’s maternal grandmother, Veronica Roberson, said during the news conference. “There’s no justification for that.” Roberson said she found out from reading the news that the state had cleared the officer, and she also saw parts of the video that had been leaked online on Wednesday. She called the lack of notice from the attorney general’s office and the leak of the footage a “slap in the face” to her family. Crump said the officers’ response – running at the vehicle with guns drawn to apprehend alleged shoplifters – was excessive and reckless. Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, previously denied that she and her friend stole diapers from the store and they have not been charged, according to state and county court records. “Diapers are something a mother needs for a child. Diapers should never cost a baby their life,” Crump said. “This decision sends a message that a black baby boy, his life, is not as valuable as the white diapers that he is wrapped in.” Martin Zummach, a lawyer representing Foster, has said the footage vindicates his client because he was in danger from the moving vehicle and had “no choice” but to fire his gun. “She came right at Hunter Foster and the other officer and he had to shoot his weapon,” Zummach said. Vellesiya Wiley has disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed towards the officers. The officer that fired the shots narrowly escaped being run over and appeared to touch the car as he was moving Charles ‘Joe’ Key, ex-police lieutenant Crump said the footage shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family concluded the same. An image of the vehicle shows its shattered right front passenger window. The family’s legal team called for the federal government to investigate the shooting. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety on Thursday released portions of the body-worn camera footage from multiple law enforcement officers, including Foster. Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi crime and community news outlet with a focus on law enforcement, posted some of that footage on its website a day earlier. The organisation’s founder, Therese Apel, is formerly the department’s communications director. The videos show Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen, as she and her friend run across the car park and enter their vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop. The vehicle then accelerates forward as Foster steps towards it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the bonnet as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother’s lap. The car continues to drive away before the video cuts out. He should never have placed himself in a position where he could have been struck John P. Gross, an expert on police use of force Two use-of-force experts reviewed the footage at the request of Associated Press but provided conflicting assessments, illustrating the complexity of the encounter. Charles “Joe” Key, a former Baltimore police lieutenant who frequently serves as an expert witness in police use-of-force cases, said that while it is a tragedy a child was killed, the shooting was a split-second decision that Foster made as the vehicle drove towards him and another officer. He said the driver of the car appeared to use the vehicle to commit assault with a deadly weapon. Wiley’s friend, who was driving the vehicle, has not been charged. “The officer that fired the shots narrowly escaped being run over and appeared to touch the car as he was moving,” Key said. “The shooting was objectively reasonable.” But John P. Gross, an expert on police use of force against moving vehicles, said Foster had used “really bad tactics”. “He should never have placed himself in a position where he could have been struck,” Gross said, adding that an accusation of shoplifting did not justify “use of deadly force on a fleeing suspect.”

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s strengths take centre stage at Apec
description: The finance ministers’ meeting cements the city’s global standing and offers momentum to expand its reach across Asia-Pacific economies.
content: Today’s global landscape is increasingly splintered. Commercial disputes, rival technical frameworks and geopolitical contests between major powers are prompting numerous nations to seek markets where stable, dependable rules still govern commerce. The successful meeting of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) finance ministers in Hong Kong offered an answer. Not only has the city’s status as the leading offshore renminbi hub and international financial centre been enhanced, but with Beijing’s support and its own strengths, it has become an ideal venue for major international summits. The next event will be the Interpol conference, which Beijing has again entrusted the city to host. The Apec meeting strengthened its members’ commitment to open commerce. Finance chiefs from Apec’s 21 economies agreed on macroeconomic policy coordination, regional cooperation on digital infrastructure financing and wider access to financial services for individuals and small and medium-sized enterprises. “We recognise that global rebalancing is in our common interest,” their joint statement said. A separate policy statement addressed “significant” funding gaps for digital infrastructure in some economies to help spread development. The gathering, chaired by Finance Minister Lan Foan, was a precursor to next month’s Apec leaders’ summit in neighbouring Shenzhen, where President Xi Jinping will meet his US counterpart Donald Trump for the third time this year. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent skipped the gathering in Hong Kong to prepare for the Shenzhen summit. Negotiators are working to line up Chinese investments in the US, and talks on extending the trade-war truce are reportedly moving in a “positive direction”. Obstacles remain, including opposition from some American lawmakers and agreed-upon tariff cuts that have yet to take effect. Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po noted how the meeting boosted foreign leaders’ confidence in Hong Kong, as he highlighted delegates’ positive feedback about the city’s positioning in Beijing’s development plan through its first five-year plan. He also observed that foreign investors were active in the city, with capital flows coming from the US, Europe and the Middle East, not just the mainland. Apec ministers have rightly focused on harnessing emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, to raise productivity, manage external risks and drive common development. For Hong Kong, the meeting reaffirmed its role as an international financial hub and highlighted the Greater Bay Area synergies. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu told ministers that, under “one country, two systems”, the city “enjoys both the China advantage and the global advantage”. He pointed to the city’s zero tariffs, low taxes and common-law system, its deep talent pool and the coming Northern Metropolis, alongside plans to grow the offshore yuan business and wealth management. The number of mainland companies with regional headquarters in the city rose to 350 last year from 252 in 2021. Encouraged by Chinese regulators, mainland firms helped Hong Kong lead global IPO fundraising last year, and more than 600 active applicants are in the pipeline. A Trade Development Council survey this year found 83 per cent of mainland firms named Hong Kong as their preferred source of “going global” support, up from 62 per cent in 2023. But complacency must be avoided. Retail investors have grown cautious and the Hang Seng Index has lost about 10 per cent this year. The Securities and Futures Commission’s freezing of HK$4.6 billion (US$590 million) in assets linked to suspected rigged listings is a reminder that the market’s reputation and confidence depend on rigorous enforcement of the rule of law, which Hong Kong actively champions. Hong Kong’s future rests on solid ground: an open capital market, a sound common-law system, the leading offshore renminbi hub and strong mainland backing. This meeting has been a confidence-booster. The city must keep evolving, from “superconnector” to irreplaceable “super value-adder”, by serving national strategies while answering regional needs and playing a unique role in the global market. Few major cities in Asia can match the city’s inherent advantages. Now is not the time to sit tight but to expand.

title: How AI microdrama Yanbian Qingmei is driving interest in an ancient Chinese calligrapher
description: By mixing romance, time travel and real history, Yanbian Qingmei has revived interest in revered Tang dynasty calligrapher Yan Zhenqing.
content: While the Tang dynasty (618-907) is synonymous with a golden age of Chinese arts and culture, its glittering reign was fractured by one of history’s most devastating civil wars. Today, the life and work of the revered Tang dynasty calligrapher Yan Zhenqing, a key figure in that 1,200-year-old tragedy, are capturing the attention of millions, partly thanks to an AI microdrama. The series titled Yanbian Qingmei, which roughly translates to Green Plums by the Inkstone, has accumulated more than 100 million views on platforms like short-video streamer Douyin, with related searches exceeding 200 million. Microdramas – ultra-short serialised stories designed for smartphone viewing – have exploded in popularity, and Yanbian Qingmei has helped drive Chinese interest in the calligrapher and politician’s legacy. The show is based on an original online story by an author who goes by the pseudonym Wanwan. The drama has generated significant hype, with some reports claiming the author single-handedly turned her literary creation into a slick microdrama using artificial intelligence (AI). However, South China Morning Post understands that author Wanwan and her childhood friend Zhang Xinyun jointly lead a creative team. Examining the story, its roots in historical record The story imagines a contemporary museum worker travelling back in time to fall in love with Yan Jiming, the calligrapher’s ill-fated nephew. Zhang says they chose the little-documented Yan Jiming because he could be sculpted into a “living person”, not merely a symbol of martyrdom in the history books. The Yan family stood against the An Lushan Rebellion, an 8th century uprising that reshaped the Tang empire. Yan Zhenqing, a regional governor, became a pivotal organiser of the resistance in Hebei, but Yan Jiming and his other relatives were slaughtered by rebel forces. In 758, after recovering his nephew’s remains, an anguished Yan Zhenqing created the Ji Zhi Wengao, which translates to Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew. Kept today in Taipei’s National Palace Museum, this piece of calligraphy is traditionally hailed as the “second-greatest work of running script under heaven”. The title was bestowed by the Yuan dynasty (1271-1368) scholar Xianyu Shu, who placed it only behind the Eastern Jin dynasty (317–420) calligrapher Wang Xizhi’s Lantingji Xu, or Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion. Xian Fang, an appraiser of Chinese paintings and a New York-based independent scholar, explains that the draft’s importance lies in the way it “preserves the traces of writing as it is happening”. Rather than allowing viewers to “directly read” Yan’s grief, the unpolished manuscript “lets us see how grief leaves traces in the act of writing”. Robert E. Harrist Jnr, a professor emeritus of Chinese art history at Columbia University, explains that the shifting ink tones and the many crossed-out characters express intense emotions. “We are watching Yan struggle with his emotions as he tries to find words adequate to express his grief.” For centuries, Yan Zhenqing’s monumental reputation rested not only on his artistic genius but also on his uncompromising moral character, eventually culminating in his own martyrdom when he refused to yield to political rebels in 785. An entry point into history Traditional Chinese aesthetics have long equated a person’s handwriting with their inner temperament, giving rise to the idea that “the writing is like the person”. Harrist calls Yan “one of the great figures in the entire history of world art” and notes that “much of Yan’s fame as an artist is closely tied to the circumstances of his life and what we know about his character as a man”. By the Song dynasty (960-1279) at the latest, Harrist adds, Yan’s bold calligraphy came to be seen as a reflection of his “uncompromising virtue in political life”. Fang notes that Yan’s importance “lies not only in how well he wrote, but in the way he further expanded the expressive range of Chinese calligraphy”, allowing the regular script to convey “solemnity, strength, pathos and even an almost monumental spiritual force”. Yet, while scholars and calligraphers have venerated his stone stele rubbings for generations, these ancient relics risked becoming alienated from modern youth and the wider global diaspora.
