By blending the emotional hook of modern romance with authentic historical reverence, Yanbian Qingmei has helped to bridge this gap. “If history and culture remain only in the language of specialists, it is very difficult for them to truly enter the lives of young people,” Fang says. “Popular culture can provide an entry point.” However, that entry point must eventually lead audiences back to the real historical record. For Harrist, the next step for these newly engaged viewers is clear. “My advice: keep looking!”

title: Profile | How Cantopop diva Paula Tsui defined an era with her contralto voice and polka dot dresses
description: Paula Tsui Siu-fung, a living legend and Cantopop superstar, has helped shape Hong Kong’s music scene for decades.
content: This is the 88th instalment in a biweekly series profiling major Hong Kong pop culture figures of recent decades. With her signature polka dot gowns, umbrella skirts and velvet-deep contralto voice that defied the high-pitched norms of her era, Paula Tsui Siu-fung did not just become a Cantopop superstar; she defined the very archetype of the Hong Kong diva. Over a career spanning more than five decades, her record-shattering live performances and unprecedented album sales have cemented her status as an enduring cultural icon, ensuring she remains a living legend among her late contemporaries such as Roman Tam Pak-sin (better known as Law Man) and Teresa Teng Li-chun. Tsui is known respectfully as Siu-fung jie, or Big Sister Siu-fung, and the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry Hong Kong recognises her as one of the city’s bestselling female recording artists of all time – she boasts more than a dozen platinum-certified albums. Her extensive catalogue moves seamlessly from Mandarin covers to Cantonese standards, including “Vanity Fair”, “Along Stream, Against Stream”, “Wind Season”, “The Long Road Ahead” and “Behind the Wedding Dress”. Her live prowess is formidable. From 1983 to 2018, she gave nearly 200 Hong Kong concerts. Notably, her 1992 concert series consisted of 43 shows at the Hong Kong Coliseum in 37 days – a feat that earned her a place in the Guinness World Records and remains her longest consecutive concert run. Forging her signature sound Tsui was born in Wuchang, Hubei province, on January 1, 1949, but grew up in Hong Kong. As the eldest of six children, she left school after Form One to support her family. She worked as a dispensary assistant and a church worker before joining her father’s barbershop to provide manicures and beauty treatments. Her path to stardom began in 1965 when the 16-year-old entered the Hong Kong Nightingale singing competition with two classmates. While her friends did not advance, Tsui beat 2,000 contestants. Her performance included a Mandarin track originally sung by Bai Guang, a Chinese singer and actress known as the Queen of the Low Voice – a fitting choice that foreshadowed Tsui’s pioneering contralto register. In an era when female Chinese singers typically possessed high-pitched, sweet voices, Tsui’s deep, husky resonance stood out. At first, her parents objected to her appearing on stage, viewing it as taboo and not something well-behaved girls did. Tsui eventually persuaded them, preparing herself by learning 500 songs before taking her first booking. To supplement the family income, she sang at the city’s hottest nightclubs. A typical evening ran from 8pm to 4am as she travelled along Nathan Road from Mong Kok to Tsim Sha Tsui, sometimes performing at more than 10 venues a night, as she later confirmed in an interview on the Shanghai Media Group’s YouTube channel. This gruelling circuit built her fan base and polished her magnetic onstage presence. “I think overnight successes are very fortunate,” she said on the TVB talk show StarTalk in 2013. “That didn’t happen for me; I accumulated my audience night by night like a savings account.” Ascent to Cantopop royalty Tsui’s recording break followed in 1969 when orchestra conductor Man Chau-po helped her secure her first official recording sessions. Travelling to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, she recorded 12 songs in two days, which were released as a series of EPs. Throughout the early 1970s, she released popular Mandarin covers, including “Lover’s Tears” and “The Moon Represents My Heart”. By the release of “Vanity Fair” in 1978, she had already recorded 21 albums – 11 of them in just five years. Composed by Joseph Koo Ka-fai as the theme song for the TVB drama of the same name, “Vanity Fair” shifted her balance towards original Cantonese material, weaving her voice into the city’s everyday soundtrack. Tsui’s popularity soon crossed borders; by 1979, she was touring North American cities to perform for overseas Chinese audiences. The 1980s proved a stellar decade for the singer, during which she helped influence the next generation of Cantopop stars. Most notably, the late Anita Mui Yim-fong won the inaugural New Talent Singing Awards in 1982 by performing Tsui’s “Wind Season”. Tsui joined music record label PolyGram in 1985, and her album Every Step, released the following year, was certified platinum. It contained the popular title track alongside “Behind the Wedding Dress”, which served as the outro for the TVB drama The Feud of Two Brothers (1986). In 1989, she received the RTHK Golden Needle Award, the highest Hong Kong music honour. The polka dot iconography Tsui’s appeal has always been as visual as it is vocal. Her long hair, 22-inch (56cm) waistline, large umbrella gowns and polka dot outfits have become the hallmarks of her image. Since her first solo concert in 1983, she has favoured elegant extravagance. After her 1987 series of shows, titled Glittering and Bright, the phrase became synonymous with her persona. “It’s my nostalgic attachment to dolls and what I think is beautiful. I can’t separate from that,” she said in the StarTalk interview when asked about her aesthetic. The polka dot dress, in particular, was solidified into Tsui’s iconography on her 1986 self-titled album Paula, where she poses with a microphone in a black-and-white dotted gown. “I’ve worn more than a dozen versions of that dress, and when reviewing older photos of me, I wore it before the album cover,” she noted in the same interview. The association is so strong that during a 2011 concert in Shanghai, the crowd kept stomping their feet not just for an encore, but for her to appear in her signature look. Beyond the glamour, Tsui has a playful side. She cycled around the edge of the stage at a 1985 show and wore a voice-activated illuminated dress in 1987. When comedian Lo Hoi-pang parodied her in a skit on the variety show Enjoy Yourself Tonight, she did not take offence. Instead, she invited him many times to join her onstage during her concerts. Fiercely guarded privacy After her record-breaking marathon of Hong Kong Coliseum concerts in 1992, Tsui became increasingly selective about her appearances. After 1995, she largely withdrew from the spotlight. She returned for a three-show engagement in Atlantic City in 2000, before staging a 23-show Hong Kong comeback in 2005. Further concerts followed in the United States, Malaysia, Macau and mainland China, alongside return engagements in Hong Kong in 2014, 2016 and 2018. Even during her periods away from the spotlight, Tsui’s cultural footprint remained ubiquitous thanks to the enduring popularity of “Joyous”. First released in 1979 as an upbeat festive anthem, the track has become a cross-generational staple. In recent years, it has found new life as a viral internet meme, frequently deployed by younger internet users to express humorous Schadenfreude, proving her music’s unique ability to resonate far beyond its original context. Despite her public visibility, Tsui has successfully avoided scandal throughout her career. Fiercely private, she kept her 1974 marriage in Canada to Albert Cheng King-hon – later a prominent Hong Kong political commentator and legislator – a secret for almost two decades. The marriage ended in divorce in 1979. Unmarried since, Tsui stands as an exemplar of a hardworking entertainment icon who has thrived on her own terms. Her legacy rests on a rare combination: the grit of a nightclub worker, the discipline of a recording artist and the commanding scale of a Hong Kong Coliseum headliner. During a 2013 interview on Commercial Radio, she was asked by the host Terry Leung Tai-loi if she felt something was missing from her life because she had not remarried. Tsui’s response encapsulated her enduring devotion to her craft. “Please don’t think I have anything missing in my life; to feel like that is a mindset,” she said. “The only thing I miss is the applause from my fans. Other than that, there is nothing missing in my life.”

title: HSBC RedCoin stablecoin launches for 3.3 million PayMe users in Hong Kong
description: The phased roll-out comes as Hong Kong pushes to establish itself as a hub for digital assets.
content: HSBC will launch its Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin in stages from Friday for more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe app, as the bank pushes to bring digital currencies into the city’s mainstream retail and investment markets. HSBC RedCoin, available only through PayMe and the bank’s Hong Kong mobile banking app, would initially support peer-to-peer transfers and peer-to-merchant payments on PayMe, according to head of PayMe Lawrence Li. Users can activate their HSBC RedCoin wallet, with no minimum balance or additional account-opening requirements. After updating the app, they can select the wallet to make instant transfers through an interface highly consistent with the current PayMe experience, he added. “The key priority in the first phase is ensuring stable service, avoiding extra burdens for customers and winning their trust,” Li told reporters ahead of Friday’s launch. The head of PayMe did not disclose a circulation target but said HSBC was optimistic about retail adoption after completing an internal pilot involving nearly 100 staff members. The trial successfully tested the full customer journey and showed smooth integration and quick user adoption, he added. HSBC plans to fully integrate the stablecoin into its Hong Kong mobile banking app by year-end. It will allow customers to instantly subscribe to tokenised asset products, including money-market funds, with a minimum investment of HK$100 (US$12.75). “Traditional investment settlement can take days, but subscribing to tokenised funds through a stablecoin enables instant settlement and significantly lowers the threshold,” said John O’Neill, managing director of digital assets and currencies at HSBC. Gold tokens and third-party funds would follow, O’Neill said, adding that HSBC was also exploring wholesale applications with designated partners and that details would be announced soon. “We began our digital asset journey a couple of years ago, launching tokenised bonds and tokenised gold, and [it] is widely accepted by the market,” said Maggie Ng, CEO of HSBC Hong Kong. So far, HSBC had supported the issuance of a cumulative US$8.3 billion of digitally native bonds globally, while tokenised gold – introduced more than two years ago in Hong Kong – had reached a cumulative traded value of US$2.5 billion, the bank said. Now, to encourage spending with the stablecoin, HSBC planned to introduce additional cashback rewards and promotions at well-known shopping and dining brands, with further details also to be announced soon, said Li, the head of PayMe. In the first phase, merchant settlement schedules would align with those used for conventional Hong Kong dollar processing, allowing businesses to adopt the service without additional investment. Settlement speeds were expected to increase in future updates, Li said. The stablecoin wallet would share existing limits with standard fiat Hong Kong dollar wallets in PayMe, without an additional tier of restrictions, he added. HSBC said it would roll out the new service to all PayMe users in stages from Friday to avoid overwhelming its servers, with full coverage expected before the weekend. Hong Kong’s stablecoin ordinance took effect on August 1 last year. HSBC and Anchorpoint, a joint venture formed by Standard Chartered, Animoca Brands and HKT, were granted licences from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city’s de facto central bank, in April.

title: Trump invokes Cold War-era Defence Production Act to boost oil production and refining
description: The move comes as surging fuel prices pose a risk for the US president in the coming midterm elections.
content: US ⁠President Donald Trump determined ⁠on Thursday that petroleum ⁠production, refining and related activities are essential to national defence, a move that could open up US funding for fossil fuel projects. In a presidential memo, Trump also invoked part of ‌the Cold War-era Defence Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels. Prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the US and Israel attacked Iran in joint action at the end of February. Since then, the ⁠conflict has limited energy shipments globally, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries ‌exacerbating the fuel shortages. The surge in costs poses a risk for Trump in the November 3 elections, as his fellow ‌Republicans try to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. A ⁠Reuters/Ipsos opinion ⁠poll that closed Monday shows just 36 per cent of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the economy. The ‌memo said that without taking the actions, the US is not able to provide enough of ‌those ‌energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, ‌permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks and supply chain limitations”. The memo did not mention ⁠specific projects that could be funded. The US averaged around 13.6 million ⁠barrels of daily crude production in 2025, making it the largest crude producer worldwide. Last week, US Vice-President J.D. Vance said the administration would ‌use the Defence ‌Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings Trump signed legislation last year that included US$1 billion in Defence Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.

title: In Focus | China’s private firms are fighting for profits. Are regulations adding to the burden?
description: With an economic slowdown adding to their woes, China’s private businesspeople lament heightened regulatory enforcement as a further strain.
content: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the second part of this series, Emma Ma speaks to businesspeople as they adapt to stepped up regulatory enforcement and deal with other economic issues the government has pledged to solve. Six years after China Evergrande Group started to show signs of insolvency – the beginning of a downward spiral that would eventually lead to the property developer’s bankruptcy and its founder sentenced to life in prison – Zhu Yinfen is still waiting to recover money the company owes to her Shanghai firm. “Evergrande still owes us 500,000 yuan (US$74,885),” Zhu said, adding that the worst problem was not the unpaid debt, but the many other clients who routinely failed to settle their bills on time. “I was quite anxious at first, but I’ve grown accustomed to it. Payment delays are rampant in the construction sector,” said Zhu, whose company supplies water-purification equipment for construction projects. While government data shows China’s private sector accounts for about 80 per cent of urban employment and 90 per cent of new jobs, its performance has become increasingly uneven. Though emerging industries such as technology and advanced manufacturing benefit from government support and attract investment, firms in traditional industries, including construction and manufacturing, have borne the brunt of an economic slowdown. Delayed payments rank among the biggest concerns of Chinese entrepreneurs. At the same time, compliance costs are rising rapidly as tax authorities step up enforcement of rules and scrutinise the collection of social insurance premiums. Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city ... payments for it have been held up for a decade Wang Xianhui, Shanghai “Dented by weaker profit expectations and faltering investment confidence, private‑sector enterprises have stepped up deleveraging,” wrote Zhang Xiaojing, a researcher at Beijing-based National Institution for Finance and Development, in a July note. The government has not ignored these issues. President Xi Jinping personally pledged to address arrears owed to private companies in a high-profile address to the country’s leading entrepreneurs in February 2025. The central government has since rolled out measures designed to help businesses weather the storm. But some businesspeople said that while the policies appeared promising in theory, they remained challenging in practice. Now, attention is turning to the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s Central Committee, to be held from Monday to Wednesday. The committee will focus on “strictly governing the party,” including measures to enforce party discipline and combat corruption. Xi has repeatedly said such efforts are needed to ensure Beijing’s policies, including those intended to benefit the private sector, are properly implemented. Payment delays evolve Wang Xianhui runs a medium-sized firm on the outskirts of Shanghai. It mainly works with local governments and major state-owned construction enterprises. According to him, a 12‑month payment cycle is considered normal for the sector, yet delays stretching beyond that time frame can also occur. Before 2020, he said, receipt of payments typically took only three to six months. “Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city in [central China’s] Hubei province, and payments for it have been held up for a decade,” Wang added. With the property market yet to recover from a prolonged slowdown catalysed by Evergrande’s default, the construction sector remains the epicentre of overdue payments. In the years since the slump, the problem has only evolved, industry insiders said. Over the past two years, Zhu said she has watched the situation shift from payment delays to debt settlement via unsold flats. “One of my clients is a major Shanghai-based developer. Starting in 2024, they began settling out contract obligations with unsold apartments in the suburban areas,” Zhu said. She added that the properties were part of the developer’s unsold inventory, and the firm offset her construction payment at the original sales price – far higher than current market rates. “Housing prices have kept falling over recent years. Local authorities set pricing for new apartments, and it is common for new-home prices to stand well above resale values – a 10 per cent to 20 per cent premium is typical in Shanghai,” Zhu said. That means if Zhu took ownership of these flats and tried to sell them, she would incur losses. On top of that, her firm would also be required to cover transaction-related taxes. “And it is not a choice between cash or property – it is either accept the apartment, or keep waiting,” she said. “It’s not limited to just one developer.” According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, total accounts receivable of China’s industrial enterprises above a designated size hit 29.48 trillion yuan (US$3.9 trillion) by the end of August, up 9 per cent year on year and outpacing the 6.6 per cent growth in revenue. To address the issue, Beijing has reiterated that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) must settle payments in cash. At a mid-September press conference, an official with the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission said cash payments to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) “must be enforced as a hard rule”. The government has also set up a website where SMEs can report delayed payments. Still, some private business owners said that while the initiative was well-intentioned, it lacked practical effectiveness. “I can sense the government’s resolve to fix these issues through the website. But we would only file a complaint there if we no longer wanted to do business with those SOEs,” Wang said. “Besides, our firm is a lower-tier contractor. That means even if we chose to submit a complaint via the website, we lack many key contracts and supporting documentation. The reality is far too complicated.” Problems with delayed payments are not unique to China, however. In Europe, business-to-business transactions generally face a 60-day deadline for fulfilment. Late payments carry statutory interest set at least 8 percentage points above the European Central Bank’s reference rate. Zhang Lin, deputy director at the research centre of Shanghai-based Far East Credit Rating, wrote in a May column for financial media outlet Caixin that Beijing could draw on Europe’s measures to impose tangible financial costs for payment delays. “What awaits settlement is not merely individual invoices, but better liquidity and stronger confidence across the economy,” he said. I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently Richard Zhu, Shanghai Paying in full This summer, Shanghai entrepreneur Richard Zhu began ensuring full social security payments are made for his employees, a process he jokingly described as “window dressing”. He heads a medical-device contract manufacturer generating 20 million yuan in annual revenue. Previously, his company had been remitting most social security contributions at the statutory minimum – more than 7,500 yuan a month for Shanghai as of this year – even though over half of his staff earned higher salaries. At his firm, he said, workers in their 20s were willing to accept lower insurance premiums to boost their take-home cash. For his older, core employees, he has always made full social security contributions, he added, as they were mature enough to understand the value of social security benefits. The informal practice is widespread among China’s SMEs as they deal with heavy operational burdens. Combined employer and employee social insurance contributions in China can reach as high as 38 per cent of an individual’s wage, a higher share than in some developed economies, including the US at 15.3 per cent and Japan at 30 per cent. Social security premiums have emerged as a significant source of public revenue. According to figures from the Ministry of Finance, national social insurance premiums hit 9.12 trillion yuan in value in 2025, outstripping the 6.89 trillion yuan in proceeds from value-added tax. “I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently. Officials flagged mismatches between their social-security contribution bases and actual payroll, ordering them to get their social-security contributions into line with regulations,” Richard Zhu said. Even though he has not received any notification from the local tax authority, he said he proceeded with the adjustments as a precautionary step – though he remains worried that non-compliance might derail his company’s partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms. A professor with close ties to the State Taxation Administration, who requested anonymity over the sensitivity of the matter, said that enforcement has ramped up this year, and that provincial governments have established specific performance targets stipulating what proportion of local enterprises should achieve social security compliance. After the change – made without reducing the pay of younger staff members to compensate – the combined outlay for social security contributions and the mandatory housing fund at Richard Zhu’s firm has surged to nearly 40 per cent of the expanding wage base, eating into the company’s profit margin. He and others in the private sector are asking a similar question: why step up enforcement of premium collection when the economy is losing momentum? “As China’s population is ageing at an accelerating pace, rigid expenditure pressures on the pension fund have risen steeply,” said Tony Peng, an independent researcher who has studied the domestic social security system for more than 10 years. “The domestic pension fund is confronted with heightened real-world pressures to balance its current-year revenues and outlays.” Those pressures compound as local governments’ fiscal positions grow strained with less revenue from land sales, he added. In the past, fiscal resources have served as a backstop for social insurance accounts whenever premium collections came up short. The fallout Peng said he believed tightening enforcement was still the correct policy direction. However, he added, “with weak domestic demand and extremely thin profit margins among private firms, a tighter enforcement ramp‑up would exacerbate their difficulties and could trigger wage cuts or lay-offs.” The repercussions already appear to be manifesting in the job market, insiders said. Confronted with narrowing profit margins, Richard Zhu opted for the simplest solution – scaling back new hiring. This summer, he slashed his recruitment quota, dropping from eight positions for engineers and office-based staff to two. Research from 2025 by Ye Jingjing, a professor at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law in Hubei province, found that heavier social security contributions led to a decline in new job postings. Beginning in 2019, China’s tax authorities took over collection of social insurance premiums, an institutional shift that triggered an earlier round of tighter regulatory enforcement. Ye’s research showed that average new job listings on one major domestic online recruitment platform dropped by 7.2 per cent in the post-2019 period relative to the 2017-19 baseline. At the same time, total social security contributions from surveyed companies climbed by 16.22 per cent. “Conditions differ from one firm to another. Labour-intensive enterprises that carry relatively high wage-to-cost ratios are more vulnerable to changes in the social security contribution base,” Ye said. Peng, the independent researcher, suggested that authorities carefully consider the pace of implementation and design of transitional arrangements. He proposed that local governments provide rebates or interest subsidies for those firms that remit full social-security contributions and have avoided staff lay-offs. This kind of “targeted compensatory support” would help incentivise some enterprises to abide by the law more willingly, he said. Richard Zhu, meanwhile, said he was choosing to stay positive. “Having spent 23 years in this business, I’ve learned it’s all about cycles. There have been ups and downs. Perhaps in another five years, all these problems will be absorbed during an economic upturn.”

title: Meet Lily Pearl Black, daughter of country singer Clint Black and actress Lisa Hartman
description: As the couple celebrate 35 years of marriage, here is everything to know about the daughter following in their musical and acting footsteps.
content: Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black celebrated their 35th wedding anniversary on October 20 this year. The country music singer and actress met backstage at Black’s concert on New Year’s Eve in 1990 and tied the knot several months later in 1991. “We strongly believe in communicating,” Hartman told Fox News when asked about the secret behind her long-lasting marriage. “It sounds so simple, but you really, really have to talk everything through. Roy Rogers said to Clint, ‘One piece of advice: Never go to bed angry.’ And it’s true. You can’t get in the car and drive away. You’ve got to talk it out if you can. A lot of times, you find it was just misinterpreted.” Black and Hartman’s daughter, Lily Pearl Black, congratulated her parents on their anniversary with a sweet Instagram Stories post featuring a throwback photo of the couple with their 2001 duet, “Easy for Me to Say”, set as the soundtrack. “Happy anniversary to my best friends,” Lily wrote. “Thank you for teaching me how to love & how to love life,” she continued. “I don’t know how I got so lucky … but I’ll never stop thanking God for the gift he gave me of y’all as my parents. I love you both to the moon and back.” Here’s everything you need to know about Clint and Lisa Hartman Black’s daughter, Lily Pearl Black. She is their only child Clint Black, 64, and Lisa Hartman Black, 70, welcomed Lily Pearl into the world in May 2001. The country musician revealed in his 2026 memoir, Killin’ Time: My Life and Music, that his wife experienced four miscarriages before they had Lily. He described his daughter’s birth as “exhaustingly joyful”. Following Lily’s birth, the couple took a step back from their careers to focus on parenthood. She is a musician With both her parents being musicians and her mother also being an actress – who shot to fame after her role in Knots Landing in the 1980s – performing was always in Lily’s blood. So it’s no surprise that she decided to follow in her parents’ footsteps. Lily was only 16 when she played her first show with her father, according to her interview with Country Town magazine in 2023. “Growing up around music and getting to see what my dad’s been doing all his life and my mum was an influence, but at the same time, it wasn’t because they were so great about letting me make my own decisions and figure out what I wanted to do with no pressure. It was about me and my decisions and wherever I ended up, so I think that made it easier for me to find my way so naturally,” she told the magazine. Lily even joined her parents on their “Mostly Hits & the Mrs. Tour” from 2021 to 2023. In November 2022, she launched her debut EP titled Songs From the Mostly Hits & the Mrs. Tour, which featured two covers and an original track written for her by her father and record producer David Foster. She is also an actress Like her mother, Lily has also dipped her toes into acting and starred in the 2012 film Flicka: Country Pride alongside her parents. Before joining her parents on tour, Lily was studying business and music at Belmont University in Nashville but made the decision to put her education on pause to pursue her musical career, according to People. It’s unclear whether Lily has since returned to continue her education.

title: Macroscope | Why market sell-offs in India and Indonesia have little in common
description: Indonesia’s financial woes are home-grown and structural – arising from failures to embrace reform – while India’s are externally driven.
content: When it comes to sentiment among Asian fund managers, Indonesia and India are distinctly out of favour. The findings of a survey by Bank of America on October 13 revealed that Asia’s fifth- and third-largest economies were the least preferred equity markets in the region. Since the beginning of this year, the Jakarta Composite Index has fallen 39 per cent, making it the world’s worst-performing stock market. India’s Nifty 50 Index, meanwhile, is down 12.7 per cent, putting it on track to record its first yearly decline following 10 straight years of gains. What is particularly troubling is that the problems faced by Indonesia and India are ones typically associated with old-fashioned emerging market crises. These vulnerabilities include declines in local currencies to record lows versus the US dollar, large outflows of foreign capital, pressure to raise interest rates more aggressively and a treacherous external environment. However, while the sell-offs in both countries share certain similarities, they are distinct from each other. Indonesia’s financial woes are home-grown and structural, stemming from the nation’s failure to fully embrace the reforms required to establish policy credibility and predictability. India’s problems, by contrast, are externally driven and accentuate policymakers’ success in making the economy more resilient and investible. The challenges confronting Indonesia are particularly pressing. On October 15, index provider MSCI said it had launched a consultation with market participants on a proposal to reclassify Indonesian stocks from “emerging market” to “stand-alone” status. This would lump Southeast Asia’s largest economy together with war-torn Ukraine and Lebanon. While MSCI had previously considered downgrading Indonesian equities to frontier market – a riskier category than emerging market – it said a one-notch downgrade “would not properly recognise the depth of the market problems”. MSCI pointed to “persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behaviour”, exacerbated by a “lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement”. On October 16, Indonesian shares suffered their sharpest daily decline since the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis. If the country is ejected from MSCI’s major equity indices, it would be the first emerging market relegated to stand-alone status for “market integrity failures” as opposed to sanctions and capital controls that triggered previous index removals. Indonesia’s lack of liquidity and transparency is symptomatic of bigger problems that have been festering for decades. Weak governance, state interventionism, democratic backsliding and the politicisation of economic policy have undermined investor confidence. Many listed firms are tightly held by founders or families, reducing the volume of shares available for public trading. Although resource-rich Indonesia has made great strides since the late 1990s, growing briskly and exploiting the energy transition, its capital markets remain underdeveloped and heavily reliant on foreign money. MSCI’s threat to remove the country from its indices, while forcing regulators to accelerate reforms, also heightens concerns about the rupiah, interest rates, growth and public finances. The risk is that bond markets punish Indonesia more severely. India faces a different predicament. At first glance, it appears to be suffering a full-blown currency crisis. The rupee has fallen against the US dollar for nine straight years to a record low. This has raised the cost of imports, reduced the value of overseas investors’ investments when converted back into dollars and made it harder to finance the current account deficit. Yet India is out of favour with foreign investors for reasons that have little to do with the management of the economy. The combination of US President Donald Trump’s tariff war and the global energy shock has added to long-standing concerns about India’s lofty stock market valuations. Moreover, India’s investment appeal has waned relative to Asia’s technology-driven markets. In the Bank of America survey, the lack of an “AI play” was the biggest concern for equity investors in India. In a report in August, Maneesh Dangi of Mosaic Asset Management said the global “growth scarcity premise” had changed dramatically in the past two years. “I’m watching the US, and now [South] Korea and other East Asian markets, deliver earnings growth that dwarfs anything India can offer, at multiples that are, frankly, cheap.” However, while the AI boom has drawn foreign capital away from India, the deterioration in sentiment has shown the country can withstand a sustained sell-off. Despite the persistent decline in the rupee and the energy crisis, inflation and the current account deficit remain relatively contained while the central bank has not had to raise interest rates aggressively. Furthermore, domestic institutional investors have provided crucial support to the stock market amid another banner year for Indian initial public offerings. Dangi said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s greatest achievement was to entrench economic stability: “Modi’s real legacy is a macro stability premium, not a growth premium.” Emerging Asia is a diverse region. The sell-offs in Indonesia and India reveal some of the most important weaknesses and strengths of Asia’s developing economies.

title: Tom Skerritt, star of Alien and Top Gun, dies at 93
description: Known for his rugged good looks and ability to shine in many genres, he took on roles ranging from an army surgeon to a spaceship captain.
content: Versatile actor Tom Skerritt, who starred in Hollywood megahits including the sci-fi classic Alien, the ⁠war comedy M*A*S*H, and the action drama Top Gun, ⁠has died at the age of 93. Skerritt, a Detroit native ⁠whose Hollywood career spanned from the 1960s to the 2020s, died on Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement. “While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives,” they said. “He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world, and helping others find and share their own ‌voices.” Known for his rugged good looks and ability to shine in a variety of genres, Skerritt delivered memorable performances in leading and supporting roles in film and television. Skerritt’s breakthrough role was a roguish US Army surgeon in director Robert Altman’s 1970 Korean war black comedy M*A*S*H, a film whose ensemble cast also included Donald Sutherland, Elliott Gould and Sally Kellerman. Skerritt played Southerner Duke Forrest as the doctors at the Mobile Army Surgical Hospital stitched up wounded troops. The film, whose popularity coincided with American unease over the Vietnam war, was nominated for five Academy Awards. In director Ridley Scott’s claustrophobic 1979 sci-fi horror Alien, Skerritt ⁠played Dallas, the captain of an ill-fated spacecraft whose crew encounters a deadly parasitic extraterrestrial creature with a surrealist look and a bad attitude. In the film’s famous ‌and bloody “chestburster” scene, Skerritt’s character is seated next to cast mate John Hurt when a baby alien violently exits the torso of Hurt’s character. Alien, an influential masterpiece whose ensemble cast also included Sigourney Weaver and Ian Holm, earned two Oscar nominations. “It is spontaneity and ‌impulse that make the difference, and that is what I felt we had with Alien. Every one of us had that immediate rapport with ⁠each other – the respect that I ⁠had for the other actors and the respect that they had for me,” Skerritt told interviewer Peter Sobczynski in 2019, while also lauding Scott’s directorial brilliance. Alien was one of several films in which Skerritt appeared that ‌featured strong female characters, in this case Weaver’s courageous character Ripley. That was considered pioneering at the time. “When I read the script, one of the things that I liked most about it was that the woman ‌becomes the ‌hero. I loved that,” Skerritt said. “The sight of women being in positions of strength and fortitude to make the right connections and decisions was what appealed to me. ‌I experienced that as well in Steel Magnolias, with the women in that. I liked the idea of women being tough and strong and influential.” In Steel Magnolias (1989), Skerritt played Drum ⁠Eatenton, husband of Sally Field’s M’Lynn Eatenton. Tony Scott, the brother of the Alien director, cast Skerritt in the key supporting role of naval aviation instructor Viper Metcalf in the ⁠1986 blockbuster Top Gun, which helped star Tom Cruise soar into Hollywood’s stratosphere. Skerritt also played Shirley MacLaine’s husband in director Herbert Ross’s 1977 ballet drama The Turning Point, and starred alongside another emerging star in Brad Pitt in Robert Redford’s beautifully shot 1992 period drama A River Runs Through It. Among other films in ‌which he appeared were: Harold and Maude (1971), Ice Castles (1978), The Dead ‌Zone (1983), Poltergeist III (1988), Contact (1997), Tears of the Sun (2003) and Ted (2012). On the small screen, Skerritt starred in the offbeat CBS series Picket Fences from 1992 to 1996, playing a Wisconsin town sheriff and claiming an Emmy as outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Born on August 25, 1933, in Detroit, Skerritt served in the US Air Force before becoming an actor, making his film debut in 1962 alongside a young Redford in War Hunt. He was the father of five children and was married three times.

title: Trump blasts basketball star LeBron James for not standing still during US anthem
description: The US president and the NBA player have been critical of one another for years, occasionally trading public swipes.
content: US President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the NBA star appeared to continue his warm-ups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia’s season opener on Tuesday. “I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. “LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot as The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at Tuesday’s game in New York. James, starting his first season with Philadelphia, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem. Trump and James have been critical of one another for years, occasionally trading public swipes. James had not made a public comment or a social media post as of Thursday afternoon about Trump’s gripe. The 41-year-old James, in his record 24th NBA season, was set to make his home debut for the Sixers Thursday night against Cleveland. Among some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics: Black shoe, white shoe James was with Cleveland in 2017 when he made a statement during an NBA game with his shoes – one black, one white, with the word “equality” in capital gold letters on the back of each. Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: “This is a beautiful country and we’re never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are.” James had called Trump “a bum” on social media and also said earlier that season of the president: “He doesn’t understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn’t understand that, and that’s what makes me more sick than anything.” Shut up and dribble James showed determination to speak out on social issues and the nation’s political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticised the four-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues. “We will definitely not shut up and dribble,” James said. “I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don’t have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they’re in.” James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards. “We know it’s bigger than us,” James said. Get to the polls James was named Associated Press’ Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helped convince many – at the peak of Black Lives Matter – who had never voted to finally head to the polls. “I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game,” James said. “But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there’s so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them.” Activist athletes AC Milan striker and former LA Galaxy star Zlatan Ibrahimovic blasted socially conscious athletes in a 2021 interview. Ibrahimovic called it “a mistake” for James and other athletes to get involved in political causes, saying they should “just do what you do best, because it doesn’t look good”. James, naturally, rejected the criticism. “I would never shut up about things that are wrong,” James said.

title: Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest hits Italy’s buffalo mozzarella output
description: Truckers are blocking deliveries over the high cost of diesel amid the ongoing Iran war.
content: A truckers’ protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of €3 million (US$3.37 million) in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said. The week-long strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left fuel pumps empty in much of southern Italy. The government approved new tax breaks for truckers on Thursday, but it was too early to tell whether they were enough to end the protest. The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain. Buffaloes have to be milked regardless of whether dairies are operating, while production rules require that their milk be turned into mozzarella within 60 hours. Buffalo mozzarella is softer, creamier and richer than cow’s-milk mozzarella. Pier Maria Saccani, director of the Consortium for the Protection of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP, said that about 1 million litres of buffalo milk produced on Wednesday could not be turned into mozzarella because of the transport blockade. The consortium oversees production standards and protects the designation of origin of the cheese in Italy and abroad. “Yesterday, no mozzarella was produced,” Saccani said, explaining it was a “€3 million block in 24 hours”. Farmers typically have only enough capacity to hold the fresh milk until dairy trucks collect it and cannot store large quantities for extended periods. “So this blockade has obviously caused panic among farmers, who say, ‘Where are we going to put it?’” Saccani added. The dairies making mozzarella cannot afford to accumulate a highly perishable product if trucks are unable to deliver it to customers. Several dairies have remained closed as a result, Saccani said, describing the situation as a “complete production blockade”. Unlike false claims this summer that production of Parmigiano Reggiano cheese was in crisis due to extreme heat, buffalo mozzarella output is indeed in jeopardy. During an extraordinary cabinet meeting on Thursday, the Italian government led by Premier Giorgia Meloni approved new measures to help truckers and farmers face higher fuel costs, bringing financial aid to those two groups to a combined €540 million in tax credits, up from €434 million. Some farmers have resorted to feeding part of the unused milk to their animals because they have nowhere to send it, Saccani said, adding that the transport disruption is also threatening supplies of animal feed and diesel needed to keep farms operating. “It’s a very, very complex and delicate situation,” he said. The blockade comes as milk producers and dairies are already confronting higher costs. Saccani said the consortium estimates production costs have risen about 30 per cent, driven by increases in animal feed, diesel, energy, plastic packaging and transport. The increases have not been fully passed on to customers, he said, leaving producers to absorb much of the additional expense and cutting into profitability across the supply chain. Buffalo mozzarella is an important industry in the Campania region, where the city of Naples is located, and in neighbouring areas of southern Italy. Saccani said that in 2025, the production of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP totalled just under 58,000 tonnes, with about 37 per cent of production exported. France is its largest foreign market.

title: Judge gives Trump deadline to sit for deposition in BBC defamation suit
description: The order came as lawyers for the UK broadcaster complained that the US president had delayed his appearance.
content: A federal judge on Thursday ordered US President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his US$10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by December 11. The order from US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance. Charles Tobin, the lawyer for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff”. He noted there was an agreed-upon date of October 16, but that Trump had cancelled it for a “matter of national importance”. Tobin said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said. Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by December 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit – unless the discovery period was extended past December 18. Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end on December 18, and the BBC’s lawyers want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defence said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also moved back. Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, Trump: A Second Chance. The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on January 6, 2021, before the storming of the US Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologised over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him. To bolster its defence, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. The parties were expected to address the issue later in Thursday’s hearing. “Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,” they argued in the filing. “He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given.” Trump’s side also argued that “Smith’s testimony would be duplicative”, because he published a lengthy report on the events of January 6 and also testified for many hours. “The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,” it argued. The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of January 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years. “It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,” the BBC’s lawyers argued. “No one forced plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. “But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim.”

title: Zuckerberg gets new Meta shares to stay in California amid billionaire tax vote
description: The move is aimed at avoiding tax impact on the CEO’s company voting power ahead of next month’s ballot.
content: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg will get a new chunk of shares in the company he founded, and in return, he has agreed to stay in California, where the company is headquartered, for at least eight more years. It is partly a financial carrot intended to keep Zuckerberg in California, where voters in November will decide whether to approve a temporary tax on wealth held by billionaires who live in the state. Meta announced the deal on Wednesday in a securities filing that coincided with its quarterly earnings report, where it said it would offer a new class of non-voting shares and give all existing shareholders a one-time bump for every share they own. That includes Zuckerberg, who owned more than 342 million Meta shares at the end of 2025, most of which are considered super-voting shares, effectively giving him more than 60 per cent control over the company, according to a filing related to its annual report. In a securities filing, Meta expressed concern that Zuckerberg’s voting power “could drop to approximately 53 per cent or lower” if he has to sell a significant portion of his shares to pay increased taxes. The deal is structured to give Zuckerberg the ability to sell shares without significantly diluting his voting power, in case California voters approve the tax measure known as Proposition 40, which could trigger “a significant, multibillion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership” in Meta, the company said in the filing. There are an estimated 39 million people who live in California. Of those, “a few hundred” have net worth of US$1 billion or more, according to the California Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is a non-partisan agency. If approved by voters, Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 per cent tax on billionaires, with 90 per cent of the proceeds earmarked for healthcare services. Some of the state’s billionaires have pre-emptively relocated elsewhere, including Google founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, and PayPal and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, according to Politico. By contrast, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has brushed off concerns. “I don’t mind paying taxes; the more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I’m OK with that,” Huang told CBS News on Sunday. “I’m not afraid of paying taxes” even if that means a US$8 billion tax bill, Huang said.

title: Hong Kong badly lags peers in Greater Bay Area AI supply chains
description: Hong Kong performs well in several areas including financial services, according to the Greater Bay Area Industry Development Index.
content: Hong Kong is significantly lagging behind its neighbours and ranks near the bottom in meeting the growing demand for artificial intelligence supply chains, according to a major index evaluating key developments across the Greater Bay Area. The finding is part of the Greater Bay Area Industry Development Index 2026, jointly released on Thursday by think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation and Dah Sing Bank. The index evaluated the performance of the 11 cities in the bay area in key sectors including trade and logistics, construction, real estate, innovation, technology and financial services. Hong Kong led overall growth among all 11 cities, with expansion of 5.1 per cent across six key industries this year. “Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Dongguan took the top three spots in the area of ‘surge in AI supply chain demand benefits advanced and hi-tech manufacturing’,” foundation vice-president Kenny Shui Chi-wai said. He added that sectors such as new materials, semiconductors and energy storage were all components of the AI hardware supply chain. The report showed Hong Kong placing ninth among the 11, lagging significantly behind some mainland cities where enterprises have long focused on highly specialised and narrowly defined segments of the supply chain. Beijing officially launched the bay area blueprint in early 2019 with the aim of developing it into one of the world’s largest economic and business hubs. In 2022, the bay area’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) exceeded 13 trillion yuan (US$1.95 trillion), up from about 12.6 trillion yuan in 2021, according to official data. The bay area covers about 56,000 sq km – 50 times the size of Hong Kong – and is home to more than 86 million people. That makes it larger and more populous than the world’s three leading bay areas – New York, Tokyo and San Francisco. The Greater Bay Area comprises Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province – Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Foshan, Huizhou, Dongguan, Zhongshan, Jiangmen and Zhaoqing. Under the 2019 blueprint, Hong Kong was to consolidate its status as an international hub for finance, trade, transport and aviation, while building closer ties with mainland cities, connecting them with the global community. According to the index, Hong Kong performed well in several areas. In financial services, the city comfortably outperformed its regional peers across multiple subcategories, including investment products, and policy support, securing the top spot. It also ranked first in trade and logistics, driven by its enduring strength as an international trade and aviation hub. In culture, sports and tourism, sports-related and tourism consumption in Hong Kong showed strong momentum, boosted by the spillover effects of co-hosting the 15th National Games last year.

title: Asian Para Games: Hong Kong win gold again as swimmer Chan Yui-lam defends title
description: City’s para athletes also win medals, two silver and three bronze, in table tennis and fencing at the Aichi-Nagoya event.
content: Hong Kong won a gold medal at the Asian Para Games for the second day in a row after swimmer Chan Yui-lam defended her 100m butterfly (S14) crown on Thursday. Chan, 23, stormed to gold at Nagoya City General Gymnasium in one minute and 5.19 seconds to finish ahead of host swimmer Aira Kinoshita, who finished in 1:05.56. Fellow Hongkonger Lau Chiu-yee took bronze in 1:07.39. The victory for the regional and Asian Para Games record-holder added to her success earlier this week when she took home the women’s 100m backstroke bronze medal on Tuesday. The success of the city’s athletes did not come from just the water in Nagoya, as there were five more medals – two silver and three bronze – in para table tennis as well as para fencing. The fencing quartet of Yu Chui-yee, Lam Ka-man, Tong Nga-ting and Fan Pui-shan brought home the women’s épée team silver medal after they lost 30-10 to China in the final. Hong Kong had earlier thrashed Uzbekistan 30-14 to reach the final. Veteran Yu said Hong Kong received a favourable draw after China, who did not compete in the two World Cup legs before the Asian Para Games, were placed on the other side of the draw. “With the new format of six bouts and 30 points, the world rankings were recalculated, and China didn’t have any rankings and so they were in the bottom half,” said the 42-year-old, who is competing in her fifth Asian Para Games. “It was more favourable for us to be in the upper half. We knew that we had a great chance of making it to the finals. “Still, we reminded ourselves that although Uzbekistan were relatively new and we may have the advantage in terms of strength, we needed to play each point well in épée because we can score points at the same time. “Knowing that China was a very strong opponent, it was all about enjoying our final and boldly trying some of the moves we had practised.” At Sky Hall Toyota, Wong Hon-lam and Lam Yan-yu reeled in a third silver medal for Hong Kong in the mixed-doubles (class 20) table tennis final. Wong and Lam lost 3-1 to Lin Tzu-yu and Su Jin-sian of Chinese Taipei, with scores of 11-9, 8-11, 11-5, 11-8. “We played rather passively today, and were somewhat pressured. Both teams performed very well in the final; it’s just that we were a little lacking in technique,” Wong said. Asian Para Games debutant Lam added that “I was merely looking to do my best” after looking at the participants’ list. “This silver medal was truly unexpected and gave us a lot of confidence,” she said. In other events, Wan Wai-lok and Wong Pui-kei, along with Yuen King-shing and Wong Ting-ting, both lost in their respective mixed doubles (class 22) semi-finals to finish with two bronze medals. Tong Chi-ming and Wong Yuen-ching also won a mixed doubles (class 14) bronze after they lost 3-2 to Chinese pair Chen Chao and Huang Wenjuan in their semi-final. Following Thursday’s medals haul, Hong Kong have now won two golds, 10 silvers and 16 bronzes.

title: Unitree developing AI system to let humanoid robots improve themselves
description: The Hangzhou-based company wants to reduce the need for manual programming, turning AI model advances into real-world robotics capabilities.
content: Unitree Robotics is developing a “self-evolving” feedback loop designed to allow humanoid robots to write code, run simulations and improve their real-world performance independently, founder Wang Xingxing said, in a move that mirrors a broader push towards “self-improving” artificial intelligence. Speaking on Thursday at a physical AI conference hosted by Unitree in Hangzhou, Wang unveiled the project, dubbed “Unitree Rehearsal”, which he called the company’s most important initiative of the year. The project sought to shift robotics development away from labour-intensive manual programming towards a continuous, autonomous feedback loop, he said. Under the system in development, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulations before running trials on physical robots. While humans could still help assess performance and provide feedback, Wang said the ultimate goal was to create an automated cycle that could exponentially accelerate the development of robotics algorithms. “In the past, every robotics engineer had to write code and debug manually, which is relatively inefficient,” Wang said. “As AI models improve, we expect them to take on more of the planning and iteration, reducing the need for human intervention.” Leading AI companies had already begun using models to generate code and gather data under human guidance, Wang said, arguing that robotics firms could follow a similar blueprint. Unlike digital software, however, robots also had to navigate environmental unpredictability and mechanical errors, he said. The comments came just days after Wang predicted that advances in OpenAI’s GPT-6 model could spur a broader robotics breakthrough within one to two years. His latest speech focused on the critical steps needed to translate AI model improvements into real-world utility. In a video shown at the event, robots developed by Unitree used GPT-6 to map routes and plan movements without task-specific training, though the presentation did not demonstrate how consistently the machines could replicate that behaviour in unfamiliar environments. While large AI models could handle robot planning and navigation, Wang said the biggest challenge was “aligning the AI model’s inputs and outputs with those of a real robot”. If that challenge could be overcome, humanoid robots could be tidying rooms on command as early as 2027, Wang suggested, though he offered 2028 as a more realistic estimate. Unitree’s upbeat road map echoed recent comments from Elon Musk. On Wednesday, the Tesla CEO told the US carmaker’s earnings call that humanoid robots could eventually become “the biggest product on Earth” and outnumber humans. He cautioned, however, that Tesla still faced about a year of development hurdles with its Optimus robot. Data, however, points to a challenging transition from laboratory to living room. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index found that robots succeeded in only 12 per cent of real-world household tasks during evaluations, despite performing significantly better in simulation.

title: EU’s idea that China is caving to pressure is ‘serious misjudgment’: ex-diplomat
description: Brussels has been emboldened by recent hybrid car deal, but China will not back down in the face of trade pressure, former diplomat warns.
content: The European Union’s perception that China is yielding to its pressure tactics on trade is a “serious misjudgment”, as Beijing proved during last year’s tariff war with the United States that it will not back down from a confrontation, a former Chinese diplomat has warned. Beijing’s willingness to compromise during trade talks with the EU earlier this month – where the two sides agreed a quota on Chinese hybrid car exports to Europe – has been taken by some in Brussels as a sign that their tougher approach is working, leading to calls for further action. But in reality, China only acted out of a willingness to safeguard its vast bilateral economic ties with Europe, and further provocations could backfire on the EU, according to Cui Hongjian, who served as a diplomat in India and Jamaica during the 2000s. “China’s willingness to reach agreements with the EU on electric vehicle export restrictions and other issues is not because we fear Europe, nor because we only respond to pressure,” said Cui, who now serves as director of the Centre for EU and Regional Development Studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University. “China has never sought trouble, but neither has it shied away from it. Even under enormous trade pressure from the United States, China has neither compromised nor bowed down,” he said during the 19th Europe-China Business and Technology Cooperation Fair in Chengdu, capital of China’s southwestern Sichuan province, on Thursday. Cui pointed to remarks by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who welcomed recent breakthroughs in trade talks with Beijing but said Brussels would continue negotiations while preparing tougher measures to address persistent trade imbalances. Speaking to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the EU must be ready to deploy trade defence instruments when dialogue failed to produce results. Others in Brussels have made a similar link between negotiations and trade protection measures. “Continued negotiations and effective safeguards are two sides of the same strategy,” said Bernd Lange, chairman of the European Parliament’s committee on international trade, in a social media post last week. At the annual three-day event, Cui said policymakers in Brussels should not misread Beijing’s intentions in trade negotiations. “China is acting out of a desire to preserve its extensive trade and economic ties with the EU and deepen cooperation in green and digital industries, not out of fear of anyone,” he added. Cui also argued that the economic differences between China and Europe – increasingly emphasised by Brussels in recent years – were nothing new, having existed since the two sides began building economic ties more than four decades ago. “Differences do not necessarily lead to disagreements, nor must disagreements turn into competition,” he said, adding that such tensions could instead drive dialogue and cooperation if both sides were willing to manage them rather than allow them to escalate into destructive rivalry. Cui likened Europe’s growing unease over its deepening economic ties with China to “pre-wedding jitters”, arguing that Brussels was hesitant to move beyond traditional trade ties towards closer industrial, investment and technological cooperation. “If China and Europe are moving from dating to marriage, Europe seems to be getting cold feet,” he said, adding that deeper integration could prove more rewarding than Brussels feared. He also proposed a new model for China-EU cooperation in green and digital industries, reversing their traditional roles by having China provide capital and technology while Europe contributes labour and market access.

title: HBO Max K-drama Make Me Tingle: Nam Ji-hyun, Kim Jae-young lead tame sex romcom
description: The K-drama streaming on HBO Max explores South Korea’s patriarchy through sex toys, but struggles to deliver on its provocative premise.
content: Lead cast: Nam Ji-hyun, Kim Jae-young South Korea finds itself at an interesting juncture in its social evolution in the mid-2020s. Following the success of works such as the 2016 book Kim Ji-young, Born 1982 and its hit 2019 film adaptation, which brought the country’s gender inequality into sharp focus, the imbalance remains stubbornly stark. People now recognise this imbalance and are unafraid to label it for what it is – “patriarchy” is no longer a dirty word. Yet change has been slow. South Korea’s rapid economic advance is one of the modern age’s great national success stories, but its social progress, which moves only as fast as generational change, could never hope to match it. Over time, this has led to a societal schism particularly pronounced in a media landscape swerving between gruelling social awareness stories and luminous metropolises filled with beautiful fashionistas. The new TVing series Make Me Tingle, featuring Nam Ji-hyun (Little Women) and Kim Jae-young (The Judge from Hell), belongs to a curious subset of recent romantic comedies about characters suffering under patriarchy who begin to emancipate themselves by diving into the world of sex toys. Previous titles include the BDSM-themed Love and Leashes (2022) – Netflix Korea’s first original film – and the JTBC series A Virtuous Business (2024), a 1990s-set drama about housewives beginning to sell sex toys. Make Me Tingle opens with what is effectively an idealised tourism video. Beautiful shots of central Seoul feature a skyline of glistening skyscrapers and ancient palaces, while hordes of attractive foreigners wander the streets, starry-eyed and posing for Instagram snaps. Amid this idealised bustle, a fashionable young woman rushes through the nighttime streets, weaving through the traditional hanok homes of Bukchon – another tourist hotspot. She stops at a particular door, catches her breath, puts on her game face and enters another world. It is still 2026, but time seems to have stopped within the walls of this Confucian domicile. The woman is Gong Yeon-su (Nam), and this is her childhood home. Her family is staunchly conservative, and now that she is on the cusp of turning 30, she is feeling enormous pressure to marry. What Yeon-su’s family does not know is that she has been dating someone for a year. She has patiently hoped for him to pop the question, not realising that he has also been waiting for something: he wants to sleep with her. With some prodding from a free-spirited colleague at her marketing firm, Yeon-su agrees to let her guard down and give her partner what he wants. However, the night takes an unfortunate turn when he insists on not using a condom. Ultimately, Yeon-su remains a virgin and the couple break up. If this experience did not shake up Yeon-su’s views on sex enough, she also crosses paths with the dashing entrepreneur Dokgo Dal (Kim), whom she first meets on a blind date. Both go out of a sense of obligation and it ends uneventfully. Yet the pair meet again later that night, following Yeon-su’s break-up. She drunkenly prowls the streets, picking up scattered condoms that are part of a product launch event hosted by Dokgo, who runs a sex toy company. Yeon-su and Dokgo encounter one another again when she becomes the marketing liaison for a new client, not realising that he is the founder of the adult toy company. As they begin to work together, these unlikely teammates gradually challenge each other. Like the other sex-positive K-romcoms that have preceded it, Make Me Tingle tackles a familiar contradiction: reconciling divergent sexual mores against a patriarchal backdrop in a medium that is inherently conservative. Dokgo’s business is successful enough that he lives in a sleek penthouse with a river view, but no characters seem to use his products. Vibrators litter the screen, but despite ostensibly being about sexual liberation, the show is unable to muster the courage to even suggest anyone is using them. The most it can do is show Yeon-su repeatedly shrivel in shame when a vibrator goes off in her handbag in various public spaces. Perhaps Make Me Tingle is building to something more daring, but if the precedents of this seemingly provocative K-media subset are anything to go by, the remaining episodes are more likely to evoke a frustrating sensation rather than a tingling one. Make Me Tingle is streaming on HBO Max.

title: Philippines’ Eala ousted as Rybakina moves into Ningbo Open last 8 on return from injury
description: First Filipino to win a WTA title loses in straight sets to Russian world No 20, while world No 1 Kazakh is cruising when opponent quits.
content: Alexandra Eala crashed out in the Ningbo Open last 16 on Thursday as world No 1 Elena Rybakina reached the quarter-finals on her return from injury when opponent Polina Kudermetova retired. Top seed and defending champion Rybakina was cruising 5-0 in eastern China when the world No 105 from Uzbekistan called it quits because of injury. Earlier, Philippine history-maker Eala suffered a battling straight-sets defeat to Diana Shnaider, the Russian world No 13 winning 7-5, 6-4 to book a quarter-final against talented American teenager Iva Jovic. The 21-year-old Eala in August became the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA title and is typically followed by a throng of fans from her country. But after beating France’s Diane Parry in straight sets in the previous round in Ningbo, in eastern China, the world No 20 came up against a far sterner test in Shnaider. The 22-year-old Russian, who is seeking to win a sixth WTA singles title, used her superior power to take the first set in just over 50 minutes. The second set was closer as Eala, who suffered a shock first-round exit to Chinese qualifier Shi Han at the Wuhan Open earlier this month, fought for survival. Shnaider put the Eala serve under severe pressure in the ninth game before breaking for 5-4, then doggedly held to seal victory in one hour and 55 minutes. The 18-year-old Jovic defeated two-time grand slam finalist Jasmine Paolini of Italy 6-4, 6-3. Moscow-born Kazakh Rybakina will face Poland’s unseeded Katarzyna Kawa in the last eight. Rybakina, 27, won the US Open for her third grand slam crown in September and usurped Aryna Sabalenka as world No 1 in New York. She was then stunned in the second round in Beijing at the start of this month, and pulled out of the Wuhan Open citing a foot injury. “Definitely not the way I wanted to finish the match,” Rybakina, also the reigning Australian Open champion, said of the injury to Kudermetova. “There is always room to improve and we’ll see how the next one is going to go.” She added: “I’m just happy being here in Ningbo again, remembering the previous memories, and hoping that I can finish the year strong and be at my best.”

title: Opinion | Europe still has no clear goal on China
description: A Europe that gives China its price list and the US its autonomy can only buy small concessions, leaving its ‘kill switch’ unused.
content: This month alone, Europe has threatened China with a trade “kill switch”, rebuked it in parliament, sent its trade commissioner on a much-trumpeted trip to Beijing and announced three new economic security instruments. The sequence exposed a European Union that has no clear goal on China, no hierarchy of priorities and has reached no agreement on what it wants from Beijing or on what it would pay to get it. China has built its European policy around this vacuum. Its method rewards patience: apply pressure, wait for Brussels to react, then offer tiny concessions on Beijing’s terms. European leaders present new instruments as proof of control, while Beijing files each one as information on Europe’s pain threshold. China knows Europe’s price better than Brussels does. Berlin and Paris opened the sequence. On October 5, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for a “kill switch” able to cut a country’s access to the single market. This is an admission of failure. Since 2019, when the EU adopted investment screening regulation and labelled China a “systemic rival”, trade tools have multiplied while the trade deficit with China grew to €360 billion (US$404 billion) last year – 2026 is set to be worse. Despite preaching “de-risking” since 2023, EU dependence on Chinese critical assets remains. Each new proposal confirms the predecessor’s failure. The European Parliament followed on October 7 with a recommendation that in effect admits it has had no consistent, unified China strategy since 2019, lists grievances and prescribes Washington as the cure, celebrating the transatlantic bond even as the US taxes European exports and pressures Europe to buy American weapons. The European Parliament condemns China’s support for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Washington is doing business with Moscow: two days after the parliament spoke, US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia; on October 16, the US paused a sanctions package on Russia. The European Parliament lives in a time that has ceased to exist: it scolds Beijing for helping Moscow and praises the ally that openly helps Russia. The commission carried its grievances to Beijing on October 8-9, armed with the June-issued ultimatum for “tangible results” and president Ursula von der Leyen’s July threat that Europe had “all the instruments on the table”. The trade commissioner returned with three “shared understandings”: China would moderate hybrid-car exports, cut tariffs on olive oil, car parts and footwear, and ease rare earth licences. Each of the three relieves pressure that Beijing created or Brussels invited. The hybrid-car surge is the commission’s own work: its 2024 tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles left hybrids at a flat 10 per cent duty. Imports of Chinese hybrid cars rose from 3,800 to 50,000 in under two years. In 25 years, China has moved from textiles to electric cars and Europe from cars to footwear – have the two economies traded places? Chinese manufacturers build cars Europeans want at prices European plants cannot match, whatever mix of subsidies, scale and engineering produced that advantage. German carmakers did the same in China for decades; nobody in Stuttgart called it a flood. The commission boasts that the deal will keep millions of Chinese cars from European roads. That means millions of cheaper cars denied to European households to protect Volkswagen’s and Stellantis’ margins. Brussels privileges a powerful lobby, sends the bill to consumers and asks them to applaud. Europe’s foreign policy establishment hailed the settlement as a geopolitical breakthrough, while the questions that matter remained off the table. Neither side has published the agreement, implementation mechanism, export volumes or a timetable. Finally, the conclusions of the October 15-16 European Council meeting invoked “macroeconomic imbalances”. Von der Leyen promised the “kill switch” would cut access to the EU “fast and immediately”, alongside a diversification instrument and a solidarity mechanism to offset Chinese retaliation. China’s commerce ministry warned Europe not to “fantasise about gaining benefits through pressure”. Deterrence works if the other side believes the threat will be executed.
