The new instruments give Beijing no grounds for that belief; they name no target and cannot enact before 2027, when their sponsors may be packing their boxes. Macron leaves office in May and Merz faces speculation about his survival; the far-right could take the lead. Those leaders have found in China a convenient alibi: an adversary far enough away that absorbs the blame for domestic failures and justifies the postponement of reforms. The primary questions are Europe’s to answer: what price it will pay for its demands and what its position between Washington and Beijing is. The first requires a retaliation doctrine the commission has never produced. It must identify the industries that would bear China’s response, the components with no alternative suppliers and the states that could split the 27 members. Without that calculation, the instruments amount to a bluff. The second question decides the rest, and time works against Europe. It retains the weight to matter to both superpowers and the exposure to need a balance between them, yet demographic change and a lack of political unity erode that weight every year. Additionally, Europe gives its leverage away for nothing. In June, it joined Pax Silica, the US-led chip and artificial intelligence pact against China, surrendering its core asset: autonomy. Beijing’s patience pays: it can wait for Europe’s leaders to change, for the next EU instrument to fail or new EU divisions. A Europe that gives Beijing its price list and Washington its autonomy will only get concessions sized to keep the kill switch unused and the next overreaction coming.

title: Hong Kong attracts another 18 strategic firms, HK$10 billion in investment pledged
description: Johnson & Johnson, Solana and Valcambi are among the latest firms to expand in Hong Kong.
content: Nasdaq-listed fintech company Solana and healthcare giant Johnson & Johnson are among the latest batch of enterprises in artificial intelligence, healthtech and advanced manufacturing to establish or expand operations in Hong Kong, bringing in more than HK$10 billion (US$1.28 billion) in investment to the city. The 18 enterprises signed agreements on Thursday with the Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES), a government unit under the Financial Secretary’s Office tasked with attracting companies of strategic importance to Hong Kong. Around half of these enterprises are from mainland China and the other half from elsewhere. They form the seventh batch of enterprises recruited under the initiative. “We are determined to create the conditions for more impact, by connecting finance, research, talent and industry more effectively,” Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said. Chan, who attended the signing ceremony with Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun, said the government also hoped to make it easier for enterprises to scale up their operations as well as products and services. Including the latest batch, OASES has attracted 142 companies across seven rounds, with the firms expected to invest HK$84 billion and create about 27,000 jobs over the coming years. Chan said investment from enterprises in the first six rounds had exceeded expectations by 30 per cent and the jobs created by 34 per cent. These companies had also taken up more than 2.8 million square feet of commercial and industrial space. Peter Yan King-shun, director general of OASES, said the latest 18 enterprises would bring in investment worth more than HK$10 billion and 1,600 jobs. “These are not trivial jobs. We are talking about really high-end jobs, focusing very much on research and development talents. Many of these jobs will help Hong Kong retain the talents that we have groomed from the universities,” Yan said. While OASES currently focuses on life and health technology, AI and data science, fintech, advanced manufacturing and new energy technology, and cultural and creative technology, Yan said he would not rule out more industries being covered in the strategic recruitment. As this year’s budget had tasked OASES with attracting aerospace enterprises, Yan said his office had been looking into it, and had already met leading firms in the sector. Strategic enterprises must submit five-year plans outlining their proposed investments and the number of jobs they expect to create, along with concrete details of their first major project in Hong Kong. Fintech company Solana, which provides instant and low-cost global transaction solutions with blockchain technology, is among the latest batch of enterprises. Chairman and CEO Joseph Chee said Solana chose Hong Kong over Japan and Singapore as its Asia-Pacific headquarters because the city was a global financial centre with the most comprehensive and sophisticated infrastructure. The law and regulations are clear and stable. He said OASES had provided support in helping the company to find an office, recruit staff and apply for work visas. “I was very surprised by the kind of support that I had … I am very impressed with all the people, how focused they are, in [helping] technology companies in Hong Kong,” he said. Chee said the company had committed to bringing in investment of at least HK$200 million to the city over the next five years, subject to the development of Solana blockchain in Hong Kong. The amount included the value brought to Hong Kong by other companies Solana had invested in or incubated. He said the company would provide its blockchain and help other companies to build things on it, and planned to hire 20 to 30 people in Hong Kong to start with. But it has no plan to issue any stablecoin or digital assets in the city. Swiss-based gold refiner Valcambi, which operates one of the world’s largest and most efficient integrated precious metals plants in Balerna, Switzerland, plans to set up a joint facility with local steelmaker Shiu Wing Steel in Lung Kwu Tan, Tuen Mun. The refinery will be the biggest of its kind in Hong Kong. The company has identified a plot of land, pending the process of changing land use to be completed. Valcambi CEO Simone Darceo Knobloch said Hong Kong would become its first expansion outside Switzerland. It planned to establish a precious metals logistics and financial hub in Hong Kong, supporting the city’s development into a world-class centre for gold refining. “What will be produced in Hong Kong will be gold bars … That’s how we want to contribute by providing physical gold in the market,” he said. Other leading enterprises on the list include Rohto Pharmaceutical from Japan, South Korea-based medical AI company Aitrics and Shanghai-based robotics firm Agibot. Additional reporting by Leopold Chen

title: Hong Kong targets financial innovation to help ease economic ‘pain points’
description: Hong Kong must work closely with partners in mainland China and across the Asia-Pacific to meet collective challenges, HKMA head says.
content: Hong Kong’s top banking regulator has called for greater innovation in the city’s financial system to help address “pain points” in the real economy, as the city works with mainland Chinese and Asia-Pacific partners to navigate a host of sustainability, geopolitical and other challenges. “True innovation in finance is not simply about chasing novelty; it’s about transforming conventional financial tools into efficient solutions,” said Eddie Yue Wai-man, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). “Hong Kong is set to push this frontier, and we want to ensure that this transformation brings tangible value also for the real economy,” he added during a keynote speech at the Asia-Pacific Financial Forum on Thursday. The comments come at a time when the city is trying to consolidate its status as an international financial centre and a superconnector linking mainland China with the rest of the world. Yue highlighted Hong Kong’s regional leadership in sustainable and resilient finance and a looming funding gap – the Greater Bay Area (GBA), for instance, will require almost US$2 trillion of investment over the next four decades to reach carbon neutrality by 2060 as planned. “In Hong Kong, we try to do what we do best, which is to mobilise capital and direct it where it’s needed most,” he said, citing the city’s growing green bond issuance. He also pointed to HKMA’s Commercial Data Interchange as a key initiative on this front. By integrating public and private data, “we help banks leverage alternative sources of information for credit assessment instead of just relying on collateral for their loans,” he explained. No single economy, no single business and certainly no single regulator can address all these challenges alone Eddie Yue Wai-man, Hong Kong Monetary Authority Yue pledged to make trade finance – a backbone of the global economy under threat from rising geopolitical tensions – more accessible for businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, calling it “a mission with high priority for us”. The HKMA chief executive also advocated for more partnerships between the public and private sectors across the Greater Bay Area, mainland China and the Asia-Pacific region at large. “No single economy, no single business and certainly no single regulator can address all these challenges alone,” he said. Speaking at a subsequent panel, Matthew Blake, managing director at the World Economic Forum, said the growing fragmentation of the global economy – brought about through industrial policies, tariffs, sanctions, investment mandates and more – had led to about US$200 billion to US$300 billion in lost productivity. “That is our new operating reality,” Blake warned, while adding that “the opportunity for the Greater Bay Area, and Hong Kong in particular, is to navigate this new environment and remain a connecting force between parties.” Regional cooperation would also help push the overseas use of China’s currency, the renminbi (RMB), said Karen Ng, head of yuan internationalisation at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong, during the panel discussion. “From the RMB internationalisation perspective, the Greater Bay Area is a very natural landscape … where synergies can be optimised,” she said. “[The region should] continue to develop and accelerate the two-way flow of capital, investments, people and talents.”

title: ‘Jensen’s nightmare’: Huawei, DeepSeek narrow AI chip ecosystem gap with Nvidia: report
description: DeepSeek is likely to rely ‘primarily’ on Huawei’s ‘already mature and well developed’ technology stack by 2027 or 2028, SemiAnalysis says.
content: Deepening “symbiosis” with artificial intelligence model start-up DeepSeek is helping Chinese tech champion Huawei Technologies catch up with Nvidia’s chip hardware and software ecosystem in a scenario that could mean Jensen Huang’s “nightmare is starting to come true”, according to a new report. DeepSeek’s latest software releases, on top of its increased experimentation with Huawei’s powerful Ascend 950PR chips, reveal that the technological gap with the US is closing, as the two firms increasingly harness their respective strengths to accelerate domestic innovation, research firm SemiAnalysis said in a report published on Thursday. The research comes weeks after DeepSeek released software tools tailored to the Ascend chip ecosystem, including six software modules that mirror ones that the Hangzhou start-up had previously developed for Nvidia chips. Among the releases was an Ascend-compatible version of TileLang, a custom programming language designed to streamline the development of high-performance kernels – essential code for operating chip hardware. The Ascend version of TileLang can help promote a more “independent and controllable” domestic software ecosystem for graphics processing units, DeepSeek said late last month. Growing symbiosis between DeepSeek and Huawei means that DeepSeek was likely to rely “primarily” on Huawei’s “already mature and well developed” technology stack by 2027 or 2028, SemiAnalysis said, “especially with the external and internal pressure to build a fully domestic Chinese ecosystem”. Beijing has made tech self-reliance a national priority amid US export controls on China’s access to advanced chips, including Nvidia’s, and chipmaking equipment. As Nvidia has increasingly found itself sidelined in the Chinese market, Huang has become increasingly outspoken about the significant impact of these restrictions on both his business and for US tech competitiveness. In a podcast aired in April, just ahead of the launch of DeepSeek’s V4 foundation model, Huang said it would be “a horrible outcome” for the US if DeepSeek optimised its models to be trained and run on Huawei chips, claiming that China “will become superior to” the US as a result. “From the software results so far and testing on 950PR, the ecosystem gap is definitely closer with DeepSeek’s help on top of Huawei’s work. Jensen’s nightmare is starting to come true,” SemiAnalysis said in its report. The latest analysis provides further details on how the two companies work together to accelerate innovation, such as DeepSeek’s testing of model-specific workloads on the Ascend hardware and software ecosystem. DeepSeek has also provided Huawei with early access to the models themselves, with Huawei announcing “Day-0” inference support – the chips that run an AI model, not the chips used to train the model – for major updates like DeepSeek V4 and V4.1. Still, the Ascend 950PR – unveiled by Huawei in March – lags Nvidia’s H100 in absolute performance, SemiAnalysis said. Nvidia began shipping the H100 in 2022. However, Huawei engineers are demonstrating “good work”, with their best Ascend kernels achieving high levels of efficiency at 99.7 per cent of their theoretical ceiling. The report also noted remaining challenges such as hardware configurations outside DeepSeek’s specific supernode set-ups, which may face compatibility hurdles for the broader industry. Most optimisations to date have focused on large-scale supernodes, leaving unresolved issues for developers attempting to run Ascend hardware on standard x86 host processors instead of Huawei’s native architectures. However, benefits from continued collaboration between the two companies could also be multiplied in the future. “Other operators serving DeepSeek can reuse kernels and deployment practices, while other labs can build new models on shared compiler capabilities,” the SemiAnalysis analysts wrote. “If these users contribute fixes and optimisations back, the gains can compound.”

title: US-China ties need more working-level dialogues, not just summits: business chamber
description: American firms welcome frequent meetings between the two leaders, but say lasting stability requires deeper engagement at working levels.
content: The president of the American Chamber of Commerce in China (AmCham China) has urged Beijing and Washington to push more negotiations down to working-level officials, saying businesses need greater long-term stability in bilateral ties than leader-level diplomacy alone can provide. Michael Hart, president of the chamber, said American businesses were encouraged by the unprecedented frequency of meetings between the presidents of China and the US, but warned that working-level officials had less time to prepare for the talks and develop substantive outcomes. “We’re feeling confident because there are two more meetings to come,” Hart said at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Wednesday. “[But] the bad part is that normally it’s the working-level bureaucrats who actually deal with clear facts, and when the two leaders are making decisions, you don’t have enough of them.” He said a US official had told him that government agencies would normally have more than six months to prepare for a leaders’ meeting, but had less than six months between the meetings held in May and September. Hart said he hoped that in 2027 negotiations would first be delegated to senior economic officials from both sides, and then “actually further down to the working-level folks”. The past year has seen dramatic swings in China-US relations, from an escalating trade war to a tentative easing of tensions. A meeting between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Busan in October 2025 helped cool trade tensions, followed by Trump’s visit to Beijing in May 2026 and Xi’s visit to Washington in September. The two leaders are expected to meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next month and at the G20 summit in Miami in December. Hart said that while the “unprecedented” frequency of leader-level meetings was “good”, American businesses still felt that bilateral ties could “go up or down” depending on decisions made by the two leaders. “US businesses or businesses in general … need much longer-term stability,” he said. “We cannot become addicted to relying on these two leaders to meet, whether it be due to structural or personal [reasons]. Fundamental problems still exist. Market access issues still exist, so there are plenty of issues to work on.”

title: 50 people beat foreign man to death in South Africa as anti-migrant tensions rage
description: The attack happened on the sidelines of a march in Durban, which has been gripped by rioting and looting in recent weeks.
content: A mob of about 50 people beat a foreign national to death on Thursday in South Africa’s port city of Durban, a flashpoint for anti-migrant sentiment, police said. Durban has been a focus of months of protests against foreign nationals, with looting and violence erupting after an anti-migrant march in the city two weeks ago. Thursday’s attack in the city centre was on the sidelines of a march, police said, without being able to say what the demonstration was about. Two men from the group approached another man, aged in his late 30s or early 40s, who was on the side of the road, police said. “It is further alleged that the victim was then assaulted by a group of about 50 people and he was declared dead at the scene,” a police statement said. The nationality of the man and the motive for the attack were unknown. Drivers with e-hailing services marched in the same area on Wednesday in a demonstration involving the March and March movement, which has mobilised protests against illegal migrants across the country for months. Two weeks ago, soldiers were deployed to central Durban as police battled to control two days of rioting and looting in unrest targeted at foreign nationals. Fourteen vehicles were set alight and businesses were looted or torched. The violence echoed weeks of protests that led tens of thousands of nationals from other African nations to flee earlier this year.

title: ‘Hong Kong would be impossible.’ Why the newest Fotografiska photo museum is in Shenzhen
description: Swedish photography museum Fotografiska opened its second Chinese location in Shenzhen in October, expanding the city’s cultural reach.
content: Contemporary photography museum Fotografiska’s newest outpost in Shenzhen is strikingly different from its original venue in Stockholm, Sweden – in the former customs building on the Stadsgardshamnen waterfront – or its Shanghai location, which opened in 2023 inside the Guang San Warehouse. In Shenzhen, a technological metropolis where sleek high-rises and futuristic cultural venues continue to emerge, the museum integrates into the modern urban landscape with a crisp white rectangular facade and expansive floor-to-ceiling windows. Opened on October 1, Fotografiska Shenzhen is the museum’s second location in China and fifth globally, following Stockholm, Tallinn, Berlin and Shanghai. It is the latest addition to Shenzhen’s expanding cultural infrastructure, after the Shenzhen International Museum of Art opened in May and the Shenzhen Natural History Museum in July. Located on the third floor of the luxury Shenzhen Bay MixC complex, the museum is surrounded by restaurants, cafes and lifestyle boutiques. Its entrance feels more like that of an upscale design store than a traditional museum. Designed by Shanghai-based studio Aim Architecture, which also created Fotografiska Shanghai, the Shenzhen branch spans about 57,000 sq ft (5,300 square metres). Its spatial concept, titled “Layers of the Future”, reflects the Stockholm museum’s vision for contemporary cultural institutions: a photography and visual arts venue that also incorporates culinary and lifestyle experiences. Liu Jie, general manager of Shenzhen Bay MixC, says the development aims to “create more natural connections between art and city life. From exhibitions to conversations, the museum offers opportunities for communities to gather, bringing lasting vitality to the Shenzhen Bay cultural district.” Fotografiska Shenzhen has a design concept store and restaurant on its lower level; five galleries across three floors – including a main hall with an 8.5-metre (27.8-foot) high ceiling for large-scale photography and moving-image installations; and the Dome Lounge, an event space on the top floor dedicated to year-round performing arts programming. The lounge was still being prepared on opening day. The restaurant, Mona, which will serve Mediterranean cuisine with Asian influences, is scheduled to open on November 4. Throughout the year, the museum will present photography, visual art and new-media exhibitions, alongside panel discussions, creative workshops, musical performances and live art showcases. The inaugural exhibition season features a line-up spanning diverse genres and artistic traditions, including “ToiletFotoPaperGrafiska”, a surreal, immersive exhibition by the team behind the magazine Toilet Paper, founded by artist Maurizio Cattelan and photographer Pierpaolo Ferrari; and Storm, by global photography and sustainability award Prix Pictet, featuring shortlisted works addressing social upheaval and environmental crisis. Also on the cards are German artist Michael Najjar’s solo exhibition Morphing Equilibrium, examining climate transformation; contemporary photographer Shi Guowei’s solo exhibition Festa, reflecting on urban festive traditions; and the group exhibition Transcendent Realities, surveying artistic practices previously featured across Fotografiska venues. The Dome Lounge, which can accommodate up to 180 standing guests, will host jazz salons, short film screenings and multidisciplinary art performances. “Many young creators are working across cross-disciplinary formats, which provides a fantastic platform for championing emerging talent,” says Christian Devillers, managing director of Fotografiska China. “Our approach to art is serious, yet we ensure it remains accessible to a broad audience,” Devillers says, noting that visitors range from seasoned contemporary art collectors to casual culture enthusiasts. “While this is challenging, we aim to strike the right balance between being an engaging destination for families, young people and serious art collectors.” To encourage after-work visits and evening gatherings, the museum opens from 6pm to 10pm from Sunday to Thursday, and until 10.30pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Shenzhen’s rapid cultural expansion makes it a strategic location for the museum group. Devillers says the city met all the criteria for expansion: a mature commercial market for brand partnerships, an engaged cultural audience, adequate space and the right development partner. “Shenzhen is the first city where all these operational elements aligned,” Devillers says. “From an economic perspective, securing and operating a comparable facility in Hong Kong would be [financially] impossible.” Tickets cost 60 yuan (US$9), and the institution expects to welcome 70,000 visitors over the coming year. On the financial realities facing contemporary art museums, Devillers says: “Virtually no museum operates sustainably on ticket revenue alone. Sustainability relies on government subsidies, patron support or commercial brand partnerships.” Fotografiska Shenzhen operates on a hybrid revenue model that includes admissions, memberships, dining, retail and corporate programming. The site was developed in partnership with China Resources Land, which co-invested 51 per cent alongside the Shenzhen Nanshan district government (holding 49 per cent). Fotografiska is the operator. Although Shanghai and Shenzhen have distinct cultural identities, Devillers says both institutions will share curatorial resources and touring exhibitions. In late October, an exhibition celebrating Fan Ho and Hong Kong photographers from the 1950s will open in Shanghai – Ho’s birthplace – before travelling to Shenzhen. “These photographers documented pivotal societal transformations and emerging generations defining new modes of style and expression,” Devillers says. “Photography as a medium captures those defining moments, anchoring visual culture and our perspectives [of looking at history] for the future.” Fotografiska Shenzhen, L3, C Zone West / Zone C, Shenzhen Bay MixC, 1218 Haide 1st Road, Nanshan district, Shenzhen, China To reach Fotografiska Shenzhen, take the high-speed train from Hong Kong West Kowloon Station to Futian Station. From Futian, transfer to Metro Line 11 (towards Bihaowan/Bitou) and get off at Houhai Station.

title: Influential patriotic educator Ng Hon-mun dies aged 100
description: City leader John Lee praises Ng, who was among first Hong Kong deputies appointed to NPC in 1975 and served as head of Pui Kiu Middle School.
content: Ng Hon-mun, an influential pro-Beijing educator and long-serving Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress who at one point called for its reform, has died at the age of 100. City leader John Lee Ka-chiu offered his deepest sympathies to Ng’s family on Sunday, praising him for his lifelong devotion to the nation and his significant contributions to Hong Kong’s smooth return to the motherland. “He dedicated his life to the cause of patriotic education, cultivating a large number of outstanding talents for the country and Hong Kong,” Lee said. “He was an outstanding educator with remarkable contributions.” Former chief executive Leung Chun-ying, a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, wrote earlier in a Facebook Post: “Deeply mourn Principal Ng Hon-mun.” Ng served as an honorary chairman of the Pui Kiu Education Foundation, which said he died peacefully in the morning surrounded by family. According to its obituary, Ng came to Hong Kong to join Pui Kiu Middle School as a teacher after graduating from Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou in 1947. During his time as principal, he spared no effort in advancing school affairs, promoting practical learning and nurturing numerous students who would later have distinguished careers, the obituary said. “Mr Ng devoted his life to loving our country and Hong Kong. With noble character and an unwavering commitment to education, he strived to foster national pride, promote exchanges between the mainland and Hong Kong, and safeguard Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability,” it said. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin praised Ng for dedicating his life to teaching and nurturing generations of students over the decades. Ng was regarded as one of Hong Kong’s most senior pro-Beijing figures and a prominent voice within the camp. He was among the first group of Hong Kong deputies appointed to the National People’s Congress (NPC) in 1975, serving for 33 years. Ng presented himself as a progressive voice in the congress, calling for reform of the legislature. In 2000, days before its annual session, he published an article in a local newspaper criticising the lack of progress in democratising the body, touching a nerve in Beijing. “Rule No 1 for parliamentary democracy is contested elections,” he wrote. “The NPC Standing Committee seats have been contested by a small number of candidates for many years, and the election has not been made more competitive.” He later recalled in one of his books that Beijing’s liaison office had advised him not to continue pressing for reform. Born in Chiu Chow in 1926, Ng spent his childhood outside mainland China with his father, a member of the Communist Party of China, moving to Thailand and Hong Kong. According to one of his books, after graduating in chemical engineering from a mainland university, Ng was arranged by an underground Communist leader in Hong Kong to become a teacher “for the needs of the revolution”. He was assigned to teach chemistry at Pui Kiu Middle School. It was the only paid job of his life; he served as the school’s principal from 1958 to 1985. There, he gave Jasper Tsang Yok-sing his first job as an English and maths teacher and became his mentor. Describing the young graduate as a “heaven-sent” talent, Ng paid Tsang HK$800 a month – more than double his own salary. Tsang would go on to found the city’s biggest pro-Beijing party, the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong, of which Ng was also a member, and become president of the Legislative Council. A lingering controversy over Ng’s time at Pui Kiu concerns the extent of his involvement in the 1967 riots, a spillover of the Cultural Revolution into Hong Kong and which killed 51 people. Although Ng was closely monitored by the colonial government at the time, he denied playing a major role in the violence. He said he had objected to students eager to join the unrest constructing makeshift bombs at the school and withdrawing from public exams. After the 1997 handover from British to Chinese sovereignty, Ng emerged as a respected and influential elder in the pro-Beijing camp. He got to know Tung Chee-hwa when both sat on the Preparatory Committee for the handover. Ng said he had “encouraged” Tung to run in Hong Kong’s first leadership election after colonial rule. He recalled Tung inviting him to his company for a conversation, during which Tung spoke of his hesitation about seeking the job. A year after Tung became leader, he awarded Ng the Grand Bauhinia Medal, the city’s highest honour. Ng occasionally made headlines with bold remarks about state leaders. In 2010, he raised eyebrows when he offered mild criticism of then president Hu Jintao, writing in a newspaper column that Hu had “attached too much importance” to Hong Kong’s richest man, Li Ka-shing, during a high-profile meeting with the businessman in Shenzhen that year. In 2011, Ng made headlines again after being invited by then premier Wen Jiabao to a private meeting at Zhongnanhai, the state leaders’ compound in Beijing. Observers said it was unusual for Wen to meet Ng alone, suggesting that the premier endorsed Ng’s reformist approach. But in his later years, Ng’s provocative remarks at times offended even younger allies in the pro-establishment camp. In 2013, he wrote that parties that mobilised others to cast blank votes in the chief executive election to force its cancellation were “surviving second-tier proteges of the evil British colonisers”. James Tien Pei-chun, then chairman of the Liberal Party, hit back, calling Ng an “outdated” figure who liked “picking up quarrels and destroying” unity. Tien’s criticism did not stop Ng from continuing to comment on politics. In 2016, when he was 91, he publicly supported CY Leung’s bid for a second term as chief executive, before later holding back and saying he needed to observe public opinion and Beijing’s inclination.

title: Pakistan risks deeper instability as political feud threatens counterterrorism efforts
description: Federal intervention in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province has inflamed tensions amid rising militant violence.
content: Pakistan’s counterterrorism campaign against Taliban insurgents risks being undermined by public resentment, following the dismissal of the opposition-led administration of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province. According to a statement issued by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s office after an emergency cabinet meeting last Sunday, the decision to impose temporary federal rule was necessitated by the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”. The KP provincial administration, led by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, had refused to support intensified military operations against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants, despite surging levels of violence over the last few years. Instead, the KP provincial assembly has passed several resolutions questioning the efficacy of counterterrorism operations and threatening to block them, while the PTI-led administration rallied resistance by tribal elders in the most afflicted districts bordering Afghanistan. According to Abdul Basit, an expert on militancy and senior associate fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore’s Nanyang University of Technology, this partisan politicking led to a breakdown in counterterrorism coordination between the federal and KP governments. This deprived the counterterrorism campaign of the “extremely, extremely critical” unanimity needed to effectively combat the rampant TTP, Basit said. Instead, the resulting “blame game” over security failures in KP made national counterterrorism policy “controversial and politicised”. Basit said this left the federal government with “no other way” than to impose an emergency in KP, where the monthly TTP casualty toll had climbed to an “alarming” 270 to 300 people. “This year is the most volatile year since Pakistan started fighting terrorism” after the September 11 attack on the US by al-Qaeda, he said. Underlying the KP administration’s intransigence was the PTI’s feud with the civil-military hybrid government in Islamabad over the imprisonment of the party’s leader and former prime minister Imran Khan, after his conviction on corruption-related and other charges. Khan’s journey from political obscurity to high office, followed by imprisonment on controversial charges, is typical of Pakistani power politics. For decades, the country’s powerful military – which has directly ruled Pakistan for roughly half of its 79-year history – has propped up lawmakers and parties, only for relations to sour and defiant politicians to be jailed, sidelined or exiled. Khan and the PTI rose to power in 2018 with the support of the military and judiciary, a year after Sharif’s elder brother Nawaz Sharif was removed as prime minister by the Supreme Court on flimsy grounds in a ruling that has since been overturned upon review. Khan’s government fell in April 2022 after the military withdrew support over its mismanagement of Pakistan’s economy, which left the country on the brink of a Sri Lanka-like default on international payments. Later that year, the head of the military’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency held an unprecedented press conference to announce it would remain politically neutral in the future. However, tensions between Khan and the generals reached boiling point in May 2023, when his arrest by security forces sparked rioting and mob attacks against military installations – some of it facilitated by serving and retired military officers, to the government’s horror. Despite a multitude of hurdles erected by federal authorities during the February 2024 general election, the PTI emerged as the single largest party, mostly due to the loyalty of voters in KP, which the party had governed since 2013. The PTI’s loss of authority there has deprived the party of its remaining leverage in the corridors of power. Ominously, public resentment against the politically dominant military and its counterterrorism operations may be the last card it has to play, analysts say. PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan called the sacking of the KP government “an extremely alarming and grave political mistake”. In a social media post last Sunday, he said the province’s people would “never accept such actions against their rights”, adding that “peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy and creating conflict between the federation and the province”. Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia initiatives at the New York-based Asia Society Policy Institute, said Pakistan’s internal divisions “make the situation more vulnerable”. Political instability had been “one of the contributors to the fragile security situation” the country had experienced over the past 20 years, Aamer said. A harmonious political situation would enable a more effective and focused security policy to tackle insurgencies in KP and western Balochistan provinces by the TTP and ethno-nationalists, respectively. “That is what the global investors also seek when they look into, say, investing in the country’s mineral sector,” Aamer said. The economic fallout from the tussle over counterterrorism policy was one of the reasons Sharif cited to justify imposing emergency rule in KP last Sunday. “I will not allow them [the PTI] to destabilise the economy,” Sharif told his cabinet. But the “genuine security crisis” was unlikely to be solved by greater central government involvement in KP, said Elizabeth Threlkeld, a former US diplomat who served in Peshawar, the provincial administrative centre. The PTI remained “widely popular” in KP and efforts to further limit the party’s political space “can backfire” at a time when the population was already under significant pressure from militant attacks and security operations, said Threlkeld, who is now director of the South Asia programme at the Stimson Centre think tank in Washington. Warning that “it is all but impossible to undertake effective counter-militancy operations without the cooperation of the affected population”, she said the dismissal of the KP administration “risks generating further resentments and driving centre-provincial tensions at a critical moment”. The inability of the government and opposition to reach a consensus on security policy “is especially concerning”, Threlkeld said. The political controversy complicated counterterrorism policy by amplifying concerns about the disruptive impact of military operations on the lives of residents in affected areas, Basit said. During past operations in the last two decades, residents have been forced to evacuate for months at a time with relatively little help from authorities, and many returned to find their homes and livelihoods destroyed. Basit feared “non-kinetic” aspects of counterterrorism policy key to its lasting success – political ownership and good governance, alongside the rehabilitation of conflict-affected areas – could remain “unfulfilled” unless Islamabad convincingly responded to the KP public’s criticism of past military operations and scepticism about the efficacy of new ones. “These are questions that the [Pakistani] state needs to answer clearly,” he added.

title: Expert explains the dangers of ‘AI slop’ for children and teens
description: A psychologist discusses the impact of content created by artificial intelligence tools.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
On social media, there is a flood of “AI slop”. This low-quality content is made by artificial intelligence (AI). Children are vulnerable to these videos, memes and more.
Dr Kitty Yeung Kit-yu is an educational psychologist in Hong Kong. She is concerned about the lack of rules for AI videos, which can be inappropriate and affect children’s learning.
Online, youth have long faced harm from a lack of protections. But now, AI can mass-produce content that is shown to children through social media’s addictive platforms. This has worsened the problem and made it harder for parents to learn how to protect their kids.
Traditional films and shows have guidelines about how old viewers should be based on the maturity of the content. But online videos have no such systems.
“I see short clips or even hour-long videos that just pop up without you needing to register for anything, and I feel the content is essentially 18 plus. They might not show highly graphic visuals, but the text and dialogue are clearly [adult content],” Yeung said.
She pointed out that parents might not look more carefully at videos with colourful animations or well-known cartoon characters.
“Even with animated characters, there are sexual elements,” Yeung said. “I believe these AI-generated videos aren’t meant for children, but they are produced in a cartoon format. If children ... watch them without questioning the content, I think it’s dangerous.”
Social media platforms also tend to show clickbait stories, which are common in AI content. Popular plots include poor characters instantly becoming rich, toxic revenge storylines or characters whose main goal in life is to marry a wealthy partner.
Yeung warned that these stories promote greed, harmful relationships and a lack of morality.
“When watching these, will children get the wrong idea about life and role models?” the psychologist asked. “It’s not that they can’t watch, but we have to teach them the context: these are just movies ... that don’t represent how most people actually behave.”
The harm could go deeper for young children, Yeung said. Toddlers aged two to three rely on what they see and hear to learn how to speak. But AI-made content shows them unnatural, robotic AI voices.
“Kids constantly hear sentences that are awkwardly chopped up, with unnatural breathing pauses, weird pitches or odd phrasing,” she said. “Are the phrases, grammar and vocal tones they are picking up actually appropriate?”
Worse still are videos with artificial gibberish .
“The kids watch the visual actions and get very entertained,” Yeung noted. “A very young child might actually think it is a real language and try to imitate it when learning to speak.”
She warned that listening to a robotic voice could affect a young child’s basic speech abilities.
Yeung urged parents to actively choose content for their children to enjoy: “Don’t just hand them a screen because they won’t sit still during meals. If you really feel you must give them a screen, you can control the content,” she said.
Rather than allowing children to scroll through short videos online, Yeung suggested directing them to platforms with built-in quality controls.
“If we really want to let children watch something, I genuinely think platforms like Netflix or Disney have many shows that are much more suitable,” she said.
“They can watch those instead of these short, low-quality clips, which I find harmful because they lack quality control.”

title: China slams Japan’s Takaichi over Yasukuni ritual offering, warns of ‘remilitarisation’
description: Attempts by political figures to pay homage at Yasukuni are efforts to ‘whitewash war crimes’ and speed up remilitarisation, embassy says.
content: China has condemned Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for sending a ritual offering to Tokyo’s war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, a move that threatens to further strain ties between the neighbours. At the start of Yasukuni’s three-day autumn festival on Saturday, Takaichi sent a ritual tree-stand offering to the shrine in her capacity as prime minister, although she did not visit in person. Minoru Kiuchi, minister in charge of economic growth strategy, visited the controversial site the same day, Japan’s Kyodo News reported. In a statement late on Saturday, the Chinese embassy in Japan strongly condemned the move. Describing the shrine as a “spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism”, the embassy said that any attempts by Japanese political figures to pay homage at Yasukuni – under whatever pretext – amounted to an effort to whitewash war crimes and pave the way for accelerating “remilitarisation”. Properly understanding and treating history was an essential prerequisite for Japan’s post-war return to the international community, the political foundation for its relations with neighbouring countries and a benchmark for whether Japan abided by its commitment to peaceful development, the embassy said. Wu Yingjie, a Japanese studies research fellow at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said Takaichi was following in the footsteps of many of her political predecessors. “Takaichi’s approach follows the balancing act maintained by most previous Japanese prime ministers – abstaining from personal visits to avoid severe international backlash while making ritual offerings to satisfy domestic right-wing allies,” Wu said. The Yasukuni Shrine honours around 2.46 million Japanese war dead, including 14 Class-A war criminals convicted by international tribunals following World War II. Asian nations that suffered under Japanese wartime aggression, notably China and South Korea, have consistently protested against visits and offerings by Japanese leaders. Wu noted that Beijing’s latest condemnation aligned with its established diplomatic position and echoed its criticisms in August, when it accused Japan of challenging the post-World War II international order. On August 15, the anniversary of Japan’s surrender in World War II, Takaichi similarly skipped a personal visit and sent an offering instead, although Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and three other cabinet members visited the shrine in person. In response to those offerings and visits, China’s foreign ministry explicitly branded Yasukuni a “war criminal shrine”. On Thursday, ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning again described the site as a “de facto war criminal shrine”, while commenting on a new documentary by Japanese public broadcaster NHK detailing the covert 1960s decision to enshrine Class-A war criminals. The latest friction deepens a frost in relations that began last November, when Takaichi suggested in parliament that a military attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially justifying military intervention. High-level governmental dialogues between China and Japan have largely ground to a halt since. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. However, Takaichi has signalled her willingness to visit China despite the diplomatic strain. She said on Friday that she intended to be in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month, parliament permitting. However, Wu cautioned that a high-level bilateral meeting was unlikely to materialise unless Tokyo made a fundamental shift in its rhetoric on Taiwan.

title: Hong Kong police to link mall CCTVs to surveillance network, security chief says
description: Chris Tang says live feeds from mall CCTVs depend on crime risks, as city’s camera target of 60,000 set to expand even further.
content: Hong Kong police are in the final stages of talks to connect security cameras at shopping centres to the force’s expanding smart surveillance network aimed at tackling crime, the security chief has revealed. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Sunday authorities were in discussions with private shopping centres to integrate their closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems, without naming the malls involved. “In fact, we see that in some places without CCTV, members of the public do not want to visit because they are dangerous and people fear becoming victims of crime,” Tang told a TV programme. “If the system requires it, I will connect and retrieve the data.” Asked whether the cameras would provide a 24-hour live feed, Tang said it would depend on the crime risk at the location. “For example, if the site is a crime hotspot, real-time monitoring might be needed. But if it’s not, footage would only be retrieved after an incident occurs,” he said. Tang was also asked whether the public would be notified that a CCTV camera was linked to the force’s network. Pointing out that many shopping centres already displayed recording notices, he said that while additional warnings were under discussion, they “may not be necessary”. Under the force’s SmartView surveillance system, CCTV feeds from public housing estates have already been connected to police networks. Tang, who previously told the Legislative Council that the government aimed to expand the citywide CCTV network to 60,000 cameras by 2028 at an expected cost of HK$4 billion (US$509.64 million), said that the final count could rise further. He explained that planned coverage for the Northern Metropolis was not included in that baseline figure. “We plan to install roughly 6,500 more there … In areas with wider expanses, a single camera may cover a broader area,” Tang said. Last year, authorities revealed that more than 5,000 cameras operated by other government departments and public bodies had already been integrated into the SmartView system. Between its launch in April 2024 and January 2026, SmartView helped police solve 899 cases, including six murders and 30 robberies, according to the force. Police also said automatic number plate recognition technology was added to the cameras in July last year, strengthening their ability to track suspicious and wanted vehicles. Tang has previously confirmed plans to integrate facial recognition technology into public camera feeds. The force has also expressed hope that SmartView will continue to evolve, saying footage could be shared with other government departments in the future if necessary. The South China Morning Post has reached out to the MTR Corporation rail operator, which runs shopping centres across the city, to ask if it was in talks with police over the surveillance integration. Separately, Tang said on a radio programme on Saturday that following the Wang Fuk Court inferno last year, collaboration with firefighting authorities in mainland China and Macau had been strengthened. In the event of a major fire in Hong Kong in the future, mainland and Macau firefighters might assist with outer-perimeter water spraying, he said. Even though firefighting equipment standards differ, through recent drills, testing and improvements, mainland fire engines coming to Hong Kong could now connect to local street hydrants using adaptor converters, he explained. Hong Kong recorded 89,137 crimes last year, a 5.9 per cent drop from the 94,747 in 2024. Cases of traditional street crimes also fell, with those involving violent crime decreasing by 15.9 per cent to 8,823, while the detection rate rose by 7 percentage points to 58.7 per cent.

title: Germany, France to tighten ‘Made in Europe’ stance, pressuring China’s auto industry
description: To qualify for public subsidies, a new proposal from Paris and Berlin says foreign automakers must shift manufacturing and R&D to the EU.
content: France and Germany have unveiled a joint position on Europe’s automotive package, with a tighter geographic definition of “Made in Europe” and a research and development requirement for cars to qualify for subsidies or public procurement, which industry insiders say would put further pressure on Chinese carmakers to invest in production within the bloc. The automotive sector’s “Made in Europe” classification would include only the 27 member states of the European Union, with an opt-in to include European partners that were part of the EU single market as of January 1, 2020, according to the document reviewed by the South China Morning Post on Friday. Despite allowing for some concessions for carmakers’ carbon emission targets in its discussions with Berlin, Paris succeeded in convincing Germany to adopt a strict definition of “Made in Europe”. “What this agreement also brings, it’s a ‘Made in Europe’ that is truly European … our position is based on the 27-member European Union, and that is what we managed to secure with Germany,” a source at the Elysee said on Friday. Starting in 2028, vehicles eligible for public-purchase support or public procurement would have to be assembled in Europe, with at least 70 per cent of total value creation in components excluding the battery. At least 10 per cent of the batteries would need to contain three principal components produced in Europe, including cells, according to the document. The legislation would mean that only a handful of countries, notably the UK – which only finalised Brexit at the end of January 2020 – and European Economic Area members such as Norway could potentially qualify, while countries like Turkey, Serbia, Japan and South Korea would be left out. Countries like the UK and Norway would only be eligible for inclusion after they adopted the European preference scheme for the car sector and aligned with relevant European anti-circumvention measures such as conditions on third countries’ investments and Europe’s trade defence measures, according to the document. This would mean that the UK, before it could be considered a European partner, would have to introduce similar tariffs on China-made electric vehicles and impose import quotas on China-made hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). London has recently been engaged in a back-and-forth with Brussels regarding tariffs on China-made vehicles. UK business secretary Jonathan Reynolds told The Guardian on Wednesday that the country would not bow to calls from other countries for it to impose higher taxes on Chinese vehicles. British trade minister Anas Sarwar told Politico on Thursday that London and Brussels should work together to tackle the challenge of Chinese cars. The tight definition might be a blow not only to Chinese brands such as BYD, which was planning a factory in Turkey, but also to Japanese and Korean brands. Tokyo has mounted intense lobbying efforts to be included as a partner, with its ambassador to the EU urging that the requirement should not “penalise” close partners, in an article in the Financial Times last month. On top of the strict “Made in Europe” definition, the joint position also outlines that carmakers should carry out “a significant share” of their R&D in the EU, without providing a specific number. “This will likely become an issue for Chinese carmakers,” said an executive of a Chinese auto brand in Europe, adding that the lack of clarity was also an obstacle for brands which are willing to invest. While many Chinese brands have R&D centres in Europe, it remains unclear whether they could meet the proposed requirement. The automotive sector has been a key point of tension between China and the EU. While both sides averted a full-blown trade war after negotiating a curb on Chinese HEV and PHEV exports to the EU, Brussels maintained the curb would not fix the trade imbalance. The president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen vowed further safeguards and said during a press conference on Friday following the European Council summit that the bloc would develop a mechanism to immediately limit access to the EU market. In a statement, also on Friday, China’s Ministry of Commerce rejected that the export cap was Beijing giving in to Europe and urged Brussels to “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”.

title: Mad rush for oxygen tanks, air purifiers in haze-choked Southeast Asia
description: Families scramble to buy devices to keep indoor air clean as toxic haze from the Indonesia forest fires persists.
content: Toxic haze from wildfires burning in Indonesia has spiked a demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say, as they work the clock on equipment providing life-saving clean air. The months-long haze has blanketed parts of Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and fuelling a rise in respiratory complaints. Families are now rushing to buy devices to keep indoor air clean. At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside Kuala Lumpur, employees were working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing. “We have seen a 35 per cent increase in sales because of the haze,” Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive’s sales team, said during a visit. “When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks,” she said. The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators. An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours. Md Noor Bin Bujang, 69, spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening. He said that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have “a shortness of breath, especially with the haze”. Mubassar Khan, a 26-year-old AA Alive technician, said an oxygen concentrator’s filter is normally replaced after 1,000 hours of usage, but the haze’s pollutants have halved its lifespan. AA Alive currently delivers around 40 rental units per day, and Firdaus said the company was able to meet the increased demands caused by the haze because they have “already experienced it every year”. Close to 60 oxygen concentrators and around 20 oxygen tanks due for a service or replacement were seen at the company’s showroom and warehouse. Experts warn prolonged exposure to haze pollutants could cause inflammation that is harmful to the body, with one classifying the situation as a “multisystem public health threat”. Juliana Jalaludin, a professor specialising in environmental health at Universiti Putra Malaysia, said she was worried that future generations could “experience a higher burden of respiratory illnesses if they are repeatedly exposed to haze and air pollution, particularly during childhood”. “The key is to reduce exposure now to protect children’s health and prevent long-term consequences for future generations,” Juliana said. Air purifier retailers, meanwhile, said sales have jumped since air quality levels started to dip in August during haze conditions. “Recently, we have seen a 600 per cent increase in sale volume of air purifier sales... from September 28 to October 12, compared with the same period last year,” regional consumer electronics retailer Courts said in a statement. “Customers are becoming more conscious of indoor air quality and are actively exploring solutions to maintain a healthier and more comfortable home environment,” a Courts spokesperson said. Singapore-based retailer Gain City said it has also seen “a significant increase in air-purifier demand”. “Demand began picking up in recent weeks, with a particularly sharp surge from October 9. Sales have since risen to nine times the level recorded at the start of the haze season in August,” the company said.

title: Hong Kong ‘optimistic’ on economic growth despite global slowdown, Paul Chan says
description: Finance chief says city is well placed to channel global capital, support mainland Chinese firms going abroad and fund AI infrastructure in developing economies.
content: The government is more “optimistic” than the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about Hong Kong’s economic growth for the year, the finance chief has said, pointing to the city’s unique position to capitalise on international capital flows and the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Writing on his blog on Sunday after attending the IMF and World Bank Group’s annual meetings in Bangkok, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said world leaders’ discussions had been dominated by two factors: the rapid disruption driven by AI and energy price surges stemming from the Middle East war. He said that while the IMF expected global growth to slow from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3.1 per cent this year, Asia’s economy would continue to expand at a faster pace. The IMF recently upgraded its 2026 real gross domestic product growth forecast for Hong Kong to 3.8 per cent, compared with the local government’s forecast of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent. Chan said the government was more “optimistic” than the IMF because Hong Kong was uniquely equipped to respond to shifting global demand. “The two immense demands are clear: developing economies require capital and technology, while mainland Chinese enterprises need international markets and professional services. Both demands converge in Hong Kong,” he said. “Here we can both channel global capital and connect with the mainland’s technology and industries. We have the conditions to enable the development of others while further elevating ourselves.” The financial secretary said he had observed that global economic performance had become increasingly polarised: growth forecasts for war-torn economies were being sharply downgraded, while economies deeply integrated with the AI supply chain were being revised upwards. Citing discussions at the Bangkok summits, Chan said that nearly 30 per cent of global import growth over the past two years was driven by AI-related goods. However, developing countries were expected to face a shortfall of 800 million jobs as 1.2 billion young people from those countries entered the workforce over the next 10 to 15 years. “Technology can either amplify competitive advantages or exacerbate existing risks,” Chan said. He also cautioned against compounding risks, including geopolitical friction, energy supply strains, inflation, extreme weather events, trade disputes and tightened financial conditions. Chan pointed to strained public finances across major economies, noting that sovereign bond yields in several Western countries had soared to roughly 20-year highs. Rising debt costs, he added, were squeezing governments’ fiscal buffers and their ability to absorb sudden external shocks. He said Hong Kong had adopted a “three-pronged” strategy to navigate these risks: channelling long-term patient capital into strategic sectors, broadening offshore renminbi instruments and managing risks through financial tools. Hong Kong should better serve as an indispensable offshore operating base and professional talent hub helping mainland enterprises go global, he said. Chan also said the city should leverage its capital markets to fund foundational AI infrastructure in developing economies, while rolling out citywide AI literacy programmes to ensure residents of all ages could adapt to technological transformation.

title: For investors, there are now just 2 kinds of offices: the best and the rest
description: The global office market has become deeply divided, with rents in prime buildings rising while others sit empty despite cutting rates.
content: From Hong Kong to New York, a deep divide is opening up in office markets around the world, as tenants compete for space in prime buildings while other properties face falling rents, low occupancy and financing pressures. The divergence reflects a global flight to quality, but also a disconnect between improving leasing fundamentals and a recovery in property values, according to analysts at Morgan Stanley and JLL. The divide is being reinforced by limited new supply in prime locations, differences in how cities remove obsolete offices, and companies’ efforts to attract talent through better workplaces. Tokyo has become the world’s most supply-constrained market with vacancy rates under 2 per cent, London leads Europe in inventory tightness, and New York City has achieved unprecedented top-tier rental rates, according to Julia Georgules, JLL’s head of research for leasing and capital markets. Hong Kong and Manhattan illustrate the K-shaped recovery. In a report released earlier this month, Morgan Stanley said headline vacancy rates masked a growing divide in which location and building quality increasingly determine performance. Scarcity in prime business districts is supporting rents despite high interest rates, while weaker locations remain under pressure. In Hong Kong, grade-A office vacancy in Central fell to 7.8 per cent in the third quarter as financial services and hedge funds fought over trophy assets, according to the US bank. Meanwhile, vacancy in less-fashionable districts such as Kowloon East was as high as 19.5 to 20 per cent, with rents continuing to decline. Manhattan shows a similar disparity. Vacancy in prime submarkets such as Chelsea and Park Avenue stood at about 5 per cent, while the Financial District’s rate was 18.4 per cent, Morgan Stanley said. The recovery in rents has yet to translate into a full recovery in property values. Gross office rents in Central had risen 7.3 per cent in the year to date, but Hong Kong grade-A office capital values remained about 50 per cent below their 2018 peak, the report said. In Manhattan, class-A rents reached US$81.94 per square foot, up 4.3 per cent year on year, while leasing volume over the preceding 12 months reached 33.1 million square feet, broadly matching pre-pandemic annual averages. Hong Kong’s sales market remains under pressure despite a rise in transactions. The city recorded about 293 office sales in the third quarter, up 25.8 per cent from a year earlier, while the value of those transactions was up 12.1 per cent year on year at HK$6.13 billion, according to Centaline Commercial. Much of the activity involved developers’ new projects, while second-hand transactions remained weak, said Mark Chan, a director in the agency’s office division. Some mortgage sales were being offered at discounts of 20 to 25 per cent compared with original purchase prices as lenders sought to recover cash, he said. The ability to remove obsolete office space is another factor shaping the recovery. Manhattan’s office construction pipeline has fallen to 2.7 per cent of existing stock, from about 12 per cent in 2019, though office-to-residential conversions are helping remove older buildings from the commercial market. Hong Kong, meanwhile, faces regulatory, planning and ownership hurdles that make large-scale conversions more difficult, leaving more existing office space competing for tenants. “Hong Kong has historically had much less ability to remove grade-A office inventory this way,” Morgan Stanley said in its report, adding that rezoning could limit future commercial supply but completed offices largely remained offices. Demand for quality is also being driven by competition for talent. Companies are increasingly treating offices as places for collaboration and productivity rather than simply as overhead costs. In Manhattan, demand from technology companies, including AI businesses, has added another source of leasing activity alongside traditional financial services tenants. “Globally, flight to quality has been the dominant narrative in the office market for the last few years,” said Georgules at JLL. “While there remains obsolete office product across markets because it has aged and fallen out of favour from an occupier perspective, supply at the top of most global gateway markets continues to decline,” she said.

title: Psychologist explains why non-stop ‘AI slop’ is harming children and teens
description: Youth have long been hurt by a lack of rules and protections online – content mass-produced by artificial intelligence only worsens this.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
The internet is drowning in “AI slop” – low-quality content generated by artificial intelligence that makes it difficult to tell what is real. Children are particularly vulnerable to this uncensored flood of videos, memes and more.
Hong Kong educational psychologist Dr Kitty Yeung Kit-yu expressed concern over the lack of regulation of AI videos, the inappropriate content in them as well as their impact on development and learning.
While the internet has long been chipping away at protections for children, AI’s ease in mass-producing content combined with social media’s addictive algorithms has exacerbated this problem – making it harder for parental supervision to keep up.
Yeung said that unlike traditional films or shows with age classifications, online videos operate without any guardrails.
“Sometimes I see short clips or even hour-long videos that just pop up without you needing to register for anything, and I feel the content is essentially [for those aged] 18 plus. They might not show highly graphic visuals, but the text and dialogue are clearly [adult content],” Yeung said.
She pointed out that parents might not be suspicious of colourful animations or well-known cartoon characters and would not examine them more closely for mature themes.
“Even with animated characters, there are sexual elements or … suggestions,” Yeung said. “I believe these AI-generated videos aren’t meant for children, but they are produced in a cartoon format. If children … watch them without questioning the content, I think it’s dangerous.”
Online algorithms could also amplify clickbait narratives popular in AI content, Yeung said. Popular tropes include impoverished characters instantly becoming billionaires, toxic revenge plots or storylines framing marriage to a wealthy partner as life’s ultimate goal.
She warned that these stories promote greed, normalise toxic relationships and blur moral boundaries regarding how people should treat one another.
“A common plot I see is a girl from a very poor family suddenly discovering she is the daughter of a billionaire. Or a girl and boy get together, and she finds out he is incredibly rich but was deceiving her,” the psychologist explained.
She expressed concern about children learning their world view from these AI-generated videos.
“When watching these, will children get the wrong idea about life and role models? Will they start thinking, ‘If I have money, I can do whatever I want,’ or ‘My goal is just to get rich so I can step on others’?” Yeung asked.
“It’s not that they can’t watch, but we have to teach them the context: these are just movies portraying abnormal lifestyles that don’t represent how most people actually behave.”
She added: “Because of this, I think there needs to be regulation, or at the very least, parents need to pay close attention.”
The harm could go deeper for young children, Yeung said. Toddlers aged two to three who rely on clear input for language development are being exposed to unnatural, robotic AI voices featuring odd pitches and fragmented grammar, the psychologist noted.
Children might enjoy the visuals, but Yeung warned that this continuous exposure to robotic cadence could compromise foundational speech skills.
“Kids constantly hear sentences that are awkwardly chopped up, with unnatural breathing pauses, weird pitches or odd phrasing,” she said. “Are the phrases, grammar and vocal tones they are picking up actually appropriate?”
Worse still are videos featuring artificial gibberish: “A very young child might actually think it is a real language and try to imitate it when learning to speak,” Yeung said.
For older children, it can be hard for them to distinguish if content has been doctored or twisted by AI.
Sixteen-year-old Angela Qian expressed concern over AI’s ability to manipulate information.
“Users with malicious intent can now fabricate convincing videos from a single text prompt,” said Angela, a Year 12 student at German Swiss International School. “Because these visual formats are inherently more engaging than plain text … viewers are far more likely to believe them.”
She added that AI-generated media was becoming increasingly difficult to spot.
“Individuals with less digital experience simply lack the tools to distinguish real content from synthetic fakes,” Angela said.
Yeung urged parents to take an active role in curating and vetting the content their children consume.
“Don’t just hand them a screen because they won’t sit still during meals. If you really feel you must give them a screen, you can control the content,” she said.
Rather than leaving children to scroll through short videos, she recommended directing them to established platforms with built-in quality controls.
“If we really want to let children watch something, I genuinely think platforms like Netflix or Disney have many shows that are much more suitable,” the psychologist said.
“They can watch those instead of these short, low-quality clips, which I find harmful because they lack quality control.”

title: China moves to cement ties with Uzbekistan amid tussle with US for Central Asian influence
description: Premier Li Qiang said the two countries should ‘strengthen solidarity and cooperation’ during a visit to Tashkent.
content: Chinese Premier Li Qiang has called for deeper cooperation with Uzbekistan in areas such as minerals and artificial intelligence (AI) as Beijing vies with Washington for influence in Central Asia. Li told President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on Saturday that Beijing was ready to strengthen strategic communication and expand mutually beneficial cooperation with Uzbekistan. He urged the two countries to step up cooperation in energy, minerals, finance and connectivity, and deepen collaboration in fields such as AI and aerospace, according to state news agency Xinhua. “In the face of a complex and turbulent international landscape, China and Uzbekistan should strengthen solidarity and cooperation and remain firmly committed to moving forward together,” he said. Li also said China was “ready to ensure the high-quality implementation of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway”, a long-delayed project that will link China and Europe through Central Asia and bypass Russia. His two-day visit to the Uzbek capital Tashkent, which ended on Sunday, comes as Beijing seeks to cement ties with Central Asia amid its deepening rivalry with Washington. The region – which holds a major global share of minerals that are vital for hi-tech industries such as manganese ore, titanium and cobalt – has emerged as a major geopolitical battleground. American Secretary of State Marco Rubio is also visiting Uzbekistan this week for the annual C5+1 meeting between the United States and five Central Asian countries. On Saturday, he said ties with the region were “important”, adding that the US wanted to “build our relationships with them”. Sergio Gor, the US ambassador to India and special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs, told a forum in New Delhi last week that Washington wanted “to be able to compete” in the region, adding that Central Asian countries were “extremely rich in critical minerals” that remained largely untapped. Li also told Mirziyoyev that China was ready to work more closely with Uzbekistan on “major issues” and step up collaboration within multilateral groupings such as the China-Central Asia mechanism and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), according to Xinhua. The Uzbek leader said his country was willing to advance cooperation with China and that the relationship had entered a “golden age”, the report added. In August, Mirziyoyev met Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, where the Chinese leader called for a “golden decade” in the relationship between the two countries. Li also met Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov on Saturday, when he made similar calls for closer practical cooperation and deeper political trust. He said China was willing to import more “high-quality and speciality” products from Uzbekistan and urged the two sides to expand exchanges in culture, tourism and education. He also said the two countries should work together to “advance an equal and orderly multipolar world”, according to Xinhua. Aripov said Uzbekistan was ready to work with China to deepen cooperation in sectors ranging from agriculture and energy to mineral resources and AI, the report added. Li and Aripov also witnessed the signing of agreements covering trade, education, customs, healthcare and poverty reduction. Li travelled to Dushanbe on Sunday for an official visit and to attend an SCO meeting. He described China and Tajikistan as “good neighbours, good friends and good partners”, according to Chinese state media.

title: ‘China haul’: why foreign tourists are shopping up a storm after Beijing policy changes
description: With easier payments and tax refunds, a greater number of foreign visitors are heading to China for shopping sprees.
content: When Grace Andrews, a US content creator, packed for her trip to China, she brought along a completely empty suitcase, dedicated solely to her shopping list. By the time she headed home, that extra luggage was bursting at the seams. In a video posted to social media earlier this month that received thousands of likes, Andrews unpacked a haul that spanned the spectrum of Chinese retail: delicate antique ceramics nestled next to trendy designer blind boxes, alongside a slew of clothing, shoes and handbags from domestic brands. As international tourism to China grows, visitors are driving a new social media trend: the “China haul”, to accompany other China-related viral trends, such as “Chinamaxxing”. Drawn by the sheer scale and variety of China’s domestic supply chains, foreign travellers are now increasingly buying everyday consumer goods instead of merely picking up mass-produced souvenirs. Last year, sales of goods bought through the departure tax refund system – which is primarily utilised by inbound travellers – increased by 95.9 per cent, outpacing the 30.6 per cent increase in the number of foreign tourists during the same period, official data showed. The surge in retail spending indicated that the “China haul” was more than a viral internet phenomenon, according to Anthony Anastasi, an assistant professor of economics at the Sino-British College, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology. “China’s domestic consumer market is itself becoming part of the attraction of visiting,” said Anastasi. “China has long produced goods for consumers around the world. What has changed is how easily foreign visitors can access its domestic market,” he added. “Expanded visa-free entry, easier payments and more convenient tax refunds reduce the barriers to visiting and shopping.” “For these tourists, a purchase only needs to beat the price of a similar item back home to feel like a bargain, as travel and lodging are costs they have already absorbed,” he explained. Such deals are easily found in a vast consumer market like China, known for its “considerable variety and, for many products, competitive prices”. Take cosmetics as an example. An eyeshadow palette from Flower Knows, a Chinese beauty brand known for its princess-style packaging, which has gained popularity overseas in recent years, costs around 100 yuan (US$14.95) on domestic platforms, around half the price on its overseas store. Aiming to stimulate its economy, China has opened visa-free travel in stages since 2023 to about 50 countries, including Australia, Russia, Singapore and most of Europe. Meanwhile, the government has ramped up efforts to ease payment hurdles for foreigners – which used to be a pain point for overseas visitors navigating China’s largely cashless society. Major payment platforms, including Tencent Holdings’ WeChat Pay, UnionPay and Ant Group’s Alipay, have enhanced interoperability with overseas e-wallets. This integration allows tourists to simply scan local QR codes and pay directly using familiar apps. At the forefront of this retail push is Shanghai. As the top destination for inbound tourists, it has set a target to nearly quintuple tax-free merchandise sales to inbound visitors over the next five years. The city, positioned as an international consumption hub, recorded 4.28 billion yuan in tax-refund sales last year, and aimed to increase that figure to around 20 billion yuan by 2030.
