Apart from the price factors, Anastasi added that, for foreign tourists, shopping in China was also about discovering products and taking part in a trend, as social media introduced visitors to items they may not have otherwise considered, against the backdrop of wider interest in travelling in China. Brooke Carline, a US tourist who travelled to China in early September, spent her shopping budget on modern items like toys, and also traditional teacups. She noted her purchases were driven heavily by the service and in-store experience. “Every store that I went into when I was in China, everyone was so helpful and so kind and so excited about you shopping in their store,” she said. “Everything that you bought came with a story and an explanation.” “I had such a good time that it was really important for me to bring back some things that reminded me of the Chinese culture.” In a September report, UBS projected that revenue from inbound travel to China would reach US$470 billion by 2040, partly driven by tax-refund optimisation and stronger domestic brands.

title: Banking on bricks: entrepreneur builds a business case for recycling plastic waste
description: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Shervin Sharghy left banking to build a business turning plastic waste into concrete paving and wall blocks.
content: Former investment banker Shervin Sharghy takes a practical approach to plastic recycling, first asking whether it makes financial sense before tackling the technical challenges. The founder of Hong Kong-based EcoBricks said the main obstacle to recycling plastic was often economic rather than scientific. Collecting, sorting, cleaning and processing waste plastic typically costs more than producing new materials from oil and gas, particularly at the small scale at which most recyclers operate. Sharghy is a finalist for the Spirit of Entrepreneurship Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. He founded EcoBricks after leaving investment banking to help tackle the global plastic waste crisis. The company turns plastic waste into concrete, the world’s most widely used material. It manufactures fully certified concrete paving and wall blocks in Hong Kong, helping to reduce waste and carbon emissions. “The first step was to prove that there is a sustainable business model,” he said. “Sustainable solutions come after.” The company developed detailed financial models alongside its technical research. Once it had demonstrated that the technology was commercially and technically viable, seed funding enabled it to establish a pilot facility and produce bricks on an industrial scale. EcoBricks believes customers should not have to pay extra for environmental benefits. It competes with conventional materials on cost and quality while helping customers reduce waste, cut costs and meet their sustainability goals. Customers can send concrete, glass, ceramics and plastic to its facility for recycling, lowering their disposal costs. They can then buy products made from their own waste. “I want to solve a problem for them first. It’s not just a case of ‘buy my brick’. It’s ‘let me help you to solve a problem’. We believe that sustainability should be a win-win.” Sino Group was an early commercial customer, with its Gold Coast development in Tuen Mun serving as a testing ground. Sharghy said an initial installation of about 700 bricks was monitored for several months before about 15,000 were installed in January 2022. Following several years of monitoring, a much larger area has now been paved with EcoBricks. The company’s cold process can handle mixed plastics and materials rejected by conventional recyclers. It can therefore work with existing collection and sorting systems, using processed plastic that might otherwise end up in landfills, incinerators or Hong Kong’s natural environment. The company has also considered what happens when its products reach the end of their useful lives. Sharghy said used EcoBricks could be recycled entirely into new ones, a capability he regarded as essential to keeping materials in use rather than discarding them. Manufacturing in Hong Kong nevertheless presents challenges. Suitable industrial sites are scarce and expensive, while heavy machinery requires space, power and appropriate land-use permissions. But Sharghy said the city also offered advantages for an early-stage venture bringing new technology to market. Its compact market and access to government, major businesses and decision makers could help new ideas gain traction quickly. “A lot of people ask us why we set up our company in Hong Kong. What really matters is the ecosystem, the infrastructure and the relationship between industry, government and start-ups,” he said. He added that Hong Kong’s stringent building standards and internationally renowned clients also helped establish EcoBricks’ credibility when approaching overseas markets. In response to customer demand, the company has expanded beyond outdoor paving to offer fire-certified internal wall blocks. It is also developing several products to help recycle more of Hong Kong’s waste. Sharghy said sustainable materials were more likely to gain acceptance when customers also had a clear financial incentive to use them. “Do it because it’s good for your business and it’s good for the planet,” he said. The Spirit of Hong Kong Awards were established in 2013 to recognise the city’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might otherwise escape public attention.

title: China’s youth draw upon Long March spirit to navigate modern uncertainties
description: Amid high unemployment and anxiety, many see lessons in perseverance and hopefulness on 90th anniversary of Red Army’s victory.
content: As China marks the 90th anniversary of the Red Army’s victory in the Long March, some young Chinese are looking to the historic journey for guidance as they face uncertainty in their lives and future. For Lyu Leiyiyi, a 22-year-old student at the Communication University of China, the spirit of the Long March offers a sense of stability at a time when people and the environment around her are changing at a dizzying pace. “People in their 20s are going through a period of uncertainty,” Lyu said. “The spirit of the Long March can help us build a more stable inner core.” This expanded perspective eventually intersected with China’s efforts to anchor young citizens in the country’s revolutionary history, such as the Long March. The Long March was a strategic retreat by the Communist Party’s Red Army between 1934 and 1936 as they sought to evade the ruling Kuomintang or Nationalist forces during China’s civil war. The Red Army covered about 10,000km (6,200 miles), crossing snow-covered mountains and treacherous marshlands while enduring hunger, exhaustion and pursuit by the KMT. The spirit, perseverance and hopefulness taken from the experience have since been consistently promoted by the party and the government as part of China’s revolutionary legacy. Lyu has visited several Long March sites, including Chishui in southwestern Guizhou province, where the Red Army’s 1935 campaign to evade Nationalist encirclement is commemorated as a model of military strategy in the party’s revolutionary history. Lyu said the soldiers’ statues and displays of the Red Army’s crude weapons brought home the hardships of the Long March and the soldiers’ determination to prevail. “It also makes me pay more attention to Long March commemorations,” Lyu said, noting her university had produced AI-generated songs for this year’s anniversary. October 22 marks the 90th anniversary of the Long March’s victory, when the Red Army’s three main forces completed their convergence in 1936. State news agency Xinhua in 2016 described the day as marking the “complete failure” of the KMT’s efforts to encircle and intercept the Red Army. Decades after the retreat, the party continues to promote the Long March’s legacy for future generations. “Each generation has its own long march, and every generation should proceed in its own way,” Chinese President Xi Jinping said while marking the journey’s 80th anniversary in 2016. Ella Shi, a 23-year-old postgraduate student in Beijing, said the Long March held a more psychological significance for her generation. “Although our material needs are largely met today, we face growing psychological pressure,” Shi said. Psychological distress is a concern among Chinese university students, with 15.5 per cent of more than 41,000 such students surveyed in 2023 reporting symptoms of anxiety, according to a 2025 study published in BMC Public Health, a medical journal. Employment uncertainty has become a common source of anxiety for university students, according to a June 2025 article in China Education Daily, a newspaper affiliated with the Ministry of Education. Shi, who is navigating this year’s graduate recruitment season, described the job hunt as her own “long march”, saying that “without inner strength and courage, it would be difficult to overcome one setback after another”. Since late August, she has submitted more than 70 job applications. Only two companies invited her to artificial intelligence (AI) pre-screening interviews, but she has yet to hear back from either. Shi initially targeted engineering safety positions but recently expanded her search to include sales roles. “I really can’t find a job in my field,” she said. China’s urban youth unemployment rate stood at 18.9 per cent in August – up from 17.9 per cent in July and a one-year high for the index. “But we must believe that we will eventually reach our destination,” Shi said, adding that perseverance was an important part of the Long March’s spirit. Andy Miao, a postgraduate student at a university in Beijing, also said that spirit helped him cope with pressures related to “studies, employment, innovation and life choices”. “The spirit of the Long March remains relevant today as it gives people the conviction, resilience and solidarity to face long-term challenges and uncertainty,” he added. Young Chinese people have “a heartfelt sense of identification with and pride in their country”, but their “expressions of these feelings are more individualised and centred on their own social circles”, according to a July article in state-affiliated magazine Defence Industry Conversion in China. Alice, a trainee teacher at a Beijing secondary school who gave only her first name, said her school had organised themed assignments, sports meets and other activities to help students learn about the Long March. “Through this process, students are encouraged to reflect on the Long March,” she said. “For universities, they organise activities related to the Long March spirit, and student societies do too.” She said a university hiking club she knew of had organised a trek to retrace the Long March route to celebrate its 90th anniversary. The Ministry of Education has called on universities to organise activities marking the 90th anniversary, including retracing sections of the route and visiting revolutionary sites and memorials, according to a notice issued in June. Alice said the spirit of the Long March remained relevant because the struggles it represented had not disappeared, even though their form had changed. “For example, competition between China and the United States continues, whether in technology or trade,” she said. The competition has intensified in areas including trade and advanced technology, as Beijing stresses the need for China to overcome external challenges and achieve greater technological self-reliance. Alice said educational activities could have an impact even if students did not visibly express their influence. “[The activities] are effective, but the spirit may have been internalised rather than outwardly expressed,” she said. However, not all young people in China were aware of the anniversary. “I had no idea,” said Lucia Dong, 25. Understanding the spirit of the Long March did not necessarily mean remembering specific dates or commemorative occasions, she added. Dong said doing her best and helping others where she could were the best ways to convey her love of the party and country. As she saw it, she had been “living by” the Long March legacy of hard work and mutual help “all along”.

title: Harvard and Cambridge to attend Hong Kong forum on role of humanities in AI age
description: Summit involving more than 50 universities to explore future of education, labour and artificial intelligence.
content: The organiser of a forum that will bring together Hong Kong and overseas universities later this month has said it hopes to spark debate on the role of humanities programmes in an era increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence (AI). The Global University Presidents and Leaders Summit, organised by the Hong Kong Association for External Friendship, will be held on October 27 and 28 at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Presidents or senior management from more than 50 universities, including Harvard and Cambridge, are set to attend the event. The heads of 10 local universities will each moderate a panel discussion on education, the future of the workforce and AI. Five government ministers from different bureaus will also attend the summit. Lawmaker and law professor Priscilla Leung Mei-fun, founding president of the association, said one focus would be the role universities could play in the age of AI, emphasising the importance of humanities programmes when developing programmes related to the technology. “Are we as institutions just blindly developing AI and competing to be the fastest? Are we going to lose our way? Should we start promoting the humanities again and place greater value on philosophers and promote human connections?” she said. “When it comes to designing a system, it is not purely about technology, which can be mechanical. The humanities cannot simply be allowed to disappear. She noted that some AI companies had begun hiring philosophy graduates to set ethical guidance and principles for the use of the technology, adding that students studying AI in the future might also need to take humanities courses. The forum would also offer a window for students and institutional leaders from outside the city to learn more about Hong Kong, she added. The trips of one student from each participating university would be subsidised, she said. “Many Westerners, especially the younger generation, have actually never been to Hong Kong. From our experience in 2024, several outstanding students mentioned that they never expected Hong Kong to be like this, as they were surprised to find English everywhere,” she said. The second edition of the forum, which was launched in 2024, will also focus on the Northern Metropolis university towns and collaboration between government, industry, academia, research and investment. The chief executive’s policy address last month confirmed that the core campus area of three university towns near the border would span up to 300 hectares. The government also opened applications for interested institutions to submit their proposals for the first university town, in Hung Shui Kiu, by the end of this year, with the results to be announced in early 2027. Leung said universities with vision would invest in the new education towns by collaborating with other institutions, as it would help them open up the enormous market of mainland China. The government earlier admitted it would be a huge challenge for overseas institutions to set foot in the university towns, as it was a self-financing project. “Prestigious universities have money to invest; the concerns are whether they have such a vision to invest in the towns and what we in Hong Kong could offer them,” Leung said. “They will see how big the Chinese market is after setting foot in Hong Kong. When they cannot directly enter mainland China, Hong Kong is their stepping stone.” She stressed that the university towns would have to close the gap that has long kept Hong Kong research from becoming an industry. “The mainland moved early, promising support for overseas talent to return to Shenzhen with their intellectual property,” she said. “Hong Kong could have done exactly the same.” She said policymakers and investors must go into university laboratories themselves to spot work with business potential. On talent retention, Leung acknowledged there was no way to stop people from leaving, but she said universities would have to compete on their own to attract the best and find partners.

title: Southeast Asia’s ethnic Chinese traders feel the China squeeze
description: From Indonesia to the Philippines, small traders say the factories supplying them have become their toughest competitors.
content: Almost every year, Kevin Stewart flies to China to find stock for his Indonesian businesses. But increasingly, the factories he visits are selling to his customers too, sometimes for less than they charge him. A data science manager in the tech sector by day, the Chinese-Indonesian entrepreneur also helps run home-living and pet-supply companies that sell to other businesses and direct to consumers, including through e-commerce platforms. Yet Chinese companies listing directly on Indonesian marketplaces are squeezing the profit margins of ethnic Chinese traders like him. “Sometimes, the sourcing quotes we get from China are actually higher than the prices at which they sell directly to the Indonesian market,” he said. Carving out a retail niche is becoming much harder, according to Stewart, who keeps track of competitors so that he knows when to stop selling an item before Chinese manufacturers flood the market with cheaper stock. He is not alone. Several Malaysian Chinese small and medium-sized businesses report being in the same double bind, with companies based in China acting both as useful suppliers and direct competitors to established local players. Bypassed brokers Smaller businesses all along the supply chain are growing increasingly concerned, according to Siwage Dharma Negara, co-coordinator of the Indonesia studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Chinese-Indonesian entrepreneurs typically derived their competitive advantages from domestic distribution networks, political access and knowledge of local culture and regulations, rather than their Chinese language skills or active commercial ties with China, Siwage said. Such strengths are valuable in sectors such as mining, industrial estates, logistics and large infrastructure projects, where Indonesian partners can provide land, licences and access to local governments. But consumer-facing sectors were different, Siwage said. There, mainland Chinese companies could leverage stronger financing to build their own supply chains and distribution networks, no longer having a need for a Chinese-Indonesian intermediary. “Cultural familiarity still helps with trust and communication, but mainland Chinese firms ultimately select partners for tangible resources,” Siwage said, while warning against fixating on ethnicity. “In Indonesia, it is usually expressed as a conflict between local and foreign businesses, not really between Chinese-Indonesians vs mainland Chinese.” Unspoken unease Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, the debate is no less contentious. In the Philippines, several Chinese-Filipino businesses approached by This Week in Asia declined to discuss their views of mainland Chinese entrants. Several cited the sensitivity of the country’s domestic political divisions and relations with Beijing. That caution reflects political divisions over how Manila should deal with Beijing, alongside long-standing tensions over maritime claims. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration has held firm on those claims while maintaining that trade and investment ties with China should continue. In March, the Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry welcomed Marcos’ proposed resumption of joint oil and gas exploration talks with China. Its president, Victor Lim, said separating territorial disputes from economic engagement reflected a “mature and pragmatic approach to statecraft”, and that energy cooperation could help secure stable, affordable supply. Yet competition complaints have surfaced before. In 2024, Robert Ace Barbers – then a congressman for Surigao del Norte – called for changes to the Philippines’ Special Investor’s Resident Visa programme, alleging that some Chinese nationals were using it to operate stores selling smuggled goods from China. “This has led to complaints from our Filipino-Chinese locals in the retail business, many of whom have suffered losses or closed down,” Barbers said, without identifying affected retailers or independently substantiating their losses. His remarks linked competition grievances to alleged abuses of the scheme, which grants visas to foreign investors who meet specific requirements. In Thailand, Narongsak Putthapornmongkol, president of the Thai-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, raised concerns about rising Chinese imports on September 2. In a survey conducted by the chamber, 27.4 per cent of respondents attributed the increase to China’s excess production capacity, which makes goods cheaper. Businesses also wanted Chinese investors to use more locally sourced materials and components. These concerns echoed a December 2025 warning from Kriengkrai Thiennukul, chairman of the Federation of Thai Industries, who has publicly identified himself as Thai-Chinese. Kriengkrai said weak domestic demand in China was driving exports and intensifying pressure on local manufacturers. Back in Indonesia, Stewart said intensifying price competition was “actually not healthy any more”. In fact, based on his own observations and conversations with his Chinese-Indonesian friends and fellow entrepreneurs, it was “killing many local businesses since they can’t compete with the prices”, he said. Yet he has no plans to stop working with Chinese suppliers, drawing a distinction between buying from firms based in China and competing against them. “So far, my suppliers have been reliable and honest,” he said.

title: The story of Jaipur jeweller The Gem Palace as it debuts at Lane Crawford Hong Kong
description: The Kasliwal family has run the Indian jewellery design business since the 18th century, counting Maharajas and modern royalty among their clients.
content: If you know the history of Jaipur, the “Pink City” so integral to Indian history and widely regarded as one of the most beautiful places in the world, you’re likely to be familiar with the story of The Gem Palace. Beyond being one of India’s most revered jewellery houses, having been appointed court jewellers by the royal family of Jaipur back in the 18th century, The Gem Palace also has a loyal following in Hong Kong, where a selection of the brand’s pieces are now available at Lane Crawford. “Our business started in 1852 officially as The Gem Palace, but prior to that we were also jewellers who were moved to Jaipur in 1727 by Maharaja Jai Singh, the founder of Jaipur, the city we come from,” says Samarth Kasliwal, who, together with his brother Siddharth and cousins Samir and Sarthak, oversees the multi-generational family business to this day. “We’ve all grown up like brothers, so we refrain from calling each other cousins.” Well over 150 years later, The Gem Palace is still creating the most extravagant and extraordinary jewellery using largely the same centuries-old methods. “We sometimes joke we have rubies running through our veins,” Samarth quips. The Kasliwals recently stopped by Hong Kong and sat down for an interview about preserving their family legacy as ninth-generation artisans of the brand. The history of your home city is really intertwined with your business, so it’s more than just jewellery; it’s also about cultural preservation. What are some of the pressures of your family legacy? Samarth: We feel this really strong sense of responsibility [towards] how people perceive Indian jewellery. We want it to be preserved as art because that’s truly what everyone working for us does. We were the first ones, in 2001, to be invited to the Metropolitan Museum of Art to display our collection and recreate some old Mughal pieces, and that really exposed the whole world to what Indian jewellery is all about. Samir: The artisans in the company have been working for our family for generations. That was very important also, to keep the skills inside the company. They are like family. Samir, where does your Italian heritage come in? Samir: I moved to India in 2009 and I prefer to run the business in Jaipur. I have a lot of clients that come from Europe because my mother is from Italy and married my dad, their uncle – and I was born and raised in Bologna, my hometown. Then I moved back and joined the family business, so I’ve been there ever since. Siddharth still lives between New York and India. My other two brothers also studied abroad. It was good to get different inputs from different cultures and bring it back to the company to run it better. We are not just specifically focused on India or just born and raised in India. In your observations coming from international places, how has that influenced how you run the business from India now? Samarth: India is a world of its own. I don’t think any of the international studies can really teach you how India runs, and that is the beauty of it. You take the good organisational methods of abroad and then input it into the Indian lifestyle. India has historically been the golden bird of the world for the longest time up until British rule. The nature over there is to create, to do something larger than life, something incredible, so we don’t want to inhibit that spirit. No matter where we studied, we come back to our roots. Between the royal legacy and all the celebrities who have worn your pieces, what is it about the brand resonates that with each of you personally when you are talking one on one with clients or presenting to whomever in the world? Samarth: Obviously the final product is an amazing thing to see, but I prefer showing the final product first and then show clients actually how it’s made. We’ve grown up in the walls of Gem Palace sorting gemstones out as kids, and now the kids of the artisans have started working with us. Even though the kids wanted to do [other] things we were like, nope, we will pay you enough so you have that incentive to continue working here. [If] one person stops, the whole bloodline of skill stops right there. Samir: The trust [our] clients have in the person they’re dealing with. We built up relationships over time, so it’s important to keep that running because it’s such a personal thing to buy jewellery. It’s not just about the value of the money that you’re spending, it’s the fact that you buy something that will stay with you for the rest of your life. Sarthak: For me it’s the creativity from start to finish, the story behind the artisan who worked for a long time – some pieces take two years to finish the filigree work – and finally, the person wearing it in the beautiful gala. It’s the whole story I appreciate most. Now there’s so much debate about synthetic versus natural diamonds. Have you seen that debate influence your business? Samarth: There are people who’ve been coming to us for a while about lab-grown [diamonds], but we’ve only been into old mine diamonds anyway – the old diamonds which were found in India, sourced from here and then went to Europe. Fortunately enough, that market is pretty much unaffected because you can replace the chemical, but you can’t replace time, and time is something which goes with old mine diamonds. History, also. They came from Indian lands. That is primarily what our clients have been coming to us for. And we all prefer coloured gemstones. Our name is Gem Palace to begin with, right? Internationally, how is Indian jewellery perceived and how has that changed over the decades? Samarth: 2001 was one of the first exhibits at [the Met’s Islamic wing], where the real beauty of Indian jewellery was out on display at museums. It was always at V&A [Museum], but they were never really appreciated in the same way until that. Sarthak: People are talking about the Patiala necklace that was made by Cartier. Tutti Frutti [is inspired by] India. Indian jewellery has always been there. It’s getting more credit. You see it [at the] Met Gala, big events everywhere. Hong Kong is such a big market for jewellery and the customers are very seasoned and know which diamonds they want. How has your reception been here? Samarth: It’s the first time we’ve come to Hong Kong on a retail level, but we’ve been coming for jewellery shows for many, many years, acquiring some of the gemstones we use in our jewellery. So many of our old clients are seeing us [at Lane Crawford] and they’re so excited. When we run into clients, everyone has an anecdote for Gem Palace, like some story or experience they’ve had with his father or my father. They would have a story which we had no clue about. That is the thing which keeps us going. We’re connected without even knowing each other. Speaking specifically more about techniques, filigree, enamelling … is there something particular you hope The Gem Palace is associated with on that degree? Samir: Enamelling. Everybody agrees because it’s really our DNA. Slowly it evolved in different kinds of collections, like in the white gold we are doing right now, platinum, titanium. We started using different kinds of material, but the base is enamelling work. Thinking ahead to the next generation, what legacy do you hope to leave behind? Siddharth: Samir and I joined the business when we were both just 20. Even as children, when we were going to Italy and France with our fathers, they would take us to the jewellery offices. It was deeply ingrained in our system. You can’t say for the next generation whether they feel the same or have the same attachment with the brand, and nowadays everybody’s in the rat race to make the business a US$100 million company and then sell it to a bigger giant. We don’t want to do that. We would not be willing to sell the business and walk away. But we can’t guarantee the future generation, if there is any. Was it only your fathers who told you to get into the business? Siddharth: Yes and no. It was like, do whatever you want to do, it’s your choice, but you’re going to be a jeweller [laughs]. Samarth: Like becoming a guitarist, but a jeweller first. Siddharth: Pre-social media, people had a lot of passions and patience, where they would come and sit with you for hours. It was a whole different experience to be dealing in jewellery. It’s a lot less personal now. 2013, 2014, we would never even put our designs on Instagram – we still avoid [it] – because [users] can just copy the thing, but they don’t know the intrinsic value of the design. We are not on the [e-commerce] platform selling online. We are one of only a few brands which I would say is vertically integrated right from the sourcing of raw material to cutting, polishing, designing. Everything’s done in-house. We don’t depend on the outside world for anything. All of this hard work, you put it out on Instagram, boom, it’s gone.

title: New property purchase disclosure rule in Japan sparks fears it may curb foreign investment
description: Rising interest rates and new legislation on nationality disclosure are raising concerns that foreign investors may reconsider real estate investment.
content: Tokyo’s implementation of a rule that requires all property buyers to declare their nationality is raising concerns among investors, according to analysts. Japan’s shift from an ultra-loose monetary policy to gradual normalisation of its interest rates was also likely to force investors to reconsider whether real estate assets were still attractive, they added. “Japan has had a really strong run for the last seven or eight years,” said Neil Brookes, head of Asia-Pacific capital markets at property consultancy Savills. “But generally, because interest rates have gone up so much, there’s definitely less demand for Japan.” The world’s fourth-largest economy netted US$27.2 billion in property investment in the first half of the year, ranking second behind mainland China in Asia-Pacific, according to data tracked by MSCI. The transaction volume, however, was 7 per cent lower than in the same period in 2025, the financial services company added. The Bank of Japan’s quarter-point increase last month brought its benchmark interest rates to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent. This raised financing costs specifically for highly leveraged property investors, which was likely to dampen demand for speculative transactions, said Yasuyuki Nozawa, president and CEO of Tokyo-based LogProstyle. The real estate and hospitality group listed on the NYSE American, which focuses on small and mid-tier companies, counted international customers as an important target market, particularly for its renovated residential properties, Nozawa said. Official data released by the Japanese government last month showed that in the six months to December 2025, foreign nationals and businesses bought 68 – or 0.7 per cent – of the 9,573 large-scale land deals in Japan. Among them, Chinese individuals and businesses were the most frequent investors, with 28 deals across a total of 42 hectares. Meanwhile, Tokyo now requires both Japanese nationals and holders of other citizenships to add nationality information when registering new property ownership or transferring property from October 5 onwards. According to Kingston Lai, founder and CEO of Asia Bankers Club, the disclosure rule was unlikely to dissuade his clients at the Hong Kong-based company from investing in Japanese real estate. “It’s a disclosure rule, not a restriction, and Japanese buyers have to declare their nationality too,” Lai said. “Our clients are mostly bankers, lawyers and business owners who go through KYC [Know Your Customer] all the time,” Lai said, referring to a compliance process. “So declaring a nationality on a title deed will not change anyone’s decision.” However, the rule was spurring clients to question whether it was “a first step towards tougher measures, like Singapore or Canada have done”, Lai said, referring to Singapore’s punitive levies on residential transactions by foreign buyers and Canada’s ban on home purchases for most foreigners since 2023. “That’s fair, but for now nothing stops a foreigner [from] buying in Tokyo or Osaka, and Japan’s real draws haven’t changed,” Lai said. Japan imposed the new rule following renewed concerns about foreign nationals buying land and property across the country, with growing alarm over the acquisition of property close to so-called sensitive sites, as well as overseas investors causing prices to spike beyond the reach of many Japanese people. “The government has been reviewing the framework surrounding property purchases by foreign nationals and has increased reporting and scrutiny in this area, so international investors need to pay close attention to regulatory developments,” Nozawa of LogProstyle said. “At the same time, Japan continues to welcome legitimate international investment and inbound tourism, both of which are important to the economy,” Nozawa added. “Clear and predictable rules are ultimately positive for serious long-term investors because they give everyone greater confidence in the market.” Amid all these changes, Nozawa said Japan remained a market where investors could access high-quality assets in major cities, a transparent legal and ownership framework, strong tourism demand and, in many cases, pricing that remained attractive relative to comparable properties in other global cities. “We also believe international awareness of Japan as an investment destination has increased substantially as tourism has recovered and more investors experience the country directly,” he said. For those looking into Japanese real estate, the asset class and its soundness should be the main priority, said Richard Hill, senior managing director and head of global research and strategy for real estate at Principal Asset Management. “When you consider foreign investment into Japan, you have to be careful about what type of investment that is,” he said. “Is it levered or non-levered? That’s a big question to begin with. Is it driven by income returns or capital returns? These are questions that investors are beginning to ask.”

title: ‘Outrageous’: Taiwan Mandopop band member allegedly assaulted by South Korean diver underwater
description: Rival diver claims self-defence, alleging Song’s group intruded on their dive site, ignored warnings to leave, and struck first.
content: Palau authorities are investigating an alleged underwater attack by a South Korean divemaster on Taiwanese musician Devon Song and his Bangladeshi divemaster. Song, a member of the music group Nan Quan Mama, posted on social media that he and his divemaster, Sobuj Patwary, were attacked by a South Korean divemaster known as “Romeo”. Song said they were diving at Siaes Corner, a popular site west of Koror, when Romeo suddenly charged at them from below, about 25 metres underwater. Romeo allegedly punched Song’s diving mask and tried to remove it, but Song managed to fend him off. Patwary stepped in to stop Romeo, who then allegedly tried to tear off Patwary’s mask and fins and remove his breathing regulator from behind. LJ, a Chinese staff member at the diving centre where Patwary works, said Patwary “choked on water many times” while trying to retrieve his rebreather. Another client escorted him back to shore. Song described the incident as a “murder” and said Patwary was nearly killed. The musician also posted video footage of the incident. Patwary later confirmed Song’s account in a social media post. He stressed that dive guides in Palau have a responsibility to “ensure that every diver returns safely to the surface”. Romeo, who runs another diving centre in Palau, later posted a statement claiming that Song and Patwary’s group had entered his team’s dive site and ignored their gestures to leave. Romeo also claimed that Patwary attacked him first and that he had acted only in self-defence. Song strongly denied Romeo’s account, calling it a “lie” and insisting that they “made absolutely no resistance underwater”. He also asked: “Even if someone intruded on your site, would you need to attack them underwater?” LJ said the group was at least 20 metres away from Romeo’s team and had not entered their area. She also claimed that this was not the first time Romeo had behaved similarly. Song said Romeo’s party had offered to settle the matter privately, but he was determined to seek justice. “His presence underwater would jeopardise other people’s lives. Any aggressive actions underwater are unacceptable,” he said. Song, who has 25 years of diving experience, said he had never witnessed “such outrageous behaviour”. He also thanked Patwary for protecting him from what he described as life-threatening danger. The case went viral after Song posted about it. Nan Quan Mama debuted in 2004 with the support of Mandopop star Jay Chou. Song also wrote lyrics for several of Chou’s well-known songs, including Maple Leaf and Step Aside. Song and Patwary’s diving centre reported the incident to local police. On October 12, Palau’s Bureau of Tourism and the Koror State Government issued a joint statement saying they were investigating the case. They also said that the individuals involved had been suspended from diving and conducting tourism-related activities pending the outcome of the investigation. The authorities added that they were “committed to protecting visitors” and “supporting responsible tourism operations”. The case sparked heated discussion online. “I suppose there might be another side to the story, but that still doesn’t justify this action,” one commenter wrote. “Imagine your dive guide being attacked and left without fins, a mask or a regulator in an area known for strong currents. This could have seriously endangered the entire group,” another wrote.

title: Grass fire at Canadian military base kills 4, injures dozens
description: Blaze during live-fire combat training leaves 19 in critical condition and triggers mass-casualty response across Alberta.
content: Flames that killed four Canadian soldiers and left 19 people in critical condition began with a smouldering grass fire that quickly grew in an Alberta base’s training area where personnel were carrying out exercises, officials said on Sunday. Officials said 39 people were in hospitals as a result ‌of the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, which Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on home soil. Winds up to 96km/h (60mph) fed the blaze which began around 4pm MDT on Saturday. But they were below 50km/h leading up to the fire, Major General Wade Rutland told reporters at a news conference. He described the sudden high winds and resulting spread of the fire as an “uncommon, rapid” event in which the flames advanced 1km in 30 to 60 seconds. “I’ve ⁠certainly never seen anything like it,” said Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, which is based in Edmonton, about 210km west of the military site. Officials ‌identified the dead as Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark. “The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost,” Carney said Sunday, adding that he had ordered ‌flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-staff to honour the victims. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said many ⁠of the injured will require “weeks and ⁠months” of specialised, intensive medical care. When the fire began, Rutland said, 85 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were in “high intensity” combat training using live munitions at the base, ‌which is located in a prairie setting. The soldiers were preparing for deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces currently have their largest international military operation. Rutland said the incident remains under investigation and declined to ‌speculate ‌on what caused the grass fire. Officials do not believe the region’s extensive oil and gas infrastructure had anything to do with the incident, he ‌said. He also ruled out “outside interference”. CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base houses the ⁠Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those affected in Saturday’s fire came from military bases across the country. Military ⁠and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in “some of the worst conditions imaginable,” Carney said. Twenty-two ground ambulances and eight air ambulances responded to the scene, Smith said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer. Military search and rescue technicians also parachuted ‌into the site, Rutland said. Health staff in ‌Edmonton said a “code orange”, or mass-casualty event, was declared to coordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright. The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6,600, is just north of the base. The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Sunday that the fire is not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist bridges the gap in accessible dental care
description: Through Smile Again, social worker Mark Cheung provides barrier-free dental care for cancer survivors and special needs groups.
content: Hong Kong social worker Mark Cheung Kai-yuen is working to make dental care more accessible for cancer survivors, people with disabilities and children with special needs who often struggle to find suitable clinics. Through Smile Again, the social enterprise he co-founded with dentist Dr Ho Kwun-yin, Cheung has adapted both the facility and the way care is delivered, with wheelchair-friendly facilities, longer consultations and tailored communication approaches. Cheung is a finalist for the Spirit of Entrepreneurship Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. The dental service originally began with cancer survivors. Ho had encountered patients who received radiotherapy or major surgery for head-and-neck cancers, with some requiring complex reconstruction in hospital. After returning to the community, they still needed routine dental care, but finding a clinic able to accommodate their medical histories and ongoing needs was daunting. There is also no dedicated dental subsidy specifically for cancer patients in Hong Kong, according to Cheung. While some elderly people and people with disabilities can qualify for existing assistance, cancer survivors may have to pay for continuing dental care themselves. The pair first tested their approach through a funded project using rented dental clinics. As people from other groups began approaching them, however, the limitations of borrowed premises became clear. The success of that project led them to establish their own barrier-free clinic, supported through a second project under the Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Fund. Patients now include elderly people, wheelchair users, people with intellectual disabilities and children with special needs. Cheung distinguishes between physical accommodations and what he calls “software” accessibility. Structurally, the clinic has step-free access, a larger treatment room that can accommodate electric wheelchairs and an X-ray machine that can be lowered for seated patients. Operationally, the practice tailors its care to each individual’s unique needs, unless a condition requires a specialist referral. Some cancer survivors, for example, may experience restricted jaw movement, muscle deterioration or swallowing difficulties after treatment, meaning even a routine cleaning requires extra time and adapted procedures. For an anxious child, staff might suggest a parent have their teeth cleaned first as a demonstration, while other patients may use an initial visit simply to familiarise themselves with the clinic and discuss their needs. Cheung and Ho split responsibilities accordingly: Ho leads the clinical practice, while Cheung oversees non-clinical operations, including fundraising, partnerships, government relations and patient communication. Keeping the model financially viable remains a challenge. The clinic has been operating for about a year, but treatments for the underprivileged still need funding support. Cheung said healthcare services require substantial upfront investment, while restrictions on advertising dental services make reaching potential patients harder. The business also avoids recommending a more expensive treatment simply because it produces more revenue. Cheung cited dental implants as an example, noting that dentures or bridges may be more suitable for patients who would struggle to maintain implants properly. “The priority is always the patient’s best interests. We recommend the treatment that is most suitable for them, not the procedure that brings in the most revenue,” he said. In addition to the Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Fund, Cheung also thanked Jing Yuan Charity Foundation, Koo’s Giving Charitable Foundation and Social Impact Partners for supporting Smile Again’s work. Launched in 2013, the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might escape public attention.

title: Chilling details emerge of mass shooting plot targeting US Hindu temple
description: Authorities say a 19-year-old told co-workers his rifle jammed at suburban Chicago site and that he ‘couldn’t wait to kill Indian people’.
content: Illinois authorities believe a 19-year-old man charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago entered the building’s car park on Sunday, hours before police arrested him near his home after receiving a tip about the alleged attack plan. Authorities announced Wednesday that they had arrested Alexandros Paporakis and provided the additional detail about his suspected movement during a news conference Thursday. The leaders of Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in a statement said a security threat had “targeted our Temple” and announced an increased security presence. Palatine Police Chief William Nord said a red Acura RDX registered to Paporakis entered a temple car park on Sunday around 12.25pm and left less than 15 minutes later. He was seen alone inside the car around 2pm near his home in another suburb. Paporakis faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle. Prosecutors have said his co-workers at a Taco Bell location called 911 after Paporakis told them he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and said Sunday would be the “special day”. Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, around 65km west of downtown Chicago, said leaders were in contact with police. “Please know that the safety of our devotees, employees and volunteers is our highest priority, and we have implemented additional security measures effective immediately, including increased armed security presence at the Temple,” a statement said. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois’ 8th congressional district, said he was at the Hindu temple on Sunday. “I visited not knowing that there was an attacker lying in wait with a sinister motive to commit a mass shooting, and only because his AR-15 weapon jammed was he not able to commit a massacre that day,” Krishnamoorthi told Associated Press on Thursday. Krishnamoorthi said he had increased his security in response to the alleged planned attack. He called on the FBI to “investigate and prosecute this particular matter as a hate crime”, and the Trump administration to release federal non-profit security grants to bolster security at religious institutions. “People are really shaken up,” he added. Aurora Mayor John Laesch said at a Thursday news conference at the Council on American Islamic Relations’ Chicago office that police were “made aware” of other scheduled celebrations and are reaching out to other temples in the area “to make sure that they know they have a number to call”. Paporakis told a co-worker on Sunday afternoon that his gun jammed and he left quickly, but promised to “retry”, according to prosecutors. He sent the co-worker a video showing an AR-style rifle and a photo of himself wearing a tactical vest, they added. Paporakis also sent the coworker an eight-page document in which he used racial slurs to describe non-white people and outlined a plot to kill as many of them as possible, according to prosecutors. He also described himself as a white supremacist and a neo-Nazi who fantasised about mass murder. Police arrested Paporakis later that day near his home in Palatine, which is located about 65km northeast of the temple. Detectives who searched his home found an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines and “hundreds of rounds” of ammunition, a gas canister labelled with a slur referring to South Asians, a tactical vest and a patch depicting Nazi symbolism, authorities say. Paporakis’ mother was questioned, but she is not cooperating with the investigation, police said on Thursday. At a Wednesday court appearance, a judge ordered Paporakis to remain in detention. His next court hearing is scheduled for October 30. “This case is in the earliest stage of what will likely be a lengthy process,” the office of the Cook County Public Defender, which is representing Paporakis, said in a statement emailed to AP. “We would remind the public that statements made by police and prosecutors are only allegations and that cases can change significantly as they continue to be investigated.” The targeting of the Hindu temple is another example of heightened threats in the last few years against South Asians in the US, according to Stop AAPI Hate, the national reporting centre for anti-Asian hate incidents. Online slurs and threats have risen significantly, co-founder Manjusha Kulkarni said in a statement. “We are grateful this violent plot was thwarted and that no one was hurt – but it doesn’t erase the fear Hindu, Indian, and South Asian people feel after years of escalating hate,” Kulkarni said. “Violence against South Asian people is not inevitable. It is fuelled when leaders stoke fear of immigrants and people of colour for political gain.” She attributed some of the anti-South Asian sentiment to the Trump administration’s rhetoric around Indian immigrants who hold work visas. She also pointed to a Texas Republican last month posting a social media video of South Asian students cheering at a University of Texas football game and referring to them as “foreigners”. The temple, like other Hindu temples and households around the country, has been celebrating Navratri, a Hindu festival that lasts nine days. It “should be a time for celebration and unity, not terror and hate,” Kulkarni said.

title: Hong Kong vies for role in robotics boom with launch of embodied AI hub
description: Hong Kong Productivity Council’s applications hub involves seven robotics companies including Unitree Robotics and Galbot.
content: The Hong Kong Productivity Council (HKPC) opened the city’s first experimental hub for embodied artificial intelligence on Thursday with the participation of seven mainland and Hong Kong companies, including industry leaders Unitree Robotics and Galbot, as the city looks to carve out a role in the global robotics boom. Located at the HKPC Building in Kowloon Tong, the Embodied AI International Applications Hub, housed under the HKPC’s industrial AI and robotics centre, features simulated real-world environments where the companies can test and optimise their latest robotic designs, ahead of potential global roll-outs. “Hong Kong’s application scenarios have an international characteristic,” said Sunny Tan, HKPC chairman, at the opening ceremony. “For many mainland robot manufacturers, they can train their robots for international application scenarios without leaving the country here.” Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong said that the hub marked a major milestone in Hong Kong’s efforts to align with national initiatives to advance in embodied AI and robotics, and pledged further government support to promote development in the field. “Humanoid robotics and embodied AI are key frontiers of the next wave of technological innovation, with tremendous potential to transform industrial operations and foster new quality productive forces,” he said. Hong Kong’s unique advantage lies in its international demand and its pool of global talent Jason Chen, Galbot The hub will initially feature a cohort of seven technology partners and eight “scenario partners” – government bodies and major enterprises that will deploy the latest robots in various application settings. These include Hong Kong’s Civil Engineering and Development Department and electronics company TCL. Edmond Lai, HKPC’s chief digital officer, said that the partnerships would address one of the main bottlenecks for the robotics industry: a lack of real-world testing environments. “Different regions are still at the stage of formulating standards for embodied AI, and this is a golden window period,” he said. “Through this training hub, we hope to establish these practices so they can be pushed forward as potential industry standards.” Following the ceremony, industry leaders and media were guided through live demonstrations from the seven robotics companies. Tsinghua University-backed Robotera showcased its M7 humanoid robot, which has already been deployed in facilities of SF Express and China Post, while domestic humanoid robot leader Unitree showcased its R1 humanoid and A2 quadruped robots, which can be used for factory inspections. Meanwhile, Shenzhen’s AI Squared Robotics and Beijing’s Galbot both showcased use of their robots in retail settings, including the preparing and retrieving of beverages. The sole local firm was Hong Kong start-up Rice Robotics, which showcased its NEX semi-humanoid robot, designed for smart libraries and educational environments. Jason Chen, senior vice-president at Galbot, said that he hoped the partnership with HKPC, and his company’s recent opening of three fully autonomous robot-staffed retail stores in the city, would popularise robots among the public. “Hong Kong’s unique advantage lies in its international demand and its pool of global talent,” he told the South China Morning Post.

title: Indonesian durian farmers stand to benefit from minister’s visit to China
description: Country’s transmigration minister says he is eager ‘to learn from China’s experience in building industry and developing rural economies’.
content: Indonesian officials, looking to alleviate poverty in their country and eyeing the rise of rural economies in China, are turning to Beijing for help that may include stoking the exports of a potentially lucrative durian crop. Indonesian Transmigration Minister Muhammad Iftitah Sulaiman Suryanagara began a seven-day visit to China on Monday, with Indonesia’s state-owned Antara news agency saying consultations with Beijing’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, companies and academic institutions were on his agenda. Before he left for his visit, the news agency quoted Suryanagara as saying that Indonesia wanted to “learn from China’s experience in building industry and developing rural economies”. The minister has held talks in China this week about modern agriculture, technology transfers and industrialisation with a view towards creating jobs in Indonesia’s “transmigration” areas. Transmigration is an Indonesian government programme that relocates poor or landless people from densely populated parts of the sprawling archipelago – home to 288 million people – to less populated ones, including rural areas. As of 2023, more than 7.2 million people had been relocated. China’s experience integrating agriculture, infrastructure development, industrialisation and “workforce quality improvement” could serve as a “reference” for developing transmigration target areas, Antara quoted Suryanagara as saying. Paramitaningrum, an international relations lecturer at Bina Nusantara University in Jakarta, said: “Focusing on developing rural areas is important for the government because it can improve the people’s living conditions and reduce poverty.” China declared in 2021 it had elim­in­at­ed extreme poverty after an eight-year campaign. President Xi Jinping attrib­uted the campaign’s suc­cess to strategies focused on households and indi­vidu­als, with tailored meas­ures to lift pro­ductiv­ity. Tax cuts, government subsidies and transitions from farm work to higher-paid labour in factory, construction and service jobs have helped raise rural incomes in China. The [Indonesian] government needs to put more attention on the fruit industry Mohamad Reza Tirtawinata, Nusantara Durian Foundation Durians grown in the Indonesian province of Central Sulawesi – along with coconuts, sugar cane and coffee raised in other parts of the archipelago – could become a “focus of the exploration” between institutions in the two countries, Antara said. China consumes about 90 per cent of the world’s durians, with the pungent spiky fruits often given as gifts on special occasions. “The [Indonesian] government needs to put more attention on the fruit industry, set higher priorities for fruit production and help loosen investment regulations, especially for durians,” said Mohamad Reza Tirtawinata, director of the Nusantara Durian Foundation. “I understand that investors from China are willing to invest in durian plantations in Indonesia, but there’s been no significant progress up to now.” Tirtawinata said last year that Indonesian durian testing, packing and shipping facilities needed improvement. Investments must be made in plantations across Indonesia to sustain a year-round harvest for the China market, he said, and growers should avoid harvesting at the same time as durian export giants Thailand and Vietnam. Suryanagara had meetings with four Chinese companies on Tuesday, including drone developer Shenzhen DJI Innovations and agricultural trading firm China National Township Enterprises. China National Township Enterprises presented contracts to acquire a combined 14,000 tonnes (15,432 short tons) of Indonesian mung beans and seaweed worth a total of US$19.59 million, Antara reported.

title: UK comedian Russell Brand in London court for rape trial start
description: Brand, 51, denies the charges relating to alleged historical crimes including rape, sexual assault and indecent assault.
content: Jury selection took place on Monday for the ⁠trial of British actor ⁠and comedian Russell Brand over alleged ⁠historical crimes including rape and other sexual offences. Brand, 51, once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters and former husband of US singer Katy Perry, faces three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and ‌one count of indecent assault relating to six women from 1999 to 2009. Brand has denied all the accusations. He arrived at London’s Southwark Crown Court wearing sunglasses and accompanied by his wife. During the hearing he sat in the dock, mostly staring straight ahead or with his eyes closed. “We are about to start ⁠the trial of one Mr Russell Brand,” the judge, Joel Bennathan, told potential jurors. “Many ‌of you will have heard of him.” The judge excluded those who said they had watched a documentary broadcast about three years ago or ‌had read a long newspaper article from the same time in which ⁠allegations of sexual misconduct ⁠were made against Brand. “Those are allegations he firmly denies,” the judge said. He later told those who ‌had been initially selected: “The defendant is clearly someone very well known. You absolutely must not carry out any research ‌at all ‌about this defendant Russell Brand.” The trial is expected to last about six weeks, ‌Bennathan said, with the jurors formally sworn in on Tuesday while prosecutors will open their ⁠case later in the week. The comedian, known for his flamboyant style and appearance, was ⁠a regular on British television screens in the 2000s and also worked as a radio presenter for the BBC. He went on to star in ‌a number of films ‌including Get Him to the Greek in 2010, the same year he married Perry. They divorced in 2012 after 14 months of marriage. In recent years Brand has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. Reporting by Reuters, dpa, Associated Press

title: Hong Kong to expand indices, derivatives and yuan-denominated products: HKEX CEO
description: Bourse operator plans new yuan products and deeper mainland China market links as it seeks to boost liquidity and attract global investors.
content: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) is planning further measures to boost market liquidity, attract more international investors and expand the use of China’s currency, including through yuan-denominated gold futures and stock trading, according to a blog post by its CEO on Monday. The plans come as the city steps up efforts to reinforce its position as a leading international financial centre, following priorities outlined in the government’s policy address and the city’s five-year development plan. “We intend to meet this moment by building a multi-asset ecosystem spanning equities, fixed income, currencies, commodities, derivatives, indices and data,” Bonnie Chan Yiting wrote. Alongside efforts to refine listing rules and attract more issuers, Chan said the bourse operator would continue working with mainland Chinese partners to add real estate investment trusts, or Reits, into the connect schemes and include yuan counters in the southbound Stock Connect programme, measures aimed at both boosting yuan usage and market liquidity. The southbound Stock Connect allows mainland China-based investors to buy eligible Hong Kong-listed shares. HKEX will also advance yuan internationalisation by expanding Hong Kong’s fixed-income, currency and commodities ecosystems. “The renminbi [yuan] is increasingly attractive as a financing and investment currency because it combines a large pool of liquidity with the prospect of long-term internationalisation,” Chan said. Investors were seeking greater access to yuan-denominated assets as well as tools to invest, finance and manage risk in yuan throughout the investment life cycle, she added. Issuance of HKEX-listed dim sum bonds rose 14 per cent year on year to 266.9 billion yuan (US$39.9 billion) as of September 24, putting the market on track for a record year. “We look to add more bond futures with different maturities over time, helping investors manage interest-rate risk across the curve and supporting a fuller offshore renminbi yield curve,” Chan said. Gold is a key part of HKEX’s strategy. Since relaunching its physically delivered US dollar gold futures contracts in July, trading volume and open interest have reached record highs, attracting banks, trading houses and gold producers. “Next, we plan to launch a redesigned renminbi-denominated gold futures contract and build more renminbi-denominated precious metals products, extending its role in commodity trading and risk management,” Chan said. Taken together, these initiatives presented a compelling opportunity for Hong Kong, she added. More indices are also in the pipeline, with HKEX exploring ways to deepen collaboration between onshore and offshore index ecosystems. Such cooperation could support product innovation while giving international investors more effective benchmarks as they evaluate and increase allocations to China’s capital markets, Chan said. “Looking ahead, we will continue broadening choices for investors, including exploring opportunities to expand our suite of equity derivatives and futures products linked to mainland Chinese and regional markets,” she said. The exchange will roll out an additional 12 single-stock option classes in November, each with weekly and monthly expiries, building on the 38 weekly stock options launched so far this year.

title: AI fuelling growth while putting Asia’s young workers at risk, IMF meeting hears
description: AI investment is propping up global growth amid energy shocks, but leaders at the IMF summit warn of a job tsunami threatening Asia’s youth.
content: An investment surge into artificial intelligence may be helping prop up a global economy battered by energy supply shocks, but the technology’s potential to cull jobs requires swift mitigation if Asia’s youth are to secure a place in the future workforce, delegates were warned at the IMF–World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday. Soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and mounting debt framed the opening of the week-long summit, which was last hosted in the Thai capital in 1991. Unusually, the US has not sent its Treasury Secretary to attend the gathering, despite triggering the energy crunch following its war against Iran, taken alongside Israel, in February. Since then, oil prices have oscillated around US$100 a barrel thanks to the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, driving up inflation and forcing governments to drain reserves or borrow heavily to cushion consumers from high costs. Yet the multi-trillion-dollar global plunge into AI and its supporting infrastructure – from data centres to printed circuit boards – had given a 3 per cent boost to a global economy bruised by successive crises, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). “AI – love it, hate it or fear it – it is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact,” said IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, citing the US, China and India as the main drivers of growth in the technology. “That shift in [to a] higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at 3 per cent, despite the fact we’re being dragged down by the energy shock,” she told delegates, including finance ministers from across the world. But the same technology serving as a sticking plaster for a wounded global economy risks undermining its workforce over the longer term unless policymakers act quickly to prepare their populations for the changes taking place. “It is a slow-moving tsunami,” Georgieva said of the impact on employment. “We estimate 40 per cent of jobs will be augmented, downgraded or eliminated. In advanced economies, [that figure is] 60 per cent. [In] low income countries, [around] 23 per cent.” “We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now … but we can be disciplined, draw lessons and act on them.” Highlighting the upside of a technology whose capabilities and speed have thrilled and horrified people in equal measure, Georgieva said Asia’s ageing societies could offset shrinking workforces and declining tax bases with AI-driven productivity gains. Advanced Asian economies could see an annualised growth increase of up to 1 percentage point from AI adoption, she said, while slower-adopting countries could gain between 0.2 and 0.8 percentage points. To realise those gains, governments were warned to take a long-term view – especially in reforming education systems to equip graduates with skills needed to survive and thrive in the coming years. “This is a whole new era,” Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam told the same panel on how smaller countries might also gain from scaled AI adoption. “We should start with the recognition that growth is going to be critical to secure good jobs, but growth is not itself going to be sufficient. There is already a divergence between growth and job creation, and AI is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive.” Global AI development remains heavily concentrated in the US and China, where leading foundation models are trained, hoovering up talent and capital as tech giants expand. The resource-intensive infrastructure like data centres is frequently outsourced to developing nations, which often lack access to the higher-paid roles and training opportunities created by the technology. To narrow that gap, Shanmugaratnam said Asian governments and private businesses must collaborate to ensure students acquire adaptable skill sets that can be continually upgraded. Education systems would have to be retooled urgently to ensure young people entered the workforce with relevant skills, he added. “The silver lining in job displacement is it’s going to happen task by task,” Shanmugaratnam said. “That gives us time to adapt, learn new skills and stay agile.” Host country aspirations The IMF was set up after World War II to stabilise the international monetary system, provide policy guidance and emergency loans to nations in crisis. But critics say its bailouts have sometimes pushed borrowing countries deeper into hardship by imposing tough spending rules. Others condemn the organisation for maintaining Western economic dominance, noting that the US retains effective veto power over core decisions. The IMF–World Bank annual meetings are held in Washington for two consecutive years before rotating to one of the institution’s roughly 190 member states every third year. Thailand, which spent nearly US$35 million to host this year’s summit, is using the event as a showcase for its own economic ambitions. The kingdom’s economy has logged growth of 1.5 to 2.5 per cent in recent years, struggling to overcome the lasting shock of the Covid-19 pandemic and trailing its regional peers such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam. Host officials are framing the summit as an opportunity to position Thailand as a stable investment destination in Southeast Asia, highlighting its regional connectivity, regulatory streamlining and readiness to attract foreign direct investment – especially in data centres and core AI supply chains. Thailand relied on billions of dollars in IMF emergency funding during the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis to pull it back from the brink. The lifeline came attached to structural reform requirements that eventually helped Thailand, alongside Indonesia and South Korea, stabilise and rebound. Yet the country faces stark challenges, notably an education system that currently struggles to produce enough technical graduates to meet the demands of expanding AI firms. Similar challenges face countries across the world as an estimated 1.2 billion young people turn 18 over the next 10 to 15 years. Across Asia, vast disparities in income, education, digital literacy and internet infrastructure persist. These divides separate developed and developing nations, as well as cities and rural areas, leaving tens of millions of young people vulnerable to white-collar job displacement and linguistic isolation from English-dominated large language models. “The most important thing is to remove the gap between youth and the system that shapes their future,” Sarah Rauzana, Chairwoman of the Asean Youth Organisation, told a separate panel. “We need to make sure youth are included in all of the policymaking process … from design to monitoring [and] implementation.” Other panellists urged governments to keep pace with innovation by cutting bureaucracy and updating regulations to support young entrepreneurs launching start-ups. “We see a lot of companies able to go regional [or] global from day one,” said Mei Chel Tan, global managing partner at the venture capital firm 500 Global. “Companies and entrepreneurs that grow with that global vision are the ones going on to create new jobs and new segments of the economy.” But government leadership was critical to ensure the benefits of AI were widely shared, she added. “In Southeast Asia, we see incredible talent … but it has to be harnessed.”

title: Meet NBA star Steph Curry’s mother, Sonya, who just remarried at 60
description: The Golden State Warriors player’s mother, who was also an athlete, posted wedding photos on Instagram but kept her new husband’s identity a secret.
content: Stephen Curry’s mother, Sonya Curry, has remarried. The 60-year-old announced her second marriage in an Instagram post shared on October 9. Quoting Ecclesiastes 3:1-14, a passage from the Bible about life and its changing seasons, Sonya reflected on her life in a lengthy caption. “A year ago my mom passed unexpectedly, while simultaneously the most amazing man came into my life! & months late, I was blessed with becoming his wife!” the mother of three wrote. “Our union is a testament to the fact that God has seen every tear I’ve cried and answered every prayer that I had regarding the type of man that would be a perfect help mate for me (if God saw that it was in his will for me to remarry)!” Her caption was accompanied by a series of snaps from her big day, while keeping her groom’s identity a secret. A photo of the wedding menu seemingly revealed his name as “Andre”. In another post about her wedding, Sonya shared pictures of her family, including the Golden State Warriors point guard and his daughter on the dance floor. In the post, the bride also revealed that the wedding was planned within two months, while reports said it was held at the Fairmont Scottsdale Princess resort in Arizona. Sonya shares three children, Stephen, Seth and Sydel Curry, with ex-husband and former NBA player Dell Curry. They wed in 1988 and divorced in 2021. Here’s everything you need to know about NBA star Stephen Curry’s mother, Sonya Curry. What is Sonya Curry’s background? Sonya Curry was born and raised in an African-American community in Radford, Virginia. She has spoken about the difficulties of growing up in poverty and said in previous interviews that she experienced racism growing up. In one incident, Sonya watched a Ku Klux Klan member riding a horse and lighting a cross in the field where she and her all-Black women’s softball team were preparing for a game, she recalled in an interview with sports and culture media outlet Andscape (formerly The Undefeated) in 2019. At her secondary school, which was “less than 1 per cent Black”, Sonya turned to sports, excelled in basketball and volleyball, and competed at the state level in 400m hurdles. She told Andscape that her athleticism shielded her from racism at school. “You had to play sports. I had to be the best to force them to play with me,” she said. How did she meet Dell Curry? Sonya’s athletic talents landed her a place at Virginia Tech as a collegiate volleyball player. While she was there, she met Dell Curry, who played on the school’s basketball team. The couple welcomed their first child, Stephen, in 1988, after marrying earlier that year. They later welcomed son Seth in 1990 and daughter Sydel in 1994. Stephen has credited his mother with doing a “great job” raising him and his siblings. “A lot of people say whatever defensive abilities I have, I get from her,” he told SF Gate in 2013. “My toughness and grittiness.” He added: “She’s a strong woman. Growing up in an NBA household, with my dad being on the road a lot, she did a great job with me and my siblings. She deserves a lot of credit for how we turned out.” Sonya and Dell separated in 2021. In 2023, Dell married Nicki Smith. She is an author Sonya published her memoir, Fierce Love, in 2022. The book chronicles her three children’s upbringing, as well as her faith and passion for education. Sonya graduated from university with a degree in education and founded the Christian Montessori School of Lake Norman in North Carolina in 1995. “I wrote Fierce Love to share my story, my testimony and my experience so that others may find strength and purpose in their own journeys,” Sonya told People in 2022. “I want to encourage others to pray continuously, live intentionally, love fiercely, and laugh daily!”

title: Global diesel shortage: why Gulf refined fuel exports lag crude oil shipments
description: From shipping bottlenecks to strikes on refineries, analysts warn the market faces a prolonged recovery.
content: Global diesel prices remain near record highs as Gulf producers struggle to restore refined-fuel exports, despite a recovery in crude shipments and pledges by more countries to release reserves. Net diesel exports from Gulf countries averaged 390,000 barrels per day in August, just over a quarter of their levels before the US-Israel war on Iran, according to the latest available data by the International Energy Agency (IEA) published in September. One obstacle to recovery is that Persian Gulf infrastructure is geared towards crude oil, making it harder to ship diesel and other refined fuels, analysts said. Zhao Xuyi, a senior analyst at Shanghai-based Guotai Junan Futures, said Middle Eastern crude exports had recovered quickly through ship-to-ship transfers, in which oil is moved between vessels at sea.
