Exporting refined fuels is more complicated, however, because different products require separate shipping arrangements. “In short, the Middle East has found a way to move crude oil, but it has yet to resolve the challenge of consistently and separately exporting six or seven different refined products,” Zhao noted. The South China Morning Post calculated that diesel prices have surged by more than 66 per cent since the Iran war began in late February. The fuel is essential for farming, heating and road freight. Against this backdrop, the Group of Seven (G7) announced on October 2 that it planned to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and refined fuel products over the coming weeks, with substantial volumes of diesel due to be released early. US diesel futures fell after the announcement but soon edged higher again. Zhao cautioned that the planned release would do little to resolve the wider supply shortage. “The scale of the release is actually very limited. That means the G7’s move can only ease the short-term diesel shortage, not the broader structural shortage,” Zhao said. “So judging by diesel price movements, I think diesel prices will stay bullish.” The pressure on supplies is also reflected in falling global oil inventories. In its report, the IEA said observed inventories had fallen by 507 million barrels since the Iran war began. “With buffers shrinking and the global refining system stretched to the limit, the need for progress in resolving the conflict in the Middle East – and the Russia-Ukraine war, which is now in its fifth year – is greater than ever to avoid further market tightening and demand destruction,” the report’s authors wrote. The supply disruption could also prolong the recovery in refining. In a research note published at the end of August, Goldman Sachs analysts projected that global refinery processing levels would return to seasonal norms only in the second half of next year, citing increasing strikes on refineries in the Middle East and Russia. A potential new source of supply emerged on Friday, however, when US President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to sell diesel immediately to US and global markets. Trump wrote on social media that he had held a “highly successful” discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to Trump, the two leaders agreed that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US, with additional volumes to follow in November. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, called the agreement “historic” in a social media post, saying “Russia-US energy and economic cooperation will continue”. Trump wrote that diesel prices would fall “in record numbers and fast”, though oil market analyst Rory Johnston offered a sharply different assessment. “I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is,” he wrote on social media. US commercial distillate inventories, which include road diesel and heating oil, stood at 100.2 million barrels for the week ending October 2, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That was about 14 per cent below the five-year seasonal average. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the government’s emergency stockpile of oil, fell to about 283 million barrels in the week ending October 2, its lowest level since 1982.

title: Co-care scheme may help prevent 9% of stroke, heart failure cases in next decade
description: Over 200,000 Hongkongers in co-care scheme as of January, with 40 per cent of those screened diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension or pre-diabetes.
content: About 9 per cent of stroke and heart failure cases may be prevented in Hong Kong over the next decade through a government co-care scheme, according to a university projection. Launched in 2023, the Chronic Disease Co-care Scheme has enrolled more than 200,000 residents as of January. Originally a pilot scheme, it was regularised in March, with about 40 per cent of those who completed screening diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension or pre-diabetes. “The co-care scheme effectively enables individuals who have not yet been diagnosed … to receive early management from a multidisciplinary team to comprehensively control cardiovascular risks,” said William Wong Chi-wai, clinical professor and chairman of the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) department of family medicine and primary care. “The results … demonstrably reduce mortality risks as well as complications associated with diabetes and hypertension.” The scheme is a part of the Health Bureau’s primary healthcare co-care network, which would run for five years and was expected to benefit 700,000 residents, said Dr Esther Yu Yee-tak, a consultant of the bureau’s Primary Healthcare Commission. The scheme provides subsidised screening for diabetes, high blood pressure and high blood lipids to people aged 45 or above through participating family doctors. If participants are diagnosed with any of those conditions, they will proceed to receive subsidised treatment and any necessary laboratory tests. According to an HKU projection, calculated based on an assumed baseline of 200,000 participants, medical literature and clinical indicators, the scheme could prevent 502 strokes, 591 cases of type 2 diabetes, 253 heart failure cases and 170 cases of peripheral vascular diseases over the next 10 years, representing a drop of around 8 to 10 per cent in disease risk, Wong said. As for chronic kidney disease, there would be a reduction of 581 cases, representing a 3 per cent dip. Alex Chu Man-yan, who works in the beauty care industry, was a participant in the co-care scheme. The 51-year-old said he had experienced occasional dizziness over a few years but did not seek medical advice. Upon referral by a friend, he did a subsidised screening and was diagnosed with diabetes. Under the scheme, Chu said he followed a personalised treatment plan devised by his family doctor, who scheduled regular blood tests to track his health. He also received eye checks to screen for diabetic complications and consulted a dietitian for advice. He found the co-payment model affordable, having to pay around HK$100 (US$13) for each doctor consultation or physiotherapy session. “I also used to buy lipid-regulating medication out-of-pocket. Under this scheme, the doctor prescribes it altogether, so I don’t need to spend extra money purchasing it myself,” Chu said. He said he regularly went running with friends after joining a health run scheme organised by the district health centre. Since joining the scheme, Chu’s blood sugar dropped significantly, and he experienced improvements in his physical stamina and mental health. “My lifestyle has totally transformed,” he said. According to an analysis by the HKU team, the major risk factors among the scheme’s participants with diabetes showed “significant improvements”, with drops in blood pressure and blood lipid levels for those who received one year of follow-up appointments. “Cardiovascular disease, despite being the leading killer in Hong Kong, is actually preventable, as long as we identify individuals with hidden risk factors early on, including diabetes and high blood pressure,” Yu said.

title: How China and the EU pressed pause on trade war – and what it took to get there
description: EU officials spoke of a ‘paradigm shift’ in wake of surprise trade deal, saying the ‘nature of the rebalancing exercise has changed’.
content: Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods. The deal, unveiled on Friday, takes some of the heat out of searing bilateral trade tensions and temporarily averts the prospect of a bruising trade war. Beijing agreed not to retaliate against Brussels’ move to curb imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which will see shipments capped at 350,000 units per year, rising at 6 per cent annually. This will leave exports at less than half the 800,000 vehicles the EU has projected will be shipped in 2026. Asked on Monday how Beijing grew to accept the concessions – after Chinese officials spent weeks rejecting the prospect of voluntarily limiting auto shipments – Brussels framed its position with a time-worn business maxim: “The customer is always right.” A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, referenced the saying. “In business, there is a saying that the customer is always right. So, as a customer, we have made the point very clearly that we are hurting, and that we will remain a customer. But the volumes and the surge that we have seen are unsustainable.” After the bloc’s 27 member states consent to the arrangement, the bloc will use a technical safeguard instrument to moderate the import of Chinese hybrid cars, likely to be in place from December 1. Once 350,000 units have been imported, others will be turned away at EU ports. The agreement, which will be in place for a four-year period, aims to halve China’s share of the EU hybrid market from the current 12 per cent. While the quota applies to all other countries, no other trading partner approaches China’s level, meaning other exporting nations stand to benefit from the cap. We want to sell more in China … but having China sell less to us is very much the political driver of the rebalancing exercise Senior EU official Chinese brands making hybrid cars in third countries, however, will be subjected to the host country’s quota. For example, a BYD car determined to have been fully made in Turkey under WTO rules of origin would not count towards China’s annual quota. From January 1, meanwhile, China will reduce tariffs on EU goods by a cumulative €4 billion (US$4.47 billion), lowering duties on items such as car parts, olive oil, ice cream and footwear. It will examine whether to broaden the granting of general licences for the export of rare earth elements to new sectors, including healthcare and medical devices, and consider granting “white list” status to those EU firms who have been granted these licences in the past. Separately, in a bid to address growing concerns from the West over trade imbalances, Beijing will cut the value-added tax export rebate rate for new energy vehicles from 13 per cent to 9 per cent from April 1, according to a notice issued jointly on Monday by the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration. Tax rebates on e-cigarette exports will also be cancelled, per the notice. The EU gave no ground, officials said, on its tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles. Instead, the conditions for reaching price undertaking agreements were reaffirmed, meaning any Chinese company wishing to benefit from a minimum price deal must negotiate with Brussels directly, rather than through their government. China has long railed against export controls on the most advanced lithography machines used to produce semiconductors – equipment exclusively manufactured by Dutch firm ASML. While the EU agreed to convey Beijing’s concerns on export controls to the member state authorities responsible, there was also little conceded on that front. The deal marks a boon for Brussels, which for months has tried to convince Beijing to take a step back from the brink of a full-blown trade war. EU officials said Chinese counterparts were amenable to an amicable solution when confronted with evidence of an “injurious” import surge backed by data, but also suggested Beijing had responded to the threat of unilateral action. The agreement came after the leaders of France and Germany threatened to deploy a new policy tool that would cut Chinese firms out of the EU market overnight, in a rare moment of unity on China policy from the bloc’s two biggest members. Despite the deal’s prevention of a more pitched conflict, trade tensions are likely to keep simmering. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will speak again via video call with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in January before another in-person meeting in March. EU officials said those sessions will be used to take stock of how the hybrid car export rules are being implemented and explore whether the strictures can be broadened to other sectors. On Thursday and Friday, meanwhile, leaders of EU member states will meet in Brussels to consider the need for new weapons to counter what they view as a threat of deindustrialisation posed by China’s industrial prowess. European politicians have characterised China’s rise in several bedrock industries as the product of undeclared subsidies and an undervalued yuan, accusations Beijing has denied. The senior official spoke of a “paradigm shift” in Brussels, with a relocation of the primary battleground in trade tensions from the market access European businesses have long sought to the continent’s reduction of Chinese imports. “We want to sell more in China … but having China sell less to us is very much the political driver of the rebalancing exercise,” the senior official said. “So the nature of the rebalancing exercise has changed, and that has very much to do with what has been called deindustrialisation, the result of what some would call the China shock 2.0.”

title: Taiwan aims to raise pilot retirement age to 58 as new F-16V jets arrive
description: Addressing fatigue concerns, chief of staff says the island’s air force has moved away from scrambling fighters to shadowing PLA aircraft.
content: Taiwan’s defence ministry plans to allow military pilots to serve until the age of 58 as it grapples with the prospect of “having fighter jets but no pilots”. The proposed retention scheme comes as the island’s air force prepares to form operational squadrons around 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighters ordered from the United States, adding pressure to an already stretched pool of experienced pilots. Under the plan, pilots could serve until they turn 58 – up from about 48 for lieutenant colonels and 52 for colonels – extending their current service limits of 26 and 30 years, respectively. The air force would also create 72 additional posts for highly qualified lieutenant colonel and colonel pilots who have served at least 14 years, allowing them to retain their rank and focus on flying rather than command or administrative duties. Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said on Monday that the arrangement was designed to keep experienced pilots in uniform when many faced a choice between remaining in the military and pursuing longer, potentially more lucrative careers with commercial airlines. Civilian airline pilots can fly until the age of 65, giving military pilots an incentive to switch careers while still relatively young. “If they can serve until 58, the gap with civilian airline pilots, who can fly until 65, will not be that large,” Koo told lawmakers. He said 57 air force pilots had retired so far this year, broadly in line with previous years but fewer than last year. All had completed their minimum required period of service. But the defence ministry acknowledged in a report to the legislature that retaining veteran pilots remained difficult, as the post-pandemic expansion of commercial aviation had increased demand for experienced aviators. The challenge is particularly pressing as Taiwan begins receiving its new F-16Vs and prepares to assign more than 100 pilots for the additional fighter units needed to operate them. The first two of the 66 F-16V Block 70s landed at Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung on October 2. They are expected to serve with the Seventh Tactical Fighter Wing, which is being organised into operational squadrons in phases. The ministry said the air force had increased pilot positions and training in preparation for the new aircraft. Its pilot staffing rate stands at 87.8 per cent, although officials said this could rise to 91.3 per cent after pilots in training qualified in January. Koo said training a military pilot took years, with those reaching the ranks of lieutenant colonel or colonel generally being among the air force’s most experienced and technically mature aviators. Under the proposed system, the 72 veteran pilots would occupy additional posts outside the regular personnel establishment, meaning they would not take positions from other officers or have to assume command roles. “Their job would simply be to fly,” Koo said, adding that they must still meet physical requirements. They would also train and mentor younger pilots while continuing to receive aviation-duty allowances and retention bonuses. The ministry submitted the proposal to the cabinet for approval on September 4 and estimates it would require more than NT$40 million (US$1.3 million) in funding. The retention push comes as deliveries of the long-delayed F-16Vs appear to be picking up. Koo said 63 of the 66 aircraft had entered production, including six reaching the flight-test stage. Two have arrived in Taiwan, two will remain in the US for training and two others are undergoing acceptance procedures. He said more fighters could pass acceptance tests this month and expressed hope that additional aircraft would arrive in Taiwan before the end of October. However, Koo stopped short of promising that all 66 would be delivered by the end of next year. He said Taipei must continue coordinating with Washington over the schedule. Lawmakers, meanwhile, have raised questions about the electronic warfare capabilities of the first two aircraft delivered to Taiwan. Air Force Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Lee Ching-jan said parts of the hardware for the AN/ALQ-254 Viper Shield electronic warfare suite had been installed, but its software remained under development. The system is designed to detect and counter hostile radar and other electromagnetic threats, providing an important layer of protection for the Block 70 in contested airspace. Koo said the electronic warfare suite still had to be integrated with other systems aboard the new fighters, with the work proceeding according to schedule. The 66 new aircraft will expand Taiwan’s F-16 fleet beyond its 140 or so older F-16A/B fighters that had been upgraded to the F-16V standard, adding to staffing demands as the military struggles with broader personnel shortages. Asked about pilot fatigue caused by staffing pressures and frequent sorties by People’s Liberation Army warplanes around Taiwan, Lee said the air force had moved away from scrambling fighters to shadow PLA aircraft on a one-for-one basis. Instead, Taiwan was using a combination of fighters already on patrol, naval vessels and land-based missile systems to monitor and respond to PLA activity, reducing strain on both pilots and aircraft. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Who is Callina Liang, the actress playing Chun-Li in the new Street Fighter movie?
description: Callina Liang talks about the traits she shares with her character, past work with Lucy Liu and Benedict Wong, and her Chinese cinema dreams.
content: When Kitao Sakurai, the Japanese-American director of a new film adaptation of the Street Fighter video game franchise, called to say she had the role, Callina Liang reacted the way anyone might expect. “I was in a park screaming at the top of my lungs,” the 26-year-old actress reveals with a giggle over Zoom. Starring Andrew Koji (Warrior) as Ryu and Noah Centineo (Black Adam) as Ken, the film allows Liang to live out her 16-bit dreams, playing Chun-Li, the franchise’s first-ever female playable character and a real fan favourite. The casting represents a full-circle moment. Growing up in Beijing, Liang spent her free time playing Street Fighter at a local arcade in Chaoyang. “My grandma would take me there, and this was always the game I gravitated towards,” she says. For an actress with an innate fighting spirit, it is no surprise she was drawn to this classic title. “I’m a huge gamer now, and I’m a big fan of fighting games,” she says. “And I always say Street Fighter was the game that got me into my love for gaming.” First published in 1987 by Japanese developer Capcom, Street Fighter is the mother of all martial arts video games, as players take on the characters of Ryu, Ken and many others, fighting each other or a rogues’ gallery of computer-controlled characters. Not even the much-maligned 1994 movie adaptation – starring Jean-Claude Van Damme as William Guile and Kylie Minogue as Cammy White – could dent the game franchise’s popularity, with more than 60 million copies sold. Liang herself has “kept playing the game” right up to the 2023 iteration, Street Fighter 6. “I have it downloaded on my PS5,” she says. Becoming Chun-Li With the role secured, she soon began working with a trainer in Toronto, Canada, where she lives – a two-and-a-half-month sprint to hone her martial arts skills. For two hours in the morning and two in the afternoon, she was lifting weights at the gym and eating a meal every couple of hours (including 12 eggs a day). “I managed to put on about 20 pounds [9kg] in a month and a half,” she says. “So it was a crazy process for sure, but it was also very therapeutic. I really enjoyed getting all my anger out, learning how to fight and to kick. Now I keep it up. I can’t stop. It’s addictive, and it’s a form of therapy.” After training ended, she moved to Sydney, Australia, for the “extremely physical” shoot. “When you’re doing a film like Street Fighter, almost all you’re doing is fighting,” she says. But while the story might be secondary to the smackdowns, she could not dismiss the fact that Chun-Li is fuelled by revenge against antagonist M. Bison (played by David Dastmalchian), who killed her father. Liang made sure she dived into the spin-off manga and anime versions. “I definitely wanted to bring my own take on the character, while also at the same time honouring her storyline and who she is in the games,” she says. Striking similarities Intriguingly, Liang did find parallels between Chun-Li and her own life. Some of them are silly coincidences. “She’s quick to anger sometimes. When I’m really hungry, I get ‘hangry’ really easily,” she chuckles. Liang also shares some vital statistics with the character – same height (169cm/5ft 6in), same blood type (A). “And when you look at her likes and dislikes in the video games, her likes are desserts, fruit and candy, and I’m like, ‘Oh, that is also 100 per cent me.’” Other comparisons are more serious. “She doesn’t really have any family members other than her father … and me too,” she says. “I don’t have any siblings, and I only have my dad. So growing up it was just me and my dad and no one else. “She’s also pretty stubborn, very headstrong, very determined,” she adds. “If she wants something, she’s gonna get it done. So I also related to her in that way … and as a woman, just navigating in this world by yourself. I moved away from my family at a pretty young age. I was in boarding school from the age of five.” Liang’s global upbringing has clearly shaped her. Canadian by birth – she was born in Vancouver but was there for a matter of weeks before her family headed to Beijing – she moved to Sydney in 2010, partly for her father’s work in real estate and partly to learn English. Four years later, she shipped out to Singapore, where the acting bug really kicked in. When she dropped out of high school to study drama, her father gave her four years to make it work – or return to education for a career in medical research. Fighting for representation After moving to New York in 2019 to further her acting studies, Liang has more than proved herself to her father. She has already worked with Steven Soderbergh in his highly effective 2024 ghost chiller Presence, opposite Lucy Liu, and the high school drama Bad Genius (also 2024), alongside Benedict Wong. Liang counts both Liu and Wong as mentors. “Not only were they such great actors who were so honed in on their craft, they also showed me that there is a place for us in this [Hollywood] world that isn’t predominantly for Asian people, so they inspired me truly,” she says. The journey has not been without its struggles. “I’m very grateful to have gotten the opportunities that I have,” Liang says, “but it didn’t come easily. “Again, you gotta find jobs that are open to casting an ethnicity without … being so specific to it. There are a lot of stereotypical roles sometimes. It’s gotten better, but I think there’s definitely still room for improvement. It’s not been easy, but I think it’s definitely a lot easier than what actors from the previous generation had to deal with – actors like Lucy and Benedict. “I’m grateful, but I’m still fighting for more,” she adds. Given her fluent Mandarin, Liang is open to working in Chinese cinema, despite noticing stylistic differences. “My family really wants me to go into the Chinese cinema world of it all,” she says. “But personally, there isn’t a huge pool for me. I just find the acting styles to be pretty different – the Western world versus the one in China. But if I ever get the opportunity to, I definitely wouldn’t turn it down. “It would be a dream of mine to use my first language in a film, doing what I love … that would mean a lot to me. And I actually speak some Chinese in Street Fighter, which is cool.” Liang flies back to Beijing two or three times a year. “My grandma still lives there, so I try and see her as much as I can,” she says. “Whenever I’m not working, I go back to China, and I spend time there because she’s getting old.” There is a nostalgia, she admits, to returning to her childhood home, even if so much has changed. “The arcade doesn’t exist any more,” she sighs. “Even the supermarket we used to go to doesn’t exist any more.” No doubt the next time she returns, there will be another change: her own fame. Gamers demanding selfies with the new Chun-Li will probably be the next challenge. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: ⁠US economists Robert ⁠Hall, Michael Woodford win 2026 Nobel economics prize
description: The two Americans have been honoured for their work on ‘smoothing out economic peaks and troughs’.
content: American-born economists ⁠Robert ⁠Hall ⁠and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy. Hall, 83, is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford, 70, with Columbia University in New York. The announcement was made in Sweden’s capital Stockholm, with the winners honoured “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. One of their key insights is that economies can only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a ⁠micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work. “The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone on Monday from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honour, it’s a surprise.” We are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences The men’s work has “provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world”, said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.” During the oil crises in the 1970s, the Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked. That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective. In separate contributions they set about taking into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy jury said. “This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affects the economy through their actions.” The economics prize, formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the ⁠final ⁠prize to be given ‌out this year. Last year, the economics award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth. Nobel honours were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace. The central bank established the economics prize in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about US$1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation. Additional reporting by Reuters, Associated Press

title: Few Hong Kong investors take interest in listing by Africa’s top phone maker Transsion
description: Shenzhen Transsion’s US$428 million offering oversubscribed just 3.5 times, sources say, as sharp decline in listing sentiment continues.
content: Shenzhen Transsion Holdings drew a lukewarm response for its HK$3.36 billion (US$428 million) Hong Kong share offering, heightening worries over market sentiment for new listings in the fourth quarter. The maker of Africa’s bestselling phones closed its bookbuilding on Monday, with preliminary figures showing the offering attracted about 14,000 applications and was oversubscribed roughly 3.5 times, according to people familiar with the matter. Retail participation in Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs) has dropped sharply since September. Out of 12 listings last month, only two – Camsense Technologies and Mech-Mind Robotics Technologies – drew more than 100,000 retail applicants, while Red Avenue New Materials Group recorded the lowest demand with just 12,645, according to the companies’ allotment results. In contrast, 11 out of 19 listings across July and August topped 100,000 applicants, with Momenta and Basic Semiconductor each surpassing 200,000. “Last month was one of the weakest periods for the IPO market in nearly two years, primarily because over 60 per cent of new listings fell below their offer price within the month,” said Jasper Chan, manager at Phillip Securities (Hong Kong). Three IPOs in September ended up with oversubscription numbers in the low single digits, representing 25 per cent of the total IPOs, compared with just two out of 65 listings garnering such tepid response between April and August. Shenzhen Transsion lacked strong fundamentals and competitive advantages, Chan said, as it faced intensifying competition in Africa from Chinese rivals like Xiaomi and Oppo. The company also did not fit into the technology or artificial intelligence themes currently favoured by the market, limiting its appeal, he added. Founded in 2013, Transsion dominates African smartphone sales through its Tecno, Infinix and iTel brands, holding 53 per cent of the market last year. Its annual revenue fell 4 per cent to 65.5 billion yuan (US$9.8 billion) in 2025 while profit plunged 53 per cent to 2.6 billion yuan, the prospectus showed. The company’s Shanghai-listed shares slipped more than 8 per cent during its Hong Kong subscription period from Wednesday to Monday, where it marketed 86.6 million shares at up to HK$38.80 each. Its Shanghai shares gained 0.84 per cent to 49.36 yuan on Monday. Investors were acting with extreme caution now, Chan said. Even if a company in a hot sector listed in the fourth quarter, investors would no longer chase concepts alone but would judge whether the company’s valuation was reasonable, he added. Transsion’s Hong Kong shares are expected to debut on Thursday. The offering was backed by 11 cornerstone investors including GIC, Shenzhen Longsys Electronics and Bank of China Wealth Management. Citic Securities is the sole sponsor of the Hong Kong listing.

title: Chinese man arrested after fabricating rooftop child grave hoax above residential flat
description: Analysis revealed that the bone fragments belonged to livestock or poultry, while the teeth were identified as fish teeth.
content: Police in southwestern China have debunked a terrifying rumour after an alarmed homeowner was told by a neighbour that bones found on her rooftop belonged to a buried young boy. On October 5, a woman surnamed Li from Chengdu, Sichuan province, told local media outlet Sichuan Observation that she had found what appeared to be a grave on the rooftop above her flat. Li bought the second-hand flat on the seventh floor in 2017 and had rented it out ever since. A neighbour recently told her that the rooftop was the burial site of a seven-year-old boy who had lived in the building and died of an illness in September 2009. Footage taken by Li showed what appeared to be bones, including teeth, buried beneath a pile of rocks and weeds. She subsequently alerted police. Li accused the previous owner of concealing the alleged grave, saying it could affect the property’s value. She sought to hold the seller accountable but was unable to contact them. The discovery caused a stir on mainland social media, with related videos attracting millions of views. “This is horrifying. No matter how much you miss your child, you should give them a proper burial, not bury them on a rooftop,” one online user commented. “If true, this could unsettle residents and send property prices tumbling,” wrote another. According to a lawyer, burials outside designated cemeteries are illegal in China. Li could also seek to cancel the property deal and claim compensation if the seller had deliberately concealed the alleged grave. However, the case took a surprising turn after police examined the bones. On October 8, police confirmed there was no grave on the rooftop, only a flower bed containing animal remains. There was no tombstone, urn or other burial-related items. Tests identified the bone fragments as belonging to livestock or poultry, while the teeth were consistent with those of fish. After checking death records and interviewing residents, police dismissed the story of the boy’s grave as a rumour traced to a 73-year-old neighbour surnamed Liu. Liu, whose motive remains unclear, received an administrative penalty. Under Chinese law, spreading rumours can carry up to 10 days’ detention and a fine of 500 yuan (US$75). In serious cases involving disruption of public order, offenders can face up to seven years in prison. One online observer remarked: “Whether driven by personal revenge or a desire for attention, spreading rumours is both foolish and shameful.” “Don’t blindly believe sensational urban legends or add to the spread of misinformation by embellishing what you hear,” warned another.

title: Mapping US chip supply chain: China accounts for far more than it appears, report says
description: US chip production relies on ‘vulnerable inputs hidden deep in upstream global supply chains’, SIA says.
content: China accounts for about 5 per cent of the equipment and materials directly supplied to the US chip industry when measured by country of manufacture, but its grip on certain rare earths needed for chipmaking is over 90 per cent, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA). While 95 per cent of the nearly US$27 billion annual spending by American chipmakers on manufacturing equipment and materials was sourced from companies headquartered in the US, Europe, and Japan, that figure dropped to 68 per cent when the value is counted by country of origin, according to SIA. Suppliers “often rely on production chains outside their country of domicile”, the SIA said in a report published on Friday. China’s share rose to 5 per cent by production site from about 1 per cent by supplier headquarters, while Southeast Asia’s jumped to 10 per cent from less than 1 per cent, it said. China’s share rises from about 1 per cent by supplier headquarters to 5 per cent by production site, while Southeast Asia is up from less than 1 per cent to 10 per cent. The figures cover equipment and materials bought directly by the US chip industry and do not capture raw materials and components sourced further upstream, where the report identified additional exposure to China. China accounts for about 95 per cent of global gallium supply and 85 per cent of tungsten supply. Gallium is used in compound semiconductors, while tungsten can be refined into chemicals used to deposit thin films during chip production, the report noted. The SIA findings also put China’s share of neodymium and praseodymium supplies, measured together, at about 95 per cent, and its share of terbium at roughly the same level. These rare earths are used in high-performance magnets for motors, robots and precision systems inside chipmaking equipment. “The equipment and materials necessary to produce semiconductors in America rely on vulnerable inputs hidden deep in upstream global supply chains,” SIA said, adding that these vulnerabilities “compound risks to the semiconductor ecosystem in the US and partner nations”. Beijing has imposed export licence requirements on specified gallium products, certain tungsten products and products related to seven medium and heavy rare-earth elements. It announced a broader set of controls last October but suspended them until November 10, 2026. The earlier licensing requirements have remained in place. Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US last month, the White House said the two countries were continuing to work on US concerns over shortages of rare earths and other critical minerals, with the aim of restoring shipments. American companies continued to face shortages of critical minerals earlier this year despite the relaxation of some controls, the South China Morning Post reported in March. The SIA has called for stockpiling priority inputs and developing alternative supplies with allies, warning that capacity for some materials could take a decade or more to build, followed by three to four years to qualify new suppliers and materials for chip production.

title: China-educated ex-US FDA official to lead Hong Kong’s medical products regulator
description: With more than 30 years’ experience in pharmaceutical regulation, Li Zili viewed as ideal head of body that will help develop city’s bioeconomy.
content: A Beijing-educated former official at the US federal drug regulator has been appointed to lead Hong Kong’s new medical products approval body, tasked with accelerating the clinical use of medicines and medical devices as part of a regulatory overhaul. Dr Li Zili, who previously worked at the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), would take up the post of controller for medical products regulation under the Department of Health on a three-year term starting on October 20, the government said on Monday. He will lead the Centre for Medical Products Regulation, to be established later this year, which aims to promote proactive “primary evaluation”, speed up the clinical application of drugs and medical devices, and give patients access to advanced products that meet quality and safety standards. Li served twice at the FDA, first as a medical team leader and later as head of global affairs at the agency’s Office of Generic Drugs. Dr Ronald Lam Man-kin, Hong Kong’s director of health, said he was confident Li could rapidly and systematically build the centre’s regulatory capability. “Mr Li possesses an in-depth understanding of international medical product regulation and public health policy, as well as extensive hands-on experience in the regulatory review and independent evaluation of innovative medical products abroad. He is an outstanding leader with vision and determination,” Lam said. He also said the establishment of the centre marked a significant milestone in Hong Kong’s reform of its medical products evaluation, approval and regulatory system. “It is also an indispensable factor in advancing the registration, regulation, research and development of medical products,” he added. Li earned his medical degree from Peking Union Medical College and completed his residency training at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, where he also obtained a Master of Public Health. A US-licensed physician and internationally recognised medical executive, Li has more than 30 years of experience in pharmaceutical regulation and global drug development. He has also held senior roles at several multinational pharmaceutical companies, including as global vice-president and head of Asia-Pacific research and development at Janssen Pharmaceutical of Johnson & Johnson. Li is a fellow and board member of the Drug Information Association. In 2013, he received a Special Contribution Award in Regulatory Science from the Centre for Drug Evaluation of the then China Food and Drug Administration, followed by a special recognition award from the US FDA in 2014 for his contributions to building regulatory capacity. Lo Yuk-lam, president of the Hong Kong Bio-Med Innotech Association, said Li was internationally recognised and fully qualified for the position. He added that Li had previously served as a consultant to the Department of Health. “Who can be qualified for the role? One must understand the US FDA, China’s National Medical Products Administration and the international regulatory system. The only candidate who fulfils all three conditions is Li Zili,” he said. Lo said the establishment of the centre was very important for Hong Kong because it would serve as a “trigger” to help develop the bioeconomy. The city’s advantage lay in safety and reliability, he said, adding that Hong Kong needed to develop its own regulatory system so that drugs approved locally would also be recognised by other jurisdictions. Lo said he expected Hong Kong to help medical companies in mainland China expand overseas and serve as a key regulatory system for the country and Southeast Asia. “We do not have a very large population. But if we can develop our own standards and regulatory system and turn it into an FDA-equivalent body, it would have a great impact on Hong Kong in 10 to 15 years,” he said. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau previously said the city was seeking recognition from the World Health Organization for its future Centre for Medical Products Regulation. The ultimate goal was to move to primary evaluation by 2030, enabling Hong Kong to assess and approve drugs independently without relying on foreign approvals. The government launched the “1+” mechanism, allowing drug makers to seek local registration for products supported by local clinical data and only one external regulatory approval, instead of two. Since it took effect in November 2023, 21 drugs had been approved as of late June.

title: Indian homes, factories hit by hours of blackouts amid more demand for coal
description: Coal-fired power stations supply about two-thirds of India’s electricity. Energy issues include extra hot weather increasing air-con use.
content: Indian factories, smelters and households are being hit by blackouts and rising energy costs as the impact of plunging coal stockpiles at the country’s power stations ripples through the economy. The weakest monsoon since 2015 has curbed hydropower output, while hotter-than-normal weather has buoyed demand for air conditioning and farm irrigation. That has seen coal-fired power stations, which supply about two-thirds of India’s electricity, rapidly burn through their inventories. Smaller factories, farmers and households are facing power cuts as demand outweighs supply on the grid. Meanwhile, large industrial customers – in metals smelting, chemicals and paper – cannot get enough fuel to produce electricity themselves due to state-owned miner Coal India prioritising deliveries to grid-connected generators. Small steel mills in the central state of Chhattisgarh are facing outages of 10 to 12 hours a day, forcing plants to reduce output, said Manish Dhuppad, general secretary at the Chhattisgarh Mini Steel Plant Association. Mills require an “uninterrupted supply of power”, he said. “Say we have hot metal inside the furnace and just before we are able to take it out, the power supply goes. By the time it comes back, the material has solidified and we need to melt it again.” The power shortage highlights the increasing role that extreme weather is having on India’s economy, with the weak monsoon driven by a record El Nino. It also shows how the country’s continued reliance on fossil fuels is limiting its ability to respond to a changing climate. Feedstock supplies at almost half of India’s coal-fired plants had fallen to less than a quarter of required levels as of October 10, according to the power ministry. A late burst of monsoon rainfall last month in coal-mining regions in the east of the country exacerbated the shortages, crimping production and also hampering rail transport of the fuel. In the northern state of Punjab, homes and industries are enduring lengthy blackouts. It is difficult to plan our operations and deliveries and affects product quality. The sudden stoppage and restart of machines also raises the risks of accidents Badish Jindal, who runs a steel wire plant Badish Jindal, who runs a steel wire plant in Ludhiana, an industrial city in the state, said frequent power cuts of three to four hours had resulted in higher energy costs, as his factory needed to shift to expensive backup generators. “The power cuts are unscheduled,” he said. “That makes it difficult to plan our operations and deliveries and affects product quality. The sudden stoppage and restart of machines as the power supply goes and comes back also raises the risks of accidents.” The country’s electricity grid has faced an average shortfall of nearly four gigawatts a day in the first 10 days of October, data from Grid Controller of India show. That is enough to power about 2 million rural Indian households, according to Bloomberg calculations. The policy to favour grid-connected power stations has left companies that generate their own coal-fired electricity at a major disadvantage, said Rajiv Agarwal, secretary general of the Indian Captive Power Producers Association, which represents the big industrial users. They are having to pay high prices at Coal India auctions and buy expensive power from the grid, he said. The firms are also having to wait months for rail transport, so those with limited operating capital are being forced to cut output, he said. Average premiums at Coal India spot sales in September jumped to 94 per cent over the base price, compared with a 59 per cent difference in August. Two of the company’s subsidiaries – Northern Coalfields and South Eastern Coalfields – charged more than a 200 per cent premium at auctions last month, data from the miner show. Coal India did not immediately reply to a request for comment. For those getting their power from the grid, bills have gone up in most Indian states over the past few years. That has been driven by a range of factors including rising coal prices and the cost of upgrades to the national electricity network. In Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous province, some villages in Shamli district are facing as much as seven hours a day of blackouts, prompting many residents to buy back-up systems that can run lights and fans, according to Devinder Singh, a local grain and sugar cane farmer. A rapid buildout of solar in the country over the last few years means there is enough power for him to irrigate his fields during the day, although problems occur after sunset, he said. “We somehow adjust,” Singh said. “My bigger concern is the rising cost of electricity.”

title: Hong Kong domestic helper arrested for alleged murder of 93-year-old woman
description: Elderly woman was found unresponsive in her flat after helper sought assistance from building security staff.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a domestic helper on suspicion of murdering a 93-year-old widowed cancer survivor she was caring for, with an investigation suggesting the elderly woman was assaulted repeatedly in the hours before her death. The woman, surnamed Kwan, was found unresponsive in her flat in Long Yiu House at Tak Long Estate in Kai Tak on Sunday morning, police said. The 52-year-old helper, hired to provide round-the-clock care, sought help from building security staff at about 8.20am, saying the woman was unresponsive and needed an ambulance. Paramedics rushed Kwan to hospital after performing emergency treatment at the scene but she was pronounced dead at 9.12am. Initial examinations found no obvious fatal injuries and no signs of a struggle or ransacking inside the one-person, 150 square foot public housing flat. “We believe that, according to preliminary investigations, friction between the two arose over time or strained relations due to overworking,” Terry Wan King-hang, acting deputy Sau Mau Ping district commander, said on Monday. “As far as we understand, the Social Welfare Department also made regular visits to the deceased. “Footage gathered by police shows that there were intermittent minor assaults daily in the past half a month or so.” Wan added that the woman did not have any children and her husband died more than three decades ago due to an illness. Police said Kwan had a history of chronic illnesses, including hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol. She was diagnosed with colorectal cancer 17 years ago and suffered a stroke more than two years ago, requiring long-term medication and regular medical follow-up checks. Her relatives arranged for the helper to care for her in late 2022, and the worker officially began the job in January 2023. According to police, security camera footage showed the helper allegedly assaulting Kwan multiple times between 8.03am and 8.10am on Sunday. The suspect allegedly hit her about 20 times on the head, face and neck with her hands in a series of attacks. She was also seen stepping on Kwan’s abdomen while moving her and handling her body in what police described as a rough and violent manner. At about 8.10am, the footage showed Kwan lying motionless on her bed. Police said the helper then attempted to wake her by feeding her water and lightly patting her before seeking outside help. Officers arrested the helper at the flat at about 3.50am on Monday on suspicion of murder. Police said a preliminary examination by a forensic pathologist found bruises on Kwan’s chest, lower abdomen, right side of the abdomen and right jaw, as well as cuts on the left side of her neck. However, no obvious fatal injuries were immediately identified. An autopsy and further forensic tests will determine the exact cause of death. The suspect remained in custody as the Sau Mau Ping district crime squad continued its investigation.

title: Former HSBC executive launches wealth platform powered by team of AI agents
description: Veteran banker says start-up aims to help ‘mass affluent’ investors manage portfolios, monitor risks and spot opportunities proactively.
content: A former top executive at HSBC has launched an artificial intelligence-driven wealth management start-up, setting her sights on a billion-dollar valuation and betting that AI can transform how individuals manage their investments and finances. Trista Sun, formerly a managing director in the international wealth and premier banking division at HSBC, said in an interview last week that her venture Equora aimed to help investors manage their finances “proactively” with AI agents, addressing large-scale needs that existing AI tools fail to meet. She said the company’s platform, a2b2.ai, featured 10 AI agents specialising in different tasks, such as tracking product maturity dates, detecting fraudulent transactions and flagging market movements that impacted their portfolios. The agents leveraged large language models (LLMs), including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Moonshot AI’s Kimi and Qwen from Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post. Users could upload portfolio statements, while the system automatically scrubbed names and account numbers before storing the data, Sun added. “I wanted to build something very, very proactive, but in the wealth and investment domain,” said Sun, who previously held several senior positions at HSBC, including executive vice-president at HSBC China. The launch comes amid a wave of increasingly sophisticated general-purpose AI agents and a growing push by major AI companies into industry-specific applications. Meta Platforms’ release of Muse earlier this month intensified the race to develop personal AI agents, while Anthropic and OpenAI last month unveiled products for financial services built on their latest LLMs. Sun, however, said “significant gaps” and user friction remained in the market. Most general-purpose AI tools lacked deep financial expertise and relied heavily on the quality of user prompts, while many financial AI solutions faced conflicts of interest because they earned commissions from distributing investment products, Sun said. She added that she had yet to see a direct competitor to a2b2. “[We want the platform to] try to serve you, be on your side, to not promote or sell things or have any other agenda,” Sun said. She said a2b2 offered four subscription tiers, with monthly fees ranging from US$3 to US$90. The company would primarily target “mass affluent” individuals and households in Hong Kong and the US, with Singapore as its third market. Sun, whose other former roles at HSBC included global head of international and cross-border business and global chief operating officer of wealth management, has set high expectations for the start-up. The platform aimed to serve 1 million “active” and “sticky” paying users within two to three years, according to Sun. Without sharing a specific valuation target for the start-up, Sun said she had been “used to managing billion-dollar businesses” throughout her career. “I’m used to that kind of scale,” she added. Sun said she was currently funding the venture herself, but Equora could seek external funding next year.

title: China Open champ Zheng Qinwen withdraws from Wuhan citing fatigue, shoulder injury
description: The 24-year-old is now ranked back among the world’s top 25 after reaching the US Open quarter-finals before lifting the trophy in Beijing.
content: Freshly crowned China Open champion Zheng Qinwen withdrew on Monday from her home tournament in Wuhan, citing fatigue and a right shoulder injury. Zheng became the first Chinese player to clinch the Beijing title on Sunday by defeating reigning Roland Garros champion Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 in the final. It was Zheng’s first WTA 1000-level triumph and her first title since winning Tokyo two years ago. “I’m very sorry to share that I will be withdrawing from this year’s Wuhan Open,” Zheng said in a statement. “Wuhan is where my tennis dream began, and the Wuhan Open is also where I made my breakthrough at the WTA 1000 level. I have always looked forward to competing in front of my hometown fans. “Since returning from injury, however, I have played a demanding stretch of tennis over the past month and a half, competing at the US Open, the Billie Jean King Cup and the China Open. “My body is feeling very fatigued after this intense run of matches.” An Olympic gold medallist in Paris 2024 and a former world No 4, Zheng underwent elbow surgery last year and missed nearly eight months of action, dropping as low as 160 in the rankings this season. The 24-year-old has enjoyed a resurgence over the past few weeks, however, reaching the US Open quarter-finals before lifting the trophy in Beijing. “Now, at 24, I’ve become more mature. I am mentally more stable than I used to be. When I am making choices on and off the court, I am more clear-minded,” she said. “I want to be a more aggressive player. It has always been my dream and ambition.” Zheng also said there is still more to come. “If not for the surgery, I could keep going higher. The surgery stopped my progress somehow. I have to start from zero again. I really want to see what I can do in the future,” she said. Zheng added that the setbacks had given her a deeper appreciation of every victory. “There have been many chapters going through this journey. I just didn’t expect that the lows this time continued that long. That is why I treasure the opportunities now. I know how much effort I have made behind each win. “Honestly, I’m eager to know what’s going to come next in my career,” she said. “Tennis is a beautiful sport. I don’t want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis.” She is now ranked back among the world’s top 25 but will not pick up any points in Wuhan, which kicks off Monday and ends on Sunday. Beijing runner-up Andreeva has also withdrawn from Wuhan, citing a change of schedule, as the Russian teenager looks to get some rest ahead of her first singles appearance at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells next month. Zheng and Andreeva join a growing list of high-profile Wuhan absentees that also includes world No 1 Elena Rybakina, last year’s Wuhan champion Coco Gauff and reigning Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

title: Smokescreen politics? Malaysians mock Indonesian official’s ‘we send oxygen’ haze defence
description: Some social media users question whether they are breathing imported air and ask how it would be sold.
content: Malaysians have reacted with sarcasm and disbelief to an Indonesian official’s claim that his country provides the region’s oxygen, as toxic smoke from forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan chokes neighbouring nations. Syahganda Nainggolan, head of Indonesia’s government communications agency, prompted the backlash after invoking his country’s forests when questioned on Saturday about the severe smog that has forced school closures and triggered health warnings across Malaysia and Singapore. “We don’t just send smoke; when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” he said in a widely circulated video published by Indonesian media outlet Kompas. “The oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia also comes from our forests.” On social media, users questioned whether they were breathing imported air and why Malaysia’s own forests appeared to have been forgotten. “Since when did we subscribe to oxygen from Indonesia?” one user wrote, while another asked, “So all this time I’ve been breathing imported oxygen?” Another user wondered whether the 50 ringgit (US$12) they had would cover the cost, asking, “How do they sell the oxygen? In packets, bottles or by weight?” Some people identifying themselves as Indonesian also criticised the remarks, apologising to their neighbours and urging commenters to distinguish officials from ordinary citizens. “As an Indonesian, I’m deeply embarrassed by some of the reckless and irresponsible statements made by our public officials,” one user wrote. Another wrote, “I’m Indonesian … so embarrassed to have an official like this … if you’re wrong, just apologise.” Malaysia’s Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Sunday that the country had offered a firefighting aircraft, three helicopters and personnel, but was still awaiting a response to letters from its disaster agency and foreign ministry. “We assume in good faith that perhaps they do not need our assistance,” he told local reporters. He said any consideration of legal action would be left to the attorney general, while favouring cooperation through the regional Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Schools in several Malaysian states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya were ordered to close on Friday as air quality deteriorated. By 10am on Monday, 23 areas nationwide recorded unhealthy air, according to Malaysian state news agency Bernama. The southern state of Johor was the worst affected, with one of its towns, Kota Tinggi, registering the highest Air Pollutant Index reading at 170. Seven stations in Johor were in the unhealthy range, alongside areas in Negeri Sembilan, Pahang, Terengganu, Melaka, Selangor and Sarawak, as well as Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya. Readings from 101 to 200 are classified as unhealthy. Singapore’s 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index ranged from 104 to 147 at 1pm on Monday, placing all five regions in the unhealthy category, AsiaOne reported. Indonesia said bilateral discussions were continuing, with its foreign minister reporting that more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed against the fires, Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported. The country is home to the world’s third-largest expanse of tropical rainforest and its largest tropical peatland area, according to the World Bank, which has documented how draining peat swamps for agriculture leaves them vulnerable to fires that are difficult to extinguish. Several commenters challenged Syahganda’s oxygen claim by pointing to marine life. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates that roughly half of Earth’s oxygen production comes from the ocean, largely through photosynthetic plankton. Most oxygen people breathe, however, comes from atmospheric reserves accumulated over hundreds of millions of years. Syahganda’s remarks echoed another controversial comment made by then Indonesian vice-president Jusuf Kalla in 2015 during a previous haze crisis. “For 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us,” Jusuf said. “They have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset.” One social media user questioned whether the same logic meant someone whose house caught fire should be grateful for free heating. “Pak Menteri, this is a public health issue, not a buy-one-free-one promotion,” the user wrote, addressing the official as “Mr Minister”.

title: Meet Emily Markus, who just married Rob Lowe’s son Matthew in a star-studded ceremony
description: The couple’s wedding ceremony was officiated by Gwyneth Paltrow, in the presence of Hollywood A-listers like Chris Pratt, Zoe Saldaña and Cameron Diaz.
content: Rob Lowe and Sheryl Berkoff’s son, Matthew Lowe, just tied the knot with Emily Markus in a star-studded wedding ceremony officiated by Gwyneth Paltrow. The wedding was held in Santa Barbara, California, on October 10 and was attended by A-listers including Katy Perry, Chris Pratt, Zoe Saldaña, Cameron Diaz and Adam Levine. Paltrow, who served as the officiant, has been a long-time friend of Rob and Berkoff, per People magazine. Rob’s brother Chad Lowe, his wife Kim Painter, and their two daughters were also in attendance. Matthew and Emily’s nuptials come on the heels of a family tragedy for Chad and Painter, whose 13-year-old daughter Fiona died by suicide in September. Here’s everything you need to know about the newlywed Emily Markus. What does Emily Markus do? Markus works as the head of social and managing director at Crown Social Agency, a social-first advertising agency based in Seattle, per her LinkedIn profile. She attended Archbishop Prendergast High School in Pennsylvania and graduated with an impressive 4.0 GPA. She went on to earn her bachelor’s degree in broadcast journalism from the University of Miami in 2017. Markus has previously worked for media companies such as BuzzFeed and ESPN. Her relationship with Matthew Lowe It’s unclear how Lowe and Markus met and how long they have been romantically involved – she first posted photos of them together on Instagram in May 2024, sharing snaps from a cute Hawaii getaway. “Hey siri, show them paradise,” Markus captioned the carousel. The couple got engaged in July 2025 and announced the news with an Instagram post featuring snaps of Lowe popping the big question. “Lord of the rings,” he jokingly captioned the post. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Malaysian PM Anwar’s new budget tackles corruption, but critics ask: is it too late?
description: Facing coalition pressure, Anwar has targeted anti-corruption in his 2027 budget, but analysts warn laws alone will not restore trust.
content: With his reformist credentials battered by coalition compromises and a looming general election, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has used his 2027 budget to launch a fresh wave of anti-corruption measures. But as his government nears its four-year mark, analysts warn that restoring public confidence will require more than additional funding and tighter legislative oversight. The measures, announced when Anwar presented Malaysia’s 2027 budget on Friday, include 1.1 billion ringgit (US$269 million) to strengthen enforcement agencies, a proposed bill to tighten oversight of government-owned entities and greater transparency in public procurement. Yet concerns persist over the independence of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC), while promised reforms – including separating the roles of the attorney general and public prosecutor – remain incomplete. Anwar, who is also finance minister, said in his budget speech that the pledges would be pursued without fear. “The most difficult reforms are those that limit our own powers,” he noted. He added that the government was drafting a Government-Owned Entities Bill to strengthen oversight of state-linked companies and statutory bodies entrusted with managing public funds and assets, aiming to prevent financial scandals that have marred previous administrations. “The bill will cover government companies and statutory bodies to prevent a recurrence of abuses such as the 1MDB scandal and the Tabung Haji and Federal Land Development Authority crises,” he said. The Government Procurement Act, due to take effect in 2027, will require greater public disclosure of government projects, including contractors and contract values. The government is also studying the establishment of a Malaysian Law Reform Commission to identify outdated legislation and legal gaps, though no timeline has been announced. But government watchdogs said such legislative measures would do little to address deeper public concerns over accountability and political meddling. “No amount of money will fix this, only political will and a genuine advancement of strengthening institutional accountability,” said Cynthia Gabriel, founder of the Centre to Combat Corruption and Cronyism (C4 Centre). She noted that while additional funding could strengthen enforcement capabilities and operations, true reform must begin by ensuring impartiality and limiting political interference. Gabriel, who also heads Environmental, Social and Governance at the law firm Halim Hong and Quek, said institutional reforms had been uneven despite Anwar’s four years in office. “Reforms have taken a step forward and often retreat two steps backwards,” she said. Gabriel cited past cases allegedly fuelled by political interference and preferential treatment, including the discharge not amounting to acquittal granted to Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi over 47 corruption charges, and the delayed release of the Tabung Haji royal inquiry report. She said political financing and freedom of information legislation were among the fundamental reforms still needed to improve financial and information transparency. “Madani [Anwar’s administration] has one more year to fulfil these, and we urge them to fast track several outstanding promises and promote institutional accountability and trust in the system,” she said. The MACC welcomed the measures in a statement on Saturday, describing them as evidence of the government’s commitment to combat corruption and strengthen governance while backing the proposal to set up the Malaysian Law Reform Commission. “As a country that prioritises progress, Malaysia must continuously update its legal framework to close loopholes and opportunities for criminal activity,” the commission said. Pressure from within The debate over Anwar’s reform programme has exposed growing tensions within his governing coalition, particularly with the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key component of Pakatan Harapan. In February, senior DAP leaders Anthony Loke and Gobind Singh Deo, both federal ministers, called for a royal commission of inquiry into allegations involving the MACC after a Bloomberg report alleged anti-corruption officers were part of a “corporate mafia” scheme to intimidate executives and facilitate company takeovers. DAP leaders argued that the government response – including establishing a special task force to investigate the claims – was insufficient to address concerns about the anti-corruption body and its former commissioner, Azam Baki. In September, the DAP pushed for two constitutional reform items to be debated in parliament: separating the attorney general’s prosecutorial powers and limiting the prime minister’s tenure. However, the DAP pushed back against calls for snap elections, arguing that the government should use the remainder of its mandate to fulfil its reform pledges. In his budget speech, Anwar said the proposed ministerial term limit failed to secure the required two-thirds parliamentary majority, but noted that efforts to separate prosecutorial powers had been examined in-depth. Experts say Anwar must deliver four core institutional reforms pledged earlier this year: a 10-year limit on prime ministerial tenure, separating the attorney general and public prosecutor roles and introducing freedom of information and ombudsman laws. “If he can deliver all the promises with the new ones announced in this budget, he would be the most reformist PM Malaysia has ever had,” said Sunway University political scientist Professor Wong Chin Huat. “Even if he is just a one-term PM, it would be his legacy,” Wong said, adding that failure to deliver could expose Anwar to accusations from both the opposition and coalition partners of making unfulfillable promises. Analysts note that Anwar has already lost political capital among voters expecting faster reforms, partly because managing a broad coalition required compromises. Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at government affairs consultancy BowerGroupAsia, said anti-corruption remained a crucial issue for urban, professional voters, but the key test was whether Anwar could deliver before the next general election. “There is a clear need for him to reassert his reformist identity and realign PH towards what had always been its true north,” he said, adding that the public would prefer to see these reforms implemented in the coming year rather than pushed onto PH’s next election manifesto. Wong added that reforms and economic concerns should not be viewed as competing priorities. “Reforms and anti-corruption and bread-and-butter issues are not a trade-off. They can go hand in hand,” he said.

title: Opinion | Cheap debt is not enough to get China’s homebuyers spending again
description: Policymakers should put more fiscal resources towards absorbing excess housing supply and restoring buyers’ confidence.
content: After repeated attempts to arrest the protracted slump in the property sector, Chinese policymakers are trying a new inducement: paying part of homebuyers’ mortgage interest. A new programme, announced in late September, offers eligible first-time buyers subsidies of one percentage point of the interest rate of mortgage loans issued by banks for up to five years, provided they take out a mortgage during the next 12 months. The offer might bring forward some purchases but it won’t deliver the sustained recovery Beijing wants because households are increasingly reluctant to borrow at all. Despite repeated mortgage rate cuts, people remain adamant about reducing the debt they are carrying. By the end of June, outstanding household mortgages had fallen year on year for 13 consecutive quarters as repayments continued to outpace new borrowing. Part of the decline in mortgage borrowing reflects a shrinking housing market. Home prices have been falling steadily since the residential property market reached its peak in 2021 – reportedly by half in some cities – so buyers also need smaller loans. Even among those who are still buying, taking out a mortgage to purchase a depreciating asset is becoming harder to justify. In Guangzhou, the share of purchases financed with mortgages reportedly fell from 45.1 per cent to 35.6 per cent from June to August. In Shenzhen, more than a quarter of existing home transactions in the first half of the year were paid for entirely in cash, up 6.3 percentage points from a year earlier. Those who cannot afford to pay in full are making larger down payments to keep down future interest costs. In other words, Chinese households increasingly want the home without the debt, a preference reflecting doubts about both future income and property values. The arithmetic is easy to follow. During the property boom, borrowing to buy made sense: it secured today’s price, while tomorrow’s gains could more than cover the interest. Falling prices have turned that calculation on its head. Waiting now offers the prospect of a better deal, while taking out a mortgage means locking in a loss on the property while paying the bank for that privilege. The mortgage subsidy programme follows an approach evident elsewhere in China’s efforts to revive domestic demand. For more than two years, Beijing has offered rounds of subsidies for households to replace cars, appliances and electronics – with mixed and diminishing success. Since last September, it has also subsidised interest on personal consumer loans. Tellingly, the subsidies have not stopped consumer credit from shrinking. Both short- and medium-to-long-term consumer loan balances fell in the first half of this year, declining by more than 1 trillion yuan (US$149.4 billion) combined. Beijing deserves credit for committing fiscal resources to the housing slump, which is something it has long been reluctant to do. Policymakers have had to weigh the need to contain the downturn against the risk of prolonging the economy’s dependence on property-led growth. For better or worse, the calculus now appears to be shifting towards immediate relief. Unfortunately, by reaching for subsidies, Beijing risks pushing on a string. A discount or a cheaper loan might be enough to persuade the average household to replace an ageing refrigerator or buy an electric car, but financing a mortgage requires confidence in earnings across much of a working life. Five years of cheaper interest offers little reassurance to those unsure they can afford the debt in the first place. After all, a home is more than a consumer purchase. It is also an investment, often the largest one a household will ever make. Reviving demand therefore requires restoring buyers’ confidence in asset value, not just making debt easier to service. Since the property downturn began, rates on new commercial mortgages have fallen from roughly 5.4 per cent in 2020 to around 3 per cent this year. Down-payment requirements have been lowered and loan terms extended, yet confidence has continued to weaken. In an ongoing survey by China Index Academy, only 9 per cent of respondents in August expected home prices to rise, down from 13 per cent a year earlier. Restoring confidence will not be easy. Rather than nudging people to borrow with more credit perks, Beijing would do better to direct its limited fiscal resources towards absorbing excess housing supply – a structural source of downward price pressure. Local acquisition programmes have been under way since 2024, but their reach has been limited by weak local finances. Central funding could turbocharge those purchases, bringing supply and demand back into balance sooner. By stepping into the market as a buyer, Beijing could send an immediate signal of confidence – one that is backed by its own money. Chinese households want reassurance that home prices have found a floor. Who better to provide it than Beijing?

title: A writer’s birthday escape to Madeira blends island adventure with a lot of pampering
description: Madeira’s Portuguese lifestyle, natural swimming pools and the luxurious Reserve at the Savoy Palace make for an ultra-indulgent break.
content: By Alan Behr Wilson Fernandes takes every tight turn, steep plunge and narrow miss of parked cars like the pro that he is, driving me in his Land Rover through the back roads of the island of Madeira. We are in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, 500 miles to 600 miles (800km to 1,000km) southwest of the Portuguese mainland, but the hill-studded landscape, challenging roads and the rotating patches of functional housing, opulent villas and open terrain remind me of Saint Barthelemy, far to our west, in the Caribbean. Wilson, who is part South African, speaks excellent English. He drives me to Paul da Serra, a broad plateau, for a view from nearly 5,000 feet (1,524 metres) above just about everything. The Fanal Forest sits atop the plateau, vivid green with the native evergreen til trees that gave the island its name. In Portuguese, madeira means “wood”. Til trees can live for centuries, and some, in laurel forests such as this one, were on the island when it was discovered in 1419. We push on. After more twists and swerves, we arrive at Porto Moniz Natural Swimming Pools. Our driver explains how to use the public baths, where waves can be heard each time the ocean crests over a recess in the barrier wall, foaming and lunging into the main seawater pool. Only after I am in the pool do I decide to follow the lead of the men one-third my age who have swum to the point where the waves break into the enclosure, there to climb and sit atop the low wall until the next wave carries them off. I succeed only in landing prone on top of the concrete, and then I am tumbling and bobbing my way slowly back to the sanctuary of the lifeguard station, swallowing saltwater, only to feign a nonchalant indifference when I resurface for good. As Wilson drives me away, I text Diana Pestana, the assistant assigned to me at my hotel, The Reserve at the Savoy Palace, to confirm my dinner reservation. The Reserve is a hotel within a hotel. The luxurious Savoy Palace, part of the Savoy Signature collection, is refined. The Reserve is grand beyond all rational expectation; but this is a birthday trip, and the years have honed my ability to pamper myself to a fine cutting edge.
