My junior suite has a large deck and a plunge pool, all with a view of the town of Funchal, a small harbour and hills seemingly shaved down by the low afternoon clouds sliding through their crests. I throw off all my clothes and land in my plunge pool, swishing around like a contented goldfish. I let the warm twilight air-dry me while lying on the chaise and then slip into the satin pyjamas left for me by housekeeping. Battling the roaring Atlantic has its place, but this is travel as nature intended. Later that evening, at Nikkei, The Reserve’s Asian restaurant, chef Wellse Khadki, assisted by Ngima Sherpa, prepares six of nine tasting courses in front of those few honoured to sit at the chef’s table. A muscular afternoon is tempered by presentations of tuna sashimi, Norwegian salmon cured in Madeira wine, and A5 Wagyu beef over rice. Each course is paired with a Portuguese wine, and dessert closes the performance with a glass of Blandy’s 10 Year Old Sercial wine. Madeira was uninhabited when claimed in 1419 by captains serving Prince Henry the Navigator. It is now home to a permanent population of about 270,000 and has notes of the Caribbean way of life so close to mainland Europe, but with a tempo and temperament authentically Portuguese. As my swim shows, I think of myself as an adventurous traveller, but The Reserve, with its helpful staff, now keeps me close to home. The maid service is a masterwork in attention to detail: I don’t recall previously returning to a hotel room to find my underpants neatly folded. I spend the next morning in my private spa on my deck, take lunch at Terreiro, a contemporary, family-style Portuguese restaurant on the secluded back lawn of Savoy Palace, and then head off on foot for a visit to town. Funchal proves surprisingly vibrant for its size. The narrow roads of the countryside are replicated, seemingly in miniature. True, there are many shops with souvenirs and the inevitable restaurant street where hawkers holding photographs of indifferent dishes virtually beg passers-by to overpay, but the atmosphere is convivial, even celebratory. The Madeira Cable Car – also known as the Funchal Cable Car – takes you up the steepest incline far enough to reach the municipality above, but riding it would be too obviously prudent. In a repeat on dry land of my struggle with the ocean the day before, I lurch and sweat the last 600 feet up a road that would have made a San Francisco street appear level. When I at last reach the entrance to the castle, staff greet me warmly and explain that they are shutting the monument down for the day. This time, I know the drill: taxi back, up to the suite, clothes off and into the plunge pool of my private spa. A short time later, I am in Laurea, the hotel’s real spa – billed as the largest in the country – massaged for a soothing hour by a skilled craftswoman named Marina. It is worth noting that, for short trips and getting around, taxis are plentiful and inexpensive, but have cash at the ready, not a card. Many choose to rent cars or motorbikes, but you need to be comfortable with conditions that test a motorist’s skills. Four-wheel drive is a must. Booking a private driver and guide in advance is also recommended. The massage puts me in the right mood for my concluding feast, at Galaxia atop Savoy Palace. It is a gourmet restaurant grounded in Madeiran ingredients and traditions. I go for the Rings of Saturn tasting menu: seven courses, one for each set of the planet’s main ring groups, expertly paired with Portuguese wines (including more Blandy’s 10 Year Sercial). Back in my room, my satin PJs are perfectly laid out on the bed, where I now neatly fold the day’s clothes. I slip into the plunge pool and text Diana my breakfast order. The sky has mellowed into a tranquil black. Orange lights decorate the hills like blooming flowers. Low clouds again waft through the peaks. All is gentle and at peace.

title: Southeast Asia takes on Big Tech to protect children online
description: Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore are making platforms answerable for children’s safety – but bans can only do so much.
content:
Earlier this year, Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it.
Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age.
“He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.”
Since March, Indonesia has had some of Southeast Asia’s strictest rules governing children’s social media use.
Yet, like elsewhere in the region, such restrictions are only as effective as the systems Big Tech platforms put in place to identify underage users – and keep them out.
From Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore, governments that once merely urged platforms to protect children are now imposing rules designed to force social media companies to take responsibility.
Indonesia’s child protection regulations have already affected how social media companies operate.
In April, Meta Platforms raised the minimum age for a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account from 13 to 16 in Indonesia, with YouTube following suit later that month. Both said they would begin a phased deactivation of accounts belonging to underage users.
TikTok, the first platform to comply with the new rules, raised its minimum age to 16 on March 28. By October, it had deactivated 9 million underage accounts, Indonesia’s digital affairs minister announced on Wednesday.
And online gaming platform Roblox now scans Indonesian users’ faces to estimate their age, restricts some communication features for children and has added age-based account limitations.
Yet youngsters still seem to find ways to skirt the rules. To combat this, Indonesia’s government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments detailing how their algorithms, age-verification and ad-targeting systems protect children.
If the platforms fail to comply, the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry has finalised a sanctions mechanism that – once codified into law – would allow Indonesia to levy fines of up to 6 per cent of tech firms’ global revenue. Applied to Meta’s reported revenue for 2025, that would amount to roughly US$12 billion (HK$94.17 billion).
Such a fine would not be without precedent. In August, Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states up to US$18 billion to settle lawsuits alleging Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to make children addicted and caused them harm.
The settlement also forced sweeping changes to how teens experience the platforms, including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks and strengthened age-verification controls.
Meta has reportedly migrated some 22.5 million Indonesian platform users across to these “teen accounts”, but for the country’s government this does not go far enough.
“While we see this as progress, we still do not consider Instagram and Facebook teen accounts to be low-risk,” Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid told reporters in Jakarta on Wednesday. “They remain categorised as high-risk.”
Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online.
In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million Malaysian ringgit (HK$19.2 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives.
Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms required to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time.
The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures.
In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate.
Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to 1 million Singapore dollars (HK$6.13 million).
App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts.
Global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front.
“A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” said Unggul Sagena, head of internet access at the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network, an Indonesian digital rights organisation that advocates for internet freedom and user safety.
“Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.”
Regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US, said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations.
“Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said.

title: How China harnesses AI microdramas to shape public opinion at home and abroad
description: A profusion of content across mainland platforms weaves culture, policies, achievements and history into engaging storylines.
content: Beijing is rapidly scaling up the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to produce short-form videos and microdramas in its publicity campaigns, aligning with directives stressing technology’s role in strengthening ideological work and guiding public opinion. In contrast to sensational tropes dominating AI content across Chinese media platforms – such as Cinderella romance, rebirth for revenge and post-apocalyptic survival – a new wave of AI-generated miniseries weaves Chinese culture, policies and initiatives, developmental achievements and revolutionary history into engaging storylines. They are mostly produced by Chinese publicity authorities and official media, usually in cooperation with private production studios and digital creators. The latest example is Tie Ji De, or The Iron Remembers, an AI microdrama created by the news media centre of the People’s Liberation Army. Its first episode was released last Thursday. The series features a unit of 128 troops safeguarding a telegraph transmitter and a hand-cranked generator with their lives during the Long March, a large-scale retreat between 1934 and 1936 by the Communist Party’s Red Army to evade the ruling Kuomintang forces during the Chinese civil war. These state-backed AI productions form part of Beijing’s broader push to modernise its official messaging, leveraging emerging technologies to steer public opinion and make national narratives more engaging to audiences at home and abroad. Beijing considers the efforts vital to maintaining political stability, fostering loyalty to the leadership and reinforcing its discourse power globally – to counter Western mainstream narratives that often frame China as threatening and authoritarian. At a 2019 study session of the Politburo, the party’s top decision-making body, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged mainstream media to boldly adapt new technologies, mechanisms and models to maximise publicity outcomes. Noting that fast-evolving technologies such as 5G, big data, cloud computing and AI were driving the expansion of mobile media, Xi pointed to the need for a “mobile-first strategy”. “By leveraging mobile dissemination, mainstream media should firmly secure the strategic high ground in guiding public opinion, providing ideological orientation, transmitting culture and serving the public,” Xi said. He reiterated the message at another Politburo study session in February last year, saying authorities “must step up positive publicity and public opinion guidance and focus on using modern science and technology to enhance social governance”. In response to top-level directives on innovative publicity, local governments and official media across China have continually refreshed their dissemination toolkits to amplify the reach of state-sanctioned ideological and cultural content. These updated channels range from building proprietary mobile apps that feature media convergence to introducing immersive virtual-reality news videos and launching digital collectibles that immortalise historical news moments. Now, with generative AI technology flourishing, the spotlight has shifted to AI-generated content. China rolled out its regulations for generative AI in 2023, requiring AI-powered content to conform to “socialist core values” – 12 principles that guide individual morality and public ethics to achieve a prosperous, harmonious and modern society under party leadership. Productions like The Iron Remembers, alongside other AI videos unveiled by Chinese publicity bodies, emerged amid the country’s AI microdrama boom. According to a report from the China Netcasting Services Association in July, 367,000 microdramas debuted in the first half of this year, with over 1,500 new AI-generated series flooding the market daily, accounting for more than 74 per cent of the total. Microdramas, usually rendered in a vertical format and lasting only a few minutes each episode, gained immense popularity before generative AI was introduced to their production process. The tool can be used across all stages, from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, all the way to post-production, creating animation or live-action-style dramas. In May, the National Radio and Television Administration launched a strategy to promote the refinement, popularisation and internationalisation of microdramas. Central to this push is the goal of producing 1,000 high-quality works annually on themes like mainstream values, historical milestones and regional cultures. The broadcasting regulator has called for leveraging AI to boost efficiency, lower costs and enhance visual quality. The Iron Remembers comes ahead of the 90th anniversary of the conclusion of the Long March on October 22. This historical journey – during which Red Army troops travelled roughly 10,000km (6,200 miles) and suffered staggering casualties – has become a symbol of resilience and sacrifice that Beijing and Chinese mainstream media frequently draw upon to bolster patriotism and foster national unity. According to Chinese media reports, the telegraph transmitter and hand-cranked generator at the centre of the series were the Red Army’s only pieces of communications equipment – so vital that a reinforced company was formed exclusively to protect them throughout the Long March. The two machines are anthropomorphised with animated eyes and ears through AI, as shown in the first episode, which details the formation of the protection unit and the troops’ plan to dismantle the heavy machinery for a river crossing. Another AI miniseries, The Hidden Gambit, similarly focusing on the party’s revolutionary history, debuted in September. Based on a true spy story, the drama follows a female operative who assumes the identity of a high-ranking official to gather pivotal intelligence for the “Yangtze River crossing campaign” – a decisive battle during the civil war’s final stage. The Hidden Gambit was produced under the guidance of Anhui provincial authorities to commemorate the party’s 105th anniversary. Publicity bodies are also turning to AI microdramas to advance grass-roots policy initiatives and social governance. Unveiled in February, the AI miniseries A Story of Town was produced by Yanqing town in Beijing to promote urban civic virtue. The storyline follows A Niu, a young man who returns to his hometown to launch a business and whose uncivil daily behaviours lead to amusing mishaps. The series charts A Niu’s growth as he adopts civic virtues, from keeping fire exits clear to avoiding unauthorised flyposting. AI microdramas are also increasingly harnessed to promote traditional Chinese culture. The Queen’s Sword, an AI series from state-owned news channel China Global Television Network that debuted on October 2, showcases the Shang dynasty civilisation of 3,000 years ago – an era historically documented primarily through oracle bones and bronze artefacts. Other recent titles include Illuminating the Lamp of Spatiotemporal Connection, which debuted last Thursday, with backing from local authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province. It showcases the intangible cultural heritage of gun deng, or “rolling lantern”, through a time-travel narrative spanning the Southern Song dynasty (1127-1279), the Republic of China era (1912-1949) and modern times. These projects closely align with Beijing’s continuing call to preserve and revitalise Chinese culture, fostering cultural confidence to counterbalance foreign cultural influence. Other AI microdramas are meant to display regional development. The Ideal of a Tree, a series set in the Tibet autonomous region and released on September 30, follows a young musician travelling there to find inspiration and connect with her grandmother’s past. In the process, the musician witnesses Tibet’s progress in modernisation and ecological conservation. The storyline also highlights young people’s reinterpretation of Tibetan culture alongside inter-ethnic exchange, thereby advancing Beijing’s vision of national ethnic unity bound by shared roots and a common future. Foreign critics and human rights groups frequently accuse Beijing of pursuing forced cultural assimilation in ethnic minority regions like Tibet. Beijing has consistently rejected the accusations. Beyond these featured productions, however, the rapid boom in AI microdramas has created mounting regulatory headaches for Chinese authorities, ranging from content plagiarism to copyright infringement and unauthorised likeness usage. Meanwhile, the market’s chaotic expansion has also led to a flood of poorly produced content. Chinese media reports say that the country’s broadcasting regulator has pulled 68,000 microdramas from the web this year alone, citing content deemed harmful, vulgar, child-inappropriate or copyright-infringing. To address industry malpractice, regulators and major platforms have stepped in with stricter oversight. In July, the broadcasting regulator published formal administrative measures regarding prior approval for sensitive or high-budget series, with a rule effective from September mandating explicit labels for AI-generated content. Streaming platforms are also taking action, banning repetitive “cookie-cutter” characters while deploying automated pre-screening tools to detect copyright infringement and unauthorised likenesses before content airs. The South China Morning Post previously reported that China’s broadcasting regulator had urged greater support for live-action drama to counter the rapid rise of AI-generated content.

title: Brake-pedal failures in luxury EV put Chinese cars’ quality in regulatory spotlight
description: Viral video of broken brackets in test of car from Huawei-backed brand prompts ministry action to step up policing of quality.
content: A safety failure spotted in tests of a Chinese electric vehicle (EV) made by a Huawei Technologies-backed luxury brand has raised doubts about the cars many consumers view as a source of national pride, and prompted regulators to step up policing of quality and reliability. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, along with three other ministry-level departments, published draft rules on Saturday that would govern testing of new car models. The move came after a video released on Thursday on ByteDance-owned car-information platform Dongchedi showed that brake-pedal brackets snapped on all three Maextro V800 EVs used in a test of emergency braking from 100km/h. “A car’s brake pedal should absolutely never fail while driving,” Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said in a commentary on Sunday. Although the specifics of the failures were still under investigation, the newspaper said the incident underscored the importance of strengthened oversight over the country’s “rapidly developed” EVs. It described the ministry’s proposed rules as a vigorous response to safety risks on Chinese roads. The Maextro V800 multipurpose vehicle is one of the most expensive EV models in mainland China, with a base price of 766,000 yuan (US$114,462). Assembled by JAC, based in eastern China’s Anhui province, it was co-developed by China’s tech giant Huawei which, through its Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, supplies technology for smart driving and digital cockpits to various carmakers. The Maextro brand said in a statement on Sunday that it would address the brake pedal issue by the end of this month. In the draft rules – published on Saturday to solicit public opinion – the ministry stipulated that sufficient vetting measures, such as 30,000km (18,641 miles) of road testing, should be completed before any new model could be offered to consumers. “The Maextro issue has exacerbated consumers’ worries about car safety,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “This is yet another wake-up call to Chinese carmakers and supply-chain vendors to focus on quality, rather than intelligence.” A fatal crash of a Xiaomi EV in March 2025 raised nationwide concerns about autonomous driving technology, leading to a recall and the summoning of more than 60 carmakers to a government conference about the technology and the ways it was being marketed. Nevertheless, China’s carmakers and automotive suppliers are seen as the vanguard of EV technology and production, buoyed by government support and consumer appetite for innovation. Nearly all of the roughly 100 carmakers in China have been developing new technologies, such as self-driving systems, to lure consumers in the world’s largest automotive and EV market. In August, vice-minister of industry and information technology Xin Guobin said at a press briefing in Beijing that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures. Some innovative designs had been recklessly installed in vehicles without sufficient testing and verification, he added. Beijing is also carrying out a nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars.

title: ‘A pack of lies’: Abby Choi’s mother rejects claims Kwong family repaid her debts
description: Cheung Yin-fa says she gambled up to HK$100,000 at mahjong parlours for ‘entertainment’, but denies debts ever led to debt collectors harassing her family.
content: The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”. Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment. Wrapping up her five-day testimony in the High Court, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts. Cheung appeared emotional as she responded to the defence’s contention that Kwong, who said he had run a restaurant in mainland China and worked as a parallel betting agent in Macau, had helped repay her debts and supported her over the years. “This Kwong family of brutes repaid my debts? Impossible,” she said. “How can he tell such a lie? Is he human? It’s all a pack of lies.” She also denied ever receiving HK$7.5 million from Kwong through a luxury watch company, saying the money was simply a return of funds she had given him via a currency exchange shop. Kwong, 31, is accused of conspiring with his father and elder brother to murder his ex-wife after parts of the 28-year-old’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were found at a flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village in February 2023. He is standing trial on a joint murder charge alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has pleaded not guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, while his two sons pleaded guilty to that charge before the trial. Prosecutors argue the family feud stemmed from the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin. The father, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the luxury home and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so that he could keep it. Under cross-examination, Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, said his client did not oppose the sale and had been asked by Choi to persuade his father to sign a power of attorney allowing her to negotiate with prospective buyers. Cheung reiterated that the entire Kwong family had been reluctant to sell the flat until she threatened legal action. Raffell cited a series of text conversations that he said showed Alex Kwong had previously given his former mother-in-law more than HK$500,000. Cheung rejected that interpretation, saying she owed Kwong only HK$150,000 for shopping expenses. She added that he had given her daughter HK$370,000 in profit from the sale of a car that his ex-wife had bought. On her gambling habits, Cheung acknowledged that she occasionally visited mahjong parlours with friends and gambled up to HK$100,000 for “entertainment”, but stressed she had never run up debts so severe that debt collectors harassed her family. Raffell suggested that Choi helped her mother clear her debts by taking out a second mortgage of up to HK$4 million from a high-rise property at the Manhattan Hill residential estate in Lai Chi Kok, which she received from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, as a wedding gift. The counsel noted that the white Toyota Alphard that Cheung had been using to travel to court in the present case was splashed with red paint in February this year, which he said was indicative of her financial difficulties. Messaging records showed that Cheung complained to Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, the chief investigating officer of the murder case, that she had been harassed by a woman she met in a mahjong parlour in Mong Kok over a monetary dispute she thought had been resolved seven years ago. Raffell also highlighted text exchanges between Cheung and Choi, in which the witness acknowledged she would occasionally play mahjong “till daybreak” and that what she owed her daughter “cannot even be repaid in this life”. Cheung dismissed Alex Kwong’s contention as smearing and stressed she did not have any outstanding debt. She also denied that her gratitude towards Choi was because she had repaid her gambling debts, saying she was simply thankful for her daughter’s support. Raffell suggested that Alex Kwong had co-owned a restaurant in Guangzhou and knew an agent who sold Richard Mille watches in Macau. Cheung admitted she had no direct knowledge of her former son-in-law’s income, apart from what Choi had told her about his failure to contribute to the support of their two children. Separately, Raffell argued that his client had been angry with Cheung for calling police after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023, despite knowing that he was wanted over his role in a HK$6.3 million theft case after jumping bail in 2015. Cheung said she was unaware that authorities were still pursuing her former in-law. She reiterated that she believed the matter had been “settled” by Kwong Kau years before Choi’s killing. During re-examination, prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC sought to counter the defence’s suggestion that Cheung’s family was not as wealthy as she had claimed. She asked Cheung to explain the jewellery and luxury items she had worn or brought to court during her week-long testimony. They included a luxury watch set with diamonds and rubies, a pair of bracelets, a diamond necklace and a pair of earrings. Cheung said the valuables – excluding the watch, which was a gift from Choi – were worth at least HK$1 million. She added that the handbag she carried to court on Monday was worth about HK$50,000, while another Hermes Birkin bag she had previously brought to court had been bought by Alex Kwong for more than HK$100,000 using her money. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Beijing police detain Yiren Digital chairman after massive product defaults
description: Authorities launch a criminal investigation into firm after defaults.
content: Police in China have detained a controller of Yiren Digital, a US-listed Chinese digital lender, after two related investment platforms failed to repay mainland investors for over four months. The Beijing Municipal Public Security Bureau said that it had recently launched an official criminal investigation into relevant companies associated with CreditEase over suspected illegal activities and had arrested controllers, including a 53-year-old male with the surname Tang and a 51-year-old female surnamed Zhao, according to a notice on Monday. In 2015, Yiren went public on the New York Stock Exchange as a consumer loan arm of CreditEase, which was established in 2006. Tang Ning is the founder and controlling shareholder of both CreditEase and Yiren. The notice came one day after CreditEase announced “a material default” on fixed-income-like products on two of its asset management platforms, after deciding to fully suspend repayments on the products on May 22. The firm attributed the decision to the scale-down and underperformance of inclusive finance and wealth management businesses. “The group may be balance-sheet insolvent, facing a significant debt shortfall,” CreditEase told high-net-worth investors in a note on Sunday, after failing to dispose of “poor quality” underlying assets in the markets. No official disclosure on the repayment scale was given so far, though the outstanding amount was estimated to be between 30 billion yuan (US$4.5 billion) and 50 billion yuan, according to Chinese media reports. Following media reports on CreditEase in May, Yiren said in a statement that it was an independent company with a separate management team and operations from its controlling shareholder. It confirmed the defaulted products were offered by “affiliates of the company’s controlling shareholder”. In Yiren’s second-quarter results released at the end of September, Tang said the firm maintained “a disciplined approach” to the credit solution business and saw an “improvement” in later-stage delinquency rates. Yiren did not immediately respond to the request for comments from the South China Morning Post. Controllers Tang and Zhao were subjected to mandatory criminal measures, Beijing police said on Monday, adding that affected investors could report their cases for the investigation and asset recovery. CreditEase said on Sunday that it remained committed to addressing the risks associated with fixed-income-like products in accordance with the law and expediting a fair payout to investors, while maintaining stable operations in loan-facilitation and other licensed businesses. It said it would attempt to accelerate the recovery of non-performing loans and the liquidation of valuable assets.

title: Singapore tops global air pollution ranks again, rolls out haze subsidies
description: Both the city state and Malaysia are grappling with persistently unhealthy air quality due to fires in nearby Indonesia.
content: Singapore again ranked as the world’s most polluted city on Monday, according to Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir, as the fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands – intensified by a turbocharged El Nino weather phenomenon – keep emitting toxic haze. The city state has rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment and schools were closed in parts of neighbouring Malaysia, as both countries grapple with persistently unhealthy air quality due to fires in nearby Indonesia. The fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses. In Singapore, the government activated schemes on Monday that allow citizens to receive affordable care for haze-related conditions. The subsidies cover conditions including “allergic rhinitis, asthma, bronchitis, conjunctivitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, upper respiratory tract infection and their complications”, the health ministry said in a statement late on Sunday. Treatment is capped at S$10 (US$7.80) for most eligible Singaporeans, and S$5 for senior citizens aged 67 and above. The city state last activated its haze subsidy scheme in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian forest fires cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks, driving up illnesses and leading to school closures and flight cancellations. In neighbouring Malaysia, schools reopened on Monday in most areas as air quality improved slightly, but remained closed across southern Johor state and parts of the capital Kuala Lumpur and central Selangor state. Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but the fires have intensified this year because of El Nino, set to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago. Experts have also pointed to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape. The transboundary haze has also disrupted regional travel. Malaysian low-cost carrier Firefly cancelled flights between Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport near Kuala Lumpur and Singapore’s Seletar Airport from Saturday to Monday as a “precautionary safety measure”, the airline said. “Given the evolving weather situation, Firefly is monitoring developments closely. Further updates on flight schedules will be communicated directly to affected customers,” Firefly said in a statement on social media.

title: DeepSeek’s cost-saving AI may lead to inaccuracy in model performance: research
description: In one example, adding irrelevant text before the same piece of computer code impaired DeepSeek’s ability to choose the correct answer.
content: New research has exposed a potential flaw in the memory-saving technology underpinning DeepSeek’s models, marking a rare challenge to a breakthrough that has helped the Chinese artificial intelligence lab close the gap with US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic with its low-cost approach. The findings were published late last month in a paper led by researchers from ByteDance and co-authors affiliated with Princeton University, Stanford University and the University of California, Berkeley. The study, which has not been peer-reviewed, said that DeepSeek’s efforts to reduce the memory needed to process lengthy inputs may come at the expense of reliability, as the models were more likely to miss the same information when it appeared in certain positions in a document. “The phenomenon appears in DeepSeek-V4, V4.1, and all compressed models we pretrained,” the paper said. The researchers tested several DeepSeek models on their ability to retrieve information from lengthy contexts of about 128,000 tokens – equivalent to roughly tens of thousands of words. They found that the retrieval accuracy of the flagship DeepSeek-V4 family of models can differ by up to 40 percentage points. They attributed the fluctuations to how DeepSeek groups and compresses information before storing it for later retrieval. While the technique saves memory, it can also make certain details harder to recover depending on where they fall within the compressed segments. In one example, adding irrelevant text before the same piece of computer code impaired DeepSeek’s ability to choose the correct answer, illustrating how seemingly minor changes to an input could affect its performance. The researchers cautioned that their findings were based on controlled experiments and a limited number of coding examples, rather than a comprehensive assessment of how frequently the problem affects real-world applications. DeepSeek and ByteDance did not respond to requests for comment. DeepSeek has made cost-efficiency a central selling point of its technology, an approach that helped propel the Hangzhou-based company to international prominence as it challenged assumptions about the enormous computing resources required to develop competitive AI systems. Such improvements are particularly significant for Chinese AI developers, which face restrictions on access to advanced US semiconductors and growing pressure to deliver competitive performance with more limited computing resources. But as developers compete to make their models both more capable and less expensive to operate, the findings highlight a challenge in balancing efficiency with reliability, particularly for applications requiring accurate retrieval of information from lengthy documents or software code. Additional reporting by Ben Jiang

title: Beijing sanctions Paraguayan and Belizean ministers over support for Taiwan
description: Belize has signed a diplomatic training deal with Taipei this year, while Paraguay has started a data centre investment project.
content: Beijing on Monday sanctioned Paraguayan and Belizean government ministers over the Taiwan issue, after the two nations sealed deals with Taipei in recent months. Gustavo Villate, Paraguay’s minister of information and communication technologies, and Francis Fonseca, Belize’s minister of foreign affairs, foreign trade, education, culture, science and technology, were placed under sanctions from Monday, the foreign ministry said. The measures include freezing their assets within China, prohibiting Chinese entities and individuals from transacting or cooperating with the pair, and denying them entry to China, including to Hong Kong and Macau, it added. The foreign ministry issued two separate statements on Monday morning, accusing the pair of “obstinately supporting … so-called diplomatic ties with China’s Taiwan region” out of self-interest. Belize and Paraguay are among the 12 countries that currently maintain diplomatic relations with Taipei. The measures under China’s anti-foreign sanction law aimed to “safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests, and to oppose separatist activities”, the statements added. “These politicians in Paraguay and Belize have acted as pawns for the Taiwan authorities’ attempt to ‘seek independence by relying on foreign forces’, making visits to Taiwan and receiving ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said later on Monday. Mao also accused “some officials” of smearing Beijing by spreading false claims about alleged cyberattacks by China. Villate’s ministry and the US embassy in Paraguay issued a statement in July saying a joint cybersecurity review found that multiple “threat actors” linked to the Chinese government had breached Paraguayan state systems. Beijing rejected the accusation at the time, labelling it “slander”. Mao also emphasised that the Taiwan issue was “the core of China’s core interests”. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In late September, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize and met with Fonseca. The two sides signed a bilateral agreement on diplomatic training to improve the professional development of Belize’s foreign service sector. Taiwan plans to invest in a US$200 million data centre in Paraguay that is expected to be operational by the end of 2027. Villate praised the plan in May, saying he hoped to use this project to build Paraguay into a regional technology hub. The country is Taiwan’s only ally in South America. On Saturday, when delivering his annual Double Tenth address marking the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te highlighted the island’s diplomatic progress. Beijing accused Lai of “stubbornly clinging” to a “separatist mindset” and playing up the alleged “mainland threat”. Lai’s speech incited cross-strait confrontation and undermined peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, said Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office. She said Beijing would resolutely crack down on separatist forces and oppose interference by external forces.

title: Australian man rejects UAE links to Flydubai cockpit attack: ‘false accusations’
description: Islamic centre chief decries claims the Flydubai co-pilot was radicalised at his organisation in Melbourne.
content: A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a Flydubai jet has hit out at “false accusations”. The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from al-Qaeda’s September 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”, according to the Emirati prosecutor’s findings published by state media last week. The prosecutor said the co-pilot first became radicalised while studying in Australia “through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks”. The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organisation known as “My Centre” managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza. Neither “My Centre” nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing. In a video posted on social media, Abu Hamza – also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi – struck back at what he called “false accusations”. “Right through the ages … those who’re righteous, they’ve always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned – and this is the way it is,” he said. “The best thing sometimes is not to say anything,” he added. “They’re going to continue accusing you … making false accusations.” He did not comment directly on the UAE prosecutor’s claims. During the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help. Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board “noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner”, according to the findings. After gaining entry, he “intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect”. The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. Police and intelligence services in Australia have said they are investigating the man’s links to the country. Police in New Zealand said last week he had spent time in the country on a six-month student visa, where he completed a portion of his flight training, national broadcaster RNZ said.

title: Goldman Sachs president urges market reforms to boost Shanghai as financial hub
description: Wall Street executive John Waldron urges clearer rules, fewer restrictions on data flow to build Shanghai into top financial hub.
content: Goldman Sachs president John Waldron has called on China to loosen foreign exchange rules, ease cross-border data restrictions and improve regulatory transparency as the country’s policymakers seek to strengthen Shanghai’s role as an international financial centre. Waldron, also the investment bank’s chief operating officer and widely seen as a front runner to succeed its current CEO David Solomon, expressed confidence in the city’s potential at an annual meeting of business leaders advising the Shanghai government. “Shanghai has an enormous opportunity to become a leading global capital market centre,” Waldron said at the 38th International Business Leaders’ Advisory Council meeting on Sunday. “Transparency, predictability and consistency are the three most important things that generate confidence in global investors … to allocate capital to this marketplace versus other global opportunities.” Responding to Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming’s question about bottlenecks to expanding cross-border and offshore financial services amid the city’s push to improve its standing as an international financial centre, Waldron pointed to a set of regulatory steps. “[This includes] clear guidance on overseas financing structures, stronger safeguards on inward and outward investment [and] being very clear and prescriptive about what those safeguards are,” he said. He also pointed to “restructuring foreign exchange regulations and simplifying capital account opening”, noting that “one of the challenges in the Chinese market is the capital account and the flow of capital into and out of the country.” Making it easier and more seamless for global talent to live and work in Shanghai is something that’s very important John Waldron, Goldman Sachs Regulators should also reform stock market ownership rules – some of which Waldron said constrained the market’s capacity to raise capital – and expedite reviews of initial public offerings, secondary equity transactions and other capital market offerings to bring the pace of capital formation closer to global standards. He also suggested assessing foreign financial institutions based on their global resources, rather than just their local entities, during regulatory and licensing reviews, saying this would give global firms greater confidence to allocate capital to the city. On Friday, Waldron met China’s Vice-Minister of Finance Liao Min in Beijing, where the two “exchanged views on China-US economic and trade relations and the two countries’ macroeconomic situations”, according to the ministry. During the Sunday meeting, Waldron also called on Shanghai to facilitate cross-border data flow and expand its pilot programme for cross-border data transfers in the Lingang New Area, a special area within the Shanghai free-trade zone. Restrictions on cross-border data transfers could create “information silos”, preventing Shanghai-based teams at Chinese companies that rely on global risk control and IT platforms from fully leveraging their organisations’ global capabilities, he noted. Waldron also urged Shanghai to make the city more attractive to international professionals by, among other measures, simplifying visa applications and establishing mutual recognition of professional qualifications and management experience for senior executives. He said Shanghai was well positioned to become a leading destination for global talent, noting that it was a city “where executives would ... be happy to live”. “Making it easier and more seamless for global talent to live and work in Shanghai is something that’s very important,” he added.

title: Adidas CEO taps outdoor sport, street dance as new China growth drivers in fierce market
description: The German company has pledged to open new stores and strengthen its e-commerce presence in China while catering to emerging youth trends.
content: German sportswear giant Adidas is bent on new fashionable outdoor and street dance apparel to sustain its growth in China amid heightened competition against domestic and international rivals, according to its CEO Bjorn Gulden. “We see that there’s a running boom and an outdoor boom [in China],” he told reporters in a media briefing in Shanghai on Sunday. “We see new sports like street dance [becoming] new activities that look to be relevant for the young people in the universities.” He said Adidas would continue to open new stores and strengthen its e-commerce operations in China to consolidate its foothold in the world’s second-largest economy. The German company, jostling against a clutch of rivals such as Nike, Puma, Anta and Xtep, reported a 13 per cent year-on-year sales jump in China in 2025 to US$4.2 billion. In comparison, Nike’s revenue in China slumped 12 per cent to US$5.85 billion. During the first six months of 2026, Adidas saw sales rise by 16 per cent year on year in China, the company said in its half-year earnings report in July. “Whatever trends we see, it will be up to us to support the businesses and the brands,” Gulden said. “I personally hope that we can see more kids doing sports.” The CEO was speaking on the sidelines of the annual International Business Leaders’ Advisory Council meeting in Shanghai. Adidas has been looking to rebuild its running business to fight against brands including Hoka, On and Brooks. In July, the company rebranded its 15-year-old Terrex line in China as Shanchuanli, which means “among the mountains and rivers”, while designing a new logo to promote its outdoor apparel sales. China’s outdoor apparel market climbed by 17 per cent to 143 billion yuan (US$21.4 billion) in 2025, according to Kung Fu Data, an e-commerce and digital marketing firm. International companies were the front runners in the China’s sportswear market before 2021, with Nike and Adidas each holding a substantial portion of the pie. But leading domestic players have made huge strides and have leapfrogged the international giants. Anta Sports leapfrogged Nike to become the largest sportswear company in China by sales in 2021. Its revenue in China reached US$11.2 billion last year, up 13.5 per cent from 2024. Anta has completed a string of acquisitions and investments around the globe since 2018. The company, based in southeastern China’s Fujian province, owns a multi-brand portfolio including international brands such as Fila, Salomon, Descente, Jack Wolfskin and Arc’teryx.

title: US can choose to deport Hongkongers under Deferred Enforced Departure scheme
description: Department of Homeland Security issues warning after Politico report states dozen of city residents under programme had been detained at airports.
content: US authorities could deport Hong Kong residents granted extended stay under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme and have not ruled out the option of doing so after a dozen were reportedly detained at local airports. “The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is not precluded from placing aliens with such temporary administrative designation into removal proceedings, nor is it currently removing them,” a department spokesman said in a reply to the South China Morning Post on Sunday evening. “Work authorisation or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States.” The remarks followed a report by US media outlet Politico that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents had detained at least a dozen Hong Kong residents under the DED programme at local airports. The DED programme – extended in 2025 until February 5, 2027, by then-US president Joe Biden – is an executive measure that protects Hongkongers from deportation and allows them to continue living and working in the country beyond the expiry of their visas. According to Politico, the Hongkongers were threatened with indefinite detention unless they agreed to be deported voluntarily and were held for periods ranging from 10 days to two months. Courts have since ordered the release of the detained residents, but they were required to wear ankle monitors and were restricted from travelling outside their immediate area. The move came amid the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown. Responding to queries from the SCMP, the department stressed that illegal aliens were not welcome in the country and that anyone who broke the law would face consequences. It added that authorities would no longer tolerate illegal aliens travelling freely within the US and were working diligently to ensure that they could no longer board flights unless departing the country as part of deportation proceedings. But the DHS declined to comment about claims by human rights groups that the Trump administration did not intend to extend the DED protection for Hongkongers. The department earlier estimated that 3,860 Hong Kong residents were eligible for the DED in March 2021. The Biden administration introduced the programme in August 2021 in response to Beijing’s promulgation of the national security law in Hong Kong the previous year. The US extended the measure by two years in 2023. Willis Fu Yiu-wai, a senior immigration consultant at Goldmax Associates, said he had handled several cases involving people under DED protection who sought to apply for US immigration visas. He noted that some had entered the US on student or visitor visas and remained under DED protection after their visas expired, while others had left Hong Kong first and stayed under the DED while seeking a pathway to permanent residency. Fu said the programme was designed only for temporary stay and that those remaining in the country would need to change their immigration status to secure permanent residency. He added that previous extensions had given Hongkongers ample time to apply for an immigrant visa. But he cautioned that as approval of immigrant visas could take years, those currently under DED protection who decided to apply only now might be unable to secure legal status before the programme expired next year. Retired Cornell University immigration law professor Stephen Yale-Loehr said that even though DED protection for Hongkongers did not expire until next year, authorities would contend the programme did not confer a legal status that could prevent such action. “Termination of DED can be challenged in court. But the Trump administration is likely to argue that it has wide discretion both to grant and terminate DED,” he said, adding that courts had previously upheld the US government’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for some countries. TPS is another humanitarian measure that offers temporary deportation protection and work authorisation to residents of areas facing conflict or natural disasters. Given the Trump administration had terminated TPS for almost all destinations, it would likely refuse to extend DED protection for Hongkongers, Yale-Loehr said. Michelle Mittelstadt, director of communications and public affairs at the Washington-based Migration Policy Institute, said the administration’s record of ending temporary protections for people from several countries under the DED and TPS programmes suggested it had little appetite to extend DED protection for Hongkongers. However, she noted that the government had not ended TPS protection for Salvadorans, suggesting there was still some leeway. US-based barrister Craig Choy Ki stressed that while DED protection was not a formal immigration status, it was intended to shield individuals from removal during the designated period. He said detained Hongkongers could seek a bond hearing before an immigration judge, appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals or challenge the lawfulness of their detention. The likelihood of deportation would depend on individual circumstances, he added, including whether they had entered and remained in the US legally and whether they had committed any criminal offences. Yale-Loehr suggested that affected Hongkongers consult an immigration lawyer about alternative ways to stay in the US, for example, by seeking employer sponsorship for a work visa or claiming asylum if they were forced to return to the city. Meanwhile, two Democratic lawmakers are pushing for the Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act, seeking to provide a pathway to green cards and ultimately citizenship for Hong Kong residents in the US currently protected under the DED programme. Their proposal drew criticism from both the Hong Kong and central governments.

title: From its Chinese architect to manga, how Asian influences abound in Los Angeles’ Lucas Museum
description: At the new Los Angeles museum designed by Beijing-born architect Ma Yansong, Asian touches are everywhere.
content: In a city known for hype-filled events, from the Oscars and Grammys to countless Hollywood premieres, the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles occupied its own stratosphere, drawing a constellation of celebrities including Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Katy Perry and Pharrell Williams. Many of the names at the museum’s September 19 grand opening were there to wish founder George Lucas, creator of the sprawling Star Wars franchise, and his wife, Mellody Hobson, well. But celebrity wattage aside, the 300,000 sq ft (27,000 square metre) museum is a jaw-dropping achievement: a sweeping, futuristic structure conceived by Chinese architect Ma Yansong and a striking new addition to the downtown Los Angeles landscape. Ma’s design uses more than 1,200 curved fibreglass-reinforced polymer panels that make it look like a levitating spaceship, integrating a tree-covered roof and an elliptical oculus allowing natural sunlight to stream into the ground-level entry. That a China-born architect shaped the building that houses this collection is fitting, because the story inside is very much a global one. Before visitors reach the galleries of Star Wars concept paintings and comic-book pages, they pass through a ground-floor exhibition on the history of narrative art. There, among samurai armour from the 18th century and Chinese scrolls from the 17th, the museum makes its case: telling stories through pictures is a human habit, not an American one. “The idea of narrative art has no geographical or chronological boundaries,” says Ryan Linkof, the museum’s senior curator. “It really is, in some ways, the oldest form of art. We use images to tell stories.” That philosophy, shaped by Lucas’ vision, gives Asian and Asian-American artists a foundational role here rather than a footnote. The ground-floor gallery gathers objects from across the world, including a 19th century Edo-period woodblock print of a Chinese story, a reminder of how tales travelled between cultures. “A classical Chinese story had migrated into Japan in the Edo period,” Linkof says, “and become a big part of that kind of visual culture of heroism.” South and Southeast Asian works, including Hindu and Buddhist figures, show “the global ways in which deities and gods are depicted”. Upstairs, the thread continues in the inaugural “Star Wars in Motion” exhibition, where Doug Chiang, the Taipei-born American film designer and artist who helped define the aesthetic of the Star Wars prequels, created the pod race sequences and the design of the surrounding vehicles, costumes and worlds. Chiang’s Podrace Crash captures the chaos of that sequence on the page, while his artwork featuring Darth Vader shows his command of one of the world’s most famous villains. The museum displays original artworks from its collection and reproductions made for the exhibition. The manga gallery features some of the form’s most important figures, from Osamu Tezuka, whose work includes the early days of Astro Boy, to Eiichiro Oda, creator of the long-running phenomenon One Piece. Also on view is Takashi Murakami’s sculpture Miss Ko² (Project Ko²) (1997), a work that shows how manga and anime imagery has moved from the page into the world of contemporary art. These properties, Linkof says, “have become some of the most widely reproduced and circulated in the history of the world”. Of One Piece, he says: “Its reach is unbelievable. There’s really almost no comparison other than maybe Star Wars.” Many of the exhibits in the museum are part of Lucas’ 40,000-piece personal collection. Lucas has been collecting art for 50 years, but largely in an American context, Linkof says. The comics collection did not originally include manga, “even though that’s such an important tradition, that has so many parallels with American and European comics. “So that’s been an area where we’ve been collecting over the last year or so, to really build that out,” he says. “Asian and Asian-American artists were also just really important to a lot of these forms,” Linkof says, citing Jim Lee, the Korean-American comic book artist who is president, publisher and chief creative officer of DC Comics. “He’s profoundly important to the history of comics in the past 30 years.” The same goes for Alfredo Alcala, the Filipino artist Linkof describes as “important and prodigious”, who is represented in both the children’s illustration and comics galleries. While the museum has a “something-for-everyone” appeal, its curators also wanted it to welcome artists who have not yet been discovered. “We really are a museum that platforms artists who really haven’t had an institutional space, in a way that has championed them,” Linkof says. “There are a lot of artists whose art most museums either don’t collect or might have one or two examples of. But we have really robust holdings.” He encourages visitors, who have been able to explore the museum since its public opening on September 22, to wander freely: to drop in and out of the two cinemas that show films on a loop, the library, the viewing terraces and the exhibition spaces. “There’s no prescribed path of the museum,” he says. “There can be as many reactions to this place as there are people who come to see it. But if people walk away with some understanding that images are not just passive things in the world, they are actually active agents in how we understand ourselves, that is a pretty big takeaway.”

title: Manchester City must make ‘own noise’ amid Premier League financial scandal: Maresca
description: Victory over Liverpool continued club’s perfect start to season, but guilty verdict hangs like cloud over every result.
content: Enzo Maresca said Manchester City must “make their own noise” to drown out the distraction of the guilty verdict on over 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules. In their first match since the bombshell ruling, City showed they are unfazed by the uncertainty over potential sanctions as they ignored the hostile Anfield atmosphere to beat 10-man Liverpool 3-0 on Sunday. City boss Maresca has made a flawless start to the daunting task of replacing Pep Guardiola. The Italian has won his eight games in all competitions to take City three points clear at the top of the Premier League. But the future of City’s title challenge likely rests on the outcome of the club’s appeal against the verdict of an independent commission. “It was not easy for the players after the last two or three weeks but they dealt with the situation very good,” Maresca said. “I said during the week we need to lean how to deal with the outside noise, but make our own noise, which is to win games. “Our fans were singing at the end, so the noise was from us.” City took full advantage after a red card for Liverpool’s Ryan Gravenberch on the hour mark swung the momentum their way. Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki struck in a 13-minute spell after Gravenberch’s dismissal as City won in front of a crowd at Anfield for only the second time since 2003. “To win 3-0 at Anfield is a great result for sure. In this moment all the organisation needs this kind of win,” Maresca added. “It’s good for us as a coaching staff, the players, the organisation. This kind of win is good for all the club.” Maresca also refuted suggestions that his celebrations would be tempered by the uncertainty of not knowing if the three points will ultimately matter at the end of the season. “You cannot imagine how happy I am,” he said. “I am here to try to prepare the games and win the games. Hopefully, I can speak about this situation when we win the appeal.” The defeat was Andoni Iraola’s first as Liverpool manager, but his side are now nine points off the top in ninth place. The Reds were blunted by the absence of injured trio Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo. Iraola, though, believed Liverpool were the better side until Gravenberch’s controversial exit for two quickfire yellow cards. “There were two different games. One until the red card and one from the red card until the end,” the Spaniard said. “We were the better team until the red card and they were better than us obviously after and scored the goals.”

title: Minibus driver hospitalised, 18 others injured, after collision with goods truck
description: Hong Kong police say accident occurred on Monday morning on Yuen Long-bound side of San Tin Highway.
content: A minibus driver has been hospitalised after her vehicle collided with a medium goods truck in Hong Kong, causing injuries to 18 others. Police said the accident occurred at around 9.22am on Monday, when a green minibus and a medium goods truck collided on San Tin Highway on the Yuen Long-bound side of the road near Fairview Park. According to police, nine men and 10 women were injured in the crash. The accident prompted authorities to close two lanes of the road, leading to severe traffic congestion. “Two men from the truck were injured, while the remaining injured were the driver and passengers from the minibus,” a police spokeswoman said, adding that the minibus driver was briefly trapped inside the wreckage before being rescued. She sustained injuries to her head, neck and legs, while the others had minor injuries. Photos circulating online showed that the front of the minibus was seriously damaged, with the driver’s side of the vehicle crushed and the windscreen shattered. The rear of the yellow truck was damaged on the left side, with debris scattered on the road. Several injured passengers sat on the roadside awaiting medical treatment. One was seen with a bandage on her forehead.

title: Chinese desalination plant cuts 60% energy use, turns waste brine into industrial salt
description: Technology may help to solve the global problem of discharging concentrated by-products of drinking water production into the sea.
content: A large desalination plant on Bohai Bay has achieved an energy efficiency breakthrough, slashing electricity consumption by more than half while converting millions of tonnes of toxic waste brine into high-value chemical salt. Situated in the Caofeidian industrial zone of Tangshan, Hebei province, the facility recently entered its trial production stage, the state-run Science and Technology Daily reported last month. This technology provides a viable pathway to solving the global challenge of discharging concentrated seawater into the sea, according to the report. The facility processes waste brine at a three-to-one ratio, yielding 1 tonne of refined concentrated seawater – with a salinity of 120 grams per litre – alongside 2 tonnes of fresh water. The refined brine is then piped directly to a chemical plant 50km (31 miles) away to produce soda ash, a fundamental raw material used extensively across the glass, metallurgical, papermaking, textile-dyeing and food industries. According to Zhao Lin, head of research and development at Tangshan Sanyou Group, the firm behind the innovation, the project boasts the largest scale and lowest energy consumption globally among comparable technologies. “For every 10,000 yuan (US$1,490) of value produced, the plant uses 60 per cent less electricity than conventional desalination methods,” Zhao told Science and Technology Daily. In the same report, Liu Lan, a senior engineer at the Ocean University of China in Shandong, described the large-scale resource utilisation of concentrated seawater as “unprecedented”. “This technology has completed the circular industrial chain linking seawater desalination, refined concentrated seawater and the salt chemical industry,” Liu said. The plant is the culmination of several years of collaborative research between universities and business. Within the pre-treatment facilities, insoluble impurities are first filtered from brine before the primary technical challenge begins: separating out divalent ions such as calcium, magnesium and sulphate. During high-ratio concentration, these ions precipitate rapidly, much like limescale in a kettle. This blocks pipes and damages membrane equipment, proving notoriously difficult to clear. Furthermore, the production line must retain the salt within the brine – an even steeper hurdle for both technical and economic viability. Following hundreds of trials, the research team successfully identified and resolved this critical bottleneck, according to the report. In September 2023, the Tangshan-based company officially launched its pilot plant. Operating five production lines simultaneously, the facility precisely intercepted calcium and magnesium ions – the minerals responsible for stubborn scaling – while successfully retaining a high-purity solution of sodium chloride, or common salt. The subsequent challenge was to increase the concentration, or salinity, of the waste brine from 40 to 45 grams per litre to 120 grams per litre. Traditional methods of forcing water molecules from a brine of such high concentration require immense physical pressure. According to the research team, this extreme pressure is not only highly energy-intensive but also threatens to warp or completely crush the fragile membranes used in the filtration process. To circumvent this, the team devised an innovative solution by dividing the concentration process into four distinct stages. They matched different membrane components to the specific characteristics of each stage and determined the optimum sequence for their connection. Yet, even with a theoretical framework established, scaling it for the production line presented a host of practical challenges, chief among them being the selection of ideal membrane components. Lead researcher Zhao Lin explained that the team rigorously tested products from mainstream domestic and international manufacturers. They conducted repeated comparisons and cross-verifications before ultimately selecting a domestic brand. In June this year, the entire production line was successfully integrated and the first phase of the project officially entered its commissioning stage. According to an official from the industrial zone where the facility is based, once the third phase is completed, the plant is expected to process nearly 100 million tonnes of concentrated waste seawater annually, substantially relieving the Bohai Bay of a heavy ecological burden.

title: Shares in Malaysia’s Genting tumble by most in 28 years
description: The gaming giant, which is grappling with mounting debt and falling profitability, announced fundraising plans through a rights issue.
content: Share in Genting plunged by the most in 28 years after the leisure group controlled by Malaysian billionaire Lim Kok Thay announced plans to raise about 1.25 billion ringgit (US$306 million) through a renounceable rights issue. The stock fell as much as 17 per cent to 1.56 ringgit, the biggest decline since 1998. The issue price would be fixed at a discount ranging between 25 and 30 per cent, Genting said in a bourse filing on Friday, adding that proceeds raised would be used to repay its borrowings and fund working capital. The fundraising comes as Genting grapples with mounting debt and falling profitability. The gaming giant in August reported a net loss for the second quarter, while total borrowings rose to 45.3 billion ringgit as of end June. “Our scenario analysis reveals not only minimal interest savings and de-gearing but also marked earnings-per-share and book value per share dilution,” Samuel Yin, an analyst at Maybank Investment Bank, wrote in a report. “We also cannot rule out more equity fundraising efforts or fewer dividends,” he said, downgrading the stock to sell from a buy recommendation. The exercise was concerning as it signalled that Genting might have limited success in trying to refinance its borrowings to longer dated ones, Yin added. The group’s unit Genting Malaysia fell as much as 8.1 per cent, the most in more than a year. Fitch Ratings downgraded Genting to BBB- in September on expectations of a slower pace of deleveraging due to substantial capital expenditure needed to expand key properties, including those in Singapore and New York. Last year, Genting’s Resorts World won a licence to operate a casino in New York City that is expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue.

title: Hong Kong’s workers fear AI-driven retirement disruptions, only 20% feel prepared: survey
description: Uncertainty is most pronounced among workers aged 30 to 39, with 61 per cent anticipating a rockier road to retirement, T. Rowe Price found.
content: More than half of Hong Kong’s working adults believe artificial intelligence will make their retirement path more unpredictable than previous generations, yet only one in five feel financially prepared for the shift, according to a survey by global asset manager T. Rowe Price. About 55 per cent of the 1,004 Hong Kong residents surveyed – all 30 or older and earning at least HK$15,000 (US$2,239) per month – said they expected AI-driven disruptions to destabilise their long-term career and income trajectories. Uncertainty was most pronounced among workers aged 30 to 39, with 61 per cent anticipating a rockier road to retirement, the survey found. “Retirement is becoming less of a single point in time and more of a journey,” said Raymond Chan, head of Greater China intermediary distribution at T. Rowe Price. “AI adds another layer of uncertainty because it could enable some people to work longer or more flexibly, while prompting others to reskill, reduce their hours or rethink when they retire.” Despite widespread concern, financial planning has yet to keep pace. Only 21 per cent of respondents said they were “fully” or “substantially” prepared financially should AI alter their employment, income or retirement timing. Although nearly 60 per cent estimated they would need over HK$5 million to retire with peace of mind – with 22 per cent targeting upwards of HK$10 million – just 15 per cent of respondents maintained a comprehensive retirement plan that was reviewed regularly. Initial financial planning leaned heavily towards short-term buffers rather than long-term growth. To hedge against AI risks, 43 per cent of workers have expanded their emergency cash funds, whereas only 28 per cent had adjusted their retirement investment portfolios. “Holding too much of a long-term retirement portfolio in cash can leave purchasing power vulnerable to inflation,” said Wenting Shen, Global Investment Solutions Strategist and Portfolio Manager at T. Rowe Price. “If people retire earlier, later or in stages, their investment horizon and risk needs may change too. That makes it important to have an investment framework that can adapt over time.”

title: China’s factories leaping straight into agentic AI and taking it global: Black Lake CEO
description: Manufacturers are bypassing traditional digitalisation and deploying AI agents across operations, Chinese software firm Black Lake says.
content: China’s manufacturing sector is leapfrogging straight into the era of agentic artificial intelligence and is now exporting that playbook to global supply chains, according to the CEO of Black Lake, a Chinese provider of cloud-based AI tools for factories. “Just as China skipped credit cards and jumped directly to mobile payments, many factories are skipping full traditional digitalisation and jumping directly to AI agents,” Zhou Yuxiang said in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. The shift marks a pivotal stage for China’s manufacturing sector. It was moving beyond its traditional advantages of low costs and reliable quality to compete on “agility”, deploying AI tools and agents from design to production so factories could meet small-batch and customised demand in time, Zhou said. The trend aligns with Beijing’s national “AI plus” initiative, which includes a target of integrating AI into 90 per cent of China’s economy by 2030. Shanghai-based Black Lake has launched a series of role-based agents that handle tasks ranging from design files and workflows to procurement, quality assurance, supply chain coordination, planning and scheduling, and equipment maintenance. Up to 40 per cent of those agents had reached full autonomy, making decisions under human supervision, according to Zhou. The remaining 60 per cent remained in a co-pilot stage where they helped employees make decisions faster, but Zhou said he expected them to evolve to full autonomy within 12 to 18 months through reinforcement learning based on engineering feedback. “Factories buy the solution for speed and, once embedded in the factory, the agent learns from human feedback,” he said. “Over one to two months, the agent catches up, eradicates errors and reaches parity with human capability.” For factory owners, AI agents were increasingly valued as manufacturers grappled with an ageing workforce and a shrinking pool of young workers willing to learn from veteran technicians, according to Zhou. Once software reaches full autonomy and robots operate without human supervision, that will represent the ultimate picture of future manufacturing Zhou Yuxiang, Black Lake As China’s manufacturing sector embraces agentic AI, Black Lake is exporting the playbook overseas, where demand is growing rapidly in Southeast Asia and Latin America. The firm’s overseas footprint initially stemmed from Chinese factories expanding operations in markets like Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Mexico. According to Zhou, this expansion later broadened as multinational companies using Black Lake’s technology in China replicated the system across their international operations, followed eventually by local, native factories overseas seeking to integrate Black Lake’s AI agents into their own production. “Agents are the result of industrial knowledge, skills and expertise [accumulated in] China’s industrial sector, which has been leading global manufacturing,” Zhou said. Demand for greater manufacturing agility was being fuelled by a new wave of globally successful “Made in China” brands such as Pop Mart’s Labubu, Zhou said.
