Unlike traditional mass-produced toys, Labubu products came in hundreds of distinct designs, requiring manufacturers to make rapid adjustments across their supply chains, he said. To tap into the trend, Black Lake launched Popzao in April, a platform aimed at riding on the explosion of demand from celebrities, museums and tourist attractions seeking to create merchandise even in small batches despite having little or no manufacturing experience. Popzao used AI agents to tokenise and automate processes ranging from design and 3D simulation to mould-making for clients, slashing fixed engineering costs from about 300,000 yuan (US$44,800) to 2,000 yuan in tokens, Zhou said. The model also lowered minimum order quantities from 20,000 units to just 100 units. The growing robotic deployment in manufacturing has also prompted Black Lake to deepen integration between AI agents and hardware systems. “We act as the central dispatcher and brain,” Zhou said. Robotics companies primarily targeted 70 per cent of factory work involving manual and low-skilled tasks, while AI agents addressed the remaining 30 per cent performed by high-skilled experts and engineers, Zhou said. “Once software reaches full autonomy and robots operate without human supervision, that will represent the ultimate picture of future manufacturing,” Zhou said.

title: Vacheron Constantin and The Met celebrate artisanal mastery with residency collaboration
description: Aspen Golann, Ibrahim Said and Joy Harvey, the three artists selected for the Artisan Residency programme, unveiled their creations in New York last week.
content: Transmission and mentorship are at the heart of Vacheron Constantin, the world’s oldest watchmaker to operate continuously for more than 270 years. Back in 1775 in Geneva, Switzerland, master watchmaker Jean-Marc Vacheron signed the company’s first apprenticeship contract. That legacy has continued over the decades at Vacheron Constantin’s workshops, where skilled artisans specialise in rare crafts passed down through generations: disciplines like guillochage, a decorative engraving technique, enamelling and gem-setting. The house has expanded its purview to support artisans outside the watchmaking industry, most recently through the Artisan Residency programme, in collaboration with The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York (The Met). Launched in May 2025, the initiative involved an 18‑month residency for three artisans working in traditional crafts. As part of the project, the artisans – selected after an open call and submissions from around the world – immersed themselves in The Met’s collections and archives and travelled to Vacheron Constantin’s ateliers in Switzerland. At an event hosted by Vacheron Constantin at The Met’s famous Temple of Dendur last week, the artisans unveiled the works they created during the residency. The three pieces couldn’t be more distinct. Each showcases the artists’ unique backgrounds and perspectives, as well as what they absorbed from working closely with The Met’s curatorial team and Vacheron Constantin’s craftspeople. Aspen Golann is a cabinetmaker and woodcarver based in New Hampshire. Her work draws on American furniture from past centuries. For the Artisan Residency programme, she created a monumental wooden vessel carved with a landscape depicting whimsical creatures and fantastical scenes. After discovering a series of 17th-century chests in The Met’s collection, she found blankets with crewel embroidery made by young women. The bas-relief on the vessel, named Crewel Cabinet, is a take on those patterns. “It’s this intimate object that both displays and demonstrates all of the constraints that these girls lived under,” she said of the blanket that inspired her piece. “The only time they could ever make anything was for a dowry, but it’s also full of their imaginations. And so there is this tension.” Golann was pleasantly surprised by how much freedom Vacheron Constantin gave her during the residency. “Artists are able to get funding for work that’s another version of something they’ve already made, but nobody will give you support and funding to make something that you can’t even describe or imagine, and you can’t even verbalise because it hasn’t existed before,” she said. “And that’s what this was; you could do anything basically. This work resembles nothing I’ve ever made before, and it allowed me to not just make something ambitious and new, but to build an entire new branch of my practice.” Egyptian-American ceramicist Ibrahim Said, who lives in North Carolina, makes vessels, vases and sculptures inspired by his background. His creation pays direct homage to Vacheron Constantin. His ceramic sculpture, Shaping Time, takes the form of Vacheron Constantin’s eight-pointed Maltese Cross, which the watchmaker adopted as its emblem and trademark in 1880. Said was impressed that the Maltese Cross serves both a functional and decorative role; it is not just a logo but also appears inside the timepieces’ movements. The motif is also painted on the sculpture. British-Italian goldsmith and jeweller Joy Harvey, based in the Northern Italian seaside town of Rimini, created a jewellery-like sculpture consisting of a headpiece inspired by a Hellenistic necklace from The Met’s collection. The crown is embellished with tiny gold flowers in guillochage, a technique Vacheron Constantin perfected. It sits atop a bunch of thorned stems meant to represent brambles creeping upon ancient ruins. She named her work Ruined Splendour. “It’s a topic that’s very close to my heart at the moment,” she said of the meaning behind her piece. “We’re seeing climate change and destruction all over the world for different reasons, so I wanted to bring different kinds of destruction to my practice because it’s what I’m feeling at the moment.” This is not the first time Vacheron Constantin has worked with pre-eminent cultural institutions, including The Met. As part of its Masterpiece on the Wrist project, the watchmaker offers clients the opportunity to create a bespoke timepiece with a hand-painted dial featuring a miniature reproduction of an artwork from the Louvre’s collection in Paris and The Met in New York. The Artisan Residency programme, however, marks a new chapter in the maison’s support of the arts and of young talent. No product is involved in this initiative, which celebrates creativity and innovation while exposing the world to niche crafts at risk of being lost. In a panel discussion the day after the event, Christian Selmoni, Vacheron Constantin’s style and heritage director, said he firmly believes young people are gravitating toward handicrafts. “You’d be surprised to see how the new generation is very much concerned about what I like to describe as the intelligence of the hand,” Selmoni said. “In ancient Greece, craftsmen were considered at the same level as philosophers or doctors. Then in the West, things changed, and we began to prefer the intellectual to the manual, but the good news is that it’s changing. Many young people are interested in watchmaking. One of my theories is that we live in such a digitalised world, but we’re very much analogue as humans and made of flesh and bones. It’s a kind of reaction, and we’re reconnecting with what we’re coming from as humans, and that’s why crafts are so important,” he added. The excitement around this project shows that this new-found appreciation for exceptional things – whether it’s a one-of-a-kind watch hand-engraved with a cityscape or a beautiful art piece with no function beyond aesthetics – is resonating with audiences looking for special pieces and meaningful interactions with those who make them.

title: ‘Just a little spark’: disability advocate on inclusion, belonging in Hong Kong
description: Faride Shroff, founder of SENsational Foundation, says hiring people with disabilities requires making suitable arrangements and matching skills to jobs.
content: Greater awareness of disability in Hong Kong has not necessarily made it easier for people with disabilities to find work, according to advocate Faride Shroff, who says tighter corporate budgets and a difficult job market have made the next stage of inclusion more challenging. Shroff, founder of SENsational Foundation, said employers that recruited people with disabilities also needed to provide guidance, suitable workplace arrangements and roles that matched individual strengths. “Every person has got certain skills,” she said. “It is finding those skills and matching them to the right job.” “It is definitely more difficult” to hire in the current economy, she said. “But I believe that any socially responsible company that wants to really make a difference will find a way. It is not charity, just pure business advantage.” Her work has earned her a place among the finalists for this year’s Spirit of Nurturing Award at the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. SENsational Foundation, set up in 2013, works with companies on disability awareness, mentoring and workplace accessibility. Shroff said the organisation also remained available after someone had been hired, helping employers and employees navigate any adjustments that might be needed. Funding has become another concern. Shroff said unrestricted funding, which allows NGOs to pay staff and keep programmes running, had become particularly difficult to secure as companies cut budgets and headcounts. Corporate support can take different forms. Shroff cited JLL, which has provided SENsational Foundation with workspace for several years. The foundation has also worked with companies including Swire Properties and Manulife on disability inclusion. Workplace design is another area where Shroff believes meaningful change can begin at the planning stage, rather than being treated as an afterthought. SENsational Foundation has conducted accessibility audits for companies, examining how offices and older buildings can be adapted for people with different disabilities. A ramp at the entrance, she said, was only the beginning. Modern technology can create barriers of its own. Shroff gave the example of office access systems that direct employees to a particular lift through a visual display. For someone with a visual impairment, audio instructions could make the same system usable without assistance. “Such innovations make a person with a disability more independent, instead of being disabled by society,” she said. Her approach follows a principle widely used in disability advocacy: “Nothing about us without us.” “When you want advice on being truly inclusive in a holistic way, do not assume. Ask us directly and engage with us,” Shroff said. She said SENsational Foundation had also been selected as Hong Kong’s representative for the Valuable 500, a global disability-inclusion initiative. Shroff has also seen what greater visibility can mean at an individual level. After disclosing one of her own disabilities during a university panel, she was approached by a student with the same condition, who said she would no longer be ashamed to tell others. The student grew in confidence and later began speaking on stage and working as an event master of ceremonies. “Young people need to have representation and role models who can change the way they think,” Shroff said. “That’s all they need, just a little spark.” For Shroff, the next step is to make accessibility a routine consideration in workplace design while addressing the bias and stigma that can exclude people with disabilities. “We need to think ahead and plan,” she said. “Together, we need to make everyone feel a sense of belonging in our society.”

title: Letters | As the US-China space race heats up, watch out for patent law
description: Readers discuss patent law in the US and China amid technological rivalry, and why Beijing might decide not to play by the West’s rules.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Over several decades, China has risen to become one of the most potent powers in the space race. In October 2024, China released a national mid- and long-term development programme for space science. Since then, China has made significant strides. In 2025, it conducted 92 space launch missions, representing a 35 per cent increase from 2024. Furthermore, China’s Tianwen-2 probe was the first to photograph Kamo’oalewa, a quasi-satellite of Earth. According to the World Intellectual Property Organization, China filed the most patent applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty in 2025, with the US in second place. As global collaboration intensifies, tech-sharing has become ubiquitous. Competitors may increasingly integrate Chinese-patented technologies into their infrastructure, thereby gaining an edge. This is averse to Chinese interests, particularly amid the development of the International Lunar Research Station, a collaboration between China, Russia and various developing countries. Patent law aims to incentivise innovation by rewarding inventors with time-limited monopolies on their inventions. If their rights can be easily circumvented by mere contrived geographical displacement, this may deter tech giants from patenting and investing in China. Indeed, they may turn to jurisdictions which allow for extraterritorial application of their patent law protections. Section 105 under Title 35 of the United States Code deems “any invention made, used or sold in outer space on a space object or component thereof under the jurisdiction or control of the United States” to be so “made, used or sold” within its territory, with few exceptions. “Control” is scantly defined and the ultimate arbiter remains US courts. In addition, US courts have held that an entity found to supply or cause to supply US patented invention(s) (and/or any component thereof) for combination abroad would still be liable for infringement. This dramatically elevates the value of US patents and attracts Chinese companies to patent their inventions in the US. However, the US government is permitted by law to use and manufacture sensitive technologies without patent-holders’ approval. This ultimately imperils Chinese interests. Rendering China’s patent law protections extraterritorial can preserve and instil confidence in home-grown innovators. This can galvanise national innovation and help realise its lofty aeronautical ambitions. Alexander Clevewood Ng, New York Lesson for the West from China’s Spring and Autumn period For centuries, Western industrial and military supremacy has fostered a civilisational “god complex”. This narrative hegemony has allowed the West to demonise geopolitical adversaries while shielding itself from reciprocal criticism. However, this strategy when weaponised against major powers like China and Russia risks triggering devastating consequences for global stability. A historical precedent from the Zhou dynasty’s Spring and Autumn period offers a stark warning. This era was defined by a decline in central imperial power, which hubristically insisted on acting as the sole governor of legitimacy, culture and etiquette. Meanwhile, the southern kingdom of Chu was often ridiculed by the elites of the Central Plains for its distinct language and customs. The breaking point arrived when the ruler of Chu, Xiong Qu, famously declared: “I am a barbarian; I will not adopt the titles and posthumous names of the Central Kingdoms.” This was a pivotal moment: liberated from the constraints of the central authority, Chu went on to become one of the strongest sovereign states tearing the empire apart. Today’s polarised geopolitical environment begs a similar question: when and why do nations fundamentally rebel against a Western-led, rules-based international order? What is the breaking point? For Russia, the answer crystallised after decades of structural alienation. Despite voluntarily undergoing painful capitalist shock therapy and repeatedly floating cooperative security frameworks, including reportedly putting out feelers about joining Nato, Moscow was dismissed as a mere “gas station with nuclear weapons”. The Minsk II ceasefire deal seems to have been used to buy time for Ukraine’s military build-ups rather than to achieve peace. If Russia, culturally and racially intertwined with Europe, could not negotiate an equitable seat at the table, what chance does China have? Beijing now faces a similar existential calculation. Ultimately, global statecraft is dangerously shifting from a calculation of what can be gained to a grim assessment of what is left to lose. Daniel Cheung, Mid-Levels

title: AirAsia founder denies state bailout talks despite insiders’ claims
description: Malaysia held talks as concerns mount over the airline’s financial health. Tony Fernandes insists he sought no rescue.
content: AirAsia co-founder Tony Fernandes met with officials from Malaysia’s finance ministry two weeks ago to discuss potential government support for Southeast Asia’s largest low-cost airline, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. The talks reflect growing government concerns about the financial health of the country’s largest domestic carrier following a spike in jet fuel prices, the people said. Discussions centred on the prospect of the government backing AirAsia’s fundraising efforts provided the airline agreed to proposed conditions, which remain under discussion, two of the people said. Details of the proposed conditions could ‌not immediately be determined. Just because I meet them doesn’t mean we’re talking about financial assistance Tony Fernandes, AirAsia co-founder Fernandes, speaking for the airline as its co-founder and adviser, said in an exclusive interview on Friday that he had met with officials from Malaysia’s finance and transport ministries during the week starting September 28 at his request. He said the discussions focused on aviation-related costs such as airport charges and fuel, not financial assistance. “Obviously, like every airline in the world, we are telling government that this is a tough period,” he said. “There have been no discussions on financial assistance with the government,” Fernandes added. “I meet with government officials all the time … just because I meet them doesn’t mean we’re talking about financial assistance.” He said he had not approached the government for help, and the government had not raised concerns with him about AirAsia’s funding or offered support. Fernandes said he was “100 per cent“ confident AirAsia could navigate the situation without state ⁠assistance, as it had during the Covid-19 pandemic. But Fernandes said AirAsia would not turn away help if offered from any government in the countries where it operates, including Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. “We will never say no to it. We would be ‌foolish to do so,” he said. He added that he had previously asked the government to help the airline secure loans from Malaysian banks rather than borrowing overseas, and still sought such support as he preferred local-currency loans with better interest rates and terms. Representatives from Alton Aviation Consultancy, which the finance ministry has hired to assess loss-making AirAsia’s funding ‌needs, also attended the meeting, two of the people with knowledge of the discussions said. Malaysia’s finance ministry declined to comment. Alton did not respond to requests for comment. Malaysian Transport ‌Minister Anthony Loke told a press conference on Monday that he had not had any meetings with AirAsia in the last two to three weeks, nor had other transport ministry officials. “They [AirAsia] may have had discussions ⁠with the Ministry of Finance. These airlines do have regular meetings ⁠with the government,” Loke said. His comments were made after the publication of reports about the meeting between Fernandes and the finance ministry. AirAsia shares were trading 5 per cent lower on Monday afternoon. The airline has ⁠been hit by soaring jet fuel costs that surged ⁠66 per cent in the second quarter from the prior quarter to an average of US$183 a barrel, stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran. The meeting followed a report last month that Malaysia’s government had asked Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air whether they could absorb AirAsia’s domestic market share as part of ‌scenario planning while authorities monitor the carrier’s financial health. AirAsia’s shares fell as much as 21 per cent to near four-year lows the next day. The government has grown increasingly concerned about AirAsia’s financial position because of the knock-on effects its weakness would have on air connectivity, tourism and related businesses such as state-linked ‌airport operator ‌Malaysia Airports Holdings, said two of the people. AirAsia controls about 60 per cent of Malaysia’s domestic aviation market and employs 26,000 people, according to Fernandes. The airline had cash and bank balances of 954 million ringgit (US$233.65 million) and current ‌liabilities of 18.4 billion ringgit as of June 30. The meeting with government officials followed a company town hall Fernandes held on September 28 at AirAsia’s headquarters, where he told staff that the airline would overcome its current difficulties, two of ⁠the people said. Fernandes said he had told employees it was a tough time for all airlines. “We’ve been through many tough times before. We will come out of it stronger,” he recalled saying. “The big difference between this and Covid ⁠is we can actually fly.” At a press conference on September 18, he said there had been no discussions with the government, the carrier had “strong liquidity” and “we do not need rescue, bailout, whatever”. AirAsia reported a net loss of 831 million ringgit for the second quarter ended June 30, hit by higher jet fuel costs and foreign-exchange losses of 331 million ringgit. The airline has said it is targeting ‌up to US$1 billion from international debt markets plus 700 million ‌ringgit in local credit facilities, primarily to refinance existing debt. Its stock has lost more than 70 per cent of its value this year. Fernandes said on Friday he expected the US$1 billion fundraising to be completed between December and February, with half used to refinance expensive loans and the rest for working capital and paying off “extended liabilities.” Fernandes said AirAsia was budgeting for 12 months of high oil prices and had yet to see demand weaken, with the percentage of seats filled above 80 per cent even though jet fuel prices had risen as high as US$200 a barrel. “Above US$200, it hasn’t been tested yet,” he said. “At some point, it will create demand destruction. I’m not sure where that point is.”

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ could undergo testing next typhoon season: Eric Chan
description: City’s No 2 official says system to provide ‘full picture of Hong Kong’, connecting traffic, flood monitoring, drainage and weather data.
content: Hong Kong’s artificial intelligence management system could take shape and be tested as early as the typhoon season next year, the government’s No 2 official has said, adding that the project will give authorities a “full picture” of the city once it is in full swing. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said the “AI city brain” system aimed to connect independent databases maintained by different government bodies. “With the invention of AI, I think it is a good idea to connect them together, so that we can have a full picture of Hong Kong,” he said. The data includes traffic information, flood monitoring and drainage systems, landslide warning systems, weather information and public inquiries and complaints under the 1823 hotline. “Before the typhoon season comes next year, hopefully we will add some of these warning and monitoring systems into our AI city brain,” Chan said. “We will use the government cloud as the system base, and use the Security Bureau’s Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre [EMSC] as our application scene.” Currently, the government’s different monitoring systems worked independently, Chan said. When a typhoon approaches the city, the EMSC goes into operation and representatives from different departments meet to share information. “But this is all being done manually and checked by our officers manually as well,” Chan said. “With this AI city brain, they will do it automatically by computer. It is far more accurate and faster.” He said a task force on the AI city brain would be established by the end of the year. Chan said that as task force chairman, he would work with staff from different government bodies – including the Security Bureau, the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau, the Development Bureau and the Transport and Logistics Bureau – to steer and monitor the project at a high level. He added that HK$200 million (US$25.5 million) had been earmarked for the first phase of the system, which included an upgrade to the 1823 complaint mechanism. By the first half of next year, authorities aimed to complete the AI city brain system’s basic design and start the first phase of construction. In the first quarter of 2028, the first phase of the platform’s development should be completed and officially launched, Chan added. The 1823 system would be connected in the third quarter of 2028, syncing emergency-related data such as fallen trees and flooding to the AI city brain. Under improvements to the complaint mechanism, AI would be used to determine which government unit should take the lead on complaints spanning multiple departments. “If no consensus is reached, the matter will be escalated to the deputy chief secretary for administration for a final decision,” he said. “With the launch of the AI city brain, we expect to speed up risk identification, speed up cross-department responses, and in the end, decrease the number of repeated complaints.” Chan said the platform’s AI functions would be trained using historical data from various departments to make predictions, helping the government take preventive measures. “With the addition of AI functions, it will help us to make a decision or a suggestion on whether anything should be done by a certain department,” Chan said, citing extreme weather events such as typhoons as an example. “So our aim is to hopefully prevent some accidents from happening. Even if we cannot prevent them, at least we can respond quickly to the accident.” The government previously said the AI city brain would take six to nine years before it could become fully operational. “In the future, when all systems are integrated into one, we can have this AI city brain operate round the clock, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. So it means that we can have the EMSC in operation all the time,” Chan said. “We can monitor the system not only during typhoon time, but also at all times. This is the final destination for our AI city brain.” The government cloud used as the base of the AI city brain would not involve third parties, which Chan called “very good protection”. He emphasised that all cross-department data sharing would strictly comply with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and would not involve residents’ movements or personal data. “It involves no personal data, so it involves no privacy issue,” he said. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced his administration’s plans to build an AI city brain in his policy address last month. Designed to enhance city management and strengthen emergency response capabilities, the platform will consolidate the big data of multiple government bureaus and create a real-time data-sharing environment.

title: Indonesia finds orangutans saved from wildfires a new home
description: After nine hours by car, boat and foot, eight endangered apes rescued from Indonesia’s worst fires in 11 years reached safety.
content: Indonesian authorities and conservation workers have successfully moved eight ⁠orangutans to a safe ⁠location after the endangered ⁠primates’ homes were destroyed by wildfires in the forests of Borneo. The Southeast Asian nation is battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, mainly on Sumatra and Borneo islands, and the ‌government has warned the blazes could continue until November, aggravated by the El Nino weather pattern. Three mother-child pairs and two adolescent male orangutans were among those rescued between August and September from several locations, the Indonesian government and wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI) said in a statement on Sunday. “Their ⁠relocation to Batu Nyambu protected forest is expected to give the eight orangutans a ‌chance to return to living naturally,” the statement read. Orangutans are critically endangered great apes found in the wild only on the ‌Southeast Asian islands of Borneo and Sumatra, with Indonesia home to all ⁠three recognised ⁠species, according to conservation group the WWF. Populations have declined due to deforestation, wildfires and poaching. The relocation ‌operation took six hours by car, one hour on boats, and two more hours on foot, with ‌the orangutans ‌in cages carried on bamboo poles. Before they were moved, YIARI conservationists checked ‌the animals’ health. YIARI CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the animals to a new location was a “necessary step” when their habitat was no longer safe. “Protection of habitats will always be a top priority to ensure orangutans continue to have safe forests to live in, but as long as their habitat remains threatened, rescue is one of the best options we can take to help them survive,” Sanchez said. The reserve was chosen due to availability of food and water sources as well as its connectivity to other forests, YIARI operational director Argitoe Ranting said. “We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat,” Argitoe said. Since August, the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency and YIARI ⁠have rescued 46 orangutans affected by fires, agency head Murlan Dameria Pane said. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to the WWF. Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned fires were burning in habitats containing 52 per cent of Borneo’s orangutan population. Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but the fires have intensified this year because of the El Nino weather phenomenon, set to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago. Experts have also pointed to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape. From January ⁠to July this year, fires burned around 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) in Indonesia. No official data for subsequent months has been released, but non-governmental organisations ‌estimate fires have burned ‌at least 600,000 hectares more since. Severe haze from the fires has caused 175,000 cases of respiratory illness in Indonesia, with the smog affecting neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia where many schools were closed on Friday as air quality deteriorated. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: educator who removes death’s stigma through culture
description: Joseph Lau takes students to cemeteries, funeral homes and heritage exhibitions, encouraging them to learn about culture outside the classroom.
content: Joseph Lau Yui-yip has taken students to cemeteries, funeral parlours and heritage exhibitions because he believes some parts of Hong Kong culture are best understood outside the classroom. Lau heads the student affairs department of Polytechnic University’s college of professional and continuing education and has spent years researching subjects ranging from funeral customs to a little-known Hakka animal dance. His work has put him among the finalists in the culture category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Launched in 2013, the awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed. Lau first became interested in funeral logistics through contacts with companies handling the repatriation of bodies overseas and, more often now, to the Greater Bay Area. One introduction led to another, bringing him into contact with funeral homes, cemeteries, government departments, end-of-life planners and people involved in preparing bodies for burial or cremation. That experience later entered his teaching. He has organised life-and-death exhibitions, been involved in the production of a song and music video on the subject, and taken students and the public to Gardens of Remembrance to learn about green burial. Lau said some went in thinking that the scattering of ashes looked casual and disrespectful. Once they had seen the garden, that misconception gave way. “Afterwards, they were more willing to talk to their families about what should be done,” he said. Lau believes those conversations should happen before a death, while people can still explain what they want. “Good preparation takes a weight off the family,” he said. Older people, he has found, are ready to talk. The young often refuse. “Death is not so frightening,” he said. His cultural research has also taken him into a very different field. Lau is one of the authors of a book published this summer on pixiu dance, a Hakka performance that brings out a mythical beast associated with prosperity and protection. The dance was placed on Hong Kong’s intangible cultural heritage list in 2014, but hardly anyone noticed, he noted. According to Lau, some people know the creature only as a decorative figure. Far fewer know that it was traditionally performed on occasions such as moving into a new home. The dance demands martial arts skills because the performer’s body is not concealed by a full costume. Lau and his collaborators have introduced the dance through research, exhibitions and workshops. Students have learned about it through talks and model-making classes. An exhibition has already been held in Wan Chai. Another will take place at Tai Kwun from October 30 to November 1. He is also planning workshops with the Tung Wah Group of Hospitals on death and art, to be held on the PolyU campus from 22 to 26 February next year. Lau has also organised Chinese cultural festivals and exhibitions covering traditional martial arts schools, bone-setting clinics, ceremonial craftwork and auspicious animal performances. In 2025, he received the Outstanding Senior Alumni Award from PolyU’s department of logistics and maritime studies.

title: China grass-roots singer shoots to fame after saving delayed Hacken Lee concert with 2-hour set
description: Rushing by taxi and shared bicycle to reach the stadium just in time, Hou took the stage with zero rehearsal and no teleprompter.
content: A grassroots singer in China rose to fame after standing in for Hong Kong singer Hacken Lee, giving an impromptu two-hour set after Lee was delayed. On the evening of September 26, the touring concert Hear Yourself, featuring six acclaimed singers from Hong Kong and Taiwan, was held in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, in northern China, Shenzhen TV reported. Lee was scheduled to give the grand finale performance. But he did not arrive in time because his flight, originally bound for the nearby city of Hohhot, had to land in Taiyuan, Shanxi province, due to hail. Lee and his colleagues took a taxi from Taiyuan to Baotou, a journey of 570km. Unfortunately, the electric car they were travelling in ran out of power along the way, forcing them to spend a long time finding another ride. The concert’s director, Zhang, came up with a plan B: he asked his friend, singer Hou Lang, to perform for the 30,000-strong crowd while they waited for Lee. Hou, a 33-year-old native of Guangdong, is a little-known singer who specialises in performing Cantonese songs. When Zhang contacted him, Hou was eating barbecue with his friends at a restaurant in Baotou. He took just a minute to agree to help Zhang and step in to save the concert. Hou took a taxi and then rode a shared bicycle to reach the stadium. At about 10pm, he appeared on stage in his everyday clothes, after giving the concert’s sound engineer a list of the songs he would perform. Without a rehearsal or an autocue, Hou – who had initially been asked to perform for half an hour – sang continuously for two hours. At 12.20am, Lee finally arrived at the concert. He bowed and apologised to the audience nine times. Lee then performed six of his signature songs on stage. After the concert, he hugged Hou for more than 10 seconds to express his gratitude. Hou said Lee had been his idol for years. He recalled that in 2010, while working as an intern at a performance company and helping to build a stage in Shenzhen, he had taken a photo with Lee. The Baotou concert audience enjoyed Hou’s performance, and very few people left the venue. “Some audience members even asked Hou to rest or drink some water. The atmosphere was very moving,” a female attendee was quoted as saying. Hou said he had felt nervous on stage because of the concert’s scale. Previously, he had performed only in front of audiences of up to 5,000 people. “I didn’t think much at the time. I just sang every song with all my heart,” he said. “I’m proud of myself for saving the concert and performing on the same stage as my idol, Lee,” Hou added. He declined an internet user’s joking suggestion that he should receive half of the concert’s revenue. “One should not receive a reward without having earned it,” Hou explained modestly. The number of followers on his social media account skyrocketed from fewer than 10,000 to 420,000 in the two weeks after the concert. Hou said he was open to music-related business collaborations but not to live-streaming sales. He asked the public not to focus on him, but instead to do more meaningful things. “I am just an ordinary person who loves music,” Hou says in his social media bio.

title: Exclusive | As AI and the Iran war loom, China’s energy technocrats are on the fast track
description: The energy careers of senior Communist Party cadres have given them technical expertise, foresight and management skills.
content: This is a special contribution from the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong. Read the full report at the end of the article. It will be available on the institute website cccw.hku.hk from October 13. With the rising strategic significance of energy, especially due to the need to support China’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, members of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee with energy backgrounds – the country’s “movers and shakers” in this strategic sector – merit closer attention. Among them are former or current power-company executives, petroleum managers, nuclear-safety officials and specialists in water administration. Many built their expertise over decades, establishing themselves as energy technocrats before taking on responsibilities beyond their original industries. Their biographies reveal a recurring route into political leadership – deep specialisation first and diversification of political experience later, highlighting the growing presence and power of this leadership cohort. More experience, greater representation Our data set identifies 34 energy sector members, including 21 full members and 13 alternates. They account for 10.2 per cent of the 205 full members, 7.6 per cent of the 171 alternates and 9 per cent of the combined membership. Three of them were elected to the Politburo in October 2022, representing 12.5 per cent of its 24 members. As of this year, their median ages are 64 among full members and 60 among alternates. By October 2022, 29 of the 34 had at least 10 years of energy experience. This included 16 of the 21 full members. Nineteen had careers spanning 20 years or more. The comparison with earlier committees further illustrates the long tenure and solid leadership experience of these energy technocrats, especially among the full members. In the energy cohort, the share with at least 10 years of energy experience was 75 per cent in the 18th committee, falling to 67.7 per cent in the 19th before reaching 85.3 per cent in the 20th. Among full members, the number with energy backgrounds increased from 15 in the 19th committee to 21 in the 20th committee; within that group, the number with at least 10 years of experience increased from nine to 16. A long apprenticeship The career of Zhang Yuzhuo, president and Communist Party secretary of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, is illustrative. He began work at a coal research institute in 1985, combining research with progressively greater institutional responsibilities. In 2002, he moved to Shenhua Group, where he held senior management positions before becoming chairman in 2014. When he joined Tianjin’s municipal party leadership and became party secretary of the Binhai New Area in March 2017, he brought more than three decades of coal-related research and enterprise experience into local government. That was a specialised career, but not a narrow one. Zhang’s progression from research to institute leadership and then corporate management placed him at different points in the relationship between technology and industrial production. The professional foundation remained rooted in the energy industry as the scale of his responsibilities expanded. This is an important feature of deep specialisation. Remaining within an industry can involve considerable movement across functions – from solving technical problems to managing people, allocating capital and taking responsibility for operations. Each role exposes a different part of the same system and offers opportunities to understand how an engineering choice becomes a financial commitment, an organisational challenge and, eventually, an operating result. The resulting knowledge is both technical and managerial. A manager who understands why a grid connection is delayed – whether due to network capacity, equipment procurement or the timing of another investment – can ask better questions of the organisations involved. Read in this light, the long careers represent an extended apprenticeship in complex systems. Their significance lies in sustained exposure to implementation – what it takes to turn a plan into a functioning operation. Repeated responsibility for delivery can sharpen judgment about whether a timetable is credible and whether the organisations involved can meet their commitments. For those who later enter government, this experience provides a practical and solid foundation for much broader and more strategic decisions. From an industry to governance The next stage changes the scope of responsibility. Among the energy cohort in the 20th Central Committee, 22 had acquired party-government experience by the 20th party congress in 2022, in local or central posts. Their careers connect prolonged work within an industry with appointments spanning a broader range of public responsibilities. Career diversification, in this context, means an expansion of governing responsibilities. The transition from responsibility for a particular enterprise or administrative field to responsibility for a wider set of institutions, interests and public priorities is a demanding task. China’s personnel framework provides institutional channels for such movement. The Communist Party has an established tradition of recruiting leaders from enterprises, universities and research institutions and allows exchanges across organisational boundaries. Technical experience can enter leadership selection through a system of party appointment and evaluation. Liu Ning, who until recently served as Henan’s provincial party secretary, illustrates the scale of that transition. He began work in the Yangtze water-planning and design system in 1983 and later became chief engineer and vice-minister at the Ministry of Water Resources. After roughly 34 years in water-related work, he moved to Qinghai province in 2017. He subsequently served as governor of Qinghai and then Liaoning before becoming Guangxi’s party secretary in 2021. By the 2022 party congress, a long specialist career had been followed by senior responsibilities in three different provincial settings. His trajectory illustrates two stages of increasing complexity. Water administration already requires decisions across connected territories and competing uses, whereas provincial leadership extends that problem across the whole economy. A water official may approach a proposed project through its implications for supply, flood protection or infrastructure. A provincial leader must place those considerations alongside employment, public finances, industrial development and social services. Earlier expertise remains useful, but its holder must now decide how much weight it deserves among competing claims. Yang Jinbai, deputy secretary of Hainan’s provincial party committee and concurrently secretary of its Political and Legal Affairs Commission, followed a parallel route through electricity. He began work in power dispatch in 1994, progressing through technical and operational positions before taking senior roles at Guizhou Power Grid, China Southern Power Grid and State Grid. In 2018, after 24 years in the power sector, he became a vice-chairman of the Guangxi regional government. He became a vice mayor of Beijing in 2020 and was elected an alternate member of the 20th Central Committee. His industrial career had already widened from dispatch and engineering to strategic planning and corporate management. The move into government expanded its scope again. In Guangxi, he concurrently headed the office responsible for planning and construction in the Beibu Gulf Economic Zone. Now his responsibilities on the Hainan party committee encompass public security, social stability and coordination across law-enforcement and judicial institutions. Yang’s trajectory makes the distinction between the two stages particularly clear. Within the power sector, his responsibilities grew around a connected set of technical and commercial problems. His move into government transferred that experience to the regional economic agenda. His subsequent appointment in Hainan shows that diversification can extend across distinct functions of party-state governance. A city cannot be governed like an enlarged enterprise. Its leadership must consider firms with conflicting interests, residents affected by development and public bodies pursuing different objectives. An investment that makes commercial sense for one company may impose costs elsewhere. A project that promises industrial growth may compete with housing, transport or public services for land and funding. For an energy veteran, this changes the central question. Experience in industry helps explain how a project can be delivered. Governing requires deciding whether it deserves to be a priority, how its costs should be distributed and what other commitments must accompany it. This is precisely the substance of the second apprenticeship of governing. Higher office calls for negotiation across departments, choices under budget constraints and engagement with interests outside the original professional community. The two stages reinforce each other. Professional depth provides a basis for scrutinising technical advice. Wider governing experience places that advice within a larger set of economic and social choices. The sequence is essential because depth and breadth address different weaknesses. Rapid movement across unrelated posts can produce extensive exposure without sustained understanding. Energy technocrats, China’s security and AI capacity This combination of deep energy expertise and broad governing experience helps officials manage the complex demands of energy security and AI development. It contributes to the rapid industrial deployment of cost-efficient open-source models, despite US chip export curbs. Energy veterans who developed technical competence alongside political judgment are uniquely prepared to anticipate and manage risks and to pursue long-term strategies. Power plants, grids and reserves take time to build, so waiting until a need becomes urgent can leave few options. Officials must judge when the benefits of early investment justify its costs and when preparing for a possible shortage is necessary. Expanding AI capacity, for example, requires power infrastructure to be planned alongside computing facilities. In Guian, Guizhou, the supercomputing centre handles AI training orders from across China. As the surrounding data centre cluster expanded, a new 500-kilovolt substation entered service three months ahead of schedule to meet demand. The project illustrates the value of coordinating power and computing investment to bring computing capacity into use sooner and provide reliable electricity for training and running AI models. Energy security also depends on investments made ahead of need. During the recent US-Iran war, oil stocks accumulated before the conflict helped China weather disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. Accumulating oil before the crisis illustrated the foresight energy planning requires – weighing demand prospects against the risk of interrupted supply. Using reserves effectively also calls for coordination across enterprises and government. China’s energy veterans can bring both industrial knowledge and governing experience to such decisions, helping the country prepare for external shocks while investing in future growth. It is no coincidence that China has excelled in energy security while confronting the dual challenges of a global oil shortage and the massive electricity demands of the AI revolution.

title: Style Edit: Louis Vuitton’s Multipass bag blends elegance with modern versatility
description: Unveiled at the French maison’s cruise 2026 show in Avignon, the slouchy bag with detachable elements can shift its shape to elevate your look for every occasion.
content: Louis Vuitton’s cruise 2026 show, held last year in Avignon, was memorable for several reasons. It made history as the first-ever fashion show held at the Palais des Papes, one of Europe’s largest Gothic palaces and a Unesco World Heritage site. It also marked a seminal moment in the brand’s oeuvre with the unveiling of a new icon: the stylish yet effortless Multipass bag. Inspired by the bestselling Express handbag, the Multipass has since become one of the maison’s signature creations, joining designs such as the Petite Malle and the Side Trunk. Boasting refined lines that combine elegance and functionality, this slouchy style appeals to a new generation. With an adjustable shoulder strap, braided chain and short handle, all removable, it transforms to suit every style, making it the ideal companion for any moment of the day. Its exceptional versatility plays out in several different ways. Worn on the shoulder, it becomes the ideal city bag. It can also convert to a cross-body for effortless freedom of movement, or be carried as a clutch or slung across the wrist for a sophisticated yet nonchalant look. The Multipass bag’s allure lies in its unique personality, which adapts to the ever-changing demands of modern life. Each season, it is reinterpreted as an endless array of personas. Crafted in monogram canvas, it becomes a classic, while grained leather versions are exceptionally refined, thanks to a stunning palette ranging from deep black to soft vanilla. Other versions feature a suede effect or Epi trompe l’oeil on suede calfskin for pure elegance. For the current fall/winter 2026 season, the Multipass takes centre stage against the backdrop of a ready-to-wear collection titled Super Nature, which proposes an architectural wardrobe designed for 21st-century nomads. Sculptural styles feature extreme shapes – capes come with exaggerated shoulders – while alpine- and mountaineering-inspired looks evoke pastoral beauty. Many looks are defined by the natural world. Flora and fauna leave imprints on the garments, while animalier patterns are woven into canvas and denim, taking on a new dimension. Craft is melded with technology to showcase the creativity of nature. Buttons draw from raw minerals and heels evoke antler silhouettes. Vegetal furs add tactile depth, while textured leather mimics natural wood. Adding an elegant finishing touch to multiple ready-to-wear looks is the latest rendition of the bag – the Mini Multipass. This miniature version is graceful and poised while still embodying all the must-have hallmarks of the full-sized style. Available in new seasonal colourways, it is carried by hand to create a fresh yet covetable look.

title: Style Edit: Burberry marks 170 years with London, New York, Seoul and Shanghai campaign
description: The British fashion house celebrates individuality with a showcase of 10 outerwear styles – including trench coats, puffer jackets and capes – on the streets of four cities.
content: A Burberry coat has always promised more than protection from the elements. It carries the practical qualities of British all-weather dressing, of course, but also a certain style: think of a collar turned up against the rain or that signature checked lining caught in motion. For its 170th anniversary, Burberry returns to that enduring idea with 170: The Anniversary Portraits, a global campaign that places its outerwear not in a studio, but on the streets and in the cities where it is worn. Photographed by Jack Day and accompanied by a film directed by Hector Aponysus, the project brings together 170 people across London, Shanghai, New York and Seoul, each interpreting one of 10 outerwear styles in a personal way. It follows in the spirit of Burberry’s 2009 Art of the Trench campaign, which turned a heritage garment into a document of individual style. This time, street-cast locals share the frame with figures from art, literature, sport and music, as well as members of Burberry’s own global team. The cast includes ballet artist Tan Yuanyuan, director Xin Shuang, volleyball player Kim Yeon-koung, singer Crush, theatre director Jamie Lloyd, model Lila Moss and footballer Nico O’Reilly. The 10 designs form a comprehensive guide to the house’s outerwear approach. At its core are the Long Kensington Heritage Trench Coat, structured with set-in sleeves, and the Long Waterloo Heritage Trench Coat, which takes a softer approach with raglan shoulders and a classic fit. The Mid-length Camden Heritage Car Coat offers a more pared-back, single-breasted line for men, along with concealed buttons. Elsewhere, familiar forms are pushed into new territories. The Leather Kensington Trench Jacket is executed in burgundy nappa leather, while the Long Cashmere Kensington Trench Coat recasts the classic silhouette in insulating cashmere. For men, the Hastings Trench Coat comes in a brushed grey mélange cashmere; for women, the Shearling Collar Cashmere Cape is lined in the house’s signature check. Glossy nylon puffer jackets meanwhile bring tonal or yarn-beige House Check into modern fabric, with goose down and feather filling and packaway hoods. Quilted pieces take their lead from classic countryside styles: the shearling-collared Quilted Nylon Rosedale Coat references the trench through its stitched check, while the Reversible Quilted Nylon Brighton Overshirt turns from shale-green to bold House Check. Daniel Lee, Burberry’s chief creative officer, describes 170: The Anniversary Portraits as a study in personality. “For 170 years, our outerwear has adapted to the weather and the way we dress,” he says. “Each portrait is different, but together they capture individuality and self-expression.” That’s an apt way to mark the milestone. Instead of treating outerwear as a static archive, the house recognises that a well-designed coat takes on new character with every wearer.

title: Style Edit: Gucci’s cruise 2027 collection takes over Times Square in New York
description: Stars like Mariah Carey and Shawn Mendes turned out for Demna’s GucciCore runway, which draws on the many ways New Yorkers dress – from pinstripes to slouchy denim.
content: New York’s Times Square hardly lacks visual stimulation. Yet for the unveiling of GucciCore, the house’s cruise 2027 collection, it chose the district’s relentless digital glow as its backdrop, treating one of the city’s loudest landmarks as the stage for a collection with everyday roots: looks that might be encountered on the streets. Before the show, Gucci filled Times Square’s screens with a montage of found footage and mock advertisements spanning Gucci Automobili, Gucci Gym, Gucci Pets and a fictional Palazzo Gucci hotel – painting a faintly surreal vision of the brand as a lifestyle rather than a logo. The show’s invitation was a brass key in an aged-leather sleeve, recalling the Gucci Galleria, a private, key-accessed space above the house’s Fifth Avenue flagship in the 1980s. The choice of Times Square is a return of sorts. Gucci opened its first store outside Italy in New York in 1953, and the city has remained a defining part of the house’s international story. GucciCore connects that history with the present, translating it into what the brand describes as a new core wardrobe – and, more specifically, a set of characters who might cross paths anywhere from Madison Avenue to Brooklyn, SoHo, Harlem or Fifth Avenue. Under creative director Demna, the cruise 2027 collection brings the city’s familiar social uniforms together. Pinstriped stockbrokers share the imagined pavement with women in casually worn shearling, skaters in soft tailoring and slouchy denim, and socialites in gowns and trouser suits. It isn’t a single New York look, but a parade of many: polished, pragmatic, excessive and casual, all represented in equal measure. The clothes display similarly contrasting approaches. Circular duvet stoles in butter-soft leather and monogrammed fabric are sculptural, while reversible technical coats and textured shearling outerwear are practical. The Web stripe, a Gucci signature since 1951, becomes a bandeau top. Technical outerwear gains goat-hair and shearling linings. Elsewhere, croc-scale sequins, beaded fringe and feather embroidery bring haute decoration to menswear without sacrificing the collection’s urban edge. Accessories reinforce the street-level variety. The signature Horsebit is reworked as a stirrup detail on severe heeled boots, set against sharp metal-tipped stilettos. Bags move between inky or jewel-toned precious leathers, wristwatch clutches with timepiece straps, and roomy, unstructured sling totes realised in new fabrications. As the fourth act in Demna’s ongoing “character studies”, GucciCore unites the visual worlds of spring/summer 2026’s La Famiglia, Generation Gucci and Primavera collections. Its central idea is refreshing: luxury can be theatrical, and belongs as much on the streets as anywhere else.

title: South Korea hails success of its first Arctic shipping trial
description: President Lee Jae Myung said it shaved 10 days off the one-way sailing time compared to going through the Suez Canal.
content: A South Korean container ship has returned from a trial voyage through the Arctic, testing an alternative route opened by melting sea ice as conflict in the Middle East disrupts global shipping. The PanStar Acro made the round trip to Europe in less time than the conventional route through the Suez Canal, officials said. The initiative has drawn concerns that increased traffic could accelerate Arctic ice loss. The Arctic route could also expose operators to sanctions-related risks because it runs along Russia’s northern coast. “The PanStar Acro, which embarked on a trial voyage along the Arctic shipping route on August 22, docked at Jaseongdae Pier in Busan Port,” the South Korean oceans and fisheries ministry said in a statement on Sunday. The vessel sailed through the Arctic’s Northern Sea Route before making port calls at Felixstowe in Britain, Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland, and returning via the same route. President Lee Jae Myung hailed the successful voyage, saying it “shortened the one-way sailing time by 10 days compared with the conventional route via the Suez Canal”. “It also allowed us to gain valuable experience operating a South Korean container ship in polar waters and to collect navigational data,” Lee said on social media. The Middle East conflict, sparked by US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, has roiled global shipping, prompting governments and operators to explore alternative routes. Environmental advocates, however, warn that expanded commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route could threaten the fragile Arctic ecosystem. Major shipping companies, including CMA-CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd, have pledged to avoid Arctic routes, citing environmental concerns. The Northern Sea Route is generally more accessible during the warmer months, when reduced sea ice makes navigation easier, although ice conditions remain unpredictable and some vessels still require icebreaker assistance. Without making any reference to the environmental concerns, Lee said the successful trial mission would help his country “prepare for the era of Arctic shipping routes”. “We will transform Busan and the southeastern region into a ‘southern maritime capital region’ and ensure that this new sea route becomes a new engine of growth,” he said.

title: At least 139 migrants dead, dozens missing after boat capsizes off Djibouti
description: UN agency says vessel carrying 305 mostly Ethiopian passengers sank on a dangerous Red Sea route to Yemen.
content: At least 139 migrants died, including 15 children, and 84 went missing when an overcrowded boat sank while heading from Djibouti to Yemen, a UN agency said on Sunday. The vessel was carrying 305 people, most of them Ethiopian, when it capsized north of the Djibouti town of Obock on the night of October 8-9, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said in a statement. “Survivors told me that the boat started to sink backwards as soon as they got in it,” Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said. “This is a devastating loss of life,” he said earlier in the statement. “Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives.” The IOM gave an initial toll of 109 dead and 116 missing, and revised it to 139 dead and 84 missing in a later statement after more bodies were recovered. Coissac said IOM teams were on the ground alongside Djiboutian authorities to provide emergency aid. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities” by trying to cross the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Yemen and then reach Gulf countries, he said. Coissac said he had spoken to one survivor of the wreck who came from the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, where rebels are battling the federal government in a recent flare-up of violence. Among the 109 bodies earlier recovered were 52 men, 42 women and 15 children – nine girls and six boys – the initial statement said. Eighty-two people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals, according to the updated toll. “Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East,” the IOM said. The IOM said it was assisting 64 survivors at a migrant centre in Obock. “Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing.” It called it “one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded” on the route. IOM spokesman Kennedy Omondi Okoth said last week that 178,000 people had arrived in Djibouti from Ethiopia from January to October this year. Since September 10, the IOM detected more than 20,000 crossings to Djibouti from Ethiopia, despite a surge in conflict in Yemen. The country is stricken by fighting between the Saudi-backed government and Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, who have joined in the regional conflict involving the US and its allies against Iran. Coissac said 150 of the people on the boat that sank off Djibouti had previously been turned back from Yemen but had attempted the crossing again. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the sea route to Yemen and the number attempting the journey increased by 18 per cent, the IOM said. A shipwreck in March 2026 left nine people dead and 45 missing. Okoth said most of the people attempting the journey were from Ethiopia or Somalia. He said many of them were ending up “stranded” in Djibouti. “No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope in a statement. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.” The IOM urged “donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti’s response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance”. The African Union Commission chairman expressed his “profound sorrow over the tragic loss of life” in a statement. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf also stressed the urgent need to “address the root causes of irregular migration, combat migrant smuggling and trafficking in persons, and promote safe, orderly and regular migration”.

title: Days after AI missile test, North Korea fires more projectiles
description: South Korea’s military confirmed Monday’s launch, which followed its own hypersonic missile test earlier this month.
content: North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul’s military said, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the countries’ heavily fortified border. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff confirmed in a statement that it had detected several ballistic missiles launched from the Pyongyang area, adding that its military “has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches”. One of the missiles flew more than 900km (559 miles) before falling into the sea, a spokesman said. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected. Japan’s Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari separately said the country had detected at least two missiles launched 17 minutes apart and that the weapons landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone. Koyari said the first missile flew about 220km (137 miles) and the second more than 910km (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path that he said suggested it might have been a hypersonic weapon. There were no reports of damage to aircraft or vessels. North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an October 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan. That missile incorporated artificial intelligence technology, said Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, at the time. It was “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it”, she said at the time. Days later, Seoul announced the successful test of its first home-grown hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV), a weapon carried into the upper atmosphere by rocket boosters or ballistic missiles before gliding towards their targets. South Korea’s presidential office said the HGV offered “a new deterrence capability capable of striking key targets within the Korean peninsula’s operational environment”. Tensions between the two Koreas have been heightened since three South Korean soldiers were injured when two landmines detonated in the Seoul-controlled area of the demilitarised zone that has served as a buffer since the 1953 armistice. A joint Seoul-UN investigation alleged that North Korea had planted the landmines over a year ago, something Pyongyang has angrily denied. Kim Jong-un in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described its neighbour as a permanent enemy amid a prolonged stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. He has so far rebuffed US President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a precondition for talks. The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favours engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric towards the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts. Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea’s conventional defence capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States. Washington unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with South Korea in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Beijing moves to steady A-share market after sharp tech sell-off
description: CSRC chair Wu Qing convenes meeting with listed firms and financial institutions after a sharp third-quarter market decline.
content: China’s top securities regulator has signalled fresh support for the domestic A-share market, convening a symposium over the weekend as authorities sought to shore up sentiment following a sharp sell-off in technology shares driven by concerns over US sanctions. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) brought together executives from listed companies and experts from securities firms and fund managers at a meeting in Beijing on Saturday to “discuss the country’s capital markets and financial conditions”, according to an online statement. The meeting was chaired by CSRC head Wu Qing, who sought views and suggestions on the current market environment. It came amid a sharp market correction. China’s CSI 300 Index fell 12 per cent in the third quarter, weighed down by a 31 per cent slump in the tech-heavy Star Market 50 index. Selling pressure persisted after the week-long National Day holiday. During intraday trading on Friday, the ChiNext Index briefly fell below the 3,000-point mark, while the Star 50 index dropped more than 4 per cent and slipped below 1,400 points. Both later pared losses and closed slightly higher amid heavy buying, which some market participants linked to government-backed funds. It was not the first symposium of its kind this year. Following a sharp market correction in July, Wu also chaired a meeting with investors aimed at boosting confidence, after which markets stabilised with policy support and fresh capital inflows. No new policy measures were outlined in Saturday’s official readout. Wu urged listed companies and industry institutions to offer suggestions and work together to improve the capital market and deliver better returns to investors. Participating experts were said to have proposed strengthening market-stabilisation mechanisms, broadening the channels through which medium- and long-term funds could enter the market, and developing “patient capital” willing to invest over longer periods. They also called for eligible listed companies to increase dividends and share buy-backs, improve investor protection, optimise listing rules, strengthen trading supervision and enhance cross-border risk monitoring. Beijing faces an uphill battle in attracting long-term overseas capital to China’s A-share market, as funds continue to flow into the United States, where stocks hit new highs last week. The regulatory push, however, coincided with signs that global active funds were ending a four-year underweight position on Chinese equities, with institutions such as Bank of America pointing to a shift towards benchmark-neutral allocations. Chinese investment banks including CCB International and Zheshang Securities warned that mainland and Hong Kong equities faced a challenging fourth quarter. Analysts expected markets to remain range-bound amid persistent expectations of higher US interest rates, tight global liquidity and a shifting sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related stocks.

title: Opinion | The game changer in Hong Kong’s gold ambition? Shenzhen’s jewellery hub
description: Serving central banks and institutions is important but adding a vibrant gold wholesale and manufacturing centre would be an ace move.
content: Beijing is building a gold-backed monetary architecture to accelerate yuan internationalisation. In this three-part series, Part 1 traces China’s path as a gold superpower, while Part 2 explores the crucial role of Hong Kong’s offshore vaulting infrastructure. Hong Kong’s ambition to become an international gold trading centre rests not only on serving the nation’s financial needs, but also on China’s booming consumer market for gold. As the world’s largest gold producer and importer, China easily absorbs hundreds of tonnes of the precious metal each year or more, an estimated 80 per cent of which is snapped up by consumers whose love of gold dates back millennia. Hong Kong has long been the primary gold market for Chinese consumers. In the early 1970s, the city’s largest jeweller, Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, established the 999.9 purity standard (meaning 999.9 parts gold per 1,000), which quickly caught on. In 2008, the Legislative Council set the Chuk Kam purity standard at 99.9 per cent, higher than the mainland’s 99 per cent consumer standard. As a tax-free port, Hong Kong levies no import duties on jewellers and no sales tax on customers, allowing it to become China’s undisputed consumer centre for gold. By 1998, the city had at least 1,300 gold and jewellery shops; today, it is widely regarded as one of the world’s top gold retailing centres. Yet, the picture has also changed considerably. Hong Kong remains an important retail centre for gold, but its future depends largely on integration with Shenzhen across the border. Best known for its meteoric rise as China’s tech capital, Shenzhen is also an equally impressive centre for wholesale jewellery and fabrication. Obscure 20 years ago, Shenzhen’s Shuibei market is now Asia’s largest jewellery wholesale hub by volume. Occupying an area only one third the size of New York’s Central Park, it houses more than 7,000 jewellery merchants and accounts for at least 50 per cent of China’s gold trading, with an annual turnover of 100 billion yuan (US$14.91 billion). The city first set out its ambition to turn Shuibei into a world-class gold wholesale and fabrication hub two decades ago, and this year it again mentioned gold and jewellery as a competitive industry in its 15th five-year plan. This dovetails neatly with Hong Kong’s goal of becoming an international gold trading centre and expanding its physical gold storage tenfold, to 2,000 tonnes by 2028. As I explained in an earlier column, a major reason for building up our vaulting capacity is to support the internationalisation of the yuan and to serve central banks and institutions in Belt and Road Initiative countries. But that alone is not enough. Bullion sitting in brand-new vaults will not generate much wealth unless it is put to use and changes hands. Serving central banks and institutions is important, but adding a vibrant gold wholesale and manufacturing centre would be the real game changer. A considerable portion of the gold used by Shuibei’s manufacturers already comes from Hong Kong. There is no official figure, but my calculation, based on various industry reports, puts it at around 20-30 per cent. Hong Kong’s plans to expand its physical gold storage aggressively and to develop yuan-denominated gold financial products will be music to Shenzhen’s ears. The reason lies in how jewellery manufacturing and gold fabrication work. Facing intense competition, foundries operate on thin margins, and it normally takes several days from order to delivery. Daily fluctuations in the gold price can shipwreck their business. The industry mitigates this risk through gold leasing and hedging. Under a gold lease, a foundry does not hold stock but borrows gold from a bank only after receiving a confirmed order. After delivery, it repays the bank with a similar amount of gold, plus interest, at a favourable time. This greatly reduces the capital the foundry must put down, as well as its exposure to price swings. Because Shuibei also supplies gold products overseas, particularly to Southeast Asian markets, its foundries can lease gold from Hong Kong, transport it to a bonded zone in Shenzhen for fabrication and export the finished goods immediately. This closed-loop operation involves no customs duties and is extremely cost-effective. Even for the domestic market, Hong Kong is attractive because of interest-rate differentials. The onshore gold leasing rate is consistently higher than the offshore rate, and the spread can sometimes be significant. Modelled on the successful Stock Connect and Bond Connect schemes, Hong Kong launched Delivery Connect in July. It establishes a direct, regulated pipeline for moving and settling physical gold between Hong Kong and the Shanghai Gold Exchange, which keeps large physical vaults in Shenzhen. This will make it increasingly easy for Shuibei merchants to lease gold from Hong Kong and take advantage of the onshore-offshore price premium. The same goes for hedging. As Hong Kong develops more gold-backed, yuan-denominated financial instruments, Shuibei jewellers will have more options to hedge against price fluctuations and manage risk. All this gives Hong Kong ample opportunity to put its burgeoning gold vaults to work. Most importantly, it creates a unique gold trading ecosystem that combines high finance, wholesale, manufacturing, retail, and onshore and offshore markets across Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Nowhere else, not London, New York or Switzerland, can offer such a comprehensive value chain. This is Hong Kong’s ace up its sleeve.

title: The timeless legacy of Chinese musical instruments
description: Uncover the fascinating evolution of instruments from ancient times to today’s orchestras.
content:
In Chinese mythology, Ling Lun is known as the person who started music. The Yellow Emperor asked him to create a system of pitch pipes. He made 12 bamboo pipes to copy the harmonious sounds of the mythical phoenix.
The history of Chinese musical instruments goes back over 8,000 years. They have changed from simple bone flutes in prehistoric times to the complex instruments used in today’s orchestras. Early Chinese societies had a vibrant musical culture that dates back to the Zhou dynasty, which was around 1046-256BC. During that time, people grouped instruments by the materials they were made of.
Today, modern Chinese orchestras are organised into four main groups: plucked strings, bowed strings, wind instruments and percussion .
The pipa is a four-stringed instrument shaped like a pear. It was likely brought to China from West Asia over 2,000 years ago. It is famous for its expressive and dramatic sound. Thus, it has occupied a key position in modern Chinese orchestras.
