The characters pi and pa in its name depict the inward and outward plucking action of playing the instrument. Many classic pieces still live on with the pipa’s help, such as Ambush from Ten Sides (1818).
The erhu, often called the “Chinese violin”, is a two-stringed instrument. It has a handle that runs through its body. It is played with a bow that moves between the strings, producing an emotional, weeping tone. This instrument has a rich history, having been used in China for over 1,000 years.
The sheng is an ancient mouth-blown instrument dating back to at least 1100BC. It is made of small bamboo pipes arranged in a circle around a wind chamber. Each pipe features a free reed made of metal or bamboo. When a finger covers a pipe’s hole, the reed vibrates, producing sound.
This musical instrument dates back to the earliest records of Chinese civilisation. Bronze bells first appeared during the Zhou dynasty. They were historically played to signify status and power.
The bianzhong serves as both a primary lead and a rhythmic anchor in modern Chinese orchestras. A full set of these bells requires two or more people to play, but smaller sets are often featured in modern concerts.

title: China’s CXMT unveils ‘key progress’ on chip structure pursued by Samsung, SK Hynix
description: Memory chip giant says its proprietary transistor design could increase storage density and improve efficiency.
content: Chinese memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has reported “key progress” on a new cell architecture to boost memory density, an innovation that competitors such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are also working on. CXMT planned to roll out a new server-memory product based on the structure by the end of 2026, president Cao Kanyu said at an industrial event in Shanghai over the weekend, according to a company statement. At the centre of the development is the “4F square” design, in which each memory cell occupies an area of four square F, with F representing the minimum line width of a semiconductor. The structure enables higher storage density by fitting more cells onto a single chip. For now, mainstream commercial dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) uses a 6F square-cell structure. The world’s leading DRAM producers are all pursuing the technology. SK Hynix unveiled its 4F square road map in 2025, while Samsung, according to a report by South Korean media outlet The Elec in April, planned to mass-produce sub-10-nanometre DRAM based on the new design by 2028. CXMT said the core of its 4F square design was its proprietary Vertical Surrounding Gate (VSG) transistor, which used a vertical gate architecture to address current leakage while significantly reducing unit area and increasing storage density. The shift from the mainstream 6F square structure to 4F square represents a fundamental transition from horizontal to vertical transistor channels. Because existing manufacturing flows could not be adapted to the new structure, CXMT had to redesign key processes to optimise the performance-to-power ratio, the company said. The memory giant, based in Hefei, capital of central China’s Anhui province, said it expected to release a new generation of DDR5 RDIMM by the end of the year. Designed for enterprise-grade servers, the new memory module will incorporate the advanced technology. CXMT did not disclose detailed specifications or a launch date. The firm said the server product required higher levels of endurance and compatibility than consumer memory products. It must support round-the-clock uninterrupted operations, withstand voltage fluctuations and pass hundreds of compatibility tests with central processing units and motherboards from different manufacturers. Since listing on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s Star Market in July, CXMT has made several moves to showcase its technological muscle. Last month, it said its fifth-generation DRAM manufacturing platform, known as G5, had entered mass production, marking another step in narrowing the gap with global industry leaders. Founded in 2016, the company said it had been researching the 4F square architecture since its inception and had published more than 300 related patent families, surpassing both domestic and overseas peers. Additional reporting by Howard Liu

title: How Hong Kong student-athletes can find careers that merge their passions
description: A study shows that more than a quarter of pupils want to work in sports, but about half do not know of jobs beyond competing or coaching.
content:
Before joining Hong Kong’s sailing team, 17-year-old Huang Ziyan thought a career in sports meant being an athlete or a coach.
She represented the city at the Asian Games in 2023 and at the Youth Sailing World Championships in 2024 and 2025. She is also a student at Harrow International School Hong Kong.
“I was under the impression that opportunities in sport were a lot more narrow ,” Ziyan said. “Going to the [Hong Kong] Sports Institute opened my eyes ... You could be a sports psychologist, a physiotherapist , a strength coach or work in sports science.”
In recent years, the city has seen huge success from its athletes. Earlier this month, Coleman Wong Chak-lam won Hong Kong’s first Asian Games tennis gold.
Not every athlete can get to this level. But a think tank is hoping to show young sportspeople how to turn their passions into a career.
In August, Our Hong Kong Foundation released a study of 1,098 secondary school students in the city.
The think tank found that 28 per cent of students are interested in a career in sports. But 56 per cent are not aware of jobs beyond competing or coaching.
Many students are unsure about how to enter jobs in the sports industry and do not have experience with them.
Our Hong Kong Foundation suggested ways to help more student-athletes learn about sports careers, such as physiotherapists, data analysts and event coordinators. The think tank recommended forming a team to organise events exposing young people to these jobs.
It also urged government departments to work together to make guidelines for how schools can support student-athletes. They should set rules on taking leave for competitions and flexible scheduling for classes and exams.
The University Grants Committee offers the Student-Athlete Learning Support and Admission (SALSA) Scheme for elite athletes.
Clara Wong led the launch of the SALSA scheme at City University (CityU).
“My goal when setting up the programme was to show athletes that sports aren’t limited to just one rigid path ... It opens up a whole new world for them,” Wong said. She is also a senior physical education officer at CityU.
“Students eventually realised that ... almost any discipline can be merged with sports.”
Wong has done this in her career. She is a former national table tennis player, and she studied accounting. She said managing the SALSA scheme was a way to combine her interests. She hopes other athletes can also find jobs like this.
Student-athletes need support as they keep up with their studies while training for their sports.
Wong said that young athletes would often focus on winning medals. But that is when mentors can step in to ask: “What will you do after graduation?”
She added: “It made me start planning ahead and take my education seriously.”
For Ziyan, she hopes to study psychology, economics or public policy. In the future, she wants to be involved in sports development in Hong Kong.
“I’m really passionate about ... increasing access to sailing and other sports,” she said. “I’m also interested in psychology because it plays a crucial role in youth development ... for athletes and youth in general.”
Ziyan added that being a student-athlete taught her many lessons.
“The skills I’ve developed as an athlete – discipline, resilience and organisation – have helped me in my studies. Similarly, being able to focus on things for a long period as a student has helped my training,” she said.

title: Letters from readers about gymnastics, choir, family and friends
description: This week, readers share their favourite pastimes and hobbies, what they’re learning in gymnastics and why they love their family.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
I enjoy being in the choir because my passion is singing. I have been learning how to sing since I was in the second grade.
I have one older sister, a mum and a dad. They always play with me and talk to me. On my birthday, they buy me gifts. My family is kind and patient, so they have many friends.
My best friend is Bella Wong because she is kind and wise. She likes McDonald’s and KFC.
I like Minecraft and Roblox because I can build anything in Minecraft and we can challenge other players. It’s fun!
I enjoy doing gymnastics in my free time. Although I am not that good at it, I try to do my best. I know how to do a split and a bridge. I am very happy about my progress! I am trying to learn to do a cartwheel, but it is very hard.
I am really thankful for my mother. She always helps me with my homework. I think she is the best mother in the whole wide world.
Some of my favourite hobbies are making art, dancing and spending time with my friends and family.
I like to colour and paint when I make art. My favourite colours are pink, blue, white and light yellow.
At school, my favourite subjects are art, music, physical education and the programme of inquiry.
Some of my friends are Saanvi, Mishka and Nairra, and my best friend is Prisha.
My Year Six teacher is Ms Gibson. She is very kind. She was my Year Four teacher, too.
My favourite things to eat are pizza, hotpot and lentils.
My favourite drinks are bubble tea, cold refreshing beverages and mocktails!

title: Lucas Lam Cheuk-lok’s top pick: ‘Don’t Trust Fish’ by Neil Sharpson, illustrated by Dan Santat
description: The six-year-old student from Kowloon Junior School shares why he loves this nature-guide-gone-wrong picture book that makes science fun and easy to understand.
content:
Do you have a book, film or television show you love? Send us your recommendations using this form .
I really enjoy reading Don’t Trust Fish by Neil Sharpson. My favourite part is when it explains how other animals evolved from fish. It makes science fun and easy to understand.
I also like how the book keeps repeating, “Don’t trust fish!” It sounds funny and makes me curious. The drawings in the book are very colourful, and the characters have cute and silly faces.
Overall, the book is very funny and colourful. It makes me laugh and learn at the same time. I would recommend it to my friends and relatives.

title: Feature of the Week: Sage Liu Hei-tung’s short story ‘The Teddy Bear’s Army’
description: The seven-year-old from Po Leung Kuk Choi Kai Yau School shares this thrilling adventure about rescuing her classmates from a terrifying teddy bear.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
I woke up in a spacious white room with purple potion-bottle-like shapes and a high roof. I saw boys from my whole school trapped in cylinders. Then I found a pickaxe strapped to my skirt, so I smashed one cylinder into pieces with it. Mason was free!
He offered to help me break the other ones. I went to break Kyle and Jayden’s cylinders while Mason went to break out Lucas and Ryan. One by one, all the boys were free.
Just as we were about to leave this place, a deep voice echoed behind me. A chill ran down my spine as I turned around – it was a giant teddy bear! It had bloody red teeth and horrifying eyes.
It shouted, “No one leaves this place without being tortured by me!” It ran towards us, holding up a shard of broken glass from the white marble floor. I decided to fight back.
I picked up sharp pieces of glass and carefully hurled them towards the teddy.
Soon everyone joined in, but it seemed like it was just giving the bear more energy than hurting it. So I said, “Everybody down the staircase!”
When we were at the bottom, tiny teddy bears with swords were waiting for us. We could not get out.
All of a sudden, our teachers burst in with the principal, holding laser guns.
They fired! The tiny teddy bears were all gone. Their leader had no choice but to surrender. Turns out it was just tired of kids disrespecting it.
A blinding, bright light forced me to squeeze my eyes shut and cover my face with my hands. When I finally opened my eyes, I saw daylight streaming through my bedroom window. It was all just a dream.

title: Advice: My parents give me different rules, so I don’t know who to listen to
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
Dealing with conflicting rules can be tricky. Family meetings can help everyone to communicate better.
To get started, the family should agree on some ground rules. Here are examples of rules you can set.
Every member of the family has a turn to share.
Do not interrupt when someone else is talking.
Each meeting should have one goal. For example, if the conflicting rule is about bedtime, then that is the only topic during the meeting. Everyone should have equal time to speak. Each person can share why a certain bedtime is best. The goal is to agree on a new rule.
Family meetings should be short so that everyone stays focused. A decision should be made by the end. If not, the topic can be paused until next time. The goal of this is to stop family arguments from continuing.
Take notes during the meeting. Then, everyone can check the rules to follow in the future.
But some parents might still struggle to agree after many meetings. Then, you may need to reach out for more help outside your family.
Social workers are experts in helping people learn healthy communication. Or perhaps your parents would be more comfortable speaking to someone they know. This could be a family friend or relative.
This question was answered by Elizabeth Jung Rowlinson, a mental health therapist at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: Drive and survive: metal plates, mental scars not enough to derail teen’s F1 dream
description: Seira Kojima will be back in her seat in Malaysia next month after overcoming physical and mental hurdles following terrifying crash.
content: Seira Kojima does not remember the karting crash that left her with metal plates and screws in places they have no business being in a 15-year-old girl, but she can describe it pretty well. She has seen video of her “rear tyre getting bumped” and the vehicle spinning through the air, and has the scars to back up the resulting injuries, which included a fracture of her right scapula, and a broken collarbone. The terrifying incident at the All Japan Kart Championship in April, which left her in an intensive care unit, would have put many off the sport for life. But the steely, single-minded, determined teen is made of stronger stuff and was back behind the wheel just three months later. An attitude that should help as she attempts to shatter one of motorsport’s toughest glass ceilings, getting a seat in Formula 1. “When I was in hospital, I was thinking only about racing,” Kojima told the South China Morning Post. “I was regretting my move [before the accident]. and I just wanted to get back and improve.” Kojima’s parents, her biggest supporters in every respect, wanted their daughter to stop racing, perhaps invest more time in the badminton, basketball and horse riding she enjoys. “I told them there was no reason for me to quit, and they said they would back me: that I should do what I wanted,” Kojima said. “I did rehabilitation every day, then I started training, had some small races in Japan, and stepped it up from there.” Fifth in the Senior FIA Karting Arrive and Drive Asia-Pacific Championship in Macau last month, Kojima began racing at 10. “I watched F1 and other motor racing on television because of my dad, then I tried karting on a small circuit in Japan,” she said. “I would only practice about once a month, but when I moved to bigger circuits it became more fun and exciting. Driving went from a hobby to my lifestyle.” At 13, Kojima, whose father is Japanese and mother Filipino, relocated with her family to Malaysia so she could regularly compete in racing series staged in the country. After entering karting’s senior bracket this year, she has transitioned to online studying at Soka International School Malaysia. “It’s difficult not seeing my friends every day, but when I go back they always say, ‘I saw your Instagram, good job’, or ‘I’m proud of you’. It feels really good, and I appreciate their support and encouragement,” she said. Kojima credits her father’s drive and generosity for her accelerated progress from beginner to contender, while she is grateful for her mother always being by her side as she circles the globe gaining competitive experience. “My dad’s personality is such that anything he does, he wants to do it perfectly, and he wants me to do the same,” Kojima said. “I just practice every week, every weekend, and spend a lot more money than other drivers, which allowed me to compete in about 30 races last year.” The first Asian finisher, Kojima placed fourth in last year’s inaugural Junior FIA Karting Arrive and Drive World Cup. The next best female was Leonie Her of France in 22nd. An invite from the FIA Women in Motorsport Commission was responsible for her appearance in Macau last month. Formula 1 has delivered few female role models. Since Italian Maria Teresa de Filippis broke the all-male stronghold in 1958, Lella Lombardi, between 1974 and 1976, has been the only woman to follow her compatriot onto the starting grid. Divina Galica, Desire Wilson and, most recently, Giovana Amati in 1992, have tried and failed to qualify for F1 races. Although she views the progress of 20-year-old Juju Noda, who competes in the Japanese Super Formula Championship, and has tested in Formula E, as evidence that women can make advances, Kojima looked to men for her racing heroes. The first name she mentioned, Nigel Mansell, competed in his last grand prix in 1995, 16 years before Kojima was born, and three years after winning his solitary world title. “It’s all because my dad likes him so much,” she said. “He overtook from the outside a lot, which is really difficult and dangerous. But it’s very cool.” Kojima also cited four-time world champion Max Verstappen as an idol. On returning to competition following her Japan crash, Kojima discovered that some of her own aggression had softened, and on occasions when she “needed to push” she would “tense or brace”. After one race, she admitted to the “fear and anxiety lingering inside me”, while during a race in Belgium her kart was slammed from behind, prompting flashbacks to the Japan incident. “I’d lost my confidence,” she said. “It was frustrating, because although you’re working really hard, you can’t achieve what you want. “It took some time to get back to being myself, but I’m now there. The senior class is fast and physically hard but I’ve got used to it. For every [practice] session and race, we decide the plan, then afterwards we review everything. I love the process, and I feel I improve with every session.” Kojima regularly competes in Europe, where larger fields and less stringent regulations make for more intense and unforgiving racing. Next month, though, she will be back on the LYL International Karting Circuit in Malaysia, where she is intimately familiar with every twist and turn, for the senior Arrive and Drive World Cup. Beyond that, she says that driving at breakneck speeds will remain the core of her existence. “Winning is important, but I’m 15 and I have a lot to learn about racing and life,” Kojima said. “I treat motorsport the same as life; I’m using my brain to learn to solve problems and improve.”

title: Hong Kong must ease listing rules to attract more angel funds and start-ups: HKEIA
description: Hong Kong could learn from the US market, where streamlined regulations foster a thriving ecosystem of angel funds and start-ups, an industry body says.
content: Hong Kong would need to ease its listing rules and transaction requirements to attract more angel funds and become a hub for start-ups to go global, according to a leading industry body in the city. The city has only around 100 active angel funds – private investment vehicles targeting very early-stage innovative enterprises. This was far fewer than Shenzhen, which had about 400 such institutions, according to Samson Tam Wai-ho, honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Electronic Industries Association (HKEIA). Besides Shenzhen, Shanghai and the United States also had many active angel funds, helping them become start-up hubs, Tam told the South China Morning Post in an interview. “Lack of angel funds and early-stage investors for start-ups is the weakest part of the capital market ecosystem in Hong Kong for us to attract start-up founders to come here,” Tam said. To solve the problem, Hong Kong needed to make it easier for angel funds to cash in their investments through listings or mergers and acquisitions, said Tam, who was also an angel fund investor in many start-ups. “In the US, it is very easy for companies to go public, which is why there are many angel funds and start-ups,” he said. “If Hong Kong could make it simple and easy for newly set up good potential start-ups to raise funds, more angel funds would be based here, and also the start-up founders would like to set up businesses here,” Tam said. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), the city’s bourse operator, is leading the charge. In September, it launched a consultation paper proposing to shorten the post-listing waiting period for spin-offs from three years to one and reduce the number of transactions requiring shareholder approval. Analysts widely saw the proposals as a way to enhance the city’s appeal as a listing destination. Established in 1980, HKEIA promotes the development and global expansion of Hong Kong’s electronics and technology industries. The association now has about 300 corporate members, including over 20 large listed companies such as Lenovo, VTech, Gold Peak Technology Group and others. The association also advises on and helps organise activities that promote the city as a fundraising hub for start-ups and a technology centre, in line with the goals of the government’s five-year plan. Hong Kong would also need to arrange more matching activities connecting start-ups with investors, Tam said. As part of these efforts, HKEIA will host a Future Industries Zone at the Electronic Fair, held from October 13 to 16 at the Hong Kong Convention & Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. The event will unveil a list of the top 100 future industries pioneers. HKEIA would also arrange for about 30 of the selected pioneers to meet with angel investors, family offices and other institutional investors, Tam said. “Hong Kong has already been very successful in helping large innovative companies to raise funds in the stock market and bond market, but it needs to also help more smaller players to raise funds and go global,” Tam said.

title: How shadow banking feeds Myanmar while starving its military
description: Myanmar’s exiles and migrants rely on informal currency swaps to fund their families while starving the military regime.
content: On a recent Friday night in a Bangkok dive bar, a group of young Myanmar exiles sang softly along to a mournful ballad played on an acoustic guitar. None among the crowd had any plans to leave, either for their homeland or home for bed. They fled war, a broken economy and forced conscription into a military that seized power in the 2021 coup. While their future in Thailand is uncertain, their ties to home are kept alive by the hard currency they send back each month to parents and siblings left behind in devastated village economies. Aung*, a 31-year-old from the government-controlled Bago region, used to work at a state-owned bank. But since fleeing Myanmar he has relied on a shadow banking system to bypass state-sanctioned remittance channels that take a hefty cut. That means most of the 3,000 to 5,000 baht (US$90-US$150) he sends home every month reaches his mother and sister. “I only use the agent in my home village. The exchange rate is better and the military does not get the money,” he said. Village-level agents are the front end of Myanmar’s “hundi” system, a network built on kinship, trust and community that can deliver money to remote hamlets within a day or two, even amid conflict. “My agent is like my brother, I trust him 100 per cent,” Aung said. Rules enacted in 2024 require migrant workers to send at least 25 per cent of their earnings home through Myanmar’s official banking channels, with non-compliance punishable by travel bans and passport confiscation. Last year, such remittances totalled US$5.6 billion, or about 38 per cent of foreign inflows, according to non-public Finance Ministry data cited by Bloomberg. That pales in comparison to the US$8 billion that Myanmar’s government estimated was remitted in 2015, though this did include money sent through both official and unofficial channels. A decade ago, total remittances were thought to account for as much as 13 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product. It is not known what that percentage is today, but it is almost certainly higher given the millions based abroad sending money back home. Foreign direct investment, by comparison, barely topped US$1 billion last year, by Myanmar state media’s own admission. The government, desperate for foreign currency to pay for essential imports, sees remittances as a quick and reliable source of cash. Money sent by relatives abroad is also a lifeline for those left behind in a nation where inflation spiked to nearly 25 per cent in June, according to the World Bank. The kyat, Myanmar’s currency, has lost about three-quarters of its value against the US dollar since the coup, its worth battered by conflict, natural disasters and economic mismanagement. Giant currency swaps Money sent home by Myanmar’s migrant workers through the unofficial hundi system rarely, if ever, crosses the border as physical cash. Instead, it operates more like a giant currency swap. In Thailand, small sums of baht collected from migrants are pooled in border towns like Mae Sot and Mae Sai to pay Thai exporters directly for goods. Myanmar importers then hand over the equivalent value in kyat to hundi agents, who distribute it to migrants’ families while charging a transaction fee of around 2 to 2.5 per cent. In Myanmar, a country that has been at war with itself for generations, this informal system has been in operation, in one form or another, for decades. It now dwarfs official banking channels and works, by comparison, like clockwork. Customers get a better deal too, enjoying an exchange rate that can be twice as high as the official rate of around 2,100 kyat to the US dollar. It works just as well for Myanmar nationals living and working in Malaysia. Ju*, a migrant from Yangon, said the hundi system was as easy to use as walking into a shop in Kuala Lumpur’s Pudu district or elsewhere in the Klang Valley, with the money arriving fast, at a better rate and without the daily withdrawal limits imposed by conventional banks. Some people “have been cheated before”, Ju conceded. “So usually, we test an unfamiliar agent by sending a smaller amount first. Usually it arrives within a day.” Chasing foreign cash In Naypyidaw, former military chief Min Aung Hlaing’s government would like some of that money. The coup leader swapped his fatigues for the title of president in April and his administration – civilian in name but military in character – needs foreign currency to pay for imports. Thailand, meanwhile, wants the influx of Myanmar migrants in the country, nearly all of whom work, to be regularised, moving millions from the shadow economy into one that is taxable, or at least more visible. As many as 4.6 million Myanmar nationals were based in Thailand as of September last year, according to the International Organization for Migration – forming what Thai government-linked think tank the Institute for Strategic Policy called “the largest single migrant-worker corridor in Southeast Asia” in a report published last month. Their remittances “are a critical source of household income and national foreign exchange for Myanmar,” the report said. “Yet the overwhelming majority of these flows continue to move through informal channels – principally the hundi system – rather than through banks or licensed money transfer operators.” Some Thai banks have partnered with Myanmar digital payment platforms such as KBZPay and AYA Pay to offer cross-border transfers at rates that now compete with the black market. But opening a Thai bank account requires a passport and other documents issued or notarised by the Myanmar embassy, creating an impossible hurdle for exiles who crossed the border illegally or fled conscription into the military. Thai authorities would also like the legions of migrant workers from Myanmar to pay into social security or health schemes so they do not place a strain on public services intended for Thai citizens. “The issue for the Thai side is we have to find a way to pay for their health, education and social facilities,” said Pana Janviroj, executive director of the Institute for Strategic Policy, suggesting that employers could start paying a small monthly contribution to welfare funds for legal employees. In the meantime, some of those who did use the hundi system “may be charged more, some are taken advantage of”, Pana warned, adding that both governments had a security interest in monitoring cross-border money flows because “a lot of grey money goes into this system”. None of this is persuading the exiles back at the bar in Bangkok. Mistrust of Myanmar’s military-backed government just runs too deep. “If I register, the government will know about me,” said Mark*, using an anglicised nickname. “Then I will have to fight in the army or they can cause trouble for my family.” He had a more fundamental objection as well. “I don’t want to give the government any money to buy more guns and bombs to use on us.” *Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

title: Japan crowns youngest winner at Asian Games
description: Primary school student Yuki Kurihara, aged 11, may be the Games’ youngest champion in history.
content:
The Asian Games has crowned teenage champions before, but this edition has witnessed stunning successes by child prodigies, culminating in Yuki Kurihara standing atop the podium aged just 11.
The Japanese primary school student demolished opponents three times his age on the way to a historic gold in esports at the games in Aichi-Nagoya.
He is Japan’s youngest Asian Games champion in history and almost certainly the youngest the games have ever seen.
Kurihara did not even react after winning the final in Puyo Puyo Champions, a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs.
The boy, who does not turn 12 until June and wants to be a train driver when he grows up, later explained that he felt “embarrassed”.

title: Rising sea levels are reshaping a California beach town
description: After years of erosion, the state is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Nino.
content:
For years, residents of one Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-coloured sand and dip their toes in the waves.
However, that walk has been cut short. Coastal erosion has been eating away at the beach in San Clemente, known for nearly a century as a “Spanish village by the sea”. The rising sea and crashing waves have pushed the shoreline landward.
It’s one of many California coastal communities grappling with the effects of rising sea levels. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California’s beaches could significantly erode by 2100.
After years of erosion, California is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Nino, a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific known to warp weather worldwide.
A recent study showed that El Nino events are getting stronger because of human-caused climate change.

title: Trump, Rubio weigh firing US ambassador to Greece: official
description: Decision on Kimberly Guilfoyle expected as State Department’s inspector general looks into reported questionable conduct.
content: US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. A senior US official said on Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely p***** off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are likely to decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled. In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the US embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her. After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here”. But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. The official said Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied. A second US official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss staff matters, said the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Wall Street Journal late last month and have since multiplied. The second official could not say if a formal investigation had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staff and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential inspectors general investigation. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Congressman Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. Since late September, the Wall Street Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Wall Street Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a US$100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The newspaper then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British newspaper The Daily Mail, said Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece. Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son, Donald Jnr.

title: How can Hong Kong support student-athletes in sports careers beyond competing?
description: Study reveals 28 per cent of secondary school pupils want to work in sports, but over half do not know roles beyond athletes and coaches.
content:
Before joining the Hong Kong national sailing team, 17-year-old Huang Ziyan thought a career in sports meant either competing for a spot on the podium or coaching on the sidelines.
“I was under the impression that opportunities in sport were a lot more narrow,” said Ziyan, who represented Hong Kong at the Asian Games in 2023 and at the Youth Sailing World Championships in 2024 and 2025.
“Going to the [Hong Kong] Sports Institute opened my eyes ... You could be a sports psychologist, a physiotherapist, a strength coach or work in sports science,” explained the student-athlete who is attending Harrow International School Hong Kong.
Recent landmark achievements – from Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s historic tennis gold at the 2026 Asian Games to Olympic triumphs by Cheung Ka-long and Siobhan Haughey – have fuelled a surge of youth interest in sports.
But not every dedicated athlete can enter the spotlight, and a think tank is hoping to show young sportspeople how to integrate their passions into a long-term career.
More than one in four secondary school students in Hong Kong are interested in a career in sports, yet 56 per cent are unaware of professional roles beyond competing or coaching, according to a study released in August by a think tank, Our Hong Kong Foundation.
The research team surveyed 1,098 secondary school students across more than 40 schools.
The NGO found that 28 per cent of students expressed a desire to work in the sports sector, but barriers included unclear entry pathways and a lack of practical exposure.
To unlock the potential of off-field roles, the think tank recommended establishing a dedicated government or NGO team to coordinate career exposure programmes.
It also urged the Education Bureau, Hong Kong Sports Institute (HKSI) and the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau to publish citywide dual-career guidelines for schools, standardising flexible timetabling , leave policies and exam rescheduling for student-athletes.
Our Hong Kong Foundation researcher Joyce Chan noted that dual-career pathways could expand athletes’ networks, sharpen their decision-making and ease their transition after secondary school.
Drawing on European Union guidelines, Chan stressed that Hong Kong needed a comprehensive framework to help schools tailor support to individual student-athletes.
“This could include a dedicated resource pack alongside local and overseas case studies,” she said.
She also urged HKSI to expand its Elite Athlete-friendly School Network, which encourages secondary schools to support student-athletes in pursuing sports while maintaining their studies. Currently, only 9 per cent of secondary schools are part of the network.
Hong Kong student-athletes mainly rely on three paths in progressing to higher education in the city.
The Education Bureau’s School Nominations Direct Admission Scheme (SNDAS) allows schools to nominate students with exceptional performance in non-academic areas – including sports – for university admission.
The Student-Athlete Learning Support and Admission (SALSA) Scheme, offered by the University Grants Committee (UGC), specifically targets elite athletes. Universities also have their own admission schemes for student-athletes.
Funding for the SALSA Scheme, however, has only been allocated until the 2027-28 academic year.
“If the SALSA Scheme becomes a regularised, permanent policy, parents won’t have to worry as much, allowing athletes to truly focus on their sport during their peak competitive years,” said Clara Wong, who led SALSA’s implementation at City University (CityU).
“They can dedicate themselves to athletic excellence knowing that the university system will provide solid support for their degree.”
Once student-athletes have enrolled, managing academic demands alongside high-performance training requires dedicated institutional support.
“My goal when setting up the programme was to show athletes that sports aren’t limited to just one rigid path,” said Wong, who is a senior physical education officer at CityU and a former national table tennis player. “Students eventually realised that ... almost any discipline can be merged with sports.”
She added that managing SALSA was a chance to integrate her sports background with her accounting degree – an experience she hoped to pass on to others.
“When athletes realise they have choices beyond just studying sports, it opens up a whole new world,” she said.
Despite the daily demands of competitive sports, Wong pointed out that student-athletes would still be held to the same academic standards as their peers.
The institutional goal, Wong noted, should be finding a middle ground that maintained academic fairness while guiding professors on alternative evaluation methods.
“As young athletes, our mindset is usually very simple: we just want to win medals and play our sport. We rarely think about what comes next,” she shared.
“Having a mentor or professional coach step in and ask a single critical question – ‘How do you plan to arrange your next three years of study, and what will you do after graduation?’ – completely changes your trajectory . It made me start planning ahead and take my education seriously.”
Wong also pushes students to get involved in sports-related initiatives outside school: “Volunteering is a great way for them to realise how big the world really is and how many opportunities exist beyond the pitch,” she said.
Rather than viewing competitive sports as a phase, Ziyan hopes to study psychology, economics or public policy as a way to stay involved in sports development.
“One thing I’m really passionate about is increasing access to sailing and other sports,” she said. “I’m also interested in psychology because it plays a crucial role in youth development ... for athletes and youth in general.”
Beyond its influence on her future, Ziyan said being a student-athlete had also shaped her holistic development.
“The skills I’ve developed as an athlete – discipline, resilience and organisation – have helped me in my studies. Similarly, being able to focus on things for a long period as a student has helped my training,” she said.

title: Six-year-old Chinese girl sets world record with Rubik’s Cube
description: Lian Yunzhi is ‘the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds’, according to CCTV.
content:
A six-year-old Chinese girl has set a new women’s world record for solving a 3x3 Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds.
Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice last month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, said China’s state broadcaster CCTV.
She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times.
Lian is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV added.
A video CCTV posted showed the small girl wearing a red bow on her head as she turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube. After solving the puzzle, she placed the cube on the table, clapped her hands and pumped a fist into the air.
Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the young girl from Chengdu was first introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class, one of various extracurriculars alongside dance and music lessons, her mother, Lin Yangxi, said.

title: Editorial | Beijing is right to reserve its fiscal firepower
description: The central government is prioritising ‘precision’ and ‘effectiveness’ in efforts to stimulate the economy, but local debt presents a harder challenge.
content: Finance Minister Lan Foan’s latest article offers an authoritative glimpse of Beijing’s fiscal compass. Its timing is telling: demand is flagging, external headwinds are stiffening and the Central Committee’s fifth plenum convenes in late October. Beneath the dry prose lies a weighty message: the real test is not only how hard to stimulate the economy but how to mend local governments’ battered finances. Stimulus comes first. The keywords are “precision” and “effectiveness”, signalling Beijing wants to avoid repeating the broad, debt-fuelled expansion of September 2024. The latest package, while significant, is narrower. It includes a rate cut for policy banks and the country’s first interest subsidy for new commercial mortgages for first-time homebuyers. This restraint is sensible. Growth is near the official target, and earlier measures, such as ultra-long special government bonds, are still being absorbed. With banks’ net interest margins at a historic low of 1.4 per cent, broad rate cuts would hurt lenders. Targeted measures coordinated by the finance ministry and central bank offer a better path. Beijing is right to reserve its fiscal firepower. The harder issue is local debt. Unresolved, it blocks any meaningful lift in domestic demand and remains a major economic risk. Lan reports about 5.8 trillion yuan (US$865 billion) of a 6 trillion yuan bond programme to swap local governments’ hidden debt has been issued, suggesting that resolution is entering its final stage. Equally telling is his warning that new hidden debt and false debt-reduction claims will be strictly investigated and punished. Deleveraging and risk control remain a priority; Beijing will not simply flood the economy with cash for short-term growth. That is the right direction, but the swap deals with existing debt, not the conditions that created it. Lan now turns to deeper structural risks, such as the operating deficits of local government financing vehicles. He stresses strengthening local public budgets, hinting they may widen tax sources and keep a larger share of value-added tax. The case is strong. Local governments carry most spending responsibilities, from social welfare to infrastructure, yet rely for revenue on land sales and transfers from Beijing, both squeezed by the long property slump. Central government spending rose 6 per cent in the first eight months, but local spending grew just 0.3 per cent, so overall general public budget spending rose only 1.2 per cent. The general budget deficit more than doubled from 2.76 trillion yuan in 2019 to 5.66 trillion yuan last year, with a record 5.89 trillion yuan budgeted this year. Short of money, authorities have withdrawn promised tax incentives and closed loopholes. In July, a 20 per cent tax was imposed on gains from offshore trusts with mainland beneficiaries or assets. In September, a 1994 dividend tax exemption for foreign individuals was scrapped. These are stopgaps. On September 28, a cabinet meeting chaired by Premier Li Qiang called on local governments to utilise unused borrowing limits. Beijing did the same in 2024 and 2025, allocating 400 billion yuan and 500 billion yuan respectively. But local governments have often used less than their quotas, suggesting more room to borrow is not the whole answer. For decades, local officials were rewarded for pumping up gross domestic product, producing breakneck construction and encouraging rampant property speculation. Beijing now wants an end to wasteful local subsidy races, hence the State Council’s planned “negative list” of entities local authorities may not subsidise. It also wants them to shift from a production-centred model to providing public services. Without steady revenue, they cannot do so. Lan’s often vague wording is understandable: policymakers must guide the public without upsetting markets while retaining leeway to act. Beyond strict fiscal policy, the greater challenge is ensuring there are bigger payoffs after years of investment and infrastructure building. Fixed-asset investment has fallen 7.2 per cent this year, a sign the old growth engine is running out of steam. As the plenum approaches, Beijing needs to turn hints into concrete reform. Lasting growth in domestic demand depends on putting local finances on a sound footing.

title: Is it fashion or is it art? Hong Kong’s Vann Jewellery falls somewhere between the two
description: Vann Kwok’s sculptural, narrative-driven jewellery pieces have been displayed in several art exhibitions.
content: While clout and trendiness may be the currency of contemporary fashion, Hong Kong costume designer-turned-jewellery artist Vann Kwok chooses to prioritise artistic narrative over social capital or seasonal hype. Kwok founded Vann Jewellery in 2019 “to create something cool and fashionable, but now, I’m a middle-aged woman”, she quips. “Being cool isn’t essential to me any more; it’s not something I feel compelled to achieve. “If people find my work cool, thank you – but it’s really a platform for self-expression. Nowadays, I treat my brand more as my way of communicating with the world.” Kwok, now in her early forties, studied fashion design at Hong Kong’s Polytechnic University, and spent most of her twenties in the local film industry as a costume designer. In 2013, she took a leap of faith and enrolled in the fashion artefact master’s programme at the University of the Arts London. She immensely enjoyed the course’s “super experimental” approach and its strong focus on material, which encouraged her to question the boundaries between art and fashion. With her “more sculptural, conceptual” work, she won in the jewellery categories at the European International Talent Support Awards in 2015 and the UK-based Arts Foundation Jewellery Award in 2016. The awards gave her visibility and partially funded her living expenses, helping her secure jobs in London, first at one of Hussein Chalayan’s stores – no longer in operation – then in Vivienne Westwood’s jewellery department. That gave her the perfect start: Chalayan is known for his avant-garde, high-concept designs, while Westwood’s jewellery leaned towards the costume category, right up Kwok’s alley. Embracing imperfection in her work In 2017, she returned to Hong Kong and by the time she founded Vann Jewellery, she was exploring the same “body sculpture” theme she had developed during her years in London. “I love looking at – and if possible, touching – sculptures, furniture and anything three-dimensional,” she says. “Flat, two-dimensional stuff isn’t really my thing. I adore colours too … my work’s always been about material and very much about the process and embracing imperfection. All these keywords are still very important whenever I create a collection.” Her new “Isekai” collection, scheduled for release in early 2027, reflects those ideas. Isekai, meaning “strange world” or “other world”, is a Japanese sci-fi fantasy subgenre that revolves around a person’s journey through an unfamiliar new dimension. In many ways, it fits with Kwok’s otherworldly aesthetic of expressive forms. “Much of my work is organic shapes, curves and fluid states that appear frozen in flow, but their development is never finished,” she says. “It means that I may decide at this moment the piece is done, but I often revisit my older work, taking it out again to continue working on it.” Kwok says that, at least in Hong Kong, her work is more popular with people from the art world than the fashion industry. In 2026, she exhibited her pieces twice in contemporary art settings. Between June and August, her work was featured among 22 artists in the “Dreamedcore” group exhibition at Gold by Serakai Studio in Wong Chuk Hang. She also showed her work at “The Pleasure-Dome of Hills: A Curated Hallucination of a Modern Literati”, a group exhibition at the Ora-Ora gallery in Central’s Tai Kwun complex, between August and October. The latter exhibition’s theme reminded her of her carpenter father’s rosewood furniture and her own experience with landscape paintings, leading her to create a new “Continuum” series comprising three pieces of earrings and brooches that explore the visualisation of qi. “It’s a mix of my childhood memories, my own design DNA and the gallery’s brief about shanshui [landscape] paintings – not about brushstroke technique, but how people historically hung them at home to create an atmosphere of peace and a contemplative mental space. That concept guided my inspiration.” Finding her niche Seven years into Vann Jewellery, Kwok seems to have finally found the perfect audience for her anti-trend, non-commercial fashion jewellery. This has been no easy task in the fashion industry, as often people’s “first question was never about the narrative”, she explains. “There are a lot of practical concerns and figures, which are correct for their world, but maybe I’m not the fittest candidate for that.” On the other hand, people in the art industry seem to be more curious about the stories she wants to tell and have an innate understanding of the sculptural and conceptual aspects of her work. When asked whether she was nervous about dipping her toes into the art world, she says it felt like the perfect time for her and Vann Jewellery’s journey. “The best part was that they never asked me to pretend to be an artist,” she adds. Instead, the curators that she has worked with so far “respect that I’m a designer and maker who works somewhere between fashion and art”. Today, she oscillates between considering Vann Jewellery a “brand” and a “project”. “I feel like if I called it a brand, people would question how I run the business, where I sell and how I sustain,” she says. “I feel bad that I kind of failed in all those commercial aspects, so I think it may be better to call it a project.” Kwok keeps an active online store with some of her pieces available on online fashion marketplace Farfetch. Every year, she releases a main collection and a collaborative collection with a local stylist. She also makes made-to-order, customised pieces. “Most importantly, I do a pop-up [event where I sell my pieces in a physical space] at the end of every year,” she says. “As for sustainability … magically and thankfully, it’s worked out for now, though I don’t know how, either.” Vann Jewellery will hold its annual pop-up at the end of October, with details to be announced. For more information, visit vannjewellery.com or @vann_jewellery on Instagram.

title: Filipino domestic helpers in Hong Kong pursue degree dreams
description: Non-profit organisation FullPhils partners with universities in the Philippines to offer online courses for domestic workers abroad.
content:
When Dyan Agonoy left the Philippines to work as a domestic helper in Hong Kong, she had to leave her family.
“I’ve missed a lot of my kids’ milestones ... I’m always the only one missing from the pictures,” she said.
Agonoy left university, married young and started a family. Without the bachelor’s degree required for many jobs, she took up domestic work abroad.
Her life changed in 2024, when she came across FullPhils, a non-profit organisation that helps overseas Filipino workers in Hong Kong earn bachelor’s degrees. The courses are fully online. The group subsidises 80 per cent of the costs, leaving students to pay about HK$600 per term.
FullPhils was founded in 2022 by Emilio Baja, when he was just 14 years old. Originally from the Philippines, Baja lived in Hong Kong for two years. He was struck by the crowds of domestic helpers gathering every Sunday in makeshift tents and on cardboard boxes.
FullPhils partners with institutions in the Philippines, including AMA University, Philippine Women’s University and the University of the Philippines, to offer domestic workers online courses where they can be full-time students.

title: Drivers face ‘longer-than-expected’ clearance times at revamped Huanggang crossing
description: Checkpoint opens after six-year redevelopment, but motorists report long waits, unfamiliar clearance equipment and unclear signs.
content: The revamped Huanggang Port has officially opened after six years of redevelopment, becoming the first border checkpoint between Hong Kong and mainland China to use a “joint clearance” system for immigration. The facility, which the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office says is the largest single-building land port in the world, opened at 6.30am on Monday. It replaces the old Huanggang Port in Shenzhen, which served Hong Kong residents arriving by shuttle bus from the San Tin public transport interchange or by private vehicle via the Lok Ma Chau control point. With immigration procedures for both the Hong Kong and Shenzhen sides integrated within the building, authorities have said clearance time will be cut from 30 minutes to five minutes for travellers on foot, and from 10 minutes to two minutes for vehicle drivers. Senior officials from Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangdong province took part in an opening ceremony at the new facility on Sunday. At the ceremony, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu called the new infrastructure “a critical milestone” in cross-border connectivity, while the retirement of the old checkpoint, in use since 1989, embodied the collective memory of generations of residents. The South China Morning Post tracks the crossing’s opening and operations on its first day. ‘Longer-than-expected’ clearance times for private cars Private cars faced “longer-than-expected” clearance times as the new port opened. Vehicles queued on San Sham Road in the morning before making their way to the new port. Police cordoned off an area as a temporary traffic buffer zone and directed vehicles from there towards the building. Driver Ho Shun-ping, in his sixties, waited 25 minutes in the buffer zone and another 30 minutes at the “integrated information collection device” before crossing the border in his car. “It actually took a long time because many drivers were using the device from the car for the first time,” he says. “They parked a bit far from the device and had to jump off the car to check, the staff inside the booth then had to help manually one by one.” Ho adds the process reversed the usual pattern at the old crossing, where it used to be “car waiting for people (crossing the border on foot), but today is the opposite”. “The overall process took longer than expected compared with my usual experience at the old crossing,” he says. Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, says unclear signs on the Shenzhen side directing drivers to the new Huanggang building also caused confusion among Hong Kong motorists. “Some drivers spent at least 10 minutes around the Shenzhen side of the border and could not tell the road signs to the new or old border,” Lee says. “I hope the Shenzhen side will update the electronic maps and road signs as soon as possible.” ‘First in line’ for a tour Members of a tour group from mainland China held up signs bearing slogans such as “New Huanggang, First in line” and “Huanggang Port debuts from centrestage” as they arrived at the public transport interchange before 9am. A 52-year-old woman who gave her surname as Kuang said she and 11 family members travelled for five hours by high-speed rail from Hunan to Shenzhen before crossing the border. “It’s great! It’s fast, it’s modernised and service is great,” Kuang says. She says she brought her 78-year-old mother to Shenzhen for the first time, along with several aunts and other family members. “This port is more convenient, unlike other ones where you have to walk for a long time,” Kuang says. The Hunan native says the family will continue their trip on Monday with a day tour of Hong Kong, including sightseeing at Victoria Harbour. Timothy Chui Ting-pong, executive director of the Hong Kong Tourism Association, says he expects local travel agencies to launch tours themed around the revamped Huanggang Port in the near future. He says the main attraction will be the “Eye of Huanggang”, an eye-shaped observation deck inside the newly reopened port building that serves as a landmark photo spot. Chui adds that some mainland tour groups visiting Hong Kong have already switched to the revamped port for their departures that day. Several agencies have also organised tours to the mainland departing from Kowloon via the new facility. Tour groups from Hong Kong were among the first visitors to the new Huanggang Port on Monday morning. Travel agency Big Line Holiday signed up 1,000 people for 20 tours departing between 10am and 1pm. Each tour includes a buffet lunch and a visit to Honghuashan Park in Shenzhen. Participants came to witness the opening of the 24-hour port. Cecilia Wong, a Yuen Long resident in her seventies, visited with her husband and brother to try the joint clearance process. “I would like to see how smooth the process of using one identity document is, but I have no plan to visit nearby spots in Huanggang,” she says. “I saw on the news that many civil servants were mobilised for stress tests, so I want to see how big the building is.” But she adds that Shenzhen Bay remains the most convenient crossing for her trips to the mainland. Weekend surge expected Eddie Choi Shun-kei, chairman of the Non-Franchised Public Bus Association of Hong Kong, says passenger demand and traffic volume will surge at the weekend as the Chung Yeung Festival is on Sunday and the related public holiday on Monday. “With the opening of the new control point and a three-day long weekend in Hong Kong, we estimate that passenger flow will reach its peak this coming weekend, especially on Sunday,” he tells a morning radio programme. “In terms of service frequency, our buses run about every 10 minutes during peak hours. However, we estimate that during the Sunday return peak, demand could be high enough to require a departure every three minutes.” As the new port building operates round the clock and allows all public transport to enter, competition will be keener among operators, he says. “But opportunities will come from the massive passenger capacity of this new control point. We expect our passenger volume to at least double from current levels,” he adds. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki also pointed to crowd management challenges at weekends. “The biggest challenge lies at weekends,” he says. Lifts alone ‘take more than 5 minutes’ Hong Kong travellers have been trying out the new Huanggang cross-border terminal for the first time, with mixed reactions. In the arrivals hall on the Shenzhen side, visitors take photos and try facilities such as a robot coffee booth. Some Hongkongers visit a comprehensive service centre on level five, where staff answer questions about transport and routes in Cantonese. Lau, in her fifties, picked up a Shenzhen tour guidebook from the centre. “We used to go to Shenzhen via Huanggang two to three times every week, and the new building is definitely more convenient than the former two-place, two-clearance arrangement,” she says, adding that she will use the new facility more often. Lee, a Tung Chung resident in his forties, took a cross-border bus directly to the new terminal in just 35 minutes. He says the journey is much faster and more convenient than the previous arrangement, which required a bus transfer to the old Huanggang Port. “The new port is really big and new. I hope other borders can also adopt this machine, because after all, having to go through two clearances takes more time,” he says. Lee adds that although he registered in advance to use facial recognition clearance, he still had to use his Hong Kong identity card. Helen Ho, 70, who travelled from Sham Tseng and uses a walking stick, says the building felt too big for her. “I don’t feel it’s actually faster as the building is so big and I have to take many lifts. And I have not been guided enough along my way,” she says. Lai, who works in the container industry and lives in Shenzhen’s Futian district, described a similar experience. He says that although joint clearance was faster, “taking all the lifts in the building for different levels feels like it already cost me more than five minutes”. Lai checked his route with staff in the building and says they answered his question, but adds that, “These people are here because it is just the first day, there will not be that much guidance after it’s been running long-term”. More than 5,000 travellers in first two hours Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung says the new Huanggang control point recorded 5,170 incoming and outgoing passengers, 60 per cent higher than expected, and 953 vehicles, exceeding projections by 30 per cent, between 6.30am and 8.30am. “We have arranged sufficient manpower and service ambassadors to provide immediate support and guidance to travellers and drivers,” Tang says. The security chief adds that a joint command centre set up with Shenzhen authorities will remain in operation “as long as it is needed”, including weekends and during the Apec meetings in Shenzhen and Hong Kong in November and late October respectively. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan says that as of 8am on Monday morning, around 1,200 people had taken public transport to enter Shenzhen via the revamped port. At the same period, around 2,000 people had boarded public transport in the city after entering Hong Kong via the revamped crossing. Chan reassures residents that public transport services will be sufficient despite three public bus routes stopping at the San Tin interchange to pick up tour groups. A public transport buffer area has been set up outside the checkpoint building, with the minister saying the area can hold 200 vehicles. “We can arrange some emergency and contingency arrangements, including stacking bus, minibus and taxis,” Chan says. The Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office says the revamped port is the largest single-building land port in the world. Clear signs and short lines at public transport interchange At the public transport interchange on L2, passengers begin streaming in after 8am. Queues are short, however, with just one line of 14 people waiting for the B13 bus to Hong Kong Island East at 8.30am. KMB staff hold up signs indicating bus stop locations and help passengers find the right route to take. A 22-year-old construction worker surnamed Shi says he finds it easy to locate the stop for the B11 bus to Tin Shui Wai, where he is heading for work. “I’ll use the new Huanggang Port if I’m not in a hurry, as the B11 bus doesn’t come that often,” he says. “The bus departs at 10-minute intervals.” A bus enthusiast from mainland China, who gives his surname as He, says he took the last shuttle bus from the old Huanggang Port to Hong Kong on Monday, then caught another bus to the revamped crossing. “I think the signage is quite clear here. The map provided by the Transport Department showing bus route locations is good,” he says. The student says transport arrangements were more chaotic at the San Tin interchange, which linked the city to the old Huanggang control point. A mainland influencer who gave his surname as Yang says travelling via the revamped port had cut his journey time from Shenzhen to Hong Kong International Airport by 30 minutes. He is due to take a coach directly from the revamped port to the airport. “It’s mainly because clearance time is shorter,” says Yang, who films travel content in Southeast Asia. Bumpy first ride Setting off as the first bus from San Tin on the substitute route for the old shuttle bus to the new Huanggang building, Citybus route B13 departed from San Tin at around 6.10am. More than a dozen passengers on board were given a first-ride certificate and a special bus notepad as souvenirs. A retiree surnamed Lee said she lived near San Tin and had come specially to take the bus and enjoy the new facility. She kept taking pictures and inspecting the new road to the new border crossing, describing it as “much wider and more beautiful than it was before”. But she noticed the bus returned to the San Tin Interchange after a few minutes’ ride. “Why are we coming back to where we started? Is the driver going the wrong way?” she asked. Another passenger replied that “the driver took the old way to the old port facility and had to head back”. Lee said she seldom used Huanggang Port, although she had continued going to Shenzhen more than two or three times a week to buy food and had meals there for years. “It’s mainly because the bus connections are not as good as those to the Futian checkpoints. And today I feel the signage at the San Tin interchange is not clear – it took me 10 minutes of asking around to find the right spot.” Lee said she was surprised the first bus could go to the wrong place: “Does that mean we cannot be the first batch to pass through clearance?” The bus headed in the right way and then stopped halfway along the road to the new building. “We have to wait until after 6.30am to enter the new facility,” a Citybus staff member told passengers. The first B13 trip arrived at the new port at around 6.36am. Staff said the bus normally took just five to 10 minutes from San Tin to the new Huanggang building. ‘Farewell to last ride’ The final Huanggang cross-boundary shuttle bus, connecting the San Tin interchange and the old Huanggang Port, departed at around 6.15am, drawing the service’s nearly three-decade journey to a close. Signs at the bus station and on the buses carried farewell messages thanking passengers for their support over the years. Some members of the public made a special trip to see the bus off. Among them was Desmond Lam, a 21-year-old university student, who arrived at 3am to catch the final trip. He brought a self-made farewell poster. “I preferred taking the bus to Huanggang Port because it’s more comfortable. I want to say goodbye to the bus with years of memories,” he says. Kelly Lai, a care worker at a home for the elderly who lives in Shenzhen for its lower cost of living, took her final ride from the old Huanggang Port to San Tin, where she transferred to a bus bound for Sheung Shui. She used to spend about 30 minutes, about half of her one-hour commute, crossing the old Huanggang Port. “I hope I can get more sleep starting tomorrow, now that I can use the new facility with faster clearance,” Lai says. Final inspections and ‘satisfactory’ opening Shortly before the revamped Huanggang Port opens, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki and security chief Chris Tang Ping-keung inspected the “joint clearance” automated lanes. Director of Immigration Benson Kwok Joon-fung and Commissioner of Customs and Excise Chan Tsz-tat also joined them. Chan, the city’s No 2 official, says the opening was “satisfactory” and that passengers he had talked to reflected a smooth clearance. Chan adds that authorities have installed 500 temporary signs inside the building and 300 more along roads leading to the checkpoint. “We will need time to familiarise ourselves with operations here. I hope that by the weekend, our staff are well familiar with procedures and capable of handling the passenger surge,” Chan says. A young man who gave his surname as Jie says he crossed the border from Shenzhen to Hong Kong shortly after the checkpoint opened to see the new development for himself. “It’s really bright and spacious overall. The mobility route for passengers is also clear,” Jie says. A Shenzhen resident who gave his surname as Liao says he crossed the border into Hong Kong at around 6.30am and returned to the mainland shortly before 7am. Liao, who lives in Shenzhen’s Longgang district, says the clearance process was smooth, with barely any queues inside the building. “The clearance was done in a minute,” he says. He adds that the revamped facility resembles an airport and is more convenient than the old Huanggang Port. “I think other ports can adopt the clearance model here too,” Liao adds. Another mainland resident, surnamed Wen, arrived in Hong Kong shortly after 7am and praised the speed of the clearance process. “It used to be so inconvenient. Now it’s so fast! Like it took 0.001 seconds!” Wen says. Dey Wu, a Shenzhen resident who holds a US passport, says clearance officials told her she was the first foreigner to cross the revamped checkpoint. The finance worker, who is in her twenties, praised the speed of clearance at the staffed counters, saying the process took less than a minute, with the two counters just “one step” apart. “I used to avoid crossing the border to Hong Kong for work, and I used to come once a month. Now, I’d be happy to come twice a week,” Wu says. ‘Joint clearance’ system The revamped Huanggang Port is the first to deploy the new clearance system. Unlike traditional clearance, which handles departure and entry procedures at separate counters, the new system allows travellers to complete clearance by presenting one identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates. Hong Kong residents, both Chinese and non-Chinese, who hold a valid mainland travel permit can use their Hong Kong identity cards interchangeably at the “joint clearance” channel for both outbound and inbound trips. However, authorities have cautioned that eligible residents should still carry both identity documents with them at all times when crossing the border at the new facility. Hong Kong and mainland residents will have to register with immigration authorities on both sides of the border to use the automated “joint clearance” channels. More than 160,000 residents had registered on the Immigration Department’s e-Channel mobile app as of noon on Friday. Hong Kong residents who cannot use the joint clearance channels can still complete clearance via staffed counters. The revamped checkpoint has 134 automated channels using the “joint clearance” system and 64 manual counters. Access by authorised public transport only Hong Kong residents can reach the revamped port by bus, green minibus or taxi. There are six daytime bus routes and three green minibus routes that end at the revamped crossing. Taxis would begin service at the new checkpoint as early as 6am, an industry source said. Up to 600 taxis will serve the checkpoint on its first day of operation. Only taxis from the city’s five premium fleets are allowed to take bookings from arriving travellers inside the building. Travellers can book their rides using the respective apps for the taxi fleets. There is no designated pickup area for non-fleet taxis but passengers can queue at the taxi ranks for urban or New Territories cabs. Expanded capacity The old Huanggang checkpoint in Shenzhen handled an average of 40,000 travellers a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people, with a daily average throughput of 9,000 vehicles and a peak of 12,000. The revamped crossing is expected to be able to handle up to 300,000 passengers a day. The Immigration Department said it expected around 100,000 people a day to pass through the new crossing during initial operations. It can also handle 15,000 vehicles a day. Guangdong’s top official, Huang Kunming, last week called on Shenzhen to use the upgraded border checkpoint to better align with Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis plan. Huang, the province’s Communist Party secretary, described the checkpoint as a key hub for cross-border exchanges. He said its “co-location” clearance arrangement was a reflection of the “one country, two systems” governing principle. Huanggang Port tours A number of tour agencies have posted advertisements on social media promoting the redeveloped border checkpoint as a new attraction for trips to the mainland, touting “five-minute clearance” at the port. One agency said bookings had risen significantly after the government announced that the revamped checkpoint would be open on Monday. Another said its first tour sold out in under three hours. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that authorities anticipated strong interest in the crossing and had allocated extra manpower, as well as drawn up contingency plans to cope with unexpected surges in passenger numbers. He said his bureau would activate its Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre to oversee operations, while a joint command centre would also be set up with Shenzhen authorities. Tang urged those who did not need to use the crossing immediately to delay their visits.

title: Laopu Gold deepens Hong Kong footprint with entire-floor lease at Central tower: sources
description: Mainland Chinese jeweller set to move into One Exchange Square to support its global expansion plans.
content: Beijing-based jeweller Laopu Gold has leased an entire mid-floor at One Exchange Square in Central to support its global expansion, according to two sources familiar with the matter. The brand was taking around 13,000 square feet at the flagship Central tower, which houses Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), one source said. The deal comes as mainland consumer firms and financial institutions increasingly anchor their presence in Hong Kong’s core business district. Recent transactions on the 36th floor of the same building fetched monthly rents of some HK$1.69 million (US$215,000), according to Centaline Property Agency data. Property consultancy firm JLL concluded the Laopu Gold deal, a source said. The jeweller and the landlord, Hongkong Land, both declined to comment. Established in 2016 and renowned for its handcrafted heritage pieces, Laopu Gold has emerged as a rare winner amid China’s consumer slowdown, benefiting from demand for gold as a safe-haven asset. Its stock price has surged more than tenfold since its 2024 Hong Kong listing, making it one of the exchange’s best performers and drawing strong investor interest. The office expansion aligns with aggressive overseas plans outlined by founder and chairman Xu Gaoming during the company’s August 26 interim results presentation, where he vowed to open flagship stores in the United States, Canada and France in 2027. Many Chinese financial institutions and major consumer brands have tended to establish large office operations in Central or Admiralty after listing in Hong Kong to enhance their brand image and attract international talent Alex Lam, Colliers Many Chinese financial institutions and major consumer brands have tended to establish large office operations in Central or Admiralty after listing in Hong Kong to enhance their brand image and attract international talent The move comes despite broader industry headwinds. A 30 per cent decline in China’s gold and jewellery consumption in the first half of 2026 and a sharp correction in international gold prices weighed on the group’s second-quarter performance, although Xu insisted Laopu faced “no earnings pressure”.
