The brand already operates three high-performing Hong Kong boutiques, including a flagship store at IFC in Central and outlets at Harbour City and on Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, which routinely draw long queues. “Many Chinese financial institutions and major consumer brands have tended to establish large office operations in Central or Admiralty after listing in Hong Kong to enhance their brand image and attract international talent,” said Alex Lam, executive director and head of Hong Kong Island office services at property consultant Colliers. Lam said in a statement on September 28 that HKEX’s transition from tenant to owner through its HK$6.3 billion purchase of its permanent headquarters in April last year showed its commitment to Central. Laopu Gold’s lease underscores a flight-to-quality trend driving Central’s office market. Prime Central and greater Central office leasing activity was up 16 per cent this year as of the third quarter, outpacing growth of 6.1 per cent across the overall office market, according to data from property consultant Cushman & Wakefield. Occupancy at landmark towers like One IFC and The Henderson exceeded 90 per cent.

title: Spark Deep Dive: Hong Kong uses AI to track rodents
description: Government is deploying thermal cameras to map areas of infestation as public hygiene concerns grow.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
The city’s rodent infestation problem is getting worse
Hong Kong resident Yau Suk-ming was startled when a rat leapt out from her kitchen blender. The rodent ran away before the 74-year-old retiree could catch it. Still, she was not surprised to see the rat. Earlier, she had noticed rat droppings in her flat in Kowloon City.
Rats can be seen around the city’s wet markets, butcher shops and fresh produce stores. They have become a cause for concern about public health and hygiene.
The number of live or dead rodents caught or collected in Hong Kong in the first half of 2026 stood at 87,105.
The annual number had risen in the past decade, from 37,169 in 2016 to 157,182 in 2025 – a 323 per cent increase.
Still, authorities have said their containment strategy is working. The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) said it was using the latest artificial intelligence (AI) technology to track and capture rodents.
For instance, thermal imaging cameras installed across Hong Kong take images at two-minute intervals from 7pm to 7am for three consecutive nights, every six months.
The system’s AI algorithm detected and counted rats from their thermal signature. It also analysed the frequency of their appearance and peak activity hours and mapped dispersal routes, a spokesman said.
This provided the rodent absence rate. The rate was measured by dividing the number of snapshots in which no rats were detected by the total number of images taken.
“A high rodent absence rate gives the impression that Hong Kong is almost rodent-free in certain districts. Yet, some residents have reported that the rat infestation problem is getting worse,” said Brian Wong Shui-hung.
He is a researcher at local think tank Liber Research Community.
According to department statistics, rodent absence rates exceeded 90 per cent across all 18 districts in the second half of last year. Eastern, Islands and Tuen Mun districts were more than 98 per cent rat-free, while Sai Kung topped the list at 99.5 per cent.
Wan Chai and Kowloon City were the only two districts with more than 10 locations recording a rat absence rate below 80 per cent.

title: Create your own rattle drum and enjoy a fun game of copycat
description: Learn the history and cultural significance of this Chinese instrument and how to play rhythmic games with friends.
content:
Ever wanted to play a drum beat, but don’t know how to play the drum? A rattle drum can solve that problem.
This traditional Chinese instrument was made of bamboo with drumheads on a pole.
Two beads were attached to it with a string. The beads strike the drum to create a rhythmic and distinct sound. The rattle drum was once a recognisable signal for street vendors and a popular children’s toy. Still, that doesn’t mean it was just for children.
Historically, the rattle drum was used in Chinese ceremonies. It was also considered a sacred instrument and used in rituals to ward off evil.
It symbolised good fortune and joy. The rhythm of the rattle drum reflected the festive atmosphere of the celebrations.
1. Paint the bottoms of the plates red. Let the paint dry.
2. Use masking tape to attach the sturdy paper straw to the centre of the unpainted side of one plate.
3. Take the two pieces of ribbon and attach a bead to each one. An easy way to do this is to thread the ribbon through the centre of the bead and tie a knot. Use masking tape to attach the free ends of the ribbon near the edge of the unpainted side of the plate, about 2cm away from the centre.
4. Place the second plate on top of the one with the straw. Make sure the red sides face outward, and the ribbons hang out.
5. Imagine the drum is a clock. Staple the plates together at the 12, 3, 6 and 9 spots on the “clock”. Ask an adult to help.
6. To make noise, hold the drum’s handle in your hands and twist it back and forth.
Now that you know how to play the rattle drum, let’s play a game!
1. With a friend, take your rattle drum and play a pattern of beats.
2. Your friend has to copy the beat you played. If they fail, you get a point. Use the table below to keep track of your scores.

title: Deep Dive: Hong Kong turns to AI to tackle rat problem
description: Government is deploying thermal cameras to map areas of infestation but experts say underlying issues, like waste management, must be addressed.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Hong Kong is using AI to detect and map rodents
More than 87,000 rodents caught in the first half of 2026
Hong Kong resident Yau Suk-ming was startled when a rat leapt out from her kitchen blender. The rodent scurried away before the 74-year-old retiree could catch it. Still, she was not surprised to see the rat. Earlier, she had noticed rat droppings in her flat in Kowloon City.
Rodents lurking below the city’s wet markets, butcher shops and fresh produce stores have increasingly become a cause for concern about public health and hygiene.
The number of live or dead rodents caught or collected in Hong Kong in the first half of 2026 stood at 87,105. The annual number had risen in the past decade, from 37,169 in 2016 to 157,182 in 2025 – a 323 per cent increase.
Despite this rise, authorities have said their containment strategy is working. The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) said it had deployed the latest artificial intelligence (AI) technology to track and capture rodents.
Thermal imaging cameras installed across Hong Kong take images at two-minute intervals from 7pm to 7am for three consecutive nights, every six months.
The system’s AI algorithm detected and counted rats from their thermal signatures, analysed the frequency of their appearance and peak activity hours and mapped dispersal routes, a spokesman said.
This provided the absence rate. The rate was measured by dividing the number of snapshots in which no rodents were detected by the total number of images taken.
“A high rodent absence rate gives the impression that Hong Kong is almost rodent-free in certain districts, yet some residents have reported that the rat infestation problem is getting worse,” said Brian Wong Shui-hung, a researcher at local think tank Liber Research Community.
According to department statistics, those rates exceeded 90 per cent across all 18 districts in the second half of last year. Eastern, Islands and Tuen Mun districts were more than 98 per cent rat-free, while Sai Kung topped the list at 99.5 per cent.
Wan Chai and Kowloon City were the only two districts with more than 10 locations recording a rat absence rate below 80 per cent.
District councillor Lam Tak-shing attributed the rise in sightings in Kowloon City to 65 active construction sites, where vibrations drive rats into public spaces.
He noted that the Highways Department has repaired broken concrete and sewage pipes off Ma Tau Wai Road to restrict rodent movement, bringing the district’s infestation largely under control.
To ensure dynamic surveillance that responded to new rat hotspots, the placement of the thermal cameras was “continuously calibrated” based on verified complaints, live and dead rodent catch figures, routine inspections and views of local communities, an FEHD spokesman said.
1. According to the information in News, which of the following statements is false? (1) The total number of rodents caught or collected has increased by 323 per cent over the last nine years. (2) Thermal imaging cameras record images for 12 hours straight every night throughout the year to calculate the rodent absence rate. (3) Sai Kung achieved the highest rat absence rate among all 18 districts at 99.5 per cent. (4) Kowloon City was the only district to report over 10 locations with a rat absence rate under 80 per cent.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (3) only C. (2), (4) only D. (3), (4) only
2. Based on your understanding of News, explain ONE reason why a high rat absence rate reported by the FEHD may not accurately reflect the actual rodent situation on the ground.
3. Do you think using AI thermal imaging technology is an effective strategy for managing Hong Kong’s rodent problem? Give TWO reasons for your stance using News and Glossary.
1. Identify ONE district in which the number of dead rodents collected increased significantly between 2022 and 2024. What trend has it been on since 2024?
2. Using the information in News, explain why this area has so many dead rodents.
Underlying issues need to be addressed to solve the city’s worsening rodent problem, experts say
Food waste and illegal dumping contribute to rat issue
Although many Hong Kong districts are reporting high rodent absence rates, that does not mean the city is rodent-free, according to Michael H. Parsons, an urban ecologist at the Centre for Urban Ecological Solutions. It could simply mean rodents have shifted to areas that were not under surveillance.
One way to gauge the scale of a rodent problem – regardless of official metrics – was to measure sightings in the daytime over a few days, Parsons added.
Ming Wai-kit, an associate professor at City University’s department of infectious disease and public health, said cities such as London and Paris face rat issues due to high urban density, food waste and ageing drainage systems.
These cities have tackled their infestations by cleaning water sources, sealing off abandoned buildings and drains, and using traps and surveillance. Ming cited Tokyo’s approach to dealing with rats, including strong public hygiene practices and proper food waste recycling.
To control rat levels in Hong Kong, authorities must address illegal dumping and improve food waste handling, Ming explained. While Hong Kong’s problem is less severe overall compared to other cities, infestations remain serious near markets, housing estates and eateries.
He suggested that the government create an online reporting system for residents to report rat sightings, helping authorities measure and contain them.
Local businesses have taken their own actions. For example, Kowloon City grocery store Chan Hing Wong Foods pays HK$700 monthly for professional pest control.
Employee Yan Chan called the service worthwhile, noting that rats could otherwise damage inventory, resulting in greater losses.
Lawrence Iu Chun-yip, executive director of the think tank Civic Exchange, highlighted the government’s integrated rodent control framework.
He urged authorities to focus on sustained outcomes, such as measuring the time required to clear a rat-infested area and observing whether the rodents returned after eradication.
In 2024, the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) launched an anti-rodent charter encouraging private stakeholders to step up inspections. In the same year, the FEHD conducted strategic anti-rodent operations at 97 priority rodent blackspots.
However, enforcement challenges persist. In July, contract workers were caught keeping trapped rats and feeding them apples and sweet potatoes instead of exterminating them, resulting in the contractor’s suspension.
Peter Leung Kwong-yuen, chairman of the Pest Control Personnel Association of Hong Kong, supported the government’s move to establish a charter aimed at rat control in residential buildings. He urged the government to step up contractor training and oversight of how workers handled the pests.
An FEHD spokesman stated that proactive inspections, enforcement, education and public complaints guide resource deployment. They urged property managers, food businesses and residents to all play their part.
1. Why are daytime rat sightings a good indicator of Hong Kong’s rodent problem?
2. Using Issue, identify and explain TWO measures that can help control or prevent rodent infestations in Hong Kong.

2. Do you think the government’s strategy for eliminating priority rodent blackspots has been successful? Explain using News, Issue, Glossary and your own knowledge.

thermal signature : the infrared heat pattern emitted by a living organism that allows cameras to identify and track it in the dark

integrated rodent control framework: the Hong Kong government’s unified, cross-departmental strategy that combines multiple methods, such as hygiene enforcement, structural repairs and waste management, to combat pest populations
anti-rodent charter : an initiative launched by the government that invites owners of residential buildings and commercial units to commit to anti-rodent efforts on their premises
priority rodent blackspots: areas that officials have deemed as needing targeted measures because they have a high concentration of rats

(any one)

Effective: Using AI thermal imaging technology is an effective strategy for managing Hong Kong’s rodent problem because the cameras can track rodents, their peak activity hours and dispersal routes using thermal signatures. Data collected also allows authorities to calibrate camera locations continuously based on complaint hotspots, routine inspections and community views. Not effective: Despite high statistical absence rates (over 90 per cent across many districts), overall rodent capture numbers have skyrocketed by 323 per cent over the past decade, showing the underlying problem persists. Relying on absence rates creates a false impression that districts are almost rat-free, potentially delaying necessary public action and hygiene measures. (accept all reasonable answers)
1. Kowloon City saw a big increase between 2022 and 2024. After 2024, the number of dead rodents collected decreased steadily from 2024 to 2026. (accept all reasonable answers)
2. A district councillor blamed the rise in rat sightings in Kowloon City on construction sites that would drive rats into public spaces.
1. The thermal imaging only works at night, but rats also move around in the day, which is also when they would cause disruptions to people’s lives. (accept all reasonable answers)
2. Cut off the primary food source that attracts and sustains rodent populations near markets and eateries / Allow residents to register rat sightings, helping authorities measure prevalence and deploy targeted resources / Repair broken concrete and sewage pipes to restrict rodent movement and prevent them from entering public spaces / Encourage private stakeholders and shopping centres to step up regular inspections, traps and other preventive measures (any two)
3. Policy charters and outsourcing rely heavily on frontline execution, but poor oversight can lead to failures in enforcement, such as contractors keeping and feeding trapped rats instead of exterminating them. To bridge this gap, the government must move beyond simply launching frameworks and instead focus on sustained outcomes by tracking concrete metrics like systematic drives to clear rats from certain districts and recording the success or failure of these drives. (accept all similar answers)
1. The number of priority rodent blackspots consistently decreased year after year. The total reduction was 19 blackspots from 108 in 2023 to 89 in 2026.
2. While the government’s strategy for eliminating priority rodent blackspots has achieved measurable progress, its long-term success remains limited due to gaps in enforcement and surveillance. On one hand, official data shows a clear reduction in citywide blackspots from 108 in 2023 to 89 in 2026, supported by AI thermal imaging and an integrated rodent control framework that drove annual rodent captures to a 323 per cent increase over the past decade. Initiatives like the anti-rodent charter have also engaged private stakeholders to step up building inspections. On the other hand, a high statistical rat absence rate does not guarantee a rodent-free environment, as thermal cameras can miss rats that shift outside surveillance zones or activity windows. Furthermore, serious implementation issues, such as contract workers feeding trapped rats instead of exterminating them, demonstrate that policy targets do not always translate to effective pest control on the ground. True success will depend on sustained oversight, managing food waste density and tracking rat recurrence rather than relying solely on blackspot counts. (accept all reasonable answers)

title: Toasted skin syndrome: why you shouldn’t leave a laptop on your skin
description: This rash, also called erythema ab igne (EAI), is caused by long-term exposure to low heat.
content:
Doctors warn that they are seeing more children with a reaction caused by resting electronic devices on their skin.
Erythema ab igne (EAI) is also known as toasted skin syndrome. It is a netlike rash caused by long-term exposure to low heat.
EAI is usually found in adults who use hot-water bottles or heating pads (see graphic). But it is becoming more common among young people who use electronic devices.
A preteen boy was diagnosed with EAI after resting his laptop on his stomach for up to eight hours a day.
Dr Mara Znagoveanu wrote about this in BMJ Case Reports. She is from the University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust.
The doctor said the patient went to the children’s emergency department with “spontaneous bruising”. Neither he nor his parents could pinpoint what caused the rash. He was well, with no trauma or symptoms such as fever or weight loss. Blood tests and scans were normal, so he went home.
Two weeks later, the patient returned to hospital as the rash had worsened. Areas of his skin were peeling.
It turned out that the boy was being home-schooled and used a laptop for learning. He rested the device on his stomach for up to eight hours a day, usually while it was charging.
The boy was later diagnosed with EAI. A number of months later, the boy’s father told doctors that the rash eventually went away.
Znagoveanu said: “EAI may be overlooked in children, especially when the source of heat is less obvious than the traditional sources such as hot-water bottles and heating pads.”
EAI is usually reversible. Once the heat source is removed, the rash improves over weeks to months.
But in some cases, it can leave permanent dark marks on the skin.
Znagoveanu explained that there were currently no official medical guidelines for diagnosing EAI in children. Doctors had to rely on a patient’s medical history and typical physical symptoms.
She added that recognising the condition early by asking the right questions could save young patients from unnecessary medical tests.

title: Listen Up: Rediscover Taiwan’s forgotten films one reel at a time
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Joshua Dummer, a production editor on SCMP’s China desk, and Young Post deputy editor Esther Cheung.
Voice 1: In a dimly lit red-brick house in central Taiwan, film hunter Wang Wei and his team carefully extract ageing film reels, preserving the delicate remnants of a cinema boom that nearly faded from history. These rare Taiwanese-Hokkien films are locally referred to as taiyupian . They thrived briefly from the mid-1950s to the late 1960s, during a time when Taiwan was under the Kuomintang government, which had fled after its defeat by the Chinese Communist Party.
Voice 2: Until the late 1980s, when the Kuomintang lifted martial law, Mandarin was promoted as Taiwan’s official language, which marginalised Taiwanese Hokkien. Despite this, independent and private filmmakers continued to produce popular black-and-white films in this dialect. Today, Taiwan is working quickly to restore these decades-old films to preserve an important chapter of its cultural history.
Voice 1: Film preservers have saved fewer than a sixth of the estimated 1,200 films produced. Arthur Chu is chairman of the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute, or the TFAI for short. He says the films’ value lies in how they have existed for such a short period of time, while representing the post-war generation.
Voice 2: The films ranged from popular operas to thrillers, comedies and romance dramas. They resonated with many Taiwanese who had been educated during Japan’s colonial rule and had limited Mandarin skills. There were even Taiwanese Hokkien versions of international blockbusters such as James Bond and Tarzan .
Voice 1: Some taiyupian were produced quickly with limited budgets to meet booming demand, which made them “crude” or even “absurd”, Chu said. But they also provided a rare visual record of everyday life in Taiwan at the time. They captured old Taiwanese dialogue and slang, becoming a valuable record for film researchers and linguists.
Voice 2: Wei, the film hunter, said that rediscovering these movies would honour those who worked so hard to make them and capture the images of Taiwan during that era. He emphasised that if the rare vintage reels are discarded or allowed to deteriorate, they will be lost forever.
Voice 1: Wei mentioned that locating Taiwanese-language films is quite challenging. He has spent the last 10 years seeking out vintage films. On one occasion, he discovered rare celluloid films at an old theatre in the US city of Los Angeles. Wei collaborates with the government-funded TFAI, which has devoted nearly two decades to locating surviving film reels. Many of these films were either lost or left to deteriorate due to the island’s hot and humid climate.
Voice 2: Ageing cellulose acetate films are also susceptible to developing “vinegar syndrome”. This chemical decay can cause the film to become brittle, warped or sticky. To repair these films, they must first be stored in a cold environment. After this, they can be repaired by hand, scanned and digitally cleaned and corrected.
Voice 1: Among those helping preserve the films is 86-year-old supplier Wang Chin-ting. He began working in the movie business in 1984 and bought a film company 12 years later. Among the hundreds of reels he collected, only a few are in Taiwanese Hokkien. These reels are currently stored at his ancestral home in Changhua, central Taiwan, where the brick house naturally provides cool, dry conditions for storage. Chin-ting lifts each reel from its flat, circular metal can and threads it through a rewinding machine. This process helps prevent the deterioration of the old films.
Voice 2: At TFAI’s restoration centre in New Taipei City, film restorer Wu Long-hao painstakingly repairs damaged reels by hand using tape, a scalpel and eucalyptus oil. Some reels are in such poor condition that we have to assume they may only survive a single pass through the scanner, he said, adding that if they snap, they are beyond saving.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): Ikebana, the Japanese art of arranging flowers
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] Ikebana, the Japanese art of arranging flowers, is a form of expression that dates back more than 500 years. It continues to blossom, quietly, not only with traditionalists but also with newcomers who find its blend of creativity and mindfulness to be restorative.
[2] Ikebana can be a bit like solving a puzzle, except there’s no fixed answer. Because each flower and human is different, there are multiple solutions. “There’s a ‘detox’ purifying factor and a healing,” said Hiroyuki Okada, 40, who began taking lessons in ikebana about seven years ago. He now teaches Ikenobo, the oldest of three major ikebana schools.
[3] Okada considers himself typical of those drawn to ikebana today: people looking for joy, purpose or solace from the daily grind or pain of modern life. “In arranging [flowers], you are dealing with the life that is there, the beauty, of course, but you find what’s in your heart,” Okada said. “You come face to face with yourself.”
[4] The Kyoto-based Ikenobo school, which is rooted in Buddhism, now has chapters around the world. Ikebana involves interacting with nature, but on a small scale – usually in a little vase. “It is about the relationship of the creator with the flowers,” said Senko Ikenobo, headmaster-designate of the Ikenobo school. Her family dates back generations to the originators of the art. Her father is the current headmaster.
[5] Jeannette Haviland-Jones, professor of social psychology at Rutgers University, said: “[Studies show] that flowers and even flower scents promote happiness in people. We suggested a coevolutionary theory for this in which flowers became the ‘pets’ of the plant world.” Besides a flower’s beauty and fragrance, the feel of its petals and leaves is crucial, like petting a kitten or a puppy, according to Okada.
[6] One traditional Ikenobo arrangement is shoka shofutai , which attempts to arrange the flowers, leaves and branches as they might look in nature, reaching towards sunlight or bending in the wind. The vase, sometimes crafted from wood or pottery, also becomes part of the arrangement’s vision.
[7] Yet the overall look is pure and simple, expressing the life cycle of flowers – from blossoming through withering – through three main elements. Shin , the tallest element, is arranged first, representing one’s core, reaching up to the sky. Soe , which is trimmed to about two-thirds the height of the shin and is placed at the side, expresses the flower’s individuality. The leaves might be slightly faded, representing the later stages of life. Tai , the third element, is the future. Choose a blossom or fresh small leaves, representing things that are being born.
[8] There are also freer, spin-off styles that look more like casual, Western-style bouquets than the textbook-oriented shoka shofutai . That may feel easier and more fun for beginners. Just as ikebana connects a person with flowers, those who practise the art say it’s also about the passing of the art over generations, connecting people.

[1] The Hong Kong Police College has become the first government department to offer a bachelor’s degree programme. The force is set to roll out the course for rank-and-file officers by the end of this year. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming announced the development after the Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications approved the college’s Bachelor of Policing (Honours) (Security and Criminal Investigation) programme.
[2] The curriculum will cover foundational and criminal investigation training. It will also offer internships, including frontline patrols, and language courses. Students will also be expected to complete a thematic report before graduating. According to the Education Bureau’s website, this programme is a part-time, in-house training course that will be valid from August 2026 until August 2031.
[3] The college was started in 2006. It was originally founded as the Police Training School in 1948. It offers many different kinds of training, including a basic programme for recruits and specialised courses for current officers. Chow said that the police have recruited 30 probationary inspectors and 362 police constables for the 2026-27 financial year. Last month, the police began a recruitment campaign at local universities.
[4] The police force has had a hard time reaching its recruitment goals since 2020. It has removed the minimum height and weight requirements. Now, candidates can wear glasses or contact lenses during eye tests. Applicants who did not pass public exams can also take a new written test in Chinese or English to qualify. As of March 2025, the force had a vacancy rate of 17.4 per cent. It plans to hire 130 new probationary inspectors and 1,140 police constables in the 2025-26 financial year.
[5] To become a police constable, you need at least level 2 in five subjects in the Diploma of Secondary Education Examination (HKDSE). Those who have a university degree usually apply to become inspectors instead. The police used to train recruits and officers at the old Police Training School. The training courses mostly focused on practical skills needed for the job, discipline and the basic legal knowledge required to carry out police duties.
[6] After the school was upgraded to a college in 2006, its courses were revised to cover leadership training. It also provided a pathway for frontline officers to pursue further studies. The force partnered with the then Open University of Hong Kong, now Hong Kong Metropolitan University, to deliver modules in the foundation training course for constable recruits. title: Open Questions | Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
description: Veteran US diplomat says containing China is impossible, but urges Washington to shore up its regional partnerships.
content: Kurt Campbell is a veteran US diplomat and strategist who has played a leading role in shaping Washington’s approach to China and the Indo-Pacific for more than a decade. He served as the White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs from 2021 to 2024 and as US deputy secretary of state from 2024 to 2025. Previously, he served as assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs from 2009 to 2013 and was a key architect of the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia”. Often described as the Biden administration’s “Asia tsar”, Campbell also helped develop the Quad and the “small yard, high fence” approach to technology competition. A former US Navy officer, Harvard professor and co-founder of the Centre for a New American Security, he is now chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a Washington-based strategic advisory firm. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. You once argued that America’s enduring advantage over China was “allied scale” rather than unilateral dominance. But China’s strategy today looks different from the one Washington confronted in 2021. China now presents itself as a champion of sovereignty, non-interference and a more “multipolar” order while expanding its diplomatic and security presence. Is this a genuine strategic shift or a new form of competition expressed in different language? What is the realistic objective of US policy towards China today? I think it is the determination of both leaders to take steps to stabilise a complex dynamic relationship between the two countries. Both leaders understand that at the current moment, it is in the best interests of both countries to get along strategically. There are a variety of reasons for that. Some of them rest in a desire to improve competitive advantage. And some are motivated by a desire to genuinely work together. My own sense is that the US is most effective as a global power when it works constructively with its allies and partners. President [Donald] Trump has taken more time and put more focus on building a stronger relationship with China than he has on working with some of his allies and partners. I very much support efforts to stabilise US-China relations. But I would like to see President Trump make more effort to stabilise relations with other partners. For instance, what we’re seeing in relations with Canada is quite shocking, suggesting that Canada is no longer one of the closest friends and partners to the US. I find the fact that Canada is seeking to join the EU quite troubling. My general argument would be that US technology strategy, US efforts to sustain the global order are best achieved not just by trying to stabilise the US-China relationship, but by also seeking to maintain a strong posture with allies and partners. So what is the realistic objective for US policy towards China? There are a number of things that are necessary for US-China relations as we head into the next critical phase. I personally believe that the path to true cooperation between the United States and China on AI is very complicated, especially since President Trump said he seeks a dialogue with China but insists on dominance. That message is a complicated one for Chinese friends to hear. It probably is a disincentive to seek true collaboration, because it suggests that the terms are implicitly or explicitly negative for China. What I think is important going forward is that both countries understand clearly the risks of frontier work, especially when researchers on both sides are increasingly voicing concerns about AI that we don’t fully understand or comprehend. It is important that both the United States and China recognise that racing for advantage in a technological space that holds such potential risk – as well as promise – raises concerns. I would commend the work that the two countries have taken to date to at least find a degree of common ground for a continuing dialogue. But I will also say that this issue is developing rapidly, and both sides are going to need to adapt their position to establish a true dialogue around potential areas of collaboration, on safety reporting and mutual engagement. The question for many of us is what is the appropriate metaphor when we think about AI. Is it nuclear weapons? Is it Covid? Is it climate change? Are there other experiences historically that we can utilise and apply to this new technology in the US-China context? I think the one thing that is unique here is the role of the labs. These are not just technological capacities. They are the most powerful economic and commercial players of modern times. They are absolutely dominant. So they will want a voice in any deliberation between the United States and China. We don’t have as many experiences in the past in which it’s not just government to government, but the most powerful commercial and technological voices as well. So are you particularly concerned about AI competition between China and the US? In the larger context, I am worried about AI writ large. I believe that the politics of AI in the United States are becoming increasingly complicated. There is a bipartisan anxiety about data centres and their development. You’re seeing many states now questioning the buildout of these large entities. There are questions about capital use. There is an incredible level of investment in AI that has taken investment from other areas. In fact, many believe that to the extent that we have economic growth in the United States currently, it is largely because of the investment in AI. But I think more directly, it is undeniable when the most senior people in various companies are calling for government intervention and restraint that alerts us that there is a problem here. Every week there is a new story of an AI entity that has escaped captivity and gone on an excursion, often creating havoc. There are also stories of engineers choosing to resign from these prestigious posts because they are worried not just about an incident but the status of humankind. Many very senior people have worried about human extinction. It seems to me that if that is a truly serious matter and debated among engineers and designers of AI, it is incumbent on us to reflect, to think about guardrails, to consider safety and to understand that there are existential issues here that in many respects transcend simple competition. Let’s talk about Taiwan and Japan. Does strategic ambiguity remain the best policy or have China’s military capabilities and pressure campaigns made greater clarity necessary? I still believe that one of the great success stories of US-China relations – this is rarely discussed – is the complex maintenance of peace and stability between the two countries with respect to Taiwan. There have been lots of tensions and disappointments, but the truth is the status quo has served the interests of the people of Taiwan. I would argue the framework that the United States and China have maintained for decades is being increasingly tested by military and political developments. But I still believe that this framework is in the best interests of all concerned. And so it is often said that we have a degree of strategic ambiguity but tactical clarity; I think that it is important for the United States to underscore our determination to maintain peace and stability. But it is also the case that a dialogue over Taiwan is handled carefully between the two leaders. It’s undeniable that this issue has come up and that it is being actively discussed. If Beijing imposed a quarantine or blockade without launching a conventional attack, would that trigger a US response? I’m out of government now. I’m not really in the business of offering views on particular scenarios. My own sense is that the more we discuss openly potential scenarios, the less it might be stabilising to the situation. If anything, they tend to draw sharp contours in a complex environment. And, in many respects, create even greater distrust. My own sense is that the United States should maintain a strong unofficial relationship with Taiwan, recognise how critical this issue is in a larger US-China relationship and manage this with care and dexterity. Despite the ups and downs, history reflects that it is possible to take the necessary steps to maintain peace and stability. And I fully expect that this can continue. On Taiwan, what is the strategic cost of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable within the broader US-China relationship? Is there any practical form of Taiwan-related cooperation that Washington and Beijing could undertake? What would a credible cross-strait dialogue look like if Beijing continues to reject engagement with Taiwan’s current government? The strategic risk of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable is that it can inject doubt into the credibility that has helped preserve cross-strait stability for decades. While there are deep differences over Taiwan, both Washington and Beijing have a common interest in crisis management, military-to-military communications and reducing the risk of unintended escalation. Given the tensions between China and Japan, what responsibility does Washington have to ensure that the US-Japan alliance remains a mechanism for deterrence rather than escalation? Is Japan primarily becoming a frontline deterrent, an industrial and technological partner or a military coequal? I would simply say that Japan is an important partner of the United States. It has a relatively small military and its defence investments are quite modest. I believe that one of the most critical paths of diplomacy in Asia is to make sure that lines of communication between Beijing and Tokyo are open. My own sense is that the Japanese would prefer to have a more open dialogue with Beijing. I think one of the issues occasionally challenging is that the historical issues still animate Beijing’s thinking about Japan. One of the things that I’ve noted is the effectiveness of Chinese diplomacy generally, their ability to reach out to countries in which they have a complex history. In particular, what we’ve seen is renewed diplomacy between China and India. I think it would be in China’s interests to open up more lines of communication with Tokyo. I do not believe that Japan is somehow an American cat’s paw. The people of Japan are deeply peace-loving. Efforts to revise the constitution or to move Japan in a more assertive direction have actually met with substantial domestic opposition. I think some of the military modernisation in Japan is indeed modest. It is designed to reflect increasing challenges in the Indo-Pacific. And remember, those do not come exclusively in the US or in the Japan-China relationship. What Japan is confronting is an increasingly hostile North Korea that is well armed and has nuclear capabilities. So Japan is seeking to play a larger role in Asia. I support that. But at the same time, I do believe there have been periods in the past where the lines of communication between Tokyo and Beijing have been much stronger. I do know that the Japanese are troubled by how difficult it has been to establish communication with Beijing. And I think just as President Trump and President Xi [Jinping] have found some common purpose and would meet in a complex time, I think President Xi and Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi can find the political courage to sit down as well. China increasingly portrays this sort of alliance – whether it’s with Japan, or trilateral cooperation with South Korea and Japan, or quadrilateral with India, Australia and Japan – as an instrument of containment. Given China’s thinking, how should Washington support their expanded security role while assuring China that these alliances are defensive? The US seeking closer relations between Japan and South Korea has more to do with their own histories than it does with China. I would simply remind Chinese friends that not every development in Asia is about China: South Korea and Japan have profound historical tensions, but they are close allies of the United States. It is only natural that the United States would seek the two countries to coordinate more closely. Each country has its own unique relationship with China. It is also the case that closer coordination among the three could have a stabilising impact across the Indo-Pacific. The Quad has not met at the leader level under President Trump, but its first incarnation in the early 2000s was a result of the tragedy that struck Indonesia and Malaysia. The terrible tsunami. I myself had been actively engaged in the Quad. Much of what the Quad was involved with in its most recent incarnation was Covid vaccine development and South Pacific issues related to education and training. I would say that the Quad was primarily about delivering well-being to underserved groups and creating more capacity. I don’t believe that any country in the Quad would support the institution becoming an alliance aimed at any one country. I see it mostly as developing common approaches to complex societal and security problems. These are four maritime democracies and each again has its own set of relationships. With Beijing, more recently, we are seeing India and China edging closer to a more substantial dialogue. I think the Quad can exist with a range of diplomatic formations in Asia. As much as anything, it helps anchor the United States in the Indo-Pacific, which is in the strategic interests of Washington. Should the Quad become more institutionalised? Or would that make it less flexible and more threatening to China? How vulnerable is it to domestic political changes in these four member states? I cannot speak to what’s expected next in the Trump administration, but there has been no discussion recently of reconvening the Quad at the leader level. I think without that, it’s difficult to sustain active forward momentum. I do not know what President Trump’s ambitions are for the Quad besides the foreign ministry meetings and a variety of other assessments. But I think at this juncture, there is no push or intention towards institutionalisation. If anything, the focus continues to be on areas which are primarily about the well-being, for instance, of Pacific island nations. One of the areas of cooperation in the past, for instance, was on dealing with illegal fishing in the Pacific, which is an issue that Pacific island nations care deeply about and do not have the capacity to address. So I do not see the institution emerging as a direct vehicle for somehow containing China. And I just think that framework is outmoded. China is a great, powerful country with deep interests across the world. It’s not possible to contain China and the most recent work towards this coming summit between the United States and China brings that point home. China is a country that needs to be engaged actively. It is not possible to think about China in the context of containment. Would a reduced US-China rivalry lessen the importance of security partnerships such as the Quad, Aukus and other minilateral groupings? If so, what implications would that have for the balance of power, deterrence and Indo-Pacific stability? Partnerships like the Quad and Aukus are valuable because countries across the Indo-Pacific recognise that many of the region’s challenges, from maritime security and technological change to supply chain resilience and disaster response, require closer cooperation. The value of these partnerships does not depend on the status of the US-China relationship. Even in a period of more stable US-China relations, these partnerships would continue to play a critical role in strengthening deterrence, building collective capacity and fostering a regional balance that supports peace and prosperity. In many respects, the greatest contribution of a grouping like the Quad is the creation of habits of cooperation, strategic trust and practical capabilities. What would the durable regional security architecture look like if it included China rather than being organised against China? Is it possible to have such a thing? We’ve had a number of efforts at regional security or regional dialogue, such as the East Asia Summit, the Asean Regional Forum, which have been established for decades. One of the challenges has been the uneven participation of the United States. We don’t attend all of the meetings. In fact, I think you’ve seen, particularly in the Trump administration, an ambivalence about regional institutions. We’ve long sought to create capacities for more dialogue and cooperation among Indo-Pacific actors. We’ve seen that at Apec. We’ve seen that at the Asean Regional Forum and in the East Asia Summit. I would go as far as to say that, by some measurements, nine of the 20 members in G20 are Indo-Pacific nations. In many respects that institutional innovation was designed to reflect the increasing importance, not just of China but of other rising nations in the Indo-Pacific. I would like to see the United States more actively engaged in that multilateral diplomacy. I do not think it is a secret that the United States is less interested and focused on that diplomacy and seeks, in many respects, to act unilaterally without constraints with other countries. I do not believe that is in America’s strategic interests. I think investing in regional architecture is important and a critical dimension of our national power. What’s your take on the US changing the name of INDOPACOM to USPACOM? It was Trump’s first administration that originally changed it to Indo-Pacific. And now they’re changing it back. I don’t know if that is a desire to return to an earlier period framework. At first, the Indo-Pacific framework was adopted by Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, and that framework was accepted by parts of the Trump administration. When President [Joe] Biden came to power, the Japanese asked for that framework to be continued. We supported that. I do not know if this is a request from President Xi to President Trump, or whether this is a rethinking by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. There are too many things that have happened in terms of Pentagon policy to speculate about why they move in one direction or another. How can Washington reassure its Asian allies and Southeast Asian countries that its partnerships do not force them to choose between the US and China? Is the current alliance-centred strategy sufficiently attentive to Asean priorities? The most important dimension here is for the United States to invest actively in regional institutions and bilateral engagements. Most of the frameworks of engagement that we have seen most recently have been around highly difficult trade relations with a variety of countries in Southeast Asia. I increasingly hear from a variety of Southeast Asian countries that they are adopting policies that allow them to maintain a degree of flexibility in engagement with both Washington and Beijing. The most effective US policy does not demand countries to make some sort of overt choice between the two. And there is a deep recognition that commercial and political ties between Beijing and Southeast Asia are only natural, as is the United States maintaining close ties in Southeast Asia. These are not zero-sum relationships. They can be mutually beneficial. What do you think is Hong Kong’s role in Sino-US relations? And how should the city move forward? It’s a complex city. It’s undeniable. It is, in many respects, a financial launching point for China’s relations with the world. It still has some characteristics of its past, but it is increasingly a Chinese city that has an extraordinarily critical and important role in the global economy. And as far as I can tell, it appears to continue to play a very dynamic role in the global financial economy. And it is continuing to be a meeting place between East and West and the financial centre of activities across the Indo-Pacific. There are other capitals that are emerging in that equation: Singapore, Tokyo and the like. But Hong Kong continues to play a vital role.

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): Brad Pitt and his dog co-star shine in ‘Heart of the Beast’
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] American writer-director David Ayer has built a career on tough-guy films featuring unlikely team-ups – from mismatched policemen Denzel Washington and Ethan Hawke in Training Day (2001) to Jason Statham and some bees in The Beekeeper (2024). However, Heart of the Beast , a soulful survival drama scripted by Cameron Alexander, represents Ayer’s best combination yet.
[2] Brad Pitt stars as retired special forces officer James Belmont, who flies into the Alaskan wilderness in his seaplane to hunt and fish, taking along his best pal, Odin – played by an equally rugged German shepherd called Uber and several stunt pups.
[3] A former combat dog, Odin has a metal leg and titanium teeth from missions that went wrong. Belmont’s scars take a little longer to spot. It is easy to see what draws them to the wilds. The scenery is absolutely stunning – from the bright, spreading glaciers to muddy, Mordor-like swamps, all handsomely shot by Mauro Fiore – and there is nobody around for miles. Well, almost nobody. “There’s nothing like the quiet of nature, a whole world all to yourself,” notes a weathered old-timer played by J.K. Simmons, who briefly interrupts their idyll.
[4] When the pair fly back to civilisation, however, Belmont suffers a heart attack at the controls. A terrifyingly realistic crash – mostly shot from inside the plane – sees Odin flung free, while Belmont is trapped in the wreckage at the bottom of a lake. Touchingly, as the plane goes down, Odin tries to protect his master, though much worse is to come for both of them.
[5] What follows is a tale as old as Jack London’s The Call of the Wild – though Belmont prefers Cormac McCarthy’s The Road . Our injured heroes are forced to trek cross-country, facing inhospitable terrain, angry predators and PTSD flashbacks as they try to reach safety.
[6] Crucially, Ayer has the confidence to build the sense of danger slowly, giving the audience plenty of time to witness the depths of their bond – and the beauty of the landscape – as the noose tightens inexorably around them.
[7] While not as dramatic as The Grey or as ambitious as The Revenant , the film still features tense moments, such as a hair-raising canyon crossing and a fearsome nighttime encounter. Along the way, Belmont requires help from his fiercely loyal four-legged friend – there is even a scene in which Odin helps him reset a bone. However, there are also some surprisingly bad CGI interlopers and a conclusion so syrupy sweet it might deter more cynical viewers.
[8] A film as stark and simple as this stands or falls on the chemistry of its leads, and both deliver. Pitt is good, but Uber is the real star of the show. To remain unmoved by their obvious love would take a heart of stone.
Source: South China Morning Post, September 22

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): AI revolutionises Japanese desserts
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Many people are worried that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) might one day threaten humanity. This has been a big topic in the news. In Japan, the technology is being used for a sweeter reason.It is helping create new desserts for sale in convenience stores. Some customers are bored with the usual egg sandwiches and rice balls. So, big retail chains are using AI to develop new products, including some surprising flavours.
[2] Lawson is one of the largest convenience store companies in Japan. It recently introduced three new food items. These included a lemon tart with pickles and a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yogurt cream. The items were launched in Tokyo and nearby areas. They were created using AI, with the idea being: “What on earth is this? But it’s delicious!” according to a company press release. “To generate ideas unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends, we used AI during brainstorming, without relying on past sales figures or market data,” the press release said.
[3] Lawson rival FamilyMart said it gave sales data to AI to help create a new dessert, which is a French-style canele pastry. This pastry is made with dough containing sweet potato puree and topped with caramel sauce. The company said the dessert is available across Japan. Like Lawson, they used AI to come up with ideas. However, humans were still part of the product development process.
[4] This was not FamilyMart’s first dessert product made with the help of AI. In July, the chain tested a new biscuit sandwich with thick milk cream. The first experiment was a success, so the company decided to use AI to help create more products. A spokeswoman said they are planning to launch more of these items.
[5] The fast-growing abilities of AI have caused a worldwide scare recently. Researchers have warned of the dangers of extremely smart computer systems that might get beyond human control. Top AI labs in the United States have asked for a joint pause on their advanced projects. Meanwhile, discussions are ongoing about how governments should manage the technology.
Source: Agence France-Presse, September 16

title: Opinion | Despite a China-India thaw, military relations are stuck in 2020
description: Xi and Modi have shaken hands, border trade has reopened and direct flights have restarted – but their armies are still not talking to each other.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping has met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi three times in the past three years. Indian pilgrims are back at Kailash, the Tibetan mountain sacred to Hindus and Buddhists. Air China has restarted flights to New Delhi. But can trust grow between two armies that meet only in a crisis? And why does the Pentagon now talk to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) more easily than India’s army does? In September, Xi made his first visit to India in nearly seven years; Beijing says it wants both countries to be “good neighbours and friends”. Later that month, US President Donald Trump hosted Xi at the White House. Two capitals welcomed Xi. But only one lets its army talk properly to China’s. The Sino-Indian thaw has reached everything except the military. Direct flights have returned after nearly six years. Three border trading points have reopened and trade now stands at more than US$100 billion a year. Leaders, traders and pilgrims cross the Himalayas. Why not soldiers? Because two of the world’s largest armies, facing each other along a disputed Himalayan border, are still frozen in 2020. They last trained together in December 2019, at Umroi in Meghalaya, in the eighth round of Hand-in-Hand, a counterterrorism exercise that began in Kunming in 2007. Six months later came the Galwan incident, the first deadly clash on the border in 45 years. Soldiers fought with clubs and stones; 20 Indians and four Chinese died. This May, Umroi hosted more than 400 troops from 12 Asian countries for the inaugural Pragati exercise. China was not among them. New Delhi’s view is that the PLA must earn its way back. The instinct is understandable. But caution is not a strategy. The question is not whether India should trust China blindly. It is whether India can afford to keep distrusting it by default. Washington has answered that question for itself. Last November, US defence secretary Pete Hegseth and his Chinese counterpart Dong Jun agreed to build channels to “deconflict and de-escalate”. In May, Hegseth became the first US defence chief since 1972 to accompany a president to China. The Pentagon treats talking to the PLA as risk management. Delhi still treats it as a concession. Is this thaw a warning that India may be left alone? It is better read as a green light. If the world’s two biggest rivals can compete and keep their generals talking, so can Asia’s two oldest civilisations. India cannot possibly be more hawkish on the PLA than the Pentagon is; yet, awkwardly, that’s what it looks like. Are the new hotlines not enough? In August, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi agreed to add two military hotlines and two meeting points for senior commanders as well as a pledge of “early and substantial” progress on settling the boundary. Beijing deserves credit. But a hotline is a fire alarm: it rings only when something is already burning. Weeks earlier, reports of a stand-off at Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh raised the alarm again. Armies that only talk in emergencies will keep having emergencies. Would engagement reward Beijing for the Galwan clash? No. The incident is the reason to talk, not the reason to avoid it. Along the Line of Actual Control, a de facto border, both armies knew each other’s positions down to the last tent but not each other’s minds. Soldiers on both sides paid for that gap. The objections are real. Pakistan received live inputs from China during Operation Sindoor, India’s four-day conflict with Pakistan in May last year, and 81 per cent of Pakistan’s recent military hardware imports are Chinese. So what should be done? First, revive Hand-in-Hand. Over eight rounds and 12 years, it was the only regular occasion where the two armies met as professionals rather than adversaries. Second, open the staff colleges. India’s Defence Services Staff College in Wellington trains officers from dozens of countries. China’s PLA Army Command College in Nanjing shapes future ground commanders. A few exchanges would let each side study the other’s doctrine first-hand. Would that expose secrets? No more than India’s exchanges with dozens of other armies do. And nothing humanises a rival like discovering that he, too, complains about the mess food. Third, give the hotlines a political spine: an annual defence ministers’ dialogue on a fixed date, whatever the mood on the border. Fourth, train together for disaster. On August 26, a glacier-rock avalanche on the Nepal-China border sent a flash flood down the Bhote Koshi river. Within days, Indian military personnel and two PLA Air Force Y-20 transport planes had landed in Kathmandu. They worked in the same disaster, but apart. Glacial floods do not recognise borders and the next one may strike between India and China. What should New Delhi ask in return? Restraint in the buffer zones, advance notice of large exercises and a joint way to investigate incidents. And why should Beijing agree? Because a quiet Himalayan front frees it to focus elsewhere and because an India that trains with everyone except China will be read by Asia as aligned against it. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will reportedly visit India later this month ahead of a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, a grouping comprising the United States, Japan, Australia and India. But Asia’s peace will not be settled in Washington. For Beijing, it means meeting openness with transparency, and having patience with India’s politics. The diplomats of both countries have done their part. Now their soldiers have to talk.

title: US Homeland Security chief dismisses risk from live-streaming execution
description: Markwayne Mullin rejects concerns that live-streaming Nidal Hasan’s firing squad death would create a martyr.
content: A top Trump administration official said on Sunday that the planned live-stream execution of the perpetrator of a mass killing of US soldiers would not pose an additional security risk to the United States. “I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” US Homeland Security chief Markwayne Mullin told CBS News’ Face the Nation, when asked if it risked turning the perpetrator into a martyr for his cause. “I think people need to understand … if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” he added. Nidal Hasan, 56, a US Army psychiatrist, shot dead 13 people and wounded more than 30 in an al-Qaeda-inspired attack at a military base at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. He would be the first person executed by a US military firing squad since 1945. The plan to publicly broadcast his death by firing squad, scheduled for December 3, was first put forward by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon on Thursday, drawing condemnation in the United States and beyond. President Donald Trump later left uncertain whether the execution would be publicly broadcast. “By showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters Saturday as he left the White House to participate in a political rally in Tennessee. “So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.” When Mullin was pressed Sunday with questions about live-streaming, he told CBS: “No one has to watch it if they don’t choose to”. Trump “leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring America’s values and bringing us … where America should be”. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned the possibility of a public execution in the US as “abhorrent”. “It’s something that I can’t say I ever want to see anywhere in the world,” he told The Rest is Politics podcast. The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder. The Death Penalty Information Centre says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: UK PM Burnham to publish Manchester City dealings after intervention draws criticism
description: Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch urged the PM to publish ‘everything’ related to his work with the club when he was Greater Manchester mayor.
content: Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the football club’s owners raised eyebrows. Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch had urged him to publish “everything” related to his work with the club as Greater Manchester mayor. City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club maintained their innocence and appealed against the verdict. Burnham said last month he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the finding, crediting them with being “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”. His office sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the prime minister was clear the judgment is serious and that where wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the consequences. Burnham said he would “put out there” everything he had done to work with the club’s owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday. He said that “the football issues are different from the investment issues”. “But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do. “I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester. “None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there. “But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they’re not the same thing.” The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd, which had majority ownership of the club.

title: UK’s Burnham says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote
description: First British leader to openly acknowledge Russian meddling warns European allies of ongoing influence efforts.
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered ⁠in the 2016 ⁠Brexit vote, as he warned voters in ⁠France and Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics. Burnham, who took over as Britain’s leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, is the first British prime minister ‌to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday. Burnham did not spell ⁠out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no details on what evidence ‌this statement was based. The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia has previously denied meddling in the ‌Brexit vote, casting Britain as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria. Burnham’s comments mark a departure from ⁠those of former prime ⁠minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian ‌interference in the referendum. Britons voted 52 per cent to 48 per cent to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since ‌World ‌War II. Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to ‌disrupt their politics. “I mean, these things are important now to put clearly on the record, ⁠and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is ⁠instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said. Britain’s government failed to establish whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum on membership of the EU, according to a report by ‌parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee ‌in 2020. The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland’s 2014 independence referendum, in which voters rejected independence. Burnham last month said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the next general election, reopening the country’s divisive debate on its relationship with the continent.

title: Saudi Arabia’s main airport hit by new Houthi strike day after deadly attack
description: Riyadh’s international airport targeted again as strikes expose vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities.
content: A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, killing one person and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there. Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”. Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire. Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added. The fresh attack on the airport killed one person – a Pakistani resident – and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on X. Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT on Monday (5am Tuesday, Hong Kong time), the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform. Multiple blasts could be heard in the Saudi capital on Sunday. “The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city. The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east – which the Houthis also said they had targeted – a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby. Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east. It said early on Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a call with his Saudi counterpart that “insisting on a military approach and disregarding a political solution would further complicate the current situation”, Iran’s state media reported. He said Tehran was ready to help “initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and facilitate the achievement of a political solution”, according to official state news agency IRNA. The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport – where three people were also killed on Thursday – as well as on Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. Although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through. The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”. Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday. A spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry said on X that one of the strikes killed a civilian and wounded five others. Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 people wounded. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before. Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath. “Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident said. The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport. Australia condemned the Houthi attacks as “unacceptable” on Monday, having earlier urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to stay indoors and “shelter in place”. Despite the warnings, Saudi authorities have indicated the 25th World Petroleum Congress and associated events, due to run from Sunday through October 15, would go ahead. The city was also scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative, Riyadh’s flagship investor gathering, later this month. Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa. On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counteroffensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said Saturday. The Houthis claimed to have repelled them. Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Republican and Democrat senators want Trump to reverse course on Russian diesel deal
description: Bipartisan coalition says lifting sanctions violates US federal law funding Moscow’s war effort.
content: Republican and Democratic US senators called on President Donald ⁠Trump on Sunday to “reverse course” on his diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it runs counter to US law barring imports of energy until Russia ends its aggression against Ukraine. “Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” the seven senators – four of Trump’s fellow Republicans and three Democrats – said in a statement. They also said that the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation of its decision, something also required ‌by law. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the statement said. It was only the latest bipartisan criticism of Trump’s deal, a shift from his party’s near-unanimous support for Trump’s foreign policy decision weeks before November 3 midterm elections that will determine whether his Republicans will retain their control of Congress. It was issued by Republican Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ron Wyden of Oregon. Tillis had said earlier on Sunday that the diesel deal may be illegal and would put American lives ⁠at risk. Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its ‌war on Ukraine. “I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis, who is retiring from the Senate in January, told NBC’s Meet the Press. Prices for diesel – used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking – are near record highs and could hurt Republicans in next month’s congressional ‌elections. Analysts have said that Trump’s agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News ⁠on Sunday that the Trump administration will follow ⁠through with the deal using existing legal authority, and the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down. “We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says ‌whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong,” Bessent told Fox & Friends. Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026”, to honour ‌the ‌South Carolina Republican and long-time Russia hawk who died in July. Some other Republicans had also criticised the diesel plan. Retiring congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said on X on Friday that “propping up Putin’s ‌war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”. Mike Pence, Trump’s former vice-president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a “betrayal” of Graham’s legacy and urged the ⁠president to “rescind” it. As Trump’s poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada. But the Senate’s ⁠No 2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel pact, telling CBS’ Face the Nation that Trump is focused on bringing costs down. “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a call on Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made it clear that the diesel deal “is in direct opposition ‌to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies ‌to create peace and stability in Europe,” his office said in a statement. In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an “energy ceasefire” taking effect immediately, but did not elaborate. Zelensky said he was still waiting to see details of that agreement. “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well,” Zelensky said on the Telegram app. There was no word from Moscow on the announcement, which followed days of US pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

title: Drivers detained after coach and truck crash in Turkey, killing 11
description: Authorities launch probe into potential wrong-way driving on western highway corridor.
content: Eleven people were killed and 27 injured in western Turkey on Sunday when a coach turned over after colliding with a truck, authorities said. The coach crashed near the entry to a motorway between the city of Bursa and the seaside city of Izmir, the governor’s office of the local Manisa district said on social media, stating the death toll.
