Emergency services rushed to the scene, Turkey’s Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said. “We are closely following the situation, in coordination with all the institutions concerned,” he said on social media. A photograph published by the news agency DHA showed the coach lying across safety barriers with its windscreen smashed. Turkish media reported that the drivers of both the coach and the truck had been detained as part of an investigation into the crash. Their health conditions were not given. Several reports said the truck involved was a tow-truck. One outlet, Hurriyet, said early indications suggested it could have been driving on the wrong side of the road.

title: Putin aide looks to boost Russian shipbuilding ties with China during visit
description: Nikolai Patrushev said to have discussed potential for Chinese shipbuilders becoming tech partners and suppliers for new Russian facilities.
content: Russia is looking to expand shipbuilding cooperation with China through technology partnerships and joint investment, visiting presidential aide and Maritime Board chairman Nikolai Patrushev said. Patrushev held talks in Beijing with Ke Jixin, Chinese vice-minister of industry and information technology, the Russian Maritime Board said in a statement on Saturday. It said the two sides discussed the possibility of Chinese shipbuilders becoming technology partners and equipment suppliers for new Russian shipyard facilities. Maritime ties are the main focus of Patrushev’s six-day trip, which began in Shanghai on Thursday. There, he visited one of China’s biggest shipyards, Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, acknowledging that cooperation between the two countries on shipbuilding was “quite limited” at present but adding that there was scope for more. “For example, we could jointly build a series of ice-class vessels at Russian shipyards, including those for Chinese shipping in the Arctic,” he said during a meeting with Waigaoqiao executives, according to a report by Russian broadcaster Rossiya-24. “This task is becoming increasingly relevant for China,” he said. “Russia is currently developing a large-scale project for a trans-Arctic transport corridor, thanks to which polar trade routes will become significantly more attractive and safe.” Moscow has stepped up efforts to develop Russian shipbuilding to strengthen defence and security, setting up the Maritime Board in 2024 to coordinate its strategy with Patrushev at the helm. Russia is also seeking to develop Arctic shipping lanes, while China is looking to the region as an alternative for its trade routes affected by escalating geopolitical tensions – creating strong potential for cooperation between the neighbouring countries. Earlier this month at the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, a think tank in Moscow, President Vladimir Putin said LNG carriers and civilian vessels for Arctic operations were being built at the Zvezda shipyard in Russia’s Far East. “We have built there one of Russia’s biggest shipyards – Zvezda – which is building a fleet of superships that even the Soviet Union did not produce. We have launched the production of LNG tankers and super large civilian ships customised for operating in the Arctic,” Putin said. “We are aware that our Chinese friends are also interested in this domain,” he added. On Friday, Patrushev visited Shanghai Jiao Tong University, which is known for its work in mechanical engineering, shipbuilding and ocean engineering. He discussed boosting ties between Chinese and Russian universities and research institutes and the potential for joint research projects and training for the maritime sector. He also toured the Yangshan Port, south of Shanghai, which has topped world container throughput rankings for 16 consecutive years. Patrushev said there were opportunities for joint investment projects. “We can implement joint investment projects to develop berthing and terminal infrastructure at Russian ports, drawing on the experience of the phased construction of the port of Yangshan, which took place over the course of a decade and a half,” he said, according to a separate Maritime Board statement.

title: Russia hits Ukraine power plants despite Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ declaration
description: Russia says Kyiv does not ‘deserve’ a ceasefire for a presidential election. ‘I do not think he deserves a respite’ says FM Sergei Lavrov.
content: US President Donald Trump has sowed more confusion, announcing an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia that sparked astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine’s Western allies. But the ceasefire appeared shaky at best as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, leading to power outages and outrage. Trump’s announcement on Sunday came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, prompting outrage by European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said on Truth Social. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well”. “It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” he told Warsaw Security Forum via a video link on Monday. “If Russia doesn’t agree to energy ceasefire – we will respond.” The Kremlin has nothing to say yet on an “energy truce” although contacts were continuing, spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, according to Tass. Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday that Kyiv did not “deserve” a two-month ceasefire that could enable it to hold a presidential election, which both Moscow and Washington have called for. “I do not think he deserves a respite,” Lavrov said after Kyiv on Sunday called for a 60-day halt to fighting in response to a fresh call from Trump to hold elections. Zelensky said on Monday that multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit in the latest attacks by Moscow and that “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day,” referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that is now used extensively by Russia. Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages – prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries it says fund the war. More recently, Trump’s war in Iran has led to oil shortages and ensuing price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections early next month. The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key Western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. Several leaders called on Russia to uphold the deal. But that support was in contrast to broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has led to mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky. Zelensky said the diesel deal was a “weak decision”, while several of Ukraine’s European allies expressed outrage and pledged to increase pressure on Moscow. Seven US senators – including four Republicans – released a statement Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelensky, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelensky pushed back, telling ABC News that “it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader”. He said that fuel prices were rising because of the war in the Middle East and the blocked Strait of Hormuz. “Everybody understands it,” he said. Germany’s foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to “fully support” Zelensky. “Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government,” Johann Wadephul said in Berlin. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country “strongly supports President Trump’s call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now”. In Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump’s call for Zelensky to be replaced. “I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president,” said 40-year-old Olesia Goncharuk. “We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people,” she said. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Wuhan’s Covid mayor Zhou Xianwang jailed for 14 years for corruption
description: Zhou, who was widely criticised for the delayed announcement that the virus had been detected in the city, was convicted of bribery.
content: Zhou Xianwang, the former mayor of Wuhan widely criticised for the initial handling of the Covid-19 outbreak, has been sentenced to 14 years in prison for corruption. Zhou used various positions he held between 2003 and 2025 – including party secretary of Huangshi, mayor of Wuhan and vice-governor of Hubei province – to “provide assistance to companies and individuals in contracting projects, business operations and administrative approvals”, Shangqiu Intermediate People’s Court in Henan said. In return, he accepted cash and property worth more than 60.5 million yuan (US$9 million), the court said. The court, which tried the case on July 9, described the sum as an “exceptionally large amount” and found him guilty of bribery. It added that Zhou, who was also fined 5 million yuan, had confessed his crimes and returned his illicit gains, which led to a lighter punishment. Zhou was placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the country’s top anti-corruption watchdog, in July last year. Zhou, 64, had climbed steadily through the party ranks in his native province of Hubei and was named deputy party secretary of Wuhan, the provincial capital, in May 2018. In September he was also appointed as the city’s mayor. When the coronavirus was first detected in Wuhan in late December 2019, the city authorities delayed the announcement – a decision that was later widely criticised. The city went into lockdown three days after a meeting of the State Council, China’s cabinet, on January 20, 2020 that told local authorities to take responsibility for their own areas. In late January 2020, Zhou told state broadcaster CCTV that “as a local government official, I can only disclose information after receiving it and being authorised”. He also defended his decision to allow more than 40,000 people to attend a Chinese New Year gathering earlier that month, which helped spread the virus. Zhou said that he and Ma Guoqiang, the former Wuhan party secretary, were “willing to resign to appease the public” as soon as the outbreak could be brought under control. Ma was removed from his post in February 2020 along with Jiang Chaoliang, the Hubei provincial party secretary. But Zhou remained in his job until 2021, when he resigned and went on to serve on the provincial and national committees of the country’s top political advisory body. Jiang has also been convicted of bribery, receiving a suspended death sentence in August. Earlier this year, he featured in a CCTV documentary about corruption, where he admitted receiving funds from a businessman in return for favours for over a decade. The latest big names snared in China’s ongoing anti-corruption drive were Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu, two former defence ministers who were given suspended death sentences in May.

title: In Focus | Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
description: China’s securities firms are pursuing global ambitions, but winning non-Chinese clients may prove the toughest test.
content: China’s investment banks spent decades trying to emulate Goldman Sachs, the Wall Street powerhouse that became a benchmark for the country’s financial ambitions and whose alumni included senior US policymakers like former Treasury secretary Henry Paulson. Today, Beijing’s goal has evolved beyond building a Chinese version of Goldman. At the Central Financial Work Conference in 2023, President Xi Jinping called for cultivating first-class investment institutions as part of China’s ambition to become a financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics. Many analysts and industry players believe the foundations are already in place. China now operates the world’s second-largest capital market after the US, while direct financing through stocks and bonds for the first time surpassed bank lending in 2025, ushering in a golden era for securities firms, they said. The next challenge lies beyond mainland China. As Hong Kong’s role in China’s capital markets expands and mainland companies invest more aggressively overseas, Chinese brokerages are increasingly pushing into international markets. “Overseas business, particularly in Hong Kong, is one of the key growth drivers for Chinese securities companies as they expand beyond their home market,” said Franco Lam, a director at Fitch Ratings. From apprentice to contender Compared with Wall Street and the City of London, China’s capital markets have a relatively short history. When China International Capital Corporation (CICC) was established in 1995 as the country’s first Sino-foreign joint-venture investment bank, its ambitions were global from the outset. Yet its bankers had little experience to draw on. Fang Fenglei, one of CICC’s founding executives, in an article published in 2018 in China Securities Journal, recalled how Morgan Stanley, one of the venture’s founding shareholders, arranged study visits for him to New York and London to learn the operations of Western financial markets, as part of what he described as a journey to “learn from the West”. The learning curve was steep. Paulson said in his book, Dealing with China, that Goldman Sachs bankers gave CICC executives and Chinese officials what amounted to a crash course in taking companies public as they prepared China Mobile’s predecessor for its Hong Kong and New York listing in 1997. The deal raised US$4.2 billion, offering an early glimpse of how quickly the gap between Chinese and Western investment banks could narrow. At the time, the relationship between Chinese and foreign investment banks was heavily tilted in favour of Wall Street, whose firms brought technical expertise and access to international institutional investors that Chinese brokerages lacked. Over the following two decades, Chinese securities firms moved beyond simply learning the mechanics of international investment banking to acquiring the networks and capabilities needed to compete overseas. A first-class investment bank should not merely be large, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent Wu Qing, China Securities Regulatory Commission Citic Securities took a major step in 2013 by acquiring brokerage CLSA from French bank Credit Agricole, gaining an established research, sales and trading platform spanning major global financial centres. More than a decade later, the group is increasingly adopting the Citic Securities International, or CSI, identity across its global operations as it gradually phases out the CLSA brand. Industry veterans liken the transition to one from apprentice to competitor. Wang Junhong, deputy CEO of Guotai Junan International, where he has worked since 2012, said Chinese brokerages spent their early overseas years as “apprentices”, often playing secondary roles on deals led by foreign banks. But as Chinese bankers accumulated experience and recruited internationally trained talent, they progressed from taking part in underwriting syndicates to leading them, Wang said. “You go from being a participant in the underwriting syndicate to becoming the lead underwriter,” Wang said in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. “The apprentice graduates. You become capable of standing on your own, and in some businesses you may even do better.” Today, Chinese investment banks were “at least on an equal footing” with their Western rivals in much of Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market, and led in some areas, Wang said. The rise of Chinese companies had also changed the equation, he said. As mainland businesses grew larger and more familiar to global investors, Chinese brokerages’ understanding of their home market became increasingly valuable. At the same time, the growth of mainland institutional investors and private wealth had created a much deeper pool of Chinese capital to support offshore transactions, Wang added. Beijing’s push for global champions Beijing is giving new momentum to a decades-old ambition as it pursues its broader goal of becoming a financial superpower. China’s securities regulator has set a goal of having two to three investment banks and financial institutions with international competitiveness and market leadership by 2035. Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), said in December that a first-class investment bank should “not merely be large”, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent. The renewed policy push has been accompanied by a wave of fresh capital. At least nine mainland Chinese securities firms had announced or completed plans to inject a combined 51.7 billion yuan (US$7.7 billion) into their Hong Kong operations as of the end of August, according to a calculation by the SCMP. Among the largest commitments, Citic Securities raised 16 billion yuan to support its international business, while Guotai Haitong Securities and Huatai Securities announced plans to inject 9 billion yuan and up to HK$9 billion (US$1.1 billion), respectively, into their offshore units to support overseas expansion. By the end of 2025, 34 Chinese securities firms had established 36 international subsidiaries with combined assets of HK$1.94 trillion, up nearly 32 per cent from a year earlier, according to data from the Securities Association of China. But Wang said the industry’s recent capital injections should not be viewed simply as compliance with Beijing’s policy directives. “When you have a good business foundation and want to do more business, you need more capital to support it,” he said, describing much of the fundraising as “proactive” expansion rather than a sign of weak overseas operations. The timing has also been favourable. A revival in Hong Kong’s IPO market and growing demand from mainland clients for offshore diversification had created new growth opportunities, especially as the recovery in mainland capital market activity remained gradual, Fitch’s Lam said. Hong Kong: the proving ground For most Chinese securities firms, internationalisation has started in the same place: Hong Kong. Wang described the city as both a “bridgehead” and a “core hub” for the industry’s overseas expansion. Its proximity to the mainland, bilingual business environment, and status as the principal offshore financing centre for mainland companies made it the natural first stop, he added. Hong Kong also provided Chinese investment banks with a market where their biggest competitive advantage – deep knowledge of Chinese companies and investors – mattered most. Mainland companies now accounted for about 78 per cent of Hong Kong’s stock market capitalisation and 90 per cent of trading turnover, according to Fitch Ratings. While mainland markets had stabilised in the first half of 2026, profitability growth across the securities sector could moderate in the second half because of a high comparison base and softer market sentiment, according to Fitch. IPO activity on the mainland also remained below levels seen in 2022 and 2023, Lam said. Hong Kong, by contrast, offered access to mainland clients through cross-border links, a broader range of investment products, a diverse international institutional-investor base and global market reach, he said. Changes to listing rules had also enhanced the city’s appeal as a listing venue, Lam added. Those advantages have translated into stronger balance sheets and a growing pipeline of capital-market business. Citic Securities generated 15.86 billion yuan in revenue outside mainland China in the first half of 2026, up 45.5 per cent from a year earlier, while net profit at its international arm more than doubled to US$829 million, according to its interim report. CICC’s overseas revenue rose 45 per cent to 9.19 billion yuan over the same period, accounting for about 35 per cent of its total revenue. Hong Kong subsidiaries of Chinese securities firms accounted for 50.6 per cent of IPO business among the city’s top 30 brokers in the first eight months of 2026, up from 35.3 per cent in 2022, according to Fitch data. The share held by foreign securities firms fell to 26.5 per cent from 29.3 per cent over the same period. Chinese brokerages were also seeking to diversify beyond the more volatile investment banking and trading businesses by expanding wealth and asset management operations, while cross-border investment schemes were creating additional opportunities over the medium term, Lam said. “If you see more opportunities coming ahead, definitely they want to put more capital into areas where there is more growth potential,” he added. Their success in Hong Kong also points to the next challenge: whether advantages built around Chinese companies, Chinese capital and a China-linked financial centre can be replicated in markets where those advantages are less pronounced. There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive Chen Zhiwu, University of Hong Kong Charting a new path The next experiment is already under way. Chinese securities firms are extending their reach beyond their traditional Hong Kong base, with Southeast Asia and the Middle East emerging as key growth markets. China Securities established a regional office in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) in late September to pursue opportunities in equity and debt capital markets, investment banking, asset management and institutional business. CICC opened its own DIFC branch a year earlier, positioning Dubai as a gateway between China and the Gulf region. Southeast Asia has become another testing ground. China Galaxy Securities has built one of the industry’s broadest regional networks, spanning Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. However, the expansion abroad has also exposed firms to the risks of operating beyond familiar markets. Everbright Securities’ investment in European sports-rights agency MP & Silva and Haitong International’s heavy losses during the offshore bond market downturn offered costly lessons. Haitong International lost a combined US$1.7 billion in 2022 and 2023 after defaults swept through the high-yield debt market, where it had become a major player. Winning local trust “There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive,” said Chen Zhiwu, a finance professor at the University of Hong Kong, referring to the next stage of internationalisation in which Chinese securities firms build substantial businesses among local, non-Chinese clients. “Internationalisation is not just about setting up an office in New York or London. That is relatively easy,” Chen said. The harder test, he said, was whether a company in Europe, Southeast Asia or Latin America, presented with a choice between a local bank, a Wall Street institution and a Chinese broker, would choose the Chinese firm to lead its IPO or advise on an acquisition. The same question applied to wealth management: would a wealthy local family be willing to “entrust millions of dollars to a Chinese institution”? Chen asked. “It means that you can make them feel you are one of us or you can be one of us.” Guotai Junan’s experience in Vietnam illustrates the challenge. Its local brokerage, acquired in 2019, ranked about 40th among roughly 80 securities firms in the country and was aiming to break into the top tier over the longer term, according to Guotai Junan’s Wang. “We want to accelerate our growth, and given our client base, capital scale and market expertise, we could become much bigger very quickly. But there are still some constraints,” Wang said. The veteran banker, who also chairs Guotai Junan’s operations in Vietnam and Macau, said an outsized presence by Chinese companies could stir local sensitivities in some overseas markets such as Vietnam. “If a Chinese company became one of the dominant players, they might feel some pressure,” he said. For Wang, Chinese investment banks would only become “truly global” when they could occupy a position in London or New York similar to the one Goldman Sachs and other global banks enjoyed in Hong Kong, and when their client base was no longer predominantly Chinese. “Ultimately, you need to serve local companies with global presence,” he said. “Can you serve an American company like Apple? Can you serve Google?” If that was the case, Wang said, “then I think you could say you have truly become global”.

title: Pakistan imposes emergency in stronghold of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan
description: The federal government and the military have accused Khan’s party of failing to curb ‌Islamist militants.
content: Pakistan’s president declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan on Sunday, the president’s office said, following allegations it had failed to tackle Islamist militancy. The constitution allows the federal ‌government to take over some or all provincial government functions during an emergency. The provincial governor will take charge with an advisory council, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad, adding that the arrangement will initially be in place for six months. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months. “The situation is so grave that you wouldn’t see any residents coming out of their ⁠houses after evening in some of the districts,” said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi. The federal government and the military have accused Khan’s party of failing to curb ‌the militants, while Khan’s party has rejected the accusation and says the federal government has failed to provide it with the funding and equipment needed. Islamabad accuses neighbouring Afghanistan of harbouring Islamist militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says that Khan’s party ‌had been sympathising with both the Taliban in Kabul and their affiliates at home. Both the Afghan Taliban and Khan’s party have ⁠denied the accusation. President Asif Ali Zardari declared an emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a ⁠federal cabinet decision, the president’s office said. The security forces and citizens had been under attack for the last two years, Sharif ‌told the Cabinet. “We can’t just act a silent spectator.” The move comes after Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party rallied for several days to pressure the government for his release, threatening to march on ‌the capital ‌Islamabad in coming days amid deepening political instability. Khan’s supporters say the military rigged the 2024 election against the 74-year-old former cricket star, an allegation the military ‌denies. “This is more of a coup disguised as emergency,” said Zulfikar Bukhari, Khan’s aide and his party’s spokesperson, adding that it risks leading to further bloodshed and instability. Ahead ⁠of the planned march, authorities detained three of Khan’s sisters and hundreds of party activists. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of chief minister Sohail Afridi ⁠of Khan’s party, one of his close aides said. The government has cut access to the capital, Islamabad, to bar the protesters from reaching parliament, blocking major highways with shipping containers and deploying tens of thousands of security forces, interior ministry officials said. The party’s last ‌large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly ‌clashes with security forces. Khan’s 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the standing of the Pakistani military. Cases against Khan have ranged from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All convictions but one have since been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing. The latest protest coincides with public discontent over inflation and rising fuel prices that has spread beyond Khan’s core supporters.

title: Tears and a song as victorious Zheng Qinwen makes China Open history
description: Chinese star stuns Russian rival Mirra Andreeva, makes history as first woman to ever win singles title at home tournament.
content: Zheng Qinwen became the first home winner of the China Open on Sunday as she beat Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4, in front of a partisan crowd in Beijing. The former world No 4 and current Olympic champion was a wild-card entry, having struggled with form and fitness after elbow surgery in 2025. At one point this year she had dropped as low as 122nd in the world. It was the 54th-ranked Zheng’s first title in nearly two years, and her first ever at the WTA 1000 level, and tears filled her eyes as she fell to the court in celebration. “The feeling was incredible to win here in Beijing … in front of my home crowd is one of my dreams,” she said during the trophy ceremony. “I’ve been through a very, very tough year.” She congratulated Andreeva on her French Open win from earlier this year before serenading the National Tennis Centre crowd with a song about chasing the “light of dreams”. The 24-year-old is the first Chinese player to win the prestigious tournament, and the first from the country to reach the final since Chen Li lost to Chinese Taipei’s Wang Shi-ting in 1996. Andreeva, who started the week ranked fifth in the world but will move to No 3 with the next update, was more consistent to start with, but Zheng grabbed back a break and stayed with her 19-year-old opponent as they battled on the baseline. Zheng saved three set points to level at 5-5 and won every single point after that, sending down an ace to take the first set. A crowd desperate to see their home-grown talent crowned champion was at times disruptive as cheers erupted before points ended and shouts for Zheng punctuated serves on both sides of the net. But the players kept their focus, holding serve until Zheng found a way through in the ninth game of the second set, firing brilliantly against the line to break and go up 5-4. A double-fault threatened to derail an imminent triumph until Zheng, defiant, sent down an ace to win on her first match point. It is Zheng’s first trophy since October 2024, when she beat Sofia Kenin in Tokyo. The players’ only previous meeting was in the 2024 China Open quarter-finals, where Zheng beat Andreeva in three sets. Andreeva, playing in her first China Open final, said it was “a very nice week” despite falling just short. “I love playing in Beijing, so of course had a very, very nice time,” she added. Zheng and ‌Andreeva are expected to ‌compete at the Wuhan Open which starts on Monday, with US Open quarter-finalist Zheng eyeing a return to the top 20 in the rankings if she can carry the momentum into the next tournament.

title: ‘A Hawaiian son’: Honolulu honours Sun Yat-sen as his landmarks vanish
description: Few buildings the revolutionary leader knew in Honolulu survive, but descendants of families who funded his cause are keeping his legacy alive.
content: Eddie Flores pressed the button at a pedestrian crossing on King Street, then pointed across the road. In the spring of 1910, Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen lodged over there, on the second floor of a shop owned by a friend and fellow party member. “It’s no longer there,” said Flores, chairman of the restaurant chain L&L Hawaiian Barbecue. “But we can more or less point out where the building is.” Much of Sun’s Honolulu has to be found this way. The church where he worshipped as a boy was pulled down in 1909. The basement where his followers met in secret was lost in a renovation. The theatre where he called for the overthrow of the Qing dynasty’s autocratic rule is now a market. And the place where China’s first revolutionary party was founded is a car park. On November 24, 1894, about 20 men gathered there, on Emma Lane, first in the house of a bank clerk named Ho Fon and then in the house next door. They formed the Hsing Chung Hui, or Revive China Society, and pledged to bring down the Qing dynasty. Their leader was a 28-year-old doctor who had gone to school a short walk away. Both houses were demolished in the 1960s. The families of the men who housed and funded him are still here. They treat his years in the islands as their own history, and they are proud of it. On November 1, Flores and a committee of Chinese-American community leaders will lead the public along that route to mark the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth. The programme includes walking tours, a lei-draping at a statue of Sun as a 13-year-old, the unveiling of a mural and a banquet in Chinatown hosted by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. Where a building is missing, a guide will stand in for it. Hawaii’s governor and Honolulu’s mayor have been invited, along with representatives from China. Flores, who was born in Hong Kong, is of Chinese and Filipino descent and a long-time supporter of causes in both communities. “We consider him to be a Hawaiian son, just like Obama,” Flores said, referring to former US President Barack Obama. “Obama was born here, went to school here.” Sun was born on November 12, 1866, in Cuiheng, a village in Guangdong province. But he once said otherwise, and it got him into the United States. The birth certificate Warren K.K. Luke, chairman of the Dr Sun Yat-sen Hawaii Foundation and chief executive of Hawaii National Bank, told the story this way. In 1904, when Sun sailed to San Francisco to raise money for the revolution, immigration officers stopped him under the Chinese Exclusion Act, the 1882 law that barred Chinese labourers from the country. “He said, ‘Well, I’m Chinese, but I was born in Hawaii,’” Luke said. “And he showed them his Hawaii birth certificate, and they said, ‘OK, you’re OK.’” It was not the first time. According to historian William Zanella, in a paper published by the foundation, Sun reportedly persuaded the American consul in Yokohama in the 1890s to issue him a passport on the same claim. The certificate resurfaced more than a century later, Luke said, when people who doubted Obama’s Hawaii birth pointed to it as proof that the islands’ records could not be trusted. The Exclusion Act was not repealed until 1943. Luke said his own father, a Hawaii-born student in Boston, had to register his birth to be sure of getting home. He sees an echo now. Hawaii, he said, was where people of different backgrounds learned to work together, and it was once held up as America’s natural bridge to Asia. “We were getting to the point where everybody would work together, and now we’re going through isolationist policies,” Luke said. ‘We’re all Zhongshan’ Sun first came to Hawaii at 12 or 13, when it was still a kingdom, to join an elder brother who had prospered as a merchant and rancher on Maui. Over seven visits he spent years in the islands. He was among neighbours. Most of Hawaii’s early Chinese came from the same county on the west bank of the Pearl River Delta, then called Heungshan. After Sun died in 1925 it was renamed Zhongshan, the name by which he is known in Chinese. “My grandfather was a supporter, but so many others in Hawaii were supporters of Sun Yat-sen as well,” said Wing Tek Lum, a Honolulu real estate executive. “The primary reason is that we’re all Zhongshan.” Family memory holds the details. When Sun spoke in public, Lum said with pride, his grandfather carried out the table and brought him a glass of water. Later, at Sun’s urging, he said his grandfather helped found a Chinese-language school that was eventually renamed for him. The family has another connection to the trail. The Lum Yip Kee Building at 88 King Street, which belongs to Lum’s family, housed a shop in 1910 whose basement Sun’s followers used for secret meetings. “It’s not just one person that created this revolution,” Lum said. “There are a lot of people involved. People going back and forth, back and forth.” Luke’s family has its own record. His wife’s grandfather gave money to the cause, he said, and kept the receipts Sun’s organisation issued in return. Chinatown’s district societies keep the memory too. The Lung Doo Benevolent Society was founded in 1891 by migrants from one part of Zhongshan. At the head of its meeting room hangs a black-and-white portrait that members say Sun gave to one of their own. It sits in a dark wooden frame between the American flag and the flag of Hawaii, above a pair of carved chairs. A wavering base Sun’s support in Hawaii was never as steady as it is remembered. Flores said the whole community “supported him wholeheartedly”. Historians describe something slower and more divided. It began small. Honolulu had about 5,000 adult Chinese men in 1894, and only about 20 of them came to the founding meeting of Sun’s society, according to Zanella, the historian. Then it nearly collapsed. In 1900, Liang Qichao, a prominent reformer who had fled China, came to Hawaii to recruit for a rival cause. Sun wanted to replace the emperor with a republic. Liang wanted to keep the emperor, under a constitution. Within six months about 90 per cent of Hawaii’s Chinese had joined Liang’s side, including Sun’s own brother. Sun returned in 1903 and won many of them back, speech by speech. One, on December 13, drew hundreds to the American Theater. The site is now Maunakea Marketplace, entered through a green-tiled gate flanked by stone lions, and it is where the new mural will be unveiled. By 1910, his rallies in Honolulu drew thousands, and more than 800 people joined his party. The enthusiasm faded again within months. When he wrote asking for money, most members did not answer, and by the end of that year only about 30 were still active. Lum acknowledged the split. Many local Chinese “unfortunately” supported the monarchists, he said. The memorials carry their own politics. The statue of Sun as a boy, given to the city of Honolulu in 2007, is the work of Hong Kong sculptor Chu Tat-shing. It stands in a small fenced park beside the Hawaii Theatre, where a city sign bans camping, alcohol, open fires and, oddly for a paved plaza, golfing and says the park is closed at night. The statue is often draped with lei. In September it wore at least two. At the other end of Chinatown, 10 minutes on foot, a bronze of the adult Sun in a long gown holds up the society’s declaration, on a base inscribed with Confucian maxims in English and Chinese. It was donated in 1984 by the people of Kaohsiung, Taiwan. In September, a purple scrawl marked its robe, and many homeless people gathered in the area around both statues. The committee is also looking past its own generation. A statewide essay competition on Sun is open to Hawaii’s high school and college students, and the winners will be recognised as part of the November 1 festivities. The last classroom Even the question of where Sun became a revolutionary is contested, politely, between two of Honolulu’s best-known schools. He spent three years at Iolani, then an Anglican school run by British teachers loyal to the Hawaiian crown. In 1882 he took second prize in English, handed to him by King Kalakaua. When Sun became notorious in 1896, the school’s bishop wrote that he had learned no republicanism there. He then spent some months at what is now Punahou, founded by American Protestant missionaries. Obama graduated from the same school in 1979. Flores said Punahou likes to boast that it educated two presidents: one of the United States and, in Sun, the first provisional president of the Republic of China. Luke believes that is where he read about Abraham Lincoln and George Washington. Flores, who is overseeing the mural, put both schools on it. “I have to be diplomatic,” he said. “I got to be on both sides.” Punahou has one advantage, and it is the rarest thing on the Sun Yat-sen trail: a building. The hall where Sun took his lessons, built in 1851, is still used as a classroom, Luke said, with a plaque on the wall. “Everybody from China comes,” he said. “They want to go take a picture.” The rest of the trail will have to be imagined on November 1. Guided tours will leave every 15 minutes through Chinatown, with guides doing what Flores did on King Street: stopping and pointing. At 10am, community leaders will drape fresh lei on the statue of the boy. Then the crowd will walk to Maunakea Marketplace, where the American Theater once stood, to unveil the mural. Draft designs by the artist Jessika Tseng, shared by the organisers, show two tall panels on the market’s facade. On one, Sun is a boy in a long blue gown, arriving in 1879 with a trunk in his hand, beneath the names of both Iolani and Punahou. On the other, he is the grown revolutionary of 1903, a rolled paper in his fist. Between them, in gold characters on red, is his best-known motto: the world belongs to all. So, by now, does Sun. Beijing honours him as a forerunner of the revolution and Taipei as the father of the nation. A Hong Kong sculptor made one of his Honolulu statues and the people of Kaohsiung gave the other. Two schools each count him as their own. On November 1, Chinatown will renew its claim: a Hawaiian son.

title: Apple’s Tim Cook kicks off China visit amid mixed signals on new iPhone demand
description: Executive’s third visit to China this year follows the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro line-up and the company’s first foldable device.
content: Apple executive chairman Tim Cook has begun his third visit to China this year, following the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro line-up and the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable device, in one of its biggest markets. Cook met Meng Fanli, governor of the southern province of Guangdong, on Sunday and said Apple was willing to expand its presence, including in smart manufacturing and sales channels. As an important manufacturing powerhouse, Guangdong had been essential to Apple’s growth in China, Cook said, citing the region’s concentration of Apple suppliers and ecosystem partners. Meng said the provincial government welcomed the American tech giant to deepen its presence through innovative products, emerging businesses, and research and development platforms, while vowing to forge a “first-class business environment” that was international, market-oriented and governed by the rule of law. Cook was then spotted at an Apple Store in the provincial capital Guangzhou, according to several social media posts by customers on Sunday. “Great to be back in China!” Cook wrote in a Saturday post on Weibo after starting his trip in Guangzhou, where he watched a local content creator use an iPhone 18 Pro to film a martial arts video. This marks Cook’s first trip to China since transitioning to executive chairman last month, when he handed the CEO role to John Ternus. As Apple CEO, Cook visited China twice earlier this year. In May, he joined a high-profile business and tech delegation accompanying US President Donald Trump to a meeting with President Xi Jinping. Other American executives in the delegation included Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. In March, Cook toured Apple stores in Chengdu and Beijing as part of celebrations marking the company’s 50th anniversary. His latest visit followed the September launch of the much-anticipated iPhone Duo, which is scheduled to go on sale on October 23, as well as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which are already available. Initial data showed the Pro handsets were well-received, although higher prices could weigh on consumer demand. Sales of the new Pro models in their first three days were 12 per cent higher than sales of the iPhone 17 Pro line-up during its entire first week last year, lifting Apple to the No 1 position by smartphone sales in China for the week of September 14 to 20, according to Counterpoint Research. However, Nikkei Asia reported last week that Apple had asked some suppliers to cut production of components for the new Pro models, raising questions about demand after the initial launch period.

title: My Take | The US and Israel have gone full rogue
description: As Israel denounces Nobel Peace laureate Navi Pillay, the US sanctions the entire International Criminal Court.
content: While Israel denounces the Nobel committee’s award of the Peace Prize to former UN human rights chief and South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the United States decides to sanction the entire International Criminal Court. Rarely has a single day shown so starkly where the international order is breaking down. On Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded its Peace Prize to Pillay “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”. Within hours, Israel compared her to Joseph Goebbels, and the United States announced sanctions on the ICC, where she sat from 2003 to 2008. The two allies had turned on the institutions that give a rules-based order its meaning. The committee described the prize as support for tribunals at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”. “An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” it said. This was an unmistakable reference to Israel and the US and their relentless assaults on the international court. Pillay, the committee added, has held states and national leaders to account and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. Pillay opposed apartheid in her native South Africa. At the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, her groundbreaking work recognised rape as a tool of genocide. She went on to serve as an ICC judge and then as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. Until last year, she chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Predictably, that infuriated Israel, which has a habit of relentlessly trying to undermine and discredit its critics. Responding to the award, the Israeli Foreign Ministry said in a statement on X: “If there were an award for lies, hatred and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a front runner.” It called accusations of genocide levelled at Israel “the biggest lie of the 21st century”. “Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell”, it said, referring to Nazi Germany’s chief propagandist during the Holocaust. That is about as unhinged an official statement as any in the annals of international diplomacy. Meanwhile, Washington added the ICC itself to its Specially Designated Nationals list, alongside violent criminals and drug cartels. Such sanctions typically force banks, insurers and software firms to cut ties. Americans who violate the underlying executive order face up to 20 years in prison. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a “rogue court” and warned: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” The Donald Trump regime’s case rests on the fact that the US, like Israel, is not an ICC member state, so the court supposedly has no judicial power to arrest their officials or soldiers. It is true that neither country is obliged to carry out ICC orders, including arrest warrants. But member states are, and that includes arresting, for example, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant as suspected war criminals if they are found within their borders. A court allowed to pursue only the enemies of powerful Western states and their allies is a tool, not a court The court is necessary because states are often unwilling or unable to investigate grave crimes themselves. For Washington, the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant were the last straw. But a court allowed to pursue only the enemies of powerful Western states and their allies is a tool, not a court. The rights group Democracy for the Arab World Now warns that sanctions threaten “the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes”, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine. The ICC has responded with dignity. “The court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” it said. Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan vowed that its work would continue. ICC member states, but especially EU countries and Nato members except the US and Turkey, now face a choice. The European Union’s “blocking statute” bars Europeans from complying with listed foreign sanctions, and in 2018 it was extended to cover US measures on Iran. Slovenia raised the need for an EU response in June 2025, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for activating the statute in May this year. In August UN experts urged the EU to activate it, and last week the ICC’s registrar asked Brussels to be ready to use it. The European Commission has still not acted. The question is not whether the ICC is flawless. It is whether the principle behind it can survive: that no leader, however powerful, is above the law with regard to genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. In a world where great powers sanction judges and vilify laureates, the rules bind only the weak. The court’s member states have repeatedly vowed to defend it. Now they must keep that promise. As the court itself warned, “History will judge this moment.”

title: Poland detains suspect in alleged plot to attack PM and defence minister
description: Online activity leads security forces to arrest man in his 60s amid a heightened nationwide security alert.
content: Polish police are investigating after arresting a man suspected of plotting an attack against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, the interior ministry said on Sunday. Searches were continuing at the suspect’s home, ministry spokeswoman Karolina Galecka said, adding: “information about this man will of course then be verified by the police”. This came after Tusk and Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that a suspect had been detained. “The man threatening an attack has been detained,” Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their “swift and decisive action”. The suspect, a man in his 60s, was arrested in the southwestern region of Lower Silesia, Kierwinski told public broadcaster TVP Info. “The services got to him through a thorough analysis of content posted online,” he added, saying the man’s “contacts and his activity on the internet are being examined”. Earlier, the interior ministry said Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz may have been the targets of assassination attempts. Galecka said police had been alerted by the State Protection Service (SOP) following reports of a potential threat against the premier and defence minister. Members of the police, SOP and Poland’s internal security agency met on Sunday to discuss the case. “We are treating this matter as deadly serious,” a spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, Jacek Dobrzynski, told reporters afterward. He said threats to Polish officials had become increasingly common but added that, in this case, there was “a strong likelihood” they could have been carried out. Poland, a member of both Nato and the EU, has been on high alert following a series of stabbings over the past week, which Tusk on Thursday denounced as a “cult of violence”. Police said Sunday that nearly 64,000 institutions had been inspected and 117 people detained following violent incidents on school grounds. In September, Polish intelligence services arrested a 17-year-old Nazi sympathiser suspected of plotting an attack against a school and a mosque. Two other minors were later detained in connection with the arrest, the internal security agency said. Warsaw, a staunch ally of Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, has repeatedly warned of Russian sabotage and hybrid warfare on Polish soil, accusations rejected by Moscow. However, interior minister Kierwinski told TVP Info that “at this stage it is probably too early to claim … that any foreign angle is possible” in the alleged assassination attempt. “It rather appears that this is a man from very radical groups, establishing very radical contacts via the internet with various people,” he said.

title: Leading Chinese mathematicians unite behind use of AI in research
description: Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, who is leading the project, warned that the country is lagging behind the US in using the technology.
content: Leading China’s mathematicians joined forces in Beijing on Sunday to launch an alliance aimed at integrating artificial intelligence into mathematical research. The Yau Laboratory Alliance for Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence is being spearheaded by Fields medallist Shing-Tung Yau, who warned that China was lagging behind the United States in using AI to advance frontier science. It will bring together eight leading institutions and aims to create a network of more than 1,000 scientists. The alliance will focus on developing specialised AI models for mathematics, using the technology to generate conjectures and formalise proofs, and building systems whose reasoning could be more easily interpreted. “A year ago, I did not think AI was this powerful,” Yau, the director of the Yau Mathematical Sciences Centre at Tsinghua University, said. He added that over the past six to 12 months he had seen AI tackle problems that mathematicians had struggled to solve. “The development of AI in mathematics is like a tsunami,” he said, arguing that Chinese mathematicians needed to organise themselves and engage with the technology rather than avoid it. The alliance was launched amid a growing debate over AI’s ability to solve advanced mathematical problems. Last week, OpenAI released 722 mathematical manuscripts grouped into 372 families of results, claiming progress on hundreds of open problems. But the company withdrew three manuscripts the following day after identifying an error that invalidated an argument and affected two related papers, while revising 14 others. Some mathematicians have criticised the speed and scale of the release, arguing that mathematical results needed careful verification, clear explanations and proper acknowledgement of previous work. Another Fields medallist, Terence Tao, has called the use of AI to be slowed down given the concerns about its negative impact, triggering a heated debate with other mathematicians who support the use of the technology. But when asked about the issue, Yau said: “Tao is a very good mathematician, but that does not mean he represents the mathematical community.” He added that the dispute should not deter mathematicians from working with AI, instead highlighting the need for closer cooperation between leading mathematicians and AI developers. He said the gap between China and the United States was particularly pronounced in frontier scientific research, especially when it came to AI systems capable of advancing mathematics and physics. Chinese models have performed well carrying out tasks for ordinary users, he said, but remained far behind leading US systems in cutting-edge research. “But if you ask them to do the work OpenAI has done over the past month, the gap is very large.” Yau said leading US AI companies had mobilised thousands of scholars and substantial industrial investment to tackle difficult scientific problems, with mathematicians helping improve AI systems while using them to investigate new questions. “The United States and the West have brought together their top mathematical experts to work with AI and explore frontier problems,” he said, adding that China’s efforts were fragmented. Scientists who attended Sunday’s launch included Xi Nanhua, the president of the Chinese Mathematical Society; He Xuhua, vice-president of the International Mathematical Union; and Tian Ye, the deputy director of the Morningside Centre of Mathematics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Besides the Yau Laboratory and Morningside Centre, other institutions involved in the alliance include Tsinghua University’s Qiuzhen College, the Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, the Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, Southeast University’s Yau Centre, the Hetao Institute of Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences and the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Zhizhen School of Interdisciplinary Mathematical Sciences.

title: The EU’s China dilemma: how to counter Beijing without alienating friends
description: Europe grapples with whether efforts to protect its industry from China mirror the US policies it previously railed against.
content: In September, the Jaecoo 7 – a budget SUV from China’s Chery Automobile – made headlines when it shifted more than 10,000 units to become Britain’s bestselling car. Christened the “Temu Range Rover” online, a nod to the cheap goods available on the Chinese online marketplace and the luxury 4X4 made by Jaguar Land Rover that it resembles, its success showed British drivers’ new-found taste for cut-price Chinese cars. Overall, 23 per cent of new cars bought in Britain last month were Chinese models, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, with several electric and hybrid models ranking highly. But days later, the booming Chinese car market was caught up in a wider European trade dispute. Britain was considering matching EU tariffs of up to 45 per cent on Chinese-made electric vehicles to gain access to European manufacturing subsidies, The Times reported. Brussels is also weighing import restrictions on Chinese-made hybrids, a category that includes the plug-in version of the Jaecoo 7. If adopted, London could be under pressure to follow suit. The EU had long wanted Britain to align on EV tariffs, fearing that the country, which left the EU in 2020, would become an entrepot for cheap Chinese cars, which it says are flooding the European market. Now, with its proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), the bloc potentially has a tool with which it can strong-arm London to follow suit. “The UK example shows that you can have a negotiation position with the IAA,” said Nils Redeker, acting co-director of the Jacques Delors Centre, a think tank. Redeker argued that the law could give Brussels leverage to pressure Britain into taking a tougher stance on Chinese car imports. The act is the EU’s major foray into industrial policy after a decades-long love affair with neoliberal governance, during which the very term “industrial policy” became dirty words. Yet, it has also raised questions among political groups in Europe and among its allies whether, in its frenzied efforts to protect its industry from China, the EU is mirroring the US policies it previously railed against. “The IAA should not – even inadvertently – penalise the companies of close partners, which have invested deeply in Europe and become part of its industrial networks simply because their headquarters happen to be elsewhere,” wrote Kazutoshi Aikawa, Japan’s ambassador to the EU, in the Financial Times last month. “Trusted international partners are part of Europe’s industrial strength,” he added. Aikawa compared the law with former US president Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act, a green-oriented stab at industrial policy that alienated Tokyo and Brussels alike. The bloc’s recent steel restrictions, aimed at curbing the impact of Chinese overcapacity, led other partners including South Korea and Turkey to complain they were caught in the crossfire. When adopted, the IAA would create rules through which EU funds, public contracts and other incentives are funnelled to EU-made products in sectors like EVs, steel, cement and clean technology, while speeding up permits for new industrial projects. The aim is to bolster European manufacturing and reduce the bloc’s dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly China. It would also impose strict conditions on large investments from countries dominating global production in strategic sectors, again primarily targeting Beijing. “European workers and the firms must benefit … China has applied this logic for 30 years,” said Anna Cavazzini, a Green member of the European Parliament, involved in drafting the chamber’s own version of the law. “The only shocking fact for me is that it took us so long to even consider investment conditionalities.” But it is not without controversy. A European preference would also disadvantage companies from partners such as Britain, Japan and South Korea, their governments argue, unless they secure exemptions, leading to negotiating scrambles such as the UK-EU talks. This has sparked a vigorous debate as to just how much the EU, in its efforts to counter China’s industrial prowess, can and should cut itself off from the rest of the world. Ignacio Garcia Bercero, formerly a top EU trade negotiator, said the bloc needed to be “extremely careful” that it does not throw the baby out with the bathwater as it heads in new policy directions. “We must not have a situation where because of legitimate concerns relating to China … we are going to be fundamentally undermining the value of [free-trade] agreements,” Garcia Bercero said. “It would be a huge mistake to … disrupt our relationship with those countries that normally [are] close allies of the EU because of these concerns.” At the EU level, some members led by Germany want to allow countries with which the EU has made a free-trade agreement to be given access to the benefits of IAA. “If you say this is all about China, then why is the Japanese ambassador writing concerned letters to the Financial Times? Why is the South Korean government telling us last week in Seoul there will be countermeasures to these proposals because this is simply an attack on us?” asked Dirk Gotink, a Dutch member of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), at a recent debate. This week, the EPP took it further: a small group of influential lawmakers from the group proposed scrapping the IAA altogether. On the other side of the ledger sits a coterie of nations led by France who want the plan to be narrow geographically and broad in scope. “This [allowing FTA partners in] would open up provisions to over 80 countries, 27 from the EU,” said Christophe Grudler, a centrist French lawmaker involved in drafting the parliament’s counterproposal. “That’s about 110 countries out of 190 in the UN. So, it’s no longer made in the EU. It’s no longer made with the EU. It’s made everywhere.” Research commissioned by the parliament suggested, however, that the debate showed Europe obsessing over details that barely move the needle economically. An EU-only “Made in Europe” scenario would increase GDP by 0.13 per cent and employment by 0.11 per cent, according to the study’s modelling. And a “Made with Europe” scenario, including selected trading partners, would lift GDP by 0.19 per cent and employment by 0.16 per cent.

title: Inside Hong Kong’s Chinese Medicine Hospital, where Eastern and Western healthcare meet
description: A writer’s consultation at the recently opened hospital reveals how it blends Chinese and Western medicine, and how to navigate appointments.
content: In the last instalment of a four-part Health Matters series on traditional Chinese medicine, Chloe Loung experiences the patient journey at Hong Kong’s new Chinese medicine hospital, where Western doctors and TCM practitioners work side by side to streamline holistic healthcare. There are no receptionists barking ticket numbers in chaotic waiting rooms at the new Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong. In fact, stepping into the complex’s sunlit atrium, you can barely hear a footstep. Hong Kong’s healthcare system has historically kept Western medicine and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) separate. For generations, accessing TCM in the city meant navigating a plethora of non-standardised clinics, and sometimes a language barrier. The new hospital, in Hong Kong’s Tseung Kwan O neighbourhood, aims to change this. Designed as a patient-first hybrid model, it offers traditional treatments – such as acupuncture and herbal remedies – and Western medicine under one roof. But what does the experience actually feel like for an everyday patient walking through the door? To find out, I book a general outpatient appointment to walk through the system step by step. The hospital’s most striking difference from a typical neighbourhood TCM clinic is its seamless accessibility. Booking via the hospital’s dedicated app links directly to the iAM Smart identity profile, with English-language options available at every step. I arrive 15 minutes early for my appointment as instructed, and immediately notice how serene the place is. Tall glass windows allow natural light to flood the wide corridors, which are free of queues. At registration, a nurse points me to a touch-screen kiosk to settle the appointment fee. I have barely taken a seat when another nurse comes to check my blood pressure, temperature and heart rate before ushering me into a room to have my height and weight measured. The silence in the waiting area, I soon realise, is by design. Instead of loudspeakers calling out ticket numbers, every patient gets a notification on their phone from the app when the next stage of their appointment is set. Minutes later, I am called in to see the Chinese medicine practitioner. After I share my symptoms – hot flushes, lower back pain and poor sleep – she performs the traditional diagnostic checks, taking my pulse on both wrists and inspecting my tongue. After telling me I have an excess of dampness and humid qi, she advises me to quit cold drinks and prescribes a course of herbal medicine to reduce the internal dampness – addressing the core imbalance rather than individual symptoms. The entire consultation lasts less than five minutes. I go to the pharmacy and collect my prescription, which is neatly sealed in a ziplock bag with clear, printed instructions alongside advice to return in five days if my symptoms don’t improve. The total visit takes less than an hour from check-in to leaving. I find that a process formerly characterised by complex explanations and manual processes has been streamlined into a swift, modern service. The core TCM consultation remains brief in my non-serious case; the real test of the hospital’s hybrid model will be in treating complex, multidisciplinary conditions – where Western doctors and Chinese medicine specialists sit in the same room. Integrated clinics treat disorders jointly Had I been more insistent about my back pain during the appointment, I would have been referred to a specialised clinic where Western and Chinese medicine practitioners work with patients together to assess patients and provide treatment for post-stroke rehabilitation, pain management, neurological disorders and other conditions. I arrange a visit as a reporter to learn how this works. This time, orthopaedics and traumatology specialist Dr Lam Kwong-chin and senior Chinese medicine practitioner Dr Yeung Chi-fung walk me through the set-up. The hospital’s integrated approach centres on bian zheng lun zhi (“treatment based on pattern differentiation”). A Western diagnosis serves as the starting point, after which the TCM practitioner identifies underlying patterns by evaluating pain triggers alongside factors such as sleep, stress, diet, tongue appearance and pulse quality. These findings distinguish, for instance, blood stasis from damp-cold obstruction or kidney deficiency. Treatment is then tailored to that specific pattern through acupuncture, herbal medicine, tui na, cupping or moxibustion, rather than being directed solely at the physical symptoms. This approach means two patients with identical MRI scans could receive entirely different TCM treatments if their underlying body patterns differ. Within the hospital’s integrated model, Western diagnostics – X-rays, MRIs, blood tests and other investigations – confirm the biomedical diagnosis, rule out red flags and provide a safety net. Western medication is used for immediate symptom relief when necessary. During a joint consultation, both doctors are present from the start. The Western medicine doctor reviews public Hospital Authority e-health records on-screen while the Chinese medicine practitioner conducts the TCM evaluation. On my visit, Yeung takes my pulse, checks my tongue and performs a physical examination to test my range of motion and to check for muscle weakness, numbness and nerve pain. In cases where imaging is needed, the Western doctor will order an X-ray or MRI on the spot – bypassing a long-standing legal barrier for Hong Kong TCM practitioners, who traditionally have not been able to order diagnostic tests independently. “In the past, if I wanted an X-ray for a patient, I’d have to send them somewhere else,” Yeung says. “But here, everything can be done much faster, which is critical in certain circumstances.” TCM is rarely used in emergencies, but Lam recalls an early patient with severe back pain and a history of gallbladder and kidney issues. A rapid X-ray revealed a destroyed spinal disc. “I combined that with his history – the biliary infections, the kidney problems – and realised bacteria had likely seeded into the disc space,” Lam says. “This was an emergency. We explained it to him immediately and sent him back to [a Western] hospital the next day for surgery.” The case, Lam says, illustrates why the collaboration matters: “He came to a Chinese medicine clinic. If he had only seen a Chinese medicine practitioner without the ability to order imaging, that diagnosis might have been missed. Instead, we caught it because we were working together.” Yeung says such cases are rare but not unheard of. “Most lower back pain we see is chronic, degenerative, mechanical,” he says. “But when there are red flags – neurological symptoms, unexplained weight loss, fever – we need to act fast. Having a Western doctor in the room makes that possible.” We ask the same questions, do the same examinations. It’s only at the treatment stage that we diverge Orthopaedics and traumatology specialist Dr Lam Kwong-chin After my examination, the practitioners agree on a joint plan: acupuncture, herbs or tui na from the TCM side paired with painkillers and physiotherapy if required. Luckily, my situation is not dire enough to warrant surgery or emergency transfers. The practitioners take me to the room next door, where Yeung inserts eight needles into my lower back and sets up a red warming lamp. I enjoy a 20-minute nap during the treatment. Yeung stresses the importance of lifestyle changes to complement prescribed treatments. “I tell patients, ‘I can give you acupuncture and herbs, but if you don’t change your habits, the problem will come back,’” he says. “A good doctor doesn’t just treat the disease – they [help] change the patient’s life.” Lam has incorporated some of that philosophy into his own practice. “I’ve learned to ask more extensively about sleep, about stress, about diet,” he says. “In orthopaedics, it’s very practical – there’s no abstract theorising. It’s about whether the patient’s pain improves, whether they can function better. “But these things matter, even from a Western perspective. Chronic pain is not just a mechanical problem; it’s biopsychosocial. The Chinese medicine approach addresses that in ways Western medicine sometimes overlooks.” Lam admits that he arrived at the hospital with some trepidation. “I don’t know Chinese medicine,” he says. “I thought they’d be talking to me about yin and yang, about … meridians – things I’d only read about in martial arts novels. But the diagnostic process is virtually identical. We ask the same questions, do the same examinations. It’s only at the treatment stage that we diverge.” That convergence is the beating heart of Hong Kong’s first dedicated Chinese Medicine Hospital – a model both doctors believe could reshape chronic pain care across the city. “At the end of the day, the patient doesn’t care whether the treatment is Western or Chinese,” Yeung says. “They care whether it works. And here, it works.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery for small growth on lung
description: The growth was ‘well-contained’ and detected at an early stage.
content: Pope Leo said ⁠on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this ‌week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure. Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was “well-contained” and caught at an early stage. “Recently, during ⁠some medical examinations, doctors found a localised nodule in my ‌lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well ‌contained.” “The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, ⁠so, following their ⁠advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The ‌operation is already scheduled for the next few days.” A nodule on the lung is ⁠a small, localised ⁠lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5 per cent of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, ‌although risk rises with age, size, and other factors. Leo, elected pope by ‌the world’s ‌cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a ‌Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is ⁠not known to previously have had health issues. The late pope ⁠Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years. The Vatican press ‌office said ‌Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health. Leo keeps a busy schedule and is ‌due to make an ‌11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake”.

title: Hong Kong hiker dies, Singaporean teen discharged after 2 trail emergencies
description: The teenager was airlifted to hospital after falling ill during a hike with two friends, while the man was certified dead.
content: At least two people were airlifted to hospital in the past two days after falling ill while hiking in Hong Kong, with a middle-aged man dying and a 17-year-old Singaporean girl discharged. The teenager was flown to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai on Saturday morning after vomiting and experiencing chills while hiking on Lion Rock, a 495-metre (1,624-foot) peak. In a separate incident, a 66-year-old man suddenly felt unwell and collapsed while hiking with his nephew in Plover Cove Country Park in Tai Po, police said on Sunday. He collapsed near Ha Miu Tin while hiking from Wu Tan Tang along the medium-difficulty Double Haven Country Trail. The Government Flying Service dispatched a helicopter to the scene and airlifted the man to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan for emergency treatment. The man, who was unconscious when taken to hospital, was certified dead at about 5pm after rescue efforts proved unsuccessful. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death. As for the Singaporean hiker, the government said she was discharged at about 10am on Saturday. Earlier that day, she had been hiking with two other 17-year-old girls when she fell ill. One of the hikers’ mothers called police for help at about 6.50am, and the Government Flying Service airlifted the teenager to hospital for treatment. The girl’s companions were uninjured and returned home. Despite it being late autumn, Hong Kong’s weather remained relatively warm and dry. Sheung Shui recorded the city’s highest temperature of 34.2 degrees Celsius (93.6 Fahrenheit) on Sunday, followed by Lau Fau Shan, Shek Kong and Ta Kwu Ling. Tai Po recorded a maximum temperature of 31.4 degrees, while relative humidity stood at 72 per cent. Hiking expert Umer Abdullah said the period between October and January was a popular season for hiking because lower temperatures and humidity could reduce the risk of exhaustion. However, he said hikers should take specific safety precautions. “Hikers must ensure they have enough warm clothes, as temperatures can drop uphill,” he said. “It is also good to have a light source because the days are shorter.” He recommended using a headlamp rather than a phone light, which occupies one hand and can affect balance. Hikers should also study their trail in detail before setting out, avoid unfamiliar routes alone, check the weather forecast and carry gear suitable for the weather and terrain, he said. If a weather warning was issued, hikers should immediately abandon the hike and seek shelter, he added. He also advised hikers to notify someone of their route and expected time of return, keep their phones fully charged and carry a power bank and a basic first aid kit.

title: Hong Kong Cyclothon bosses sorry for route chaos, angry riders call city ‘capital of fails’
description: Cycling association chiefs say earlier accident caused confusion, leading to bottleneck, riders being diverted away from original 32km route.
content: Cycling bosses issued a fulsome apology on Sunday after furious riders branded The Sun Hung Kai Properties Hong Kong Cyclothon a “bike-pushing festival” and the city “the international capital of embarrassing fails”. A chaotic end and mid-race route change in the 32km (19.9 mile) ride prompted myriad complaints from competitors, with most angry at being turned away from Ting Kau Bridge and then finding themselves forced to complete the course on foot. In a lengthy statement, the Cycling Association of Hong Kong China said a lead vehicle had been responsible for taking some cyclists in the wrong direction, with an earlier accident involving two entrants in the 56km event causing the confusion. Those who took to social media to angrily complain about the day also raised concerns over the gridlock towards the end of the race, while others pointed to safety issues, claiming they had been diverted into oncoming traffic.
