Giving riders the opportunity to speed over bridges and along roads usually the preserve of motor vehicles is one of cyclothon’s biggest pulls, and the 32km route took in Cheung Tsing Tunnel, Ting Kau Bridge, Nam Wan Tunnel and Stonecutters Bridge, while the longer distance included Tsing Ma Bridge, Ting Kau Bridge, Stonecutters Bridge and the Central Kowloon Bypass “To ensure the injured received immediate medical treatment, on-site staff had to temporarily move traffic cones placed at the entrance leading to the Nam Wan Tunnel to clear an emergency lane for ambulances to enter the scene as quickly as possible,” the association statement said. “Due to the repositioning of the traffic cones, the lead vehicle for the 32km category misjudged that the cyclists’ route to Ting Kau Bridge had been altered. It failed to turn onto Ting Kau Bridge according to the original route and instead continued straight towards the Nam Wan Tunnel. “As this location was a downhill stretch where riding speeds were high, all following participants had no choice but to follow towards the Nam Wan Tunnel to ensure safety.” The association said it offered its “most sincere apologies for the disappointment and inconvenience” caused. While previous editions were held in Tsim Sha Tsui, this year organisers switched the start and finish to West Kowloon Cultural District. The annual event featured rides of 56km and 32km open to the public, a 100.4km UCI Class 1.1 road race that attracted professional teams from overseas, and a CEO Charity and Celebrity Ride. Earlier in the day, disgruntled cyclists had taken to social media to vent their anger, with one “officially declaring the Hong Kong Cyclothon the most failed cycling event in the world”, and suggesting it should be cancelled. Course safety and organisation also came under fire from those who had paid HK$280 (US$36) and HK$600 to enter, depending on which distance they cycled. “Traffic jam and bike-pushing festival,” said one. “U-turn arrangements were terrible and signs were unclear. Merging required riding against oncoming traffic – almost had a collision!” Even before things got under way, there were complaints about organisation, with a lack of bus timetables and stops leaving one rider complaining that “trying to figure out how to get to the starting line is giving me a headache”. The venue’s single access route for entry and exit resulted in competitors having to dismount towards the beginning and end of the ride. One social media commenter said organisers’ calculations for the 32km race involved 26km of riding, sandwiched by 3km of walking. “They might as well partner with Oxfam Trailwalker next time,” they added. Another rider suggested a name change to the “Hong Kong Bike-Pushing Festival”, and said the route had meant it was “total gridlock when leaving”. The annoyance spilled over to drivers who were locked in traffic jams, with some complaining they had been in their cars for two hours. “Either be like the Hong Kong Marathon and announce road closures well in advance, or expect people to get furious just seeing a bicycle right now,” one wrote. One rider said they had “felt stupid” after believing organisers’ promises to provide protective tape for bikes loaded onto shuttle buses. “They were tacked together too loosely, [it was] super easy [for them] to get scratched,” she said. “Never mind my old frame, but my boyfriend literally just bought a brand new, expensive bike. If it’s really scratched up, it’s both physically and emotionally painful.” The Soudal Quick-Step rider, Paul Magnier of France, won the UCI road race in two hours, three minutes and 30 seconds. Vincent Lau Wan-yau, the best-performing Hongkonger, came home 19 seconds back to place 32nd in the 93-man field. Nonetheless, it is the race-day mayhem that will live longer in the memory of riders. “Damn it, get ready to be blasted by complaints,” one rider said, while another wrote: “Hong Kong: The international capital of embarrassing fails.”

title: ‘Special-forces’ travel: Chinese woman wins admiration after climbing 5 famous peaks in 5 days
description: Challenge aligns with ‘special forces style’ travel trend that has surged in popularity among young Chinese people recently.
content: A woman from southwestern China has climbed five famous mountains in five provinces in five days, earning widespread admiration on social media. The climber, surnamed Peng, began her journey in her hometown of Guiyang, Guizhou province, on September 23, the Xiaoxiang Morning Herald reported. She climbed Mount Hua in northwestern Shaanxi province the following day, then Mount Heng in neighbouring Shanxi province on September 25, Mount Tai in eastern Shandong province on September 26, Mount Song in central Henan province on September 27, and finally another Mount Heng in Hunan province on September 28. The five mountains are collectively known as China’s Five Great Mountains, celebrated for their natural beauty and historical and cultural significance. According to the report, Peng climbed during the day, then pressed on with her journey and slept on trains at night. Peng, 27, said she came across a themed tour inviting the public to climb the five mountains in an effort to “deeply understand China”. As a mountain-climbing enthusiast, she was drawn to the idea. She decided to take on the challenge in late September to mark her 10,000th day of life. Peng used an app called Liang Bu Lu to record her hiking routes and check in at designated spots atop each mountain, as required by the event organiser. At the end of her journey, she received a certificate confirming that she had climbed the Five Great Mountains. Peng took between four and nine hours to climb each mountain, and walked as many as 39,000 steps a day. She climbed up and down the mountains on foot, except at Mount Hua and Mount Heng in Hunan, where she climbed up on foot but took a cable car down. The entire trip cost her 4,000 yuan (US$600), Peng said. She said she felt exhausted after climbing the final mountain but recovered quickly after resting that evening, without experiencing muscle soreness or fatigue. By the end of the challenge, she had lost 0.5kg. Peng admitted that she had felt uneasy before setting off because she had never hiked for so long or at such intensity. She said she completed the challenge smoothly, partly thanks to help from strangers along the way. “Don’t be afraid to start alone. You will meet some good-hearted fellow travellers,” Peng was quoted as saying. She advised the public not to attempt the five-mountain challenge without careful consideration. “You should take your own physical condition into consideration and prioritise your safety when doing outdoor activities,” Peng said. The challenge is part of a so-called “special troop style” travel trend that has gained popularity among young people in recent years. These physically demanding trips involve visiting many tourist attractions in a short period and on a low budget. The story has captivated social media users in mainland China. “She is a heroine. I admire her,” one online observer said. “Brilliant, Little Sister. You won’t be defeated by difficulties in the future,” another remarked.

title: How Taiwan’s military manpower shortage is undermining its ability to fight
description: Concerns are mounting over its ability to recruit elite troops and whether it will be able to operate its new US equipment.
content: Taiwan’s military is grappling with a worsening manpower shortage, with its volunteer staffing rate remaining below the 80 per cent target for a third consecutive year and concerns mounting over the impact on combat readiness, according to the island’s legislature. The shortages extend deep into frontline formations – including infantry, artillery, missile and air defence units – raising questions over whether Taiwan will have enough trained personnel to operate and maintain the vast quantities of new weapons entering service, observers said. A Legislative Yuan Budget Centre assessment of the government’s proposed 2027 budget warned this week that persistent personnel shortages could increase workloads and training demands on serving troops while affecting readiness. Defence ministry figures cited by the centre showed that the number of staff positions successfully filled by volunteers peaked at 88.52 per cent in 2020 before falling below 80 per cent in 2023. It dropped to 75.93 per cent in 2024 and stood at 77.31 per cent at the end of last year. A separate Budget Centre assessment of this year’s supplementary budget put the rate at 76.62 per cent at the end of June. More significantly, numerous Category I formations – elite troops expected to fight on the front line of any conflict – remained below the 80 per cent staffing benchmark. They included army infantry, mechanised infantry, special operations, artillery, armour, anti-armour and territorial defence units, as well as Marine Corps infantry, armour and artillery formations. Naval fleet and shore-based missile units, air force missile units and the military police’s 202nd Command were also below the threshold. The centre warned that the shortages could hinder the training and long-term retention of the specialised personnel needed to operate new weapons as Taiwan accelerates military procurement amid growing pressure from the People’s Liberation Army. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Analysts said sophisticated weapons required highly skilled personnel who often needed lengthy training. “If volunteer staffing remains below 80 per cent, it will become increasingly difficult to train and retain enough operators,” said Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society. If the situation continued, the island’s armed forces were likely to experience a difficult period in which “there are weapons, but not necessarily enough people to operate them”, he said on Thursday. Lo said the military should restructure its forces and reallocate manpower rather than rigidly trying to keep its existing organisation fully staffed. Military analyst Lu De-yun, a former defence ministry press secretary, said shortages directly eroded operational effectiveness. “First, you have to extend people’s duty hours, which increases fatigue,” Lu said. “Second, you may have to operate systems with fewer personnel. If a system is supposed to be operated by 10 people, you may have to make do with nine or eight. That will reduce the effectiveness of the weapons system.” He said shortages were particularly burdensome for junior non-commissioned officers (NCOs), who could simultaneously be responsible for personnel, discipline, training and administration. The problem could become more pronounced as Taiwan takes delivery of new US weapons, including 66 modernised F-16 fighter jets, while expanding its missile and unmanned capabilities. Hsu Chiao-hsin, a legislator with the main opposition Kuomintang, has questioned whether the air force will have enough pilots for the new fighters alongside its existing fleet. The air force, however, has said that despite some pilots leaving early or declining to extend their service, its pilot staffing rate remains above 90 per cent. Chieh Chung, a researcher with the Taipei-based Association of Strategic Foresight, said the headline figure could conceal a more serious problem – the loss of experienced pilots needed to train and lead younger aviators. Taiwan plans to form another fighter wing and add 107 flight officers to operate the 66 new F-16Vs ordered from the United States in 2019. The first two aircraft were delivered last week after repeated delays. However, funding for bonuses designed to retain experienced flight officers would fall by about 4 per cent next year, marking a fourth consecutive annual decline, Chieh noted. He said the trend suggested the departure of experienced pilots had yet to ease. “Even if overall pilot staffing meets requirements, flying units could lack enough experienced majors and lieutenant colonels to serve as instructors, flight leads and mission commanders,” he warned. That meant the air force’s combat capability would not necessarily increase in proportion to the expansion of its fighter fleet, he said. The manpower shortage is also acute among enlisted personnel, the main pool from which NCOs are drawn. Chieh said NCO shortages could be particularly damaging because they formed the operational backbone of units and were often more familiar with missions and procedures than newly assigned officers. The Budget Centre also warned of longer-term demographic pressures. The number of men eligible for compulsory service fell below 100,000 for the first time in 2023 and is projected to fall below 80,000 next year. Ruling Democratic Progressive Party legislator Chen Kuan-ting said the irreversible decline in Taiwan’s young population meant it was unrealistic to insist on keeping traditional large formations fully staffed. He called for “greater use of drones, automated surveillance and artificial intelligence systems to reduce manpower requirements in areas including logistics, surveillance and reconnaissance”. The defence ministry said it had been working to stem personnel losses, improve recruitment and retention, relax some entry requirements, raise allowances for several categories of military personnel and improve pay and living conditions.

title: Meet Archie Renaux, who plays Johnny Warren in HBO’s War
description: The British actor, who co-stars with Sienna Miller and Dominic West in the series, was an air-conditioning engineer and model before his acting break.
content: Archie Renaux stars as the ambitious lawyer Johnny Warren in HBO’s latest legal drama War. Starring Renaux, Sienna Miller and Dominic West, the anthology premiered on October 1. Its first season follows the high-profile and multimillion dollar divorce between social media mogul Morgan Henderson (West) and his film star wife Carla Duval (Miller). The show also follows the estranged couple’s attorneys from rival law firms Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne. Renaux’s character, Johnny, becomes central to the show’s plot as it emerges that the Taylor & Byrne solicitor is actually a mole for Cathcarts. Here’s everything you need to know about Archie Renaux. He worked as an air-conditioning engineer Archie James Beale, who is known professionally as Archie Renaux, was born in November 1997 in Kingston upon Thames in the UK. He is reportedly of English and Indian descent. Although Renaux’s love for acting started young, he chose to pursue a conventional career path and was working a 9-5 apprenticeship as an air-conditioning engineer, like his grandfather. However, Renaux quickly realised that he wanted to give acting a real shot. Kick-starting his acting career “It took me doing an apprenticeship to realise I wasn’t happy,” Renaux told W Magazine. “Whilst I was young, I knew I had to try [acting].” The Morbius actor quit his job and enrolled himself in weekend acting schools. After a short modelling stint, another career path that Renaux discovered he did not enjoy, the actor landed his first on-screen role in the 2018 drama film Feline. Since his debut, Renaux has been steadily building his career and has starred in films such as Voyagers (2021), Catherine Called Birdy (2022) and Alien: Romulus (2024). He is a father Renaux has been in a long-term relationship with his partner Annie O’Hara. The couple welcomed their first child together, a daughter named Iris, in 2020. “Spending time with my daughter, watching her films, playing her games has allowed me to see the world from her point of view, through her eyes,” Renaux said about his daughter in an interview with Polimoda in 2024.

title: 4 Tokyo cafes that serve Hong Kong-style milk tea, from Chenputon to Victoria 1842
description: Hong Kong milk tea is thriving in Tokyo’s cafe scene, with many spots offering black tea menus, egg tarts, dim sum, pineapple buns and more.
content: Hong Kong milk tea – a mainstay of cha chaan teng, or Hong Kong-style diners – is taking on a new role in Tokyo’s cafe culture. According to the Japan Tea Association, the country is in the midst of a “third black tea boom” and more cafes are offering black tea menus. Even convenience stores are revamping their takeaway drink options, with 7-Eleven, for example, expanding its Seven Cafe tea machines to around 2,000 stores in early 2026. Suntory also released a Hong Kong-style milk tea under its Craft Boss soft drinks line earlier this year. There is even a growing trend of nunkatsu where usually young women enjoy upscale afternoon tea and take photos for social media. Against this backdrop, there is room for variety in the tea scene. While Taiwanese milk tea or English tea are far more familiar to Japanese consumers, a small number of new cafes have added Hong Kong-style milk tea to their menus. Here is where to try it in the Japanese capital. 1. Urushi to Hibi, Hatchobori Hong Kong’s afternoon tea culture has become the centrepiece of a space lined with lacquerware cups, chopsticks and jewellery. A dark wooden counter is laden with freshly baked egg tarts and scones, setting the stage for the tea theatre taking place behind it. Co-founders Lei Shengyu, Zhang Qingyue and Ji Qiuzi dove deep into Hong Kong milk tea culture after seeing its parallels with the world of crafts. They began following the work of Cui Hanpeng, a Shenzhen-based Hong Kong-style milk tea practitioner and champion of the 2024 National & Greater Bay Area KamCha Competition (HK Milk Tea), who works to spread the craft to younger generations. After studying theory and extraction methods online in Japan, they travelled to Shenzhen to take part in one of Cui’s workshops. They practised daily and even took part in the KamCha competition’s Shenzhen regionals in November 2025. They continued practising after returning to Japan. In January 2026, they felt ready to launch Urushi to Hibi as a full-fledged cafe. 1/F, Glanffice, 1-28-33 Shinkawa, Chuo City, Tokyo 2. Victoria 1842, Ichigaya More than a cafe, Victoria 1842 opened in September 2024 as a Hong Kong culture hub: a cafe, bookstore, goods shop and event space that hosts cultural exhibitions. Order milk tea, or perhaps yuen yeung (coffee with milk tea) with an egg, or bubble, waffle, and then enjoy them in the second-floor cafe. The dark wood space emulates colonial Hong Kong under British rule with antique furniture and framed photos of the city’s past on the wall – but it also comes with Wi-fi and charging spots for those wanting to get some work done. “We want to make this a space where people feel comfortable to just sit down and read,” says Eliza Wong, who assisted with interior styling and runs the Victoria 1842 social media account. Victoria 1842 Building, 15-10 Haraikatamachi, Shinjuku City, Tokyo 3. Ippai Cha, Korakuen The latest newcomer, Ippai Cha, opened in January 2026. According to Qi Bing, the store manager, the shop imports its tea leaf blend from Hong Kong and boils it for one hour to produce a deep, rich flavour. The tea is then strained eight to 10 times through a cloth filter for proper aeration and reduced astringency. It also bakes bolo bao, or pineapple buns, fresh daily – available with a variety of fillings and also in cocoa and matcha flavours. For those undecided, staff are quick to recommend the classic, sliced open and filled with a generous slab of Hokkaido butter. The shop gets extra bonus points for cute cat art depicting the four stages of making Hong Kong milk tea. 1/F, Monarch Mansion Korakuen, 2-24-11 Kasuga, Bunkyo City, Tokyo 4. Chenputon Hong Kong Tea Room 1946 Also invoking the British colonial era is Chenputon Hong Kong Tea Room 1946, which opened in February 2023 as the most tea-focused venue of the Cantonese restaurant group Chenputon. Located in the upscale business district of Marunouchi, its menu sits between Hong Kong cafe, dim sum restaurant and British tea room. It offers a decadent afternoon tea, replete with a cake stand laden with sweet and savoury bites, including its signature pork and shrimp siu mai, and Chinese and black teas served in British Burleigh teacups. There is no need to get too extravagant, though. Here, you can enjoy Hong Kong-style milk tea in classic Black & White cups with a warm egg tart on the side. B1/F, Shin-Marunouchi Building, 1 Chome-5-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda City, Tokyo

title: From Abby Choi to the ‘Hello Kitty’ killing: Hong Kong’s most shocking crimes
description: Hong Kong may be known as one of the world’s safest cities, but it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes.
content: The alleged murder and dismemberment of Abby Choi Tin-fung in 2023, which prosecutors say was linked to a dispute over a luxury flat, has once again gripped Hong Kong as the trial over the 28-year-old socialite’s death entered its second week. Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of her body. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, has pleaded not guilty to the same charge. All three men deny murdering Choi. While Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the world’s safest cities, it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes. 1. Plaza Hollywood stabbings (2023) Just months after Choi’s alleged murder, two women were stabbed to death in a frenzied knife attack at the Plaza Hollywood shopping centre in Diamond Hill by a man suffering from severe mental illness. News of the unprovoked attack, captured on CCTV, spread widely online and heightened safety concerns at a time when the city was still recovering from the Covid-19 pandemic. Szeto Sing-kwong, 43, a former warehouse worker, wandered through the shopping centre with an unsheathed knife he had just bought before encountering Fong Hiu-tung, 26, and Lau Kai-hei, 22, outside a Sasa cosmetics shop. CCTV footage showed Szeto repeatedly stabbing one of the women in an attack lasting nearly a minute. The second woman tried repeatedly to intervene but was herself slashed and stabbed. Fong sustained 27 knife wounds and Lau eight, according to medical evidence. Both died from blood loss and respiratory failure. Szeto later pleaded guilty to two counts of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, after prosecutors accepted that an acute relapse of paranoid schizophrenia meant he should not be held liable for murder. Last month, the High Court ordered him to receive indefinite mandatory psychiatric treatment and supervision at Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre in Tuen Mun, noting that he continued to show limited insight into his condition. 2. British banker turned double murderer (2014) British banker Rurik Jutting tortured and killed two Indonesian women in his Wan Chai flat between October and November 2014. Jutting tortured 23-year-old Sumarti Ningsih for three days, subjecting her to what the court described as increasingly cruel violence using a belt, sex toys, pliers and his fists, before slitting her throat on or about October 27. Her body was later found in a large black suitcase. Five days later, he took 26-year-old Seneng Mujiasih, also known as Jesse Lorena Ruri, back to his flat and cut her throat. It was reported that his murder spree was triggered by the break-up with his fiancée. Jutting was sentenced to life imprisonment for two counts of murder in 2016. He later appealed to the Court of Final Appeal, which dismissed his final attempt after just eight minutes. 3. Son’s gruesome slaughter of parents (2013) Henry Chau Hoi-leung, then 29, killed his parents in a rented flat in Tai Kok Tsui and placed their dismembered heads in a refrigerator. Chau had planned to murder his father, Chau Wing-ki, 65, and mother, Siu Yuet-yee, 63, for six months. He told the court he hated his parents and blamed them for his failures in life and love. He killed and dismembered the couple at a flat belonging to his friend, Angus Tse Chun-kei. Tse said Chau had threatened to harm his own mother, prompting him to help pack and dispose of some body parts at sea. Chau was caught after sending text messages confessing to the killings, having earlier filed a missing persons report and made an online appeal for help finding his parents. Forensic officers believed some of the couple’s body parts had been cooked, microwaved and salted. Others were decomposing when found. In 2015, Chau was convicted of two counts of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Tse was sentenced to one year in prison for preventing the lawful burial of bodies. The case inspired the 2022 film The Sparring Partner. 4. The ‘Hello Kitty’ case (1999) In one of Hong Kong’s most horrifying cases, 23-year-old nightclub hostess Fan Man-yee was kidnapped and tortured by three triad members before her death. Her head was later placed inside a Hello Kitty doll. Fan was abducted and held in a flat in Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, after the men accused her of stealing HK$4,000 (US$510) from one of their wallets. She was held for nearly a month in the flat, which was filled with Hello Kitty toys. The attackers, believed to have been under the influence of drugs, were suspected of torturing her in the days before her death. After she died, the men dismembered her body, boiled the flesh to conceal the smell of decomposition and discarded other remains. They kept her skull and sewed it into the head of a large Hello Kitty toy. The case came to light when a 13-year-old girl told police she had been having nightmares and felt “haunted” by a ghost. She was the girlfriend of one of the three killers and had occasionally joined them in assaulting Fan. In exchange for immunity, she testified against the men, who were convicted of manslaughter. Because only Fan’s skull, a tooth and some internal organs were recovered, the court heard there was insufficient evidence to determine whether she had been murdered or died from another cause, such as a drug overdose. The three men were sentenced in 2000 to life imprisonment for manslaughter, false imprisonment and preventing Fan’s lawful burial. One had his sentence reduced to 18 years after a retrial. 5. The ‘Rainy Night Butcher’ serial killings (1982) Perhaps Hong Kong’s most infamous serial killer, night-shift taxi driver Lam Kor-wan murdered four women in the 1980s after picking them up as passengers on rainy evenings. He drove them to secluded locations, strangled them with wires, photographed their bodies, dismembered them and preserved body parts in containers at his home. Lam was arrested in 1982 after attempting to develop photographs of his victims at a Kodak shop in Mong Kok. The shop manager alerted police, who ambushed Lam when he returned to collect the pictures. Although the photographs suggested there may have been more victims, Lam was ultimately charged with the murders of four women police were able to identify. The court heard that he had eaten part of one victim’s intestine and, according to evidence, including photographs and videos, engaged in necrophilia. Lam was sentenced to death, but the sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment.

title: Why are mainland China’s tax officials suddenly so interested in my Hong Kong MPF?
description: China’s push to tax offshore trusts is supposed to target the super-rich. So why are mainland officials asking me about my Hong Kong MPF?
content: For the past few months, this newspaper has extensively covered China’s ongoing clampdown on tax avoidance, especially its push to tax the income of super-rich families held in offshore trusts. We never expected to become targets of the campaign ourselves. But there have been signs in recent weeks that officials are starting to take an interest even in the incomes of South China Morning Post journalists, with several of us being contacted by the tax man. First, a colleague with our Beijing bureau received a text message from the city’s tax service, issuing a “warm reminder” to declare any holdings in “offshore trusts”. “To further assist you in fulfilling your tax obligations and help you avoid tax risks, you are kindly requested to promptly notify us of any offshore trust holdings and complete the required tax declaration and payments,” the message read. “We thank you for your cooperation and full support.” Then, at the end of last month, I received a polite yet baffling phone call from Shanghai’s municipal tax bureau, which had taken a particular interest in Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) – the city’s compulsory retirement savings scheme. “Sorry for disturbing you,” the caller said. “We understand that the MPF has been categorised as a type of offshore trust, and so we wonder if we could gather some information.” She then asked to check my mainland China tax payments during my two-year stint working in Shanghai, before demanding details about the monthly contributions that I and my employer make to my MPF account in Hong Kong. I explained to her that the MPF was a de facto pension fund mandated by Hong Kong law for all wage earners, and so it was a bit far-fetched for mainland tax officials to label it an “offshore trust” – a tool usually seen as the preserve of the wealthy. “Just like Hong Kong’s Inland Revenue Department won’t try to collect tax from social security accounts in mainland China, it would be utterly outrageous if the mainland moved to tax the MPF, a pension and retirement savings fund,” I said. In response, the official quickly apologised for the abrupt call and any impression that she was “chasing taxes”. “It’s nothing more than part of our routine work collecting and updating records,” she assured me, adding that she would mark down my statement and that normally no further actions would follow. But I took the opportunity to continue the discussion, telling her it would be better if mainland tax authorities could clearly define what they consider to be an offshore trust, taking into consideration the fact that people overwhelmingly feel that pension funds like the MPF should be spared. The official said she would “relay” my suggestions to her supervisors, adding that – as a frontline worker – she was told to make these calls. I also pointed out that the policy could potentially affect Shanghai’s ability to lure global talent. “As mainland China’s most prominent commercial and financial hub, tens of thousands of people from Hong Kong and abroad work in Shanghai,” I said. “Many of them may reconsider Shanghai if their offshore savings and pensions are taxed.” She concurred. The call ended with her repeatedly stressing that I was not facing a tax demand and that the tax bureau was simply “canvassing” some individuals to gauge their opinions. “Personally, I also think pension and retirement savings, in whatever form, should not be taxed,” she said. Beijing has launched an effort to tighten its tax enforcement policies over the past couple of years, which has included new measures to collect taxes on overseas income and assets such as offshore trusts, cross-border insurance policies and overseas equity investments. The campaign is designed to boost the finances of local governments, which have come under strain as land sales have plunged amid China’s property downturn and an economic slowdown has affected tax revenues. In July, China’s Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration announced that all income in offshore trusts would face a flat 20 per cent tax. The tax applies at each stage of a trust’s life cycle: the transfer of assets into the trust, income earned during its operation, as well as its eventual closure. Many economists have pointed out that China, like any country, has the right to collect taxes based on its laws and plug tax loopholes as it sees fit. But concerns have still been raised that the campaign could lead to aggressive tax enforcement, with inconsistent, unpredictable actions – sometimes applied retroactively – that stifle economic vitality at a time when China needs to boost confidence among consumers and businesses.

title: Opinion | If Hongkongers’ support for Legco is waning, it isn’t just lawmakers’ fault
description: Despite Legco having become more efficient, public perception of the legislature isn’t overwhelmingly positive. The administration’s approach hasn’t helped.
content: Rita Fan Hsu Lai-tai, Hong Kong’s first post-handover Legislative Council president, recently dropped a political bomb. She revealed that one of her friends had been telling her that a legislature with 90 seats costs a lot more than one with 60 and that “I kind of agree with that”. The basic maths behind the statement cannot be refuted: 60 is two-thirds of 90. Even though Fan didn’t bring up the topic herself – she was asked the question by the host during a radio show – it was shocking that a political veteran of her calibre would suggest considering the reduction of Legco seats to cut costs. Funding is not the main issue at play here. Reducing the discussion to dollars and cents does not properly address the real problem, which is public perception. First, a quick breakdown of how we arrived at the current number of Legco seats. The legislature expanded from 60 to 70 seats for the 2012-16 term. This was part of the 2010 constitutional and electoral reform package, which also increased the number of Election Committee members from 800 to 1,200. Naturally, there was a cost to adding 10 more seats to the council, but the addition was seen as worth it. Then, the 2021 electoral overhaul took the number of Legco seats from 70 to 90 and completely reconfigured Legco’s composition. There is a gap between public expectations and the perception of how lawmakers are performing their roles and duties. Fan did touch on this in her interview, pointing to the personal conduct of lawmakers and stressing that they should always behave with caution and avoid breaking the law, however minor the infraction. She cited recent misconduct by Legco members. “Lawmakers should not only convey the thoughts of residents but also serve as role models for them,” she said. It is true that misconduct by Legco members erodes public trust in them. Without that trust, the council’s perceived value diminishes. Lawmakers have been embroiled in legal troubles and controversy before, though, and reducing the size of the legislature did not come up. Answering why Legco’s size and cost are now an issue requires considering something beyond personal conduct. The skirmishes inside the chamber that used to make news have dissipated with this better-behaved, more patriotic Legco, so the most largely mundane work lawmakers do goes unnoticed. Incidents like the recent one at a district office of two lawmakers are more likely to garner headlines. A disgruntled resident reportedly threw red paint at the joint office because the lawmakers were “being unhelpful”. Such an episode leaves a greater impression on the public than lawmakers praising one of their own for being well-spoken, which also recently made the news. A survey last year by the PoD Research Institute found that only 29.6 per cent of respondents expressed satisfaction with Legco’s performance while 50.6 per cent were dissatisfied. While we don’t need fights to return to the legislature’s chambers, we do need to know that quality debate is taking place and that our lawmakers are making constructive contributions to the city. That means doing more than just airing any idea that comes to their minds. One noteworthy bad example of late is the suggestion to hold a Mark Six lottery for families of newborns to help boost the city’s anaemic birth rate. Legislator and former police officer Joe Chan said last month that the government could collaborate with the Hong Kong Jockey Club to set up a Mark Six-style award ranging from HK$1 million (US$127,000) to HK$4 million for newborns. Two years ago, lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu had suggested that displaying photos of babies in government offices would encourage more civil servants to have children. These are not valuable contributions to Hong Kong’s future. The biggest issue by far stems from the unintended consequences of how Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has conducted his business with Legco. During his unprecedented speech to lawmakers at the oath-taking ceremony in January, Lee spoke at length on how he thinks legislators should do their job. That gave the impression that Legco members did not know how to do their jobs. He did not mention the legislature’s constitutional role of monitoring the government. In addition to this, the way Lee and his team have treated lawmakers who have been critical of their policies is making it harder for the city’s legislators to carry out their work. Despite Legco having become more efficient, the public’s perception of the council has suffered as a result of the administration’s approach.

title: Man arrested after 23,000 bogus customer service scam calls in over a week
description: The 24-year-old man is believed to have applied for a large number of SIM cards under a company name.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a 24-year-old man over an alleged scam operation that made more than 23,000 fraudulent calls in over a week by impersonating e-commerce customer service representatives, with one victim losing more than HK$100,000 (US$12,741). The force said on Sunday that the man was suspected of operating a call centre for a syndicate that posed as online shopping platform staff and tricked victims into transferring money for a variety of reasons. Senior Inspector of the Commercial Crime Bureau Liu Long-kwan said the syndicate claimed there were problems with goods the victims had purchased and that they needed to be returned or refunded. “These fraudsters would use various excuses, such as charging deposits or handling fees, or falsely claiming that the victims’ bank accounts would be charged a steep annual fee, to demand that victims transfer money into bank accounts they provided,” Liu said. In a Friday operation, police raided a residential flat in Tseung Kwan O and arrested the man on suspicion of fraud. Officers seized a large batch of SIM cards, a modem-pool device, four mobile phones, a computer and a tablet. Liu said police believed the man had been using the unit as a hub for making fraudulent calls. He added that the man had applied for a large number of SIM cards from telecommunications companies under a company name. The newly registered phone numbers from these SIM cards were linked to recent telephone fraud cases in which scammers impersonated customer service staff of e-commerce companies to obtain money from victims. Liu said the modem-pool device, which had made more than 23,000 automated calls to local phone numbers in over a week since it began operating, could be remotely controlled through a software programme installed on the computer found in the Tseung Kwan O flat. He noted that one of the phone numbers among the seized SIM cards was linked to a recent customer service fraud case in which the victim lost more than HK$100,000. The man is currently being detained for further investigation. Liu said police urged the public to verify a caller’s identity if they received calls from unknown sources, and to remain vigilant if the caller asked for money. He also reminded the public not to sell SIM cards registered in their own name to others, warning that they could face criminal liability if the cards were misused for fraud.

title: China cinemas tap into Zheng tennis fever gripping country ahead of women’s final
description: Venues across mainland will broadcast Zheng Qinwen’s women’s singles final against Mirra Andreeva after National Tennis Centre sold out.
content: Cinemas across China will throw open their doors for a special showing on Sunday, but it isn’t the latest blockbuster fans are flocking to see – it’s tennis star Zheng Qinwen. The Olympic champion has finally broken her country’s China Open curse, and will be the first home player to compete in a singles final, men’s or women’s, since Chen Li lost to Chinese Taipei’s Wang Shi-ting in 1996. With the National Tennis Centre in Beijing selling out, cinemas across the mainland have opted to show the match against fourth seed and French Open champion Mirra Andreeva on their giant screens. The pair will battle it out on the Diamond Court, two years after Zheng beat her Russian rival in the quarter-finals at the same venue. Whoever comes out on top, the tournament will get a first-time women’s singles champion. Win or lose, reaching the last two marks a dramatic turnaround for Zheng, who was handed a wild-card entry after enduring a miserable run of form as she recovered from an elbow injury. A “no retreat” mindset has delivered the 24-year-old’s most consistent tennis in some time, and taken her live ranking from No 54 to No 28, a significant improvement given she had plummeted as far as No 122 in July. “I’ve faced many tough opponents along the way, including today, and I’m very happy to reach the China Open final,” Zheng said after her 7-5, 6-2 semi-final win over Elise Mertens on Saturday. “It’s an honour to be the first Chinese player in the final here, but the job isn’t finished yet.” Reflecting on a difficult spell when her ranking fell outside the top 100, she recalled accepting the reality of playing US Open qualifiers and following her coach’s instructions without complaint, as she “no longer had the leverage to argue”. “I took a much more humble approach during that time and rediscovered myself,” she said, adding that she had not even thought about making the final at the start of the week. “I’m glad that I can be the first one. But still, I know the battle is not over. Tomorrow I will face a tough opponent. There is one more match to go. I would say I would stay humble and let’s see for tomorrow.” Standing between Zheng and the trophy is a 19-year-old who will be No 3 in the world when the rankings are next updated. She will be the youngest player to have reached that spot since her compatriot Maria Sharapova did so in 2005. The Russian said she had little concern about playing Zheng in front of a passionate home crowd, but acknowledged her rival had been “playing better, she’s been beating a lot of great players”. Still, Zheng needed three sets to get past her first four opponents, before finding her rhythm to see off Elina Svitolina and Mertens. Andreeva, meanwhile, has not dropped a set and blasted past Nikola Bartunkova in the semi-finals, winning 6-2, 6-2. Zheng is not the only home player in action on Sunday. Zhang Shuai and partner Katerina Siniakova will take on Gabriela Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani for the women’s doubles title.

title: Can Saudi Arabia’s 2034 Fifa World Cup survive the Middle East’s escalating wars?
description: Escalating conflicts threaten to leave billions in Gulf sports infrastructure stranded, casting doubt on the region’s mega-event strategy.
content: When 60,000 football fans gathered in Jeddah for the Arabian Gulf Cup on Tuesday, they inadvertently highlighted the vulnerability of major sports events hosted by Gulf monarchies to the wars raging across the region. The previous day, Saudi Arabia resumed strikes on Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi rebels after a four-year ceasefire collapsed. That truce had originally followed a Houthi attack on an oil facility near Jeddah’s Formula One track during a practice session. While the two-week football tournament went ahead as planned, lingering risks were highlighted on Wednesday when a Houthi air strike on Riyadh’s international airport killed three people, including a Saudia Airlines captain. Analysts say the threats from the Houthis and Iranian air strikes against Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states – Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman – do not bode well for the region’s ambitious sporting calendar. If these conflicts drag on or end inconclusively, the resulting uncertainty could undermine coming major events, including the 2030 Asian Games in Qatar, as well as the 2034 Fifa World Cup and Asian Games in Saudi Arabia. While regional instability was not unique to the Gulf, it would weigh heavily on host decisions, according to Guy Burton, a Brussels-based international relations researcher and co-host of The FootPol Podcast, a sports show focusing on the intersection of football and politics. Security considerations are built into every major event bid, but the Middle East presents particular challenges. “What is distinctive in this context is the volatility,” Burton said, noting how difficult it was to predict whether threats would escalate or subside. Past hosts have always had to manage security risks ranging from crime to state-sponsored threats – such as London hosting the 2012 Olympics following the events of September 11, 2001, and Britain’s involvement in the wars on terror. Diversification under pressure But the risks do not end with security concerns. Gulf monarchies have invested heavily in sports to diversify their economies away from dependency on oil and gas revenues. “The pressure on that model now comes from material realities, in particular less certainty over government revenues as hydrocarbon exports come under strain,” Burton said. If conflicts disrupt these events, the tens of billions of dollars invested in stadiums, hotels, airports and airlines could be left redundant, along with the economic policies underpinning them. As if to drive the point home, the Bahrain Formula One Grand Prix scheduled for April was postponed and relocated to Malaysia and the Saudi Grand Prix cancelled outright, incurring an estimated US$200 million in losses. That followed the March cancellation of the Finalissima football match in Qatar between Spain and Argentina. Similarly, the Esports World Cup was moved from Saudi Arabia to France in May, though this did not derail Riyadh’s gaming ambitions. In August, a consortium led by its sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), finalised its US$55 billion leveraged buyout of Electronic Arts – the largest transaction of its kind. The 2027 test According to Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, fellow for the Middle East at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, “the next big test” would be the AFC Asian Cup across Saudi Arabia in early 2027. “That experience will be closely studied for what it may portend for future large-scale events in the Gulf,” Ulrichsen said, including the Fiba Basketball World Cup in Qatar later that year. Risk-averse investors in these and other coming events will be watching closely. Simon Chadwick, a professor of Afro-Eurasian sport at the Emlyon Business School in France, said regional stability was paramount. Without a lasting peace, Chadwick warned, long-term ambitions – such as the 2030 and 2034 Asian Games, the 2034 Fifa World Cup and Qatar’s confirmed bid to host the 2036 Olympics – faced serious challenges. Qatar spent US$240 billion on infrastructure for the 2022 Fifa World Cup, aiming to reuse those assets for future events. But war and political instability risk turning that infrastructure into costly white elephants. Only US$6.5 billion of that spending went to stadiums, putting into perspective the US$22 billion Saudi Arabia is pouring into venues for 2034. “This year is really challenging historic strategic decisions,” Chadwick said. Fears over viability have already led the PIF to shelve a number of unprofitable projects, including LIV Golf after US$5 billion in losses. In contrast, the acquisition of EA Sports is seen as a step in the right direction, reflecting a shift towards building a sustainable domestic ecosystem – incorporating intellectual property ownership and a joint venture with Lenovo – rather than relying solely on hosting single events. Nonetheless, active conflicts in the region had “certainly complicated” the Gulf’s ambitions to become a global sports hub, Ulrichsen said. The long lead-up to the 2034 World Cup provided some cushion, but officials in the region were hoping 2026 was “a one-off rather than the start of a longer-term pattern of uncertainty and unpredictability”, he added.

title: China’s rich coastal cities to see sea-level rise up to 20% higher than global average
description: Even if global warming is limited to 1.5 degrees Celsius, scientists warn China’s densely populated coastline faces flooding this century.
content: International scientists warn that rising sea levels driven by melting Antarctic ice will be 15 to 20 per cent higher in cities such as Hong Kong and Shanghai compared with the global average. They said gravitational shifts caused by shrinking Antarctic ice would redistribute water across the globe, causing higher ocean levels along China’s densely populated coastlines. “Even if we limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit], the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious goal, Antarctica still has a 92 per cent chance of losing mass this century,” said lead author Lin Yucheng, an assistant professor at City University of Hong Kong’s school of energy and environment. “For port-based megacities like these, [rising sea levels] means more frequent and costly shocks. Without effective adaptation and coastal protection, which is very costly, large numbers of people may eventually need to relocate,” the climate scientist said. Lin collaborated with researchers from institutions in Australia, Britain, New Zealand and the United States to evaluate how the mass loss of the Antarctic Ice Sheet threatens coastal communities far away from the Earth’s south pole. In their paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Geoscience on September 30, the team said effective management of the risks to densely populated coastal communities required rapid emissions reductions in line with the Paris Climate Agreement. The study found that Antarctica, a massive frozen expanse larger than China and India combined, was highly likely to lose mass this century. “We tried thousands of different Antarctic models and found we are highly certain that Antarctica will cause sea-level rise higher in Shanghai and Hong Kong than global average – 15 to 20 per cent more than global average,” he said. When asked when the above-average rise in sea levels would happen in the Chinese cities, Lin said “almost immediately”. “Once Antarctic ice enters the ocean, the water is redistributed within weeks to a few months. So it is already happening, and it applies to every centimetre of sea-level rise that comes from Antarctica,” he explained. “If we do not cut greenhouse gas emissions fast enough, we found a potential domino effect that could add up to 25cm (9.8 inches) of sea-level rise from Antarctica alone by 2100 – enough to permanently flood the homes of more than 10 million people.” According to Lin, this domino effect begins with greenhouse gas emissions causing the ocean surrounding Antarctica to warm. As the warm waters thin the floating ice shelves, these weakened shelves break apart. Consequently, the glaciers formerly held in place by the shelves flow faster into the ocean. To put 25cm of sea-level rise in context, he said global sea levels had risen by about 20cm since 1900. “Yet that is already the fastest rise in at least 4,000 years, and its impact on coastal extremes is profound. Human-driven sea-level rise at about 15cm has quadrupled the frequency of extreme coastal flooding worldwide since 1900,” Lin said. He pointed to his recent study that found rising sea levels caused by human activity were responsible for more than 70 per cent of extreme coastal flooding days in Hong Kong between 2010 and 2018. “Antarctica alone could add up to 25cm by 2100, and about 29 to 30cm in Hong Kong and Shanghai. That comes on top of rise from other sources, such as melting of the Greenland ice sheet and mountain glaciers, and warming oceans that make seawater expand,” Lin said. Known as the “sleeping giant” of rising sea levels, Antarctica’s vast scale means it reacts slowly, accounting for roughly 10 per cent of global sea-level expansion between 2006 and 2018. “The worry is that once it starts losing ice, or ‘wakes up’, it keeps going for centuries,” Lin said. “So 25cm by 2100 is only the start. “In the most extreme simulations from a recent international ice sheet modelling project, Antarctica alone adds up to about 7 metres (22.9 feet) by 2300.”

title: Annabelle Ho’s climate education concerts mix violin, film and environmental awareness
description: The violinist and activist is the founder of ClimateXArt, a performance and climate change awareness initiative aiming to educate and inspire.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension , with exercises based on the story we’ve written.
Annabelle Ho Wai-shan’s fingers flew across the neck of her violin. Behind her, scenes from the Japanese animated film Spirited Away played on a screen. In the Studio Ghibli classic, a powerful River Spirit is infected with human pollution. The main character pulls out what becomes a heaping pile of rubbish from the grateful spirit’s body.
Ho finished playing and the scene behind her ended. She began talking about Hong Kong’s own pollution and waste problem. She also noted groups doing environmental work in the city.
The concert is part of Ho’s ClimateXArt project. She founded it on Earth Day 2023. Since then, the violinist has hosted multiple concerts that mix musical performance with climate education. It has reached some 1,450 people.
“The way we treat our planet is ultimately how it treats us back,” Ho said. “While our environment is facing severe damage – some of it irreversible – it is never too late to stop further degradation and do everything within our power to restore what we can.”
The 28-year-old works on the project alongside her full-time job. She wants her music to start a conversation about climate change.
“I often think about how to make the next generation really understand [what’s important] … and inspire them to do it themselves, without pushing them,” Ho said.
After graduating from university, Ho helped out at a TEDx programme. There, she was impressed by a teen who spoke about ocean protection.
“I thought since she could do it, I could do it too,” Ho said.
The experience encouraged the violinist to join climate action projects. She began to wonder: could she use music to talk about the environment?
She held her first collaborative performance at a cafe in Central.
It was the first time she combined Studio Ghibli films, classical music and climate change awareness. The performance was informal and experimental . Some came because they liked Studio Ghibli films and the music. Others were simply curious.
This showed Ho that music could bring people into a conversation about climate change even if it was not the reason they walked through the door.
“Music is a really good ‘soft’ approach. It doesn’t force you … it gives everyone room to talk,” she said.
At the end of every performance, Ho connects the film scene to environmental issues in Hong Kong. She wraps up by explaining solutions offered by local organisations.
Audience members learn what is available in Hong Kong, “which can help them take individual climate action”, she said.
In 2023, the violinist performed twice at the 28th United Nations Climate Change Conference, or Cop28. At the conference, Ho learned how climate change is experienced differently around the world.
She recalled a conversation with representatives from a small, developing country. They were curious how Hong Kong had “so much money” for green policies.
“I saw they really wanted to do something but were very powerless because they had no money,” Ho said. “Their anxiety really awakened me.”
Ho has given guest lectures at Hong Kong universities and local organisations. She discusses how music can inspire climate action.
The violinist said she occasionally feels frustrated when audience members seem uninspired by her performance and its message. But she reminds herself that it may be one step towards caring for the environment.
“I don’t mind if they just listen to the music. I’m also very grateful they gave me time to speak and were willing to listen,” she said.

title: Disney+ K-drama Merry Berry Love: Ji Chang-wook goes to Japan in hollow romantic comedy
description: This Japan-South Korea co-production with Mio Imada as a strawberry farmer opposite Ji’s Seoul designer aims squarely for low-hanging fruit.
content: Lead cast: Ji Chang-wook, Mio Imada Cross-cultural media ties between Japan and South Korea continue to blossom with Merry Berry Love, a rural romance starring Ji Chang-wook (The Worst of Evil) and Mio Imada (Trillion Game). Co-produced by South Korea’s CJ ENM and Japan’s Nippon Television, the show airs locally on Nippon TV and streams globally on Disney+. Although written and directed by South Korean creatives, the story unfolds largely on Charo Island, in rural Japan. Imada plays Karin Shirahama, a plucky farmer who has spent years trying to secure official recognition for her strawberry patch. Despite losing overworked staff and facing repeated setbacks, she puts on a brave face. Karin also suffers from a mysterious illness that flares up when her heart rate increases. Across the sea in glitzy Seoul, celebrated spatial designer Lee Yu-bin (Ji) has just landed the biggest deal of his career. He delegates the paperwork to a friend and business partner, only to discover that the man has scammed him. Yu-bin’s reputation and finances are left in tatters. His luck takes a turn when he inherits a small plot of land in Japan. With little else to his name, he travels east, hoping to sell it and start over. Little does Yu-bin know that Karin and her strawberries already occupy the land. Even before they realise this, the pair lock horns several times during Yu-bin’s misfortune-prone journey to the island. At the end of the opening episode, a devastated Karin returns to her ravaged strawberry patch to find Yu-bin casually eating the last of her cherished berries. Her heart monitor goes off and she collapses into his arms in classic K-drama fashion. Perhaps “classic” is a little too generous here, as Merry Berry Love aims squarely for low-hanging fruit at every turn. This is partly by design, as broad comedy travels better across cultures than subtle humour, but the resulting confection feels hollow, even by K-drama romcom standards. Despite their global success, South Korea’s film and drama industries face a domestic market crisis, driven in part by declining local demand and soaring production costs. South Korean companies are consequently more open than ever to international collaborations. While South Korea has been building ties with markets such as Hollywood and emerging Southeast Asian territories, its exchanges with Japan have been among the most visible in recent years. Around this time in 2025, Netflix released two South Korea-Japan co-productions: the big-budget satire film Good News and the romantic comedy series Romantics Anonymous. Both screened at the 30th Busan International Film Festival. Netflix returned to Busan in 2026 with the manhwa adaptation The Blue Road. Merry Berry Love is a glossy affair with major star pedigree in the form of Ji, but its eagerness to please and cautious cross-cultural storytelling result in a procession of cliché-riddled set pieces. Individually, they look the part; taken together, they quickly tip into parody. Similarly, Yu-bin and Karin are skeletal characters stitched together from familiar archetypes. Attractive on the surface, they offer nothing under the hood, and the opening episode makes little effort to flesh them out. Merry Berry Love is effortless and easy-going, but with only one 45-minute chunk of light entertainment a week, veteran K-drama fans may want to approach this as a snack, rather than a meal – or perhaps wait a few weeks to build up a few hours of content to binge. The linguistic mix also feels oddly inconsequential. Yu-bin does not speak Japanese, but his communication difficulties are no greater than those of the typical aloof city slicker in the familiar K-drama fish-out-of-water routine. Before long, he seems to understand everyone just fine. International co-productions are a notoriously difficult balancing act, and the urge to find shared emotional, comic and dramatic beats is understandable. But a series still needs a reason to exist. Cute title aside, Merry Berry Love has yet to show that anything meaningful is ready to sprout from Karin’s ruined patch. Merry Berry Love is streaming on Disney+.

title: NBA China and Shanghai Jiushi sign deal to drive development of players, coaches
description: Collaboration is first of its kind between league and club in China, and follows on from 2025 agreement covering national teams.
content: A new deal signed by NBA China and Shanghai Jiushi will see the league help the Chinese Basketball Association side with the development of its players, coaches and front office. The collaboration with the reigning CBA champions is the first of its kind, and comes as the Dallas Mavericks and Houston Rockets clash in two pre-season friendlies in Macau. According to a statement released by the NBA, the agreement will cover four key areas: elite player development, competition opportunities, coach training and front office executives. For players who show promise, there will be access to international basketball development programmes, while the club will get the chance to take part in “events and competitions conducted by the NBA in China and across Asia”. Among those will be the NBA Shanghai Basketball Festival, NBA-organised invitational tournaments, and other future competitions in the region, the statement said. Troy Justice, the NBA’s senior vice-president, head of international basketball operations, said the deal was part of the league’s “long-standing commitment to supporting basketball development in China at every level”. “We look forward to working together to develop the next generation of elite players, coaches and front office executives,” he added. Shanghai Jiushi youth players have already had the opportunity to train in the United States, something the club’s chairman, Wang Zhenwei, said would contribute to their development. “This collaboration marks an important step in our efforts to expand the club’s international development initiatives,” Wang added. “With a focus on elite player development, the agreement reflects a practical and complementary approach that will create long-term growth opportunities for both organisations. The collaboration builds on the multi-year agreement between NBA China and the CBA, which was announced during last year’s games at The Venetian Arena between Brooklyn Nets and Phoenix Suns, and covered the country’s national teams and some of the best young players.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: Gaza nurse’s obstacle-laden road to becoming a professor
description: Border closures and travel restrictions prevented Hammoda Abu-Odah from leaving Gaza on six occasions. Today he is a lauded Hong Kong nursing professor.
content: On six occasions, Hammoda Abu-Odah, a Gaza nurse-turned Hong Kong scholar was offered an opportunity to study overseas. But each time, border closures and travel restrictions prevented him from taking them up. Abu-Odah had obtained a nursing degree in his native Gaza but set his sights on an academic career abroad. He kept working, teaching and conducting research, despite the many challenges that prevented him from leaving. Finally, on the seventh attempt, he made it to Hong Kong, where he eventually completed his doctorate at Polytechnic University in 2022 after receiving a Hong Kong PhD fellowship. “If I had given up after losing six scholarship opportunities, I would not be here in Hong Kong teaching today,” he said. His journey has placed him among the finalists in the perseverance category of the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Sino Group. Launched in 2013, the awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed. Among other honours, Abu-Odah’s doctoral work received the Distinguished Thesis Award from PolyU’s faculty of health and social sciences in 2022, and, earlier this year, he was selected as one of the top 10 finalists for the Aster Guardians Global Nursing Award out of more than 134,000 entries across 214 countries and economies. Abu-Odah had not planned for a career in nursing. His father had hoped he would become a doctor, but medical school fees were beyond the family’s means. “I told him, why not nursing?” Abu-Odah recalled. “We would still be in healthcare and our goal would still be to support patients.” He also made a promise to his father. “I told him I would become a professor in the future,” Abu-Odah said. Once he began training, he began to see the value of nursing. “Nurses are the backbone of the healthcare system. Patients and their families need our emotions and our feelings. They need us to spend time with them.” That outlook later drew him towards cancer and palliative care. One experience in Gaza remains especially vivid. Abu-Odah met a woman in her mid-30s with metastatic breast cancer and two children. Her greatest fear was what would happen to them after her death. “She told me, ‘I am not worried about myself. I am worried about my children,’” he recalled. “Our concern is often not about ourselves. It is about the next generation.” Another patient, an elderly man with a brain tumour, required treatment outside Gaza but was unable to cross the border. He died two weeks later, reinforcing Abu-Odah’s commitment to improving access to palliative and cancer care. Now an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s school of nursing, his research covers cancer supportive and survivorship care, palliative and end-of-life care, patient-centred communication and culturally responsive interventions. He also serves as the nursing representative for Palestine on the WHO Regional Palliative Care Expert Network for the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Hong Kong has become home for his family too. Five of his six children were born in Gaza, but the youngest was born in Hong Kong. He ultimately chose to continue his academic career in the city rather than take up an offer in the United States. His family’s wish to remain in the city was an important consideration, he said. His own setbacks have taught him lessons that he passes on to students. “Obstacles may close the road you expected to take, but they do not have to end the journey,” Abu-Odah said. “You find another way, keep moving forward and never give up.”

title: Urn with Anita Mui’s ashes missing from Lantau monastery as family appeals for help
description: Family of late Hong Kong Cantopop star says police made ‘no progress’ after three-month investigation, with case causing ‘immense distress’.
content: The urn containing the ashes of late Hong Kong Cantopop star Anita Mui Yim-fong was discovered missing from a monastery three months ago, the singer’s family has revealed, saying police have made “no progress” in their investigation and that the incident has caused “immense distress”. A police spokesman said on Sunday that the force had received a report on July 18 that an item stored in a Lantau monastery was suspected to have gone missing. The case has been classified as a “request for police assistance” and is being investigated by Lantau district crime squad. No arrest has been made so far, the spokesman said. Mui’s family made a public appeal for information on the whereabouts of the ashes in a statement issued on Saturday, Mui’s birthday. The singer, who died in 2003 aged 40, would have been 63. The statement, reposted by one of the singer’s biggest fan groups – the Anita Mui International Fan Club – on its Instagram account, said police had made no progress after a three-month investigation. “This incident has brought immense distress and mental torment to Mui’s family. Coupled with the earlier passing of Mui’s mother, the family is now enduring a dual blow, suffering both physically and emotionally,” the statement said. The statement revealed that a fan first discovered that the urn had gone missing from a columbarium at Po Lin Monastery on Lantau Island while paying tribute to Mui on July 18. The monastery is located on the Ngong Ping plateau and is the site of the famous Tian Tan Buddha or Big Buddha. The fan discovered that the screws on the door panel of the niche housing Mui’s ashes had come loose, and the urn inside was missing. The fan notified Mui’s family, who made a police report. The statement added that there was no portrait at the niche as the family wanted a low-profile arrangement. Police said they would continue to maintain contact with the family and relevant parties and follow up appropriately. Another fan club, the 1,000-strong Mui Nation, said on Sunday that it was shocked to hear about the loss of the urn and called for the monastery’s management to review its security arrangements and explain what had happened. “The incident is extremely absurd, against any moral standards and is a shock to those who love and respect Ms Mui Yim-fong,” it said. Po Lin Monastery said it would not comment on the case as it was under investigation. It was understood that Mui’s family did not receive any extortion call demanding payment for the return of the ashes. No other urns at the columbarium appear to have gone missing. One fan wrote on social media: “My heart hurts so, so much. Mui went through so many trials and so much suffering in her lifetime. Why do so many bad things still happen even after she’s gone?” “This is so utterly classless,” another fan commented. “Whoever stole her ashes should go to hell.” Posting on Threads, Mui’s apprentice, singer-actor Patrick Tam Yiu-man, said he hoped police would recover the urn soon. “I really do not understand why there is such negligence,” he added. Mui’s family also expressed hope the ashes would be recovered as soon as possible. The family appealed to Mui’s friends, fans who had previously visited to pay their respects and the general public for help. The family said anyone who visited the columbarium on or before July 18 and had noticed anything suspicious should get in touch immediately. They also appealed to those who drove to the columbarium to provide relevant car-cam footage. Those who had any clues, photos or videos should contact the Lantau district crime squad at 3661 1938 or the WhatsApp Hotline at 4740 1308, the family added. Anti-triad officers have arrested a man in connection with the suspected theft of urns from a columbarium in Sha Tin in November last year, after containers holding the ashes of legendary kung fu master Lau Kar-leung were allegedly stolen between May and August last year.

title: Tariffs, millions in extra costs, Iran war: Trump’s policies hammer US firms
description: ‘Frustrating would be one word,’ a CEO says, as US manufacturers struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.
content: For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminium product manufacturer in the US state of Ohio, President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs – and recently, the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive. Rende is CEO at Shapes Unlimited, one of many American producers smarting from Trump’s economic policies as the midterm election approaches. “Frustrating would be one word,” Rende said. “And I think that we’re sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power,” he added. Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries. Besides aluminium, the duties hit steel and autos too, while US trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country. Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty. Trump’s spiralling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries. Grievances over Trump’s trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favour as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November’s vote. Rende’s company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminium building products used in fixtures like fences. Trump’s tariffs on aluminium have steadily climbed, from 10 per cent during his first presidency to 25 per cent and then 50 per cent last year, and Rende has felt the impact. “This year alone, it’s upwards of US$4.5 million to US$5 million in additional costs,” Rende said. “There’s only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat,” he added. “So, we absorb a healthy portion.” These added costs include steeper transport fees, as fuel prices surged with the US-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are “upwards of US$6,500 per container” of goods from suppliers, Rende said. As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly. Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump’s trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions. “It’s been difficult for businesses to manage,” Miller said from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. “I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views.” Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s duties, the US leader has since reinstated many of them. Deteriorating US-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other’s products after trade negotiations collapsed in August. “We’re selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers,” Miller said. He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada this year, but progress has slowed. Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, said he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely. These are a “mixed bag” for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members. Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said. Canada is also Ohio’s biggest export market, with a third of Ohio’s exports going to the country. “Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times,” he said. The Iran war adds to stresses, raising freight costs and hitting aluminium supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East. With a lack of new US aluminium smelters, Coviello said: “We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defence and medical industry.” But he added: “We have to be careful when you’re talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the US.”

title: Trump’s new spokeswoman is a ‘devoted fan’ who lived in Beijing and speaks Chinese
description: White House press secretary worked at a leading Chinese law firm and learned enough of the language to occasionally surprise people.
content: Before she addresses the world from behind the White House briefing room podium this week, 42-year-old Katie Zacharia has a story that stretches far beyond Washington’s power corridors. Years before US President Donald Trump appointed her as his new press secretary, she lived in Beijing, worked at one of China’s leading law firms, and learned enough Chinese to occasionally surprise people. Her reported experience in China spans international law and a communications role with a non-profit organisation focused on the children of migrant workers, alongside her later career in conservative politics in the US. She also served briefly earlier this year as spokeswoman and deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security. Most recently, she served as senior communications adviser to Truth Social, owned by the Trump Media & Technology Group. Zacharia is replacing Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as press secretary at the end of August to spend more time with her family after the birth of her second child. Leavitt is now joining Fox News as an on-air contributor and is expected to host her own show. Announcing Zacharia’s appointment on Truth Social on Friday, Trump hailed her “unblemished record of support” and said she was a “loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning” and a “devoted fan and member of MAGA”. China watchers say this combination could draw particular attention as the Trump administration navigates its increasingly consequential relationship with Beijing. Her background could take on added significance in the coming months, as Trump engages with President Xi Jinping at the Apec summit in Shenzhen and the Group of 20 summit in Miami, where US-China trade, technology and security tensions could feature prominently. According to Denis Simon, a senior fellow at the Quincy Institute, a think tank in Washington, Zacharia’s “Beijing experience gives her a potentially useful perspective”. “She has had an opportunity to encounter China through commercial law and non-profit work rather than only through American political debate,” said Simon, a long-time China scholar. He described Zacharia’s years in Beijing as “much more meaningful than simply joining even a high-level delegation or visiting as a tourist”. “Working in a Chinese office for two years could have helped her develop a more substantial appreciation for Chinese culture and the dynamics of the business world,” Simon said. From Malibu to Beijing Zacharia studied law at Pepperdine University’s Caruso School of Law in Malibu, California before moving to Beijing, where she worked as an associate on the international practice team at Zhong Lun, one of China’s leading commercial law firms. According to her LinkedIn profile, she worked at the firm from August 2011 to June 2013, at a time when the country was becoming an increasingly important player in global trade and investment. “Zhong Lun is one of China’s leading corporate law firms, often grouped among the country’s so-called red circle firms – a term roughly comparable to the ‘magic circle’ firms in London or ‘white shoe’ firms in New York,” said Sida Liu, a professor of law and sociology at the University of Hong Kong. He highlighted that although the firm had earlier strengths in areas such as real estate and Japan-related work, by the early 2010s – around the time Zacharia worked there – Zhong Lun had developed into a broad, full-service commercial law firm. “That period was also one in which many elite Chinese law firms were actively expanding their international practices and hiring foreign-trained lawyers to support cross-border work,” Liu added. Zacharia has said that her work included serving as outside counsel connected to the World Bank Group. During her time in Beijing, she also held a fundraising and communications role with Compassion for Migrant Children, though the extent of her direct involvement in the non-profit’s programmes is not clear.
