Her husband, Tyler Zacharia, was in Beijing during the same period, working in private equity focused on emerging markets. Language skills One of the more unexpected details of Zacharia’s background is that she retained some Chinese language skills after leaving China. She reportedly knows enough basic Chinese to occasionally interject in a conversation and catch people off guard. Available descriptions characterise her level as basic, rather than suggesting that she can conduct complex diplomatic or legal discussions in Chinese. Experts say even limited language skills can offer a degree of familiarity with another society that is not always common among political communications officials in Washington. But they caution that knowing a few phrases is not the same as having deep insight into Chinese politics or policy. “The more consequential issue is whether she draws on that experience to communicate with greater sophistication about China, or whether her role is primarily to convey the administration’s existing positions as forcefully and loyally as possible,” Simon argued. He added that for a White House press secretary, the latter responsibility was fundamental. “The real test will be whether her earlier professional exposure to China adds nuance to the administration’s public communication, without assuming in advance that it will change either her own political views or those of the president.”

title: What’s in a name? What China and Trump call AI reveals how they see its future
description: While the term AI dates back to 1956, the Chinese version offers a different take on the relationship between humans and intelligent machines.
content: US President Donald Trump wants to banish the word “artificial” from artificial intelligence, saying it makes one of the world’s most consequential technologies sound “fake”. Across the Pacific, however, China’s name for the technology has long carried a different connotation – one that places humans, rather than artificiality, at its centre. Trump last week signed an executive order directing US federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence”, or AI, with “Super Intelligence”, or SI, in official communications, websites and policy documents. The White House said the new terminology better reflected the rapidly advancing capabilities and “limitless opportunities” of the technology. While the term “artificial intelligence” dates back to 1956 – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy at a landmark workshop at Dartmouth College – the history of its Chinese counterpart offers a different perspective on the relationship between humans and intelligent machines. The history of China’s AI term China adopted its term for the technology, rengong zhineng, from the Japanese jinkō chinō, which uses the same characters, according to Shuang Frost, an associate professor at Aarhus University who researches Chinese AI translation. The first two characters, rengong, combine ren (human) with gong (work or labour), while zhineng refers to intelligence. Frost said rengong zhineng can therefore be translated literally as “human-made intelligence”. “‘Artificial’ can suggest something synthetic or opposed to the natural and human; rengong explicitly reminds us that this intelligence is the product of human work,” Frost told the South China Morning Post. That distinction took on particular significance as AI emerged as an academic field in China around 1980. Viewing the technology through a Marxist lens, early Chinese theorists saw AI not as a competing “alien intelligence”, but as a tool built to extend and transform human potential, Frost said. While not every Chinese speaker consciously thinks of that history when using the term, “the human is linguistically much harder to remove from rengong zhineng than it is from ‘artificial intelligence’”, she added. In China, there is a running joke that some AI-powered products contain more rengong than zhineng – more human labour than intelligence. This refers to the workers who have historically labelled data and performed behind-the-scenes tasks needed to make automated systems work, Frost wrote in a book chapter tracing the history and translation of Chinese AI terminology in Machine Decision is Not Final. While Trump’s move to adopt “super intelligence” seeks to elevate the technology by emphasising capabilities beyond human intelligence, Frost said greater capability did not automatically make the Chinese term obsolete. An intelligence could become extraordinarily powerful and still be “human-made”, she noted. China’s terminology debate China also had its own debate over what to call the technology. In March, an online commentary published by People’s Daily argued that the ubiquitous English abbreviation “AI” was an unsatisfying way to describe a technology becoming deeply embedded in everyday Chinese life. It proposed finding a shorter, catchier Chinese alternative to complement the formal term rengong zhineng, pointing to home-grown names such as diannao (“electric brain”) for computer, and shouji (“hand machine”) for mobile phone. Chao Han, an associate professor in the department of Chinese Studies at the National University of Singapore, said the Chinese debate centred on “accessibility, linguistic identity and public communication”. A shorter Chinese label could prove useful while preserving the established term rengong zhineng, said Chao, whose research lies at the intersection of translation studies and natural language processing. Frost noted that the US and China naming debates differ fundamentally in intent. While Trump argues AI has outgrown its English name, the Chinese debate centres on why an English abbreviation is replacing an established native term. Still, the different terms should also not be read as evidence of neatly divided American and Chinese world views, Frost cautioned. Chinese technological vocabulary has always been “profoundly transnational”, arriving via Japan while drawing heavily on Western scholarship, she said. “Concepts change as they travel,” Frost said. “They are not simply imported intact from one culture into another.” The future of rengong zhineng Still, rengong zhineng could eventually face a conceptual challenge of its own. As AI systems take on a greater role in training and upgrading subsequent models – a process known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) – humans could become increasingly distanced from the direct production of machine intelligence, Frost said. That raises a fundamental question: how “human-made” must a system remain to justify being called rengong zhineng? “Ironically, its future difficulty may arise not because AI becomes too intelligent to be called rengong zhineng, but because it becomes less visibly rengong – less visibly the product of human making,” Frost said. In that scenario, language may adapt once again. “Perhaps chaoji zhineng could supplement it for a specific capability category and in specific contexts,” Chao said, referring to chaoji – the Chinese term for “super”.

title: India’s cockroach party leaders freed as election chief protests mount
description: Demonstrators in New Delhi demand Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation following allegations surrounding a nationwide voter roll revision.
content: The leaders of India’s youth-led online “cockroach” movement were released on Sunday, their lawyer said, a day after they were detained to thwart a major protest against the chief election commissioner. The leaders pledged on Sunday to continue their campaign against the election commissioner, hours after they were released. Thousands of protesters were detained before Saturday’s planned demonstration in New Delhi, according to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which called on supporters to keep taking to the streets despite strict security measures. Saturday’s rally was meant to be the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision, demanding the resignation of the head of the Election Commission of India. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before they could disembark from their flight after arriving in the capital from Mumbai. Ratna Singh, the CJP’s head lawyer, said in a social media post that Dipke and the others had been released by an executive magistrate’s court. She said they had been released on the condition that they made “no breach of peace for one year”. Dipke, wearing a white shirt, was driven away in a black vehicle soon after walking out of the court. In a social media post soon after his release, Dipke took aim at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India,” he said. “Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully.” Activist and social media influencer Dhruv Rathee, detained from his home, was also released. Authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital on Saturday, detaining thousands to prevent protesters from gathering at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar protest site, the CJP and Indian media reports said. Police have not commented on the detentions. On Sunday, there were no signs of any major gathering of protesters around the Jantar Mantar site despite calls from the CJP to march there. Election authorities say the revision was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries. According to media reports, it resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists. Critics say the process has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. The election commission has rejected allegations of wrongdoing. India’s Supreme Court was set to hear a petition in a special sitting on Sunday against the closure of Delhi metro stations and train services on Saturday. The metro stations were opened on Sunday but there was a huge security presence at exit and entry gates. The CJP has won millions of followers on social media since it was launched by Dipke in May as a satirical movement. Protests organised by the CJP against exam irregularities in July forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi’s administration. Saturday’s detentions triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi’s government was stifling dissent. In Geneva, the UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those “arbitrarily detained” in Delhi. The CJP as well as opposition leader Rahul Gandhi have vowed to press ahead with protests despite the crackdown. Gandhi said his Congress party “and the youth of the country will once again take to the streets in large numbers” on Monday. “The more Modi and his government crack down, the more the anger of Gen Z and students will grow,” he said.

title: Huanggang Port a ‘milestone’ for connecting Hong Kong, Greater Bay Area: John Lee
description: Countdown to launch of facility begins as city leader says crossing is part of Hong Kong’s efforts to align with national development strategy.
content: The revamped Huanggang Port checkpoint is a “critical milestone” for the connectivity of the Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong’s leader has said, as the city and Shenzhen count down to its launch on Monday. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said at a ceremony on Sunday that the Huanggang control point was a “landmark project” built and shared through the joint efforts of Hong Kong and Shenzhen. “Hong Kong unveiled its first five-year plan last month to proactively align with the national 15th five-year plan, allowing the city to better integrate into and serve the overall development of the country. The plan proposed to facilitate cross-border passenger flows and elevate customs clearance efficiency,” he said. “The opening of the revamped Huanggang checkpoint represents an explicit action for Hong Kong to align with the national development strategy and deeply engage in the construction of the Greater Bay Area.” The new building will start operations at 6.30am on Monday. The existing Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang crossing will cease operations at the same time, ending nearly 40 years of service. “Since it started operations in 1989 … it has served hundreds of millions of travellers and witnessed increased cross-border traffic and embodied collective memories of several generations of citizens,” Lee said. He called the revamped Huanggang Port the most important 24-hour land boundary passenger checkpoint, with a designed daily capacity of 200,000 passenger trips. That figure will rise to about 300,000 passenger trips upon the completion of the MTR’s Northern Link project. “With the stronger transport connection between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the flow of people, goods, capital and information between the two cities will be more efficient, further driving the deep integration of the Greater Bay Area,” he added. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung and Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also attended the ceremony, along with senior Guangdong provincial and Shenzhen municipal officials. Xue Huaming, an official from the Office of Port of Entry and Exit of the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government, said crowd control and security measures were in place to prepare for a large number of travellers using the revamped port when it opened, and pledged to ensure a smooth clearance experience. “We expect that in the initial period after the port opens, a large number of travellers will visit and ‘check in’ at the new Huanggang Port, including experiencing the clearance process. We will provide better service,” Xue said. “The port authorities of both Hong Kong and Shenzhen will coordinate emergency preparations for peak travel flows. We have already put in place relevant diversion and control measures, and have streamlined the on-site clearance flow, to ensure that everyone has a better experience during the process.” Xue stressed that Hong Kong and Shenzhen had conducted more than 200 rehearsals before the port opened, covering emergency plans and contingency arrangements to ensure the control point was ready to go into service. He expected the port to handle 100,000 to 200,000 passenger trips a day in the initial period, up from the current 50,000. Finance chief Chan wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday that the new infrastructure, the world’s largest single-building land control point, would bring Hong Kong closer to mainland China. “It will be very convenient for business travellers, visitors and residents who frequently travel between Hong Kong and Shenzhen,” he said. Under the “collaborative inspection and joint clearance” model at the crossing, the clearance time for travellers will be cut from about 30 minutes to around five minutes. Eligible passengers will be able to complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates. Chan added that, together with an Apec finance ministers’ meeting to be held in Hong Kong later this month, these developments showed how the city was strengthening regional economic ties through infrastructure and major events. The existing checkpoint in Shenzhen handled an average of 40,000 travellers a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people, with a daily average throughput of 9,000 vehicles that went up to a peak of 12,000. The revamped checkpoint will have a daily capacity of 200,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles. Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, described the opening of the crossing as a crucial step for the development of the Greater Bay Area and the Northern Metropolis. “[The port] will significantly facilitate cross-border collaboration in industrial innovation within the Greater Bay Area and promote the free flow of talent. It will also inject substantial foot traffic and economic vitality into the Northern Metropolis and across other districts,” he said. Lo added that efficient and convenient cross-border clearance arrangements would be essential to fostering collaboration in the innovation sector between Hong Kong and the mainland, calling on the government to continue improving connectivity across other cross-border infrastructure and institutions.

title: Paul Chan highlights 4 priorities ahead of Apec finance ministers’ meeting this month
description: Hong Kong finance chief says focus will be on fiscal policies that support livelihoods, digital infrastructure financing, inclusive finance and young talent.
content: An Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong this month will focus on fiscal policies that support livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance and young financial talent, underlining the city’s role as an international financial centre, the finance chief has said. “These four priorities are areas of strength for Hong Kong and fields in which we can make an active contribution,” Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday. “Hosting the finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong highlights the central government’s strong support for the city and reflects the city’s status as an important international financial centre in the region.” About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from Apec’s 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21 at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. It will be the first time Hong Kong has hosted the event. Chan noted that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) gathering, alongside Monday’s opening of the revamped Huanggang Port border crossing, showed how Hong Kong was strengthening regional economic ties through infrastructure and major events. He outlined Hong Kong’s efforts and strengths in the four areas on the meeting’s agenda, noting that the city had been training students and young professionals in green finance, asset and wealth management, and fintech. It provided internships and educational courses to help the younger generation better understand regional markets and emerging businesses. Chan added that more than 150 young volunteers had been recruited to help at the Apec meeting, offering them a valuable learning experience outside the classroom while allowing visiting guests to experience the enthusiasm and hospitality of the city’s youth. On green finance, Chan emphasised the city’s role in connecting regional projects seeking funding with investors looking for transparency through green bonds, transition finance, project certification and professional services. He noted that about US$38 billion in green and sustainable bonds had been issued in Hong Kong in 2025, ranking first in the Asian market for the eighth consecutive year. Chan also highlighted the city’s efforts to advance inclusive finance, citing the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Commercial Data Interchange platform, which allows small and medium-sized enterprises to give banks consent in advance to access operational data from different sources, improving the efficiency of loan approvals and easing financing difficulties. The finance chief also said Hong Kong could foster deeper exchange and collaboration among Apec governments, financial institutions, investors and tech companies, allowing public resources to play a guiding role and mobilising more market capital to support the development of the regional digital economy and artificial intelligence. Beyond the four priorities, Chan said Hong Kong would also showcase its strength as an international insurance and risk-management hub, which could help facilitate regional collaboration amid increasing climate risks. “Our insurance-linked securities services, captive insurance companies and ‘Marine Specialty Risk Pool’ can cooperate with regional partners,” he said. “Catastrophe bonds and speciality underwriting can provide additional protection and financing tools for regional infrastructure investment and climate-risk response. “These open up broader markets for Hong Kong’s financial, insurance and professional services sectors.” He added that he expected dignitaries attending the meetings to learn about Hong Kong’s latest developments in innovation, technology and urban construction, while experiencing the city’s cultural and artistic vitality and charm. China is the host of this year’s Apec meetings, with the annual economic leaders’ gathering to be held in Shenzhen in November.

title: This Gen Z designer nearly left the industry. Now, he is redefining luxury fashion
description: Kenneth Chow, founder of Chow Chow, blends luxury with sustainability, crafting bespoke designs while overcoming industry challenges.
content: “I’m not a fashion person,” says Kenneth Chow, founder of independent fashion label Chow Chow. During our interview, he wears a simple striped shirt and answers without pretension. “I barely buy new clothes,” he says, laughing. Despite his simple approach to fashion, Chow’s business focuses on refined craftsmanship, intricate designs and handcrafted luxury. His designs, embellished with crystals and pearls hand-stitched on dark-coloured silks, play with perceptions of geometry and linear structures. From women’s gowns and corsets to men’s cashmere jumpers, Chow’s pieces can range from HK$3,000 (US$380) to nearly HK$40,000. The fashion entrepreneur, now in his mid-twenties and based in London, has been running Chow Chow for his elite clientele since 2024. But his journey here was not without setbacks. For one, he is a young designer often underestimated by his industry peers – so he declines to disclose his exact age. “I’ve been judged a lot by my age in the workplace, and I just want my work to speak for itself,” he says. From high school programmes to launching a label Born in Canada to Hong Kong and Chinese-Japanese parents, Chow spent his youth between Vancouver, Hong Kong, Japan and mainland China. He first got into fashion through a specialised programme at his Canadian high school, where he spent hours learning how to design and sew. He remembers these sessions as an “escape” from his usual school environment, in which he experienced bullying and struggled with his mental health. Despite the reluctance of his parents, who wanted him to pursue a more stable career, Chow left home to pursue fashion. While he nearly failed high school, he competed and ranked in national tailoring competitions such as the 2018 Skills Canada National Competition. He was then selected as one of two Canadian candidates for the WorldSkills Competition and spent a year in full-time, government-funded training, competing to represent Canada on the world stage. “It was definitely like a gamble,” he says. “But at the same time, this was all that I knew. This was what I was good at, so that was what I chose to do.” Chow moved to London and apprenticed under master tailors on Savile Row – the London street famous for traditional bespoke tailoring and heritage brands. Instead of enrolling in a fashion institute programme, he chose to gain practical skills. “Sometimes I would think, ‘Would I have a better network?’ or ‘Would I have more connections?’”, if he took the more traditional route. Yet, Chow does not regret his decision, believing he otherwise would not have gained much else from academia. Chow had started to find his footing; then the Covid-19 pandemic hit. The world was in lockdown, and he was let go from his apprenticeship after his former employer died by suicide. Distressed and disillusioned, “fashion was like the last thing that I wanted to do any more,” Chow recalls. His applications for new jobs resulted in rejection letters, and he began looking at “option Bs”, seeking employment in the film industry within costume departments, where he could still work with textiles. Luckily, British bridal fashion house Alonuko offered him a position as a tailor. He had no bridal experience, but the designer took a chance on him. “That really changed my life trajectory … I’m sure I would have left fashion if I hadn’t got that job,” says Chow, who worked there for five years, often staying awake up to 24 hours to work, making his way up to a managerial position. While his five-year tenure at the company fostered both his needlecraft and self-evolution, the ambitious tailor eventually wanted something more. “I had an itch in me,” he says. “If I could build someone else’s dream, why couldn’t I build my own dream?” A made-to-order system rooted in environmentalism Chow Chow was founded in 2024. While Chow now has a small team of artisans, it is still very much an “all hands on deck” situation, and the designer does much of the tailoring. He works 17 hours each day. “Every day is still a challenge,” he says. “You’ve caught me like still at the very beginning of the journey.” Decision fatigue is the biggest challenge he points to as a business owner. His first collection, “Chapter 23”, was inspired by television moments from his youth, capturing the veil between reality and fantasy. It is perhaps a manifestation of the two career paths he was torn between just a few years ago. One of these pieces was even worn by corporate strategist and influencer Sommyyah Awan on the Toronto International Film Festival red carpet in 2025. Most of Chow Chow’s projects are made-to-order, customised pieces. “I think my most favourite experience is connecting with clients and seeing how they’ll change my design or request different alterations, tweaks, customisations to fit their personality,” the tailor-founder says. “I’m a people pleaser,” he adds, laughing, “I like understanding what their needs are.” But, more than that, this made-to-order system is driven by Chow’s own philosophy on environmentalism. A self-proclaimed “tree-hugger”, Chow is primarily concerned with reducing waste in a textile industry dominated by fast fashion. His most recent collection, released this year, strays slightly from the geometry of his earlier collections and prowls towards the organic silhouettes of the natural world. Interested in exploring texture, he drew inspiration from shells and wings while staying true to his signature mosaics of beadwork. Looking ahead, Chow is keeping his cards close to his chest. “I do have specific goals, but I keep my goals to myself a lot,” he says. “I’m not superstitious. I’m just a very private person.” Still, he is transparent about the brutality of running your own business from the ground up. “It’s difficult. If you have another option, maybe consider it,” he says with another laugh. “I wouldn’t tell everyone to follow their dreams. You have to know what cards you’re dealt with and how much, I guess, suffering you can take.”

title: Unsung turtle conservation heroes in Malaysia’s Sabah unite to fight poachers
description: A group of volunteers is helping to stem the illegal trade of protected turtles by monitoring the movements of poachers.
content: Roziah Jelali has a tip or two on catching a turtle poacher: carrying a pair of binoculars and having patience in spades are key to doing the job well. The 36-year-old Malaysian volunteer ranger once spent three months in Sabah tracking a man whom she suspected of illegally capturing protected turtles. Once thriving off the azure seas of Omadal Island in the Malaysian state, many turtles had been hunted down, killed and sold for their meat, according to conservation experts. Recounting the 2023 incident, Roziah said she patrolled the beach from dawn daily to keep an eye on the poacher. She would scribble detailed notes on her target’s movements at her stilted home, backed by tips from her network of part-time conservationists on nearby islands. “Every day after my patrol, I would sit near my house with my binoculars and watch him. He was initially operating on Bum Bum Island, then he came to Omadal,” Roziah told This Week in Asia. “He would kill the turtle at sea, then when he returned, he would cut it open and cook it on the boat.” Her careful surveillance led to the rescue of a live turtle and a crackdown against an illicit ring selling turtle meat in the waters of Omadal and the town of Semporna. Using Roziah’s information, wildlife officials caught the poacher and an accomplice. They were accused of illegally catching five turtles, four of which were butchered for their meat. Roziah did not learn the anti-poaching skills on her own. She received training from Sabah’s Wildlife Department and WWF-Malaysia while learning more about the rich biodiversity off the state’s east coast, such as the seagrass, sea grapes and green turtles. She and four other women are part of a volunteer watchdog committed to protecting the marine life that once thrived around Omadal Island but has been threatened with extinction due to poaching. They are also adept at craftwork, regularly weaving pandan leaves into mats and baskets. Their husbands also have strong links with the sea, as its sustainability is crucial to their jobs as fishers. As volunteers with the Women’s Association of Omadal Island (WAPO), the women would share findings with their peers. According to WAPO chairwoman Sitti Rasah Haji Abdul, the association has not recorded any turtle landings on Omadal and other nearby islands since last year. In the past, turtles would lay their eggs in guarded hatcheries, and this would help prevent attacks by predators like monitor lizards or theft by villagers. While Sitti is disappointed about the disappearance of nesting turtles, she is determined to do her part to bring about their safe return. Widespread illegal trading Sea turtles have been a fully protected species under Sabah’s wildlife conservation laws since 1997. According to marine life experts, the presence of these turtles is a key sign of a healthy marine environment. Through their grazing, green turtles contribute to the growth of seagrass meadows, which store carbon that is biologically essential for fish and shellfish. Nesting turtles also help move nutrients from the sea onto beaches and keep jellyfish populations in check. But the threat of illegal trading faced by turtles extends beyond Malaysia’s Borneo shores. The waters surrounding Sabah form part of the trafficking corridor spanning the Sulu-Celebes Seas between Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia, according to the wildlife trade monitoring group Traffic. Turtle eggs are particularly prized by poachers, according to Elizabeth John, Traffic’s communications manager. The Sulu-Celebes Seas accounted for most of the illicit wildlife trade activities involving turtles between June 2003 and September 2021, according to the latest available data in a Traffic report released in 2023. “Our records from that study period showed cases of stockpiled dead green sea turtles, the discovery of live hawksbill turtles with missing scutes in the north of Sabah and other turtle parts seized several times in the Semporna district,” John said. While Sabah’s law enforcement agencies have been active, the state continues to be a hotspot for illegal turtle trade. “The seizure cases in Semporna district included people from island communities instructed by middlemen to poach turtles at turtle foraging grounds,” John said. In November last year, police and wildlife authorities raided premises in Semporna and seized 570 hawksbill turtle scutes weighing 17.8kg (39lbs) and valued at US$3,450, believed destined for the black market. They arrested two people, including a foreign national. Daunting challenge Between eastern Sabah and the southern Philippines, the Celebes-Sulu Sea provides ready cover for wildlife criminal gangs to hide among fishers, cargo and passenger boats, said Ramli Dollah, a lecturer and maritime security expert at the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities in Universiti Malaysia Sabah. “The same boats, operators, routes, landing points and intermediaries can move people or different types of goods,” said Dollah, who referred to their system of “co-riding and camouflage”. The vast area in Sabah and beyond poses a formidable challenge for enforcement agencies to catch poachers and smugglers, according to Dollah. Maritime security specialist Nazery Khalid, an adjunct professor at the University of Malaysia, Terengganu, said the vast Sulu-Celebes Seas were difficult for poorly resourced Malaysian and Philippine authorities to patrol. “There may be cooperation among them in areas such as intelligence sharing, but without maintaining boots on the ground in the form of operationally fit vessels, traffickers can operate with impunity or outmanoeuvre the enforcement agencies’ vessels,” he said. Sitti and Roziah consider their roles as complementary to those of the enforcement agencies as they pursue the common goals of boosting Malaysia’s turtle population and conservation of other species. “If not me, then who will do it for the generations to come?” Sitti said. “As long as I am still able to carry out conservation work, I will continue.” Sitti added that she and the volunteers faced constant risks of potential confrontation with turtle poachers and stormy weather when they were out on boat patrol. These challenges do not faze Roziah. “We must have courage and determination. That is the most important thing,” she said.

title: Admission scores fall for Hong Kong physiotherapy courses amid jobs crunch
description: Budget constraints and an unprecedented rise in the number of new practitioners entering the market have taken their toll on profession.
content: Admission scores for physiotherapy degree programmes at three Hong Kong tertiary institutions fell by as much as 10 per cent this year compared with 2025, amid gloomy career prospects in the sector, the latest data shows. The decline prompted the professional body for physiotherapists to call on the government to halt healthcare funding cuts in the next budget, saying they had contributed to a jobs crunch in the sector. Across four institutions, 23 per cent of students admitted to physiotherapy programmes this year had ranked the course outside their top three choices, up from just 2 per cent in 2025. The figures suggest that more first-year students did not consider physiotherapy their preferred field of study. The fall in both popularity and admission scores came after the government announced last year that recurrent public expenditure would be cut by 1 to 2 per cent in 2025-26, with the arrangement extended to 2027-28. These budget constraints coincide with an unprecedented increase in the number of new practitioners entering the market. Physiotherapy graduates are facing a jobs crunch and have voiced their difficulties finding work. Polytechnic University, the first publicly funded institution in the city to offer an allied health programme, recorded a 57 per cent drop in the number of students picking the programme among their first three choices, from 581 in 2025 to 246 this year, according to the Joint University Programmes Admissions System (Jupas). Jupas is a platform through which students sitting the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) apply for government-subsidised bachelor’s degree programmes. Admission score data also shows that the programme’s average DSE score, with subject weighting applied, fell from 329.3 last year to 303.6 in 2026, the largest decline among PolyU’s undergraduate courses. PolyU’s department of rehabilitation sciences said it had no comment. The figures come as education authorities reduce the number of subsidised places for physiotherapy at three self-financing institutions by about a third for the 2027-28 academic year. The three programmes will see a sharp reduction in places, with total intake falling 31 per cent from 175 in 2026-27 to 120 in 2027-28. At Tung Wah College (TWC), the number of applicants placing its programme among their top three choices fell from 369 in 2024 to 281 in 2025 and down further to 224 in 2026, marking a 40 per cent drop in two years. Its mean admission score fell 10 per cent from 22.2 in 2025 to 20 in 2026. TWC has been approached for comment. The median admission score for the physiotherapy programme at Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU) also fell from 25 in 2024 to 22 last year and 20 in 2026 – a 20 per cent drop in two years. A spokesman for HKMU said the university’s physiotherapy programme had been accredited by the Allied Health Professions Council and graduates were eligible for registration as qualified physiotherapists in Hong Kong. At Saint Francis University (SFU), the number of students who ranked the programme among their top three choices fell by 37 per cent, from 508 in 2025 to 319 in 2026. An SFU spokeswoman said the university would review its student intake in line with society’s demand for these professionals. She stressed, however, that demand for healthcare professionals would continue to rise as the city’s population aged rapidly. Admission scores refer to the total marks students obtained in the DSE, which uses a seven-level grading scale. The highest grade, level 5**, equals seven points, while level two is equal to two points. Alexander Woo Chuen-hau, president of the Hong Kong Physiotherapy Association, noted that all the programmes had filled their places. Woo said entry scores did not necessarily determine graduates’ future performance and demand for physiotherapists remained high because of the rapidly ageing population. Woo called on authorities to increase healthcare funding, noting that government coffers were expected to record a surplus next year. He also encouraged prospective students to consider their interest in the profession. “If you like it, go for it and study hard,” Woo said. “The road ahead may not be completely smooth. Graduates might not secure their dream position immediately, but employment opportunities are still out there.”

title: Denuclearising North Korea would ‘defy history’: analyst
description: Security expert Jenny Town says Washington and others should abandon the goal and instead focus on arms limitations and crisis talks.
content: The denuclearisation of North Korea has become an “increasingly improbable” goal and the United States and its allies should move beyond it to devote their diplomatic efforts to talks on arms limitations and crisis communication, the director of the US-based North Korean analysis website 38 North said. Recalling the 20 years since North Korea carried out its first nuclear test on October 9, 2006, Jenny Town said in a written interview that “a pivotal moment” in Pyongyang’s weapons development came in 2017 when the country’s first test-firing of an intercontinental ballistic missile took place. Even without fully showcasing ICBM capabilities, the test changed “the nature of the threat and the way US allies viewed the credibility of US extended deterrence”, Town said, referring to the US commitment to using its military capabilities, including nuclear weapons, for protection of its allies and deterrence against attacks. “While reassuring allies of security commitments is a persistent challenge, North Korea having both theatre and long-range capabilities – able to reach the US homeland as well – has exacerbated decoupling fears in South Korea,” she added, noting that such fears will “only grow” as Pyongyang works to improve the credibility of its strategic weaponry. North Korea carried out nuclear tests six times through September 2017, claiming the most recent one was that of a hydrogen bomb to be loaded on an ICBM. Later that year, North Korea declared its nuclear force complete. According to Town, senior fellow at the Stimson Centre, which houses the 38 North programme, Pyongyang had shown willingness on several occasions in the past to make concessions to improve the security environment on the Korean peninsula as a whole, which could have led to containing its nuclear development programme. “But during many of those moments, the US simply wasn’t interested,” she said, partly due to scepticism about whether the intentions were sincere. “In many ways, North Korea learned that the only time the US would take it seriously and be willing to talk was when it did provocative things.” Town said “one of the biggest missed opportunities” was the working-level talks between the two countries on denuclearisation in Stockholm in October 2019, which followed three meetings between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. At the first-ever US-North Korea summit in Singapore in 2018 during his first term, Trump agreed with Kim that Washington would provide security guarantees to Pyongyang in exchange for the “complete” denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula. But in the February 2019 summit in Vietnam, the two fell short of bridging the gap between Washington’s denuclearisation demands and Pyongyang’s calls for sanctions relief. At the subsequent working-level talks, Pyongyang said the US side came to the negotiations “empty-handed”, indicating that the talks broke down. “If the US gone into that meeting with a counter-offer, something perhaps smaller but workable to demonstrate a reason to keep negotiating, rather than starting all over, it might not have worked but would have at least tested what was still possible when North Korea was still willing to engage,” she said. North Korea’s mission of its development of the destructive weapons has also evolved, with the 2022 nuclear use law making the country declare that its status as a nuclear weapons state has become “irreversible”. “In the past, the North Korean nuclear programme was always discussed in conditional terms – ‘as long as the US maintained its hostile policy,’” Town said. “That is no longer the case. North Korea is no longer trying to justify why it needs nuclear weapons but already considers itself a ‘responsible nuclear weapons state.’” “To be fair, there is no precedent of a state building a sovereign nuclear weapons capability to this extent that has ever voluntarily reversed course,” she added. The closest precedent was South Africa, but it had only six nuclear weapons and had greater stakes in reintegrating into the international community. “The idea that North Korea would be willing at this stage to reverse course at any price is a pretty extraordinary belief and would defy history.” As for the outlook, the expert on Northeast Asian security issues said Pyongyang’s preconditions for talks are a “tall order” from where the US and its allies stand today because they are “not just a matter of ‘not talking about denuclearisation up front’, but declaring a denuclearisation agenda is over”. At the same time, she said, continuing to push for denuclearisation has prevented “dialogues about risk reduction, crisis communication and response, arms limitations, doctrine and other things”. “Denuclearisation, when North Korea is so far advanced in its deterrent development, is an increasingly improbable task. Continuing to hold this as the heart of our diplomatic efforts limits our own agency in dealing with North Korea,” she added.

title: New vs old: why new-builds are far outselling used homes in Hong Kong
description: New homes are selling fast while used property sales have remained sluggish. The two trends appear to be linked, analysts say.
content: A clear divide has opened up in Hong Kong’s property market in recent months: sales of new-build homes have surged, but the recovery in the secondary market has remained far more modest. The contrast between the two segments is not a coincidence – and is likely to persist for some time, according to analysts. The trend is largely being driven by developers slashing prices on new-builds to clear their inventories ahead of expected interest rate rises in the coming months. This is making new homes more affordable for buyers and diverting attention from the used property market, analysts say. Sales of new residential properties have bounced back strongly from a slump in July, rising more than 95 per cent to hit about 1,500 in September, according to data from Centaline Property. The total value of those transactions jumped by 31.8 per cent to reach HK$20.88 billion (US$2.66 billion). The secondary market, however, has remained sluggish. Just over 3,000 used homes were sold in September, a decline of 337 compared with July. The value of those transactions also fell by HK$2.31 billion to HK$24.76 billion. Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties, said the primary market had significantly outperformed the secondary market because new housing projects were attracting buyers with low prices, whereas owners in the secondary market were holding firm on their asking prices. “Over the past two or three months, developers have priced new projects in line with – or even below – market rates,” he said. “Combined with flexible payment terms and mortgage incentives, this has significantly siphoned off purchasing power from the secondary market.” The first phase of The Sterling – a new project in Cheung Sha Wan developed by China Resources Land – is an example of the recent wave of discounting. An initial batch of 102 flats hit the market in mid-August at an average price of just HK$17,880 per square foot – and all of them sold out on their respective launch days. It is easy to see why buyers were interested. The prices per square foot were similar to those of homes recently sold on four neighbouring residential estates, all of which are over 20 years old, according to agents. Average transaction prices on the estates – Liberte, The Pacifica, Banyan Garden and Aqua Marine, known collectively as the “four little dragons” – hovered between HK$16,600 and HK$17,400 per square foot, agents said. One investor surnamed Chan said he had originally been scouting for undervalued properties in the “four little dragons” area, but subsequently decided to enter the lottery to buy a home in The Sterling instead. “Prices of new homes are comparable to those of secondary properties, yet the new developments are 20 years younger and the investment potential is greater,” he said. “Plus, with the incentives offered by developers, using leverage is more advantageous than with resale homes.” Anson Tsang, chief associate director at Hong Kong Property Services, said the launch of The Sterling had led to a 20 per cent fall in viewings on nearby used developments. “The ‘four little dragons’ recorded only 12 and 13 transactions in August and September, respectively – a sharp decline of more than 60 per cent from the 36 transactions recorded in the year’s high in January,” Tsang said. State Residence – another new project in North Point developed by Chow Tai Fook – has also offered steep discounts. In mid-September, the first batch of 50 flats came on the market at just over HK$20,600 per square foot. The price is 15 per cent below the average for other new developments and secondary-market properties in the area, and as much as 40 per cent lower than some unsold flats in other new projects nearby, according to agents. There are a total of 194 flats in State Residence, and 189 of them sold within 13 days of being launched. Chris Wong, executive director at Century 21 Sunrise, said the sales launch for State Residence had led to a 25 per cent drop in secondary market transactions in the North Point area. One buyer surnamed Ng said he had been going on viewings at relatively new developments in the area in September – such as Diva in Tin Hau and Fleur Pavilia in North Point – but dropped those plans to submit a purchase application at State Residence as soon as the sales launch began. “Sellers in the secondary market are asking aggressive prices and are standing firm, with only a 1 to 2 per cent room for negotiation,” he said. “I’d rather switch to buying at a new development.” It was a similar story with phase one of The Atlas, a new residential project in Yau Tong by Yuexiu Property. The first 128 flats at the development were offered at a price of just HK$13,988 per square foot – the lowest price seen for a new development in urban Kowloon in a decade. Norey Tsang, senior area sales manager at Midland Realty, noted that one-bedroom flats on the secondary market in the New Territories currently cost between HK$3 million and HK$4 million – a price range comparable to The Atlas. Many buyers who had been looking at small secondary-market flats had therefore shifted their focus to enter the sales lottery for The Atlas phase one, Tsang said. Chan of Ricacorp Properties expects developers to continue launching projects at market or even below-market prices and employ incentive strategies to attract buyers, as they focus on reducing their inventories. “The secondary market will remain under pressure as a result,” he said. “New home projects continue to outperform the secondary market in terms of pricing, payment terms and the advantages of off-plan sales.” Chan added that the gap between the two was unlikely to narrow in the short term. The pattern of a strong primary market and a weak secondary market would persist through October, he said. “In the medium to long term, the situation hinges on inventory levels,” he explained. “The gap will only narrow once low-priced primary market flats are gradually absorbed or secondary market owners deepen their price cuts.”

title: Nanotechnology expert Antonio Facchetti joins HKUST from Georgia Tech in the US
description: Facchetti, co-founder of a company that makes flexible transistors for displays, has joined the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
content: Materials scientist and chemist Antonio Facchetti, formerly of the Georgia Institute of Technology in the United States, has joined the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology as a chair professor in its newly established department of materials. Facchetti, who was elected to the US National Academy of Engineering last year for his “contributions to the engineering of commercially viable electronic materials and devices”, researches semiconductors, dielectrics for thin-film and electrochemical transistors, sensors, batteries and photovoltaics. The nanotechnology professor is also the chief technology officer and co-founder of Flexterra Corporation, a company that produces flexible transistors, which can make e-Paper and OLED displays flexible. His research also covers flexible and sustainable thin-film electronics, transparent electronics for see-through displays and polymers for energy storage. “HKUST’s vibrant research culture and relentless pursuit of innovation provide an ideal platform for advancing groundbreaking materials research,” Facchetti said, according to a social media post released by the department on October 1. “I look forward to collaborating with university colleagues and students to push the boundaries of functional materials and translate fundamental scientific breakthroughs into innovative technologies that address real-world challenges,” he said. The HKUST Department of Materials, established in July within the school of engineering, said in the post that Facchetti “possesses extensive experience bridging fundamental materials science, molecular engineering, device technology and industrial translation”. “His interdisciplinary expertise will further strengthen the department’s research capabilities in advanced functional materials and emerging technologies, while creating new opportunities for collaboration – both within HKUST and with academic and industry partners in China and internationally,” it added. The department said its goal was to “gather leading scholars in materials science, engineering and intelligent technology to address global challenges and national strategic needs in energy, health and sustainable development”. In addition to the National Academy of Engineering, Facchetti is a fellow of the National Academy of Inventors, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the Materials Research Society, the European Academy of Science and the Royal Society of Chemistry. Before joining HKUST, Facchetti was a professor and Hightower Chair in the school of materials science and engineering at Georgia Tech, which he joined in 2022. He has been an adjunct professor of chemistry at Northwestern University in Illinois since 2002. Facchetti received his PhD in chemical sciences from the University of Milan. He has published more than 600 research articles and holds more than 120 patents. His H-index of 141 places him as a highly cited researcher. His accolades include the 2009 Italian Chemical Society Research Prize, the corporate 2011 Flextech Award, the 2016 American Chemical Society Award for Creative Invention and the 2017 Giulio Natta Gold Medal from the Italian Chemical Society. Recognised as a Highly Cited Researcher from 2014 to 2024, he was named among the top 100 materials scientists of the decade from 2000 to 2010 by Thomson Reuters and was inducted into the Advanced Materials Hall of Fame in 2019.

title: Letters | 5-year plan must preserve what makes Hong Kong distinctive
description: Readers discuss the rest test of the city’s first five-year plan, the art of building a legacy, and the choice of music for Trump’s state dinner with Xi.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan should not be judged simply by its resemblance to mainland planning, nor by the number of targets it contains. Its real test is whether long-term policy coordination can strengthen the qualities that make Hong Kong internationally valuable. Overseas observers are likely to focus first on whether deeper integration with national development can coexist with Hong Kong’s international character. Access to the mainland remains central to the city’s appeal, but its distinctive value also rests on predictable regulation, common-law institutions, free capital flows, professional services and global talent. Integration will enhance Hong Kong’s role only if these advantages remain credible. The second test is economic diversification. The plan’s emphasis on artificial intelligence and the Northern Metropolis reflects a sensible effort to reduce dependence on finance, property and traditional services. Yet spending targets alone cannot create an innovation economy. Success should be measured by whether university research produces viable companies and products, whether start-ups can scale and whether skilled workers can build long-term careers in Hong Kong. The Northern Metropolis will be the clearest test of implementation. It must become more than a large property and infrastructure project. Housing, transport, universities, laboratories, private investment and cross-border coordination must develop on compatible timelines if the area is to form a genuine innovation ecosystem with Shenzhen. Long-range planning can improve continuity and make public investment more disciplined. But it also carries risks: agencies may chase numerical targets, public funds may favour fashionable sectors and rigid priorities may struggle to keep pace with technological change. Hong Kong therefore needs strategic government without displacing market judgment. International confidence will not be secured by a comprehensive blueprint alone. It will depend on transparent implementation, measurable outcomes and policy flexibility. Hong Kong need not choose between national integration and global relevance. Its challenge is to prove that the two can reinforce each other – and that planning can provide direction without weakening the openness and institutional trust on which the city’s competitiveness depends. Alan Tang, policy researcher, POD Research Institute Legacy building is more than capital growth In today’s world, a critical dimension remains missing from global wealth governance: a profound understanding of how a true legacy is actually attained through philanthropy and is more than capital growth. As the custodian of a young Section 88-approved organisation in Hong Kong, I reflect on a few universal realities. Institutional synergy serves as a shield. Driving structural breakthroughs in public space demands an ecosystem of trust, regulatory commendation and rigorous compliance. This reality is epitomised by our successful drive to include next-generation chronic lymphocytic leukaemia therapy options in the Hospital Authority Drug Formulary with Samaritan Fund coverage. When family capital seamlessly collaborates with academia, community and government, the synergy translates into human progress. True ESG (environmental, social and corporate governance) requires a decisive shift from labels to deeds. Led by a dedicated, nimble board of trustees operating under a strict institutional charter, and seamlessly assisted by an esteemed advisory board and professional practitioners, I ensure global pharmaceutical partnerships are translated into verifiable socio-economic substance. Aligning a legacy with core family values begins with foundational wealth preservation – through structures that shield a family, support future generations and build lasting resilience. Then, balancing classical risk mitigation with capital appreciation helps ensure private wealth serves a transcendent purpose. As Prospero, the sorcerer in Shakespeare’s The Tempest, observes amid the transient architecture of mankind: “The cloud-capped towers, the gorgeous palaces, the solemn temples, the great globe itself, yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve … We are such stuff as dreams are made on”. It is through a meaningful philanthropic legacy that a family’s shared philosophy may outlive wealth architecture. Mike Cheung, founder, Cypress Charitable Trust The moon represents Sino-US relations President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States was widely seen as a success. However, antagonistic voices from Taiwan seized on how “The Moon Represents My Heart” was played on the harp, suggesting the Americans’ choice of music for the state dinner would have been a pain in the neck for Xi. The song was popularised by Teresa Teng, who was hugely popular across the Chinese-speaking world. Although Teng was loyal to Taiwan, I don’t see the choice of the song as provocative. Rather, the mellow song was played at an opportune time, when a full moon was rising over the White House and auguring well for harmonious Sino-US relations. Randy Lee, Ma On Shan

title: Chinese retiree devotes life to photography after tumour shrinks post-bucket-list trip
description: Driven by a new-found motivation to live, Wang has spent her pension on advanced gear, travelled to 30 countries to pursue bird photography.
content: After spending all her savings on a month-long trip to Antarctica following a cancer diagnosis, a woman from southwestern China discovered that her tumour had shrunk. Wang Ying, 67, is an amateur wildlife photographer who has photographed more than 1,200 bird species. In 2013, as she was preparing to retire from her job as an administrator at a school in Kunming, the capital of southwestern China’s Yunnan province, Wang was diagnosed with a form of thyroid cancer. Doctors urged her to undergo surgery immediately, the Shanghai Morning Post reported. The diagnosis was a crushing blow. “If I were to die, I wished to die somewhere far away. I absolutely did not want to have surgery,” she recalled. Wang then decided to travel to Antarctica to photograph penguins. She had been an enthusiastic bird photographer for decades. Her savings were not enough to cover the month-long trip, which cost 150,000 yuan (US$22,000), so Wang’s mother helped pay the difference. In Antarctica, Wang most wanted to photograph a mother penguin feeding her chick, she said. While other tourists left the icy land, Wang stayed outside for a long time despite the harsh conditions: temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius, gale-force winds and heavy snowfall. At last, she captured the moment a mother penguin returned from fishing and fed her chick. “I took pictures of this precious moment. I was so happy! Seeing them walk together and look for their home, I felt very touched,” Wang was quoted as saying. After returning from Antarctica, Wang went to hospital for a check-up. To her surprise, she found that the tumour had shrunk since her previous examination a month earlier. Doctors told her that she did not need surgery for the time being, but should continue to monitor her condition closely. Wang said the experience had rekindled her hope and given her great motivation to live. Since then, she has devoted her time and money to bird photography. She has visited more than 30 countries, spending her entire pension on advanced photography equipment. Wang plans to visit the US, Peru and several African countries this year and next. “After travelling to many places and seeing a variety of things, I have come to terms with changes in life. I won’t make a fuss about some issues now,” Wang said. Wang’s story has attracted widespread interest on Chinese social media. “This case again shows that physical health is related to mood. A good mood and a good rest can improve immunity, leading to the destruction of tumour cells,” one internet user commented. Another person noted: “Thyroid cancer is not very aggressive and has a high survival rate. But after all, it is good to see her get better in such a short time.”

title: Japan’s Sumitomo Bakelite expands China chip packaging materials output amid AI boom
description: The investment underscores the growing importance of advanced packaging materials in the semiconductor supply chain.
content: Japanese semiconductor materials giant Sumitomo Bakelite plans to expand production of advanced chip packaging materials in China and Singapore, marking the second such announcement for its Chinese operations in less than four months as artificial intelligence drives demand for more sophisticated semiconductors. The Tokyo-based company said on Friday that it would add production lines for mould underfill (MUF) materials and compression-moulding granules at its facilities in Suzhou, eastern China’s Jiangsu province, and Singapore. The company did not disclose an investment amount. The expansion is expected to roughly double the company’s production capacity for MUF materials and triple that for compression-moulding granules compared with current levels, according to its statement. The Suzhou lines will be installed as part of an expansion of an existing factory completed in 2024, with production scheduled to begin in fiscal 2030. The Singapore lines, also to be added to an existing facility, are expected to begin operations at the end of fiscal 2028. The investment underscores the growing importance of advanced packaging materials in the semiconductor supply chain, as the AI boom drives demand for more powerful chips with increasingly complex packaging structures. Sumitomo Bakelite said demand for advanced semiconductors used in generative AI and communications satellites was growing rapidly, particularly in China and Southeast Asia, requiring packaging technologies capable of accommodating larger, thinner and more densely integrated chips. MUF materials are used to fill microscopic gaps around semiconductor connections while encapsulating the package, helping improve reliability and manufacturing efficiency. Compression-moulding granules allow manufacturers to produce larger packages with reduced warpage to improve chip reliability. Global revenues for semiconductor packaging materials rose 9.3 per cent to US$27.4 billion in 2025, according to industry association Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International, known more as Semi. China is the world’s second-largest market for semiconductor materials, which include wafer fabrication materials, with revenue of US$15.6 billion, behind Taiwan’s US$21.7 billion. Chinese semiconductor makers are also stepping up investments in advanced packaging. In September, Shanghai-listed Biwin Storage announced plans to invest 4.5 billion yuan (US$672 million) in a new phase of its wafer-level advanced packaging and testing project, building on earlier investments in technologies including 2.5D packaging and redistribution layers. The latest announcement comes less than four months after Sumitomo Bakelite disclosed a separate expansion plan for its Suzhou facility, when it said new production lines would increase its semiconductor encapsulation materials capacity in China by about 30 per cent, with operations expected to begin around December 2028. The Japanese company has manufactured semiconductor packaging materials in China since 1997, gradually expanding its production footprint to meet growing local demand. Sumitomo Bakelite is one of the world’s largest suppliers of semiconductor encapsulation materials, with an estimated global market share of about 40 per cent, according to figures previously disclosed by the company. The expansion also comes as the Japanese materials maker seeks to strengthen its position in the global advanced packaging market through acquisitions. In January, it agreed to acquire part of Japanese electronics manufacturer Kyocera’s chemical materials business for around 30 billion yen (US$189.6 million), including operations producing semiconductor encapsulation materials and bonding pastes. The transaction, expected to be completed by the end of October, also covers chemical materials operations in Wuxi, another manufacturing hub in China’s Jiangsu province. Sumitomo Bakelite said the acquisition would add further MUF and compression-moulding materials capacity to its existing operations, strengthening its supply network across Japan, China and Southeast Asia.

title: Could Thai durian export duty mean higher prices, higher quality in China?
description: Proposed levy part of a draft bill aimed at establishing a fund for research and ‘sustainable’ development of the sector.
content: A Thai government proposal to charge export duties on durians, a major cash crop, could raise prices for the fruit in China – its primary market – along with the quality, analysts said. Thailand’s draft bill to establish a fund for research and “sustainable” development of the durian sector would include the collection of fees, the government’s public relations department said last month. Southeast Asian media outlets and agricultural publications have tipped the export duty to be as high as 2 baht (5 US cents) per kilogram. That extra cost could be passed on to Chinese supermarkets, analysts said. China consumed more than 90 per cent of the world’s durians, HSBC analysts said in a report published in 2023. “I think there will be some impact on prices because somebody along the supply chain has to bear the additional cost,” said Lim Chin Khee, an adviser to the Durian Academy, a Malaysian institution that trains growers. “Some exporters may absorb part of it, but eventually some of the cost could be passed on to buyers and consumers in China.” If Thailand spent the fund revenue on improving durian quality, consumers would notice that too, analysts said. “Thailand’s proposed durian levy is intended to offset things the industry needs collectively,” said Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a professor of international relations at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok. The sector needed more “quality control”, traceability, research, pest surveillance and Thai durian brand protection, he said. If the Thai duty goes ahead, it may open more opportunities for other durian-producing countries Lim Chin Khee, Durian Academy “But if it does not achieve these aims, the levy risks becoming just another cost imposed on a successful export sector,” Thitinan said. Thailand shipped US$5 billion worth of the pungent, spiky fruits to China in the first eight months of this year, more than for all of last year, according to Chinese customs data. In China, Thai durians have an edge over other Southeast Asian producers due to strong logistics and quality control. Chinese consumers knew enough about durians to pick fruits according to quality, not just price, Lim said. Durian exporters from Thailand’s chief rival, Vietnam, were stung last year after Chinese inspections found “excessive levels” of two potentially harmful substances in shipments. “I have seen prices go up and down like the share market,” Lim said. “When one country’s cost becomes too high, buyers naturally start looking for alternatives. So if the Thai duty goes ahead, it may open more opportunities for other durian-producing countries, but ultimately we still have to compete on quality.” The Thai Durian Association and the Thai Fruit Traders and Exporters Association oppose the proposed duty as a financial burden and have said exporters were unlikely to absorb the cost, Southeast Asian media outlets reported. Thailand has not set a date to implement the proposed export levy. “At issue is … who pays among domestic players,” Thitinan said. “Thai exporters would pay the levy, but this cost can be pushed back to farmers through lower farm prices.”

title: Should Hong Kong increase the local student quota for international schools?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
Earlier this year, it was reported that eight international school operators in Hong Kong failed to meet the government’s non-local student admission targets.
This policy for international schools, which aims to maintain a majority of non-local students, is designed to preserve the schools’ “international” character.
Yet clinging to this outdated quota not only threatens the financial viability of these institutions but also ignores Hong Kong’s evolving demographic composition and role in a new global world order.
Thus, Hong Kong should increase the quota for local students at international schools, as failing to do so ultimately hinders Hong Kong’s competitiveness domestically and internationally.
The government requires international schools to maintain a non-local student ratio of at least 70 per cent. But this quota has become difficult to fulfil as Hong Kong’s expat population – long the primary targets for international schools – has fluctuated.
Beyond impracticality, this quota perpetuates a narrow vision of what it means to be “international.” True international education is defined not by a student’s passport but by the curriculum and the exchange of ideas in the classroom. A school does not cease to be international simply because more students hold Hong Kong passports.
Critics argue that admitting more local students to international schools would accelerate the enrolment decline currently plaguing Hong Kong’s local schools, potentially forcing some to shut down. However, this argument assumes a zero-sum game in which local and international schools are direct competitors for the same pool of students.
International schools offer a distinct curriculum and environment, meaning that a local student who enters an international school has not been “taken away” from the local system. Rather, this student likely would have sought an overseas education regardless.
Barring local students from international schools using quotas does not guarantee they will stay in the local system. Instead, it may push them abroad, which drains Hong Kong of both talent and tuition fees.
Increasing the quota for local students at international schools would benefit Hong Kong and mean greater access to education, diversity and choice for all.
International schools in Hong Kong are facing difficulties in enrolment as they cannot meet their quotas for non-local students. According to the city’s Education Bureau, the proportion of non-local students at some schools had fallen to as low as 39 per cent in the last academic year, compared with targets of 50 to 98 per cent.
To help these schools and keep them safe from the risk of closure, some have suggested increasing the quota for local students. However, I completely disagree, as this does not solve the problem and also has drawbacks for students.
Hong Kong has long been known as a global city. It even ranked as the most international city in Asia in the Asian Cities Internationality Index 2025. The index is compiled by global market research firm Ipsos and was commissioned by the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
Still, the drop in the number of international students illustrates how the city’s status as an international one is declining. Increasing the number of local students at international schools will not help this reputation.
Moreover, raising the quota might intensify the “ rat race ” among local students, heightening academic pressure. They may not have felt as much pressure to win a spot when they knew there were fewer ones available for them.
Pupils applying for international school likely also come from highly competitive academic backgrounds, so adding more places may only increase the sense of competition.
There is also a risk that students might not adapt to the different teaching style.
Hong Kong’s various international schools base their curricula on those from Britain, the United States, Australia and other countries. The general learning environment at an international school in Hong Kong differs significantly from that of a local school, which could pose challenges for students and staff.
Instead of raising the quota for local students, we should focus on exploring additional ways to boost non-local enrolment. For instance, the city can enhance its overall talent-attraction policies, streamline visa procedures for overseas working families and promote Hong Kong’s international system to global communities. These measures can increase the number of foreign pupils.

title: New HK$122 million lifeguard outsourcing contract sparks public spending concerns
description: Firm awarded new contract to supply services at six pools despite failing to provide required staffing on seven occasions previously.
content: A controversial decision by Hong Kong authorities to award a lifeguard and first aid services contract worth more than HK$122 million (US$15.6 million) to a company previously found to have failed to provide the required staffing at swimming pools has sparked concerns over whether public funds are being used prudently. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department on Saturday defended the decision, saying it was satisfied with Spotlight Enterprises’ performance over the past two years and that it had strictly followed the government’s procurement procedures. The department outsourced services at six public swimming pools in September 2024 in a trial scheme to tackle long-standing lifeguard shortages, awarding two contracts worth a total of HK$75.9 million to Spotlight Enterprises for two years of services. The pools were Island East, Tai Kok Tsui, Lam Tin, Tung Cheong Street, Tsing Yi Southwest and Ping Shan Tin Shui Wai. A report by the Audit Commission last year said the contractor had failed to provide the required staffing on seven occasions between August 2024 and August 2025. However, the department took up to 305 days to deduct payment from the contractor and up to 311 days to issue default notices. Some of these incidents were not recorded in monthly performance appraisal reports, as required. At the time, the department told the commission that it would review the trial scheme’s implementation when the contract expired in July this year. Nevertheless, according to the Government Logistics Department’s website, the company was awarded another tender in July. The contract was extended from two years to three, and its value rose to HK$122.78 million, representing a 7 per cent increase on an annualised basis. The contract works out at an average of around HK$568,400 per swimming pool per month and a monthly budget of HK$50,000 per lifeguard as the contractor is required to deploy 68 staff members for the six pools each day. While the contractor’s pay rates are unknown, a civil service lifeguard’s salary starts at around HK$19,000 to about HK$27,000, according to a job posting. Nick Wu Kai-wing, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong and Kowloon Life Guards’ Union, criticised the arrangement as a waste of public funds. “All six swimming pools are smaller in scale. They did not need many lifeguards,” he said. According to Wu’s understanding, the six pools had no manpower problems to begin with, and that some lifeguards who had worked there were posted elsewhere to make way for the outsourced staff after the first contract was awarded. He said Hong Kong faced a lifeguard shortage only in summer, and that the situation had recently improved because the union had worked with the government to cover extra shifts. Some public swimming pools also close in winter, with their lifeguards redeployed to ones that remain open all year. Wu said outsourcing services at the six pools had led to an oversupply of lifeguards in winter, especially among those from summer-only facilities. He urged the authorities to limit the outsourcing arrangement to the summer peak season rather than all year. Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu urged the department to consider testing seasonal outsourcing arrangements at public pools to see whether it could save money. “We could make some comparisons and then gradually implement the arrangements,” said Tang, chairman of the Legislative Council’s home affairs, culture and sports panel. He suggested dividing swimming pools into groups, with some using year-round outsourcing contracts and others hiring external lifeguards only during peak seasons, allowing the department to compare their cost-effectiveness. Tang warned that a highly concentrated market among service providers could undermine the expected benefits of outsourcing, stressing the need to guard against anticompetitive practices in government tendering. The department said it was satisfied with the contractor’s performance. “Over the past two years, all six swimming pools operated smoothly, and outsourcing lifeguard and first aid services was found to be effective,” it said. “All swimming pools remained open to the public and did not close due to a manpower shortage of lifeguards.” The department said it had strictly followed government procurement procedures by reopening the tender for the services and taking into consideration price, management plans, innovation proposals, bidders’ experience and relevant certifications. “The increase in the new contract price is mainly due to the tight manpower supply in the market, which requires the contractor to offer competitive pay and benefits to recruit lifeguards, as well as establish a backup manpower deployment mechanism to keep the pool facilities open,” it said. “Rising inflation has also increased the operational costs in technical input and management.” It added that the trial was part of a multipronged approach to address the recruitment challenge, saying the number of private swimming pools had increased to around 1,400, while the number of people joining the life-saving industry was declining.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: biotech firm eyes cervical cancer test breakthrough
description: Phase Scientific founder Ricky Chiu is drawing on his firm’s pandemic experience to advance early detection methods through urine-based HPV testing.
