content: Hong Kong biotech entrepreneur Ricky Chiu Yin-to is seeking to make cervical cancer screening easier through urine-based HPV testing, using sample-concentration technology developed by his company. His company, Phase Scientific, made its name during the Covid-19 pandemic through its rapid antigen test, Indicaid. The product received US emergency-use authorisation in July 2021, was used in Hong Kong community testing and sold in more than 30 countries. At the start of the pandemic, the firm employed 20 to 30 people. Its headcount later peaked at around 400, while monthly production reached as many as 30 million rapid tests. Chiu said business during the pandemic gave the company the funds, manufacturing experience, team and technology to pursue longer-term research after demand for rapid testing subsided. “Covid gave us the capital, the experience and the team,” he said. “The question was what problem we wanted to tackle next.” He chose to reinvest the company’s Covid profits into cancer research. Phase’s technology concentrates material already present in a liquid sample before testing. For cervical screening, a woman collects her urine, which is then processed in a laboratory to concentrate the biological material researchers want to detect. “If you have five particles in a whole cup of water, the test may not be able to detect them,” Chiu said. “But if you can concentrate that cup into one drop and keep those five particles there, you have a much better chance of finding them.” The work has earned Chiu – the firm’s founder, chairman and chief executive – a spot as a finalist in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Sino Group to honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed. A scientist by training and the main inventor behind Phase’s technology, Chiu co-founded the company in California in 2015 before moving its headquarters to Hong Kong. A meeting with Professor Dennis Lo Yuk-ming, known internationally for his work on circulating DNA, encouraged Chiu to consider applying the technology to liquid biopsy and cancer diagnostics. At the time, Lo was Li Ka Shing professor of medicine at Chinese University and director of the Li Ka Shing Institute of Health Sciences. He became CUHK vice-chancellor and president in January 2025 and remains Li Ka Shing professor of medicine. One of Phase’s current areas of focus is urine-based HPV testing. The company is taking part in a mainland Chinese clinical study covering about 17,000 women, with around 9,000 having participated by the time of Chiu’s interview. A separate Hong Kong study is being conducted with the University of Hong Kong with government innovation funding. Chiu said large-scale clinical evidence would be needed before a new screening method could gain acceptance among doctors, regulators and the public. “Before you convince ordinary people, you first have to convince the doctors and the authorities that it really works,” he said. He believes urine self-sampling could make cervical screening easier for women who might be reluctant to undergo conventional sample collection. Phase is also researching whether the same concentration method could help detect tiny traces associated with other early-stage cancers, including liver and lung cancer. Chiu said blood testing at an early stage could be difficult because the amount of detectable material in a single tube may be extremely small. Urine offers another possibility because far larger volumes can be collected and concentrated in the laboratory. He described that work as a research goal, not a finished product. More than two decades after leaving Hong Kong to pursue science in the United States, Chiu now sees biotechnology as part of the city’s economic transition. “If Hong Kong is to make this transition, people need to see that it can succeed. I hope we can be one of the examples that proves it can.”

title: More support needed for ethnic minority children with special needs, charity says
description: Heep Hong Society says its pilot project in Hong Kong helped 95 per cent of participating children improve, but calls for services to expand into more districts.
content: A non-profit children’s education organisation in Hong Kong has urged the government to expand support services for preschool-aged ethnic minority children with special needs to more districts, after a pilot project found that 95 per cent of participants showed improvement. Heep Hong Society said on Sunday that many ethnic minority families faced multiple barriers when seeking support for children with special educational needs (SEN), including language difficulties, financial constraints and cultural stigma. According to the Education Bureau, early identification of special educational needs is vital to ensuring children receive timely intervention and support. Children must have a diagnosis to attend government-funded Early Education and Training Centres or Special Child Care Centres, which provide preschool rehabilitation services for children with special needs. According to official statistics provided by the Social Welfare Department, the number of non-Chinese-speaking children receiving preschool rehabilitation services through such centres rose to 968 in the 2025-26 school year, from 741 in 2023-24. Dr Kwok Chun-chuen, deputy chief executive officer for services at Heep Hong Society, said many Hong Kong families with children who had suspected special needs already struggled to access the support they required. “For the [ethnic minority] families, the situation is even worse because of the language barriers and lack of information,” he said. “They may feel helpless. They may feel like they don’t know how to help their children.” He noted that it could take up to a year to receive a government assessment, while private assessments were often beyond the means of ethnic minority families, many of whom earned well below the city’s median income. Joy Wong, a project manager at the organisation, said some ethnic minority families were unaware of what special educational needs were, while cultural stigma also persisted in certain communities. To address these gaps, Heep Hong Society ran Project Embrace from March 2023 to February 2025, providing assessments, diagnoses and support services for ethnic minority children aged six and below. The organisation served 171 ethnic minority families with children who have special educational needs, 70 of whom received developmental assessments. Families paid HK$500 (US$64) for the service, which Heep Hong Society said was about HK$5,500 less than the average cost of a private equivalent. Assessments were conducted within about two months. The organisation provided interpretation mainly in Nepali, Urdu and Hindi – the dominant languages among Hong Kong’s South Asian ethnic minority communities. According to a social impact assessment of the programme by Oxfam Hong Kong’s research team, 95.7 per cent of participants improved in areas including activity participation and following instructions. Improvements were also recorded across six developmental areas, including fine motor skills, cognitive ability and social-emotional development. Meanwhile, 87.7 per cent of parents who took part said they better understood how to support their children, while 84.4 per cent said they were more aware of available resources. Cherry, a Filipino Hongkonger born and raised in the city who took part in the programme, has two sons aged 11 and four who have been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Cherry, who asked to be identified only by her first name, said her elder son was diagnosed late, during the Covid-19 pandemic, meaning she was unable to secure the services he needed in time. So when she began to suspect that her younger son, Ethan, might also have autism, she said she became “hungry for information”. Ethan was already on the waiting list for a government assessment, but she could not afford a private one. “Of course, I had a lot of worries,” she said. “I really didn’t know where to reach out to before Project Embrace.” She said she was referred to the programme through a local NGO. After enrolling Ethan, she noticed improvements in his communication skills and learned how to interact with him more effectively. “This significantly reduced my caregiving stress,” she said. Kwok said that as the number of children born to ethnic minority families increased, more needed to be done to ensure those with special educational needs received proper support. The organisation called on authorities to allocate more resources to dedicated ethnic minority service units within Social Welfare Department-funded Parents/Relatives Resource Centres. Of the 23 centres in operation, only five have units dedicated to ethnic minority communities. It also urged the government to increase the number of government-funded Early Education and Training Centres and Special Child Care Centres offering English and multilingual services according to district needs. At present, there are only two Early Education and Training Centres and one Special Child Care Centre dedicated to English-language teaching. All three are on Hong Kong Island and can accommodate a total of only 126 children. Wong said that although Project Embrace had ended, Heep Hong Society would continue to offer fast-tracked early assessments for ethnic minority families. The group also announced the launch of Project Bond Beyond Words, a new programme that will focus primarily on supporting parents of children with special needs. “They are the person who will go through the lifelong journey with the child,” she said. In a response to the South China Morning Post, the Social Welfare Department said it had provided subsidies to Special Child Care Centres and Early Education and Training Centres admitting ethnic minority children with special needs since the 2019-20 school year. The subsidies were intended to enhance training, parent communication and family support, it said. The department also said it had provided resources to nine Parents/Relatives Resource Centres in districts with larger ethnic minority populations. Since October 2025, each centre has had two additional peer supporter posts, “with flexibility to employ ethnic minorities peer supporters based on district needs”, it added. “The department will continue to review demand for preschool rehabilitation services among [ethnic minority] children and consult stakeholders on future arrangements in due course.”

title: Why warm welcomes can’t stop Malaysia’s doctor exodus from Borneo
description: Over a third of doctors offered permanent posts in Sabah and Sarawak are no-shows, driven away by isolation, costs and career doubts.
content: On Facebook, public hospitals in Malaysia’s Bornean states have been rolling out “Selamat Datang” [welcome] banner posts to embrace medical staff reporting for duty. Tawau Hospital on Sabah’s east coast recently published a group photograph welcoming newly arrived medical officers. Kinabatangan Hospital posted similar banners hailing arrivals across various departments, while in neighbouring Sarawak, Kapit Hospital accompanied its greeting with a portrait of a newly arrived doctor. But behind the warm online welcomes lies a dilemma for Malaysia’s healthcare system: more than a third of doctors offered permanent posts in Sabah and Sarawak have failed to report for duty. The no-shows highlight the difficulty of persuading medical professionals to relocate to the country’s Bornean states. Doctors cite family separation, uncertain career prospects and difficult working conditions as major hurdles – with many questioning whether to stay even after heeding the call. Speaking in parliament on Thursday, Malaysian Health Minister Dzulkefly Ahmad said 382 out of 1,055 medical officers offered permanent appointments in East Malaysia had not reported for duty. While the 36 per cent no-show rate was an improvement from 42 per cent in 2025, Dzulkefly said it was still not a result to be proud of. Hard choices For Dr S*, accepting a permanent appointment in Sabah meant leaving her family in Kelantan to build a new life alone. The doctor moved from Kota Bharu to Sabah’s east coast in late September after her family encouraged her to accept the permanent offer. She said she had initially considered remaining on a contract in her home state. Malaysia introduced fixed-term contracts for junior doctors in 2016 amid a shortage of permanent positions, making permanent appointments highly sought-after for their greater job security. But accepting the post came at a price: moving from Kelantan to Sabah cost S nearly a month’s salary. Even after subsidies and reimbursements, she was still about 2,000 ringgit (US$489) out of pocket, mainly covering upfront rent and basic necessities. “I have been adapting to the new environment, culture and language. The workload is demanding because we have a shortage of medical officers,” S said. “But I also have support from my specialists, nurses and fellow doctors … Even small things, like invitations to share meals, are very meaningful when you are far from family.” Despite the support, S does not envisage staying indefinitely. “For now, I see about two years as the maximum period I can serve away from my family,” she said, adding that while she might consider staying up to five years if her family could join her, her ultimate goal was to return to Kelantan. Other doctors have chosen not to take the leap at all. Dr AN*, another contract doctor, declined a permanent appointment in Sarawak to continue serving in Kelantan. “My own health needs and my mother’s illness factored into my decision to stay in Kelantan as a contract [doctor],” she said. AN appealed the placement decision, but after this was rejected, she chose to remain a contract employee and reapply for a permanent position in the future. Asked if she would have accepted under different circumstances, AN said: “My decision is final. I want to continue serving in my home state.” The limits of incentives The experiences of S and AN reflect the reasons outlined by Health Minister Dzulkefly in his response to Pulai MP Suhaizan Kayat in parliament. Besides family separation, health and financial and logistical challenges, Dzulkefly said that doctors often declined postings due to a preference for urban facilities, concerns over future specialist training and difficulties ensuring eventual transfers back home. To address these concerns, Dzulkefly said he had directed the ministry to study and implement a dedicated 30 per cent quota for specialist training for medical officers serving in Sabah and Sarawak. “Today, our Hadiah Latihan Persekutuan [Federal Training Award] has 1,650 places, so 30 per cent – around 500 places – will be specifically for those who are in Sabah and Sarawak,” he told parliament. Sarawak MP Kelvin Yii welcomed the announcement but added that stronger career incentives should be accompanied by better pay, improved accommodation and clearer posting terms. “Each posting should state the specific location and the duration of service from the start,” Yii said in his statement on Thursday. Dr A. Iswaran, who now works in private practice in Kuala Lumpur, described a different frustration: wanting to stay in East Malaysia but being unable to secure a permanent role. After serving as a contract house officer and medical officer in Sarawak and Sabah, Iswaran contacted health authorities in 2021 offering to remain in Sabah if allocated a permanent position. His request was not granted and he later declined an extension of his contract. Official correspondence he shared directed him to the standard federal appointment process, explaining that permanent roles fell under the health ministry subject to approval from the Public Service Commission. Iswaran also recalled having to rent private housing with colleagues because staff quarters were not provided, noting that the additional allowances failed to cover rent, utilities and security deposits. During all of this, Iswaran was single. “I only had myself to look out for,” he said. Dr R. Dinesh, a private doctor from the Klang Valley, was posted to Sarawak in 2014 – before the 2016 introduction of the contract system for junior doctors. “If you [were] single and male, you [were] gonna be posted to Sabah or Sarawak,” Dinesh said, recalling the expectation among his peers after they completed their housemanship training in Putrajaya. Though he preferred Peninsular Malaysia, he decided to see the move as an adventure. That included squatting at a friend’s place for a fortnight while starting work because there was no initial lodging and local hostels were full, and having to wait two months for relocation expense reimbursements. Beyond reporting for duty To ease the transition for new hires, Dzulkefly told parliament that the ministry had begun releasing placement results earlier and allowing eligible officers to claim full transfer allowances covering travel, meals and hotel accommodation. But the Malaysian Medical Association (MMA) warned that official placement numbers might not necessarily reflect the reality on the ground. In a statement on Thursday, MMA president Dr Sivanaesan Letchumanan said that feedback from the association’s Sabah branch suggested several hospital departments were experiencing a net reduction in medical officers. As a result, some doctors were forced to work on-call shifts every other day, with individual shifts lasting between 24 and 33 hours. “Are the reported placements translating into an actual increase in doctors serving at healthcare facilities where they are most needed?” the statement said. The association called for a facility-level breakdown of arrivals and departures, including clarification on whether official figures included doctors already serving in Sabah who had chosen to remain. Addressing broader healthcare reforms, the government committed under Malaysia’s 2027 budget, tabled on Friday, to offer permanent positions to more than 9,000 contract doctors next year. While the MMA welcomed the commitment in a statement on Friday, it stressed that job security alone will not solve regional shortages unless backed by a comprehensive workforce-retention strategy. The association also called for better incentives, improved working conditions and clearer career-development opportunities in Sabah and Sarawak. “Ultimately, progress must be measured not merely by the number of doctors reporting for duty but by whether healthcare facilities have sufficient manpower to deliver safe, timely and quality care to the rakyat [public],” the MMA added. For doctors like S in Sabah, while her colleagues’ support has helped her settle in, accepting a posting was different from deciding to stay. “In the long run, I still want to return to serve in my home state and be closer to my family,” S said. *Names have been changed to pseudonyms as the doctors are employed by the Ministry of Health and are not authorised to speak publicly.

title: Japanese primary student becomes youngest winner at Asian Games
description: Primary school student Yuki Kurihara, aged 11, may be the Games’ youngest champion in history.
content:
The Asian Games has crowned teenage champions before, but this edition has witnessed stunning successes by child prodigies, culminating in Yuki Kurihara standing atop the podium aged just 11.
The Japanese primary school student demolished opponents three times his age on the way to a historic gold in esports at Aichi-Nagoya.
He is Japan’s youngest Asian Games champion in history and almost certainly the youngest the Games have ever seen.
Kurihara did not even react after winning the final in Puyo Puyo Champions , a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs.
The boy, who does not turn 12 until June and wants to be a train driver when he grows up, later explained that he felt “embarrassed”.

title: Opinion | Hangzhou is doubling down on tech – minus the viral hype
description: Beyond kickboxing robots and DeepSeek, the city is making a strategic pivot and betting on tech champions that build the infrastructure powering China’s next AI cycle.
content: A year ago, a Unitree robot kickboxing could light up social media. When DeepSeek released its latest open-source artificial intelligence (AI) model, developers around the world rushed to test it. This year, however, Hangzhou’s latest technology bets have barely made a ripple. The city’s “New Eight Steeds” – eight deep-tech companies in fields ranging from smart glasses and inference graphic processing units (GPUs) to compute-in-memory chips and space computing – are a very different proposition from the “Six Little Dragons” that have made Hangzhou a focus of the global tech conversation. Most of them operate further up the industrial chain, serving companies and institutions rather than consumers. That helps explain why the new cohort has struggled to capture the public’s attention. It also raises an uncomfortable question: has Hangzhou’s technology marketing playbook stopped working? The scepticism is understandable. Some mock Hangzhou’s eagerness to turn tech companies into a branding exercise. The “Six Little Dragons” have yet to produce many businesses with proven profitability, yet the city has already moved on to another coterie. The financial markets have provided ammunition. Unitree’s market value surged to about 444.9 billion yuan (US$66.4 billion) after its August listing before tumbling by more than half by the end of September. Manycore Tech, another member of the group, saw its shares slump from a post-listing high of HK$48.50 (US$6.20) to around HK$7. The pullback has complicated Hangzhou’s technology narrative. For two years, milestones by Unitree, DeepSeek and others were presented as evidence that the city had created the right ecosystem for breakthroughs. The markets offered a reality check, exposing how some companies still fell short on basics such as revenue, profit and commercialisation. However, the comparison with the new group is flawed. The products of the “dragons” were naturally suited to social media: dancing robots, films generated by AI models, brain-computer interfaces that come with an unmistakable human-interest hook. The new “steeds” sell something much less visible: infrastructure. It is difficult to explain an inference GPU in a short video. Compute-in-memory architecture does not make for an obvious viral post. Space computing is harder still. Their value depends on the industrial ecosystem built around them. That matters because Hangzhou is making a broader strategic pivot. At the end of 2025, the city said it aimed to become China’s leading city for AI innovation during the 15th five-year plan period, moving beyond its previous identity as a digital economy hub. Hangzhou is building institutions to support that bet. It has introduced the country’s first local regulation for embodied intelligence. Its “3 plus N” industrial fund cluster exceeds 300 billion yuan in total, with longer investment periods, more flexible requirements and higher risk tolerance for deep-tech investment. The formula is simple: legislation provides boundaries and state funds supply long-term capital. The challenge is whether Hangzhou can turn that institutional design into actual industrial results. The first test is patient capital. Chipmakers normally need several years to achieve yield consistency, win customer validation and ramp production. Space computing could take longer. Government-backed capital can tolerate longer fund life cycles and exit timelines, but only if investors are willing to stay patient when companies generate little publicity or deliver weak returns. The second test is turning “opening application scenarios” into actual orders. These companies need customers, not mere policy documents. Smart glasses companies must find industrial and security deployments. Space computing companies need customers who are willing to pay. Meaningful first orders from governments or state-owned enterprises would be more consequential than any city branding campaign. Hangzhou also has to accept that it is not competing alone. Beijing has advantages in AI research and Shenzhen in supply chain depth, while Shanghai draws on its industrial base, research institutions and global business links. Hangzhou’s potential edge lies in combining open-source technology, hardware entrepreneurship and a relatively flexible regulatory environment. DeepSeek and Unitree showed it could produce globally visible AI and robotics companies. The new cohort is a harder bet: can that ecosystem extend upstream into chips, robotic components and in-orbit computing? Alibaba is an unavoidable part of the equation. At its flagship Apsara Conference last month, Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu Yongming described the coming period as the machine intelligence era and identified “AI models, AI chips and the AI cloud” as its three foundations. The company is targeting more than 20 gigawatts of global data centre capacity by 2032 and plans to roll its Zhenwu V900 chip into mass production in the first quarter of 2027. For Hangzhou’s chip and computing companies, Alibaba offers both a rich ecosystem and a formidable competitor. They need niches within or alongside its expanding AI infrastructure. The “Six Little Dragons” put Hangzhou in the global spotlight because their products are easy to see, test and share. The new “steeds” are designed to make the city relevant to the next-generation AI infrastructure. It would be a mistake to judge them by the speed at which DeepSeek or Unitree became globally known. Hangzhou’s challenge is no longer simply to produce companies whose products people can easily understand and to which they can relate. It is to build companies that other parts of the AI economy cannot easily do without. The “dragons” helped Hangzhou get noticed. The “steeds” are an attempt to make it indispensable in the AI race going forward. If that bet works, Hangzhou’s next tech success story might not arrive as a viral video or market meme. It could instead emerge quietly, embedded in the chips, machines and data centres powering China’s next AI cycle.

title: Bar Association urges proxy cap, electronic voting to curb building bid-rigging
description: Association chairman Jose-Antonio Maurellet expresses reservations about a proposal limiting proxies to only two classes of people.
content: The Hong Kong Bar Association has suggested capping the number of proxies a person can hold at homeowners’ meetings, without restricting who may act as a proxy, stressing that improving transparency and introducing an electronic voting system could help to deter abuse in large-scale maintenance procurement. Speaking to the South China Morning Post, association chairman Jose-Antonio Maurellet expressed reservations about a government proposal to restrict an owner’s representative to a relative or another owner in the same estate to minimise external interference in building management affairs. “Proxy right is a right which is derived from private ownership. So, we think it might be a little bit too onerous to say you can only proxy to these two classes of people,” he said. “We tend to think a better approach, perhaps, is to increase the level of transparency.” These suggestions formed part of the association’s submission on the government’s proposal to amend the Building Management Ordinance, prompted by the fire at the Wang Fuk Court housing estate, which killed 168 people and displaced about 5,000. The independent inquiry investigating the inferno exposed alleged systemic bid-rigging and anticompetitive behaviour at the estate, where a HK$336 million (US$43.1 million) renovation project was under way at the time of the tragedy. Maurellet said possible ways to increase transparency included requiring proxies to be lodged 96 hours in advance and displaying proxy arrangements in the building podium 48 hours before the meeting. The association, the professional body for the city’s barristers, suggested that property management companies could examine signatures, conduct random audit calls on a proportion of proxy holders, launch a review of irregularities or even report cases to police. Although past corruption investigations had shown that property management firms could play a role in bid-rigging, Maurellet said: “The question is not what is perfect, but within the existing structure that people can actually afford in real life, who are the possible contestants? “We think that property management companies probably, at the first instance, are the best gatekeepers for the time being.” He also proposed setting up an electronic voting platform, which could help reduce the number of proxies. “The beauty of this is that you really cut out the proxy, you cut out the middleman, because you can vote yourself … Hopefully, that will increase the degree of participation and the voting [turnout],” he said. Authorities have suggested that a person may only hold one proxy in buildings with 50 flats or fewer. In buildings with more than 50 flats, a person may be allowed to hold 20 proxies, or less than 2 per cent of the total number of flats, whichever is lower. While surveyors and some politicians had reservations about the ceiling, the association’s submission deemed a statutory cap an “appropriate and proportionate safeguard” and could address the concern of “undue concentration of voting power”. Maurellet added that the proxy ceiling could be devised on a sliding scale based on contract value, but procurements of large-scale building maintenance and those with high values and related to safety should adopt stringent arrangements. Another proposed amendment floated by the government is higher attendance requirements and voting thresholds for decisions on large-scale and high-value maintenance procurement at incorporated owners’ meetings. Under a proposed three-tier system, projects in the highest tier – those worth more than HK$120,000 per flat – would require 20 per cent of owners to attend the meeting, while 10 per cent or 200 owners would need to vote in person. The other two tiers, for projects worth HK$30,000 or HK$80,000 per flat, would have lower quorum and in-person voting thresholds. While supporting the proposed tiered system, the association suggested that an affected owner or interested party should also be able to seek directions from the Lands Tribunal to avoid paralysing the decision-making process. Maurellet said the government should also give the tribunal more power to address exceptional circumstances related to owners’ corporation meetings. The court had said that it had no jurisdiction to modify statutory rules when the administrator of Wang Fuk Court applied to postpone a meeting requested by owners. The association also proposed giving authorities greater power to intervene when the management committee of an owners’ corporation was dysfunctional. For example, authorities should be able to intervene if a committee refused to convene a meeting requested by at least 5 per cent of the owners, or repeatedly failed to comply with safety notices. Maurellet also expressed hope that the government would consider giving individual owners the right to apply to the Lands Tribunal if an incorporated owners’ committee unreasonably refused to take enforcement action on a safety-critical breach of the deed of mutual covenant. The deed of mutual covenant is a binding legal document setting out a building’s management rules. Maurellet said he hoped the proposal would encourage incorporated owners to take their duties more seriously. He said he believed such reforms might require more funding and resources for the Lands Tribunal, but noted that it should be “manageable”.

title: As clock ticks on China’s commercial land leases, renewal plans allay investors’ concerns
description: With leases on more than US$14 billion of land set to expire within 20 years, Guangzhou and Shanghai lead way in proposing solutions.
content: Groundbreaking land-renewal policies recently announced in Guangzhou and Shanghai represent a step forward in stabilising China’s commercial property market and shoring up investors’ confidence amid Beijing’s efforts to revive the real estate industry, according to officials and industry analysts. The new rules governing the leasing of land for commercial and industrial use will also facilitate the issuance of exchange-traded real estate investment trusts (Reits), a financing tool that developers can use to replenish their coffers. “The policies effectively address the regulatory loopholes regarding the renewal of expired non-residential land-use rights,” said Yan Yuejin, deputy director of the E-House China Real Estate Research Institute. “They mark a significant milestone for the authorities and market players to revitalise existing property assets, drive urban renewal and stabilise market expectations.” The Guangzhou and Shanghai governments have proposed that non-residential property owners pay land-use fees equivalent to no less than 70 per cent of the fair market price to extend leases after expiration. In mainland China, land is owned by the government. Developers and owners pay fees to secure land-use rights under lease agreements with the authorities. In early 1990s, when Beijing began deregulating the real estate market, it granted leases of 40 years for land earmarked for commercial properties like shopping centres, 50 years for factory sites and office buildings, and 70 years for residential developments. Some commercial property leases are due to expire in the coming years, sparking fears about their value and the effects on their users’ legal rights and interests. Guangzhou promulgated detailed land-renewal policies in April, with Shanghai following suit at the end of July. Since then, Xiamen and Hangzhou have also released similar frameworks for regulating coming lease extensions. More than 1 trillion yuan (US$14.2 billion) of non-residential properties have leases that will expire within 20 years, according to property services firm Cushman & Wakefield. Top policymakers will take a cautious stance on the land-renewal issue Wang Feng, Ye Lang Capital CBRE has estimated that 30 million square metres (322.92 million square feet) of office and retail property assets in 18 major Chinese cities will have remaining land tenures of less than 20 years by 2030. The Beijing-based Grandall Law Firm said in a report published in August that detailed operating guidelines were needed to ensure leases could be extended smoothly, with fairly priced land-use fees. Wang Feng, the chairman of Shanghai-based financial services group Ye Lang Capital, said it would “take some time before the central and local governments map out clear-cut rules to facilitate transactions and maintain market order”. “The real estate market is of vital importance to the national economy and top policymakers will take a cautious stance on the land-renewal issue,” Wang said. “Those policies in Shanghai and Guangzhou are viewed as trial runs and can be adjusted in future.” Brokers said office building prices in Shanghai had plunged 30 to 40 per cent from their peak amid a national property crisis that started in 2021, prompting local investors to hunt for bargains. Yan said the renewal policies had effectively allayed investors’ concerns about Reits backed by commercial properties because lease extensions meant they could generate stable and sustainable returns. Reits allow asset owners to raise cash from valuable but ­illiquid assets without losing control of them. The investment vehicles also give investors the opportunity to collect regular dividends, with income generated by the underlying properties. The mainland’s first four exchange-traded Reits backed by commercial properties made their trading debut in Shanghai on June 18 after raising a combined 20.3 billion yuan.

title: How Manchester City could repeat Uefa victory and hit back at Premier League
description: Respected lawyers identify City’s best grounds for argument when appeal is heard, but expect severe punishments if pleas fall on deaf ears.
content: Manchester City have a puncher’s chance of successfully contesting the ruling that they were guilty of all charges relating to flagrant breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, but should their argument fall flat, the 10-time English champions can expect to be clobbered with swingeing penalties. Those are the views of Luca Ferrari and Daniel Gore, specialists in sports and litigation law, respectively, after City were found guilty by a three-person independent commission of 80 charges of financial wrongdoing between 2009 and 2018, and another 34 of failing to cooperate with the subsequent five-year investigation. Preparing to face Liverpool on Sunday in their first match since the verdict became public, the club were said to have employed “sham” contracts to inflate revenue and reduce costs to the overall tune of more than £900 million (about US$1.2 billion) over the period in question. Citing the precedent of Everton being docked six points in 2023-24 for a single £20m rules infringement, Gore said: “If you extrapolate that to £900 million, they could be looking at hundreds of points [270].” Manchester City accumulated 240 points over the past three seasons. “Expulsion is a tricky one … if you kick them out of the Premier League, it’s not automatic that the Football League would accept them in any of their divisions,” Gore said. His “gut sense” is that City will be hit with a “big points sanction”. “Perhaps one that applies for a number of seasons, or that lasts as long as the length of the breach,” he said. Regardless, Ferrari and Gore, both partners at law firm Withers, believe the lawyers in City’s corner have grounds to fight the commission’s ruling, but that the club should narrow in on the strongest strand of their argument. That means not pursuing their claim that the safety of the verdict was compromised by the length of time it took to reach. “It’s going to be a very difficult argument for City to succeed with,” Gore said, adding that the panel “covered itself” when writing about the weight of transcripts and submissions the case generated. “We’ve not seen the multiple appendices, but these were sophisticated arbitrators, who produced a comprehensive judgment.” Ferrari said: “The judgment makes the point that part of the reason they had difficulties in ascertaining facts was the conduct of Manchester City throughout the proceedings.” Indeed, Gore said the club’s combative defence in the original hearing, coupled with their obfuscation, would “put them on the back foot in any appeal”. “The human nature of an appeal judge is probably going to question why they would be so aggressive at resisting.” Where Ferrari and Gore believe City have “their main shot” is in their insistence that sponsorship deals were part-financed by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club’s owners. “It was pretty damningly rejected by the tribunal at the first stage, but we know there was a lot of analysis of politics and governance in Abu Dhabi,” Gore said. “We don’t yet know the nuances, but I think their main shot would be to say [the panel] got it wrong on the analysis of where the money came from.” Manchester City were found to have engineered inflated commercial arrangements, where sponsors footed base sums and the club’s owners covered the shortfall. The manoeuvring added £830.69 million to their revenue over the nine-year period under investigation, leading the panel to conclude that City “gave the misleading impression to third parties in its financial statements and any required FFP [financial fair play] returns that its commercial revenues from sponsorship agreements were far, far greater than was in fact the case”. “[City] can argue that you can’t judge the right price for anything in this world,” Ferrari said. “That it depends on how badly you want it, how important it is for some government-linked entities to boost their images, or to have success. “Are you judging only by economic standards, or should you also judge the value of something from the associated benefits and success?” A new three-person independent panel will hear City’s appeal, while the original independent board is poised to reconvene to determine the sanctions that should be imposed on the club in the event that their pleas are rejected. Back in 2020, City had a two-year Champions League ban rescinded, and a £25.4 million fine substantially reduced, after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled Uefa had not established that the club’s owners had disguised equity funding as sponsorship revenue. “Manchester City scored a technical knockout against Uefa but that case was about the same issues as this one,” Gore said. “This uncovers what Uefa believed but couldn’t prove, and there could be another attempt from them to take action.” City will learn their fate within 30 days of the appeal being heard. Should it go against them, they would have recourse to a second appeal. Everton had their original 10-point deduction cut to six, while, in more recent years, Nottingham Forest and Leicester City unsuccessfully challenged points punishments. Burnley successfully claimed that Everton’s transgressions contributed to their relegation, and in June, the Merseysiders were ordered to pay the Championship club £35 million. Gore said he did not know whether that “judgment, methodology and analysis would survive appeal”, but he expects rivals to similarly seek financial reparation from City. “I think every club will explore it, but we’re a long way away from that sort of action. We might be many years away from the end of this.” Ferrari added: “Technically, the challenge [in gaining compensation from City] would be that there’s a degree of speculation when you’re trying to link football results to breaches of financial regulations.” Regardless of how the rest of this episode unfolds, it has raised legitimate questions over the integrity of football’s spending restrictions. It was little wonder that Karl Heinz-Rummenigge, the former chief executive of Bayern Munich, was such a staunch proponent of financial fair play (FFP) when it was agreed in 2009 and implemented two years later, given the concept enshrined his self-sustaining club’s position at the top of German football. “The original aim of sovereign fund owners with unlimited resources was to reduce costs, increase revenues and turbocharge to the top level,” Ferrari said. Had City not won eight Premier Leagues between 2012 and 2024, those titles would have been shared between Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, the three English clubs that most benefit from rules that impede aspirational rivals in the transfer market. The billionaire-owned pair of Newcastle United and Aston Villa have recently sold key players to comply with financial stipulations. “What the regulations have missed is the creation of a clear pattern that allows for an entrepreneurial project that makes sense,” Ferrari said. Rummenigge’s predictable counter is that “unlimited equity injections from owners would usher in a ruinous arms race”. “From an entrepreneurial perspective, it would make sense to start with a club like Eintracht Frankfurt or Paris FC [if spending rules were not so rigorously enforced],” Ferrari said. “Like challenger banks, you would need to allow overspending to reach a point where you had a sustainable position at the higher level of football.” Gore believes that “financial regulation in sport is here to stay”, but that “nobody can find the right mix or balance for that tension”. “Right now, it means clubs with bigger commercial footprints have more sustainable models, because they generate more cash.” If the pecuniary rules are not going anywhere, then neither is the hunt for loopholes in them, according to Gore. “Elite sport is about really fine margins,” he said. “That used to be on the pitch, but now it’s trying to find a little margin off it. “As long as there’s elite competition, there’ll always be someone trying to find a way around regulations.”

title: Who rules Negeri Sembilan? Royal row tests Malaysia’s constitutional order
description: What began as a customary dispute over a throne has left an administration purged and a state in legal limbo.
content: The dust has yet to settle in Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan, where a royal row has led to the fall of a state government and left the public wondering who, exactly, is in charge. Observers warn that the months-long constitutional crisis could create ripple effects well beyond the state’s borders, testing the entire nation’s systems of monarchy and government. The dispute centres on which of two men: the incumbent, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, or his intended replacement, Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar, is the legitimate ruler of Negeri Sembilan. It all began on April 19, when the state’s four territorial chiefs, known as undangs, issued a joint proclamation removing Muhriz from the throne over allegations of misconduct and naming Nadzaruddin as his immediate replacement. Negeri Sembilan is the only Malaysian state whose royal house practises an elective monarchy instead of automatic succession by birthright. Rooted in a centuries-old matrilineal customary system called adat pepatih, succession is decided by the four undangs, who are constitutionally empowered to choose the state’s ruler, bearing the official Malay title of Yang di-Pertuan Besar. Muhriz’s office disputed the April 19 decision, however, arguing that there was no evidence to support the claim and that two of the undangs seeking to dethrone him had been removed from their positions before the proclamation was made. This led to the group of four filing an application for a judicial review in May at the Seremban High Court, seeking to compel the state’s chief minister to sign and carry out their proclamation. The political drama also spread beyond the royal court. A week after the proclamation, all 14 elected Umno state-level representatives announced they had quit the state administration – led at the time by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition – for failing to carry out the order. Aminuddin Harun, then the chief minister, said it was not for him to decide on the status of the ruler as that responsibility fell on the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang, the state’s highest customary council. The walkout left PH with a razor-thin majority in the 36-seat state assembly, enough to force a state election in August that saw the United Malays National Organisation win power back after less than a term as a junior partner in the state government. At Muhriz’s behest, veteran state Umno leader Ismail Lasim was appointed as chief minister on August 2, a day after the state election. A few days later came the appointment of his 10-member state executive council, made up almost entirely of party colleagues. Barely a month into its term, the council issued a September 15 statement unanimously backing the undangs’ April 19 proclamation. The Attorney General’s Chambers in Putrajaya later rejected this move, stressing that the proclamation did not meet constitutional requirements. The state secretary of Negeri Sembilan also refused to carry out the order, citing the federal attorney general’s position. Retaliation from the palace came swiftly. On September 20, Muhriz decreed that the entire state executive council, minus the chief minister, was to be dismissed with immediate effect for violating its oath of office by seeking to remove him as ruler. Councillors were then barred from their offices, as police tightened security at the state administrative building. “It’s been a disaster for the state government,” said Lim Wei Jiet, a practising lawyer and constitutional legal expert. “You have one chief minister without any executive councillors to assist in the administration of the state.” The absence of an executive leadership may not have an immediate effect on how Negeri Sembilan is run, thanks to established laws and state-level administrative procedures. But analysts said problems could arise when civil servants needed the authorisation of senior figures to proceed, as the row between the executive council and state secretary over gazetting the April proclamation showed. “The greatest immediate danger is not necessarily the complete paralysis of government, but the emergence of competing centres of constitutional authority,” said Awang Azman Pawi, dean of the University of Malaya’s Academy of Malay Studies. “The longer this uncertainty continues, the greater the risk that what began as a royal and customary dispute becomes a problem of governance.” The fallout from the royal ruckus also threatens to spread beyond Negeri Sembilan, especially with the attorney general’s direct intervention in the interpretation of the state’s constitution. By drawing a line in the sand, the federal government has placed itself in direct conflict with a state administration, observers warn. “Obviously two positions cannot be correct at the same time. It has to be resolved one way or another, either through the courts or otherwise,” Lim said. “It’s not ideal, and this will not set a good precedent moving forward if there are differences in the selection of the ruler in other states, [especially] when it conflicts with the federal government’s position.” Meddling in royal affairs is a risky proposition for Malaysian politicians. Malaysia’s nine royal houses are widely considered sacred, especially by the Malay-Muslim majority who make up about 60 per cent of the country’s 34 million people and whose support is vital for any political party seeking legitimacy to govern. Awang Azman said any attempt to exploit a royal dispute for political advantage would likely bring only short-term gains. More importantly, he said it risked unravelling the country’s constitutional system, in place since independence from Britain in 1957. “It is a test of whether Malaysia’s constitutional system can manage an exceptionally complicated dispute involving written law, customary authority, elected government and the royal institution without allowing those institutions to collide irreparably,” Awang Azman said. “Winning the immediate argument is less important than ensuring that, when the dispute finally ends, the authority of the Negeri Sembilan government, its constitutional monarchy, its adat [customary] institutions and the rule of law all remain intact.”

title: Tiger kills man who entered big cat enclosure at UK wildlife park
description: The animal was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident.
content: A man died on Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said. Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1.35pm, but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said. The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated. “We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,’’ the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website. Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its “Land of the Tigers” attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-metre (yard) raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or play in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

title: The plague isn’t history. Where it still exists, how it spreads and a cure
description: While modern medicine treats the plague effectively, awareness and quick action remain crucial to stopping it from spreading.
content: To most, the plague is an ancient nightmare, a scourge that wiped out tens of millions in medieval Europe and killed more than 20,000 people in colonial Hong Kong between 1894 and 1929. A recent death at a plague research facility in Siberia is a stark reminder that the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, was never eradicated. While modern medicine has transformed the former “Black Death” into an easily treatable bacterial infection, the disease continues to circulate quietly across the globe, claiming lives whenever humans cross paths with infected wildlife. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). There are an average of about five human cases per year in the United States, according to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, mostly in rural areas of the American West. A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia. The case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing shows no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined. “People think the plague is gone; it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It’s not. It’s here among us,” says Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the UK. “Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you’re not going to get rid of the bacteria.” Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here is what to know. Plague can attack lymph nodes, lungs and blood People in Siberia have been dying of plague for at least 5,500 years. The earliest evidence of a form of the disease was found in teeth from ancient hunter-gatherers north of the region’s Lake Baikal. Thousands of miles away and centuries later, Hong Kong became the epicentre of the third plague pandemic in May 1894, when a severe outbreak of bubonic plague hit Hong Kong, concentrated in the densely populated Sheung Wan district. More than 2,000 people died of it in the city that first year. From 1894 to 1929, more than 20,000 cases with a mortality rate above 90 per cent were reported in Hong Kong. The last two cases were reported in 1929, and no cases have been recorded in the city since. Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague – also called the Black Death – are both caused by Yersinia pestis. During the Hong Kong outbreak, Swiss-French doctor Alexandre Yersin isolated the pathogen responsible for the plague in a makeshift lab in Kennedy Town. The bacterium was named in his honour. The bacterium spreads naturally among rodents such as rats and prairie dogs. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease. The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes, most commonly in the groin, armpits and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic in the US state of Ohio and Hong Kong’s Centre for Health Protection. There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria and infects the lungs, while septicaemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO. Bubonic plague often develops into the other two forms of plague if untreated. Plague can spread through fleas or bodily fluids Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also catch the plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend extra care when handling dead or sick animals. The plague can also spread through respiratory droplets from someone with pneumonic plague. “If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn’t travel very far,” says infectious disease specialist Dr Glenn Wortmann of the MedStar Washington Hospital Centre in Washington. “So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague.” That is why “the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the US will not happen”, he says. Antibiotics can treat the plague The plague was never eradicated, but we have got better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans. The plague can be cured with early antibiotic treatment. The key is to get to a doctor fast – otherwise the plague can be deadly. There is a vaccine, but the WHO recommends it only for people at high risk of infection, such as laboratory and healthcare workers. There is no strong evidence that vaccines work against the pneumonic form. There is no plague vaccine available in the US or for general public distribution in Hong Kong. Instead, local health authorities rely on continuous rodent and pest control, as well as early antibiotic treatments. Additional reporting by staff reporter

title: Editorial | Cooling-off period bill should protect more consumers
description: There is no reason not to give consumers in sectors other than fitness and beauty the same leeway to reconsider prepaid deals.
content: Yet another high-profile business collapse has exposed how vulnerable Hong Kong consumers remain when they pay large sums upfront for service contracts stretching over a long period. The abrupt closure of Hotstone Yoga, after a decade in business, has left hundreds of customers facing potentially millions of dollars in losses. The incident has once again highlighted the risks for consumers paying hefty prices upfront for discounted services over a long period. It also renews calls on the government to strengthen consumer protection by widening the scope of a proposed statutory cooling-off law to cover more sections of the wellness market. Hotstone Yoga announced late last month that it would cease operations immediately, citing “business operations and other actual circumstances”. Customs and Excise Department officers later arrested a 61-year-old director for allegedly violating the Trade Descriptions Ordinance by accepting payment when there was no reasonable ground that the relevant service could be delivered within the prescribed time or a reasonable period. The chain ran seven studios across the city at its peak, offering yoga, dance and fitness classes. Some customers said they were still being encouraged to buy course packages days before the company shut down. Earlier, the department had received 381 reports involving contracts worth about HK$4.07 million (US$518,633), while the Consumer Council had logged 286 complaints involving claimed losses of HK$3.91 million. The figures later rose sharply, with the authorities receiving close to 700 reports involving about HK$7.8 million in contracts. The numbers underline the severity of the matter. Just a month ago, three people were arrested in connection with a beauty chain accused of using high-pressure sales tactics. The department had received no fewer than 38 relevant calls for help, with reported losses ranging from HK$1,800 to more than HK$200,000, amounting to more than HK$3 million in total. The two cases are unrelated. But they show consumers are often placed in a disadvantageous position. In the latest incident, some customers paid handsome money in return for discounted classes over a long period. While prepayment usually offers customers lower prices and businesses a degree of financial certainty, the arrangement actually transfers the risk to the customer. Some yoga packages reportedly cost as much as HK$29,700 for 180 classes. One customer said she had paid HK$11,880 for 63 classes and used only 19 before the studios shut down. Another individual loss reportedly reached HK$46,000. The Consumer Council has strongly advised customers to avoid high-value prepayment for fitness and beauty sessions to minimise losses in the event of the contractor failing to provide the services. The closure of the yoga chain is yet another cautionary tale against locking oneself into a long service contract that requires hefty payment upfront. The savings from such bargain deals can hardly cover the losses when things go wrong. The practice of businesses luring customers to sign long service contracts has been an issue of concern. This is not helped by a long-standing culture of high-pressure selling among some traders. Thankfully, a proposal is under way for a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid fitness and beauty contracts, with the relevant amendment bill scheduled to be introduced to the Legislative Council as early as the first half of 2027. Officials earlier said there were no plans to extend the coverage to dance and yoga studios, saying there were relatively few complaints against such venues. Some lawmakers have urged the authorities to review the scope of the law amendment in light of the evolving trends in the wellness market. Indeed, the spirit of consumer protection is arguably the same regardless of the services involved. There is no reason not to give consumers in other sectors the same leeway to reconsider deals involving front-loaded payment arrangements. It would become a serious loophole if other businesses could take advantage of the limited statutory coverage to continue preying on vulnerable customers. The last thing consumers need is more business collapses and losses prompting the authorities to put in place the right legal protection.

title: Write to Win: What would be the toughest and easiest part of a day without electricity? (Round 5)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form . The deadline for voting is 12pm on Tuesday, October 13.
Neptune: The impact of a day without electricity would vary significantly depending on the season and the location. For instance, if it were winter in London, the nighttime would likely be the most challenging, as a lack of electricity means no heating, which would be quite uncomfortable due to the cold. However, right now, we are in Hong Kong, where the temperature is around 30 degrees Celsius every day. In this heat, enduring the scorching, humid afternoons without air conditioning would feel like being stuck in a large sauna for too long. It’s worth noting that it’s generally easier to suffer from heatstroke than from hypothermia, so staying cool would be a major concern. Additionally, without electricity, ice cream and cold drinks would be inaccessible, making the afternoons quite uncomfortable. On the other hand, the nighttime would be more bearable. Although there would be no artificial light, we could always channel our inner cavemen and use fire as a light source. From candlelit dinners to refreshing baths or showers, a lack of electricity might even allow us to romanticise life a bit more.
Mercury: Boom! The lights went out immediately. Terrified, I would instinctively shrink down and hug my parents. Since childhood, I have suffered from severe nyctophobia; darkness plunges me into sheer horror. A day without electricity would be absolute torment. The hardest part would be the overwhelming anxiety and constant, nagging fear that prevents me from completing daily tasks or sleeping soundly. However, the easiest part of this experience would be the forced break from digital distractions. Without the glare of screens or the buzz of notifications, my life would become completely quiet. This sudden silence would encourage my family to gather around candlelight, sharing stories and laughter. Ultimately, the very darkness that triggers my deepest fears would also create an opportunity to bond with my loved ones and find safety in their presence.
Mars: A day without electricity would be both exhausting and challenging. The most difficult aspect would be enduring the physical and mental discomfort. Staying in a stuffy room without air conditioning would be unbearable, and the intense anxiety of being disconnected from my friends would only add to my distress. I would constantly wonder what they were discussing and dread missing out on their gossip the following day. Feeling restless without my usual entertainment would make the hours drag on painfully. On the other hand, the easiest part would be the sudden boost in my productivity. Without the distraction of my phone, all interruptions would vanish. Knowing that nights would leave me with no light or that using candles would only make the room hotter, I would naturally work much faster. It would become surprisingly effortless to focus and complete all my tasks before sunset, demonstrating that a digital break can simplify life.
Jupiter: Hong Kong boasts one of the most efficient power supply systems in the world, yet I was surprised to find myself without electricity for nearly a day a few months ago. One Sunday, my building experienced a maintenance issue that caused a power outage. Those hours without power brought my family closer together. With no electricity, we turned to books, played board games, and engaged in conversations to replace our usual screen time. The hardest part was enduring the summer heat without air conditioning, which led us to fan ourselves and search for forgotten power banks to recharge our portable fans and emergency lights. During this time, I thought of my grandparents in India, who grew up without smartphones and continue to live freely without constant connectivity. They find entertainment in spending time with friends and family, a quality I aspire to cultivate. Let’s disconnect from our devices and reconnect with our loved ones because the cherished moments we share are far more valuable than any photo.
Venus: A sudden blackout that leaves us without electricity can turn an ordinary day into an unexpected adventure. The easiest part would be the break from screens. With no Wi-fi, my school’s online portal would be completely inaccessible. That means no homework notifications, no deadlines on Google Classroom and no emails about school. For a few blissful hours, I could imagine myself as a poet, reading a book by the window like a mysterious main character. However, the hardest part would hit when reality set in. Facing a completely dead phone would trigger panic, leaving me totally cut off from my social media and friends. In today’s world, staying in the loop is essential. On top of that, without air conditioning, my room would quickly turn into a sauna, making me a sweaty, dramatic mess. Surviving this challenge would definitely not be easy.

title: How a museum masterpiece’s life-size replica sparked rare US-China collaboration
description: Beijing team’s results based on 14th century Yuan dynasty mural hailed for ‘profound historical and practical significance’.
content: For anyone who has visited the Chinese galleries at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, there is one work that stops them in their tracks. Stepping into Gallery 206, home to Chinese Buddhist art, visitors are met by a monumental wall – over 15 metres wide and 7.5 metres tall (nearly 50 feet by 25 feet) – covered in a Buddhist assembly so vast and majestic that it momentarily erases the Manhattan bustle outside. Here stands the Medicine Buddha, a 14th century Yuan dynasty (1279-1368) mural originally from Guangsheng Temple in central China’s Shanxi province, glowing with mineral pigments and filled with serene deities. The work left a lasting impression on Zhang Jian, director of the Meticulous Painting Institute at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, who visited the Met three times before 2023. “The moment you step into the hall, you are overwhelmed by its awe-inspiring energy and ancient brilliance,” Zhang said. “But back then, I never connected it to my own work. It was only when I later stood inside the dilapidated main hall of Guangsheng Temple in Shanxi that the two spaces clicked in my mind.” The revelation sparked a groundbreaking journey. Over the next three years, Zhang led a team of Chinese artists and scholars in working just inches away from the masterpiece, painstakingly recreating every crack, faded line and historical scar to render a life-size replica. Most surprisingly, they even uncovered mistakes the Met’s own restorers never saw. The 700-year-old treasure left China in 1928, was cut into sections and sold by impoverished monks for 1,600 silver coins to repair a collapsing temple roof. More than 10 million Chinese cultural artefacts have been lost overseas since the opium wars of the mid-19th century, mostly through wartime looting and illegal trafficking. After changing hands through international dealers, Medicine Buddha was officially donated to the Met in 1965 by Dr Arthur M Sackler. While the physical repatriation of lost relics remains an arduous task, Zhang proposed an ingenious alternative: a visual homecoming through forensic, research-based copying – an exacting art form that replicates not just lines but hundreds of years of decay and restoration. At a time when US-China relations face headwinds across trade, technology and geopolitics, cultural collaboration has carried on without fanfare. On September 24, the first day of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US, the fruits of this cross-continental effort were unveiled in an exhibition at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing. Featuring a life-size replica of the mural among a collection of traditional Chinese and Buddhist paintings, the exhibition is scheduled to run until November 15. “This systematic research-based copying is both an academic challenge and a cultural responsibility,” Zhang said at the opening ceremony. “We are exploring a wall painting protection methodology with distinct Chinese academic characteristics, allowing ancient murals to re-enter contemporary cultural life,” he added. Jason Sun, the Met’s curator of Chinese art, described the results achieved by the team in Beijing as having “profound historical and practical significance”. “They offer deep insights and guidance for the future restoration and resplicing of ancient wall paintings at the Met,” Sun said. “We look forward to continued friendly cooperation.” The project is the culmination of an initiative launched by the Chinese National Academy of Arts. In line with Beijing’s broader strategy to elevate cultural heritage preservation as a pillar of national rejuvenation, the institute launched its mural initiative in 2016. The effort was backed in 2017 by the China National Arts Fund, a state-endowed philanthropic fund established in 2013 and approved by the State Council, China’s cabinet. For 13 years, central fiscal allocations have poured billions of yuan into hundreds of thousands of projects preserving national treasures and nurturing conservators. This momentum was reaffirmed in September, when Beijing issued its 15th five-year plan for cultural heritage protection and preservation. The sweeping joint directive explicitly prioritises the systematic conservation of ancient murals and ancient architecture, urging the leveraging of national funds and cross-border partnerships to build autonomous knowledge systems and talent pipelines. The document also emphasises intensifying research into Chinese artefacts held overseas, tracing their provenances and deepening international cooperation in restitution and museum exchanges. Over the past decade, the institute has surveyed and copied classic murals across more than 40 cave temples, monasteries and tombs along the ancient Silk Road in Shanxi, as well as Gansu province, the Tibet autonomous region and the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. By 2023, with help from the US embassy and consulates across China, academic links were established with the Met. In 2024, the partnership was formalised, with the Met granting full authorisation and sharing ultra-high-resolution digital images. Zhang’s team travelled to New York five times, spending seven to 10 days during each trip inside the Chinese gallery. The Met granted them unprecedented access – “the only such conditions in the world”, as Zhang put it – allowing them to set up isolated work zones and use specialised hydraulic lifts to examine high sections up close. “The Met staff actively coordinated with visitors for us,” said Meng Ying, an artist on the team. “Though our lifts and lighting equipment occasionally blocked sightlines, visitors were remarkably understanding.” “Many Chinese and foreign tourists came up to greet us warmly when they realised we were recreating this masterpiece for audiences back home,” Meng added. While most mural reproductions are painted on smooth paper or silk, Zhang’s team insisted on the ancient technique of painting directly on a mud-and-straw plaster base. To ensure absolute authenticity, they sourced raw soil from the immediate vicinity of the original temple. Most clay-based copies only reach about 80 per cent accuracy, but the team pushed for 95 per cent. Matching colours under dim museum lighting was a challenge. On every trip to New York, the artists carried dozens of handmade mud test tiles and giant prints to lay on the gallery floor, comparing them directly against the original. “It wasn’t just about picking a colour,” explained Han Maoyuan, another artist on the team. “Lighting, digital cameras and printing all change how a colour looks. We had to tweak our paints over and over again on site.” Rather than painting on a smooth modern wall, the team layered their mud base in two stages to copy both the original texture and the scars left by past restorers. “Real accuracy means respecting every chapter of the painting’s history, including its scars,” Han said. According to Wei-Cheng Lin, an associate professor of Art History at the University of Chicago and faculty director of the Dispersed Chinese Art Digitisation Project (DCADP), such physical marks bear unique historical weight. Fragmentation was the “necessary evil” that allowed these fragile images to be separated from crumbling walls and kept alive in art museums today, Lin said. “The indelible cuts witnessed a tumultuous period of the early 20th century, when the cultural significance of ancient Chinese artefacts was still in limbo,” he added. “That fragmentation transformed the mural painting from a religious image into an artwork.” The most surprising finding came when the team discovered that the Met’s earlier restorers had made several errors when reassembling the fragments. In one case, the restorers decades ago misread the neck lines and misaligned the Medicine Buddha’s head by 5cm (about 2 inches). “Western restorers are masters of chemistry and material conservation, but they were less familiar with the compositional logic of traditional Chinese brushwork and central-axis symmetry,” Meng said. “In Buddhist iconography, the central Buddha must project a dignified, perfectly aligned presence.” When Zhang presented digital reconstructions to Met curators, initial surprise gave way to realisation. Curators accompanied the Chinese artists back into the gallery to inspect the mural at close range. “They were astonished and admitted the tilt was real,” Meng recalled with a smile. “When we returned to New York for our next trip, a Met expert joked: ‘Ever since you pointed out that the Buddha’s head was shifted, the more I look at it every day, the more crooked it seems.’” Far from causing friction, the discovery strengthened mutual respect. “They truly appreciated our academic rigour and our willingness to point out and correct errors,” Meng said. “After all, this is what true academic exchange is all about. Meaningful academic exchange thrives precisely on asking questions and raising doubts.” The team’s traditional craftsmanship has also been amplified by 21st century technology. They used high-precision cameras and MacBooks for data capture and iPads on lifts for colour matching. The blend of ancient heritage and modern tech caught international attention when Apple executive chairman Tim Cook visited the team’s project workshop during his trip to Beijing for the China Development Forum in March. Cook observed how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools were being applied to cultural preservation, from colour correction to virtual image reconstruction, according to Chinese media reports. “I see AI as an amplification of the human, not as a replacement of humans,” Cook was quoted as saying after observing the workflow. “You saw today some things that were being done to make life much easier in terms of recreation … whether it’s colour correction and some of the things that you saw posted here, all of those things can be driven by AI. I would advise, ‘Don’t fear it, embrace it.’” Cook later shared his thoughts on social media, saying: “A new generation of art researchers is bringing China’s cultural treasures back to life.” Digital projects aimed to “re-envision our cultural heritage in a virtual world that transcends spatial and temporal limits”, added Lin, whose team at the University of Chicago has extensively digitised other dispersed Guangsheng Temple murals across American institutions. “At this level of understanding, collaboration on a global scale becomes necessary, and the digital paradigm we try to build could be extended to other cultures as well,” he said. DCADP seeks to digitally restore scattered Chinese relics to their original heritage sites. It has collaborated with multiple Chinese institutions, including the Taiyuan University of Technology, the Tianlong Mountain Grottoes Museum, Tsinghua University and Xian Jiaotong University. Across the United States, the Beijing team’s work has triggered a ripple effect. They helped the Cincinnati Art Museum in Ohio and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Missouri reidentify the exact original positions of their own Guangsheng Temple mural fragments. Inspired by the Met project, both institutions are now actively negotiating with the Chinese National Academy of Arts to initiate similar research-based copying projects for their collections, according to Han. Later in October, the Met is to co-host an international symposium in Beijing about Chinese murals with the academy, marking the first time the New York institution has jointly held a major academic conference in China with a national research body. The debut of the exhibition at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum also took place against a broader diplomatic backdrop. On September 24, the first ladies of China and the US toured Chinese artworks and a gallery dedicated to Asian design at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art. Peng Liyuan praised the US for returning lost Chinese artefacts in recent years and urged both sides to forge deeper cooperation on cultural heritage. Cultural heritage preservation has emerged as a fruitful front in Sino-American cooperation. Since signing their intergovernmental memorandum of understanding to prevent the illegal import of Chinese cultural artefacts in 2009, the US has facilitated the return of more than 700 lost artefacts to China. And just days before the exhibition in Beijing opened, US Homeland Security Investigations handed over 58 cultural relics and fossils at a ceremony at the Chinese embassy in Washington.

title: This week in PostMag: the collectors preserving art, design and cultural heritage
