description: What makes a collector tick? This week, we explore the pursuit of rarity, the preservation of heritage and the pleasure of owning beautiful things.
content: What drives the urge to collect? Does collecting ever become a habit, rather than a passion? Ultimately, what brings more fulfilment: amassing quantity or curating quality? A torrent of questions floods the mind when it comes to understanding the raison d’être of collecting. But rather than hear from me, a non-collector – all I accumulate is white hairs, at an astonishing speed – our dedicated Collecting issue happens to be the perfect stage for PostMag’s managing director, Eugene Tang, to share his experience on the subject, and what, in the infinite universe of “things” one can possibly collect, captures his attention: “I collect junk, in my wife’s view. Cufflinks are an easier, cheaper and more readily accessible distraction. I also collect contemporary art, [though] less of it now in Hong Kong since space is at a premium. But the real passion of my pursuits is celadon ceramics; old stock and bond certificates (scripophily); and the works of a Chinese painter named Zhu Da, better known as Bada Shanren. “My passion is driven by the quest for rarity, and the journey during the quest. I definitely go after quality, not quantity. In celadons, I do extensive research, travel to old kiln sites throughout mainland China to study the shards and sniff the old clay. I talk to people involved in the ecosystem of finding old ceramics: the heirloom sellers, gravediggers, buyers, resellers, auctioneers and collectors. I visit museums, attend auction previews and view famous collections to learn what the genuine pieces are, before committing to buying. “My journey is similar in scripophily: research, research and more research to eliminate the cottage industry of reprints and fakes. When one comes across a genuine piece – like the 1917 Bank of China stock certificate I found in a soon-to-be-demolished Beijing bookshop more than 20 years ago – the joy in the serendipity is truly memorable. “Bada Shanren is more aspirational – a fantasy, even. His works are beyond my reach. An album was up for auction at Sotheby’s on October 8, with an estimate of HK$60 million [US$7.65 million] to HK$80 million. He lived during the dynastic shift between the Ming and Qing. As the descendant of an aristocrat, he expressed his grief and anger at the changing circumstances through his work. Openly expressing such dissent was treasonous at that time. Yet, he was able to communicate sarcasm, cynicism and discontent with the flick of a paintbrush through the rolled eye of a fish or a mynah, set against a minimalist backdrop. I consider it the highest form (and an early progenitor) of dissident art, or anti-establishment art.” Others, meanwhile, collect for the sake of preservation. Earlier this year, the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation was founded to safeguard the city’s rich maritime history, with five wooden craft, hand-built in the 1930s, to its name already, thanks to generous patrons. What lives have these boats lived in the past century, and what grand adventures have they seen? Alex Sherr speaks with the organisation to hear their stories. Even more interesting is when the notion of “collecting” is interpreted through an unusual perspective. It took many years for Vo Thanh Vuong – 2019 winner of Top Chef Vietnam – to be honest with his cooking and embrace the flavours of his heritage in his fine-dining menus. Doing so, however, led him to a Michelin star. Hei Kiu Au follows the fisherman-chef out to sea to learn how he sees the ocean’s bounties as a “living archive” and how fermentation is central to his mission of recording his past. Elsewhere, one might simply collect for the sake of being surrounded by beauty and craftsmanship. Broadcasting legend Robert Chua Wah-peng opens his “home museum” to us for a tour of the fruits of his decades-long “labour” of acquiring Chinese antiques. At 80, he is now thinking about sharing the joys of his beloved collection with the world. And with that, enjoy the read.

title: Meet Thomas Eisenhood, Jessica Simpson’s rumoured new boyfriend
description: Following her split from former NFL tight end Eric Johnson, the pop star was recently spotted in New Mexico with the Nashville-based touring engineer and saxophonist.
content: Jessica Simpson seems to be cosying up to her rumoured new beau. On October 5, TMZ reported that the 46-year-old singer and actress was spotted enjoying a Sunday morning walk at Albuquerque’s Balloon Fiesta Park with 33-year-old musician Thomas Eisenhood, whom she was first linked to in April. According to TMZ, the pair had been dating for roughly three months when the outlet broke the news in April. A source confirmed the relationship to People, adding, “[Simpson is] happy. She’s in a great place, excited for her future.” Simpson split from her husband of 10 years, Eric Johnson, in January 2025. She shares daughters Maxwell Drew, 14, and Birdie Mae, seven, and son Ace Knute, 13, with the 47-year-old former NFL star. Neither Simpson nor Eisenhood has personally commented on the romance rumours. So, who is Thomas Eisenhood? What’s his background? Eisenhood was born on February 8, 1993, per Cosmopolitan, and is based in Nashville, Tennessee. According to his LinkedIn profile, he attended Loyola University New Orleans, where he double-majored in psychology and philosophy. Based on his Instagram posts, he seems to be close with his parents and has a younger brother. What does he do for work? View this post on Instagram A post shared by tom (@lowercasetom) Eisenhood is a freelancer in the event production and operations business, per his LinkedIn. He worked as a media assistant in college and founded the alternative rock band Stoop Kids in 2012. The band moved to Nashville for better opportunities than it was getting in New Orleans and to be closer to their Nashville-based manager, they revealed in an interview with Atwood Magazine. Eisenhood was a saxophonist and background vocalist for the group until they went on an indefinite hiatus in 2023. Eisenhood has also worked as a front-of-house engineer and stagehand, with experience in video and music studio production, festival networking, tour management and production management. He had a lifeguard licence from the American Red Cross, which expired in 2016. How did he meet Jessica Simpson? Simpson and Eisenhood met through their shared circle of music industry friends, per TMZ. They have reportedly been spending time together when the “I Wanna Love You Forever” singer visits her Nashville home. In June, a source told Us Weekly that the two have been touring together “on and off for the past few months” and because of Eisenhood’s busy touring schedule, the couple “spent a lot of time together by working closely”. The insider described Eisenhood as “a very low-key guy” and added that Simpson “likes that about him”.

title: Opinion | In AI, India’s choice needn’t be between a US leash or Chinese hook
description: What matters most is the ability to take any AI model – American or Chinese – make it serve Indian needs, prove it works and keep it running.
content: On June 12, two of the world’s most capable artificial intelligence models went dark. An American export directive barred foreigners from using Anthropic’s two flagship AI models, and because the company could not check every user’s nationality, it switched them off. Access returned on July 1 but the warning is clear: India’s AI future can be switched off from Washington. In September, Beijing came calling. At the Brics summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping promised China would “be a pioneer in establishing a Brics AI open-source community”. It is a seductive offer. Chinese open models are capable, cheap and free to adapt; once downloaded, no one in Washington can take them away. But this is a choice between a leash and a hook. American access can be yanked away overnight. Chinese models cannot be switched off once downloaded, but they arrive with Beijing’s sensitivities built in. Asked whether Arunachal Pradesh is an Indian state, DeepSeek’s chatbot declined to answer. No country of 1.4 billion people should run its banks, courts and public services on either. Delhi’s response so far has been to chase size. Start-up Sarvam AI plans to build a trillion-parameter model; so does state-backed BharatGen. The government is reportedly exploring an anchor investment of up to 200 billion rupees (US$2.08 billion) in a new frontier AI fund, on top of the 103.7 billion rupees the “IndiaAI Mission” approved in 2024. This is a race India cannot win, and does not need to compete in. That money cannot keep India at a frontier that American laboratories move every few months. Most of the 12 companies chosen two years ago to build public-welfare AI have reportedly drifted away from that work because the government has no way to buy what they build. There is still no independent institution to verify whether funded models perform as claimed. India is weighing a bigger cheque with no public scorecard for the last one. The deeper failure is a lack of urgency about the foundations. India generates nearly a fifth of the world’s data but has less than 5 per cent of its AI computing power. Every accelerator in the IndiaAI Mission’s subsidised pool is foreign-designed, overwhelmingly by Nvidia. In January 2025, a US rule capped how many advanced chips India could import until it was rescinded that May. Nearly five years after Delhi approved a 760-billion-rupee semiconductor programme, no Indian fab is in commercial production, and Tata’s Dholera plant will reportedly start production at 90 nanometres rather than the promised 28nm. Power is barely planned for. The government expects AI data centres to add 26.3 gigawatts to national electricity demand by 2031-32, and Google’s US$15 billion data centre project is already battling water concerns. India’s information technology secretary concedes “denial happens all the time”. Yet the response has been announcements, not urgency. Owning the biggest model is not sovereignty. Sovereignty is the power to adapt models to Indian needs, run them on Indian power and hardware, and evaluate them independently. An application programming interface (API) is a lease a foreign government can cancel. Open weights, downloaded and run at home, are an asset. They can be audited and retrained: a model that will not discuss Arunachal Pradesh can be fixed through post-training. Post-training costs a small fraction of pre-training, and it is where small teams can match far larger models on the tasks that matter to them. In my published research, an agent that automates this step lifted a small model’s pass rate on one task from 84.9 to 99.3 per cent. Other middle powers have worked this out. Singapore built recent versions of its SEA-LION models by further training open base models such as Google’s Gemma. Switzerland’s Apertus publishes its weights, training data and methods. South Korea funds several teams for its national model and cuts those that fall behind. Five steps would change the game. First, stop grading our own homework: create an evaluator independent of funders and builders, with private tests in Indian languages, and publish every result. Second, no milestones, no money. Third, fund adaptation, data and computing access so that hundreds of Indian teams can post-train open models for agriculture, health, law and public services. Fourth, never depend on one supplier: diversify across American, Chinese, European and Indian open weights. Fifth, treat power and chips as AI policy: guarantee clean, firm power for computing, and build a chip road map on the packaging and testing plants India has, rather than waiting until 2028 for the first wafer. Pre-training still matters, and India should build competitive base models of its own. But sequence matters. The capacity to adapt and evaluate pays off now and makes every later rupee accountable, while power and chips decide whether any of it is truly India’s. India does not have to choose between Washington’s leash and Beijing’s hook. It can use both while owning what matters most: the ability to take any model, make it serve Indian needs, prove that it works and keep it running whatever is decided in Washington or Beijing. That, not a trillion parameters, is what AI sovereignty looks like.

title: 9 dead, including children and pregnant woman, in shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania
description: The gunman, who was related to most of the victims, was also found dead at the scene.
content: A man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pennsylvania, before taking his own life as well, authorities said on Saturday. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims in the previous day’s shooting, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman. Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door shortly before 5pm on Friday, he said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran towards him, before returning inside. Police arrived to find the two women dead outside. Inside they found the bodies of a five-year-old boy; a one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor. “Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference. “But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole.” Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. “They knew something was going on at that house,” he said. “We have to figure out what that is.” Lorah said officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots. No additional shots were fired after that. “Sounds that may have been mistaken for gunfire came from flashbang devices – chemical munitions – used by Swat officers,” he said. Governor Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration’s “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who spoke directly to the victims’ families during the news conference. “I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier,” she said. “But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.” District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continues. “Please do not allow rumours, speculation or unverified information to add to the pain that these families are already experiencing,” she said. Erie is about 190km (120 miles) north of Pittsburgh.

title: Isaias kills 4 in US, leaves 670,000 without power
description: The hurricane weakened to a post-tropical cyclone after making landfall, but hazardous conditions remain.
content: Four people died after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, and about 670,000 residents in Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi were still without power as the storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Two of the deaths resulted ‌from trees falling on homes, according to local media and authorities. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Centre said. The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as a priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. “They’re going to make assessments this morning, ⁠and I think that’ll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration,” DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen ‌had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. About 420,000 customers in Florida, 190,000 in Alabama, 43,000 in Georgia and 17,000 in Mississippi had no power as of midday Saturday, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. A separate storm on the Pacific Ocean, Rachel, was moving towards the coast ‌of northern Baja California on Saturday, bringing wind gusts and increased tides, which left another 7,000 people without power in California. Alabama’s emergency management agency said ⁠the downed trees and power lines made ⁠travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. “Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” it posted on social media. A category 2 hurricane when it ‌hit Florida’s coast and the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, Isaias is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell said it ‌was beginning to ‌redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets in the Gulf, while Chevron was advancing efforts to redeploy staff to its platforms and seeking to restore full production. “Remobilisation ‌of crews will continue through Sunday,” it said. Despite the progress, about 69 per cent of oil output and 57 per cent of natural gas production in the US Gulf of Mexico remained shut ⁠on Saturday, slightly down from Friday numbers, the Marine Minerals Administration said. Some 113 production platforms representing 30 per cent of the total remained evacuated, according to the agency. US President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane ⁠preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was “under control”. The US Energy Department said on Saturday it authorised an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to address supply disruptions due to the hurricane. Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and ‌Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available ‌to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on social media. “There’s also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we’ve had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on,” DeSantis told Fox News early on Saturday. In the coastal city of Pensacola, a lack of drinking water was a problem, the mayor said. Pensacola airport, Florida’s 10th largest, was damaged by the storm and is closed to commercial flights until further notice.

title: Why freaky shoes from Saint Laurent, Chanel and Dior are trending
description: From Alexander Skarsgård’s clear brogues to controversial designs by Schiaparelli, Margiela and Chanel, conceptual footwear has everyone talking.
content: There is something quite deliciously subversive about a freaky shoe. Feet of course already hold a hint of perversion – some people are really into them, while others find them repellent. But shod those feet in a shoe that people can find both compelling and strange? Well actually, that’s fashion catnip. Visceral proof can be found in those who have made the freaky shoe their signature, such as the aristocratic, enigmatic and entirely iconic Daphne Guinness, who always wears a pair of vertiginous Alexander McQueen Armadillo shoes. Their hoofed shape is perhaps the dictionary definition of a freaky shoe. The latest in a long history of unsettling yet alluring footwear – we could include the kinky little lace-up boots that women wore in the Victorian era – is the sole-less sandal that Matthieu Blazy debuted at the Chanel cruise show in Biarritz earlier this year. The shoes – recently worn by Chanel girl Margaret Qualley at the London premiere of Ridley Scott film The Dog Stars – featured a delicate structure that tied around the ankle, leaving the rest of the foot entirely bare. Obviously, it immediately divided the internet, which is always part of the fun. The same could be said in recent years of the balloon pumps that Jonathan Anderson sent down the runway when he was at Loewe, the flower-adorned ones at Anderson’s Dior and the gold “toe” shoes that Daniel Roseberry has created for surrealist fashion house Schiaparelli. Not to mention how the Margiela split-toe Tabi shoe – once the kind of shoe worn only by a true fashion insider – has reached both cult and mainstream status. Emma Kalfus, a stylist and co-founder of independent fashion magazine Side-Note, says the freaky shoe is especially resonant right now, both on the runway and off it. In part, she says, because fashion loves being contrary. “The freaky shoe is definitely having a moment. From Chanel’s barefoot shoes at cruise 2027 to barely-there pumps, fairy tale jelly shoes and transparent Perspex brogues, footwear is becoming increasingly conceptual and increasingly strange. But perhaps that’s the point? The fashion world is obsessed with staying ahead, and designers are being pushed further and further into the realms of newness, creating shoes that are as much conversation pieces as they are commercial propositions,” she says. Kalfus points to the invisible lace sock pumps by Ukrainian designer Evikrv that were on the Area runway during New York Fashion Week in September – and which immediately sold out – as an example of how, and why, the freaky shoe is right for now. The jelly shoes shown at Chloé, says Kalfus, also fit squarely into what she calls “fashion girl fantasy”. “With their nostalgic, almost fairy tale-like quality, they’re the kind of shoe that feels simultaneously ridiculous and irresistible and are now filtering down to the high street.” The translucent shoe is indeed trending. As Kalfus notes too, the clear perspex brogues at the Saint Laurent menswear spring/summer 2027 show, also worn by Alexander Skarsgård at the London premiere of his film Wicker were particularly kinky. The thing about a divisive shoe also, as with anything that colours outside the lines: someone has to go first. “The audience was divided, but that’s arguably part of the appeal. There’s something fetishistic about a completely transparent shoe, and you can imagine its most committed fans wearing it long before the rest of us have decided whether we actually like it,” says Kalfus. Perhaps the most compelling reason for the continued fascination with the freaky shoe, though, is that it demands a certain level of taste. Or indeed, it’s not for everyone. “I think what all of these shoes have in common is that they demand a reaction,” says Kalfus. “They’re not necessarily designed to be universally beautiful, they’re designed to feel new and that’s what we’re craving most right now: not another version of something we already know, but something strange enough to make us look twice and something to talk about.”

title: Trump demands Ukraine get new president, lashes out at Zelensky
description: A day after unveiling a diesel deal with Putin, Trump accused Kyiv of contributing to global fuel shortages by striking Russian refineries.
content: US President Donald Trump has called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing him of rejecting multiple opportunities to end the war with Russia. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday. “Zelensky could have settled this war many times, many many times, and he chooses not to,” Trump said. The US president suggested that Ukrainians should choose a new leader capable of negotiating an agreement to end the war. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does,” Trump said. He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin was interested in ending the war. “Russia would like to make a deal … but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal,” he told reporters. “President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly.” Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago, in February 2022. Putin has repeatedly rejected proposals for an unconditional ceasefire, while US-led diplomatic initiatives have also failed to produce a breakthrough. Trump also accused Zelensky of contributing to global diesel shortages by ordering strikes on Russian oil refineries. The accusations came a day after Trump announced an agreement with Putin for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to help ease global fuel shortages. Washington plans to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel to allow the deliveries to proceed. The Kremlin confirmed the agreement, which drew swift criticism from Zelensky. “He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump said. The US president said he had warned Zelensky against targeting Russian refineries because of the impact on global fuel supplies. “Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries,” Trump said, recounting his warning to the Ukrainian leader. He demanded that the attacks cease, saying: “He better damn well stop.” Crude oil and diesel prices surged following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian energy infrastructure as part of its efforts to weaken Moscow’s ability to finance and sustain its war. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after surviving US execution attempt
description: The Death Penalty Information Centre says she is the first person to live after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
content: Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, her lawyers said on Saturday. Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her lawyers said in a written statement. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said. Pike had been hospitalised since surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her on September 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point she was on a ventilator, and her lawyers did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with help. The Death Penalty Information Centre says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. Pike’s lawyers said in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed”. The failed execution brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution As the process got under way, Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

title: Palestinian leader Abbas postpones elections to September 2027
description: Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, after which Hamas seized control of Gaza.
content: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday postponed legislative elections due next month until September 11, 2027, and called a presidential poll for the same date, blaming Israel and ‌the security situation in the Palestinian territories for the delay. Abbas’ decree cited “obstacles posed by Israeli measures” and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions for “free, fair and inclusive elections”, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported. The decree called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza to vote. There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead next month. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-2006, after which Abbas’ rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists. Abbas has ruled by decree since ⁠his presidential mandate expired in 2009. The Palestinian Authority held municipal elections in April in the West Bank and in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, the only city ‌in the enclave to participate. The vote was the first election held in Gaza since 2006. The decree said Israeli military attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel’s continued withholding of ‌Palestinian tax revenues, created challenges to preparing for and holding elections this November. In Gaza, the decree pointed to “exceptional security and humanitarian conditions”, ⁠the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the ⁠lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police. Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to Gaza and East ‌Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said. There was no immediate Israeli comment on Abbas’ announcement, with officials unavailable for comment on Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath. Israel typically bans the Palestinian Authority from holding elections in ‌East Jerusalem, territory ‌it captured in the 1967 war and later annexed in a move most countries do not recognise. The decision to postpone followed consultations with Palestinian factions ‌and political forces. It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address challenges facing the electoral process. Two Palestinian officials said on Thursday that leaders of Abbas’ Fatah movement and rival Hamas had agreed at a meeting in Cairo ⁠on Wednesday to postpone the elections. An August poll by the West Bank-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research showed declining support for both Hamas and Fatah, which many Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank blame for their continuing political divisions. The delay comes just ‌weeks after Abbas reaffirmed the November election ‌timetable in his September 24 address to the UN General Assembly, as he sought to advance internationally backed reforms. Abbas had committed in writing to French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to hold presidential and legislative elections as part of France’s recognition of a Palestinian state in September 2025. France’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that holding the elections was essential and it welcomed the launch of an EU election observation mission.

title: Houthi attack on Saudi airport kills 12, injures hundreds
description: Calling the strikes ‘not acceptable’, Trump said the US was ‘going ⁠to look at’ joining Saudi campaign against Houthis.
content: At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in an attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, as the Iran-backed Houthis escalate a campaign they launched this summer. The dead from the third attack this week on the airport included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, ‌the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, 309 were wounded, officials said. Yemen’s Houthis warned airlines, travellers and airport workers on Sunday to stay away from Saudi airports. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina,” the Houthis said in a post on social media. “We urge everyone to take ⁠our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions.” US President Donald Trump said on Saturday Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, some in critical condition after the attack, which occurred without warning. The two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport this week left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defence capabilities as it wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group. The Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the attack, but a Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond. Trump, asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes ⁠on the Houthis, told reporters: “We may. We’re going to ⁠look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.” Calling the attacks “not acceptable”, Trump said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks on the airport, saying they “demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life”. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned Saturday’s strike, reiterating that ‌attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and must cease immediately. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have said these killed civilians including women ⁠and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims. Saudi Arabia entered ‌the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous ⁠year, pushing out government forces. The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, ⁠freezing the conflict. That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country’s third-largest ‌city, Taiz, under siege. On Saturday, all flights were diverted from Riyadh and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, ‌the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on social media after the attack that the group had “shut down Riyadh international airport”. The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations. One witness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then ‌multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport. An injured traveller said they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport ‌before ‌part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. The US embassy in Riyadh said it “strongly recommends all US citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas”. Earlier Houthi attacks had prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences. Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

title: Resurgent home favourite Zheng Qinwen charges into China Open final with Mirra Andreeva
description: Ex-world No 4 becomes first Chinese player to reach final ⁠in Beijing, where she will face Russian she defeated in their only previous match.
content: A resurgent Zheng Qinwen charged into the China Open final on Saturday, beating Elise Mertens 7-5, 6-2, and will play Mirra Andreeva for the title at her home tournament. It is another step in the Olympic gold medallist’s injury comeback, following a gritty showing at last month’s US Open, where she reached the quarter-finals. Zheng, a former world No 4, had struggled with her form since needing elbow surgery in 2025 and is a wild-card entry in Beijing. “I had a great performance tonight,” said Zheng, who became the first Chinese player to reach the final ⁠in Beijing. But she told the crowd: “I would not say I’m back. I would say the best version of me is still coming in the future.” Zheng dropped just three points as she eased into a 3-0 lead, punching winners into the corner with searing accuracy. Her game faltered afterwards as she needed to warn the crowd to “stop speaking” before Mertens levelled to 4-4, but held her nerve to win the first set on the first time of asking. She carried that momentum into a dominant second set, closing out the match with 43 winners across the one-hour-and-a-half affair to secure her second clash with Andreeva, having beaten ‌the Russian when they met in the 2024 Beijing quarter-finals. “I always want to give my best here. It’s like the fifth grand ‌slam for me,” said Zheng. Earlier, Russian teenager Andreeva snagged the first spot in Sunday’s final, brushing aside Nikola Bartunkova 6-2, 6-2. “I wanted to play aggressive today,” said the 19-year-old, ranked five in the world. Andreeva raced into a 4-0 lead in the first set as 34th-ranked Bartunkova double-faulted twice before giving away the fourth game. The 20-year-old Czech made 20 unforced errors across the 74-minute match and was outplayed by the French Open champion, who sent down 27 winners. Bartunkova saved the first match point but Andreeva triumphed on the second without much more fuss. “She’s a very tricky opponent to play against … she sometimes manages to hit rockets out of nowhere,” Andreeva said. “I tried to be brave no matter what,” she said, adding that she calmed some nerves by playing the card game Uno with her coach before the semi-final. As fourth seed, Andreeva was the highest-seeded player left in the tournament by the quarter-finals after a run of upsets saw the departures of Elena Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff. The Russian player’s 50 match wins put her in a tie with Jessica Pegula for most on tour, according to the WTA, and she is set to move up two spots in next week’s rankings.

title: Are Chinese military aircraft already using a new joint air facility in Laos?
description: Recent satellite imagery shows twice as many K-8/JL-8-family trainer aircraft on site as Laos’ air force is thought to possess.
content: Chinese military aircraft may already be using a new joint aviation facility in Laos, with satellite imagery showing twice as many K-8/JL-8-family trainer aircraft there as the Laotian air force is assessed to possess. Eight of the two-seat trainer and light-attack aircraft were visible at Ban Keun Airport in commercial satellite imagery taken on September 30, according to Reuters, which first reported the images. More than two dozen military and support vehicles were also visible. The image was taken a day after the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy formally began operations at the airport, with a People’s Liberation Army delegation attending the inauguration. Beijing says the jointly maintained and operated centre is intended to strengthen training for Laotian air force pilots. The Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force is assessed by the IISS Military Balance 2026 to operate about four K-8Ws. The South China Morning Post could find no public record of Laos acquiring a new batch of K-8-family aircraft. Possible explanations for the discrepancy include additional Laotian aircraft not reflected in published inventories, aircraft assigned to the new academy or the presence of Chinese military aircraft. Chinese military aviation analyst Andreas Rupprecht said he believed PLA Air Force aircraft were among the eight visible at Ban Keun. “In my opinion, not only possibly but certainly, since there are eight aircraft to be seen there and Laos itself only owns four,” he said, adding that the imagery could show four Laotian K-8Ws alongside four JL-8s from the PLA Air Force. Rupprecht also pointed to apparent differences in their colour schemes, noting that Laotian K-8Ws had been seen in camouflage while PLA aircraft of the type commonly use a much lighter-coloured livery. A satellite imagery expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more cautious in his assessment. The expert said four aircraft were covered by tarpaulins, while the remaining four appeared lighter in colour – possibly consistent with Chinese aircraft – but sunlight reflection prevented a definitive identification. Timothy Heath, China expert and founder of security research firm Perceptum, called the four-and-four interpretation “very plausible”. But according to Brian Hart, deputy director of the CSIS China Power Project, even if some of the aircraft were operated by the PLA, their presence would not necessarily signal a significant expansion of Chinese air power in the region. “These aircraft do not provide China any significant new ability to project air power in the region,” Hart said. “They are primarily trainer aircraft.” The imagery also shows Ban Keun has the capacity to accommodate considerably more aircraft than Laos’ existing jet-trainer fleet, which Military Balance lists as comprising about four K-8Ws and three Yak-130s. The satellite imagery expert said the apron appeared to contain about 24 marked parking positions suitable for small aircraft such as the K-8/JL-8. Few other facilities were yet visible, although construction was continuing, and the number of positions could indicate that aircraft would travel to Ban Keun for training, with enough space to accommodate joint training. More broadly, Ban Keun occupies a distinct place in China’s small overseas military footprint. Hart said in an interview when the centre opened last month that Ban Keun was China’s first acknowledged overseas military facility centred on air power. According to official Laotian reporting, cooperation at the centre will include joint training and exercises, personnel development, humanitarian assistance and other areas. If PLA aircraft were among those visible, their presence would demonstrate actual Chinese military aviation access to Ban Keun, said Isaac Kardon, an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University’s school of advanced international studies. “Training and a strategically useful military presence can coexist,” Kardon added, saying that the main questions were who operated the aircraft, under whose command and with what permissions. In January 2024, nine JL-8s from the PLA Air Force’s Red Falcon aerobatic team flew to Laos for celebrations marking the Lao People’s Army’s 75th anniversary, showing that Chinese military aircraft could operate from Laotian territory temporarily. PLA aircraft have also temporarily used partner airfields in countries including Russia, Pakistan and Thailand for exercises and training. What would distinguish Ban Keun from those temporary deployments, Kardon said, is whether the PLA had “reliable access” – an arrangement allowing it “to return and use the facility predictably, rather than negotiating each deployment as a separate event”. He said an enduring PLA operating location would require three elements together: “reliable access, sustained support and a recurring operational role”, including personnel and facilities capable of maintaining, fuelling and supporting Chinese aircraft over time. Kardon said fuel storage, maintenance facilities and communications would be relevant indicators, although they could also support an ordinary training establishment. Calling Ban Keun a PLA aviation base would require clearer evidence about its standing mission, command arrangements and China’s control of the facilities, he added. Hart said the joint facility’s location meant that even if China stationed more capable aircraft there in future, it would not fundamentally change the PLA’s ability to project air power in the region because Chinese aircraft could already reach the area from bases in China. “Still, operating from there could help China to build experience with overseas basing – a valuable stepping stone if the PLA seeks to open bases farther afield in the future,” he added. Whatever Ban Keun’s eventual status, the facility’s significance was primarily political and institutional, Heath said. “This base not only shows China’s growing influence in Southeast Asia,” he said. “It clearly demonstrates China’s expectations of its Belt and Road Initiative partners.” At the same time, Kardon cautioned that permission to train Laotian pilots did not automatically imply permission for Chinese aircraft to conduct regional intelligence or combat operations. Ban Keun could represent “an aviation application of the Ream model”, he said, referring to the China-Cambodia Joint Training and Support Centre at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. “A standing, jointly supported aviation facility that enables repeated or extended Chinese deployments would be a meaningful development,” Kardon added. “Whether Ban Keun meets that description remains to be established.”

title: Russian attacks kill 20 in Ukraine after Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin
description: The diesel deal contrasted a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month to clamp down on Russia’s oil and gas revenues.
content: Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow’s war in Ukraine. Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said on Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded in the attack. Missiles also struck Kyiv in a daytime attack on Saturday. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said four people were wounded. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4½ years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days. Trump said on Friday he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote Saturday on social media. He said the attacks showed Moscow understood “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities”, adding that “different signals are needed”. Zelensky said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days. In a post on social media, Zelensky also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and said that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones. “It is important to continue working together to protect people and limit Russia’s ability to wage this terrible war,” Zelensky said. Trump had been set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. Instead, the American leader announced on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. In Kyiv, people gathered at a memorial to fallen soldiers on Independence Square greeted the deal with a mix of anger and resignation. “Trump has once again shown his true face,” said Oleksandr Petrenko, 26. “He didn’t care about the situation, the shelling or the destruction of our homes. All he’s interested in is oil or the fuel prices and how much Americans have to pay.” “Knowing Trump, he tries to manipulate the markets. He’s got an election coming up soon,” Petrenko said. “So he needs to emphasise to his voters that petrol will be cheap. But it won’t be effective.” For Oksana Yakunina, a financial adviser from Kropyvnytskyi, the announcement “didn’t really come as a surprise”. “Trump has been working with Putin for a long time,” she told Associated Press. Trump’s announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelensky said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy”. He framed it as an investment in the war that could prolong it. “It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said. According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelensky called it “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners”. Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war. “I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelensky said.

title: 127 arrested as Hong Kong police bust Vietnamese-led loan-sharking syndicate
description: The group allegedly charged borrowers HK$100 a day for every HK$10,000 borrowed, with the compounded rate reaching 3,700 per cent a year.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested 127 people in a six-month undercover operation against a Vietnamese-led crime syndicate accused of running loan-sharking rackets charging interest rates of up to 3,700 per cent, as well as illegal gambling and unlicensed bars in West Kowloon. The syndicate is also alleged to have helped illegal immigrants find shelter and work, with police raiding eight premises on October 8 and 9. Among those arrested were 10 alleged core members, including the suspected leader, a Vietnamese woman holding a Hong Kong identity card. “The group’s operations were very closed, recruiting only among its compatriots,” Superintendent Chiew Tsi-huen of the Organised Crime and Triad Bureau said on Saturday. Police said they believed the syndicate had operated for at least a year. Senior Inspector Christopher Pumar, also of the bureau, said the group used grocery shops and an association for Vietnamese residents as fronts. It allegedly provided illegal immigrants with temporary accommodation and counterfeit Hong Kong identity cards or construction worker cards, charging HK$2,000 to HK$2,500 per document to help them find work. Police said most of the syndicate’s core members were Vietnamese nationals holding recognisance forms. The group also allegedly ran several illegal gambling venues offering baccarat and Vietnamese card games, as well as two unlicensed bars that offered cheap alcohol and drugs. Its main income came from loans charged at HK$100 a day for every HK$10,000 borrowed. With interest compounded, the effective annual rate could reach 3,700 per cent – far above the legal maximum of 48 per cent – police said. The syndicate allegedly also drew borrowers into illegal rotating credit schemes, with each scheme comprising 20 members who paid HK$5,000 every 10 days into a HK$100,000 pool. The suspected leader decided who received each payout, while members faced hidden fees and an unclear distribution of funds. Debtors unable to repay were allegedly threatened, assaulted or unlawfully detained. Some were also pressured to traffic drugs, police said. The group had separate teams to promote loans, collect debts and carry out violent offences. Its services were offered only to Vietnamese residents in Hong Kong, making the syndicate harder to investigate. Many debtors, concerned about language barriers and their immigration status, often did not seek police help, officers said. The 127 arrested – 55 men and 72 women aged 23 to 92 – included 37 Vietnamese nationals. Police seized more than HK$2 million in cash and valuables, along with loan records, counterfeit-document-making equipment, gambling tools and drugs. They also confiscated a car worth about HK$400,000 from the suspected leader’s home. All those arrested remained in custody as police investigated their backgrounds and the source and movement of funds. Officers did not rule out further arrests.

title: China’s Zhejiang province calls to limit tech giants’ power over online traffic
description: Communist Party authorities in eastern China urge greater oversight of internet platforms, warning that algorithms amplify social divisions.
content: Communist Party officials in eastern China’s Zhejiang province have called for greater oversight of major internet platforms and their “traffic power”, warning that online traffic and algorithms had evolved into a force capable of shaping public discussion and sentiment. The publicity department of the Zhejiang provincial party committee published the commentary on social media on Thursday, saying traffic could no longer be viewed simply as a data resource. Zhejiang’s capital city, Hangzhou, is a major Chinese tech hub. The department argued that public feed traffic should be treated as a semi-public utility rather than “a private asset owned by tech platforms”. It accused platforms of prioritising clicks and commercial interests over the public interest. Online platforms have considerable control over content visibility, deciding which posts and topics receive exposure or are taken down, according to the department. It said platforms promoted low-value or sensational content through trending lists and recommendation feeds, while topics related to technological development, social welfare and livelihoods tended to be suppressed. “Over time, this could weaken the public’s understanding of social realities and reduce attention to and participation in public affairs,” the department said. In September last year, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) took action against top social media platforms Weibo, RedNote and Kuaishou after they “failed to fulfil their primary responsibility for managing online information content” by displaying celebrity gossip and “trivial matters” on their trending lists. The three platforms have hundreds of millions of monthly users each. The commentary also warned that platforms amplified disputes through traffic recommendations, triggering wider discussion and user-generated content that could potentially deepen social divisions. Recommendation algorithms select and rank content based on a user’s online activity and preferences, helping platforms generate traffic and keep users engaged. Because of this, researchers have raised concerns that users might be exposed to a narrower range of views, reinforcing stereotypes and polarisation. The recommendation processes used by platforms, along with their decisions on account bans and whether to boost or limit content, often “operate as a black box”, the article said. “The platforms’ social influence is not matched by corresponding accountability,” it added. The department called for regulators to clarify the boundaries of platforms’ power, strengthen oversight of platform rules and introduce tougher constraints and penalties for promoting low-value content and amplifying disputes. It also urged platforms to tighten their content management and make their rules more transparent. Chinese authorities have been carrying out a “Qinglang” campaign – a series of online clean-up efforts launched in 2016 and led by the CAC. More than 60 rounds of crackdowns were carried out between 2021 and August of this year, according to an August article by CAC head Zhuang Rongwen in the Communist Party magazine Dangjian. Penalties and other enforcement measures against major platforms have become a regular feature of the Qinglang campaign. Over the past two years, several major platforms, including RedNote and Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, have “updated their recommendation algorithms to promote more positive content, give users greater control over their feeds, diversify recommendations and improve algorithm transparency”, according to the CAC. Several platforms have also introduced rules for managing trending content and accounts, according to company announcements. Dong Chenyu, an associate professor at Renmin University of China’s school of journalism and communication, said major Chinese platforms had little incentive to pursue gains by promoting attention-grabbing content that drives traffic and engagement at the expense of the public interest. “The most direct consequence of pursuing such short-term gains is that you can expect to be fined,” Dong said on a podcast posted on Douyin’s official safety and trust centre account.

title: Senior civil servants could face disciplinary action over Tai Po fire if named in report
description: Civil service chief says she will not rule out launching disciplinary action if any public servants are named in coming investigation report.
content: Senior public servants found accountable for last year’s deadly Tai Po fire could face disciplinary action if named in an investigation report that a government-appointed panel is expected to submit this month, Hong Kong’s civil service chief has said. Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan also said on Saturday that a support unit was being set up to assist the Public Service Commission if investigations into officials’ “administrative responsibilities” were eventually launched. “If the [investigation] report clearly pinpoints an individual [official] and points out what he or she has done inadequately, or there is prima facie evidence established, I would not rule out the possibility of launching disciplinary action directly,” she told a radio programme. “Otherwise, if system failure is said to be a main issue, the Public Service Commission could also probe the officials’ administrative responsibilities.” Yeung was referring to the two-tier administrative accountability system, implemented in July as part of reforms pushed by the city leader John Lee Ka-chiu to improve governance. A first-tier investigation covers relatively minor problems and will be handled by department heads. Serious or systemic government problems, or cases that involve permanent secretaries or department heads, will trigger second-tier investigations conducted by the commission. It is understood that a special task force is being set up under the commission to follow up on efforts to establish accountability for the fire and will be led by former sports commissioner George Tsoi Kin-pan and former deputy secretary for security Benjamin Mok Kwan-yu. Yeung declined to comment, saying the deployment was a “normal” exercise as preparations were being made in the wake of the commission’s expanded roles. Yeung reiterated that the government would decide what to do next after receiving the report of the committee looking into the fire tragedy but promised that accountability would be pursued. She added, however, that the government might not make the commission’s investigation report fully public, citing the need to protect privacy and confidentiality. The devastating fire at the Wang Fuk Court housing estate in Tai Po claimed 168 lives last November. A judge-led committee was appointed by the government last December to investigate the cause of the blaze and make recommendations. During its hearings, the panel was told that the government’s lax monitoring and heavy reliance on the contractors’ self-supervision were partly to blame. The panel’s 30 evidential hearing sessions, held over five months, exposed how the use of non-fire-retardant materials such as scaffolding nets and polyfoam boards, the removal of fireproof windows from emergency staircases and the deactivation of fire alarms at the estate, which was under renovation at the time, led to the rapid spread of the flames. Victor Dawes, the committee’s lead counsel, also singled out four government bodies for failing to heed fire risks in the run-up to the disaster – the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit. The committee is expected to submit a report by the end of this month. Meanwhile, Yeung said in Saturday’s interview that 41,000 government employees across about 100 job grades had been covered in the first phase of a revised civil service appraisal scheme launched this month. Under the revised system, staff performances are assessed on a six-level rating scale, with about 5 to 10 per cent of those deemed to have underperformed not being granted a salary increment. Yeung said the figures were not rigid targets. She also said the scheme would be reviewed after two years to see whether any adjustments were needed. Some of the job grades covered in the first phase of the Performance Appraisal Enhancement Scheme for Civil Servants include traffic warden, structural engineer, social work officer, government counsel, hawker control officer, court interpreter and architect, according to the bureau.

title: 2 men die in float festival accidents in Japan
description: Accidents often occur during the highlight of such parades in which the floats make turns without stopping.
content: Two men died and more than a dozen others were injured Saturday when floats overturned during annual festivals in Osaka Prefecture. In Izumisano, a 51-year-old man became trapped beneath a float that overturned while he was riding it with other participants, police said. He was later pronounced dead at a hospital, while seven others were injured. A float at a different event in Izumiotsu also toppled, killing a 48-year-old man who was among those trapped underneath, according to the prefectural police. He had been riding the float when it overturned. Nine others were injured. Both accidents occurred as the “danjiri” floats were being manoeuvred around corners, the police said. Danjiri floats are pulled through city streets entirely by human power in festivals that originated as prayers for a good harvest in the southwestern part of the prefecture. Accidents often occur during “yarimawashi”, a highlight of the parades in which the floats make turns without stopping. On October 3, 11 people were injured when a float toppled in Sakai, another city in the southwestern part of the prefecture.

title: Singapore not ideal for sprints, say Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton after chaotic race
description: Red Bull driver says ‘we shouldn’t host a sprint where you can’t pass’ after he claims first win in city state as nine cars retire.
content: Singapore’s Formula 1 circuit needs redesigning and lacks entertainment value for a sprint race, Saturday’s sprint winner Max Verstappen and runner-up Lewis Hamilton said after the 20-lap race involved little overtaking. Rain delayed the start of the inaugural sprint at the ‌Marina Bay Street Circuit, and with overtaking almost impossible, the only drama came in the form of collisions and a record nine retirements. “I think we shouldn’t host a sprint where you can’t pass,” Red Bull’s pole sitter Verstappen told reporters after notching his first victory at the circuit. “I’m fine, I just do my thing … but it’s not what I like. The overtake mode, it barely does anything here. You don’t really gain a ⁠lot on the straights … we need to have a longer straight or like more of a proper hairpin to ‌overtake.” Mercedes’ George Russell spun into the wall on the final turn of the first lap when he was leading the sprint while the two McLaren cars collided on the last lap ‌while chasing the final podium spot. The big beneficiary of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s “papaya spat” on the last lap was Kimi Antonelli, who inherited fourth place having started seventh on the grid, and stretched his championship lead over Russell to 89 points. Russell has a grid penalty for Sunday’s Grand Prix, meaning the 20-year-old Antonelli could take another big step towards becoming Formula 1’s youngest-ever champion. ‘It was the rain that ⁠made it exciting’ In between, six of the 20 laps ran behind a ⁠safety car, which is ⁠commonplace in Singapore because of crashes, while 11 of the 16 race wins have come from pole position. “I love the race here, [but] I was ‌just saying to Max, I think they need to change the track to maybe a longer straight somewhere in order to allow it to be truly ‌a great ‌racing circuit,” Hamilton said. “It’s a great track to drive over a single lap and qualifying, but … there’s like ‌one place, really, that you could potentially get close to overtaking. “I thought it was fun, but if it was dry, ⁠that would have been probably the most boring race for you to have watched. It was the rain that ⁠made it exciting.” Reduced-distance sprint races, with eight points going to the winner, are held on Saturdays with sprint qualifying replacing the usual second Friday practice sessions. Singapore’s was the sixth and final sprint race this ‌season and it is not ‌on next year’s 10-event sprint calendar, though another city circuit on the schedule is Monaco – a venue Ferrari’s hometown hero Charles Leclerc said was not ideal. “I don’t think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general,” said Leclerc, who finished third in Singapore’s sprint. “Here or Monaco, I don’t think it adds anything to the weekend.” Verstappen had kept his pole position after escaping a penalty ⁠for overtaking under a yellow flag on Friday but the Dutchman made a slow start as Russell stormed ahead and Hamilton swiftly ‌moved up from sixth to third. “The start was horrendous again, so that’s definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have ⁠something like that tomorrow, ⁠that’s your race over if nothing crazy happens,” Verstappen added. “After that, you just want to keep it calm and under control because you know that you can’t pass ‌around here.” ‘Silly mistake’ for Russell Russell said a miscalculation caused him to spin out at the last corner. “I came through the corner, had more battery deployment than I thought. ‌Pushed me ‌a little bit wider than I hoped and then I just went on the white line,” Russell said. “Yeah, silly mistake. Big, ‌big consequences.” The qualifying session for Sunday’s race was delayed because of the rain. The start was delayed because of heavy rain, making it the second week running that a Formula 1 race had started late. Last week’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was first held up by a downpour, then because several cars’ software failed to cope with the wet conditions. The FIA issued a software update which was also being used in Singapore this week.

title: Nearly 80, Korean artist Kang Myonghi talks about ‘What Remains to be Seen’
description: Kang Myonghi explores time and emotion in her Hong Kong exhibition through her abstract interpretations of natural landscapes.
content: At nearly 80, South Korean artist Kang Myonghi retains the creative energy of her youth. She remains active in her studio, with her commitment to international projects undiminished. In recent months, she has visited Hong Kong twice to prepare for “What Remains to be Seen”, her first solo exhibition at a gallery in two years. The only pause in her working routine came during the 2020 pandemic lockdowns. Travel restrictions did little to stem her creative output, however. Being confined to Jeju Island sparked a new realisation six decades into her illustrious career – the shift is reflected in about 20 works, produced between 2020 and 2026, on show at the Villepin art gallery in Hong Kong’s Central until November 15. “The pandemic marked the beginning of a pivot where I began to perceive time along a horizontal plane rather than from a fixed, single-point linear perspective,” Kang says. She is referring to the eye-level horizontal line that divides a composition, rather than the conventional vanishing point used to create an illusion of three-dimensional depth on a flat surface. Kang is known for abstract interpretations of natural landscapes, shaped by her deep appreciation of classical Chinese poetry and ink painting. Her inspirations include the poet Wang Wei and artists Zhao Mengfu and Wen Tong. A seasoned traveller, Kang has made multiple trips to the National Palace Museum in Taipei to study classical ink masterpieces first-hand. How she captures what she sees “She is not merely depicting landscape as scenery,” says Rishika Assomull, senior director at Villepin, standing before Wollabong, a 2026 canvas depicting Jeju’s famed oreum, or small volcano cones. “This work captures multiple perspective angles simultaneously, creating the impression that the landscape floats in mid-air. It is not a literal rendering of physical reality; she is painting her sensory experience of the terrain – the feel of the wind against her skin or the subtle vibration of the horizon.” Assomull recalls Kang’s account of travelling alone through the Gobi Desert in the 1990s and setting up her easel in the vast wilderness. For hours, Kang felt no inclination to touch brush to canvas, opting instead to absorb the surroundings in silence. “When the impulse to paint finally arrived, night had fallen,” Assomull says. “She was gripped by fear, alone in the desert darkness. What she finally rendered was not the physical desert landscape, but her emotional response upon confronting that immense expanse.” Kang says her creative impulse comes from observing a subject and striving to respond to it “faithfully”. “To me, a painting is the remnant left behind after pushing through paralysing fear and immense hesitation, which I then contemplate countless times,” Kang reflects. “The fact that I can continue painting by using those very marks as a lever never ceases to astonish me, filling me with joy and gratitude.” Creative from an early age Kang was introduced to art as a child in Daegu, South Korea, in the years following the Korean war (1950-1953). Raised by a single mother who worked as a civil servant, she was encouraged to pursue her creative interests from an early age. She went on to study at Seoul National University’s College of Fine Arts before moving to Paris in 1972 to refine her work while immersing herself in traditional East Asian art, poetry and philosophy. Over the course of her career, Kang has earned international acclaim for work that bridges figuration and abstraction. Rather than simply depicting landscapes, she seeks to capture physical sensations and emotions – wind, light and fear among them. Working in oil and pastels, her visual vocabulary is defined by lyrical, calligraphic marks, luminous colours – including pigments she formulates herself – and recurring botanical motifs such as camellias. Her work reflects a meditative engagement with time, memory and nature. Kang has since moved beyond her formal academic training. Her adventurousness as a traveller and an artist has led her to embrace spontaneous irregularities within her work. Rather than pursue pristine execution, she views compositional challenges and unexpected marks as vital components of her creative process. “She feels that without an imperfection, a painting cannot fully mature,” Assomull explains, pointing to the 2026 work Le ruisseau de la vallée d’Andeok, where delicate graphite lines remain visible beneath layers of oil paint. “In daily life, our instinct when encountering a mistake is to erase it immediately. But when Kang encounters an unexpected mark, she sits with it, absorbs it and works in dialogue with it, believing that is how one ought to engage with life’s uncertainties.” A fascination with pink Kang feels challenges always lie in wait as she paints while observing an object. “Walking into those problems on the canvas only opens up another level of questions and problems,” she says. “In other words, I am always pushing to the furthest point I can see. Each solved difficulty yields a fresh one, and it is simply what the act of seeing demands.” Her current artistic inquiry centres on the colour pink, inspired by wildflowers around her Jeju studio. “Pink is such a strange, elusive colour,” she reflects, noting that it evokes distant memories. In the blossoms she sees the shade of pink present in a 10th century Song dynasty hibiscus painting she admires; the semi-precious red stones she encountered in Mongolia; the delicate transparency of azalea petals cherished by her late friend, the Swiss artist and photographer Meret Oppenheim; the filtered light streaming through Yemeni stained glass; and the robes worn by Christ in frescoes by the Italian painters Masolino da Panicale and Gentile da Fabriano. “All these echoes live at the core of the problem I must answer to,” she says in her calm, soft voice. “When my mind and body are fully aligned, when the pink I seek is finally ‘true’, I will pick up my brush and set that stroke onto the canvas.” “What Remains to be Seen” runs at Villepin, 53-55 Hollywood Road, Central, until November 15. For more information, visit villepinartcn.com.

title: Cracks in security? Qing dynasty ceramics damaged in British Museum display
description: Incident involving 300-year-old Jingdezhen ceramics puts museum display safety under global scrutiny.
content: Two Chinese ceramics at the British Museum have been damaged while on display and are being restored, sparking fresh debate over how museums should safely exhibit fragile cultural treasures. The museum confirmed on Friday that a bowl had fallen from its shelf and landed on a small box on the bottom shelf, damaging both pieces. “Both objects are already with our expert conservation team for complete restoration,” the museum said. The museum, which said the incident occurred on October 4, noted that while the shelf and mount showed no signs of failure, it would continue to investigate how the pieces were damaged. Photos circulating on social media show ceramic shards inside a four-tier display cabinet featuring items from the Sir Percival David Foundation of Chinese Art. A bowl catalogued as B629, originally positioned at the centre of the top shelf, appears to have fallen to the bottom tier, smashing another piece, item 634. According to the museum’s website, both damaged ceramic pieces date to the Kangxi period (1662-1722) of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), originating from Jingdezhen in China’s Jiangxi province. The museum’s website says they are “not on display”. The B629 item, labelled by the museum as “bowl with ladies engaged in cultural pursuits”, is 216mm (8.5 inches) in diameter and 80mm high. The underglaze blue ceramic depicts women in a terraced garden admiring a painting, playing a traditional stringed instrument and taking part in board games while surrounded by attendants, trees and mountains. According to the museum’s description, the artefact is “a very fine copy of a 15th century Ming porcelain bowl”. Item 634 is a circular porcelain box with a low-domed cover, 66mm in diameter and 25mm in height. The centre of the lid depicts a Buddha’s hand citron rendered in a pencilled style with underglaze cobalt blue, framed by peach branches and camellias. The lower section of the box is decorated with a peach branch and a floral spray. Room 95, where the damaged ceramics were displayed, was closed following the incident and reopened the next day after the broken fragments were removed from the cabinet. The gallery houses nearly 1,700 objects, showcasing some of the finest Chinese ceramics in the world from the 3rd to the 20th century. The collection was donated to the museum by the Sir Percival David Foundation. The incident has sparked debate on Chinese social media over how museums should protect fragile works. “I am more concerned with why the accident happened, how the artefacts will be restored and how similar incidents can be prevented in the future,” said Pan Jinyu, a Chinese-speaking tour guide in London, in a social media post on Thursday. Pan, while noting this was not the first time the British Museum had made headlines for artefacts being damaged or lost, said: “What is more disappointing than the damage itself is that mainstream UK media have not reported on this yet.” The incident was not the only vulnerability at the London institution. The museum was rocked by a major scandal in 2023, when an internal investigation revealed that about 2,000 artefacts had been stolen, damaged or lost from its storehouses over several years. The revelation triggered global outrage over the museum’s security protocols, leading then director Hartwig Fischer to step down.

title: Meet singer Olivia O’Brien, who just called Pete Davidson ‘an absolute joke of a human being’
description: Davidson is known to have dated a long list of celebs, including Margaret Qualley, Kaia Gerber, Emily Ratajkowski, Ariana Grande, Kim Kardashian and Phoebe Dynevor.
content: Amid online backlash over his recent comments on female influencers, Pete Davidson is getting called out by singer-songwriter Olivia O’Brien, who labelled the Saturday Night Live alum “an absolute joke of a human being”. During an interview with Variety, Davidson mocked influencers and said that he finds the career path “insane” and “lame”.
