The comedian went on to specifically target female influencers. “It’s bad, and it makes me sad, you know,” Davidson said in the interview. “And girls are just talking to themselves on there, and they’re like, ‘OK, come get ready with me.’ And I’m like, ‘Who the **** are you? What do you do? Nothing. What the **** is this?’” he shared. “They make 40 million a year. What? And then I’m like, ‘The world’s broken.’” He continued, “There [are] girls my age that go on TikTok, and they’ll, like, mutter like a thing and then do this, like, dance. And I’m like, ‘What the **** are you doing?’ This is insane. Does no one else see how ******* insane and lame this is? And these girls are like super famous. Like, everyone’s like, ‘Oh my god, I can’t believe [it].’” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Variety (@variety) The internet quickly clapped back at Davidson, with several commenters calling out the comedian, who famously dated Kim Kardashian between 2021 and 2022. “Imagine dating the biggest influencer of all time and still having these thoughts? Like what?” one user wrote under Variety’s Instagram post featuring a clip from the interview. “But he literally does nothing and also makes US$40 million?” another user chimed in. O’Brien, who reportedly dated Davidson in 2020, added fuel to the fire when she responded to an Instagram post that criticised Davidson’s recent comments. She accused him of “sleeping his way to the top”, Davidson is famously known for having a long list of celebrity ex-girlfriends, including Kim Kardashian, Margaret Qualley, Kaia Gerber, Emily Ratajkowski and Ariana Grande (to whom he was briefly engaged). “I was dating him in 2020 and found out we were no longer together by seeing on The Daily Mail’s Snapchat that he went public with a more famous woman, lmaooo,” O’Brien wrote. “He is an absolute joke of a human being,” she added. In another comment, she wrote: “Not sure how he has the time considering we were texting 24 hours a day and falling asleep on FaceTime when we weren’t together. Busy boy! Lmfao.” Here’s everything you need to know about Olivia O’Brien. What is Olivia O’Brien’s background? Olivia O’Brien was born in Thousand Oaks, California. In a 2018 interview with music blog Ones To Watch, O’Brien described her childhood as “terrible” and shared that her classmates bullied her. “If you did anything that was different, they just hated you. I skipped third grade too, and I got so much shit for that,” O’Brien said. Despite being an academic achiever, O’Brien said music had always been her only passion. When she was in secondary school, O’Brien started posting song covers on SoundCloud and experimenting with fashion on social media, which she said invited more bullying. Around 16, American singer and rapper Gnash discovered O’Brien and reached out to her for a collaboration after he came across her covers of his songs. O’Brien also sent him a voice note of her original song “I Hate U, I Love U”, which became a hit for the two of them and kick-started her musical career. Since then, the songstress has released several singles and launched her second album Pixie this July. She is bisexual O’Brien is openly queer and came out as bisexual in an X post in July 2022, writing: “I’m pretty sure everyone already knows I am bisexual based on my behaviour but like … yeah I am”. Pete Davidson has denied dating her In 2021, celebrity gossip site Deuxmoi posted an anonymous tip that said “I have it on good authority that Pete and Phoebe [Dynevor] are in fact an item. He ended things with B-list pop star/influencer he had been seeing before Phoebe.” In 2022, O’Brien appeared on an episode of the BFFs With Dave Portnoy, Josh Richards and Brianna Chickenfry podcast, where she admitted she was the “B-list” pop star Deuxmoi mentioned. “Yeah, Pete. I didn’t think that anyone knew about that, I really didn’t,” she said. “He’s hot, he’s funny, and he’s sweet; he’s a really sweet guy. That was October of 2020. He texted me and was like, ‘I’m seeing someone else so I can’t.’” O’Brien added: “I cannot believe you guys found that; that’s really crazy. You’re the first people to ever ask me about that, and I really thought that no one knew about that. Breaking news. Oh, god. Two years later.” Davidson, however, quickly denied ever being involved with O’Brien. “There is no truth to this,” he told E! News in 2022, adding that he and O’Brien “were friends and hung [out] a few times”. In response, O’Brien took to her Instagram Stories and said: “News outlets are taking things I said in an interview (after being asked a VERY specific question) wayyy out of context. I never claimed to date anyone. Stop trying to start weird drama over me texting someone two years ago. Jesus Christ.”

title: 3 injured in Poland’s third youth stabbing attack in 4 days
description: Two school attacks earlier in the week left one dead and several others wounded, including children.
content: Three people were injured in a ⁠stabbing attack at ⁠a further education ⁠college in Warsaw on Saturday, police said, the latest in a series of incidents that have stoked concerns in Poland about copycat violence among young people. On Friday, thousands of ‌police visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after two stabbing sprees by teenagers in as many days sparked rumours of potential further attacks, fears that Saturday’s incident is likely to intensify. “At 12.30pm today, we received a report ⁠of an incident involving the use of a dangerous weapon,” police spokesperson Jakub ‌Filipiak said. “One person was injured and transported to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Two other bystanders ‌also sustained injuries but did not require hospitalisation.” He said the ⁠attacker was ⁠a 21-year-old student of the college. State news agency PAP reported that the victims ‌were two 17-year-old girls and a 24-year-old woman who had come to submit enrolment documents. Preliminary ‌police findings ‌indicated that the attacker and victims did not know one ‌other, PAP reported. Police said on Saturday they had inspected some ⁠50,000 facilities since Friday and detained 76 people. Authorities had previously said ⁠most of the people detained were teenagers who had made threats online. On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted ‌camera killed a ‌caretaker and injured two teachers at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital.

title: Taiwanese leader welcomes talks between Washington and Beijing ‘to reduce risk of war’
description: Beijing says William Lai’s Double Tenth speech was ‘stirring up confrontation’ as he accused the mainland of trying to change the status quo.
content: Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has welcomed talks between Washington and Beijing aimed at reducing the risk of conflict. Lai’s annual Double Tenth address on Saturday, marking the anniversary of the foundation of the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name, also called for democracies to work together to safeguard regional peace and for the Taiwanese people’s right to exist to be respected. He also warned that mainland China was trying to put pressure on the island to change the status quo, but Beijing accused him of “stirring up confrontation across the Taiwan Strait”. “Lai Ching-te’s speech disregarded facts … misled the public and revealed sinister motives, constituting a performance true to form by a ‘pragmatic worker for Taiwan independence’,” said Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office, using a label Lai had previously attached to himself. Zhang also accused him of “stubbornly clinging” to a “separatist mindset” and playing up the alleged “mainland threat”. She said Beijing would resolutely crack down on separatist forces, oppose interference by external forces and safeguard peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. She also said Beijing would promote “peaceful and integrated” cross-strait relations and “advance the great cause of national reunification”, but did not address his comments about the talks with Washington. On Saturday, Lai said: “We welcome the US and China managing their competition through dialogue to reduce the risk of conflict and war.” Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump met last month in Washington, where Xi urged Trump to handle the Taiwan question prudently and oppose independence. Lai added that maintaining regional peace and stability required rejecting “distortions of World War II history”, respecting the Taiwanese people’s right to exist and joint efforts by democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to preserve the status quo. During their meeting, Trump and Xi highlighted their countries’ alliance during World War II, prompting criticism from Taipei, which says it was the Republic of China government, rather than the People’s Republic of China – established only in 1949 – that fought alongside the Allies. Beijing has described such arguments as “a betrayal of history”. Saturday’s address was Lai’s third Double Tenth speech since taking office in May 2024. The annual address has traditionally served as a platform for the government in Taipei to outline its policies, and is closely watched by Beijing and the international community for signals about cross-strait relations. Speaking outside the Presidential Office Building in Taipei, Lai said: “China continues to exert pressure through military and grey-zone activities in an attempt to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.” Faced with the “expansion of authoritarianism”, Lai said Taiwan’s resolve was not only about its own survival but also about “whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules and that powerful countries cannot deprive people of the right to determine their own future”. Lai also warned of the challenges posed by “red supply chains”, a term commonly used in Taiwan to refer to supply chains centred on mainland China. “Peace cannot rely solely on wishes,” he said, adding that Taiwan would continue to strengthen its defences and use its strengths in sectors such as semiconductors to develop a more self-reliant defence system. In last year’s address, Lai outlined plans for a missile shield dubbed the “T-Dome” to counter growing military pressure from Beijing. He also said Taiwan’s defence spending would pass 3 per cent of gross domestic product this year and reach 5 per cent by 2030. On Saturday, Lai said the increase in defence spending was not intended to provoke, but to deter war. He also said Taiwan was willing to engage in dialogue with the mainland, but insisted that it must take place on an equal and dignified footing. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. It has stepped up its pressure on the island since Lai, whom it views as a “separatist”, took office and has since conducted several large-scale military exercises around the island, including one that came days after his first Double Tenth speech in October 2024. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main arms supplier and international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. Washington, however, is bound by law to arm Taiwan for self-defence and opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force. On Saturday, Lai avoided repeating some of his more contentious remarks from earlier addresses, including the assertion two years ago that Taiwan and the mainland “are not subordinate to each other”. Zhu Songling, a professor at the Institute of Taiwan Studies at Beijing Union University, said Lai’s speech was largely in line with expectations, noting that he did not use other provocative phrases. His welcome for the dialogue between Washington and Beijing reflected Lai’s “awareness of new developments in US-China relations and the situation across the Taiwan Strait”, Zhu said. “The broader US-China relationship clearly has a significant impact on the Taiwan issue,” he added. However, Zhu said Lai’s pro-independence position remained unchanged, and he was increasingly framing Taiwan’s security in international terms and linking it to democratic values. “The speech placed greater emphasis on repackaging the separatist narrative around Taiwan independence in terms of democracy and international engagement,” he said. Wang Kun-yi, head of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, said Lai had maintained a hard line with his comments accusing the mainland of pressurising Taiwan. While the speech broke little new ground on cross-strait policy, it suggested that improving US-China relations could make Lai more cautious, Wang said. He said Lai had shown “greater strategic flexibility” than in previous speeches, indicating that “Taipei must take into account the impact of US-China interactions on the situation across the Taiwan Strait.” “The Lai administration supports efforts by Washington and Beijing to reduce tensions, while stressing that Taiwan’s interests must not be sacrificed in negotiations between major powers,” he said. Wang Jianmin, a cross-strait specialist from Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, also said Lai’s most significant comments were those about the talks between Washington and Beijing. “To some extent, he is endorsing the idea of the US and China jointly managing regional stability,” Wang said, adding that they should be understood in the context of Taiwan’s pro-US stance rather than a shift in his view of Beijing. Wang added that Lai had not mentioned cross-strait exchanges, which had become constrained under his ruling Democratic Progressive Party. “He is not a pragmatic Taiwan independence advocate, but a radical one,” Wang said. Tang Shao-cheng, a research fellow at the Institute of International Relations at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University, said there was “no sting” in Lai’s comments, but they still fell far short of what Beijing wanted to see. “The new international environment shaped by Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States is highly unfavourable to Taiwan independence forces, prompting Lai to make some adjustments to his rhetoric,” Tang said. He said Lai appeared to be adapting to this environment, describing it as a “positive development, but it is far from enough”. Tang added that Beijing would look at Lai’s actions, such as his policy on cross-strait tourism, rather than his words. During Saturday’s speech, Lai also highlighted Taiwan’s economic performance, saying the island’s annual economic growth was expected to exceed 11 per cent, its highest rate in 39 years. He also pledged to make Taiwan a “city upon a hill” – invoking a biblical metaphor widely used in the United States to invoke a model for others to follow. Lai also outlined a range of policy priorities, including expanding social benefits, tackling drugs and strengthening Taiwan’s advanced technology industries.

title: Hong Kong records 21 mpox cases since August, high-risk groups urged to get jabs
description: The latest case, involving a 29-year-old man, brought the total number recorded in Hong Kong this year to 30.
content: Hong Kong has recorded 21 cases of mpox since August, accounting for 70 per cent of this year’s total, prompting health authorities to urge people who engage in high-risk sexual contact to take protective measures and get vaccinated to reduce their risk of infection. The latest case, involving a 29-year-old man, brought the total number recorded in Hong Kong this year to 30, comprising 23 local cases and seven imported ones, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Saturday. Twenty-one cases, or 70 per cent of the total, were recorded since August. Epidemiological investigations showed that all 21 patients reported engaging in high-risk sexual behaviour during the incubation period, including having sex with male strangers or multiple partners, and having sex without a condom, the centre said. Most of the patients had not been vaccinated against mpox, it added. Genetic analysis of the virus also found that some cases had identical genetic sequences, suggesting they might have shared a common source of infection, with multiple transmission chains existing among the population of men who have sex with men. “The CHP once again urges individuals who have engaged in high-risk sexual contact, particularly with strangers, to remain vigilant and take appropriate personal protective measures, including receiving the mpox vaccination and avoiding high-risk sexual contact, so as to lower the risk of infection,” it said. The centre also noted that more than half of the patients diagnosed in recent months with mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, had used dating apps to find casual sexual partners. “In some cases, patients were unable to contact their newly met sexual partners, which hinders effective contact tracing and the implementation of corresponding prevention and control measures,” it said. It urged people to keep their sexual partners’ contact details to make contact tracing easier. The latest case under investigation involved a 29-year-old man who developed a papule – a small, solid, raised bump – on his buttock on September 28. He later developed rashes on his limbs and buttock, as well as a fever and swollen lymph nodes. He attended an outreach vaccination service organised by the centre on October 8. Staff noticed his symptoms and arranged for him to receive isolation treatment at Princess Margaret Hospital in Kwai Chung. His clinical specimen tested positive for the mpox virus. The patient was in a stable condition, the centre said. He had high-risk sexual contact with a man in Hong Kong during the incubation period, it added. The centre said it was continuing its epidemiological investigation of the case and would report it to the World Health Organization. Hong Kong has recorded 114 mpox cases – 90 local and 24 imported – since 2022, all involving male patients. Mpox is a zoonosis – an infectious disease that can be transmitted from animals to humans – caused by the monkeypox virus. Infection can occur through contact with the virus from infected animals or people, or contaminated materials. People can become infected through bites or scratches from certain wild animals, such as some species of primates, rodents and squirrels, or through direct contact with their body fluids. Human-to-human transmission is mainly through close contact with infected individuals, such as skin-to-skin, mouth-to-mouth, mouth-to-skin and sexual contact. The likelihood of transmission through respiratory droplets is relatively low. The Department of Health provides mpox vaccination services for high-risk groups, including people who engage in high-risk sexual practices, such as having multiple sexual partners, sex workers or people who have had a sexually transmitted infection in the past 12 months.

title: Retired China Olympic champion diver sparks debate after reality show reveals toxic parenting
description: Her parents reportedly controlled her bank cards, and her mother refused to let her use her savings for investments.
content: A former Chinese Olympic diving champion’s quest for independence has struck a chord online, after her mother’s controlling behaviour drew widespread criticism following their appearance on a reality TV show. Zhang Jiaqi, 22, grew up in a modest Beijing family and went on to win gold in the women’s synchronised 10-metre platform event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020. Her youthful charm and exceptional talent have also attracted 3.3 million followers on Douyin. Zhang began diving at six, won her first national title at 12 and went on to claim dozens of gold medals at home and abroad. But success came at a steep physical cost. Years of gruelling training left her with injuries to her shoulders, back and feet, while some of her joints still ache in damp weather. She retired last November. Since then, Zhang has pursued financial independence through public speaking, fashion events and live-stream sales. In August, Zhang and her mother, Xiao Yingjie, appeared on Hunan TV’s reality show My Little One, where tensions in their relationship came to light. Throughout the programme, Xiao repeatedly chastised her daughter for minor habits, from leaving a tag on her clothes and ordering takeaways to keeping an untidy room. Even sitting on the floor to put on her shoes drew criticism from Xiao, who lamented that her daughter’s life was “a complete mess.” According to mainland Chinese media reports, Zhang felt she had been raised by the national diving team rather than by her parents. She accused her mother of prioritising medals over her feelings, rarely taking her wishes into account and expecting her to be anything but “ordinary.” Zhang recalled that her grandmother would offer her treats after training, while her mother urged her to eat less to control her weight. More controversially, her parents reportedly held all three of her bank cards. When she asked to use some of her savings for investment after retiring, her mother refused, arguing that she was “too young to understand.” Xiao also opposed her daughter’s move into live-stream selling. Undeterred, Zhang has been learning about product selection, on-camera presentation and audience engagement. She is also studying English, pursuing an international diving referee qualification and learning to drive. Her ultimate goal is to achieve financial independence and buy a home of her own. On October 4, Zhang reflected on their strained relationship in a social media post, expressing hope that they could find a healthier balance. “Mum, like any ordinary girl striving to build a life, I want to take charge of my own destiny and become a more well-rounded, fulfilled person,” she wrote. Her predicament has prompted debate about traditional Chinese parenting, which is often regarded as harsh. “A world champion, yet her own mother cannot see a single virtue in her. Many Chinese parents regard anything that falls short of their expectations as a flaw,” one commenter observed. Another was more scathing: “Zhang has every right to her hard-earned prize money. It is not for her parents to squander on holidays.” “Her mother fears losing control as Zhang grows more independent, so she keeps putting her down to regain her authority,” said a third.

title: Meet Primetime actor Skyler Gisondo, Ella Rubin’s rumoured boyfriend and viral meme star
description: The 30-year-old, who broke into acting through a Pizza Hut ad, is starring in A24’s Robert Pattinson-led psychological thriller – but how did he rise to internet fame?
content: Skyler Gisondo, who starred in A24’s psychological thriller Primetime alongside Robert Pattinson, is no stranger to viral fame. His 2015 red carpet photo became an internet meme, and recently he returned to the spotlight as the media speculates about his romantic life. Gisondo is rumoured to be dating Sterling Point’s Ella Rubin. The pair have been spotted attending events together since January 2024, when the 30-year-old actor accompanied Rubin to the premiere of her Apple TV miniseries Masters of the Air. Gisondo also referenced his “girlfriend” in a 2025 interview with Young Hollywood, where he said he discovered himself on wikiFeet, a website that shares celebrity foot photos. “My girlfriend might have sent it to me,” the actor said then. This January, Gisondo and Rubin attended the Vanity Fair and Amazon MGM Studios awards-season party together. While neither Gisondo nor Rubin has confirmed their romance, here’s everything you need to know about the actor and beloved internet meme, Skyler Gisondo. What is Skyler Gisondo’s background? Gisondo was born in Palm Beach County, Florida, in July 1996 to parents Ron and Stacey, both of whom worked as ocean engineers. Gisondo was only six years old when he fell in love with television and would watch films on repeat until he memorised the dialogue, he told The Beach Reporter in a 2016 interview. He would also direct his siblings and parents to re-enact West Side Story. “I was so passionate about acting,” he said during the interview. “I would do anything to entertain or to make people laugh.” When his family later relocated to California for his father’s job, Gisondo’s mother started sending photos of the budding actor to various agencies. Soon, he landed his first acting gig in a Pizza Hut commercial. What roles has Skyler Gisondo played? The Pizza Hut advertisement led Gisondo to work on more commercials for two years before he went on to star in television shows and films. In 2003, Gisondo landed a role in an episode of the comedy series Miss Match starring Alicia Silverstone. Working consistently throughout the years, he has amassed over 70 acting credits and starred in projects such as Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb, The Amazing Spider-Man 2 and Superman. How did Skyler Gisondo become a meme? Yes he does 😭 https://t.co/I9MUpfMheb — Gracie (@graciem120001) October 5, 2026 Aside from acting, Gisondo became internet famous in 2022 after fans discovered a 2015 red carpet image of him and started making memes from it. Several netizens claimed that he possessed a typical “boy-next-door look”. The memes continued in 2023 and are making the rounds again in 2026, featuring captions such as “the kid you befriend at the hotel pool for the entire day as a kid and then never hear from ever again”. Another meme read, “he def left school early for a dentist appointment and came back with McDonald’s for lunch”. Gisondo has been a good sport about the memes and is using the 2015 red carpet photo as his Instagram profile picture. “As an actor, the dream is to make stuff that means something to people, that they care about and that resonates. To see that reflected in this way, whether it’s in memes or just in any kind of positive sentiment, it’s so sweet and fulfilling,” Gisondo said about the memes in a recent interview with Variety.

title: Hong Kong police smash alleged Thai prostitution ring, seize HK$13 million cash
description: Seven men, aged between 44 and 54, arrested for suspected human trafficking and money laundering, force says.
content: Hong Kong police have dismantled a local syndicate allegedly running a vice ring involving Thai women, seizing HK$13 million in cash (US$1.66 million) and freezing HK$5 million in suspected crime proceeds. The force said on Saturday that it arrested five local men and two foreign men, aged between 44 and 54, for allegedly running a prostitution ring in the Tsim Sha Tsui district by luring Southeast Asian women to work as sex workers in Hong Kong. Four core members, including three brothers and one Thai national, were arrested on suspicion of human trafficking, living off the earnings of prostitution of others, causing prostitution and money laundering. Nine sex workers from Thailand, aged between 19 and 33, were also arrested on Friday during an undercover operation for allegedly breaching their conditions of stay. Superintendent Gar Kam-lam of the crime unit at West Kowloon headquarters said the syndicate members in Thailand would entice women to fly to Hong Kong and arrange for them to stay in hotels in Tsim Sha Tsui, covering their flights, meals and accommodation to provide sexual services in exchange for money. “We found that the syndicate operated quite meticulously,” he said. “They also advertised for them online and on Telegram, using photos and videos to attract customers.” On Thursday and Friday, officers broke into a flat in a private housing estate in Tuen Mun, which acted as the syndicate’s operations centre, and arrested two core members who were contacting clients and the sex workers via Telegram at the time. During the operation, police seized disposable towels, condoms and HK$13 million in illicit proceeds, including HK$400,000 in cash believed to be the syndicate’s earnings in the past two days. Senior Inspector Yip Yan-wa of the district crime squad team said the four core syndicate members used their personal bank accounts to process the proceeds of their crime and also transferred funds overseas. “We successfully froze four bank accounts operated under individual names by criminal syndicates, totalling over HK$5 million, successfully preventing the transfer of these proceeds.” Officers also seized two computers from the syndicate’s operations centre. One computer was operating an online social media platform, advertising and updating the schedules of each sex worker to attract clients. The other computer contained detailed daily client schedules for each sex worker, recording the contact numbers of sex workers and their clients. The case will be mentioned in Kowloon City Court on Monday.

title: China unveils AI-powered robot designed to help farmers breed better strains of wheat
description: The prototype device was designed to use a ‘vast amount of breeder experience’ when assessing crops for their breeding potential.
content: China has unveiled a smart robot prototype designed to assist with wheat breeding in the latest step in its ongoing drive to advance agricultural technology and bolster food security. The robot made its public debut at a recent seminar on wheat breeding, state-run China Science Daily reported on Friday. Traditional wheat breeders rely on a wealth of accumulated experience to identify and select strains with superior traits from tens of thousands of hybrid offspring. But this requires manual assessment in the field – a process that is both labour intensive and subjective. The robots are designed to reduce this workload using an advanced navigation system, high-definition cameras and vision algorithms. Crucially, the robot is not merely a passive scanner. According to the research team, it has been trained to exercise autonomous judgment similar to that of a human breeder. The seminar heard that in trials the smart machine – measuring over 2 metres (6.5 feet) in length, width and height – had successfully halted in front of the crop it was inspecting. It then used its robotic arm to envelop a single wheat ear, allowing eight micro-cameras to capture detailed images from multiple angles. Moments later, a full suite of quantitative data, including grain count and ear length, was generated. Wang Hongwei, a scientist at Shandong Agricultural University’s state key laboratory of wheat breeding and co-leader of the project, told the newspaper that a defining feature of the robot was the integration of “a vast amount of breeder experience” into its training model. To achieve this, the research team planted 2,000 diverse wheat genetic materials in a range of different environments. Each plant was photographed individually and breeding specialists were then brought in to score and assess the images. The results were then fed into the system and translated into machine-readable data. This information was then used to build an intelligent decision-making model for the robot, which carried out rapid, large-scale screening as well as the evaluation and marking of crops that could be used for future breeding. This model and its advanced imaging system were first used to carry out the preliminary screening of individual plants in the field, identifying candidates worthy of further investigation. Then it sprayed paint on the target plants to be inspected by a human. The research team has reached a preliminary agreement with Shandong Jizhi Biotech, a firm specialising in gene technology and intelligent breeding applications, to develop a commercialised AI wheat-breeding robot, the report said. Earlier this year, the central government unveiled a blueprint for overhauling China’s vast agricultural sector over the next five years using cutting-edge technology. The State Council, China’s cabinet, pledged to significantly strengthen research and development within the sector and set targets for increasing the contribution of technological advances to farm output. The document called for the wider adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in agriculture, outlining plans to use the technology for crop breeding, detecting pests and diseases, and forecasting crop yields.

title: Chinese nickel investors brace for headwinds as Indonesia weighs smelter freeze
description: Jakarta's proposed restrictions could reshape the foreign-backed supply chains feeding critical sectors, from stainless steel to electric vehicle batteries.
content: Chinese investors could face significant disruption if Indonesia imposes a moratorium on new nickel smelters to curb global overproduction and protect local industries across its vast minerals sector, analysts said. Indonesia was weighing a halt to the construction of smelters that produce semi-finished nickel products amid a global supply glut that had driven down commodity prices, state news agency Antara reported, citing energy and mineral resources minister Bahlil Lahadalia. Semi-finished products, including nickel pig iron and nickel matte, make up about 50 to 60 per cent of Indonesia’s total output, Antara reported. The proposed restrictions were part of the energy minister’s efforts to strengthen the country’s industrial structure, it added. Nickel pig iron is primarily used to make stainless steel, while nickel matte is used in electric vehicle batteries. Chinese investment accounts for about 75 per cent of Indonesia’s nickel refining industry, according to an estimate by the US-based Centre for Advanced Defense Studies. . “Chinese investors are likely to be significantly affected because Chinese companies and capital play a major role in Indonesia’s nickel mining and smelting industries,” said Nukila Evanty, an Indonesia-based member of the Asia Centre research institute’s advisory board. “Chinese investors should reconsider and selectively scale back new smelting capacity, particularly projects producing intermediate nickel products in an already oversupplied market.” Indonesia held more than half of the global nickel market in 2023, according to a study by Rafi Adis Subarna, an analyst with Jakarta-based political risk consultancy KRA Group. Jakarta’s six-year-old ban on raw nickel ore exports had spurred the expansion of domestic mining and production, he argued in the study, citing strong global demand for products such as electric vehicle batteries and an influx of investment in smelting facilities. Chinese investment had “supported” Indonesia’s expansion of nickel processing capacity over the years, Goldman Sachs said in a February commentary. But that growth had contributed to an oversupply, weighing on prices since 2023, it added. If a moratorium takes effect, Chinese-invested companies planning conventional smelting capacity expansions could face delays or be forced to cancel projects, particularly where profit margins were already narrow, said Siwage Dharma Negara, a principal fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Jakarta’s “regulatory uncertainty” posed a bigger concern, he added. “If the government frequently changes investment conditions, investors may postpone their expansion or eventually pull back from the country.” Indonesia should evaluate whether it had the domestic capabilities, technology and equipment to operate its own nickel smelters under a moratorium, said Zhao Xijun, a finance professor at Renmin University in China. Chinese enterprises had the necessary expertise and would invest in other countries, from Africa to Latin America, if Indonesia made it difficult, he said. “Then the loss is Indonesia’s,” he added. “The mines would still be there with no one to develop them.” Evanty from the Asia Centre advisory board said Chinese investors should prioritise improving existing facilities and diversifying into higher-value products, all with “stronger” environmental standards. The Indonesian energy and mineral resources minister’s team was preparing a recommendation for President Prabowo Subianto to decide which segments of the semi-finished nickel smelting sector would be restricted, Antara said.

title: Guangdong yachts to sail into Hong Kong from Friday under southbound scheme
description: The scheme will allow Guangdong yachts to berth at designated Hong Kong locations, with about 300 mainland yacht masters already qualified to navigate local waters.
content: Guangdong-registered yachts will be allowed to sail into Hong Kong waters from next Friday under a new travel scheme, the city’s transport minister has confirmed. Writing in her weekly blog on Saturday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said the maiden voyage ceremony for the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme would be held on launch day. “Building on the groundwork laid by the Northbound Yacht Travel Scheme, the maiden voyage ceremony for the Southbound Yacht Travel Scheme marks a two-way journey of maritime connectivity,” she said. Chan made the announcement after the Marine Department and the Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration signed work arrangements last month to establish a framework for cross-boundary yacht travel between the two places. The move is in line with the government’s goal of developing Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as set out in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest policy address, both unveiled last month. Beijing approved the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Individual Yacht Scheme in June, allowing Hong Kong yacht owners to sail to designated ports under a broader strategy to develop the “yacht economy” in the Greater Bay Area. Authorities have also introduced arrangements covering the certification, training and examination of mainland Chinese yacht masters seeking to navigate Hong Kong waters. Chan previously said about 300 mainland yacht masters had obtained the required qualifications. Under the southbound scheme, mainland vessels will berth in designated areas monitored through a dynamic, real-time system that allows authorities to manage berth traffic. Meanwhile, ahead of the eighth anniversary of the opening of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge, Chan said traffic on the mega bridge had continued to rise, particularly during the National Day “golden week” holiday. She said passenger flow through the bridge exceeded 670,000 between October 1 and 7, while two-way vehicular traffic reached more than 170,000 trips. Chan also said the booking requirement for Northbound Travel for Hong Kong Vehicles – which allows Hong Kong cars to drive to Guangdong – had been removed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays since September last year. “The government is in discussions with the Guangdong provincial government to extend the booking-free arrangement to other non-peak weekdays,” she said.

title: Opinion | Better protection needed as violent cryptocurrency robberies surge
description: A mature financial ecosystem must give cryptocurrency investors and their families credible ways to remain safe.
content: Cryptocurrency’s promise of financial freedom carries a cost the industry must confront: growing wealth can make its owners more attractive targets for violent criminals. Protecting digital assets while treating the physical safety of their holders as a personal matter is an inadequate approach to financial security. The industry must take responsibility for designing products and services which account for the reality that people can be threatened into surrendering their assets. The rise in “wrench attacks” – physical violence or threats used to force someone to surrender cryptocurrency – exposes this vulnerability. A wallet may resist sophisticated hacking while its owner remains vulnerable to coercion. When one person can immediately authorise the transfer of substantial wealth, that person and their family can become targets of criminal coercion. Violent criminals extracted over US$30 million from cryptocurrency holders in the first half of the year. If that pace continues, annual losses could exceed last year’s US$58 million. The industry has reason to expand its definition of investor protection beyond the risks of price volatility, account theft and platform failure. Worldwide, 46 incidents were documented through to late June – physical coercion is a serious financial security risk. A portfolio may multiply in value while its owner’s security arrangements remain unchanged. Research has identified a correlation between bitcoin prices and reported physical attacks, but correlation alone cannot establish how much of the increase is attributable to price movements, adoption, information exposure or improved reporting. And the threat can outlast a rally. Once someone becomes known – or is simply believed – to possess substantial cryptocurrency wealth, that reputation may persist. Last December, masked intruders attacked a cryptocurrency investor at his home in Solihull, England, and threatened his pregnant wife. He transferred cryptocurrency worth hundreds of thousands of pounds during the 45-minute ordeal. In March, Hong Kong police received a report that a man had been assaulted in a Hung Hom hotel and robbed of cryptocurrency worth about HK$5.3 million (US$675,342). Silver worth a further HK$800,000 was also reportedly taken. These cases reveal an uncomfortable limitation of digital security. A transaction system can check whether the required cryptographic authorisation has been supplied. That does not establish whether the person supplying it is acting freely. A holder threatened with violence may complete every required security step while acting entirely against their wishes. Self-custody makes this problem especially important because it can place extensive financial authority in one person’s hands. That authority has genuine benefits: direct ownership, portability and reduced dependence on an intermediary. It also changes who must manage the consequences of coercion. Conventional finance faces coercion too. Bank customers can be threatened and institutional controls can fail. But withdrawal limits, independent approvals, delays and checks for unusual activity can create opportunities for intervention. These arrangements impose costs on legitimate users, yet their protective value deserves recognition when financial products are evaluated primarily for speed and convenience. Advice to avoid publicising wealth can be useful, but it cannot substitute for institutional responsibility. People can be exposed through records they were required to provide or through information they never intended to disclose. Responsibility for violence remains with the perpetrators. The industry’s response should therefore address both custody design and the services surrounding it. Multiple independent approvals can reduce reliance on a single key or device. Delayed withdrawals and transaction limits may reduce the amount accessible during a short period of coercion. None of these mechanisms guarantees physical safety. They introduce complexity and criminals may continue threatening despite technical restrictions. Blockchain records can help criminal investigations although traceability does not automatically provide the power to freeze or recover assets. Recovery is possible in some cases: after the rescue of kidnapped Ledger co-founder David Balland and his partner, French authorities said almost all the cryptocurrency paid as ransom had been traced, frozen and seized. That outcome depended on investigators, operational intervention and institutional cooperation. It shows how the practical protection of digital ownership continues to depend on public systems. Financial losses capture only part of the harm. An unsuccessful extortion attempt can still leave a person injured, a family displaced or a child traumatised. Even complete recovery of stolen funds cannot restore the sense of safety lost during an attack. As cryptocurrency fortunes grow across market cycles, the industry must recognise that wealth changes its owners’ exposure to crime. Security promises should be tested against what happens when a customer is frightened, isolated or protecting a loved one. A rising valuation can make an investor wealthier. A mature financial ecosystem must also give that investor – and the people around them – credible ways to remain safe.

title: Disney+ K-drama Between Steps: Kim So-hyun, Choo Young-woo in Ahn Pan-seok’s final romance
description: Kim So-hyun and Choo Young-woo star as a fashion major and a robotics PhD student in this slow-burn romance from the late Ahn Pan-seok.
content: Lead cast: Kim So-hyun, Choo Young-woo Latest Nielsen rating: 2.36 per cent Kim So-hyun (My Lovely Liar) and Choo Young-woo (The Tale of Lady Ok) share the screen in this university-set slice-of-life drama, which teases a slow-burn romance between two frustrated young adults trying to find their place in a society that does not always play by the rules. Between Steps is notably the final drama from veteran director Ahn Pan-seok, whose credits include the romance Something in the Rain and the jaunty corporate thriller The Art of Negotiation. The Korean drama industry was left reeling this summer when Ahn died suddenly of a brain haemorrhage at the age of 64. In Between Steps, Kim plays Lim Yu-jin, a driven fashion major whose celebrated professor recognises her talent and takes her under her wing to fast-track her career in academia. However, Yu-jin’s life falls apart after she defends a friend from a drunk senior attempting to force himself on her. Rather than support her students, Yu-jin’s professor chooses to cover up the incident. When Yu-jin refuses to apologise to the senior for involving the police, the professor expels her from the department. Meanwhile, Park Min-jae (Choo) is pursuing a PhD in the university’s engineering department, where he works in a robotics lab. Min-jae was once a promising competitive swimmer but a rare form of cancer resulted in the loss of one of his legs. Although the illness has since gone into remission, his bitterness over the future that was robbed from him remains. Yu-jin and Min-jae’s lives intersect in several ways early in Between Steps. Their first encounter is innocuous, with the pair unknowingly falling asleep on each other’s shoulders on the subway. Things escalate, however, when Min-jae comes to Yu-jin and her friend’s aid following their late-night altercation with the senior. Min-jae takes them to a police station but refuses to tell the officers that he witnessed the incident – because he arrived afterwards. The headstrong Yu-jin quickly sours on him. Despite this early bump in the road, Min-jae and Yu-jin are destined to cross paths again. In need of a new major, Yu-jin applies to the university’s robotics lab, which is recruiting a new member, unaware that Min-jae is a part of the team. Yu-jin’s fashion background does not make her a natural fit for the lab, but it intrigues those reviewing her application. She ultimately beats out another, more obvious candidate and joins Min-jae and his three male colleagues. All three take an immediate interest in her after Min-jae insists there is nothing going on between them. Exploring the gradual romance that blossoms between two people whose life experiences have made them cautious, if not outright mistrustful, of others, Between Steps is especially reminiscent of Ahn’s 2024 series The Midnight Romance in Hagwon. Compared with the glossy, almost fantastical romances that tend to dominate K-drama schedules, Ahn’s series usually feature muted, recognisable colour palettes and focus on earthier, cagier characters struggling to balance responsibility, desire and necessity in a society where honesty and ability are not always rewarded. As a result, Between Steps stands out from many of its peers. However, as one of the more dour entries in the K-drama romance genre, it may not be to everyone’s taste – particularly those seeking a guilt-free escape from their own stressful lives. On the other hand, those who appreciate shows that refuse to sugarcoat human relationships may find it refreshing. That said, Between Steps is not as smooth a ride as The Midnight Romance in Hagwon. At times, the series struggles to balance its two competing impulses – sincere drama and crowd-pleasing asides. The dramatic beats largely feel natural, while the comic interludes don’t always land the same way. Between Steps was written by Min Hyo-jung, known for classic dramas such as Full House and Cats on the Roof, and marks her first K-drama writing credit in 21 years. Min began her career with Ahn, who directed her debut script, Speak with Your Eyes, in 2000. Years after she stopped writing, Ahn sought her out once more, leading to her return to the screen. Playing prickly characters who bristle at life’s disappointments, Kim and Choo take some time to warm to. Choo, coming off a banner 2025 that saw him break out in four roles, including The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call, imbues Min-jae with a naturalistic air. Kim does not feel quite as comfortable in her role, although there is plenty of time for that to change. Between Steps is streaming on Disney+.

title: China hails ‘constructive’ trade talks with EU as both sides seek ties in AI, new energy
description: The two sides have ‘huge cooperation potential’ in new energy, AI and green low-carbon fields, China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Saturday.
content: Chinese and European Union representatives agreed to explore cooperation in areas including new energy and artificial intelligence during their just concluded trade talks, which Beijing described as “equal, professional and constructive”. The two economies “have huge cooperation potential in new energy, AI, services trade, the digital economy and green low-carbon fields”, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in an interpretation released on Saturday, following the second round of China-EU trade talks in Beijing on Thursday and Friday. Both sides reaffirmed their positioning as key trading partners and agreed to handle economic and trade differences within the WTO framework, promoting “balanced and forward-looking” trade ties, the ministry said. “Both parties believe the [trade consultation] mechanism is operating smoothly and efficiently. The successful convening of the second regular meeting marks a new starting point, not an end point,” it said. They held “in-depth” discussions on electric and hybrid vehicle trade and “prevented the situation from escalating”, with the EU set to advance its minimum import price mechanism and review procedures in the EV anti-subsidy case, it said. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters on Friday that Beijing had promised to cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “several million cars” over a four-year period. The two sides were ready to discuss market access issues in areas such as medical devices and agricultural products, and would continue talks on the regulation of cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, the commerce ministry said. Discussions on EU-backed financing for renewable energy projects using inverters from “high-risk” suppliers – which Brussels said did not target any particular country – would also continue. Both parties “explored the possibility” of introducing mutual facilitation measures for the compliant trade of dual-use items between China and the EU, according to Saturday’s readout. They agreed to strengthen policy communication, keep global supply chains stable, and support the “substantive launch” of a process for the “mutual delisting” of sanctioned firms under their respective legal frameworks. This week’s meetings in Beijing unfolded against a backdrop of mounting trade tensions over the EU’s record deficit with China, the EV anti-subsidy case, EU foreign-subsidy probes, China’s rare earth export controls, and mutual market-access and procurement barriers.

title: How DNA ‘fingerprinting’ is keeping Malaysia’s green turtles safe from poachers
description: Decades of conservation have helped Malaysia’s green turtles recover, but tight budgets, fuel costs and poachers threaten progress.
content: As dawn breaks on Mataking Island off Sabah’s east coast, a tiny green turtle crawls across the sand, driven by instinct towards the surf before disappearing into the ocean on a journey that could cover thousands of kilometres. Where it goes is impossible to know, but with a huge dose of luck on its epic travels, it may return to the same Malaysian beach decades later to lay eggs of its own. The hatchling is one of tens of thousands that emerge from Sabah’s beaches each year, as the species continues a remarkable recovery after decades of conservation efforts to reverse its decline. Today, Mataking Island – a teardrop-shaped outcrop in the Celebes Sea – is a luxury diving retreat. At low tide, a sandbar dubbed “Moses Crossing” connects its smaller islets, where visitors are greeted by green turtles of all sizes grazing on seagrass among the reefs. Green turtles have staged a miraculous comeback in recent years. In 2025, they were reclassified from ‘endangered’ to ‘least concern’ – becoming the first marine turtle species to move out of the threat categories on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, which tracks the global extinction risk and conservation status of animals, plants and fungi. Science has played a vital role in protecting these shelled aquatic reptiles. When they hatch, they are just a few inches long and weigh about as much as a single battery – yet as adults, they grow up to 1.2 metres (4ft) in length and weigh a hefty 200kg (440lbs). Now, tiny tissue samples are giving conservationists something close to a genetic address. By allowing scientists to trace where turtles originate, the technique is an important tool in combating wildlife trafficking, as turtles continue to be targeted by poachers for their meat and eggs, which are sought after as exotic delicacies in parts of Vietnam and China. “Turtles don’t stay in one place. They cross borders,” marine biologist Juanita Joseph told This Week in Asia, explaining the need for a system to “fingerprint” the reptiles. Joseph is working at the University of Malaysia Sabah to help build ShellBank, a global DNA database of marine turtle populations. Every two to four years, mature females return to the exact beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. But in between, they cross vast stretches of ocean to reach feeding grounds far beyond Malaysia’s borders. In Sabah’s Turtle Islands Park, conservation efforts date back decades, with more than 20,000 nests recorded annually. Since 1977, Sabah Parks said more than 14 million hatchlings had been released from these islands. It is a recovery that stands out against a bleaker global backdrop for wildlife. The WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026, published on Thursday, identified a 73 per cent decline in monitored vertebrate wildlife populations between 1970 and 2022. Daudi Sumba, chief conservation officer at WWF International, said concerted action is crucial to sustaining these gains, pointing to the green turtle as a rare bright spot. “If those efforts stop, we can lose recovery,” Sumba said. “Positive tipping points and self-reinforcing feedback loops can help keep recovery on track and sustain it over the long term.” But major challenges remain to ensure green turtles stay a conservation success story, Sabah Parks director Maklarin Lakim told This Week in Asia. “These are marine parks and there are no boundaries that we can physically fence off,” he said. “We do not have many staff [and] the assets we have, such as boats, are also limited … costs are high, especially with the price of fuel now.” Given these constraints, Sabah Parks’ marine protectors are not overly celebrating the green turtle’s improved status on the Red List, pointing to concerns over the much rarer hawksbill turtle. “Even though we are happy about one species, for another species we are worried,” Maklarin said. Lifelong protection For marine biologists, building a complete picture of the population and habits of a creature on the move for most of its life is a constant challenge. “If you want to save turtles, it’s not just one particular component at the beach. It’s the whole sea turtle life cycle,” said Gavin Jolis, marine species strategy manager at WWF-Malaysia. Major green turtle populations in the region span Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Thailand. A turtle nesting in Sabah may travel to feeding grounds near the Philippines or Indonesia, exposing it to threats beyond the reach of Malaysian conservation authorities. The ShellBank database aims to track the health of nesting populations, their migration paths and how they navigate lives at sea that can span several decades. Similarly, DNA collected from turtles at feeding grounds, from carcasses or taken from trafficked products can be matched back to their population of origin. Joseph said her team began collecting genetic samples from Malaysian nesting beaches in 1998 and from feeding grounds in 2011, with those samples now contributing to ShellBank. But the database remains a work in progress as researchers gather enough samples across nesting populations to fully map the region. Unlike satellite tracking, which follows individual animals and can be costly, genetic profiling enables researchers to map connections across entire populations. Samples from turtle meat, shells or other products seized across the region can reveal whether they originated from populations in Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines or further afield. “ShellBank is a tool. It’s only one of the tools that’s gonna help us with [the] conservation of turtles,” Joseph said. As the sun peeks over the horizon on Mataking, a bale of turtle hatchlings scrambles across the sand, tiny flippers carrying them towards an ocean they will explore for decades to come. The surviving females will eventually rely on their internal navigation systems to return to these same shores to lay the next generation of eggs – sustaining a cycle that conservationists have spent decades fighting to protect. “‘Least Concern’ does not mean ‘no concern’,” Jolis said of the IUCN reclassification. “What it does show is that long-term conservation action is working.”

title: Can China’s dancing robots swing some new business partners in Africa?
description: Performances are about marketing China as a technology partner, analysts say, but it is not clear if they will translate into factory deals.
content: At events marking China’s National Day in Africa on October 1, robots provided the entertainment. In Luanda, Angola, dancing robots amused guests and ambassador Zhang Bin called the industry “a small snapshot of the Chinese economy’s move towards innovation and higher-quality development”. In Brazzaville, Congo, nearly 400 guests – including Congolese officials and Chinese business representatives – watched on as a robot dog performed. Guests also interacted with a robot dog at a Chinese New Year reception in Johannesburg, South Africa in February. Such displays at diplomatic and commercial events across Africa are symbolic of China’s push to become a technology partner in the region, according to analysts. But they said broader adoption of Chinese industrial robotics in African factories would depend on whether the technology could solve worthwhile problems – and whether local technicians could install and maintain it. Bulelani Jili, an assistant professor at Georgetown University in Washington, said that – beyond the spectacle – the robot displays aimed to present China as a provider of advanced technology rather than just a source of extractive investment or low-cost goods. He said they were also “a form of technology diplomacy” that put robotics alongside China’s offerings in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and telecoms. Chinese carmaker Chery brought two robots to the July opening of its Rosslyn plant near Pretoria in South Africa. Its humanoid robot Mornine interacted with the presenter of the event, while its robotic dog Argos appeared in an exhibition area. Both belong to Chery’s robotics business, AiMOGA, which says its robots are used in over 50 countries and 100 scenarios. In April, at GITEX Africa – a tech and start-up show held in Marrakech, Morocco – Huawei also had a robot on show, alongside technology for finance, healthcare and government. Georg Stieler, managing director for Asia at Stieler Technology & Market Advisory, said having a robot at such events made China’s pitch as a technology partner “tangible in a way a speech about industrial capabilities does not”. Chinese diplomats have put robots on stage elsewhere, including at a National Day reception in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. That event made headlines with images of humanoid robots dressed in Saudi clothing performing a traditional Ardah sword dance. It is all about image projection, according to Stieler. “The robot on stage is not necessarily the product being sold; what is being marketed is China as a technology partner,” he said. He added that low labour costs weakened the case for buying a robot simply to replace workers in some African markets, while limited local capacity to install and maintain them added to the expense. Stieler expected robotics to follow Chinese manufacturers that were already operating in Africa. He said Chinese companies with plants on the continent were more likely to automate their own lines than win new robotics business through diplomatic performances. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre, said Beijing was trying to capitalise on its success with AI and robotics to present itself as a tech leader for the Global South. He said China was already working with Global South nations on technology such as batteries – giving the example of its investment in Morocco – but that it was not clear how it might partner with African nations on robotics. “The real test will be whether China will invest significantly in R&D and engineering talent development in African nations,” he said. Jili said the robot displays could lead to pilot projects or commercial agreements, but their value to African countries would depend on local skills, the involvement of African firms and researchers, and the ability to maintain and govern the technology. “The salient question is not only whether robots attract attention, but also who owns, maintains, governs and benefits from the technological systems they introduce,” he said.

title: New mechanism to strengthen oversight of renovations after Tai Po fire: minister
description: Home affairs minister says mechanism will encourage rational discussion among owners and stop traders exploiting disputes over major renovations.
content: A three-tier dispute resolution mechanism could help Hong Kong homeowners strengthen oversight of major renovation projects and prevent exploitation by “unscrupulous traders”, according to the home affairs minister. The city’s building management challenges came under the spotlight after the deadly blaze at Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court in November 2025. The estate was undergoing a HK$330 million (US$42.3 million) renovation when the fire broke out, killing 168 people and displacing nearly 5,000 residents. An independent committee investigating the blaze earlier uncovered evidence pointing to suspected bid-rigging and connected bidding companies, among other concerns. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen told a radio programme on Saturday that the proposed mechanism could better handle disputes among property owners and foster a more constructive environment for building management. “When major renovations are required, if owners can engage in rational discussions throughout the process and listen to different opinions … it will undoubtedly strengthen management and oversight,” she said. “If property owners cannot unite and work together rationally to resolve disputes, unscrupulous businessmen could easily take advantage of these loopholes. When they see two parties at odds, they could manipulate one side to gain its support while sidelining the other.” The three-tier mechanism, introduced in last month’s policy address, is among a series of proposed rules designed to plug regulatory gaps exposed by the fire. Under the first tier, district council members would intervene early to help neighbours resolve disputes through negotiation. If the issues remain unresolved, the councillors would refer the parties concerned to professional mediation services provided by the Home Affairs Department. The final tier would be to take the case to court. The mechanism is expected to take effect next year. Mak said authorities had been providing mediation training to district council members, who are expected to play a bigger role by not only making referrals but also actively facilitating communication among the parties across all three tiers. Other proposals include requiring a technical briefing before owners vote so that homeowners can ask questions, prohibiting the rescheduling of owners’ meetings without a valid reason and requiring more parties to declare their interests. All would require amendments to the Building Management Ordinance. A public consultation on the proposals ended last month. On youth development, Mak dismissed concerns over the rising youth unemployment rate, saying the problem was not unique to Hong Kong. “Youth unemployment above the overall rate did not just happen in Hong Kong, but also in many parts of the world,” she said. Government statistics show the unemployment rate among people aged 20 to 29 rose to 9.1 per cent between June and August, well above the overall rate of 3.8 per cent. “What we need to do is not just create more jobs to counter unemployment, but equip our young people with the skills they need to meet those challenges through different measures,” she said. For example, the authorities had worked with the Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport to provide 200 three-month technology internship places, she said. Mak said many companies were satisfied with the interns’ performance and had offered them full-time positions. “Many young people said they did not expect to enter the industry before the internship programme … we will expand the quota, hoping more tech start-ups can provide such opportunities for our youth,” she said.

title: A fortune, a HK$72m flat and a family feud: inside the Abby Choi murder trial
description: Court hears claims that financial dependence and threats over a flat sale drove the killing, while the defence disputes the family’s reliance on the Hong Kong socialite.
content: A bitter family dispute over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat allegedly led a retired police officer and his two sons to murder socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung three years ago, a Hong Kong court has heard. The trial over the 28-year-old model’s killing, which shocked Hong Kong and attracted international attention, started after a one-week delay caused by unresolved preliminary issues and jury selection. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, told the High Court how her relationship with her daughter’s former in-laws deteriorated, accusing them of clinging to her family’s fortune and having “bitten the hand that fed them”. Giving evidence for the prosecution, Cheung became emotional at times as she accused Choi’s former in-laws of living in luxury without contributing to the upbringing of the two children her daughter had with her ex-husband. She wept in the witness box while watching footage of her daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat on February 21, 2023, the day she was last seen alive. “My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her kindness to the wrong people. This family really bit the hand that fed them.” Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial after pleading not guilty to murdering her. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial. The killing came to light after some of Choi’s dismembered remains were discovered in a 600 square foot flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village on February 24, 2023. Inside, police found a hammer – the alleged murder weapon – a meat mincer, two cooking pots containing Choi’s remains, and multiple saws and knives. The prosecution alleges that the killing stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his sons to help kill her so he could keep it. Prosecutors have described the alleged murder as a carefully crafted plot in which each defendant played a role. It allegedly involved renting the village flat, driving Choi to the remote location on the pretext of collecting her daughter from school, and striking her with a hammer during the journey. Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC suggested that money was the motive and highlighted the significant wealth gap between the two families. Choi’s stepfather, Choi Cho-san, was described as a wealthy businessman who provided a monthly allowance of more than HK$1 million to support his wife, Cheung, Choi and the model’s two stepsisters in Hong Kong. The court heard that Choi received a HK$41 million flat as a wedding gift from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, who also came from a wealthy family, although the couple never formally registered their marriage. She was also said to have received more than HK$300 million from the Tam family over the years. The Kwong family, according to the prosecution, was far less affluent. Kwong Kau’s wife, Jenny Li Sui-heung, and their two sons were said to be unemployed, while he relied on an annual pension of HK$145,000 after retiring from the police force in 2006. The court also heard that Kwong Kau had worked as a taxi driver, although his lawyer disputed this. Cheung testified that her daughter had registered the Kadooria flat in Kwong Kau’s name to avoid HK$9 million in double stamp duty, with the understanding that he would hold it on trust for the two children she had with Alex Kwong. But when Choi indicated in June 2022 that she wanted to sell the flat and move the children closer to their school in Tuen Mun, Kwong Kau allegedly attacked her and threatened to kill her and her entire family if she went ahead. In a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, Choi complained that her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years. She also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in her former father-in-law’s name. Cheung said she and her daughter had supported the Kwong family for years but received nothing in return. She told the court that Alex Kwong had obtained more than HK$70 million from his ex-wife after saying he would invest the money in luxury watches. He also persuaded Choi to lend him her credit card to pay his living expenses in mainland China while he was evading justice over his involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case, Cheung said. Anthony Kwong received HK$2 million from Choi to run an egg waffle shop in Sham Shui Po, according to Cheung. He became Choi’s stand-in chauffeur in early 2023 after he and his mother repeatedly urged her to give him a job, the witness added. The court also heard that Choi gave Kwong Kau a monthly allowance of HK$20,000 and paid more than HK$200,000 towards his medical expenses when he was seriously ill. During cross-examination, defence lawyers challenged Cheung’s account of their clients’ financial dependence on Choi. Anthony Kwong’s lawyer, Trevor Beel, said his client had never received substantial financial support from Choi. He said the egg waffle shop had been set up at her request because her two children loved the snack. Oliver Davies, representing Kwong Kau, described his client as a businessman with considerable savings who had contributed half of the Kadooria flat’s HK$60 million purchase price in 2019. He challenged Cheung’s account of her husband’s wealth, arguing that Choi Cho-san was “constantly in debt” and could not have afforded to give her HK$1 million a month. Davies also pointed to the limited assets Choi left behind, suggesting that she was not particularly wealthy either. Cheung will face further cross-examination by Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, when the trial resumes on Monday.

title: Trump casts doubt on Pentagon plan to live stream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
description: Bipartisan outrage and UN condemnation have followed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to stream Nidal Hasan’s death sentence.
content: US President Donald Trump cast doubt on Friday on whether authorities will live-stream the firing squad execution of the perpetrator of a deadly attack on American soldiers, a plan that has drawn broad and bipartisan condemnation. Nidal Hasan’s execution – scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 – is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945. A Pentagon official said on Thursday that the execution would be streamed live, after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said “we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public”. But Trump, who supports the death penalty in this case, left uncertain whether the execution would be publicly broadcast. “They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump said. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes.” Earlier on Friday, Vice-President J.D. Vance told journalists who asked about the planned live stream that he did not “know that that’s actually going to happen”. “This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Vance said, but added that if the execution was broadcast live, “I’m not going to be watching it”. Representative Austin Scott of Trump’s Republican Party said he supported executing Hasan but “live streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that”. Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice” but that public executions were “the kind of thing Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?” Technology firms YouTube, Meta Platforms and X did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether they would allow the execution to be streamed on their platforms. TikTok directed questions to its policy banning depictions of “graphic incidents and violence” including “the shooting of an individual”. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the plan, saying in a message on Friday that “the live streaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture”. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”. Hegseth said it would be the military’s first firing squad execution since World War II. “People need to understand that … there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said in a video shared on Thursday on official Pentagon social media accounts. The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder. The Death Penalty Information Centre says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916. According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran. Amnesty’s Justin Mazzola said on Friday that the death penalty was “a violation of human rights”, and that streaming Hasan’s execution “would only compound the cruelty”. Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralysed from the waist down. Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013. Court-appointed defence lawyers expressed concern that he was seeking execution. The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaqi, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

title: Hong Kong to expand community recycling after shelving waste-charging scheme
description: Environment chief Tse Chin-wan also pledges review of permitted profit levels of city’s two power companies.
content: Hong Kong will strengthen its community recycling network with measures such as round-the-clock automated collection points after scrapping its waste-charging scheme due to strong public opposition, the environmental chief has said. Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan on Saturday also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when their control agreements with the government expire in 2033. He added that the government would boost clean energy imports from mainland China. Tse expressed confidence that Hong Kong would achieve the four binding goals on environmental protection outlined in the city’s first five-year plan, unveiled last month. Under the plan, the government set out goals to reduce carbon intensity, increase the share of zero-carbon energy used to generate power, and improve air and surface water quality. The government shelved the twice-delayed waste-charging scheme in 2024 even though it had previously said the direction was among the key methods for Hong Kong to attain carbon neutrality as garbage was the city’s third most significant source of emissions. Tse said the government would instead step up the city’s recycling efforts. “We’ve been talking about waste reduction through refuse collection or reduction for decades,” he told a radio programme. “We once considered imposing municipal waste charging but due to public opposition and backlash, we will strengthen the Green@Community initiative instead.” Green@Community is a citywide community network covering all 18 districts to promote recycling. Together with smart recycling bins, the community recycling network has more than 800 public collection points. Tse said with the expansion of Green@Community coverage, Hong Kong’s waste volume had decreased by about 1,000 tonnes over the past three to four years. “We plan to introduce automation to the Green@Community facilities, allowing recycling stations to operate 24 hours a day, which will provide more convenience for the public. There will be greater public participation,” he said. He added that the Green@Community mobile application currently had 1.2 million registered users. “By turning waste into energy, we’re confident of achieving the zero landfill target,” he said. Tse also pledged to review the permitted profit levels of the city’s two power companies when their control agreements with the government expire in 2033, and to increase imports of clean energy from the mainland. “We also aim to increase the proportion of zero-carbon electricity imported into Hong Kong from the mainland to 60 to 70 per cent, which is believed to help lower local electricity tariffs at that time.
