We’re now in discussion with some mainland units,” he said. He said authorities had asked for the transmission capacity of the Daya Bay cable to be increased. The government would also apply for funding from the Legislative Council to construct a large-scale power reception station on reclaimed land in Tseung Kwan O Area 132, as well as build new transmission cables from the mainland to import large amounts of zero-carbon energy into Hong Kong. “We’ll set up a working group. The government will conduct a cautious and comprehensive review, including each of the roles, the project details and financial arrangements, etc,” he said.

title: How to zoom through new Huanggang Port crossing at Hong Kong’s border
description: Here is your guide to registration, clearance and transport at revamped crossing opening on Monday, promising five-minute processing times.
content: The Huanggang Port will open on Monday after more than six years of redevelopment and rounds of preparatory drills. The 24/7 checkpoint will be the first to adopt the “joint clearance” model, where passengers can complete both departure and entry clearance in a single three-gated automated channel. As the final checks are carried out, the South China Morning Post explains what you need to navigate the new checkpoint. 1. Do I need to register for ‘joint clearance’? Yes, Hong Kong and mainland Chinese residents will have to register with immigration authorities on both sides of the border to use the facilities. Hong Kong residents can register in several ways: City residents must also ensure they have already registered with mainland authorities to use e-channels before they can use the “joint clearance” automated channel. They will need to travel to the mainland via any other land checkpoint to complete registration there first, or they may also register at the existing Huanggang checkpoint before it closes at 6.30am on Monday, when the new building opens. Children under seven cannot use the automated channels and must be accompanied by their parents at staffed counters to complete clearance. Those aged seven to 17 can use the “joint clearance” channels once their parents have registered them. Other Hong Kong residents who cannot use the joint clearance channels can still complete clearance via staffed counters. Mainland residents can complete Hong Kong registration at the enrolment office on the fifth floor or at the gates of the “joint clearance” channels. 2. How do I get to the checkpoint? Travellers in Hong Kong heading to and from the revamped Huanggang Port can only use authorised public transport services – buses, green minibuses or taxis – to reach a public transport interchange on level two. Both urban and New Territories taxis can drop off passengers from the public transport interchange inside the checkpoint building. Passengers using cross-boundary coach services, encompassing routes departing from Mong Kok, Yau Tsim area, Kwun Tong, Wan Chai and Tsuen Wan, can also use the revamped facility. Passengers must alight for immigration clearance. 3. Where do I go for clearance? After alighting from public transport and cross-boundary coaches, passengers enter the building on level two. Travellers will need to take escalators to reach the departure hall on level five to complete immigration clearance. Passengers using cross-boundary private cars will have to alight and proceed to a separate clearance hall at level one (M) near the car clearance lane to enter Shenzhen. 4. What is the clearance procedure? The crossing is the first to adopt the “joint clearance” model, where passengers need only present one identity document required by their destination to complete both departure and entry. The process will be handled by 134 e-channel machines each equipped with three gates, rather than the usual two. Travellers can also use 68 staffed counters. Authorities have said the “joint clearance” model will cut the previous clearance time from 30 minutes to five. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung announced in August that residents who hold valid home return permits can use either the document or their Hong Kong identity cards for “joint clearance”. However, residents were urged to carry both when using the revamped crossing. 5. What about drivers? Private car drivers eligible to travel between the city and Guangdong province can use the “joint one-stop” vehicle lane on level one of the building. Departing drivers must first pass through a customs kiosk, where ad hoc inspections will be carried out. They will then arrive at an “integrated information collection device”, which will collect identity and biometric information for five departments of Hong Kong and Shenzhen authorities to confirm clearance. Those using the vehicle clearance lane for the first time will need to give permission for information collection after placing their identity documents in the device, but no advance registration is required. Drivers need only present their identity documents once to the device to obtain clearance from Hong Kong’s Customs and Excise Department, Immigration Department and Department of Health, as well as Shenzhen’s immigration and customs authorities. With clearance obtained, drivers can drive through to Shenzhen. They can pick up their passengers at a private car pickup zone on the mainland side of level one. A Hong Kong government spokesman earlier said drivers currently authorised to drive between Guangdong and the city under an existing quota scheme with closed road permits for Heung Yuen Wai, Shenzhen Bay or Sha Tau Kok checkpoints could not directly use the revamped crossing. Drivers with permits for the three above-mentioned checkpoints can only drive through the Lok Ma Chau control point or revamped Huanggang Port from midnight to 6.30am daily. Only drivers with a closed road permit for the current Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang control point route can drive through the revamped Huanggang Port at any time. 6. What about public transport in Shenzhen? Travellers can go down to basement levels one to three in the building to take public transport, which includes the metro line seven, taxis and buses. A high-speed intercity railway linking Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Dongguan will be connected to the revamped crossing in the future. Mainland authorities have not yet released an estimated time to finish the Huanggang section of the railway, but tunnelling work began in July. 7. What transport options in Hong Kong? For returning Hongkongers, the arrival hall is located on level four of the building. After arriving in the city, they need to take escalators down to level two to exit the checkpoint via the public transport interchange, where they can line up for buses, minibuses, coaches or urban and New Territories taxis. Only taxis from the city’s five premium fleets are allowed to take bookings from customers inside the building. Travellers can book their rides using the respective apps of the taxi fleets. Other ride-hailing services will not be available inside the boundary control area. A pre-booked fleet taxi waiting area set up inside the port building features a service station and a display panel for arrival information. Those who have pre-booked a fleet taxi should register at the service station by showing the vehicle registration mark to the fleet’s taxi ambassadors. They will deploy the corresponding vehicles waiting in a public transport buffer area to the dedicated pickup area to ensure passengers can board quickly and smoothly. The buffer area is located in the boundary control area, a two-minute drive away from the port, and public buses, minibuses, coaches and taxis must wait there during peak periods to avoid congesting the bridge leading to the new building.

title: Opinion | Truth needs a treaty in this age of AI disinformation
description: When algorithmic lies threaten world peace, international law must step in to protect verified facts and defend reality.
content: Imagine this: one major power launches an operation against another’s ship in a sensitive strategic zone, acting on intelligence that the vessel is carrying sanctioned goods. The operation sparks a major international incident that brings the two powers to the brink of war. Unlikely as this may sound in today’s hi-tech world of sensory awareness, it did almost happen. In mid-September, it was reported that the US military was on the verge of launching an operation against a Chinese ship near Iran, which intelligence suggested was carrying components for a nuclear weapons programme. The intelligence came from the US Special Operations Command Pacific in Hawaii, where an analyst had used an AI chatbot to examine the vessel’s manifest. The system wrongly identified the cargo as nuclear-linked. Filed as an intelligence report, the information set a military operation in motion. According to media reports, US aircraft were already airborne with military personnel preparing to board the Chinese ship when the AI-generated identification was finally found to be false and the operation halted. Whether intentionally or otherwise, the management and manipulation of information has become a major threat to global peace and security. Disinformation is now easier to use in ways that are harder to detect and harder to combat, while the suppression and manipulation of the truth has become an important means of escalating and prolonging conflict. How, then, can truth be protected? The urge to lie and misinform is as natural a human instinct as the urge to be open and honest, perhaps more so. As 20th century political philosopher Hannah Arendt observed: “No one … has ever counted truthfulness as a political virtue.” Yet just as international conventions safeguard access to health, asylum and food, so there is arguably an urgent need to safeguard access to fact-based information, so that people can trust what they see and hear, and judge the veracity of what they are told. Accurate, evidence-based information is an essential ingredient of peace. Advanced technology, artificial intelligence included, has made it easier than ever to distort, to mislead and to entirely fabricate information, with the result fast becoming a weapon for sowing fear and escalating conflict. Disinformation – not only outright falsehoods, but also manipulated partial truths – can now be used to determine the course of real events and, like other weapons of mass destruction, may need to be governed by international convention. It was once possible to combat what we called propaganda using access to independent media. But today’s information operations, employing the tools of pervasive social media, AI and cyber tools, are much harder to defend against. Setting aside the financial and political constraints on contemporary media, it is increasingly governments, even those subject to public scrutiny, that seek to mislead their people and withhold accurate information. For these reasons, defending access to information and ensuring its unimpeded flow in ever more challenging environments becomes a responsibility of the global commons. One approach would be to make it the duty of the United Nations to protect the flow of accurate information as part of its mission to safeguard peace and human security. That could begin with broadening the mandate of the UN’s special envoy for digital and emerging technologies, Under-Secretary-General Amandeep Singh Gill. He has warned that new technology could soon bypass cybersecurity defences, accelerate armed conflict and erode public trust through deepfakes and misinformation. “When we cannot tell the difference between what is true and untrue, what is reality or imaginary, then we lose this shared sense of an understanding of facts,” he said at an ethics and technology conference in May. Gill is spot on, but he needs the authority to lead on ensuring that people have access to accurate information, much as they have rights to health and safety. A first step would be to outline processes that everyone can agree on for labelling deceptive or misleading content, much like media fact-checkers already do. The UN could also raise funds for digital literacy programmes, especially in poorer countries. In a world swamped with disinformation, digital news literacy should be a core component of education. These and other measures could eventually be framed as a General Assembly resolution to codify new standards of information protection. Such standards could build on existing norms of cyber behaviour and extend to the output of AI labs, which are churning out ever more sophisticated models that help to confect convincing fakery. It will not be easy. The usefulness of manipulating the truth makes agreements on information protection hard to imagine. Facts, and the way they are presented, can obviously be viewed subjectively. Whose truth prevails is often contested. Platforms, locally trusted messengers and AI companies would all need to play a part. More visible watermarking of AI-generated content could be helpful, for example. An internationally recognised information protection agency would need a mandate and the means to effectively monitor, provide the resources for training and ensure access to verified truth in any given context. Just like the World Food Programme or the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, it would equip stakeholders with the means to better monitor and protect truth. The UN already has a Department of Global Communications, but its mission is narrowly defined as providing information that supports “the aims and work of the United Nations”. Offering a platform for effective communication is not the challenge the world faces; protecting information and ensuring its veracity is. Some might say the world doesn’t need a new international mechanism. But this cannot be left to civil society alone – it requires the force of international law and convention. If the truth goes unprotected, the future becomes more dangerous: polarisation and disagreement more easily escalate into conflict, and the obstacles to mitigation and mediation will be insurmountable. Michael Vatikiotis is a Senior Adviser at the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue, he previously reported on conflicts across Asia for some 30 years.

title: Gen Z overtakes older collectors as art market spending rebounds globally: report
description: Young wealthy collectors emerge as the top spenders, while mainland China and Hong Kong remain key hubs, report says.
content: Gen Z high-net-worth collectors have overtaken older generations as the art market’s biggest spenders, with average fine art expenditure more than twice that of older collectors, helping drive a global sales rebound to nearly US$60 billion, according to the latest Art Basel and UBS market insights. The surge came as mainland China and Hong Kong continued to play pivotal roles in the global art market’s growth, according to the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026, released earlier this week. Global art sales returned to growth in 2025, rising 4 per cent year on year to an estimated US$59.6 billion and ending two consecutive years of decline. Market activity remained highly concentrated, with the United States, the United Kingdom and China accounting for 76 per cent of global art sales by value. Authored by Clare McAndrew, founder of Arts Economics, the report surveyed high-net-worth collectors across 10 key markets. It found that family remained the primary motivation behind collections, cited by 28 per cent of respondents overall and 40 per cent of Gen Z collectors. “China maintained its position as one of the world’s leading art markets, while Hong Kong continued to play a central role in the Asian art ecosystem, with several high‑value sales and early signs of macroeconomic stabilisation this year,” said Adrian Zuercher, co‑head of global asset allocation and co‑head of global investment management in the Asia-Pacific region at UBS Global Wealth Management CIO. “Against a backdrop of moderating inflation and improving regional fundamentals, these dynamics reinforce Asia-Pacific’s growing importance on the global art market stage.” Driven by auction activity, US art sales reached US$26 billion despite trade uncertainty, while UK sales increased to US$10.5 billion. In China, sales rose to US$8.5 billion, helping stabilise the market despite property-sector headwinds and economic concerns. Beneath that resilience, however, lies a changing wealth landscape. Mainland China’s billionaire population expanded to 539 individuals with a combined wealth of US$2.18 trillion, from 450 billionaires with US$1.88 trillion in wealth previously, according to the report. At the same time, the country’s millionaire population fell to 5.3 million from 6.3 million amid broader economic pressures. Mainland China’s art trade also reflected tighter market conditions. Art imports totalled US$900 million and exports reached US$700 million, representing about 3 per cent of global imports and 2 per cent of global exports. The report also pointed to a broader transformation in collecting behaviour. In the 2024 survey, millennials were the main drivers of market activity, while Gen Z was largely viewed as an emerging and digitally native segment. By 2025, high-net-worth collectors had increased their average allocation to art to 20 per cent, while interest in newly discovered artists reached 66 per cent. By 2026, Gen Z had become the highest-spending demographic among wealthy collectors, having spent more on fine art in 2025 and the first half of 2026 than any other generation surveyed. Digital engagement deepened, artificial intelligence-powered research tools reached mainstream adoption, and buying decisions increasingly focused on rarity and quality. Some Hong Kong industry participants, however, believe regional buying behaviour differs sharply from the global Gen Z trend. “For now, the Asian market still relies heavily on seasoned collectors aged 45 and above, who generally have more experience in art collecting and [greater] financial capacity than Gen Z,” said Heiman Ng, founder of Art Prince Advisory. “Gen Z’s tastes appear to lean more towards luxury goods and trendy collectibles, such as watches, jewellery, handbags and Pokemon cards, rather than rare modern art or antiques, which carry higher knowledge barriers and price points.”

title: Photos: El Nino’s wrath causes extreme weather events worldwide
description: The recent floods and wildfires across the globe are linked to this climate phenomenon and are expected to persist until 2027.
content:
Have you noticed an increase in extreme weather events in recent months? While climate change is a major factor, the recent flooding, storms and wildfires can also be attributed to the El Nino phenomenon.
This warm phase in the Earth’s climate system raises the temperature of the Pacific Ocean and causes significant disruptions worldwide every two to seven years.
Currently, the El Nino event is particularly strong and is expected to continue until 2027.
As climate change continues to warm the planet, we can expect more frequent extreme El Nino events in the future. These photos show just some of its recent devastating effects.

title: Herb to trend: the rising popularity of coriander in Hong Kong cuisine
description: Discover how coriander adds flavour and health benefits to exciting new dishes.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Once considered merely a garnish, coriander is experiencing a surprising rise in popularity. Thanks to viral trends on social media, this unassuming herb is now being used in dishes like ice cream and egg tarts.
Kathy Ng Yiu-fan, a senior nutritionist at Kat-Spirit Nutrition Centre in Hong Kong, noted that this interest stems from locals becoming more health-conscious and eager to experiment with new flavours.
“The herb’s rise reflects a broader shift in Hong Kong’s dynamic food culture towards adventurous, experience-driven dining,” she said.
In Hong Kong, fresh coriander is commonly used alongside spring onions, Chinese celery and garlic chives. Each of these herbs has a distinct flavour and role in recipes. Coriander has a sharp, citrusy and pungent taste. It is often added at the end of cooking, for instance, on steamed fish. Also, it is frequently used in dipping sauces for hotpot.
Ng said: “This helps make greasy or strongly flavoured dishes taste lighter and fresher.”
Spring onions have a light onion flavour that is slightly sweet. They are often combined with garlic and ginger and are commonly used in stir fries and dipping sauces.
Chinese celery has a strong aroma and a spicy, bitter taste. It is tougher and more fragrant than Western celery. Unlike Western celery, it is usually not eaten raw; it is typically stir-fried with meat or cooked in soups.
Garlic chives have a strong flavour and are often cooked on their own.
According to Ng, coriander aids in digestion by helping the stomach process food. It may also help to balance blood sugar levels and protect the heart by lowering blood pressure and reducing bad cholesterol.
Additionally, coriander contains antioxidants that support brain health and protect the skin from sun damage. For optimal nutritional benefits, it’s best to consume the leaves raw or to stir them in just before serving, as high heat can destroy their benefits.
Ng added: “To help your body absorb fat-soluble nutrients like beta-carotene, eat the leaves with healthy fats such as olive oil or avocado.”
Coriander seeds can be crushed and lightly toasted. Drinking them steeped in hot water can also help soothe stomach cramps and support digestion.
But Ng pointed out: “Even though coriander is packed with healthy nutrients and antioxidants, adding a tiny sprinkle of it to a Portuguese egg tart doesn’t make the dessert healthy.”
The butter, white flour and sugar outweigh the herb’s benefits.
“A better option is to make your own coriander-infused breakfast,” Ng said.
“Here is a recipe that is a quick, savoury upgrade to the classic local cafe egg sandwich. It gives you protein to power through your study sessions while the fresh coriander cuts through the richness of the eggs.”
Wash and chop the coriander leaves and stems into small pieces.
In a bowl or mug, whisk together the eggs, light soy sauce and chopped coriander.
Put sesame oil in a small pan on medium heat. Pour in your mixture and gently scramble for 60 to 90 seconds, until it is no longer runny.
Put the warm scrambled eggs between two slices of bread. Cut the sandwich in half and enjoy.

title: Violinist and activist Annabelle Ho uses musical concerts to inspire climate action
description: Through her ClimateXArt project, Ho has reached more than 1,450 people through 25 concerts that mix performances and climate education.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension , with exercises based on the story we’ve written.
As Annabelle Ho Wai-shan’s fingers flew across the neck of her violin, scenes from the Japanese animated feature Spirited Away played behind her. The Studio Ghibli film itself is an attractive draw, but its message is part of what makes this concert so unique.
In the film, a powerful River Spirit is infected with human pollution. The main character pulls out what becomes a heaping pile of gunk-covered waste from the relieved, grateful spirit’s body.
As Ho finished playing, the scene behind her concluded. She took the opportunity to transition into a message about Hong Kong’s own pollution and waste problem, pointing audience members to groups doing environmental work in the city.
Since its inception on Earth Day 2023, Ho has reached more than 1,450 people through concerts that mix musical performance with climate education. The project is aptly named ClimateXArt.
“The way we treat our planet is ultimately how it treats us back,” Ho said. “While our environment is facing severe damage – some of it irreversible – it is never too late to stop further degradation and do everything within our power to restore what we can.”
The 28-year-old works on the project alongside her full-time job, leveraging her music to bring audiences into a conversation about climate change.
“I often think about how to make the next generation really understand [what’s important] … and inspire them to do it themselves, without you pushing them,” Ho said.
Ho has played the violin since she was six, but her climate advocacy journey only began around 2020. After graduating from university, she applied to help with a TEDx programme that explored social issues. There, she was impressed by a teen speaker advocating for ocean protection.
“I thought since she could do it, I could do it too,” Ho said. The experience encouraged the violinist to join climate change awareness projects.
Ho soon began to wonder: why not use music to talk about the environment? She held her first collaborative performance at a cafe in Central. It was the first time she combined Studio Ghibli films, classical music and climate change awareness.
The performance was informal and experimental. Some attendees came because they liked Studio Ghibli films and the music. Others were simply curious.
That mix showed Ho that music could bring people into a conversation about climate change even if it was not the reason they walked through the door: “Music is a really good ‘soft’ approach. It doesn’t force you … It gives everyone room to talk,” she said.
Ho handles everything, from marketing and partnerships to performance design, on her own. Concert tickets are priced to help cover the costs of venue rentals and audience gifts. Music is selected based on what audiences may recognise, such as scores by Joe Hisaishi, the Japanese composer behind many Studio Ghibli films.
At the end of every performance, Ho connects the film scene to environmental issues the audience might encounter in Hong Kong, such as waste reduction and ocean protection. She wraps up by explaining solutions offered by relevant local organisations and brands.
Audience members learn what is available in Hong Kong, “which can help them take individual climate action”, she said.
At one memorable concert, Ho invited her violin students to play, giving them a chance to gain experience and confidence, and be part of climate action.
Ho’s music and environmental education have taken her to bigger international stages – the violinist performed twice at the 2023 United Nations Climate Change Conference, or Cop28.
At the conference, Ho learned how climate change is experienced differently around the world. She recalled a conversation with representatives from a small, developing country who were curious how Hong Kong had “so much money” for green policies.
Despite concern about their country’s environmental situation, they faced severe limitations in fundraising.
“I saw they really wanted to do something but were very powerless because they had no money,” Ho said. “Their anxiety really awakened me.”
Ho has gone beyond concerts when it comes to climate education. She has given guest lectures at Hong Kong universities and local organisations, discussing how music can help inspire climate action.
One topic she has explored is sustainability within the music industry. She has examined how concert tours generate carbon emissions and the eco-friendly practices some bands have adopted, such as Coldplay encouraging fans to use recyclable wristbands and take public transport to venues.
When asked what advice she has for young climate activists, Ho was straight to the point: “When there’s a chance, just grab it.” She suggested launching a pilot programme and finding a mentor who builds confidence.
The violinist said she occasionally feels frustrated when audience members seem uninspired by her performance and its message. But she reminds herself that it may be one step towards caring for the environment.
“I don’t mind if they just listen to the music. I’m also very grateful they gave me time to speak and were willing to listen,” she said.

title: Open-source AI is Europe’s only path to tech independence, says Alibaba chairman Joe Tsai
description: Tsai argues that US export controls on advanced technologies have fuelled the development of China’s AI ecosystem.
content: Embracing the open-source approach is the only way for Europe to achieve technological independence, Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai said, pointing to China’s own open-source drive as a blueprint for innovation under constraints. For Europe, which shares China’s deep roots in traditional manufacturing, the open-source approach presented a unique opportunity, Tsai said, highlighting that factories in the region possessed highly valuable manufacturing data. “You don’t want to feed it into some closed-source API. You want to maintain those data and be able to take open-source models and then further train your model, and improve it for your use,” he said. The comments, which were made by the Alibaba co-founder earlier this week at the Wave tech event in Italy, came as Alibaba itself is doubling down on the open-source approach to become a leading player in the global AI boom. Tsai described the company’s current era – from 2023 onwards – as its “AD period”, pivoting away from past unfocused expansion to a strict dual focus on e-commerce and full-stack AI. Tsai, who co-founded Alibaba with Jack Ma and others in 1999, became the group chairman in 2023. The Hangzhou-based tech giant was using the US$25 billion free cash flow generated by its e-commerce operations to fund AI infrastructure and model development, Tsai said, adding that the group had doubled capital expenditure on computing infrastructure every year for the past three years. On US-China tech competition, Tsai drew a sharp contrast between the current strategies of AI developers in the two countries. “Chinese companies are open sourcing their innovation, they write papers,” he said. “The American closed-source labs don’t write papers any more because they don’t want to share.” Tsai argued that US export controls on advanced technologies have fuelled the development of China’s AI ecosystem. In an analogy that he has used previously, Tsai likened US firms to children born in resourced, wealthy families, while noting that China has more motivation to work hard and innovate because it does not have the same resources. Alibaba has been making an aggressive push through this approach, as highlighted by the company’s announcements at its annual Apsara Conference in September. During the event, the company debuted the Zhenwu V900 processor, billing it as “the most powerful AI chip in China today”, and teased plans to train an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters. Looking forward, Tsai predicted that AI would go beyond a stand-alone novelty to become an integral part of everyday life over the next few years. “Five years from now, we won’t be talking about AI per se,” the 62-year-old said. “AI would have been infused in every aspect of our business. For the same reason, we don’t talk about the internet today, but the internet is everywhere.” Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Could Indonesia’s ‘content governor’ rival Prabowo for the presidency in 2029?
description: Dedi Mulyadi’s blend of populist policies and social media savvy has made him one of Indonesia’s most talked-about politicians.
content: Dressed in his trademark white shirt and traditional Sundanese headcloth, West Java Governor Dedi Mulyadi stood near the barren slopes of Mount Wayang. Announcing a new initiative to pay hundreds of local farmers to replant its forests and shield the region from flooding, he delivered a line perfectly pitched for the cameras tracking his every step. “I am a leader who does not want obedience caused by poverty,” he declared on September 26. “I want obedience caused by prosperity.” It is this blend of populist rhetoric, grass roots problem-solving and relentless social media promotion that has transformed the 55-year-old former motorcycle taxi driver into one of Indonesia’s most talked-about politicians. Having won a landslide gubernatorial election in late 2024 as a member of President Prabowo Subianto’s Gerindra party to lead Indonesia’s most populous province, Dedi’s massive online following and recent strong poll numbers have ignited speculation that he could mount a serious bid for the presidency in 2029. A July simulation by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) placed Dedi at 35 per cent in a multi-candidate presidential preference test, leaving Prabowo trailing far behind at 14.5 per cent. A subsequent August survey by Tempo Data Science produced similar results, placing Dedi above 40 per cent and Prabowo around 15 per cent. The 2029 presidential election is some time away, but analysts say Dedi’s poll numbers have raised an awkward question for Gerindra: could the governor who rose to prominence under its banner eventually become its chairman’s rival for the presidency? Strength in ‘authenticity’ Dedi’s ascent has been propelled by his mastery of social media. His primary YouTube channel has 9.2 million subscribers and generates tens of millions of views every month, earning him the nickname “Gubernor Konten”, or “content governor”. Rather than broadcasting dry policy speeches, his feed operates more like a populist reality show: he intervenes in neighbourhood disputes, hands out cash to the elderly and recently made headlines by offering a 50-million-rupiah (US$3,200) personal bounty to anyone who could catch pickpockets or muggers. In a July survey conducted by Lembaga Survei Indonesia (LSI), public satisfaction with Dedi’s performance across West Java reached a staggering 95.4 per cent. Djayadi Hanan, executive director of LSI, observed that Dedi’s grass roots appeal combined political cultivation spanning a quarter-century, as he climbed from local councillor and two-term regent of Purwakarta to national lawmaker, with an instinctive command of social media that starkly contrasted with the archaic outreach methods of his older peers in the political circle. Dedi’s “main strength is authenticity”, Djayadi said, a trait he shared with Prabowo’s predecessor, former president Joko Widodo, who also rose from humble origins to national fame by branding himself a man of the people. “By contrast, you cannot imagine President Prabowo Subianto making social media content hugging a taxi driver or eating at a street vendor without people viewing it as staged,” Djayadi added. According to Burhanuddin Muhtadi, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute, Dedi’s surging profile outside his home province is not merely a product of his social media activities. His poll numbers also reflected a growing public weariness with the central government, Burhanuddin said. He added that Dedi’s huge popularity should not be attributed to just his political strengths. “Part of his rise also reflects negative sentiment towards the Prabowo government. Dedi projects a more down-to-earth, accessible image, whereas Prabowo has a much more high-profile presidential persona.” Going ‘offside’ With the surge in Dedi’s online presence, his content creation has begun to raise eyebrows within Jakarta’s establishment. In August, in the wake of a magnitude-7.7 earthquake, Dedi travelled to East Nusa Tenggara to personally deliver relief assistance. While framed as an act of humanitarian solidarity, his excursion beyond West Java’s borders drew intense chatter, with critics questioning why he was leveraging a distant crisis to elevate his national profile. For some analysts, Dedi’s manoeuvres risk crossing an unwritten line in a political system where institutional loyalty is prized above personal popularity. While Dedi has earned a reputation as an on-the-spot problem solver, venturing beyond his provincial boundaries risks overstepping his mandate, said Aditya Perdana, a political science lecturer at Universitas Indonesia. By attempting to intervene in crises outside West Java, Aditya argued, the governor was increasingly playing “offside” in the eyes of party elites by projecting influence where he had no jurisdiction. His widening ground engagement has likely not gone unnoticed inside Prabowo’s party, which Dedi joined only in 2023 after decamping from Golkar, according to analysts. “The potential main friction lies in Prabowo’s inner circle in Gerindra, who may perceive Dedi’s activities outside of West Java as his political warm-up agenda for the 2029 election,” said Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political researcher at the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN). Gerindra’s bind Publicly, Gerindra has dismissed the polling disparity between the two men. After the release of the SMRC report, the party’s daily executive chairman, Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, brushed off pollster’s figures, saying surveys could “fluctuate” from one cycle to the next. Djayadi has noted Dedi’s “strategic ambiguity” by routinely deflecting questions about his national ambitions and insisting he remains focused on his present position. “I am currently just thinking about how to be a successful governor,” Dedi told reporters last month when pressed on his 2029 prospects. “Now is not the time for that.” As for Prabowo, while Gerindra elites have already publicly pushed him to run for a second term, the 75-year-old incumbent has so far refused to commit, stating repeatedly earlier this year that he would not run in 2029 if he felt his administration had underperformed. Should Prabowo decide to run, Dedi has been touted by some observers as the president’s running mate. But Burhannudin said voter data suggested that such an alliance could fail. “One complication is the emerging ‘anyone but Prabowo’ sentiment,” Burhanuddin explained. “If Dedi becomes the running mate of an incumbent whose popularity has been declining significantly ... some voters who currently support Dedi could instead move towards Anies or Gibran,” he added, referring to former Jakarta governor Anies Baswedan and Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, both of whom are also seen as potential 2029 contenders. “We should not assume that all Dedi supporters would automatically follow him into a Prabowo-Dedi ticket. Some may prefer Dedi precisely because they see him as an alternative to the incumbent.” Nor can Gerindra sideline Dedi and order him to remain an obedient campaigner on Prabowo’s behalf without consequence, Burhanuddin said. “The publicly available survey data suggest that, if Dedi is removed from the presidential-choice simulation, Anies and Gibran benefit more than Prabowo,” he added. Another possibility is that Dedi could leave Gerindra to seek a ticket elsewhere. This prospect has become plausible following a landmark Constitutional Court ruling last year that abolished the minimum requirement of 20 per cent of the vote for a political party before it could nominate a presidential candidate, which has opened a back door for popular independents to contest in an election for the top job. “This significantly changes the strategic environment,” Burhanuddin said. “Other parties that lack a sufficiently popular presidential figure of their own may be interested in nominating Dedi for president.” Long road to 2029 Dedi, however, faces the daunting task of sustaining his populist aura given the relentless public scrutiny. While his personal approval rating remains sky-high, his governance record is not without blemishes. In June, the turbulent rollout of West Java’s public school admissions system left thousands of parents frustrated after their children failed to secure places at state schools, prompting Dedi to issue a public apology. With West Java facing a projected 3.4-trillion-rupiah deficit, Dedi announced last month that he was halting all new provincial projects to avoid taking on massive debt. The polling landscape, however, remains far from uniform. A nationwide survey conducted in late August by pollster Median offered a counterweight to earlier findings, placing Prabowo in the lead with 32.4 per cent support, followed by Dedi at 20.6 per cent and Anies at 20.5 per cent. Three years is a long time in Indonesian politics, Burhanuddin warned, and early regional momentum can easily evaporate as the stakes rise. “His current popularity is real, but sustaining it until 2029 will depend on whether his personal appeal can survive the much harder tests of governing performance, greater national scrutiny and the changing political environment.”

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: explorer inspires youth through glacial field trips
description: Wilson Cheung’s unconventional path to career in glaciology helps him mentor young people through hands-on field science.
content: When Wilson Cheung took Hong Kong secondary school students into the Swiss Alps this summer, terrain he had once been able to reach had become inaccessible. Glacier melt and thawing ground had destabilised parts of the mountain, while rockfall made fieldwork more hazardous. Only weeks earlier, Cheung had completed a roughly 1,700km (1,056-mile) scientific snowkite traverse across Greenland in 2026. The journey took him across the ice sheet while he continued collecting data in one of the world’s most extreme environments. “We can see it in the measurements, but when we are actually there, we see the physical changes in front of you,” he said. Cheung is a finalist for the Spirit of Perseverance Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. His route into glaciology was far from conventional. Cheung grew up in a low-income family and struggled with English at school. With little money at home, his mother often sent him to the library, where the air-conditioning was free and there were plenty of books to read. After graduating from Baptist University and struggling to find suitable work, polar explorer Rebecca Lee Lok-sze became an important influence. She introduced him to Richard Bach’s Jonathan Livingston Seagull, the story of a bird unwilling to accept the limits imposed by its flock. Cheung said a person’s starting point should not determine how far they could go. In his view, school results capture only one point in someone’s life; what follows depends on the choices and actions that come afterwards. His studies eventually took him to Canada, where he completed a PhD in glaciology at Queen’s University. His doctoral research examined decades of glacier change in Auyuittuq and Sirmilik national parks in the Canadian Arctic. Cheung said he did not gauge success by how much he earned. He cared more about the knowledge and experience gained, and whether his work could contribute something useful. He now gives young people opportunities to experience field science themselves. On the Swiss trip, students were asked to observe each glacier closely and explain how it differed from the previous one. By the end of the programme, the students had a grasp of what the ice and surrounding terrain could tell them, he said. Some participants in his youth programmes have since pursued their own paths. One later studied in Tasmania and went on to work in Antarctica. Another headed to France to train as a mountain guide. Cheung also recalled a girl who had repeated a year at school and was considering giving up on an examination she feared. He promised that if she passed, he would send her a postcard from the Arctic. She did, and he kept his promise. Donors including Christine Yu and Cyrus Cuthbertson have helped fund his youth programme, while PlayHard Hong Kong has supplied some of the field equipment. Cheung hopes that support could reach pupils who might otherwise be unable to take part. Years of polar fieldwork have also taught him that even careful plans can unravel. On his first assignment in the Canadian Arctic in 2022, a helicopter due to collect him was involved in an accident before reaching him. Cheung waited for 10 days before he could leave. The pilot was seriously injured and had to be taken to hospital. “Being able to come home, see my mother and talk to her, that’s success,” he said. The lesson from the polar regions, he said, is to prepare carefully while accepting that conditions can change without warning. “We make a plan so that we have a plan to change,” he said. “Every day you wake up to a different problem, and you have to find a way to solve it.”

title: Bling Empire’s Dorothy Wang is back. This time, it’s her wedding, her rules
description: The socialite shares how using her own production firm enabled her to control the narrative in Dorothy’s I Do, now streaming on YouTube.
content: For Dorothy Wang, documenting her life is hardly new territory. After years of appearing on reality television, including Rich Kids of Beverly Hills, Bling Empire and Bling Empire: New York, the socialite-entrepreneur and heiress – her father Roger Wang is the billionaire founder of Chinese real estate company Golden Eagle International Group – has spent much of her adult life sharing her life with the public. But when she met lawyer Brandon Yankowitz through mutual friends in 2022, she found herself in a relationship with someone who did not even have an Instagram account. Now, with Dorothy’s I Do, Wang has returned to the public sphere. The five-part docu-series is now available on YouTube; the final episode will air on October 11, 2026, to marked the couple’s first wedding anniversary. She also recently announced that she was expecting their first child. The series reveals the meticulous yet occasionally chaotic three-month planning process behind the couple’s sumptuous nuptials at the Collegio alla Querce in Florence, Italy. Viewers get a glimpse of her style choices – couture gowns by Oscar de la Renta, Giambattista Valli and Prabal Gurung – as well as more intimate moments, including Wang’s conversion to Judaism for her husband and the traditional Chinese tea ceremony that kicked off the wedding festivities. How Wang is taking control of her own narrative “I always would say I would do it if it was right,” Wang tells the South China Morning Post of returning to reality TV. “I think for me, and in the time I am in my life, I’m not really joining an ensemble cast, and I’m not just going to be talent for hire.” Reality television is notorious for dramatic contrivances. To avoid that, Wang produced the series herself under Chez Yankowitz, the production company she and her husband established. The couple also brought on board producer Gennifer Gardiner, who previously executive produced Rich Kids. Wang wanted to maintain control of the creative process from the outset. “I’ve been in this industry a long time, so I know that when things go to a network or a studio, there are certain things that they’re looking for and try to change the story,” Wang says. “But we wanted to maintain full control of our story and how we wanted it to be shared. “I knew that if it was the right project, if I could have my hand in it, help create and produce it, then that would be a story that is interesting for me to tell.” Yankowitz was not necessarily opposed to reality television, but it had never been his world; he had never watched the shows Wang appeared on. Accompanying her around New York and on their travels, however, gave him a first-hand look at the connections she had built with viewers. “People would come up to me so nicely, so politely and just be like, ‘Are you going to come out with anything soon? We miss you.’ He saw that many times first-hand,” Wang says. Those encounters helped Yankowitz understand that her relationship with her audience was more than a by-product of being on television. It was a genuine connection, built over years of affording people glimpses into her life. A whirlwind Florence wedding Dorothy’s I Do begins around three and a half months before the wedding, coinciding with the most intensive phase of planning. Wang describes the production as organic, with the couple assembling a team of camera operators, sound technicians and editors she had worked with before. “It really felt like a coming home series for everyone,” she says. The compressed planning schedule was deliberate. Wang says she had never been someone who spent her childhood imagining her wedding or researching destinations where she might one day get married. Nor was she particularly eager to spend a year immersed in wedding preparations at the expense of her everyday life. Planning, she says, meant spending considerable time with unfamiliar people and less time with the friends and family who were part of the couple’s everyday lives. Rather than prolong that disruption, Wang and Yankowitz decided to concentrate the preparations into a few months. “We felt that no matter what, we would be stressed anyway,” Wang says. “We would rather be stressed for three and a half months than take out a year of our regular, lovely lives.” Choosing Florence also involved considerable deliberation. The couple considered Lake Como and Paris before settling on the Tuscan capital, drawn by the combination of history, culture and contemporary luxury they wanted their guests to experience. “We wanted to bring our guests and our family somewhere where they could explore, walk around and just have a good time,” Wang says. “And we really felt that Florence was the perfect mix of that.” Unscripted moments and future plans Watching the footage back has given Wang a new appreciation for the smaller, unscripted moments between her and Yankowitz. She finds herself noticing the way he looks at her, even when she is simply walking out of a room. “I really am sentimental,” she says. For Wang, the series is more than a record of a lavish destination wedding; it is a keepsake she and her husband can revisit and share with loved ones for years to come. “I think that we have created the best memory time capsule wedding video to show our children and grandchildren in the future,” she says. “We’re proud of it.” That does not mean the story is an unbroken celebration. Wang says the final episodes reveal that some things did not go according to plan, and she hopes viewers planning their own weddings will take away practical lessons from the couple’s experience. She is particularly candid about her frustrations with an industry that, in her view, does not always deliver the services couples expect. Ultimately, she hopes the YouTube series conveys something more enduring than the stresses of organising a wedding. The couple’s first year of marriage has reinforced her sense that getting through the planning process together was an achievement in itself. While the preparations could be stressful, she describes married life as a welcome contrast. “Marriage, while you’re not wedding planning, is a delight and a breeze,” she says. “If you can get through the wedding planning process, you can conquer it all.” Even the title, she says, is symbolic. “Dorothy’s I Do, to me, just means saying yes,” she says. “It means giving your word, surrendering to the future, and giving your 100 per cent.”

title: Australia says it won’t buy Russian fuel despite Trump’s diesel agreement
description: Canberra will maintain its import ban to block revenue for Moscow’s war effort, citing sufficient domestic petrol and diesel reserves.
content: Australia has no need to buy fuel from Russia and said that purchases from there would remain barred so that the country did not benefit from the invasion of Ukraine. “We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, said on Saturday at a press conference in western Sydney. “We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East. What the United States does is a matter for them, but we won’t be changing our approach.” President Donald Trump announced on Friday a series of cargoes beginning this month totalling about 13.5 million barrels initially. He is working with Russian President Putin to release Russian diesel supplies into global markets, a move that upends years of sanctions as the White House seeks ways to tame soaring fuel prices ahead of the US midterm election. Bowen also said that Australia had 43 days’ worth of petrol, two days more than a week earlier, while diesel stocks sat at 31 days’ worth, one day less.

title: The hidden heartbreak of losing a pet in Singapore and Malaysia
description: When society minimises the bond owners share with an animal, owners can be left to suffer in silence, counsellors say.
content: Growing up in a Malay family in Singapore, Hafeez Hassan feared dogs. He never expected to mourn one like a sibling. “Maybe that is what I have been grieving all along … The experience of loving something that I was taught I was not supposed to love,” he said. Even as an adult, walking his former partner’s husky Pieces in public made Hafeez anxious that a relative might see him, or that he might be judged for being close to an animal whose saliva and waste are regarded as ritually impure by many Muslims in the region. Touching or holding a dog is not sinful, according to the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore. Though it did note in a 2014 advisory that other schools of Islamic jurisprudence had different views on dogs. Hafeez, who is a dance choreographer and movement coach, did not immediately seek counselling when Pieces died. Years passed before he started to talk openly about what the loss meant to him with George Chan, a loss and grief counsellor in the city state whom Hafeez knew from their work together on dance productions and musicals. Disenfranchised grief Hafeez’s experience is one that counsellors in Singapore and Malaysia say they recognise all too well. Those in the profession call “disenfranchised grief”, a term for a loss that is not openly acknowledged or socially supported, and that others may not readily understand or accept. A dead pet can bring on such a feeling when owners sense the bond they had with an animal is being minimised or dismissed. “The moment they feel like they have to defend their grief, it becomes a very lonely thing,” Chan said. What is lost is often more than just an animal, according to grief counsellors. It can be the routines that were built around the pet, or the absence of a steady companion that helped an owner through upheavals and challenging times. Some clients come to Chan specifically because their pets have died. For others, the grief only surfaces while they are working through other issues such as a divorce or the death of a parent. Chan’s sessions often begin with the pet’s name and what kind of companion it was. “I’m not trying to understand death,” he said. “I’m trying to understand the relationship.” For owners who had to decide whether to euthanise their pet, guilt over acting too soon or waiting too long was often part of the grieving process, Chan said. “Sometimes it is easier to hold on to a guilt story than to accept that you were completely helpless … with guilt, you can still blame yourself, the vet or someone else,” he said, adding that the alternative was to admit there was nothing more the owner could have done. He sets no fixed number of sessions for his clients and does not regard grief as a problem to be solved. “My job is not to fix a five-week-old grief, you grieve because you loved,” Chan said. Lifelines after loss In Malaysia, PiePie Pet Memorial has made follow-up care part of its services, rather than treating the farewell ceremony as the end of its role. Manager Tan Chien Yung said the company began formally tracking counsellor follow-ups in 2022, with more than 4,000 bereaved pet owners receiving such support in the years since. Last year, the pet funeral and cremation services provider recorded around 1,250 follow-ups with grieving owners, up from 1,030 the year before. So far in 2026, some 850 owners have been contacted. Not all follow-ups result in a dedicated grief support session. In fact, only 21 owners had booked a complimentary session since 2022, Tan said. “The purpose of the service is not to encourage more people to attend counselling,” he said. “It is to make sure that no pet owner feels they have to navigate their grief alone.” Tan Su Wen, a licensed counsellor who works part-time with PiePie on its follow-ups, usually calls about a week after the final farewell, or sooner if funeral staff report that an owner appeared particularly distressed during the ceremony. “Some owners feel a degree of closure after a formal send-off,” she said, adding that guilt was a common concern among those owners who sought help after euthanising a pet or losing one to an unforeseen accident. Like Chan, she finds that many owners struggle with the shock of a sudden death or the loss of an animal companion that had become part of the family. For Adam Ishak, her help really mattered. Samuel, his orange Persian-Maine Coon mix, died in late February at the age of 12, after a year-long battle with feline chronic kidney disease. As the cat’s condition worsened, Ishak and his wife opted for euthanasia to spare it further suffering. Their advice to other owners is to look out for possible signs of the disease and seek veterinary advice early. Ishak, who has lived with cats all his life, said Samuel “left a mark on my life like no other”. The PiePie team’s support had been invaluable, he said, especially the “certificate of life … which is hanging above his ashes in our home”. Every day, the couple light a candle and say Samuel’s name, based on a traditional Central American belief “that a life dies three times: when the body dies, when it is interred and when its name is spoken for the last time”. “Because of the last ‘death’, I believe Samuel is still alive for as long as we remember him,” Ishak said. Enduring taboos While losing a dog or cat is the most common reason people see a pet bereavement counsellor, grief is not necessarily dictated by the pet’s species or size. Chan noted a tendency for society to create a hierarchy even within pet loss, assuming the death of a dog carried more emotional weight than that of a bird, fish or reptile. Most of his clients were dog owners, but he said he had also counselled someone grieving a bird. At PiePie, grief-support appointments have mainly involved dogs and cats, but also rabbits and hamsters. The company has even held a farewell for a pet fish. Hafeez got another dog after Pieces’ passing. Ali, a shih-tzu, has been with him for six years. But there are still family gatherings at which Ali is not welcome. “There is something painful about loving an animal deeply while knowing that a relationship is considered forbidden or unacceptable by parts of your own community,” Hafeez said. “And the more I think about it, the more that hurts, not because I need everyone to relate to dogs the way I do, but because I would genuinely love for my family to meet someone who has become part of my family too.”

title: Worker prospects in Hong Kong hair, beauty sector not cut and dried amid staff shortages
description: Despite 4.9 per cent vacancy rate, salons in Hong Kong face hiring challenges as many do not see hair and beauty care as rewarding career path.
content: Hongkonger Terrence Wu Chung-ting puts on an apron, picks up a comb and massages hair essence into a client’s scalp during a treatment for hair loss. But eight years ago, Wu’s job could not have been any more different. A finance graduate from one of the city’s top universities, he was then a marketer for beauty products and focused on sales. But when he saw untapped potential in Hong Kong’s hairdressing industry, he boldly switched careers from a white-collar to a blue-collar profession, training to become a scalp therapist. Wu, now in his mid-thirties, recalled starting from scratch by learning basic tasks such as shampooing and blow-drying hair. Beauty care and hairdressing were recently highlighted in the government’s midterm manpower projection report as a job category expected to see a manpower crunch. The report said the city’s workforce was expected to shrink by about 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages forecast across industries involving both skilled technical workers and low-skilled labourers. There were 49,800 workers in the beauty care and hairdressing industry in 2025, with a 4.9 per cent vacancy rate, according to statistics from the Labour and Welfare Bureau. The industry would need 2,440 more workers, with hairdressers specifically in demand. An industry expert said salons struggled to fill junior vacancies because roles with low entry requirements attracted mostly young people who constantly changed jobs, resulting in high turnover. Noting the staffing problems in the industry, Wu said salon assistants might not be aware of the career prospects in the hair care sector. “I think most people do not really know much about hair and scalp treatment, and that could be the cause of the manpower shortage in this industry,” he said. “They don’t even know about the position of a scalp therapist, so they don’t consider this a viable career path,” Wu said. Unlike traditional salons where assistants must do the grunt work of cleaning the salon before learning haircutting techniques and other skills, the training of a scalp therapist focuses on developing knowledge, including a basic understanding of scalp health. In Wu’s salon, a single hair and scalp treatment session can range from HK$1,000 (US$127) to more than HK$2,000 depending on the client’s needs. When he first started, Wu studied the stylists from traditional hair salons, learning how to blow-dry and style women’s hair and other skills. “I guess that to outsiders, it might seem unexpected – they probably wonder why someone highly educated would choose to go into blue-collar work,” he said. “But I see this as an industry where you can actually make good money. Even though it’s hard work, the returns are worth it.” Nelson Ip Sai-hung, founding chairman of the Federation of Beauty Industry, acknowledged that young salon assistants often came and went because they knew the shops were always hiring for junior roles. But scalp treatment was a step up and represented a “high-value-added” item in the industry, he said. “I think it is pretty attractive to youngsters … honestly, [the treatment] is a high-value transaction, which means the revenue will be high too,” Ip said. In addition, the title of “therapist” made a good impression and conferred a certain status that was “not just an ordinary apprentice”, he added. Elaine Wan Yee-man, director of United Beauty Group, said it was difficult to hire beauticians for massage and facial services, as the work was physically demanding and many preferred to be therapists who operated equipment instead. “The biggest problem we face in recruitment is that candidates divide themselves into therapists and beauticians. They feel being a beautician is quite an ordinary role, but there should not be such a prejudice,” she said. “I think a proper facial should include massage – pressing the face, shoulders and neck – that is what makes it a full treatment.” Wan said the industry was struggling to attract new blood because apprentice salaries ranged from HK$10,000 to HK$18,000 a month. The “bundled arrangements” that once guaranteed workers a basic pay regardless of their output had also been scrapped, creating a sense of income instability for new hires. “When the market was good, everyone was poaching staff. It was really important to have bundled arrangements, and workers could push their salaries up really high,” she said. “But now the market is genuinely worse, so a lot of us in the beauty industry have already cancelled the bundled arrangement.” She added that there was still demand for beauticians who provided facial treatments manually, as many customers were willing to pay for these traditional treatments.

title: At a Shenzhen market, ‘golden week’ tourists flock to buy discount gold jewellery
description: A dip in gold prices and the holiday week draw tourists and shoppers to Shuibei wholesale market.
content: For Xiao Lei, a gold seller in Shenzhen’s Shuibei district, China’s week-long National Day holiday has meant a rush of customers and a heavier workload, as shoppers flock to buy jewellery at lower prices. Shuibei, a sprawling gold and jewellery trading district in a city better known for its technology industry, is one of China’s largest wholesale hubs for the precious metal. Xiao said customer traffic at her shop had risen sharply during the holiday. “We’ve had all kinds of customers, including tourists from Jiangsu and Zhejiang who are using the long holiday to come here and buy gold,” she said. “But most are young people from here in Guangdong.” The holiday was only part of the attraction. Xiao said Shuibei’s gold price had fallen from more than 1,000 yuan (US$149.1) per gram last week to about 945 yuan on Wednesday. “A lot of people are waiting for prices to fall before buying,” she said. “They pick out the pieces they like in advance, then buy as soon as the price comes down. They believe gold will keep gaining value over time, and a lot of young people are buying gold jewellery as an investment.” The buying rush reflects gold’s dual appeal as an accessory and a store of wealth. Weakness in China’s property market, volatile stocks and falling deposit rates have encouraged some households to seek other places for their savings, while geopolitical uncertainty has added to the metal’s appeal. Yet prices have retreated in recent weeks as a stronger US dollar, elevated Treasury yields and expectations of further US interest-rate increases weigh on gold. Spot bullion traded near US$4,130 an ounce on Wednesday, after peaking above US$5,300 in January. Wedding purchases were another source of demand, according to Yan, a seller in Shuibei, who said Guangdong’s year-end wedding season was approaching. Customers can get the designs they like without paying extra for the brand name Alice Zhou, jewellery seller Many Chinese brides traditionally receive “five golds” – earrings, necklace, ring, bangle and anklet, with regional variations – often presented by the groom’s family as wedding gifts. Pointing to a necklace popular with wedding buyers and priced at about 23,000 yuan that day, Yan said the design had sold out twice during the week. “We restocked five last night, and they were all gone this morning,” she said. But Yan said younger shoppers were also coming to Shuibei as they were less willing to pay the premiums charged by established jewellery brands. Gold jewellery priced at about 945 yuan per gram in Shuibei could cost around 1,300 yuan at some well-known domestic chains, she said. In Shuibei, prices were linked to international gold prices, with workmanship charges typically adding a few dozen yuan per gram. “Compared with my generation – those of us born in the 1970s – young people care less about the brand and more about the craftsmanship and gold purity,” she said. “You can pay a big premium for a brand, but when you sell the jewellery back, the price still follows the international gold market, and a lot of young people don’t want to pay that extra.” The appeal of familiar designs at lower prices was evident at another stall, where seller Alice Zhou pointed to pieces resembling those sold by international luxury houses such as Buccellati and Van Cleef & Arpels, as well as Chinese jewellers Chow Sang Sang and Laopu Gold. “Our craftsmanship is just as good, sometimes even finer,” Zhou said. “Customers can get the designs they like without paying extra for the brand name.” Such similarities also carry risks. Yan said sellers were wary of copying branded pieces too closely. “We don’t reproduce branded designs exactly. At most, we make something similar,” she said. “If we were sued, the losses would be far greater than the profits. A lot of designs here tread that line.” She said fewer sellers were offering Louis Vuitton-inspired pieces after the luxury house sued Chinese tea chain Molly Tea over trademark infringement. By Wednesday, the final day of the holiday, Zhou said the crowds had thinned somewhat from their earlier peak. “From October 1 to 5, there were so many customers I barely had time for lunch,” she said. “People even had to queue just to ask about a piece.” Zhou said not all her customers were Chinese, and that she had served more than a dozen people from the US, Britain and Russia over the past week. “As brands such as Laopu have become popular overseas, more foreigners have taken an interest in Chinese gold craftsmanship,” she said. “Though they tend to prefer pieces with diamonds.” For Zhang, a tourist from Inner Mongolia autonomous region, the latest price drop was reason enough for one final visit before his flight home. He planned to buy another piece of gold jewellery for his mother. “I bought a bracelet here two days ago for more than 4,000 yuan,” he said. “Now the ring I had my eye on is 460 yuan cheaper, so I’ve come back to buy it before my flight.”

title: Singaporean teenager flown to hospital after falling ill during Lion Rock hike
description: Girl, 17, suffered chills and vomited during early morning hike with two friends.
content: A Singaporean girl has been flown to a hospital after falling ill during a hike with two other friends at Hong Kong’s Lion Rock, according to police. The force received a report on Saturday from the mother of one of the hikers at about 6.50am. Her daughter called for help after the 17-year-old Singaporean friend vomited and experienced chills during their hike at Lion Rock, a 495-metre-high mountain. Police later arrived at the scene while the Government Flying Service deployed a helicopter to airlift the teenager. The girl, who remained conscious, was sent to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai for treatment. The other two girls, both 17, sustained no injuries and returned home.

title: Letters | Before we trust AI, we must trust each other
description: Readers discuss the artificial intelligence race, and putting people first in mental health decision-making.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The artificial intelligence race is often regarded as a purely technical issue. It is a prisoner’s dilemma instead. As algorithms play a larger role in domains ranging from credit scoring to military operations, the main risk stems not from malfunctioning code but from deep-seated mistrust among the nations developing these technologies. Automation is rewriting the social contract. When algorithmic systems determine outcomes such as mortgage approval or judicial sentencing, they introduce asymmetric power dynamics. The design of these systems keeps their underlying logic hidden behind corporate confidentiality. The result is a dangerous new kind of bureaucracy where life-altering decisions cannot be transparently challenged or appealed. This indistinctness also affects public discourse where people confuse human free speech with automated amplification. Social media platforms often rely on free speech protections to defend recommendation engines optimised for advertising engagement, but algorithmic code holds no constitutional rights. That’s why regulation should focus less on what is said and more on how it’s shared, especially by limiting automated processes that can turn fringe grievances into widespread issues. With the quest for artificial general intelligence, the threat shifts from online arguments to systemic collapse. The tech sector is caught in a trap. Tech giants and nation-states fear that pausing for safety assessments could lead to a loss of technological leadership, yet rushing ahead means deploying systems with black-box mechanisms no one fully understands. Trust cannot be established when incentives to breach safety agreements remain significant. Technological solutions alone cannot tackle underlying political and economic problems. To avert a catastrophic race to the bottom, we need a governance framework based not on ambiguous corporate ethics boards but on rigorous, verifiable treaties. This framework must prioritise democratic accountability, transparency and collaborative action. As Henry Kissinger argued in his later years, just as the nuclear era necessitated the International Atomic Energy Agency to monitor fissile material, the AI era requires the equivalent international authority. Regulating AI means building a system that strengthens human dignity and operation. Trust is the missing ingredient in the future of AI. Ross Cheung, PhD candidate, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Put people first in mental health decision-making This year’s World Mental Health Day theme, “Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change”, reminds us that meaningful mental health reform cannot be achieved solely through professional expertise, policy directives or service targets. It must be shaped with people who have experienced mental health challenges and the systems intended to support them. The history of mental health reform reflects an expanding understanding of what people need. Deinstitutionalisation challenged the assumption that long-term psychiatric hospitals should be the centre of care. Rehabilitation subsequently emphasised residential support, vocational opportunities and reintegration into community life. Psychosocial approaches further highlighted relationships, participation, dignity and quality of life. The recovery movement takes this further: it asks what gives a person meaning, purpose, hope, identity and a valued place in society beyond a diagnosis or a list of symptoms. This is why language matters. Official documents have sometimes used labels such as “ex-mentally ill”. Such terms can reduce a person to a past illness and imply that their primary identity is defined by it. Increasingly, we use “people in recovery” or “people with lived experience”. These expressions signal a change in mindset. People come first, their experiences carry knowledge and recovery is a personal, non-linear journey rather than a professional verdict. People with lived experience should not be invited only to tell moving stories at public events while decisions are made elsewhere. Their expertise should inform the planning, design, delivery and evaluation of mental health policies and services. Genuine co-production can help services identify practical barriers that professionals might overlook, respond more closely to what people actually need and strengthen accountability to those who use them. The World Health Organization similarly calls for people with lived experience to influence policies, services and decisions, not simply to be heard after the fact. This World Mental Health Day, let us ensure lived experience is represented at every table where decisions are made. Real voices must have real influence. That is the foundation of real change. Dr Candice Powell, CEO, Mind HK

title: Will Taiwan issue derail Washington and Beijing’s latest reset? Analysts are sceptical
description: The opening of a new representative office and former leader Tsai Ing-wen’s US visit may have a limited impact, diplomatic observers say.
content: Recent interactions involving the US and Taiwan are not expected to derail the current momentum in relations between Washington and mainland China, according to diplomatic analysts. Beijing was taking a pragmatic approach to navigating the complexities of the Taiwan issue, they said, but the fate of a US$14 billion arms package for the island remained a key concern. During President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to the United States, Xi urged his hosts to “adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwanese independence”. On Monday, Taiwan’s former leader Tsai Ing-wen started a week-long visit to the US on the same day that the island’s foreign minister attended the opening of a de facto consulate in Arizona. Tsai’s itinerary included a meeting with former US House speaker Nancy Pelosi and a speech to Stanford University on Taiwan’s role in global stability. It is Tsai’s first trip to the US since her eight-year spell as leader ended in May 2024 and also her first meeting with Pelosi since the then speaker visited Taiwan in 2022 – a move that triggered large-scale military exercises around the island by the People’s Liberation Army and a continued stepping up of military pressure since then. Her publicly released itinerary suggests she will remain in California throughout the trip. Beijing has yet to respond publicly to Tsai’s visit, but her trips to Japan and Europe after leaving office have prompted the mainland’s Taiwan Affairs Office to affirm its opposition to independence for the island. “At this point, it remains to be seen what kind of political arrangements, if any, the United States will make for Tsai Ing-wen’s visit to the US, or whether the visit will be merely symbolic,” said Zhu Feng, professor and dean of Nanjing University’s School of International Studies. He added that from Beijing’s perspective, there was no need to be “completely confrontational” over the Taiwan issue, pointing out that Tsai was no longer the island’s leader. Zhu said the visit further illustrated the complexity of the Taiwan issue in China-US relations and it was not something that could be “resolved overnight”. On Wednesday, Tsai spoke at a conference on technology and national security at Stanford, where she accused Beijing of carrying out “grey zone” activities – ways of exerting pressure without resorting to all-out warfare – around Taiwan. She also called for greater industrial cooperation between the island and its democratic partners, saying this would not only strengthen Taiwan’s own security but also “the stability of the Indo-Pacific and the resilience of the wider democratic community”. Meanwhile, Taiwan’s foreign ministry described the opening of a new de facto consulate in Arizona as a “milestone in the Taiwan-US economic and trade partnership” that would help strengthen exchanges in areas such as economics, technology, education and supply chains. As part of a three-day visit to the US, the island’s foreign minister Lin Chia-lung attended the opening of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Phoenix on Monday. Meanwhile, the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, defended Donald Trump against criticisms that he was too soft on Beijing over the Taiwan question. He wrote on social media that Trump was “as strong on Taiwan as I’ve ever seen anybody” and had authorised 50 per cent more arms transfers to Taiwan than any US president since 1979, the year Washington formally established diplomatic relations with Beijing. He also said the US stance on Taiwan had not changed, adding: “We don’t support independence. We don’t support coercion either.” Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The US, in common with most countries, does not recognise the island as independent but is opposed to any attempt to seize it by force. Washington is also legally committed to supplying Taiwan with arms to defend itself and last week the island finally received two F-16V fighter jets that had been due to arrive earlier this year. They were part of a NT$247.2 billion (US$7.8 billion) package of 66 F-16Vs approved in August 2019 during Trump’s first term.
