Zhu and other analysts said Beijing was now more concerned about a US$14 billion weapons package for Taiwan that has been on hold for months awaiting Trump’s approval. Zhu said it was possible that the US president would approve the deal before next month’s midterm elections as he sought to portray himself as securing greater benefits for Americans. Trump signing off on the package would damage China-US relations, “but I do not think this would overturn the consensus on cooperation”, he said. Shi Yinhong, an international relations professor at Renmin University, said recent engagements between Washington and Taipei had not produced any major results and were unlikely to affect the next possible meeting between Xi and Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November. “The most notable development concerning Taiwan in the context of China-US relations is Trump’s continued delay in making a decision on a major new arms sale to Taiwan,” Shi said. But he added that Washington would continue to support the island and suggested the delay was “a tactical move” on Trump’s part.

title: Your Voice: Dogs and public safety, Hong Kong’s traditional eateries and phone scams (letters)
description: This week, readers analyse the threat fighting breeds pose and urge young people to preserve city’s culinary lineage and protect the elderly from phone scams.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
For decades, the Hong Kong government has been toiling to create a more inclusive society by introducing more pet-friendly policies.
In July, a dog-inclusive dining scheme was rolled out, and it was well-received among restaurant owners and dog lovers. However, within just a month, 31 licensed eateries decided to pull out of the scheme, and 70 warnings were issued by authorities during environmental hygiene and food safety inspections.
The withdrawals show that the policy has room for improvement. Worse still, recent incidents of dog attacks and the animals running amok in public areas have also sparked public concern.
A more comprehensive review of pet-friendly initiatives in the city is needed. Not only do dogs present risks to restaurant hygiene, but they also pose a threat to public safety.
On August 20, a woman was found unconscious at a dog training centre in Ta Kwu Ling. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Closed-circuit television footage uncovered that the woman was mauled by a mongrel dog after trying to lead it to the cage. The dog was later found to have some pit bull ancestry, a fighting breed.
The government should ponder how to monitor dogs that carry genetic traits from fighting or dangerous breeds. It must also consider how to prosecute dog owners if they wrongly declare their pets’ DNA.
Preceding the mauling, an unleashed 60kg dog killed two small canines in Yuen Long. This incident also spread fear and panic among pet owners, specifically when walking their four-legged furry creatures in public areas.
These events tell us that regulations on leashes and dangerous dogs must be tightened to ensure everyone’s safety.
The pet-friendly dining scheme should be suspended temporarily to allow time for cultivating responsible pet ownership. Many complaints and non-compliance cases regarding the dining scheme centred on dangerous dogs entering eateries or dogs near food preparation areas.
Restaurants are retail outlets and customer-oriented. Even if their frontline staff offer verbal advice to pet owners, it is the responsibility of owners to follow rules and keep their dogs under control. Warnings should not be restaurants’ sole responsibility but one shared with pet owners.
The government should ensure pet owners are fully aware of the mandatory leash rules and sanitation practices to guarantee everyone’s safety.
Public safety is always a priority. It does not mean the scheme should be discontinued forever, nor that the pet-friendly initiative is bringing us down the wrong path.
A necessary halt is a pragmatic move. Polishing the current dining scheme will foster bonding between man and pets. Reviewing the overall pet-friendly initiative will pave the way for a more harmonious, stable and sustainable environment.
Choi Wing-yu, Christian Alliance S.C. Chan Memorial College
I am writing to share my reflections on Young Post’s cover feature “Cooking up a storm” published on September 14. Chef Mel Ng’s inspiring story deeply resonated with me, shedding light on a critical issue that our city can no longer afford to ignore: the alarming rate at which Hong Kong’s traditional eateries are vanishing.
As a secondary school student witnessing the steady erosion of our local food culture, I believe Ng’s journey offers a masterclass in how the younger generation can intervene.
Seldom do we realise that these historic restaurants are far more than mere commercial entities; they are the living, breathing repositories of our collective memory and cultural identity. But sentimentality alone cannot shield them from harsh economic realities.
What struck me most about Ng was her pragmatic approach. Recognising that traditional masters possess unparalleled craftsmanship but often lack modern marketing acumen, she astutely leveraged her business background and social media platforms to throw these struggling shops a lifeline. This synergy between heritage and modernity is precisely the catalyst our culinary industry desperately needs.
Armed with their digital literacy, tech-savvy youngsters can revitalise old-school brands. Not only can they breathe new life into precarious businesses, but they will foster a profound cross-generational connection – one that will allow youth to appreciate the grit and dedication of our culinary elders.
Schools should pioneer entrepreneurship projects that pair students with local food stalls. Ultimately, preserving our culinary lineage requires a shift from passive nostalgia to proactive innovation. It is my sincere hope that more young people will step up to ensure these flavours do not dissolve into history.
Chan Chun-wing, Po Leung Kuk Ho Yuk Ching (1984) College
Many elderly residents in Hong Kong have fallen victim to phone scams that cost them significant life savings. It is crucial that we tackle this problem.
Most, if not all, of the elderly population were born before the internet was as widely used as it is today. There is a clear technology gap between younger and older generations, and the lack of digital safety knowledge leaves older adults vulnerable to phone scammers looking to exploit them.
To tackle the root of the problem, the government can help educate the elderly on how to distinguish between real and junk calls. The government can broadcast educational videos on television, which is the main source of information for the elderly.
As young people, we also play an important role in helping prevent the elderly from being scammed. We are tech-savvy, so we can teach them scam-prevention tips, such as installing anti-scam mobile apps to help block potential scam callers.
Protecting our elderly in the digital age is a shared responsibility for the government and residents. With concerted efforts from both the government and young people, we can help keep the elderly safe online in today’s digital era.
Recent social media posts have disparaged the thumbs-up emoji, crediting the rejection to Gen Z. But why is the emoji so disliked?
A 2022 Forbes article declared that Gen Z had cancelled the thumbs-up emoji. Once a symbol of simple agreement or acknowledgement, the emoji representing the motion of putting your thumb up has turned into a mark of annoyance and passive aggression.
As a young person who uses the thumbs-up emoji constantly, however, I struggle to understand how the simple gesture can be taken so negatively. Although I can imagine some use the emoji to quickly leave a conversation or to send insincere agreement, I take the thumbs-up to say “I agree” or “Yes, understood.” I don’t register the hostility of a very common gesture and a useful emoji.
Of course, there are situations where the emoji is absolutely not appropriate. If someone is seeking consolation or advice, one should not send a single emoji as a response.
However, in situations where you set up a meeting place to hang out, send a reminder or even just notify someone, the emoji should be fine – and a “thank you” could accompany it. At the end of the day, I would argue that sending the thumbs up emoji is better than leaving someone on read.

title: Trump slams Norway and Nobel committee after missing out on Peace Prize
description: The US president lashed out after former UN official Navi Pillay was awarded the prize, claiming the decision discredited Norway.
content: US President Donald ⁠Trump reiterated his complaints on Friday about not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize, calling it a disgraceful and embarrassing decision that had left a ‌stain on Norway, which hosts the Nobel committee. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” Trump told supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York. He added that the snub was “just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country”. Trump unleashed on Norway hours after the committee awarded this year’s prize to Navi Pillay, a South African judge and human rights lawyer. Pillay serves as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice in The Hague, and last year chaired the UN commission that investigated Israel’s retaliatory war in Gaza and concluded that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration had committed genocide against Palestinians, a finding that the Israeli government firmly denounced. She previously served as an appeals judge on the International Criminal Court. Trump called Pillay a “mystery person” and “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of” during ‌the campaign rally. “I never heard of the person. Nobody did … I know a lot of people. I’ve never heard of this particular person. But congratulations anyway.” Pillay was attending the Nuremberg Forum, a gathering to discuss international law in the German town that hosted the trials of Nazi leaders after World War II, when she learned she had won. The news was met with applause by the audience. “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” Pillay joked. Each year of ‌his presidency, Trump has expressed disappointment at his failure ⁠to ⁠win the prize. Trump campaigned aggressively in 2025 to be awarded the prize, arguably the most prestigious award in global diplomacy. The Nobel committee was unswayed then, instead awarding Venezuelan opposition figure Maria Corina Machado the prize. She later gifted her medal to Trump, prompting the Nobel Institute to release a statement saying the prize could not be revoked, shared or transferred. “This is an indelible stain on the country of ‌Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said. He ‌listed ‌a number of conflicts that he claimed a ‌role in resolving and said he had helped prevent wars ⁠from breaking out between North and South Korea and Japan and ⁠North Korea, without providing evidence. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited ‌by a handful of ‌radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation. And we will not forget, Norway,” he said. Hours after Pillay received the Nobel Prize, the Trump administration unveiled fresh sanctions against the ICC, which the White House has long accused of unfairly targeting the US and Israel. It was not immediately clear if the sanctions were intended as a response to the Nobel announcement. The move would impose financial punishment on any entity that does business with the ICC, a move that US allies including the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Canada and Japan warned would have a “significant impact” on the court, its staff and their families. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: Blind musician with rare birth disease plays her heart out
description: Born with Hirschsprung’s disease, Cassie Li has had a lifetime of health issues. But the 17-year-old continues to learn, perform and inspire others.
content: A year after a seven-hour surgery in Hong Kong in 2025, Cassie Li Pui-ying was on stage at Queen Elizabeth Stadium, playing the drums before an audience of more than 2,500 people. She heard the applause but could not see who it came from. That March night was organised by Live Theatre, which her mother Marine Mak also helps run. Li sang, spoke and played the drums. The group gives visually impaired students a stage to perform on. Despite having been through several serious health scares, what comes across is Li’s faith, optimism and cheer. She moves people. For the second year in a row, the 17-year-old has been named a finalist in the perseverance category of the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Launched in 2013, the awards honour individuals and groups whose work might otherwise go unnoticed. Recounting her tribulations in the past year – only the latest in a lifetime of health challenges – Li said she struggled to accept her situation when she was readmitted to the intensive care unit of Queen Mary Hospital in 2025. “I wanted a normal life. Why another operation?” she said. But her surgeon, who has looked after Li since childhood, was reassuring. “If you believe us, we’ll help you. And you’ll be all right,” she recalled him saying. Born with Hirschsprung’s disease, Li lacks the nerve cells that push food through the gut. Doctors once expected her to live only about 10 months. She cannot eat as others do, and is fed intravenously each day. She is blind in her left eye and has only 10 per cent of sight remaining in her right. Li spent years of her childhood going in and out of hospital. She often had little appetite. But music captivated her from a young age and, despite her disability, she learned how to play different instruments. She is currently in Form Four on an adapted curriculum and hopes to take applied learning in music. Apart from drumming, she is learning to play the guitar and to write music on a keyboard. Enlarged sheet music helps, while tactile markers on the guitar frets and a tuning app make playing easier. She learns how to play songs note by note, and by ear, and enjoys performing while leaving the mixing to others. Li said she hopes eventually to pursue a career in music, whether through performing, songwriting or other work in the industry. Li has drawn on her years of struggle, not only with her health problems but also in other personal experiences, to build resilience and to help others. Her father passed away six years ago, when she was just 11, but what she carries today is not a sense of loss but the fondest memories of him. “This moment was very sweet,” she said, describing a photograph of him holding her as a young child. Li said she was grateful for all the people who had supported her over the years, including her mother, her teachers and all the doctors and nurses in the paediatric ward at Queen Mary Hospital. Their encouragement and care, she said, had helped her through difficult times and continued to motivate her to keep learning, performing and looking ahead.

title: Why a Communist Party boss had a coffee shop date with Chinese content creators
description: When Jilin province’s party chief met influencers at a cafe, he had a number of messages in mind.
content: The setting may have been casual but the choice was not when the Communist Party boss of a northeastern Chinese province sat down with digital content creators at a coffee shop on Wednesday. Jilin province party secretary Huang Qiang invited the influencers to the relaxed setting of the Songyuan Coffee Shop in Changchun to encourage them to “actively promote mainstream values and spread positive energy”. According to a local government statement, Huang and the participants also exchanged views on key promotional priorities, including publicity for the Winter World University Games in Changchun in January, cultural tourism and the region’s revolutionary history. The choice of the informal venue broke with the rigid protocols of traditional Chinese officialdom. While many politicians in the West hold “coffee hours” or casual meet-and-greets in everyday public spaces, few officials in China would use such informal settings to communicate a political message. Instead, the events would normally take place in venues ranging from internal meeting rooms within municipal government centres and tiered auditoriums to grand ballrooms and multipurpose halls at designated hotels. The meeting came 100 days before the winter games, an event that is expected to draw thousands of participants from around the world. The discussion was an attempt to harness the storytelling power of the content creators, with Huang saying that this was a chance to elevate the region’s profile. “[We] must seize the key opportunity of the Changchun Winter World University Games to step up international communication, and present to the world a credible, lovable and respectable China, alongside a Jilin that is warm-hearted, vibrant and full of promise,” he was quoted as saying. Huang urged the influencers to be “people-centred” by using accessible language, and to dig deep into Jilin’s unique history and ecology to produce high-quality cultural content. He also called on them to champion traditional Chinese virtues to promote an authentic and welcoming regional image. The Songyuan cafe was chosen as a backdrop to convey that message. The building was originally the residence of the commander of the Japanese Kwantung Army during Japan’s invasion of China. It was repurposed as an official reception facility and then reopened last year to the public as a coffee shop. The rebirth of the building represents the province’s broader efforts to prioritise heritage protection by advocating the adaptive reuse of historical architecture. The cafe also rolled out drinks with local flavours, such as “ginseng coffee” – infused with Jilin’s prized medicinal herb – and “frozen pear coffee” – inspired by the region’s winter delicacy. Huang also presented the content creators with two books on Jilin’s regional development and revolutionary history to guide their digital storytelling.

title: Chinese police crack real-life ‘Breaking Bad’ drug lab, arresting ex-chemistry professor
description: Retired academic masterminds drug operation, designs process, uses personal connections to secure illicit lab space across 5 Chinese cities.
content: Police in eastern China recently dismantled a cross-border drug-trafficking gang that allegedly involved a retired chemistry professor and a master’s degree holder in producing narcotics. The case went viral in China, where social media users dubbed it “China’s Breaking Bad,” after the American crime drama that aired from 2008 to 2013. The series is widely regarded as one of the greatest TV shows of all time. In China, all five seasons scored above 9 out of 10 on the country’s best-known ratings site. During a routine inspection of a pharmaceutical technology company in 2024, police in Shandong province noticed that it had bought unusually large quantities of six chemicals used as key ingredients in etomidate. Etomidate is a narcotic drug that has often been misused in e-cigarettes known as “zombie vapes.” Long-term use of high doses can be fatal. China placed the substance under control in 2023. Police discovered that a man surnamed Huang was behind the purchases. He had a master’s degree in chemistry and had spent years selling e-cigarettes in Shenzhen. He worked at the pharmaceutical company for just three months before quitting. Police suspected that Huang had bought the ingredients to produce etomidate. Their investigation found that he travelled frequently between Zibo, in Shandong, and Shenzhen, and spent several days at a time with Wu, a retired chemistry professor from a local college. Investigators later revealed that Wu was the key figure in the production of etomidate. He had designed and refined the manufacturing process and used his connections to secure laboratory space in factories across five Chinese cities, ostensibly to develop new medicines. According to Shandong police, the pair took care to produce only etomidate’s precursor chemicals in China, then transport them to Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia for conversion into the finished product, in an effort to avoid legal risks. While Wu and Huang oversaw production, an e-cigarette seller and international logistics business owner surnamed Wang arranged for the chemicals to be moved in small quantities and for the manufacturing equipment to be transported. Police said they needed to dismantle the entire cross-border drug-manufacturing and trafficking network at once to bring its members to justice. If they found only precursor chemicals in China, they would be unable to prove a crime or make arrests. It took Chinese police nearly two years to gather sufficient evidence and coordinate with their counterparts in Vietnam and Thailand. In March and April, police dismantled seven of the gang’s bases across Cambodia, Vietnam and Thailand. China Central Television reported that they arrested 71 people and seized 73kg of etomidate, five tonnes of active ingredients and multiple pieces of laboratory equipment. Police discovered that Huang had made five million yuan (US$750,000) from the illegal operation. The case remains under investigation, and the suspects are awaiting trial. Under China’s Criminal Law, anyone who sells, transports or manufactures 50 grams or more of heroin may face at least 15 years in prison, life imprisonment or the death penalty, as well as confiscation of property. In previous court cases, judges have calculated sentences by treating each gram of etomidate as equivalent to 0.4 grams of heroin. “Zibo Heisenberg,” one netizen joked, referring to the alias used by Walter White in Breaking Bad. “Making drugs must be easy for chemistry experts, but most wouldn’t do it because there are more important things than profits,” another commented.

title: Malaysia urged to police its firms in Indonesia as haze shuts schools
description: With six regions shutting schools, civil society groups say accountability must extend to Malaysian corporate interests across the border.
content: Malaysia is facing renewed pressure to clamp down on its companies over their alleged links to forest fires abroad, as recurring haze from Indonesia continues to disrupt schools and daily life despite years of regional efforts to tackle the problem. On Thursday, Malaysia ordered schools to close across several states, including Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and the Rompin district in Pahang, while sporting events scheduled for the weekend were cancelled. The latest closures follow findings by environmental watchdogs Greenpeace and Pantau Gambut alleging links between Malaysian and Singaporean corporate interests and fire hotspots in Indonesia’s Kalimantan. The findings have intensified calls for Putrajaya to take action on companies linked to fires abroad, rather than rely on regional cooperation that has yet to prevent recurring haze crises. On Wednesday, Greenpeace Malaysia and civil society groups marched to parliament, demanding stronger legislation to investigate companies linked to fires that have contributed to the ongoing haze crisis. “Malaysia must have the legal power to investigate and hold companies accountable where credible evidence links them to environmental harm beyond our borders,” Greenpeace Malaysia campaign manager Heng Kiah Chun said in a statement. “A transboundary haze law cannot remain on the drawing board while communities continue to bear the health consequences of haze year after year.” Members of parliament received the memorandum from Greenpeace on Wednesday, with Bandar Kuching MP Kelvin Yii saying authorities had struggled to gather evidence, investigate and enforce laws against entities outside the country’s jurisdiction. Bukit Bendera MP Syerleena Abdul Rashid said the recurring impact on schools, air quality and public health demanded stronger regional action. “We already know the cause. Now we need action,” she said, according to local news outlets. Malaysia has sought to draft a transboundary haze law since 2019, with the previous Pakatan Harapan government agreeing in principle in February 2020 to develop a framework that would give authorities powers to pursue companies over activities abroad. The proposal was championed by former environment minister Yeo Bee Yin after the severe haze crisis in 2019. But the proposal was not advanced after a change of government. The new administration argued that its ability to pursue companies for activities in foreign jurisdictions was limited, particularly without cooperation from foreign authorities. As civil society groups press for the law to be revived, Malaysia faces the challenge of holding its companies accountable for environmental damage beyond its borders. Experts say targeted legislation and continued cooperation with Indonesia would be needed. Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of environmental politics and governance at the University of Malaya, said the country had a responsibility to ensure its companies operated responsibly abroad but currently lacked the jurisdiction to take action against them for misconduct in Indonesia. “If the Malaysian law is revived and passed according to this ‘Malaysian entities only’ format, it should be quite effective,” Varkkey said. She said a revived law should focus on Malaysian entities operating overseas whose activities had caused haze at home, rather than adopting Singapore’s broader approach of pursuing companies regardless of nationality. Such a focus could deter Malaysian companies while signalling to Indonesia that Malaysia was also overseeing its own entities. Singapore enacted its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014, allowing authorities to pursue Singaporean and foreign entities whose conduct abroad causes or contributes to unhealthy haze in Singapore. Under the law, perpetrators can face criminal or civil liability for activities such as land clearing by fire, with companies facing fines of S$100,000 (US$78,000) per day of haze pollution, capped at S$2 million. Varkkey said Malaysia’s proposed legislation could also ease diplomatic tensions following Singapore’s adoption of its haze legislation, which Indonesia has viewed as interference. “Limiting the legislation to Malaysian entities could give Indonesia diplomatic space to deal with other companies while avoiding diplomatic sensitivities of an extraterritorial law,” she said. However, other experts said giving Malaysian authorities powers to pursue companies abroad would not solve the enforcement problem that derailed the legislation six years ago. Renard Siew, climate adviser at the Malaysia-based Centre for Governance and Political Studies, said any transboundary haze law would need clear standards of liability, credible evidence, meaningful penalties and due process if it was to become more than a symbolic deterrent. “A company’s responsibility should not stop at Malaysia’s borders simply because its operations are offshore,” Siew said, but cautioned that detecting fires alone did not establish who started them or prove corporate wrongdoing. Greenpeace Malaysia, Greenpeace Indonesia and Pantau Gambut identified Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong (KLK), through its reported ties to Indonesian entity Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana, among the top 20 entities linked to findings on fires in Indonesia in 2026, according to a report released on Monday. The analysis drew on data tracking haze sources from August to October 1, the groups said. Greenpeace said Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana had also been identified as having fires on its land in a separate 2019 report. The findings do not, by themselves, establish that KLK or the Indonesian entity started the fires or was legally responsible for them. “Forest and peatland fires that continue to persist are not part of a natural cycle but a reflection that economic expansion based on global commodities is valued more highly than the lives of citizens,” Greenpeace said in a statement. Separately, Greenpeace Indonesia said its analysis identified 5,540 smoke-source points across Indonesia between August 8 and September 20. Of these, 774 were within 210 oil-palm plantation concessions and 859 within 115 licensed forestry concessions. The figures indicate the locations of detected smoke sources, not proof that concession holders caused the fires. KLK rejected suggestions that Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana was responsible for the fires, saying most had originated outside its concession area and had since been extinguished. “As a Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil member, we uphold our zero burning policy aligned with its principles and criteria,” KLK said in a statement on Tuesday. “We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations.” Experts say the dispute shows why legislation alone may not be enough, as Malaysia’s ability to pursue companies beyond its borders ultimately depends on obtaining evidence, establishing liability and enforcing it against those found responsible. While Asean cooperation matters, cooperation without enforceable obligations risks becoming a cycle of statements followed by the same crisis. “The biggest failure is not a lack of regional commitments; it is the gap between commitments and consequences,” Siew said. He said the fundamental problem was no longer the lack of regional commitments but the failure to translate those promises into consequences. “When schools close, the costs are borne by the public, while those responsible may face limited consequences. This is fundamentally an accountability failure.”

title: Coastal erosion, rising sea levels are reshaping a California beach town
description: The state is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Nino.
content:
For years, residents of one Southern California beach town could walk a mile along a stretch of cream-coloured sand and dip their toes in the waves.
But coastal erosion has been eating away at the beach in San Clemente. The rising sea and crashing waves have pushed the shoreline landward.
It’s one of many California coastal communities grappling with the effects of rising sea levels. Nearly a decade ago, scientists forecast that more than half of Southern California’s beaches could significantly erode by 2100.
California is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Nino, a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific known to warp weather worldwide. A study has shown that El Nino events are becoming stronger due to human-caused climate change.

title: In Focus | This womb for rent: why are some Chinese cities hubs for illegal surrogacy services?
description: Industry insiders say Wuhan and Guangzhou are the two major Chinese hubs for surrogacy agencies.
content: It was like something out of a movie: blindfolded, her cellphone confiscated, Miranda was being driven in a van carrying only other women. When she attempted to strike up a conversation with the passenger next to her, the driver made her move to another seat. The silence stretched for 45 minutes before the blindfolds were removed and the vehicle pulled up at what appeared to be a resort-style compound. “I only knew the site lay on the city’s outskirts, nothing more,” said Miranda, who declined to give her full name. “They did not want me to learn the precise location. That was standard procedure every single time I was taken there.” The facility was a surrogacy house in Wuhan, capital of central China’s Hubei province and Miranda’s hometown. Chinese law says assisted reproductive technologies can only be performed by permitted medical institutions for married couples dealing with infertility, and only for medical purposes. Those using such technologies for surrogacy can be fined or face criminal charges. ‘Professional’ services “I knew it was illegal, of course, but surrogacy was a forced choice for me, and it was my last hope of having my own baby,” Miranda said. She opted for it following two second-trimester miscarriages caused by moderate intrauterine adhesions, which complicate pregnancy by damaging the uterine lining and shrinking the space required for a fertilised egg to develop. About five years ago, she learned about the Wuhan surrogacy agency from a friend in Shenzhen. Her first impression was that the facility was clean and well-equipped. She described the agency as “professional”, while noting the irony of applying that term to an illegal operation. “The doctors they arranged came from top local hospitals,” Miranda said. “For egg retrieval, a doctor and anaesthetist would come to the house, and nurses would make home visits for the ovulation-induction injections. But for key examinations, they would drive me to hospitals.” Two years later, her son was born in a Wuhan hospital. The baby’s birth certificate listed the names of her husband and the surrogate mother. After obtaining her son’s household registration document, Miranda asked the surrogate mother to sign a contract waiving her parental rights. She paid more than 600,000 yuan (US$89,454) to the Wuhan facility, with roughly a third going to the surrogate mother. Miranda said the agency told her that most of its clients turned to surrogacy for the same reason: their uteruses were no longer medically viable to carry a pregnancy. Others were seeking to avoid exhausting rounds of hospital treatment. China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists Olivia Ngan, University of Hong Kong Government concerns An analysis released in March by Frost & Sullivan, a consultancy firm, said the number of infertile couples in China had risen from 54.8 million in 2020 to 60.6 million last year, and was projected to climb to 74.4 million by 2035. While surrogacy may appear to be the solution for women like Miranda, Chinese policymakers consider it a practice carrying far more risks than benefits, and the authorities are adamant that surrogacy activities – in any form – are prohibited. In 2021, when deputies to the National People’s Congress – the country’s top legislature – suggested allowing legal surrogacy to prevent repeated illegal operations, the National Health Commission replied that “surrogacy severely harms women’s health rights and interests”. The practice “objectifies women and gives rise to a string of grave social problems, including human trafficking, and can cause ethical crises within the family and society”, it said. The authorities renewed a clampdown on underground surrogacy networks last month. Two laboratories, one in Wuhan and the other in Changsha, the capital of neighbouring Hunan province, were shut down for offering surrogacy services. Wuhan’s municipal health commission said eight people had been detained, police were investigating and “any illegal activities” would be severely punished. This month, the health commission in Taicang, part of Suzhou bordering Shanghai, said it had carried out inspections together with police at an alleged surrogacy facility following online tip‑offs. It has yet to release its findings. They were not the first crackdowns by national and local regulators targeting surrogacy operators. In the second half of 2023, a 14-department task force headed by the National Health Commission rolled out a targeted nationwide campaign. It sought to root out crimes stemming from the unauthorised use of assisted reproductive technology, including commercial surrogacy and illegal egg harvesting. “China’s restrictive stance on surrogacy is consistent with concerns expressed by many policymakers and ethicists,” said Olivia Ngan, research assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s school of clinical medicine. “The central ethical concern is that commercial surrogacy may lead to the commodification of women, reproduction and children.” She said critics argued that “when pregnancy becomes a paid service, there is a risk that economically vulnerable women may be pressured into acting as surrogates, raising concerns about exploitation, coercion and unequal power relationships”. ‘One-stop service’ “Demand for surrogacy does not arise in a vacuum,” Ngan said, noting that those who had experienced infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss or related medical conditions could have a profound desire for genetically related children. Propelled by such desires, China’s underground surrogacy industry now provided “one-stop service”, said Karen, a Shanghai resident who also declined to give her full name. She married late and struggled with infertility for over five years. By the time she turned 45, her diminished egg quality meant scant prospects for wholly natural conception. That was when Karen began exploring alternative options outside hospital care and was surprised to discover that the underground industry offered everything she needed. She opted for the same agency used by Miranda. “The eggs I bought were relatively affordable,” she said. “I paid around 10,000 yuan because the donor – a woman in her twenties – did not have a top-tier educational background. “The surrogate mothers were typically in their thirties. The agency told me that all of them had previously given birth, and it only recruited women from southwestern China’s Yunnan or Guizhou provinces because they tended to come from relatively low-income backgrounds.” After the eggs were successfully fertilised with her husband’s sperm, the agency matched Karen with a surrogate mother. Industry insiders said Wuhan and Guangzhou, the capital of southern China’s Guangdong province, were the two major Chinese hubs for surrogacy agencies, drawn by convenient transport links and relatively lower living costs, which helped keep overall expenses down. China recorded a crude birth rate of 5.63 per thousand people last year, less than half the 12.95 per thousand in 2016, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Block or channel? Ngan said that as China’s population aged and fertility rates remained low, “reproductive aspirations and reproductive health needs may become even more prominent social issues”. To address infertility, China provides assisted reproductive technology services, with more than 600 medical institutions having been approved to deliver them or serve as human sperm banks by June last year. At a news conference in June this year, the National Health Commission said the success rates for assisted reproductive technology services in China had reached internationally advanced levels. “Following comprehensive interventions, 80 per cent to 90 per cent of couples experiencing fertility difficulties are able to conceive naturally,” a commission official said. However, that means multiple fertility treatments fail for 10 per cent to 20 per cent of women who are unable to carry a pregnancy. Professor Kirsty Horsey, from the school of social sciences and humanities at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom, said: “Prohibition [of surrogacy] tends to make people seek alternatives, like going overseas or entering into more dangerous clandestine and potentially unethical arrangements. It is not unknown for trafficking and surrogacy to be connected, but ‘feeding’ this market by prohibitions really does not help.” Chinese media have reported that because legal surrogacy services were unavailable, some people had sought them out overseas, with the US serving as one of the top destinations. Several high-profile Chinese actresses have been caught up in overseas surrogacy controversies in recent years, leading to some of them being effectively banned from the entertainment industry. Beyond the United States, the UK, Canada and New Zealand also permit altruistic surrogacy, while banning the commercial arrangements allowed in America. Australia is conducting a review of its laws related to surrogacy. Ngan said many countries that permitted surrogacy only allowed altruistic arrangements, where surrogates were reimbursed for expenses but received no payment for carrying a pregnancy. “This approach seeks to reduce commercial incentives and the risk of exploitation,” she said. Horsey said overseas experience in jurisdictions with regulated surrogacy showed that “having a regulated and safe form of surrogacy available to infertile couples – with involvement of legitimate clinics, counsellors, lawyers, et cetera to give their respective advice and guidance – would legitimise a particular form of or route through surrogacy, meaning people would not have to resort to dangerous underground arrangements which are also likely to be less ethical”. Miranda said that without surrogacy, “women like me” who were basically incapable of conceiving babies, even with modern medical help, “might never have children”. “So I don’t believe this government-led clampdown will fully stamp out the business,” she said.

title: Japanese brewer designs ‘wobbly’ beer glass to encourage responsible drinking
description: A craft brewery in Japan has developed a U-shaped glass that tilts unless balanced with water, promoting healthier drinking habits.
content: A craft beer producer in central Japan is hoping that its U-shaped “wobbly” glass will encourage people to drink water along with their beer, in a bid to prevent excessive alcohol consumption and dehydration. The “Wobbly Beer Glass by Yona Yona Ale”, produced by Yoho Brewing based in Nagano prefecture, has been on sale since August amid growing awareness of the need for responsible drinking. The idea is that the glass, divided into two sections, will tilt if a balance between beer and water is not maintained. Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, in guidelines released in 2024, encourages people to alternate between drinking alcoholic beverages and water to slow intoxication. Kyoko Kitano, the employee in charge of developing the glass, was inspired by conversations with a colleague about forgetting to sip water while drinking with friends. The company created seven prototypes over about eight months to develop a design that would not lead to spills. A survey of 636 regular drinkers conducted for the company found that while 75 per cent were aware of alcohol-induced dehydration, 75 per cent admitted they failed to consume enough water while drinking alcohol, with most saying they simply lost track once tipsy. Liver specialist Dr Satoshi Ogata said that while drinking water does not eliminate alcohol’s toxicity, alternating beer with water slows the drinking pace and prevents rapid spikes in blood alcohol concentration, while replacing fluids lost through increased urination. The glass holds about 270ml (9.13 fluid ounces) each of beer and water, filled up to its pinched waist, and sells on pre-order for 13,750 yen (US$87). “I will be happy if the glass we developed helps spread healthier drinking habits,” Kitano said. Since 2015, Yoho Brewing has been producing lower-alcohol beer and limiting alcohol-serving hours at outdoor events. “As a beer producer, we believe it is important to continue thinking about responsible drinking,” said Moe Sakai, in charge of public relations of the company.

title: Opinion | Modi and Xi can’t bridge the India-China divide by themselves
description: Building trust requires tackling deep-seated misgivings among bureaucrats and citizens. Easing visa restrictions, facilitating dialogue and collaborating on shared goals are the places to start.
content: Last month, President Xi Jinping travelled to New Delhi to attend the Brics summit – his first visit in seven years. On the summit’s sidelines, Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an in-depth conversation that explored topics of shared interest between them, such as leveraging open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) for mutual benefit. Even so, such sanguine signals were soon drowned out by a spate of downbeat headlines. One recent story warned of the “asymmetric” relationship between the two, with China’s manufacturing dwarfing India’s. Another reported Delhi’s renaming of 28 sites in Ladakh, situated near the heavily contested Line of Actual Control. For keen observers of Sino-Indian relations, such dynamics are by no means a new phenomenon. Positive reassurances from the top leadership are welcome, yet they take time to percolate through to the policy level. Impediments to warming ties, on the other hand, are aplenty – especially concerning territorial claims. Conversations with informed stakeholders suggest a stark disparity in strategic frameworks. While the Chinese leadership views the border issue as one among several other dimensions to the bilateral relationship that can be set to one side, Indian leaders view the border issue as the foremost priority in negotiations with China. Given such core differences, while summits of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Brics bloc of emerging economies in recent years have paved the way for the ongoing detente, there remains significant mistrust between the two countries’ bureaucratic apparatuses. Such mistrust is mirrored by the wider public, especially since the 2020 Galwan Valley clashes. A 2024 survey found that 89 per cent of surveyed urban youth viewed border conflict with China as the greatest challenge to India’s foreign policy. A Tsinghua poll a year prior revealed that more than 50 per cent of Chinese respondents held an unfavourable view towards India. It did not help that people-to-people exchanges were effectively frozen during the Covid-19 pandemic, which saw the suspension of direct flights between the two countries for five years. Visa restrictions have made studying one another up close extremely difficult for scholars and students. Ultra-nationalist propaganda poured fuel on the fire and amplified unhelpful stereotypes. This need not be the way. I had the pleasure of visiting Delhi twice this year, in March for Raisina Dialogue and October for the Kautilya Economic Conclave. On both occasions I visited Jawaharlal Nehru University, where I exchanged views with astute, aspiring China scholars on topics ranging from involution to how China does AI. They came to Hong Kong in April. It dawned on me during our conversations that proactive trust-building requires more than time – it demands starting with small, provable steps. I have three suggestions. First, people-to-people exchanges must be bolstered through reciprocal lowering of visa restrictions and travel barriers. Delhi could resume tourist and conference e-visas and issue longer-period, multi-entry visas to Hong Kong passport holders, which would mirror Hong Kong’s 14-day visa-free entry for Indian passport holders. Given that mainland and Hong Kong passports are distinct, there need be no worry that this overwhelms the Indian security vetting system. At the same time, Beijing should ease the stringent restrictions on Indian journalists. Both sides should recognise that even as tensions flare up, accurate reporting with quality assurances is preferable to an information vacuum which spurs vitriolic speculation. If the above arrangements work out successfully, then Indian tourist and conference e-visas should be resumed for Chinese applicants. Meanwhile, Beijing should expedite and streamline business visa applications for executives, engineers and technical specialists. Second, China must recognise that the widening trade deficit in its favour does its image in India no favours. Prolonged weaponisation of chokepoints could spark an unwarranted push for decoupling. To bridge policy differences and chip away at the underlying mistrust, the two bureaucracies could take a leaf out of the Boards of Trade and Investment mulled by China and the United States and establish comparable working groups and bilateral dialogue mechanisms. The Indian Ministries of Commerce and Electronics and Information Technology could jointly explore this idea through focused engagement with their Chinese counterparts. In exchange for better market access into India for Chinese corporations, Beijing should enforce tighter regulations against the overseas excesses of its private enterprises, as well as encourage them to undertake technology exchange in relatively non-sensitive domains, such as automobiles, solar panels and lithium batteries. The crystallisation of such efforts calls for reviving the two joint industrial estates in Gujarat and Maharashtra. If these parks can meaningfully create new jobs and generate state government revenue, this would show Chinese investment in India can benefit the wider community, as opposed to Chinese firms alone. Third, China and India should build working-level trust through fighting for the Global South. There are clear domains where Indian and Chinese entrepreneurs can collaborate on global public goods needed by many emerging economies, such as pharmaceuticals, renewable energy and food. Both sides must resist the temptation to impose chokepoints for strategic leverage. Sub-national entities, such as individual states in India and provinces in China, can also play a crucial role in amplifying national-level efforts. The southern state of Tamil Nadu has a long history of trading with China. With its sizeable Indian diaspora and potent financial linkages with India, Hong Kong is the prime location for the convening of conferences and workshops on South-South financial collaboration. Trust is easily broken and hard to build. The road to more robust Sino-Indian relations remains long and arduous, yet it is imperative that we start somewhere and do so now.

title: India’s ‘cockroach’ movement leader detained as capital locks down
description: Police detained youth leader Abhijeet Dipke at Delhi airport and have deployed thousands of officers to block a major anti-government rally.
content: Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the “cockroach” youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a demonstration demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district, and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a rally organised by the ‌cockroach movement. The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi. But the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began. A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India’s financial hub, Mumbai. There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. However, small protests broke out elsewhere in the city, including at a popular crafts market and the memorial to freedom movement leader Mahatma Gandhi, with protesters shouting slogans demanding Kumar’s resignation. “Long live the revolution,” some young protesters chanted in central Delhi as police chased them and dragged scores of others into buses to be taken away, even as more arrived, a Reuters witness said. “This is violating the rights of the people and the ⁠country will not tolerate this any more,” Yogendra Solanki said as police escorted him away. Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed ‌in Delhi, the group said in a statement. Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft. “I have come to be arrested, arrest me … I am not afraid of you guys,” he said. “No, this is not an arrest,” one officer replied. “Please cooperate.” The movement condemned what it ‌called the “authoritarian detention” of its leaders, demanded their immediate release and said the protest would continue regardless. CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders’ whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke’s grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral. Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal and Arvind ⁠Kejriwal of Delhi were also detained, TV channels showed. Representatives ⁠of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released. Some lawyers protesting outside the Supreme Court were also picked up and later freed, according to the ‌president of the court’s bar association. There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. Across the sprawling capital of about 20 million people, security forces mounted checkpoints on major roads and at city entry points. Police officers boarded buses searching for protesters, while vehicles were subjected to ‌inspections. Barricades and ‌concrete blocks stopped traffic, while anti-riot vehicles mounted with tear gas guns were stationed on key routes. The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that ‌election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls. Protests have gathered momentum since last week, when the Indian Express newspaper reported that two election commissioners had questioned and disagreed with Kumar over revisions that removed roughly ⁠130 million names from voter lists. Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing. The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses ⁠opposition parties of spreading misinformation because they have failed to win elections. Nonetheless, the near-daily protests pose a new challenge for Modi, just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit. The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027. Saturday’s restrictions showed Modi’s government had “officially waged war against its own people”, K.C. ‌Venugopal, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress party, ‌said. BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said democracy had prevailed over mob rule. Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world’s largest democracy. Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died. The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

title: Lack of heat action plan leaves Hong Kong’s vulnerable residents at risk, experts warn
description: Extreme heat may have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in the city over the space of a decade, new research shows.
content: Environmentalists and academics have voiced concerns over the omission of a systemic heat-health action plan in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and latest policy address, warning that relying on “common sense” is failing to protect vulnerable residents from rising temperatures. Their comments came as new research from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) found that extreme heat might have contributed to as many as 3,238 excess deaths in the city over 10-year study period. In response to the South China Morning Post’s queries about the lack of a cross-departmental heat action plan for vulnerable groups, a government spokesman said there were ongoing efforts to “elevate the response capabilities of the government and the community”. Environmentalists noted that neither the five-year blueprint nor the annual policy address, both delivered by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in September, included a comprehensive plan for a systemic, overarching heat-health action plan to address urban heat. A new management system known as the “city brain”, which aims to improve interdepartmental collaboration during extreme weather, was proposed in the policy address. The World Health Organization outlines eight core elements for heat-health action plans, including governance, early-warning systems, surveillance and outreach. Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner Prudence Yeung said: “Through high-level political commitment, such as including a heat action plan in the policy address or the five-year plan, [the government] could ensure heat adaptation and resilience as a citywide priority, and provide a foundation for investment in heat resilience infrastructure, research and public awareness.” A Greenpeace survey, released in August, found that nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported physical or mental distress during periods of extreme heat. That month the city logged its hottest single day – August 9 – since records began in 1884. In a study currently under peer review, Professor David Bishai, director of the school of public health at HKU, and other researchers revised figures from research in 2024, estimating that heatwaves in Hong Kong between 2014 and 2023 may have contributed between 1,455 and 3,238 excess deaths. The earlier estimate was 1,677 excess deaths. Bishai’s projection was based on demographic data from the Census and Statistics Department, temperature data from the Hong Kong Observatory and relative risks derived from local research. A simulation was used to estimate heat-attributable deaths under different definitions of a heatwave. These preventable excess deaths had largely gone unrecognised as they were preventable exacerbations of underlying illnesses, rather than heatstroke, which was rare, Bishai said. “Enacting an action plan in the face of extreme heat can be helpful in reducing death rates … We know that just leaving it to common sense is not working, because we are still seeing these excess deaths during heatwaves,” he said. “It’s like running a marathon. The heart rate goes up, the blood vessels dilate, blood is shunted away from the brain into the hands and feet so that you can sweat more. And it is a very bad stress test that people’s bodies fail at those ages with those pre-existing conditions.” Bishai cited Paris, where a heat action plan featuring proactive welfare checks on the elderly was projected to have cut heat-related mortality by around 77 per cent following heatwaves in 2003. Hong Kong’s heat measures are activated when the Observatory issues a “very hot weather” warning, triggering the opening of temporary shelters in community halls. According to government figures, the 19 shelters that operated overnight on very hot evenings served between 120 and 210 users a day in June and July. The Labour Department issues heat-stress alerts for outdoor workers – recently revamped following criticism – while the Department of Health provides public health advisories. Ren Chao, an HKU professor who specialises in climate-responsive design, pointed to a gap between heat warnings and government-led community relief. She called for government intervention through more heat shelters and public health education, as well as ventilation and electricity bill subsidies. Heat-risk mapping was also crucial to visualise areas experiencing hot days and nights, which varied across districts, and served as a powerful tool for communicating heat risks to the public, she said. Ren said the government could consider adopting a coordination framework similar to that of its existing typhoon response panel to develop a heat action plan. In a reply to the SCMP, the Home Affairs Department said care teams would remind households in need of measures to stay cool during hot weather, but it did not provide information on the number of visits carried out on hot days. A Development Bureau spokeswoman said the government was committed to enhancing urban forestry resilience and integrating greening into public works and new developments, to “build a more sustainable, climate-resilient and liveable Hong Kong”. The Observatory had been closely providing meteorological data and meteorological advice to help government departments formulate appropriate responses to heat, a spokeswoman said.

title: New Taipei-Hong Kong subsea route opened to cut risk and meet AI demand
description: New path launched through underwater network to tackle recurring disruptions and surging data workloads, RETN says.
content: One of the world’s biggest network service providers has opened a new subsea route between Taipei and Hong Kong to strengthen the system against repeated underwater cable disruptions around the island. Britain-headquartered RETN said the new route would take its total to six serving Taiwan: four connecting Taipei and Hong Kong, and two linking Taipei and Tokyo. “Like many island economies, Taiwan’s international connectivity relies heavily on subsea cables, which creates exposure to risks such as concentration where multiple systems share similar corridors or landing points, alongside ageing subsea cables, natural hazards and fishing activities,” the company said in a statement on September 28. “We aim to address recurring subsea disruptions and support growing demand for data-intensive workloads such as artificial intelligence, cloud, and high-performance computing. “The additional independent international paths provide greater flexibility and resilience when individual cables are impaired, helping maintain service continuity during periods of widespread subsea disruption.” The new route passes through an existing set of cables. According to the Washington-based Global Taiwan Institute, the island is connected to about two dozen undersea cables. Most of the world’s international internet traffic goes through a global network of submarine fibre-optic cables measuring 1.5 million km (932,000 miles). Globally, around 150 to 200 subsea cable faults occur each year. According to the International Cable Protection Committee, “around 70 to 80 per cent are caused by accidental human activity, such as commercial fishing activity and ships’ anchors, rather than sabotage”. Between 2018 and 2022, cables connecting Taiwan to the Matsu Islands were severed 27 times, with further incidents recorded in 2025. Taiwanese authorities have previously said there was no evidence of deliberate tampering by Beijing. The fragility of the global network was underscored in 2024, when four severed Red Sea subsea cables severely disrupted Asia-Europe-Africa telecommunications. While initial estimates pointed to a 25 per cent drop in Europe-Asia data traffic flow, RETN puts the actual data traffic disruption closer to 70 per cent based on its network diagnostics and feedback from major internet service providers in Southeast Asia. The crisis highlighted the dangers of concentration, where multiple cables sharing the same corridors or facilities trigger cascading congestion, latency spikes and packet loss. “Those lessons informed our decision to launch six physically diverse subsea routes for Taiwan, engineered to avoid shared chokepoints and to operate alongside terrestrial alternatives such as TRANSKZ,” it said. TRANSKZ is a 15,000km terrestrial route connecting Frankfurt to Hong Kong via Central Asia that it developed and runs. It diverted 60 to 70 per cent of affected traffic during the 2024 Red Sea cable crisis. RETN said that while it did not own the subsea cables, the company monitored them from network operations centres in Latvia’s capital Riga and Hong Kong, used data centres and landing points in different locations and “diverse equipment vendors and terrestrial corridors so that an incident at one site does not affect all routes”. “DDoS protection and network‑level security services further help keep customer services online during cyber incidents, even when physical infrastructure is under stress,” it said, referring to distributed denial of service attacks.

title: Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to US police, hit government sites
description: Safety concerns grow as Claude automated tests trigger rogue form entries across government sites, sparking criticism of delayed disclosures.
content: An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, authorities said on Friday, criticising the company for taking two months to report the incident. It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite ‌instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms. The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings. “I may have information regarding this case,” Anthropic’s model wrote in its submission. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that ‌time period. Please ‌contact me if this information is relevant.” The brackets featured in Anthropic’s statement. According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder. The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case. Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties ⁠were. “Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm,” Federal Trade Commission director of public affairs Joe ‌Gabriel Simonson said on social media. This process was “not optional”, he said, adding that the US government’s newly created AI body, the Super Intelligence Force, would fulfil its responsibility. The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called “unauthorised ‌and fraudulent use of government and other systems”. The incident echoed other recent cases of unintended behaviour involving AI models, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face. In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologised for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance ⁠of an AI agent exploiting a government website. The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision. Anthropic published a report on Friday outlining multiple types of “unintended” actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website. Other organisations affected included the White House and other US government agencies, the report said. The newly revealed incidents “had minimal real-world impact” and were “significantly less severe” than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said. The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting “basic” coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees and using short URLs to get around other limits. In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a ⁠fee. Another instance revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university. Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs. Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now “until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures … reliably catch behaviours like these”, the report said. Philadelphia police said the phoney tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Centre for vetting. They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised. Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said. The company alerted the department on Wednesday, and the two sides met the following day. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the department said. Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide”. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added. Knowingly giving false ‌reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanour under Pennsylvania law, which specifies “a person”, however. This includes “information relating to an offence or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offence or incident”. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Reflections | The Chinese emperor whose death sparked a mystery that remains unsolved 1,000 years on
description: Was Song dynasty founder Zhao Kuangyin’s sudden death the doing of the brother who succeeded him, like Czech St Wenceslas 40 years earlier?
content: A human skull was carried into a Czech town in late September as part of the country’s observance of St Wenceslas Day, officially the day of Czech statehood. The public holiday honours Wenceslas, the 10th century ruler later venerated as the patron saint of the Czech lands and the “Good King Wenceslas” of the familiar Christmas carol. Wenceslas (Václav in Czech) was born around 907 and became ruler of Bohemia as a teenager. Raised as a Christian, he promoted Christianity – then relatively new to the region – and helped consolidate the early Bohemian state. His political orientation towards the Christian rulers of the German realm was not universally welcomed at home. In the autumn of 929 (some sources place his death in 935), he was murdered at Stara Boleslav, about 24km (15 miles) from central Prague, apparently at the behest of his younger brother Boleslav, who succeeded him. Wenceslas’ death transformed him into a martyr. His cult developed rapidly, and over the centuries the assassinated monarch became enveloped by legend. Wenceslas came to be seen not simply as a saint but as a protector of the Czech lands and a potent symbol of political legitimacy and statehood. His name and image appeared on coins and royal insignia. In modern times, the equestrian Statue of St Wenceslas became the symbolic focal point of Wenceslas Square in Prague. The square has witnessed both jubilant crowds and defiant demonstrations during some of the defining moments of Czech history in the 20th century: the proclamation of Czechoslovak independence in 1918, the Soviet-led invasion of 1968 and the Velvet revolution of 1989. That symbolism has not remained confined to history books. Every September, pilgrims converge on Stara Boleslav, where Wenceslas was murdered, for the National St Wenceslas Pilgrimage. His relics are normally kept in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague, but around his feast day on September 28, they are taken to Stara Boleslav for veneration. This year, the skull arrived from Prague on September 27, while a new silver reliquary containing a fragment of the saint’s remains was presented publicly during the pilgrimage. The human skull, preserved for more than 1,000 years, remains part of a living national and religious tradition. Wenceslas’ death in a fratricidal struggle has an intriguing parallel in Chinese history. Around 40 years after his murder, an emperor on the other side of the world died suddenly after a private encounter with his younger brother. Zhao Kuangyin, known posthumously as Emperor Taizu, founded the Song dynasty in 960 and ruled until his unexpected death in 976. His younger brother, Zhao Guangyi, succeeded him. The circumstances of Taizu’s death became one of China’s enduring historical mysteries. According to the traditional story, Taizu and his brother met privately at night for drinks in the autumn of 976. Attendants and guards, who had been given strict orders to remain outside the palace apartment, reportedly saw the shadows of the two men moving frantically behind the papered windows and heard the sound of an axe. By morning, the emperor was dead and his brother had succeeded him. But here, as with Wenceslas, historical fact is entangled with legend and hearsay. The surviving records don’t establish that Taizu was murdered. The official dynastic histories presented his death as the result of an illness, but later accounts generated competing explanations and suspicions about his younger brother’s role. Modern historians continue to debate how much weight should be given to these later narratives. Two rulers, two deaths and two younger brothers who emerged from the aftermath as successors. Wenceslas’ death ultimately produced a saint whose skull is still publicly venerated in Czech Republic. In China, Taizu’s sudden passing left behind a historical mystery that has endured for a thousand years.

title: Esports body founder hopes Asian Games medals, perception change help grow Hong Kong gaming
description: City’s first ‘M’ Mark esports event, Blast Premier Rivals Hong Kong, returns next month after selling out AsiaWorld-Expo arena last November.
content: The founder of the Esports Association of Hong Kong (ESAHK), Erik Yeung, is hoping a perfect storm of changing perceptions, Asian Games success and a wider talent pool can help continue the growth of the gaming scene in Hong Kong. Competitive gaming has been a huge growth market in Asia and became an official medal event at the Asian Games in 2023, and was back again in Japan last month. China has dominated proceedings, winning seven gold medals across the two Games. Three of those came at this year’s Games in Nagoya, where Hong Kong also picked up bronze medals in Honor of Kings as well as the Fighting Games Team event, which combined Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8 and KOF XV. Esports has become a much more mainstream offering in recent years and the city’s first “M” Mark esports event, Blast Premier Rivals Hong Kong, sold out the arena at AsiaWorld-Expo last November, with more than 30,000 fans attending the event across the three days. It also generated HK$600 million (US$76.5 million) in economic impact and drew 36 million hours of global viewership. Blast Premier returns to the city next month, and has kept its ‘M’ mark status. Yeung said Blast Rivals and this year’s LCK Cup, which was held at Kai Tak Arena, were “crucial” to the development of the region’s esports scene and a driving force in helping improve perceptions of competitive gaming as a whole. “I think the ecosystem in Hong Kong has changed a lot,” Yeung said. “From the beginning, we always thought there should be more competition, but we didn’t know how to do it. Now, we have the facility to do it, not just in terms of venues but the support of the government and the subsidies. “Traditionally, parents regarded esports as entertainment rather than a traditional sport. Things have changed a lot in recent years due to the Asian Games – this year you can see a lot of athletes came back with medals and it feels like things are changing a lot. “It’s really become part of the sports, and it’s changed the perspective of not just parents but schools as well. We can see the traction for it and people are starting to believe it’s good for the development of the youth as well.” Esports at the Asian Games encompasses events across 13 games, with China including 23 athletes in its delegation, while Hong Kong took 43. Nine of the latter were responsible for securing the bronze medals, and Yeung said that success had already caused a significant shift in how esports was viewed in Hong Kong. “Five years ago, if you’d have asked me how close we were to esports being put alongside traditional sports, I would say we had a long way to go. If you asked me today, I think we’re really close,” Yeung said. “I think if you ask anyone now, many would say it’s kind of like a traditional sport – this was the second time we took part in esports for the Asian Games and we’re expecting more medals from our athletes in the future.” A huge part of the success has been in the education sector, with the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) offering a Master of Arts in Esports Management programme to students. Many of those students come from the mainland and Yeung believes leveraging that is crucial in helping the industry in Hong Kong to flourish. “We deliver more than 15 talks to different schools every year and we engage with different universities as well. The Education University organises an esports master course and many of us have taken part as lecturers and I’m one of the professors,” Yeung said. “In the Masters programme, I think more than 70 per cent of the students come from the mainland. The local Hong Kong industry isn’t that big, but the esports industry on the mainland is huge. “We may not have enough of a market locally to nurture people, but if we position ourselves as the window and work together with the mainland market, then it will be huge. “One advantage the mainland can’t provide is that we’re an international scheme. Here, you can get in touch with events like Blast and can get along with people from different cultures. That’s Hong Kong – which I think brings the mainland a lot of value as well.”

title: Southeast Asia battles Big Tech to protect children online
description: From Indonesia to Vietnam, governments are making platforms answerable for children’s safety – but bans can only do so much.
content: Indonesia officially barred under-16s from using “high-risk” social media earlier this year. But that hasn’t stopped the son of one Jakarta-based writer from using it. Aged 14, he already had accounts on Instagram and TikTok – among the platforms Jakarta said children would be banned from using – as well as popular video game Minecraft and gaming platform Roblox. To register, he simply lied about his age. “He can access everything,” Inne Abidin said of her son. “His friends use everything too.” Since March, Indonesia has had some of Southeast Asia’s strictest rules governing children’s social media use.
