Yet like elsewhere in the region, such restrictions are only as effective as the systems Big Tech platforms put in place to identify underage users – and keep them out. From Malaysia to Vietnam, the Philippines and Singapore, governments that once merely urged platforms to protect children are now imposing rules designed to force social media companies to take responsibility. Patchy compliance Indonesia’s child protection regulations have already had an effect on how social media companies operate. In April, Meta Platforms raised the minimum age for a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account from 13 to 16 in Indonesia, with YouTube following suit later that month. Both said they would begin a phased deactivation of accounts belonging to underage users. TikTok, which was the first platform to comply with the new rules, raised its minimum platform age to 16 on March 28. By October, it had deactivated 9 million underage accounts, Indonesia’s digital affairs minister announced on Wednesday. And online gaming platform Roblox now scans Indonesian users’ faces to estimate their age, restricts some communication features for children and has added age-based account limitations. Yet youngsters seemingly still find ways to skirt the rules. To combat this, Indonesia’s government has given tech companies until the end of the year to complete comprehensive self-assessments detailing how their algorithms, age-verification and ad-targeting systems protect children. If the platforms fail to comply, the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry has finalised a sanctions mechanism that – once codified into law – would allow Indonesia to levy fines of up to 6 per cent of tech firms’ global revenue. Applied to Meta’s reported revenue for 2025, that would amount to roughly US$12 billion. Such a fine would not be without precedent. In August, Meta agreed to pay a coalition of US states up to US$18 billion to settle lawsuits alleging Facebook and Instagram were deliberately designed to make children addicted and caused them harm. The settlement also forced sweeping changes to how teens experience the platforms, including daily usage limits, overnight usage blocks and strengthened age-verification controls. Meta has reportedly migrated some 22.5 million Indonesian platform users across to these “teen accounts”, but for the country’s government this does not go far enough. “While we see this as progress, we still do not consider Instagram and Facebook teen accounts to be low-risk,” Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid told reporters in Jakarta on Wednesday. “They remain categorised as high-risk.” Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost Unggul Sagena, digital rights advocate For Southeast Asia, the unavoidable question now being asked is whether governments can turn the threat of penalties into real change. “In my view, the level of cooperation comes down to a few factors: how valuable the market is, how credible the government’s enforcement is, whether the rule threatens the platform’s global business model, how closely it aligns with obligations they already meet elsewhere and whether it carries legitimacy,” said Unggul Sagena, head of internet access at the Southeast Asia Freedom of Expression Network, an Indonesian digital rights organisation that advocates for internet freedom and user safety. As the region’s largest economy, the sheer size of Indonesia’s consumer market – as well as its risk-based approach to online child protection – lent its arguments and regulations weight that smaller countries lacked, Unggul said. “Global platforms are complying,” he said. “Even if not yet fully.” Part of the reason for the changes is the legal machinery Indonesia already has in place, including a regulation passed in 2020 that obliges platforms to act on government takedown orders within tight deadlines, as short as four hours in urgent cases. “The government has also taken the issue directly to headquarters,” Unggul said, noting that the communications minister met representatives from Meta’s global public policy and safety leadership team in New York last month to push for faster deactivation of underage accounts. “Child protection is hard to oppose publicly, so resisting it carries a high reputational cost,” he added. Still, Indonesia’s proposed fine framework has yet to be legally codified and many question marks remain over how it will ultimately be implemented. Unresolved issues include how to collect fines from companies with no local assets, how to accurately verify global revenue “and what due process exists when the same ministry writes the rules, judges compliance and imposes the sanction”, Unggul said. Blocking sites, meanwhile, “hurts Indonesian users more than the companies”, he said. “And the government can order [content] removals, but it still has little visibility into how the platforms are actually designed.” The threat of high fines could push platforms to invest more in safety-by-design and high-privacy defaults for children, said Indriyatno Banyumurti, executive director of ICT Watch, an Indonesian civil society organisation focused on digital literacy. But he warned that legal clarity and consistent enforcement were key, stressing that child safety “should not depend solely on voluntary corporate commitments”. Indriyatno said much would depend on how violations were defined, how compliance was monitored, how evidence was assessed and whether sanctions could be applied fairly and consistently. Regional rules Indonesia’s social media ban may have been Southeast Asia’s first, but it is far from alone in trying to make Big Tech take responsibility for children’s safety online. In Malaysia, rules in force since June now bar under-16s from opening or maintaining social media accounts and require platforms to verify users’ ages. Companies that fail to comply face fines of up to 10 million ringgit (US$2.5 million), with further penalties for ignoring regulatory directives. Vietnam is considering a draft decree that would limit under-16s to a view-only mode of social media, preventing them from posting content, commenting, sharing or reacting to other posts. Accounts would have to be registered using a parent or guardian’s details under the proposed rules, with platforms compelled to block age-inappropriate material and place caps on children’s online gaming time. The Philippines’ approach has been more piecemeal. It already legally forces internet providers to block child sexual abuse material or face heavy penalties and has used regulatory pressure to squeeze direct concessions from platforms. Lawmakers are also considering introducing age limits and other measures. In August, Meta and Roblox agreed to strengthen age checks, parental controls and content takedowns following talks with Philippine authorities over child safety and online radicalisation. A spate of school shootings this year also spurred officials in Manila to order Reddit and Discord to appoint local representatives to coordinate on online threats. Discord was briefly blocked before agreeing to cooperate. Singapore requires social media giants to shield users, including children, from harmful material under its Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Act that came into effect in 2023, with non-compliance carrying a financial penalty of up to S$1 million (US$781,500). App stores have been legally required to verify the ages of users who want to download age-restricted material in the city state since April this year. And an Online Safety Commission, launched in June under legislation passed last year, has the power to order the immediate removal of harmful content and restrict offending accounts. While these efforts have helped effect some change, analysts say the results have been uneven. “Platforms do respond, but market size is a factor they consider,” said regional tech policy adviser Paco Pangalangan, a technology and human rights fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School in the US. “A large market might get more attention, while a smaller one might get a slower, more minimal version. Whether there’s a law matters too.” By his count, most of the big social media companies do not even have in-country representatives in five of Asean’s 11 member states. “So there’s often no real channel for regulators or civil society to raise problems,” Pangalangan said. Strength in numbers Individual governments, especially those that represent sizeable markets with credible enforcement mechanisms, may be able to force social media platforms to comply with their rules. But global technology companies can also opt to deal with countries one by one, which analysts and advocates say makes it harder for smaller markets to exert sustained pressure. One solution could be to present a more united front. “A regional coalition can push Big Tech to create child-friendly ecosystems in ways no single country can,” Unggul said. “Individually, each Asean country is a market platforms can afford to deprioritise. Together, the region is not.” Pangalangan said that, taken as a whole, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations could leverage the region’s more than 400 million social media users to strengthen its hand in negotiations.. “Collectively, we have a market that platforms can’t afford to simply deprioritise,” he said. “If we can agree on common standards, including requirements around how platforms are designed, there’s less room for platforms to play one country off against another or just wait things out.” Allan Cabanlong, Asean regional director for cybersecurity and cloud services provider CyberCX’s regional cyber advisers programme and a former assistant secretary at the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, agreed that collective action could hand regional governments greater bargaining power. “A broom with one strand cannot sweep,” he said. “We have hundreds of millions of users in Asean. If the Philippines were to stand alone, it would not be listened to.” As this year’s Asean chair, the Philippines could push the protection of children online higher up the regional agenda, Cabanlong said, while the bloc could also work to strengthen its existing mechanisms for digital regulation. Asean would not be starting from scratch. Its declaration on the protection of children from online exploitation and abuse, adopted in 2019, and associated regional plans of action already recognise online harm to children as a cross-bogrder issue. Other frameworks on personal data protection – and a declaration on safe and responsible social media use, adopted last October – widen that scope to include online radicalisation and AI-related risks. But few observers expect a single, regional law on children’s social media use to be the end result. “Asean does not necessarily have to start by creating one identical social media law for all member states,” said Ysrael Diloy, executive director of Stairway Foundation, a non-profit children’s rights organisation in the Philippines. “Given differences in national legal systems, regulatory structures and capacities, that may not be the most realistic starting point.” Indriyatno agreed that a more realistic approach would be for Asean to agree on common expectations for factors such as risk assessments, minimum standards of platform accountability, privacy defaults for children and cooperation on cross-border cases. “Regulators could also develop more compatible requirements for platform transparency and information sharing,” he said. Alejandro Reyes, chief strategic officer of non-profit organisation AI Safety Asia, said national regulators would also need to share information and cooperate more closely. “If Singapore identifies a serious failure in a platform’s child-safety systems, its counterparts in Malaysia, the Philippines and elsewhere should have access to those findings,” he said. “Joint investigations, shared technical expertise and coordinated enforcement would make it harder for companies to exploit differences between national regulatory regimes.” Such a baseline would not demand identical laws, but it would provide common ground in dealing with companies that straddle borders. It would also carry risks. “The concern here is that child protection is part of a much broader framework of government control over online content and expression,” Reyes said, urging caution given the differences in countries’ legal systems, political priorities and enforcement capacity. Other issues, according to Unggul, include the fact that Asean members currently compete for technology investment, have very different track records when it comes to free expression and make decisions as a bloc by consensus. “Collective leverage only works if it is credible and rights-based, and that is where civil society across the region must make sure the coalition strengthens accountability rather than state control over content,” he said. “Child safety must not become cover for censorship. Bargaining power comes not only from penalties but from legitimacy.” Limits of laws Governments can restrict access, require age verification and impose penalties on platforms, but they cannot regulate the behaviour of children and families, online child safety experts say. Fandy Zulmi, programme manager at the Centre for Child Study and Protection in Indonesia, pointed to recent Communications Ministry data showing that three out of five Indonesian children had falsified their age to access restricted platforms. Without stronger digital literacy, parental involvement and robust reporting mechanisms, Indonesia’s social media ban for children might simply move the risks “somewhere else”, he said. “It is still too early to conclude that the policy has effectively deterred children from going online,” Fandy said. Indonesia’s implementation challenge begins with the fact that there are between 60 million and 80 million children in the country whose circumstances differ enormously, according to Diena Haryana, founder of the Sejiwa Foundation, a Jakarta-based child welfare organisation. “Where they live, what education their parents have, what digital parenting awareness the parents have, whether the parents themselves have digital skills – all of that varies massively, especially between somewhere like Jakarta and rural areas,” she said. Some parents used social media platforms to keep children occupied while they worked, Diena said, while others were more aware of the risks involved with giving their children unfettered access. “We all need to work much harder to make sure children understand what the regulation is, why it exists and how implementation should actually work,” she said. But ultimately, it is the platforms themselves that bear the brunt of the responsibility for child safety, according to Pangalangan. “They already know where many of the harms are,” he said. “They don’t need a law to fix things they control in their own products.”

title: China wants 5 innovative drugs with US$1 billion returns by 2030. Which might they be?
description: Beijing is attempting to have at least five pharmaceutical products with annual global sales of more than US$1 billion.
content: The increasing global appeal of Chinese firms’ novel therapies has propelled the country’s rise as a biomedical powerhouse, but China has yet to produce a drug to rival all-time best-selling Western blockbusters in sales. Beijing has set ambitious new five-year targets to boost its global presence, including at least five products with annual global sales surpassing US$1 billion by 2030. The goal is achievable, according to some analysts. Jefferies’ head of Asia healthcare research Cui Cui noted that Chinese biopharmaceutical companies contributed over 50 per cent of the global deal value in the first half of 2026, adding that their “competitive efficiency and speed” would drive global commercialisation. Meanwhile, Julia Pian, a senior associate at Atlas Venture, wrote in a blog post last week that the quantitative goals set out in China’s five-year plan were “well within reach”, based on the current trajectory. Mark Kong, executive director of equity research at DBS Hong Kong, also expressed confidence that China would reach its targets, including having Chinese first-in-class innovative drugs accounting for at least 25 per cent of the global total by 2030. This proportion was about 22 per cent at present, up from 4 per cent in 2016, according to Kong. Here are five of the top contenders to meet Beijing’s US$1 billion sales target by 2030. BeOne’s zanubrutinib The drug from BeOne Medicines, formerly BeiGene, is one of two Chinese pharmaceuticals that have already exceeded US$1 billion in annual global revenue. Zanubrutinib treats blood cancers, including mantle cell lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. It works by inhibiting Bruton’s tyrosine kinase, an enzyme that helps certain blood cancer cells survive and grow. Sold under the brand name Brukinsa, the drug was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2019. Last year, zanubrutinib reached US$3.9 billion in global revenue, dethroning its main competitor, AbbVie and Johnson & Johnson’s jointly owned ibrutinib, which brought in US$2.87 billion in 2025. Legend Biotech’s ciltacabtagene autoleucel Legend Biotech’s cancer medicine ciltacabtagene autoleucel, jointly developed and commercialised with Johnson & Johnson and sold as Carvykti, has also met Beijing’s target, bringing in US$1.9 billion in global sales in 2025. Targeting multiple myeloma, or cancer of the bone marrow, Carvykti is a type of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, which modifies a patient’s immune cells to identify and eliminate cancer cells. Intense competitive pressure, however, may stymie Carvykti’s future growth, according to a July UBS report. Similar treatments, including Johnson & Johnson’s own product Tecvayli and Gilead’s anito-cel, were expected to gain traction and crowd the market, UBS said. Akeso’s ivonescimab Chinese biotechnology firm Akeso’s flagship cancer drug ivonescimab was a strong candidate for hitting the US$1 billion sales milestone by 2030, according to Jefferies’ Cui. Ivonescimab famously beat Merck’s Keytruda in lung cancer trials in 2024, a milestone that earned Akeso praise for creating Chinese biotech’s “DeepSeek moment” last year. British drug maker AstraZeneca announced last week a US$2 billion equity investment in US firm Summit Therapeutics, which holds the exclusive rights to develop and commercialise ivonescimab outside China. Ivonescimab’s global sales could reach US$8.5 billion by 2032, according to a June report by Evaluate, a pharmaceutical industry data platform. BeOne’s tislelizumab Tislelizumab, sold under the name Tevimbra, is BeOne Medicines’ second-highest-grossing drug. A so-called PD-1 inhibitor, the drug works by blocking a cancer cell’s PD-L1 protein from binding to the T cell’s PD-1 receptor, enabling the immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells. It is used to treat gastric and esophageal cancers, among others. Tevimbra reached US$737 million in global sales in 2025, increasing 18.8 per cent from 2024. Its main competitors include Merck’s Keytruda, the company said in its 2025 annual report. Kelun-Biotech’s sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) Sichuan Kelun-Biotech Biopharmaceutical’s antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) sac-TMT, which the company licensed to Merck for commercialisation outside China, was also a promising candidate for reaching US$1 billion in global sales by the end of this decade, Cui said. ADCs deliver cancer-killing drugs directly to tumour cells in a targeted manner, and Kelun’s sac-TMT treats tumours including breast cancer and lung cancer. While Kelun has not disclosed the drug’s 2025 sales figures, the company reported 2.05 billion yuan (US$305.76 million) in total revenue for the year and identified sac-TMT as its core product.

title: Our cheat sheet for the best things to do in Hong Kong, October 10-25
description: Indulge in a post-run pasta party for a good cause, let go of your remorse at the “What We Regret Most” exhibition, pick up a limited-edition boba tea and dive into a nostalgic Hong Kong-style afternoon tea, spiced up by European craftsmanship.
content: EAT THIS Jimmy’s Kitchen Local flavours merge with British traditions at Jimmy’s Kitchen, which is marking nearly a century of culinary history with a Nostalgic Hong Kong afternoon tea. Combining Hong Kong food references with European craftsmanship, the menu, available until November 30, features savouries such as typhoon-shelter prawn with cucumber and black-bean mayo, pastel de nata topped with Baikal caviar, curry fish-ball skewers and pineapple bun filled with Iberico ham and salted butter. Sweet offerings include a Hong Kong milk-tea tiramisu, peanut-butter toast with hazelnut and condensed milk, and more, alongside scones. Guests can pair their bites with a curated selection from Jing Tea. M/F, Pedder Building, 12 Pedder Street, Central DO THIS Pici Pasta Run 2026 Are you a runner who is crazy about carbs and eager to contribute to a good cause? Here is the perfect opportunity to combine your passions: the annual Pici Pasta Run returns on Sunday, October 25. Choose between 5km (starting in Causeway Bay) and 10km (starting in Kennedy Town) for your long-distance challenge. Both routes converge at Pici Taikoo Place for a glorious post-exercise carb celebration, where handmade pasta, drinks and desserts await. Entry is set at HK$250 per person, with all proceeds going to Mind HK, to fund mental-health initiatives that provide early-intervention psychological support. Come in your best costumes – there will be prizes. Pici, Lincoln House, Taikoo Place, 979 King’s Road, Quarry Bay. For tickets, click here SEE THIS What We Regret Most We all have regrets, whether big or small. At this group exhibition, running until October 27, visitors are invited to ruminate on those feelings through 40 or so stories and objects submitted by the public on the themes of remorse, collective healing and vulnerability. “What We Regret Most” turns the tables on regret to honour the messy, funny and shameful moments we all experience but rarely confess to. From regretting a wedding (but not the marriage) to regretting getting swept up in the Barbie fad and bleaching one’s hair – only to suffer permanent hair loss – the stories touch on health, romance, work, family, friendship and more. The Garage @ Heath, B/F, 36-44 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui DRINK THIS Honolulu Cafe x Chatime Honolulu Cafe’s masterful tea-brewing meets Chatime’s trendsetting boba innovations this autumn for the ultimate crossover event. Featuring the Hong Kong cha chaan teng’s signature tea bases, premium coffee beans and heritage-driven craftsmanship, combined with Chatime’s star ingredient – chewy tapioca pearls, freshly prepared on a daily basis – the two industry giants have created four limited-edition speciality drinks: coffee with pearl, milk tea with pearl, milk tea and coffee with pearl and Ceylon tea with pearl, with customisable levels of sweetness and served hot or cold. Hong Kong-style boba, anyone? Shop 360, 3/F, Moko, 193 Prince Edward Road West, Mong Kok; Shop 205, 2/F, The Southside, 11 Heung Yip Road, Wong Chuk Hang; Shop 107, 1/F, Nina Mall 1, 8 Yeung Uk Road, Tsuen Wan

title: Meet Hong Kong designer Ed Ng, co-founder of AB Concept
description: Ng’s projects ranged from the Spago Shanghai restaurant at The St. Regis on the Bund to porcelain tableware made with Japanese manufacturer Noritake Design.
content: Founded in Hong Kong in 1999 by designer Ed Ng and architect Terence Ngan, AB Concept has since expanded to become a global firm with offices in Kyoto, London, Taipei and Milan serving clients across even more locations, from New York to Beijing. It is now widely recognised as a pioneering force in luxury design, having established partnerships with leading high-end hospitality brands such as Four Seasons, The Ritz-Carlton, Rosewood Hotels, Waldorf Astoria and W Hotels. Specialising in bespoke, narrative-driven interiors, AB Concept is also renowned for its collaborations with master artisans around the world, creating luxury products like designer chairs and handblown glass lighting through its R&D labs in Kyoto and Milan. Notable collaborations include a capsule collection of couture rugs created in partnership with Hong Kong-based Tai Ping Carpets and a line of sculptural fine porcelain tableware made with Japanese manufacturer Noritake Design Collection, which was unveiled at Milan Design Week last year. One of AB Concept’s latest projects, Spago Shanghai at The St. Regis on the Bund, which was revealed last year, brings to life both the studio’s design philosophy and the storied history behind Spago and the St. Regis hotel brand. Blending Art Deco accents, curvature and motifs – an homage to Spago’s Hollywood heritage and Californian cuisine – with panoramic views of the Shanghai skyline, the space glamorously exemplifies the East-meets-West ethos which makes The Bund such an enduring cultural crossroads of a destination. From the polished marble and bronze of the dramatic entrance to the expansive gazebo chandelier which looms over the lounge and bar area, every detail is meant not only to exude a sense of luxury but also to immerse guests in an environment of spatial storytelling. That same philosophy applies to AB Concept’s projects closer to home, like the revamped event and hospitality suites at Hong Kong’s Aberdeen Marina Club. Eschewing any sense of pretension or the stuffy feel associated with private members’ clubs, AB Concept’s redesign instead focuses on the Club’s legacy as a Hong Kong institution for generations of families. Floor-to-ceiling windows and warm timber finishes thus allow natural light and views of the surrounding marina to be the star of the show, creating a harmonious sense of continuity between the Aberdeen Marina Club interiors and its external environment. Hong Kong, Ng writes, is a place that “recognises and rewards” this sort of originality in design. “Heightened real estate values mean every square metre demands highly articulate, intentional design solutions, leaving little room for superficial styling,” Ng continues. He believes that interior designers in the city have matured and adapted accordingly, shifting away from what he describes as “performative luxury” towards more thoughtful spaces that are layered with both meaning and functionality. All in all, AB Concept’s global footprint reflects Hong Kong’s standing as a benchmark for international design and the unique cultural acuity which makes the city’s architects and designers the most in demand in the world. For Ng, the reasoning behind the tiny territory’s outsized influence on global design is clear. By bringing together “local practitioners, international studios and cross-border clients under one roof,” he writes, Hong Kong’s design scene remains an “open, interconnected ecosystem” which “continuously nurtures creative talent”.

title: How much alone time is too much? Experts on differences between recharging and withdrawal
description: Taking time to recharge is natural, but when does isolation become a problem? Mental health experts explain and give tips on reconnecting.
content: You spend the evening alone on your couch, decline a party invitation or prefer to stay at home instead of going out to a pub or cafe. Some people withdraw, consciously or unconsciously, from social interactions. Sometimes it is just a phase that can help you recharge your social battery. If it is prolonged, however, it can be harmful to your health. People naturally need time for themselves, say, after partying or during stressful periods in their lives. It is perfectly normal to keep to yourself a couple of evenings a week – for a while or regularly – to pursue hobbies or rest, according to Dr Tatjana Reichhart, a psychiatrist, psychotherapist and resilience coach based in Munich, Germany. “If withdrawal is self-chosen and you deliberately use the time for yourself, we wouldn’t call it social withdrawal, but rather ‘me time’”, to replenish energy by recharging your mind and body, Reichhart says. She says it is problematic, though, if work regularly leaves you too exhausted to pursue hobbies or get together with friends. “This isn’t quality time and generally won’t restore energy levels,” she says. ‘Me time’ versus harmful isolation “Social withdrawal can be an avoidance strategy to steer clear of negative feelings,” says Klaus Nuyken, a psychologist based in Hamburg. Someone who declines an invitation for fear of being judged – “They’ll surely think I’m dumb” – is acting dysfunctionally. While avoidance tamps down fear in the short term, it remains and grows stronger over time. You can fall into a vicious circle. If you withdraw from social interactions, you don’t receive any positive feedback either. This, Nuyken warns, can reinforce the proclivity to withdraw. “Social withdrawal is closely linked to mental illnesses such as depression and anxiety disorders, and is typically an illness symptom,” he says. In the case of depression, social withdrawal is largely due to the accompanying listlessness and loss of interest or pleasure in normal activities. Avoidance plays the main role in anxiety disorders but can also result from a traumatic experience or be a symptom of certain personality disorders. Affected people usually don’t at first realise they are retreating from social engagement and are not doing themselves any favours. “This is why it’s important to reflect,” Reichhart says. “For example, how satisfied and refreshed are you before and after an evening alone in front of the TV set?” Then you can make a mental comparison: how would you feel after spending the evening with a friend or pursuing a hobby? Resuming social interactions can be particularly difficult if you have been avoiding them for a long time. If a mental illness is causing this behaviour, you should seek professional help. Depression should be treated. Taking small steps to reconnect If mental illness is not the cause, Reichhart advises reviewing your social network: who is part of it? Who would you like to get back in touch with? Common interests such as sport can be a good way to re-establish contacts. She also advises marking firm times in your calendar for social contacts so that they are not forgotten amid the normal stresses of everyday life. Taking small steps is the best way to start socialising again. “Instead of going to a party, you could meet up with just one, very familiar person, or you could first send a message,” Nuyken says. And instead of inviting someone over to your home, you could meet in a cafe. This way you can better control how long the get-together lasts. Nuyken also recommends using a technique that is an element of depression therapy: structure before pleasure. This means, for example, that you resolve to send a message to a long-time acquaintance at 10am even if you don’t really feel like it. “It makes positive experiences possible,” Nuyken says, adding that waiting until you are motivated can exacerbate the problem “because it usually doesn’t happen”. Something else that can help you to break out of your self-imposed isolation is what Nuyken calls coexistence. By this he means meetings during which you don’t have to talk to each other the whole time – going to the cinema, for instance, “experiencing something together not involving deep conversation”. No matter how you go about it, it is important to spend time with others again, Reichhart says, noting that loneliness is a risk factor for many illnesses, not only mental ones. “We’re social beings, and relationships with other people are our lifeblood,” she says.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong, crowned world’s freest economy again, can’t rest on its laurels
description: The city’s decision to remain a free port, despite a challenging geopolitical environment and US tariffs, is a testament to its commitment to economic freedom.
content: Hong Kong has been ranked the world’s freest economy for the third consecutive year, and for the ninth time in the last 10 years. Despite the almost unbroken grip on the coveted ranking by the Fraser Institute, a top Canadian think tank, it is not to be taken for granted. The Hong Kong government sets great store by continued recognition of the city’s economic freedom because it is fundamental to its competitiveness. For example, after the city lost first place to Singapore in 2023, on regulatory and legal environment grounds among other reasons, officials vigorously disputed every one of the criticisms, pointing to “factually wrong” and “unfounded” statements. In fact, the relevant data was two years old – the latest available – and dated back to the Covid-19 pandemic and the aftermath of social unrest in Hong Kong. A claim that the city’s ranking was likely to fall even further proved to be unfounded. The latest Fraser Institute report, compiled by the Vancouver-based public policy research organisation using data from 2024, ranked Hong Kong first among 165 jurisdictions. Hong Kong scored 8.53, down 0.02 from the previous year. Switzerland scored 8.45, up from 8.38 the previous year and lifting it ahead of Singapore into second place behind Hong Kong. The city state, which scored 8.43, was followed by New Zealand with 8.38 and the United States with 8.21. Among other major economies, Britain ranked 13th, Japan 17th, India 86th and mainland China 108th. The report assessed regulation, openness to international trade, the size of government, the legal system, property rights and the stability of the currency. It also measured people’s freedom to make economic decisions in their countries or cities. Fraser Institute senior fellow Matthew Mitchell said: “Global economic freedom fell during the pandemic as policymakers imposed new regulations, raised barriers to trade, increased government spending and taxes, and then printed money to pay for the spending.” The think tank said that although governments had begun to reverse these policies, economic freedom generally had not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. A factor in Hong Kong’s ranking in the future – if not this time – is likely to be the government’s reaction to US President Donald Trump’s announcement in April last year of a global tariff regime: unequivocal affirmation of the city’s free-port status. The tariffs treated Hong Kong on a par with mainland China. Beijing enacted reciprocal tariffs to match US rates. Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po condemned the US levies as a violation of world trade rules and vowed the city would maintain its free-port, zero-tariff status. Confirming Hong Kong would not apply retaliatory tariffs on US goods, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said it would focus instead on diversifying markets and seizing opportunities in mainland China. The decision enhanced Hong Kong’s status as an international trading centre. Under the “one country, two systems” framework, Hong Kong remains a free port. A government spokesman said the Fraser Institute report once again affirmed Hong Kong’s strengths as a free-market economy and its open, efficient and fair business environment. “Amid increasing global economic uncertainties and rising trade protectionism, Hong Kong remains firmly committed to maintaining its free-port status, zero-tariff policy, and simple and low tax regime, providing a secure, stable, fair, predictable and internationalised business and investment environment for investors and entrepreneurs from around the world,” he said. Factors that may have weighed on Hong Kong’s ranking, leading to a drop in its overall score, include government-led investment such as bond issuance, the impact on the currency through the US dollar peg amid interest rate rises, and perceptions of the legal system arising from political events and security laws. Rankings are not everything but still important. Hong Kong should not rest on its consistent achievement of top ranking. Amid geopolitical and economic tensions, the government needs to redouble its efforts to spread the story of a competitive, open economy, with a free flow of information and the rule of law under an independent judiciary.

title: Top 10: How would you help kindergarteners with special educational needs feel valued?
description: If readers taught a class for a day, these are the creative steps they would take to be supportive and inclusive of children with special educational needs (SEN
content:
Our next question: If you could invent an AI tool to make student life easier, what would it do? To take part, drop us a line via this form by 12pm on Tuesday, October 13 .
Jayden Lee, 16, Carmel Secondary School: As a student with mild autism, I have experience with how my kindergarten teachers helped me integrate with other students. I think letting pupils engage in diverse activities, even something as simple as taking part in other classes, helps them feel valued by the school. Moreover, some young pupils are hyperactive and do not take part in naptime properly. To make them feel treasured, you could reward them for doing activities that do not come easily to them. For example, you could say, “If you sleep like a log this time, when we turn the lights on again, you can play with the Legos over there.” This makes the pupils feel accomplished. Lam Yuen-ying, 16, Lung Kong WFSL Lau Wong Fat Secondary School: I would design a “Superpower Wall” to showcase each SEN child’s unique talent, such as drawing or storytelling. I would also organise sensory play games. These activities will highlight pupils’ individual strengths, foster empathy and help SEN kids feel accepted, cherished and truly valued.
Nicole Chan Cheuk-ying, 17, Shatin Tsung Tsin Secondary School: I would ask each student to create their very own drawing based on how they see themselves. While they draw, I would ask them questions about their strengths. After they finish drawing, I would ask the children to praise each other’s drawings, as feeling celebrated by peers boosts pupils’ confidence, especially children with special educational needs. The process also encourages expression, allowing them to share their unique perspectives of the world.
Reno Lee, 15, Fung Kai No 1 Secondary School: I would create a safe space with a visual schedule and a simple welcome ritual that would help every child feel secure. Story time would be multisensory, with props and movement, so all could join at their own level. Each child would have a meaningful role and a way to decompress. A rotating buddy system would build bonds and empathy. Sylvia Tang Sum-ying, 14, Leung Shek Chee College: I would set up a “calm corner” in the classroom, complete with books, toys and some colouring pens. I would explain to the class that anyone who feels overwhelmed, tired or in need of space can come here to rest and recharge. I think this corner would also help them feel valued.
Joey Lam Tang-ching, 13, St Mary’s Canossian College: I would create a corner dedicated to story time, featuring puppet shows. Traditional schools often have rigid structures, and students with special educational needs often have less awareness of their surroundings. A story corner will help these students interact, integrate and take part in performances, helping uncover their special talents. Angel Law Siu-yau, 12, Shatin Pui Ying College: I would host a group drawing activity on a big canvas. Pupils would use drawings to share their small acts of kindness, like holding doors for the elderly. SEN students could act as story‑leaders in sharing how they help others. This activity empowers them, building empathy and making them feel truly valued. Nolan Chan Wing-him, 16, CCC Kung Lee College: I would create a small problem or puzzle and ask them to help me solve it. For example, opening a “tight” bottle cap. Then, I would thank them to ensure they know they are appreciated.
Aegis Lam Hang-yu, 12, King Ling College: As an autistic person myself, one reason we might not talk is that we do not think we have good topics to discuss. If I led a kindergarten class for a day, I would talk about the television series My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic . In the show, the ponies go on adventures and solve problems with their friendships. This would give the children something to discuss. Hazel Huew, 15, Christian Alliance S.C. Chan Memorial College: I would create cards for every child. In the morning, each pupil would decorate their small card to explain how they would like to say hello and show me when they need a break. They would also add one thing they are good at. I would help children who cannot write use drawings, stickers, photos and symbols, and I could also write for them. We would keep the cards together using a ring. Before partnered play or group time, pupils can peek at a friend’s card and understand how they would like to be included, maybe by waving, signing, pointing or being allowed to sit quietly. This would make communication easier and more engaging for pupils with special educational needs. It would help them feel valued because their way of communicating is respected, their strengths are seen and their classmates have a simple, kind way to connect with them.
Last week we asked students: “If you taught a kindergarten class for a day, what creative steps would you take to help pupils with special educational needs feel valued?”
This question has been sponsored by Yew Chung College of Early Childhood Education (YCCECE), Hong Kong’s only higher education institution dedicated to early childhood education and child development.
Building on over 90 years of Yew Chung experience and its “Learning Through Play” approach, the College offers government-recognised undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in early childhood education, child development, psychology and family counselling.

title: Trump picks Truth Social’s Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary
description: Zacharia, a lawyer who frequently appears on conservative news outlets, is an adviser for the US president’s social media platform.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he has appointed Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for his Truth Social platform, to serve as White House press secretary following Karoline Leavitt’s departure in August. He said Zacharia ‌has an “unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter”. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The New York Times first reported the news of her appointment. The selection will put Zacharia at the ⁠centre of the White House’s public messaging operation in the final stretch before next month’s midterm elections, when Trump’s agenda ‌and his party’s control of Congress will be put before voters. Zacharia said in a social media post that she welcomed the appointment and looks forward to “working with the White ‌House press corps, and with reporters across the country” to get Trump’s message out. Trump’s approval rating fell ⁠to 32 per cent – the lowest ⁠of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living and the Iran war, a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll ‌found. The selection of Zacharia underscores the close ties between Trump’s administration and his broader political and media operation. It comes after Trump Media unveiled in ‌July ‌that for a fee it would give banks and trading firms “the fastest” access to posts from influential Truth Social ‌accounts, such as the president’s, whose posts often move global markets. Zacharia has worked as a senior communications adviser for Truth ⁠Social, the Republican president’s social media platform, and the Trump Media and Technology Group since June, according to her LinkedIn page. She ⁠briefly served as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security before departing in March. Zacharia, a lawyer who frequently appears on conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax, previously worked as a legal adviser for ‌Fix California, a conservative group ‌that aims to address what it described as “the left’s stranglehold” on state politics. The group was founded by Richard Grenell, who has served as Trump’s envoy to Venezuela and the interim president and executive director of the Kennedy Centre in Washington. Zacharia interned at the White House during President George W. Bush’s administration.

title: Panama rocked by 2 powerful earthquakes, multiple aftershocks
description: The 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude tremors caused buildings to collapse and prompted evacuations across the country.
content: Two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks struck Panama on Friday afternoon, collapsing buildings near the epicentre and prompting evacuations across the country, the US Geological Survey said. The earlier quake, felt as far away as neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (six miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 10km. The USGS initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7. Visibly shaken residents of Panama City gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday. “We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” said Rosendo Dominguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck. “Everyone is outside, scared.” Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt. Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months. Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela’s La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people. Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino called for calm on Friday, saying on social media: “What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder.” Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers. Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonome, around 150km (93 miles) from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported. Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million travellers in 2025, said it would temporarily suspend operations and activate evacuation plans. It said operations would resume once security conditions had been checked. The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the key global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialised technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage. The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centred in nearby Costa Rica killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas de Toro region. Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama’s border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates. Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire”, a 40,000km (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. The National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning on Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. It warned that waves ranging from three to nine feet (one to three metres) above tide may occur in some coastal areas of Panama. Alerts were also issued in El Salvador and as far as Chile’s Easter Island, about 3,500 km (2,175 miles) off Chile’s mainland coast. Chile’s government placed the island under a precautionary advisory. Nearby countries sent messages of support on Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times”. “Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he said on social media. The US embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.

title: Exclusive | What are the concerns and priorities behind the new language used to define China-US ties?
description: The two sides have now agreed to include principles such as ‘respect’ and ‘fairness and reciprocity’ that reflect their different priorities.
content: When China and the United States agreed in May to frame their relationship as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”, the phrase left many observers trying to guess what it actually meant. Four months on, they have added an elaboration that offers further insight into the two sides’ respective priorities. After presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington last month, the two sides pledged to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity”. According to people familiar with the matter, the new phrasing was agreed following a diplomatic back and forth in which Washington had pushed for the relationship to be defined by “fairness and reciprocity”, while Beijing insisted that “respect” be written in as well. Sources said US officials had been pushing for their preferred wording to be added since the Beijing summit in May. At the time, the White House used the phrase “fairness and reciprocity” in a fact sheet but China’s statements did not. They said Beijing had initially resisted the use of those words but softened its stance in the run-up to the September summit after securing Washington’s agreement to describe relations as being built on mutual respect. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi offered the clearest insight into the latest wording after last month’s summit. He said respect meant “respecting each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, respecting each country’s choice of social system and development path, and respecting the other side’s core interests and major concerns”. He also said fairness involved pushing for mutually beneficial cooperation, handling differences through dialogue and “not seeking unilateral absolute advantage”. And reciprocity, he added, meant that the two countries were “equal in sovereignty, that neither side stands above the other, [and] that neither engages in hegemonic or bullying behaviour”. China’s insistence on the principle of respect reflects the importance Beijing attaches to sovereignty and “core interests”, a term used to describe issues such as Taiwan. Xi emphasised Beijing’s position on “safeguarding national reunification and territorial integrity” at the recent summit, urging the US to “adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwanese independence and handle the Taiwan question with caution”. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser on US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said the Trump administration did not want to give the impression it had uncritically accepted China’s framing of their relationship. By attaching the “fairness and reciprocity” language, Washington made its acceptance an “ongoing negotiation instead of a discrete decision”, he said. China, meanwhile, wanted to engage the US as a “near-peer”, believing it had the upper hand in shaping the relationship. “By stipulating such an expansive conception of ‘respect’ – one that includes its ‘core interests and major concerns’ – China can frame virtually any competitive actions that the United States takes as undercutting the framework,” he said. “Beijing feels confident in taking that step because President Trump is keen to maintain both a cordial rapport with President Xi and a tactical thaw in bilateral relations.” David Arase, resident professor of international politics at the Hopkins-Nanjing Centre, said: “The US pushed to add ‘fairness and reciprocity’ because it wants China to meet US norms and legal standards of free-market trade and investment relations conducted on the principle of reciprocal and equitable market access.” He also said Beijing had pushed for the wording about respect – including respect for a country’s chosen political system – because it wanted to reserve the sovereign right to “maintain its extensively party-state regulated and state-owned financial and industrial model of trade and investment relations with the US to maintain its existing political and economic system”.

title: As I see it | The EU is its own worst enemy
description: From industrial decline and debt woes to political polarisation, Europe’s crisis is home-grown – and blaming China won’t fix it.
content: Another day, another hardline statement from the European Union. This week, the European Parliament voted by a landslide for a significantly tougher China position, despite long-standing Beijing lobbying. The report labels China a “decisive enabler” of Russia, calls for a “continuous” European naval presence and joint exercises in and around the Taiwan Strait, and describes Beijing’s industrial policy as an “existential threat to the EU”. “[T]his parliament can send a clear message: no more dumping, no more spying and fair competition,” said its lead author, the Belgian lawmaker Hilde Vautmans. The message may be clear; its wisdom is not. European warships near Taiwan will not make Beijing back down. Reunification is the one issue on which Beijing will never compromise. This came after France and Germany demanded a new trade weapon, set out in a joint paper and a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. It threatens to cut off access to the EU market when third countries cause severe distortions. In effect a kill switch, it would grant the European Commission dramatic new powers to respond swiftly. Brussels wanted to present a united, hardline front ahead of the crucial negotiations with Beijing this week. But France, Germany and the union itself were negotiating from a position of profound weakness, without the traditional backing of Washington, which has even turned hostile. France faces a mounting fiscal crisis. Students have led violent mass protests against austerity cuts, while bond markets signal deep discontent. Borrowing costs have hit their highest in 24 years, now exceeding those of Italy and Greece. Debt has surged to €3.6 trillion (US$4 trillion) – 119 per cent of gross domestic product – during Emmanuel Macron’s presidency, and a hung parliament hampers consolidation. Analysts warn of a self-fulfilling spiral in which rising debt-servicing costs widen the deficit and push borrowing costs higher still, raising fears of euro-zone contagion requiring European Central Bank intervention. The far right’s rising polls before next year’s presidential election add uncertainty. Germany’s growth has stalled since 2020, with latest projections of roughly 1 per cent this year, and that’s considered high. Rising energy costs, bureaucracy and crumbling infrastructure have hurt manufacturing and the chemical industry, while Chinese competition has undercut its traditional strengths in cars and high-end machinery. Frustration has fuelled record gains for the far-right Alternative for Germany, notably in eastern states such as Saxony-Anhalt. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government languishes at historic lows in public approval, and executives from Siemens, Mercedes-Benz and Deutsche Bank have warned that right-wing extremism threatens investment and talent recruitment. Europe led in technology in the 1970s but has stagnated since 1990, missing both the IT and artificial intelligence revolutions. Its labour productivity lags America’s by 20 per cent; only two of the world’s 100 most valuable hi-tech companies are EU-based. While America’s leading companies change each decade, Europe’s remain dominated by German carmakers. Tesla and SpaceX flourished through venture capital as Europe’s auto and space industries declined. Rigid labour laws, a fragmented single market, excessive regulation and a lack of business leaders able to mentor and invest in entrepreneurs have stifled a genuine start-up ecosystem. Only about 30 per cent of the reforms prompted by Mario Draghi’s 2024 competitiveness report have been implemented, and these prove insufficient. Brussels must drastically simplify rules such as the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act, which have reduced venture capital investment. China, meanwhile, learned from the US and is now a close rival. While America’s leading companies change each decade, Europe’s remain dominated by German carmakers Ordinary Europeans pay the price. The costly decoupling from cheap Russian fossil fuels brought record energy bills and supply shortages, driving inflation in the euro area to a peak of 10.6 per cent in 2022. Black Sea blockades disrupted grain supplies and raised food costs. The bloc has committed vast sums, including a €90 billion loan programme for Ukraine, while managing millions of refugees. Ageing populations resisting reform, and elites dismissive of voter grievances, notably over immigration, fuel populism and democratic erosion. Europe’s moral authority has also suffered. As then EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell acknowledged, the bloc stands accused of double standards. It called Russia’s targeting of Ukrainian infrastructure “acts of pure terror” and imposed comprehensive sanctions, yet has struggled to condemn comparable violations in Gaza. The perceived hypocrisy has alienated much of the Global South and weakened the soft power on which EU influence rests. Caught between America, Russia and China, European leaders should recognise Beijing may be the least of their worries. They can make China a trading partner or an existential enemy. China can live with either outcome. The EU cannot.

title: Port of LA, key US point for China imports, has best-ever quarter despite trade uncertainty
description: Port of Los Angeles, the US’ leading gateway for imports from China, had its busiest three-month period on record from July to September.
content: The Port of Los Angeles, the largest container port in the United States and the country’s leading gateway for imports from China and other Asian countries, had its busiest three-month period on record from July through to September, despite persistent uncertainty over tariffs and shifting global trade supply chains. “If there was ever a time for a drum roll, this is it,” said Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, during a media briefing on Friday. “July through September was our best quarter in port history at almost three million TEUs [twenty-foot equivalent units]. Stretch it back to June, and we moved almost four million container units. That’s the strongest four-month stretch that we’ve ever had,” he added. TEUs are a standard industry measure of cargo capacity based on the volume of a single 20-foot shipping container. Seroka cited several factors behind the increase, including a reduction in tariffs from 2025 levels, strong consumer demand ahead of festival season and continued operational challenges at the Suez and Panama canals. The port’s imports rose 19 per cent year-on-year in September, while exports increased by a more modest 10 per cent. “Outbound volumes remain softer than normal, which reflects the ongoing challenges facing American farmers and manufacturers,” Seroka noted. While China’s share of imports through the LA port has declined from roughly 60 per cent in 2018 to a projected 40 per cent in 2026, it remains the port’s largest source of imports, followed by Vietnam. US imports from China totalled US$308 billion in 2025, down close to 30 per cent, according to data from the US Trade Representative office. US imports from Vietnam rose 42 per cent in the same period. Willy Shih, a professor at Harvard Business School, said countries like Vietnam and Mexico have seen “a lot of growth” in their imports to the United States, but they still rely on “Chinese intermediate goods”. “So companies, in some sense, are rearranging the final assembly step while the upstream dependence remains,” he said during a discussion at the LA port media briefing. Speaking about last month’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington, Shih said that the economic outcomes remained modest and both sides had decided to “kick the can down the road”. Washington and Beijing agreed to keep their Busan trade truce in place until January 10, 2027, extending it by two months beyond its original November 10 expiry, and launched the Board of Trade mechanism, listing non-sensitive products worth up to US$30 billion on each side that would be eligible for tariff reductions. Xi and Trump are due to meet again next month at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, and again in December at the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida. Despite the frequent meetings and announcement of the trade framework, Shih argued, the situation for traders remains uncertain given the mismatch between Washington’s “transactional approach” and Beijing’s “strategic approach”. “People need a longer horizon where they can have some stable framework, a stable set of rules to engage in their planning,” Shih said. “So until our leaders get together and get some stability, we are just going to have to be in an environment where people are planning contingencies and creating options.”

title: Who is Briley King, Marcus King’s wife dubbed ‘country music’s most hated’?
description: Marcus King’s controversial wife, Briley, recently announced her music career – here is everything to know about the singer and entrepreneur.
content: Briley King, who is married to country musician Marcus King and has been labelled “country music’s most hated wife”, announced in September that she was hard-launching her own music career. After occasionally joining her husband on stage for a few couple duets, Briley debuted her first release, Huswife, on September 17, which includes her debut songs “Bad Guy” and “Keepin’ Caroline”. Unfortunately, her foray into the music scene has not been well received by many who have flooded Briley’s social media with comments accusing her of being a “fame-chasing ‘nepo wife’”, as per the Daily Mail, who ran an article dubbing her “country music’s most hated wife”. Several netizens have accused Briley of being disingenuous, with a Reddit user writing in a forum: “I think there’s an insincerity in the way she has presented herself and her intentions. History shows that she has been chasing fame and a music career for most of her life, but since being with Marcus, she’s acted as if this wasn’t something she wanted and it just happened/was pushed on her.” Briley, however, is seemingly unbothered and recently responded to all the hate she has received with an Instagram post on October 5 featuring a snap of herself and the caption “12 hour work day, this most hated wife gig is keeping me busy”. So who is Briley King? Here’s everything you need to know. Briley King is a North Carolina native Briley King, born Briley Hussey, was born and raised in North Carolina. As a child, she participated in various activities including dancing, singing, gymnastics, theatre, basketball and softball, as per her profile in City Lifestyle. But it was singing that King was most dedicated to. When she was seven years old, her parents reportedly told her she would have to fund herself if she wanted to take singing lessons. Determined, she sang on the streets until she’d collected enough money. Despite her love of singing, King graduated with a degree in communications from East Carolina University and kick-started her corporate career in litigation before moving into finance. How did she meet Marcus King? Briley first met Marcus King, the lead singer, guitarist and founder of The Marcus King Band, in 2021 after she attended one of his concerts with her friends for her 30th birthday. She later posted a photo of herself at his concert and tagged King’s personal Instagram account, only to receive a personal message from him, which led to their first date. The couple was engaged seven months later. “I fell in love, hard!” King told People about first meeting Briley. “She waltzed up on my bus like she owned it, and I was taken with her sweet Southern drawl. She asked to connect to the Bluetooth, blared Linda Ronstadt and Aretha Franklin and we sang and danced till it was time for the bus to leave. I told her the next morning to quit her job and marry me instead.” The couple tied the knot in February 2023. She’s an entrepreneur Briley is also an entrepreneur and launched Little Bird Trucking, a hat company, in 2023. The brand came to be after Briley started wearing trucker hats on the daily because life on a tour bus meant she never knew when her next hair-wash day would be. The company’s name is inspired by King’s nickname for her (“little bird”), and her father, who is a long-haul truck driver. Since launching Little Bird Trucking, the brand has become a staple among country musicians, with several big names, including Post Malone, sporting the label’s hats.

title: Trump announces major diesel deal with Russia ahead of US midterm elections next month
description: Shock move reverses years of US pressure on Moscow over Ukraine war, as the president seeks to lower spiralling fuel costs.
content: US President Donald Trump has opened the American market to Russian diesel, reversing years of sanctions pressure on Moscow just three weeks after signing a law to punish buyers of its energy, as record fuel prices threaten his party in next month’s midterm elections. Trump said on Truth Social on Friday that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin had reached the supply deal in a phone call that had been expected to focus on suspected plague cases in Russia. According to Trump, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and an additional one million tonnes after that. A further three million tonnes would follow “within a short period of time”, depending on the condition of Russia’s refineries, he said. “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said that lowering fuel prices for Americans – especially farmers, ranchers and truck drivers – was his “greatest priority”. He also reiterated that “Iran will not have nuclear weapons”. Later on Friday, Putin said in a Kremlin statement that Russia was ready to supply oil and oil products to the United States and global markets, adding that this would help the global economy as a whole. The call had originally been scheduled to discuss suspected plague cases in Russia, but Trump abruptly announced the major energy agreement. Diesel agreement ‘will benefit the world’, says Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, said on X that “Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world”. Shortly after the announcement, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a general licence authorising all transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading or import of diesel of Russian origin, including imports into the United States, until April 7, 2027, five months after the midterms. The licence sets no cap on volumes. Its only stated exclusion is for debits from accounts held at US financial institutions by Russia’s central bank, its National Wealth Fund or its finance ministry. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the move a sign of weakness. “Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness,” he said on X. “We count on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one.” Trump’s focus on energy prices comes less than a month before the US midterm elections on November 3, with fuel prices now a central campaign issue. A poll from the Associated Press-NORC Centre for Public Affairs Research shows 65 per cent of US adults now blame Trump’s policies more than factors outside his control for persistently high costs. Two overlapping wars have driven the broader energy crisis. Since February 28, 2026, the US and Israel have been at war with Iran. Iran hit back with missiles and drones and effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz. About 25 per cent of the world’s oil and petroleum products shipped by sea, and about 19 per cent of liquefied natural gas, normally pass through that strait. The war has now lasted more than seven months. Most commercial oil shipments have stopped, and energy prices worldwide have surged. Ukraine continues large-scale drone strikes on Russian refineries Meanwhile, in the Russia-Ukraine war, Ukraine has launched sustained large-scale drone strikes on Russian refineries. Russia’s refining output fell 30 per cent year-on-year in June, hitting its lowest level in more than 20 years, and the Russian government banned diesel exports in July to protect domestic supply. The two wars combined pushed US diesel prices from about US$3.71 a gallon before the war to a record US$6.52 on September 22. As of October 9, the day the deal was announced, the US national average remained US$6.28 a gallon. Those costs have fed into consumer goods, adding to US inflationary pressure. It remains unclear how much the phone agreement will affect oil prices. The three million tonnes in follow-on deliveries are explicitly conditional on “the condition of Russian refineries”. Given that Russia itself faces a fuel crisis, actual export volumes could fall short of what was promised. The global market is also extremely tight, with both China and Russia restricting fuel exports. The United States had previously asked European allies to release emergency diesel stocks and warned that if Europe did not act, Washington might limit its own diesel exports. The agreement also represents the biggest loosening of US energy sanctions on Russia since the 2022 Russia-Ukraine conflict. Last month, Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that included sanctions on Russian officials, banks and “shadow fleet” tankers, banned all new US investment in Russia, and directed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas. That policy has now undergone a major reversal, greatly reducing the likelihood that the sanctions will be implemented. Senate Democrats have repeatedly criticised Trump for easing sanctions on Russia, calling the move “a dangerous and indefensible gift to Putin.” Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, expressed his dissatisfaction, writing in a statement on X: “This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia. “Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he’s lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels.”

title: Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Israeli airport, UAE says
description: The planned suicide attack was inspired by the events of September 11 in the US, public prosecutors believe.
content: An Omani Flydubai co-pilot had intended to seize a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight and crash it into a terminal at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport on September 30 in a suicide attack before he ‌was thwarted by the captain, the UAE attorney general said on Friday. Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi’s statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened. Flydubai was not immediately available for comment. The plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors think, as a result of their criminal investigation launched on October 1. It ⁠found the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport”, the state ‌news agency WAM reported. It is the first public confirmation of the co-pilot’s September 11 inspiration. The aircraft was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with a crash axe, typically ‌kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies. The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 feet (4,900 metres) ⁠in 30 seconds before ⁠the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The suspect was transferred to the UAE, Flydubai’s ‌home country. Investigators examined Flydubai’s recruiting procedures and found the suspect had met all professional and security requirements, including holding a pilot’s licence ‌and ‌providing a certificate of good conduct. “However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to ‌carry out a terrorist plot,” Al Shamsi added. He said the 29-year-old had worked for airlines in different countries including Oman Air ⁠before joining Flydubai in January 2026. The investigation found there were signs of the suspect drifting towards “extremism and terrorism” as early ⁠as 2017, while he was studying in Australia. Royal Air Maroc has said that he underwent three months of training there in 2025, but that his application to work for the airline afterwards was rejected. UAE officials have ‌not identified the suspect; however, a person ‌with direct knowledge of the matter said he had been identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Al Shamsi said the suspect had told investigators he had prepared psychologically and physically for the attack by viewing material promoting terrorism and taking boxing lessons. Saudi Arabia has launched a separate safety investigation into flight FZ1073, sources said.

title: No Kyrie Irving yet, but Mavericks, Rockets still put on a show for NBA China Games fans
description: Point guard still to return from injury break, but fans still enjoyed an entertaining contest as well as a look at famous faces on sidelines.
content: Dallas Mavericks fans will have to wait just a little bit longer to see Kyrie Irving in their team’s colours for the first time in almost two years, after he sat out Friday’s 135-117 pre-season loss to the Houston Rockets in Macau. Even without the flashy point guard running things, however, the two Texas clubs still put on a show for the thousands that packed into The Venetian Arena for the second year of NBA China Games. When the 34-year-old does finally return after an injury break that began in March last year, he will have a new head coach directing him from the sidelines, with Dusty May making the step up from the collegiate game to the professional ranks this season. Like many, May said he was “just excited” to see the veteran guard back on the court, but added the “unbelievable leader” had still been a valuable asset during his recovery from the torn left ACL he suffered in a game against the Sacramento Kings. “He’s a wealth of knowledge, and so we’re encouraging him to share as much of that with everyone as possible,” May said. “There have been several times in practice when you’re watching him play and you realise how much gravity and leverage he provides for the other guys. “I think that’s one area where we can make a big improvement offensively. Simply having a floor general like him on the court, with a young group, I think, will open up a number of things. “The tension that he garners allows everyone else to have a little bit more space and a little bit more, I guess, creativity to play because of the attention that’s on him.” Irving might not play until Sunday, but he and Rockets star Kevin Durant have still been the main draws this week; however, even they did not elicit the roar that greeted the sight of former Houston centre Yao Ming sitting court side. Yao was just one of a number of famous faces who made their presence felt on Friday, with Mavericks owner Patrick Dumont, former England football captain David Beckham, three-time NBA champion Dwyane Wade, Alibaba founder Jack Ma and Brooklyn Nets owner Joe Tsai – also a founder and co-owner of Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post – also sitting nearby. Not far from the star-studded bench was former NBA sensation Jeremy Lin, sitting alongside boy band Mirror star Keung To, while NBA legends including Chris Bosh, Ray Allen, Mitch Richmond and Metta World Peace were all present, as was Chinese women’s basketball rising star Zhang Ziyu. Among those who made the trip for the five day basketball festival at The Venetian Macao was Liang Xiaoye, who paid four times the 888 yuan face value of her ticket on the secondary market. The teacher from Hangzhou, who was celebrating her birthday in Macau, said that as well as the basketball, she had been drawn by the appearance of China’s Winter Olympics gold medallist Wang Meng. The legendary short-track speed skater, who won four Olympic titles between 2006 and 2010, appeared at the NBA House as a crossover guest. “This Friday offered a perfect trifecta for me: experiencing the basketball I love, seeing my favourite speed skater, and celebrating my birthday,” said Liang, who arrived in Macau on Thursday as part of a 30-strong tour group. Fans came from near and far for the event. The Tranquille family – Melissa, David and Chante – made the trip from Perth, Western Australia, as part of Chante’s 21st birthday celebrations. The trio spent five days in Hong Kong before moving on to Macau, and mother Melissa estimated they had spent around A$21,500 (HK$118,000) on the “once-in-a-lifetime experience”.
