Although eager to watch stars on both sides, the family said they leaned slightly towards Dallas, and especially Irving. “I just love the way he handles the ball, his defence … his personality,” Melissa Tranquille said. “On and off the court he’s just a great, great guy.” In his absence, it was Rockets guard Fred VanVleet who stole the opening night’s show, knocking down three straight from beyond the arc to give his side – listed as the visitors – the lead. Heading into his second season, Cooper Flagg lived up to the expectations of head coach May, who said in a pregame press conference that the first overall pick in the 2025 NBA Draft could “score three levels, and make defensive plays on and off the ball”. The small forward lived up to his coach’s billing, easily topping the Dallas scorers’ table with 19 points, despite playing only the first half. Flagg connected on back-to-back baskets and a three-pointer to get his team going early in the second quarter. But with the rest of the team capable of only four baskets in the entire 12 minutes, and Flagg troubled with four personal fouls, the Mavericks saw the deficit balloon to 20 points at half-time, and they trailed 65-45. There was no way back for the “home team” after the restart; Rockets star Durant scored 15 points in 23 minutes as his team went on to down the Mavericks by 18 points. Turkish centre Alperen Segun also finished with a triple-double, tallying 16 points to go with 10 rebounds and 10 assists. Altogether, six Rockets players reached double figures. With both teams sporting their fair share of international players, with Serbia, Switzerland, France and Spain all represented, Rockets head coach Ime Udoka said basketball was “a worldwide sport with people bringing their experiences from everywhere”. “It’s like coaching is catching up as far as that aspect goes,” the 49-year-old from Oregon said. “There is obviously a larger influx of players now, and coaching as well. So, it’s great to get different perspectives from people that have coached and played in different parts of the world.”

title: US slaps sanctions on ICC, hours after ex-judge wins Nobel
description: The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, and the move puts the US on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
content: US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order” and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. “The court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” it ‌said in a statement. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment.” The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. ‌Friday’s move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself. “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement. “That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.” ICC Deputy Prosecutor Khan said the sanctions “must be condemned”. “The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing,” Khan said. “Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions.” Washington has long been angry over ICC ⁠arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan which the ICC has since closed. The court, founded in 2002 ‌to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the Nato alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in ‌the Netherlands, an EU and Nato member. Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work in international criminal justice, served ⁠as a judge on the ICC’s Appeals ⁠Chamber from 2003 to 2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”. “An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the ‌victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” the committee said. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns. He did not provide further details, but ‌a senior ‌State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licences “to protect American interests”, an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions. US sanctions typically ‌bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation. The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials ⁠during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025. Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect ⁠of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance. The court’s registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called “blocking mechanism” that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions. In his statement, ‌Rubio said the United States had delayed its sanctions ‌hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defence, to rein in the court,” Rubio said. “We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly,” Rubio said.

title: Hong Kong lawmakers back 5-year plan as firms urged to align with blueprint
description: Liaison office chief calls on mainland firms to align themselves with five-year plan and play a greater role in city’s economic development.
content: Hong Kong’s legislature has passed motions supporting the city’s first five-year plan and thanking Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu for his latest policy address, while Beijing’s top representative in the city urged mainland Chinese enterprises to align themselves with the government’s blueprint. At the close of a three-day Legislative Council debate on Friday, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki thanked lawmakers for their suggestions, saying they would help improve governance. “The process of formulating the city’s five-year plan and the in-depth discussion at the Legislative Council have demonstrated a positive interaction between the administration and the legislature, with both striving for the best for Hong Kong,” he said. “I believe that, as long as we work together, remain proactive and pragmatic, we will be able to fully implement the five-year plan, create a better future for residents and make Hong Kong a bridge connecting China and the world.” While backing the two motions, lawmaker Junius Ho Kwan-yiu said the five-year plan had plenty of content but lacked concrete targets. Ho pointed to the document’s description of annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth as remaining “within a reasonable range” and Lee’s explanation that Hong Kong’s economy was subject to external factors. “I hope the government can show more determination,” Ho said. Lee unveiled the annual policy address last month alongside the five-year plan, which aims to align Hong Kong’s development with the national development strategy. The two documents set out initiatives to accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject and strengthen the city’s position in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology. Some lawmakers highlighted the government’s coming tasks, such as rebuilding public confidence in the malpractice-plagued building maintenance market following the deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court in November last year that killed 168 people and displaced about 5,000. Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan urged the government to consider setting up a statutory body to supervise building maintenance works and introducing third-party construction cost assessments, among other measures, to stamp out back-room deals and bid-rigging. Fellow lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu backed a suggestion to establish a dedicated authority to monitor building renovations, saying that overcoming gridlock was an “inevitable reform”. Separately, Zhou Ji, director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong, urged mainland enterprises operating in the city to align themselves with the government’s first five-year plan and play a greater role in its economic development. Speaking at a reception hosted by a business group on Friday, Zhou outlined three expectations for mainland firms, including that they capitalise on Hong Kong’s advantages under the “one country, two systems” principle to cultivate new growth drivers. He also called on companies to leverage Hong Kong’s position as a gateway to international markets, work closely with the government’s task force supporting mainland businesses expanding overseas, and attract more enterprises to establish a presence in the city. Zhou further urged firms to strengthen their grass-roots engagement and charitable work to improve residents’ livelihoods and sense of well-being.

title: K&K offers extra warranty to One Stanley homebuyers amid building defects furore
description: The under-pressure developer will offer buyers a six-year structural warranty, as it tries to contain growing uproar over alleged construction issues.
content: Developer K&K Property has announced plans to offer a six-year structural warranty to homeowners at its luxury One Stanley development, as the company seeks to move on from a growing furore over alleged construction defects at the complex. “As the developer of the One Stanley development project, we attach great importance to the recent public attention surrounding one of the detached houses in the project,” the company said in a statement released late on Friday. One Stanley, a collection of luxury houses and flats on the southern side of Hong Kong Island, was thrown into disarray last weekend when the government announced it was launching an investigation into work quality issues at the development. “In addition to our original three-year defect liability period, we will provide [a] six-year structural warranty calculated from the completion date,” the company said. “Furthermore, we will arrange property inspections for owners and buyers by independent qualified professionals and bear the relevant costs, with specific arrangements to be notified separately.” The government probe has threatened to disrupt the project, with banks reportedly taking a more cautious approach to mortgage applications and at least one property agency suspending most viewings at the complex while the investigation was under way. K&K Property has been in discussions with the buyer who made the original complaint over building quality issues, proposing that both sides jointly hire an independent professional to conduct further inspections, according to the statement. “However, a consensus could not ultimately be reached, and the arrangement was not implemented,” the company said. “The two parties subsequently held discussions regarding the transaction arrangements and related demands, but no agreement was reached.” The developer said “there is no obvious danger regarding the overall building structure”. However, experts have called for stronger homebuyer protections, including implementing a mandatory period for buyers to rescind contracts when statutory violations are discovered. The company noted that it had “immediately contacted owners who have completed their transactions and is progressively reaching out to buyers whose transactions are currently under way”.

title: Developer of One Stanley pledges 6-year warranty and checks amid steel bar probe
description: K Wise offers extra structural coverage and free independent inspections for owners, buyers following claims of missing steel reinforcement.
content: The developer of One Stanley has offered flat owners a six-year structural warranty and free independent property inspections amid an investigation into suspected steel reinforcement deficiencies at the seaside luxury residential development in southern Hong Kong. K Wise, a subsidiary of One Stanley developer K&K Property, addressed the brewing scandal on Friday, a week after allegations of substandard work were reported by a local property media outlet, issuing a statement outlining remedial measures for homeowners and buyers completing transactions. “The company understands that the incident has caused concern among property owners, buyers and the public, and will make building safety and safeguarding the interests of owners its top priority,” K Wise said. “On top of the three-year defect liability period already provided by our company, we will also offer a six-year structural warranty from the date of completion of the purchase.” It added: “[We will] ... also arrange independent, qualified professionals to conduct property inspections for owners and buyers, and all costs will be covered”. The online property news platform claimed that an on-site inspection of a house found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts of the home. The number fell short by as much as 75 per cent from the approved building plans, according to the report. The property in question is a four-bedroom, 3,000 square foot (278 square metre) detached house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024 for about HK$100 million (US$12.7 million). The irregularities were subsequently spotted by engineers and contractors hired by the owner during internal renovations, according to the report. The owner made a report to the Buildings Department, which revealed last week it had been carrying out inspections at the development since March. The department has also asked the developer to submit a report. In Friday’s statement, K Wise said it had contacted the owner of the detached house in question to discuss follow-up plans. It said it had proposed that “both parties jointly hire an independent professional to conduct further inspections to clarify the circumstances”. But no consensus was reached, according to K Wise. Both sides had also discussed related claims but no agreement was reached either, the company said. “Regarding the private contracts and legal matters between the two parties, our company is not prepared to make further comments,” K Wise said. On follow-up actions, the company said it had contacted owners who had completed their transactions and was continuing to reach out to buyers who were currently in the process of making a transaction. “As the investigation is ongoing, it is not appropriate for our company to comment on unverified technical matters at this stage so as to avoid making speculations or biased judgments before the completion of the investigation,” it said. The South China Morning Post has learned that 24 transactions were recorded at One Stanley between March and September.

title: Travel agencies tout Huanggang Port tours, but security chief urges later visits
description: Tour firms promote revamped port including “five-minute clearance” as an attraction, with one agency reporting 10 groups booked for its opening day.
content: Hong Kong travel agencies are offering tours featuring “five-minute clearance” at the revamped Huanggang Port when it opens on Monday, but the security chief has urged those who do not need to use the crossing immediately to delay their visits. Three days before the port’s official opening, the South China Morning Post on Friday found a number of tour packages advertised on social media that promoted the redeveloped border checkpoint as a new attraction for trips to mainland China. An advertisement posted by Sino Step Travel Services on its Facebook page said: “Early access to the Huanggang Port for a brand new clearance experience!” Marketing manager Cici Chung Ka-lam said: “Since the government announced early Friday that the checkpoint would open at 6.30am on October 12, inquiries and bookings have risen markedly, with many residents eager to experience ‘five-minute clearance’.” She added that the checkpoint complex had “become a key selling point” of the agency’s tours. Big Line Holiday began preparing tours through the new checkpoint in early September and started selling short-haul trips to Guangdong priced at about HK$1,000 to HK$2,000 (US$127 to US$254). Sales director Kit Chan said the first tour sold out within two to three hours of going on sale. The agency now has 10 groups departing next Monday, each with about 40 people, most of them older travellers. “We have trained all our call centre and frontline staff to stress the new Huanggang checkpoint as the biggest selling point, which has the ‘joint inspection’ system to make clearance much faster and more efficient,” he said. “The two-border, two-check arrangement at the old Huanggang checkpoint was always a bit troublesome,” Chan said, adding that “many tour members told us that having to pull their luggage and transfer from buses was very inconvenient.” Chan said the company would arrange more tours through Huanggang if the checkpoint operated smoothly and passenger numbers remained manageable. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday authorities had allocated extra manpower and drawn up contingency plans to cope with unexpected surges in passenger numbers, anticipating strong interest in the crossing. “We understand that during the initial opening, some tour groups may view Huanggang Port as a new attraction, lingering a little longer during border clearance to take extra photos, which we consider completely understandable,” he said. “We have fully anticipated this situation. At the same time, we appeal to members of the public who are in no real rush to consider experiencing the facility at a later date.” Tang also warned that travellers should proceed with border clearance as soon as possible after entering the building, as failing to do so could constitute a breach of the law. The checkpoint will be the first to adopt the “joint clearance” model, where passengers can complete both departure and entry clearance in one three-gated automated channel.

title: Anthropic claims Chinese AI firms secretly use Claude. Is it true?
description: If the claims are true, Beijing’s main concern would not be intellectual property theft or model copying, but data security, says one analyst.
content: Did Chinese AI companies secretly tap US models to close the technology gap? That is the central question hanging over China’s tech sector following a wave of allegations from Washington and American AI lab Anthropic. According to a joint advisory by the National Security Agency, FBI, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency last month, Chinese AI developers have been systematically extracting capabilities from US frontier models to reduce their own computing, electricity and research costs. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent similarly warned in July that Chinese firms were engaged in large-scale “distillation”. Specifically, Anthropic claimed Chinese AI developers used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to siphon reasoning data from its flagship model, Claude – and in some cases even used the US model as a covert back end for their own apps. Here’s a closer look at whether the accusations hold water – and why Beijing is taking those claims seriously. What are Anthropic’s allegations? Anthropic accused Chinese developers of conducting “industrial-scale” distillation, a technique in which outputs from a more capable “teacher” model are used to improve another model. While model distillation is a common practice across the AI industry, Anthropic claimed Chinese firms crossed ethical lines. According to a report published by the company last month, Chinese labs circumvented usage restrictions through fraudulent accounts and third-party proxy services to harvest Claude’s output and reasoning traces at scale. Anthropic reported that over just 10 days, Moonshot routed almost 300,000 user requests, primarily to the Opus model. The Chinese company utilised a proxy network of 5,380 fraudulent accounts largely based in Singapore and Japan, Anthropic claimed. Furthermore, Anthropic alleged that some companies used Claude as a hidden back end. This meant users believed they were interacting with a domestic Chinese model when their queries were actually being processed by the US firm’s servers, the firm said. Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment. How strong is the evidence? Industry analysts are divided over the credibility and attribution of Anthropic’s findings. Konstantin Pilz, co-founder and fellow at the Washington-based Centre for Technology and Statecraft, considered the claims credible, noting that they reflected the intense pressure on Chinese developers facing US chip export restrictions. “To not fall further behind on AI model performance, Chinese AI companies have to use adversarial distillation on a large scale,” Pilz said, suggesting that distillation allowed domestic developers to leapfrog expensive reasoning data generation. Ben Hayum, a research assistant at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said Anthropic had long been able to gather threat-intelligence signals that could detect and attribute distillation attacks. However, other experts argued that pinpointing direct blame on Chinese AI companies was not always straightforward. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, noted that third-party proxy services – or “transfer stations” – might be the real culprits. These proxies might secretly divert user requests to Claude to obtain and sell reasoning data without the direct involvement of the Chinese AI labs, he said. Wang Zebin, an investment manager at Shenzhen-based private equity firm JG Investment focused on large language models and embodied intelligence, said Anthropic’s report “does not provide enough concrete examples to independently verify how those companies obtained or used the model outputs”, adding that the specific distillation methods described in the report were questionable. Why might Beijing be concerned? Chinese regulators were reportedly investigating domestic AI labs following Anthropic’s report. According to a report by The Information last month, the Cyberspace Administration of China questioned seven developers named by Anthropic before narrowing its focus to DeepSeek and Moonshot. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment. If the report was true, the main concern for Beijing would not be intellectual property theft or model copying, but data security, according to Pilz. Anthropic claimed that some of the prompts sent to Claude contained sensitive information from state-affiliated organisations and companies, as well as names, email addresses, and other corporate data. Re-routing sensitive data to American AI model providers may pose a “very significant security issue for China”, Chan said, adding that it would be “even more severe” than exposing search histories because users share so much data with AI. Coding requests in particular can leak underlying IT infrastructure or login credentials. “China should be seriously questioning this,” Hayum said, noting that regulators must evaluate whether they can trust domestic tech firms to safeguard sensitive data and manage emerging cybersecurity risks. Even if the allegations were true, however, Chan expected Beijing to handle the matter discreetly to avoid publicly validating Anthropic’s claims. Additional reporting by Minxiao Chang

title: China’s Pacific ties not part of ‘geopolitical rivalry’, Wang Yi tells island leaders
description: As US and China vie for influence in South Pacific, top diplomat stresses that Beijing remains a reliable partner to developing countries.
content: China’s cooperation with the Pacific islands is not part of a geopolitical competition, top diplomat Wang Yi told a delegation of politicians from the region on Friday. The comments come as Beijing and Washington vie for influence in the South Pacific. “China’s engagement with Pacific island countries is a form of South-South cooperation based on mutual assistance and support,” Wang said, according to a statement from the Communist Party’s International Department. “This cooperation does not interfere in the islands’ internal affairs, impose political conditions, engage in geopolitical rivalry or target third parties, nor is it subject to interference by third parties.” Wang made the remarks during a meeting in Beijing with a joint delegation of Pacific island politicians led by Tonga’s Deputy Prime Minister Viliami Latu. Wang said China’s diplomacy consistently stood with developing and smaller countries, describing Beijing as a reliable partner to Pacific island nations. “China supported the islands in pursuing development paths suited to their national circumstances and chosen by their own people, as well as in safeguarding their sovereignty, security and development interests,” he said. He urged the islands to continue upholding the one-China principle, saying Taiwan’s return to China after World War II formed an important part of the post-war international order. The delegation members described China as “a good friend and partner”, thanking Beijing for its long-standing help with their economic and social development, according to the department’s statement. They said the Pacific islands would continue to uphold the one-China policy and deepen cooperation with Beijing in infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, education, disaster prevention and relief, and capacity building. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Beijing has sought to persuade Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies in the region to switch formal recognition from Taipei to mainland China. Nauru, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands have all severed formal ties with Taipei and established diplomatic relations with Beijing. However, the Solomon Islands has since sought to rebuild ties with Washington, signing an agreement allowing US Coast Guard vessels to patrol its waters alongside local police officers. The diplomatic contest is unfolding alongside growing competition in the South Pacific, with Beijing seeking to deepen its diplomatic and economic ties while Washington and its allies offer new funding. At this year’s Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau, Washington and Canberra unveiled a joint US$580 million aid package for the region. In a parallel move, the US and New Zealand also pledged US$50 million and NZ$17.5 million (US$9.8 million), respectively, to upgrade a former World War II port in the Cook Islands. China’s expanding role has also drawn scrutiny from Australia and New Zealand. In July, the two countries criticised Beijing after it launched a ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine into international waters in the South Pacific, citing short notice and a lack of transparency. Despite the intensifying competition among outside powers, Pacific island leaders have stressed that regional security and development priorities should be determined by the island nations themselves.

title: Netflix K-drama The Blue Road: Son Suk-ku, Eita Nagayama hunt a vicious serial killer
description: This Netflix ‘buddy cop’ drama stars Son Suk-ku and Eita Nagayama as detectives from Korea and Japan working on the same serial killer case.
content: Lead cast: Son Suk-ku, Eita Nagayama Son Suk-ku and Eita Nagayama team up for the transnational crime thriller The Blue Road, Netflix’s upcoming K-drama in which they play rival detectives on the trail of a viciously creative serial killer whose crime spree spans South Korea and Japan. Adapted from the 2002 manhwa (Korean comic) – itself a cross-border collaboration steered by Takashi Nagasaki (aka Keishi Edogawa) and Gaya Kwon – and set against the backdrop of the 2002 World Cup co-hosted by the two nations, the show is much more than a straightforward murder mystery. Directed by Han Jun-hee (D.P.) and adapted by Cho Yu-jin (Pilot), The Blue Road plunges deep into the strained relationship between the two Asian powerhouses while also embracing the humorous dynamics of the mismatched buddy cop genre. The first three episodes of The Blue Road just premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, ahead of the show’s streaming debut in November. The body of a young woman is discovered in a disused building in Shinjuku, Tokyo. Her limbs are broken and horribly contorted, while her bloodstream is coursing with a new designer drug. A sinister slogan written in her blood on the wall above reads, “One fear breeds infinite fear, and all methods are concealed.” Renegade detective Hiroshi Inose (Nagayama) is assigned to the case. While examining the crime scene, he gives chase to a suspicious individual taking photographs. The stranger is revealed to be South Korean police detective Kim Seok (Son), who has been sent to Tokyo as part of an official joint investigation after a similar murder in Seoul. The connection between the victims appears to be the narcotic they were both using, known as Speed K. This clue leads the detectives to a local dealer, Takahashi (Yosuke Kubozuka), then to an ice-cold yakuza madame (Kim Shin-rok) and finally to “the photographer”, a hitman who terrorised yakuza gangs and collected photos of his gruesome crimes. However, after interrogating him in prison, the detectives realise that he is merely a copycat, emulating an even more gruesome killer whose crimes date back to 1980s Korea and who appears to have resurfaced. As is customary in these narratives, reluctant partners Kim and Inose clash in their opening exchanges, refusing to trust one another or disclose all the information their respective departments have on the case. Fuelling the rivalry is the lingering resentment over the two countries’ tumultuous past, brought to a boil by the World Cup matches playing out in the background. Soon enough, however, the pair set aside their differences and work together to catch the killer. When a woman is abducted in Seoul, the action shifts back to Korea, with Inose following his new partner to continue tracking the killer on Kim’s home turf. Digging deeper, they discover the origins of the mysterious slogan left at the murder scenes, which harks back to a violent general from Korea’s Joseon era (1392-1897), whose reign of terror may still be admired by a few dedicated radicals. Rarely does a month go by without a new thriller about a wildly inventive serial killer dropping on one of the streaming platforms. At first glance, The Blue Road might seem destined to disappear into the endless stream of content. However, its tonal shifts – from gruesome murder to barbed banter – as the two charismatic leads trade jabs while pursuing a potentially monstrous adversary make for a surprisingly engrossing watch. With a potent backdrop of unresolved conflict and resentment always threatening to erupt into a full-blown clash, The Blue Road has plenty to distinguish it from the competition. And while the series remains largely grounded in reality, a few teasing, unexplained elements tip the mystery into a more fantastical realm. Kim suffers from strange visions that sometimes manifest as shadowy figures lurking in his periphery and, at other times, as torrents of gushing blood. Meanwhile, a drug addict who witnessed the initial murder in Shinjuku claims the killer was more monster than man, taking the form of a giant tiger. In the third episode, the investigation points to a highly plausible suspect and unveils a potential – and undeniably hideous – motive behind the crimes. But viewers are best left to discover these details for themselves when the series launches. With five episodes still to air and Jung Jae-young confirmed to appear, though he has yet to make his debut, it would be reckless to take any of these revelations at face value. It is safer to assume that what we have seen is merely the tip of the iceberg. Based on the episodes screened so far, however, The Blue Road has us hooked. The Blue Road starts streaming on Netflix on November 20.

title: Why a ‘confrontational posture’ won’t help China in the Arctic
description: Chinese think tank says Beijing ‘still has considerable policy space’ in the region after US, Denmark and Greenland sign new security pact.
content: China should avoid taking a “confrontational posture” over a new security pact between the United States, Denmark and Greenland as it might end up being excluded from engagement on the emerging Arctic order. That was the warning from Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies (NISS), a Chinese think tank, in a report released on Wednesday. It also said the US was unlikely to turn the northern polar region into its “exclusive strategic backyard”. The report noted that Russia as well as America’s Nato allies including Canada and European nations could constrain how far a “northward Monroe Doctrine” would go. The new pact signed by the US, Denmark and Greenland on September 22 allows America to establish two new military bases in Greenland and gives it a formal say in vetting foreign investment in “sensitive” sectors on the world’s largest island, an autonomous Danish territory. Those sectors include but are not limited to critical infrastructure and resource extraction. The deal also bans states outside the Nato transatlantic security alliance from establishing military installations or deploying troops in Greenland without the consent of all three parties. Observers have said the agreement could have an impact on Beijing’s engagement in the Arctic because its activities in the region could face more scrutiny, while its efforts to develop polar shipping routes could be challenged. The NISS report echoed those views, saying that the deal would raise the political bar for Chinese capital, research and infrastructure projects to enter parts of the Arctic. “But China still has considerable policy space,” the institute said in the report, which was posted on social media. It noted that the Greenland agreement would not alter the rights of countries outside the region to take part in scientific research, navigation and global governance in the Arctic under international law. It said the pact also did not empower the US to close off the Arctic Ocean’s high seas or legitimate international shipping lanes. But the institute did caution against two “misjudgments” when assessing the impact of American policy on Chinese interests in the Arctic. “First, overestimating the speed of ice melt and the commercial value of shipping routes, leading to duplicated investment,” the report said. “Second, treating all Western restrictions as a denial of China’s legitimate rights and interests, thereby reinforcing the other side’s security concerns through a confrontational posture.” Still, the report said China remained the extra-regional force that the US was “most explicitly” seeking to guard against in the Arctic. The Donald Trump administration has designated the western hemisphere as Washington’s top foreign policy priority. That approach was framed in the 2025 National Security Strategy as the “Trump Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine”, invoking a policy from more than 200 years ago that warned European powers against interfering in the affairs of the Americas. Before the agreement was reached with Greenland and Denmark last month, Trump had repeatedly threatened to annex Greenland, citing national security concerns and the need to counter potential influence from Beijing and Moscow in the melting Arctic. Unlike the US and Russia, China is not an Arctic littoral state. Beijing described itself in a 2018 white paper as an “important stakeholder” in the region and a “near-Arctic state”. The NISS report said the Greenland security deal was a sign that the Monroe Doctrine’s scope – which traditionally focused on Latin America – was extending further north. “[Washington] is taking the Arctic as an extension of North America’s homeland security perimeter, using military denial, investment screening and alliance rules to restrict foreign activities at the northern end of the Americas,” the institute said. “Greenland’s particular value lies precisely in the convergence there of minerals, infrastructure and Arctic-North Atlantic routes, making it the most direct intersection of resource security and military security in the US ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’.” But the report also noted that the Arctic was not a no man’s land that the US could unilaterally carve up, and most of the land and offshore resources in the region were already subject to clearly defined sovereignty and jurisdiction. “The ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’ also has clear limits,” it said. The report was released a day before the Arctic Circle Assembly – the biggest annual international gathering on Arctic affairs – began in Reykjavik, Iceland on Thursday. American activities in the Arctic and China’s role in the region’s affairs are both on the agenda at the conference, which runs until Saturday. The Arctic has become a new flashpoint for great-power rivalry in recent years, as climate warming and record-low sea ice open the region to shipping and resource extraction. In its report, the NISS said the Greenland deal was unlikely to change Russia’s established presence in the region, but it could help the US to restrict rival powers’ access to strategic space in the northern reaches of North America. Russia has the world’s densest network of Arctic ports and the largest icebreaker fleet, while the Arctic shipping corridor known as the Northern Sea Route runs along its coast. The report also pointed to Canada’s long-standing claim that another sea lane – the Northwest Passage – lies within its territorial waters, noting that Ottawa could be wary of Washington trying to dominate the Arctic. In addition, the NISS noted that Finland, Sweden and Norway all had their own resource, shipping, local governance and security interests in the Arctic, and that they could seek to retain a degree of policy autonomy while maintaining security cooperation with the US under the Nato framework. It also argued that, given the European Union’s increased investment in recent years in Greenland’s communications, energy, mining and infrastructure, it might be hard for the US to “unilaterally securitise” those areas in future. “Russia’s coastal advantages, Canada’s sovereignty claims, the autonomous interests of the Nordics and the EU and China’s continued participation all limit the expansion space of the ‘northward Monroe Doctrine’,” the NISS said. “The US can strengthen its influence on specific areas, but it will find it difficult to turn the entire Arctic into an exclusive strategic backyard.” It said the key to China’s future policy on the Arctic would be improving scientific research and shipping, expanding industrial cooperation, taking part in multilateral rule-making and continuing Arctic engagement. “[China should] avoid being excluded from the process of shaping the future Arctic order while respecting Arctic states’ sovereignty and local community interests,” the report concluded. It said China should continue investing in areas including polar science, sea-ice forecasting and ecological monitoring, improve the foundations for its involvement in Arctic shipping, and increase the transparency of commercial projects. The institute also called on Beijing to remain involved in setting international rules on Arctic shipping, fisheries, environmental protection and ocean governance.

title: NBA China Games draw fans from near and far, Irving just one of the star attractions
description: Houston Rockets, Dallas Mavericks get the 2026 matches under way at The Venetian Macau, where a China Olympian is an equally big draw.
content: Basketball fans draped in the red of Houston and blue of Dallas flooded into The Venetian Macau on Friday ahead of the first of this year’s NBA China Games. The exhibition between the Rockets and Mavericks forms the centrepiece of a five-day basketball festival that tipped off on Wednesday and will conclude with a second match between the two on Sunday. Crowds gathered hours in advance of the opening tip-off, and lengthy queues snaked past the prominent NBA House entrance archway along the carpeted concourse of the Cotai Expo. Inside the venue, fans flocked to NBA merchandise exhibits, food pop-ups, and interactive set-ups including shooting challenges and video game stations. The event also featured photo sessions with NBA legends including Ray Allen, Chris Bosh, Carlos Boozer, and Jeremy Lin, alongside appearances by celebrities including Hong Kong singer Keung To, rapper MC Jin, and K-pop artist Evan. For the thousands in attendance, the event offered more than just elite basketball, and it provided a stage for deeply personal milestones. Among the crowd was Liang Xiaoye, who said the premium ticket she had been forced to buy on the secondary market had been worth every penny. The teacher from Hangzhou, who was celebrating her birthday in Macau, said that as well as the basketball, she had been drawn by the appearance of China’s Winter Olympics gold medallist Wang Meng. The legendary short-track speed skater, who won four Olympic titles between 2006 and 2010, appeared at the NBA House as a crossover guest. “This Friday offered a perfect trifecta for me: experiencing the basketball I love, seeing my favourite speed skater, and celebrating my birthday,” said Liang, who arrived in Macau on Thursday as part of a 30-strong tour group. “She showed me that even in your 30s or 40s, you can still step out of your boundaries, explore new fields, and continuously progress. I consider this a stage that accompanies my own growth.” Determined to attend, Liang turned to the secondary market after standard tickets sold out. “I paid four times the original 888 yuan face value,” she said. “Someone at the entrance just asked if they could buy it from me for 3,500 yuan, and I immediately said no. I have to watch this. The price doesn’t matter; the multi-layered significance of today makes it completely worth it.” The international draw of the event was equally evident among fans travelling from farther afield. For the Tranquille family – Melissa, David, and Chante – attending the NBA China Games in Macau was the culmination of a long-planned family celebration after flying in from Perth, Western Australia. The trip combined a five-day stay in Hong Kong to mark Chante’s 21st birthday with four days in Macau specifically for the games. The journey required a substantial financial commitment. The family spent A$7,000 (US$4,883) on game tickets alone, alongside A$4,500 on flights and around A$10,000 for accommodation. “We’ve worked hard, very hard, to be able to come and experience this with our kids,” Melissa Tranquille said. “And it’s definitely worth it. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience for us.” Securing access required ordering tickets as early as June as soon as sales opened, though high demand left the family sitting in separate sections. “I ordered our tickets back in June as soon as they went on sale,” Melissa Tranquille said. “I couldn’t get seats all together, so my husband and I are sitting separately … but we really wanted to be here.” While eager to watch star players on both sides, specifically Dallas’ Kyrie Irving and Houston’s Kevin Durant, the family leaned slightly towards the Mavericks as a team. “I just love the way he handles the ball, his defence … his personality,” Melissa said of Irving. “On and off the court he’s just a great, great guy.” Chante added her praise for Durant: “I think he’s super funny, I think he’s a great basketball player … and I can’t wait to watch him play.” Despite the long travel and logistical effort, the family expressed complete satisfaction with the fan experience and venue management at The Venetian. “We think they’ve done a fantastic job,” Melissa said. “The whole NBA House has been amazing … the way it’s set up, you can walk through all of it, it’s not too crowded, and the experience is amazing. It’s organised very well.” For local fans and foreign workers alike, the event offered a rare opportunity to experience an authentic NBA atmosphere close to home. Clifford Paderanga, a 32-year-old Filipino living and working in Macau, attended the event on his rest day alongside his girlfriend. A Dallas Mavericks supporter for more than a decade since the Dirk Nowitzki era, Paderanga was eager to catch a glimpse of his team and star guard Irving. “In the Philippines before, I never had a chance to go to this kind of event,” Paderanga said, adding that he was still trying to get a ticket to one of the games. “I don’t care how much it costs, as long as I can still afford it.”

title: US lawmakers push green card bill for Hongkongers, but observers doubt success
description: Broad Republican opposition to immigration expansion and tight legislative calendar expected to derail Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act.
content: Two US lawmakers are pushing for a bill that would allow Hongkongers in the country to apply for permanent residency, but authorities and observers have dismissed it as a political move unlikely to succeed. Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, and Representative James McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, announced the Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act, seeking to provide a pathway to green cards and ultimately citizenship for Hong Kong residents in the US currently protected under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme. Introducing the bill, Merkley accused Beijing and Hong Kong authorities of continuing to “undermine the fundamental rights and freedoms of Hongkongers”. “The United States must protect Hong Kong residents who have sought refuge in America,” he said. “Congress must take action and enact our legislation to ensure Hongkongers residing in the US do not have to fear deportation.” The proposal drew criticism from both the Hong Kong and central governments. A Hong Kong government spokesman denounced the remarks as “unfounded and biased”, saying that authorities “steadfastly safeguarded the rights and freedoms enjoyed by Hong Kong people as protected under the law.” The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement to the South China Morning Post that Hong Kong affairs were purely China’s internal matters, in which no foreign government, force, organisation or individual could interfere. “China urges some members of the US Congress to stop pushing for the review of relevant bills concerning Hong Kong and to stop meddling in Hong Kong affairs and interfering in China’s internal affairs,” it said. Wilson Chan Wai-shun, co-founder of the Pagoda Institute think tank, said on Friday that the bill was very likely to perish in the current legislative session, and there would be insufficient time to process the proposal in the next session before DED protection expired on February 5, 2027. He explained that US lawmakers would focus on campaigns surrounding the midterm election in November, while the new batch of lawmakers, to be sworn in in early January, could not process the bill quickly because they would have to handle procedural matters. “If it cannot be realised within the current legislative session, there will not be enough time in the next session to cover the date when DED expires,” he said. “Then effectively, it would become useless.” DED is an executive measure that temporarily protects Hongkongers from deportation and allows them to work, but does not offer permanent legal status. It was introduced in 2021 by the Biden administration in response to Beijing’s imposition of the national security law on Hong Kong and was extended twice in 2023 and 2025 by the then president. It is not yet clear whether US President Donald Trump will renew it. Under the proposed bill, Hong Kong permanent residents and their families staying in the US relying on the programme would be able to apply for permanent residency, provided that they had been staying in the country continuously since January 15, 2025, without having returned to Hong Kong or mainland China. The proposal comes amid the Trump administration’s broader immigration crackdown, including moves to end Temporary Protected Status – which shields migrants from deportation and allows them to work – for people from more than a dozen countries, including Venezuela, Haiti and Honduras. Chan said although the Republicans’ and Democrats’ stances on China remained highly consistent, the bill also involved migration issues and might leave the Republican Party, which controls both chambers of Congress, with reservations. “[Republicans] do not have to explicitly object to the bill, but could just insist that it be deliberated through normal procedures,” he said. “In that case, the bill is already dragged to death.” Keeping full control over DED gives Trump significant leverage both as a diplomatic bargaining chip with Beijing and on domestic immigration, according to Chan. Merkley’s office told the SCMP that the issue had drawn Republican support before, citing the bipartisan Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act that Marco Rubio, then a senator and now secretary of state, introduced in 2021. Congress had tried multiple times to help Hongkongers settle in the US, without success. Two bills introduced in 2020 – the Hong Kong Victims of Communism Support Act and the Hong Kong Refugee Protection Act – would have offered Hong Kong residents asylum or priority refugee status. In the same year, the House passed the Hong Kong People’s Freedom and Choice Act, which would have given Hongkongers temporary protected status. However, Republican Senator Ted Cruz blocked it in the Senate, arguing it could let Chinese spies into the US.

title: Opinion | With war project, US tech ecosystem is beginning to look a lot like China’s
description: The US is moving towards a fusion of the government and the military-industrial complex – the Chinese model from the opposite direction.
content: The world’s wealthiest man has just been appointed to a Pentagon commission that will help decide what the future of warfare looks like. Elon Musk, alongside Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House speaker Newt Gingrich, is to lead “Project Meridian”. It follows a strategy by this White House that moves government and the tech sector ever closer. Project Meridian goes much further than the influence of defence contractors in Washington. It marks the beginning of Silicon Valley arriving at the halls of power, where the future of warfare itself is being imagined. The post-war years have been marked by an ever-closer relationship between American defence contractors and the government. This was exactly the convergence president Dwight Eisenhower warned against in his 1961 farewell address. Even with the revolving door between industry and government, and billion-dollar lobbying efforts, the structure of the relationship was clear: government would set the direction and contractors would bid to enact it. The founding political ideology of Silicon Valley was deeply libertarian. Despite its early ties to the military, the Valley imagined itself as a counterweight to Washington’s political power. By building new technology and tearing down old conventions, the Valley’s leading lights would reimagine and reinvigorate the spirit of democracy, or at least that was the story they told themselves. Consequently, they saw any attempt to regulate their business as a threat to that civilisational mission. The dawn of the age of artificial intelligence (AI) created a new part of the global defence economy, a booming sector of companies that carry as much DNA from Silicon Valley as from traditional weapons manufacturers. These neoprimes create the platforms on which weaponry can be automated and simplified. They have openly rejected the old model, in which contractors create systems for a future defined by the Pentagon. They are building the software – AI-enabled, as is the demand of the 2020s – through which that future can become real. At this intersection, they find the old dependence on state contracts for their growth clashes with Silicon Valley’s belief that they should be the ones building the future. As Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel put it: anyone opposing these “disrupters” view of the future of AI is tantamount to the Antichrist. To him, it is a mortal sin to put guardrails on the new world being built. In the pursuit of ambition, this new sector has shed its old libertarian ethos and instead doubled down on its belief that rapid, unencumbered advancement should override any checks on its power. With Project Meridian, that has been given force. Two tech leaders whose companies hold billions of dollars in Pentagon contracts are now tasked with defining what the future of warfare will require – and thus stand to benefit from it. Here, the American relationship between technology and the state is beginning to look a lot like its Chinese counterpart, albeit from different directions. Historically, China’s tech sector has seen itself as part of the national project of its emergence as a great power. Beijing sets the strategic direction, and with many companies having set up Communist Party committees, the phone works both ways. That is especially true for AI, which Beijing sees as the vanguard of its economic transformation in the unfolding century. The People’s Liberation Army has been relying heavily on civilian AI vendors and research institutions as it attempts to leverage China’s well-educated society to build the region’s dominant military. The distinction between the two matters as they engage in a great power conflict. Chinese and American technology are increasingly a proxy for the kind of power they project into the world. Beijing offers a version in which there is little meaningful difference between the state and industry. Washington, at least in theory, offers open space for private innovation. That distinction still matters, but less and less. If the most important American AI firms are now the ones deciding the future of war, then the myth of neutrality emerging from the private ownership of these companies is gone. Relying on the leaders of these companies to make important decisions will shape the state that sponsors the process. The Chinese model of technological development has long been one in which private innovation happens inside a political system that sets its direction. The American version is now arriving at the same integration from the other side. The private sector, as it always has, is pulling the state towards its own incentives. The result, accidentally, is that America’s tech ecosystem is beginning to resemble China’s, albeit from the opposite direction. Both systems are arriving at a fusion between the industry and the state while preserving their native pathologies. That convergence leaves the world without a meaningful alternative to a technological system that operates as an arm of a political mandate.

title: Elon Musk’s Starlink row in India exposes Asia’s deeper battle over satellite power
description: Musk claimed Indian tycoons are blocking Starlink, but analysts say security fears and state control are driving Asia’s satellite pushback.
content: Elon Musk’s accusation that powerful Indian business interests are blocking Starlink’s entry into India has sparked a political row, but analysts say the dispute also highlights security concerns, regulatory hurdles and strategic calculations shaping the satellite service’s expansion across Asia. In a post on social media, Musk said Starlink was licensed in more than 165 countries and had spent five years complying with Indian laws and regulations. “So why still no licence? Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he wrote, suggesting Reliance Group chairman Mukesh Ambani – one of India’s wealthiest tycoons whose sprawling conglomerate has a major footprint across the economy – might wield undue influence over the licensing process. The post drew a sharp response from Rahul Gandhi, leader of India’s main opposition party. “Welcome to India, Elon. Wait till you discover the other guy,” Gandhi said, apparently referring to Gautam Adani, another prominent Indian billionaire whose infrastructure and energy empire has expanded rapidly in recent years. Gandhi has frequently accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and its ruling Bharatiya Janata Party of favouring Ambani and Adani. The Indian government said its regulatory framework for satellite communication services was fair and non-discriminatory. Raj Kapoor, president of the India Blockchain Alliance, said Musk’s accusation overlooked the intense scrutiny Starlink was likely to face from security regulators across Asia. “It is a foreign-controlled satellite network with the ability to provide connectivity across political borders and potentially bypass conventional terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure,” Kapoor said, adding that Indian security agencies had been scrutinising infrastructure localisation and whether user traffic could be routed outside domestic jurisdiction. “Calling this an oligarch conspiracy is good politics on X but a poor reading of what is actually happening,” Kapoor said, pointing to past seizures of Starlink terminals from separatist militants in India’s Manipur state and from a drug-smuggling vessel off the coast. “That tells a security agency that the network can be reached by people the state cannot see.” Starlink’s regional expansion has run into regulatory hurdles, security concerns and geopolitical resistance in several Asian countries, including Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Nepal. Kapoor said the regulatory concerns differed across jurisdictions and should not be generalised. Starlink’s launch in Sri Lanka faced delays over regulatory assessments, data monitoring processes and national security vetting before receiving approval in mid-2025. In Vietnam, it launched nationwide operations in August under a tightly controlled five-year pilot programme. Globally, Starlink has expanded rapidly across more than 160 countries, serving millions of customers. “One of the reasons for the rapid expansion of Starlink has been how quickly countries have licensed it,” said Simon Baker, a UK-based senior research director for satellite and non-terrestrial connectivity at market research firm IDC. “The service offers productivity gains to many services with poor telecoms infrastructure and this has encouraged them to overlook security issues for the time being. However, as Starlink use grows, the conditions imposed on it could increase in many places,” Baker added. Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based technology policy adviser to governments, said security concerns among Asian countries were “entirely genuine” because satellite networks bypass land-based infrastructure, raising questions over data sovereignty, surveillance and national defence. “States require concrete guarantees that domestic user data remains localised and that authorities retain crisis management capabilities,” Lian said. “These regional delays are not anti-innovation roadblocks; they are standard sovereign prerogatives. India’s methodical approach reflects a sovereign state establishing equitable telecommunications rules.” The delays facing Starlink’s application in India stemmed mainly from complex regulatory requirements, Lian added. India’s telecommunications market is currently dominated by Reliance Jio Infocomm and Bharti Airtel, which together control more than 80 per cent of the market. Reliance is expanding its own satellite ambitions through Jio Satellite Communications and a joint venture with Luxembourg-based satellite operator SES. While OneWeb and Starlink are among the providers granted preliminary satellite communications licences in India, none has yet received spectrum allocation or launched full commercial services. The government said that all applicants must undergo mandatory security assessments before spectrum allocation. An uneven landscape Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said that India’s market structure was heavily concentrated among a small group of large companies. “Under such an industrial organisation, it is not unusual for foreign entrants to find the competitive conditions less than ideal,” Lim said, noting that entering a market dominated by established players was always difficult, regardless of an entrant’s technological advantage. The dispute between Musk and New Delhi also reflects growing geopolitical overlay in economic policymaking. “It does not help that the Indian government has had its own share of friction with the United States,” Lim said. India has indicated that trade negotiations with the United States have largely stalled, with its willingness to make further concessions to Washington reaching a limit. US lawmakers have also enacted sanctions legislation authorising discretionary tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil, a move aimed partly at India’s continued energy trade with Moscow. Lim noted that while Musk’s companies had “deep pockets” they should “expect no favours from Indian policymakers”. Despite regulatory hurdles, proponents argue that Starlink offers significant benefits to Asian economies by delivering high-speed digital connectivity to remote and disaster-prone regions. But Lian said that Starlink’s Asia-wide roll-out “will be a marathon, not a sprint”. Kapoor predicted a segmented roll-out across the region: while some Asian countries would adopt Starlink rapidly, others would impose strict localisation rules, and a third group would pursue domestic or allied satellite alternatives. “India does not want to exchange dependence on one set of telecoms gatekeepers for dependence on a foreign satellite network,” Kapoor said. “It wants the benefits of Starlink without surrendering strategic autonomy.” Satya Gupta, president of the VLSI Society of India and a veteran telecoms industry executive, said the controversy highlighted the need for India to develop its own satellite service. “We should aim to have this over the next five to seven years. This is the future of the internet for a range of services,” Gupta said. “We have all the ingredients and we need to put it together.” India has already emerged as a major global hub for low-cost small satellite manufacturing and cost-effective space projects. Gupta said India could develop its own satellite services and offer them to regional neighbours, including Sri Lanka and Nepal.

title: ‘You’re not ugly’: Chinese driver’s kindness to blind passenger wins millions of hearts online
description: Driver befriends Ou and pledges to drive him for free between Chengdu and his hometown – over 200km away – whenever he needs a ride.
content: A video of a ride-hailing driver in southwestern China reassuring a blind passenger about his appearance has gone viral, touching hearts across mainland social media. The driver, surnamed Wang, recently picked up a visually impaired passenger in Chengdu, Sichuan province, and helped him into the car after the platform flagged the booking as requiring accessible service. Wang later clarified that passengers who register with disability certificates have their bookings automatically marked as accessible service requests, rather than being assigned to specific drivers. The passenger, surnamed Ou, asked whether Wang had been reluctant to accept the booking after learning he was blind. “What’s the big deal? People should understand each other. Everyone needs a helping hand sometimes,” Wang replied. Ou said he lost his sight to a fever when he was one year old, leaving him in complete darkness for the past 48 years. His mother died when he was three, and his father passed away several years ago. Ou now earns a living as a massage therapist. Overcome with emotion, Wang rolled up his car window to hide his tears from passers-by. Ou then took off his sunglasses, explaining that he wore them to conceal what he considered his unattractive appearance. “Brother, you’re not ugly,” Wang reassured him. Moved by the remark, Ou offered Wang a 20-yuan (US$3) tip, saying: “Just from those words, I know you are a good person.” The pair exchanged contact details and arranged a return journey. Ou later offered Wang a 100-yuan cash gift and a mobile phone credit top-up, but Wang declined both. Wang said that respecting Ou meant treating him as an equal, rather than defining him by his disability. “If you ever run into trouble, I’ll be there to help you, whether you give me money or not,” Wang promised. The two men have since struck up a friendship and shared a meal, according to Chengdu media. Ou, who has never married and has no children or savings, described the encounter as an unprecedented source of warmth. Wang, meanwhile, said he admired Ou’s resilience and optimism. A military veteran, he dismissed his own gesture as a small act of kindness. He has also pledged to drive Ou free of charge between Chengdu and his hometown, more than 200km away, whenever he needs a ride. The video, uploaded by Wang, has received more than 7.4 million likes and widespread praise. “Empathy is the essence of kindness,” one online observer commented. Another wrote: “They are healing each other. Ou is remarkable. Despite being blind for almost his entire life, he has managed to earn a living through his own skills.”

title: Chinese researchers make Arctic-to-Antarctic call using rival to Musk’s Starlink
description: The Guowang network’s deployment is at an early stage, with around 180 satellites in orbit compared to Starlink’s 11,000.
content: Polar researchers have used a would-be Chinese rival to Elon Musk’s Starlink to make a satellite video call between the Arctic and Antarctic – the first publicly reported test of the Guowang constellation. The call highlights the growing capabilities of the country’s satellite constellations, according to state media. Beijing has been accelerating the development of its low-Earth-orbit constellations in recent years, particularly as the US-based Starlink showed its wartime value by helping Ukraine resist the full-scale Russian invasion. China has barred foreign satellite communications services from its territory over data security concerns. The near-real-time call took place in late September between researchers on three Chinese Arctic expedition ships – the Xuelong, the Jidi and the Tansuo-3 – and personnel at China’s Qinling Station in Antarctica, according to state broadcaster CCTV. The delay on the call was reportedly below one second. The Guowang constellation is operated by the state-owned China Satellite Network Group. The network’s deployment is still at an early stage – satellite launches began in December 2024 and just over 180 satellites of a planned 13,000 are now in orbit. The Arctic researchers also tested Guowang’s ability to support real-time communication between research vessels and China’s National Marine Data and Information Service, sending data files and voyage logs. The test marked “a major step towards China achieving independent and controllable communications in the polar regions, while ensuring that data remains within the country and improving data security”, the report said. According to the report, the maximum uplink and downlink speeds recorded during the polar tests were around 30 megabits per second (Mbps). By comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink typically provides download speeds of between 25Mbps and 220Mbps, depending on location and network conditions. A 30Mbps satellite link would be enough for most tactical communication and could potentially support real-time control of uncrewed systems, according to Chinese online military observers. However, the coverage, total data capacity and availability of the 180-satellite Guowang network remain limited compared with the 11,000-satellite Starlink. It also lagged behind in capabilities critical to military communications such as network resilience and resistance to jamming, observers said. China Satellite Network Group wants to have 400 satellites in orbit by the end of 2027 to provide Guowang coverage across China. In the longer term, the network is expected to deploy about 1,300 satellites by late 2029 and ultimately reach 12,992 satellites by 2035. Besides Guowang, China is also developing the Qianfan constellation, which aims to have 15,000 satellites. The network began launching satellites in August 2024, and there were 256 in orbit as of last month. The state-backed operator, Shanghai Spacesail Technologies, has said it aims to have 324 satellites in space by the end of this year.

title: China agrees to slash EU hybrid car exports in half, putting brake on trade war
description: The agreement will see Chinese hybrid vehicle exports decline by ‘several million cars’ in the coming years, EU trade chief says.
content: The European Union and China have “reached an understanding” that will cut Chinese hybrid car shipments to the bloc by “more than a half”, in a temporary salve to trade tensions that have threatened to boil over into a full-blown trade war. Speaking after marathon trade talks in Beijing, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said the deal would see China slash its hybrid car exports “by several million cars” over a four-year period. “This is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tensions, and I very much appreciate that,” Sefcovic told reporters in the Chinese capital. The sides also agreed to expedite EU applications for rare earth mineral export licences and improve market access for goods including car parts, olive oil and textiles, which Sefcovic said could be worth “almost €4 billion” (US$4.5 billion) in current export value. Beijing said it had received assurances that the EU and its members would “facilitate specific priority licences to China among dual-use sectors”, without naming the industries in question. The parties agreed to give advance warning of export controls, “improve the transparency of listing and delisting procedures” and work towards delisting companies that have been named. The latter is significant as powerful EU members are considering a new weapon that could instantly exclude firms from the single market. Brussels said its incoming inverter ban was not aimed at any particular country, despite EU officials confirming it was intended to wind down a heavy dependence on China. The Chinese commerce ministry described the talks as “equal, professional and constructive”, but Commerce Minister Wang Wentao made it clear that he was not happy with the EU’s newly assertive stance, expressing “concern over the recent trade and economic restrictions imposed by the EU”. He added that “China is not the root cause of the EU’s problems, but rather a partner in resolving them”. The ministry added that Wang had “urged the EU to work with China to properly handle frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation”. For Beijing, however, the big prize could be preserving the status quo as far as possible, given the economic importance of exports and the closure of the US market to many Chinese goods. “Judging from the details released by the EU, China appears to have made significant concessions on several issues. Whether these concessions will lead to corresponding adjustments by the EU on trade restrictions and market access remains to be seen over the coming months,” a commentary published by Geopolitechs, a website specialising in Chinese policymaking, said. Sefcovic, meanwhile, said EU national leaders would decide next week whether China’s concessions were enough, but downplayed the likelihood of an all-out tariff war. “It’s very easy to declare a trade war or any war, but it’s very difficult to stop it,” he said. “So therefore, I put so much emphasis on negotiations, and I’m glad that today I can present to you the outcome.” Sefcovic declined to share further detail on the arrangement on hybrid cars – shipments of which have ballooned in recent months – but hinted that it could follow a recent import curb the bloc placed on Chinese steel. “There are different techniques,” he said. “If you look in recent couple of months, I think you would find the answer.” A source briefed on the talks suggested that it would be a safeguard measure, by which the EU is able to place quotas and tariffs to urgently curb import surges. This is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing Maros Sefcovic, European commissioner for trade Earlier in the week, EU sources had explained that the bloc was seeking a “proof of concept” deal in a single sector – hybrid cars – which would be seen as a test of whether Beijing was negotiating in good faith. A joint statement by the two sides, published following two days of negotiations, said that talks would continue over reducing tariffs and creating minimum price deals that would allow Chinese electric vehicles to enter the EU market at a lower duty rate. The 16-point agreement listed a series of deliverables from the latest round of talks, with the two sides set to meet for further discussions in March next year. Most of these centred on further talks over long-standing trade disputes, including over medical equipment and power inverters. Sefcovic – who met with Wang and Vice-Premier He Lifeng – had been pressing Beijing to cap exports of hybrid vehicles, as a recent surge in shipments to Europe had led to fears within the bloc that its car industry could be hollowed out. “We never had the level of intensity of our exchanges and contacts as we have [had] over the last three to four months with our Chinese counterparts,” Sefcovic said. “I want to say that this was done in good faith, and this is the result of very intense work.” But he cautioned that the outcomes laid out in the joint statement would not be enough by themselves to reduce tensions between the two sides. “I often say that genuine negotiations deserve a real try. Therefore, I appreciate my counterparts’ engagement. Having said that, this is far from the end. It is a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing,” Sefcovic said. “As President von der Leyen has said, dialogue needs results, and where the dialogue cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to ensure rebalancing.” The latest talks came amid rising tensions between China and the EU over a range of trade issues, with calls growing in Europe for Brussels to take firmer action to curtail a surge in Chinese exports to the bloc. Next week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will brief EU national leaders on the results of the talks with Beijing, as the European Commission seeks instruction on how to respond to what is now widely described in Europe as a “China shock 2.0”. Member states have been coalescing around a tougher approach, shown by a joint paper from the governments of France and Germany – leaked on Monday – which called for a weapon to cut countries or firms perceived to be cheating on trade out of the EU market almost instantly. The commission is then likely to present a series of new trade tools before the end of the year. It was also expected to launch a flurry of investigations aimed at quickly curbing Chinese imports in sectors including chemicals, plastics and automotive, though it remained unclear on Friday whether the progress in Beijing would alter those plans. Businesses responded positively to the Beijing talks. The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU (CCCEU) welcomed the “pragmatic outcomes”, saying they showed both sides’ “willingness to handle trade frictions and stabilise bilateral trade relations through dialogue”. The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association said “this announcement is a positive step in easing trade tensions between the two” sides. Pascal Canfin, a lawmaker who manages the China file in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told the South China Morning Post that the hybrid deal was “a very first step towards rebalancing our trade relationship”. “But while dialogue has delivered a first result today, we are under no illusion: the imbalance is systemic,” Canfin said. “We will therefore have to go further, and we must of course not give up on using our trade defence instruments to safeguard our economic security.”

title: 17 key takeaways from Malaysia’s 2027 budget - ‘live with dignity’
description: The government is projecting slower economic growth and higher inflation in 2027 as it seeks to narrow the deficit.
content: Malaysia plans to spend 460 billion ringgit (US$112.6 billion) under its 2027 budget, expanding welfare assistance and tax relief while retaining fuel subsidies as households contend with higher living costs. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who is also finance minister, presented the spending plan in parliament on Friday as his government faces pressure for an early election following a series of state poll defeats. Anwar said the budget should be judged on “whether more people can live with dignity” as the government forecast slower economic growth and higher inflation next year while targeting a narrower deficit.
