content: As Russian President Vladimir Putin watched the final stage of the massive Tsentr-2026 military exercise in the Urals recently, Chinese troops were training alongside forces from Russia, Belarus and other countries. More than 47,000 military personnel joined the exercise, which incorporated lessons from the war in Ukraine. The symbolism extends beyond Chelyabinsk. From Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to Chinese military exercises with Belarus – and now China’s participation alongside Russian and Belarusian forces in Tsentr-2026 – Eurasian developments are connecting two strategic theatres once considered largely separate: the Euro-Atlantic and Indo-Pacific. Against this background, a new strategic triangle is quietly taking shape among the United States, Japan and Poland. It is neither a formal trilateral alliance nor necessarily another cold war. Rather, it may represent a new architecture of deterrence in what I described in my book Peaceful War as the long competition between the US and China – a contest conducted through trade, technology, diplomacy, military preparedness, alliances and competing visions of international order. This peaceful war unfolds within what I call an age of “fragmented interdependence”. These nations compete strategically while remaining economically and technologically dependent upon one another. Yet the immediate catalyst for the Washington-Warsaw-Tokyo triangle lies less in China than in Russia. Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine transformed Poland’s security environment. As a frontline Nato state bordering Ukraine, Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region, Poland accelerated military modernisation and deepened its relationship with Washington. Warsaw has authorised preparations for negotiations on a permanent US military base; Poland already hosts the forward headquarters of the US Army’s V Corps in Poznan and major American infrastructure at Powidz. Then the Indo-Pacific moved unexpectedly closer. In July 2024, Chinese troops conducted the Eagle Assault exercise with Belarus near Brest, close to Poland’s frontier. Beijing described it as counterterrorism training – not an operation directed against Nato, the transatlantic security alliance. Yet Chinese forces were exercising in a country that facilitated Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Tsentr-2026 now adds Chinese training alongside Russian and Belarusian forces on Russian territory. That helps explain why Poland’s rapidly developing relationship with Japan deserves greater attention. The Warsaw-Tokyo connection is not new. During the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05, Polish independence leaders looked to Japan as imperial Russia’s adversary. The most compelling humanitarian chapter came in 1940. Chiune Sugihara, Japan’s consul in Lithuania, issued transit visas that enabled thousands of Polish Jews to escape German-occupied Poland through the Soviet Union and Japan. Long before today’s strategic partnership, Polish and Japanese interests – and human destinies – were intersecting across Eurasia under pressure from great-power conflict. In April this year, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi elevated bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership. Significantly, their joint statement declared Euro-Atlantic and Indo-Pacific security to be closely interconnected, opposed attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion, condemned Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and called for deeper cooperation with like-minded partners and stronger alliances with the US to enhance national defence capabilities. This strategic logic was captured by Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski when he observed that “the defence of Poland’s national interest – including the defence of Polish sovereignty – often begins 1,000km from our borders”. His formulation helps explain Warsaw’s strengthening strategic partnership with Tokyo and its broader engagement with other Indo-Pacific partners. Japan occupies the eastern maritime frontier of America’s alliance system – facing China and nuclear-armed North Korea. Poland occupies Nato’s eastern continental frontier – confronting Russian power and instability in Belarus. The US connects them. Yet this is not simply an anti-China coalition. Poland maintains a comprehensive strategic partnership with China; Japan remains economically intertwined with China; and Washington simultaneously competes, negotiates and trades with Beijing. This apparent contradiction is precisely fragmented interdependence. The US-Japan-Poland triangle may therefore be better understood as deterrence rather than containment: Poland contributing to stability on Nato’s eastern flank, Japan to the strategic balance in the Indo-Pacific, and the US connecting two increasingly interdependent security theatres. Nonetheless, this deterrence may carry danger. If Washington interprets every Chinese initiative as expansion while Beijing sees every American alliance as containment, the security dilemma could transform peaceful competition into military confrontation. Poland and Japan can show that strong alliances need not require closed economic blocs and that deterrence can coexist with dialogue. The 21st century may therefore be defined neither by another cold war nor – one hopes – by a hot war. Instead, it increasingly resembles the peaceful war I described years ago. It sustained competition for economic, technological, diplomatic and strategic advantage among powers that remain profoundly interconnected. In this age of fragmented interdependence, the Washington-Warsaw-Tokyo triangle may become an important new architecture of deterrence. Its success should not be measured by whether America prevails over China or China retreats before America. Rather, the more consequential question is whether deterrence can preserve peace while the peaceful war continues – and whether great power competition can ultimately contribute to a more peaceful world. The opinions expressed here are solely those of the author.

title: Why Asian parents are trapped in a private tuition arms race
description: From Singapore to South Korea, fear of falling behind fuels a costly cycle of extra lessons despite the toll it takes on children.
content: Grace often hears other Singapore mothers debating how much private tuition their children need. Some rush to enrol their offspring in multiple classes before they turn five, while others try to resist the pressure to add lessons outside school. She enrolled her two children, now aged four and seven, in Chinese tuition when they were three to give them greater exposure to their ancestral tongue. “Neither of their parents speaks fluent Mandarin at home … I guess there is some degree of pressure involved too,” said Grace, 38, the founder of a creative agency. Her dilemma reflects a wider tension across Asia, where parents continue to invest in private tuition to give their children an academic edge, despite growing concerns over the stress placed on young learners and the widening gap between families who can afford extra classes and those who cannot. In Singapore, a recent survey found that parents were spending more on tuition and enrichment classes than ever before, despite widespread concerns that children are already devoting too much time to them. The survey of 1,500 primary school parents by the Institute of Policy Studies found that nearly nine in 10 agreed children in the city state were spending too much time on private classes, even as overall expenditure on extracurricular activities had increased. Seven in 10 parents said they would spend more on such classes if they had the resources, while around half admitted feeling pressure because other parents did so. The report, published last month, noted that parents were increasingly seeking both academic success and holistic development for their children, creating tension when one was perceived to come at the expense of the other. “Concerns about school placement, future pathways, wider social comparisons and their own desire to safeguard their children’s opportunities can make it difficult for parents to act fully on their holistic preferences,” the report stated. The dilemma is not unique to Singapore. Across Asia, in education systems where families compete for limited opportunities, parents can find themselves paying for tuition even when they believe the collective pressure damages children’s well-being. Ong Ee Cheng, an associate professor of economics at the National University of Singapore, described the situation as a “thorny” paradox as everyone would be “better off” if no one sent their children to private tuition. “But if I send my kid to tuition and you don’t, my kid will do better than yours, and vice versa,” she said. “Ironically, when we both send our kids to tuition, we’re worse off than if neither of us had done so.” The competition has fuelled demand for private education in Singapore, where parents spent an average of S$677 (US$529) a month on tuition this year – an increase from S$318 a decade ago. House of Hows, a tuition centre offering classes for primary, secondary and junior college students, has more than 1,000 prospective students on its waiting list. Founder and lead tutor Laura Oh warned against viewing all tuition spending simply as a fear of missing out. While some parents viewed extra classes as a way to secure an advantage, she said many were increasingly prioritising stress management and helping children find enjoyment in learning. Other than Chinese lessons, Grace has enrolled her children in swimming, netball and art classes to develop their interests outside the classroom. “It’s important for parents like us to recognise their interests early in life and provide them with as much help as possible early on,” she said. Educational arms race Across the region, the private tuition industry continues to expand as parents try to give their children a head start. But observers warn that these advantages extend beyond the classroom, reinforcing socio-economic divides as academic perks translate into better access to further education and, potentially, the job market. Students whose parents can afford private classes are more likely to do well in entrance examinations, experts say, with those advantages potentially creating inequalities that continue into employment. Nathan Peng, an assistant professor of political science at Singapore Management University, said countries that sorted students through high-stakes national examinations at a young age were particularly vulnerable to widening social divides. “Even if all schools were equally good, the earlier you test a child, the more the results reflect family background rather than schooling, because the child has spent less time in the formal education system,” he said. “And the more a society believes credentials reflect someone’s ‘true’ potential, the less likely it is to ask how much adversity different candidates overcame to reach the same point.” The pressure to secure an advantage can begin long before formal schooling starts. Ong said well-off parents in Singapore, China and South Korea often engaged in what she termed an educational arms race well before primary school. The effects of private tuition on social mobility could be more pronounced in countries with high levels of inequality, she added. “Unfortunately, many countries in Southeast Asia and Asia fit the bill.” In Malaysia, gaps in the quality of public education could leave children reliant on extra help to keep up, said M Niaz Asadullah, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka. Learning gaps caused by under-resourced public schools disproportionately affected poorer families, who were less able to pay for private lessons, he said. “Tuition markets can expand both because schools leave learning gaps and because families compete for limited opportunities,” Asadullah said. “The risk of widening inequality depends on how unequally families can participate in that competition.” Can policy curb the trend? The challenge for governments across the region is addressing both sides of the problem: fixing shortfalls in public education while curbing intense competition for scarce educational opportunities. In South Korea, households spent about 29.2 trillion won (US$21.8 billion) on private education in 2024 – a 60 per cent increase from a decade earlier. In April, authorities announced measures banning private tutoring academies or cram schools, known locally as hagwons, for children under three and capping preschoolers’ time spent in such lessons at three hours a day. Singapore has also attempted to reduce academic pressures. In 2021, the government replaced aggregate scoring for the Primary School Leaving Examination with wider scoring bands, allowing students to be graded on their individual learning mastery rather than relative to their peers. In 2024, full subject-based banding replaced streaming scores to reduce academic labelling. Asadullah urged regional governments to provide free, targeted tutoring through state schools, prioritising disadvantaged students, while ensuring classroom instruction was good enough to make private tutoring unnecessary. Peng said early support was crucial as children often started school from very different academic baselines. “Governments should help narrow gaps in family resources from pregnancy through early childhood, including nutrition, learning materials and parents’ knowledge of child development,” he said. Other observers acknowledged that policy fixes alone could not dismantle the culture of tutoring without a wider shift in how families and societies defined success. “If there were more emphasis on overall well-being – including mental and emotional – and less on material wealth, perspectives may start to shift to ensuring children are happy, resilient and confident,” Ong said. “But of course, that’s more likely if parents know that even if their children fall, there’s only so far that they can fall.”

title: Why the Dajiao Festival on Hong Kong’s Kat O island is held once every 10 years
description: As Kat O welcomes visitors to its Dajiao Festival, heritage advocates hope to reconnect younger generations with the island’s traditions.
content: On a typical day, Kat O – a tranquil island within the Hong Kong Unesco Global Geopark, in the northeastern waters of the New Territories – sees just a small number of visitors, who arrive mostly for a scenic hike through its heritage trails. However, with an island-wide festival taking place from October 11 to 15, things are about to get lively. In the run-up to the festivities, villagers are busy completing a giant bamboo theatre, traditional puppets and parade lanterns, while local artists finalise their installations and performances. It has been a decade since the Dajiao Festival was last held on Kat O. Visitors can look forward to Cantonese opera performances at the temporary bamboo theatre, colourful parades, sacred rituals, a traditional Dajiao vegetarian biscuit called Key Lo Bicky (also known as Qi Lu Bing) and the Kat O Dajiao Arts Festival, a contemporary art event taking place throughout October. “The parade on the third day is particularly grand,” says Desmond Wong, senior conservation manager for cultural heritage at the Hong Kong NGO The Conservancy Association. “We have invited traditional Chaozhou Yingge dancers, as well as the Unicorn Dance and Fish Lantern Dance troupe from Sam A village in Sha Tau Kok, both of which are national-level intangible cultural heritage.” A folk tradition to give thanks Dajiao – also known as Da Chiu – is a traditional Taoist sacrificial rite tracing back to the Qing dynasty. Originally practised by China’s imperial court and state officials, it gradually evolved into a community folk tradition in rural villages and fishing communities, where it is held to thank the deities – most commonly Tin Hau, the goddess of the sea – for past harvests and seek their continued blessings. Villages typically engage Taoist priests, or naam mou sifu, to conduct the rites in autumn, although the frequency and customs vary considerably among clans and regions. One of the largest islands in the northeast New Territories, at 2.35 sq km (0.9 square miles), Kat O – nicknamed Crooked Island due to its twisted shape – has just 50 residents. Kat O’s community comprises Hakka villagers and boat-dwelling seafaring families. Unlike Dajiao festivals elsewhere, which are commonly known as Tai Ping Ching Chiu (the ritual for peace), Kat O’s celebration is called On Lung Ching Chiu (the ritual for settling the dragon). People “believe that, every 10-year cycle, the place where they reside develops a lung mak (dragon vein)”, Wong says. In addition to thanking the deities and performing rites for the departed, villagers must replenish the dragon vein’s vitality to ensure the community’s continued peace and divine protection. During the On Lung ritual, the priest and villagers climb the mountain to a designated site, where they replace a jar of “dragon water”. Drawn from an ancient well in Kat O’s Sai O village, the water is used to replenish the dragon vein. Elsewhere in Hong Kong, Dajiao celebrations are held more frequently. Cheung Chau’s Tai Ping Ching Chiu, better known as the Bun Festival, takes place every year, while other clans hold theirs every three, five or eight years. The least frequent on record is the Liu clan’s Tai Ping Ching Chiu in Sheung Shui, held only once every 60 years. “The next one will take place in 2066. I probably will not be around to see it,” Wong says with a chuckle. For each Dajiao, the clan selects representatives to perform the rituals on behalf of the village. When the Liu clan held theirs in 2006, it chose a young child in the hope that he would live to see the next festival 60 years later. “He might not have understood the full significance back then, but when the time comes, he will carry vivid memories of it,” Wong says. Many of these rituals are passed down through the generations. In the past, villages maintained Dajiao manuals, which recorded everything from the height of the bamboo scaffolding and festive couplets to purchasing lists, daily prayers and fundraising guidelines. Today, villagers rely on video archives to preserve this knowledge for future generations. For a festival devoted to giving thanks to deities, a 10-year interval may seem lengthy, let alone one of 60 years. “That isn’t determined by choice, but by divination,” Wong says. “Villagers consult the deity through a sacred ritual, and the deity indicates whether the cycle can be shortened.” On Tung Lung Chau, for example, Dajiao is held every three years – a frequent cycle that costs more than HK$1 million (US$127,400) each time. “They attempted divination to ask Tin Hau whether they could extend the cycle to once every five years,” Wong says. “But Tin Hau did not grant approval, so they maintained the three-year interval.” I felt it would be a great loss if the festival vanished Sze Ka-yan, of music NGO Fragrant Village Many of Kat O’s native villagers now live elsewhere in Hong Kong or overseas, so the role of Dajiao has evolved from a purely religious ritual into a force that binds families and communities together. “The Dajiao Festival serves an essential role in reuniting overseas residents and scattered villagers as they gather on the island once more,” Wong says. “In previous editions, returnees travelled back from as far as the UK.” The Conservancy Association, led by Wong, and Fragrant Village, a local music NGO founded by Sze Ka-yan, are two key organisations supporting Kat O’s community as it revives the island’s festival. Sze, a performing arts graduate specialising in traditional village songs, visited Kat O two years ago for field research. There, she learned of the concerns among the village elders, all of whom are over 60. “They told me the coming festival would likely be the final Dajiao on Kat O because younger generations knew little about the customs, and it would be difficult for the elders to organise it once they reached their seventies,” she says. “I felt it would be a great loss if the festival vanished.” Wong says: “Dajiao encompasses far more than religious rites; it represents a rich ecosystem of intangible cultural heritage: Cantonese opera, bamboo scaffolding techniques, traditional feasts and paper crafting.” Together, the two organisations are breathing new life into the festival by introducing the Kat O Dajiao Arts Festival, which runs until October 25. Sze has invited eight visual and performance artists to create site-specific works inspired by the Dajiao tradition. Among them is Karlie Wu, a Kat O descendant born and raised in Glasgow, Scotland, who feels a deep connection to the island. A decade ago, she filmed footage of Kat O’s Dajiao, which she has edited into a video artwork presented alongside works by Shenzhen artist Yip Man. Artists Jaffa Lam and Lee Man-sang have constructed an installation from recycled umbrella ribs woven into a roof, reflecting on Dajiao as an act of homecoming. Sze has also invited mainland Chinese folk singer Xiao He to perform a concert. Xiao directs the Nursery Rhyme Program, travelling to rural villages to record traditional nursery rhymes and folk music – a mission that closely aligns with Sze’s efforts to preserve Kat O’s heritage. Xiao will perform local Hakka folk songs, fishermen’s chants and the Kat O Public School anthem inside Kat O’s bamboo opera shed. Wong hopes the contemporary programming will attract international visitors and younger audiences, cultivating a new generation of heritage advocates. He is also helping the Kat O community apply for intangible cultural heritage funding. “We hope this innovative model serves as a reference for other regional Dajiao festivals,” he says. Sze remains optimistic that more young descendants of Kat O villagers will return. “Preserving culture requires sustained, long-term commitment – building meaningful relationships with the community and creating events that engage descendants near and far,” she says. “We hope to use art to weave these connections, uniting the community and reviving Kat O’s precious heritage.” The Kat O Dajiao Festival runs from October 11 to 15 and the Kat O Dajiao Arts Festival until October 25.

title: China charges tech firm with smuggling restricted ‘dual-use’ optical lenses out of country
description: As Beijing tightens export controls on strategic technologies, the case highlights risk of criminal prosecution for companies.
content: Chinese authorities have charged a Shenzhen-listed firm and its chairman over smuggling restricted “dual-use” optical lenses out of the country, in a case that lawyers said underscores the growing risk of criminal prosecution for export control violations as Beijing tightens restrictions on strategic materials and technologies. Nanjing Wavelength Opto-Electronic Science & Technology, which manufactures optical components used in infrared thermal imaging, and chairman Huang Shengdi were among five defendants charged with smuggling goods prohibited from import or export, according to a company filing on Thursday. The other three were a former director and former employees of the company’s international business department. The total value involved in the case was 20.1 million yuan (US$3.0 million). Prosecutors in Shanghai alleged that the company and the individuals exported controlled optical lenses without obtaining the required export licences for dual-use items, which can serve both civilian and military purposes, between August 2023 and April 2025. The case underscores the compliance risks facing Chinese manufacturers as Beijing expands export controls of dual-use items and the materials used to make them amid intensifying tech rivalry with the US. Since August 2023, China has imposed export controls on gallium and germanium, two important materials used in semiconductor manufacturing. It later also added graphite, rare earths and other materials to its export restrictions. According to Wavelength’s latest half-year report, its infrared thermal imaging lenses are made from optical materials such as germanium and silicon. Chen Yao, a Shanghai-based lawyer and senior joint partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, said the case was unusual because violations involving dual-use items had often resulted in administrative penalties rather than criminal prosecution. The case also highlights how export control violations could become a major unexpected risk for companies listed on China’s A-share market, Chen added. The investigation began in April 2025, when customs authorities in Shanghai started reviewing the company’s exports over the preceding three years. They later concluded the company was suspected of exporting germanium-containing lenses under falsely declared material descriptions before referring the matter to anti-smuggling investigators. Wavelength said in June that it had suspended the export business related to the investigation. The business accounted for a relatively small share of annual revenue and formed part of its infrared optics operations. The precise lens models, declared materials and export destinations involved have not been publicly disclosed. The company’s misdeclaration of the material composition of its goods took the case beyond an administrative violation for failing to obtain an export licence and into the realm of criminal smuggling, where the potential consequences are far more serious, said Li Fan, a Hefei-based lawyer and partner at the Lantai Partners. “For businesses, export control compliance is no longer just a legal paperwork exercise,” he said. “It must be built into every stage of the export process, from product classification and order screening to customs declarations, to help guard against criminal liability.” The case is not the first in which Chinese companies have faced penalties or criminal proceedings over the unauthorised export of controlled materials. In May, superhard-material producer Monte-Bianco Diamond Applications said it had been fined 910,000 yuan for shipping state-controlled dysprosium in April 2025 without the required export licence. In April, Puyang Refractories said prosecutors had indicted the company and several executives for smuggling after finding that management had mislabelled more than 1,240 tonnes of natural flake graphite as general graphite powder to bypass export controls between April 2024 and March 2025. Wavelength said Thursday that its case had yet to go to trial, leaving its outcome and potential impact on profits uncertain, but the proceedings were not expected to have a material impact on its ability to continue operating.

title: Beijing and Manila trade blame over South China Sea medical mission
description: The Philippines also reports seeing 101 Chinese vessels near contested features in September, nearly double August’s total.
content: China and the Philippines have traded accusations over a medical evacuation near the disputed Second Thomas Shoal, with Manila also reporting a near-doubling of Chinese military and coastguard vessels around contested South China Sea features in September. The latest exchange centred on the evacuation on Thursday of an injured Philippine serviceman from the BRP Sierra Madre, a Philippine naval vessel grounded on the shoal decades ago. Known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines, the shoal is one of the region’s major flashpoints. The Philippine Coast Guard accused China Coast Guard vessels of obstructing the emergency evacuation, including by using a water cannon in an apparent attempt to block a Philippine patrol ship from reaching the shoal to retrieve the injured serviceman. The incident delayed the mission by nearly 10 hours and forced the Philippine vessel to withdraw for safety reasons, although the water cannon did not hit the ship, according to Philippine Coast Guard spokesman Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela. The injured man was eventually evacuated by rubber boat at a rendezvous point farther from the shoal and was reported to be in stable condition. China’s coastguard rejected the Philippine account on Thursday night. Spokesman Jiang Lue said Philippine Coast Guard vessel 4409 had approached waters near the shoal to transfer one injured person from a ship that Beijing called “illegally grounded”. Jiang said China had immediately allowed the medical evacuation on humanitarian grounds, permitting the transfer by small boat and providing necessary help while handling the operation in accordance with Chinese laws and regulations. He accused Manila of “disregarding the facts, reversing right and wrong and attempting to mislead public opinion”, repeating Beijing’s claim to sovereignty over the Spratly Islands and their surrounding waters. He also urged the Philippines to stop what he called “infringement and provocation” and “unfounded hype”. Separately, Manila said on Thursday that it had monitored 101 Chinese navy and coastguard vessels around four contested features in September, compared with 56 in August, according to a tally by the Armed Forces of the Philippines. Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, the Philippine military’s South China Sea spokesman, described the increase as part of a strategy by China aimed at achieving what he called “mission kill” by undermining Manila’s ability to sustain operations in the disputed waters. The vessels were recorded near the Philippine-garrisoned Thitu Island and Second Thomas Shoal, as well as Sabina Shoal and the Chinese-controlled Scarborough Shoal. The Chinese build-up sought to “break our people’s resolve to keep what is ours”, Trinidad told Agence France-Presse. Manila has also accused Chinese military and coastguard forces in recent days of harassing Philippine aircraft and vessels near Scarborough Shoal and in the Spratly Islands, known in China as the Nanshas. Beijing, in turn, has accused the Philippines of conducting provocative activities and violating Chinese airspace and maritime rights. China has also rejected Manila’s account of a separate September incident in which the Philippines said a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine fisheries bureau boat, saying the Philippine vessel bore full responsibility. Second Thomas Shoal has been the scene of repeated confrontations between the two countries, including collisions, water-cannon incidents and disputes over Philippine resupply missions to the Sierra Madre outpost. China claims most of the islands and rocks in the South China Sea, including Second Thomas Shoal, and rights over their adjacent waters despite a 2016 international arbitral ruling that rejected the legal basis of Beijing’s expansive historic-rights claims. Beijing refused to take part in the arbitration and dismissed the ruling as “illegal and void”, while Manila regularly cites it in support of its maritime rights.

title: Malaysia budget: healthcare boost, Malay businesses to get more public projects
description: The US$112.6 billion budget will see higher spending in education, healthcare, welfare, subsidies, SME support and others.
content: Malaysia’s government will boost spending on social welfare while maintaining subsidies to rein in the cost of living under its 2027 Budget unveiled on Friday, as Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim seeks to shore up public support while under pressure to call for an early general election. Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) has suffered bruising defeats in a series of state elections since December, as voters expressed disapproval of his administration’s failure to deliver on promises of reforms, which had helped the ruling coalition to secure the largest share of parliamentary seats in the 2022 polls. Malaysia’s next general election is due by February 2028. He faces the prospect of presenting possibly the last budget of his term, as his federal partner but state electoral rival Umno demands immediate snap polls, emboldened by its decisive victories over PH in the recent Johor and Negeri Sembilan elections. Anwar, who is also finance minister, presented an expansionary budget of 460 billion ringgit (US$112.6 billion), with increased spending on education, healthcare and infrastructure along with higher wages and aid for small and medium enterprises (SMEs). “It must be stressed that the national budget is a moral statement of a responsible government. Malay traditional intelligentsia has long placed justice and trust as the core of governance,” Anwar said when presenting his budget in parliament. He said the government expected to spend at least 80 billion ringgit (US$19 billion) on subsidies next year. This includes an estimated 40 billion ringgit to sustain fuel subsidies at pump stations and a 6.7 per cent increase in cash handouts to 16 billion ringgit. The higher subsidy bill takes into account expectations of a prolonged energy crisis caused by the US-Israel war on Iran, which has already forced Malaysia to revise its 2026 budget estimates higher to 444.1 billion ringgit, Anwar said, from the initial target of about 419 billion ringgit. “We have to remember that the cost-of-living issue is already there even before the Iran war started in February this year,” Irwan Shah Zainal Abidin, a senior associate fellow at Universiti Utara Malaysia’s Economic and Financial Policy Institute, told This Week in Asia. “Maintaining the fuel subsidies is more about not making things worse rather than addressing the issue of living costs pressure.” Middle-class Malaysians will benefit from a 1 per cent reduction to their 2027 income tax assessment, and there will be a new tax relief ceiling of 12,000 ringgit to accommodate additional categories including maternity care and elderly care for grandparents, AI subscriptions and vaccination for pets. The package will offer some relief, but its impact on middle-income purchasing power will be modest, according to Doris Liew, an economist specialising in Southeast Asian development. Those earning below the taxable threshold would not benefit from the tax relief, while families facing high housing, childcare and eldercare costs could remain under pressure, particularly single-earner households and workers with irregular income, she said. “For these households, stronger earnings and more affordable essential services matter more than modest tax saving.” The government will also raise the minimum wage for unskilled workers to 2,000 ringgit from 1,700 ringgit currently from June next year, while the wage floor for semi-skilled workers will be set at 2,500 ringgit for the first time. Anwar said the government, supported by government-linked firms and major corporations in primary sectors such as banking and oil and gas, had paved the way for more reasonable wages in the country. “Hence, I urge all private employers to do the same,” he said, adding that companies could only claim tax breaks on salaries paid through bank accounts to close loopholes that had long enabled the hiring of undocumented workers. To win over the country’s Malay-Muslim majority, the government will expand their business access to nearly 70 billion ringgit worth of small-scale public projects, funding and investments, besides procurement opportunities with national energy giant Petronas and government-linked companies. The country’s Malays account for 60 per cent of Malaysia’s 34 million population and whose support is vital for political parties to secure legitimacy to rule. The government will also cut the cost of elderly care, allowing full service tax exemption for annual care centre fees of up to 96,000 ringgit. The government will also allocate 1.3 billion ringgit for cash aid targeted at elderly citizens. The budget will allocate 1.5 billion ringgit for welfare aid for the disabled, including raising the wage floor by 300 ringgit to 2,000 ringgit for companies claiming benefits for their disabled employees and a 600 ringgit monthly payout for families and caregivers of disabled and bedridden individuals. “The continued move towards more targeted assistance should help improve the efficiency of government support while reducing leakages. Subsidy reform continues to protect vulnerable households without unduly increasing the cost of living,” said Arshad Mohamed Ismail, group chief executive at local ratings firm Malaysian Rating Corporation. To boost healthcare, the government will spend 47.7 billion ringgit in 2027 to build and upgrade facilities and improve access to primary and outpatient care and recruit at least 9,000 doctors on a full-time basis in the public health sector. Education will get a combined budget of nearly 100 billion ringgit, to cover the construction of new schools and food aid for students at primary, secondary and university levels, besides lower repayment requirements for government student loans and tax breaks for companies that help their workers with government-back study loan repayments. For local businesses, income taxes for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) will be brought down by 1 per cent to help cushion the blow from rising operating costs, while factories can claim sales tax refunds for machinery, spare parts and equipment sourced from local traders or distributors. The Malaysian central bank will also offer an additional 5 billion ringgit in funding in 2027 for SMEs affected by the Iran war, adding to the 5 billion ringgit set aside for this year. A total of 6 billion ringgit will be set aside to develop tech capabilities among Malaysians, which includes providing 100,000 free subscriptions to new AI applications on the market. In an uncharacteristically blunt assessment of its own performance, the government said in its 2027 Economic Outlook Report that it had fallen short of delivering on promises to keep prices low, narrow the wage gap and improve healthcare access. The report, released ahead of Friday’s budget, cited limited welfare coverage for self-employed and informal workers, fragmented delivery of targeted cash aid, substandard student performance, a chronic shortage of specialist doctors and escalating medical costs. “Despite significant progress, Malaysia’s social protection landscape continues to face challenges in providing adequate and comprehensive protection across different forms of employment and household circumstances amid the rising cost of living,” the report said. The government said it was on track to narrow the country’s deficit to 3.3 per cent next year through more efficient subsidy mechanisms, improving on the revised target of 3.6 per cent for 2026. Inflation is expected to range between 1.8 and 2.8 per cent in 2027, likely tracking higher in the first half of the year due to carry-over effects from higher energy, food and other input costs before easing as the year progresses. The economy is forecast to grow by 4.8-5.3 per cent this year before moderating slightly to 4.2-5.2 per cent in 2027, buoyed by resilient domestic demand and sustained global demand for Malaysia’s semiconductors and AI-related products.

title: Singapore Grand Prix: George Russell to go ‘all out’ as Kimi Antonelli nears Formula 1 title
description: Mercedes driver fastest on Friday in ⁠only practice session ⁠for race as Briton looks to bounce back from Sepang disappointment last weekend.
content: Mercedes driver George Russell said he will need to throw everything he can at stopping, or even just delaying, Kimi Antonelli’s march to the Formula 1 title – but that will not be easy from the back of the grid at the Singapore Grand Prix. Russell, who won last year’s race in ‌Singapore, ⁠was fastest in ⁠the only practice session on Friday. With the Marina Bay Street Circuit hosting a ⁠sprint this year on Saturday, drivers had just one practice session available – albeit in ‌the daylight – to get to grips with the track ahead of sprint qualifying under the lights later on ‌Friday. Russell clocked one minute and 32.274 seconds at the dusty ⁠circuit on the ⁠streets of Singapore, nearly two-tenths of a second faster than Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc while ‌reigning F1 champion Lando Norris was third-fastest. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 84 points, ‌was only ‌seventh-fastest behind Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, McLaren’s Oscar Piastri and Red ‌Bull’s Max Verstappen – the fastest driver on medium tyres. At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last Sunday, Russell was third, with Mercedes teammate Antonelli ahead of him in second, when his power unit suddenly failed, leaving him with a penalty this week for an engine change. After that, this week it is “all-out attack, just trying to enjoy the weekend”, Russell said on Thursday. “Obviously not an ideal situation, but Singapore is a place I love and I’ll try and carve my way through the pack.” Russell said Singapore was “probably the second-bottom of the list” in terms of the ease of fighting back after a penalty and predicted he might need to serve another for an engine change before the season is over. It is a big contrast from the last time Antonelli had to serve a penalty. Mercedes changed his engine for the Italian Grand Prix in a planned move, calculating that overtaking was easy enough at Monza that he could limit the damage. He did far more than that and took a statement victory in his home race. Antonelli could clinch title in Texas Antonelli finished second behind Max Verstappen in Malaysia for his sixth podium finish in the past seven races, moving him 84 points clear of Russell in the standings. With 33 points on offer across Singapore’s sprint race and grand prix, if Antonelli scores 16 points more than Russell this week, he would have a shot at sealing the title at the United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, on October 25. Lando Norris might have a fix for his McLaren’s straight-line speed problem, but this weekend could still spell the end of his title defence if Antonelli outscores the McLaren driver by 18 points. Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen could also be eliminated from contention. Rain, haze, heat could test drivers Singapore is always a tough test for drivers because of the heat and humidity. This week, add in a haze of air pollution from forest fires in nearby Indonesia, too. Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas has plenty of first-hand experience of the local conditions after cycling from Sepang to Singapore this week. There is also a chance of rain affecting the action on Saturday and Sunday. Not only is a wet street track a tricky proposition, but there will be extra scrutiny on the cars after a software bug on a wet track caused the start to be delayed in Malaysia last week. The FIA said the software fix that was rushed out for Sunday’s race was ready for use again in Singapore and a new version is coming for the US Grand Prix.

title: Chinese optical chip stocks extend rout amid fears of potential US curbs
description: Upstream laser chip suppliers bore the brunt, suffering steeper declines than downstream optical transceiver manufacturers.
content: Renewed fears of potential US trade curbs on next-generation optical transceivers for data centres have sent shares of Chinese suppliers tumbling, deepening a sell-off across artificial intelligence supply chain stocks. Shares of Chinese optical chipmakers extended their losses for a second straight session on Friday despite reassurances from major suppliers, while China’s benchmark CSI 300 Index slid 1.3 per cent by the midday break to its lowest level since August last year. Upstream laser chip suppliers bore the brunt of the market downturn, suffering steeper declines than downstream optical transceiver manufacturers. In Shanghai, Yuanjie Semiconductor Technology dropped 6.5 per cent on Friday, following a 20 per cent daily-limit plunge on Thursday, the first session after China’s week-long National Day holiday. Fellow laser chip supplier Everbright Photonics fell 5.4 per cent after a 20 per cent limit-down plunge a day earlier. In Shenzhen, Dongshan Precision fell 3.4 per cent on Friday after hitting its 10 per cent daily decline limit on Thursday, while Shanghai-listed Shijia Photons was up 3.4 per cent following a 17.4 per cent loss the day before. In contrast, major optical transceiver makers saw milder losses on Friday, with market leaders Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink falling 2.5 per cent in Hong Kong and 2.19 per cent in Shenzhen, respectively. The sector-wide sell-off was triggered by an October 1 research report by Morgan Stanley, which warned that the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) could introduce restrictions on Chinese-made optical transceivers as early as this month. The report noted that any potential measures would most likely target next-generation 3.2-terabit-per-second (3.2T) products. Optical transceivers are critical components in AI data centres, converting electrical signals into optical signals to enable high-speed data transmission between servers and computing equipment. According to the US investment bank, Washington could consider a regulatory approach allowing Chinese-made optical transceivers into the US market if at least 65 per cent of their bill-of-materials (BOM) value originated from US-based companies. Reports emerged in August that Washington was considering restrictions on Chinese optical transceivers, though the FCC’s finalised rules in September did not specifically target the products. However, Morgan Stanley’s latest report noted that a local-content mandate would put heavy pressure on upstream suppliers, favouring American makers of laser chips and other components at the expense of Chinese rivals. Major Chinese suppliers moved to reassure investors that any potential US measures would have a limited impact on their near-term operations. In a stock exchange filing on Thursday, Dongshan Precision said the 65 per cent US-content requirement was based on market speculation rather than official regulatory policy. The company said optical chips accounted for no more than 10 per cent of its transceivers’ total BOM costs, adding that it had sufficient flexibility to adjust its supply chain. It did not rule out the possibility of establishing manufacturing facilities in the US if needed. Meanwhile, an Everbright Photonics representative told Chinese news outlet National Business Daily that commercial production of 3.2T optical transceivers was not expected until 2028 or 2029. With current market demand anchored to 800G and 1.6T products, any restrictions targeting next-generation modules would have a limited immediate effect on the company, the person was cited as saying.

title: Ex-university student jailed for 7 years for rape, sexual assault and voyeurism
description: Defendant, 31, committed offences against five women, with some of the crimes taking place at EdU orientation camps.
content: A Hong Kong court has sentenced a former university student to seven years in prison for raping and sexually targeting five women, with some of the crimes taking place at orientation camps. The 31-year-old defendant was sentenced on Friday at the High Court after a jury found him guilty of one count of rape, another of voyeurism and three counts of indecent assault. The five convictions concerned offences committed between January and August 2023. The defendant, identified only by his initials YLH, was a fourth-year student at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdU) in Tai Po at the time. He denied the allegations, and the victims testified at his trial. At a joint school orientation camp in July 2023, the defendant was playing a drinking game with a male student, Noah, and another woman in a room. When Noah left, the defendant took advantage of the woman and groped her several times. He then escalated the assault and raped her that night. The following month at an EdU camp, the defendant secretly observed a woman showering before pulling open her shower curtain. At the same camp, he also molested two other women. On one occasion, he approached one of the victims at a campfire and touched her thigh. Another victim, who was not associated with any of the camps, also said the defendant sexually assaulted her in January that year inside his car after the pair had a drink in Central one night. The court heard that the defendant offered to drive the victim home, but instead took her to Kowloon Peak – a secluded area – where he molested her when she was unable to escape. Citing the victim impact reports, Madam Justice Esther Toh Lye-ping said the woman who was raped suffered from moderate depression and anxiety. Toh handed down a six-year sentence for the offence of rape. She ordered the defendant to serve a consecutive term of one year and one week for the remaining four charges.

title: Exclusive | Bessent may skip Apec in Hong Kong to focus on Trump’s Shenzhen visit, sources say
description: US Treasury secretary expected to meet Chinese vice-premier in Shenzhen ahead of summit in November as trade truce extension takes priority.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may skip a meeting of Apec finance ministers in Hong Kong later this month to focus on preparing for President Donald Trump’s historic visit to Shenzhen in November, sources told the South China Morning Post. Bessent is expected to meet Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in Shenzhen ahead of Trump’s visit – when Trump will again hold talks with President Xi Jinping – as the two sides look to secure a longer extension of the bilateral trade truce, which is due to expire on January 10. With that taking priority, it is understood that Bessent wants to focus on the Shenzhen meeting. Washington will instead send a deputy to attend the gathering of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation finance ministers in Hong Kong. Erin Browne, Treasury undersecretary for international affairs, is the leading candidate to head the US delegation on October 20 and 21, a source familiar with the situation said. Browne has been involved in the economic negotiations with China, working under Bessent on follow-through to the trade truce and on the bilateral investment dialogue meant to hold Beijing to its commitments. The sources requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak on the record about the itineraries of senior US officials, or about the highly sensitive arrangements surrounding US-China diplomacy. A second source said Bessent was not keen to travel to Hong Kong in October, citing his schedule and the proximity of the leaders’ meeting, set for November 18 and 19 across the border in Shenzhen. “Bessent’s top priority for his autumn travel calendar is accompanying President Trump on his official trip to Shenzhen for Apec, where both presidents are expected to solidify a delicate bilateral economic understanding,” the source said. During Xi’s state visit to Washington last month, the two sides extended their trade truce by two months to January 10 and agreed in principle to support each other across the Apec and Group of 20 agendas, seeking to stabilise global markets and to establish a more predictable framework for trade negotiations. Against that backdrop, the second source said, Washington’s focus had “naturally shifted towards ensuring the high-level meeting between the two top leaders in Shenzhen yields tangible economic dividends, rather than dispersing executive focus across preliminary ministerial gatherings”. “Logistically, it simply makes no practical sense for Secretary Bessent to cross the Pacific twice in less than four weeks,” a third source involved in international economic policy discussions told the SCMP. “Hong Kong is a long way … and he is already confirmed to be in China alongside President Trump in November.” The source added that Bessent had a demanding schedule as host of upcoming G20 finance events, which required substantial preparation. “Apec is not the primary venue for global financial architecture or macroeconomic rebalancing. Those discussions traditionally take place within the G20 and the International Monetary Fund,” the third source said. “As such, the Treasury secretary’s absence from the finance ministers’ meeting is not really material to substantive global policy.” A further source also said Apec was “not involved in important global financial and macroeconomic matters” and was “largely a forum for trade and investment facilitation and liberalisation”. The meeting was therefore not a high priority for Bessent, the source said. Another person familiar with the situation added that it should not come as a “surprise” and there was “no chatter” about Bessent attending at all. A separate source said the absence should not be read as a snub to Hong Kong or to Apec since Bessent had “already participated prominently” in Trump’s economic diplomacy with the region, “including representing Trump at the 2025 Apec leaders’ informal dialogue”. Washington has long treated the finance ministers’ meeting as optional for the Treasury secretary. US Treasury secretaries have only attended four Apec finance ministers’ meetings held overseas since the turn of the century: Suzhou in 2001, Chiang Mai in 2003, Hanoi in 2006 and Kyoto in 2010. Most of Bessent’s predecessors have sent deputies to lead delegations at the meetings. Former Treasury secretary Janet Yellen attended only once during her four-year tenure, in 2023, when the United States hosted Apec in San Francisco and she chaired the meeting, and otherwise delegated representation to her deputies. For Hong Kong, hosting the meeting remains a significant milestone, underscoring its role as Asia’s premier international financial centre and as a bridge between mainland China and global capital markets. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Tuesday pledged a “high quality” experience for guests, as the city works closely with Beijing to assist delegations with registration. About 500 guests – including finance ministers and senior officials from the 21 member economies – are expected to attend. Hong Kong is hosting the meeting for the first time, at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Lee said the government would continue close communication and cooperation with Beijing’s Ministry of Finance on the arrangements. Beyond the official sessions, it will host a welcome dinner, seminars and visits for delegations. Additional reporting by Nayan Seth and Dewey Sim

title: 5 horology highs in September, from Geneva and Bangkok watch fairs to new Rolex
description: Roger Federer sported the new Rolex Perpetual Padellone at the Laver Cup, while Matthew McConaughey wore the relaunched Cartier Roadster at the Emmys.
content: September is when the weather always cools, and the world of high horology heats up after a summer lull. Geneva Watch Days kicked off the month with a bang, growing to 71 brands and welcoming more than 2,500 visitors this year. As one of the year’s most talked-about watch fairs, it also set the stage for House of Brands to relaunch Gallet. Meanwhile, Bangkok Watch Week represented Southeast Asia as collectors descended upon Thailand to see novelties, meet other enthusiasts and hear brands share insights. Beyond that, Jaeger-LeCoultre and Rolex made splashy releases and Matthew McConaughey wore a Cartier Roadster to the Emmys. Here are our top high horology moments for September. Geneva Watch Days goes from strength to strength It’s been another bumper year for what is arguably becoming the second-largest annual watch fair on the high horology calendar. This year, 71 brands and over 2,500 collectors, clients and enthusiasts descended on the Rotonde du Mont-Blanc from September 2 to 6 to see almost 400 new watch releases in the metal. Visitors also heard talks from industry professionals, took part in watchmaking challenges, and bid on 16 lots at a charity auction organised by Phillips in Association with Bacs & Russo, raising 115,500 Swiss francs (US$139,110) for the Geneva Watchmaking School to support apprentices through the Pierre Amstutz Fund. Established and independent brands alike saved momentous releases for the week. Tudor revived its Northflag line with a METAS-certified GMT tool watch, and Tag Heuer revisited the Monza chronograph with a carbon-forged case and a flyback chronograph with a black dial and red accents. Breitling paid tribute to one of its most famous wearers – jazz trumpet legend and the original Prince of Darkness himself, Miles Davis – by releasing the Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41, a nod to the Navitimer Ref. 806 mk5 Davis wore. On the more independent side, Vianney Halter imbued his aesthetic signatures into Bulgari’s Octo Finissimo, rendering a watch that looks as though it could belong in both individual catalogues. De Bethune and MB&F both went jump hour – the former gave us the DB25 Digitale, featuring a starry blue titanium dial as is the maison’s signature, along with a minutes wheel at six o’clock. MB&F reimagined 82-year-old Vincent Calabrese’s Baladin watch from 1989 to give us the M.A.D.3 Vincent Calabrese. The pink version is exclusive to the brand’s Tribe members and friends of the brand, whereas the blue is available via MB&F’s traditional raffle system. House of Brands relaunches Gallet Perhaps most notably at Geneva Watch Days, the House of Brands – which comprises Breitling and the previously relaunched Universal Genève – revived Gallet on its 200th anniversary by bringing back historic models tailor-made for exploration. The Flying Officer was first released in 1939 as an early tool for intercontinental pilots or passengers tracking multiple time zones, while a later piece, the Multichron Pilot, was released 30 years later for largely the same purpose but built with a chronograph and using more durable materials. Both reappear in Gallet’s current line-up, alongside an array of classic bicompax chronographs under the Gallet Classics line, including the Tribute to Multichron Yachting Big Eye, which has a tidal indicator in red and blue at three o’clock. Bangkok Watch Week On this side of the globe, Bangkok cemented its place as one of Southeast Asia’s premier watch meccas as developer Siam Piwat hosted Bangkok Watch Week at Siam Paragon from September 22 to 27. More than 45 haute horology brands and independent watchmakers met collectors, industry leaders and enthusiasts to discover over 200 novelties and take part in an expanded symposium. The 18 sessions covered everything from brand craftsmanship to the future of watch culture. Highlights included Franck Muller and Vacheron Constantin discussing their signature Crazy Hours and Historiques American 1921 models, as well as a keynote from House of Brands CEO Georges Kern on brand legacy. The Laver Cup and Emmys – prime time for prime watches If you’re not a watch convention type of person, it seemed that even in September, tennis tournaments were a stellar opportunity to catch high horology on the wrists of the rich and famous. Roger Federer attended the Laver Cup in just a button-down, but flashed the newly released Rolex Perpetual Padellone (more on that later), while Jonah Hill, courtesy of Wristcheck, was spotted at the US Open with a Naoya Hida & Co. NH Type 1D in steel, adding to a year of explosive exposure for the independent Japanese watchmaker. Off the courts, stars showed out at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles for the 78th Emmy Awards. Hublot, Rolex and Vacheron Constantin dotted the red carpet, but perhaps most interesting was Matthew McConaughey discreetly sporting a blue-dialled Cartier Roadster, relaunched this year in a distinctive tonneau case with a date aperture. New releases Even outside watch fairs, brands kept up with huge releases. Rolex may have given us the biggest splash of all. After introducing the Settimo seven-link bracelet on the dressy 1908 line, Rolex now presents a similar silhouette in Everose gold and platinum. Inspired by the mid-20th-century reference 8171, the Rolex Perpetual Padellone offers an annual calendar with a pointer date, day-month aperture, and moonphase. Jaeger-LeCoultre also made waves this month with massive releases across several models. The Master Hybris Artistica Minute Repeater Cosmotourbillon has a tourbillon which completes a counter-clockwise revolution after one sidereal day (23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds). The Duometre Grande Complication à Grande Sonnerie adds two types of chiming to 13 other complications including a flying tourbillon and a retrograde perpetual calendar. Last but not least, the Calibre 101 returns via the 101 Secrets, hiding the time behind a bracelet set in a gradient of pink sapphires. Extremely round cases for smaller watches also seemed in vogue this month, as Blancpain released the ultra-small yet chic Lady B and Louis Vuitton reprised its Monterey in ceramic after launching the model last year. The Lady B features a striking bubble-shaped case with hidden lugs coming in at just 19mm and 2.9 cubic centimetres in volume, a perfect visual accent for more slender wrists, whereas the Monterey comes in a more standard 37mm – still 2mm down from the October 2025 version in yellow gold.

title: China holiday travel spikes, global funds shift: 5 figures investors are watching in China
description: A Kowloon residential site sale and Hong Kong’s MPF gains shape the week’s market narrative.
content: Hong Kong’s property market showed renewed strength as a Kowloon residential site fetched its highest price in nearly five years, while the city’s pension funds posted solid gains despite a September setback. Meanwhile, global investors returned to Chinese equities after years of caution, as US Treasury yields surged to multi-decade highs. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. China records 2.14 billion passenger trips over National Day holiday China recorded 2.14 billion cross-regional passenger trips during the seven-day National Day holiday, averaging 306 million journeys a day, up 0.7 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Transport. The holiday box office fell 36.5 per cent to 1.165 billion yuan from a year earlier, according to National Film Administration data reported by CCTV, though this year’s holiday was one day shorter than last year’s. US 10-year Treasury yield hits 24-year high of 5.36 per cent The benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.36 per cent on Wednesday, its highest level in 24 years, as rising oil prices and persistent inflation concerns triggered another sell-off in government bonds. The 30-year yield also reached a 24-year high of 5.7 per cent, although a strong US$39 billion auction of 10-year notes later helped ease selling pressure, suggesting that higher yields were attracting investors back into the market. Hong Kong’s MPF gains nearly HK$100 billion in first nine months Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund generated HK$96.9 billion (US$12.34 billion) in investment gains over the first nine months of the year, delivering an average return of 6.2 per cent, according to MPF Ratings on Wednesday. The gains came despite a setback in September, when the city’s compulsory retirement scheme lost HK$25.1 billion, or 1.47 per cent, across its 382 investment funds. Global funds end four-year underweight stance on Chinese equities Global active long-only funds have raised their allocations to Chinese equities to benchmark-neutral levels, ending four years of underweight positioning, according to Bank of America. The shift, observed across nearly 2,800 funds managing US$562 billion in Chinese stocks, reflects renewed interest in relatively cheap valuations and artificial intelligence opportunities, although analysts cautioned that it did not necessarily signal a bullish turn. Kerry Properties pays HK$4.31 billion for Kowloon residential site Kerry Properties acquired a residential plot in Ho Man Tin for HK$4.31 billion (US$549 million), according to Hong Kong’s Lands Department on Tuesday, the highest price paid for a residential site in Kowloon in nearly five years. The Fat Kwong Street site fetched HK$20,738 per square foot of gross floor area, reflecting developers’ renewed appetite for prime residential land amid expectations of resilient demand for luxury homes.

title: Legal arguments delay trial over murder of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi again
description: Nine-member jury told to return on Monday as lawyers debate legal issues, delaying cross-examination of Choi’s mother.
content: The murder trial of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has been delayed again while the court addresses legal issues raised by lawyers in the high-profile case. Deputy High Court Judge Brian Keith told the nine-member jury on Friday that the hearing would resume on Monday after the legal arguments concluded. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, had been expected to face cross-examination by counsel for Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, on the fifth day of her testimony. He is standing trial on a joint murder charge alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35. The elder Kwong, a former police sergeant, has also pleaded not guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial. Parts of the 28-year-old influencer’s dismembered remains were found at a village house in Tai Po on February 24, 2023. Prosecutors allege that the trio killed Choi over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria development in Ho Man Tin. They allege that Kwong Kau, the registered owner, resented Choi’s efforts to sell the property and enlisted his two sons to help kill her and dispose of her remains. In earlier testimony, Cheung said the Kwong family had relied on her family’s wealth without contributing to the support of Choi’s two children with Alex Kwong. She described Kwong Kau as a “cunning old fox” and alleged that his two sons were skilled at coaxing others into doing their bidding.

title: 11 premises raided over alleged bid-rigging to supply virtual reality systems to schools
description: Hong Kong’s competition watchdog searches suspects’ offices and homes after complaints of price-fixing over deals worth HK$10 million.
content: Hong Kong’s competition watchdog has raided 11 offices and homes over alleged bid-rigging for contracts to supply virtual reality (VR) systems to schools and non-profit organisations, with the deals valued at HK$10 million (US$1.3 million). The Competition Commission revealed on Friday that it had secured warrants and searched the 11 premises, including those of several IT service and equipment providers, other firms and the residences of several suspects, in an operation the previous day. The companies were accused of engaging in bid-rigging, price-fixing, market-sharing and exchanging competitively sensitive information when providing quotations for VR equipment and software installation services to various schools and non-profit organisations, the watchdog said. The commission said the searches were prompted by earlier complaints alleging that some IT suppliers had engaged in anti-competitive conduct when submitting quotations for VR systems, such as preparing tender documents for other suppliers and companies so they could act as sham bidders. “The commission followed up on the case and was satisfied that there was reasonable cause to suspect that a contravention of a competition rule had taken place,” it said. The watchdog said it would proceed with its investigation and requested the relevant parties to produce documents and information. “Rapid advancements in VR technology have led to its widespread usage across various fields,” it added. “This case concerns schools and non-profit organisations, and the suspected anti-competitive conduct involved may ultimately result in reduced choices or increased costs for these organisations, thereby compromising the efficient use of public resources.” In March, the commission took legal action at the Competition Tribunal over six undertakings involving eight companies and 12 individuals linked to building maintenance projects worth nearly HK$700 million. The legal action targeted alleged corruption and anti-competitive practices in the syndicate’s bids for projects at 11 housing estates and buildings between April 2022 and September 2023. One of the estates was Wang Fuk Court, where 168 people died in an inferno in November last year. In July, the commission revised its tender clauses so that bidders using them would be required to make a statutory declaration that they had not engaged in collusion on a project, amid calls to criminalise bid-rigging. On the maximum penalty, the watchdog earlier said a proposed seven years’ imprisonment would only be the minimum and the penalty could be raised to 10 years in jail. The commission will also launch a study into the city’s auto fuel market amid a surge in prices, according to its chairman, Jat Sew-tong. The sector has faced long-standing allegations of price-fixing.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: scientist’s soybean research pushes agricultural frontier
description: Lam Hon-ming’s groundbreaking work on soybean genetics and varieties has led to cultivation in mainland China, contributing to country’s food security.
content: When Professor Lam Hon-ming returned to Hong Kong after completing postdoctoral work in the United States in 1997, he was fixated on one question: how can science help feed the country and the world? He found that soybeans offered part of the answer. In addition to its nutritional value, the crop can fix nitrogen levels in the soil, reducing reliance on chemical fertiliser, and some varieties can be bred to tolerate drought and salinity. Lam went on to spend almost three decades studying soybean genetics and developing varieties suited to marginal land. “I wanted to work in agricultural research because it is important for everyone, although relatively few people were doing it,” said Lam, the director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s State Key Laboratory of Agrobiotechnology. “Coming from a low-income family in Hong Kong myself, I understood how important access to food and opportunities can be for people from disadvantaged backgrounds.” His research has since moved well beyond the laboratory. Lam and his collaborators published work in the scientific journal Nature Genetics in 2010 examining genetic diversity across wild and cultivated soybean genomes. Four years later, his team reported a gene associated with salt tolerance in wild soybean in another publication, Nature Communications. Ordinary soybeans fail where salt has built up in the soil. Irrigation and dry weather leave that salt behind, and large stretches of farmland in northwestern mainland China cannot support a normal crop. That science has been applied to breeding non-genetically modified soybean varieties that can cope with difficult growing conditions. Several varieties produced with mainland partners were approved for cultivation, including in Gansu province. From 2016 to 2024, the cumulative area planted with three varieties exceeded 100,000 hectares (247,105 acres). “To me, it shows what Hong Kong science can contribute to mainland agriculture,” said Lam. Lam’s soybean work received a Gold Medal with Congratulations of the Jury at the 50th International Exhibition of Inventions Geneva in 2025. “You cannot simply come in and tell farmers what to do,” he said. “You have to work with them, understand what they need and find something that works locally.” That approach has also taken his research overseas, with collaborators in Pakistan, Bangladesh and Cambodia, as well as projects and discussions elsewhere in South Asia and Southeast Asia. “Every place has different soil, temperatures and growing seasons,” Lam said. “Varieties have to be selected for local conditions and sometimes tested for two or three seasons before anyone can be sure they will work.” Lam is quick to share the credit. He recalls his wife supporting him when he used his own salary for early field trials. The Lo Kwee Seong Foundation and Lee Hysan Foundation also supported his field work, and the two organisations generally contribute to science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) education. More recently, colleagues and private investors have backed projects over the longer timelines common in agriculture. His work has earned him a place as a finalist in the innovation category of the Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post. Lam is now working to ensure years of research can continue beyond academic papers and his own career, including through commercial applications in agriculture and food. “When I was younger, I always wanted to be the one charging ahead,” he said. “Now I want to create the conditions for others to take the work forward. If the next generation can carry it further than I did, that is enough for me.”

title: Hong Kong needs tougher inspection regime, experts say after CK Asset building fiasco
description: Hong Kong lawmakers call for more inspectors and barring of errant contractors from government tenders after serious lapses at Kwun Tong project.
content: Lawmakers and engineering sector leaders have called for a review of Hong Kong’s building inspection mechanism and a blacklist to bar errant contractors from government tenders, after a developer said half of the city’s first privately built “starter homes” project will be demolished due to shoddy steel work. The government should review the inspection regime and increase its supervisory manpower, lawmakers and engineers said on Friday, calling for inspectors to be stationed at construction sites of privately built subsidised housing estates rather than relying on spot checks. The call came after the Buildings Department said on Thursday it had approved property developer CK Asset Holding’s plan to tear down and rebuild three of the six blocks at the Anderson Road development in Kwun Tong, with remedial work continuing on the rest. Earlier investigations found that the steel reinforcement in parts of the towers diverged significantly from approved plans, with fewer reinforcement bars used than required. Engineering sector lawmaker Aaron Bok Kwok-ming said on Friday that any violation of construction standards should be punished and prosecuted, while stressing that such cases remained rare. “Hong Kong carries out some HK$250 billion (US$31.8 billion) of construction work every year, and cases like this remain a small minority,” he told the media. “But the government should review whether the level of supervision needs strengthening and allocate more resources and staff to engineering teams, as that cost is only a very small portion of the overall project.” CK Asset said the remedial proposals it submitted to the government were too “time-consuming” after an engineering consultant spent nearly two years investigating the three buildings in question and came up with the planned solutions. Bok said demolition was an extreme step rarely taken in the industry, as building designs incorporated substantial safety margins and redundancy that allowed localised defects to be fixed through minor strengthening works. Bok added that whether the project would remain profitable after demolition was for the developer to assess, but that he doubted that the margins were large enough to absorb such a cost. The Anderson Road development is a “starter homes” project, under which the government invited private tenders to help first-time buyers ineligible for subsidised flats under the Home Ownership Scheme. The project comprises about 2,930 flats, at least 1,000 of which are to be sold at 80 per cent of market price to Hongkongers who have never owned residential property and meet income and asset limits. Construction was halted in October 2024 after the steel reinforcement discrepancies came to light. The city’s corruption watchdog said in May last year that 10 people had been arrested over the case for alleged bribery, conspiracy to defraud and use of false documents. Some of the suspects were related to the project’s former main contractors, Aggressive Construction Engineering, and Superb Interior Contracting, the South China Morning Post learned earlier. CK Asset named China Railway Construction Group Company as the new contractor. The fiasco has intensified growing concern in recent months over local construction standards. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu stressed the importance of building quality ahead of an Executive Council meeting earlier in the week, saying the Development Bureau would table proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance before the end of the year to tighten regulation and stiffen penalties for malpractice and shoddy work. Lawmaker Scott Leung Man-kwong said the case could dent confidence in the public-private partnership model, under which developers building subsidised housing largely police themselves and the government intervenes only when problems emerge. “For subsidised housing built with private sector participation, authorities should follow the practice for public housing and station teams at construction sites to monitor work, so problems are caught during the process rather than at the spot check stage,” he said. Leung is a member of the Housing Authority and its subsidised housing committee He also called for an integrity regime within the public works system, including a blacklist that would bar contractors found guilty of major violations, shoddy work or corruption from bidding on government contracts for a specified period, on top of criminal prosecution. “Restrictions need to be tougher than they are now to strengthen deterrence and prevent such failures from happening again,” he said.

title: Why Hong Kong’s Cantonese restaurants are closing – and who is saving them
description: As the city’s Cantonese restaurants vanish at a rate of nearly one a week, a new generation of chefs and restaurateurs asks what can be saved – and what must change.
content: The last basket of dim sum is sold, the roller shutter comes down, and another Cantonese restaurant in Hong Kong closes. Nine months into 2026, this scene has already played out at least 30 times. The causes are familiar – sky-high rents, thin margins, rising costs, and dining habits reshaped by the pandemic years. Legislative Council figures show that between 2018 and 2025, the number of Cantonese restaurants and banquet halls in Hong Kong fell from 1,790 to 1,500, representing a 16 per cent drop, or nearly one fewer every week over seven years. Across generations, local restaurants have carried the everyday life of Hong Kong. But as spending habits and tastes change, what disappears may be more than places to eat. For nearly 40 years, Hong Kong Chinese Chefs Association president Ricky Kong has carried on his family’s three-generation culinary legacy. Today, as the trade faces mounting pressures, his focus has broadened to preserving the craft and ensuring there is a next generation to carry it forward. “When we entered the trade, the kitchen was run like a military boot camp. Every day, the master would scold us. Management is much more flexible now. The starting salary for a Chinese chef isn’t low, about HK$22,000, but fewer and fewer young people are willing to join,” he says. With fewer juniors on staff, restaurants are replacing some handwork with pre-prepared dishes.
