And when a dish is split between factory production and restaurant reheating, what is lost is not only the process but the passing of a craft from master to apprentice. “Some traditional dishes, like Golden Coin Chicken and Pipa Bird’s Nest, require so much labour that few restaurants can spare the staff and time,” Kong says. “Where kitchens once employed someone solely to pick crabmeat, many now use canned crab.” Kong understands he cannot save the entirety of Cantonese cuisine but must be selective. At his restaurant Lion Rock, he has curated an Intangible Cultural Heritage Banquet showcasing traditional techniques behind Hong Kong salted fish and shrimp paste. For Kong, passing on Cantonese cuisine means giving its craftsmanship a future, not keeping it in the past. While some old establishments bow out, the century-old Lin Heung Tea House has chosen to evolve. Under new management, the team behind it brings more than 20 years of Lan Kwai Fong nightlife experience to the traditional teahouse. “We adjust the menu to each branch’s clientele,” says marketing director Yin Wong, who is also an electronic music producer. Yin highlights how dishes at the teahouse’s airport branch are boneless and foreigner-friendly, while dishes in Tsim Sha Tsui lean spicier to cater to mainland visitors. Machines are gradually replacing time-consuming handwork. Once that stops, we lose not just a technique, but a piece of who we are ArChan Chan, Ho Lee Fook The reinvention goes beyond the menu. To revive the old tradition of “night tea”, the Tsim Sha Tsui and airport branches operate 24 hours, while the Sheung Wan flagship screens live sports on a nine-metre LED display. Alongside retro Cantopop parties and celebrity collaborations, these changes are drawing back a generation no longer in the habit of going to a teahouse. If old names are using new methods, how does a younger generation of chefs find the balance? “I grew up in Sham Shui Po. One of my first memories of Cantonese food is going to a dai pai dong with my whole family,” says ArChan Chan. She remembers wok-fried baby bok choy with garlic and clams in black bean sauce – simple dishes whose wok hei and flavour captivated her as a child. Years later, after working in Australia and Singapore, she returned to Hong Kong to head Ho Lee Fook and began rethinking which traditions should stay and which practices can change. “One skill I fear will eventually be lost is making har gow wrappers by hand,” she says. “Machines are gradually replacing time-consuming handwork. Once that stops, we lose not just a technique, but a piece of who we are.” Yet she is no stickler for tradition and is against the habit of using baking soda to tenderise meat. “We gain texture and lose taste,” she notes. It is not just Cantonese restaurants and dining houses; traditional cha chaan tengs are also innovating. In 2025, after their father passed away, Lavitt Ko and Theo Ko, then only 25 and 23, took over Kam Shun in Tai Wai. “Unlike our parents’ generation, young people today don’t go to a cha chaan teng every day,” remarks Lavitt. To entice them back, they installed speakers in the restaurant, with DJs playing upbeat music and live beatbox performances, and launched a “Milk Tea Rave” inspired by the coffee rave trend. “At first, the neighbours found it novel. They’d pass by and ask what we were doing, and many regulars stayed to join in and support us,” Lavitt says. Gradually, word spread and now guests visit from Sai Kung, “two hours by bus” says Theo, to take part. The brothers insisted on maintaining the booth seating from when Kam Shun first opened, and on preserving the cha chaan teng’s human warmth. “The waitress remembers what regulars like. Sometimes a customer doesn’t have to say a word, she already knows what they want,” the pair say. “This is a community connection. It’s what we most want to keep.”

title: Japan angry after Russia seeks extradition of ICC chief targeted by US
description: Tokyo condemned Moscow’s move against Tomoko Akane and eight other officials, pledging to ‘take the appropriate path of action’.
content: A senior Japanese government spokesperson said it was regrettable that the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office had requested that Dutch authorities extradite International Criminal Court president Tomoko Akane and eight other officials. “Time and again we have conveyed to the Russian side that measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unfair and unacceptable. We find it regrettable that the Russian side has nevertheless requested various nations to extradite these individuals,” Japan’s Deputy Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said at a regular news conference on Friday morning. “We hope to take the appropriate path of action, including issuing further protests against the Russian side regarding this unjust measure, based on continued communication with the ICC and other signatories,” Ozaki added. Akane is on Russia’s wanted list, along with other ICC officials, over the court’s 2023 arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin on allegations of war crimes in Ukraine. She and other ICC members were tried in absentia and sentenced to prison terms by a Moscow court in 2025. The latest development comes amid increasing pressure on the ICC from countries including Russia and the United States, raising questions about how Japan will support the court as its closest ally works to dismantle the institution. Akane has also been sanctioned by the US following accusations that it has unfairly targeted the US and Israel in the wake of its investigation into the conflict in Gaza. The incident represented a rare public point of friction between Japan and the US, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi initially came under fire for not condemning the action beyond calling it “regrettable”. She has since taken the issue up with US President Donald Trump himself in a meeting held in September. “We have consistently supported the ICC in accordance with our efforts to uphold the rule of law and we will continue to do so,” Takaichi said during a parliamentary session held on Friday morning.

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: youth-led charity supports young cancer patients
description: Timothy Chan founded Youth Cancer Hong Kong so young patients can speak openly with others who understand what diagnosis and treatment mean at their age.
content: Timothy Chan Chi-fung was 19 when a testicular tumour sent him into a Hong Kong hospital system largely designed for children or much older adults. Neither door quite fitted. His experience eventually led him to found Youth Cancer Hong Kong, a contribution that has earned him a place as a finalist in the community category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards. The awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, were launched in 2013 to recognise individuals and organisations whose work contributes to Hong Kong and its communities. Chan was diagnosed in 2019 with a mixed germ cell tumour of the testis. He underwent surgery within two weeks of his diagnosis, followed by two cycles of chemotherapy. He lost his hair and his studies at university were interrupted. But he eventually recovered. Now in his sixth year of follow-up checks, Chan, now 26, is pursuing a master’s degree in psychology at the University of Hong Kong and is determined to become a clinical psychologist working with people affected by cancer. Youth Cancer Hong Kong grew out of accounts Chan posted online about his diagnosis, treatment and the lack of people his age to talk to. Other young patients began writing to him, and those exchanges prompted them to form a mutual support group, Stars of Life, in July 2022. A year later, Youth Cancer Hong Kong was registered as a charity. Today, its community numbers about 400 to 500 people who were diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 39, with at least 10 newcomers joining the group each month, often through Instagram. The city recorded 4,579 new cancer cases among a similar age group – 20 to 40 – in 2023, according to the Hospital Authority’s Hong Kong Cancer Registry. “The most fundamental support is that you are not alone,” he said. At gatherings, conversations can be strikingly direct. “What cancer have you got? Which chemo? Which targeted drug? Which doctor? These are subjects that families may find painful to hear repeatedly, while fellow patients understand them immediately,” Chan said. The group relies largely on donations from patients and families who have used its services. About 28 volunteers, including doctors, nurses, social workers, occupational therapists, students and a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner, support its work. Peer support is a major part of that work, pairing new patients with people who have been through similar experiences. Clinicians also translate overseas information on adolescent and young adult cancer, including fertility issues, which can become an urgent concern when chemotherapy threatens future plans for children. Public education is another major strand of their work. Through school talks where young patients share their personal experiences directly with participants and an exhibition at Central Market, topics that are rarely discussed openly are brought into public conversation. Chan has also spoken at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s medical faculty for three consecutive years. The sessions give future doctors an opportunity to meet patients close to their own age and consider how best to communicate with them. “If you have been the patient, you talk differently,” he said. His longer-term hope is for Hong Kong to establish dedicated youth cancer support as part of the public healthcare system, bringing psychological, fertility and social services together. Turning 18, he said, did not suddenly make someone an adult with different needs. Youth Cancer Hong Kong also supports families when members die. Chan often returns to an idea from the 2017 American film Coco – that people finally disappear when they are forgotten. “For as long as you remember what they changed in you, they’re still around,” he said.

title: Hong Kong faces limited impact if Fed curbs access to US dollar funding facility: analysts
description: A US lawmaker has asked Fed chair Kevin Warsh to review Hong Kong’s access to an emergency funding facility, citing Beijing’s global yuan push.
content: A US lawmaker’s call for a review of Hong Kong’s access to a Federal Reserve facility that provides short-term US dollar funding would have limited impact on the city as it is not a regular source of financing, according to analysts, who said any restriction could instead weaken the US dollar’s global dominance. John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, has written to US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh urging a review of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s (HKMA) access to the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities (FIMA) repo facility, which provides short-term US dollar liquidity to foreign central banks, according to a statement published by the committee on Tuesday. Moolenaar asked Warsh to respond by Wednesday on whether the Fed should allow the HKMA to retain access to the facility. He cited the authority’s role in supporting the People’s Bank of China’s efforts to expand yuan internationalisation, particularly after the PBOC introduced a new yuan-denominated repo facility modelled on the FIMA programme in June. The Federal Reserve told the South China Morning Post in response to an inquiry: “We have received the letter and plan to respond”. A Hong Kong Monetary Authority spokeswoman said: “We do not have any comment to offer.” Hong Kong bankers and traders said losing access to the FIMA facility would have little impact on Hong Kong because it was designed to provide emergency funding, rather than serve as a regular source of financing. The facility was introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic and became a permanent standing facility in July 2021. The HKMA has also introduced a temporary US$10 billion liquidity facility using the FIMA repo arrangement and has not disclosed usage data, but bankers said they rarely used it at all after the pandemic. Limiting HKMA from accessing FIMA repo would only lead the international world to cut down their reliance on the US dollar Jasper Lo, independent analyst “The US committee itself is only advisory, and its suggestions do not always turn into reality,” said Wilson Chan Fung-cheung, an adjunct professor at City University of Hong Kong. The Fed, Chan added, was unlikely to restrict the HKMA’s access because the facility was created to protect global financial stability during crises. “The current proposal by the committee chairman only focuses on political tensions and has not considered the importance of global financial stability,” said Chan, who worked as a banker for three decades before turning to academia. “I do not think HKMA or the Hong Kong banking sector would suffer much if we cannot use these FIMA repos,” Chan said. “The city’s Exchange Fund has a total size of HK$4.46 trillion [US$568 billion], which can fully support the Hong Kong dollar and the local financial system with no need to use the FIMA repo.” Jasper Lo, a veteran foreign exchange trader and independent analyst, also predicted that the Fed would not allow political pressure to influence the market. “The US has tried to continue the US dollar’s dominance. Limiting HKMA from accessing FIMA repo would only lead the international world to cut down their reliance on the US dollar,” he said. “For banks in Hong Kong, they have no difficulties attracting US dollar deposits.” Hong Kong banks held HK$9.4 trillion in US dollar deposits at the end of August, higher than their HK$8.8 trillion in Hong Kong dollar deposits, according to HKMA data. Lo attributed the trend to the higher interest rates available on US dollar deposits compared with those on Hong Kong dollar deposits. Additional reporting by Teresa Frontado

title: China proposes ‘basic safeguards’ to cover expanding gig workforce but gaps remain
description: The draft requires that payment cycles not exceed one month and holiday work be paid at a higher rate, but it does not specify by how much.
content: China has issued a draft of its first formal regulation to extend labour-law protections to the country’s rapidly growing ranks of gig and platform workers, a major segment of an expanding flexible workforce within the country’s tough job market. Platform workers, such as ride-hailing drivers and those engaged in food deliveries – a group totalling 84 million who often face irregular pay and intense workloads – will be entitled to basic labour protections covering pay, rest periods, workplace safety and more, according to the draft published on Thursday for public comment. However, it only sets minimum standards for working conditions, falling far short of the protections currently afforded to workers in formal employment, according to the document from the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security. “[The] government has finally taken action on the long overdue occupational security issues of workers who have not established clear labour relationships,” said He Wenjiong, a professor at Zhejiang University who specialises in social security. The move comes as a rising number of Chinese turn to flexible work amid decreasing formal job openings amid an economic slowdown, raising concerns among the top leadership and members of the public over their rights, he added. The nation’s ninth national survey of the workforce in 2023 showed that China had about 402 million workers, with roughly one-fifth in “new forms of employment”, meaning they earned a living by providing labour through internet platforms under platform rules and instructions. The number is part of a broader flexible workforce that was estimated to total more than 200 million as of last year, according to a report co-issued by hiring agency zhaopin.com and Jinan University in February. Even during this summer’s typhoon weather, when a customer placed an order, I had to go – otherwise the platform would reduce the number of future orders assigned to me Shen Qilan, Shanghai “The new regulation cannot address all the issues, but it at least establishes some important principles and puts in place several basic safeguards – for example, ensuring that wages will no longer be delayed, and protecting workers against occupational injury,” He said. The draft requires that payment cycles not exceed one month and that work done on holidays be paid at a higher rate, but it does not specify by how much. It also demands that platform companies join the government’s occupational injury protection scheme for workers, but the companies are not mandated to provide social insurance such as pensions and medical coverage. On the right to rest, the regulation calls for “reasonably determining” maximum daily and weekly working hours and making them public. Shen Qilan, who takes orders from a domestic-service platform to provide cleaning and cooking services for households in Shanghai, said she currently had none of the proposed protections. “Even during this summer’s typhoon weather, when a customer placed an order, I had to go – otherwise the platform would reduce the number of future orders assigned to me,” she said. “If it’s something extremely important, like getting married or a spouse’s death, you can request not to take orders, but only for two or three days at most,” she said. In March, the human resources ministry said at a press conference that 17 provinces across China had run pilot programmes for occupational injury protection for gig workers, with more than 25 million people enrolled.

title: What is authentic Chaoshan cuisine? 3 top chefs across Guangdong may have to agree to disagree
description: With Chiu Chow cuisine interpreted differently across Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Hong Kong, three chefs weigh in on what gives the regional fare its soul.
content: At Shenzhen’s The Bay by Chef Fei, a dish of fish simmered with bamboo shoots in plum juice and pickled vegetables is plated individually and served to diners one by one. At Chiu Tang in Hong Kong, diners sit at round tables, share stories, sip oolong tea and reach for morsels from communal dishes. As Chaoshan cuisine, traditionally rooted in coastal neighbourhoods and late-night street food stalls, moves into luxury restaurants and is reimagined through French-style tasting menus and fine-dining plating, a dialogue unfolds between international innovation and preserving the soul of the streets. Talk to the people doing the cooking, and one question keeps surfacing: does the soul of Chaoshan food live at the table or in the flavour – and who gets to call it authentic? When chefs talk about the soul of Chaoshan cuisine, also called Chiu Chow cuisine, they usually mean three things: the freshness of the ingredients, the heat of the wok, and the informality of the table. The first two can travel. The third is harder to plate. Three chefs with roots in the region give three different answers. In 2026, the cuisine is stepping onto the international stage. “More and more international professional catering awards are paying attention to Chaoshan cuisine,” says Huang Jinghui, head chef at The Bay by Chef Fei in Shenzhen. “How to establish stable production standards in different regions, let more young customers understand this innovative aesthetic, and make the experience and expression more in line with the contemporary context, are all issues that must be faced,” he says. Chef Chen Xiaodong has called his Guangzhou restaurant, Chao Yue, “a love letter I wrote to Chaoshan”. But a love letter has to be read in a language the reader understands. For Chen, Chaoshan’s modernisation runs parallel to Cantonese cuisine’s broader identity, where innovation isn’t a rejection of the past but part of the tradition itself. “A pioneering spirit runs through Cantonese cuisine; it has always embraced change,” he says. Chen points to Chaoshan’s deep roots, from fishermen venturing far out to sea to the traditions of fishmongers and fish rice born of ritual offerings, which give the cuisine a mythic dimension that transcends simple street food. Despite the name, fish rice contains no rice: whole fish are gently poached in brine until the flesh turns silky, served as the meal’s staple in place of grain. To share this traditional delicacy with food lovers worldwide, Chen has presented it as a refined dining experience. While the traditional version uses barramundi, he chooses a fattier fish, slow-cooks it at a low temperature, and rolls it into delicate fish rolls. These are topped with a crispy, fish-shaped skin, rolled out with a pasta machine to achieve a texture as light and airy as a soda cracker. Thus, a refined version of fish rice was born. Huang was born and raised in Chaoshan, and he sees the region’s cuisine transforming into a Western-style tasting menu as a way to create rhythm. “The tasting menu does not alter the core essence of the cuisine, but rather enhances its rhythm and layers, allowing well-heeled diners at home and abroad to savour Chaoshan flavours from a more nuanced perspective,” Huang explains. His poached threadfin fish comes with pickles, plum sauce and the umami that defines Chaoshan pickled vegetables. It is served in individual portions to ensure precise temperature control and consistent texture at the moment of tasting. “Shenzhen has a huge Chaoshan population, and Chaoshan cuisine has a strong urban background here,” Huang says. The city’s fast pace, diversity and mature high-end dining scene made it a natural place to pursue what he calls a more balanced expression between tradition and refinement. Cheung Lam-por, executive chef of Hong Kong’s Chiu Tang, also comes from Chaoshan – Puning, to be precise – but he is not convinced reinvention is the way forward. Cheung emphasises that sharing dishes is a traditional custom rooted in Chaoshan life, which Western-style single-serving dishes cannot replicate. From a practical cooking perspective, many Chaoshan dishes are collectively cooked in the same wok or clay pot. Serving them family-style keeps the dishes hot and preserves their true taste; dividing them into individual portions cools them faster. “From a cultural perspective, sitting around a shared dining table symbolises unity and warmth,” Cheung says. “Everyone eats from shared dishes in the centre, which not only brings people closer together, but also promotes lively conversations and strengthens family bonds. This is a communal experience that individual plating cannot replicate.” For Cheung, ultimate luxury is not expensive wine pairings but Chiu Chow traditions and pre-meal rituals that cannot be outsourced. Guests are greeted with hot towels, served a pot of freshly brewed kung fu tea to cleanse the palate and offered a few simple home-made peanuts and pickled vegetables to stimulate the appetite. It is a heartfelt welcome gesture in Chaoshan culture and, in his view, the meal’s point. Here is the fault line. Huang plates his fish individually to guarantee precise temperature at the moment of tasting. Cheung warns that split dishes cool down and lose their true taste. Each is sure the other’s method fails the food, and each describes something different: the bite versus the meal. For Cheung, the shared table is not merely a serving style – it is the meal. For Huang, the format is a container for flavour. For Chen, refinement is how tradition survives. Three chefs, three answers to one question: does the soul of Chaoshan cuisine live in the format or in the flavour? Perhaps that is where the soul lives: neither in the format nor the flavour, but in the refusal to let the question go. It is best debated, of course, over a shared clay pot, with the tea already poured.

title: Philippines thought Pogos were gone. Corruption and AI still power them
description: Recent raids reveal persistent corruption and tech-enhanced operations keeping the scam hubs alive despite the 2024 ban.
content: Two years after the Philippines banned its notorious offshore gaming hubs, or Pogos, a recent crackdown on hundreds of foreigners has highlighted a worrying trend of embedded corruption that still enables the sector to thrive. In September, the National Bureau of Investigation raided a call centre-style facility in Makati City, arresting more than 120 Chinese nationals linked to an alleged illegal trading and “lust scam” that tricked local and foreign victims into sharing explicit videos, which were later used to blackmail them. The enforcement blitz continued this month as police swooped on two scam hubs in the southern province of Zamboanga Sibugay. About 244 foreigners, mostly Chinese citizens along with two Cambodians, were arrested in an operation the Bureau of Immigration dubbed the “largest Pogo bust”. It said the suspects were housed at one of the raided properties while undergoing identity verification before their deportation. The foreigners are also accused of working without valid visas, being involved in illegal online activities, lacking proper documentation and illegally entering the country. Same old playbook The latest raids reflect a long-standing suspicion that Pogo elements have not entirely left the country since a ban introduced in 2024, according to Winston Casio, a former deputy operations director of the Presidential Anti-Organised Crime Commission (PAOCC). The PAOCC – an agency attached to the president’s office – spearheaded a series of nationwide Pogo raids in 2023–24, which unearthed evidence of human trafficking and torture and also led to the jailing of former Bamban mayor Alice Guo over her role in setting up a scam centre. Casio said government agencies needed to reconcile their figures to determine if the recent arrests related to new arrivals or were of foreign nationals who went into hiding after the 2024 Pogo ban announced by President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Before 2024, at least 10,000 foreign Pogo workers were granted a permit to stay in the Philippines beyond the 59-day grace period allocated for their repatriation. But Casio, citing Bureau of Immigration data, said only 8,000 actually left. At one point, up to 400,000 overseas Pogo workers were estimated to be in the country. “So there’s a discrepancy in the numbers and those numbers were never reconciled after the ban took effect,” he said. This Week in Asia has contacted the Bureau of Immigration for comment. Casio said the recent raids in Makati City, Alicia and Siay happened in the same hotspots where unlicensed Pogos were previously located, noting that these operations appeared to have “simply hid under the radar of the national agencies”. He added that the recent arrests raised questions about the suspects’ immigration status. “Did they enter the Philippines prior to the ban? If so, then they are part of the number that had yet to be deported then,” he said, adding that if the suspects arrived afterwards “then we have a problem”. Casio also called for a review of the 14-day visa on arrival scheme for Chinese nationals that was introduced in January in a bid to boost tourism. “They have to check when these individuals arrived in the Philippines. Did they take advantage of the visa upon arrival specifically given to Chinese nationals?” Analysts say the scammers are operating along much the same lines as before, but have adapted to the current hostile political climate surrounding Pogos. In the latest round of arrests, authorities found some of the alleged fraudsters operating out of a tent in Alicia. “In security, we have what is called ‘hiding in plain sight’ … they’re just in a tent. Who would suspect an operation of that gravity in a tent?” said Allan Cabanlong, head of cybersecurity provider CyberCX’s Asean cyber advisers programme. Cabanlong, who is also a former assistant secretary of the Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology, said the set-up was “planned” to aid the scammers’ easy escape. ‘There’s AI now’ Artificial intelligence likely made the scammers’ existing business models and modus operandi more agile, Cabanlong said. “There’s AI now, so the scams of before are much more intense today,” he said. “If they target a pool of victims, they can reach 100 per 10 minutes … the tradecraft is similar, though some are more sophisticated and improving.” Inadequate funding, tech infrastructure and corruption hobbled Manila’s efforts to tackle a “digital arms race” in the scam industry, Cabanlong added. “We admit the criminals have money for that. But the government can barely even manage the bidding and on top of that there’s graft,” he said. “So how do you catch up, if you’re not procuring what you need to build your capacity and build your workforce against current scam techniques?” Casio suggested that the Philippines should work with foreign agencies to bridge technological gaps. “You have to make sure you go after the big bosses,” he said. “We need to coordinate with foreign counterparts because they’re more technically competent in following the digital footprint and the money trail.” Most of the remaining Pogos were in the central and southern Philippines, Casio said, allowing fraudsters to evade national agencies and continue in business by only dealing with local bureaucrats or law enforcement. He said the Pogos that were still operating could use dirty money to influence the country’s next presidential election in 2028 and corrupt local politicians willing to conceal such operations, calling the latest raids merely “catching small fry”. “What we’re talking about here is public corruption, plain and simple … they’re obviously looking for politicians who could support them,” he said. “That’s the difficulty. They don’t want to talk about the real difficult things, the elephants in the room. Let’s not kid ourselves.”

title: How the Qing dynasty’s imperial workshops turned the emperor’s visions into exquisite art
description: A Hong Kong Palace Museum exhibition showcases 157 treasures produced by some of China’s finest artisans who worked in the palace’s ateliers.
content: At first glance, the peach-shaped box with coral inlay appears to be carved from red lacquer. But the piece – made specifically to celebrate the birthday of the Yongzheng Emperor (1678-1735) – is, in fact, a gold-bodied box with a surface overlaid with red coral. Each fragment of the vivid gemstone is cut and set so precisely that the joins almost disappear, creating a shimmering mottled crimson skin. It is a deliberate exercise in restraint, executed entirely in one medium and, unusually for an imperial commission, left completely unadorned: no enamel, no gilding, no carved decoration, just the clean, taut lines of the vessel, a simple handle and the cool grey sheen of polished metal. It is one of 157 national treasures currently on show at the Hong Kong Palace Museum as part of the “Design for the Forbidden City: Imperial Workshops of the Qing Court” exhibition. Other must-sees include beautiful jade works such as the “Myriad Cycles” box with 12 zodiac animals. On loan from the Palace Museum in Beijing, the collection tells the story of the sprawling production network that supplied the court with everything from daily necessities to ornamental masterpieces. It showcases not only the era’s finest artisans and, as in the case of the red coral box, the taste of their very important client – the emperor. “Through some of these items, you can even see their personalities,” Hong Kong Palace Museum curator Dr Yi-Li Hou says. Known as the Zaobanchu – Office of Manufacture – these imperial workshops operated as high-end custom studios that produced luxury goods inside the palace, for the palace. They were established in the late 17th century under the Kangxi Emperor (1654-1722), and for the next 200 years, the Qing court ran what amounted to its own vertically integrated manufacturing empire. At its peak, it encompassed more than 40 specialised ateliers producing everything from imperial robes and jade carvings to firearms and astronomical maps. “You’ll see that the Qing people were completely eclectic,” Hou says. “They mixed materials, styles, influences, which were, in many ways, very modern.” The first workshops were in the Yangxin Dian, or the Hall of Mental Cultivation, within the inner court, but they were not confined to the Forbidden City. A branch was established at the Yuanmingyuan, the Old Summer Palace, during the Yongzheng reign (1722-1735), and by the Qianlong period (1735-1796), hundreds of rooms were added and workshops in the capital had also been relocated there. The institution also operated a national production network, sending designs and models to specialised facilities in Suzhou, Hangzhou and Guangzhou for certain crafts. Beneath this administrative layer, the workshops were divided into ateliers, offices, factories and halls. The roster changed over time, but surviving records list more than 40 distinct units, including a glass factory, clockmaking office, enamel workshop, jade workshop, armoury, cannon workshop, map office and even an eyeglasses workshop. The emperor would not hesitate to tell them himself exactly how he wanted them to do it Hong Kong Palace Museum curator Dr Yi-Li Hou The imperial workshops produced three broad categories of goods. First were the bespoke imperial commissions, the personal objects ordered by the emperor himself, without regard to cost. Second were prototypes for items needed in larger quantities. For these, the Zaobanchu determined the decoration, form and specifications, frequently producing a sample before passing the design to other official workshops for mass production – princely robes and furnishings, for instance, were standardised through the Zaobanchu before being manufactured elsewhere. Third, and perhaps most consequentially, came technological development. Under the Kangxi Emperor, Western artists and craftsmen – among them the Italian Jesuit missionary and painter Giuseppe Castiglione (Lang Shining) – worked alongside Chinese artisans, and techniques such as painted enamel (falangcai), certain porcelain glazes and imperial glassware were developed or refined within the Zaobanchu. “Archives reveal a very hands-on approach, and emperors would directly tell their ministers what to do, according to their own preferences and styles,” Hou says. “The emperor would not hesitate to tell them himself exactly how he wanted them to do it.” The objects are intensely personal and reveal as much about the emperors’ tastes and temperaments as about Qing craftsmanship. The exhibition at the Hong Kong Palace Museum showcases the workshops that operated under Qing emperors Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong. One highlight is an antler armchair built from deer hunted by the Kangxi Emperor. Rather than being carved from a single block of wood, its frame is assembled from the branching antlers of the deer, shaped and fitted so that the natural curves and forks of the horns form the arms, legs and supports of the chair. The result is a piece that looks organic and almost skeletal, its surface retaining the irregular texture of raw antler. Decades later, his grandson, the Qianlong Emperor, replaced its backboard and inscribed it with a poem, transforming a piece of furniture into a private memorial to his grandfather. In it, he writes that he “dare not sit upon it, ever in awe and admiration”. Contemporary observers were struck by the concentration of talent. The workshops – colloquially known as the Baigong Fang or “workshop of 100 crafts” – recruited the finest craftsmen from across the empire and gave them access to premium materials such as rosewood (huanghuali), red sandalwood (zitan), gold, silver, gemstones and mother-of-pearl. The Zaobanchu’s surviving archives – known as the huoji dang, or “work records” – capture a running dialogue between the throne and the workshops. They record not only what was made, but who ordered it, what materials were used, how long it took and, crucially, what the emperor thought of the result. Entries frequently show emperors rejecting finished pieces, ordering modifications, or demanding that an object be remade entirely. The archives also preserve something unexpectedly human: the identities of the individual craftsmen themselves. The Zaobanchu was a high-security precinct within the Forbidden City and entry was strictly controlled. Craftsmen had no photographs to identify them, so they were issued wooden identification tablets – known as gongpai – that recorded their place of origin and distinguishing physical features. These modest wooden tags are among the few objects in the exhibition that commemorate the talented artisans themselves. “They didn’t have photographs before, so they would write where you were from – for the imperial workshops, which place you were a craftsman from – and what facial features you had,” Hou says. “We saw this tablet. On it was written that one of the artists was yellow-complexioned and bearded.” “Design for the Forbidden City: Imperial Workshops of the Qing Court”, Hong Kong Palace Museum, West Kowloon Cultural District, 8 Museum Drive, Kowloon. Programme and ticketing information can be found on the Hong Kong Palace Museum website.

title: China warned Myanmar syndicates, Trump urged Xi to talk to Takaichi: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From Abby Choi’s HK$72m flat wasn’t a gift to France and Germany seeking new trade weapon, here are highlights from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. China tried 3 times to talk crime families out of scam business in Myanmar: CCTV China tried three times to persuade powerful families in northern Myanmar to shut down scam operations before Myanmar police carried out large-scale arrests in 2023, according to a new documentary broadcast on Chinese state television. 2. Trump urged Xi to talk to Takaichi and lift export curbs on Japan, sources say US President Donald Trump pressed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to roll back China’s export curbs on Japan during their meeting in the US, urging talks between the Chinese and Japanese leaders as Tokyo seeks to manage mounting pressure from Beijing. 3. Abby Choi’s HK$72m flat was never meant as a gift to former in-laws, court told The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has accused her former in-laws of living off her family’s wealth, stating that her daughter never intended to gift them a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat she had bought for her children. 4. Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province. 5. France, Germany seek new EU weapon to instantly cut off market access for China In the strongest sign yet of a shifting European Union policy on China, the leaders of France and Germany have demanded a new trade weapon that would cut off access to the EU market when third countries cause severe distortions. 6. ‘A show of strength’: US F-35 stealth jets join Indian air drills US F-35 stealth fighters have joined Indian warplanes for military exercises near the Pakistan border in recent days, marking the first time America’s most advanced multirole combat aircraft has taken part in joint drills in India. 7. Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years An elderly man in central China, who has spent the past 21 years making ends meet as a scavenger, experienced a remarkable stroke of luck when he discovered that his pension fund contained over 420,000 yuan (US$63,000).

title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: firm uses 3D-printed tiles to restore coral reefs
description: Archireef has helped to conserve or restore reefs in Hong Kong, Singapore, UAE and Saudi Arabia and monitors the results, says co-founder Vriko Yu.
content: In 2014, a University of Hong Kong research team watched two years of reef restoration work collapse in Sai Kung. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department had asked the researchers to speed up coral recovery. Cement structures were placed on the seabed and coral began to grow. But as the colonies became larger, they became unstable. “They have no roots,” said Vriko Yu Pik-fan, then a doctoral student on the project. “The bigger they got, the less stable they were.” That failure eventually led Yu to co-found the company, Archireef. After cement, metal and plastic had all been tried, Yu’s team turned to clay. Using 3D printing, they produced terracotta reef tiles designed to give coral larvae a porous, pH-neutral surface to attach to. The company was incorporated in Hong Kong in 2020 to commercialise the research. “A useful solution should not be confined to the lab,” Yu said. Her work has earned her a place among the finalists of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards in the sustainability category. The awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, were launched in 2013 to recognise individuals and organisations whose work contributes to Hong Kong and its communities. According to Archireef, close to 10 hectares (24.7 acres) of marine habitat have been conserved or restored across Hong Kong, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Today, much of its value comes after the tiles have been deployed. Port operators, developers and other clients who are legally required to mitigate the environmental impact of their projects increasingly need evidence of what has survived, what species have returned and whether restoration has worked. “We help them spend less, or lose less,” Yu said. “The cost of the sea used to stay off the accounts.” Archireef now uses environmental DNA, photogrammetry and camera imagery analysed by software to monitor marine life. At monitored Hong Kong sites, 95 per cent of deployed coral was still alive three years after installation, according to the company. “Restoration is the intervention,” Yu said. “The product is knowing, defensibly, whether it worked.” The Hong Kong-registered company now owns three Gulf subsidiaries and keeps its research team in the city. “Our roots are here. Our research team is here,” Yu said. “The availability of the right mix of talent is why we stay.” She also credits improvements in Hong Kong’s water quality with making coral restoration possible. Referring to the Harbour Area Treatment Scheme, she compared conservation with improving personal health. “If a person smokes, they stop first,” she said. “Then they exercise.”

title: Hong Kong national security police charge man over seditious social media posts
description: Man, 52, accused of provoking hatred towards central and Hong Kong governments, but police reveal no details of alleged seditious posts.
content: Hong Kong national security police have charged a man with publishing seditious material on social media, but only informed the press after the defendant appeared in court and declined to provide details of the alleged crime. The force’s National Security Department said on Friday it had charged a 52-year-old man for posting seditious material with the intent to provoke hatred towards the central authorities, the Hong Kong government and the judiciary. The defendant attended the first hearing on Wednesday afternoon, according to the force’s statement. Contrary to its usual practice when charges under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance are filed, the department issued no media statements when it brought the defendant before West Kowloon Court. The man was charged with a count of knowingly publishing material with a seditious intention, but no details of the allegations were included in the department’s press release on Friday. The force said officers arrested the defendant on July 9 in Eastern district. The South China Morning Post asked police for details of the case, including whether the defendant was on remand or released on bail, but the force declined to provide any information.

title: How is AI changing the game for people studying ancient Chinese texts?
description: As technology makes classical works more accessible, experts discuss what role AI should play in helping us learn about history.
content:
For generations, working with ancient Chinese texts has been a painstaking task.
Specialists would spend years identifying unfamiliar characters, copying manuscripts by hand, adding punctuation to texts written without it, comparing different editions and tracing references across thousands of years of records.
But artificial intelligence (AI) is now changing that process, not only by helping to preserve fragile manuscripts but also by transforming how ancient texts are recovered, studied and shared.
As China increases its efforts to digitise a huge collection of ancient works, universities and technology companies are helping to turn the country’s rich literary heritage into an open digital resource.
An example of this is Shidian Guji, an online database of more than 70,000 ancient works. All of them are freely available to the public. It was launched in 2022 and jointly developed by ByteDance and Peking University in Beijing.
The database provides tools for searching and reading classical works, including modern language versions of ancient texts and chatbot-based interactions that help users explore them. In July, Shidian Guji published a collection of almost 2,000 traditional scientific works covering fields such as astronomy, mathematics, agriculture and engineering.
Sun Xianbin is a researcher at the Institute for the History of Natural Sciences at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. He told Shangguan News that the digital archive held centuries of China’s “indigenous knowledge system”.
This concept has become more popular in recent years, as Beijing tries to promote ideas rooted in China’s intellectual traditions rather than imported Western concepts.
Beyond technology’s ability to help people access classical Chinese texts, AI-driven digitisation also offers a way to facilitate the “digital return” of ancient manuscripts from overseas. Millions of Chinese texts are kept in collections in countries such as Japan, South Korea and the United States – partly as a result of war and social upheaval.
Several projects have been set up to make these works available to the public.
One is run by the Harvard-Yenching Library in the United States. It has made digital copies of more than 6,000 rare Chinese books available online. These include some works that are valuable because no surviving copies exist in China.
But even when ancient texts are digitised, they can be difficult for non-specialists to read.
Tsui Lik-hang is an associate professor from the department of Chinese and history at City University of Hong Kong. He said AI was helping to remove barriers for modern readers by adding punctuation, glossaries and translations for classic works.
“Much premodern Chinese material is inaccessible not because it is locked away, but because it is unreadable to most people,” he said.
But Tsui warned users to be aware of which elements were supported by historical sources and which were created by AI.
For Tsui, AI’s value lies beyond preserving ancient texts – the more difficult stage is after digitisation when “interpretive operations” are needed to create usable research materials. These operations can include punctuating the text, identifying people, offices, places and dates, as well as annotating allusions.
Tsui said such tasks were “until recently mostly done by hand”, but machine learning had become increasingly useful in assisting with them. Handwritten text recognition was also improving rapidly with AI models, he added.
Tsui said historians had always sensed connections between certain authors, texts and historical periods – but proving them often needed a great deal of reading and note-taking. But now, he said AI tools could help him shift from studying a single written letter to finding patterns across “hundreds of documents by various different authors”.
But Tsui said AI should not become a substitute for directly engaging with historical sources.
“Historical research is … a trade in which scholars find pleasure in reading, interpreting [and] explaining,” he said. “If we always let a predictive machine sit between ourselves and the sources, we lose that.”
He also warned that large language models sometimes made up names, dates or citations, and their “confidence” could make it hard for non-specialists to spot issues.
More importantly, Tsui added: “Interpretation in the humanities is multiple and contested by nature. An AI model returning one confident reading could flatten that.”
Historians, he added, should play a role in shaping these AI systems, which could not replace historians.
“Historians and humanities scholars are trained critics and readers of all kinds of sources. We weigh evidence, argue over meaning and context, and go deep,” he said. “This is precisely what we need in the age of AI models.”

title: Former Greentown China head charged for taking bribes over stake in real estate project
description: Hong Kong corruption watchdog charges Zhang Yadong for taking HK$20 million in bribes from mainland Chinese developer for stake in latter’s project.
content: Hong Kong’s corruption watchdog has charged the former head of a listed company for allegedly accepting HK$20 million (US$2.5 million) in bribes from a mainland Chinese property developer in exchange for acquiring a stake in the developer’s real estate project. Zhang Yadong, 58, who was chairman of Greentown China Holdings from 2019 to 2025, faced a count of conspiracy to accept advantages, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Friday. The case was mentioned at Eastern Court on Friday. Prosecutors alleged that between January 2020 and March 2023, Zhang conspired with his son, a middleman, a shareholder of an estate developer in Dailian, Liaoning province, and others to accept bribes totalling HK$20 million from the shareholder in exchange for Greentown China acquiring equity interests in the developer’s project. An ICAC investigation revealed that the shareholder had been pitching a Dalian real estate project to Greentown China since 2019. Zhang allegedly solicited bribes from the shareholder through the middleman to facilitate Greentown China’s acquisition of the project for 440 million yuan (US$65.6 million). “The bribes were suspected to have been deposited into the bank account of the defendant’s son in multiple payments through the middleman,” the watchdog said.

title: Letters | Hong Kong should invest in natural infrastructure to harvest hope
description: Readers discuss hope as a social resource worth investing in, and international action against cross-border scams.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to the letter, “Hong Kong’s mental health narrative must instil a sense of hope” (September 23). Your correspondent is right. Hope is not simply a personal emotion. It is a social resource shaped by the environments we inhabit, the relationships we build and the futures we imagine together. Hong Kong’s mental health challenges are well documented. Focusing solely on symptoms risks overlooking the broader conditions that sustain well-being. If we are serious about restoring hope, we must look beyond clinics and counselling rooms and pay greater attention to the natural and social foundations of mental health. Evidence from Shenzhen suggests happiness is closely linked to better self-rated health among children. Strong family relationships, friendships and a sense of safety are significant contributors to well-being. Research also indicates that well-being is transmitted across generations: parents’ happiness is positively associated with that of their children. Hope and happiness are therefore not only individual experiences but family and social assets that can either flourish or diminish over time. The implications extend beyond personal lives. A society experiencing declining well-being may face lower productivity, weaker social trust and greater disengagement from collective aspirations. “Lying flat” reflects more than economic anxiety. The phenomenon can also be understood as a response to a perceived absence of purpose, belonging and hope. If mental health is shaped by our surroundings, natural capital deserves greater attention. One underappreciated pathway is our relationship with water. Hong Kong is surrounded by the sea and blessed with reservoirs, rivers, streams and wetlands. Emerging research highlights the value of water encounters, viewing water not merely as a resource but as a medium through which people connect with nature, community and place. Time spent in blue and green spaces can reduce psychological distress, strengthen nature connectedness and improve well-being. Whether walking along Tolo Harbour, exploring Tai O’s waterways or cycling along the Shing Mun River, such encounters foster a sense of belonging and stewardship. Mental well-being also depends on social capital. Research shows that friendships, community participation and a sense of safety are strongly associated with better health and happiness outcomes. In an increasingly fragmented society, mutual respect, trust and meaningful social connections are essential. Hong Kong has long invested in physical infrastructure. We should now invest with equal ambition in the natural and social infrastructure that sustains human flourishing. Hope grows when people feel connected to nature, to place, to one another and to a shared future. Wanxin Li, visiting professor, School of Public Policy and Management, Tsinghua University, and adjunct associate professor, Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chinese University of Hong Kong Phnom Penh Declaration on scams is a starting point The letter, “Phnom Penh Declaration on online scams short on details” (October 3), correctly notes that international commitments must result in action. Cambodia views the Phnom Penh Declaration as a starting point for enhanced international cooperation against cross-border criminal networks, not as the conclusion of the process. Cambodia does not claim to have eliminated all scam operations. While some smaller, less visible activities persist, authorities have dismantled the large compounds that once operated openly. We are now targeting the criminal networks behind these operations. Since July 2025, Cambodian authorities have investigated 832 suspected scam locations and conducted operations at 663 sites. Eighty-six scam compounds have been dismantled. We have referred 446 cases, involving 3,927 individuals of 29 nationalities, to the courts, including alleged ringleaders. The Anti-Corruption Unit has addressed four cases involving 15 senior officials and law enforcement officers. Authorities have frozen over US$300 million in scam-linked bank accounts. Last month’s International Conference on Combating Online Scams in Phnom Penh brought together representatives from 28 countries and seven international organisations. Participants adopted the Phnom Penh Declaration, committing to stronger cross-border investigations, intelligence sharing, action against criminal financial flows and enhanced protection for victims. The declaration does not replace national law enforcement or practical international cooperation. Its purpose is to strengthen both. Because criminal networks move people, money and operations across borders, governments must work together to pursue those responsible, recover illicit assets and prevent closed operations from re-emerging elsewhere. The challenge now is implementation. Cambodia is committed to working with international partners to turn these commitments into sustained action. Neth Pheaktra, minister of information, Royal Government of Cambodia

title: 160,000 Hongkongers register for ‘joint clearance’ ahead of Huanggang Port opening
description: Security chief says extra manpower will be deployed and high-level command centres activated, including joint operations with Shenzhen authorities.
content: More than 160,000 Hong Kong residents have registered to use “joint clearance” e-channels ahead of the revamped Huanggang border crossing’s opening on Monday, with extra manpower to be deployed and command centres activated to ensure a smooth start. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said on Friday that his bureau would activate its Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre to oversee operations. A joint command centre will also be set up with Shenzhen authorities. “We will monitor passenger and vehicle flows as well as surrounding traffic to monitor and coordinate departments on-site to ensure a smooth opening,” Tang said. More than 160,000 residents had registered on the Immigration Department’s e-Channel mobile app as of noon on Friday, Jacky Wong Ki, assistant director of control, said. Confirming an earlier South China Morning Post report, the government said the crossing would open at 6.30am on October 12, replacing the existing Lok Ma Chau-Huanggang port as the sole round-the-clock clearance point. An opening ceremony will be held on Sunday. Tang said the 6.30am start, rather than midnight, was intended to manage vehicle passage requirements. “At 6.30am, only cars with a permit to cross at Huanggang Port can use the checkpoint, whereas at midnight, cars with permits for other checkpoints can also use the revamped port,” Tang said. The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau said that 45 insurers in Hong Kong had agreed to extend the geographical limit of their mandatory motor and employees’ compensation insurance policies to the Hong Kong port area of the crossing, without policyholders incurring extra costs. The bureau said that although the port area had been established since July 31, insurance contracts were not automatically extended to cover that area, prompting the government to negotiate with the industry over the arrangement. The effective start of the new arrangement was backdated to July 31, it added. The expanded Huanggang facility will be a strategic, round-the-clock control point with new technologies and customs clearing equipment deployed for the first time at a land crossing. Top Guangdong official Huang Kunming visited the facility on Thursday and called on Shenzhen to use the upgraded border checkpoint to better align with Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis plan, according to state media. Huang, the province’s Communist Party secretary, called the checkpoint a key hub for cross-border exchanges. He said its “co-location” clearance arrangement vividly demonstrated “one country, two systems”, the governing principle of Hong Kong. Tang said the revamped checkpoint was well-equipped to handle passenger and vehicle flows at the existing Huanggang control point. He said the existing checkpoint in Shenzhen handled an average of 40,000 travellers a day and a peak flow of 65,000 people, with a daily average throughput of vehicles at 9,000 and a peak at 12,000. The revamped checkpoint’s capacity of 200,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles a day would be sufficient, he added. Tang said the existing control point would cease operating as the revamped checkpoint opened and the relevant roads would be closed. Huanggang Port will only permit ride-hailing through pre-booked licensed taxi fleets, with no designated pickup areas for non-fleet or unbooked taxis. Chau Kwok-keung, chairman of the Hong Kong Taxi and Public Light Bus Association, said the restrictions on non-fleet taxis were unfair, noting that the government had not consulted the trade before announcing the measure. “A fleet taxi can be pre-booked and driven right in, but what convenient arrangement is left for non-fleet taxis that rely on picking up passengers on the spot?” he said. There are about 2,000 active fleet taxis and 2,400 fleet taxi drivers in service, according to the government. Chau said he expected heavy footfall at the new port, but doubted the taxi trade would benefit significantly with numerous bus routes covering districts across the city. “Passengers opting for buses over taxis is a certainty. As for whether demand at night or from business travellers will gradually build up – that remains to be seen,” he said. Chau said the trade would gather data once the port opened to assess the impact on ordinary taxis, adding that a long-term balance had to be struck between fleet and non-fleet taxis. Wong Tai-hoi, fleet operations manager at Sino Development (International), said the company would deploy around 100 taxis to the new port on Monday. “We expect the new port will draw large crowds and business will be good,” he said. He noted that pre-bookings had yet to pick up as opening details had not been confirmed. Lawmaker Chan Siu-hung said the government should consider reserving pickup and drop-off points for ride-hailing and private cars once the port’s operations stabilise. He added that the introduction of fleet taxis could diversify point-to-point transport and offer premium services, while travellers with lighter bags could still board urban or New Territories taxis from designated waiting areas. “Depending on a passenger’s actual needs – bulky luggage, mobility assistance, or travelling in a larger group – fleet taxis can offer a range of vehicle types to choose from,” he said. The revamped port is connected by public bus routes to different areas, including Yuen Long, Tai Po, Eastern, Kai Tak and Tuen Mun, with three franchised firms – Citybus, KMB and New Lantau Bus – operating on site. The opening of the checkpoint was an opportunity for Shenzhen to further align with the Northern Metropolis, Huang said, referring to the 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) development near the border with mainland China. Shenzhen should also step up personnel exchanges and economic activities with Hong Kong, and support the cross-border innovation cooperation zone, Huang added. Hong Kong’s immigration authorities met their Shenzhen counterparts on Wednesday to discuss arrangements at the facility. Under the co-location arrangement, the city’s government has set up a Hong Kong area in the building, which is on the Shenzhen side of the border. The port uses a “joint inspection” clearance system, a first for border crossings. Unlike traditional clearance models, which require passengers to complete departure and arrival processes at separate counters, the new arrangement allows them to complete both steps at once by presenting one identity document required by their destination. In a social media video clip, Hong Kong customs said it had installed an “active millimetre-wave detection system” – the first of its kind for land border crossings – in the Huanggang facility. The system can detect items concealed under clothing and was designed to enhance clearance efficiency and enforcement accuracy. It was tested in previous large-scale drills ahead of the facility’s opening. Additional reporting by Edith Lin

title: Can China use its widening US yield gap to boost the yuan’s global role?
description: Beijing could leverage the yuan’s low interest rate to increase the currency’s worldwide use, an expert says.
content: China should seize a window opened by the widening US-China yield gap to strengthen the financing, hedging and asset-absorption systems behind the yuan, turning its cyclical low-interest-rate advantage into lasting global use of the currency, according to a researcher from a Beijing-based governmental think tank. The 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.22 per cent on Thursday, compared with 1.69 per cent for Chinese government bonds on their first trading day after the National Day holiday – a gap of about 3.5 percentage points, compared with a record 3.7-percentage-point gap on September 9. Jiang Zhenlong, an associate research fellow at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Finance and Banking, argued that higher US yields weakened the appeal of yuan assets and added pressure on the exchange rate and capital flows, but also raised dollar funding costs. “The China-US yield inversion presents an asymmetric effect: pressure on the asset allocation side and benefit on the financing side,” he wrote in the latest issue of China Money Market, a central bank-affiliated magazine. Borrowers have responded, with Jiang citing international media data showing yuan bond fundraising – onshore and offshore – had topped 1 trillion yuan by early September, a record. But demand for yuan financing does not necessarily mean demand to hold yuan assets, he wrote, pointing out that “China’s financial market still lacks sufficient capacity to absorb and retain global capital”. Official figures reflect the problem – the yuan made up 2.11 per cent of global official reserves in the second quarter, against 56.70 per cent for the US dollar, per International Monetary Fund data. Jiang also warned that the wider gap may encourage carry trades – borrowing yuan, selling it and buying higher-yielding foreign assets – which could create persistent selling pressure on the currency. So far, the yuan has held steady at about 6.7 per dollar. He called for measures including tying yuan borrowing to real trade and investment, bolstering offshore liquidity during stress, expanding longer-dated hedging tools and tracking how borrowed yuan was used to separate genuine financing from carry trades. Hong Kong, the main venue for offshore yuan bond sales, has been expanding its tools. To bolster risk management for international investors, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing launched the offshore market’s first five-year Chinese government bond futures on August 3. Local authorities were also exploring a seven-day offshore yuan liquidity tendering mechanism to broaden banks’ access to short-term funding, Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Eddie Yu said last month. “The yuan’s low-interest-rate cost advantages can truly become a long-term driver of internationalisation only if it is embedded in real economy and trade activity,” Jiang wrote. Improving the liquidity, convenience and collateral function of yuan assets was “more important than simply chasing yield levels,” he added.

title: First stop, Bangkok: Japan volleyball chiefs eye Asia expansion, global influence
description: Top tier of Japan’s domestic SV League will play regular-season games in Thai capital this weekend as officials seek regional growth.
content: Japan’s top volleyball competition will stage regular-season matches overseas for the first time this weekend, in a strategic push to transform itself into an Asian league. The SV League will host women’s matches on Saturday and Sunday in Bangkok, and plans to take men’s games there in January. Launched in October 2024 as the successor to the former V League, the revamped professional competition features 10 men’s teams and 14 women’s teams competing in a regular-season and playoff format. Officials said their long-term focus was on “looking beyond Japan and building lasting connections with players, clubs, leagues and fans across the region”. The ultimate goal would be to become a “leading professional volleyball league that represents Asia on the global stage”. Thailand had been picked as the league’s inaugural overseas destination because of its passionate volleyball fan base, historical sporting ties with Japan and strategic role as a gateway to the broader Southeast Asian market, officials said. While domestic operations in Japan remain the league’s primary foundation, league bosses consider international expansion to be vital to its long-term growth, with the hope it unlocks new revenue streams in broadcast rights, regional sponsorships and digital engagement across Asia. The objective is “not simply to export Japanese volleyball, but to build relationships in which leagues and clubs in Japan and across Asia can move forward together”. To facilitate regional integration, the league is adjusting its roster regulations starting in the 2026–27 season. The on-court limit for foreign players will increase from two to three, which – combined with one player under the Asian quota – will allow teams to field up to four international players simultaneously. The move coincides with a growing presence of Southeast Asian talent in Japan. Six Thai players will compete in the SV League during the 2026–27 season, including legendary setter Nootsara Tomkom for Aleeza Aichi and Hattaya Bamrungsuk for SAGA Hisamitsu Springs. The Bangkok fixtures build on existing regional cooperation. SV League maintains an operational partnership with South Korea’s Kovo league, while Japanese clubs have previously held training camps in Vietnam and the Philippines. In 2025, Japanese clubs Tokyo Great Bears and Voreas Hokkaido took part in pre-season matches organised by Taiwan’s professional league. However, league officials confirmed there are no immediate plans to stage regular-season matches in Hong Kong or mainland China, noting that future expansion across Asia will depend on strategic alignment, fan interest and local partnership conditions.

title: Sacred splashes: ancient Chinese ritual of ‘elephant washing’ for good fortune
description: The tradition came to an end in the late Qing dynasty, after a parade elephant went rogue, crushed a general’s carriage, and killed a eunuch.
content: In ancient China, royal families washed elephants to pray for good fortune – until one elephant went rogue and brought the tradition to an end. Elephants had been spotted and documented in China as early as 4000 BC. They are believed to have once been familiar animals in the Central Plains before gradually migrating south to more remote regions. From the Han dynasty (202 BC–220), elephants were presented as tribute to the royal court. They carried deeply auspicious meanings: the Chinese word for “elephant”, xiang, is a homophone for auspiciousness, xiang – the core half of ji xiang, which means “good fortune.” Royal families began domesticating elephants during the Jin dynasty (266–420). In the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1912) dynasties, elephants became more closely associated with the imperial honour guard, where they were trained to embody royal majesty in ceremonies. It was around this time that the tradition of washing elephants took hold. Every year during the sanfu, or “dog days of summer,” trainers led elephants to the river outside Xuanwumen Gate for a bath. The procession could include as many as 30 elephants. At its height, the event became a festive occasion, drawing crowds to the riverbanks to watch the elephants bathe. The magnificent scene was described in detail in the 17th century travel guide A Sketch of Sites and Objects in the Imperial Capital, written by Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng. According to the authors, the elephants splashing in the water had the “momentum of a rising dragon.” They also noted that the bath could not last too long, or the animals would become agitated and fight. The ritual is said to have been linked to a classic Buddhist story in which monks bathe the white elephant ridden by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. “Washing an elephant,” or xi xiang in Chinese, is also a homophone of a phrase describing the state of transcending all forms and appearances. In traditional Chinese painting, the act of washing elephants became a distinct subject. The theme flourished during the Ming dynasty, inspiring works by masters such as Ding Yunpeng and Cui Zizhong. The renowned Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) calligrapher and painter Zhao Mengfu also painted Bathing an Elephant. The tradition came to an end in the late Qing dynasty, after an elephant went rogue during a parade in 1884. It crushed a general’s carriage, killed a eunuch and tried to escape through the Meridian Gate. The elephant was eventually captured, but the court no longer dared to include elephants in its ceremonies. The remaining elephants were sent to the Beijing Agricultural Experiment Station, an early predecessor of today’s Beijing Zoo, where they spent their remaining years.

title: New York mayor urges Trump to remove ICE after driver with child in car is shot
description: Zohran Mamdani speaks out after ICE wound man with a 5-year-old boy in the back seat.
content: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday he would ask US President Donald Trump to remove federal immigration agents from the city as tensions flared over the latest shooting involving ICE. The New York Police Department said a man had been shot around 4pm in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of the Bronx during an altercation with federal agents. Mamdani and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) later confirmed that the shooting occurred during an operation of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency responsible for Trump’s immigration crackdown. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that agents were attempting to “to arrest a criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.” It did not state how many officers fired their weapons or why. “ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital,” the DHS spokesperson said. The department initially claimed that the person targeted had associations with a Dominican gang, but later issued a revised statement removing that sentence. Mamdani said that a five-year-old child was in the car when the altercation occurred. “This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” the Democratic mayor said on X, adding that he had called the president. “When we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities,” he added. Trump, a Republican, heavily criticised Mamdani before he took office in January, but the two men have since struck a surprisingly warm relationship. Several hundred protesters gathered peacefully at the scene of the shooting Thursday evening to express opposition to Trump’s crackdown. Many people then moved to the nearby hospital where the victim was being treated. Tensions with the police escalated when some protesters attempted to prevent cars from leaving the hospital, before being moved away from the entrance by law enforcement, who set up barriers. New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted to X Thursday, saying she expects “federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident”. “This incident is another reminder of the unchecked, rampant violence ICE has been spreading throughout our communities,” said Murad Awawdeh, president of the New York Immigration Coalition. “We demand an immediate investigation into the shooting, the release of the body camera footage, and accountability for any ICE agents who used excessive force.” ICE has been involved in several high-profile shootings this year, including the killing of two US citizens in Minneapolis, which sparked angry protests. New York, a Democratic stronghold, is one of several US cities that bars its police force from assisting with federal immigration enforcement.

title: Singapore film festival rejects South Korean party’s calls to drop The Assassin(s)
description: Organisers said the political thriller will open the festival amid growing backlash in South Korea over claims of historical distortion.
content: The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) is standing by its decision to screen South Korean political thriller The Assassin(s) as its opening film, despite calls from South Korea’s conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP) to withdraw it over allegations of historical distortion. The film, directed by Hur Jin-ho and starring Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho, has drawn criticism in South Korea over its fictionalised portrayal of a real-life 1974 assassination attempt on then president Park Chung-hee, which resulted in the death of his wife, first lady Yuk Young-soo. SGIFF said it was aware of the discussions surrounding the film but would retain it as the opening title of its 37th edition, which runs from October 21 to November 1. “SGIFF respects the creative vision of the filmmakers behind The Assassin(s), which remains the festival opening film of our 37th edition,” the festival said. “The film was selected through SGIFF’s independent curatorial process for its artistic merit and contribution to contemporary Asian cinema. “The filmmakers have described the film as a work of cinematic imagination that combines historical events with fictional characters and situations. “It was not made to establish historical conclusions, distort facts, or serve any political purpose. SGIFF presents the film in that context, as a creative work.” Set in South Korea in 1974, The Assassin(s) follows a detective investigating a shooting during a presidential event after discovering that evidence at the crime scene contradicts the official account. The film draws on the real assassination attempt against then president Park on August 15, 1974, during a Liberation Day ceremony in Seoul. Park survived the attack, but his wife, Yuk, was fatally shot. The gunman, Mun Se-gwang, was held responsible for the attack and South Korean authorities at the time concluded that he had acted under instructions linked to North Korea. However, the film raises questions about the possible involvement of the former president and South Korean intelligence officials in the incident. The fictional interpretation has angered conservative groups and politicians as they argue that the film unfairly implicates Park in his wife’s death and misrepresents an established historical account. The controversy reached Singapore when the PPP sent an open letter to SGIFF executive director Jeremy Chua on Tuesday, urging the festival to reconsider its opening film selection. According to South Korean media platform Asia Business Daily, the letter was issued in the names of the party’s 109 National Assembly members. “We express deep regret over the choice of The Assassin(s) as the opening film and urge you to reconsider this decision immediately,” the party said. “While we respect artistic freedom and the independence of film festivals, creative freedom does not mean freedom from responsibility regarding historical facts.” The party argued that selecting a film to open an international festival carries particular significance because it reflects the festival’s values and editorial judgment. The objections have extended beyond the film’s Singapore screening. According to South Korean newspaper The Chosun Daily, critics have circulated instructions on social media encouraging people to petition SGIFF, Singapore’s embassy in South Korea and the Singapore Tourism Board’s Seoul office to withdraw the film.
