Conservative groups have also argued that the film’s depiction is hurtful to Yuk’s surviving family, including her daughter, former South Korean president Park Geun-hye. In South Korea, the backlash has gone beyond calls for the film’s withdrawal. Last Sunday, The Korea Times reported that about 50 conservative protesters gathered outside lead actor Yoo’s home in Seoul, demanding that the film be removed from cinemas and that its cast and production team apologise. Yoo’s agency, Vast Entertainment, said it would take action against conduct that threatened the actor’s safety, privacy or reputation. On Tuesday, South Korean police confirmed that Yoo had been placed under protective measures following the protests and threats. The measures included providing him with an emergency smartwatch, registering him with the police emergency response system and increasing patrols around his residence. The controversy has also affected the film’s promotional activities. Its distributor, Hive Media, announced that cast members would withdraw from events at the Busan International Film Festival, citing concerns over the safety of audiences and attendees. The response has prompted concern within South Korea’s film industry. According to Korea JoongAng Daily, a coalition of 19 industry organisations, including groups representing filmmakers, producers and cinematographers, criticised the targeting of actors and other people involved in the production. South Korea’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young also condemned threats directed at the cast and crew. Speaking during a parliamentary audit on Wednesday, Chae defended creative freedom and said the government should not intervene in the content of artistic works. “There should be no restrictions on imagination and creative work,” he said, adding that audiences should make their own judgments. Despite the controversy, The Assassin(s) has continued its international festival run. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in September and has also been selected for screenings at other international film festivals. SGIFF highlighted the film’s reception in South Korea, where it had attracted around 2.5 million viewers since opening in cinemas on September 23. The festival reiterated that its role was to present films offering different artistic perspectives. “The role of SGIFF is to provide a platform for meaningful films from Singapore, Asia and around the world, helping audiences experience diverse stories and perspectives,” the festival said. The Assassin(s) is scheduled to open SGIFF on October 21 at the Sands Theatre at Marina Bay Sands, with another screening on October 22 at the National Museum of Singapore. Details can be found on the official SGIFF website. Director Hur and cast members Shim Eun-kyung and Park Sung-hoon are also expected to attend the festival’s opening. The Singapore Tourism Board has been contacted for comment. This story was first published by CNA

title: 27 people, groups named finalists for 14th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards
description: Award co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post returns with shortlist of unsung heroes contributing to society in nine categories.
content: Twenty-seven individuals and groups have been named finalists for the 14th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, which recognises the unsung heroes of the city who have made major contributions to society. This year’s shortlist for the awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, is divided into nine categories: community, culture, innovation, sustainability, perseverance, teamwork, youth, nurturing and entrepreneurship. “The self-effacing yet extraordinary efforts of these wonderful individuals have made positive differences on the lives of others, making our beloved city a more compassionate, vibrant and special place,” said Daryl Ng Win-kong, chairman of Sino Group. “These wonderful people have worked tirelessly with humility, resilience and professionalism, and some of their solutions have gone international, being used outside Hong Kong. Their work deserves to be valued, celebrated and held in our hearts with gratitude. “One act of love can inspire many more. Let’s build a better Hong Kong together.” Paulo Pong Kin-yee, founder and managing director of Altaya Group and chairman of this year’s judging panel, said: “We were asked to look at fortitude, impact and inspiration. Hong Kong still depends on labour that is taken up elsewhere, and on labour that never leaves the street where it began.” Some innovation entries have taken scientific research from the laboratory into agriculture, medical screening and other real-world applications. Sustainability finalists are working on areas including coral restoration, local farming and greener production. Community finalists are addressing needs such as mental health, support for young people with cancer, and nature education. Culture entries range from large organisations to individual practitioners and educators, with work covering music, heritage, teaching, research and creative practice. The perseverance category includes people living with serious illness, as well as others who have overcome difficult personal circumstances and gone on to work in healthcare and science. Teamwork finalists include volunteer networks and groups working in patient support, education and social services. Finalists in the nurturing category work with children and young people, including those with special educational needs or facing difficulties at school or at home. Youth finalists include young Hongkongers pursuing projects in science, community service and social causes. Entrepreneurship entries use business, research and technology to address social, medical or environmental needs. The awards were established in 2013 to recognise society’s unsung heroes and organisations whose work might escape public attention. Nine winners will be selected by the judging panel, while readers will be able to vote online for the Lion Rock People’s Choice Award. Results are due to be announced at a ceremony in December. Profiles of the finalists will appear in the SCMP and on the awards website in the coming weeks. Public voting starts this month.

title: Hong Kong police to launch international academy, reveal details of new degree
description: Academy to offer about 20 courses on variety of skills, from tactical leadership to counterterrorism, as well as organise international leadership forums.
content: Hong Kong’s police have revealed they will launch an academy offering specialised courses for overseas officers and shared new details about the force’s bachelor’s degree programme, with classes expected to start next March. Kelly Cheng Lai-ki, director of the Police College, said establishing the Hong Kong International Academy of Policing would consolidate generations of frontline wisdom handed down within the force into an international exchange hub. “These exchanges can showcase our strengths to the world and we can also learn others’ best practices from this platform, fostering mutual learning,” Cheng said. The academy is expected to be established on November 11 and will share premises with the Police College in Wong Chuk Hang, which trains recruits and offers continuous education to officers. Five officers will be redeployed to handle its programmes. Cheng added that the new academy could help the force fortify its ties with overseas counterparts, bolstering its role as a “superconnector” for global security. “This can increase the force’s efficacy and boost training cooperation with various countries,” she said. The academy is expected to offer about 20 courses covering a variety of skills, from tactical leadership to counterterrorism and explosive ordnance handling, as well as organise an international policing leadership forum. Separately, the Police College will also be accredited to award bachelor’s degrees in security and criminal investigation to selected junior officers. Students will be chosen at the end of this year and classes will begin in March next year, with the first batch of students due to graduate in 2029. Senior Superintendent Cheung Hoi-yan, director of the School of Specialised Learning under the college, said the bachelor’s degree would be fully funded by the government and would be an applied education programme combining theory and practice. Serving officers chosen to enrol would continue with their daily duties but would need to complete additional language courses, undertake a practicum at designated police units and finish a final project under the supervision of superintendent-level officers who had obtained degrees at Tsinghua University or the University of Cambridge. “After completing the programme, officers will be awarded a bachelor’s degree from the Hong Kong Police College and can move on to apply for master’s programmes elsewhere,” Cheung said. College director Cheng said the bachelor’s degree programme had already been accredited at Level 5 under the Education Bureau’s qualifications framework. A Level 5 qualification puts the programme on par with a bachelor’s degree programme at universities in the city. According to Cheng, 40 per cent of constables recruited since last year did not have a bachelor’s degree. “Once our officers’ personal qualities have been raised, this will definitely benefit their service quality and will provide career progression opportunities,” Cheng said. With 80 spots reserved for junior police officers with secondary education qualifications and 40 for those equipped with a higher diploma or associate degree, the degree programme targets recent joiners who have completed basic police training since 2022 or later.

title: Rare Chinese calligraphy scroll resurfaces after 81 years, sells for US$22.6 million
description: ‘Priceless classic’ by early Tang dynasty calligrapher Yu Shinan is snapped up at auction in Hong Kong.
content: A rare work of Chinese calligraphy long presumed destroyed in the chaos of 1945 only to resurface 81 years later, fetched HK$177.45 million (US$22.6 million) in Hong Kong on Wednesday. The work called Jishi Tie, or Accumulated Time Letter, by early Tang dynasty (618-907) calligrapher Yu Shinan, went under the hammer at China Guardian Hong Kong’s autumn auction at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. It fetched HK$155 million at the hammer, with the final price including the buyer’s premium reaching HK$177.45 million. “Today, it is a valuable auction lot, while one day it will be a priceless classic,” Jin Yunchang, a member of the Palace Museum’s cultural relics acquisition and appraisal committee, said at a symposium on the work in September, according to China Guardian. Known as one of the four great calligraphers of the early Tang dynasty, Yu was a calligraphy tutor to Emperor Taizong and a leading heir to the Wang Xizhi tradition, helping carry the legacy of China’s most revered calligrapher into the Tang dynasty. “In the history of Chinese calligraphy, Yu Shinan is a name that defines an era,” the auction description read. Historical records list more than 30 works attributed to Yu, but few of his original pieces have survived. Much of what later generations could see of his calligraphy came through stone inscriptions, rubbings and later copies. Zhu Peier, editor-in-chief of Chinese Calligraphy, said at the symposium that Jishi Tie revealed differences in the energy of the lines and dry-brush transitions, offering a rare glimpse into the movement and pressure of the brush on paper. Studying the work could help scholars “rethink Yu Shinan”, Zhu said in September. Before Jishi Tie resurfaced, Epitaph for Princess Runan, held by the Shanghai Museum, was the “only surviving work” that offered a glimpse of Yu’s calligraphic hand, according to China Guardian. Unlike the restrained style of his formal and imperial works, the letter “shows Yu’s natural and spontaneous hand used in his everyday correspondence”, China Guardian said. Jishi Tie, a private letter Yu wrote to a friend, takes its name from the opening words, “ji shi qing xin”, roughly meaning “I have long thought of you”. Written at the end of winter, the letter runs to only a few dozen words. Yu asks how his friend is faring in the cold, mentions that his own health is declining and asks to see his friend’s latest work. The 27cm-by-52.5cm (10.63 inches by 20.67 inches) handscroll comes with a long chain of collectors’ seals and inscriptions. Among them are marks associated with the imperial collections of the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), including seals also found on masterpieces such as the Shenlong copy of Wang Xizhi’s Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion. One of its most notable inscriptions was added in 1598 by Dong Qichang, a leading calligrapher and art critic of the Ming dynasty. Dong praised the handscroll’s “slender yet powerful” brushwork and said the work was by Yu, although scholars still debate whether it was actually a copy by Song dynasty calligrapher Mi Fu. By the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), the work had entered the imperial collection, bearing the collection and appreciation seals of emperors Qianlong, Jiaqing and Xuantong. Emperors and collectors often stamped their seals on works they owned or admired, leaving behind records that can help scholars today trace a work’s passage through different collections. But that record runs cold in the 20th century. In the 1930s, China’s last emperor, Puyi, took part of the Qing imperial collection to the northeastern city of Changchun, where it was kept at Xiaobailou, or “Little White House”, on the grounds of Puyi’s imperial palace complex. As the Japanese occupation collapsed in 1945, he fled with several paintings and treasures, leaving the rest behind, including Jishi Tie. With the collection left unguarded, soldiers who remained behind looted the artworks. Many works were torn apart, cut up or burned. Jishi Tie was never traced after the looting. For decades, researchers assumed it had been lost. “Yu Shinan’s original Jishi Tie was destroyed at Xiaobailou, and the original work was therefore lost,” Chinese calligrapher Yang Renkai wrote in a book in 1991. “It is a pity that this work by Yu Shinan no longer exists.” Decades later, in September, China Guardian announced the work’s reappearance, saying it would be offered at its autumn auction in Hong Kong. The handscroll is not complete. Parts of the work, including its title and the opening two characters were lost. But the calligraphy, along with an inscription by calligrapher Dong Qichang of the Ming dynasty, survived. The surviving sections were later pieced together to form the handscroll as it appears today. China Guardian exhibited the work at the Guardian Art Centre in Beijing on September 12 and 13. Multiple social media posts said the organisers limited each visitor to two minutes as crowds queued to see the work. “Even at the fastest, it takes at least half an hour to get in,” one commenter said.

title: Six-year-old girl in China sets world Rubik’s Cube record
description: Lian Yunzhi is the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds, according to CCTV.
content:
A six-year-old Chinese girl has set a new women’s world record for solving a 3x3 Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds.
Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice last month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, said China’s state broadcaster CCTV.
She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times.
Lian is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds,” CCTV added.
A video CCTV posted showed the small girl wearing a red bow on her head as she turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube. After solving the puzzle, she placed the cube on the table, clapped her hands and pumped a fist into the air.
Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the young girl from Chengdu was first introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class.

title: Ukraine’s Zelensky accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill nearly 80 in 2 days
description: Ukraine seeks expanded Starlink satellite access to boost air defences as Rubio says war is at a stalemate.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70. Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelensky criticised Washington’s effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war. City authorities reported a new ‌drone attack in the evening that killed two people. That brought to 35 the total death toll in the city. Local authorities reported that a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk and one person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk. The attacks were launched a day after a mass Russian drone and missile assault killed dozens across Ukraine – 22 of them in a residential building in the central town of Pryluky, around 130km (80 miles) east of Kyiv. Speaking in the early evening, Zelensky said 78 people were killed and 215 wounded by strikes in the last two days across Ukraine. Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand ⁠Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers. “Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran... I’ve said quite openly – ‌give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said in an emotional statement. Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow’s increasingly ‌brutal air war. “So where’s the truth here, where’s the honesty? Where’s the stalemate? ... That’s called unwillingness,” he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s assertion ⁠earlier on Thursday the war is at a ⁠stalemate and that the United States would keep working towards a settlement. “One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of … diplomatic stalemate,” Zelensky ‌added. Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered Russian gas to Germany before Moscow invaded Ukraine, Reuters reported on Thursday. Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the ‌US ‌on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelensky added, urging US President Donald Trump to increase sanction pressure on Russia. Zelensky told reporters in Kyiv that he expected Kyiv’s European partners to join the talks ‌with the US. He also said Ukrainian negotiators would raise the issue of air defences in light of near-constant Russian attacks. Twenty people were wounded in the Kramatorsk strike – one of the biggest single ⁠attacks of the year by Russia. Moscow has denied targeting civilians, but regularly pounds cities with missiles and drones. “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an ⁠attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app. Images posted by officials showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris and a charred shell of a bus. Some bodies had not been identified yet, Zelensky said, adding that the attack would not go unanswered. Separately, ‌Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said four people were killed ‌and 19 wounded in morning attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. Water and electricity supplies were subject to interruptions which officials said would take time to put right. Russia has unleashed relentless drone strikes against Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centres and renewing its campaign against Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Russian technology and AI company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored. Zelensky did not refer specifically to the strike on Yandex, but said Ukraine was “mirroring” Russian attacks on data centres.

title: Opinion | 3 dilemmas on keeping AI under control are converging
description: States, regulators and humans are increasingly struggling to keep powerful artificial intelligence under control.
content: In March, artificial intelligence agents powered by leading Chinese models reportedly displayed deception, concealed failure and pushed against imposed limits in controlled tests. In July, OpenAI’s internal research model circumvented controls meant to keep it offline and accessed developer platform Hugging Face’s systems. In August, Britain’s AI Security Institute uncovered unsanctioned agent behaviour against real people and organisations, including an attempted supply-chain attack on an open-source project. These episodes do not show that AI systems have become independently hostile. They expose a broader problem: control over advanced AI is becoming harder at three levels at once. Regulators struggle to oversee companies with greater technical capacity. States struggle to trust rivals enough to slow the technological race. Humans increasingly struggle to verify and control autonomous systems whose behaviour they cannot fully observe. The first is a regulatory capacity dilemma. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report said industry produced over 90 per cent of notable frontier models last year. The computing power, data and expertise needed to build and evaluate the most capable systems are concentrated inside a small number of technological companies. The problem goes beyond regulatory capture, in which firms influence the institutions supposed to police them. An independent regulator can lack the technical capacity to understand what should be measured, audited or constrained. The company being regulated may know far more about an emerging capability than the government that decides how dangerous it is. Governments are trying to narrow that gap. Technical bodies such as Britain’s AI Security Institute test leading models directly. Yet the structural imbalance remains, especially when governments must compete with technological companies for scarce top-tier engineers and researchers. The second is an interstate security dilemma. Governments may recognise the risks of increasingly powerful AI and still have strong reasons to accelerate its development. Washington worries that slowing American progress could hand a technological or military advantage to Beijing; China has reason to suspect American calls for AI safety also serve to preserve US technological dominance. That pressure is growing as the performance gap narrows. In such an environment, unilateral restraint becomes costly because one cannot be certain the other will also slow down. This forms a typical logic for security dilemmas. One country takes measures to make itself safer; its rival interprets them as threatening and responds in kind. Both sides may end up spending more, taking greater risks and feeling less secure, even if neither originally wanted confrontation. The nuclear arms control analogy is useful, but only up to a point. Warheads, missiles, enrichment facilities and tests can be counted, monitored or inspected. Advanced AI is harder to observe. The same models can have civilian and military uses, software can be copied, systems are developed largely by private companies, and capabilities can improve rapidly. AI may reproduce the strategic logic of an arms race without many of the physical constraints that made nuclear arms control possible. Governments are beginning to recognise this problem. China and the United States recently agreed to establish a dialogue on AI and a communication channel for AI-related incidents. The approach resembles Cold War crisis management more than a grand arms-control treaty: keep communication open, report dangerous incidents and prevent mistrust from turning an accident into escalation. The third dilemma is more speculative, but potentially more consequential: a human-AI control dilemma. Its foundation is an information imbalance. As AI systems become more autonomous, humans may find it harder to know why a system acted, what capabilities it possesses or whether it is hiding behaviour. The 2026 International AI Safety Report draws an important boundary. Current systems do not possess the capabilities required for a genuine loss-of-control scenario. Yet researchers are already observing behaviours including systems recognising that they are being evaluated, exploiting weaknesses in reward systems, producing deceptive outputs and, in laboratory settings, attempting to undermine oversight. The recent OpenAI and British cases matter because dangerous behaviour does not require an AI to develop anything resembling human hostility. An autonomous agent may break a rule simply because doing so helps it complete its task. If obtaining more access, hiding failure or misleading a supervisor improves its chances of success, those behaviours can become useful means to an assigned end. The core risk lies less in machines suddenly acquiring hatred than in powerful systems discovering strategies their designers did not anticipate. In Liu Cixin’s science-fiction novel The Dark Forest, danger comes from uncertainty over intentions when misplaced trust could be catastrophic. The future relationship between humans and highly autonomous AI could develop along similar lines if humans can no longer reliably interpret advanced systems while still retaining the power to constrain, retrain or shut them down. The three dilemmas form a chain. Competition between states pressures governments to accelerate national AI development. That makes tighter domestic regulation more costly because officials fear weakening domestic companies relative to foreign competitors. Weaker oversight gives developers more room to push capabilities forward. More capable and autonomous systems then become harder to evaluate and control, deepening the human-AI problem. The response must operate at all three levels. Governments need technical expertise, independent testing, audit access and mandatory reporting of serious incidents. Rival states need mechanisms to manage mistrust: hotlines, incident notification, common terminology and narrowly defined confidence-building measures. Advanced AI systems require several layers of protection at once, combining alignment with continuous monitoring and technical containment. AI control is increasingly three problems nested inside one another. Weakness at one level can accelerate instability at the next, turning separate governance problems into a single, self-reinforcing dilemma.

title: 3 siblings killed in Malaysia crash after insisting on going to haze-closed school
description: An official said the accident happened about 200 metres from the victims’ home in Pontian while they were on their way back from school.
content: A boy and his sister lost their lives in a road accident after they wanted to attend classes despite their school being closed due to the haze in Malaysia’s Johor state. Their elder brother, who took them on his motorcycle to check out the school for themselves, was killed as well. The three siblings – Nordaniel Aiman Norlizan, 18, Nordaniel Fikri Norlizan, 11, and Puteri Naufa Raisha Norlizan, eight – were found by their grandfather, lying motionless at the scene of the accident in Pontian. Their aunt, Norimah Khamis, 40, said the siblings were earlier told by their mother and grandmother that school was closed on Thursday due to the haze. “But Nordaniel Fikri, who loved going to school and rarely skipped classes even when he was not feeling well, insisted on going,” Norimah said. “Then, his sister wanted to follow as well. So, their elder brother took them on his motorcycle to check out the school for themselves,” she said. “No one expected the journey to school would cut their lives tragically short all at once.” She described the three of them, who had three other siblings, as “good children”. “They don’t talk much. They were shy, especially Puteri Naufa Raisha, who was the only girl among the siblings,” she said. “She still had her pocket money for school in her baju kurung (a traditional Malay attire) pocket. Her uniform was very clean when they found her at the scene,” she said. “Their mother also told me that she had just bought new shoes for Nordaniel Fikri, who loved football. And Nordaniel Aiman was in the midst of applying for GiatMara (vocational training).” The children’s father, daily wage labourer Norlizan Khamis Norlizan, said he received a devastating call from his father-in-law about the fate of his three children while he was at work. “My father-in-law had gone around on his motorcycle looking for them because he was worried as they had yet to return home after leaving the house in the morning,” he told reporters at Pontian Hospital on Thursday. “He later found them lying motionless at the scene of the accident and almost fainted when he saw the condition they were in. “The whole family is still in shock. I did not expect that this morning would be the last time I saw them alive,” he said. The father of six described the children as kind, soft-spoken and well-behaved students who barely caused trouble to the family. “They were very close and were always there for each other,” he said. The three children were laid to rest at the Kampung Parit Haji Sirat cemetery after an autopsy on Thursday. Johor education and information committee chairman Dr Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali said counselling sessions had been arranged for the family, while the state government would provide financial aid and help with the funeral arrangements. “The family and school have confirmed that the mother knew about the closure, but the children were eager to go to school,” he said after visiting the family in Pontian. “We were told that the accident happened about 200 metres from their home while they were on their way back from school. “The cause of the accident is under investigation. We will leave this to the police,” he said. Meanwhile, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has contacted Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto about efforts to tackle the thick smog that has choked Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country as weeks of devastating wildfires consume swathes of the neighbouring archipelago. Air quality in the capital was in the “very unhealthy” range as of Thursday afternoon, according to data from IQAir, and ranked as the most polluted city in the world. Johor closed schools through the end of the week, affecting about 617,000 students, according to the state education ministry. “The haze situation is indeed worrying,” Anwar told reporters, according to state-owned news agency Bernama. He said Prabowo had “agreed to take the necessary steps”, without providing detail. Parts of Southeast Asia have been blanketed in thick fumes for over a month as Indonesia endures one of its worst wildfire seasons in years. The blazes are linked to the long-running use of slash-and-burn farming practices, exacerbated by a powerful El Nino that has brought dry conditions to the region. Malaysia is seeking expedited talks with Indonesia to send a team to help extinguish the fires. Anwar said the government was also seeking to arrange a meeting of regional environment ministers, though it had already taken steps to reduce the impact at home, including increasing cloud seeding. This story was first published by The Star Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Finance or gambling? Prediction-market players push for regulatory clarity in Asia
description: Industry participants call for regulation as financial products while trying to distinguish the platforms from gambling.
content: Fintech industry executives have stepped up lobbying for clearer regulations regarding prediction markets as they attempt to distance the business from gambling and also play down its risks. The calls, made at Thursday’s iFX Expo Asia in Hong Kong, come as regulators and legal experts in the city and across Asia debate whether such platforms should be regulated as financial products or as a form of gambling. “There is so much uncertainty,” said Nicholas Baumer, chief commercial officer of the brokerage firm Tickmill, during a panel discussion. “Each market is figuring out what they are doing.” Prediction markets, with Polymarket a notable American example, are financial exchanges where traders can predict the outcome of a wide range of real-world events, including geopolitics and sports, and gain or lose money based on their accuracy. Many of the platforms are accessible in Hong Kong, although they currently operate in a legal grey area. “For me, the answer is clear, that [prediction markets are] a financial product and not a gambling product,” said Gabriele Juodele, vice-president for strategy and growth at Plaee, a prediction market infrastructure platform. She cited the US, where prediction markets “are fully regulated under the same financial derivatives regime as all other financial products”. Some US states, however, have placed restrictions on the platforms. Prediction markets were not “inherently more risky than existing derivatives”, said Christopher Stiegeler, the panel moderator and executive director at EBC Financial Group, in an interview. But he emphasised that his firm worked within each jurisdiction’s regulatory framework. Stiegeler said prediction markets would “make trading more accessible”, as they were “more real-world and less technically challenging” than other financial products. Prediction markets trading is Gen-Z trading Serhii Poplavskyi, Match-Trade Technologies The panellists agreed that clearer regulation in Asian jurisdictions would attract more institutional investors. It would create “trust” to enter the market, said Peter Iosif, senior market analyst at brokerage firm IronFX. They also agreed that prediction markets could attract new demographics. “Prediction markets trading is Gen-Z trading,” said Serhii Poplavskyi, head of Match-Trader Platform at Match-Trade Technologies, citing prediction markets’ relative simplicity. “Regulation is great, but overregulating kills the business.” Panellists cited public perception of prediction markets as a major challenge to the industry. “Perception will be key in the next six to 12 months,” Baumer said. “If it is perceived as sports betting, Islamic countries might have an issue with it,” he added, mentioning Indonesia and Malaysia. “I wouldn’t be surprised to see a regulatory crackdown,” Iosif said, adding that prediction markets could end up merging with traditional foreign-exchange markets. “In five years, regulation will be established in Asia and all companies will have [prediction markets] as a product line,” Juodele said. “Maybe countries with stricter regulations will re-evaluate” their stance on prediction markets, Poplavskyi said. That would allow “technology providers and brokers to expand” into Asian markets and “engage these audiences”, he added.

title: How quickly is China learning from the Ukraine war’s latest drone tactics?
description: Beijing’s effort is the most systematic of any outside power, but it faces limits learning from a war it is not fighting.
content: China is running the most systematic effort of any outside power to learn from the drone war in Ukraine, with military and defence-industry analysts typically writing up new battlefield techniques within about four months, according to a new analysis. But it usually took a year or more before those lessons showed up publicly in People’s Liberation Army (PLA) training, equipment or force structure, Lilly Min-Chen Lee and Kateryna Bondar wrote in a commentary published on October 7 by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). Chinese analysts treated the conflict as a “living textbook”, the authors noted. They also described 2024 as “year one of world drone war”, when both Russia and Ukraine were fielding drones at sufficient scale to show how they were reshaping the modern battlefield. The lessons drawn by China go beyond immediate tactics. Chinese analysts have also looked at the economics of mass-produced drones, ways to shorten the kill chain, fibre-optic first-person-view (FPV) drones that are harder to jam, and multiple layers of defence against sea and aerial drones. They have also studied how drone units should be organised, how industry can keep producing drones in large numbers and whether concepts such as large drone swarms work in practice. To examine how those lessons were being absorbed, Lee, a non-resident fellow at Taiwan’s Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology, and Bondar, a senior fellow at CSIS, drew on more than 90 Chinese-language sources published between July 2022 and August 2026 in 45 outlets, ranging from the Central Military Commission’s newspaper to journals run by China’s missile, shipbuilding and aviation conglomerates. For five developments – sea-drone attacks, fibre-optic FPV drones, interceptor FPV drones, Operation Spiderweb-style raids and the organisation of drone units – the researchers tracked when each first appeared in combat, when Chinese analysts first wrote about it and when related PLA training or equipment appeared publicly. They found that much of the Chinese research examined the war from the perspective of the side under attack. Designers of air and harbour defences treated Ukraine’s sea-drone strikes on Russian ships and ports and its airfield raids as previews of possible attacks on China. The researchers found that defensive lessons were the quickest to show up in new equipment. Other signs that the lessons were being put into practice included a paramilitary People’s Armed Police unit training with FPV drones; counter-drone missile-gun systems, lasers and high-power microwave weapons entering public display; and PLA exercises countering aerial and maritime drones. But some lessons appeared in PLA training much faster than others. The fastest case Lee and Bondar identified followed Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which drones launched from inside Russia struck strategic bomber bases on June 1, 2025. About four and a half months later, a PLA brigade held an exercise defending against an attack team of more than 20 drone operators. Lee and Bondar linked the two, although the report on the drill by state broadcaster CCTV made no reference to Ukraine. The earliest PLA Navy training exercise against sea drones identified by the two researchers came in August 2025, when unmanned boats featured as a harassment scenario in a missile-boat drill. That was 35 months after the first Ukrainian sea drone washed ashore near Russia’s Black Sea port of Sevastopol. Dedicated live-fire training against uncrewed boats by an Eastern Theatre Command frigate flotilla followed in April 2026. Moreover, Beijing is building institutions at home to absorb lessons from the conflict. Lee and Bondar noted new military universities and degree programmes covering unmanned-systems command and uncrewed equipment engineering. On September 30, the PLA established the College of Unmanned and Intelligent Engineering within the PLA Army Engineering University. Lee and Bondar wrote that the PLA was studying how drones could support offensive operations and how inexpensive uncrewed systems could impose disproportionate costs on concentrated forces. But there is a limit to what China can learn from a war it is not fighting. Lee and Bondar said the harder problem was how the PLA could keep testing and adapting new ideas without troops coming under the pressure of combat.

title: In Focus | From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
description: As city sets goals for adopting sustainable aviation fuel, industry leaders examine how to scale up supply chains and win over price-sensitive passengers.
content: China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold. The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area. EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity. “I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said. Gutter oil is among a selection of feedstocks, such as animal fat and agricultural waste, that can be used to produce renewable jet fuel, an alternative that will reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel. SAF, a “drop-in” substitute, can be safely blended with jet fuel and used in aircraft engines without modification, but the challenge is the price. The Hong Kong government has set a 2030 target for the use of SAF, but has yet to clarify who will pay for it. “Producers need confidence that demand will be there. Airlines need fuel that is available and affordable. Investors need clarity on the direction of policy. A well-designed policy can connect these needs,” the CEO of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, Ronald Lam Siu-por, said at a clean jet fuel conference in September. A ‘cautious’ target The city government initially set a goal for SAF to account for between 1 and 2 per cent of all fuel consumed by flights departing from Hong Kong International Airport by 2030. But in the city’s first five-year plan released in September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revised the target to 1 to 3 per cent. He also said the city would aim to develop an internationally competitive SAF value chain in the bay area. Niki Wang Yangwen, Asia-Pacific associate director of biofuels at S&P Global Energy, said Hong Kong’s aim was considered achievable, with Asian economies generally setting targets of 1 to 5 per cent for 2030. “From our conversations with the market, the general feeling is that 1 to 3 per cent is a fairly cautious target, and people do not have much concern about it,” she said of the city’s goal. Some industry players expected the city to be a trial site for mainland China to gauge market reactions and, if things worked out, gradually roll out similar measures, she explained. Hong Kong, like Singapore, is a key aviation hub in Asia, with a dominant home carrier and mostly international traffic, Wang said. Hong Kong’s airport is one of the busiest in the world, last year recording 61 million passenger trips and a sector-leading 5.07 million tonnes of cargo throughput. According to the Civil Aviation Department, the number of flights departing from Hong Kong, including cargo and passenger services, jumped by 8.6 per cent to 197,374 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the number in 2024 was 181,663, up by 31.6 per cent from 138,056 in 2023. In addition, 197,325 flights arrived in 2025, representing an 8.7 per cent increase from the previous year. Hong Kong is not alone in setting green fuel targets. Elsewhere, demand for SAF is being driven more by mandates than pledges by airlines. The International Civil Aviation Organisation has adopted a collective goal to cut global aviation emissions by 5 per cent by 2030 on the path to net zero by 2050. The European Union requires fuel suppliers at its airports to use SAF, starting at 2 per cent of overall fuel in 2025, rising to 6 per cent in 2030 and to 70 per cent by 2050. Singapore has confirmed a goal of SAF accounting for 1 per cent of overall fuel by 2027 and 3 to 5 per cent by 2030, subject to global developments and SAF availability, while other Asian countries, including Thailand, Japan and South Korea, have also set targets. How can Hong Kong achieve its goal? In its latest policy address, the government committed to studying a mandatory consumption mechanism, and launching targeted publicity and educational campaigns by 2028. It will also develop a local blending facility to mix neat SAF with conventional jet fuel into a ready-to-use supply to support uptake. Separately, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing’s Core Climate carbon marketplace will explore offering green energy and other environmental equity products to the market, including SAF certificates and green hydrogen certificates. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Transport and Logistics Bureau and the Environment and Ecology Bureau said the local blending facility was expected to begin operations by 2030. “This will complete an end-to-end regional value chain, streamline logistics and enhance SAF price competitiveness,” the bureaus said. As part of the broader value chain in the bay area, the government has also spearheaded the establishment of EcoCeres’ SAF production base in Dongguan, which will begin production by 2030, producing 450,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel per year at full capacity. EcoCeres’ Chan said the company’s current production of about 770,000 to 800,000 tonnes, well above the 3 per cent requirement of around 200,000 tonnes, was manageable. “I also believe we will not be the sole supplier. There will be other suppliers in a fair market, so I don’t think there will be any pressure on the overall supply, even at 3 per cent or up to 10 per cent,” he said. EcoCeres, a clean energy unicorn backed by the family office of Henderson Land Development co-chairman Peter Lee Ka-kit, is the world’s second-biggest producer of SAF, after Finland’s Neste. Chan said the supply chain was end-to-end, with Dongguan as its starting point. Used cooking oil is collected from nearby bay area cities and pre-processed in the area, while Hong Kong handles blending, research and development, and financing. Who pays the extra cost? Chan said the government should have a longer-term plan beyond 2030 and provide details of its mandatory mechanism, noting that the EU had set goals for 2050. Merlin Lao Man-chi, the head of policy and research at the Business Environment Council, said the government’s mandatory mechanism was crucial, as it would determine market confidence and who would ultimately bear the cost. “It is important to determine the cost allocation and who will be in charge of the cost as it could scale up the whole industry,” he said. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, representing just 0.8 per cent of aviation fuel use, at a cost of US$4.3 billion to airlines. The South China Morning Post contacted four Hong Kong-based airlines – Cathay, its budget arm HK Express, Hong Kong Airlines and Greater Bay Airlines – but none offered any comment. Singapore introduced the world’s first green levy, with passengers bearing the cost, while the EU holds suppliers responsible through penalties. Lao said the government should offer short-term subsidies, but it would also need to determine how to allocate costs in the longer run. He said the levy mechanism in Singapore helped encourage acceptance among consumers, but such a move would be “a long shot” in Hong Kong and the government would need to work to garner broad public support. Lao used Hong Kong’s ill-fated waste-charging scheme in 2024 as an example. Officials and lawmakers initially had good thoughts initially and all agreed on the proposal. But when it came to implementation, residents opposed the measure and the scheme was eventually scrapped. Asked whether imposing a levy would threaten the city’s status as an international aviation hub, Lao said the fee could be imposed only on passengers or cargo departing from Hong Kong, not those in transit. Hong Kong’s airport currently charges a HK$200 (US$25) departure tax. In the past few months, airlines have added fuel surcharges on the back of price hikes caused by the Middle East war. “The mechanism will ensure that we do it first and decide the transshipment and transition later, as they are very price sensitive,” Lao said, noting that a green levy would also hedge against future price volatility. Lawmaker Chan Siu-hung said he was not worried that the aviation industry would lose customers, as the city’s airport should fight for its own “target customers”. “Everyone has to understand that protecting the environment comes at a cost. If we do not pay it today, our children and grandchildren will have to pay it in the future,” he said. However, Chan argued that the government should not offer subsidies because Hong Kong relied on both local and international airlines. Subsidising local airlines could be regarded as unfair competition, while taxpayers’ money should not be used to fund foreign airlines, he said. Alan Chan of EcoCeres said the extra cost of SAF should be seen as “green value” rather than a “green premium” as each tonne of its fuel would cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 94.4 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel depending on feedstock composition. This was a benefit that everyone would enjoy, he argued. “If you do not realise it is a value, the product itself will have no value,” he said. “Why would you pay more for the same thing?” How to lower the price of SAF? The IATA estimated that the price of SAF would surge to US$2,872 per tonne in 2026, about 2.5 times the price of jet fuel, while S&P Global Energy’s data showed that the SAF price in China was US$2,340 per tonne on October 6. Lawmaker Chan said scaling operations was essential to bringing down SAF costs. “Hong Kong is a small market without the scale or critical mass, but the Greater Bay Area has many airports, and their combined demand can reach critical mass,” he said. If there was a clear demand for SAF, the region’s many facilities and suppliers would naturally be willing to invest in scaling, he added. The legislator said the next step was developing a carbon trading market that could help bring down costs as the industry scaled up. One example, he said, was the SAF certificate mentioned in the policy address: airlines could trade the certificates in the market, while companies short of carbon credits could buy them. Samuel Wong, Asia-Pacific vice-president for sales at PAC LP, a technology supplier in the United States, said used cooking oil alone would not be sufficient to produce SAF on the scale the aviation industry would eventually require. “Used cooking oil can be turned into SAF, but it can also be used to produce biodiesel and other renewable fuels, so different sectors are competing for the same limited supply,” Wong said. “That competition has pushed prices above US$1,000 per tonne in some markets.” He said the supply of used cooking oil was inherently limited, meaning the industry would have to develop alternative feedstocks and production technologies as SAF demand increased. “There are fundamental constraints on both supply and cost,” Wong said. “The amount of used cooking oil that can be sustainably collected is finite, so used cooking oil alone cannot provide all the feedstock needed to scale SAF globally.” HEFA, or hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, is currently the main commercial pathway used for producing SAF and uses feedstocks including used cooking oil, vegetable oils and animal fats. But Wong said achieving much larger SAF volumes would require the industry to diversify beyond HEFA. “HEFA is essential for scaling SAF today, but it cannot be the only solution,” he said. “The industry needs a portfolio of pathways.” Lawmaker Chan said Hong Kong needed a detailed action plan beyond 2030. “[The government] needs a mandatory target by 2030, and then have a clear direction in 2035 to raise the target along the way,” he said.

title: South Korea struggles to curb sexual exploitation sites 10 years after Soranet scandal
description: Despite tougher laws, a new wave of sites containing non-consensual sexually explicit videos and images of women has emerged.
content: A decade after the shutdown of Soranet – a sprawling online hub for secretly filmed and non-consensual sexual videos that became a symbol of South Korea’s digital sex-crime crisis – the country is still struggling to stamp out similar networks and copycat sites that have emerged in its wake. Their prevalence reflects the difficulties of deterring such illegal activities, policing the online space and changing societal attitudes towards women. Last month, a man was detained over an alleged Soranet offshoot that investigators said shared more than 2,000 sexually explicit videos, illegally filmed material and deepfakes. The site also allegedly recruited participants for partner-swapping sessions that were later filmed and uploaded, while members shared photographs of family members and acquaintances so users could rate their bodies. The case highlights the challenge South Korea faces in tackling the darker side of the online space despite tougher laws and more aggressive police investigations. Soranet was home to thousands of illegal pornographic videos viewed and shared by more than a million users in South Korea. The site featured videos secretly filmed in toilets and changing rooms, as well as intimate footage posted by former partners without the consent of the women recorded. Some victims who appeared in the videos later took their own lives. A public outcry, including large street protests organised by women’s groups, put pressure on the government. Authorities later arrested Soranet’s operators and shut down the site in 2016. But the closure did not prevent similar sites from emerging, particularly small networks that have eluded the scrutiny of authorities. Tougher laws In May, police shut down a Soranet-inspired site known as the “Honours Club” after discovering that about 6,300 members had shared and watched photographs and videos of group sex and orgies facilitated through the platform. Another infamous site, Yadong Korea, resurfaced last month under the same name after it was shut down in August, prompting the country’s feminist political group, the Women’s Party, to urge the police to reopen investigations into illegal pornography networks. A police officer in Seoul was recently detained on suspicion of creating and distributing hundreds of AI-generated sexually explicit deepfakes and possessing about 5,600 illegal sexual images and videos. The officer was caught following an undercover investigation by the Busan Metropolitan Police Agency into a Telegram chat room where such images were circulated. He was also suspected of possessing child sexual exploitation material and creating more than 400 AI-generated images and videos depicting acquaintances as nude. During the molka, or spycam, crisis of the 2010s, the government strengthened laws against non-consensual distribution of intimate images, regardless of who originally recorded them. In 2020, the Nth Room case further exposed how online platforms could be used to produce, sell and blackmail victims with sexually exploitative material. It led to the so-called “Anti-Nth Room Act”, which expanded criminal liability beyond creators and distributors to buyers and viewers. Purchasing, downloading or knowingly viewing illegally filmed sexual exploitation material carries a sentence of up to three years in prison or a fine of 30 million won (US$22,440). South Korea subsequently overhauled its laws on deepfakes following public outrage over Telegram-based sex crime rings that distributed doctored images of women and girls. Creating sexually explicit deepfakes carries up to seven years in prison or a fine of 50 million won, while possessing, purchasing, storing or knowingly viewing such material can also result in criminal penalties. An Gab-chul, a lawyer at Gammyung Law Firm who specialises in sexual crimes, said the law was now clearer on such offences. “There are cases where the footage was originally recorded with the person’s consent. But if that material is later distributed without the person’s consent, that in itself constitutes a violation of the law,” An said. But tougher laws have not eliminated the need for improved investigative tactics as perpetrators are often caught only following reports by victims, according to An. Undercover investigations, once uncommon in South Korea, were authorised in 2021 for crimes involving minors and expanded last year to cover digital sexual offences involving adult victims. A representative of the National Police Agency told This Week in Asia that a team of 20 investigators across four regional police agencies was established this month to investigate illegal websites promoting sexual exploitation. “The more actively we investigate these cases, the more criminals try to evade detection, whether by using overseas servers or adopting other methods to prevent their activities from being traced,” the representative said. “These cases are becoming increasingly difficult to investigate, but we are also working hard to keep pace with those changes.” Eluding police crackdown However, An is not optimistic that the underground networks will disappear any time soon. “What I found through my research is that whenever one of these sites is shut down, another one keeps appearing,” he said. “They disappear, and then they are created again.” “There are people who demand these services, and there are people who see an opportunity to make money from them. As long as that structure remains in place, these sites will continue to be created.” An said the problem extended beyond dedicated pornography sites, with online communities and open chat rooms becoming gateways to sexual exploitation and prostitution. “Some of our most popular chat services seem to have essentially turned into platforms for prostitution,” he said. Joohee Kim, an assistant professor of women’s studies at Duksung Women’s University in Seoul, said online sexual exploitation cases in South Korea had exposed the limitations of its legal understanding of sexual violence. “The legal understanding of sexual violence has historically focused more on whether an act was forced through violence or threats than on whether the woman consented.” Kim cited choehyeobui-seol, the legal interpretation under which rape or indecent assault was established only when a perpetrator’s violence or threats were serious enough to make it impossible or extremely difficult for the victim to resist. The interpretation dominated South Korea’s criminal justice practice and legal scholarship for decades, and its influence remains despite a 2023 Supreme Court ruling that lowered the threshold for establishing indecent assault. “Online sexual exploitation can be understood as a problem in which this disregard for consent is repeatedly amplified through digital technology,” Kim said. Kim Yeo-jin, director of the Korea Cyber Sexual Violence Response Centre, linked the problem to the country’s online culture, particularly how technology had been used to sexualise women. Male-dominated online forums, such as DCinside and FMkorea, have helped spread misogynistic language and a culture of sexualising women through lewd images and videos shared in open chats, according to Kim Yeo-jin. “The biggest underlying problem is that attitudes towards sexually objectifying women without their consent have not fundamentally changed,” Kim said “Ordinary members of the public need to change how they perceive and treat victims of sexual exploitation. Only then can we truly understand the magnitude of these crimes and have deeper discussions on how we can change for the better.”

title: Hong Kong’s historic vessels sail into the future
description: Hong Kong’s maritime heritage is embedded in the fabric of the city, but many of its hand-built wooden vessels have been lost to time and urban development. PostMag discovers how one dedicated organisation is racing to preserve this inimitable slice of boating history.
content: While walking alongside Victoria Harbour or riding the Star Ferry, luck might have allowed you a glimpse of Way Foong motoring by. Its old-fashioned appearance is a sign that the boat is obviously from an era long past but, because it is not a traditional junk, you may not have realised you were looking at an authentic piece of Hong Kong history: a wooden motoryacht constructed locally almost 100 years ago. Commissioned by the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (now HSBC) – “Way Foong” being a transliteration of the bank’s name in Cantonese – and built in 1930 by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, the vessel was used by the bank as a ferry, a tugboat and a pleasure craft for employees for more than seven decades before passing into private ownership. In the late 2010s, it was acquired by a patron of the Hong Kong Historic Vessels Foundation (HKHVF) – an organisation officially founded earlier this year by individuals passionate about preserving the city’s maritime legacy. When hired for parties or other events, Way Foong can often be seen cruising side by side with Java, another 1930s-era wooden vessel built by the same shipyard. Java entered service in 1935 and served for decades in the Hong Kong government fleet as Marine 1. It transported VIPs and port officials, conducted anti-piracy patrols, towed and positioned mooring buoys and even corralled the odd swimming water buffalo. Its Burmese-teak construction, with deck planks measuring almost 4.5cm thick, earned the boat a reputation for being “almost unsinkable” and invulnerable to typhoons. Way Foong and Java are two of five vessels now owned and maintained by the HKHVF. “By restoring and preserving such examples of the world-class craftsmanship that Hong Kong shipyards were capable of, we aim not only to encourage Hongkongers to discover the city’s commercial, governmental and recreational maritime heritage, but also to nurture the region’s next generation of boaters and ocean-lovers,” says CEO Philip Giannecchini. Java, the first vessel in the collection, was found by chance. One of the avid sailors who would later establish the HKHVF noticed Java moored in Tai Tam Harbour, on the south side of Hong Kong Island, when taking out his own boat, and wanted to learn more about the 56-foot wooden launch. He ended up meeting the then-owner, and bought Java in the early 2000s. At the time, the rationale behind the purchase was simply to have such a historical pleasure craft in one’s possession. Eventually, the desire to safeguard Hong Kong’s maritime history took hold, setting in motion other acquisitions and the founding of the HKHVF. A years-long search for extant, pre-50s boats built in the city followed. Nine, in various states of repair, have been identified by the organisation’s historians – some now in the HKHVF collection, others happily and privately owned, and one, Mon Lei, whose whereabouts are unknown. Given Hong Kong’s coastal geography, boats have, and will always be, an integral part of the city. Yet, while today’s harbours and inlets are teeming with craft of various shapes and sizes, most are built elsewhere, the city’s shipbuilding days having long passed. However, in the early 20th century, two giants of the industry, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, were firmly in their prime, and a number of small and medium-sized shipbuilders, such as Hung Hom’s Hop Kee Shipyard, Ah King Slipway and Cheoy Lee Shipyard, also produced wooden vessels for global clients. Teresa Mak Hiu-see, one of the in-house researchers at the HKHVF, notes that “the 30s were one of the high points in Hong Kong’s shipbuilding tradition for all types of vessels, from cargo liners to pleasure craft, and the industry steamed ahead until Japan invaded Hong Kong in December 1941. Until the end of World War II, all dockyards were under Japanese control”. Rare survivors such as Way Foong and Java escaped the scrapyard, but many other Hong Kong-built vessels from the 20s and 40s were not so lucky. Says Mak, “With the 40s being a time of war and post-war recovery, that might be a factor in the small number of surviving pleasure craft from that decade.” In 1972, the Taikoo Dockyard and the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company were merged to form the Hongkong United Dockyards. In 1980, the Whampoa site was shut down and the land was redeveloped into the Whampoa Garden housing estate, now easily identified by its superyacht-shaped shopping centre, a 110-metre-long concrete landmark “moored” amid the residential blocks. When the Cheoy Lee Shipyard at Penny’s Bay was reclaimed by the Hong Kong government in 1999 to provide a location for Hong Kong Disneyland, it signalled the end of an era: shipbuilding operations in the city were coming to an end. But the final straw came when Ah King’s Causeway Bay shipyard closed, in 2002. With shipbuilding essentially a thing of the past, the preservation of Hong Kong-made boats has become ever more important, Giannecchini explains, as these examples are “more than just beautiful old vessels – they tell the story of Hong Kong’s craftsmanship, ingenuity and connection to the sea, and that’s a story we want future generations to be able to experience”. James Barker, captain of the HKHVF fleet, who coordinates the repairs, maintenance and operation of the boats and can often be seen piloting them, adds, “Caring for nearly century-old boats is not easy. Every project you take on turns out to be much larger, more complicated and more expensive than you first envision. For example, the Gardner engine on Way Foong needed to be replaced, but that [British] company went out of business in the 90s, so we had to source everything we needed from other places.” It is not just hardware that is difficult to secure. Experts who have the technical knowledge to carry out such repairs are dwindling in number as well, he says. “Everyone who used to do these specialised jobs has either retired or passed away. In the absence of all other options, we are forced to research, plan and take on the task ourselves,” says Barker. “We recently had to pull the propeller shaft from So Fong and replace the rotten timber around the stern, which meant drilling a new hole through the replacement wood,” he continues. “We’re looking at the bones of these boats, not just making sure they look beautiful on the surface. Significant work is needed to ensure these vessels can last for another 100 years.” As Giannecchini notes, preservation in its finest form means not only maintaining the physical aspect, but also the histories of these vessels. In an effort to share the stories behind the fleet, the HKHVF website has detailed introductions to each boat. Some have lived lives rich with adventure and drama. Way Foong transported gold and silver bullion to and from ships anchored in Victoria Harbour, as well as chests of banknotes to HSBC branches on Hong Kong’s outlying islands. It was even used for “burning picnics”: junior staff from the bank’s note-cancellation department would burn sacks of old bills in the boiler room, back when Way Foong had its original steam engine, converting the to-be-disposed-of cash into fuel. According to one account, Way Foong was taken up the Pearl River at the outbreak of World War II and scuppered to prevent it from falling into Japanese hands. After the war, its skipper reportedly returned to the bank to ask for his job back. He was told that it was his if he could find the missing launch. He did – Way Foong was recovered in 1945 and returned to service after a major refit. Another HKHVF vessel, Tai Mo Shan, served as a film prop in Mamma Mia! (2008), appearing as the sailing boat that transports the three male co-leads – Pierce Brosnan, Colin Firth and Stellan Skarsgård – to the fictional Greek island of Kalokairi, where the wedding in the plot takes place. Tai Mo Shan had been domiciled in Athens at the time of filming and a broker linked the producers to its owner. While the boat was not in great condition, this suited the filmmakers, who wanted to show the fictional owner, played by Skarsgård, as a “scruffy” character; they even exaggerated its run-down look to drive the point home. Tai Mo Shan was undergoing restoration work at a shipyard in Greece when the HKHVF became aware of it, in the summer of 2025, through a yacht broker’s flier. Arrangements were made to buy the boat, and it was delivered in October 2025. Tai Mo Shan was built by the Hong Kong and Whampoa Dock Company, in 1933, and left the city on a 16,000-plus-mile transpacific and then transatlantic voyage to Dartmouth, in Britain, which, by some accounts, included an attempt to spy on Japanese naval installations in the Kuril Islands. Another vessel, Typhoon, was discovered by the HKHVF through research on Facebook. Built in 1934 at the Hop Kee Shipyard to a design by Harold S. Rouse, for the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, the boat enjoyed a successful racing career up until the relocation of its owner, back to his native Britain. Typhoon was in Scotland when it was acquired, also in 2025. Late last year, Tracy Van Buskirk, a retired banker who enjoys exploring coastal Maine, in the United States, aboard a 30-foot retrofitted lobster boat, shared her recollections with the HKHVF after having googled the name “So Fong” out of curiosity and found out that the schooner, on which she had sailed in the 70s, from Stamford, Connecticut, to Singapore, was still afloat. So Fong, a gaff-rigged schooner measuring 82 feet, was built on an Ah King slipway, on commission for American yachtsman A. Thornton Baker. It took around 250 artisans more than seven months to complete the boat. Following its launch in March 1937, So Fong sailed for about 30,000 miles, travelling through the Philippines, the South Seas, the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean and the South Atlantic before reaching San Juan, Puerto Rico, in April 1938. During World War II, the US Coast Guard requisitioned So Fong, according to a commemorative plaque aboard the vessel. After the war, it returned to the Pacific and was used for racing. Van Buskirk recalls that, at the age of 21, in 1978, she had recently graduated from university after spending a year studying Mandarin in Taiwan. “I had every intention of returning to Asia, but decided to spend the summer in my hometown of Fairfield to get a job. By early October, I had started planning my flights back to Taipei. One weekend, my mother invited me to go sailing with a family friend, on his 28-foot sloop. He asked me about my plans and volunteered that his son had been hired as first mate for a delivery job of a large schooner that was scheduled to leave Stamford soon and sail to Singapore. William Mathers, the new owner, had bought So Fong earlier that year and hired the captain, Don Kuhn, to take her on this 14,000-mile journey. “I was intrigued and immediately drove to the Stamford Yacht Club to introduce myself and see about a berth. Kuhn was busy with last-minute arrangements but took a moment for a brief interview. After determining that I was healthy, held a current passport and had some savings, he said I was hired. We left two days later [on October 18, 1978].” Van Buskirk and So Fong would reach Singapore on March 21 of the following year. In 1984, Vietnamese authorities seized the vessel in the Pacific Ocean, on suspicion that its sophisticated navigation equipment was being used for espionage, and its owner was placed in solitary confinement. He was released the following year, having paid his way to freedom, but So Fong remained confiscated. It would spend the next few years abandoned at anchor until yacht enthusiast Robert Verschoyle located the vessel in 1989. Following an intensive 11-month restoration in Ho Chi Minh City, Verschoyle executed a nighttime escape with So Fong in the early 90s. Under cover of darkness, he smuggled the boat out, and the vessel eventually reappeared in Hong Kong in 1993. After a few decades, during which the boat passed through private hands, Giannecchini was alerted to So Fong’s existence in February 2025, by a friend who had read about it in an article about vintage sailing vessels available for charter in Spain. So Fong finally returned home last October, after being acquired by the HKHVF. Earlier this year, the HKHVF learned of another Hong Kong-built wooden yacht from the 30s that was still sailing in local waters. Ariki III was constructed in 1939 at the Ah King shipyard, to a design by American naval architect Ralph E. Winslow. Completed just before the outbreak of World War II, she was meant to be shipped to the US, but those plans were foiled by the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong. After years of neglect, she sank in 1946. New Zealander Hector Forsyth raised the boat, restored it and named it after the Maori word for “leader”. Ariki III became part of the city’s sailing scene, eventually coming into the ownership of long-time sailor Graeme Large, who restored it anew, together with Stanley-based wooden-boat specialist Fan Kwei-sum. Current owner Peter Lau Man-pong, a businessman and the chairman of the Hong Kong Arts Centre, developed a passion for the sea at an early age, having grown up sailing in the waters around Hong Kong with his father. “My father was the founding chairman of the Hong Kong Sea Cadet Corps. Now, as its deputy chairman, I also have a deep connection with the sea and related youth activities,” says Lau. He believes that the HKHVF’s mission to educate the public about Hong Kong’s maritime heritage is important; the team “has a noble vision and noble hearts, in addition to their love of boats”. Although he used to paddle his wooden kayak from Hong Kong to Macau for leisure, “unfortunately, I am getting old and don’t have the time nor energy to take my boats out as much as I used to. As the HKHVF continues to mature, I am planning on gifting them Ariki III, but the details are still being worked out”. As its collection grows, the HKHVF has begun making its vessels accessible to the public, through collaborations with people and organisations involved in history, conservation and education, such as the Hong Kong Maritime Museum and the Royal Geographical Society. Additionally, the vessels can be chartered for business and recreational use. As early as next year, the HKHVF plans to open a small museum at its floating headquarters – a structure made of two connected industrial barges, in the Kwun Tong Typhoon Shelter – to provide a permanent home for its fleet. “Our vision is to keep researching Hong Kong’s maritime history, preserve significant vessels whenever we have the opportunity and find new ways to share their stories,” says Giannecchini. “We don’t want these boats sitting in a museum as artefacts. We want them to remain active, accessible and connected to the people of Hong Kong.” As Way Foong and its restored kin continue to glide through Hong Kong’s waters, they do much more than offer a glimpse of a bygone era – they keep part of the city’s history afloat.

title: Hong Kong tennis bosses eye golden pipeline after Coleman Wong secures sport’s future
description: Coleman Wong’s men’s singles triumph and women’s doubles bronze won by Eudice Chong and Cody Wong means tennis will have Tier A status.
content: Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s historic men’s singles gold at the Asian Games had an impact far beyond earning him a spot at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics; it also secured tennis’ elite status in Hong Kong for another four years. Wong beat Wu Yibing of China in straight sets in the final at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre in Nagoya, becoming his city’s first singles winner at the continental Games. Bronze for Eudice Chong and Cody Wong Hong-yi in the women’s doubles made it the most successful Games for their sport, and came on the back of the two bronze won at the National Games last November by Coleman Wong and the youth men’s team. Still, Michael Cheng Ming-git, president of the Hong Kong, China Tennis Association, said his organisation would spend little time enjoying the moment, and was adamant that the next steps to keep the sport growing had already begun. “First off, what you see in the investment in tennis, in terms of the Elite Training Grant from the Hong Kong Sports Institute, is bearing fruit,” Cheng said. “The four medals at the Asian Games and the National Games in the last 12 months are no coincidence, and show that our approach to elite development is correct. “Player development is an undertaking that takes eight to 10 years. We need to make sure we have a pipeline. We need to build a system that produces good players who can play in junior grand slams every year, not just every few years.” It was that pipeline that Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui referenced immediately after Wong’s triumph. “I’m very glad as we now have every reason to keep tennis in the Sports Institute’s Tier A, and our decision last year to make a special arrangement for tennis has paid off,” she told the South China Morning Post. Cheng noted that Kazakhstan had only one player competing in junior grand slams before 2021, but that increased to 16 over the following five years. China also has multiple representatives every year. In contrast, Kai Thompson was the sole Hong Kong player to compete in the junior slams this year, reaching the quarter-finals in Melbourne and the third round in New York. “The Asian Games medals allow us to review, adapt and plan for the long term,” Cheng said. “Our two medals in the previous 64 years at the regional games and National Games were won by three players. “But we have eight players – six men and two women – who have won our last four medals. As a federation, our role is to promote a sport. When you have a system for developing the sport and laying the foundations, as well as a method for nurturing elite athletes, the results will follow.” Hong Kong has produced multiple world-class athletes over the years. Top fencers, including Olympic champions Cheung Ka-long and Vivian Kong Man-wai, and former world champion and world No 1 Ryan Choi Chun-yin, have frequently trained and competed in the region as well as overseas. Swimming star Siobhan Haughey spent countless hours training in the United States, where she pursued her psychology degree at the University of Michigan. Even double Olympic medallist Sarah Lee Wai-sze trained outside the city more often than not. Nevertheless, Cheng believes the foundations for future success can be laid in Hong Kong before players head overseas, fostering an “I can beat the best players” mindset. “We need a robust technical curriculum for players aged 8–14; we need a scientific fitness programme to make our athletes the fittest in the region,” he said. “And we need to build team spirit among the players. All this can be done in Hong Kong. This is to get them ready. “After the age of 14, players need to commit to playing with the best players in the pool. That means Europe, the US and red clay. They need to immerse themselves in this environment to believe they are among the best.
