Vance told Reuters that Iran must make “meaningful” reductions in its enrichment capacity. The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied. Trump has repeatedly cited productive or ongoing diplomatic talks with Iran without any results. He’s also repeatedly threatened military escalation against Tehran, sometimes without ordering new attacks. Trump added on Thursday that a US naval blockade of Iranian exports would remain in place. Yet fresh tanker attacks by Iran threaten to curtail a recent uptick in oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz: UK Maritime Trade Operations reported nine attacks in the waterway so far in October. And while oil shipments through Hormuz are approaching pre-war levels with the US military’s assistance, the recent spate of Iranian attacks have already helped trigger another surge in oil prices. The US has moved its B-1B bombers from the Royal Air Force base in Fairford, England, citing terror threats. The base had been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran earlier in the conflict, but the warplanes were hastily removed following the arrests of a number of men outside the base. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it’s likely Iran was involved in the plot, with Trump saying the bombers were removed to lower the security risks. British officials told Bloomberg they’re concerned Trump’s decision will embolden Tehran and Moscow to use more proxies to carry out sabotage attacks. European officials are already struggling to contend with a Russian campaign of so-called hybrid warfare attacks across the continent, with attempted attacks in Germany and elsewhere. Back in the Middle East, the Iran-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen also struck two airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia in the past two days, killing three people and injuring dozens more, in a blow to one of Washington’s key partners in the Middle East. The US is currently opting out of taking a direct role in a Saudi-backed counteroffensive to take back Houthi-claimed territory, but Saudi Arabia’s allies could come under pressure to become more involved as ballistic missiles are fired towards Riyadh. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: US Senate candidate fires back after Trump misnames him ‘Mohammed’
description: Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed says US president is ‘struggling’ following post making baseless terror links.
content: A Muslim candidate for US Senate accused Donald Trump of “struggling” on Thursday after the president misnamed him “Mohammed” on social media amid increasingly bitter exchanges between the two men. Trump attacked the left-wing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed on his Truth Social platform, baselessly accusing him of being a “Terrorist Sympathizer”. El-Sayed, an Arab-American running for a Michigan senate seat that could decide which party wins the US upper chamber in knife-edge midterm elections next month, said “I think Donald might be struggling a little bit”. “He thinks my name’s Mohammed ... My name’s Abdul, and you know it. And the only reason he won’t say it is I keep ripping you,” El-Sayed said at a campaign event in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “So try again and get it right because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly,” he added to laughter at a restaurant photo-op, where he was joined by Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer and Delaware Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester. Like many Muslim men, El-Sayed’s middle name is Mohamed, but he does not use it publicly. Trump and his supporters have fixated on El-Sayed, accusing him and his family of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and the al-Qaeda jihadist group. Trump said El-Sayed, locked in a knife-edge race with Republican Mike Rogers, was the “best friend” of “America Hating Hasan Piker”, the left-wing influencer who campaigned for El-Sayed during the Democratic primary. The Michigan Senate seat, open because Democratic Senator Gary Peters is retiring, is considered essential to Democratic hopes of regaining the Senate. The party aims to retain the Michigan seat in Democratic hands while wresting four other seats in the 100-member chamber from Republicans. The midwestern state backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election, even as Democrat Elissa Slotkin narrowly defeated Rogers for Michigan’s other Senate seat. El-Sayed was backed by progressive leaders including Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Elizabeth Warren, as well as the United Auto Workers union. His platform includes healthcare for all, higher taxes on billionaires, ending unconditional US military aid to Israel and reducing the role of corporate money in elections.

title: UK counterterror police arrest 2 inside airbase used by US
description: Latvian nationals held under the National Security Act after security breach at RAF Molesworth.
content: British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday. The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by ‌the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain. Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran. The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100km (60 miles) north of London, ⁠and raised the alarm. Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were ‌arrested inside the base. They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being rearrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under ‌the National Security Act 2023. RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command ⁠operations, as well as ⁠a Nato intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations. Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 145km west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran, which denied any involvement. The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used ‌by US ‌forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford. “We’re ‌very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this ⁠incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a ⁠statement. Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city. Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said. “We are highly ‌vigilant about potential threats to ‌our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defence minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X. A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement. “We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

title: US suspends Microsoft, major IT firms from green card programme
description: IT firms including Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini will also be suspended from the programme, officials say.
content: The US government ⁠is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and ⁠several large IT firms from a programme that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency, senior US officials have announced, citing alleged fraud, and as part ‌of an effort to push companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Thursday. Vance said the programme required companies to advertise jobs in the US before applying to the Department of Labour to show they needed to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American staff. “They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it,’” Vance said. “And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants.” “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.” Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. Secretary of Labour Keith Sonderling added that some of ⁠the largest IT firms in the world would also be suspended from ‌that programme, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. “We will not accept any new or process any ‌pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said. Microsoft did ⁠not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment. Under the PERM process, employers seek certification from the Department ‌of Labour that there is no qualified, willing or available US worker for a ‌specific job. ‌It is a step required before filing petitions for most employment-based ‌green cards. Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would ⁠be investigated for allegedly bringing in international students to undercut American ⁠wages. Labour Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. “We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or ‌visa abuse are compromising federally ‌funded research,” D’Esposito said. “If an American university is breaking the law to save US$1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal.” Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: UK police accept ex-prince Andrew search warrants must be ‘legally quashed’
description: Thames Valley Police said it agreed the warrants were not properly granted by the courts but that the investigation into Andrew continues.
content: British police on Thursday said that search warrants they secured to search properties linked to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been issued unlawfully and must be quashed, but that the investigation into King Charles’ younger brother was continuing. Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in ‌public office in February, linked to his relationship with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and searches were carried out at properties in Sandringham, eastern England, and Windsor. The arrest of the senior royal, eighth in line to the throne, was unprecedented in modern times and a Reuters photo of the ashen-faced former prince leaving the police station made front pages around the world. However, Mountbatten-Windsor, who has not made any public comment since his arrest, subsequently launched a legal challenge and applied for the search ⁠warrants to be quashed. Thames Valley Police said it now agreed these had not been properly granted by the courts. “We accept the position that ‌the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed,” it said. “Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during ‌the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation.” At a hearing ⁠at London’s High Court on ⁠Thursday, Judge Nicholas Hilliard said the force was applying to keep the seized property, which Mountbatten-Windsor was opposing, and the issue would not be settled until next year. Thames Valley Police said it had not returned any material to the royal other than that which was not deemed to be connected to their investigation. While the quashing of ‌the warrants ‌is an embarrassment, it does not stop the police investigation which began after the release of millions of documents by the US Department ‌of Justice relating to Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor, the second son of the late Queen Elizabeth, has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein and said he ⁠regrets their friendship. The offence of misconduct in public office, which carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, can relate to any serious wrongdoing – from ⁠sharing confidential information to corruption and sexual misconduct. Police have said their investigation, which relates to Mountbatten-Windsor’s time as a British special representative for trade, between 2001 and 2011, would be lengthy and incredibly complex. He was forced to quit all official royal duties in ‌2019 over his ties with Epstein and ‌was then stripped of his titles and honours by his older brother last October after further revelations about their relationship. Epstein was found dead in his Manhattan prison cell in August 2019 in what was ruled a suicide. Meanwhile, a Buckingham Palace source has said the former prince had been told that money provided from private funds by his brother the king should not be used to fund his legal challenge.

title: Washington’s transactional Taiwan policy puts Indo-Pacific at risk, ex-US officials warn
description: The United States has ‘not been in a weaker position in the western Pacific’ than now, former American commander says.
content: Washington’s policy towards Taiwan is increasingly tied to its relationship with Beijing, according to former American officials who also warn that the war on Iran is weakening US military readiness for a potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait. During a fireside chat in an annual symposium hosted by the Global Taiwan Institute in Washington on Wednesday, Brent Christensen, former director of the Taipei Office of the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT), said Washington’s policy towards the self-ruled island had seen a “discontinuity”, becoming “less independent” from its China policy in the current administration. Christensen said that while the security relationship between the US and Taiwan remained “very robust”, there was “a huge increase in US demands for burden sharing, or for Taiwan to do more of its own production of weapon systems and increase defence spending”. He also said there was a big increase in demand for Taiwan’s hi-tech investment in the United States. Building on Christensen’s argument, Laura Rosenberger, a prominent China hawk who served at the National Security Council in former president Joe Biden’s administration and was chairwoman of the AIT under Biden, said she was “concerned” about the characterisation of arms sales as a “negotiating chip” with Beijing, indicating a “fundamental departure” from traditional US policy framework on Taiwan. “I think it’s a very problematic one, and particularly because it’s not just been a rhetorical one but one where we have seen a US$14 billion arms sale that was pre-notified to Congress not move forward,” Rosenberger said, adding there was no sign the sale would progress, which “is a deep concern”. “It is a question of a broader range of support for the security relationship.” The officials’ remarks contrasted with earlier remarks by Taiwan’s envoy to the US, Alexander Yui Tah-ray, who said Washington had made clear there was no change in its position on Taiwan and that US-Taiwan relations remained “robust”. The remarks came after recent summits between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, where the issue of Taiwan remained a point of friction between the two leaders. During the summit with Trump in Washington last month, Xi reiterated hopes that the US would oppose “Taiwan independence”, urging the US to handle the Taiwan issue with caution. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as independent, but Washington is opposed to any use of force in the strait and it is committed to supplying it with arms. Under the Six Assurances – six foreign policy guidelines given by the US to Taiwan in July 1982 – Washington has pledged not to consult Beijing before deciding on arms sales to Taipei. Even though Washington has reiterated that the broader US policy towards Taiwan remains unchanged and it transferred two F-16V fighter jets – approved during Trump’s first term – to the island after the September summit, the second Trump administration has indicated a highly transactional and leverage-focused approach to Taiwan compared with previous administrations. In May, Trump cited the US$14 billion weapons package as a “very good negotiating chip” to help maintain a trade truce, holding up its approval. The administration earlier announced a separate US$11 billion arms sale to Taiwan in December, which drew a strong reaction from Beijing. Trump has also called on Taiwan and Indo-Pacific allies to share the defence burden in the region, pressuring them to increase their military spending in the face of potential armed conflict with Beijing in the Taiwan Strait. Mark Montgomery, who served as commander of Carrier Strike Group 5 aboard the USS George Washington, whose homeport is in Japan, told the symposium session the US had “not been in a weaker position in the western Pacific” than now. He said the US war in Iran created Beijing’s possible “illusions” of military action against Taiwan, as the US diverted its carrier strike groups from the Indo-Pacific to the Middle East. According to Montgomery, there are no US destroyers or aircraft carriers actively operating in the western Pacific, as the USS Abraham Lincoln and USS George Washington – which were both scheduled to be deployed in the Indo-Pacific this year – had been sent to the Middle East. He said it could eventually create a “readiness bathtub”, or steep decline in available combat forces, for 18 months and beyond, causing US Navy and Air Force readiness in the region to “fall off a cliff”. “The longer we do this mission, the deeper the trough,” Montgomery said. “If we’re there till next June, or between next March and next June, that’s my guess on this extra deployment, this is going to impact us through late 2028, through 2029, 2030. So that’s the first big problem.” In addition to moving its carriers, the US has transferred critical munitions, missile defence systems and military assets from the Indo-Pacific theatre to the Middle East to support operations and replenish stockpiles amid the ongoing conflict with Iran, where Montgomery said the US had “grossly insufficient numbers”. He said that beyond military implications, Taiwan remained significant for its production of the semiconductors needed for advanced US weapons, such as its fighter jets. He said Beijing should learn from the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine that large-scale offensive operations were difficult, and that any armed confrontation harming Taiwan’s semiconductor industry could “destroy” the world economy and be a major loss for mainland China. “This president [Trump] fundamentally does not understand the value of Taiwan,” Montgomery said. “We absolutely want Taiwan to be successful. We need it to be successful, and we need it to not be coerced by China.”

title: Police called in, venue blacklist planned after fans abuse coach Wang Hao at WTT China Smash
description: Table tennis crackdown on extreme fans coincides with scrutiny over team management after unwell world No 1 Sun Yingsha suffers shock exit.
content: Chinese table tennis authorities have called in police and announced plans for venue blacklists as they crack down on extreme fan behaviour, after men’s head coach Wang Hao was swarmed and verbally abused by a crowd of extreme fans at the WTT China Smash. The crackdown coincides with mounting public scrutiny over team management and athlete overwork, after world No 1 Sun Yingsha suffered a shock early exit while competing with a fever on Wednesday night. The off-court turmoil unfolded on Tuesday at Beijing’s Shougang Park during the WTT event, when men’s head coach Wang was surrounded by a crowd of around 100 fans as he walked towards the parking area. The crowd shouted profanities and chanted “put Lin Shidong in top singles” and “Wang Hao step down” as they aggressively questioned his coaching line-up decisions. When the crowd continued, Wang pulled out his phone to record video evidence before reporting the incident to on-site police officers to demand intervention. Later that day, Wang’s wife, Yan Boya, posted a video on Weibo sent by a fan at the scene, writing: “I don’t understand how competitive sports turned out like this …” The demand for “top singles”, a term referring to a team’s No 1 player being picked to face the opponent’s strongest competitor, stemmed from the recent Asian Games. Fans criticised Wang’s decision to name Wang Chuqin as top singles and rising star Lin Shidong as third singles in the men’s team final, where China lost gold to Japan. After Lin later defeated Wang Chuqin 4-0 in the men’s singles final, fans argued Lin should have led the team. Under China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law, disrupting order at major public events or harassing and insulting staff carries penalties ranging from warnings and fines of up to 1,000 yuan (US$150) to 10 days of detention. On Wednesday, the Chinese Table Tennis Association (CTTA) issued a formal statement pledging to combat extreme fan misconduct, confirming it had assisted personnel in reporting cases to public security organs and was pushing to establish a stadium blacklist system. The CTTA noted that abusive behaviour, rumour-mongering and personal attacks against coaches and players had “spread from the venue to the internet, and from the internet back to the scene”. It revealed that athletes had been disturbed during matches, coaches faced courtside verbal abuse and gestures, and personnel received a relentless barrage of “abusive text messages, harassing calls and social media private messages”, severely disturbing their training and daily lives. “The Chinese Table Tennis Association always places the physical and mental health and long-term development of coaches and athletes in an important position,” the statement read. Moving forward, the CTTA would “push for the establishment of a venue blacklist system and strengthen on-site order”, adding that false claims regarding team management, player usage and tactical arrangements would be handled in accordance with the law. Calling for a “rational, civilised and inclusive table tennis culture”, the association urged that “love should have warmth, expression should have boundaries, and the arena should have order”. The off-court hostility coincided with a major upset on Wednesday evening, when world No 1 Sun was knocked out in the women’s singles round of 32, losing 1-3 to Thailand’s 101st-ranked Orawan Paranang, Sun’s career-worst finish at a WTT Smash event. Sun had arrived directly in Beijing after competing in three events under heavy physical strain at the Asian Games. She revealed she suffered a high fever the night before the match, leaving her physically compromised despite the fever subsiding on match day. Visible fatigue led to uncharacteristic errors, particularly in key points during the third and fourth games. The loss triggered a heated online debate, fuelled by Taiwanese commentators Zhou Dongyu and his co-host, who argued during the broadcast that a “good coaching team should forcefully require an athlete to rest” when unwell, prioritising physical state over results to prevent serious injury. They noted Sun was visibly pushing through physical distress, with delayed reaction times and compromised footwork. The commentary trended on social media, with fans questioning why the CTTA did not allow Sun to rest after the Games, pointing out that male players had received injury breaks while Sun faced heavier physical consumption, leading to accusations of differential treatment. Speaking at a post-match press conference with no Q&A session, Sun praised Paranang’s performance and acknowledged that winning and losing were normal in sports. “I really wanted to play well at this tournament and deliver a great performance for everyone. Today’s result is indeed regretful,” Sun admitted, noting that despite feeling unwell, she fought hard but fell short of expectations. Looking ahead, Sun stated her top priority for the next two weeks would be physical recovery before resuming training for the coming WTT Champions France. She also urged the public “not to over-speculate or worry”, reassuring fans that her condition was manageable and asking for encouragement as she prepared to return.

title: UK signals ‘openness’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet programme
description: British PM Andy Burnham is in Berlin for talks focused primarily on security, including the launch of a new partnership aimed at hybrid threats.
content: The United Kingdom is “open” to Germany joining an international coalition to build the next generation of fighter jets, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced. Speaking in Berlin on Thursday, during his first visit to the German capital since taking office, Burnham said he “indicated” to Chancellor Friedrich Merz Britain’s “openness” to the country joining the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP). Initially a pact between the UK, Italy and Japan to build a sixth-generation fighter jet, GCAP welcomed Canada as an “observer nation” in July. Informally dubbed “Tempest”, the new jets will be equipped with technology including AI and next-generation sensors, as Western nations seek to maintain air superiority over threats from rival powers like Russia and China. Germany’s own FCAS fighter jet project with France collapsed earlier this year. Burnham travelled to Berlin on Thursday for talks with Merz focused primarily on security, including the launch of a new security partnership aimed at hybrid threats. The pair also ratified the UK-German Kensington Treaty, which was signed in July last year and commits the two nations to deeper cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and growth. “We are talking today about defence collaboration, and I’ve indicated to the chancellor, in our discussion prior to this ratification, our openness to Germany joining GCAP, the next generation of fighter aircraft,” Burnham said, speaking alongside Merz at the Chancellery. “And that is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our partners Italy and Japan, in relation to that as well.” There has been mounting speculation that the ⁠founding countries of the GCAP could open the door to Germany after the FCAS collapse. Germany is viewed by some defence experts as a suitable partner given its growing military budget and the ‌fact that ‌it already works on the Eurofighter Typhoon with the UK and Italy. From Britain’s point ‌of view, adding another country at a time when its military budget is under strain ⁠would help share the cost burden, but Japan may need convincing. Italy has also said in the ⁠past it would be open to new countries joining to help share the cost. In brief remarks to journalists, Burnham also stressed the importance of countering hybrid attacks, saying it was something both countries were “facing on a regular basis”. Last month, the British government summoned a senior Russian diplomat to protest against an “egregious and reckless attack” at Germany’s Leipzig airport, a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. A drone carrying explosives was found near Ukrainian cargo planes in August, but failed to explode and was subsequently defused. Investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby and a third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later. “It makes sense to face these threats together and to support each other in countering them, as well as countering interference in our democratic processes as well, and being stronger together when we face these threats,” Burnham said. Addressing the wider relationship with Germany and Europe, Burnham said he was “committed to securing deeper cooperation” with the EU at a summit with the bloc “towards the end of the year”. He said: “We’ve had an excellent discussion today, and we will look to see if we can turn the summit into a good outcome for the EU, but also for the UK as well.” Additional reporting by Reuters

title: 1 dead in Poland’s second school knife attack in 2 days, amid ‘copycat’ fears
description: Two others were injured in the incident at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials say.
content: A 15-year-old former pupil killed one employee and injured two others at a Polish primary school on Thursday wearing a helmet-mounted camera, the second school stabbing in two days, possibly in response to an internet challenge, authorities said. A 37-year-old woman who ‌worked as a caretaker had died in the latest attack, which took place at around 9am local time in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw, officials said. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at another school in Ostroleka, northeastern Poland, and police detained a 17-year-old in Sierpc in north-central Poland on suspicion of planning an attack. “We fear a grim copycat phenomenon,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk told an emergency meeting. “We are facing an extraordinary situation … for the first time, we ⁠are dealing with a killer who wore a helmet-mounted camera, intending to film the knife attack.” It was not clear whether the ‌attack was actually filmed. He ordered police to visit schools daily in an effort to prevent further violence. A police spokesperson said authorities had information that the incidents could be related to an internet challenge ‌and that this was being investigated. Tusk praised the heroism of two teachers at the ⁠school who were injured as ⁠they tried to stop the attacker. Head teacher Krzysztof Ochmanski said he had heard a scream and ran into the corridor. “He wounded me with the blade of ‌a rather long knife – he had three knives on him – and hit me with the handle,” he told the public broadcaster Polskie Radio RDC. “By then, I had managed ‌to restrain ‌him.” A Reuters reporter saw an air ambulance flying away from the school, where a small crowd had gathered. The father ‌of one child, waiting outside the school, said pupils had not yet been allowed to leave, but were safe. Footage on public ⁠news broadcaster TVP Info showed what appeared to be the attacker being handcuffed and put into a police van. Inspector Katarzyna Nowak, director ⁠of communications for national police, said serious offenders were becoming younger across Europe. “Over the past few months in Poland, we have seen arrests of teenagers who were preparing to carry out attacks … So, this is indeed a problem ‌we face, and one we must ‌acknowledge,” she told TVP Info. Interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said the 17-year-old detained in Sierpc had mentioned plans to do “something dangerous” on school grounds. “Data recovered from electronic devices revealed online searches regarding how to orchestrate such a violent event,” Kierwinski said. Police found two knives in his possession.

title: Can China match up with Meta’s Muse in race to harness AI agents?
description: Analysts say agent harnesses could shift more of AI sector’s value away from foundational models and towards software layer.
content: Meta Platforms’ breakout Muse personal AI agent is shining a spotlight on a new battleground in artificial intelligence – one in which China’s biggest internet companies are already jostling for position. Launched on September 8, Muse surpassed 2.5 million downloads in its first two weeks and topped free-app rankings on Apple and Google’s US app stores. Its popularity has drawn fresh attention to the emerging market for what are known as agent harnesses. Unlike chatbots, which merely respond to prompts, agent harnesses provide underlying AI models with persistent memory, tool access and the autonomy to execute more complex tasks. Meta says Muse operates across the web and connected services like email and calendars, and can help users fill out forms, make purchases and book travel while remembering their preferences. Industry analysts said agent harnesses could shift more of the AI sector’s value away from foundational models and towards the software layer. Analysts at financial research and brokerage firm Bernstein said in a recent report that the main prize was “context lock-in”: the more an agent learned about a user’s habits, history and workflows, the more useful – and harder to replace – it could become. That dynamic could favour Chinese internet giants Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding – the owner of the South China Morning Post – whose sprawling ecosystems encompassed messaging, payments, e-commerce, workplace software and cloud computing, the report said. Muse’s success had revived investor interest in the value of such integrated ecosystems, said Winnie Wu, head of Asia-Pacific equity strategy and co-head of China equity research at Bank of America. “With a chatbot, it doesn’t have a differentiation point,” Wu said. “It’s about whether the agent can get things done for you.” Local front-runners As the paradigm shifts, Chinese tech heavyweights are deploying their own agent strategies to capture market share. Tencent stood out on the consumer side, Bernstein said, with its WorkBuddy workplace agent having taken an early engagement lead among third-party productivity harnesses in China, ahead of rivals including ByteDance’s Trae and Alibaba’s QoderWork. The analysts said Tencent could take “a small leap of faith” towards building something similar to Muse by making its WeChat social media platform the front-end interface for the operation of its Xiaowei agent behind the scenes. Xiaowei, which entered beta testing in June, is designed to execute tasks through WeChat mini programs rather than simply answer questions. By leveraging native access to WeChat search, mini-programs and WeChat Pay, Xiaowei could turn Tencent’s ecosystem – which processes trillions of yuan in annual transactions – into a powerful data flywheel, the Bernstein report said. Deepening agent usage would lock users further into Tencent’s services while generating high-quality, real-world data to refine future AI models, it said. The Bernstein analysts said Alibaba was pursuing a more enterprise-focused strategy, integrating agents across QwenWork, DingTalk, Taobao and Alibaba Cloud. The company could use existing enterprise data and workflows to embed agents more deeply into corporate operations, they said, with greater adoption to drive demand for its Qwen model and cloud computing services. ByteDance could emerge as a contender through Feishu, its workplace collaboration platform. Bernstein said the company’s hyperscaler capacity could allow it to expand further into enterprise agents, but it had yet to demonstrate the same ecosystem position as Tencent in social communications or Alibaba in enterprise software. Competition is also emerging outside China’s internet giants, particularly in coding. Bernstein said DeepSeek Harness and Z.ai’s ZCode ranked eighth and eleventh respectively among the coding tools it tracked on OpenRouter by 30-day token usage, although global players such as Anthropic’s Claude Code remained well ahead. Manus, the Chinese-founded agent start-up that briefly became part of Meta before resuming independent operations, is also moving closer to the personal-agent model. Last week, it unveiled Manus 2.0, including a new agent harness called Cascade, and Cue, a dedicated personal-agent app. Analysts said the emerging competition suggested the AI race could increasingly move beyond model performance to models that know their users best. Hurdles in China However, Bank of America’s Wu cautioned that the Muse model might be harder to replicate in the Chinese market. She said China’s mobile internet was dominated by “guarded” ecosystems that could make it difficult for an agent to operate seamlessly across services. Tasks involving WeChat or Alipay, for example, might require access that an agent controlled by a rival platform could not easily obtain. Consumer behaviour posed another challenge. Chinese users had historically shown less willingness than their counterparts in the United States to pay recurring subscriptions for software, Wu said, raising questions about how personal agents would be monetised. There was also the cost of running them. Agents such as Muse could require substantially more computing power – a constraint faced by China – than conventional chatbots, Wu added.

title: CK Asset to demolish 3 blocks at starter homes project after steelwork scandal
description: Developer says rebuilding three of six blocks in Hong Kong is most time-saving solution, two years after substandard steelwork halted construction.
content: Three of the six residential buildings at CK Asset’s “starter homes” project in Hong Kong will be demolished and rebuilt in what the developer called the most “time-saving” solution, two years after a scandal over substandard steel reinforcement work halted construction. The Buildings Department said on Thursday that it had approved demolition plans for three blocks at the Anderson Road development in Kwun Tong, while remedial work was under way at the other three. Earlier investigations found significant discrepancies between steel reinforcement installed in parts of the six towers and the approved plans, including fewer reinforcing bars than required. Ten people were also arrested in connection with the project on suspicion of bribery and other offences. CK Asset said the remedial proposals it submitted to the department required investigation and verification, a process it described as “extremely time-consuming”. “Previously, the engineering consultant spent nearly two years conducting investigations for three of the six buildings and proposing remedial measures accepted by the Buildings Department,” a spokeswoman said. “Therefore, after evaluating the options based on efficiency and cost-effectiveness, we determined that demolishing and rebuilding the remaining three buildings is the most time-saving solution.” The developer named China Railway Construction Group as the new contractor. It also cited the department as saying there was no obvious structural danger at any of the buildings. The department confirmed that the developer planned to demolish and rebuild three buildings. “The Buildings Department has received and approved the relevant demolition plans, but the department has not yet received an application to commence the demolition works to date,” it said. It added that it had approved a remedial proposal submitted by the structural engineer for the other three buildings and lifted the stop-work order in May. It understood that remedial work had begun progressively since then. The development is a “starter home” project, for which the government invited tenders to help first-time flat buyers who are ineligible for subsidised housing sold under the Home Ownership Scheme. The project will provide about 2,930 flats, with at least 1,000 to be sold at 80 per cent of the market price to Hongkongers who have never owned residential property and meet income and asset limits. The Housing Bureau said it would keep in close contact with the department and follow the project’s progress closely. “We will continue to urge the developer to complete the relevant flats as soon as possible, provided that construction quality and safety are ensured,” it said. The bureau noted that the project was part of the city’s subsidised housing supply, while the overall forecast completion for subsidised sale flats between 2027-28 and 2031-32 was 72,700. “The progress of an individual project will not constitute a huge impact on the overall supply,” it said. CK Asset subsidiary Art Champion Investment won the bid with a land premium of HK$4.9 billion (US$625.7 million). The project has been embroiled in construction quality concerns since August 2024, when the department received a report alleging problems with steel reinforcement work. Construction at the site was halted in October that year. The city’s corruption watchdog said in May last year that it had arrested 10 suspects in connection with the project, over alleged bribery, conspiracy to defraud and use of false documents. Those arrested were an employee of the main contractor, five proprietors, operators or employees of subcontractors, and four site supervisors at an engineering consultancy. In August last year, the department initiated 205 prosecutions against registered general building contractors and related professionals. The project’s initial contractor, Aggressive Construction Engineering, lost its operating licence in 2023, leaving it unable to carry out building work. Superb Interior Contracting took over the project later that year.

title: Netflix K-drama Dead-End Job: Squid Game meets supernatural horror in uneven thrill ride
description: A man takes on a series of bizarre jobs to escape debt of his own making in this splashy, effects-heavy K-drama series.
content: Lead cast: Lee Jae-wook, Go Min-si, Kim Min-ha, Lee Hee-jun In Dead-End Job, Lee Jae-wook (Alchemy of Souls) stars as a desperate loser who takes a series of dangerous, increasingly bizarre part-time gigs to escape crippling debt. Netflix’s latest high-concept K-drama series blends humour, horror and social commentary into a kinetic, if tonally wayward, thrill ride with an intriguing supernatural twist. The first four episodes have just premiered at the Busan International Film Festival, ahead of its streaming debut later this month. Fans of Squid Game will immediately see the parallels between that epoch-defining series and Dead-End Job, a directorial debut from Kim Da-min, writer of 2024’s A Killer Paradox. In both shows, ordinary citizens at the end of their tether volunteer for get-rich-quick schemes with potentially lethal consequences. In Dead-End Job, Hyeok-jun (Lee) loses everything, including his mother’s life savings, to an online investment scam and is contemplating suicide when he stumbles upon the Spider Staffing Agency. Inside, the mysterious Mr S (Lee Hee-jun) proposes an unbelievable job opportunity – a one-night shift at a secluded convenience store that pays 50 times the going rate. With nothing left to lose, Hyeok-jun agrees. He soon finds himself saddled with a shifty-looking colleague (Choi Hyun-wook) and fending off swarms of giant moths, a grotesque insect woman and a giant rat-like demon – all to earn a pay cheque. After miraculously surviving unscathed and receiving a wad of cash for his efforts, the temptation to continue filling Spider’s vacancies proves impossible to resist. Hyeok-jun is soon approached by Yeon-joo (Go Min-si, Sweet Home), an accident investigator working for a labour institute. She claims that everyone who has passed through Spider’s doors is either missing or “develops a problem”. While she seems on the level, Hyeok-jun is not ready to give up his cash cow just yet. Because his pay doubles after every completed job, his second assignment – a deranged road trip with a blowhard manager (Yoon Kyung-ho) and a bizarre circus mime (Yoon Byung-hee) – will pay 100 times the usual wage. Hyeok-jun’s younger sister, Ji-yoon (Kim Min-ha, Pachinko), is also on his case. Understanding her brother’s situation only too well, she soon finds herself called upon to visit Spider Staffing Agency and enrol in a mind-bending part-time job of her own. While tearing tickets at a famously haunted cinema, she is plagued by images from her own troubled past and confronted with the truth: the world we know is only half of reality. On the other side is a dark, malevolent spirit realm, separated by a fragile barrier that these assignments help maintain … until they fail. There is no shortage of ambition in Dead-End Job, but there is a definite lack of focus. Each of the four episodes screened for Busan audiences is wildly different in tone, hitting familiar but eclectic touchpoints, making it tricky to get a handle on the bigger picture. Episode one taps into the age-old notion of staying overnight in a haunted house, popularised by Shirley Jackson’s 1959 novel The Haunting of Hill House and more recently by the hugely successful Five Nights at Freddy’s video game and film franchise. Episode two strikes a markedly different tone. Much of the oddball road trip is played for laughs, with a smattering of supernatural surrealism as Hyeok-jun’s clown-like companion slowly reveals his magical powers. The episode builds to a horrifying climax that should delight Stephen King fans with its reverent nods to both It and Carrie. Genki Kawamura’s 2025 Japanese horror film Exit 8, itself adapted from Kotake Create’s video game, appears to exert an influence on episode three, which sees Hyeok-jun attempt a deceptively complicated milk delivery run through a sinister block of flats that shifts, revolves and repeats in much the same way as the subway station in Exit 8. And so it goes on. Behind all the visual showboating and otherworldly mischief, however, the show builds on a foundation of pressing social concern. Hyeok-jun’s plight is entirely self-inflicted, due to his addiction to online stock trading, a widespread issue across South Korea that has seen many fall into crippling debt in recent years. Simultaneously, the narrative’s ethical stance – and Spider’s guiding principle – is that honest hard graft is what society needs to preserve its integrity and breed good moral fibre in younger generations. How Dead-End Job will succeed in striking an effective balance between its attention-grabbing thrills and grounded messaging remains to be seen, but based on what has been revealed so far in this splashy, effects-heavy adventure, Netflix might be taking the biggest gamble of all. Dead-End Job starts streaming on Netflix on October 30.

title: South Korea test-flies its first home-grown hypersonic weapon
description: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung hails the test as a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities.
content: South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities. There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it was a major step in strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place. The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and manoeuvred both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean peninsula theatre of operations”. Lee stressed that South Korea “must secure our security through our own strength”, and also inspected the country’s most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North. Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in landmine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South’s military and the US-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology. North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong-un expands his military nuclear programme while taking an increasingly hard line towards Seoul. Kim has so far rebuffed US President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearisation as a precondition for talks. The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favours engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric towards the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts. Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea’s conventional defence capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim. In its latest weapons test on October 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000km (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone. South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700km, while Japan’s defence ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680km. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, claimed the differing flight estimates by the two US allies showed they were incapable of properly tracking such a missile during its flight and would therefore not be able to intercept it.

title: Is the Philippines using new anti-spying laws to silence critics?
description: Proposed updates to a 1941 law could impose life sentences for broad offences, raising fears the law could be weaponised against dissent.
content: A Philippine bill expanding the country’s espionage law to cover peacetime activities is raising concerns among journalists and legal experts, who warn that its broad provisions could stifle free expression and restrict public scrutiny of national issues. The House of Representatives approved the measure on September 17, paving the way for a broader definition of espionage than under the current law, which dates to 1941 and focuses on wartime spying. The Senate is considering a similar version. Senator Panfilo Lacson, a former military official before becoming the national police chief who also crafted the controversial 2020 Anti-Terrorism Act, has defended the need for the new law, arguing that current statutes did not address modern peacetime espionage. Lacson said in an explanatory note for his Senate Bill No 33, which will form the basis of the Senate version, that authorities arrested five people for spying last year, including cases involving aerial drones photographing military facilities on Palawan island, as well as the detention of a Chinese national near the Commission on Elections office in April 2025, allegedly with a device used to intercept mobile phone traffic and track location data. The proposed law would also sharply increase penalties. Unlawfully photographing or sketching defence installations currently carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison or a fine of up to 2,000 pesos (US$32). The proposed amendments would raise the penalty to life imprisonment without parole or good conduct allowances, alongside fines ranging from 10 million to 20 million pesos (US$159,000 to US$317,000). But critics say the bill does more than merely update the law to deal with modern forms of espionage, potentially giving the state powers that could be weaponised against legitimate dissent and public scrutiny. Renee Co, representing the Kabataan (Youth) Party List, said the bill would authorise the Anti-Money Laundering Council to not only investigate and freeze the assets of suspected spies, but to forfeit them outright. Under the current Anti-Terrorism Act, the council can temporarily freeze assets but requires a court order to seize them following forfeiture proceedings. However, both the House and Senate draft versions of the espionage bill would grant the council direct forfeiture powers. Sarah Elago of the Gabriela Women’s Party warned the measure opened the door to suppressing legitimate criticism. “The bill also expands the definition of ‘critical infrastructure’ to shield private corporate interests by including telecommunications, energy and food security under the umbrella of espionage protection,” Elago said, adding that it “effectively bans the public from scrutinising the industries that most affect their lives”. Antonio Tinio, deputy minority floor leader representing the ACT Teachers Party List, said that while efforts to introduce amendments were welcome, “our essential critique is that some definitions and the scope of coverage remain so overly broad … that this can be used as an instrument to suppress the fundamental rights of our citizens to free expression – the right to dissent – in the name of national security”. ‘Chilling effect’ on journalism John Ted Cordero, president of the Economic Journalists Association of the Philippines and a reporter for GMA News, said that he personally believed “the proposed law would have a chilling effect on economic journalists’ coverage amid fear of being jailed and slapped with huge fines”. Cordero highlighted provisions in the Senate version that classified harming “critical infrastructure”, which includes banking and finance, as spying. “The criminalisation of ‘unauthorised’ possession of classified or sensitive state financial information – such as leaked loan agreements, internal fiscal or debt restructuring documents and anti-money-laundering alerts – could negatively affect how journalists verify, handle and publish such information,” Cordero said. He warned that reporters could face espionage charges simply for possessing physical or digital copies of sensitive financial documents, regardless of whether the intent was for public interest reporting. “News outlets might ultimately refuse to run critical scoops based on leaked documents about public debt [or] sovereign risks out of fear,” he added. “This could turn reports on the financial situation of the country into passive amplifiers of state press releases … [and] damage market transparency as investors rely on the free press to gauge the true fiscal health of the country.” Vergel Santos, a retired publisher of BusinessWorld and free press advocate, said he felt there were still enough legal protections to guarantee freedom of the media in the Philippines. “Of course, being oriented to all sorts of bogeymen, the likes of Lacson are inclined towards ultraconservative measures that can lead to repression – that’s why he always wants stiffer terms and penalties,” Santos said. “The draconian Terrorism Act is an example.” Barry Gutierrez, a criminal law professor at the University of the Philippines, distinguished between the two versions, saying he was less concerned about the House bill, viewing it mainly as an update to the 1941 law. Most provisions in both versions simply restated existing legal frameworks, he said, such as the extraterritorial application of the law under the Revised Penal Code and that disloyalty provisions were strictly confined to public employees. But Gutierrez warned that the Senate draft contained “extremely problematic” definitions, highlighting its expanded use of “disloyal acts or words” to apply to “any person”, not simply public employees. “This is therefore a free speech regulation that must be subjected to the highest degree of scrutiny, as it potentially exposes any person who may express criticism of the government to liability for ‘disloyalty’,” he said. The definition of “interference” similarly covered “any person”, Gutierrez said, and was broad enough to penalise ordinary political commentary. The Senate version “has the clear potential for overbroad application and abuse of the law to clamp down on critics and the media”, he added.

title: WTO nearly doubles trade volume forecast as AI surge counters Middle East disruptions
description: Merchandise trade shows ‘surprising’ resilience amid Middle East conflict, economist says, as same shock dents services forecast.
content: The World Trade Organization (WTO) has nearly doubled its forecast for merchandise trade volume growth this year amid a stronger than anticipated surge in artificial intelligence-related capital investment. The group raised the forecast to 3.9 per cent from an earlier prediction of 1.9 per cent, it said in its global trade outlook report published on Thursday. “It is somewhat surprising that [merchandise trade growth] is so resilient to all the shocks that have been going on,” said WTO chief economist Robert Staiger. Besides the accelerating AI investment boom, the expansion was also supported by trade resilience to the Middle East conflict as supplies were diverted and new suppliers stepped in to help the global economy mitigate downward pressure on trade, he said. Meanwhile, the WTO lowered its forecast for growth in services trade volume this year to 3.3 per cent from 4.8 per cent, citing depressed travel and tourism, as well as higher global fuel input costs stemming from the conflict. In 2027, trade volumes in merchandise and services were expected to grow by 4.1 per cent and 6.4 per cent, respectively, pending “a timely resolution” of the war, according to the report. While making up less than 15 per cent of world trade, AI-enabling goods accounted for 47 per cent of the growth in global merchandise trade, in value terms, in the first half of 2026, offsetting declining shipments of oil, natural gas and fertiliser, the report said. The AI-enabling category includes a broad range of items, from raw materials that go into circuit boards to finished chips and systems, as well as data-centre needs such as power and cooling equipment. Export of such goods is dominated by East Asia excluding China, which represented 40.4 per cent of total export value in 2025, followed by Southeast Asia at 23.2 per cent. China, North America and Europe accounted for 13.6 per cent, 11.5 per cent and 10.6 per cent, respectively. East Asia excluding China also held the top spot for imports of AI-enabling goods at 27.4 per cent, with China and North America in second and third place with 20.1 per cent and 19.9 per cent, respectively. Europe’s share was 12.3 per cent. China’s share of AI-enabling goods imports fell between 2015 and 2025 as the country’s domestic production of the relevant items grew, according to the report. With the top 10 economies representing roughly 80 per cent of all trade in AI-enabling goods, the resilience of the category’s growth was an open question, according to Staiger, though he added that the trade showed no signs of slowing down yet. “I think there is a valid concern, or if not concern, at least a thought that one would want to make sure that the AI boom is not going to drive other concerns under the rug, so to speak,” he said. “And given that it is narrowly defined in terms of both its sector and also regions, it does tend to mask the headline numbers … to mask the very real disruptions that are occurring in certain regions.” The report also identified other risks, including the accelerating US-China decoupling, which the WTO said had become the main driver of bloc divergence, while the broader pattern of bloc-based fragmentation had not continued to intensify. Amid growing trade frictions among major economies, Staiger also made a case for the WTO’s continued utility and the resilience of the rule-based system. He cited MIT economist Lester Thurow’s famous declaration in Davos in 1989 that The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade – the WTO’s predecessor – was dead. The pronouncement was contradicted several years later when the WTO was founded, Staiger said. “There was often a view that the rules-based system was on its last leg, and yet it continues,” he said. “Those basic principles do have an economic line that is, in some sense, timeless, to help economies solve problems that they have in the international arena on trade policy.”

title: Did a US warship lose power while chasing a Chinese destroyer in the South China Sea?
description: PLA Navy officer tells state media the unnamed foreign ship’s ‘radar stopped transmitting and its navigation lights went dark’.
content: The Chinese navy says it had a rare South China Sea encounter involving a foreign warship that lost power, propulsion and radar while following a People’s Liberation Army destroyer, an account that resembles incidents this year involving US Navy destroyers in the region. The incident occurred when a foreign vessel conducted aggressive close shadowing of the PLA Navy Type 055 destroyer Zunyi during routine training by the Chinese vessel, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Wednesday. The CCTV report did not identify the foreign warship or specify the date or exact location of the encounter. Zhang Jun, an officer aboard the Zunyi, told the broadcaster that his ship had accelerated in high-speed cruise to force the foreign follower to speed up and keep pace. “During the stand-off, [suddenly its] power and electricity all went out. Its radar stopped transmitting and its navigation lights went dark. That lasted for nearly half an hour,” Zhang said, adding that the Zunyi continued operating normally. The description bears some similarities to two US Navy destroyer accidents this year, although there is no evidence the foreign vessel involved with the Zunyi was American or that the US destroyer incidents were linked to Chinese naval activity. The USS Higgins, an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer homeported in Yokosuka, Japan, had an electrical-system failure on April 28. The outage reportedly lasted “several hours”, although the US Navy did not say where the incident occurred or what mission the ship was conducting. A statement from the US Seventh Fleet said the Higgins, which was commissioned in 1999, “experienced a loss of power throughout the ship” before it subsequently restored its power and propulsion systems. “Initial reports indicate an electrical malfunction, which may have produced sparking or smoke that ceased once power was removed,” the US Navy said. In a separate incident on July 24, the USS Benfold, another ageing Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, “reported an engineering casualty involving its generators, causing a loss of power” while transiting the South China Sea, according to the US Navy. It was travelling with the USS George Washington carrier strike group towards the Middle East. The 30-year-old ship was left stranded without normal electrical power for four days before being towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for repairs. Official US statements have not linked either vessel’s electrical failure to any mission or encounter involving Chinese military ships. There has been no statement from either the Pentagon or the US Navy stating that Chinese naval forces were present during those incidents. The 13,000-tonne Zunyi is one of the PLA Navy’s 10 most advanced Type 055 destroyers in service. Since entering service in 2023, it has served as a major command, air-defence and information node and has been integrated within Chinese aircraft carrier groups, according to the CCTV report. The broadcaster said the ship had engaged in “many close encounters” with foreign warships and aircraft. Zhang expressed confidence in his ship’s readiness when facing such tense circumstances. “Why would I be nervous ... As long as they are within my missile range, I am sure I can destroy them,” he told CCTV.

title: Hong Kong’s Coleman Wong looking ahead to rest, meals with friends after ‘hectic’ 2 weeks
description: Asian Games champion returns home after playing in Hangzhou, Nagoya and Shanghai, and is likely to finish his season playing in Asia events.
content: Tennis star Coleman Wong Chak-lam said he longed for nothing more than some decent rest at home and eating with friends after he returned to Hong Kong from a hectic two weeks involving three different cities. Off the back of a quarter-final appearance at the Hangzhou Open, Wong won five matches on the trot to win Asian Games gold in Nagoya, before breaking into the Shanghai Masters main draw following back-to-back wins in the qualifiers. Following his loss to Quentin Halys of France in straight sets in the first round, Wong returned home on Thursday with the gold medal he won in Japan still around his neck. “I have yet to celebrate my Asian Games victory; I flew to Shanghai the day after the final, and then started playing the next day,” he said. “I really need some rest, there aren’t any plans yet. “I had been playing for two weeks nonstop. It was really hectic, I have no idea about my training plans yet but I think I need to rest for maybe 10 days first.” From winning his first ATP Challenger title in Jiujiang in May to overcoming then world No 12 Jiri Lehecka – the highest-ranked opponent in his career – at the Los Cabos Open in July, the Hongkonger broke into the world’s top 100 and was ranked as high as No 92 in August. Becoming the city’s first man to win a singles title at the continental Games, which has earned him a place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, had made this the best year of his career so far, Wong said, but he added that he was taking nothing for granted. “I grew up always wanting to participate in the Asian Games and the Olympic Games, so of course, I am very happy with my victory,” he said. “But I have to keep practising; it’s still a long road ahead but this medal was also an affirmation [of my hard work]. “I have to keep my head down and carry on. There is still a lot to learn, there are still many skills I have yet to master. I feel like I can still improve, but the results showed that I am heading in the right direction. “I will continue to believe in myself and my team. Be it improving my serve power or my stamina, I need to work on all fronts to close the gap with the world class players.” After cracking into the top 100, Wong said his next target was “naturally the top 50 in the world”. “It almost felt crazy to be inside the top 100, but I’ll keep pushing myself because it’s never enough,” he said. “I want to do better on the tour, and hopefully I can get some great results at the Olympic Games two years later.” With little more than two months left in the current season, Wong hinted that he expected to base his remaining season in and around the region, instead of travelling long hours to Europe. This month there are ATP Challenger Tour events in Guangzhou, followed by those in Seoul or Ningbo. There are also stops in Taipei, Matsuyama, Kobe and Yokohama in Japan in November. The 22-year-old also revealed he expected to base his off-season training in Mallorca, in a similar fashion to the one he had in Norway – with local star Casper Ruud – at the turn of the year. “My coach [James Allemby] has been planning for that already, and I was told quite some top players will be heading to Spain this year for pre-season – among them would be Alexander Zverev – so I think that’s where I am going to be before the new season starts.”

title: Opinion | It’s time for China to offer more than statements on Hormuz
description: Beijing does not need to replace Washington as a security guarantor, but it can use its unique access to resolve the crisis.
content: Two summits in five months between US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping have produced shared language but not an open Strait of Hormuz. After the May meeting in Beijing, there was little sign the two sides agreed on how to end the war. Xi’s visit to Washington yielded no breakthrough on Iran, though Xi backed a return to the interim US-Iran agreement. Last week, Trump rejected a truce proposal from Iran and said he was considering resuming US bombing of Iran after the midterm elections next month. The one line the US and Chinese summit readouts shared – that “no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways” – is a principle, not a procedure. That is the problem in a nutshell. Seven months into the war that began on February 28, China’s diplomacy has been rich in principles and thin on procedures. Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Iranian counterpart Seyyed Abbas Araghchi on September 16 that the region’s security architecture was imperfect and needed reform and strengthening. That is the right diagnosis. Beijing does not need to replace Washington as the Gulf’s security guarantor. However, it does need to show that its access can produce something more durable than another call for restraint. China’s stake in the region is real and goes beyond Iran. It imported about half its crude oil and almost a third of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Middle East in 2025, according to Columbia University’s Centre on Global Energy Policy. Beijing has also absorbed much of the energy shock, cutting crude imports from 11.7 million barrels a day in February to less than 9 million by late May, accounting for about 74 per cent of the decline in global crude imports. The more difficult question is leverage. Gulf governments have been under direct fire, with the UAE alone reporting being targeted by at least 2,800 Iranian missiles and drones between February 28 and the April ceasefire. They will want to know whether Beijing is prepared to use its standing with Tehran. Analysts have noted that Wang has stopped short of pressing Iran and offered no concrete mediation plan. That does not mean Beijing should coerce Tehran. It means China should say what it will actually do: put proposals on the table, name a venue and be clear about what it will ask of Iran as well as of the United States. Credibility with Gulf countries has to be built on specifics. The 2023 agreement between Saudi Arabia and Iran shows what is missing. China helped broker the deal in a genuine act of convening power. However, the International Crisis Group found that progress in restoring relations had plateaued after the initial rush of reopened embassies and visits by senior officials. Normalisation is not crisis management. A reopened embassy does little when a commercial vessel is attacked and there is no agreed channel for the parties to talk. China could lend its support to a standing Gulf crisis management mechanism, one with a deliberately modest mandate that is built alongside Iran and the Gulf states. It could cover direct lines of communication, a shared procedure for reporting maritime incidents, emergency consultations when tensions spike and agreed protocols for protecting civilian shipping and critical infrastructure. The mechanism would not settle political disputes or replace security partnerships. Rather, its purpose would be to keep miscalculations at sea from becoming a wider war. The 1972 US-Soviet Incidents at Sea agreement did not end their Cold War rivalry, but it made collisions less likely to spiral out of control. Building blocks for the mechanism already exist. In the first week after the US and Israel attacked Iran, China held talks with Tehran so crude oil and LNG from Qatar could safely pass through the strait. Oman has acted as an intermediary among Iran, the US and other Gulf states, as has Qatar. Pakistan has put itself forward as a mediator and co-authored a five-point plan with China in March. Gulf states could still reject the mechanism, and their reasons should be respected. There is a lack of consensus as the war has widened the gap between Saudi Arabia – which has taken a more accommodating approach towards Iran – and the UAE, which is more hawkish and aligned with the US. Any mechanism must be regionally owned and encompass functions every participant can accept. There is logic behind China’s reticence to directly involve itself. Military entanglement in the Gulf could be costly and hard to end. However, if its partners conclude that its influence works for trade and investment but not in a crisis, China’s economic weight will not turn into political confidence. The test is not whether China can replace the US in the Gulf. It is whether its influence can keep any miscalculation from spilling over into a wider war.

title: Why the traditional Chinese practice of nominal age makes people up to 2 years older
description: Under xu sui, babies are born at age one, a relic of ancient China lacking a numerical zero until Indian monks introduced it 1,000 years ago.
content: Age calculation in China is probably one of the most confusing aspects of Chinese culture, even for Chinese people themselves, because two systems are used. One system is the international standard: a person’s age is calculated from their date of birth. The other, the traditional nominal-age system, or xu sui, adds a year at the start of each lunisolar year. Under the xu sui system, a person’s nominal age can be up to two years greater than their actual age. The system is more commonly used in rural China and among older generations. As a result, misunderstandings about age sometimes arise in China. One netizen said that a friend who was a paediatrician once complained that a child’s grandmother said the child was two, when in fact the child was only five months old – a misunderstanding that nearly led to a misdiagnosis. Under the xu sui system, a person is considered one year old at birth. One explanation often cited is that China did not have the number zero until an Indian monk introduced it during the Tang dynasty (618–907). Meanwhile, China had begun calculating people’s ages before Qin Shi Huang unified the country in 221 BC, in order to assess their eligibility for taxes and corvée labour. Although xu sui adds a year to everyone’s age at the same time, the date on which ages increased varied across different dynasties. For example, during the Qin and Han dynasties (221 BC–220), ages increased at the time of the official household registration, which took place in August. During the Tang dynasty, the date for the annual age increase was moved to the first month of the lunisolar calendar, laying the foundation for today’s practice of adding a year on lunisolar New Year’s Day. One piece of evidence that ancient Chinese people calculated age according to the lunisolar year is the literati practice of “writing on New Year’s Day”. On that day, men of letters would write a poem or create a painting with auspicious meanings to pray for good fortune in the coming year. Some literati, including Zhang Yu of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) and the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) poets Wang Yue and Wang Shizhen, wrote about their ages increasing on New Year’s Day. It is said that before the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) issued the country’s first Household Registration Law in 1911, shortly before its collapse, official records listed only people’s birth years – not their birth months or dates. In today’s China, official age is calculated from a person’s birthday, in line with the international standard. Younger generations are also increasingly abandoning the xu sui system so they do not feel quite so “ancient.”

title: At least 33 dead in Russian bomb blast in east Ukraine stronghold
description: Authorities describe it as a targeted strike on civilians in the city of Kramatorsk.
content: A ⁠Russian bomb attack on ⁠the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk ⁠killed at least 33 people, authorities said on Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow. Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, ‌which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelensky described it as a bus stop. Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. “For them [the ⁠Russians], a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill ‌as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app. There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies ‌targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets ⁠during its full-scale invasion ⁠that began in February 2022. Moscow’s forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk ‌and other cities in Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region. Russia has demanded that ‌Ukraine ‌cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, ‌which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow’s battlefield gains in the region has significantly ⁠slowed this year. Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key ⁠fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying “we have no right to risk” citizens’ lives. Thursday’s attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air ‌attack across Ukraine, primarily ‌targeting the country’s power grid. Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defences.

title: How expanded Japan-US military exercises could complicate PLA planning over Taiwan
description: This year’s Keen Sword exercise will feature US and Japanese forces deploying mobile missile systems to Yonaguni Island near Taiwan.
content: Japan and the United States will rehearse moving anti-ship missiles, air defences and communications networks onto islands near Taiwan this month in an expanded military exercise that analysts say could complicate Beijing’s planning for a Taiwan or East China Sea conflict. Keen Sword 27, which runs from October 19 to 29, will involve about 45,000 Japanese personnel, 6,100 vehicles, 40 ships and 260 aircraft, up from about 33,000 personnel, 30 ships and 250 aircraft in 2024. About 12,000 US troops are reportedly expected to take part. France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines, which were observers in 2024, are listed as participants this year alongside Australia and Canada. Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, said Japan and the US were “building out their ‘wall’ strategy in the East China Sea”. He said that meant reinforcing and “fortifying” Japan’s southwest islands and rapidly moving forces and anti-ship weapons there to hinder the movement of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) through nearby straits during a Taiwan contingency. “The operational problem Keen Sword is built around is clearly the one the PLA poses,” said Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute. He said that meant “holding the southwest islands, defending them against missile and air attack” and keeping Chinese surface ships at risk along the first island chain. Japan does not present Keen Sword as preparation for war with China; its Joint Staff says the exercise trains responses to “various contingencies”. Tokyo’s latest defence white paper, however, describes China’s military activities as its “greatest strategic challenge”.
