The exercise’s clearest link to a potential Taiwan contingency is the activity planned for Yonaguni Island, just over 100km (62 miles) from Taiwan. Japan will temporarily deploy Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles and Type 03 medium-range air-defence systems, while the US Marine Corps will bring its Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (Nmesis) anti-ship missile platform and its Marine Air Defence Integrated System (Madis). They will move equipment through Yonaguni Airport and Kubura fishing port. Communications training will connect Yonaguni with Ishigaki and Miyako islands. Murano described the Type 88 deployment alongside Nmesis as “something like a test of a Japanese version of EABO”, referring to the US Marine Corps’ concept of Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations – operating mobile forces from dispersed temporary bases in contested maritime areas. In a conflict, Murano said, Nmesis deployed on Yonaguni could cover waters between the Japanese island and Taiwan, as well as areas to Taiwan’s north and east, including approaches the PLA Navy could use to operate east of Taiwan or enforce a blockade. Even then, the Taiwan Strait itself would remain “largely out of range”, with Nmesis at most able to reach its northern entrance, he added. Murano noted that to engage ships beyond the horizon, Nmesis would rely on targeting data from other sensors and platforms. Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said the significance of the Yonaguni deployment lay less in exactly which waters the missiles could cover than in showing that US anti-ship capabilities could be “rapidly deployed to an island close to Taiwan”. Tokyo has said it has no current plan to permanently station anti-ship missiles on Yonaguni. Matsuoka said that made the temporary deployment significant as a test of whether such systems could be moved there quickly during a crisis. She described the drills as both an “operational rehearsal” and a “political signal”, stressing the “important distinction” between testing an option and committing to it. Repeated rehearsals, however, could “lower the practical and political barriers” to deploying the systems in a future crisis, she added. Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, was more sceptical of the deployments’ military weight. Given China’s growing missile and naval capabilities, he said, such Japanese and US military assets were “likely irrelevant in halting a Chinese military operation”, but could still affect Beijing’s calculations by raising the risk of drawing Japanese and US troops into any such operation. The wider international participation in Keen Sword could further complicate Beijing’s calculations. Hughes said the Philippines’ involvement was particularly significant, as it suggested Japan and the US were extending their “wall strategy” farther south along the first island chain. Maslow said the wider participation was evidence of an Indo-Pacific security architecture that had “moved beyond symbolism”. Matsuoka noted that repeated participation in exercises such as Keen Sword could build familiarity among the forces involved without obliging their governments to intervene over Taiwan. For Beijing, she added, it could reinforce perceptions that “a wider group of states is becoming integrated” into a US-Japan-centred regional security network. Beyond the widening foreign participation, Keen Sword 27 will also be the first iteration of the exercise since Japan established its permanent Joint Operations Command in March last year. The programme has expanded from 10 training areas in 2024 to 15 this year, including separate cyber, information, space, electromagnetic and distributed-operations components. Murano said closer coordination between the new command and US forces was likely to concern the PLA because it could allow Japanese and US anti-ship and air-defence capabilities to be employed together “from early in a crisis”. A distributed posture also meant the PLA “cannot simply concentrate on Taiwan”, he said, but would have to “find, track and suppress many small, mobile targets”, diverting surveillance assets and munitions while stretching its timeline. However, the measures designed to complicate PLA planning could also deepen strategic mistrust. Matsuoka warned they could be interpreted in Beijing as preparations for conflict, feeding a cycle of mainland Chinese countermeasures and Japanese and US responses. Maslow argued that this cycle could also make repeated military deployments to Japan’s southwest islands increasingly routine, embedding them further in Tokyo’s regional contingency planning. With any further deployments in the area, he said, “security tensions with China are bound to intensify”. Hughes said that despite concerns in Tokyo over Washington’s security commitments under US President Donald Trump, the military side of the alliance told a different story. “The substance of US-Japan alliance planning and interoperability is only further tightening and integrating,” he said.

title: Haze not ‘a threat’ to Singapore Formula 1 race, but entertainment activities may be curbed
description: Transboundary haze from Indonesian fires has pushed city state’s air quality to unhealthy levels, but track activity will not be affected.
content: Motorsport’s governing body said transboundary haze from Indonesian fires, which pushed air pollution in Singapore into unhealthy levels on Thursday, did not “represent a threat” to this weekend’s Formula 1 race in the city state. Singapore’s air quality again crossed the threshold, making it one of the most polluted cities globally, according to the Swiss-based air monitor IQAir. “Air quality levels are being monitored by the relevant local authorities, and appropriate contingency measures are in place should conditions worsen,” the FIA said in a statement. If the haze worsened “and depending on the pollution level, there may be some restrictions on outdoor activity focusing mainly on entertainment activities rather than the Paddock environment and the circuit”, the FIA said late on Wednesday. But “based on the latest information available, air quality and haze are not forecast to represent a threat to track activity or the conduct of the event”, it said. Singapore Grand Prix organisers too said they were unconcerned about the haze, despite IQAir’s website showing the nation-state as the world’s third-most-polluted major city after Kuala Lumpur and Kinshasa, with an air quality index (AQI) reading of 174. The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks. Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous. Singapore’s National Environment Agency data showed all five regions in the city state recorded “unhealthy” levels of air pollution. Singapore and Malaysia have been surrounded by a milky haze for more than a month as smoke drifted across from uncontrolled fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands. The possibility of haze is just one of the “many potential issues” that are covered in the overall contingency plan for the race, Singapore GP said in a statement. An F1 spokesperson said: “There is absolutely no risk to the event and the conditions where the event is taking place are not at any level of concern.” However, the FIA’s F1 race director Rui Marques issued a heat hazard warning on Thursday, saying that both Saturday’s sprint and Sunday’s race would be run at times in a heat index greater than 31 degrees Celsius (87.8 degrees Fahrenheit). Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled to the Singapore GP from Malaysia after retiring from Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang circuit, said: “I ‌don’t feel like it’s that extreme ‌yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.” Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton said he had “much bigger issues to focus on. So I haven’t noticed anything while I’m outside, apart from the fact that we struggled to land because of smog”. “The fact is we’re all here.” On the track, defending Singapore champion George Russell’s title challenge is hanging by a thread ⁠after his retirement in Malaysia handed Mercedes ⁠teammate Kimi Antonelli firm control of the championship battle. The Marina ⁠Bay Street Circuit has a history of delivering drama under the lights, and Russell desperately needs some luck to go his way after a power unit failure while running third at Sepang allowed Antonelli to stretch his advantage to 84 points. Russell had arrived in Malaysia buoyed by a dominant victory in Azerbaijan and would have hoped to reinforce his title credentials before his car failed ‌with five laps remaining. With little time to rest as Formula 1 heads into the final leg of its triple-header on the streets of Singapore, Russell faces a very different challenge as he looks to keep his slim title hopes alive. The Briton won last year’s race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit but is set to start from the back of the grid on Sunday after Mercedes confirmed he had no engines left in his season’s allocation of four. Russell will need a new engine for the sprint weekend and had hoped to take the penalty at ⁠the US Grand Prix in Austin, where overtaking is easier than the tight and slow Singapore track where 11 of the 16 races have been won from ‌pole. The 4.927km-long Singapore circuit features 19 corners with walls so close they punish even the smallest errors while heat and humidity make it one of the season’s most physically demanding races. Antonelli’s objective is far simpler. The Italian finished a distant fifth last year – more than half a minute behind Russell – but he does not need a victory. As the season draws ‌to a ‌close, all he needs to do is keep Russell behind him and avoid handing momentum back to his teammate.

title: Amid battle for AI edge, Hong Kong presses HSBC over Singapore hub decision: sources
description: HKMA raises questions over bank’s decision to establish an AI centre in Singapore despite Hong Kong being its largest market, sources say.
content: As Hong Kong and Singapore compete for leadership in businesses ranging from foreign exchange trading to wealth management, the battleground has extended to artificial intelligence, with both cities vying to attract investment from HSBC Holdings and other major corporations, according to industry players. The issue came into focus after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) questioned HSBC about its decision to set up an AI centre in Singapore, despite Hong Kong being its single largest market, a source familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post. HSBC announced in late July that it would establish an AI centre in Singapore by the end of the year and hire 100 AI specialists there. The announcement came just a few days after the bank agreed to sell its Singapore life and health insurance business to Germany’s Allianz for S$2.7 billion (US$2.1 billion). The source said the HKMA had been in discussions with HSBC since the announcement. An HSBC spokesman declined to comment. The issue gained additional relevance after Hong Kong unveiled its five-year development plan last month, identifying AI investment and development as a priority. “This appears to be classic competitive regulatory signalling in the Hong Kong-Singapore rivalry,” said Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary ­president of the Institute of Securities Dealers. By raising the issue with HSBC, the HKMA was sending a signal to major banks and corporations that Hong Kong should be given priority when decisions were made on AI investments, Chan said. “Banks with significant Hong Kong operations should give serious consideration to developing or placing high-value functions, including AI development, in the city rather than defaulting to Singapore or other centres,” Chan said. Kenny Ng Lai-yin, a strategist at Everbright Securities International, said Hong Kong could not solely rely on government initiatives if it wanted to become an AI hub, and instead would need substantial investment from large corporations. It was natural for the HKMA to check on HSBC’s decision to base an AI centre in Singapore because it would affect where AI talent, computing resources and investment capacity were ultimately concentrated, Ng said. To compete with Singapore, Hong Kong should actively seek to attract banks’ AI investments, research teams and high-value technology functions, said Stephen Law Cheuk-kin, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants (HKICPA) and a private-equity investor. “The policy objective should be to make Hong Kong a place where banks choose to develop and deploy AI because the ecosystem is strong and commercially attractive. Hong Kong is already doing all this,” Law said. HSBC’s decision did not mean the bank was reducing its commitment to Hong Kong, Law added. HSBC group CEO Georges Elhedery said in a post-results briefing in August that Hong Kong remained an important centre for the bank’s AI investment. “In Hong Kong, we already have a strong team of 150 AI specialists, and we continue to grow the team,” Elhedery said. “We are progressing at pace and building an AI research institute in Hong Kong focused on research, capability building, ecosystem development and the commercialisation of innovative technologies. We will share more in the coming months.” Tommy Ong, managing director of financial advisory firm T.O. & Associates Consultancy, said it was reasonable for Hong Kong to seek an appropriate level of AI investment from institutions that generated most of their revenue in the city.

title: Washington, Brussels forge ‘multilateral coalition’ against China’s industrial surge
description: As US rallies most G20 members to pressure Beijing on overcapacity, experts warn China could retaliate.
content: Most G20 members, including the European Union, signed a US-led joint statement calling for action to eliminate industrial overcapacity, a move experts say reflects a coordinated effort by Washington and Brussels to assemble a “multilateral coalition” to pressure Beijing amid growing trade imbalances. In the statement, issued by the Office of the United States Trade Representative on Wednesday, the US and 14 other economies agreed to “take effective actions” to address structural excess capacity in several sectors such as electric vehicles, batteries, semiconductors and solar panels. Signatories included the trade ministers of Argentina, Australia, Canada, the EU, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Poland, Turkey, the UK and US. China, Brazil, Indonesia, Russia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa – also G20 members – were not signatories. The statement, which did not name China, also urged countries to end “non-market” policies and practices that distort markets and perpetuate excess production. The agreement was reached on the sidelines of an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Trade Committee meeting. It came just days after G20 trade ministers failed to reach consensus on the issue at a meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Following the G20 meeting, China’s commerce ministry said most participating economies held differing views on excess industrial capacity, while Washington said only a “handful” of ministers had opposed efforts to establish a pathway for cooperation. The joint statement meant the US wanted to “use the overcapacity narrative to assemble a multilateral coalition to put pressure on China”, said Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University. While this strategy had been pursued since the Biden administration, the US was amplifying it further now, he added. At the same time, Europe wanted to use the statement to demonstrate a willingness to align with the US in pressuring China, Zhao said. “While US-Europe relations face significant challenges and their shared policy objectives are limited, pressuring China over capacity issues is one of the few areas where their goals genuinely overlap.” Similarly, Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s School of International Studies, said the statement marked “a clear attempt by the EU to capitalise on Washington’s current momentum to further suppress China”. Zhu said the recent joint appeal by the leaders of France and Germany for tougher measures to address market distortions “aimed to further curb China’s production capacity”. He added that China should not assume it was just a “formal threat” from Europe, as it could turn into new trade measures. In recent years, the US and the EU have objected to what they see as excess supply of some Chinese exports. In response, they have imposed tariffs on products ranging from solar panels to electric vehicles. Beijing has consistently pushed back on the claims. In response to the French and German appeal, a commentary published by state broadcaster CCTV on Wednesday said that if the EU pressed ahead with discriminatory measures, China would “respond firmly” to defend the legitimate interests of its industries. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic was in Beijing on Thursday for two days of talks with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, seeking progress on efforts to narrow the growing trade deficit with China before a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels next week. Zhao expected China to continue talks with the US and the EU, but warned Beijing could hit back if Washington and Brussels use the issue to impose “discriminatory” trade measures on China.

title: China’s central bank slams currency manipulation claims as EU trade talks begin
description: The bank said China did not need to devalue the yuan to boost exports – and those accusing it of doing so were ‘dodging accountability’.
content: China’s central bank published a position paper on the yuan exchange rate on Thursday, arguing that China has no need to gain a competitive edge through devaluing its currency and has never resorted to deliberate devaluation. The report was published on the same day that China and the European Union kicked off a fresh round of trade talks, with growing European calls for a stronger yuan to help address the bloc’s widening trade deficit with China. “Global economic imbalances are deeply intertwined with shifting global division of labour, inherent flaws in the international monetary system, and persistently high fiscal deficits and high consumption in some countries,” the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said. “Attributing one’s decline in industrial competitiveness, weakened fiscal discipline and complicated structural issues simply to others’ exchange rates is nothing but shifting the responsibility for adjustment onto others and dodging accountability.” The report said past experience did not suggest that a stronger yuan negatively affected China’s trade expansion, nor that a weaker yuan boosted exports. The country’s share of global exports rose in each of the three periods since 2005 when the yuan had appreciated strongly against the US dollar, according to the report. Meanwhile, its share fell in 2016 and 2022 – both years in which the currency weakened. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic met for their first day of trade talks on Thursday. Sefcovic said in a social media post that both sides were “working hard to rebalance EU-China trade” and reiterated that the talks in Beijing should deliver tangible results. The PBOC report is “a direct response to accusations of renminbi undervaluation”, according to Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. Shao Yu, chief economist with the Sci-tech Innovation Centre at Fudan University’s School of Management, echoed this view, saying the paper could also serve as an extra bargaining chip for China in its negotiations with Europe. Europe has long accused China of using currency manipulation to boost its exports. Earlier this week, France and Germany proposed handing the EU the power to rapidly cut off third countries’ access to the European market if they caused severe distortions, such as “restrictions of currency convertibility or currency manipulation”. French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz raised the issue of the yuan exchange rate at a joint press conference in July, arguing the currency was undervalued by 25 to 30 per cent. Merz also previously floated the idea of a Plaza Accord for China, which triggered some controversy given the accord’s negative image in China. The PBOC argued that China’s trade had become “significantly less sensitive to exchange rate movement” as the country climbed up the value chain. The global currency market had grown too large for sustained intervention to have a meaningful effect, it added. Yuan trading averages more than US$800 billion a day, about 80 per cent of which takes place offshore, according to the PBOC. As a result, no central bank could shift the underlying trend of an exchange rate and no country could make itself more competitive through prolonged devaluation, it argued. The central bank also said there was no straightforward relationship between a country’s exchange rate and current account. It cited the South Korean won and the Japanese yen, which both weakened during the first half of 2026 even as their countries’ current account surpluses grew. The top priority for the PBOC is stability, and it would welcome a gradually strengthening yuan with stability as a prerequisite, according to Xu. “The PBOC and the broader Chinese authorities seem keen to facilitate China’s structural rebalancing, although they do not want to create the impression that they are being forced by other countries to do so,” he said. Additional reporting by Sylvia Ma and Xinyi Wu

title: China nominates Song Li for WHO chief as agency faces funding shake-up from US exit
description: If elected, she would be the first mainland Chinese director general of the United Nations health agency.
content: China has nominated health official Song Li to run for director general of the World Health Organization, the foreign ministry confirmed on Thursday. If elected, Song would be the first person from mainland China to head the United Nations health agency. China previously backed Margaret Chan, a Hong Kong-born doctor and former director of health of Hong Kong, who served as WHO director general from 2007 to 2017. Song’s nomination comes as the WHO faces a major funding shake-up following the US withdrawal from the organisation, while China has pledged to increase its financial support. Speaking at a regular press conference in Beijing, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said China believed that, if elected, Song would help the WHO “play a more positive role in improving the health and well-being of all humanity”. “Against the current backdrop of challenges to multilateralism, global health faces a difficult and demanding task,” Mao noted, adding that the role of the director general would be “particularly important” as the WHO navigated a changing global landscape. “China’s nomination of Dr Song Li demonstrates China’s willingness to work with all parties to build a community of health for all, and reflects China’s firm support for multilateralism and the WHO,” Mao said. Song has worked in maternal and children’s health for more than two decades and has experience in health policy and international cooperation, according to the WHO. She previously worked at China’s National Health Commission, where she served as director general of its Department of Women and Children’s Health. Since October 2023, Song has served as a member of the secretariat of the All-China Women’s Federation. China previously nominated Song to run for regional director of the WHO’s Western Pacific Regional Office in 2023. The US formally left the WHO in January, completing a withdrawal ordered by US President Donald Trump soon after he returned to the White House last year. The US had been the WHO’s largest financial contributor, and its departure has left the agency facing a significant funding gap. Washington also owes about US$260 million in unpaid assessed contributions. China last year pledged an additional US$500 million to the WHO over the next five years. Beijing is one of the agency’s largest sources of funding. Under the WHO’s 2026-27 financing scale, China accounts for more than 20 per cent of assessed contributions, while the US remains assessed at 22 per cent despite its withdrawal. The WHO became a focal point of US-China tensions during the Covid-19 pandemic, with Washington accusing the agency of being too close to Beijing while China accused the US of politicising the crisis. Early in the outbreak, WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus worked closely with Chinese officials and met President Xi Jinping in Beijing in January 2020. Washington increasingly challenged the WHO’s handling of the pandemic and its relationship with Beijing. In April 2020, Trump accused the agency of being “China-centric” and threatened to halt US funding. The tensions have persisted beyond the pandemic. In a report last year, the WHO said it was still seeking information from China needed to assess the origins of Covid-19. Beijing has rejected suggestions that it failed to cooperate. Song’s nomination comes as Beijing seeks to play a larger role in multilateral institutions, including UN agencies. Six other candidates – representing Saudi Arabia, Belgium, Qatar, Botswana, Indonesia and Spain – have already made their bids public on the agency’s website. The WHO is expected to publish the full list of candidates early next month. Tedros is due to complete his second term as director general in August of next year.

title: Hong Kong police arrest students as alleged key figures in HK$2.16 million scam ring
description: Officers arrest 10 suspects linked to fake job ads, dating scams and bogus concert ticket sales, with students making up most of the victims.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested two tertiary students suspected of being key members of a fraud and money-laundering syndicate behind fake job advertisements, dating scams and bogus concert ticket sales. The force said on Thursday that officers had arrested 10 people in an earlier operation targeting the syndicate, which allegedly swindled victims – mainly students – out of more than HK$2.1 million (US$267,578). The suspects, five men and five women aged between 13 and 68, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud and money laundering, according to Superintendent Leung Chi-hang of the regional anti-deception unit in New Territories South. Leung said two of those arrested, a man and a woman studying at different tertiary institutions, were a couple and suspected core members of the syndicate. The operation covered cases involving 43 victims, about 60 per cent of whom were students who had fallen prey to shopping scams. Chief Inspector Lam Chun-hong of the regional technology and financial crime unit in New Territories South said the syndicate allegedly posted fake modelling recruitment advertisements on social media between October 2024 and May this year. “Under the pretext of making salary payments, they tricked jobseekers into using phone numbers provided by the syndicate to register electronic wallet accounts, which were then manipulated [by the suspects] as puppet accounts to receive funds from scams,” he said. Lam said the syndicate subsequently used at least eight such accounts to receive funds from at least 43 online shopping and dating scams. “In the scams, the fraudsters would purportedly claim to sell concert tickets to swindle money,” he said. “They would then funnel most of the scammed funds through multiple transfers into their personal accounts, laundering the money through everyday expenditures at luxury massage parlours, tertiary institution canteens and medical clinics.”

title: Alibaba’s AI cloud revenue set to surge over 50% as investment blitz pays off: analysts
description: The Chinese tech giant is expected to post a more than 50 per cent jump in AI cloud revenue for the September quarter, according to analysts.
content: Alibaba Group Holding is expected to report a 50 per cent revenue surge for its cloud and artificial intelligence unit for the September quarter, driven by strong returns on its aggressive AI investments, according to analysts. Analysts across several financial institutions projected revenue growth for the Chinese tech giant’s AI Cloud and Compute Services unit to have accelerated in the three months ended September 30, up from the 45 per cent growth seen in the preceding quarter. The unit’s profit margins are also expected to rise, signalling progress in Alibaba’s efforts to monetise its massive AI investments. Jefferies projected the segment’s profit margin to reach 12.3 per cent for the quarter, while Singapore-based brokerage Longbridge Securities forecast an EBITA (earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation) margin of about 15 per cent, up from 12 per cent in the June quarter. The earnings preview followed a strong showing in the June quarter, when Alibaba’s AI cloud segment – which began including the T-Head chip business that quarter – posted 48.4 billion yuan (US$7.2 billion) in revenue, its fastest growth rate in 22 quarters. Revenue for Alibaba’s AI Lab and Applications segment was projected to grow 20 per cent year on year, accelerating from a 16 per cent expansion in the previous quarter, Longbridge estimated. The unit – which is separate from the AI cloud business – encompasses the company’s AI model labs, the Qwen Consumer Business Group and workplace platform QwenWork. The brokerage expected losses for the unit to narrow to between 10 billion and 11 billion yuan for the period. Overall group performance was also expected to pick up. Jefferies estimated that Alibaba’s total September-quarter revenue would rise 9.6 per cent year on year, marking a slight improvement from the 9 per cent revenue growth recorded in the previous quarter. Despite Alibaba’s heavy capital expenditure, profits from the group’s cloud business are expected to offset the quarterly losses from the AI Lab and Applications segment by the end of December, according to Jefferies analysts Thomas Chong and Zoe Zong. The forecasts follow a slew of announcements at Alibaba’s annual Apsara Conference in September. During the event, the company debuted the Zhenwu V900 processor, billing it as “the most powerful AI chip in China today”, and teased plans to train an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters. The Hangzhou-based company also outlined ambitions to scale its Alibaba Cloud global data centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032. To fuel its AI ambitions, Alibaba issued HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) worth of new shares in August, with the firm planning to invest the proceeds to boost its full-stack capabilities, including by expanding its AI infrastructure. It was the company’s first share placement since its Hong Kong listing in 2019. Alibaba chairman Joe Tsai highlighted the company’s bet on full-stack AI capabilities at the annual Wave tech event in Italy on Wednesday. “We have distribution capability because of our very large e-commerce ecosystem, where we can apply AI to benefit our users and also our corporate clients,” he said, adding that AI would “be infused in every aspect of our business” over the next five years. Meanwhile, Alibaba’s core e-commerce business remains in a transition phase amid fierce domestic competition. Jefferies expected quarter-on-quarter losses for its quick-commerce unit to narrow to about 9.8 billion yuan. Alibaba shares dropped 1 per cent to HK$104.30 on Wednesday, amid a broader retreat of Chinese tech stocks in Hong Kong. The company is expected to report its September-quarter earnings in November. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: India aims to anchor military ties with US as Indo-Pacific ‘resident power’
description: Despite trade tensions, a top US naval officer’s New Delhi visit signals that Washington remains keen to anchor India as a security partner.
content: A second visit by one of the top US naval officers to India this year has raised expectations that the two countries can insulate their growing military ties from trade tensions. US Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, who leads the US Pacific Command, is scheduled to leave India on Thursday after spending six days meeting with senior Indian defence officials and others. The talks, which follow Paparo’s visit to India in February, come as Washington weighs further tariff pressure on India over its purchases of Russian oil and the trade imbalance in Delhi’s favour. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday that negotiations for a trade deal with the United States had reached a plateau, the strongest acknowledgement by Delhi that talks on market access had stalled since they started in February last year. “Trade tensions will not break the India-US military relationship, but they can put a ceiling on it. India does not want a security partnership where economic coercion becomes a test of political loyalty,” said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Delhi-based think tank Indic Researchers Forum. “The military channel will remain open, but trust deepens when both sides see each other as partners, not instruments,” he added. India and the US have continued to deepen defence cooperation in recent years, including through expanding military exercises and closer coordination on maritime security in the Indo-Pacific. Paparo’s visit comes shortly after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, where the two sides sought to ease trade tensions while leaving broader differences in their relationship unresolved. Given the uneasy understanding reached between Washington and Beijing, India has an opportunity to continue positioning itself as a key security player in the Indo-Pacific, according to Balakrishnan. “India sees itself as a resident power in the Indo-Pacific, not as Washington’s counterweight to China. Its priority is a stable Indian Ocean, secure sea lanes and freedom of action,” he said. “New Delhi will cooperate with the US, Japan, Australia and others, but without accepting a bloc mentality that limits its strategic autonomy,” Balakrishnan added. Indo-Pacific stability Uday Chandra, a professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University, said Paparo’s discussions with Indian defence officials took place just weeks before US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visits India on October 19, indicating that Washington is keen to maintain engagement with India on regional security matters. Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation, said that Washington wanted to remove any apprehension among its partners that it would pull out or reduce its security role in the Indo-Pacific. However, the dynamics could change if the US were to continue putting pressure on its partners to bear a greater share of its security burden overseas, Mishra said. He cited comments by US President Donald Trump calling on Australia, Japan, South Korea, France and the UK to deploy their warships to help secure the Strait of Hormuz, a key gateway for the delivery of oil and gas supplies, where Washington deployed its third aircraft strike group last week. India would be wary of any US demand for security cooperation in areas such as the Strait of Hormuz other than the Indo-Pacific, Mishra said. Chandra said both countries saw the importance of putting security cooperation high on the agenda despite their trade differences. “Admiral Paparo’s second visit this year suggests that military-to-military engagement may continue despite friction on other fronts. If tariffs become part of a longer pattern of economic coercion against India, they will inevitably affect political trust on both sides,” he added. Nonetheless, India would have to ensure that it is not a “junior partner in an American-led security architecture” in areas such as protecting the region’s sea lanes, according to Chandra. “Cooperation with the US is extremely useful for these purposes, but only as long as it strengthens its strategic autonomy. Constraints imposed by US domestic or foreign policies need to be tiptoed around,” he said.

title: Canada’s Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for ‘inventive’ spin on classics
description: The Canadian poet and essayist’s work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix.
content: The winner of this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature is Canada’s Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair. The 76-year-old won “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”, the Swedish Academy said on Thursday. Carson is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work which ranges from opera librettos to literary criticism and verse novels such as Autobiography of Red from 1998. Her style ⁠is exemplified in Norma Jeane Baker of Troy from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the ‌stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play Helen and Marilyn Monroe. Ingrid Carlberg, the academy’s the permanent secretary, said she had briefly spoken to Carson. “We didn’t have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.” “They’re all crazy,” Carson said of the decision to honour her, in an interview with public broadcaster RUV in Iceland where she has lived part of the year since 2008 and has become a citizen. Asked by RUV on a blustery roadside if she thought the Nobel would change her readership, Carson, holding tightly to her cap so it would not blow away, replied: “I’ll get a sticker on the front of my books.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday lauded Carson’s win. Her works featured “wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own”, Carney said on social media. “She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, calling the award “an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada”. Born in Toronto in 1950 and educated at the city’s university, Carson has taught at several universities in North America including McGill, Michigan, New York and Princeton. A professor of classics with a background in dead languages, literature, anthropology and history, Carson was described by The New York Times in 2001 as “one of the great pasticheurs”. Her unique contemporary poetry earned her several key literary prizes in the 1990s, including the 1996 Lannan Award and the 1997 Pushcart Prize. The academy said almost all of Carson’s literary production “has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning”. It singled out her poem Nox, printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her brother who died in 2000, as “an unforgettable work”. “Palpable here is a deep sense of loss that works its way up from below. The result is a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” the academy said. Carson’s wide-ranging influences, from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Bronte, led “to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms”, said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel Literature Committee. Carson has said that she considers herself a visual artist as much as a literary one. “I think of making a poem as making an object. I have always thought of ⁠them more as drawings than as texts, but drawings that are also physically enterable through the fact of language,” she said in an interview with Canada’s CBC Radio One in 2016. Poetry, she says, may be more attuned to the fast modern-day life than long-form writing. “I ⁠think it’s probably more useful than prose right now because it’s faster and everybody is in a hurry so basically it’s good because it is brief,” she told the Icelandic broadcaster on Thursday. Carson had been among the favourites to win this year’s prize, according to bookmakers Ladbrokes, and takes a place beside luminaries such as ‌Alexander Solzhenitsyn, ‌Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award, which often divides opinion among book lovers. Last year, the academy picked Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai. The academy has been ‌lambasted for ignoring some of the literary titans of the last 120 years such as Leo Tolstoy, Woolf and Jorge Luis ⁠Borges, criticised for snubbing US authors – though it gave the prize to singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in 2016 – and accused of being too ⁠obscure in its choices. Defenders say the academy has made popular picks, such as Colombia’s Gabriel Garcia Marquez in 1982 and Doris Lessing in 2007, arguing that part of its task is to highlight lesser-known literary traditions and ‌encourage readers to broaden their horizons. There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel Literature Prize was first awarded in 1901. The Literature Prize is the fourth award announced each year, following the Nobel Prizes in Medicine, Physics and Chemistry. The Peace Prize will be announced on Friday in Oslo, the only Nobel award not presented in Stockholm. The week concludes on Monday with the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Each Nobel Prize this year carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about US$1.2 million). The prizes will be formally presented to the winners at a ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death of Swedish inventor and Nobel Foundation founder Alfred Nobel (1833–1896). Reporting by Agence France-Presse, Reuters, Associated Press and dpa

title: Meet Nicole Kidman’s daughter, Faith Margaret, who was at Chanel’s SS27 show in Paris
description: The youngest child of the Practical Magic 2 actress turned heads at Paris Fashion Week, where her sibling, Sunday Rose, walked the Miu Miu runway.
content: Nicole Kidman just turned Paris Fashion Week into a family affair. On October 5, she stepped out with her youngest daughter, Faith Margaret Kidman Urban, for Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel spring/summer 2027 presentation. A day earlier, the 15-year-old attended Valentino’s Antibiblioteca show at the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève to support her elder sister, 18-year-old Sunday Rose, who walked during Alessandro Michele’s showcase for the brand. Nicole Kidman & Faith Urban arriving at the Chanel Spring/Summer 2027 show at Paris Fashion Week. pic.twitter.com/WHeUuXDeIQ — L’avoir Magazine (@lavoirmagazine) October 5, 2026 Both Faith Margaret and Sunday, whom Kidman shares with ex-husband Keith Urban, joined their mother for Paris Fashion Week last year. In March, the trio was spotted at Chanel and Charles Finch’s Annual Pre-Oscar Dinner at The Polo Lounge in Beverly Hills. Nicole Kidman arrives at the Chanel fashion show, accompanied by her two daughters, Sunday and Faith, on monday, october 6, in Paris. 💛 pic.twitter.com/CtfKQuwmcJ — Nicole Kidman Daily 🪄 (@dailykidman) October 6, 2025 So, what do we know about Faith Margaret Kidman Urban? She was born via surrogacy Faith Margaret Kidman Urban was born on December 28, 2010, in Nashville, Tennessee. Kidman and Urban – who separated in 2025 and finalised their divorce this January – welcomed their youngest daughter via gestational surrogacy due to Kidman’s fertility struggles. “The love I felt … she [the carrier] was the most wonderful woman to do this for us. We were in a place of desperately wanting another child,” the actress recalled on Australia’s 60 Minutes. Faith Margaret’s name supposedly comes from the fact that her parents “never gave up faith they’d have another child together”, a friend of the former couple told People. She got her middle name, Margaret, from Kidman’s grandmother. Faith Margaret has two half-siblings, Bella Kidman Cruise, 33, and Connor Cruise, 31, whom the Babygirl actress adopted with her first husband, Tom Cruise. Where did she grow up? Faith Margaret grew up in Nashville, where her father relocated from Australia in 1992 to pursue his country music career. Kidman, who was born in Honolulu to Australian parents, considers her daughters Nashvillians. “They have a southern drawl. They have some Aussie. They have an unusual mix. They’re hybrids,” the Practical Magic 2 star told People. Kidman raised her daughters without phones or social media, per Vanity Fair. Speaking to L’Officiel in 2024, she revealed that her children often tag along when she travels for work and have lived in Morocco, France, Australia, England, Scotland, Ireland, Vietnam and Hong Kong. What are her interests? Faith Margaret played the violin as a child, per Vanity Fair, but she has branched into acting in recent years. In 2019, she appeared in two episodes of Big Little Lies, which stars her mother, and voiced Beatrice and Sophie in The Angry Birds Movie 2. The following year, she guest-starred in an episode of the thriller series The Undoing, in which Kidman plays a psychotherapist, and Hugh Grant plays her husband. According to People, Faith Margaret is also interested in cars.

title: Retail properties offloaded for losses in weak market as revaluations spark bank concerns
description: Hong Kong retail property prices have fallen by up to 70 per cent since 2018, says Centaline Commercial managing director.
content: Several retail properties sold recently by prominent Hong Kong investors have been offloaded at a loss – a trend analysts attributed to banks maintaining a tough stance on debt collection. Stanley Poon Chi-ming, managing director at Centaline Commercial, said retail property prices had fallen by 30 to 70 per cent from their 2018 peaks. That meant any sales in the current market – especially of properties bought around a decade ago – would essentially result in a loss. “Many retail property owners are facing bank demands to cover mortgage shortfalls following property revaluations, forcing them to sell at low prices to raise cash and repay their loans,” he said. “Some are even facing financial distress and defaulting on their mortgage payments, leading banks to require them to sell their properties.” Veteran investor Yeung Fun-bun, the chairman of Kam Wah Holdings, recently sold a ground-floor shop at 250 Castle Peak Road, Cheung Sha Wan, for HK$22.8 million. The property has a gross floor area of about 1,596 square feet, translating to a price of about HK$14,286 per square foot, according to market sources. Yeung listed the property for sale at HK$55 million last year, but it ultimately changed hands for HK$32.2 million less – a 58.5 per cent reduction. He bought the shop for HK$54 million in February 2018 and held it eight years, incurring a loss of HK$31.2 million or 57.8 per cent. The property is leased to the Ki’s Roasted Goose restaurant chain for HK$84,000 a month, offering the buyer a rental yield of 4.4 per cent. Another veteran local investor, Choi Pak-nang, incurred a paper loss of HK$36 million on a ground-floor shop at 207A Tung Choi Street, Mong Kok, that he recently sold following 14 years of ownership, according to market sources. He sold the property, with a gross floor area of about 1,100 square feet, for HK$27 million, or HK$24,545 per square foot. Some property owners who are pressed for cash have no choice but to sell at a lower price Stanley Poon, Centaline Commercial Choi bought the property for HK$63 million in November 2012 and sold it for 57 per cent less. It is leased to an aquarium shop until 2028 at a monthly rent of HK$115,000, meaning the buyer is expected to achieve a yield of about 5.1 per cent. Early this week, Shop A on the ground floor of the Yee Fat Building at 10-16 Portland Street, Yau Ma Tei – which is occupied by the Kung Fu Dim Sum snack shop chain – changed hands for HK$11 million, according to market sources. The sellers, Ma Tin-ming and Ma Tin-chung, founders of the BKT Group food and catering company, bought the property for HK$15 million in February 2014 and held it for 12 years, incurring a paper loss of HK$4 million or 26.7 per cent. Centaline Commercial’s Poon said it was not a good time to sell shops, because prices were “so low”. “Some property owners who are pressed for cash have no choice but to sell at a lower price – such cases have become more frequent recently,” he said, adding that banks had not eased up on debt recovery efforts. “It appears that banks have held off for a while, giving owners time to sell the properties themselves. However, sales may not have materialised; the only option left is to take possession and sell them as foreclosed properties.”

title: Development chief dismisses fears Northern Metropolis supply will hit office sector
description: Incoming supply in the megaproject is primarily for the I&T sector, Bernadette Linn tells lawmakers.
content: Hong Kong’s development chief has dismissed concerns that commercial floor space in the Northern Metropolis megaproject will further depress the city’s struggling office market, stressing that incoming supply is primarily for the innovation and technology (I&T) sector. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho told the Legislative Council on Thursday that the 1 million square metres (10.8 million square feet) of economic floor space to be provided in the megaproject next to the Shenzhen border over the next five years was unrelated to traditional office supply. She was responding to a question from real estate and construction sector lawmaker Augustine Wong Ho-ming, who voiced concern during a debate on the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy address that the additional commercial floor space could aggravate already high office vacancy rates in non-prime locations. “Hong Kong is currently undergoing economic restructuring and a reshaping of corporate operating models. Office vacancy rates outside the prime areas remain high,” Wong said. “When planning industrial space in the Northern Metropolis, has the government comprehensively reviewed and timely adjusted the planning of commercial land and the pace of land sales outside the Northern Metropolis?” According to Rating and Valuation Department figures, the vacancy rate of private offices stood at 17.6 per cent in 2025, the highest in more than four decades. Office prices and rents also fell by 13.6 per cent and 3.2 per cent year on year, respectively, in the last quarter of 2025. Linn said the new commercial floor area in the metropolis, which aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into a technology hub and serve as an economic engine, would not dampen the subdued office market. “This 1 million square metres of economic floor space primarily comes from land in the Lok Ma Chau Loop area and the San Tin Technopole,” she said. “It is floor space for the innovation and technology industries and is unrelated to traditional commercial floor space.” Linn added that the government was preparing to launch the second “large-scale land disposal” project for the Fanling North new development area and had been in contact with interested developers, following the tender announcement for the first pilot site in Hung Shui Kiu in August. She also said the government would continue implementing diversified land-development approaches to facilitate businesses’ participation in the Northern Metropolis and continue rolling out administrative measures to cut red tape and accelerate development. The second day of the three-day Legco debate also covered artificial intelligence (AI) risk governance and tourism. Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok echoed a proposal by lawmakers to publish guidelines for minors’ use of artificial intelligence before completing the review of AI risks and related legislation. He stressed the importance of education in the proper use of AI, noting that the guidelines would also target parents and teachers to help guide children in protecting themselves. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said that Hong Kong received 40.7 million tourists over the first three quarters of this year, a 12 per cent year-on-year increase. During the seven-day National Day “golden week” break, the city also recorded 1.41 million inbound trips by mainland visitors, above expectations. Law said she was confident the city could meet its full-year target of 53.8 million visitors. She also noted that the International Lantern Spectacular in Victoria Park, organised by the Hong Kong Tourism Board, had attracted 730,000 visitors and had successfully boosted nearby restaurants and retail businesses. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu last month unveiled the annual policy address alongside the five-year plan, which aims to align Hong Kong’s development with the national development strategy. The two documents set out initiatives to accelerate the Northern Metropolis and strengthen the city’s position in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

title: Marcos says Philippines ‘resigned’ to managing South China Sea dispute
description: Speaking in Singapore, the Philippine leader warned a simple misstep at sea could trigger an out-of-control clash.
content: The Philippines is “resigned” to managing its long-standing dispute with Beijing in the South China Sea and avoiding dangerous escalations, President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said on Thursday. At the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore, Marcos said: “I don’t know if we can find a resolution to the problem, but we are resigned to just being able to manage the problem, so that we do not have mistakes, we do not have misinterpretations. “My greatest fear is that some seaman, some soldier, just makes a mistake, and that mistake turns into something that goes out of control.” But the Philippine president reiterated Manila’s sovereign rights over the waterway, which he said were backed by international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. “We refer to it as the West Philippine Sea,” Marcos said before an audience of over 400 chief executives, entrepreneurs, and investors. “It’s been on the western side of the Philippines, you know, since time immemorial.” Beijing has rejected a 2016 arbitral tribunal ruling in The Hague, which found no legal basis for its claims in the South China Sea under its nine-dash line. China considers the ruling illegal and non-binding, while Manila relies on it to assert its maritime rights. Tensions between the two nations have intensified in recent months. On Monday, Beijing accused Manila of violating its airspace near the disputed Scarborough Shoal, which China refers to as Huangyan Island. In response, the Philippine military said a Chinese fighter jet had interfered with a “routine military patrol”. Chinese state media quoted a foreign ministry spokesman calling the Philippine flight a serious violation of Beijing’s sovereignty and jurisdiction and an attempt to undermine peace and stability in the waterway. To de-escalate the regional flashpoint, China and the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations have held monthly meetings to discuss a long-awaited code of conduct, aiming to finalise the document by the end of the year. Marcos acknowledged the delays that had plagued the finalisation of the code, but insisted he remained optimistic and that good progress was being made. “Sometimes it’s a bit frustrating that just the definitions of ordinary words are becoming bones of contention,” Marcos said. “But we are determined to come to an agreement and to hopefully de-escalate the situation.” De-escalating the conflict, which was now “deeply embedded” and affecting the livelihoods of his citizens, was imperative, he added. Filipino fishermen have reportedly faced increasingly restricted access near Scarborough Shoal, a rich fishing ground effectively controlled by the Chinese coastguard since a 2012 stand-off. During a meeting with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn last month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Beijing was ready to work with Asean to fully implement the code, adding that peace and stability in the waterway benefit all countries in the region. At the conference, which speaker line-up includes Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Singaporean counterpart Lawrence Wong, Marcos added that all Asean member states agreed the code was “absolutely necessary” to avoid difficulties and “incidents”. Last month, Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin voiced concern that an “unexpected incident” in the South China Sea could spill over into Malaysia, prompting Kuala Lumpur to strengthen its national defence capabilities. Speaking later in the day, Wong said all parties involved in discussions were sincere and focused on achieving an amicable solution. He added that Singapore would continue facilitating negotiations as Asean chair next year if they did not conclude before then. “We are not a claimant state, but our stance has always been that we want to uphold international law, Unclos and freedom of navigation,” he said.

title: Police fire tear gas at barricaded Paris high school as pupil protests continue
description: French police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when pupils began protesting to demand more education funding.
content: Pupils barricaded a secondary school in northeastern Paris with rubbish bins on Thursday before police moved in with tear gas, as France’s nationwide protests showed few signs of ending. The Helene Boucher high school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday. Riot police gathered in side streets as pupils converged on the school. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid being recognised. At least a dozen demonstrations supporting the pupils’ movement were planned across France later in the day, including a rally at Place de la Bastille in Paris, where tear gas and a water cannon were fired at protesters. Police have made more than 6,600 arrests since late September, when pupils, most of them under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, according to the Interior Ministry. The Education Ministry said 375 schools were fully or partially closed on Thursday. While the number of school closures was down compared with Tuesday, pressure is mounting on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. The protests against the underfunding of schools — many of them struggling with dilapidated facilities and insufficient staff - have drawn troublemakers not concerned about the aims of the protest movement as well as unions and political groups. In a television address, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalised, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults”. He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles”. France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said. At the Lycee, 18-year-old university student Emma Khelil came to offer support to those at the barricades at her former high school. She told Associated Press that she is really concerned about police violence. “We’re here to defend our rights, not to lose an eye or a hand,” Khelil said. She also said that she had noticed insulation problems and water leaks in the school building and had even seen rats on occasion. Other pupils confirmed that they had also seen rats. She was not convinced by Lecornu’s efforts to calm the situation. “I don’t think the movement is going to lose momentum. As long as things don’t change, we’re going to see the movement grow stronger, and potentially a convergence of struggles, especially with the next presidential election coming up,” she said. Not long after she spoke, police surrounded a nearby square. The crowd surged and tear gas was fired. Smoke from burning rubbish nearby hung in the air at Place de la Republique as hundreds of high school and university students prepared to march towards Place de la Bastille, the demonstration’s focal point. Some carried signs bearing their schools’ names; others held placards reading “More money for repression than for our education” and “Who protects us from the police?” “We’re here, we’re demonstrating and we won’t stop. Until October, November, December if necessary. Nothing will stop us,” said Sofia Ferdials, 18, a student at Paris 8 University. Dounia Gergeon, a 39-year-old school librarian, said she joined the demonstration at Place de la Bastille because she shared pupils’ concerns and worried about a broader crisis facing young people anxious about their futures. At the middle and high school where she works, time was set aside for pupils to discuss their demands. “They do not feel supported,” she said. “They feel cornered and forced to work under these conditions.” Authorities deployed tear gas and a water cannon at the protesters, some of whom hurled projectiles at riot police. France is not the only country to be dealing with pupil-related protests. In Belgium, Willy Demeyer, the mayor of Liege, issued a ban on public gatherings until midnight on October 16, citing a “real, serious and imminent risk” of further clashes and vandalism. City police said they used water cannon and tear gas on Wednesday to hold back several hundred protesters. Authorities sent emergency text messages advising shopkeepers to close due to rioting. Nearly 90 people were arrested and several police were injured. Police reinforcements were sent from the capital, Brussels, and from Antwerp, and more are coming. Smaller protests have been held in Mons and Charleroi. Belgium’s Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said on social media that the “perpetrators will have to answer for their actions before the courts”. The Belgian protests, organised through online chat groups, include demands for more teachers and smaller classes as well as complaints about education reform in Belgium but are also probably inspired by events in France. Pupil protests have spread to several Italian cities, though on a much smaller scale and over a broader set of domestic grievances. Activists have explicitly invoked the French movement with the slogan “let’s do as they do in France”, while organising school occupations, assemblies and marches. In Turin, pupils occupied several secondary schools over building conditions, education funding and increased military spending. In Rome, pupils occupied one school and walked out of another, while pupils in Naples added opposition to a planned migrant detention centre to their demands.

title: Kremlin aide visits China amid speculation about potential Xi-Putin-Trump meeting
description: Nikolai Patrushev will hold maritime talks, but his trip is being watched for signs that a summit is planned for November.
content: An aide to Russia’s president arrived in China on Thursday for a visit that will be closely watched for signs of preparation for a possible trilateral summit with the US during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting next month. Nikolai Patrushev, who is also chairman of Russia’s Maritime Board, was set to hold talks with Foreign Minister Wang Yi, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Wednesday. Leading a delegation that included representatives from government agencies, major logistics firms, shipbuilders and scientific and educational institutions, Patrushev would “hold talks on Russian-Chinese cooperation in the maritime sector”, Russian news agency Interfax quoted the Maritime Board as saying. This was Patrushev’s first visit to China as chairman of the Maritime Board, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Thursday, noting that Wang and other department chiefs would meet with him to exchange views on bilateral relations and cooperation on maritime affairs. “China is ready to take this visit as an opportunity to work with Russia to deepen strategic communication, promote practical cooperation and keep providing new momentum for the development of China-Russia relations in the new era,” she said. While Beijing and Moscow have steadily expanded their maritime ties in recent years – including the development of Arctic shipping routes, joint naval exercises and scientific expeditions in polar regions – Patrushev’s visit has attracted attention beyond maritime affairs. The former intelligence officer, who has been the president’s aide since 2024 and served as the secretary of the Security Council of Russia from 2008 to 2024, is the first high-level Russian official to visit China since President Xi Jinping had a summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington late last month. With Xi and Trump having agreed to extend their countries’ trade truce and work towards “constructive strategic stability”, global attention has now turned to whether Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin could meet during November’s Apec summit in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen. Speaking at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club last Thursday, Putin seemed to be receptive to a three-way encounter, saying that such a meeting during the Apec gathering “is certainly possible”. “To a large extent, this will depend on China as the host of the event. But I repeat: meetings are always beneficial as they allow for an exchange of views and a clarification of positions,” Putin said. “The most important thing is to single out the issues that could lay the foundation for such a trilateral summit; the key is to define the agenda for these negotiations.” “However, this will undoubtedly depend to a large degree on the hosts of the event – in this case, President Xi Jinping,” he added. Diplomats have also weighed in on the potential summit. Speaking to Russian newspaper Izvestia late last month, Zhang Hanhui, China’s ambassador to Moscow, said such a meeting would “be very beneficial for the development and formation of a multipolar world”. “Because Russia, America and China are UN Security Council permanent members; they are world powers. The future of this world depends on us,” Zhang said.

title: Who is Michael Douglas’ son, Cameron? The actor’s new memoir recounts their troubled relationship
description: The Fatal Attraction star is opening up about his life in One Helluva Ride – but what do you know about his son Cameron, whom he shares with ex-wife Diandra Luker?
content: Michael Douglas has made a series of explosive claims in his new memoir, One Helluva Ride. The actor and film producer comes clean about cheating on his first wife, Diandra Luker, with actress Kathleen Turner while on the set of the 1984 film Romancing the Stone. Other candid revelations include details of his previously strained relationship with his eldest son, Cameron Douglas, whom he welcomed with Luker. In his book, which was published on October 6, Douglas writes about Cameron’s years-long struggle with substance abuse, which eventually led to his arrest on a drug-dealing charge in 2009. He was sentenced to five years behind bars for federal drug trafficking and distribution. Although Douglas now shares a close relationship with Cameron, he said he refused to write to his son while he was in prison. Douglas also declined to attend group therapy sessions with Cameron while he was in rehab for drug addiction. “I love Cam, but we went through a really rough time,” Douglas explained to The Times about his decision to distance himself from his son. “I’m telling my story, man, and the [reality is] you do everything you can for your kids, but I lost a half-brother from an overdose,” the Fatal Attraction actor continued. In 2004, Douglas’ half-brother Eric died of an accidental overdose. He was 46 years old. “To watch your own father be in his eighties, dealing with group therapy sessions with his son? I said I’m not going to do that. I said I’m not going to go into my seventies and eighties going to rehab sessions,” Douglas continued, adding, “I love my kids, but you know, I have an entitlement to a right to live a life.” So, what else do we know about Cameron Douglas? Read on to find out. His parents divorced in 2000 Cameron Douglas was born in 1978 to parents Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker. Douglas and Luker wed in 1977 after only eight weeks together; he was 32, and she was 19, per The Times. According to his new book, Douglas was unfaithful throughout his first marriage and recounts his various affairs, including with actresses Kathleen Turner and Jeanne Tripplehorn. The Oscar-winning actor hints that Luker had also been unfaithful. The couple ultimately parted ways in 2000. He wrote a memoir too In his own memoir Long Way Home, published in 2019, the now 47-year-old says his relationship with Douglas was influenced by the friction the Basic Instinct actor experienced with his own father, Kirk Douglas. Cameron recounts occasionally having physical altercations with his father and resenting his fame. “Every son admires his own father, but everyone in the world admired mine,” he wrote. Cameron was only 13 years old when he started smoking cannabis, and by his late teens, he was using cocaine and soon became addicted to heroin. Cameron’s substance abuse only led his relationship with his father to further deteriorate. Originally jailed for five years in 2010 for drug possession and distribution, Cameron was ordered to serve two additional years in prison for smuggling drugs into the correctional facility. During his time in prison, Cameron began journaling and writing poetry. With encouragement from his father, he started penning a memoir following his release. The father-son duo has since mended their relationship. Cameron is also close to his stepmother, Catherine Zeta-Jones. He is currently following in his famous father and grandfather’s footsteps and pursuing a career in acting. He appeared in the 2023 television miniseries The Crowded Room and had a role in the 2025 film Looking Through Water. Is Cameron Douglas married? Cameron became a father for the first time in 2017 when his then-girlfriend Viviane Thibes gave birth to their daughter Lua Izzy. They also share a son, Ryder, who was born in 2020. Cameron and Thibes split in 2024 and share custody of their two children, per Daily Mail.

title: South Korea to recall ambassador from Ukraine amid POW dispute
description: The two countries have been at loggerheads since Zelensky disclosed the transfer of the prisoners captured on the battlefield early last year.
content: South Korea said on Thursday it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine in response to a deepening diplomatic row over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul. The two countries have been at loggerheads since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last month disclosed the prisoner transfer, sparking anger in Seoul, which said it had placed their families in North Korea at risk. The recall also comes days after a media report alleged more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, had been shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August, sparking accusations Seoul was helping alleviate Russian fuel shortages. “The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.” In Kyiv, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry said it was open ‌to renewing a constructive dialogue with South Korea despite Seoul’s decision to recall the ambassador. A spokesperson said the South ‌Korean envoy was invited to the ministry this week to ⁠hear the ⁠Ukrainian position on the matter. “We believe that diplomacy should prevail over emotions,” the spokesperson said. “Despite Seoul’s ‌decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to resuming constructive dialogue, even if it will take ‌some ‌time.” Since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, North Korea has become a key ally of the Kremlin, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology. South Korea’s spy agency estimated last year that about 2,000 North Korean troops had been killed in the war, while a more recent assessment put the number killed or wounded at around 6,000. Ukraine’s hopes of armament supplies from Seoul have been complicated by the row over Zelensky’s disclosure. South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war. Seoul had already summoned Kyiv’s ambassador and threatened unspecified “further measures”, and President Lee Jae Myung has demanded an official apology over the prisoner revelation. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga has referred to the incident as a “diplomatic misunderstanding”. A report in Britain’s Guardian newspaper this week has threatened to deepen tensions, with allegations of fuel shipments to Russia coming as Ukraine has struck refineries deep in Russian territory while Moscow has been launching an all-time high of missile attacks. An adviser to Zelensky said this week that the alleged diesel shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies, remarks Seoul slammed as “factually incorrect” and “inappropriate”. Seoul has been part of a coalition of countries with enhanced export controls on Russia and its ally Belarus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But South Korea’s foreign ministry on Thursday issued a statement saying that even if the fuel had originated in South Korea – something it argued had not been established – that would not fall foul of the country’s export ban. “Refined petroleum products, including commercial diesel and aviation fuel, mentioned in The Guardian’s report, are not subject to South Korea’s export controls against Russia,” it said, noting that overall exports to Moscow had more than halved since the war’s start. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Record prize money, better flow, Hong Kong event key to LPGA’s 2027 schedule
description: Hong Kong tournament will be the richest in Asia and brings a three-week swing through the region to an end.
content: The LPGA Tour’s 2027 schedule features 33 tournaments, a record US$147 million in prize money and an itinerary that does not have players bouncing across the country. LPGA Commissioner Craig Kessler released the plan for next season on Wednesday and emphasised routing, quality of courses and prize money, and the schedule has ticked several of those boxes. Hong Kong appears on the calendar for the first time in 50 years, with the Futu Ladies World Championship in the first week of March ending a three-week Asia swing, which starts with the Honda LPGA Thailand and takes players to the HSBC Women’s World Championship in Singapore, before heading to The Clearwater Bay Golf and Country Club. From there, the game’s best head to Hawaii for back-to-back tournaments on the Big Island and Maui. The first stop is the new Nanea Cup with a US$4 million purse for 95 players and 25 amateurs at five colleges competing in separate events held concurrently. Then it’s over to Kapalua’s Plantation course, the most recognisable course in Hawaii because it hosted the PGA Tour’s season opener for 25 years. Asia to Hawaii takes the LPGA Tour straight to the West Coast Swing – Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles – before the first major of the year in Houston at The Chevron Championship. “Our schedule impacts every stakeholder, but our athletes remain at the heart of how we build it. Our progress is evident in how our athletes and the entire LPGA ecosystem will move around the world next year, creating more opportunities to rest, recover and ultimately operate more efficiently,” Kessler said. The Hawaii events are the same week as The Players Championship and Arnold Palmer Invitational at Bay Hill, and that wasn’t an accident. The idea was for viewers to go from the PGA Tour events right into the LPGA in the evening hours. The three majors that rotate courses take them to Inverness Club in northwestern Ohio for the US Women’s Open, Congressional Country Club for the KPMG Women’s PGA and Royal St George’s for the AIG Women’s British Open. Royal St George’s, the first English links where the Open Championship was played, has held the men’s Open 15 times dating to 1894. This will be the first time it hosts the Women’s Open. The USGA chose to stage the US Women’s Open from June 3 to 6, the same week as the Jack Nicklaus-hosted Memorial Tour a little over two hours away in Dublin, Ohio. Four tournaments are missing from 2026 – the Women’s Scottish Open, LPGA Blue Bay in China, the Aramco Championship in Las Vegas and the Kroger Queen City Championship in Cincinnati. Hong Kong, which will be the richest women’s tournament in Asia with a US$3.4 million prize purse, has replaced Blue Bay, which has been held on Hainan Island for the past couple of years. Aramco has been replaced by a Saudi Golf-funded tournament in the UK – the course has not been announced – that will precede the Women’s Open. Also back is the Hanwha International Crown, held in non-Solheim Cup years and a team event based on countries. That will be at Lake Merced, a highly rated course in San Francisco. Eighteen tournaments have at least a US$3 million prize fund. That does not include the five majors, which have an average purse of US$10.72 million. The LPGA said nearly 20 tournaments have enhanced perks such as hotels, flights or other transport.

title: Bruce Lee ballet, Marina Abramovic work to lead WestK Performing Arts Centre’s debut season
description: The WestK Performing Arts Centre is slated to open in Hong Kong in 2027, with a Bruce Lee ballet and Wong Fei-hung dance drama on the cards.
content: Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District Authority has unveiled the inaugural line-up for its highly anticipated WestK Performing Arts Centre (WestK PAC). The new arts hub, 10 years in the making, is slated to open in summer 2027 and will be marked by an ambitious series of world-class performances. The opening production will premiere the dance drama Wong Fei Hung in July 2027. Inspired by Wong Fei-hung, one of China’s most enduring martial arts legends, the production brings together creative talents from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Guangdong to reimagine the folk hero for modern audiences through a fusion of contemporary dance and martial arts. Hong Kong Ballet, announced earlier as the first company to take up residence at WestK PAC, will premiere Bruce Lee: Hong Kong Legend in September 2027. With the set and costumes designed by Oscar-winner Tim Yip Kam-tim, the work celebrates Lee’s journey from Hong Kong to international stardom and his influence on martial arts, cinema and pop culture. Another world premiere will feature British choreographer Sir Wayne McGregor’s Tenderness Data, a piece inspired by research into physical intelligence, artificial intelligence and emerging quantum technologies.
