The commission is one of several international partnerships established during the Hong Kong International Cultural Summit held during Art March earlier this year. Serbian conceptual artist Marina Abramovic, winner of the Golden Lion for Best Artist at the 1997 Venice Biennale, will present the Asian premiere of Marina Abramovic: Balkan Erotic Epic. Drawing on Balkan folklore, ancient rituals and traditional mythology, the work – widely regarded as one of Abramovic’s most ambitious projects – interweaves dance, music and performance art to explore eroticism, spirituality and the human body as a site of power, mystery and transformation. Performance dates for these two blockbusters will be announced in due course. Other headliners set to make their Hong Kong debuts at WestK PAC are Thus Have I Heard: A Play Inspired by The Diamond Sutra (October 2027) and City of Floating Sounds (December 2027), two cross-cultural arts productions co-commissioned by WestK. The former, directed by Hong Kong theatre veteran Tang Shu-wing, brings together a cast from Hong Kong, Shanghai and India to weave ancient Buddhist philosophies on identity and enlightenment into a multidimensional narrative. Meanwhile, City of Floating Sounds, composed by pianist and vocalist Huang Ruo, fuses Chinese folk traditions with contemporary orchestral music into an immersive experience. Audiences will take part in a citywide mobile sonic journey featuring the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra before gathering for a live performance by the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra. The Impossible Trial, the first original Cantonese musical commissioned by WestK Performing Arts and co-produced with the Hong Kong Repertory Theatre, will make a grand return in spring 2028, marking its third rerun in Hong Kong. WestK PAC stands as Hong Kong’s first purpose-built venue dedicated exclusively to dance and theatre. The complex will house four performance spaces including the 1,450-seat Grand Theatre, the 600-seat Medium Theatre, the 270-seat Studio Theatre and the 148-seat The Hall, as well as a dedicated Resident Company Centre, Dancehouse and state-of-the-art rehearsal facilities. Combined with the six performance spaces across the Xiqu Centre and Freespace, it forms the WestK theatre cluster: an interconnected network of 10 performance venues with a total seating capacity exceeding 4,500, set to host world-class dance, theatre and musical productions spanning large-scale international works, original creations and experimental multidisciplinary projects. Earlier this month, the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority recorded a deficit of HK$998 million (US$127 million) in the 2025-26 financial year, up from HK$769 million in the same period a year earlier. The authority has indicated the increase is mainly due to higher operating costs related to preparing for the opening of WestK PAC.

title: Uniqlo sees profits soar in China despite Beijing-Tokyo tensions
description: The Japanese clothing brand saw its China sales recover over the past year despite ongoing political tensions and China’s consumer slowdown.
content: Fast Retailing, the parent company of Japanese clothing retailer Uniqlo, has defied the ongoing political tensions between Beijing and Tokyo and soft consumer sentiment in China to log a rebound in sales and profits on the Chinese mainland. The Japanese firm said the 2026 financial year, which ended in August, had been a period in which its mainland China business had “made steady progress, with encouraging steps indicating a return to growth”, according to its annual report released on Thursday. The company’s full-year revenue on the Chinese mainland climbed 3 per cent year on year in local currency terms, while business profits rose by roughly 18 per cent. Hong Kong and Taiwan also saw increases in full-year revenue and profit over the period, the group said. The improved performance was partly driven by ongoing structural reforms, with Uniqlo rolling out a revamp of its store network in mainland China with a focus on refined site selection and higher operational efficiency, the company said. The chain has opened more large-format stores and closed many smaller underperforming outlets. The Greater China region – covering mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan – constitutes the group’s second-largest market globally after Japan. The region’s total sales hit 724 billion Japanese yen (US$4.6 billion) over the same period, up 11.3 per cent year on year, while profit came in at 112 billion Japanese yen, up 24.6 per cent. Fast Retailing’s Hong Kong-listed shares have risen 34 per cent so far this year and closed at HK$37.30 on Thursday morning, up 0.81 per cent from Wednesday. Trading of its Hong Kong depositary receipts on the Hong Kong stock exchange was suspended from 1pm on Thursday at the company’s request, and will resume on Friday. The upbeat market reaction comes even as political tensions between Japan and China weigh on bilateral economic ties. Beijing issued a travel advisory in November urging citizens to avoid travelling to Japan, after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi indicated that Tokyo could intervene in the event of an armed conflict in the Taiwan Strait. The move triggered a wave of flight cancellations between the two countries and a plunge in Chinese tourism to Japan. Once a top destination for Chinese travellers, Japan was not even among the top 10 most popular travel hotspots over the just-concluded National Day holiday, according to Chinese online travel agency Tuniu Corp.

title: National security police arrest 2 over alleged seditious social media posts
description: Pair suspected of managing YellowInsurance and publishing posts that allegedly incited hatred against Hong Kong’s constitutional order.
content: Hong Kong national security police have arrested two people, including an insurance broker, on suspicion of publishing seditious posts on social media. A police spokesman said on Thursday that officers from the National Security Department had arrested a man and a woman, both 38, on Tuesday on suspicion of doing an act with a seditious intention under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. “The two arrested people, including a male licensed insurance broker, were suspected of operating pages on various social media platforms and publishing seditious posts that incite hatred against the constitutional order of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region,” the spokesman said. A source said the pair were suspected of managing social media pages for YellowInsurance, a platform accused of posting content supporting the 2019 anti-government protests and arrested protesters, as well as smearing the central and Hong Kong governments. The source identified the man as former pro-democracy activist Wong Ka-ho, who later became a financial consultant at a local investment firm and had held an insurance intermediary licence. The woman was a friend of Wong and did not hold such a licence. Selling insurance products is a regulated activity in Hong Kong, and brokers must hold a valid licence issued by the Insurance Authority. The source said YellowInsurance had been active on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, but a South China Morning Post search on Thursday found that the pages were no longer available. “After the national security law came into effect, this page switched to ‘soft resistance’ to fan anti-China sentiment and sow chaos in Hong Kong,” the source said. The source added that the messages were conveyed through “surreptitious means”, such as hashtags and acrostic poems. The platform was also accused of promoting the banned protest song “Glory to Hong Kong” and other “yellow” vendors that supported the protesters. Under the ordinance, anyone convicted of the offence faces up to seven years in prison.

title: Hong Kong child abuse case prompts calls to watch for signs of psychological harm
description: Welfare experts urge vigilance over subtle changes in children’s behaviour as video of girl carrying beer highlights difficulty of detecting hidden abuse.
content: Psychological abuse can be hard to detect, Hong Kong welfare experts have warned, urging social workers and teachers to look for subtle changes in children’s behaviour amid outrage over a viral video showing a girl carrying heavy bags of beer as her stepfather called her “useless”. Welfare groups said on Thursday that emotional and verbal abuse were among the most common yet least recognised forms of child abuse. Signs often emerged through changes such as social withdrawal and anxiety, they said, but the harm could be as serious as physical injury. They urged professionals working with children to consult the Social Welfare Department even when suspected cases fell short of the serious harm threshold for mandatory reporting. Their calls came after police on Wednesday arrested a man and a woman on suspicion of ill-treatment of a child. The previous evening, their 10-year-old daughter had been filmed carrying two heavy bags of beer at Fu Tai Estate in Tuen Mun, with her backpack torn and gaping open. The video showed the man, who was accompanied by two other children, snatching back one of the bags and calling the girl “useless” when bystanders intervened. The girl’s mother, 32, and stepfather, 38, were released on bail on Thursday and must report back to police later this month. The Social Welfare Department was also following up on the case. Although the girl had no visible injuries and her stepfather claimed the heavy loads were intended to train her muscles, experts said excessive physical demands and verbal abuse could cause lasting psychological harm to children. Maple Lau Siu-kwan, executive director of the NGO Against Child Abuse, said repeatedly making a child carry loads beyond their age or physical capacity was itself a form of abuse. She cited Department of Health guidance suggesting that a child’s load should not exceed 10 per cent of their body weight. “In this case, the public could already tell from common sense that this was beyond what the child could bear,” she said. “Exceeding a child’s physical capacity can endanger the body, and whether it is a one-off incident or a persistent one, it deserves our attention.” Lau said child abuse fell into four categories – physical abuse, neglect, sexual abuse and psychological harm – with the last being the most difficult to detect. “Psychological harm comes with behavioural signs, such as anxiety or unusual unhappiness. We must stay alert and keep observing and assessing continuously, so we can help the child and identify problems early,” she said. She urged professionals covered by the mandatory reporting ordinance, which applies to 25 categories across three sectors, to seek advice from the Social Welfare Department’s Family and Child Protective Services Units whenever they noticed warning signs. “Even if the case may not amount to serious abuse under the ordinance, there is a good chance the child and the family need help, support and protection. The child comes first, and that is our guiding principle,” Lau said. She also encouraged parents to adopt positive discipline and non-violent communication. Hong Kong’s Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse Ordinance, which took effect in January this year, requires education, social welfare and healthcare professionals to report cases in which a child is suspected of suffering serious harm or being at real risk of it. Billy Wong Wai-yuk, executive secretary of the Hong Kong Committee on Children’s Rights, said singling out one child for heavy chores, as in this case, reflected a common pattern in which abuse targeted one child while their siblings remained unharmed. “Families often use the other children, who appear unharmed, as a smokescreen. Meanwhile, the abused child will almost always protect the parents when outsiders ask questions,” she said. Wong said psychological harm was difficult to detect because children often suffered in silence for long periods, living with constant anxiety while symptoms emerged only gradually. “Teachers and social workers may be the first to notice when grades suddenly slide, the child loses interest in everything or stays tense all day. That is the moment to step in and conduct a home visit,” she said. “Many children feel guilty for getting so many people involved and for their parents being arrested. These situations must be approached with great care and patience, so the child feels safe and is reassured that this is not their fault.” The girl’s school, Lutheran Tsang Shing Siu Leun School, said on Wednesday that social workers and teachers had provided counselling to the pupil and her family. The Education Bureau said it was “highly concerned” and confirmed that the school had activated its crisis management team. Additional reporting by Edith Lin

title: To retire or not to retire? Malaysia divided over working past 60
description: Calls to raise the retirement age come amid warnings over inadequate savings, and experts say a one-size-fits-all policy could hurt workers.
content: Chew Kin Wah spent seven seasons gracing Malaysian television screens as “Kee Tat” in the hit sitcom Kopitiam in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Now 61, the Malaysian actor is still working, albeit more selectively, taking projects when the right offers land on his table. “There is no thought of retiring when you are doing something you enjoy,” he told This Week in Asia, adding: “Money helps. Never fight with money.” For Chew, working beyond 60 is a choice. But for many Malaysians, the question is less about whether they want to keep working than whether they can afford not to. Calls to raise the country’s mandatory retirement age above 60 have reignited debate over whether Malaysians should remain in the workforce longer. Longer lifespans are colliding with inadequate retirement savings and growing concerns over whether older workers can realistically stay employed across vastly different occupations. Shahril Ridza Ridzuan, a former CEO of the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), Malaysia’s mandatory government-backed retirement scheme, recently called for a review of the retirement age. “The reality is that many Malaysians will continue working,” Shahril said at the International Social Wellbeing Conference last week, arguing that older people should be given more opportunities to stay economically active. The EPF caters for private-sector and non-pensionable public sector workers, with more than 18 million registered members. Shahril pointed to low wages as part of Malaysia’s retirement problem, arguing that while the country’s contribution rates were relatively high, low salaries meant many workers still failed to accumulate adequate savings. As of May 31, only 38.3 per cent of active formal-sector Malaysian EPF members aged 18 to 60 had reached the “basic savings” benchmark set for their age group, according to figures provided to parliament. Under the EPF framework, the basic savings target at age 60 is 390,000 ringgit (US$95,000) – an amount intended to provide a minimum monthly income of 1,625 ringgit (US$400) over a 20-year retirement. A greying population The economic argument for keeping older Malaysians in the workforce has been building for years. Malaysia’s rapid transition into becoming an aged society was highlighted by a World Bank report published in 2020. It projected that the share of Malaysians aged 65 and older would rise from more than 7 per cent in 2020 to 14 per cent in 2044, reaching 20 per cent by 2056. “Slower population growth and the shrinking relative size of the working-age population could account for about one-third of the decline in headline gross domestic product growth by 2050,” said the report titled “A Silver Lining: Productive and Inclusive Ageing for Malaysia”. It found that only 45.2 per cent of Malaysians aged 55 to 64 were employed, well below levels seen in high-income economies, while three-quarters of EPF members had less than 250,000 ringgit in their accounts by age 54. But advocacy groups insist that longer life expectancy does not justify raising the official retirement age. “Raising the retirement age needs to consider health span and not chronological age alone,” said Cheah Tuck Wing, chairman of the Malaysian Coalition on Ageing, noting that such a move risked forcing people to work through years of declining health. Cheah said flexible models such as phased retirement should be supported by early lifestyle interventions, preventive healthcare and age-friendly urban planning. “Extending the retirement age above 60 should be flexible, voluntary and sector-sensitive,” he said. “A blanket increase in retirement age is not practical and inequitable.” Increased flexibility Employers also prefer flexibility, arguing that keeping older Malaysians employed does not require shifting the retirement age from 60 to 65. The Malaysian Employers Federation said older workers brought valuable experience and institutional knowledge, but warned that a five-year increase would impose a “one-size-fits-all” solution across various industries and occupations. “The realities of a professional, managerial or advisory position can be very different from those involving physically demanding, safety-sensitive or shift-based work,” federation president Syed Hussain Syed Husman told This Week in Asia. It favours systems that offer older Malaysians opportunities to keep earning a living without an automatic right to remain in the same role on the same terms. Syed Hussain suggested options such as part-time employment, reduced hours, fixed-term contracts, consultancy and mentoring roles or redeploying older staff to less physically demanding positions. He said the federation believed that raising the mandatory retirement age across the board from 60 to 65 “may not be the most appropriate and practical approach for all sectors, occupations and workers”. Unequal burden Not all of Malaysia’s workforce shares the same ability to continue working past 60. Cheah said lower-income Malaysians were more likely to have physically demanding jobs that became harder to do with age – even though they were often the least financially prepared to retire. Higher-income workers, by contrast, could more easily extend their careers. “White-collar professionals can work into their sixties or seventies, bringing experience and maturity to the workforce,” Cheah said, adding that workers in sectors such as construction could face physical limitations that made extending their working lives more difficult. In July, government spokesman Fahmi Fadzil said the cabinet had decided to keep the mandatory retirement age at 60. Yet the government’s 13th Malaysia Plan signals a push to keep older citizens economically active, targeting an increase in labour-force participation among those aged 60 to 64 to 38 per cent by 2030, from 36 per cent in 2024. For Chew – a former quantity surveyor who began acting professionally in 1997 – working past 60 felt natural. While selective about his roles, he feels age matters less than whether the work is still worth doing. “I think the sixties are the new forties because of access to healthcare and fitness routines, so it makes more sense to retire at 70,” he said.

title: Iron cage beds at elderly home in Thailand fuel anger, owner defends ‘innovation’
description: Thai authorities have shut down the nursing home, saying they also plan to bring charges against the owner.
content: A care scandal has erupted in Thailand after a nursing home was exposed for confining old and sick residents in beds covered by iron cages with barely a foot of space above their heads. Images of bedridden patients at the Sothornchai Nursing Home in Kanchanaburi, western Thailand, have shocked Thais since they were shared earlier this week on the television current affairs show Hone Krasae. Thailand is projected to be a super-ageing society in the coming years, with authorities warning of a care crisis and a shortage of money to meet the complex needs of the elderly. A 63-year-old whistle-blower who spoke to Hone Krasae said she was held for over two years at the facility after she was taken there against her will by her son and daughter-in-law, both of whom were seeking control of her cosmetics business. It prompted an inspection of the nursing home by health officials who issued damning findings about standards in the overcrowded home, saying they would close down the facility and consider bringing charges against the owner. The home was licensed to house 50 beds but had more than double that number and kept residents with physical ailments, dementia and complex psychiatric needs, according to a statement by the Department of Health Service Support released on Tuesday. Describing horrific conditions including “rooms with iron bars that could be locked from the outside”, the statement said beds “had been modified with additional iron structures resembling cages to enclose and confine the service recipients in another layer”. Psychiatric patients had been illegally admitted to the nursing home, which was not registered as a medical facility and ill-equipped to deal with their needs, it added. Ying Pornsermsiri, the facility’s owner and a former nurse, defended the use of the bed cages, telling reporters on Wednesday that it was for the protection of the residents. “Had I not put up the cage on their bed like this, these patients would have fallen. They’re incoherent, they don’t know what they’re doing, they would climb all day long,” she said, according to local media reports. In later comments, she doubled down on the use of the cages as an “innovation” in the care sector, seemingly impervious to the anger felt among the Thai public upon seeing the images of frail elders inside the cages. Thailand is the second-fastest ageing nation in Southeast Asia after Singapore. Thirty per cent of Thais are expected to be elderly – or aged 60 and over – by 2035, according to the World Bank, although Thai authorities say that marker could be reached earlier. Facing a labour crunch and spiralling care costs, successive governments have outlined various strategies to cope with the demographic crisis. But they have faced a shortage of funds to pay for pensions, hospices, long-term nursing and medical care. At the same time, Thailand is trying to draw wealthy foreigners from China, Japan, Europe and the US as it positions itself as a global hub for retirement and nursing homes with its trained medical staff, modern care facilities and hospitals. “We’re seeing more quality nursing homes for the elderly emerging, but ordinary people can’t access them,” Ekkapop Sittiwantana, a palliative care expert and an MP for the opposition People’s Party, told This Week in Asia. “We have the personnel, but we don’t have the budget. We don’t have a long-term care system. The additional funding would have to come from taxes or a fund – something no government has ever dared to do because they’re afraid of losing votes.” Inevitably, the responsibility of long-term care falls on family members, while some elderly people have to stay in basic nursing homes with a lack of protection, according to Sittiwantana. “So society has to think together about whether we’re ready to invest collectively in insurance – in guaranteeing protection for the vulnerable – so that when we’re in a state of dependency, we’ll have professionals to care for us.”

title: China’s AI chipmaker Biren tumbles 12% as it seeks US$510 million in share placement
description: The capital injection marks the firm’s second share placement since its Hong Kong listing in January, following a previous round in July.
content: Shares of artificial intelligence chipmaker Shanghai Biren Technology tumbled more than 12 per cent in Hong Kong on Thursday amid plans to raise HK$4 billion (US$510 million) through a share placement, as competition with other Chinese Nvidia challengers intensifies. The sell-off followed a stock exchange filing by the Hong Kong-listed company on late Wednesday, which revealed it had engaged placing agents on a “best effort” basis to issue 130 million new shares at HK$31.08 apiece. The offering price represents a roughly 10 per cent discount to the stock’s closing price of HK$34.44 on the previous day. The new shares would account for around 5 per cent of its total issued shares as of Wednesday, according to the filing. Biren shares dropped to as low as HK$30.24 before closing down 11.9 per cent at HK$30.36 on Thursday. The capital injection marks the firm’s second share placement since its Hong Kong listing in January, following a previous round in July that raised HK$7 billion, bringing its combined fundraising from the two recent placements to more than HK$11 billion in just three months. The move adds to a broader frenzy of massive fundraising efforts across China’s semiconductor sector this year, as domestic Nvidia challengers increasingly tap equity markets to bankroll Beijing’s mandate for tech self-reliance. Rivals Moore Threads and MetaX, both listed in Shanghai, have announced plans for a flotation in Hong Kong. Biren said its latest fundraising was driven by “faster than anticipated” progress in developing its new-generation AI processors and growing demand for computing power. Its new-generation product had completed initial testing and entered post-silicon validation, bringing it closer to customer sampling and commercial production, according to the filing. The company plans to allocate about 70 per cent of net proceeds from the new share placement to secure manufacturing capacity, procure components and prepare for the commercial launch of its next-generation products. Another 20 per cent would be used to strengthen research and development (R&D) capabilities and its software ecosystem, while the remaining 10 per cent would support working capital and general corporate purposes, according to the filing. The latest fundraising comes as Biren reports rapid revenue growth, reflecting China’s expanding market for domestically developed AI processors, although the company has yet to turn a profit. In the first six months of 2026, its revenue surged around 21-fold to 1.24 billion yuan (US$184.9 million), driven largely by increased sales of its intelligent computing solutions. Its net loss narrowed to 377 million yuan, compared with 1.6 billion yuan a year earlier. Despite the improvement, Biren continues to spend heavily on developing its processors and related technologies. R&D expenses rose 40.7 per cent to 804 million yuan in the first half.

title: Macroscope | How Japanese bond yields, Chinese competition are stoking euro-zone fears
description: China has exploited the EU’s ineffective integration while Japanese bond investors fear the financial consequences of reform failures.
content: When the governor of the Bank of France feels it is necessary to point out that “France is not Greece during the euro zone crisis”, it is clear there is a confidence problem at the heart of Europe’s monetary union. While there are stark differences between the current threats facing the single currency area and those that almost tore apart the bloc in 2012, bond investors can smell blood. Worryingly, France – the euro-zone’s second-largest economy, which was previously treated by investors as part of the bloc’s safe core – is the main cause for concern. On October 2, the yield on French 10-year bonds hit 5 per cent, its highest level since 2002. France is paying more to borrow than Greece and Italy, once the euro-zone’s riskiest borrowers. In a sign of the degree to which the sell-off in French debt has revived fears about the financial fragmentation of the bloc, the additional interest rate France pays to borrow over safe German bonds has risen to its highest level since 2012. “The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot,” said Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank. France is clearly being singled out because of strong political resistance to fiscal austerity, the prospect of far-right leader Marine Le Pen winning next year’s French presidential election and the toxic mix of high public debt and anaemic growth. One of France’s vulnerabilities is its heavy reliance on foreign demand for its government debt. Overseas investors own 58 per cent of the country’s bonds. Moreover, Japan is the largest holder of French debt outside the euro zone, according to JPMorgan data. This is why Japan’s bond market has emerged as a source of risk. While French bonds used to offer attractive returns, the surge in Japanese yields during the past year, coupled with mounting concerns over France’s fiscal irresponsibility, has changed the calculus for Japanese investors. On a currency-hedged basis, French bond yields are not high enough to compensate Japanese investors for the country’s political and fiscal risks. Japanese bonds, by contrast, provide local investors with a decent return without the exposure to French sovereign risk. Signs that Japanese investors have begun to sell French debt come amid growing speculation about the repatriation of Japanese money – particularly pension fund assets – out of foreign bonds and back into Japanese debt. “We suspect the latest round of rapid [French bond] selling over the past week might have been fuelled by Japanese portfolio rebalancing,” TS Lombard said. However, the stress in euro-zone debt markets is a far cry from the panic that engulfed the bloc in 2011-12. The current financial vulnerabilities are idiosyncratic as opposed to systemic, at least for now. The real crisis is in the economy. While the European Central Bank can suppress bond yields by intervening in markets, it cannot fix the deep-seated structural problems confronting Europe. According to Robin Brooks of the Brookings Institution, the euro-zone sovereign debt crisis “never really ended”. The big difference, however, between today’s threats and those 15 years ago is the rise of China. Nowhere is the impact of the “second China shock” more apparent than in the euro zone. The European Union was largely shielded from the first shock in the 2000s when a flood of low-cost Chinese goods upended the business models of manufacturers in the West, especially in the United States. The second, which began in 2020, is far more threatening to Europe. China’s formidable manufacturers are outcompeting European producers in advanced industries that were once the preserve of European firms. Germany is the most exposed. In 2013, China accounted for 5 per cent of global car exports. Last year, its share had risen to 15 per cent, on a par with Germany’s. Fierce competition at home, huge industrial scale, generous subsidies, a vast pool of engineering talent and an undervalued exchange rate have contributed to Chinese firms’ aggressive expansion in Europe, squeezing out domestic producers. Yet while the severity of the competitive threat has caused Germany to align itself more closely with France in calling for a tougher response in the EU’s acrimonious trade negotiations with China, it has also accentuated and exacerbated the euro-zone’s home-grown failings. ING believes geopolitical and trade tensions “could be the nudge Europe needs” to increase corporate investment by deepening the single market and liberalising labour markets, yet structural adjustment has long been the euro-zone’s biggest weakness. Bond markets have turned on France partly because of the country’s unwillingness to engage in reforms. The euro-zone’s economic woes run deep and are rooted in the partial and ineffective integration of the bloc. China has exploited this vulnerability while Japanese bond investors fear its financial consequences.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, October 9-11
description: A story-led exhibition, a fundraising cabaret and a mental health awareness campaign are just a few things to look out for this weekend.
content: As the weather cools in October, it is finally pleasant enough to venture out on weekends, so it is time to trade the indoor hustle for this season’s best offerings. This weekend’s line-up brings together meaningful community events, immersive storytelling and unique local flavours across the city. Here are five things to do in Hong Kong this weekend. 1. ‘What We Regret Most’ “What We Regret Most” is a community-driven, story-led exhibition that invites people to embrace the messy, awkward and shameful decisions everyone makes, rather than erase or ignore past mistakes. The public submitted about 40 stories and objects, each carrying a different story imbued with longing or regret, and showcased in this free exhibition. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Heath 慶方 (@heath_hk) On show until October 27, the programme also includes guided meditations on letting go of the past, a “wall of regrets” for visitors and a series of performances. The Garage @ Heath, B/F, 36-44 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 2. Little Bao x Regent Hong Kong From now until October 31, luxury hotel Regent Hong Kong presents “Hong Kong at Heart”, a month-long residency featuring chef May Chow – founder of modern Chinese restaurant Little Bao – at The Lobby Lounge. Chow, partnering with the Regent’s executive chef Calvin Choi, brings her signature playful reimagining of the classic bao. Each creation draws inspiration from local classics, from comforting Chiu Chow noodles and lively dai pai dong seafood to familiar cha chaan teng dishes, nostalgic dim sum and sweet street treats. Highlights include the salt-and-pepper kuruma prawn bao and an ice cream bao inspired by put chai ko, a steamed, sticky rice pudding. Restaurant bookings can be made via the Regent’s online booking platform. Regent Hong Kong, 18 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui 3. Hong Kong Players’ ‘What a Pair!’ September was Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, while October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month. In a mission to raise money for cancer support and research, non-profit theatre organisation Hong Kong Players will perform a one-night-only fundraising cabaret, What a Pair! The performance features local actors, singers and volunteers performing in duos to showcase musical duets and comedic duologues reminiscent of Shakespeare’s dramatic plays. Enjoy a fun night out while supporting a good cause, because all proceeds from ticket sales directly support cancer research and care initiatives. Two shows – one at 5pm and the other at 7.30pm – are scheduled, and tickets are priced at HK$250 (US$32). Click here for more information. Fa Gai, G/F, Wyndham Mansion, 32 Wyndham Street, Central 4. The Green Ribbon Campaign OCD and Anxiety Support Hong Kong (OCDAHK) will host its 12th annual Green Ribbon Campaign on October 10, World Mental Health Day. Taking place across two public booths in Central – at Theatre Lane and outside Central Tower – the campaign provides a stigma- and pressure-free environment to encourage mental health conversations between parents and children. Additionally, charity merchandise will be available for purchase to raise funds for Rainbow of Hope, OCDAHK’s low-cost counselling clinic supporting individuals affected by anxiety, high stress and depression. Available items include signature metal green pins, well-being Post-it notes, tumblers and more. Visit the official website for more information about the organisation. 5. Primetime The latest entry in the journalism movie category that includes the likes of Network (1976), Shattered Glass (2003), Nightcrawler (2014) and Spotlight (2015), Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime turns the lens on Dateline NBC, the US news magazine show, and in particular the work of Chris Hansen, the presenter of To Catch a Predator – a disturbing segment that began in 2004. The show aimed to sniff out and expose internet paedophiles who attempted to lure underage children into meeting them. Played with oil-slick excellence by Robert Pattinson – who also serves as a producer – Hansen is a suited-and-booted showman who steps in once predators are caught on camera with a decoy. Inspired by real-life events – in particular, a sting operation that went disastrously wrong – Oppenheim’s film asks us to consider the ethics and dangers of such crusading television shows, and how complicit we might be as an audience howling for justice. Read the full review here. Primetime is in cinemas now.

title: In Indonesia, will VP Gibran’s ‘diploma-gate’ haunt his future after court ruling?
description: The Constitutional Court ruled to keep Gibran as VP, but doubts over his education spark impeachment calls and threaten his political future.
content: A legal challenge to the vice-presidency of Indonesia’s Gibran Rakabuming Raka could haunt his political future even though he has survived damning court findings on his educational qualifications. The Constitutional Court on Tuesday dismissed a petition to unseat the son of former president Joko Widodo, ruling that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing. But it also found no convincing evidence that Gibran’s overseas education met the minimum high-school qualification required for presidential candidates. Legal experts say the ruling has shifted the battleground to parliament and law enforcement agencies, potentially opening a Pandora’s box for Gibran. Political observers, however, doubt President Prabowo Subianto would risk a confrontation that could destabilise his government. Gibran, who ran on the 2024 ticket alongside Prabowo – capturing 58.59 per cent of the vote – is likely to retain his office for now, but analysts say he will be dogged by questions over his future political career. Delivering the judgment on Tuesday, Chief Justice Suhartoyo argued that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing to dispute the presidential election result because they were not contestants in the race. “Consequently, the court rules that their petition be declared inadmissible,” he said. Although the court unequivocally stated it was in no position to disqualify the vice-president, it noted there was “no convincing evidence” to confirm that Gibran had completed an education equivalent to Indonesian senior high school. In a news conference after the ruling, lawyer Refly Harun, one of the plaintiffs, quipped to reporters that it was unprecedented in Constitutional Court history for a ruling to bring celebration to both sides of a trial. “The defendant is happy because he still gets to keep his vice-presidency, for now. But we are also happy because we’ve satisfactorily proved that he doesn’t have a high school diploma,” Refly said, adding that the ruling should shame Gibran into resigning. Known locally as “Gibran’s diploma-gate”, the saga erupted on September 10 when 12 plaintiffs, led by constitutional law expert and former deputy minister of law and human rights Denny Indrayana, filed a petition with the court. In their complaint, they accused Gibran of manipulating his secondary school degree equivalency certification. Under Indonesian election law passed in 2003, presidential and vice-presidential candidates must have completed senior high school or its equivalent. According to his educational record, Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore, where he completed his O-Levels, before taking a pathway programme at UTS Insearch in Sydney, Australia. He subsequently attained his bachelor’s degree in marketing from the UK’s University of Bradford via the Management Development Institute of Singapore in 2010. The petitioners asked the court to nullify his vice-presidency on grounds of fraud. Herlambang P. Wiratraman, an associate professor and director of the Research Centre for Law and Social Justice at Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia, told This Week in Asia that the Constitutional Court had delivered a sound ruling that had gone as far as its legal remit allowed. “I see it as a vigorous nudge at getting the other state institutions to act on the verdict and do their jobs under the constitution,” Herlambang said. State administrative law scholar Bivitri Susanti, who testified as an expert witness for the plaintiffs during the court’s two-week proceedings, agreed that the ruling opened up other legal avenues for Gibran’s removal. “The House of Representatives can now legally start a process of impeachment against the vice-president,” she said, adding that law enforcement agencies should also initiate an investigation into Gibran for alleged forgery to strengthen the impeachment case. “So the ball is in the politicians’ court now.” On Wednesday, a group calling itself Advocators For Upholding National Ethics, Morals and Integrity filed a police report against Gibran for falsifying his educational record. “But I suspect the police will stop short of conducting an actual investigation,” said Made Supriatma, a political analyst and visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Made said Prabowo would want to prevent the issue from escalating into a full-blown political crisis. “The ramifications for an impeachment process would be too volatile and unpredictable for his administration.” Prabowo has so far steered clear of the controversy, offering no public comment. However, Syahganda Nainggolan, recently appointed head of the Government Communications Agency, said in a podcast on Monday that the president had “long been aware of Gibran’s fake diploma, but saw it as a non-priority for the government to tackle”. Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at Jakarta-based pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, pointed to another aspect of the debate he believed was being overlooked. “As a guardian of democracy, the court should’ve borne in mind that limiting elected office to people of certain educational backgrounds is elitist, if not non-inclusive,” Saidiman said. He questioned using formal qualifications as a benchmark for public officials, pointing out that most Western democracies did not impose educational prerequisites on elected political leaders. He also questioned the plaintiffs’ motives in targeting Gibran’s overseas education as a legal loophole. “It’s obvious they had a target on his back with this manoeuvre, with the end game being his political demise – either through removal from office or by barring him from future elections on technicalities.” But Made said that what Gibran did with his education documents was essentially illegal. “He sought to circumvent existing regulations through falsification, and that is always wrong.” Analysts are divided on whether the court’s findings automatically bar Gibran from running again for vice-president or president in the future. “This constitutional blight on his persona should strongly dissuade political parties from nominating him as a candidate,” Bivitri said. In contrast, Saidiman saw the ruling as no impediment to Gibran’s future candidacy, provided a proper degree equivalency certificate could be obtained from the Ministry of Education. Gibran has publicly denied not having completed his secondary education. “If I hadn’t graduated from high school, I wouldn’t have been able to enrol at a university. Please bear in mind I finished my tertiary education in Singapore,” he told reporters on Wednesday. Made said that Gibran might retain his current post but would likely not emerge unscathed. “His political legitimacy will greatly suffer as a result,” Made said. “And this will come back to haunt him again and again.”

title: Hong Kong IPO boom at risk as cornerstone backers get cold feet, sources say
description: At least one listing postponed, while bankers scramble for investors to keep other offerings on track, according to sources.
content: Exuberance among cornerstone investors in Hong Kong’s booming initial public offering (IPO) market seems to be fading, forcing some issuers that had hoped to list this month to postpone their offerings. With more than 60 per cent of new listings in the third quarter now trading below their issue prices, cornerstone investors – who typically receive guaranteed allocations in exchange for holding shares for six months – are reconsidering whether to subscribe to coming deals, according to people familiar with the matter. At least one IPO originally planned for October had to be delayed until next month at the earliest after some institutional investors pulled out of verbal agreements to be cornerstone backers, they said. “Bankers are now scrambling to find replacements,” said the people, who asked not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly. The slowdown follows a weak showing among the city’s largest debuts this year. Out of the nine Hong Kong listings that raised more than US$1 billion in the first three quarters, six are now trading in the red. For example, Chinese energy-drink maker Eastroc Beverage has plummeted more than 60 per cent from its issue price since its debut in February. “Even if they don’t exit entirely, some say they want to reduce their investment size or go back through their internal investment committee,” the people added. “Issuers with high valuations and unclear earnings are especially affected.” This post-IPO weakness had severely undermined long-term investor confidence, particularly amid ongoing market volatility, said Edward Au Chung-hing, southern region managing partner at accounting firm Deloitte China. Funds raised through Hong Kong IPOs reached US$48.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, marking the highest level for this period since records began in 1980, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. However, as of September 30, out of 31 companies that listed in the city during the third quarter, 20 – more than 60 per cent – fell below their offer prices. Among them, electronic test equipment manufacturer Rigol Technologies, medical device maker Medcaptain Medical Technology, Chinese autonomous driving firm Momenta and Beijing Tong Ren Tang Healthcare Investment have all seen their share prices halved from their offer prices. Blockbuster IPOs launched during the quarter also performed poorly. Only Innolight’s shares remain above its issue price, while Shein and Luxshare are currently trading 27 per cent and 20 per cent below their issue prices, respectively. Sovereign wealth funds and private equity firms such as GIC, Hillhouse and Temasek actively took part in Hong Kong’s IPO market, but most have recorded paper losses. Temasek subscribed to a total of more than US$500 million worth of shares across Chaozhou Chaozhou Three-Circle, Eastroc Beverage, Luxshare, and Innolight, but three of these investments are now sitting on losses. Over the past few years, the number of international cornerstone investors in Hong Kong IPOs has steadily recovered, reaching a recent high this year. Beyond traditional Asian investors, long-term funds from the Middle East, Europe, North America and the Asia-Pacific region have continued to increase their participation, said Bonnie Chan Yiting, CEO of bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), last month. Among the top 10 largest IPOs this year, seven had cornerstone allocations account for nearly 50 per cent of their total fundraising – mostly for companies listed in the first half of the year. In contrast, Shein, which listed in the third quarter, had a cornerstone allocation of only 22 per cent. For smaller listings like RoboTechnik Intelligent Technology and Shenzhen Longsys Electronics, cornerstone participation stood at 35 per cent and 18 per cent, respectively. “Investors will become more selective and cautious, and investment amounts may decrease, but this will not deter companies’ ambition to list in Hong Kong,” Au said.

title: Police recover HK$30 million in gold swapped for fabric softener in hotel theft
description: Two men held and all 30kg of gold recovered after travelling companion allegedly let accomplices into the hotel room to swap granules for eight bottles of softener.
content: Hong Kong police have recovered about HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) worth of stolen gold and arrested two men in connection with an elaborate hotel-room swap in which 30kg of gold granules were replaced with eight bottles of fabric softener. The force said it received a report early on Wednesday from a mainland Chinese man who said about 30kg of gold granules, valued at around HK$30 million, were suspected to have been stolen from his luggage in a Kwun Tong hotel. The gold had been replaced with eight similarly weighted bottles of fabric softener and a friend travelling with him in the same room had disappeared. Police traced the suspects using the city’s surveillance camera network. A man was arrested in Tai Po at noon on Wednesday, and officers found a room card for a hotel in the same district on him. They went to the hotel room and recovered all of the gold. Another suspect was arrested while attempting to leave Hong Kong at the Lo Wu control point. Chief Inspector Tang Tsz-hin, of the Kwun Tong police district, described the case as “meticulously planned”. “The mastermind is the victim’s travelling companion, who is suspected of arranging for two other men to buy the fabric softener in advance and book an adjacent hotel room,” he said. “When the victim briefly went downstairs for a cigarette, his friend opened the door to let the two men into the room to steal the gold. The culprits managed to swap out 30kg of gold in just two minutes.” The suspects used different modes of transport after the crime in an attempt to mislead investigators, police said. Tang revealed the two male suspects, aged 27 and 41, were Chinese nationals holding two-way permits – travel documents issued by mainland authorities for visits to the city – and were being held for inquiries. The victim also came to Hong Kong on a two-way permit and mainly bought and sold gold at licensed institutions. The man travelling with him was a friend with whom he had worked for months. Police said they believed the alleged mastermind had already left Hong Kong before the victim filed his report and were searching for him. Under Hong Kong law, theft carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment.

title: China and other energy importers lead shift from oil to clean energy, report says
description: Clean capacity grows three times faster across China, India and Europe than in Middle East, North America and Russia, DNV says.
content: China and other energy-importing countries are expanding clean energy capacity three times faster than energy-exporting nations, according to a recent report on the global energy transition. The shift reflects growing determination among governments to reduce reliance on imported oil and gas, a trend reinforced by disruption of shipping via critical chokepoint the Strait of Hormuz, according to risk-management firm DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook released on Wednesday. Over the last five years, the share of non-fossil energy in the primary energy mix across China, India and Europe has increased by 2.2 percentage points, compared with a gain of just 0.7 percentage points across the Middle East, North America and Russia, the report said. “Transition strategies are now more heavily linked to national interests,” said DNV CEO Knut Orbeck-Nilsen. “Fossil-importing nations are accelerating the adoption of clean energy technologies to reduce exposure to volatile fuel markets, while many fossil-exporting countries are transitioning more slowly.” The US-Israel war on Iran that started in February remains stuck in a costly stalemate of deadlocked talks and ongoing threats to shipping through the strait. The DNV findings carry particular significance for China, a major buyer of oil and gas from the Middle East and other regions, as it prioritises energy security through domestic production and renewable deployment. Already a dominant player in clean energy manufacturing, it is now, along with other import-reliant economies, accelerating its transition at a pace far exceeding that of exporters, according to the report. While the disruption from the war in the Middle East was “among the most severe in history”, its impact had been “moderated by strategic reserves, particularly in China”, DNV said. The report predicted that the Middle East’s share of global oil production would drop to around 40 per cent in 2050, down from a 50 per cent projection made last year, according to the firm. China’s dual role as both a major importer of fossil fuels and a global supplier of clean energy technologies – solar panels, wind turbines and batteries – positions it uniquely in this shifting landscape. In Europe, China and India, absolute electricity demand would grow by 62 per cent on average over the coming two decades, the report projected. North America, the Middle East and Russia would also electrify due to efficiency gains and cost advantages, but at a slower pace – a 47 per cent increase over the same period, according to DNV. “China is setting the pace for electrification,” the report said, estimating electricity would supply more than 50 per cent of the nation’s final energy demand by 2060, an 85 per cent increase from 27 per cent currently. The report projected that by 2050, the world would reduce emissions by 44 per cent from today’s levels. But that will not even be halfway to net-zero emissions, it added. Beijing has stated goals of peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060, driven in part by energy security concerns.

title: Chinese team says its all-in-one mini artificial pancreas offers next-gen diabetes care
description: Smartphone-controlled prototype offers a patient-friendly design for automated insulin delivery.
content: Chinese scientists have created a wearable all-in-one device combining a glucose sensor and insulin micropump that they say paves the way for a fully autonomous mini artificial pancreas, although it has so far only been tested on mice. Unlike existing commercial systems for managing diabetes that typically require patients to wear two separate patches for monitoring and hormone delivery, the new prototype combines both functions in a single coin-sized device. Researchers from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China said their smartphone-controlled intelligent device offered a shift for next-generation diabetes management. “We present a wearable closed-loop insulin micropump that enables a miniaturised artificial pancreas in diabetes therapy,” the researchers said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Microsystems & Nanoengineering on September 29. Equipped with an electrochemical insulin micropump and a microneedle glucose monitoring unit, the device autonomously suppressed blood sugar spikes when tested in type 1 diabetic mouse models. With an outer diameter and thickness of about 2cm (0.8 inches), the device is smaller than commercial insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitoring devices on the market, according to the researchers. “This highly integrated, miniaturised design offers a compelling paradigm shift for next-generation patient-friendly diabetes-management systems,” the team said. Diabetes is a disease where the pancreas does not produce enough insulin – the hormone that controls glucose levels in the blood – or when the body is unable to effectively use the insulin it produces, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Unmanaged diabetes can cause complications such as heart disease, kidney failure, stroke, blindness, limb amputation and death. According to the International Diabetes Federation, about 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes, with the number estimated to exceed 850 million – or 1 in 8 adults – by 2050. People with type 1 diabetes do not produce enough insulin and need to take it to survive. This form of diabetes is not preventable and there is no cure. Type 2 diabetes, which affects the vast majority of diabetics, is an often preventable form that can involve impaired insulin production or insulin resistance. Blood glucose levels can be managed through diet, exercise and medication, along with insulin administration. In 2022, more than half of people aged 30 and above living with diabetes worldwide did not take medication to treat it, with coverage the worst in low and middle-income countries, according to the WHO. Insulin management has shifted from manual injections towards automated delivery and hybrid closed-loop systems that pair wearable insulin pumps with continuous glucose-monitoring sensors. “Despite these clinical triumphs, the realisation of a fully autonomous, highly integrated and patient-friendly artificial pancreas remains hindered by the fundamental architectures of current commercial devices,” the Chinese team said. Even in leading automated delivery systems, the sensor functions as a separate unit. Existing pumps also typically rely on mechanical or electromagnetic drives, which can make the devices rigid, bulky and energy intensive. The team’s new device has an electrochemical micropump, a hydrogel microneedle monitoring unit that uses glucose-responsive fluorescence to measure blood sugar levels, and a wireless low-energy Bluetooth control circuit controlled via smartphone. When the device senses high blood sugar, the control circuit is activated to output an electrical current. This drives electrodes within the micropump to electrolyse water and generate gas, causing pressure that pushes against a latex membrane to deliver insulin into the body. “As the blood glucose level gradually returns to baseline, the system automatically suspends drug delivery. Thus, an intelligent theranostic loop without manual intervention is established,” the paper said. A smartphone application can also be used to monitor glucose levels and execute personalised treatment interventions. In testing, the device functioned stably in typical environmental temperatures. According to the team, the micropump and control circuits allow for extended wear exceeding 20 days, while the hydrogel microneedle patch is designed to be modularly replaceable more frequently. By comparison, market-leading glucose sensors such as the Dexcom can be worn for 10 to 15 days, while leading patch pumps like the Omnipod require changing every three days. The team tested its new device in mice and found that punctures from the microneedle patch disappeared within 15 minutes and said the therapeutic efficacy of the micropump matched that of traditional manual insulin injections. To transition from mice to humans, the team said dosing requirements must be carefully considered – maintaining an ultra-compact device would require higher concentration insulin formulations. “This ultra-compact and wireless paradigm transcends the dimensional limitations of traditional devices, providing a viable patient-friendly blueprint for the future of personalised diabetes care,” the researchers said.

title: US AI firm Anthropic enables Chinese-language options for Claude chatbot
description: Analysts say overseas Chinese communities are the likely target, rather than any plan to enter the mainland China market.
content: US artificial intelligence company Anthropic has introduced Chinese-language options to its Claude chatbot in supported markets, even as it continues to block users from mainland China. Checks by the South China Morning Post on Thursday confirmed that Claude’s web interface now lets users select simplified and traditional Chinese as their preferred on-screen language. China also briefly appeared as a billing country option before disappearing from the settings. Users on X have shared screenshots showing UnionPay, China’s dominant bank card network, as a payment option at checkout. The SCMP was unable to independently confirm whether UnionPay payments were active. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. While the updates sparked speculation among some Chinese users that Anthropic might be preparing to ease access restrictions, analysts said the features were likely to target overseas Chinese communities rather than signalling any plan to enter the mainland market. Poe Zhao, a China technology analyst and the founder of Hello China Tech, said the changes aimed to serve Chinese-speaking users in supported markets such as Singapore, Malaysia, Taiwan and North America. “Offering a product in Chinese and serving users in China are two different decisions,” Zhao said. “Anthropic can do the first without the second. “The official supported-region list is the best indicator of its strategy, and it has not changed.” Su Lian Jye, chief analyst at Omdia, agreed that Anthropic appeared to be targeting the global Chinese diaspora rather than attempting to “warm up the Chinese market”, describing the localisation as a commercially significant step to enhance user experience. The distinction highlights the balancing act facing Anthropic as it seeks to expand Claude’s global footprint while enforcing some of the industry’s strictest controls against access from mainland China. The updates follow what appeared to be a recent tightening of Anthropic’s geographical restrictions. Last week, several Hong Kong users reported abrupt account suspensions after accessing Claude via virtual private networks (VPNs). Mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau remain excluded from the San Francisco-based company’s official list of supported regions. The line between Chinese-speaking users overseas and users based in China will always be difficult to draw precisely Last month, Anthropic accused Chinese AI developers, including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, of conducting “industrial-scale” distillation using fraudulent accounts and proxy services to harvest Claude’s outputs and reasoning traces. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also repeatedly warned of the risks to the United States’ national security posed by China’s AI advances, urging Washington to maintain strict export controls on advanced chips and equipment. Analysts expect Anthropic to carefully screen new account sign-ups to maintain its enforcement policies without loosening standards. “The line between Chinese-speaking users overseas and users based in China will always be difficult to draw precisely, given VPNs, foreign payment cards and resold accounts,” Zhao said. “Anthropic relies on payment checks, IP detection and account reviews to manage it. I don’t expect this change to make those rules looser.” Su added that Anthropic might shift towards tighter identity verification to distinguish between the two user groups, which could provoke further friction with Beijing. Anthropic’s strategy reflects a broader trend among American AI companies. Earlier this year, OpenAI began recruiting staff to serve Chinese-speaking clients despite keeping its services blocked in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau. Industry experts said the move highlighted the growing global influence of Chinese-speaking developers.

title: NBA star Kyrie Irving’s deeply held connection with China a case of ‘paying it forward’
description: Dallas Mavericks star guard gets bulk of attention in build-up to NBA China Games in Macau thanks to personal, professional ties to the nation.
content: No offence to Kyrie Irving’s Dallas Mavericks teammates or, for that matter, the Houston Rockets, but there is no question who will get the loudest cheers on Friday and Sunday in the NBA China Games. Nor is there any doubt which player will attract the most cameras and reporter questions during Thursday’s Mavericks-Rockets Media Day, which is projected to be covered by more than 400 journalists, most of them from China and other Asian countries. China’s love fest with Mavericks star guard Irving, 34, dates well over a decade. During a quiet moment of reflection after Wednesday’s practice in Macau’s Venetian Arena, The Dallas Morning News asked Irving why he engendered such strong feelings in the country, and vice versa. “Well, when you come here at 19 years old, it’s hard not to make friends and get to know everybody,” he said. “I think initially coming over here, I didn’t know what to expect, and it’s grown on me ever since because of just the amount of support that I get. “As soon as I land and get off the plane, fans are waiting at the airport. I get to the hotel, fans are waiting at the hotel. I go to the weight room, the fans are waiting in the weight room. They just love sport here. They love basketball. They love what we bring to the culture, as well.” It is no coincidence the global sportswear and equipment company with which Irving is so personally aligned, Anta, is based in Jingjiang, having been founded there in 1991. When Irving signed with Anta in July of 2023, it was a natural fit. He did not just sign with the company; he became its chief creative officer. He plays an active role in brand direction, design and marketing. And it is certainly not happenstance that these NBA China Games will bookend a big day for Irving and Anta. Saturday will mark the global release of the Anta Macau Pack, debuting with two of what is expected to be four new colourways: the KAI 3 “Hearts” and KAIBRID “Spades”. Macau, of course, is known as the Las Vegas of Asia. It is the only place in China that has legalised gambling. The Friday and Sunday pre-season games against Houston here in the Las Vegas Sands-owned Venetian Arena mark Irving’s return to the court from a 19-month absence following his left ACL tear of March 3, 2025. Irving and Anta have dubbed this “The Return” season. During a promotional visit to China in June, Irving shocked an 18-year-old superfan in China by dropping into his home in Shanghai, unannounced. Just another, albeit famous, case of Irving and China connecting on a personal level. “What we represent, especially in America, they follow what we release – whether it be apparel, whether it be shoes or whether it be quotes on our Instagram,” Irving said. “Or whether it be outfits that we’re wearing. “They really enjoy our freedom to express, and I think that’s something that connects me. I have a very liberating spirit that I like to offer. Give a lot of hugs. I take walks around the town. “I’ll surprise fans at their house or their apartment. Just do little things to make sure I’m staying engaged because the love is just continuing to grow. Mainly for me, it’s about paying it forward.” Irving tore his ACL in March 2025 during the first quarter of the Mavericks’ ‌loss to the Sacramento Kings. He stayed on the court to make two free throws before leaving the game in tears. Irving missed the final 20 games of the 2024-25 season after the injury. He averaged 24.7 points, 4.8 rebounds, 4.6 assists and 1.3 steals in 50 games that season, before also sitting out the 2025-26 campaign. “Conditioning is going ⁠great,” Irving told reporters ahead of the game against the Rockets on Friday. “I feel great. ‌Just going through the rigours of just the contact and being in this combative sport. “Just practices, games within practice that we have, or scrimmages, just ‌really testing out where I am. I feel like I’m still unlocking things ⁠in my instincts and ⁠my proprioception and just getting used to just being able to play high-level basketball consistently. “Practices do wonders but the ‌game is, it can’t be recreated. So I’m excited to strap up my boots, get out there, throw on my uniform, play ‌in ‌front of these great fans here, and continue to have a strong pre-season.” Irving’s return comes ‌as the Mavericks continue to reshape their identity following the blockbuster trade that sent Slovenian Luka ⁠Doncic to the Los Angeles Lakers in February 2025. The franchise is now building around reigning Rookie of ⁠the Year Cooper Flagg, the top pick in the 2025 NBA Draft, with first-year coach Dusty May at the helm after his national title-winning stint at Michigan. “I’m really ‌excited to be able ‌to share the court with Kyrie. He’s obviously a special, special player,” Flagg, 19, said.

title: Abby Choi’s ex-father-in-law ‘cunning old fox’ who clung to her wealth, court told
description: Socialite’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, rejects defence claims that Kwong Kau paid HK$30 million towards an upscale flat at centre of dispute.
content: The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has described her daughter’s former father-in-law as a “cunning old fox” who clung to her family’s fortune, dismissing his lawyer’s claim that he paid HK$30 million towards an upscale flat at the centre of a bitter dispute between the two families. Cheung Yin-fa told the High Court on Thursday that her daughter had given Kwong Kau a monthly allowance of HK$20,000 (US$2,548) and paid more than HK$200,000 towards his medical expenses when he was seriously ill. She appeared emotional when defence counsel suggested that Kwong, a former police sergeant, could afford a Rolls-Royce and a seven-seater car because he had made money from business activities in mainland China since retiring from the force. “This is definitely impossible ... He couldn’t even afford his meals; how could he spend HK$6 million to HK$7 million on a Rolls-Royce?” Cheung said on the fourth day of her testimony. “He had no money when he was about to die. Had my daughter not used her credit card to give him HK$200,000, he’d have been [expletive] dead in half an hour.” Asked about Choi’s decision to take back what she had given to the Kwong family, Cheung said: “Because his foxtail was exposed, so she had to cut ties with them and take things back. This old fox, Kwong Kau, is very cunning.” Kwong, 68, allegedly enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old model and dispose of her body in February 2023 after she tried to sell a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Cheung said the flat was registered in Kwong’s name to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty, and that her daughter never intended to give the property to the family. Kwong is standing trial on a joint charge of murder alongside his sons, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31. The elder Kwong has also pleaded not guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial. In their opening statement, prosecutors suggested that money was the motive for the crime and highlighted the substantial wealth gap between the two families. During cross-examination, Kwong Kau’s defence counsel, Oliver Davies, argued that the Choi family was not as wealthy as Cheung had claimed in earlier testimony. Instead, he portrayed Kwong Kau as a businessman with considerable savings, who was able to contribute half the HK$60 million purchase price of the flat in Kadooria in 2019. Davies said Kwong stood to gain nothing by agreeing to become the flat’s owner at the risk of being prosecuted for tax evasion. Cheung dismissed the lawyer’s contentions and said the two families had agreed that Kwong was simply holding the property on trust for the benefit of the two children Choi had with Alex Kwong. Davies cast doubt on Cheung’s depiction of her husband, Choi Cho-san, as a successful merchant and questioned how he was able to give her a HK$1 million monthly allowance when he was regularly in debt. Land Registry records showed the elder Choi, whose name was written as Tsoi Chor-sang, had pawned Cheung’s former home at Whampoa Garden three times and taken out a mortgage before he sold it for HK$12 million in 2019. Cheung acknowledged she was aware of her husband’s financial difficulties, while revealing she had been receiving his money via a currency exchange shop. Davies said Abby Choi, despite leading a luxurious lifestyle, was not rich either, and she did not leave behind a vast amount of assets at the time of her death. The court heard the influencer had less than HK$6.5 million in her three bank accounts, and the total value of her stocks was about HK$5.5 million as of February 2023. While she owned a property in the Manhattan Hill residential complex in Lai Chi Kok, it had an outstanding mortgage of HK$10 million. Cheung said she had no idea about her daughter’s finances but reiterated that the socialite had been providing for her former in-laws until her death. “Their whole family had been living off the blessing of the two grandchildren [the two children Choi had with Kwong]. Their greed knows no bounds,” she said. Davies also said Choi was unable to repay a HK$5 million loan taken out by her husband, Chris Tam Fong-chun, when he gambled in Macau during the Covid-19 pandemic. Cheung said the repayment was only delayed because the casino concerned closed down shortly after the trip to Macau. She also denied that Tam was a gambling addict. Counsel Andrew Raffell, representing Alex Kwong, suggested that Cheung had been tailoring her evidence to fit the police theory about how the alleged murder came about. Cheung said she was merely cooperating with police. Raffell described his client as a gentle and introverted man who had been bullied by his father and was less mature than Choi during their school years. Cheung said her former son-in-law had indeed been a good person before, but added that he was also good at currying favours. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Britain downscales and renames Jerusalem consulate after Israel orders closure
description: Now operating as the ‘UK Mission’, London says it will continue ‘vital services’ following a row over West Bank settlements.
content: Britain and Israel announced on Thursday that the nearly 200-year-old British diplomatic mission in Jerusalem would stay open at a smaller scale and with a new name, in a compromise after Israel ordered the consulate shut in a sanctions dispute. Under the last-minute agreement, Britain will rename the consulate, founded in 1839, as the “UK Mission” in the city. Israel said 20 British diplomats including the ‌consul general would depart, leaving just seven working at the mission in a limited role. Britain said it had withdrawn some diplomats “temporarily”, intended to build back its presence, and would hold off on reciprocal measures for now. The agreement appeared to ward off a major diplomatic crisis between long-standing allies. In recent days, sources had said Britain had been prepared to consider ejecting Israeli diplomats if the mission were closed. Israel had issued a 30-day deadline last month for Britain to close the consulate, after London announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including a ban on trade in goods from there. In a statement, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon ⁠Saar said the consulate would formally end operations but that some British diplomats would be allowed to continue working there. Saar’s British counterpart, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, said his country did ‌not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate. The consulate is in a part of the city Israel captured in a 1967 war, which Israel later annexed in a move that most countries do not recognise. Following discussions with Israel, “our Consulate General building ‌will not be closing, and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from today”, Miliband said. It would continue to “deliver vital services and our ⁠work with the Palestinian people.” On Thursday morning workers in the consulate removed a plaque reading “British Consulate General” and another sign for its consular section. The British flag was still flying over the building. Saar said Israel and Britain had ‌reached an understanding on Wednesday night to prevent a further deterioration in relations between the two countries, and that Britain had agreed not to take any measures in retaliation. Miliband said Britain had “temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families ‌to ensure ‌their safety and security” and that it would work in the coming months to build back its presence. “We will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway ‌and credible,” Miliband said in a statement. Last week, Britain’s top national security adviser Jonathan Powell visited Israel in a bid to keep the consulate from closing. Britain’s minister for the ⁠Middle East, Stephen Doughty, told Sky News that London was engaged in ongoing talks with the Israeli government, and that it deeply regretted Israel’s actions in relation to its consulate. “Our ⁠building remains open, our staff remain doing important work,” Doughty said. “We retain a presence in Jerusalem ... and it is very important that work is able to continue.” The closure order does not affect Britain’s embassy in Tel Aviv, which handles diplomatic relations with Israel’s government. The consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood ‌of East Jerusalem, has handled Britain’s relations with ‌Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, and provided consular services to Palestinians. The British sanctions announcement, and Israel’s order to close the consulate, mark a new low in a relationship that has deteriorated over the past three years. Britain has repeatedly criticised Israel over its actions in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, which faces an election later this month, has accused Britain’s governing Labour Party of being hostile towards Israel.

title: Anwar’s push to return Myanmar to Asean sparks criticism over weakened leverage
description: The Malaysian leader’s pledge to visiting President Min Aung Hlaing comes without securing ‘significant concessions’, critics say.
content: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Thursday said Malaysia would do “whatever is possible” to strengthen cooperation with Myanmar and fully reintegrate the diplomatically isolated nation into the Asean fold. The pledge came during an unusually high-profile official welcome for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing, despite Malaysia’s position that such engagement does not amount to recognition of his government. Min Aung Hlaing inspected a guard of honour in Putrajaya before holding private talks with Anwar for about 40 minutes, drawing criticism that the prime minister was giving up leverage over the former junta chief at a time when the country was pursuing Myanmar’s cooperation to repatriate thousands of its nationals. Naypyidaw, a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, was also seeking greater regional legitimacy, as its political leaders had been excluded from the bloc’s summits since 2021 for failing to implement a peace plan calling for an end to violence, inclusive dialogue and humanitarian aid. Asean has continued to engage Myanmar while withholding political-level representation, with the bloc’s approach tied to progress on its Five-Point Consensus. Anwar said Malaysia would “do whatever is possible” to boost ties and “ultimately take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of Asean”.
