He acknowledged differences over democratic reform but praised Min Aung Hlaing’s willingness to listen, recalling earlier assurances about engaging all parties to prevent further violence. “But how you do it, the mechanism, of course, is up to you as a leader of the country,” Anwar said. “But I want to just stress the importance that we have never reneged [on] that responsibility to express our views.” Min Aung Hlaing became Myanmar’s president in April following a military-organised election widely criticised by Western governments and rights groups, and has since visited Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. “This visit marks my fifth trip to an Asean member state and my ninth overseas trip since assuming the duty of president,” he said. Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul hosted him in August and pledged support for Myanmar’s full participation in Asean. Anwar also thanked Myanmar for financing repatriations, saying 10,493 nationals had been returned by air and sea, with another 3,000 to 4,000 detainees to follow. “Very, very few, hardly any country, in my experience, are willing to accept this repatriation in large numbers at their own expense, as you have shown,” he said. His office clarified that those awaiting return were part of an existing 5,000-person programme, whose first group of 1,476 left Malaysia on September 29. Min Aung Hlaing said Myanmar would expedite returns and send a naval ship, while inviting Malaysian investment in agriculture and infrastructure. “I firmly believe that enhancing our bilateral economic cooperation will bring highly practical economic benefits and joint opportunities for the people of both countries,” he said. He described Malaysia as Myanmar’s fourth-largest trading partner and ninth-largest investor. Diplomatic dividends Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Anwar had surrendered bargaining power. “I strongly believe Anwar, who I do respect greatly, has actually given away leverage that he, a skilled diplomatic actor, could have used to secure significant concessions,” Kurlantzick told This Week in Asia. “I think his decision thus was a major mistake. The broadening legitimacy offered to the Myanmar regime, with really little asked for in return, does not make much sense at all.” Blake Berger, deputy director of Verve Research, said bilateral engagement was allowing Myanmar’s leadership to regain acceptance without meeting Asean’s demands. “While it may be a stretch for Anwar to secure every member’s agreement on Myanmar’s return to the Asean fold, he may not need to, given the junta’s success in engaging bilaterally with a number of regional states,” Berger said. He questioned whether repatriation cooperation would increase Malaysia’s influence, as “the junta has so far made none of the political concessions Asean has sought since 2021”. Malaysia describes the returns as voluntary, but the UN refugee agency said it had no access to assess the previous group’s protection needs or consent, questioning whether decisions made in detention were freely taken. The returnees had been held in Malaysian immigration detention centres and it remains unclear whether Rohingya Muslims – a persecuted minority largely denied citizenship in Myanmar – were among them. Rights groups have warned that those sent back could face persecution or forced military conscription. Anwar last month rejected accusations that Malaysia was disregarding their safety, arguing that continued engagement with Myanmar was necessary to resolve long-standing issues. He said his government would pursue further talks to arrange returns. Josef Benedict, an Asia researcher with CIVICUS, accused Anwar’s government of ignoring warnings about persecution and urged it to engage Myanmar’s opposition and civil society. “Any guarantees they provide cannot be trusted at all,” he said of Myanmar’s leadership, calling for independent monitoring of returnees. Myanmar news outlet Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Wednesday that migrant workers in Malaysia had staged a work stoppage against the visit of the president, with organisers saying it showed opposition to normalising relations. The welcome comes as an International Criminal Court prosecutor’s application for Min Aung Hlaing’s arrest remains pending over alleged crimes against humanity involving the deportation and persecution of Rohingya Muslims in 2017. Malaysia’s foreign ministry has defended engagement as consistent with Asean’s approach to peace and reconciliation. Myanmar’s Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union, which brings together political and armed resistance groups, condemned the trip on Thursday. “Receptive diplomatic hosting of Min Aung Hlaing at the head-of-state level stands in direct contradiction to these established principles,” it said in a statement, citing Malaysia’s stated commitment to democracy and human rights.

title: China’s National Day holiday sees uptick in longer trips, overseas travel
description: Extended holiday boosts long-distance travel, yet plummeting box office sales underscore challenges.
content: China’s National Day holiday saw travel remain broadly stable as the break – an extended length of time compared with 2025 – supported longer-distance trips, though cinema cooled sharply, offering mixed signals on efforts to revive consumer spending. Over the seven-day break, which ended on Wednesday, China recorded 2.142 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 306 million a day, up 0.7 per cent year on year, according to the Ministry of Transport, as reported by state broadcaster CCTV on Thursday. Analysts from China International Capital Corporation (CICC) said in a note on Thursday that the growth in passenger travel had slowed, potentially reflecting “the drag from higher oil prices on road travel”. Oil prices have remained elevated amid persistent concerns over Middle East supply disruptions and rising risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Specifically, road passenger trips averaged 280.26 million a day, while China’s railways handled an average of 21.70 million passengers per day during the break, up 12.7 per cent year on year, according to the transport ministry. Air passenger numbers averaged 2.42 million a day, broadly in line with last year’s level. Trains were more popular than planes for economic reasons, independent civil aviation analyst Li Hanming said. For some, this year’s customary National Day week effectively absorbed another holiday, the late September Mid-Autumn Festival. That combination expanded the break for students and company employees who were allowed to combine the two holidays. “The Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays allowed people to extend their break to 13 days by taking three days of annual leave, lengthening the travel window and releasing demand for longer-distance and more in-depth trips,” the CICC analysts said in the note. Booking platform Trip.com said that domestic travel saw a “clear shift” towards longer distances. Outbound “long-haul” travel expanded as well, the platform said in a statement to the South China Morning Post, with trips lasting eight days or more rising to 42 per cent of outbound trips. It found double-digit growth in travel to Italy and Spain, plus a doubling of trips to New Zealand. During the National Day holiday, China recorded 15.46 million inbound and outbound trips, averaging 2.21 million a day, up 6.7 per cent year on year, according to data from the National Immigration Administration on Thursday. Outbound trips by mainland residents rose 9.3 per cent year on year, while inbound trips by foreigners increased 5.4 per cent. Those entering under visa-free policies rose 9.2 per cent. On the cinema front, China’s National Day holiday box office came in at 1.165 billion yuan (US$173,897.5 million), according to data from the National Film Administration reported by CCTV on Thursday. The figure was down 36.5 per cent from the 1.835 billion yuan recorded during the same holiday period last year, although the 2025 National Day film season ran for eight days, one day longer than this year’s seven-day holiday. The average ticket price during this year’s National Day film season was 36.41 yuan, down 0.77 per cent compared to the same period last year, according to the National Film Administration. The data underscored challenges for Beijing’s efforts to bolster domestic consumption, which remains sluggish. Retail sales, a key gauge of consumer spending, rose just 0.4 per cent year on year in August, slowing from 0.6 per cent in July, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Meanwhile, growth in turnover at major commercial areas during the National Day holiday improved slightly compared with the 2026 Dragon Boat Festival and Mid-Autumn Festival holidays, the CICC report said. It cited data from the Ministry of Commerce showing that foot traffic and turnover at 78 major shopping areas monitored by the ministry rose 3.4 per cent and 5.3 per cent, respectively, in the first three days of the holiday from the same period last year.

title: World’s 50 Best Bars 2026: Hong Kong’s Bar Leone takes top spot for second year in a row
description: The neighbourhood bar in Sheung Wan has been named world’s best bar once again; three other Hong Kong bars also make the list.
content: Hong Kong’s Bar Leone has been named the world’s best bar for the second consecutive year, following its No 3 placement in the Asia edition of The 50 Best Bars list in July. The Italian cocktail bar, founded by Lorenzo Antinori and Justin Shun Wah in 2023, is known for its convivial atmosphere and impeccably made drinks rooted in classic mixology. The results for the global ranking of The 50 Best Bars – now in its 18th edition – were announced during a live ceremony held in Milan, Italy, on October 7. The recognition caps off Bar Leone’s impressive string of accolades since opening three years ago: it received Asia’s Best Bar in 2024 and 2025, but narrowly missed out on a hat trick this year, ceding the No 1 spot to Guangzhou’s Hope & Sesame. In 2025, it made history as the first bar from Asia to top the World 50 Best Bars ranking, previously dominated by names from the US and UK. Hong Kong bars continued to impress voters this year, as the city is tied with Paris and New York for the most venues – four apiece – in the top 50, with Argo at the Four Seasons Hong Kong returning to the list as No 25. Also ranking for the first time are Antinori’s Montana bar (No 36) and Gokan (No 41); the latter’s founder, Shingo Gokan, was also recognised with the Industry Icon Award. Elsewhere in Asia, Bangkok has three bars in the top 50, including Bar Us (No 4), Dry Wave Cocktail Studio (No 27) and BKK Social Club (No 30). Singapore and Tokyo landed two bars each, with Jigger & Pony (No 18), Nutmeg & Clove (No 38), Bar Benfiddich (No 44) and Virtu (No 48). Seoul’s sole representative, Zest, came in at No 7. Bar Leone’s accolade tops off an exciting season for the founders, who recently announced a partnership with Rosewood Hong Kong to launch a new bar concept in November. title: North Korea decries medical aid, says ‘nothing to give or receive’ from Seoul
description: North Korean leader Kim’s sister said the neighbour must show ‘respect’ to mend ties instead of indulging in ‘political provocation’.
content: North Korea’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ‌leader Kim Jong-un, denounced on Thursday South Korea’s plans to provide medical equipment aid to Pyongyang, calling it a “political provocation” and violation of its sovereignty. In a statement carried by state media KCNA, Kim criticised Seoul for publicising its efforts to obtain United Nations sanctions exemptions for a medical aid package, saying Seoul had “insulted” North Korea by referring to shortages of medicines and medical equipment and deteriorating health conditions. “The ⁠hostile nature of inter-Korean relations and South Korea’s identity can never change,” Kim said, adding that North Korea’s position ‌is that there is “nothing to give or receive” from South Korea. Kim, a senior official in the North’s ruling Workers’ Party, said Seoul’s aid proposal was intended to showcase ‌South Korea’s “goodwill” in contrast to North Korea’s rejection of the help, calling the effort a ⁠politically motivated scheme. Seoul secured a ⁠UN sanctions exemption in May to ship medical equipment worth about US$6.8 million to a hospital in Pyongyang, according to South Korean media reports. The ‌plan involves sending more than 1,400 medical items, including diagnostic and surgical equipment, by late November, although Seoul’s unification ministry said the proposal remained subject ‌to consultations ‌with North Korea, the reports said. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has sought to reopen dialogue with ‌North Korea and expand humanitarian cooperation despite repeated rebuffs from Pyongyang. Kim also linked the aid issue ⁠to a recent mine blast dispute, accusing Seoul of simultaneously pursuing humanitarian outreach while escalating tensions over the mine incident ⁠that wounded South Korean soldiers near the demilitarised zone last month. “If there is truly a desire to restore inter-Korean relations, South Korea should first show respect, consideration and sincerity in each of its ‌words and actions,” Kim said. Seoul ‌says the incident was caused by North Korean mines and has warned of diplomatic and military responses, while Pyongyang has denied planting the mines and described the incident as a fabrication. South Korea’s unification ministry said Seoul would not be “swayed by each development” in North Korea’s response and would continue efforts to ease distrust between the two Koreas.

title: How Puma fits into Chinese sportswear maker Anta’s plan to challenge global rivals
description: Puma joins a growing stable of international brands as Anta builds a multi-brand platform aimed at capturing different consumer segments.
content: China’s biggest sportswear maker, Anta Sports, has strengthened its challenge to global rivals such as Nike and Adidas by becoming the largest shareholder in Puma, the German brand recognised worldwide for its sports and casual footwear. The Hong Kong-listed company completed the acquisition of a 29.06 per cent stake in Puma from Artemis, the investment vehicle of France’s Pinault family, in an all-cash deal valued at €1.51 billion (US$1.7 billion). “The stake is expected to boost Puma’s performance in China,” said Fu Yifu, a special research fellow at Su Merchants Bank in Nanjing, capital of eastern China’s Jiangsu province. The deal closed on Wednesday with the transfer of more than 43 million shares, Anta said in a filing with Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing on the same day. The purchase extends Anta’s string of global sportswear acquisitions and investments since 2018. It first announced the investment in Puma in January. The group’s multi-brand portfolio already includes international brands such as Fila, Salomon, Descente, Jack Wolfskin and Arc’teryx. “Anta excels at embedding global brands into China’s business ecosystem,” Fu said. “Established European brands are grappling with growth bottlenecks, and the two sides are essentially strategically complementary. Anta will most likely continue acquiring international brands.” Fu said China’s sportswear market had shifted from channel expansion to refined operations. “Success rests on local insights, supply-chain agility and brand storytelling,” Fu added. Anta’s shares rose 0.6 per cent to HK$71.80 on Thursday. The stock remains down 11 per cent this year. Although sportswear demand in mainland China remained subdued, Anta’s multi-brand portfolio continued to capture faster-growing categories and consumer segments, HSBC said in a recent research report. Ding Shizhong, chairman of Fujian province-headquartered Anta, said the global sporting goods market “continues to offer significant growth opportunities as more people embrace active lifestyles and increase their participation in sports”. The value of a multi-brand group “lies in helping each brand realise its full potential by leveraging the capabilities and resources of the broader group”, Ding added. In the first six months of the year, revenue from Anta’s other brands rose 44.2 per cent year on year to 10.69 billion yuan (US$1.6 billion), according to its interim results. Puma generated sales of €278.3 million in mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan during the same period, up 2.7 per cent year on year and accounting for 7.9 per cent of group revenue. Anta’s premium brand portfolio was projected to deliver a compound annual sales growth of about 20 per cent through 2030, according to consultancy Morningstar.

title: US judge blocks release of alleged Beijing agent accused of filming Taiwan leader’s son
description: Defence had argued the case was based on a ‘single day’ of surveillance and wasn’t proof she would flee, but a federal judge disagreed.
content: A federal judge on Wednesday ordered Wanying “Heather” Zhang be held in custody, after her lawyers – who had fought to keep her out of jail – said she “looks forward to establishing” her innocence at trial. They argued that the US government’s case centred on a single day of alleged surveillance in Seattle and was not evidence that she posed a flight risk. US Magistrate Judge Steve Kim sided with prosecutors, who told him that Zhang’s parents and siblings lived in China and that her brother had a history of working with the Chinese government. “The alleged surveillance began and ended on a single day, September 1, 2025,” Zhang’s lawyers wrote in a brief opposing her continued detention. The government’s complaint, they said, “charges a single violation” of the unregistered-agent statute arising from that day in Seattle. “For purposes of this detention hearing only, Ms Zhang accepts the allegations of the complaint as true, as the court must at this stage,” the brief said. “She does not concede them. She contests the charge and looks forward to establishing her innocence at trial.” In a brief filed for Wednesday’s detention hearing, the defence argued that the timeline was central to the question of whether Zhang should remain in custody while the case proceeds. The lawyers wrote that the alleged surveillance took place on September 1, 2025, while the communications cited in the case ended in October 2025. The argument came three days after the FBI arrested Zhang, 34, at Los Angeles International Airport as she prepared to board a one-way flight to China. The FBI has said the flight was bound for Shanghai. The US government filed its criminal complaint in secret and seized her US passport. The FBI found no Chinese passport. The case has drawn attention because Washington accuses Beijing of using an American citizen of Chinese origin to conduct surveillance against the son of Taiwan’s leader, William Lai Ching-te, on American soil. According to the FBI, Zhang and an associate filmed outside the suburban Seattle home of Lai’s son on September 1, 2025. Zhang allegedly sent photographs and video, along with vehicle licence-plate numbers, to a handler in China. Messages cited by prosecutors include: “Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one” and “I am videorecording”. Zhang is accused of acting in the US as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government, a federal offence carrying a potential sentence of up to 10 years. She has not been indicted and is presumed innocent. The defence said the government was using Zhang’s arrest at the airport and her one-way ticket to China to argue that she might flee. Her lawyers pointed instead to the 13 months between the alleged surveillance and her arrest, during which she travelled abroad, including to China, and came home each time. “A person cannot avoid proceedings she does not know exist,” the filing said. “A person who means to flee to China does not fly there and come home, again and again, to her husband and daughters.” Zhang’s lawyers said the trip that ended with her arrest had been planned weeks earlier so she could visit her mother. She delayed the trip until after her daughters’ birthdays, the brief said. Her lawyers also said she routinely bought one-way tickets and purchased return flights separately. The defence also challenged a pretrial services report, relaying the case agent, that Zhang may hold Chinese citizenship, a factor cited in support of keeping her detained. The brief said the agent identified no source. Zhang came to the US in 2014 and became a US citizen in 2020. She has worked in Orange County real estate for roughly a decade and has been married since 2017 to a US citizen. The couple’s daughters are eight and five, and the family lives in an Irvine home purchased in 2021. “Ms Zhang earned her place here,” the defence wrote. “Her husband, her daughters, her home and her work are all here, and she is not leaving them.” Under the defence proposal, if released, Zhang would be placed under GPS monitoring and home detention and barred from airports. Her family and a friend would also put up more than US$800,000 in guarantees, with the Irvine home – which the defence said had at least US$700,000 in equity – offered as security. The judge rejected that proposal. Zhang is due back as early as October 19 for a preliminary hearing, unless prosecutors indict her first. Zhang’s case is the latest in a run of prosecutions accusing Chinese-Americans in the US of acting for Beijing without notice. The outcomes have been mixed. In New York, Linda Sun, a former aide to governors Andrew Cuomo and Kathy Hochul, and her husband, Chris Hu, are awaiting a retrial. A Brooklyn jury deadlocked in December 2025 on charges that Sun acted as an unregistered agent and that the couple laundered money and took benefits in exchange for shaping state access and messaging. Judge Brian Cogan set a retrial for January 18, 2027. Prosecutors have since added a money-laundering conspiracy count. Both have pleaded not guilty. In California, Eileen Wang, the former mayor of Arcadia, pleaded guilty in May 2026 to acting as an illegal agent and resigned. She admitted that, before she was elected, she posted pro-Beijing material at the direction of Chinese officials. She is awaiting sentence. Her then-fiancé, Yaoning “Mike” Sun, pleaded guilty to the same charge and is serving four years in jail.

title: SOTY 25/26: Visual Artist category finalist transforms everyday items into art
description: Hong Kong teen artist blends anxiety awareness, cultural memory and bold creativity to inspire change.
content:
Hillary Lee Hiu-lam is an emerging contemporary artist who transforms fragments of daily life – from food to packaging – into meditative and whimsical works of art.
At 17, she lives with an anxiety disorder and channels her creativity to remain calm and inspire others.
“Everyday things are my starting point – the little patterns on product packaging, the way a box unfolds, a scrap of handwriting – they all trigger ideas,” said the Form Six student at The Chinese Foundation Secondary School.
“A repeating motif can suddenly remind me of waves seen on a family trip, and that ordinary detail expands into a full scene in my mind. I collect these moments carefully.”
These projects began when Hillary was still a child.
“Once, I transformed an empty chicken essence box into a tiny theatre by putting a sound device inside so that opening it set off an alarm,” she recalled.
Hillary uses mixed media to create her pieces, from boxes, birthday cards and even food. She draws with watercolour and charcoal pencils.
For her three-dimensional pieces, she chooses materials that resonate with her and allows them to guide the storytelling. Additionally, she takes photographs, gathering visual fragments that later appear in her artwork.
“The ordinary is where I find the extraordinary,” she explained.
Art has freed her from a fear of mistakes that once defined her: “Growing up, I was terrified of making mistakes; I thought art had to be beautiful in a certain way, like something an artist would approve of,” she said.
That changed in Form Four, when she realised that art did not have to fit into one format – it could be messy and still be true.
“The turning point was a piece made from food. I deliberately changed the recipe, altered the gelatin-to-water ratio, used gelatin to preserve ingredients, sliced them into tube shapes and reassembled them into a new form. Familiar textures and colours disappeared so the work no longer looked like food,” she recalled.
“That experiment taught me to embrace accidents and let the materials lead.”
Her process is improvisational: “When I start a piece, I rarely follow a rigid plan. I make a rough sketch, break the idea into separate parts and let the materials tell me what to do next,” Hillary noted.
A drawing might evolve into a three-dimensional installation; a hand-drawn mark could be layered onto product packaging; a sculpture might be built from objects that come together to form a narrative.
Last year, she entered a 3D Model Design Competition with her classmates, where they won first runner-up and bagged the award for greatest cultural value.
“We mixed bamboo with old Hong Kong symbols and icons, reworking traditional motifs into a contemporary structure,” she said.
Judges told her the bamboo piece brought back memories they thought were lost to the younger generation, she noted.
“Seeing them smile, hearing them say we’d taken them back to the old streets, I felt how art could heal: it could reawaken fond memories,” she said.
“I want my work to tap into collective experiences and remind people of things they’ve lived through together.”
The healing power of art is central to Hillary’s approach.
“I see art as a way to accompany people and ease the stress of study and everyday life,” she said.
For instance, she discovered ways to engage with people while operating a small portrait booth at a school open day.
“I did not rush and began chatting with each sitter, and added patterns and designs they liked. Those conversations became part of the portraits,” she said. “When visitors received the drawings I had made of them, their faces lit up with this quiet happiness.”
Hillary and her classmates have created artwork for charity, such as a piece made with buttons her grandmother had saved over decades.
“I stitched them into a dinosaur form, layering buttons of different sizes and patterns and weaving in colourful strings to show how love is tied and passed down through generations, which is the theme of this piece,” she said.
“It carried traces of different eras and felt like a family archive turned into playful sculpture.”
They exhibited and sold their work to raise money for charity at the Project RE:DINO exhibition in July.
The positive response showed Hillary that creative work can connect personal histories with real social needs.
Looking ahead, Hilary wants her art to both heal and provoke thought, and she plans to study art therapy at university.
Her outstanding achievements earned her a place as a finalist in the Visual Artist category in the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.

title: Exclusive | German President Steinmeier targets China trip as Berlin sharpens trade stance
description: Trip coincides with Merz’s Asia tour as Berlin and Paris advocate new EU mechanism to exclude rule-breaking trade partners.
content: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is planning to visit China in the coming weeks, even as relations between the two countries sour over trade, according to multiple sources familiar with the arrangement. It will mark the first official visit to China since 2018 for Steinmeier, a former foreign minister whose decade-long tenure as president ends in March next year. The visit will coincide with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s trips to Japan and South Korea this month. When asked about the visit on Thursday, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said the ministry had no details to offer at this point. Germany’s president is the head of state, while political power sits mainly with the chancellor and government, making Steinmeier’s a largely ceremonial role. The president does, however, represent Germany abroad. The trip will be watched closely for signs of further cracks in the Sino-German relationship. Berlin has pivoted dramatically in recent weeks towards a more hardline approach to China on trade amid fears that its manufacturing heartlands will be hollowed out by intense Chinese competition. On Monday, the South China Morning Post reported that Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron had co-signed a paper calling for a new trade weapon that could see China or other trading partners deemed to be flouting the rules excluded from the giant EU single market, almost immediately. Steinmeier, a Social Democrat, has been on a political journey of his own in recent years. Previously a staunch supporter of the Ostpolitik thread that ran through post-Cold War German politics, promoting openness to Russia and other Eastern powers, his position shifted notably following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In interactions with Chinese leaders since then, including a call with President Xi Jinping in December 2022 and a meeting with the visiting Premier Li Qiang in June 2023, he called for Beijing to use its clout to help bring the war to a close. In a speech last summer, Steinmeier spoke in favour of a carefully calibrated de-risking from China, even if it was couched in the language of partnership. “We want good relations with China, and we are working towards that. At the same time, we must continually readjust our relationship with China without slamming any doors. But we must insist on further reducing asymmetries – that is, differing levels of market access,” Steinmeier said. In the intervening year, however, mainstream German politics has shifted significantly. It has become common belief that the symbiosis between the two economies – whereby German manufacturers made the machinery to kit out China’s factories – has worn off. These same factories have swiftly moved up the value chain to become fierce rivals of their erstwhile vendors. A security thread runs through the relationship now as well. On Wednesday, the German government blocked the sale of large parts of Hamburg logistics company Zippel to Chinese state-owned shipping giant Cosco because of security concerns. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardised the resilience ⁠of Germany’s and the EU’s supply chains,” the economy ministry said in a statement. While Steinmeier does not manage these policies, they are likely to be discussed when he meets Xi this month. It will mark the first major German diplomatic trip to China since Merz went there in February. Upon returning from stops in Beijing and Hangzhou, the conservative leader told the Bundestag that he could “envisage” a free-trade agreement “in the longer term … with the People’s Republic of China”. That moment, however, appears to have passed. The EU’s trade chief arrived in Beijing on Wednesday for two days of crucial talks with counterpart Wang Wentao. Brussels has been pressing the Chinese side to make a voluntary commitment to cap the exports of a single product, understood to be plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, which would be seen as a positive deliverable from months of intensive talks. Should this approach fail, it is likely that tariffs and quotas would be slapped on this product in the form of a safeguard mechanism supported by Berlin. German support for tariffs in this sector is a marker of how quickly its stance on China and trade in general has changed. Less than two years ago, Berlin unsuccessfully lobbied other EU capitals to vote against tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles, which were adopted in October 2024.

title: Man arrested after red paint splashed at joint office of ‘unhelpful’ lawmakers
description: Suspect, 66, accused lawmakers of ignoring his complaints, while police say no national security or triad elements involved.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a man for allegedly splashing red paint at the joint office of two lawmakers whom he accused of being unhelpful. A source said on Thursday that police had arrested the 66-year-old man over the incident at the office shared by Kowloon East lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu and insurance sector legislator Chan Pui-leung. The force said it received a report at 6.40am from a security guard at Sau Mau Ping Estate that red paint had been splashed at an office in the estate’s Sau Chi House. Officers made the arrest after reviewing surveillance footage. According to the source, the suspect carried out the attack after his complaints were not followed up by the two legislators, whom he accused of failing to help him with even a single case. The insider also confirmed that no national security, debt-related or triad elements were involved. Police have classified the case as criminal damage and it is being handled by a criminal investigation team under the Sau Mau Ping police district. In a joint statement, Tang and Chan condemned the alleged act and thanked police for their “swift” response. They added that the office had resumed operations and reminded staff to pay extra attention to personal safety.

title: Why China’s new air force base in Laos could rattle Vietnam
description: Hanoi likely to view the Ban Keun facility as Beijing’s bid to ‘encroach into its area of influence’ in Vientiane, analysts say.
content: A newly opened China-backed air force training centre in Laos could unsettle Vietnam, even as it aims to modernise Vientiane’s military and balance defence ties among Beijing, Moscow and Hanoi, observers say. China’s National Defence Ministry said last Tuesday that the joint support and training facility at Ban Keun Airport in the Laotian capital would strengthen the expertise of local air force pilots and was “not directed against any third party”. “The establishment and operation of the two institutions reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, aligning with domestic laws of both countries, as well as international law and common practices,” the ministry said in a statement. It added that the installation, widely described as China’s third overseas defence base, “contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation, as well as promoting regional peace and stability”. China’s other two military facilities are in East Africa’s Djibouti and Ream Naval Base in Cambodia. Operational activities have already begun at Ban Keun, with satellite images taken on September 30 by Vantor showing what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets ‌and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built. Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates, said the facility indicated that Laos was looking to juggle defence relations between China, Russia and Vietnam. “As Vietnam continues to maintain close defence partnerships with Russia, Laos could look to China as a counter balance,” Rahman said. Modernising its air force and roping in China as a potential supplier and partner were also high on Vientiane’s agenda, but the move has another dimension: “a competition between Vietnam and China for influence in Laos”, he said. Given Vietnam’s long history of exercising political, military and strategic sway in Laos, Rahman said Hanoi may see the latest development as “China encroaching into its area of influence”. He added that Beijing could also monitor military activities in southern Vietnam by developing Cambodian naval and air defence facilities. “Vietnam could be surrounded by China from the north and China-friendly regimes in Laos from the west and Cambodia from the south,” Rahman said. ‘Chosen partner’ Beyond keeping an eye on Vietnam, the Laos facility signalled China’s deepening competition with the United States for influence in mainland Southeast Asia, he said. Hanoi and Beijing maintain a quietly tense relationship driven by a complex strategy of balancing intense economic interdependence against maritime territorial disputes in the South China Sea. Rahman noted that China has the ability to monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam if it decides to install the 700km (434 miles) YLC-8B long-range radar system. Security analyst Olli Pekka Suorsa said from Vientiane’s perspective, Beijing appeared as an ideal partner to help develop the country’s small, capacity-constrained air force, which has sent its pilots to China for training. “The [facility] is of great importance to the [Laos air force] and its future development road map,” Suorsa said. The assistant professor of security at the Rabdan Academy in Abu Dhabi said “China has become the chosen partner” for the modernisation of Laos’ air force, whose SAIC LE500 and Hongdu K-8 jets are also Chinese-made. He added that Chinese flight instructors would be sent to the new facility in the future, allowing local pilots to complete their military flight training syllabus entirely in Laos. Vientiane could also seek to acquire budget-friendly Chinese combat jets, including the JF-17 and FTC-2000, Suorsa said. Describing reports that the airfield would be occupied by Chinese combat aircraft as implausible, Suorsa said the facility had limited infrastructure and runway to support a large Chinese air force contingent. With a single 2,000-metre runway, Suorsa said it was relatively short for military operations as Chinese airbases under the Southern Theatre Command generally had runways of about 2,500 metres. In addition, China already had a significant airbase network close to Laos and Vietnam across Yunnan and Guangxi provinces, as well as on Hainan Island, under the Southern Theatre Command, he noted. “For operations in mainland Southeast Asia, the PLA Air Force has a broad network of bases that provide it with significant reach,” Suorsa said, adding that China’s growing fleet of aerial refuelling aircraft could further extend the reach of its tactical and strategic aircraft without the need to base them in Laos. “Taken together, the fear of China using the new facility as a forward base is likely overblown,” he said, adding that China’s military and civilian aid to Laos had been extensive over the past two decades, including in the Kingdom’s aviation sector. Simon Creak, an associate history professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore and modern Southeast Asia historian, said the training, equipment and infrastructure benefits for Laos were clear. “A joint facility like this delivers something Laos cannot develop by itself,” Creak said. Though Laos has similar arrangements with China in other areas of development and infrastructure, it was the first time the country used this model to strengthen its military capacity, he said. “It is unprecedented in this sense.” Laos and China have long-standing defence ties that include holding the “Friendship Shield” drills and providing modern military equipment, maintenance support and training to Vientiane. Keith Barney, an associate professor at the Australian National University and country expert on Laos, said there was a broader connection between the Ban Keun air facility and the US$6 billion Laos-China Railway, both built with Chinese support. During the 2024 exercise near Vientiane, the rail link was used to move personnel and military equipment. Vehicles were unloaded at a station some 25km from Ban Keun. Ban Keun’s under-construction runway could potentially be extended from 2,000 metres to 3,000 metres (9,842 feet), enabling longer-range aircraft to operate from there, Barney said. “Infrastructure can have both civilian and military uses and infrastructure can become strategic,” he said, adding that the facility could potentially acquire wider logistical or operational functions over time. Barney said Laos’ need for Chinese financial support might constrain its room for manoeuvre in negotiations with Beijing, including over military cooperation and access to infrastructure. “I would not assume that this means China has imposed particular terms on Laos in the case of Ban Keun, but the wider debt relationship is relevant to understanding the context in which such agreements are made.” Laos faces a severe debt crisis with public and external debt exceeding up to 118 per cent of its gross domestic product, struggling to meet its financing and repayment obligations. Massive financial losses in the state-run energy sector and heavy infrastructure overborrowing from Chinese banks have largely contributed to the situation.

title: Did Portuguese breads and pastries shape Hong Kong’s most iconic baked goods?
description: Portuguese merchants brought breadmaking to Asia centuries ago. Today, echoes may be found in Hong Kong pineapple buns and sha yung egg puffs.
content: Francisco Oliveira, the Portuguese founder of bakery brand Santa Nata, was reminded of home when he tried Hong Kong’s iconic pineapple bun for the first time. “When I ate the pineapple bun, I immediately thought of the pao de deus,” he says, referring to a popular Portuguese baked treat he has eaten since childhood. Translated as “bread of God”, pao de deus is a brioche found in pastry shops across Portugal. It is generously slathered with sugar and coconut before baking to create a golden, crumbly topping that bears an uncanny resemblance to the buttery crust on a pineapple bun. However, the flavour calls to mind the filling of another famous Hong Kong baked good – the cocktail bun. Oliveira was motivated by these similarities to include pao de deus alongside Santa Nata’s signature pastel de nata as a launch product at the London-based brand’s first Hong Kong store, located in the Central neighbourhood. A cross-cultural baked good Oliveira’s version of pao de deus is tweaked for the Asian market, with a fluffy shokupan-like dough and a filling of coconut paste and egg custard. “I’ve already had a couple of Hong Kong customers tell me how similar our pao de deus is to the pineapple bun,” he says. While the pineapple bun’s origins remain contested, a popular theory suggests it was inspired by Japan’s melonpan, created in the 1920s by an Armenian baker in Tokyo. Given the influence the Japanese had on Hong Kong’s gastronomic landscape during the World War II occupation, the connection between the pao de deus and the pineapple bun starts to make sense. After all, the Portuguese introduced breadmaking to Japan and the wider region during the Age of Discovery from the 15th to the 17th centuries. In fact, the Japanese word for bread, pan, comes from pao in Portuguese. But the pineapple bun is not the only Hong Kong baked good that might have a Lusophone heritage. Although today an icon of Chinatown bakeries around the world, paper-wrapped sponge cakes did not appear on Hong Kong bakery shelves until the 1950s. They share many similarities with Japan’s castella, which itself is derived from a fluffy cake known as pao de lo that Portuguese traders brought to Nagasaki, on the Japanese island of Kyushu, in the 1500s. There are also the deep-fried sugar egg puffs known as sha yung, the earliest known records of which appear in 17th century Chinese scholar Qu Dajun’s seminal work, New Discourse on Guangdong. Aside from documenting Cantonese culture in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, Qu was interested in the customs of Portuguese merchants and mariners who arrived in southern China during these periods. While spending time among them, he may have come across their version of the sha yung – a golden fritter dusted in cinnamon sugar and named sonho, meaning “dream”. Ringo Chan, executive pastry chef at the Four Seasons Hong Kong hotel, notes the similarities between sonho and Chinese sha yung. He says the traditional sha yung he grew up eating and loving were eggier than sonhos and did not contain cinnamon, but that the concept and the technique of controlling the frying oil temperature were alike. “I think this is something Hong Kong people would readily embrace,” Chan says. “If we started making [sonhos] here, they might even become more popular than Portuguese egg tarts.” While Chan, an industry veteran who also sits on the committee of the Hong Kong Bakery and Confectionery Association, has extensive knowledge of how other cultures helped shape the city’s sweet tooth, he admits that he has heard “almost zero accounts” of Portugal’s influence on its local cuisine. “We have very minimal knowledge about Portuguese pastries in Hong Kong,” he says. “Most people here only know about the pastel de nata, but even the pastel de nata we are familiar with is actually the Macau egg tart.” This Asian variation is a bestseller at the Four Seasons Hong Kong (where it is also available in pandan and kaya flavour), and Chan describes it as sitting somewhere between a Hong Kong egg tart and the Portuguese original. Ironically, even though Macau was a Portuguese colony for more than 400 years, the recipe for its famous egg tart was created only in the late 1980s by British entrepreneur Andrew Stow. The ambiguity of food history “One of the issues about the Portuguese legacy of a specific area we reached is that we were probably the first Europeans to arrive,” says Frederico Duarte, one of the co-founders of Fabrico Próprio, a multidisciplinary project dedicated to the design of Portuguese confectionery. In Asia, the British arrived later, staying throughout the 19th and 20th centuries as industrialisation stabilised societies and documentation of consumption habits improved, Duarte says. “When you’re trying to look for Portugal’s footprints, they’re much older,” he says. “They’re sometimes like an echo, kept only in words or in a taste memory.” It does not help that even in Portugal, the significance of what has literally been the bread and butter of its people is often overlooked. Duarte describes Portuguese pastries as “affordable and very available”. As a result, he says, these staples are not seen as worthy of attention. He notes, however, that in recent years, there have been growing efforts to document this part of the country’s food history. But tracing Portugal’s gastronomic legacy is a daunting task. “Portugal was a very open country, even from the beginning, and the territory was very dispersed,” Duarte says, referring to the wide network of trading posts it established during its early days of global exploration. Aside from fuelling commerce, these feitorias facilitated cultural exchange in multilateral and often non-linear ways. For a taste of this type of cross-pollination, one can turn to the pastel de coco, which looks like the long-lost cousin of Hong Kong’s coconut tart, right down to the halved glacé cherry often adorning its toasted top. The Portuguese may have conceived the pastry, but its key ingredients – coconut and sugar – came from places such as Brazil and India. Even when it comes to sonhos and their resemblance to sha yung, Chan and Duarte say similar fried-dough desserts exist in other European cultures, making it difficult to attribute full credit to the Portuguese. But perhaps this is what the Portuguese should be recognised for – spreading food knowledge, ingredients and techniques in ways that blurred cultural boundaries and allowed new dishes to rise from the recipes of others. As Duarte puts it: “The biggest contribution the Portuguese made to world culture is ambiguity.”

title: Naked, gilded Trump statue goes on display at EU Parliament
description: Satirical ‘Orange Plague’ artwork depicting the US president atop a smaller man unveiled in Strasbourg.
content: A gilded statue of US President Donald Trump naked went on display in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg on Tuesday. Danish artist Jens Galschiot is exhibiting the satirical statue, titled “Orange Plague” and also known as “King of Injustice”, at the parliament’s headquarters in the eastern French city. It shows the president sitting naked on the shoulders of a much smaller man. In his hand, he holds a long golf club. Including its pedestal, the statue is around 2.5 metres tall and, according to the artist, is coated with 23-carat gold. An orange cloth covering it was removed when it was unveiled on Tuesday. The statue stands at one of the parliament’s busiest intersections connecting two buildings. It is scheduled to remain on display through Thursday. The artist was invited by Danish left-wing member of the European Parliament Per Clausen. “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage,” Clausen said. Business cards placed beside the sculpture quote the “King of Injustice” as saying: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under the burden. I would do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back”. Galschiot describes Trump as one of the greatest obstacles to solving climate change. Galschiot is also the creator of the “Pillar of Shame”, an eight-metre-tall sculpture commemorating victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown. The artwork previously stood at the University of Hong Kong for more than two decades, and the artist has been trying to secure its return.

title: Mouthing Off | First hotels, now wine. Is Michelin scraping the barrel with its new guides?
description: The people behind Michelin have added vineyard grading to restaurant and hotel guides, watering down the brand even further.
content: Confession time. For a food writer, I am woefully below average in terms of wine knowledge. My immediate family members are not drinkers. I was never properly introduced to wine appreciation. At college, my friends chugged beer. To me, a wine cooler was a wimpy drink, not a mini-fridge for storing bottles, with temperature and humidity controls. Honestly, until recently, I could not even spell oenology or viticulture without consulting a dictionary. But I do know a pathetic and desperate publicity scheme when I see one. This summer, the people behind the Michelin restaurant guides moved into wine ratings. Instead of countries, they focus on specific wine regions, ranking estates as brands. In July, Michelin unveiled its first guide to Burgundy, in France, with its Bordeaux selections announced in September. A total of 94 Burgundy producers and 83 Bordeaux producers were awarded either three grapes – the highest distinction – two grapes or one grape. Winemakers who fell just short were “selected” for recognition, much like restaurants that have yet to receive a Michelin star or Bib Gourmand plaque. Instead of assessing individual wines, Michelin decided to examine each winery’s entire portfolio using “five universal and consistently applied criteria” – the quality of agronomy (which seems to mean how good their dirt is), technical mastery, identity, balance and consistency. In short, the question is not how good an individual bottle is, but how good a producer’s overall output is year after year. But wine is even more subject to personal preference than food. The differences between wines can be subtle, and inspectors will inevitably judge them according to their own palates. If your taste buds match with theirs, great. If not, the guide will be pointless. If you think the arguments over whether a restaurant deserves a Michelin star are intense, wait until wine snobs start feuding over wineries that can release dozens of bottles each year. Burgundy produces both red and white wines, and has 84 official Appellations d’Origine Contrôlée (AOC). The region is home to more than 1,000 vineyards, some of which may have dozens of owners, each producing their own distinctive bottles. Does Michelin really expect its jurors to evaluate every estate properly, year after year? Michelin may want to present itself as a new authoritative reference for wine, but to me, it is compiling wine guides for beginners. True connoisseurs already know legendary producers such as Domaine de la Romanee-Conti, Domaine Leroy and Domaine Coche-Dury. Those who swirl their glasses and talk about raspberry notes and oak tannins are probably more interested in specific vintages in a producer’s catalogue. Two years ago, Michelin began diversifying by ranking luxury hotels, handing out one to three keys for properties it deemed worthy of its standards for outstanding stays. Sadly, nobody seems to care, because hotels already have a more established five-star rating system based on facilities, service and luxury. Rather than expanding its reputation, Michelin is actually diluting the brand by trying to rank every form of hospitality luxury. And how has it even proven its expertise in hotels or wine? It is also no secret that, to finance these supposedly impartial listings, Michelin has signed sponsorship deals with tourism boards for some of its restaurant guides. Conflict of interest, anyone? Ultimately, Michelin is first and foremost a tyre company. It started its restaurant guide in 1900 to encourage French drivers to get out on the road. It is not very smart of the company to promote drinking and driving now.

title: US wraps up military mission in Iraq, giving Baghdad room to strengthen China ties
description: Analysts say Beijing will pursue energy and commercial deals after American withdrawal but will not seek to fill a security role.
content: The US has ended its military mission in Iraq, a move analysts said could give Baghdad more room for diversified partnerships and indirectly benefit China’s energy and commercial interests. But they cautioned that the shift was unlikely to create a power vacuum for Beijing to fill, with China lacking both the ambition and capacity to take on the US security role. The United States formally ended its Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq on September 30, completing a withdrawal agreed on in 2024 under the administration of former US president Joe Biden. The mission, launched in 2014 to fight Islamic State, has been replaced by an Iraqi-led security effort, while Washington has said it will continue targeted training and intelligence support. The move caps a turbulent two-decade US military presence that began with the 2003 invasion, which ousted Saddam Hussein and empowered a Shiite-led government. Washington withdrew its forces in late 2011, only to return less than three years later to fight Islamic State. For China, the significance of the withdrawal may lie less in replacing the US than in the greater room it could give Iraq to diversify its foreign relationships. China is not looking to replace the US or inherit its role as Washington scales back its presence Li Weijian, Shanghai Institutes for International Studies Li Weijian, a researcher at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said the diminished US involvement could give Iraq more autonomy in dealing with external powers. “A reduced US presence in Iraq and a scaling back of its Middle East posture actually benefits nations like Iraq that are seeking a more balanced diplomacy,” Li said. He said Iraq and other Arab states in the region had already been seeking to lessen their reliance on the US – beyond just the security sphere – potentially creating more willingness to cooperate with China. “US dominance has failed to bring genuine peace to the region,” Li said, adding that “China welcomes multilateral cooperation and diversified diplomacy”. China has long had economic interests in Iraq, particularly in its energy sector, alongside infrastructure projects in the country. Li said those interests did not depend on the US withdrawal. He said China had been working with Iraq for decades and that many Chinese projects would continue regardless of the US presence. “China is not looking to replace the US or inherit its role as Washington scales back its presence,” Li said. Jesse Marks, founder of Rihla Research and Advisory, said it was still too early to determine whether the US move represented a broader withdrawal of American forces from the region. “The current drawdown is as much a political decision as it is a practical one,” Marks said. “Ending that mission does not necessarily mean ending the broader US security relationship with Iraq.” The US withdrawal therefore does not necessarily amount to a major opening for Beijing, according to Marks. “Beijing will keep pursuing energy and commercial deals in the absence of a larger US military presence, but it will not fill a US security role. At least not now,” he said. Washington’s influence in Iraq would continue to rest primarily on diplomacy and security ties rather than competition with China over infrastructure or energy, he added. Kenneth Katzman, a senior fellow at the Soufan Centre, a New York-based think tank, echoed that view. “China does not envision a security role in Iraq,” Katzman said, citing Beijing’s lack of force-projection capabilities and ambition to take on such a role. Instead, he said, China’s interests were concentrated on energy, including securing supplies and investing in Iraq’s large energy industry. “China might play a role [in] helping Iraq get its oil out and developing its oil, but a security role? No,” Katzman said. The withdrawal comes as Baghdad tries to balance close security and political ties with both Washington and Tehran – a rarity in the region. Pro-Tehran factions have long demanded an end to the US presence, with Iraqi militias stepping up attacks on US forces in Kurdistan following late-February strikes on Iran by the US and Israel. The US withdrawal has also raised concerns about the ability of Iraqi forces to contain Islamic State remnants and manage the influence of Iran-backed armed groups. For China, greater Iranian influence or renewed instability would not necessarily be beneficial, Marks said. “China’s economic interests benefit most from a stable Iraqi state capable of protecting energy infrastructure and maintaining predictable relationships with multiple external partners,” he said.

title: Reporter’s notebook: my week with Huawei’s new US$3,500 trifold phone
description: The Mate XT 2 offers a tablet-sized screen at paperback weight – for an eye-watering price. Here’s what it’s actually like to use.
content: When I took out the US$3,500 Huawei Mate XT 2 over a family dinner during China’s “golden week” – the long National Day holiday in early October – the trifold phone quickly became the centre of discussion: my father and his peers took turns playing with the device, marvelling at the sleek design while debating whether it was true innovation or pure luxury. It wasn’t the first time unfolding its massive 10.2 inch display raised a few eyebrows at dining tables during the week I spent trying out the Huawei Mate XT 2. On high-speed trains and in restaurants, the device occasionally drew curious looks from other passengers and diners. While the Chinese market is no stranger to foldable smartphones of various designs, ranging from book-style to clamshell, the Mate XT 2, launched in early September, is Huawei’s first double-hinge phone that folds inward to form a U-shape, and has also drawn widespread attention as the most expensive handset in the company’s history. Having always been a slab phone user myself, finding even the iPhone Pro Max cumbersome, I used the device with a mix of curiosity and scepticism. Huawei made a unit of the Mate XT 2 with 1-terabyte storage available to the South China Morning Post for this hands-on experience. A phone, or a tablet? The moment I got my hands on the Mate XT 2, I couldn’t help but marvel: it was lighter than I had expected. That turned out to be the reaction from many of my friends and family when they held this 299-gram (11-ounce) gadget, roughly the weight of a standard paperback novel. The expansive display drastically changes the everyday smartphone experience. When unfolded across three panels, the screen feels as spacious as a tablet while being much thinner, offering a more intuitive layout for watching videos. The protective case featuring an adjustable kickstand that comes with the phone makes it easier to watch videos. Though the inner creases remain quite visible, they were not too distracting for full-screen viewing. When folded, it turns into a 16.5cm (6.5-inch) phone with a 12.3mm (0.48-inch) thickness. The massive screen also proved to be a game-changer for productivity. For those who spend their day drafting documents, reviewing text-dense reports and juggling multiple chat and email threads at the same time, the display allows smooth multitasking all at once. Despite its size, I could keep what I saw to myself, as double tapping on the outer screen can activate the privacy shield mode that blacks out the screen for people nearby, and you can choose to apply the feature to specific apps. A decent camera with new tricks Like Huawei’s other flagship models, the Mate XT 2’s camera system features vibrant colours and rich detail, capturing a range of images, including my playful cat and a full moon. The new form factor also unlocks new photography tricks such as bending the phone into a standing mode to take selfies or group shots from a table. Huawei has tried to bring some of its top imaging technologies for its slab flagship to the trifold phone, but packing a four-camera system into an ultra-thin chassis still creates a prominent camera bump on the back. Apart from the hardware engineering, software performance running on Huawei’s latest HarmonyOS 7 was smooth throughout my daily use. Connecting to Wi-fi, switching between apps, and browsing resource-heavy websites were completely lag-free. More importantly, even during long video streaming or multi-window sessions, the phone did not noticeably overheat. Yet, switching to a new ecosystem proves to be a steep onboarding curve for me. I went to great lengths retrieving a long-lost Huawei account, which included providing my real name and national ID number for verification, to have a full experience of apps and core features in Huawei’s own ecosystem. Extra effort for smaller hands Meanwhile, with all its technical innovations, the physical presence constantly reminded me that this phone wasn’t built for everyone. As a female user with smaller hands, handling the trifold device required constant caution and effort. The size and weight make it challenging to navigate one-handed, and the device slipped straight out of my shallow pockets twice over the past week, which I blame on the design of women’s clothing that rarely features pockets deep enough for larger devices. Still, for users who possess larger hands, deeper pockets – in both senses – and a demand for mobile multitasking, I believe it has an undeniable appeal as an innovative gadget, as well as a status symbol.

title: Letters | Don’t overlook eye health as Hong Kong ages
description: Readers discuss the importance of protecting eyesight, legislating against bad behaviour on public transport, and bus service quality.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. World Sight Day falls on October 8 this year. It is a timely reminder that protecting sight should be part of how we think about ageing well, not something we consider only after vision begins to fade. Hong Kong is a fast-ageing society, but vision is still too often overlooked in conversations about ageing well. Good eyesight helps older people move around safely, manage daily tasks, stay socially connected and maintain their independence. When vision deteriorates, the impact can extend far beyond the eyes, increasing the risk of falls, isolation and loss of confidence. At The Fred Hollows Foundation, we have seen through our work around the world that sight can transform lives at every age. Many causes of vision loss, including cataract and uncorrected refractive error, are preventable or treatable. A pair of glasses, timely screening or a sight-restoring operation can help a person continue reading, working, caring for family members and participating in the community. Eye health is also a smart investment. The Value of Vision report, released at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and co-authored by The Fred Hollows Foundation, found that every dollar invested in addressing avoidable vision loss can return US$28 in benefits. This makes eye care one of the most cost-effective ways to support health, productivity and dignity as populations age. Regular eye examinations, early detection and accessible care can help more people prevent avoidable vision loss and live independently for longer. Eye health should be treated not as an afterthought, but as part of everyday preventive healthcare. To bring this global message closer to Hong Kong, The Fred Hollows Foundation Hong Kong is launching a local World Sight Day campaign with Tai Ma Sing and Run Grandma Run. It encourages the public to learn more about eye health and take simple steps to protect their sight. As Hong Kong builds a healthier and more age-friendly society, regular eye checks, early detection and greater public awareness can help more people live fuller, safer and more connected lives. Cyrus Pow, head of Hong Kong and Macau, The Fred Hollows Foundation Legislate against bad behaviour on public transport Updated regulations in Singapore, under which passengers can be fined up to S$500 (US$390) for offences such as putting their feet on seats or playing loud audio on public transport, have prompted discussions on whether Hong Kong should follow suit. When commuters are already enduring cramped and stifling journeys, the last thing they want is being forced to listen to someone else’s blaring audio. Such behaviour also deprives passengers of precious time to rest or read quietly during their daily travel. It could have a negative effect on mental health. While bus companies and the MTR have launched campaigns to promote commuting etiquette, such efforts appear not to have yielded results. The Hong Kong government is going to great lengths to enhance the livability of our city. Perhaps eradicating undesirable behaviour on public transport is no less important than curbing second-hand smoke. It is high time we seriously considered whether legislation is necessary. Nathaniel Mong, Tuen Mun Are better bus services a bridge too far? Bus announcements in Hong Kong tell passengers to behave properly: not to eat or drink, not to cut fingernails, to set phones to silent mode. Of course, passenger behaviour can be disturbing, but what about the bus companies themselves? Are they offering proper bus services? Bus companies have reduced bus services in the city recently. Citybus has shortened the route 5X service period with the last bus departing at around 7.30pm, while KMB has also shortened route 89B and reduced its service time. The Transport Complaints Unit received 4,056 complaints and suggestions regarding franchised buses in the first quarter of this year. More than half of them referred to KMB and affiliated Long Win Bus, while about a fifth referred to Citybus. Meanwhile, the MTR received far fewer – 354 – complaints and suggestions. It is important to note that the MTR has had higher ridership than bus services in recent years. Perhaps some passengers have had enough of deteriorating bus services and are taking the MTR instead. Karl Shieu, Mong Kok

title: ByteDance heads first SCMP Plus Going Global 100 ranking
description: Social media giant beats out Foxconn Industrial, Shein and BYD in new SCMP Plus ranking of China’s global champions.
content: TikTok owner ByteDance is China’s Going Global champion, according to a new SCMP Plus databank tracking mainland companies’ overseas expansion efforts. The social media giant topped the debut SCMP Plus Going Global 100 ranking ahead of Apple assembler Foxconn Industrial Internet, online fashion retailer Shein and electric vehicle (EV) maker BYD. More than 2,000 companies were assessed as part of the research project, which assigned each contender a weighted score based on overseas revenue, reliance on foreign markets and the pace of overseas growth. About two-thirds of the Going Global 100 members are technology or consumer companies, such as carmakers, reflecting how private businesses are driving China’s overseas growth through the development of cutting-edge technology and the creation of their own global brands. Private manufacturers are also now outpacing state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in overseas expansion, as they move beyond being assemblers for multinational brands and look to escape cutthroat price wars at home. “Private firms have started to dominate, given the growing prominence of consumer electronics, e-commerce platforms, digital tech, EVs and green tech and even light manufacturing,” said Jayant Menon, senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. The Going Global 100 database is exclusively available to subscribers of SCMP Plus, the premium data and news offering from the South China Morning Post. ByteDance boosted overseas sales by nearly 50 per cent last year, according to Chinese media reports. The company generated more than 30 per cent of its revenue from overseas markets, up from 25 per cent a year earlier. Its rapid growth was driven by e-commerce business TikTok Shop, which recorded a 70 per cent surge in gross merchandise value. The company, founded by Zhang Yiming – Asia’s richest man, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index – has also reached US$4 billion of annualised artificial intelligence revenue, the highest reported figure among Chinese businesses. AI investment weighed on profit last year. Still, the company is building data centres in countries including Thailand and Brazil to support international expansion. The prominence of private technology companies marks a sharp shift from the early years of the Belt and Road Initiative, which was launched in 2013 to build overseas infrastructure and strengthen trade links. SOEs then dominated China’s overseas expansion, sending engineers, builders and financiers abroad to work on megaprojects. “In the past, it was heavy industry and infrastructure, which are already nationalised in China,” said Charles Chang, finance professor at Fudan University in Shanghai. In 2023, China shifted the focus of the Belt and Road Initiative to smaller, more remunerative projects after parts of the programme became saddled with debt and faced opposition in some countries. Now, private Chinese companies are striving to build globally recognised brands as part of an official “going global” strategy, moving beyond their traditional role as low-cost assemblers (see SCMP Plus fact sheet). Domestic overcapacity and profit-sapping price wars are also prompting businesses to look overseas for growth. China’s own market is beset by a years-long property slump, weak consumption and employment jitters. The shift towards offshore markets helped boost China’s outbound direct investment by 11.1 per cent last year to a record US$214 billion, according to an annual report jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce and two other state economic bodies in September. That made China the world’s second-largest source of global capital, trailing only the United States. Outbound investment has picked up since 2021, when China introduced new policies to support overseas e-commerce expansion. Before that, an investment boom came to a crashing halt in 2017, when the government tightened foreign-exchange controls. Technology-related industries were among the fastest-growing destinations for China’s overseas investment last year. Spending on information transmission, software and information technology services surged by 88.3 per cent to US$13.1 billion. Chinese tech companies are also leading a shift towards developing and selling new products worldwide. They thrive in online entertainment, AI, e-commerce and autonomous driving (see SCMP Plus fact sheet). Among the more visible brands offshore are AI platform DeepSeek, drone maker DJI and video-game development company miHoYo. Chinese carmakers have also come to dominate the global EV market, helped by competitive pricing and technological advances, including batteries. BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor are among leaders of the overseas push amid domestic price wars and rising global demand for cars that are environmentally friendly (see SCMP Plus fact sheet). The Going Global 100 members have expanded across the world, with 88 having a presence elsewhere in Asia, 78 in North America and 71 in Europe. Southeast Asia is a major investment destination because of geographical proximity, local manufacturing expertise and free-trade agreements. BYD, for instance, opened a US$490 million EV factory in Thailand in 2024. Southeast Asia offered Chinese firms a nearshoring haven in countries whose exports were subject to lower US tariffs than exports from China itself, said Menon of the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Wages remained lower on average than in China, he added. While SOEs had pulled back on aggressive projects abroad to cut risk, Menon said China was now working with private firms intent on going global. Government funds offered financing, for example, while infrastructure-building consortiums overseas led by SOEs could subcontract to private tech and manufacturing firms. Fudan University’s Chang said some SOEs had invested in private firms to capture a share of overseas-growth dividends at a time of domestic market saturation, particularly in sectors where China was strong, such as robotics and consumer electronics.

title: As China and the EU begin crunch trade talks, optimism is in short supply
description: Observers on both sides are braced for more turbulence – and mainly hope Beijing and Brussels can avoid a full-blown trade conflict.
content: As China and the European Union began a fresh round of trade talks in Beijing on Thursday, observers on both sides appeared to agree on one thing: a big breakthrough was unlikely. Chinese firms based in Europe said they hoped the talks could achieve some “limited progress” to help stabilise the trade relationship, while European analysts remained cautious about the potential outcome. “They’re bound to get some results,” said a Chinese source with knowledge of the talks, adding that EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic “will not go home empty-handed”. The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU called on both sides to make full use of the Trade and Investment Consultations (TIC) mechanism to manage differences, push for solutions and send clearer signals to businesses. “Even limited progress that improves predictability and reduces the risk of further escalation would be meaningful for companies in both Europe and China,” said an executive at a Chinese renewable energy firm in Europe. Chinese firms in the automotive, medical equipment and chemical products industries are bracing for more trade frictions in the months ahead, according to another Chinese executive based on the continent. Yuyuan Tantian, a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster China Central Television, published an article on Wednesday urging both sides to “maintain strategic patience” and said current negotiations enabled China and the EU to “verify trade flows in sectors such as plug-in hybrid vehicles and chemicals together through a joint monitoring mechanism”. Many on the European side agreed that it was in no one’s interest for talks to break down, but stressed that Sefcovic would be under pressure to bring back significant results to satisfy policymakers in Europe. With concerns rising that a “China shock 2.0” could decimate its industrial base, frustration has grown in Europe over a perceived lack of progress in the EU’s trade discussions with China. On Monday, France and Germany proposed a “rapid response” trade tool giving the European Commission the power to swiftly cut a third country deemed a threat – such as China – out of its market. While China-EU trade relations are complex and issues take time to resolve, it was important for China to show some forward movement, according to Ignacio Garcia Bercero, a senior fellow at Bruegel and former director at the European Commission’s trade department. The best-case scenario would be for China to recognise that the EU needs to take action to protect some of its sectors, Garcia Bercero said. “China should understand that normal actions under World Trade Organization rules are not escalations,” Garcia Bercero said, adding that both sides should not let policy actions interrupt dialogue. Beijing may offer small compromises to calm certain member states and turn them against the Franco-German “rapid response” tool, but such measures would not be enough to solve the wider imbalances in the trade relationship, according to Marc Julienne, director of the Centre for Asian Studies at the French Institute of International Relations. A source from France’s Elysee Palace said the proposed trade tool would enable the EU to take necessary action to protect businesses while trade talks with third countries progress, as Europe could not afford to wait “for months” on the outcomes of dialogues while certain sectors faced pressure from unfair competition. “China and Europe are likely to head towards a more intensified trade tit-for-tat situation,” Julienne said, cautioning that for now neither side wanted a trade war.

title: Data centre opposition is growing in Australia. Is there a middle ground?
description: At least three data centre plans have been shelved recently amid fears over water and power supply, noise levels and environmental damage.
content: Australia may have vast tracts of land and political will to support the growth of the artificial intelligence industry, but the development of data centres to power the technology is proving more challenging. Last month, property developer Goodman Group withdrew its application for a 90-megawatt data centre in Lane Cove, on Sydney’s lower north shore, after months of opposition from residents about the potential impact on their electricity and water supplies, noise pollution and other concerns. In a press statement, Goodman said it had considered changes in the policy and regulatory environment, as well as feedback from residents. It is not the first time that a developer has pulled the plug on a proposed data centre in Australia this year. In May, GreenSquareDC shelved its plan for a 120MW data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs. A much smaller proposed data centre in Katoomba, in New South Wales’ Blue Mountains, was also withdrawn by MAK Urban Group in June. Although the projects were in two different states, residents had raised similar concerns – that the large resource-hungry facilities would be located too close to their homes and schools, and could cause environmental damage. Rob Nicholls, a senior research associate at the University of Sydney, who recently gave evidence to a New South Wales legislative inquiry on the development of data centres, said these facilities had run ahead of current land-use categories.
