Developers typically looked for sites with convenient access to high-capacity electricity networks, fibre-optic connections, water and sewerage, Nicholls said, adding that these requirements favoured established industrial estates. Yet he said such sites had often been designated for warehouses and lighter industrial uses, located near residential neighbourhoods, schools and waterways. Existing telecommunications infrastructure could fit into the plans of data centre developers if they were scaled down, Nicholls added. “I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see lots of Telstra telephone exchange buildings hosting small inference-level data centres.” Residents push back Sasha Titchkosky, from the Lane Cove Responsible Planning group, explained to This Week In Asia why residents were up in arms over the data centre plan, saying it would be built just 20 metres (66 feet) away from the nearest house, close to a nursery and conservation bushland. Residents were concerned about the constant noise and fire hazards created by diesel backup generators, air pollution and water use, Titchkosky said. While the community was not totally opposed to having a data centre, the scale of the Goodman plan meant it was not suitable for Lane Cove, she added. “We would say that data centres fit into the heavy-industry kind of classification because of their impact.” In Hazelmere, community members and Trillion Trees Australia objected to GreenSquareDC’s planned facility, which would have been located near a school, residential areas and Helena River, a major environmental and cultural landmark. Kate Herren of Trillion Trees Australia said the conservation charity was not wholly against the development of data centres. “We understand the need for it, but there needs to be very careful consideration of the impact of these developments on the environment and the local community,” she said. Herren said planning staff from the City of Swan, the local government area in Perth, had recommended rejecting the GreenSquareDC plan, as operating diesel backup generators overnight could exceed the residential noise limit. The developer withdrew the proposal before local authorities could assess the data centre’s feasibility. Titchkosky and Herren said the communities they served were part of the Australian Community Alliance for Responsible Data Centres, an informal network sharing information and strategies on proposals for such facilities. The alliance has called for a moratorium on new approvals while local governments develop stronger safeguards for communities and the environment. Nicholls and his University of Sydney colleague Deanna D’Alessandro have proposed a “dual-gate” approval process for data centres that sets a threshold for power usage. Under their proposal, conditional planning permission and breaking ground on construction would hinge on electricity and water companies guaranteeing adequate supplies for data centre operators. In addition, the researchers have proposed using recycled water and restricting drinking water supplies if levels drop too low. Guidelines for development Australia’s federal and state governments have been taking steps to address community concerns. In March, the federal government’s Department of Industry, Science and Resources published a document stating that data centre expansion must meet certain national expectations for operators to retain their “social licence to operate”. The document also states that new facilities should enhance clean-energy generation or storage, minimise water use, engage communities and indigenous groups early in site selection and pay their share of infrastructure upgrades. “New data centres and AI infrastructure should not place upward pressure on energy prices and should make a positive contribution to Australia’s energy transition,” it said. New South Wales state has introduced a separate policy framework requiring developers seeking approval for energy and water infrastructure to meet environmental and efficiency standards and avoid shifting costs to households and small businesses. Data Centres Australia, an industry association and lobby group, has said the sector is already subject to extensive regulation. Belinda Dennett, the association’s CEO, has rejected claims that data-centre construction and operation are unregulated, citing existing planning, building, environmental, water, electricity and critical-infrastructure laws. “What is disappointing is that some continue to perpetuate the myth that this sector is unregulated,” she wrote in a social media post in September. That same month, the association issued a media statement welcoming the federal government’s consultation on nationally consistent standards for AI infrastructure. Calling for one set of rules at the national level, Dennett said in the statement that “a clear and certain framework is better for communities and better for investment than a patchwork of different rules across the country”. The association also said its members had adopted voluntary commitments on energy, water, community consultation and transparency. These include pledges to engage communities before and during approvals on land use, noise, traffic and amenities, minimise water use, choose recycled or non-potable water where available, and fund their own energy and water connections. Opposition in the US Several industry players, including Data Centres Australia, have noted that objections against data centres in Australia appear to mirror the backlash in the United States. In July, Blackstone-owned QTS terminated its Digital Gateway project in Virginia after years of planning and regulatory review. A month later, developer Stillwater withdrew its permit application for a proposed US$1 billion facility in Georgia. The US also saw multiple protests against data centres across 42 states on July 18, as opponents expressed concerns over water and energy use, and transparency in approvals. Despite differences over how the data centre issue has evolved in the two countries, the communities’ concerns are the same, according to Titchkosky. “It’s the same impact in terms of diesel generators, the pollution, light, the heat impact, and the water and noise issues,” she said. “What the US situation showed us was what the future could look like if you just allowed unfettered data-centre development.”

title: Helper arrested for allegedly slapping five-year-old boy after he refuses to eat
description: Hong Kong police receive report from boy’s mother, who accused helper of hitting her child after checking indoor security camera footage.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a foreign domestic helper for allegedly slapping a five-year-old boy who refused to eat his meal at a Kowloon City flat. Police received a report at about 11.57pm on Wednesday from the boy’s mother, who said her son had been ill-treated by her 37-year-old helper at their home on 97 Hau Wong Road. Police said the woman checked the flat’s surveillance cameras after her son told her he had been slapped by the helper. The footage allegedly showed the helper hitting the boy with her hand at around 9pm on Wednesday while feeding him, after he refused to eat his meal. Initial investigations suggested the helper had struck the boy’s face. The boy, who complained of pain in his face, was sent to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei for a medical examination. The Filipino helper, who had been employed by the family for about a month, was arrested for ill-treatment or neglect of a child or young person and was detained for investigation. The case is being handled by the Kowloon City district criminal investigation unit.

title: Workers, mostly Indian, building US consulate in Milan agree to record settlement
description: Potentially life-changing sums averaging US$50,400 begin under historic US$35 million labour exploitation deal.
content: Foreign workers building the vast new US consulate compound in Milan signed agreements at a Milan hotel Wednesday securing payouts averaging €45,000 (US$50,400) each for alleged labour abuses while working for an American construction company. More than 60 labourers, mostly from India, signed the deals Wednesday to receive their share of a €31 million (nearly US$35 million) settlement agreed last month with Alabama-based Caddell Construction. The signings began Tuesday. Prosecutors say it is the largest settlement ever for labour exploitation in Europe. Each worker signed a document seen by Associated Press agreeing not to discredit Caddell and not to disclose the individual payments. Caddell said in the document that the settlement was not an admission of liability. Individual payments are to be made within 30 days of the signing. The workers saw the potentially life-changing sum in black-and-white for the first time at the signings - with the highest reaching nearly €90,000 (nearly US$101,000), said Francesco Brigatti, the court-appointed administrator working to return the consulate construction site to legality. The payouts combine unpaid overtime, reimbursement for housing illegally deducted from their pay and hefty damages personally sought by investigating Prosecutor Paolo Storari, Brigatti said. “The damages component alone amounts to 60–70 per cent of the overtime total,” Brigatti said, well above the 10 per cent to 30 per cent that he said is more customary in such cases. Dilip Ram, a 43-year-old mason from India, has worked at the Milan consulate site for more than two years. He said the money would go a long way to helping his family of five back home in the Indian state of Bihar. “Things are better now than before … we get more rest now,” Ram said, after signing the deal. “This has led to a lot of change. This settlement will be good. Because the workers had troubles, that’s why this settlement has been applied.” Over two days, 115 workers signed the deals, with the procedure continuing next week. Prosecutors say workers were paid less than US$2 an hour, were illegally docked money for housing and denied overtime for working up to 10 hours a day, six days a week. They also were allegedly subjected to threats and not given proper medical care when they were injured on the job. Most of the workers were from India, but also Nigeria, Kenya and Bangladesh. Workers from India reported having to pay €5,000 (US$5,600) to recruiters to get the jobs, but the settlement did not directly address abuses in India, where prosecutors could not investigate, officials said. The investigation against Caddell remains open, pending the payouts, which are expected to be completed by February. Two managers under investigation for extortion and facilitating illegal immigration remain under house arrest. Caddell’s settlement includes about €11.2 million (US$12.5 million) for Italy’s social security coffers and workplace injury insurance. Under the deal, the workers are also getting permits to work in Italy even off the Caddell site. Caddell, a major contractor for US embassies and consulates worldwide, said in June that it was cooperating fully with Italian authorities, reviewing its global subcontractors and consultancies for compliance with labour laws, and working with authorities to protect workers on the project. “Caddell continues to cooperate in good faith with the appropriate authorities throughout this process, and we remain focused on the care and well-being of the people working on an important project,” the company said Wednesday. The US State Department has said it is investigating the allegations made by prosecutors and that US law enforcement is working with Italian authorities. Last week, it added that it is following the case closely. “The US government has zero tolerance for illegal activity,” it said. In all, nearly 480 workers can expect payouts - some 300 still working on the site, another 100 elsewhere in Italy and the rest in their home countries.

title: China boss gifts top employees new BMWs to protect them from harsh weather commutes
description: Ma attributes her company’s prosperity to the collective effort of her employees, believing they should directly share in its success.
content: A restaurant boss in China has received widespread online admiration for gifting brand-new BMWs to her top-performing employees because she hated seeing them brave harsh weather on electric bikes during their commutes. Ma Yanli, owner of a beef hotpot chain headquartered in Jiaozuo, in central Henan province, took some of her workers to collect their new BMWs on September 24. The cars, each priced at 300,000 yuan (US$45,000), had been bought by Ma two weeks earlier with full payment, Henan TV reported. “I am so thrilled! I dared not think about this before,” one of the lucky employees, Li Jie, was quoted as saying. “On the way to the BMW showroom, Boss Ma just told me she would gift me a big toy.” A brand-new white BMW was registered in Li’s name that same day, and she did not have to pay a cent for it. Ma also did not ask Li to sign an agreement in exchange for the gift. Ma said she first came up with the idea of gifting BMWs to her employees last winter. Like most of her colleagues, Li used an electric scooter to commute. One early morning, Ma saw Li arrive at the restaurant with her face flushed bright red from the cold. Her ears had turned purple, and her hands were stiff from the chill wind. Seeing this made Ma feel sorry for Li, who had worked at the restaurant for eight years. “I said to myself: I can sit in my car and enjoy warmth and convenience during transportation. Why can’t she?” Ma said. “I have achieved success in my career. But my company’s prosperity is attributed to the collective efforts of all my employees. So I must let my workers also benefit from the success of my company,” added Ma, who has worked in the catering industry for two decades. Besides Li, another worker, Liu Yingying, received a grey BMW. “My boss told me you work hard and your performance is excellent. You deserve this car,” Liu told the media. This was not Ma’s first generous gesture towards her staff. On traditional Chinese festivals, she usually gives them daily essentials and cash bonuses. Bosses who give gifts to their staff or offer generous pay often draw significant attention in China. Cui Peijun, chairman of Henan Kuangshan Crane Company, is nicknamed “the boss who loves distributing money most” because of his generosity towards his workers. Before the Spring Festival last year, he gave his staff a total of 180 million yuan (US$27 million) in bonuses, equivalent to two-thirds of the company’s profits from the previous year. Every International Women’s Day, Cui gives each of his 2,000 female employees 800 yuan. In August each year, workers from rural areas receive 1,000 yuan from him as a “grain reaper subsidy” to help them rent harvesters for their families’ crops.

title: Will Huanggang Port opening boost spending at Shenzhen’s border retail shops?
description: Service staff are bracing for influx of visitors, but say they fear shoppers will bypass border establishments for major commercial belts.
content: Retail businesses in Shenzhen are gearing up for the imminent opening of the revamped Huanggang Port at the border Hong Kong shares with mainland China, but some fear the area still lacks commercial appeal to make travellers stay. After six years of redevelopment, the expanded checkpoint is due to open on October 12, according to a source. It will adopt the “joint inspection” model for immigration clearance, which is expected to cut the previous clearance time from about 30 minutes to five minutes. Authorities have said the port will initially be able to handle 100,000 passenger trips a day, with capacity potentially rising to 300,000 in the future. The Bosen Dental clinic opened a new branch across from the new facility in August. Its other branches are also located near border crossings such as Futian and Liantang, as well as one near Shenzhen North railway station. “Of course, we all hope the new crossing will open soon to bring us more guests,” the manager of the clinic’s Huanggang branch said, noting the company chose the site to attract customers crossing the border. “Hong Kong residents make up most of our customers,” said a clinic staff member handing out promotional fliers along the border street. “We open where there is a need.” Several other dental clinics have also set up promotional booths at the Huanggang Checkpoint metro station. “We’re promoting here in anticipation of the new border crossing opening,” a sales staff member from Maiya Dental said. Lawson, a convenience store chain, opened a branch in August near the new immigration facility, where it also rents space to run a courier shop. It plans to hire an additional staff member next week after the official opening, specifically to serve Hong Kong customers sending parcels across the border. “The store is targeted at earning money from Hongkongers,” a service staff member said. Two restaurants also opened near the new building in August, anticipating customers from across the border. A woman could be seen standing outside a tea restaurant, trying to attract diners in Cantonese. “Our goal is to welcome Hong Kong foot traffic from the new crossing,” said a waitress working for another Chiu Chow restaurant. “We expect at least a 300 to 400 per cent increase in our sales.” Zhou Qunhui, manager of the 7-Eleven at the Huanggang Checkpoint station, said she was excited about the opening because her store was next to a tunnel connecting with the new building. “We had planned to install some new equipment in the store and prepare more popular foods and products that may attract Hong Kong customers,” Zhou said. “Our business in recent years has always been steady, neither poor nor good, but I am really betting on the new opening to at least double our sales.” However, other retail employees harboured doubts about whether faster clearance and larger crowds from the crossing would translate into higher spending or even encourage travellers to stay longer. “I’m not sure whether the new port will bring us more guests, because there is no commercialisation,” said the manager of Bosen Dental. “Only centralised commercial areas can attract customers.” Pointing to shops near the clinic, he noted that many remained under construction or were even empty despite the site being located directly across from the new building in what is largely a ground-floor area of a residential complex. “More customers will only come if there are enough choices for entertainment, like food and drinks and massages.” A manager of a hotel about a 10-minute walk from Huanggang Port said hotels were already struggling due to the area’s waning attractiveness. “Once the border gets more convenient public transport, we will only lose more customers, as most of them will directly take a taxi or metro to other districts,” the manager said, referring to Futian district as “having larger commercial areas and more new hotels”. “There is no commercial district [around Huanggang]. If this large residential area had one, say a night market, a food street or even just a shopping centre slightly closer, then we can say we are in a good position.” The Huanggang checkpoint sits next to the Futian checkpoint, and it takes about 15 minutes by subway to reach the core commercial zones around the Shopping Park and Convention and Exhibition Centre stations, known as a major shopping belt drawing many visitors from Hong Kong.

title: In Focus | The ‘G2’ illusion? After Xi-Trump summit, China wants equality while the US seeks deals
description: White House pageantry casts Beijing as an equal – unsettling India and raising questions about China’s Global South status.
content: Washington and Beijing may have signed an agreement built around “reciprocity”. But a more consequential question remains unresolved: does it mean equal status for Beijing? Countries without a seat at the table are watching that ambiguity closely. The spectacle of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington – the tarmac greeting, the flyovers, the state dinner – has been interpreted less as courtesy than as a statement of rank. Some argue that China is no longer being treated as part of the Global South, but as the US’ peer. But “reciprocity” does not necessarily mean the same thing to both sides. For the United States, reciprocity is transactional: a concession matched by a concession, a deal measured by what each side gets in return. For China, it means equal standing: the recognition that Beijing should be dealt with not as a subordinate power being managed by Washington, but as a peer. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi made that meaning explicit as the visit ended. In remarks released by state news agency Xinhua on September 26, he said reciprocity meant the two countries were “equal in sovereignty”, that neither side stood above the other, that concerns were handled “on an equal basis” and that cooperation developed “in a balanced manner”. According to analysts, US President Donald Trump’s embrace of “G2” diplomacy and the extraordinary choreography of his reception for Xi give Beijing an opportunity to turn the language of a transaction into the image of parity. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the reception showed that Washington valued Beijing’s international weight and was willing to “invest political resources into improving ties” – a signal that could “set the stage for future negotiations and inter-agency cooperation”. But he cautioned against reading the symbolism too far. “Reception protocol alone is not enough to conclude that both sides have accepted a ‘G2’ framework,” Sun said, referring to the idea of a “Group of Two”, or a global duopoly with China and the US as the world’s leading powers. “If ‘G2’ merely emphasises the importance of US-China coordination to global affairs, that indeed reflects reality,” he said. “If it implies the two countries jointly dominating the world and making decisions on behalf of other nations, that goes beyond any conclusion this meeting can support.” “China is more concerned with whether the relationship is equal, whereas the US side is more focused on whether specific trade-offs are worthwhile,” Sun added. Trump’s warmth towards Xi appears personal rather than institutional. The White House “still stresses that the US should exercise leadership from a position of strength”, he said. What matters, he said, was “whether the US can respect China’s right to development and core interests in concrete policies, and accept addressing differences through consultation on an equal footing”. That gap is the “G2” illusion: the two sides can sit across the same table while attaching very different expectations to what the relationship means. Sourabh Gupta, a senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, was blunt: a US-China “G2” is not emerging. “Trump aside, much of his administration and the beltway political establishment seek rivalry with China. But China won’t play ball,” he said. “Just as one cannot clap with one hand, so also the two sides are stuck between uneasy coexistence and the drift towards rivalry.” The same logic applies to the economy. China wants interdependence; much of the US would rather decouple. The result, Gupta said, was “a mediocre and deteriorating economic equation that might appear stable at a given moment, but which masks a deeper strategic hollowness”. In that condition, a “G2” was “a far-fetched assumption”, he added. Xi Jinping does not want a G2 that governs the world together with the United States Ken Moriyasu, Hudson Institute Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South Programme at the Quincy Institute, said “a sweeping G2” was unlikely. “[But] limited G2s may emerge down the road that create bargains in certain spaces in which outright competition is too costly or risky for both. AI is such an area,” he added. The chances of a resolution rise if neither side can prevail easily – which he noted was the present reality – and if both see mutual benefit, a condition he said had yet to be observed. Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, argued that Beijing did not even want to be part of a duopoly. “Xi Jinping does not want a G2 that governs the world together with the United States,” he said. According to Moriyasu, Xi wants a “new model of major-country relations” in which the two powers respect each other’s political systems, core interests and spheres of concern while avoiding confrontation. He said Beijing’s preferred order was more multipolar than a “G2” – closer to the UN Security Council, with five major powers standing above the rest. As the weaker power, Gupta said, Beijing “harps on sovereign equality in its dealings with Washington, much as New Delhi continually does so in its dealings with Beijing. It is a function of weakness, and strict reciprocity viewed as an equaliser.” He added that the US had stood “head and shoulders above its peers for the past 75 years” and treated sovereign equality as “a notional concept” while leveraging its advantages for “transactional gain”. The Global South question These observations land on a larger question: whether China still belongs in the Global South category it has long claimed. Shidore drew a distinction between the treatment and the label. “Most certainly, Washington treats China very differently from any other Global South middle power,” he said. “China is being recognised as a great power, a recognition that China has itself long craved. With President Trump, it has received it without any reservations.” Moriyasu went further. “I doubt many countries in the Global South now look at China and see a fellow Global Southerner,” he said. “If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck. China is now a full-fledged great power.” Gupta rejected the binary. China “can be a great power and still remain very much a part of the Global South”, he said, calling it a “bundle of contradictions” that could sit at the global head table and still be “a great power within the confines of the Global South’s rise”. If Washington deals with Beijing as a peer, however, China begins to look less like the most powerful member of that camp and more like one of the powers sitting above it. That reading has landed hardest in New Delhi. Indian officials and commentators watched the Chinese leader’s Washington visit with a familiar dread: a US-China “G2”, long feared in private, was being staged in public. Trump was receiving Xi as a peer. India in the audience Ivan Lidarev, a research fellow at the National University of Singapore’s Institute of South Asian Studies, said the fanfare had sparked “unease and jealousy” in India. “New Delhi has long feared the emergence of a US-China G2 through which the two sides will manage the world and South Asia,” he said. Trump has refrained from using the phrase “G2” in recent days, though he has framed his encounters with Xi in those terms since their summit in South Korea last autumn. To Brahma Chellaney, a New Delhi-based strategic analyst, Trump’s language was more revealing than the pageantry. “The writing on the wall is clear: Trump sees America and China as the world’s two pre-eminent powers that should cooperate in managing global affairs, despite their intense rivalry,” he wrote on social media. “For America’s allies and strategic partners, especially in Asia, that signals a profound shift in Washington’s strategic world view.” For some Indian observers, the summit pointed to “how far China is ahead of India”, Lidarev said, with the US increasingly treating China as an equal superpower. He said it also threatened the two-decade bedrock of US-India ties – which were “built on counterbalancing China” – just as those ties were strained over trade and oil sanctions. Jabin Jacob, a professor at Shiv Nadar University, said India would not read much into the pageantry. “It certainly understands that [the meeting] does not fundamentally alter the trajectory of US-China relations,” he said. “This is competitive more than it is cooperative.” Lidarev noted that India’s fears about the Xi-Trump meeting included the possibility of joint Sino-American oversight of the Indo-Pacific, a technological duopoly in AI and semiconductors, and US concessions on Taiwan that could embolden Beijing. “Fortunately for India, none of these concerns were justified,” he said. But more frequent Trump-Xi meetings still raise the prospect of a real “G2” at India’s expense. Lidarev said he did not expect a major recalibration following the summit, but Delhi would pursue a thaw in ties with Beijing and adopt a “less US-leaning position”. Jacob said India had to reset its policy towards both powers anyway, because its compromise-heavy stance, driven by economic strain and reliance on Russian oil, was “suboptimal”. That need would become more urgent if US-China ties evolved into a genuine duopoly. Shidore said that if such an arrangement emerged, even in just a few sectors or specific regions, other countries would find less room for independent policy. “Rather than exploit the competition between Beijing and Washington, these states will have to conform to rules jointly defined by the two great powers, rules against which they will have little capacity to resist,” he said. He added that the pressure would be less about choosing a side than “falling in line with an arrangement they had no voice in shaping”. “We are not there yet,” he said. “It remains to be seen if we will get there.”

title: Domestic helpers in Hong Kong pursue degree dreams they put on hold
description: Non-profit organisation FullPhils partners with universities in the Philippines to offer online courses for domestic workers abroad.
content:
When Dyan Agonoy left the Philippines to work as a domestic helper in Hong Kong, she had to leave her family behind.
“I’ve missed a lot of my kids’ milestones ... I’m always the only one missing from the pictures,” she said.
Agonoy left university, married young and started a family. Without the bachelor’s degree required for many jobs, she took up domestic work abroad.
Her life changed in 2024, when she came across FullPhils, a non-profit organisation that helps overseas Filipino workers in Hong Kong earn bachelor’s degrees.
The courses are fully online. The group subsidises 80 per cent of the costs, leaving students to pay about HK$600 (US$76) per term.
FullPhils was founded in 2022 by Emilio Baja when he was just 14 years old. Originally from the Philippines, Baja lived in Hong Kong for two years. He was struck by the crowds of domestic helpers gathering every Sunday in makeshift tents and on cardboard boxes.
FullPhils partners with institutions in the Philippines, including AMA University, Philippine Women’s University and the University of the Philippines, to offer domestic workers online courses.

title: Style Edit: Hogan marks 40 years of luxury sneakers with cinema
description: The Italian luxury shoemaker celebrates its legacy dating back to 1986 with short films, limited-edition Cool Blue sneakers and scholarships for students at a Rome film school.
content: Before the luxury sneaker became a wardrobe staple, Hogan had already identified the opportunity in a shoe that could move comfortably between casual and cachet. The Italian brand marks its 40th anniversary this year by revisiting that founding instinct: a belief that well-made footwear should accommodate the pace of modern life without compromising on design or craftsmanship. Founded in 1986 within the Tod’s Group, Hogan began with the Traditional, a streamlined, cricket-inspired shoe defined by a pared-back elegance. Its next landmark arrived in the 1990s with the Interactive, developed after Andrea Della Valle observed women commuting in trainers before changing into smarter shoes for work. The resulting sneaker, recognisable by its bold “H” and softly contoured profile, offered an early answer to an increasingly familiar question: why should comfort stop at the office door? That idea has continued to shape Hogan’s offerings. Over four decades, the label has expanded from footwear into bags and apparel, introduced silhouettes including the ultralight Olympia, H-Stripes, Hyperlight and Cool, and collaborated with figures such as Karl Lagerfeld. Its approach has remained rooted in a certain Italian practicality – clean, expressive and designed to be worn rather than saved for an occasion. For the anniversary, Hogan has chosen cinema as a way to revisit its history. Four emerging Italian directors from the Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia have each made a short film centred on an iconic shoe and a different decade. Nicolò Folin’s Celeste looks back to the 1980s through the Traditional; Sarah Narducci’s Nine Hundred places the Interactive in a midnight skating story at the turn of the millennium; Gregorio Mattiocco’s Never Off casts the Olympia as a constant amid a diva’s escape from the paparazzi; and Paoli De Luca’s Lola Rebel finds freedom and reinvention in the Hogan Rebel. The partnership will also provide five three-year scholarships for students at the Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia, supporting training in directing, acting, screenwriting, editing and production design. It is a practical extension of the campaign’s emphasis on new perspectives and creative momentum. The milestone is marked, too, with the Hogan Cool Blue Limited Edition. Available in selected boutiques and on Hogan.com, the shoe updates the clean lines of the Hogan Cool with a deep-blue pony-effect leather upper, H86_26 graphics on the outsole and matching laces. As Hogan turns 40, its anniversary is a reminder that a true everyday icon is made to adapt: footwear conceived for people in motion, with enough character to carry its history forward.

title: Boy, 13, rescued after climbing onto air-conditioning unit to escape fire in flat
description: Hong Kong firefighters rescue boy who was home alone on Wednesday night, while his mother has been arrested on suspicion of child neglect.
content: Hong Kong firefighters have rescued a 13-year-old boy who climbed out of a window onto an air-conditioning unit to escape a fire that broke out in his flat, while his mother has been arrested on suspicion of child neglect. Police received reports at 7.54pm on Wednesday that a fire had broken out in a flat at Tsui To House, one of the blocks of Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong. Online video showed the boy, wearing only his underwear, climbing out of the window and onto the condenser unit as thick black smoke filled the flat. Firefighters deployed a ladder to reach the boy and pulled him to safety. Around 70 residents were evacuated. The blaze was extinguished at about 8.25pm. The boy, who was suspected to be ill from smoke inhalation, was taken to United Christian Hospital in Kwun Tong for treatment. A preliminary investigation found the fire was caused by a charger in the living room, and police said the incident was not suspicious. Officers later believed the boy had been left home alone. His 42-year-old mother, surnamed Ho, was arrested for ill-treatment or neglect of a child or young person under her care and detained for investigation. The case is being handled by the Kwun Tong district criminal investigation unit.

title: Yemen’s Houthis claim strikes on Saudi airports, killing 3
description: Attacks on Riyadh and Abha airports mark a sharp escalation of the war in neighbouring Yemen.
content: Saudi authorities said Wednesday three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom’s international airports, including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. The Iran-backed Houthis have claimed a wave of attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, which came as Riyadh-backed forces pressed a counteroffensive against the group’s territorial gains. Since Yemen’s civil war reignited in July, more than 200,000 people have been displaced within the country, the United Nations said Wednesday. The Houthis claimed an attack on Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition – which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight against the group – vowed retaliation. The Houthis later claimed another attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Thursday and repeated a warning – “for the last time” – to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace. “On Tuesday and Wednesday … Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities,” Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said in a statement. An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said. The attacks wounded 36 people, it added. In a subsequent statement, the coalition directly blamed Houthi fighters for the strikes and vowed a response. “The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished,” it wrote on X. The coalition said it had retaliated by striking 82 “legitimate military targets”, including missile facilities, command centres, communications systems and Houthi gathering sites. Yemen’s government declared a major counteroffensive against the Houthis this week, claiming to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha. But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by Agence France-Presse have not reported any major changes on the ground. Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Wednesday that the group had targeted Riyadh’s airport in an “accurate” strike that “led to a disruption of air traffic”. The Saudi-led military coalition said on X it “destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform” used in the attack. The Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in Aden, the interim capital for Yemen’s government. The government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport. The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, Houthi spokesman Saree said, claiming they had “hit their targets accurately”. It is the second time this week Houthis claimed to have attacked Riyadh’s main airport. Saudi Arabia has led an international coalition fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance. The coalition said Monday it was providing air support for the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive. After four years of ceasefire, the Houthis claimed last month they had seized Yemen’s entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years. New clashes on Wednesday in Yemen’s west left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps said. Saba also reported that a Houthi missile wounded five civilians in Taiz, a city held by government forces. Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade. The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.

title: Protect the middle? Why Southeast Asia should care about a vulnerable class
description: Recent shocks have exposed how the middle class can fall through the cracks of the region’s safety nets, analysts say.
content: As households across Southeast Asia face rising prices, higher borrowing costs and insecure jobs, analysts say governments should do more to protect a middle class that drives consumer spending but can fall between the cracks of social protection systems designed primarily for poorer households. The issue has come into sharper focus in the Philippines, where the Asian Development Bank Institute urged the government in September to provide targeted support for the middle class to protect its purchasing power and avoid a drag on economic growth. Bambang Brodjonegoro, dean and CEO of the institute, said Philippine officials should focus their efforts on the middle class, which made up the bulk of household consumption. “For the Philippines to revive its economic growth, the attention needs to be on how to increase the purchasing power of the middle class and to not let the middle class shrink,” Brodjonegoro told local media on the sidelines of a forum on September 17. The Philippines’ inflation rose to a four-month high of 7.2 per cent in September, adding to pressure on household finances. Maria Monica Wihardja, an economist and fellow of the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s media, technology and society programme, said the Philippines was “one of the most affected countries in the Asean region” by the US-Israel war on Iran because of its high dependence on oil transported through the Strait of Hormuz “and its twin energy and current account deficits” Governments across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations faced difficult trade-offs between fiscal constraints and expanding social protection, Wihardja said. “Recent shocks have significantly affected the middle class because they are the income class that spends a lot on fuel, takes loans and works in sectors that have been affected by a series of external shocks, but at the same time they are not covered by any safety net programmes unlike the poor and the vulnerable,” she said. In addition to the impact on individual households, economists say middle-class consumption is also an important source of growth. “When middle-class households have to cut back sharply on consumption, growth can suffer,” said Jose Ramon Albert, a senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute for Development Studies. The Philippines recently launched a social assistance programme called “Uplift” to ease recent price spikes, but Albert said it was only designed to help poor and low-income households. “We do not have a programme designed for the middle class as such … a middle-class family hit by a shock may obtain help, but must seek assistance and undergo assessment,” he said. Wihardja said the issue was especially apparent in Indonesia, where the middle class was shrinking. An analysis published last October by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace also highlighted gaps in social support for the aspiring middle class, who miss out on cash transfers, scholarships and subsidised health insurance. It found that households between the 50th and 80th percentiles saw a drop in real consumption between 2019 and 2022, whereas the bottom 20 per cent saw gains, thanks to government safety nets. Such findings raise a broader question about whether state support reaches households that are above the poverty line, yet remain vulnerable to sudden economic shocks. According to Albert, Indonesia and the Philippines face a similar challenge, in that the bulk of their middle class live on between US$8 and US$16 a day and are at risk of falling back into poverty. Vietnam’s middle class, by contrast, has a much higher concentration of people at the upper end of the income scale. “But income or consumption levels alone do not establish resilience. Assets, debt, insurance and job security also matter,” he said. “The contrasts lie in the mix of exposures: how much household income comes from informal work or small enterprises, reliance on remittances, exposure to food and fuel prices, and access to insurance and other protection.” For policymakers, the question is therefore not simply whether to create a new welfare category for the middle class, but how to make current safety nets more responsive when households begin to struggle. Wihardja said protecting middle-class purchasing power through targeted measures would be a wise move, given that this group was a primary driver of consumer demand for goods and services – but such assistance need not come through direct subsidies. “It can be done by making sure that the quality, accessibility and affordability of public infrastructure and services, from transport to education, are improved so the middle-class households don’t have to opt for more expensive private services,” she said. Vietnam offers an example of how broad-based measures can also benefit middle-income households. The Vietnamese government has temporarily held value-added tax at 8 per cent instead of the usual 10 per cent across most goods and services. Meanwhile, state school tuition, from nursery through to secondary education, became entirely free nationwide from September 2025. Personal income tax allowances have also been raised, offering financial relief to eligible working families. Not every country faces the same challenges, however. “There are common global and regional patterns or causes of increasingly insecure middle class but there are also country-specific differences,” Wihardja said. In Thailand, she said many middle-class households were burdened by high debt, while the Philippines was heavily dependent on remittances from abroad. For regional governments, creating more resilient societies will entail extending access to basic services and protection against major risks to more than just low-income households. “When a crisis hits, governments should be able to extend temporary support quickly to those who need it, including middle-class households that are not poor in normal times but are pushed to the edge by a shock,” Albert said. That would require comprehensive social registries, clear eligibility criteria and benefits capable of scaling up during economic downturns, he said, as well as more robust social insurance for health, unemployment and old age. But Wihardja said short-term protection was only part of the answer. Governments also needed to focus on quality job creation, industrial upgrading, AI-related supply chains and the green transition, she said, as technological change could affect jobs previously considered secure, including white-collar work in high-value service sectors. “At the macro level, middle-income countries need to have policies that can support structural transformation towards higher-value, higher-productivity sectors and jobs including skill- and knowledge-intensive industries,” she said.

title: Elon Musk hits out at ‘certain oligarchs’ for blocking Starlink in India
description: Responding to Musk’s apparent dig at Mukesh Ambani and Sunil Bharti Mittal, New Delhi said its regulations were ‘fair’.
content: Elon Musk accused unnamed rivals of blocking SpaceX’s Starlink satellite broadband network in India, an apparent swipe at billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Sunil Bharti Mittal. SpaceX has been awaiting approval from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to offer Starlink service in India, where companies controlled by Ambani’s Reliance Industries and Mittal’s Bharti Airtel have spent years building formidable positions in telecoms. “Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people,” Musk said on social media. “You can guess who they are …” India’s two biggest private telecoms operators, Reliance Jio Infocomm and Bharti Airtel, together account for roughly 910 million broadband subscribers, more than 80 per cent of the country’s market, according to the latest government data. India’s Ministry of Communications said on Thursday that the government had a “fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework for all telecommunication services”. It made no mention of Musk, but only a post “being circulated in social media regarding the fairness of India’s regulatory framework for satellite communication services”. It added telecom licences had been granted to satellite services “as part of its commitment to enable provision of satellite communication services in India”, without specifying the names of the companies. Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent after regular business hours. India had effectively frozen final approvals for Starlink’s commercial launch due to security concerns. Security agencies under the country’s home ministry withheld clearances for the low-Earth orbit service to begin operations, people familiar with the matter said in June. Starlink has secured a satellite communications licence in India but is still waiting for the security clearances as well as spectrum before it can switch on commercially. Speaking at an industry conference in New Delhi on Wednesday, Lauren Dreyer, vice-president of Starlink business operations, said the company has spent five years working with Indian regulators and had built its network specifically around the country’s security requirements, with “controls at every layer” and Indian user data kept within India. “We’re standing ready to serve India once India is ready,” she said. Bharti is one of the largest shareholders in Eutelsat Communications, operator of the Eutelsat OneWeb satellite network that is one of Starlink’s biggest low-Earth orbit competitors worldwide. Airtel has separately partnered with SpaceX to offer Starlink to its Indian customers, an illustration of the complicated alliances emerging around the market. Reliance has its own satellite ambitions through Jio Satellite Communications and its joint venture with Luxembourg-based satellite operator SES. Jio, OneWeb and Starlink are among the three companies that have received India’s satellite-communications licences, although none has yet fully switched on commercial service. Jio Platforms, Reliance’s telecoms and digital services arm, is preparing for what may be the biggest initial public offering in India’s history later this month. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: More global investors eye Chinese equities, ending 4-year underweight run, bank says
description: Chinese assets likely to continue attracting attention amid relatively low valuations and elevated external uncertainties, analyst says.
content: Global investors are taking another look at Chinese equities after years of cautious positioning, drawn by relatively cheap valuations and opportunities in artificial intelligence, although an end to persistent selling does not indicate an outright bullish turn, according to analysts. Global active long-only funds have raised their average allocation to Chinese equities to benchmark-neutral from underweight since June, according to a recent Bank of America analysis of 2,767 global funds. The change ended four years of underweight positioning, with the funds managing US$562 billion in Chinese stocks, the bank added. Meanwhile, BlackRock remained neutral on Chinese equities but saw opportunities in physical AI, according to its fourth-quarter global outlook published in September. UBS Asset Management also said in a report published on October 1 that China remained “a key opportunity”, citing attractive valuations in selected sectors including technology, AI and advanced manufacturing. “Chinese assets are likely to continue attracting greater attention from global investors,” said Kenny Ng, a strategist at Everbright Securities International. “Valuations, particularly in Hong Kong, remain relatively low, while external uncertainties remain elevated.” Risks including persistently high US Treasury yields, mounting US government debt, geopolitical tensions and the US midterm elections could increase market volatility, making Hong Kong and mainland Chinese equities “attractive from a diversification perspective”, he said. The shift also came as concerns over China’s economic outlook eased. The MSCI China Index traded at about 10.2 times forward earnings as of September 30, below its 10-year average of 11.7 times, while exchange-traded funds focused on China and Hong Kong recorded US$19 million of inflows in August, reversing US$1.94 billion of outflows in July. However, some analysts cautioned against interpreting the shift in positioning as a broad return of foreign investors to Chinese equities. “The shift is more a stop to the selling, not a broad bullish turn,” said Louis Wong, executive director at Phillip Capital Management. “What changed is investors’ buy-in to China’s attractive valuation”, along with a perception that the Chinese economy had performed better than feared. Interest is concentrated in AI semiconductors and equipment, data-centre power and grid infrastructure, as well as selected internet platforms with visible cloud growth Louis Wong, Phillip Capital Management Foreign exposure to Chinese equities would “edge up gradually and moderately”, Wong said. With the 10-year US Treasury yield at around 5.3 per cent, investors faced a high hurdle for adding exposure to a market still associated with policy and geopolitical risks, he added. “[Global investors’] interest is concentrated in AI semiconductors and equipment, data-centre power and grid infrastructure, as well as selected internet platforms with visible cloud growth,” Wong said. Disappointing economic momentum, slow AI earnings growth, tighter US export controls or further weakness in the yuan could derail the shift, he added. Wang Qi, chief investment officer at UOB Kay Hian’s wealth-management division, was more cautious, saying he had yet to see a genuine shift in global investor sentiment towards Chinese equities amid higher US interest rates. Global investors would need to see a “sizeable and effective” stimulus by the Chinese government before significantly increasing their exposure, he said.

title: Opinion | Beyond the summit: how US-China relations could still unravel
description: High-level optics from Xi’s state visit cannot hide underlying friction – over tech exports, investments and domestic politics – that threatens to pull ties back off track.
content: This year’s Chinese National Day reception in Washington felt noticeably jollier than those I have attended in recent years. The mood was more relaxed and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng’s opening speech was upbeat. He even joked about the panda ambassadors at his own expense. The cheerful tone followed President Xi Jinping’s short but successful state visit to the US, during which his counterpart, President Donald Trump, gave him an unprecedented high-level reception that would have flattered even the most fastidious of guests. Yet the mood outside the embassy was decidedly different. The opposition Democrats criticised Trump’s cosying up to “communist” China as another example of his misguided foreign policy, a betrayal of American allies and even a sell-out of national interests. The mainstream media, locked in a feud with Trump over his ban on media access to the White House, either downplayed the visit or focused on its lack of tangible progress. Even the president’s allies admitted in private that the timing “was not right” to expect a major breakthrough. With the midterm elections just weeks away, the polarisation of American politics can only deepen. Even among Trump’s supporters and the business community, there is little agreement on what deals to seek with Beijing. Americans certainly want China to lift its rare earth export controls, but there is no consensus on what to offer in return. Relaxing the US ban on advanced chips to China meets strong opposition. At the risk of oversimplification, there are two camps. One argues that the restrictions will only push Beijing to accelerate its own chip development, and that it is in American interests to allow a controlled flow of advanced chips to China to maintain its “chip dependency”. The other believes that China will pursue an alternative chip industry regardless, and that selling advanced chips would merely buy Beijing time. This camp holds that the US should double down on the restrictions, particularly as nobody can be sure whether China, or any other country, can really build an alternative system independent of American-controlled components. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su sat at the head table at the state dinner Trump hosted for Xi, but the South China Morning Post was told that chip controls were never on the negotiating table. That suggests the hawks on this issue are in the driver’s seat. There is similarly no consensus among Americans on regulating artificial intelligence, or “superintelligence” as the White House calls it. Some see regulation as a power grab by a handful of tech giants. Advocates of the open-source approach want to know how standards would be set, who would be responsible for verification, and how, even if a common set of standards could be agreed. The Chinese proposal to include chip controls in the bilateral AI dialogue only complicates matters. The same is true of allowing more Chinese investment, or Chinese-owned electric vehicle and battery factories, in the United States. As the SCMP reported, some Chinese company executives travelled to Washington in the hope of a last-minute agreement that might open the door to US investment, but it proved futile. It is telling that just a few days after Xi’s visit, Ford CEO Jim Farley warned that the US must carefully consider whether to admit Chinese carmakers to the American market, lest it become another Europe – a reference to the explosive growth of Chinese cars there. Farley wants to work with the Chinese only in areas where America can acquire technologies it lacks, which is hardly something Beijing will be excited about. Beyond business, matters are even more complicated. It is widely known that Taiwan is Beijing’s absolute red line. Trump showed remarkable restraint on this sensitive issue throughout Xi’s visit, but even for him, the Chinese request that he openly oppose Taiwan independence was a bridge too far. There is considerable pushback on the issue, even among Trump’s supporters. The president has delayed the latest round of arms sales to Taiwan, partly helped by supply shortages for more urgent needs elsewhere, but how long the administration can keep the lid on is an open question. In his speech, Ambassador Xie highlighted the good rapport between Xi and Trump, which has become the most critical ballast stabilising the bilateral relationship. Western media wrote about how Trump caged the China hawks. Yet it is always risky to predict the American president’s behaviour. He has been careful to maintain his relationship with Xi, but his China policy can change course drastically at any time. Those who accuse Trump of going soft on China would do well to remember that he launched an unprecedented trade war against Beijing just 18 months ago. Trump has still to make a historic trip to Shenzhen, home of Huawei, BYD and DJI, and Xi will visit Miami. But the focus of these meetings will be more on international affairs, compared with their summit in September. The whispers in Washington are that, besides the lack of American consensus, US allies alarmed at the unprecedented reception Xi received are also working hard to lobby Washington to push back. Japan is the most obvious example, but it is hardly the only country that feels this way. If there is no significant progress between Beijing and Washington by the time of the G20 summit, it will give the US, the European Union, Japan and others an opportunity to press China on issues such as the trade imbalance and rare earth controls. Added to this is uncertainty over the impact of the midterm elections, which many predict will go badly for Trump. How will the president react? Will he shift his focus to domestic issues, take a more conciliatory approach, or double down? Dabbling in the arcane art of Trumpology is a career hazard. None of this is to gainsay the positive results of Xi’s state visit, about which Beijing has plenty of reasons to feel pleased. But it would be dangerous to assume smooth sailing for China-US ties from here on. The next three months will determine whether strategic stability can truly emerge, or the relationship could go off the rails again.

title: End ‘wholesale restrictions’ on Chinese EVs in US, experts say
description: They call for America to engage with carmakers and battery manufacturers ‘strategically’, saying protectionism is ‘an act of self-harm’.
content: The United States should engage with Chinese carmakers and battery manufacturers “strategically”, using targeted safeguards instead of the current “wholesale restrictions”, which could lead US carmakers to lose global market share, according to experts. “We need to consider strategic partnerships,” said John Helveston, an associate professor at George Washington University, during a discussion on Tuesday. “So not just wholesale restrictions, but look at some of the best opportunities and let automakers pursue things like licensing agreements and other agreements with some targeted safeguards,” he added. Sourabh Gupta, resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, described the practice of protectionism in a globally scaled and competitive market as “an act of severe self-harm”. The comments came days after efforts to explore possible Chinese investments stalled during President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, amid growing opposition from members of Congress and US carmakers. The South China Morning Post earlier reported that differences between Washington and Beijing over potential investment announcements played a key role in blocking Chinese businesses from joining Xi’s delegation, despite a small group of Chinese executives being in the US capital. A person familiar with the issue said the group was expected to include representatives from Chinese electric-vehicle companies, which had expressed particularly strong interest in investing in the US. The two countries also remained divided over the Board of Investment, one of the outcomes from Xi and Trump’s summit in Beijing in May. Another source said the two sides had explored potential deals ahead of Xi’s visit, including one involving Chinese batteries, but the talks failed to produce an agreement. The official accounts after the summit showed that the plan had made no progress. The US fact sheet repeated its May reference to the investment board, while the Chinese readout did not mention it. Currently, Chinese carmakers face tariffs of more than 120 per cent, as well as restrictions on China-linked software and hardware under a connected vehicle rule designed to address data security risks posed by foreign technology. Congress has also moved to tighten restrictions, with bipartisan lawmakers introducing several House and Senate bills targeting China-linked electric vehicles in the US market. Despite opposition from car manufacturers and lawmakers, Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of allowing Chinese companies to set up shop in the US. “If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” he told Fox News last month. China dominates EV sales globally. “Europe has 4 million cars sold last year, but China is on a different scale. China sold more EVs last year than the US sold of all vehicles,” Helveston said during the discussion. “The advantages today are structural, not from unfair advantages from the government. The narrative of China dumping subsidies into the industry is overblown and misses a lot of other important things,” he added. Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies argued that Chinese carmakers “operate at a competitive level that has no peer”. “Fundamentally, the strength of China’s automakers derives from the excellence of their end-to-end integrated and intelligent manufacturing ecosystem back home as well as the creative remodelling of car interiors,” he said. Helveston cited a Rhodium Group report from February: the BYD Seal’s per-car cost advantage over the Tesla Model 3 from direct government grants is only US$304 – just about 5 per cent of the total gap in their cost structures. The bigger differences came from things like vertical integration. BYD makes nearly everything on the car in-house, down to the windscreen wipers, so it does not pay suppliers for those parts – saving US$2,369 per car. It also has much lower overheads thanks to local R&D, which adds another US$1,766 per car. “People think about lower-cost labour in China and imagine line workers in the manufacturing plant. That’s not really the difference,” Helveston said. “Because Tesla also has Chinese workers in its plants over there. The difference is that they have Chinese engineers, who are much less expensive to pay than a Silicon Valley engineer,” he said. “The US is kind of excluding Chinese companies right now. Reasons include protecting local automakers and security threats. “Banning Chinese EVs does not buy you the security that you think it does because every connected car is a nightmare, not just Chinese ones,” Helveston said, pointing to growing cybersecurity risks associated with connected cars in the US. He used Tesla as an example showing how companies could enter another country. “Even China – highly concerned about national security – didn’t ban Tesla outright. Instead, it set targeted rules: Tesla had to store data in China, use Baidu Maps instead of Google Maps, and avoid sensitive areas like military bases.” Tesla complied and built its Shanghai Gigafactory. The lesson: clear rules can protect security while still allowing market access, which is more reasonable than a blanket ban. If the US continued on its current path, Helveston feared American carmakers would shrink from being global players to a US-only market – maybe not even including Mexico and Canada – and fall behind on EVs. He suggested keeping North America integrated; not imposing tariffs on Canada and Mexico; and using real security standards, not just bans based on country of origin. He also called for an end to the policy back-and-forth, urging bipartisan support for recognising EVs as the future of the auto industry, rather than simply as an environmental technology, and incentivising them until they reach maturity.

title: Mainland Chinese arrivals beat last year’s ‘golden week’ figures despite shorter holiday
description: Arrivals topped 1.41 million over the seven-day holiday, as malls and hotels reported brisk trade.
content: Hong Kong recorded more mainland Chinese visitor arrivals during the National Day “golden week” holiday than predicted, surpassing last year’s total despite the break being one day shorter as malls and hotel operators reported brisk business. The city welcomed more than 1.41 million mainland arrivals during the seven-day holiday, exceeding the government’s forecast of 1.29 million, according to Immigration Department figures. More than 1.4 million mainland visitors arrived during the same holiday last year, when the break lasted eight days, from October 1 to 8. The government said on Thursday that the fireworks display on October 1, which drew 378,000 people, was among the most popular draws. It added that 1,140 mainland tours involving 41,000 visitors entered the city, with 60 per cent of them staying overnight. Echo Huang Shaomei, executive director and CEO of New World Development, said footfall at the group’s flagship K11 Musea mall reached a record for a National Day golden week holiday, while tourist spending rose by 26 per cent year on year. She said jewellery and watches remained popular with mainland visitors, with one transaction worth nearly HK$2 million (US$254,846). She added that sales of athleisure products also grew strongly, driven by the opening of American brand Alo Yoga’s first store in the country. “This further underscores the success of the brand upgrade programme that our team has pursued over the past two years, strengthening K11 Musea’s position as a premier destination for visitors during peak tourism seasons, while continuing to attract and broaden its high-net-worth customer base,” Huang said. She added that more internationally renowned brands were set to open at the shopping centre in the fourth quarter. A Henderson Land Development spokeswoman said spending on jewellery, electronics, premium dried seafood and dining was strong. Rewards and promotions targeting residents and tourists had helped stimulate consumption, she said. “Overall, both footfall and turnover at the group’s major shopping malls recorded double-digit year-on-year growth,” she said. The developer attributed the gains to government efforts to promote major events, a stabilising trend in Hongkongers travelling to the mainland to spend and its own marketing campaigns. Judy Chow Shuk-man, general manager for leasing at Sun Hung Kai Properties’ leasing agency, said many restaurants at Moko in Mong Kok and New Town Plaza in Sha Tin served two or more sittings at dinner. At Yoho Mall in Yuen Long, new brands attracted families from within and outside the district, with long queues during peak dinner hours, she said. Spending per head was similar to last year. “The trend of residents heading north has stabilised significantly,” Chow said. “Yoho Mall has carried out a large-scale refresh of its brands this year, introducing more than 75 new brands. “Together with different themed activities, this has successfully retained many local family customers.” She said the mall’s proximity to border crossings also made it convenient for visitors from elsewhere in the Greater Bay Area. Chow said themed pop-ups at New Town Plaza, including a Miss Dior cafe and shops featuring Pompompurin and Harry Potter, had attracted residents and tourists. Moko also recorded a marked increase in overseas visitors, including those from Southeast Asia. The developer was confident about the outlook for retail and dining businesses in the fourth quarter, she said, with Halloween, Christmas and New Year’s Eve offering further opportunities to boost spending Swire Properties said its malls, including Pacific Place in Admiralty, Cityplaza in Taikoo Shing and Citygate Outlets in Tung Chung, recorded higher sales over the past week. The government said the city’s overall occupancy of hotel rooms reached 90 per cent, about the same as last year. Peter Tam, deputy general manager of Metropark Hotel Mong Kok, said the hotel had performed strongly during the holiday, “hitting 100 per cent occupancy” from October 1 to 3, with the average daily rate peaking at HK$1,300. “Demand was led by solo travellers, with only a small group component at the start of the holiday, underpinned by mainland leisure travel,” he said. Tam added that most guests booked short stays of two to three nights. Room rates peaked in the first three days before falling notably by October 6. Many mainland visitors also headed to ecologically sensitive areas in Sai Kung. Sai Kung district councillor Chris Cheung Mei-hung said some locations came under pressure and facilities had not fully kept pace with numbers, although crowd control during the holiday was better than in previous peak periods. “These include Kiu Tsui Chau and Hap Mun Bay. On October 1, some 1,160 visitors headed to Po Pin Chau and about 2,020 to Kiu Tsui Chau, while a green group recorded more than 3,000 people landing at Hap Mun Bay in a single day,” he said. Cheung described high visitor numbers but low spending as “a warning sign”, pointing to changes in behaviour. “Many visitors now are backpackers or people who take ‘fast-paced’ trips, going straight to Po Pin Chau or Kiu Tsui Chau but leaving quickly, often without stopping in Sai Kung town centre,” he said. “While some restaurants around Sai Kung Pier have seen an increase in business, others are still empty with hardly any customers.” Additional reporting by Chris Tsang

title: Japan ‘considering ownership’ of nuclear submarines as regional rivalries worsen
description: Proposed changes could allow research into developing a domestically built nuclear-powered submarine without a firm decision on acquiring a fleet.
content: Japan is expected to float the idea of acquiring a fleet of nuclear-powered submarines in revised security documents to be released later this year, with analysts suggesting that Tokyo’s initial aim is to promote discussion of the issue and overcome the public’s concerns. Analysts acknowledge there will inevitably be pushback from some sectors of society in the only nation to have suffered a nuclear attack, but say there is a growing recognition that regional rivalries are worsening and Japan needs to do more to guarantee its own security. Quoting government sources, the Yomiuri newspaper reported on Wednesday that an expert panel set up to consider changes to the National Security Strategy and other key security documents would state that Japan was “considering ownership” of nuclear submarines. This would permit initial research into developing a domestically built nuclear-powered submarine without a firm decision on acquiring a fleet. If public support was adequate, the project could be given the green light to proceed, it added. “Attitudes in Japan have changed a lot in the last decade or so,” said Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Sophia University. “Anyone who is paying attention to national security issues has grown much more realistic about all the challenges surrounding Japan and has become more accepting of recent military programmes.” In recent years, these include the introduction of Japan’s first aircraft carrier since the end of World War II, a reinterpretation of export rules that now permits Japanese firms to sell weapons overseas and plans to acquire long-range missiles that can be launched from submarines, among others. “I expect this new document will mention that nuclear-powered submarines are necessary to act as a deterrent, while there is also the impact of South Korea’s decision to also obtain nuclear submarines,” Anno said. “That could easily be seen as a justification for Japan doing the same and I think that logic would help convince some that having a nuclear-powered submarine is no longer a taboo and is at least an option.” Experts say a Japanese nuclear-powered submarine is at least a decade away, however. “Japan’s current conventional fleet has already adapted many advanced technologies and that has helped it expand the time it remains submerged, but Japan is still behind what the US and Chinese navies can do,” said Joseph Kristanto, a maritime security analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies. “China, in particular, is developing its submarine capabilities quite rapidly and is able to operate ballistic missile submarines in the South China Sea and elsewhere,” he said. “In order for Japan to be able to track those boats, it would need nuclear-powered vessels.” Kristanto agrees there will be reluctance in some quarters to adopt nuclear technology, in part because of the destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, but also due to lingering fears from the disaster at the Fukushima nuclear power plant in March 2011. Yet resistance to nuclear power in general has abated and new plants are being built, suggesting that the public may be gradually coming around to the idea. “I would not describe this as Japan joining a submarine arms race, but there is certainly a sense of competition among Asian countries and a feeling in Japan that it cannot afford to be left behind,” he said. While nuclear-powered submarines are arguably less effective in the shallow waters within the first island chain, which stretches from Japan’s Okinawa prefecture through Taiwan and down to the Philippines, Kristanto said he did not believe that Japan deploying a new class of submarines into the Pacific could be considered the first step in the creation of a full blue-water capability. “A nuclear-powered submarine is just one element of a blue water capability and Japan would need surface ships if it wanted to operate a long way from its own ports,” he said. “Japan does not have that capability now and I do not think it would be sustainable over the long term.” While outright opposition to nuclear-powered submarines joining the Japanese fleet is inevitable, the suggestion has a lot of support from conservatives in Japan. In April, the Japan Institute for National Fundamentals released a policy proposal calling for debate on the nation developing a nuclear capability, including nuclear weapons. “The rapid and diverse expansion of nuclear forces by China and North Korea is making the threat to Japan become more real,” the report by the right-wing think tank said. It called on the government to “examine the appropriate form of nuclear deterrence for Japan and take the necessary measures at the earliest possible time”. While the policy paper said it adhered to the concept of the abolition of nuclear weapons, it noted that such an ideal was becoming increasingly unattainable as countries such as North Korea and China invested heavily in atomic weapons. It also pointed out that there were credibility issues concerning Japan’s security alliance with the US under President Donald Trump and urged Tokyo to take steps to reduce its reliance on Washington for security.

title: Newly united Hong Kong aiming to overcome key absences on T20 World Cup mission
description: City team missing stars old and new in Malaysia, as head coach Kaushal Silva eyes twin-objectives of qualification and increasing talent pool.
content: Deprived of the player he called “the future of Hong Kong cricket”, and also without one of the city’s greatest batsmen for the beginning of a winding 2028 T20 World Cup qualifying campaign this week, Kaushal Silva looked forward to a time when key absences were covered by oven-ready replacements from a growing talent pool. Head coach Silva’s 14-man party for the first round of qualifiers in Malaysia features only four players from the last Hong Kong team to compete in a major tournament at the 2016 T20 World Cup. It is relatively long in the tooth, nonetheless, with eight men who are 30 or older, including Ehsan Khan, the off-spin bowler, who will turn 42 before the turn of the year. The inclusion of the exciting 16-year-old batsman, Reyansh Sharma, nods towards Silva’s wish for regeneration, and helps lower the squad’s average age to 30.07. Nizakat Khan, Hong Kong’s second-highest T20I run scorer, is missing as he takes a tentative step back from international cricket. The gifted 18-year-old middle-order batsman, Shiv Mathur, meanwhile, is beginning his economics degree at the University of California, Los Angeles. Silva said that Mathur was “still in our system”, and that in the United States he would join coaching camps, adhere to Hong Kong-prescribed gym programmes and play club cricket. “He’ll be in touch with cricket, and with me,” Silva said. “We’ll be getting him on board whenever he’s available. He’s the future for Hong Kong cricket and we don’t want to lose him.” If Mathur is a diamond in the rough, Silva wants to see the day when Hong Kong boasts a glittering cast of young prospects. A former Sri Lanka wicketkeeper-batsman, whose 39 Tests yielded centuries against Bangladesh, Pakistan and Australia, Silva said: “[Producing more players] is the main thing in my job.
