The vision is to have 15 to 20 who can compete at international level and, if needed, immediately replace some of these players”. Silva acknowledged that Hong Kong’s limited domestic structure was working against him, and that “the number of players we’re producing is not what we need”. Along with his Cricket Hong Kong, China bosses, he plans to send “A” teams on more tours, and field promising players more frequently in one-day fixtures where “the ranking doesn’t matter as much as in T20Is”. “Getting the next generation of players international exposure, then transitioning them to the [senior] team is important,” Silva said. Hong Kong have had to quickly erase the disappointment of rain washing out their Asian Games quarter-final against Pakistan, who progressed as the higher-ranked team. “I’m from a Test-playing nation, but I feel the struggles and challenges that associate nations are going through,” Silva said. “These opportunities to showcase our talents, and see where we are against high-quality teams, matter a lot. “I think things can be changed and arranged in a way that’s beneficial for both teams.” Anshy Rath, the dependable opening batsman, advocated for reserve days to be introduced to the quadrennial Games tournament, after Hong Kong played seven matches, including qualifiers, to book what would have been a marquee date with world No 6 Pakistan. The city team are down at No 24 in the global standings. Nonetheless, left-hander Rath, 28, said the “pretty good cricket” Hong Kong have mustered of late had delivered “positives going into the World Cup qualifiers”. Having seen his team “start to fight” in recent tournaments, Silva warmed to that theme. At the ACC Premier Cup last month, where they finished third, Hong Kong recovered from a seemingly hopeless position to beat Malaysia following a super over. In an earlier victory over world No 17 Nepal, Babar Hayat and Ehsan Khan added an unbroken eighth-wicket stand of 128 to lift Hong Kong from the depths of 133 for seven. Equally, the pronounced dips that Hong Kong have experienced in the past few years are becoming fewer and further between. “We’re showing lots of character, and playing together as a team,” Silva said. “There’s still room to grow, so that we’re more consistent, because we can still be up and down.” A member of the 2016 T20 World Cup team as an 18-year-old, Rath credited Silva’s ability to “manage different cultures” for uniting a dressing room that has been known to splinter. “[Silva] cares about everyone, not just his star players, and he treats everybody the same”, Rath said, adding that he had not known a more unified squad since his international debut 12 years ago. “When you’ve been around for as long as some of us have, you tend to let go of the small things. “The core group has been through thick and thin together, and relationships build over time. Kaushal is a very good man to guide us with his expertise. When you add that to some of the talented individuals we have, cricket in Hong Kong is on the right path.” Beginning their T20 qualifying campaign against hosts Malaysia on Thursday, Hong Kong will have to banish the demons from a startling collapse against the same opponents two years ago that cost them their chance to reach this year’s T20 World Cup. The top two from a group that also features China, Saudi Arabia, the Maldives and Singapore advance to the next stage. “This is crucial for us,” said Silva, who acknowledged that competing in Australia and New Zealand in two years would “benefit our board financially, generate lots of recognition for the sport in Hong Kong, and help at grass-roots level”. “World Cups provide immense exposure, and being there would encourage more people in Hong Kong to start following cricket and falling in love with it”. Destined to leapfrog Nizakat Khan and, in time, Hayat, to become Hong Kong’s leading T20I run scorer, Rath will shoulder a lot of responsibility in Malaysia. “We’re believing in ourselves and not worrying about the opposition,” he said. “We’re going in with the attitude that if we play our good cricket, we can beat anyone.”

title: Top SS27 runway beauty looks from Chanel, Dior, Gucci and more
description: From Louis Vuitton’s shimmering fringe to bold feathered lashes at Rick Owens, here is a round-up of the standout looks from the spring/summer 2027 fashion weeks.
content: Beyond the eye-catching fashion at the biggest spring/summer 2027 ready-to-wear shows in New York, London, Milan and Paris, the hair and make-up also offered plenty for beauty aficionados and style watchers, from confetti accents to ink-black pouts and more. Coach Some of the models at Coach clearly had a fabulous time celebrating the brand’s 85th anniversary as they walked the runway covered in foil confetti in a rainbow of colours, clinging to their skin, hair and clothes. Why not try this whimsical and utterly fun look for the coming festive season? Khaite & Prada The next time you leave your house in a rush, consider your messy mane a high fashion statement. We love that the models at Khaite (in New York) and Prada (in Milan) sported intentionally untidy and frizzy hair this season – think totally tousled, bedhead volume and lopsided bouffants. Simone Rocha Make-up artist Thomas de Kluyver crafted fabulous floral eyebrow appliqués for models at the Simone Rocha show during London Fashion Week. One style featured Blade Runner-esque metallic hues, while the other mixed pink, green, white and blue bugle beads to harmonious effect. Gucci Sam Visser was the mastermind behind Gucci’s electrifying make-up looks, which are currently living rent-free in our minds. Think of it as a sharper, more intense and more sultry take on defined lips and traditional smoky eyes. The clean girl aesthetic is officially out and the messy girl era is in. Dior We caught two different trends at the Dior show: a micro-thin metallic eyeliner worn across the models’ upper lash lines and a solid, glittery wing on the outer corners of their eyes. Both techniques focus light on and around your eye and are easily achievable, requiring minimal products and just a couple of minutes of your time. Chanel & Saint Laurent A bold red lip will always be a vibe. Some models at Chanel and Saint Laurent during Paris Fashion Week wore statement lippy in shades ranging from bright crimson and deep red through to burgundy. Choosing the right red depends on two factors: your skin’s undertones and what event you are dressing for. Schiaparelli At the Schiaparelli presentation, there were a few models that sported a beautifully striking black lip – commanding immediate attention and significantly altering the appearance of their skin. The look, also seen at Schiaparelli’s fall/winter haute couture show in 2025, was envisioned by legendary make-up artist Dame Pat McGrath, who often collaborates with the maison. Rick Owens Otherworldly beauty is making a comeback. At Rick Owens, models walked the runway looking entirely unconventional but utterly charming in jet black sclera lenses and gigantic feathered lashes, often intentionally misaligned. The make-up harmonised with the tone of the collection, which featured futuristic ensembles in black or else pale neutrals. Louis Vuitton Could bejewelled headpieces be the next big thing? Models at a retro-futuristic Louis Vuitton show donned dazzling diamond trims over their foreheads, giving a blunt, shimmering fringe. Perhaps it’s time to ditch convention and opt for something more theatrical instead.

title: Governments in Southeast Asia promote reading to combat literacy decline
description: Initiatives like book distributions and reading rewards aim to inspire lifelong reading habits among the youth.
content:
Singaporean Najwa Alhabshi remembers spending her teenage years poring over literary classics such as F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby and George Orwell’s 1984 . But as work commitments grew, finding time to read became harder, and her smartphone took over.
“Life got in the way – it was work, a lack of time, and eventually, the phone screen,” the 35-year-old tutor said.
Across Southeast Asia, governments are stepping in to get people reading again. Concerns are growing over falling literacy rates, shortened attention spans and declining critical-thinking capabilities.
Indonesia launched a countrywide plan to distribute more than 5.5 million books to primary and secondary schools. Neighbouring Malaysia is handing out 100 ringgit (HK$192) vouchers to more than 2.2 million students to spend on its national digital book marketplace.
Last month, Singapore launched an initiative that pays citizens to read. Under the scheme, users earn 20 virtual coins for every reading session lasting at least 15 minutes. Recording one session a day for 50 days accumulates 1,000 coins, which can be exchanged for 1 Singapore dollar (HK$6.12).
A global study by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development found that students are now reading at a level previously expected of those a year younger. The study also found a decline in skills such as evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources and critical thinking.
Overreliance on artificial intelligence (AI) threatened the development of reading skills, said Portia Padilla, a professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman.
“If you do not think while reading, you are not truly reading,” Padilla said, adding that readers should use AI to challenge their assumptions rather than form judgments.
While government intervention and incentives can nudge people to pick up a book, experts say they do little to build intrinsic motivation and cultivate lifelong habits.
Reading should be viewed as a commitment rather than a short-term campaign, she added, urging support across the whole ecosystem, including public policy, language development programmes and supportive environments at home and in the community.
Providing dedicated spaces for reading – such as quiet public zones or after-hours book clubs – could offer another way to build momentum, said Loh Chin Ee from the National Institute of Education in Singapore.
For Najwa, the battle begins at home. To instil a love for reading in her five-year-old son, she limits his screen time to just 15 minutes a month. Her son reaches for short illustrated books when he wakes up.
“Beyond just expanding vocabulary, reading does so much more for our children,” she said. “Books are portals to a different world – through them, imagination lives.”

title: ‘China already has spies’ at US AI labs, former Anthropic researcher warns
description: Jacob Coxon alleges Beijing can close any technological gap with the US as it has ways to ‘steal our progress at any time and catch up’.
content: Former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon said he was 90 per cent certain that China already had spies inside both US artificial intelligence (AI) companies, without providing evidence. Coxon made the allegation in an interview with entrepreneur Patrick Bet-David on the PBD Podcast, arguing that China could steal advances from leading US AI labs and quickly close any technological gap. “Right now, if we just stopped, they would try and catch up. But I think one really important thing people don’t realise is that China already has spies at OpenAI and Anthropic,” Coxon said. “China has the ability to hack at any time. If we pull ahead, that doesn’t give us a big lead. They can just step in, steal our progress at any time and catch up.” Asked by Bet-David how certain he was that Chinese spies were already inside the companies, Coxon replied: “Ninety per cent. Yeah, it’s almost certain that they have.” Reacting to Coxon’s comments on social media, Paul Triolo, an expert on China’s technology policy and cybersecurity, said: “Sorry, but this seems really irresponsible.” Coxon’s remarks could also raise concerns inside US AI labs, which rely heavily on talent from China. Researchers from China accounted for 38 per cent of the top AI talent working in the US, slightly ahead of Americans at 37 per cent, according to the MacroPolo think tank. Three years earlier, Chinese researchers represented 27 per cent of top AI talent in the US, compared with 31 per cent for Americans. The comments come days after Washington and Beijing agreed to launch an AI dialogue focused on the technology’s “risks and benefits” during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US, with the next round scheduled for November. The two sides also agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” to discuss AI-related incidents. Coxon, who spent three years working on pre-training research at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic in September, warning that the two companies were racing towards self-improving AI without adequately addressing the risks. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote on social media in September. His resignation and comments drew widespread attention and sparked debate over whether leading AI labs were adequately addressing safety concerns, along with calls to slow development. However, the Trump administration has rejected calls to slow down, citing the global competition with China for AI dominance. US President Donald Trump has instead backed industry self-regulation, meeting leading AI executives at the White House last month and endorsing a voluntary agreement for companies to monitor and audit their own AI systems. He described the agreement as “morally binding”. As Chinese companies have closed the gap with US firms in frontier AI models, American technology companies and Trump administration officials have increasingly accused Beijing of copying or extracting capabilities from US models to accelerate its own development. “The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation. So, the Chinese distil our models, and they can never get ahead of us,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last month. “It’s kind of like if you’re looking over someone’s shoulder, copying their homework, you can never get a higher grade than they do.” Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones. China has rejected US allegations, terming distillation “a common practice in the AI sector”.

title: Editorial | Kai Tak Hospital promises to set new benchmark for public healthcare
description: The hospital, now the city’s largest, addresses pressure on medical services in Kowloon with state-of-the-art clinical infrastructure.
content: Hong Kong has long prided itself on the quality and coverage of its public healthcare system. But it has not opened a hospital on the scale of the new one at Kai Tak, on the old airport site, for decades. Recent stand-alone developments like the North Lantau or Tin Shui Wai hospitals are significantly smaller. It is important that the opening goes smoothly. About 350 patients on day one is an impressive start, but that is expected to reach 1,800 a day by year’s end. The opening of Kai Tak Hospital is a historic milestone for public healthcare in Hong Kong. The HK$36 billion hospital is the city’s largest. With 2,400 inpatient beds, 37 operating theatres and state-of-the-art clinical infrastructure, it enhances the city’s diagnostic capabilities, treatment capacity and overall patient access. For years, demographic shifts and an ageing population have put increasing pressure on public medical infrastructure, particularly across the dense urban corridors of Kowloon. Kai Tak Hospital addresses this structural challenge. It serves a catchment area of more than 1.8 million residents spanning four major districts: Yau Tsim Mong, Kowloon City, Wong Tai Sin and Kwun Tong. By absorbing patient volume and gradually taking over services from Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan, the hospital marks a new era in acute and specialised clinical care. It can be expected to enhance diagnostic processes across multiple disciplines. Advanced diagnostic and radiology suites, an automated blood sample system and integrated pathology laboratories promise to expedite them. Early detection drives better outcomes, particularly in fields like oncology and neurosurgery. The hospital will offer specialised day services for clinical oncology, surgery, and obstetrics and gynaecology, alongside diagnostic tools that reduce wait times for screenings and imaging. Treatment resources receive a similar upgrade. The hospital will have Hong Kong’s largest pharmacy department, spanning 2,000 square metres. It will introduce the first automated dispensing system in a public hospital, capable of processing up to 3,200 prescriptions daily. When the hospital’s second operational phase reaches full swing in 2028, its 24-hour accident and emergency department – three times larger than that of Queen Elizabeth Hospital – will function as a primary regional trauma centre. Hospital administrators have adopted a strategic, phased roll-out, beginning with the Family Medicine Integrated Centre, offering hundreds of daily outpatient consultation slots for chronic disease management and routine illnesses. Other services will also be provided gradually this month, including allied health services, diagnostic and interventional radiology, pathology, pharmacy, day services for clinical oncology and obstetrics and gynaecology. Major clinical services, including inpatient care and surgery, will begin in 2028 when the second phase starts. The real test may come as more patients go to Kai Tak. Transport connection problems can be expected, given that the hospital is 30 minutes’ walk from the nearest MTR stations. Patients travelling from Kowloon or MTR stations can use one of 10 bus routes or six green minibus routes serving the hospital. The routes connect the hospital with Kai Tak, Kowloon Bay, Sung Wong Toi, To Kwa Wan, Wong Tai Sin, Ngau Tau Kok, Kwun Tong and Yau Tong. That said, it may at first be a challenge for many elderly patients to find their way to the new hospital, which is located on the old airport runway. Once services transfer from Queen Elizabeth Hospital, the Jordan site will be redeveloped into Hong Kong’s first integrated ambulatory care hospital, with centres for cataract surgery, radiology and radiotherapy. Kai Tak Hospital will also serve as the interim teaching hospital for the city’s third medical school, which is being established by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Once enhanced diagnostic resources and treatment capacity come together with improved patient access, Kai Tak Hospital promises to set a new benchmark for public healthcare.

title: In this 60-year-old Hong Kong home filled with things, every object tells a story
description: A 1,700 sq ft flat in Pok Fu Lam was transformed into a vibrant, eclectic home, showcasing cherished possessions and clever design solutions.
content: There is a lot going on inside this 1,700 sq ft (158 square metre) Pok Fu Lam flat, which rejects the pared-back minimalism typical of Hong Kong homes. And that is what sparks joy for designer Rosheen Rodwell, founder of Rosheen Rodwell Interiors. When redesigning a flat, she prefers clients to hold on to their cherished possessions rather than start afresh. “A home should always tell the story of people who live there,” she says, “and I love incorporating people’s treasures, collected over the years, into my projects.” The 60-year-old, three-bedroom, two-bathroom flat on Hong Kong Island was last renovated 20 years ago and was due for a cosmetic refit. Happily for the budget, the existing floor plan could be left largely intact, so Rodwell focused on smaller tweaks better suited to the three-person household and on giving the family’s belongings the setting they deserved. Curating those possessions was part of the brief. Over the years, the well-travelled family’s “treasures” had become a melting pot of cultural and architectural influences, crying out to be brought together cohesively. Appropriately, Rodwell framed them against gallery-white walls, with bespoke timber reliefs adding drama. The impact of those tweaks was considerable. Take the dramatic, pitch-black archway she inserted into the formerly completely open-plan living and dining area. Serving no structural purpose, the archway was installed to visually separate the room’s two functions. Spatial zoning was further achieved by a sisal rug in the dining area and a Persian rug in the sitting area, which opens onto the seafront balcony. These adjoining spaces share solid wood flooring retained for its beauty and refreshed with dark mahogany stain. Both zones now also benefit from an elegant moulded dado. “I quite like the feel of a wooden floor that has been walked on for years,” Rodwell says. “Replacing it would have been wasteful, and it’s hard to find anything of such good quality these days.” Note the finishing details, such as brass toggle switches with matt black back plates. “In design, you need to pay attention to the things that your client interacts with every day, like switches,” she says. “How should they feel when you touch them? How should they look?” The social zone also presented opportunities for more exposed woodwork, one stable-style kitchen door where the bottom can be closed to contain the family’s dogs, with the top half left open to allow light and air in. Another is a pair of double-opening Jefferson doors split vertically in the hallway leading to the bedrooms and bathrooms. Though different, both sets of doors are connected design-wise by the rounded frame. The kitchen – with its butcher block island, bright white cabinetry, deep ceramic sink and aged brass tapware – looks straight out of a country farmhouse. Look down and you will see shallow drawers at floor level disguised as kickboards. Look up and there are antique-look brass spotlights imported from Britain. Most of Rodwell’s lighting is sourced overseas because she finds the brass in Hong Kong “can be a bit orange”. “I prefer an unlacquered metal that develops a patina over time,” she says. Realigning the main bedroom en suite’s layout saw the shower placed front and centre to a spectacular view of the South China Sea. It also allowed for additional bathroom storage and the retention of an extra-long tub the owners had custom made years earlier. Rodwell splurged on Carrara marble around the bath but saved on the floor, using inexpensive mosaic tiles bought in Mong Kok, which she acid-washed to remove their sheen. Similarly, in the main bedroom, luxury Pierre Frey and Ralph Lauren fabrics cohabitate with inexpensive pelmet trims sourced from a vendor in Sham Shui Po. For the child’s bedroom, Rodwell cocooned the bed inside a canopied nook. Behind the navy-and-white striped curtains are bookshelves fitted above the custom bedhead, and the inside wall is decorated with his posters and photos. Apart from the touted psychological benefits of a nest bed for young ones, this concept is also the most efficient use of space, allowing a wardrobe and desk to dovetail into the design. The third bedroom is used as a study, with a pull-out divan bed for occasional guests. It contains two desks, allowing both partners to work from home. Here, the hero design feature is a wide, sculpted timber cornice linking banks of shelving for the couple’s vast book collection, making the space feel more like a cosy English library. From an eclectic collection of furniture, homewares and mementos spanning decades and design styles, Rodwell has created an interior full of life and colour. There was just one design challenge that rankled. The expensive German windows installed 20 years ago, and still good as new, would, like the flooring, have been wasteful to replace. Opening inwards made them difficult to accommodate curtains or blinds and, in the case of the dining room, impossible. “That made my head explode – seeing a window undressed really bothers me,” she says. “But in the end, I had to let it go.” Living room Bespoke sofa designed by Rosheen Rodwell Interiors. Coffee table from Taobao. Persian rug, Chinese cabinet, artworks, candles on wooden stands, low chest and table on balcony, all from the client’s collection. Terracotta tiles outside, in herringbone pattern, from Hop Hing Lung Material (Tel: 2511 3013). Balcony chairs from Ikea. Antique brass spotlights from Corston Architectural Detail. Living and dining area Decorative archway designed by Rosheen Rodwell and built by Chin Tool Decoration (Tel: 9093 3930). Cane chest and black-and-white striped lampshades from Ikea. Lamp bases on prayer table from Sum Ngai Brass. Dining chairs from Taobao. Tablecloth from The Ginger Jar Lamp Co. Round-edge stable door to the kitchen designed by Rosheen Rodwell. Kate Spade for Visual Comfort hanging lampshade and wall lamps from Lumino Collection (Tel: 2736 2338). Sockets and switches from Soho Lighting. Original solid wood floor, sanded and re-stained by Chin Tool Decoration. Son’s room Child’s nest bed designed by Rosheen Rodwell. Ralph Lauren curtain and pelmet material from Avante Garde Designs. Matchstick stripe wallpaper from Woodchip & Magnolia. Bronze drawer pulls from Willow & Stone. Main bedroom Ottoman and cushions designed by Rosheen Rodwell and available on her website; fabric from Altfield. Headboard upholstered in Ralph Lauren fabric from Avante Garde Designs. Pendant light from Pooky. Main bedroom en suite Bullnose trim Carrara marble from Famous Stone (Tel: 9023 7892). Taps from Perrin & Rowe. Toilet from Nitto Hardware & Sanitary Ware (Tel: 2677 0998). Mosaic floor tiles from Chun King Building Materials (Tel: 2398 0488). Ceiling light from Pooky. Twin basins from Oscar Bath and Kitchen. Taps from Perrin & Rowe. Oak veneer cabinetry and mirrors designed by Rosheen Rodwell and built by Chin Tool Decoration. Chrome handles Perrin & Rowe. Towel rails from Nitto Hardware & Sanitary Ware. Wall lights from Pooky. Library/guest room Joinery with sculpted cornice, bookshelves and wardrobe, designed by Rosheen Rodwell. Divan bed by Chin Tool Decoration. Wall lamps from Etsy. Hallway Jefferson doors designed by Rosheen Rodwell and made by Chin Tool Decoration. Brass hinges and sockets from Kinetic Hardware (Tel: 2575 7721). Dado moulding designed by Rosheen Rodwell. Overhead lights from Pooky. Wall light from Lumino Collection. Kitchen Kitchen, including butcher’s block, designed by Rosheen Rodwell and made by Chin Tool Decoration. Brass handles and drawer pulls from Devol. Quartz benchtops and splashbacks from Sunlight Marble Engineering (Tel: 2397 8689). Farmhouse sinks from ABI Interiors. Aged brass taps from Perrin & Rowe. Main ceiling light from Elstead Lighting.

title: Hong Kong banks grow cautious on One Stanley mortgages amid investigation
description: Banks are taking a cautious approach to mortgages related to the luxury Hong Kong development, which faces building defect allegations.
content: The furore over alleged construction defects at luxury development One Stanley threatens to cast a shadow over Hong Kong’s recovering super-prime property market, as banks hold off on mortgages and property agents suspend viewings at the complex while an investigation continues. “Most [banks] are adopting a wait-and-see approach,” said Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services, adding that lenders were likely to take a more cautious approach to mortgage applications at the development while the investigation was under way. Loan approvals would be assessed on a “case by case” basis, said a banking industry source, adding that lenders would look at whether buyers had a high net worth or were otherwise considered reliable customers. A property agent handling sales at One Stanley, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said their company had suspended viewings at the development unless clients proactively requested a visit. The agency had yet to receive any further explanation from developer K&K Property about the status of One Stanley, the agent added. One Stanley, a collection of luxury houses and flats on the southern side of Hong Kong Island, was thrown into disarray over the weekend when the government announced it was launching an investigation into work quality issues at the development. Buyer interest has not completely disappeared, however. Louis Ho Siu-tong, a senior associate director at Centaline Property covering The Peak and Southern district, said agents received three to four requests for viewings over the weekend. The developer had made no new arrangements regarding viewings, he said. The mixed response comes amid a rebound in Hong Kong’s “super-prime” residential market, with transactions for homes worth at least HK$100 million (US$12.75 million) accelerating in recent months as mainland Chinese buyers return to trophy assets in areas such as The Peak, according to Centaline Property. One Stanley has been part of that recovery. Since January, 27 properties – including 11 houses and 16 flats – have been sold at the development, transaction records show. A Mongolian mining family bought a house for HK$247 million in January, while another house sold for HK$151.08 million in July. The Building Department’s investigation relates to allegations that one house at One Stanley had up to 75 per cent fewer steel bars in some areas than specified in the approved construction plans. The department has asked K&K Property to investigate whether similar problems exist elsewhere in the development and said it would conduct random inspections of selected properties. Concern is spreading among professionals involved in property transactions. Polly Chu, a partner at law firm Hugill & Ip who focuses on property transactions, said concerns over safety and structural defects were expected. She was organising a seminar to gather views from authorised persons, bankers, valuers and dispute-resolution specialists, which may help “clarify their rights” and clear their doubts, she added. K&K Property did not respond to requests for comment. One property industry executive described the incident as an isolated case, saying Hong Kong had few comparable examples. The latest sale at One Stanley was registered on September 30, two days before online property news platform WuChatProp first reported the alleged construction defects. One Stanley comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats. Transaction records show 13 flats and 10 houses remain available for sale. Albert Luk, a representative of the owner of the affected house, said he did not rule out the possibility that more owners could come forward after the authorities release their findings. Raymond Cheng, a veteran property analyst and research director at Mingze Capital International, said the incident would create “short-term noise” but he expected its impact on luxury home sales to be limited because K&K was a relatively small developer. “The issue may lead to buyers being more selective or preferring to buy units from traditional big developers rather than small developers, who may need to offer lower prices to attract buyers,” Cheng said.

title: After losing both legs, snowboarder Neil Tsui sets his sights on the Paralympics
description: Neil Tsui, who spent nearly a decade in Hong Kong, tells PostMag about choosing grit over limitations after losing both his legs and setting his sights firmly on the next Winter Games.
content: I was born in 1981, in Surrey, south of Vancouver, in Canada. I’m the youngest of four – three boys and one girl. My father is Chinese, originally from Shanghai. He left during the communist revolution and moved to Macau and then Hong Kong. My mother is Brazilian, originally from just outside São Paulo. They met in Brazil and immigrated to Canada in 1970. My upbringing was very outdoors. Everywhere you go, there are mountains and ocean. I got into snowboarding when I was about 13 years old. It’s my favourite thing to do. I went to Earl Marriott Secondary School, and didn’t go to university, much to my parents’ frustration. I loved carpentry, was a petrolhead and enjoyed fixing cars with my brothers. Then, I worked in sales. I had a great life, friends, family. But as I approached 30, I felt that if I didn’t leave, I was never going to go. I went to visit my sister, who was living in Hong Kong, and just like everyone else, I fell in love with the city. So, I got a job working in business development and marketing for professional services. From 2011, for three years, I lived in Mid-Levels and was a recruiter and really enjoyed it. I was then approached about a technology role within recruitment. It was a start-up, an American firm, and that was a great experience. The start-up was based in San Francisco, but we launched it in Asia. I later worked for another tech company, Phaidon. In 2019, my sister and her family left Hong Kong, and I felt ready for my next move. I moved with the company to Singapore in September 2020. I’d met my (future) wife, Sarah, on a dating app in 2019. We finally met in person in May 2021 and an attraction was that she loved wakeboarding, like me. We got married in 2023. Six weeks after we arrived back from our honeymoon, I had an eczema spot on the back of my leg. My dermatologist gave me a cortisone jab but made me get a blood test as I had also been taking Olumiant, a strong drug for alopecia, for six months. I then went wakeboarding on Sentosa beach, where the water is filthy, and, in the evening, started getting chills. My fever got worse and I collapsed on the bathroom floor. We got a taxi to the hospital. My blood pressure was spiking and I passed out. The following day, my wife told me I had developed sepsis and gone into septic shock. I had necrotising fasciitis, which is a flesh-eating disease. My whole body was shutting down. I was put into an induced coma, so that my body could fight to stay alive. My sister flew out from Amsterdam and my mother-in-law came from Britain. For three days, my wife just held my hand, staring at a heart monitor, not knowing if I was going to make it. Miraculously, after four days, I started turning around – my heart, my kidneys on dialysis, everything was starting to turn around. They woke me up 10 days later. My legs were covered in bandages. And all I could see were my feet, which had gone this kind of blue-purple colour. Three of my doctors came in and told me they had given me an inotrope drug – it’s what they give anyone who goes into serious septic shock. It redirects all the blood flow to your torso, to preserve your vital organs. As a result, your extremities – such as hands, feet, even your face, your nose – get cut off from adequate blood flow. So, they stood by the bed and explained all of this, and then said, “We’re going to give you a bilateral amputation. We’re going to amputate both your legs below the knee.” All I could picture was my wife, who I’d been married to for six weeks, pushing me in a wheelchair. And then I thought about my dad. My parents started out as broke immigrants. And my dad’s outlook is: if you fall, it’s up to you to pick yourself up. In my head, it just clicked – “OK, you’re going to own this” – and I opened my eyes and looked at the doctors and said, “Can I still snowboard?” And they said yes. I was lucky to be alive. I typed into Instagram: “Amputee Snowboarding”. And it came up with a Canadian athlete named Tyler Turner. He’s the first Canadian to win a gold medal for snowboarding, at the 2022 Beijing Paralympics. And he was the same as me – a double amputee below the knee. I wrote to him and then we talked for an hour and a half. He told me to harness the snowboarding as that would get me through my recovery. As a joke, he said they were always looking for double-amputee athletes for the Paralympic team. In my head, it clicked – getting on the team would be my North Star. Four days later, I had the first leg amputated. (Tsui has undergone 17 surgeries in total.) A couple of months later, I got my first set of prosthetics. I felt so tall! I had an incredible physiotherapist, who worked with me on my core, and knew about my snowboarding goal. I just kept building up my strength and balance, and started playing tennis again and riding a bike. I met Tyler in the summer of 2024 and we went surfing together in Tofino, on Vancouver Island; it was an instant bond. He asked me if I wanted to go to the Netherlands in November 2024, to get my classification for the Paralympics and, since I was living in Singapore, I hadn’t even been on a snowboard yet. I went to Trifecta Singapore, a sports facility with an indoor Snow Arena for practising snowboarding and skiing using hi-tech simulators. I couldn’t even balance. I was there for an hour and I couldn’t let go of the bar long enough. When I got home, I ripped my legs off and was on the floor, absolutely broken. Sarah encouraged me to go and meet Tyler and get the classification. Two weeks later, I was in the Netherlands, at SnowWorld Landgraaf, an indoor ski resort. I strapped my snowboard on and we went up in the chairlift and Tyler filmed. As soon as I started going, it just clicked. I did a big carve right, a big carve left, and then I just ripped all the way to the bottom without falling. I was screaming and hooting. The video is quite ridiculous; I’m literally whooping the whole way. And I’m crying. I was so elated and, all the way down, I was saying, “We did it!” I was just thinking about Sarah and how this was for us – this is what had got us through a hellish year, to get to this moment. It was 366 days after my right leg was cut off. I did two runs and went to get my classification. We now have a son, he’s nine months old, and we are moving back to Canada next year. Canadian Olympic snowboarder Mark Fawcett said I need to spend as much time on snow as I can. I’m still aiming for the Paralympics in 2030. We bought a house on Vancouver Island. By the time of the next Winter Paralympics, in 2030, in the French Alps, I’m going to be 49. Three years ago, I was getting my legs amputated and I’m now snowboarding with Mark, one of the godfathers of snowboarding. I now do public speaking at corporations and at schools. I’m not trying to be some sort of inspirational person. I am just trying to be the old Neil, who just loves activity. But, obviously, I know there is a lesson in there. The irony is that it took me losing both of my legs to feel limitless. I won’t know until literally a month or two before the actual Games if I’m on the team. It’s a lofty goal and a total gamble, but you need to stay the course. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

title: Trump says he deserves Nobel Peace Prize but has doubts he will get it
description: The US president has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace between Ukraine and Russia.
content: US President ⁠Donald Trump, who waged war ⁠with Iran and has ⁠yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on Wednesday that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize but acknowledged doubt about his chances. “I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said of the ‌2026 award, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Friday. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.” Since his return to the White House last year, Trump has repeatedly said he deserves what may be the world’s most prestigious award. “It is about that time,” Trump told ⁠reporters in the Oval Office. “But I was very honoured to receive it indirectly last time by ‌the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.” Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her 2025 Nobel ‌Peace Prize medal to Trump in January as she sought US support ⁠for her efforts ⁠in Venezuela. Trump said he should get the prize after wading into eight conflicts since taking office last ‌January. The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Trump, though there is no way of ‌verifying that. Parties ‌to some conflicts Trump claims to have resolved dispute the US president’s diplomatic ‌role, and fighting has flared again in some of those regions, including the Democratic Republic ⁠of Congo and along the border between Cambodia and Thailand. A resolution to Russia’s war ⁠in Ukraine has eluded Trump, who promised to end it on the first day of his second White House term. US-Israel strikes on Iran have ‌led to a seven-month simmering ‌conflict that has upended global energy supplies and driven fuel prices up before November’s midterm elections. Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court and the special rapporteur for the Palestinian Territories are among the favourites to win this year.

title: Trump to give Musk top US science medal
description: Tech bosses Sergei Brin, Jensen Huang and Lisa Su will also receive the National Medal of Science.
content: President Donald Trump will present close ally Elon Musk and other tech bosses with the top US scientific award at a ceremony on Thursday, the White House said. Google co-founder Sergei Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD chief Lisa Su will also receive the National Medal of Science at the “Science: A New Golden Age” summit. Computer mogul Michael Dell and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will get the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the top award in its field. “The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology. These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation,” White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said in a statement on Wednesday. SpaceX and Tesla tycoon Musk has returned to Trump’s good graces after they fell out last year over his role heading the cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. He was also the biggest donor to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Musk and Huang were both at Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping last month. Along with other tech bosses, they were also at the White House last week for talks in which tech chiefs promised to self-regulate against possible threats from artificial intelligence. Trump has dismissed warnings that AI could wipe out humanity, insisting it is crucial for what he calls the “Golden Age” of the US economy in his second term. But Trump’s Republican Party could lose control of Congress in midterm elections next month amid voter concerns over the Iran war and the cost of living.

title: Rubio touts US power, calls on Europe to emerge from ‘slumber’
description: The US secretary of state warned that Western civilisation is ‘at a crossroads’ between ‘national power’ and decline.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday flexed American power and called on Europe to shake off its “long slumber” in a rousing speech delivered beneath the Acropolis in Athens. “We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” Rubio said in a speech attended by senior Greek officials at Pnyx hill, praising ancient Greece’s civilisation as the cradle of Western democracy. “Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginning of a generational shift, skyrocketing defence spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programmes, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defence commitments” made last year at the Nato summit in The Hague, he noted. But Rubio also warned that Western civilisation now finds itself “at a crossroads” between “national power” and decline. The ancient Greeks “understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it”, he said. “This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim … not just for our country but for the whole of our civilisation,” said the former senator, who is seen as a possible successor to Donald Trump. “Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads. The next decade will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline,” Rubio said. The US under President Donald Trump has made its choice, according to Rubio. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defence, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future,” he said. His speech was packed with historical references and glorified heroes of antiquity such as Alexander the Great but also the conquistador Hernan Cortes. It followed an address in February when Rubio argued that Europe was threatened by mass immigration and called for it to defend Christian civilisation. Earlier on Wednesday, Rubio, who arrived from Iceland as part of a European tour, underlined the “critical” US alliance with Greece. He flagged the energy sector and announced a joint agreement on information-sharing on drug trafficking and terrorism. Rubio took part Wednesday in a “strategic dialogue” with Greece on regional and energy security amid high tensions triggered by the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and was later hosted by conservative Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. Because of its location in the Mediterranean, at the crossroads of many transit routes, Greece is particularly exposed to the threats posed by migration, human trafficking and various forms of terror, Rubio said. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have highlighted the fragility of energy supply routes, and Greece is positioning itself to become a key hub in southeastern Europe, particularly for the transport of natural gas. Recently opened gas pipelines and port infrastructure have enabled Greece to contribute to the energy corridor through Eastern Europe to Ukraine. Rubio concludes his European trip with a visit to Portugal on Thursday.

title: Exclusive | Trump urged Xi to talk to Takaichi and lift export curbs on Japan, sources say
description: The Chinese president wasn’t receptive to the requests during last month’s summit, warning of the risk of Japanese militarism.
content: US President Donald Trump pressed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to roll back China’s export curbs on Japan during their meeting in the US, urging talks between the Chinese and Japanese leaders as Tokyo seeks to manage mounting pressure from Beijing. People familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post that Xi also warned Trump about the growing risks of Japanese militarism during their sit-down in Washington last month. According to the people, while the issue was not one of Trump’s top priorities, the US leader raised Japan’s grievances over Chinese export restrictions – including on rare earths – that have squeezed Japanese industries. The people – who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly – said Trump framed the Chinese measures as a threat to American industries reliant on Japanese suppliers. As a result, he said they were an indirect violation of the US-China trade truce reached in Busan last October. Trump also called for Xi to meet Japanese leader Sanae Takaichi, urging Beijing to repair its ties with Tokyo, the people added. They said the Chinese leader was not particularly receptive to Trump’s requests, instead saying Beijing’s dispute with Tokyo should be kept separate to – and should not affect – the US-China relationship. According to the sources, Japan had earlier pushed for talks between Takaichi and Xi during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month but Beijing rejected the request, instead offering a meeting with Premier Li Qiang. The sources said Tokyo had signalled that Takaichi would not accept a meeting with Li in place of Xi. Xi visited Washington as China’s ties with Japan remain in a deep freeze. Over the decades, China-Japan relations have been mixed as a result of deep historical wounds, geopolitical enmity, their territorial dispute in the East China Sea as well as economic interdependence and cultural affinity. Bilateral ties have plunged sharply since last November after Takaichi said a Taiwan contingency could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan that would justify a military response. The remark and her refusal to retract it infuriated Beijing, which views Taiwan as a “red line” that must not be crossed and has been long wary of Tokyo’s military expansion. In retaliation, Beijing cut official and cultural exchanges at all levels, axed flights to Japan – once a favourite destination for Chinese tourists – and banned exports of dual-use products, including rare earths and other critical minerals, to Japan’s defence industries. Meanwhile, Japan has deployed offensive missiles and conducted military drills in its southwest islands close to Taiwan, and intensified its security alliance with the Philippines, which also has engaged in tense disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea. Takaichi met Trump just one day before he welcomed Xi to Washington. Right after the Xi-Trump summit concluded, Trump called Takaichi, giving her what she described as “detailed explanations” of the talks. “Japan and the United States have now become the most trusted allied nations, and we confirmed our commitment to jointly contribute to peace and stability in the region and the world,” she said on social media. The official readouts from the White House and Beijing on Xi’s three-day visit last month did not explicitly mention Japan but both leaders made references to Japan’s wartime actions in the official talks at the White House and the state dinner. A Chinese statement outlining the deliverables reached between the two leaders described the countries as “allies in World War II” that “fought side by side to win the war”. Xi raised the same point at the White House state banquet. “Over 80 years ago, the Chinese and American people stood shoulder to shoulder in the fight against Japanese militarist aggressors,” he said. “Such a friendship, forged in blood and fire, will surely live on through the generations.” Diplomatic engagement has been largely limited between the two neighbours until recently when there were initial signs of a thaw. Last week, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year. Wang said bilateral ties were facing a “severe situation” and urged Japan to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leadership regarding Taiwan. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. In a policy address on Monday, Takaichi called China an “important neighbour”, pledging to build a stable relationship with Beijing despite the ongoing diplomatic chill. “We will work to ensure communication on shared challenges, promote dialogue to safeguard our national interests, and build a constructive and stable relationship,” she said.

title: Meet Stephanie Seymour’s daughter, Lily Brant, who made her runway debut at Paris Fashion Week
description: The 21-year-old, who has Naomi Campbell as her godmother and grew up around the late Tunisian-French couturier Azzedine Alaïa, recently walked a show for his brand.
content: Stephanie Seymour’s daughter Lily Brant has become the latest nepo baby to walk the runway at Paris Fashion Week. Bearing a striking resemblance to her supermodel mother, the 21-year-old made her runway debut for French luxury house Alaïa. She joins the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin’s daughter Apple Martin, who walked for Chloé, as well as John Travolta’s daughter Ella Bleu Travolta, who walked for Miu Miu. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lily Brant (@lily.brant) Here’s everything you need to know about Stephanie Seymour’s mini-me daughter, Lily Brant. She is Stephanie Seymour’s youngest child Lily Brant was born in 2004 to Stephanie Seymour and Peter Brant. The couple are also parents to sons Peter and Harry Brant, whom they welcomed in 1993 and 1996, respectively. In 2021, Harry tragically passed away from an accidental drug overdose after battling addiction for several years. Seymour also has a son, Dylan Thomas Andrews, from her previous marriage to guitarist Tommy Andrews. Brant reportedly has five older children from his first marriage. Lily Brant’s connection to Alaïa Thanks to her supermodel mother, Lily was introduced to fashion at an early age. In fact, she revealed in her recent interview with Vogue that there was a deeper meaning behind her walking for Alaïa at Paris Fashion Week, having grown up around the maison’s late designer. Seymour had been a long-time muse to Azzedine Alaïa and the two shared a close relationship; she reportedly called him “papa”, and Lily grew up attending family dinners at his house. “He was always just the sweetest presence and had such a kind soul; he would always give me hugs, and he treated me like family,” Lily told Vogue. She is following in her mother’s footsteps Lily is signed to Ford Models, which helped launch Naomi Campbell, who is also Lily’s godmother. Beyond the runway, Lily also spent two summers interning at Alaïa. She took up various roles, including working for the PR team, cutting fabrics at the atelier and working behind the scenes at shows. “Everyone there is so sweet and talented and genuine, and it feels like home,” she told Vogue about Alaïa. “I feel so lucky that I got to walk in the show, and that I got to work there, and that I just have this special connection.” When she is not busy practising her catwalk, Lily is a student at Washington University, where she is majoring in film and media studies with a minor in business of the arts, per her LinkedIn.

title: Opinion | Can the Gulf aviation superhub model survive the war?
description: The problem is not that war disrupts flights, but that this time, the hubs of Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi have become part of the battlefield.
content: For decades, the Gulf superhubs of Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi performed an improbable trick. They redirected millions of people travelling between the West and Asia to connect through their airports. Last year, the three airports handled about 182 million passengers, three times the traffic at Hong Kong airport. Dubai alone handled 95.2 million, the highest ever recorded by an airport. The Gulf’s hub-and-spoke model – funnelling passengers through a central airport to multiple destinations – created economies of scale that redesigned global commercial aviation flows through a routing system solid enough to become the new standard of travel between West and East. When the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February, Iranian retaliation targeted all three hubs. Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International was struck, with the airport reporting one death and seven injuries; Dubai International suffered damage to a concourse; Doha was also targeted. Airspace emptied and flights were cancelled or diverted. For those wealthy enough to escape by private jet, charter prices initially tripled. War-risk insurance for a single private-jet journey to the region reached as much as US$50,000. By the first half of 2026, passenger traffic at Dubai International had fallen by 31.3 per cent year on year. On September 30, a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia after its co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft. The disruption raises an uncomfortable question: was one of modern aviation’s great successes built around a vulnerability hiding in plain sight? The Gulf hubs engineered their dominance. Each hub consisted of an airport paired with its own airline, creating the frictionless closed system key to their industrial efficiency: Dubai started Emirates in 1985, Doha Qatar Airways in the 1990s and Abu Dhabi Etihad Airways in 2003. Their governments combined vast hydrocarbon wealth with a fortunate location and imported everything else. Aircraft came from Airbus and Boeing, financed through international leasing markets. Low-cost labour and highly paid executives and managers came from abroad. Migrant workers account for over 80 per cent of the United Arab Emirates’ resident population. Dubai’s financial centre established an English-language common-law court system. The physical environment had to be negotiated too. These desert cities depend on fresh water from desalination plants, which can be targeted, on air conditioning for enormous terminals through summers hotter than 40 degrees Celsius, and on imports for up to 90 per cent of food in the UAE’s case, along with equipment and technology. Airports and fleets were built on a scale wildly disproportionate to local passenger markets. Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad operate more than 700 aircraft, with modern widebody jets worth well over US$100 million apiece when new. Cathay Pacific Airways, by comparison, ended 2025 with 159 passenger aircraft. The infrastructure is equally extraordinary. Dubai has approved a US$35 billion expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, designed eventually to handle as many as 260 million passengers a year – almost three times Dubai’s passenger record. Yet one input cannot be negotiated: proximity to Iran and some of the world’s most contested airspace. Superhubs’ traffic concentrations are both their strength and weakness. Feed more destinations through one airport, and every additional connection makes the network more useful. Interrupt that airport, and disruption propagates through the same network with equal efficiency. The Middle East endured wars while Gulf aviation expanded. The problem is not that war disrupts flights, but that in this specific war, the Gulf’s hubs have become part of the battlefield. This also creates an opportunity for Asian and Western operators to recapture passengers. Chinese airlines have one clear advantage: unlike many Western competitors, they can still cross Russian airspace. Finnair says a Shanghai-Helsinki flight that took around eight hours now takes more than 12, while Chinese competitors retain the shorter routing. Shorter routing means less fuel and flight time, allowing airlines to fly expensive aircraft more often, increasing productivity. Chinese airlines added as many as 2,900 flights to Europe this summer, including 1,120 by Air China. Singapore, Istanbul and European hubs are likely to compete too. None of this means that Emirates, Qatar Airways or Etihad is doomed. Their networks, fleets and infrastructure took decades to accumulate, and their governments have formidable resources to keep supporting them. The question is whether geopolitical exposure is turning from an occasional disruption into a permanent condition. The Gulf aviation miracle was ultimately an exercise in assembling a constellation of imported tangible and intangible assets. Aircraft, capital, technology, expertise and labour could all be brought to the desert. Even drinking water could be manufactured. For four decades, geography was the superhubs’ greatest asset. The current test is whether geography becomes their greatest liability – and whether some of the traffic they drew from Western and Asian operators will now find its way back to them.

title: Maduro and wife to face new US charges over alleged torture of Americans
description: Venezuela’s former president and spouse jailed in New York on drug counts await expanded indictment.
content: Ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges ‌in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official said on Wednesday. The new charges could come as soon as Thursday, according to the official, who was briefed on the investigation. Maduro, who led Venezuela for 13 years, and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on January 3 and brought to New York ⁠to face drug trafficking charges. They have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial starting ‌June 1, 2027. A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, declined to comment. Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests ‌for comment. The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Wednesday. Details of the ⁠new charges, including ⁠the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available. Maduro’s tenure was marked by tensions with the United States. Washington accused ‌his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions such as relief from financial sanctions. Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during ‌Maduro’s tenure ‌included five oil executives arrested on corruption charges. They were freed in 2022 in exchange for ‌two of Flores’ nephews who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking. Others detained included two former ⁠US Army Special Forces members who were arrested in Venezuela in 2020 in connection with a botched raid ⁠aimed at ousting Maduro. They were freed in 2023 as part of another prisoner swap. Since Maduro’s capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has ‌increased cooperation with the Trump ‌administration. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been held in a federal jail in Brooklyn. Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Thursday to urge US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to release her from jail before trial for health reasons. Prosecutors oppose her release.

title: Madrid woman whose eviction ignited Spain’s housing protests dies at 87
description: Rallies over Maricarmen Abascal and the country’s housing crisis mount as trade unions call a nationwide general strike.
content: Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old Spanish woman whose dramatic eviction last month sparked mass housing protests that led to an early election, has died, the Madrid tenants’ union said on Wednesday, as thousands demonstrated over her death. Abascal had been in hospital for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her eviction on September 23 from her home of more than 70 years, when police and social ‌workers removed her by stretcher. Her case ignited protests over a mounting housing crisis including a shortage of homes and surging rents. Activists camped out in a major Madrid square. Following news of Abascal’s death on Wednesday, thousands marched from the square, Puerta del Sol, towards parliament, chanting: “This is not a death. It’s a murder!” A cause of death was not announced. “This was a completely avoidable death that symbolises the drama that is the housing crisis in Spain,” said 36-year-old marcher Dario Gomez in Madrid. Demonstrators also held protests in Barcelona. Trade unions on Wednesday announced a nationwide general strike ⁠over housing issues on November 11. The protests, along with parliament’s rejection last week of decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Prime Minister ‌Pedro Sanchez to call an early election for November 29. Sanchez is seeking to shift the political narrative from his government’s handling of a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta and a series of corruption cases involving his Socialist ‌Party and his family to the housing crisis, hoping to tap into growing resentment over rising rents. “Now, following her passing, ⁠we are left with the example ⁠of the fight she waged and the legacy Maricarmen has left behind. And, above all, we will honour what she always asked of us: ‘Fight, keep fighting for what is yours,’” the ‌tenants’ union said in a statement. Sanchez lamented Abascal’s death in an X post. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today,” he wrote. The leader of Spain’s centre-right ‌opposition ‌People’s Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, said on X that Abascal’s death shouldn’t be politicised. There should be “no campaigns, no political parties, no other interests here,” he ‌wrote. “In the face of someone’s death, respect is all that matters.” Abascal was evicted after an investment fund bought her house. Several days ⁠later, her lawyer said she reached an eight-year agreement with her landlord that would allow her to return home and pay rent at the same ⁠prior amount. She had planned to sign the deal once she felt better, but never had the opportunity to leave hospital. A neighbour of Abascal, whose home was near Madrid’s famed Retiro Park, said she was shaped by living through Spain’s authoritarian Franco regime, which ended in ‌1975. “She was a fighter, with very ‌clear ideas, a somewhat broad sense of justice, and, above all, perhaps a social conscience and ideas about solidarity,” he said. Guillermo Ruiz, 31, an audiovisual specialist at the mass march, said he felt pessimistic about change. “The best homage we can pay to her is to continue the fight, continue to mobilise, fight for a dignified life and that what happened to her doesn’t happen to anyone else.”

title: New York’s famed Chrysler Building finally finds a buyer
description: Real estate firm Tishman Speyer and other investors will inject US$235 million into refurbishing the ageing art deco landmark.
content: A US real estate firm announced on Wednesday it is buying the Chrysler Building and will undertake a vast makeover of the art deco landmark that dominates New York’s skyline. The Chrysler Building, which was opened in 1930 as a symbol of exuberance and modernity, had faced several years of uncertainty over its ownership. Tishman Speyer, a commercial landlord, said it and other investors will inject US$235 million into the property to refurbish its ageing interior and exterior. They will also pay rent to Cooper Union, a New York college that owns the land on which the Chrysler Building stands, as part of a 150-year ground lease. Tishman Speyer is no stranger to the famous 77-story office tower: the developer bought the lease at auction in 1997 and finished fully divesting from it in 2019. Investors now plan an intensive programme to modernise the mechanical, electrical and air conditioning systems. The 61st floor, whose exterior features a tribute to the radiator caps of early Chrysler vehicles, is to be converted into a dining space with access to outdoor terraces. The project also includes restoration of the facade and polishing of its famous stainless steel crown. The goal is to enable it to compete with the more modern skyscrapers in the city.

title: US issues first outbound investment fine over Chinese robotics AI deal
description: Parent of Plug and Play Tech Centre fined US$200,000 for failing to report a roughly US$92,000 investment in Shanghai robotics AI firm.
content: The US Treasury on Wednesday announced its first penalty under rules governing American investment in sensitive Chinese technologies, revealing a US$200,000 fine against the parent of Plug and Play Tech Centre for failing to report an investment in a Shanghai robotics AI company. The Treasury said on Wednesday that Amidi, LLC failed to submit a required notification after its Chinese fund subsidiary invested around US$92,478 in Shanghai Qiongche Intelligent Technology Company Limited, known as Noematrix, on April 19, 2025. The penalty was issued in July but announced on Wednesday. It exceeded twice the investment amount. The case provides the first concrete example of enforcement under the Outbound Investment Security Programme, which took effect in January 2025 and governs certain US investments in Chinese artificial intelligence, semiconductor and quantum computing businesses. The programme prohibits some transactions and requires investors to notify the Treasury of others. Its requirements also cover certain investments made through overseas entities controlled by US persons. The Treasury identified Amidi’s violation as a failure to notify it of the transaction. The announcement did not describe the investment as prohibited or allege wrongdoing by Noematrix.The South China Morning Post contacted Amidi and Noematrix for comment. Amidi is the parent entity of the organisation operating as Plug and Play Tech Centre, the Treasury said. Noematrix develops “embodied AI”: models and software that enable robots to understand their surroundings and perform physical tasks. The company lists logistics, household services and food processing among its applications. Its financing announcements have named Plug and Play China among its investors, alongside Prosperity7 Ventures, a fund under Aramco Ventures, and other investment firms. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the announcement underscored the department’s commitment to protecting US national security through investment security measures. Christopher Pilkerton, assistant secretary for investment security, said the programme addressed advances in key technologies by countries of concern that could pose national security risks. “We will continue to ensure that investors comply with the requirements established under the programme,” he said. The Treasury said it discovered the transaction through regular compliance and market monitoring. The announcement did not explain how it calculated the US$200,000 penalty.

title: Canada will not allow assisted suicide for those with only mental illness
description: The government is seeking to close debate on one of the country’s most controversial healthcare issues.
content: Canada will not allow medically assisted suicide for people whose only condition is mental illness, the justice minister said on Wednesday, seeking to close debate on one of the country’s most controversial healthcare issues. Canada legalised assisted dying for those at the end of life in 2016. The right was extended to those suffering from serious and incurable illnesses in 2021, even if death was not “reasonably foreseeable”. Initially, Canada was to allow assisted death regardless of condition by 2024, but that date was pushed back three years, with the government saying it wanted to make sure that the already overwhelmed mental health system was ready. Without government action, people exclusively suffering from a mental illness would have had access to assisted suicide in March, when the exclusion was set to expire. But Justice Minister Sean Fraser told reporters on Wednesday that Canada’s Liberal government plans to pass legislation that will prohibit assisted suicide for people whose only underlying medical condition is mental illness. “Canada has made a decision not to move forward with the expansion [of assisted suicide],” Fraser said. “While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach.” Fraser’s announcement follows recommendations from an advisory panel which in June urged the government not to expand assisted suicide rights. That panel raised concern about the lack of mental health support in communities across the country, and the risk that suffering patients would choose death because they could not access care. The committee also highlighted debate among mental health experts as to whether mental illness could ever be deemed incurable. A majority of Canadians support the right to assisted suicide, but in recent months some medical professionals have called for a review of the policy, including how patients receive approval to end their lives. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Trump wants to turn his Florida golf course into a presidential retreat
description: White House explores converting West Palm Beach club into a Camp David-style getaway for future leaders.
content: US President Donald Trump wants to turn his luxury Florida golf course into retreat for future American leaders modelled on the historic Camp David getaway, the White House said on Wednesday. The plan would make the Trump International Club in West Palm Beach – where the 80-year-old billionaire often spends weekends on the fairway – into an official sanctuary for his successors. “The United States government has asked to look into developing a presidential retreat at Trump International Golf Course in Palm Beach for future presidents, so they can hold important meetings and utilise the amenities of a world-class property,” a White House official said on condition of anonymity. The official stressed the security at Trump’s course, where gunman Ryan Routh shot at the then-presidential candidate in September 2024. “The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement and happens to be a highly rated golf course. “These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat.” Palm Beach international airport was renamed after the city’s most famous resident earlier this year. A lawyer representing the Trump course wrote to local officials in September comparing the proposed retreat to Camp David, Windsor Castle in Britain and France’s Elysee Palace, The Washington Post reported. Trump is not a fan of Camp David, having visited the presidential bolt-hole in the scenic Maryland hills near Washington on only a handful of occasions during his two terms in office. Where other presidents have made frequent journeys and hosted historic foreign summits there, Trump prefers to spend his downtime at his golf courses in Florida and New Jersey.

title: US proposes US$70,000 fee for foreign students to work after graduation
description: Schools would have to pay for graduates’ initial OPT participation, with a further US$30,000 charge, affecting thousands of Chinese students.
content: The United States has proposed requiring universities and other certified schools to pay US$70,000 for each foreign student entering a post-graduation work programme, a measure that could sharply raise the cost for thousands of Chinese graduates seeking employment experience in the country. The Department of Homeland Security announced on Wednesday that the proposed fee would apply to initial participation in Optional Practical Training, or OPT, with a further US$30,000 charge for subsequent participation. The full proposed rule, released in the Federal Register after DHS announced the measure, also cites concerns involving Chinese students and Beijing as part of the administration’s justification for tightening the programme. DHS pointed to a 2020 visa-fraud case involving at least 2,693 people, primarily Chinese F-1 students seeking OPT, and noted that one student associated with the operation was later convicted of acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government. The department also cited congressional concerns about Chinese nationals taking part in US science and technology programmes and previous proposals to restrict OPT eligibility for people affiliated with entities owned or controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. Nearly 62,000 Chinese students took part in OPT in the 2024-2025 academic year, according to the Institute of International Education’s Open Doors report. The programme allows eligible students on F-1 visas to work in jobs directly related to their field of study. Schools would have to pay before recommending a student for OPT, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services would not grant employment authorisation without payment, DHS said. Although schools would be responsible for paying the fees, the proposed rule says they could pass the cost to students or employers. That raises questions about whether institutions would continue recommending students for the programme and how participants would finance the charges. NAFSA: Association of International Educators criticised the proposal, saying it would deepen uncertainty for international students and undermine the US economy. “International students don’t take opportunities from Americans, they create them,” said Fanta Aw, the association’s executive director and chief executive. Aw said OPT allows international students to gain practical experience while helping to fill shortages in high-demand STEM fields and generating jobs for American workers. The association plans to submit detailed comments outlining its concerns about the proposal. “Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labour, or a prize for those who game the system,” a DHS spokesperson said in the announcement. The department said the fees would combat fraud, improve oversight and protect American workers. It cited schemes involving false employment and “pay-to-stay” arrangements that exploit student visa rules. Michael Clemens, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins University and a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, disputed the administration’s argument. “No research whatsoever supports the government’s claim that this policy will protect American workers,” he said to the South China Morning Post. Clemens said US-trained, highly skilled foreign workers increase productivity, benefiting American workers across sectors and skill levels. He warned that the proposed charges would sharply restrict access to the principal route international graduates use to remain and work in the country and hurt innovation and entrepreneurship. “The loss will be hard to see: it will be counted in inventions never made, firms never founded, races against other countries lost,” he said. “It will not be easy to hold accountable the people who caused it. But the loss will nevertheless be colossal.” Eligible F-1 students can generally receive up to 12 months of OPT at each education level. Graduates in designated science, technology, engineering and mathematics fields may qualify for a further 24-month extension. The charges remain a proposal. DHS said it would accept public comments from October 8 through November 9 and could revise the rule after reviewing submissions. The proposed rule would take effect 60 days after publication of a final rule. Existing OPT approvals and school recommendations issued before that date would not trigger the fee, although later requests could be subject to the new charges.

title: France halts use of stun grenades in policing of student protests
description: Protests show no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed, and more marches planned for Thursday.
content: The French government said on Wednesday it was pausing the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests, after a 15-year-old boy’s hand was blown off during a clash with riot police, fuelling protesters’ accusations of police brutality. Protests showed no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept across the country, and unions representing high-school students, teachers and other workers planning more marches for Thursday.
