The ‌wave of protests has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace French President Emmanuel Macron. At Lycee Lamartine, a high school in central Paris, protesters sang the Marseillaise, chanted slogans and performed Mexican waves as they blockaded the entrance to the school. “We saw there were lots of crumbling walls, a shortage of teachers in public schools, absent teachers,” said Gabriel Fillieule, who used to attend a public school but now goes to a private one. He and others said they were protesting to demand better learning conditions for all. While most of Wednesday’s blockades were peaceful, police used tear gas and pushed back protesters in a ⁠street barricaded by rubbish bins outside Sciences Po university in central Paris. Rights groups, labour unions, students and some opposition politicians have accused the police of using disproportionate force to quell the wave of protests. Interior ‌Minister Laurent Nunez said he had ordered the suspension of the use of stun grenades following an incident in the northern city of Lens on Monday in which there was a “strong possibility” the firing of a stun grenade had caused a teenager to lose his hand. “I am suspending their use for the ‌high school students’ movement until light has been shed on what happened in this case,” said the minister, who added that 18 incidents in total had been referred to ⁠the police inspectorate for investigation. Protesters have said ⁠they blame poor learning conditions for a sharp drop in French teenagers’ scores in reading and maths over the past decade. French 15-year-olds scored 43 points lower in reading in 2025 than in 2015, according to the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment, the ‌biggest drop among the OECD countries. Their maths scores also dropped the most. But the government, under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, has little spare cash to address students’ complaints of teacher shortages, ageing school buildings and inequalities between schools in affluent ‌and poor ‌areas. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has acknowledged the “legitimate” demands of France’s students but also described the unrest as the most violent student demonstrations in decades. Education ‌Minister Edouard Geffray told parliament that 24 high schools had been damaged by fire or vandalism to the extent that they would remain closed for weeks, meaning some 30,000 students would receive no in-person ⁠teaching until they reopened. He estimated it would cost €20 million to €30 million (US$22 million to US$34 million) to fix the damage. Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, the front runner according to opinion polls, said those who damaged schools ⁠should pay for the repairs rather than taxpayers. The government has adopted a similar stance and has a bill going through parliament that aims to set up such a system. Elsewhere in Europe, where budgets have been under pressure as governments respond to successive cost-of-living and energy crises, students in parts of Belgium staged similar protests. In the Belgian ‌city of Liege in the southern French-speaking Wallonia region, ‌at least 107 people had been arrested in connection with student protests this month, the Belga news agency reported. Teachers are also on strike. In Portugal, the main teachers’ union FENPROF launched an indefinite strike in mid-September over working conditions, with teachers refusing to do any unpaid work beyond the 35 hours a week mandated by law. And in Spain, teachers’ unions have been protesting against conditions in state schools. Teachers in Madrid plan a strike on October 14 to press demands including a reduction in hours, smaller class sizes and higher salaries.

title: Singapore’s air pollution worst in world as haze shuts Malaysia schools
description: Air quality levels in Singapore were in the ‘very unhealthy’ range as of Wednesday afternoon, according to data from IQAir.
content: Singapore’s air pollution worsened to the highest in the world as haze from Indonesia wildfires blankets the region days before the city state’s annual Formula One weekend. Air quality levels in Singapore were in the “very unhealthy” range as of Wednesday afternoon, according to data from IQAir. Nearby Kuala Lumpur, which was earlier in the top spot, ranked as the second-most polluted city globally. In the Malaysian state of Johor, about 140km (87 miles) northwest of Singapore, some 200 schools, kindergartens and nurseries in the district of Bahu Pahat were ordered to close on Wednesday due to the haze conditions, local media reported. Dry conditions were forecast for the next few days over most of southern Southeast Asia, keeping the risk of fires and transboundary haze elevated, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said in its latest outlook. Its data also pegs air in all five regions of the city at unhealthy levels. A spokesperson for Singapore GP Pte Ltd, which organises the F1 race, said on Tuesday that it would work closely with relevant agencies “to assess the situation before making any collective decisions regarding the event” should haze cause visibility, public health or operational issues. An F1 spokesperson said conditions were not at any level of concern. Swathes of Southeast Asia have been clouded in choking smog in recent weeks as Indonesia battles one of its worst wildfire seasons in years. The uncontrolled blazes stem from the long-running use of slash-and-burn agricultural practices, but fire conditions have been exacerbated by an intensifying El Nino that is parching the landscape. The number of hotspots last month was the highest since 2015, when a regional haze emergency caused widespread disruptions and diplomatic tensions, according to the Forestry Ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi. Environmental group Greenpeace has identified more than 20 palm, pulp and sugar companies, including several with links to Malaysia and Singapore, whose land concessions contained sources of smoke from the fires. Last week, organisers of the Kuala Lumpur Standard Chartered Marathon cancelled a kids’ race on health concerns, while pressing on with other race categories, including the full and half marathon distances. Still, top finishers of the full marathon clocked times that were slower than recent years. The marathon was cancelled in 2015.

title: China’s thorium-229 nuclear clock beats Vienna’s on stability, studies show
description: Chinese and European teams in ‘fierce but friendly’ competition to develop the next-generation timepieces.
content: Initial results from the world’s first two working nuclear clocks indicate that China’s timepiece is about six times as stable as the one in Vienna, according to papers published this week by the journal Nature. The clocks were developed independently but both the Chinese team, led by Tsinghua University in Beijing, and the researchers at Vienna’s TU Wien used thorium-229 nuclei embedded in crystals to keep time by the steady rhythm of the atom’s core, rather than the electrons whirling around it, as in atomic clocks. When Nature reported in June that the two teams had separately developed the radical new devices, Thorsten Schumm, a member of the European team, said that “now we have a fierce but friendly global competition”. According to the latest papers, the Beijing scientists also showed that two crystals grown separately kept the same time – a sign such clocks could be reliably reproduced, they said. Meanwhile, the Vienna team used its clock to hunt for dark matter, without success. Ding Shiqian, who led the Tsinghua team, told the South China Morning Post that moving the clock’s tick from electrons to the nucleus mattered because the nucleus was much smaller than the atom and less disturbed by stray electric and magnetic fields. “In the long term, this could allow nuclear clocks to reach extremely high accuracy,” he said. But the significance went beyond simply building a “better clock”, he added. The thorium nucleus reacted to the laws of physics very differently from the electrons in atomic clocks, so comparing the two kinds of clocks could reveal tiny shifts in nature’s constants or traces of dark matter. The clocks could also have practical uses, Ding said. Today’s best atomic clocks are extraordinarily precise, but they remain complex laboratory systems. “A solid-state nuclear clock could potentially be made much more compact, robust and easier to operate. If that becomes possible, it could bring optical-clock-level precision out of specialised laboratories and allow such precision to be deployed much more broadly in the real world,” he said. His team also found that two crystals made separately gave the same tick, agreeing to within about three parts per 10 trillion. The tick also matched earlier measurements by physicist Jun Ye’s group at JILA, a research institute run by the University of Colorado Boulder and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which used different crystals and different equipment. That showed the clock’s tick “is not simply a property of one particular crystal, but can be reproduced across independently prepared samples and laboratories”, Ding said. He called it “an important step” towards turning the nuclear clock from a laboratory demonstration into a reliable standard. While the work heralds a new generation of more precise, robust and compact timekeepers, for now neither nuclear clock is as stable as the best atomic clocks, which keep time by tracking electrons as they jump back and forth between two energy levels. For more than seven decades, atomic clocks have been the world’s most precise timekeepers, underpinning everything from satellite navigation to the official definition of the second. In 2003, Germany-based physicists Ekkehard Peik and Christian Tamm proposed a clock built around the atom’s nucleus instead, as it was so tiny and tightly bound that it would be less disturbed by stray electric and magnetic fields that can throw off atomic clocks. However, most nuclei need far more energy to make such jumps than any existing laser is capable of triggering. Thorium-229, a rare radioactive form of the metal, is the exception: its nucleus can be switched with a nudge of ultraviolet light. That quirk – which comes from a near-perfect balance between the forces holding the nucleus together – also makes thorium-229 extremely sensitive to tiny shifts in the basic forces of nature. This characteristic makes physicists hopeful that nuclear clocks could help in the hunt for dark matter and eventually test whether the constants of physics are truly constant. It took many years to pin down the exact energy of the thorium jump, with scientists first managing to trigger it with lasers only in 2024. For the latest studies, both teams shone ultraviolet laser light through a tiny crystal laced with thorium-229 and tuned the laser until the nuclei soaked up the most light. That point became the clock’s “tick”. The Chinese team made its ultraviolet light by firing laser beams through cadmium vapour heated to 600 degrees Celsius (1,112 Fahrenheit) – hotter than a wood-fired pizza oven. The Tsinghua researchers used this bright beam to light up a crystal that was smaller than a grain of rice yet packed with about a million billion thorium nuclei, according to the paper. The Vienna team’s crystal held about 200 times as many thorium nuclei, and its ticks were checked against an atomic clock across the city through 10km (6.2 miles) of optical fibre. But the researchers in Vienna found the tick varied slightly depending on which part of the crystal the laser passed through, so that the clock kept a slightly different time each day it was switched on. Both teams said the road ahead would have its hurdles. According to the Tsinghua team, thorium-229 is so scarce there is almost no room left to experiment with how the crystals are made. Better crystals – with the thorium spread more evenly and with fewer internal flaws – would help every part of the crystal keep the same time and sharpen the tick, the Vienna team wrote. Together with more powerful lasers, such improvements could eventually make nuclear clocks competitive with – or even better than – today’s best atomic clocks, the researchers wrote. title: 10 injured in knife attack at school in northeastern Poland
description: A 19-year-old suspect, who was among those hurt, was detained shortly after the incident.
content: Ten people were injured in a knife attack at a ‌school in Ostroleka in northeastern Poland on Wednesday, the town’s mayor said, with police detaining the 19-year-old suspect, who was among those hurt, shortly after the incident. Masovian Regional Governor Mariusz Frankowski told reporters that nine people had been taken to hospital but that none of them was in a ⁠life-threatening condition. “The injured ⁠included five students, two teachers and two bystanders, as well as the perpetrator, ‌who inflicted self-harm,” he said. Police said the suspect was a student at the school and that he had attacked people with ‌a machete. They confirmed that bomb disposal experts were checking the attacker’s ⁠backpack but were unable ⁠to say if anything had been found. Authorities identified the suspect only as Jakub Z., in line with Polish privacy laws. He was arrested on a riverbank less than 1km (a half mile) from the school after fleeing the scene, according to police. He was wounded at the time of his arrest in what prosecutors said was a result of “self-mutilation”. The young man was taken to a hospital. The attack took place at ‌a vocational school for teenagers. Fire brigade spokesman Adrian Stupski told state news channel TVP Info that students ‌had ‌barricaded themselves into classrooms in self-defence before they were evacuated. Authorities said the attack ‌happened about 11am local time. Police said they detained the suspect about 20 minutes ⁠after the attack and posted a photo on social media showing a man they appeared to ⁠have apprehended lying face down in a wooded area. Town hall spokeswoman Katarzyna Ogniewska told reporters that all schools in Ostroleka were closed ‌and that children were safe. The ‌motives behind the attack were unclear. Such incidents are rare in Poland, but in September police detained a 13-year-old suspected of planning an attack and found a knife in his bag. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: 24 luxury houses at One Stanley sold amid probe into alleged construction defects
description: Experts call for stronger homebuyer protections in Hong Kong, including mandatory period during which purchase contracts can be rescinded.
content: Two dozen luxury houses at One Stanley have been sold since Hong Kong authorities launched an investigation into alleged structural defects in March, with buyers including local and international businesspeople. The transactions have prompted experts to call for stronger homebuyer protections, including implementing a mandatory period for buyers to rescind contracts when statutory violations are discovered. The South China Morning Post learned that 24 transactions were recorded at One Stanley between March and September. The government launched a probe into construction quality at the development in March. Lingnan University Professor Yau Yung, a surveyor who researches building illegality, urged stronger consumer protections for first-hand property buyers. “I have suggested a mandatory time frame during which buyers can rescind purchase contracts if severe defects or statutory violations are discovered,” he said. Buyers of the 24 homes included local entrepreneurs, mainland Chinese executives and international businesspeople, with several of the properties featuring sea views, sources said. The Buildings Department said on Saturday that it had launched an investigation into work quality issues at One Stanley, which sits in one of the most expensive neighbourhoods in Southern district, and had requested information from the developer, contractor and relevant professionals. The department sent staff to carry out an on-site inspection at a house in March after receiving a complaint from an owner regarding the structural safety of the floor slabs of the property in January. It said its previous inspections did not find any imminent danger. The development comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats in total. The issue came to light after a report published on Friday by online property news platform WuChatProp alleged that an on-site inspection of a house at One Stanley found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts, falling short of the number in the approved building plans by as much as 75 per cent. The owner reportedly bought the property in 2024 for about HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) and discovered quality issues when he started renovations in August last year. The Buildings Department said in a reply to the SCMP on Tuesday night that it would be inappropriate to comment further with the investigation under way. The department added that it had instructed the developer to inspect similar houses and residential units within the development and submit a report. As the regulatory authority, the department also said it would proactively carry out random checks on selected units and audit other current projects managed by the building professionals and contractors involved to ensure overall structural safety. K Wise, the estate seller, has three directors: Law Kino, Ng Shun-yee and Raymond Law Ka-kui. Raymond Law is the youngest son of late textile tycoon Law Ting-pong, one of the founders of Bossini. Law Kino is the mogul’s grandson. According to the Buildings Department, it issued occupation permits to 32 standalone houses and 11 low-rise blocks at One Stanley in July 2023. The document stated that Wong Ming-yim was the project’s authorised person and Benny Lai Siu-lun was the registered structural engineer. Sales information of One Stanley indicated that Wong was from DLN Architects. According to the firm’s website, Wong was a deputy managing director at the company founded in Hong Kong in 1972. Lai is believed to be the executive director of SYW & Associates, as the company’s phone number matches with the contact of Wong on the department’s structural engineers’ register. According to an SCMP check, Lai appears to be one of the members of an independent review panel that looked into the partial collapse of the Married Inspectors’ Quarters building at the Central Police Station in its early days. While declining to comment on the specific development, former lawmaker and lawyer Doreen Kong Yuk-foon noted a recent surge in construction defect cases across the city, highlighting an urgent need for enhanced legal protections for homebuyers. She added that latent structural issues often emerged years after projects were finished, yet statutory liability for Hong Kong builders remained strictly limited. She said that holding developers accountable for defects was exceptionally difficult for homebuyers, particularly when project entities underwent voluntary winding-up shortly after selling all flats. To address these loopholes, the government should overhaul existing regulations, including restricting developers from swiftly initiating voluntary winding-up proceedings upon completing sales, she said. However, a barrister specialising in property law said whether a developer should stop selling properties after identifying issues was a commercial decision. “Having to halt the sales of the entire development just because of an issue at one flat is somewhat hard to justify from a commercial perspective,” the industry player said. “A development may involve 1,000 flats. If that were the policy, it would discourage developers from investing or selling properties. We need to strike a balance.” The barrister added that a developer who knew about work-quality issues and still sold its properties also bore the risk of compensating buyers in the future. Additional reporting by Eric Jiang

title: More than 300 hopefuls sign up for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll
description: Several seeking committee subsector seats refuse to comment on possible second term for leader John Lee, saying they are currently focused on winning votes.
content: More than 300 people signed up for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll as the nomination period opened on Wednesday, vying for seats on the body that chooses the city’s leader. The nomination period for committee subsectors for the November 22 election will run until October 20. The 1,500-member body will select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year. The Registration and Electoral Office received 305 nominations for candidacy on Wednesday. It also received two nominations from designated bodies proposing members for the Election Committee. Registered subsector voters will elect up to 982 representatives to the committee. They will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies. Hopefuls submitted nomination forms throughout the day, including heavyweights from various sectors. But they all said it was premature to comment on the next chief executive race. Clement Chan Kam-wing, chairman of the Consumer Council who is running for a seat in the accountancy subsector, said he would push for Hong Kong to strengthen its position as an international financial hub. Wai Chi-sing, former managing director of the Urban Renewal Authority, is contesting a seat in the engineering subsector and said the next chief executive should address the need for better alignment between the Northern Metropolis and older urban districts. Renowned filmmaker Derek Yee Tung-sing and Hong Kong table tennis team coach Li Ching formed part of a 15-member team contesting the sports, performing arts, culture and publication subsector. They declined to say whether the team would support current leader John Lee Ka-chiu should he run for a second term. Wong Po-kee, honorary deputy secretary general of the Sports Federation and Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China, only said: “We will work hard to win voters’ support. We will talk about the future later.” In the labour subsector, the Federation of Trade Unions put forward 46 representatives, including former lawmakers Aron Kwok Wai-keung and Michael Luk Chung-hung. The Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions also nominated 12 members to stand in the subsector, which has 60 seats. A coalition of 14 educators signed up to contest the education subsector, calling on prospective chief executive candidates to address teaching staff shortages and demographic changes. The 1,500 members will be responsible for nominating and selecting the city leader next March and electing 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029. The committee comprises five sectors representing 40 subsectors, ranging from commercial, financial and professional groups to labour unions, district representatives and Hong Kong representatives on national bodies.

title: Why China’s export engine may hit a ceiling as trading partners face limits
description: Exports likely to keep growing in near term but could face pressure in the years ahead, analysts say.
content: While China’s export engine still has room to grow, many of its trading partners may be approaching the limit of how much more they can absorb, which could place a ceiling on further growth over the coming years, according to a Goldman Sachs report. “At least over the next few years, there is still room for Chinese exports to maintain their strong momentum,” analysts said in the report led by the American investment bank’s chief China economist Hui Shan on Wednesday. “Over the longer term, however, stronger economic growth in importing economies will be required for continued Chinese export gains.” Even under the bank’s most conservative projection, China’s real exports could grow by 8 per cent annually in the near term, despite the country posting a record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus last year. Much of that momentum was driven by supply-side factors in China, according to the report, with export volumes rising since 2021 even as profitability across industries declined. In the automotive sector, for example, export value nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025, while profit margins fell from 6.4 per cent to 4.8 per cent. The Goldman Sachs analysts warned that the country’s export growth could face a longer-term constraint as it increasingly depends on overseas markets to absorb more Chinese goods. A growing number of trading partners were already running large trade deficits with China, which could eventually constrain their ability to increase imports further, they added. “Trading partners’ trade deficits cannot rise indefinitely,” the report’s authors said. “The sharp increase in the number of countries already facing large and still-rising deficits with China points to balance-of-payments constraints for some of China’s trading partners.” In 2025, 82 countries recorded trade deficits with China exceeding 3 per cent of gross domestic product, up from 24 in 2005. Of those, 67 were low-income countries, some with limited foreign-exchange reserves to finance persistent deficits, according to the report. Together, those countries accounted for 44 per cent of China’s total exports. Beijing has long faced criticism from Western governments over its export model. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen recently warned that a “second China shock” was already hitting Europe and pledged to use all available tools to rebalance trade. Amid growing concern among Western politicians about China’s widening trade surplus, the Politburo – a major decision-making body led by President Xi Jinping – in July called for efforts to “expand the scope for mutually beneficial international economic and trade cooperation” and “promote more balanced trade development”. China’s cumulative trade surplus reached US$805.51 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up about 3 per cent from the same period last year, according to customs data. The latest trade figures are set to be released next week.

title: Can ‘neutral’ Malaysia stay above the fray in the US-China tech rivalry?
description: Speaking at a tech event, Malaysia’s defence minister says the country is ‘non-aligned’ in ‘every domain’, including in cyberspace.
content: Despite Malaysia’s insistence that its long-standing non-alignment policy extends to cyberspace, analysts say the country’s reliance on American and Chinese technology could make such a stance difficult to sustain amid the rivalry between the two superpowers. Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin said on Monday that Malaysia would “always remain neutral” in cyberspace, arguing that cyber threats could come from non-state actors and should not be viewed solely through the lens of geopolitical contestation. “As a principle of the country, we are non-aligned. We are neutral, and it goes into every domain,” Nordin told reporters at the Cyber Digital Services, Defence & Security Asia 2026 event. “Cyberattacks can come from anybody from anywhere, and it may not come from a state actor.” Analysts warn, however, that Malaysia’s reliance on foreign technology could leave critical systems exposed to disruptions if a major power confrontation were to result in sanctions, export controls and other curbs. “Neutrality in foreign policy does not make our digital systems neutral,” said Murugason R. Thangaratnam, a cybersecurity consultant and adjunct professor at the University Malaysia of Computer Science and Engineering. He cited Malaysia’s telecommunications networks, cloud services and defence systems, as well as other critical infrastructure that relied on technology from the US, China and elsewhere. “Malaysia need not take a side to be pushed towards one,” he said. “Malaysia can remain politically non-aligned, but in cyberspace non-alignment is a policy aspiration, not a technical reality.” Malaysia has previously faced the ripple effects of the superpower tech rivalry. In March last year, then investment, trade and industry minister Tengku Zafrul Abdul Aziz said the US had asked Malaysia to closely track high-end Nvidia chips entering the country amid concerns that some could be diverted to China in violation of Washington’s export controls. In July, Malaysia introduced a Strategic Trade Permit requirement for the export, transhipment and transit of high-performance AI chips of US origin, including those not listed as strategic items. The Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry said the measure was intended to close regulatory gaps as it reviewed whether chips should be added to Malaysia’s Strategic Items List. Balancing act In recent years, Malaysia has sought to avoid dependence on any single tech supplier. The country’s first 5G network, operated by Digital Nasional, was built using equipment from Swedish tech giant Ericsson, while its second 5G network was developed in partnership with ZTE, a partially state-owned Chinese tech company. Malaysian mobile telecoms services provider U Mobile also opted to partner with Chinese multinational corporation Huawei Technologies to deploy the second 5G network. Farlina Said, director of cyber and technology policy at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies Malaysia, said the country could be considered technologically non-aligned, with infrastructure such as its 5G networks drawing on innovation from East and West. “The landscape may differ if we are looking at military applications,” Farlina said, explaining that in the sensitive security domain, Malaysia must consider the compatibility of systems used by its partners. Diversification was important to prevent a single point of failure, and for international investors to feel safe and secure about their systems in Malaysia, she added. Ainiuddin Wahid Abdul Wahab, a professor from the Department of Computer Systems and Technology at Universiti Malaya, said that having a diversified tech supply chain did not mean that Malaysia would not face any risks. Any major power conflict, sanctions and export controls could affect operating systems, security patches and cloud services, forcing organisations to move to other technological ecosystems or face serious disruptions, Wahab said. “The biggest risk is not the hardware but the lifeline that keeps it running, such as cloud services, software updates and proprietary standards,” he added. “The safeguard is to map our dependencies and prepare backup plans early.” In 2021, the Malaysian government announced a push to expand cloud services across the public sector. Its government cloud programme uses four commercial providers: Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, TM Cloud Alpha and Amazon Web Services. Farlina noted that under the US CLOUD Act, Washington could require foreign entities to hand over data, raising questions over digital sovereignty during a geopolitical crisis. “There are incidents which illustrate how legal orders could still apply across borders, especially if companies are headquartered in the specific [US] state,” she said. Last year, a Microsoft France executive told a Senate inquiry in Paris that he could not guarantee that data belonging to citizens of France would never be handed to a foreign authority without the approval of the French government. In a further example of the blurred tech boundaries, the signing of a partnership agreement in July between Malaysia’s National Cyber Security Agency and Huawei Technologies Malaysia covering areas ranging from cryptology to AI security has prompted concerns of Washington’s possible objection. In 2023, the US and European Union warned Malaysia of national security and investment risks over its 5G roll-out and Huawei’s potential role in the network, with US ambassador Brian McFeeters warning that “untrusted suppliers” could expose the Southeast Asian country’s infrastructure to security risks. Ultimately, Malaysia has to ensure that its critical digital infrastructure can continue to function even during a political crisis between the major powers, according to Murugason. “Malaysia does not need to choose between Washington and Beijing,” he said. “It needs to ensure that, in a crisis, no one else can make that choice for us.”

title: Review | The Mage review: Josie Ho scavenges lost souls in supernatural detective thriller
description: Josie Ho stars as a former fortune-teller who crosses paths with a policeman investigating gruesome murders in this Pang Brothers film.
content: 2.5/5 stars A seemingly deranged rubbish collector makes for an unorthodox cinematic sleuth. Yet this is precisely the conceit of The Mage, a supernatural whodunnit that pairs the pungent outcast with a cynical police detective to make sense of a spate of gruesome deaths in Hong Kong. Beneath the grime is Josie Ho Chiu-yee. The billionaire heiress has long exhibited a fascination with the wealth spectrum’s lower end in the stylised horror films produced by her own studio, 852 Films, having previously starred as a struggling homebuyer in Dream Home and a troubled property investor in the Tokyo-set Onpaku. The Mage plays like Keeper of Darkness meets Limbo, blending the former’s spirit-guiding premise with the latter’s rubbish-filled procedural grit. In it, Ho gleefully offends every nostril as Lan, a former fortune-teller now burdened with a crippling phobia of water after a client (Sabrina Ng Ping) jumped from a building and landed at her feet during a torrential downpour. Seeking redemption, Lan dedicates herself to scavenging the scattered souls of those who met unnatural ends. Her routine of collecting haunted objects soon intersects with the investigation of Sergeant Wong (Carlos Chan Ka-lok), whose suspicion is raised by her penchant for loitering at death scenes. Wong’s personal life is unravelling following the decision of his ex-girlfriend and forensic colleague (Kathy Yuen Ka-yee) to abort their child. His attitude towards Lan shifts when she temporarily opens his “third eye”, granting the grieving officer a glimpse into the spirit world and prompting him to forge an alliance with the eccentric mage. For its first hour, The Mage is diverting as a darkly comic character study. Twin brothers Oxide Pang Chun and Danny Pang Fat (The Eye), co-directing for the first time since 2013’s Out of Inferno, infuse the grim proceedings with a levity that anchors the fantasy elements within a prickly odd-couple dynamic. When this uneven thriller – penned by Danny Pang and Zheng Wei – unveils its devious design, however, tension leaps out the window. Viewers are somehow expected to be intrigued by Lan’s mysterious master, whom the protagonists suddenly believe to be the mastermind behind the deaths. This pivot lands with a thud. Iman Taheri, 852 Films’ newly signed actor, delivers an exceedingly campy turn as Wong’s boss. Elsewhere, German Cheung Man-kit – again auditioning to be Hong Kong cinema’s go-to brute for abrupt bursts of action – shows up for a messy climax that mistakes chaotic pugilism for narrative resolution. While The Mage’s striking occult aesthetics hint at a compelling vision, its sleuthing plotline is hopelessly fumbled. For all its entertaining build-up, the mystery-solving third act proves frustratingly indecipherable amid a barrage of superstitious mumbo jumbo. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Sri Lanka’s ex-first lady arrested in charity corruption probe
description: Shiranthi Rajapaksa is facing allegations that her charity misused US$30,000 in donations collected for a children’s hospital.
content: Sri Lanka’s anti-corruption authority arrested former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa on Wednesday over allegations that her charity misused donations collected for a children’s hospital. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s government has revived long-dormant corruption investigations involving members of the once-powerful Rajapaksa family, which dominated Sri Lankan politics for nearly two decades. The 73-year-old wife of former president Mahinda Rajapaksa was arrested in Colombo and driven to the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) for further interrogation. “The arrest is in connection with her Siriliya Saviya Foundation,” a CIABOC official told reporters at the Rajapaksa home in the capital. She is due to be taken before court later on Wednesday, when a magistrate will decide if she can be released on bail. Her lawyer, Manoj Gamage, told reporters that she denied the allegations made against her and would contest the charges of misappropriating donations raised for charity. The CIABOC also arrested the former head of a state-owned bank in connection to a 10 million rupee donation (US$30,000) to the charity, the agency said. Pradeep Kariyawasam, the then chairman of the National Savings Bank, was accused of donating public funds to the Rajapaksa charity without following proper financial regulations. Shiranthi Rajapaksa travelled to Singapore on September 16 for medical treatment, and was served with a summons at Colombo airport to provide a statement to police about her charity. She flew back on Monday after filing a court petition seeking to prevent her arrest, but the hearing for anticipatory bail was fixed for October 12. Police said authorities wanted to question Shiranthi Rajapaksa over the 10 million rupees in donations collected by her Siriliya Saviya charity for a PET scanner intended for a local cancer hospital for children. Investigators told a court that the scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government, but the charity allegedly continued to solicit donations and misused the funds. Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money had not been misappropriated. Other members of the family have also faced legal troubles. The former first lady’s eldest son, opposition lawmaker Namal Rajapaksa, is in remand custody over allegations linked to a 2013 Airbus aircraft deal signed during his father’s presidency. The Rajapaksa family has consistently denied the corruption allegations and dismissed the cases against them as politically motivated. Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president from 2005 to 2015 and remains one of Sri Lanka’s most influential political figures, despite the decline in the family’s fortunes since mass protests ousted his brother, Gotabaya Rajapaksa, from the presidency in 2022.

title: India-born US citizen drives research into light at sanctioned Chinese school
description: At the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Arup Neogi’s team explores how light and sound interact.
content: “Science has no borders,” Arup Neogi, an India-born scientist who works at a US-sanctioned university, told Chinese state media. Neogi’s speciality is photonics, the study of generating, controlling and detecting light. At the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) in the southwestern city of Chengdu, he leads a team exploring the interconnection between light and sound. This university has one of China’s top electronics and communication programmes and has been on the US “Entity List” since 2012. Inclusion on the list subjected the university to sanctions on academic exchanges and technology procurement. The university was added to the list because it was accused of acting as a proxy for the Chinese Academy of Engineering Physics, which had previously been sanctioned over its role in China’s nuclear programme. Neogi was born and raised in India, obtained his first doctorate in his home country and his second in Japan before working in the US for around two decades and becoming an American citizen. In 2014, he began to collaborate with UESTC, and in 2022 joined the university full-time. “As a foreigner working in China, I really like this state of affairs because I can gather different thoughts and perspectives together,” Neogi said in an interview published in Chinese by state-run Science and Technology Daily on September 17. “Especially in today’s era when global challenges such as climate change are intensifying, we need this kind of cooperation even more.” He leads a team focused on creating photonic chips and nanophotonics. “One growing area the group is interested in is manipulating sound using light for deep-sea communications and ultrasound imaging,” he was quoted as saying. In 2024, he received the China Government Friendship Award, the highest honour for foreign experts who have made significant contributions to China’s development. He won the award for developing an acoustic diode for underwater sound wave control at UESTC. After the award ceremony, Neogi was invited to attend a reception celebrating the 75th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China, at which Chinese President Xi Jinping delivered a speech. In addition to his scientific work, he helped cultivate China’s optical expertise. In the past few years, he helped UESTC enrol several overseas researchers, according to the university. He also helped many Chinese students apply to study abroad, young Chinese teachers apply to international programmes, and Chinese teachers attend international conferences. The South China Morning Post contacted Neogi for comment.

title: Hong Kong and Indonesia can deepen green finance ties, Jakarta envoy says
description: Special envoy Mari Elka Pangestu also says city’s common law expertise and financial services can support country’s push to attract family offices.
content: Hong Kong and Indonesia can deepen cooperation in green finance as their ties strengthen, the country’s special envoy for international trade has said, adding that the city’s common law expertise can support the nation’s efforts to attract family offices. Hong Kong also played a vital role as a conduit channelling mainland China investments to Asean, Mari Elka Pangestu told reporters before delivering a lecture at the University of Hong Kong on Wednesday. Pangestu is the Indonesian president’s special envoy for international trade and multilateral cooperation, as well as vice-chairwoman of the country’s National Economic Council. Following efforts by the Hong Kong government to tap the Asean market, ties between the city and the bloc had prospered, she said, noting the region was the city’s second-largest trading partner. The bloc comprises the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor. Hong Kong and Asean merchandise trade grew at 7.6 per cent annually on average over the past five years, reaching HK$1.66 trillion (US$211.5 billion), or 15.3 per cent of the city’s total trade, in 2025. “Moving forward, what we would like to see is kind of more the complementarity between what Hong Kong can offer and what Asean has. And I think the real potential is probably in financial connectivity and green bonds, sustainable finance and infrastructure investment, because Hong Kong is a financial centre,” Pangestu said. Noting that both sides were eager to develop green finance, she described the sector as highly complementary. She said the surge in global fuel prices had heightened the urgency for renewable energy production across Asean countries, creating emerging investment opportunities such as the electric vehicle market. “What we need to do is align the green bond standards and taxonomies and mobilise private capital for Southeast Asia’s energy transition,” Pangestu said. She added that Hong Kong could support Indonesia with its expertise in financial and legal services, as well as its talent pool, particularly in the country’s drive to attract family offices and investors. “We have been told by investors that what [they] want is common law, because it apparently provides the most legal certainty when you have disputes,” she said. “So I can see that we will probably come and look for legal expertise in Hong Kong, say for those who are very experienced with common law, and then also to run financial services.” Edward Chen Kwan-yiu, honorary professor of the university’s business school and the distinguished economist after whom the lecture series is named, echoed the view that Hong Kong must strengthen collaboration with Asean. Chen said the government should diversify investment sources for the Northern Metropolis and attract capital from Asean. The megaproject aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land along the mainland Chinese border into a technology hub and create a new economic engine. Chen also highlighted Hong Kong’s strength as the world’s largest offshore renminbi hub in promoting trade. “Using renminbi is a great advantage to Asean countries. The borrowing cost is much lower than the US dollar ... And the transaction cost is much lower because it is direct exchange,” Chen said. In June, the People’s Bank of China, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Bank Indonesia signed an agreement to implement a currency transaction framework for the direct exchange and settlement of Indonesian rupiah and Chinese yuan in cross-border trade and investment activities. However, Pangestu acknowledged that only about 10 per cent of trade between Indonesia and China was currently settled in renminbi, which she described as a relatively small share, despite the practice beginning to gain traction. She attributed the modest figure to limited business awareness and availability, while noting that the Indonesian central bank had been promoting renminbi settlement to mitigate volatility of using the US dollar. She also commented on Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last month, saying that it had helped stabilise Sino-US ties despite lingering uncertainty. “A stable floor is good enough for now, because at least then you can do your relative calculations,” she said. “I think we have now, even though there is still risk and uncertainty, we kind of have an idea of where the uncertainty is, at what level this is going to be stabilising ... and I think businesses have figured out how to manage this in terms of the supply chain disruptions.” Pangestu also addressed challenges facing the Indonesian economy as its currency fell to historic lows against the United States dollar this year. She noted that many countries had seen currency weakening due to the stronger American dollar and higher US interest rates, while domestic factors such as investor confidence in Indonesia had also played a role. She expected Indonesia’s economy to grow by more than 5 per cent this year, saying the government had recognised the weak consumer spending caused by higher borrowing costs and was working to improve the investment environment to support stronger expansion.

title: Opinion | US and China must set rules before autonomous fighters cross paths
description: Rapid military AI development makes agreed limits on mission scopes, operational areas and target parameters an urgent priority.
content: In December 2022, a Chinese J-11 fighter came within metres of a US RC-135 surveillance plane over the South China Sea, according to the US military, which criticised it as an unsafe manoeuvre. China, however, held the American crew responsible and claimed the RC-135 had suddenly veered towards the Chinese jet despite repeated warnings. Both sides released video footage, yet neither accepted the other’s account of the incident. This and other such close encounters involved human pilots. The next one may involve aircraft with no one on board. On September 30, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans for a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command to scale up autonomous and robotic capabilities across the US military. The Pentagon has requested US$54.6 billion for accelerating the development and adoption of autonomous and unmanned systems in the 2027 financial year, up from US$225.9 million the year before. China is moving in the same direction. In November last year, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force released footage of its GJ-11 stealth drone flying alongside a J-20 fighter. In January, state broadcaster CCTV said a single soldier could control a swarm of more than 200 drones, which could plan their own flight paths when jammed. As these aircraft become more autonomous, two questions arise: How much leeway should operators allow them? And how can states demonstrate that the aircraft stay within designated limits? In a July live-fire test of a collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) – an uncrewed combat jet designed to fly alongside a piloted fighter – the US Air Force stressed that such aircraft “will not autonomously employ weapons”. However, the July test was conducted in a controlled environment. Over the South China Sea or the Taiwan Strait, the situation can change in an instant. These aircraft may operate far from their operators, where communications are easier to jam, and may be given prior permission to choose and engage targets without human approval for each engagement. The US Air Force’s assurance is a policy decision, and policy decisions can change. The Pentagon’s own directive on autonomy in weapon systems is now being rewritten. A June presidential memorandum gave the Pentagon 90 days to update it, but the new version was still unpublished in late September, according to The Washington Post. Beijing, for its part, offers little visibility into how it reviews new autonomous weapons. That is why the agreement reached during President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month matters. The two sides will set up a channel for AI-related incidents, hold an AI-specific dialogue in November and sign a memorandum on military crisis communications. But the real test of such a channel will come when an American autonomous fighter and a Chinese GJ-11 get too close. Each government would then need to know, within seconds, whether a human operator or the autonomy software took any decision, and whether the aircraft remained within its authorised limits. A hotline would serve little purpose if both sides are not willing to share this information, and US President Donald Trump has already said there will be limits on what the US tells China. Then there is Geneva. At the seventh review conference of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, from November 16 to 20, states will decide whether to begin negotiating rules on autonomous weapons. The non-binding text agreed in September could serve as a basis. Neither side needs to ban these aircraft. What they could agree on, in the AI dialogue and in Geneva, is that commanders must set limits for every mission, based on its targets, operating area and the threats they expect to face. The International Committee of the Red Cross’ proposed limits on targets, operating time, geographical area and scale offer a useful starting point. But limits only matter if the aircraft follow them in combat, even when they lose contact with their operators. Aircraft that cannot complete an engagement within these limits should have to end it or seek further input from an operator. States should test whether their aircraft do this, and tell each other how they tested. Even with tests, though, verification would be hard. Former US Air Force secretary Frank Kendall argues in his book Lethal Autonomy that a requirement for human approval of lethal engagements could be circumvented and hidden with little technical effort. A state might demonstrate a safeguard in a trial and remove it afterwards. Yet Kendall himself suggests making a designated official and organisation responsible for testing and verifying that such systems comply with the laws of war, as is done with airworthiness certification. Washington and Beijing could each adopt that idea, which would give them something concrete to report through the new AI-related incidents channel. In 2022, despite pilots and videos on both sides, the two governments could not agree on what happened. With autonomous aircraft, there will not even be a pilot to question, and any account would depend on software logs and whether either side is prepared to share them. Washington and Beijing should use their AI dialogue in November and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit in Shenzhen to decide what the new channel will report, before an uncrewed combat aircraft loses contact with its operator over contested waters.

title: Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies
description: Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
content: ⁠Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones on Wednesday, the country’s transport ministry said, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified. Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched ‌a counteroffensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold. The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, a US ally. On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy ⁠it, but gave no details of casualties or damage. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. ‌There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport. Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government ‌sources say. Fierce clashes have taken place, with the Houthis claiming they have repelled attacks. On Monday the Yemeni government said it had reached Mocha, which sits ⁠at a junction with a supply route ⁠to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim had been premature, according to Yemeni military officials on the ground and analysts. Hussam Radman, a researcher at the Sanaa Centre, a Yemen-focused think tank, said pro-government forces including the Giants Brigade, ‌a conservative Sunni Salafi group that has led the counteroffensive, were trying to take control of Dhubab and to advance in the mountains to its east. Control of those highlands would allow for government forces to more easily advance up the ‌rest of ‌the coast, he said. Along Yemen’s coast to the east, one missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, ‌the transport ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it ⁠added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control. The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, ⁠seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement. The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the ‌Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as ‌a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations. Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported. In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

title: Why do Hong Kong’s Election Committee polls matter as nominations open?
description: The South China Morning Post examines who is running, what to watch for and how committee will choose city’s next leader.
content: The nomination period opened on Wednesday for election to the 1,500-member body responsible for choosing Hong Kong’s next chief executive and 40 lawmakers. The Registration and Electoral Office received 305 nominations for candidacy on the first day of the window. The South China Morning Post explains the significance of the poll, who has signed up and what to watch for. 1. What is the Election Committee and why is it important? Wednesday marked the start of the two-week nomination period for the 2026 Election Committee Subsector (ECSS) Ordinary Elections, scheduled for November 22. Up to 982 subsector representatives will be elected to the city’s top electoral college. They will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies. Together, the 1,500 members will be responsible for nominating and selecting the chief executive next March and electing 40 of the Legislative Council’s 90 members in 2029. The Election Committee comprises five sectors representing 40 subsectors, ranging from commercial, financial and professional groups to grass-roots organisations, district representatives and Hong Kong representatives on national bodies. The body was revamped in 2021 as part of Beijing’s electoral overhaul to ensure only “patriots” govern Hong Kong. It expanded from 1,200 to 1,500 seats with the addition of a fifth sector comprising politicians, including deputies to the National People’s Congress. 2. Who has signed up? Hopefuls from at least four subsectors submitted nomination forms throughout the day. Some arrived at government offices carrying placards and chanting slogans. Each nomination form must be endorsed by at least five voters registered in the relevant subsector. Renowned filmmaker Derek Yee Tung-sing and Hong Kong table tennis team coach Li Ching were among a 15-member team contesting the sports, performing arts, culture and publication subsector. The team was backed by lawmaker Kenneth Fok Kai-kong. The Federation of Trade Unions put forward 46 representatives for the labour subsector, which has 60 seats. They included former lawmakers Aron Kwok Wai-keung and Michael Luk Chung-hung. The federation’s chairman, Stanley Ng Chau-pei, said the hopefuls represented unions across a range of industries, including transport, logistics and public utilities. A coalition of 14 educators also signed up to contest their subsector. They urged prospective chief executive candidates to promptly address teaching staff shortages and demographic changes. 3. What should I watch out for? Attention will focus on how many subsectors require a contested election and which ones they are. In the 2021 poll, seats in 23 subsectors were filled uncontested. Some politicians have said Beijing “encouraged competition” to build an electoral atmosphere, although national security vetting remains in place to ensure only “patriots” can run. Before the 2021 electoral system overhaul, the committee was regarded as a “highly contested battleground”, particularly in professional subsectors such as education. Pro-democracy and pro-establishment candidates competed fiercely for seats elected by individual voters. Those seats are now chosen through corporate voting. 4. What happens next? After the two-week nomination period closes, the Candidate Eligibility Review Committee will vet the nominations and confirm which candidates are eligible, taking advice from the Committee for Safeguarding National Security. On November 22, registered voters in contested subsectors will cast their ballots to determine the final line-up of elected members. Electoral Affairs Commission chairman Mr Justice David Lok Kai-hong inspected preparations at the returning officer’s office at Tamar on Tuesday. Lok also chairs an independent commission investigating the deadly Tai Po fire last year. He reminded returning officers to ensure the elections were conducted in an “open, honest and fair manner”.

title: Hong Kong police arrest 17 more over HK$137 million ‘crash-for-cash’ scam
description: Commercial crime bureau operation brings total arrests to 55 as authorities investigate 669 cases.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested 17 more people linked to a suspected “crash-for-cash” scam syndicate as authorities investigate 669 suspicious claims totalling more than HK$137 million (US$17.4 million). Among those arrested was an insurance claimant accused of filing 12 compensation claims worth more than HK$3 million. Officers from the commercial crime bureau arrested the 17 claimants aged 27 to 49 between September 9 and Tuesday on suspicion of fraud, bringing the total number of people arrested to 55. Police said these new batches of suspects were linked to 63 civil compensation claims arising from traffic accidents, involving a total of HK$25 million. One of the arrested individuals allegedly filed 12 separate claims seeking about HK$3.64 million. Officers seized a batch of documents and mobile phones during the operation. The force began investigating what they regarded as a new form of “crash-for-cash” scheme after receiving reports since January from insurance companies, related organisations and members of the public alleging fraudulent behaviour in traffic accident compensation claims. Officers have so far received 669 suspicious cases involving claims worth a combined HK$137 million. Preliminary investigations suggested 461 of the cases were connected to the same law firm. Drivers involved in traffic accidents reported being approached long after collisions and facing what they claimed were unjustified demands for substantial compensation. Some alleged that multiple cases involved the same law firm and doctor, raising suspicions of an organised operation. Between February and this month, police carried out four enforcement operations and arrested a total of 55 people. Three of them have been charged with offences including fraud, attempted fraud and perverting the course of justice. The remaining 52 suspects have been released on bail pending further investigation and are required to report back to police between the middle of this month and mid-November. Police said they would continue taking action against suspected “crash-for-cash” fraud syndicates. Among those arrested earlier, a 37-year-old driver and his wife, 38, a registered nurse, were previously charged in connection with the investigation with a total of 20 offences, including fraud and perverting the course of justice. The pair failed to appear in court when the case was mentioned on June 25, prompting the court to issue arrest warrants.

title: 14 years after Nirbhaya gang rape horror, has India progressed on women’s safety?
description: Several reported rape cases in New Delhi recently show that the rights and safety of women are still being trampled upon, lawyers say.
content: Bhavya Gupta was a Grade 4 student when the 2012 horrific gang rape and murder of a medical college intern who was on a private bus in New Delhi, which sparked nationwide outrage and led to the execution of four attackers, prompted her teacher to mention the case in class to raise awareness about women’s safety. “My teacher gathered all the girls in the classroom and told us about it, and after that our school uniform changed from skirts to pants. I also remember adults around me talking about the case in a victim-blaming way, asking why she was out so late with a guy, as if she was partly at fault,” said Gupta, who is now a 25-year-old communications professional based in the Indian capital. The victim, 23, who later died from her injuries, was dubbed Nirbhaya – the fearless one – as she could not be named under Indian law. The political fallout from the tragedy was swift, with analysts attributing the then ruling Congress Party’s losses at the local and national levels to the case. Fourteen years later, another gang rape of a 17-year-old girl, along with a string of other similar cases, has raised questions about whether the country has progressed from the Nirbhaya case. The incident last month in a prominent South Delhi park, close to the prestigious Lady Shri Ram College, prompted street protests expressing outrage and calling for enhancement of women’s safety. Observers say legal red tape and a male-dominated mindset that fails to respect women have led to their rights and safety being eroded. They warn that the reported cases are only the tip of the iceberg, and short memory after the initial national outrage has perpetuated the vicious cycle. “Things have got worse, not better,” Gupta said. “I am not in a position to fix the system, so I focus on what I can control. I avoid going out at night, I do not go to isolated or poorly lit areas, and I share my location with my parents whenever I travel.” Delhi authorities are mulling implementing security measures, including restricting access to public parks after dark. Lady Shri Ram College has shifted classes online after the incident, triggering debate on whether its measures are appropriate. On Monday, the Supreme Court called for stronger measures to prevent crimes against women in the capital. “We must ensure that every woman in National Capital Territory Delhi feels safe, whether walking at 10pm or travelling by metro or road,” the court said. Three other recent assaults on minor girls in Delhi preceded the park incident, including the gang rape and murder of a 16-year-old girl last month. Protesters point out that stronger punishments passed after the landmark Nirbhaya case have failed to improve safety for women on the ground, with data showing more than 80 reported rapes daily across India. Divya Swamy, a partner at D&Y Law Chambers, said that while there had been some improvement in law enforcement since 2012, women still had to make decisions to protect themselves daily, such as avoiding areas deemed unsafe. Legal changes had expanded the range of related actions punishable under the law, she said. “But the trial process itself is so burdensome for the victim that it usually leads to low reporting [of crimes].” The latest protests had “reignited the discourse around women’s safety”, Swamy said, and that violations against women were “more common than we know”. Aparna Mittal, a lawyer and founder of Samana Centre, a leading anti-discrimination consultancy, said the persistently high number of rape and sexual assault cases had led to many women feeling unsafe in India. “If you look at the cases, they are unfortunately happening every day in India. We must also remember that many such cases go unreported, so the official numbers we see are lower than the actual cases that occur,” she warned. While peaceful protests against gender-based violence are happening, the state machinery and institutions tasked with prevention, investigation and punishment are not “functioning adequately or timely”, according to Mittal. “Many women struggle to register their police complaints, especially when the perpetrators are well-connected and privileged. The process of investigation is often marred with loopholes, and judicial verdicts are inevitably delayed because of a multitude of reasons,” she added. Patriarchal mindset Anecdotally, some cities such as Mumbai and Bengaluru were safer than Delhi, but even in these places there was “no guarantee of women’s safety”, Mittal said. “Personally, I may feel safer in Mumbai and Bengaluru than Delhi. In Mumbai, I can take a local cab at 11pm, but in Delhi, I will never do it.” To bring about changes, Mittal called for a transformation away from the “patriarchal mindset” in the country. “All this learning has to start in nursery schools and homes – respecting women, treating women as equals, and not looking at women in an over-sexualised manner,” she said. Mittal cited how India’s patriarchal society had led companies to assume that women were not good enough for top management and people on social media “body-shaming” women over their choice of attire. Gupta is aware of the societal bias against women. She recounted how she was alone at night when she experienced a long delay on a bus journey between the city of Dehradun and Delhi and frantically looked for another female passenger to feel safe. She wore an iron bracelet that she believed could ward off evil and act as a standby weapon if she was facing danger, Gupta said. “Depending on where I am, I will cover up with a long shrug or dupatta [scarf] over what I am wearing, not because I want to, but because I have learned that how I dress can affect whether I get harassed.”

title: Chinese consortium to build Latin America’s longest cable-stayed bridge in Brazil
description: A public-private partnership including two Chinese engineering conglomerates is due to complete the Salvador-Itaparica Bridge by 2031.
content: Chinese contractors will build Latin America’s longest cable-stayed bridge, a trans-bay span in Brazil, as their latest stamp on new infrastructure overseas. A consortium of Chinese companies is set to construct much of the Salvador-Itaparica Bridge, which is due to become the region’s biggest cross-sea project supported by cables once completed in 2031, Chinese and Brazilian media said. They would contribute to a 46.8km (29-mile) project including 12.4km crossing the Bay of All Saints along the Atlantic Ocean and a 682-metre (2,237-foot) span. A piling ship built by a subsidiary of state-owned China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) left from Jiangsu province in eastern China on Sunday to reach the bridge site in 45 days, Xinhua reported. A piling ship helps build bridges by driving structural columns deep into the seabed. The bridge will be built under a public-private partnership including China Communications Construction and CRCC. Brazilian news outlet Brasil 247 said the consortium would also operate and maintain a surrounding highway system. A cable-stayed bridge uses steel cables attached to vertical towers that together support the weight of the road. Brazil represents a good bet for China as a “politically friendly” country where Chinese contractors have already built infrastructure for power transmission, ports and telecommunications, said Evan Ellis, a research professor of Latin American studies at the US Army War College’s Strategic Studies Institute. “Brazil is a welcoming environment now for the Chinese, politically and economically,” he said. “A lot of investment is already there, there’s a huge internal market and many other infrastructure projects have already been done.” But the results of Brazil’s October 25 presidential run-off election between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro could complicate the political landscape. The senator, son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, aims to steer Brazil’s diplomatic and economic position away from China towards the US. He has promised US President Donald Trump’s administration access to Brazil’s rare earths to cut US reliance on China. The bridge also extends China’s push to build infrastructure throughout Latin America where money can be made, Ellis said. Other projects include the Chancay Megaport in Peru and the Coca Codo Sinclair Dam in Ecuador. Brazil’s bridge, which broke ground in July, will link people from the cities of Salvador and Vera Cruz in 15 minutes rather than the one-hour ferry rides available today, Xinhua said. Shipping times for locally produced grain, cotton and fruit would be slashed as well, the news agency said.

title: Abby Choi gave HK$2m for waffle shop to ‘bootlicker’ ex-brother-in-law, trial told
description: Mother of slain model gives account of strained ties with Anthony Kwong and says she was planning to buy new HK$20 million flat in Tuen Mun.
content: The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has told a court that her daughter’s former brother-in-law was a “bootlicker” who coaxed her into funding an egg waffle shop and hiring him as a driver months before her death. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, said on Wednesday that Anthony Kwong Kong-kit had frequently sought financial support from her daughter before he allegedly joined his father and younger brother in a plot to murder her in February 2023. “It is during the time when we were still on good terms that he kept saying he could not find a job. He is a really good bootlicker begging for mercy,” she said on the third day of her testimony at the High Court. Kwong, 35, was Choi’s stand-in chauffeur when the 28-year-old model was allegedly attacked during a car journey she thought was to fetch her daughter from school on February 21, 2023. He is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father Kwong Kau, 68, and his younger brother, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is Choi’s ex-husband. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial. The killing allegedly arose from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell the luxury home and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so he could keep it for himself. Cheung previously testified that the relationship between the two families broke down in June 2022. The elder Kwong was reportedly so opposed to the sale that he threatened to kill Choi and her whole family if she pressed ahead. During cross-examination on Wednesday, the witness said the flat’s intended sale was part of her daughter’s effort to reclaim possession of assets she had given the Kwong family over the years. “[She] realised this family was not good, so [she] wanted to take back the things she owned,” Cheung said. She said her daughter had planned to spend about HK$20 million on a new flat in Tuen Mun for the two children she had with Alex Kwong, which would be closer to their school in the same district, although no purchase was made before the influencer’s death. Defence counsel Trevor Beel, representing Anthony Kwong, sought to challenge Cheung’s suggestion that his client had been living off the influencer’s wealth before the alleged offences. He claimed Choi’s former brother-in-law became her stand-in chauffeur at her request after she dismissed her previous driver in November 2022. But Cheung maintained that Anthony Kwong and his family had persistently asked her daughter to hire him because he was jobless. She said Choi reluctantly agreed to hire him on a three-month provisional basis, but still complained to her that he drove “very dangerously”. The witness said Choi had also given Anthony Kwong about HK$2 million to run an egg waffle shop in Sham Shui Po after her former in-law begged her for money. Cheung said that Anthony Kwong visited her “almost every day” for dinner after Choi stopped financing the business and the shop folded. But Beel contended that Choi had never made significant financial contributions towards Anthony Kwong’s living expenses. The shop, he said, was set up by Choi simply because her two children loved egg waffles. Cheung rejected that assertion and said Anthony Kwong did not repay anything Choi had lent him. The court also heard on Wednesday that a police officer involved in handling the murder trial had approached Cheung via WeChat after she gave evidence on Tuesday. The officer, identified as Detective Police Constable Ko Yan-kit, asked Cheung about the address of a flat at Whampoa Garden, which she said she co-owned with her husband. Instead of supplying the address, she told the officer that she had given wrong evidence about the property’s ownership earlier in the day. “Today I was angry … About Whampoa Garden, a long time has passed and at that time, I thought [the property] was registered jointly under our names, but I was mistaken because it was so many years ago,” she wrote in a message sent to Ko on Tuesday night. Cheung told the court she was mistaken in previously claiming her daughter had not registered the Kadooria flat under her mother’s name because she would be required to pay double stamp duty due to the Whampoa Garden property. Instead, the witness said on Wednesday the Kadooria flat was registered in Kwong Kau’s name because he was jobless and could “run around” for the influencer. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: ‘No more dumping, no more spying’: European Parliament hardens line on China
description: Report calls Beijing an ‘existential threat’ to industry and urges naval exercises around Taiwan Strait.
content: The European Parliament voted for a significantly tougher China position on Wednesday, despite strong and long-standing lobbying from Beijing to tone down its official stance. The chamber backed stronger actions against Beijing, stating it is a “decisive enabler” of Russia, calling for a “continuous [European] naval presence and joint exercises” in and around the Taiwan Strait, and urging swift action to counter Beijing’s industrial policy, which it described as an “existential threat to the EU”. Lawmakers voted by a landslide to adopt the report on Wednesday. In total, 454 lawmakers voted in favour, 86 voted against and 110 abstained. The paper does not directly affect the European Union’s China policy, but helps crystallise the tougher China consensus that has developed in Brussels since the parliament last changed its official line in 2023. In that period, relations between the EU and China have worsened, despite many believing that the return of US President Donald Trump last year would bring the sides closer together. Instead, trade tensions have soared, while fears have deepened about Beijing’s cosy ties with Moscow as Russia’s war on Ukraine shows no sign of ending. The parliament has been rocked by several China-linked espionage scandals, even as the chamber moved to normalise ties with Beijing last year. “We have watched China test the limits of international law. Tomorrow, this parliament can send a clear message: no more dumping, no more spying and fair competition,” the report’s lead author, Hilde Vautmans, a centrist Belgian lawmaker, said in a debate on Tuesday evening. For Beijing, the adoption of the report may be disappointing. For several years, it has devoted huge lobbying resources to the European Parliament – and with some success. Last year, while the broader EU-China relationship was in free fall, the European Parliament normalised its ties with Beijing, leading to a flurry of visits and exchanges.
