Beijing lifted its sanctions on lawmakers that had been in place since a bilateral sanctioning blitz in 2021 relating to reports of human rights violations in Xinjiang, which Beijing denies. Records show a heavy Chinese presence in the parliament, while sources say Chinese diplomats had been lobbying to alter the text of the parliament position paper. Parliamentary disclosures show that Vautmans met mainland Chinese delegations six times in the process of drafting the text this year. She met Taiwanese representatives three times and the World Uygur Congress twice. Previous drafts were scrubbed of the term “systemic rival”, an official designation of China by the EU since 2019, which sources says was removed by Vautmans as she sought to assuage voices from the parliament’s Socialist and Democratic group. The term was returned to the adopted text. Nonetheless, Beijing may be content with the success of two amendments proposed by the socialist grouping, which sought to soften the report’s framing. These amendments restored the term “comprehensive strategic partnership” to the text to describe the EU’s ties with China. They stressed avoidance of decoupling and bloc confrontation and preserving dialogue and cooperation, while downgrading security and deleting reciprocity as central organising principles. Those amendments were adopted in roll-call votes on Wednesday afternoon. The Chinese mission to the EU did not respond to a request for comment about its lobbying activity or the report itself. The divisions among parliamentary groups were on display. Socialist and left-wing group members broadly called for more engagement, while centrist and right-wing groups were largely more hostile. “China is a systemic rival … There is only one language that China understands: not the language of diplomacy, but the language of strength,” said Engin Eroglu, chair of the parliament’s China delegation and a frequent visitor to Beijing. Parliament vice-president Javi Lopez – a socialist ally of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez – took a different tack. “Firmness does not mean confrontation … our relations with China cannot be based on a two-bloc bipolar idea of a world, which is dangerous and unproductive,” he told the chamber during Tuesday’s debate. A day before crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing, the parliament’s report urged a more hardline approach from Brussels. It said Chinese industrial overcapacity “threatens to hollow out the EU’s industrial core” and the country’s EV market was a “big threat” to Europe on security and economic terms. “The EU reserves the right to pursue unilateral measures under its economic security strategy wherever engagement with Chinese authorities proves ineffective or insufficient,” the report read. It accused Beijing of being “a decisive enabler of Russia’s illegal and unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine, serving as the largest provider of dual-use goods and helping it circumvent sanctions”. China says it is neutral in the war and that it continues normal trade with Russia. On Taiwan, meanwhile, it urged the EU to “work with member states and other democratic partners in the region on closer security coordination, including a continuous naval presence and joint exercises, to reinforce stability in the region”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including all EU members and the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: ‘Nothing is left’: deadly floods slam Thai economy and strain Bangkok ahead of IMF meeting
description: Monsoon floods in Thailand have killed 60, battered key industries and sparked unrest ahead of next week’s IMF-World Bank meeting.
content: Monsoon floods in Thailand have killed 60 people since mid-September, officials said, as surging waters exact an increasing economic toll – destroying homes and crops, killing livestock and flooding factories. Bangkok buckled at the end of September as 300mm (11.8 inches) of rain – around one month’s worth – hit its creaking drainage system over just three days. The floodwaters have largely retreated from the capital, giving city officials crucial breathing space to clear the stinking, slurry-like mess left by stagnant water in Bangkok’s east and to dredge canals ahead of renewed storms forecast to roll in from Saturday. Hundreds of millions of dollars in damage has been done to the capital alone, as homeowners race to apply for complicated government compensation schemes. Authorities say they have contingency plans in place should the floods return, threatening the IMF-World Bank annual meeting scheduled to take place in the capital early next week, an event expected to draw thousands of global delegates. While Bangkok enjoyed a rare day of respite on Wednesday, eastern provinces including Chachoengsao and Prachin Buri faced rising waters as tidal rivers pushed floodwater back into vast tracts of land used for agriculture and industrial estates. The Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation said 19 people had died in Prachin Buri so far – the highest toll among the 27 affected provinces – with nearly 190,000 people impacted nationwide. The province is home to hundreds of factories, including new artificial intelligence infrastructure ranging from data centres to printed circuit board facilities that the government has positioned as key drivers of economic growth. Videos posted on social media show fast-flowing water reaching rooftop levels, with residents cowering on upper floors filming the devastation as dark storm clouds pour unrelenting rain onto metres-deep floods. In hard-hit Chanthaburi province, the nation’s main fruit-growing hub famed for its durian harvest, residents spoke of obliterated homes and businesses. “My house and restaurant are completely destroyed – nothing is left,” Wararat Kunam, 53, told This Week in Asia, sharing an image of her refrigerator swept into a nearby tree by floodwaters. “At its peak, the water was several metres deep, submerging the entire first floor. We couldn’t move our belongings in time because the water came very fast.” Wararat said she was grateful that her 200-tree durian orchard sits on higher ground for now, meaning the lucrative harvest may survive a punishing rainy season as she prepares for forecast El Nino-driven drought next year. Others who joined the durian boom driven by surging Chinese demand have not been so lucky, with tens of thousands of rai (1 rai = 0.16 hectares) affected. “If a durian tree is submerged for three days, its root system cannot breathe, and the tree will die standing. Farmers have to start counting from zero again, and production costs also start over,” she said, noting that durian trees take up to five years to bear fruit, making them a high-risk investment. “It has always been like this – the area is inherently fragile,” Wararat added. “When it floods, it floods for real; when it’s dry, it’s brutally dry.” The floods have also hit the agricultural supply chain. Drowned livestock and submerged poultry farms have led the Commerce Ministry to urge egg exporters to slash overseas shipments by up to 50 per cent over the coming weeks to ensure domestic supply. With the floods ongoing, the government has yet to calculate the overall economic impact. But losses are mounting across tourism – after Bangkok’s main airport was temporarily paralysed by flooding – as well as in clean-up costs and direct compensation. Thailand’s annual monsoon typically replenishes reservoirs and feeds crops ahead of the dry season as water flows down from swollen northern rivers into the Chao Phraya – the country’s central arterial waterway – before emptying into the Gulf of Thailand. This year, however, rainfall has been erratic and intense, overwhelming natural drainage systems and straining the infrastructure of Bangkok, a sinking city built on soft clay. The political costs are mounting too. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has come in for heavy criticism over a perceived slow response when Bangkok flooded late last month. Political rivals accuse him of failing to lead relief efforts, particularly in the hardest-hit eastern provinces, while government focus appears split between flood response and hosting high-profile international dignitaries at next week’s IMF-World Bank gathering. “What we are seeing is a failure in the government’s management of the situation,” opposition leader Natthaphong Ruangpanyawut, head of the People’s Party, told parliament on Wednesday. “The prime minister should be sitting at the head of the table, directing all agencies to work effectively and provide targeted assistance. Instead, he has distanced himself from the problem, choosing to visit field kitchens rather than answer questions.”

title: Hong Kong tech index to harness fast-growth companies in bid for better performance
description: Compiler unveils revenue threshold in plan to expand index to 50 firms after falling behind global peers amid lack of AI exposure.
content: Hong Kong’s stock index compiler will add 10 fast-growing companies with at least HK$500 million (US$64 million) in annual sales into the city’s technology-focused benchmark in a bid to revitalise an index that has missed out on artificial intelligence-driven gains. The threshold is among a set of new measures Hang Seng Indexes Company will use to reform the Hang Seng Tech Index, which is referred to as Hong Kong’s answer to the Nasdaq but has lost its shine relative to global peers, falling 23 per cent so far this year. The gauge’s most heavily weighted constituents – Chinese tech giants including Tencent Holdings and Meituan – have failed to spark investor excitement amid the frenzy for AI developers and related stocks, such as memory chipmakers. By comparison, the Nasdaq 100 and the chip-heavy Korea Composite Stock Price Index have hit records multiple times this year. “We want [the tech index] to be forward-looking by picking some emerging companies by sales growth,” said Anita Mo, CEO at the firm, which has compiled the city’s major market indices including the flagship Hang Seng Index since 1969. In December, Hang Seng Indexes will expand the tech gauge by 20 constituents to 50 members. Half of the new additions will be the fastest-growing firms with sales of HK$500 million or more in two consecutive financial years, irrespective of market capitalisation. The other 10 additions, like the 30 current members, will be chosen by market cap, subject to a minimum average daily turnover of HK$100 million over the preceding three months. For comparison, major indexes across the world focus on liquidity and market valuation. “By introducing the growth stream, we hope that if [the smaller firms] could be included earlier, the index could enjoy their success,” said Daniel Wong, head of product management at the compiler, in a media briefing on Wednesday. The two thresholds aim to counter the market’s concern that the liquidity of smaller companies could hinder effective fund tracking, Wong added. After the tech gauge’s May quarterly review, Hang Seng Indexes in June replaced Kingdee International Software and Kingsoft with MiniMax and Z.ai – which is also known as Zhipu and trades as Knowledge Atlas Technology – in an effort to capture market enthusiasm for emerging Chinese AI models. However, share prices for the two new members peaked in March and June, respectively, meaning the gauge missed out on most of their gains. The company said it would retain its quarterly review mechanism, while the maximum weight of any single constituent would be reduced to 8 per cent from 10 per cent. In addition, it said it would implement most of the measures proposed in a consultation in August, including removing industry requirements and expanding sub-themes to 24 from 16. The new list of index constituents will be announced on November 20 and will take effect on December 7. “We hope to grow together with the Hong Kong market through the indexes, strengthening our role as ‘superconnector’,” Mo said.

title: Russia glosses over Stalin-era repression in reinvented museum
description: The ‘Museum of Memory’, which has elbowed out the Gulag History Museum, is set up to commemorate the ‘genocide of the Soviet people’.
content: In a Moscow museum that once housed evidence of Stalin-era repression, serene family scenes flickered on a screen as a narrator hailed the tranquillity of pre-World War II life in the Soviet Union. The museum – set up to commemorate the “genocide of the Soviet people” – has elbowed out the award-winning Gulag History Museum, a harrowing collection that had for years cast a light on the killings and imprisonment of millions under Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin. But since Russia launched its assault on Ukraine in 2022, such criticism of the country’s past has been cast as unpatriotic, scrubbed from textbooks and the official narrative. Instead, the Kremlin has doubled down on glossing over the horrors committed under Stalin, rehabilitating the dictator and erecting statues and busts of his likeness across the country. The Gulag History Museum was “temporarily” closed in 2024 on allegations of fire safety violations. Its exhibits “moved to storage”, according to a guide at the new museum. “From now on, the history of the repressions will remain a murky area, and our shared history will remain distorted,” a Russian woman who fights to preserve the Gulag memory said on condition of anonymity. That history is grim from both perspectives. Up to 18 million people were imprisoned by their government in the Gulag system between the 1930s and early 1950s, accused of being traitors and enemies of the state. Historians generally accept that at least 1.5 million of them died, with some suggesting the real figure is higher. Another 3 million to 5 million died in the man-made Holodomor famine in Ukraine in the 1930s and 1.6 million were either executed or died as a result of forced population transfers, according to Soviet archives declassified decades later. World War II, meanwhile, inflicted its own deadly toll – the Soviet Union suffered the highest casualties, with 20 million to 27 million people estimated to have died, both civilians and military. On speakers throughout the new museum, a narrator recounts how during World War II – which Russia calls the “Great Patriotic War” and says started with the 1941 Nazi attack on the USSR – “our homeland faced violence never seen before”. There is not a word about those arrested, executed or imprisoned in the gulag, the Soviet Union’s vast network of prison labour camps. Despite its bombastic display of the official Kremlin narrative, the “Museum of Memory” has kept a low profile so far. It offers only guided tours to small groups by prior arrangement. On its website, it says it welcomes “above all” veterans of the Ukraine war and their families, as well as students and schoolchildren. Inside, the handful of visitors follow an AI-generated story of an imaginary family – the Lebedevs – recalling horrors endured during the Siege of Leningrad, in concentration camps and villages that were razed to the ground. “It’s a composite image. Each member of this family has several prototypes,” the guide explained. The scenes were, he reassured, “filmed with the participation of real actors”. Giant screens display recreations of bunks in Nazi concentration camps and the entrance to the Auschwitz-Birkenau death camp. Around the hall are waxwork-style figures – women and children, their clothes torn and bloodstained, being held at gunpoint by Nazi soldiers. Critics have balked both at the closure of the original Gulag museum and at the content of its replacement. Much was created by AI, as the museum has chosen not to include first-hand accounts from the period. The final room is dedicated to the Nuremberg trials, where Nazi officials were tried and convicted between November 1945 and October 1946. “All wars end in peace, and all crimes are judged by a court,” the guide said. Maxime Novikov, a 43-year-old historian on the tour, said he was “pleasantly surprised that part of the new museum is dedicated to Russian territories that were under Nazi occupation”. But its predecessor was “unique”, he said with a sigh. Closing it was “most likely a political decision aimed at making people forget the history of the Gulag … which is a disturbing history. It is, after all, the history of the KGB”, the Russian intelligence services, he added. Since launching its offensive on Ukraine, Russia has ramped up the jailing of dissenters and ushered in strict military censorship to outlaw criticism of the authorities. Lina, a 72-year-old doctor, said she found it “terribly sad … that this place of memories – the place where we could have taken our children and grandchildren – no longer exists”. “There are dark chapters in history that we must nevertheless be aware of. And yes, history undoubtedly repeats itself,” she said. “It could happen again in an even more terrible way than before.”

title: Hong Kong’s Wine and Dine Festival to feature extended hours, 10% more booths
description: Tourism board to roll out ‘Hong Kong Gourmet Month’ after four-day festival from October 29 to November 1.
content: The annual Hong Kong Wine and Dine Festival in late October will extend its opening hours until 1am on two nights and feature 10 per cent more booths, with the Tourism Board rolling out a gourmet month throughout November to boost visitor spending and encourage longer stays. Organised by the board under the theme “Taste the World’s Best”, the festival will be held from October 29 to November 1 at the Central Harbourfront, opening at 7.30pm on the first day and 1pm on the following days. The board expects the event to attract 168,000 visitors this year, slightly higher than last year’s 160,000 attendees. For the first time, the event will extend its opening hours until 1am on October 30 and 31. The four-day festival will be followed by the “Hong Kong Gourmet Month” in November, featuring more luxury dining activities. “Through these initiatives, we aim to encourage visitors to stay longer and spend more, creating additional business opportunities for the trade,” board chairman Peter Lam Kin-ngok said on Wednesday. Lam said this year’s festival would be held on a larger scale, with more than 340 booths, an increase of more than 10 per cent from last year. The event footprint would also be extended to Tamar Park, he added. Key highlights for the event include the Grand Wine Pavilion, a designated area for premium wine, and the Tasting Room restaurant featuring five renowned chefs. The Grand Wine Pavilion will bring together fine wines and delicacies from around 31 countries and regions, including Australia, Canada and South Korea. It will also feature wine selections from top Bordeaux chateaux, including renowned bottles such as Mouton Rothschild Pauillac 1er Cru 1982, a prized wine from one of Bordeaux’s “first growth” estates and the legendary 1982 vintage. At the Tasting Room restaurant, diners can enjoy dishes made by Michelin-star chefs Edward Lee, Yoda Chen Zhiping and Thierry Marx, presenting a limited all-new, 10-hand collaborative banquet. The event will also showcase local “Only in Hong Kong” flavours through innovative combinations such as black sesame soy milk pudding tart. It will also bring together 26 hotels, each serving up its signature dishes, such as Hong Kong-style satay beef bun from the Kowloon Shangri-La in Tsim Sha Tsui and three signature pandan cakes with coconut ice cream from The Fullerton Ocean Park Hotel in Southern district. Immediately following the festival, the board will roll out “Hong Kong Gourmet Month”, presenting limited-edition dishes and dining discounts throughout November. Festival-goers can also present their ticket stubs to enjoy exclusive offers at selected restaurants, retailers and business associations. Tickets will be available online for American Express cardholders via Trip.com from Wednesday until October 12, after which sales will be open to the general public. Tasting passes, grand wine passes and tickets for the Tasting Room’s “Taste of Time” banquet and other dining events will be available for public purchase from October 12.

title: 60% of Hong Kong’s suspected student suicides involved children aged 15 or below
description: Figures provided by Education Bureau also reveal principals had referred about 17 high-risk students to Hospital Authority every month since December 2023.
content: Hong Kong education authorities have revealed that at least 60 per cent of suspected student suicide cases in the last three academic years involved children aged 15 or below, urging schools to avoid giving excessive homework so pupils can lead a balanced lifestyle. The Education Bureau also told lawmakers on Wednesday that school principals had directly referred 547 students at high risk of suicide to the public health system over the past 2½ years. On average, principals had referred about 17 high-risk students to the Hospital Authority every month since December 2023. In a written response to the Legislative Council, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin revealed that the respective numbers of suspected student suicide cases reported to her bureau by primary and secondary schools were 30, 33 and 23 in the three school years between 2023 and 2026. The proportions of cases involving students aged 15 or below were 60 per cent, 67 per cent and 65 per cent, respectively. In Hong Kong, youngsters aged 15 are studying in either Form Four or Form Five. “Each case has its unique underlying reasons, and the age distribution of students involved may also fluctuate from year to year,” Choi said. Primary and secondary schools must report all suspected student suicide cases to the bureau so it can provide support. The Hong Kong Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention at the University of Hong Kong earlier estimated that there were 976 suicide cases, or 13 per 100,000 residents, last year – a slight decline from 2024, based on data provided by the Coroner’s Court. While rates declined across nearly all age groups, the figure rose among those aged under 15 to 2.9 per 100,000, the highest level since 2016. There is limited data on suicide rates for the under-15 demographic around the world. The suicide rate for children aged 10 to 14 is generally between 0.2 and 0.8 per 100,000 across most members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, according to a study published by the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry in April. The rates were 0.3 in the United Kingdom, 0.9 in the United States and 1.2 in South Korea. In 2023, the government adopted a three-tier mechanism to provide immediate help to students at high risk of suicide or who show signs of severe mental distress. It focuses on early identification and immediate assistance by prioritising the students using school resources, and in more severe situations, activating an off-campus network for outside help. Under the system, principals can directly refer severe or acute cases to the authority’s psychiatric specialist services for urgent intervention. The mechanism covers Primary Four to Form Six students. Choi revealed that 855 cases had been referred to the off-campus support network teams between December 1, 2023, and July 31 this year. She added that 547 cases were referred by principals to the authority’s psychiatric services. “Both international and local studies have suggested that suicide, including attempted suicide, is a complex issue influenced by the interplay of various factors, mainly related to interpersonal relationships including family, social or relationship problems and personal issues such as learning and school adjustment, depressed mood and mental illness,” she said. To ensure students led a balanced life, the bureau had asked schools to view homework through the frame of “quality rather than quantity” and to develop a coordination mechanism so teachers did not assign too much, Choi told lawmakers. “To cater for students with diverse learning needs, primary schools should arrange a tutorial session in the afternoon as far as possible for students to finish some or all of their assignments under teachers’ guidance,” she added. The minister also pledged that the government would strengthen training for professionals working at schools, such as social workers, guidance counsellors and educational psychologists to ensure early identification of students at higher risk of suicide. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: How will new longer-range aircraft boost Manila’s South China Sea surveillance?
description: The more ‘other countries aid the Philippines, the more likely that they will take an interest’ in the waters, analyst says.
content: The Philippine Coast Guard will receive three longer-range aircraft from the US, two of them modified for improved surveillance, giving Manila greater reach and endurance to monitor Chinese coastguard, naval and research vessels across the South China Sea. Under a US$39.6 million contract awarded by the United States Navy on September 28, the three second-hand, extended-range King Air 350-series aircraft will be fitted with extended-range fuel systems, upgraded Garmin avionics and high-frequency radios. Two will also carry King Air Maritime Domain Awareness intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance systems. The work is expected to be completed by September 2028. Observers said the twin-turboprop aircraft could allow the coastguard to reach distant patrol areas – such as Scarborough Shoal, the Spratly Islands and waters around Batanes in the northern Philippines – more quickly, and remain over them for longer. The agency is already deploying aircraft to such areas to monitor and challenge Chinese activity. On September 27, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) sent the Cessna 208 Grand Caravan PCG-2081 to locate and challenge China Coast Guard vessel CCG-3303 near Cabra Island, Occidental Mindoro province, visually confirming the ship and issuing repeated radio challenges. Raymond Powell, executive director of the SeaLight Foundation, noted that while the PCG’s existing single-engine surveillance aircraft could locate Chinese vessels, it had “little endurance or sensor capability to stay and observe” them. He said the two King Airs fitted with mission suites would allow crews to “loiter, evaluate, document completely and return home with time-stamped evidence” – even if Chinese military aircraft forced them away from the immediate area. The King Air aircraft could extend the PCG’s surveillance reach into the Luzon Strait and around Batanes, where it had historically been able to devote “almost no persistent surveillance” to the movement of PLA Navy and Chinese research vessels, according to Powell. The three King Airs would make it easier to have aircraft available, even during training and maintenance operations, said Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute. This additional capability would allow the PCG to respond “more consistently, swiftly and effectively to vessels that are further afield”, he said. Peter Layton, a visiting fellow at the Griffith Asia Institute and a former Royal Australian Air Force officer, said the King Air’s two engines would provide an added safety margin on long overwater flights. He also expected the aircraft to have “a much better nighttime capability”, which could extend coastguard surveillance into the night. Washington’s move to support its Southeast Asian ally comes as Philippine surveillance flights continue to encounter Chinese military aircraft around contested waters. On October 3, a Philippine Air Force C-208 Caravan patrolling near Scarborough Shoal encountered two Chinese military aircraft. Manila said one, a J-16 fighter, repeatedly manoeuvred dangerously close to the smaller plane. Beijing said the C-208 had “illegally intruded” into what it called the territorial airspace over Huangyan Island, its name for Scarborough Shoal. The People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command said Chinese forces tracked and monitored the aircraft and issued warnings to expel it, accusing Manila of “provocative acts”. Bosack said Beijing could similarly seek to curtail King Air operations through “radar lock incidents, unsafe manoeuvres around the aircraft or deployment of flares” once they entered service. Timothy Heath, director of China and security research firm Perceptum, said the King Airs were unlikely to significantly change Beijing’s response given that China could continue sending military aircraft to challenge Philippine flights around disputed areas. He said the King Airs had “longer duration and potentially more surveillance capabilities” but added that their addition “doesn’t fundamentally change the situation”. Detecting Chinese activity does not necessarily give the Philippines the surface assets needed to respond, and while the King Airs could help Manila decide which incidents warrant deploying its limited surface assets, they cannot stop Chinese grey-zone activity. The PCG “simply cannot dispatch ships to address every Chinese boat in its maritime areas of responsibility”, Bosack said. However, Heath noted that improved surveillance could provide “earlier warning” of Chinese operations and help Manila determine which coastguard or military assets to send, reducing the chances of Philippine forces being surprised or outmatched. Powell said evidence gathered during longer surveillance flights could help Manila “strip away deniability” by providing a more complete record of Chinese activity, strengthening its ability to challenge Beijing’s account of disputed encounters. The King Air programme is the latest example of foreign partners helping Manila fill gaps in its maritime monitoring and enforcement. Australia has provided the Philippine Coast Guard with drones and training. Japan, which has already financed 12 PCG vessels, is funding a further five and France is supporting Manila’s purchase of 40 OCEA patrol boats through export-credit insurance and direct market-rate loans. Heath noted that wider foreign involvement could ultimately matter more than the aircraft themselves because “the more the other countries aid the Philippines, the more likely that they will take an interest” in what happens in contested waters. This mattered because information gathered by Philippine surveillance aircraft could also provide US forces with “useful data” on PLA activity during a Taiwan crisis, he said.

title: China’s open-weight AI models are winning global users. Who is capturing the value?
description: Chinese AI labs face intense competition from platforms hosting their models, highlighting the challenge of turning widespread adoption into sustainable revenue.
content: China’s open-weight artificial intelligence models are taking off globally, but much of the money they generate is flowing to third-party providers rather than the companies that create them, according to a new study. Developers including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI make their model weights – essentially the “brains” of their AI systems – freely available for download. This strategy, which has accelerated global adoption over the past two years, allows other companies to run the models on their own servers and modify them independently. While the approach has boosted adoption, it has also exposed developers to intense competition as rival platforms host the open models on their own infrastructure and offer access at lower prices. By contrast, companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic in the United States keep their models closed and maintain tight control over access and pricing. Hangzhou-based start-up DeepSeek, for example, captured only about 8 per cent of estimated customer spending on its models accessed through third-party aggregator OpenRouter, according to a report released on Tuesday by US research institute Epoch AI. Beijing-based Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, faces a similar challenge. Within a day of the lab releasing the weights for its GLM-5.3 Flash model in August, 12 third-party providers were offering access to it through OpenRouter. Twenty days later, the number had risen to 26, with eight providers charging less than Z.ai. Over the same period, Z.ai’s share of GLM-5.3 Flash tokens served through OpenRouter plunged from 88 per cent to 22 per cent. Its daily token volume dropped 70 per cent even as overall use of the model rose 17 per cent, Epoch AI reported. The figures suggest Chinese developers face a significant disadvantage when attempting to capture revenue from direct access to their models. Z.ai reported a gross margin of 24.6 per cent for its application programming interface (API) platform in the first half of this year, up from 18.9 per cent in 2025. The platform lets customers use Z.ai’s AI models in their own applications and tools. By comparison, Epoch AI estimated that US rival Anthropic achieved a gross margin of 85 per cent by offering its closed-weight Opus 4.8 model exclusively through its own API. DeepSeek was an “outlier” among open-weight developers, with estimated gross margins of between 70 and 80 per cent because of the company’s low inference costs, according to the report. Even so, third-party hosts still captured much of the end-user demand for DeepSeek’s models. US firms, meanwhile, have been able to capture more revenue directly from users through lucrative subscription plans for their closed models. Anthropic, for example, had “aggressively” monetised users, according to a report on Monday by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. About 7.3 per cent of Claude’s paying subscribers were on the company’s most expensive individual plan, which starts at US$100 a month, the report said. The monetisation gap between US and Chinese AI developers remains wide. China’s six leading AI developers – ByteDance, Alibaba Group Holding, Z.ai, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and MiniMax – collectively generated about 10 per cent as much AI revenue as OpenAI and Anthropic combined as of September, Epoch AI estimated. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Chinese developers are experimenting with new licensing agreements and commercial partnerships that could allow them to capture more of the revenue generated by third parties using their models. In July, Beijing-based Moonshot AI released its Kimi K3 model under a licence requiring some large providers that offer the model as a service to enter revenue-sharing agreements. Moonshot had also sought up to 30 per cent of the revenue generated by Kimi K3-related services on major cloud platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, Reuters reported in August. Kimi K3 was launched on Amazon last month. Z.ai is adopting a similar strategy. On Monday, Amazon added GLM-5.3 to its Bedrock platform, giving businesses access to it through the US cloud giant’s servers. Chinese tech media outlet Star Market Daily reported that the arrangement included usage-based revenue sharing with Z.ai. Such agreements could give Chinese AI developers a way to benefit from the distribution advantages of open models while retaining a greater share of the revenue they generate, Epoch AI said in the report, though it remains too early to judge how much revenue the new arrangements could produce.

title: Clockenflap 2026: Hayley Williams, Keshi, Malcolm Todd unveiled for Hong Kong festival
description: Paramore frontwoman Hayley Williams and multi-instrumentalist Keshi have been announced as co-headlining acts for Clockenflap 2026.
content: US singer-songwriters Hayley Williams and Keshi have been announced as co-headlining acts for Clockenflap 2026, Hong Kong’s biggest music and arts festival taking place from December 4 to 6. Williams, who became a prominent voice in the 2000s as the frontwoman of pop-punk band Paramore, made a triumphant return last year with her single “True Believer”, a critique of religion-based capitalism and politics in the United States. Born in the US state of Mississippi, Williams formed Paramore in Tennessee in 2004. The band’s second album, Riot!, brought it mainstream fame in 2007, and Williams became one of the best-known female voices in pop-punk. In 2008, Paramore’s “Decode” was the lead single for Twilight, a romantic fantasy film that has become a defining feature of 2000s pop culture. Paramore’s hit 2014 song “Ain’t It Fun” won best rock song at the 57th Grammy Awards. Since launching her solo career in 2020, Williams’ appearances with Paramore have been infrequent. In 2025, she announced the band would be taking a break while she pursues her own projects. Paramore performed in Hong Kong in 2011 at the AsiaWorld-Expo. Clockenflap 2026 will mark Williams’ first time playing in Hong Kong as a solo musician. Williams, 37, is widely known as one of the most politically outspoken musicians in the US. During the George Floyd protests in 2020, she temporarily handed over her official Instagram account, which currently has 4.7 million followers, to a youth-led activist group to highlight their work and share resources in relation to the Black Lives Matter movement. In 2024, she described US President Donald Trump’s leadership as a dictatorship. In 2025, she said transphobes were not welcome at her shows and joined the “No Music for Genocide” campaign, which blocked her and Paramore’s music in Israel. Keshi, real name Casey Thai Luong, was born in Texas to Vietnamese immigrant parents. A self-taught multi-instrumentalist, he adopted the moniker “Keshi” from a childhood nickname when he posted his debut single, “Over U”, on SoundCloud in 2017, and gained some online traction. He was trained as a nurse at the University of Texas at Austin but quit his job as an oncology nurse and signed with Island Records in 2019. He has become known for his falsetto vocals and blend of lo-fi pop and alternative R&B. In 2024, he released his second studio album, Requiem, paired with global headlining tours. He performed at Hong Kong’s AsiaWorld-Expo and AsiaWorld-Arena as part of his “Epilogue” (2023) and “Requiem” (2025) tours. Keshi will headline on Friday, December 4, while Williams will top the bill on Saturday, December 5. The Clockenflap 2026 line-up also includes English shoegaze legends Slowdive, who played their first Hong Kong gig in a decade in 2024; 23-year-old American indie bedroom pop player Malcolm Todd; American rockers Queens of the Stone Age; South Korean indie band Hyukoh; Scottish alternative rock darlings The Jesus and Mary Chain; and Kim Gordon, the bassist, guitarist and vocalist of alt-rock legends Sonic Youth. Social media posts purporting to show the full act line-up had been circulating the day before Clockenflap’s official announcement. While many of the names listed in the unverified posts have been confirmed, artists such as Hong Kong pop group Goodnight Lillie and South Korean rapper Luci Gang are missing from the official announcement. Clockenflap 2026 takes place at Central Harbourfront from December 4 to 6. Tickets for the three-day weekend are HK$2,180, while a single-day pass is HK$1,380. General ticket sales begin 3pm HKT on Saturday, October 10.

title: Anti-terror arrests in Indonesia highlight challenge of combating ‘virtual’ groups
description: Suspects have organised online meetings for indoctrination and training, the Indonesian counterterrorism force says.
content: The recent arrests of 11 suspected terrorists by authorities in Indonesia underline how terrorism remains a persistent security challenge, with analysts warning that militant networks are communicating online through smaller and decentralised cells despite stronger enforcement. The Indonesian National Police’s counterterrorism force, Special Detachment 88 (Densus 88), said on Sunday that 11 suspected terrorists had been arrested in raids across West Java, Central Java, Central Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, Riau and North Maluku provinces since its operations began on Friday. “The suspects are believed to be affiliated with Daulah Islamiyah and other terrorist networks,” Densus 88 spokesman Mayndra Eka Wardhana said in a statement. Wardhana said that the suspects communicated with each other through “virtual rooms”. “Early investigations indicate that the suspects from various regions were connected virtually. They utilised online meetings for indoctrination, training and network consolidation,” he said. Daulah Islamiyah refers to radical Islamists whose goals are aligned with Islamic State (IS) ideology. Several suspects allegedly took part in militancy training, such as physical and shooting drills, and other activities linked to preparations for terrorist acts, Wardhana said. Densus 88 has also arrested other alleged terrorists earlier this year. In May, eight suspected terrorists linked to the IS-affiliated Jamaah Ansharut Daulah (JAD) network were arrested in Central Sulawesi. The suspects spread radical propaganda through social media posts, videos and other content. Last year, Densus 88 arrested 51 suspected terrorists, a drop from the 196 arrested in 2024, according to data from the national police. Asked by This Week in Asia about the estimated total of active members and supporters of Daulah Islamiyah in Indonesia, Wardhana said that he could not reveal the number due to it being “excluded information”. He also declined to mention the force’s strategy to detect the terrorist cells’ online groups. More nimble cells The recent operations highlight how extremist ideology continues to sprout in smaller, decentralised and harder-to-detect cells two years after the landmark dissolution of Jemaah Islamiah (JI). “From 2023 to 2025, we can indeed say there were zero terror attacks [in Indonesia], but the terrorist networks are always there,” said Chaula Rininta Anindya, an assistant professor of international relations at the University of Indonesia. “The extent of the terrorist networks that form online is difficult to detect. The chat groups are usually numerous. Their development is rapid, while communication platforms are becoming more varied. We don’t know what tools they use to support their discourse.” Radical mindsets – “based on religion or nihilistic violent extremism” – also posed a problem in other Southeast Asian countries, such as Singapore and the Philippines, Chaula said. In July, three Singaporean teenagers aged between 14 and 19 were arrested after they were allegedly self-radicalised by violent extremist ideologues and planned to carry out separate attacks, Singapore’s Internal Security Department said. According to Chaula, the drop in overall attack statistics in Indonesia is made possible due to its stronger legal framework on counterterrorism. In May, the government issued a presidential decree to eradicate terrorism through national preparedness and counter-radicalisation. Under a 2018 law on terrorism, law enforcement is authorised to arrest suspected terrorists pre-emptively without having to wait for their planned actions to be carried out. In June 2024, leaders of JI disbanded the group, which was responsible for multiple bombing attacks in Indonesia in the early 2000s. However, not all members of JI “agreed to rejoin the Indonesian republic”, according to Tegar Bimantoro, a criminologist with the Institute of Andi Sapada. Some of them might have formed cells to “consolidate” their networks and connected through digital platforms, he said. Tegar warned that it would be “very dangerous” if a recidivist were to return to extremism or rejoin a terror cell. “Someone who has been in prison already has access to materials on bomb-making, for example. It would be especially dangerous if they pass on their knowledge to their followers,” Tegar said. A study on terrorist recidivism published by S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore released on Friday estimated that 4 to 11 per cent of 1,200 former terrorists who had undergone a deradicalisation programme in Indonesia over the past decade subsequently reoffended. In November, Densus 88 arrested five suspected terrorists for allegedly recruiting more than 110 children into terrorist networks via social media, online games and encrypted messaging since the end of 2024. One of the five suspects was a former prisoner affiliated with the JAD. In April, Eddy Hartono, head of the National Counterterrorism Agency (BNPT), told reporters that a chat feature in one online game had been used as a “recruitment tool”, dubbing the practice as “digital grooming”. Economic reintegration Tegar said that sustained counterterrorism in Indonesia would depend not only on arrests but also on commitment to social reintegration and economic empowerment over the long term. “When their economy is good and their basic needs are met, I think ideological concerns can be put on the back burner. The current phenomenon is that the economic well-being of these former terrorist convicts is still below standard,” Tegar said. “Today, ideology should not be a main issue when discussing terrorist convicts. We need to talk about reintegration, how they can live sustainably.” Chaula urged Jakarta and BNPT to work together with local governments on additional oversight or social support for former convicts, who typically would return to their hometowns following their release from prisons. “To ensure more effective or intensive monitoring, local governments must be involved. This includes ensuring former terrorist convicts’ reintegration into society, employment, or even simple support for their families, such as schooling for their children. These are things that will be easier to accomplish when local governments are involved,” she said.

title: ‘Ensuring dignified life’: how an app keeps advanced cancer patients out of hospital
description: HKU’s SUPPORT+ mobile app, offering weekly symptom tracking and nurse follow-up, has attracted 76,000 registered users since 2022.
content: Advanced-stage cancer patients could spend half as long in hospital and avoid more than a third of unplanned admissions if a symptom-tracking mobile app is added to their routine care, according to new research from the University of Hong Kong. The SUPPORT+ mobile app, developed by HKU’s clinical oncology department, provides symptom-management information and a direct line of communication with healthcare staff. Launched in 2022 with private backing, the app has attracted 76,000 registered users, including 2,800 families with cancer patients. “Advanced-stage cancer patients often experience severe, worsening symptoms such as pain, shortness of breath, fatigue and loss of appetite … if those problems were not handled early, it could increase the risk of hospitalisation and emergency department visits,” said Clinical Associate Professor of Practice Wendy Chan Wing-lok, who developed the app. “Repeated hospitalisations will not only affect their quality of life but also cause a strain to their carers and the healthcare system.” The two-year study, running from January 2023 to February 2025, covered more than 1,200 patients with advanced-stage cancer who had stopped anti-cancer treatment and were receiving community-based palliative care across six public hospitals. Patients were randomly divided into two groups: one receiving standard care – regular clinic visits and nursing support – and the other receiving standard care plus app support. App users submitted weekly symptom reports and received automated management advice, with severe symptoms triggering an alert and a nurse follow-up within one to two working days. Over an 18-week period, the two groups were evaluated on quality of life, self-efficacy, emergency department visits, length of hospital stay and other outcomes. “For most of our patients with advanced cancer who have stopped anti-cancer treatment, what matters most is not necessarily the length of their remaining life but rather maintaining a comfortable environment and ensuring a dignified, high quality of life moving forward,” Chan said. Of the 1,214 patients enrolled, 633 contributed complete outcome data. Patients receiving both standard care and app support reported a slower decline in quality of life and greater confidence in self-care. About 29 per cent of patients receiving usual care experienced unplanned hospitalisations during the study period, compared with 17 per cent of those receiving app support – a 40 per cent reduction. The standard-care group stayed in hospital for an average of 7.3 days, while the app-supported group averaged 3.4 days, a 50 per cent difference. Emergency department visit rates were similar between the two groups. Chan said she hoped the app could be more widely adopted in public hospitals, but that would require additional resources. Currently, the team had only three nurses due to limited resources, with care focused on patients who had just begun anti-cancer treatment, as side effects often emerged in the first 12 weeks, she said. “Our team needs more resources to hire more nurses, and we need experienced ones that are able to answer questions of patients or their carers on the phone and provide the best advice after looking at the medical records,” Chan said. One carer who benefited from the app, surnamed Chan, is now looking after her 79-year-old mother, who was diagnosed with stomach cancer in March. Chan recalled struggling to care for her mother after discharge, when she had a feeding tube and a gastric juice drainage tube. On one occasion, she noticed the gastric juice volume in the collection bag had doubled and was mixed with blood. She contacted the nurse immediately and received clear instructions on when to monitor at home and when to go to hospital. Beyond medical advice, the nursing team also monitored Chan’s mental well-being, reminding her that caring for herself was essential to caring for her mother. “Without the app, I would have taken my mum to the emergency department a dozen times,” Chan said.

title: Manchester City legend David Silva comes out of retirement for Hong Kong stint
description: Spaniard signs on with local Premier League new boys Supreme Sha Tin three years after drawing line under illustrious career.
content: Supreme Sha Tin have pulled off an astonishing coup after tempting David Silva out of retirement and into a short-term deal with the ambitious Hong Kong Premier League club. World Cup winner Silva hung up his boots three years ago following an enormously decorated career with Valencia, Manchester City and Real Sociedad. Nonetheless, the 40-year-old was unable to resist the opportunity with newly-promoted Supreme, who this week appointed Englishman Tom Ballantyne as their head coach, and he could make his debut as soon as next week. Jim Wong Chi-chuen, the innovative player-owner who has bankrolled Supreme’s speedy rise through the leagues, told the South China Morning Post that Silva could potentially figure against Football Club at Hammer Hill Road Recreation Ground on October 18. Should that match come too soon, the Spaniard would appear for the first time on November 7 against BC Rangers at the same worn-out venue. The owner of 125 international caps, Silva won two European Championships, in 2008 and 2012, either side of the 2010 World Cup triumph with his country. He scored in Spain’s 2012 4-0 final demolition of Italy. During 10 years with Manchester City, where he moved from Valencia in 2010, Silva won four Premier Leagues and two FA Cups, although those honours have been placed under a cloud after the English club were found guilty last week of more than 100 breaches of the league’s financial rules. Regardless, the slight midfielder was unquestionably one of the best and most creative footballers on the planet throughout his time in England, having first gained global prominence as part of an exciting Valencia team. Silva retired in summer 2023 after sustaining a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee following three seasons with Real Sociedad. Supreme have come up to the local top flight with a bang. Unveiling popular Hong Kong girl group Collar as ambassadors on the eve of the season, they attracted more than 3,000 fans to their opening fixture, a 3-1 away victory over Eastern at Mong Kok Stadium. The 4,592 crowd for their 3-0 defeat by Lee Man, also at Mong Kok, the following week represented the highest local league attendance since 6,489 watched a title decider between Kitchee and Lee Man in May 2023. Since purchasing the club three years ago, in its previous guise as Sun Source, Wong estimates that he has pumped in around HK$5 million [US$637,000] of his own cash, as Supreme climbed from the Third Division to the Premier League in successive seasons. They signed a partnership agreement this summer with First Division Sha Tin, enabling Wong, 35, to take a team from his home district into the top tier. The managing director of Live Nation Electronic Asia, Wong introduced live music performances for home matches this season, although Supreme are lodging at unprepossessing Hammer Hill, while Sha Tin Sports Ground is given a makeover. Supreme’s uplifting start to the season has given way to a reality check, and head coach Kenneth Kwok Kar-lok, hired during the close season, left after Kowloon City had inflicted their third straight defeat last month. Wong, who failed in an audacious bid to sign former Chelsea and Manchester United forward Juan Mata earlier this season, this week appointed Ballantyne, who at 41 is only one year Silva’s senior. The coach was most recently in charge of Devonport City in the second tier of Australian football. In the past week, Supreme have also confirmed the signings of versatile Spaniard Aitor Aldalur, 34, the 24-year-old Japanese midfielder Seito Takatori from Eastern District, and Matheus Dantas, 28, the Brazilian centre-back who was a cornerstone of Kitchee’s championship-winning campaign last season.

title: Like father, like son: Chinese duo build mini national engineering marvels in home lab
description: Beyond science education, Duan senior instils patriotism in his son, hoping he grows into ‘a useful person for the country and society’.
content: A Chinese father-and-son duo established a home laboratory to create miniature models of China’s significant national strategic hardware, captivating many online with their skill and passion. Duan Yanjuan, a 13-year-old second-year junior secondary school student in Shanghai, has already replicated turbojet engines, pulse detonation engines, and an electromagnetic aircraft launch system, with assistance from his father, Duan Changzhi. The inspiration for replicating the electromagnetic aircraft launch system stemmed from news coverage of the Chinese aircraft carrier Fujian’s sea trial in 2024. He was thrilled to witness the system used by the advanced carrier. For both him and his father, crafting models from scratch served as an educational experience to understand how the system functions. It took the duo a year to successfully replicate the system, composed of an accelerating mechanism powered by 100 electromagnetic coils and a power recycling system designed to recover surplus electricity. They revealed that their next project would involve replicating a turbofan engine. Their goal is to create a miniature replica of one significant piece of Chinese national strategic machinery each year. Both Duan senior and his wife fully support their son’s hobby. They allocated a 10-square-metre space in their 63-square-metre flat as their home laboratory, where various replicas have been crafted over the past few years. Moreover, Duan senior has been guiding his son in scientific experiments since he was just three years old. Graduating with degrees in communication engineering and law from the prestigious Tongji University, Duan senior noted that he had to acquire substantial knowledge in physics and aerodynamics to understand the functioning of engines and systems. The family has also invested 200,000 yuan (US$30,000) in materials and equipment, including a 280mm aperture planetary telescope and a solar telescope, to inspire Duan junior’s interest in the universe. Additionally, the family hosts three open days each year to showcase their creations, welcoming over 40 neighbouring families to their home lab. Duan junior introduces their replicas and the operating principles behind those systems to his peers and guides other children in conducting scientific experiments. He also occasionally shares videos online where he presents their projects. One video of him explaining a turbojet garnered 90,000 likes and 10,000 comments. Despite dedicating significant time to their scientific endeavours, Duan junior’s school, Shanghai Jincai North Secondary School, is supportive as it prioritises STEM education and encourages students to be curious and experimental. In addition to scientific education, Duan senior consistently teaches his son about patriotism, hoping he becomes “a useful person for the country and society.” Duan junior expressed his ambition to study national defence science and technology at a military academy in the future. “Children’s interests and enthusiasm should be cherished and supported, as they can influence them for life,” commented one online observer. “I can already see a future scientist in him. Keep up the great work!” praised another.

title: Hong Kong’s third-quarter GDP grows, but external risks persist: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief says economy supported by strong exports and tourism traffic, as lawmakers debate city’s five-year plan and policy address.
content: Hong Kong’s economy continued to expand in the third quarter of this year, driven by strong exports and tourism, the finance chief has said, while warning of risks including the Middle East war and global inflation. Addressing lawmakers during a debate on the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy blueprint on Wednesday, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also reiterated that he was confident the economy would grow by between 3.5 per cent and 4.5 per cent this year. He noted that gross domestic product grew by 5.1 per cent in the first six months, the strongest half-year performance in nearly five years. “Recent figures show that Hong Kong’s economy continued to expand in the third quarter of this year,” he said. While confident growth would hit its full-year target, the government would continue to monitor potential risks, the minister added. “Of course, unfavourable external factors persist: volatile situations in the Middle East may spill over into energy markets and global inflation,” Chan said. “We will also closely monitor inflation trends in major economies, the policy directions of major central banks, as well as the risks arising from trade protectionism and the global artificial intelligence boom.” Chan noted that the value of merchandise exports surged by 52 per cent year on year in July and August, extending a run of double-digit growth to 19 months. Visitor arrivals continued to rise, with preliminary figures showing a 9 per cent year-on-year increase in the third quarter, bringing the total for the first nine months to about 41 million, he added. Chan also highlighted strong stock trading activity and an active initial public offering, noting that funds raised exceeded HK$388 billion (US$49.4 billion) in the first nine months, surpassing last year’s total. He said the economy’s momentum had been hard-won and Hong Kong should stay focused on high-quality development in its next phase. The legislature began a three-day debate on the two policy documents on Wednesday, with the first session focusing on the economy, finance, aviation, logistics and trade. Chan’s remarks followed calls from lawmakers for the government to strengthen Hong Kong’s roles as a global offshore renminbi powerhouse, gold trading centre and aviation hub. Finance sector lawmaker Ronick Chan Chun-ying said he expected the Northern Metropolis to drive wider use of offshore renminbi, citing growing demand for green infrastructure and financing for innovation and technology (IT). He urged the government to introduce more offshore renminbi products, such as dual-currency cross-border bonds with Shenzhen, and support high-quality IT companies in issuing renminbi bonds. These measures could attract investment to the megaproject while advancing Hong Kong’s development as an offshore renminbi centre, he said. As the government sought to establish Hong Kong as an international gold trading centre, Chan suggested approaching the People’s Bank of China and the central banks of India and Southeast Asian countries about storing their reserves in the city. Lawmaker Jonathan Stuart Lamport, who represents the business sector, called for greater support to help large enterprises establish a presence in the Northern Metropolis and expand its trade networks. Such efforts would give the megaproject a clearer direction and boost overseas investors’ confidence, he said. He also proposed building an exhibition and convention centre in the new development. Legislator Kenneth Fok Kai-kong said Hong Kong’s airport had fallen behind rivals such as Singapore and Dubai in the race to become a major air transit hub. He urged the government to consider following Singapore’s example by adopting an open-skies policy of deregulation to secure more routes. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu last month unveiled the annual policy address alongside the five-year plan, which aims to align Hong Kong’s development with the national development strategy. The two blueprints set out initiatives to accelerate the Northern Metropolis megaproject and strengthen the city’s position in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology.

title: Despite rising yields and political gridlock, France not facing a debt crisis: analysts
description: Experts are urging calm amid surging borrowing costs, though they cite ongoing risks.
content: Despite the recent surge in French borrowing costs that pushed the country’s 10-year bond yield spread with Germany to a level unseen since the euro zone crisis, analysts are urging calm, saying France is not facing a debt crisis but cautioning that future uncertainties remain. “The short answer is no, this is not a debt crisis,” said Stephane Colliac, senior economist at BNP Paribas. France’s effective interest rate is lower than the rising market yields, at slightly above 2 per cent, around the same level as that of the Netherlands, Colliac said, adding that France has faced the same inflation as most advanced economies due to conflicts in the Middle East and higher yields. French politicians have been worrying about rising debt and a budget deficit, but cutting the deficit has proven difficult in a National Assembly where no political group wields a majority. Since late 2024, discussions over the national budget have led to the collapse of two governments. France already has the third-highest debt-to-gross-domestic-product ratio in the EU after reaching 117 per cent during this year’s first quarter, behind only Greece and Italy, according to the latest Eurostat data. It rose further to a record level of 119 per cent in September with the government struggling to bring its annual deficit down. The current crisis was triggered mainly by markets pricing the risks in French domestic politics, according to Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis. These include the government missing this year’s deficit target, no clear majority in parliament to pass next year’s budget and a presidential election in April, all amplified by higher global yields. Europe’s second-biggest economy was unlikely to drag the bloc into another Greek-style sovereign debt crisis, she said, due to the differences between the Greek and French economies. When the government announced the plan for this year, no one expected the war in Iran to break out Stephane Colliac, BNP Paribas “Greece lost market access as a small economy with a current-account crisis. France funds itself in euros, has a deep domestic savings base and sits inside the European Central Bank’s framework … The euro zone risk is spillover in spreads if the budget fails, not a Greek-style rescue,” Garcia-Herrero said. A passed budget for 2027, even a modest one, would help remove a lot of the premium from French yields, she added. Deutsche Bank’s global head of macro research Jim Reid wrote in a note on Monday that the markets might have “already overshot.” The problem for Paris was its political stalemate, Colliac said. With no clear majority in parliament, he added, it would be difficult for the government to pass a budget that made tough cuts and adhered strictly to its plan to bring the deficit down to 3 per cent. Global uncertainties would also impact its execution. “When the government announced the plan for this year, no one expected the war in Iran to break out,” he said. Analysts also said the debt issue was unlikely to have a major impact on the trade conflict front with China. France was more vulnerable to interest rate shocks due to its high debt level, but less so to trade shocks, since France’s exports lay in high-value-added sectors such as luxury and aeronautics, according to Colliac. France running a larger deficit would not change the tools that matter most in practice, such as EU trade defence, regulation and procurement, said Garcia-Herrero. She cautioned that higher interest costs and a tight budget left less room for subsidies and a government tied up in a budget vote was less free to open a second, expensive area of policy action.

title: Meet Heidi Klum’s youngest daughter, Lou Samuel, who turned heads at Paris Fashion Week
description: The supermodel’s youngest child with ex-husband Seal recently made her first fashion week appearance at the Vivienne Westwood SS27 show.
content: Paris Fashion Week is easily one of the most highly anticipated fashion events of the year, but for Heidi Klum’s youngest child, daughter Lou Sulola Samuel, the trip to the French capital was an “early birthday present”, the 53-year-old supermodel told Vogue. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Heidi Klum (@heidiklum) Lou, whom Klum shares with her ex-husband, musician Seal, turned heads at the Vivienne Westwood spring/summer 2027 show on October 3, days ahead of her 17th birthday on October 9. It was Lou’s first fashion week outing, but she confidently posed alongside her mother and even attended Business of Fashion’s BoF500 Gala with her. “To be honest, I’m totally nervous because it’s my first time,” she admitted to Vogue. So, what else do we know about Lou Sulola Samuel? She has 3 siblings Lou Sulola Samuel was born on October 9, 2009, in Los Angeles. Her eldest sibling is 22-year-old Leni Olumi Klum, whose father is the supermodel’s ex, Flavio Briatore. Seal adopted Leni when she was five. Lou has two brothers: Henry Günther Ademola Dashtu Samuel, 21, and Johan Riley Fyodor Taiwo Samuel, 19. Leni and Henry are models, while Johan is an artist, per People. When asked about advice from her siblings, Lou told Vogue, “I don’t really get any advice from my siblings, but by watching what they do and seeing that they’re succeeding – and we all grew up the same way – that gives me so much confidence.” She is close with her parents Seal has doted on Lou since she was born. In a statement announcing her birth, he wrote, “From the moment she looked into both of our eyes, it was endless love at first sight.” Lou shares her mother’s love for Halloween and was even spotted at her annual party last year. “If anyone has the major block about dressing up and that stuff, it would be my Lou,” Klum told People. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Heidi Klum (@heidiklum) In 2024, the teenager stepped out with her father and siblings for the Los Angeles premiere of The Book of Clarence (2023), which is directed by her uncle, Seal’s brother, Jeymes Samuel. Lou is also close to Heidi’s current husband, Tom Kaulitz, who calls himself an “extra dad” to her children, per People. What has she said about having famous parents? Speaking to Vogue, Lou revealed that being in the spotlight was “part of life” for the Samuel siblings, but she is now ready to carve her own path. “Now that I’m actually going to a real fashion event and experiencing high fashion first-hand, I can somehow express myself more and officially show who I am, instead of just walking around and being photographed,” she mused, emphasising that this step “really means a lot to me”.

title: Kagan, Soai win Nobel Chemistry Prize for solving chemical asymmetry puzzle
description: The scientists were honoured for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
content: Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a long-standing riddle of asymmetric “mirror image” molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing, the award-giving body said on Wednesday. Soai, 76, is Japanese, and Kagan, 95, is French, and their work built on a discovery by the 19th century French chemist Louis Pasteur. “This is the most exciting day in my life, I am very glad to share this prize with professor Henri Kagan,” Soai said, speaking by phone to the Nobel Prize press conference, adding ‌he had been out shopping when receiving the news. The Nobel committee was still trying to contact Kagan, the third-oldest person to be awarded a Nobel Prize, to inform him. French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated the laureates on X, calling it an immense honour for the country. “A recognition suited to a lifetime of research,” he said. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke by phone to Soai on Wednesday, saying that she was “proud” of his achievement, Kyodo reported. Kagan’s work has long been seen as influential on the field and the then French research minister complained to the Nobel Foundation in 2001 when Kagan was left out that year. The prize instead went to two American and one Japanese scientists for work in the same field. The chemistry Nobel, always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, followed those for medicine and physics announced on Monday and Tuesday. Many of the molecules essential to life exist in two forms that ⁠are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands. Yet living organisms almost exclusively use only one version, a phenomenon known as “homochirality” – from the Greek word for hand – that has puzzled chemists for more than a ‌century. This year’s prize was awarded for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favour a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals. “The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need ‌methods for selectively preparing them,” said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry. “In developing such methods the findings of this year’s laureates are important. They provided powerful ⁠tools for that,” he said. The first link in the chain in solving the problem was work by Pasteur, who died a few years before the Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901. He was looking at tartaric acid, important in the production of wine, and noticed that bacteria only ferment one of ‌the two forms of tartaric acid – that which is naturally found in grapes. With the other there is no fermentation. That proved that some substances occur in two forms and that they have different properties, sometimes very damaging to health. How to create the right form of a chiral ‌substance was ‌a problem not solved until Kagan and Soai were able to produce asymmetric reactions, creating an excess of one form. The importance of the work is illustrated by the case of the thalidomide scandal in the early 1960s, ‌when thousands of children were affected by birth defects caused by a sedative, thalidomide. When researchers analysed what had happened, they realised that it was the active substance’s mirror image that caused the harm. Established ⁠in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars. Nobel, a chemist ⁠by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank. Sometimes overshadowed by more famous laureates in the fields of physics, literature and peace, the chemistry awards have still recognised many influential discoveries such as nuclear fission and genetic sequencing techniques. Last year’s chemistry award went to scientists ‌Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for the development ‌of so-called metal-organic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of fresh water. The laureates will receive their medals from Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. The awards are followed by a lavish banquet at Stockholm City Hall. They also share 12 million Swedish crowns (US$1.2 million), as well as the fame of winning arguably the world’s most prestigious science award. The peace prize, the only Nobel not presented in Sweden, is awarded separately in Oslo.

title: South Korea signals military exemption cuts for athletes after Asian Games backlash
description: Celebrations by some of country’s gold medal-winning football players has sparked calls for change to rule that rewarded success at Games.
content: The reward of a military service exemption for gold medal-winning South Korean athletes could be abolished or reduced in future after public backlash to some controversial comments from winners at the Asian Games. Three players from the men’s football team came under fire for comments following South Korea’s 1-0 win over Japan in the Asian Games final last weekend in Japan. All three apologised but a broader debate had already reignited over whether athletes should receive special treatment for sporting achievements, particularly as ordinary citizens – and even members of BTS, the globally famous K-pop group – had to complete their mandatory service. Criticism intensified on Tuesday and, on Wednesday, Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Choi Hwi-young told the National Assembly’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Committee that the alternative military service exemption system for artists and athletes “will inevitably have to be scaled back.” “It is true that the system has contributed to helping outstanding artists and athletes maintain and develop their abilities,” Cho said. “However, the values attached to fairness and public perceptions of military service have changed. I agree that the system should be comprehensively reviewed once again.” Most South Korean men must start 18 to 21 months of military service by the age of 28. Since 1973, however, Olympic medallists and Asian Games gold medallists have been able to replace the full term with a supplementary service which consists of three weeks of basic training. Three of the soccer players, including Yang Min-hyuk, who created the winning goal against Japan, made comments that were viewed as insensitive. “The medal and winning the championship weren’t important. I played the game with only one thing in mind – the reward of a military-service exemption,” said Yang, who joined Tottenham Hotspur in 2025 and is currently on loan at Belgian club Westerlo. Newcastle United midfielder Park Seung-soo posted a photo on social media showing him wearing a cap associated with soldiers who have completed their service. In a post-match interview, captain Lee Gi-hyuk held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military.” A number of politicians, including Ahn Cheol-soo of the People Power Party, said it was time to change. “Some players’ remarks after the match were outrageous,” Ahn posted on social media. “Even the captain bragged about not having to serve in the military. Are all the young people who enlist every year fools?” Former lawmaker Yoo Seong-min said the flippant comments had provoked resentment and asked: “Is it really fair that BTS has to serve in the military while Asian Games gold medallists are exempt?” In a Korea Herald editorial Tuesday, the newspaper declared that the practice was outdated. “South Korea now stands shoulder to shoulder with the world’s leading nations,” the newspaper said. “The days when finishing first in Asia could meaningfully enhance the country’s national prestige are long gone. It is time to reconsider.” That was the message from Defence Ministry spokeswoman Chung Binna during a press briefing in Seoul. “Ultimately, we have plans to cut back or scrap the supplementary service, including one designed for artists and athletes,” Chung said. The football players were among many winners from the Asian Games who qualified for the military exemption. Golfer Tom Kim won the men’s singles on Saturday after flying across the Pacific when the Presidents Cup competition ended so he could compete in Japan. Asked about the military exemption, he took the gold-medal approach. “I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” he said. Sixteen South Korean baseball players are also exempt after defeating Japan 3-1 in the Asian Games final. So are three South Koreans who won gold in esports, an event at the Asian Games.

title: Ex-Buddhist monk who founded Thai Aids hospice convicted of embezzlement
description: Alongkot Poonmook, who was forced to leave the monkhood last year after he was arrested, has been sentenced to 50 years in prison.
content: A former Buddhist monk in Thailand was convicted on Wednesday of misusing donations to a highly praised hospice he established for people with HIV/Aids and given the maximum term of 50 years in prison. Alongkot Poonmook, formerly known as Phra Ratcha Wisutthiprachanat, was forced to leave the monkhood after he was arrested last year along with an associate, Seksan Sapsubbsakul, who served as a fundraiser for the project. The Central Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct Cases found both men guilty on multiple counts of embezzlement and money laundering. Some Buddhist temples in Thailand are extremely wealthy because worshippers donate large amounts as a way of making religious merit, and the country has seen cases of senior monks being accused of misappropriating temple funds. The case has drawn widespread attention since questions about the handling of funds for the hospice emerged online and prompted an investigation. The court sentenced Alongkot to a cumulative 742 years in prison, while Seksan received more than 386 years, but those sentences were automatically reduced to the legal maximum of 50 years.
