The men were also ordered to return more than 300 million baht (about US$9 million) to the hospice at Wat Phra Bat Namphu temple in the central province of Lopburi, where Alongkot had served as abbot. The temple has long been a revered institution in Thailand, where most of the population are Buddhist, but its image has been dented by the financial scandal. Alongkot’s hospice was considered a pioneering humanitarian project when it was established in 1992, but it became less relevant after the development and distribution of antiretroviral drugs to treat HIV. Alongkot later expanded the hospice to offer treatment to people suffering from other serious ailments. The temple also runs various charities providing funding for the education of underprivileged children.

title: Nasa releases striking image of dawn on Mars
description: Curiosity rover captures scene an hour after sunrise while climbing Mount Sharp in Gale Crater.
content: Nasa has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth’s planetary neighbour. Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, ‌a 5km-tall (3-mile-tall) mountain rising from the crater floor. The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover’s Mastcam camera about an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved cliffs in the distance. “The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far. We think it once was windblown sediment, maybe sand or maybe even ash that blew into the crater from nearby volcanic activity. After the sediment ⁠hardened into rock, aeons of wind carved up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs,” said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of Nasa’s Jet Propulsion ‌Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist. The yardang layer most likely formed about 3 billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16km across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp. “However, the yardang layer doesn’t appear to be part of the continuous stack ⁠of layers that make ⁠up the layer-cake of Mount Sharp. It was added on a little later. It’s above what geologists call an unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before ‌new layers were deposited on top,” Vasavada said. The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of 1km in elevation, the most ever climbed on ‌Mars, according ‌to Nasa. Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a period of the planet’s geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have ‌learned more about bodies of water – lakes and streams – that long ago covered this region, at a time when Mars was wetter and warmer ⁠than the cold and desolate place it is today. Vasavada said Nasa hopes Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at ⁠which time it will use its instruments to scrutinise the geology there. Curiosity has been studying the geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harbouring microbial life. It is one of two Nasa rovers ‌operating on Mars. The Perseverance rover is ‌currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere. Curiosity’s new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly. “This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky. But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It’s like Earth, but it’s definitely Mars,” Vasavada said.

title: Why Morgan Stanley sees more upside in Hong Kong offices than New York towers
description: Improving rents and vacancy rates in Central may support stronger returns for Hong Kong landlords, US bank says.
content: Higher interest rates have weighed on property markets in both Hong Kong and New York, but Morgan Stanley sees greater upside potential in the Asian financial hub – particularly the office segment – in the months ahead, according to its latest report. The US investment bank highlighted the similarities between two of the world’s leading financial centres, pointing out that Hong Kong’s monetary policy moved in lockstep with the US Federal Reserve, while both cities faced limited land supply, expensive housing and office demand that was closely tied to the finance sector. “Higher rates transmit differently into these two cities,” said a team of authors led by Praveen Choudhary, head of Hong Kong and India property research at Morgan Stanley. “Scarcity matters more than rates. We prefer Hong Kong landlords over New York City office owners or Hong Kong developers.” The office cycle had turned in both cities after years of elevated vacancy rates following the Covid-19 pandemic, the report said. Recovery was concentrated in the best locations, it added. The vacancy rate in Manhattan’s class A office market fell 2.1 percentage points year on year to 10.6 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, bringing leasing back to pre-pandemic levels, while rents rose 4.3 per cent, Morgan Stanley said. Manhattan’s office capitalisation rate stood at about 8.5 per cent in the second quarter of the year, near the upper end of the range seen since 2003. In Hong Kong’s overall prime office market, the vacancy rate dropped to 12.5 per cent in August from 13.5 per cent a year earlier. Central led the recovery, with rents rising 7.3 per cent as vacancy declined to 7.8 per cent from 11.2 per cent. Capital values, however, remained 50 per cent below their peak levels. “The more important similarity is within each city,” the report said. “Manhattan’s strongest submarkets are already at roughly 5 to 10 per cent vacancy, while weaker areas remain in the mid- to high teens.” It added that Hong Kong showed the same pattern. “Central is tightening first, while Kowloon East remains materially oversupplied,” the report said. “We therefore think location and building quality matter more than the headline vacancy rate.” Morgan Stanley said it expected Hong Kong’s office property cycle to follow a path similar to New York’s. “Operating fundamentals are recovering faster than asset values in both cities,” the report said. “We think this set-up is particularly relevant for Hong Kong landlords with exposure to prime office.”

title: How closer China-US ties – and more Xi-Trump summits – could work in Iran’s favour
description: Better links between Beijing and Washington offer more opportunities than threats, Iranian researcher says.
content: China and the US – Iran’s key partner and its chief adversary – found firmer common ground on Tehran at the Washington summit last month, and further head-of-state diplomacy could work in Iran’s favour, according to analysts. Iran was on the agenda when the presidents of the United States and China met in Beijing in May and again in Washington in September. There was no direct reference to Tehran in Beijing’s statement after the May summit, but following the September meeting China was more specific, saying it and the US agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment against developing nuclear weapons. In an eight-point consensus, the two powers also agreed that no country or organisation should impose tolls on international waterways, according to the Chinese foreign ministry. Chinese state news agency Xinhua also reported that Xi Jinping said in Washington that China hoped that the US and Iran would resolve their conflict through dialogue, prompting thanks in a social media post from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Donald Trump and Xi are expected to meet twice more this year, creating opportunities for dialogue despite Iran’s fears that it could be reduced to a bargaining chip in great-power competition, observers say. Niu Xinchun, director of the China-Arab Research Institute at Ningxia University, said the shift in China’s statements between the two summits showed that Beijing and Washington had “built greater alignment on Iran than before”. “This demonstrates that exchanges between the two nations are increasing and their consensus is expanding,” he said. A more stable US-China relationship was “undeniably beneficial” for Iran, because it gave Tehran an additional and “potentially far more effective” channel to communicate with and influence Washington, Niu said. Iran has relied on regional powers such as Pakistan and Qatar to communicate with the US. Russia had also offered to mediate, but its strained ties with Washington made it a poor fit for an effective diplomatic bridge, Niu said. “On the flip side, Iran harbours a concern typical of smaller powers – the fear of ultimately being used as a bargaining chip in major-power dealings,” he said, adding this was why Tehran sent its top diplomat to Beijing for talks just days ahead of Xi’s US trip. During the discussions with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi reaffirmed Beijing’s support for Tehran, called for a political resolution with Washington and warned against regional tensions spilling over into Yemen. Araghchi also visited Beijing in May shortly before Trump’s state visit to China. Iran harbours a concern typical of smaller powers – the fear of ultimately being used as a bargaining chip in major-power dealings Niu Xinchun, Ningxia University Xi and Trump are expected to meet twice more this year – once at Apec in Shenzhen in November and again at the G20 in Miami in December. With the Middle East conflict already in its seventh month and no end in sight, it is likely to be a recurring topic between Xi and Trump. Ali Salehian, a senior researcher at the Tehran-based Governance and Policy Think Tank, said Iran did not need to panic over closer US-China engagement, citing the consistency of Beijing’s policy on the Middle East and Tehran’s resilience to withstand political shifts. Salehian also saw “more opportunity than threat” for Iran in improved US-China diplomatic ties. “We see opportunities – similar to the mediation role China played between Iran and Saudi Arabia,” he said. Salehian said Tehran had sought to deepen strategic ties with Beijing, a position not likely to change in the near future. Beijing could also become an economic “anchor of stability” for the Middle East but it needed to go beyond its “wait-and-see” approach by being proactive in regional affairs and translate ideals such as “multipolarity” and “Global South solidarity” into action. Jesse Marks, founder of Rihla Research and Advisory, a Washington-based consultancy focused on the Middle East, said Iranian authorities would be sceptical of improved Sino-American ties but there was confidence in Tehran that “Beijing will not abandon them politically”. He noted that there was a fundamental internal clash between Iran’s diplomatic class and the country’s most powerful military branch, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “Both sides understand that China is unlikely to help the Trump administration end the war, but the bigger issue is the internal struggle for identifying a clear, united Iranian state position on engagement with the US,” Marks said. Diplomatic efforts between Iran and the US have stalled since Trump rejected an Iranian proposal – conveyed through Qatar – to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict. In addition, Washington is reportedly preparing to send a third aircraft carrier to the region and Trump has threatened to resume military action after the midterm elections in November. In Tehran, Iran’s top diplomat has said the country is “ready for real diplomacy” but would remain steadfast even in an “apocalyptic war”. According to Marks, Beijing had the “legitimacy and economic weight” crucial for Iran’s post-war reconstruction and global reintegration, a role that other powers, like Russia, could not easily replicate. However, Marks said, while warmer ties between Xi and Trump could improve coordination on Iran’s nuclear programme, this was highly unlikely to fundamentally change regional realities as China was “not a major player in Middle East security”. “Iranian rigidity towards a ceasefire negotiation comes at the expense of Chinese energy interests in Hormuz. So, Chinese leaders have to balance how it encourages Iran back to the negotiating table without undermining their position once at the table.” Jodie Wen, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy who specialises in the Middle East, said China’s cautious approach to the region avoided US-style heavy-handed intervention and was a conscious strategic choice rather than a reflection of limited capability. She said China and the US remained the decisive players on the Iran issue, as both European and regional actors had limited leverage and capacity. “The significance of the US-China summit lies in the positive signal it sends – namely, that when Washington and Beijing build a foundation of strategic stability, regional tensions can begin to ease.”

title: Opinion | US risks ceding AI governance leadership to China and the EU
description: The voluntary agreement involving US tech companies that Trump announced rests largely on self-policing, in contrast to the approach taken by Brussels and Beijing.
content: Standing alongside prominent technology executives, US President Donald Trump announced a voluntary agreement under which major artificial intelligence (AI) companies will use internal controls and monitoring, outside audits and board oversight to manage risks. The White House calls the commitments “morally binding”, but the accord does not create a comparable system of legal enforcement. The administration’s logic is understandable. AI is becoming a source of economic and military power, and Washington does not want regulation to slow American companies while China races ahead. But what happens when the country developing many of the world’s most powerful AI systems tells the rest of the world that the companies building them should largely police themselves? That question cannot be confined to Washington. A model may be developed in California, trained on American computing infrastructure, incorporated into a product sold in Europe and eventually used in Asia or Africa. Its consequences do not stop at the boundary of the country where it was developed. Europe has taken a different approach. The European Union’s AI Act imposes binding obligations on providers of general-purpose AI models, with additional requirements for systems considered to pose systemic risk. Meanwhile, China is combining domestic regulation with an active effort to influence the international discussion. The Chinese government has been explicit about that effort. Its 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan calls for international cooperation, capacity building and a more inclusive framework for AI governance. In July 2025, Beijing also proposed the World AI Cooperation Organisation and said the United Nations should remain the principal channel for global AI governance. That organisation moved from proposal to reality in July 2026, when 29 countries signed the agreement establishing it in Shanghai. My recent work has led me to conclude that China increasingly sees international scientific engagement, standards and networks as part of its broader technological strategy. Beijing is trying to combine greater technological self-reliance with a more expansive role in global scientific and technological affairs. Technological leadership and institutional leadership are not the same thing. The United States can remain ahead in important areas of AI and still lose influence over the rules that govern the technology. If Washington’s principal answer is that frontier AI companies should police themselves, other governments will take notice. Some may adopt similar arrangements. Others will conclude that systems with consequences across national borders cannot be left primarily to corporate judgment. The likely result is a patchwork of rules: American companies operating under a voluntary US framework, European users facing detailed legal requirements, and governments elsewhere developing their own approaches. Developing countries have a particular stake in this debate. Many want the economic benefits of AI without becoming permanent consumers of technologies whose standards are established elsewhere. China has understood this concern and has made AI capacity building and cooperation with the Global South part of its international message. Its September 2025 AI+ International Cooperation Initiative calls for policy exchange, practical cooperation and broader access to the benefits of AI. Washington should recognise the appeal of that message in countries seeking a larger voice in setting technological rules. Moreover, US-China competition in AI could become a security dilemma. Neither government has to want an arms race for competitive pressures to produce something resembling one. That is why communication between Washington and Beijing matters. The two governments do not need to settle their larger differences before discussing practical questions: how should dangerous model capabilities be tested? What information should be shared after a serious AI incident? How should cybersecurity risks be handled? When should military applications require additional safeguards? Caroline Wagner and I have argued for “smart openness”: maintaining useful channels of US-China scientific engagement while applying appropriate security safeguards. Earlier work with Richard Applebaum made the case for continued engagement to preserve US visibility in China’s rapidly changing research system. None of this requires a single global AI regulator. A more practical objective would be narrower: common terminology for serious risks, broadly comparable testing procedures, mechanisms for reporting major incidents, cooperation on cybersecurity and reliable channels through which governments can communicate when an AI-related event crosses borders. The United Nations is beginning to build some of that capacity. In February, the General Assembly appointed 40 members to an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, intended to provide independent assessments of the technology’s opportunities, risks and impacts. The issue is not whether the US should copy Europe’s AI Act or China’s governance model. It is whether Washington intends to help shape international rules for a technology in which American companies and research institutions have enormous influence. If Washington leaves the international governance question largely unresolved, Europe will continue to regulate, China will continue promoting its own ideas, and developing countries will have to navigate between them. American technological leadership once gave the US an extraordinary voice in shaping international rules. AI offers Washington another opportunity. The choice is whether to use that influence – or allow the rules to emerge piecemeal from competing governments, companies and international institutions. The answer will shape not only America’s AI industry, but the international technological order around it.

title: ‘Stylish’ Italian, ‘iconic’ Indian, Xinjiang: a French chef’s Hong Kong restaurant picks
description: Guillaume Sejourne of Le Colvert shares where he eats steak and regional Chinese lamb dishes, and an Indian spot he keeps returning to.
content: Guillaume Sejourne is the head chef and founder of Le Colvert, a restaurant in Sai Ying Pun, Hong Kong, specialising in French pressed duck. He spoke to Andrew Sun. I grew up in the French countryside in Soissons, near Paris. My earliest culinary memories are rushing from school to my grandma’s house to eat meat with some delicious vegetables from her garden. She would always prepare extra portions to feed the neighbourhood cats. I have now been in Hong Kong for more than 12 years and love it more and more. It has such a large variety of cuisine. Everyone can find something to their taste. I have done a bit of exploring, and I think Ba Yi (43 Water Street, Sai Ying Pun. Tel: 2484 9981) is one of the best Chinese restaurants for Xinjiang cuisine. I love its lamb leg dishes, flavourful soups and bao. Jimmy’s Kitchen (M/F, Pedder Building, 12 Pedder Street, Central. Tel: 2526 5293) is another long-standing institution that reopened in 2024. It is well known for classics such as the baked Alaska, which has inspired us a bit in making our own flambé desserts. When it comes to guests visiting Hong Kong, BluHouse (G/F, Rosewood Hong Kong, Victoria Dockside, 18 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 3891 8732) is definitely on my list. The rotisserie theme, the fresh pasta and the delicious tiramisu, paired with the stylish environment of the Rosewood Hong Kong, make it a culinary destination. La Vache! (various locations including 48 Peel Street, SoHo. Tel: 2880 0248) is a place to consider for a celebration. The staff are just so good at things like celebrating a special event or singing a birthday song for you or your friend. Ping Pong 129 (G/F, Nam Cheong House, 129-135 Second Street, Sai Ying Pun. Tel: 9158 1584) is a really cool bar. It is a place I like to go with the team once in a while. It specialises in gin, serving all sorts of cocktails with the spirit as a base. The retro decor and atmosphere make it a good option for a quick debrief after a long shift. Gaylord Indian Restaurant (5/F, Prince Tower, 12A Peking Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2376 1001) has been in Tsim Sha Tsui for ages. I was invited there once many years ago, and since then I go at least once a year. It is such an iconic location for Indian cuisine. It reminds me of the old days of Hong Kong. The naan, tandoori and curries are something to revisit regularly. Overseas, my favourite culinary destination remains Paris, where there is good food everywhere. I recently discovered Le Train Bleu (Place Louis Armand, Gare de Lyon, Paris. Tel: +33 1 43 43 09 06). The name refers to the restaurant’s location in the Gare de Lyon. It is like a museum stuck in the old days where garçons de salle (waiters) would flambé dishes tableside, like a whole lamb leg or crepes Suzette. It really is my favourite place in the world, and Le Colvert is partly inspired by this amazing vibe.

title: Israel continues demolishing buildings in Gaza a year after ceasefire
description: With almost the entire population homeless, displaced Palestinians face an unrecognisable landscape.
content: It’s perhaps the most dramatic wound inflicted on the Gaza Strip by Israel’s military campaign over the past three years: the city of Rafah, once home to a quarter million people, has been erased. Satellite imagery shows the Israeli military has systematically razed the southern city and other towns and districts to the ground and in some places ploughed away the rubble. Demolition, using bulldozers and explosives, has continued unabated since the Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal reached a year ago, as the military solidifies its hold over the around 60 per cent of the territory that it still controls. Gaza’s mangled landscape is just one of the wounds on top of wounds that the enclave’s 2 million Palestinians have endured since Israel launched its campaign to destroy Hamas after the militants’ October 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel. More than one out of every 10 people from Gaza’s pre-war population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire. While nearly every family mourns dead or cares for wounded, most also had to move multiple times to escape fighting and Israeli evacuation orders. With almost the entire population homeless, the coastal territory is now effectively one of the world’s most populated tent cities. Ramshackle canvas and nylon shelters blanket beaches and former agricultural lands and fill empty lots. Little is likely to change for the foreseeable future. While the ceasefire deal stopped the offensives and heaviest bombardment, Israel hits tents, cars and buildings almost daily in strikes that it says target Hamas members – but that regularly kill women, children and other family members. People no longer have to flee from place to place, but few can rebuild homes because Israel bars most construction material from entering Gaza. The ceasefire agreement’s plan for the large-scale reconstruction of Gaza has never got off the ground because Israel and Hamas have failed to reach a deal on disarming the militant group. Gaza’s population is squeezed into about 40 per cent of the tiny territory, and Israel’s military controls the rest. Satellite imagery by Planet Labs PBC shows that the vast majority of buildings in the Israel-held part have been bulldozed or exploded down to piles of rubble, much of it after major fighting ended a year ago. The Israeli military says it demolishes buildings to prevent their use by Hamas militants or to destroy the group’s tunnel networks. But a UN-appointed expert said in a February report that the scale of destruction of civilian housing and infrastructure in Gaza “is unprecedented even by the terrible standards of modern warfare since the 20th century”. The report warned that it could constitute a crime against humanity or reach the level of genocide, which under international law includes “deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction”. Israel rejects accusations of genocide, saying it targets Hamas militants and their infrastructure that are interwoven with civilian areas. The Planet Labs imagery shows at least 50 Israeli military outposts built throughout the Israeli-held part of Gaza, at least 18 of them constructed since the ceasefire began. Many have been put on top of former neighbourhoods where the rubble of demolished buildings nearby has been cleared away. Most of Rafah was razed before the ceasefire, but images show that troops continue to demolish the few remaining buildings. Several abandoned UN buildings have been spared, as well as a municipal sports field that now appears to contain a military base. A new base also stands on what was once the main intersection of the southern town of Beni Suhaila. Levelled over the past year, the town is now a wasteland intersected by a spiderweb of dirt paths that were once streets. In Jabaliya in the north, most of the al-Awda Hospital Complex was reduced to rubble in recent months, as were a number of UN-run school buildings, satellite images show. Jabaliya was once home to the Gaza Strip’s biggest refugee camp, home to some 120,000 refugees and tens of thousands of other residents in a densely built urban district. Now one of the few buildings still standing is the octagonal-shaped Indonesian Hospital, empty since troops shut it down in June 2025. The Israeli military built a new base nearby. Similarly, most of Beit Hanoun, once a town of some 70,000 people in Gaza’s far northeast corner, and Shijaiya, a Gaza City neighbourhood founded 800 years ago, are now block after block of levelled houses and residential towers. An increased flow of aid and commercial products brought Gaza back from famine that arose in some areas last year under a months-long Israeli ban on food and other goods. But most of the population remains dependent on international relief. Jobs are few, mostly connected to selling in the market. Thousands of bodies remain buried under buildings smashed by Israeli strikes. Since the ceasefire, Gaza authorities have slowly been going from site to site to try to find them.

title: Renault’s plan for Chinese EV motor assembly in small French town sparks job loss fears
description: As EU-China trade talks near, the Renault plant shows the hard reality of creating jobs in a shrinking industry, even with Chinese partners.
content: In the industrial heartland of Normandy, more than 100km (62 miles) away from Paris, lies the small town of Cleon. Home to fewer than 5,000 residents and a Renault factory, the town and its environs are a near-perfect reflection of the current state of France’s rust belt, where economic activity and jobs are dwindling – the factory’s workforce has shrunk from almost 5,000 to 3,124 in 10 years. Yet the planned arrival of an assembly line from Chinese firm Shanghai E-Drive next year, in collaboration with Renault to produce EV motors, drew a mixed reaction. While Renault hailed it as an example of the group’s dedication to the factory, some workers voiced concerns: the assembly line would create only a handful of jobs, they said, and its products could directly compete with the plant’s other wares, risking further unemployment. The politician who helped foster the deal also urged stricter made-in-France policies to encourage Chinese firms to bring more production to France to save jobs. As the EU and China head into another round of talks to address their trade imbalances, with the loss of European jobs in the automotive sector being a major concern for Brussels, the Cleon plant is a sign of the tough reality of creating employment in an industry that analysts said is bound to shrink, even with Chinese investment. This is why some argue only stricter made-in-EU rules can save what remains. “It will only create 27 jobs in total across all teams … it’s an assembly line and it works without workers; unfortunately there is no longer the need for many people,” said Will Audoux, secretary of the factory’s branch of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of the country’s largest trade union federations. Like many of the other electric motor assembly lines the workers had already seen, this one would be highly automated, they said, adding robots would be soon to arrive. The situation is further complicated by the fears of many workers that the new assembly line would be helping to make a motor that competes directly with the 6AK, which the factory manufactures from start to finish. Therefore, the arrival of Chinese motors could paradoxically be putting more jobs at risk at the factory, according to David Bellanger, chief of the factory’s CGT branch. Production of the 6AK involves seven workshops and around 350 workers – from foundry and machining to winding and assembly – while the Shanghai E-Drive model will only be assembly, with some logistics, according to Bellanger. All things considered, he said, the new line might cost more jobs at the plant than it brings. In a statement to the South China Morning Post, Renault declined to confirm the number of jobs the assembly line would bring and maintained that the two models would meet different customer needs. Alma Dufour, the local member of parliament from the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) party, helped foster the deal, even going so far as to visit the Chinese embassy and ask for help. But even she agreed this was far from enough, and certain protectionist policies needed to be put in place to incentivise Chinese firms to produce more in France. The issue, according to Dufour, was the rubric France uses to decide whether an EV qualifies for its purchase subsidy. She said it was not fine-grained enough, as the parts that make up the motor are not really taken into account. “In my view, it will depend on the regulations … if the regulations get tougher, Shanghai E-Drive will follow on component manufacturing here. I don’t see any particular obstacles for them,” Dufour said. She went to visit Shanghai E-Drive’s headquarters in China in May and met the group’s executives. “They made me understand that their strength was precisely to take advantage of tariff barriers or protectionist measures to set up early, and so benefit from the market ahead of competitors who would arrive later,” she said, adding that from the company’s point of view, France’s policy to shut out made-in-China EVs from receiving state subsidies gave the firm an edge compared with its other Chinese competitors. The problem is you have all this fixed cost, you have these fixed factories, all this tooling and all these people … you basically do not need them any more Harald Hendrikse, European head of autos research at Citi France currently uses a system that calculates the environmental score of each EV model. As it takes into account the carbon footprint of a model’s production and shipping, including where the car and its battery were made, the scoring favours cars made in Europe. Nevertheless, even with tougher made-in-Europe policies, analysts warned that the continent’s automotive industry would be likely to shrink under the transformations brought by the EV revolution. An internal combustion engine car has 3,000 parts, while an EV has fewer than 1,000 parts, reducing the need for parts and people and lowering added value across the supply chain, according to Harald Hendrikse, European head of autos research at Citi. “The problem is you have all this fixed cost, you have these fixed factories, all this tooling and all these people … you basically do not need them any more,” he said. If Europe wants to keep some level of employment in the automotive sector where jobs are bound to shrink, it needs some kind of made-in-Europe law, according to Hendrikse. For him, technology transfer was not important from a job-saving perspective, because European carmakers had access to Chinese technologies through their branches and partners in China. The point was for the EU to accept a level of inefficiency in exchange for maintaining a certain level of industrialisation in the bloc. “Either way clearly there will be fewer people employed in the industry … but the ones that we do keep, we need to keep in Europe,” he said.

title: Travellers must use authorised buses, taxis at Huanggang Port, Hong Kong authorities say
description: Residents must use licensed taxi fleets as other ride-hailing services will not be available inside boundary control area.
content: Travellers heading to and from the revamped Huanggang Port must use authorised public transport services only, including pre-booked licensed taxi fleets, as other ride-hailing services will not be available inside the boundary control area, according to the Hong Kong government. At a press conference on Wednesday, transport officials also urged travellers not to rush to use the new port in the initial phase of its operations. Ahead of the expected opening of the Huanggang Port on Monday, the Transport Department explained the public transport arrangements connecting the revamped Huanggang Port to different parts of Hong Kong. Sharing maps of the port’s Public Transport Interchange and its pickup points for franchised buses, urban and New Territories cabs, officials reminded those who wanted to book ride-hailing services to use only licensed taxi fleets. “A pre-booked fleet taxi waiting area set up inside the port building features a service station and a display panel for fleet taxi arrival information,” said Amy Tse Sen-yee, assistant commissioner for transport. While people arriving by taxi can simply get out at the public transport interchange, travellers departing the port must follow another procedure. “Passengers who have pre-booked a fleet taxi should register at the service station by showing the vehicle registration mark to the fleet’s taxi ambassadors. They will dynamically deploy taxis waiting in the public transport buffer area to the dedicated pickup area to ensure passengers can board quickly and smoothly.” According to the department’s website, there will be no areas at the new building for pre-booked cabs that are not part of a taxi fleet, in order to maintain smooth and orderly traffic flow. Ride-hailing services will not be available as the building is within a restricted area. Transport authorities did not respond directly when asked why taxi fleets were designated to provide ride-hailing services. Hong Kong has five taxi fleets with more than 2,000 vehicles in service. The fleets were introduced last year to provide premium services and address long-standing complaints about cabbies, from cherry-picking trips and overcharging passengers to a lack of electronic payment options. Tse said urban and New Territories taxis, as well as fleet taxis, must obtain a queue ticket at a public transport buffer area before proceeding to the taxi ranks to pick up passengers. The buffer area is located in the boundary control area, a two-minute drive away from the port, and public buses, minibuses, coaches and taxis must wait there during peak periods to avoid congesting the bridge leading to the new building. At the press conference, Deputy Commissioner of Transport Candy Kwok Wai-ying urged residents to use suitable checkpoints for border crossings and to avoid rushing to use Huanggang Port. She also reminded those who used the new port to avoid lingering at major interchanges and to plan sufficient time for customs procedures. “Members of the public are urged to use other land and rail border crossing points based on their needs for travelling between Shenzhen and Hong Kong and not rush to the new port for crossing the boundary,” she said. The Huanggang Port will be the city’s first checkpoint to use the “joint inspection” model for immigration clearance, with mainland Chinese and Hong Kong immigration gates located side by side across 134 channels. Travellers will need to present the travel document required for their destination and pass through a single electronic clearance machine equipped with three gates, rather than going through separate counters. After presenting their travel document, they will pass through two gates for biometric data collection and identity verification. Kwok said the new Huanggang Port public transport terminal connected to nine MTR stations and four bus interchanges to ease the pressure on other modes of transport. The port also provides more comprehensive transport facilities than other control points – including overnight buses and minibuses, as well as 24-hour cross-border buses to the city centre – to expedite passenger flow. Daytime bus routes include B10 and B11, operated by KMB, departing from Kwai Tsui Estate Public Transport Interchange and Tin Fu Bus Terminus in Tin Shui Wai, respectively. North Lantau Bus will operate route B12 from Wu Kai Sha Station Public Transport Interchange. Citybus will operate routes B13, B14 and B15 from Island Resort in Siu Sai Wan, Olympic Avenue in Kai Tak and Castle Peak Bay, respectively.

title: China’s missile lidar model; world’s most accurate atomic clock: 7 science highlights
description: From China’s higher education reform to claims surrounding BeiDou’s satellite, here are some highlights from SCMP’s recent science reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on science from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Chinese researchers say missile lidar model can spot US F-35 at up to 61.5km A computer simulation developed by Chinese researchers suggests that a missile-borne system with the latest light detection and ranging system, or lidar, could detect and track an F-35 stealth fighter at up to 61.5km (38 miles) at night. 2. ‘Everyone can attend university’: China unveils sweeping higher education reform China has unveiled an overhaul of its university system, urging institutions to develop distinct roles as demographic change, a tighter job market and industrial upgrading alter the country’s skills needs. 3. Chinese commercial reactor achieves nuclear fusion with clean hydrogen-boron fuel In a first, a Chinese company has achieved high-parameter hydrogen-boron plasma control, marking a “significant and valuable” advance in research into neutron-free magnetic confinement fusion. 4. China offers 15-year research grants to the world’s brightest young scientists China is offering the world’s brightest young scientists generous 15-year research grants for free exploration, as the country accelerates its drive to become a global science powerhouse. 5. Singapore builds world’s most accurate atomic clock, leaves US and China in dust A small Singaporean research team has beaten scientists in China and the United States to build the world’s most accurate atomic clock. 6. Claims China’s BeiDou satellite was refuelled in orbit could change space race Chinese researchers appear to have revealed a previously unknown satellite-to-satellite refuelling operation in high Earth orbit, putting the country at the forefront of a technology that could reshape the space race. 7. Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province.

title: Singapore to charge American man over perfume theft spree at Changi Airport
description: If convicted, the 47-year-old faces up to seven years’ jail, a fine or both.
content: A 47-year-old man will be charged on Thursday over a series of perfume thefts at Changi Airport, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) said on Wednesday. The thefts date back to November last year and involved almost S$1,410 (US$1,102) worth of perfume, the police said in a news release. SPF said it was alerted to the first theft on November 5, 2025, after a retail assistant discovered that a box of perfume was missing from a shop’s display shelf. Closed-circuit television footage showed that the American had stolen a box of perfume valued at S$331 from the shop in Changi Airport’s Terminal 3 transit area at about 7.38pm on November 4, 2025, SPF said. Further investigations revealed that he stole three more boxes of perfume, which were worth S$646 in total, from two shops in the Terminal 2 transit area later that day, police said. Officers from the Airport Police Division managed to identify the man, but he had already departed Singapore, they added. The man returned to Changi Airport for a connecting flight on the morning of April 24 this year. Preliminary investigations revealed that he stole two more boxes of perfume from two shops on this occasion, SPF said. The first box he stole at about 7.15am was priced at S$236.90 and the second one taken around six minutes later was valued at S$195.40, police said. The man left Singapore after the second round of alleged thefts but was arrested on September 25 while transiting through the airport again. He will be charged on Thursday with five counts of theft in dwelling. Those convicted of the offence face up to seven years’ jail, a fine or both. This story was first published by CNA

title: Asian investors turn to housing, real assets as global tension shakes market confidence
description: Advisers’ interest in real estate jumps while private credit falls amid trade friction, energy security fears and softer Chinese demand: report.
content: Amid various macro uncertainties, interest in private credit declined sharply to 48 per cent from 71 – among alternative investments – while interest in real estate jumped to 52 from 39 per cent, according to the 2026 Asia Advisor Survey released today by financial technology company iCapital. This marks a sharp decline for private credit, which was the leading area of interest among Asian advisers in 2025. In addition to real estate, advisers are also turning to other real assets, with interest almost doubling to 31 per cent. “The rotation towards real assets comes as geopolitical disruption and energy security concerns have increased focus on inflation resilience and tangible assets,” the report says. Interest in venture capital, at 39 per cent, also marked a double-digit increase. This was “consistent with a robust capital markets backdrop in Asia in 2026, particularly for AI-related portfolio companies”, according to the report. The report includes findings from 62 respondents in Hong Kong and Singapore, who work across various wealth management channels and serve a client base of at least 50 per cent individuals and families. The results come at a time of trade policy uncertainty, a Middle East energy shock, softer Chinese demand and continued uncertainty around US inflation, interest rates and the dollar. Against this backdrop, positive sentiment by Asian advisers about their local economy, the US economy and the global economy was cut roughly in half, hovering just above 40 per cent for each of them. Asia marked the steepest sentiment decline of any region surveyed. But the intent to allocate wealth in alternative investments has risen, with 28 per cent of respondents saying they plan to invest more in alternative investments over the next year, compared with only 5 per cent in last year’s survey. The rise in allocation intent against the decline in overall positive economic outlook suggests that advisers were “treating alternatives as a long-term portfolio allocation rather than responding to near-term conditions,” according to the report. Alternatives have become “structural rather than tactical allocations”, the report highlighted. Nevertheless, alternatives were not yet common among Asian clients. Of the advisers who had some clients invested in alternatives, over half said the majority – more than 90 per cent – of their clients did not. “Seven in 10 Asian advisers now use alternative investments, but the asset class reaches only a narrow share of their clients,” the report summarises. The report describes compliance and regulatory concerns as the fastest-growing challenge to incorporating alternatives in firms’ investment models, cited by 59 per cent of respondents, up from 44 per cent in 2025. The biggest challenge remains difficulty in assessing liquidity and risk exposure across asset classes, at an unchanged 62 per cent. The Asia report is part of iCapital’s second annual Global Advisor Survey, which included 870 respondents across 15 countries globally.

title: Malaysia’s Melaka sets election date as BN, PAS near alliance against Anwar
description: The November 14 contest comes close on the heels of BN’s strong wins, adding pressure on Anwar’s PH amid shifting electoral strategies.
content: Malaysia’s Melaka will hold a state election on November 14 as the Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition nears a pact with Islamist rivals, leaving Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s alliance facing another difficult contest after a string of recent defeats. The filing of nominations would begin on October 31 and early voting on November 10, Election Commission chairman Ramlan Harun said on Wednesday. A total of 687,897 registered voters are eligible to elect the state’s 28 assembly members, with 15 seats needed for a simple majority. The local legislature was dissolved on September 23. BN won 21 seats in the 2021 state election, while Pakatan Harapan (PH) secured five and opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) two. Melaka, south of Kuala Lumpur, is home to a Unesco-listed historic port whose shophouses, churches and fortifications reflect centuries of Asian trade and Portuguese and Dutch rule. BN’s potential tie-up with the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) would pile more pressure on Anwar’s PH as his federal governing partners increasingly seek electoral gains through deals with the opposition, analysts say. BN starts the Melaka campaign on a strong footing following a 48-seat landslide victory in Johor in July. It also won the Negeri Sembilan election in August alongside PN, where the two parties took 25 of 36 seats. Those successes preceded an Umno congress last month at which party president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi – who remains Anwar’s deputy prime minister – demanded an early national election. “GE16 is the decisive moment for us to reclaim the mandate to lead,” Zahid told delegates, referring to the next general election, due by early 2028. BN and PH have governed Malaysia together since the inconclusive 2022 election. However, Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, said renewing that partnership in Melaka would contradict BN’s efforts to distance itself from Anwar. “I find it personally difficult to fathom a surprise BN-PH tie-up for Melaka as BN would then have to make a U-turn in its positioning,” he told This Week in Asia. “This flip-flop political manoeuvre adds to optics risk for BN and also puts into question whether the bloc can be a sincere coalition partner for both PH and PN later on.” Partners in waiting Zahid said on Sunday that negotiations with potential partners were 95 per cent complete, with an announcement expected after the election dates were fixed. But he remained open to negotiating an electoral pact with PH, local media reported. BN has insisted on defending all 21 seats it won in 2021, a condition caretaker chief minister Ab Rauf Yusoh described as non-negotiable, according to state news agency Bernama. PH, meanwhile, has explored cooperation with Malay-based Bersatu, although its components differ over widening the alliance, with Amanah open to outside partners despite the Democratic Action Party’s opposition. Last month, Anwar confirmed discussions with Bersatu but said no decision had been made, leaving negotiations to PH’s election committee. “We should not be arrogant. If people say they are ready to discuss, then we discuss. That is how politics works,” he said, according to Bernama. “We have also discussed it with Bersatu. There is no decision yet. I leave it to the committee. I am focusing on running the country.” Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University Malaysia, said resolving seat swaps would strengthen BN and PAS, while PH was searching for a different approach after defeats in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. “If they can do that and it seems it’s close to a deal, they’re going to go into Melaka so much stronger,” Syaza said. She expected PH to struggle even with Bersatu’s support, but cautioned that agreements among leaders would count for little without committed campaign workers and supporters willing to vote for candidates from another party, particularly where BN made way for PAS. “These negotiations have always been at the leadership level. But at the end of the day, elections are about machinery and grass-roots support,” she said. Getting supporters to vote would be the main challenge, as new party alliances “might affect motivation and eventually turnout”, she added.

title: Singapore must be able to say ‘no’ to US, China to preserve trust: foreign minister
description: Vivian Balakrishnan says Singapore must maintain trust with Washington and Beijing without becoming a proxy for either.
content: Singapore occupies a “peculiarly sensitive existential point” as it seeks to retain strategic options amid a great power rivalry, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan has said, doubling down on the city state’s stance of refusing to take sides. He also warned that the global landscape would remain unsettled if China and the United States failed to address their respective domestic issues. Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit 2026 in Singapore on Wednesday, Balakrishnan identified maintaining trust with both Washington and Beijing – whose relationship was in a “difficult phase” – as a key challenge. The city state had to assure both superpowers that it would remain useful without serving as a proxy for either, he said. Balakrishnan warned that assets and investments would leave Singapore the moment it lost its ability to say no – a position which might be easier said than done. “For us, this is a peculiarly sensitive existential point. What do we have in Singapore? We’ve got a wonderful location, but everything else depends on trust,” he said. Washington was economically crucial due to its heavy investments and technology ties, Balakrishnan said. The US was Singapore’s top source of foreign direct investment inflows last year at S$35.2 billion (US$27.5 billion), according to data from Singapore’s Department of Statistics. He also acknowledged Chinese sentiment that Singapore should base its foreign policy on shared cultural ties. “My colleague in China will regularly say to me: ‘Of all people in the world, you – meaning Singapore – should understand us the best, linguistically, culturally, historically and so on and so forth.’ Actually, what he means is, you should agree with us.” Balakrishnan urged both superpowers to tackle internal challenges for the collective global good. Washington was being pulled apart by income inequality and political division, while Beijing faced an ageing population and economic imbalances, he said. China’s economy has experienced a prolonged imbalance, with resilient exports supporting industrial activity while weak consumption and investment weigh on domestic demand. “It’s not just about competition. It’s not just for contestation or rivalry, but until and unless you get a rebalancing of domestic politics, followed by a new paradigm, a new world order internationally, we are going to be in unsettled times,” he said. The countries that emerge stronger amid the erosion of global order would be those that master new technologies, such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology and energy, Balakrishnan added, calling for global regulatory frameworks in these sectors. “There are emerging threats and great potential in AI and synthetic biology … If you want to move fast, you also need to have good brakes, and you need to have international standards,” he said. While establishing global frameworks was increasingly difficult, it was still possible, Balakrishnan said. He pointed to Singapore’s consistent position that transit through international waterways was a right rather than a privilege. At the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, Balakrishnan urged global leaders to collectively reject the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea was “absolutely crucial” for Singapore, Balakrishnan said, noting that about 40 per cent of global trade traversed the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. “When we look at the Strait of Hormuz, even without taking sides, any full-frontal assault on this regime of the right of transit passage for ships and aircraft over straits used for international navigation is a full-frontal threat to our business model,” he said. In April, then Indonesian finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa floated the idea of charging vessels to cross the strait, though he later backtracked on the proposal. Asked about Singapore’s chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year, Balakrishnan said the city state was aiming for deeper integration within the bloc, alongside broader partnerships with both traditional and non-traditional allies, such as the European Union. “We want to do stuff with Africa, South America, Pacific Islands, across Canada as well – a trans-Pacific strategy,” he said. Despite regional challenges – including Myanmar’s civil war, an unresolved Thailand-Cambodia border dispute and simmering tensions in the South China Sea – Balakrishnan expressed confidence in the bloc, pointing to healthy economic growth in member states such as Vietnam and Malaysia. “If we can thread the needle, and not just for Singapore, but for Asean as a whole, I think we’ve got quite a compelling narrative and great potential for Asean,” he said. “So I’m still an advocate. I’m a believer in Asean.” Global frameworks and cooperation At a separate event later that afternoon, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam warned that the domestic economic problems facing the US and China could have wider consequences for the global economy. Speaking at the 2026 IMF Annual Meetings Curtain Raiser in Singapore, Tharman said the US needed to address its growing fiscal deficit more forthrightly, warning that government borrowing was already absorbing an “inordinate” share of global finance. He also said China’s efforts to rebalance its economy were in its own interest as well as the world’s and could help create a more stable form of economic interdependence. But both countries faced difficult adjustments, Tharman said. Raising China’s domestic consumption would be a “multi-year task” that would require measures including pension reforms and increasing the share of national income going to households. “We must understand the complexity of the task, and that adjustments will take time,” he said. “But in the meantime, find ways for the relationship in trade and investment between the major economies of the world to be put on a more stable footing.” The remarks came during a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the curtain-raiser event ahead of the IMF and World Bank Group’s annual meetings in Bangkok next week.

title: Russian strikes kill 24 across Ukraine after Zelensky warning
description: Russian missiles and drones hit residential and civilian sites in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
content: At least 24 people were killed in Russian strikes across Ukraine on Wednesday, including four young children who died when a missile slammed into a residential block in the north of the country as they slept. Windows shattered in the powerful blast in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, reducing one half of the five-storey building into a smoking pile of charred concrete and twisted metal. President Volodymyr Zelensky said three of the 18 victims of the strike were just 12 months old while another was aged eight. Seven other children were among dozens wounded and one child was among 15 rescued, he wrote on social media, accusing Russia of knowingly striking “ordinary cities, ordinary life”. “The continued use of missiles against Ukraine, against our people, our children, is an absolutely deliberate choice of terror,” he said. “We were at home, sleeping,” Olena Sayun, a 40-year-old massage therapist, said at the scene of the blast. “Our windows blew out. Thank God, we covered the child with our bodies. My husband got a few cuts on his back and I did too … The child just had a nervous breakdown, got very scared. We immediately ran to the bathroom and then, while everything in the apartment was being blown apart, we stayed in there.” “All our kids are about the same age – 10, 8, 14, 11,” she added. “They all played in our courtyard, on the playground, every single day. We knew them all very well.” The strike, which locals said happened at about 6.30am local time, came after Zelensky on Tuesday warned of a “massive” Russian attack, particularly targeting energy infrastructure. Two people were killed when missiles slammed into high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others lost their lives in Oleksandriya, he added. In the capital, Kyiv, two people died in a fire caused by a strike in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood, the city’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Kyiv has come under increased attack in recent weeks as winter approaches, with air raid sirens wailing nearly constantly to warn of incoming Russian strikes. Worried residents hunkered down for the night in subway stations overnight, hauling duffel bags, sleeping mats and blankets. “We grabbed our things and came here, we live right next door,” said Iryna Rybalchenko, who works in a bank, sitting on the platform wrapped in a dark hoodie and surrounded by bags. “The whole of Kyiv is in a state of fear. We were stuck at work today and everyone – our group chats, our bosses – were messaging us to be careful.” Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight against several regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Poltava, Ukraine’s air force said. Zelensky, who called it “one of the most vile strikes” in the nearly five-year conflict, said some were shot down but ballistic missiles were “the greatest challenge” and new air defences were essential to help Ukraine defend itself. “I don’t see any military significance in this at all,” said Yuliia Shamrai, 31, who works in online marketing and lives near the stricken building in Pryluky. Asked why they had been hit, she added: “Just to break people, the civilian population that was peacefully sleeping.” Kyiv mayor Klitschko warned last week the capital should now be on a war footing after repeated strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure. Scheduled power cuts on Tuesday plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness to ease the pressure on the battered grid, and generators cranked into life. The air force said on Wednesday morning that it had intercepted five ballistic missiles, as well as 39 cruise missiles and over 100 drones. Ukraine has been struggling to down the new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, as well as the ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept. Concern has mounted about rising civilian casualties on both sides, as Ukraine also steps up its long-range attacks on Russian targets it says are vital to its war effort. “The children were absolutely terrified. Whenever there’s heavy shelling, we try to head underground,” said Daria Medvedeva, 36. Zelensky said Ukraine’s “just responses” to Russian strikes saw it hit two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions, as well as the Black Sea.

title: Former nursing student jailed for stealing from hospital patients and colleagues
description: Hong Kong’s District Court sentenced Leung Ho-fung, 29, to two years and four months in prison after pleading guilty to 11 counts of theft.
content: A former nursing student at a leading private hospital in Hong Kong has been jailed for two years and four months for stealing cash, credit cards and a phone from patients and colleagues, causing losses of at least HK$59,000 (US$7,517). Leung Ho-fung, 29, was sentenced at the District Court on Wednesday after pleading guilty to 11 counts of theft. He admitted stealing an iPhone, HK$6,500 in cash and nine credit cards from four patients and four colleagues at Hong Kong Sanatorium and Hospital in Happy Valley between September 19 and October 23, 2024. He also used some of the stolen cards to make purchases totalling HK$52,875 at an Apple store on three occasions. In mitigation, Leung told Deputy District Judge Derek Lai Kim-wah that he was heavily in debt and needed money to get by at the time of the offences. The court heard that he had declared bankruptcy after accumulating debts of at least HK$300,000. According to court documents, Leung was on a nursing placement at the hospital and had been assigned to a ward on the 20th floor. Five patients reported losing personal belongings during their stays between September and October. Police arrested Leung after linking him to the thefts. Officers found five of the stolen credit cards in his pocket when they searched him. During a police interview, he admitted stealing items from patients’ bedside cabinets and his colleagues’ lockers in a changing room. Defence lawyer Joe Chan Wai-yin told the court that Leung’s financial difficulties were partly due to poor money management. Leung had also fallen victim to a scam and suffered a five-figure loss, Chan said. “Now he knows that he should not have done it under any circumstances. He feels stupid,” Chan said. Judge Lai said Leung had abused his position in the ward to steal items over a five-week period. With help from his relatives, Leung had paid more than HK$59,000 in compensation for the stolen items.

title: Hong Kong’s non-public schools to increase tuition fees by up to 4.75% for 2026-27
description: Education Bureau approves fee hikes amid rising costs and inflation pressures affecting private, DSS and international schools.
content:
Hong Kong’s private, semi-private and international schools in Hong Kong have been authorised to increase their tuition fees by an average of 4.75 per cent, 4.07 per cent and 4 per cent, respectively.
On Tuesday, the Education Bureau announced that as of August 31, it had received fee adjustment applications from 185 schools for the academic year 2026-27.
They comprised 49 semi-private schools under the government’s Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS), 74 private schools and 62 international ones.
One application from an international school was still being processed, the bureau said.
Tuition fees at DSS schools were set to rise by 4.07 per cent on average for the new academic year, it added.
Fees would increase by an average of 4.75 per cent at private schools and 4 per cent at international ones, according to the bureau.
Last year, DSS schools were allowed to increase fees by 4.64 per cent on average for 2025-26, and by 4.8 per cent in the year prior, the most in five years.
Private and international schools got the green light last year to raise fees by 4.62 per cent and 4.6 per cent, respectively.
According to the bureau, DSS schools must provide budgets and justifications in their applications for fee increases, and it would also examine whether the institutions had carried out consultations.
DSS schools were also required to set aside no less than 10 per cent of their total tuition revenue for fee remissions and scholarships to cater to students who could be affected by family financial difficulties, it added.
The co-educational Christian Tai Po Sam Yuk Secondary School is set to implement one of the largest fee increases for next year, raising its tuition by 25 per cent rise from HK$12,400 to HK$15,500 (US$1,580 to US$1,975) for Form One.
Elite institutions such as Diocesan Boys’ School, Heep Yunn School and St Paul’s Co-educational College applied for 4.2 per cent rises, with the new fees ranging from HK$45,585 to HK$87,800 a year for Form One.
Creative Secondary School in Tseung Kwan O applied to increase its fees from HK$96,250 to HK$99,990, a 3.9 per cent rise.
Dion Chen, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Direct Subsidy Scheme Schools Council, said every institution’s fee hike had to go through a procedure that involved consulting different stakeholders.
“The price increases require approval from the school management committee, following consultations with the parent-teacher associations, and the proposals are subject to approval from the Education Bureau,” he said.
“I believe that the increase in every school has its relevant justifications, which are accepted by the bureau.”
Chen pointed out that a reduction in government funding, pay rises for civil servants and inflation could contribute to rising school fees.
“The number of teachers at DSS schools is higher than at public schools, so the government’s subsidy might not cover the additional salary increases for their teachers,” he said.
“New measures such as promoting AI or STEAM education, smaller classes or hiring more teachers to offer a diversity of electives could also contribute to the rise in fees.”

title: Bangkok’s culinary stars fade amid rising costs, tighter budgets and fewer tourists
description: Several globally renowned restaurants like Canvas, Keller and Villa Frantzén have shut their doors, even as competition rises from Vietnam and Malaysia.
content: Earlier this year, Bangkok’s F&B scene pulled off a coup. At Asia’s 50 Best Bars awards in Macau, eight venues from Asia’s “City of Angels” crowded the list – rankings historically dominated by Hong Kong and Singapore – with four more in the 51-100 tier. The city’s restaurant honours tell a similar story – Sühring recently joined Sorn in holding three Michelin stars, and Bangkok claims nine spots on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants, more than any other city. The tourism figures are equally bullish: Bangkok again ranks as the world’s most visited city, with food-led travel a stated priority for visitors. Clearly, Bangkok’s food and beverage scene is commanding more attention than ever before. And yet, on the ground, the picture is less rosy. On the producer side, the economics have turned brutal. According to the Thai Restaurant Association, restaurant sales in the second quarter of 2026 fell 30 to 50 per cent. Over the same period, costs climbed 15 to 20 per cent, driven by higher prices for ingredients, fuel, electricity, rent and labour. Delivery apps promised an escape route, but they have become a trap of their own. Restaurants hand over a commission on every order and must fund aggressive promotions and marketing to stand out in a crowded field. And in Thailand, alcohol sales are effectively prohibited on delivery platforms, eliminating for most restaurants a major source of revenue. And that is just on the producer side. On the consumer side, rising prices and stagnant wages have squeezed household spending. And despite Bangkok’s international appeal, tourist numbers have taken a dent this year, owing to a mix of higher aviation fuel prices, uncertainty in the aviation hubs of the Middle East and increased competition from neighbouring Vietnam and Malaysia. The result is visible across the city. Restaurant openings have fallen by as much as 50 per cent, and the damage reaches well beyond small eateries. Several high-profile, internationally renowned establishments like Canvas, Keller and Villa Frantzén have also had to shut their doors. “Institutions are suffering. Just one example: a friend and colleague told me last night that they’re losing 500,000 baht a month. They’ve been open like 15 years, and did well up until recently.” That’s the report from Dave Cleland, former chef-owner of Tina’s, a neighbourhood New Orleans restaurant in Sathorn that closed last year, despite awards and glowing reviews. “Places that even four or five years ago were packed on a Saturday night are empty now.” Cleland believes the middle of the market is being hollowed out – mid-range restaurants caught between rising input costs and shrinking discretionary spending. It is a pattern economists elsewhere have dubbed the “K-shaped” recovery: growth flowing to the luxury and budget ends of the market while the middle stagnates. He is similarly sceptical of the marketing economy that now determines which restaurants get noticed. Mid-range venues with limited budgets struggle to compete for attention against operators who can pay for it. “There’s this obsession with everything being social media. When you invite influencers, they expect something. It used to be a free meal was enough. Now they want 20,000 to 40,000 baht. [This] monetisation of food journalism. It’s not even journalism. It’s whatever you’d call it that is wrecking it.” Cleland is equally bearish about the focus on the highest-end consumers, largely tourists – a model especially stark in a city where dinner for two at a fine-dining restaurant can cost the equivalent of a month’s income for many Thais. Frankly, he says, tasting menus have become too expensive. “The market is overrun by this obsession that fine dining has to be this one thing. And for bars – I like a place where I can get a proper martini, but I’m not paying 500 baht.” Despite this gloomy prospect, at least at the lower end the government has provided a stimulus in the form of the “Thai Chuay Thai” (Thais helping Thais) programme. Under this scheme, Thai citizens pay only 40 per cent of the cost for food from small vendors, with the government covering the remaining 60 per cent (capped at 200 baht) alongside additional benefits for state welfare recipients. Grab and Line Man, the country’s two main delivery apps, have also joined in to provide a raft of further incentives for Thai Chuay Thai spending. Still, Cleland refuses to write the city off. “Yes, there’s a pivot right now, and yes, restaurants will close. But look around you: Bangkok is a city of eaters. We have the talent, we have the consumers, we have the locations. I have to have faith in this city.”

title: Israel marks 3 years since October 7 attack that sparked war in Gaza
description: Sombre tributes take place as political debate intensifies weeks before Israel’s national vote.
content: Israel marked the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Wednesday with silent tributes, new strikes on Gaza and intense political debate, weeks before elections in which the country’s deadliest day will be front and centre. At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads in silence – although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the dead. Both at Nova and the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another site of mass killings three years earlier, loud explosions echoed from across the Gaza border during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite a ceasefire officially in place for the past year. Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the territory, most of which has been reduced to rubble in relentless bombing in retaliation for the worst attack ever against Israel. At the Nova site, Katia Zohar, whose daughter Bar Zohar was killed at age 23, called the start of the attack at 6.29am, “the minute that changed our lives forever”. “Sadly I remember everything,” Zohar said. “The moment she called for me to come and pick her up because there were missiles in the air. Then the second time when she called from the road, screaming that they were shooting at her.” Anna Davitashvili, 53, paid tribute to her eldest son Shaun, who was killed at 25 at Nova alongside friends, by playing the last track of techno music that the party-goers were dancing to when the attack began. “I feel him here. I’m terribly sorry that I couldn’t save him, I couldn’t help him get out of this massacre,” she said, tears filling up her eyes. On October 27, Israel will hold elections for the first time since the attack, with polls showing a tight race for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in three years has ordered the massive offensive in Gaza and fought wars against Hezbollah in Lebanon as well as Iran, whose cleric-run government backs Hamas. At the Nova site, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister seeking to oust Netanyahu, told reporters of the attack: “This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land.” The centre-left Democrats Party put online footage of the attack, without commentary. “A government that for three years has not destroyed Hamas’s rule is a government dangerous to Israel,” Democrats leader Yair Golan said. Netanyahu marked October 7 with official ceremonies in Jerusalem on Monday, which was closer to the anniversary on the Jewish calendar. He said there would be “no forgiveness for the murderers” and vowed never to allow rule in Gaza by Hamas, which has faced major losses but remains in control of part of the territory. October 7 delivered a deep shock to the psyche of Israel, which has prided itself on protecting its borders despite long odds. Israelis had a more triumphant narrative last week when passengers helped foil an attack by the co-pilot of a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, although questions were soon raised about why he was allowed to fly. On October 7, Palestinian fighters breached the border, storming southern Israel with gunfire, rockets and grenades. A total of 1,221 people died, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Militants also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead. The last live hostages were freed a year ago as part of a US-brokered ceasefire deal in which Hamas stopped firing into Israel. Israeli attacks have subsided but not stopped, with Netanyahu vowing to kill anyone involved in the attack. Israel’s military offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

title: Last chance saloon: EU presses China for a sign to prove trade talks can work
description: Brussels hopes Chinese commerce ministry will agree to modest ‘proof-of-concept’ arrangement at top-level meetings in Beijing.
content: The European Union’s top trade mandarins depart for Beijing on Wednesday for two days of intensive negotiations but expectations in Brussels are measured as to what the talks will deliver. Maros Sefcovic, the EU’s trade chief, will meet his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, on Thursday and Friday – three months after their last encounter in Brussels, when the Europeans set an October deadline for signs of a rebalancing in the trading relationship. Non-stop working-level talks have proven difficult, with the lopsided trade balance showing little sign of narrowing. Indeed, Beijing’s enormous trading surplus with the 27-member bloc has expanded further in the intervening quarter. However, Beijing is believed to no longer outright reject the suggestion that there are problems in its trade ties with Europe. Brussels hopes that by the end of Friday, Beijing’s Ministry of Commerce will agree to moderate its exports in a single sector, in a “proof of concept” arrangement that could be extended to further sectors, according to people familiar with the talks. Even a narrow outcome such as this would allow both sides to declare the early rounds of what has been named the Trade and Investment Consultations a success. “The Sefcovic talks in Beijing will determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table, and whether those offers are substantial enough to change the underlying dynamics,” said Andrew Small, director of the Asia programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations. Beijing could hope to retain broader access to the lucrative European market at a time when its economic reliance on exports is growing. Nonetheless, minor progress is unlikely to deter the EU from taking the task of rebalancing into its own hands later this year. The bloc is convinced that China’s model of state capitalism and subsidised competition is putting its own manufacturing sector in jeopardy. Surges in cheap imports from China in key sectors are blamed for the loss of thousands of factory jobs across Europe’s industrial heartlands, particularly in Germany. Chinese firms that were valued customers and suppliers for German manufacturers have hurtled up the value chain to become ruthless competitors. German officials are convinced that behind the cutthroat competitiveness lie undeclared Chinese state subsidies, an undervalued currency and other forms of support. The dynamic has led to an unprecedented Franco-German alliance on China policy that seems set to push the EU in a much more hawkish direction. “The consensus for European action on China is finally in place after Germany’s caution had long held back a more robust EU approach,” Small said. On Monday, Paris and Berlin co-signed a paper calling for, among other things, a new trade weapon that would allow the EU to cut China out of its market immediately – a dramatic step-change from a German government that has for years been reluctant to take Beijing to task on trade for fear of retribution. A letter signed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, laid out the reasoning behind the move. “We need a credible instrument in the hands of the commission to allow for decisive and systemic reaction, i.e. activation by reversed qualified majority, and for powerful measures up to an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed,” it read.
