The letter marks an unlikely alliance: Paris has for years been the cheerleader for more protectionism and industrial policy, with Berlin often the biggest obstacle. According to Bernd Lange, the European Parliament’s top trade lawmaker, “the European Council has finally woken up”. “With Germany and France, two heavyweights have recognised that we need a change of course when it comes to trade defence instruments. They must be quicker and easier to deploy to protect against unfair market distortions,” he said. The bloc is also creating a tool to force EU firms in key sectors to broaden their supplier base to avoid dependence on imports that could be weaponised. This diversification instrument is likely to be laid out, along with a solidarity fund to compensate firms hit by trade retaliation, in early December. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday that it hoped “France and Germany … refrain from encouraging the EU to frequently resort to protectionist tools, and certainly not politicise or oversecuritise economic and trade issues, so as to avoid taking the wrong path in the wrong way and ultimately harming themselves”. Leaders from the 27 EU members will meet next week in Brussels where they will be debriefed on the Beijing talks. At the last such meeting in June, only Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez spoke up against a tougher trade policy. With the socialist leader calling a snap election in November and trailing in the polls, China could soon find it has few defenders at Europe’s top table. “Today, everyone is on high alert,” Pascal Lamy, former chief of the World Trade Organization, told Le Monde on Tuesday. “We need a Plan A to deal with China: that’s what Sefcovic is doing. He’s trying to negotiate measures with the Chinese that they themselves would take to curb their exports or their dumping in certain sectors,” he said. “But it’s doubtful that this will be enough. So we also need a Plan B.”

title: Singapore-born British artist Kim Lim’s legacy explored in Hong Kong exhibition
description: At the show’s opening, Kim Lim’s sons reflect on her minimalist sculptures and photography, and growing up with two artist parents.
content: The late Singapore-born British artist Kim Lim has recently garnered a much-deserved resurgence of international attention. Following major showcases at Tate Britain in 2020 and the National Gallery Singapore in 2024, the diverse oeuvre of the artist is now on view at Axel Vervoordt Gallery in Hong Kong. Titled “Source”, the exhibition takes its name from her 1988 granite sculpture Source II. Lim specialised in printmaking and sculpture, frequently carving directly from wood or stone to create abstract forms that embodied a powerful minimalism. Despite being the only female and non-white artist featured in the 1977 Hayward Annual exhibition, she was largely overlooked by the mainstream art world following her death from cancer in 1997, aged 61. Today, her estate is managed by her sons, Alex and Johnny Turnbull. To mark the opening of the Hong Kong exhibition, the brothers joined curator Bianca Chu to reflect on their mother’s creative legacy. “When I was thinking about how to begin the curatorial framework, I wanted to go back to her writings,” Chu says during a panel discussion at Axel Vervoordt Gallery in Wong Chuk Hang. Lim’s own descriptions of Source II, noting its “compact energy” and “brooding quality”, stuck with the London-based curator. “I think this archaicness and the novelty of her work are what I find incredibly fascinating,” Chu says. “You could be looking at a piece and think it could have existed in nature without any intervention. But at the same time, upon closer inspection, you realise it is very considered.” Chu also observes Lim’s work through the lens of Chinese philosophy, particularly in how it relates to breath, silence and attention. She notes the Taoist concepts of yin and yang, as well as the tension that emerges between absence and presence. “I feel that very strongly when you stand in front of her work, that you are both engaging with something that is palpable and very physical, and at the same time there is so much unseen, but you can feel,” Chu says. How Kim Lim rejected convention Born into a well-connected family of Singaporean socialites in 1936, Lim came of age amid the background of British colonial rule, the Japanese occupation and a cosmopolitan culture. Expected to join her class of debutantes, she instead charted her own course, moving to the United Kingdom in 1954 to study art at Saint Martin’s School of Art (now Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design) and Slade School of Fine Art in London. However, Chu argues that Lim’s true education stemmed from her extensive trips to Egypt, Turkey, France, Japan and Cambodia, which fundamentally shaped her understanding of light and rhythm. In her writings, Lim described a profound sense of awe when encountering major architectural and sculptural landmarks. The Axel Vervoordt Gallery is also displaying a small collection of Lim’s photography, much of which she developed herself in a darkroom at her Camden Square home in London. Chu highlights this sensuous, image-making aspect of Lim’s practice that is often forgotten. The curator focuses on what Lim was paying attention to, what she chose to preserve and how those memories transformed through her processing into physical artworks. Through her writing and photography, Alex and Johnny have continued to learn more about their mother and their father, the Scottish artist William Turnbull. “I kind of view my mum in an analogy – a personality like an iceberg,” Johnny says. “She was a small person, but beneath it is enormous resolve and strength.” He recalls how she would single-handedly move large-scale stones, occasionally using electric drills to facilitate her hand-carving. “To be an artist at that time, to just have the kind of self-belief … through periods of maybe not getting validation … is really quite extraordinary,” he says. Growing up with two artist parents was not the relaxed, bohemian experience many might assume. “I think we had the strictest parents out of any of my friends. They were Scottish and Chinese. What do you expect?” Alex notes with a laugh. He points out that both parents grew up during wartime in the 1940s. “They were quite strict, so we had to do our chores and wash these sculptures,” he says. Despite being discouraged by their parents from entering the arts, both brothers defied expectations and became musicians. This musical connection feels fitting when considering Lim’s own perspective on her art. In a 1996 interview, Lim famously remarked that the spaces in between her works were as important as the things themselves, likening them to the spaces between musical notes that prevent chaos. As Chu says, “She talked about the possibility of understanding something beyond sight, which I thought was a very revealing thing to say for a visual artist.” “Kim Lim: Source”, Axel Vervoordt Gallery, 21/F, Coda Designer Centre, 62 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Wong Chuk Hang, Tuesday-Saturday, 11am-7pm. Until January 30, 2027. For more information, visit axel-vervoordt.com.

title: US firm ArriVent’s plunge shows risks facing China’s biotech expansion into global markets
description: US-listed ArriVent lost nearly half its value after a Chinese-licensed cancer drug failed a late-stage trial.
content: US firm ArriVent BioPharma’s shares plummeted after a late-stage trial failure involving a cancer drug licensed from China, a setback that analysts said highlighted the challenges facing Chinese biotech companies expanding overseas. New York-listed ArriVent closed down nearly 47 per cent on Tuesday after reporting that its cancer treatment firmonertinib failed to meet its main goal in a phase 3 trial. Firmonertinib was originally developed by Shanghai Allist Pharmaceuticals to treat non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), targeting a mutation known as an epidermal growth factor receptor exon 20 insertion. ArriVent acquired the exclusive rights in 2021 to develop and commercialise the drug outside China, becoming one of the earliest US biotechnology firms licensing Chinese drug assets. The company said its phase 3 trial failed to demonstrate that firmonertinib could significantly delay disease progression compared with standard chemotherapy treatment. ArriVent chairman and CEO Bing Yao said in a statement that the “disappointing” results were “not what we hoped for”, and that the company was evaluating the full trial dataset to determine the “most appropriate development path” for the drug. Tony Ren, head of Asia healthcare research at Macquarie Capital, said many “out-licensed Chinese drugs are starting to face their moments of truth as they come under more rigorous scrutiny and higher global standards”. Ren noted that while firmonertinib won approval in China in February as a second-line treatment, ArriVent’s trial evaluated the drug as a first-line therapy for the same type of mutation. As more Chinese drugs enter global trials, we should expect more visible failures alongside the successes David Zhang, Trivium China In cancer, first-line therapies are the standard initial treatment, while second-line options are typically used when the first therapy fails or stops working. “It is quite common for a drug to succeed in later line settings but fail in early settings,” Ren said. The failed overseas trial highlighted a key reality for Chinese drug makers – that commercial success in China did not guarantee clinical success in new indications or overseas markets, said David Zhang, an analyst at Trivium China. Allist’s firmonertinib is approved in China for three types of NSCLC treatment and generated about 3.14 billion yuan (US$468 million) in sales in the first half of 2026. The company said in August that the drug helped lift its first-half revenue by nearly 40 per cent from a year earlier. Shanghai-listed Allist did not trade on Wednesday because mainland China’s financial markets were closed for the National Day holiday from October 1 to 7. Chinese biotech firms have expanded rapidly overseas in recent years as global pharmaceutical giants increasingly turn to China for innovative therapies. Zhang said the rapid growth in cross-border partnerships did not eliminate the risks inherent in drug development. “This setback highlights the clinical uncertainty that remains even for an established product,” Zhang said. “As more Chinese drugs enter global trials, we should expect more visible failures alongside the successes.”

title: Climate change and farming gave rise to ‘genetically distinct’ Beijing swan goose: study
description: New population of the migratory waterbird has emerged in the Chinese capital over the past century, according to researchers.
content: Climate change and agricultural development have brought a new goose population to China with unique migratory patterns, a study has found. In an article on the Chinese Academy of Sciences website, researchers from the CAS Institute of Zoology said they had discovered a “genetically distinct” population of swan geese that emerged in Beijing over the past century. They said the timing of their arrival coincided with environmental shifts in the region during the early 20th century – namely climate warming, the expansion of rice fields and the development of irrigated agriculture. “This study provides new evidence for understanding the underlying mechanisms of how migratory animals respond to rapid environmental changes, and also offers a scientific basis for the conservation and management of migratory waterbirds in East Asia,” according to the article posted on September 17. The researchers published the findings of their study in the peer-reviewed journal Science Bulletin in mid-June. It was conducted by scientists from the CAS institute’s State Key Laboratory of Animal Biodiversity Conservation and Integrated Pest Management, the Beijing Milu Ecological Research Centre, and other institutions. The swan goose (Anser cygnoides) is a migratory species endemic to East Asia. Its wild populations mainly breed in Mongolia, Russia and Northeast China, migrating south for the winter along inland and coastal routes. Due to its dwindling population, the swan goose is listed as an endangered species by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. While historical records show no evidence of the species breeding locally in Beijing, recent field surveys indicate a dramatic shift, according to the paper. Breeding populations are now established around the capital and their migratory routes differ markedly from previously recorded swan goose populations elsewhere in the region. To trace the origins of the Beijing flock, the researchers conducted whole-genome resequencing on samples collected from wild swan geese in Beijing and Mongolia, as well as from domestic geese. The genetic data revealed that the Beijing birds show a clear divergence from both domestic and other wild populations, though they remain most closely related to wild lineages in eastern Mongolia and Northeast China. The researchers concluded that the Beijing population had likely splintered from their eastern Mongolian ancestors within the last 100 years. “The timing of this divergence aligns with significant environmental changes in Beijing and its surrounding areas since the early 20th century,” the Institute of Zoology researchers wrote, highlighting regional warming and the rapid expansion of irrigated agricultural land. These shifts likely created the ideal ecological conditions for the geese to establish a new local population. To track the birds’ altered habits, researchers fitted 16 swan geese with GPS transmitters at Beijing’s Milu Park – a natural wetland habitat – during the 2020 and 2022 breeding seasons. By November 2024, the team had amassed 163,887 tracking data points. The monitoring exposed a distinct “partial migration” pattern: while two-thirds of the flock migrated south in the autumn as expected, the remaining third stayed in Beijing to overwinter. With the swan goose listed as a Class II state-protected animal in China – covering rare or endangered species – the paper concluded that understanding these rapid shifts in migratory strategies and population dynamics was critical for effective conservation planning.

title: Viral trapped shark in South Korea brings tourism, retail windfall to Busan
description: ‘Bukangi’ has attracted over a million visitors, boosting the local economy, as vendors capitalise on the stranded shark’s fame.
content: A marooned three-metre-long (nine feet) shark in South Korea has drawn more than a million visitors to the coastal city of Busan, boosting local retail sales and triggering a trademark war, as authorities rush to stop opportunistic vendors from cashing in on the viral phenomenon. The shark, nicknamed “Bukangi” in reference to the park where it has become trapped, has become an internet darling and tourist sensation after non-stop local media coverage about multiple failed efforts to encourage it back into the open ocean. Busan authorities have moved to capitalise on the frenzy. The city has appointed the shark – which experts believe is a dusky shark – an honorary ambassador, giving it a starring role in local promotional campaigns. Some 1,062,800 people have visited the park to see the shark since September 19, the Busan Infrastructure Corporation said. Bukangi is the latest example of how wildlife straying into urban environments can become tourist sensations supercharged by the internet, boosting the local economy. In 2018, a mandarin duck – native to East Asia – went viral as it settled in New York’s Central Park, sparking themed merchandise. The same year, Londoners were thrilled by a beluga whale frolicking in the River Thames. In the week after the shark appeared in mid-September, CU convenience stores near the park reported a 76.7 per cent jump in sales compared with earlier in the month, according to BGF Retail, which operates the popular chain. Sales of tangentially shark-related products, like the Jaws Bar ice lolly, were up 26.5 per cent nationwide, it said. Busan has warned it will take action against any efforts to trademark the Bukangi name for private commercial use. “Bukangi has grown into a new symbol of Busan,” mayor Chun Jae-soo said in a statement. “I will ensure that this name, created with the public, is not used exclusively by any single individual.” Yet the business opportunities the shark presents may be limited. Yun Jin-ho, director at Choin Marketing Lab, said that while local store owners may be nimble enough to release shark-related products, the animal’s eventual departure makes it tricky for larger companies to act. “People love it because it’s a chance event that could vanish at any moment,” Yun said. Once the shark goes back to its natural habitat, “the random and unusual nature of it will become but a memory”, Yun added. Last month, the city’s coastguard and fire department officials unsuccessfully tried to escort the Busan shark back to the ocean with high-pressure hosepipes and loud noise. A second rescue attempt last week involved a wide net to bring it closer to the exit. The next day, the shark had swum further inland, sidestepping the net. Scientists at the National Institute of Fisheries Science will continue to monitor its movement and health, said Kim Hyun-woo, its senior researcher. Experts say once the water dips in temperature, the shark is likely to return to the ocean on its own, though the longer it stays, the weaker it will get. “It’s been about eighteen days since it has eaten,” said Choi Youn, professor emeritus of fish taxonomy and ecology at Kunsan National University. The shark may be attracted to the magnetic field created by the undersea cables along the waterway, Choi added. Sharks are known to use Earth’s magnetic fields to orient themselves and navigate the ocean.

title: French school protests: Why are students protesting and what’s the latest update
description: Riot police fire tear gas in Paris and elsewhere as more than 250,000 rallied nationwide for school funding and better classroom environments.
content:
After a weekend lull, French riot police fired tear gas at crowds in Paris and elsewhere in the country on Tuesday, as more than a quarter of a million people mobilised across the nation, according to government figures, to support secondary school students demanding education funding.
Pressure is mounting on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron. There had been at least two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors.
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Pupils also blockaded schools while large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities.
The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fuelling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
Protests first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September. Teachers and students mobilised against a lack of staff at a lycée, or high school, in Creteil, in the southeastern outskirts of the French capital.
From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, with protests even in high schools of smaller towns.
Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
“We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.”
From the outset, pupils focused on perceived inequalities in the school system, saying that teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement are not as good for students in disadvantaged neighbourhoods – despite the promise of France’s national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Placards held up by the first protesters in Creteil read “Too many inequalities, we’re disgusted”, “Education is a right, not a privilege” and “Sorry to bother, it’s for our future,” according to photos posted by Clémence Guetté, the district’s lawmaker at the National Assembly, France’s parliament.
Pupils elsewhere complained that during summer heatwaves they roast in classrooms without air conditioning, and they freeze in winter. French media broadcast videos of scampering rats, collapsed ceilings, leaks, broken furniture and other woes, all filmed in dilapidated schools.
“The public needs to know that conditions for studying are no longer what they were for us,” said Sophie Bordy, a 50-year-old literature teacher in Paris. “It has deteriorated significantly.”
Education spending is one of the costliest items in the state budget Macron’s government is proposing for 2027. It has earmarked 65.5 billion euros (HK$577 billion) for schools, more than the 63.4 billion euros for defence
Pupils also complain of long hours. In high schools, classes often start at 8am and can last to the early evening. French high schoolers’ compulsory school hours are among the highest in Europe, according to European Union figures.
“I see the teachers more than my family,” read one young girl’s placard photographed by Le Parisien newspaper.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students’ concerns and find solutions.
Responding to criticism of police tactics, Lecornu pledged that any “accidents” would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a “lie”.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn’t make “any sense to hit minors”.
“Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
The violence is “absolutely unbearable”, Le Coq said.
Interior Minister Nunez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers’ riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend from immediate difficulties like fuel prices that have soared because of the US-Israel war on Iran to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron.
Against that backdrop, pupils’ complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
“You say ‘young people are the future,’ so listen to them,” read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.

title: Letters | Hong Kong’s ethnically diverse communities must drive solutions for youth
description: Readers discuss the systemic barriers faced by ethnically diverse children in the city, and house arrest in Malaysia.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Education is widely described as the catalyst for breaking barriers and ending intergenerational struggle. However, Hong Kong’s school system, where systemic barriers remain entrenched, continues to marginalise ethnically diverse children. Instead of believing in their capacity to thrive, too many pupils are treated as lost causes, held back by a culture of low expectations. Many young people like me move through secondary school carrying low self-esteem and self-worth, painfully aware of how easily we could be dismissed. Now that we’re on the other side, contributing positively to Hong Kong’s economy and society, we feel an urgent desire to turn our lived experience into constructive solutions. We want to support the next generation of ethnically diverse youth: to give them hope, motivate them and guide them through planning for a future they can believe in. Those who have been through the system’s failures often understand the solutions best, which is why I joined EmpowerU in 2020 to co-found the PowerThru education programme for ethnically diverse youth. PowerThru has supported over 1,100 ethnically diverse secondary school students. We work with ethnically diverse working professionals and tertiary youth to create career-exploration “taster” courses and guidance workshops, where students explore their post-secondary options. When students meet mentors they can relate to, they feel understood, cared for and inspired to see new possibilities for themselves. But the fix doesn’t stop at just disseminating information. First, we need to train educators and social workers to recognise the root causes behind why ethnically diverse students are lagging behind academically and psychosocially, and why many have a pessimistic outlook on their future. We need to carve out intentional spaces for honest conversations, where educators come together to share practical strategies from experience. Second, solutions must be driven by people with lived experience who serve the community with dignity and respect. I have attended events and programmes for ethnically diverse “beneficiaries” that have left me feeling more frustrated and furious. Hong Kong still has a strong top-down, charity mindset that sees communities as requiring handouts and nothing more. Programmes designed to put people first encourage resilience and can bring real systemic change. Weeks into the new academic year, I cannot help but notice how familiar these problems remain. Without changing our fundamental approach to education and community work, we risk circling the same challenges and asking, again and again: “What is wrong with ethnically diverse youth?” Sumichhya Gurung, PowerThru programme director, EmpowerU In Malaysia, a house could be turned into a prison Malaysia’s Pardons Board agreed last month to allow disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak to serve out the remainder of his jail term under house arrest. Malaysia does not have a specific law governing house arrest. But a house can be a prison under the Prison Act 1995. Section 2 defines prison as “any house, building, enclosure or place, or any part thereof, declared to be a prison under Section 3 and shall include the grounds and buildings within the prison enclosure and also the airing grounds or other grounds or buildings belonging or attached thereto and used by prisoners”. Section 3 empowers the relevant minister, by notification in the gazette, to declare “any house, building, enclosure or place, or any part thereof, to be a prison for the purposes of this Act for the imprisonment or detention of persons lawfully in custody and may in like manner declare that any such prison shall cease to be a prison for the purposes of this Act”. The first declaration under Section 3 was way back in 1998, three years after the act came into force. The last declaration was only five months ago, in April, when the home minister declared all buildings and areas situated on Lot PT 5347 of Mukim of Pelangai, Bentong district, Pahang state to be a prison for the purposes of imprisonment or detention of persons lawfully in custody. So, if Najib is to serve out the remainder of his jail term under house arrest, which is not currently provided for under the law, the designated house can and should be declared a prison first. Mohamad Hafiz Hassan, lecturer, Faculty of Law, Multimedia University, Malaysia

title: Lionel Messi calls time on Argentina career, says not playing will be ‘deeply painful’
description: Lionel Messi ends international career with two goals in 3-0 victory over Benin, tells fans it is ‘saddest day of my career’.
content: Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the “saddest day of my career” on Tuesday in Buenos Aires after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin. Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and teammates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina. “It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the crowd. “Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here. “Not coming any more is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.” Messi said that returning to the Monumental – where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup – was bittersweet. “Now I’m here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you. “But now I’ll be on that side [with the fans], supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united,” he said. Messi, though, said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where the South Americans battled through to the final only to lose to Spain. Messi said the emotional roller coaster of that tournament – which included a 2-1 defeat of bitter rivals England in the semi-final – had taken a toll. “Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” said Messi. “We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again. “In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big. “We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close.”

title: Hong Kong police arrest parents of 10-year-old girl made to carry bags of beer
description: Parents held on suspicion of ill-treatment after video shows girl carrying heavy bags of beer to Tuen Mun residential estate, while school has offered help.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested the parents of a 10-year-old girl after a viral video showed her carrying heavy bags of beer and being berated by her father as he confronted bystanders concerned about her welfare. Police said they received a report at about 10.30pm on Tuesday that a girl in a school uniform was seen carrying two bags containing numerous cans of beer to a building at Fu Tai Estate in Tuen Mun. A spokesman said officers from the New Territories North regional child abuse investigation unit arrested the girl’s father, 38, and mother, 32, in Tuen Mun on Wednesday afternoon on suspicion of ill-treatment following further investigation. The pair remain in custody pending further inquiries. In a previous update, the force said the 10-year-old girl was found to have no visible injuries. The case has been classified as a “request for police assistance” and referred to the same investigation unit and the Social Welfare Department for follow-up. Her school, Lutheran Tsang Shing Siu Leun School, said social workers and teachers had intervened after learning of the incident, offering help and counselling to the pupil and her family. “We love every child and will never tolerate any behaviour that harms children’s rights or their physical and mental health,” the school said on social media. At least two videos circulating on the social media platform Threads show the girl carrying a large bag of beer in each hand. Her backpack also appears badly torn in both clips. One video shows her in school uniform walking up a staircase with the bags. The other shows her alongside a man and other children as bystanders question why she is carrying both bags and ask whether another child can help. During the exchange, the man becomes angry, snatches one of the bags from the girl and calls her “useless”. The family told media later on Tuesday that the incident was a misunderstanding and the man arrested was said to be the girl’s stepfather. The man said he asked the girl to carry the beers as a way to build her muscles, adding that he would use other methods in the future. The girl said it was the first time that she was carrying six packs of beer, each containing four 500ml cans, in one go, and admitted that it was tiring. “I started from carrying two packs, then gradually to four packs, but I had never carried six packs before,” she told the media. But she said her parents cared for her and that the damaged backpack she was carrying in the video was not her school bag and she had torn it herself. The school said it was looking into the incident and would continue to monitor the situation and provide appropriate support to the family. It also urged the public to stop sharing the footage and related information to protect the child’s privacy and psychological well-being. The school appealed to the public to give it space to handle the matter and refrain from harassing, pursuing or following the pupil and her family to avoid causing further harm or fear. The Education Bureau said it was “highly concerned” about the incident, adding that the girl’s school, social workers and police had intervened and were following up on the needs of the pupil and her family. The school had activated its crisis management team, it added. The bureau vowed to continue to maintain close contact with the school and provide support.

title: The Hong Kong siblings who bond over fitness reveal why endurance runs in this family
description: Joanne Nixon and her brother, Elliot Froidevaux, have transformed their lives through running. Now, keeping active is a family affair.
content: In the punishing world of Hong Kong endurance sports, few events command as much respect as the Hong Kong Four Trails Ultra Challenge (HK4TUC), a gruelling 298km (185-mile) test across the city’s major trail networks. While 51-year-old ultra-runner and coach Elliot Froidevaux has conquered the challenge twice, his journey from a 100kg (220lbs) heavy smoker to elite trail runner was no solo effort. Standing next to the Swiss-born, Hong Kong-raised Froidevaux is his older sister, Joanne Nixon, a 53-year-old marathoner and Hyrox competitor who turned to running as a retreat through family illness, a demanding career and midlife reinvention. Nixon, also born in Switzerland and raised in Hong Kong, has built an impressive endurance résumé, completing countless half-marathons, 12 full marathons and challenging events such as the Oxfam Trailwalker, Action Asia and Green Power races. She recently took on her first Hyrox women’s singles race in May 2026, and already has her sights set on another Hyrox competition and the Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon, both in January 2027. Her love affair with running began with a misunderstanding. In 2003, while chatting to a stranger at a bar, she thought he was asking for her phone number. Only later did she realise he was asking where to collect his race bib for an upcoming marathon. “Luckily, he called me anyway,” she says. The stranger would eventually become her husband, and together they would have two children, now aged 16 and 14. ‘Running is the only time that is entirely mine’ For Nixon, running began as a leisurely weekend ritual, jogging 4km with her father along Bowen Road. “Then I fell in love with Charlie, a passionate runner, who persuaded me to run the New York Marathon in 2004,” she says. Together, they trained for the race while raising HK$100,000 for the Hong Kong Cancer Fund. Her parents flew to New York to watch the couple finish the race, even though her mum was fighting stage four cancer at the time. “The incredible atmosphere, the roaring crowds, had me hooked,” shares Nixon, who still does much of her training along Bowen Road and around Happy Valley on Hong Kong Island. Running became her coping mechanism. Between a demanding career, raising two children and supporting parents through illness, it gave her space to breathe. “Running is the only time that is entirely mine. It makes me feel strong, grounded and resilient,” says Nixon, marketing director for the Hong Kong retail chain Bookazine. Balancing training with real life has come with its share of hurdles – “from needing surgery [for a broken and dislocated toe in January 2020] after a flip-flop mishap walking the dog, to putting everything on hold to support my parents through hospital stays, or the kids being sick on race day”, Nixon says. More recently, Nixon powered through a Hyrox competition while recovering from a painful case of frozen shoulder. The setback served as a wake-up call to prioritise mobility and recovery alongside her mileage. That includes a focus on stretching pre- and post-runs. Her brother is her hero. “Elliot is living proof that if you set your mind to a goal, you can achieve it,” says Nixon, who grew up with her brother at the secluded Sea Ranch development on Lantau Island in the 1980s, after their family arrived in Hong Kong in 1979. “We swam in the sea nearly every day, played tennis and learned judo. We hiked over the hills as kids to get to English lessons in the next village.” From unable to run to ultra-marathons Froidevaux’s path to fitness was markedly different. Having taken up smoking at school, he spent much of his twenties carrying extra weight and struggling even on relatively easy hikes. The turning point came in 2007, shortly before the birth of his eldest daughter, when his wife delivered an ultimatum: quit smoking. Seeking help, he visited a Chinese medicine practitioner. “I went to him on a Friday evening. He told me to stop smoking that day and gave me a herbal tea to drink every four hours. Every cigarette I tried to sneak in tasted so awful with the tea that I stopped completely,” he says, noting he has not smoked in nearly two decades since. It would take several more years for Froidevaux to fully embrace endurance sports. In 2010, he began playing competitive squash for the Hong Kong Football Club and discovered his stamina lagged behind veteran players. “I incorporated interval sessions and hill repeats into my training and, inspired by my brother-in-law Charlie, an active trail runner, decided to give the sport a try,” he says. Over the next 12 years, he shed 27kg and has maintained his weight at 76kg to 78kg since. By 2016, he was ready for his first official race, the King of the Hills Half Marathon in Tai Po. “After my first race, I realised this was not going to be as simple as turning up and doing well,” he says. Yet the challenge only deepened his fascination with endurance sports. Before long, he was signing up for demanding races, progressing from the Moontrekker 30km and Action Asia HK50 to Lantau 70, the 9 Dragons 50 Miles and the prestigious HK100. Then came the pinnacle: the HK4TUC. “It took five years of racing, training and building a running résumé worthy of earning a coveted place in the event,” says Froidevaux, who completed the gruelling challenge in both 2022 and 2026, and has finished 10 ultra-marathons spanning more than 100 miles. In 2023 alone, he covered 520km across three ultra-marathons in six weeks. Nutrition and strength training are key At the height of his HK4TUC training, he logged up to 200km a week. Today, returning from injury, he averages around 70km. “As we get older, our bodies need longer to recover, and we can’t tolerate the same training loads we could when we were younger,” he says. A series of injuries, including Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis and recurring ankle sprains, forced him to reduce his volume. Success in endurance sport, he learned, requires patience as much as perseverance. Strength training is now a non-negotiable part of his routine; after a bout of patellar maltracking – misaligned kneecap movement – left him struggling on stairs, targeted strength work and cross-training helped restore his function. His approach to nutrition is equally pragmatic. “The demands of high-volume training require sufficient fuel,” he says. “Apart from creatine and occasional supplements to address deficiencies, I rely on carbohydrates to power the demands of running and make sure I eat enough protein. “Running ultras is a fast track of living life, with high highs and low lows. It teaches you how to adapt, keep moving forward and stay humble,” says Froidevaux, who draws inspiration from American ultra-runner Sally McRae and Japanese athlete Tomokazu Ihara. What began as informal online coaching helping runners plan their training gradually evolved into a new career. Encouraged by his family, Froidevaux left his previous line of work to coach full time in 2023. Setting an example Today, running is a family affair. Nixon’s husband and children regularly take part in events including the AVOHK 5k, The Peak 24 Hour Race, Team Fear and Run Hong Kong. “My son Cody has raced alongside his uncle, Elliot, and Elliot’s daughter, Nellie, now at university, has already completed multiple half-marathons,” Nixon says proudly. “The passion for running runs through our family.” Though the siblings no longer train together as often – “Elliot is far too fast for me now,” Nixon laughs – their shared outdoor background remains their foundation. During the pandemic, the extended family swapped intense runs for long group hikes across Hong Kong’s hills. “It was a wonderful escape from the reality of Covid and a chance to spend time outdoors together,” she says. Being active, for her, is also about setting an example. “I want my children to see that their mum can challenge herself, push her limits and achieve difficult things,” she says. For people in their fifties looking to get active, both siblings offer simple advice. “Put your shoes on and get out the door,” Froidevaux says. “If that means walking before you run, then walk. Give yourself a purpose, whether that’s signing up for a race, setting a challenge or joining a running group.” Nixon agrees. “You’d be surprised what you can achieve when you truly put your mind to it,” she says. “If I can do it, so can you. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the greatest. Just be yourself, do it your way, and most of all, enjoy it.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: China’s ‘city of the future’, Xiongan, hunting high-value tech firms: sources
description: New area aims to cultivate five companies valued at or above 10 billion yuan, 10 worth more than 5 billion yuan, and 100 core firms.
content: China’s Xiongan New Area is accelerating its hunt for technology firms as the city, designed partly to house state-owned institutions relocated from Beijing, moves to nurture its own industries, according to people familiar with its plans and local officials. Officials were looking to attract tech companies that could reach valuations of 10 billion yuan (US$1.4 billion), hoping some would list on stock markets, including Hong Kong’s, in the next few years, sources said, adding that the key sectors would span artificial intelligence, satellite internet and robotics. Xiongan was pursuing a three-year developmental goal dubbed “511”, which aimed to cultivate five companies valued at or above 10 billion yuan, 10 worth more than 5 billion yuan, and 100 core firms, local officials said. The ambitious targets first surfaced at a media briefing in June by Zhang Yingjie, deputy head of the new area’s bureau of industry, information technology and data, according to The Paper, a digital news outlet based in Shanghai. Xiongan authorities did not immediately respond to a request for further details. Established in April 2017 under a plan championed by President Xi Jinping, Xiongan, dubbed China’s “city of the future”, spans three counties and surrounding areas in Hebei province, about 100km (62 miles) southwest of Beijing. It was designed to ease pressure on Beijing by moving some universities and state-owned enterprises from the capital, while creating a new engine of regional growth. State-owned enterprises have anchored the first wave of arrivals. China Satellite Network Group and China Huaneng, a major power generation company, have moved their headquarters to Xiongan. Since 2023, Xiongan has attracted 157 second- and third-tier subsidiaries of central state-owned enterprises. PDD Holdings, the owner of the Pinduoduo and Temu online marketplaces, established a digital services subsidiary there in May that has already hired more than 5,000 people, Xinhua reported. However, sources said that simply moving state firms’ headquarters would do little to establish a lasting technology industry if their suppliers, researchers and business operations remained elsewhere. One expert familiar with the local authorities’ thinking said the relocation of a corporate headquarters gave you “a building rather than a supply chain”. Measures released by Xiongan authorities in April call for officials to map the supply chains of relocated state firms and encourage private companies to take part in their procurement, technical research and projects testing new applications. China Satellite Network Group offers an early example. After moving to Xiongan in 2024, by September it had become an anchor for a 69-firm aerospace information cluster, according to official figures. Meanwhile, Xiongan has also attracted a growing number of laid-off tech professionals and solo entrepreneurs from Beijing who are seeking to strike out on their own, as advances in artificial intelligence models and agents make it increasingly feasible to build “one-person companies” (OPCs). At a workshop at Xiongan AI Industry Park late last month, participants spent an afternoon building AI-assisted WeChat mini-programmes, a low-cost test of a business idea and an essential social media tool for running OPCs. Five produced initial prototypes by the end of the session, according to the organiser. Xiongan has moved to support OPCs with dedicated incubators and subsidised computing resources. Four AI-focused OPC communities opened in May, offering more than 60,000 square metres (645,800 square feet) of space along with help on company registration, technical training, legal and financial matters, and finding customers. Under a support programme introduced this summer, qualified early-stage founders can receive six months of free computing capacity and AI model tokens. The new area is also developing shared workspaces and services to connect solo founders with financing and potential projects. For all the resources Xiongan could put behind its technology recruitment drive, the question facing any company mulling a move was straightforward, the expert said: “Is there enough business to be done there?”

title: Paris Fashion Week: Louis Vuitton SS27 at the Louvre
description: Amid warming weather, Nicolas Ghesquière turned to simplicity and lightness while preserving the French luxury maison’s signatures.
content: Just days after French president Emmanuel Macron bestowed the insignia of Chevalier de la Légion d’honneur (Knight of the Legion of Honour) on Louis Vuitton’s women’s artistic director Nicolas Ghesquière at the Élysée Palace, the designer unveiled the brand’s spring/summer 2027 collection on the last day of Paris Fashion Week. For the show, Ghesquière turned the courtyard of the Louvre museum into a futuristic cityscape with flying cars painted with the brand’s signature Damier pattern and reminiscent of spaceships. The runway was paved to look like a race track. The set was meant to evoke a modern urban jungle and the chaos of daily life in a metropolis; it was envisioned in contrast to the lightness of the clothes, Ghesquière explained in a post-show interview with editors. “I wanted to express a sensation of simplicity and a feeling of purity with this collection,” he said. “But the construction behind it and making things extremely light and the simplification [are] extremely complex.” The first couple of looks – soft dresses and separates in pastel hues that gently caressed the body – set the tone for a parade of streamlined outfits in fabrics like jersey that billowed and bounced as the models walked at breakneck speed. Ghesquière is known for his structured, architectural garments, but he wanted these clothes to feel like swimwear and almost like a second skin. Reflecting on Louis Vuitton’s origins as a trunk maker, Ghesquière noticed that, throughout its long history, the company has worked to make trunks lighter and flatter so they could travel more easily. That idea inspired him to strip things down and deconstruct garments, “to take off as much as possible and keep just what is essential”. When conceiving this range, Ghesquière also thought about the heatwaves France and Europe have been experiencing. “The world is getting warmer, and we all wear layers,” he said. “We need a different wardrobe and to think differently; it’s almost like you have to weigh the clothes these days to see if they perform.” With barely any patterns or embellishments – except for crystal fringes that some models wore on their foreheads like sparkling bangs and a couple of beaded looks – the collection was Ghesquière’s take on minimalism, something very new for him. Even the bags, Louis Vuitton’s most important category, were mostly pared-down, except for a few models adorned with gold hardware in the shape of Louis Vuitton’s signature monogram flower. Some were shaped like letter envelopes in the brand’s signature epi leather, similar to the ones Louis Vuitton fashion-show invitations come in every season. Footwear ranged from men’s brogues with silver soles to zippered ankle booties and square-toe heeled shoes with luggage-tag uppers. Long-time fans of Ghesquière’s work and of his unparalleled ability to combine futuristic elements with historic references are likely to be surprised by the simplicity of this collection. This easy dressing feels right for the times we live in, when people need clothes with a purpose and layers they can shed to suit unpredictable weather patterns.

title: 521kg of meth seized from Laos private jet bound for Manila, not Malaysia: police
description: Malaysia’s Narcotics Crime Investigation Department said its officials would visit Laos to get further information on the cross-border gang.
content: The 521kg (1,148lbs) of suspected methamphetamine seized by Laotian authorities from a private jet was not sourced from Malaysia, with the drugs believed to have originated in Laos and been destined for Manila, the Philippines. Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Hussein Omar Khan said police were informed by Laotian authorities on Tuesday that the cross-border smuggling attempt had been foiled at Luang Prabang International Airport last Thursday. Hussein said the private jet had initially departed from Subang airport in Malaysia without any cargo before flying to Luang Prabang. “The drugs seized were meant for the Manila market in the Philippines and not the Malaysian market,” he said in a statement. “The aircraft departed Subang for Luang Prabang without any cargo before it was believed to have been used to transport the drugs from Laos to Manila,” he said. Hussein said the aircraft arrived in Luang Prabang at about 11.30am, while two vehicles arrived at the airport at about 1.30pm. Several airport personnel then helped transfer 23 bags from the vehicles onto trolleys to be loaded onto the aircraft. An inspection of the bags found 500 packages of suspected methamphetamine weighing 521kg in total. Earlier, media reported that a Malaysian was among 13 individuals detained by Laotian authorities following the discovery of 521kg of crystal methamphetamine aboard a private jet in the country last week. Hussein said police had launched an investigation and would send several NCID officers to Laos to question those involved and obtain further information on the syndicate, particularly its links to Malaysia. Laotian authorities had earlier said the operation was launched following information received on September 21 about a planned cross-border smuggling operation. This story was first published by The Star

title: Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spaces to flip to neighbours for profit
description: Residents argue that parking is a vital community asset that should not be monopolised by anyone seeking financial gain from resale.
content: A woman in central China invested 14 million yuan (US$2 million) to acquire 196 parking spaces in a residential community, later selling them at a significant mark-up, which led to furious residents suing her. The lawsuit centred around a residential block, the name of which was not disclosed, located in Changsha, Hunan province. The property project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, many were sceptical about the community’s prospects due to a lack of essential public facilities such as shops, schools, and public transport options. Consequently, there was little interest in both the flats and the parking spaces, according to Hunan TV. Despite this pessimism, a woman surnamed Wu snapped up 196 parking spots in a single transaction, representing 40 per cent of the project’s total parking inventory, for a sum of 14 million yuan. The developer, facing severe cash constraints, agreed to her purchase. Wu expressed confidence in the community’s future growth after reviewing the regional development plans issued by local authorities. As she anticipated, the area experienced rapid development, resulting in the swift sale of homes within the block and a surge in demand for parking spaces. To safeguard her investment, Wu installed parking locks to prevent unauthorised use of her spaces. She began leasing some spots at 500 yuan (US$75) each per month, effectively doubling the original rental price set by the developer in 2018. She declined requests from residents seeking a reduction in rent to 300 yuan. Subsequently, she listed her parking spaces for sale at about 100,000 yuan (US$15,000) each, with some priced up to 80 per cent higher than their original values. Many residents felt Wu should sell them at the original rates. Wu’s actions incensed local residents who struggled with a shortage of available parking. A government official was dispatched to mediate the dispute, but his efforts proved ineffective. An undisclosed number of residents formed a collective to bring Wu to court. This group contended that parking spaces are integral to a community’s infrastructure and should not be monopolised by an individual profiting from resale. They urged the court to annul the purchasing contract between Wu and the developer. In February 2024, a local court in Changsha ruled in favour of Wu. The court stated that when the property developer offered the parking spaces for sale, all residents had the opportunity to buy them but chose to forgo that right. Instead of adopting a wait-and-see approach, Wu seized the opportunity by securing funding and assuming the market risk on her own. Consequently, her bulk purchase was deemed legal, with the court noting that no law restricts the number of parking spaces one individual may own. The case gained renewed attention on social media in China in late September, stirring considerable online debate. “There is nothing wrong with this woman. The developer did ask other residents if they wanted to buy, but they chose not to,” one online user supported Wu. Another person commented: “This woman is wealthy and evidently astute.” Conversely, a user argued: “Parking spaces in a community should prioritise meeting the needs of its residents. It’s unjust that many spots remain vacant while others struggle to find parking. I suggest the court annul Wu’s purchase contract.”

title: Malaysia’s Myanmar bet? Repatriations pave way for diplomacy
description: Malaysia’s move ahead of Min Aung Hlaing’s visit has raised concerns that Asean’s efforts to resolve the Myanmar civil war would be futile.
content: Malaysia’s repatriation of Myanmar nationals ahead of a visit to Kuala Lumpur by the war-torn country’s leader appears to mirror efforts by other Asean countries seeking to mend ties with Naypyidaw. Several Asean members have stepped up engagement with Myanmar at the bilateral level recently, raising questions about whether a gradual normalisation between the bloc and the country could undermine efforts to end its civil war, according to analysts. Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia arrived in southern Yangon on Sunday, regional government minister Nay Lin Tun said. Under the repatriation scheme – which has drawn criticism from human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency – 1,479 returnees were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship. They are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals slated for phased repatriation from Malaysia, where more than 10,300 others remain in immigration detention centres, according to the country’s home ministry. The repatriation coincided with preparations in Kuala Lumpur to host Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing, who arrived in Malaysia on Wednesday for a two-day trip. Min Aung Hlaing, the former leader of Myanmar’s military junta who was elected president in April after a controversial election several months earlier dominated by an army-backed party, would be among several foreign leaders visiting Kuala Lumpur in October, state news agency Bernama quoted Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil as saying last week. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since a 2021 coup led by Min Aung Hlaing ousted the National League for Democracy government. Rejecting accusations that Malaysia was returning the Myanmar nationals without regard for their safety, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month that continued engagement was necessary to resolve long-standing ⁠issues, adding that his government would hold more talks with Myanmar to facilitate additional returns. Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor of international relations and human rights at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia’s repatriation efforts had raised concerns. “I would be careful about calling this definitively a quid pro quo unless we know what was actually agreed between the two sides,” Khoo said. “Still, given the timing of the repatriation and Min’s upcoming visit, it is difficult not to see a connection.” She added that the move could set a worrying precedent if the migrant issue were to become part of wider talks with Myanmar. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees was denied access to the Myanmar nationals, preventing any assessment of whether their return was voluntary, according to media reports. “Malaysia can pursue its national interests, but those interests should not come at the expense of basic protection safeguards,” Khoo said, noting that Thailand had repeatedly deported Myanmar nationals. “The danger is that, as governments focus on getting people out of their own countries, much less attention is paid to whether it is actually safe for them to go back,” she added. According to rights group Fortify Rights, Thailand worked with Myanmar to forcibly return more than 3,500 Myanmar nationals via the Ranong-Kawthaung border crossing between February 2024 and late 2025, a practice that continues today. Khoo noted that Malaysia’s former foreign minister Saifuddin Abdullah was particularly critical of the junta and pushed for the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations to engage a wider range of actors in Myanmar’s conflict. “But that approach also had its limits,” Khoo said, citing poor progress on Asean’s Five-Point Consensus, with Malaysia and other members of the bloc failing to translate strong language into tangible changes in Myanmar, referring to the bloc’s peace plan adopted in 2021 to tackle the crisis in Myanmar. The Anwar administration is more inclined to resolve concerns with Myanmar at the bilateral level, such as repatriation and practical security cooperation, according to Khoo. In recent months, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam have hosted Min Aung Hlaing, while Asean foreign ministers had initiated what officials described as a “calibrated re-engagement” with his government in July. While maintaining open lines of communication was crucial, allowing bilateral interests to drive normalisation without progress on ending the civil war, dialogue and humanitarian access was not an ideal way to deal with the Myanmar crisis, she said. “Taken together, they [these meetings] begin to look like a gradual normalisation of his [Min Aung Hlaing’s] government without a corresponding improvement on the ground. That weakens Asean’s collective leverage,” Khoo said. On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR) urged Malaysia not to confer legitimacy on Myanmar’s leadership by signing agreements or issuing joint statements. “[Malaysia should] extend no further invitations to Min Aung Hlaing,” the advocacy group said, calling on Kuala Lumpur to suspend repatriations until the safety of the returnees could be guaranteed. “Malaysia should not be receiving Min Aung Hlaing at all. Every red carpet rolled out for him tells the people of Myanmar, who live under air strikes and forced conscription, that the region has made its peace with what is being done to them,” said APHR chair Mercy Chriesty Barends. Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia, said Asean and the global community had failed to take firm action to improve the Myanmar situation. He pointed out that Malaysia also sent back large numbers of Vietnamese boatpeople in the 1970s and 1980s. “As with previous spans of military rule in Myanmar, the regime will gradually come to be accepted, or at least tolerated, by most if not all,” Oh said. “That’s just the cold, harsh fact of realpolitik.” Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute, said Bangladesh, which shelters more than 1.2 million Rohingya from Myanmar, had taken a different approach by not returning displaced Myanmar nationals to their country. “This is more of a one-of-a-kind situation in which Anwar is seeking to bolster his domestic political credentials in response to recent setbacks at the ballot box,” Marston said. Following the ruling Pakatan Harapan coalition’s losses in elections in Negeri Sembilan and other states, Anwar has rolled out populist policies and promised to carry out various reforms. While Malaysia continued to focus on the Five-Point Consensus in line with Asean’s stance, Marston said the bloc and Kuala Lumpur differed in terms of their actions in dealing with Myanmar. “[This] leaves room for ambiguity and uncertainty regarding the direction of their policies,” he added.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong’s AI city brain must understand how people really speak
description: A city brain that grasps communication which moves between languages is likelier to make good decisions as it centres how people live, work and interact.
content: Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s vision of an “AI city brain” is bold and timely. An integrated system linking data across transport, public works, environmental monitoring and emergency response could help Hong Kong manage risks more proactively and coordinate services more effectively. The initiative is highly commendable. It also raises a critical question: can a city brain truly understand a city if it does not understand how its people communicate? The truth is that communication is rarely monolingual in Hong Kong. People like myself move between Cantonese, Mandarin, English and other linguistic resources every day, often within a single conversation. This is not a problem to be solved. On the contrary, it is one of Hong Kong’s greatest strengths. The city’s advantage lies in its biliterate and trilingual population. When policymakers discuss multilingualism, they often focus on how many languages people can speak. An equally important question is how people move between them. A multilingual person possesses multiple languages. A translanguaging person draws on them dynamically according to context, audience and purpose. Language use is not like a fixed set of separate mental compartments. It is a flexible system that allows people to convey and negotiate meaning, relationships and identity in real time. The distinction is not merely semantic. A system built around multilingualism might classify a caller as being “Cantonese-speaking” or “English-speaking” and route the call accordingly. A system built around translanguaging would recognise the same caller might move between languages within a single sentence and that the movement itself could carry information. The first approach treats language as a fixed attribute, the second one treats it as a dynamic resource. This matters because the proposed AI city brain will interact with human behaviour, not just infrastructure. The government should therefore include linguists and cognitive scientists in its development. Language is not simply another data set. It is one of the primary ways through which people experience public services, report emergencies and communicate their needs. To see why this matters in practice, consider a realistic emergency scenario. During a typhoon, a hotel receptionist calls 999. She begins in Cantonese, switches briefly to English to describe technical details about the building, then returns to Cantonese to reassure frightened guests nearby. The information conveyed is not merely linguistic. The language shifts themselves reveal context, urgency and social dynamics. An AI system designed around rigid monolingual categories might capture the words but miss part of the meaning that could help save lives at a critical moment. A language-aware system should not replace the human operator. It should preserve the linguistic context of the call, flag possible misunderstandings and suggest clarification questions. This is not about automating empathy. It is about giving human decision-makers better information so they can exercise judgment more effectively. Emergency management is particularly relevant because the first phase of the AI city brain focuses on the Security Bureau’s Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre. In crises, communication can become more fluid rather than less. Research suggests people do not necessarily choose languages deliberately under stress. They draw on whatever resources are most accessible at the moment. This does not mean artificial intelligence (AI) should infer people’s intentions from every language shift. Rather, it should recognise when multilingual communication creates uncertainty, preserve the original wording and encourage clarification rather than premature conclusions. In emergency response, recognising uncertainty can be just as important as recognising meaning. This is especially important for vulnerable populations. Public systems are not designed only for the majority who can navigate them easily. They must also serve those who struggle most when circumstances become difficult. No one should be left behind. The same logic extends beyond emergency response. Consider Macau’s gaming sector. A dealer might interact with a Mandarin-speaking visitor, an English-speaking tourist and a Cantonese-speaking local within a short period. The skill involved is not simply speaking three languages. It is moving between them smoothly while managing expectations, relationships and cultural cues. As AI systems become more involved in customer support, public services and decision-making, they will increasingly encounter similar patterns across the Greater Bay Area. Should these systems merely classify people according to language categories, or should they recognise how language is actually used in real life? Hong Kong is uniquely placed to address this challenge. Our competitive advantage is not simply that many residents know more than one language. It is that people routinely connect linguistic, cultural and professional worlds. Cantonese anchors our everyday life, English connects the city globally and Mandarin links Hong Kong to national development. Much of the city’s success comes from moving between these worlds rather than remaining within one of them. An effective AI city brain should reflect that reality. A city brain that understands multilingual communication is more likely to make sound decisions because it is built around how people actually live, work and interact. Hong Kong’s future competitiveness might depend not on speaking more languages but on understanding the value of moving between them. If our AI city brain is intended to serve and understand the city better, it should also understand the people who make the city what it is.

title: US military in Japan’s Okinawa imposes night curfew after marine’s arrest over murder
description: Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson said ‘incidents like this demand we pause for reflection’.
content: The US military in Okinawa will impose a curfew from midnight to 5am for a month starting Friday following the arrest of a marine on suspicion of robbing and murdering a local woman, its regional coordinator said on Tuesday. All US military personnel on Okinawa will also observe a 48-hour operational pause from noon on Wednesday, during which there will be “no off-base liberty, including a complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base”, said Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson, Okinawa area coordinator of US Forces Japan. “Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Watson said of the murder case. “Discipline is the individual and collective commitment to make sound decisions, look after one another, and always do what is right.” The announcement came after local police arrested Devin Ballard, a 20-year-old US marine stationed in the southern island prefecture, on suspicion of robbing and murdering Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha on Saturday. The case sparked outrage in Okinawa, which hosts the bulk of US military installations in Japan. Meanwhile on Wednesday, Okinawa Governor Genta Koja held talks with Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo, where the latter vowed that the government would discuss with the United States what effective steps to take to prevent such incidents from happening again. “Every time an incident occurs, we have been calling for measures to prevent a recurrence. I cannot help but say that the US military’s enforcement of discipline and human rights education are not functioning at all,” Koja said. Koja also called for a review of the bilateral Status of Forces Agreement, under which US military authorities retain custody of US military personnel they arrest for suspected off-duty crimes while those arrested by Japanese authorities remain in Japanese custody. In response to a question about whether the restriction on Japan’s judicial power under the agreement is a factor behind repeated occurrences of crimes and accidents caused by US military personnel, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi on Tuesday said the government will “continuously examine” the nature of the agreement. Motegi added that Japan will discuss with the US “effective” measures to prevent crimes by US military personnel.

title: Hong Kong’s MPF has gained nearly HK$100b this year despite September loss: report
description: MPF members made gains of over HK$20,000 on average in the first nine months of 2026, despite losing HK$5,000 in September, report finds.
content: Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) recorded a loss in September but still made overall gains of nearly HK$100 billion (US$12.8 billion) over the first nine months of the year, according to data from MPF Ratings released on Wednesday. The 382 investment funds under the MPF schemes delivered a 6.2 per cent average return in the first nine months, despite losing 1.47 per cent in September, the consultancy found. In monetary terms, they earned HK$96.9 billion over the first three quarters but lost HK$25.1 billion last month. The MPF is the city’s compulsory retirement savings scheme and covers 4.97 million members. On average, each MPF member saw their pension savings lose HK$5,060 in September, but they still gained HK$20,161 over the first nine months, the MPF Ratings data showed. “September saw concurrent losses in equities and bonds. With multi-decade-high US Treasury yields, inflation concerns and economic slowdown risks, it may appear that conventional diversification strategies are ineffective,” said Francis Chung, chairman of MPF Ratings. Chung, however, urged investors to maintain their diversification and long-term investment views and not worry too much about short-term market volatility driven by interest rate moves and geopolitical tensions. Pension regulator the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority (MPFA) also warned against a short-term strategy for MPF investments. Such an approach could lead to members “buying high and selling low” and incurring unnecessary losses, the MPFA said in a statement on Wednesday. “MPF is a long-term investment spanning over 40 years,” the statement said. “Attempts to predict the future market trend would prove to be futile.” Instead, members should diversify their MPF investments to mitigate risks, it added. Total MPF assets stood at HK$1.68 trillion (US$215 billion) as of the end of September, up HK$130 billion from the end of last year, reflecting investment gains in the first nine months of this year and ongoing member contributions, the consultancy said. On average, each member had HK$338,950 in their MPF account as of the end of September. Hong Kong and mainland China equity funds – the most popular investment choice among MPF members, accounting for more than one-third of total assets – lost 3 per cent in September but gained 1.6 per cent overall in the first nine months, the data showed. This reflects wider market performance, as Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index lost 3.7 per cent in September but still rose 6.4 per cent over the first nine months of 2026. In September, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate for the first time in three years, signalling the start of a new cycle of rate rises and causing global stock and bond markets to become more volatile. Money market funds, which invest in bank deposits, were the best performers in September, with a modest 0.2 per cent gain, while yuan bond funds posted a 0.1 per cent gain. Every other fund category recorded a loss in September. On a nine-month basis, Asia equity funds were the strongest performers with a return of 24.3 per cent, followed by Japan equity funds with an average gain of 20.8 per cent. Global equity funds rounded out the top three with a 13.4 per cent average gain. Global bond funds were the worst performers over the nine-month period, falling 3 per cent, followed by Hong Kong dollar bond funds, which were down 2.5 per cent, and Asia bond funds, which lost 2.3 per cent. In the first nine months, mixed-asset funds – which invest in both equities and bonds – posted average gains between 7.9 per cent and 9.5 per cent, with funds with higher stock exposures performing better, MPF Ratings data showed. The default investment strategy (DIS) fund – a type of mixed-asset fund that automatically switches investments between stocks and bonds based on age-based risk profiles – also reported a gain in the first nine months. The DIS with a higher stock exposure had a 7.3 per cent return in the first nine months, while the one with more bond exposure reported a 0.7 per cent investment gain. Chung expected the MPF to post a positive return for 2026 as a whole.

title: China’s DeepZang AI aims to transform Tibetan language tech, promote ethnic unity
description: Seminar attended by the LLM’s developer discusses expanding multi-dialect translation, public service integration and cross-regional AI.
content: Creators of China’s first Tibetan-language AI model have pledged to speed up upgrades aimed at promoting ethnic integration. Approaches to advancing the large language model, DeepZang, were discussed at a seminar on Monday that brought together representatives from research institutes, universities and enterprises, according to state-run portal Chinanews.com. It said the event held in Hohhot, in China’s northern Inner Mongolia autonomous region, addressed issues such as improving Tibetan artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and expanding the model’s application into multilingual simultaneous interpretation. Speakers included Tenzin Norbu, the model’s founder, who vowed to continuously refine Tibetan AI technologies and advance their practical use. He also emphasised the use of technological innovation to “foster ethnic interaction and integration” and support digital development in ethnic minority regions. DeepZang’s launch in March came roughly three years after the unveiling of Monlam AI, a Tibetan-language LLM developed by Monlam Tibetan IT Research Centre, a non-profit organisation based in Dharamsala – the Indian hillside town that has hosted the 14th Dalai Lama and the Tibetan administration-in-exile since 1960. Tibet remains a top priority in ethnic and religious affairs for Beijing, which has consistently bolstered domestic Tibetan studies to regain control of international discourse on the issue. DeepZang is part of this broader effort to reshape global narratives around Tibet with its own authoritative data and technology. These efforts are also reflected in Beijing’s push since 2023 to use the romanised Pinyin name “Xizang” instead of “Tibet” in English articles, projecting its sovereign narrative globally. China’s policies in ethnic minority regions including Tibet have been a major focus of Western governments and rights groups, which repeatedly accuse China of human rights violations. Beijing steadfastly denies any wrongdoing. In March, China passed its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which is designed to counter Western ideological influence and lay the legal foundation for assimilating minority groups. The law took effect in July. DeepZang has been trained on nearly 70 million Tibetan texts and over 30,500 hours of audio covering the language’s three main dialects. It powers AI chat, real-time translation and speech-to-text features across Tibetan, Chinese and English.
