Tibetan AI technologies have long faced low-resource challenges due to unique linguistic structures, dialect variations and scarce digital corpora, making precision and versatility difficult to achieve. Monday’s Chinanews.com report said that DeepZang had continuously broken bottlenecks, “bridging key technical voids in the field and bolstering China’s technology ecosystem for ethnic language AI”. As cited in the report, Tenzin Norbu noted that AI development in other Chinese ethnic minority languages also faced low-resource constraints, making cross-regional and cross-linguistic collaboration essential. The seminar also outlined future plans to integrate DeepZang into sectors including public services, education, healthcare and local governance, while “empowering the digital transmission of fine traditional Tibetan culture and ensuring that all ethnic groups equitably share the benefits of technological progress”.

title: Land sales offer only temporary relief for West Kowloon arts hub, experts warn
description: Property development cannot replace a sustainable long-term funding model for the West Kowloon Cultural District, experts say.
content: Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District is betting on property development to ease its financial pressures amid a widening operating deficit, but experts have warned that land sales will only provide temporary relief and cannot replace a sustainable long-term funding model for the arts hub. The warning comes as the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority prepares to tender a prime residential site in the first half of next year, a potentially lucrative project that property experts expect to attract interest from major developers. Norry Lee, a senior director at property consultancy JLL, said the site’s location and potential harbour views made it attractive, particularly for larger flats targeted at wealthier buyers. “If you are talking about larger flats, especially those with sea views, there will definitely be demand,” he said, adding that the development was likely to appeal to major developers given its scale and prime location. The development will have a total gross floor area of about 129,000 square metres (1.39 million square feet), including 108,000 square metres of residential space and about 20,000 square metres for retail, dining and entertainment. Lee said the residential portion would account for most of the project’s value, with the commercial component relatively small by comparison. He estimated the development could be worth close to HK$20 billion (US$2.55 billion), based on an accommodation value of about HK$15,000 per square foot and recent transactions for nearby areas. “If you have HK$20 billion and can generate a 5 per cent return, that is HK$1 billion a year,” he said, noting that this would roughly match the authority’s latest annual operating deficit. But Lee said the bigger question was what the authority did with the proceeds after the development was sold. “If it is a land sale, it is a one-off,” he said. “Once you sell it, it’s gone.” Lee said investing the proceeds or otherwise using them to generate recurring returns could provide a more lasting source of funding for operations. The authority recorded an underlying operating deficit of HK$998 million in 2025-26, up by 30 per cent from a year earlier, even as self-generated operating income rose by 19 per cent to a record HK$768 million. It expects to receive an upfront payment when the Zone 2B project is awarded, followed by further instalments as the development progresses. The authority has also turned to borrowing to bridge the period before major commercial projects begin generating income, securing a HK$3 billion 10-year loan facility from ICBC (Asia) and issuing two five-year bonds totalling HK$700 million. Lawmaker and town planner Andrew Lam Siu-lo, a former authority board member, said using property income to subsidise cultural facilities had been part of the district’s financial model from the outset. He noted that the property market had stabilised, improving prospects for next year. “I don’t think it is being too optimistic, because it really would be a turning point,” Lam said of the tender. But it was important to distinguish between the district’s capital and operating needs, he added. The district still required funding to complete the remaining facilities and related works, so proceeds from property development could first help meet capital requirements before any surplus was available to support daily operations, Lam said. How long the proceeds could sustain the district should therefore depend on the eventual tender outcome and how the funds were managed, he noted. “For its long-term operation, stable revenue ultimately cannot come from one-off income,” Lam said, adding that the district needed to strengthen its core revenue streams, including ticket sales, sponsorship and cultural merchandise. He also rejected the idea that cultural institutions could realistically be expected to fully pay for themselves. “If anyone assumed that a cultural district could be entirely self-sufficient, that was a misjudgment,” he said. “I don’t see government museums or performing arts venues achieving a balance between revenue and expenditure. This isn’t unique to Hong Kong; it’s the same globally.” Cultural policy advocate Ada Wong Ying-kay, who served on several committees and boards during the district’s early development, went further, saying criticism of the arts hub’s finances had been “very mean”. Wong compared the district with museums, performing arts venues and libraries operated by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, saying public funding of such facilities had long been accepted without an expectation they should recover their full costs. Against that, she described the district’s overall cost recovery rate of about 40 per cent as “amazing”. She also pointed to efforts to increase income through merchandise, venue rentals, commercial events and fundraising, describing its approach to operating cultural facilities as entrepreneurial. “Almost all cultural institutions around the world, whether of a similar scale to West Kowloon, larger or smaller, cannot be financially sustainable on their own,” she said. Major cultural institutions instead tended to rely on hybrid funding models combining public funding, commercial revenue, corporate support and philanthropic endowments, she added. Wong argued that the HK$21.6 billion lump-sum funding granted by the government in 2008 should be viewed more as an infrastructure investment than an expectation that the district would thereafter operate without public support. “Would [other world cities] say: ‘The HK$21.6 billion was more than a decade ago, and now that you’ve used it up, go and sell land’?” she added. Wong said relying on property sales alone merely postponed the question of how the district should ultimately be funded. “You asked whether selling land is sustainable. The answer is no,” she said. “However many sites there are, eventually you will run out of them.” Hong Kong needed a broader discussion about how its flagship cultural institutions should be funded, particularly as the city sought to strengthen its role as an East-meets-West centre for international cultural exchange as laid out in the city’s first five-year plan, as well as by Beijing, she said.

title: As bear attacks rise in Japan, fearful residents change daily routines
description: A foreign resident who has been attacked multiple times says he now carries bear spray and a baseball bat when he visits his lodge in Gunma.
content: Jeff Kingston used to take long walks with his dogs across the hills of Gunma in central Japan. But not this year. He has good reason. Kingston says he has encountered bears in those mountains more than 100 times over the years and been charged by aggressive bears around a dozen times. In 2014, a black bear knocked him down and attacked him across the skull with its claws, leaving a gash that required nine stitches. “This year, I have actively refrained from going into the hills precisely because I want to avoid encounters,” said Kingston, an American academic who lives in Tokyo but has a lodge in Gunma. “And when I do go, I always carry bear spray and a baseball bat just in case.” His caution reflects a wider concern in Japan, where bear encounters have surged in recent years, including in residential areas and farmland, prompting authorities to warn people to take extra care as the animals prepare for winter. The rise in encounters has exposed a more fundamental problem – Japan does not have a clear picture of how many bears it has, where they are moving or how local populations are changing. A record 13 people died in bear attacks in the 2025 financial year, with 238 reported injuries, while the public logged more than 50,000 bear sightings over the period. In the present financial year so far, there have been six fatalities and 49 people injured. Around 60 per cent of attacks have happened in mountain forests, while up to 30 per cent occurred in residential areas or farmland. Prefectural authorities across Japan are warning the public to be cautious over the coming months as bears fatten up before going into hibernation, with competition for food increasing the likelihood of encounters. In some parts of Japan, the risk is more acute because the yields of some staple crops have been poor this year. Gunma prefecture cautioned residents and visitors on Monday that acorn and chestnut crops had fallen recently, and as such, hungry bears were likely to seek food in country villages and even the suburbs of large towns. The prefecture has created an online map plotting bear sightings and offered tips on what to do in the event of an encounter. People are instructed to back away slowly while facing a bear, avoid making loud noises that might provoke an attack and, if possible, keep an obstacle between themselves and the animal. Kingston said the changing risks had led many people to alter their routines to avoid potential bear encounters. “I was talking a few days ago with a lady in her 80s in the village, and she told me that she was cutting down all her persimmon trees because bears like the fruit at this time of year, while a hunter had to be called into another village nearby because a bear was in the graveyard,” he said. Kingston’s own brush with a bear could have ended far more seriously, as he was only saved when his dogs came to his rescue and drove the bear away. Just last week, Kingston said he suffered a nightmare about being attacked by a bear. In an effort to get a better grasp of the number of bears in Japan, as well as how far they can roam, the density of local populations and other data that might help reduce encounters with humans, the Environment Ministry in June began a comprehensive survey to replace piecemeal efforts that had previously taken place at the prefectural level. More than 800 automatic trail cameras have been placed in forests, managed woodland and mountainous areas in the northern Niigata prefecture and the six prefectures that make up the Tohoku region. The ministry intends to expand the programme to other prefectures with bear populations in the next four years. “The ministry is using two methods to monitor the bear population,” said Hifumi Tsuruga, a bear expert at the Hokkaido Research Organisation. “The camera traps allow researchers to identify each bear by the unique markings it has on its chest and it can then be tracked.” A second method is placing hair traps to catch the hair of passing bears, which is then used to obtain their DNA, and combining this with statistical modelling to estimate the number of bears. “Before, there was no common method for gathering this data and monitoring the bears, as it was all done at the prefectural level,” Tsuruga said. A fragmented system could lead to a miscounting of bears when they cross prefectural boundaries, giving an inaccurate picture of the total population, according to Tsuruga. Prefectures also used different methods to track numbers, with some preferring camera traps to statistical models, leading to further inconsistencies, he added. Hokkaido is not presently taking part in the scheme. But Tsuruga said there had been a sharp increase in bear sightings across Japan’s most northerly prefecture. “Hokkaido killed more than 2,000 bears last year, so the population certainly fell, but I do not believe even that many being culled will lead to a dramatic decrease in the total number of bears,” he said. “This year, the situation has been calmer. I do not expect that they will cull as many as this year.” Tsuruga said that the fruit that bears enjoyed – such as persimmon – was in short supply going into winter and this might encourage more of them to venture closer to human habitation. On Friday, a man driving in a rural district of Hokkaido encountered a bear and its cub in the road, with the mother caught on a camera repeatedly attacking the vehicle. Last month, a black bear was spotted on a camera on Mount Takao, a popular day-tripping and hiking spot in western Tokyo. City officials declared a level one alert and told visitors to exercise caution in the area.

title: Hong Kong cycling coach in hurry for success after hiring France Olympic superstar
description: Herve Dagorne in race against time to produce champion from city, as Frenchman welcomes compatriot Kevin Sireau to world-class coaching team.
content: After completing the interminable process of assembling a world-class coaching team that “knows what it is to win”, Herve Dagorne said he needed to “hurry up” and deliver a champion Hong Kong cyclist before time runs out on his reign. The appointment of two-time Olympic silver medallist Kevin Sireau to lead the city’s sprint squad was the final piece in a particularly tricky jigsaw that head coach Dagorne has been attempting to piece together for the past two years. Also a three-time world champion, Sireau began work on Monday, joining a staff that also features Mickael Bouget, the former Swiss track cycling head coach, and Remi Anase, who helped mastermind fellow Frenchman Benjamin Thomas’s 2024 omnium Olympic gold. Also enlisted are Cheung King-wai, the 2006 Asian Games points race champion, Anthony Peden, the ex-New Zealand sprint head coach who led Hong Kong to a shock men’s team sprint bronze from the recent Games, and road endurance chief Ben Kersten, a 2006 Commonwealth Games gold medallist. Having previously come close to capturing 2004 Olympic team pursuit champion Bradley McGee, and another Australian in Tim Decker, who had an eleventh–hour change of heart, Dagorne said he had “slept a bit better in the past two weeks now that we have everyone on board”. While not going so far as to say that his elite crew was tasked with turning water into wine, Dagorne acknowledged that “we don’t have the greatest physical talent in Hong Kong”. Nonetheless, in Ceci Lee Sze-wing and a small pool of promising youngsters, Dagorne reckons the city has sufficient talent for him to start doing more than just “reaching my KPIs”. He met his five-medal target from the Asian Games bang on. Himself a two-time Olympian, Dagorne said: “I wanted coaches who know what the Olympics are; what it is to win big races. “Most of all, though, I wanted them to live in Hong Kong, to invest in the culture here and to share the passion I have for the city and the squad: then we can work on a long-term vision. “If Hong Kong Sports Institute [HKSI] lets me work with the team until my retirement, I will build something that has a legacy.” Dagorne was coaching France’s endurance riders, including omnium silver medallist Bryan Coquard, when Sireau bagged the second of his Olympic team sprint silvers in 2012. “I’ve always had a good relationship with him, and it’s a real pleasure to have him with us,” Dagorne said, adding that the 39-year-old, who claimed his first Olympic medal in Beijing in 2008, “did not get all the tools he expected” during nearly three years in charge of India’s track sprint squad. “He’s a young coach, we’ll support him, and HKSI will give him all the tools,” Dagorne added. The manner in which Dagorne and his staff are squeezing every drop from their resources brings to mind the phenomenon of “marginal gains”, popularised by divisive former British Cycling and Team Sky manager Dave Brailsford. “We’re building something to train a champion in Hong Kong,” Dagorne said. “There’s huge motivation among all the coaches to use the scientific assessments, the nutrition service and the fitness training centre. “We have the multidisciplinary team to help us because we don’t have the greatest physical talent”. Indeed, Dagorne said he currently had nobody at his disposal who boasted either the “massive talent” or “natural genes” of Sarah Lee Wai-sze, Hong Kong’s bronze medallist from the 2012 and 2020 Olympics. “Ceci has the potential but she’s not there yet … so we need to be good in every aspect,” the Frenchman added. Poised to turn 60 in January, Dagorne is keenly aware of the march of Father Time. Appointed in March 2024, six years after he joined the city coaching staff, following three years as Kazakhstan head coach, Dagorne said: “HKSI rules don’t allow you to continue coaching past 65, so I need to hurry up and continue the work. “We’ve had some very good results in the past two years, but I couldn’t do everything I wanted. We reached my KPIs, but it’s not enough. The Olympics are ‘tomorrow’, and it’ll be very hard, but we have to be ready to perform. “We also need to increase the detection and development of young athletes. “I don’t treat this like a job, it’s a passion, and I’m lucky that [my bosses] trust me for the moment.” What of Ceci Lee, one of Hong Kong’s greatest current athletes, but also one of its biggest sporting conundrums? An Asian Games Madison silver medallist alongside Chloe Leung Wing-yee, Lee was utterly dejected after some of her old mental demons returned in an omnium event where she had publicly targeted victory but managed only bronze. “For a gold medal, it’s not enough to be good physically, which she was,” Dagorne said, referencing the super-fit Lee winning the tempo race in the four-discipline competition. “There are different pillars of performance, like technique and psychology, and she doesn’t have those.” Dagorne drew a clear distinction between Lee, who “was stressed about whether she’d get gold”, and the titanic Yumi Kajihara, who was not in peak condition but “hungry for gold and only calculating how to win”, as she stormed to her third straight title. While Lee will “continue to work with [HKSI] staff” to convert the tension that still surfaces around major competitions into “strength and motivation”, the 25-year-old’s immediate objective is to string together a series of displays that reflect her ability at next week’s UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai. “We’re taking care of her wellness, because she’s really disappointed, but she did come back with two medals,” Dagorne said, adding that Lee was capable of registering top-12 finishes, at least, in the global event. “She has the physical and technical skill to really compete in the scratch and elimination races,” Dagorne said, pointing to the three UCI Track World Cup medals that Lee claimed this year. Charles Ng Pak-hang will compete in the world championships individual pursuit, but Hong Kong do not have sufficient ranking points for Franco Chu Tsun-wai to go in the omnium, after the 25-year-old’s Asian Games silver from the event “came easy to him”, according to Dagorne. “He was flying and in a flow state,” the coach said. “He was so strong that he could commit some small tactical errors. All day, he was confident, sometimes overconfident, but it was a great performance.” Regardless, Dagorne said there was a “big gap, physically” between Chu and the world’s best riders. “Our next target is for him to reach world level, especially now that we have Olympic qualification coming,” Dagorne said. A large 2028 qualifying points bounty is on offer in Shanghai, with the next chance for the city cyclists to fill their boots coming in the Asian Track Championships in Malaysia from January 31. Hong Kong’s endurance riders will stage a camp on Hainan Island from November 16 to December 10, then transfer to Tasmania for a heap of races in the Tascarnivals series. From there, they will link up in Adelaide with the sprint contingent, who will undergo the first part of their winter training in Melbourne. For Dagorne, there is no time to waste.

title: IMHO, these 6 formal phrases for professional success are the GOAT
description: Internet slang doesn’t belong in formal writing, so check out these tips for communicating in a clear, impactful way.
content:
In today’s fast-paced digital world, effective communication is more important than ever. As we navigate different forms of interaction – such as emails, reports or formal presentations – the choice of language plays a crucial role in conveying professionalism and clarity.
The use of abbreviations and slang can undermine the seriousness of our message. By understanding and using full words and formal phrases rather than casual shorthand, we can ensure our messages are received with the gravity and respect intended.
Meaning: considered the absolute best in a specific field Alternatives: champion, best, number one or greatest of all time Example: When it comes to basketball, Michael Jordan is the greatest of all time.
Meaning: to see or read something so funny that you can’t help but laugh Alternative: use the whole phrase instead of the acronym Example: That joke was so funny that I couldn’t help but laugh out loud.
Meaning: masterful, outstanding or highly successful Alternatives: excellent, amazing, extraordinary or spectacular Example: Have you seen that new zombie movie? It’s amazing!
Meaning: by reason of; due to Alternatives: “Because” is acceptable in some writing – just spell the word out. However, phrases like “due to” sound more professional. Example: The game was cancelled due to the rain.
Meaning: used either to label a brief summary of a long text or to complain that a passage of writing is too lengthy Alternatives: summary, recap, review or rundown Example: Give me a recap of the book; I didn’t read it!
Meaning: in my personal view; I think Alternatives: If you are writing a persuasive essay, you can use the phrase “in my opinion”. For other forms of formal writing, choose phrases that show there is evidence to back your claims, such as “based on my assessment”. Example: Based on my assessment of the data, Hong Kong’s summers are getting hotter.

title: Meet Ella Bridgland, founder of Studio Ella in Hong Kong
description: The interior architect, who moved to the city from London, crafts high-end interiors, blending art and emotion in challenging urban spaces.
content: Formerly an associate at Joyce Wang Studio, interior architect Ella Bridgland now heads up her own firm, Studio Ella, which she started in 2022. Bridgland relocated to Hong Kong in 2017 after having worked for some of London’s most prominent design and architecture firms and has since carved out a niche for herself in the city’s design scene, specialising in high-end residential and boutique commercial projects. Beyond offering bespoke furniture design, art advisory and interior architecture services, Studio Ella is also an art consultancy and sells a number of homeware products. Last year, Studio Ella unveiled its first luxury show flat commissions at 33 Kennedy Road, a project which highlighted Bridgland’s particularly personalised approach to design, as well as her eye for art. Works by local artists such as Arrow Lai Siu-wai and Kanny Yeung aren’t seen as just decorative but are finishing touches which round out the personality of the space, each unit being inspired by a different aesthetic depending on who might be living there – be it a young professional going for a chic, modernist studio, or a couple looking for a calm, minimalist home. For Bridgland, art helps not only to transform the mood of a space but also to create a sense of hierarchy through the addition of considered focal points, injecting personality into a home. This human touch is also what makes Studio Ella one of the most exciting design firms to watch in Hong Kong today. Even in a place where property values are often seen as markers of status and the norm of vertical living makes quality design uniquely challenging, Studio Ella projects prioritise emotional resonance above all else. A designer with internationally lauded expertise and experience, Bridgland cites the city’s “addictive” pace and energy as the reason for its design culture, adding that it “makes things feel possible”. “[Hong Kong] is constantly being built, stripped back and remade,” she continues, “and that gives the city a particular creative tension. That immediacy, combined with the city’s silly heat, density and ‘can-do’ attitude, makes design here feel instinctive, physical and alive.” However, she acknowledges that “the city needs to do more to encourage creative vocations and attract international talent. It’s a hard grind, requires passion and an absolute dedication to detail. It pulls you in every direction all at once. This needs to be recognised and rewarded.” On where the future of Hong Kong design is headed, Bridgland writes that “the proximity to possibility” is still what drives the city to embrace innovation and move forward. “Hong Kong has ideas, ambition and international perspective,” she adds. “The Greater Bay Area gives us extraordinary access to making, prototyping and turbo speed.” As for what comes next? “I would like to see the city treat design not merely as superfluous decoration,” Bridgland says, “but as part of the city’s cultural infrastructure – something worth investing in, protecting and striving for better. Function is the very minimum. It has to look great, be beautiful and improve the quality of lives at every scale.”

title: Russia says no risk of epidemic following plague institute worker’s death
description: Russia’s health watchdog says it is winding down precautionary measures it put in place and has shared its latest information with the WHO.
content: Russia’s health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death. Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has ‌prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump, and which saw about 200 people initially placed in quarantine. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said in a statement it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO. No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90 per cent of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens. It said Shipilova had been ⁠vaccinated and had therefore been “immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked”. It did not say though what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how ‌she fell ill. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the WHO in Geneva, said in a statement on X earlier on Wednesday that his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened. “WHO has requested further information ‌to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia ⁠of undetermined cause,” he said. “Timely, complete ⁠and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed ‌the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures. When asked about the WHO’s request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it ‌came to ‌using media reports as a reference for what was happening. “There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting ‌about this situation is false information,” Peskov said. He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a ⁠Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO’s questions. Some Western media outlets have reported – citing unnamed “Russian media” – that a second person in ⁠Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague. Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died, although some bloggers on social media were making – without evidence – such assertions. Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had ‌nothing further to add on the matter beyond ‌what Tedros – who was due to give a press conference later on Wednesday – had already posted on X. Tedros’ call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident. The European Union on Wednesday also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the reported death. “We think that it’s necessary to have reliable epidemiological and microbiological findings,” European Commission spokeswoman Eva Hrncirova said. The EU was in contact with experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control on the matter, she said, adding “we follow the situation very closely”. Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or Covid-19. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: In pictures: the evolution of school uniforms in Hong Kong
description: From traditional qipao designs to navy-inspired sailor collars, how Hong Kong school uniforms evolved through changing culture, campus rules and shifting global fashion trends.
content: Since 1918, when St Paul’s Girls’ College (now St Paul’s Co-educational College) became the first Hong Kong school to introduce a mandatory dress code – a qipao top with matching trousers or skirt, to build a unified identity – school uniforms have become a highly visible facet of the city’s cultural identity. Uniforms became mandatory in virtually all primary and secondary schools after the second world war, when a massive wave of migrants from mainland China caused student enrolment to explode. The outfits were intended to promote equality, erase social-class indicators and demarcate large student bodies. Whereas boys tended to wear sharp, suit-like outfits and girls signature qipaos, New Method College broke ground in the 1970s with Japanese sailor-inspired uniforms while international schools introduced a more relaxed, casual dress code. Today, school-uniform culture has shifted towards functionality and comfort, with many schools favouring breathable, low-maintenance designs over strict formality. Manufacturers such as Kam Lun Tailors and Fung Cheong Shun have witnessed this evolution first-hand, having continuously offered modern solutions to meet the needs of schools and their students. Here’s a look at how South China Morning Post photographers have captured the evolution of school uniforms over the decades, reflecting changing youth culture, campus rules and shifting global fashion trends.

title: Editorial | 3 years on, Hong Kong’s investment body has proved its worth
description: As HKIC helps the city show that ‘effective market’ and ‘capable government’ can coexist, it must also improve transparency.
content: Three years after Clara Chan Ka-chai took the helm as its first chief executive, Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC) has proved its worth despite a difficult global economic climate. Her reappointment as chief executive for a further three-year term, beginning on October 9 is a fitting acknowledgement of that record. When HKIC was unveiled in the 2022 policy address, it had its critics. Some argued that Hong Kong’s prosperity was built on laissez-faire, not government investment, and that the state should leave capital allocation to the market. But times have changed, not only in Hong Kong and mainland China but around the world. There is a clear case for a well-run investment company, established and wholly owned by the government, that can make better use of fiscal reserves to strengthen the local economy and its industries. HKIC is not a conventional sovereign wealth fund, and not merely because Hong Kong is a city rather than a city state. Singapore’s Temasek seeks long-term profitability with a global reach, to benefit Singaporeans over generations. HKIC, which was given HK$62 billion in initial capital, has a more extensive mandate to raise local productivity and competitiveness, not profitability alone. Its focus on hard and core technology, biotechnology and green energy is meant to nurture strategic industries, placing long-term value for Hong Kong alongside financial return. By the measures it has published, HKIC has done well on several fronts. As of the end of 2025, the net internal rate of return on its portfolio had reached 14 per cent. Total investment income for 2025 exceeded HK$6.4 billion, a year-on-year increase of about 175 per cent. The corporation has invested in more than 200 companies. Eleven are already listed in Hong Kong, and more than 30 have submitted or plan to submit listing applications in the city this year. The most quoted figure is that every Hong Kong dollar invested by HKIC has attracted more than eight dollars in international long-term market capital, up from over four dollars in March 2025. That multiplier deserves some caveats. It appears to measure private co-investment drawn in alongside public money. Moreover, 71 per cent of the portfolio was placed in hard and core technology, as designed, and since most of these holdings are unlisted, the reported gains rest on valuations, not realised returns. Even with these qualifications, the figures are impressive for a young investment company, publicly owned or not. As the portfolio matures, HKIC should disclose more accordingly. Realised and unrealised gains ought to be reported separately. The public should be told how unlisted investments are valued, and how the corporation weighs commercial returns against strategic goals as a whole. None of this implies any shortcoming, only that public trust is built on transparency. Such detail matters all the more because HKIC’s role is set to grow in importance. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan states explicitly that the government will use HKIC as “patient capital” to actively pursue co-investments. The 2026-27 budget, for its part, said the government would arrange for a capital injection into the corporation “in a timely manner”. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has insisted that “the five-year plan is not a planned economy”. HKIC is where that claim will be tested as it becomes a key facilitator in the growth of the city’s sectors in finance, innovation and technology, and emerging industries. This, of course, also means actively supporting the development of the tech-oriented Northern Metropolis and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area. If HKIC maintains its investment discipline and stays independent, it will demonstrate that an “effective market” and a “capable government” can coexist. HKIC has earned the confidence expressed in its chief executive’s reappointment. It has deployed capital carefully and patiently, drawn in serious international partners and helped replenish the city’s listing pipeline. Those are real achievements for such a young institution. But as more public money flows its way, public transparency is expected to grow in step.

title: How Broadway Cinematheque, Hong Kong’s longest-running art house cinema, is thriving at 30
description: Opened in 1996 in Yau Ma Tei, Broadway Cinematheque continues to defy the streaming era with independent classics and fresh local voices.
content: While cinemas worldwide have suffered waves of closures over the past decade, Hong Kong’s longest-running art house theatre has bucked the trend. As Broadway Cinematheque celebrates its 30th anniversary, shifting audience preferences appear to be playing to its strengths. In November 1996, Broadway Cinematheque (often simply called BC) opened in Kowloon’s Yau Ma Tei district as one of Hong Kong’s few cinemas screening international films that would not otherwise make it onto the city’s commercial circuit. Founded and run by Edko Films – which operates the wider Broadway cinema circuit – the venue relied on a hybrid model for years, showing blockbusters alongside niche releases to sustain business operations while subtly converting mainstream cinema-goers. “The idea was that if those commercial films were sold out elsewhere, people would buy tickets here, discover our art house posters and decide to catch an independent film next time,” says Didi Wu, director of BC. “Before the internet, it wasn’t easy to access films from unfamiliar realms. It was only through film buyers and distributors that audiences were introduced to international non-English language films, discovering new cultures and shaping their film appreciation.” Streaming services have since transformed audience behaviour, moving viewers from theatre seats to home sofas. According to government figures, the number of operating cinemas in Hong Kong dropped from 61 in 2020 to 52 by mid-2025 – a 15 per cent decrease. In January 2026, the residential Ma On Shan area lost its only cinema. “Streaming hit hard a few years ago and disrupted the traditional ecosystem, but over time, the industry will find new ways to restructure and survive,” Wu says. “Much like theatre or other art forms, it just won’t exist as a mass-market phenomenon any more, but things always find a way.” BC has returned to its artistic core three decades after its inception: for its 30th-anniversary “bc30 bc it’s cinema!” programme, running from October 8 to December 16, it is spotlighting film festival darlings, cult classics and films from emerging local directors. Curating for the community The “bc of you” curation will rerun 30 timeless classics and forgotten gems picked out by long-time supporters of the venue. Crowd-pleasing titles include Fruit Chan Gor’s Made in Hong Kong (1997), Alejandro G. Inarritu’s Amores Perros (2000), Guillermo del Toro’s Pan’s Labyrinth (2006), Ann Hui On-wah’s The Way We Are (2008) and Charlotte Wells’ Aftersun (2022). Oliver Chen Ying-ji, a Hong Kong- and New York-based filmmaker and “bcinephile” – a BC member – praises the venue’s curation. “The selection of films is one that truly tries to be on par with the international independent cinema scene,” he says. “For a filmmaker like myself, it’s essential to have this singular access to world cinema and to know there’s a community here in Hong Kong that yearns for it together.” Wu, who joined BC’s programming team in 2013, believes that “streaming, social media and internet culture have altered the audience’s perception of timelines”, citing today’s frequent revival of old memes and nostalgic media. Mostly, she notes a shift in cinema-goers’ attitudes. “People don’t necessarily care about first-run releases any more. They are still important, but audiences don’t mind rewatching films in the theatre for memory’s sake or to introduce them to someone else,” she says. “It has become a statement of ‘This is what I love.’ That’s why globally, re-releases and restorations have expanded significantly.” Cheng Yu-shing, a programmer at BC, says the selection was not about “an official Cinematheque narrative”. The team hand-picked the movies after interviewing cinephiles, filmmakers and film workers for a crowdsourced retrospective. “We discovered really organic connections between specific films and the community,” Cheng says. “For example, Before the Rain [a 1994 Macedonian war film], which screened about a month or two after we opened, was brought up independently by a few people when asked which single film they associated with BC. Some might have forgotten it, but this film left a huge impression and was incredibly eye-opening for those who experienced BC’s grand opening.” Cheng’s conversations with film enthusiasts also led him to wonder: “What makes a film a timeless classic?” He recalls watching The Secret in Their Eyes (2009) at BC and enjoying how it “catered to both highbrow and mainstream tastes, packaged as a genre crime drama”. “Back when audiences weren’t familiar with Argentine cinema, this film blew up suddenly and attracted huge crowds with its slick cinematic technique and great storytelling,” he adds. “Revisiting gems like this makes you realise how outstanding they remain today.” Finding a niche in the streaming era Amid fatigue with the homogenised, highly predictable films of recent years, Wu thinks the market is “shifting towards a niche direction” and increasingly favouring non-linear narratives and complex storytelling. BC is well positioned to benefit from this. Cheng adds, “When the mainstream film industry seems to be lacking compelling stories or intellectual property, art house cinemas might find their footing more easily during this transitional period. It’s hard to generalise; post-pandemic pessimism suggested streaming would destroy the film industry, but we may have passed that low point.” He says Letterboxd, a film discovery platform founded in 2011 that grew exponentially during the pandemic, has been a major catalyst in transforming how film buffs communicate. Before, people centred on the screening experience; now, cinephiles have extensive discussions about specific films that become cultural touchstones and identity symbols for the community. Aftersun, for example, has become a popular rerun at BC. “This reflects a shift among contemporary film-goers,” Cheng says. “Instead of traditional and solid plot structures, audiences are now more drawn to films expressing intense emotions.” Spotlighting independent voices BC’s 30th-anniversary line-up includes a special presentation of The Water Will Carry Us (2026), a local independent film not to be confused with the 2025 Taiwanese-Malaysian festival film The Waves Will Carry Us. The first feature funded by Hong Kong Metropolitan University, The Water Will Carry Us follows an elderly dragon boat club boatman struggling to overcome the loss of his son in a maritime accident years ago. It is a poignant drama that explores themes of loss, family and closure. Wu explains that she decided to showcase the film because she initially had low expectations for what was essentially a university project. The film, however, turned out to be a pleasant surprise, proving that it is possible to make something worthwhile with limited resources. “Passion and dedication matter most,” she adds. “Often, the tighter the resources, the more explosive the creativity. So I hope Hong Kong creators can harness that mindset and not let budget constraints hold them back. Loving what you do is key to doing it well.” BC will also highlight 10 international art house selections from the current year’s festival circuit, including Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine and James Gray’s Paper Tiger. Other anniversary events include a “bc Birthday Party”, a film quiz, a music performance by Hong Kong musician Olivier Cong, and “Tai Kwun Movie Steps – Asia Unseen: A Different Cinematic Journey”, with more details to be announced in due course. title: Hong Kong’s first-store appeal grows as more Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands arrive
description: Brands from the three overseas markets account for 36 per cent of new entrants, matching mainland Chinese retailers, amid tourism recovery.
content: Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands have increased their share of new entrants in Hong Kong’s retail property market by 7 percentage points to more than one-third in the first nine months of 2026, while the demand for shops from mainland Chinese brands has slipped, according to Cushman & Wakefield. A slew of new brands helped lift the combined share of Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands to a three-year high, according to Cushman, which said it expected the trend to continue. This year, Japanese fashion brand Cullni opened an outlet in Wan Chai, while second-hand goods retailer Ragtag took space in Hysan Place in Causeway Bay. South Korean footwear brand Khiho entered Hong Kong through a store at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui. Thai brands also launched outlets, with woven-bag seller Sugar Monday opening at Telford Plaza in Kowloon Bay and gelato retailer Blendies choosing K11 Art Mall in Tsim Sha Tsui for its first overseas location. Together with other brands from the three markets, they accounted for 36 per cent of newcomers to Hong Kong this year through September, up from 29 per cent in 2025, Cushman said. Mainland Chinese brands made up 36 per cent of newcomers to Hong Kong in the first nine months of this year, down from 38 per cent in 2025, while other markets accounted for the remaining 28 per cent. Supported by the recovery in regional tourism, Hong Kong offers brands a strategic platform to enhance their visibility among both local consumers and tourists John Siu, Cushman & Wakefield “We believe the market is now entering a period in which many overseas brands are testing and refining their business models to better suit local demand,” said John Siu, managing director for Hong Kong at Cushman. “Expansion activity among mainland Chinese brands remains ongoing, although the pace has moderated compared with a year ago.” Hong Kong’s retail sales rose by 8.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, according to the latest data from the Census and Statistics Department. Visitor arrivals during the same period increased 11 per cent year on year, fuelled by an influx of mainland Chinese and long-haul international tourists, according to the Hong Kong Tourism Board. “Supported by the recovery in regional tourism, Hong Kong offers brands a strategic platform to enhance their visibility among both local consumers and tourists, while serving as a launch pad for expansion into Greater China and other Asian markets,” Siu said. The recovery has also been aided by lower occupancy costs. High-street retail rents across the four core shopping districts of Causeway Bay, Central, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui were about 50 per cent lower than their 2019 peak levels, Cushman said. Entrepreneur Jennifer Kim is one of those expanding in Hong Kong. The South Korean national has added a new location for Seoul Recipe – her deli, takeaway and dining outlet serving healthy and affordable Korean cuisine. The new branch, which held its soft opening last week, is located at Champion Tower on Garden Road in Central. The outlet had eight tables, which could accommodate a maximum of 16 diners, and measured about 800 square feet (74 square metres), Kim said in an interview. “Our food is affordable and its quality is very good,” she said. “I realised that in Central, it’s difficult to find a good meal that would only cost you HK$100 [US$12.75], and that’s the market we are serving.” Kim said Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector remained challenging as residents continued to travel to Shenzhen for dining and shopping, attracted by lower prices, but added that her catering business was performing well. “It’s tough … but we also know that Hongkongers and tourists here need at least one decent meal,” she said. “That’s usually lunch and, for many [people], going to Shenzhen for lunch is not possible.” More locations would help introduce Seoul Recipe’s food to a wider customer base, which influenced the decision to lease a prime space in Central, Kim said. Founded in 2017, the Seoul Recipe group is a Hong-Kong based Korean food importer, manufacturer and distributor. In addition to its two deli outlets, the group operates Danji, a casual Korean restaurant in Wan Chai, as well as food-delivery and catering services for private and corporate events. Cushman forecast that high-street retail rents would post low single-digit annual growth across districts this year, while rents in the food and beverage sector would remain under pressure. So far this year, retail rents in Causeway Bay, Central and Mong Kok had risen between 1.6 per cent and 1.9 per cent, while rents in Tsim Sha Tsui had declined by 3.2 per cent, according to Cushman.

title: US citizen arrested in connection to Canada school shooting
description: James Cody Bryant allegedly advised shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar and offered to live-stream attack.
content: US authorities arrested ⁠a person in Washington state on Tuesday ⁠who they accuse of providing advice and offering to live-stream a deadly mass shooting carried out earlier this year in Canada. James Cody Bryant, 30, was detained on a charge of conspiracy to murder people in a foreign country in connection to the shooting at ‌Tumbler Ridge, according to the Department of Justice. The charge carries a penalty of up to life in prison. Bryant was in repeated contact with the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, offering technical advice, sending money, including for the shoes to be used during the attack, and agreeing to live-stream the event, law enforcement officials said. “James Cody Bryant had the information and ability to alert law enforcement ⁠and even discussed that possibility with the shooter, but he chose not to, and he encouraged and offered assistance ‌to a murderer,” Acting US Attorney for the Western District of Washington Neil Floyd told reporters. Court records did not immediately list a lawyer for Bryant. Nine people, primarily children, ‌were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in one of Canada’s worst ⁠mass shootings. Van Rootselaar, ⁠18, who had suffered from a series of mental health problems, killed her mother and stepbrother at home before shooting dead a teacher and ‌five young students at her former school in Tumbler Ridge, a settlement of around 2,400 in the Canadian Rockies, according to police. Van ‌Rootselaar then died by suicide. Bryant, who officials ‌said they understood identifies as female, agreed to live-stream a ⁠feed of the attack and broadcast it “in a way that would maximise notoriety for the shooter”, Mike Herrington, FBI ⁠Seattle special agent in charge, said. The live stream on Twitch was shut down after about 20 seconds, officials said. “Without Bryant’s misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the live stream, we don’t ultimately ‌know if the shooter would have ‌gone through with the crime,” Herrington said. “We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the live stream without Bryant broadcasting it, and was depending on Bryant to amplify the live stream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media.” If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: China’s economy to slow as global growth stays solid, US think tank report says
description: Overcapacity and continued property slump weighing on domestic demand, Peterson Institute for International Economics reveals.
content: China’s economic growth is expected to slow further next year as export strength fades and weak domestic demand persists, even as the global economy remains resilient, according to a new outlook from the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE). The Washington-based think tank projects China’s GDP will grow 4.6 per cent this year and 4.3 per cent in 2027, down from 5 per cent growth in 2025, according to its semi-annual Global Economic Prospects report, released on Tuesday. The report said overcapacity and the property slump are weighing on domestic demand while export strength is expected to fade. Karen Dynan, a PIIE senior fellow and former top official at the US Treasury Department, presented the outlook at the institute’s event in Washington. “China in particular, I’m looking for a further slowing of aggregate demand,” Dynan said. “It’s weak.” PIIE’s latest 2026 forecast is slightly higher than the 4.5 per cent it projected in April, while its 2027 forecast is unchanged. But the tone has shifted as the spring report described Chinese exports as strong, with the property slump the main drag. Dynan said she expects China’s export boom to fade as trade restrictions increase, removing a key support for an economy already weighed down by soft domestic demand. She noted that China has benefited from exporting goods that support the global AI buildout. She declined to be more specific about the restrictions, saying the trade situation is too fluid. The forecast broadly aligns with official data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics. China’s economy grew 5 per cent year on year in the first quarter, beating market expectations and keeping the country on track to meet its full-year growth target without near-term stimulus, analysts said. However, economic growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, down from 5 per cent in the first quarter and marking the slowest quarterly expansion since late 2022. Global growth ‘solid’ The report, titled “Global Growth Remains Solid in a Challenging Environment”, projects the world economy will grow 3.2 per cent this year and 3.1 per cent next year, despite the war with Iran and uncertainty over energy prices. “It’s fair to say that we are in a challenging environment right now, given the adverse events of the last couple of years, and yet global growth is holding up,” Dynan said. She also predicted that the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates three more times in the coming months amid inflation concerns. In the US, she said the artificial intelligence boom would continue to propel growth, with GDP forecast to expand 2.3 per cent this year and 2.2 per cent in 2027. Chip exports and fiscal expansion are supporting Japan’s growth. China set its growth target for this year at “4.5 to 5 per cent”, a slight shift from the “around 5 per cent” goal that had been the recent norm, as the economy grapples with weak domestic demand, a prolonged property downturn and rising external risks. Despite the slowing outlook, President Xi Jinping and Chinese state media have stressed confidence in the economy’s resilience as China begins its 15th five-year plan from 2026-30. “Our country’s economy has forged ahead under pressure, shifting towards new drivers and higher quality, and demonstrating strong resilience and vitality,” Xi said at his annual National Day address, according to state news agency Xinhua.

title: Ex-CIA official accused of stealing US$40 million in gold bars pleads guilty
description: David Rush faces up to 20 years in prison after fabricated covert programme cost the US government US$194 million.
content: A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over US$40 million, according to court records. David Rush fabricated a “highly classified” government programme to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus “sensitive government activity” to obtain the gold bars, the filing says. Rush’s fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately US$194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department. The losses included over US$1.8 million in privately chartered flights that Rush authorised for personal use at the US government’s expense. Under questioning from investigators, Rush admitted that he provided a foreign government official with information about the identity of a secret source for the US government, a new court filing says. The filing doesn’t specify which country the foreign official represented. Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake programme that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorised by high-ranking US officials. “Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions,” the court filing says. Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on January 28 in Alexandria, Virginia. Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorise the release of US$100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday’s filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately US$145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four “luxury” properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says. In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly US$46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honourably discharged from the US Navy in 2015. “Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush’s crimes. “David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly US$2 million in US currency and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent’s affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year. During a hearing in June, defence lawyer Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn’t charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as “basically a non-issue” and “nothing more than a sensational titbit”. She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement. “Mr Rush never claimed they were his,” Carmichael said. Carmichael declined to comment on Rush’s guilty plea after Tuesday’s hearing. Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former US Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor’s degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master’s degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York. Investigators determined that he didn’t serve as a US Navy pilot and didn’t attend either school. Rush enlisted in the US Navy in 1997 and was honourably discharged from the US Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

title: In Focus | After cordial Xi-Trump summit, could China’s US dollar pivot cause tremors?
description: Beijing is building a financial safety net around the yuan while reducing exposure to US Treasuries – a strategy that could draw increasing scrutiny from Washington.
content: As President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump talked tariffs, agricultural quotas and critical minerals at last month’s closely watched summit in Washington, an “elephant in the room” loomed over the discussion: China’s efforts to gradually diversify away from US dollar assets. Beijing has gradually been cutting its holdings of US Treasuries while pushing to expand the yuan’s global use and developing alternative financial architecture. While these issues may not have featured in the summit’s official communique, they have not gone unnoticed by economists and investors – or by policymakers on both sides of the Pacific. Charles Chang, a finance professor at Fudan University, said topics such as China’s holdings of US debt were likely to have been raised during the talks, although he added they were unlikely to result in a formal agreement similar to those covering trade. “Unlike tariffs, which can be set out as part of a policy framework, sovereign debt management involves actual capital allocation and is highly sensitive, making it unlikely to be formally addressed in official statements,” Chang noted. “However, from a strategic perspective, Beijing’s ongoing reserve diversification does serve as an important piece of leverage in these high-stakes bilateral negotiations.” These moves, together with Beijing’s push to internationalise its currency and develop alternative payment infrastructure, are viewed by some analysts as largely defensive measures rather than an attempt to displace the US dollar. But they cautioned that any efforts to protect China against potential US financial pressure could themselves become a long-term source of friction between the two countries, particularly if Washington sees them as weakening its currency’s international role. Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well Matteo Giovannini, Centre for China and Globalisation The Treasury retreat Long regarded as one of the safest assets in global markets, US Treasuries have come under increasing pressure as investors grapple with the more than US$40 trillion federal debt burden and the prospect of interest rates continuing to remain high amid stubborn inflation. A global sell-off in government bonds in recent months has pushed long-term Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, with both the 10-year and 30-year yields recently rising to their highest levels since 2002. Underscoring this retreat, Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages Norway’s US$2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, recently proposed a significant reduction in its exposure to US government bonds. Short-term market factors have played a role, but the latest unease about American government debt has also fed into a broader debate over “de-dollarisation”. Barry Eichengreen, a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, described this latest wave as different from previous episodes, as questions mount over the strength of American political institutions and the durability of its geopolitical alliances. Japan, one of Washington’s long-standing allies, cut its US Treasury holdings for three consecutive months to US$1.1 trillion in July, according to the latest data from the US Treasury Department. Once Washington’s largest foreign creditor, China continues to diversify its foreign reserves away from US Treasuries as uncertainties in the bilateral relationship persist. The shift has also coincided with growing concern among Chinese officials and academics over the risks of relying too heavily on the American currency. China dropped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year, and its holdings fell to an 18-year low of US$618 billion this July, according to the US Treasury Department – though questions remain over whether headline figures tell the full story. Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote last month that China’s state-owned banks held substantial dollar assets offshore that were not included in the country’s official reserves. At the same time, Chang said China’s massive US Treasury holdings might give Beijing some potential leverage because a deliberate sell-off could destabilise markets. “Beijing can also use modest, short-term increases in its holdings to send a friendly signal, particularly when the Treasury market is under pressure,” Chang said. “It is a reciprocal diplomatic dynamic – if China shows goodwill, it would naturally expect certain concessions from the US in exchange.” Some analysts argued that China also had an interest in preventing a disorderly crisis in the US Treasury market, even as it continued to gradually reduce its stockpiles. “Beijing still has significant dollar exposure, so a sharp Treasury sell-off would hurt China as well,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “I would therefore distinguish between gradual diversification and actively destabilising the market.” China’s continued trimming of Treasury holdings was nevertheless part of a broader shift in the market’s investor base, Giovannini noted, making it “more sensitive to supply-demand pressures.” Wiring a safety net Alongside China’s diversification away from US dollar-denominated assets, Beijing is building financial infrastructure that could give it more options for cross-border payments and trade. That includes efforts to expand the international use of the yuan and systems such as the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) and Project mBridge. CIPS provides an alternative channel for cross-border payments to Western-dominated networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly known as Swift. Project mBridge, meanwhile, is a multilateral platform designed to ease direct settlements using digital currencies issued by central banks. Both initiatives have made headway, though the pace of growth has varied. The value of transactions processed through CIPS grew at a double-digit pace for several years before rising by just 2.7 per cent last year, official data showed. Transaction value then rose 11.9 per cent year on year to 100.9 trillion yuan (US$14.9 trillion) in the first half of this year, according to the People’s Bank of China’s annual yuan internationalisation report released last month. By the end of June, CIPS had 210 direct participants and 1,619 indirect participants, with services reaching 192 countries and regions, the report said. Analysts said Beijing’s main objective was to make China’s financial system more resilient and reduce its vulnerability to potential sanctions or other restrictions. “I would see this as building a safety net, consolidating global financial influence and even laying the groundwork for the future – but not as an effort to replace the US dollar, which is not something that could be achieved in the foreseeable future,” said Chang of Fudan University. He added that meaningfully challenging the US dollar would require China to fully open its capital account – the rules governing how freely money can move in and out of the country. Any such move would require Beijing to surrender greater control over the exchange rate and could undermine its export-driven economic model, he said. Data also underscores how far the yuan remains behind the US dollar as a reserve currency. The yuan accounted for 2.11 per cent of global central bank reserves in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 56.7 per cent for the US dollar, according to the International Monetary Fund. The purpose of projects such as mBridge, Chang argued, should be understood primarily in terms of making cross-border trade and payments easier in regions that had often been underserved by the US financial system. “Once you establish payment infrastructure, you can build trust and facilitate capital flows, which also opens the door to broader financial services,” Chang said. Project mBridge has brought together the central banks of mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Macau, which joined in June. Saudi Arabia joined the project in 2024 but ceased taking part in May of last year. Even if replacing the US dollar is not Beijing’s intention, analysts cautioned that a larger global role for the yuan could still be viewed in Washington as a challenge to the dollar-based financial system. “Parts of Washington will treat even a regional yuan system as a strategic threat, because payments infrastructure is dual-use: trade convenience plus sanctions resilience,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis. These concerns could lead to greater scrutiny of CIPS links and correspondent banks, she added. Washington has also shown sensitivity to potential challenges to the US dollar’s dominant role, including Trump threatening to impose 100 per cent tariffs on Brics countries if they move to create a new currency or replace the dollar. Brics, a grouping of major emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members. Garcia-Herrero forecast a future of “managed coexistence”, with the US dollar retaining its role as the global reserve and invoicing currency while the yuan expands across Asia, energy markets and China-centric trade. She also expected “occasional political flare-ups when either side talks [about] ‘weaponisation.’” Giovannini, also an AsiaGlobal Fellow at the University of Hong Kong, expressed a similar view, saying concerns in Washington could become more pronounced if the yuan expands its role in trade and financial infrastructure across the Global South. “This could also create a feedback loop, with US financial leverage encouraging China to build alternatives, and those alternatives in turn increasing US concerns about dollar primacy,” he said.

title: US seeks US$100 million bail each for Chinese-born couple in surrogacy child abuse case
description: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang allegedly had nannies beat children at their California mansion and watched on surveillance cameras.
content: Los Angeles County prosecutors are seeking bail of US$100 million each for a Chinese-born couple charged on Tuesday with conspiring to abuse young children who were born through surrogacy and raised in their California mansion. Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, allegedly directed nannies to physically punish the children, watched the beatings through an extensive surveillance system and coached children before police arrived to deny the abuse, according to a felony complaint. At least 14 surrogate-born children, some as young as two months old, were abused, the district attorney’s office said. It said the couple were accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in the home to repeated physical abuse. “The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. Prosecutors cited the risk that the defendants would flee and the nature and extent of the alleged crimes in recommending the bail amounts. Both defendants are charged with felony conspiracy to commit child abuse, between April 2021 and May 2025, and with being accessories after the fact for allegedly helping a nanny avoid arrest. Xuan also faces a separate felony child abuse charge and five counts of dissuading a witness. Zhang faces four counts of dissuading a witness. If convicted as charged, Xuan faces up to 17 years and four months in prison and Zhang up to 11 years and eight months, according to the district attorney’s office. The South China Morning Post has sought comment from Mitchell Krems, who has represented Xuan in related child custody proceedings. It was not clear whether either defendant had a lawyer in the criminal case. The alleged abuse came to light after police responded to a report that a two-month-old boy had suffered a head injury, the district attorney’s office said. Prosecutors allege that a nanny, Chunmei Li, struck the infant on May 4, 2025, and that Xuan and Zhang did not obtain medical treatment until two days later. Zhang allegedly told hospital staff the baby had fallen from a bed. When detectives came to the home on May 7, Zhang and Li gave the same false account and the couple directed officers to the wrong bedroom, the complaint alleges. Li has been charged separately with felony child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death and faces up to 12 years in prison. According to the complaint, about 32 motion-activated cameras recorded video and audio throughout the home, with live feeds displayed on a large television beside the couple’s desks in their shared office. Prosecutors allege the system recorded nannies repeatedly striking children on each of 11 consecutive days, from April 27 to May 7, 2025. On April 30, Xuan allegedly told a nanny who was striking a child to hit harder, then joined in, delivering open-handed blows to the child’s head and lifting him by one arm while continuing to strike him. On May 4, Zhang and Li allegedly laughed as they watched footage of a nanny striking a child with a shoe. The next day, the couple allegedly met the nannies and discussed the importance of disciplining children without leaving visible marks. Before police arrived on May 7, Xuan and nannies allegedly undressed several children to check them for marks, and Zhang told a nanny to put away the sticks used to strike the children. The couple also allegedly told children to deny they had been beaten. The nannies shown in the footage are described in the complaint as uncharged co-conspirators. The complaint also alleges that the couple ran a surrogacy agency, Mark Surrogacy Investment LLC, from the home and gave false information to women recruited across the United States to carry more children for them. One surrogate was allegedly told Zhang was a single mother struggling to conceive and learned only during a second pregnancy for the couple that they already had about 16 children. Zhang kept a spreadsheet that, as of May 7, 2025, listed 21 children by name and date of birth, prosecutors allege. Xuan has told investigators that he fathered 22 children, all but two of whom were born to surrogates, according to the Los Angeles Times. The Wall Street Journal, in an investigation published in August 2025, identified both defendants as Chinese-born. It reported that Xuan came to the United States from Xinjiang and that the couple ran a Los Angeles-area property business with partners based in China. Zhang told the Journal that her experience of China’s one-child policy had motivated her to have a large family. She denied selling children and said the couple could provide for them. Xuan told a Chinese-language outlet that they were both US citizens, according to the Journal. The Arcadia household had already been featured in the US debate over birthright citizenship before charges were filed. At a congressional hearing in March titled “Protecting American Citizenship: Birthright Citizenship for Illegal Aliens and Tourists”, Peter Schweizer, president of the Government Accountability Institute, cited surrogacy arrangements with Chinese ties as part of what he described as the exploitation of birthright citizenship. “Even more insidious is the use of surrogacy in the United States to produce children for senior CCP officials and elites,” he wrote in his testimony. He cited the Arcadia case as a “prominent example”. “These cases highlight a largely unregulated surrogacy industry in states like California, where over 100 companies with ‘surrogacy’ in their names are owned by Chinese individuals,” he wrote. The criminal complaint against Xuan and Zhang does not allege any link to the Chinese government. Amanda Frost, a law professor at the University of Virginia who also testified at the hearing, challenged that argument in an interview with the SCMP in March, arguing that separate issues had been conflated. “Nothing about President Trump’s executive order would address that,” Frost said. “If there’s a problem with abuse of surrogacy relationships, that’s a surrogacy regulation question, which is a state law matter.” The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump vs Barbara on June 30, striking down the Trump administration’s executive order restricting automatic citizenship for children born to parents in the country unlawfully or temporarily.

title: Christa Pike conscious and speaking after botched execution in US
description: Tennessee death-row inmate who survived two doses of lethal drugs is being treated at a hospital while shackled to her bed, lawyers say.
content: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers said Tuesday, six days after the state’s failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection left her unconscious and on a ventilator. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as executioners attempted to put her to death last Wednesday for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered. Her survival raises further questions about her medical and legal future. Her lawyers said her prognosis remains unclear and that she faces a long recovery. “Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” lawyers for Pike said in a statement. “Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented.” Her lawyers said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”. As recently as Sunday, Pike’s lawyers said she had remained unconscious and on a ventilator. Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery”. But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her. “She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.” A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalised Tuesday. Pike’s lawyers are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection. The lawyers are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the September 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.
