Pike’s lawyers said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask outgoing Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole. “Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her lawyers said. Lee halted further executions following Pike’s hospitalisation and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”. US Senator Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican candidate to replace him, called on the state to explore other methods of execution to ensure it can continue carrying out capital punishment. In addition to questions about competency – whether Pike can understand why she would be put to death – Pike has strong arguments that it would be cruel and unusual for the state to try again to execute her, said Deborah Denno, a Fordham Law professor who has studied execution methods for 36 years. It could also violate the prohibition on double jeopardy, trying or punishing someone twice for the same offence, Denno said. In other recent cases, states have been allowed to try again after failing to establish a suitable intravenous line, she said, but Pike is the first person to survive after the lethal drug was actually administered. “They carried out every aspect of the execution,” Denno said. “She didn’t die, but every process they intended, they did it.” Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo, who handled capital cases as a public defender in Los Angeles, called the failed execution horrible but said he doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double-jeopardy grounds, should it decide to do so. “There’s nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she’s been through,” Russo said. But, he added, “I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die – to be executed – not to suffer an attempt at execution.”

title: As I see it | Can’t Uygurs drink Starbucks and taste American freedom?
description: US Congressman says it’s OK for America to sell massive bombs to Israel but not coffee in Xinjiang.
content: “Morally bankrupt”? Was Michigan Republican John Moolenaar talking about himself? Last week, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China demanded that Starbucks “immediately reverse course and close its stores”. The coffee chain’s crime? It opened two stores in Urumqi – the capital of Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region – in the city centre’s Grand Bazaar and its international airport. The way Moolenaar talked about it, you would think Starbucks was committing genocide and crimes against humanity, or at least being complicit in them. A committee press release said: “This week, Starbucks opened stores in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is committing genocide against Uygurs and other minorities.” Moolenaar said in the release: “This is a shocking and morally bankrupt decision by a company that prides itself on social responsibility. Every cup sold in these stores ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uygurs. Starbucks should immediately reverse course and close its stores in Xinjiang.” I don’t know, maybe the Uygurs and other minorities might sometimes want to take a break from constant oppression by Han Chinese and buy an American cuppa or a frappuccino? There is a danger, I admit, that they might be compelled to work as baristas under China’s forced labour regime. While Moolenaar expresses outrage at Starbucks trying to sell a few more cups of coffee, he and the majority of US members of Congress, including most of those on his committee, have gone out of their way to support Israel with massive bombs that vaporised humans during the war in Gaza. Granted, there are a few honourable exceptions. You don’t see Moolenaar and his kind jumping up and down as the Trump administration now prepares to sell Israel 60,000 heavy bombs. The whole world knows what Israel has used them for since October 7, 2023. The latest sale, worth US$2.8 billion, reportedly includes 2,000lb (907kg) bombs such as 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrators. The MK-84 is an unguided general-purpose bomb built for blast and fragmentation against buildings. It can kill or injure people hundreds of metres away. The BLU-117 looks like the MK-84 but can be fitted with precision-guidance kits and has a thermal protective coating for safer storage. The I-2000 Penetrator is a “bunker buster” with a much thicker, harder casing, designed to punch through hardened structures before detonating. Together, these and other powerful weapons have killed tens of thousands and displaced millions in Gaza and southern Lebanon. Then US president Joe Biden’s administration paused some deliveries of 2,000lb bombs in 2024 because of criticism from rights groups about civilian deaths. Current US President Donald Trump resumed such arms sales to Israel after taking power the following year. The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Project on Defense Alternatives says a 2,000lb bomb blast severely damages, injures or kills everything within 35 metres (115 feet). Preliminary research suggests Israel has used these bombs more often since the Gaza war began. One example is the October 31, 2023 strike on the Jabalia refugee camp, which killed dozens of civilians. The UN Human Rights Office said that strike could amount to a war crime. According to an Al Jazeera investigation, Gaza civil defence teams have documented 2,842 Palestinians who “evaporated” in blasts, leaving almost no remains. Experts and witnesses attribute this to thermal and thermobaric weapons. The investigation links US-made MK-84 and BLU-series munitions to these disappearances. Metal powders have reportedly been added to the explosive mix to push temperatures to 2,500-3,000 degrees Celsius (4,500-5,400 Fahrenheit). The sales come despite reports that US munition stockpiles are being depleted during the war with Iran. I strongly recommend the following reports related to Palestine for Moolenaar’s reading pleasure: Amnesty International (December 2024) International Criminal Court (November 2024) Human Rights Watch (December 2024) B’Tselem (July 2025) International Association of Genocide Scholars (August 2025) Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention (December 2023) Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (July 2025) United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory (August 2025) The congressman has been a consistent and staunch supporter of Israel. He unfailingly supports military and foreign aid packages to the country and has publicly called for unwavering alignment with it. These include his April 2024 vote in favour of a US$26 billion US aid package designated to support Israel’s military operations. So, selling Israel 2,000lb bombs that vaporise women and children is perfectly fine, but selling chocolate mocha and espresso in Xinjiang? Now that’s complicity in genocide and crimes against humanity.

title: Trump says Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing backlash
description: White House defends Nebraska rally remarks as California Democrats denounce comment.
content: US President Donald Trump suggested to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska that Iran could “take out” a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, drawing a swift rebuke from California’s Democratic leaders and some fellow Republicans. Trump, speaking at a political rally in the state’s farm belt on Monday, discussed American wartime economic sacrifices and said he was determined to “see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did”. “And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high, ‌it’s a small price to pay,” he told the crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertiliser and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war. “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon,” he said. “It’s essentially almost over with,” Trump went on. “But it’s going to end very soon, and it’s going to end one way or the other.” On Tuesday, the White House dismissed criticism of the remark. “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a ⁠nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung said in a social media post. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” Trump ‌has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously played down his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil. The comment in rural Nebraska, a state Trump won with more than 55 per cent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run ‌cities in California, a solidly Democratic state the president often criticises. Monday’s comments prompted a backlash from California officials. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, denounced the Republican president as “deranged and dangerous”. “After ⁠sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, ⁠Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” he wrote on X. Newsom, who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, juxtaposed a video clip of Trump ‌in Nebraska with mention of the president’s previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration. California’s early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday. The president’s Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state ‌in ‌recent years, including this year’s gubernatorial election. Newsom championed the redrawing of California’s congressional map last year to favour Democrats in this year’s election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to redraw its map to boost Republicans. One of the ‌Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from Trump’s remarks. “I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, ⁠but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” he wrote on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” US ⁠congressman Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump’s comment was “unhelpful”. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump’s comment “could potentially compromise our safety”. Appearing on MS Now on Tuesday, Bass disputed Cheung’s assertion that Trump’s comments were being misinterpreted by a “freaked out” media. “Well, I’m ‌not sure that he understands that we can hear what ‌the president said,” Bass countered, adding that Cheung’s defence of Trump’s remarks “has no connection to the words that came out of the president’s mouth”. Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population. More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego, including Naval Base San Diego, the largest on the US west coast. “My constituents – including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families – are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump’s stupid war,” US congresswoman Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post.

title: EU wants to track potential rogue efforts to block out the sun
description: Rising temperatures are sparking fears that governments or private actors could launch unsanctioned experiments to try to alter the climate.
content: The European Union has launched a €35 million (US$39.4 million) tender to fund research and coordination on, among other things, detecting rogue efforts to alter the Earth’s atmosphere by blocking out the sun. The EU’s Horizon Europe arm, which funds research and innovation, launched the call for projects on Tuesday as part of an early stage effort to coordinate action on so-called Solar Radiation Modification, a nascent and controversial technology that could be used to cool the planet should temperatures rise to critical tipping points. In a report last month, the UN warned that global temperatures are set to cross the key 1.5 degrees Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years, and could climb as high as 2.6 degrees without changes to current policies. The effects of climate change are already being felt with wildfires, droughts, hurricanes and severe floods happening increasingly frequently. That has led to concerns that governments or private actors could launch unsanctioned experiments to try and alter the climate at a regional or global level with potentially dangerous side effects. So far there is little in the way of international agreements to control or monitor such a move, and some scientists have called for an international non-use agreement on such solutions. “This robust monitoring framework should be designed to detect and attribute outdoor experiments and deter potential unilateral deployments by private or state actors,” the tender published by the EU said. The tender makes clear that deployment and field experiments are out of the scope of the project.

title: Hong Kong approves average fee hikes of up to 4.75 per cent for non-public schools
description: Authorities approve tuition adjustments for private, DSS and international schools, as institutions note increases must involve consulting stakeholders.
content: Hong Kong’s private, semi-private and international schools have been given the green light to raise tuition fees by an average of 4.75 per cent, 4.07 per cent and 4 per cent, respectively. The Education Bureau said on Tuesday it had received applications from 185 schools as of August 31 to adjust tuition fees for the 2026-27 academic year. They comprised 49 semi-private schools under the government’s Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS), 74 private schools and 62 international ones. One application from an international school was still being processed, the bureau said. Tuition fees at DSS schools were set to rise by 4.07 per cent on average for the new academic year, it added. Fees would increase by an average of 4.75 per cent at private schools and 4 per cent at international ones, according to the bureau. Last year, DSS schools were allowed to increase fees by 4.64 per cent on average for 2025-26, and by 4.8 per cent in the year prior, the most in five years. Private and international schools got the green light last year to raise fees by 4.62 per cent and 4.6 per cent, respectively. According to the bureau, DSS schools must provide budgets and justifications in their applications for fee increases, and it would also examine whether the institutions had carried out consultations. DSS schools were also required to set aside no less than 10 per cent of their total tuition revenue for fee remissions and scholarships to cater to students who could be affected by family financial difficulties, it added. The co-educational Christian Tai Po Sam Yuk Secondary School is set to implement one of the largest fee increases for next year, raising its tuition by 25 per cent rise from HK$12,400 to HK$15,500 (US$1,580 to US$1,975) for Form One. Elite institutions such as Diocesan Boys’ School, Heep Yunn School and St Paul’s Co-educational College applied for 4.2 per cent rises, with the new fees ranging from HK$45,585 to HK$87,800 a year for Form One. Creative Secondary School in Tseung Kwan O applied to increase its fees from HK$96,250 to HK$99,990, a 3.9 per cent rise. Dion Chen, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Direct Subsidy Scheme Schools Council, said every institution’s fee hike had to go through a procedure that involved consulting different stakeholders. “The price increases require approval from the school management committee, following consultations with the parent-teacher associations, and the proposals are subject to approval from the Education Bureau,” he said. “I believe that the increase in every school has its relevant justifications, which are accepted by the bureau.” Chen pointed out that a reduction in government funding, pay rises for civil servants and inflation could contribute to rising school fees. “The number of teachers at DSS schools is higher than at public schools, so the government’s subsidy might not cover the additional salary increases for their teachers,” he said. “New measures such as promoting AI or STEAM education, smaller classes or hiring more teachers to offer a diversity of electives could also contribute to the rise in fees.”

title: 4 Indonesian seamen kidnapped by Somali pirates return home
description: The men were among 17 crew rescued a week ago when maritime police stormed the Palau-flagged MT Honour 25 tanker that was hijacked in April.
content: Four Indonesian seamen who were kidnapped and held hostage by Somali pirates aboard an oil tanker for more than five months arrived back home on Tuesday. The men were among 17 crew rescued a week ago when maritime police from the semi-autonomous region of Puntland in northern Somalia stormed the Palau-flagged MT Honour 25 tanker that was hijacked in April. Before the vessel could be recaptured, the pirates had already killed five crew members – three Pakistanis, an Indian and a Myanmar national – according to a Puntland police statement. The four Indonesians were received at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport by their families and officials including Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir. In a welcome ceremony, Arrmanatha thanked the ship’s Indonesian skipper Ashari Samadikun for helping ensure the surviving crew members remained safe during the rescue. “I would also like to thank the families for their patience … because it is not easy to wait for news, not knowing the fate of their children, their husbands on board the ship,” the minister said. Ashari expressed regret for the deaths of the five crew members. “I sincerely apologise to the families of my five deceased crew members. I couldn’t keep my promise to bring all my crew members back safely,” he said through tears. Puntland police said the Honour 25 had 18,500 barrels of oil on board. Sixteen pirates were detained in the rescue operation, while others “fled towards the shore and moved inland”, police added. Somali piracy has seen a resurgence, with at least 15 attacks since April, the highest number since 2013. Puntland police have faced criticism for failing to act against a new pirate network that has been highly active in the region this year. Days before the Honour 25, they rescued another oil tanker, the Sibu 1. But several pirates arrested in the operation escaped while being transferred to jail. Puntland police also responded recently to the hijacking of the MT Eureka, forcing pirates to run the vessel aground before abandoning it and disembarking the crew. All crew were later “confirmed safe”, according to police, while the pirates fled ashore.

title: UK police arrest seventh man linked to security incident at US-run airbase
description: Police say the 22-year-old was detained on Tuesday in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
content: British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offence over a security incident at a US-run military airbase in England that authorities have linked to Iran. The arrest is the seventh in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford, located 160km (100 miles) west of London, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during this year’s war. Five British men in their 20s were detained near the perimeter of the base in the early hours of September 27, and a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London on Thursday. All six have been released on bail under investigation. Counter Terrorism Policing said a British national was detained on Tuesday in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives “continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry” and “remain committed to investigating all possible angles”. Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area late at night. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the United Kingdom saw “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was. Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. The United States moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it is unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests. US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he did not want to tempt “the enemy” by having the bombers there. “We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he said in Washington. He said the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran”, but did not offer details. British officials have declined to comment on reports that the bombers were moved because of fears of a drone attack on the base. The prime minister’s spokesman, Tom Wells, said on Monday he was “not going to comment on foreign nations’ military operations”. But he insisted that RAF Fairford is safe. The mysterious incident near the base came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on UK soil. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50 per cent in the six months to December 2025. UK officials also say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in the UK and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

title: Iceland is ‘critical outpost’ for security, Rubio says during visit
description: The US secretary of state’s visit comes amid his country’s push for greater influence in the Arctic region.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Iceland had long been a “critical outpost” for security during a visit to the island, as his country pushed for greater US influence in the Arctic region. His trip comes after US President Donald Trump has stirred up the power balance in the region by making threats to buy or annex Greenland. The United States signed a security pact with Denmark and Greenland in late September that will allow Washington to establish two new military bases there, drawing the autonomous Danish territory further into US orbit. Rubio said at a news conference that Iceland had long served as “a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behaviour and deterring our adversaries”. He added: “There’s interest in doing more together, and obviously if there’s opportunities that make sense for both countries, it’s something we would pursue.” Rubio arrived in Reykjavik on Monday and has held talks with Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir and top diplomat Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir. They covered topics including geothermal energy, data centres and the pharmaceutical industry. With competition on the rise in the Arctic, Iceland has regained status as a strategic player, even as the island continues to rely heavily on the US for security. At the start of September, Trump sparked new controversy by sharing an AI-generated map that appeared to show all of North America, the Caribbean, Greenland and Iceland as “the United States of America”. In response, Reykjavik summoned the US ambassador and called the image “wholly inappropriate”. Gunnarsdottir said on Tuesday the issue had now been dealt with. She also welcomed the US deal with Greenland, adding that her country would continue strengthening ties with Washington. Trump again signalled his obsession with Greenland on Sunday, posting on his Truth Social platform an AI-generated image of his face looming over what appears to be its landscape, accompanied by the words “Hello, Greenland!” Icelanders voted in late August 52.8 per cent to 47.2 per cent against resuming negotiations on joining the European Union, which have been frozen since 2013. Since gaining independence in 1944, Iceland has never had a military. It relies on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) for its security and on a bilateral defence pact signed with the US in 1951. The US had a continuous presence at a military base at Keflavik until 2006, but is looking to consolidate its control over Arctic access routes coveted by Russia and China. “We obviously had an enduring presence here that ended in 2006, not because of anything that was going wrong, but because we shifted forces to other parts of the world,” Rubio said. “The reality of it is, the world has changed over the last 20 years.” After Iceland, Rubio continues to Athens to participate in a “strategic dialogue” with Nato member Greece on regional and energy security, according to the State Department. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have laid bare the fragility of energy supply chains, and Greece is positioning itself to become a key hub in southeastern Europe for natural gas transport. The visit follows media reports about possible conflicts of interest involving the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former fiancee of Donald Trump Jnr and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom. In a letter addressed to Rubio, Congressman Gregory Meeks sought clarification of a Wall Street Journal report alleging she had stated the US could create “political change” in European countries. Rubio later wraps up his European tour with a brief stop in Lisbon. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Rising electricity needs put Southeast Asia’s energy security at risk: report
description: The International Energy Agency report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity and diversify where they get their power.
content: Risks to Southeast Asia’s energy supplies are multiplying faster than nations are coming up with solutions to meet rapidly rising demand for electricity, according to an International Energy Agency report released on Tuesday. Southeast Asia has a seemingly insatiable appetite for energy, but the region is now in a pinch as energy costs rise, partly due to the Iran war. Fast-growing Southeast Asian economies also need more electricity to power data centres and keep homes and businesses cool. To boost regional energy security, the report says Southeast Asian nations should share electricity among each other and diversify where they get their power. But countries face multiple hurdles, from territorial conflicts between neighbours to differing types of national energy markets, according to analysts, who warn these barriers may keep the region vulnerable to energy shocks. “Southeast Asia is one of the world’s most dynamic regions, but its rising needs for energy to power its economic growth face challenges in an increasingly uncertain global energy landscape,” Fatih Birol, the IEA executive director, said in a statement. With the Iran war now bleeding into its seventh month, the IEA warns energy security issues among the Association of Southeast Asian Nations will intensify as the region’s electricity demands outpace growth in power generation. Rapid industrialisation, urbanisation and rising living standards are driving Southeast Asia’s energy demand, which has risen almost 30 per cent per person over the last 10 years. From now until 2030, the IEA forecasts demand will expand at an average annual rate of 5.4 per cent because of demand for cooling, data centres and industry. The energy crisis stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been a wake-up call for Southeast Asia, which has suffered fuel shortages and soaring costs. Unlike their wealthier East Asian neighbours Japan and South Korea, countries in Southeast Asia have limited energy reserves and fewer resources for dealing with the crisis. To survive, countries went into a state of energy triage to conserve power, while also burning more coal and buying Russian crude oil. But as the conflict lengthened, it also led to new policies for cleaner power – from nuclear energy agreements, to solar power subsidies and incentives for buying electric vehicles. That can help diversify the region’s energy sector, according to Amy Kong, with Zero Carbon Analytics. “The Iran war has given governments a bit of a reality check,” she said. If Southeast Asia wants to improve its energy security, nations need to continue diversifying energy supply sources and routes, make greater use of domestically available energy resources and accelerate electrification alongside efficiency improvements, according to the IEA. Countries needed to act, and move faster, said Putra Adhiguna, with the Jakarta-based Energy Shift Institute. “Southeast Asia is at a crossroads,” he said. “There needs to be much more drastic change in how the region adopts the energy transition and diversifies its traditional energy sources.”

title: Hong Kong’s rising fencing star Harris Ho confident of gold at Youth Olympic Games
description: ‘I had a one-week break after the Asian Games and that’s enough for me. I am ready to get going again,’ the 17-year-old says.
content: Rising fencing star Harris Ho Shing-him said for the coming Youth Olympic Games he only had one goal in mind: to win the gold medal. Hong Kong have never won any individual gold medals at the Youth Olympic Games since their inception in 2010, and while teenager Ho had “no idea” who he might face in the capital city of Senegal, he was determined to succeed. “I had a one-week break after the Asian Games and that’s enough for me. I am ready to get going again,” the 17-year-old said. “I am confident that I can win the gold medal, so finishing in the top four barely fulfils my coach’s requirement for me. My goal is the gold medal.” Ranked No 26 in the world, the young Hongkonger revealed what he hoped to achieve in the new season. “I want to crack into the top 16 of the world. It’s not easy but it’s important to have a goal for myself,” he said. “Because if I don’t, I probably won’t have a direction to pursue improvement. “No one knows how this is going to end, so I am going to do all I can, and then see how it goes.” The Youth Olympic Games come after a busy summer for Ho, who had previously competed at the last world championships on home soil in July and then the Asian Games in Nagoya, where he won the men’s foil team silver medal. He also recently won a local junior competition in Hong Kong. “I think I will be in Japan [later this month] for the World Cup and the start of the new season,” Ho said. “After the Youth Olympic Games, I am going to fly to Mallorca immediately, rest a day and be ready for the second World Cup. “I wasn’t really paying attention to the additional focus on me after the Asian Games, and I am only treating the Dakar Games as one of the tournaments. It’s just about performing at my level, doing my part regardless of what the others are saying about me. “I know that these multi-sports games used to have an athletes’ village but unfortunately this isn’t the case in Japan and Senegal. It was the one thing that I wanted to experience most.” Arguably the biggest star of the delegation heading to Senegal, Ho was one of the three athletes who had recently competed at the Asia Games in Japan. The other two were swimmer Man Wui-kiu and table tennis player Su Tsz-tung. Altogether 15 athletes – 10 fewer than the previous edition in Buenos Aires in 2018 – will compete in 12 sports, including athletics, badminton, rowing, windsurfing and wushu, which was made a medal event for the first time. Originally scheduled for 2022, the Dakar Games were postponed due to the global pandemic and mark the first Olympic event to be held in Africa. The Games run from October 31 to November 13. Hong Kong managed to win at least one medal in each of the three previous editions for a total of six silvers and two bronze.

title: Chinese team creates ‘lifelike’ hydrogel that changes shape for smart devices
description: Light-activated hydrogel that can evolve with living tissue may ultimately help make more flexible brain-computer interfaces and robots.
content: Chinese researchers have developed a “lifelike” shape-changing hydrogel they say could provide a platform for next-generation developments, such as flexible tissue engineering scaffolds, brain-computer interfaces and humanlike robots. Inspired by living organisms, the team created a light-triggered system called STERS, which uses liquid metal particles to generate slow, self-sustaining chemical reactions that allow a hydrogel to change its structure over time. Capable of growing and changing alongside living tissues, this adaptive system could inspire next-generation biomedical materials and devices. It could also have broad implications in fields such as regenerative medicine and soft robotics, according to the researchers. “This novel approach enables programmable, lifelike morphological evolution in hydrogels, spanning microscopic to macroscopic scales, minutes to weeks, and single to multiple transformation cycles,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Matter on September 4. Living organisms rely on physical structural changes – such as colour changes and directional growth – to adapt, grow and evolve. Scientists are actively developing smart synthetic materials and devices inspired by these dynamics. Du Xuemin, study author and a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, said he had long been engaged in research on smart materials and had previously drawn inspiration from species such as sensitive plants, whose leaves fold inward when touched, and the chameleon. Du said in an interview that the field of smart materials had advanced rapidly, with shape reconfiguration accelerating from slow speeds to the millisecond range. Materials in development include shape memory alloys, which can bounce back and forth between set shapes when triggered by external stimuli such as temperature changes. “However, after conducting extensive research in this area, I returned to the perspective of living organisms,” Du said. “I realised that while organisms undergo rapid shape changes, they also undergo slow long-term evolutionary transformations,” he said, pointing to wound repair and embryonic development as examples. Tissue engineering often uses scaffolds loaded with active substances to promote healing, but Du noted that existing materials either transformed too rapidly or lacked shape-morphing abilities. “So I wondered if we could mimic these slower morphological transformation processes in nature to construct slow, shape-morphing materials,” he said. To achieve this, the team developed a liquid metal-based system inspired by active chemical species being released in cells to drive morphological changes. The STERS or “spatiotemporally evolving reactive species” system integrates gallium-based liquid particles that produce reactive species and vinyl monomers that help drive that production and the polymerisation of the hydrogel, thus creating building blocks for the gel to change shape. The system is activated by near-infrared light, and a single exposure can sustain the STERS system for up to four weeks. The researchers said this worked because the liquid metals generate reactive species through cycles of surface oxidation when exposed to environmental elements, followed by the removal of the oxide layer to re-expose the metal and allow the reaction to repeat. To test their system, they used the hydrogels to guide stem-cell differentiation into bone and neural-like cells. “Furthermore, we modified the surface of a brain-machine interface electrode with this material to monitor how electrical signals evolve during rat embryo development,” Du said. “This allows precise detection of changes in brain waves, offering a new technique for studying brain activity during embryonic development and advancing brain science.” The material’s transformation rate and magnitude can be tailored to match embryonic brain changes, as development patterns are already well understood in existing literature. Du said the use of liquid metals, which can pose biological safety risks to tissue, was another safety consideration. To mitigate this, the team packaged the materials using a sandwich structure to safely and effectively encapsulate the material and avoid leaks to surrounding tissue, he said. Du said he believed there were opportunities for the STERS system in other fields such as robotics. For robots to become more humanlike, he said, their sensing capabilities, skin and other physical characteristics must also align with humans. The system also holds promise for sensing applications. The team created a hydrogel that gradually changes colour over the span of a month, serving as a long-term visual indicator. However, Du noted that several hurdles remained for long-term clinical applications, including precisely matching the material’s transformation timeline to specific tissues, exploring even slower shape morphing and achieving on-demand control of the transformation process using external stimuli. For now, he said, the system could be used as a sensor or for laboratory demonstrations in tissue engineering and brain-machine interfaces.

title: Registration on both sides of border needed for Huanggang ‘joint clearance’
description: Around 100,000 travellers a day are expected to use the revamped crossing when operations begin.
content: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese residents will have to register with immigration authorities on both sides of the border to use automated “joint clearance” channels at the revamped Huanggang Port crossing, with around 100,000 travellers a day expected to use the control point when operations begin. Hong Kong’s Immigration Department would deploy sufficient manpower to help passengers register at the checkpoint, assistant director Jacky Wong Ki said on Tuesday. “The whole registration process at the automated channel is very quick, it takes a few seconds to complete,” Wong said. The “joint clearance” model will enable passengers to complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document required by their destination and passing through a three-gated automated channel. Authorities said the new system could reduce the typical clearance time from about 30 minutes at the existing Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang crossing to five minutes at the revamped Huanggang Port building. The passenger clearance facilities at the existing Huanggang control point will permanently cease operations when Huanggang Port opens. A source earlier said the revamped checkpoint was expected to open on October 12. Adult Hong Kong residents can register in several ways: via the department’s mobile app for e-channel services; at the first gate of the automated channels; at an enrolment office on the fifth-floor departure hall; or at kiosks on the fourth-floor arrival hall and on the fifth floor. City residents must also ensure they have already registered with mainland authorities to use e-channels before they can use the “joint clearance” automated channel. They will need to travel to the mainland via any other land checkpoint to complete registration there first, or they may also register at the existing Huanggang checkpoint before it closes. Parents can also register children aged from seven to 17 to use the “joint clearance” automated channels via the e-channel app, the enrolment office and kiosks at the checkpoint. They will need to bring proof of parentage and their children’s identity cards to register. Mainland residents can complete Hong Kong registration at the enrolment office on the fifth floor or at the gates of the “joint clearance” channels. Drivers will use a “joint one-stop” vehicle clearance lane for departure and entry clearance at an “integrated information collection device”. Those using the vehicle clearance lane for the first time will need to give permission for information collection after placing their identity documents in the device, but no other registration is required in advance. A department spokesman said around 100,000 passengers were expected to pass through the revamped Huanggang Port each day in the early stages of operation. Its capacity could reach handling 300,000 passengers a day when the northern line of the MTR enters service by 2034. Passengers in cross-boundary vehicles will have to alight to complete clearance at an adjacent departure hall. Chiang Yi-lee, assistant commissioner at the Customs and Excise Department, said clearance time for drivers at the revamped Huanggang Port would be cut to two minutes. Currently, vehicles crossing the border via the Lok Ma Chau/Huanggang route take around 10 minutes to complete clearance. Drivers first spend around two minutes completing Hong Kong customs procedures, take five minutes to cross the Lok Ma Chau bridge, and then complete mainland clearance at the current Huanggang crossing in another three minutes. At the revamped crossing, drivers could pass through the customs kiosk and complete clearance at the information collection device within two minutes, Chiang said. The average daily throughput this year at the Lok Ma Chau and Huanggang crossing was 8,000 vehicles a day, she said. “With the commissioning of the new Huanggang Port, we expect more or less the same or a bit higher,” Chiang said.

title: Hong Kong land sale stuns market as HK$4.3b bid hits 5-year Kowloon high
description: Kerry Properties wins Ho Man Tin plot at price 38 per cent above top market estimate, signalling confidence in luxury home demand.
content: Kerry Properties has won a land plot in Ho Man Tin for HK$4.31 billion (US$549 million), the highest price paid for a residential site in Kowloon in nearly five years, as developers show confidence in demand for luxury homes. The site on Fat Kwong Street sold at HK$20,738 per square foot of gross floor area, the highest land premium for a residential site in recent years, according to Vincent Cheung, managing director of valuation firm Vincorn Consulting and Appraisal. The last time a Kowloon residential site fetched more than HK$20,000 per square foot was in October 2021, when Lai Sun Development paid HK$22,465 per square foot for a site on Broadcast Drive in Kowloon Tong. Kerry’s winning bid was 38 per cent above the upper end of market estimates, which ranged from HK$9,000 to HK$15,000 per square foot, according to industry sources. The government received 10 tenders for the site before Friday’s deadline. It was the only Kowloon site included in the government’s land sale programme for the 2026-2027 financial year, and the only residential site offered for sale in the third quarter. The aggressive bidding reflected developers’ optimism about luxury home demand, especially from investors, Cheung said. The site, formerly occupied by a saltwater service reservoir and a temporary works area for the Highways Department, is close to existing luxury projects near Ho Man Tin MTR station. James Cheung King-tat, a surveyor at Centaline Surveyors, said the site’s location made it a rare opportunity to secure land in an established luxury residential area. After accounting for construction costs and a reasonable profit margin, the completed project would need to sell at nearly HK$40,000 per square foot of saleable area, he added. The 55,649-square-foot site has a maximum gross floor area of 207,750 square feet and is expected to accommodate around 250 flats. The successful bidder must also build an elderly care centre and a community centre, and carry out works on an access road connecting the development to Fat Kwong Street. “We are confident in the project’s prospects and will draw on our extensive experience in luxury residential development to create a landmark high-quality residential project in the area,” said Calvin Tong, Kerry’s director and general manager. “Ho Man Tin is a rare prime residential location in urban Kowloon, with excellent connectivity and well-established community amenities.” Kerry Properties has been actively replenishing its Hong Kong land bank, securing four sites for a combined HK$6.47 billion this year, including purchases in Shau Kei Wan, Mid-Levels West and Kowloon Tong. The company planned to “invest very actively in the future”, Tong said when the company presented its first-half results on August 24. Additional reporting by Chris Tsang

title: Catalan separatist leader Puigdemont set for Spain return after arrest warrant lifted
description: Puigdemont was accused of using public funds to organise an independence referendum, which the courts said amounted to embezzlement.
content: A Spanish judge on Tuesday lifted an arrest warrant for exiled former Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, paving the way for his return to Spain ahead of a general election in November. Supreme Court judge Pablo Llarena made the move after Spain’s Constitutional Court backed extending a 2024 amnesty law to include the crime of embezzlement. The law was aimed at easing tensions in the wealthy northeastern region following its failed 2017 independence bid, Spain’s worst political crisis in decades. About 400 people involved in the independence push have benefited from the amnesty, but Puigdemont, who headed Catalonia’s regional government when it held a banned independence referendum and attempted to secede from Spain, had been excluded. Puigdemont was accused of using public funds to organise the referendum, which the courts had said amounted to embezzlement. He fled to Belgium in 2017 to avoid detention after the referendum and remained the subject of an arrest warrant. Spain’s Supreme Court initially ruled that the amnesty law did not apply to those, including Puigdemont, investigated for embezzlement. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the lifting of the warrant, saying it would allow Catalonia to “look to the future”. “We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time,” he added at a Madrid news conference. Puigdemont briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 after almost seven years in exile, appearing before thousands of supporters and vowing to continue the fight for Catalan independence. He then disappeared before the regional parliament’s vote to install Socialist Salvador Illa as Catalonia’s leader, evading a police operation to arrest him before returning to Belgium. The amnesty law was passed to secure the backing of Catalan separatist parties, whose support allowed Sanchez to remain in power after a 2023 election produced no clear majority. Spain’s right fiercely opposed the amnesty law, with the mainstream conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox arguing it undermined the rule of law. The two parties frequently accused Sanchez of trading political support for the votes of Catalan separatists and staged large protests against the amnesty law. Puigdemont’s Junts party later withdrew support for the government, accusing Sanchez of failing to fulfil commitments, including the amnesty for its leader. Junts on Friday voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez’s minority government amid nationwide protests. The party’s seven seats were key for passage of the decrees. The defeat of the measures led Sanchez on Monday to call a snap vote for November 29. The next general election was due by August 2027. Since Puigdemont fled, Junts has seen its support decline as the Catalan independence movement has lost momentum and a new far-right separatist party, Alianca Catalana, has emerged as a rival.

title: US firm to make battle-tested drones in Taiwan, boosting supply chain resilience
description: Drawing on Ukraine war lessons, Aevex’s drones are 3D-printed, easily modified and built to resist electronic warfare.
content: Two combat-tested American drones could become part of Taiwan’s expanding unmanned arsenal as the island seeks to build a “drone shield” against the People’s Liberation Army. California-based defence technology company Aevex Aerospace is working with Taiwan’s Coretronic Intelligent Robotics Corporation (CIRC) to produce its Vandal and Onyx drones locally, combining lessons drawn from the war in Ukraine with the island’s electronics and manufacturing capabilities. Both aircraft have been tested under combat conditions in Ukraine, where intensive electronic warfare has helped shape their development, according to Aevex executives. Vandal, the smaller of the two, is designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, as well as electronic warfare and precision strikes. According to Aevex, the electrically powered aircraft can carry a 4.5kg (10lbs) payload and fly more than 460km (286 miles), while its low-signature design is intended for contested environments. The larger Onyx can carry 13.6kg, and has a range exceeding 270km and an endurance of up to 2.8 hours. Its modular payload bay can accommodate sensors and equipment for surveillance, targeting, communications or precision strikes. Both are designed to operate when satellite navigation is degraded or unavailable – potentially important in a cross-strait conflict in which the PLA would be expected to employ extensive electronic warfare. Aevex integrates the drones with its CompassX navigation architecture, which uses technologies including computer vision to operate in GPS-denied or degraded environments. Together, the systems could provide complementary capabilities ranging from persistent reconnaissance and targeting to electronic warfare and precision strikes, with ranges extending well beyond Taiwan’s coastline. But analysts said their significance for Taiwan could lie as much in how they are produced as in what they can do in the air. “The Aevex-CIRC production model could be particularly useful during a conflict because 3D printing could allow Taiwan to manufacture replacement drones rapidly rather than relying entirely on overseas resupply,” said Lu De-yun, a former Taiwanese defence ministry press secretary. “In wartime, 3D printing could be used to rapidly produce thousands or even tens of thousands of drones in Taiwan,” Lu said. Containerised 3D-printing facilities could also be moved between locations, dispersing production and supporting a “high-low” force mix combining advanced weapons with large numbers of cheaper systems, he said. According to Aevex, its ForgeX 3D printer also allows drones to be rapidly modified in response to battlefield requirements. Such resilience could become critical if the PLA imposed a blockade or disrupted supply routes across the Pacific, Lu added. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Announcing the partnership in Taipei on Friday, Aevex chief growth officer Murali Krishnan said the Ukraine war had created a rapid feedback loop in which information from frontline operators was passed to engineers, incorporated into designs and returned to production. Taiwan would “inevitably fight a little bit differently” from Ukrainian and Russian forces, he said, but lessons about what worked and what did not could be applied to the island. That experience is being paired with the local engineering and manufacturing capabilities of robotics-maker CIRC. CIRC chairwoman Ann Wu said flight-control systems, edge computing and payloads for locally produced aircraft would be developed and supplied by the Taiwanese company, while motors and batteries would also be sourced on the island. The drones would be produced at CIRC’s Zhunan facility in northwestern Taiwan, where capacity could reach 4,000 aircraft a month depending on demand, she said. The partnership comes as Taipei pursues a broader effort to turn Taiwan into a major unmanned-systems manufacturing hub, creating a military “drone shield” and what officials hope will become another strategically important technology industry alongside the island’s semiconductor sector. Economic affairs minister Kung Ming-hsin said on Monday that Taiwan needed more than 200,000 drones to create a deterrent effect, with components and software sourced from what he called a “non-red” supply chain, meaning one free of mainland Chinese products. He said local production was crucial to avoid shortages during a crisis. He added that global demand for supply chains free of mainland Chinese components offered Taiwan an opportunity to become an important part of “democratic supply chains”. The economics ministry recently raised its forecast for the value of Taiwan’s drone industry in 2030 from NT$40 billion (US$1.3 billion) to NT$50 billion. The government is also implementing a six-year, NT$44.2 billion unmanned-vehicle industry development programme covering government procurement, technological support and testing facilities. Lu said the combination of government spending and demand for supply chains free of mainland Chinese components was making Taiwan increasingly attractive to foreign drone companies. Foreign manufacturers had commercial reasons for seeking Taiwanese partners, but their technology and operational experience could also strengthen the island’s defences and help local companies enter global markets, he said. Krishnan described the logistical challenge facing Taiwan as the “tyranny of distance”, saying local production could reduce reliance on moving replacement systems across the Pacific during a crisis. Aevex senior vice-president of growth Craig Anders said the partnership was therefore intended to go beyond a conventional arms sale. “Some companies will talk about working with Taiwan, but what they really mean is they’re going to sell to Taiwan,” he said. “That is not what we are doing. What we are doing is bringing technology to Taiwan and working with our partners to allow that to happen from Taiwan itself.”

title: End of an era: Lionel Messi prepares to hang up Argentina boots with monumental farewell
description: Some 85,000 fans will be on hand to watch the 39-year-old idol perform his wizardry in a friendly against Benin in Buenos Aires.
content: Lionel Messi will pull on Argentina’s sky blue-and-white jersey for the last time on Tuesday and enjoy an emotional farewell in front of his adoring fans in a stadium with a name to match his legacy: Monumental. Some 85,000 Argentina fans will be on hand to watch the 39-year-old idol perform his wizardry in a friendly against Benin that brings down the curtain on his 21-year international career. Millions more will be following the action in South America’s largest arena, Buenos Aires’ Monumental Stadium, on television. The most-capped player in Argentine history is hanging up his boots two and a half months after losing the World Cup final to Spain. “I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote when announcing his international retirement in August. On Monday, he took part in his last training session with the team at the complex that bears his name in the Buenos Aires suburb of Ezeiza. “You can’t ask for more, that’s it,” Nahuel Nieva, a retail worker who took the day off work to watch his hero train, said. Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated. No effort has been spared for the send-off of a player considered one of the game’s greatest ever. Several of the teammates with whom he reached football’s pinnacle in Qatar, and who will lead the post-Messi team, will play in the game, including defender Cristian Romero, midfielders Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernandez, and forwards Julian Alvarez and Lautaro Martinez. After the game the captain’s armband will pass to Romero. Coach Lionel Scaloni has vowed to try to fill the “void” left by his talismanic captain and the signs from the next generation, some of whom weren’t even alive when Messi debuted with the team in 2005, are auspicious. In their first games since the World Cup final last week, minus Messi, Argentina thrashed Bolivia 4-0 in a friendly in Cordoba on Wednesday before running rings around Burkina Faso on Saturday at Monumental stadium. Franco Mastantuono and Gianluca Prestianni, two of Argentina’s brightest new hopes, both scored their first international goals against Burkina Faso in a 7-0 romp. The results helped lift the gloom of the defeat in the World Cup final when Argentina and a visibly tired Messi were outplayed by Spain and resorted to thuggish tactics which have been punished with bans and fines for a number of players. Messi is not only Argentina’s record appearance-maker but also its leading scorer with 125 goals in 207 games, as well as a record 68 assists. La Pulga (The Flea) won the eternal gratitude of Argentines – and sealed his place as rightful heir to Diego Maradona – in 2022 when he ended their 36-year World Cup drought in Qatar. During his time with the national team, Argentina were also crowned 2005 World Youth Champions, 2008 under-23 Olympic champions and they won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024. They also won the 2022 Finalissima, a match between the champions of South America and Europe. But there were tears along the way too, notably after Argentina’s defeat by Germany in the 2014 World Cup final in Brazil, their loss to Spain in this year’s final and their shock humiliation by Chile in the 2016 Copa America final. One detail remains unclear, however: who will inherit Messi’s coveted number 10 jersey? “Until Leo’s game, we won’t give the number 10 to anyone,” Scaloni said. “After that, we’ll see.”

title: Opinion | Would China agree to slow AI development? That’s the wrong question
description: Meaningful US-China action on frontier AI requires two things: a safe space for technical experts to collaborate and pressure on leading companies to act.
content: The latest US-China summit covered a wide range of topics including artificial intelligence (AI). However, the official readouts from both countries did not touch upon an issue that has generated heated debate: whether the United States and China should agree to pause or slow down the development of frontier AI. That absence has triggered considerable discussion. During my recent visit to New York, many US friends asked whether Beijing would ever agree to some form of arrangement. Before predicting whether China would say yes or no, we need to unpack several other questions first. The first question we need to clarify is who we are talking about when we ask, “What does China think?” If you ask people in China’s AI safety community, I expect many of them to be seriously concerned about frontier risks and already working on these questions. We can see this from the AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 recently published by the National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of the Standardisation Administration of China. If you ask Chinese AI companies struggling to survive and facing restrictions on access to advanced computing power, that question might seem rather distant from their immediate reality. If you ask ordinary Chinese people, many of whom still see technological progress as a way to improve their lives and worry more about being left behind, talk of existential risks and pausing frontier AI might sound like something from a sci-fi movie. There is no one firm answer from “China”. The second question is more basic. What exactly counts as frontier AI? According to recent estimates based on publicly released models and benchmark performance, the leading Chinese frontier models remain around eight months to one year behind those in the US. There is also concern in China that as US restrictions on access to advanced chips and computing power become stronger, this gap will become ever bigger. The capability gap changes the debate. While OpenAI’s newly launched GPT-6 Astra has sparked renewed discussion over whether artificial general intelligence (AGI) has arrived, Chinese frontier labs still struggle to use limited compute to develop the best possible models while reserving enough resources for safety evaluations. Z.ai recently delayed the public release of the weights of its GLM-5.3 model after finding that its cybersecurity capabilities required additional testing and safeguards. It shows that some Chinese developers are already confronting the trade-off between rapid release and safety evaluation. The third question is more technical. What exactly would constitute a slowdown? Would limits apply to training runs, compute, model capabilities or deployment? How could compliance be verified? Who would have both the technical capacity and the political legitimacy to conduct such verification? Until these questions are answered, it is not realistic to expect a definite answer from any government to the larger question of whether it would agree to slow down. There are also several aspects of the Chinese context that need to be understood. In China’s modern history, technological development has usually been associated with economic growth and improvements in everyday life. For many Chinese people, the fear is more that they will be left behind and not benefit from advancements in technology. In addition, Chinese discussions about technology have traditionally put the emphasis on balance. There is an old Chinese saying, guo you bu ji, which basically means that going too far is no better than falling short. The dominant tone of policy language is about balancing AI development and security, innovation and governance. The idea that technological development itself should be stopped because of a future catastrophic scenario seems to be a philosophical dilemma that has much less resonance in mainstream Chinese public debate. It is also true that the discussion cannot be separated from the wider deterioration in US-China technological relations. Years of US restrictions on advanced chips, semiconductor equipment and sanctions on Chinese companies have created a perception in China that Washington is seeking to constrain China’s technological development. Without fully understanding the complexity of US domestic politics and the differences among the Trump administration, Congress, AI companies and other stakeholders, Chinese observers can easily ask if “pacing” is another instrument for maintaining US technological superiority while slowing down China. Rather than waiting for a definite answer from China, perhaps we should think about what can be done to create an environment in which governments are more ready to take action when the question becomes more urgent. As China and the US prepare for the next round of intergovernmental dialogue on AI, frontier risks can be part of the agenda. There should also be a safe space for technical experts from both countries to work on possible governance frameworks. During the Cold War, the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs created space for scientists from different sides of the geopolitical divide to work through some of the most difficult questions surrounding nuclear weapons and arms control. AI is obviously different from nuclear weapons, but the underlying idea remains useful. When official negotiations are difficult, scientists and technical experts need places where they can explore what is technically possible before governments are ready to negotiate. What is more important is that frontier companies need to be encouraged to begin by taking measures themselves, including investing more in safety evaluations, developing clearer release thresholds, testing models for loss-of-control risks and publishing evidence about which safeguards actually work. If Chinese and American companies can compete over who develops better safety evaluations, stronger safeguards and more credible solutions, that will be the kind of competition that people welcome.

title: How traditional Chinese medicine is shaping Kazakhstan’s health system
description: Partnership is latest move by Beijing to engage the resource-rich country amid expanded ties in energy, security, trade and infrastructure.
content: China has pledged to expand its health partnership with Kazakhstan by helping the Central Asian nation integrate traditional medicine directly into its national healthcare system, shifting away from simple product exports. The Chinese embassy in Kazakhstan on Monday called for the alignment of high-level policy to enhance bilateral health cooperation for both countries’ benefit. “Both nations should promote the qualitative upgrading of cooperation in smart healthcare, hi-tech diagnostics and treatment, the pharmaceutical industry and public health … extending the lifespans of their peoples for generations to come,” said Cheng Kefan, the embassy’s interim charge d’affaires, at a medical seminar organised by the GX Foundation in Astana. The move represents just the latest policy partnership between Beijing and Astana. Kazakhstan was the first country to endorse the Belt and Road Initiative following the China-centred trading network’s announcement in 2013. In recent years, the resource-rich nation has expanded ties with China in energy, security, trade and infrastructure, aligning the initiative with its own infrastructure programme to become a major Eurasian transit hub. Beijing likewise attaches great importance to its ties with Astana, elevating bilateral relations in 2019 to a “permanent comprehensive strategic partnership” – one of the highest tiers in China’s diplomatic framework. At Monday’s seminar on emerging trends in medical science, the embassy stressed that strategic guidance from both heads of state served as “the most fundamental and powerful driving force” behind China-Kazakhstan ties. Chinese President Xi Jinping has travelled to Kazakhstan six times during his presidency, making the country tied with the United States as his second most visited foreign nation. Russia remains Xi’s top global destination at 11 visits. In June last year, the Chinese leader attended the second China-Central Asia Summit in Astana, underscoring Beijing’s deep engagement with the region. Cooperation between China and Central Asian countries in recent years has focused increasingly on healthcare initiatives – often referred to as the “health silk road” – and joint scientific technology sharing. Traditional Chinese medicine has emerged as central to their collaboration. Beijing has promoted practices such as acupuncture and herbal cultivation, established a dedicated traditional medicine centre in Kazakhstan and drawn young Kazakhs to pursue medical studies in China. In addition, China is sharing with Central Asia its overarching healthcare model that uses traditional medicine alongside modern Western medical practices, according to industry professionals attending Monday’s seminar. Hong Kong in particular could offer a practical blueprint for countries including Kazakhstan seeking to integrate their own indigenous practices into national frameworks, according to Ko Wing-man, a specialist in orthopaedics and a Standing Committee member of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, China’s top advisory body. The city’s unique regulatory framework independently licenses Chinese medicine practitioners, safeguarding traditional practice without forcing it into Western medical models or leaving it unregulated, Ko added. He said Chinese medicine clinical protocols had been established for 20 to 30 clinical conditions in Hong Kong, and further support existed in dedicated traditional Chinese medicine hospitals. Ko called Hong Kong’s registration system for Chinese medicine “exemplary”, adding that “nowhere else has this stringent requirement” for traditional remedies. “We ask for a very high standard of safety and efficacy. But we do not adopt the FDA type of reduction of research approach, which requires you to separate and isolate all chemical compounds,” the doctor said, referring to the US Food and Drug Administration, which regulates health products in America. “This can be an equivalent of the FDA in traditional medicine, especially in the belt and road area.” Beijing has sought to expand the global reach of traditional Chinese medicine, aiming to train 1,300 overseas health workers across belt and road countries through 2027. Traditional Chinese medicine has already gained popularity among local communities in Kazakhstan, according to Emily Chan Ying-yang, CEO of the GX Foundation, a Hong Kong-based charitable organisation offering medical and public health humanitarian help to belt and road countries. Chan said the GX Foundation had received many inquiries from among the 30,000 patients it had treated in Kazakhstan. She described the primary challenge for bilateral health cooperation as one of tailoring policies and strategies to local needs across different regions. Chan said Astana and Beijing shared clear complementary strengths, noting that Kazakhstan’s vast territory created high demand for primary care and telemedicine, while China excelled in producing low-cost, portable medical devices. “The whole concept of remote primary care remains a theoretical model without those devices to tell what problems patients have [and] whether they need to be sent to the city or can stay in the village,” she added. Chan stressed that technology alone was inadequate and that future efforts would focus on local capacity building, such as providing rural workers with standardised guidelines, proper training and “true community ownership” over the technology.

title: India opposition lawmakers detained over protest against election chief
description: The march is a fresh political challenge to PM Narendra Modi, months after similar protests forced the resignation of his education minister.
content: Indian police detained several opposition lawmakers in the capital of New Delhi on Tuesday for trying to breach barricades during a protest march to demand the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists. The march presents a fresh political challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi midway into his ‌third term, just months after similar protests forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks. Parties opposing Modi’s government along with members of the popular “cockroach” youth movement protested against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after the Indian Express newspaper reported divisions in the poll body last month. The reported differences over the lists and voter registration procedures stoked concern about the neutrality of the commission, led by a Modi government appointee. “The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government,” Congress ⁠president Mallikarjun Kharge, told reporters as the march began. “We are fighting to save our democracy.” Lawmakers carried placards, waved ‌the national flag and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1km long, or less than a mile, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of Delhi. Some carried placards calling Kumar a ‌traitor and accused the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of snatching away the right to vote, while they sat on the road outside ⁠the panel’s office, demanding to ⁠meet him. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka and several more stood on police barricades there, waving the national flag and calling for Kumar to resign. Hundreds of ‌security personnel, some wearing riot gear and carrying batons, tried to stop Gandhi and other lawmakers from entering the election commission. Police did not immediately comment on the detentions. “After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in the country and attack institutions,” BJP spokesman Sambit Patra told ‌reporters before Tuesday’s protest. TV channels said the Gandhi siblings were among those briefly detained before being released. The duo sought entry through the grounds ⁠of the state radio office next door, where they sat in protest under a tree after the route was blocked, the channels ⁠said. Congress and other parties say the revised voter lists benefit Modi and his party. Kumar has not commented on the issue, but the commission and Modi’s BJP denied the accusations. Tuesday’s event is the latest of a series of ‌almost daily demonstrations by student organisations, political ‌parties and the “cockroach” movement, which began last week. India’s Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear requests for its intervention in the accusations against the poll body’s voter drive, and the conduct of its chief. If “there are decisions against the law … We will take care of it,” the court said at the hearing, after the petitioners accused the poll body of bias.

title: As China’s AI race accelerates, ‘model fatigue’ becomes the next challenge
description: Frequent upgrades, falling prices and fierce competition make it harder for new AI models to stand out, analysts say.
content: On September 22, the global artificial intelligence landscape spun on its axis within a matter of hours. In Beijing, Xiaomi engineers went live with an unusual broadcast, streaming the training run of their new MiMo-V2.6 model. In San Francisco, Anthropic unveiled its frontier Opus 5.5 model. About an hour later, OpenAI crashed the party with the surprise release of its GPT-6 Sol and Luna models. For tech executives and developers trying to keep pace, it was just another overwhelming day in the AI trenches. But while Silicon Valley is beginning to grapple with what some have dubbed “model fatigue”, China’s hyper-competitive tech sector is experiencing the phenomenon on steroids. The one-day barrage – coming on the heels of major roll-outs from Z.ai, DeepSeek, Tencent Holdings, Alibaba Group Holding and Moonshot AI – shows how companies are churning out upgrades so rapidly that individual breakthroughs are struggling to command the spotlight. “If anything, there may be more model fatigue in China,” said Rui Ma, a tech analyst and founder of the Tech Buzz China newsletter. “People are exhausted by the pace, but they’re also excited that the ecosystem is moving this quickly.” Where the economic pressure falls Analysts said model fatigue manifested differently in the world’s two largest AI markets. While US businesses wrestle with whether incremental performance gains justify the costs of switching models, the burden in China falls more heavily on developers. As models become deeply embedded in consumer apps and cloud platforms, the rapid pace of releases has triggered brutal price wars. “In China, fatigue is about economics. Each new generation [of models] resets the price floor,” said Lionel Sim, founder of AI research firm The AI Capitol. Customers increasingly responded only to genuine leaps in capability or meaningful price cuts, with incremental updates drawing little attention, he added. Leia Wang, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said Chinese users tended to be more price-sensitive, making brand loyalty difficult to build at the model level. The model layer was the “least sticky layer”, Wang said, adding that tech giants like Alibaba attempted to lock in users by integrating models directly into broader cloud ecosystems. That economic pressure was evident throughout the latest release cycle. DeepSeek slashed its V4.1 Flash application programming interface (API) prices to as low as 0.02 yuan per million cached input tokens during off-peak hours. Z.ai claimed its GLM-5.3 Flash model outperformed the previous iteration at 10 per cent the cost, while Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash charges 1 yuan (14 US cents) per million input tokens. Xiaomi took a different route with MiMo-V2.6, holding API prices steady while promoting “higher intelligence at the same price”. Its live stream also showcased a push towards recursive self-improvement (RSI), a process in which AI systems enhance their own capabilities without human intervention. Even US developers are adjusting to the pricing squeeze. Anthropic cut operating costs for Opus 5.5 by 40 per cent compared to its predecessor, while OpenAI halved API prices for its GPT-6 Sol and Luna models relative to promotional rates for GPT-5.6. There are now too many model names, benchmark claims and frequent upgrades for every release to receive sustained attention. However, this does not mean demand for AI is weakening Poe Zhao, Hello China Tech The race that will not slow The relentless pace has continued despite growing calls from some industry leaders to slow down. Just 10 days before launching Opus 5.5, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged the industry to temper the pace of frontier AI development, citing mounting safety risks. Those calls have met strong resistance in China, where researchers and state media commentators have framed proposals to slow development as a strategic attempt to preserve the US’ technological lead. For Chinese developers, slowing down was simply not an option, analysts said. “There are now too many model names, benchmark claims and frequent upgrades for every release to receive sustained attention,” said Poe Zhao, a China tech analyst and founder of newsletter Hello China Tech. “However, this does not mean demand for AI is weakening.” Zhao said enterprise clients tended to prioritise stability, predictable output, integration costs, data security and technical support over marginal improvements in benchmark scores once AI systems were deployed in production environments. A new model became commercially significant only when it enabled entirely new tasks, substantially reduced errors, or drastically slashed operating costs, Zhao added. [China] is an ultra-competitive market, and if you stop shipping, you risk disappearing from the conversation Rui Ma, Tech Buzz China Specialisation as a survival strategy To survive the churn, Chinese tech firms were carving out niches rather than competing solely on general benchmark scores, Tech Buzz China’s Ma said.
