ByteDance, for instance, has leveraged its short-video strengths by rapidly upgrading its Seedance video-generation models. Meanwhile, Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba, has focused on healthcare, with its AI health app AQ amassing 150 million users, the firm said. The stakes remain high as AI monetisation accelerates. Alibaba reported that revenue from AI-related products grew at a triple-digit rate for a 12th consecutive quarter, boosting its cloud and AI division by 45 per cent year on year in the June quarter. Z.ai and MiniMax have also posted surging sales as they shift towards paid enterprise offerings, although massive infrastructure spending continues to keep much of the sector unprofitable. “This is an ultra-competitive market, and if you stop shipping, you risk disappearing from the conversation,” Ma said. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

title: Elderly man found dead, wife hospitalised after smell reported at Hong Kong flat
description: Man, 81, had died in flat at One Madison in Cheung Sha Wan, while woman, 73, was found in semi-conscious state and taken to Caritas Medical Centre.
content: An elderly man was found dead and his wife was taken to hospital after authorities responded to a report of a foul smell from a flat in Hong Kong on Tuesday. Authorities received a report at about 5.20pm from security staff at One Madison, a residential building on Castle Peak Road in Cheung Sha Wan, after an unusual odour was detected from the flat and the occupants had not been seen for some time. Firefighters were called to the scene and forced entry into the flat. The man was found in the bathroom, and the woman was in the kitchen area. Paramedics confirmed that the man, 81, had died in the flat. The woman, 73, was found in a semi-conscious state and taken to Caritas Medical Centre, where she regained consciousness. Police are looking into the circumstances surrounding the incident. The cause of death has yet to be determined.

title: Greenpeace catches Hong Kong geopark ‘golden week’ visitors damaging marine life
description: Green group urges visitor caps after recording incidents of damaging behaviour across popular nature spots during holiday period.
content: About 100 incidents of visitors catching sea cucumbers and digging up sea snails and clams were recorded at a popular spot in Hong Kong’s Unesco-listed geopark on a single day of the National Day “golden week”, a green group has found, following similar incidents last year. The Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung was also strewn with rubbish on a separate day, Greenpeace said on Tuesday. At nearby Long Ke Beach, the group recorded nearly 90 instances of environmentally damaging behaviour, including climbing trees, littering and disturbing wildlife. A Greenpeace site inspection on October 4 recorded 3,010 visitor arrivals at Hap Mun Bay, at the southern end of Sharp Island, also known as Kiu Tsui Chau. Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner Ha Shun-kuen said additional public funding and manpower allocated during golden week had failed to contain the damage. Measures included the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department’s (AFCD) deployment of more than 100 personnel to hiking and tourist hotspots, as well as a reservation system at Po Pin Chau. “This indicates that strengthening enforcement only after overcapacity is exposed at individual tourist spots is merely a piecemeal ‘painkiller’ approach that fails to tackle the continuously expanding problem of overtourism at its source,” he said. Between October 1 and 5, Greenpeace conducted field surveys at several Sai Kung hotspots, including Hap Mun Bay within the geopark, the Po Pin Chau section near the East Dam and Long Ke, to count visitors and record damaging behaviour. At Hap Mun Bay on October 4, the group recorded more than 100 incidents involving visitors collecting marine life or coral remains. These included catching live sea cucumbers, using metal tools to dig out sea snails and clams, and picking up coral skeletons. At 3pm that day, as many as 23 visitors were digging at the same time, with no officers seen patrolling or intervening, the group said. The waters of Hap Mun Bay support coral communities, but the government’s proposed marine park boundaries cover only the eastern and western sides of Sharp Island, excluding the bay, according to Greenpeace. The group warned that concentrating enforcement efforts within the proposed marine park could push crowds towards Hap Mun Bay, putting pressure on its coastal ecology. Ha said only seasonal closures of the Po Pin Chau trail for restoration work could effectively protect the natural environment. Greenpeace urged the government to immediately assess the visitor capacity of all countryside hotspots across Hong Kong and set a cap for each location. In the longer term, the group called for an ecotourism policy that prioritised conservation, required routine monitoring of visitors’ environmental impact and set out measures to address it. A government spokesman said on Friday that to address visitors’ inappropriate behaviour causing harm to marine life at Sharp Island, the AFCD would collaborate with the Leisure and Cultural Services Department to promote respectful behaviour and marine conservation messages. These included reminding visitors and swimmers to care for marine ecology and refrain from catching or disturbing marine life, he said. Last October, Greenpeace documented similar behaviour on an overcrowded Sharp Island, where tourists dug up sea stars, sea urchins, sea cucumbers, conches and clams. The group also recorded littering, illegal fires lit for cooking and trampling on coral. In August, a real-name booking system was launched to better manage crowds at Po Pin Chau. The AFCD previously carried out enforcement operations on Sharp Island during mainland China’s National Day golden week holiday, stepping up patrols at popular snorkelling spots and along the coast.

title: School protests sweep France in most violent student demonstrations in decades
description: Rallies draw 250,000 nationwide following a fortnight of unrest originating in Paris’ suburbs.
content: Demonstrations swept across France on Tuesday as teachers and parents took ⁠to the streets with high school pupils on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent student demonstrations in decades. Police fired tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups on the fringes of marches in Paris, Strasbourg, Rennes and Toulouse, among other cities. The marches drew more than 250,000 people in dozens of cities, the interior ministry said, though organisers said 450,000 had participated. The protests, in which a teenager lost a hand on Monday, were the latest manifestation of public anger in a country where support for populist parties on the far-right and far-left has surged ahead of a presidential election in the spring. The government is under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, and has struggled with basic tasks such as passing a budget since President Emmanuel Macron’s allies lost their majority in a 2024 parliamentary vote. Lecornu told lawmakers at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had so far been injured in clashes, “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system”. His office said more than 700 police officers were also hurt. Macron has convened Lecornu and other senior ministers at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, broadcaster BFM reported. US President Donald Trump said the protests were evidence of “out of control” migration in France. “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country,” he posted on Truth Social. The students’ demands do not concern religion or immigration, but focus instead on understaffing and lack of funding. ⁠Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party has not linked the protests to France’s migration policy. Lecornu’s office did not respond to a request for comment. In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up handmade signs bearing phrases such as “The state has ‌killed national education”. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city. Paris police said clashes in the capital resulted from some 300 people, most hooded or masked, facing off against security forces, and that the protest generally unfolded without major incident elsewhere. Several storefronts were damaged. The Interior Ministry said 488 people had been arrested and 48 security personnel ‌were injured on Tuesday. The student protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris before spreading nationwide. Students complain about schools facing basic maintenance problems, from water leaks to rat infestations. “There is ⁠such a gap between the elites and us,” said ⁠Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg. The High School Students Union said more than half of France’s high schools were blockaded or had closed for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online. Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against ‌minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and in some places deteriorated into urban violence. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted for unspecified crimes, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said on Monday. “They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters,” said Omar Slaouti, a high-school ‌teacher ‌in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris. “If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake.” Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the ‌students’ leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day and the need for longer lunch breaks. The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, ⁠who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October. Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government’s words were not enough: “That’s all fine and dandy, but that’s ⁠not what’s going to change the daily lives of our children,” she said. Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult. The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France’s growing debt, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push the cost of borrowing higher. The surge ‌in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the ‌broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policymakers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in. Le Pen, the far-right Eurosceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring’s election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens. French spending on education has lagged inflation and the country’s students are trailing their OECD peers in overall performance, data from the PISA 2025 assessment shows.

title: Saudi-Iran war risk grows as Riyadh resumes Yemen bombing
description: Backed by Western and regional allies, Riyadh’s renewed campaign against the Houthis threatens to blow Tehran’s proxy war wide open.
content: Iran and Saudi Arabia are edging dangerously closer to direct conflict, analysts warn, after Riyadh resumed major air strikes on Yemen’s Tehran-allied Houthi rebels this week, ending a four-year lull. More than 100 Saudi warplanes bombed rebel positions on Monday, enabling Yemeni government forces to retake much of the Red Sea coastal territory the Houthis seized last month. The Houthis had been aided by embedded Iranian military advisers. Analysts expect the Houthis to retaliate by intensifying drone and ballistic missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are expected to supply weapons and targeting intelligence to their partners in so-called Axis of Resistance. Casualties on all sides are also likely to rise as the war widens and draws in more international players. On Monday, Pakistan and Turkey said they would “provide agreed forces and military capabilities and rapidly deploy them in Saudi Arabia” under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement all three signed in August. Pakistani military advisers are reportedly already embedded with Yemeni government forces, providing the intelligence and communications support needed to coordinate operations against the Houthis. Western powers are also backing Saudi operations against the Houthis and their Iranian advisers. The US military has reportedly sent a specialised task force of more than 100 advisers to Riyadh, while Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refuelling for Saudi aircraft and French air defence units have taken on defensive responsibility for repelling Houthi air attacks on Saudi oil-export infrastructure. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have moved to end their dispute over support for rival Yemeni anti-Houthi factions. Despite all this, Tehran believes it has “little choice” but to continue supporting the Houthis, “even at the risk of direct war with Saudi Arabia”, according to Ali Alfoneh, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Arab Gulf States Institute and author of Political Succession in the Islamic Republic of Iran. He said Tehran’s fear of the US and Israel resuming air strikes “deepens Iran’s dependence on regional allies” such as Yemen’s Ansarallah, the Houthi movement’s official name. The Houthis had been “extremely useful” in pressuring Saudi Arabia, said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, but their successes now risked becoming “strategically counterproductive” for Tehran if they produced the sort of international coalition that the Iranians had “spent years trying to prevent”. Pakistani and Turkish military involvement, renewed operational cooperation between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and British and French deployments around Saudi Arabia were “all warning signs for Tehran”, he said. Krieg expects Iran to continue supporting the Houthis while simultaneously trying to “calibrate their escalation” and avoid politically explosive incidents that would further internationalise the conflict. Examples include mass casualties at the pilgrimage cities of Mecca and Medina, the killing of Western military personnel or the closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects trade between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. Alfoneh said disrupting shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz straits, and targeting regional energy infrastructure, remained “Tehran’s only means of inflicting pain on the global economy and mobilising an anti-war lobby”. Without these tools, he said Iran risked suffering the fate of Saddam Hussein’s Iraq between the 1991 Gulf War and the 2003 invasion: “impoverished by sanctions and an embargo, hollowed out and vulnerable to a US ground invasion”. Strategic ambiguity Iran would not risk its “core military capabilities”, such as longer range drones and missiles capable of striking Israel, in support of the Houthis, said Dave Des Roches, a retired Pentagon official and senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum. For Tehran, he said, the Houthis were an “economy of force operation” that served “Iranian interests, not the other way around”. Despite international concern about the Houthis’ recent seizure of key locations around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, it was too early to tell “who will actually put skin in the game”, said Barbara Slavin, a distinguished Middle East fellow at the Stimson Centre think tank in Washington. Both Iran and Saudi Arabia would prefer that “this remains an indirect fight with Yemenis on both sides of the political divide paying the price”, she said. At the same time, analysts expect Iran to keep publicly denying operational control over the Houthis, while preserving diplomatic backchannels with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, as well as the Gulf mediators Oman and Qatar. Krieg said ambiguity was central to Iran’s strategy of retaining the military leverage that the Houthis provided without accepting responsibility for their every action. “The danger is that this strategy may be reaching its limits,” he warned. Western intelligence reports say Iran’s assistance goes well beyond weapons transfers; it includes technical expertise, intelligence, mission planning, missile and drone preparation, targeting support, electronic warfare and battle-damage assessment. But it would be wrong to describe every Houthi operation as being directed from Tehran, Krieg said, adding that the Houthis retained their own leadership, interests and operational autonomy and Iran “cannot reliably switch them on and off”. Nonetheless, the more Iranian military personnel became embedded in Houthi operations, and the more Saudi intelligence was able to identify and strike those networks, “the harder it becomes to keep the Saudi-Houthi war separate from the Saudi-Iranian confrontation”, Krieg said. “That is probably the most serious escalation risk over the coming weeks,” he added.

title: ‘It’s not a secret’: the rise of Thai chic as fashion brand Amr de Saison hits Hong Kong
description: Thai fashion is having a global moment and Thai brand Amr de Saison is taking full advantage of that to bring timeless looks to Hong Kong.
content: Once overlooked by the global fashion industry, Southeast Asian couture and craftsmanship are now stepping into the spotlight as labels from Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia and neighbouring countries start to gain widespread admiration. “People always say it’s like a kept secret,” says Verawat Chinpilas, 38, co-founder and creative director of Thai fashion brand Amr de Saison. “But, no, it’s not a secret. You just weren’t looking.” Founded in Bangkok in 2022, Amr de Saison blends relaxed everyday essentials with urban tailoring. The brand has eight physical locations in the Thai capital and recently made its international debut with a pop-up exhibition in Hong Kong at Lane Crawford in Harbour City, with an exclusive line that features curated favourites by Thai actress Miu Natsha. Crafted in classic silhouettes, the brand’s garments ranging from 1990s-style denim jeans and relaxed baseball tees to cashmere cardigans are created to achieve timelessness. “The philosophy was always about doing wardrobe essentials reinterpreted in a way that the products last longer, with better cutting quality, a bit of craftsmanship and good materials,” Verawat says. He and his co-founder, plus chief marketing officer Pitchaya Songskulchai, 32, had always aimed to create pieces that were “as seasonless as possible”. Rather than chasing micro-fashion trends, the two are focused on producing garments that are both aesthetically and practically evergreen. “We want our products to blend seamlessly with other items in our clients’ existing wardrobe,” Verawat adds. Before founding Amr de Saison, Verawat was a multi-label buyer who attended Paris fashion shows every season. He was inspired by the effortless Parisian chic aesthetic, which he then sought to combine with his Asian roots. Today, he believes in the idea of dressing the “global citizen”, an aesthetic that is “borderless in terms of both gender and also culturally”. A moment in the spotlight But are timeless and simple synonymous with each other? Verawat thinks they are two different things. A timeless garment is one that you feel excited to wear “time and time again” and something that you can just grab out of your wardrobe no matter the occasion, he says. “It’s something that happens a lot with our feedback from our clients – when they wake up, they don’t have to think about what they want to wear. They just grab it.” Most of Amr de Saison’s fabrics and garment production are manufactured at local facilities in Thailand, though some are also outsourced to Japan and mainland China. Launching a pop-up exhibition in Hong Kong felt like a “natural” step for the brand. Hundreds of thousands of Hong Kong tourists flock to Thailand each year, and vice versa. Verawat can see that Thai brands and culture are finally getting their due on the global stage, with the help of popular Thai music and tourism ambassadors such as Lisa from the K-pop girl group Blackpink, who is Thai and proudly promotes the country’s culture. He cites Miu as another example of talent bringing Thailand to the forefront. “I think there’s a lot to offer in Bangkok,” Verawat says. “There’s so many up-and-coming brands, so many designer brands.” He specifically highlights designer handbag brand Boyy as a Thai brand that truly can outcompete Western brands. The pop-up at Harbour City wraps up on October 22. Despite being optimistic about plans for future pop-up exhibitions and even permanent store locations, Verawat wants to remain cautious about international expansion. He certainly hopes that Amr de Saison will have more opportunities to work with Lane Crawford and other Hong Kong brands in the future. But using the same philosophy that he approaches his fashion with – one built on timelessness and longevity – he does not buy into the idea of mass production and rapid growth. “If our business is going somewhere overseas to a new market, I feel like we should have a good partner,” he says. “Someone that understands us as a brand and also sees the same vision and also [can] expand us diligently – not too fast.”

title: Who is DWTS pro dancer Hailey Bills? Her uncle Val Chmerkovskiy has slammed ‘nepo baby’ claims
description: The 20-year-old, who partnered with reality star Sarah Jane Nader on Season 35 of Dancing with the Stars, previously toured with choreographer Derek Hough.
content: Season 35 of Dancing with the Stars introduced viewers to a brand-new pro dancer, Hailey Bills. However, she’s no stranger to the ballroom. The 20-year-old is the niece of veteran DWTS pro dancers Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Johnson through her mother, Johnson’s older sister Stacy Bills. Hailey Bills was part of the DWTS troupe last year and a junior pro on Dancing with the Stars: Juniors, where she competed alongside Tripp Palin under Johnson’s coaching while Chmerkovskiy judged. The pair was eliminated early, and Bills joked about it on The Joe Vulpis Podcast. “The drive home with Val was really awkward,” she recalled, adding, “we actually went to dinner, and he gave me his whole pep talk, and I know he was sad about it.” On Season 35 of DWTS, Bills partnered with Love Thy Nader star Sarah Jane Nader and they were the second couple eliminated. When The Hollywood Reporter published an article describing the dancer as a “nepo baby”, Chmerkovskiy called it “nonsense”. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Hollywood Reporter (@hollywoodreporter) So, what do we know about Hailey Bills? Read on to find out. What is Hailey Bills’ background? Hailey Bills was born on May 18, 2006. She is the oldest of five siblings: Jake, Luke, Kade and Gracie. She grew up in Utah, Illinois and Frisco, Texas. Several of Bills’ maternal relatives are dancers, but her mother initially did not want her to get into dancing. “[My mother] taught Jenna, she was her director, and then she taught her other sisters. So, she was done with teaching, she was done with the comps [and] did not want me to dance,” Bills told Mackenzie Couch’s Stop Talking Kenz podcast last year. Bills played football as a child, but after taking a dance class in Chicago, she fell in love with the art form. Her mother also became “the most influential dance teacher” she ever had, Bills wrote in a 2023 article for the Dance Teacher magazine. She has won multiple dance awards In Frisco, Bills joined the Prodigy Dance and Performing Arts Centre and began dancing competitively at age six. She won the Mini Female Best Dancer title in 2017 and the Teen Female Best Dancer in 2022 at The Dance Awards. In 2018, she starred in DWTS: Juniors. Bills continued her training at Utah’s Center Stage Performing Arts Studio and later attended Brigham Young University, where she joined the dance team, the Cougarettes. Her mother is currently the team’s co-head coach. Bills has also toured with dancer and choreographer Derek Hough. Is Hailey Bills single? Bills’ current relationship status is unknown, but on the 34th season of DWTS, she was linked to contestant and eventual winner Robert Irwin. The 22-year-old is the son of the late Australian conservationist Steve Irwin. Neither confirmed the romance rumours.

title: Indonesia to take delivery of first Chinese J-10CE fighter jets in 6 months, report says
description: When they arrive the southeast Asian nation will become the third international operator of the aircraft, after Pakistan and Uzbekistan.
content: Indonesia is expected to receive its first Chengdu J-10CE fighter jets in six months, according to an Indonesian media report, which would make it the third international operator of the Chinese-made aircraft. Jakarta confirmed an order of 42 of the 4.5-generation fighter jets – known as Vigorous Dragons – last October, with an approved budget of US$9 billion. The first delivery is expected in April though it is not known how many aircraft will be delivered, Indonesian news outlet Republika Online reported on Monday, citing sources with knowledge of the matter. Indonesian Air Force Chief of Staff Marshal Mohamad Tonny Harjono did not give an update on the order but asked for patience from the public, saying “just wait” for the Chinese Vigorous Dragons to arrive, according to the report. The J-10CE – the export variant of the J-10C – was developed by Chengdu Aircraft Corporation (CAC). Its relatively low cost compared to Western fighter jets and flexible supply arrangements have drawn buyers seeking to modernise their air force fleets. News of the Indonesian delivery schedule follows the formal induction of the J-10CE into the Uzbekistan Air Force. State television broadcast footage of at least six J-10CEs taking part in a ceremony in August, confirming Uzbekistan as the second foreign operator of the fighter jet after Pakistan. Uzbekistan has reportedly procured 24 J-10CE fighters, though the exact order size, delivery schedule and financial terms of the contract have not been disclosed. Also in August, Bangladesh reportedly submitted a draft proposal to buy 20 J-10CE fighters for an estimated US$2.2 billion, pending final approval from the country’s Ministry of Finance and the Armed Forces Division. Azerbaijan has also emerged as a potential new customer. CAC’s parent company, Aviation Industry Corporation of China, had a full-scale J-10CE mock-up on show at the Azerbaijan International Defence Exhibition in Baku last week. It was painted in Azerbaijani Air Force markings with the serial number “27-001” and carried model missiles. This was interpreted by military observers as a tailored sales pitch to Azerbaijan, while Chinese media suggested that the display also indicated Baku’s growing recognition of the J-10CE. While Azerbaijan has not confirmed it will buy the J-10CE, it is already operating the JF-17 Block III, a fighter jet jointly developed by CAC and Pakistan. A few other countries are also reportedly considering the J-10CE, such as Egypt and Algeria, though none of them have confirmed a purchase. Until recently, Pakistan was the only confirmed foreign buyer of the J-10CE. The single-engine multirole fighter attracted international attention after the Pakistan Air Force claimed it shot down Indian aircraft – including French-made Rafales – using J-10CEs during a military conflict in May 2025.

title: Hong Kong return collapsed because football bosses can’t forgive me, Andersen says
description: Popular former head coach now in charge of Myanmar believes he was punished for opting to leave city’s top job in the first place.
content: Jorn Andersen was on the brink of a sensational return as Hong Kong head coach earlier this year, only for talks to collapse and pave the way for interim boss Roberto Losada’s permanent appointment. Enormously popular with supporters after ending the city team’s 55-year wait to reach a major tournament at the last Asian Cup finals, Andersen ultimately accepted a “great offer” from Myanmar back in July. He had been unemployed for two months after leaving Yunnan Yukun when the local football association sounded him out in February about replacing Ashley Westwood, who left following Hong Kong’s Asian Cup qualifying defeat by Singapore last November. Andersen met with recently departed technical director John Morling, the general secretary, Charles Cheung Yim-yau, and board member Johnny Woo Wai-man. “When they called me, I said to my wife, ‘Maybe we’ll go back’,” Andersen told the South China Morning Post. In charge of Hong Kong for 2½ years before he resigned in May 2024 to take over at then-China League One club Yunnan, Andersen said: “A lot of people wanted me back, but the ones who decided ultimately didn’t want to do it. “I think they were so disappointed the last time I left, and they haven’t forgiven me.” Along with the two parties not being aligned over financial terms, the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) would not agree to Andersen’s request that he be released from his deal should an attractive approach come from elsewhere. After taking over Yunnan midway through the 2024 campaign, Andersen guided his new team to the second-tier title. He led them to eighth in their debut Chinese Super League campaign, but had decided before the end of the season that he would leave because “this club was new [established in 2021] and not so professional”. “Everything I asked for – new players, better organisation – they said, ‘no’,” he added. “I took the risk of not signing a new contract, and went back to Europe to rest. I thought I would join another Chinese club.” Ultimately, negotiations with “two or three big clubs” broke down. “In China they have people sitting in the top positions who don’t understand football,” Andersen said. “They come from outside, or from the government, and they make bad decisions.” Nonetheless, having previously harboured reservations over managing on the mainland, Andersen’s 18 months with Yunnan “changed my mind”. “The training facilities were great, the players lived and ate together, and there were big crowds,” he said. “It’s much more professional than Hong Kong. There’s more money, so they have better foreigners: maybe second and third level, whereas in Hong Kong the overseas players are fourth level. The Chinese players were not of such high quality, but I’ll go back if I have the chance.” After six months back in Germany, where he spent time with his children and three grandchildren, and became a regular in the stands at Eintracht Frankfurt, the club where he scored a Bundesliga-high 18 goals in 1989-90, Andersen had grown restless. He needed only “three or four days” to accept an offer from Myanmar that was more financially rewarding than the one Hong Kong had proposed, having asked the team’s German former bosses Michael Feichtenbeiner and Antoine Hey about the country’s political climate. “They said, ‘What everybody says about war and the military, you’ll never see anything’, so I decided to go and sign the contract,” Andersen said, adding that the Myanmar Football Federation had agreed to the exit clause their Hong Kong counterparts rebuffed. “My wife’s always more positive than me. When we went to North Korea [for nearly two years as national team boss from May 2016], I said, ‘We have to think, it’s a big decision’, but she said, ‘We go’. She always wants to do something special.” Living in a “good city” in Yangon, Andersen has discovered a domestic football scene that is “one step better than Hong Kong”. “But they don’t have much money for foreigners, they have not so good local players, and not many stadiums, so I’m a bit disappointed with the league level,” he said. “The training centres are not like Hong Kong, they are worse. “But the national team is OK. We have a good base; an old stadium, but it’s big, and in 2½ months we’ve already played two tournaments.” Andersen immediately recast expectations in Myanmar, overseeing a statement 4-1 Asean Hyundai Cup away win over the Philippines, before his depleted team lost to a late Cambodia strike to exit the recent Fifa Asean Cup in Hong Kong. “I try to let them play with more freedom: more offensive, more aggressive, more high pressing,” Andersen said. “The players, the fans, everybody likes it. When the players see we can have some success, they buy into it. The biggest problem is we don’t have lots of good players, maybe about 12, so when some are missing, it’s hard.” While managing Hong Kong, Andersen frequently aired his frustrations over players’ fitness and the substandard quality of football administration in the city. “We got a little bit better tactically, and the players’ conditioning became a little bit better,” Andersen said. “But it was all poor in my time. One of my reasons for leaving was that I couldn’t see how they could improve much more. [HKFA] are the same as my club in China, they’re not professional enough. “I don’t want to criticise, but you see who is at the top of the Hong Kong FA, and they’re not football people.” Englishman Morling recently jumped ship for a role in the United Arab Emirates. His predecessor, Carlos Anton, left to become sporting director at Saudi club Al-Qadsiah, having previously quit a HKFA coaching post to work in Kuwait. This summer, Darren Arnott resigned as under-23 boss for the Football Cub head coach job. A troubling brain drain also saw Andy Foster resign as head of coach education last October. “It’s a bit like, you are here because you didn’t find something better, but when a better offer comes, you leave very quickly,” Andersen said. Still, Andersen has retained enormous affection for Hong Kong football and his former players. He was “disappointed” watching the Singapore qualifier last November, when the city team led 1-0 at half-time, then “went back, stayed there and waited”. “I don’t know what [Westwood] said at half-time, but Singapore couldn’t attack in the first half,” Andersen said. “In the second half, Hong Kong invited them to score two goals, then they started attacking again, but it was too late.” Andersen is hoping that the city’s football chiefs give Losada a fair crack. “He knows every player, and everything about Hong Kong,” Andersen said. “He understands football, he’s a good coach, and the players like him. When you bring a foreign coach, it takes six months for them to understand everything. I have felt that myself. I think it’s the right thing for Hong Kong to take some coaches who’ve been working here.” The counsel of Feichtenbeiner and Hey speeded Andersen’s crash course in Myanmar football, and he talks optimistically about engineering improvement. Andersen also spoke to his friend Jurgen Klopp, now in charge of Germany, about the Myanmar challenge. “He’s already making a big difference in Germany,” Andersen said. “Nobody was talking about the national team, now everybody is talking about them. “He knows this business. When I was in Hong Kong, he was Liverpool manager. He said, ‘All the best [with Myanmar]’. He understands that everybody has to take what he can get.” At 63, Andersen retains the physique of a man who could still deliver an effective centre-forward’s shift. “I feel good, not old or tired,” he said. “I was on the way to stopping after China, but I wanted to work again. I want to stay coaching for some years, I can’t stay at home.” Could he one day be enticed back to Hong Kong? “I can’t say never, but with these people on the board, I don’t think so,” Andersen said. “They were disappointed and angry with me for leaving. But I got an offer from China that was better than they could manage, and I wanted to try something new.”

title: Asian Games star Ryan Choi, top jockey Vincent Ho honoured in 10 outstanding persons award
description: Ho is the first jockey to win the award after he and Choi represented the city at home and abroad over the past several months.
content: Elite Hong Kong athletes Ryan Choi Chun-yin and Vincent Ho Chak-yiu have been named among the recipients of this year’s Ten Outstanding Young Persons award. The pair have represented the city at home and abroad over the past several months, with Choi winning two silver medals at the Asian Games last month, in the men’s individual foil and men’s team foil categories. Ho, meanwhile, captained Hong Kong’s first ever Shergar Cup team to an impressive second place at Ascot in August and is the first jockey to win the award. In a statement, the Hong Kong Jockey Club congratulated Ho on “the remarkable achievement” and said the award recognised the 36-year-old’s “continued drive for world-class excellence and his contribution to society”. Andrew Harding, the Jockey Club’s executive director, racing, called it “particularly meaningful” because it was a first in the 54 editions of the award. “Vincent’s journey is defined by his resilience and never give up attitude, as well as a constant desire to learn, improve and better himself,” Harding said. “This is best exemplified by his partnership with Hong Kong racing’s former champion Golden Sixty, and how he has returned to the saddle stronger from serious injuries. “Vincent’s deep-rooted passion with the horse sports stems from equestrian and through the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s Apprentice Jockeys’ School before becoming an internationally renowned jockey, reflecting his talent and determination. “His pursuit of world-class excellence, together with his utmost professionalism, rigid discipline and highest integrity, have made Vincent a role model for young people and an outstanding ambassador for Hong Kong racing. “Vincent has shown that lasting success comes not only from talent, but also from perseverance, humility and a commitment to doing things the right way. We are proud of Vincent, and we look forward to seeing him race to even greater success as he continues to inspire future generations through his passion and pursuit of excellence.” Other award winners included: Alfred Yeung Yui-shing, the principal of SKH Kei Wing Primary School and founder/head coach of the Endeavour Running Club; musical therapist Chung King-man; Dr Doris Lam Pui-ying, a clinical assistant professor in paediatric dentistry at the University of Hong Kong; Dr Eric Lam Wing-kit, a deputy consultant pathologist at Tuen Mun Hospital; City University associate dean professor Cao Zhiyin; Dragon Wan-sang, executive chairman of the Hong Kong Youth Exchange Promotion Association and Chan Hiu-man, founder of OSP Sports Physiotherapy and Hydrotherapy Centre. Carol Wong, chairwoman of the Ten Outstanding Young Persons selection committee, said those awarded were “truly outstanding”. “In the golden era of AI, when excellence is achievable by almost everyone, it has become more challenging than ever to be truly outstanding,” she said. “Nevertheless, I see something in common in each of the nine awardees this year, something that AI cannot replicate: it is the human touch that they offer as an inspiring leader to help others thrive.”

title: Singaporean massage parlour boss added to US ‘worst of the worst criminal aliens list’
description: Prostitution ring operator Jing Emtage becomes the third Singaporean named on the US list ahead of her deportation.
content: A Singaporean woman has been added to a US list of “the worst of the worst criminal aliens,” becoming the third citizen from the city state to appear on the register, after convicted sex offender Amos Yee and money launderer Lim Seok Pheng. Jing Emtage, 54, was sentenced in July last year to two years and two months in prison on seven counts of second-degree promoting prostitution across multiple Washington state massage parlours she ran with her husband, Gerald Emtage. Gerald Emtage, 49, was handed a jail term of three years and two months for the same offences following an investigation launched in 2021. Both also received concurrent 12-month sentences for money laundering. According to prosecutors, the couple – who were arrested in 2023 – made “significant profits from the commercial sexual exploitation of dozens of women” while “living in a home valued at over a million dollars”. While the defendants “hid hundreds of thousands of dollars in their home, there are no state records of any wages paid to their victims required to provide sexual services to strange men”, local news outlet Seattle Weekly reported, citing court documents. Police said Jing Emtage transported women between businesses, and an inspection of her phone revealed messages discussing operations, including collecting money and delivering condoms. Jing Emtage ran a massage therapy business in Singapore before moving to the United States in 2018, where she met her husband. She was diagnosed with throat cancer after her arrest. According to her sentencing memorandum, she “believes that her current health issue is her karmic punishment for her immoral decisions”, Federal Way Mirror reported. She is currently being held at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) processing centre in Washington state awaiting deportation after being added to the list maintained by the Department of Homeland Security. Before her inclusion, Yee was the first Singaporean named on the register when it was launched in December 2025. The controversial blogger was deported to Singapore in March after serving a prison sentence in the US for child pornography and sexual grooming – a return criticised by Singaporean Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam. “I wish the Americans had kept him,” Shanmugam said on a podcast in April. In February, Lim became the second Singaporean added to the list – which contains around 46,000 people – following her arrest for money laundering. The DHS does not publish a breakdown ranking origin countries by total numbers on the list, which highlights non-citizens convicted of crimes and targeted by ICE as part of US President Donald Trump’s sweeping anti-immigration crackdown. However, US media reports show South American countries dominate the database, which also includes citizens from Asian nations such as India, Bangladesh and Laos. The DHS said it “will not stop until every illegal alien is off our streets and out of our communities, so they can no longer threaten the lives, dreams and futures of American citizens”. But many people appearing on the list do not fit its description. In February, CBS News cited an internal DHS document showing that fewer than 14 per cent of the roughly 400,000 immigrants arrested by ICE during Trump’s first year back in office had charges or convictions for violent crimes such as robbery, kidnapping or sexual assault. In response, the government said that the “fake news seems to think that illegal alien drug traffickers, drunk drivers, burglars, and those with weapons charges – whom they classify as ‘non-violent’ offenders – should be left alone, allowed to roam freely within the United States. Not under this administration”.

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo taps Widodo’s allies as advisers amid falling approval rating
description: By co-opting Widodo’s allies to the presidential advisory council, no opposition against Prabowo can be built through them, an analyst says.
content: Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto is seeking to keep potential rivals in his inner circle as he faces growing political pressure by appointing influential figures from across the political establishment to a presidential advisory council, according to analysts. The council, which advises the president on the direction of government policy but has no power to set or control it, comprises allies of former presidents, political commentators and Muslim leaders. “These are figures who have influence, connections and mass followings. By keeping them in Prabowo’s orbit, Prabowo can feel a bit more at ease that no opposition is being built outside through these figures,” said Yoes Kenawas, a political analyst with the Indonesian Survey Institute. On Friday, Prabowo designated 26 political figures, civil society representatives, Muslim leaders, businessmen and activists to the council, which had been vacant since he became president in October 2024. Prabowo already has a separate board of special advisers whose 10 members counsel him on matters including politics, security, defence, energy, labour, health and haj. The move has taken on added significance after Thursday’s cabinet reshuffle, which saw several figures linked to former president Joko Widodo move out of key government positions even though some of them were appointed to the council. One such member is Pratikno, who chairs the council. He previously served as a minister during Widodo’s two-term presidency and as Prabowo’s coordinating human development and culture minister, and was replaced by former foreign minister Sugiono in the cabinet reshuffle. Muhammad Qodari, another ally of Widodo, was appointed as the council’s secretary after having worked as head of Prabowo’s Government Communications Agency. The council’s vice-chairman, Hatta Rajasa, is an in-law of former president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, under whom he served as minister of several different portfolios, including transport and coordinating economic affairs. Prabowo also recruited Budi Gunawan, a close aide of former president Megawati Sukarnoputri and former coordinating minister of politics and security affairs in his cabinet, to the council. The other council members include vocal political commentator Rocky Gerung, former Constitutional Court chief justice Anwar Usman, who is Widodo’s brother-in-law, prominent Muslim scholar Quraish Shihab, Sinta Nuriyah Wahid, widow of former president Abdurrahman Wahid, and Said Aqil Siradj, former leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, the country’s largest Muslim group. Gerung said the council would not advise Prabowo on “technical” issues but rather on “ethical” matters, whereby its members would “provide deliberations regarding the direction of the government policies to ensure they align with the president’s vision”. “Members of the Presidential Advisory Council need to contemplate, evaluate and even fantasise about the future of the republic, like some kind of an oversight committee,” Gerung told reporters on Friday. According to Gerung, the council would also be responsible for “shaping public perception so that they align with the president’s perception”. Expanding coalition Yoes said Prabowo’s choice of appointments was due in part to his falling public support levels. “Prabowo is currently experiencing a significant drop in his approval rating compared with last year. Therefore, he needs to bring these elites under his sphere of influence.” In August, Prabowo’s approval rating declined to 51.1 per cent, down from 81.2 per cent in November, according to a survey by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting. Prabowo’s electability was at 14.5 per cent, behind West Java Governor Dedi Mulyadi, who was preferred by 35 per cent of the survey respondents, the pollster said. Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political researcher at the Indonesian National Research and Innovation Agency, said that the council’s composition showed that Prabowo was feeling pressure over criticisms of his policies. Prabowo has repeatedly labelled critics, academics, experts and journalists as “foreign stooges”, “black foreigners” or “stupid” in his speeches. “The president realised there was a blunder when he criticised [experts]. That’s why he appointed them to the government. While he doesn’t directly monitor social media every day, there are elements within the palace who monitor social media conversations and reactions to the president’s statements,” Wasisto said. While appointed directly by the president, as a “non-structural institution” within the presidential palace, the council “does not hold a strategic position”, Wasisto said. “The council doesn’t control policy or programmes. It’s merely a consultative body whose information is reserved exclusively for the president,” he said. Relationship with Widodo Prabowo’s latest political shake-ups have raised questions about his ties with Widodo, as several of his loyalists have been set aside. While some of Widodo’s allies have joined the advisory council, Prabowo has reassigned police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, another Widodo loyalist, to the presidential chief of staff in Thursday’s cabinet reshuffle. “It could mean that Prabowo was feeling insecure as Jokowi began his political manoeuvres. Jokowi is now a member of the Indonesian Solidarity Party, and he has visited some regions, including the earthquake-affected areas in East Nusa Tenggara,” said Nicky Fahrizal, a political researcher with the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia, referring to Widodo’s nickname. “Even though Jokowi’s key figures were removed [from the cabinet], they weren’t discarded. They were still embraced,” said Fahrizal. According to Yoes, a sweeping dismissal of Jokowi’s loyalists from Prabowo’s administration is akin to “an open war with Jokowi”, which could be “dangerous for Prabowo”. “For Prabowo, it is quite difficult to separate himself from Jokowi because his approval rating is dropping. A political elite who is openly opposed to Prabowo can easily consolidate all voices that don’t like Prabowo,” Yoes said. On Thursday, Widodo told reporters that the cabinet reshuffle was “President Prabowo’s prerogative authority”. “Listyo Sigit has served as national police chief for five years and eight months, so it’s time [for him to be replaced],” he said.

title: Fire breaks out on rooftop of residential building in Hong Kong’s Mong Kok
description: No casualties reported as firefighters battle blaze with one water jet after items stored on the rooftop catch fire.
content: Firefighters battled a fierce rooftop blaze at a residential building in Hong Kong’s Mong Kok district for around an hour on Tuesday before dousing the flames. The Fire Services Department received a report at about 5.20pm that items stored on the rooftop of the 26-storey Block B of Shun King Building on Nelson Street had caught fire. No casualties were reported, while 40 residents fled the building. Firefighters tackled the blaze with one water jet. Strong flames and thick black smoke could be seen billowing from the top of the building. The smoke was visible from a considerable distance. The fire was put out at about 6.40pm. Preliminary investigations suggested that candles used for worship on the rooftop accidentally ignited nearby combustible materials, causing the fire. The cause of the blaze is not considered suspicious.

title: Hong Kong’s Generation Y unhappiest amid housing and economic pressures, poll finds
description: Hong Kong’s happiness index falls to 5.87, staying below passing level of six out of 10 for fourth year, but remains above 2024 low.
content: Hong Kong’s Generation Y residents – those aged 30 to 45 – are the city’s unhappiest age group, largely because of dissatisfaction with economic and housing conditions, a poll has found. The Hong Kong Happiness Index stood at 5.87 out of 10, according to a survey of 1,039 adults conducted by HK.WeCare, an initiative under non-profit organisation Wofoo Social Enterprises. The score remained below the passing level for a fourth consecutive year, despite an overall upward trend since 2024. More than 40 per cent of residents reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms. Respondents also reported only moderate levels of community belonging and trust, scoring 3.13 and 2.81, respectively, out of five. Both factors were found to be directly linked to happiness. At a briefing on Tuesday, lawmaker Andrew Lam Siu-lo said problems could arise when people became disconnected from their families, communities or society at large without adequate support. “In our interpretation of the Happiness Index, this manifests as being relatively unhappy,” Lam said. “It is also our hope that everyone can use this index as a tool to think together about how, ultimately, we can rebuild a happy city.” He added that it was important to monitor whether isolation among individuals would worsen as artificial intelligence and social media exerted a growing influence on society. The index fell to 5.87 from 5.95 last year but was higher than the 5.63 recorded in 2024, its lowest level since 2018. Hong Kong residents generally reported satisfactory levels of happiness between 2018 and 2022, with scores above six out of 10. The latest survey, conducted this summer among baby boomers and members of Generations X, Y and Z, found that Generation Y respondents had the lowest scores for happiness, health and family relationships. They also reported the lowest satisfaction scores of any age group in areas such as governance, political and social conditions, and the media, while baby boomers expressed greater satisfaction in these areas. Generation Y participants accounted for almost half of all respondents. Among them, unmarried respondents reported average happiness and life-satisfaction scores of 5.18 and 5.13 out of 10 respectively. Their married peers with children reported higher average scores of 6.01 and 5.94. Nearly 30 per cent of Generation Y respondents described their economic situation as “poor”, while housing-satisfaction scores among Generation Y respondents were below six out of 10. Unmarried respondents recorded an average score of 4.44. Sylvia Chan May-kuen, HK.WeCare’s co-chairwoman, said the dissatisfaction might be linked to interpersonal relationships. “That is why we emphasise that the family is a very important place and a major source of happiness,” she said. “When relationships between people face problems in a space that isn’t very spacious, it creates a lot of friction.” Generation Z respondents also reported more frequent conflicts among family members than other age groups. Chan urged residents to spend less time on screens, strengthen face-to-face connections and get adequate rest to maintain a healthy, balanced lifestyle. The government should also encourage businesses to adopt family-friendly measures that better supported employees and their families, said Tik Chi-yuen, another co-chairman of the platform. A biennial study by the Mental Health Association and the Chinese University of Hong Kong found in March that one in three Hong Kong adults had moderate to severe symptoms of depression, almost three times the rate recorded in 2012. Generation Z respondents, who spent substantial time on screens, were the most affected, the study found.

title: Review | Mastermind review: Louis Koo plays detective in ludicrously bad Hong Kong mystery thriller
description: Viewers expecting a gritty whodunit will be sadly disappointed in Mastermind, riddled as it is with hollow tropes and zero forensic logic.
content: 1/5 stars A fine line separates a labyrinthine murder thriller from an infuriatingly fragmented mess. With Mastermind, emerging Hong Kong writer-director James Hung Ling-ching (The Seventh Lie) crosses it with reckless abandon, delivering a detective mystery with such irredeemably awful plotting that genre fans will rarely have felt so insulted. Set over a single, relentlessly storm-soaked night in H City – a fictional, dystopian metropolis of 5 million starved of proper rule of law – the film begins with a battered corruption witness, Earl (Yeung Wai-lun), escaping to the run-down East Precinct police station to seek protection. Unfortunately, Maximo (Louis Koo Tin-lok), the weary but righteous captain who hears him out in a detention cell, is rendered unconscious. An hour later, Earl is discovered shot dead inside the locked records vault of the city’s castle-like police headquarters some 10km (6.2 miles) away. The body is found by Sonny (Ci Sha), Maximo’s protege, who kicks the door open after noticing the blood pooling outside. We can only assume this locked-room setting was conceived by someone unfamiliar with physics, as the blood helpfully flows in one direction straight out from under the heavy door. The alleged fatal bullet happens to be Maximo’s antique keepsake, and the ostensibly wicked inspector Si (Simon Yam Tat-wah) immediately declares the captain the prime suspect. Shockingly, everyone then agrees to grant Maximo seven and a half hours of unrestricted crime-scene access to clear his name before daybreak. Clues are haphazardly dropped – such as a perfume scent around the forensic scientist Lluvia (Amy Lo Wai-man) that pays off arbitrarily later on – while intelligence chief Prins (Tse Kwan-ho), a cigar-chomping villain type, arrives at this inconvenient hour to demand vault evidence, a suspicious coincidence that goes comically unremarked upon. Attempting to manufacture unearned emotional heft, Hung also tacks on a tragic backstory involving Maximo’s deceased son, alongside a treasured piccolo for Sonny – whose father was perhaps killed by Si – that serves minimal narrative purpose. As Mastermind bombards the audience with frantic twists and reversals, genuine forensic deduction is deemed frivolous. The villains’ meticulous plan to quietly conceal incriminating evidence even spirals into an explosive finale – a deeply counterproductive approach to keeping a clean record in the official system. Seeking entertainment beyond this frustrating whodunit premise, capped by an absurdly efficient sci-fi gadget in the final act, proves futile. The film’s fight and shoot-out sequences are so shoddily assembled that they obscure the action choreography, compounding the pervasive sense of waste. Following My First of May (2025), a similarly superficial melodrama, Hung is fast confirming his storytelling brand: assembling genre ingredients galore – locked rooms, framed officers and planted evidence – without the substance or wisdom to connect them. Mastermind is a hollow facade, proving that poor lighting alone does not a noir make. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Construction worker jailed for life for killing bus driver after smoking dispute
description: Tam Yun-chiu attacked Ho Lok-man, who had confronted him about smoking while they waited for a lift at Amoy Gardens in Kowloon Bay.
content: A construction worker has been sentenced to life in prison for murdering a man who confronted him about smoking while they were waiting for a lift at a private housing estate in Hong Kong. A High Court jury on Tuesday found Tam Yun-chiu, 52, guilty of killing Ho Lok-man after hearing that he repeatedly punched the victim in the face, knocked him to the ground and kicked his head on the podium floor of Amoy Gardens in Kowloon Bay on September 19, 2023. Ho, a 48-year-old bus driver, became embroiled in a dispute with Tam after reprimanding him for smoking while they waited for the lift. Security camera footage showed Tam following Ho after the pair left the lift. He began the assault by pushing Ho against a railing before repeatedly kicking him in the head after he fell to the ground. Tam then left Ho lying on the floor, unresponsive. After regaining consciousness, Ho called an ambulance and was taken to hospital. He was discharged the following day. Shortly after returning home, however, Ho began vomiting and lost consciousness. He was taken back to hospital, where he underwent emergency brain surgery. Ho died in hospital on October 1. An autopsy found that his cause of death was a head injury. In a police statement, Tam admitted attacking Ho, saying he rarely got into arguments but had been enraged by the victim’s attitude that day. “He was swearing at me, so I lost it and hit him,” Tam said. After the verdict, Mrs Justice Judianna Barnes Wai-ling imposed the mandatory life sentence, describing the case as tragic. She said Tam came from a good background but had nevertheless committed the serious offence of murder.

title: Public outcry as China nurse dies after on-duty brain bleed, but death ruled not work-related
description: Under Chinese law, an employee’s on-duty illness is only deemed work-related if they die at the workplace or within 48 hours of emergency treatment.
content: The death of a 30-year-old nurse in southwestern China from a brain haemorrhage while on duty sparked outrage after authorities refused to classify her death as work-related. Chen Jiajia, a supervising nurse in the medical imaging department at Guizhou Maotai Hospital in Zunyi, experienced a severe headache and began vomiting while working on August 4, according to Dafeng News. Her colleagues swiftly rushed her for emergency treatment, and she subsequently underwent a craniotomy after being diagnosed with acute brain herniation. Chen remained at the first hospital for treatment until the early hours of August 14, when an ambulance transferred her to a hospital in Chongqing. Specialists there declared her brain-dead. She was later taken back to her hometown, and according to her mother, Lin, she stopped breathing about five minutes after arriving home. The sudden loss left the family devastated, and Chen was buried on a plot of land beside the family home. Her family later requested that Maotai Hospital apply for official recognition of her death as work-related. On September 17, the Zunyi Human Resources and Social Security Bureau rejected the application, ruling that Chen did not meet the statutory criteria because emergency treatment continued for 10 days. Under Chinese regulations, an employee who falls ill at work may have their death deemed work-related if they die at the workplace or within 48 hours despite emergency treatment. Families in recognised cases may receive funeral subsidies, dependent pensions, and a lump sum death benefit. This year’s one-time benefit is about 1.1 million yuan (US$164,000). Her mother shared with mainland media that she could not accept the loss of her daughter within 48 hours. “Even with a one-in-ten-thousand chance, we would still have tried to save her,” she stated. The family is preparing to request an administrative review of the decision. Chen underwent annual health checks and had no known underlying illnesses, according to her family, who described her workload as demanding and noted that she was sometimes called back to the hospital at night. A divorced mother, Chen was raising an eight-year-old son. She had previously been recognised as an “Outstanding Healthcare Worker” and had participated in local Covid-19 prevention efforts in 2021. Her death has ignited widespread discussion online, with many questioning whether the 48-hour threshold creates a perverse incentive for families facing life-or-death medical decisions. “No parent will give up on their children as long as there is a little bit of hope,” one online observer commented. Another urged local authorities to reconsider their decision, adding: “Chen was a dedicated nurse who cared deeply for her patients. How a society treats those who care for others reflects its true values.” The case resonates with another controversy from April, when a programmer in Shenzhen, southern China, died in a toilet shortly after clocking in for work, leaving behind two children. The local social security authority determined that his death was not work-related because he “was not at his desk” or “logged onto his computer” before he died. Such disputes are not uncommon in China. In July last year, a security guard in Xian died after arriving at work an hour early to prepare for his shift. His employer denied compensation on the grounds that his death was unrelated to his job, prompting public outrage.

title: Chinese brands drive global consumer 3D printer boom with ease of use, lower pricing
description: Shenzhen-based companies account for 90 per cent of the global consumer 3D printing market, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
content: For Toronto-based product designer Alex Vong, buying his first 3D printer was not about experimenting with a niche technology – it was about finding a reliable tool for his creative business. After watching several YouTube reviews, he eventually chose a machine made by Shenzhen-based Bambu Lab. “A 3D printer is something I’d rather buy once, and buy the best,” he said. “I’m not buying multiples unless I have the space for it.” Vong has been using the 3D printer to produce the shell of an interactive, retro art toy modelled after an Apple Macintosh desktop computer. “They understand that user experience matters for every kind of user, not just enthusiasts who enjoy dialling in settings,” he said. “You hit print and get consistent quality without needing to understand what’s happening underneath. And if you do want to go deeper, the advanced options are there.” Once viewed as a niche technology reserved for laboratories and tech enthusiasts, 3D printing – a process that builds objects layer by layer from digital designs – is moving into the mainstream as consumer-grade machines become easier to use and more affordable. Chinese brands, meanwhile, have emerged as leading players in the sector, leveraging their advantages – and the manufacturing advantages of the country at large – to turn complex hardware into consumer products. Shenzhen, home to many of China’s major consumer 3D printer makers – including Bambu Lab, eufyMake, Anycubic, Elegoo and Creality – accounted for 90 per cent of the global consumer 3D printing market, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Chinese companies’ strengths in engineering, supply chain coordination and large-scale manufacturing have helped turn the technology into reliable, user-friendly and affordable products Bambu Lab, Shenzhen The scale of China’s expansion is also reflected in export data. In the first eight months of 2026, China exported more than US$1.9 billion worth of 3D printers, with shipments reaching 5 million units, a 90 per cent increase in volume from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. “The key factors [in our competitiveness] are the improvement of China’s smart manufacturing capabilities and efficiency advantages brought about by a complete supply chain,” Bambu Lab said in a written response to the South China Morning Post. “Consumer 3D printers are complex hardware systems … Chinese companies’ strengths in engineering, supply chain coordination and large-scale manufacturing have helped turn the technology into reliable, user-friendly and affordable products.” Those attributes, according to the company, have aligned well with changing user priorities. Consumers, who once focused on whether a 3D printer would work, now pay more attention to ease of use, reliability and the broader product ecosystem, which is driving growth in the global market. More affordable pricing has also contributed to the rapid growth of Chinese 3D printer brands, Bambu Lab said. A single unit from major Chinese brands can cost as little as around US$200, according to information on supplier websites. Overseas markets currently account for a significant share of sales for China’s consumer 3D printer makers. Shenzhen-based Creality disclosed in its prospectus that 74 per cent of its 2025 sales were from abroad, while Bambu Lab said overseas sales that year accounted for about 70 per cent of its total. Bambu Lab attributed a portion of overseas demand to the mature maker communities in those markets, where interest in DIY technology has been strong. Domestically, demand for 3D printers is expanding rapidly. Manufacturing output rose 29.9 per cent year on year in August, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics. Industry insiders said the growth was mainly driven by consumer-grade machines, Shanghai-based media outlet Cailian Press reported in August. The Chinese government pledged policy support for the niche market. In a guideline released in late August, 3D printers were identified by Beijing as a product category with the potential to boost consumption.

title: Meet Bo Bryan, country star Luke Bryan’s high school quarterback son
description: The eldest son of the ‘Play It Again’ singer recently scored six touchdowns in a school game to lead his team to victory, and has earned offers from three universities.
content: Country music star Luke Bryan’s son Bo Bryan is making headlines for his skills on the gridiron as quarterback, after he scored six touchdowns and led Battle Ground Academy to a 41-36 victory against Franklin Road Academy on September 25. “Well, just super impressed. Obviously, crosstown rival, big rival, big game. His senior year. You know, he’s learning as he goes,” Luke Bryan told USA Today about his son’s performance after the game. “I mean, everything that happens to him this year is the first time he’s had all these pressure situations. The ups, the downs. “He came out, we got behind. He threw a pick that actually turned into a touchdown for them. And then for the team to battle back and for him to really have an incredible second half … can’t be more proud as a dad,” Bryan continued. Here’s everything you need to know about Luke Bryan’s rising star quarterback son, Bo Bryan. He is Luke Bryan’s eldest child Luke Bryan and his wife, Caroline, were college sweethearts and dated on and off for several years before eventually tying the knot in December 2006. The couple welcomed their first child, son Thomas Boyer Bryan, in March 2008. Little Bo was named after his father, whose real name is Thomas Luther Bryan, and his middle name comes from his mother, whose maiden name is Boyer. “I’m over the moon! Everyone is doing great! My fishing buddy is finally here!” the proud father wrote in a statement when Bo was born. “I thought being on stage was an amazing feeling, but there is nothing that can top watching my wife bring our son into this world. There is no way I would have missed this for anything.” Bo is the older brother of Tatum “Tate” Christopher Bryan, who was born in 2010. The “Play It Again” singer and his wife also helped raise his nephew Tilden and nieces Jordan and Kris after their parents, Ben and Kelly Cheshire, passed away. The Cheshire siblings lost their mother, Bryan’s sister Kelly, in 2007. Several years later, in 2014, their father Ben died of a heart attack. He is eyeing a college football career While Bo may have grown up in the spotlight of his father’s fame, he has chosen to pursue a different career as an American football player. Bo is set to play the sport as a collegiate athlete and has already received offers from three universities: Austin Peay State University, the University of Tennessee at Martin, and the University of North Alabama.

title: ‘Neutrino Man’ Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics
description: The Belgian-American scientist was honoured for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
content: Belgian-American particle physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel ⁠Prize in Physics for his work creating an Antarctic observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that can reveal otherwise inaccessible information about the cosmos. Halzen, 82, realised that pristine ice at the South Pole could be used to track such neutrinos, sometimes known as “ghost particles” for the way they pass through the Earth without a trace, only interacting with matter extremely rarely. “The messengers bring information from the cosmos,” Eva Olsson, of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a press conference. “They open the door to distant galaxies and tell us about ‌the processes of exploding stars.” The interactions registered by the IceCube observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, according to the academy. In 2014, the US-based Smithsonian magazine dubbed Halzen “Neutrino Man” when giving him one of its Ingenuity Awards, acclaiming him for an “amazing experiment [that] heralds the beginning of a new era in astronomy”. It even published a comic illustrating his life: How One Physicist’s Pursuit of the Cosmos Took Off in Antarctica. The observatory – in effect a telescope that shows neutrinos instead of light – is set in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, which extends to a depth of 2,500 metres below the surface near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. More than 5,000 sensors await blips from the nearly massless high-energy neutrinos, which unlike other particles do not lose energy ⁠or change direction, in the hope of tracing their paths back to exploding stars, gamma-ray bursts, and cataclysmic phenomena involving black holes and neutron stars. They can expect to register about one per day. Halzen, a professor at ‌the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the United States, first presented his idea in 1988 for capturing neutrino traces at the South Pole, but the project was not completed until 2011. “I have to emphasise how lucky I was because, when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, ‌including myself,” Halzen told the press conference by telephone. Neutrinos are electrically neutral, undisturbed by any magnetic field, which means that, in contrast to electromagnetic waves such as visible light, the direction ⁠from which they arrive points directly back to their source. The observatory has determined that high-energy neutrinos originate within but also far outside our own Milky Way galaxy, setting in motion an interstellar quest to find the objects and processes that create them. Through the long winter at the South Pole, ‌when bringing anything in or out is difficult as temperatures below minus 50 degrees Celsius (minus 58 Fahrenheit) preclude even aircraft landing, a skeleton crew of “winterovers” has to maintain the observatory. The station, home to many other activities, can house as many as 150 people and has an industrial kitchen, dining room, gym ‌and ‌even a greenhouse. Last week it celebrated the sun’s return above the horizon after six months of night with a six-hole ice-golf tournament. An extension, IceCube-Gen2, encompassing 8 cubic kilometres of ice, is planned to become operational in ‌2033 and will be able to detect 10 times as many neutrinos, including much weaker ones. Halzen said the main fruits of his work were yet to be seen and that it was too early to say exactly what ⁠it could reveal about the universe. “The real excitement is that I cannot answer that question yet,” he said. “This is just an introduction to the science, the astronomy is still to come.” Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever congratulated Halzen on the recognition of “a life dedicated to unravelling the greatest secrets of the cosmos through its most minuscule manifestations”. The physics laureate receives an award of 12 million Swedish crowns (US$1.2 million). Past winners include several other neutrino research pioneers, for instance Japan’s Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald from Canada in 2015. The Nobel Prizes were established under the will ‌of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was ‌built in part on the invention of dynamite. Physics was prominent in Nobel’s will and the prize remains one of the discipline’s highest distinctions. Over the decades, it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity’s understanding of the universe. Among past laureates are some of the most celebrated figures in science, including Albert Einstein, Marie and Pierre Curie, Max Planck and Niels Bohr, whose work helped establish the foundations of modern physics. The prize is presented in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death.

title: Kenya reports first Ebola case imported from DR Congo after patient dies
description: The Kenyan man, who fell ill about a month ago and was treated in the DR Congo, died after returning to the country, authorities say.
content: Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister said on Tuesday, after a Kenyan man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo died after returning to the country. The DR Congo declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May. The deadly disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years. Kenya has never previously reported a case. Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DR Congo – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said a team was heading to Kenya to provide assistance, and its director general Jean Kaseya would also visit in the coming days. The Kenyan citizen, who has not been named but was referred to as a 40-year-old businessman, fell ill around a month ago and had been treated in the DR Congo, Health Minister Aden Duale told reporters. He travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and then flew to Nairobi on Saturday. Duale said the man was suffering “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”. The man’s relatives took him to a Nairobi hospital, where he was confirmed positive for the virus, before he “regrettably passed on last night at around 11.30” local time, Duale said. Arrangements for a “safe and dignified burial” were planned for later on Tuesday, in line with public health standards. Kenyan authorities have identified 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but none have tested positive for Ebola so far. Authorities are pursuing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight, and that potential quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” Duale said. More care was needed at border entry points as “diseases know no boundaries”, Patrick Amoth, director general at the health ministry, told reporters. “The failure is the system that did not work,” he added, questioning how someone with such obvious symptoms was able to travel. As of Friday, the World Health Organization had recorded 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases since the emergence in the DR Congo of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment. After starting in the northeastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the north and east. The virus has hit unstable regions in the vast central African country where armed clashes and violence, alongside a critical lack of resources, have hindered the health response. Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province which borders Uganda. Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year for the creation of an Ebola facility for US citizens at Laikipia Air Base, about 200km (125 miles) from Nairobi.

title: Hong Kong remains world’s freest economy as Switzerland overtakes Singapore
description: Annual Economic Freedom of the World report compiled by Canada’s Fraser Institute ranks city first among 165 jurisdictions.
content: Hong Kong has retained its status as the world’s freest economy in the latest annual ranking by a top Canadian think tank, although its score has declined in recent years.
