Switzerland overtook Singapore to claim second place in 2026, pushing the city state down to third in the league table released by the Fraser Institute on Tuesday. The Economic Freedom of the World report, compiled by the Vancouver-based public policy research organisation using data from 2024, ranked Hong Kong first among 165 jurisdictions. “Despite a precipitous decline in economic freedom since 2018, Hong Kong remained the world’s most economically free jurisdiction in 2024, the latest year for which we have data,” the think tank said. According to the latest data, Hong Kong scored 8.53, down 0.02 from the previous year. It was the only jurisdiction in the top 15 to record a decline in its score. Switzerland scored 8.45, up from 8.38 the previous year. Singapore, which scored 8.43, was followed by New Zealand with 8.38 and the United States with 8.21. Among other major economies, Britain ranked 13th, Japan 17th, India 86th and mainland China 108th. Ireland recorded the highest increase in its score among the top 10, rising by 0.11 points, although it remained in sixth place. The report assessed regulation, openness to international trade, the size of government, the legal system, property rights and the stability of the currency. It also measured people’s freedom to make economic decisions in their countries or cities. “Global economic freedom fell during the pandemic as policymakers imposed new regulations, raised barriers to trade, increased government spending and taxes, and then printed money to pay for spending,” Matthew Mitchell, senior fellow at the Fraser Institute and a co-author of the report, said. The think tank said that although governments had started to reverse these policies, economic freedom in the average country had not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels. The 10 lowest-ranked countries were Congo, Egypt, Malawi, Algeria, Iran, Myanmar, Libya, Sudan, Zimbabwe and Venezuela. A government spokesman said the report once again affirmed Hong Kong’s strengths as a free-market economy and its open, efficient and fair business environment. “Amid increasing global economic uncertainties and rising trade protectionism, Hong Kong remains firmly committed to maintaining its free port status, zero-tariff policy, and simple and low tax regime, providing a secure, stable, fair, predictable and internationalised business and investment environment for investors and entrepreneurs from around the world,” he said. Gary Ng, senior economist for the Asia-Pacific region at Natixis, said Hong Kong had an edge over other jurisdictions, thanks to its free flow of capital and talent, and low-tax regime. But Ng said the city’s performance in certain categories, such as the size of government, might have led to the drop in its overall score. He noted that the city had seen more government-led investment, such as increased bond issuance, adding that other countries had been doing the same thing. In the report, government size is measured in terms of consumption, subsidies, investment, top marginal tax rates and ownership of assets. Ng also noted that the city’s standing in the sound-money category could have been affected by the US rate rises, given Hong Kong’s currency peg to the US dollar. Sound money is measured in terms of money growth, the standard deviation of inflation, inflation in the most recent year and foreign currency bank accounts. Ng said the city’s score for the legal system category was based on surveys and respondents’ perceptions could have played a role. “In the future, Hong Kong should continue to focus on maintaining its edges,” Ng said. Retired economist Thomas Yuen Wai-kee noted that national security laws and political events might have affected the overseas perceptions of the city’s legal system. “The government has been explaining and reflecting Hong Kong’s situation to the outside world … It takes time for them to understand, as long as they find that Hong Kong has not changed and is business-friendly,” he said. Yuen also stressed that increasing government intervention in the market was not a big issue, as the city’s monetary and fiscal policies could not be changed easily and were “cornerstones of the economy”. Apart from the pegged exchange-rate system, the city’s mini-constitution, the Basic Law, stipulated that the government had to avoid deficits, he said.

title: Why India is getting serious about ending the Ukraine war
description: US tariff threats and drone strikes on an Indian-owned factory are pushing Delhi to shift from passive advocacy to active peacemaking.
content: India’s recent push to become more involved in helping end the Russia-Ukraine war comes as the costs of the conflict continue to mount for New Delhi, amid the threat of US tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy and a recent drone attack on an Indian-owned pharmaceutical plant in Ukraine. Sunday morning’s drone attack destroyed a large part of Kusum Group’s factory in Sumy, killing one person and injuring several others. The company, which has manufactured generic medicines in Ukraine since 2009, said the attack was particularly devastating as its warehouse had already suffered a drone strike in April last year. The Ukrainian embassy in India condemned the attack in a social media post. “The barbarians do not care that the factory belongs to Indian owners,” it wrote. “The hypocrites continue talking about the ‘historic friendship’ between India and Muscovy. In reality, death and destruction are the true face of Russian fascism, hidden behind the mask.” The aggressor does not care that this is not a military target. It does not care that this is a pharmaceutical factory producing critically needed medicines. The barbarians do not care that the factory belongs to Indian owners. The hypocrites continue talking about the “historic… https://t.co/vrQqKsAHGQ — Ukraine in India (@UkrembInd) October 4, 2026 India’s government has not issued an official statement about the attack, but External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said on Sunday that Delhi was in talks with both Moscow and Kyiv on issues including the safety of Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports. Jaishankar added that India had in recent months become “a little bit more involved beyond advocacy” as it sought to help address shared concerns. The disclosure came weeks after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to shift from “endless war” to an “end of war”, speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on August 31. Both warring sides have publicly acknowledged India’s more active peacemaking role. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Friday that Kyiv had received a proposal from India aimed at helping end the conflict, calling it the “most comprehensive” of four proposals submitted by different countries, while Putin said on October 1 that Modi had some “good ideas” for finding a mutually acceptable solution. Analysts say the longer the war continues, the higher the indirect costs will be for India – particularly as it tries to balance ties with the West and Moscow, long seen by Delhi as a trusted ally. “The attack on the Kusum plant makes the war less distant for India because Indian commercial interests are directly affected,” said Uday Chandra, a professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University. Washington’s signing into law of a bill on September 18 that empowers US President Donald Trump to impose tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas “is more consequential for India” because it raises the economic cost of large-scale purchases of Russian oil, Chandra said. “Neither development will, of course, alter India’s relationship with Russia. Yet both give New Delhi clear material stakes in an early negotiated settlement to the war,” he said. India has been a major importer of Russian oil in recent years, taking advantage of discounted supplies amid Western sanctions. In September, it imported around 1.75 million barrels per day, down from some 2.1 million barrels per day in August, according to vessel-tracking data from data analytic platform Kpler. Jaishankar said on Monday that India launched the latest round of talks with Russia and Ukraine in July following attacks in the Black Sea that killed and injured Indian sailors. That India was looking to move “beyond advocacy” was significant, Chandra said. “India seems to be emerging as an intermediary on logistical matters in which both sides have something to gain: Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports and defence arrangements. This pragmatic and incremental approach suits India nicely,” he said, adding that such an approach allowed India to preserve its ties with Moscow while building credibility with Kyiv and Western capitals. The recent drone attack on another Kusum facility would make it easier for Kyiv “to present this as a pattern rather than an isolated incident”, Chandra added. “Ukraine has a concrete example with which to argue that Russian military actions are now damaging Indian economic interests too,” he said. Priyajit Debsarkar, a London-based author specialising in South Asia, said Delhi was likely to view such an attack on an Indian company overseas as “something very serious”, though its response would likely be confined to “diplomatic manoeuvring”. It was too early to conclude that Russian drones had deliberately attacked the facility, which was at risk because of its location in a conflict zone, he added. Swaran Singh, a former professor of diplomacy and disarmament at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s School of International Studies in Delhi, said both the drone strike on the Kusum factory and the prospect of additional US tariffs gave India incentives to act as a “facilitator” to end the conflict. “Higher stakes do not mean India can impose a settlement; its credibility rests precisely on retaining access and trust on both sides,” he said, pointing to Jaishankar’s recent comments. “This is essentially quiet, issue-based intermediation, rather than formal mediation in the conventional sense. India is unlikely to become a full-time peace broker with a single grand formula.” Singh added that India could not realistically tell Russia to “withdraw” or accept Ukraine’s terms, but it did have influence. “Delhi is able to tell Moscow that the military option is increasingly producing diminishing strategic returns while imposing growing economic and diplomatic costs,” he said. “India can urge Putin to use Russia’s military position to negotiate from strength rather than continue an open-ended war.”

title: 2026 Bangkok floods: Sinking capital fuels fury over Thailand government inaction
description: The city’s worst flooding in 15 years has the Thai capital at breaking point, with growing anger as the continuous heavy rain becomes an emergency disaster.
content:
As floodwaters surged from drains in Thailand’s capital city, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping unscathed; she had bought the car less than a month earlier.
“I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.”
Relentless rain paralysed Bangkok in September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days. The city, long plagued by sinking, went underwater. Not all of it, but enough of the city’s east and northeast to offer a terrifying insight into what may lie ahead as this year’s “super” El Nino climate pattern intensifies.
In the Khlong Chan neighbourhood of Bangkok’s Bang Kapi district, Fon – whose full name is Siraprapha Sangseeluem – was still stranded in her block of flats five days after the deluge.
Her scathing assessment of the authorities’ handling of the floods? “I can say only one thing: the government is totally useless,” she said.
Some of Fon’s neighbours have been even less diplomatic. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was met with a volley of abuse when he arrived to distribute relief to the flats on September 27.
The reception was similar in several places Anutin visited that week with his cabinet ministers and the media, in a city that largely did not vote for him. His Bhumjaithai Party did not win any of Bangkok’s constituency seats in February’s general election.
Anger has boiled over in recent days at a government that seemed blindsided by a calamity meteorologists had warned was brewing, but which city and central authorities alike played down in the days before it struck.
Anutin’s own campaign boast that his party would make the country “so rich, you won’t know what to do with your money” has come back to haunt him. “I feel so rich”, chanted crowds of angry residents sarcastically as he arrived to distribute food and water.
Speaking to reporters on September 30, Anutin acknowledged the backlash. “I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough,” he said. “The fact that people scolded me, criticised me … rest assured that I’ve heard you and I’m not ignoring you.”
Critics are unconvinced, however. “If the measurement of the prime minister’s job is to manage the situation, to bring calm, a sense of trust … then he fails miserably,” said political commentator Voranai Vanijaka.
On September 25, as floods swallowed Bangkok’s roads, homes, shops and restaurants, residents struggled to find their bearings. Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, normally hypervigilant, appeared caught off guard by the speed and scale of the rising water. He apologised days later for delayed warnings and a slow start to the relief effort.
Anutin, who is also the interior minister, cut short a diplomatic visit to London to oversee the response. His initial absence was nonetheless felt in Thailand’s highly centralised, hierarchical political system, with key officials seeming reluctant to make snap decisions without him.
Last week, opposition lawmakers blasted the government’s flood response, criticising everything from slow warnings to the sluggish relief effort.
Rain and floods are unpredictable in Thailand, and it lacks the comprehensive flood defences found in Singapore, Shanghai or Amsterdam. It is the failing of successive Thai governments, but critics still say Anutin was caught flat-footed.
As the planet heats to unprecedented, dangerous levels, extreme weather events are becoming ever more erratic and destructive, presenting governments everywhere with challenges many are ill-prepared to meet.
Last month, Japan’s capital logged 35 consecutive days of rain – its longest streak on record – while wildfires continued to rage in Indonesia’s Kalimantan region, sending toxic haze across borders to Singapore and Malaysia.
Thailand’s recent floods have cost at least 40 people their lives, with estimates of the damage running to hundreds of millions of US dollars.
In Bangkok, the floods were the worst in 15 years, filling drains and canals to capacity and affecting roughly one-tenth of the capital. The country’s southern provinces, where the rainy season typically peaks between November and January, are now bracing for a similar onslaught.
Bangkok’s misfortune has been decades in the making. The city’s ever-expanding urban sprawl is slowly sinking into the soft clay beneath it.
Concrete has spread upwards and outwards far faster than investment in infrastructure, especially drainage – effectively turning the built-up city centre into a basin with few natural outlets or floodplains.
It floods easily in large storms and in the increasingly common “rain bombs” that dump vast quantities of water on the city in a matter of hours.
In 2011, the worst floods in recent memory submerged the north of Bangkok, killing dozens and leaving parts of the capital up to two metres (6½ feet) under water for weeks on end.
This year’s floods, which may not be over yet, were the result of ceaseless rains overwhelming drains and inundating entire neighbourhoods, including affluent ones, with filthy, sludge-filled floodwater.
On Tuesday, Anutin’s cabinet approved a 160 billion baht (US$4.8 billion) plan to divert floodwaters away from the capital. It includes a new canal to relieve pressure on the Chao Phraya River, which currently carries run-off from northern and central Thailand straight through Bangkok. But that project is slated to take eight years to complete.

title: 8 public officers in Singapore referred to police after property review
description: The review identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to unannounced MRT stations.
content: Eight public service officers have been referred to Singapore police after a review of 191 officers’ property transactions, Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing has told parliament. The review followed a working paper by the US-based National Bureau of Economic Research, which identified 2007 to 2011 as the period of concern. The Public Service Division (PSD) extended the scope to 2014 as a matter of prudence, Chan said on Tuesday, because many new MRT station locations continued to be announced after 2011. Based on administrative records, PSD identified officers in agencies involved in rail planning who bought property between 2007 and 2014 close to locations later announced as MRT stations, he said. PSD assessed factors including the officer’s role at the time, whether the officer had access to relevant non-public information, and the timing and circumstances of the transaction. Of the 191 officers, eight were found to have cases that warranted further examination, said Chan, who is also defence minister. Further checks are ongoing. “This could be due to the specific circumstances surrounding the purchase, or that we currently do not have adequate information to exclude the case from further review. We have referred these cases to the police,” he said. He stressed that a referral did not mean that wrongdoing had been established, and that police would look into the facts independently and due process would be followed. The government would consider what the review revealed about the effectiveness of existing safeguards and the gaps to address, he said. Members of Parliament asked whether more safeguards were needed, such as more systematic cross-checking and extending declaration requirements to other family members or cohabitants. Chan said the public service “regularly reviews its rules and has strengthened them over time”. “We will consider what the present review tells us about their effectiveness and whether there are gaps to address. Any further measures should be proportionate to the risks and practical to implement, while allowing legitimate personal transactions to proceed with appropriate oversight,” he said. “Even with strong safeguards, no system can eliminate the possibility of wrongdoing entirely. We must therefore continue to reduce the opportunities for abuse, maintain effective means of detection, and act firmly where evidence of wrongdoing emerges.” According to Chan, access to sensitive information is controlled and given on a need-to-know basis. Such information is subject to security classification and handling requirements, system and physical access controls and, where appropriate, audit, monitoring and project-specific safeguards. Officers must also follow declaration and approval requirements for personal interests and transactions. Since the 1990s, all officers have had to declare purchases of private property and, every year, any non-owner-occupied properties they hold. “These requirements have been progressively tightened over the years. Today, where an officer possesses non-public information relevant to a transaction that he or she proposes to undertake, the officer must seek approval from the head of agency before proceeding,” Chan said. The requirements also cover other personal transactions where the officer has relevant non-public information, and extend to transactions involving officers’ spouses and financially dependent children. “More broadly, an officer must not pass non-public information to a relative, friend or any other person for private gain. Doing so would breach the applicable rules and may also constitute an offence under the law, including the Official Secrets Act,” he said. Agencies handling particularly sensitive information may add requirements according to the risks involved. Chan cited the Singapore Land Authority, which requires officers in relevant departments to declare to human resources any sale of property or land by themselves, their spouses or financially dependent children. Contractors, consultants and other people outside the public service who could access sensitive government information were also bound by confidentiality, conflict-of-interest and information-handling requirements, he said. Officers could also report suspected wrongdoing to their supervisors, human resources or agency heads, which would give agencies another way to learn of possible misconduct, he said. Asked whether more safeguards were needed to protect public officers’ confidentiality, Chan said different considerations were involved. The National Bureau of Economic Research report’s authors identified the property buyers through the Singapore Government Directory Interactive, an online database that lists the names, email addresses and office telephone numbers of a large number of public officers. It is freely accessible in Singapore and overseas. The directory was pared down from July 1 to combat the risk of scams. “Certain information on property transactions and ownership is already publicly accessible for legitimate reasons. Separately, some information about civil servants’ appointments and responsibilities also needs to be available in the public domain,” Chan said. “We should not restrict access to such information simply because it may be linked across different sources. At the same time, the government will continue to ensure that personal information about public officers which does not need to be made public is appropriately protected.” Chan said the government had no information about who funded the research, but emphasised it was assessing the working paper’s claims on their merits, including the methodology, available evidence and underlying facts. This story was first published by CNA

title: Opinion | Short trade truce can’t paper over realities of US-China relationship
description: As long as the US’ transactional strategy towards China remains unchanged, the rhythm of crisis and managed de-escalation will continue.
content: The recent US-China summit yielded a narrow, caution-filled outcome for bilateral trade: a two-month extension of the Kuala Lumpur trade truce, which now expires on January 10 next year. This reprieve eases fears of immediate tariff escalation and shows that head-of-state diplomacy can still curb spiralling confrontation. Yet the short timeline exposes the wide gulf separating the two sides’ priorities. China’s position has been unambiguous: removal of all punitive tariffs and restrictive measures imposed since 2018. Beijing has repeatedly stressed that no one wins in a trade war. Even so, it responded to the extension with goodwill. The Ministry of Commerce said the pause gave both sides time to take stock of implemented consensus and deliver stable, predictable policy conditions for businesses. Washington offered a different narrative. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent portrayed the two months as a compliance review, accusing China of failing to fully meet its commitments. He and other US officials did not celebrate the pause, instead speaking of obstacles remaining before any longer truce could be agreed. That framing is not merely diplomatic semantics. It reveals that the window is less about creating breakthrough conditions than about serving domestic political needs while positioning Washington for a possible tougher line after this year’s midterm elections. The subtext is familiar: the truce is Washington’s to grant or withdraw, China is the reluctant performer and any extension is a concession rather than a mutual interest. That framing is good politics in an election season and good leverage in a negotiation, but it is a poor description of how the supply-chain dispute actually started. Rare earths sit at the centre of Washington’s public justification of its actions. Beijing maintains that it manages dual-use items lawfully, approves compliant civilian applications and is committed to global critical-mineral supply-chain stability. The US complaint that rare earth export volumes have not bounced back fast enough ignores the self-inflicted nature of the friction. China exported 512 tonnes (564 tons) of rare earth magnets to the United States in August, down 13 per cent year on year and 20 per cent lower than July. The same Trump administration that demands smoother trade flows has also maintained broad pressure through its own tariffs and export controls, expanded Section 301 actions and treated China’s capacity to produce semiconductors, batteries and clean energy as a threat. When a supplier is also the target of systematic containment, constrained deliveries are the predictable result. If the US expects China to meet its rare earth supply demands, then Beijing has every reason to demand that Washington lift its restrictions on advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence technology. When Washington treats chip export controls as a non-negotiable red line, Beijing cannot be expected to forego aligning its rare earth export policies in the same direction. Since the US considers chip restrictions essential to its national security, China naturally reserves the right to treat export controls and supply security as legitimate sovereign tools. Any substantive resolution of rare earth and technology restrictions requires an equitable package deal, not a one-sided agreement. Beyond the fight over rare earths, the two-month trade truce extension serves US President Donald Trump’s domestic political purposes. By framing the short reprieve as a sign of US strength, with Washington keeping China on a leash, Trump leaned on his familiar playbook of projecting an image of himself as a negotiator holding all the cards. In the wake of his “Liberation Day” wave of global tariffs in April last year, Trump attempted to portray himself as holding a commanding position. He told reporters that Chinese President Xi Jinping initiated a phone call with him to seek a tariff deal, a claim China’s Foreign Ministry rejected. The election timeline makes Trump’s political motive clearer. The US midterm elections take place on November 3, with the 120th Congress set to take office in January. The brief extension avoids any difficult decisions during the election window for an administration facing voter anxiety over inflation. The extra two months are long enough to claim progress while short enough not to have to impose further tariffs or escalate the trade war. The same choreography is visible on Iran. Rather than opting to pursue a definitive military or diplomatic victory before the midterms, Trump has indicated he expects to resume bombing Iran after the election. The pause is not peace in either conflict but a holding pattern until domestic political turbulence clears. The two-month extension is a microcosm of the broader US-China economic relationship. Washington views the truce as a tactical pause that buys time to shore up domestic support. Meanwhile, it is gearing up to extract concessions from China through trade truce extensions. This playbook is nothing new. Former US president Joe Biden vowed to scrap Trump’s punitive tariffs on the campaign trail yet kept them in place as a bargaining chip when in office. The broader lesson is that a trade truce is not a foundation for lasting stability. As long as the US’ strategy towards China remains unchanged, the rhythm of crisis and managed de-escalation will continue. For Beijing, the right response is not to chase a longer truce for its own sake but to condition any extension on concrete US moves, such as scrapping punitive tariffs and easing tech controls. In return, China will be in a position to grant approvals for verified civilian rare earth and magnet orders while keeping national security safeguards as a negotiated position.

title: China’s Transsion, Africa’s top phone maker, targets US$500 million Hong Kong listing
description: The Shanghai-listed smartphone manufacturer behind Tecno and Infinix is eyeing an October 15 trading debut in Hong Kong.
content: Shenzhen Transsion Holdings has begun to take investor orders for its Hong Kong listing, with the maker of Africa’s bestselling phones offering 86.6 million shares at a maximum price of HK$38.8 per share, according to the company’s prospectus on Wednesday. The public offering will run from October 7 to 12, with the company expected to list on October 15, seeking to raise up to HK$3.36 billion (US$428.1 million). With the overallotment option, the deal size may grow to the equivalent of about HK$3.8 billion, confirming an earlier report. The share price reflects a discount of 38 per cent from the 53.8 yuan closing price on September 30 in Shanghai. A total of 11 cornerstone investors have agreed to buy HK$1.24 billion worth of Transsion shares. They include Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC, Shenzhen Longsys Electronics and Bank of China Wealth Management. The cornerstone tranche would account for up to 40 per cent of the total funds set to be raised, Transsion said. Founded in 2013, Transsion leads the African mobile phone market. Its three brands – Tecno, Infinix and iTel – sold more than 91 million handsets last year and captured 53 per cent of the regional market share, according to the company’s regulatory filings. The Shenzhen-based company has expanded into other markets such as Latin America and Southeast Asia, though its brands have no presence in the firm’s home market. The budget-phone maker has also faced growing challenges in recent years, including intensifying competition in Africa from rivals such as Xiaomi and Oppo. Rising chip procurement costs have also forced the company to raise retail prices. Transsion’s annual revenue fell 4 per cent to 65.5 billion yuan last year, while profit plunged 53 per cent to 2.6 billion yuan, according to the company’s filings. Despite a rebound in revenue and earnings in the first half of this year, its Shanghai-listed shares were still down about 70 per cent from their 2021 peak and have fallen 16 per cent this year. Citic Securities is the sole sponsor for the Hong Kong listing, according to the company’s prospectus.

title: Bali or Europe? Retired Hong Kong couple builds an ‘alpine’ retreat in the mountains
description: After three decades in Hong Kong, a former construction executive and her hotelier husband have opened a resort in Bali’s cool, misty north.
content: “At the moment, it’s about 23 degrees Celsius [73 degrees Fahrenheit],” says new hotelier Cheryl Kwok, looking out of her window on a recent overcast afternoon. “The rainy season is just about to start, so we’ve got a little drizzle. At night, it might drop to 14 or 16 degrees.” It may come as a surprise that Kwok, a native Singaporean and former Hong Kong resident, is based in Bali. The island is not exactly known for sweater weather or heated swimming pools, but that is precisely what she offers at her newly opened Buyan Lakeside Villas. Unlike Bali’s hot and humid tourist traps such as Canggu, Denpasar and Seminyak, Kwok’s retreat sits high up in the mist-covered mountains of north Bali, at an elevation of 1,300 metres (4,265 feet). One of the four sacred lakes of the island, Lake Buyan is surrounded by tropical rainforest and enjoys a cool, almost alpine climate. “We first came up here when Covid happened,” says Kwok, who previously lived in Canggu. “We spent a few days here, went to the golf course [the Handara Golf & Resort, set within an ancient volcanic caldera] and thought the area was beautiful. There was literally nothing else, not a decent restaurant for miles and nowhere luxurious to stay. That’s when I thought, ‘Why don’t I build something?’” Kwok and her husband, Gary, worked in Hong Kong for 30 years. She was a construction industry executive; he worked in hotels. They maintained a home in Bali for holidays, flying there two or three times a year. When Gary retired in 2014, they decided to reverse the arrangement: living in Bali full time and returning to Hong Kong a few times a year to see friends and stock up on goods that are difficult to find in Indonesia, such as Chinese preserved sausages. “We wanted a change of scenery and a different lifestyle,” Kwok says. “But after about 10 years of doing nothing – hanging out by the pool, having lunch and seeing friends – you feel there’s no structure to your day. I was really itching to do something.” Buyan Lakeside Villas took three years to build and comprises five cottages overlooking the lake, along with an independent restaurant, Pepper Lane Cafe. Each lodge is designed for country-style comfort, with thoughtful environmental considerations and primarily locally sourced materials. The property may also be the only resort in Bali with working fireplaces. In the garden, Kwok is even growing roses and other flowers that would not survive the heat further south. “The idea was that, since we are in the mountains, surrounded by greenery, with Christmas trees and fir even, it’s almost like we’re in Europe,” Kwok says. “I thought, ‘Why build a Balinese house up here? Why not build something a little bit different?’ I have always loved these sorts of A-frame European homes, and I think they are really suitable for the area. “We sourced all our materials from Indonesia and made everything inside sort of Indonesian, but in a more luxurious, modern style.” Contrary to her description, the vibe is less luxurious than it is modest and tasteful. Kwok is not aiming for ostentation, but for a design that complements the tranquillity of the surroundings. Guests can hike scenic trails and fish in the lake, but other watersports are discouraged; motorised boats are prohibited on the lake. This sense of calm is a sharp contrast to the overdevelopment of south Bali. Over the years, heavier traffic, increased noise and the influx of backpackers, surfers and yoga influencers have blighted some of the island’s more serene destinations. “When we first came to Bali, Canggu was really quiet,” Kwok says. “There wasn’t much going on. Even my kids said, ‘Oh my God, we’re so far away from Seminyak.’ Now Canggu is a crazy area, with traffic, bars and nightclubs, hotels, restaurants, everything. So we felt like we had to escape again.” A string of reports about foreigners disrespecting local culture and digital nomads failing to contribute to the local economy have left a further black mark. In July, a Canggu-based running club was accused of discrimination for not letting local Indonesians join its activities. The controversy prompted politicians to threaten action and led to the club’s Dutch organisers being barred from the country. In some ways, Kwok’s villas represent a different path for Bali tourism. The question is whether the resort will remain an outlier on an island increasingly associated with mass tourism – or whether the secluded retreat will help turn north Bali into the next big Instagram hotspot, bringing the selfie circus with it? “Definitely, there are certain areas [in the south] that are overbuilt, with too many bars and restaurants,” Kwok says. “The way the roads are structured, there’s not much room for expansion. “There’s been quite a lot of interest in this area [in the north]. Land prices have started to go up. There’s a little construction going on around us – not big developments but small holiday homes. People come up here at weekends for holidays.” This is a dilemma facing many of the world’s most popular tourism locales. Success eventually brings a backlash, while overdevelopment destroys the very qualities that made a place attractive in the first place. Kwok believes smaller resorts such as hers, together with infrastructure that keeps pace with growth, will keep tranquil Lake Buyan intact. “I think the government is trying to [encourage] more tourists to visit the north, which is a lot less populated,” she says. “The good thing is they are starting to build a new airport on Bali’s north to ease growth. They know they need to develop different types of tourism, not just the beach lifestyle. “We have tons of beautiful waterfalls, hot springs, even fishing on the lake. There are cocoa and coffee plantations to visit. All these things are underrated.”

title: West Kowloon arts hub deficit widens to HK$998 million as operating costs rise
description: ‘We will have more revenue in the coming months such as from the upfront fees from the tender of the residential project,’ authority CEO Betty Fung says.
content: The authority managing Hong Kong’s arts hub in West Kowloon recorded a wider deficit in the 2025-26 financial year but expects to generate more income next year by putting a residential development project out to tender. The West Kowloon Cultural District Authority’s deficit ballooned to HK$998 million (US$127 million) in the year to March 31, from HK$769 million in the same period a year earlier. The increase was mainly due to higher operating costs as it prepared the new WestK Performing Arts Centre, which is expected to open in autumn 2027. Revenue jumped 19 per cent to HK$768 million in 2025-26, driven by growth in ticket sales, sponsorship and sales of intellectual property and creative products, according to a document submitted to the Legislative Council on Tuesday. “The deficit is still within control, below the HK$1 billion level,” authority CEO Betty Fung Ching Suk-yee said. “We will have more revenue in the coming months such as from the upfront fees from the tender of the residential project.” In 2024, the government conditionally relaxed a build-operate-transfer restriction on residential development in Zone 2, allowing the authority to generate income and helping the arts hub avoid running out of money. Fung said the site’s first residential package, known as Zone 2B, would be put out to tender in the first half of 2027, with completion expected in 2031. While the relaxed framework permits a maximum residential gross floor area of 170,280 square metres across the entire Zone 2 site, the Zone 2B package slated for tender covers up to 108,500 square metres of residential space. It also includes about 20,000 square metres earmarked for retail, dining and entertainment facilities. Fung said the development was expected to have more than 1,000 three- to four-bedroom flats and 500 parking spaces. Operating costs rose 13 per cent to HK$1.85 billion in 2025-26, driven by expanded operations, including preparations for the new performing arts centre, rising visitor numbers, and higher facilities management and technology costs. The authority’s staff costs rose 12 per cent to HK$638 million, while other operating expenses increased 17 per cent to HK$846 million. Fung said the M+ museum and the Hong Kong Palace Museum each achieved a cost recovery rate of about 50 per cent in 2025-26, on a par with or higher than those of major cultural institutions worldwide, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, Tate in London and the Centre Pompidou in France. According to the document submitted to Legco ahead of discussions on Monday, the Hong Kong Palace Museum’s cost recovery rate rose to 56 per cent, from 44 per cent the previous year, while M+’s increased to 47 per cent, from 44 per cent. Overall, the authority’s basic operating cost recovery rate, excluding interest income, improved to 40 per cent, from 37 per cent in 2024-25. In February, the authority secured a HK$3 billion, 10-year loan facility from ICBC (Asia) as part of a broader financing plan to ease cash-flow pressures while it develops new sources of revenue.

title: Mox, BOCHK, ZA Bank and Citibank apps land among Asia-Pacific’s 10 best, study says
description: HSBC’s app drops from third to eighth place among Hong Kong rivals as additional features translate to poor experience, consulting firm says.
content: Banking apps from Mox Bank, Bank of China (Hong Kong) (BOCHK), ZA Bank and Citibank Hong Kong are among the top 10 in Asia-Pacific, according to a study exclusively previewed by the South China Morning Post. Sia, an international consulting firm, assessed 145 banking apps in 20 markets in Europe, Asia and Australia using 100 criteria, including functionality, user experience and feedback, with each receiving a score from 0 to 100. The app from digital lender Mox Bank – backed by Standard Chartered, in partnership with Trip.com, HKT and PCCW – ranked first in Hong Kong and fifth in Asia-Pacific with a score of 67, according to the annual Mobile Banking Benchmark study, to be released later this month. BOCHK ranked second in Hong Kong and seventh in Asia-Pacific with a score of 65, ZA Bank ranked third in Hong Kong and eighth in Asia-Pacific with 64 and Citibank Hong Kong ranked fourth in Hong Kong and ninth in the region at 63. All four have improved their apps and moved up in the global ranking compared with last year. Citibank Hong Kong climbed the most, jumping 51 notches to 45th, while ZA Bank rose eight spots to 44th, BOCHK edged up three notches to 42nd and Mox moved up 11 positions to 27th. The top scoring app in Asia-Pacific was Commonwealth Bank of Australia with a score of 78, followed by three apps from lenders in mainland China: Ping An Pocket Bank in second with a score of 75, China Merchants Bank in third at 69 and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in fourth at 68. DBS Digibank took the sixth spot at 66 and National Bank of Australia finished 10th at 61. Jack Campbell, senior financial services consultant at Sia, said Hong Kong mobile apps made big improvements, matching an international trend, particularly in the areas of providing predictive personal financial management tools and artificial intelligence chatbots that can execute app functions. “The banks are trying to retain the space where you can grow your personal wealth on their apps as a one-stop shop,” Campbell said. “We have seen great growth in terms of investment scores and insurance scores across the board in Asia-Pacific, especially in Hong Kong.” HSBC, the city’s biggest lender, scored 57.9 points, falling from third in Hong Kong last year to eighth this year, while its global ranking dropped 13 notches to 54th. “HSBC has released a lot of features – almost too many features,” Campbell said. “According to a recent media report from June, [the bank’s app] offered about 600 journeys and features released in 2025. This has not translated well in their app from a pure user experience perspective.” Overall, Hong Kong banks’ apps lagged behind many mainland banks and Western lenders in terms of teaming up with partners to provide non-bank transaction services, according to the report. No Asian lenders cracked the global top 10, which was dominated by European banks, the report showed. Globally, the app from Belgium’s KBC Group ranked first with a score of 83, taking the top spot for the third straight year. It was followed by UK-based digital bank Revolut’s app and French digital bank BoursoBank’s app, both at 82. Camilo Ramirez, head of financial services at Sia Hong Kong, said European lenders’ mobile apps had more AI functions and partnerships that supported features such as shopping, buying tickets and obtaining advice, while most Asian banks were still more focused on banking transactions.

title: How Singapore’s local cafes compete with Chinese coffee giant Luckin
description: Cheap drinks and app ordering helped Luckin expand fast, but independent cafe owners say personal connection beats pure convenience.
content: When Chinese coffee giant Luckin Coffee moved into the unit next to his neighbourhood cafe in Singapore, Folk Yard owner Chew Yit Shan grew nervous. Luckin launched with an aggressive promotional deal of S$1 (78 US cents) per cup, served in just two minutes. In the first few months following its arrival, Chew saw sales at his independent cafe drop by 15 per cent. But once the initial hype had died down and the promotions ended, Chew said regular patrons returned and coffee sales bounced back. “We had to explain to customers that we offer something different. It’s the simple things, like knowing the baristas and coming back to the same places in the neighbourhood,” Chew said. “There’s a level of interaction and familiarity that becomes part of their routine, and that goes beyond the product itself.” Chew, who opened Folk Yard in 2022, said that Chinese brands like Luckin worked because of their “incredible purchasing power and economies of scale”. “I don’t think there’s a point where we can compete with them purely on price and convenience. What we can offer is individuality – something that is unique to us and can’t be replicated at the same scale,” Chew said. Last month, Luckin announced it had hit its 100th-store milestone, just three years after making its overseas debut in the city state. The chain now operates 103 outlets in Singapore, with up to six more reportedly planned by the end of the year. Its mobile app, which allows customers to order and pay in advance before picking up in-store, now has some 1.9 million users in the city state. Globally, the brand operates more than 36,000 stores across China, over 150 in Malaysia and more than 20 in New York. Satish Kumar, a 40-year-old civil servant, said he became hooked after his first sip of Luckin’s coconut velvet latte two years ago. While local coffee – affectionately known as kopi – is a cheaper alternative at S$1 to S$2 a cup, Kumar said Luckin had a different appeal. “I got addicted after trying [it] because it tastes good to me, and I prefer lattes to kopi,” Kumar said. “They also now have a lot of different flavours and it’s so easy to order on the app.” ‘Like tech stores’ Singapore’s specialist coffee market was estimated to be worth about US$327 million last year, with Luckin capturing roughly 24 per cent of the market share. Starbucks, which entered Singapore in 1996, held about 34 per cent, according to Weihan Chen, insights lead at market intelligence consultancy Momentum Works. Chen said the arrival of Chinese drink chains had raised the level of competition, particularly around convenience, product variety, pricing and the speed of new product roll-outs. Yet Chen cautioned against framing Chinese chains as simply replacing local cafes, noting that consumers support very different drink formats, and these brands often compete for different occasions. Nathanael Lim, Asia-Pacific insight manager for beverages at Euromonitor International, said Luckin’s rapid rise in Singapore reflected its ambitions beyond China. “Unlike local brands, Luckin combines substantial financial backing with its playbook centred on digital ordering, frequent limited-edition product launches and strong app-based loyalty programmes,” Lim said, adding that Luckin’s scale gave it advantages in supply chain sourcing and operational efficiency. Seshan Ramaswami, an associate professor of marketing education at Singapore Management University, pointed out that Luckin stores typically had limited seating, keeping overheads low while minimising staffing requirements. App-based ordering also gives the brand a huge database to use for real-time customer analysis. Drawing from its experience in China, Luckin fine-tunes its customer relationship management to offer targeted discounts that drive repeat purchases. “This sort of rapid expansion is not always successful, of course – so much depends on consumer loyalty as well as competitive reaction,” Ramaswami said. “But if the taste and the value perception at Luckin’s prices catch on, it could force other chains to change their product mix or even close some stores in the proximity of its outlet.” Lawrence Loh, a professor of strategy and policy at the National University of Singapore Business School, noted that beyond menu options or marketing strategies, brands like Luckin used novel scaling models that rapidly expanded the number of physical stores to secure long-term market share, even at the expense of short-term profitability. “Brands are often like tech stores at the shopfront, which not only reduces labour costs but adds a modern feel that appeals to customers, particularly the younger generations who are always on the move,” Loh said. Deep-pocketed foreign players would often outbid competitors for retail space while constantly reinventing their products, he said, adding that the coffee experience they offered went beyond the menu to embrace culture, community, corporate social responsibility and the “cool” factor attached to being a patron. “Of late, Chinese brands seem to be able to offer this totality in overseas markets even better than the incumbent brands,” Loh said. But Denise Lum, co-owner of independent local cafe Maxi Coffee Bar, said she did not see Luckin as a competitor because it catered to a completely different consumer. “Luckin probably attracts a distinct customer base – people who really care about convenience, price, efficiency, technology and all of that. We cannot compete in that space … All we can do is build on what we feel makes our shop special, which is the customer experience,” she said. “For them, it’s a scale game. For us, it’s not a breadth but a depth game.” Opening a new outlet for Maxi Coffee required careful consideration, Lum said, regardless of whether capital was readily available. “Growth has to be intentional. It’s very much about the neighbourhood and less about just wanting to grow. It’s about identity and community building,” she said. Folk Yard’s Chew agreed that Luckin customers appeared to want convenience and low prices, whereas his clientele were looking for something else entirely. “Our customers are people who are looking to slow down,” he said. “They’re not just coming in for a coffee; they’re coming for the experience, the interaction and the sense of community.” Looking ahead, Momentum Works’ Chen said Luckin would face challenges in maintaining its large network of stores. “Opening stores quickly demonstrates that there is consumer demand, but sustaining a large network requires strong store-level economics, local management and supply chains,” Chen said. “As they expand into more countries, the challenge becomes how much of the system developed in China can be replicated and how much needs to be localised.”

title: Abby Choi called ex-father-in-law ‘old crook’ amid HK$72m flat row, court hears
description: Hong Kong socialite’s mother tells murder trial former in-laws attempted to turn her children against her over bitter property dispute.
content: Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her former father-in-law an “old crook” as she accused her ex-relatives of turning her children against her when she tried sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat, a court has heard. Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023. Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial. “My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her heart to the wrong people. This family, this family really bit the hand that fed them.” Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial at the High Court after pleading not guilty to murdering the model on February 21, 2023. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial. The killing allegedly stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s attempts to sell it and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so he could keep it for himself. Cheung said on Monday that her daughter had bought the property in 2019 for her children and partly as a personal investment, but she registered it in her former father-in-law’s name to avoid double stamp duty. She stressed that Choi had never intended to give the flat to her former in-laws. Giving evidence for a second day, Cheung said Kwong Kau became furious when her daughter first told him in June 2022 that she intended to sell the flat. He threatened to kill her entire family if she went ahead, Cheung said. The elder Kwong signed a power of attorney authorising Choi to negotiate the sale only five months later, after Cheung threatened to sue him. Choi aired her grievances in a series of audio messages to her mother in October and November 2022, saying her former in-laws were ungrateful despite her having supported their lavish lifestyle for years. “She does not cherish her blessings at all,” Choi said in an apparent reference to Li, who is not a defendant in the case. “[They are] not grateful to me even while leading such a lifestyle.” The influencer also expressed regret at having registered a property in Hainan province and a Rolls-Royce in Kwong Kau’s name. Cheung said Kwong Kau and his wife also disparaged her daughter in front of the two children she had with Alex Kwong and told them not to listen to their mother. The court heard that Choi and her mother had further discussions in November 2022 about how to get Kwong Kau to sign legal documents authorising her to negotiate the sale. Choi suggested that the elder Kwong, whom she called an “old crook”, “scum” and a “stinking bastard”, was deliberately delaying the process and would play tricks on them unless the matter was settled quickly, the court heard Cheung said her daughter wanted to sell the property as soon as possible and was willing to lower her asking price by a few million dollars because Kwong Kau could revoke the power of attorney at any time. The model also complained that the Kwong family had prevented her from speaking to her two children by phone while she was attending a fashion event in France during the Lunar New Year holiday in January 2023. Cheung told the court she received her final message from her daughter at around 2pm on February 21, saying she would pick up her daughter from school. Fear for the model’s safety grew that night when Choi’s husband, Chris Tam Fong-chun, informed Cheung that she had gone missing. Cheung said she called Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s temporary chauffeur at the time, but he appeared impatient and insisted the influencer had got out of her car after an argument over the phone. She said her former relative gave conflicting answers when pressed to explain Choi’s whereabouts. He also allegedly suggested that she might have got drunk and become lost, even though she normally avoided alcohol. Cheung said she and Tam reported the case to police shortly before midnight, much to Alex Kwong’s dismay. “He said: ‘Damn you! Why didn’t you alert me when you called police?’” she said. “I said to him: “Damn you! I reported my daughter’s disappearance to police. What does it have to do with you?” When Cheung suggested that Alex Kwong and his father must have taken Choi somewhere, her former son-in-law replied with a question: “Why did you say so?” “I called the whole [Kwong] family but nobody cared,” the witness added. Defence counsel Trevor Beel, representing Anthony Kwong, argued the elder Kwong was reluctant to sell the flat during the economic slump linked to the Covid-19 pandemic. “I suggest, madam, that it would be understandable that Kwong Kau would not be keen to sell the property at that time, because the property price was low,” he said in cross-examination. Cheung disagreed. “The money wasn’t his. What did he stand to gain? We were entitled to reclaim [the flat]. He had no say on it,” she said. Some members of the public burst into laughter when Cheung recalled her exchange with Alex Kwong, drawing a stern warning from lead prosecutor Charlotte Draycott SC. “It’s important for the public to remember that this is a woman who has lost her daughter,” she said. “If you want to laugh, you go outside.” The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Southeast Asia urged to step up war against AI-powered scams through data sharing
description: While scam organisations are using agentic AI to expand, regional countries face unwieldy rules on cross-border data exchange, experts warn.
content: Governments and financial institutions in Southeast Asia urgently need to find a way to safely and quickly share data if they hope to contain a surge in scams, cybersecurity experts warn, as artificial intelligence enables criminal operations in the region to expand their reach rapidly. Criminal enterprises stole as much as US$114 billion from victims across the Asia-Pacific in 2025, according to a United Nations report released in July, more than triple the amount from two years earlier, aided by AI and other technology. The scourge of scams and financial crime could become worse with the adoption of agentic AI, which experts say could allow criminals to automate and scale their operations with unprecedented speed. As such, regulators and institutions in the region need to prepare for a worst-case scenario and establish effective mechanisms to safely share data across borders, allowing them to identify and disrupt scam operations before they spread and do damage. “At the moment it is not about whether we can win [against criminal enterprises]. It’s about how badly we lose,” Martin Smith, Asia-Pacific compliance and financial crime industry adviser with enterprise AI firm SymphonyAI, said in Kuala Lumpur on Tuesday at a panel discussion on financial crimes. Smith’s assessment follows an earlier warning by on-chain intelligence platform TRM Labs, which pointed to scam syndicates investing heavily in training agentic AI agents to target multiple victims across different languages, all at the same time. Fully trained AI agents will remove the need for a large workforce and enable fully remote operations, allowing syndicates to exponentially increase their scale and reach while becoming more difficult to catch, according to TRM Labs. Smith said regulators and institutions in the region continued to lag behind criminal enterprises as they were stuck operating in their silos, hindered by unwieldy rules on cross-border data sharing that made it difficult to collate information to help weed out criminal activity. Raymond Ram, president of Transparency International Malaysia, said governments, enforcement agencies and financial institutions needed to expand their cooperation to include exchange of financial data that could help pinpoint criminal money trails. “We cannot depend just on [mutual legal help]. We need more data sharing between financial authorities,” Ram said. Shamir Rajadurai, a criminologist, said an institutional response was vital as individuals would stand no chance against the large scale of criminal enterprises targeting their money. “These criminals are operating at an organisational level. So we need to get organisation versus organisation, fight fire with fire,” Shamir said.

title: From cabin crew to cockpit: Malaysian woman’s AirAsia pilot dreams take off
description: Suriati Sukardi said her journey with the airline showed ambitions could soar with determination and ‘a bit of luck’.
content: She spent some of her teenage years helping her mother at a sundry shop in Malaysia after school, and throughout that period kept a dream of achieving something higher alive. Now, 36-year-old Suriati Sukardi is a pilot, flying AirAsia’s commercial A320 and A321 Airbus aircraft. Before that, she had landed a job as the airline’s flight attendant and served the company for eight years since 2017 while continuing to eye and seek an opportunity to climb further in her career. In 2019, her prayers were answered when she was offered the chance to take up aviation lessons, completing her course to become a pilot in 2022. “However, I faced a brief challenge thereafter because I had difficulty landing a job as a pilot so I had to return to stewarding while continuing my search,” Suriati said. Two years later, a position opened up and she was offered the chance to fly the Airbus A320 and A321. “After so many years, I am finally soaring above with AirAsia and living the dream I once held close to my heart,” she said. Though navigating her career in a white tunic now, Suriati will always cherish her memories donning the red uniform, serving the aisles thousands of metres above the ground. “This is a reminder for myself and hopefully others that dreams can become a reality with determination, a bit of luck and a lot of hard work,” she said. This story was first published by The Star

title: North Korea’s DMZ landmines sabotage the South’s peace push
description: Seoul is seeking an apology for last month’s border blast even as Pyongyang fortifies a line it now treats as a permanent frontier.
content: North Korea’s laying of landmines along its heavily fortified border with the South has laid bare how misaligned the two nations have become over their de facto land boundary, after three South Korean soldiers were wounded in an explosion last month. Seoul blames Pyongyang for the blast near the military demarcation line (MDL) on September 21, in which one soldier lost a foot. On Tuesday, its Foreign Ministry said in a statement it was preparing a response to force an apology for the blast, without going into specifics, further urging the North to hold talks on the poorly signposted MDL. Military personnel from both sides are technically forbidden from crossing the MDL under their 1953 armistice agreement. As the precise centre line of the 4km (2.5-mile) wide demilitarised zone (DMZ) that bisects the Korean peninsula, it serves as the effective land border between North and South Korea. But the 250km (155-mile) long line is sparsely marked, with few of the more than 1,200 original markers that were installed over seven decades ago still in place. A joint investigation by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that at least four mines at the site of last month’s blast, 10 metres (32 feet) south of the MDL, were deliberately planted by the North. Forensic evidence, including explosive residue and mine fragments, pointed to Pyongyang’s culpability, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement on Monday. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said in a statement on Friday last week that the fortification work was meant to “cut off the relationship forever” with the South. She also called South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s peace overtures a “farce”. Boundary creep North Korea began fortifying the border in 2024, clearing vegetation, laying new minefields, building tactical roads and installing barbed-wire fences. Major General Yang Jin-hyeok, director of operations for Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, told reporters on Monday that “up to 7,000 personnel” had been deployed every day this year along the entirety of the MDL as part of the fortification effort. Fences, minefields and road construction in the area were about halfway complete, he said, with the work expected to be complete within two years. North Korean troops have crossed the MDL more than 50 times this year, according to the South’s military, the vast majority occurring since August on the eastern portion of the boundary. Soldiers are thought to have pushed as far as 20 metres (66 feet) south of the line, the Joint Chiefs said. By contrast, Seoul detected just 17 incursions last year and nine in 2024. Compounding matters is the fact that Pyongyang’s interpretation of the MDL’s location differs from that of Seoul and the UN Command. Yoo Yong-won, a lawmaker from the opposition People Power Party, told broadcaster MBC on Thursday that such discrepancies had also been an issue under the South’s past conservative administrations, with repeated proposals for talks receiving no reply. The North was “taking advantage of the poorly marked MDL to move its border fortification work slightly southward”, Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told This Week in Asia, adding that he expected more incidents to occur in future. ‘Next to impossible’ South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young has proposed that the two Koreas meet to reverify and firmly establish the location of the MDL. He rejected the People Power Party’s calls to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts, suspended since June 2025, as “irresponsible and dangerous”. “Stoking hatred and hostility is not politics,” he told reporters on Friday. “The role of politics is to transform that hatred and hostility into mutual respect and peaceful coexistence.” Chung reportedly clashed with Foreign Minister Cho Hyun at last Thursday’s National Security Council meeting, after Cho had proposed unilateral sanctions against North Korean cyber activities. Chung was quoted as saying such sanctions were unrelated to the border blast and would not be appropriate at a time when Seoul was pursuing dialogue. The country’s military, meanwhile, has responded with broadcasts and warning shots whenever North Korean troops approach or cross the MDL. Yang Moo-jin, a political scientist and professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Pyongyang was attempting to turn the armistice line agreed in 1953 into a permanent border between “two hostile states”. “As long as the North sees the line as an impregnable border while the South sees it as a poorly marked line that should be clearly redrawn”, then dialogue over the issue would be “next to impossible”, he said. Yang warned of a further flashpoint at sea. The 1953 armistice left the western maritime boundary between the two Koreas unsettled, so the UN Command unilaterally drew the so-called Northern Limit Line, which Pyongyang has never recognised. An agreement was reached in 2018 to turn the area into a maritime peace zone, but it was never fully implemented due to recurring military tensions and unresolved border disputes. “Should the North, emboldened by its recent naval build-up, extend its fortification work from the land border into the sea off the western coast, it would be a potential source of conflict,” Yang said.

title: Villa keeper Suzuki eyes Asian Cup atonement after ‘very bad’ display in 2024 defeat
description: New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki believes Japan can win tournament this time around after previously losing in last 8 to Iran.
content: Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki said he is confident Japan can win next year’s Asian Cup and thinks his “very bad” performances were responsible for their quarter-final exit two years ago. Suzuki, who has impressed in the Premier League since joining Villa in the summer, made a string of mistakes at the 2024 Asian Cup in Qatar as Japan were bundled out in the last eight by Iran. But he believes he is a better player this time around and backed Japan to end their 16-year wait for the continental title when the tournament starts in January in Saudi Arabia. “The last time, I played for the first time, I played very bad and I led the team to defeat,” the 24-year-old said after Japan’s 2-1 friendly win over New Zealand in Tokyo on Monday. “This time I experienced a lot of things and I played at the World Cup and I’m playing in the Premier League, so I have confidence. I want to help the team and we are confident to win the Asian Cup.” Suzuki joined Villa from Italian side Parma and has slotted straight in after replacing Argentina’s Emiliano Martinez, who left for Chelsea. He has also helped Japan win home friendlies against Uruguay, Venezuela, Ecuador and New Zealand in the past two weeks. The win over Ecuador came via a penalty shoot-out in the semi-finals of the four-team Kirin Cup, with Suzuki making a decisive save. He said he had “settled in” at Villa, where he was named player of the month for September. “I like the environment, I like the way we play, the way the manager plays, so I’m very comfortable,” he said. “There is more intensity and the speed is faster so it’s not easy to adapt, but I’ve played four or five games now and I find something that I have to improve more. I want to improve more and more.” Suzuki impressed at this year’s World Cup in North America, where Japan lost 2-1 to Brazil in the last 16. Japan will face Brazil again in a friendly tournament in Singapore in November, in their last set of tune-ups before the Asian Cup. Japan have been drawn in a first-round group with holders Qatar, Thailand and Indonesia in Saudi Arabia. “The Asian Cup is not easy,” Suzuki said. “We need to stick together, but this time I think I’m more confident. I’ve experienced a lot of things, so we will see.”

title: Nvidia-backed Reflection AI challenges Chinese dominance in open-weight models
description: Reflection says its Beam model requires three to four times less inference compute than comparable open models to reason through problems.
content: An Nvidia-backed US start-up has unveiled an open-weight model to challenge China’s dominance in freely available artificial intelligence, releasing a system that early third-party testing suggests could be one of the most token-efficient open models in its class. Reflection AI on Monday debuted Beam, its first open-weight model built for coding, reasoning and agentic tasks. The US firm said Beam was “competitive” with GLM-5.2 from Z.ai – also known as Zhipu AI – and was “approaching” Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max on coding and agentic workflows, although Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 remained ahead in “raw capability”. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Built on a “mixture of experts” approach, Beam distributes workloads among specialised networks. Reflection said this architecture allowed the model to activate just 23 billion parameters per task out of a total of 501 billion, substantially undercutting the compute demands of Z.ai’s GLM-5.2, which activated 40 billion out of roughly 744 billion parameters. According to Reflection, Beam requires three to four times less inference compute than comparable open models to reason through problems, enabling users to run AI workloads faster and cheaper. While official independent benchmarks have yet to be released, benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis said evaluation was under way. The firm noted that “early indicators suggest Beam will be one of the most token-efficient open models we’ve seen for its level of intelligence”. The launch comes amid growing efforts in the US to counter the global rise of Chinese open-source AI developers, including DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot AI and Z.ai. In July, Nvidia and US tech giants including Microsoft, Palantir and Meta Platforms signed a public letter calling for the US to support a domestic open-weight AI ecosystem and avoid “premature restrictions” on downloadable models. The initiative also drew backing from IBM, OpenAI and Google. Washington is also supporting the open-weight push. At a congressional hearing last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged American companies to develop more open-weight models, warning against allowing a handful of closed-model developers to dominate the industry. Reflection has become part of that effort. The company has partnered with the Pentagon and US Department of Energy and has struck agreements to develop AI systems for US allies including South Korea. Chinese open-weight AI developers have become increasingly embedded in the global ecosystem, with even US tech giants turning to their models to meet customer demand. On Monday, Amazon said its cloud unit Amazon Web Services (AWS) added Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 to its Amazon Bedrock platform. AWS will share revenue with Z.ai based on model usage, according to Chinese tech media outlet Star Market Daily. The addition follows AWS’s launch of Moonshot AI’s flagship Kimi K3 model last month under a similar revenue-sharing deal. Reflection, founded by former Google DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, has raised over US$4 billion since its launch in 2024. It reached a US$25 billion valuation before releasing its first model. Nvidia backed the start-up with US$800 million and provided it with vital chip access, alongside venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Disruptive and 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jnr is a partner. Laskin said China’s grip on open-weight AI has left businesses and governments with limited Western alternatives for models they can actually control. “The only way to own intelligence is, by definition, if it’s open,” he said in an episode of the Sources Podcast published Monday. Beam is undergoing final red-teaming – where developers simulate cyberattacks and prompt exploits to test safety limits – and is available to a limited group of early users. Reflection plans to release the model weights later this month, alongside fine-tuning tools.

title: China tried 3 times to talk crime families out of scam business in Myanmar: state media
description: Series outlines how joint operations brought down major border compounds amid warning criminal syndicates are relocating near Thailand.
content: China tried three times to persuade powerful families in northern Myanmar to shut down scam operations before Myanmar police carried out large-scale arrests in 2023, according to a new documentary broadcast on Chinese state television. The three-part documentary, jointly produced by China’s Ministry of Public Security and state broadcaster CCTV, began airing on Monday. It shows obstacles faced by Chinese authorities in pursuing criminal networks and scam groups operating in northern Myanmar across the border. Chinese authorities said earlier this year that judicial proceedings against two out of the four main criminal syndicates had been concluded, while noting that major scam groups in northern Myanmar had been dismantled in November 2024. Some 15 core members of syndicates have been executed for a range of crimes, from murder to fraud and human trafficking, while one person who had been sentenced died before the executions were carried out. Telecoms and online scams became a major problem in China in the 2010s, fuelled by the spread of mobile phones, the internet and online payments. The documentary said 80 per cent of telecoms and online fraud crimes that targeted Chinese nationals were committed overseas, with northern Myanmar accounting for a significant share. It said jurisdiction was a key obstacle to China’s efforts to combat cross-border scam operations, requiring Chinese authorities to pursue multiple approaches. Talks with Kokang’s four major family-run syndicates were among the efforts disclosed for the first time in the programme. The Bai, Wei, Liu and Ming families built extensive political, business and armed networks in northern Myanmar’s Kokang, a predominantly ethnic Chinese region bordering Yunnan province in southwestern China. Footage of Bai Yingcang, a senior member of the Bai family who was executed in February, showed him saying Chinese officials had warned the groups several times to eliminate scam operations “unconditionally”. During one meeting, representatives of the four families and a Chinese delegation held talks for three hours in a small, makeshift structure on the Myanmar side of the border, but the talks ended without any clear progress. Bai quoted Ming Xuechang, head of the Ming family, as saying at the time: “If we stop, we have nothing to eat.” Ming died by suicide in November 2023 as Myanmar authorities moved in to arrest him. Crimes linked to the Bai family involved more than 20 billion yuan (US$2.9 billion) in gains from fraud and gambling while the Wei family was linked to more than 5 billion yuan in fraud-related funds, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported last October, citing the Ministry of Public Security. A 2023 United Nations report said at least 120,000 people across Myanmar might be held in situations where they were forced to carry out online scams. Those trapped in scam centres face beatings, abuse and, in some cases, murder. At the peak of distress calls, Chinese police were receiving 40 requests a day from family members for help to free victims held by the criminal organisations, according to the documentary. It said collecting evidence overseas to prosecute perpetrators was another major challenge, as Myanmar authorities were initially uncooperative and ongoing conflict risked destroying evidence. “Fighter jets from Myanmar flew over our heads and dropped bombs on the battlefield [on the Myanmar side]. All we could think about was making sure our evidence was not destroyed by the fighting,” Na Xin, a senior criminal investigator with the Kunming Public Security Bureau in Yunnan, told the programme. “Myanmar authorities had maintained that no Chinese nationals had been killed in the beginning,” Na said. Chinese police retrieved several bodies a day after negotiations with the Myanmar side. Chinese investigators later entered the core areas of the compounds to conduct further searches and collect evidence, according to the documentary, which said information relating to homicide, gambling and fraud and gathered through multiple rounds of investigation was returned to China. “Cross-border investigations require cooperation to obtain, preserve and lawfully share evidence that can support a prosecution,” said Xu Peng, a research fellow at the Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute at the University of Manchester. Joint operations by authorities from both sides led to 59,000 suspected telecoms fraud offenders being repatriated to China, according to Chinese authorities. Some 76,486 people were arrested between October 5, 2023 and September 29 this year, in operations targeting online scam and illegal gambling sites in Myanmar, the military-run Myawady news portal said last week, citing Myanmar’s president, Min Aung Hlaing. Kota Watanabe, a lecturer in global and regional studies at Toyo University in Tokyo, said the disruption of scam operations in northern Myanmar could be attributed to pressure from the Chinese government, but scam activities continued to expand in other parts of the country. “The regime [in Myanmar] has been complicit [in] and benefiting from the scamming operation through bribes, and its crackdown measures were only a show,” Watanabe said. He said scam compounds had proliferated in areas along the Myanmar-Thai border under the protection of armed groups with ties to Myanmar’s military. Scam operations in other parts of Myanmar had continued to expand, Watanabe noted. This was partly because China did not have “as much influence on local armed groups and militias protecting scamming operations as in the China-Myanmar border areas due to the geographical distance and the lack of historical ties”. In a recent case, a Shanghai music teacher went missing after travelling to Thailand on September 24.
