A police investigation later traced his phone signal to Myanmar, although authorities have not determined what happened to him. Surachanee “Hammerli” Sriyai, CEO and co-founder of S&I Strategic Advisory, said global economic pressure was among the factors allowing scam operations to persist. “Poverty and the global economic downturn make people [so] desperate that they’re willing to take a chance for ludicrous job opportunities,” she said. “Without adequate social safety net programmes, people will continue to be vulnerable to trafficking.”

title: Ukraine attacks Moscow region with 650 drones as both sides step up strikes
description: Russian state media calls overnight assault the second-largest on the capital area in two years.
content: A massive attack involving 650 drones targeted Moscow overnight, leaving at least two dead, Russian authorities said on Tuesday. Most of the drones were destroyed by air defences at long range, including 105 intercepted as they approached the capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on Telegram. Russian state news agency Tass reported it was the second-largest drone attack on the capital region in the past two years. The dead included a 71-year-old man pulled from under the rubble ‌of a house and a 20-year-old ⁠man ⁠found in a nearby village, Andrei Vorobyov, the governor ⁠of ⁠the Moscow region, said. A warehouse was also set ablaze, ‌local authorities ‌were cited as saying by Tass. Both Ukraine and Russia have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months on civilian and industrial targets, including energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea. Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones. Russia has said it plans to increase strikes on infrastructure targets, including in Kyiv, as winter approaches. Ukraine says its long-range strikes have neutralised more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow’s ability to supply its forces during its 4½-year-old invasion. The Defence Ministry said late Sunday that recent strikes on refineries in cities, including Moscow, Yaroslavl, Ust-Luga, Perm, Saratov and Syzran, had disabled 51 per cent of Russia’s oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified.

title: Gone in 40 seconds: how a Chinese rail station handled 1 million trips in a day
description: Holiday demand pushed Guangzhou South station past 1 million trips on October 1, with bullet trains departing every 40 seconds at peak hours.
content: A railway station in Guangzhou has set a national record for trips in a single day and drawn attention for the frequency of bullet train departures – one every 40 seconds – during this month’s holiday period, according to the Guangdong provincial government. Guangzhou South Railway Station handled 1,252 train services and just over 1 million trips on October 1, the start of the seven-day National Day holiday across mainland China, the publicity department of the province’s Communist Party committee said on its WeChat account. Crossing the 1 million-trip milestone was a first for China, it added. At peak periods that day, trains departed every 40 seconds, an interval the publicity department said was “faster than people could scroll through short videos”. By comparison, at Tokyo Station, combined shinkansen departures reach up to 24 trains per hour during peak periods, averaging one bullet train leaving every 2.5 minutes. Guangzhou South was designed to handle high traffic volumes, said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a think tank associated with the provincial government. As one of five major railway hubs in Guangzhou – Guangdong’s capital, with a population of 18.7 million – the station has 15 platforms and 28 tracks. Guangzhou moved early to integrate its subway system, intercity railways and high-speed railways to make travel relatively “seamless”, Peng added. For the October holiday, Guangzhou South also operated 202 overnight high-speed services, accounting for about one-sixth of all trains departing the station on a single day, according to the publicity department. China State Railway Group had projected a record 284 million passenger trips during a 16-day period covering the National Day break and the Mid-Autumn Festival in late September. To prepare for the holiday rush, Guangzhou South expanded transfer areas and departure lanes, improved passenger information services and added train services based on wait-list demand data, the publicity department said. The additional services strengthened links with major cities including Shenzhen, Changsha, Nanning, Zhuhai, Zhengzhou and Chongqing, it added. Guangzhou South connects with a total of 196 cities, including Beijing and Hong Kong. “When you add all this together, it’s not rocket science to see why Guangzhou South is as busy as it gets,” independent railway specialist David Feng said.

title: Japan PM Takaichi defends skipping G7 online meeting
description: She did not offer a specific reason for her absence from the session that focused on coordinating a response to diesel prices in the West.
content: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi defended her absence from a Group of Seven online meeting, responding over social media to some critics who questioned why she did not attend despite her apparently free schedule. “This was a last-minute meeting arranged by the chair, France, and allowed for substitute representatives. I understand that UK Prime Minister Burnham did not attend in person and had someone fill in for him, and that European Council president Costa was also absent,” she posted on Monday evening. She was at her official residence and was not meeting anyone while the meeting was being held, according to local media. The post underscores her preference to pore over documents and work solo from home. In late August, the Nikkei newspaper reported that Takaichi had not left her official residence on most weekends and public holidays since becoming prime minister, in comparison to the previous three prime ministers who spent between 3 per cent and 16 per cent of weekends and public holidays entirely at home. Takaichi did not offer a specific reason for her absence, but her post suggested the short notice and agenda, which focused on coordinating a response to diesel prices in Europe and the US, were factors in her decision not to attend. “While the outcome of this meeting was a decision to implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of oil reserves, Japan has already been releasing reserves and has no plans for any new measures at this time,” she said. Kazuya Endo, the deputy minister for foreign affairs, filled in for her, Takaichi added. Michito Tsuruoka, a professor at Keio University specialising in global security, questioned the reasoning behind Takaichi’s decision to skip the session. “It’s a poor move to suggest that the absence was acceptable simply because the issue at hand primarily concerned the West. Such a rationale implies that Western nations could likewise skip meetings when the focus shifts to issues involving Asia or China,” he wrote on social media. “The G7 has long pursued the principle that its members’ concerns are inextricably linked,” he added. The G7 is a bloc consisting of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. The EU is also represented within the G7. Takaichi also opted out of attending an online meeting regarding the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, hosted by France and the UK in April. She instead issued a written message and had Keiichi Ichikawa, a senior diplomat and secretary general of the National Security Secretariat, attend in her place. An analysis of her official schedule through July showed she met finance ministry officials 50 per cent less often than the country’s previous two leaders and held the fewest Cabinet Office meetings of any prime minister over the past 14 years.

title: Hong Kong’s Hermitage Capital stays devoted to top-tier tech stocks amid jitters
description: ‘Even when sentiment is at its lowest’ and confidence is ‘under severe pressure’, keep buying top-tier technology companies, founder says.
content: Even as geopolitical frictions and market swings unsettle venture investors, Hong Kong-founded Hermitage Capital is sticking to a global strategy of backing frontier technology companies wherever they emerge. With a US$1.5 billion war chest that is 80 per cent in US dollars, with the remainder in renminbi, the private equity firm is ramping up investments across artificial intelligence, semiconductors and robotics, mainly in the US and China, capitalising on a market turnaround triggered by the breakout success of names like DeepSeek since last year. “Even when sentiment is at its lowest and valuations and confidence are under severe pressure, we need to keep adding to top-tier technology companies,” said Sean Xiang Yuqiu, the firm’s founder and CEO, in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. Since announcing a three-year plan last year to invest US$500 million in AI and robotics globally, Hermitage had already deployed more than US$200 million, Xiang said. Founded in 2017 by the former JPMorgan Chase banker, the firm counts institutional investors and wealthy family offices across Asia among its backers, accounting for about 80 per cent of its capital, with others in the UK and Canada. Xiang adheres to a straightforward, unyielding investment thesis through geopolitical turbulence, market swings and business downturns: “Global, long-term, only the best.” That conviction was forged during a steep market downturn. Amid Beijing’s regulatory tightening on internet platforms and property, alongside tightening US export controls, global sentiment towards mainland assets had plunged since 2022. “Global interest in Chinese assets after 2022 didn’t decline gently – it fell off a cliff,” Xiang recalled. This economy’s concentration of engineers, manufacturing capabilities and ability to turn pressure into technological improvements may be unmatched Sean Xiang, Hermitage Capital In response, Hermitage pivoted to a dual-track strategy. Its New York office, originally set up to raise US capital for Chinese deals, shifted to sourcing and evaluating American firms. Today, Hermitage’s portfolio of more than 30 companies is split roughly evenly between China and overseas markets, predominantly the US. Yet, Xiang remains firmly convinced of China’s industrial resilience. US semiconductor restrictions, he said, forced domestic chipmakers to turn designs into commercial products faster and secure local customers. “Once the geopolitical headwinds have been weathered, the world will gradually recognise a simpler truth: this economy’s concentration of engineers, manufacturing capabilities and ability to turn pressure into technological improvements may be unmatched,” Xiang said. Hong Kong serves as the essential bridge for this strategy. Xiang described the city as an “operating system” for global investing, linking capital, tech companies and supply chains through an internationally recognised institutional and legal framework. Its time zone helped Asian fundraising, while its capital markets offered a natural exit avenue as portfolio companies matured, he added. Hermitage typically enters at series B through D rounds, taking a high-conviction approach by backing its top picks across multiple market cycles. The company has taken part in 13 funding rounds for cross-border payments unicorn Airwallex since 2019, five rounds for autonomous-driving chipmaker Horizon Robotics and three for graphics processor developer MetaX Integrated Circuits. Horizon Robotics listed in Hong Kong in October 2024, while MetaX debuted on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-style Star Market in December 2025. Converting interest into action, Xiang said, required strong discipline. Moving from liking a company to investing required 10 times the resolve and effort, he said, adding that building a large position and holding it over the long term each required another tenfold increase. Foundation models were the sector to bet heavily on in 2023 and 2024. Physical AI is the sector to bet heavily on now Sean Xiang, Hermitage Capital “Just liking it is meaningless,” he said. “You’re only a spectator.” Growing demand for transparency and control was reshaping how Hermitage interacted with its investors, Xiang said. Family offices increasingly preferred single-deal, special-purpose vehicles over traditional decade-long blind-pool funds, seeking more visibility on entry valuations and exit timelines, he said. In terms of sector strategy, Hermitage has selectively locked in gains by trimming earlier bets on large language models to focus on the next frontier. “Foundation models were the sector to bet heavily on in 2023 and 2024,” Xiang said. “Physical AI is the sector to bet heavily on now.” The firm’s pivot comes amid volatility in Chinese humanoid robotics equities, driven by sobering market expectations. Unitree Robotics, for instance, plunged nearly 60 per cent from its peak after its high-profile debut on Shanghai’s Star Market in August, as investors recalibrated sky-high growth assumptions. Acknowledging that frontier technology start-ups were “born expensive”, commanding valuations well ahead of commercial orders and real-world data, Hermitage said it was selectively targeting robotics, self-improving AI and enabling hardware. Recent deals include US humanoid robot maker 1X, AI research automation developer Recursive Superintelligence and Chinese robotics-chip developer D-Robotics. Lessons from earlier hardware cycles had refined the firm’s risk management, Xiang said. Disappointments in solid-state battery investments from 2021 – where mass production lagged behind schedules – taught the firm to size initial tickets more conservatively, committing larger follow-on capital only as operational milestones were met, he said. Ultimately, Xiang said he measured portfolio bets using a “worry-to-return ratio”. “You want to have the lowest worry per unit of return,” he said, adding that the goal was to own businesses that the firm could hold through downturns without constantly questioning their durability.

title: John Lee promises ‘high-quality’ experience for Apec finance meeting guests
description: City leader says Beijing is handling attendee registration without confirming whether US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is among the guests.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to provide guests attending this month’s Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting with a “high-quality” experience, as the city works closely with Beijing to assist delegations with the registration process. About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which will be hosted by Hong Kong for the first time at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. Asked whether US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent would attend the summit, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday only that the Ministry of Finance in mainland China was handling attendee registration. “The Hong Kong government will continue to maintain close communication and cooperation with the Ministry of Finance to assist the delegation in completing the registration procedures,” Lee said ahead of an Executive Council meeting. “The government will fully support the Ministry of Finance’s work and provide the delegation with a high-quality conference experience. We will make further announcements when there are updates.” Lee added that beyond the official sessions, the government would host a welcome dinner, seminars and visits for delegations, and generally organise the meeting well. He said the gathering would pick up discussions from previous sessions, focusing on the global and regional macroeconomic and financial situation, fiscal policies supporting livelihoods and development, financing for digital infrastructure, and advancing inclusive finance. The gathering would also strengthen exchanges and cooperation among finance officials of Apec member economies, Lee noted. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said earlier that authorities would put in place security arrangements, including contingency plans for potential terrorist attacks, and would safeguard hotel, venue and transport security, given the expected attendance of many ministerial-level officials. He also pledged to minimise disruption to residents’ daily routines. The gathering will be the first Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States last month, during which the two countries agreed that their leaders would support each other in hosting the Apec forum and the G20 summits later this year. The annual Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting will be held in Shenzhen in November.

title: John Lee urges public to tune in to Legco debate on city’s 5-year plan, policy address
description: Hong Kong legislature set to discuss concept and details of city’s first five-year blueprint and latest policy address from Wednesday to Friday.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has urged residents to pay close attention to a coming three-day debate on the city’s inaugural five-year plan and latest policy address in the legislature. The debate on the two policy documents is set to begin on Wednesday morning and continue until Friday, according to the Legislative Council’s agenda. “I look forward to tomorrow’s Legislative Council debate, during which government officials and lawmakers will conduct an in-depth discussion on the concept and details of the five-year plan,” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday, adding that the sessions would be attended by government officials led by Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki. “I encourage everyone to pay close attention, as this will help you better understand the importance and significance of the five-year plan, as well as how the policy address will implement the plan’s first-year initiatives.” Last month, Lee unveiled the last annual policy address of his current tenure alongside the city’s first five-year plan, which aligns with the national development strategy. The five-year blueprint included plans to double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy. The city leader said that he had attended a discussion with Legco members following the release of the blueprints, while major officials had also held policy briefings for different panels. “Lawmakers’ views reflected that they supported the objectives and policy directions of the five-year plan and policy address, and had also made suggestions in different areas,” he said. The five-year blueprint, a seven-part document described by Lee as “an action agenda” for Hong Kong’s medium and long-term development, lists 105 indicators, including 22 major targets covering economic and innovation development, livelihood issues and environmental protection.

title: Hong Kong prepares reforms, accountability measures ahead of Tai Po fire report
description: City leader John Lee pledges to pursue accountability and implement comprehensive reforms as soon as possible after receiving independent committee’s report.
content: Hong Kong authorities have made “a series of preparations” to implement reforms and pursue accountability ahead of the final report of an inquiry panel on the Tai Po blaze later this month, the city’s leader has said, pledging to act “as soon as possible”. It was understood that the government has established a dedicated task force under the Public Service Commission, led by former deputy secretary for security Benjamin Mok Kwan-yu and former commissioner for sports George Tsoi Kin-pan, to investigate alleged official failings linked to the deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday that the government would study and follow up on the recommendations of the judge-led independent committee investigating last November’s disaster, adding that details would be announced after he received the report. “The government has already made a series of preparations,” Lee told the media before a meeting of the city’s key decision-making Executive Council. “Upon receipt of the independent committee’s report, the government will, based on its contents, implement comprehensive reforms as soon as possible and pursue accountability.” The government established the task force under the Public Service Commission, an independent statutory body that advises on civil service appointments and promotions, to conduct an internal investigation into the fire and pursue accountability. Directorate-level civil servants, including Mok and Tsoi, are understood to have been posted to lead the task force’s work, and while senior they do not hold top rank. By comparison, the internal investigation into the 2012 ferry collision near Lamma Island was led by Joseph Lai Yee-tak, who at the time served as permanent secretary for transport and housing (transport), holding the highest rank in the civil service. However, Lee stopped short of disclosing the scope or timeline of the internal investigation. He also pointed to the seven priority reforms for the building maintenance, safety and construction sector laid out in his policy address last month. They include considering the criminalisation of bid-rigging, launching new tender invitation and evaluation services for homeowners, introducing a smoking ban at construction sites, and strengthening the regulation of fire service installations and equipment. The smoking ban was introduced in July. The fire, which broke out on November 26 last year, killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents, making it the city’s deadliest blaze in decades. At the time, the eight blocks were covered in scaffolding as part of a HK$336 million (US$42.85 million) facade-renovation project. The independent committee was set up in December last year and began its inquiry in March. It identified a series of “human factors” that led to the blaze, including the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, the placement of combustible polyfoam boards over windows and the deactivation of the fire alarm system. The panel also found that government departments had failed to supervise the safety of the renovation work and had taken no action despite repeated complaints from residents about fire risks, including unsafe materials and workers smoking on site. In his closing submissions, the committee’s lead counsel, Victor Dawes SC, singled out four government bodies for their alleged failure to heed fire risks in the run-up to the disaster: the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit. The committee is expected to submit its report to the government by the end of October, one month later than originally scheduled, due to the complexity of the disaster and the time needed to review the large volume of documents.

title: Turkmenistan grows its arsenal of Chinese air defences as Russia’s role shrinks
description: Amid regional instability, Central Asian nations look beyond Moscow for arms as the war in Ukraine drains Russian stocks.
content: Turkmenistan has added the FK-2000 missile-and-gun system to its growing arsenal of Chinese-made air defences, highlighting Beijing’s expanding role in the Central Asian weapons market once dominated by Russia. At least 10 FK-2000 vehicles – along with an array of other Chinese-made military equipment – could be seen in footage of Turkmenistan’s Independence Day parade in Ashgabat on September 27. Developed by the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation, the FK-2000 is a mobile air defence system combining missiles and twin 30mm (1.1-inch) cannons with on-board radar and electro-optical sensors. The system is designed to counter aerial threats including aircraft, helicopters, drones and precision-guided weapons. Its missiles can target aircraft at ranges between 1.2km (0.75 miles) and 25km, according to the state-run People’s Liberation Army Daily. Its missiles can target precision-guided munitions, including cruise missiles, at ranges between 1.2km and 10km. Other paraded Chinese-made equipment in Turkmen service included DJI Matrice 30T drones and Norinco’s Sky Saker FX80 unmanned aerial vehicle. Also displayed was a radar identified by Turkmen state media as a “YLS-18A”. While its designation resembles that of China’s YLC-18A, a comparison by the South China Morning Post based on publicly available images found differences in the vehicle configuration. Parade footage showed the radar vehicle immediately ahead of Chinese-made DWL-002 electronic surveillance systems. The precise identity of the radar remains unclear, but its appearance alongside the DWL-002 underscores the range of Chinese-made sensors already in Turkmenistan’s air-defence inventory. It also remains unclear how extensively Turkmenistan’s Chinese sensors and missile systems are linked through a common command, control and communications network. As far back as 2016, Turkmenistan was already displaying Chinese-made FM-90, KS-1A and FD-2000 surface-to-air missile systems alongside YLC-series radars. An analyst familiar with Chinese systems said the latest acquisitions appeared to be part of a broader modernisation of Turkmenistan’s air defences using Chinese equipment. The FK-2000 partly overlaps with the short-range FM-90 but combines missiles, cannon and its own sensors on a single highly mobile platform, giving Turkmen forces another way to intercept low-altitude threats including drones and precision-guided weapons. Turkmenistan has long been diversifying away from Russian arms, adding suppliers from Turkey, Italy and Israel, making the latest Chinese additions part of a broader procurement strategy rather than a wholesale shift towards Beijing. Yet the latest additions are also notable because they highlight China’s expanding role as a weapons supplier to one of Central Asia’s most closed and formally neutral states. Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia programme at the Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, said Turkmenistan’s long border with Iran and Ashgabat’s proximity to the country could also be a factor in its interest in strengthening air defences. Iran has been at war with the United States and Israel since February, with missiles and drones playing a major role in the fighting. Hostilities have largely paused in recent weeks, but talks have stalled and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in place. “I could imagine that Turkmenistan is very concerned to be located next to an active war zone,” Goldstein said, adding that this could make the country more willing to invest in its armed forces, “perhaps especially in upgrading its air [drone] defences”. Beijing has also been expanding its military exports elsewhere in Central Asia. Uzbekistan operates Chinese-made air-defence systems and in August confirmed the acquisition of J-10CE fighters, while Tajikistan operates the Chinese HQ-17AE short-range air-defence system. Footage circulating online appears to show Y-9E military transport aircraft bearing Kazakh Air Defence Force markings, although neither Kazakhstan nor China has publicly confirmed an acquisition. Goldstein said the trend also reflected Russia’s need to devote its air defence production to its own requirements, particularly to counter Ukraine’s long-range attacks, while advances in Chinese military technology were opening new markets for Beijing. “Russia is distracted and also quite tapped out,” he said, adding that Beijing’s “rise through the ranks of military technology is opening up new markets for Chinese arms exports”. A 2024 Caspian Policy Centre analysis found Russian arms deliveries to Central Asia in 2021–23 were 23 per cent lower than comparable levels in the previous decade, while Russia’s share of newly promised weapons by volume fell by 35 per cent. More recent data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute also shows a sharp wider decline in Russian arms exports.

title: India sizes up US F-35 stealth jets in landmark first on home turf
description: Joint drills offer New Delhi a glimpse of fifth-generation US air power, though analysts say Washington is keeping its top tech under wraps.
content: US F-35 stealth fighters have joined Indian warplanes for military exercises near the Pakistan border in recent days, marking the first time America’s most advanced multirole combat aircraft has taken part in joint drills in India. The US jets’ participation in the drills “signals a degree of military confidence and interoperability that is difficult to manufacture through communiques”, Sushant Singh, a South Asian studies lecturer at Yale University and former Indian Army officer, told This Week in Asia. “It also allows India to compare Western networked air-power concepts with its mixed Russian, French and indigenous fleet.” Analysts say the F-35s’ participation in Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 offers India’s military insights into how modern, fifth-generation fighters operate, as it struggles to get its own Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft project off the ground. It also serves as a test bed for cross-platform synergy and operational readiness. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Official Instagram Page Of IAF (@indianairforce) Apart from the United States, Australia, the United Arab Emirates, France, Germany, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are taking part in the drills, alongside several observer nations, according to India’s defence ministry. US ambassador Sergio Gor confirmed in a social media post on September 27 that six F-35 Lightning IIs and more than 200 US Air Force personnel were joining Tarang Shakti 2026, which is being held at Jodhpur Air Force Station in Rajasthan state, about 200km (124 miles) from the Pakistan border, from September 26 until next Monday. Sameer Patil, director of the Observer Research Foundation think tank’s Centre for Security, Strategy and Technology, said Indian officials would be measuring the F-35’s performance against the Russian-developed Sukhoi Su-30MKI, which forms the backbone of India’s air force. “They will also assess the aircraft’s stealth characteristics,” he said, noting that India’s fifth-generation fighter project had been held up by the complexities of achieving ultra-precise stealth manufacturing, as well as difficulties securing a suitable jet engine. Rajeswari Pillai Rajagopalan, a security analyst and resident senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, agreed that the presence of operational fifth-generation US fighters in India for joint drills for the first time offered Indian pilots and air force leaders a unique opportunity to observe and learn. “Equally significant is the fact that there are several different [Indian] fighters including Rafales, Su-30MKIs and Tejas alongside the F-35, which will also validate how different aircraft from different generations can operate together in a mission,” she said. Guarded secrets US President Donald Trump publicly stated last year that Washington was considering selling F-35 stealth fighters to India, but security analyst Olli Pekka Suorsa said that New Delhi’s close defence ties with Moscow made such a move unlikely. The US Air Force was also likely keeping “the aircraft’s true low observability a secret” by masking the F-35s’ true radar profile with the use of specialised, bolt-on radar reflectors, said Suorsa, an assistant professor of security at the Rabdan Academy in Abu Dhabi. Such capabilities were typically only “demonstrated in high-trust exercises like those between Nato allies, amongst other F-35 operators, or in war”, he said, referring to the transatlantic security alliance. Nor would the US reveal the aircraft’s true electronic countermeasures capabilities, Suorsa said, though Indian pilots would likely get a good idea of the F-35s’ basic manoeuvres and aerial performance. American pilots would likewise get to fly against India’s Russian-developed Su-30MKIs, which, alongside the S-400 surface-to-air missile system, continued to form the core of India’s air power capabilities, he said. Tarang Shakti 2026 is being held against the backdrop of disputes over US tariffs, disagreements over India’s Russian oil imports and differing approaches to regional security, including US engagement with Pakistan. Yet arms sales appear to have continued uninterrupted, according to Patil, who pointed to India’s purchase of the US-made FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank guided missile system in August. “While certain disagreements remain, both countries share converging threat perceptions in the Indo-Pacific,” Patil said. Singh, the former military officer, said US-India defence cooperation had acquired a “strategic logic resilient to political turbulence”. “F-35 participation is therefore a hedge against diplomatic volatility, and not evidence that disagreements have vanished,” he said. The US identified India as a critical partner in its latest National Security Strategy, released late last year, calling for improved relations “to encourage New Delhi to contribute to Indo-Pacific security”. Against that backdrop, Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 was “a show of strength and resilience”, Rajagopalan said.

title: ‘I’ve always loved food’: Yan Can Cook’s Martin Yan on his culinary journey
description: Yan talks about his big TV break, writing cookbooks and why he’s endorsing Hong Kong restaurateur Dan Gan’s Exotica Umami marinade sauce.
content: Martin Yan Man-tat first appeared on Canadian television in 1978 as a fresh, enthusiastic 29-year-old chef eager to teach people about Cantonese cooking. He has since become one of the culinary world’s most renowned figures, recognised for his cooking show Yan Can Cook and catchphrase, “If Yan can cook, so can you!” Nearly 50 years on, the celebrity chef – who was born in Guangzhou, moved to Hong Kong as a teenager and later left for Canada and the United States – remains as zealous as ever in spreading culinary knowledge and discovering new approaches in the kitchen. “I’m still working because I love what I do,” says Yan, who turns 78 this December. “Nowadays, I just do things that I love, things that I enjoy, [but] I’ve always loved food, and I’m passionate about it.” His latest interview with the South China Morning Post comes on the occasion of his endorsement of Exotica Umami – Ex M for short, a marinade sauce developed by Hong Kong restaurateur Dan Gan and launched earlier in 2026. Although Yan only started testing it in his own kitchen about a month ago, the umami-rich marinade impressed him and piqued his interest so much that he decided to help promote it at no cost. “I’m not an innovator, but as a food scientist and a chef, when I see something nice and new and innovative that works, I definitely want to try it myself and introduce it to other people,” Yan says. “It’s not about money – I did not charge [Gan] my fee to do it – but [it’s about products that] elevate texture, moisture retention and taste sensation.” Yan’s journey to success In the late 1960s, at age 19, Yan enrolled in the food science programme at the University of California, Davis in the United States. To make ends meet, he worked a series of food-related jobs outside class: kitchen hand, server, private caterer and, perhaps most importantly, cooking class instructor. In the mid-1970s, he went to Canada to help a friend who had recently left Hong Kong to open a Chinese restaurant in Calgary, Alberta. In the witty, friendly style that Yan Can Cook fans have come to love, he made the space his own and turned the job into a life-changing gig. The restaurant was “not too far away from the local television station”, he recalls. “A lot of the producers and directors would come and eat, and I would tell anyone, ‘Don’t look at this chop suey, chow mein menu. You tell me how much you want to spend, and I’ll cook for you.’ “I ended up making friends. One day, one of the chefs from InterContinental got sick, and I was invited to appear [on a cooking segment] as the replacement. “I got on once, they asked me to come back to do it twice; after the second time, they asked me to go up there and offered me 130 shows.” He adds with a hearty laugh: “I just did it [because] I’d never seen that kind of money before. I never wanted to be successful. I didn’t know how people would respond. I was the first Asian chef ever to host a daily show. It became very popular.” That was 1978, on the eve of his 30th birthday. In 1982, Yan Can moved from Calgary to San Francisco, where it became Yan Can Cook. Since that first appearance, Yan has filmed more than 3,500 episodes, making it the longest-running cooking show by a Chinese chef, broadcast in more than 50 countries. From television to cookbooks Although he is less active on television these days, Yan still writes cookbooks. At the start of 2026, he published his 36th cookbook, Best of Yan Can Cook, featuring more than 110 hand-picked recipes from his internationally celebrated programme, still on air as reruns around the world. His 37th and most recent cookbook, My Asian Kitchen: My Top 100 Asian Favourites, is inspired by his “travelling all over”. Yan has just returned from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, where he took part in and donated to a fundraising event for a local orphanage during the Mid-Autumn Festival. To a chef, travelling is often a mode of continuous research. While Yan thinks many professional chefs are taught to revere tradition and tend to be “very conservative” and resistant to change, as a food scientist, he is not afraid to embrace new practices. “I was the one who introduced combi-ovens and induction burners to a lot of chefs around the world,” he adds. “Our lifestyle has changed. When we were little kids, everybody had to go to the wet market to buy freshly slaughtered pork. Now, when you go to the supermarket, a lot of [meats] are chilled or frozen.” He explains that Ex M is an innovation that can “open up” and activate the protein inside frozen meat or seafood, bringing out “that freshness, that umami” and “the intrinsic quality” of the ingredient – which, to him, “totally changes the concept of cooking”. With his many decades of kitchen experience, Yan believes that cooking is “always evolving with new products and equipment – all of which are very important for chefs”. “It’s like how we were all driving diesel cars; now it’s electric cars. The whole world is changing and moving along. It just takes time.” On November 23, 2026, Yan will host an Exotica Umami dinner at New World Millennium Hong Kong Hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, with more details to be announced.

title: AirAsia chief’s jab backfires, Singaporeans going ‘car-lite’: 7 Asia highlights
description: From Japan’s strict visa rules to the Indian pilot hailed as a hero, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. AirAsia chief mocks Singapore Airlines’ food – and social media hits back AirAsia co-founder Tony Fernandes has caused a stir online after taking aim at Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) in-flight meals, claiming the food served by the carrier lagged behind his own airline’s offerings. 2. Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years. 3. No more welcome mat? Japan’s tough visa rules spur foreigners to look elsewhere Five years ago, Sarah and her husband were optimistic about Japan’s economic future and were expanding their small businesses across several sectors. Today, that optimism has been replaced by concern over a sense of hostility towards two hard-working foreigners who feel they have contributed to the society that they have worked hard to fit into. 4. Philippines’ uranium find a ‘vital’ boost for nuclear energy ambitions Researchers have identified a potential source of uranium in a long-explored mining district in the southern Philippines, as Manila moves to establish nuclear power and expand its critical minerals industry. 5. From Ed Sheeran to Massive Attack: Gaza rows spark Southeast Asia backlash American rapper Macklemore lost his spot on British pop star Ed Sheeran’s US tour after speaking up for Palestinians, but in Malaysia it was Sheeran’s music which ended up being pulled from the airwaves. 6. Sinking city, rising rage: Bangkok’s floods fuel fury over government inaction Bangkok, a city long plagued by a sinking feeling, went fully underwater. Not all of it, but enough of the city’s east and northeast to offer a terrifying teaser of what may lie ahead as this year’s “super” El Nino climate pattern intensifies into 2027. 7. Indian pride swells as Flydubai pilot who saved 174 lives hailed as hero An Indian pilot’s extraordinary bravery during an apparent mid-air hijack attempt has ignited a wave of national pride, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailing the pilot as a hero for saving 174 lives on a Flydubai plane – adding a dramatic chapter to a career that began almost by chance.

title: Random checks to be carried out at luxury Hong Kong estate for substandard work
description: Government will strengthen regulations and impose stiffer penalties to deter violations and uphold building standards, city leader says.
content: Hong Kong’s building authorities will conduct random sampling and inspections at the remaining properties of a luxury development in Stanley where substandard work was uncovered at one house, as well as at other projects undertaken by the contractor and professionals involved. The Buildings Department revealed the move on Tuesday night, hours after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the city would strengthen its regulatory regime and impose stiffer penalties to ensure strong deterrence against building violations, following a series of scandals over substandard construction, including the latest one at One Stanley in Southern district. The department said it had asked K&K Property, the developer of One Stanley, to conduct an investigation into similar detached houses and flats in the development and to submit a report. “As the regulatory body, the department will also proactively perform random sampling and inspections on selected units,” it said. “Furthermore, the Buildings Department will conduct random spot checks on other current projects managed by the building professionals and contractors involved, in order to ensure building safety.” The development comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats in total. Lee pledged to safeguard the high professional standards of the construction industry in the wake of the debacle involving the house, where the number of steel bars reportedly fell short of the figure in approved building plans by as much as 75 per cent. The owner reportedly bought the property in 2024 for about HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) and discovered quality issues when he started renovations in August last year. While declining to comment on details of the latest incident amid an ongoing investigation by the department, Lee highlighted that such issues concerned the professional standards, quality and safety of construction works. Lee said he was concerned as to whether those involved in the works had discharged their duties properly and whether the contractor had carried out the works in breach of requirements. “I have asked the Development Bureau to monitor the investigation of this case and construction work standards as a whole, to raise the regulatory regime and penalties under the law, to ensure strong deterrence and to severely punish those involved in any violations,” he said. The department said over the weekend that it had launched an investigation into the One Stanley project, which sits in one of the most expensive neighbourhoods in Southern district, and had requested information from the developer, contractor and relevant professionals. The probe began in the wake of a report by property news platform WuChatProp, which alleged that an on-site inspection of the house had found that insufficient steel bars had been used. The investigation is the latest concerning construction standards. In September, the Housing Authority found issues with concrete samples from three public housing blocks under construction in Tung Chung, prompting further review and testing. A month earlier, 24 of the 28 lifts in Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block were deemed unfit for use. The widespread installation defects delayed the full commissioning of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year. Lee earlier vowed to pursue accountability for that case as well. The city leader said on Tuesday that the Development Bureau would proceed “at full steam” to submit a proposed amendment to the Buildings Ordinance this year to strengthen regulation and enhance penalties for malpractice and substandard performance. “We must safeguard the high professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong’s construction works,” he said. Vincent Ho Kui-yip, a former president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, welcomed the government’s move, expecting tougher penalties and faster prosecution or disciplinary action. As more new blood joined the sector and the number of construction projects was expected to rise, tighter regulations could send a clear signal encouraging professionals to act with greater rigour, he said. However, Ho stressed that he did not believe the recent incidents pointed to systemic problems, and he cautioned against adopting overly stringent rules, such as requiring government approval at every stage of a project, which could significantly slow them down. “This is a culture issue; merely imposing fines of HK$10 million or HK$20 million cannot solve the problem,” he said, stressing the importance of education to improve practices. “We should not be overly strict on every single detail … If frontline workers and professionals are living in fear, it may become harder to get enough people to take part in construction projects.” Lawmaker Andrew Lam Siu-lo, a professional urban planner, called on the government to conduct a comprehensive review of the regulatory regime. Some professionals still harboured a mentality of taking chances and failed to fulfil their responsibilities, he said. “No matter how high the penalties are, it can be difficult to catch offenders because of challenges in gathering evidence or other practical constraints … Some professionals simply collect their payment and perform their duties without carefully verifying the construction work,” Lam said. “We need to examine this issue more thoroughly and find ways to counter this mentality of taking chances, whether through more frequent random inspections or even a demerit-point system.” Lam also suggested authorities make greater use of technology in supervision to reduce reliance on manual inspections. Lawmaker Michelle Tang Ming-sum, a civil engineer, said she was concerned that a manpower shortage and the need to fast-track projects were leading frontline workers to bypass standards to save time. She urged the industry to ensure projects met safety standards. “As you can see from earlier incidents, such as those involving cut-short screws, many of these cases stem from a rush to complete work and the pressure to keep to schedule,” she said. “I am worried that we might swing from one extreme to the other. I do not think that would be ideal.” Tang said she expected the government to expedite the proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance, but cautioned that some cases might involve subcontractors who were not registered professionals bound by the industry’s laws. She expressed doubt that simply raising penalties would create sufficient deterrent and suggested authorities increase spot checks as an additional safeguard.

title: China taps ultra-deep oil reserves 6,000 metres deep as global energy turmoil continues
description: Advanced drilling technology and offshore expansion are fuelling plans to boost domestic supply by 2030.
content: China is accelerating ultra-deep oil and gas development to expand domestic supply amid global energy uncertainties, with advances in exploration and extraction technologies unlocking harder-to-recover resources. One key frontier is the resource-rich western region of Xinjiang, where PetroChina’s Hade-Fuman oilfield has produced more than 26 million tonnes of oil equivalent from reservoirs more than 6,000 metres underground, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday. Wells deeper than 6,000 metres are generally classified as ultra-deep wells, where extraction is highly challenging due to extreme pressures and temperatures deep underground. The Hade-Fuman oilfield is located in the Taklamakan Desert and comprises two fields: Hade and Fuman. The latter was China’s largest ultra-deep oilfield, with oil and gas resources exceeding one billion tonnes, according to PetroChina. The reserves were discovered in 2021, following the company’s breakthroughs in geological understanding and exploration technologies that helped unlock complex oil and gas reservoirs buried deep underground. To tap the Fuman field, PetroChina said it had developed specialised drilling tools and technologies, successfully drilling wells with an average depth of more than 8,300 metres – a distance almost equivalent to the height of Mount Everest, the world’s highest peak. Chinese oil giants have stepped up domestic oil and gas exploration as Beijing seeks to strengthen energy security. The importance of such efforts has become more pronounced amid this year’s global energy turbulence, as disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for Gulf oil and gas exports, have underscored vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains. Under a five-year plan dedicated to the oil and gas sector, China was targeting a domestic supply of 440 million tonnes of oil equivalent by 2030, while 20,000 km of new long-distance oil and natural gas pipelines would be added, bringing the national network to 220,000 km – enough to circle the Earth more than five times. Last year, China’s total oil and gas production reached a new high of 420 million tonnes of oil equivalent, with crude oil output hitting a record 216 million tonnes. Beyond ultra-deep reservoirs in the desert, China is also expanding offshore oil and gas development. Among the latest is the Liuhua oilfield, located off the coast of Zhuhai in Guangdong province. Discovered in the late 20th century, the field has undergone redevelopment since late 2024, with advances in China’s deepwater development technologies helping to improve extraction efficiency in challenging offshore conditions. The field’s cumulative crude oil output exceeded two million tonnes as of Saturday, CCTV reported.

title: Q&A | Designer Azeeza Khan on her CFDA Genesis House win, New York Fashion Week and Law Roach
description: Style sits down with the Chicago-based creative, whose designs have been worn by stars like Barbra Streisand, Beyoncé and Jennifer Lopez.
content: Designer Azeeza Khan has spent the better part of 15 years building a fashion empire on her own terms, in her own way. For one, Khan is still based in her hometown of Chicago, away from the American fashion epicentre of New York and the Hollywood machine in Los Angeles. “We’re at Kith, Revolve, Shopbop, all those places, so we have reach,” she explains, but she hopes to expand her eponymous label’s physical presence with a secondary office outside Chicago. “LA is one of our top-selling consumer markets, but the fashion capital is New York with production and events,” says Khan, whose flagship store can be found on Chicago’s Magnificent Mile, next to established luxury names like Gucci and legacy department stores like Saks Fifth Avenue, where her designs are also stocked. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Azeeza Khan (@azeeza) Khan also rejects the traditional fashion week calendar and seasonal trends, incorporating subtle nods to her Indian heritage in the most tasteful of ways. “When I first started, my first Paris showroom was a massive undertaking because I thought I had to do it,” she says, “and that’s when we were onboarding Barneys and Revolve and Saks. I was spending a lot of money to keep up, and now I [only] want to do it in the right way, a fashion show and things of that nature.” Barbra Streisand, Beyoncé, and Jennifer Lopez have all worn Khan’s pieces. Her distinctly authentic approach to building a fashion business is clearly resonating. Recently named a recipient of this year’s CFDA Genesis House AAPI Design + Innovation Grant, Khan will receive US$60,000 in funding and mentorship from leading fashion figures to continue growing her brand and participate in a design challenge in Seoul, South Korea. We catch up with the designer to hear more about the milestones she has reached so far and the next stages of her business. Tell me about the Genesis House grant. There is this misconception that these grants are aimed at younger brands, whatever that means. How does this support you as a more mature brand, so to speak? It’s a full circle moment. As a new designer 15 years ago, before social media, influencer seeding, and all that, it was a different landscape. [I gained] credibility engaging with the CFDA early in my career – the team and the institution it is for America. They cast a pretty wide net [with applications]. Every year, CFDA focuses on a handful of talent; it really changes their business. I still feel as vulnerable and naive as I did on day one. I’m still self-invested. It’s just as much work as it was 15 years ago, if not more today. I welcome the platform and mentorship. How do production processes, supply chain issues and all that differ in Chicago versus New York? Chicago was a great development ground. From a commercial standpoint, it’s very strong for many retailers. Definitely a lot of spending power. We have a great base of private clients. It’s a small-pond, big-fish concept. It has its benefits, but your relationships are [in New York]. Likewise, I’m always invited to cool things I can’t make it to. Access is limited. The number one thing that’s been challenging is talent acquisition. I have to recruit good people out of [New York and Los Angeles]. Production, sampling, seamstresses and patternmakers – I do all that in New York. What about showing at New York Fashion Week? We are looking at doing our first actual presentation in February. You heard it here first, and now that I’ve said it, I have to do it [laughs]. We are manifesting. We’re also working on our first-ever raise, investment, for the business. Now it makes sense. I was against it. Now I feel I’ve grown the brand to where I can grow it. What scaling challenges have you encountered that led you to this conclusion? I personally did not pay myself my first pay cheque until 2022. A very modest pay cheque. Any money I made from anywhere, we put right back in [the business]. Even when I do get investment, I would be in that [dollar-conscious] mindset. We still ship out all the e-commerce from our showroom. It lets me quality-check everything, but it’s definitely limiting in growth. So we’re looking at strategic capital, specifically. It’s not just about money. It’s about hiring the right CEO because I never wanted to be the entrepreneur. I started this creative pursuit, and 10 per cent of my day is spent on creative. The biggest thing is to get back to making dresses I want to wear. I started chasing that commercial product, losing my creative vision while chasing dollars. I used to do a ton of artisanal embellishment. I would go [to] our own embroidery house in India at least three, four times a year – and I haven’t had bandwidth to do that in the last three to five years. Growing up Indian-American, how has your heritage inspired your work? Bespoke is such a big business [in India]. You walk down the street and there’s a tailor and custom dressmaker every block. You don’t really buy off the rack. I started learning how to cut and sew there under a Catholic Indian [who] would make wedding and American [style] dresses for her community. Because of that, I was able to learn [to make] dresses. Otherwise, if I had gone to a local tailor, I’d be making saris, more native dressing. Why are South Asian brands more famous now? Luxury fabrications, artisanal embroidery. A flower on a shirt: you have that drawn, then convert it to a print chalked onto the fabric, then you stretch the fabric like a canvas and embroider with threads of metal wire. In all these places in Paris, once they prototype it, they take it to India to get it done. That is our craft; that’s the most unique and applauded. Translating that onto American silhouettes was always exciting to me. Why has intricate embroidery on free-flowing silhouettes become your signature? The first person to ever call the brand elegant was Virgil [Abloh]. Everybody was in very form-fitting dresses [back then]. All the buyers [said my dresses had] too much volume. The poof sleeves I did – my reference was the show, Dynasty – we gave it to Barneys, and nobody had it. Now they’re everywhere. I can’t look good in a bandage dress; I just don’t have the body proportions for it. Speaking of Virgil, how have Chicago connections and culture shaped your brand and collaborations, like the athleisure line with Nike? Is there anybody else you’d like to shout out? When Virgil did The Ten with Nike, I started engaging with them at that time. I was wearing my dresses and wearing comfortable, cool shoes. I was a sneakerhead. That was the pairing I’d done: Nikes and dresses. Nike recognised that and really leaned into the feminine part of that world. On the record, [they’ve] said I’m their first South Asian collaborator as well. Today it’s not novel. But 15 years ago it was different. The Reinsdorfs, who own the [Chicago] Bulls, are private clients. But the first person we have to give a nod to is Law Roach. He’s the truest of Chicago kids. Virgil was a pioneer; he would literally be the next Karl Lagerfeld if he were continuing on his trajectory. But Law is so himself and supportive to people like me. He wrote my referral letter for the Genesis [House grant]. Someone else really cool is an artist by the name of Runsy. She does a lot of work with Nike. We’ve been talking about her sketching my next fabric prints.

title: Letters | Xi-Trump meeting mattered more than was first apparent
description: Readers discuss what the summit achieved, the last word on AI adoption, and AI writing.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The latest meetings between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping ended, yet again, with little to show in the way of a breakthrough. What grabbed international headlines was the pageantry, from Trump’s unprecedented greeting of Xi on the tarmac to a personal tour of the US$5 million granite helipad. “He’s an expert on stone aside from many other things,” Trump later told reporters. “And he loves good granite.” Pointing to these displays, observers were quick to dismiss the meetings as insubstantial. But that misses the bigger picture. The meetings helped stabilise a volatile bilateral relationship and, in doing so, laid the groundwork for future engagement. Even without achieving a grand bargain, the two sides made progress on three fronts. First, the tariff truce that was set to expire has been extended to January 7. Going into the summit, markets anxiously watched to see whether the arrangement that lowered triple-digit tariffs would lapse and send both sides back into a tit-for-tat trade war. That it didn’t suggests both sides still see reason for optimism. Washington is broadly content with China’s follow-through on its commitments, though the extension runs only two months, which implies that Washington is not satisfied enough to offer more. Second, both sides have agreed to open talks on a military crisis-communication pact that would restore channels between their armed forces. Beijing scaled back military contact in 2022, cutting off command-level communication between US and Chinese officers. Those ties have only recently begun to recover as relations thawed. The talks signal a shared interest in keeping lines of communication open, which is essential to stopping minor incidents from spiralling. In 2023, for instance, when a US fighter jet shot down a suspected spy balloon, then US defence secretary Lloyd Austin tried to reach his Chinese counterpart, only for Beijing to decline, saying Washington had not created the “proper atmosphere” for dialogue. Third, the two sides now have a dedicated platform for discussing artificial intelligence. That is no small feat. Trump has fiercely opposed global efforts at AI governance, and Washington and Beijing remain an ocean apart on everything from advanced chips to how the technology should be regulated. Even so, an AI-specific dialogue is scheduled for November to discuss risks and benefits. None of this amounts to a breakthrough, and it would be a mistake to pretend otherwise. But stability itself, in a relationship this fraught, is already an important achievement. Allen Zhang, research assistant, The Heritage Foundation Majority should have the last word on AI adoption For far too long, the preset default is that we will accept new technology unless we tell innovators otherwise. This approach is lame. Nobody should decide what is suitable for all of us. No matter how great those behind the new inventions are, the majority of us should have the last word on adoption. Artificial intelligence, which is all the rage right now, is a good case in point. The very people involved in this new technology are calling out the danger of it getting out of control, even decimating the human race. So why have they invented it? Could they be committing a heinous crime against humanity for being so callous about it? Why are we following the herd instinct and blindly adopting it? There is still no cure for cancer in general. Should not resources be directed at more urgent purposes? If both human labour and intellect are replaced, what do we have to exist for? This perhaps is the final frontier for humankind. Lee Teck Chuan, Singapore How not to write like AI I refer to “Don’t let AI take over our human creative expression” (September 24). I am your reader in Moscow whose letters occasionally appear in the press abroad, including your paper. Once I facetiously asked a Western AI if it assumed I was a Russian AI designed to promote the Kremlin’s propaganda in the West. The reply was that I was not since an AI can’t have relatives, while I am regularly mentioning my grandfather, my grandmother, my uncle and last but not least my aunt. Mergen Mongush, Moscow

title: Malaysia’s queen comforts family of girl found dead at school, pledges to get justice
description: Raja Zarith Sofiah also took part in a prayer meeting as Irene Sofiya’s father called for stronger school safety.
content: The father of 16-year-old Irene Sofiya said he drew comfort from Malaysia’s Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah and her assurance that she would do what she can to help seek justice for his daughter. Mohd Khairool Faisal Khyar, 42, said he deeply appreciated the queen’s concern and words of encouragement during her visit to the family home in Kampung Selamat, Johor, on Monday. “Raja Zarith Sofiah was very considerate and we greatly appreciate what she said to our family during this difficult period for us. Her Majesty told us to be patient with what had happened and said she would try to do what she can to help find justice for my daughter,” he said after the visit. Mohd Khairool, an engineer, said securing justice for his only child was now his main priority following the tragedy. He said he had received his daughter’s postmortem findings but declined to elaborate. Mohd Khairool also expressed gratitude for the public’s support following Irene’s death at her school last week. “I am very grateful and appreciate all the support. I hope that in the future, something like this will not happen to someone else’s child. I hope the matter will be addressed and resolved,” he said. Asked what he wanted to see from the education ministry, Mohd Khairool said greater priority should be given to school safety. “Safety in schools. It must be strengthened so that parents can feel assured when sending their children to school,” he said. Earlier, Raja Zarith Sofiah, accompanied by Che’ Puan Mahkota Khaleeda Johor, the wife of Johor regent Tunku Ismail, visited the family. The meeting began with the recitation of prayers led by Batu Pahat kadi (an Islamic legal official) Mohd Fauzi Bachok. Raja Zarith Sofiah also presented a personal contribution to the family to help ease their burden following Irene’s death. Before leaving, both the queen and Che’ Puan Mahkota Khaleeda were seen wiping away tears. Also present were Ayer Hitam MP and MCA president Dr Wee Ka Siong and Yong Peng assemblyman Ling Tian Soon, who is also a Johor state executive councillor. Meanwhile, the secondary school in Yong Peng where Irene was found dead continued its regular operations on Monday. A parent, who declined to be named, said students were asked to remain at school slightly longer as the administration held an emergency assembly. However, the parent expressed uncertainty about what the assembly addressed. On Saturday, Irene was pronounced dead at her school hall after suffering multiple injuries to her head and body, according to Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad. Police have detained a 16-year-old male student and obtained a six-day remand order to assist investigations. The case is being investigated under Section 302 of the Penal Code. This story was first published by The Star

title: Paris Fashion Week: Chanel and Sacai SS27 highlights
description: Matthieu Blazy envisioned swifts and swallows as symbols of lightness and freedom, while Chitose Abe spliced fabrics and leather with hardware like zips.
content: Another very long day in Paris began at 10am with a lovely show from Japanese label Sacai and ended more than 10 hours later with Chanel. Those two brands couldn’t be more different, yet both are rooted in real clothes imbued with just the right amount of fantasy. For spring/summer 2027, Chanel’s artistic director Matthieu Blazy turned the Grand Palais into a starry sky with a moon surrounded by flocks of white birds with their wings spread as if about to take flight. Models walked on an iridescent surface, similar to the one at Blazy’s debut show last year. The show teaser, unveiled a couple of days before the event, was a series of stunning black-and-white photographs taken by British photographer David Bailey. One was a still of a bird’s nest with a bird flying away. Before the show began, birdsong played in the background – you get the gist. This is not the first time Blazy was inspired by avian creatures at Chanel – his first haute couture collection for the brand was also bird-themed – but this time around, the swifts and swallows he dreamed up were envisioned as symbols of freedom and lightness. The show opened with a white slip dress featuring a feather flower at the bosom that was so light and delicate, it almost looked like a negligee. Since joining Chanel, Blazy has brought lightness and joy to the house, a lighthearted escapism that is still based upon clothes women actually want to wear. Take the way he reimagined the Chanel jacket, one of the house’s signatures. The ones in this collection were more stripped down and pared-back than in previous shows, even when embellished with sequins, feathers or tiny flowers; they were “worn as a second skin against bare flesh, as lightly as a perfume”, as the collection notes put it. A couple of jackets were paired with nothing underneath, their wing-shaped closures barely holding them together and replacing Chanel’s double-C buttons. Despite the theme, the bird references were few and far between. A quilted jacket was embroidered with clouds and birds reminiscent of an Asian landscape, while a billowing gown with a train evoked a serene blue sky filled with cloud formations. A couple of terrific looks featured tweed miniskirts slashed at the side, worn with matching cropped jackets. They were great examples of how to reinvent the Chanel suit while still retaining its essence. The most unexpected look in the show was a trench coat made of what looked like upcycled fabric held together with tape, perhaps a nod to Blazy’s days at experimental house Margiela. Chanel is known for its must-have bags, but Blazy is also doing a remarkable job with footwear. Square-toe pumps with sculptural heels, Chanel’s famous two-tone motif rendered in animal prints or deep colours like burgundy, mesh heels with gold trims – it was difficult to take your eyes off the models’ feet. Handbags ranged from streamlined styles adorned with the Chanel double-C logo in gold – the first and last looks were accessorised with an actual archival bag that had belonged to Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel herself – to extravagant models in colourful patterns and a minaudière shaped like an empty birdcage, its former resident already on the way to explore a faraway land. While it’s easy to dismiss the bird theme as a tired and gimmicky cliché, as the models walked out for the finale to a remix of Britney Spears’ “Gimme More”, it was hard not to feel the positive energy in the room and the infectious sense of wide-eyed wonder that has made Blazy’s revamp of Chanel such a success story. The great thing about Sacai is that you can recognise its garments as soon as you see them. Chitose Abe has built such a strong signature aesthetic for the label that it must be hard to evolve the look season after season without deviating from the brand’s DNA. For spring/summer 2027, the designer worked with fabrics such as satin and materials like leather, slicing them open and adding hardware like zippers to change the silhouette of garments like pencil skirts and bomber jackets. Crystal and gold embellishments, trompe l’oeil fur prints, and varsity logos from the “University of Sacai”, printed with the slogan “A Moment of Becoming”, rounded out the well-edited collection.

title: Temperatures in Hong Kong drop to 23 degrees Celsius
description: Sunny intervals are expected during the day, with temperatures peaking at around 29 degrees.
content:
Hong Kong saw its lowest temperatures so far this autumn, dropping to about 23 degrees Celsius (73 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday morning.
According to the Hong Kong Observatory, the cooler weather was caused by a dry northeast monsoon.
“A dry northeast monsoon will bring mainly fine weather to the coast of Guangdong in the next couple of days. It will be windier and slightly cooler in the morning over the region,” the forecaster said.
“The monsoon is expected to moderate slightly in the latter part of this week to early next week.”
The forecaster added that the mercury would rise gradually from 23.3 degrees, but the temperature difference between day and night would be relatively large over inland areas.
The weather will be mainly cloudy and dry on Tuesday, though sunny intervals are expected during the day with temperatures peaking at around 29 degrees.
It will be mostly fine and sunny from Thursday through to next Wednesday, with temperatures ranging between 25 and 32 degrees Celsius, according to the forecaster.

title: Trump approves firing squad execution for US military base shooter Nidal Hasan
description: Decision sets up the first execution by the US military in decades following the Pentagon’s recommendation for 2009 shooting.
content: US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 people at a military base in 2009, the Pentagon said on Monday. Hasan’s execution for the attack at Fort Hood in Texas – which also wounded more than two dozen people – will be the first carried out by the US military since 1961. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth “has recommended – and President Donald J. Trump has approved – death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a post on X. “The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote. Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the al-Qaeda-inspired mass shooting at Fort Hood. He chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. Court-appointed defence lawyers expressed concern that he was seeking execution. Muslim of Palestinian descent, opened fire on November 5, 2009, at a medical facility in the sprawling Fort Hood base, which served as a staging point for soldiers to deploy to combat zones in Iraq and Afghanistan. Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralysed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack. The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaqi, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen. While mass shootings in the United States are common, they are rare at military facilities. In 2025, a soldier opened fire at a US military base in the state of Georgia, wounding five fellow troops before he was tackled and apprehended. In 2019, a US sailor fatally shot two people and wounded a third at a base in Hawaii, while a Saudi military student shot dead three people at a military facility in Florida the same year. A Kuwaiti-born US citizen attacked two military installations in Tennessee in 2015, killing four Marines and a sailor. The FBI concluded the violence was inspired by a “foreign terrorist group”. Two years earlier, a man killed 12 people and wounded eight at the Washington Navy Yard in the US capital, before being shot dead by officers.

title: Chinese actress Li Bingbing credits success to younger sister who acts as manager, confidante
description: Li notes the considerable sacrifices her younger sister made for her career, asserting that she could die for her.
content: From a humble working-class family in northeast China to becoming a celebrated actress on the Hollywood stage, 53-year-old Li Bingbing’s ascent has never been a solo journey. At the heart of her decades-long career is her younger sister, Li Xue, 51, who transitioned from journalism to become Li Bingbing’s manager. Together, they co-founded Hesong Entertainment, a talent company that has represented performers across generations. The sisters have long been recognised as one of China’s most prominent sibling partnerships in the entertainment industry. Li Bingbing boasts over 42 million followers on Weibo, and Sohu News estimates her personal wealth at over 1 billion yuan (US$150 million), although this figure has not been independently verified. She has consistently credited her sister for her success, stating, “Without my sister, I would not be where I am today.” Li Bingbing remains unmarried and childless. According to The Paper, she plans to leave her assets to her sister’s two children. Born in Wuchang, Heilongjiang province, the sisters grew up in a modest household. Their parents worked as factory labourers, and the family once rented a home from their neighbours. When Li Bingbing enrolled in the Shanghai Theatre Academy, her family faced financial strain following her mother’s surgery. To alleviate this burden, she supported her sister’s education through advertising work and minor acting roles. Li Bingbing once reflected: “I can endure hardship myself, but I could not bear to see my sister suffer.” When Li Xue became her manager in 2000, Li Bingbing was still struggling to find her footing in the film industry, while contemporaries like Zhang Ziyi and Zhou Xun had already risen to prominence. Recognising her sister’s potential, Li Xue focused on selecting projects that could elevate Li Bingbing’s career. Her choices proved transformative. She guided Li Bingbing towards Feng Xiaogang’s A World Without Thieves in 2004 and The Knot in 2006, significantly increasing her visibility. This culminated in Li Bingbing winning Best Actress at the 2009 Golden Horse Awards for The Message. Li Xue later identified opportunities beyond China’s film market, encouraging her sister to take part in the Chinese-American production Snow Flower and the Secret Fan in 2011. This pivotal move opened the door to Hollywood projects, including Resident Evil: Retribution, Transformers: Age of Extinction, and The Meg, as well as collaborations with international luxury brands. Her role also encompasses ensuring her sister’s well-being. In 2015, when Li Bingbing fell seriously ill while filming in Australia, Li Xue halted production and brought her home for treatment, despite online speculation portraying Li Bingbing as a “diva” on set. However, their close professional partnership has not been without challenges. Li Bingbing has acknowledged that the sisters often clashed over work decisions, with their most significant dispute resulting in more than three months of no contact. Yet, these disagreements have never diminished their bond. Li Bingbing has highlighted the considerable sacrifices her sister has made for her career, describing Li Xue as a confidante and asserting: “I could die for her, because she is my sister.” Meanwhile, Li Xue derives happiness from her work, viewing their partnership as a means to realise her own worth. The sisters’ enduring collaboration has fascinated many on mainland social media. One online user noted: “They truly complement each other. The elder sister stands in the spotlight, while the younger sister maps out the broader vision. Sisters are natural allies.” “A healthy relationship isn’t devoid of conflict, but rather one that can recover and progress. They exemplify how partners can support each other over time,” commented another.

title: Bangkok braces for fresh chaos as possible floods threaten IMF-World Bank summit
description: Large trucks and four-wheel-drive vehicles will be deployed to transport over 15,000 delegates if roads flood this weekend.
content: Bangkok is preparing for possible flooding as more than 15,000 delegates are due to arrive for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group.
