The Thai capital could receive about 50mm (two inches) of rain a day from October 11-13, coinciding with the start of the week-long gathering of finance ministers, central bankers, executives and other delegates from the institutions’ 191 member countries, according to Surapong Sarapa, the Meteorological Department’s head of forecasting. The preparations come shortly after a late-September deluge dumped more than 304mm of rain on Bangkok over several days, flooding roads and homes, disrupting flights and temporarily shutting factories. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has instructed agencies to prepare for severe flooding and avoid a repeat of the travel chaos that accompanied the September deluge. Large trucks and four-wheel-drive vehicles will be available to transport delegates if roads flood, while hundreds of pumps are being positioned to drain water. Officials have drawn up contingency plans tied to floodwater levels. At 152mm, authorities would accelerate drainage to keep routes open for more than 400 motorcade vehicles. At about 254mm, electric BMWs would be replaced with buses; at about 508mm, delegates would be directed onto Bangkok’s rail network. In an extreme scenario in which floodwater reaches three metres (10 feet), the meetings would be cancelled. “There must be no disruptions like those seen last week,” Anutin said. The coming rain is not expected to be as severe as the September event. It should be more widespread but shorter-lived than the persistent downpours that overwhelmed Bangkok’s drainage system last month, Surapong said in a phone interview. Still, the wider water system has limited capacity to absorb another deluge. Major reservoirs in central Thailand were about 91 per cent full as of Monday, increasing the risk of flooding if heavy rain persists. One major dam was already above its normal capacity, raising the prospect of more water being released downstream towards provinces surrounding Bangkok, according to Hannarong Yaowalers, a Thai water-resources advocate. Officials say the central areas where many delegates are staying are designed to drain water relatively quickly into the Chao Phraya River. The river is currently about one metre (3.3 feet) below Bangkok’s flood barriers, leaving some capacity to absorb additional water, government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises said. The IMF-World Bank meetings are an important showcase for Thailand as it seeks to attract investment and position Bangkok as a regional business and financial centre. “Hosting this meeting is an important opportunity for Thailand to create economic value, expand trade and strengthen confidence in Thailand internationally,” Anutin said.

title: In Focus | Beijing’s policy advisers map out how post-reunification Taiwan could be governed
description: Mainland Chinese scholars discuss varying levels of autonomy for the island based on how reunification is achieved.
content: In 2019, President Xi Jinping became the first Chinese leader to publicly call for the exploration of detailed proposals for governing Taiwan after reunification. Seven years later, the first proposals from a handful of the mainland’s leading research institutes have either been finalised or are nearing completion, the South China Morning Post has learned. Rather than setting out a single fixed model, scholars involved in those studies told the SCMP there should be different scenarios based on how reunification was achieved, with peaceful reunification granting Taiwan the largest scope of autonomy under Beijing’s “one country, two systems” framework for post-reunification governance. “The earlier Taiwan engages in talks with the mainland, the more bargaining power it would have, and therefore the greater the space it would have to shape the terms. That is almost inevitable,” said Chen Xiancai, a Taiwan affairs professor at Xiamen University. Chen said that, given the state of cross-strait relations, one scenario he considered “highly viable” would be forcing Taiwan into reunification talks by applying pressure across the political, military and international arenas. While this does not represent Beijing’s official policy, Chen said he believed some of the measures had already been employed in recent years, and that a blockade of the island could not be ruled out if deemed necessary in the future. The sooner they talk, the better the terms The study led by Chen, the director of the university’s Centre for Taiwan Studies, is among the research projects undertaken by mainland Chinese scholars since Xi’s landmark speech to explore a “two systems” Taiwan. These projects have not yet been published. Xi’s call built on the “one country, two systems” model, which was first formulated by former Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s as a possible solution to the Taiwan question. It has already been implemented in Hong Kong and Macau. Under the formula, which holds that there is only one China, the island could retain its existing economic and social systems and enjoy a high degree of autonomy after reunification. In that 2019 speech, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-standing position that peaceful reunification remained “the best approach”, saying the “one country, two systems” formula was designed “precisely to accommodate Taiwan’s actual conditions”. Seven years after the speech, Beijing has said little publicly about how it would seek to govern Taiwan following reunification. However, Tsinghua University and Xiamen University have finalised their studies on the subject this year, with another one conducted by Peking University close to completion, according to academic sources. The studies do not represent Beijing’s official policy, but serve as a reference for policymaking and offer a rare glimpse into academic discussions about the possible terms of a future settlement across the Taiwan Strait. A recurring theme discussed by scholars involved in the studies is that the circumstances under which reunification took place would determine the extent of autonomy granted to Taiwan. “If reunification were achieved entirely through peaceful means, with the two sides negotiating now, Taiwan’s room to manoeuvre – or the powers and status it might retain – could potentially be greater than those of Hong Kong and Macau,” Chen said. But if reunification were achieved through what Chen described as “compelled reunification”, Taiwan could be offered a Hong Kong- or Macau-style model, or possibly “even less autonomy” than the two special administrative regions, he said. “Compelled reunification” – or bitong – is a term coined by mainland scholars to describe an approach between complete peaceful reunification and a full-scale attack. This approach, they argue, means reunification is compelled after Beijing deploys a range of political, economic, military and diplomatic measures. “However, if Taiwan does not accept the goodwill offered by the mainland or its policy of peaceful reunification, and instead forces the mainland to resort to military means, Taiwan will have fewer bargaining chips, and its room to manoeuvre will be severely curtailed,” Chen said. Other heavyweight policy advisers have echoed this point, including Li Yihu, a lawmaker and Taiwan specialist at Peking University, who warned last year that if Taiwan left Beijing no choice but to reunify by force, the island’s autonomy would be the same as an average province. Discussions among scholars about a detailed plan for Beijing to govern Taiwan have grown in the past month. On September 12, more than 20 mainland scholars, led by Wang Jianmin of Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, reached a 12-point consensus on a plan for Taiwan at a seminar in Beijing. Their proposal included maintaining a People’s Liberation Army presence on the island and introducing patriotic education. However, another scholar, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Taiwan-related academic research on the mainland was far more diverse than the 12-point proposal, which did not represent the full range of views among mainland academics. The discussion was joined by Li Ci-ze, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education. In a proposal published in August, Li argued that after peaceful reunification, Taiwan should be able to retain its direct elections for the island’s top executive official and legislature while “fully retaining” its opposition parties. Beijing said it was pleased to see the proposal, without hinting at whether it agreed with the details. Chang Ya-chung, head of the Taiwan-based Sun Yat-sen School advocacy group, said the two sides should take gradual steps towards signing a peace deal before discussing the details of post-reunification governance. He made the comments during his trip to Beijing to attend last month’s Xiangshan Forum security conference, and later elaborated on them in an article. When asked about Chang’s remarks, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office said it welcomed suggestions from Taiwan’s people, and “the sooner and more extensively” the Taiwanese held such discussions, the more benefits they would see. ‘Compelled reunification’ The strategy of “compelled reunification” is highly feasible under current cross-strait conditions, according to Chen, though Beijing authorities have never publicly acknowledged the idea. “What we mean by ‘compelled reunification’ is essentially the use of certain measures to shape, guide or pressure the Taiwan authorities towards reunification,” Chen said. He argued that this was a special form of “peaceful reunification”. “It is carried out within the broader policy of peaceful reunification, but its distinctive feature is the use of pressure,” he said, adding that it could encompass military, diplomatic, economic and legal measures. “Compelled reunification does not necessarily mean a military conflict. It would not necessarily be like the Russia-Ukraine war, where the PLA would have to enter Taiwan or launch a landing operation on the island.” A blockade could also be one possible form of pressure under such a scenario, he added. In recent years, Beijing has conducted large-scale military exercises around Taiwan, including drills that have simulated elements of a blockade and involved coordination between the PLA and mainland China’s coastguard. Chen said the approach also had historical precedents in the Communist Party’s handling of the civil war against the Nationalists before 1949. He cited the case of the “Beiping model”, referring to the peaceful takeover of Beiping, now Beijing, by the Communist Party in 1949. The Communist forces’ military advantage in north China, including the seizure of Tianjin and the siege of Beijing, forced the Nationalist defenders to agree to a peaceful takeover by the PLA in Beijing. Although Chen said the approach did not represent an official policy of Beijing, he believed that elements of such a strategy had already been put into practice, with pressure extended across military and international arenas. In the military domain, PLA exercises in recent years have pushed beyond the Taiwan Strait median line, an unofficial boundary that has long served as a de facto buffer between the two sides. After then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022, Beijing intensified military exercises around the island, and PLA aircraft have increasingly crossed the median line. Diplomatically, Beijing has stepped up efforts to restrict Taiwan’s international space. A total of 10 countries have cut off diplomatic ties with Taipei since 2016, when the island’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party came to power. In April, Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te was forced to postpone his visit to eSwatini, the island’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa, because three countries along the flight route – Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar – revoked flight permits for Lai’s aircraft, according to Taipei. Integration push The idea of “one country, two systems” appears to be highly unpopular in Taiwan. More than 80 per cent of people in Taiwan oppose the “one country, two systems” formula, according to a poll in August conducted by Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council. However, mainland scholar Chen argued that peaceful reunification remained possible, saying Beijing was seeking to integrate Taiwan with the mainland and gradually shape public opinion in favour of reunification. “It’s not that the prospect of peaceful reunification has disappeared. That’s why both the government and academia are still discussing it – the prospects for peaceful reunification remain strong,” he said. He argued that Beijing’s growing power was one factor, and “internationally, the situation is also moving in the mainland’s favour”. He added that the stability of Sino-American relations as well as Washington’s stance on Taiwan were things Beijing could work on to create a more favourable environment for its reunification goals. It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee? Chen Xiancai, Taiwan affairs expert After meeting Xi in May, US President Donald Trump said of Taiwan: “I’m not looking to have somebody go independent.” The American leader also described a US$14 billion arms sale to the island as “a good negotiation chip”. Chen said Beijing could not rely on any single political party in Taiwan to support reunification, and that Beijing sought to work with pro-reunification forces across the island and use cross-strait integration to influence public opinion. “Our approach to reunification is to win people’s support. We are not simply trying to work through individual political parties,” he said. He added that public opinion in Taiwan could ultimately change policy, though it would take time. Wang Huning, Beijing’s fourth-ranked official and its top official overseeing Taiwan affairs, last year outlined what he described as “seven betters” that Taiwan could enjoy through reunification, covering areas including infrastructure, the economy, energy and disaster relief. The remarks marked a rare effort by a senior Chinese leader to explicitly spell out the potential benefits of reunification for people in Taiwan. Beijing has in recent years promoted greater cross-strait “integration”, particularly through pilot projects in the coastal province of Fujian. These initiatives have been presented as potential models for future cross-strait arrangements while also serving as a means of increasing pressure on Taipei, according to Chen. For example, construction of the mainland section of a bridge between the Fujian city of Xiamen and the Taiwan-controlled island of Quemoy is nearing completion. The necessary connecting infrastructure is already in place for it to eventually link up with Quemoy, also known as Kinmen. Chen said Beijing had taken the initiative in showing the potential benefits of reunification while maintaining pressure on Taiwan’s authorities. “It’s like dating. If a man wants to pursue a woman, shouldn’t he take the initiative and buy her a coffee?” he said. “We have the financial resources and the machinery. We can get these projects built, continually putting pressure on Taiwan while making people in Kinmen feel that they stand to benefit.”

title: Opinion | Hong Kong’s bridge of gold completes China’s yuan ambition
description: With Shanghai pricing the contracts and Hong Kong handling offshore vaulting, Beijing is building a gold-backed route to currency internationalisation.
content: Beijing is building a gold-backed monetary architecture to accelerate yuan internationalisation. In this three-part series, Part 1 traces China’s path to becoming a gold superpower, while Part 3 explores Hong Kong’s unique role in the emerging gold trading ecosystem. In 2013, one-third of the world’s traded gold passed through Hong Kong. That year, the city imported 1,158 tonnes of bullion, overtaking India, the traditional top buyer. For all our love of the glittering metal, little of it stayed in our vaults. It mostly went straight to mainland China, where strict controls meant the bulk of its gold imports had to transit through here. Little did we know that things would soon be turned upside down. In 2014, China relaxed restrictions, allowing more mainland banks to buy foreign gold without routing it through Hong Kong. Net gold flows to the mainland via the city fell to 863 in 2015, then to 245 tonnes in 2019, before reaching a nadir of 67 tonnes in 2020, according to a Hong Kong Legislative Council report. Just as Hong Kong’s gilded days as the region’s premier gold hub seemed over, things flickered back to life. Bullion flowing into the city has surged since 2020, rebounding to 942 tonnes last year. Now, Hong Kong has set itself the goal of becoming an international gold trading centre, with plans to increase storage capacity tenfold, from 200 tonnes to 2,000 tonnes by 2028. What has happened is a structural shift in Hong Kong’s role: from a simple gateway to a critical link in the nation’s push for financial security and the internationalisation of its currency. China’s yuan strategy has changed fundamentally since 2014. It has moved away from pursuing full capital account convertibility and integration into Western-dominated systems. Instead, it has pivoted towards building an alternative cross-border payment system independent of the US dollar. As the undisputed global trade superpower, China persuades others to settle their transactions in yuan, yet has no intention of relaxing its capital controls. But for others to hold the yuan as they do the US dollar or euro, foreign central banks must be confident the currency will hold its value and can be converted into tangible collateral. Enter gold and the offshore yuan market. The People’s Bank of China ranks fifth globally in sovereign gold reserves, yet it has far more room to expand than other major central banks. Gold accounts for 65-75 per cent of the foreign exchange reserves of the US, Germany, France and Italy but makes up less than 10 per cent of China’s massive US$3.4 trillion reserves, which remain dominated by the US dollar and foreign currency bonds. The US-led sanctions against Russia were a wake-up call for Beijing, and the urgency to build up gold holdings is now structural. China has been the world’s No 1 gold producer since 2007, churning out about 380 tonnes a year, all of which it keeps. It is also becoming the largest importer, snapping up more than 1,000 tonnes so far this year. Its relatively opaque reporting makes it a guessing game how much physical gold the government has amassed, but Beijing is clearly hoarding for strategic reasons. By steadily replacing US dollar assets with physical gold, China signals that a vast, neutral “hard asset” backs its national balance sheet. That strengthens foreign confidence, particularly among the non-Western Global South, in holding yuan-denominated debt or trade balances. Historically, gold trading, pricing and physical clearing have been concentrated in London and New York. China is building its own centres, and Shanghai and Hong Kong could form the axis of this parallel Eastern infrastructure. In 2014, it established the Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE) international board, which focuses on physical transactions and sets its own standards, pricing and clearing protocols, distinct from those of the dominant London Bullion Market Association. The London bullion market still commands more than 70 per cent of global daily trading volume, but the SGE’s share has risen to 16 per cent. Most importantly, the SGE dominates global physical gold trading, which involves physical delivery and vaulting. Beijing has also introduced yuan-denominated gold contracts on the SGE and expanded offshore gold vaults in Hong Kong. This allows trading partners, particularly Brics nations and Middle Eastern oil exporters, to accept yuan for their commodities, immediately convert it into physical gold in Hong Kong and ship it home. This process, known as “gold convertibility”, makes accepting yuan far less risky for China’s partners. In effect, China is building Shanghai as the gold pricing and clearing centre, and Hong Kong as the vaulting and delivery point for foreign clients. Our common law system, free flow of capital, safe and secure environment, and highly efficient professional services make the city an ideal place for countries to diversify their gold holdings away from London and New York. Central banks from Belt and Road Initiative countries can vault their gold here and use it as collateral to raise yuan-denominated capital at a lower cost. Without full convertibility, the yuan serves mainly as a medium of exchange. Now, physical gold stored in Hong Kong can serve as a store of value. Linking the two completes the jigsaw, and no place can do it better than Hong Kong. On September 23, the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) announced plans to launch a yuan-denominated gold futures contract early next year. This will allow Asian and Global South counterparties to price, trade and settle physical bullion directly in yuan, and it underpins the city’s ambition to become a global gold trading centre and aggressively expand its storage capacity. Our future as an international financial centre in the coming decades depends on whether we can develop the offshore yuan and gold businesses for the nation. If we can be the bridge of gold for the Global South, Hong Kong’s position will be vault-secured.

title: Hong Kong temperatures drop to 23 degrees Celsius on Tuesday morning, lowest this autumn
description: Weather will be mainly cloudy and dry on Tuesday, though sunny intervals are expected during the day with temperatures peaking at around 29 degrees.
content: Temperatures in Hong Kong dropped to about 23 degrees Celsius (73 Fahrenheit) on Tuesday morning, the lowest so far this autumn. According to the Hong Kong Observatory, the cooler weather was caused by a dry northeast monsoon. “A dry northeast monsoon will bring mainly fine weather to the coast of Guangdong in the next couple of days. It will be windier and slightly cooler in the morning over the region,” the forecaster said. “The monsoon is expected to moderate slightly in the latter part of this week to early next week.” The forecaster added that the mercury would rise gradually from 23.3 degrees, but the temperature difference between day and night would be relatively large over inland areas. The weather will be mainly cloudy and dry on Tuesday, though sunny intervals are expected during the day with temperatures peaking at around 29 degrees. It will be mostly fine and sunny from Thursday through to next Wednesday, with temperatures ranging between 25 and 32 degrees Celsius, according to the forecaster.

title: Experts urge wider One Stanley checks, tighter paperwork after steel bar shortfall
description: One house in luxury development reportedly found to have up to 75 per cent fewer steel bars than specified in the approved building plans.
content: Hong Kong’s building authorities should consider inspecting the remaining properties in a luxury residential development and tightening work process documentation after one house was found to have used insufficient steel bars during construction, experts have said. Their suggestions followed the Buildings Department revealing at the weekend that it had launched an investigation into work quality issues at One Stanley in Stanley, one of the most expensive neighbourhoods in Southern district, and had requested information from the developer, contractor and relevant professionals. Referring to the development, which comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats in total, the department said the irregularities did not “pose obvious danger”. Lingnan University’s Professor Yau Yung, a surveyor who researches building illegality, said the department could consider inspecting the rest of the development to play safe. “It is possible that the other properties will have similar issues if they involve a systematic error, an omission or malpractice,” he said. Edward Chan Sai-cheong, past chairman of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers’ structural division, said the results of the investigation would determine whether the department had to check the remaining properties. “It has conducted many tests. First, it should decide whether it is an individual case or a systematic situation. Secondly, it should also decide whether it involves a serious problem,” he said. Chan said some owners might have concerns about a site-wide inspection as they did not wish to be troubled, while others might want to hire professionals for inspections before escalating the issue to the department. The issue came to light after a report by online property news platform WuChatProp alleged that an on-site inspection of a house at One Stanley found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts, falling short of the number in the approved building plans by as much as 75 per cent. The owner reportedly bought the property in 2024 for about HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) and discovered quality issues when he started renovations in August last year. The developer, K&K Property, said on Sunday that it was highly concerned about the incident and was investigating. It said that if any party was found to have made construction or other related errors, the company would carry out any fixes needed to the property and hold the relevant parties accountable according to the law. The department, which issued an occupation permit for the development in July 2023, said it had received a complaint about the structural safety of floor slabs in January this year. Subsequent inspections found irregularities in the concrete cover of one of the beams and in the steel reinforcement of some slabs. Yau of Lingnan University said the incident involved the quality of concealed work, which relied on technical staff from the contractor for supervision. He added that the department generally would not check such work when it issued an occupation permit unless there was an obvious issue. Yau said the department could consider using penetrating radar for future assessments but warned it might require additional manpower and significantly lengthen the process. He called for strengthening documentation of the work process. “In the future, in some hidden works, such as installing steel bars and waterproofing the kitchen and toilet … Whether these works have been done correctly and thoroughly, I think there should be plenty of technology available that can help keep records of them,” he said. “In case of any disputes, it will be easy to pull up those records to judge whether things were done right or wrong in the first place.” Yau added that strengthening documentation requirements could also deter contractors and developers from cutting corners. Chan, the engineer, said the idea of strengthening documentation could be explored, noting that the department currently required certain work procedures to be recorded. He said existing rules on the supervision of new building works under the Buildings Ordinance were sufficient, as the law stipulated that the contractor had to deploy technical staff to supervise procedures. An industry expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused the department of trying to downplay the severity of the issue. “Claiming there is no imminent danger simply means the structure will not collapse immediately, but it undoubtedly poses serious long-term safety risks,” the expert said. He stressed that every engineering project must strictly adhere to established design standards, approved architectural plans and standardised protocols, particularly regarding concrete quality. Addressing the impact on affected property owners, he said the use of defective building materials should in theory give them legitimate grounds to rescind their purchase agreements.

title: Marine’s arrest for murder in Japan fuels anger over US military presence
description: Residents say the killing of an Okinawan woman shows they are paying the price of shouldering Japan’s heaviest security burden.
content: The alleged murder of an Okinawan woman by a US marine has raised questions over the American military presence on the island, piling pressure on its newly elected governor just as the prefecture assumes greater importance in Japan’s regional security strategy. Anna Yagi, 39, was found dead at a hotel in Naha in the early hours of Saturday morning. A postmortem determined she died from suffocation. The killing sparked protests the following day, with around 100 people rallying outside the prefectural government building on Sunday, while social media filled with demands for greater Japanese control over US bases. Yagi was identified on security cameras entering the hotel with Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, a lance corporal with the US Marine Corps based at Air Station Futenma. Ballard was seen leaving the hotel some hours later, allegedly with Yagi’s bag. Japanese police arrested Ballard on Sunday in Okinawa City and told local media he had denied all knowledge of the incident. Analysts said the killing could stir further opposition to US military bases in Okinawa, though they doubted that Japan’s central government would allow its security relationship with Washington to be damaged. Go Ito, a professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo’s Meiji University, said the case had revived memories of the abduction and rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl in 1995 by three US servicemen, which triggered weeks of protests across the prefecture. “This will inevitably remind people of 1995, and it could not have come at a worse time for the new governor,” he said. “Much will depend on how he responds, but I can very easily see a strong backlash among ordinary Okinawan people if they feel he has not done enough.” Governor Genta Koja took office on September 30 after successfully campaigning on economic issues rather than the US base dispute that has dominated local politics for decades. “This is an extremely malicious incident that will cause great anxiety among the residents of the prefecture and city. I feel intense anger,” Koja reportedly said on Monday after summoning the head of the local foreign ministry office and the top-ranked official of the Okinawa Defence Bureau to file a protest. “I strongly urge the Japanese and US governments to take responsibility and implement effective and fundamental measures, including a review of the Japan-US Status of Forces Agreement, to ensure that such an incident never happens again.” Ito said the backlash would likely force Tokyo to accelerate the transfer of US marines to a new base in the coastal ward of Henoko, as it spurred calls for “the return of Futenma to Okinawan control and the transfer of several hundred US troops to Guam”. The proposed closure of the base in Futenma and the scaling down of the US military presence in Japan’s most southerly prefecture had been in the works for more than 30 years, he pointed out. Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo’s Waseda University, said that while Japan had to preserve its security arrangement with Washington, the situation would leave Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi walking a diplomatic tightrope. “What happened in 1995 was the trigger for the relocation of Futenma, and now we have had a fatality. So it is clear there are going to be political ramifications,” he said. “The Takaichi administration is going to do everything it can to maintain good relations with the US.” Takaichi’s condemnation was swift and strong, and while chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara echoed that message, he made it clear that the US and Japan should work together to ensure such incidents would not recur. Ascione said Takaichi had worked hard to build a good personal relationship with US President Donald Trump, positioning herself as a successor to former prime minister Shinzo Abe. “Takaichi does not want a rift in the alliance although at the same time she has to be seen to be upholding Japanese sovereignty at home,” he said. “She has to straddle that line and strike the right balance between the domestic and international pressures.” Still, the prime minister would “not allow” any friction in the US-Japan security alliance “to deepen to such an extent that it would affect the alliance or the security role of Okinawa itself”, Ascione said. Okinawans have been taking to social media to vent their anger, with the online pages of the local Ryukyu Shimpo newspaper flooded with angry comments about the attack and what many see as Japan’s powerlessness to act. “Eighty years after the war, the Japanese government is still being extorted by the US, and I believe we are still under occupation,” read one message. Another commentator asked: “If a nation cannot exercise sufficient judicial power or access rights over foreign military bases within its territory, isn’t it essentially no different from a ‘colony’?” There are an estimated 30,000 active-duty US military personnel on Okinawa, along with 25,000 family dependents and 25,000 civilian contractors appointed by the US Department of Defence. The southern prefecture, which comprises less than 1 per cent of Japan’s total land mass, accounts for 70 per cent of the land used for US military bases in the country. Koja’s immediate predecessor, Denny Tamaki, was elected in 2018 on a platform of reducing the US military presence in Okinawa.

title: Proposed Asian football reforms threaten to kill Hong Kong’s World Cup hopes
description: Continental governing body advocating for Nations League that would reshape Asian and World Cup finals pathways.
content: As Hong Kong bathed in the afterglow of their Fifa Asean Challenge Cup triumph on Saturday, the level-headed Sun Ming-him cautioned that World Cup qualification remained a pipe dream for Roberto Losada’s team. What Sun, one of Hong Kong’s best players, did not know as he spoke was that despite the World Cup swelling to 48 teams this year, and another 16 potentially joining mammoth future editions, the city side’s qualifying task could soon become all but impossible. It has been reported that on Tuesday the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) will outline to its members proposals for a Nations League that would redraw pathways to the Asian and World Cup finals. Split into first and second divisions of 18 teams, with the continent’s lowliest 11 sides competing in a third tier, the new biennial competition would begin in 2030, following a pilot edition over the preceding two years. Asian Cup qualifying matches would be kicked into the long grass, with all 18 top-tier teams guaranteed spots in the next finals, likely to be staged in 2032, and six more berths up for grabs from the second echelon. Currently ranked No 30 in Asia and 153rd globally, Hong Kong would almost certainly end up in the second division, barring an unexpected nosedive, but needing to defy considerable odds to repeat their 2023 Asian Cup finals appearance. What’s more, for any chance of playing in the 2034 World Cup, the city team would need a top-two finish in the 2030-31 Nations League. That would earn promotion to the 2032-33 edition’s top tier, which is set to supply all nine Asian teams for the 2034 tournament in Saudi Arabia. The Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) has been approached for comment. Before news of the prospective revamp emerged, Sun said that beating Cambodia to win the inaugural Fifa Asean competition had represented a “new start for us under a new head coach”. “We have to improve step by step, improve our Fifa ranking and be ready for the next qualifiers,” he said. It has been suggested that 2030 World Cup qualifying will begin next March, largely replicating the most recent format, where Hong Kong finished bottom of their second-round group behind Iran, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. These preliminary qualifiers would be used to determine the pilot Nations League’s divisions. The HKFA is yet to tell anyone who or where its representative team will play in next month’s Fifa window, but whatever the future looks like for Hong Kong, Sun is assured of a prominent role. Blessed with the football IQ to fill any outfield position, other than centre-half, the 26-year-old said: “I’ve become more efficient in different positions and, psychologically, I’ve learned to be calmer when I’m playing, which has been the most important thing [in my development]. “I still prefer a forward position, whether it’s striker, right-wing or left-wing, because it’s where I feel most natural, and what I trained for when I was young.” Sun is primarily employed at left-back by his Chinese Super League (CSL) club, Tianjin Jinmen Tiger, where he has signed renewed terms to stay after this season. Hong Kong head coach Losada managed Sun for 2½ years at Eastern before the player left in February 2024 to join the now-defunct Cangzhou Mighty Lions. “Playing in the CSL, with good training and strong opposition, gives you something extra, and he has really improved,” Losada said. “I know what he can give me, and we can take more advantage of his attributes when he is playing in a forward position.” While the mooted Nations League would probably consign Hong Kong to second-rung football in perpetuity, they would at least have a gateway to major finals. For the flotsam and jetsam occupying the third tier, their current routes to summer tournaments, however convoluted, would be barricaded. That would be a huge shame for the likes of world No 202 Timor-Leste, who played some fabulous football in their two Asean Cup matches in Hong Kong, and 197th-ranked Pakistan, who accepted the hospital pass of an elite Fifa Asean Cup invite and duly drew 2-2 with the Philippines, then gave Vietnam a fright in a 4-2 defeat. The top-tier Asean place became available after India withdrew in favour of marquee friendly dates with Panama, Brazil and Uruguay. Sun said: “If we played strong opponents like Brazil and Uruguay, it would be a brilliant opportunity for us to identify the differences between great teams and us. “It’s important to understand [where gaps exist] because that’s how you improve as a team. “I’ve already had such a long journey, but I still want to contribute more and help [Hong Kong] get better.” Told that he had reached 48 caps against Cambodia, Sun was genuinely astonished. He acknowledged, nonetheless, that he really should have more than three international goals. Playing as a second striker, Sun scored a fabulous header in the 4-0 victory over Laos that launched Hong Kong’s Fifa Asean Cup campaign; then, from left midfield, he supplied the precise cross for Matt Orr to open the scoring against Cambodia. “I need to work on my finishing technique and my decision making,” Sun said. “If I get better in those areas, I’ll score more. You can always continue improving your football intelligence and physicality, too.” Certainly, Sun locating his shooting boots would be a significant boon for a team that is heavily reliant on Orr and Everton Camargo for goals. Of their 21 wins from 55 matches since June 2022, only six have come without a goal from either Orr or Camargo, who, after scoring Hong Kong’s second against Cambodia from the spot, told the Fifa website that 2030 World Cup qualification was possible if “we keep working hard and raising our levels”. “I really believe in the future of this team,” Camargo added. Still, Orr last week acknowledged that Hong Kong were a “team in transition”, while Losada warned that “we’re in a process of changing some things and, sometimes, the team will look erratic”. The coach accepted, too, that it would take more than victories over Laos, Brunei and Cambodia, three teams whose average world ranking stands at No 187, to win over the more sceptical Hong Kong supporters. Citing the example of Gavin Lee, who masterminded Singapore’s 2027 Asian Cup finals qualification but is now under fire following one win and four defeats from six matches, including a 6-0 capitulation against Malaysia, Losada said: “Our job is always on the line. “I understand the fans are sometimes frustrated. When things don’t work, or the team doesn’t do well, they have the right to express their opinions. “We’ll keep going and keep believing in what we want to do.” As familiar with Losada’s methods as anybody, Sun said: “He’s been in Hong Kong a long time [16 years], he’s played and coached here, and he knows the football environment. He can help us become a better team because he knows what every player needs. “The World Cup is still too far from us. We need to learn from every match, the good parts and our drawbacks, and try to improve every time.”

title: How designers are making adaptable sizing for the Ozempic era
description: Designers including Ester Manas, Issey Miyake and Sacai are pioneering clothes that don’t need replacing with every weight gain or loss.
content: Ozempic continues to make headlines in the fashion world and not just because everyone is still on some form of GLP-1 weight loss medication. Ozempic-proof wardrobes are becoming a necessity as women are looking for clothing they can keep wearing even when their dress size is in a continual state of flux. Sizing has always been a thorny issue, which is why more brands have expanded their ranges to be more inclusive. This, however, doesn’t address the Ozempic effect, where women may move between multiple sizes in a very short time. In an ideal world, buying a complete new wardrobe of different sizes could easily solve the problem, but this isn’t exactly sustainable. As such, women are looking for clothing that not only looks good, but that can adapt to their ever-changing size needs. “It’s been driven by a mix of everything at once,” says Ester Manas, an LVMH Young Designer prize finalist and co-founder of her eponymous clothing line. “There’s the sustainability angle, and there’s the fact that bodies change all the time, for a thousand reasons that have nothing to do with a drug or a diet. And there’s just women being done with the idea that they need a ‘before’ and ‘after’ wardrobe. “The Ozempic conversation is just the latest trigger for something that’s been building for years. The real shift is that women don’t want their clothes dictating how they’re allowed to feel in their own body,” she says. Adaptable or adjustable clothing isn’t exactly a new phenomenon. Japanese brand Issey Miyake solved Ozempic dressing long before it ever became a problem with his Pleats Please line, which offers adaptive sizing achieved by using perfectly engineered pleats made from a stretch polyester jersey. Every item moulds to changing body shapes without losing form or style, making it a godsend for women who don’t fit conventional sizes. Fellow Japanese brand Sacai is also popular thanks to its hybrid styles and deconstructed silhouettes. Details such as integrated belts, drawstrings or wrap structures allow for easy adjustments while relaxed cuts combined with structured panels make fits especially forgiving. Phoebe Philo, a designer lauded for making clothing for “real women”, approaches her eponymous label with this philosophy of built-in transformability. Details such as strategic zippers and adjustable waists on trousers and jackets allow the wearer to change the garment’s silhouette, drape and tightness on a whim. Hidden stretch panels in all of Rick Owens’ leather jackets have made them a cult favourite item with women everywhere. “I think most women have a side of their wardrobe that they instinctively go to when they are up or down a size. The trick is to build that part of your wardrobe deliberately,” says Lupe Puerta, founder of The Floorr, a digital platform for personal shoppers and stylists. “I do believe in intelligent, fluid design: beautiful cuts, fabrics and proportions that still make a woman feel great and that can move with you through a size or two without ever looking like they were designed to do so,” she says. Also providing a stylish solution are a host of independent brands whose collections are built around the premise of offering women clothes that grow with them – literally. British brand The Female Archetype features styles that can be adjusted between multiple sizes thanks to cleverly engineered systems within the garments themselves. Japanese denim jeans come with adjustable waists while a tailored blazer features a panel system on the side seams that can be altered to accommodate six different clothing sizes. Manas’ line offers one-size-fits-all pieces crafted from fluid, stretch-friendly fabrics and silhouettes that move with the body. “Versatility is more about styling, and how many ways you can wear something. Adjustability is structural, it’s built into the pattern itself,” explains Balthazar Delepierre, co-founder and designer of Ester Manas. “We design flexible patterns from scratch, carefully engineered to accommodate as many body shapes and sizes as possible within a single garment. Ruching, elastics, drawstrings, adjustable straps – they’re all tools in service of that same idea: the pattern does the adapting, not the wearer. It means a dress bought today can still make sense on a very different body, or a very different day, months or years later.” Those not wanting to buy new clothes can also invest in accessories and other tools that transform your clothing. Kitdo, the brainchild of fashion stylist Denise Ho, is a stylish and innovative magnetic fashion accessory that can change the look and fit of multiple items like shirts, skirts, and even dresses. “Kitdo is about giving women more freedom with the clothes they already own. Clothes don’t truly feel like yours until you can put your own twist on them. It gives women that ability to take a piece and make it feel personal, rather than being limited by how it was originally designed to be worn,” she says. As women continue to come to terms with their ever-changing bodies, adaptable clothing may start to appear in wardrobes everywhere. “This is the opposite of a passing moment: it’s a correction to decades of an industry that designed for an imagined ‘ideal’ body instead of real, changing ones. We think it’ll become essential simply because it’s more honest design,” says Manas.

title: Backlash forces Trump to pay for TV ads featuring himself
description: US president agrees to use personal and Maga committee funds following criticism over spots ahead of midterms.
content: US President Donald Trump ⁠on Monday said taxpayers will no longer ⁠pay for television ads featuring him shortly before the November congressional elections after widespread criticism of the campaign-style spots. Ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties have criticised the three nationally broadcast ads, which celebrate a “golden age of America”, and called ‌for independent investigations. In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”, but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers and said either he or his Maga PAC would fund the ads. Trump’s Maga Inc political action committee has about US$400 million. A White House ⁠official who spoke on condition of anonymity told Reuters that going forward the ads would be ‌paid for by the PAC. Lawmakers have questioned whether public funds are being used to promote Trump politically, while other critics say the spots may violate long-standing ‌restrictions on government propaganda and political activity. Democratic lawmakers said last month that the ⁠White House transferred US$20 million ⁠in Homeland Security Department funds to air the ads, including one that closely resembles a 2024 Trump campaign ad, and ‌sought independent probes. The ads have run during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming. The New York ‌Times reported that ‌Trump personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV ‌spots, citing sources. One ad features Trump declaring that “America will never be a communist country” while ⁠a chorus repeats the words “love me”. Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising ⁠a “golden age of America”. The ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday called for an independent ‌investigation, calling it a “staggering ‌misuse of public funding and breach of public trust”, after two Democratic congressmen last week urged a probe. FCC Chair Brendan Carr, a Republican named to his position by Trump, last week said the ads were appropriate and rejected a request to investigate them.

title: Antwerp: a well-seasoned melting pot of Rubens, diamonds and Belgium’s only Chinatown
description: Antwerp may be the cradle of Flemish culture but you do not have to wander far from its spectacular railway station to discover other facets of the city: the dazzling diamond district, Belgium’s only Chinatown and a vibrant mix of multicultural influences.
content: Tourists visiting the Belgian city of Antwerp are usually drawn by its reputation as the cradle of Flemish culture. This was home to the Baroque painter Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), whose masterpieces decorate churches across the city, including St Charles Borromeo Church and the soaring Cathedral of Our Lady. Grand squares and marketplaces are lined with flamboyant Renaissance guild-houses and palatial merchants’ mansions dating back to a golden age, at the beginning of the 16th century, when Antwerp’s port was the undisputed capital of world trade. And then there is the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, which showcases an unparalleled collection of Low Countries old masters, from Rubens, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625) and Jan van Eyck (1390-1441) to modern artists such as René Magritte (1898-1967), Rik Wouters (1882-1916) and James Ensor (1860-1949). But Flemish heritage is just one face of this city of 568,000 people. On closer inspection, the city reveals itself to be a colourful melting pot of cultures, cuisines and religions, those of generations of immigrants who have chosen to make their home in Antwerp. Jews began to settle in the city after their expulsion from Spain in the late 15th century, and their descendants transformed it into a global centre of the diamond trade. Belgium’s 19th century empire resulted in immigration from the Maghreb and Central Africa, and after World War II, a wave of settlers from Hong Kong and mainland China arrived, creating what is today the only official Chinatown in the country. The latest additions to the city’s cosmopolitan character have been refugees fleeing conflict in countries such as Afghanistan, Syria, Iraq, Somalia and Ukraine. Just 40 minutes north by train from the Belgian capital, Brussels, Antwerp’s late-19th century Central Station has a lavish dome, a sweeping marble staircase, frescoes and stained-glass windows that periodically win the building awards for “World’s Most Beautiful Station” in travel magazines. Walk out of what locals call their “railway cathedral” and you plunge into a harmonious clash of cultures: on one side, the ornamental pagoda gate at the entrance to Van Wesenbekestraat that marks the beginning of Chinatown; on the other, Pelikaanstraat, home to a tight-knit Orthodox Jewish community and its diamond stores. One-hundred-and-twenty boutiques full of glittering, dazzling diamonds and gold jewellery are crammed into this single square mile, though it is a wonder how they all survive when they seem to be selling the same items. “I came to Antwerp 35 years ago, from Israel, though my family is originally from Georgia,” says Yosef Degan, standing proudly next to a replica of a gold bullion bar in his temptingly named store, Be Very Rich. “I am one of the last authentic goldsmiths here, because apart from dealing diamonds, I specialise in buying old gold, melting it down and creating my own unique jewellery designs.” Although Yiddish is the lingua franca for the hundreds of Jewish dealers, brokers, cutters and jewellers working here, and the kippah skullcap and tzitzit trouser tassels can be seen everywhere, Degan insists that his community remains discreet. I take his recommendation to have lunch nearby, at Hoffy’s, a kosher diner filled with noisy diamond dealers, whose owners, three Hoffman brothers, explain their Hasidic Ashkenazi culture to customers through their unique cuisine: in my case, a slow-cooked cholent of baked beef and vegetables, kugel potato pancakes, veal schnitzel, poached gefilte fish and salt-beef pastrami. Another world awaits through the jewel-toned archway that stands at the entrance of Van Wesenbekestraat, ablaze in radiant reds and brilliant golds and proudly flanked by two sculpted stone lions. Attracted by the city’s port, Chinese sailors and dock workers began settling in Antwerp from the early 20th century. They were followed in the late 1940s by larger numbers of mainly Cantonese-speaking immigrants from Hong Kong (particularly the New Territories) and southern China, who were escaping political turmoil and a lack of jobs, and were drawn by a post-war European revival and what was known as the “chop-suey boom”. As with all Chinatowns, the restaurant business was the obvious line of work for most of these new immigrants, and from the 70s, the closeness to Antwerp’s railway station helped solidify Van Wesenbekestraat and the surrounding area as a genuine community. Recognised as Belgium’s sole official Chinatown in 2001, the neighbourhood’s culinary scene has mushroomed from the early Cantonese restaurants to an eclectic kaleidoscope of Thai, Philippine, Malaysian and Nepalese eateries. A dozen bustling Asian supermarkets rub shoulders with two martial-arts schools, traditional-medicine establishments, a lion-dance school and the Fo Guang Shan Belgique Temple, located not in an ornate pagoda but in a simple Flemish house on a terraced row, painted a distinctive yellow, with a wrought-iron-framed window in the front door. Much of the fare on offer in Chinatown is cheap and cheerful street food – hand-pulled noodles, char siu pork, wonton soup, even the classic sweet and sour chicken – but two addresses stand out, both just off the main drag of Van Wesenbekestraat. Fong Mei opened more than 30 years ago and its classic Cantonese cuisine – more than 50 handmade varieties of dim sum alongside steamed fish with ginger and coriander, lacquered roast duck, beef-tripe soup and duck tongue – has been recognised by Belgium’s Michelin Guide. The decor is delightfully kitsch, with red lanterns, giant photos of Hong Kong, even a poster depicting a dragon boat powering through a village scene and celebrating Chinese-Belgian friendship. The proprietor at the hole-in-the-wall Ni Shifu Sichuan Cuisine & Fondue, “Master Ni”, as the chef-owner describes himself, came to Antwerp 25 years ago, from Chengdu, and still does not speak a word of Flemish or English, but he certainly cooks up a storm in his tiny kitchen, dressed in shorts and a T-shirt, bent over his smoky wok. His dan dan noodles are wickedly spicy, the best I have eaten outside Asia, with the small dining room packed with a mix of Flemish locals, Antwerp Chinese and savvy visiting foodies. Ni Shifu has been singled out for Michelin praise for its authentic Sichuan cuisine and booking in advance is recommended. Antwerp’s crucial bridge to the world, the docks – alongside the Scheldt river – are still among the busiest in Europe, but much of the surrounding Het Eilandje neighbourhood has been redeveloped. Its cutting-edge architecture includes the abstract pile of towering red-sandstone blocks that is the MAS maritime, history and cultural museum and Zaha Hadid’s metallic Port House, which resembles the shimmering prow of a floating ship. Less conspicuous is the old red-brick warehouse that houses the Red Star Line Museum, a memorial to the millions of emigrants who passed through Antwerp on their way to a new life in North America. This intensely personal collection graphically illustrates the stories of some of the two million people who transited through Antwerp between 1873 and 1924, often after a long, tortuous journey from Central or Eastern Europe. Here, they endured medical examinations, disinfection and exhaustive immigration checks before finally being allowed to board a Red Star Line ship bound, in most cases, for New York. Most were fleeing poverty and persecution, little different from today’s migrants, and the anonymous tales are just as moving as those of the more famous émigrés who set sail on the Red Star Line: theoretical physicist Albert Einstein, composer Irving Berlin and future Israeli prime minister Golda Meir. Just around the corner, in the Montevideo area – Antwerp’s quays are named after the exotic ports that produce was exported to and imported from – celebrity chef Nick Bril has just relocated his two-Michelin-star restaurant, The Jane, into a minimalist dining room, a striking departure from its original location, in a deconsecrated chapel downtown. “Choosing Het Eilandje felt like a very logical step,” explains Bril, who has appeared on television in Belgian reality show Special Forces: Who Dares Wins, has served as a judge on Celebrity MasterChef Vlaanderen and is a renowned DJ. “It is an area where Antwerp’s history and future come together in a very natural way. The city has always drawn its strength from its openness to the world, and though our cuisine is firmly rooted in Belgium and in the products that surround us, it has always been influenced by experiences beyond our own borders.” Gert de Mangeleer is present for every service in his kitchen at the two-Michelin-star Hertog Jan at Botanic, overseeing a tasting menu that is his own interpretation of a Japanese omakase experience. “When I decided to open my restaurant in Antwerp, it was the perfect inspiration for my cuisine: this cosmopolitan harbour city that is an entrepôt for spices and exotic produce from around the globe,” says de Mangeleer, who gained prominence as part of the Flanders Kitchen Rebels campaign, a movement of young, talented chefs who brought a modern, rebellious attitude to traditional Belgian gastronomy. His diners are tempted with dishes such as Japanese binchotan-grilled Wagyu beef served with locally smoked eel sauce, crispy veal sweetbreads, steamed dumplings of spinach dim sum and a sauce of Zeeland oysters. One of Belgium’s two three-Michelin-star restaurants, Zilte, stands in the old docks area of Antwerp, but a favourite haunt of local chefs and sommeliers – evidenced by the fact that it’s open on Mondays, a traditional day off for restaurant staff – is the casual bistro Invincible. Here, animatedly supervising a brigade of cooks, Kenny Burssens interprets traditional Flemish cuisine, sautéing crunchy Brussels sprouts with bone marrow, and pairing tiny girolle mushrooms with tender chunks of milky cows’ udder, or line-caught cod with the salty sea-vegetable salicorne. The wine list includes vintages from little-known Belgian vineyards. A little different is a meal at Samenloop, a restaurant that occupies the ground floor and cobbled courtyard of the Maagdenhuis, which was opened in 1552 as an orphanage for girls and also houses a museum and a chapel. The recently opened Samenloop is a social project for refugees: its waiters from Afghanistan and Palestine, and kitchen staff from Eritrea, the Maldives and Colombia are offered hospitality training so they can better integrate into society. One of a changing cast of celebrated chefs (for two months from November, it will be Karen Shu, an American-Filipino chef with a restaurant near Antwerp who is known for vegan and plant-based cuisine) collaborates by selecting recipes from the homelands of the refugees and adapting them into a tasting menu: crispy Nepalese pani puri surprisingly stuffed with chopped local asparagus; traditional Syrian falafel with fresh green peas; a light Ukrainian strawberry sernik cheesecake. Another string to Antwerp’s bow is its reputation as a cutting-edge capital of European fashion. The Fashion Museum, known as MoMu, is a hotbed of creation, its studios and ateliers training the next generation of designers. The city broke onto the international fashion scene in the 80s, with the rise of the Antwerp Six: revolutionary stylists who all graduated from the city’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts and colonised the pages of Vogue, Elle and Harper’s Bazaar. “[Antwerp] is the perfect place to work,” one of the six, designer Walter Van Beirendonck, told Surface Magazine in 2016. “It’s not expensive, it’s quiet and it’s close to Paris, Milan and London. The art is great, the food is good, you can live well. There’s a real sense of possibility here.” The visionary designs and eye-catching fashion shows of the likes of Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester and Van Beirendonck can now be seen at the MoMu exhibition “Antwerp Six”, which runs until January 17, 2027. Another innovative temporary show can be found at the monumental Royal Museum of Fine Arts, with its colonnaded facade, neoclassical architecture, marble staircase and huge exhibition rooms. “KMSKA x Young Fashion Designers” (until November 8) gives free rein to 10 young graduates from the Antwerp Fashion Academy to create fashion sculptures influenced by pieces in the museum’s collection, inspiration having come from the dramatic flowing robes with cascading folds of fabric often depicted by Rubens and the revolutionary slashed canvases of Lucio Fontana (1899-1968). A fitting way to end an exploration of eclectic, multi-ethnic Antwerp is to head for the Theaterplein square on a Saturday, the venue for the Exotic Market. As Chinese immigrants were arriving after the end of World War II, migrants from countries such as Spain, Greece, Turkey and Morocco settled here, too, bringing the spices and ingredients of their native cuisines. They started selling their wares at the Theaterplein every Saturday, at what was first termed the Foreigners’ Market. Teeming with locals and tourists from 8am to 4pm, this is more a multicultural, all-day party than a commercial centre, where the cava flows and food trucks serve customers sitting on temporary terraces a kaleidoscope of global cuisine: cheesy Turkish börek; plump Tibetan momo dumplings; Pakistani palak paneer; Peruvian panini; North African couscous and tagines; Vietnamese glass noodles. And to remind you that this is still Antwerp, there are also Flemish specialities, such as matjes (herrings), local oysters and bowls of karakol, a tasty soup of whelks and celery.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong has scope to build on record Asian Games medal haul
description: The city’s total of gold medals has increased but maintaining the high-performance momentum will be challenging in some sports.
content: Hong Kong athletes’ record medal haul from the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, could hardly have been better timed. It comes soon after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu launched the city’s first five-year plan, which enshrines sport as a pillar of the city’s economic and social development until 2030. Our athletes’ success boosts the sport segment of the plan almost from the beginning. Key initiatives include big cumulative increases in sport funding and in the number of full-time elite athletes trained at the Hong Kong Sports Institute over the next five years. The city’s total of 54 medals was just one more than in the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou in 2023. But it includes 11 gold medals – three more than in the previous games, and 19 silver, also three more, while 24 bronze medals fell short of the 29 awarded in 2023. Competitors won gold across multiple disciplines including swimming, wushu, rowing, squash, sailing, tennis, windsurfing and rugby sevens. Some gold-medal winners are already familiar to sports fans, like multiple Olympic medal-winning swimmer Siobhan Haughey, tennis player Coleman Wong Chak-lam and the rugby sevens players. Wong, a relative newcomer on the international scene, is the first Hongkonger to secure entry to the Olympic tennis tournament. Sailing and windsurfing sparked optimism about the next generation, with water sports claiming four golds. Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet, boys’ and girls’ windsurfing champions, are a case in point. Hong Kong delegation chief Wong Po-kee said the successes demonstrated “the continued emergence of sporting talent in Hong Kong”. He echoed a social media post by the chief executive, who hailed the example set by those athletes who had shown everyone “that as long as you work hard and have dreams, you can break through your limits and achieve great results”. Lee thanked the squad for “showing us that Hong Kong can cultivate so many outstanding athletes who can compete and win against top Asian athletes on the international stage”. Lee’s social media post also referred to the “billions of dollars invested annually” to train the city’s elite athletes, adding that he was pleased “to see that the government’s investment is beginning to bear fruit”. But maintaining the high-performance momentum will be challenging. The reality remains that this is Haughey’s last Asian Games, with no one at the top level ready to fill her shoes. The same goes for Olympic fencing gold medallist Cheung Ka-long, who is in the twilight of his career, and retired Olympic fencing gold medallist Vivian Kong Man-wai. There is an argument that Hong Kong is enjoying a golden age of generationally talented athletes and that young athletes show promise. For example, teenage swimmers Yeung Hoi-ching and Gilaine Ma, who reached the finals of their events, gave hope for the next games in Doha. But there are questions about the way some sports are trying to develop their next star. Hong Kong has again been found wanting in track and field. Continued failure may require some form of intervention. Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui has pointed to the funding approach taken with tennis. Tennis was allowed to retain its Tier A elite funding designation as a high-performance sport at the Hong Kong Sports Institute because of evidence that long-term investment would ultimately pay off. Importantly, the sport development plan is not confined to the elites but involves the whole community. It includes accreditation, hosting and funding of M-mark mega-sport-related events for competitions, such as the Hong Kong marathon and Hong Kong Sevens, to boost tourism and drive the local event economy. The Hong Kong Jockey Club has awarded HK$37.5 million in cash incentives to the city’s medallists. More support from non-government channels would be welcome. China topped the gold-medal table for a record 12th straight Asian Games, securing 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals – its best-ever haul at an overseas Asian Games. The next Asian Games, at Doha, in 2030 or 2031, will serve as a benchmark of Hong Kong’s sporting progress under the five-year plan. Meanwhile, it is time for both teams to get better prepared for the Los Angeles Olympics.

title: What does the Busan International Film Festival’s new pathway to the Oscars mean for Asia?
description: Festival director Jung Han-seok discusses how Busan is now a direct track to eligibility for the Oscar for best international feature film.
content: The Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) opens its 31st edition today with a renewed sense of relevance and prestige as it celebrates its newly minted status as an A-list festival accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF). This globally recognised industry benchmark “gives us clear and tangible external validation”, says Busan festival director Jung Han-seok in an email interview with the South China Morning Post. “BIFF’s international standing and value as a film festival have long been widely recognised … I hope this recognition will further strengthen the confidence that international film professionals and filmmakers have in BIFF.” Even more significantly, as of this year, BIFF will be one of only six major festivals – and the only one from Asia – to provide a pathway of eligibility for the Academy Award for best international feature film. A new route to the Oscars Unlike in every other category at the Oscars, films are not deemed eligible for the best international feature film award by screening publicly in a major US metropolitan area for at least one week during the calendar year. Instead, each country/region submits one film to officially represent it. Hong Kong’s submission this year is Juno Mak Chun-lung’s Sons of the Neon Night. Taiwan has submitted Chen Yu-hsun’s A Foggy Tale. Meanwhile, South Korea’s entry, Venice Silver Lion winner Possible Love from director Lee Chang-dong, is considered by many to be a strong favourite. At the time of writing, mainland China has yet to announce its submission. Previously, this meant that no other film from these countries and regions was eligible for consideration for that award. This year’s amendment changes all that: whichever film wins the Busan Award for best film at this year’s festival is automatically eligible for consideration for the Academy Award for best international feature film, regardless of the country it hails from or the official selection submitted by that country. “I see this as another meaningful confirmation of BIFF’s international standing,” Jung says. “More importantly, I believe it gives filmmakers a very concrete incentive to submit to, and be selected for, our competition. We have already seen a noticeably more proactive and positive response to BIFF’s competition from key industry figures across Asia.” The other festivals providing this new pathway to the Oscars include Berlin, Cannes, Venice, Toronto and Sundance. Industry commentators are already speculating on how these new inroads might help films covering politically sensitive topics, or filmmakers who lack support from their home nations. Jung says he has seen such possibilities raised in a number of articles, but it is still too early to draw any firm conclusions. He remains excited, however, that BIFF might become an even more crucial destination for filmmakers with competitive ambitions. “With this new pathway, some filmmakers may now be able to envision a longer-term strategy that begins with winning the Busan Award and continues into an Oscar campaign. That can clearly provide meaningful motivation in terms of both promoting their films and increasing their international visibility and value.” Jung reveals that he met with members of the Academy leadership in Cannes earlier this year after the announcement was made, and that key representatives are expected to attend the Busan festival. “Our ultimate goal is not simply to identify films for the Academy Awards,” he says. “I do not think this will fundamentally change our programming strategy. Programming BIFF’s competition is a highly complex process that requires us to consider many different factors.” Beyond the Academy Awards While this new status may well draw more attention to a festival that is already regarded as the Cannes of Asia, there is plenty more on offer. “This was not something we deliberately set out to design, but as the festival came together, a number of important events naturally emerged that celebrate the achievements of major women in cinema,” Jung says. “Michelle Yeoh will receive the Asian Filmmaker of the Year Award, while Ann Hui [On-wah] will receive the Camellia Award, which honours women in film.” The director goes on to highlight a programme featuring luminaries such as Isabelle Huppert, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Charlotte Gainsbourg and Judith Godreche, all attending the festival to meet with audiences. “I think that, in itself, is a sign that the festival is moving in the right direction,” Jung says. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs until October 15. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: How a Hong Kong property investor still made US$30 million – after a 40% price cut
description: Low-profile veteran investor slashes price of Tsim Sha Tsui retail portfolio, but still secures a 12-fold return after four decades.
content: Amid concerns over rising interest rates and a weak retail property market, a long-time investor has sold a portfolio of prime street shops in Tsim Sha Tsui – held for more than four decades – and locked in a profit of nearly HK$237 million (US$30.2 million) despite accepting a deal more than 40 per cent below his original asking price. The portfolio of retail shops in Cheung Lee Commercial Building and the podium of Wing Lee Building, both on Kimberley Road, changed hands for HK$256.8 million, according to Land Registry data. The seller, low-profile investor Ng Kan-hoi, had previously listed the assets for a combined HK$430 million before slashing the price by 40 per cent. Ng acquired the properties for a combined HK$19.84 million between 1979 and 1987, during the tense Sino-British negotiations over Hong Kong’s return to mainland Chinese rule and a stock market slump that pushed property prices to depressed levels. After holding the assets for more than 40 years, he realised a gain that was almost 12 times his original investment. When the market was booming, you might not have been able to buy these retail shops even for HK$600 million or HK$700 million Edwin Lee, Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management Edwin Lee, founder and CEO of Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management, said the transaction involved a large portfolio with a substantial total value, but the price per square foot was relatively low because it was difficult to find a buyer for the entire package. “When the market was booming, you might not have been able to buy these retail shops even for HK$600 million or HK$700 million,” Lee added. The properties included the basement and ground, first and second floors of the Cheung Lee Commercial Building at 25 Kimberley Road, with a total gross floor area of about 21,871 square feet. The first and second floors have been leased since May last year to century-old restaurant Lin Heung Tea House for about HK$250,000 a month, equivalent to roughly HK$23 per square foot. The ground-floor tenant is cha chaan teng operator Lok Tin Cafe, while the basement is leased to mainland Chinese karaoke chain Mei KTV. Those assets were ultimately sold for HK$202.8 million, or about HK$9,273 per square foot. Additionally, Shops 6-10 on the ground floor of Wing Lee Building at 27-31C Kimberley Road, with a total gross floor area of about 2,731 square feet, sold for HK$54 million, reflecting a price of about HK$19,773 per square foot. They are currently leased to a noodles restaurant. According to Chinese media reports, Ng had long owned more than a dozen commercial properties in Tsim Sha Tsui, including assets on Cameron Road and at Haiphong Mansion. The sale marks the second major disposal by Ng in recent months. In June, he sold the entire ninth floor of Far East Finance Centre in Admiralty for about HK$165 million, according to Land Registry data. After holding the property for 18 years and reducing the asking price by as much as 38 per cent, he made a profit of only about HK$11.2 million or roughly 7 per cent.

title: US seeks to revoke citizenship of 2 China-born men convicted in Beijing-linked cases
description: Former US Navy sailor Jinchao Wei and Florida resident Ping Li are among 40 people named in DOJ announcement.
content: The US Justice Department (DOJ) is seeking to revoke the citizenship of a former Navy sailor convicted of spying for China and a Florida man convicted of conspiring to act as an agent of Beijing, it announced on Monday. Jinchao Wei and Ping Li are among 40 people facing denaturalisation actions in what the department described as the largest batch of such filings under the Trump administration. The civil proceedings remain pending, with no determination of liability, the DOJ said. The case against Wei was filed on September 30 in the Southern District of California, while the case against Li was filed on October 1 in the Middle District of Florida. Wei was convicted of espionage and export offences in August 2025 and sentenced in January to 200 months in prison, or 16 years and eight months. But the same jury acquitted him of naturalisation fraud, according to the DOJ’s announcement of his sentence. While serving aboard the amphibious assault ship USS Essex, Wei passed photographs, technical manuals and other sensitive naval information to a Chinese intelligence officer in exchange for more than US$12,000, according to evidence presented at trial. DOJ alleges that Wei concealed criminal conduct when he became a citizen in May 2022 through military service. It also cites his discharge under other-than-honourable conditions before completing five years of honourable service. Li was sentenced to four years in prison in November 2024 for conspiring to act as an agent of China without notifying the US attorney general. According to his plea agreement and court filings summarised by prosecutors, Li admitted working at the direction of China’s Ministry of State Security from at least 2012. He supplied information about Chinese dissidents, pro-democracy advocates and Falun Gong practitioners, as well as information from his employers in telecommunications and information technology. DOJ argues that Li’s conduct shows he did not meet constitutional allegiance requirements at the time of naturalisation. The announcement came a day after the FBI arrested Zhang Wanying, a Chinese-born US citizen, at Los Angeles International Airport on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of Beijing. Authorities allege that she conducted surveillance in Seattle on a close relative of a Taiwanese government official. The allegations against Zhang have not been proven, and the DOJ’s denaturalisation announcement did not include her. US law permits courts to revoke naturalisation obtained illegally or through concealment of material facts or deliberate misrepresentation. Filing a civil complaint does not, by itself, revoke citizenship.

title: US accuses mainland China of targeting Taiwan leader’s family in surveillance case
description: FBI says US citizen Zhang Wanying filmed William Lai Ching-te’s son’s home and vehicles in Seattle before trying to fly to Shanghai.
content: The United States has accused mainland China of hiring an American citizen of Chinese origin to surveil the family of Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te, days after President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington. The Federal Bureau of Investigation on Sunday arrested 34-year-old Zhang Wanying at Los Angeles International Airport, alleging that she attempted to flee the country and charged her with acting as an unregistered agent for the Chinese government. The FBI accused her of surveilling the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family in Seattle last year, filming their home and vehicles and sharing the footage with handlers in China. “The Chinese government allegedly sent an operative to surveil the family of Taiwan’s President ON AMERICAN SOIL – photos, video, license plates – then she tried to hop a flight back to Shanghai. Wrong move,” FBI Director Kash Patel wrote on social media. Zhang appeared in the US District Court in Los Angeles on Monday for an initial hearing, with a second hearing scheduled for Wednesday to determine whether she will be released on bail or remain in custody. She has not been formally indicted yet.
