On Tuesday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that he was “not familiar” with the situation, but “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative”. In an affidavit filed with the US District Court in Orange County, the FBI did not identify the surveillance target, referring to him only as “a close relative of a Taiwanese government official”. The FBI later identified him on social media as Taiwanese leader Lai’s son, whose name is Ting-Yu Lai. It alleged that Zhang, a resident of Irvine, California, travelled to Seattle in September last year with another person to conduct surveillance. “She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection. She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offence,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, said on social media. Lai’s office condemned what it called “barbaric acts” and said that “such behaviour should not be tolerated in the civilised world”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. According to court documents, Zhang is facing charges under 18 USC section 951, a federal criminal law that forbids acting inside the United States as an undisclosed agent of a foreign government without giving prior notification to the US attorney general. A violation is a felony and usually carries a maximum penalty of up to 10 years in prison, a fine, or both. A RedNote account believed to belong to Zhang and identified by the South China Morning Post appears to place her in Seattle in early September 2025, matching the timeline in the federal complaint. The account, named “美美哒 Heather” – the complaint gives “Heather” as Zhang’s alias – posted on September 2, 2025, with a US location tag. The Chinese-language post reads: “Seattle airport must be the least efficient international airport in the US? Security line took an hour.” The complaint does not cite the post. According to the federal criminal complaint and affidavit, Zhang stayed in touch for years with a former classmate in Beijing whom the FBI calls “PRC Official 1”. The US authorities believe that when Zhang met Official 1 in China in January 2025, Official 1 directed her to obtain information about an Irvine address previously associated with a Taiwanese elected official. “Based on my training and experience and conversations with others involved in the case, it is likely that PRC Official 1 tasked ZHANG, while ZHANG was visiting China, to obtain information about this address,” FBI agent Kevin Holt wrote in the affidavit. “I know that China’s Intelligence Services often tasks individuals visiting China while they are in China in order to evade US government scrutiny.” In June 2025, Official 1 introduced Zhang to another purported Chinese government official, whom the FBI calls “PRC Official 2.” Official 2 later met Zhang in China, according to the complaint. In a July 7 WeChat exchange, Official 2 referred to “our thing last time” and said he had intended to provide Zhang with “some assurance”. On September 1, 2025, while outside the Seattle home, Zhang messaged Official 2, “Saw him. Young male,” and said she was video-recording, according to the document. She sent two licence plate numbers and a video of the house. A week later, she asked her travel companion to AirDrop her the Seattle pictures rather than send them over WeChat or text. On September 11, Official 2 asked Zhang for pictures of the house. Zhang told him that her friend had deleted the pictures. No message in the complaint explicitly tells Zhang to surveil the house. The FBI affiant interprets Official 2’s references to “our thing” and “assurance” as referring back to their June 2025 discussion of a “US house”. Dennis Wilder, a former senior US intelligence official and a China expert, expects that the arrest will have limited influence on the ongoing US-China talks, as the two leaders are scheduled to meet twice more this year. “This will have minimal impact on Sino-US relations,” he posted on X. “Spy games are an accepted superpower competition and have been forever.” Who is Zhang Wanying? According to a LinkedIn profile under her name, Zhang has been CEO of Alphabet Investment Management since 2017. She has also worked on the Douglas Elliman sales team for Metropolis, a luxury residential development by Greenland, a Chinese company and a Fortune Global 500 firm. A representative from Douglas Elliman confirmed her employment but said she had left the company nearly a decade ago. “I am the only native Chinese speaking in the team,” Zhang wrote on LinkedIn, where she described herself as “detail oriented, action oriented” with “excellent negotiation and relationship management” skills. She earned a bachelor’s degree in public administration from the University of International Relations in Beijing in 2014 and a master’s degree in public administration from the University of Southern California in 2016, with a concentration in real estate.

title: Trump says US moved bombers from UK airbase after threats
description: Comments contradict Secretary of State Marco Rubio following sudden departure of B-1 aircraft from RAF Fairford.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran ⁠had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase. The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week, five British men were arrested near the base – which Iran’s Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target – on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. “We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “So we had a threat and if we’re going to be ‌threatened, we just move them and that sort of alleviates that. And we actually know the people that made the threat.” When asked if they were linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran”. Earlier on Monday, Vice-President J.D. Vance said the US moved the bombers out of an abundance of caution. “We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States [and others], so we are being extremely cautious, and that’s all I’d say about that,” Vance told reporters. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot. He said the Pentagon is “constantly reallocating resources where they need to be”. A Nato military source had said on Monday: “It is still believed ⁠that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK”. While much about the incident remains unexplained, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any plot was probably backed by Iran. Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any ‌plot are baseless, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on social media: “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree”. Rubio said on Monday the US had confidence in the security of all its bases. Fairford, located 145km (90 miles) west of London, is one of the most ‌important European bases for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B-1 aircraft. It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the ⁠Middle East, although its bombers are not stationed there permanently. During ⁠the current conflict, the US has had permission to use Fairford only to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, or so-called defensive strikes. London had refused permission for the US to use British bases for offensive strikes on Iran. That approach has strained ties between the ‌US and Britain, typically one of Washington’s closest allies. A Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday that all US bombers that had been deployed to Fairford had headed to their home stations in the US. The Pentagon said the US bomber force remained ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities “anywhere, anytime”. The New York Times, citing two US ‌officials, said ‌the US had rushed over the weekend to move the bombers after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. It said some of the planes had left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled. A US official declined to comment. ‌The British government also declined to comment, although a spokesman for Burnham said the base was safe. Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the short term reduce US capacity “to quickly surge ⁠sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat”. But he noted that the use of Fairford was already limited given London’s stipulation on defensive strikes. The aircraft could now potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf, to reduce ⁠the need for more air-to-air refuelling to cover the additional distance, but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, he added. In the early hours of September 27, five British men in their 20s were arrested after being seen running into fields from three white vans parked near the base. Police said no explosive devices were found but a quantity of petrol was present. The ‌men have since been released on bail. A sixth man, ‌a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail. Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had planned “big damage” and that it might have been connected to Iran. Trump later said he would not have released the suspects on bail. A senior Nato military official said the removal of the bombers would have no impact on the alliance: “Nato’s defensive agility towards any aggression remains unchanged and unmatched thanks to the unity, strength and combined capabilities of 32 nations”. The Wall Street Journal first reported the removal of the US bombers.

title: My Take | Hong Kong must scrap housing plan and preserve golf course
description: Court ruling shows building housing on the Old Course makes no sense as city strives to become a leading host of international sporting events.
content: The hotly contested court battle over government plans to build 12,000 public flats on Hong Kong’s oldest golf course has played its final round. The government decided not to appeal against a ruling that held its approval of an environmental impact assessment (EIA) report on the project to be unlawful. This is better than pursuing a further attempt to persuade the courts to uphold a fatally flawed process. Now, a broader review of the plans can be undertaken in light of the Court of Appeal’s judgment in favour of the Hong Kong Golf Club. There are many lessons to be learned from the affair. The Court of First Instance found in 2024 that the process by which the EIA report was prepared and approved was littered with errors and breaches of the law. Almost all of those findings were endorsed by the Court of Appeal. The case has its roots in the previous administration’s bid to ease the city’s housing crisis with a desperate search for land on which to build public estates. It announced in 2019 that 32 hectares of the golf course would be developed. This was a popular move at the time. The issue pitched the community’s need for affordable housing against the exclusive golf club with its privileged members. However, of all the places to build a housing estate, this was an unlikely one. The Fanling golf course, as the court said, is regarded as one of the “finest and most scenic” in Asia. It is the only venue in Hong Kong capable of staging elite international tournaments. The area earmarked for development covers eight holes of the Old Course, which dates back to 1911. It is the oldest in China and a valuable remnant of the “golden age” of golf in the early 20th century. The development would have led to its destruction. The cultural significance and heritage value of the site should have been obvious, but the impact of the housing plan on this “architectural gem” was not properly evaluated. There was also a lamentable failure to adequately assess the potential for the development to negatively affect the site’s ecology, which includes endangered species. The court found the public consultation process to be inadequate. Additional information on important areas of the assessment was provided only after the consultation. There was also a failure by the government to fairly consider detailed submissions made by the club on the late additions. Conditions attached to the approval of the EIA report effectively required the plan to be redesigned and rethought, which could have made it “quite a different creature” to the one the public was consulted on, according to the court. One of the most striking parts of the judgment dealt with areas in which the EIA report did not comply, as required by law, with the technical memorandum and study brief. This revealed alarming failures to sufficiently consider the possible impact of the project on flora and fauna, notably trees, moths and bats. The fate of the critically endangered Chinese Swamp Cypress tree is a glaring example. The court said such trees on the site make up 15 per cent of the global population and 29 of them are estimated to be more than 100 years old. The EIA process failed to properly assess the potential “devastating and irreversible” impact of the development on the trees, which are highly sensitive to changes in their environment. The judgment highlights the need for careful, comprehensive and fair consideration of the effect of even relatively small developments on the environment. The law was amended in 2023 so that EIA reports are only required for areas exceeding 50 hectares, rather than the previous 20. As Hong Kong seeks to push ahead with ambitious development plans, it must not overlook the need to strike the right balance and protect the environment. Last week, the government stressed that solving the housing problem is top of its agenda. Progress has been made in recent years, and the search for sites is not as frantic as in the past. The huge Northern Metropolis development is expected to feature 150,000 homes. The golf course is within the boundaries of that project and is intended to provide a “green corridor” at its heart. Building housing on the Old Course makes no sense, especially as Hong Kong strives to become a leading host of international sporting events. The housing plan is back at the first tee. The master stroke would be to now abandon it and allow the iconic golf course to be preserved.

title: Mainland Chinese favour diplomacy to achieve Taiwan reunification with caveats: survey
description: China Pulse study also reveals faith in the US remains low, although still support for engaging with Washington on trade and security issues.
content: Mainland Chinese prefer coercion over military force to settle the “reunification question” with Taiwan, and their opinion of the US remains low, although they favour engaging with Washington on trade and security. These are the results from the latest survey of mainland citizens, conducted between April 16 and June 26. This straddled the first summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing but came before the second one in Washington last month. “The Chinese public attitude towards Taiwan fits very well with domestic messaging on Taiwan in China,” said Nick Zeller, lead researcher with The Carter Centre, which conducted the biannual China Pulse survey with Emory University. “Peaceful cross-strait relations are far and away the preferred option. But if de jure independence were declared, if Taipei says, ‘We are now formally governing ourselves,’ you are going to see a military response.” Mainland favorability towards Taiwan was the highest of any other economy at 61 out of 100. The survey of 2,500 people found opinions split on unification by force. Preferred responses if Taiwan declared independence included attacking Quemoy and Matsu islands at 77 per cent; conducting a naval blockade at 59 per cent; and economic sanctions at 56 per cent. Those who favoured non-coercive approaches preferred greater cultural exchanges and trade promotion at around 82 per cent, and eased work and residency policies at some 72 per cent. Notably, respondents who opposed the use of force rose significantly after Trump visited Beijing, to 40 per cent from 32 per cent. This may have reflected the transactional president’s decision to delay a US$14 billion arms sales package to Taipei and his comments on the plane home and in a Fox News interview that weapons sales were a “very good negotiating chip for us, frankly”. On their view of the US, mainland public sentiment remains low, falling slightly to 32 out of 100 since the last survey six months ago. Nearly three-quarters viewed the US as a national security threat, led by concern over Taiwan and trade, with younger and better-educated Chinese the most dovish after the May summit. Zeller said he expected the same trend to continue when results are polled from last month’s summit in Washington and the coming Xi-Trump meetings at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen and the G20 in Miami. “The US and China are both going to be locked in a sort of frenemy convergence,” he added, “but still looking for opportunities for cooperation”. While faith in education exchanges has fallen sharply, there were calls for ongoing engagement involving national security, trade and, less so, science and global security. “These findings should be read as cause for cautious optimism for those seeking more stable US-China relations,” the survey said, but added: “The Chinese public continues to express low favourability towards the United States.” Added Zeller: “My master key for understanding how they see the US is: we don’t like you, but we’re as strong as you, so we’ll work with you.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. Turning to the rest of the world, Chinese belief in their country’s superiority rose from an already “staggering” 89 per cent to 95 per cent after the May summit. The Chinese view of most countries other than the US fell after the summit, led by Singapore, Iran and Russia, although Russia was among those viewed most favourably with a rating above 50 indicating a net positive view. “Accompanying this increased nationalist belief in China’s superiority, Chinese favourability towards most other countries in this survey decreased in the spring and summer of 2026,” the survey said.

title: Jeffrey Archer, British novelist and former politician, dies at 86
description: Author who sold over 300 million books leaves a legacy shaped by high-office drama, prison, and literary success.
content: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Monday. Archer sold over 300 million copies worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers like ‌his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less and 1979’s Kane & Abel. His final novel, Adam and Eve, was due to be published on Tuesday. Kate Elton, HarperCollins’ UK CEO and Archer’s editor, said in a statement: “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers – and a true friend”. Archer was also a prominent Conservative politician, who briefly served as a lawmaker before becoming ⁠a senior party official under then-Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s. But he was as well-known for his very ‌public downfall. In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 (US$660,450) in damages. The case returned to the ‌public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London’s first elected mayor in ⁠1999. A former friend ⁠accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. ‌He served two years, during which time he wrote A Prison Diary. The trial of Archer’s libel case, which was ‌heard ‌in front of a jury, became notorious for the judge’s summing up of evidence given by Archer’s wife Mary. “Remember ‌Mary Archer in the witness box,” the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. “Your vision of her will probably never ⁠disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?” And, of Archer, ⁠he added: “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?” Archer’s reputation as one of the most colourful figures in British public life did no harm to his literary ‌career. His books were sold in ‌119 countries, HarperCollins said. He spent several years on The New York Times bestseller lists. He was due to speak about his final novel this weekend at the Cheltenham Literature Festival and had recently appeared on radio shows to promote the book. HarperCollins said he had died suddenly and peacefully, “between writing sessions”.

title: Exclusive | Beijing wanted more from Xi’s state visit to Washington
description: Sources say US knocked back proposals such as engagement with the business community and public, talks on AI and security issues.
content: Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington in September was steeped in pageantry. The Chinese president received two 21-gun salutes in three days, watched a flyover by the powerful B-2 stealth bomber, and viewed the founding documents of American democracy at the National Archives. US President Donald Trump called his summit with Xi a “great meeting” and rated it a “12 out of 10”. Xi was also positive, saying “everything is done to the highest order of perfection, and there is thought in every little detail”. But according to people with knowledge of the matter, Beijing had wanted more from the trip. The sources told the South China Morning Post that Beijing had pushed for a more ambitious programme for Xi’s first state visit to the United States in more than a decade. Beijing suggested Xi could engage with the American business community and public, pushed to raise dozens of diplomatic and security issues with Trump, and proposed talks on artificial intelligence between Chinese and American executives, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to media. But none of those pitches made it to the itinerary of what ended up being a tightly choreographed visit – albeit one that was hailed by both sides as historic and productive. In the lead-up to the trip, Chinese officials are said to have contacted the embassies of other nations in Washington to compare notes and plan what one source called a “grand visit” for Xi. The source said officials were trying to find out what sort of reception the Trump administration might give Xi, and the activities that could be offered for his itinerary. A separate source said Beijing wanted to know what the Americans had done for other visiting foreign dignitaries, hoping to “take the best of all the different programme options”. People familiar with the matter also told the SCMP that Chinese officials had floated the idea of Xi holding a dialogue with US business leaders or speaking to students at a top university in Washington or New York. They said the Trump administration had knocked back those suggestions, citing the need for the visit to be reciprocal and mirror Trump’s May trip to Beijing. US officials were also said to be wary of giving Xi a platform to amplify his views. In 2015 – the last time Xi made a state visit to the US – he had extensive engagements with American business leaders. During that week-long trip that took him from Seattle to New York and Washington, Xi visited Microsoft’s headquarters in Redmond and toured Boeing’s factory in Everett. Xi also visited Lincoln High School in Tacoma on that trip, where he engaged with teachers and students and delivered a speech touching on building a better future for US-China relations, according to a Chinese readout of the school visit. The eventual itinerary for Xi this time was largely similar to Trump’s visit to Beijing, where he was welcomed with a state banquet at the Great Hall of the People, served tea at the Zhongnanhai compound – where China’s top leaders live and work – and taken on a stroll with Xi through the Temple of Heaven. In Washington, Xi was welcomed with a state dinner in the White House’s East Room, served morning tea in the Red Room, and he also visited the National Archives with Trump. One striking difference was that, while no Chinese executives accompanied Xi to Washington in September, American business leaders – including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk – travelled with Trump to Beijing in May and attended a state banquet at the Great Hall of the People. American business executives also attended the state dinner Trump hosted for Xi at the White House but the extent of their engagement with the Chinese leader remains unclear. The sources also said there were initial discussions to bring together executives from top Chinese and American tech firms to discuss artificial intelligence, in a governmental effort to boost cooperation on AI. But that suggestion did not materialise, with the US citing national security concerns. China and the US did agree, however, to establish an AI dialogue to “exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI” and to set up a communication channel for AI incidents, according to readouts from the two sides. As Xi’s visit neared, Chinese officials grew anxious that the summit’s agenda had narrowed almost entirely to trade, leaving little room for other diplomatic and security issues, according to the sources. Beijing then put forward a list of more than a dozen such issues for Xi to raise with Trump, they said. But the White House rejected the suggestions, saying Trump would only engage on issues involving Iran, alongside planning for the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and Group of 20 summits. China is hosting the Apec gathering in Shenzhen in November while the US will host the G20 summit in Miami in December. In readouts after the Xi-Trump meeting, both countries said they would “support each other as respective hosts” of the events. Iran was also mentioned in the statements, with the two leaders agreeing that Tehran should not develop nuclear weapons and that no country or institution should be allowed to impose tolls on an international waterway. A White House factsheet of the meeting said the two leaders also discussed global concerns including Russia and North Korea.

title: Former American Idol singer Caleb Flynn sentenced to life for wife’s murder
description: Ohio court imposes maximum term on ex-pastor Caleb Flynn after jury rejects staged burglary claim.
content: A former music pastor in Ohio who appeared briefly on American Idol was sentenced Monday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, after a jury convicted him last week of murdering his wife while he was having an affair. The judge said Caleb Flynn, 40, used his Christian faith to manipulate others and showed no remorse for actions marked by “layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty”. With tears rolling down his cheeks, Flynn apologised to his family just before being sentenced, starting with his two young daughters, who were home when he shot his wife in her sleep. He called their births the “greatest joy in this life”. Although he said he accepted responsibility for his words and decisions, Flynn remained adamant that he was innocent. “As I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife,” he said. Prosecutors said Flynn staged a home invasion in February and claimed a burglar killed his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old teacher and volleyball coach. In his 2013 appearance on American Idol, Flynn credited his wife with encouraging him to chase his dreams on the singing contest. He did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood. During the trial, Flynn didn’t testify on his own behalf, nor did anybody else. Family members, including Ashley’s parents, spoke in favour of the harsh sentence Monday, while saying they had forgiven Flynn because they didn’t want her legacy to be hatred. Her sister, Kayla Keyt, said Flynn’s actions have scarred their entire church community, prompting children to run into their parents’ bedrooms to make sure their fathers haven’t killed their mothers. As a family member read a statement written by his daughter Ava, Flynn sobbed uncontrollably as a pile of tissues grew on the defence table in front of him. At one point, it appeared he might fall over. “Mommy was the perfect person,” her statement said. “The absolute perfect person. What did she ever do to you to make you hate her so much?” In her statement, his daughter Alyssa said she wouldn’t visit him in prison. During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their house in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. He sent a text message to his lover the night before the shooting, saying: “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” prosecutors said. During the trial, Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. She told jurors that Flynn said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her. The gun used to kill Ashley Flynn was not found at the scene, and his lawyers told jurors that investigators found no evidence that Caleb Flynn fired a gun that day. Prosecutors said his fingerprints and DNA were at the scene and that his devices showed him moving around the house, even though he claimed he was asleep at the time of the shooting. The jury found him guilty of multiple counts, including murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.

title: Bogota mayor presses Chinese-led consortium for more metro workers as auditors flag delays
description: Colombia’s comptroller found road works 52 per cent behind on the US$5.75 billion line, due for trial runs in September 2027.
content: Bogota mayor Carlos Fernando Galan has called on the Chinese-led consortium building the city’s first metro line to send more workers to its stations, after the country’s top auditor warned that delays in several parts of the project could push back its opening in March 2028. “We are entering a critical stage, which is the final stretch,” Galan said in an interview published by local news magazine Semana on Monday. “We have to ask Metro Linea 1 to get moving and put more staff in the stations.” The consortium, in which China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) holds 85 per cent and Xi’an Metro the rest, won the 24km (15 miles) elevated line in 2019 in what is still the largest international tender taken by a Chinese company in Latin America. The contract is worth about US$5.75 billion. Galan said the works remained within acceptable margins of the schedule, with the viaduct and trains on track and most of the fleet already in Bogota. Stations, public space and communications systems were falling behind, however, and he said the real test now was getting every part of the system to work together before the deadline the city has set. Galan said he wants construction finished by September next year so the line can begin several months of trial runs without passengers, with the viaduct due for completion in January or February. “It’s complex and we have to adjust some things to get there,” he said. Those dates depend on a project that was already behind plan at the end of August, when city figures put the line at 82.33 per cent complete against the 86.79 per cent its schedule had called for, according to the Comptroller General’s Office. By then more than 18km (11 miles) of viaduct had been built and 19 of the 30 trains delivered, but the office found much wider gaps elsewhere when it took over fiscal oversight of the line in September. Road and public space works lagged their schedule by 52.34 per cent, while stations and access points were 19.24 per cent behind and systems and equipment 18.58 per cent. Leonidas Narvaez, who runs the state-owned Bogota Metro Company, acknowledged the delays in an interview last month and said his team had already asked the consortium to hire more people and speed up station work. Video complaint Pressure on CHEC in Bogota had been building since August, when the local media published a video recorded in April showing the legal representative of local subcontractor Union Temporal Metrobuild handing 60 million pesos (US$19,000) in cash to a commercial manager of a CHEC unit. Metrobuild, which made beams and substructures for the viaduct, told prosecutors the money had been demanded before an overdue invoice would be signed off. The consortium gave a different account, saying the cash was a “provisional retention” agreed upon while Metrobuild fixed defects in its work and that the meeting had been filmed covertly. The Bogota Metro Company filed its own criminal complaint and informed the multilateral banks that help finance the line, though prosecutors have not announced any charges. The case has not held up the project’s funding, and last week Colombia’s finance ministry authorised the city to borrow up to 1.3 trillion pesos (US$400 million) from BNP Paribas to pay its share of the costs. CHEC’s parent company has been on Washington’s radar since 2020, when the US Commerce Department added several of its units to the Entity List over their role in building artificial islands in the South China Sea.

title: International Criminal Court unseals arrest warrants for Taliban ministers
description: Court in The Hague accuses Afghan leaders of crimes against humanity stemming from curbs on women.
content: The International Criminal Court on Monday gave more details about arrest warrants issued last year for two Afghan education ministers accused of committing crimes against humanity through the Taliban government’s restrictions on women and girls. The warrants, for Habibullah Agha, minister of education, and Neda Mohammad Nadeem, minister of higher education, were issued on September 9, 2025 and remained under seal until Monday. The two officials are accused of gender-based persecution linked to policies that have barred girls aged over 12 from school and excluded women from higher education following the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021. While the ICC warrants were likely to increase international pressure on Taliban authorities, the Afghan government said it does not recognise the body. “We are bound by the rulings of Islamic sharia and its courts, not by intelligence entities or so-called courts,” chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in a statement. “Afghanistan calls on such entities not to make claims beyond their authority and jurisdiction.” The two warrants against the ministers were issued after the ICC, in July 2025, authorised warrants for Afghanistan’s Supreme Taliban Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Supreme Court President Abdul Hakim Haqqani, parts of which have been made public. Both Agha and Nadeem have played key roles in implementing the supreme leader’s vision for Afghanistan. “There are reasonable grounds to believe” the suspects committed “the crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds”, the court said. It said the persecution was directed against women and girls, and the deprivation of their fundamental rights was committed “in connection with” other alleged crimes under the Taliban government’s policies, including “imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance”. The court said the alleged crimes were committed in Afghanistan from the Taliban’s takeover until at least January 20, 2025. The ICC’s disclosure of the warrants came the same day the UN Human Rights Council urged the Taliban authorities to repeal their “worsening” and “systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan”. The council’s 47 member countries unanimously criticised that discrimination “and the harms that it has entrenched, which are unbearable, unjustifiable and should shock the conscience of humanity”. The ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II said it decided to unseal all four warrants, with redactions, after concluding that doing so would not unduly affect ongoing investigations and could “prevent the commission of further crimes by the suspects”. Publication could also “promote cooperation by the international community … in relation to the situation in Afghanistan”, it said. Afghans across the country have told Agence France-Presse journalists of severe mental health problems tied to the education ban, with teenage girls and women mostly staying at home. Afghan universities are now men-only zones, where smartphones are banned and students can be chastised if their beards are not long enough. Some women and girls have tried to continue their education by studying online, but their efforts are hampered by internet and electricity problems across Afghanistan. Women are increasingly absent from public life and need to abide by a strict dress code when they leave home, covering everything but their eyes. They are banned from most jobs and a host of public places, including parks, and must have a close male relative escort them on long journeys. The higher education ban has led to staff shortages in hospitals, multiple healthcare workers have said, as women are no longer allowed to qualify as doctors.

title: Separatists win Quebec election in fresh test for Canada’s Carney
description: Parti Quebecois secures minority government as the incoming leader promises a future independence referendum.
content: Separatists won provincial elections in Quebec on Monday, with a promise to hold a vote on leaving Canada after US President Donald Trump leaves office, testing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s message of national unity. But the Parti Quebecois fell short of a majority government in Canada’s French-speaking province, offering some solace for the federalist camp. The PQ win still upends Canada’s political landscape as the country confronts a trade war and annexation threats levelled by the United States. It also comes just two weeks before Canada’s oil-producing province of Alberta, an economic powerhouse, holds a vote on whether it wants to begin the process of leaving Canada. The results make PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, a 49-year-old lawyer known by his initials PSPP, Quebec’s next premier. At a jubilant victory party in Montreal, he invoked “the courageous struggle” francophones have endured in a part of the world increasingly dominated by English speakers. That struggle “will find meaning when (francophones) obtain their own country,” he said. “We deserve it,” he added, calling a referendum a chance “to decide what our national future will be”. Carney congratulated PSPP, saying that “building a stronger Quebec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada”. The prime minister is popular in Quebec, and the separatist win was not seen as a repudiation of his stance towards Trump, whose confrontational policies have infuriated Canadians. Instead, the PQ’s rise after more than a decade in opposition has been tied to frustration over affordability and an enduring desire to protect the French language in a majority anglophone country. Surveys suggest that only about 30 per cent of Quebecers want independence, but PSPP has maintained he would call a referendum on leaving Canada, just not while Trump is in office. He has said a decision on Quebec’s independence “requires conditions that allow for an informed and calm debate”. That should not be “hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president,” he added, ruling out a referendum until at least 2029. Quebec has held two previous votes on leaving Canada. Federalists won comfortably in 1980, but the 1995 result was excruciatingly close, with just 50.58 per cent voting to stay in Canada. The PQ replaces a party, known as the Coalition for Quebec’s Future (CAQ), that advocated strongly for the province’s distinctive culture within Canada, without supporting separatism. Lacking a majority, the PQ will struggle to advance its separatist agenda. The two largest opposition parties after Monday’s vote, the Liberals and Conservatives, both declared they would never back a referendum on independence. PSPP may not have majority backing for an independent Quebec, but his plans to target the British monarchy appear far more popular. Canada is part of the British Commonwealth. King Charles, Canada’s head of state, is represented in Ottawa by the governor general. Lieutenant governors represent the monarchy in the provinces, including Quebec. In a 2025 Leger poll, 87 per cent of Quebecers said they felt no attachment to the British monarchy, and only 31 per cent expressed a favourable view of King Charles. PSPP has said his government could cut off funds for the lieutenant governor, calling it a “masquerade that wastes money”.

title: Russia plays down plague reports after lab worker death
description: Dozens quarantined as technician at anti-plague institute dies from what officials say was unexplained pneumonia.
content: Russia on Monday sought to play down reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as US President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help. Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region, sparked alarm. “We’re looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia. “We’ll help them, we’ll help them as much as we can.” The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube. Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility. As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating. But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease. Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said on Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that “the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology”. He said on Telegram that Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that “no microorganisms linked to the young woman’s professional work were found in her biological samples”. He added that there had been “no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention” since the woman’s death. Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was “stable”. “The situation remains under our control and that of the experts.” Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to “rely on Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements rather than … rumours and speculations”. Plague is endemic to Siberia, location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among wild mammals in the region’s vast wilderness. While cases occur annually in other parts of the world – notably Africa – human infections in Russia remain rare. The disease can manifest in several forms, most notably pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious variant and spreads via respiratory droplets. Bubonic plague, the more common form, is transmitted by infected fleas. Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization. The reports would be closely watched in Washington, where memories of the Covid-19 pandemic that started in Trump’s first term are still fresh. Trump has strongly backed the theory that the disease was due to a leak from a laboratory in Wuhan, China. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said his country was monitoring the Russia situation but saw no “cause for alarm”. “There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” Rubio told reporters before taking off for a visit to Iceland. “So we’re watching and monitoring it closely. I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we’re doing that.” Experts said the reported response in Russia appeared “proportionate”. “It appears that measures are being implemented to quarantine any potential contacts and prevent any onward transmission,” Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology, Imperial College London, said in a commentary. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: US to announce US$150 million for Alaska power lines as Vance visits battleground state
description: The US vice-president will also rally voters for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is in a re-election battle with Democrat Mary Peltola.
content: The US Energy Department will announce US$150 million in new funding for power lines in Alaska on Monday as Vice-President J.D. Vance visits the state, where Republicans are ‌fighting to hold a critical Senate seat in the November midterm elections. Vance is set to rally voters for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight re-election battle with Democrat Mary Peltola. Flipping the seat is key to the Democratic Party’s strategy to take control of the US Senate and recent polls have Peltola, a former member of the US House of Representatives, leading Sullivan. The energy plan ⁠is the latest in a series of economic and investment announcements US President Donald Trump and his administration have highlighted ahead ‌of the midterm elections amid voter concerns over the Iran war and high petrol prices. Under the Energy Department plan, the Trump administration will tap federal funds to help construct ‌359km (223 miles) of new electrical transmission lines linking the Beluga power station on Alaska’s southern coast ⁠with Healy in the ⁠state’s interior, an administration official told Reuters. The corridor between Beluga and Healy covers major ports and nearly three-quarters of the state’s roughly 735,000-person population. ‌The total cost of the project is US$400 million, the official said. A New York Times poll that concluded on October 1 ‌placed Peltola ‌ahead by 7 percentage points. Other polls indicate the race is about even. Alaska, with its far-flung and ‌rural population, is often difficult for pollsters to gauge. Trump unveiled plans last week for South Korea to invest some US$200 ⁠billion in US projects, including for an Alaska liquefied natural gas pipeline. But Seoul quickly said the pipeline would ⁠only proceed if certain commercial and legal conditions were met. Both Sullivan and Peltola have made affordability – and energy – primary issues in their campaigns. Sullivan supports drilling for oil and gas in Alaska’s protected ‌wilderness and has called on Trump ‌to ban diesel exports amid the economic fallout from conflict with Iran and the Russian war in Ukraine. Peltola has called for refining more oil and natural gas in Alaska but does not support drilling for resources in the environmentally fragile wilderness. She has also advocated for federal tax credits for solar, wind and hydropower projects.

title: 2 killed, including student, in ‘horrific’ school bus crash in Florida
description: The bus was transporting 39 people to Winter Haven High School when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and caused the crash.
content: A school bus flipped over onto its roof during a multivehicle crash in central Florida on Monday morning, killing two people – including a 10th grade girl – and injuring several others, authorities said. Some 39 people were on the school bus that was headed to Winter Haven High School in Winter Haven when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and caused the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said at a news conference. “It was a horrible crash,” Judd said. “It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life.” The bus had been travelling along a Winter Haven road shortly after 6am local time when an oncoming car crossed the centre line and crashed into the side of the bus near the rear wheels, Judd said. The impact ripped the tyre off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming jeep, which caught on fire. One person in the jeep died. Judd said five to seven people were transported to the hospital with potentially traumatic injuries and that one person remained in critical condition early on Monday. The bus was transporting 39 people in all – 37 high school students, the bus driver, and the bus driver’s daughter. Judd said first responders spent the first several hours getting people to the hospital, identifying them and reuniting students with their parents. “I think this is the most horrific bus tragedy we’ve had in decades, as far back as I can remember,” Judd said. Just over a month ago on September 3, another Polk County school bus was involved in a crash in Lakeland. Authorities said no students were on the bus at the time, and one person had injuries that were not life-threatening. Polk County Public Schools Superintendent Frederick Heid said students practised drills on how to leave a bus that was involved in an accident. “This event could have been far worse. You can see the condition of the bus, you can see its current positioning,” Heid said. The sheriff and superintendent held their news conference directly in front of the overturned bus, which had come to rest in a ditch beside the road. Helicopter video taken by WESH-TV later in the morning showed a horrific crash scene. The front end of the school bus was a mangled mess of metal, and it appeared to be missing one of its four back tires as it lay on its roof. Justin Sharpless, chairman of the Polk County school board, asked the community to come together to support the family of the girl who died, as well as the school and school staff. “There are really no words that can take away the pain of losing a young person,” he said.

title: US search for missing airmen in China gains new attention after Xi-Trump summit
description: Access to crash sites and wartime Chinese archives is key to resolving about 700 cases and bringing missing US servicemen home.
content: For more than eight decades, the remains of US fighter pilot Morton Sher lay unrecovered in China. A photograph of a memorial to him in a Hunan village eventually helped investigators find where his plane crashed in 1943. Sher was buried in his hometown of Greenville, South Carolina, in December 2025, a homecoming that offers a rare example of what US-China cooperation can achieve for families of missing servicemen. That cooperation has now drawn fresh attention. After the recent summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, Beijing said that the two militaries had agreed to continue cooperating in the search for the remains of missing US servicemen in China. The account also said the militaries would seek to conclude a separate memorandum on military crisis communication and prevention “as soon as possible”, but it did not specify new recovery missions or arrangements for access to sites and records. For American investigators, cooperation means permission to search crash sites and access to wartime records that could show where to look. “All of our work starts with a historical study aspect,” said John Figuerres, a senior operations officer at the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA). Records of battles, aircraft crashes and possible prisoners of war help investigators decide where to dig, and access to Chinese archives could help historians establish what happened to missing Americans. “Both getting to sites and that exchange of information are important things with China,” Figuerres said. China occupies a distinctive place in the agency’s work: it is the only country where DPAA has missing Americans associated with four conflicts, namely World War II, the Korean war, the Vietnam war and the Cold War. DPAA said just over 700 US personnel are missing in China across the four. The work was already under way before the summit. Since 2024, DPAA has conducted two pre-deployment site surveys, three investigation missions and two recovery missions in China, the agency said. This past August and September, two teams worked in southern China. A 12-member US recovery team excavated what is believed to be a World War II crash site and recovered possible human remains, while a nine-member investigative team surveyed multiple locations in Hunan and interviewed witnesses to prepare case proposals that could lead to future recovery missions. Officials from the People’s Liberation Army and provincial and local governments assisted both teams, DPAA said. US and Chinese scientists are due to hold a joint forensic review of the recovered evidence later this month, the agency said. DPAA periodically communicates with the PLA Archives to share information on unresolved cases involving both countries, the agency said. The two sides are developing an archival exchange for the 2027 US financial year, which began on October 1. For the US military, the search extends a battlefield commitment across generations. Figuerres called it part of the “warrior ethos”, the end point of never leaving a fallen comrade behind, and a “sacred obligation” to families waiting at home. Sher’s case shows how such a search can unfold. He flew with the 23rd Fighter Group, which carried on the legacy of the Flying Tigers, the American volunteer pilots who fought for China against Japan. Sher himself had crashed in China before: engine damage forced him down near a Chinese village in October 1942, according to a US military account, and residents welcomed him with a feast and helped him return to base. The banquet, he told an Army newsletter, “turned out to be one of the biggest surprises of the trip”. On August 20, 1943, the 22-year-old US Army Air Forces pilot was killed while intercepting a Japanese aircraft headed towards Hengyang. US forces located the crash site, but his remains were not recovered. That changed in 2012, when a private citizen brought a photograph of the village memorial to the attention of the Joint POW/MIA Accounting Command, a predecessor of DPAA, prompting years of research. During the 2024 excavation, the team found possible human remains and equipment. Anthropological analysis, other evidence and DNA testing led to Sher’s identification in June 2025. Such identifications are painstaking. At DPAA’s laboratory in Hawaii, which the agency describes as the world’s largest skeletal identification laboratory, scientists may begin with fragments that are difficult to distinguish from animal bone or debris. Dr Jennie Jin, a DPAA scientist, said anthropologists examine bones for clues such as age and healed injuries, then compare their findings with military files, dental records and DNA results. Anthropologists initially examine remains without knowing the case details, which helps guard against bias. DNA can be a limited guide. Age and chemical treatment can damage it, Jin said, and a genetic match may narrow the search without establishing a single identity. She recalled a Korean war case in which DNA results narrowed the possibilities to five men. An anthropologist spotted two old fractures, and in one serviceman’s file, Jin found a letter from his mother describing injuries to her son’s forearm and lower back. “Ooh, I found him,” Jin remembered thinking. The man was identified and buried beside his mother. But the work starts long before the laboratory, in China’s villages, and it depends on people who remember where an aircraft came down. Figuerres said teams had met local residents who still remembered the US role in the second world war and had maintained tributes to fallen airmen. Jin, who investigated three World War II crash sites in China in 2017, recalled a memorial residents had assembled for American personnel. Her team found no leads at those sites, she said, but residents and Chinese counterparts were helpful. Historians from the two countries are also beginning to meet regularly, Figuerres said, and building those relationships is an important part of gaining information that could help resolve cases. For Sher’s family, the search ended with a funeral. DPAA said his sister, who is 93, received his remains. His nephew, Bruce Fine, said that right before his last mission the pilot had turned down an opportunity to return home as an instructor. On August 19, 1943, Sher wrote to his parents about his decision to stay in China: “I let another pilot take that instructing job, for I find things too exciting here to leave right now.” He was killed the next day.

title: Bid to turn 14 subsidised Hong Kong sale flats into subdivided homes raises abuse concerns
description: Home Ownership Scheme flats are deemed a form of social welfare and should not be used for profiteering, lawmaker says.
content: The owners of 14 subsidised sale flats have applied for a grace period to comply with Hong Kong’s new regulatory regime for subdivided homes, the housing minister has revealed, raising concerns that public resources were being abused. The cases were disclosed on Monday at a Legislative Council housing panel meeting when lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung asked Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin about the use of subsidised sale flats as subdivided units for renting. Chong said flats sold under the government-subsidised Home Ownership Scheme were deemed a form of social welfare and should not be used for profiteering. Ho said that it was against the law for an owner to lease a subsidised sale flat without having paid the premium. “The penalty is severe, with a maximum fine of HK$500,000 (US$64,000) and one-year imprisonment [under the Housing Ordinance],” she said. “If the owner has paid the premium and wishes to renovate it into a basic housing unit, as Chong has said, there are still some technical considerations … There are some structural restrictions.” Under the Basic Housing Units Ordinance, subdivided flats must fulfil a set of minimum standards to be recognised as a “basic housing unit” that can be leased legally on the market from March next year. Existing landlords can apply for a three-year grace period to carry out alterations, with registrations open between March this year and next February. Ho said landlords of about 73,600 subdivided units had registered for the grace period, involving more than 20,000 complete flats. She described grace-period applications from owners of subsidised sale flats as “rare”, involving 14 cases, or 0.07 per cent of the 20,000 homes. However, she stressed that the government would monitor the situation closely. While leasing subsidised sale flats with the premium unpaid was illegal, Ho said there were structural constraints and that some structures could not be removed easily. She said creating a window in an exterior wall for lighting or ventilation would be subject to building-plan restrictions. She added that estates had different designs and the exact structural restrictions would depend on the building plans of individual estates. Chong urged the government to clearly state whether the 14 properties could be rectified without contravening the Deed of Mutual Covenant, a legally binding document covering all flat owners of a building and governing its management and regulations. He also suggested that the authorities should consider explicitly banning owners of future subsidised sale homes from turning their properties into basic housing units. Separately, Ho said the authorities had so far received recognition applications from landlords of 184 subdivided homes and certified 42 of them as basic housing units. Ho said the applications were coming quicker than she expected, and foresaw that more properties would apply for accreditation. Under the regime, a basic housing unit should have an area of at least 86 square feet (8 square metres) and a 2.3-metre (7½-foot) ceiling height, a separate waterproofed toilet and an operable window. The requirements also cover fire safety, hygiene and other standards. Landlords must hire specified professionals to confirm their properties comply with the minimum standards.

title: ‘There will be no Hamas rule in Gaza,’ Netanyahu vows at October 7 memorial
description: The Israeli prime minister also says he stands with victims’ families and the nation shares their grief.
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday vowed there would be no Hamas rule in Gaza as he attended a memorial event marking three years since the militant group’s October 7, 2023 attack. Monday is a national day of remembrance for the deadliest day in Israel’s history, with flags lowered to half mast on public buildings from 6.29am, the time the attack began. Speaking during a state ceremony at the Mount Herzl military cemetery in Jerusalem, Netanyahu said “we have achieved enormous accomplishments, but there are still missions ahead of us, and we intend to complete them”. “There will be no Hamas rule in Gaza,” he added, vowing to continue targeting anyone who was involved in the attack or who held hostages. In a separate speech later on Monday, Netanyahu said he stood with victims’ families and the nation shared their grief. “There is no forgiveness for the murderers, the torturers, the arsonists. There is no forgiveness for the destroyers, the looters, the kidnappers,” he said. Later in the speech, a heckler shouted: “You didn’t protect my son and 1,200 others killed on October 7 – shame!” leading Netanyahu to briefly pause the address. The Hamas-led attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Militants also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive that has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the territory’s health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Since a ceasefire was declared last October, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,440 people in Gaza, according to the ministry. Plans for Gaza’s post-war governance have begun to take shape, but the issue remains largely unresolved in practice. Since Hamas’ October 2023 attack, Israel has fought wars on several fronts, including against Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon. During his speech on Monday, Netanyahu also vowed to keep striking Hezbollah to “create an opportunity for peace with a country whose people, for the most part, want peace with us”. Netanyahu also hit out at the clerical leadership in Iran, where Israel and the United States launched a joint attack on February 28, triggering the Middle East war. “We will not allow the ayatollah regime in Tehran to threaten our existence,” Netanyahu said, adding the Iranian leadership was “weaker than it has been since its establishment”.

title: France school protests: teenager’s hand blown off after picking up grenade
description: The 15-year-old appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot officers in Lens and it exploded in his hand, a source says.
content: A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday picking up a police grenade as students across France demanded better classroom conditions in a days-long wave of protests that have erupted into blazes and barricades at some schools while disrupting lessons at hundreds nationwide. Some students returned to classrooms but others maintained protests outside their schools, ahead of larger demonstrations expected on Tuesday in what a secondary school students’ union has dubbed “Act III” of the movement. Authorities said the teenager was injured in the northern town of Lens. A police union source said he appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police and that it exploded in his hand. Since late September, students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of schools, complaining of teacher absences, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings ill-adapted to rising temperatures, among other grievances. “It’s clear the education system isn’t working,” said Alma, a pupil at the Lycee Charlemagne in central Paris. The unrest ignited just months before 2027 elections that will determine the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron. The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing hard-left activists of having hijacked the protest movement. “They think that just because they’re letting us express ourselves on a platform, on the internet, we’ll stop blocking access and being angry, but this anger has been here for years,” said Simon, a pupil also at the Lycee Charlemagne. The French Human Rights League (LDH) on Monday accused security forces of using disproportionate methods against protesters, many of whom are legally minors. “We can see that in the instructions given to the police, there is no directive to show restraint, even though they are dealing with children,” LDH president Nathalie Tehio said. More than 400 out of France’s 3,700 high schools, known as lycees, were partially or totally closed on Monday morning, the education ministry said. In central Paris, dozens of teenage students demonstrated outside a school while passing cars honked their horns. Some classmates made their way inside to attend lessons. “We’re missing our lessons to give you one,” read one cardboard sign outside the Turgot high school in Paris. In Bordeaux, in the southwest, some students returned to the classroom while others continued to demonstrate in the presence of riot police. Some protesters outside the Gustave Eiffel high school set off fireworks in the direction of police, who responded with tear gas, but overall the situation remained calm, Agence France-Presse reporters said. The movement started on September 17 at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, in support of teachers striking over a lack of staff and resources. It gained momentum and spread across France, at times spiralling into vandalism, including the destruction of bus shelters, the burning of school entrances and clashes between protesters and security forces. Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister. More than 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them minors, have been arrested. Protesters have also accused police of using excessive force, and internal investigations have been opened into at least three instances of alleged police brutality. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Sunday urged local authorities to prioritise filling gaps left by long-term teacher absences and unfilled posts. He called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country’s often-dilapidated school buildings. The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of drawing on public funds. Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon defended the bill. “When you have 14-, 15-, 16-year-olds who, at 9am, are burning bus shelters or – perhaps even more seriously – the high school where they study, that raises the question of parental responsibility,” she told the Europe1/CNews broadcaster. Lecornu has said the draft law could allow compensation payments to be recovered from family allowances and housing benefits while preserving a minimum income threshold. The head of the main CGT labour union, Sophie Binet, slammed what she called a “populist announcement”, which she said would “end up targeting the most vulnerable families”.

title: France, Germany call for new weapon allowing ‘immediate cut off’ of China from EU market
description: Strategy laid out in joint paper and letter to EU chief signed by the leaders of the two largest members of the bloc and seen by the SCMP.
content: In the strongest sign yet of a shifting European Union policy on China, the leaders of France and Germany have demanded a new trade weapon that would cut off access to the EU market when third countries cause severe distortions. The tool would effectively act as a kill switch, allowing Brussels to respond rapidly to systemic distortions, potentially immediately. It would grant dramatic new powers to the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch, which manages trade policy for the 27-member union. The strategy was laid out in a joint paper written by the bloc’s two largest members, as well as a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen – both of which have been seen by the South China Morning Post – ahead of a crucial period of EU-China negotiations. “We need a credible instrument in the hands of the Commission to allow for decisive and systemic reaction, i.e. activation by reversed qualified majority, and for powerful measures up to an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed,” the letter, signed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, said. While neither document names China, and both make clear that any new instruments would have to be country-agnostic, they are laden with language ordinarily seen as bywords for China’s policies, including “unsustainable trade deficits with key partners”, “structural excess capacity”, “dumping, excessive and across the board subsidies”, and currency manipulation and undervaluation. Unlike existing trade-defence tools, this tool would tackle distortions beyond traditional dumping or subsidies, including political or economic pressure and currency manipulation, and could apply from a single product to an entire sector. To prevent single capitals from blocking its use, the commission could deploy the instrument unless a qualified majority of EU members oppose it. The unnamed instrument is one of a suite of new recommendations by the French and German governments, which have previously sparred on China policy but have come closer together in recent months, with Berlin’s position shifting notably amid a surge in Chinese imports in key sectors, which officials say amounts to a “China Shock 2.0”. “It is important to hear that there is a European consensus today that these imbalances are unsustainable,” an Elysee source said. “We want this dialogue [with China] to lead to concrete measures, not dialogue that leads nowhere. So, there is, I believe, a very clear Franco-German determination and a very clear European determination to say that we are not the ones who want a trade war, but that we are determined to enforce fair competition rules.” The paper also calls for a new diversification instrument to reduce dependencies and force companies to spread their sourcing risks, and the more frequent and rapid deployment of trade investigations. Berlin and Paris specifically call for urgent targeted measures in chemicals, some plastics and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The documents set the stage for talks between the EU’s trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday and Friday. Next week, they will help set the tone for a summit of EU leaders in Brussels, where they will discuss what to do about what is considered an existential problem for European industry. France hopes the talks in Beijing will produce a negotiated settlement, but it is understood that major EU parties have grown impatient waiting for China to change. “There comes a point where we also have sectors that have been facing unfair competition for months and cannot be left waiting on the uncertain outcome of a dialogue when it comes to specific sectors,” said the Elysee source. “So what we expect, while making progress on this dialogue, and while this dialogue delivers results, is that concrete measures can be taken so that the sectors that have been suffering for months can benefit from some protection.” Olof Gill, a trade spokesman for the European Commission, said “we very much welcome the letter” to von der Leyen. “This is a valuable contribution to the ongoing debate on how the EU can best address geoeconomic risks and global macroeconomic imbalances,” Gill said. “It aligns with the work of the European Commission and the president’s clear stance on competitiveness and the approach to trading partners, including China.” Since reports of the new tool surfaced last week, it has been variously compared to the US’ Section 301 tariffing tool and the bloc’s own anti-coercion instrument (ACI), which was adopted three years ago, but has lain dormant since, despite what is viewed as a rise in coercive behaviour towards Europe from both the United States and China. The Elysee source said that the proposed tool would be more pre-emptive than the ACI, which is a retaliatory weapon. “There, the purpose is to put an end to coercion. Here, our objective is to have an instrument that is genuinely dissuasive,” they said.

title: Hong Kong IVF clinic cleared to resume all services after embryo specimen mix-up
description: Regulator says Heal Fertility in Central can resume all 17 treatment services covered by its licence after implementing improvement measures.
content: A Hong Kong fertility clinic that had most of its services suspended for mishandling embryo biopsy specimens from two patients has been cleared to fully resume all treatments after implementing improvement measures. The Council on Human Reproductive Technology said on Monday that Heal Fertility in Central could resume all 17 treatment services covered by its licence from Tuesday, after members reviewed the findings of a follow-up inspection and confirmed the clinic had properly implemented the required corrective measures. The clinic had been barred from providing 14 of its 17 licensed treatment services since July 8 following the embryo biopsy specimen mix-up involving two couples. It had only been allowed to continue three services related to the storage of gametes and embryos while investigations were under way. The controversy emerged after Heal Fertility and the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s pre-implantation genetic testing centre notified the council on June 17 that embryo biopsy specimens sent for genetic testing were suspected of having been replaced by other specimens. According to the council, tests later established that there had been no mix-up of the embryos stored at the clinic and there was no evidence that any embryos had been wrongly implanted. In July, the council said initial findings suggested the incident might have been caused by human factors and launched an investigation. In August, police classified the case as suspected fraud after investigators concluded that a former Malaysian embryologist might have made mistakes while handling embryo biopsy specimens and subsequently provided false information in an attempt to conceal them. The woman left Hong Kong for Malaysia shortly after being interviewed by police and resigned from the clinic. Police later placed her on a wanted list. The regulator said it held a special meeting on September 3 and accepted the investigation committee’s conclusion that “the main cause of the incident may involve intentional unlawful conduct by an individual”. It nonetheless found room for improvement in the clinic’s operations and ordered it to carry out a series of enhancement measures before services could resume. A surprise inspection was conducted on September 22 to assess implementation of the measures. According to the council, Heal Fertility refined its sample-handling procedures, strengthened staff training and upgraded laboratory management and security systems. Improvements included installing CCTV surveillance, fitting biometric locks on cryostorage tanks and enhancing sample identification and verification procedures. The council also noted that the principal personnel involved in the incident had left the clinic and that new staff had been recruited and trained. “The council was satisfied and convinced that Heal Fertility had refined its internal sample-handling procedures, strengthened staff training, and upgraded laboratory management and security systems in accordance with the council’s requirements,” it said. The regulator added it would continue to closely monitor the clinic’s performance to ensure the provision of safe and quality reproductive technology services. It has also begun reviewing the Code of Practice on Reproductive Technology and Embryo Research, including incident-reporting arrangements and biological sample security procedures, with the exercise expected to be completed next year. Heal Fertility welcomed the regulator’s decision and said it would resume IVF and other reproductive services from Tuesday. The clinic said it would contact existing clients to explain the latest arrangements and schedule treatment according to their wishes.

title: How is China planning to build on its ‘engineer dividend’ in tech war with US?
description: Ministry of Education has announced plans to offer an extra 76,000 undergraduate places at top universities by 2030.
content: As China seeks to build on its “engineer dividend” – the advantage created by a vast pool of engineers built up over decades – it is directing more talent towards artificial intelligence and other hi-tech fields central to its competition with the US. The push comes as fresh graduates face mounting pressure to find jobs, underscoring the challenge of aligning China’s expanding higher education system with the needs of its changing economy. But Beijing has a narrow window to act, an education expert said, with the number of students entering the country’s higher education system expected to peak in the coming years before entering a longer-term decline. Last month, the Ministry of Education announced plans to expand undergraduate enrolment at the country’s top universities by 76,000 places between 2027 and 2030. The expansion would “strengthen basic and frontier research and drive breakthroughs in key technologies, building a strong force to support major national strategic priorities”, Guo Peng, the head of the ministry’s development planning department, said at a news conference in Beijing. It would focus on training talent for strategic industries and fields facing acute shortages, including AI, integrated circuits, biomedicine and new energy, he said.
