The government would draw on central-budget funding and ultra-long special treasury bonds to support new campuses and improvements to dormitories, canteens, sports facilities and laboratories at the elite universities, Guo said. The nurturing of tech talent has become a prominent factor in the race between the United States and China to develop cutting-edge technologies, with Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek and Kimi K3 narrowing the gap with American rivals and fuelling jitters in Silicon Valley over the sustainability of the US lead in frontier AI. Bloomberg reported last year that China’s “engineer dividend” was paying off, citing data showing the number of engineers in the country surged from around 5.2 million in 2000 to some 17.7 million in 2020. China employed 41 per cent of the world’s leading AI researchers last year, pulling ahead of the US at 34 per cent, according to a study released last week by the Carnegie China think tank. Despite that growing pool of Chinese talent, shortages persist in specialised sectors. According to a campus recruitment report by hiring platform 51job, there were 25 job openings for every applicant in integrated-circuit design this year, 15 for every applicant in algorithm engineering and 14 for every applicant in autonomous driving. Some leading universities have announced plans to expand enrolment in those fields this year. Southeast University said it would add 600 places for disciplines including AI, integrated circuits and robotics, while Xidian University’s enrolment plan added 400 places, focusing on high-demand fields such as communications, integrated circuits and AI. After the demographic peak passes in about a decade, what will happen to these institutions? Xiong Bingqi, 21st Century Education Research Institute The expansion is part of a broader plan to add more than 100,000 undergraduate places at China’s “double first-class” universities by 2030. The universities had added 62,000 places since 2024, Guo said. The “double first-class” initiative is a performance-based funding programme that aims to turn more than 100 Chinese universities and their top departments into global academic heavyweights akin to the US’ Public Ivies. The expansion was also a response to the expected peak in the college-age population by 2032 while also preparing for the longer-term decline in the number of students, said Xiong Bingqi, director of the Beijing-based 21st Century Education Research Institute and an authority on Chinese education policy and reform. “In the coming years, the number of National Higher Education Entrance Examination candidates is expected to increase in many parts of the country, so if the overall admission rate is to remain unchanged, universities will also need to expand their enrolment,” he said. At the same time, students and parents were placing greater emphasis on access to high-quality higher education, Xiong said, creating additional pressure to expand places at leading universities. But expanding other types of institutions could create a different problem once the number of students began to decline, he added, saying: “After the demographic peak passes in about a decade, what will happen to these institutions?” National Development and Reform Commission chairman Zheng Shanjie told a news conference in March that China’s student populations for junior high, senior high and higher education would peak sequentially in 2026, 2029 and 2032. To manage that rolling wave of demand, Zheng said the government’s priorities for the next five years would include expanding high school capacity and building undergraduate capacity at top universities.

title: Authorities investigate viral drone footage of National Day fireworks display
description: Hong Kong’s Civil Aviation Department investigating suspected illegal drone flight over Victoria Harbour after mainland Chinese visitor posts fireworks footage.
content: Hong Kong aviation authorities are investigating suspected illegal drone flying over Victoria Harbour during last week’s National Day fireworks display, after privately shot footage of the show went viral online. The footage drew the attention of local internet users after a mainland visitor, who came to Hong Kong during the “golden week” holiday, posted clips of the 23-minute display on his social media account over the weekend. The man, who calls himself Su Fan on RedNote, a popular platform among mainland Chinese users, described himself as a professional from Yunnan province. When some users asked whether he had permission from the authorities to film the show with a drone in a no-fly zone, he replied: “No need to bother”. Criticism has since flooded his account. The clips appeared to have been removed and could no longer be found on his account by Monday afternoon. Some users also accused authorities of lax law enforcement. In response to a South China Morning Post inquiry, the Civil Aviation Department said on Monday that it was following up on the case in accordance with established procedures. “Operations exceeding the operating requirements and/or operations within restricted flying zones are advanced operations and require prior permission from the Civil Aviation Department and/or the relevant authorities,” it said. Offenders face a fine of up to HK$100,000 (US$12,742) and up to two years’ imprisonment upon conviction. In 2025, police also caught a mainland visitor operating a drone without permission in a restricted zone at Edinburgh Place in Central during the National Day fireworks display.

title: Yemen forces drive Houthis from Bab el-Mandeb Strait as Saudi allies pledge troops
description: Coastal push aims to secure Red Sea oil route; Pakistan and Turkey join regional force as rebels target Riyadh.
content: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces staged a lightning advance on Monday to retake the coast around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait up to the city of Mocha, the government said, pushing the Iran-backed Houthis out of most of the areas they seized last month. In response, the Houthis said they had attacked key locations in Saudi Arabia including the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, the Abha international airport and the Khamis Mushait military base. The claims could not be immediately verified. Saudi Arabia and Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Yemeni forces of ‌the internationally recognised government, backed by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha late on Monday and Houthi fighters were retreating into the highlands, four government sources said. The Defence Ministry said the city had fallen. The advance, if confirmed, would loosen the Houthis’ grip on a vital Red Sea oil route already roiling energy markets alongside Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, though the group could still strike vessels with drones from other positions. Fighting has raged along several front lines in Yemen for weeks since a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said late on Monday that naval forces carried out a military operation in Yemen’s Red Sea governorate of Hodeidah. The government forces had already ⁠taken key positions including an airstrip in the Dhubab district at the mouth of the strait whose seizure by the Houthis last month sent shock waves through energy markets. Reuters could not independently verify the extent of the government gains. The ‌Houthis, who have controlled many of Yemen’s more populous areas including the capital Sanaa since 2014, said the Saudi-backed government’s claims were baseless. Meanwhile, the Houthis themselves made important advances near the third-largest city of Taiz, gaining sections of a mountain road to leave government forces besieged, according to five military sources with the Yemeni government. One government source denied the road had ‌been cut. The group also threatened to attack traffic in Saudi airspace. The escalating conflict has prompted Riyadh’s allies to act. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh on ⁠Monday to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities in Saudi ⁠Arabia under their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement. The fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis in Yemen, the poorest state in the Arab region. The UN migration agency said on Monday that 184,000 people had been displaced since the war resumed. Yemen’s internationally recognised president, Rashad al-Alimi, swore on ‌Sunday to fight “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia”. Saudi Arabia said on Monday it had attacked hundreds of targets to provide air cover for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Yemeni ground forces. The Yemeni government said it had launched attacks on several fronts including in Sanaa province. The ‌Houthi-run ‌health ministry said two people had been killed and seven wounded in strikes on the province’s Sanhan and Sa’wan districts. While the war has raged on several fronts, the heaviest fighting has been in the ‌southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around Taiz. The Houthis damaged a culvert on the Taiz-Aden road, making it impassable, and on Sunday their fighters made new advances into the town of al-Turbah, five ⁠government military sources said, though another government source denied this. A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head ⁠of Yemen’s interim presidential council. The advances left Taiz, a city with a population of over half a million and a garrison of thousands of government fighters, surrounded by Houthi forces, the government military sources said. In a statement following their meeting, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan accused the Houthis of attempting to target Islam’s holiest sites, Mecca and Medina. “The Parties also condemned in the strongest terms the attempted targeting of Mecca and Medina, as well as the continuing attacks targeting cities and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom, reaffirming their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity,” the statement said. The “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, signed in August, is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack on all.

title: Japan, Australia boost economic security ties with finance dialogue
description: The two countries’ finance ministers will meet regularly to promote cooperation across a broad range of economic themes.
content: Japan ⁠and Australia ⁠have agreed to establish an ⁠annual finance ministers’ dialogue aimed at deepening cooperation in financial and economic policy, as well as strengthening bilateral collaboration on economic security. Under ‌a memorandum of understanding signed on Monday that is effective for five years, the two countries’ finance ministers will meet regularly to promote cooperation across a broad range of economic themes. “Recognising ⁠that Japan and Australia’s economic and security futures are ‌deeply connected, the Finance Ministerial Dialogue will enhance bilateral cooperation on economic security matters,” the ‌memorandum said. “We will work together to promote stable economic growth in the Indo-Pacific region and around the world,” Japan’s finance chief Satsuki Katayama said during the signing ceremony. Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said closer Australia-Japan cooperation was “more important now than ever”, adding the two countries “can seize new economic opportunities” by building on their complementary strengths. The framework will focus on creating ⁠opportunities ⁠to enhance mutual energy and fuel security, investment in critical minerals, as ‌well as building “transparent, diversified, sustainable, and secure supply chains including in ‌the defence industry ‌sector”, it said. The mechanism marks Japan’s third ‌ministerial-level finance dialogue with a major regional partner. Tokyo ⁠established similar frameworks with South Korea and China in ⁠2006, although no Japan-China finance ministers’ dialogue has been held since 2018. Australia, a major supplier of ‌natural resources ‌to Japan, is one of the country’s key sources of liquefied natural gas. Australia is also rich in critical minerals, including rare earths. Additional reporting by Kyodo

title: Mainland Chinese arrivals to Hong Kong surged at start of ‘golden week’ holiday
description: City enjoyed initial rush of visitors on National Day before arrival growth eased, with lawmaker calling for more nighttime events.
content: Mainland Chinese arrivals to Hong Kong surged at the start of the National Day “golden week” holiday before easing towards last year’s levels, with a lawmaker attributing the early rush partly to the city’s fireworks display and tourists making the most of a shorter break. Immigration Department figures showed that 277,304 mainland visitors arrived on October 1, up 19.1 per cent from 232,751 on the first day of last year’s holiday and 25.1 per cent from the 221,644 recorded in 2024. “The fireworks were certainly a major factor,” lawmaker and China Travel Service chairman Perry Yiu Pak-leung said, noting that this year’s seven-day holiday was one day shorter than last year’s, prompting some visitors to start their trips earlier. However, growth moderated sharply after the first day, with mainland arrivals rising by 5.4 per cent year on year to 234,007 on the second day, remaining basically unchanged at 221,566 on the third day and edging up by 2.3 per cent to 206,180 on the fourth day. In total, 939,057 mainland visitors entered Hong Kong during the first four days, about 7 per cent more than the 877,833 recorded over the same period last year and 14.5 per cent more than the 820,315 in 2024. The figures also showed an unusually large gap between arrivals and departures on the first day, when only 49,798 mainland visitors left the city, resulting in a net inflow of 227,506. That gap narrowed substantially from the second day, with departures outnumbering arrivals on both the third and fourth days. Yiu said nighttime attractions could play an important role in encouraging visitors to stay overnight rather than return to the mainland on the same day. “If there are good programmes at night, they will prefer to stay,” he said. “Whether there are programmes worth staying for has a big impact on whether visitors are willing to remain in Hong Kong.” Yiu noted that the hotel sector had reported bookings of more than 90 per cent on the first day of the holiday, while the industry expected overall occupancy during the break to reach about 90 per cent. He pointed to the National Day fireworks and the extended lantern display at Victoria Park as events that could encourage longer stays, adding that tourists hoping to visit several attractions naturally required more time in the city. The influx was felt beyond traditional tourist districts, with large crowds also heading to countryside destinations and spots popularised on mainland social media. The trend has renewed questions over how authorities can prepare for sudden surges at places that may not have been designed to handle large numbers. Sai Kung district councillor Edwin Cheung Chin-pang said the adoption of a reservation system at Po Pin Chau might have pushed some visitors towards other countryside attractions, including Ham Tin Wan, which did not require bookings. He said authorities should monitor mainland social media platforms such as RedNote to identify destinations that were suddenly gaining popularity and prepare for an influx of visitors. “Sometimes a place suddenly goes viral on social media because someone posts a set of beautiful photos,” Cheung said. “These places can become popular very quickly and it can be difficult to predict.” He suggested the government establish a system to track such trends, enabling relevant district authorities, police and other departments to prepare before crowds arrived, even if imposing a reservation system was not immediately necessary. Cheung, who visited Po Pin Chau during the holiday, said he also encountered visitors who were unaware of the booking requirement and had arrived expecting walk-in access. He recommended promoting the reservation requirement across mainland booking platforms used for high-speed rail and air travel. Cheung also renewed his call for introducing a deposit or fee for reservations, pointing to the high proportion of no-shows. “Even though it is a real-name reservation system, there is no penalty or deposit, so making a booking comes at no cost,” he said. Social media posts by mainland visitors also showed large crowds at popular attractions during the first days of the holiday. Users posted images and videos of busy streets in Tsim Sha Tsui during the fireworks display One visitor described Kennedy Town as “packed to bursting” on the third day of the break, noting long queues had formed for trams, waterfront photo spots and cafes despite the overcast skies. They advised visitors to avoid peak periods or allow extra time. Other posts complained about rubbish left behind after the fireworks. One commentator urged visitors to carry rubbish bags and dispose of their waste rather than leave it on the streets. The government has forecast that about 1.29 million mainland visitors will enter Hong Kong during the seven-day holiday.

title: Opinion | AI microdramas are a test case for China’s next big export wave
description: A quiet shift is happening in China’s services exports as its competitive manufacturing capabilities start moving into entertainment content.
content: China’s US$1.2 trillion goods trade surplus last year has focused attention on electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels and industrial overcapacity. Tariffs, anti-subsidy investigations and localisation requirements have followed as trading partners respond to China’s manufacturing scale. Yet the less visible shift is happening in services. Services exports rose by 17.1 per cent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, while exports of personal cultural and entertainment services surged by 57.8 per cent. China still runs a trade deficit in services, which are nowhere close to replacing manufacturing. But digital services can scale up globally without factories, containers or ports. Microdramas generated by artificial intelligence (AI) offer an early example. China industrialised the format domestically: one-to-three-minute episodes, rapid plot twists and cliffhangers designed around smartphone viewing and payment. The sector’s revenue rose from less than 1 billion yuan in 2020 to an estimated 100 billion yuan (US$14.91 billion) last year. Chinese-backed platforms such as ReelShort already have sizeable overseas audiences. Rather than simply exporting Chinese television, these companies are exporting a production system built around audience data, rapid localisation, performance marketing and, increasingly, AI. Chinese factories became formidable by shortening product cycles, compressing costs, producing many variants and quickly scaling up whatever sold best. AI allows content producers to apply the same logic to entertainment. China released about 430,000 microdramas in the first eight months of 2026, as much as 13 times all of 2025, with AI accounting for over 90 per cent. The productivity gains explain the rapid adoption. South Korean producer Vigloo cut production from three months to one and costs to about one-fifth using AI. Shenzhen studios using ByteDance’s Seedance have achieved a similar compression. But the advantage is not just cheaper video generation. China has an ecosystem capable of turning AI output into commercial content quickly and at scale. That matters because microdramas are built for rapid experimentation. Producers can see within the opening episodes whether viewers are staying, then redirect marketing spending towards titles gaining traction and abandon those that do not. Lower costs also mean more bets. While a traditional studio may spend months developing several expensive projects, an AI microdrama producer can launch many titles, read audience behaviour quickly and scale up only the winners. Breakout successes are few and far between – only 0.48 per cent of AI microdramas released on Douyin in the first half of 2026 exceeded 100 million views. Still, microdramas may be a better risk model than committing millions to a long-form production: microdramas make failures far easier to discover. Yet scale is creating its own problems. Beijing is now pushing the industry towards greater quality, originality and copyright protection, effectively telling a sector built for speed to slow down. iQiyi shows how this is no longer a fringe format. Built around premium long-form drama, iQiyi saw its short-form titles take the top domestic market share for the first time in the second quarter this year, even as group revenue fell by 5 per cent year on year. Its response has been to push deeper into AI and short-form production. Microdramas may not explain its wider revenue pressure, but they are reshaping the economics of it. More than a fad, microdramas are a test case. They show how China’s industrial strengths can be applied to digital services, creating exports that scale globally without the factories, shipping lanes and tariff exposure that define physical trade. A microdrama crosses borders through an app. There is no container to inspect and nearly zero marginal distribution cost, even as AI lowers the cost of translation, dubbing and localisation. Digital products can still face restrictions. TikTok’s case shows how the effect of national security and platform regulation can substitute for those of tariffs. But policies designed for manufacturing overcapacity work less neatly when the export is entertainment, software, intellectual property or attention. China is applying familiar manufacturing capabilities to services: speed, scale, cost control, rapid experimentation and a ruthless elimination of weak products. Only the output has changed. Entertainment adds another dimension because stories shape perceptions. AI amplifies not only output, but also the assumptions and stereotypes embedded in it, especially when algorithms reward those narratives with traffic. I have seen Chinese microdramas cast the United States as a bully and use a fictional small Southeast Asian country as shorthand for money laundering and corruption. Repetition can still normalise such portrayals. China spent four decades building an export machine around physical goods. If the same economics spread through gaming, online literature, entertainment, apps and AI-enabled services, China gains another channel for globalisation that is less dependent on factories and harder to address with conventional tariffs. Services will not replace China’s manufacturing engine any time soon. Rather, the competitive capabilities built in manufacturing are beginning to migrate into services. China’s trillion-dollar goods surplus is visible at the port. Its next export wave may increasingly arrive through the smartphone.

title: Man, 74, lost control of paraglider in strong winds, probe into fatal crash finds
description: Retired Hong Kong police officer was lifted off the ground backwards and into thick cloud cover before crashing on Lantau in 2024.
content: A 74-year-old retired Hong Kong police officer lost control of his paraglider in strong air currents and suffered multiple injuries after crashing on Lantau Island, a probe into the fatal 2024 accident has found. A report published by the Air Accident Investigation Authority on Monday detailed the incident involving the pilot at Sunset Peak, Hong Kong’s third-highest mountain, on June 17, 2024. The authority urged paragliding groups to stress the importance of thorough risk assessments before flights. According to police records from the time, the unnamed pilot went to Pak Kung Au on Lantau with five friends to paraglide. Equipped with walkie-talkies, he was the first in the group to take off solo from a designated paragliding site on the 869-metre (2,850 feet) peak. He had 27.7 flying hours from 95 flights between July 2023 and that month. The investigation found that strong winds had lifted the pilot off the ground backwards during a reverse launch, a take-off technique used in paragliding. The man had planned to fly down to Lower Cheung Sha Beach in a two- to three-minute trip, the investigation report said. But shortly after take-off, strong updrafts lifted the paraglider – a high-performance BogdanFly X-wing – higher and into thick cloud cover. The man’s companions previously said a sudden gust of wind swept him into dense clouds in the direction of Pui O. They advised him over the radio to deploy descent techniques but received no response, the investigation revealed. The pilot made brief radio contact with his companions at about 3pm, saying that he was injured and stuck in a tree, but could not reach his phone to transmit his location before going silent. Rescuers located him unconscious at 9.25pm on a slope near a section of the Lantau Trail. He was taken to North Lantau Hospital at 2.40am the next day and pronounced dead on arrival. The authority’s final investigation concluded the pilot lost effective control of the paraglider due to strong atmospheric lift while flying inside cloud cover, resulting in a collision with terrain and impact with a tree that caused multiple injuries. The cause of death was multiple severe blunt force trauma injuries to the face, limbs and torso, the investigators reported. During the incident, recorded wind speeds at nearby Cheung Chau reached 22 to 28km/h (14 to 17mph), with gusts peaking at 38km/h – well above recommended site limits. Additionally, low cloud cover completely engulfed the peak area. The report highlighted that flying into clouds violated the Hong Kong China Paragliding Association’s site guidelines – which explicitly warn against entering clouds due to nearby air traffic – as well as the Civil Aviation Department’s safety guidance requiring paragliders to operate under visual meteorological conditions and remain clear of clouds at all times. Following the investigation, which adhered to International Civil Aviation Organization standards, the authority issued a safety recommendation to both the Hong Kong China Paragliding Association and the International Paragliding Association. It urged both organisations to re-emphasise to all local participants the critical importance of conducting thorough risk assessments to ensure flight risks were kept as low as reasonably practicable.

title: Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi-final, Zheng Qinwen survives another 3-set test
description: Novak Djokovic qualifies for final after Russian is defaulted for hitting ball into crowd, injuring spectator; Chinese star through to last 16.
content: Daniil ⁠Medvedev ⁠was disqualified ⁠from his China Open semi-final clash with Novak Djokovic after ‌hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd, hitting a spectator in the eye. Earlier on Monday, home hope Zheng Qinwen survived another three-set test to advance to the last 16, while former world No 1 Iga Swiatek staged a comeback in Beijing. World No 5 Medvedev was trailing ‌his semi-final 7-5, 5-3 and had lost ‌a point when he ⁠hit ⁠the ball coming off ‌the wall. The spectator, who was ‌sitting in ‌the first row, ‌clutched his left eye ⁠and appeared to be in ⁠pain as he walked out of the ‌gallery, ‌assisted by stadium staff. The chair umpire and tournament supervisor came down onto the court to talk with Medvedev, who did not appear to put up much of an argument with the disqualification. Medvedev then walked to the net and shook hands with Djokovic. The incident was reminiscent of when Djokovic was kicked out of the 2020 US Open for accidentally hitting a line judge in the throat with a ball. “A bit of a shock, to be honest,” Djokovic said. “I honestly didn’t see what happened. I hope that person is not badly injured. On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil, because I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match ... I am sure that Daniil didn’t want to do this intentionally. It just happens.” Medvedev has a history of on-court behavior issues. He was fined €6,000 (US$7,000) for unsportsmanlike conduct after he smashed his racket seven times during a 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at the Monte Carlo Masters earlier this year. Djokovic will play Alex de Minaur for the title on Tuesday. China’s Zheng was put to the test as she endured her third three-setter of the tournament when she beat Czech player Marie Bouzkova, 7-6, 4-6, 7-5. Zheng, who reached the quarter-finals of the US Open last month on the back of a return to form, voiced frustration in each set at movement outside the court, including as she tried to salvage the second set on Bouzkova’s serve. But she pulled out some of her most accurate tennis to clinch the last two games and win the match when 27th-ranked Bouzkova fired long. “I gave everything,” said Zheng, who had already spent more than five hours on court in the first two rounds. “Truthfully speaking, I felt a lot of pressure today,” the 23-year-old told her home crowd, thanking fans for their support but commenting on distractions during play. “Sometimes I’m a bit screaming in Chinese because I really see you guys are moving, but next match I hope I will be better on this.” Zheng, the current world No 54, next plays 118th-ranked Alina Charaeva, who sent out top seed Elena Rybakina in the second round. Swiatek overcame frustration to cling on as her opponent served for the set, dominating a must-win tiebreak to beat Croatia’s Donna Vekic 4-6, 7-6, 6-2. “I was just angry, wanted to change something, because clearly it wasn’t working,” the 25-year-old from Poland said on court. “Sometimes if you care a bit less because you’re … probably going to lose, it also helps you a bit,” she later told reporters. She will face American teenager Iva Jovic for a spot in the quarter-finals. Australia’s de Minaur advanced to the final when Hubert Hurkacz retired because of an apparent injury midway through the second set of their semi-final on Monday. De Minaur led 6-4, 3-2 when Hurkacz – who was barely able to run for balls in the second set – stopped playing. The nature of Hurkacz’s injury was not immediately clear.

title: People’s Daily 10-day series highlights potential of AI, private sector in 15th 5-year plan
description: The 10 articles ran under the pen name ‘Jinxuan’, widely believed to be associated with the National Development and Reform Commission.
content: China’s Communist Party’s mouthpiece has published a 10-day series highlighting the prospects and resilience of the country’s economy under its 15th five-year plan, following President Xi Jinping’s closely watched meeting with US President Donald Trump. The series, published by People’s Daily from September 25 through the National Day holiday period, ran under the pen name “Jinxuan”, which is widely believed to be associated with the National Development and Reform Commission, the country’s top economic planner. The articles covered economic priorities under the 15th five-year plan, from new growth engines such as the BeiDou satellite navigation system, artificial intelligence and biomanufacturing to domestic demand and private sector development, underscoring the economy’s potential and resilience. “China has the world’s largest and most comprehensive manufacturing system, a vast consumer market, enormous market space, well-developed infrastructure and a strong pool of talent … its growth momentum and economic resilience as a major country continue to strengthen,” one of the articles said. “Our products are gaining increasing favour, while the resilience and security of industrial and supply chains continue to improve, giving us greater confidence in responding to various risks and challenges.” The article roll-out came as Beijing sought to set the tone in the first year of its 2026-30 development blueprint, amid sluggish domestic demand, rising external uncertainty and persistent tech rivalry with the US. The series also came ahead of the fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee, slated for October 26 to 29, which is likely to be the most important gathering ahead of next autumn’s national party congress, a five-yearly event marked by significant top-level reshuffles. One of the articles called for stronger safeguards in key areas including food, energy, water, cybersecurity and biosecurity, as well as tighter regulation of AI and greater protection of Chinese citizens and organisations overseas. “We must remain confident and rise to the challenges … strengthen bottom line thinking, effectively prevent and defuse various risks, and enhance economic and social resilience,” the article said. Last week, China’s central bank announced a fresh package of measures to boost the real economy, cutting an interest rate for policy banks and introducing the country’s first interest subsidy for commercial mortgages. Separately, Economic Daily, a state-run newspaper focused on economic affairs, published a commentary on Monday hailing the growing global reach of Chinese manufacturing and services. “China’s hi-tech products continue to sell well overseas,” the commentary said. “Beyond the products themselves, capabilities in technology, supply chains and services are also expanding globally, with more Chinese companies shifting from selling products to building ecosystems.”

title: Sincere to close Central department store after 126 years as lease expires
description: Hong Kong’s oldest Chinese-owned department store seeks new premises after failing to renew lease, leaving just one location in Mong Kok.
content: Hong Kong’s first Chinese-owned department store, Sincere, will close its historic branch in the city’s central business district in December after 126 years of retail history. The company revealed, however, that it would seek a new location in Central or Sheung Wan. Economists cautioned, however, that despite strong retail sales in the city overall recently, the market had changed, and running physical stores had become highly challenging. Sincere announced on Sunday that the flagship store would shut in early December after lease renewal talks with the landlord broke down ahead of the tenancy expiring on December 31. “As a result, the Central store will cease operations in early December and reinstatement work on the premises will commence thereafter for handover to the landlord,” the company said, without specifying the final date of the branch’s operation. It added: “The company will continue looking for suitable venues in the Central or Sheung Wan area to establish a new outlet for its department store operations. “However, up to the date … no suitable premises have been identified yet.” The closure leaves the Mong Kok outlet at King Wah Centre as Sincere’s sole remaining bricks-and-mortar department store in the city, alongside its e-commerce platform. The company once operated three branches in the city but closed its Dragon Centre store in Sham Shui Po, where it had been a neighbourhood fixture for three decades, earlier this year. The closure of the Central store came as a surprise to some amid a broader recovery in local retail performance. Government statistics released last week showed retail sales in August rose 5.6 per cent year on year to HK$32.1 billion (US$4.09 billion), marking a 16th consecutive month of expansion. Over the first eight months of the year, sales climbed 8.5 per cent compared with the same period in 2025. Lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai, who represents the wholesale and retail sector in the legislature, said: “Competition from online shopping has been very keen. Especially for operators of physical stores, they have to pay high rents. “I am not suggesting that there is no future for department store operations. But rent is a big challenge.” Economist Simon Lee Siu-po shared Shiu’s views and said the city’s retail landscape was stuck in a difficult position, despite the recent rebound in sales. “It is picking up, thanks partly to the tourism boom,” he said. “But the figures show it is still very weak when compared with the past.” For example, the retail sales figure for August 2018, before Covid-19 hit, was HK$38.2 billion, compared with HK$32.1 billion for this past August, he noted. “People’s shopping habits have changed, and online shopping is very common now. It is too expensive to run physical department stores,” Lee said. Rumours about the closure of the Central branch have been brewing since early this year, and news of the closure drew mixed reactions online. “A 100-year-old base is gone,” one user wrote on Discuss.com.hk. “It is a bit sad. Times have changed too fast.” Another noted: “An end of an era.” One commentator was less sympathetic, saying: “Traditional department store operation is old school. Things are not very cheap there. Plus the boom of online shopping.” The windows of the branch on Des Voeux Road Central have been covered with posters saying “final clearance, nothing to be left”. One of the sales assistants, who had worked at the branch for 10 years, said: “It’s sad. We will miss the regular customers.” She said the company had yet to brief staff members about further arrangements. Founded in 1900, Sincere Company is one of Hong Kong’s oldest retail groups. Founder Ma Ying-piu and his friends opened the store upon returning to Hong Kong from Australia, where they had been inspired by David Jones, an upmarket Sydney department store. Sincere was a pioneer in Hong Kong retail, becoming the first store to hire women as shop assistants, introduce fixed pricing without bargaining and issue formal purchase receipts. In the 1980s, Sincere and its main rival Wing On – founded in 1907 – agreed to close on alternate Sundays so employees at both stores could have regular days off. While retail remained the company’s core business for decades, Sincere began to suffer losses in the 2010s as local shopping habits evolved and its image was seen as outdated among younger consumers. In 2021, third-generation owner Philip Ma King-huen resigned as chairman and CEO after Shenzhen-based Realord Group Holdings acquired all of the company’s listed shares.

title: Empty classrooms on remote Greek island signal crisis across Europe
description: Falling enrolment across Greece this year prompted authorities to close 75 schools.
content: Chryssa Ntalaka’s classroom has become an object lesson in subtraction. The sole teacher in the last school on the idyllic Greek island of Kalamos has a shorter list of students every autumn. This year, just two. On September 23, the sixth graders sat at Ntalaka’s table beneath the whiteboard, in front of rows of unused desks and benches. When they head to middle school on Greece’s mainland next year, her school will be mothballed. Toys and picture books still sit on shelves in the nearby kindergarten since it was closed three years ago. “Usually, teachers are placed on these islands against their wishes,” Ntalaka said. “Whereas for Kalamos there are teachers and kindergarten teachers, as far as I know, who want to come – but there are no children.” Falling enrolment across Greece this year prompted authorities to close 75 schools and suspend or extend suspension of classes at more than 400 others. It is a situation playing out across Europe and beyond. The region has 16 of the world’s top 20 oldest nations, particularly in southern Europe, according to the independent World Population Review. And its remote communities act as an early warning system: mountain villages and small islands are among the first places where schools and services disappear in a deepening cycle of population decline. Some 17 million people live on more than 4,000 islands across the European Union; Greece has about 200 of them. “Closing schools leads to young people not staying and to them leaving,” said Byron Kotzamanis, co-founder of the Institute of Demographic Research in Athens. “Leaving means fewer and fewer people – fewer and fewer births. It means depopulation and dead settlements that will become nursing homes.” Commuting across the sea each day Kalamos’ year-round population is just 80. A decade ago, it had 40 children in local schools and public day care. “It was very nice. We played together every day. We went to [primary] school every morning,” Antonis Aivaliotis, a high school senior, said during a ferry ride in the predawn light. Aivaliotis is among Kalamos’ seven teenagers who today make a choppy crossing to school on the mainland. They miss class on days when strong winds pose a risk. He spent several years as a student of Ntalaka’s class, which at the time was a single room with children of all ages. Ntalaka has often been the lone teacher during her 20 years at remote schools. Half that time was in Kalamos, located not far from Odysseus’ home island Ithaca in The Odyssey. She fell in love with Kalamos’ unspoilt beaches that are a magnet for yacht tourists. She learned to dive and became an accomplished spearfisher. But she will have to leave. All it would take for her school to remain open would be the arrival of two families. She and town officials have desperately sought to spread the word, but there is no sign of any comers. “We’re very welcoming and we’re trying. That’s what we want to do, even right now – for someone to hear us,” Ntalaka said. “The sooner, the better.” As for Aivaliotis, he sees moving away after graduation as an inevitability. “Of course I would like to stay here,” he said. “I love Kalamos. It is my home. But there’s no development at all.” Islands fight to keep schools open Ageing countries are struggling to keep their island schools open, with limited success. Croatia had invested €4.6 billion (US$5.1 billion) in its islands over the past 10 years, Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said in June. That includes 20 kindergartens being built or expanded, and renovation of primary schools and sports arenas. Croatia’s parliament, the Sabor, in January passed an Islands Act aimed at improving life for islanders. The rate of population decline on small, remote Croatian islands is similar to that of the mainland. Japan faces grimmer demographics. In the decade through 2023, the population of over 250 remote islands covered by a government support programme fell 19 per cent, almost double the national rate, according to the most recent government data. Nearly 1 million people lived on those islands in 1955, and 340,000 by 2020. This has led to a shortage of people to operate ferries and other transport, worsening economic contraction on remote islands. Japan’s government says maintaining residents is crucial to national security and has provided subsidies to lure people to work in tourism, fishing and other industries. Some islands have managed to recruit students from elsewhere. On remote Oki Islands, for example, 74 of the 132 students at a fisheries high school were drawn there through family relocation programmes. And on the Italian island of Stromboli, formed by the tip of a volcano, a school reopened last month after 20 years with a single student. Italian junior schools normally need at least 15 pupils, but exceptions are granted to remote islands because a school’s closure can accelerate depopulation. Images broadcast on Italian television showed six-year-old Aysha wearing a purple backpack almost as big as her body and holding her mother’s hand as she walked through the narrow streets of Ginostra to her first class inside the village’s local church. Europe’s population is growing older Aris Alexopoulos, head of the OECD’s Crete Centre on Population Dynamics, says Greece’s population will fall as low as 8 million, from 10.5 million, by 2050. Young people were becoming a minority, he said on the sidelines of a demographics conference in Athens on September 21. The trend extends across the European Union: 3.55 million babies were born in 2024, roughly half the 1964 peak. Its fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.34 children per woman, well below the 2.1 level needed to maintain a stable population. Greece was among a few countries with rates below 1.25. In June, the EU announced it would develop a strategy for islands, aiming to address the problem of shrinking populations, among others. Themis Christophidou, director general for regional and urban policy at the European Commission, said in an email that the EU had spent €146 million over the past five years to modernise schools on four Greek island clusters, specifically to counter demographic decline. “Mobility is one of Europe’s strengths, but people should leave by choice, never because of neglect or missing investment,” she wrote. “That starts with quality public services, with education at their heart.”

title: Adrian Cheng, former scion of Hong Kong’s NWD, expands K11 brand in Xiamen
description: Company touts foot traffic and sales growth for Xiamen project combining shopping with wetland park, cultural events.
content: Adrian Cheng Chi-kong, former heir apparent to Hong Kong’s New World Development (NWD), is expanding his K11 cultural retail business in mainland China, launching a venture of his own as his family’s property group grapples with heavy debt. Xiamen K11 Select, developed by Cheng’s K11 by AC Group along with state-owned Xiamen Rail Transit Group in the city in the southeastern province of Fujian, has attracted more than 2 million visits since its opening on September 22, with sales rising 32 per cent week on week, according to a statement on Monday. With 95,000 square metres (more than 1 million square feet) of space, the complex houses around 200 brands, including about 80 making their national, provincial or regional debuts. “China’s first wetland conservation-focused retail, art and cultural tourism landmark in Xiamen has delivered strong operating results since opening, signifying the success of the ‘cultural commerce’ model developed over the past 16 years,” Cheng said at an opening ceremony. The project extends Cheng’s cultural retail concept into ecotourism, linking the shopping complex to an 85-hectare wetland park through a 1km elevated walkway. The development also offers art exhibitions, restaurants and public spaces, illustrating his push to build destinations that extend their appeal beyond shopping. Cheng resigned as New World’s CEO in September 2024 and later left the board of Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, the family’s investment holding company. He launched Almad Group in 2025, with K11 by AC pursuing cultural retail and entertainment ventures separate from NWD. The Xiamen opening comes as NWD sells assets and cuts costs to ease its debt burden. On Wednesday, NWD reported a net loss of HK$26.8 billion (US$3.42 billion) for the year ended June, as it booked HK$18.3 billion in impairments and provisions tied to the early termination of its flagship 11 Skies mall project. During a results briefing, the group’s CEO Echo Huang reiterated that Xiamen K11 Select was not part of NWD’s business and that Cheng’s investments and asset-light management operations had no connection to the group. The grandson of late tycoon Cheng Yu-tung and son of property developer Henry Cheng, Adrian Cheng founded K11 in 2008, and spearheaded the development of projects including Hong Kong’s K11 Art Mall and K11 Musea.

title: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
description: By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative.
content: India has sold its Akash air-defence missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, giving it a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to become a major global arms exporter. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”. Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming. It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets. The Akash programme has also been updated with newer variants, such as Akash Prime and Akash-NG, which feature upgraded sensors and other improvements. Its export to Central Asia comes amid India’s wider push to sell its air defence systems to a region where Russia has traditionally been the dominant arms supplier and China has been gaining ground. Armenia became the first international customer for the Akash in 2022, attracted by the system’s relatively low cost as well as Russian supply shortages and rival Azerbaijan’s growing drone fleet, said Atul Kumar, a fellow at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation’s strategic studies programme. For Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, Kumar said acquiring the system was a way for them to diversify their defence suppliers beyond Russia and China. “Turkmenistan has already acquired a number of Chinese air-defence systems and the Akash is expected to complement them by fulfilling the mid-layer role in its air-defence architecture,” he said. For Russia, Kumar said India entering the Central Asian defence market was likely preferable to the region moving close to Nato or Chinese military standards. But the presence of Indian military hardware along China’s western flank would be an unwelcome development for Beijing, he said – not least because it had sought to establish itself as the region’s preferred military supplier. “India is actively promoting defence exports and expanding private-sector participation through various policy initiatives, incentives and defence corridors,” Kumar said. A third option Russia’s weapons exports have decreased since it invaded Ukraine, but data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute shows the Kremlin is still Central Asia’s main arms supplier. China has reportedly been catching up, however, especially in Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Kazakhstan bought 11 per cent of Russia’s major arms exports between 2020 and 2024, while Tajikistan still heavily relies on Russian equipment and military assistance, the institute’s data shows. Armenia, meanwhile, has been cutting back on Russian weapons and turning to new suppliers such as India and France. The Akash offered high-end air defence capabilities at a fraction of the cost of Western alternatives, said Rahul Wankhede, a research analyst at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in India. “The system is supported by domestic manufacturing lines … and additional orders placed by India’s own armed forces,” Wankhede said. “So this assures potential buyers of supply chain reliability, quick replenishment and a comprehensive training package.” In addition to its own arms, India could provide Central Asian nations like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan with support for Russian-origin systems, Wankhede said. “So it’s a dual advantage for both sides.” Unlike China, Russia or the United States, India was not looking to create dependencies through weapons sales, he said, making it an attractive partner for nations looking to balance their strategic relationships. “The Akash system will have a wider export base in the future since it’s a purely defensive system,” Wankhede said. “This marks India’s emergence as a credible defence exporter on the global stage.” ‘Battle-hardened’ Russia’s current preoccupation with preserving surface-to-air missile supplies for its own use had created an opening for India, said Aleksei Zakharov, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation think tank in Delhi. “After procuring the Akash-1S systems, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, similar to Armenia, are likely to consider importing other Indian military equipment, including radar systems, artillery and missiles,” Zakharov said. Part of the appeal of the Akash was that it was “a battle-hardened system”, said Antoine Levesques, senior fellow for South and Central Asian defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, citing its use in last year’s brief air war with Pakistan. “Foreign sales of Akash provide added evidence that India’s exports of defence articles are picking up pace,” he said. “Feedback from those sales will allow India to fine-tune other defence products it is preparing for export markets.” Foreign sales of Akash provide added evidence that India’s exports of defence articles are picking up pace Antoine Levesques, defence analyst India’s friendly relations with Central Asia meant it could position itself as a reliable partner, said Rajiv Kumar Narang, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analysis. India wanted to increase its defence exports but it would take time to achieve this, he said, as Delhi worked to improve its offerings. The South Asian nation currently ranks 31st for global arms exports, shipping an estimated US$4 billion of weapons last financial year. C. Uday Bhaskar, director of the Society for Policy Studies think tank and a former Indian naval officer, said that “modest exporter” India was unlikely to try to directly compete with Russia. Given the two countries’ work on the Brahmos missile system, Delhi “would proceed in a prudent manner”, Bhaskar said, adding that competition with “China is a different story”.

title: Seoul probe reveals border mine blast caused by North Korea
description: South Korea’s military says the North deployed up to 7,000 workers to install mines and fences this year.
content: South Korea ⁠said on Monday that a ⁠recent border blast that seriously wounded two ⁠of its soldiers was caused by mines planted by North Korea. North Korea, which has been fortifying its border with South Korea since April 2024, deployed up to 7,000 workers to install mines and fences this year, with some 50 incidents of ‌crossing the border, according to a briefing on Monday by the South’s military. The two Koreas are still technically at war after their 1950-53 war ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty. “Based on the findings of joint investigations with the United Nations Command and scientific evidence, it is officially determined that our soldiers conducting regular operations in the demilitarised zone [DMZ] were wounded ⁠severely by an anti-personnel mine installed south of the military demarcation line by North Korea under its ‌so-called fortification work,” Kwon Dae-won, vice-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told a briefing. The mine that exploded on September 21 was believed to have been ‌planted about a year ago, Kwon said. “Our military strongly urges North Korea to ⁠apologise sincerely to our soldiers ⁠injured by the mine blast and immediately remove mines installed in violation of the armistice agreement,” Kwon said, adding that the ‌army conducted operations on Monday to remove North Korean mines and it would continue if Pyongyang did not remove them voluntarily. Last ‌week, the ‌UN Command said after joint investigations with the South Korean military that another North Korean anti-personnel ‌mine was identified on the South Korean side of the military demarcation line bisecting the 4km (2.5-mile) ⁠wide DMZ, calling it a violation of the Korean war armistice. On Friday, North Korea’s Kim Yo-jong, ⁠the influential sister of leader Kim Jong-un, said South Korea’s accusation was “groundless” and dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology. Last year, the South Korean administration of President ‌Lee Jae Myung proposed talks with ‌North Korea to open dialogue with North Korea and ease tensions. It suggested setting a clearer boundary along the border to avoid the risk of potential military clashes, but North Korea has not responded to any calls for dialogue since it defined South Korea as a “hostile” nation in 2023.

title: How Vietnam’s twist on Hainan chicken rice tells a rich story of migration
description: In Hoi An, on Vietnam’s central coast, com ga is a dish steeped in migrants’ history and tangy flavours.
content: Hainan chicken rice, known for its tender, poached chicken and fragrant rice flavoured with chicken stock, is one of the many great Asian comfort foods. Paired with a trio of chilli, ginger and soy dipping sauces, every bite offers a customisable balance of rich, nostalgic flavours. The original dish hails from Hainan, a Chinese island province, where traditionally it is made with local Wenchang chicken. The dish evolved as Hainanese natives emigrated to Southeast Asia, with Vietnam’s com ga being perhaps the most distinct variation. In Hoi An, on Vietnam’s central coast, com ga – which translates as “cooked rice” and “chicken” – has the same tenderness as Hainanese chicken rice but a brighter medley. It features golden rice, shredded chicken with a tangy, herbal twist, and sweet heat from a sticky red chilli jam. Here, rice serves as the warm foundation of a salad. The classic Hoi An method is similar to that in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand: free-range chicken is gently poached in a broth with ginger and shallots, then removed and shredded. The poaching liquid cooks the rice, which is first toasted in chicken fat. Often, the rice is cooked with turmeric, which contributes to its yellow hue. Once the rice is ready, the shredded meat is scattered over it with sliced white onion, Vietnamese coriander (rau ram) and crisp green papaya. A small savoury bowl of broth, often containing chicken offal and cubes of blood, makes the meal more substantial. “Com ga is almost unrecognisable from Hainanese chicken in Singapore and Malaysia,” says Dobee Lam, executive chef of Sep, a modern Vietnamese restaurant in Central on Hong Kong Island. He notes that the biggest difference is the dressing, which includes fish sauce, lime juice, garlic, ginger and chillies. The other accompanying sauces set Hoi An’s version apart. Unlike the fresh red chilli sauces served with Singaporean or Malaysian chicken rice, the chilli condiment is closer to a jam. In the Vietnamese version, chillies are cooked with tomato, garlic, oil, sesame and seasoning until thick and glossy. Rather than for dipping, it is stirred through the chicken and rice. Diners can use lime, fresh chilli, fish sauce and soy sauce to adjust the balance of a dish that is richer and more refreshing than its culinary cousins in the region. From portside community dish to fine dining While food history is never straightforward, com ga fits within Hoi An’s maritime past. From the late 16th to the early 18th century, the town was a major Southeast Asian port where Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese and European traders converged. After the fall of the Ming dynasty in 1644, Chinese arrivals to the port sought both trade opportunities and refuge. Like many merchants in the region, they formed a vital commercial network, bringing shipping knowledge, trading capital and connections that helped make Hoi An one of Indochina’s busiest ports. The Hainanese were one strand of this broader Chinese – or Hoa – community, alongside other regional groups. Their enduring architectural legacy is the Hainan Assembly Hall on Tran Phu Street, a traditional compound built for gathering and worship, mirroring their ancestral halls in mainland China. These spaces gave a far-from-home community somewhere to meet, pray, honour ancestors, settle business and preserve collective memory. By the late 19th century, this separate Hainanese presence was, if not disappearing, thinning out. The Chinese families who had lived there for generations and married locally were increasingly woven into Vietnamese society. The demographic distinction grew less visible, even as halls, shrines, cooking and kinship survived; like the chicken dish, the cultural distinctions blurred. At La Sen at Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai, chef de cuisine Tran Thanh Cong takes this local template seriously enough to refine it rather than dilute it. He renders chicken fat, sautés it with lemongrass, shallot and turmeric, stirs in raw rice, then cooks it in chicken stock. The chicken is marinated with lime, chilli and fish sauce before it is seared, while his papaya, carrot and white onion pickle is soaked briefly in iced water for crunch, then lightly dressed with fish sauce. Though it is a fine-dining chef’s version of com ga, the familiar pleasure remains: silky smooth chicken and hot scented rice among an intriguing medley of textures. “The biggest difference is the chilli jam,” Cong says. His is slow-cooked with sugar until it is gently sweet rather than aggressively hot: “When we mix it with the chicken, the flavour is very nice.” His other quiet intervention is the soy sauce. “Outside, it’s just a soy sauce,” he says, but at La Sen, he folds in shallot oil, steeps the mixture with fried shallots, strains it and adds a touch of sugar. That extra onion depth is a small detail that makes the sauce feel like the next step in the evolution of this dish. A conduit for hospitality That is perhaps why com ga deserves attention. It signifies not only the journey but also the assimilation of the Hoa community into the Vietnamese whole. Its broth carries the economy of a poached bird; its rice remembers Hainan; its herbs, lime, fish sauce and chilli jam represent central Vietnam. At La Sen, Cong’s refinements do not erase the dish’s local character. Instead, they bring its complex layers into focus: fresh chicken, fragrant rice, crunchy pickle salad and the slow cooking of the chilli jam. For Cong, the dish is a conduit for hospitality. When a guest asks why the sauce is sweet, why rau ram is there or why the rice is yellow, the meal becomes a conversation about place, travel and inheritance. “I say: ‘The dish comes from China, but we use ingredients from Vietnam.’”

title: Meet Chad Lowe’s eldest daughter Mabel, who paid tribute to her late sister Fiona
description: The 17-year-old, who made her screen debut in 9-1-1: Nashville, recently wrote a tribute and shared childhood photos of her late younger sibling on Instagram.
content: Chad Lowe’s family confirmed the tragic news of his 13-year-old daughter Fiona’s passing in a statement shared with People on September 29. “We are deeply heartbroken by the loss of our beloved Fiona,” the Emmy-winning actor’s family said. “Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time,” the statement continued. It also included contact information for a Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the US. While Lowe’s family did not provide a cause of death, the database for the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner later confirmed that Fiona died by suicide. Lowe, the younger brother of actor Rob Lowe, and his wife, Kim Painter, also have daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10. After her sister’s passing, Mabel wrote a tribute for Fiona on Instagram, sharing a series of childhood pictures of herself and her late sister. “I love you so much Fiona. I wish your short time here was easier and [I] hope your mind is at ease now. I will honor you forever and keep your memory alive. I love you, [I] hope you knew just how much,” her post read. Here’s everything you need to know about Chad Lowe’s 17-year-old daughter, Mabel. She is Chad Lowe’s eldest child Lowe and Painter welcomed their first child, daughter Mabel, in May 2009. Adorably, young Mabel was the ring bearer at her parents’ wedding in August 2010. Lowe and Painter would go on to welcome Fiona and Nixie in 2012 and 2016, respectively. Before marrying Painter, Lowe was married to actress Hilary Swank from 1997 to 2007. They have no children. She is a budding actress Like her father, known for roles in television shows such as Life Goes On and Pretty Little Liars, Mabel has also taken the Hollywood path. According to her Instagram bio, the budding actress is signed to AEFH, a Los Angeles-based talent agency. She made her on-screen debut in 2025 with a role in an episode of 9-1-1: Nashville, per her IMDb. On her 17th birthday in May earlier this year, Lowe marked the occasion with an Instagram post, writing, “Please join me in wishing this beautiful soul a most happy 17th birthday!!” “I love you soooo much @mabellowe_ !! I’m so proud to be your Dadda,” he continued. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Why the PLA’s Z-10 attack helicopter is taking a bigger role at sea
description: Aircraft was built to hunt tanks and support ground troops, but a broader maritime role means it can operate closer to Taiwan.
content: Built to hunt tanks and support ground troops, the People’s Liberation Army’s main attack helicopter is increasingly being prepared for operations at sea. Crews of the Z-10 are training to fly from ships – a shift that could give Beijing extra firepower in an amphibious assault on Taiwan. Manufactured by AVIC subsidiary the Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation, the Z-10 entered service with the PLA Army in late 2010. It began documented shipboard trials in 2014, when Chinese navy imagery showed a Z-10 landing on the Baxianshan Type 072A tank landing ship. The attack helicopter’s maritime role has gradually expanded since then. In 2020, army helicopters practised landing, refuelling and rearming on a civilian semi-submersible. The PLA has also operated Z-10s close to the Taiwan Strait. Defence intelligence publisher Janes said satellite imagery from December 2020 showed 12 of the aircraft at the Yuanqian helicopter base on the Fujian coast opposite Taiwan, while it was still under construction. Four years later, images appeared to show eight Z-10s aboard another semi-submersible. And in November of the following year, state broadcaster CCTV said the Type 075 amphibious assault ship could carry the army-operated helicopter. Together, the coastal presence and shipboard trials could allow the PLA to operate Z-10s closer to Taiwan, where they could escort troop-carrying helicopters, attack coastal positions and support troops ashore. That could be important because Janes estimates the Z-10’s combat radius at 114km to 294km (70 to 182 miles), depending on the configuration. At the lower end, that is less than the roughly 130km width of the Taiwan Strait at its narrowest point. That range limitation also helps explain the PLA’s interest in semi-submersibles. An analysis published in June by the US Army War College’s China Landpower Studies Centre said the PLA Army would likely rely on such ships and other flat-deck vessels as forward refuelling and rearming points in any attack on Taiwan. The PLA has also tested how the Z-10 could be used against targets at sea. Footage aired by CCTV in 2023 showed Z-10s from the Eastern Theatre Command’s 73rd Group Army firing rockets at simulated maritime targets off Fujian. Such training points to a possible role against small boats or other targets at sea, not just positions ashore. Official footage released this February showed Z-10s, Z-20s and Mi-17s from a PLA Army brigade taking off from a land base and training together out at sea, illustrating how attack and multirole helicopters could be used together in maritime operations. That broader maritime role is notable because the Z-10 was developed mainly for battlefields on land. China’s first dedicated attack helicopter emerged from a programme that drew on foreign expertise. Kamov general designer Sergei Mikheyev said in 2013 that the Russian bureau had secretly designed the helicopter’s baseline configuration for China in 1995 – a preliminary design known as Project 941 – before further development continued under Chinese direction. The first prototype flew in April 2003. Pratt & Whitney Canada also supplied 10 engines for development aircraft in 2001 and 2002, while production versions later switched to Chinese power plants. The tandem-seat helicopter carries a chin-mounted 23mm cannon and can be armed with anti-tank missiles, rockets and short-range air-to-air missiles, giving the PLA Army a purpose-built platform for anti-armour strikes, close air support and armed escort. The Z-10 has also continued to evolve in PLA service. Upgraded versions have appeared with extra armour, upward-facing exhausts intended to reduce their infrared signature, a new identification system and a new BeiDou antenna. The PLA is also testing how the helicopter can work with drones. Chinese reports citing CCTV said crews practised engaging a drone with the helicopter’s cannon in 2026, while another exercise paired Z-10s and Z-20T assault helicopters with a KVD-002 drone. A separate analysis published by the China Landpower Studies Centre said the exercise showed coordination between helicopter crews and drone operators, but did not show that Z-10 crews themselves controlled the drone. The IISS Military Balance 2026, published by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, lists about 200 Z-10s in service with the PLA Army and another eight Z-10Ks with the air force’s Airborne Corps. China also adapted the Z-10 for the export market. The resulting Z-10ME made its public debut in 2018 at Airshow China in Zhuhai. Six years later, a demonstrator at the Singapore Airshow was shown with additional features including a mast-mounted millimetre-wave radar and directed infrared countermeasures. Pakistan inducted the Z-10ME into army aviation service in August 2025, becoming its first and so far only confirmed foreign operator. The number of Z-10MEs acquired by Islamabad has not been publicly disclosed. The Z-10 is considerably lighter than the US-made AH-64E Apache, which is also operated by the Taiwanese army. Janes puts its maximum take-off weight at an estimated 7 tonnes, about 3.4 tonnes less than the Apache’s maximum operating weight. While the figures are not strictly like-for-like, the gap reflects the Z-10’s smaller overall design, which gives it less scope to add fuel, armour, weapons and other equipment. That helps explain why China is also looking at a larger attack helicopter. The country is now testing a new design commonly referred to as the Z-21, though the designation remains unofficial. First seen in 2024, the tandem-seat aircraft is substantially larger than the Z-10. Separate test flights in 2026 have shown it carrying external fuel tanks and, on another occasion, a mast-mounted radar. The June analysis said the fuel-tank tests pointed to an emphasis on longer-range missions and assessed that the new attack helicopter could enter PLA Army service by the end of 2027, though China has announced no service date. Its larger size could also provide more capacity for fuel, armour, sensors and weapons. In an amphibious assault on Taiwan, the analysis said, the Z-21 could operate alongside Z-10s and Z-19s during beach landings or escort Z-20 transport helicopters in air-assault operations.

title: Chinese ‘Coffee Grandma’ learns brewing to save son’s cafe, inspires female independence
description: To perfect her latte art, Zhao mixes dish soap with hot water to mimic milk foam and uses soy sauce as a stand-in for coffee.
content: An 86-year-old grandmother in China has become a social media sensation for operating a coffee shop for over a decade – a business she took over from her son in 2015, despite having no experience with coffee at the time. Zhao Qiying, affectionately known as the “Coffee Grandma,” revealed that the shop, located in downtown Qingdao in eastern China’s Shandong province, was nearly bankrupt due to her son’s lack of business acumen, according to the Peninsular Metropolis News. At that time, Zhao was disheartened by the passing of her husband. Her son suggested she manage the coffee shop to help distract her, advising her to merely serve as a doorkeeper since few customers visited the outlet. Despite her initial reservations, Zhao wanted to learn how to make coffee for customers. However, no institution was willing to accept her as a student due to her age, prompting her to take matters into her own hands. She taught herself through coffee-making books and received tips from her son, gradually honing her skills. Zhao mentioned that the most challenging aspect was mastering latte art. To practise, she innovatively used washing powder in boiled water to mimic milk and soy sauce as a substitute for coffee liquid. After six months, Zhao had become proficient in preparing 10 types of coffee and cooking quick meals, including spaghetti and French fries. In recent years, her cafe has thrived, attracting customers from various age groups. Many patrons praise Zhao’s coffee, describing it as “authentic and free from excessive frills,” while others admire her spirited nature. “Grandma Zhao is in excellent health. She always sits up straight,” said a regular customer, Liu, who remarked on Zhao’s vitality. “She is remarkable for making coffee on her own. Her story inspires us. We young people should strive to overcome challenges like she has,” Liu added. Zhao occasionally receives help from her close friend of over 30 years. She expressed that running the coffee shop can be hectic, but she prefers it to idling at home. “I enjoy chatting with my customers. They come from all over the country, sharing breaking news or customs from their hometowns,” Zhao shared. “I impart my life philosophy to them: to live for oneself and not through others,” she added. Zhao once advised a female customer not to rush into marriage but to focus on independence first. Her son encourages her to continue running the coffee shop as long as her health permits. An internet user who visited Zhao’s cafe commented on social media: “I told her, ‘Grandma, I hope my later years will be as fulfilling as yours.’ She replied, ‘Yours will be even better than mine.’ I truly admire this grandma.” Another online observer remarked: “It feels like my dream has come true in this cafe.”

title: Nobel Medicine Prize awarded to US-German trio for work on optogenetics
description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were honoured for their research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
content: American Karl ⁠Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday for developing optogenetics, a technique that uses light to control individual nerve cells in the brain. The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, had been selected for their “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”. “This method [optogenetics] makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” said Thomas Perlmann, secretary general of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute. Anna Wedell, a professor in genetics and a member of the Nobel Committee for ‌Physiology or Medicine, said a new era in neuroscience had opened but it was only the beginning. “For the first time we can actually start to understand how the brain processes information and how different neurons interact across the brain,” she said. The trio will share a prize sum of 12 million Swedish crowns (US$1.2 million). Announcements will follow in the coming days on this year’s Nobel physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics prizes, with the winner or winners of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to be announced on Friday. Deisseroth said he was still awake in the early hours when he was called from Stockholm. “I was not yet asleep, being a night owl, and now I don’t think I’ll be able to sleep for quite a while,” he said. Deisseroth was training to become a neurosurgeon when he encountered patients he could not help at a psychiatric clinic. That encounter – ⁠witnessing suffering he had no tools to treat – prompted a question that would define his career: why does the brain work so differently in different people? The answer would come from an unexpected place: an alga, and two German scientists ‌driven by equally simple curiosity. Hegemann, fascinated by exploration and unknown territory, began investigating in the early 1990s how the alga Chlamydomonas reacts to light in half a millisecond. He hypothesised that a single protein both captured light and acted as an ion channel. Nagel tested this hypothesis by injecting Chlamydomonas genes into frog eggs, discovering channelrhodopsin-2 – a light-sensitive ion channel. In 2003, Nagel and ‌Hegemann published findings showing the protein could be introduced into human cells to generate electrical impulses using light. Deisseroth showed the technique in rat nerve cells in 2005, and the method was named optogenetics in ⁠2006. One scientist at Hegemann’s Max Planck Institute in Frankfurt in ⁠2007 recalled researchers taping optical fibres salvaged from Christmas decorations to microscopes. “We didn’t really know how it worked. We didn’t really have any tools,” said Dima Kuzmin, a neurochemist at the time. “And it was massively exciting.” The three laureates’ research is now providing insights about brain disorders. Animal models ‌are being used to understand schizophrenia, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, epilepsy and addiction – conditions that affect millions of people worldwide and have limited treatment options. Deisseroth used optogenetics to control the movements of mouse whiskers by activating specific nerve cells in the motor cortex. He also used light to wake sleeping mice, confirming that specific ‌nerve cells ‌control wakefulness. “There are mouse models of dementia, epilepsy, addiction. By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in mice, we can understand where to look in humans,” Wedell said. Researchers are also applying the technique to try to restore ‌vision to people blinded by retinitis pigmentosa – a progressive eye disease – by inserting a light-sensitive protein into the retina. They also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, potentially allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices. “When you think ⁠about it in the retina, all patients need to do is open their eyes and you have the light. So it makes a lot of sense as a potential therapy,” said Paul Bresge, CEO of US biotechnology company Ray Therapeutics, ⁠which is developing a therapy to treat retinitis pigmentosa. The most advanced of the treatments are autism spectrum disorder therapy by a US-based biotech company MapLight, co-founded by Deisseroth, and a vision restoration medicine for retinitis pigmentosa by Nanoscope, also based in the United States, though both are still some way from reaching patients.
