Manuel Valero, researcher at Barcelona-based Hospital del Mar, where he heads the Neural Computation Laboratory, said optogenetics had “allowed us to ‌push the boundaries between science and science fiction”. “In laboratory animals, we ‌have managed to control emotions, create false memories or even recover lost memories in models of Alzheimer’s disease,” Valero said. “Perhaps the great promise it has yet to fulfil is precisely one of its founding promises: its ability to treat diseases of the human brain.” Each laureate’s path reflected their distinct character. Hegemann developed an early fascination with exploration, viewing scientific research as charting unknown territory. Nagel had worked as a teacher, opened a cafe and taken up hang gliding as a hobby. The suffering witnessed by Deisseroth at the psychiatric clinic drove him to seek deeper understanding of the brain through research rather than clinical practice alone.

title: HKMA licenses Bakai Bank, city’s first from Central Asia
description: Bakai Bank, one of Kyrgyzstan’s largest lenders, set up in Hong Kong as China and Central Asia’s trade links are increasing.
content: Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has granted a banking licence to Bakai Bank, marking the first Central Asian bank to set up in Hong Kong amid closer ties in the economy and trade flows between China and the region, according to a statement on Monday. Bakai Bank, one of the largest lenders in Kyrgyzstan, will operate as a restricted licence bank in Hong Kong. It will be the 17th restricted licence bank in Hong Kong. Under the licence, it can take deposits of at least HK$500,000 (US$63,776) and conduct corporate banking and merchant banking business, but not retail businesses. Andreas Meletiou, CEO of Bakai Bank Hong Kong, said the lender wanted to use Hong Kong as a platform to expand in the region. “We have chosen Hong Kong as our first stop of international expansion because it offers a very strong platform for us to play the role as the bridge between Central Asia and Asia-Pacific,” Meletiou said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Bakai Bank will be the first bank to ever establish presence outside Kyrgyzstan, and the first bank from Central Asia to ever establish a presence in Hong Kong. It is an important milestone for Central Asia as a whole, especially considering the evolving relationship between Central Asia and East Asia.” Hong Kong has made efforts to expand commercial ties with Central Asia, with Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu leading the city’s first delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June. Central Asia, a five-country region comprising Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan and Tajikistan, is located at the heart of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013 to promote trade flows. Mainland China became the largest partner of Central Asian countries for the first time last year, with total value of trade in goods reaching US$106.3 billion, up 12 per cent compared to a year earlier, according to data from the Ministry of Commerce. “Central Asia is a key part of the Belt and Road Initiative for China. When trade routes are being challenged, and especially [as] the sea-bound trade routes are becoming riskier in the current geopolitical landscape, Central Asia is getting more prominent,” Meletiou said. China’s exports to Central Asia were US$71.2 billion last year, led by machinery, electrical and hi-tech products, while China’s imports from Central Asia were US$35.1 billion, including agricultural and industrial goods. Meletiou said the bank now had 35 staff and would expand to about 50 in the future. It would target serving companies with their needs for payment, foreign exchange and financing in trade and other investment in Central Asia and mainland China. “We strongly feel that we are at the right place at the right time,” he said. “The market opportunity and the Hong Kong government initiatives are aligned with our strategy for us to play the bridging role between these two parts of the world.”

title: Formula 1 to investigate software bug in Malaysia race; Verstappen wants ‘lesson learned’
description: Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, Red Bull’s eventual race winner Max Verstappen among several affected by glitch at Sepang circuit.
content: Formula 1’s governing body has promised a full investigation into a ⁠software bug that caused chaos ⁠and forced the start of Sunday’s Bahrain ⁠Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted with drivers feeling like they were in battery-powered cars made of Lego. Ferrari’s seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull’s four-time champion and eventual race winner Max Verstappen were among several affected by the glitch on a formation lap after ‌torrential rain and a long delay at Malaysia’s steamy Sepang circuit. Verstappen compared the experience to a “Lego race” held at Silverstone before the British Grand Prix, while Hamilton, the sport’s most successful driver of all time, had to stop his car on track and restart it in what he said was a career first. “It was like the Lego race,” Hamilton said. “Same speed.” The on-board algorithms that decide how and when to deploy the car’s electrical hybrid power were seemingly thwarted by the drivers using less acceleration than usual to deal with the slippery conditions. “It’s not what you want in the sport,” said Verstappen, who earned his first win of 2026 and the 72nd of his decorated career. “I hope there is a lesson learned.” After a season in which the Dutch driver has struggled to adapt to changes to Formula 1 cars, the rest of the field was able to feel his pain for a day. Those new cars struggled to operate ⁠in the wet conditions, leading to an initial 40-minute delay at the start and then another 53-minute ‌delay when software issues plagued some cars, including Verstappen’s. “It was very hectic with a lot of different things in the start,” Verstappen said. “No power, so you have ‌to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call ⁠with the intermediates, and ⁠after that, step by step, we moved our way forward.” The episode was the latest in a difficult first season for the new era of cars and engines, ⁠with drivers at the pinnacle of motorsport unhappy since the opening race with the power units’ increased electrical component ‌and the need for energy management. The governing FIA said afterwards that “an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led ‌to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars”. “As a result, the FIA technical ⁠department removed the energy ⁠limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, ‌enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race. “This issue had not been detected by the FIA ‌or the ‌teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power ‌unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.” The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis told reporters the lack ⁠of pre-season testing in wet conditions had played a part in the chaos. “Some cars went very slowly, almost came ⁠to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely,” he said. “That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to ‌start again. “I think if we had ‌had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.” Sepang was the first race weekend of the season with wet conditions, although the track dried during the race. “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time,” Tombazis said. When the race finally started, Verstappen dropped from his position on the pole ‌into third place before passing Kimi Antonelli on Lap 13, and went on to win from there, finishing 2.3 seconds ahead of the ‌standings leader. ‌Hamilton was third after rallying from 18th place. “It’s a really nice one, after the year ‌that we’ve had and the progression that we’ve made,” Verstappen said. “I’m incredibly proud of everyone, and it’s just ⁠super nice to win here.” Formula 1 moves on to Singapore for a night race and sprint this weekend.

title: Ex-prince Andrew takes UK police to court to ‘quash’ Epstein affair search warrants
description: The 66-year-old is challenging Thames Valley Police over searches of his former and current homes on royal estates.
content: Britain’s disgraced ex-prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched a legal challenge over search warrants for his royal homes issued before his February arrest, Britain’s judiciary confirmed on Monday, in an unprecedented royal move in modern times. The judiciary confirmed the High Court was to hold a private hearing on Thursday, as King Charles’ brother challenges Thames Valley Police over the searches in Windsor, west of London, and Sandringham, eastern England. The force arrested the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten, on his 66th birthday on February 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his links to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Andrew was released the same day after hours of police questioning but remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in his associations with the American financier. His shock arrest prompted King Charles to issue a statement insisting “the law must take its course”. The Daily Telegraph reported the legal challenge late on Sunday. The newspaper noted it was the first time a member of Britain’s royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649. It said his legal team wanted to examine whether the search warrants granted by a judge sitting at London’s Old Bailey court – formally known as the Central Criminal Court – were lawful. A Palace source said Andrew had been told ⁠that money provided from private ⁠funds by his brother the king should not be used to fund his legal challenge. Andrew’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The judiciary’s press office said “the case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026”. Andrew’s arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the ex-prince, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections. The government has even considered passing a law to remove him from the line of succession. Scandal has engulfed the king’s younger brother since one of Epstein’s accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoir that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager. The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a US civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability. The Thames Valley Police investigation follows new revelations from documents relating to the American financier released by the United States earlier this year, including emails in which Andrew appeared to share potentially confidential information with him. In one November 2010 email seen by Agence France-Presse, Andrew appeared to share with the US financier reports on his visit to several Asian countries. Epstein had been convicted in the United States in 2008 of procuring a child for prostitution. At least nine British police forces confirmed they were looking into claims – some related to Andrew – stemming from the batch of some three million Epstein files released by the US authorities in January. However, the Thames Valley investigation appears to be the most advanced. Its officers, who swooped on the remote Sandringham royal estate in eastern England to detain Andrew, searched his home there and his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, west of London. The raid in Windsor lasted six days. In response to Andrew’s legal challenge, Thames Valley Police said in a statement that its “investigation into misconduct in public office continues”. “We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained,” it added. “As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.” Additional reporting by Reuters

title: US defence experts to work inside Taiwan military HQ under reported pact
description: Move would mark a key upgrade in military ties but sparks domestic concern over budget growth and loss of strategic autonomy.
content: A reported plan to station US defence personnel inside Taiwan’s military headquarters would take mutual cooperation into the heart of defence planning, potentially angering Beijing while raising questions over Taipei’s policymaking autonomy and military secrecy. According to Taiwanese media reports at the weekend, the Pentagon plans to send one official from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Policy and one expert from the Institute for Defence Analyses (IDA) to work on a long-term basis at the defence ministry’s headquarters in Taipei. The two would aid policy coordination and combat capability assessments under an expanded “Taiwan-US Defence Ministry Joint Cooperation Assessment” programme that would run from this year to 2028, according to the reports. The programme has a total budget of more than NT$471 million (US$14.8 million), including NT$152.5 million this year for expenses such as US personnel and consultancy costs, travel, research equipment and data collection, and interpreting for classified-level meetings. If confirmed, the arrangement would mark a significant change from the existing US military presence in Taiwan, where American personnel have generally worked as trainers or through the American Institute in Taiwan, Washington’s de facto embassy on the self-ruled island. The reports said the US representatives could provide on-site advice on overall defence planning, war games for Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises and assessments of major weapons procurement programmes. Taiwan’s defence ministry did not confirm details of the reported arrangement. On Sunday, it said only that Taipei and Washington continued to deepen military exchanges to strengthen the armed forces’ overall defence capabilities and resilience. It declined to elaborate on how the cooperation would be implemented. On Monday afternoon, a representative for the US Department of Defence said it had no comment on the reports. Wang Ting-yu, a legislator from Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party, has described the reported arrangement as a “major upgrade” in military cooperation. He said on Monday that in addition to hundreds of US military instructors – sometimes referred to in Taiwan as “American English-language teachers” – helping to train Taiwanese forces, US representatives would now work directly inside the defence ministry. “This means US personnel will directly enter the core of Taiwan’s defence policymaking establishment, assisting with policy coordination and assessments of combat capabilities,” Wang said, describing it as an upgrade of direct military cooperation “to the highest level”. But Ma Wen-chun, a legislator of the main opposition party, the Kuomintang, questioned the sharp increase in spending on the cooperation programme, saying its annual budget had risen more than twelvefold compared with earlier years. “Supporting Taiwan-US military exchanges and cooperation, and supporting national defence, does not mean the budget can be allowed to grow without restraint,” Ma said. She questioned how many US personnel would come to Taiwan, how many meetings would be held and what concrete benefits the programme would deliver. The defence ministry had yet to provide specific answers, she said. Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei, said it had long been an “open secret” that serving and retired US military personnel were in Taiwan to provide training and advice and had taken part in Han Kuang exercises. But stationing personnel directly inside the defence ministry would be considerably more sensitive. “Beijing is certain to protest and could respond with measures such as expanded military exercises and intimidation,” he said, adding that this could explain Taipei’s reluctance to publicly confirm the arrangement. He said he did not expect the US personnel to wear uniforms because that could be interpreted as a more formalised US-Taiwan military relationship and might further provoke Beijing. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any unilateral change to the cross-strait status quo by force and has been committed to supplying it with weapons. Despite the closer cooperation, Zivon Wang said he did not believe US representatives would dictate Taiwan’s defence strategy. “Many aspects of Taiwan’s military strategy are already closely linked with those of the United States,” he said. “Their main purpose in Taiwan would be communication and coordination rather than directly controlling Taiwan’s defence policy or strategy. Taiwan would retain the leading role.” He acknowledged that US representatives were likely to gain access to at least some classified information, noting that the two sides already shared intelligence on People’s Liberation Army exercises and other activities. However, he said it was less clear how sensitive the information available to them would be, which could depend partly on the broader US-China relationship. James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based international relations and strategic studies scholar, cautioned that embedding US personnel in the defence establishment could gradually increase Washington’s influence over Taiwanese decision making. While the arrangement would represent “a significant upgrade in security ties”, Taiwan’s defence decisions could become increasingly influenced by US strategic planning and priorities, he said. “If US national interests were ever to diverge from Taiwan’s interests, Taiwan could find itself facing an uncomfortable strategic dilemma, with limited flexibility to pursue an independent defence posture.” Chen further argued that the asymmetrical nature of the relationship left Taipei with relatively little leverage and could make it difficult for the island to resist US policies that did not fully coincide with its interests. Ho Jeng-sheng, vice-chairman of the Taiwan External Relations Research and Development Association, on Monday drew a distinction between benefiting from US expertise and becoming strategically dependent on Washington. “The question is how far that cooperation should go before defence autonomy turns into outsourcing Taiwan’s defence,” he said. US intelligence, technology, war-gaming models and strategic advice could help Taiwan improve its capabilities, Ho said, but decisions on defence policy, military command and force deployment ultimately had to remain in Taiwanese hands. “The United States can have a seat at Taiwan’s defence conference table, but it cannot occupy the head of that table,” Ho said. “Military cooperation between the two sides can be upgraded, but Taiwan’s defence autonomy cannot be downgraded.”

title: Opinion | Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
description: With resale transactions outpacing new home sales for the first time, stabilising the existing housing stock has become vital.
content: For decades, China’s property sector was defined by spectacular scale: farmland transformed into suburbs, skylines rising across regional hubs and, more recently, the prominent unravelling of heavily indebted developers. Yet beneath those dramatic changes, a far quieter and more consequential transformation is taking shape. Official figures published by the National Bureau of Statistics in September reveal that secondary market home transactions have surpassed new residential builds in volume. Nationwide registered resales reached 549 million square metres, signalling that housing demand in China has not vanished. Rather, it appears to have structurally migrated. This marks a departure from the previous growth model. For a quarter of a century, following the end of the old welfare housing system in 1998, China’s property market operated on a high-velocity loop: developers acquired municipal land, pre-sold unfinished apartments, collected buyer cash and funnelled those advances into their next projects. That mechanism turned residential construction into the primary economic engine of the country. That engine is now losing momentum. What is emerging is not merely a smaller version of the old market but a different market altogether. The centre of gravity is shifting – from developers selling a promise of tomorrow to households trading the homes of today. The shift reflects not only a change in policy but a change in how households think about housing itself. For years, policymakers responded to property downturns with a familiar toolkit: lower down payments, cheaper mortgages and local incentives to clear unsold homes. But those measures are increasingly running up against a more fundamental reality. The question is no longer simply whether homes can be made cheaper to buy but whether households still have compelling reasons to buy them. China is no longer a country suffering from a simple shortage of housing. Urban living space has risen to 42 square metres per person, while property remains the dominant component of household wealth. Under those conditions, buying a home is no longer simply a bet on rising prices. For many families, it is also a decision about protecting an asset that already represents a large share of their balance sheet. The crisis of the presale model has reinforced that caution. After years of stalled projects and developer defaults, buyers have become more sceptical of paying for homes that exist mainly on paper. Existing properties offer something increasingly valuable: certainty. They can be inspected, occupied and transferred immediately. The second-hand market also performs another function that the new-home market has struggled to provide: price discovery. The secondary market has increasingly become where the real value of housing is negotiated. This creates an awkward policy problem. Measures designed to make new homes more attractive can unintentionally put pressure on old ones. New projects have increasingly offered larger usable spaces, better layouts and other features that make existing apartments look less competitive. What helps one segment of the market can therefore weaken the perceived value of another. That matters because housing is not merely a consumption good in China. It is also the largest store of wealth for many households. When the value of existing homes falls sharply, families feel poorer, become more cautious and may postpone other forms of spending. Existing properties offer something increasingly valuable: certainty. They can be inspected, occupied and transferred immediately For policymakers, this changes the objective. Supporting new construction may boost activity in the short term. But preserving confidence in the enormous stock of homes already owned by households has become a separate economic priority. There is, however, a difficult trade-off. A healthy market for existing homes can help stabilise household wealth but it does little to revive the fiscal and financial machinery built around new construction. Resales generate neither the land transfer revenue on which local governments once relied nor the presale cash flow that enabled developers to finance their next projects. Collapsing land sales leave local treasuries with a severe fiscal deficit. Adapting to this shift, state-backed champions like China Resources Land and China Overseas Land and Investment are abandoning volume expansion for asset management and urban renewal, pivoting from converting land into new flats to extracting long-term value from existing urban stock. Recent policy changes point in the same direction. Greater emphasis on completed home sales and tighter requirements around presales raise the standards for new development and may reduce the supply of future projects. The shift offers no easy substitute for the old growth model. China cannot simply replace millions of newly built flats with an equivalent volume of second-hand transactions and expect the same economic effects. Existing home sales can redistribute wealth and establish market prices, but they do not generate the same demand for land, construction, materials, credit and local infrastructure. China’s housing market is therefore entering a period in which protecting wealth may matter more than expanding scale. The country is unlikely to return to an era when residential construction could serve as a near-limitless engine of economic growth. For much of the past generation, progress was visible in the changing skyline. In the years ahead, it may be measured less by how many towers are added than by whether the homes already standing can preserve enough value and liquidity to give the families who own them a sense of security. After decades of building at extraordinary speed, China’s housing market is entering a different era, one in which progress can no longer be measured by how many homes are added, but by how much value the existing housing stock can retain.

title: Coleman Wong wins Asian Games tennis gold, first in Hong Kong history
description: The young athlete’s victory – which has secured his spot at the 2028 Olympics – has also helped the city reach a record medal count at the games.
content:
Anyone watching tennis player Coleman Wong Chak-lam win his historic men’s singles title at the Asian Games might have wondered if he even knows what pressure is.
The 22-year-old Hongkonger needed just one chance at victory over China’s Wu Yibing, ranked No 111 in the world. Winning would also come with a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
The manner of Wong’s 6-2, 6-4 triumph at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre would suggest it is the 99 players ranked above him who should worry.
Wong’s gold was the eighth the city’s athletes had won in Japan. Windsurfers Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet added two more soon after, making it the most Hong Kong has ever won at a single Games.
Within the city’s overall medal count of 54 is a record 11 golds, three more than in 2023.
“Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the colour,” Wong said. “But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement.”
He also acknowledged the role his family played in getting him to this stage of his tennis career.
“Since I was young, my family always had the mindset of, ‘OK, if you want to do it, just go for it’,” Wong said.
He hopes his success can convince other families in the city to take a leap of faith in sports.
“Sometimes parents in Hong Kong might feel, ‘Ah, is that doable?’ They overthink it. Instead, if kids want to do it, let them give it a try first. This is a huge influence my family had on me,” said Wong, who graduated from Diocesan Boys’ School and won the Sportsperson category in the 2021/22 Student of the Year Awards.
“I went abroad and out into the world to try at a very young age. Losing and winning didn’t matter; it was about going out to improve.”
Wong and Wu are no strangers on the court. Three years ago at the Games in Hangzhou, Wong knocked out his mainland rival in the third round; last November, Wu beat Wong in the semi-finals of the National Games.
“He’s a really good player, and we always have a great match every time we play each other,” Wong said. “You can’t think that much at that moment because it’s so fast, and the game, the margin is so slim. So I was just trying to focus on what I can do at that point.”
The groundwork for Wong’s win was done in the first set when the only real moments of menace for Wong came from the three lucky breaks that involved the ball hitting the net and dropping in Wu’s favour.
Otherwise, the silver medallist’s game in the main was characterised by a succession of unforced errors at inopportune moments, namely when winners sailed long on crucial points.
It was a closer affair in the second set, with the pair going toe to toe, and Wu showed signs of the form that once made him world No 54.
“Obviously I was a little bit nervous because I’ve never been to this stage before, but it was tough,” Wong said. “The whole match was really close.”
Wu had every opportunity to hold the game, but he hit potential winners long or wide and struggled with his first serve.
At 5-4 down and with the match on the line, Wu hit Wong’s first serve out and then could only watch as the Hongkonger’s power did the rest.
Having won, Wong sank to the floor in celebration before rushing over to the coaches’ box to embrace friends and family.
The next generation of Hong Kong athletes will have an opportunity to watch Wong on the Olympic stage in Los Angeles, as long as he remains in the top 500 players in the world.
“It’s a very happy moment indeed,” Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui told the South China Morning Post. “I’m very glad as we now have every reason to keep tennis in the Sports Institute’s Tier A, and our decision last year to make a special arrangement for tennis has paid off.”
Michael Cheng, president of the Hong Kong China Tennis Association, felt Wong’s gold and the bronze won by women’s doubles pair Eudice Chong and Wong Hong-yi the day before showed “that the long-term investment is bearing fruit”.
Cheng added: “I’m thrilled because it shows the structural alignment is right and hopefully the pipeline will come.”
Wong, meanwhile, has two years before the Olympics, but he won’t be resting on his laurels.
“I feel my current form is pretty good, and I want to keep maintaining it and continue improving, because I feel it’s never enough,” he said. “I still have 99 players ahead of me [in the ATP rankings], so I’ll keep climbing.”

title: Why Josie Ho is diving back into the macabre for her new horror-crime thriller The Mage
description: Ho, who plays a spirit medium in the film, talks about non-traditional horror, her doctor-turned-co-star, and taking on atypical roles.
content: During a whirlwind September press tour in Thailand, Josie Ho Chiu-yee cuts a glamorous figure at the centre of the Bangkok International Film Festival, where she even receives a royal souvenir from Thailand’s Princess Ubolratana Rajakanya Sirivadhana Barnavadi, a prominent patron of Thai cinema. But what Ho, a daughter of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun, has come to promote is much darker and grittier: her latest feature, The Mage. As both lead actress of the horror-meets-crime thriller and de facto co-producer through her production company, 852 Films, Ho dives back into the macabre realm that first defined her producing chops. In the film, when a series of grisly deaths rocks Hong Kong, garbage collector Lan (played by Ho) must use her skills as a spirit medium to locate souls trapped inside discarded items and guide them to reincarnation. When police officer Wong (Carlos Chan Ka-lok) notices the scavenger woman at every crime scene, he begins investigating her as a prime suspect – before the two eventually team up to confront a greater evil. Ho’s vision for the project was shaped in part by her time on the jury at the 2018 Sitges Film Festival, a prestigious showcase for fantasy and horror cinema, where she was told to look out for films that “don’t look like traditional horror”. “It doesn’t have to be ghosts, or locking up two little girls in the basement with a clown,” she tells the South China Morning Post during a quieter moment in Bangkok. “We don’t want those; we want new stuff.” The Mage “is not just a horror movie; it’s really a drama”, she says. “For me, in every single film, I look for the humanity of the character and her moral values.” She also notes at the film’s press conference that she believes The Mage is ultimately about karmic retribution. With her husband Conroy Chan Chi-chung taking the producer credit, Ho was relatively hands-off in the film’s creation. “Usually for 852 Films, we come up with our own ideas, and we find a scriptwriter, or we lure a director into developing it with us. But this time, it’s pure Pang Brothers [the film’s co-directors] – Danny Pang Fat’s idea [to be precise].” A laid-back approach to a gritty shoot Pang pitched the idea to Ho, and she fell in love with it immediately. Ho, who started filming The Mage the very next day after having been abroad for her husband’s surgery following a life-threatening ruptured aorta, admits she “didn’t really have a chance” to read the script before shooting. “It was an entirely different method from how I [typically] research and explore different angles or different choices in each scene,” Ho says. “We’re old friends with Pang, so I think it has a lot to do with trust.” Recalling their collaboration, Ho says that Pang would explain what he wanted before filming each scene. This laid-back approach allowed her to improvise. The Mage’s production featured demanding physical stunts and extensive set rigs. Pang even recalls refusing to film a scene unless the production team could spend extra money to fill Lan’s entire bedroom with water. “My only request was, ‘Please don’t let it be the water from the raining car trucks,’” Ho says, laughing. “Please find some better water. Because I have to be soaked in the water and garbage.” The cast worked with real rubbish rinsed in water, and also filmed at actual refuse sites. As a self-professed germaphobe, Ho found it a daunting yet necessary task, even if it resulted in her developing a painful eye stye after extended exposure to the grime. A doctor on call sheet Fortunately, she has a medical professional on call. As Ho shuffles through her gruelling schedule in Bangkok, one thing remains constant: the Iranian doctor-turned-actor Iman Taheri by her side. Ho and Chan signed Taheri, who previously worked as Chan’s doctor, to 852 Films as an actor after learning about his showbiz dreams. In The Mage, Taheri plays an English-speaking police chief who dismisses spirits. This was Taheri’s first acting role. Because of Taheri’s determination to study cinema, Ho says she was not too concerned about his greenness or lack of Cantonese skills when signing him. Taheri now lives with Ho and Chan, and looks certain to remain their favourite person; Ho responds with a resounding no when asked if she will sign any other actors in the future. “In my past career as a surgeon, I was trained to be in control,” Taheri says of his approach. “I was attached to the facts, and I was attached to knowing everything beforehand. But a big part of acting is to let go.” Ho adds that Taheri “has a Greek mythology god-type body shape”, contrasting him with the more feminine-presenting male celebrities in the current limelight. “There used to be a lot of ‘men’ in our Hong Kong cinema, and suddenly they’re all gone,” she continues, before expressing the hope that Taheri can take the lead in popularising that look – especially with The Mage 2, the planned sequel that has already wrapped up filming and entered post-production. Alongside the challenges of producing independently, Ho is focused on the broader horizon of regional storytelling. She believes a “pan-Asia” movement is the next step in Asian cinema, especially after learning that Hollywood executives often do not see the value in supporting Asian arts. Taheri similarly speaks of a return of the “magic of the Silk Road”, envisioning a resurgence of vibrant cultural and artistic exchanges across the continent. “I hope that Iman can bring us over and beyond the Silk Road,” Ho says. “I’m partially Persian and … I really want to try to go to Iran.” She also notes that Taheri is the first “Iranian connection” she has made. Embracing the anti-heroine Reflecting on her career, Ho admits she often chose roles critics would not typically expect from a billionaire’s daughter to distinguish herself from her family name. She still takes on these bizarre roles, as is obvious in The Mage, but no longer as a deliberate act of self-demarcation. “I wasn’t quite happy then,” she says, referring to a time when she faced mean-spirited tabloid headlines. “But now I’m pretty comfortable with being myself.” Her company 852 Films gave her a new sense of freedom. In Dream Home (2010), one of its first projects, Ho played an “anti-heroine”. “In Hong Kong, they didn’t know that word – they just called me a villain,” she explains. “A lot of jobs were offered to me, fortunately, but even Hollywood asked me to become the villain. I was kind of stereotyped into [playing] that. So when Danny Pang had this role for me [in The Mage], I immediately blindfolded myself and jumped right into it.” As The Mage prepares to haunt cinemas across Asia in the coming weeks – having secured distribution in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam – it is perhaps Ho’s turn to prove that the future of independent filmmaking lies not in playing it safe, but rather in diving blindly into the dark.
