title: Southeast Asia starts to rethink its AI data centre boom: ‘at what cost?’
description: With Thailand pausing projects and Malaysia facing grid pressure, regulators are learning that hosting the AI boom comes with a heavy cost.
content: Southeast Asian governments are learning some hard truths about the data centre boom they spent years working to attract, analysts say – it promises jobs, digital infrastructure and a foothold in the AI economy, but the rapid buildout is also straining power grids, land and regulatory systems. “There is this enthusiasm to attract investments, but now it raises the question: at what cost and at what speed?” said policy researcher Mark Manantan, a research fellow for the Centre for Global Security at La Trobe University. At first, governments had good reason to aggressively compete for data centre investment, said political economist Alvin Camba, a non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Indo-Pacific Security Initiative. “They bring in large investments, support cloud and AI infrastructure, and governments worry about being left behind,” said Camba, who is also director of research at US-based AI firm Lyvi. “In that sense, not having enough capacity looked worse than having too much. The problem is that governments understood the upside much better than the downstream costs.” That tension is now pushing governments across the region to take a closer look at data centre projects. Last week, the governor of Indonesia’s West Java province ordered an immediate halt to construction at a site run by Singapore’s BDx Data Centres following an inspection, reportedly because key permits had yet to be issued, including the project’s environmental impact assessment. BDx, which runs data centres for cloud companies and other enterprises across Asia, broke ground on the 640-megawatt AI data centre campus in Jatiluhur on September 22. On September 4, Thailand paused work on 166 data centre projects – 49 of which were under construction and 117 awaiting approval – while government agencies drew up nationwide standards governing resource use, locations, safety and economic benefits. “These are different levels of government responding to different regulatory gaps,” Manantan said. “The buildout outran the rule book.” Stricter rules will not automatically make Southeast Asia less competitive, according to Camba, as investors do not necessarily need the most permissive regulatory environment. “They need to know that they can actually secure power, water, permits and connectivity and continue operating predictably,” he said. “The countries with reliable infrastructure and predictable rules may actually be more competitive than the ones that simply approve everything.” Singapore was one example of this, he said, with Johor also moving in the same direction as it continued to attract large investments. “Investors can live with rules, but not with unpredictability,” Manantan said. “Competitiveness will depend less on how loose the rules are and more on how coordinated and predictable they are.” Taking stock The recent rethink also lent regional governments more bargaining power, Camba said. “If electricity and water are scarce, they can ask what exactly they are getting in return. That could mean local procurement, renewable power, technology transfer or more investment in domestic AI capacity.” James Guild, an assistant professor of political economy at the Indonesian International Islamic University, said the regulatory interventions were a response to the rapid acceleration of data centre investment across the region. “Investment is pouring in, there are lots of project approvals and applications, and this is possibly straining regulators’ ability to keep up,” he said. “A pause or slow-down gives them time to adjust and maybe seek to get more value out of these projects.” Analysts say the same factors that make Southeast Asia attractive to data centre operators – cheap land, governments eager for investment and affordable power and water – are now becoming constraints. “Once enough projects arrive, those resources stop being abundant,” Camba said. He pointed to Malaysia’s Johor state as a clear example. “It initially attracted enormous investment precisely because those inputs were relatively cheap,” he said. “However, Malaysia is now becoming more selective because the data centre pipeline has grown large enough to pressure power and water resources.” In other words, data centres not only consume scarce resources, they also change the economic realities of the areas that host them. In July, a developer’s consultant withdrew an application to reassess the feasibility of a potential site in Kota Damansara, near the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur, after the local council received nearly 300 objections to its development. At a public hearing in Iloilo province, the central Philippines, in August, residents and farmers protested against a proposed 50MW AI data centre so vociferously that its Norwegian investor withdrew the application days later. Public protests Although public backlash does not appear to be the primary driver of government decisions, analysts say addressing criticism is essential to mitigate the political cost of such projects. “Another important question is whether the demand for data centre services will be sufficient to justify such massive investment outlays,” Guild said. “People are starting to question that assumption even in the US, and it’s worth considering in Southeast Asia as well where so much of economic activity is still informal sector work.” Camba said the objections emerging around individual projects reflected a broader question about who would ultimately bear the costs of the AI data centre buildout. “The pushback comes from the fact that governments competed for these projects before fully understanding what hosting them at scale would mean,” he said. “They understood the investment figures and the strategic argument, as well as the fear of falling behind. What they understood less clearly was what happens when dozens of projects start competing for the same power, water and land.” Public opposition mattered, “because it turns those abstract infrastructure costs into something politicians must respond to”, Camba added. In Bangkok, for example, repeated odour complaints eventually forced the government to send inspectors to a data centre site last month, where they discovered more than 200,000 litres (53,000 gallons) of diesel being stored without a permit. In the Philippines, the government’s US-backed Pax Silica hub – aimed at boosting the country’s AI and semiconductor capabilities while attracting infrastructure investment – has similarly caused the local costs and benefits to be put under the microscope. “Governments sold these projects based on investment and technological competitiveness, but the public experiences them through land use, power demand, water use and local disruption,” Camba said.

title: Spain’s prime minister calls early election as housing becomes a national flashpoint
description: Defeated on housing measures in parliament, Pedro Sanchez gambles on a November 29 vote.
content: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced early general elections on Monday after his government suffered a bruising legislative defeat last week on emergency measures related to the country’s housing crisis. The vote will be held on November 29. In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month. Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees introduced by Sanchez’s government that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation. The setback sparked wide speculation that Sanchez would move up a national election that would have otherwise taken place next year – and seize on his base’s anger over the rejected housing measures. In an address to the nation, Sanchez on Monday argued that a broader progressive coalition in parliament would allow Spaniards to tackle the biggest issues facing their country today. “The time has come, therefore, for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country,” Sanchez said. “Whether you wish to join that far-right wave – which rolls back progress wherever it governs – or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility. Whether you want our country to move backward or continue moving forward,” he said. Sanchez, 54, has been Spain’s prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-standing leaders. He has become one of the leading international progressive heads of government thanks to his defence of migration, his diplomatic efforts to defend Palestinians and his criticism of the American and Israeli war against Iran. He has also enjoyed one of the fastest-growing economies in the developed world in recent years. But back home, the Spanish leader has been hemmed in by a series of legal cases involving his Socialist party as well as his wife and brother, who both deny wrongdoing. He has also struggled to account for this summer’s border crossing by tens of thousands of mostly Moroccans into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where a humanitarian crisis remains two months after the initial crisis. He has led a coalition minority government along with the left-wing junior partner Sumar since 2023. But his reliance on several smaller parties to get anything done has hamstrung his legislative ability. Throughout his political career, Sanchez has earned a reputation as a political escape artist capable of winning elections he looked set to lose. Speculation around whether he would call snap elections centred on the momentum that his party may now have around affordability issues, while the opposition Popular Party – which holds the most seats in parliament already – is likely to define the contest around corruption and the ruling government’s mismanagement of the Ceuta crisis. “Sanchez is choosing this moment because it is arguably the best time to do so, given that the issue of housing frames the electoral conflict or debate in terms that are highly favourable to [his party’s] position,” said Oriol Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. “Sanchez can frame the election – or has realised he can frame it – in very classic left-versus-right terms,” Bartomeus said. The Socialist leader will face Popular Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who aims to take control of the government. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” Feijoo said Monday after the announcement of the snap election. “These are not elections like previous ones in our democracy. This is about Spain defeating Sanchez and what he represents,” he said. The formal dissolution of parliament will need to be approved by the cabinet, which Sanchez has convened for later on Monday.

title: Hong Kong lawmakers say 5-year tax incentive too short to entice major innovative firms
description: Lawmakers back incentive plan but argue that five years not enough to attract firms to establish headquarters or expand operations in city.
content: Hong Kong lawmakers have backed the government’s proposed tax incentives for large innovative companies, but many said on Monday that the planned five-year concession period is too short to attract major firms to establish headquarters or expand operations in the city. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in his policy address last month said the government planned to submit a bill introducing preferential profits tax rates of either 5 per cent or 8.25 per cent, which was half of the city’s standard corporate tax rate of 16.5 per cent, for selected innovative enterprises for up to five years. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told lawmakers at a meeting of the Legislative Council’s financial affairs panel that the incentives would be limited to specific sectors, including advanced manufacturing, finance, logistics and supply chain management, as well as to companies establishing headquarters in Hong Kong. “The special tax rates [scheme] will set a high threshold, with only very large companies that have big expansion plans in Hong Kong and hire many people here qualifying,” Hui said. He did not specify the qualifying thresholds, saying they would vary by industry. Many innovative companies do not earn any money in the first 10 years of operation, so they would not need to pay tax anyway Alan Chan Chung-yee, Legislative Council While lawmakers said they supported the proposal, many questioned whether a five-year tax concession would be sufficient to influence investment decisions. “Many innovative companies do not earn any money in the first 10 years of operation, so they would not need to pay tax anyway,” said lawmaker Alan Chan Chung-yee at the meeting. “The tax incentives would last for only five years and are not attractive to them. A prolonged period of 10 or 15 years may be more appropriate.” Lawmaker Nick Chan Hiu-fung said overseas companies considering relocating their regional headquarters would likely take a longer-term view. “The chief financial officers of many of the largest international technology companies look at the long term,” Nick Chan said. “If the tax reduction only lasts for five years, it is hard to convince their board of directors to move their headquarters here.” Hui said five years should be sufficient, pointing out that Singapore offered similar tax incentives that also lasted for five years. “Companies can apply to renew the five-year period if they continue to expand in Hong Kong for another five years,” Hui said. “Tax incentives are only one of the reasons for companies to come to Hong Kong, as they also eye business opportunities here.” Several lawmakers also raised concerns that the scheme could be abused. Hui said the proposal would differ from other industry-specific tax incentives that were granted automatically once a company reached a certain threshold. Instead, each application would require approval from a committee led by Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po. “The approval process would prevent tax avoidance, and companies would need to report to the government on whether they have implemented their expansion and hiring plans,” Hui said. In an interview with the South China Morning Post last month, Paul Chan said a handful of leading firms from emerging industries were expected to come to Hong Kong in the coming months, with the incentive scheme expected to take effect from the tax year starting on April 1, subject to legislative approval. The panel also discussed whether Hong Kong should extend stock market trading hours to keep pace with other exchanges that have extended or plan to extend their trading hours, including Nasdaq, London and South Korea. Hui said any such move would require careful study. “We would need to have a detailed exploration of the proposed trading hours and whether such a move can really bring benefits to the market, as a longer trading time may only spread turnover over a longer period,” Hui said.

title: 8 more firms from Belt and Road Initiative countries apply for IPOs in Hong Kong
description: Trade promotion chief Frederick Ma says interest in Hong Kong’s capital markets has surged in Central Asia since official delegation visited region in June.
content: Eight more companies from countries belonging to Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative have applied to list in Hong Kong, the city’s trade promotion chief has revealed. Frederick Ma Si-hang, chairman of the Trade Development Council, also said on Monday the city’s economy would benefit from improving China-US ties. Speaking on the sidelines of the Global Youth Powerhouse Summit, Ma said interest in Hong Kong’s capital markets from Central Asia had surged after a high-level delegation led by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu visited the region in June. “During my trip to Kazakhstan, its sovereign fund, which holds controlling stakes in many local companies, said it was interested in leveraging Hong Kong, an international financial centre, and its capital market to raise funds,” he said, without disclosing the identities or sectors of the applicants. “According to my understanding, eight companies from countries under the Belt and Road Initiative had filed for initial public offerings to the Hong Kong stock exchange.” More than 100 companies from belt and road countries are listed in Hong Kong, boasting a combined market capitalisation exceeding HK$340 billion (US$43.3 billion). China’s initiative aims to improve trade and infrastructure connectivity across global markets. Weeks after the delegation visited Central Asia to forge deeper business links in June, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, the country’s national railway operator, filed for a dual listing in Hong Kong alongside its domestic exchange. Ma added that the Hong Kong economy would benefit from improving Sino-US relations after Chinese President Xi Jinping met his US counterpart, Donald Trump, in Washington last month. “A good relationship between US and China is going to help,” he said, pointing to easing tariff concerns after Xi’s visit. The two superpowers have since pared back tariffs imposed on each other. “We [will] continue to do good business, particularly in the AI and semiconductor sector,” Ma said. Last month, the council raised its forecast for Hong Kong’s export performance for the year to between 42 and 47 per cent growth, up from its June prediction of “more than 20 per cent”. The council attributed its optimism to “robust” and sustained global demand for electronic products, driven by growth in the artificial intelligence sector.

title: Chinese doctors shrink lung tumour for baby still in mother’s womb, using needle
description: In ‘new milestone’, technology works by vibrating water molecules to create intense heat, destroying tumour tissue from inside out.
content: Chinese doctors have performed an unprecedented surgery to save an unborn child who developed a fast-growing tumour. A medical team from Shenzhen and Hong Kong recently completed a challenging, precise reduction of a foetal chest tumour while the baby was still in the womb, offering new hope to families facing similarly dire prognoses. Jointly performed by doctors from Shenzhen Baoan Women’s and Children’s Hospital and the Chinese University of Hong Kong, the procedure was detailed and published on August 20 in the peer-reviewed journal Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology. This marks China “stepping to the global forefront” in the field of minimally invasive interventional treatments for solid foetal tumours, according to the mainland science media platform Advanced Life Science in a September 15 article. The 40-year-old mother was 22 weeks pregnant when her foetus was diagnosed with microcystic congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), the medical report said. CPAM is a rare congenital condition caused by the abnormal growth of lung tissue during embryonic development. While benign, it is a rapidly growing lung tumour that can lead to heart failure and hydrops, a severe accumulation of fluid. Scans revealed a solid tumour measuring about 5cm (2 inches) and occupying the foetus’ entire right chest cavity. It severely compressed the heart and lungs and had already caused ascites, a dangerous build-up of fluid in the abdomen. Standard treatments usually involve draining large fluid pockets or cutting off a tumour’s main blood supply. However, because this specific growth consisted of tiny cysts and lacked a central blood vessel, traditional methods were ineffective. To save the infant, the medical team adopted a novel approach. Guided by high-definition, real-time ultrasound imaging, the team precisely mapped a route. They smoothly inserted a fine ablation needle – a thin, specialised medical probe – through the mother’s abdomen, the uterine wall and the foetal chest wall, reaching directly into the core of the tumour. The microwave technology works by vibrating water molecules to create intense heat, essentially destroying the tumour tissue from the inside out. The active heating process was exceptionally fast, taking a mere two minutes in total. Doctors closely watched the heat spread on their monitors to ensure the baby’s healthy organs remained unharmed. The results were immediate. Just three days after the procedure, the tumour’s volume had decreased significantly, and the fluid build-up was completely gone. The infant was delivered via caesarean section at 37 weeks, weighing 2.9kg (6.4lbs). At birth, the baby achieved a perfect score of 10 on the Apgar scale – a quick test used to check a newborn’s physical condition – indicating excellent overall health. At four months of age, the infant remains symptom-free and has required no surgical intervention. According to the Advanced Life Science article, the success of the surgery was not only a highly challenging clinical rescue but also set “a new milestone” in the international history of maternal-foetal medicine.

title: Days after Xi-Trump summit, Taiwan opens de facto consulate in the US
description: No Washington stop planned during the three-day visit to Arizona’s semiconductor corridor, sources said.
content: Taipei’s foreign minister is in Arizona this week to open a de facto consulate and tour the state’s semiconductor corridor, just days after US President Donald Trump wrapped up the pageantry of a state visit for President Xi Jinping. Lin Chia-lung, Taiwan’s foreign minister, arrived in Phoenix late on Saturday for a three-day visit that highlights the deepening economic ties between Washington and Taipei. His visit will not include stops in Washington or meetings with anyone at the State Department, according to two sources familiar with the matter. A trip to Washington just days after Xi’s visit could have risked a blow-up with Beijing, which used the September 23-25 summit to press the US to harden its line on Taiwan. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including the island’s main international partner, the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force and is legally bound to supply it with weapons to defend itself. Taipei framed Lin’s trip as economic rather than political. “The unveiling of the office in Phoenix also symbolises the Taiwan-US economic and trade partnership moving towards a new milestone,” it said in a statement on Sunday. According to the statement, Taipei will use public-private collaboration to deepen ties with Arizona and New Mexico “in trade, culture, education and supply chains”. It will also provide frontline services to Taiwanese companies and expatriates, and “anchor Taiwan’s influence in the southern United States”. The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Phoenix will be Taiwan’s 14th representative office in the US. As well as presiding over the office’s official opening, Lin will meet Taiwanese investors and expatriate leaders, and call on Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs and Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego. Lin will also witness the signing of a memorandum of understanding between the Arizona Commerce Authority and Taiwan’s National Innovation and Entrepreneurship Association. Ingrid Larson, managing director of the American Institute in Taiwan, flew in from Washington to accompany Lin throughout the trip. The programme includes a visit to a Taiwan artificial intelligence (AI) and biomedical display centre. “Minister Lin’s trip is mainly aimed at understanding the practical needs of Taiwanese companies’ layout in the United States, so as to help them build closer links with local governments, industry and communities,” the ministry said. Larson’s presence, it added, showed “the importance both sides attach to deepening local and industrial cooperation”. The Arizona trip also comes as the US and China compete over the advanced-chip supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) remains the key producer of leading-edge chips, including the AI accelerators sold by Nvidia and AMD. Trump has pushed to move more chip production to the US to reduce reliance on Taiwan, while restricting Beijing’s access to advanced chips. He initially tightened those controls, including on Nvidia’s H200, before later allowing Nvidia and AMD to sell some advanced chips to mainland Chinese clients in exchange for a share of the revenue. Top-end Blackwell processors remain restricted. The contrast was visible at the White House state dinner for Xi. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his AMD counterpart Lisa Su – both born in Taiwan and dependent on TSMC – were seated at the head table with Trump and Xi. The new representative office is seen as Taipei’s way of serving the companies and families that have followed TSMC to Phoenix, where it is building a cluster of chip factories. About 300 babies were born to TSMC-related employees in Arizona over five years. TSMC’s first factory in Arizona began mass production in late 2024. A second is finished and due to start production in the second half of 2027, while a third is still under construction. According to a New York Times report in December 2024, about half of TSMC’s roughly 2,200 Arizona employees were brought over from Taiwan. The company later put the Phoenix workforce at about 3,000, including hundreds from Taiwan, with a target of about 6,000 once the second and third factories are running. The transfer of employees led to a lawsuit that remains open. Deborah Howington, a TSMC talent-acquisition executive, sued the company in August 2024 in federal court in San Jose. She accuses the company of an “anti-American” culture that favoured Taiwanese hires, recruited them through a confidential “Asian headhunter” and sidelined workers who were not Taiwanese. Lin’s Arizona stop follows a week in Belize and Guatemala, the two remaining countries in Central America with official diplomatic ties to Taipei. Over the weekend, Taipei also announced plans for former leader Tsai Ing-wen to deliver the opening keynote address at Stanford University on Wednesday, on her first US visit since leaving office in 2024. The Stanford Gordian Knot Centre for National Security Innovation said that during Tsai’s eight years in office, Taiwan had strengthened its position in critical technologies and semiconductor manufacturing. The island had also deepened partnerships and invested in defence “amid an increasingly complex security environment in the Indo-Pacific”, it said. Tsai will also speak on Thursday at an event hosted by Stanford’s Hoover Institution on democracy, resilience and global security. The events come less than two weeks after Trump hosted Xi in Washington, when the two sides extended their trade truce into early 2027 and Xi urged the US to “oppose” Taiwan independence. In May, after his own state visit to Beijing, Trump said he was holding “in abeyance” an arms sale to Taiwan, described as a package worth about US$14 billion, calling it a “good negotiating chip” with Beijing.

title: Malaysia eyes permanent F1 comeback despite travel chaos at Bahrain GP
description: Six-hour traffic jams failed to dampen the mood after more than 260,000 fans packed Sepang for its first Grand Prix in nine years.
content: Malaysia was aflush with Formula One fever this weekend, rekindling talk of permanently bringing the race back to the Southeast Asian nation after a long hiatus – despite days of traffic chaos that left thousands of fans stranded for hours. More than 260,000 people flocked to Sepang International Circuit in Selangor state for the Bahrain Grand Prix, which was originally meant to be held in April but had to be postponed and relocated away from the Persian Gulf island nation due to security concerns arising from the US–Israel war on Iran. It marked the first time since 2017 that Malaysia and the punishingly technical track at Sepang had hosted a Formula One race. And Sepang delivered drama in spades, with Red Bull Racing’s Max Verstappen earning his first win of the season as teams scrambled to adapt their strategies after a sudden deluge. The downpour triggered widespread technical failures and tyre-choice headaches on a track that transitioned from wet to dry. Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was so impressed with the spectacle that he declared his government was actively exploring the possibility of bringing Formula One back to the country. “I’m looking forward to it. We’re discussing,” he said in a brief chat with Sky Sports commentator Martin Brundle ahead of Sunday’s race. “You see, I’m wet, drenched, but I am very excited. You see, the entire country is rejoicing.” Off the track, however, public sentiment was more mixed. While Formula One fans were largely thrilled with how the race panned out, their experience was soured by the logistical nightmare of getting to and from Sepang. View on Threads Local media reported “extraordinary congestion” on Sunday, with thousands of vehicles stuck in traffic for more than six hours after the race had ended at 6.30pm. Shuttle buses meant to transport ticket holders to their cars were delayed by hours, leaving many motorists to trek as far as 10km (6 miles) along the highway to reach their vehicles. Traffic was similarly chaotic on the previous two days, when practice runs and qualifiers were held, with one attendee saying she “broke down and cried for an hour straight” after seeing a man with a physical disability struggling but getting no help. ‘We can do it’ Malaysia was chosen as the host of this year’s Bahrain Grand Prix in July, under a deal that saw Bahrain’s state-run circuit retain full operational authority over the event’s commercial side, including ticket sales and providing hundreds of marshals and other race officials. Local fans were quick to defend Malaysia’s hosting of the event, laying the blame for any issues with the race squarely at the feet of the Bahraini race organisers. One video that did the rounds on social media showed Sepang circuit chief executive Azhan Shafriman Hanif handing out free water to fans queuing for their shuttle buses after Bahrain’s official workers had reportedly already left the circuit. this is the way to KLIA btw, people choose to walk instead of waiting for shuttle .... i even saw a mom pushing her kid stroller in the dark trying to walk to KLIA because the line for klia shuttle doesnt even move weih 😭😭 sumpah sedih pic.twitter.com/7ckzXxP0Sx — nin dawg #GoingToSepang (@63orgeous) October 2, 2026 Despite the logistical fiasco, the sheer number of fans who turned up for the race was a clear indicator of the economic potential a revived Malaysian Grand Prix could bring, Mokhzani Mahathir, president of the Motorsports Association of Malaysia, told national news agency Bernama. “I was surprised to see people turning up even for practice on Friday. Yesterday’s qualifying session was also packed,” he was quoted as saying. Mokhzani – whose father, former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, first brought Formula One to the country – said he was “sure” that a revived race at Sepang would have a significant “economic impact and multiplier effect”. “In terms of the circuit’s capability, we can do it,” he told Bernama. Sepang hosted a Formula One race every year for 19 years until 2017 and remains a regular fixture on the MotoGP calendar. Last year, more than 190,000 fans flocked to the track to watch Alex Marquez of Gresini Racing narrowly defeat Spanish compatriot Pedro Acosta of Red Bull KTM Factory Racing. In 2024, the latest year for which government figures are available, MotoGP generated an estimated 694 million ringgit (US$157 million) in economic returns for Malaysia, or roughly 6.3 times the amount invested. Putting Malaysia back on the Formula One calendar would cost at least 300 million ringgit per year, according to Sepang’s projections. Yet the investment could be worth it. Hong Leong Investment Bank has estimated that this weekend’s race generated roughly 1.3 billion ringgit in total revenue. Malaysia’s prime minister certainly seems hopeful for the race to return. “Hope we meet again in Sepang. Insya-Allah!” Anwar wrote in Malay on social media after the race, using the Arabic phrase for “God willing”.

title: Abby Choi’s HK$72m flat was never meant as a gift to former in-laws, court told
description: Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, says Kwongs were ‘penniless’ and ‘did not buy a single tin of baby milk formula for their grandchild’.
content: The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has accused her former in-laws of living off her family’s wealth, stating that her daughter never intended to gift them a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat she had bought for her children. Cheung Yin-fa on Monday recounted how her family maintained an amicable relationship with her former son-in-law, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, and his family after he and her daughter separated in 2015, only for the relationship to break down over the sale of an upscale flat seven years later. Kwong, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial at the High Court after pleading not guilty to murdering the model on February 21, 2023. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial. Cheung, the first prosecution witness to give evidence, said the Kwongs were “penniless” and had never treated her family to a meal or contributed anything towards the upkeep of the two children Choi had with her ex-husband. “Never did [the Kwongs] buy a single tin of baby milk formula for their grandchild … I have never been treated to a meal by Kwong Kau’s family, not even yum cha,” she said. The witness said Alex Kwong was skilled at coaxing others into doing him favours. After his divorce from Choi, Kwong, who was wanted in connection with a HK$6.3 million theft case, successfully convinced his ex-wife to lend him her credit card to cover his living expenses in mainland China while he was evading justice. She said Kwong had also received more than HK$70 million from Choi, claiming the money was for investing in luxury watches, until her daughter stopped financing him further because he failed to make any profit. The killing allegedly arose from a family feud over the sale of a HK$72 million flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. Kwong Kau, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill the influencer so that he could keep it for himself. Prosecutors suggested in their opening statement that money could be the reason for the crime, highlighting the significant wealth gap between the two families. The court heard Choi’s stepfather, Choi Cho-san, was a successful businessman who once operated three Chinese restaurants in Hong Kong. He returned to his native Hainan province in 2004, while continuing to support Cheung, Choi and her two stepsisters in Hong Kong with a monthly allowance of more than HK$1 million. Cheung said she first met Alex Kwong when the then 15-year-old Choi brought him home for dinner after they became friends at an international school. According to Cheung, Kwong’s mother and elder brother spent their time “idle at home”, while his father worked as a taxi driver after leaving the police force. Choi began dating Alex Kwong when they were both 17, and she became pregnant shortly after they started living together at a flat next to her family home. She gave birth to her first son in June 2013 before marrying Kwong three months later. After giving birth, Choi took a finance course, while earning a substantial income through investment and modelling work to cover her own expenses. Cheung said she had never seen Alex Kwong work while he was living next door. The witness said her family had maintained a good relationship with the Kwongs after the couple separated in 2015, and they would frequently visit Hainan with their grandchildren. She said the Kwongs never paid for anything on those trips apart from buying their own air tickets. In late 2015, Choi started dating another former schoolmate, Chris Tam Fong-chun, who was from an “extremely wealthy” family. The two held a wedding banquet the following year, although they never formally registered their marriage. Cheung said Tam and his father, Tam Chak-kwan, loved the influencer dearly, giving her more than HK$300 million over the years for investment. She added that her daughter’s relationship with Alex Kwong had also improved before the two families clashed over the Kadooria flat in June 2022. Cheung said her daughter bought the flat in 2019 and spent HK$9 million on renovations to give the two children she had with Alex Kwong an ideal place for their upbringing. The socialite also intended to sell the flat at an appropriate price in the future. Alex Kwong’s mother, Jenny Li Sui-heung, the two children and two maids lived in the flat from 2019 until February 21, 2023. Kwong frequently stayed at the flat, whereas his father stayed there intermittently before June 2022. The witness stressed her daughter had only registered the property under the name of her former father-in-law to avoid paying double stamp duty. Asked whether Choi had any intention to gift the property to the Kwong family, Cheung said: “That was impossible. Their whole family was fed by us.” The court heard the Kwongs snubbed the socialite’s proposal of selling the flat and moving her two children closer to their school in Tuen Mun. Cheung said Kwong Kau was particularly averse to the idea, threatening to harm her daughter if she insisted. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Kai Tak Hospital starts first phase of operations, treats 350 patients on day 1
description: Chief executive of public hospital – positioned to be Hong Kong’s largest – says daily number of patients projected to reach 1,800 by year end.
content: Hong Kong’s Kai Tak Hospital launched its first phase of operations, treating about 350 patients at its family medicine centre on Monday, with the daily number projected to reach 1,800 by the end of the year. While patients welcomed the service, lawmakers called for more frequent feeder transport and better publicity about transit options. Positioned to become Hong Kong’s largest public hospital once fully operational, Kai Tak Hospital opened its family medicine integrated centre on Monday to treat patients with stable chronic conditions and mild one-off illnesses. Patients began arriving at the specialist outpatient clinic block at 8.30am, while dozens of volunteers in blue vests were stationed along the way to direct them. All 350 daily consultation slots at the centre were fully booked by 11am. Dr Eric Cheung Fuk-chi, the hospital’s chief executive, described initial operations as “smooth” despite a handful of patients mistakenly showing up for blood tests. “The relocation of services to Kai Tak Hospital [from Queen Elizabeth Hospital] is the largest hospital relocation project in Hong Kong’s history, so it will be carried out in a phased manner,” he said. Cheung said specialist outpatient services would be added on October 26, after which neurosurgery and some oncology patients could also be treated. He expected the daily patient flow to reach about 500 by that stage. On November 12, the department of medicine, the hospital’s biggest specialty division, will begin operations. Cheung said the number of patients seen daily would reach 1,800 by the end of the year. On Monday morning, a Tai Wai resident surnamed Lau praised public transport connections to the facility, saying he had a better experience at Kai Tak Hospital compared with his previous clinic. “Everything was well-organised and orderly. Apart from the directional signs, many staff members and security guards at the hospital greeted me and asked if they could help,” Lau said. Hossain Chowdhury Shamimara, a housewife in her fifties who had also been transferred to Kai Tak Hospital, praised the facility for its spaciousness and the smooth and punctual service she received. “I’ve also been to Queen Elizabeth Hospital before. That’s also good, but not as open a place. This one is open, with a lot of lighting and windows, and the staff are also very nice,” she said. She added that she took an Uber from her Tsim Sha Tsui home to the hospital because she was unfamiliar with the district, but found it difficult to find a bus on her return trip after her appointment. She ended up choosing a bus that ran only every 30 minutes. A total of 10 franchised bus routes and six green minibus routes currently connect directly to the hospital from districts across Kowloon. At Kai Tak MTR station, one of the closest stops, additional road signs were installed along the route from inside the station to the bus interchange outside Airside shopping centre. The connecting ride on new bus route 22S took the reporter 12 minutes to travel from Airside to the hospital, although the service was still not yet listed on Google Maps. Speaking on a radio programme on Monday, lawmaker Kitson Yang Wing-kit expressed concern that many residents still did not know how to travel to Kai Tak Hospital and called on facility management to step up transit publicity. Yang also urged authorities to increase the frequency of transport services connecting different districts with Kai Tak Hospital, so residents would not have to wait longer than 10 to 15 minutes for a bus or train. Lawmaker David Lam Tzit-yuen said on the same programme that the hospital’s opening would lead to a more balanced distribution of medical resources across Kowloon Central and Kowloon East, making healthcare far more accessible for residents in Kowloon East. Addressing complaints of limited direct bus services, Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau, who visited the hospital in the afternoon, said patients needed time to adapt to the new environment and transport routes. Describing his journey to the hospital as “convenient”, Lo said he took the MTR from Admiralty to Kai Tak station, where he took a connecting bus. He said that authorities hoped to use a phased approach to roll out services in Kai Tak Hospital, starting with those of lower risks first. “The family medicine clinic opening today is a soft launch [for the hospital],” Lo said. “The hospital has a lot of equipment, which must be tested through actual use to see if there are any issues.” Additional reporting by Vivian Au

title: Hong Kong poised for first listed property debt fund as banks pull back
description: Private equity firm Gaw Capital lines up US$291 million pipeline of deals as banks scale back exposure to riskier property lending.
content: Private equity firms are moving to plug a commercial real estate funding gap as traditional banks pull back, with one fund filing to launch Hong Kong’s first listed property debt vehicle. Gaw Capital, a Hong Kong-based real estate private equity fund which managed US$35.6 billion in assets as of late 2025, filed to list its Gaw Capital Real Estate Private Debt OFC on Friday, seeking to become the first property-focused private debt fund on the Hong Kong stock exchange’s main board. The fund has identified a HK$2.29 billion (US$291 million) pipeline of deals across Hong Kong, Australia, South Korea, Thailand and the Maldives, with most projects targeting internal rates of return of more than 10 per cent per annum. Banks have been retreating from higher-risk commercial real estate lending and large-scale projects as stricter capital requirements under the Basel framework increase the risk weighting applied to property loans, creating a substantial funding gap. The Basel framework is a set of international banking regulations that forces traditional banks to hold more capital against risky property loans, making it more expensive for them to lend to commercial real estate. Gaw Capital said the real estate and infrastructure private debt market in the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East was expected to exceed US$161.4 billion by 2025 and reach US$372.7 billion by 2030. Private debt’s share of real estate financing in Asia-Pacific was projected to rise to 12.8 per cent in 2030 from 8.4 per cent in 2026. The fund aimed to provide quarterly distributions, although dividends were not guaranteed, Gaw Capital said. It would be managed by Gateway Capital (Hong Kong), with DB Trustees (Hong Kong) serving as custodian. Property private debt provides non-bank, asset-backed loans to real estate projects, offering a higher-yield strategy that has historically been limited to institutional and high-net-worth investors. Structured under Hong Kong law as a closed-ended Open-ended Fund Company, more commonly known as OFC, the fund does not permit share redemptions, meaning investors seeking liquidity must trade their holdings on the Hong Kong stock exchange. The initiative aligns with a goal set out in the Hong Kong government’s 2024 policy address to open new retail distribution channels for private funds and strengthen the city’s status as an asset management hub. Qualified alternative asset funds with an expected market capitalisation of at least HK$780 million and a focus on generating stable income are eligible to list in Hong Kong without undue impediments, according to a circular issued by the Securities and Futures Commission last year. Jefferies is the sponsor of the deal.

title: China’s record-breaking Asian Games spark introspection despite dominance ahead of Olympics
description: Success in pool and track and field plays out alongside shortcomings in strong disciplines, such as table tennis, badminton and weightlifting.
content: Midway through the Asian Games, China’s sports minister felt the need to issue a rallying cry despite the country again overwhelmingly dominating proceedings. A week into competition, the delegation had already racked up 125 gold medals, won more swimming titles than ever before and were so far clear of the rest that one American press outlet half-jokingly suggested changing the name to the China Games. In the final reckoning on Sunday, China’s tally was as follows: 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals for a total of 341. Their nearest challengers, Japan, could not even muster half the number of golds, and in overall terms finished 72 behind at the end of the Games. Still, Gao Zhidan, the team’s chef de mission in Japan and president of the Chinese Olympic Committee, was obliged to address what was seen by those at home as some disappointing performances in disciplines where their athletes have traditionally been strong, among them table tennis, badminton and weightlifting. Losing the men’s team table tennis final for the first time in 36 years, and to the hosts no less, brought a level of introspection you might otherwise associate with a failing programme. While state media discussed the lack of depth in the team and generational transition, with the likes of Sun Yingsha and Wang Chuqin confirming this was likely their last continental Games, Gao urged the team to “remain clear-headed”. The fact Lin Shidong beat Wang to men’s singles and mixed doubles gold, and the women’s singles final was also an all-China affair, with Wang Manyu getting the better of Sun, would not suggest a sport in crisis. Gao did however point to some shortcomings in “depth of talent”, “match management” and “form adjustment”, and Wang’s comments about the whole process of playing feeling “rather exhausting” will have been noted too. “Through the World Cup, world championships, for some reason, I haven’t been able to find the same feeling I used to have on court,” he said after losing to Lin. “I can’t find that enjoyment of competing out there. That’s something I have to really reflect on.” In badminton, gold was restricted to the women’s team and the mixed doubles, while China was not represented in either the men’s or women’s singles finals. It was one of the areas that Gao said served as a wake-up call, although China served some of their own to rivals either in Japan or watching from afar. Of the delegation’s 815 athletes, 548 were competing in an Asian Games for the first time, and the likes of teenager sprinter Chen Yujie will certainly have made people sit up and take notice. Track and field is where those envious of China’s power in other sports have started when suggesting the country’s Olympic success lacks big wins. Dominating every aspect of diving, for example, is not considered the same as winning the blue-riband events, which at the global Games have always involved running, jumping and throwing. But in the latter of those at least, China again has world-leading talent. Teen javelin star Yan Ziyi needed just one throw to win gold in Nagoya. Her first attempt of 70.46 metres was a Games record, and no one else came close. Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi took silver with 62.70m. Barring serious injury or poor performance on the day, there is nothing to suggest that Yan, who is still only 18, will not be dethroning her Japanese rival in Los Angeles in less than two years. There was also a Games and Asian record in women’s hammer, with Zhang Jiale, 19, throwing a mighty 78.27m for victory. In Paris, that would have blown Canadian gold medallist Camryn Rogers, who hit 76.97m on her fifth attempt, out of the water. “I have thrown further than this, at a competition in Huai’an, China,” Zhang said. “I did not feel this one got everything out of me. I did not feel I had the speed on it. “For my first Asian Games, though, I think it was pretty good.” China took more athletics gold than any other team, winning 17 overall, although in a worldwide context, not all titles are created equal. Chen set a Games record in the women’s 100m, coming home in 11.06 seconds. By comparison, the fastest time globally in 2026 was the 10.62 seconds American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden put down at the World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest last month. The five quickest finishes of the year are 10.80 seconds or below. How much speed Chen, or men’s 110m hurdles champion Chen Yuanjiang, can find between now and 2028 remains to be seen, but one area where Chinese athletes are still producing world-beating times is in the pool. Yu Zidi, who turns 14 this month, was already a power in her sport before becoming a triple Games gold medallist, winning the 200m butterfly, the 200m individual medley and the 400m individual medley. Zhang Zhanshuo, who is 19, became the first swimmer in Asian Games history to win seven gold medals at a single edition. Away from sports in which China traditionally wins medals, there was gold in climbing’s individual speed events, BMX freestyle and esports. Yang Siqi, meanwhile, won silver in women’s shortboard surfing, her country’s first Asian Games medal in the sport. Gao called the Games a “mid-term exam” for the next Olympics. Some athletes have come through with flying colours, others scraped a passing grade and others have some serious work to do. Zhang Xin, secretary-general of the Chinese delegation, said the focus would “immediately turn to preparations for the Los Angeles Olympic Games, moving faster to address our shortcomings, shore up weak areas and improve our overall competitive level”.

title: Huawei, Qualcomm strike multi-year patent agreement across 5G, AI
description: Cross-licensing deal includes Qualcomm’s purchase of specific Huawei US patents across compute, AI and networking, Chinese firm says.
content: US chip giant Qualcomm has agreed to pay to licence and acquire patents from China’s Huawei Technologies for the first time as part of a “multi-year, broad patent licence agreement” covering 5G, computing and artificial intelligence. The deal involved cross-licensing between both firms’ patent portfolios, the Shenzhen-based firm said in a statement on Monday, adding that it included Qualcomm’s purchase of specific Huawei US patents across compute, AI, networking and other technologies. The transaction did not involve any other business cooperation and remained subject to regulatory approvals, Huawei added. The value of the deal was not disclosed. The two tech powerhouses settled a dispute in 2020, with Huawei agreeing to pay Qualcomm US$1.8 billion in back licensing fees. Meanwhile, Huawei has been pushing to monetise its vast patent portfolio in telecommunications, audio and video to boost returns on its continuous investments in research and development. The latest deal not only showed “the value of Huawei’s innovations”, but also recognised Qualcomm’s “foundational contributions to modern communication technologies”, said Alan Fan, Huawei’s chief intellectual property officer, in the statement. John Han, executive vice-president and general manager of Qualcomm Technology Licensing, said the agreement “reaffirms industry recognition of Qualcomm’s 5G technology leadership” and “likewise reflects Qualcomm’s recognition of Huawei’s continued innovation and intellectual property in 5G and other technology fields”. Including the Qualcomm deal, Huawei’s total contract value from patent licensing agreements has exceeded US$6.9 billion since its first such income from Motorola in 2011. Huawei has expanded the influence of its intellectual property through more than 260 licensing deals with major global tech firms including Nokia, Samsung and Amazon, alongside domestic smartphone rivals like Oppo, Vivo and Xiaomi, according to the company. Prior to the Qualcomm deal, Huawei settled disputes with US personal computer giant HP in August via a multi-year global patent cross-licensing agreement covering their respective Wi-fi patents. According to its annual report, the telecoms giant invested 192.3 billion yuan (US$28.7 billion) into research and development in 2025, equal to nearly 22 per cent of its total revenue. One of the world’s largest patent holders, Huawei held 165,000 active granted patents worldwide as of 2025. In 2022, Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei urged the company’s intellectual property team to step up efforts to turn its vast pool of patents into revenue via “reasonable pricing” and to “generate an appropriate return” on its investments. In June, Huawei announced that it would start charging royalties for its Wi‑fi 7 technologies, the newest wireless standard, with the rate set at 50 US cents per unit. A key player in Wi-fi licensing, Huawei’s patent licensing deals covered 1.6 billion devices globally by the end of 2025, the firm said. Additional reporting by Iris Deng

title: If BTS has to serve, why are South Korean sportsmen, artists exempt: ex-lawmaker
description: South Korean football captain Lee Gi-hyuk has come under fire for celebrating the exemption during his team’s Asian Games gold medal win.
content: A former South Korean lawmaker has called for the abolition of the military exemption system granted to outstanding national athletes, arguing that military service should not be used as an incentive for achievements in sports or the arts. Yoo Seong-min’s remarks came amid controversy over comments made by members of South Korea’s men’s football team, who recently won its fourth consecutive Asian Games title, regarding the military benefits they received. South Korea defeated host Japan 1-0 on Saturday in the men’s final in Toyota, near Nagoya. Afterwards, the team’s captain, Lee Gi-hyuk, smiled as he held up his gold medal to reporters and said: “I’m not going to the military.” Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to perform between 18 months and two years of military service before the age of 28. But the government rewards Asian Games gold medals and Olympic medals of any colour with an exemption, meaning they will carry out just weeks of light basic training instead. Exemptions are a sensitive topic in South Korea, and athletes usually shy away from talking about it. The 26-year-old Lee, a defender who plays in the domestic K League, apologised on Sunday for “the thoughtless remarks I made and the way I behaved after the match, things I should not have said or done, both as captain and as a player”. In a social media statement, he said he was “caught up in the happiness, adrenaline and excitement of the moment”. “I am deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us,” he said. “As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking. I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions. I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty.” Asian Games football is contested between under-23 squads, but three overage players are allowed. The golfer Tom Kim also earned a military exemption after winning gold at the Asian Games on Saturday. Yoo called for the abolition of all military exemption criteria for athletes and artists in a social media post on Sunday. “The flippant remarks and behaviour of football and baseball players who won gold medals at the Asian Games over military exemption have provoked resentment among many people,” he said. He stressed, however, that the issue should not be reduced to criticism of individual players. “Basically, this is a matter of principles and a matter of the system concerning military exemptions. It would be right to abolish all military exemption criteria in sports and the arts altogether,” he said. “Looking solely at the effect of enhancing national prestige, there are few young people who have done as much as BTS. Is it really fair that BTS has to serve in the military while Asian Games gold medallists are exempt?” He argued that “the idea of promoting sports and the arts through military exemption as an incentive is itself outdated” and that it amounted to the state itself recognising the nation’s military service duty as something to be avoided. Yoo also pointed to the continuing controversy over fairness in determining who qualifies for military exemptions. “Even with the same gold medal, controversy over fairness will not disappear regardless of where the line is drawn – whether exemptions should apply to the Olympics, the World Cup or the Asian Games, why silver and bronze medallists should not qualify when gold medallists do, or how far exemptions should extend to the numerous domestic and international competitions in the arts,” he said. “The development of sports and the arts can be supported in many other ways. Outstanding athletes and artists may receive appropriate rewards for their achievements, but it is difficult to justify using military service itself as a form of reward.” He added that fairness and equality in military service were “of utmost importance” in South Korea. “Rather than continuing to adjust the line between who qualifies for military benefits and who does not, we should now eliminate the line itself.” This article was first published by The Korea Times Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: How a Los Angeles church was reborn as a hotel – and why more could follow
description: Once a Presbyterian church built in 1931, the boutique Hotel Lucile opened after more than a decade of controversy and transformation.
content: There is a cross on the roof, stained glass windows and a choir loft upstairs, but this whitewashed three-level building near Sunset Boulevard in Silver Lake, Los Angeles, is no longer a house of worship. It is the Hotel Lucile, a 25-room boutique lodging that opened in September 2026 with a restaurant and bar in the high-ceilinged sanctuary where church-goers once gathered. This opening follows more than a decade of controversy and transformation, including a community debate, bankruptcy and the arrival of a new hotelier in 2020. It also brings further energy to the Sunset Junction area, Silver Lake’s main walkable hub, which is already home to stylish spots including the Silver Lake Farmers Market, Taiwanese restaurant Pine & Crane, sports bar 33 Taps and the Photobooth Museum. The new hotelier is Santa Barbara-based Casetta, which specialises in adapting older structures and has properties in California and New Mexico, including Casa Cody in Palm Springs. Guests at Hotel Lucile will find many reminders that the building was built as Bethany Presbyterian Church in 1931. They will also see plenty of updates, including 25 guest rooms, a 225 sq ft (21 square metre) pool and a rotating display of more than 100 contemporary artworks (many for sale). The organ loft is now a meeting space. The choir loft has been retooled as a zone for coffee and drinks. The rooftop is a lounge with downtown views. After serving as a church for most of the 20th century under varying names, the building was informally adapted for multiple uses, including stints as an antique shop, filming location and the backdrop for the interactive horror theatre experience Delusion. “The building has lived several lives,” Hotel Lucile general manager Anthony Gutierrez says in an email. “It has always been a place for people to gather.” This church-to-commerce transition is not unique. Across the city and the country, declining attendance has left many religious buildings empty, often leading to conversions. In Downtown Los Angeles, the restaurant and event space known as Redbird + Vibiana was previously St Vibiana’s Cathedral, deconsecrated by the Catholic Church after suffering damage in the 1994 Northridge earthquake. In Beachwood Canyon, the Monastery of the Angels was built as a private mansion and rebuilt by the Catholic Church in 1948 as a monastery. In early 2026, Homeboy Industries bought it from the church and began remaking it into Home of the Angels, a “recovery campus” for people affected by trauma, substance use disorders and involvement in the justice system. More church conversions may follow, thanks to a California law that was passed in 2023 to allow faith-based groups and non-profit colleges to avoid some local restrictions when converting buildings into affordable housing. Meanwhile, the Hotel Lucile begins a new chapter, retaining interior arches, masonry, woodwork details and a rooftop cross that the hotel will keep alight at night. The old church bell, however, will remain silent. Because the hotel has no on-site parking, it will rely on valets and street parking – already tight in the neighbourhood – to accommodate the cars of overnight guests and restaurant diners. The rates begin at US$441 a night, plus a US$50 amenity fee. To start, management is offering a “locals’ rate” of 15 per cent off for guests who can show a California state ID. “We did preserve as much as we could of the original beams and stained glass,” says Laney Langenstein, who oversees strategy and marketing for Casetta. Guest rooms have minibars – curated by Erewhon and other partners – and Langenstein notes that hotel staffers will also push a martini cart that will “go through the hallways and see if anybody thinks it’s cocktail hour”. The dinner-only restaurant Sous Sous will draw upon cooking traditions of southern France and the American South, seating up to about 120 and occasionally offering live music. A hotel cafe will be open to guests for breakfast and lunch. The hotel’s new look was produced by Casetta and design firm Electric Bowery. Children are permitted at the hotel, but not encouraged by the layout. Of the 25 rooms, 24 have a single king bed and one has two queens. Most rooms have showers, not bathtubs. There is one suite, which has its own courtyard patio and fountain. Now that the hotel is about to open, feelings among locals are mixed. “When they tried to get a permit for the hotel, we all went to speak against it. But they got the permit,” says Jin Chang, long-time owner of nearby Big Mac’s Liquor on Sunset. Now Chang is neutral about the hotel opening and relieved that his row of shops already has its own dedicated customer car park. “What’s the definition of progress?” asks VJ Kesh, a long-time neighbourhood resident. “Is this hotel a reflection of Silver Lake? Hell, yes. So I’m in favour.”

title: Wellcome operator DFI Retail seeks buyer for fully leased shopping centre on The Peak
description: The 8,974 square feet Dairy Farm Guildford Road Shopping Centre will be sold via a public tender that closes at noon on November 19.
content: DFI Retail, the food and beverage unit of Hong Kong-headquartered conglomerate Jardine Matheson, is looking to sell its mall at The Peak, one of the city’s wealthiest neighbourhoods. The entire commercial portion of the Dairy Farm Guildford Road Shopping Centre will be sold via a public tender closing at noon on November 19, according to sole agent CBRE. The property is near The Peak campus of the German Swiss International School. The mall consists of a two-storey retail podium with a gross floor area of about 8,974 square feet (834 square metres), together with multiple car parking spaces. The shopping centre is currently 100 per cent leased out to various tenants including Wellcome Supermarket, real estate agencies and a cafe among others. The property’s location was “supported by an exceptionally affluent resident base, plus about 1,300 students and families from the German-Swiss International School from more than 30 different countries around the world, providing strong and sustainable spending power for the property’s retail offerings”, said Avan Pau, senior director of CBRE Hong Kong capital markets. In addition, about 200 affluent families were anticipated to move into the area after the ultra-luxury residential development at Mansfield Road, led by Wheelock Properties, was completed in 2028, Pau said. This would further strengthen local spending power and enhance the long-term retail and commercial value of the property, Pau added. DFI Retail is also set to take over more than 1,100 Starbucks outlets across Asia as part of a deal with Maxim’s Caterers, in which the latter would buy back 50 per cent of its stake held by the Jardine Matheson unit. Jardine Matheson bought a 50 per cent interest in Maxim’s in 1972, before transferring the stake to Dairy Farm, now known as DFI Retail. The Wu family retains 50 per cent of the business via the company Hongkong Caterers. Hong Kong’s retail market is on a path of gradual recovery. Sales in the first eight months of the year rose 8.5 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Friday.

title: Hong Kong outlines 4-step AI talent plan to help graduates navigate job market
description: Permanent Secretary Kevin Choi says government aims to boost digital literacy at ‘population scale’, viewing AI as catalyst rather than threat.
content: Hong Kong has unveiled a four-step artificial intelligence (AI) “talent ladder” strategy to counter entry-level job shock and foster industry leaders by treating the technology as a “catalyst, not a threat”. Permanent Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Kevin Choi Kit-ming warned on Monday that the “entry-level shock” was genuine because AI performed well in many routine tasks that traditionally formed the core of a graduate’s initial role, such as basic coding and first-line customer service. Speaking at the Global Youth Powerhouse Summit for young technology leaders, Choi added that the government was investing in AI “at a population scale” to elevate overall digital literacy, rather than trying to “shield young people” from the tool. “In Hong Kong, we view AI not as a threat, but as a catalyst … We are building a comprehensive ‘talent ladder’ to take emerging professionals from foundational literacy to industry leadership,” he said. Citing a recent report showing 70 per cent of Hongkongers were proficient AI users, with 20 per cent being “super users” who harnessed AI agents for daily tasks, Choi said the city enjoyed a strong starting position to make the workforce transition. The first rung of the four-step “talent ladder” involved eliminating price and accessibility barriers to AI tools, upskilling workers with large-scale educational programmes and promoting adoption among students, researchers and working professionals. Under the second step, the government planned to “convert active learners into practical innovators” with a series of higher education and advanced talent-nurturing initiatives, Choi said. The third step focuses on building an ecosystem that drives synergies between research and industry, followed by a fourth one aimed at establishing an infrastructure and policy environment conducive to innovation. “A ladder needs solid ground, and for Hong Kong that foundation is a deliberate strategy of balancing robust innovation with responsible governance,” he said. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revealed in his latest policy address that the government would study ways to refine its AI governance framework to tackle AI-enabled crimes and clarify liability boundaries for disputes caused by use of the technology. Authorities will also examine a governance framework for AI agents, while assessing the technology’s broader impact on the workforce. Speaking at the same event, Lee said Hong Kong’s role was becoming more vital as mainland China went from strength to strength in the global AI race. “Geopolitical tensions, rapid technological advances and economic uncertainties are reshaping the landscape for your generation. Hong Kong thrives on changes and always emerges stronger from challenges,” he said. “For you, Hong Kong is where careers are built, talent is nurtured and global horizons are within reach.” He highlighted the city’s Northern Metropolis megaproject, which was aimed at turning 30,000 hectares (74,130 acres) of land bordering the mainland into an economic powerhouse and housing hub, as an arena where opportunities would unfold for young people. Lee also noted his policy address included internship schemes, in which authorities would partner with the private sector to offer 30,000 placements for university students and fresh graduates over two years, including 10,000 focused on science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields The event also featured Ilaria Chan, founding chairwoman of the technology policy think tank Tech for Good Institute, who argued that AI development must take social well-being into account, rather than focus solely on “winning”. “We think about civil society first, and we think about the balancing between commercial interests and what is right for society, and that is where the government comes in,” she told a panel discussion. “That is why we need to have the right public-private partnership to have responsible AI adoption.” While praising the technology’s power, Chan urged young people to remain “people-savvy” and build lasting human connections to understand the world beyond their own echo chambers. Fellow panellist Cindy Chow, executive director and CEO of the Alibaba Hong Kong Entrepreneurs Fund, which supports start-ups, said the public and companies should be encouraged to explore how the technology could be used, while recognising the importance of discussing AI governance and ethics. “It is only through trying that you know what is really helpful for your organisation or for your specific position,” she said, describing efforts to discourage people from trying the technology as “the most damaging”. Alibaba Group owns the South China Morning Post.

title: China develops plant to extract hydrogen, fresh water and uranium from the sea
description: Scientists improve on existing technology, plugging an overlooked energy leak to achieve a potentially profitable green solution.
content: Chinese scientists have built a small, stable co-production plant that uses one system to extract hydrogen and fresh water from seawater, while also recovering uranium and bromine and improving electricity use efficiency by about 15 per cent. The team, led by Deng Dehui and Liu Yanting from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, improved on an existing technology that is both costly and power hungry, according to a paper in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Energy. Producing hydrogen from seawater in a process powered by renewable energy is an important route to green hydrogen, but both of the two main approaches have their drawbacks. In the direct seawater electrolysis method, the high levels of chloride ions react with the anode, corroding the electrode, while calcium and magnesium ions form scale on the cathode and reduce efficiency. The second approach is a two-step route: first, desalinate the seawater and then electrolyse it. Reverse osmosis or distillation turns seawater into pure water, which is then used to make hydrogen. The Chinese scientists proposed an improved technology based on the mature second route, with its expensive desalination equipment and high electricity requirements, according to the study that appeared on September 15. In 2023, the team built a small 25-kilowatt unit, based on the desalination technology, that the China Petroleum and Chemical Industry Federation rated as internationally leading. The researchers then scaled up the design, building a 250kW plant and targeting an overlooked power leak. Calculations showed that the system could turn a profit because it used energy efficiently, the paper said. In existing commercial systems, at 80 to 90 degrees Celsius (176 to 194 degrees Fahrenheit) about 30 per cent of electricity becomes low-quality waste heat that is hard to recover and is usually removed by cooling water systems – further increasing energy and freshwater consumption. To solve the problem, the team linked the electrolyte with a desalination unit, sending waste heat from electrolysis directly into a vacuum distillation tower where it drives seawater to boil and evaporate at a low temperature of 40 to 50 degrees. The vapour is then condensed into fresh water. According to a Chinese Academy of Sciences press release, the system produces enough fresh water to run the electrolyte and still leave extra. Salt, uranium, bromine and other marine resources could be extracted from the remaining concentrated seawater in multiple stages, it said. The 250kW unit can produce 380,000 standard cubic metres (about 13.4 million standard cubic feet) of hydrogen per year, with purity reaching 99.9999 per cent. It also produces 256 tonnes of fresh water, the scientists said. The study found that compared with traditional alkaline water electrolysis for hydrogen, the system improved electricity utilisation by 14.4 per cent. It also ran stably for 40 days under daily start-stop conditions with no obvious decline. Deng wrote in the paper that a cost analysis showed the system was more economically competitive than the traditional two-step process of pre-desalinating seawater and then electrolysing it for hydrogen. According to the paper, the system holds promise for highly profitable hydrogen production, with an estimated average cost of US$2.1 per kg when electricity costs are at US$0.033 per kilowatt-hour from onshore wind, and US$2.9 per kg at US$0.049 per kWh from solar power. Hydrogen currently sells for about US$3.9 per kg. Deng also said that future research should focus on developing better catalysts, improving recovery of waste heat from electrolytes and using artificial intelligence to optimise process parameters and maximise overall system performance and efficiency.
