title: India seeks to be ‘a little bit more involved’ in ending Ukraine war: minister
description: The external affairs minister’s comments point to a more active role for Delhi after years of taking a cautious approach to the war.
content: India is taking a more direct role in efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, engaging both sides on issues including shipping and reducing hostilities, Minister of External Affairs S. Jaishankar has said. Speaking at a security conference over the weekend, Jaishankar said India in recent months has become “a little bit more involved beyond advocacy”. The comments point to a more active role for New Delhi after years of taking a cautious approach to the war, in part because of its long-standing ties with Russia. “We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard. We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” he said, adding that talks have also covered energy shipments and “non-attack possibilities”. India has called for a halt to the fighting but has been reluctant to criticise the Kremlin, abstaining from United Nations votes condemning the war. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the conflict during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan in late August. Jaishankar said dialogue and diplomacy were essential to ending the war. He added that India’s relationship with Russia had evolved over the years and now spanned energy, space and trade. When Modi met Putin on the sidelines of the Brics summit last month, the two pledged to deepen ties, underscoring their close relationship even as Washington pressed Delhi to distance itself from Moscow. The US has sought to use its position as India’s top trading partner to pressure Delhi to stop buying Russian oil. India’s purchases initially declined before picking up again during the Middle East war. Russia is also a major supplier of weapons to Delhi. The Indian military has hundreds of Russian-made fighter jets, as well as several S-400 air-defence systems that were used during the four-day conflict with Pakistan in May 2025.

title: Letters | Tanzania could offer test of Hong Kong’s belt and road ambitions
description: Readers discuss the city’s role as a connector between capital and Belt and Road Initiative markets, the proliferation of online scams, and payment in renminbi.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Last month, Hong Kong had been promoting its role as a financing and professional services hub for Belt and Road Initiative expansion. Tanzania offers a useful reminder that signing deals is only the beginning. More than 6,000 participants attended Hong Kong’s Belt and Road Summit in September, as the city highlighted finance, legal services, insurance and capital-market access to companies expanding into emerging markets. Tanzania is relevant to that strategy because China’s economic presence there has grown quickly. China-Tanzania trade reached US$11.28 billion in 2025, up 27 per cent year on year, while infrastructure cooperation includes major transport and energy projects. The 153rd Inter-Parliamentary Union Assembly in Arusha, Tanzania, will examine the less visible side of those investments. Governance, public trust, extractive industry oversight and economic opportunity are central to the October 5-9 meeting. Tanzania has built a stronger physical economic platform. Dar es Salaam port moved 33.7 million tonnes in 2025-26, compared with 27.7 million tonnes a year earlier. Electricity capacity stands at about 4,075 megawatts and real gross domestic product grew 5.9 per cent last year. Those numbers make the country more investible. They also increase the importance of contracts, regulation, procurement, logistics and dispute resolution. Port expansion provides a clear example. Rising cargo volumes have increased the number of trucks moving around Dar es Salaam, creating pressure on roads outside the port even as terminal efficiency improves. Physical capacity can therefore develop faster than the systems surrounding it. For Hong Kong, which wants to act as a connector between capital and belt and road markets, that gap is commercially important. Arusha will not produce Hong Kong’s next infrastructure transaction. It will address something equally important to financiers: whether the institutions behind such investments are capable of keeping them working after the signing ceremony. Jasper A. Kwayu, director, InAfrika Providence Limited Crack down harder on cybercrimes In the past few years, there have been many reports about scam victims in Hong Kong. Recently, a veteran investor lost HK$7 million (US$892,000) after clicking into a fake website. It looked so much like that of a real securities firm that he entered his information. As a consequence, shares were sold from his portfolio and replaced with low-value stocks. In another case, a man in his 70s was cheated of HK$13 million by someone who convinced him that investing in cryptocurrency would bring him huge rewards with little risk and that his money could be withdrawn at any time. Also, a retired woman and online shopper was cheated of HK$3 million. She was sent a text by a supposed courier claiming the goods she ordered were accidentally damaged, then led to call the supposed customer service of a well-known courier company. She was told she would be compensated at three times the price of the goods after a bank account verification process. Eventually, she was asked to enter a verification code provided by the scammers several times, unwittingly transferring money to them. In the past two months, one of my bank accounts showed receipt of substantial sums of money from unknown sources, although this was not reflected in the available balance. Phone calls from mainland China (where no one would call me on my mobile phone) or the area code +881 (indicating a satellite phone number) would come in. Out of caution, I never took these calls. The tricks used by crooks change all the time. Regrettably, even when the police catch the culprits, they turn out to be small fry – usually just money mules. The government should crack down harder on these crimes. The legislature should promptly and seriously consider harsher laws to punish these unscrupulous elements. Harry Lam, Quarry Bay Payment in yuan is easier said than done I refer to the report, “HK metal storage tops 30,000 tonnes” (September 19), in which Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu talked about settling payment for services, such as buying Dongjiang water, in yuan. One would assume that the drive to internationalise the yuan is supported by the central government. However, when my company tries to pay our suppliers in mainland China in yuan, we are punished by a 10-13 per cent surcharge. Our suppliers claim that when we pay in yuan, they no longer get “export support”, the abolition of the value-added tax. So we either have to pay the surcharge – or pay in US dollars. One can only hope that the water supply doesn’t come with the same surcharge. Roland Guettler, Lai Chi Kok

title: Paris Fashion Week: Miu Miu and Valentino SS27
description: Gigi Hadid and Olivia Colman walked for Miu Miu, while Alessandro Michele’s library-themed show for Valentino blended high fashion with philosophical musings.
content: Two Italian brands – Miu Miu, Prada’s sister label, and Valentino, the Rome-based haute couture house – were the headliners of day seven of Paris Fashion Week. Here’s the lowdown on the two shows. Miuccia Prada is giving her Miu Miu customers what they want for spring/summer 2027. Everything that has made Miu Miu such a success story – from preppy staples like pleated tartan skirts to athleisure essentials like track pants – was in the show. Most looks paired wardrobe classics, such as V-neck sweaters, with activewear like asymmetrical sports bras. Named Here and Now, the collection was a parade of everyday clothes – “quotidian”, the show notes called them – and pieces that we’ve all seen at Miu Miu before. Distressed leather (which was actually suede laminated with wax), crushed satin, crystal embellishments, retro prints – you name it. It was a very self-referential collection, but then again, Miu Miu has built such a strong visual vocabulary that there is nothing wrong with mining your own archives from time to time. A couple of looks were even reminiscent of big sister Prada, something that only Miuccia Prada can pull off with such confidence. The brand’s long-term collaboration with New Balance returned with the New Balance x Miu Miu RC150, a retro silhouette that will be a hot item once it drops in stores. The label also unveiled a denim range in partnership with American brand Wrangler, offering original jeans from the 90s upcycled into new models and embellished with Miu Miu’s signature shoelace fastenings. Miu Miu has had a few blockbuster seasons recently, including a very good – albeit polarising – spring/summer 2026 show that celebrated the humble apron. This very customer-friendly collection is much more straightforward and to the point. “Let’s not overthink it,” Miuccia Prada seemed to suggest with these clothes, and just create desirable pieces that women and men actually want to wear. As always at Miu Miu, actors such as Olivia Colman and Emma Corrin were part of the very diverse line-up of models who walked in the show. The Valentino spring/summer 2027 show invitation was a booklet titled Antibiblioteca: Catalogue of the Unread, which included a list of 68 books with brief synopses and basic information like their ISBN numbers, resembling a library catalogue. The concept of the antibiblioteca (antilibrary in English) refers to books we accumulate but don’t necessarily read, which can come in handy for research or other purposes and hold the potential for discovery. That idea led Valentino’s creative director, Alessandro Michele, to reflect on the purpose of a fashion collection. Like a pile of books in a personal, or even public, library, a fashion collection is made of outfits that will be worn and cherished; garments that will appear only in a show and then as fleeting images online; and creations that will be acquired but never actually worn in real life. “A fashion show dedicated to what remains possible” is how Michele described it in the booklet, which listed made-up books such as What Fungi Teach About Time by Kenji Watanabe and The Reluctant Invention of Negative Numbers by Dev Raghunathan (clearly not your average beach reads, even if they actually existed). Valentino also asked guests to bring a book to the show to be donated to local libraries. Michele loves an obscure reference, but his esoteric concepts usually translate into striking garments that, while not for everyone, never fail to elicit a strong reaction from those witnessing his mesmerising shows. The show took place at the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève, a historic university library on Paris’s Left Bank, where models walked around study desks surrounded by bookshelves. As soon as the first model – clad in a sexy black bustier paired with a matching tight skirt – walked out, a remix of dance songs, including Madonna’s Music, started to play. The loud rave music felt out of place in those hallowed halls, and so did the clothes, a mix of glamorous evening wear and boudoir dresses that were a far cry from the ensembles you’d expect to see in a library. That was a choice, explained Michele in a post-show chat with editors, adding that staging a show in a library was a dream come true. A few pieces, including a T-shirt and a couple of baseball caps, were emblazoned with the phrase “Villain Teen”, a play on words that echoed the brand’s name and referenced the mischievous attitude associated with the word “villain”, the designer said. Michele is the fashion world’s unofficial philosopher – he recently published a book co-written with an actual one. This show was yet another example of his wondrous mind, although his reset of Valentino, which he joined two years ago after a stellar tenure at Gucci, is still a work in progress. A highlight of the collection was the menswear, which was very desirable and felt more attuned to the needs – and wants – of today’s luxury consumers.

title: Kai Tak Hospital opens this week: what you need to know before visiting
description: Hong Kong’s largest public hospital begins phased operations on Monday, starting with family medicine and specialist outpatient services.
content: Hong Kong’s largest public hospital, built on the former airport site in Kai Tak, began its first phase of operations on Monday after more than a decade of planning and preparation. The South China Morning Post looks at the hospital’s key features and what its opening means for the city’s healthcare development. 1. What makes Kai Tak Hospital special? With a gross floor area of roughly 500,000 square metres (5.38 million square feet) and 2,400 beds, Kai Tak Hospital will be Hong Kong’s largest public hospital. It will gradually take over services from Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan. The hospital, which cost more than HK$36 billion, comprises five buildings on the site of the former airport’s south apron. Major facilities include 37 operating theatres and a 24-hour accident and emergency department. It will also house Hong Kong’s largest pharmacy, the first in a public hospital to use an automated dispensing system capable of handling up to 3,200 prescriptions a day. Planning for the hospital stemmed from the 2013 policy address, when then-chief executive Leung Chun-ying said the government would reassess demand for medical facilities in Kowloon and expedite development of the reserved hospital site in the Kai Tak Development Area. The project was included in the government’s HK$200 billion first 10-year hospital development plan in 2016, which positioned it as a new acute hospital for the area. 2. Which services will open first? Services will be introduced in two phases. The first began on October 5 with the opening of the family medicine integrated centre, which will initially offer about 350 consultations a day – with 100 for existing patients. The centre will provide family medicine outpatient services for patients with stable chronic conditions, as well as those with relatively mild one-off illnesses such as the flu or gastroenteritis. It will also offer nursing services, including drug injections and wound dressing. Patients can make appointments through the Hospital Authority’s HA Go mobile app or by telephone. Specialist outpatient services from several Queen Elizabeth Hospital departments, including medicine, surgery, neurosurgery and clinical oncology, will transfer to Kai Tak in batches from late October. Other services will also roll out gradually this month, including allied health services, diagnostic and interventional radiology, pathology, pharmacy, day services for clinical oncology and obstetrics and gynaecology. Major clinical services, including inpatient care and surgery, will begin in 2028 when the second phase starts. 3. Will emergency services be available? Although the hospital has a helipad and is designated as a trauma centre, its 24-hour accident and emergency service will not begin until 2028. When operational, Kai Tak’s accident and emergency department will be three times the size of that of Queen Elizabeth Hospital. 4. How can patients get there? Patients travelling from Kowloon or nearby MTR stations can use one of 10 bus routes or six green minibus routes serving the hospital. The routes connect the hospital with Kai Tak, Kowloon Bay, Sung Wong Toi, To Kwa Wan, Wong Tai Sin, Ngau Tau Kok, Kwun Tong and Yau Tong. The bus routes are: 5R, 15A, 20A, 20X, 22, 22M, 22S, X6C, 11A and 17A The green minibuses are: 22A, 68, 86, 88A, 90A and 90B It takes about 30 minutes to walk from the hospital to the nearest MTR stations: Kowloon Bay, Ngau Tau Kok or Kai Tak. 5. What does the opening mean for other hospitals? Once services transfer from Queen Elizabeth Hospital, the Jordan site will be redeveloped into Hong Kong’s first integrated ambulatory care hospital, with centres for cataract surgery, radiology and radiotherapy. Kai Tak Hospital will also serve as the interim teaching hospital for the city’s third medical school, which is being established by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The hospital will serve more than 1.8 million residents in four districts – Yau Tsim Mong, Kowloon City, Wong Tai Sin and Kwun Tong. It will work closely with Kwong Wah Hospital, another major healthcare facility in Kowloon, on emergency services. It will provide emergency and pathology support to the adjacent Hong Kong Children’s Hospital.

title: Asset manager Schroders to expand in Hong Kong after merger with Nuveen, CEO says
description: Government actions are making Hong Kong ‘a more appealing location for private markets professionals’, Richard Oldfield says.
content: UK fund house Schroders will increase investment and headcount in Hong Kong after being acquired by US asset manager Nuveen, according to Schroders’ global CEO. “Hong Kong is a critical interface for mainland China through schemes like Wealth Management Connect,” Richard Oldfield said in an online interview with the South China Morning Post on Friday. The scheme, launched in 2021, allows investors in the Greater Bay Area to buy wealth-management products across borders. Underpinning Schroders’ aim to increase investment in the city was the government’s first five-year plan, announced last month, which would enhance integration between the city and the mainland market, Oldfield said. “While there are no immediate plans to move to larger offices, headcount in Hong Kong has already increased over the last nine months,” he said. “We are going to increase headcount in Hong Kong in the future. I am very excited about the work that the Hong Kong government is doing to make Hong Kong a more appealing location for private markets professionals to come live and work.” Oldfield unveiled the expansion ambition for Hong Kong, as well as Asia, just a day after US asset manager Nuveen completed its acquisition of Schroders on Thursday, creating a giant financial firm with about US$2.6 trillion of assets under management, based on the two firms’ data as of the end of June. After the takeover, Schroders would continue to operate independently for 12 to 18 months with Oldfield in charge, according to the company. Investment strategies would remain unchanged, but the sales teams of the two firms would collaborate during that time, Oldfield added. The new combined group would become Europe’s second-largest asset manager after Paris-based Amundi, which had US$2.7 trillion in assets under management, according to LSEG Data and Analytics. Hong Kong is one of Schroders’ key Asian hubs, and the combined group manages US$320 billion of assets in Asia, representing around 12 per cent of the total. “Asia is the fastest growing part of the world, and therefore what we expect to see as Schroders and Nuveen is that the portion of our assets grows at a faster rate in Asia,” Oldfield said. “Asia is not an adjunct to our strategy. It is actually central to our future growth. The combination of Schroders and Nuveen gives us a much broader set of capabilities to serve clients, particularly in the areas of wealth, retirement, and private markets, which are especially important in the region.” The Asia-Pacific region has provided Schroders’ fastest growth globally over the last 12 months, driven by two sources of capital: international investors who want to diversify their investments in the region and growth in local client investments as the middle class expands. “Our sales teams need to come together, and that is because I cannot have a client in Hong Kong have someone from Schroders knock on the door at 10 o’clock and then another team from Nuveen knock on the door at 11 o’clock,” he said. Although Beijing has tightened control on cross-border investments since May and added a 20 per cent tax levy on overseas investments in July, Oldfield said he remained bullish on the long-term growth of Hong Kong and mainland China. The growing number of wealthy clients and the ageing population’s higher demand for retirement savings solutions supported that outlook, he said. Schroders conducts onshore business in mainland China via a joint venture with Bank of Communications, while its Hong Kong unit serves offshore clients.

title: Pro-Israel Samoa prime minister apologises for Nazi gesture in leaked video
description: Schmidt has previously voiced his support for Israel and has committed to opening an embassy in Jerusalem by the end of the year.
content: Samoa’s prime minister apologised on Monday after video surfaced showing him saying “Heil Hitler” and making a Nazi gesture. Prime Minister La’auli Leuatea Schmidt said the footage was from a family gathering almost 20 years old and was never meant to see the light of day. “The footage shows me using the words ‘Heil Hitler’ and participating in a gesture associated with Nazi Germany in a private family gathering – not intended for the public,” he said in a statement. “Whatever the context or intention at that gathering twenty years ago, I recognise that those words and gesture were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt, and I apologise for using them.” Schmidt has previously voiced his staunch support for Israel and has committed to opening an embassy in Jerusalem before the end of the year. “I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said. He wore a Jewish prayer shawl when he was sworn in as prime minister in 2025, entering the room to the sound of a ceremonial shofar horn. “I stand for Israel, the land of God,” he said at the time, according to local media. “Samoa will stand up and support the holy land of God.” Deeply religious Pacific nations like Samoa hold strong beliefs in Old Testament prophecy, which holds that Jews are destined to one day return to the Land of Israel.

title: The Live Conversation: Education Beyond the Checklist
description: The International Schools Festival puts the spotlight on new approaches to education and how best to go about the application process
content: Over 1,700 parents, students and educators attended the International Schools Festival – Hong Kong Island 2026. Held at Hong Kong Ocean Park Marriott Hotel on September 19, it featured 46 schools and education advisers, and offered families guidance on admissions, curricula, university applications and future education planning. Across five parent talks and 10 school-led information sessions, speakers returned to one central message: education should not be driven by fear or the pursuit of a perfect résumé. Whether choosing a primary school or planning for university, families should focus on well-being, curiosity and adaptability. A new approach to admissions At the morning panel session entitled, “Rethinking the Admissions Journey,” school leaders challenged the idea that primary admissions should be treated as a test children must be trained to pass. Instead of rehearsed answers, they said schools want to see curiosity, confidence, emotional readiness and a child’s natural ability to communicate and engage with others. At English Schools Foundation’s (ESF) Kennedy School, principal Brenda Cook said they do not look for one fixed type of applicant profile. “We don’t have a particular child that we’re looking for at ESF. We welcome everybody.” While ESF is in many ways non-selective, children still need sufficient expressive and receptive English to access learning confidently and flourish. Cook added that parent interviews are intended to help schools understand the child, not judge the parents. For Ross Dawson, primary principal at Victoria Shanghai Academy (VSA), the key question is not which school has the strongest reputation, but which best fits the family. “There are so many great schools in Hong Kong; it’s about finding the right fit for your family,” he said. “I always say to parents, you’re not applying to your school just for your child, but your whole family.” Dawson encouraged parents to consider a school’s educational philosophy, language environment, homework expectations and approach to learning. In a bilingual school such as VSA, language proficiency is also important, particularly for older children learning in both English and Chinese. The importance of fit was echoed by Dr Cora Hui, head of school at Christian Alliance PC Lau Memorial International School, who urged families to take a more holistic approach. Beyond more traditional notions of learning, parents should consider character development, wellness, social connection, the school’s play-based approach and expectations for parental involvement. “We want to find a good match,” Hui said, highlighting the importance of balancing physical activity, social bonding and academic rigour. That broader view of readiness was reinforced by Jane Thomas, head of primary at Australian International School Hong Kong, who said well-being is central to admissions. “We want well-being to come first and we will not apologise for that. We know that when children are settled and they feel happy and want to learn, the learning will come.” Preparing for an AI future The conversation moved from primary admissions to future pathways in the panel session “Navigating Higher Education in the AI Era: Future Degrees, Smarter Applications, Strategic Planning”. As AI reshapes learning, university applications and career planning, speakers urged families not to respond by trying to predict the future too precisely. Instead, Dr Spencer A Fowler of Li Po Chun United World College of Hong Kong; Michael Hirsch of ESF West Island School; Kevin Li of Crimson Education; and Helena Murchie of the French International School of Hong Kong all pointed to adaptability, intellectual curiosity, communication and the confidence to keep learning as skills likely to outlast any supposedly “safe” degree choice. Fowler said AI should not be treated as a shortcut for homework. Used responsibly, it can provide more personalised support and help students engage with real-world problems. “There can be so much more learning in real time where these AI tools and algorithms can support students in a unique way that would be very difficult to provide with teachers and peers,” he said. The question of authenticity was also central to the discussion. Hirsch described AI-generated applications as “a new version of an old, old problem,” noting that students have always been able to receive inappropriate help from parents, tutors or others. He suggests using AI as a research and thinking partner to better understand universities, courses and their own motivations. Li said “AI is the democratisation of knowledge,” but families should not lose sight of the fundamentals of university preparation: strong academic performance, positive relationships with teachers, credible recommendations and meaningful activities. Murchie, meanwhile, added that schools must balance technology with academic integrity and human development. “Employers, universities, they want to know what you can do with those grades,” she said. That means students need to demonstrate problem-solving, creativity and the ability to explain and defend their work – skills that may become even more important as AI tools become more common. Across both panels, speakers encouraged families to take a less anxious approach to education planning. As Fowler put it: “Have fun with your kids. Explore with your kids.” The festival offered a timely reminder that, even in an increasingly competitive and technology-driven education landscape, the qualities that matter most remain deeply human: curiosity, resilience, empathy, confidence and the ability to keep learning. title: Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years
description: Handing Ru the bank card, a social worker advised him to keep it safe, spend wisely, and beware of telecom scams.
content: An elderly man in central China, who has spent the past 21 years making ends meet as a scavenger, experienced a remarkable stroke of luck when he discovered that his pension fund contained over 420,000 yuan (US$63,000). In late September, the 71-year-old man, surnamed Ru, received a bank card linked to his pension account, which revealed a balance of 424,204 yuan, as reported by Changde Daily. Completely unaware of his entitlement to pensions over the decades, Ru sobbed as he spoke to the media: “It goes without saying that I am happy. I never expected this to happen. I am grateful for the support from the social assistance authority and other related government departments.” For the past 21 years, Ru has been scavenging to earn a living in Changde, Hunan province. In the early 2000s, he was laid off from a state-owned shop in Zhuzhou, also in Hunan, where he received an undisclosed amount of compensation. Ru had worked at this shop for 30 years after graduating from a technical school. He quickly squandered the compensation because he was someone who “loved enjoying life.” Once the money ran out, he fell into debt and experienced conflict with his relatives, which drove him to start collecting rubbish. He later moved to Changde and has lived there ever since. In the winter of 2024, Wu Jinhui and his colleagues at a social assistance station in Changde discovered Ru living in an abandoned building. Initially, Ru refused their suggestion to move to a relief shelter due to a strong sense of self-esteem, according to Wu. Officials had frequently provided him with essential daily necessities and assured him of support before he eventually agreed to relocate to the shelter, where he also revealed his personal details. Wu explained that under China’s retirement policies, Ru reached the pension age in 2015 and became eligible for pensions after that. His pension amounts to about 3,700 yuan (US$550) a month, accumulating to over 420,000 yuan over the last 10 years. Ru mentioned that after being dismissed from the state-owned shop, he assumed he needed to pay for endowment insurance for many years before qualifying for the pension. Due to his financial situation, he did not pay for the insurance. Without a mobile phone, Ru has been disconnected from social developments and is unaware of the country’s retirement regulations. He has remained single throughout his life. According to Chinese law, individuals who have paid premiums into the social insurance system for at least 15 years are entitled to receive a pension upon reaching retirement age. The retirement age for Chinese men, which stood at 60 in 2015, is now being gradually raised to 63. Wu noted that Ru had worked at the state-owned shop for 30 years, during which time his employer deducted portions of his salary for premium payments. While handing the bank card to Ru, Wu advised him to keep it safe, spend the money wisely, and stay vigilant against telecommunication fraud. Ru stated that his immediate priority is to rent a flat in Changde, and he plans to visit his hometown of Zhuzhou in the future. The news has sparked significant buzz and discussion among the public. “With so much money at hand, I think his relatives will come to visit him quickly,” commented one internet user. Another said: “Kudos to these officials. They have done an excellent job in helping a poor old man.”

title: Is Hong Kong’s drive to eliminate substandard housing doing more harm than good?
description: Advocacy group warns that some subdivided flat tenants are struggling to resettle and are becoming worse off under the new housing regime.
content: Housewife May and her three children were overjoyed last September when they moved into a 200 sq ft subdivided flat in Kwai Tsing, a Hong Kong district with one of the city’s lowest average monthly household incomes. For years, the 50-year-old single parent had lived in a squatter hut with her son and two daughters, where they had to climb hundreds of stairs daily. They later moved into a 100 sq ft subdivided flat before securing their current place. Located on the 15th floor of a lift-equipped building, their home has windows, two partitioned bedrooms, a dining room, a toilet and a kitchen. The subdivided flat also has room for a small sofa and a dining table, giving the school-aged children a proper space to do their homework instead of on their beds. Relying on a monthly government subsidy of around HK$17,000 (US$2,170), the family could only afford to pay HK$8,300 for rent. But her landlord recently gave her four months’ notice to move out by November as he planned to quit the subdivided housing market as a new regulatory regime was rolled out in March. “I even begged my landlord to stay in the market, but he and his family did not want the hassle,” she said. May’s family is among those struggling to resettle, as authorities aim to wipe out substandard housing under the Basic Housing Units Ordinance by setting minimum requirements for subdivided flats and recognising qualified ones as “basic housing units”. The Hong Kong Subdivided Flats Concerning Platform, an advocacy group, said tenants such as May were facing a decline in living standards under the new basic housing units regime. A recent survey by the group found that many of the families with relocation needs over the past year had moved to other substandard homes or even squatter huts and industrial buildings. As Monday marks the UN’s World Habitat Day, which advocates for the basic right to adequate shelter, the group has suggested that the government provide a stable supply of transitional housing and review its long-term housing strategy. May has been looking for a transitional flat to move into in the same district where her children attend school. But the clock is ticking. “I am still waiting for an offer. We have to live nearby … My younger daughter cannot carry anything heavy after undergoing back surgery. I have to send her to school and pick her up every day. I cannot move too far,” she said. Transitional flats, rolled out in 2018, are short-term housing operated by NGOs on idle sites and properties for residents who are queuing for public rental housing or facing urgent accommodation needs. As of June, more than 19,100 homes were in operation. The group said not all tenants facing relocation could secure a better living environment, according to its survey of 647 subdivided flat households that responded between March and June. Fifty-nine families said they had moved home over the past year, with only five relocating to transitional flats or short- or long-term public rental housing. While 16 households moved to subdivided flats that appeared to meet the new minimum requirements, the remaining 38 families either resorted to substandard subdivided homes or illegal properties such as squatter huts and industrial buildings. “Many resettlements are not for improving living quality or moving up the housing ladder,” advocacy group member Lai Kin-kwok said. One such tenant is a 50-year-old woman who wished to be addressed by her surname, Then. She initially lived in a 100 sq ft subdivided flat with a window but moved to another subdivided home in an industrial building. She was evicted by her landlord, who planned to sell the property rather than fix it to comply with the new standards. The new requirements include a minimum size of 86 square feet, a waterproof toilet and other safety and hygiene conditions. Despite paying a similar monthly rent of more than HK$4,000, her new home is stuffy and humid with no windows. She also faces safety risks, with her home located next to a food factory. The cleaner, who earns about HK$13,000 a month, considered moving to another district but was unsure if she could secure a new job. “Other properties in the district are over my budget. They are leased for at least HK$5,000,” she said. Despite a small number of evictions, Lai warned that it was an emerging problem, especially when the future of transitional housing remained uncertain. He noted that the city’s first five-year plan, announced in mid-September, no longer mentioned transitional housing, which operated on sites that had to be returned to the government or private owners at some point. According to Lai’s analysis of the available data, projects totalling about 12,770 transitional homes, or more than 66 per cent of the existing stock, may have to cease operation next year. It coincides with the enforcement arrangement from March 2027, as authorities will take action against landlords letting substandard subdivided flats, except those covered by a three-year grace period. Sites offering about 4,100 transitional flats are also set to be returned in 2028, while projects with another 1,300 homes may end in 2029. About 3,400 transitional flats may remain until 2030 or beyond. The government will fully enforce the regime from March 2030, as the grace period ends. Lai noted that the government still had 30,000 short-term flats under its light public housing scheme to accommodate residents, but one-third of the supply was located on a prime site in Kai Tak that was set to be returned for development by 2031. “Without proper planning, the city’s capacity in handling resettlement may be compromised … Meanwhile, tenants may resort to a hidden and dangerous housing market that lacks protection,” he said. He urged the government to clarify the transitional housing policy, adding that it could also rent recognised subdivided homes or basic housing units and lease them to residents in need. Such a move could provide more housing in urban areas for the low-income working class and incentivise landlords to renovate their properties. The Housing Bureau said the proposal was not viable, as it could be perceived as the government subsidising landlords to profit and drive up rent. It added that only about 400 transitional homes were to cease operating in 2027-28, while an extra supply of 120 transitional flats would be ready by the fourth quarter of 2027. “Regarding the operation of transitional housing after 2027-28, we will continue discussions with developers who lent the land, encouraging them to actively consider extending the land use for ongoing transitional housing projects. The response so far has been positive,” the bureau said. It added that the bureau would proactively coordinate with government departments that currently loaned sites without immediate long-term development plans, aiming to extend the operation of such transitional housing projects. It said it would ensure operators were prepared for exiting projects in advance, such as helping tenants to relocate. It added that it was confident that households in need would be able to improve their living environment with the supply of transitional housing and short- and long-term public rental housing. The advocacy group said authorities should take enforcement action and monitor whether landlords might circumvent the regulations by leasing the entire property to a single tenant while secretly subleasing units within the flat to others. The bureau noted that a single tenancy agreement involving multiple tenants and subleasing could still be subject to liability. Lai also called for a review of the city’s long-term housing strategy set out over a decade ago, which he deemed could not cover the impact of the latest policies. With the aim of building more public rental housing flats, selling more subsidised flats and stabilising the property market, this year’s report forecasts a demand of 420,000 homes in the coming decade. It maintained an estimated demand of 127,500 flats from inadequately housed households as it was still early to assess the new regime’s impact. He suggested building a comprehensive housing ladder, as well as addressing the accommodation needs of subdivided flat tenants and low-income families ineligible to apply for a long-term public rental home.

title: In Focus | Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
description: Temu is quickly losing its shine in the face of a wave of global regulation. Can the platform reinvent itself?
content: In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot. “Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig. The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience. That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data. The platform’s breakneck rise continued to gain momentum from there, bringing Chinese-style e-commerce to markets around the world. However, three years on, Temu’s initial business proposition is being rewritten amid a wave of global regulation, with rising customs barriers eroding some of the advantages that made its cut-to-the-bone prices possible. At the heart of the change is a simple issue: shipping a dress directly from a warehouse in China to doorsteps in America or Europe is no longer as simple – or cheap – as it was a couple of years ago. Temu’s ability to offer such ultra-low prices was built on two main factors: its vast, well-oiled Chinese supply chain and a clever distribution strategy that allowed the firm to avoid paying hefty import tariffs. [PDD] has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature ... and reusable supply chain system Chen Tao, Analysys International On the supply side, Temu could draw on parent company PDD Holdings’ years of expertise operating Pinduoduo – one of China’s largest e-commerce platforms, which has built a sprawling supply chain with deep roots in the Chinese manufacturing sector. PDD “has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature … and reusable supply chain system”, said Chen Tao, an e-commerce analyst at consultancy Analysys International. Temu had effectively copied Pinduoduo’s business model and rolled it out globally, Chen added. The model allows Temu to draw on China’s sprawling network of factories, suppliers and cross-border merchants, which is able to produce and ship goods at a scale and cost unmatched anywhere else in the world. Since China began opening its economy in the late 1970s, specialised clusters for producing particular products have formed across the country, concentrating factories, suppliers, logistics firms and skilled workers into dense, tightly woven ecosystems. In southern China’s Guangdong province, for example, the city of Dongguan is known for electronics and toys, while Shenzhen is a hub for electronics. Foshan specialises in furniture, and Zhongshan is a major centre for lighting products. Vast trading and logistics networks have formed alongside these manufacturing clusters, helping factories reach buyers around the world. Yiwu, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, has developed a gargantuan wholesale market where hundreds of thousands of vendors sell almost any small product imaginable to overseas buyers – from toy cars to Christmas decorations. The city is home to well over 260,000 cross-border e-commerce businesses, according to non-exhaustive local government data. Temu estimates that about 40 per cent of its merchants are based in the city. Another critical piece that made the economics work for Temu was the once-permissive trade policy in some of its largest overseas markets including the US, according to Chen. In the US, the long-standing “de minimis” exemption allowed individual shipments worth less than US$800 to enter the country without the duties normally imposed on larger commercial imports, helping make it economical for Temu to ship low-cost goods directly from Chinese suppliers to American doorsteps. It had become a major conduit for Chinese cross-border commercial parcels entering the US. About 60 per cent of the more than 1 billion packages that entered the US under the de minimis exemption in fiscal 2023 came from China, according to US Customs and Border Protection data. Temu paired that trade advantage with its fully managed model, under which Chinese merchants supplied the goods while the platform handled much of the overseas sales process, from pricing and marketing to cross-border logistics. “For a small merchant, the cost of shipping a small batch is very high,” Chen said. “But with a platform like Temu, many small batches of goods can be consolidated,” significantly reducing logistics costs. At Temu’s scale, analysts said, orders from different merchants could be gathered in China and transported together across the Pacific, spreading freight costs across huge volumes of parcels while retaining their identities as individual consumer shipments for US customs and qualifying separately for de minimis treatment. China’s low-cost supply base, Temu’s fully managed model and duty-free treatment of small parcels allowed the platform to sell to consumers an ocean away while keeping inventory in China until they ordered. However, that formula was attracting scrutiny almost as quickly as Temu was attracting shoppers. In April 2023, just two months after Temu’s first Super Bowl appearance, research staff at the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a congressional advisory body, identified the de minimis exemption as one of the regulatory advantages helping Chinese e-commerce platforms expand in the US. The report said the huge volume of low-value packages made it harder for US authorities to inspect shipments and enforce trade rules, while also pointing to accusations against Temu over product quality and copyright infringement. The commission said Chinese e-commerce platforms were particularly well positioned to benefit from de minimis because their goods were typically shipped as individual low-value parcels. Temu did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The formula that once worked like magic began to quickly unravel in the US in May 2025 – four months after Trump was sworn into office – when the Trump administration ended de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from mainland China and Hong Kong. The exemption was later removed for shipments from all countries in August. The change struck at one of the central advantages of Temu’s original model: goods could still be made cheaply in China, but getting them into the hands of American consumers suddenly became more expensive. The impact was swift. Temu’s daily US users fell 48 per cent in May compared with March, according to Sensor Tower data cited by Reuters. Analysts said the policy change threatened to weaken Temu’s low-price proposition by raising the cost of the direct-shipping model that had powered its expansion. The new taxes would significantly increase the cost of shipping low-priced goods directly to overseas consumers and potentially push up retail prices, Chen said. That posed a particular challenge for Temu because many of its customers were price-sensitive, meaning higher prices risked driving some away, he added. Zhang Zhouping, executive director at Ben Se Think Tank, a cross-border commerce consultancy, echoed Chen’s view. “Taxes on small parcels erode the low-price advantage, while tax, logistics and compliance costs pile up,” Zhang said. “If those higher costs are reflected in final prices, price-sensitive consumers could be affected.” In response, Temu began moving goods closer to American shoppers. The company had already started recruiting US-based sellers and rolling out what it called a “semi-managed” model in 2024, under which merchants took greater responsibility for moving and stocking their goods overseas. Under the semi-managed model, merchants take on more responsibility for overseas logistics and warehousing, shifting inventory closer to consumers and reducing reliance on individual parcels shipped directly from China. The change makes Temu less dependent on the cross-border shipping model vulnerable to changing tariff rules, but introduces more inventory, warehousing and local fulfilment costs into the supply chain. By early 2025, about 20 per cent of Temu’s US sales were being shipped by local sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse, cited by Reuters. The end of de minimis accelerated that transition. The pressure is not confined to the US. The European Union has also tightened rules on low-value e-commerce imports. Since July, goods worth less than €150 (US$177) entering the bloc have been subject to an interim €3 customs duty for each different category of goods contained in a parcel, ending the previous duty-free treatment ahead of a broader overhaul of the EU customs system. The change has particular implications for Chinese e-commerce platforms, as some 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, with 91 per cent coming from China, according to the European Commission. Other markets have moved in the same direction. Thailand began imposing a 10 per cent customs duty in January on imported goods worth 1,500 baht (US$46) or less, which had previously been exempt from customs duties. South Africa has also tightened tax treatment of low-value e-commerce parcels. Together, the changes point to a broader erosion of the favourable treatment for low-value parcels that helped Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms expand internationally, increasing the pressure to rethink a model built heavily around shipping inexpensive goods directly from China to overseas consumers. PDD has acknowledged the consequences. At the company’s latest earnings call, Zhao Jiazhen, PDD’s co-chairman and co-chief executive, said cross-border orders in affected markets would face “lower fulfilment efficiency and higher costs”, which would have a “considerable impact” on parts of its business. For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world … In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power Wang Xin, Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association In the longer term, Zhao said Temu would bring in more local merchants and accelerate investment in local warehousing and fulfilment infrastructure to “integrate more deeply into every market we serve”. That marks a significant pivot for a platform whose original appeal rested partly on reaching overseas consumers without building out the extensive local infrastructure associated with established global e-commerce businesses such as Amazon. Another response could be geographic diversification, with Chinese platforms accelerating expansion into markets beyond the US and Europe where regulatory conditions differ, Ben Se’s Zhang said. Analysys International’s Chen said Temu was unlikely to abandon its original model altogether. Instead, he expected it to combine direct shipping where it remained economical with overseas warehouses and locally held inventory elsewhere. But the transition may ultimately involve more than changing how Temu gets goods to consumers. It could also change what it sells. If the low-price strategy becomes less effective, Temu could increasingly turn towards branded products carrying higher margins and more moderate prices, Chen said. PDD has already taken a significant step in that direction. In March, the group announced Xinpinmu, a strategic project to develop and operate its own brands by combining the supply chain resources accumulated by Pinduoduo in China with Temu’s overseas reach. The group has injected 15 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion) into the project and plans to invest a total of 100 billion yuan over three years, with the venture developing brands across different product categories and markets for global consumers. “Temu’s rapid growth over the past three years was a key leap made possible by the strength of China’s supply chain, and has also created a new opportunity to upgrade and reshape the domestic supply chain,” Zhao said when announcing the initiative. Three years after Temu promised Americans they could “shop like a billionaire”, the factories capable of producing a US$8.99 dress cheaply have not disappeared, nor has the vast Chinese manufacturing ecosystem behind them. What has changed is the economics of getting that dress from China to consumers thousands of kilometres away, and, increasingly, the kind of goods PDD wants those factories to sell. Those economics could shift again as Washington and Beijing continue to negotiate the terms of their trading relationship. During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month, tariffs and other trade issues were high on the agenda as the world’s two largest economies seek to manage a fragile detente. For Temu and other Chinese cross-border e-commerce companies, the stakes of that meeting are high, as their low-price model is particularly sensitive to tariffs and trade rules that raise the cost of moving goods from Chinese factories to US consumers. For some in the industry, however, the changing environment is accelerating a broader push to upgrade China’s cross-border e-commerce sector beyond its reliance on low prices. “For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world,” said Wang Xin, president of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, in an interview with state broadcaster CCTV earlier this year. “In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power,” she said.

title: Style Edit: Boucheron’s ivy motif blooms with new Lierre de Paris high jewellery creations
description: Creative director Claire Choisne reimagines the leafy emblem that has flourished in the jeweller’s designs for more than 150 years.
content: Ivy has a way of making itself at home. It climbs, curls and spreads with little regard for where it is supposed to stop, taking over walls and trees with its fast-growing natural architecture. For Frédéric Boucheron, that freedom was precisely the attraction. Of all the plants that appeared in his jewellery, ivy became one of the most persistent – a fitting symbol for a jeweller who was drawn to nature in its less orderly forms. The motif entered the Boucheron archives in 1870 and, by the end of the decade, had become one of the house’s defining designs. Frédéric Boucheron used ivy in his original 1879 drawing for the Question Mark necklace, which was brought to life two years later. The maison would continue to evolve its depiction of the plant. In the 1920s, its stems were reduced to delicate trails of gold; in 2012, Lierre de Paris gave the motif a more assertive high jewellery interpretation. More recently, ivy appeared on a much larger scale in Boucheron’s 2025 and 2026 Histoire de Style collections, where it seemed to grow across the body rather than simply decorate it. Creative director Claire Choisne now returns to the plant and the Lierre de Paris collection with a more intimate proposition. Her latest collection comprises nine pieces, all in white gold and diamonds, but the monochrome palette does little to tame the subject. Instead, it sharpens the contrast between the brilliance of the stones and the organic forms they describe. Three rings allow the ivy to travel across the hand. One stretches over two fingers, while even the small and medium versions each show three leaves opening across the fingers. The smallest ring has a corresponding pendant, creating a set that carries the same composition from hand to neckline. Elsewhere, a supple necklace without a clasp wraps around the neck like a branch that has found its own path. The earrings are deliberately mismatched, with two asymmetric pairs designed to be worn in different configurations. Ivy brooches take the idea further. Their spiral fastening allows them to be placed on a jacket, dress or even in the hair, alone or clustered together. They have the looseness of an accessory picked up and rearranged rather than a jewel fixed into a single prescribed position. Much of the collection’s impact, however, comes down to how convincingly the plant has been rendered. The leaves are sculpted rather than simply outlined, with open-worked backs beneath the diamond pavé that allow light to pass through. Veining is articulated with enough delicacy to make the leaves appear almost botanical, while their softly rounded tips prevent the pieces from becoming overly precise or mechanical. That balance is where Boucheron’s interpretation becomes interesting. Ivy is inherently unpredictable; high jewellery is an exercise in control. Here, the maison’s artisans use extraordinary precision to recreate something that, in nature, grows without it. The result is jewellery that retains the irregularity and movement of a climbing vine while revealing the meticulous handwork required to make it appear effortless. For Boucheron, ivy has never been merely a pretty botanical motif. It has represented freedom from the beginning. More than 150 years later, under Choisne’s direction, the maison is still finding new ways to let it grow.

title: Style Edit: Chaumet expands the Joséphine collection, inspired by the French empress
description: The new additions to the signature line, launched in 2010, bear the pear-shaped motif, designed for those who mirror the free spirit, taste and elegance of its historic muse.
content: Joséphine de Beauharnais, Empress of France from 1804 to 1810 during her marriage to Emperor Napoleon I, remains one of the most iconic figures in French history. A byword for style, she became known for her patronage of the arts and her exquisite taste, surrounding herself with creative people and helping to shape their work. An innovator who redefined the artistic preferences of her era, she established the wildly influential empire style of architecture and decorative arts, using her own residence – the grand Château de Malmaison near Paris – as the canvas for a revolution in aesthetics. Two centuries after her reign, in 2010, she was honoured in fitting style, when Chaumet celebrated its 230th anniversary with the launch of a collection that bears her name. It celebrates a number of styles that Joséphine herself popularised: the imperial tiara that once adorned her head has been reimagined as a series of rings, and there are innovative renditions of the pear-shaped diamonds she so loved, alongside the graceful “V” shapes inspired by the aigrette, an ornament worn on the hair. The aigrette appears in several of the latest pieces in the collection, including those in the Joséphine high jewellery parure. Its most dazzling appearance is as an openwork bracelet in which the aigrette patterns of three bands of pavé diamonds intersect, with brilliant-cut diamonds arranged in a pear shape as its centrepiece. Brilliant-cut diamonds are similarly arranged into pears across the new Joséphine earrings, inspired by the Bourbon-Parma tiara Joseph Chaumet created in 1919. The pear shape also finds a home at the heart of the Triomphe de Chaumet ring, where a sapphire creates a dynamic contrast with the purity of a band of white diamonds. A Joséphine ring, now available in rose gold, showcases a 0.5-carat pear-cut diamond, offset by aigrette-shaped lines of pavé diamonds. A pear shape also defines a new Joséphine watch, available in rose gold and steel, studded with diamonds and encircling a white dial. The aigrette again comes to the fore in a new collection of pendants and earrings. The pendants, available in rose and white gold, come in versions where the “V” is adorned with either Akoya pearls or mirror-polished gold beads. On another set of necklaces and earrings, the “V” becomes a graphic chevron, with a textured relief pavé setting in white gold.

title: Malaysians choose family over shopping or holidays, domestic travel data shows
description: The dominance of family-related travel has presented opportunities for hotels, local attractions.
content: Malaysians delight in visiting family and friends, so much so that these visits made up 44 per cent of domestic travel. They enjoy seeing their loved ones even more than shopping (21.6 per cent) and holidaying (13 per cent), as shown in the latest numbers from the Statistics Department on domestic tourism in the second quarter of this year. The 44 per cent recorded is even higher than last year’s trend in domestic tourism where “visiting relatives and friends remained the primary purpose of domestic travel, accounting for 35.6 per cent”. The dominance of family-related travel has presented opportunities for accommodation providers, particularly when visitors prefer to stay near their relatives rather than in their homes. Budget hotels could cater to these travellers through competitive rates, family rooms and convenient locations near residential areas and town centres, Malaysia Budget and Business Hotel Association national president Sri Ganesh Michiel said. The trend could also benefit smaller hotels in secondary towns, where affordability, convenience and cleanliness are key considerations. Michiel said that hotels needed greater flexibility to accommodate shorter stays and family gatherings, while tourism infrastructure in smaller districts should improve to address accessibility, transport and connectivity challenges. For these travellers who were visiting their families, he said that the need for hotel rooms was especially crucial during festive celebrations, weddings, funerals and family gatherings. Malaysian Association of Hotels president Christina Toh said that social media had helped popularise lesser-known attractions since the Covid-19 pandemic, encouraging visitors returning to their hometowns to explore surrounding areas. “People who return to their hometowns to visit relatives are now more likely to explore attractions nearby, rather than spending all their time with family at home,” she said. Malaysian Association of Tour and Travel Agents president Nigel Wong said travel agents could turn family visits into broader tourism experiences. Citing data from the Statistics Department which showed that the average length of stay rose from 2.49 nights in 2024 to 2.56 nights last year, he said that this was an indication that travellers could be encouraged to spend more time at their destinations. Travel agents could offer add-on experiences such as food trails, shopping excursions, heritage walks, nature activities and evening programmes which could fit around their visits, Wong said. “The objective is not necessarily to extend the trip longer, but to encourage visitors to spend an additional day, one additional meal or one additional activity within the local economy.” This article was first published by The Star

title: Opinion | Hong Kong can speak better Mandarin but not at the expense of Cantonese
description: The nation’s rise makes communicating in Mandarin practical. However, we should have room to respond to the evolving realities around us.
content: One of Hong Kong’s top high schools made the mistake of apparently banning Cantonese from graduation videos. Only English and Mandarin were permitted, according to “language standards” issued to Form Six students. The guidelines said that if Cantonese was detected in video submissions, the audio would have to be muted and sound effects redone. A post on the matter quickly went viral last month, a backlash erupted and the authorities stepped in. Good Hope School acted swiftly, activating its crisis management team and clarifying its policy not only to students but also to the wider community. It offered a genuine apology and reassured the public that it was not and would never be its ethos to “constrain the mother tongue of any child entrusted to our care”. Disaster averted. The question of how things came to that remains, however. The principal said the slide in question hadn’t been revised before dissemination. But at some point, it seems, someone at the school with decision-making powers decided it would be OK to “mute” Cantonese, which is spoken by about 95 per cent of the population. No language policy can be separated from politics. It was a contentious issue in Hong Kong’s past, going back to the days of imperialism, when language was an instrument of power and a device for alienating the voice of the people. In Hong Kong, Chinese was not recognised as an official language until 1974. Every so often, debate heats up again about the use of language in this city. Last November, controversy erupted after it emerged that a school would permit students to use simplified Chinese characters in written assessments and exams. Former Hong Kong chief executive Leung Chun-ying spoke out against the measure, which was aimed at accommodating new students from the mainland. Leung argued that these students must accustom themselves to traditional Chinese characters, like other students in this city. Leung got himself in a bind 10 years ago with social media posts that contained a few simplified Chinese characters. Those were very different times though. Radical localism was quick to pounce on just about anything, politicising issues while feeding off social angst. The Education Bureau didn’t help matters; it actually tried to suggest primary school pupils learn simplified Chinese characters. Pushback came even from Jasper Tsang Yok-sing, then Legislative Council president, who said the idea should not be raised without thorough consideration and deep thinking. Hong Kong’s official language education policy aims for biliteracy and trilingualism. Any attempt to thwart that would be misguided. There is already growing anxiety over whether Hong Kong is becoming “just another Chinese city”. The language we speak and write is an issue that goes to the heart of our identity. With the phenomenal rise of the nation, Hong Kong’s renewed role as a superconnector definitely makes communicating in Mandarin and simplified Chinese characters practical and necessary. But that does not require that we ban Cantonese or limit its use. Upholding and protecting “one country, two systems” – under which our way of life, arguably including our use of language, is safeguarded – means that we should have room to respond to evolving realities around us. Encouraging the use and understanding of Mandarin is far wiser, and some are already naturally playing catch-up. The Legislative Council made a historic study trip to Beijing in July. At one point during a long exchange session, Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, made a lighthearted suggestion that our lawmakers should improve their Mandarin skills. Sure, that would improve communication and it need not be at the expense of other Chinese dialects. Our lawmakers have never been called on to defend their use of Cantonese at home. Hong Kong is an international city, and this is something we are, and should be, very proud of. We aspire to be an inclusive society, open to diversity and welcoming to people from different cultures and backgrounds. Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong has been very comfortable speaking Mandarin in the Legislative Council and other public settings. Our government has been working hard to celebrate, promote and protect local culture, including our culinary traditions and heritage sites. This year, the city is launching “Hong Kong Halloween Month”. How this festival came to be celebrated in Hong Kong in the first place is part of who we are. Perhaps it was seized on as an excuse for everyone to let their hair down and bring vibrancy back to our nightlife. One way or another, our culture, history and collective experience should be recognised.

title: FBI chief Kash Patel and country singer Alexis Wilkins announce engagement
description: Pair share social media post as country artist quips she ‘got the law involved’.
content: FBI Director Kash Patel is engaged to his country singer girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, the pair announced in a post to X on Sunday evening. Wilkins, 27, posted a black-and-white photo of herself standing with Patel, 46, flashing her hand in front of them to show off her ring with the caption: “Went and got the law involved”. The two have been dating since before Patel took over as head of the FBI in 2025, when she attended his swearing in. The country singer and political commentator released her debut album in 2023. Wilkins has been affiliated with conservative groups and writes on her website that she “honours country tradition while adding relevance and current commentary”. Patel, who reposted Wilkins’ photo, has faced criticism for travelling on government aircraft on trips that have no known or apparent law enforcement purpose, including using an FBI jet to fly to State College, Pennsylvania, for a pro wrestling event where Wilkins performed the national anthem. ❤️💍 — Kash Patel (@Kash_Patel) October 4, 2026 Photos posted to social media by Wilkins afterwards showed the couple smiling while she held an oversized golden championship belt. Wilkins also made headlines as a performer at President Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall as part of America 250, as other artists pulled out of the event after finding out it was not a non-partisan celebration.

title: HKU eyes Northern Metropolis expansion to boost research capacity, attract talent
description: New research vice-president Anderson Shum says megaproject offers space HKU needs for hardware such as new dry and wet labs.
content: The University of Hong Kong (HKU) is looking to secure more laboratory space in the Northern Metropolis university town to expand its research capacity and attract talent, its new vice-president for research has said. Professor Anderson Shum Ho-cheung, who took up the vice presidency in August, also called for more government funding, saying grant applications took time and returns on investment could be slow. Shum said the university’s research development would align with the government’s emphasis on integrating education, technology, industry and talent to expedite the development of the Northern Metropolis as laid out in the policy address. He described a closed-loop strategy moving discoveries from the laboratory to industry and back. Top talent drives breakthrough research, industry partnerships and start-ups translate it into applications, and successful ventures feed new research problems back to scientists. “When our start-ups do well and form new industries, those industries bring new questions back to our scientists, and the cycle keeps going,” he said. “Talent draws talent. Researchers hope to work alongside other talented people. When the density of talent gets higher, the attraction for talent will only increase.” HKU recently recruited two Nobel laureates, Sir Andre Geim and Ferenc Krausz, and one Fields Medallist, Ngo Bao Chau. Shum said talent assessed a university’s development potential through its hardware and that the Northern Metropolis offered the opportunity to meet those needs. “If a researcher needs to run a certain kind of infectious disease experiment and there is no laboratory with the required biosafety level, you can hire them, but they still cannot do their work,” he said. The Northern Metropolis plan which was included in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the policy address announced last month, included three university towns in San Tin, Hung Shui Kiu and Ta Kwu Ling, spanning more than 1,000 hectares to develop the city as an innovation hub. Funding is expected to be self-financing, with the government providing land and loans and institutions free to tap their reserves or issue bonds. The Hung Shui Kiu site is expected to be ready this year, with universities able to begin bidding this month. Shum said HKU needed new laboratories in the Northern Metropolis, including dry labs for computation and data work, wet labs for handling biological and chemical experiments, and AI facilities. “The government has set out a forward-looking vision that education, technology, industry, talent and urban building should develop together as five elements of Northern Metropolis, and we need close communication across all five to make it most effective,” he said. Shum, a biomedical engineering scholar, has spent years in university leadership. He was HKU’s associate vice-president for research and innovation between 2021 and 2024. He was then appointed as City University’s research vice-president, a post he held until he returned to HKU this year. He also sits on an expert group under the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit advising on research strategy. Under Shum, HKU has launched RISE – short for research, innovation, strategic partnerships and entrepreneurship – a platform consolidating research funding, intellectual property, technology transfer and start-up incubation. “Turning research into products is never easy. Raising funds, writing business plans, passing regulatory approvals – every step is difficult, and returns can be years away,” he said. “That is why we need funding from both the government and the university, so our researchers can give full play to their creativity.” On university-industry collaboration, Shum said companies should be brought in early, highlighting that firms best understood where their products needed to improve, whereas scientific questions were better tackled in universities. “If industry tells us early that a material is difficult to mass produce, or that a chemical will struggle to win approval, we can have that conversation early and make the whole translation process more efficient,” he said. Shum will also front the university’s flagship Innovation Week from October 12 to 16, bringing more than 1,000 representatives from government, industry and academia together to showcase over 120 innovations. “We hope Innovation Week can improve science popularisation and lift our overall innovation and science literacy to another level, which is an important social mission of the university,” he said. He added that raising public awareness of science mattered for technology transfer, drawing inspiration from the community and keeping the university closely tied to society.

title: Meet the real animals behind ‘five styles’ kung fu
description: The southern Chinese martial art form was inspired by the tiger, crane, snake and leopard as well as the mythical dragon.
content:
In the beloved animated film Kung Fu Panda, a clumsy, lovable panda transforms into a martial arts master. This captivating fictional tale holds some truth. The original creators of Chinese martial arts were inspired by animals – though the panda was not one of them.
The kung fu in the film is called “five styles” and is a southern style of Chinese martial arts. It is inspired by one mythical animal, the dragon, and four real animals: tiger, crane, snake and leopard. Read on to learn more about the real animals that inspire kung fu techniques and movements.
This feline is known for being powerful and fierce, so it is a symbol for strength and bravery in kung fu. As a king of beasts, the tiger often shows relentless aggression when hunting its prey.
When fighting in the style of a tiger, people should take a firm step forward to help power a punch with a burst of force.
This bird often stands elegantly on one leg to conserve energy, saving its strength for when it takes flight. With long necks, wide wings and delicate feet, cranes are considered graceful birds with balance and power. Kung fu movements inspired by this animal are both soft and fierce, with arms that stretch out for every strike and transition .
The “snake hand” technique imitates the fangs and fluid strike of a snake. Just like the reptile’s accuracy in killing its prey, this move is targeted and direct.
The snake style also features unpredictable footwork inspired by a snake’s smooth, fast movement. It allows the martial artist to attack from the least expected direction.
The leopard is an excellent hunter. Despite being the smallest of the large cats – a group that includes tigers, lions and jaguars – leopards can run up to 58km in an hour. The agile beast closes in on its target before striking with explosive power. Inspired by these lightning-fast movements, this style of kung fu focuses on quick attacks.

title: Laotian man freed from eSwatini jail 14 months after US third-country deportation
description: Around 500 have been deported to African countries that are not their home nations since the third-country programme began last year.
content: A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to eSwatini under Donald Trump administration’s immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said. Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to eSwatini – where he has no ties – in July 2025, in the early days of the Trump administration’s secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation programme. Chomsavanh’s US-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had been informed that he was being deported to eSwatini only shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago. Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said. Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported with to eSwatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the US, but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini’s administrative capital, Mbabane. “He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything,” Nguyen said. “He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.” He said in a separate interview that Chomsavanh had left eSwatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos. The eSwatini government did not immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release. Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was seven, his lawyer said. Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that are not their home nations since the third-country programme began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations. Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the US, some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. ESwatini, which is Africa’s last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid US$5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. eSwatini has received around 30 deportees so far.
