The programme, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they have not been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticised by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the US and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent. The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the US when their home countries might not immediately take them back. Last month, a US appeal court upheld a judge’s ruling to halt the programme, because it did not give immigrants facing removal from the US time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there. The US Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow the Trump’s administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December. The programme has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held.

title: University students explore China’s cultural spirit
description: The youth are revitalising heritage by exploring Beijing’s hutongs, Guangzhou’s trade and Hong Kong’s global culture.
content:
As Ou Aki walked through Beijing’s centuries-old narrow streets, known as hutong, she began to look beyond the brick walls and tight lanes.
Instead of just seeing old neighbourhoods, the Peking University student saw communities finding new ways to keep their history alive.
“It’s an attitude of maintaining old things while making new repairs, constantly changing and evolving ,” said Ou, who is 22.
“They are not only trying to preserve the hutong ... but also continue to make changes to attract younger, vibrant generations.”
Ou grew up in Japan. She had always been interested in cultural places. Still, it wasn’t until she joined the fifth “Bi-city Youth Cultural Leadership Programme” that she saw how heritage could become part of everyday life in China.
The Hong Kong Palace Museum arranged the eight-week programme. It brought together 22 university students from mainland China and Hong Kong. They went on field visits and did internships.
Participants looked at how heritage, cultural spaces and community projects shape modern China.
Eamon Chang Shang-chen is a psychology student at Beijing Forestry University. He travelled to Beijing, Guangzhou and Hong Kong. This journey helped him see how each city plays a role in China’s growth and development.
The 22-year-old student described Beijing as a city with a lot of history. He said Guangzhou was shaped by a long history of trade and openness. Chang added that Hong Kong shares Chinese culture with the world while also welcoming influences from other countries.
He believes this reflects a collective spirit : “Every city has a very important role,” he said. “These different characteristics complement each other.”
He also spent four weeks doing an internship at the East Kowloon Cultural Centre. This experience inspired him to explore psychodrama. Psychodrama is a kind of therapy in which people act out scenes from their lives to understand their feelings.
Serene Yu Sum-in is a student at Hong Kong Shue Yan University. The 19-year-old is studying arts, culture and technology.
Yu said she noticed a value in all the cities she travelled to: respect.
In Beijing, she observed how community projects were designed around residents’ needs. In Hong Kong, she saw cultural spaces embracing people from different backgrounds.
When she visited Longxi Art Society, a community-based cultural group in Foshan, she was impressed by its commitment to children’s art education and art therapy.
“All of these people really respect others’ ideas,” she said. “No matter your age or your background, they make you feel welcome.”

title: IPL stars dominate India’s Hong Kong Cricket Sixes squad
description: Bhuvneshwar Kumar, veteran of 229 international appearances, leads ‘one of strongest India sides’ for 2026 tournament.
content: The Hong Kong Cricket Sixes is set for a “quantum leap forward” after headliners India announced a squad for this year’s tournament composed almost exclusively of players who competed in the 2026 Indian Premier League. Bhuvneshwar Kumar, a veteran of 229 international appearances, will captain a side that also features his Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) teammate, and fellow reigning Indian Premier League (IPL) champion, Krunal Pandya, as well as the former India all-format bowler Thangarasu Natarajan. Since the Sixes was revived in 2024, India, who claimed their solitary Hong Kong title in 2005, have delivered a pair of slapdash tournament performances, twice crashing out at the group stage. They lost nine of their 10 matches over the past two editions. After assembling a seven-strong squad that features only one player who did not make it into the middle during the latest IPL, the Kolkata Knight Riders top-order striker Rahul Tripathi, the Indians will expect an upturn in fortunes when the three-day 2026 Hong Kong Sixes gets under way on October 30. “We are very grateful to the Indian cricket authorities for their support in helping us put together arguably one of the strongest sides that has represented India in the history of the Sixes,” said Anurag Bhatnagar, Cricket Hong Kong, China’s (CHKC) director of marketing and commercial. “This will surely prove to be a quantum leap forward in terms of viewership and further validation for this iconic tournament.” Last month, CHKC announced a partnership with Indian enterprise JSW Sports, which includes co-ownership of IPL giants Delhi Capitals among an enviable sporting portfolio. Among this year’s Indian Sixes contingent, the Delhi franchise has provided Natarajan, whose lone Test appearance came in India’s series-clinching three-wicket victory over Australia in Brisbane in January 2021, and 32-year-old former international middle-order batsman Nitish Rana. The JSW tie-in was forged with a view to the Sixes “going global”, according to Bhatnagar, with plans in place to introduce an additional competition every year, until a worldwide series of five or six events has been established. Pakistan will defend their Hong Kong title at Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground, after the 12-team line-up was confirmed on Friday. In right-arm swing merchant Kumar, 36, India come with a player who played 21 Tests, 121 ODIs and 87 T20Is during a 10-year international career, and claimed the wickets of Sai Sadharsan and Jason Holder in RCB’s IPL final victory over Gujarat Titans in May. Kumar also won the IPL with Sunrisers Hyderabad in 2016, when his 23-wicket haul made him the tournament’s most prolific bowler. Spinning all-rounder Pandya, who has made 19 T20I and five ODI appearances, was also on the winning side in this year’s final. Leg break bowler and huge-hitting batsman Rahul Tewatia, another member of the India party for Hong Kong, was in the beaten Gujarat team, with whom he won the IPL in 2022. Shashank Singh, the 34-year-old Punjab Kings all-rounder, and Kolkata’s Tripathi, 35, who played five T20I matches in 2023, are also in India’s Sixes squad. India squad for Hong Kong Cricket Sixes: Bhuvenshwar Kumar (c), Krunal Pandya, Shashank Singh, Rahul Tewatia, Nitish Rana, Rahul Tripathi, Thangarasu Natarajan.

title: Rigid goals not set in Hong Kong’s 5-year plan to allay fears of planned economy: Tse
description: Hong Kong constitutional affairs chief Janice Tse also says government exploring administrative measures to protect same-sex couples’ rights after bill veto.
content: Hong Kong refrained from setting overly rigid economic indicators in its first five-year plan to avoid fuelling concerns that it was moving towards a planned economy, according to the city’s constitutional affairs minister. The current priority should be hitting targets instead of dwelling on accountability mechanisms for potential shortcomings, Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse Siu-wa said. Tse also emphasised the government’s efforts to explore administrative measures to protect same-sex couples’ rights after lawmakers vetoed a bill last year meant to recognise their partnership in line with a court ruling, although she offered no timeline. Last month, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, outlining initiatives to speed up the Northern Metropolis megaproject and cement the city’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology to align with the nation’s development strategy. The “action agenda” for long-term development set out 22 major targets covering economic and innovation development, livelihood and environmental protection. Only five are binding targets, while the remaining 17 are anticipatory goals, such as annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth “within a reasonable range” and achieving “steady growth” in imports and exports. Amid doubts over the blueprint’s lack of binding goals and the vagueness of key economic indicators, Tse stressed that overly rigid indicators could jeopardise Hong Kong’s image as a free-market economy. “What is the most difficult part of setting quantified indicators? If they are too rigid, some people will say Hong Kong is running a planned economy,” said Tse, who spearheaded the document’s coordination and drafting. “However, if you do not set indicators, some people will criticise you for lacking commitment. Or if you set anticipatory goals, people might ask whether there is no need for accountability if you fail to meet the targets.” She added that long-term planning and development inevitably involved uncertainties, making it almost impossible to predict free-market economic figures with precision. She cited GDP growth sensitivity to global trade and tourism’s vulnerability to unforeseen shocks such as the Covid-19 pandemic. She reaffirmed the administration’s determination to meet the goals listed in the blueprint, but stopped short of detailing how officials would be held accountable if targets were missed. Instead, she said the priority should be on closing gaps when targets fall short. “The government hopes to achieve any quantified indicator. If risks arise or we identify a gap during assessment, we should catch up and do better,” Tse said. “We should not, right after setting an indicator, immediately start thinking about what happens if we fail to meet it.” Under the blueprint’s implementation mechanism, which included dynamic monitoring, midterm assessment and final reporting, the administration would continuously review progress, policy priorities and resource adequacy rather than conducting only annual reviews, Tse said. Although the government previously rejected calls to adopt mainland Chinese practices of conducting third-party reviews by think tanks and research institutes, Tse said public and professional groups’ feedback and criticism, lawmakers’ concerns and the central government’s oversight already formed a robust accountability system. “Many residents, professional groups and think tanks have been closely monitoring the five-year plan. Every day, numerous articles published in various newspapers discuss what should be done and whether enough has been achieved,” Tse said. “In fact, these already amount to third-party assessments. They come uninvited, but we are very grateful … and many of them reflect the concerns of different industries.” She also sought to assure that even though the document would not be revised, policy execution would remain agile and responsive to market dynamics. “The market will tell us how to adjust. Hong Kong has always been entirely market-led, but the government needs to provide support,” she added. When asked why the five-year blueprint did not address political reform, Tse said a stable environment under the current system was key to the economy, development and people’s livelihoods. But she noted that the document only charted a course for the next five years, making it difficult to predict outcomes in the long run as the broader environment could change. Following the overhaul of Hong Kong’s electoral system in 2021 to ensure that only “patriots” can hold power, Beijing published a white paper saying that the move fostered favourable conditions for universal suffrage of the chief executive and the Legco, as outlined in the Basic Law, the city’s mini-constitution. Tse, a retired civil servant, was appointed the constitutional and mainland affairs chief in March, filling the vacancy left by Erick Tsang Kwok-wai, who stepped down in January due to poor health. With only about 10 months remaining in the current government term, Tse declined to divulge whether she intended to stay on to oversee implementation of the five-year plan, describing the question as an issue “outside her radar”. “I have a lot on my plate; this is not an issue I need to be concerned with at the moment,” she said. “The five-year plan’s continuity does not depend on any individual; the planning has been written down.” Turning to the debate over same-sex couples’ rights in the city, Tse said her bureau had been exploring administrative measures after the veto of the Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill last September and would announce details once they were finalised. But she added that her bureau already faced a heavy workload, including organising three major elections by the end of next year. The bill was the government’s answer to a 2023 ruling by the Court of Final Appeal, which gave authorities two years to draw up laws to set out “core rights” for same-sex couples. Tse dismissed claims that the delay had undermined the rule of law. “The government has made efforts. We submitted the bill to the legislature, but it was voted down … So you cannot say the government did not try or that it placed a low priority on the matter. We did make the effort,” Tse said. “[The bill] could not get through. That is the reality. Having accepted this reality, we are now considering ways forward. Do you think it is easy?” She sidestepped a question of whether the government could resolve the issue before her term ended in July next year, saying: “I am confident that I will accomplish many things during my term, because this is my responsibility.”

title: Letters from readers: Favourite subjects, hobbies and remembering beloved pets
description: This week, students share what they do at school, sports they enjoy and memories of a treasured family member.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
My favourite subject in school is art, but I love to read books, too. I have a pet hamster at home called Hazelnut. I used to have a dog named Clifford, but he got cancer.
My favourite places to go for holiday are Vietnam and Thailand. If I could change the world, I would end world hunger.
My hobbies are playing football and badminton. I started to enjoy them when I was in Primary One and now I play almost every week.
I like these sports because they are not only fun but also help me stay healthy and make new friends. When I joined the interschool swimming competition, I was nervous at first, but once I jumped into the water and started swimming, I felt very excited. Although I did not win the championship, I learned the importance of persistence and effort.
I once won first place in a friendly swimming competition, which made me very proud.
It’s been more than three months since you crossed the Rainbow Bridge, and we still have not been able to get over losing our big brother. We love you so, so much – we don’t have enough words to describe our love for you.
When we turned around to look at you, we would see you just sitting there, looking at us with concerned eyes, but so calm and quiet. You were the best dog ever! You brought us so much joy and comfort.
Thank you for your unconditional love and companionship. Thank you for coming into our lives.

title: Carrie Wong Ka-yuet’s top picks: ‘The Dragonsitter’ and ‘KPop Demon Hunters’
description: The 8-year-old student from Po Leung Kuk Tan Siu Lin Primary School shares her favourite book and film.
content:
Do you have a book, film or television show you love? Send us your recommendations using this form .
I recommend a book called The Dragonsitter by Josh Lacey. I like it because it’s a very funny book. It is about a boy named Eddie. His uncle, Morton Pickle, has a pet dragon.
His uncle is on holiday, so Eddie has to take care of the dragon. But the dragon burns up everything in the house and even tries to attack the neighbour’s cats!
Thankfully, Uncle Morton comes up with a solution – feeding the dragon chocolate. At last, the problem is solved.
The film I would like to recommend is KPop Demon Hunters .
The hunters are Rumi, Zoey and Mira. They are trying to create the Golden Honmoon so that demons cannot attack the world ever again.
Before the Honmoon can be sealed, the demon king Gwi-ma sends a demon boy band to defeat the hunters.
But there’s a twist! Rumi is half-demon because of her father.
She tries to hide her demon patterns from her friends. By the end of the movie, her friends learn about her demon side and they still sing together.

title: Feature of the Week: Clement Cheung’s visit to Heureka Science Centre in Finland
description: The student from Kwai Ming Wu Memorial School of the Precious Blood shares what he learned at the innovative educational destination.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
In Finland, they teach people to think like an inventor, helping students develop innovative skills and improve their creativity. But how exactly do they do that?
I think it’s because they don’t always stay in the classroom to learn. I’d like to introduce you to the Heureka Science Centre, one of the country’s most famous educational destinations.
Now you may be thinking, “It’s just a science centre, right?” Yes, but it’s also a whole new dimension for creativity! People can take part in hands-on experiments and explore science.
I have actually visited the science centre. There are dozens of exhibitions to see, from learning about the Ice Age to freshwater reserves. There’s even one where you can experience riding a bicycle in mid-air! These exhibitions let you learn about the concepts of history, gravity and more.
Now, some people may believe this is irrelevant to innovation. But the centre teaches us about many issues that need to be resolved, such as how climate change and human activity can cause great harm to nature.
We can also learn how human activity affects water availability and the water cycle.
By highlighting these major problems, Heureka inspires visitors to find solutions, helping us innovate and reach new levels of creative thinking.
If you find yourself in class wondering, “Can this stop extreme weather from happening?” or “What can we actually do to help innovate mankind?” then the Heureka Science Centre might be your best teacher.

title: Legendary lessons from Confucius: treat others as you want to be treated
description: The ancient Chinese philosopher, known as Kongzi, taught that everyone should be treated with dignity.
content:
More than 2,500 years ago, a wise man named Confucius lived in China. He is also known as Kongzi. He was born Kongqiu in 551BC in eastern China.
Back then, the country was filled with fighting and chaos. Confucius wondered how to make communities peaceful again. He believed that respect was key to creating people who could help improve society.
Confucius wanted to change the world by being a public official. But he found more success as a teacher. His students recorded his lessons in The Analects .
He believed that respect is like a thread that sews a society together. He taught his students that everyone – from powerful rulers to common citizens – should be treated with dignity.
When he died in 479BC, Confucius left behind many students. His teachings would continue to influence China for thousands of years.
One of his famous teachings is called the “Golden Rule”: “Do not do to others what you would not want them to do to you.”
Think about how that works in your daily life. If you do not like being teased, do not tease your classmates. If you want people to listen to your ideas, make sure to listen when they speak.
Confucius believed that when we show respect at home to our parents and siblings, it will spread to our community and beyond.
He also taught that we should never stop learning. Confucius believed he could learn something valuable from every person he met, even a child. He showed that true wisdom does not come from knowing everything. It comes from having an open and respectful mind.

title: Despite logistical problems, world records prove Asian Games were a hit, says top official
description: Olympic Council of Asia director general says ‘numbers are facts’, pointing to 54 world, 11 junior world and 89 Asian records in Aichi-Nagoya.
content: The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) said ⁠that a near 20 per cent jump ⁠in revenue, strong viewership figures and ⁠a slew of world records proved the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games were a success, despite logistical problems plaguing the multi-sport showpiece. The Games saw a catalogue of mishaps, from athletes bused to the wrong venues to the North Korean national anthem being played for the South Korean hockey team. There were not enough beds for the more than 17,000 athletes and officials, a larger number than the Olympics. Countries also complained of being stranded for up to six hours at the airport on arrival. However, the Games produced some elite performances, although sometimes in front of rows of empty seats. Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said “numbers are facts” as he launched an impassioned defence of the Games before the closing ceremony. He pointed to the 54 world, 11 junior world and 89 continental records set at the Games as evidence of effective ⁠organisation. World records were broken in sports including swimming, shooting and weightlifting. “This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes,” he said. “The athletes cannot perform if they don’t sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don’t have good transportation. “We are here to present to you the evidence,” he added. The number of participants had ballooned following a flurry of late entries – around 2,000 more than projected. With no dedicated Athletes’ Village, participants were housed in ‌a mix of hotels, container-style living units and a cruise ship. Satoshi Murate, secretary general of the organising committee, apologised after the unexpected increase strained accommodation and transport networks, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms and small beds. However, Al-Musallam said the accommodation was “very well received by the athletes” and provided a sustainable model for future Games. He added that at a time when the Games must be sustainable and financially viable, the Aichi-Nagoya model ‌was one worth copying. “We are happy to see that there is no big financial burden in the organising committee, and there is no ‌white elephant ‌staying in Nagoya or any place.” The revenue increase, measured against the Games in Hangzhou three years ago, ‌came mainly from digital growth and stronger viewership figures, with India’s hockey and cricket matches against Pakistan drawing ⁠large TV audiences, OCA officials said. Al-Musallam also said the Games had provided a moment of unity during a ⁠time of geopolitical turmoil. “When you look to the news, conflict everywhere – in Asia, outside Asia,” he said. “Economic problems everywhere. But look at Asia, how united we are in sport.” Tayyab Ikram, chairman of ‌the Games Coordination Committee, acknowledged the logistical problems but said they had overcome them by working together. “There is no Games without challenges. There is no Games without initial interruptions,” said Ikram, who also heads the International Hockey Federation. “In future, we would like to see more sustainable solutions, more improvement and innovation … but without compromising on the athletes’ conditions.”

title: Quant funds are ‘necessary’ to China’s ascent as financial powerhouse: investor
description: Beijing would be remiss to regulate quantitative trading too tightly, as the sector plays ‘important role’ in financial market, executive says.
content: Beijing has tightened scrutiny of quantitative trading funds in recent months amid fears they add to market instability. Yet a leading investor believes the future is bright for China’s quant funds, as they are “necessary for a developed economy”. Seth Huang, the head of Aris Capital, said quant funds had such a clear advantage over retail investors on China’s capital markets that the situation could be described as “a war with some using machine guns and others butcher knives”. Quant funds have been making rapid progress in China, with the number of funds managing more than 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in assets jumping by 18 this year, according to domestic media reports. The sector’s growth is mostly down to the funds’ strong performance, according to Huang, who is also an associate adjunct professor of finance at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “Last year, 95 per cent of CSI 1000 quant index-enhancement funds generated positive excess returns,” he added, meaning they beat the CSI 1000 – China’s flagship small-cap index. On average, quantitative index-enhancement funds across indexes outperformed their benchmarks by 16.75 per cent, reaching an average return rate of 45.08 per cent, according to the Chinese Securities Journal. But quant funds were currently less accessible to ordinary investors in China compared with other markets, a result of Beijing’s relatively tight regulation of the sector. “In the United States, the largest quant funds manage pension funds and endowments, so essentially they manage the money of teachers, firefighters and garbagemen,” Huang said. “In China, the government does not let quant funds manage pensions or state money.” This raises questions about who benefits from quant funds’ strong performance. A large portion of quant funds are market makers: they provide liquidity when retail investors, who are market takers, take liquidity away Seth Huang, Aris Capital Quant funds have faced criticism in China over recent months, with some arguing they can amplify market swings. But Huang argued that the funds could have a positive effect on the equity market – including for retail investors. Certain quant funds cushion price drops by providing quotes to the order book when retail investors rush to sell, he pointed out. “A large portion of quant funds are market makers: they provide liquidity when retail investors, who are market takers, take liquidity away,” Huang said. For these reasons, Huang said Chinese regulators would be remiss to further tighten regulations over quant funds. They play an important role in China’s maturing market, even if regular retail investors are not directly invested, he added. AI is adding to the arsenal of technological weapons at quant funds’ disposal, according to Huang. “I used to run a research team of around 20 people,” he said. “Today, I can have four good researchers using AI tools and get perhaps three times as much research done. It’s extraordinary.” AI also changes what quant funds can model. “Financial markets contain non-linear interactions among thousands of variables that are difficult to specify manually,” Huang explained. While traditional models simplify these interactions, “modern machine-learning models can examine much richer relationships”. When asked about Hong Kong’s role in China’s rising quant fund sector, he said the city had historically been a “middleman of capital, not a strategy originator”. “The incentive to create something new with top talents is much smaller in Hong Kong compared to the mainland,” he said, adding that China was “increasingly” developing its own quantitative ecosystem.

title: As US bears down, export powerhouses China and Vietnam establish closer transport links
description: Two countries working to enhance cargo and passenger flows using trains, planes and ships.
content: Neighbouring China and Vietnam, two manufacturing giants, are building out railways, adding flights and boosting cargo links to leverage their geographic proximity for another boost in trade and tourism that will help both weather pressure from the US. The two countries set aside political disputes last year to step up economic ties, and analysts said they were now improving both the quality and quantity of transport links. “Overall, I see the China-Vietnam connectivity story moving from relatively simple border trade towards a much more integrated manufacturing, logistics, tourism and supply chain corridor,” said Jack Nguyen, Vietnam CEO of business services platform Ascentium. The economies of both countries rely heavily on manufactured exports to other countries – the United States, around Asia and in Europe. China also supplies raw materials to Vietnamese plants, and Vietnam ships electronics and machinery in the other direction. The Vietnamese government has launched a US$320 billion investment plan covering transport and logistics through to 2030, Swiss private banking group J. Safra Sarasin said in a research note released last month. American tariff increases since April 2025 have made trade with the US more expensive, and Washington is scrutinising Vietnam’s potential use as an export transshipment route from China, where tariffs may be higher. “I would say there is a growing element of hedging,” Nguyen said. “As US tariffs and non-tariff barriers create more uncertainty, Vietnam and China have strong incentives to deepen their transport, supply chain and trade links and diversify their markets.” China and Vietnam have made progress this year on three railway lines that promise to increase freight shipments and passenger trips across their 1,297km (806 mile) land border. In August, Vietnam added US$3.36 billion in funding for the construction of the standard-gauge Lao Cai-Hanoi-Haiphong line, which would synch up tracks in the two countries by 2030, Xinhua reported. For the separate Haiphong-Ha Long-Mong Cai line, the two countries agreed in March on a technical assistance project for the railway’s standard gauge, according to Vietnam’s Ministry of Construction. The ministry is also finalising an investment outline and pre-feasibility study this year for a US$5 billion Hanoi-Dong Dang railway project due to be rolled out in 2035. China and Vietnam expected railways to reduce congestion at highway border crossings and promote tourism, said Carl Thayer, an emeritus professor at the University of New South Wales who has long studied Vietnam. Nguyen said the projects were intended to create “more efficient” supply-chain corridors, cut logistics costs and reduce transit times while linking Vietnam’s manufacturing base and ports more directly with China’s extensive rail network. Winnie Lam, a veteran business adviser based in Ho Chi Minh City, said railway links at two border crossings currently used older infrastructure and narrow-gauge systems. Railway trips were “not too common” due to the different track standards, she said. To further facilitate trade, a logistics arm of Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Ltd said last month it would extend its SuperLink China Direct service to Vietnam. The extension would give Vietnamese enterprises a “more convenient and cost-effective logistics and air-road intermodal solution” for shipments to or from China, Hong Kong Air Cargo Industry Services said, adding that it had already set up a trial scheme. A record 8.6 million passenger seats are available on China-Vietnam flights this year, up from 7.7 million last year, according to aviation market intelligence firm OAG. Vietnam received about 5.3 million mainland Chinese visitors last year, Xinhua reported, up more than 40 per cent year on year. The Vietnamese government said China was the country’s largest source of foreign tourists last year and in the first half of this year, when about 2.7 million visitors arrived. In April, budget carrier VietJet announced five new routes connecting Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City to four tourist destinations in China. Another carrier, Vietravel Airlines, began a route between Ho Chi Minh City and the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen in August, the Vietnam+ news portal reported. Chinese airlines entering the Vietnam market and capacity increases by larger carriers explained the growth, OAG chief analyst John Grant said. “For the Chinese airlines, Vietnam is a good market, relatively short in sector lengths and with growing volumes of trade and tourists travelling in both directions,” he said. China also opened the 134.2km (83.4 mile) Pinglu Canal last month, creating a new gateway linking Nanning, the capital of southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, to the Gulf of Tonkin, known as the Beibu Gulf in China, which spans the two countries’ maritime border. With the canal’s opening, a new freight route linking Nanning with Can Tho in Vietnam had begun operation, Chinese state broadcaster China Central Television reported.

title: Boucheron CEO Hélène Poulit-Duquesne on Histoire de Style and Carte Blanche
description: Poulit-Duquesne discusses her creative partnership with Claire Choisne, building the iconic Quatre line, and servicing high jewellery collectors.
content: In 2020, Hélène Poulit-Duquesne, CEO of Boucheron, made a bold move in the very traditional world of high jewellery. High jewellery – or haute joaillerie in French – is a very niche segment of the jewellery industry, akin to haute couture in fashion. Think one-of-a-kind creations made with the most precious metals and rarest stones, often requiring years of handiwork. Founded in 1858 and the first jeweller to be based in Paris’ Place Vendôme, Boucheron is known for its unique approach to the craft. Every year, creative director Claire Choisne is given free rein to come up with out-of-the-box collections that defy expectations of what high jewellery looks like. Six years ago, Poulit-Duquesne faced a dilemma. After internal discussions about the avant-garde nature of Choisne’s work, the CEO decided she didn’t want to stop the creative director from pushing the envelope or to ask her to only deliver more client-friendly designs. Instead, she decided to introduce two lines each year. Histoire de Style, unveiled every January, celebrates Boucheron’s heritage, while Carte Blanche, unveiled every July, is about breaking boundaries. “I was really pushing, pushing Claire to be creative and at the same time, the sales teams were telling me, ‘It’s too creative, too difficult to sell, some clients are very traditional’. So, at some point, I was so upset about these never-ending discussions that on a weekend, I decided alone, myself, that I would split into two.” Happily, Poulit-Duquesne found that each collection appealed to different people: those looking for investment pieces gravitated towards Histoire de Style while more adventurous collectors were drawn to Carte Blanche. “They love the craziness and the innovation behind the pieces, and they collect them like [they do] contemporary art,” she says of the latter. We not only want Boucheron to move, but we want the whole industry to move Hélène Poulit-Duquesne “Most of what we’re selling to clients, you never see,” she explains. “It’s the signature pieces like the Question Mark that are going directly from the atelier to [them]. You also need to have icons in high jewellery.” Invented in 1879 by house founder Frédéric Boucheron, the Point d’Interrogation (Question Mark in English) necklace is one of the most innovative designs in the history of jewellery. Over the years, Choisne and her team have reinvented the piece, presenting it with everything from archive-inspired feather motifs to botanical shapes such as leaves. Speaking of icons, Boucheron’s bestselling Quatre line – a four-band design introduced in 2004 – has become the brand’s most instantly recognisable signature, thanks to its graphic lines and mix of different materials such as gold and ceramic. “You cannot develop a jewellery maison if you don’t have an icon but you do not decide yourself which icon,” says Poulit-Duquesne. “It’s the clients who decide. When I joined the company [in 2015], I knew instinctively, even if the house was very small at the time, that around me, people in the know were talking about Quatre. I knew it was already an icon, even if it’s a [relatively] new icon because it was designed in 2004.” While the lion’s share of Quatre’s sales comes from its rings – up to 80 per cent, Poulit-Duquesne says – Boucheron has expanded the range with bracelets, earrings and necklaces. Quatre also has a big following among men, a rarity in the female-dominated fine jewellery category. Thanks to Quatre’s popularity, especially over the last decade, Boucheron has become one of the success stories of parent company Kering, owner of brands including Gucci, Saint Laurent, Balenciaga and Bottega Veneta. Kering acquired Boucheron in 2000 but the maison often felt like an afterthought at the group, which focused its resources on its fashion and leather goods division. “When I joined 11 years ago, I had a meeting with [Kering owner] François Pinault and I said to him that on top of growing the house, which I will do, I have a duty to train him, to train the group,” Poulit-Duquesne says. “I spent so many hours telling the story of jewellery and high jewellery. It was like a training process for the last 10 years, explaining that jewellery takes time and that whatever you create is for eternity. It was a process of educating a group that now really understands what high jewellery is about.” Boucheron’s increasing international footprint is a sign that Kering is paying attention. While the house’s top two markets are still South Korea and Japan, where the brand has a long history – it first entered Japan in 1973, for instance – in 2024 it landed in the US, where it already operates three boutiques. Boucheron only opened its first store in China in 2018, although it has a much longer history in Hong Kong, where Poulit-Duquesne admits that the brand has not focused enough on the local clientele. “The local clients in Hong Kong know pretty much everything. They’re really in the know and very knowledgeable about stones,” she says. “Hong Kong has been relying a lot – too much probably – on inbound travellers but it’s probably because we’re still a small maison that we didn’t take care enough of the great clients living in Hong Kong.” That is set to change with a revamped and expanded boutique at Pacific Place mall, which will play a key role in the brand’s effort to cater to those local customers, a demographic that is very different from the tourists travelling from mainland China and the rest of Asia to shop in Hong Kong, the CEO explains. As a veteran of the jewellery industry, Poulit-Duquesne is an avid collector of stones herself and still travels the world to acquire precious gems for the maison. She couldn’t be happier that the rest of the luxury world is finally taking notice of the untapped potential and excitement surrounding the previously very low-key world of jewellery, and of Boucheron in particular. “Frédéric Boucheron used to be super innovative so if we want to respect the past and to pay tribute to Frédéric, we still have to innovate today; it’s part of our DNA,” she says. “Some brands don’t think that way because they’re a little bit stuck in the past. Claire and myself are the right people in the right place because we have that kind of innovative spirit. We’re obsessed with progress. We not only want Boucheron to move, but we want the whole industry to move, both creatively and technically.”

title: Malaysia’s Anwar set to unveil crowd-pleasing budget as political pressure rises
description: Experts are predicting handouts and subsidies, increased education and healthcare spending, and measures to support lower-income Malaysians.
content: Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim is expected to roll out a populist budget on Friday aimed at placating voter concerns over the cost of living and access to essential services, experts say, as the prime minister seeks to shore up support ahead of a general election that could be called as soon as next year. Anwar’s coalition government is under mounting pressure amid a deepening feud with Umno. The Malay nationalist party, a key partner in Anwar’s administration, has demanded a snap poll after defeating the ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition in recent state elections. The political fallout could force Anwar to call for a national election ahead of the February 2028 deadline – especially if PH fails to secure a strong result in the coming Melaka state poll. Anwar is expected to present an expansionary budget for 2027, with experts predicting higher cash handouts and targeted subsidies, increased spending on education and healthcare and measures to support higher wages and skills training for lower-income Malaysians. The measures could include higher monthly cash aid for household necessities, special financial help for civil servants and pensioners, expanded government-backed pension and insurance for gig workers, and possible adjustments to electricity pricing to cushion the impact of rising costs, according to a research note by Singapore banking giant UOB. “Anwar is likely to use Budget 2027 to rebuild political confidence around cost-of-living issues and address the government’s weak support among Malay voters,” said Asrul Sani, associate vice-president with strategic advisory and business consulting firm The Asia Group. The prime minister has struggled to build support among the Malay-Muslim majority, which accounts for roughly 60 per cent of Malaysia’s 34 million population, leaving him heavily reliant on Umno. That partnership has come under strain after Umno scored convincing victories over PH in back-to-back state elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan, forcing Anwar to recalibrate his political strategy. Early start Anwar had already sought to get ahead of Friday’s budget with a slew of policy measures announced over the past month to ease cost pressures on households. Monthly subsidised petrol quotas were restored to 300 litres (80 gallons) per person from September 1 after an earlier cut in response to the energy crisis triggered by the Iran war. Pickup truck drivers were given a higher monthly quota of 400 litres of diesel. On August 30, he announced a 50 per cent hike in funding for school maintenance, raising the total allocation to 1.5 billion ringgit (US$367 million) to cover all school categories over the whole of 2027. Anwar also posted on September 24 that micro-businesses and small and medium enterprises – which account for over 90 per cent of registered businesses in Malaysia and are the largest source of employment – would be granted access to 6 billion ringgit in financing and limited exemptions to tax requirements. But with much of its bandwidth taken up by soaring fuel subsidies, the government has little fiscal space to add more goodies to its budget bag. It had already spent 38 billion ringgit on fuel subsidies over the first half of 2026, about 61 per cent higher than initially budgeted, said Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid, chief economist at Bank Muamalat. “Given that global crude oil prices are likely to stay elevated, the government is expected to provide a higher allocation for the fuel subsidies for 2027,” he said. “At the same time, the government would need to maintain a narrower fiscal deficit going forward in order to contain the government debt ratio to 60 per cent at some point. So the government has less fiscal headroom.” Anwar will also need to stave off pressure from Umno to include measures that could bolster its political position at his expense, while at the same time presenting a budget that can pacify long-time supporters angered by his administration’s perceived failure to deliver on promised reforms. Friday’s budget will be “politically critical” for Anwar, as it gives him a chance to reset the political narrative and show that his government is responsive to voter concerns, according to Asrul. “Anwar’s challenge is to give voters enough to feel the government is responding, without weakening the country’s fiscal credibility,” Asrul said.

title: What is leung cha, Hong Kong’s bitter herbal teas?
description: The traditional cooling concoctions are medicinal – and trendy.
content:
Before modern pharmacies and over-the-counter painkillers, there was leung cha . The intensely bitter herbal “cooling teas” were brewed in massive brass cauldrons in Hong Kong’s traditional open-front shops.
For many, the dark, earthy, grassy mixtures are an acquired taste. But for generations of locals, they are century-old remedies served in ceramic bowls. The “medicine” is used to help sore throats, flush out seasonal “dampness” and reset bodies run down by stress.
According to records from Hong Kong’s Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, there were at least 385 Chinese herbal tea shops in the city as of late 2025.
This network operates alongside hundreds of commercial chain outlets and Chinese medicine dispensaries.
The practice of drinking cooling teas originated in China’s southern Guangdong province, Lui Ka-chun said. He is a Hong Kong author and food writer.
Younger people’s focus on wellness has made leung cha popular once more, Lui said.
“Over the past few months, I’ve noticed that young people are super health-conscious,” Lui shared. Many of them are in their twenties, he added.

title: Vintage treasures reveal Hong Kong’s hidden stories
description: Alfred Lee’s shop showcases nostalgic items, preserving history for future generations.
content:
What do an old Beyblade, a Coca-Cola yo-yo and a 1980s McDonald’s napkin have in common?
According to Alfred Lee, owner of the vintage store SapGau, these items each reveal unique stories about Hong Kong’s history.
Since he was a child, Lee, who is now 27, has had a passion for collecting vintage toys and common objects.
His vintage store SapGau, which means “to rediscover the old” in Cantonese, is located in an industrial building in Tsuen Wan. The shop is filled with items from Hong Kong dating from the 1960s through the 1990s.
“I like the stories behind them, the history. I learn things I didn’t know, and that’s what I enjoy,” said Lee, who works as a freelancer to support his vintage shop.
“I want to know its history so I can pass these stories on to the next person.”
Some of Lee’s earliest acquisitions were classic Hong Kong-made toys from his childhood, as well as other popular items like Beyblades and Gundam figures.
As he grew older, Lee’s enthusiasm for collecting deepened. Four years ago, he rented a space for his first vintage store in an industrial building in Kwun Tong.
But as his collection grew, the warehouse became too crowded.
He then relocated to his current shop in Tsuen Wan, where he can showcase his collection more effectively.
One of Lee’s notable collections began when his father took him to explore street markets and bought him a used Coca-Cola yo-yo. In the latter half of the 20th century, the American beverage company promoted its international presence by selling various yo-yos in different countries.
Years later, Lee’s father gifted him a unique tin yo-yo from his own assortment . Lee eventually learned that it was one of the first Coca-Cola yo-yos made in Hong Kong.
“Who knew it would turn out to be ... so precious?” Lee said.
That discovery sparked a challenge: “If I already had the hardest one to find, why not collect all the others?”
Lee now estimates that he owns over 1,000 Coca-Cola yo-yos, which feature about 300 designs from Hong Kong, Japan, the Philippines and Mexico, created between the 1960s and 2000s.
Although some of Lee’s items may seem unusual, his goal is to “find the things Google can’t show you”.
“Things that are more about everyday life – museums might not necessarily have them,” he said. “But everyday items are more down-to-earth, showing how people’s living conditions really were at the time.”
Through his shop, Lee also tracks how Hong Kong has changed over time – for example, how piggy banks show technology’s impact on our approach to saving money.
“In the past, piggy banks were everywhere, but children today don’t necessarily have them,” Lee explained.
Although Lee began collecting long before vintage styles became trendy, he has noticed growing interest from adolescents .
Some come in searching for Pokemon cards and end up discovering older items around them. Others come specifically looking for decorative pieces that were popular in the past.
Lee believes that part of this trend is driven by curiosity about an era they never experienced. “People are curious about what life was really like,” he said.
He believes his work is particularly important for preserving sentimental belongings that people would otherwise discard.
“Do you think everyone wants to throw things away?” Lee asked.
But Lee’s shop gives some of these objects a second chance.
“Whether it’s helping Hong Kong conserve some stories, or keeping these stories because I like them myself, I think it’s about preserving a story for everyone,” Lee said.

title: A new generation in China’s centuries-old porcelain city
description: Jingdezhen pottery-making history spans more than 2,000 years.
content:
Chinese porcelain artist Chen Qing has one vivid memory of her grandfather. She remembers the only time he wrote down the formula for her family’s distinctive red pigment.
Chen’s grandfather asked her mother to memorise it. Then, minutes later, he burned the paper. The secret has since been passed down only by word of mouth from one generation to the next.
Her family has made porcelain in Jingdezhen since around 1860. The city is in China’s central Jiangxi province.
Jingdezhen is known as China’s porcelain capital. Its pottery-making history spans more than 2,000 years. It began during the Han dynasty. The city’s porcelain sites were added to Unesco’s World Heritage List in 2026.
Jingdezhen’s artists have maintained techniques that were once used to make porcelain for the imperial court. Chen’s ancestors adopted some of those traditions after the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, which ended the monarchy.

title: Editorial | China must ensure R&D funding flows to where it matters most
description: China’s expenditure on research and development now exceeds the OECD average but private sector spending on basic research lags the US.
content: China’s spending on research and development (R&D) has reached a milestone worth celebrating, a testament to Beijing’s sustained commitment to science and technology. It hit a record 2.8 per cent of gross domestic product last year, exceeding 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) and beating the average for Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) member states. Yet, there is still a long road ahead as the nation strives to lead the world at the technological frontier. The 2.8 per cent covers all R&D, including that funded and performed by businesses and the private sector. As a share of output measured by purchasing power parity, China now matches the United States. Put simply, a yuan buys considerably more laboratory time, and engineering and scientific talent, at home than its dollar and yen equivalent in America and Japan. By that measure, China’s total R&D spending has climbed from about 72 per cent of the American level a decade ago to roughly parity today. Its research workforce, nearly 8 million strong, is the world’s largest by some margin, as Beijing’s five-year plan notes. Scale, however, is not the same as strength. Two issues stand out: insufficient investment in basic research, and the relatively modest participation of the business sector. Basic research accounts for only about 7 per cent of China’s total R&D spending, compared with 17 per cent in the US and 15 per cent in the European Union. The imbalance is understandable. A country playing catch-up naturally concentrates on application rather than frontier research. But the cutting edge is forged in frontier research; without it, China risks remaining second in the race. Beijing evidently recognises this. This year’s government work report makes spending on basic research a priority. The share has only recently crossed the 7 per cent threshold for the first time. Over time, there is reason for optimism that China will catch up. The second weakness is more urgent and harder to address. America’s standing as a science and technology superpower rests not only on the shoulders of its government but also on its business and private sector. Its leading technology companies spend far more on frontier and basic research, often without any clear commercial opportunity, at least in the short term. By comparison, Chinese businesses largely confine their spending to applications or research that promise immediate commercial returns. There is a notable exception. Huawei, the national telecommunications champion, devoted more than 21 per cent of its revenue to R&D last year, equivalent to 192.3 billion yuan. It is hardly surprising that it has delivered some of the most significant breakthroughs, such as the Tau scaling law, a new approach to advancing chip performance beyond conventional transistor shrinking. Without that depth of commitment, such a breakthrough would have been impossible. Other Chinese companies, including top-tier technology giants, fall short of matching that ambition. The private sector, in general, is more efficient and innovative than public institutions, and China’s problem is that private sector participation in basic and frontier research trails America’s. Yet this is not merely a matter of corporate will. The government, too, must create a more conducive environment, one in which long-horizon research makes commercial sense. Intellectual property protection has been greatly improved. Firms willing to invest in discoveries that may take a decade to bear fruit deserve protection. Hong Kong, with its established legal framework, has played a genuine role for the nation. Equally essential is patient capital, investment willing to wait years rather than quarters for a return. Here, China and its private sector enjoy an advantage over US companies constantly looking at the next quarter’s earnings. Beijing has proved it can spend at the scale of a scientific superpower. The next task is to ensure that money flows to where it matters most, and that the country’s most dynamic companies are given the confidence and incentives to take on missions, not just look at the balance sheet. Only then will parity in spending translate into leadership in discovery.

title: Can HRT help prevent dementia? New research suggests it might, depending on key factors
description: As debate continues over whether hormone replacement therapy can protect against dementia, new studies suggest timing and formulation are key.
content: This is the 99th instalment in a series on dementia, including the research into its causes and treatment, advice for carers and stories of hope. Will using hormone replacement therapy (HRT) preserve a woman’s brain health and protect her from dementia or not? The debate continues. Various studies have looked at the effects of menopause and hormone treatment on the brain – and dementia risk. Some have suggested that HRT has no impact on brain health in older women, and that it has a neutral effect, while others have suggested that it increases dementia risk. But newer research shows a positive correlation between the use of hormone therapy and a lowered risk of dementia. What type of hormone therapy a woman uses and when she is introduced to it along her menopause journey seem to make a difference. Among the recent studies is one from Stanford University, in the United States, which found that women over 50 who used oestrogen-only hormone therapy had 35 per cent lower odds of exhibiting Alzheimer’s pathology when their brains were analysed postmortem. A study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia in August 2026 examined more than 180,000 postmenopausal women in the UK and found that those taking HRT – also known in the US as menopause hormone therapy (MHT) or hormone therapy (HT) – had a 10 per cent lower risk of developing any type of dementia and were 16 per cent less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. Another 2026 study published in The Journal of the American Medical Association (Jama) found that the earlier menopause set in, the more likely women were to experience cognitive decline later in life. This included women who had undergone “surgical menopause” – the removal of the ovaries (an oophorectomy, frequently accompanied by a hysterectomy), often performed to treat reproductive cancers. These women were also more likely to show faster accumulation of white matter hyperintensities – small, stroke-like lesions visible on brain MRIs that signal tissue damage. Researchers suggest frequent hot flushes during perimenopause and menopause may serve as a key biomarker for this underlying vascular stress. Oestrogen helps guard against such damage by supporting healthy blood vessel function and regulating brain glucose. Because the brain is the body’s most energy-demanding organ – consuming roughly 20 per cent of its blood glucose despite accounting for just 2 per cent of body weight – oestrogen’s drop directly compromises its primary fuel source. This is why researchers view hormone therapy as potentially brain-protective – if started during an optimal window. However, the exact formulation matters as much as the timing: Oestrogen-only – safe only for women who have had a hysterectomy. It carries lower risks and shows the strongest link to brain health benefits. Combined therapy (oestrogen + progestin) – required for women with a uterus to prevent endometrial cancer. Body-identical HRT – transdermal oestrogen (patches or gels) combined with natural progesterone mirrors the body’s natural hormones, offering a safer profile than older synthetic oral pills. Those who had a surgical menopause early and were introduced to hormone therapy immediately afterwards benefited from even more profound effects. The risk of dementia in this group fell by 26 per cent. And women who started HRT at younger ages – between 46 and 56 years old – had a lower risk of developing dementia than those who started treatment later in life. Many people, women included, often don’t appreciate that menopause is a brain-driven transition, which is why it affects nearly every system in the body; oestrogen receptors are found far beyond a woman’s reproductive organs – in her heart, blood vessels, bones, gut, skin and brain. Oestrogen functions like a key that fits into these receptor “locks”, switching bodily functions on or off. Up to 40 symptoms can result from oestrogen declines during menopause, with symptoms affecting roughly 80 per cent of women. Some are widely recognised, such as vaginal dryness and loss of libido. Others are less expected: heart palpitations, frozen shoulder, dry eyes and persistent hot flushes. These hot flushes are not just uncomfortable; they also disrupt sleep, which can contribute to depression – itself a significant dementia risk factor. Notably, women face roughly twice the lifetime risk of both depression and Alzheimer’s disease compared with men, a correlation researchers are still working to fully explain. Dr Susan Jamieson is an integrative medical doctor who set up a pioneering well-woman clinic in Hong Kong in 1994 and has been supporting women through menopause with bioidentical HRT for years. She says the perimenopause to menopause transition is considered a critical period in its neurological function, and may help to explain why so many more women than men suffer from dementia. The brain is not static, she says. It changes “in response to different amounts of hormones” – in particular, oestrogen. Jamieson explains that the brain undergoes a biological crisis during transition through perimenopause and menopause. It is supersensitive to the falling oestrogen levels, so it needs to reprogramme itself and alter its chemical behaviour. In effect, the substantial oestrogen decline triggers something like an inflammatory response in the brain, which prompts a shift in its metabolic processes, which in turn leads to the many symptoms, including those hot flushes. The Women’s Health Initiative study published in 2002 is widely blamed for setting back HRT research and practice. Its findings were applied broadly to all women, rather than accounting for the age of the participants – many of whom were a decade past menopause – or the specific type of therapy used. As a result, many women missed out for years on a treatment that “remains an important option for managing menopausal symptoms and may significantly improve quality of life for many people”, according to Dr Tom Blackmore, research programmes manager at Alzheimer’s Research UK. Ultimately, it is a woman’s quality of life that is the crux of the matter: how she feels is what should determine whether a woman uses hormones during the transition to menopause. HRT is neither a panacea nor a poison, Blackmore stresses, and should not be presented as a guaranteed shield against dementia “or something women should fear”. Rather, it is a treatment designed to ease some of menopause’s most disruptive symptoms, potentially helping women sleep better, stay socially engaged, avoid depression, or remain physically active through reduced joint pain. These outcomes align closely with modifiable risk factors for dementia prevention identified in research in the journal The Lancet. As Jennifer Bruno, one of the authors of the Stanford study, puts it: “The most important message is that dementia risk in women has many contributing factors, and hormone therapy is just one piece of a much larger picture that we’re still working to understand.” Like what you read? title: From yo-yos to piggy banks, unwrap Hong Kong’s quirky history
description: Dive into vintage store owner Alfred Lee’s treasure trove where nostalgia meets fascinating tales of the past.
content:
What do an old Beyblade, a Coca-Cola yo-yo and a 1980s McDonald’s napkin have in common?
According to Alfred Lee, owner of the vintage store SapGau, these items each reveal unique narratives about Hong Kong’s history.
Since he was a child, Lee, who is now 27, has had a passion for collecting vintage toys and common objects. His fascination started when he observed his father collecting items manufactured in Hong Kong.
“I don’t do this because I like the aesthetic. I like the stories behind them, the history. I learn things I didn’t know, and that’s what I enjoy,” said Lee, who works as a freelancer to support his vintage shop.
“I want to know its history so I can pass these stories on to the next person.”
SapGau, which means “to rediscover the old” in Cantonese, is located in an industrial building in Tsuen Wan. The store is filled with items from Hong Kong dating from the 1960s through the 1990s.
As reflected in the store’s name, Lee aims to help visitors reconnect with the beauty of the city’s past.
“I want to help everyone find their own memories from the past through old objects,” he said.
Some of Lee’s earliest acquisitions were classic Hong Kong-made toys from his childhood, as well as other popular items like Beyblades and Gundam figures.
“Just owning them made me happy,” he recalled.
As he grew older, Lee’s enthusiasm for collecting deepened. After graduating from secondary school, he began setting up pop-up stalls at local markets to display and sell his items.
Four years ago, he rented a space for his first vintage store in an industrial building in Kwun Tong. But as his collection grew, the warehouse became congested .
He then relocated to his current shop in Tsuen Wan, where he can showcase his collection more effectively.
His shop is packed with items that easily could have ended up in a landfill. He sources these treasures from nearby thrift stores and international flea markets.
A significant portion of the toys Lee collects from Hong Kong can be traced to a catalogue he discovered, which featured local items produced during the 1980s.
“It became like a ... guide – [I was] trying to find the actual items listed in the book,” he said.
One of Lee’s notable collections began when his father took him to explore street markets and bought him a used Coca-Cola yo-yo. In the latter half of the 20th century, the American beverage company promoted its international presence by selling various yo-yos in different countries.
Years later, Lee’s father gifted him a unique tin yo-yo from his own assortment. Lee eventually learned that it was one of the first Coca-Cola yo-yos made in Hong Kong.
“My dad gave it to me as if it were junk. Who knew it would turn out to be so hard to find and so precious?” Lee said.
That discovery sparked a challenge: “If I already had the hardest one to find, why not collect all the others?”
Lee now estimates that he owns over 1,000 Coca-Cola yo-yos, which feature about 300 designs from Hong Kong, Japan, the Philippines and Mexico, created between the 1960s and 2000s.
Although some of Lee’s items may seem unusual, such as a collection of unused 1980s McDonald’s napkins, his goal is to “find the things Google can’t show you”.
“Things that are more about everyday life – museums might not necessarily have them,” he said. “But everyday items are more down-to-earth, showing how people’s living conditions really were at the time.”
Through his shop, Lee also tracks how Hong Kong has changed over time – for example, how piggy banks show technology’s impact on our approach to saving money.
“Back then, piggy banks represented a strong saving mindset,” Lee explained.
“Today, keeping cash sitting around loses value to inflation, so people invest instead. Simple items like that reveal shifts in our economy, technology and culture.”
Lee also studied toy details from the 1960s to the 1980s and discovered how manufacturing has changed over time – earlier packaging relied on hand-painted artwork while later versions shifted heavily towards photography as cameras became more accessible.
Although Lee started collecting long before vintage styles became popular, he has noticed a growing interest in Hong Kong’s old culture among young people. He has seen an increase in the number of secondary school students visiting his shop.
Some come in searching for Pokemon cards and end up discovering older items around them. Others come specifically looking for decorative retro pieces, such as old banknotes, clocks and lamps.
Lee believes that part of this trend is driven by curiosity about an era they never experienced.
“I think there’s a bit of longing – a sense that life was better before. People are curious about what life was really like,” he said.
Lee personally finds the 1980s appealing as “it just seemed like people lived more comfortably, with fewer worries”.
Despite his emotional attachment to his items, he does not see himself as the last owner of these objects – if a visitor shows a genuine passion for a specific item, Lee is happy to pass it on.
“I’m just an intermediary ,” he explained. “I’m just someone who owned them for a moment.”
Lee believes Hong Kong’s limited living space makes his work particularly important for preserving sentimental belongings that people would otherwise have to discard.
“Do you think everyone wants to throw things away?” Lee asked. “Most of the time it’s just because there’s no choice.”
But Lee’s shop gives some objects a second chance.
“Whether it’s helping Hong Kong conserve some stories or keeping these stories because I like them myself, I think it’s about preserving a story for everyone,” Lee said.

title: Spark Deep Dive: China tightens taxes with new offshore trust policy
description: New rule on the mainland aims to control money flowing over the border and nail loopholes that allow billionaires to avoid paying the government.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Beijing has launched a wave of measures over the past few months to prevent people from avoiding tax
Recent offshore trust rule aims to close loopholes that benefit the wealthy and better control money crossing the border
Beijing has begun tightening controls on the flow of money leaving mainland China. The government wants to stop people from avoiding taxes and reduce the amount of money leaving the country.
Major companies have been punished for helping mainland investors illegally buy overseas stocks. Banks in Hong Kong have also become tougher on mainland customers applying to set up accounts.
In late July, Beijing announced that offshore trusts would now be subject to China’s personal income tax . This closed a loophole that had allowed wealthy Chinese families to protect large amounts of money from taxation. Offshore trusts are also a way for Chinese entrepreneurs to transfer wealth to the next generation.
The new tax rule could complicate this process.
The policy charges a 20 per cent tax on the gains from offshore trusts that have mainland Chinese beneficiaries or that hold assets from the mainland.
The rule will apply when a trust is set up or closed. It will also apply whenever any income from the trust is given out. It will affect any gains dating back to as early as January 1, 2023.
Beijing has offered a 90-day grace period for people to declare if they put mainland Chinese assets in offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025.
The issue has become a hot topic in China. Children of the late Zong Qinghou – the billionaire founder of drinks company Wahaha Group – launched a legal battle for control over offshore trusts.
The trusts had assets worth about US$2 billion (HK$15.68 billion).
For Beijing, offshore trusts are a serious issue. They have allowed the country’s wealthiest families to avoid paying tax on large amounts of assets.
The Chinese government is struggling to earn income because property values have been dropping. This is one reason Beijing needs more money from taxes.
Last year, Chinese authorities collected 1.62 trillion yuan (HK$1.89 trillion) in income tax revenue, an 11.5 per cent increase from 2024.
The increase can be attributed to officials ensuring that more people follow new rules, as well as the closing of tax loopholes.
The new policy for offshore trusts could seriously damage China’s billionaires. A large amount of their overseas income is connected to offshore trusts.
The new rules have also raised concerns in Hong Kong. The city has long been a place for rich Chinese investors to set up offshore trusts. They are drawn in by Hong Kong’s low tax rate and strong privacy protections. It is also the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub.

(2) The policy sets a 20 per cent tax on gains from offshore trusts with mainland links at every stage, including set up, income movement and closing. (3) The rules could make it easier for Chinese people to share their wealth with the next generation who are in other countries. (4) Beijing is cracking down on tax avoidance because the government needs funding as property values fall.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (3) only C. (2), (4) only D. (3), (4) only

offshore trusts: a legal arrangement in which someone transfers ownership of certain assets to a manager in a different place. This is often a way for wealthy people to avoid paying taxes or to transfer their assets to their heirs.
personal income tax: a direct government tax on an individual or a household’s net earnings, wages, investment gains and other income
beneficiaries: an individual or group designated by the person who creates a trust to receive benefits from its assets and income
assets: anything, tangible or intangible, that has economic value to its owner or could have economic value in the future
The government has offered a 90-day grace period for people to declare if they put mainland Chinese assets in offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025. This measure should encourage individuals to voluntarily self-report before the tax rules tighten.
The new offshore trust policy worries wealthy Chinese families because they routinely use offshore trusts to protect their assets from tax and to easily transfer assets to their heirs. Under the new tax rule, these people face higher tax burdens and can no longer use this “loophole” to protect their wealth.
Since 2021, billionaire wealth in mainland China has declined gradually, with a small rebound in 2025. Since 2022, billionaire wealth in Hong Kong has held steady at under US$500 billion. (accept all reasonable answers)
Many wealthy Chinese people choose to put their money in offshore trusts in Hong Kong because of the city’s low taxes and strong privacy protections, which can help them save more money and make it simpler to transfer wealth to the next generation.

title: US Coast Guard suspends search for 6 aboard crashed medical aircraft
description: Rescue crews locate debris field off the Massachusetts coast after Bermuda-to-Boston flight vanishes in a storm.
content: US Authorities on Sunday suspended the search off the Massachusetts coast for six people on an air ambulance that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The US Coast Guard said authorities searched more than 7,081km (4,400 miles) over a span of 66 hours for the four Canadians and two people from Bermuda who were on board. “Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s northeast district, said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.” The Federal Aviation Administration contacted the Coast Guard at 2am Saturday that it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G100 carrying six people over the Atlantic Ocean. Searchers later Saturday found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Lake had said at a news conference on Sunday. US Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities searched a vast area using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters. The depth of the water around the debris field was around 27 metres. The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport. Air traffic audio indicates that the plane may have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot. That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. “Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation lawyer. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”

title: Amid France’s heatwaves, Nile crocodile eggs hatch on their own in a zoo
description: The European country is usually not hot enough for this species from sub-Saharan Africa to hatch on its own.
content:
France’s heatwaves have led to a strange outcome. At a wildlife park, 10 Nile crocodiles hatched without human help for the first time.
In the wild, Nile crocodile eggs incubate in underground nests. But zoos usually hatch them in controlled incubators. Staff closely monitor the temperature and humidity.
“For the first time, we had an incubation that took place entirely under natural conditions,” Samuel Martin said. He is the director of the zoo in the town of Pierrelatte.
La Ferme aux Crocodiles says it is Europe’s largest wildlife park with a focus on reptiles.
On August 22, visitors saw 10 Nile crocodiles hatching without human help. They told staff, but the excitement quickly turned into concern. Martin said this birth showed the effects of climate change since France is not usually hot enough for Nile crocodiles to hatch on their own.
A Nile crocodile egg must be kept between 30 and 34 degrees Celsius for about three months. This is how the embryo will grow and hatch.
The temperature when the eggs are incubating can decide if the babies will be male or female. If the temperature is around 31 degrees or below, the hatchlings are female. Higher temperatures produce more male babies (see graphic).
This species lives in sub-Saharan Africa, where temperatures are usually warmer than in France. But France had three heatwaves this summer. The country saw a record 52 days of extreme heat. Climate change has made these conditions worse.
Because the hot weather lasted so long, the sand at the French zoo stayed warm from the sun. This created the perfect environment for the Nile crocodiles to hatch naturally.
All 10 hatchlings are doing well. Staff will watch over them in the nursery before they are shown to visitors.
At the zoo, Martin said species coming from “hot countries are feeling comfortable” in the heatwave. But he added that those from places that are not very hot or cold might suffer more.

It is a winning combination for Hong Kong. Last year, it overtook Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub, riding a wave of blockbuster listings by Chinese technology companies. But some worry Beijing’s tax clampdown on offshore trusts poses a threat.
Analysts, however, stressed that the new mainland policy was in line with international practices.
