title: Listen Up: British museums battle climate change to protect historic collections
description: Staff use technology to protect collections from heatwaves and other extreme weather.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the provided script for help.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Graeme Acres, a production editor on SCMP’s Hong Kong desk, and Cathy Hilborn Feng, SCMP’s health and wellness editor.
Voice 1: As visitors peered at skeletons and preserved animals in a zoological museum during a heatwave in Britain this summer, staff focused on a different attraction: a computer screen glowing with red and green temperature indicators. With each one linked to a sensor in a different display case, the system allows staff at the Grant Museum of Zoology in London to see when an exhibit is in danger of overheating.
Voice 2: Last year, during a hot spell, staff arrived one morning to find that an antique specimen jar had blown out amid the heat. It contained a tabby cat that was nearly two centuries old. By monitoring temperatures in the display cases, staff hope to prevent damage to other exhibits by identifying which exhibits need to be decanted in advance.
Voice 1: Tannis Davidson is the head of zoology at the 200-year-old collection that is home to some 100,000 specimens covering every major animal group. She said they wanted to safeguard the collection for at least the next 200 years so that students, researchers and members of the public could enjoy it and learn more about the natural world. But she said curators were having to deal with a whole new set of challenges due to climate change and extended periods of high temperatures.
Voice 2: Emma Howard Boyd is the chair of the independent National Heat Risk Commission. According to Howard Boyd, the impact of climate change is no longer a distant threat but a present-day reality affecting the cultural sector. The heatwave earlier this year forced the closure of many London cultural attractions, including the Young V&A museum, Cutty Sark museum ship and Tower Bridge.
Voice 1: Artworks also require careful monitoring of temperature and humidity levels to prevent damage, according to Claire Teasdale of the National Trust heritage body. She explained that having more storms, wet weather and extreme weather was affecting everything.
Voice 2: Teasdale manages the collections at Cragside, a 19th century mansion in northeastern Northumberland. Cragside is home to an important art collection. It was built to cope with Victorian rainfall levels and not 21st century rainfall levels, Teasdale said. She added that rain and sunshine both increased levels of potentially damaging humidity. Six of Britain’s 10 wettest years have occurred since 1998, the Met Office said.
Voice 1: John Calautit, a lecturer in sustainable and low carbon technologies at University College London, said installing air conditioning was not a silver bullet for large spaces and historic buildings often subject to highly restrictive building regulations.
Voice 2: But he said experts were developing alternatives to provide ventilation and cooling based on windcatcher principles used for centuries in architecture. He explained that this ventilation system attached to a roof could capture air at higher altitudes. He added that it brought airflow into the space at a higher volume. Modern-day systems incorporate some form of low-energy cooling and have already been commercially produced and used in Middle Eastern countries.
Voice 1: Howard Boyd argues that museums and historic properties need to explore all options for climate resilience. She envisages a future in which venues become community hubs offering people a refuge from the heat. An initiative launched in June highlights venues where people can find local spaces to keep cool.

[1] Half smiling through crinkled eyes, Moussa Ndiaye watched a combine machine harvest his northern Senegal rice paddy. He expected a good haul, but not just of grain. His field is part of a study that aims to fight one of the world’s major parasitic diseases and increase rice yields by adding fish to paddies. The fish can then be caught and sold for profit: a rare win-win-win for local farmers.
[2] In Senegal, rice and fish are ubiquitous dietary staples and practically a matter of national pride. Growing the two side-by-side is logical, those involved say. Such nature-based solutions are part of a growing trend in science, and so far, the results have been promising. In the pioneering study, fish eat snails that cause the parasitic disease schistosomiasis. The fish also fertilise the rice with their faeces.
[3] Ndiaye’s village, Lampsar, is in the lower valley of the Senegal River, near the border with Mauritania. People here have long lived off fish from the waterway, not ones reared in rice paddies. “Since our youngest age, since our grandparents, we have fished. We’re Waalo-Waalo,” the 80-year-old said, referring to an ancient kingdom that people in the region still identify with.
[4] The area is also known for schistosomiasis. It is a disease caused by parasites released by freshwater snails, which are common in the paddies. Ndiaye has had the disease three times. His sons who work in his fields have also contracted it. It causes symptoms ranging from itchy skin to organ damage, and even death. It can be treated with medicine, but that does not prevent reinfection or mitigate the time and money lost from missed school or work.
[5] The World Health Organization estimates 254 million people require preventative treatment and that 94 per cent of those needing treatment live in Africa. Transmission of the disease has been reported in 79 countries, it says.
[6] Scientists introduced Nile tilapia, which fertilise the fields, and African bonytongue, which eat schistosomiasis-causing snails, into the paddies. More than 40 farmers across multiple villages participated in a pilot study and follow-up research. “It’s not just a one-hit punch; we’re really tackling a lot of challenges,” said Emily Selland of the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, the United States. She is a lead author of a paper on the pilot study published in the journal Nature Sustainability.
[7] “We came at this from the disease angle first,” she said. But then there was “the nutrition angle, the economic angle, the sustainability and ecological angle”. Her research found that adding fish boosted rice yields by 25 per cent and increased revenue for rice-farming households. There were also fewer snails in fields with predatory fish.
[8] At an aquaculture facility at Gaston Berger University (UGB) in the city of Saint-Louis, Nile tilapia rippled the water’s surface in a large concrete basin. From here, some 15 minutes southwest of Lampsar, the fish will head to research paddies belonging to AfricaRice. The centre will conduct similar studies but in a controlled environment. “Our intention is that, once we have the expected results, this be scaled up across many African countries,” said Ali Ibrahim, a regional representative for AfricaRice.
Source: Agence France-Presse, September 15

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): Why nasal strips aren’t a ‘miracle cure’ for snoring
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
https://collaborate-next.scmp.work/groups/Young%20Post/boards/3f4bbec1-64cf-4ee6-b8d9-e1fab69a426d/d13bddf6-fe9e-4118-b2ac-b3fea8eb4503/f98cd616-d1ec-440e-ba30-269940ea8bbc/article_viewer?userId=5fb6cccf69e544000109e0bc&viewMode=true
[1] Nasal strips are available without a prescription and are easy to use. However, ear, nose and throat specialists say they aren’t a sure-fire cure for snoring. The strips carry few risks beyond occasional skin irritation. This could happen around the area where the adhesive is applied, according to Germany’s Professional Association of Ear, Nose and Throat Doctors. People who snore do not need to worry about trying them.
[2] The experts say the strips only help in a small number of cases. They might be useful when snoring is caused by a narrowing in the nasal passage. This could happen because of a cold or allergies. A 2016 analysis reviewed multiple studies. It found that the evidence on nasal strips remains mixed. Some people respond to the treatment; others do not.
[3] Gently lifting the sides of the nose with the adhesive strip can provide some relief in cases of clogged and narrow nasal passages. However, the effect has not been proven scientifically. It has also not been proven that nasal strips provide more oxygen during sports. Your doctor will likely tell you that the cause of snoring often lies in the throat. In those cases, a strip on the nose is not useful.
[4] The UK’s National Health Service (NHS) advises people who snore regularly and feel tired during the day to see a doctor. These issues may indicate sleep apnoea. It is a condition where breathing stops and starts during sleep. Without treatment, sleep apnoea can lead to additional health problems. These include high blood pressure and an increased risk of stroke.
[5] These tips can help reduce or even stop snoring. Sleep on your side if possible. To avoid rolling onto your back, place a small pillow or a piece of foam behind you. Sleeping in a raised position using thick pillows or a foam wedge can also help. Ensure fresh air in the room but avoid draughts. The ideal bedroom temperature is between 14 and 18 degrees Celsius.
[6] Avoid eating too late, too heavily or too much protein in the evening. Avoid sleeping pills where possible. A doctor may also advise people who snore to lose excess weight. Source: dpa, September 14

title: Open Questions | Zheng Yongnian on China-US realism and battling for the upper hand before the next summit
description: Political scientist evaluates China-US relations, AI dialogue, and why head-of-state diplomacy remains vital for global stability.
content: Zheng Yongnian is a political scientist in China and a government adviser. His academic work is mainly about contemporary China, particularly politics, the country’s transformation and its external relations. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. Many have offered a lukewarm assessment of the Xi-Trump summit in Washington, citing the lack of a breakthrough. What is your take? There are two primary views right now. One is nihilism, which holds that China and the US are ultimately bound to fight for global dominance – that the world isn’t big enough for two superpowers. The other is idealism, which expects all differences to be resolved in a single step. We should assess China-US relations with realism. The fact that both countries have managed to get to where they are today is already no small feat. China and the US will remain somewhere between a de facto G2 and a formal G2 for a long time, navigating between being two de facto superpowers and exercising joint governance. As two major powers, China and the US naturally have distinct national interests. We must recognise that cooperation and competition coexist. Everyone must keep a floor in mind, acknowledging that conflict between China and the US would only bring about the destruction of the world, whereas their cooperation can lead to win-win outcomes. China has published its list of deliverables and the United States has released its fact sheet of the event. What did the summit achieve? The summit delivered the best outcome within the range of expectations. Although the two sides framed the results differently, that is because they have different priorities. Two aspects stand out. The first is economic and trade relations, which I think have become more stable. That is very important. According to our assessment, about 70 per cent of the Chinese and US economies are highly complementary, while 20 to 30 per cent are competitive, such as the hi-tech sector. The summit essentially confirmed the structural complementarity between the two economies and further consolidated the consensus that economic and trade ties are indeed the ballast of the bilateral relationship. Even in the hi-tech field, there is common ground. As for “super intelligence” and “artificial intelligence” (AI), that is a distinction in technical wording but not a substantive one. The consensus [the establishment of the bilateral AI dialogue] is a positive trend. The second aspect is political trust. China-US relations need to proceed in three steps: first economic and trade ties, then politics and finally security. The Chinese list of deliverables and understanding reflects such a sequence. The Chinese statement announced eight points of consensus, but the most important element is the one that follows them – that we consider the “ninth point” even though it was not described in this way. That is about military-to-military communication and security. Still, security issues are not ready to be addressed, as the level of bilateral political trust remains insufficient. Perceptions that the other side poses a security threat are high in both the US and China. Many so-called security threats are perceived, rather than real. Tackling this will require building a lot of political trust through frequent communication between the two countries’ leaders. Without that, it could get challenging. President Xi [Jinping] and President [Donald] Trump are on track to meet twice more this year, which is remarkable. For the leaders of China and the US to meet four times in a single year on different occasions is unprecedented and might not happen often in the future. Looking ahead to the next two summits, a task should be to further expand and strengthen the economic and trade ballast while making the consensus on stability bigger, stronger and deeper. After trust has gradually built up, it would be somewhat easier for the two countries to then work on security issues. This is not an impossible mission. Speaking of the “ninth point”, only the Chinese readout said the two militaries “agree to conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible”. The White House’s fact sheet did not include this, although the US has long called for keeping military-to-military communication open. Instead, it mentioned Trump’s call for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, China and Russia. How do you read those differences? Of course, what the US highlighted were the issues of its concern, such as the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Korean peninsula and the war on Iran. The Beijing side’s emphases, though not explicitly written out, remained on Taiwan and the South China Sea, which are our most significant security concerns. From the Chinese perspective, these are issues of sovereignty that transcend security. Still, they manifest as security issues and call for more communication. There is an implicit shared understanding regarding those fields, namely, both sides need to cooperate. To address the Taiwan question and the South China Sea, Beijing needs US cooperation. Likewise, Washington needs the Chinese side’s cooperation to resolve the major challenges on its agenda. You said Beijing and Washington should work together to make the consensus on stability bigger, stronger and deeper. What should they do to ensure a durable, stable relationship that outlasts Trump’s presidency? There are both certainties and uncertainties. The certainty is the minimum baseline for the stability of the bilateral relationship, which is that the two countries cannot come into conflict. This is a consensus not only between China and the US but also between the Democratic and Republican parties in America. The consensus has been even clearer [since the summit]. Such a consensus will go beyond Trump’s current term and likely endure for much longer. This is grounded not only in the reality that the China-US relationship rests on a foundation of strength but also in the common recognition by both sides that a conflict between the two countries would not merely affect themselves; it would throw the entire world into chaos. Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different. Zheng Yongnian Meanwhile, there is still much that can be done. First, shaping the future of China-US relations hinges on high-level summits. Communication between the heads of state should continue. This will continue even if the Democrats return to power or another Republican takes office. It is impossible for China and the US to absolutely not engage. Second, both sides should continue to enlarge and strengthen the economic and trade ballast. For China, this is a force to help keep US capital engaged. As long as American interests are deeply embedded in China’s economy and China’s in America’s, there is a foundation to build on. Economic interdependence does not necessarily prevent war but it can encourage everyone to be more rational and continue to expand bilateral trade and investment reciprocally. Third, it is critical for bureaucracies on both sides to earnestly materialise the consensus rather than undermine it. That involves communication and coordination between the two countries’ respective bureaucratic apparatuses as a whole, not just their diplomatic services. Fourth, the overall media environment needs to improve. Mutual criticism is fine, but demonising each other is not. We talked about the American press’ unfriendliness towards China. Chinese media should also tone down their rhetoric about the US being finished, degraded or in decline. Both sides should practise empathy. If the Chinese press attacks the US all day while American outlets constantly attack China, it will only worsen public sentiment in both countries. Will Trump’s high-level reception for Xi’s Washington visit put Beijing in a stronger position for their potential bilateral encounters during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting in November and the G20 gathering in December? The summit gave both nations greater confidence to face and discuss problems directly, rather than shunning them. As for the high-level reception offered by President Trump to President Xi, this reflected reciprocity. When Trump visited China in May, Beijing also arranged warm hospitality for him. This is a good trend. Major powers truly should show mutual respect. It is often difficult for a major power and a small nation to get along with each other due to the gap in strength. However, it is actually easier for major powers to deal with each other, as their strengths are matched, allowing for genuine equality. From the perspective of the different civilisations they each represent, China and the US are also bound to cooperate rather than be in conflict. In the sphere of media discourse, there are overly simplistic interpretations of one another on both sides. We should see the reality of the two countries rather than solely look through the lens of ideology and moral sentiment. How might the two further bilateral summits this year help manage or shape the China-US relationship, especially given that the US midterm elections will be held before those meetings? Apec is about economics and trade. It grew during the heyday of globalisation and free trade. One of the largest concerns in the region has been that security issues have come to dominate the agenda, overshadowing economics and trade. When security becomes the overriding focus, it can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy where everyone actually ends up less secure. It is not that the US no longer wants to trade now, but it is adjusting its approach. China and the US can do a great deal not only on the bilateral dimension but also on advancing economic development across the entire Asia-Pacific. It is feasible to build on good interactions between the two countries to steer Apec back towards economic cooperation and trade facilitation, which would benefit all sides. China is well positioned to contribute a lot in this regard, including on energy, agricultural goods and rare earths. We should think about how to use the positive momentum to take the China-US relationship into its next phase, rather than simply maintaining the current situation. After all, standing still can mean stepping back. After the four summits this year, how can the momentum be sustained into next year? You have emphasised the importance of stable economic and trade ties. Should we be concerned that while the two-month trade truce extension would offer a window of opportunity, the outlook could again become uncertain? First, we should recognise that Trump’s trade war is not directed exclusively at China. China is just one part of his broader trade war, which has also targeted US allies. If China has the capacity to expand economic and trade ballast, why not do so? We should not struggle for the sake of struggling. Struggle must have a purpose. In fact, there is plenty of room for cooperation between China and the US. For instance, both countries are confronting the question of how a major power manages its borders. Many of the problems facing the US come from its immediate neighbourhood, including illegal immigration and drugs. China also faces challenges, such as telecoms fraud operations in Myanmar and Cambodia. China-US ties are not like the US-Soviet relationship. Never before in history have two economies this large been so closely interconnected. The two countries can build consensus not only at greater depth but also across a wider range of areas. And effective policy implementation will lay the foundation for credibility and trust. Even if there are no formal meetings next year [as there were in May and September], there will still be the annual Apec and G20 gatherings, as well as many other potential occasions. There are many ways for communication. We do not have to worry too much. Replicating this year’s high frequency of bilateral summits may not be necessary, but head-of-state diplomacy will certainly continue. The key is not to lose the momentum, which is hard won. China and the US could mobilise the positive forces for the bilateral relationship in both countries. Negative forces undoubtedly exist too, on both sides. For example, we see constant talk of “China is going to defeat America” or “America must defeat China” within the two societies. We need to shape a favourable media and social environment, which is crucial. Take China’s unilateral opening-up measures in recent years to welcome more American visitors; both sides should do more of what benefits China-US relations, rather than framing the relationship in terms of who defeats whom. Neither side can defeat the other. When the two sides agreed in May to build “constructive strategic stability”, the White House cited demands for “fairness and reciprocity”. China echoed the two points this time, and both sides added “respect”. What is your take on this development? China certainly values respect, as the US has long been accustomed to exercising hegemony. I have argued that managing two variables is crucial to handling China-US relations properly. First, China must manage its own rise. What we consume and do not consume and how much we consume all affect global markets, and even China-US relations. It is not that the world should applaud simply because we have risen. The way China rises matters a great deal. It is not enough for us to feel that we are rising; other countries must also come to regard China’s rise as a positive development and welcome it. That would constitute a successful and peaceful rise. The Chinese modernisation also emphasises the path of peaceful development. Second, the relative decline of the US must be managed too. [In a de facto Group of 2] the US has had a considerable psychological adjustment. It is no longer as arrogant or dismissive of others as it once was, and it has come to view China as a much more equal counterpart, as evidenced by speaking of “respect, fairness and reciprocity”. That is beneficial for China. But the more this is so, the more humble China should be. Nations are like people – feelings and face matter. It is important to be mindful of the US’ psychological position. It would be unwise to show no consideration for that or adopt an attitude of kicking someone when they are down. Narratives such as “the East is rising and the West is declining” still resurface from time to time in public discourse. Is this view still open to question? I have said that great powers are not to be defeated. If the US were to fail, it would not be because China had defeated it, but because of problems within itself. And the same holds true for China. China and the US can only coexist. Neither can defeat the other. If one were to defeat the other, the result would be the destruction of the world. China now should go for smart diplomacy, approaching foreign policy through reason and wisdom rather than simply acting on instinct. Great powers must shoulder their responsibilities. Managing the two variables discussed [in the previous answer] is one example of doing so. A country does not become a great power by defeating another. No one would like such a great power, and it will end up defeating itself. At this summit, both presidents recalled that China and the US were allies during the World War II. Shortly after the meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Trump and exchanged views primarily on issues related to China, including security. Meanwhile, new stand-offs have emerged between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea. With Beijing and Washington agreeing to build constructive strategic stability, how should China manage its relations with US allies in the region, particularly Japan and the Philippines? These countries are also actively strengthening security ties between themselves. Could that in turn affect China-US relations? [The de facto G2] has implications for many so-called middle powers. Countries such as France, Germany, Canada and the United Kingdom, which have fewer geopolitical disputes with Beijing, are not choosing sides between Beijing and Washington in managing their relations with the two powers. Meanwhile, Japan appears to be trying to play the role of an “Israel in East Asia”. It likely feels that the US is now paying less attention to protecting it, so the country seeks to take security into its own hands and, based on that, keep Washington tied to its side. But there are limits to this approach. As long as China and the US have enough trust between them, Japan and the Philippines will have little role to play. As a relationship between major powers, China-US relations constitute a structure within which Japan and the Philippines can only make some autonomous choices. No matter what [Japan and the Philippines] do, they cannot themselves become a structure. On Taiwan and the South China Sea, there is still considerable room to explore in future exchanges between Beijing and Washington. For Beijing, Taiwan and the South China Sea are matters of sovereignty. For the US and Japan, these are issues of geopolitical space. Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different. On the basis of mutual respect and reciprocity, we can talk with the American side over how to ensure US interests in the western Pacific. Addressing the Taiwan question and South China Sea issues does not mean Beijing wants to exclude Washington from the region. Likewise, we can also talk with the US about how to assure China’s interests in the eastern Pacific, including in Latin America. These are reciprocal matters the two sides can discuss. That rests on the deeply intertwined nature of China-US relations, and the two countries not carving so-called spheres of influence. Once the Taiwan question is resolved, we could welcome US warships and aircraft carriers making port calls at the island openly, just as we once welcomed American military vessels to dock in Hong Kong. The two sides should work together to manage the Pacific and the world as a whole instead of trying to exclude each other. Will the dynamics of Sino-US relations and Beijing’s posture vis-a-vis Washington during this summit affect how middle powers, including Japan and the EU, approach their relations with China? They have already begun to change. We should go back to the realistic dimension when looking at international relations. Since the dawn of the modern era, an idea originating from Europe holds that all states are equal. This is an ideal, not a reality. As countries differ in size and strength, we cannot assume that they are fully equal at the starting point. But we can strive for equality. Every nation has its own positioning in international relations. If a country does what it ought not to do, or fails to do what it should, that is not helpful to its own national interests and is not sustainable. Under the de facto G2 context, both China and the US are repositioning themselves. Other countries will also be doing the same. This is a structural issue that could shape international relations for decades. The boundaries of the China-US relationship may gradually become the boundaries of international relations as a whole. The bounds set by the two countries for the bilateral ties could also define red lines that other states should not cross. Neither side’s release mentioned Taiwan. Trump said he and Xi “didn’t talk about it too much” at the summit. Should there be concern that the question has been shelved? How might Beijing and Washington approach Taiwan in future exchanges? The fact that Taiwan was not mentioned in the documents does not mean the two sides did not consider or discuss it but only indicated they had not yet reached a broader consensus on it. Indeed, there is a concern that Taiwan could become the focal point of a conflict if it is not handled carefully, potentially undoing progress on all other work. But as we talked about earlier, Taiwan is not a subject that cannot be discussed. Many specific issues need to be gradually untangled. If the dialogue simply consists of China accusing the US of being “a force from outside the region” while Washington levels the similar charge against Beijing, it goes nowhere and the two sides could drift towards conflict. But adopting a more mutually inclusive mindset can make a difference. The US is still a significant actor in the western Pacific. Similarly, China’s influence in Latin America is growing. Every issue has its origins and its solutions. There are always solutions other than war. We should not underestimate human wisdom. China made no mention of rare earths and critical minerals in its own list of summit outcomes, although the US repeated its concerns in its fact sheet. Does this signal a firm stance by Beijing on the issue, and how might it affect competition in this domain? The US is looking to reinforce its toolkit, looking for additional means. China is doing the same, like the case of AI start-up Manus. This is reciprocity – and you can only negotiate for reciprocity when you have the strength to back it up. If political trust between China and the US gradually builds and both sides move towards the same direction, I do not think rare earths will be a problem. But if [political trust] deteriorates, more points of friction could emerge. Rare earths serve as a countermeasure for China but the country’s purpose is rather simple - zhi ge wei wu [a Chinese idiom meaning “true martial virtue lies in stopping warfare”]. If the US weaponises something to pressure us, China has tools of its own to push back. Still, as long as the US remains rational, the Chinese side would not cut off rare earth supplies. China and the US have agreed to establish an AI dialogue. Given their differing approaches to the technology and divisions within the US on AI slowdown, what concrete outcomes can we expect from AI discussions between the two countries? First of all, when it comes to AI development, there is little consensus within China or the US, let alone between them. Domestically, the US is currently split into two camps on AI: one believes AI can solve many of our problems, while the other fears it could bring about doomsday. But China and the US do share a consensus on the security risks posed by AI; what remains to be mapped out is the specifics of what they should discuss. The two countries also follow different models of AI development. Trump supports accelerated development with no regulation. China, at least theoretically, tries to balance development with security. AI requires multilevel discussion between China and the US. Technology and capital circles essentially dominate the discourse about AI. Trump aligns himself with them, further reinforcing their power. Talk of regulation and slowing down AI development in the US has gone on for a long time but with little real progress. These issues cannot be driven by commercial companies – they can only be tackled by governments. AI will undoubtedly serve as a major platform for future US-China discussions, much like nuclear weapons did between the US and the Soviet Union. [Former US secretary of state Henry] Kissinger’s final visit to China was also aimed at easing AI negotiations between Beijing and Washington. Despite their different rhetoric on AI, both sides share the consensus that discussion between them is necessary. When people talk about AI today, they are effectively talking about China-US relations, as its technology and production capacity are highly concentrated in the two countries. Trump has confirmed his intention to attend the Apec summit, further raising global expectations for the event in November. What impact do you think this could have on the host city, Shenzhen? And how do you view the frequent comparisons between Shenzhen and Hong Kong? This is certainly a boon for Shenzhen. The entire Pearl River Delta, including Shenzhen and Hong Kong, has an export-oriented economy, for which China-US relations are paramount. Every twist in the relationship would be reflected immediately in Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Hong Kong and Shenzhen can also be key to implementing the consensus reached by the Chinese and US leaders. If local governments and businesses do more to foster China-US friendship, it benefits not only themselves but the whole country. With the relationship enjoying such good momentum, I expect the Apec summit in Shenzhen to be a great success. It will also mark the first visit to Shenzhen by a sitting US president since the Chinese special economic zone was founded more than four decades ago. Shenzhen can be proud in showing the world what it has achieved but should also stay humble. Although Shenzhen is a city that buys globally and sells globally, it still has things to learn from Hong Kong when it comes to institutions and mechanisms, and the internationalisation of people. Apec is a test for Shenzhen. Although much is arranged by the central government, the local side will shape the atmosphere of the summit on the ground. I hope that, through the coming Apec summit, Shenzhen can gradually move closer to Hong Kong, though the city still has a lot to learn.

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): How Nikita Kuwadekar’s health journey and drive led to Busy Brew
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
Read the following text and answer the quiz below.
[1] Few would guess that Busy Brew, Hong Kong’s first plant-based canned coffee brand, is run by a 23-year-old. One could be tempted to see it as an entrepreneur fairy tale. A student spots a gap in the market and builds a cult following for her canned oat milk lattes. Then she lands incubation funding and watches the product fly off the shelves in some of the city’s largest retail chains.
[2] But Nikita Kuwadekar, the founder of Busy Brew, will be the first to tell you that the journey has not been easy. Kuwadekar was born in Hong Kong, where she was also raised, with a congenital condition. She needed open‑heart surgery while still in secondary school. Determined not to fall behind, she overhauled her diet, cutting dairy and sugar to accelerate her recovery.
[3] The physical benefits were immediate. Kuwadekar’s skin cleared and her energy returned. But she also made a discovery that would eventually shape her career. “I realised I was lactose intolerant, and that like, 90 per cent of Asians and almost 68 per cent of the world are too,” she said. “That’s nuts. Because everything around us is dairy: bubble tea, coffees, every canned coffee on the shelf.”
[4] As a first-year student at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Kuwadekar noticed the only grab‑and‑go coffee options were loaded with milk powder and sugar. “If you look at the ingredients of what’s on the shelf, it’s actually pretty terrible,” she said, citing stabilisers, additives and preservatives. The gap in the market became impossible to ignore. “Coffee should be accessible, and it should be healthy,” she said.
[5] Kuwadekar was 19 at the time. Faced with spending up to HK$60 on an oat milk latte every day, she thought: “Why doesn’t this exist in a can?” She entered various university pitch competitions with her idea for Busy Brew. This helped bring in funding. Then she entered an incubation programme by Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation. The organisation was set up by the government in 2001 to foster innovation and technology development. It gave Busy Brew the resources to become a company.
[6] Kuwadekar spent more than two years refining her recipe through relentless customer testing. She eventually landed on a vanilla oat milk latte formula with zero additives. Now, the drinks are stocked at Hong Kong chains like City’super and Louder, as well as the online retailer HKTVmall.
[7] In 2026, Kuwadekar won the Spirit of Youth Award at the 13th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards. She is part of a generation rewriting the rule book on climbing the career ladder – by not climbing it at all. For many young entrepreneurs, the appeal of starting a business is not only about going against the corporate grind but also about aligning work with personal values. Kuwadekar’s business is the product of her own health journey. “Anytime I see someone drinking it, I genuinely feel like I know them,” she said. “The community we’ve built is incredible.”
Source: South China Morning Post, September 15

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): New Yorkers queue for HK$470 loaves of bread
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] The humble loaf of rye bread has found new fame in New York. Here, people have been queuing in the SoHo neighbourhood to pay US$60 (HK$470) for a loaf of Austrian sourdough.
[2] The loaves weigh about 1.5 kilograms each and are baked in a two-tonne oven imported from Germany. “The bread is going down really well,” Tim Auer said. He is the son of Martin Auer, the founder of the shop Rye.
[3] The family from Graz runs a third-generation family business in Austria with 45 branches. “We thought: The one thing we are really exceptionally good at – that’s what we’ll bring to New York,” Auer said. A slice of the bread can be purchased with fish eggs, chocolate spread or chives and butter.
[4] The shop has attracted attention because of its price. Its September opening was met with backlash on Instagram. Auer said he understood the “outrage” over the price. “Most of the people who said that were not in New York,” he said. In New York, he explained, there was no negative feedback. “This is one of the most expensive cities in the world, one of the most expensive streets in this most expensive city. They should take a look at what an apartment costs here.”
[5] All the raw ingredients for the bread are imported, Auer added. Even the counter was made from a tree sourced in the Styria region of Austria. The bread is not cheap even by New York standards. An ordinary loaf in the city of millions costs on average just a few dollars. Artisanal sourdough bread is available in many bakeries for under US$20.
[6] Hearty rye bread is an everyday staple in Austria and Germany, but is far less common in the United States. New York has been experiencing a boom in artisanal bakeries and sourdough breads for years.

title: US removes bombers from UK base after security incident
description: Redeployment from RAF Fairford comes as British authorities link thwarted plot to Tehran.
content: The US Air Force has removed its bombers stationed at a US-run military airbase in England used to strike Iran following an investigation into a planned terror attack at the RAF Fairford base. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity. Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers fly out of the base on Sunday. The move comes as US President Donald Trump weighs options for his war on Iran – including new strikes – despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks. “We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is – it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters on Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and released on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. Trump had said those involved in the plot had planned “big damage”, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the “hands of a foreign actor”. UK officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue. RAF Fairford, located 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier, as well as the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – are heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers in the region as early as the end of October. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: My Take | Dario Amodei’s American AI imperialism
description: The Anthropic CEO and AI pioneer discovers the age-old ‘China threat’ card works as well for Silicon Valley as for Washington.
content: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei seems to believe that he, the American artificial intelligence (AI) industry and the United States are the only ones who should have the right to determine the fate of humanity. While he pays lip service to involving other democracies in AI development, which ones remotely approach the technological capacities of the US and China? Do other non-democratic developing countries not count? His self-belief is far more dangerous than mere commercial greed. Like Peter Thiel, the venture capitalist and Silicon Valley power broker who warns of the Antichrist while taking on many of its trappings, Amodei and his AI industry embody the very danger he warns against. Like many Washington politicians, Amodei routinely casts China as the AI bogeyman while urging the US and his own industry to lead the world, dominate frontier technology and make everyone else abide by their rules. Last week, Anthropic warned of the potential danger posed by Chinese firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, saying the open weight model showed a troubling mix of powerful hacking abilities and weak safety constraints. Come again? Exactly which country’s AI companies have been responsible for rogue agents breaking out to hack others? In a recent essay, Amodei said a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world” and called for measures to restrict China’s progress. “If we execute these measures well, I believe they would slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next 3-5 years,” Amodei wrote. Yet he also concedes that global pacing will require cooperation with China, which he describes as “the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities”. It is a plain and glaring contradiction, understandable only in the context of Amodei’s lust for power while he claims the moral high ground. China’s foreign ministry has described his claims as “fearmongering”. Consider the commercial motive. Tech companies have strong incentives to portray AI as more powerful and dangerous than it is. Cast it as a technology that decides national security and the future of civilisation, and it automatically enjoys unprecedented financial support from the private sector and the government. Companies in the industry become “strategic infrastructure”, which raises their policy importance and barriers to entry and boosts their valuations. Anthropic is preparing for an IPO that could make Amodei one of the world’s richest men. Meanwhile, Anthropic and the wider American AI industry face growing competition from Chinese open-source models, which challenge their closed-source approach on cost, performance and developer ecosystem. Curbing Chinese access to American models and technology protects that monopoly. The BBC reported that some observers saw his essay as “less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology”. Chamath Palihapitiya, an investor and co-host of the “All-In” podcast, wrote that Amodei “makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic”. In two September videos, finance analyst and YouTuber Patrick Boyle examined the sudden calls from Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman to slow AI development. He noted that they came in the same weeks that Anthropic and OpenAI were preparing IPOs and funding rounds valuing them at more than US$2 trillion. He asked whether the safety alarm was real, a bid for regulatory capture, or both. The sums involved are enormous. Boyle also explains why critics ranging from Michael Burry to David Sacks have called the slowdown self-serving. “Pacing”, as some critics have noted, could act as a “soft cartel”, protecting the market dominance and high valuations of frontier labs while disadvantaging smaller competitors and open-source projects. Amodei is, of course, joining the political chorus in Washington. Time and again, the all-purpose “China threat” is trotted out whenever the most powerful and richest segments of America, those with vested but hidden interests, want to scare the public. The latest version serves the same purpose: preserve US dominance and inflate the strategic value of frontier companies against the threat of the Chinese bogeyman. On the other hand, China is championing AI as an open resource, a public good to be shared wherever possible and at more affordable rates. Its open-source models have reportedly recorded more than 10 billion cumulative downloads. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue told CNBC in August that China is winning. Perhaps he has reason to be wary of American labs: his company was hacked by rogue AI agents from OpenAI. The distillation row follows the same script. Days before Amodei’s essay, Washington accused top Chinese AI firms of conducting malicious, industrial-scale “model distillation” to systematically copy American AI technology. This politicises and weaponises a common technical and commercial practice – one that China’s Commerce Ministry noted is used by many AI companies – and applies double standards. Amodei’s essay specifically urges a crackdown on it. All major AI companies, including those in the US, have helped themselves to unauthorised material from across the internet to train their AI models. Anthropic itself paid US$1.5 billion to settle a class-action lawsuit filed by authors over pirated books. China has been an active participant in international AI governance, including at this year’s World AI Conference and the High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance. It was US President Donald Trump who last week rejected global AI governance in favour of the American AI industry’s self-governance, which is exactly what industry insiders wanted. Effective governance balances safety and development through dialogue, risk assessment and multilateral coordination, not blockades, accusations and gaslighting the public. If AI is as dangerous as Amodei says, no single nation or company should be trusted with the keys, least of all one that profits from the panic.

title: Serb separatist Dodik declares victory for his party in Bosnia election
description: Milorad Dodik credits support from Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump as ally secures seat in country’s tripartite presidency.
content: Bosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday that was shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992–95 war. Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that have sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia. Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war. With nearly 90 per cent of votes counted, Dodik’s ally Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55 per cent of votes to take one of the three seats in the country’s tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by around 30 percentage points. Speaking at a news conference late on Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska’s assembly, and credited US President Donald Trump’s “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s support for the election win. “No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. “We will not give up, but continue for our people ... I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.” Around 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament, and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs. With over 94 per cent of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipovic of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegovic, by fewer than three percentage points. Both Filipovic and Becirovic declared victory in their races late on Sunday before all votes were counted. Bosnia’s Central Election Commission said 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42 per cent that was down by around 8 per cent from Bosnia’s last election in 2022. Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war. Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia’s national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country. At his party’s final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead”. “It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian ambassador Igor Khalabukov. Such political and ethnic divisions – in which the country’s Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines – have blocked Bosnia’s progress towards joining the EU despite the bloc’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to work together for reform. One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades after the war that started in 1992, after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions. Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladic, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes. Bosnian Serbs view Mladic as a hero despite his conviction by a UN court over the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995, and other atrocities. Sunday’s election was the first time Bosnia used electronic identification of voters and ballot scanners to prevent irregularities or organised voter manipulation, which have cast doubt on the fairness of previous elections. On Sunday morning, Associated Press journalists reported seeing multiple polling places where voting could not begin on time because of difficulties with the new digital technology. Bosnia’s election commission announced late on Sunday that some polling stations that had experienced disruptions earlier in the day would be permitted to remain open past the 7pm cut-off. On Sunday, some voters in Banja Luka expressed concern that the new digital systems could confuse older voters. Republika Srpska’s interior ministry said in a statement that of 1,957 polling stations in the entity, there had been delays at 201.

title: Netanyahu orders security review of flights to Israel after cockpit attack
description: Omani co-pilot’s attempt to bring down Tel Aviv-bound Flydubai plane sparks a political row and calls for an investigation.
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a security review of international flights to Israel on Sunday, after an attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound plane from Dubai. Netanyahu “has instructed the head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel”, a statement from the premier’s office said. Calls have mounted in Israel for an investigation into the security lapse that allowed the Omani co-pilot of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday to attempt to bring down the aircraft after stabbing the Indian captain. Israeli media has reported that the co-pilot intended to crash the aircraft on Israeli territory. Critics have focused on how a pilot from a country with no diplomatic relations with Israel was cleared to operate a flight bound for Tel Aviv. Transport Minister Miri Regev rejected responsibility for the failure, saying security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines falls under the remit of the Mossad and Shin Bet, Israel’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies. A 2024 report by the state comptroller found there was no clear division of responsibility for the security of foreign airlines operating in Israel, and recommended that the government address the issue. Israeli media have reported that pilots from countries hostile to Israel have repeatedly flown into the country in recent years. Keren Terner, who previously served as director general of the transport ministry and is now running for parliament for the opposition, blamed Regev for the security failure, noting that the Civil Aviation Authority was under the “direct subordination” of her ministry. “You are responsible for the security of foreign companies. Not the Shin Bet, not Mossad. You. That’s what the government decided and that’s what the law stipulates,” Terner wrote on social media. Opposition leader Yair Lapid dismissed Netanyahu’s announcement of a security review as a “sham investigation”. “The chain of failures that preceded the incident could have led to a disaster of historic proportions, and this is how an Israeli prime minister responds?” Lapid wrote on social media. “Just as Netanyahu escaped an investigation into the October 7 massacre, he is now running away again,” he added. Gadi Eisenkot, a leading challenger to Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 election, wrote on social media that “in a proper and functioning government, the minister of transportation would have submitted a letter of resignation last night”.

title: Iran tells US there is no military solution to war as talks hit impasse
description: Tehran’s top diplomat vows a stronger response to any fresh confrontation as diplomacy over the Strait of Hormuz stalls.
content: Iran’s top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States’ war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse. A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure. The main point of contention remains Iran’s attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday that another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile. “If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. “There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict. The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations. Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation. The US has imposed its own counter-blockade of Iranian ports and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it. On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz “reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room”, though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded. The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel’s origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG (liquefied natural gas) carrier. But as Iran faces growing queues at petrol stations due to the impact of the Middle East war, the country’s oil minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned, the president’s office said on Sunday. Hamid Bovard, the CEO of the National Iranian Oil Company, “has been appointed as acting Minister of Oil by a decree from the president”, said the presidency statement carried by state media. Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait. Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. US President Donald Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks and renewed military operations. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Sunday the US had expressed its views on the proposal and said it was being reviewed. “The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures,” he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA. “Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario.” Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being “in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues”. “We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required “an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions”. The United States and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – a goal it has long denied pursuing – though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shock waves through world energy markets. The United States has not struck Iran since September 1 but it has recently pursued a fresh military build-up in the region. US media outlet Axios reported that top Trump cabinet members met on Friday to discuss the war in Iran, as well as the conflict in Yemen, where the Tehran-backed Houthis have been fighting government forces and attacking Saudi Arabia.

title: Hundreds of schools close as France braces for more protests
description: After a weekend lull, high schoolers are expected back at the barricades for a fresh wave of demonstrations.
content: Up to 500 schools across France will be totally or partly closed on Monday because of a wave of student protests that has shaken the country, the education minister said. Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, said Education Minister Edouard Geffray on Sunday, adding that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement. He described the closures as chiefly a security precaution ahead of large-scale protests that the leaders of the movement have called for Tuesday. The teenagers at French high schools, known as lycees, say that their studies are being ruined by high teacher absence rates, overlong school days and dilapidated facilities, as well as other grievances. Geffray said the number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday but vowed there would be a “partial, progressive return to lessons”. More than a third of the 468 schools in the wider Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital will be shut on Monday as a result of the protests, Valerie Pecresse, the right-wing president of the region, told broadcaster Franceinfo. The movement began at a Paris school on September 17 but grew last week into nationwide protests marked in places by outbursts of violence involving teenagers and the security forces, which have used tear gas and truncheons against the students. At Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, students took turns expressing their grievances at an open-air meeting Sunday. When you are a student from one of the deprived districts, said one student, “The violence is unleashed”. She referred in particular to one student who had lost his teeth to a police rubber bullet and another who had been hit in the eye. One 16-year-old boy, Campion, held a placard that read: “They say they are listening to us but prefer to gas us”. “I don’t understand why the government deploys so much force against a case that is valid: our education, our future,” he said. Geffray, in his statement, spoke of far-left infiltrators who had “hijacked’ the movement “and engaged in extreme violence”. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students,” he said, adding that 78 education staff members had been injured. “They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system,” Geffray said. Organisers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from the government. In a bid to address the protesters’ concerns, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Sunday urging local authorities to prioritise filling gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts. He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country’s often-dilapidated school buildings. More than 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement. A 16-year-old was detained on Sunday over the assault of a teacher in the southern town of La Ciotat. The teacher, 59, was struck and doused with petrol on the sidelines of a high school student protest on Friday. A group of youths was last week filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in Belfort in eastern France in images that caused an outcry among officials. Two youths, Bulgarian nationals aged 15 and 17, have been arrested and investigated for suspected aggravated violence, the prosecutor said. One of the youths, whom the policeman had tried to arrest before being beaten, has now filed his own attempted murder complaint, his lawyer said. The France branch of Amnesty last week slammed “disproportionate police violence” in tackling the demonstrations and said students must be allowed to express their grievances. “Authorities must allow young people to exercise these rights without fear of being hit by tear gas grenades or batons, or being arbitrarily taken into police custody,” said Amnesty France president Anne Savinel-Barras. But Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stated that security forces “are not cracking down on young people” but rather “protecting” school and university students wishing to “peacefully voice their demands”.

title: Police detain dozens at Russian Communist Party rally in Moscow
description: Demonstration marking 1993 uprising sees arrests after protesters chant slogans including ‘For fair elections’ and ‘Down with the Tsar’.
content: Police in Moscow detained about 60 people at a rally on Sunday held by Russia’s Kremlin-friendly Communist Party, the party said. The party said in a statement that the detentions happened as the rally was ending and that its Moscow branch was working to get those who were detained – mostly young people – released. The rally marked the anniversary of the Kremlin’s 1993 crushing of a parliamentary uprising. The Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti said protesters chanted slogans including “Freedom for political prisoners”, “for fair elections”, and “down with the tsar”. The rally came as public frustration has been simmering in Russia during the intensifying Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country. The strikes have hit oil refineries and warehouses, caused fuel shortages and disrupted daily life, including in Moscow. The October 1993 violence capped a long stand-off between president Boris Yeltsin and hardline lawmakers who opposed his painful free-market reforms. After Yeltsin ordered parliament disbanded and demonstrators supporting the lawmakers tried to seize the state television broadcasting centre, he sent in the military, which used tanks to shell the parliament building. Authorities said 123 people were killed, while unofficial estimates put the toll in the hundreds. The Communist Party has been a leading force in parliament since the 1990s, led for more than three decades by 82-year-old Gennady Zyuganov, a former Soviet official. Throughout Putin’s rule of more than a quarter of a century, the communists have criticised some aspects of government policy but have carefully avoided any criticism of him. They steadfastly support the war in Ukraine.

title: Brazil heads to run-off between Lula and pro-Trump Senator Flavio Bolsonaro
description: Right-wing senator takes surprise first-round lead over Brazil’s 80-year-old president.
content: Brazil’s presidential election will go to a run-off on October 25 between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who has promised the Trump administration access to Brazil’s rare earths to cut US reliance on China. With 99.9 per cent of ballots counted from Sunday’s vote, Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, had 47.07 per cent of votes and Lula had 45.11 per cent, triggering an automatic run-off. Lula, who at 80 is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, had led a Datafolha poll published ahead of the vote, 45 per cent to 40 per cent. Lula said he had expected to win outright in the first round, while 45-year-old Flavio Bolsonaro told supporters the result showed Brazilians were ready for change. Former governors Ronaldo Caiado of Goias and Romeu Zema of Minas Gerais, social media figure Renan Santos and author Augusto Cury, who between them took about 8 per cent, never reached double digits in polls. White House visit and a letter from Rubio Ahead of the vote, US President Donald Trump said he was following the election “very closely”, calling Brazil “a very important country” while stopping short of an explicit endorsement – a departure from his recent endorsements in elections across Argentina, Chile, and Colombia. Flavio Bolsonaro had met Trump at the White House in May and promised a “long-term strategic partnership” on rare earths, with “shared re-industrialisation” between the two countries. He later said Brazil would join the US-led Shield of the Americas initiative if he won, Axios reported, and his rallies have featured large US flags and pictures of Trump. Brazil has the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves after China. The senator has called the country “the only real alternative to China for the free world” for those minerals. In June, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote to thank him for a “generous offer” to put a transition team “at Washington’s disposal” if elected. Three months later, news site Amado Mundo published a 22-page presentation with the campaign’s logo on every page, written in English by close ally Andre Marinho and reportedly shown to the Rockbridge Network, a donor group founded by US Vice-President J.D. Vance. It promised a “parallel supply system” with Washington and said Brazil would not become “structurally dependent on Chinese processing chains”. Marinho, who was running for governor of Rio de Janeiro and lost the race on Sunday, said the file had nothing to do with the campaign. In a podcast interview last week, Lula said Beijing could be a partner “bringing technology to us” and praised Chinese investors for being “bold” as the US and Europe were largely leaving Latin America. In September, Lula signed a law creating a council under the presidency to oversee critical minerals policy, with powers to review foreign stakes in projects it deems strategic and grant tax credits for processing until 2034. Chinese miner CMOC has owned niobium mines in Goias since 2016. In April, USA Rare Earth agreed to buy the Serra Verde rare earth mine in the same state for about US$2.8 billion. Record trade, falling investment under Jair Bolsonaro China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. In the first eight months of this year, after Washington placed a 25 per cent tariff on a range of Brazilian goods in July, exports to China rose 15 per cent and sales to the US fell 9.7 per cent, according to official data. But even though he adopted a more virulent rhetoric against Beijing in private, former president Jair Bolsonaro - in office from 2019 to 2022 and now serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election - tried to maintain a polite relationship with China publicly. He went to Beijing in October 2019 and hosted President Xi Jinping at a Brics summit in Brasilia the following month. His foreign minister, Ernesto Araujo, resigned in March 2021 under pressure from senators over his treatment of China. Exports to China also hit records of US$87.7 billion in 2021 and US$89 billion in 2022, though much of that came from commodity prices rather than volume, since Brazil’s average export price rose 29.3 per cent in 2021 and volumes only 3.2 per cent, according to the Getulio Vargas Foundation. Yet, Chinese investment in Brazil fell 78 per cent in 2022 to US$1.3 billion, the lowest since 2009, according to the Brazil-China Business Council. Of the US$4.7 billion in Chinese projects announced that year, only about a quarter went ahead. Total foreign direct investment nearly doubled to US$90.6 billion. Filipe Figueiredo, a historian and geopolitical analyst who hosts Brazil’s most popular foreign affairs podcast Xadrez Verbal, expected much the same from a Flavio Bolsonaro government. “We will probably have a decrease in investment and perhaps episodes of diplomatic crises.” Some of Jair Bolsonaro’s allies wanted Brazil out of Brics, and Flavio Bolsonaro’s manifesto ignores the bloc. Figueiredo noted that the bloc’s membership guarantees Brazil “a high-level audience with the leadership of China at least once a year” and that this would be “a diplomatic benefit that is very difficult to give up”. Chinese car plants and ports could be held back “whether by China, by Brazil or by pressure from the United States”, in his view. Commodities are another matter, since the US grows soy and competes with Brazil for buyers. “The United States will not buy the amount of iron ore that China buys from Brazil. Chinese demand cannot be met by any other country,” he said. Washington’s pressure would centre on critical minerals, Figueiredo said, and in some sectors it already worked as an unofficial veto on Chinese money. Chinese arms maker Norinco had been favourite to buy defence manufacturer Avibras before it went to Globe Investimentos, a Brazilian group with large US operations, Figueiredo said. “We can certainly say there was pressure from the United States, and the construction of another solution.” Flavio Bolsonaro’s suggestion that he could name his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro foreign minister was, for Figueiredo, “the big unknown”. In 2020, Eduardo Bolsonaro angered Beijing by comparing China’s handling of Covid-19 with the Soviet cover-up of Chernobyl. “Not only China, but all the other governments will look at him and be fully aware that he only holds this post because he is the son of a former president and the brother of the current president,” Figueiredo said. Beijing would probably treat him as “an unreliable partner”, he added. “Using the words of Ernesto Araujo, there would be a risk of Brazil becoming a kind of pariah.” Yet, Figueiredo said China “without a doubt” had prepared for a Flavio Bolsonaro presidency. “They certainly did not go to sleep trusting in the polls and the strength of our friendship.” Race for endorsements Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies also did well in Senate and state races. In Sao Paulo, Brazil’s largest economy, Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, a minister under Jair Bolsonaro, won re-election in the first round. Caiado was expected to declare a vote against Lula’s Workers’ Party, according to local newspaper Folha, while Gilberto Kassab, who leads Caiado’s Social Democratic Party, was expected to campaign for the president. Renan Santos may be harder to win over. In September he accused the Rockbridge Network of financing Flavio Bolsonaro’s run “illegally”, a claim the men he named as its Brazilian operators denied. Even so, throughout the campaign he positioned himself as an anti-establishment candidate and went so far as to say during the first presidential debate of the election that he did not want the votes of those planning to vote for Lula.

title: Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea, says Zelensky
description: The Ukrainian president on Sunday said Russia shared the technology ‘because North Korea helped them with missiles’.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday ⁠he believed Russia ⁠may have shared jet-drone technology ⁠with its long-standing ally North Korea. In recent weeks, Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-drones against Ukraine, which so far has no effective means of countering them other than using ‌combat aircraft. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, ⁠Zelensky told journalists: “Yes, of course.” “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I ‌don’t know about the ballistic and etc, but I think, yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles,” he added. South ‌Korea and Western countries have previously voiced concerns that Pyongyang may ⁠be getting help ⁠with weapons development from Moscow in return for its help in the Ukraine war. Thousands of North Korean ‌soldiers were sent to Russia to gain combat experience in the war. Seoul and Kyiv have been ‌locked ‌in a diplomatic dispute since Zelensky announced at the United Nations General ‌Assembly last month that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war ⁠captured while fighting for Russia to South Korea. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung ⁠on Friday threatened unspecified measures against Ukraine unless Kyiv acknowledged a confidentiality agreement that Seoul says covered the transfer and issued an apology. “South ‌Korea asked us to ‌give them North Korean soldiers. By the way, according to their constitution, they are their citizens … so we gave them these two guys,” Zelensky said, without alluding to Lee’s comments.

title: UK Green Party votes to define Zionism as racism, triggering backlash
description: Israel bans leader Zack Polanski as Jewish groups and ruling Labour condemn conference motion.
content: The UK’s left-wing Green party voted Sunday to define Zionism as racism at the party’s annual conference, drawing sharp backlash from three British Jewish groups, the ruling Labour Party and Israel’s government. Members of the Green Party, which has five MPs in Britain’s 650-seat parliament and which enjoyed a boost in recent local and special elections, backed the motion at the party’s conference, with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against. Israel’s foreign ministry, declaring the resolution “a clear antisemitic text”, announced in retaliation Sunday evening that Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar was barring the Green party’s leader, Zack Polanski, from entering Israel.
