According to the motion, Zionism would be “treated as any other form of racism” and the party supports the establishment of a “single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine”. The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination. “This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership,” a Green spokesperson said. The Greens have enjoyed a surge in popularity under the charismatic leadership of Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government’s stance on the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza. However, Polanski’s popularity has taken a hit in recent months, polls show, following several missteps. “This motion would make the Green Party the first electorally significant UK political party in living memory to adopt what appears to be an overtly antisemitic political platform,” three Jewish community groups said in a letter to the party ahead of the vote. “We also emphasised the implications for the safety and welfare of all British Jews,” the heads of the Board of Deputies, Community Security Trust and Jewish Leadership Council warned. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, called the Green party’s decision “a disgrace”. “Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people, and it forms the basis for the Jewish people’s right to a state and a national home in the Land of Israel,” Herzog said on X. Bridget Phillipson, chair of the ruling Labour Party and Minister for Women and Equalities, also condemned the Green Party’s conference decision. “It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel’s right to exist,” she said in a party statement. The motion laid bare divisions in the party with Polanski – who is currently running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer’s London constituency – skipping the vote. Despite at least three out of five Green MPs opposing the motion, Polanski said last week that the “displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people” was “clearly racism”. United Nations investigators have accused Israel of committing “genocide” in the war in Gaza, a finding that Israel has rejected. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Hong Kong woman with knife arrested after demanding cash, Octopus cards at MTR station
description: Police later trace suspect to Tsz Ching Estate and arrest her after finding her inside flat speaking incoherently, source says.
content: Police have arrested a woman on suspicion of attempted robbery after she allegedly brandished a knife at staff at an MTR station customer service centre and demanded Octopus cards and cash. A source familiar with the case told the South China Morning Post on Monday that the woman, a Hong Kong resident surnamed Lai, was armed with a ceramic knife and demanded all Octopus cards and HK$100 (US$13) banknotes from staff at the Diamond Hill MTR station customer service centre on Sunday evening. “When the staff refused the request, the arrestee used the knife to ... [bang on] the glass of the customer service centre, damaging the ceramic knife,” the insider said. The source noted that the woman later fled towards Plaza Hollywood after the failed robbery attempt. After reviewing CCTV footage, the force traced her to a green minibus, which she took to Tsz Ching Estate. She was seen entering Ching Fai House at the estate and taking a lift to the fourth floor. Officers later raided a flat in the building under a search warrant and arrested the suspect. They found the woman speaking incoherently and sent her to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei for treatment, the source said. Investigators also found an appointment slip from a public hospital’s psychiatric centre in the flat, the insider added. The incident has been classified as an attempted robbery and the force will continue its investigation.

title: Supporters of Pakistan’s ex-PM Imran Khan begin ‘long march’ to Islamabad
description: Authorities have been preparing for weeks for the arrival of demonstrators in Islamabad after the march was postponed.
content: A march protesting against the imprisonment of former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan kicked off in northwest Pakistan on Sunday after talks to avoid the demonstration stalled. Authorities have been preparing for weeks for the possible arrival of demonstrators in Islamabad, with the march planned by supporters of Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party originally slated for September 27 and then postponed until Sunday. Videos posted on PTI’s official social media showed supporters coalescing in different areas in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which is ruled by the party, and setting off in convoys as part of the “long march”. Sohail Afridi, the chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said earlier on X that the demonstration in support of Khan would go ahead. Discontent over Khan’s incarceration has mounted in recent months, particularly over the 73-year-old’s medical treatment and access to him by doctors and family. PTI has also called for the release of Khan’s three sisters, whose arrests last month further heightened tensions. Opposition politician Allama Raja Nasir Abbas said last-minute talks between the government and representatives from PTI were in “deadlock.” Abbas told Geo TV, a popular private news channel, that negotiators had hit an impasse over demands that included access to Khan by his doctor. Khan, a hugely popular former cricket star, has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges ranging from corruption to treason and inciting violence, following widespread anti-establishment riots in May 2023. He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralising his popularity. Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a geopolitics expert, said the protests were “fundamentally driven by economic factors,” with the Iran war affecting fuel prices in Pakistan and food prices rising on the back of the war in Ukraine. “Day-to-day life has become a real struggle for ordinary Pakistanis in recent years,” said Willasey-Wilsey, who is with the UK-based Royal United Services Institute. “Imran Khan is the focal point for all opposition to the government,” he added. ‘Popular support’ James Dorsey, a fellow at the National University of Singapore, said Khan was “essentially a populist leader” with “a genuine popular movement that had broad popular support”. “That’s why I think you’ve seen the determination by the government to prevent [the protesters] from entering Islamabad,” Dorsey said. Afridi, the chief minister, said the demonstration was to begin in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday and make its way to Khairabad, 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday. “The army and police are very capable of defending Islamabad and the government is not under any immediate threat,” Willasey-Wilsey said. “But the problems for Pakistan are piling up,” he added. Dorsey said that with Pakistan’s security concerns, particularly following its unresolved February 2026 war with Afghanistan, Islamabad would look to avoid escalation in the face of the protests. “It’s a problem for the government, but I don’t think it’s an existential threat,” he said. Further phases of the plan would be announced in Khairabad, Afridi said, without specifying when demonstrators could arrive in the Pakistani capital. Authorities in Islamabad have blocked main access routes to the capital with double-stacked shipping containers in preparation for the protest, obstructing traffic and public transit. The Supreme Court ruled in August that Khan should be moved to a civilian hospital for treatment, but authorities instead returned him to prison after a short stay at a government-run hospital.

title: China swimmers Yu Zidi, Zhang Zhanshuo among Asian Games stars who could light up LA Games
description: Games MVPs Yu and Thai Boonson Puripol among Asia’s best athletics, swimming hopes of shining at 2028 Olympics, along with a weightlifter.
content: The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya close on Sunday, bringing the curtain down on a fortnight of competition featuring some record-breaking performances. Among the best performers were the two athletes named Asian Games MVPs: 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi and Thai track and field sprinter Boonson Puripol. Yu, who won all three of her individual events with ease, said “I’m no prodigy” after being named the women’s MVP on Sunday. The schoolgirl, who looks poised to take the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics by storm, won the 200m butterfly, 200m individual medley and 400m IM in Games-record times to underline her rare talent. Her times were among the fastest in the world this year and she is already the youngest swimming world championships medallist in history after winning a relay bronze last year aged 12. But for all that, she said: “I don’t think I am what people describe as a prodigy. “I will continue to train hard, push myself and work alongside young athletes across Asia to inspire more young people to love and take part in sports, especially swimming.” Yu will be 15 when the LA Olympics come round and is likely to be a major medal threat with the world watching. Thailand’s Boonson, who did the 100m–200m sprint double, was named the men’s MVP. “I’m very happy and very honoured for my family, my country, and the Asian running community,” the 20-year-old said. Asked what he will do with his US$25,000 prize money, he said: “The money will go to my family and my self-development for goals in the future.” The Los Angeles Games are already in his sights after breaking the Asian Games records in the two sprints. “This time there were a lot of global athletes at this event, so the MVP gives me a lot of confidence that I can make the podium in LA,” he said. Here are four other athletes who starred and look primed to make an impact at the LA Olympics. Zhang Zhanshuo, swimming (China) With Yu grabbing the headlines, Zhang went slightly under the radar. But the 19-year-old went home with seven gold medals, the most by any swimmer in Asian Games history. He did it with panache, too, sitting on the lane divider and slowly counting off all seven on his fingers after bringing home the last one. Zhang scorched to the men’s 400m freestyle title in a Games-record time and also won individual titles in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, as well as three relays. Shin Ohashi, swimming (Japan) The 17-year-old said he wanted to set a world record at his home Games – and he did just that. Ohashi, who admits to loving junk food, clocked an astonishing two minutes 04.83 seconds to slice more than half a second off the previous 200m breaststroke world record held by China’s Qin Haiyang. The record continued Ohashi’s stunning rise and marked him out as the man to beat in Los Angeles, where he could face French superstar Leon Marchand. Yan Ziyi, athletics (China) The formidable Yan will just have turned only 20 when the LA Games roll around, but already the Chinese javelin thrower looks destined for the top. She demolished the Asian Games opposition with her first and only throw of 70.46 metres, breaking the Games record. It was the sixth-best throw of all time. Yan hurled a colossal 71.74m in May, second only to the world record of 72.28m set by the Czech Republic’s Barbora Spotakova in 2008. Ri Song-gum, weightlifting (North Korea) The tiny weightlifter gave North Korea an explosive start to the weightlifting campaign and next will be hunting the one honour missing from her career: an Olympic medal. The 1.40m (4ft 7in) pocket powerhouse set three new world marks in the 49-kilogram class as she entered the record book as the only woman to clinch three successive Asian Games weightlifting golds. She is also a double world champion and has been untouchable in her weight division since North Korea emerged from Covid exile in 2023. North Korea weightlifters have not taken part in the past two Olympics, so Los Angeles could be the 28-year-old’s only shot at Olympic glory.

title: 1,500 Hong Kong residents tour revamped Huanggang Port border crossing
description: Members of the public learn about public transport arrangements, immigration and customs clearance, and passenger-friendly facilities.
content: More than 1,500 Hong Kong residents toured the revamped Huanggang Port border crossing on Sunday as authorities pushed ahead with preparations for its opening. A Security Bureau spokesman said that participants took franchised buses or cross-boundary coaches from various districts to reach the crossing and were shown the new port building in groups. “The event effectively enhanced participants’ understanding of the public transport arrangements, immigration and customs clearance and passenger-friendly facilities at the port building,” the spokesman said. City authorities conducted four drills in August, testing facilities and simulating emergency situations at the revamped checkpoint between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. A source previously said that authorities were aiming to open it as early as October 12. Residents were first taken to the public transport interchange at the crossing to learn about various links for travelling to and from the checkpoint. Afterwards, they were invited to connect to the building’s free Wi-fi. Unlike other free government Wi-fi services, users do not need to visit a landing page to log in when connecting to the wireless network at the revamped crossing. Volunteers from the Fire Services Department and the Correctional Services Department led Sunday’s group tours. Members of the public were introduced to the design of the building and could visit the departure and arrival halls. Authorities also introduced the “joint inspection” clearance system to participants, which will be available at 134 e-channels at the checkpoint. Unlike traditional clearance models, which require a passenger to complete departure and arrival processes at different counters, the joint inspection model allows a passenger to complete both departure and arrival clearance by presenting one identity document required by their destination. The revamped Huanggang Port crossing will be the first to adopt the new model. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung previously announced that both Chinese and non-Chinese residents holding a valid mainland travel permit could use that and their Hong Kong identity cards interchangeably for the joint inspection clearance. Tang met participants on Sunday’s tour. His bureau’s spokesman noted that many residents had responded positively to the tour.

title: Hotstone Yoga closure losses rise to HK$7.8 million as 694 customers file reports
description: Customs arrests 61-year-old director as investigation looks into whether unusual sales activity preceded the chain’s abrupt shutdown.
content: Losses linked to the abrupt closure of Hotstone Yoga have risen to nearly HK$8 million (US$1 million), with close to 700 reports filed by affected customers in Hong Kong, according to authorities. The Customs and Excise Department said that as of 6pm on Sunday, it had received 694 reports relating to the yoga chain, involving service contracts worth about HK$7.8 million. The Consumer Council said it had received 416 complaints by 5pm the same day, with claimed losses totalling HK$5.42 million. Hotstone Yoga announced on Wednesday that it would cease operations immediately, citing “business operations and other actual circumstances” after “careful consideration”. The company had operated for more than 10 years. At its peak, it ran seven studios across the city – in Central, Causeway Bay, Aberdeen, Jordan, Tsuen Wan, Sha Tin and Kwun Tong – offering yoga, dance and fitness classes. The closure came after some customers said they were still being encouraged to buy course packages days before the company shut down. Earlier reports indicated that some packages cost as much as HK$29,700 for 180 classes. Customs launched an investigation into the closure and last Friday arrested a 61-year-old director of the company on suspicion of wrongly accepting payments in violation of the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. The department said it was examining the company’s financial and operational situation before the closure, as well as whether there had been any unusual sales activity. In a notice issued through a law firm and posted outside one of its studios, Hotstone said it would pay employees’ September wages and refund class fees for that month by October 5. However, some customers have expressed doubts about whether they will receive refunds and have sought help from authorities and the Consumer Council.

title: China urged to build ‘system’ to protect expanding overseas interests
description: Analysis calls for strategic shift, with more diplomatic engagement to reshape the rules and deeper security cooperation with other nations.
content: Beijing has been urged to do more to protect its overseas interests with a call for diplomatic engagement to reshape international rules and deeper security cooperation with other countries. As China’s expanding global footprint comes under pressure from geopolitics and restrictions from the West, a Chinese analysis posted on the Global Security Research social media account has called for a major shift in strategy. The author was not identified, but the account regularly posts analysis and commentary on Chinese national security ranging from nuclear issues to supply chains and technological sovereignty. It called for Beijing to move beyond crisis management and focus instead on prevention and cooperation when it comes to the country’s interests abroad. “The primary task is to build a systematic, complete and highly coordinated overseas interests security protection system,” said the analysis, which was posted last month. To do that would require “streamlining responsibilities across diplomacy, commerce, security and military departments to form a unified national approach”, according to the analysis. It highlighted the need to reshape international rules through diplomatic engagement, urging Beijing to “actively participate in global security governance and improve rule systems in the global investment, trade and maritime fields”. The analysis also called on Beijing to deepen security cooperation with countries where China has interests – particularly Belt and Road Initiative partners – including on law enforcement, counterterrorism and transnational crime. It said joint working mechanisms should be set up to protect Chinese companies and personnel on the ground. By the end of last year, more than 50,000 Chinese companies were operating overseas across 190 countries and regions, according to Ministry of Commerce data. The ministry data showed that China’s cumulative outbound investment has remained in the global top three for the past nine years. Outbound direct investment totalled US$174.38 billion in 2025 – a 7.1 per cent increase from a year earlier. But as China’s overseas investment has increased, new dangers have emerged beyond the traditional and non-traditional security risks, according to the analysis. They include legal compliance risks, unpredictable policy changes and foreign sanctions, all of which “interweave and amplify each other, making responses increasingly difficult”. It said “growing politicisation” of Chinese investment was also a concern for Beijing. The analysis said some countries used state power to suppress foreign enterprises and that national security was used as a pretext for protectionism, in an indirect reference to the United States. “Previously, going overseas mainly meant competing on cost and service,” it said. “Now you also have to guard against major powers flipping the table.” It comes as Chinese state-owned and private entities increasingly face foreign curbs ranging from export controls to investment screening and financial sanctions targeting Chinese enterprises globally. In a case earlier this year, Panama took control of two container ports on the Panama Canal after its Supreme Court annulled contracts that had allowed Hong Kong firm CK Hutchison Holdings to run them, calling them “unconstitutional”. The ruling came after pressure from US President Donald Trump. Beijing has sought to strengthen its legal arsenal to protect its interests overseas, most notably through its 2021 Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law which enables authorities to penalise entities that enforce measures deemed harmful to Chinese sovereignty. Resource nationalism has also been an obstacle for Chinese mining investors. For instance, Indonesia’s 2020 ban on raw nickel exports forced foreign companies to process the metal onshore. That prompted Chinese investors to start scaling back their operations earlier this year and threatening to withdraw from the Indonesian nickel industry due to production quota cuts and foreign exchange controls. Chinese mining operations face political and legal challenges across Latin America and Africa, while undersea cable projects have encountered resistance on national security grounds in multiple regions. The US Federal Communications Commission enforces a presumption of denial for cable-landing licences linked to foreign adversaries, effectively blocking Chinese firms from connecting submarine cables to US territory. The Pacific Light Cable Network – originally planned to link Hong Kong with Los Angeles – had its Hong Kong segment dropped entirely. China’s vulnerability along key maritime routes was also highlighted in the analysis, which argued that the security of shipping lanes was critical to energy and mineral imports as well as supply chains. “As Chinese supply chains have globalised, critical components, raw materials and production are now scattered globally,” it said, adding that they were exposed to geopolitical conflict, logistics disruptions and deliberate supply chain ruptures. The analysis warned that disruption at chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca could affect China’s economic stability. “We must strengthen technological support using big data, artificial intelligence and satellite remote sensing to build a global risk monitoring and early warning platform,” it said. “This will enhance risk identification, assessment and warning capabilities, enabling dynamic monitoring of global hotspots, key projects and critical corridors.”

title: China Eastern reports passenger to police over cabin crew kneeling row
description: Agitated flyer used ‘vulgar and offensive language, and threatened to kick the flight attendant’, carrier says, places him on no-fly list.
content: China Eastern Airlines has reported a male passenger to the police for allegedly disturbing order, after a flight attendant was filmed kneeling in a cabin aisle to apologise for bumping his elbow with a service trolley. In its second statement on the incident, the carrier said on Saturday that it believed the actions of the passenger amounted to disturbing order aboard a civil aircraft and had severely infringed upon the employee’s personal dignity. The airline added that it had banned the individual from flying with them. Footage of the incident aboard a flight from Hefei in Anhui province to Dalian in Liaoning province started circulating online on Monday. According to the airline, the cabin crew member accidentally bumped the sleeping passenger’s elbow with a trolley during the drinks service. She apologised immediately and repeatedly, but to no avail. “The passenger became agitated, using vulgar and offensive language, and threatened to kick the flight attendant, demanding that the flight attendant accompany him to the hospital after landing,” China Eastern said on Wednesday in its first statement on the incident. Chinese media reports citing the original uploader of the clip said that the passenger refused to accept the flight attendant’s apologies, prompting her to kneel repeatedly to beg for forgiveness. China Eastern also said that the attendant had repeatedly reminded passengers to mind the meal trolley. It did not say why she knelt. The flight attendant was offered immediate care and support and has since returned to duty as normal, according to Wednesday’s statement. The airline added that medical personnel examined the passenger upon landing and confirmed the bump did not result in any serious injury requiring further treatment. “The company has formally reported the aforementioned infringement and disturbance to the public security authorities,” China Eastern said on Saturday. The footage – filmed by a fellow passenger – has ignited debate over the pressure on cabin crew from complaint-driven evaluation systems, which can play a big role in staff appraisals. According to the official Beijing Daily, passenger complaints are directly tied to the performance evaluation and career advancement opportunities for cabin crew. “It’s not just about losing money for a single complaint – it impacts the flight attendant’s overall annual performance rating, which factors in both bonus points for commendation letters and deductions for complaints,” the newspaper quoted a veteran flight attendant as saying. Reducing complaint rates is an equally critical operational metric for airlines. Globally, rating agencies such as Skytrax also factor passenger complaint volume into their airline evaluation criteria. Beijing Daily quoted another aviation insider as saying that an airline’s complaint volume could directly affect its ability to secure flight rights and landing slots. Shanghai-based China Eastern is one of the country’s three major state-owned carriers, operating an extensive domestic and international network. Addressing the controversy on Friday, Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily said the passenger’s “relentless” demands despite the flight attendant’s apologies went far beyond legitimate rights protection, violating her personal dignity and crossing legal bottom lines. Under China’s civil aviation laws, verbal abuse or assault of crew members, as well as “picking quarrels and provoking trouble” aboard civil aircraft, are strictly prohibited. “No professional in any line of work should be subjected to such malice on the job,” the newspaper said in a commentary. It added that when facing aggressive behaviour, airlines must intervene, secure evidence and hand over offenders to police upon landing. “Unconditionally backing down just for ‘customer satisfaction’ to keep the peace will only encourage unreasonable passengers to push their luck, leaving frontline employees stripped of their sense of professional security,” the commentary said.

title: Hong Kong issues amber rainstorm warning
description: Observatory says squally thunderstorms are expected over Hong Kong, while intense gusts reaching 70 km/h could affect the city.
content: The Hong Kong Observatory issued an amber rainstorm warning on Sunday evening, with the signal remaining in place for more than two hours. The weather forecaster issued the alert – the lowest level in a three-tier warning system – at 8.20pm and cancelled it at 10.30pm. “A few squally thunderstorms are expected to occur over Hong Kong,” a spokesman for the Observatory said in the evening. Showers would be heavy at times. The forecaster also warned that intense gusts reaching 70km/h (43mph) could affect the city. It said there would be flooding in some low-lying and poorly drained areas, as well as possible flash floods from heavy rain. The amber rainstorm signal signifies that heavy rain exceeding 30mm (one inch) in an hour has fallen or is expected to fall generally over Hong Kong. The Observatory said the weather on Monday would be cloudy with occasional showers. “A cold front is moving across the coast of Guangdong gradually and bringing showers and squally thunderstorms to the region,” the spokesman said.

title: South Korean Asian Games footballers’ joy over national service exemptions raises ire
description: Social media users say there should be rethink over policy under which Games gold winners, Olympic medallists are exempted from military duty.
content: What was meant to be a few glorious moments could spark policy reform in South Korea after post-match comments from a couple of gold-medal-winning footballers triggered heated debate. South Korea beat hosts Japan 1-0 at the Toyota Stadium to win their fourth straight – and seventh overall – men’s football title at the Asian Games, leading to 20 of the 23-strong squad earning exemptions from military service. While the exemption was not an exclusive perk for the country’s footballers but for all athletes who win gold medals at the regional games, or reach the podium at the Olympic Games, it was the comments of two current players that fuelled the latest round of debates about the 53-year-old policy. “Medals and trophies don’t matter; our only reward is exemption from military service,” midfielder Yang Minh-yeok said. Team captain Lee Gi-hyuk – who reportedly had to report to the army in nine days – said “I don’t have to report to the army now!” while waving his gold medal. Nineteen-year-old defender Park Seung-soo also showed off his cap signalling his exemption on social media on the night of the victory. In response to those comments, South Korean lawmaker An Cheol-su on Sunday asked: “Is the military a despicable place? “The Asian Games’ exemption from military service should now be reconsidered. It’s truly heartbreaking that a member of the national team, an athlete who fights under the Taegeukgi flag, would have such limited awareness,” he said. “It was practically a blatant mockery; even the team captain boasted in an official interview that he ‘didn’t have to serve in the military’. They have completely forgotten the respect and affection that this country and its people once gave them because of that ‘glorious goal’. “Aren’t there many athletes who win gold medals without being exempt from military service? It’s simply outrageous to grant military service exemptions to national team members who bring shame to the country and despise the military.” The 26-year-old Lee, a defender who plays in the domestic K League, has since apologised for “the thoughtless remarks I made and the way I behaved after the match, things I should not have said or done, both as captain and as a player”. In a statement on Instagram he said he was “caught up in the happiness, adrenaline and excitement of the moment”. “I am deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us,” he said. “As an adult I should have thought carefully before speaking. I deeply regret having spoken so carelessly, and I will continue to reflect on my actions. “I sincerely apologise to all the fans who have supported us wholeheartedly and who are doing their utmost to fulfil their military duty.” In 1973, then-president Park Chung-hee introduced a military service exemption and reduction system for elite South Korean athletes and artists. The policy allowed athletes to earn alternative service or exemptions by winning a gold medal at the Asian Games, or a medal of any colour at the Olympics. Under this framework, qualifying medallists had to complete only basic military training and a brief period of community service instead of full active-duty military service. Current key figures in the South Korean football team, including the likes of Son Heung-min, Kim Min-jae and Lee Kang-in, were examples of players who resolved their military service issues by winning Asian Games gold medals. Needless to say, the players’ comments immediately caused an uproar among South Korean social media users. “The South Korean football team has found a way to win gold medals and still get criticised: abolish military service exemptions! Those soldiers who diligently serve in the military must be furious,” said one commentator. Another said: “The system was established 50 years ago, when people all over the world couldn’t distinguish between North and South Korea. Now, winning a gold medal only pleases the person involved; the general public isn’t even that interested. “K-pop and K-culture are what enhance our country’s prestige. Of the 20 million foreign tourists who visit South Korea annually, at least 50 per cent are directly or indirectly influenced by K-culture.” There were also comments suggesting that the military service exemption should be granted to only “the top three best players” in the final. While their neighbours were busy arguing about whether Asian Games medallists should be exempted from military service, Chinese social media users somehow found a way to belittle those who performed better than them. A Weibo post titled “Only the Japanese team could not smile during the Asian Games men’s football awards ceremony” was among the hot topics, suggesting that China were happy to be back on the podium after 28 years. It came after China drew 2-2 with Uzbekistan before winning on penalties to claim bronze in the men’s football event. The last time the Chinese men’s football team were on the Asian Games podium was in 1998, when they beat Thailand 3-0 in the play-off. “Hopefully, we can win silver or gold next time. Although the chances are slim, it still gives people a glimmer of hope,” said one Weibo user. Referring to China’s senior team losing 5-0 to Pakistan in Chongqing on Friday, another Weibo user said: “I suggest that the senior national team be disbanded here and now and this U23 team be promoted directly.”

title: China’s police, sightseeing operators snap up Bell helicopters despite safety concerns
description: Buyers hover around the small aircraft as sales soar and private jet use dives, making China the vendor’s second biggest Asia-Pacific market.
content: A range of public and private-sector Chinese buyers have acquired a total of 44 small-model Bell helicopters, often for sightseeing and corporate travel. This makes China the vendor’s second biggest market in the Asia-Pacific, with growing demand for more despite safety concerns surrounding rotary-wing aircraft, an aviation services firm said. China lagged behind only South Korea in the total number of five-seat Bell 505 Jet Ranger X helicopters, according to a statement by the Hong Kong-based Asian Sky Group. Its manufacturer, Texas-based Bell, was the world’s second biggest brand of turbine helicopters in 2024 to 2025 after Airbus, the Rotortrade dealership said in an annual industry report. The model launched in 2014 has sold a total of 700 worldwide. Customers in China include police agencies, corporations and operators of aerial sightseeing trips, Asian Sky Group consultancy services director Dennis Lau said. In its statement, Asian Sky Group said the helicopters had been “deployed on a variety of missions” in China. The 505 model is now used in China mostly for tourism and sightseeing, but customers increasingly want to carry out “utility” missions, Bell’s China country manager Liam Zhu said. Utility refers to flights for transport, infrastructure support or public safety. Its use is “expanding beyond tourism” now into agricultural and forestry operations, Zhu added. Most South Korea-based Jet Ranger X helicopters were operated by the armed forces in “training and utility roles”, according to the company’s statement. Helicopter purchases in China show a continued interest in private aircraft as a soft economy tempers the use of business jets. The number of business jets in mainland China fell to 243 in 2025, from 249 in 2024 and 270 in 2023, Asian Sky Group has previously said. China’s ultra-wealthy are parking their jets offshore to sidestep tougher compliance rules at home, while corporate executives are downgrading to commercial flights, according to analysts. Safety remains a latent concern across helicopter brands, Lau added. Most recorded Bell accidents globally were due to pilot errors, training, collisions or weather problems rather than mechanical issues, US Federal Aviation Administration-approved pilot examiner Dave Dziura indicated in an analysis on the consultancy SafeRotors’ website. However, helicopters in general fly at a higher risk of accidents compared to fixed-wing aircraft. At least two sightseeing helicopters have crashed in China since 2023 as general aviation increases. Demand for the Jet Ranger X has been growing in China among customers who can pay the “entry-level” price, Lau said. The Bell helicopters often sold for less in China than a comparable model made by Airbus, he added. Lau said many buyers would see the Jet Ranger X as a “step up” from Robinson-brand helicopter models that were also common in the country for civilian use. The Bell model had more power and a larger cabin.

title: Opinion | How the ‘G2’ effect of Xi-Trump summit is reverberating through Asia
description: When the world’s two biggest powers speak of respecting each other and swap stories about a war against Japan, the message is clear.
content: For American and Chinese people interested in the outcome of the latest summit between China’s President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, their conclusions could not be more different if they turn to the media and pundits for guidance. Chinese state media spared no superlative, echoing the official description of the summit as: forging the right way for the major powers to get along and writing a new chapter in ties. It played up the fact that Trump gave Xi the highest-level reception and met him at the airport, the first time since 1962 that a US president has done so for a visiting leader other than a pope. By contrast, US media and pundits were almost united in dismissing the summit as heavy on symbolism and light on substance, noting that both leaders played down their stark differences and delivered little more than a two-month extension of the trade truce and a new dialogue on artificial intelligence. Both camps may be off the mark. Chinese state media went over the top. But US commentators were too harsh, ignoring what the summit showed: the arrival of “G2” and its effects are being felt in Asia, particularly in Japan and Taiwan. The idea of a US-China Group of Two framework was first floated by American thinkers in 2005; Trump revived it at the Busan summit last October. His turnaround is striking. For nearly eight years, Washington took on China across the board, from trade to technology and chips. Now Trump has rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s first state visit to the US in 11 years. Beijing may not embrace the G2 label in public, but Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the visit was meant to put ties on an equal footing. The pageantry and pomp showed Washington was finally treating Beijing as an equal. Interestingly, the two leaders agreed to build a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”. Fairness and reciprocity have long been Washington’s words, used to demand China play fair in trade and investment. Intriguingly, they also recalled that China and the US were World War II allies. The significance should not be underestimated, for two reasons. First, the message seems that while the two countries may not become allies again, they can once more work together on bilateral issues and global challenges. Second, the reference to the wartime fight against Japanese militarism has practical weight for regional stability, particularly for Beijing’s ties with Tokyo and Taipei. At the welcome ceremony, Trump said American and Chinese “common interests” had “even made us allies in World War II” while Xi went further at the state dinner, saying the two peoples stood shoulder to shoulder “against Japanese militarist aggressors”. The White House readout repeated the point. This is more than history. It boosts Beijing’s narrative against Tokyo at a fraught time. Ties have worsened since last November, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Taiwan crisis could draw a Japanese military response. Since then, Beijing has run propaganda and economic pressure campaigns, accusing Japan of reviving militarism. The joint references to World War II left Tokyo confused and uneasy. Takaichi said she would not comment on every word; Trump called her for about 20 minutes to brief her. The speed of that call says something about how much reassurance is needed. The World War II talk also unsettled Taiwan, since America’s allies in China then were mostly Kuomintang forces, not Communist troops. And Taiwan itself was played down. Xi urged Washington to oppose Taiwan independence. The White House statement did not mention the island. US ambassador to China David Perdue said in a post-summit interview that US policy has not changed. Then he added something intriguing: Trump asked Xi “at one point” whether China wanted to buy American weapons. Trump denied it, said Perdue was probably talking about Taiwan but added “maybe it’s a good idea” to make such an offer to Beijing. Perdue also said the two men would continue to discuss arms sales to Taiwan, which sits badly with the US pledge in 1982 not to consult Beijing on the matter. All this follows Trump’s pause on a record US$14 billion package after the Beijing summit in May. He called the sale a “very good negotiating chip” with China. The two leaders also discussed Russia, North Korea and Iran. Trump pushed for three-way arms control talks with Russia and China, though China has long refused to join such talks and the White House readout did not say it agreed. Shenzhen may offer a chance. The Kremlin said Russian President Vladimir Putin plans to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit there in November and a three-way meeting with Trump and Xi had been “discussed”. The G2 is not a done deal. Trump is the outlier in a cabinet full of hawks, and he is as well known for his deal-making as for his unpredictability. The November midterm elections, when Democrats are widely expected to win back the House, add more uncertainty. But the two men will meet again in Shenzhen and at the G20 in Miami in December, which would make four meetings in one year. The summit has also locked in stability between two economies in open confrontation until last year. To be sure, the two major powers will keep competing hard on AI and other frontier technologies, but the summit shows they can still work together where their interests meet. The rest of the world does not need a formal G2 to feel its effects. When the two biggest powers speak of respecting each other and swap stories about a war against Japan, the message is loud and clear.

title: On-site staff, hotline deployed as Kai Tak Hospital starts phased operations
description: Family medicine centre opens on Monday at city’s largest hospital, specialist outpatient and blood-taking services to follow in late October.
content: Hong Kong health authorities will deploy on-site staff and step up support via a dedicated hotline for patients visiting Kai Tak Hospital amid booking and transport queries as the city’s largest public hospital begins its phased opening. From Monday, Kai Tak Hospital’s family medicine integrated centre will start operations, while specialist outpatient services and automated features in the hospital’s blood-taking services are scheduled to launch in late October. Dr Eric Cheung Fuk-chi, cluster chief executive of Kowloon Central and Kai Tak Hospital chief executive, said services would be rolled out in a “gradual approach”. “This is the largest hospital relocation in Hong Kong’s history. As a result, we must proceed with caution to ensure that patient care and service quality remain entirely unaffected,” Cheung said. The family medicine centre, which opens on Monday, will treat about 350 outpatients daily: 100 existing patients from the public hospital system and 250 additional slots for the public. The centre will handle patients with relatively mild conditions such as flu or gastroenteritis, as well as those with episodic or chronic diseases. It will also offer vaccinations and general nursing care. Equipped with a dedicated pharmacy, the centre can operate fully independently. Nutrition and occupational therapy services will also be launched on Monday. To assist the public, a task force has been set up to contact patients about the new arrangements, while a hotline will be available seven days a week to answer queries. Staff in blue vests will be stationed at the lobby and clinical departments from Monday to help patients on the ground. Specialist outpatient services will be rolled out in phases from late October. The blood-taking station, also starting in late October, features an automatic specimen transport system that dispenses tubes automatically, cutting blood collection time to within five minutes. The clinical oncology day centre will commence service in November. The hospital also houses the city’s largest pharmacy. With 21 counters, it will introduce an automated dispensing system in the first quarter of 2027, slashing medication waiting time to an average of 30 minutes. The hospital, a 2,400-bed facility with 37 operating theatres, is set to take over services from Queen Elizabeth Hospital and become a healthcare hub for Kowloon. Spanning a total gross floor area of 500,000 square metres, the hospital complex comprises five blocks. The specialist outpatient clinic block, where the family medicine centre is located, and the oncology block are scheduled to commence services in the coming months. The remaining three blocks, covering acute services, administration, and education and training, form the facility’s second phase, with major clinical services including inpatient, surgical, and accident and emergency services available in 2028.

title: India election chief faces calls to resign from protesters, opposition
description: The protesters say a nationwide voter-roll revision exercise launched last year has disenfranchised millions ⁠of eligible voters.
content: Thousands of young protesters and opposition parties staged protests in the national ⁠capital and Mumbai on ⁠Sunday, demanding the resignation of Election Commission Chief ⁠Gyanesh Kumar, as police detained demonstrators for a third consecutive day. Opposition leaders Raj Thackeray and Uddhav Thackeray led protests in Mumbai calling for the scrapping of revisions to the electoral roll and Kumar’s resignation. In Delhi, protesters started gathering in the early evening and police started detaining some of them, ‌according to a witness. Some demonstrators breached police barricades and surrounded vehicles carrying detained demonstrators, climbing onto them and laying on the road to block ⁠their path, the witness added. “Police dragged me by my hair,” said Aahna Singh, an activist and political science student at Jawaharlal Nehru University who ‌was protesting. “The police are resorting to brutality.” Many demonstrators were later released, though police registered cases against some for allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in the capital. The protesters say a nationwide voter-roll revision exercise launched last year has disenfranchised millions ⁠of eligible voters by removing them from electoral rolls. They allege the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party. ‌The Election Commission and the BJP deny the allegations. “I just want to tell the ruling party this much … We are angry about how you are wielding that power. It’s ‌the people of this country who should decide who sits in power and who sits in opposition, not ⁠the Election Commission,” Raj ⁠Thackeray said. The protests are likely to intensify over the next few days as an alliance of India’s opposition parties plans to launch protests to “save ‌democracy” with a march to the Election Commission office on Monday. The Gen Z Cockroach Janta Party has announced plans for a major rally in Delhi ‌on October ‌10. The demonstrations represent the latest in a series of youth-led challenges to Modi’s government – unprecedented in his 12 years ‌in power. In July, student protests forced the removal of the federal education minister following a leak of question papers ⁠for a national medical college entrance examination, marking the worst political crisis of Modi’s third term in office. Rim Jhim Sharma, a ⁠resident of Soniya Vihar in Delhi who came to the protest site, said before being detained that many from her locality have been stripped of their voting rights. “We are here for protest and this ‌is our right. We will take ‌our India back from Modi,” she said. Kumar has not responded to demands for his resignation or commented on the protests. The Election Commission says the exercise is designed to remove duplicate, deceased, or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, the commission directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.

title: Hong Kong woman loses HK$21.5 million in cryptocurrency scam
description: Clerk, 60, was duped by a fraudster posing as an investment expert she met online.
content: A 60-year-old Hong Kong woman has lost more than HK$21 million (US$2.7 million) in a cryptocurrency scam after a fraudster posing as an investment expert she met online duped her. The clerk reported the case to police on Saturday, saying she had befriended an individual claiming to be an investment specialist on “Baby Kingdom”, a popular online parenting forum and community website, on March 15 this year, a source said. The fraudster duped her into investing on a fake cryptocurrency platform that promised high returns. Believing the pitch, she remitted HK$19 million to the fake website. Subsequently, an accomplice posing as a platform compliance officer contacted her, claiming that her account had been involved in money laundering and demanding funds to clear her name. Acting on the instructions, the victim transferred an additional HK$1.2 million. She eventually alerted police after being asked to make further payments. Between March and September, the victim lost about HK$21.5 million in total. The case has been classified as obtaining property by deception and handed over to the Sau Mau Ping district investigation team. Earlier this year, a 67-year-old retired foreign businessman lost HK$84.8 million after meeting an online fraudster on social media who developed a romantic relationship with him over WhatsApp. Posing as a cryptocurrency investment expert, the fraudster persuaded the victim to download a fake trading application and transfer digital assets into designated crypto wallets over a six-month period.

title: Curtain comes down on Asian Games after 2 weeks of turmoil, record-breaking performances
description: Rugby player Cado Lee leads out remaining Hong Kong delegation at closing ceremony, which features customary handover to the next host, Doha.
content: The curtain came down on the Asian Games on Sunday, with officials hoping the fortnight in Japan would be remembered not for the chaos dogging every step but for the athletic performances that brought more than 150 world, junior and continental records. In keeping with the overall approach of the Games, the closing ceremony was a strange affair, one that felt a little like adults trying to be cool in a room full of teenagers. The fact it took place in front of rows and rows of empty seats at a venue that even at the height of the athletics competition was nearer to being empty than full did not help. Neither did the slow trickle of athletes who entered during their parade. With many of those who competed already at their next event or at home, the ones who remained did what is common on such occasions: mixed freely, laughed and joked, and took selfies. Cado Lee Ka-to led a smiling Hong Kong group, mostly made up of his rugby sevens teammates and sailors, into the Paloma Mizuho Stadium while a video of highlights played in the background. Hideaki Ohmura, the president of the local organising committee, told those at the ceremony that he believed local support for athletes had come because their “outstanding performances touched our hearts and gave us courage, hope and inspiration”. Earlier, in a closing press conference, suggestions that the organisational issues would ultimately overshadow any significant athletic endeavour were shut down by Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) director general Husain Al-Musallam. The Kuwaiti pointed to the 54 world, 11 junior world and 89 continental records set in Nagoya, Tokyo and elsewhere, and said it was an achievement that “does not come without the best environment”. “The athletes cannot perform if they don’t have transportation,” he said. “The athletes cannot perform if they don’t ‌have good healthcare. The athletes cannot perform if they don’t eat food. Numbers talk, it’s ⁠evidence. We are here ⁠to present you the evidence.” Hong Kong chef de mission Wong Po-kee would argue otherwise, and he praised the city’s athletes for delivering “outstanding performances, despite the difficult circumstances”. “Their determination, perseverance and willingness to overcome challenges made these remarkable achievements possible. Their accomplishments made us all proud.” Next up will be Doha, which organisers are still branding as 2030, although the expectation is there will be a five-year gap as the Games switch to being in the year before an Olympics, with more events doubling up as qualifiers. The sovereign state staged the Games 20 years ago, and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, the country’s prime minister and foreign minister, said it was an honour to take over “responsibility as the next hosts”. “Doha 2030 will build on the legacy of Doha 2006 while looking ahead to a new generation of athletes, fans and communities across Asia,” he added. “We will approach this responsibility with humility, partnership and a deep respect for the cultural diversity and aspirations of our continent.” Much of the event after the Games officially closed centred on Doha, and the entrance of Qatari equestrian Jassim Al Kuwari on Red Raiden to collect the OCA flag provided one of the brighter moments. Things picked up a little bit thereafter, with an earnest MC dressed like a game show host trying to convince athletes to dance with performers before a singer in a gold kimono and fireworks brought proceedings to a close.

title: Malaysia repatriates 1,500 Myanmar nationals despite UN risk warnings
description: The returnees have been convicted of staying illegally and other immigration violations in Malaysia.
content: Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals who were sent back from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city on Sunday despite warnings from the UN refugee agency and rights groups that conditions for return remain unsafe. Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on February 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition and plunging large parts of the country into conflict. The returnees, including 86 women, have been convicted of staying illegally and other immigration violations in Malaysia, according to reports from Myanmar state media. They were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship last Tuesday. They arrived in southern Yangon early on Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said. The returnees are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where 10,388 others were being held at immigration detention centres, according to Malaysia’s Home Ministry. The UN high commissioner for refugees and rights groups have criticised the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. “Under international law, the government of Malaysia is obligated to uphold the principle of non-refoulement and prevent the return of individuals to situations where they face a real risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations,” Kelley E. Currie, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said in a statement on Thursday. “In my assessment, the risk of refoulement in the present circumstances is substantial.” It was unclear if any of the returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who are facing persecution in Myanmar and have been denied citizenship. Myanmar Foreign Ministry official Han Win Aung said that the repatriation involved “genuine citizens”. Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants. Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s military-backed government who was sworn in as president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia this month to discuss the refugee and migrant issues.

title: Beijing fights invasive moths with parasitic wasps and caterpillar-catching contests
description: They have blanketed trees in the Chinese capital and surrounding areas this summer, posing a threat to hundreds of species of plants.
content: Authorities in the Chinese capital are releasing more than a billion parasitic wasps and encouraging caterpillar-catching competitions to try to contain the spread of the invasive North American fall webworm. The caterpillars have blanketed trees in Beijing and surrounding areas this summer, spinning clouds of greyish-white webs as they eat their way through foliage. The insects are the fuzzy larval stage of Hyphantria cunea and metamorphose into adult white moths. While not harmful to humans, they pose a threat to hundreds of species of plants, China Science Daily reported on Friday. According to the article written by Chen Min, a professor at Beijing Forestry University, this generation of larvae has a greater risk of spread than usual, making control measures more difficult. Chen said a warm winter and a rainy summer were providing ideal conditions for the pest to thrive, with the wet weather washing away pesticides. To combat the outbreak, municipal workers have taken physical measures such as removing webs and trapping moths as well as spraying pesticides. Nearly 3,000 monitoring sites had been set up around Beijing to guide control efforts, state news agency Xinhua reported last week. Community efforts were also launched to combat the outbreak, including caterpillar-catching competitions and calls for people to report infected trees. Beijing has released 1.1 billion Chouioia cunea – a species of parasitic wasp discovered in the 1980s that acts as a natural predator for the pest – to try to suppress the population, according to the China Science Daily report. The fall webworm is native to North America – found across the United States, Canada and Mexico – and was accidentally introduced to Europe in the 1940s, according to the University of Massachusetts Amherst. It has since spread through Europe and Asia as an invasive species. Chen said the pest was first discovered in China in 1979 and was now found in 13 provincial-level areas. In the US, native populations of the moth are typically kept below damaging levels due to natural predators, according to the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Chen said the caterpillar targeted many plant species, including common Chinese street trees such as mulberry, ash and plane varieties. A single female moth can lay hundreds of eggs and three generations of the insect emerge each year. The present outbreak is the third generation, but the first – which emerges around May – is the most important to target, according to another Xinhua report on Saturday. Chen noted that this year’s concentrated outbreak in China exposed gaps in control efforts, showing that measures required better synchronisation and adaptation – particularly as climate change expands the pest’s suitable habitats.

title: TCM or Western medicine for sports injuries? Why this Hong Kong athlete chose both
description: Asian Games fencer Janelle Leung and experts in TCM describe its growing acceptance among athletes for smarter injury recovery.
content: In the third instalment of a four-part Health Matters series on traditional Chinese medicine, Aidyn Fitzpatrick speaks to a Hong Kong fencer studying TCM and local practitioners to see how athletes, both elite and amateur, are using TCM alongside Western medicine for smarter injury recovery. Fresh off helping Hong Kong clinch a bronze medal in the women’s foil team event at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, fencer Janelle Leung Ya-lei – ranked 53rd in the world – knows the fine margin between peak performance and high-stakes injury. In April 2026, she sustained a partial tear to her ankle ligament, just seven days before the Cairo Foil World Cup. Away from Hong Kong and with limited access to her regular medical team, Leung looked to her Chinese medicine knowledge from her ongoing studies at Baptist University, where she was admitted to the Bachelor of Chinese Medicine and Bachelor of Science in Biomedical Science programme in 2023. Each night after training, the 21-year-old chose to treat a few acupuncture points that stimulate the ankle for better blood flow and reduce swelling and pain. “It helped with my recovery a lot,” she says, “allowing me to train right before the competition and get into the main rounds.” A marriage of East and West In a cross-cultural city like Hong Kong, when a runner rolls an ankle on a trail, or a gym-goer develops a stubborn shoulder – or a star fencer sustains an injury far from home – the question is rarely whether to choose Chinese or Western medicine. More often, it is how to use both. Dr Cheung Yung, a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) practitioner, sees a broad range of the city’s active population. Runners most commonly arrive with sprained ankles and torn calf muscles, he says. Hikers and trail runners complain of Achilles pain. Pickleball, padel and tennis players, whose sports demand abrupt stopping and starting on hard courts, often bring knee complaints. Cheung separates these presentations into two broad groups: accident or accumulation. The former includes a lateral ligament sprain after a misstep, or a calf tear after an underprepared muscle is used abruptly. The latter comprises injuries as a result of repetition – elbow tendinopathy that causes pain and forearm weakness, for example, or golf-related low back trouble. In assessing an injury, he uses the classical Chinese medicine framework of looking, listening, asking and feeling, alongside palpation of the affected area. He also screens for factors including metal allergies, blood-thinning medication and blood disorders that may make acupuncture unsuitable. Patients’ X-rays and other imaging can help refine the picture. But his clearest advice is also the most conventional: if an athlete cannot bear weight, has dramatic swelling, or has serious pain, the hospital comes first. “A break or a full rupture is a surgeon’s problem, and no amount of needling changes that,” he says. ‘The same diagnosis, the same goals and the same recovery plan’ That blend of clinical need and cultural familiarity shapes athletes’ choices in Hong Kong. Many “tend to first seek help or advice from a Western medicine doctor to get a referral to physiotherapy or an X-ray,” says Dr Hon Sze-sze, a senior lecturer in sports management at Baptist University. Insurance requirements can play a part, she adds, but so can prior experience: “I have seen athletes who have tremendous faith in Chinese bonesetters.” At the same time, “The best integrated care is not multiple practitioners working separately,” says Professor Amy Ng Pui-pui, clinical assistant professor and co-deputy director of the Master of Community Health Care programme at the University of Hong Kong. “It’s multiple practitioners working from the same diagnosis, the same goals and the same recovery plan.” A family doctor helps establish the diagnosis, spot red flags and arrange imaging or specialist input. Physiotherapists lead exercise-based rehabilitation. A Chinese medicine practitioner may help with managing symptoms. For athletes, having many experts working together can guard against a seductive but risky equation: less pain equals “healed”. It does not. Ng says recreational athletes commonly go to one of two extremes after injury: they push through pain and return too early, or stop moving altogether. For most musculoskeletal injuries, neither is ideal. “Return-to-sport decisions should be guided by objective measures such as strength, function, movement quality and sport-specific testing,” she says. Cheung makes the same point at his clinic. For an uncomplicated soft-tissue injury, he looks for reduced swelling and bruising, less pain and restored joint movement. Yet he advises patients to wait another two weeks after those signs have disappeared before returning to sport, because the tissue is still rebuilding. “Pain-free is not the same as ready to train,” he says. The point is especially salient for athletes who feel pressure to resume training quickly, whether for a race, league fixture – or global competition. Once Leung was back in Hong Kong, physiotherapy at the Hong Kong Sports Institute became essential in order for her to target her ankle and progressively regain strength before she was ready to return to the rigours of fencing. She describes the relationship between the two healing conventions as “mutualism”. Western sports medicine handles the structure of an injury – using X-rays or MRI, then progressively strengthening the injured area. TCM, she believes, can support pain and swelling management and the quality of recovery. “The real challenge to each athlete post recovery isn’t ‘Can I return to the field?’,” she says, “but ‘Can I fence at the same quality and intensity consistently without burning out or getting injured easily again?’” The evidence broadly supports her experience. Acupuncture has its strongest case as an adjunct for pain and symptom relief, particularly when discomfort prevents someone from taking part fully in rehabilitation. Major pooled studies confirm acupuncture outperforms both standard care and placebo treatments for persistent joint and muscle pain, though its effectiveness varies depending on the specific injury. Clinical reviews also show promising results for acute ankle sprains and tennis elbow, even if researchers note limitations. Troy Sing, a Chinese medicine practitioner and former Hong Kong rugby player, puts the limits plainly: “Acupuncture does not strengthen or stretch muscles, and it does not suture ligaments or tendons,” he says. Sing refers patients for conventional assessment when needed and tracks progress with pain scores, range of motion and clinical findings. That approach captures TCM’s sensible role in a sports-recovery programme: symptom relief that enables movement and rehabilitation, not symptom relief that licenses a premature return. When movement is the best medicine For certain overuse conditions, exercise is the treatment. Structured tendon-loading programmes are first-line care for Achilles tendinopathy – a condition that can cause pain, stiffness and swelling of the Achilles tendon connecting the calf muscle to the heel. Physiotherapy is also indispensable where technique, posture or training errors must change. Chinese therapeutic massage may have a role after acute inflammation subsides, and mind-body movement practices can be helpful in longer term pain management. Cheung prescribes lin gung – combining qigong, joint mobility, muscle work and breathing – for chronic symptoms, and suggests qigong as a warm-up before more demanding exercise. Trials of tai chi and reviews of qigong and related mind-body exercise point to potential benefits for chronic musculoskeletal pain and function, particularly in the spine and knee, though they should not be presented as substitutes for diagnosis or individually tailored rehabilitation. At the same time, not every popular recovery trend is backed by strong data. Cheung is cautious about cupping and uses it sparingly in his clinic. Large-scale reviews evaluating cupping in both amateur and elite athletes found the evidence supporting its performance and recovery benefits remains weak and low-quality. He also sounds a warning about topical muscle rubs. Products containing methyl salicylate, or wintergreen oil, can deliver an aspirin-like drug through the skin. Used sparingly over a small area, they are generally safe, but large amounts, use over extensive areas or broken skin, wrapping, heat and exercise can raise systemic exposure. Athletes should disclose medications, supplements and herbs to every practitioner involved in their care, he says, and should not assume “natural” means risk-free. Hong Kong’s sport-for-all ambitions make the joint use of TCM and Western medicine increasingly relevant beyond elite squads. “A good support network would include an understanding coach, a caring but firm fitness trainer, a medical practitioner who understands the sport’s demands and a lot of patience and discipline from the athlete,” HKBU’s Hon says. In other words, for the city’s runners, weekend footballers, hikers, gym regulars – and star fencers – using TCM in recovery is ultimately not a choice between needles and physio. “Chinese medicine and Western medicine balance each other out,” Leung says, “making the whole medical field more complete through playing different roles during the recovery process.” At the same time, there is a sequence to follow: diagnose properly, rule out structural damage, manage pain safely, rebuild capacity, then test the movements the sport actually requires. TCM can have a valued place within that sequence – but don’t be tempted to skip the sequence entirely. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Most G20 trade ministers reject US call for curbing excess capacity, China says
description: Ministry of Commerce says issue was ‘highly controversial’ at G20 trade meeting last week, contrasting with US statement.
content: Most trade ministers from the world’s largest economies disagreed with calls to curb excess industrial capacity at a Group of 20 (G20) trade meeting that ended on Thursday, according to China’s commerce ministry, a view that contrasts with a US statement that a “handful” of countries objected. “The issues related to excess industrial capacity and forced labour have been highly controversial,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday about the two-day G20 Trade Ministerial Conference in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Because most member states held differing views, the meeting failed to produce an outcome document on the relevant issues, the spokesperson added. A statement from US trade representatives on Friday said that a “handful” of trade ministers rejected to creating a “pathway towards cooperative action” on excess capacity and “non-market” policies such as forced labour, without naming the involved countries. The differing viewpoints from the US-chaired meeting mean that industrial supply will be the focal point of the second round of China-EU trade talks set for Thursday and Friday in Beijing. In addition to overcapacity and forced labour, trade representatives at last week’s meeting – where the US set the agenda – also did not agree on a proposal to adjust the principles behind most-favoured-nation (MFN) status in world trade. They did make a joint statement denouncing the weaponisation of food through coercive measures. For years, the US and European Union (EU) have been highlighting what they see as excess supply of some Chinese exports and have imposed various tariffs on the goods, varying from solar panels to electric vehicles. China consistently pushes back on the claims. In late July, the commerce ministry said in an official statement that China’s industrial subsidies and insufficient domestic demand did not necessarily lead to overcapacity, warning that protectionism would only disrupt global trade and supply chains and risk the long-term growth of the global economy. In a separate statement on Friday, China’s top international trade representative Li Chenggang said the country firmly objected to the issues of overcapacity and forced labour being used as pretexts for unilateralism and protectionism. “China is open to dialogue and cooperation on industrial policy with all parties, enhancing mutual trust through strengthened policy coordination and facilitating the healthy and sustainable development of global industries,” added Li, who was promoted last month from international trade negotiator at the Ministry of Commerce. During the meeting in Wisconsin, Li also met or had brief talks with representatives from 11 member countries, according to the Friday statement. On the MFN system, the Ministry of Commerce said most attending states believed that undermining the principle would seriously damage the very foundations of the multilateral trading system. A US statement, in contrast, said there was willingness among “an increasing number of members” to discuss how it could be improved. For the coming G20 Miami Summit in mid-December, China was willing to work with the chair state and all members while sticking to consensus and collaboration, the ministry spokesperson said on Sunday.

title: China’s only monogamous emperor: why Hongzhi refused a harem, remained dedicated to wife
description: While Emperor Hongzhi certainly loved his wife, his traumatic childhood likely played a decisive role in his unique monogamy.
content: It is no secret that Chinese emperors had many women in their lives, and the imperial concubine system was a significant feature of feudal social structures. Ming-era (1368–1644) emperors could have upwards of 9,000 consorts, ostensibly to ensure an heir. Unfortunately, these women often existed in gilded prisons, barred from leaving the palace grounds and frequently subject to the wrath of a cruel emperor. However, one leader stands out for doing just the opposite; the Hongzhi Emperor (r. 1487–1505) is remarkable for being the only emperor who chose a life of monogamy. He was devoted to Empress Zhang (1471–1541) throughout his life and seemingly did not engage in any affairs, much less maintain a systematic harem. His loyalty appears to stem from genuine love and affection, but historians also suggest that Hongzhi’s monogamy – and notably, his rejection of concubines – was influenced by a childhood filled with murder and intrigue that could rival modern period dramas. The source of Hongzhi’s caution was his father’s favourite consort, surnamed Wan. She was ruthless in eliminating any threats to her standing in the palace, which inevitably included any potential heirs. Hongzhi was born to a low-ranking palace woman surnamed Ji, which immediately placed him in danger. At one point, Wan actively sought to track down and eliminate any possible heirs, sometimes including their mothers. A group of loyal servants, aware of the baby’s significance, raised him in the servants’ quarters for six years. During this time, he developed a deep bond with his mother, compounding his tragic upbringing. Hongzhi’s father, the Chenghua Emperor, was unaware of his son’s existence for five years. However, upon discovering him, he quickly proclaimed the boy as his heir apparent, which offered some protection but, unfortunately, not to his mother, who died under suspicious circumstances shortly thereafter. The theory is that this traumatic family history, coupled with his affection for his mother and love for his wife, led Hongzhi to embrace monogamy. Hongzhi’s personal loyalty to the empress was further reinforced by his deep devotion to Confucian ideology, which emphasised the sanctity of marriage. Nevertheless, the Emperor’s loyalty may have had negative repercussions, particularly regarding the powerful roles wielded by his brothers-in-law. These two brothers were famously corrupt, exploiting their influence for personal gain and engaging in selfish behaviour that tarnished the reputation of an otherwise well-respected emperor. Hongzhi fell ill in 1505 and passed away shortly thereafter, leaving behind a legacy defined by high competence and a true devotion to the Confucian values many other emperors only pretended to uphold.

title: Helpers, employers voice concerns over Hong Kong plan to import carers in 2027
description: Foreign domestic carers will be paid 10 to 20 per cent more than general helpers, labour chief Chris Sun says.
content: A pilot scheme to import hundreds of foreign domestic carers from next year to look after elderly Hongkongers has sparked concern among both helpers and employers after the city’s labour minister revealed further details, including the salary level. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Sunday that the carers would be equipped with both specialised elderly care skills and general domestic capabilities, and would first need to complete a 150-hour course in their home country. “We now need to find a professional organisation in Hong Kong for a mechanism to ensure they finish the course and are truly equipped with those skills, because I understand that in the pilot scheme, residents will be concerned whether the workers can perform their tasks,” Sun said on a television programme. The pilot scheme was expected to start in the second half of next year, he added. Hong Kong currently has around 380,000 foreign domestic helpers, mainly from the Philippines and Indonesia, who carry out general housework duties in their employers’ homes. The Social Welfare Department has sponsored around 1,000 of these workers to undertake a 10-hour course to learn first aid and basic elderly care. Sun said the intended specialised carers would complete a course that would be similar to existing training for professional carers, to equip them with more advanced skills. The course would be designed and accredited by authorised professional bodies in the industry that are recognised by the government. Sun added that these carers would still be expected to take on housework duties and would be paid 10 to 20 per cent more than their generalist counterparts. Their pay scale mechanism would also be similar to that of foreign domestic helpers. The government announced on Friday that the minimum wage for domestic workers would rise by 2.35 per cent to HK$5,220 (US$670) per month, with the new rate applying to all contracts signed on or after Saturday. Employers would have to provide free food to their helpers or pay a food allowance of HK$1,236 a month. Separately, Sun said authorities would consider a new model of publicly built care homes for the elderly that would be run by private operators. “If the community is mainly low income, we will still mainly provide subsidised services. If the community is middle class, then we think we can provide more options for the market,” he said on the same programme. An estimated 1.98 million people, or 26 per cent of the population, are aged 65 or above. The figure is projected to rise to 36 per cent of the population by 2046, or 2.95 million people.
