Stress has also emerged as a concern in recent years, as murder-suicide tragedies involving elderly carers and family members have made headlines. In June, Sun commented on a case in which a 70-year-old man was found hanging in his Kwai Chung flat, while his 78-year-old wife was discovered unconscious there and later pronounced dead, calling it a tragedy. A survey by the NGO Suicide Prevention Services last year found that 37 per cent of 942 carers polled reported a high level of stress. Eman Villanueva, spokesman for the Asian Migrants’ Coordinating Body, expressed concern that the heavy workload of domestic chores paired with full-time care could force carers to become “round-the-clock workers”. It would be especially hard on those who would need to look after elderly residents with conditions such as dementia or who required constant care, he added. Villanueva said that compared with full-time local carers, who were paid between HK$17,000 and HK$25,000 a month for domestic duties and elderly care, the proposed figure for foreign carers of roughly HK$6,000 to HK$7,000, was very low. He urged the government to study the current proposed rate. He also urged the government to clarify accountability should accidents occur to the elderly in scenarios such as when carers were cleaning the flat or when they went out to get groceries. He added the government should remove elderly care as part of the duties of helpers going forward. “If foreign domestic helpers will still be allowed to take care of the elderly, then many will just hire them and pay them less than to hire a carer,” he said. Chrystie Lam Haa-iu, president of the Coalition of Global Home Service Sustainable Development, representing employers, said the 10 to 20 per cent increase in salary for foreign carers, on top of providing food and accommodation, could create a significant financial burden for grass-roots and lower-middle-class families. She added that the 150 hours of overseas training for foreign carers was only half that required for local health workers, leading to concerns as to whether the training was sufficient for foreign carers to handle complex needs such as handling feeding tubes or managing chronic illnesses. Lam also urged the government to address operational details before the trial scheme began. “Without clear guidelines on liability and refund mechanisms, employers are worried that hiring under this new scheme carries an unfairly high financial risk,” Lam said.

title: Hong Kong should review reducing number of Legco seats to cut costs, Rita Fan says
description: ‘A friend of mine always says keeping 90 seats costs a lot more than 60, and I kind of agree with that,’ first post-handover Legco president says.
content: Hong Kong’s first Legislative Council president following the city’s return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997 has suggested reviewing the number of seats in Legco, citing the need to use public funds properly. Rita Fan Hsu Lai-tai also said on Sunday that Hong Kong and Shenzhen authorities had discussed the development of a plot at the two cities’ border before the 1997 handover, but the plan failed because of opposition within the government. Fan made the remarks during an appearance on a radio show, in which she was asked by the host whether the current 90 seats in Legco were “too many”. “A friend of mine always says keeping 90 seats costs a lot more than 60, and I kind of agree with that,” she said. Fan said authorities had to “discuss and review it” in the future, while also cautioning that she was not in a position to make any substantive suggestions as she had stepped back from politics. The number of seats was increased from 60 to 70 for the 2012-16 Legco term. The number then rose to 90 after Hong Kong’s electoral system was revamped in 2021 to introduce 40 seats elected by the Election Committee, while ensuring only “patriots” could take part. Twenty of the 90 seats were directly elected by residents, while the remaining 30 were picked by professionals from functional constituencies. Fan, whose son Andrew Fan Chun-wah is a lawmaker from the Election Committee constituency, said she would not offer any practical advice to her successors, as each term of Legco would face different challenges. But she stressed that lawmakers should always behave with caution and avoid committing even minor legal breaches, citing a recent series of misconduct by Legco members. “Lawmakers should not only convey the thoughts of residents but also serve as role models for them,” she said. “When they lose confidence in you, how would they entrust you to convey their thoughts?” In July, former Election Committee sector lawmaker William Wong Kam-fai resigned from the legislature after he was arrested and prosecuted for dangerous driving, after he allegedly drove and crashed his vehicle while in an intoxicated state. Earlier, Hong Kong Island West representative Judy Chan Kapui was fined HK$2,000 for driving on the wrong side of the road and received a written warning from Legco’s Supervisory Committee. In the two-hour programme on Sunday, veteran politician Fan also talked about the late Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive. Fan praised Tung as a visionary leader, who made various forward-looking plans during his tenure, including some that ultimately stalled because of various factors. She revealed that after Tung and she were picked for leadership roles before the handover, the party boss and mayor of neighbouring Shenzhen had met them to discuss a proposal to develop the Lok Ma Chau Loop, or Hetao, at the border into a technology hub. “Their dedication to working with us was very obvious, but the discussions led nowhere because some prominent figures in the Hong Kong government at the time thought the timing was not right,” she said. The 87-hectare loop is now divided into two technology parks managed by Hong Kong and Shenzhen, respectively. Both sides will work on easing the flows of human and innovative elements, such as data and biomedical samples, to form synergies for research and industrial applications. Fan added that Tung was keen on pushing forward this initiative, which led to the establishment of Cyberport as a technology powerhouse of Hong Kong.

title: Taipei’s dilemma over history deepens with Xi-Trump praise of WWII Flying Tigers
description: Taiwan’s ruling party uneasy that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the US has ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties.
content: Taipei’s dilemma over its history during World War II appeared to deepen as Beijing and Washington looked to the Flying Tigers as a source of connection and goodwill during last month’s Xi–Trump summit. US President Donald Trump’s description of China as an American ally during the war has raised concerns in Taiwan that what could have been a valuable historical connection with the United States ended up benefiting Beijing’s ties with Washington. The dilemma resurfaced after Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping repeatedly invoked wartime Sino-US cooperation during Xi’s visit to Washington last week. Trump described China and the US as World War II allies and praised the Flying Tigers – a unit of American military personnel who helped defend mainland China against Japanese air attacks – while Xi recalled the two countries fighting “side by side” against Japanese militarism. A White House fact sheet later said the two leaders recalled that the US and China “were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war”. The episode has put Taiwan’s independence-leaning ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an awkward position. Some argue that the island’s long-running efforts to emphasise a distinct Taiwanese identity over the pre-1949 history of the Republic of China (ROC) – Taiwan’s official name – have inadvertently created space for Beijing to claim that legacy. When China fought Japan alongside the Allies, it was represented by the ROC government, which was overthrown in 1949 on the mainland when Communist forces won the civil war and established the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Taipei objected to the wartime reference during the Xi-Trump summit, with Deputy Foreign Minister Wu Chih-chung accusing Beijing of trying to replace the ROC’s wartime role and describing the effort as part of Beijing’s “narrative diplomacy”. The dispute has in fact exposed a dilemma for the DPP, which is now invoking the ROC’s wartime legacy internationally after years of seeking to distinguish Taiwan’s history and identity from that of mainland China. Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang, which ruled the ROC during the war, accused the William Lai Ching-te administration of invoking the pre-1949 republic only when politically useful. The KMT government retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, and the island retains ROC as its formal name. KMT communications director Chen I-hsin said Lai had emphasised the “end of the second world war” – a term Japan uses for its defeat – during last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations rather than “victory in the war of resistance against Japan”. Chen accused the DPP of deliberately distancing itself from the ROC’s mainland-era history. However, Chuang Jui-hsiung, the DPP’s legislative caucus chief executive, said the “China” that fought alongside the US was indeed the ROC and that “diplomatic language between major powers is often deliberately vague and should not be overinterpreted”. The controversy has nevertheless highlighted a broader contest between Taipei and Beijing over who inherits the international historical identity of wartime China. According to Wang Hsin-hsien, director of the National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Relations in Taipei, while Beijing has long maintained this wartime narrative, what sets this instance apart is that the American account also referred simply to “China” in the context of World War II. “Trump wants something in the short term, while Xi wants a long-term discourse and narrative,” Wang said. Washington appeared interested in invoking wartime cooperation to help stabilise Sino-US relations, he added, and Beijing was pursuing a broader historical argument involving the second world war, Taiwan and the post-war international order. Together with Beijing’s commemorations of what it has called Taiwan’s “restoration” to China following Japan’s surrender in 1945, such arguments were gradually forming a “legal chain”, Wang continued. If Washington increasingly accepted the same historical framework, the ROC’s role could be “taken away wholesale”, he said. Yen Chen-sheng, a researcher at the same institute, added that the DPP’s distancing Taiwan from ROC history risked abandoning a valuable historical connection with the US. That relationship stretched from wartime cooperation and the ROC’s status as a founding member of the United Nations to close political and security ties between Taipei and Washington after the Chinese civil war, Yen said. The ROC was a founding member of the UN before the global body voted in 1971 to recognise the PRC as the only lawful representative of China at the United Nations. The debate has also spread online, where critics have accused the DPP of protesting against Beijing’s “erasure” of the ROC while playing down the same name itself. “On the one hand, they’re quietly pushing Taiwan independence and de-Sinicisation,” one critic said. “On the other, they pretend to be deeply upset and aggrieved. It’s really ugly.” Beijing has rejected Taipei’s objections. Its Taiwan Affairs Office said victory in the war belonged to the entire Chinese nation while acknowledging that Communist and Nationalist or KMT forces fought on different battlefronts. It also said the establishment of the PRC in 1949 represented a change of government rather than a change in China’s international legal identity, underpinning Beijing’s status as the inheritor of the historical role of the wartime Chinese state. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The historical dispute could become more consequential if Washington increasingly adopted the same terminology, analysts said. Wang said repeated American references simply to “China” – without distinguishing the wartime ROC from today’s PRC – could gradually strengthen Beijing’s ability to define that history internationally. “At least on the issue of the second world war, we really need to be careful.”

title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits, pledges aid
description: Merz and Zelensky were due to meet as Germany and Ukraine neared a deal for a new package of military support worth more than US$1 billion.
content: Russia struck a bridge in Kyiv on Sunday soon after Germany’s chancellor arrived in Ukraine’s capital on a surprise visit to demonstrate European support in the face of an upsurge in attacks. Air raid sirens blared across Kyiv, urging residents to shelter soon after Friedrich Merz arrived under tight security, with warnings of approaching Russian attack drones. Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko then confirmed that a strike had damaged the road surface on the Northern Bridge – one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of the city over the Dnipro River which have been struck in recent days. Images posted on messaging channels appeared to show a missile slamming into the structure, sending a fireball into the air. Klitschko has said that Kyiv – largely spared from the devastation wrought near the front lines in nearly five years of conflict – should now be on a war footing due to the upsurge in attacks. A spate of round-the-clock attacks has hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure. Merz said the country “needs all our support in the coming weeks.” “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he added. President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged Ukraine’s Western allies for more military support, including advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia’s new fast-moving jet-powered drones. Merz and Zelensky were due to meet, and government sources in Berlin said they were expected to agree a new package of military support worth more than US$1 billion. It includes combat drones and satellite technology to help Ukraine hit Russian launch sites, as well as for the joint production of anti-jet drones, the German sources said. “This support addresses the most significant current gap in Ukraine’s air defence system. The impact is expected to be rapid and tangible,” a source said. Military support Merz this week called for unity against Russia within Nato and the European Union as well as his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise. There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia’s crosshairs, including from covert attacks, if it is not stopped in Ukraine. On Saturday, Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying “massive” new air strikes would hit the city. The Russian foreign ministry declared in a statement that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning.” Moscow had issued a similar warning in May, but leaders from countries supporting Ukraine have defied the Russian warnings and continued to make visits. “The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!” EU ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on social media on Sunday. Mathernova said separately that “nobody is moving,” although European embassies always had contingency plans, including for winter, she added. Russia has admitted deliberately targeting Ukraine’s energy sector as winter approaches. Last year, similar attacks knocked out power and heating for days on end as temperatures plummeted to -20 Celsius. In Kyiv, which is home to some three million people, residents have begun mulling what to do if that happens again. The government has also suggested that the vulnerable and disabled should consider leaving. Merz’s trip was expected to announce some 350 million euros to help provide generators, transformer stations and grid repairs, German government sources said.

title: Russian exporters fight to win back Chinese buyers amid fallout over fake goods
description: Products falsely marketed as Russian are undercutting sales for legitimate exporters from the country, people in the industry say.
content: At a two-day trade exhibition in Hong Kong earlier this week, Vera Nikitina, a representative of Russian confectionery producer Belyov Pastila Manufacture, was looking for new buyers – while also trying to reassure them that the company’s products were genuinely made in Russia. The company made its first attempt to enter China in 2019, before beginning regular shipments and establishing a local office in 2022-23. Its sales grew in 2024 amid booming Chinese demand for Russian consumer goods. That year, Russian consumer goods became somewhat of a retail craze in China, as blue and white so-called Russian goods halls packed with chocolates, sausages, bread and bottles of vodka began popping up in shopping streets and malls across the country, often playing Russian music and displaying Cyrillic signs to draw in shoppers. The boom, however, did not last long. The company’s sales began to deteriorate the following year after Chinese media exposed how locally made products were being marketed as Russian imports, Nikitina said. “After Russian consumer goods became increasingly popular, many locally made products began appearing on the market under the guise of Russian imports,” she said. “This made Chinese consumers more sceptical of Russian products in general and ultimately hurt our business.” We were not the ones selling fake Russian products. But we are the ones paying the price Vera Nikitina, Belyov Pastila Manufacture The company has since opened accounts on Chinese social media platforms in an effort to reintroduce its brand and demonstrate the origin of its products. “We were not the ones selling fake Russian products,” Nikitina said. “But we are the ones paying the price.” The influx of Russian goods followed a broader realignment in trade, after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Western sanctions and the departure of many international brands from Russia. Trade between China and Russia subsequently expanded in both directions, with Chinese cars and other products filling gaps in the Russian market, and Russian food and consumer goods gained visibility in China. Bilateral trade reached a record US$244.8 billion in 2024. By the second half of that year, Douyin live streams and other online channels were promoting Russian products ranging from confectionery, sausages, honey and alcohol. Registrations of businesses associated with Russian goods rose by more than 20 per cent to 841 by the end of 2024, according to corporate database Qichacha. By early 2025, more than 3,500 such businesses were registered nationwide, although the figure covered related companies rather than shops alone. The boom soon attracted scrutiny. Media investigations and regulatory inspections beginning in late 2024 found that some stores were using Russian imagery to sell goods made in China or third countries, triggering a consumer backlash that also damaged confidence in genuine imports. Less than a year after such stores began spreading across Chinese cities, many were shutting their doors. Multiple outlets in Hangzhou had closed and others were holding clearance sales by July, according to a report by Sichuan Online last year. Evgeny Bazhov, the Russian Export Centre’s chief representative in China, acknowledged that the rapid expansion of loosely branded Russian goods stores had confused consumers and harmed legitimate exporters. “The Russian image was sometimes used as a marketing concept, while the actual origin of individual products was not always clear,” Bazhov said. “This inevitably creates confusion for consumers and can affect genuine Russian producers as well.” The centre was responding by working with verified exporters and importers, strengthening official Made in Russia sales channels and developing platforms through which consumers could check the origin of products, he said. But rebuilding trust would depend on transparent sourcing and reliable distribution rather than marketing alone, Bazhov added. “Simply being ‘Russian’ is no longer enough,” he said. “Made in Russia should become a quality and traceability proposition, not just a national image.” The confusion extended beyond questions about where products were made. Kiro, a representative of the Russian vodka brand Legend of Kremlin, said buyers at Chinese trade fairs frequently asked whether Russians normally drank vodka containing 60, 70 or even more than 80 per cent alcohol – far above the traditional 40 per cent strength of Russian vodka. “When I hear this, I have to explain that a so-called Russian spirit with such a high alcohol content is almost certainly a locally produced Chinese drink being presented as imported Russian vodka,” he said. Such products had not only distorted buyers’ understanding of Russian spirits, Kiro said, but also undermined trust in genuine imports. “It is indeed a significant reputational blow for authentic Russian products, which is why organisations like the Russian Export Centre are actively taking measures to combat the appearance of counterfeit Russian goods on Chinese store shelves.”

title: 66% of Hong Kong’s 8-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, experts warn
description: Association finds 67 per cent of six-year-olds have insufficient hyperopic reserve, urging parents to start eye checks at age three.
content: Two-thirds of Hong Kong’s eight-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, optometrists have predicted, citing a shrinking “hyperopic reserve” that normally helps delay nearsightedness. The Hong Kong Association of Private Practice Optometrists released the findings on Sunday from a screening of more than 3,500 pupils at eight primary schools conducted between November and May, urging parents to begin comprehensive eye checks when children turned three. The association found that 67 per cent of six-year-olds had less hyperopic reserve than the recommended standard of 0.75 dioptres (75 degrees), while 24 per cent were already short-sighted. Hyperopic reserve refers to the natural longsightedness children have at birth. It gradually diminishes as the eyes grow and acts as a protective buffer against shortsightedness. Children who exhaust this reserve too early face a higher risk of developing myopia. Citing mainland Chinese research suggesting 62 per cent of children with insufficient hyperopic reserve will become short-sighted within two years, the association projected that 66 per cent of the surveyed six-year-olds could be myopic by 2028. “If we do not intervene in time, more than 60 per cent of eight-year-olds could be short-sighted within two years, bringing high myopia and the heavy burden of related eye diseases,” said Queenie Yip Siu-lai, the association’s president and chairwoman of its task force on children’s eye health policy recommendations. “This is a crucial opportunity to safeguard the eyesight of Hong Kong’s children.” A cross-border study in June found the average hyperopic reserve of seven-year-olds in Hong Kong was 78 degrees – well below the European average of 144 degrees and Australia’s 132 degrees. Benny Tam Bing-tin, vice-chairman of the task force, said a child’s hyperopic reserve could be affected by factors including home size and time spent outdoors. “Hyperopic reserve is something children are born with and cannot be restored, just as myopia cannot be reversed,” Tam said. “The key is to identify children with insufficient reserve early and intervene in time.” The association urged parents to start regular comprehensive eye checks from age three to catch problems early. It also advised families to spend more time outdoors, limit screen time, maintain proper reading distance and posture, and ensure children get enough rest. It called on the government to establish policies to manage children’s short-sightedness and enhance public education. A separate survey in September, involving 67 association members, found nearly 80 per cent of parents did not have their children’s eyes checked until vision problems arose or screenings failed – suggesting low awareness of the issue. Seven-year-old Owen failed an eye screening two years ago. His grandmother took him to an optometry clinic, where he was found to be 100 degrees short-sighted in his left eye and 850 degrees in his right. His condition worsened over the last summer holiday: 150 degrees in the left eye and 1,050 degrees in the right one. Owen’s grandmother recalled he already had uneven eyes in kindergarten and leaned to the left while writing, but she did not link it to vision problems at the time. After being prescribed myopia control glasses, his grandmother limited his screen time to one to two hours a day and enrolled him in more activities, including running, swimming and badminton. His short-sightedness has since stabilised.

title: Opinion | China’s hospital ships project a different kind of naval power in Africa
description: A surgery performed or a child delivered safely aboard a PLA medical vessel can leave memories long after the ship has departed.
content: When the Auspicious Ark entered Dakar, Senegal, on September 25, the scene looked closer to a public health mission than a naval deployment. Senegalese people and members of the Chinese community were waiting at the port as the vessel arrived for the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to Senegal. The Auspicious Ark is a PLA Navy vessel. That places the visit within a wider Chinese maritime presence in Africa, something more often associated with anti-piracy patrols, port calls, training missions and questions over overseas access. Now, it reaches people through consultations, surgeries and exchanges with local medical staff, giving China’s naval presence a quieter and more personal form. The contrast was already visible in Mauritania, the ship’s previous stop. During its seven-day stay in Nouakchott, a woman with a high-risk pregnancy sought help and gave birth aboard the vessel. That evening, the ophthalmology team completed its first cataract operation of the visit. The ship handled more than 1,600 patient visits in a single day. The Auspicious Ark brings a welcome capability into port: a functioning medical system that can begin treating people within hours of arrival. The ship, on its first overseas mission, has 18 clinical departments, eight operating rooms and a medical team of more than 100 people. It can carry out more than 60 types of examinations and procedures, while a shipborne helicopter extends its emergency rescue range. Such missions have become a regular part of China’s naval diplomacy. It began in 2010 with the Peace Ark. That ship carried out the first 10 deployments, while the Silk Road Ark took over the 11th mission. The Auspicious Ark is now undertaking the 12th – a mission expected to last more than 200 days. Repeated visits give the programme much of its weight. Since its first overseas deployment, the Peace Ark has called at 49 countries and regions and treated more than 370,000 people. In 2024 alone, it spent 215 days at sea, saw 82,980 patients and carried out 1,392 operations across Asia and Africa, giving these missions a familiarity that a single port visit could never create. The Auspicious Ark arrived on familiar ground. Chinese medical teams have worked in Senegal since 1975, with more than 300 professionals treating an estimated 3.5 million patients, according to Senegal’s health ministry. In Senegal, the current programme includes hospital exchanges and community activities alongside treatment aboard the ship. Medical cooperation carries less political baggage than a basing arrangement or a major arms deal, yet it still brings Chinese personnel into regular contact with officials, hospitals and local communities. For Dakar, the appeal is straightforward: useful medical support on terms it can shape. For Beijing, the visits deepen ties with officials and institutions. China’s maritime role in West Africa has expanded through other channels. Chinese warships have made port calls around the Gulf of Guinea, held joint drills and supported training for regional countries. Beijing has hosted maritime security officials from 18 Gulf of Guinea countries as piracy, oil routes and the safety of commercial shipping have pushed naval cooperation higher on the agenda. Security cooperation around the Gulf of Guinea usually reaches the public indirectly, through training programmes, port visits or agreements between defence ministries. For a patient treated for cataracts or a doctor working with visiting specialists, the Chinese naval presence is experienced through a service with clear personal value. The visits are brief, and national health systems still face shortages of staff, equipment and financing once the ship leaves, yet the programme has become a recurring part of Chinese naval activity overseas. These vessels are military assets, built to support naval operations and provide medical care during emergencies or conflict. Crews learn how to operate across distant seas, while visits to African ports depend on coordination with local authorities. China has spent years building the reach that makes such missions possible. Its Gulf of Aden escort programme has run since 2008, giving PLA Navy crews long experience away from home waters, while China’s military base in Djibouti provides a permanent foothold near one of the world’s busiest sea lanes. Hospital ships depend on that logistical depth. Months-long deployments require replenishment, crew rotation, maintenance and experience in distant waters, turning medical diplomacy into something a navy must first have the capacity to sustain. In West Africa, maritime exercises and security cooperation often remain distant from ordinary life. While the political effect of a hospital ship visit is difficult to measure, a consultation, an operation or a child delivered safely aboard a Chinese naval vessel can leave a memory long after the ship has sailed. The Auspicious Ark will eventually leave Dakar and continue its mission. But chances are, some of its reach will remain in places no chart can mark.

title: Hong Kong’s Asian Games medal haul gives reason to be cheerful but reckoning awaits for some
description: Sailing and windsurfing certainly provide reasons for optimism, but only some members of Hong Kong Sports Institute are succeeding.
content: When Cado Lee Ka-to carried Hong Kong’s flag into the Paloma Mizuho Stadium on Sunday, he did so at the head of what remained of the most successful Asian Games delegation in the city’s history. While only a handful of the 580 athletes who made up the team attended the closing ceremony, their impact will be felt far beyond the past fortnight, although it may be in what wasn’t achieved that a lasting legacy is created. At first glance, an overall medal count of 54, only one more than the previous best of 53 in Hangzhou, might not necessarily warrant the jubilation that has been flowing through the Hong Kong camp in recent days. But as with any number, it only tells part of the story. Within that lies a record 11 golds, three more than in 2023, and in Guangzhou in 2010 and Jakarta eight years later. The 16 silvers have become 19, and bronze is down from 29 to 24, which earned the recipients a collective HK$37.5 million from the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s athlete incentive fund, showed what chef de mission Wong Po-kee said was “the continued emergence of sporting talent in Hong Kong”. Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges, the club’s CEO, passed on its “sincere congratulations to every medallist on their success” and said the city’s athletes had “truly inspired us all”. “Once again the Hong Kong delegation showed our city’s can-do spirit with an outstanding display of skill, resilience and true sportsmanship,” he added. “We are proud to recognise the delegation’s achievements at the 20th Asian Games.” Sailing and windsurfing certainly provided reasons for optimism. Water sports were responsible for four of the golds collected in Japan, and the relative youth of the likes of Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet, boys’ and girls’ champions in the latter discipline, were a bright counterpoint to some of the disappointments of the Games. The chef de mission’s words echoed those of city leader John Lee Ka-chiu, who in a lengthy social media post on Sunday hailed the example set by those athletes who had shown “everyone through their achievements: as long as you work hard and have dreams, you can break through your limits and achieve great results”. “Regardless of the final results, the athletes’ achievements are a testament to their long-term hard work and their unwavering determination on the field,” Lee wrote, before thanking the squad for “showing us that Hong Kong can cultivate so many outstanding athletes who can compete and win against top Asian athletes on the international stage”. What was missing, however, was an acknowledgement that only some members of the Hong Kong Sports Institute are delivering on that promise. Entering a competition and being good enough to be there are not the same thing. Among this year’s Mongolian delegation was 42-year-old golfer Anarbat Jargalsaikhan, his country’s men’s national amateur champion. At the end of the first round on Wednesday, Jargalsaikhan was dead last on 26-over-par, some 31 shots behind early leader Wong Wai-hsuan of Chinese Taipei. The pair may have occupied the same Kasugai Country Club East Course, but they were not playing the same game. In Hong Kong the disparity is reflected in results. Rugby and fencing occupy one end of the spectrum as the gold standard by which the rest should be judged, at the other end sit the likes of athletics. And even fencing will be asking questions of itself, given it returned fewer medals this time and has been unable to settle on adequate replacements for Olympic gold medallists Cheung Ka-long and Vivian Kong Man-wai. Still, when meeting the press on Sunday in Nagoya to discuss his views on the past fortnight, Wong, who is also the honorary deputy secretary general of the Sports Federation and Olympic Committee, repeated a common talking point from officials involved in the city’s sporting success. “Before we left Hong Kong for these Games, we said that while everyone in competitive sports focuses on the medal count, medals are not the ultimate goal for a sports association or an athlete in any single event,” he said. “We will not use the medal count as a rigid KPI to demand anything from our athletes.” In many ways that is a sensible approach. While Siobhan Haughey, who was again solely responsible for the gold medals swimming contributed to the cause, was ensuring her place as the city’s greatest ever athlete, the next generation were showing some signs of life. Teenagers Yeung Hoi-ching and Gilaine Ma might not have won individual medals, but reaching finals gave hope for the next Games in Doha, by which time their more illustrious teammate will most definitely have retired. And yet, elsewhere, there must now be balancing of the books. Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said as much on Saturday after Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s men’s singles gold. Tennis had previously been given special dispensation to retain its Tier A status because there existed evidence that the government’s “long-term investment” would ultimately pay off. With no medals and no hope of winning one, athletics is among those sports in danger of losing funding, and special measures in its case might be the saving of the sport in the city, especially if it forces changes at the Hong Kong, China Association of Athletics Affiliates. Lee’s social media post dealt heavily with the “billions of dollars invested annually” to train the city’s elite athletes, adding that he was pleased “to see that the government’s investment is beginning to bear fruit”. Coleman Wong has certainly done that, although his road to the top involved leaving his hometown early and challenging himself outside the Hong Kong bubble. “If you keep playing only inside Hong Kong or Asian competitions where you can’t play against these world-class players, it’s actually very difficult,” he said. “It’s like a swimming pool – if you stay in Hong Kong and don’t venture out into the sea to swim, it’s impossible to compete, because the gap in strength is too big.” The philosophy is the same with the men’s sevens team, who Wong Po-kee called “a source of pride” after Saturday’s triumph. Captain James Christie said despite his side’s overwhelming dominance of their competition, it was “harder to stay at the top” than to get there in the first place. “The teams are always gunning out for you, so it’s huge [to win],” he said. “We’ve been preparing for this since the last one, three years ago. Onto the next, onto the fourth one [in Doha in 2030 or 2031].”

title: ‘Lucky dog’ Sylvester Stallone, 80, on fate, insecurity and his Rocky road to success
description: With a film career spanning 50 years, the star looks back on his life, from unwanted child to struggling actor to Hollywood success story.
content: Fifty years after Sylvester Stallone pulled off one of Hollywood’s all-time long shots with Rocky (1976), the star of the Oscar-winning film still identifies with the character who for many embodies the outsider proving all the naysayers wrong. But he no longer claims to be an underdog. “It would be so disingenuous to say you’re an underdog, ‘as he said from his penthouse’,” Stallone says, on a high floor of a luxury Manhattan hotel. “Yeah. Come on. I am a lucky dog.” Stallone, who turned 80 in July, is among the most successful film stars and filmmakers in history. He has generated billions of dollars through such blockbuster franchises as Rocky, Rambo and The Expendables and portrayed some of the most memorable film characters. And he is still working, starring as mobster Dwight “The General” Manfredi in the Paramount+ series Tulsa King. Stallone has been reliving his early years as a struggling actor-writer who somehow convinced United Artists to back his modest story of a journeyman boxer’s shot at the heavyweight championship, and even allow him to play the lead despite having little acting experience. His memoir The Steps was published on September 29 and a fictionalised and semi-authorised version of his story, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky, will arrive in cinemas in November, with Anthony Ippolito in the starring role. (Farrelly spoke about the film with Stallone, who was otherwise uninvolved.) Rocky, which beat Taxi Driver and All the President’s Men among others to win the best-picture Oscar in 1977, is one of those classic films that only seem to benefit from their backstory; Stallone’s own journey to the Oscars stage echoes his character’s improbable rise. As he writes in The Steps, he was a hard-luck case, an unplanned and unwanted child who seemed to face endless discouragement right through the production of Rocky, when he feared every day on the set might be his last. Stallone was in Manhattan to promote his book, but spends much of his time at the Palm Beach, Florida estate he shares with his wife, Jennifer Flavin, 58. Even when – especially when – he is talking about his rare fortune, Stallone speaks in a warm, rumbling, offhand manner, a kind of private street talk that suggests he doesn’t believe it all. In 2025, he was honoured at the Kennedy Centre in Washington. His award was presented by US President Donald Trump, who had previously named Stallone, Jon Voight and Mel Gibson his “ambassadors” from an otherwise liberal Hollywood. Stallone once called Trump “the second George Washington”, but he has contributed to both Republicans and Democrats and broken with conservatives by calling for stronger gun control laws. He also condemns war, including the Iran war, as a story of sending people into a “meat grinder while the military complex is making zillions of dollars”. “I do believe that you have to defend yourself. But to go on the offensive?” he says, adding that he would prefer not to be known as a “political figure”. “I love the common architecture of trying to just survive. That’s noble,” he says. “To be a politician, that’s a different animal.” Here the actor also talks about fate, insecurity and why he is probably better off for his unhappy childhood. Why write this book? “I was approached a few times [over the years] and the one thing I didn’t want to write about is my life. It’s this ambivalent roller-coaster ride. It’s not always the most pleasurable ride. And I thought, ‘What am I known for?’ Pulling off this minor miracle in 1976, which falls under the heading of inspiration. That’s what I want to do. Because the character was an inspiration, I wanted to tell the people how it all came to be.” Insecurity is a great motivator Sylvester Stallone How hard was it to relive some of those early memories? “It was very hard because I spent 50 years burying that stuff. And it’s like you come across a lost city, and you start to become your own spiritual archaeologist, digging down. And it’s not pretty. But I didn’t want this to be, ‘Oh, woe is me.’ Everyone has issues and a lot worse than me. I just wanted to touch on the essence because I still have this conundrum. “If everything was really nice, maybe I wouldn’t be here, you know what I mean? If I didn’t have that insecurity which drives us. You know, insecurity is a great motivator.” For people at your level of success, do you find they all have that sense of insecurity, that drive? “I think so – especially the ones that are desperate to do better and constantly pushing it. For example, I don’t have to do my dialogue for another month before we start Tulsa King. I’m up every morning at 5 o’clock, studying until literally it’s like breathing. Now, that’s probably insecurity, but that’s the way I approach it.” When was the last time you actually watched Rocky in its entirety? Did you look at it while working on the book? “No, I didn’t. You know what I see. You’re sitting there and going through messages and somebody who’s 18 has put it on the internet or on TikTok. And how would this person relate to an 80-year-old guy? They’re not, though. They’re not relating to me. It’s that character.” Young people know about Rocky. “In retrospect, that to me is the greatest gift. You know, you write something – I’m just trying to get some footage on myself. I’m just trying to write something really simple. I didn’t ever expect it to be in more than one or two theatres. So all this is a tsunami of good luck. It [Rocky] tapped into something that I cannot take credit for.” Now you have a movie about you, I Play Rocky, coming out. “How strange is this? A movie about me being in a movie.” What did you think of it? “It’s fantastic. And the kid [Ippolito] did a great job. This is so odd. They usually do this when you’re dead and gone. It’s 50 years almost to the day when it came out and if he gets nominated … It’s so surreal. “I have to give Peter Farrelly, the director [credit]. I never in a million years had any confidence this would work. But he said that to the everyday person, this is kind of a fantastic journey. Rocky is fiction, this is real. And that’s what people are holding on to.”

title: China lashes out at Xinjiang ‘lie’ after US lawmaker urges Starbucks to close new stores
description: Beijing rejects human rights abuse claims, saying region ‘enjoys social stability, economic prosperity, ethnic unity and religious harmony’.
content: Beijing has hit back at a US lawmaker’s criticism of coffee chain Starbucks for opening its first stores in Xinjiang, rejecting the allegation that China has committed human rights abuses against the far-western region’s mostly Muslim Uygur population. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Saturday said claims of “genocide” in Xinjiang were a “blatant lie” and accused the “US group” who raised the suggestions of attacking Beijing for political purposes. “Today’s Xinjiang enjoys social stability, economic prosperity, ethnic unity and religious harmony,” Guo said, adding that China would provide more opportunities for foreign businesses to invest and operate in the country. His remarks came after John Moolenaar, the Republican chairman of the US House Select Committee on China, urged Starbucks to close its newly opened outlets in Xinjiang. “This is a shocking and morally bankrupt decision by a company that prides itself on social responsibility,” Moolenaar said on Thursday. “There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the [Chinese Communist Party] has detained more than a million Uygurs and is stripping them of their faith, language and culture,” he said. Last week, Starbucks opened two stores in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang, marking the coffee chain’s entry into the region. One is located in the city’s Grand Bazaar tourist area and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport. The Grand Bazaar outlet – described by local authorities as Starbucks’ first intangible cultural heritage-themed flagship store in China – incorporates elements of Xinjiang architecture and culture and offers drinks and products “inspired by the region”. Starbucks is seeking to deepen its presence in China after finalising a joint venture in April with Chinese private-equity firm Boyu Capital, which holds a 60 per cent stake in the coffee giant’s China retail operations. The joint venture has said it aims to expand Starbucks’ China footprint significantly, with the company citing the country as a key growth market. The Xinjiang expansion has nevertheless put the US coffee chain in the middle of a long-running dispute between Washington and Beijing over alleged human rights abuses in the region. The United States has accused China of widespread abuses against Uygurs and other Muslim minorities, including forced labour. Beijing has repeatedly rejected the allegations, saying its policies in Xinjiang are aimed at combating terrorism, separatism and religious extremism. Washington has also sought to restrict imports linked to Xinjiang. The Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act, signed into law in 2021, aims to block imports from Xinjiang to prevent goods linked to alleged forced labour from entering the US market. In July, the US Department of Homeland Security expanded its Xinjiang-related entity list by 30 per cent to 187 companies, covering industries including food, cotton, pharmaceuticals, metals and lithium. Beijing then condemned the move as “economic coercion”. Starbucks did not immediately respond to a request for comment. As of the end of September, Starbucks had 8,342 stores in mainland China. The company opened its first mainland China store in Beijing in 1999.

title: 5 dead in 3 weeks: are Indonesia’s whale strandings on the rise?
description: Recent whale and whale shark deaths have raised concern in Indonesia, but experts cite ocean shifts, human activity and smartphone reporting.
content: A cluster of whale and whale shark strandings across Indonesia – five in the past three weeks alone – has raised questions over whether such incidents are becoming more frequent, with experts pointing to a mix of environmental shifts, human activity and improved reporting as possible explanations. On September 25, a whale shark became stranded and died on a beach in Aceh province, just days after a decomposed whale carcass was discovered in a mangrove in Riau province. Another whale was found dead in West Java on September 21, just two days after a whale shark stranded and died in South Sulawesi. The latest incidents began on September 12, when a dead whale shark washed ashore in Bali. The recent deaths reflect a longer-term rise in reported whale shark strandings across the archipelago. A 2025 study by the Elasmobranch Institute Indonesia and Konservasi Indonesia recorded fewer than 10 whale shark strandings per year from 2011 to 2019. From 2020 onwards, however, that average jumped to more than 22 cases a year. Published in Scientific Reports, the study linked strandings to seasonal and oceanographic conditions – including sea-surface temperatures, wave height and marine productivity – particularly in areas affected by seasonal upwelling, an oceanic process where wind-driven currents pull cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the surface, drawing feeding marine life closer to coastlines. But researchers have said that increased smartphone use and social media reporting could account for much of the apparent rise. While whales are marine mammals and whale sharks are the world’s largest fish, both species are endangered, making the circumstances behind their deaths a pressing conservation concern. Still, scientists say it is too early to determine whether the five recent incidents are directly linked. Speaking about the Aceh incident, Miftach Tjut Ade, a traditional fishing community chief who oversees maritime issues across the province, said it was rare to come across a stranded whale shark. “It seemed to be accidental and local residents tried everything they could to push it back to sea,” he said. “But it was too heavy.” Mark Meekan, an adjunct senior research fellow at the University of Western Australia’s Oceans Institute, said strandings had been recorded for centuries and there were many theories about why they occurred. “In the past, a stranding on a remote Indonesian island would not have made the press. But these days, everyone has a smartphone connected to the internet and social media, so [they] can alert a much wider audience.” What causes strandings? The causes of individual strandings can be difficult to establish, particularly when carcasses are found in advanced stages of decomposition. Regarding the whale found in Riau’s mangroves, Ahlul Fadli, an advocacy and campaign manager at the Indonesian Forum for the Environment in Riau, described it as “a rare discovery”, but said the decomposition had hindered efforts to identify it. Official test results from the National Research and Innovation Agency in Jakarta were still pending. Ahlul warned against speculation without solid data, but highlighted key threats from human activity. He said disturbances to ocean activity, including seismic operations, military sonar and high-intensity noise from shipping, could disorient whales, while marine pollution was another possible factor. “It is possible the animal ingested solid waste, such as plastic, which obstructed its digestive system, triggering health complications or death,” Ahlul said. Meekan said navigational errors involving echolocation, geomagnetic anomalies and social behaviour could also cause individual whales or entire pods to beach themselves. For whale sharks – which are solitary, slow-moving filter feeders that spend much of their time near the surface – colliding with ships and pollution are the primary human-driven hazards. Brad Norman, a research fellow at Perth’s Murdoch University and whale shark scientist, warned against drawing conclusions without a full review of the cases. He also said it was “very hard to be sure” whether strandings globally were on the rise and that it was “too early to say” whether seasonal and oceanic patterns might be factors. “It is important that we collate strandings from across the globe and analyse these for trends and potential threats,” he said. “We need to study this further, then maybe we will have a better understanding.” Iqbal Herwata, a focal species conservation senior manager at Konservasi Indonesia, said that while the five recent incidents occurred in areas with a history of strandings, the timing differed from historical patterns. “The influence of climate variability, including El Nino, requires further study – specifically by analysing data on sea temperatures, currents and marine productivity,” Iqbal said. Strengthening the response With the causes of many strandings still uncertain, preventing them is difficult. Meekan said understanding the cause of each incident was important, but some factors were easier to address than others. “For individual strandings where the cause is man-made, such as entanglement in fishing gear or pollution, the solution to the problem is in our hands,” Meekan said. In Indonesia, Konservasi Indonesia is working with marine conservation organisation SeaLife to strengthen the response to strandings along Java’s southern coast – a known hotspot for whale shark incidents. “These efforts aim to ensure local teams and stakeholders possess the capacity to respond to incidents, handle live whale sharks and conduct necropsies on deceased animals,” Iqbal said. “This is expected to improve rescue success rates while providing the scientific evidence needed to determine appropriate preventive measures.”

title: More Hong Kong homes sell at a loss despite signs prices have bottomed: agents
description: There were at least 100 loss-making transactions for secondary homes in September despite prices edging higher, agents say.
content: Despite signs that Hong Kong property prices could have bottomed out and begun rebounding in August, market sources said at least 100 secondary residential homes were sold at a loss in September, up from at least 81 the previous month. Hong Kong’s property market dodged an immediate setback from the US Federal Reserve’s rate increase in September, and agents estimated that home prices could end the year 15 per cent higher than a year earlier. The positive trend, however, did not generally apply to the secondary home market, agents added. Loss-making secondary-home transactions last month were recorded across Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories, spanning both the luxury and mass-market segments. The losses ranged from more than 10 per cent to as much as 30 per cent, according to sources. Sai Kung, long regarded as Hong Kong’s traditional enclave for luxury homes, continued a years-long trend of secondary-home transactions completed at a loss, sources said, adding it had extended to high-value, low-density developments including Mount Pavilia, The Mediterranean, Hebe Villa and Casa Bella. Frankie Liu, sales director at Century 21 Goodwin Property, said many homeowners who sold at a loss in recent years did so because they were emigrating or downsizing, leaving them with little choice but to accept lower prices. Last week, a 695-square-foot high-floor flat at The Mediterranean changed hands for HK$8.38 million (US$1 million). The owner bought the property directly from the developer for HK$12.36 million in April 2019. The transaction generated a paper loss of HK$3.98 million, representing a decline of about 32 per cent. In late September, a detached house at Hebe Villa, with a saleable area of 1,870 square feet and a 1,510-square-foot garden, sold for HK$21 million after a HK$4 million price cut. The owner bought the property for HK$25.88 million in September 2009, resulting in a loss of HK$4.88 million, or about 19 per cent. Sai Kung has traditionally been popular among expatriate residents. But Liu said US-China tensions and the political turmoil in Hong Kong in recent years had prompted many expatriates to leave the city and sell their homes. “This year, however, there has been a resurgence in property purchases by expatriates in Sai Kung,” Liu said. “Although the proportion of foreign buyers has not yet returned to pre-2019 levels, it has rebounded from the low of around 10 per cent seen between 2020 and 2021 to more than 20 per cent today.” The latest data from the Rating and Valuation Department showed that Hong Kong’s private residential property price index edged up 0.2 points month on month to 320.5 points in August after a one-month decline in July. The picture remains mixed in the mass-market segment. In Tuen Mun – a hub for mass-market housing – at least 13 secondary-home transactions were completed at a loss in September. Last week, a mid-floor flat measuring 428 square feet at Beneville changed hands for HK$4.6 million, after a HK$250,000 price reduction, resulting in a loss of HK$980,000, or 17.6 per cent, for the owner after a three-year holding period. A flat at Le Pont with a saleable area of 737 square feet and a 775-square-foot garden changed hands for HK$8.58 million in September. The owner incurred a loss of HK$3.37 million, or 28 per cent, after holding the property for eight years. Kit Lam, senior associate director at Ricacorp Properties, said owners were willing to sell at a loss mainly because they remained uncertain about the market outlook. However, because most homeowners in Tuen Mun owned only one property for self-occupation, they were “generally” reluctant to sell at a loss, Lam added. “This has resulted in a market stalemate and a drop in secondary-home transaction volumes from more than 100 deals in May and June to about 70 last month,” Lam said. “Properties whose owners are genuinely willing to sell at a loss account for about 15 per cent of all listings.” Loss-making transactions had also spread to subsidised homes, agents said. Wing Lee, an agent at Full Mark Property, said a low-floor 434-square-foot flat at King Shan Court in Ngau Chi Wan changed hands last week for HK$3.1 million on the open market after a HK$600,000 price reduction. The owner incurred a loss of HK$230,000 after holding the property for two years. Louis Chan, vice-chairman and CEO (residential) for the Asia-Pacific region at Centaline Property, said homes bought near the market peak in the first half of 2021 would almost certainly be sold at a loss today, as current prices remained nearly 20 per cent below those levels. “I believe the property market is currently in a consolidation phase,” Chan said. “I predict that for the remainder of the year, prices will rise by 3 to 5 per cent, and the number of residential properties sold at a loss will gradually decrease.” Lam of Ricacorp Properties said there was little evidence that losses were “deepening” across the market because relatively few owners were rushing to exit the market despite a range of personal and financial pressures.

title: Flight to Okinawa diverts back to Hong Kong after suspected landing gear fault
description: The flight encountered a suspected incomplete landing gear retraction issue after take-off, Hong Kong Airlines says.
content: A flight bound for Okinawa returned to Hong Kong airport on Sunday morning after its landing gear was suspected to have failed to fully retract after take-off. Hong Kong Airlines said the crew of flight HX676, which departed at 8.57am, decided to return to ensure safety, in line with standard procedures. “[The flight] encountered a suspected incomplete landing gear retraction issue after take-off,” the airline said. The aircraft landed safely at 10am, with no injuries reported on board. The airline immediately arranged an alternative flight for the 160 affected passengers, delaying their trip by about 2½ hours. According to the carrier’s website, the replacement flight departed at 12.07pm. The aircraft is undergoing a comprehensive inspection. The airline said it had reported the incident to the relevant authorities and would fully cooperate with any subsequent investigation. “Flight safety is always Hong Kong Airlines’ foremost priority,” it said. “We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused to our passengers and thank them for their understanding and cooperation.” The Airport Authority said the flight had requested to return to the airport and that airport crews were placed on standby.

title: Hong Kong’s IPO haul more than doubles to HK$388b in first 9 months: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief says amount raised has surpassed whole of 2025, while HKIC’s CEO says over 30 portfolio firms preparing to apply for listings this year.
content: Funds raised through initial public offerings in Hong Kong more than doubled year on year to over HK$388 billion (US$49.4 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, already surpassing the total amount for the whole of last year, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po has said. Adding to the positive outlook, Clara Chan Ka-chai, CEO of the government-owned Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), noted on Sunday that more than 30 of its portfolio firms were preparing to apply for Hong Kong listings this year. Paul Chan also revealed in his weekly blog that the average daily turnover on Hong Kong’s stock market from January to September stood at HK$272.9 billion, representing 6.4 per cent year-on-year growth. “The yields of long-term US bonds have risen to a 24-year high, which has heightened investor concerns over global economic prospects and inevitably dampened recent sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market,” he said. “Nevertheless, short-term market volatility will not derail the broader trend of global asset allocation and supply chain restructuring.” He cited Middle Eastern interest in the Hong Kong market, saying capital from the region in the city’s new listings had increased significantly, with portfolios extending from property to technology, logistics and capital markets. “[Middle Eastern] business sectors are actively exploring investments in warehousing and logistics. With its extensive expertise in this area, Hong Kong stands out as one of their preferred partners for prospective collaboration.” Separately, the HKIC’s Clara Chan told a radio show that 11 out of its more than 200 portfolio companies had listed in Hong Kong, while over 30 would apply for initial public offerings (IPOs) this year. Established in 2022 to manage HK$62 billion in government funds, the HKIC is tasked with both achieving reasonable investment returns and fuelling the growth of companies of strategic importance. In 2025, the corporation recorded HK$6.46 billion in investment income, up 175 per cent year on year. It represented a net internal rate of return, or IRR, of 14 per cent. The HKIC had been criticised for lack of transparency in its financial statements, as it did not offer a breakdown of the sources of its investment income. Chan, whose term as CEO was extended for three years on Friday, said that the figure was composed of equity and credits, both realised and unrealised. “Beyond simple figures, what is more important is … whether our portfolio companies can achieve technological breakthroughs and bring momentum to Hong Kong’s long-term development in particular fields,” she said. “For us, the socioeconomic benefit in the long run is more important than the financial return.” The corporation’s annual report also outlines plans to launch a venture capital fund denominated in offshore yuan, as Hong Kong pushes to expand the use of the Chinese currency and consolidate its status as a global offshore yuan hub. Chan expressed confidence in the project, saying that the corporation had played a vital role in guiding market funds to targeted areas, as every Hong Kong dollar it committed could leverage HK$8 of investment from the private sector. She also revealed that the corporation would announce the formal launch of its internship programme in the coming week as part of its talent initiatives. According to her, the placement programme would be divided into summer and winter cohorts each year, with each batch hiring about 10 students. She added that students at local universities would be prioritised. “We acknowledge that young people play a significant part in innovation and technology, as well as Hong Kong’s development,” she told a radio show. “We hope that young people can take part in the growth of the HKIC, and meanwhile, we hope to understand the world more rapidly and accurately through the lens of them.” In his blog, Paul Chan also touched on the robust performance of the city’s tourism sector during mainland China’s National Day “golden week” break. The seven-day golden week holiday runs from October 1 to 7. The city has welcomed more than 1 million mainland visitors in the first four days of the break, representing growth of about 4.1 per cent year on year. “In fact, other than mainland visitors, we also saw considerable growth in the number of tourists from Europe, America and emerging markets,” he said.

title: Japan’s Takaichi presses US after marine arrested over murder-robbery of woman
description: Davin Ballard is accused of killing Anna Yagi and taking her wallet and backpack at a hotel in Okinawa.
content: A 20-year-old US marine was arrested on Sunday in Japan’s Okinawa prefecture on suspicion of robbing and murdering a local woman, police said. Davin Ballard stationed at the Futenma Airbase is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, and taking her wallet and backpack in the early hours of Saturday at a hotel in Naha, according to the Okinawa prefectural police. The suspect has denied the charges, they added. Ballard was seen entering the hotel with Yagi, who was found dead on Saturday morning, police said, adding that she died from suffocation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a social media post that it is “extremely regrettable” that such a heinous crime occurred and that her government has asked for full US cooperation in the investigation and the strengthening of military discipline. “The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation with the investigation,” as well as ⁠the tightening of discipline and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence, she said. Defence Minister Shinjiro ‌Koizumi said: “Such an incident is unacceptable and I am deeply outraged.” Japanese Vice-Foreign Minister Takehiro Funakoshi lodged a protest on Sunday morning with US Ambassador George Glass against the marine’s alleged involvement in the case, the foreign ministry said. In their telephone conversation, Glass told Funakoshi that the US side would fully cooperate with the investigation and take all measures it can to prevent a recurrence, the ministry said. Glass wrote in a post on social media that he had called Okinawa Governor Genta Koja, “offering our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues”. The US embassy in Tokyo also said on social media, “We extend our sincere condolences to the victim’s family.” “As an investigation is under way to determine the facts of the case, the United States is communicating and cooperating with the Government of Japan and local authorities,” it said. The US Marine Corps said in a statement it was “actively cooperating with Japanese authorities in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a marine”. A police officer questioned and detained the suspect when he was walking alone on a street in Naha’s entertainment district late on Saturday. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based marines are stationed ‌in Okinawa, which the US held from the end of second world war until 1972. Their ⁠presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and ⁠the conduct of personnel. Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison. In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. In the same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after a drunken US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver. The 1995 rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen sparked mass protests. Additional reporting by Reuters, Agence France-Presse

title: Freshwater crayfish raised in Xinjiang desert nip away at China’s food security fears
description: Government encouraging saline-alkaline aquaculture and inland fisheries to diversify food supplies and put abandoned land to use.
content: On the edge of western China’s Taklamakan Desert, in a county where sand covers 90 per cent of the land, an unlikely harvest is heading to market: Australian freshwater crayfish. As China begins its National Day “golden week” holiday, a farm in Maigaiti county, in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region’s Kashgar prefecture, is pulling 250 to 300kg (551 to 661lbs) of the premium crustaceans from its ponds every day. Native to Australia’s rivers and streams, freshwater crayfish are now being raised in one of the most remote and arid corners of China. The project is part of a broader government push to develop saline-alkaline aquaculture and inland fisheries, diversify food supplies and put abandoned land and water to use. As a result, aquatic foods once rare in southwestern Xinjiang are increasingly appearing on local dinner tables. Wu Zhijun, who co-runs the farm with his brother, said it was his fourth year trying to breed freshwater crayfish under the “East Crayfish Move West” technology-transfer programme, which had brought know-how from Rizhao, a modern marine aquaculture hub in eastern China’s Shandong province. “At first, a local official assigned to support Xinjiang noticed a lot of abandoned saline-alkaline pits and ran an experiment to see if they could be used,” he said. “Once they managed to keep the crayfish alive, we started learning how to do it.” The introduction of recirculating aquaculture systems, greenhouses and techniques for regulating saline-alkaline water has made it possible to raise shrimp and fish in parts of arid Xinjiang where it had once been considered impractical. Wu was among the earliest participants. This year, he stocked his ponds with 400,000 crayfish fry and said he expected output to approach 8 tonnes (8.8 short tons). Wu said most were sold in Kashgar prefecture, with a small amount shipped to major cities elsewhere in China, including Zhengzhou and Shanghai. “Health-conscious, upmarket consumers would pay more for my products than for crayfish from other parts of China, as Xinjiang has little industry and relatively clean water, giving the crayfish a healthier environment,” he said. But farming was made more difficult by wide day-night temperature swings, slightly alkaline water and long, costly logistics – with the shipment of feed to his farm costing an extra 1,000 to 2,000 yuan a tonne (US$135 to US$271 a short ton). Known for its cotton, Xinjiang has frequently made headlines in state-controlled media in recent years for turning idle saline-alkaline land and water resources into niche aquaculture facilities, farming species ranging from red swamp crayfish and Chinese mitten crabs to trout and silver cod. The aquaculture area across Kashgar prefecture now spans 1,733 hectares (4,283 acres), with total aquatic product output of 13,600 tonnes, valued at 208 million yuan (US$31 million), the prefecture government’s publicity department said in a report last month. Relative to its population of 1.4 billion, China is short on arable land and water resources – a continuing source of insecurity amid intensifying global geopolitical risks. In response, Beijing has been promoting the development of previously abandoned land and water resources in recent years as one means of ensuring self-sufficiency. The agricultural goals outlined in the nation’s latest five-year plan, released earlier this year, proposed “steadily advancing the comprehensive utilisation of saline-alkaline land” and said China would “develop aquaculture on saline-alkaline land in suitable areas in the west”. Xinjiang accounts for one-third of China’s saline-alkaline land, according to Zhang Jiasong, a researcher from the Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences’ South China Sea fisheries research institute. By conducting aquaculture in the region, the soil’s salt and alkali content could be biologically absorbed, making the land available for future agricultural and livestock use, he told state broadcaster China Central Television last month. Doing so allowed China to “maintain land-based aquaculture ponds in the east, while turning barren saline-alkaline land into production bases for high-quality protein”, Zhang said. When its aquaculture industry grew big enough, Xinjiang, sitting on the eastern edge of Central Asia, could not only supply other parts of China but also see its products reach landlocked countries along the China-Europe Railway, he said. But Wu, the crayfish farmer, said that while the sector had attracted widespread attention by exploiting its geographic niche, it had also been affected by China’s weak consumer sentiment over the past couple of years. When the first large batch of crayfish was harvested in 2023, 2 tonnes sold out over the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, he said. Sales the next two years were not as brisk, he said, adding that “this year demand is even weaker than last year, because the whole industry is doing poorly and consumption is sluggish”.

title: How to safely interact with dogs and what to do if someone gets bitten
description: Hong Kong veterinarian Dr Angel Ngo offers tips for protecting you and your pet from unknown or aggressive dogs.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
In the wake of recent deadly dog attacks, Hong Kong officials have intensified checks on dog owners across the city. The clampdown has put many pet owners on high alert.
Dr Angel Ngo, a vet with her own clinic in Hong Kong, explains Hong Kong’s rules and how owners can best protect their pets.
Under Hong Kong law, breeds such as pit bull terriers, Dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa, Fila Brasileiro and their crossbreeds are classified as “fighting dogs”. There are many restrictions for fighting dogs when they are out in public. For example, they must be kept on a leash no longer than 1.5 metres and be muzzled.
Some of the fear around fighting dogs stems from their strength, Ngo explained.
“Large dogs are not more aggressive than smaller ones, but any reaction from them has a much higher risk of severe injury,” said Ngo, who is also the founder of Once And For All, a local social enterprise for animals.
Beyond specific breeds, there is also the category of “known dangerous dogs”. This includes any dog, regardless of breed, with a history of attacking or biting a person or domestic animal, resulting in severe injury or death. In addition to the collar and muzzle, they must also be neutered or spayed.
“This reduces their hormones and helps them feel more mellow ... reducing aggression,” Ngo said.
Ngo said that interactions with dogs can escalate in an instant.
“When I walk my own dog, I constantly scan my surroundings. If an unfamiliar dog approaches, I make sure I have enough time and distance to step in and pick my dog up before an incident can occur,” she said.
Ngo recommended using a well-fitted harness rather than a standard neck collar. She explained that when a reactive dog wearing a neck collar is suddenly pulled back, all the force is concentrated on their neck. This can put pressure on the trachea, which, in extreme cases, can cause airway collapse and spinal damage.
A proper harness distributes the pressure across the chest and shoulders and helps protect the dog’s neck and airway.
Fighting or aggressive dogs should also wear a muzzle. The vet said a well-fitted basket muzzle works best as it still allows the animal to pant, drink water and eat treats. She advised against the duckbill “quack” muzzle popular among many Hong Kong dog owners.
“If a muzzle is too restrictive, a dog will often try to rub its face against the ground or paw at its nose to force it off. This discomfort only worsens any underlying aggression or irritability,” she explained.
Ngo said dogs can sense how we feel. If a person is anxious or aggressive, a dog is more likely to feel threatened and attack.
“Most dog bites happen because people do not understand dog body language or because they invade the dog’s personal space,” she said.
Do not stare into a dog’s eyes and never put your face near a dog’s face because animals may see it as an attack.
Do not make quick motions at a stranger’s dog, as this can seem threatening. Always ask the owner for permission to pet it first.
If the owner agrees, then you should kneel down and wait for the animal to show interest in you. Allow it to sniff you. Only pet the dog once it shows relaxed, friendly behaviour, such as wagging its tail or leaning against you.
“Learning to read a dog’s body language is the best way to prevent dog bites,” Ngo said.
If you or someone nearby is bitten by a dog, prioritise stopping the bleeding. You can also gently encourage a small amount of bleeding to help flush out bacteria. Wash the wound under warm, running water with mild soap for five to 10 minutes to prevent infection.
Ngo said to avoid applying rubbing alcohol as it destroys healthy tissue and delays healing. Always make sure to see a doctor immediately.
Get the owner’s contact details, the dog’s microchip number and rabies vaccination history. If the owner is unsure about the vaccination history, the microchip number can help trace it through the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD).
Legally, every dog bite must be reported to the police. Ngo said that while people often try to settle these incidents privately, an official report allows authorities to monitor for rabies. It also helps them assess whether the animal qualifies as a dangerous dog or a banned fighting breed.
“AFCD officials and vets handling these situations aren’t unreasonable; they are simply following government regulations and rules, which is to protect people and animals,” Ngo said.

title: Trump, burger, Hormuz: meet the Iranian team behind billboard war on US
description: The striking visuals help people to grasp ‘the overall context of what is going on in the country’, the head of Designers’ House says.
content: Huge billboards on the walls of Tehran mocking US President Donald Trump and depicting American drones under the boot of an Iranian soldier are providing a chronicle of Iran’s war with the United States and Israel. Khaneh-ye Tarrahan, or Designers’ House, produces the billboards with anti-US messaging for prominent locations in Tehran where they are seen daily by large crowds of passers-by, including the city’s famed Valiasr Square. The team created a towering portrayal of Trump’s lips sewn and his mouth muzzled by the Strait of Hormuz waterway at the centre of the Iran war, accompanied by the words “At the breaking point”. “When news breaks, the team mobilises: ideas are generated, the graphic designers are briefed and we collaborate,” said Mostafa Kafaei, 32, who manages the studio. As he spoke, people worked on projects at several desks in the office. It features a whiteboard for brainstorming, while photos of martyrs and ideas adorn the hallway wall. Kafaei’s studio, which includes a dedicated media-monitoring team, works under one of the country’s biggest state-run media conglomerates. The billboards are sponsored by the government and used to convey its messages far and wide.
