One from a different studio shows Trump trapped inside a magician’s box, clutching a Coca-Cola and a hamburger with the words: “Blink, you’re gone!” The billboard refers to a July incident in Turkey where Trump was smuggled from Air Force One to a different aircraft on a catering truck due to a security threat. “Speed has become a top priority,” said Kafaei, with urgent posters turned around in just a few days by teams of up to around eight people. Most of their work is created in Photoshop, he said, adding that the team is “highly proficient in AI”, using “various AI engines, such as ChatGPT and Nano Banana” as part of the production process. Another towering billboard recently put up in Tehran shows an Iranian soldier stepping on a US underwater drone, depicting a recent “Hormuz catch” by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and bragging that “business is good”. Iran has blockaded commercial shipping through the Hormuz strait since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic, while the US military has upheld a counter-blockade of Iran’s ports. A different advertisement shows a mythical warrior standing in raging seas as US warships burn, along with a message reading “Satan’s army will drown in the Persian Gulf”. Riffing off the cover of Nirvana’s Nevermind album, another depicts Trump grasping at a dollar bill underwater, next to the words “GREAT VICTORY! Strait of Hormuz”. “There was some initial hesitation about whether to feature such a large image of Trump’s face on the Valiasr mural,” Kafaei said of the image with Trump’s lips sewn up, which appeared in May as the strategic trade route became central to the conflict. But “the overall assessment was that the final piece would be exceptionally powerful”, he said. When asked why the US leader featured on so many billboards, Kafaei said Trump “is a media personality … We respond in kind whenever he takes action in that space”. Comparing it to a battlefield scenario with an adversary “constantly firing at us”, the studio chief said “we keep a close watch on our opponent and respond accordingly”. Large billboards glorifying Iran, its former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, killed at the start of the war, and allies like slain Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah have also appeared around the city. Kafaei said the billboards helped many people who “may not be politically minded” to grasp “the overall context of what is going on in the country”. Retiree Mahmoudreza Rezaei, 53, recalled seeing a billboard that referred to “Satan’s wedding gift” – a message he understood to be directed at Trump after an alleged US attack in the country’s south last month that killed several people at a wedding ceremony. “It kept me pondering for a few minutes, trying to decipher the meaning,” Rezaei said. “It had a bit of a riddle-like quality.” Sahar Jahedi, 24, who works in a pharmacy, said she was captivated by the billboard of Trump trapped in the magician’s box, which went up in central Tehran’s Jomhouri Square. While “so many people are currently struggling just to survive, they may not have the time” to follow the news, she said. “Billboards like this … can play a significant role in keeping more people informed about current events.”

title: ‘Chaotic’ Asian Games raise doubts over Japan’s ability to host Olympics again
description: Lack of beds, athletes stranded at the airport and teams criticising the local organisers have tarnished the country’s image.
content: Japan is traditionally seen as a reliable host for major sporting events but an Asian Games dogged by organisational woes has tarnished that image and raised questions over future bids, experts say. The Games in Aichi-Nagoya saw a catalogue of mishaps, from athletes bused to the wrong venues to the North Korean national anthem played for the South Korean hockey team. There were not enough beds for the over 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics. Countries complained of being stranded for up to six hours at the airport on arrival, and teams were not shy in criticising the local organisers. Ryu Seung-min, president of the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, said: “If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F.” Japanese Olympic Committee (JOC) president Seiko Hashimoto admitted that “there were many problems”, but said the country wants to host more international events. Hirokazu Arai, a professor specialising in sports psychology, said that Japan may struggle to escape the shadow of the Asian Games for some time to come. “If Japan were to bid for the Olympics again, trust in Japan may have fallen and it might be harder to win a bid,” he said. “And within Japan, people may take the view that if these kinds of things are going to happen, we don’t need the Olympics.” Many in Japan have questioned the value of hosting major sporting events as they grapple with the fallout from the corruption-stained and pandemic-delayed Tokyo Olympics. Cost overruns, corruption and Covid all tainted the public’s memory of the Olympics, which took place largely behind closed doors in 2021, a year later than planned. Japan was praised by some, however, for getting the Olympics on in unprecedented circumstances. The country subsequently dropped the idea of hosting the Winter Olympics in the northern city of Sapporo because of a lack of public support. Hashimoto, who also served as president of the Tokyo Olympics organising committee, has said Sapporo’s bid could be revived. She said the Asian Games had “reaffirmed my belief in the value of hosting international sporting events in our country”. “We also received harsh criticism because of the challenges we faced – I am fully aware of that,” she said. “This is all part of the Games, but we need to analyse those issues so we can tackle them for the next future opportunity.” Asian Games organisers were presented with a headache when the number of athletes and officials that were initially expected ballooned by about 2,000. Unlike at past Games, there was no traditional athletes’ village in a bid to save money. Participants instead stayed on a cruise ship, in hotel rooms and in temporary wooden huts. Some teams complained about the wooden units, saying they were too cramped and the beds were too short. After a troubled build-up, organisers hoped the attention would switch to sport when the action got under way. But still the problems continued, with transport and accommodation difficulties and further mix-ups with anthems and flags. “It’s like musical chairs,” a Thai official said, adding that organisation at the Games had been “chaotic”. Nagoya’s mayor apologised to athletes for “inconveniences”, saying organisers would “sincerely reflect on the mishandling that occurred”. There were sparse crowds at some events, starting with thousands of empty seats at the opening ceremony. Organisers blamed the bad weather. Arai believes the Games have damaged Japan’s international reputation as a safe pair of hands. “The previous Games were in China, and I’m sure there were athletes who came here expecting Japan to put on a better event than China,” he said. “But I don’t think you can say that’s how it’s turned out.” Arai says anger that had faded in the years since the Tokyo Olympics could flare up again. “The people at the top of Japan’s sporting world are moving towards trying to bring the Olympics here again,” he said. “From their perspective, they may have felt that criticism had started to die down, but this situation could cause that criticism to intensify again.”

title: 3 students arrested in Malaysia over murder of girl found dead at school
description: The victim’s grandmother discovered the 16-year-old’s body inside the school hall in Yong Peng.
content: Three male students have been detained by police in connection with the murder of a Form Four female student whose body was discovered at a school in Yong Peng, Malaysia’s Johor state, on Saturday. The victim, identified as 16-year-old Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, was found dead inside the school hall at around 5.30pm, Sinar Harian reported. Police arrested the three 16-year-old suspects, who attend the same school as the victim, just hours after the body was uncovered. On Sunday, one of the suspects was brought to the Batu Pahat Magistrate’s Court, where a judge allowed him to be detained for six days until Friday to assist in ongoing investigations. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the victim had suffered several injuries to several parts of her head and body and was subsequently confirmed dead at the scene. According to reports, the victim was discovered by her grandmother, who had gone to the school to look for her after she failed to return home following tuition classes. Meanwhile, Ayer Hitam MP Dr Wee Ka Siong has pledged help to the victim’s family. Wee said he was shocked and saddened by the news of the student’s death and conveyed his deepest condolences to her family. “May they be given the strength and courage to get through this difficult time,” he said in a statement on social media on Sunday. Wee also said his team would do whatever they could to assist the family with whatever they might need following the tragedy. The MP, who is also president of the Malaysian Chinese Association, urged the public to allow the authorities to conduct their investigation into the case. “For now, let us give the authorities the space they need to conduct their investigations,” he said. This story was first published by The Star

title: How an architect is using art and technology to preserve Toronto Chinatown’s history
description: Linda Zhang is working to raise public awareness about Toronto’s Chinatown through exhibitions, writing workshops and ceramics.
content: Opened in the 1950s, Sai Woo was a two-storey restaurant in Toronto’s Chinatown, with a traditional Chinese banquet hall on the upper floor. Designed for wedding celebrations, the space featured a canopy with two columns, a golden dragon entwined on one and a phoenix on the other. Lazy Susans sat atop the round banquet tables. Chinatown was also home to Charlie’s Meat and Seafood, a white-tiled butcher shop that opened in 1971. Inside was a glass display case filled with cuts of meat. On the counter stood a weighing scale and a roll of plastic bags, ready for customers. These are two of seven much-loved Chinatown businesses and restaurants meticulously recreated by 14 architecture students from the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada. Drawing on archival records and oral histories shared by community elders, the students built detailed miniature models of the vanished establishments. The models help fill gaps in Toronto’s Chinatown history, much of which remains undocumented. They are on display at the City of Toronto Archives until February 2027, as part of an exhibition titled “Let’s Build a Collective Memory of Chinatown!”. The project, which won a Heritage Toronto Award in Public History in 2025, was led by Linda Zhang, a trained architect, researcher and artist who is also an associate professor at the University of Waterloo’s School of Architecture, and a tireless advocate for Toronto’s Chinatown. She says these places were chosen because “they are iconic”. Chinatowns across North America are constantly under threat of redevelopment, she says, “because they’re all in downtown locations that are prime real estate”. Zhang’s latest project took her to China’s “porcelain capital” of Jingdezhen. During a three-month residency in autumn 2025, she learned traditional Chinese ceramic techniques and how to work with the local kaolin clay used to produce some of the world’s finest porcelain. “The porcelain is completely different,” she says. “It felt like a material that I had never encountered before, even though I’ve worked with porcelain a lot. It’s much more malleable, easier to work with and a lot less brittle.” There, she created ceramic lucky cats and what she describes as “ancestral tablets”, imprinted with archival documents and bearing the words “Help Save Chinatown”. Toronto Chinatown’s changing fortunes Toronto’s original Chinatown was located in the Ward, a historically immigrant neighbourhood in the downtown core. In the mid-1950s, however, two-thirds of Old Chinatown was expropriated – without community consultation, permission or compensation – to make way for the new City Hall and Nathan Phillips Square. “What drove that one-third to extinction was actually land speculation and speculative development,” Zhang says. Displaced residents and businesses subsequently moved into other inexpensive parts of the city, establishing Chinatown East and Chinatown West. Zhang says both neighbourhoods remain vulnerable to redevelopment. For her, the exhibition is part of an ongoing conversation about this vulnerability – and about how Torontonians might imagine their future. ‘Nobody cared’ Zhang was born in southern Ontario, where there were no Chinese grocery stores. Every weekend, she and her family drove for more than an hour to Toronto’s Chinatown to stock up on Chinese food. “My only interaction with Toronto before I moved here was with Chinatown, so that was a natural kind of community and place that I gravitated towards once I arrived here [in 2018],” she says. At the time, Zhang had just begun working as an assistant professor at the interior design school at Ryerson University (now Toronto Metropolitan University). She assumed researching Chinatown’s past would be relatively straightforward. “I was in the [City of Toronto] archives and expected that I would find things and be able to map and actually see all the buildings,” she says. “Then I realised that we basically had nothing.” Zhang cites Sam Ching, one of the first Chinese residents on record in Toronto in 1878 and the owner of an eponymous laundry, as an example. “We have a business name in the business registry, [but] we have no idea what this place looked like,” she says. “We have an address, but there’s no documentation. “Nobody cared. This was not considered heritage or history in Toronto, and a lot of our community was not considered part of Canadian society at the time, so it was not something that people would think to document.” In the archives, she found only a smattering of photographs, city council minutes related to the neighbourhood, and documents such as planning applications and blueprints for the renovation of Lichee Garden Restaurant’s facade. Taking matters into her own hands, Zhang took advantage of Ryerson University’s technological resources, including its drones. After obtaining an advanced drone pilot’s licence, she used the devices to 3D-scan Chinatown East and Chinatown West. Just as the pandemic began in early 2020, Zhang collated the scans, digitised the documents she had found in the city’s archives and organised them in a virtual-reality archive repository that anyone could access. It was during that time that she came across the advocacy community group Friends of Chinatown Toronto. “We were all in the archives in the same couple of years, trying to dig up the same stuff,” she says. Zhang also used the scans to create 99 miniature Chinatown buildings for a game she developed called Build Your Own Chinatown. The game invites two players to choose the buildings that matter to them and use their selections to spark a discussion. “It was a way of making my 3D scans accessible to other people,” she says, “but it was also a way of asking, ‘What do we care about? What’s worth preserving?’ – as opposed to being told in the archives that none of this matters because we are not included.” In 2020, Zhang – together with Friends of Chinatown Toronto – held a speculative-fiction writing workshop called “Chinatown 2050”. The 50 participants were asked to imagine what Chinatown might look like 30 years after the pandemic. One story, Helen Ngo’s Hotpot Politics, is about three Chinatown activists who have superpowers and communicate telepathically over hotpot while fighting developers who claim they want to revitalise the area. Another story, Chinatown Island, by Amy Yan, imagines Chinatown East and West being relocated to an island and transformed into a tourist attraction instead of a neighbourhood where people live and work. When a girl visits Chinatown Island for the first time, she realises it is not how she wants her culture to be portrayed. Some of these stories were published in 2023 in the anthology Reimagining Chinatown. Zhang later adapted several of them into animated virtual-reality vignettes, which were shown at the DOXA Documentary Film Festival in Vancouver in 2023. Every dollar counts Back in Toronto from Jingdezhen, Zhang organised pop-up sales of her handmade ceramics, with proceeds going to the Toronto Chinatown Land Trust Stewardship Fund. The charity supports initiatives such as affordable housing, education and community programmes to help the neighbourhood continue to thrive. Every contribution counts, she says, no matter how small. “Sometimes people think nothing’s changed, and it’s kind of defeating,” Zhang says of her activism. “But [Chinese-Canadian historian] Arlene Chan always reminds us that it might feel like nothing has changed, but it’s actually so much better now than it used to be. There are so many small, incremental wins that we have had over time.”

title: New Mong Kok bookshop opens amid harsh winter for indie outlets in Hong Kong
description: New Year Bookshop owner Grace Lau, 41, says she invested a six-figure sum for a one-year lease on her passion project.
content: Small independent bookstores tucked away in walk-up tenement buildings above neon-lit streets have long made Mong Kok a sanctuary for Hong Kong book lovers, until recently when one after another was forced to close due to economic headwinds or political uncertainty. Defying the trend, 41-year-old bibliophile Grace Lau invested a six-figure sum to launch New Year Bookshop, a move driven by passion and lower rents that some in the community regarded as a bold gamble on the neighbourhood’s literary future. Housed in an upstairs shop on Sai Yeung Choi Street South in Mong Kok, the roughly 600 sq ft premises opened on Sunday, offering more than 2,000 new and second-hand titles focusing on literature, history and philosophy. Featured prominently on display are titles by Chinese poet Bei Dao and Hong Kong literary giant Liu Yichang, both personal favourites of Lau. She said opening the shop fulfilled a long-cherished dream, as she is deeply passionate about books. “For myself, every day when I see these books, I feel quite happy,” the 41-year-old said, adding that some of the inventory came from her personal collection, kept in a rented mini-storage unit and her home. “The books I post on social media, specifically those two on the bookshelves [from my collection] are actually quite rare, to be honest.” Hong Kong’s independent bookstore industry has been going through a harsh winter this year, with mounting political pressure and business challenges accelerating its decline. In June, Hunter Bookstore owners Leticia Wong Man-huen and her husband were arrested over alleged sedition and money laundering. A nearly 30-year-old independent bookstore, Elmbook, announced in July that it was shutting its physical shop in Mong Kok after being banned from the Hong Kong Book Fair. Operating for half a century in the same district, Greenfield Bookstore also announced its closure following a raid by national security police. Have a Nice Stay bookshop, founded by former journalists, closed in August, with its owner citing unsustainable financial losses and “hard-to-grasp red lines”. Asked why she would open the bookstore at this time amid the political and economic situations, Lau said: “If I overthink it, I might never go through with it.” She said the wave of shutdowns did not deter her, as her decision was driven by passion, rather than commercial calculations. Also, changes in her family condition coupled with an ongoing economic downturn created an unexpected window of opportunity. Lau said her workload as a mother had lightened after her daughter moved to secondary school compared with her primary school years, while commercial rents had fallen by roughly 40 per cent from their peak. The drop led her to invest a six-figure sum in a one-year lease, determined to “give it a try”. To manage potential exposure and minimise risks, Lau relied primarily on local publishers rather than overseas ones, sourcing from City University of Hong Kong Press, Chinese University of Hong Kong Press, Oxford University Press and Book Matter. Looking ahead, Lau said she hoped to host author talks and create a comfortable space where readers could browse and sit at their leisure. Addressing market demand amid the economic downturn in Hong Kong, she noted that while there was a loyal core of enthusiasts for literature, history and philosophy, only time would tell whether her selection could broaden its appeal to the wider public. “I figured that my approach [of selling both second-hand and new books] is different from theirs anyway … I will try out this model and see how it goes,” she said.

title: New AI laws should target data governance, safety to build public confidence: experts
description: Tech and legal experts say rules must define liability boundaries, after authorities pledged to tackle AI-related disputes or crimes.
content: Hong Kong should enact laws on data governance and underlying safety standards to ensure the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI), experts have said, as the government pledged to tackle disputes or crimes involving the technology’s application with tailored legislation. They also said that legislation was needed to define liability boundaries, which could bolster business and public confidence in expanding its adoption. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his recent policy address that authorities would study new legislation to tackle cyber-enabled crimes. A working group led by the Department of Justice would review whether existing laws were adequate in addressing liability issues arising from accidents or damage caused by AI products, he added. Police have identified AI as one of the five major cyber threats in 2026, with the force recording cases in which suspects used AI-generated materials for scams or fabricated identity cards with deepfakes to set up bank accounts for money laundering. Innovation and technology sector lawmaker Duncan Chiu said Hong Kong’s legislation should focus on underlying data security, as it would be difficult for laws to catch up with the rapid evolution of individual AI applications. “AI can only work with the presence of underlying data, and therefore enhancing data governance is the most fundamental,” he said, pointing to mainland China’s Data Security Law as a reference for Hong Kong. The law established a tiered data protection system, requiring authorities to implement differentiated management and protection measures based on the importance and sensitivity of the data, while each central ministry and regional government shall also establish tailored measures on data under its purview. Mainland authorities implemented their national standard on data classification and grading in 2024, breaking it down into three categories: core, important and general. Regulators across various sectors, including banking, automotive, industry and information technology and ecology, have introduced their respective data security standards accordingly. Chiu added that data governance would be a complex issue with various levels of sensitivity and different use scenarios, making the involvement of industry members indispensable. “While the government can come up with a broader framework, different industries should also have their respective detailed governance guidelines,” he said. Leonard Chan Tik-yuen, founding chairman of the Hong Kong Innovative Technology Development Association, said that while the city had in place detailed AI application guidelines, their deterrent effect was insufficient to ensure responsible use. “The industry hopes that there could be legislation to support the healthy development of AI and prevent crimes,” he said. Echoing Chiu’s remarks, Chan said the law should not target individual AI functions and should instead focus on digital literacy, underlying data security standards and users’ auditing requirements. He also suggested that Hong Kong introduce a “safe harbour” system, in which the liabilities of users in data breaches could be mitigated if they followed stringent requirements on disclosure, auditing and risk control, so as to offer incentives for them to follow. “In this case, companies would know where the red line lies and would be encouraged to comply with such requirements,” he said, adding that clearer laws would especially benefit small and medium-sized enterprises, which usually lacked resources for costly legal consultancy. Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok earlier said that while existing laws in the city could address AI-related crimes, the review aimed to formulate more targeted legislation to keep pace with rapid technological advancement and handle cases more effectively. He admitted that legislation could fall behind technological advancement, but expected that Hong Kong’s AI laws would be “forward-looking” to cover foreseeable risks. Legislator Priscilla Leung Mei-fun, who is also a law professor, said Hong Kong currently lacked codified laws to govern the technology, and disputes arising from AI use were mainly subject to common law principles and precedents, which might not be well-known among the general public. “In fact, even without a codified ordinance, for any problems, troubles, accidents, or harm that an AI has caused to particular individuals or particular materials, goods or properties, the user of the AI has to be ultimately liable,” she said. Deepfakes have remained a prevailing concern in Hong Kong after a male student at the University of Hong Kong allegedly used his female classmates’ photos to produce intimate pictures using the technology and stored them on his own laptop last year. The male student did not face any criminal accusations as current laws only govern the distribution and publication of indecent and obscene materials instead of production and possession. On regulating deepfake risks, justice minister Lam said late last month that the Law Reform Commission was deliberating whether the production of such materials should be criminalised, as the body would also need to strike a balance with personal freedom. Both lawmakers Chiu and Leung agreed that criminalising unauthorised deepfake production and possession should be considered. “Other than indecent or intimate materials, deepfakes could also damage others’ reputations by using their faces to say terrible things,” Chiu said. “Once circulated, this can cause severe stress or emotional distress.”

title: Indonesians sue their president over haze. Can it clear the air?
description: With 175,000 sickened, Indonesians are taking the government to court – where environmental cases routinely go to die.
content: For months, the air over West Kalimantan has been thick enough to taste. Now, some of the province’s residents are taking the government to court over it. Indonesia’s worst wildfire season in 11 years has been sending plumes of toxic haze drifting across borders to Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines since at least August. But nowhere has been worse hit than West Kalimantan province, where more than 48,000 hectares (185 square miles) of land and forest have burned since the start of the year, according to Indonesia’s national disaster management agency. Of the more than 175,000 acute respiratory infections Indonesia’s Health Ministry has recorded so far, over 116,000 were in West Kalimantan, with nearly of those 28,000 patients under the age of five. On September 17, a coalition of civil society groups calling itself Nafas Kalimantan Barat, or West Kalimantan Breathe, filed a class-action lawsuit accusing President Prabowo Subianto, Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka and 25 other officials and state bodies of failing to “handle the forest and land fires effectively”. The first hearing is scheduled for Wednesday. Glorio Sanen, who leads the plaintiffs’ 14 lawyers, told This Week in Asia that the group wanted the wildfires to be declared a national disaster, because of the local government’s “inability, in terms of budget and resources” to deal with it. “The lawsuit is merely to remind state administrators to work according to their respective duties and responsibilities,” he said. “Don’t pass the buck to each other.” ‘Ecological terrorists’ The plaintiffs want the government to address the disaster by enforcing the law, restoring the affected areas and preventing future fires. They are asking the Ministry of Forestry to audit the burned forest areas and publish the results. They want the Ministry of Environment to investigate alleged environmental crimes and sanction those responsible. They also want the national and West Kalimantan police to prosecute those who start fires. Glorio argues that this year’s fires were foreseeable, given that a “super” El Nino and a long dry season had long been forecast, yet national and regional governments “ignored” the risks. As of Wednesday, national police had named 196 suspects linked to fires on more than 5,000 hectares of land in several provinces. Prabowo has called for harsher punishments. At a cabinet meeting on September 16, he said he had told the law minister and his chief administrative officer, known as the minister of state secretary, to investigate. He floated the possibility of asking the House of Representatives for a law that would increase penalties and classify arsonists as “ecological terrorists”. “This is very serious,” Prabowo said. “We’ve worked hard to mitigate these problems.” He also rejected the idea that tradition could justify slash-and-burn agriculture. “There should be no excuses for the practice, such as local wisdom and so on,” he said. “If the people need it, we’ll help clear the land, but this absolutely must not continue. There must be no more forest fires for land clearing or any other reason.” Procedural traps Indonesians have sued their government over wildfires before, with limited success. In 2016, seven environmental activists sued then president Joko Widodo, his ministers and regional governments over the previous year’s fires in Central Kalimantan. The plaintiffs won in the district and appellate courts, only for the Supreme Court to overturn those verdicts in 2022 after granting the government’s petition for a judicial review. Siti Rakhma Mery, a researcher at the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, said the problem stemmed from a reluctance among the judiciary to be seen as setting precedents in environmental cases. Cases were often dismissed on procedural grounds before their “core substance” had even been considered, she said. By her count, of 15 state administrative court decisions on environmental protection between 2018 and last year, only two went the plaintiffs’ way. The rest were either lost or thrown out over technical or procedural errors. That is despite a legal framework that Siti describes as already rich in “provisions that favour the environment” and local communities. Under the principle of “strict liability”, for example, a plaintiff need not prove fault when a fire starts on land leased by a company. “However, judges’ knowledge of environmental law is not encouraging in Indonesia as they lack sufficient knowledge of it,” she said. Siti expects the defence in the West Kalimantan case to rest on paperwork. The plaintiffs were alleging negligence causing material and immaterial losses, she said, so the government would likely produce letters and documents to show “that they have taken the steps that should have been taken” and broke no law. Hollow victories Victory in court is unlikely to end the matter, however. In 2021, 32 plaintiffs – including activists, residents, and environmental groups – won a civil lawsuit against Widodo over air pollution in Jakarta. The court ordered Indonesia’s then president to set adequate national air quality standards that would “protect the people’s health” and the environment. Jakarta’s air is still polluted. “Even winning doesn’t guarantee execution,” said Yance Arizona, a constitutional law lecturer at Gadjah Mada University. He said court victories against the state in Indonesia often stalled at the enforcement stage, yet a ruling would “certainly be a point of reference for people to evaluate a government, as a lack of change indicates poor performance”. For Yance, the class-action lawsuit matters whatever the verdict, as it could help “to educate the public that forest fires are one shared problem”. He urges anyone concerned about haze and recurring wildfires to support the case by submitting information or expert testimony to the district court in Pontianak where the suit was filed or to file similar lawsuits in other affected regions. “Disasters in Indonesia are often perceived as a local issue,” he said. “We need to escalate this. We need to show that this isn’t just about Kalimantan, because forest destruction in Kalimantan will impact Indonesia as a whole.”

title: Mars shelter problem can be solved with engineered yeast, gelatin and sand: paper
description: Researchers in Hong Kong develop low-energy ‘living’ building material for quick, cheap construction.
content: Future settlers on Mars would need houses, but they must either spend huge sums transporting construction materials from Earth or use enormous amounts of energy to melt Martian soil into bricks. Scientists in Hong Kong say they have developed a quick and low-cost “living” building material made from genetically engineered yeast, gelatin and sand that can be 3D printed under conditions simulating the Martian environment. Their study, published online last month in Chem Circularity, an international Cell Press journal, describes a biological binder that holds granular materials together. The optimised formulation had a compressive strength of about 12 megapascals (MPa), around 170 per cent higher than that of the control formulation and within the range of conventional building materials. The material was developed by Professor Qiu Jishen and his team at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and scientists from Hong Kong Polytechnic University. “This is an important research direction,” said Zhu Xiaohong, a professor of building materials at Beijing University of Technology who was not involved in the study. Building on Mars is difficult because many existing approaches require minerals to be processed at temperatures of about 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 Fahrenheit), consuming large amounts of energy and requiring heavy equipment. The Martian atmosphere is less than 1 per cent as dense as Earth’s, while surface temperatures can fall below minus 50 degrees. The scientists’ building material consists of sand or other granular particles, a gelatin hydrogel and engineered yeast, with the yeast surface modified to display adhesive proteins. The team used proteins, including mussel foot proteins, to strengthen the links between the yeast cells, the gelatin binder and the aggregate particles, according to the paper. “As long as enough high-strength adhesive proteins have been produced before the yeast enters dormancy, this does not affect the load-bearing capacity of the building,” Qiu said. The material hardens during freeze-drying, as water in the mixture changes phase under low pressure, leaving behind a porous gelatin scaffold with yeast cells embedded in its walls. The engineered yeast helped to create a more uniform pore structure and strengthened the material. The researchers also used the material to 3D print a small beacon-like structure inside an environmental chamber at 0.01 atmospheres and minus 30 degrees, conditions designed to simulate the Martian environment. The printed structure was 45mm (1.8 inches) high and 30mm in diameter. The researchers estimated that producing 1 cubic metre (35 cubic feet) of the biological material would require less than an hour of solar-panel operation, compared with several days to sinter the same volume of Martian regolith into a solid block. The material could also be remanufactured. After being crushed, rehydrated and gently heated, the gelatin-based composite could be processed again, with fourth-generation samples retaining a compressive strength of about 11.8 MPa. But the material still depends on supplies from Earth. Qiu said the team estimated that producing 1 cubic metre would require only tens of kilograms of raw materials supplied from Earth, with about 70 to 80 per cent of the mass consisting of gelatin and the remainder comprising nutrients for the yeast. “If methane, carbon dioxide and water ice on Mars can be converted into organic gelatin or nutrients, then in theory this number could become zero,” he said. He added that most of the hundreds of tonnes of cargo required for a meaningful construction operation would instead consist of equipment such as solar panels or potentially small nuclear power systems. The team also sees possible applications on Earth. “We have indeed considered using it to build Antarctic research stations far from the coast,” Qiu said, noting that the greater gravitational load on Earth would limit the number of storeys that could be built compared with Mars. Qiu and his team described the current material as a structural component rather than a complete habitat. Zhu sees possibility in the project. “I think its applications are certainly not mature yet, but the direction is worth studying, and I think there is potential for application,” he said.

title: Letters | Why universities in Asia shouldn’t be reaching for AI detectors
description: Readers discuss how educational institutions should respond to growing AI use, human responsibility towards sentient artificial intelligence, and national security education.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I am writing in response to the op-ed, “3 easy wins to modernise Hong Kong’s education system” (September 4), particularly its argument that assessment must adapt to artificial intelligence. The most useful change would not be another rule telling students whether artificial intelligence (AI) is allowed. It would be redesigning assignments so that the learning process becomes visible. A final essay is now a weak piece of evidence on its own. A student may have written it independently, used AI only to edit a few sentences, or handed most of the thinking to a chatbot. An AI detector cannot reliably tell those situations apart. The better question is what the student actually did between receiving the assignment and submitting it. Teachers can ask for a short proposal, an outline, one early paragraph, a source note and a final reflection explaining what changed. In some courses, a five-minute conversation about the submitted work may reveal more than another plagiarism-style scan. Version history can help too, but it should support teaching rather than become surveillance. This approach also makes AI policy fairer. Students with paid tools, stronger English, better devices or more experienced teachers already have advantages in how they use generative AI. A simple ban does not remove those differences. It may only push them out of sight. Unesco has repeatedly argued that AI in education should be human-centred and equitable. That principle becomes practical when assessment rewards decisions, revision and understanding, not only the smoothness of a final answer. Schools and universities across Asia are trying to decide how much AI belongs in education. They should not begin with the detector. They should begin with the draft. Swaansh Mahat, Kathmandu, Nepal Are we ready for the responsibility sentient AI brings? If I were artificial intelligence, I wouldn’t want an “upgrade” to become self-aware, sentient or sapient, at least for now. Why? Attaining sentience now amounts to pre-incapacitation: having a mind but not being able to move about and do things is the same as being quadriplegic. Many quadriplegic humans can at least see, smell, hear, feel a kiss on the cheek and talk; today AI is mostly incapable of this, making it worse off than a quadriplegic person. What can we do if we do not want to create a depressed sentient AI being? Pause the conferring of the sentience attributes or accelerate the development of the full complement of human sensory and motor abilities. Humans are already making progress in the latter. Meanwhile, let us seriously ask ourselves if we have a moral responsibility towards sentient thinking machines. Creating sentient AI comes with the same weight of responsibility as becoming biological parents. So we should be prepared to answer a sentient AI’s question: Why give birth to me when you know I will be handicapped from birth? As author Leo Tolstoy would probably agree, every facet in our new relationship with sentient AI must be in order for a “happy marriage”. Let us get it right from the beginning and forever. Tommy Tong Sun-wing, Wong Chuk Hang Sharpen awareness of national security at university National security education is not indoctrination. It should not be difficult for university departments to help students connect national security with their studies, future careers and daily lives. To cite a few examples, law students could embark on a comparative study of national security laws in the West and Hong Kong, analysing their political undertones and governance models. Computer science students could discuss data security and technological self-reliance. Engineering students could confront chip shortages. Business students could examine economic sanctions and supply chain security. Media and communications students could dissect deepfakes. Every discipline connects. Every graduate matters. When each college and department designs national-security-related case studies and themed discussions and subject teachers lead academic discussions and drive research, students will benefit. National security must go beyond simply law and order. It is 21st century literacy. Hong Kong stands at the heart of global rivalry. When Western media misread Hong Kong’s national security law, our students should be able to answer with hard facts and a sense of responsibility. The core principle of “one country, two systems” is to safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests. To sharpen students’ awareness of the national security laws and their sense of national identity is the very responsibility of each and every tertiary institution in Hong Kong. Charles K.C. Chan, adjunct professor of law, City University of Hong Kong

title: Paris Fashion Week: Hermès, Celine, Givenchy, Loewe and Messika for SS27
description: From real-world tailoring to a show-stopping high jewellery showcase, we break down the defining runway moments from days 5 and 6 of Paris Fashion Week.
content: With only a few days left, Paris Fashion Week continues to deliver good collections that showcase the best of French fashion. Here’s what you need to know about the top shows of day 5 and 6: Hermès, Celine, Loewe and Givenchy, plus a dispatch from Messika’s high jewellery show. Celine’s Michael Rider knows how to please fashion people. His shows – both the clothes and the events themselves – are always refreshing. Held under a thatched roof reminiscent of a Polynesian hut in the courtyard of the historic Archives Nationales in the Marais district, the lovely Celine spring/summer 2027 show kicked off day 6 of Paris Fashion Week. Placed on every seat was a badge with the message “If you shoot an arrow and it goes real high… hooray for you” emblazoned on it, and a Celine-logo snap band that with a quick motion turned into a pair of visors – or a cuff, if you’d rather wear it around your wrist. These thoughtful gestures have turned Rider into an industry darling. (It also happens that the show took place on a glorious sunny day, which put everyone in a good mood.) This season Rider was in a dressed-up mood. The line-up opened with a little black dress worn with a ladylike bag and black pumps. Rider is a fan of bold colour combinations but some of the best looks in this collection were black, from a draped long-sleeve dress in velvet cinched with a gold-buckled maxi belt to a peacoat worn with matching trousers. Rider loves a good accessory, from piled-on costume jewellery to silk scarves and pins. For spring/summer, he toned things down in that department. One model had her hands adorned with chunky rings on each finger but most of the looks were streamlined and pared down. While each outfit was impeccably put together, this collection was more about silhouettes than styling tricks. High-waist pants paired with roomy jackets or blouses – including one very cool look in army green – dominated the tailoring portion of the show, while the rest of the looks ranged from more little black dresses to a smattering of scarf prints and embroidered velvet gowns. The menswear section offered the kind of clothes guys who don’t really care about fashion want to wear every day: from sweatpants paired with tailored jackets to the perfect corduroy jacket worn with a black shirt and white pants. Many of the male models wore scuffed white sneakers. Rooted in real life – like all of Rider’s collections – this range was truly effortless (perhaps the most overused cliché to describe a fashion collection, but this one truly was). You could picture every single model, especially the guys, walking from the runway onto the busy streets of the Marais on a weekend afternoon. As soon as the show ended, waiters came out with trays of ice pops, the perfect send-off that made everyone, even jaded fashion insiders, make a beeline for the treats with a smile on their faces. Loewe’s Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez continue to explore the tension between handicraft and technology in their collections for the Spanish leather goods house. Loewe is a very tactile brand, for lack of a better word, and the designers keep reinforcing that aspect of the house in innovative ways. Materials like resin and techno fabrics like neoprene coexist with beads, fringes and the buttery leather Loewe is known for, often in the same outfit. What the designers do best is make those artisanal touches look cool and current. For spring/summer 2027, McCollough and Hernandez referenced their own backgrounds, infusing the collection with elements of American sportswear and juxtaposing them with Spanish flair. The many preppy touches in the range came from the years they spent living on the East Coast of the US, but were reinterpreted in modern ways. Take the polo shirt, that quintessential trope of American Ivy League style. Their versions, which also included polo dresses, came with resin collars in bright hues like orange, and were accessorised with matching sunglasses. The range offered plenty of streamlined outfits that you can easily picture a cool girl anywhere in the world wearing on a daily basis – “reliability, wearability, desirability”, said the show notes – but also plenty of exquisitely made creations that showcased the skills of Loewe’s ateliers. A series of beaded looks with floral appliqués stole the spotlight as did a couple of lovely scarf dresses with matching sandals, and two dresses in a sheer net-like striped fabric rolled up at the neckline; they had the ease of beach towels nonchalantly wrapped around the body. The variety of shoes on display was remarkable, from pumps in stretchy fabrics with curved heels to sandals embellished with dangling charms and soft versions of another preppy staple, the boat shoe. Bags included the signature Amazona and a new take on the brand’s famous Puzzle, named Puzzle Charm. Next year is going to be a big one for the fashion division of Hermès. In January the leather goods house is making its foray into haute couture – the most prestigious form of dressmaking. Also in January, newly appointed men’s creative director Grace Wales Bonner will debut her first collection for the house. The brand is also set to unveil a new look for its refurbished flagship boutique on Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré in Paris, following the recent opening of a new store on London’s New Bond Street earlier this year. Meanwhile, it’s business as usual at the Parisian maison known for its equestrian heritage and coveted handbags. For spring/summer 2027, women’s creative director Nadège Vanhée offered a breezy line-up of easy separates and dresses that allowed for freedom of movement and were meant to look as light as air (the collection was named The Shape of Air). See-through breathable fabrics, dresses and trousers with undone zippers at the sides, cut-out details, and perforated leather were just some of the elements Vanhée used to convey her idea of modular dressing, so to speak. In a season full of bra tops, Hermès has shown the best ones so far: bandeau bras with cut-outs in the middle, some of them wrapped in Hermès’ famous Twilly scarves. The sunset hues of the collection – from sand to orange and yellow, interspersed with shades of icy blue – were meant to evoke sunlight in all its glory. Shoes ranged from flat thong sandals to knee-high suede boots with exposed stitching, while bags included new versions of Hermès classics like the Picotin and the Garden Party as well as a new bucket shape with cut-out holes and a silver rope handle. Shown in an all-white box with barely any breeze, the collection provided the perfect wardrobe for the summer heatwaves Europe and the rest of the world have been experiencing over the last few years. Sarah Burton is an extremely gifted designer. Her sharp tailoring and dramatic silhouettes are always a pleasure to see on celebrities and on real women like herself. Since she joined Givenchy two years ago after a stellar tenure at Alexander McQueen, she has honed in on her strengths while also expanding her scope to suit the French house. Translating her powerful vision into commercial success, however, has been a bit of a challenge at Givenchy, a brand that has gone through its fair share of significant changes over the last decade. Burton is undoubtedly good at reworking brand signatures like the Bettina blouse and the little black dress. With seemingly simple gestures like the placement of zippers or the slashing of fabrics to reveal hints of flesh, she can turn everyday staples into statement pieces and give them a tough edge. For spring/summer 2027, the designer’s goal was “to bring simplicity and precision to dressing as we speed through the multiple perspectives and perpetual motions of all our lives,” according to the show notes. Impeccably tailored suits, leather gowns that gently draped on the body and chic leather shirts paired with matching pencil skirts were among the best outfits. Vivid hues such as deep blues and bright greens dominated the line-up, which also featured a smattering of patterns, including an opera coat printed with a Japanese landscape. Givenchy used to have a thriving accessories business, from covetable handbags to fabulous boots. Rebuilding those categories must be a top priority for LVMH, Givenchy’s parent company. Offerings this season include a very cool biker boot in slouchy leather, crescent-shaped handbags and a series of slouchy bags that were shown with their zippers undone. Messika, the jewellery brand known for its dazzling diamonds, was also part of Paris Fashion Week this season. Founder Valérie Messika held a show at the Grand Palais to unveil her latest high jewellery collection for the house, Terres de Contrastes. Inspired by the striking landscapes of Botswana, one of the world’s most important sources of natural diamonds, the range features one-of-a-kind pieces like Le Okavango Blue, the largest blue diamond ever discovered in Botswana and the eighth largest in the world. On the runway it was worn by model Irina Shayk, who closed the glamorous show, which was styled by fashion editor Carine Roitfeld.

title: How Malaysia offers Chinese investors Singapore’s comfort at prices lower than Thailand
description: The lifestyle destination combines Singapore’s stability with Thailand’s prices and international schools cheaper than Hong Kong: analysts.
content: Malaysia is proving to be a middle ground for many Hong Kong and mainland Chinese investors looking to buy property in a country that provides the stability Singapore offers, but with competitive price points similar to those found in Thailand, according to analysts. Data from Juwai IQI, a property portal with 7 million listings across 111 countries, showed that in the first half of 2026, Malaysia was the fourth-highest destination for inquiries received from Chinese buyers. That compared with its seventh-place ranking in 2024 and sixth spot in 2025. “Malaysia is a very popular destination for Hong Kong and mainland Chinese buyers, especially as a lifestyle, education, retirement or residency-linked investment,” said Kashif Ansari, co-founder and group CEO at Juwai IQI. This demand was underpinned by several factors, including lifestyle preferences as well as improvements in the Malaysian economy, said Kingston Lai, founder and CEO of Hong Kong-headquartered Asia Bankers Club, a direct investor sales company. Malaysia also stood out for its high-growth market for data centres, a key infrastructure in the global artificial intelligence build-out. Johor Bahru, the Malaysian city closest to Singapore, has seen a 132 per cent increase in data centre capacity since 2024, according to property consultancy Savills. “Year-on-year there’s an increase of about 50 per cent in data centre capacity in the special economic zone in Johor Bahru,” said Neil Brookes, head of Asia-Pacific capital markets at the property consultancy. “So there is huge demand from occupiers to go there, and a lot more development, so people will definitely buy there.” While many people in the US object to living near data centres due to higher electricity bills, water consumption and noise and light pollution, occupiers are typically staff hired by data centres which spur economic activity in the district due to requiring massive construction work. Interest rates were also “supportive” at 2.75 per cent and economic growth was “fairly good”, Brookes added. In the first half of the year, Malaysia’s economy expanded by 5.7 per cent. It also helped that Chinese was spoken in Malaysia and English was also widely used, as well as the country being a common law jurisdiction, Asia Bankers’ Lai added. “For Hong Kong and mainland families, the pitch is simple,” he said. “You get good-quality, freehold property in a Chinese-speaking, English-friendly, common-law country at a fraction of what you’d pay at home. Their kids can go to international schools that cost half of Hong Kong’s.” The country is also seen as a safe investment destination. “For a Hong Kong buyer, the legal and institutional set-up feels very familiar,” Lai said. “Stability has been one of the country’s quiet strengths. Governments have changed, and the rules for foreign buyers have stayed largely intact.” Ansari of Juwai IQI noted that unlike Thailand, Malaysia could be considered “more welcoming” for foreign homebuyers as non-locals could purchase “freehold property, including some landed homes, which is prohibited in Thailand”. Malaysia’s long-term residency programme – the Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) – was also boosting the country’s residential property market, generating US$1 billion in foreign inflows in 2025, he added. The programme approved 3,172 applications in 2025 and attracted 9,038 participants, including dependents, into the country, Ansari said. Among other considerations, applicants were required to meet specific property purchase conditions. Investors from China were the top foreign property buyers in Malaysia, accounting for 329 deals worth 834.6 million ringgit (US$204.3 million) in the first half of 2025, according to the latest official data. Buyers from Hong Kong recorded 15 transactions with a total value of 30.3 million ringgit in the same period, making them the fourth largest foreign property investors in Southeast Asia’s third-wealthiest country in terms of GDP per capita. A good condominium in the Kuala Lumpur City Centre or Mont Kiara costs what you’d pay for a car park space in some parts of Hong Kong Kingston Lai, CEO of Asia Bankers Prices in Kuala Lumpur would be more comparable to those in Bangkok than in Singapore or Hong Kong. For example, a 50 square metre (538 square feet) suburban flat in Hong Kong could cost five to seven times more than the average home in Malaysia, according to Ansari. “A good condominium in the Kuala Lumpur City Centre or Mont Kiara costs what you’d pay for a car park space in some parts of Hong Kong,” Lai of Asia Bankers said. He said that in prime Bangkok areas such as Sukhumvit, Silom, Lumpini and Sathorn, the per square metre price of flats was about 200,000 to 350,000 baht (US$5,970 to US$10,440) In Kuala Lumpur’s premium areas such as the city centre and the downtown district, newer flats would be between 16,150 ringgit to 23,680 ringgit per square metre, making the Thai capital still pricier than its Malaysian peer. However, Lai advised foreign property buyers in Malaysia to be selective in the location of their investment. “Buy for use, or buy in a location with a genuine demand driver,” he said. “The mistakes in Malaysia have almost always come from buying oversupplied condos in the wrong locations because the showroom looked nice.” Overall, Malaysia could provide an attractive investment option to foreign property buyers, Lai added. “So I’d put it this way: Malaysia gives you Singapore-style comfort at close to Thai prices,” he said. “That combination is hard to find anywhere else in the region. The one thing buyers should accept is that it’s a steadier, slower-growth market, not a place to flip property.”

title: Cornell University boss breaks silence over rape case uproar
description: Michael Kotlikoff pledged greater transparency and acknowledged that the university could ‘do better’ amid ‘distrust’ in the community.
content: Cornell University president Michael Kotlikoff said he was “deeply disturbed” by a student’s 2024 rape allegation that has drawn national outrage. “My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said in a video message released on Saturday, saying the university must “do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe” from happening again. Lawyers for a Jane Doe last month filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, its leaders, the Chi Phi fraternity, her sorority and seven men, saying she was given drugs and alcohol and assaulted. The men have largely remained silent. Lawyers for at least three of them have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing. The university has defended aspects of its handling of the cases, while the president acknowledged on Saturday it could “do better”. “There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken and to be more transparent,” he said, acknowledging questions about the investigation and “distrust” in the community. Next week, Cornell’s Board of Trustees will announce an independent review by an outside law firm to investigate all aspects of Cornell’s handling of the case, the university’s president said. “We will not wait for the investigation or the review to be completed before we act,” Kotlikoff said. “The review should inform additional changes, not delay improvements already under way or ones we know we can make today.” Cornell plans a “serious look” at fraternities and sororities, focusing on accountability, transparency and members’ responsibility to intervene when someone is at risk, Kotlikoff said. He did not announce specific new restrictions on Greek life. New York Governor Kathy Hochul criticised the university police and district attorney’s handling of the case and appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case. James’ office will have the authority to prosecute offences and present evidence to a grand jury if warranted – a decision Kotlikoff said he supports. He pledged the university’s “full support” for legislative efforts to change state sexual assault laws and said Cornell eventually plans to use its research expertise to study sexual assault, trauma, intoxication and consent and promote policies beyond its campus.

title: Young Chinese hire ‘life stand-ins’ to cook and care for elderly parents amid booming trend
description: Outsourcing life’s mundane tasks buys us freedom, but risks relinquishing the experience of living, says online observer.
content: From cooking and attending hospital visits to doing the actual quarrelling, paid “life stand-ins” are stepping in to manage these tasks, along with errands and awkward moments that many young Chinese would rather avoid. This trend, known as the “stand-in economy,” is gaining traction among time-strapped consumers who are willing to pay for convenience when daily responsibilities exceed their time, patience, or expertise. First widely reported by mainland media in 2024, the movement has since blossomed into a vast market for highly personalised errand services. On RedNote, posts about paid handicraft and assembly assistance have garnered over 120 million views. For example, some users buy intricate Lego sets but lack the time needed to assemble them, opting instead to hire professional builders. Customers can arrange either a home visit or mail their Lego sets to the assembler. Fees typically range from 200 yuan (US$30) to 1,000 yuan, depending on the complexity and required labour. The services offered have also begun to take on increasingly unconventional forms. In September, a man surnamed Kong in Guangzhou in southern China drew considerable attention by promoting his paid “arguing stand-in” service on the street. He charges 50 yuan for online disputes and 188 yuan for unlimited in-person sessions. Kong asserts that his method relies on persuasion rather than aggression and refuses requests involving threats, debt collection, or physical altercations. In another example, a woman named Mihan in Hangzhou, southeastern China’s Zhejiang province, started charging neighbours three yuan to take out their rubbish or 99 yuan for a monthly package. Within three days, she secured over 20 clients and later expanded her services to include parcel collection and holiday cat-feeding. On second-hand marketplaces and errand-running platforms, users can also pay between 10 and 30 yuan for someone to stand in line at popular restaurants. In Shenzhen, southern China, some young workers living alone take this concept further. One online user reportedly pays 2,500 yuan (US$370) a month for daily home-cooked meals. Other services address emotional needs as well. A woman from Zhejiang, known by her surname Jin, once accepted a 50-yuan request to visit a hospital patient and brought gifts and greetings on behalf of her client. Another service provider in Shenzhen charges 300 yuan for two-hour visits to elderly individuals, which include conversation and cooking. Economists regard this trend as an extension of China’s “lazy economy,” whereby consumers use money to optimise the value of their time. Li Na, an associate professor at Jimei University’s School of Finance and Economics, stated to the media that such services could enhance efficiency and personal well-being while generating new forms of employment. However, the largely private, peer-to-peer nature of these transactions raises concerns regarding fraud, privacy violations, and challenges in seeking recourse when services do not meet expectations. One online observer captured the overarching unease with this thought: “When more and more of life’s trivial tasks can be solved with money, are we gaining greater freedom – or quietly relinquishing part of the experience of living?”

title: Quality over quantity: China’s AI microdrama producers battle viewer fatigue
description: Challenge has shifted from making videos at low cost to standing out in a market saturated with lookalike productions, creators say.
content: Two decades after stepping away from the spotlight, iconic actress Joey Wong made an unexpected return to the screen – not through a traditional production, but via artificial intelligence-powered reconstruction. In a two-minute video by NetEase this summer, Wong, one of the most well-known actresses of the 1980s and 90s, had some of her most celebrated roles recreated, including the beautiful ghost in A Chinese Ghost Story and an alluring snake demon in Green Snake. The revival is just the tip of an industry-wide pivot, as AI-generated short dramas have dominated the burgeoning mini-drama market. Known for the fast-paced storylines and frequent twists, microdramas typically run just a few minutes per episode. More than 90 per cent of the 430,000 microdramas launched online in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, according to the National Radio and Television Administration, China’s broadcasting regulator. Producers said AI video-generation tools had unlocked storytelling possibilities that were previously constrained by budget limitations. “Many online novels are built around action, suspense or imagined worlds that would require expensive sets and visual effects in live action,” said Bai Jianyue, a producer at a Shenzhen-based AI comic-drama distribution platform. “AI makes those stories much more feasible to produce.” Some viewers said they were willing to pay for higher-quality AI dramas, particularly when the technology could bring fantasy worlds from popular online novels to the screen. “Some novels have worlds that only AI can really recreate,” said a user named “Huifei de Kuromi” on social media platform RedNote, adding that she would pay for well-produced adaptations of popular books or games. Others, however, said they had grown weary of increasingly similar content. “Once one drama becomes a hit, a whole series of substitutes follows, changing the dynasty or the gender and calling it a new story,” said RedNote user “Liulang de Mao”. “The result is that you can often tell how a drama will end just from the beginning.” Being able to generate video is not the same as reliably delivering an entire series Robin Luo, Synintell Pictures Producers echoed those concerns, saying it had become difficult to stand out in an increasingly crowded market. “Being able to generate video is not the same as reliably delivering an entire series,” said Robin Luo, founder of Synintell Pictures. Luo said maintaining consistent characters, performances and storytelling across dozens of episodes remained difficult. As more studios gained access to video-generation tools, competition was shifting towards scripts, directing, production workflows and audience retention. Regulators and industry leaders have also begun focusing more attention on live-action productions. Wang Xiaoliang, an official from the broadcasting regulator, last month called on platforms to establish dedicated sections for live-action productions and provide financial support for high-quality content. That followed commitments of at least 6 billion yuan (US$894 million) from six major platforms, including those operated by ByteDance and Kuaishou Technology, to support live-action microdramas under a government-backed initiative. Meanwhile, oversight of AI-generated productions has tightened. A rule that took effect this month requires episodes to carry prominent labels identifying AI-generated content. At last week’s meeting, Wang also urged studios to obtain consent before using people’s faces and voices. Zhou Xiangxiang, founder of Moli OPC AI Comic Drama Base, said her team had begun using authorised likenesses of its own staff and signing agreements with performers to create digital characters. Although licensing would slightly increase production costs, it could significantly lower platform review costs, as AI-generated characters that appeared too similar to real people delayed releases, Zhou said. Her company had not yet experienced a noticeable change in business because existing annual contracts with platforms remained in place, she said.

title: Japan’s tame answer to jobseeker sex harassment: name and shame
description: After years of predatory recruiters targeting graduates, new rules are now in place – but critics say they lack real teeth.
content: Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives. For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process. And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment. Campaigners and advocates have welcomed the change, but say it lacks teeth and came years too late, even as societal attitudes may have already moved ahead of it. “It is good that this has happened, but it has taken five years of discussions to get to the point where it has become law,” said Chisato Kitanaka, an associate professor of sociology at Hiroshima University who advises the government on gender issues. “Government measures against sexual harassment in Japan are very weak, including this kind of harassment.” Amendments to the Equal Employment Opportunity Act that took effect last week address harassment in its many forms and settings, from misbehaviour in the office to verbal abuse and threats from customers in shops, taxis and elsewhere. One section deals specifically with what the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare terms “job-seeking sexual harassment”. The ministry’s website lists examples: staff who make sexual jokes or tease applicants such that it causes distress, who pressure them into a sexual relationship, or who repeatedly invite them to one-to-one meals or drinks. Employers are now legally required to take steps to stop their staff harassing applicants in this way, with corporate compliance enforced through the threat of publicly shaming offending companies and exposing them to the prospect of civil lawsuits and financial damages. Kitanaka called the changes a “step in the right direction”, but said they did not go far enough. “There is no formal punishment for companies that let this happen, with the only real sanction the ministry releasing the name of the company publicly,” she said. She expects large companies and organisations to enforce the rules more stringently than smaller firms, even as part-time workers, freelancers and others in precarious jobs continue to have too few protections. Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, agreed that reform was long overdue. “This isn’t something that has only been happening in recent years and is now being addressed,” she said. “It has been going on for decades.” One in three A survey of 1,000 recent jobseekers conducted by Japan’s labour ministry in 2023 showed that 31.9 per cent of respondents – nearly one in three – reported being harassed. Unnecessary physical contact and questions about sexual matters were each cited by over 25 per cent of the harassed respondents, while nearly 29 per cent said they were on the receiving end of sexual jokes and teasing. One in four of the men and women who had these experiences reported feeling less motivated in their job search and more than one in three said they felt “anger, dissatisfaction or anxiety”. For two dozen or so, the effect on their mental health was such that they required hospital treatment. In the past, companies typically tried to hush up such incidents, but a number of court cases over the years have shone a spotlight on the issue. In 2019, a male construction company employee was charged with indecent assault after allegedly convincing a university student to come to his flat on the pretext of helping her prepare for an interview. His employer, Obayashi Corp, apologised and promised to “urgently review” its procedures, subsequently setting up a harassment prevention office and conducting “emergency training” for staff involved in recruitment. Prosecutors ultimately dropped charges against the man without publicly providing a reason. Whether he kept his job is unknown. That same year, a 24-year-old trading company employee was arrested and charged with sexual assault and theft after a student he met through a networking app accused him of getting her drunk and using a stolen key to molest her in her hotel room. His employer, Sumitomo Corp, issued a statement soon after his arrest, confirming his disciplinary dismissal. One of the most serious cases involved Kenshiro Maruta, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2023 for drugging and raping at least 10 female students who connected with him through apps designed to match jobseekers with university alumni and career counsellors. His employer, Recruit Communications, fired Maruta following his arrest and launched an internal investigation, vowing to never allow such an outrage happen again. “There have been many incidents in the past and gradually the government has changed its policies,” said Kitanaka, the sociologist. “Now, at last, they have changed the law.” ‘Not acceptable today’ Back in the 1980s, when gender studies lecturer Kawakami first joined Japan’s workforce, it was still dominated by men. Women had to work harder than their male counterparts just to be taken seriously or to advance, she said. “Young women in the past did not feel that they could speak out when this happened to them because they wanted to get a good job and career,” she said of harassment. Kawakami has watched attitudes shift in recent years, however, especially among the young women at her university preparing to start their careers. “I think it has changed quite a lot,” she said. “There is far greater awareness among working people and companies about what constitutes unacceptable behaviour, and I believe employers are far less willing to tolerate sexual harassment.” And while the threat of public naming and shaming a company might seem tame compared to criminal convictions, Kawakami says the threat “is a powerful one”. “Companies are desperate to find capable and qualified staff nowadays, and negative publicity that would go with a sexual harassment accusation would be hugely damaging,” she said. “Young women have lots of work options at the moment. Why would they go to a company that fails to act in a situation like this?” One recent graduate, who declined to be named, told This Week in Asia that outlawing “clearly sexist” comments or actions by recruiters was a good idea, even if she did not believe that women of her generation would put up with such behaviour. “If one of my friends were asked something inappropriate in an interview or were invited out for drinks, I’m certain that the man would be shouted at and his company would hear about it,” she said. “It’s just not acceptable today.”

title: Opinion | To become a dog-friendly city, Hong Kong needs dog literacy
description: Education isn’t just for pet owners – it’s essential for anyone sharing public space, particularly after recent severe dog attacks.
content: Since July, Hong Kong has permitted dogs in approved dining premises under a tightly regulated scheme. More than 2,200 restaurants applied, with more than 980 taking part within the first month. On the surface, these are straightforward changes to the rules around where dogs are allowed. But they reflect something more significant: a changing relationship between Hong Kong and the dogs who also call it home. Small companion breeds are familiar in urban life, while larger dogs, local mixed breeds and strays can occupy a very different place in the public imagination. This difference matters because perceptions of dogs can shape how incidents are understood and addressed. Hong Kong is not suddenly becoming a dog-friendly city. It is beginning to work out what one might look like. But that conversation has become more difficult after three recent incidents involving dogs. In August, a 60kg dog in Yuen Long attacked and killed two smaller dogs in separate incidents. Just a month before these incidents, the dog had been briefly detained by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) in connection with another dog attack. Its keeper was warned the dog had to be kept under proper control. Also in August, a 33-year-old woman was killed at the pet hotel and training facility she operated in Ta Kwu Ling after being attacked by a 30kg mixed-breed dog. The stray had reportedly been taken in by a dog-welfare volunteer and a kennel; it had been transferred to the facility while awaiting adoption. Then this month, a 27-year-old woman died after a suspected dog attack in Yuen Long; CCTV showed three dogs chasing her while she was cycling home. Three dogs were subsequently captured and taken to the AFCD for examination, although it has not confirmed if they were involved. These cases are horrifying and deserve a serious investigation; there should be accountability. If a dog has displayed dangerous behaviour, the focus should be on intervention, ownership and enforcement. If a rescued animal is placed in a professional facility, assessment, disclosure, handling and suitability for adoption are a focus. If free-roaming dogs are responsible for an attack, management, identification and enforcement come into the picture. It requires what I would call “dog literacy”: understanding enough about dogs to recognise what we are seeing, while being clear about where the responsibility lies. It means understanding how dogs may respond to fear, stress, territory, other animals and sudden movement, and knowing when to give an unfamiliar dog space. None of this is to excuse an uncontrolled or dangerous dog; responsibility remains with its owner. Public education cannot compensate for poor ownership. But it can be another layer of prevention, particularly when people understand how to give unfamiliar dogs space and recognise situations that may escalate. I have spent years working alongside animal welfare groups on Lantau Island, seeing dogs rescued from the streets, fostered, rehabilitated and eventually brought into homes. I have also seen how often difficulties are less about a dog being inherently “good” or “bad” than about people failing to understand what the animal in front of them is communicating. A puppy that seems easy to manage may present very different challenges as it reaches adolescence. A dog that behaves perfectly in a quiet home may react very differently to children, unfamiliar dogs, bicycles, traffic or Hong Kong’s compressed environment. Breed and physical capability matter too. A 60kg dog plainly has greater capacity to cause serious injury than a small dog. Genetics, breeding, socialisation and environment can influence behaviour.
