But breed is not behaviour, and a label cannot tell us everything about an individual animal. There is another part of this discussion that receives less attention: what happens to rescued and abandoned dogs. Rescue organisations also face constraints around space, facilities and resources. If Hong Kong wants fewer dogs on the streets, it also needs somewhere lawful and suitable for rescued animals to go. A dog-friendly city also has to work for people without dogs. Some may be frightened of them, uncomfortable around them, or have cultural or religious reasons for preferring to keep a distance. Some simply do not want to share a restaurant, lift or pavement with an animal. Those preferences deserve to be respected. As dogs become a more visible part of public life, basic knowledge about them should become less niche, giving Hong Kong a chance to examine owners’ responsibilities, enforcement, education and support for animal welfare organisations. We do not need everyone to become an expert on dogs. But we can become better at recognising that different dogs, circumstances and risks require different responses. Working alongside animal welfare groups has changed the way I see dogs. I notice things I once would have missed: when a dog is uncomfortable, needs space or its attention has suddenly shifted. That does not make me able to predict every dog behaviour. It simply makes me less likely to mistake one situation for another. As dogs become a more visible part of public life, Hong Kong has a chance to build that understanding into how we share our streets, restaurants and other public spaces. That means teaching ourselves and our children to recognise dogs’ boundaries, respond appropriately and understand the responsibilities that come with owning one. The three cases were horrific and deeply tragic. They were also different. Recognising those differences is part of what dog literacy should mean.

title: Trump shares Senator Tom Cotton’s phone number in daylight saving time clash
description: The US president urges people to call the Arkansas Republican, who opposes making daylight saving time permanent.
content: US President Donald Trump shared online the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator on Saturday in an escalating dispute over making daylight saving time permanent. In a social media post, the president urged people to call a phone number he said belonged to Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican who opposes the Trump-backed Sunshine Protection Act. The act would end the twice-yearly practice ‌of changing clocks by one hour. Trump says most Americans want more afternoon sunlight, but Cotton has argued the change would plunge early risers into darkness in winter. “Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump said on social media. Cotton did not directly respond to Trump’s statement, but posted on social media: “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.” When Reuters called the number Trump gave ⁠for Cotton, it went directly to a voicemail box that did not identify itself as belonging to the senator. Supporters of permanent daylight saving time say adjusting clocks disrupts sleep and increases road ‌accidents, while critics argue later winter sunrises would leave children travelling to school and commuters heading to work in the dark. Trump on Saturday published three social media posts – one in the morning and two in the afternoon – focused on daylight saving time. In a subsequent five-minute session ‌with journalists at the White House, he spent more than half the time talking about the twice-yearly practice of changing clocks by one hour. Most US states have ⁠observed the time switch since the 1960s. Clocks ⁠this year are slated to switch back to standard time on November 1. “It discombobulates everybody,” Trump said, complaining to reporters that losing afternoon daylight caused lateness for meetings and dinner and made it difficult to play more than ‌14 holes of golf. He also suggested that more daylight would reduce crime. “You know who wants it? The farmers want it. You know who wants it? Sports want it,” Trump told reporters before heading to a campaign rally in Ohio. “Professional sports ‌and amateurs ‌that would like to play tennis at night, would like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes.” Trump, an avid golfer, earlier shared an ‌October 1 letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, writing: “The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments.” After Cotton published his ⁠statement, the president responded with a post that framed the matter in political terms. “Give the Republican Party a Senatorial WIN, for a change! … TAKE THE WIN TOM, JUST TAKE THE WIN! ⁠YOU NEED IT, AND SO DOES OUR BELOVED REPUBLICAN PARTY!” Trump said. Cotton is running for re-election but his race is not considered competitive, as Trump received more than 64 per cent of the Arkansas vote in the 2024 presidential election. The US House of Representatives passed the bill in July, but Cotton is not alone in the ‌Senate. Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, this week ‌called the bill “dead as disco” and said he did not think that Senate Majority Leader John Thune would bring the measure for a vote. The offices of Cotton and Thune did not respond to requests for comment. Saturday’s post targeting Cotton is not the first time Trump has shared a senator’s phone number to make a point. During his first presidential campaign in 2015, Trump read Senator Lindsey Graham’s phone number at a rally and dismissed the South Carolina Republican as an “idiot”. They later reconciled, with the late Graham becoming one of Trump’s highest-profile allies in Congress.

title: Hong Kong’s cancer research drawing global attention, says leading body’s chief
description: Cary Adams, CEO of the Union for International Cancer Control, hails the city’s tobacco control record as an example for others.
content: Hong Kong is playing a central role as part of a broader regional hub for research breakthroughs, the head of a leading global cancer organisation has said, adding that the city’s success in reducing its smoking rate has set an example for others to follow. Cary Adams, CEO of the Union for International Cancer Control, praised the city’s tobacco control efforts as the organisation held the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong for the first time late last month. “We’ve all become aware globally that the centre of intense research and breakthrough is coming from this part of the world,” Adams told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the congress. “It was important for us to be here so we can understand what is happening in China, what is happening in Hong Kong.” Recalling his attendance at a cancer conference last year, Adams described the growth in research activity in China. “It’s inspirational to see the research that’s going on in China and the volume of oncologists and researchers, academics working in this space,” he said. Adams said he was confident that further breakthroughs in understanding and treating cancer would come from China and elsewhere in Asia. “We want to be in the centre of where the research is taking place. That’s certainly one of the big reasons that we came to this region,” he said, explaining why the major cancer event was held in Hong Kong. Adams said other places hoped to learn from the city’s tobacco control efforts, which had helped bring its smoking rate down from 23.3 per cent in 1982 to 8.5 per cent last year. “This is unheard of around the world,” he said. “Coming to a place where they have been so incredibly successful, a lot of our community will come here, they want to know how that’s been achieved, what’s been done by the government. “They can go back to their countries and say, look, Hong Kong did it, we could do it. So that’s the source of inspiration that we’re looking for.” Tobacco use is a risk factor for cancer and was among the themes discussed at the congress in Hong Kong. Data published by the World Health Organization in 2024 showed that the global prevalence of tobacco use had fallen gradually, from 32.7 per cent in 2000 to an estimated 19.8 per cent in 2025. But as of 2024, 40 countries had yet to adopt any evidence-based tobacco-control measures. Hong Kong is striving to become an international hub for health and medical innovation, an ambition outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and included in policy addresses since 2023. Adams said the congress, which brought together over 2,000 healthcare delegates from more than 124 countries, could help the city achieve that goal by creating opportunities for ideas and partnerships. Professor Anne Lee Wing-mui, vice-chairwoman of the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society, which organised the congress in the city, said Hong Kong could make a greater contribution to the global fight against cancer. “Even though Hong Kong is small, we’re not small in terms of impact,” she said. Lee, a leading clinical oncologist in Hong Kong, said some cancers, such as liver and lung cancer, had different characteristics in Asian and Western patients. That gave Hong Kong an opportunity to conduct its own research and supplement existing knowledge, she said. She added that between 2021 and 2025, there were 12,000 cancer-related academic papers that had at least one co-author from Hong Kong, and 15 per cent of them were published in top journals. As Hong Kong sought to expand its research as part of its efforts to become an innovation hub, Lee said the city had already established credibility and trust in conducting studies to international standards. “It would be good to shift some of the research here to this part of the world because it’s much more cost-effective,” she said. “It’s much less expensive to conduct a clinical trial, and you need a variety and diversity of patient population to really come up with good data.” As Hong Kong strengthens its research ties with the mainland, including through the establishment of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone near the border, Lee said the city could draw on the Greater Bay Area’s population of 86 million for trials and studies. The bay area is a development blueprint that aims to turn Hong Kong, Macau and nine other cities in Guangdong province into a hi-tech economic and business powerhouse. Adams said collaboration with the mainland could give Hong Kong an edge in cancer research. “The number of oncologists, the number of researchers, the number of patients. The numbers are extraordinary,” he said. “That is a key competitive advantage when it comes to research in cancer treatment and care.”

title: Performing under pressure helps produce record-setting gold, medal totals for Hong Kong
description: Tennis star Coleman Wong, windsurfers, rugby teams help city to best showing since 1954 – and equestrians might add to that figure on Sunday.
content: There has been a common theme running through Hong Kong’s Asian Games gold medallists when it comes to talking about the pressure of being on top: Siobhan Haughey and James Christie both referred to it as a privilege, and it would not be a surprise to discover it is an entirely alien concept to Coleman Wong Chak-lam. Before Saturday, Hong Kong had never won a medal in men’s tennis at the Games, let alone gold. Faced with making history, adding another title to the city’s growing collection and securing a spot at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years, Wong did not even blink while wrapping up a straight-sets victory against Wu Yibing. Neither did the men’s rugby sevens team, who won their competition for the third straight time. In a seemingly inexorable march to the final over the course of three days, Hong Kong outscored their opponents 200-14, and then just for good measure thumped China 26-0 to win gold. Without peers in Asia, they have not lost at the Games since being beaten 24-12 in the 2014 final by Japan, and captain Christie said his side now wanted to be “bigger in the world”. “Being top of Asia is good, but we’re not happy to settle there,” he added. The victory was a fitting end to a record-setting day for Hong Kong’s athletes, who have now collected more gold, more silver and more medals in total than any of their predecessors dating back to the city’s first inclusion in the Games in 1954. In between Wong and the rugby team, windsurfers Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet added two more golds and the day ended with 11 – three more than a Hong Kong delegation have ever managed at a Games. The overnight tally, which included sailing silvers and bronze for the women’s rugby sevens team, stood at 54, with 19 and 24 of the other two metals respectively. The city’s equestrians may yet add to that figure on Sunday, just hours before the closing ceremony begins. By almost every metric, Hong Kong’s athletes have more than answered the challenge laid down by the city’s leader ahead of the Games. During the flag presentation ceremony, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu had exhorted them to “achieve even greater success” than the then-record display in Hangzhou. China, meanwhile, will again top the medal table, although with fewer across the board than when they hosted in 2023. With no riders competing in the final round of the individual jumping competition, the 169 golds in a total of 341 is some way short of the 201 and 383 last time. Hosts Japan have narrowed the gap slightly, improving to 83 golds and 269 overall from a position of 52 and 188. On Saturday, Wong started Hong Kong’s gold rush, taking the first chance he got to wrap up a 6-2, 6-4 victory while looking for all the world as though he were just firing down aces on the practice court, and not on the verge of doing something special. “Obviously I was a little bit nervous because I’ve never been to this stage before, but it was tough,” Wong said. “The whole match was really close.” Wong and Wu are no strangers on or off the court. Three years ago at the Games in Hangzhou, Wong knocked out his mainland rival in the third round; last November, Wu beat the 22-year-old in the semi-finals of the National Games. When they do clash, there is rarely much between them, making Saturday’s 93-minute final something of an outlier, no matter what Wong said afterwards. “Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the colour,” Wong said. “But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement.” Victory, when it came, prompted an emotional rush to the coaches’ box and hugs with friends and family, most of it witnessed by Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui. That next generation will have an opportunity to watch Wong on the Olympic stage, which Law said was “way more than a ticket to LA 2028 for himself, which is by itself a great achievement too”. “It’s a very happy moment indeed,” she told the South China Morning Post. “I’m very glad as we now have every reason to keep tennis in the Sports Institute’s Tier A, and our decision last year to make a special arrangement for tennis has paid off.” In a later television interview, Law said she was “thrilled” by the performances of all the city’s medal winners, adding that the government’s “investment in sports over the years has begun to bear fruit”. Wong was keen to highlight the influence of his parents, who said that if he wanted tennis badly enough, he should “just go for it”. The world No 100 was not convinced it was a common approach in the city. “They [other parents] overthink it,” Wong said. “Instead, if kids want to do it, let them give it a try first. This is a huge influence my family had on me.” Cheung, who claimed gold in the girls’ windsurfing, deferred school for a year to chase her Asian Games dream with the backing of her parents who told her “do what you like and don’t let yourself have a chance to regret it”. Law said the success highlighted how the athletes were becoming “more professional and elite”, although Wong’s attitude immediately after winning gold may sum it up best. Asked about the Olympics, the 22-year-old said the exciting prospect was “going to be amazing”, but there was plenty to do in the two years before then. “I feel my current form is pretty good and I want to keep maintaining it and continue improving, because I feel it’s never enough,” Wong said. “I still have 99 players ahead of me [in the ATP rankings], so I’ll keep climbing.” Additional reporting by Ng Kang-chung

title: Sinking city, rising rage: Bangkok’s floods fuel fury over government inaction
description: The Thai capital’s worst flooding in 15 years turns campaign promises into punchlines and threatens foreign investment.
content: As floodwaters surged from Bangkok’s drains, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping the floods unscathed. She had bought it less than a month earlier. “I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision last weekend to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.” Relentless rain paralysed Thailand’s capital this September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days. Bangkok, a city long plagued by a sinking feeling, went fully underwater. Not all of it, but enough of the city’s east and northeast to offer a terrifying teaser of what may lie ahead as this year’s “super” El Nino climate pattern intensifies into 2027. In the Khlong Chan neighbourhood of Bangkok’s Bang Kapi district, Fon – whose full name is Siraprapha Sangseeluem – was still stranded in her block of flats five days after the deluge. Her scathing assessment of the authorities’ handling of the floods? “I can say only one thing: the government is totally useless,” she said. Some of her neighbours have been even less diplomatic. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was met with a volley of abuse when he arrived to distribute relief to the flats last Sunday. The reception was similar in several places Anutin visited last week with his cabinet ministers and the media, in a city that largely did not vote for him. His Bhumjaithai Party did not win any of Bangkok’s constituency seats in February’s general election. Anger has boiled over in recent days at a government that seemed blindsided by a calamity meteorologists had warned was brewing, but which city and central authorities alike played down in the days before it struck. Anutin’s own campaign boast that his party would make the country “so rich, you won’t know what to do with your money” has come back to haunt him. “I feel so rich”, chanted crowds of angry residents sarcastically as he arrived to distribute food and water. I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Anutin acknowledged the backlash. “I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough,” he said. “The fact that people scolded me, criticised me … rest assured that I’ve heard you and I’m not ignoring you.” Critics are unconvinced, however. “If the measurement of the prime minister’s job is to manage the situation, to bring calm, a sense of trust … then he fails miserably,” said political commentator Voranai Vanijaka. On September 25, as floods swallowed Bangkok’s roads, homes, shops and restaurants, residents struggled to find their bearings. Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, normally hypervigilant, appeared caught off guard by the speed and scale of the rising water. He apologised days later for delayed warnings and a slow start to the relief effort. Anutin, who is also the interior minister, cut short a diplomatic visit to London to oversee the response. His initial absence was nonetheless felt in Thailand’s highly centralised, hierarchical political system, with key officials seeming reluctant to make snap decisions without him. On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers blasted the government’s flood response, criticising everything from slow warnings to the sluggish relief effort. Rain and floods are unpredictable and the lack of comprehensive flood defences of the kind found in Singapore, Shanghai or Amsterdam is the failing of successive Thai governments. But critics still say Anutin was caught flat-footed. “As a leader, you are the man in charge, and you have to take control of the situation,” Voranai said. “What he chose to do instead – hit the streets, pass out food, apparently pass out cash, walk through [flood]water with no shoes on – was political marketing. Political marketing is always part of politics … but he can’t forget to be the man in charge.” Hotter, wetter, deadlier As the planet heats to unprecedented and dangerous levels, extreme weather events are becoming ever more erratic and destructive, presenting governments everywhere with challenges many are ill prepared to meet. As of Wednesday, Japan’s capital had logged 35 consecutive days of rain – its longest streak on record – while wildfires continue to rage in Indonesia’s Kalimantan region, sending toxic haze across borders to Singapore and Malaysia. Thailand’s recent floods have cost at least 40 people their lives, with estimates of the damage running to hundreds of millions of US dollars. In Bangkok, the floods were the worst in 15 years, filling drains and canals to capacity and affecting roughly one-tenth of the capital. The country’s southern provinces, where the rainy season typically peaks between November and January, are now bracing for a similar onslaught. Bangkok’s misfortune has been decades in the making. The city’s ever-expanding urban sprawl is slowly sinking into the soft clay beneath it. Concrete has spread upwards and outwards far faster than investment in infrastructure, especially drainage – effectively turning the built-up city centre into a basin with few natural outlets or floodplains. It floods easily in large storms and in the increasingly common “rain bombs” that dump vast quantities of water on the city in a matter of hours. In 2011, the worst floods in recent memory submerged the north of Bangkok, killing dozens and leaving parts of the capital up to two metres (6½ feet) under water for weeks on end. This year’s floods, which may not be over yet, were the result of ceaseless rains overwhelming drains and inundating entire neighbourhoods, including affluent ones, with filthy, sludge-filled floodwater. Drowning in delays On Tuesday, Anutin’s cabinet approved a 160 billion baht (US$4.8 billion) plan to divert floodwaters away from the capital. It includes a new canal from Chai Nat province that aims to relieve pressure on the Chao Phraya River, which currently carries run-off from northern and central Thailand straight through Bangkok. But that project is slated to take eight years to complete and critics say more needs to be done about the country’s sclerotic decision-making in the meantime. Thailand’s hulking bureaucracy meant overlapping agencies were often left duplicating work as they deferred to one another, said Winyu “John” Wongsurawat, an actor turned political commentator and podcaster. “When a crisis hits, they turn to the prime minister. Only then does the prime minister come in and say, ‘OK, do this.’ The crisis passes, and the water recedes before any real solution is reached,” he said. “This isn’t limited to Bangkok. We can see it happening all over the country. Bangkok gets more attention because people there are louder, let’s be honest, it’s the capital.” The central provinces of Ayutthaya and Ang Thong regularly endured weeks or months of flooding, Winyu said, “but just don’t make big news”. A government that is prioritising growth and foreign investment now faces a conundrum. Most of Thailand’s data centres, and the supply chains for printed circuit boards and semiconductors that go with them, are being built in and around Bangkok, central Ayutthaya and the country’s eastern provinces. All are low-lying and highly flood prone. The 2011 floods hammered the electronics and car industries of Thailand’s central provinces. How a government with a sky-high ratio of debt to gross domestic product will pay for far-reaching flood resilience, public compensation and clean-up costs that climb each year remains unclear. Other long-term economic risks are also emerging. “Repeated calamities from floods in Bangkok and other provinces pose challenges to Thailand’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination,” said Pavida Pananond, a professor of international business at Thammasat Business School. Companies pouring billions of US dollars into tech infrastructure “would be at a higher risk given Thailand’s frequent floods”, she said, adding that the latest deluge came just as the nation was trying to attract more foreign investment “in the era of global supply chain shifts”.

title: 7 thematic jewellery collections for October: Bulgari, Chanel, Sabyasachi and more
description: Bibi Van Der Velden’s scarab rings, Bulgari’s Tubogas bracelets and Sabyasachi’s Byzantine-inspired Met Gala pieces lead this month’s stand-out jewellery releases.
content: Rooted in ancient symbols and Renaissance architecture, this season’s stand-out jewellery collections bring fresh energy to iconic motifs and precious gemstones. Bibi Van Der Velden From ancient Egypt to the art deco movement, the scarab motif has been a near-constant in jewellery. Dutch designer Bibi Van Der Velden is a big fan, with her scarab rings becoming a signature of her brand. The designer recently expanded her collection with The Scarab Pinky Rings, five smaller rings designed specifically for the pinky. Made in yellow gold embellished with white diamonds, the five creations are adorned with colourful stones ranging from ebony and malachite to pink opal, turquoise, spinel and tourmaline. Bulgari Bulgari never shies away from eye-catching colour combinations. The Roman jeweller’s Tubogas bracelets each feature a rubellite, tourmaline or tanzanite as the centrepiece, flanked by complementary accent stones as well as diamonds. All three pieces successfully combine chromatic extravagance with sleek geometric lines. Chanel One of Chanel’s signature motifs, the camellia takes pride of place in this tiered necklace. Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel famously started wearing a white camellia pinned to her belt in 1913 and later continued with it in her creations. Since then, the flower, which famously doesn’t have a scent, has appeared in pieces ranging from handbags to jewels. In this multi-strand necklace, the petals of the delicate flower are recreated in yellow gold and diamonds. Mara Paris The geometry of Mara Paris’ jewels is meant to evoke the architecture of the buildings surrounding the brand’s recently opened showroom on Rue de la Paix in Paris. Designer Ayça Özbank also looked at the facades of Italian palazzos and the work of Italian Renaissance thinkers such as Leon Battista Alberti and Andrea Palladio. Those references translate into pieces where reeded surfaces and asymmetrically set diamonds create striking shapes that evoke motion and fluidity. Sabyasachi Luxury Indian house Sabyasachi begins a multi-year collaboration with The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York with a high jewellery collection that pays tribute to the art of the Byzantine Empire. The range, which debuted at New York Fashion Week last month, features statement pieces such as a necklace with a tiger-claw pendant inspired by a 12th century bone-ivory carved panel depicting animals, and a wrist cuff re-creating the engravings of a 3rd century Roman frieze. Spinelli Kilcollin If you’re a fan of the marquise cut, the recently launched Wren line from Los Angeles-based Spinelli Kilcollin is especially for you. The pointed, elongated form of the marquise cut diamond takes centre stage in the necklaces, rings and earrings of the collection. Like all Spinelli Kilcollin creations, the Wren pieces stand out for their modular construction, allowing the diamonds and bands to move and adapt in sync with the wearer’s movements. Type Founded by Panamanian designer Sara Bassan, Type is a jewellery brand to watch. Its Leggo collection is great for those who approach jewellery like fashion while still appreciating timeless creations made with precious gemstones. Perfect for stacking, the playful range includes graphic pieces embellished with gems like amethyst and tourmaline, and necklaces and bracelets with fringe accents in white diamonds. Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Editorial | No silver bullet for Hong Kong’s falling birth rate
description: The government is right to acknowledge cash handouts are just one part of a broader strategy to make raising children viable.
content: Despite a government cash incentive for young couples to have children, Hong Kong’s birth rate continues to fall. It is driving the ageing of a society in which one in four people is projected to be 65 or over by 2028. Unless the trend is arrested, one in three residents is projected to be 65 or over by the 2040s. One projection puts the number of elderly residents at 2.74 million by 2046. Granted, it is not all bad news. One reason for the population ageing is increased longevity. But the fact remains that we can expect proportionately fewer younger people to support more elderly residents, while proportionately more people may need elderly care. As a result, three years ago, the government launched its HK$20,000 baby-bonus scheme to lift the birth rate, setting aside HK$2.28 billion (US$291 million) to fund it over three years. The Labour and Welfare Bureau reported that, as of February, more than 40 per cent was unclaimed. Declining fertility remains the broader trend. Hong Kong saw a record low of only 31,714 registered births in 2025 – a far cry from official projections made in 2024 that the number of births could rise from about 32,500 in 2022, during Covid-affected times, to around 39,000 a year. By April, the disappointing outcome had prompted the government to review the scheme six months before it was due to end. Meanwhile, the number of births has continued to fall. The city recorded 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026, the lowest since official records began in 1962. And in the first eight months of this year, the city saw only 19,255 births, a 10 per cent drop compared with the same period in 2025. A survey of 1,166 young people aged 13 to 29, released last year by the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups, found that only 36.5 per cent were interested in having children, while 30.6 per cent did not want any at all. The reasons for such disinterest are understandably varied and highly personal. Job insecurity in the age of disruption by artificial intelligence, the costs of education and an unwillingness to make lifestyle trade-offs are likely to play a part. Nonetheless, the government has doubled down on the baby bonus commitment, with added tax and housing incentives. In his recent policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu not only extended the scheme for another three years, but also raised the cash bonus for second and subsequent children to HK$30,000, and the tax allowance for such children from HK$140,000 to HK$160,000. Other measures include waiving stamp duties for families who buy properties from one year before to two years after childbirth, capped at HK$20,000, and raising the mortgage loan-to-value ratio for families with newborns applying for subsidised flats to ease their down payment burden. As University of Hong Kong economics professor Michael Wong pointed out, the lack of affordable housing was a critical problem for young families. The goal is to create a conducive environment for childbearing, Lee said. This includes addressing not just financial pressures but also workplace demands and childcare needs. It is worth noting that women make up just slightly more than half of university students and graduates in Hong Kong. As childcare still tends to fall on women, if higher-educated women are to balance raising children with a professional life, they need access to affordable quality childcare while working, and job and income protection while parenting. The baby bonus cannot address such structural issues. The revamped scheme should be monitored for opportunities for family-friendly outcomes apart from handouts, which can soon be exhausted by normal child-rearing expenses. Lee rightly acknowledged that even if economic factors were the main considerations, no single payment could guarantee an increase in births. “These are very personal matters,” he said. The authorities had sought to ease the burden on working parents by expanding childcare and after-school care services. Along with economic measures, that is the right approach to tackling a complex issue. To really make a difference, the government should consider further enhancing these schemes.

title: Fibre or protein – which is more important? ‘It’s about balance,’ experts say
description: Dietitians explain why protein and fibre are key for the body, what foods they are in and how many of us should be eating much more fibre.
content: With proteinmaxxing and fibremaxxing trends both taking over, it can be difficult to understand which is more important. Should we focus on eating enough protein each day and hitting our targets, or should fibre be the priority for gut health and well-being? To answer these questions, we spoke to two dietitians, who shared their expert advice and explained how protein and fibre can complement each other. “Both are important,” says Dr Linia Patel, a UK-based women’s health dietitian, performance nutritionist and author. “It comes back to this idea that nutrition is never about nutrients in isolation. We see from evidence when we look at whether it’s longevity data or just weight management data – it’s about dietary pattern and it’s about balance.” What is protein? “When I think about protein, I’m going to talk about the biochemistry first,” Patel says. “Protein is a bit like Lego. You basically have these Lego pieces which are amino acids that are put together to form a beautiful design. Within those amino acids, some are non-essential and some are essential. “This brings me back to the idea that protein is important because there are essential amino acids that we can’t make from our body and we must get from our diet – protein is one of these multitasking nutrients.” Patel says protein is involved in everything from protecting muscle mass – including during weight management – to providing building blocks for immune cells and neurotransmitters, which carry messages between nerve cells. How much protein should be consumed in a day? Laura Tilt, registered dietitian and head of science at ready-meal supplier Field Doctor in the UK, says the recommended daily protein intake is around 0.75 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.34 grams per pound) per day. “Most people are eating over that amount – around 1.5 grams per kilo of body weight – but it will differ from person to person,” she adds. Patel says that with so much varying information and figures about protein consumption online, it is understandable that people may feel confused. “There are various conversations happening in the media that can get confusing and the amount is not black and white,” she says. Patel adds that it is not just about eating one big portion of protein but about spreading the intake throughout the day. “It’s about finding that sweet spot – and that sweet spot exists even for protein intake,” she says. “It’s not about overdoing it – you want to find the balance so that you are still able to bring in other key nutrients.” What is fibre? Patel explains: “Fibre is a type of carbohydrate.” “It sits in the overall macronutrient of carbohydrate and it’s found in plant-based foods. It’s basically a nutrient that we as humans cannot fully digest. “When we eat fibre, we don’t really just eat fibre for ourselves – we eat it for our gut microbiome – and in our gut microbiome are bacteria, viruses and fungi. Particularly, the bacteria in our microbiome love fibre – it’s like giving them their favourite thing.” Patel compares the body to a hotel containing numerous guests. “It’s this relationship between us and our guests,” she says. “If we give them the food they really like, they will use fibre to digest it to produce what we call short-chain fatty acids. These then do a whole host of things for our hotel, such as keep it clean, reduce inflammation and help our mood. “Fibre is really powerful because it indirectly helps us be healthier in the long run.” Tilt adds: “It helps to feed the gut bacteria in our large intestine. It plays a role in satiety so it helps us feel full after eating and it’s a short-term day-to-day thing for preventing constipation because it helps bulk out and soften our stools. “Longer term it can help to reduce our risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and bowel cancer.” How much fibre do we need? “The recommendations for fibre intake are 30 grams a day,” Patel says. “Again, splitting that fibre up is recommended; otherwise it will impact your digestive health.” However, many people are getting well below 30 grams. “There’s a massive gap we need to fill,” Patel says. “However, you also need to remember that with fibre, it’s slow and steady. It’s not about sprinting. “If you haven’t been eating a lot of fibre, you need to make sure that you’re increasing it slowly so that your digestive system and gut bacteria can adjust. “Make sure you’re hydrated, too.” What foods contain fibre? Fibre is primarily in pulses and legumes, whole grains, nuts, seeds, and fruit and vegetables. “The big dent is in your whole grains and your lentils and pulses,” Patel says. “If you want to bridge the gap and get foods with both protein and fibre, then the big thing is beans and legumes. They’re inexpensive, they contain per 100 grams about eight or nine grams of protein and about seven to eight grams of fibre. “Blending some white beans into a pasta sauce or adding some lentils into a curry or bolognese – those small changes actually help bridge the gap between protein and fibre.”

title: Latvia’s Andris Kulbergs wins big in election shadowed by Russia
description: Prime Minister Kulbergs, who is expected to form a pro-Ukrainian coalition, pledged to keep a hard line towards Moscow.
content: Latvian lawmakers on Sunday planned to begin negotiations to form a new government following a parliamentary election in which pro-Ukraine Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ‘s four-party coalition emerged with 35 per cent of the vote. The United List party is expected to take 42 seats in parliament, and a multiparty coalition will be needed to govern in a splintered political landscape. Parties must take at least 5 per cent of the vote to win parliamentary seats. The election saw a voter turnout above 51 per cent, according to election data. Nearly 1.56 million people in the nation of more than 1.8 million were entitled to choose the 100 members of the single-chamber Saeima for a four-year term. A businessman ⁠and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into ‌Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths. Latvia, like its Baltic neighbours Lithuania and Estonia, strongly supports Ukraine in its fight against Moscow’s invasion. It borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus. Saturday’s vote came as the small republic on Nato’s eastern flank contends with growing concern about potential Russian aggression. Last month, Kulbergs made a last-ditch attempt to prevent the removal of two Russian billionaires from the European Union’s sanctions list. Under his leadership, Latvia is likely to continue its strongly pro-Ukrainian course. Latvia’s economy has underperformed its Baltic neighbours for more than a decade and Kulbergs has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said. “Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that he can do ⁠things differently, bring some fresh energy,” he said. “This means the responsibility is huge. People expect him to deliver, but the question remains ‌whether he has the team to do it.” Kulbergs ‌pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line towards Moscow. “Any economic ties with Russia ⁠makes us weak. Yes, it ⁠can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters at his party’s headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of ‌the win. “It’s remarkably good. I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said. Th centrist United List was followed by the populist, ‌Maga-style Latvia First, ‌which was on 13.2 per cent. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote. Third in ‌the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.8 per cent, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hardline approach to the ⁠Kremlin, at 9 per cent. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5 per cent of gross domestic product, ⁠one of the highest levels in Nato. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority. Although pro-Russian parties increased their representation, Kits said they remained ‌sidelined and were unlikely to influence government ‌policy. The ethnic Russian minority ‌in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life that many see as discriminatory. Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and Nato allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south. Additional reporting by Bloomberg, Associated Press

title: Write to Win: What has been your favourite age to be, and why? (Round 4)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form . The deadline for voting is 12pm on Tuesday, October 6.
Mercury: Twelve years old was definitely a golden age for me because that was the year I transitioned to Form One. In my school, most students automatically move up to the secondary section. I remember the exact moment the realisation hit me: all my best friends were going to the same school. The sheer relief and excitement were indescribable. I was bursting with joy, knowing our friendship wouldn’t be cut short by going to different schools. We didn’t have to say heartbreaking goodbyes or face the intimidating world alone. Instead, we got to keep our daily routines intact. We could still meet at the same bus stop, eat lunch together and spend our commuting time laughing and gossiping.
Jupiter: My favourite age has always been six. In 2019, my family planned a holiday to Langkawi, Malaysia, which became one of my earliest and most cherished memories. We visited the archipelago’s famous Kilim Geoforest Park and savoured the city’s fragrant coconut rice dishes. I remember the little details vividly – like the hotel manager’s advice on handling mischievous monkeys and my six-year-old self running towards the balcony, only to collide face-first with the glass door. That trip remains unforgettable not just for the memories I made, but also because it was my last holiday before Covid-19 reshaped our lives. For me, being six meant experiencing joy, curiosity and family bonds that I will always treasure.
Venus: My favourite age was 12 because it strikes the perfect balance between childhood and independence. At 12, I officially became a pre-teen. I was old enough to hang out with friends on my own and even grab lunch for myself, which made me feel like an “adult in training”. I could enjoy staying up a bit later and try to understand adult conversations. However, the best part is that I still qualified for cheaper children’s tickets at theme parks and cinemas. At the same time, I did not have to worry about academics before starting secondary school. I got a taste of freedom while feeling grown-up.
Mars: My favourite age was 13, the year I was in Form Two. Now, as a Form Three student facing the immense pressure of choosing elective subjects, I often long for that carefree time. At 12, I was still adapting to the new secondary school environment and making friends. By the time I turned 13, although I still had schoolwork, it was much lighter, allowing me plenty of time to have fun with my friends. We grew incredibly close and made every school day memorable. After school, we would play volleyball and enjoy dessert together. In that wonderful year, true companionship blossomed without the weight of heavy academic stress. It remains the ultimate oasis of my early teenage years.
Neptune: Every moment in life can only be felt and lived once. While I can’t deny that my childhood was perhaps the most peaceful period of my life, it pales in comparison to the calamity and excitement I experience now at 17. As much as I cherished those earlier years, they are behind me. The new opportunities I have and the thrill of not knowing what comes next or who I will meet make this age my favourite, even though managing lessons and extracurricular activities is much more challenging. Ultimately, it’s not just the memories that make 17 my favourite age; it’s the fact that I am living in this moment that makes it so valuable.
Earth: Seventeen is my favourite age because it holds a sense of nostalgic magic. I have always been afraid of growing up, so this age feels like a precious sanctuary – a final line before the heavy expectations of the adult world take over completely. For me, this age exists in a delicate balance between the carefree days of youth and the impending dawn of adulthood. It is particularly special because this is when my world has begun to change. It is the time when I have started to take on real responsibilities, such as making important decisions about my future and universities. These experiences at 17 represent a beautiful, fleeting threshold where I can still enjoy being a teenager while gradually transitioning into adulthood.

title: China and Africa boost law enforcement ties in crackdown on cross-border cybercrime
description: Police cooperation allows Beijing to expand its security role without formal alliances or a large military footprint, observers say.
content: From online-gambling rings in eSwatini to SIM swapping in Kenya and cybercrime networks in Zambia, a wave of cross-border fraud is drawing African governments and China into closer security cooperation. China hosted East African security ministers and police chiefs in Lianyungang, Jiangsu province, on September 10 for talks on terrorism, kidnapping, online fraud and other cross-border threats. China’s public security minister, Wang Xiaohong, said Beijing would strengthen law-enforcement cooperation with East Africa and work jointly against terrorism, kidnapping, unlawful detention, and telecoms and online fraud. On the same day, China launched the International Alliance Combating Telecoms and Cyber Fraud, with 46 founding countries including Kenya. China said the alliance would promote regular law-enforcement cooperation, professional training, joint drills and coordinated action against cross-border telecoms fraud. Beijing seeks to protect Chinese citizens, companies and projects in Africa, where it has vast commercial interests, while African governments are seeking better access to police training, technology and intelligence sharing. Observers say police cooperation allows China to expand its security role without formal alliances or a large military footprint. According to Alessandro Arduino, an associate fellow in international security at Britain’s Royal United Services Institute, the Lianyungang initiative against telecoms and online fraud fits into Beijing’s broader effort to expand its security engagement with Africa under China’s Global Security Initiative. “Cyberfraud, an endemic problem in Africa, provides China with an especially useful entry point, as it is a genuine transnational security problem but one that also directly affects Chinese citizens and investments across Africa,” Arduino said. He added that Beijing was working through multilateral institutions and established policing networks, including Interpol, while promoting China-initiated mechanisms for intelligence sharing and coordinated law-enforcement operations. At the local level, Arduino said, “China is steadily expanding the training of African police and security officials, capacity building that is explicitly included in the China-Africa security agenda.” Just weeks before the Jiangsu talks, China warned its citizens to leave eSwatini over alleged telecoms fraud and gambling crimes. Chinese nationals and organisations already in eSwatini should “evacuate or relocate to relatively safer areas such as South Africa as soon as possible”, it warned in an August 25 advisory. The warning followed police raids in March on suspected illegal online gambling centres in and around Mbabane, Eswatini’s capital. Forty Chinese nationals arrested during the raids reportedly remained in detention in late August. Similar investigations are under way elsewhere in Africa, including in Zambia where authorities in August detained 79 people, including 11 Chinese nationals, in a raid on a suspected cybercrime operation in the capital Lusaka. On September 1, four Chinese nationals appeared in court in Kenyan capital Nairobi over an alleged SIM-swapping and money laundering scheme. Fraud networks have also targeted African jobseekers, including Kenyans, Ugandans and Ethiopians, who have been lured by false job offers to scam compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos. In May, Kenya’s foreign minister, Musalia Mudavadi, told lawmakers that 751 Kenyans had been rescued from scam compounds in Myanmar between 2022 and 2026. A further 406 were rescued in Cambodia in the first four months of this year, while 29 had been repatriated from Laos. “Over time, three Kenyans have reportedly lost their lives in the scam compounds due to illness, while one expectant lady passed on after the scammers attempted to forcefully terminate the pregnancy,” Mudavadi said. Beijing has signed dozens of public security and law enforcement agreements with African countries, including a deal in Beijing in 2024 with 14 members of the Eastern Africa Police Chiefs Cooperation Organisation. According to Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank Hudson Institute, China increasingly views telecoms fraud, cybercrime, kidnapping, human trafficking and related transnational crimes as threats that originate outside its borders and require coordinated international responses. Beijing had moved from an initial focus on trade and infrastructure towards police cooperation, counterterrorism, intelligence sharing and security capacity building, Odgaard said. The new International Alliance Combating Telecoms and Cyber Fraud “reflects an effort to build institutionalised security cooperation around issues where China sees growing governance gaps and direct national interests”, she added. However, Odgaard argued that the alliance was “unlikely to become a direct alternative” to established international and regional policing organisations any time soon. The involvement of 46 founding states, 34 observers, the United Nations and Interpol suggested it would initially complement existing organisations rather than replace them, she explained. However, over time, it could “evolve into a China-led security platform”, according to Odgaard. She said: “Because the alliance was initiated, hosted and largely shaped by China, it gives Beijing greater agenda-setting influence over transnational policing, training, technology transfer and law enforcement cooperation.” Georg Lammich, a senior researcher in international relations and African politics at the University of Duisburg-Essen in Germany, said African governments were seeking closer cooperation with China to gain access to training, technology, intelligence sharing and investigative capacity. “This should not simply be understood as China exporting a security model to Africa. There is also demand from African governments for additional partners and additional law-enforcement capacity,” said Lammich, who is also an affiliated researcher at the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. “Police cooperation gives China a way to deepen security relationships without relying on formal alliances or a large permanent military presence.”

title: Opinion | Baby bonuses fail to address the fear of falling behind
description: In highly competitive societies like Hong Kong and Singapore, subsidies and parental leave can’t overcome the cultural pressure keeping young couples from starting families.
content: When one of my seniors from medical school was pregnant during her surgical residency, she planned the exact date of her C-section so she could complete her training on time. When I asked why she didn’t consider taking maternity leave to recuperate afterwards, she said she couldn’t bring herself to lag behind her peers. “I didn’t want motherhood to slow me down,” she said. In medicine, it is common for women to delay childbearing until after their early career years, often into their mid-thirties or later. When I speak to friends in professional careers such as law, accounting and consulting, they echo a similar sentiment. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address on September 16 included an increased newborn bonus of HK$30,000 (US$3,800) for second and later children and extended the scheme for three years. Less than a month earlier, Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s National Day Rally speech promised almost S$70,000 (US$55,000) in direct support for every child. Two cities with record-low birth rates have both reached for cash. Hong Kong’s bonus has run since 2023 and paid out about HK$1.56 billion to more than 77,000 applicants as of the end of August. Births in the year to June were only 29,700, roughly half the 59,800 of a decade earlier. Singapore’s resident fertility rate fell to a record low 0.87 births per woman in 2025 despite similar support. The pattern starts early. Parents in both cities know what a child needs to get ahead: kindergarten interviews and tutorial centres in Hong Kong, Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) and enrichment classes in Singapore. Singaporean households spent S$1.8 billion on private tuition in 2023; in Hong Kong, parents invest more than HK$1 million in their child’s education from primary school to university – about three times the global average. Cash lowers the price of starting a family but doesn’t touch the price of falling behind. Subsidies don’t help a child underperforming at school or a parent pausing a career to raise one. Nirmala Rao, professor emeritus of education at the University of Hong Kong, sees the same thread running through both moments. “The cultural environment that shapes the anxieties of parents and children at the starting gate of education may also influence an adult’s hesitation at the crossroads between career and parenthood,” she said. The two cities are built the same way: globally connected financial hubs where talent is abundant and resources are scarce. Growing up in either, you imbibe the logic of survival early: work hard, be extremely good at what you do and watch your feet so you don’t trip. That mentality starts in school and carries into the workplace. In cities this contained and with social circles this established, everyone knows what everyone else is doing. Peer comparison is hard to shake. I did well enough to get into a good high school. Later on, I entered medical school, surrounded by the same friends. Years later, I work alongside those same people in the healthcare system and observe their career progression. Parenthood is essentially a forward-looking project, a bet on the future and a lifelong commitment. It’s hard to imagine a prospect of that sort as enticing; you already feel drained by keeping up in such a fast-paced society, much less bringing a child into one. When I picture having a child, my mind drifts to the paperwork, the parent-volunteering hours needed to get into the right kindergarten and the endless exams that follow through school. The thought makes me shudder. As reluctant as I am to subject my future child to the stress and competition I went through, could I bear to hold back? Eventually, the toll of excellence that parents levy on children becomes the burden children must carry. Neither the baby bonuses nor enhanced parental leave packages offered by both governments resolve the deep-seated structural and cultural issues at play preventing young couples from aspiring to have children. In an increasingly competitive world, a cheque can’t compete with a bet you’re weighing across the next few decades. Real change won’t come from subsidies or better leave policies, even though these matter. It has to come from what we consider a successful life. Protected parenting time or part-time job tracks don’t fix anything on their own if slowing down is still seen as falling behind. What counts as “having made it” has to change, or the choice of parenthood will keep looking irrational to the people making it. My senior was able to return to her studies and light clinical duties three weeks after giving birth. She completed her training on schedule.

title: Tennessee prisons chief resigning after botched execution of Christa Pike
description: Pike, one of the youngest US women ever sent to death row, is unconscious and on a ventilator after surviving two doses of a lethal drug.
content: The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning, Governor Bill Lee announced on Saturday, the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s stunning failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital. Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, will step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership. It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while an independent review determined what happened on Wednesday when the state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred,” Strada said. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Pike was taken to a hospital from prison on Wednesday night, where she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday. Hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and, as of late Thursday, were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital, which the state uses to execute prisoners, lawyers said. The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believes the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol”. Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said “it does nothing to help Christa now”. “What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.” Pike’s lawyers said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but could not get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again. Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital. Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department. When Strada was in Arizona, that state in 2022 resumed executions after a nearly eight-year break, following criticism about a 2014 execution that took about two hours as well as difficulties obtaining certain drugs.

title: Probe launched into luxury One Stanley project over alleged steel bar shortage
description: Buildings Department pulls in developer and contractors after report claims house has up to 75 per cent fewer steel bars than approved.
content: Authorities have launched a probe into the building quality of a luxury residential development in one of Hong Kong’s most expensive neighbourhoods in the Southern district after receiving a complaint from an owner that insufficient steel bars were used during construction. The Buildings Department said on Saturday it was “highly concerned about the incident” relating to One Stanley in Stanley, but stressed that its previous inspections did not find any imminent danger. The department said it would hold interviews with the developer, contractors and other relevant parties responsible for the development. Public concerns have been brewing since Friday after a report by the online property news platform WuChatProp alleged that an on-site inspection of a house found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts of the property. The number fell short by as much as 75 per cent of the approved building plans, according to the report. The property in question is a four-bedroom, 3,000 sq ft house, which the owner reportedly bought in 2024 for about HK$100 million. The irregularities were subsequently spotted by engineers and contractors hired by the owner during internal renovations, according to the report. The owner reported the case to the department but accused officials of inaction. In a statement on Saturday, the department confirmed it had received a complaint about the structural safety of the floor slabs in January this year. Officers conducted an inspection in March and determined that the overall building structure did not pose any significant danger, it said. “The [department] then launched an investigation into the case and also wrote to the registered structural engineer of the development, requesting a report and relevant information, including test reports and certificates for the materials concerned,” the department said. Inspections between June and September found that the concrete cover of one of the beams at the ground floor was not installed with wire mesh as required by the approved plan, and the steel reinforcement of some slabs deviated from the plan as well. The department was satisfied the irregularities would not “pose obvious danger”, but said it had been monitoring the situation and further investigations would be conducted. “The [department] … has written to the relevant parties, including the authorised person, the registered structural engineer, the registered contractor and the developer of the development, requesting interviews to assist in the investigation and to provide information,” it said. It warned that if the investigation found that any building professionals or contractors had violated the Buildings Ordinance, it would definitely follow up in a serious manner, including prosecuting and taking disciplinary action. One Stanley is at No 128 Wong Ma Kok Road. The upmarket residential development by K&K Property comprises 32 detached houses and 11 low-rise blocks containing 50 flats featuring sea views, with unit sizes ranging from about 1,800 square feet to over 7,000 square feet. The building contractor is Treasure Construction Engineering, a wholly owned subsidiary of China State Construction Development Holdings. The latest news posted in mid-August on developer K&K Property’s website said that strong sales had been registered at the project and another buyer had snapped up two “apartment units” at a total price of HK$47.4 million. According to news reports in late August, more than 50 units had been sold. In a statement, the developer said it was highly concerned and investigating the incident and would make necessary remedies to the affected property. “Our company has always placed great importance on the quality and safety of its development projects. “According to the information released by the Buildings Department, the department believes that the overall building structure of the property does not pose any significant danger. “Our company is currently conducting a detailed investigation and verification of the matter, including following up and reviewing relevant information with relevant professionals, and will fully co-operate with the [department’s] investigation,” it said. “If, upon investigation, any party is found to have made errors in construction quality or other related matters, the company will certainly provide remedial measures to the affected property in accordance with the laws and regulations and will hold the relevant parties accountable according to the law.”

title: Fifa Asean Cup: Gianni Infantino incurs Hong Kong fans’ wrath as city team claim trophy
description: Hosts beat Cambodia for silverware as Kai Tak Stadium crowd deliver lusty verdict on Fifa president’s leadership.
content: More than 30,000 Hong Kong fans gave Gianni Infantino their raucous verdict on his leadership of world football on Saturday, before and after watching the city team beat Cambodia 2-0 to be crowned inaugural Fifa Asean Challenge Cup champions. Infantino, the Fifa president, was lustily booed when he delivered the trophy to the pitch alongside local football association president Pui Kwan-kay before kick-off. When he returned to present the spoils to Hong Kong, the stadium PA was raised to an offensive, ear-splitting volume to drown out the jeers. In between, Matt Orr adroitly turned home a 41st-minute Sun Ming-him delivery, and Everton Camargo converted from the spot shortly after half-time as Hong Kong handsomely avenged an insipid 2-0 defeat by the same opponents four months ago. A substantial number of the 31,374 Kai Tak Stadium crowd chanted about a “Fifa mafia”, the words emblazoned on one banner, among other insults aimed at the global governing body. Roberto Losada, the Hong Kong head coach, refused to be drawn on whether Infantino should serve a fourth term as Fifa president after the Swiss lawyer’s plot to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was exposed this summer. “It’s not my job to say that; I have enough with my job,” Losada said. “I will focus on that and nothing else.” On securing silverware just four months after being appointed, Losada added: “We won the Chinese New Year Cup, but today Infantino gave us the trophy, so it’s beautiful. “The fans were the 12th player. They gave the breath that the players needed during the tough times in the game. Playing 12 against 11 made a huge difference.” Earlier in the day, Infantino posted on Instagram images of himself alongside Pui and Eric Fok Kai-shan, chairman of the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA), from a children’s coaching session at the Jockey Club HKFA Football Training Centre. Fifa ambassadors Dimitar Berbatov and Pedro, formerly of Manchester United and Barcelona, respectively, were also present. Fok and Pui both embraced Infantino as Tan Chun-lok, Hong Kong’s outstanding captain, hoisted the silverware. In a rather saccharine message accompanying the social media pictures, Infantino praised an “inspiring grass roots football activity, bringing joy, active play, and the right tools to children so they can chase their dreams”. “Empowering young girls and boys through sport is what our mission is all about, because football belongs to everyone everywhere,” Infantino added. Globetrotting to seal votes ahead of March’s presidential election, the 56-year-old can be expected to next surface on Monday in Indonesia for the final of the top-tier Fifa Asean Cup. The hosts will play Thailand after progressing on goals scored following an eye-popping 9-2 win over Bangladesh on Thursday. Struggling for fluency and creativity, Hong Kong rarely tested Keo Soksela in the Cambodia goal. Their intensity, energy and urgency overwhelmed the visitors, nonetheless, as the relentless pair of Tan and Wu Chun-ming threw a blanket over Cambodia forwards Iago Bento, Andres Nieto and Sieng Chanthea. “If it was a friendly I’d have rotated players, but we had to try to get the result and I take responsibility,” Koji Gyotoku, the head coach, said after he picked his strongest team against Timor-Leste on Wednesday, when Losada changed nine players for the victory over Brunei. “I regret that we lost but the atmosphere in the stadium was great.” Striker Chanthea had one first-half attempt comfortably held by Pong Cheuk-hei, while Nieto’s most notable contribution was to crumple to the floor following an apparent butt from Tsui Wang-kit. Both players were booked; in the case of Nieto, probably because Zhakypbekov Sanzhar, the referee, had grown tired of his gamesmanship. Philip Chan Siu-kwan twice shanked good openings off target, while Camargo had a strike from an acute angle deflected wide, before the dependable Sun aimed over a precise ball for Orr to net his third goal in three matches. A goal scorer against Laos in the opening group fixture, Sun said: “This has been a great opportunity for us, and we are so happy to get this result with our great fans.” Having benefited from the VAR ruling that decreed Tsui did not deserve a red card, Hong Kong had the video officials to thank again when they were awarded a 58th-minute penalty. Trying to fasten onto a low cross from Orr, Chan tumbled over the awkwardly outstretched leg of Cheng. Camargo smacked the loose ball into the body of Takaki Oze, but play was brought back for Sanzhar to check his screen. A chant of “penalty” rolled around the arena, the official obliged, and Camargo did the rest. “It’s been an amazing tournament for us, and we got the result we committed to,” Losada said. “We’re in the process of changing some things and during this time we’ll sometimes look erratic. In this competition we’ve proved we have the tools. We still have a lot to improve but we’ll ensure the future of Hong Kong football.” An HKFA spokeswoman intervened to stop Losada answering when he was asked about plans for the November Fifa window. “Today is a day to enjoy, and from tomorrow we’ll start to work again,” Losada said.

title: Chinese art takes long march home from US museums
description: Works amassed by America’s Gilded Age tycoons are returning to Chinese hands as wealthy collectors reshape a centuries-old art trade.
content: Christie’s auctioneer Rupert Banner leans forward with practised showmanship as bidding stalls on a rare Yongzheng bowl near New York’s iconic Rockefeller Centre. He pauses as if willing offers from thin air, scanning dozens of in-person buyers and phone banks connecting with China, London, Texas. It will be a bad look if the frenzy abates for this delicate peach-decorated bowl highlighted on Christie’s glossy Chinese sale catalogue and online advertising. But bidding soon resumes with a realised price of US$2.05 million, the sale’s top porcelain result. The bowl is among over 100 items from the Art Institute of Chicago, part of a broader generational transition as rarefied relics amassed by 19th century American Gilded Age “robber barons” return to Chinese hands after gathering dust for more than a century in Western museums. Then it is the turn of lot 1032, an archaistic zun-form vase once owned by finance magnate Charles Schwab. “They’re off and running,” says Banner, before a Chinese man snags it for US$40,960. “China lost many relics to the West because of corrupt officials,” the new owner says. “We started losing our best relics to the West after the Song dynasty, lost on the Maritime Silk Road, with Guangzhou among the key ports. I want to bring this back to Guangzhou.” The “wealthy farmer” from Jiangxi, who is in his 40s and dressed in black sportswear and trainers, does not give his name like many in the discreet art trade. “The West is in decline, and it’s only fitting,” he says, adding that he will donate it to a Chinese museum. His next stop: France and Italy to repatriate more treasures. Institute sales from the two-day event total US$17.3 million, led by a waistless Huanghuali daybed at US$3.2 million. For Chinese art collectors, items from US museums hold special cachet, given their prestige and assurances against counterfeiting. “The pieces that have museum provenance are absolutely the focus of any collector,” said Angela McAteer, Chinese works of art department head at rival auction house Sotheby’s. “In a category that’s plagued by not only fake pieces but fake provenance, fake catalogues, fake labels, you name it, a de-accession piece with that provenance is watertight.” Provenance – ensuring items are not fake or stolen – and de-accession – essentially selling unneeded stuff from your attic – are among the rarefied art world’s special language, along with good title, burned art and white-glove sales. US museum auctions also offer a recent workaround. After US President Donald Trump’s 2025 tariff bender, imported Chinese art faced up to 12.5 per cent taxes – and in some categories double – evidence that even art cannot avoid geopolitics, spurring US-sourced sales. A few months ago, after intense lobbying, the US Trade Representative agreed to exempt fine art. Recent auctions include items from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Brooklyn Museum, San Francisco Asian Art Museum and Honolulu Museum of Art. “Every major museum in America has had to grapple with this. These American tycoons were buying all this Chinese art and donating thousands of objects,” said Vicki Paloympis, Christie’s Chinese department head, navigating half-opened crates ahead of the public viewing. “Insurance is high, storage is expensive, and they have all these pieces that are duplicates and triplets.” Another factor, adds McAteer, is that museums display fewer objects these days, leaving more in storage. Asian museums tend not to de-accession given strict heritage-protection laws, although private or corporate museums with underfunded endowments sometimes do. Japan’s Fujita Art Museum faced a cash crunch before its hugely successful 2017 US$262.8 million sale. And last month’s heavily subscribed Okada Museum of Art Hong Kong auction of rare Chinese ceramics yielded HK$174.7 million (US$22.3 million) after its founder, pachinko magnate Kazuo Okada, faced a US$50 million legal dispute involving casino mogul Steve Wynn. Hong Kong faces fewer art-sale restrictions than mainland China. But museum sales are hardly exempt from criticism. “Some people were nationalistic. They wrote saying, look, American museums are getting rid of Chinese art because they don’t like Chinese culture,” said Tao Wang, the Chicago institute’s Chinese art curator, after months spent teeing up the sale. “But we made statements, and people realised what the de-accession purpose is, to upgrade and enhance.” De-accession at accredited US museums follows exhaustive legal, ethical and curatorial standards, including restrictions on how proceeds can be spent after some early scandals. “There are some people who dig in their heels and say museums shouldn’t sell their treasures, blah, blah,” said Eric Zetterquist, an artist and gallery owner. “I­t’s a much more natural process than people realise.” Rising prices have given US museums further incentive to houseclean. The global Chinese fine art auction market rose from US$200-300 million in 1995 to US$5 billion in 2015 before settling at US$1.75 billion last year, according to industry estimates, with huge upside. A single Andy Warhol image of Brigitte Bardot sold in May for US$24.8 million, more than the entire Okada collection. Long wary of the trade, Beijing has increasingly welcomed collecting while keeping a close eye on corruption, capital flight, tax evasion and political dissent. “This is not a flashy Rolls-Royce, so Chinese people can still buy and not feel like the government’s going to come down on them,” said Zetterquist. “And the government wholly encourages people to buy Chinese masterpieces and bring them back to China.” Wang’s career mirrors the dramatic arc of China’s art market. Born in Yunnan in 1962, he lived through the 1966–1976 Cultural Revolution, watching art and books burned in the river and the anti-“Four Olds” campaigns that saw museums closed. His early formal education was patchy. But he was a voracious reader, helped by an uncle who slipped him two “huge” Chinese literature books from a boarded-up library and by private calligraphy lessons. “The artist was professional. But not like a professional painter. He drew cinema posters,” Wang said. “It was far from the capital, so artists had more freedom … There was no payment. You just had to know someone.” Provincial universities reopened in 1977 and his clandestine reading helped him get into college at 16 alongside 30-something classmates. Graduating from Yunnan Normal, he headed to Beijing for further studies and then to London in 1986 where he saw his first proper museum. After receiving an art history PhD in 1993, he taught at SOAS University of London and University College London before moving to Sotheby’s in 2012 and Chicago in 2015. “At the bottom of my heart, I’m an academic,” he said, adding that he never imagined Chinese art would reach such heights. In 2011, China’s Hurun Rich List listed 271 mainland US-dollar billionaires, though Wang says that 600 was probably more accurate. That year, Chinese art accounted for nearly half of global art auction revenues. Since then, curators say, Chinese collectors have become increasingly knowledgeable. “The nouveau riche are now people who made their fortunes in the 80s and 90s and are sending their kids to Vassar,” said Zetterquist. “Their taste is much more sophisticated.” Porcelain holds a particular fascination, especially items like the peach bowl made in imperial kilns.
