Chinese buyers last month pored over items in Christie’s pre-auction galleries, sometimes holding them for extended periods. “Chinese people have a special relationship with ceramics because they in many ways invented them,” Wang said. The rarity of top-end pieces and the centuries-long struggle to crack the recipe saw Westerners similarly fixated. American shipping fortunes after 1800, some built on the illegal opium trade, spurred early interest. But demand exploded among Gilded Age steel, oil and banking magnates. The focus was initially on decorative Qing dynasty ceramics as political instability opened Chinese imperial collections and tomb excavations. Later decades saw their tastes refined towards older, rarer Song, Tang and Zhou dynasty items. “These things were considered to be what aristocrats, old money, collected, and so that’s what the robber barons wanted,” Zetterquist said. The original Morgans, Rockefellers and Fricks eventually died, leaving their collections to museums. More than a century later, some of those objects are passing to wealthy Chinese collectors. But even timeless art weathers trends. Chinese collectors tend to shun Tang dynasty horses and other funerary items favoured by Westerners. “There’s the idea that the tomb has been invaded, so to speak, and the spirit of the deceased has been left without things that he or she needed,” said Robert Mowry, a senior consultant and Harvard Art Museums’ curator emeritus. “The ironic thing is, a lot of other things that Chinese collectors are interested in, like ancient bronze vessels, like ancient jades from the Zhou dynasty, came out of tombs as well. But no one worries about that in terms of the spirit of the deceased seeking revenge.” Chinese have also frequently sniffed at “export” Chinese art, often larger items in bold colours, some even adorned with lavish gold frames targeted at foreigners after the 16th century. “People were just filling up crates and bringing them home,” said Zetterquist. “Think about the aesthetics of the Gilded Age. It was a lot of googly gook, shiny things with cachet.” Of particular interest for new Chinese buyers are items associated with past emperors, especially Qianlong’s 1735–1796 reign. “The nouveau riche collectors, it’s all about Qianlong. If Qianlong liked it, it must be good,” said Mowry, even though some imperial items were made in lots of 100,000. “If somebody visits the White House, they’re going to leave with some kind of gift,” he added. “When it’s made for the palace, everyone thinks it’s made for the emperor. Well, not everything was.” But imperial provenance provides a certain assurance, curators said. “The brand new fakes can be very convincing,” said Mowry. “Qianlong? Come back tomorrow, we’ll have some more for you … There’s the idea: if we buy it in the US or Europe or wherever, and it’s been out of China for a long time, like 40 years, it’s probably OK.” While patriotism may drive some Chinese bidders, others less so, he added. “They’re virtually all dealers,” said Mowry. “There’s nothing wrong with that. But to mask it all as repatriation is part of the truth, but not the whole truth.” Wang said museums should treasure their collections as a mother does her children, even when they’re banished. “They’re going to a better home,” he added.

title: Houthis say they struck Aramco oil facility, as Saudis hit Sanaa
description: The foes have traded strikes since the rebels seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait.
content: Yemen’s Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital on Saturday, where flames and smoke were seen, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive last month. Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that “Saudi enemy aircraft” hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting “Saudi aggression” against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties. Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city. In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said. While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites. The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at Aramco’s Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah channel earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen’s northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group’s strongholds. It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July. After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east – a region that is larger but much less populated. Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait. They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said that 26 troops had died. The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis. While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third largest after Sanaa and Aden. The Houthis also said on Friday that Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours. Saudi authorities, meanwhile, reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border. Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump. On Saturday, US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials. The meeting was not officially announced.

title: US to deploy NMESIS anti-ship system on Japanese island closest to Taiwan for first time
description: Unprecedented deployment to Yonaguni, 110km from Taiwan, during joint drills this month comes amid high tensions between Beijing and Tokyo.
content: The US is set to deploy one of its signature anti-ship missile systems to the Japanese island closest to Taiwan, an unprecedented move that comes as tensions in the region between Beijing and Tokyo continue to simmer. The ground-based US uncrewed missile platform known as the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) will be deployed on Yonaguni Island in Japan’s Okinawa prefecture during biennial joint exercises this month, according to the regional bureau of the Japanese defence ministry. It will mark the first NMESIS deployment on Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island lying just about 110km (62 miles) from the eastern coast of Taiwan, although the US military operated the system elsewhere on Okinawa last year. The deployment during the Keen Sword joint exercise moves the system closer to Taiwan than during the Resolute Dragon joint drills in September last year. Then, NMESIS was stationed on Okinawa’s Ishigaki Island – roughly 127km east of Yonaguni and about 240km from Taiwan. NMESIS will also return to Ishigaki as part of the Keen Sword exercise, which runs from October 19 to 29. According to the Okinawa Defence Bureau press release, the NMESIS deployment will support training at the Yonaguni garrison. The Japan Self-Defence Forces and US military will set up a joint coordination centre on-site, conduct island-defence tabletop drills, and train to coordinate with Japanese and US equipment deployed at other garrisons. “Various types of Japanese and US equipment are scheduled to be deployed to coordinate with the joint coordination centre,” the bureau said, adding that specific training details remained subject to change. The highly mobile and rapidly deployable island defence solution is used by the US Marine Corps in sea denial and littoral protection to target and sink enemy warships from coastal or island positions, with a range of more than 185km. If deployed to Yonaguni during a conflict, the jamming-resistant system could threaten enemy vessels trying to operate east of Taiwan – an area where Beijing has stepped up coastguard patrols, naval operations and scientific research activities to assert its sovereignty. Beijing said its moves were a countermeasure to maritime boundary talks announced in May between Japan and the Philippines – discussions it has dismissed as “illegal and invalid”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and its ally Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Ties between Beijing and Tokyo remain at their lowest point in decades following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s controversial remarks about Taiwan in November. She said a military attack on or naval blockade of Taiwan by Beijing could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, justifying a military response. On Monday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told a visiting Japanese business delegation led by former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya that it was a “pressing task” for Tokyo to “correct the erroneous words and deeds of its leaders on the Taiwan question as soon as possible”. Meanwhile, Tokyo is also moving to station air-defence missile units on Yonaguni. Beijing’s foreign ministry has accused Japan of using “so-called defence and counterstrike” capabilities as a cover to boost its “deployment of a series of offensive weapons and equipment including missiles in regions close to China”. “This is essentially an attempt to build a forward fortress of military confrontation which threatens regional peace and stability,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in April. US forces also deployed NMESIS during their joint annual Balikatan exercise with the Philippines earlier this year. The system was stationed in the Batanes Islands, the Philippines’ northernmost province sitting roughly 142 to 190km south of Taiwan. It marked the second time the system had been deployed during Balikatan, after making its debut during last year’s joint drills. Chinese military analysts warn that NMESIS could give US-Philippine forces a potent sea-denial tool, enabling them to put enemy ships at risk without deploying large surface combatants. In an update on implementation of the 2026 National Defence Strategy submitted to Congress on September 22, the Pentagon wrote that even as President Donald Trump’s administration worked to avoid confrontation with China, “we continue our efforts to strengthen deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain, with the goal … of ensuring that ‘aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive, and war deemed irrational’.” Okinawa and the Batanes Islands are widely seen as key nodes of the first island chain, running from the Kuril Islands through Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines down to Borneo, and marking the Chinese mainland’s near seas from the wider Pacific. This month’s Keen Sword exercise will also see US forces make their first deployment of the Marine Air Defence Integrated System, or MADIS, to Yonaguni. The mobile, short-range air-defence weapon is built for the US Marine Corps to track and destroy drones, helicopters and low-flying aircraft. “The NMESIS and MADIS represent a significant step forward in the Marine Corps’ modernisation efforts,” US Marines based in Okinawa said when receiving both systems in June.

title: How US-China RISC-V collaboration is deepening despite chip rivalry
description: RISC-V chipmakers are expanding beyond automotive, industrial and Internet of Things applications into physical AI and data centres.
content: As global adoption of the open-source RISC-V chip architecture accelerates, US intellectual property provider MIPS is collaborating with Chinese firms at an unprecedented level, according to a senior executive, highlighting how cross-border cooperation persists despite intense tech rivalry between Washington and Beijing. MIPS, which was acquired by US chipmaker GlobalFoundries last year, was driving RISC-V standardisation “very closely with China”, chief technology officer Yankin Tanurhan said during a media briefing in Shanghai in September. The effort formed part of broader initiatives under governing body RISC-V International to unite global players – including US, European and Chinese entities, as well as academia – to standardise technologies ranging from artificial intelligence to microcontrollers and data centre servers, he said. This cross-border collaboration is the latest sign of how China’s domestic RISC-V sector is accelerating its push into the mainstream, bolstered by faster industrial adoption and policy boost. The remarks by Tanurhan echoed those by Qi Xiaoning, a chip veteran at Chinese e-commerce and AI giant Alibaba Group Holding, which is an active player in China’s RISC-V sector through its research arm Damo Academy. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Major companies from around the world were working together “as one unified ecosystem” on the RISC-V open-standard chip architecture for edge – processing data locally on devices – and cloud applications, Qi said at the SCMP China Conference 2026 in Hong Kong in July. RISC-V, short for fifth-generation reduced instruction set computer, is an open-standard instruction set architecture that enables developers to design central processing units (CPUs). The architecture is managed by the non-profit RISC-V International. The technology has surged in popularity in China because it is free to use and modify, offering a path for Beijing and domestic tech firms to reduce their reliance on proprietary foreign architectures, mainly Intel’s x86 and Arm. Broadening its appeal over the past year, RISC-V chipmakers have expanded beyond niche applications – such as automotive components, industrial equipment and Internet of Things devices – into next-generation computing and physical AI. Beijing-based Eswin Computing Technology is set to become the first pure-play RISC-V chipmaker to list on the Hong Kong stock exchange, with its initial public offering scheduled for October 9, a move signalling capital market confidence in the commercial viability of open-source chips. The growth rate of RISC-V global shipments has surpassed both x86 and Arm due to its “openness, energy efficiency, cost effectiveness, and customisability”, Liu Shuai, vice-president and chief marketing officer of Eswin Computing, said at an industry event in September, adding that the company was building a “RISC-V plus AI” ecosystem with its partners. Meanwhile, MIPS highlighted major progress in high-performance computing. Tanurhan said the company’s RISC-V platform had achieved mass production in AI data centres, counting 13 of the world’s top 15 AI and data centre infrastructure chip suppliers among its customers. Another growth catalyst is physical AI – the integration of AI into mechanical systems like autonomous vehicles and robotics – where China is rapidly emerging as a global epicentre. MIPS told the SCMP that its Chinese clients, who initially developed RISC-V chips for Advanced Driver Assistance Systems, or ADAS, have successfully repurposed the designs for humanoid robotics. “Robotics, especially humanoid robotics, receives immense attention in China and is developing very well,” said Tanurhan. “The testing ground and application ecosystem here is robust enough to support developers through that critical ‘last mile’ of R&D.” Beijing is also stepping up policy support for the architecture. RISC-V chip development was officially designated as a core pillar of China’s 15th five-year plan for the electronics and information technology industry in a policy document released in September, embedding the architecture into a state-level strategy. Despite heightened market competition, Tanurhan said the US company maintained deep talent ties with its Chinese peers. “Most of the Chinese RISC-V IP companies in one way or another are coming from my teams of the past. We are very well related to each other,” he said, adding that MIPS retained a competitive advantage through its global reach and scale. “None of those companies have more than 700 engineers [as MIPS does] to supply quality products to the market.”

title: ‘No brainer’: growing trend of Chinese tourists seeking luxury on business-class flights
description: Chinese holidaymakers are increasingly upgrading to ‘premium travel’ to make their well-earned leisure time more pleasurable, say insiders.
content: Business-class flights, once largely the domain of company reps on paid trips, are becoming more popular among tourists in China who do not mind spending a bit extra for a comfortable ride from start to finish, industry insiders said. Businesspeople once occupied 90 per cent of the spacious seats, but have lost that edge to leisure travellers who can buy their way out of economy class but not into first class, said Wong Hong, director general of the 18-member Association of Asia Pacific Airlines. “Now you see families, couples and retirees,” Wong said. “The rising profile of young travellers and the upper middle-class segment has some appetite for premium travel.” Industry-wide data shows the share of Chinese fliers choosing premium economy or above rose from 10 per cent in 2023 to 10.8 per cent last year, and 14.8 per cent on long routes outside East Asia, said Subramania Bhatt, CEO of the marketing and technology firm China Trading Desk. China Trading Desk found in a September survey of more than 15,000 Chinese outbound travellers that around 12 per cent had flown business class on their most recent international trip. Earlier surveys did not track the trend. “Affluent leisure travellers appear to be becoming more important,” Bhatt said, citing a “greater willingness to pay for comfort on longer flights”. Fares for the more comfortable seats – that also come with lavish meals, boarding priority and early deplaning privileges – normally run two to five times higher than economy class. Growth in business-class ticketing among tourists has been apparent in Asia outside China too, Wong said. Worldwide, searches for first-class and business-class flights on the Trip.com booking platform expanded by 99 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026. Henry Wang, 24 and a newly minted manager at his firm, flies business class 10 to 20 per cent of the time when off shift, most often between Shenzhen and the Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang area. He said airlines were likely to offer price deals for those flights and the business-economy class gap could be as narrow as 300 yuan (US$45) per ticket. A business-class ticket cost the same on those routes as flying economy from Hong Kong to Shanghai, he found. “Additionally, the business cabin can offer more travel and rest experiences, like priority check-in, a lounge and preferential boarding,” Wang said, adding he sometimes took the trips with family or friends. Connecting business-class fares may also be cheaper than nonstop alternatives, an incentive for self-funded travellers, Bhatt added. Yi Tingxuan, a 23-year-old marketing assistant from Beijing, has taken more than 15 business-class trips since his first in 2020, a jaunt to the southwestern city Guiyang to visit a friend during his teenage years. Each trip was for tourism or family visits. The longest haul took him from Seoul to Atlanta. He cannot afford first-class airfare, but said he found that one-way business-class flights around China cost as little as US$200. “It’s a no-brainer,” Yi said. “Why not? I can afford it and I get more comfort.”

title: North Korea test-fires intermediate-range missile amid mine blast tensions
description: The launch came a day after she had ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologise over the September 21 landmine blasts.
content: North Korea said on Saturday it test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile that it claimed has manoeuvrable flight capabilities designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan. The latest test comes amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas over border landmine blasts. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said her brother supervised the test of the missile, which she described as strategic, implying it was designed to deliver nuclear weapons. She also said it could change its flight trajectory at low altitudes and was equipped with unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities that she claimed would make it highly difficult to intercept. Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone. The South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, did not immediately comment on Kim’s claims. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said early on Saturday it detected the North Korean missile being launched from the eastern coastal Wonsan area and flying more than 700km (435 miles). Japan’s Defence Ministry later said it detected the missile flying about 680km. Kim argued in her statement that the differing flight details between the neighbouring US allies proved they could not properly track the missile in flight. “Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points,” she said. “There is no way to avoid this attack.” The launch came a day after she ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologise over the September 21 landmine blasts, which occurred about 10 metres (38 feet) south of the countries’ military demarcation line, injuring three South Korean soldiers. South Korea said a joint inspection of the site with the US-led United Nations Command found the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea. The command later determined that the North violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-1953 Korean war. The South has also called on the North to halt its recent border fortification efforts, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers, which have accelerated after Kim Jong-un in 2024 abandoned his government’s long-standing goal of reconciliation with the South and declared Seoul a permanent adversary. Kim Yo-jong, possibly the second-most powerful figure in Pyongyang, dismissed Seoul’s demands over the mine blasts as “utterly pathetic” on Friday, saying the North intends to cut ties with the South forever. In a statement on September 30, she denied North Korean responsibility for the blasts and threatened to retaliate if South Korea fires on North Korean troops fortifying the border. Saturday’s launch at Wonsan was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including missile tests, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship, as Kim Jong-un continues to flaunt his growing nuclear programme despite US calls to revive diplomacy. Wonsan was also the site where the North on September 20 tested what state media described as a hypersonic missile system, part of a broad range of weapons North Korea has developed in recent years that are designed to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan. The various hypersonic systems tested by North Korea have included solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles that were first unveiled in 2024. The South’s joint chiefs said on Saturday the military stepped up surveillance and vigilance for possible further launches from North Korea and was closely sharing information with the United States and Japan. Seoul’s presidential national security office called for North Korea to immediately halt its repeated ballistic launches, calling them a violation of UN Security Council sanctions and a “serious act that does nothing to help manage the current situation”. The US Pacific Command said the launch “does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies”. Kim Jong-un has largely abandoned diplomacy with Washington and Seoul since his nuclear negotiations with US President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019, and he has made Moscow the new focus of his foreign policy, sending thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. Following years of intensified testing, Kim now has an extensive arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles, including long-range weapons potentially capable of reaching the US mainland and shorter-range systems that threaten South Korea and Japan. Trump in August scaled back a major military exercise with South Korea in an apparent effort to restart diplomacy with Kim, who has condemned such drills as rehearsals for invasion. North Korea has so far rebuffed Trump’s outreach. It says Washington must first abandon its “hostile policy” – a term Pyongyang has traditionally used to describe US-led sanctions and joint US-South Korean military exercises – and drop denuclearisation as a precondition for talks.

title: Hong Kong public universities’ non-local fees jump by up to 26% as quota expands
description: HKU medicine, dentistry fees more than double to HK$590,000, with online users on RedNote saying hikes are ‘going too far’.
content: Hong Kong public universities will raise undergraduate tuition fees for non-local students studying general courses by up to 26 per cent in the 2027-28 academic year, marking the sharpest increase in recent years as institutions adjust to an expanded quota. Non-local students admitted to the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) medicine and dentistry programmes will face the steepest jump, with annual tuition rising by 137 per cent to HK$590,000 (US$75,187) to recover the high costs of clinical training. Seven of the eight public universities have published their 2027-28 non-local tuition fees, with the average increase standing at 17 per cent compared with the current academic year. The cumulative hike for 2027-28 represents a 41 per cent rise since 2023-24, when the non-local quota stood at 20 per cent of local places. The latest increases far exceed the 6 to 13 per cent annual rises seen over the past three years, following the government’s decision to lift the non-local quota to 40 per cent in 2024-25 and up to 50 per cent from this academic year. Four of the seven universities that have announced fees increased their non-local undergraduate rates by 20 per cent or more. In July, rankings firm Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) warned that Hong Kong’s high living costs and the region’s steepest tuition fees in East Asia continued to deter international applicants. By comparison, the National University of Singapore charges international students around HK$205,000 annually for business and HK$244,000 for computing in the current academic year. The fee hike generated some discussion on the Chinese social media platform RedNote, with some describing the surge as “going too far”. “The value for money in studying in Hong Kong has dropped a lot, but lots of parents still really want [their children] to go,” one user named Landwave said. But universities said the adjustments reflected teaching costs, international benchmarking and cost-recovery principles. They stressed that scholarships remained available, with the Chinese University of Hong Kong and the Education University of Hong Kong (EdU) planning to expand such schemes. HKU, which raised fees by 12 per cent for other undergraduate courses apart from medicine and dentistry, said non-local students in STEM programmes would pay HK$280,000 next year – HK$31,000 more than the current rate – while non-STEM courses would cost HK$250,000, up by HK$26,000. “The adjustments to tuition fees are part of HKU’s ongoing efforts to review and align its fee structure with the costs of providing high-quality education, especially for medicine and dentistry, which are inherently costly due to the need for top professors, cutting-edge equipment and intensive clinical training,” a spokesman for HKU said. “While the tuition fees are increasing, they remain significantly lower than those of comparable top universities overseas, particularly those in the UK and North America.” The university added that it would offer scholarships to students who met admission criteria and demonstrated outstanding performance. City University (CityU) and Baptist University both raised fees by 26 per cent, or HK$50,000, to HK$240,000 per year for non-local undergraduates in 2027-28. A CityU spokeswoman said the university regularly reviewed its fee structure to ensure competitiveness and reflect programme quality. A spokeswoman for Baptist University said the fee levels reflected the full cost of education for non-local students. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) will increase non-local undergraduate fees by 21 per cent, from HK$215,000 to HK$260,000 – a HK$45,000 rise. It said the adjustment was not tied to its proposed medical school, which is funded separately. The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) is raising non-local undergraduate fees by 20 per cent, or HK$40,000, to HK$240,000 for 2027-28, saying it remained committed to high-quality education. CUHK, which increased non-local fees by 23 per cent and 20 per cent in 2025-26 and 2026-27 respectively, will raise them by a further 7 per cent. Non-local undergraduates entering in 2027-28 will pay HK$230,000 annually, up from HK$214,000 in 2026-27. EdU raised non-local undergraduate fees to HK$210,000 from HK$180,000 – a 17 per cent increase – though its 2027-28 rate remains the lowest among the universities that have announced fees. The fee increases come as the government opened applications last month for proposals to establish the first university town in the Northern Metropolis at Hung Shui Kiu, saying “favourable consideration” would be given to institutions that do not require government loans to build facilities. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said last month that no institutions had expressed financial viability concerns about establishing a presence in the university town, noting they could generate revenue by admitting non-local students. Government figures showed the non-local student intake reached 27.1 per cent of local places in 2025-26, representing around 20,093 students, with more than 70 per cent from mainland China. Only Lingnan University had not announced its 2027-28 non-local fees as of Friday.

title: Police smash burglary ring that recruited illegal immigrants for 25 break-ins
description: The force says the syndicate targeted village houses and upscale homes during holidays when residents were away.
content: Hong Kong police have busted a burglary syndicate that recruited illegal immigrants and is believed to be behind at least 25 break-ins across the city in recent weeks, with stolen cash and valuables exceeding HK$3.6 million (US$458,773). Six people aged 31 to 45 – five mainlanders and a local resident – were arrested in a Friday operation following a review of surveillance footage, police said. Three of the mainland suspects, all men, were illegal immigrants. Another two – a couple – are believed to be the masterminds, who entered Hong Kong on two-way permits, travel documents issued by Beijing authorities for visits to the city or Macau. A local man arrested in the operation acted as the group’s driver. Acting chief inspector Ng See-hin, of the New Territories North Regional Crime Unit, said the syndicate had been active since late August, adding that it was allegedly linked to at least 25 burglaries at village houses and upscale homes in Yuen Long, Tuen Mun, Sheung Shui, Tai Po, Sai Kung, Ma On Shan and Aberdeen. Ng said the group took advantage of recent long holidays and major festivals, when many residents were overseas or dining out. “They have a clear division of labour,” he said. “The masterminds arranged for the mainland men to enter Hong Kong illegally and recruited a driver to transport them between target areas and their hideout.” “They mainly target houses with lax security in quiet and secluded locations. They would pry open doors and windows while the owners were out dining or on holiday, or enter through unlocked doors and windows to steal gold jewellery, cash, watches and other valuables,” Ng added. The total reported loss exceeded HK$3.6 million, with the largest single loss of about HK$600,000 at a property in Aberdeen. “Some of the stolen property was recovered, including cash, jewellery and handbags. The total value is about HK$600,000,” he added, stressing that the force believed it had smashed the syndicate. The six were still being detained for questioning on Saturday afternoon, according to Ng. Ng also urged flat owners to remain vigilant and take simple precautions, such as locking windows and doors before leaving home. “Most burglaries are opportunistic in nature. Burglars take immediate advantage of what they perceive to be lax security,” Ng said. “The public should avoid keeping too many valuables or large amounts of cash at home.” Under the Theft Ordinance, the maximum penalty for burglary in Hong Kong is 14 years’ imprisonment.

title: Why John Carpenter’s Big Trouble in Little China is both problematic and progressive
description: John Carpenter’s cult classic, which bombed at the box office, blended problematic elements with progressive representation for the 1980s.
content: In 1986, a strange coincidence occurred in Hollywood. Despite the industry having previously shown little interest in the subject, two major Chinese-themed fantasy films were released in the same year: John Carpenter’s Big Trouble in Little China and the Eddie Murphy vehicle The Golden Child. Ever the cynic, Carpenter refused to believe in serendipity. “How many adventure pictures dealing with Chinese mysticism have been released by the major studios in the past 20 years?” he asked Starlog magazine. “For two of them to come along at the exact same time is more than mere coincidence.” Coincidence or not, when Carpenter was offered both projects to direct, he chose the more interesting of the two. Playing like a long-lost Indiana Jones film, Big Trouble in Little China was a raucous, racially charged action-comedy with horror elements, and it had an equally unlikely origin story. It started life as Lotus, an 1880s-set mystical Western written by first-timers Gary Goldman and David Z. Weinstein, inspired by Tsui Hark’s 1979 film The Butterfly Murders and San Francisco’s 19th century tong wars. Hollywood, of course, had other ideas, and W.D. Richter (director of 1984’s The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension) was hired to update the action to modern-day San Francisco’s Chinatown, although a healthy dose of absurdity remained. “I’d wanted to make a kung fu movie since I saw [1972 Shaw Brothers film] Five Fingers of Death,” Carpenter told Medium. “In general, martial arts movies had an incredible amount of violence combined with a narrative naive charm.” A genre-bending adventure Big Trouble in Little China sees restaurateur Wang Chi (Dennis Dun), all-American trucker Jack Burton (Kurt Russell), lawyer Gracie Law (Kim Cattrall) and friends infiltrating a secret world underneath Chinatown to rescue Wang’s fiancée, Miao Yin (Suzee Pai), from evil sorcerer Lo Pan (James Hong) and his warriors, The Three Storms (Carter Wong, Peter Kwong and James Pax). Cue thrilling martial arts sequences, imaginative monsters (designed by the late, great Screaming Mad George) and impressive sets where Carpenter stages captures, fights and chases. It is consistently funny, inventive and exciting, if problematic. A Chinese brothel and human trafficking ring is the “acceptable” front for the villain’s supernatural shenanigans, and Lo Pan himself is an evil Fu Manchu-style figure espousing all sorts of mystical claptrap. No wonder Jackie Chan turned down the role of Wang. However, the film is also more progressive than might be expected. Despite audience assumptions to the contrary, Wang Chi is the real hero, with Jack as his hapless sidekick. Dun, who had just appeared in Michael Cimino’s mean-spirited Year of the Dragon (1985), was glad to play a regular second-generation American rather than another racial stereotype. As Jack puts it, “I thought what we were here, racial differences aside, was a couple of old friends, both of us Californians.” In the 2017 book The Official Making of Big Trouble in Little China, Russell said, “I’ve never played a hero who has so many faults. Jack is and isn’t the hero. He falls on his ass as much as he comes through.” Cattrall’s Gracie, meanwhile, proves extremely resourceful. “I’m not screaming for help the whole time,” she said. “I think the humour comes out of the situations and my relationship with Jack Burton. I’m the brains and he’s the brawn.” Because the openly racist Year of the Dragon had left such a nasty taste, the filmmakers met Chinese community leaders and hired a casting director who had worked with many Chinese-American actors. The result is one of a handful of Hollywood films – ever – to feature a majority Asian cast. From Chinese-American character actors such as James Hong and Victor Wong (playing tour guide Egg Shen), to Hong Kong stars such as Carter Wong, known for Golden Harvest pictures like Hapkido (1972), to Hollywood’s favourite henchman Al Leong (1987’s Lethal Weapon, 1988’s Die Hard), the ensemble boasts a roll-call of surprising range and breadth. Big Trouble easily passes the Race Bechdel Test. Indeed, it is hard to imagine another Hollywood picture that features two old Asian men – Wong and Chao-Li Chi (as Wang’s uncle) – discussing Chinese mysticism in detail with the heroine, or one that has its Caucasian lead complain, “Hold on, I’m feeling like an outsider here.” It is regrettable, however, that the female Asian characters barely speak a word. Commercial failure and cult legacy After playing well with test audiences, the film bombed at the box office. This could be because of audience racism, its confusing-sounding, genre-bending plot, or because, as Russell claimed, it was buried by the studio. The fact that James Cameron’s all-conquering Aliens (1986) came out a fortnight later cannot have helped. In the years since, Big Trouble in Little China has become a cult classic, but at the time its failure sent Carpenter back to independent cinema. “The experience was the reason I stopped making movies for the Hollywood studios,” he said. “I won’t work for them again. I think Big Trouble is a wonderful film, and I’m very proud of it. But the reception it received, and the reasons for that reception, were too much for me to deal with. I’m too old for that sort of bulls***.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Chinese troops line up for Russia’s Tsentr-2026 exercise as military ties tighten
description: The mass drill involved tens of thousands of personnel from SCO countries to apply lessons from Ukraine war, Moscow says.
content: Chinese troops have taken part in a mass multinational exercise in Russia featuring new anti-drone and ground robot systems – drills that Russian state media said “applied lessons” from the Ukraine war. The troops were among more than 47,000 military personnel involved in the Tsentr-2026 – or Centre-2026 – drills in the central western Chelyabinsk region from Monday until Saturday. The Russian Ministry of Defence said the strategic command-and-staff exercise applied combat lessons from the Ukraine war to “repel external aggression in the Central Asian direction”. Russian President Vladimir Putin observed the drills at the Chebarkul Training Ground on Friday and met foreign military attaches, state news agency Tass reported. Russia invited contingents and observers from the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member countries to the event. During the exercise, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) trained alongside troops from Russia, Belarus, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia and Tajikistan, the PLA Daily, the mouthpiece of China’s military, reported. The report said the Chinese troops were deployed to the exercise via a combination of road, rail and air transport. They took part in reconnaissance and guidance, coordinated obstacle breaching, coordinated attacks, and battlefield first aid exercises with troops from other nations during the preparatory stage, it said. The execution phase began with command and control exercises, followed by live-fire drills organised into three operational stages, focusing on actions such as multidimensional reconnaissance, integrated information and firepower strikes, target guidance, multi-axis assaults, and rapid pursuit and destruction of the enemy, it said. The PLA Daily said the drills’ operational planning and live-fire manoeuvres helped to “consolidate multilateral traditional friendship and improve joint action capabilities”, while allowing the Chinese military to test its logistical reach, troop deployment capability, and combined arms coordination in unfamiliar terrain. According to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, the PLA deployed a combination of Type 99A main battle tanks with drones, uncrewed ground vehicles and helicopters, during the exercise, showcasing its growing integration of crewed and unmanned systems. The PLA deployed drone swarms to provide precise target data to ground combat groups, with tactical unmanned aerial vehicles, armed helicopters and unmanned ground combat vehicles coordinating strikes against targets, the report said. Multiple waves of firepower assaults were launched against enemy defensive positions using a “small-group, multi-waves” tactic. The report also said that all the troops involved in the exercise were stationed underground to avoid drone strikes. State-owned news agency Sputnik said the drills featured mass drone use, ground robots, electronic warfare, precision weapons, mobile assault units, and newer systems, including Geran-4/5 drones, Zarya lasers and the Izdeliye 347 missile system, offering a glimpse of how rapidly drone, counter-drone warfare had evolved, driven by the Ukraine war. The Centre-2026 exercises are the latest manifestation of China-Russia military cooperation, which has progressed from periodic, heavily scripted war games to highly complex joint deployment operations involving advanced hardware and deep command integration. The drills cap a busy summer for the two militaries. In late June, Chinese and Russian air forces conducted their 11th joint strategic air patrol over the Sea of Japan. And in late July, the navies of the two countries wrapped up a joint maritime patrol following a mission in the Pacific Ocean, an operation explicitly aimed at improving joint operational capabilities. Beijing and Moscow maintain that they do not have a formal military alliance but these regularised air and naval patrols, combined with large-scale land exercises, reflect a shift towards deeper strategic coordination. For the PLA, which has not engaged in major combat operations in decades, training alongside battle-tested Russian forces offers access to crucial operational experience from the Ukraine war, especially drone warfare.

title: ‘Cancer saved me’: Hong Kong survivor finds new purpose ahead of canoe challenge
description: Raymond Lo, 75, says liver cancer diagnosis three decades ago taught him to live differently, and he is now preparing to paddle 65km to support others.
content: Thirty-one years ago, Hongkonger Raymond Lo Shu-yuen was diagnosed with stage four liver cancer and had a quarter of the organ removed. Now 75, Lo said the illness, despite its physical and mental toll, had taught him invaluable lessons about ageing, health and making the most of life. “I can say that the cancer itself saved me,” he said. “Why? If I did not have this illness, I would not have changed my past lifestyle such as working hard like a dog, eating a lot of junk food, doing no exercise or workouts, keeping no pets and other lovely animals.” Today, he is preparing to embark on a 65km (40 mile) solo canoeing challenge between Tung Chung and Ma Wan, aiming to raise funds for cancer patients and promote public health awareness. Lo was diagnosed with liver cancer in 1995, at the age of 44. He said he had no symptoms until a routine physical check-up revealed a shadow on his liver. Subsequent CAT scans and blood tests confirmed the disease. Though initially shocked, he said he quickly accepted the diagnosis. As a hepatitis B carrier, he faced an increased risk of serious liver complications, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. Surgery successfully removed a quarter of his liver. During his recovery, he said he felt weak, lost his appetite and tired easily. More than the physical pain, he said, he feared being unable to work and support his wife and three children – two sons and a daughter aged between 10 and 16. “How could they survive without me? My wife was a housewife over 40 years of age and my children were all at school,” he said. “I could overcome the physical pain in my whole body but could not manage economically for my family.” To ease the stress, Lo left his job at a large logistics company, where he earned about HK$50,000 (US$6,371) a month, and joined a smaller firm for roughly half the salary. It was then that he began making changes to cope with the illness – changes that later became lifelong habits. He adopted a healthier, more balanced diet, eating vegetables and fruit he had grown himself, including sweet potatoes, pumpkins and papayas. He also took in a dozen abandoned and stray dogs at his place in Sham Shek Tsuen, a village on Lantau Island. “The activities kept me very busy and I had no time to think about my illness,” he said. Alongside embracing a healthier lifestyle and developing a love of animals, Lo returned to canoeing, a hobby he had neglected for years. He first took up the sport after finishing secondary school in 1971, when he joined the Auxiliary Medical Service to learn first aid, ambulance work and life-saving skills. He volunteered as a canoe lifeguard for more than eight years in areas including Repulse Bay, Shek O, Big Wave Bay and Stanley. He also served as a lifeguard trainer and canoeing instructor for new members of the service. He later left the service after the birth of his first child to spend more time with his family. While looking for ways to stay healthy during his recovery from liver cancer, he returned to canoeing and fell in love with the sport all over again. He bought a second-hand canoe for about HK$6,000, which remains his favourite because of its manoeuvrability. Lo said canoeing helped him stay focused and build self-confidence while enjoying nature. “While canoeing, I can enjoy the sea, the landscape, the sky, the waves and currents,” he said. “I can canoe fast and slow. I don’t have a route to follow. I can move freely in the water.” Lo now paddles at sea five days a week. He also works as a canoe instructor and has taught about 100 students. Alongside his regular workouts and lessons, Lo has taken on a new task: preparing for a solo canoeing challenge in support of the Hong Kong Cancer Fund, to raise funds and awareness for cancer patients. For the 65km endurance challenge, he will paddle non-stop for more than eight hours across open water between Tung Chung and Ma Wan. Lo said he came up with the challenge after witnessing friends and colleagues die from various cancers in recent years. Some were in their forties or fifties and left families behind. “Within the past 10 years, I have had a number of my friends and past colleagues who have died from various cancers,” he said. “They did not take any medical examinations or check-ups. They thought they were healthy. They went on drinking alcohol, smoking cigarettes and eating a lot of junk food.” He added that he hoped the challenge would raise public awareness of the importance of regular health check-ups and a healthy lifestyle. Lo said potential difficulties on the solo journey included heavy rain, strong winds and, in particular, lightning. He planned to set off in mid-October, depending on the weather. “My main focus right now is that I must have a healthy body and live a vibrant, fulfilling life,” he said. “Cancer has transformed me into someone who knows how to have fun and live life with enjoyment. It has built up another whole new life for me.”

title: US, China botanists sign landmark proposal on cooperation, global issues and projects
description: Botanical societies of both countries sign joint plant science cooperation initiative in China’s Taian to tackle pressing global challenges.
content: The botanical societies of the United States and China have signed a plant science cooperation initiative, vowing to strengthen bilateral ties and foster an open scientific community to tackle global issues. The joint initiative was signed during a Sino-American botany conference last month in Taian, in China’s eastern Shandong province, which brought together hundreds of experts from institutions in both countries. The conference, held from September 19 to 23, aimed to “further deepen botanical exchange and cooperation between China and the United States and to establish an international platform that fosters interdisciplinary integration in plant science”, according to the Botanical Society of China. Topics such as conservation, plant biotechnology, climate change and an international plant megaproject were discussed, the China Science Daily reported. In proposals under the initiative, the Botanical Society of China and the Botanical Society of America noted that plant science was a critical pillar for addressing global ecological issues, particularly as climate change intensifies. “Now more than ever, our scientific communities share a vital responsibility to maintain and strengthen international collaboration,” they said. “Open academic interchange is vital for addressing global challenges, promoting the cross-border flow of talents, insights, as well as data and scientific methodologies sharing.” The societies said they remained committed to ensuring that international cooperation was an “uninterrupted bridge” for progress and that they would improve mechanisms for cooperation, including academic exchange, joint research and resource sharing. The conference and joint initiative came just ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s highly anticipated visit to Washington and summit with US President Donald Trump. While scientific collaboration between China and the US has taken a major hit in recent years because of heightened geopolitical tensions and anti-China initiatives, the botany and plant science communities have continued to maintain cooperation. Harvard China Fund executive director Dorinda Elliott has written about how “Covid and worsening US-Chinese relations haven’t stopped that collaboration [between botanists] – despite the difficulties in international travel during the pandemic.” The collaboration included the sharing of specimens and joint research, she says in the article on the Harvard China Fund website. In 1972, then-US president Richard Nixon took a redwood sequoia sapling to China on a visit that ended decades of isolation between the two countries. The tree is still living at the Hangzhou Botanical Garden. In 1978, a delegation from the American botanical society visited China to tour institutes and carry out exchanges with Chinese scientists, laying the groundwork for future collaborations and visits. A paper published in the journal BioScience the following year by a member of the delegation said that Chinese scientists “admitted openly the great gap in science between our country and theirs; they are determined to catch up by the year 2000”. The first Sino-American botanical expedition in China was conducted in 1980, where researchers collected thousands of samples that were distributed to botanical institutions globally, according to Harvard University’s Arnold Arboretum. In the 2026 Nature Index, which tracks high-quality research publications, the Chinese Academy of Sciences ranked first among leading institutions in the field of plant biology, with Chinese institutes making up all but one spot in the top 10. China overtook the US in the Nature Index biological sciences ranking last year, though the US continues to be a leading country in the field. Plenary and keynote speakers for the 2026 Sino-American Conference included researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Peking University, Fudan University, Yale University, Harvard University and the University of British Columbia. Zhong Kang, also known as Chong Kang, president of the Chinese Botanical Society, told the conference that deepening strategic cooperation was a pragmatic move between the societies to focus on the long-term development of the field, according to the China Science Daily. The two botanical societies urged the plant science community to expand research into fundamental biological processes. This work would aim to enable environmental conservation and the sustainable production of food, fuels, pharmaceuticals and industrial products, they said under the initiative. “We must build bridges, not silos, to realise the conceptual and technological innovation that will be required to meet the challenges of increasing demand for resources in the face of global change,” they pledged. They also proposed that research standards and frameworks be set for the responsible development of plant science, including frontier areas such as synthetic biology and biotechnology.

title: Meet Will Arnett’s rumoured new girlfriend, Guess heiress Emma Marciano – who’s 28
description: The Arrested Development actor is reportedly dating the Los Angeles creative who runs Mimchik – worn by Blackpink’s Jennie, Kristen Stewart and SZA.
content: Will Arnett cannot stop gushing over his new girlfriend. On a September 28 episode of his podcast SmartLess, which the 56-year-old hosts with friends and former co-stars Jason Bateman and Sean Hayes, the actor was grilled about his new relationship. When Bateman asked him for an “update on [his] love life and domestic life”, Arnett revealed that things are “going really well” for him and his new partner. “I’m very happy, very, very happy,” he said, but refused to share what he imagined the relationship would look like in five years. “I’m in a place now where I’m really trying my best to just deal with what’s in front of me,” he emphasised before insisting they focus on their guest, Seth Meyers, instead. So, who is the mystery woman who stole the Arrested Development star’s heart? According to People, it’s 28-year-old Los Angeles native Emma Marciano. Here’s everything you need to know about Emma Marciano. What is Emma Marciano’s background? Emma Marciano is fashion royalty. Her father is Guess founder Maurice Marciano, and her mother is footwear designer Nathalie Marciano, whose father owned the luxury footwear brand Charles David, where she served as creative director. Nathalie Marciano is also a Hollywood producer who has executive-produced films like Love, Wedding, Marriage (2011) and The Duel (2016). She founded the production company 26 Films, which focuses on films that create social impact, and co-founded Art Firm Advisor, LLC, where she leads business development and marketing strategy. Nathalie is also an art collector and philanthropist. Emma Marciano has a sister named Olivia, who is the founder of The Middle Project, a handmade art and objects company. What does Emma Marciano do? In an interview with Sixtysix Mag in July, Emma revealed that she studied documentary filmmaking at New York University. Instead of going into that field, she followed in her parents’ footsteps and joined the fashion industry. “Growing up, such a huge part of my life [was spent] going into my dad’s closet and stealing absolutely everything he had,” she recalled in a 2023 interview with Vogue. Emma is also inspired by her mother and called her “one of the most chic people [she has] ever come across” in the interview with Sixtysix Mag. Speaking to Tmrw Mag, Emma acknowledged that her family background has helped her career, but also said it “holds [her] back” and that there are “really big shoes to fill”. Emma, who once did a one-year apprenticeship at Guess, per WWD, is the co-founder and creative director of fashion brand Mimchik. She launched the Los Angeles-based womenswear brand with her and Olivia’s childhood friend Mia Kazovsky. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Emma Marciano (@emmamarciano) Emily Ratajkowski, Blackpink’s Jennie, Addison Rae, Kristen Stewart, and SZA have been spotted wearing Mimchik.

title: Chinese woman, 60, gives birth to second child in 2 years, sparking debate
description: Brushing off public disapproval, Zhang says she feels young and healthy, and is confident in her choice to give birth at an older age.
content: A 60-year-old woman in China has captured attention on social media for giving birth to a baby girl, just two years after welcoming a son. She made the decision to have children at a later stage in life after enduring the loss of her only child four years ago, as reported by the Red Star News. The infant girl, weighing 2.8kg, was born on September 17 through caesarean section at Zhumadian Central Hospital in Henan province, central China. Her mother, identified by the surname Zhang, expressed her joy, stating: “I am so happy! I have a son and a daughter. My life is so fulfilling. The two kids will keep each other company and won’t feel lonely.” Her two-year-old son, affectionately nicknamed Guoguo, was excited to meet his baby sister, singing a popular nursery rhyme to welcome her at the hospital. Zhang shared her perspective, saying she feels youthful and is unconcerned about the disapproval from others regarding her choice to have children at an older age. “In my eyes, I am only 28 years old. I believe I can live a long life,” she remarked. Her confidence in her health stems from her family’s legacy of longevity. “My father passed away at 100, and my mother is currently 94 with good vision and hearing. She can even climb stairs on her own. I believe I am as healthy as they are. I’m confident that by the time I die, my children will be grown and married,” Zhang added. It remains unclear whether her pregnancies involved in vitro fertilisation. Zhang Hualian, an obstetrician at the hospital, noted: “She had a son at 58 and a daughter at 60. Pregnancies at her age are rare in China.” The doctor commented on Zhang’s upbeat demeanour during her latest pregnancy, stating: “She appeared more relaxed than during her previous pregnancy.” Zhang mentioned that she prepared meals and managed household chores while carrying her fetus. Initially, her husband had reservations about her decision to have children, concerned about her age. Zhang reassured him by asserting: “I’m fine with this.” Previously, the couple had only one child, like many families in China. This child, whose gender was not specified, tragically died in 2022, although the cause of death was not mentioned in the report. News reports frequently highlight families who have lost their only child and subsequently choose to have children later in life. Earlier this year, a 62-year-old woman in northeastern China’s Jilin province also welcomed a baby girl one year after the death of her only son. “No one understands my sister’s insistence. No one understands the pain of losing her only child,” the woman’s sister said on social media.

title: Asian Games: Hong Kong’s men make it a hat-trick of rugby sevens golds, women win bronze
description: Hong Kong’s men sweep past China in entirely one-sided affair, after women beat Thailand to third for second Games running.
content: There are very few certainties in life, although Hong Kong’s men winning rugby sevens gold at the Asian Games could well be one of them. A 26-0 win over China on Saturday sealed a third consecutive title for the city’s team at the Games, and it is now 12 years since they last lost a match at the multi-sport event. Their mainland opponents had already been beaten 22-0 in a Pool A game on Friday, and a first-half double from Harry Sayers ended any threat of an upset. Bryn Phillips added a third, and converted all three as well, ensuring there was no way back for China. With little need to press the issue in the second half, the only additional score came seconds after the restart, with Juan Esono Mba Oyana crossing in the corner. When it was suggested to Phillips that the performance had been a nice way to finish the week, his response was to point out that it had been the culmination of four years of hard work. “All the effort, all the dedication from everyone, the investment – it’s just amazing to go out there and put it together, and come away with a performance that we can be proud of,” said Phillips, who three years ago had been forced to watch from the stands as Hong Kong won gold. “It’s been awesome to be a part of that.” Sayers, meanwhile, will have little time to dwell on the achievement. Along with his teammates, attention will now turn to the Asian Seven Series in Sri Lanka in two weeks, before he changes focus to the 15-a-side game and the Rugby World Cup next year. While he would not have it any other way, turning 30 last week prompted a moment of introspection around the legacy to be left to some of the children he coaches by the gold medal win, which will secure the sport’s status for another four-year cycle. “I coach so many kids in Hong Kong, so them having that opportunity is about leaving the jersey in a better state than when I got it,” Sayers said. It was a good all round for Hong Kong rugby, with the women’s team beating Thailand to win bronze for the second Games in a row. A 7-5 triumph exactly mirrored the result in Hangzhou in 2023, and Natasha Olson-Thorne agreed it had again been “a little close for comfort”. “We knew it was going to be a tight game with Thailand,” she said. “They always challenge us, they’re always pretty physical, so we knew going into it that it was going to be a tough one.” Up a player early on after Thailand’s Salinda Phaekhwamdee was sent to the bin, Hong Kong battered away at their opponents’ defence and it was only a matter of time before space opened for Chloe Chan to cross. Gabriella Rivers added the extras and the city’s women were up and running. Thailand finally got on the board with half-time beckoning and Dion Akwaja raced clear down the left to score in the corner. Wannaree Meechok missed a difficult conversion, keeping Hong Kong just ahead at the break. It was largely one-way traffic after the restart, with Thailand desperately trying to find a way through and Hong Kong’s defence slamming the door on every occasion.

title: ‘Balanced and acceptable’: labour chief defends helper wage rise amid criticism
description: Chris Sun says the 2.35 per cent increase to HK$5,220 reflects Hong Kong’s stronger economy, but unions and employers’ groups remain unsatisfied.
content: Hong Kong’s stronger economic performance over the past year was the reason for raising the monthly minimum wage for foreign domestic helpers by 2.35 per cent, the labour minister has said, amid disappointment from both unions and employers’ groups. Defending the government’s decision to raise the monthly minimum wage to HK$5,220 (US$665), Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the government sought to keep the annual adjustment mechanism “balanced and acceptable”. Speaking after a radio programme on Saturday, Sun said: “If you look back, the average annual increase has been between 2 per cent and 2.5 per cent for many years. “If you look at the overall data, Hong Kong’s economic performance this year is better than last year, which everyone can see.” The new wage level will apply to all contracts signed on or after Saturday. However, the government has kept the monthly food allowance for helpers who are not provided with free meals unchanged at HK$1,236. The announcement drew criticism from both helpers’ groups and employers’ associations. The Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions had earlier proposed raising the minimum wage to HK$6,670 and the food allowance to HK$2,770. Employers, meanwhile, had called for a pay freeze, citing cost-of-living pressures on families that might reduce employment opportunities for helpers. Last year, the government raised helpers’ minimum wage by 2.2 per cent, from HK$4,990 to HK$5,100, while leaving the food allowance unchanged. Sun said authorities had considered data including inflation, employers’ income and Hong Kong’s overall economic performance when assessing this year’s increase. “After considering this data, the government made a comprehensive decision on whether to adjust the minimum wage for that year, and if so, by how much,” he said, adding that a pay freeze had been implemented during the pandemic. “We strive to ensure that the entire adjustment mechanism is balanced and acceptable to Hong Kong. “I think this will ensure that Hong Kong continues to operate smoothly because many families need the help of foreign domestic helpers.” About 380,000 foreign domestic helpers work in Hong Kong, most of them from the Philippines and Indonesia. While many earn the minimum wage, others command higher salaries depending on their experience and families’ caregiving needs. According to the latest salary survey by HelperChoice, a Hong Kong-based recruitment platform, the average monthly wage for a helper was HK$5,559 in 2026, down 2.8 per cent from HK$5,722 a year earlier. The survey, based on more than 1,000 job advertisements posted on the platform between September 2025 and August 2026, also found that salaries were highest on Hong Kong Island and lowest in the New Territories.

title: Opinion | Can Britain really afford to diverge from EU tariffs on Chinese EVs?
description: Unless London can turn its independent tariff policy into real bargaining power with Beijing, it will lose more by being shut out of an integrated European industrial framework.
content: The European Union’s demand that Britain raise tariffs on Chinese cars exposes an awkward truth about post-Brexit trade. Britain might have left the EU, but it cannot easily escape the bloc’s industrial policy. According to the Financial Times, EU officials have told Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain needs to align more closely with EU trade policy towards China if it wants British manufacturers to avoid discriminatory treatment under the bloc’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules. The proposal is tied to a larger European effort to favour locally produced goods in public procurement and state-supported schemes, including the automotive sector. The timing is not accidental. China’s car export machine is accelerating. Its electric vehicle (EV) exports in August rose 33 per cent year on year to more than 284,000, while year-to-date exports as of the end of August were more than 2.1 million, up 53 per cent year on year. Almost 95,000 of those exports went to Europe in August. Following its anti-subsidy investigation in 2024, the EU has imposed countervailing duties ranging from 7.8 to 35.3 per cent on Chinese battery EVs. In contrast, Britain has retained a standard tariff regime that is less punitive towards Chinese cars. That has helped turn the UK into an important market for Chinese manufacturers. Chinese-made cars accounted for 14 per cent of British new-car sales in 2025, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. Refusing to follow Brussels preserves something economically valuable for London: competitive pressure in a market undergoing a transition to EVs. Chinese manufacturers bring lower-cost models, rapid product cycles and intense competition. Higher tariffs would ultimately be paid through some combination of lower margins for manufacturers, higher prices for consumers or reduced choice. At a time when Britain is trying to accelerate electrification, that is not a trivial consideration. There is also a strategic advantage in retaining an independent tariff policy. Britain can use access to its market as leverage in negotiations with Beijing and other trading partners rather than automatically signing on to the EU’s choices. The UK is a significant trading partner for China, and Chinese goods accounted for 11.2 per cent of British goods imports in the 12 months to July. Maintaining room for manoeuvre could matter as supply chains, technology restrictions and industrial subsidies become increasingly entangled with geopolitics. However, Europe remains the gravitational centre of British automotive manufacturing. The EU received 60.4 per cent of UK vehicle exports in 2025, while EU-made cars represented 61 per cent of British sales. The British and European industries are also deeply intertwined through components, batteries, investment and logistics. That makes the “Made in Europe” regime potentially more consequential than the tariff. European procurement incentives, subsidies and other industrial preferences that discriminate against British-made vehicles or products with insufficient European content could put British manufacturers at a competitive disadvantage in their largest export market. The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders estimates UK-EU automotive trade at around €80 billion (US$90.8 billion) a year and warns that exclusion from the EU initiative could erode scale and investment on both sides. Following Brussels’ advice could therefore buy London something valuable: insurance against fragmentation of the European automotive market. The immediate pay-off from this would be continued access to procurement and incentives while maintaining integrated supply chains. It could also reduce the risk that manufacturers react to regulatory divergence by moving future investment away from continental Europe. There is also a geopolitical dividend. More harmony would imply that Britain is ready to work with its European neighbours on economic security at a time when China’s industrial surplus is becoming a key concern for advanced economies across the board. Commerce Minister Wang Wentao has called on Europe to avoid protectionism while signalling Beijing’s support for Chinese carmakers investing inside Europe. That points to a future where the location of production is almost as important as the nationality of the company. However, tariff alignment is not without costs. Britain would be helping protect European producers from Chinese competition while imposing additional costs on British consumers and potentially weakening one of the forces accelerating the EV transition. It could also reduce London’s bargaining power with Beijing without guaranteeing that Brussels will grant British companies full access to its “Made in Europe” benefits. The real choice isn’t whether to be tougher or softer on China. It is between two models of economic sovereignty. One gives Britain more freedom to set its own tariffs and foster competition; the other gives deeper integration into the industrial ecosystem on which much of British manufacturing still depends. The uncomfortable lesson for London is that tariff autonomy is only valuable if it can be turned into a concrete economic or strategic advantage. If not, London could find that the threat of exclusion from Europe’s industrial market gives Brussels considerable leverage.

title: Mala, coriander, congee? This UK doctor sells Cantonese-inspired bread from home
description: Doctor by weekday, baker by weekend, Hai Lin Leung runs her award-winning microbakery Lucky Yu from her East London home.
content: Every fortnight in Walthamstow, East London, a sign with a hand-painted goldfish pointing towards a kitchen window appears on the side of a residential building: “Lucky Yu Bakery pick up”. On the other side of that window is Hai Lin Leung, a general practitioner selling Cantonese-influenced baked goods from her home – think congee sourdough, bolo bao (pineapple buns), gai mei bao (cocktail buns) and more. There is no shopfront, set opening hours or seating; yet queues regularly spill down the street from her house. Customers pre-order online or turn up on the day, collecting their bakes through the window of Leung’s kitchen. “Starting Lucky Yu was like a ‘Swiss cheese effect’ where all the holes magically align,” Leung laughs. “Normally [the phrase is] used to describe something when bad things happen, but in this case it’s something really good.” Lucky Yu was founded in 2023 and quickly developed a following, with pop-ups at London bakeries including Bake Street and Quince Bakery and recognition from the Good Food Guide as one of the UK’s 50 best bakeries in 2026. Despite being awarded, Leung is still reluctant to call Lucky Yu a bakery at all. Partly, she says, that is impostor syndrome. Mostly, it is because she does not think of it as a separate business. Lucky Yu is woven into her life, squeezed around her day job as a doctor. A connection long in the making Leung’s connection to food began long before she started baking. Her Hong Kong-born parents grew up in Stanley and Mong Kok, and both moved to Liverpool, a port city in England, in 1975. Unlike many other Chinese immigrants at the time, neither followed the familiar route into the British-Chinese restaurant and takeaway trade. Her father studied computer software at a polytechnic. At the same time, her mother made clothes, opened a small boutique and eventually took over an Eccles cake factory, converting it into a production kitchen supplying spring rolls to restaurants and takeaways. In 2018, when Leung was working as a locum doctor in London, and had more control over her hours, she began volunteering one day a week at Better Health Bakery, a social enterprise that has since closed. Baking had started as a hobby, but the experience changed how she saw the craft. She learned how to work at scale, practising producing dozens of loaves at a time. Four years later, she took a year out of medicine and completed a six-month diploma in bread and pastry at The School of Artisan Food, in Nottinghamshire. For her final assessment, she had to develop a recipe with a story behind it. The result was a round, sesame-coated sourdough loaf incorporating soy sauce and rice congee, which has since become one of Lucky Yu’s signatures. The idea began with Leung’s interest in ancient grains and the crops used in China centuries ago. She researched historical references while studying heritage wheat varieties, then began experimenting with rice, soy, sesame and barley alongside wheat. “Congee is something we eat for breakfast and bread is also eaten for breakfast,” she explains. “How can I smush these ideas together and create a loaf?” The answer was simple maths, she says. She calculated how much water went into the congee, how much salt was in the soy and how much liquid each ingredient contributed, then adjusted the dough accordingly. This curious ethos runs through Lucky Yu’s menu. Mainstays like pineapple buns and cocktail buns sit alongside more experimental creations such as spring onion, fuyu and Parmesan buns; mala tomato jam, goat’s curd and coriander buns; and mushroom char siu puffs. What inspires her? Many of her ideas begin on the cycle to work, when she deliberately switches off her phone and lets her mind wander. Her notes app is filled with things she still wants to make. One long-standing ambition is a salted egg yolk custard cream biscuit. “It’s been in my brain for a long time, and I really can’t wait to get that out,” she says. Leung’s inspiration draws from several worlds that she is part of: Hong Kong bakeries, Japanese bread-making and the European kitchens where she trained. She has staged at the pastry kitchen in nose-to-tail English restaurant St John and the now-closed Japanese bakery Tetote Factory, as well as Swedish bakery Bageriet in Covent Garden. Her time at St John, in particular, changed what she wanted Lucky Yu to be. She became interested in seasonality, good produce and the techniques she had learned in professional kitchens. Rather than deciding everything had to belong neatly to one tradition, she decided it did not matter. “I have full freedom to make whatever it is that I want to make,” she says. That freedom is important because Leung has no desire to force her food into a particular category. It is not a statement about fusion, but simply the things she wants to eat and make. “I’m not doing it because I think there’s a gap,” she says. “I just do it because it feels very natural to me.” Lucky Yu’s small scale gives her another kind of freedom and flexibility, but during baking weeks it can still be punishing. She continues to work her medical shifts, finding time to order the ingredients in bulk, prepare dough in the evenings, then start baking at 2am on Saturday before opening the kitchen window at 10.30am. Her partner, George, now helps with the morning set-up, clearing the kitchen, arranging the display and setting up payments. What began as one collection window has become two, with friends helping to serve customers and restock shelves. Leung is due to finish her general practitioner training in November 2027. She expects medicine to remain part of her working life and cannot imagine making Lucky Yu her sole source of income either. A full-time bakery, she says, would probably break her within a month. “I know that is not sustainable, but I think opening a full-time bakery is really, really hard,” she explains. “I don’t think that I’m in a place to consider that now, but I would never say never.” Making connections What is unique about selling her bakes out of her kitchen window is the direct relationship and community she has fostered with her customers and neighbours.
