On difficult or exhausting days, standing at the window and seeing customers excited about what she has baked can make the early mornings feel worthwhile. “Customers travel, they use their time, spend their hard-earned money, and then they write me nice messages,” she says. Baking, she explains, has given back to her in a way that feels deeply rewarding and restored her faith in humanity. “It’s made the world so much less full of strangers and so much more full of neighbours.” For Leung, baking is a way of making room for something she loves without having to turn it into a full-time job. It has also challenged her ideas about what a career should look like. “I’m developing these two careers side by side,” she says, “but it feels sort of unconventional, but still legitimate, I think.”

title: As Saudi Arabia steps up war against Yemen’s Houthis, Pakistan set to play support role
description: To rally support among Pakistanis for the move, Islamabad and Riyadh have highlighted the Houthis’ recent drone attack on Mecca.
content: Pakistani troops are expected to take over various defensive functions for Saudi Arabia to enable the Middle East country to fight an all-out war aimed at defeating Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. According to defence analysts, Pakistani troops are not expected to participate directly in ground offensives against the Houthis being planned by Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s squabbling government factions. Instead, their primary objective would be to free up Saudi forces to focus on what is likely to be a sustained conflict involving hundreds of thousands of Yemeni fighters on both sides. “Saudi Arabia needs Pakistan to help defend Saudi Arabia so that Saudi forces have greater freedom to operate against the Houthis,” said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London. That means air and missile defence personnel, radar and early warning, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-drone capabilities, electronic warfare, intelligence fusion and command-and-control support. Pakistan can also provide maintenance, munitions support, training, operational planning and potentially additional aircraft and unmanned systems for defensive patrols and surveillance. Riyadh would value Pakistani surveillance, intelligence and potentially naval support around the Red Sea and Saudi approaches, Krieg said, particularly as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which straddles Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea in Africa, had become increasingly contested. Dave Des Roches, a retired Pentagon official and senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said the Saudis wanted the Pakistanis to deploy across the “full range of military operations”. The Pakistanis would likely not agree to such a comprehensive role, while the scope of the functions to be assumed by Pakistani forces and their area of duty would be under intense negotiation between both sides, he added. According to Saudi political scientist Nawaf Obaid, some specialist Pakistani military units may already be providing intelligence and command-and-control support. Writing for Al Jazeera English on September 26, Obaid claimed Saudi and Pakistani joint terminal attack controller (JTAC) teams were already “embedded” with major Yemeni government formations in the north of the country. They are being pitted against Iranian military advisers, whom Western intelligence agencies reported as having played a critical role in the Houthi seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month. Obaid said the Saudi-Pakistani JTAC teams were “restoring an authenticated link” between government forces on the ground and the Saudi-led joint forces command strike system, following its disruption last month by Revolutionary Guards advisers who were supporting Houthi military communications. The system reportedly operated by the Saudi and Pakistani JTAC teams was far more advanced than its Iranian counterpart, he wrote. Its deployment has enabled Saudi warplanes and drones to mount a sustained aerial counteroffensive against the Houthi command structure and massing ground forces. According to Yemeni military spokesmen, several Revolutionary Guards advisers have been killed in “government” air strikes. Security officials in Islamabad remain tight-lipped about the specifics of Pakistan’s role in the Saudi-Houthi conflict while privately telling journalists that their silence should not be misconstrued as a sign of inaction. In April, Pakistan deployed some 8,000 troops, a squadron of JF-17 fighters co-developed with China, and Chinese-built HQ-9 long-range air defence systems to Saudi Arabia under their mutual defence pact signed in September 2025. At the same time, political and military leaders have ratcheted up rhetoric about the extent of Pakistan’s commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia. “We are bound by this arrangement to defend Saudi Arabia. That means whatever means that are available at our disposal, they’ll be available to Saudi Arabia also,” Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Al Jazeera on Wednesday. To rally public support among their mostly Muslim populations, the Saudi and Pakistani governments have cloaked preparations for the decisive conflict in religious garb. Riyadh has accused the Houthis of carrying out drone strikes against Islam’s two holiest shrines in Mecca and Medina in recent weeks, allegations that the Yemeni militia has dismissed as propaganda. Echoing the Saudi narrative at the United Nations General Assembly on September 26, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the first alleged drone attack on Mecca last month had “provoked the anger of Muslims throughout the world”. Any threat to the security and sanctity of the two holy mosques “constitutes a red line that must not be crossed under any circumstances”, Sharif warned. Des Roches saw the alleged Mecca attack as a “requirement” for Pakistani public opinion to support any enhanced military action against the Houthis, given some suspicion about the motives for defending Saudi Arabia. “Pakistanis in particular know how things work in the Gulf, and they are extremely proud of their armed forces,” Des Roches said. “Defending Mecca and Medina could meet the requirement.” Sharif’s declaration at the UN coincided with three other significant developments on the same day. The grand mufti of Saudi Arabia Saleh bin Fawzan bin Abdullah al-Fawzan issued an edict validating the actions of Saudi-led coalition forces against the Houthis. “Preserving this great entity, defending its borders, repelling aggression against it, and punishing anyone who seeks to encroach upon even an inch of it, are among the greatest duties and the best acts of devotion, for which lives and souls are sacrificed in pursuit of God’s pleasure,” Fawzan declared in a written statement. The military commanders of the Mecca Defence Alliance – comprising Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey – also met in Riyadh for the first time to “explore measures supporting” the Saudis under the pact signed in August. In addition, the leader of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashid al-Alimi issued a call for general mobilisation with the unprecedented goal of comprehensively defeating the Houthis. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reiterated this goal in his annual address to the kingdom’s consultative assembly on Wednesday. Krieg expected Pakistan to be cautious about the distinction between defending Saudi territory and conducting offensive operations inside Yemen. “That distinction is politically useful to everybody,” he said. Britain and France are adopting “essentially the same principle” but in different ways to enhance Saudi Arabia’s resilience, according to Krieg. If Pakistan helps protect Saudi airspace, France protects oil infrastructure to enable oil exports via the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and British air force tankers keep Saudi aircraft airborne for longer, Riyadh can focus more on its operations in Yemen. “The interesting consequence is that all these defensive contributions can indirectly enable a more offensive Saudi posture,” Krieg said. “Defensive burden-sharing can therefore become an offensive force multiplier without any of those partners formally joining the war.”

title: Wuhan joins major Chinese cities in shift towards completed-home sales
description: Reforms focus on improving housing supply and delivery rather than boosting demand, analysts say.
content: A complete supply-side transformation of China’s housing market is likely to take precedence over any immediate revival in homebuyer demand following Wuhan’s overhaul of new-home sales, according to property analysts. Wuhan, capital of the central Chinese province of Hubei, is the fourth major economic hub – after Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou – to encourage a broader transition towards completed-home sales. “These measures do not directly stimulate demand, but they will drive a structural shift on the supply side,” said Yan Yuejin, deputy director at E-House China Research and Development Institution. The rules were likely to steer buyers towards completed homes and higher-quality inventory, Yan added. Li Guozheng, director of China Index Academy’s central China market research centre, said the policy sought to balance delivery risks, buyer protection and developers’ funding pressure. “This will help enterprises transition while supporting a smooth market adjustment,” he said in an interview with domestic media on Thursday. Under regulations issued on Thursday, residential projects on land sold after August 28 can open pre-sales only after a building’s main structure has been topped out, while developers are encouraged to prioritise completed home sales. Projects on land acquired before that date without construction permits will generally be subject to the new rules. However, developers may continue to use the previous presale framework until the end of 2027 if district authorities determine projects can be delivered on schedule. The measures implement an August 28 directive issued by national housing, land and financial regulators instructing local governments to prioritise sales of completed homes on newly sold land. Pre-sales remain permitted, but under stricter conditions, and mortgages on pre-sold homes will be issued only after projects are completed, according to the official notice. The policy overhaul comes as China’s property market continues to diverge across regions. Average new-home prices in first-tier cities edged up 0.1 per cent month on month in August, while prices in second-tier cities slipped 0.1 per cent. Wuhan, generally classified as a second-tier city, has faced greater pressure. New-home prices dropped 1.7 per cent year on year in August, while resale prices slumped 6.3 per cent. To ease cash flow, the local government said developers operating under the previous regime could apply for bank guarantees to replace up to 30 per cent of escrow funds reserved for project completion. Developers of land acquired after the national directive must pay at least half the land premium within six months and the remainder within a year, or within two years with regulatory approval. Yan said similar policy roll-outs across major cities highlighted a broader shift towards tighter supervision of developers’ funds, alongside targeted credit support aimed at lowering financing costs. He added that the changes were expected to have their biggest impact on developers as investment models were “likely to undergo some changes”.

title: Latvia holds election as concerns over Russia, inflation dominate
description: The Nato member views Russia as its main security threat and has significantly increased defence spending amid the Ukraine war.
content: Latvia will vote on Saturday in an election shaped by concerns over neighbouring Russia and the cost of living, but the result is not expected to steer the country off its pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course. The centre-right United List party of incumbent Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs is at the head of the race, with over 14 per cent of the vote, according to the SKDS institute. His coalition, however, is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain ground by focusing on economic concerns in the least affluent of the three Baltic states. The current governing coalition is made up of United List, New Unity, the Union of Greens and Farmers and the National Alliance. Polls suggest the bloc is unlikely to retain power in its current form after the vote. Criticised as pro-Russian by its detractors, the populist Sovereign Power party, led by Julija Stepanenko, is polling at over 9 per cent and could become the second-largest party in Latvia’s 100-seat unicameral parliament. The party has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases to defence spending, instead highlighting domestic economic problems. Despite its gains, the party is unlikely to enter government because most major parties have ruled out cooperation with it. Another populist force, Latvia First, led by businessman Ainars Slesers, could prove a more viable coalition partner. The Progressives, a pro-European social democratic party advocating stronger social protections and continued support for Ukraine, are polling around 6 per cent. With roughly one in five voters still undecided, the final composition of the next parliament remains uncertain. Fourteen electoral lists are contesting the election, but polls indicate only seven are likely to clear the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter parliament. Security remains central to political debate four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Latvia, a member of Nato and the European Union since 2004, views Russia as its principal security threat and has significantly increased defence spending in response. It has sharply increased its defence spending since Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Kyiv, now allocating nearly 5 per cent of its GDP to defence. Most parties expected to enter parliament support maintaining military spending at elevated levels and continuing help to Kyiv. Economic issues nevertheless remain crucial to voters. Rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline all feature prominently in campaign debates. Voting patterns among Latvia’s large Russian-speaking minority are also changing. Once concentrated behind the Harmony party, which lost parliamentary representation in 2022, many voters are increasingly making choices based on economic and social issues rather than identity politics alone. Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex. Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday. Exit polls are expected shortly after polling stations close.

title: Prison term ‘karma’, says Hong Kong man freed after 26 years in Philippine jail
description: Tang Lung-wai, 55, says he learned how to be a proper human being while locked up in Manila for a drug offence he insists he did not commit.
content: On his 29th birthday, Hong Kong bartender Tang Lung-wai boarded a flight to the Philippines for a holiday that would change his life. He ended up spending 26 years in jail in the country. Now 55, Tang spent years fighting his drug-related charges, insisting that he had been framed. But he told the South China Morning Post that he did not view those lost decades solely through the lens of bitterness. “At first, I felt a lot of resentment about being framed like that. But in the end, it’s no use holding onto so much resentment. Since you’re already in jail and since you cannot change what has already happened, you just have to change yourself to adapt to this environment,” he said. Tang, who returned to Hong Kong on Tuesday after being released from prison, said he considered his 26 years behind bars “karma” for being a “b*****d” to his family, whom he had ignored, the friends he had betrayed and the girlfriends he had cheated on. “What I learned in prison is how to be a proper human being,” he said. “It is like heaven arranged for me to learn how to be a proper person. Once I have learned it, they let me out.” Being able to walk out safe and sound, Tang considered himself to have repaid all his karmic debt. ‘Troubled kid’ Tang was arrested in Manila in July 2000 for possession of methamphetamine, also known as Ice, and remanded in custody. He was convicted more than a decade later, in 2011, and handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines can mean up to 40 years in prison. A Manila court ruled in July that his sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct. He was deported and returned home on Tuesday night. Reflecting on his life behind bars, Tang said prison had changed him profoundly. Growing up in a Kwai Chung public housing estate, Tang was the middle child in his family. As a teenager, he fell in with neighbourhood street gangs. “People could tell right away that I was a troubled kid,” Tang recalled, stressing that he was never a triad member and had no criminal record in Hong Kong. He fought for years to prove his innocence, arguing that he was not in the Philippines when surveillance related to the crime was carried out on June 1, 2000. He visited the country on June 19, 2000. Tang said he believed he came to the attention of police when co-defendant Cheung Tai-on, a casino worker whom he knew through friends, picked him up at the airport. They travelled together for a few days. He recalled that Cheung later admitted to telling police his whereabouts after he himself was arrested. On July 18, police pulled Tang from a taxi outside his hotel in Manila. He was taken to a police station where he claimed he was beaten up and extorted for money in exchange for his release. Police then placed him in a flat in Quezon City, Metro Manila, with other co-defendants and staged a raid, finding 8kg of Ice inside, he said. He said they were forced to admit the crime at gunpoint. Tang recalled he was furious with Cheung and assaulted him several times while they were remanded in a police cell. But as time passed, he forgave him. Cheung once took the blame for him after he was caught keeping a mobile phone, a banned item in prison, and was kept in solitary confinement for a month. Cheung died of a heart attack in prison in 2016. “When he died, I could not believe I cried. I really cried. I think it’s a pity,” he said. Low profile for survival Tang spent 11 years in custody before he was convicted. He was remanded for eight months in a police cell before he was sent to Quezon City Jail – infamous for overcrowding and poor living conditions – where he said he spent his worst few years. He said the prison was like a small community with shops, restaurants and wet markets operated by inmates, as well as gyms, churches and hospitals. “Never use a Hong Kong perspective to think about the Philippines,” he said, adding that the rich could even build houses inside the prison. “You can live a different life depending on how much you have in your pocket.” At first he had no money to secure a bed from the inmate leader and slept on the ground, sometimes by a drain or outside a toilet, jostling with other prisoners, he said. Conditions were so bad that he caught a skin disease. “I was always starving,” he said, as prison only served small pieces of meat, a small bowl of rice and some bread. “I was so poor that I had no money to buy toothpaste,” Tang recalled, adding that he used his fingers to rub salt on his teeth to clean them. He earned extra food by washing clothes for wealthier Chinese inmates, looking after their children, who were allowed to stay in prison during family visits, and helping out in restaurants. Tang said he saw gang fights and murders inside the prison and to survive he kept a low profile. “Some prison officers did not know my name after all these 26 years,” he said. He began writing letters to appeal for help in 2003. As a British National (Overseas) passport holder, he first wrote to the British embassy in Manila. “It took me seven hours to write. There was no AI. I just looked it up in the dictionary,” he said. He later received allowances of 10,000 pesos every three months from the embassy. He also called the Hong Kong Immigration Department for help. Into prison routine After Tang was convicted in 2011, he was transferred to the notorious New Bilibid Prison in Manila. Following an appeal for help, he received around HK$10,000 in donations. He shared some with Cheung, and spent 10,500 pesos to buy himself a 40 sq ft room with a bed from an inmate leader. He spent the remaining 6,500 pesos to buy his first smartphone and secretly kept it. Tang used his smartphone to learn how to use social media and began writing articles on Facebook about his life in prison. He later published two books, which earned him public attention and donations from readers. However, he received two years of solitary confinement as punishment in 2018. Tang said his prison life over the past few years had been quite routine. He lived in a large cell with 70 other foreigners. Waking up at 10am, he hit the gym in the morning and then went to the market to buy food, paid for by other prisoners, and prepared lunch for them. He then took a nap and went jogging in the afternoon. After preparing dinner for other inmates, he played on his mobile phone. Tang said that he had picked up conversational Tagalog but could not fully follow the television news. Back in Hong Kong, apart from getting a driving licence to make a living, Tang said he also wanted to offer help to troubled youth and obtain a first aid certificate so that he could rescue anyone in an emergency. He also plans to write a third book to record his experiences and anecdotes from prison. “Hong Kong people have helped me a lot. I also wish to contribute to this society,” he said. While he had lost the prime years of his life in which he might have had his own family, Tang said he would just go with the flow. “After these 26 years, there may be something even worse in my life that lies ahead. I don’t know. But I will be stronger in adversity,” he said.

title: Chinese lithium mine registers wider vein, bolstering Beijing’s battery supply
description: A deposit in Sichuan has registered over 1 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, adding to China’s stores of the valuable metal.
content: China has announced the expansion of the resource base for a major lithium deposit in the southwestern province of Sichuan by about 70 per cent, strengthening the country’s potential long-term supply for the metal – an essential component in the production of batteries for electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage. After recent detection efforts, the Jiada Lithium Mine has registered about 1.05 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent in the deposit, bringing its total resources to 2.53 million tonnes, state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday. The increase reinforces the mine’s status as a major hard-rock lithium deposit. Dazhong Mining, the project’s developer, said in a filing that the additional resources had passed review and registration by the Ministry of Natural Resources. They comprise 33.52 million tonnes of ore containing about 423,800 tonnes of lithium oxide, with an average grade of 1.26 per cent. The addition represents a 70.5 per cent increase from the previously registered 1.48 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, according to the filing. The company estimates that the deposit’s initial mining area, with an approved extraction scale of 2.6 million tonnes of ore a year, could support annual production of about 50,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate at full capacity, though it was still completing procedures to obtain mining and operating permits. Lithium’s utility in the manufacturing of EVs, energy storage systems and consumer electronics makes access to the metal a strategic concern for China, as its battery and clean-energy firms grow into world leaders. The country has substantial domestic deposits. In January 2025, the China Geological Survey said exploration breakthroughs had increased China’s share of global lithium reserves to 16.5 per cent, placing it second worldwide by the agency’s estimates. Yet China remains heavily reliant on overseas supplies, counting on overseas sources for about 60 per cent of its lithium resource supply in 2025, according to a report by the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association. It imports lithium concentrates from countries including Australia, Zimbabwe and Brazil, while Chile and Argentina are its main sources of imported lithium carbonate. Jada lies within a lithium belt that stretches across West Kunlun, Songpan and Garze in China’s west, which measures about 2,800km (1,740 miles) and forms part of what Chinese geologists call the “Asian lithium belt”. The region is a major concentration of the country’s hard-rock lithium resources, according to Xinhua. Wang Denghong, director of the Institute of Mineral Resources at the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, was quoted by Xinhua as saying the additional resources would strengthen western Sichuan’s lithium resource base, bolster domestic supply security and “help reduce dependence on foreign sources”. The expansion follows other major exploration gains. In Sichuan, local authorities announced a breakthrough at the Murong deposit in Yajiang in 2024, identifying about 990,000 tonnes of lithium oxide. And in July last year, central China’s Hunan province announced that its Jijiaoshan deposit contained 490 million tonnes of ore holding 1.31 million tonnes of lithium oxide. Overall, China identified eight new lithium deposits nationwide in 2025, according to a report published by the China Geological Survey. The expansion comes amid a broader mineral exploration campaign, launched in 2021, to strengthen domestic supplies of energy resources and strategic minerals and improve supply chain security.

title: ‘Better than expected’: 73,800 subdivided flats apply for 3-year grace period
description: Landlords who applied between March and August qualified for a waiver of HK$3,000 in recognition fees per subdivided flat until February 2029.
content: More than 73,000 owners of subdivided flats in Hong Kong have applied for a three-year grace period to meet the government’s minimum standards, a figure the housing chief has described as “better than expected”. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin said on Saturday that authorities received around 73,800 applications during the “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Units Ordinance, which closed on August 31. The tally represented nearly 70 per cent of the city’s estimated 110,000 subdivided flats, with 42 already certified as compliant, Ho told a radio programme. “The progress is better than I expected,” she said. “We expect that as we gradually enter the three-year grace period, as people become familiar with the certification process and find suitable renovation companies and professionals to handle it, the certification numbers will rise.” Ho urged remaining landlords to register before the grace period began next March. “We hope all landlords will register first, regardless of what you decide to do in the future, whether you continue operating or not, or rectify the current situation to make it compliant,” she said. Under Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, authorities aim to eliminate substandard subdivided flats in residential buildings by 2030 by boosting supply and cutting public housing waiting times. Landlords who applied between March and August qualified for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in recognition fees per subdivided flat until February 2029. A second six-month registration round, offering smaller fee discounts, is now under way and will complete the overall one-year application period. From March next year, only subdivided flats that meet minimum requirements and are certified as “basic housing units” may be legally leased, except for those covered by the grace period. The grace period runs from March 2027 to February 2030, giving landlords time to refurbish and certify their properties. Landlords must bear renovation and certification costs and pay the government HK$3,000 per subdivided flat for recognition as basic housing units. On the same programme, Ho revealed that 90.6 per cent of Wang Fuk Court owners had returned signed letters accepting the government’s buy-back offer. She spoke three days after the first batch of about 100 homeowners selected their replacement flats earlier this week. Following last November’s fire at Wang Fuk Court, authorities launched a HK$7.8 billion plan to buy back flats at the eight-block subsidised housing estate. Under the scheme, participants can use the cash compensation to purchase a flat on the private market or join a special sales exercise to buy new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement. Ho said a dedicated explanation team accompanied around 30 households daily, assisting them through the process, as many comprised elderly residents who needed time to consult their families. Public housing estates with faster completion times, such as those in Kowloon Bay and Fanling, proved popular as residents wanted to move into their new homes as soon as possible, she added. Ho said the remaining 10 per cent of owners who had not signed sale and purchase agreements should complete the process by October 15. “If they ultimately decide not to sign a contract with us, we will consider it a refusal to sell,” she said, adding that they would be grouped with the 13 households that did not sign letters accepting the acquisition offer. “We will handle these cases later. For example, we might need to consider legislation to address this.”

title: Restaurant business grows 10% on first 2 days of break as arrivals top 2018 peak
description: Tourism chief confident city will reach annual target of 53.8 million visitors earlier than expected.
content: Mainland Chinese visitor arrivals in Hong Kong during the first two days of the National Day “golden week” surpassed the pre-pandemic total for the same period in 2018, as a catering sector representative reported a 10 per cent year-on-year increase in restaurant receipts. The tourism chief expressed confidence on Saturday that the city would reach its annual target of 53.8 million visitors earlier than expected. The city recorded 511,311 arrivals from the mainland on Thursday and Friday, according to Immigration Department figures, edging past the 508,578 recorded during the same period in 2018. The first day of the break drew 277,304 mainland visitors, up from 247,626 on the opening day in 2018. The second day welcomed 234,007, compared with 260,952 that year. More than 568,000 Hong Kong residents departed from the city on Friday and Saturday, representing a 14 per cent increase from the same period in the previous year. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Saturday that mainland tourists on the first day had surpassed the pre-pandemic high, with many visitors also arriving early for the Mid-Autumn Festival. “Visitor numbers over the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend rose 28 per cent, so if the golden week still posts a 5 per cent increase on top of that, it is actually quite a lot,” she said. Asked whether the city would reach its 53.8 million visitor target ahead of schedule, Law said she was very confident despite the challenges posed by global conditions. “The global conditions, particularly in Southeast Asia, do pose challenges, as short-haul travellers’ willingness to spend and to visit Hong Kong has been affected by high airfares overall,” she said. The 53.8 million target, set by the government at the start of the year, represents an 8 per cent increase on the 49.89 million arrivals recorded in 2025. Law said authorities would also “go out more” to understand travellers’ preferences. The minister said she hoped to return to markets such as Southeast Asia to step up promotion once global conditions stabilised. She added that events such as the Victoria Park Mid-Autumn lantern carnival, organised by the Tourism Board and the retail and catering sectors, had drawn a strong response and showcased the city’s East-meets-West appeal. Simon Wong Ka-wo, president of the Hong Kong Federation of Restaurants and Related Trades, said the catering industry’s performance during the first two days of the golden week holiday “exceeded expectations”. The industry’s turnover on October 1 reached HK$320 million (US$40.78 million) thanks to the fireworks display, Wong said. Restaurants recorded a 10 per cent year-on-year growth in business due to the increase in mainland visitors, some of whom hailed from more distant cities, stayed for longer and had higher purchasing power. Wong said he believed the momentum would be sustained for the rest of the week and that the number of mainland visitors could potentially surpass the government’s estimate of 1.29 million visitor trips for the period. “Conversely, the trend of local residents, particularly middle-aged and older demographics, heading north to mainland China for consumption shows signs of cooling off,” he said. “They are increasingly realising that the value-for-money between the Greater Bay Area and Hong Kong is narrowing and travelling north requires a significant amount of time and effort.” Wong said the special holiday promotions and discounts by many Hong Kong restaurants were able to attract tourists and locals alike, with some eateries even seeing long queues. At Langham Place in Mong Kok, a manager surnamed Chow at GoodDay Cafe said the shop had received more customers than usual. “It’s around 20 per cent above our usual flow. Since the shops here mainly serve tourists, our business moves in tandem with visitor arrivals,” he said. Away from the tourist hotspots, crowds thinned. Wendy Kwok and Jo Leung, owners of HappyJo, which sells local snacks and rice dishes at Dragon Centre in Sham Shui Po, said the food court was only half-full during the past two days. “Our customer flow was about 30 per cent down. Saturday seats at the food court are usually fully packed, but now there are still empties,” Kwok said. Meanwhile, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said bookings for the Southbound Travel Scheme for Guangdong Vehicles to enter the city had exceeded its daily quota of 200 during the National day holiday. The quota was increased to 200 per day in July and expanded to nine cities in the bay area. “During these few days of the National Day break, we’ve seen the booking numbers for the southbound scheme exceed the quota of 200, and almost reached 300. This has met our expectations as there are ups and downs in the bookings on normal days, but it will rebound very well during holidays.” As to whether the government planned to increase the quota, Chan said they were preparing to expand the scheme to all 21 cities in Guangdong province by the first quarter of next year. “We will continue to discuss with the Guangdong authorities and closely monitor the implementation situation of both the southbound and northbound schemes to see if there is a need,” she said. Additional reporting by Cannix Yau

title: Asian Games: windsurfers’ golden double takes Hong Kong to record medal haul
description: Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet win respective boys’ and girls’ events to take the number of golds won in Japan into double figures.
content: Hong Kong windsurfers Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet both won Asian Games titles on Saturday, taking the city’s gold medal count into double figures for the first time since its athletes started competing in the multi-sport event in 1954. With Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s triumph in the men’s singles little more than an hour earlier securing a record-equalling eighth gold, victory on the water made it nine and 10 for the delegation in Japan. Not even a lack of wind at Kaiyoh Yacht Harbor could spoil the day, and with just one race possible, the overnight results carried greater weight than they might have otherwise. As such, Wong and Cheung claimed gold after building a healthy lead after 10 races in previous days. Wong, 18, won six of his 11 races to finish top of a six-strong fleet with 13 points. Masato Kozono of Japan took silver, while Singapore’s John Wong Tze-xiang finished with bronze. “I’m super, super happy. I can’t imagine it – when the race committee announced that we’ve done all the races, I was so relieved, immediately so happy,” he said. “It’s a big achievement, just unbelievable. “I think my week is quite consistent. I did many races for the first place and I think I made fewer mistakes than other competitors. This achievement just proves how hard I worked for the past few years, and that the hard work pays off.” In the girls’ event, 17-year-old Cheung won nine races, with Japan’s Akari Oshima taking silver ahead of Thailand’s Chanatkan Charoensuk. Hong Kong’s previous best gold medal haul was eight, which the city’s athletes managed three times: 2010, 2018 and 2023. Head coach Chan King-yin, who famously won two golds and one bronze at the Asian Games, said the pair’s success was a result of a two-year plan. “Four of our young windsurfers, including Wong and Cheung, paused their studies in June last year to train as full-time athletes,” he said. “Both of them had participated in the iQFOiL Youth and Junior World Championships in Spain in July, and Cheung finished No 11. “As for Wong, he might not be the strongest among us but he is clever, very smart on the racecourse, and is good all-round. Both of them are our future.” Insufficient wind meant the men’s and women’s races were scratched, leaving Ma Kwan-ching to take silver in her event. China’s Li Wenqi, who finished first in nine of the 10 races, won gold, while Japan’s Rina Nijima took bronze. “I have done [windsurfing] for 22 years, in Hong Kong and around the world,” veteran Ma said. “I’m so happy to finish my third Asian Games with the silver. “I’ve been chasing the gold for 12 years, but unfortunately I didn’t [win] the gold medal after more than 10 years [of trying]. I am 29. But I’m still happy. I enjoy the sport a lot.” In sailing, Huang Zixi and Tiago Cheng de Villemor Salgado added one silver and one bronze to the overall table in the girls’ and boys’ dinghy events. Saturday’s early medals took Hong Kong’s total to 52, just one shy of the record 53 they managed in Hangzhou. The men’s and women’s rugby teams have still to finish their tournaments, however, with the men facing China in their battle for a third consecutive title, while the women take on fierce rivals Thailand in a repeat of the bronze medal clash in 2023. Any addition to the 10 gold, 19 silver and 23 bronze medals already in the bag would make this the most successful Games in Hong Kong’s history.

title: Unsung Eats: 5 best places to eat in Milan during the World’s 50 Best Bars awards
description: Step away from the cocktail circuit this October for saffron risotto, Japanese-Italian twists, fermentation-led tasting menus and more.
content: Milan, Italy’s fashion capital and home to this year’s World’s 50 Best Bars awards ceremony, offers bites as exquisite as its reputation. For those checking out the awards this month, be sure to make time for the city’s food scene, which is every bit as compelling as its bar culture. Alongside traditional trattorias, a new generation of chefs with fine-dining pedigrees steps away from rigid traditions, experimenting with fermentation menus, sustainable work hours, and a fusion of cultures. Meanwhile, one of the city’s beloved trattorias offers a refined take on Milan’s speciality dishes, from saffron risotto to Cotoletta alla Milanese. Trattoria del Nuovo Macello View this post on Instagram A post shared by Trattoria del Nuovo Macello (@trattoriadelnuovomacello) This trattoria may be recommended in the Michelin Guide, but its slightly out-of-reach location means tourists staying in the centre often overlook it. Trattoria del Nuovo Macello is named after the slaughterhouse previously housed across the road. Today, the restaurant is distinctly private, homey and welcoming, serving regional dishes with modern refinement. The risotto alla Milanese – saffron risotto – is rumoured to be the best in town. They also offer a heavily discounted weekday lunch set, although the dishes vary daily. Location: Via Cesare Lombroso, 20, 20137 Milan Must-order: Risotto alla Milanese, Cotoletta alla Milanese Spore Ristorante View this post on Instagram A post shared by SPORE (@spore_ristorante) Italy sticks to its traditions, but the big city has plenty of ambitious restaurants. Spore specialises in fermentation, with elements of koji, garum and miso woven throughout the tasting menu. It serves only tasting menus to avoid food waste, and the dishes change seasonally. Location: Via Passo Buole Near N. 4, 20135 Milan Must-order: The five-course €50 tasting menu will allow diners to get a taste of the restaurant’s ethos Bentoteca View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bentoteca Milano (@bentotecamilano) Opened by Japanese chef Yoji Tokuyoshi, Bentoteca is a Japanese restaurant that celebrates Italian ingredients while staying true to Japanese flavours. The result is an electric fusion of the two cultures, such as tuna ossobuco (translating to “bone with a hole”), turning one of Milan’s favourite meat dishes unexpectedly pescatarian. Location: Via S. Calocero, 3, 20123 Milan Must-order: Taste a range of their classics and specials through their omakase menu, and add on the popular drunken chicken – marinated in sake, cooked on the grill and served with sardella sauce, a Calabrian fish sauce. Sandi Sandi is a modern bistro mostly open for lunch, except on Fridays, when it also opens for dinner. Shifting away from the rigidity of typical restaurants, Sandi is a breath of fresh air in how they operate and the dishes they serve. The plates are rooted in Italy’s ingredient-forward mindset and skilfully elevated by chef Laura Santosuosso. Location: Via Francesco Hayez, 13, 20129 Milan Must-order: Their latest seasonal menu Nebbia View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nebbia Milano (@nebbiamilano) Nebbia is a contemporary bistro rooted in Milanese cuisine and edited through the chefs’ fine-dining backgrounds. The minimalistic dining room is bright and spacious, while the food brings bursts of colour – from seafood starters such as marinated trout to a range of pastas with unexpected flavour combinations. Location: Via Evangelista Torricelli, 15, 20136 Milan Must-order: Fegatini, pan brioche e cipolla caramellata – pâté with buttery brioche and caramelised onions

title: Overwhelmed by city life? Slow down with these yoga and mindfulness exercises
description: Use the anchor breath to bring your focus back and relieve tight shoulders with the eagle arms pose.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
While city life is exciting, it can also feel overwhelming. The bright lights, constant noise and crowded spaces can be exhausting.
This constant busyness can overload your nervous system, making it hard to relax and sleep.
Yoga and mindfulness can help restore balance to your body. You can try these exercises at home or even while you are out and about .
No matter how stressful things are, you can always find a peaceful place inside yourself.
This breathing exercise brings your attention back and calms your nervous system.
Think of your breath like an anchor, keeping you steady. To begin, stand or sit up tall and place one hand on your belly. Close your eyes to help block out distractions. Breathe in and out through your nostrils.
Try to notice how your breath moves the hand that is on your belly. To stay focused, you can think of the words “breathe in” as you inhale and the words “breathe out” as you exhale. Try to slow your breathing while making sure it still feels comfortable. Repeat this for five rounds or more.
After a busy day moving around a city, this position calms the mind, releases tightness in your legs and improves blood circulation . It might even help you sleep better.
To start, sit in front of a chair. Lie down on your back and lift your calves and feet onto the chair with your toes pointing towards the ceiling. Use a pillow or your hands to support your head. Feel free to close your eyes.
Stay here for a few minutes and focus on your breathing. You can practise anchor breath here.
To come out of this position, bend your knees into your chest and roll to one side. Lift yourself up slowly.
This pose releases tightness from your shoulders, which can be caused by feeling stressed, hunching over a computer or carrying heavy bags. You can practise this at home or on public transport.
Begin in a seated or standing position. Hook your right arm under your left arm and then wrap your arms around each other so that your left palm touches your right fingers.
Squeeze your arms together. Gently lift your elbows while relaxing and pushing your shoulders down. Make space between your arms and face. Take five breaths here before repeating this with your left arm under your right arm.
This version of child’s pose can be practised on a chair instead of a mat. No matter where you are, you can sit down and stretch your lower back while taking a quiet moment.
Start by sitting on a chair and leaning forward.
Bend your arms and bring your right elbow to your right thigh and your left elbow to your left thigh. Rest your head in your hands.
If there is a table in front of you, you can cross your forearms and rest your head on them. Close your eyes if that feels comfortable.
Focus on your breath and stay here for as long as it feels good.

title: Hong Kong Airport Authority to reshape 11 Skies as a high-end tourism landmark
description: Transport chief Mable Chan says the project will align with the Airport City development, aiming to create an entertainment hub with minimal public investment.
content: The Airport Authority will reposition the 11 Skies commercial project after taking it over next April, with the government expecting it to become a high-end tourism landmark with minimal public investment, the transport chief has said. After developer New World Development (NWD) announced on Wednesday that it would return the 11 Skies project to the authority next April, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Saturday that the two sides had reached an agreement on commercial and contractual principles. “From the government perspective, we are pleased and welcome to see both sides trying to resolve this matter as far as practicable,” she told a radio programme. The handover includes an entertainment complex and three office towers. Debt-ridden New World will provide more than HK$3 billion (US$382.3 million) in cash or equivalents, following major losses. On Wednesday, the authority said it was taking forward the project “full steam ahead” and aimed to create a unique entertainment hub that would open in the 2028-29 financial year. Chan said the authority would align the project with its Airport City development, with the aim of making 11 Skies a core landmark for high-end tourism activities. Airport City is a development blueprint to expand Hong Kong International Airport as a key aviation hub while creating a new destination for business and leisure. “The agreement allows the Airport Authority to set a clear road map and timetable to take over and reposition the project,” she said. “We expect the authority to turn the project into a core landmark for high-end aviation, luxury retail, arts and culture, tourism and water sports like yachting.” She added that a dedicated team would upgrade the offices, shops and restaurants in the original 11 Skies plan, adding more experiential activities for passengers, particularly those in transit. Chan said the authority would align the project with the opening of Airport Terminal 2 at the end of 2027 and the completion of AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 in 2028, allowing visitors to enjoy concerts. The project would also integrate with autonomous vehicles to provide smart transport through a “SkyCity Corridor” linking the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge. “The project will provide seamless connections for passengers from around the world. Travellers can experience Hong Kong’s business, entertainment, dining and tourism without leaving the airport area,” she said. She added that the authority also planned to invite expressions of interest next year for two future tenders: an art storage facility and a marina bay in Airport City. On government investment in the project, Chan said that under Hong Kong’s five-year plan, the government would oversee the authority’s Airport City development to ensure it required minimal public investment. “The authority must conduct careful commercial operational estimates including calculating its rate of return for each item to keep its own direct investment to a minimum. We also hope to attract investors into the project which will be put to tender for every smaller item,” she said. The 11 Skies project was intended to complement the authority’s plan to develop Skytopia, a HK$100 billion landmark surrounding Hong Kong International Airport, with commercial, cultural, leisure and entertainment elements. The HK$20 billion 11 Skies development was originally expected to include three grade A office towers totalling 52,955 square metres (570,000 square feet), alongside about 247,000 square metres of retail and dining space – 70 per cent of the entire project.

title: G20 countries divided over US call to curb excess industrial capacity
description: The US call for cooperation to eliminate goods produced with forced labour from supply chains drew support from only Mexico and Argentina.
content: A “handful” of Group of 20 trade ministers rejected US calls to curb excess industrial capacity and “non-market” policies, the US Trade Representative’s office said on Friday, exposing divisions within the group of major economies. The US, this year’s G20 chair, issued the statement ‌a day after a trade meeting in Milwaukee that revealed that only two countries – Mexico and Argentina – signed on to a US-led statement calling for more work and cooperation to eliminate goods produced with forced labour from supply chains. The rejection from the vast majority of G20 countries follows the Trump administration’s imposition of tariffs of 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent on goods from 59 countries and the European Union over allegations that they fail to adequately enforce bans on forced labour. USTR is also conducting a second “Section 301” tariff investigation into 16 trading partners that show signs of excess industrial capacity. The probe is widely ⁠expected to lead to new duties in coming months. The USTR statement did not name countries that objected to the excess-capacity statement. But China had objected to ‌a similar G20 statement denouncing forced labour and non-market economic policies that lead to excessive exports at a finance leaders’ meeting a month ago in North Carolina. “The draft ministerial statement was supported by all but a handful of members, a few of whom ‌firmly rejected creating this pathway towards cooperative action” on excess capacity, the statement said, adding that this “severely disappointed” the US G20 presidency. China’s excess ⁠industrial capacity and industrial subsidies have been ⁠key themes of the US-led G20 ministerial meetings so far this year. Beijing has rejected claims that its industrial policies have created excess capacity, accusing Western countries of using the issue to justify ‌protectionist measures. The US said that G20 trade ministers reached consensus on denouncing the weaponisation of food trade, with members agreeing that trade in food or agricultural inputs should not be used as a tool for ‌economic or ‌political coercion. In that G20 joint statement, the ministers defined the weaponisation of food as measures to “slow, stop, block or direct the flow of food and agricultural ‌inputs” to exert coercive pressure to extract unrelated geopolitical concessions. “We condemn food weaponisation, as it poses a significant humanitarian and economic threat,” the G20 trade ministers ⁠said. After pressure from US President Donald Trump that included the threat of a US diesel export ban, Group of Seven countries on Friday agreed to release some ⁠100 million barrels of diesel reserves to try to drive down record-high US diesel prices. The fuel is widely used in agricultural production. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Thursday that he did not seek a joint statement on a fourth discussion topic, reforming the “most favoured nation” (MFN) system of published, unconditional global tariff ‌rates that underpin the World Trade Organization. MFN tariffs have defined the global trading system since the end of World War II. Greer has argued that the MFN principle has been abused by non-market-oriented economies such as China that have subsidised industries, but it does not allow these countries to be treated differently. The US statement said some G20 members had expressed a willingness to consider changes to MFN, including expanding exceptions to the principle and issuing new legal interpretations to enable greater use of existing exceptions.

title: Asian Angle | PAS wants urban Malaysia’s vote. Can it win over urban Malays?
description: The Islamist party has been working to prove it has a sound economic agenda and the ability to carry it out.
content: A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters. PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno. PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life. Currently, PAS controls the state governments of Kedah, Kelantan, Perlis and Terengganu. In the 2022 general election and various state polls the following year, PAS made inroads into states previously controlled by Umno, such as Perak, Pahang and Selangor. These states, however, are more urbanised, economically developed and demographically diverse, and campaigning on a platform of Islamic credibility to govern was not enough to attract Malay voters there. They may be religiously conservative but will not blindly vote based on faith alone. The results of the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections this year show that the more urbanised west coast and southern states pose a challenge for PAS. The only way for PAS to expand its presence is by allying with Malay nationalist parties such as Umno and the newly formed Wawasan. A nationwide poll in April by the Merdeka Centre showed that 81 per cent of Muslim Malays listed economic concerns as the country’s main challenge. About 53 per cent of Malays feel the country is going in the wrong direction. Most of those making less than 4,000 ringgit per month (US$980), many of whom are Malays, feel the same. PAS is targeting these voters, and it is clear that their top priority is the economy. PAS’ aim is to show them it has a sound and feasible economic agenda and, more importantly, the technocratic chops to carry it out. At its annual congress, or muktamar, last month, PAS sought to convince the Malaysian public of its ability to govern. The party put forth reformist-like motions, such as the creation of a Royal Commission of Inquiry on the so-called corporate mafia; increasing protection of healthcare workers and ramping up rice production to augment food security. Whether PAS can convince voters of this reformist, welfare-focused vision remains a challenge in the months leading up to the general election. PAS has some ground to cover from its posturing of the past decade. After purging the “professional” faction in 2015, PAS has since adopted a more ethno-religious stance. It has fused Islamism and Malay nationalism and coalesced around its hardline president, Abdul Hadi Awang. The image turns off many Malays who are pious but do not buy into PAS’ divisive rhetoric. Hence the appeal of technocrats in PAS who are seen as the party’s moderate face. Since 2018, PAS has been showcasing technocratic leaders such as Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, the chief minister of Terengganu, and Syahir Sulaiman, MP of Bachok in Kelantan. Ahmad Samsuri holds a PhD in aerospace engineering from the University of Leeds and is a protege of Abdul Hadi. Syahir has a private sector background, having worked with the Sime Darby Group before becoming a full-time politician in 2018. PAS regularly uses the Samsuri administration in Terengganu as an example of the party’s governing achievements. But PAS might be overstating its case. As an oil-producing state, Terengganu is highly dependent on oil royalties from the federal government, which make up about 80 to 90 per cent of its budget. Such royalties played a big role in the Samsuri administration’s ability to fulfil its populist agenda in its first term from 2018 to 2023. This was primarily due to the unimpeded flow of revenue from the then Perikatan Nasional federal government, of which PAS was part. The dynamic changed after 2022 when the current Madani federal government took over. These royalty payments are now subjected to onerous conditions set by Putrajaya. This affects the Samsuri administration’s visibility significantly, as the federal government can now claim credit for the payments. The federal government has also opted to develop the state directly by funding myriad projects such as a new hospital in Dungun and a 60 million ringgit (US$14.7 million) poverty eradication programme. But are the technocrats in PAS actually more religiously moderate compared with the hardline ulamas in the party? Given that PAS seeks to propel an ideologically driven movement, party members must go through a regimented indoctrination process, such as regularly attending usrah (guided study sessions). In short, a PAS technocrat can be as dogmatic as a religious scholar; the only difference is that one wears a suit and a tie while the other wears a robe and a turban. Authority over matters of faith and ideological underpinnings still resides with the ulama council. Economic policies formulated by the party’s technocrats have to get a religious imprimatur from the ulamas. As Malaysia heads into the 16th general election, PAS needs to make a case for its governing ability to hesitant Malay voters in urban and semi-urban areas. This is especially so when development in PAS strongholds still lags behind Pakatan Harapan-governed areas like Selangor and Penang. Working with Umno would help PAS leverage the former’s vast experience and proven track record in government. In the 2022 general election and various 2023 state polls, PAS combined forces with Bersatu, allowing it to penetrate Malay-majority areas outside its strongholds. As a result, PAS increased its parliamentary seats from 18 to 43 and made inroads in Perak, Selangor and Pahang. There is a similar dynamic now with Umno, but a key difference is that Umno is stronger than Bersatu and would not want to play second fiddle to PAS in this partnership. The tussle for dominance will be a key dynamic as the general election looms closer. If PAS decides not to ally itself with Umno, it would face a tough challenge in persuading the sceptical Malay electorate to put their trust in its mixed technocratic record. Dr Azmil Tayeb is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is an Associate Professor at the School of Social Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

title: Flydubai plane attack: co-pilot had been banned from flying over extremist views
description: The UAE has cancelled all flights to Israel, complicating travel for hundreds of passengers who fly between the countries on a typical day.
content: The Flydubai co-pilot who officials said nearly crashed a Tel Aviv-bound flight with 182 people aboard was barred from flying by his native Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said on Saturday. The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, according to three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat. All spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked with the cockpit’s crash axe and tried to take control of the sharply plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” on Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before passengers and others rushed in and subdued him. The new details raised questions about how thoroughly Flydubai vets potential employees, and how the co-pilot’s presence on a flight filled with Israeli passengers got past Israel’s strict security protocols. Israel’s government has said it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots of nations without diplomatic ties from flying there. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations. The UAE government has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses. The incident occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, that sparked the war in Gaza. It also came weeks before a highly contentious election in which security, and October 7 security failures, have been central issues. Separately, a regional official and a person familiar with the matter said the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. The official said he was moved to an administrative job at Oman Air. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. They gave no details about the alleged extremist views. The co-pilot was later hired by UAE-based airline Flydubai, the person said. It was not immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The Gulf diplomat said he had undergone standard security checks before being hired, but it appears that the checks focused on whether he had been convicted of criminal charges and did not go deeper into examining his background for potential signs of radicalisation. The regional official also said security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments. The Gulf diplomat said investigations were trying to establish whether the co-pilot acted alone or “has any connection with any extremist groups”. The regional official said the co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian. He obtained Omani nationality from his father, also an Omani national. The regional official also said the co-pilot had travelled to Syria, with no details. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation”, but provided no evidence. There was no immediate comment on Saturday from Israel’s government. A Flydubai spokesperson said in an email that the airline could not comment beyond its official statements and acknowledged “there are many questions at this stage”. There was no immediate comment from Oman Air, and Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident. In a statement to the AP, Royal Air Maroc, Morocco’s national carrier, said the co-pilot “completed a three-month theoretical training period with the airline in 2025, as part of the pre-employment process. At the end of this training period, his application was not selected for employment”. There were no details. Keith Coles, a spokesperson for Buckinghamshire New University in England, said that al-Hammami previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management there but “did not undertake any pilot training”. There were no details on the timing. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. Airlines are generally required to carry crash axes in the cockpit that could be used in an emergency to break open a window to escape or break open a panel to access a fire. The captain, who was badly wounded in the axe attack, has said he used his remaining energy while being attacked to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the flight while passengers screamed. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of the rudder was torn away, and aviation experts have marvelled that it did not crash. Flydubai has said crew travelling on the plane helped to stabilise the plane and land. They have not yet been publicly identified. Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE. The passengers, most of them Israeli, flew home later on Wednesday on a separate plane, to cheers.

title: Is adopting Chinese fashion appropriation or appreciation? Artisans weigh in on the debate
description: The owners of Hong Kong’s Sindart and Qipology discuss when brands using traditional designs is cultural promotion – and when it is not.
content: As international fashion companies increasingly incorporate traditional Chinese design elements into their collections, accusations of cultural appropriation have flooded social media. In recent years, brands such as Zara and Adidas have been criticised for adopting Chinese tailoring features such as Mandarin collars and pankou, or frog buttons. While Zara drew backlash for mislabelling these elements as generic “fireman clasps” without acknowledging their heritage, Adidas sparked debate over how it framed and marketed its “New Chinese Style” collections to global audiences. But what do the masters and artisans of these centuries-old crafts actually think? Miru Wong Ka-lam is the third-generation owner of Sindart, a shop in Jordan, Kowloon, that offers a refreshingly nuanced perspective. Founded by her grandfather in 1958, it is one of Hong Kong’s last handmade embroidered shoe shops. Wong sees the growing interest in Chinese design elements not as something to be condemned, but celebrated. “I feel quite happy about it, actually,” she says. She explains that while traditional Chinese-style clothing is reserved for special occasions in local culture, and often seen as old-fashioned or tacky by younger generations, its popularity among foreigners has shifted Chinese views on when and where to wear these designs. Rather than seeing Western brands’ adoption of Chinese elements as theft, Wong sees it as cultural promotion, one that benefits even traditional artisans like herself. “When I see big brands using Chinese cultural elements in their designs, I think it’s a good thing,” she says. “It promotes the culture not just to foreign customers, but to local Hong Kong customers. It helps them understand that they can be bolder about wearing their heritage.” Similarly, Julie Liu, founder of modern qipao label Qipology, believes the trend benefits Chinese culture. Her collection ranges from A-line silhouettes with pockets, velvet cocktail dresses and Mandarin-collar tops designed to pair with jeans. “I like the trend and I think it’s great,” Liu says. “It’s actually great for business. It makes people more aware, and some people purposely look for brands that offer these designs.” Is it cultural appropriation? For Wong, the difference between cultural appreciation and appropriation comes down to one thing – understanding. “You can’t just copy something wholesale,” she explains. “You need to know the story behind it. With Chinese traditional designs, like certain buttons, garments or patterns, you need to know if there are any taboos. For example, some patterns are only meant to be worn by people who have passed away. If you take that and use it casually, that’s not OK.” Liu says a common mistake she sees in qipao designs is placing the buttons on the left instead of the right – a placement that symbolises death. Wong has seen a similar issue with funeral shoes, which traditionally feature embroidery on both the sole and the upper that uses sacred or ceremonial patterns. Customers often overlook this significance, brushing them off as merely a “beautiful design” or an “interesting touch”. “They just think the shoes are lovely, and some would continue to wear them anyway even after I tell them the true meaning,” Wong says. “I guess they don’t mind, but others could get offended. If you’re going to use a pattern, you should know what it means.” These are details that mass-market brands might easily miss. “If you don’t really look into the history, you might not be aware,” Liu says. “So when they start using things that are not lucky, not prosperous, or not respectful – or incorrectly used – then I feel like they should be a little more careful.” The cultural appropriation debate has raged online for years, perhaps most memorably when American teenager Keziah Daum wore a qipao to prom and faced a wave of criticism in 2018. Liu sees such incidents differently. “We actually have a lot of clients from the US – mostly people from the US – who ask, ‘Is it culturally appropriate for me to wear a qipao?’” she says. “I say, ‘Yeah, it’s completely fine.’ As an Asian or Chinese person, it’s actually nice to see you wear it.” Is it cultural appreciation or cultural appropriation? For Wong, the key is balance. Her innovations, including slip-resistant soles and more comfortable fits, are practical improvements that make the shoes suitable for everyday wear. She continues to produce traditional embroidered shoes alongside modern designs – pointed-toe heels, denim slippers, Mary Janes – ensuring the craft evolves without losing its soul. “I think you have to keep making traditional styles,” she says. “You can have a new product line, that’s fine, but you can’t just take a traditional design and change it so much that it loses everything that made it Chinese. You have to keep at least one part of the business making traditional pieces.” Liu says, “When you’re a brand, and you take elements, and you use it correctly, then it’s appreciation. “When you do excessive – like if you interpret it in a way that’s overly sexual or revealing – it’s insulting, especially because these types of clothes, and particularly the qipao, are inherently elegant.” Wong’s most cherished memory speaks to the deep cultural resonance of her craft. She was once invited to speak on a panel alongside William Chang Suk-ping, the legendary costume and art director for Wong Kar-wai’s In the Mood for Love (2000) – a film synonymous with the cheongsam and embroidered slippers. “You don’t have to copy everything exactly,” Miru Wong says, “but you have to do your research. Understand the culture. Don’t just take something and paste it somewhere else. If you’re going to use a Chinese pattern, know what it means – and if you’re selling it, explain it to your customers.” Liu has spotted Chinese influences in unexpected places. She recently saw a Mexican fashion brand create jackets and shirts with Mandarin collars paired with Western-style trousers. Another European brand, she notes, has released whole collections featuring Oriental-style buttons on big coats. “Even this year, you see brands integrating Mandarin elements,” she says. She cites Amsterdam-based Rohe as an example of a non-Chinese label embracing Chinese design cues. “So it’s quite interesting how even brands that are not specifically Chinese are integrating these elements into their collections,” she says. However, as with all fashion cycles, Liu knows the “China-maxxing” trend will eventually move on. But for her, that is not a concern. Trends come and go, she says with a shrug. “If it’s not Chinese elements, it’ll be something else – next it’ll be Mexican Aztec prints or Indian sandals,” she says. “There’s always going to be brands using other cultures as inspiration. “There’s always going to be people who are OK with it and people who are so negative about everything. “It’s like politics. There’s no need to be so angry all the time.”

title: China returns to top 100 in gender parity ranking for first time since 2016
description: Performance in economic participation and opportunity powers rise to 96th from 103rd place in annual World Economic Forum report.
content: For the first time in a decade, China has returned to the top 100 out of 145 economies in an annual global report assessing gender equality. China closed 69.9 per cent of its gender gap in 2025, rising to 96th place from 103rd the previous year and increasing 1.3 percentage points, according to the 2026 Global Gender Gap Report published by the World Economic Forum (WEF), an international non-profit organisation based in Switzerland. It marks the first time China has been ranked in the top 100 since 2016, when it placed 99th. This year, China ranked higher than a few major economies in the region, including South Korea (101), Japan (117) and India (131). However, it ranked below Singapore (31), Bangladesh (79) and Vietnam (84). The annual report said that nearly every economy tracked since its inception in 2006 had advanced in gender parity but that full parity was 120 years away. According to the WEF, the economies are evaluated across four dimensions: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. China owed much of its improved standing to economic participation and opportunity, with parity at 72.3 per cent, ranking 57th globally. Indicators include estimated work income and the rate of labour-force participation. Compared with 2006, China’s score in this category rose 10.3 percentage points. In educational attainment, China went up 5.3 percentage points to 98.8 per cent, bolstered by achieving full parity in tertiary enrolment in 2009, as well as a progressive two-decade improvement in adult literacy, which moved up from 91 per cent in 2006 to 96.6 per cent in 2026, the report said. Yet, the report found that the country’s gender gap in sex ratio at birth continued, at 0.907 – roughly 91 girls born for every 100 boys – while the benchmark stood at 0.944, or 94 girls for every 100 boys. Partly because of that, China’s score on the health and survival sub-index came to 94.8 per cent, ranking 144th. One area that has changed little over the past two decades is political empowerment. In 2025, China scored 13.5 per cent, ranking 111th. All three indicators in the category – women in parliament, women in ministerial positions and years with a female head of state – remained unchanged from the previous year. In 2022, for the first time in two decades, there were no women on China’s 24-member Politburo, a situation that remains today. This was also cited as a concern in a 2023 report by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women. This pattern could also be observed globally, the WEF said, adding that women held just 19.1 per cent of CEO roles, while only one in 10 ministerial portfolios held by women was considered to be of high influence. “Women have reached the C-suite and cabinets but are underrepresented in roles carrying the greatest economic and political influence,” the report said. And in the growing field of artificial intelligence, women are less represented in AI firms than in non-AI firms. While women accounted for 44.8 per cent of the contributor-level roles in non-AI companies, they occupied 36.6 per cent of such jobs at AI firms. Yaqiu Wang, a human rights researcher and fellow at the University of Pennsylvania, said it was encouraging that China’s score had improved and that it had returned to the top 100 after several years. But its 96th position remained a disappointing result for the world’s second-largest economy and a leading technological power, Wang added. “China’s extraordinary advances in wealth and technology have not been matched by comparable progress in women’s rights,” she said. “Persistent problems – including the skewed sex ratio at birth and the scarcity of women in senior political positions – reflect deeply rooted preferences for sons and assumptions that men are better suited to lead.” Official policy had also impeded progress, Wang added, saying Chinese authorities had restricted independent women’s rights groups and censored online discussions of sexual harassment, employment discrimination and other gender issues. According to Jia Wang, assistant professor in the department of applied social sciences at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, women’s labour-force participation trailed men’s by 14 points and their estimated earnings were only 63 per cent of men’s. Women also did about 2.6 times as much unpaid care work as men, and hiring discrimination against women of childbearing age persisted, she said. As Jia Wang saw it, closing such gaps still required specific measures, including more balanced parental leave, affordable childcare, stronger anti-discrimination enforcement and clearer pathways for women into leadership. “If Beijing wants to achieve genuine progress rather than simply improve its ranking, it should enforce existing prohibitions against gender discrimination in hiring, increase women’s representation in senior political and economic positions, address the continuing sex-ratio imbalance and stop suppressing independent feminist activism,” Yaqiu Wang said. “Expanding educational and economic opportunities matters, but lasting equality also requires women to be free to organise and speak.”

title: No more welcome mat? Japan’s tough visa rules spur foreign businesses to look elsewhere
description: Despite a surge in foreign residents leaving Japan, Tokyo is sticking to higher fees for business manager visas and permanent residency.
content: Five years ago, Sarah and her husband were optimistic about Japan’s economic future and were expanding their small businesses across several sectors. Today, that optimism has been replaced by concern over a sense of hostility towards two hard-working foreigners who feel they have contributed to the society that they have worked hard to fit into. New regulations that took effect on Thursday mean the two Britons, who have been in Japan for more than 10 years, now face significantly higher costs for visa extensions. The cost of a business manager’s visa – until recently their long-term plan – has jumped from 5 million yen (US$31,666) to 30 million yen.
