The permanent residency fee similarly leapt 20 times to 200,000 yen, while additional barriers include an annual income of 5.75 million yen, or above the Japanese average, much higher pension contributions and Japanese language requirements. Combined with rising prices and the continued weakness of the yen, Sarah and her husband are now bringing forward their plans to leave Japan. “We have always had a dream of setting up a godo kaisha [the Japanese equivalent of a limited liability company], but these changes mean that it is out of reach now,” said Sarah, who did not give her real name out of concern about possible complications during her next visit to the immigration office. “To operate our business as a godo kaisha, we would need either permanent residency or a business manager visa, and the new regulations make either of those hard to get,” she said. “We always thought we would be in Japan for as long as we were enjoying life and earning a living, but things have changed in the last 18 months or so,” she said. “Now, we’re beginning to ask ourselves whether it is time to go.” Those were common sentiments in the foreign community of small business owners in Tokyo, she said, with social media awash with people looking for employment outside Japan or announcing their departures from the country. According to the Nikkei business daily, 953 foreign nationals living in Japan who previously held business manager visas had left the country in the first half of this year, almost four times as many as in the same period a year earlier. Similarly, applications for business manager visas plunged 96 per cent in the five months after the changes were announced, with the high capital requirement of 30 million yen the biggest hurdle for most small foreign companies. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi previously said tackling the growing number of foreign residents of Japan was a key issue in her manifesto ahead of the February general election, which her ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won by a landslide. Several other right-wing parties – notably Sanseito and The Conservative Party – were perceived to be taking votes away from the LDP on the immigration issue in the months before the vote, prompting Takaichi to adopt a firmer stance. In a social media post just days before the new visa rules took effect, Takaichi justified the changes, saying she was aware of concerns and feelings of “unfairness”. “To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies towards foreign nationals are orderly and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely,” she wrote. For the government, the changes are aimed at clear benefits: limiting the number of foreigners who choose to settle in Japan permanently, winning the support of voters and bringing in new funds for the government. Officials have claimed the visa cost increases are necessary because previous figures were too low and well below other comparable countries. Permanent residency now costs 200,000 yen (US$1,269) in Japan, compared with the UK’s Indefinite Leave to Remain fee at £3,226 (US$4,261), Australia’s Skilled Independent permanent visa at A$6,135 (US$4,255) and a US green card at US$1,440. Not everyone is enamoured with the new policies, however, with the Mainichi Shimbun declaring in an editorial last month that the revised laws “disregard human rights and should be withdrawn”. Others point out that it is a foolhardy move given Japan’s tumbling birth rate, an ageing population and chronic shortages of workers across virtually every business sector. Much has been made of foreigners driving municipal buses and taxis and working in 24-hour stores, hospitals and other jobs that few Japanese want to take. With higher hurdles and lower earning power due to the weak yen, foreigners will inevitably start to look elsewhere, according to analysts. “There is a lot of frustration among small business operators and managers, people who have come to Japan to build a business but now face far higher capital requirements and are leaving,” said Martin Schulz, chief policy economist for Fujitsu’s Global Market Intelligence Unit. “Large Japanese companies are looking for skilled managers, engineers and others to come here to support their operations, but it is very bad signalling when the restraints go up,” he said. “It was already difficult to find these people because the yen is weak and wages are low in comparison with other countries, and firms are going to struggle even more to attract talent.” Some foreign owners of firms in the service sector say they have seen the pressure being ramped up in recent years. “I’ve been in this business for 40 years, and we never had any issues over our staff for the first 30 of those years,” said Andy Lunt, owner of the Shin-Hinomoto izakaya bar in Tokyo’s Yurakucho district. “But we have been raided twice, and they took away two of my employees.” The restaurant employs part-time staff on student visas, which set a maximum limit on hours they can work to support themselves. While enforcement personnel would typically glance at the relevant papers in the past, Lunt said he was not taking any more chances now. “They are checking up on people’s papers a lot more, and the message I’m hearing is that Japan is not going to tolerate this any more.”

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong to relax ad rules for broadcasters to boost business edge, minister says
description: Commerce chief Algernon Yau says TV rules will be eased so local broadcasters can better compete against online streaming platforms.
content: Hong Kong authorities plan to relax restrictions on indirect advertising for broadcasters amid fierce competition from online and streaming media, the commerce minister has told the South China Morning Post. In a wide-ranging exclusive interview, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said many broadcast operators had requested to review the Generic Codes of Practice for Television to improve the business environment, and the government had responded. “They’re saying that the competition from other media is very strong, and it’s very difficult for them to survive, and then we have to be up market and then match the practice internationally,” Yau said on Thursday. In the annual policy address released last month, the government pledged to review the code to ensure that regulations keep pace with the times and that diversified, quality programmes were broadcast, expanding the reach of the ‘Hong Kong Brand’ in the Asia-Pacific region. Yau said the review would include examining the current restrictions on how much English and Putonghua programmes could be broadcast, as well as indirect advertisements during TV programmes. “Now it’s very restrictive. Even though you are drinking a can of soda drink, you cannot have their logo, they have to cover it up. But we are going to relax that,” he said. Yau also said other advertising restrictions could be relaxed in the future, such as for the promotion of alcohol. His bureau would discuss with other bureaus how to ensure the changes did not have any negative impact on the public, while at the same time giving the broadcasting industry more flexibility and freedom. “[Their] life is getting more difficult with more online [media], streaming, and all these are not under very stringent control, not just by Hong Kong, internationally. No country is having very, very effective rules controlling streaming and online media,” he said. Asked if the government had any plans to place restrictions on online and streaming media, Yau said it was very difficult to control the content being published online and other jurisdictions faced the same challenge. The minister said the bureau would aim to conduct a consultation in the last quarter of this year and produce recommendations next year. He said the review process would likely extend beyond the current government’s term, but the five-year plan could ensure policy continuity. “I don’t see any problem at all if there’s a change of the government or government officials in the next term,” he said. The review would be a “total review with all media” and not just broadcasting. “The whole idea in the policy address is to facilitate the media and the creative industry, like TV, film, etc, so that they can have a new ecosystem in doing business,” he said. The government had earlier proposed a legal amendment to protect copyrighted works from being used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. Yau said it would be “premature” at this moment to amend the Copyright Ordinance in view of the rapid development of AI and the different views received during public consultation. Any legal amendment would be “reviewed at the right time”. “It’s premature, too early. Even though we change it, it will have to be changed tomorrow and then the day after tomorrow. Because AI is evolving too quickly. You don’t know what is going to happen tomorrow,” he said. “Two mega countries having AI are the United States and China. And if both of them are going to have some amendment changes and that will be followed by other countries and economies, then we can have a look to see whether it is practical and applicable to Hong Kong as well,” he said. Yau said the government would issue guidelines by the end of this year if possible for business sectors and individuals on how to develop AI, with details to be discussed with the sector.

title: Letters | Phnom Penh Declaration on online scams short on details
description: Readers discuss Cambodia’s efforts to combat scams, the booking system for football matches at Hong Kong’s Kai Tak Sports Park, and Trump’s tariff approach.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The adoption of the Phnom Penh Declaration at last week’s international conference on online scams contains welcome language on international cooperation and victim protection. However, the 11-point statement ultimately leaves some of the hardest questions unanswered. Its commitments are voluntary and non-binding, with no agreed funding mechanism, timetable or concrete details on how governments will pursue criminal networks across borders or recover stolen assets. Cambodian officials rightly point to hundreds of recent investigations and raids. Yet numbers alone cannot answer the central question of accountability: who owns, finances and profits from these scam compounds, and how far up the chain have investigations reached? That question has become harder to ignore. US Treasury sanctions against Cambodian senators Ly Yong Phat and Kok An, together with recent calls by congressional leaders to investigate other senior figures – including the deputy prime minister, Neth Savoeun, who delivered the conference’s closing remarks, and Hun To, the cousin of Cambodia’s prime minister – have intensified scrutiny of possible links between scam networks and politically connected figures. Sanctions are not criminal convictions, but allegations involving figures of such prominence make it all the more important for Cambodia’s own institutions to show what has been investigated and what those investigations have found. There is still little public information on how many cases have resulted in convictions, how much money has been recovered and returned to victims, or whether influential facilitators face the same scrutiny as lower-level operatives. The declaration’s promise to protect trafficked people must also be matched by evidence that coerced workers are being identified and protected rather than simply detained or deported. If the Phnom Penh Declaration is to “break the criminal chain”, investigations will have to extend beyond the compounds themselves and into the financial, corporate and political networks that have allowed this industry to operate on such a scale. Mu Sochua, Nobel Peace Prize nominee and president of the Khmer Movement for Democracy Major football matches should have cash ticket booths Tournament organisers and Ticketflap have made a deeply misguided decision by enforcing a strict digital-only ticketing policy for the Fifa Asean Cup 2026 matches at the Kai Tak Sports Park. By eliminating traditional on-site cash ticket booths, the organisers have effectively locked out a generation of loyal, elderly football fans who are not tech-savvy or familiar with navigating complex online booking platforms. Worse still, fans are being forced to pay a HK$30 “service fee” per ticket to a middleman platform, a levy that equals a significant amount of the actual ticket price for lower-tier seats. This feels less like a convenience fee and more like direct exploitation of local sports fans. This rigid digital mandate is not only difficult for the elderly to comply with but could also expose ordinary people to cybersecurity risks. When a government invests billions of public funds into building a world-class facility like the Kai Tak Sports Park to promote local sports, the entry barriers should be lowered, not raised. Forcing fans through digital hurdles and high booking fees for regional games will only guarantee rows of empty seats. The Football Association of Hong Kong, China, and the operator of Kai Tak Sports Park must urgently reintroduce physical cash ticket booths at stadium gates. Public sporting events must remain safe, affordable and accessible to every member of our community – especially our seniors. George Woo, emeritus professor, Hong Kong Polytechnic University Matter of time before world turns against Trump’s US Canadian prime minister Mark Carney has said Canada will decide its own partnerships (“Trump threatens EU over ‘hostile’ proposal to make Canada associate member”, September 17). If the entire world joins hands with free-trade agreements and stop prioritising its relationship with the United States, will US President Donald Trump be as powerful as he believes he is today? There is a lot of discomfort with the way Trump has been handling global affairs. Does he realise it can cost the US everything it has built over the last 250 years? By making the world turn against the US economy, he is gambling with his country’s future and creating the false impression that he is winning the tariff war or any war for that matter. Rishi Teckchandani, Mid-Levels

title: Asian Games: cool, calm Coleman Wong says winning gold akin to ‘unlocking an achievement’
description: Hongkonger thanks family for his victory, which also clinches a spot at LA Olympics; city officials say investment in game is ‘bearing fruit’.
content: Siobhan Haughey called “pressure a privilege” on her way to adding yet more Asian Games gold to an already glittering resume – anyone watching Coleman Wong Chak-lam win his historic men’s singles title on Saturday might have been left wondering if he even knows what pressure is. The Hongkonger needed just one chance to wrap up a straight sets victory over China’s Wu Yibing, and for all the world looked as though he was just firing down aces on the practice court, and not on the verge of doing something no man from the city had ever done before. Just to add to the occasion, victory came with a place at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, as long as Wong remains in the top 500 players in the world. The manner of his 6-2, 6-4 triumph at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre would suggest it is the 99 above him who should have cause for concern. “Obviously I was a little bit nervous because I’ve never been to this stage before, but it was tough,” Wong said. “The whole match was really close.” Wong and Wu are no strangers on or off the court. Three years ago at the Games in Hangzhou, Wong knocked out his mainland rival in the third round; last November, Wu beat the 22-year-old in the semi-finals of the National Games. When they do clash, there is rarely much between them, making Saturday’s 93-minute final something of an outlier, no matter what Wong said afterwards. “He’s a really good player, and we always have a great match every time we play each other,” Wong said. “You can’t think that much at that moment because it’s so fast, and the game, the margin is so slim. So I was just trying to focus on what I can do at that point.” What Wong did was grab gold at the first time of asking, having finally broken his opponent in a mammoth ninth game of the second set that featured eight returns to deuce and largely summed up Wu’s day. The world No 111 had every opportunity to hold the game, but as with much of the first set, he hit potential winners long or wide and struggled with his first serve. At 5-4 down and with the match on the line, Wu hit Wong’s first serve out and then could only watch as the Hongkonger’s power did the rest. “Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the colour,” Wong said. “But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement.” The groundwork to that was done in a first set when the only real moments of menace for Wong came from the three lucky breaks that involved the ball hitting the net and dropping in Wu’s favour. Otherwise, the silver medallist’s game in the main was characterised by a succession of unforced errors at inopportune moments, namely when winners sailed long on crucial points. Wu was broken twice in three games in the first set, and having battled to hold in his first two service games quickly found himself 5-2 down. Two typically fiery aces settled matters in Wong’s favour soon after. It was a closer affair in the second set, with the pair going toe to toe, and Wu showed signs of the form that once made him world No 54, with the accuracy of the scorching groundstrokes finally returning. Then Wong forced an opening, piled through it and, on having won, sank to the floor in celebration before rushing over to the coaches’ box to embrace friends and family, while officials including Secretary for Culture, Tourism and Sport Rosanna Law Shuk-pui looked on. Wong’s gold was the eighth the city’s athletes had won in Japan. Windsurfers Wong Tsz-ho and Cheung Tsz-yuet added two more soon after, making it the most Hong Kong has ever won at a single Games. “This gold medal is actually very important to me, and everyone finds it very moving,” Wong said. “But we also shouldn’t forget, since I was young, my family always had the mindset of, ‘OK, if you want to do it, just go for it’. “Sometimes parents in Hong Kong might feel, ‘Ah, is that doable?’ They overthink it. Instead, if kids want to do it, let them give it a try first. This is a huge influence my family had on me. “If my family hadn’t been so reassuring in letting me try … I went abroad and out into the world to try at a very young age. Losing and winning didn’t matter, it was about going out to improve. So I think this is very important.” That next generation will have an opportunity to watch Wong on the Olympic stage, something he called amazing, and which Law said was “way more than a ticket to LA 2028 for himself”. “It’s a very happy moment indeed,” Law told the South China Morning Post. “I’m very glad as we now have every reason to keep tennis in the Sports Institute’s Tier A, and our decision last year to make a special arrangement for tennis has paid off. “The win is also a great boost to our Victoria Park redevelopment plan.” Michael Cheng, president of the Hong Kong China Tennis Association, felt Wong’s gold and the bronze won by women’s doubles pair Eudice Chong and Wong Hong-yi the day before showed “that the long-term investment is bearing fruit”. “I’m thrilled because it shows the structural alignment is right and hopefully the pipeline will come”. Wong, meanwhile, has two years before the Olympics, but he won’t be resting on his laurels. “I feel my current form is pretty good and I want to keep maintaining it and continue improving, because I feel it’s never enough,” he said. “I still have 99 players ahead of me [in the ATP rankings], so I’ll keep climbing.”

title: Your Voice: Protect Hong Kong’s abused children, debating social media bans (short letters)
description: This week, students write about the city’s child protection laws, regulations banning some platforms for under-16s, student stress and cats in restaurants.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
I am writing to express my strong support for updating Hong Kong’s child protection laws. It is alarming that our current legal framework dates back to an era before smartphones and social media existed.
Young victims face threats like sexual harassment and abuse of trust. Worse still, expecting traumatised children to remember exact dates and locations of repeated abuse places an unfair burden of flawless memory on them.
The proposal to criminalise grooming and introduce a specific offence for continuous child sexual abuse is an essential step forward.
As students and members of society, we must ensure that our laws actively protect victims rather than penalising them for losing their memories.
If you are facing issues such as domestic violence or sexual abuse, help is available. In Hong Kong, dial 999 in an emergency, text 18281 for CEASE Crisis Centre’s 24-hour crisis support with sexual violence hotline, or contact Hong Kong’s Social Welfare Department at +852 2343 2255 . See a full list of resources here .
I am writing in response to the South China Morning Post article “Addiction is irreversible: Hong Kong urged to ban under‑16s from social media”, published on August 8.
To combat the youth mental health crisis, several countries have introduced laws banning those under 16 from using social media. Following this trend, Hong Kong has also been urged to implement bans.
As far as I am concerned, this move is a double-edged sword. Bans could improve youth mental health and foster a positive online atmosphere, but they fail to account for the rights of young digital-age users.
Additionally, they overlook practical difficulties, as they require advanced technology and cost money. On the other hand, self-disciplined students can use social media to share educational resources, connect with like-minded friends they may not meet in person and seek mental health support.
Both perspectives offer valid insights into youth social media bans, and there is no doubt that these opinions come from people who truly care about children.
All in all, social media bans are not a perfect solution. Instead of simply restricting access, governments should combine proper legislation with guidance to help teenagers use social media in a healthy way.
Joanna Lu Tsz-ning, Christian Alliance SC Chan Memorial College
As a Form Six student, I’ve watched classmates skip lunch to cram for the Diploma of Secondary Education exam. Last week, a classmate fainted during a mock exam; she had been studying for 12 hours a day for weeks.
Hong Kong treats Form Six like a “one-shot race” to university. Schools focus on grades over well-being, and parents often push their kids to sacrifice everything for success. A survey by the Education Bureau found 70 per cent of Form Six students feel severely stressed.
We need schools to offer free counselling sessions and reduce homework loads.
Parents should also prioritise rest over revision. A 30-minute daily walk or chat with family can ease stress more than an extra hour of studying.
Let’s stop treating Form Six students like machines. They deserve to learn, not just survive.
Edmond Ng Yuet-wang, Christian Alliance S.C. Chan Memorial College
I strongly believe that allowing cats into local dining establishments is a progressive step forward that benefits pet owners, restaurant operators and the wider community alike.
Pet ownership in Hong Kong has seen remarkable growth in recent years. According to government statistics, over 100,000 households kept cats as of 2018, a number that continues to rise rapidly.
Furthermore, organisers of the Hong Kong Cat Expo 2025 estimated the city’s annual cat economy at an impressive HK$2.4 billion. Restricting these beloved animals from public dining spaces ignores the economic potential and social reality of our city.
Opening doors to felines allows eateries to tap into this lucrative market, expand their customer base and generate vital revenue to offset Hong Kong’s notoriously high commercial rents.
Simple rules, such as requiring that cats be leashed, restricting them from dining tables and creating cat-friendly zones or operational hours, can easily ensure that non-cat owners and those with allergies dine comfortably.
By implementing thoughtful regulations, Hong Kong can foster an inclusive, compassionate and vibrant dining culture that benefits business owners and customers alike.

title: More Chinese banks likely to adopt AI rules after Ping An move: analysts
description: Other listed mainland lenders are expected to introduce similar governance frameworks as regulators tighten oversight of AI use.
content: After Ping An Bank became the first listed Chinese lender to formally adopt rules governing its use of artificial intelligence, analysts said more mainland institutions were likely to follow, with the move setting an early benchmark for how far the sector can go in applying the technology. The Shenzhen-listed bank said in a filing on Wednesday that its board had approved AI management measures, following a regulatory push for banks to strengthen oversight of AI use. The full rules have not been made public. No other listed bank in mainland China had announced similar measures, according to comments Ping An Bank recently gave to domestic media outlets. The lender also said its board’s strategy committee would oversee AI-related matters, with checks at “every stage of development and use” and mechanisms for data security, algorithm risk, ethics review and responsibility tracing. It would classify AI risks by level and fold them into an overall risk-management system. The measures implement guidelines issued in June by the National Financial Regulatory Administration. These guidelines hold banks and insurers responsible for the AI systems they use and require boards to establish oversight mechanisms. The bank had rolled out more than 450 large-model AI use cases by the end of June, in areas including marketing, investment advice, compliance and risk control, according to its interim report. More banks in China and globally will move towards this direction Gary Ng, Natixis Several other banks were working to implement the guidelines and expected to issue similar governance rules, Shanghai-based financial news agency Cailian Press reported. All 42 A-share listed banks mentioned AI in their interim reports this year, it added. Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators, said the announcement provided limited detail, including how the technology would be deployed in practice. “But I believe this is the future trend for financial institutions,” he said. Given the range of mainland regulations involved, it would take time to see how far regulators were prepared to allow banks to expand their use of AI, Tang added. Gary Ng, senior economist for the Asia-Pacific region at Natixis, said AI adoption “must come with governance, particularly in finance, where the protection of customers and financial stability” were critical. “More banks in China and globally will move towards this direction,” Ng added. The development comes as Hong Kong officials urge local financial institutions to prepare for a new wave of autonomous AI systems and position the city as a hub for international compliance standards. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday that the city could offer “trusted solutions” in areas including AI model training, cross-border data flows, privacy protection and dispute resolution. He cited the city’s common law system, internationally connected standards and professional services sector as key advantages. In March, Hong Kong’s financial regulators expanded a supervised sandbox for generative AI, originally launched for banks in 2024, to include the securities, insurance and pensions sectors. Tang said many Hong Kong banks and insurers had already adopted AI to reduce operating expenses, particularly compliance-related costs. Ng said Hong Kong could be “a perfect place to test and apply the standards of different jurisdictions in an increasingly fragmented world”.

title: Your Voice: ‘Pre-learning’ in Hong Kong education; appreciating China’s heritage (long letters)
description: This week, one student shares her thoughts on learning the school curriculum before the semester starts, while another reflects on China’s progress.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Kaen Lu, SKH Chan Young Secondary School
During the summer holiday, the term “pre-made child” went viral on social media. It refers to the phenomenon in which parents have their children learn the coming semester’s school curriculum during the summer holiday. This has sparked widespread discussion on issues such as advanced learning and the city’s educational environment.
Online forums reveal a wide spectrum of opinions, but most agree that it reflects the intense academic pressures students face today.
In Hong Kong, academic results serve as the primary measure of a student’s worth. Those with top grades are recognised and celebrated. Conversely, students gifted in non-academic areas often receive little acknowledgement. This dynamic pushes many to prioritise outcomes over the learning process itself.
Hong Kong has a fast-paced curriculum, and most schools can only complete the syllabus just before the final exam. The final chapters of most textbooks are usually the most challenging. Hence, students who do not have enough time to prepare for exams often perform poorly.
In contrast, “pre-made” students who learn all the material before the semester begins have ample time to practise and become more familiar with the topics. Knowing this fact about Hong Kong’s school system creates an extra “invisible” pressure that forces students to pre-learn.
Students taking admission tests for school transfers often encounter questions covering material from the next academic year. Those hoping to move to a better school are therefore compelled to learn ahead. In this way, Hong Kong schools themselves, through the design of assessments, promote pre-learning.
Every coin has two sides. Evidence suggests that children who study the next semester’s content during their holidays gain confidence. However, students may also become overwhelmed when they do not have time to relax during their holiday, and they are likely to have to make trade-offs among learning, travelling and other hobbies.
In addition, “pre-learning” may have a far-reaching impact on student mental health. Education blogger “Brain Planet” used a brilliant analogy in an article discussing this practice: true previewing is when a child opens a new textbook themselves, hits a part they don’t understand, gets stuck, frowns and ponders, and then has an ‘’aha!’’ moment of clarity.
This moment of “getting stuck and then figuring it out” is important for a child. Not only do they gain knowledge, but their brains grow. Studying the material ahead during the summer holiday, often with the guidance of their parents, cuts out this crucial growth process with a single stroke.
Ultimately, students respond to pre-learning in different ways. Rather than following the crowd or rejecting it outright, they might benefit from a more tailored approach: one that considers each child’s pace, interests and well-being.
Chloe Chan Sze-ching, Kiangsu-Chekiang College (Shatin)
Standing on the Great Wall, you can almost hear the sound of ancient camel bells ringing along the Silk Road. Now, look across the land, and you will see high-speed railways slicing through the mountains, connecting cities at breathtaking speed.
True revival means honouring our heritage while boldly shaping a future driven by creativity, unity and global responsibility. A nation’s revival must begin with confidence in its own culture.
For centuries, Chinese civilisation has illuminated the world with its philosophy, art and inventions.
The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics perfectly embodied this, blending ancient wisdom with dazzling, cutting-edge technology. It showed the world both a timeless and modern China.
A tree grows tall only because its roots run deep. Similarly, a nation that truly knows its past can embrace the future without losing its soul. Spiritual confidence must walk hand in hand with innovation and shared prosperity.
Consider China’s technological leaps, including 5G networks connecting millions, renewable energy farms reshaping the landscape, and the Chang’e missions leaving footprints on the far side of the moon as the Tiangong space station orbits overhead.
These are not just headlines; they are symbols of a nation pushing the boundaries of possibility.
China’s achievements are not confined to laboratories. The historic triumph of lifting millions out of poverty proves that true rejuvenation must be inclusive. Strength is meaningless if it leaves people behind.
Furthermore, the Belt and Road Initiative echoes the ancient Silk Road, building roads, ports and digital connections that foster mutual development across continents. China’s advanced model seeks economic and innovative prosperity. If culture is the root and innovation is the engine, then the youth are the pilots steering this journey forward.
The dream of renewal is ultimately carried by the younger generation, who are responsible for blending tradition with tomorrow. We see it in the guochao trend, where young entrepreneurs and artists integrate classic Chinese aesthetics into fashion, music and everyday products, making heritage cool and globally appealing.
Revival is not about dominance or isolation; it is about contributing a unique voice and concrete solutions to a shared future for all humankind.
The Chinese dream, at its heart, connects with the dreams of people everywhere for a peaceful, green and prosperous world.
Reviving China is a magnificent journey of cultural rediscovery, technological breakthrough and global contribution. Every tradition you honour and every bridge of understanding you build with the world adds to that story. This is how we carry on five thousand years of culture.

title: Should Hong Kong ban prepaid beauty and fitness contracts?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
Prepaid contracts have become increasingly popular in Hong Kong’s beauty and fitness industry. Consumers are often persuaded to pay thousands of dollars upfront in exchange for discounted prices on long-term memberships.
While this may sound beneficial, it has repeatedly led to financial losses and consumer exploitation when businesses suddenly close or fail to deliver their promised services. Therefore, I strongly believe Hong Kong should ban prepaid contracts for beauty and fitness services.
First, a prepaid contract places consumers at financial risk; once customers have paid a large sum of money in advance, they lose control over their money, given how volatile the market is. For example, a beauty salon or gym could suddenly close, go bankrupt or simply refuse to cooperate.
In 2024, the closure of Physical Fitness, a gym chain, led to more than 1,700 complaints and around HK$60 million in prepaid losses. This shows how these contracts can devastate and hurt ordinary consumers.
The Hong Kong government has also acknowledged that prepaid contracts expose consumers to considerable financial risks. It has noted that they require stronger consumer protection, highlighting the huge fiscal risks they pose.
Second, prepaid contracts encourage unethical sales tactics . As businesses will receive a substantial amount of money before they have to provide any services, employees are often pressured to persuade consumers to purchase the most expensive packages rather than focus on improving the quality of service.
According to city authorities, beauty and fitness services account for nearly 90 per cent of complaints involving improper sales tactics. Individuals often enter into long-term contracts under the pressure of aggressive commercial practices, including a barrage of phone calls and emails over just a few weeks.
I think some may argue that prepaid contracts allow customers to enjoy lower prices and help businesses secure stable cash flow; however, discounts should never come at the consumer’s expense.
The government should look into alternatives that protect both consumers and companies. These include pay-per-visit systems, monthly subscriptions and more.
Despite the convenience they offer, prepaid contracts – agreements in which a customer pays in advance for goods or services to be delivered over a future period – are viewed negatively because they require long-term commitment.
The public generally accepts this type of contract for services like phone SIM cards and education programmes. However, over the last six years, there have been about 5,000 complaints tied to prepaid contracts for gyms and beauty parlours in Hong Kong.
One could argue we should ban prepaid contracts for beauty and fitness venues. But these contracts benefit customers because they prevent unforeseen price hikes.
Imagine you are happily paying for a service, but one day, the price increases. You would be annoyed that you did not opt for a package deal where you’d be safe from a price change. And your shoes would wear out from the time and energy you used to find a new, more affordable source: something called “shoe-leather costs”.
Prepaid contracts provide the investment needed in the beauty and fitness industries due to the high cost of rent and equipment. For instance, a treadmill can cost anywhere from HK$20,000 to HK$100,000.
An upfront sum from customers means businesses can make these purchases and use additional resources to improve their services and environment for customers.
Banning prepaid contracts for these industries risks pushing small businesses out of the market and reducing competition.
Competition incentivises businesses to improve their quality and reduce their prices to attract customers. A reduction in the quality of businesses will risk reducing investment in Hong Kong’s wellness markets as customers opt for personalised home gyms or go to major branches and corporations.
Prepaid contracts also protect both businesses and customers. With hundreds of competitors around Hong Kong, having a prepaid contract secures business without worry of customers leaving a gap in their revenue. Additionally, prepaid contracts create an obligation for customers to receive services from a business with flexible scheduling and without worrying about missing a session.
A ban on prepaid contracts risks higher costs, poor quality and fluctuating revenue.

title: Viral video of 9-month-old Chinese baby climbing mountain steps sparks safety concerns
description: Parents say they prioritise their son’s interests and emotional growth, while keeping him safe.
content: A video of a nine-month-old baby climbing steps at a mountain tourist site has gone viral, igniting heated debates about his family’s parenting style. Filmed at a mountain resort in central China’s Hubei province, the clip has garnered 200,000 likes and 17,000 comments on a popular short video platform. Footage shows the baby’s mother closely accompanying him, while he wears kneecaps for protection as he enjoys the outdoor activity. Some viewers expressed shock at the video, questioning whether the parents were “pulling up the seedlings to help them grow.” “Is it really appropriate for a baby this young to climb a mountain like that?” one commenter asked. However, most responses were supportive. One individual noted: “He is the only one who truly ‘climbs’ the mountain.” “I admire this parenting style. Unlike those who are overly cautious about their children getting a bit dirty, parents like this foster a child with strong immunity,” remarked another observer. “You could put a pair of gloves on him to protect him from sharp objects along the way,” offered a different suggestion. The baby’s father, surnamed Huang, shared that this was Wenwen’s first mountain climb. Wenwen quickly mastered the skill, having begun climbing at six months old, and was already able to navigate staircases by eight months. The couple felt confident in Wenwen’s ability to climb the mountain after seeing him adeptly tackle staircases in their neighbourhood. Huang mentioned that both he and his wife are outdoor enthusiasts, and their son appears to have inherited this passion; he exhibits signs of restlessness when indoors for too long. “We took him to climb the mountain not to train him, but to help him expend energy,” Huang explained. While passers-by often expressed admiration for Wenwen’s remarkable skill at the mountain, he remained focused, absorbed in the beauty of the flowers and plants along the ascent. Huang acknowledged that climbing the mountain has brought “positive energy” to their son: “His mood improved significantly, and he fell asleep quickly after the climb.” The couple emphasise the importance of valuing their child’s feelings and encouraging him to explore his interests while ensuring his safety. They noted that some parents expressed a desire to emulate their parenting approach, advising them to ensure close supervision by at least three adults during mountain climbing activities. They also recommended selecting mountain resorts with gentle paths and not forgetting protective gear for their children. Going forward, they plan to take Wenwen mountain climbing every two weeks and to introduce him to camping soon.

title: Malaysia is building a new research corridor across Asia to meet China’s rise: scientists
description: From next-gen semiconductors to advanced catalysts, scientists are navigating geopolitical boundaries to focus on mutual discovery.
content: When chemical engineer Ahmad Zuhairi Abdullah joined Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) 22 years ago, Western institutions dominated the field, from global research infrastructure and high-impact publications to the greatest breakthroughs. Two decades later, the centre of gravity has moved eastward, says Zuhairi, now a professor with the USM school of chemical engineering in Penang. “[Not much was known] about China at that time when I joined the university. I knew that they had quite a number of good universities and I was aware of their publications because some of them I referred to in my research work,” he said. “But definitely nothing much was heard in terms of collaboration with Chinese counterparts. Now, you see a lot [of scientists and students] coming here,” for studies, research and fostering collaborations, Zuhairi added. “Chinese scientists are very advanced in materials science,” he said, pointing to the high volume of publications and contributions to scientific journals. As China rises as a scientific powerhouse and Malaysia diversifies its research networks to find collaborators closer to home, partnerships in critical domains – from semiconductors to sustainable energy materials – are increasingly shaping regional innovation. “China is very aggressive and opening its doors to collaborations, which is shifting from probably 10 years back [when] it was quite close to their own things,” Zuhairi said. He also observed that China was making an effort to include Southeast Asian partners in its research ecosystem, with some provincial funding programmes requiring Chinese scientists to work with researchers from the region. At the Joint Laboratory of Biomass Chemical Engineering, inaugurated in January, researchers from USM and Huaqiao University in China’s southeastern coastal province of Fujian are working together to turn organic waste and plant material into useful products, as well as developing sustainable energy materials and low-carbon technologies. According to Zuhairi, one of the common research interests between the two countries lies in combining Malaysia’s abundant agricultural waste with China’s advanced process engineering. Malaysia’s massive palm oil sector generates vast quantities of biomass, including pressed fibre and kernel shells which contain lignin, a bonding agent in plants that was traditionally treated as a low-value by-product in the pulp and paper industry. Zuhairi’s research aims to develop specialised catalysts to break down the lignin – the second most abundant biopolymer after cellulose – into smaller molecular fragments. “Lignin is converted into phenolic substances, [which] will be a feedstock for the conversion into something more valuable,” he said. These valuable renewable chemicals include adhesives and fuel additives to improve fuel performance and reduce emissions. While chemical engineering lays the foundation for sustainable materials, advanced hardware and semiconductors are pushing the Malaysia-China corridor into critical hi-tech domains. At USM’s Institute of Nano Optoelectronics Research and Technology (INOR), director Mohd Zamir Pakhuruddin is leading research into wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride, solar cells and nanophotonic devices. The institute has broadened its international research partnerships over the past two years to work with scientists in China, Japan and Saudi Arabia, diversifying beyond its long-standing ties with research institutions in Germany and France. It has established collaborations with leading Chinese institutions in semiconductor research, such as Chongqing University, Fudan University, Harbin Institute of Technology, Hunan Institute of Technology and Nanjing University. For Zamir, an associate professor in advanced photovoltaic materials and devices, working across borders is a necessary step towards advancing technology, with the global supply and manufacturing chain for chips an example. “To be able to realise high-end semiconductor devices, there is no one country that can do that alone. The same goes for the collaboration of the academy as well,” he said. “We need our partners to be able to complement somewhere across the value chain of the fabrication.” Malaysia aims to move beyond its back-end chip assembly and testing role towards integrated circuit design, high-end manufacturing and niche equipment, as outlined in its 10-year road map, the National Semiconductor Strategy released in 2024. “The very goal of the national semiconductor strategy is to enhance the capacity of the nation to be stronger in the front end while leveraging the current strength in the back end,” Zamir said. When asked about the growing trade friction and technological competition between Washington and Beijing, Zamir said that science and collaborations “should remain open”. “Malaysia is in the neutral position politically because we do not favour sides. We do not choose sides anyway. The same goes for our academic collaboration. It is more of a diversification of our international partners that we have done in recent years,” he said. Among INOR’s Chinese collaborators is the Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT), an institution subject to US sanctions and one of the “Seven Sons of National Defence” – universities directly under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. In this partnership, the Malaysian and Chinese researchers are co-developing space solar cells with high radiation resilience for low Earth orbit satellite applications. Asked about how the institute manages its partnership with HIT, Zamir said jointly agreed proposal terms defined the scope of their cooperation. “In the areas that we agreed to collaborate, I believe these are the areas that are open for collaboration and we should leverage as long as the areas are open for exploration,” he said. Zamir acknowledged that some fields were restricted but emphasised focusing on open avenues: “For the areas that are open for collaboration, we go by the first principle [that] science should be open and let’s leverage each other’s strengths to win together.” Over his multiple trips to various Chinese cities in the past two years, Zamir said he observed that Western export controls and sanctions had accelerated China’s push towards domestic self-sufficiency. “But in science, I think the bright side is it is pushing the capability of the nation to develop your very own technology – from science to technology, to eventually realising technology on the production floor,” he said. At USM’s school of physics, deputy dean and associate professor Ahmad Fairuz Omar said that global cooperation endured as fundamental scientific inquiry continued to transcend borders. “Science is very universal,” Fairuz said. “From our engagement with all different parts of the world, including China … everybody is passionate about knowledge.” In May, the school hosted scientists from the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics’ College of Physics, who shared insights into using AI in research, nuclear physics and quantum-enabled space exploration technologies. They also explored potential collaborations in fields such as cosmology and materials fabrication. Fairuz pointed to his research using optical spectrometers to measure fruit quality metrics like sweetness, pH and firmness across different wavelengths as an area of potential for collaboration with China. “The final intention is [to] find out several wavelengths that can specifically cater for the measurement of that particular quality of the fruit. That is what we are looking for. But the tricky situation is that fruits are really diversified.” Looking to build “common understanding on this diversified world”, he said, “we can see that there are many researchers from China also working on visible near-infrared spectroscopy, particularly on agriculture”. “[With] the growing number of people working in this area, hopefully that will be some sort of meeting point.” Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: Reporter’s notebook: can canal connection give a lift to economic backwater?
description: Apple tech specialist says it could make it easier for gadgets made in Vietnam to enter massive Chinese market.
content: During a recent reporting trip to the economic backwater of Nanning, the capital of southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, the Pinglu Canal and US tech titan Apple’s latest product launch were on nearly everyone’s lips. The canal, which was officially opened on September 16, was built to make Guangxi a maritime logistics gateway for landlocked provinces in southwestern China and a nexus for trade with Southeast Asia. But many Nanning residents are not sure they will feel any immediate benefits in their daily lives, despite the regional government’s promotions of the waterway’s prospects. A week before the canal opened, Apple staged its biggest new product launch of the year in California, and the new line-up of gadgets went on sale across China, including in Nanning, on September 18. They could become a shining example of the canal’s ability to reorganise economic geography and turn grandiose visions into something tangible. Some popular Apple products that are assembled in Vietnam – ranging from wireless AirPods earbuds and Apple Watch wearables to HomePod smart speakers and other accessories – may make use of the new canal to reach Guangxi faster, and from there move on to other parts of the massive Chinese market, according to a “Genius Bar” tech specialist at Apple’s store in Nanning. He made that optimistic forecast while being overwhelmed by a scrum of would-be buyers asking when they could get their hands on their desired products. Before the opening of the canal, some Apple products and other sea freight from Southeast Asia had to pass through Guangzhou’s port before reaching Guangxi and southwestern cities like Kunming, Chengdu and Chongqing, with the detour adding more than 500km (311 miles) to their journey. Hopes are also high that the canal, which connects interprovincial rivers and railway lines to the Gulf of Tonkin, will help revive Nanning’s sluggish economy. Home to 9 million people, the city’s annual economic output ranks just 49th across all cities in China, and its 4.7 per cent gross domestic product growth lagged the national average. The canal’s opening coincided with the 23rd China-Asean Expo in the city, where Chinese officials, including first-ranked Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang, spoke at length about how it may become a catalyst for trade and development. At the expo, a representative from a Bruneian marine technology company told me she had read South China Morning Post reports about the canal. Many Asean businesses had become familiar with Nanning and the rest of Guangxi thanks to the annual expo, she said, and were eager to study the benefits of enhanced connectivity. Despite the widespread enthusiasm about the canal among foreign exhibitors, many were unable to visit it due to its remote, rural location outside Nanning. Local officials said people were welcome to visit the canal on their own, without providing much help. Reporters from Hong Kong, Taiwan and Southeast Asia were offered a guided tour of a canal exhibition hall that featured a sand table model. Many complained that even getting around Nanning was a hassle during the expo, with residents having to navigate multilayered security checks, and taxi passengers travelling from the airport subjected to AI-powered scans of faces, IDs and bags. Shops in a massive underground commercial plaza between the expo venue and a nearby subway station were ordered to shut for six consecutive days during the event to ensure safety and keep those not attending the expo at a distance. One Singaporean reporter told me the Guangxi authorities had been a bit clumsy in handling the spike in attention sparked by the expo and the opening of the canal. But there is a palpable sense in Nanning that the region is on the cusp of a big transformation. Crowds continue to pack the city’s Apple Store, pointing to the market potential for international brands in an ethnically diverse part of China that is far from its bustling eastern metropolises. More infrastructure-powered commerce may once again modernise a Chinese region, following the successful pattern pioneered by well-connected coastal regions.

title: Why a film about a dictator has South Korea at war with itself
description: A blockbuster about the 1974 assassination attempt of former president Park Chung-hee is causing a political backlash.
content: Like many films released during Chuseok, South Korea’s national mid-autumn harvest festival, The Assassin(s) shot right to the top, selling more than a million tickets in its first four days. But the box-office success of the film about the 1974 assassination attempt on former president and military leader Park Chung-hee was quickly overshadowed by calls to halt screenings, as well as a police complaint against the film’s director and producers. Park loyalists and conservative politicians are claiming the film, directed by acclaimed filmmaker Hur Jin-ho, distorts history and defames Park and his administration. Park, who came to power after a 1961 military coup, remains one of the most divisive figures in South Korean history. His authoritarian rule coincided with one of the world’s fastest periods of industrialisation, but his government was also marked by political repression and restrictions on civil liberties. As the controversy spills beyond the cinema, several actors cancelled audience greetings. Global star Lee Min-ho, who plays a freedom-fighting journalist, abruptly called off a public appearance at next week’s Busan International Film Festival. Actors have faced a wave of online abuse, while calls to boycott the film and products advertised by its cast have circulated on social media. The backlash has reignited a much older argument over how South Korea should remember the Park era, and whether unresolved political divisions are shaping how the public interprets its history. Choosing a side Sam Park is among those who have decided not to watch the film. “People are pointing out that there are similarities between the film and North Korean propaganda films,” the 30-year-old brand designer said. The film’s cast and crew have been labelled “communists” and “North Korean sympathisers”, a common accusation directed at liberals by South Korea’s political right. “Above all, this is a tragedy from relatively recent history, with surviving family members who are still alive today. The filmmakers should have been even more careful to distinguish between historical fact and creative interpretation, even while exercising their freedom of expression.” The Assassin(s) centres on the incident during a ceremony marking the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese rule. Mun Se-gwang, a Zainichi Korean living in Japan who was identified as a North Korean sympathiser, attempted to shoot Park but missed, killing then first lady Yuk Young-soo instead. While the film does not identify accomplices, it raises the possibility that people within the presidential office or intelligence authorities may have been involved. Park’s son, Park Ji-man, asked the President Park Chung Hee Memorial Foundation to demand that screenings be halted – as he did in 2005 over The President’s Last Bang, which depicted the night of Park’s assassination in 1979. The foundation issued a joint statement on Thursday calling for the film’s production company to formally apologise and take down the movie from theatres. A former People Power Party city councillor on Tuesday filed a police complaint against Hur and the film’s producers, accusing them of defamation and spreading false information by implying that Park was involved in his wife’s assassination. On Friday, the conservative civic group New Freedom Solidarity said it had submitted plans to the police to stage rallies outside the home of actor Yoo Hae-jin, who plays a police officer investigating the assassination in the film. “We are asking the actor to also appear in right-wing movies so that there is a political balance,” Kim Sang-jin, the leader of the civic group, told Yonhap News Agency. For Ellie Chung, who recently watched The Assassin(s), the controversy has brought renewed attention to an event she knew little about. “I expected there to be controversy because the film deals with the authoritarian regime and the era of Park Chung-hee,” she said. “But the film is being used for political purposes due to its historical context, and I think it has gone too far.” The production team denied having political intentions, saying the film used cinematic imagination rather than attempting to “prove a new historical conclusion”. South Korean courts have previously grappled with similar disputes over films based on true stories. In relation to the 2003 film Silmido, about a team recruited to take out North Korean assassins, relatives of those portrayed as criminals sought to halt screenings, but the court upheld the filmmakers’ freedom of expression. The President’s Last Bang was also given the go-ahead but with three scenes using documentary footage removed. Unresolved history The controversy is ultimately about how South Koreans interpret their past, according to Park Jong-rin, a professor of history education at Hannam University. “It’s not really about facts, but the difference in interpreting the events that took place. This is the nature of looking at history,” he said. “When you look deeper into the different voices reacting to the movie, it’s really about how people have not come to a consensus on the legacy of the Park Chung-hee administration.” Lee Taek-gwang, a philosophy and cultural studies professor at Kyung Hee University, said the dispute was rooted in South Korea’s democratisation struggle in the 1980s. “Ultimately, this issue is connected to the forces that emerged in the 1980s – the democratisation movement that opposed military dictatorship and sought to establish a new political order and the authoritarian regimes of the earlier period that brought on a generation of economic development,” he said. Films such as The Man Standing Next, another dramatisation of Park’s assassination, and 12.12: The Day had sought to reinterpret modern Korean history, Lee said, contrasting with efforts, particularly from conservatives, to normalise Park’s legacy. The use of popular culture to establish a political identity and world view was a distinctive feature of South Korean society, which went through several periods of civil democratic movements, he added. “South Korea is still a country where these historical arguments remain unresolved,” Lee said. “A decade ago, people assumed neoliberal forces would simply continue to dominate influence, but we are now seeing the rise of far-right movements.” The film’s critics, however, say their objections are not simply political. Park Hye-eun, chief editor of The Screen movie media publication, said audiences had every right to criticise a film they found inaccurate or objectionable. “What concerns me is that the head of a major political party singled out a particular film and called on people not to watch it, while also filing criminal complaints against the filmmakers and bringing the film into the political arena,” she said. “That seems less like the exercise of an audience member’s right to criticise and more like political power intervening in the cultural sphere.” Park said the controversy had ultimately led her to view the film through a different lens. “The film is actually trying to say that we should live in a society where anyone can ask questions and anyone can try to provide answers to those questions,” she said. “Perhaps the film is ultimately asking what a mature society should look like. Maybe it’s a society where anyone is free to ask questions, and where people are mature enough to listen to and consider the answers.”

title: Just Saying | Hong Kong vs Singapore in tackling bad behaviour
description: It’s not a competition, but a comparison and a call for a spanking rather than caning.
content: Singapore is doing something about uncivilised behaviour on public buses. The city state has started enforcing new regulations that carry an immediate fine of up to S$500 (US$390) if you put your feet up on seats, play loud audio on your phone or make a nuisance of yourself in other ways such as eating, drinking and littering. This aligns with existing rules governing passenger conduct on Singapore’s MRT railway system. Did you know we have long had similar regulations for Hong Kong’s MTR network under its own by-laws? Probably not, because nobody cares, but they do exist. For instance, playing audio loudly on trains is punishable by a fine of up to HK$2,000 (US$250). The same penalty applies for uncouth behaviour such as placing your feet on seats and for ignoring eating or drinking bans. Not only that, using profanity and language deemed offensive carries a fine of HK$5,000. If the MTR actually enforced this particular by-law, it would collect a revenue bonanza. Rushing the train doors when they’re already closing, with the warning beeps going off, should earn you a penalty of HK$2,000 as well. It should but it won’t because the difference between Hong Kong and Singapore is that many of these rules are just there for lip service. Nobody bothers to follow or enforce them in one jurisdiction, while they are taken more seriously in the other. You can resurrect the usual tropes about personal freedoms and repression in this comparison, in which we’re somehow supposed to take comfort in the assumption that at least it feels less controlling here than in Singapore. But if it’s about curtailing the freedom to behave badly in public and shared spaces, then bring on that Singaporean-style repression. There is the concept of liberty, which is the freedom to act responsibly within an accepted legal and social framework without being a nuisance to others. Then there is licence, which is the entitlement to do whatever you want with zero regard for societal norms and the rights of others around you. Millions of people in this city can’t be bothered with basic courtesy and social graces. These include holding the door open for someone right behind you, resisting the urge to furiously jab the “close door” button to deny someone entry into a lift even as you’re making eye contact, waiting for people to alight first before storming onto trains and many other daily acts of incivility and social ineptitude. There is a lot of pent-up rage out there. This is reflected in a whole lot of honking in Hong Kong as rude and impatient drivers blast perceived irritants such as fellow motorists slowing down or getting stuck in front of them, children, cardboard-collecting grannies and even wheelchair users who fail to get out of their way in time. Also in their way, as well as everyone else’s, are the mobile phone zombies. These people have their noses buried in their electronic pacifier while sauntering along the most crowded streets and walkways in the world with infuriating apathy and total disregard for the natural flow of human traffic. The cocooned self-indulgence of these sidewalk narcissists and human roadblocks everywhere we go is as exhausting in its nonchalance as it is frustrating in its main-character syndrome. They expect the entire sea of humanity to conveniently part and warp around their immovable bodies like ignorable background noise. This is not a problem unique to Hong Kong, but there is a difference that makes it all the more egregious here. While most of the world measures population density per square kilometre, Hong Kong’s 7.5 million residents are crammed into just 25 per cent of its total land area – the rest is uninhabitable or designated as protected areas and country parks. That means when we talk in terms of volumetric hyper-density – how people actually fit into public space – we are in a different league. Vertical urbanism accommodates us, but when we pour out of our anthills to go about our daily business on the ground, the congestion is next-level. On the streets of Mong Kok, for example, academic studies have shown that the population density can be up to 600,000 people per square kilometre, even though the figure for the wider district is 130,000 people, which is still one for the record books. On an average footbridge or elevated walkway in Mong Kok, density can be up to 3.5 people per square metre. This is insane, and it is also why people who make it worse should not be dismissed as harmless manifestations of first-world problems. These miscreants with mobile phones are directly and constantly escalating stress levels in an already high-strung society. Why can’t we have a law against it, just like we have one penalising the misuse of mobile phones while driving? Should you feel the urge to pause in mid-stride to check your phone while walking elbow-to-elbow with 1,000 fellow humans at any given time, pull over to the side and get your dose of instant gratification without obstructing the rest of us. If that sounds unrealistic, remember that people said something similar about banning smoking in public spaces some decades ago. Look how we pressed ahead with it and prospered. Comparisons to Singapore bring to mind what the late Lee Kuan Yew said when he was accused of infringing on personal liberties by micromanaging public behaviour: “I say without the slightest remorse, that we wouldn’t be here, we would not have made economic progress, if we had not intervened on very personal matters – who your neighbour is, how you live, the noise you make, how you spit, or what language you use. We decide what is right. Never mind what people think.” What a splendid man, unafraid and unapologetic about putting facts before feelings to get things done for the greater good. And what a pleasing thought, imagining what he would have done about the mobile phone menace if he were still around today. Sure, pearls would be clutched and token noises sounded, but most of us would appreciate the net improvement in the quality of life. I’m not advocating the introduction of caning in Hong Kong, mind you, but perhaps a bit of a spanking is long overdue.

title: Hongkongers lose HK$220 million to customer service scams in August
description: Scammers are taking real-time control of victims through direct calls or tricking them into installing malicious apps, police warn.
content: Scams involving fraudsters posing as customer service officers caused losses of over HK$220 million (US$28.2 million) in August in Hong Kong, more than triple the monthly average in the first seven months of the year, police have said. The police force also warned that scammers had shifted their modus operandi from using phishing links to taking real-time control of victims through direct calls and screen sharing, or tricking them into installing a malicious app that turned mobile phones into a credit card reader. Hong Kong recorded 29,670 scam cases in the first eight months of 2026, up 4.5 per cent from 28,379 in the same period a year earlier, with losses rising by 3.8 per cent to HK$5.2 billion. About 17 per cent, or around 5,000 cases, were customer service scams, which incurred total losses of nearly HK$700 million. The number of such scams soared from a monthly average of about 480 in the first seven months to more than 1,680 in August. Losses exceeded HK$220 million in August, more than triple the monthly average of the previous seven months. More than 1,600 cases in August involved scammers making phone calls and posing as customer service staff from banks, logistics firms and telecoms companies. The remaining 80 cases involved message-based scams. Superintendent Rachel Hui Yee-wai of the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau said the fraudsters’ shift away from phishing links reflected the evolution of scams as the public grew wary of such tricks. “They no longer just send you a link. They call you directly, and instantly they are working on your emotions,” she said. “If they want to take everything in your account, they have to operate with you, step by step, in real time. When you get stuck, they guide you on the spot, even via screen sharing. That gives them far greater control over the victim than a link ever could.” She urged the public to verify any customer service claim through official channels found independently – never through contact details provided by the caller. Chief Inspector Wong Cheung-hing of the bureau said police had identified two new methods used by scammers. In the first, victims are tricked into downloading a malicious application on their phone and then instructed to enable near-field communication (NFC), the technology behind contactless payments, and tap their credit cards on the phones for “verification” or “refund” purposes. They unknowingly hand over their card data, after which fraudulent transactions follow. “When the victim notices unauthorised transactions and questions them, the scammer claims a refund is due and asks them to tap the card again, completing a second theft,” Wong said. The second method involves scammers posing as courier staff who claim a parcel cannot be delivered and that compensation is due. They then guide victims to log in to their own online banking and add the scammer’s account as a new payee. Claiming the account has to be verified, the scammer gives the victims a string of digits as a “verification code” and tells them to enter it into the payment amount field, sending the sum to the fraudster’s account. Police cited two cases in August with combined losses of nearly HK$8 million. In one case, a 74-year-old businessman, who received a phishing text impersonating a courier firm, called the customer service number provided and gave his account details, losing HK$3.4 million. In the other case, a 53-year-old housewife returned a call from scammers posing as Taobao customer service staff who promised her compensation for “a damaged parcel”. After logging into a fake website and her online banking account, she added a scammer-controlled account as a payee and entered a “verification code” in the amount field, transferring HK$4.46 million. In response to the rising losses, police said they had stepped up action on three fronts: taking down scam websites and their operators; intercepting bulk scam texts at the telecoms level; and arresting those who laundered the proceeds. More than 1,500 fake sender IDs had been blocked in the first eight months of the year, while the force’s Scameter app logged over 500,000 public scam reports during the same period, more than 40,000 of them courier-related. On the industry side, major courier firm SF Express said it had stopped sending customer notifications by SMS in 2025, pushing all updates through its official app instead. Chun Yuk-ying, head of public affairs and communications at SF Express, said the switch had cut the firm’s scam victimisation rate from 5.03 per cent to 0.65 per cent.

title: In Focus | China has dominated tungsten for decades. Can US cash in Central Asia loosen its grip?
description: Kazakhstan is at the centre of US efforts to build a new supply chain for the metal, but analysts say China’s lead will be difficult to overcome.
content: The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold. Global tungsten prices have surged more than 200 per cent since May 2025, according to commodity and energy information provider Argus Media, adding urgency to efforts to develop alternative supplies. The soaring costs followed Beijing’s export controls on selected tungsten products introduced in February 2025 in a market already facing tight mine supply and increased demand from the defence industry. The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits. According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of manufacturing drill bits had risen by as much as 50 per cent over the past year. The company is responding by shifting production towards steel-bodied models, even as bits containing more tungsten typically last longer when cutting through hard, abrasive rock. Rival Varel Energy Solutions has made a similar calculation. “Without any stabilisation in tungsten pricing, manufacturers will be forced to transition to steel alternatives,” chief commercial officer Jayme Sperring told Reuters in a report published in May. China accounted for nearly 80 per cent of mined tungsten globally, producing about 3.7 times the output of the rest of the world combined, according to data from the US Geological Survey. Its dominance extends beyond mining into processing and manufacturing, making it difficult for new producers to compete simply by bringing more of the metal to market. Prized for its hardness and heat resistance, tungsten is used in industrial tools and some military equipment, including armour-piercing ammunition and missiles, as well as in semiconductors and electronic components supporting AI hardware and data centres. The US is a major consumer but has recorded no commercial tungsten mine production since 2015. That dependence has made overseas projects increasingly important to Washington’s efforts to secure supplies. A new front in the race In April, US mining investment firm Cove Capital acquired a 70 per cent stake in two deposits in Kazakhstan’s Karaganda region: Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty. Their combined estimated development cost is US$1.1 billion, though both remain at the engineering and feasibility study stage, with production targeted for around 2028. Financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory That timetable contrasts with Chinese-backed investments in the country. Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources already operates the Boguty Mine in Kazakhstan’s Almaty region after the facility began trial production in November 2024 and entered commercial operations in April 2025. Another proposed tungsten investment, involving Kunxin International Investment and Kazakhstan’s SP Saryarka Tungsten, was among more than 60 agreements signed at Hong Kong’s Belt and Road Summit in September, though few details were disclosed. This difference in development timelines had given China an immediate advantage in the supply chain, according to Liang Yan, Kremer Chair Professor of Economics at Willamette University. Boguty was already producing, she added, while the US-backed projects still needed to complete studies, secure financing and build their facilities. Liang argued Kazakhstan could become a “vital producer of tungsten”, citing the Central Asian nation’s more than 2 million tonnes of forecast resources and saying it could eventually supply about 15 per cent of annual global mine output. “I don’t think US financing can neutralise China’s lead in processing capacity and commercial scale,” said Liang, who is also a non-resident senior fellow at Boston University’s Global Development Policy Centre. The challenge goes beyond bringing new mines into production. Kazakhstan, Liang suggested, would also need to develop more local refining capacity if it wanted to build a supply chain less dependent on China. Without such capacity, new mines might still have to send concentrate to Chinese processors if alternative facilities faced delays or cost overruns, Liang said. Liu Wenjing, a member of the Astana International Financial Centre’s Executive Council for the Mining Sector and founder and principal adviser of Elistra Advisory, acknowledged that US financing could significantly lower the barriers to building an alternative tungsten supply chain. But, she cautioned, “financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades”. China’s advantage spanned much of the tungsten supply chain, Liu said. That includes processing mined ore into concentrate and producing ammonium paratungstate (APT), an important intermediate material used to make tungsten products, and making finished products such as cemented carbides. Geography also matters. Kazakhstan borders China while shipments bound for Europe and North America face longer routes, including across the Caspian Sea. “The US has effectively recognised that investing in overseas mines alone will not solve the problem,” said Liu, who previously served as board secretary of Jiaxin. That strategy is reflected in Washington’s investments in processing capacity at home, including plans to convert tungsten into APT. In mid-September, Washington announced a US$450 million investment in Elmet Group through redeemable preferred shares. “This shows that US strategy is moving beyond securing ore towards filling the gap in midstream processing,” Liu said.
