The same logic applies to transport, as Northern Katpar is being designed to reach international markets through the Trans-Caspian route. The plans, according to Liu, suggested Western-backed projects were addressing how the metal would reach buyers, not just where it would be mined. The cost of dependence This push to develop alternative supply routes has only intensified since China introduced export-licensing requirements in February 2025, the same day new US tariffs on Chinese goods took effect. While Beijing said the controls were intended to safeguard national security and fulfil its non-proliferation obligations, they were widely interpreted as part of the broader trade and technology rivalry between the two superpowers. At the same time, China has authorised only 15 companies to export tungsten under its state-trading system for 2026 and 2027. Products covered by the 2025 controls remain subject to separate export licences and end-user checks. Chinese customs data showed that exports of tungsten products by weight fell 25 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026. Exports of sodium tungstate plunged 94.9 per cent, while shipments of ammonium paratungstate, an important intermediate material, dropped 89.3 per cent. Exports of tungsten-related products from China to the US also fell 21 per cent by volume year on year over the same period. Shipments of unwrought tungsten and tungsten carbide stopped altogether, while exports of tungsten bars fell 42 per cent. Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory The restrictions, along with tight mine supply and rising demand, have added upwards pressure on prices. Fastmarkets, a global price-reporting agency specialising in metals and mining, assessed global tungsten concentrate prices at US$2,500–2,800 per metric tonne unit from May 29, up from US$750–850 at the start of 2026 – an increase of about 230 per cent. The price pressure is reaching manufacturers. MSC Industrial Supply, a major US distributor with nearly US$4 billion in annual sales, told an investor conference in New York last month that tungsten-related input costs had surged by about 500 per cent. “They have stabilised, but the ripples through the supply chain aren’t over yet,” chief executive Martina McIsaac said during the event, adding that suppliers were continuing to raise prices at different rates depending on their inventories and access. Higher costs are also prompting Washington to look beyond new mines for additional supply, including recycling. On August 27, it imposed a one-year ban on exports of tungsten scrap to retain material for US processors. According to materials research platform Material Insights, recycled tungsten provided about 25 to 30 per cent of global supply and was particularly important to the US because it lacks domestic mine production. The scramble goes global For Kazakhstan, the main question may be how quickly proposed mining and processing projects can be brought into operation. The country still accounts for less than 3 per cent of global tungsten mine output, though Liu said new projects could significantly increase its share. “If Jiaxin International’s Boguty mine continues to expand, and Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty come into production as planned, Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China,” she said. EarthRarest, a strategic metals research and investment platform, made a similar assessment in a report shared with the South China Morning Post. It estimated that Kazakhstan’s 2.8 per cent share of global mine production represented about one-eighth of production outside China. “An additional reliable source can matter to buyers diversifying their purchases well before it changes China’s overall lead,” EarthRarest said, adding that the US could help finance mines, processing facilities and transport links, particularly alongside purchase commitments. But it cautioned that it remained unclear whether the projects could produce at competitive costs and deliver reliably. “The reviewed evidence does not establish that finance alone removes a cost or scale disadvantage,” EarthRarest said. Kazakh tungsten could potentially reach Western buyers without passing through China if the required mining, processing, transport and customer arrangements all proved workable, according to the report. For the proposed large Kazakh projects, however, “a fully independent route remains a project objective rather than an established operating fact”. Yet Kazakhstan is not merely choosing between Chinese and American investors. Astana is also seeking to move beyond its traditional role as an exporter of raw materials and develop more of the tungsten supply chain at home. The Kazakh government’s 2023–2027 geological development strategy called for expanded exploration, digitised geological records, improved mining infrastructure and greater investment in research and skills. A separate government plan covering rare and rare earth metals through 2028 called for modernising existing facilities, introducing more advanced processing technologies and attracting investment from a wider range of international partners. Kazakhstan is only part of a broader effort by governments to secure tungsten supplies and capture more value from their mineral resources. In late August, Britain’s National Wealth Fund announced an investment of up to £71 million in Tungsten West to support the proposed restart of the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon. The project is targeting full-scale production in the first quarter of 2027. Resource-producing countries are also tightening their grip on the metal. Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade has proposed removing tungsten from the list of minerals permitted for export. It has not specified how long the proposed restriction would last and has stressed that it would not amount to a permanent ban. Zimbabwe went further in September, suspending exports of antimony and tungsten in all forms, including ores and concentrates, until further notice. The government said the measure was intended to encourage mining companies to refine and process more of their minerals domestically, allowing the African nation to retain more value before export.

title: Reflections | The surprising history of beer in China, from li to Tsingtao
description: From ancient China’s fermented grain drink li to the founding of Tsingtao Brewery, China has a long history of brewing.
content: Munich’s Oktoberfest was never on my travel bucket list. But it offered a chance to meet up with good friends from Hong Kong and their adorable toddler, Joshua, who go to the festival every year as a family. So there I was, spending a weekend at Theresienwiese, surrounded by bewildering varieties of beer and their drinkers. The annual Oktoberfest, first held in October 1810 to celebrate a royal wedding, is about more than just beer. There are amusement rides, games, stalls selling things you never knew you needed, and, of course, a staggering smorgasbord of hearty Bavarian food, which I happily enjoyed. Still, beer remains Oktoberfest’s main draw. And this is where I must drop the bombshell: I do not like beer. Some quirk of my biology means that even a single glass leaves me feeling bloated and very uncomfortable. Over that weekend, I was hoping nobody would notice that I was nursing a single tankard of leichtbier (“light beer”) throughout each day while discreetly drinking copious amounts of fizzy water. Beer enthusiasts will probably be happy to know that thousands of years ago, people in ancient China made li, an early fermented grain drink whose brewing method shares a fundamental principle with beer. Archaeological evidence found near Xian, in China’s Shaanxi province, shows broomcorn millet, barley and other grains were used in brewing as far back as 5,000 years ago. Other evidence suggests malted grains had been adopted by the Shang dynasty (1600-1046BC). The key was sprouted grain. As grains germinate, they produce enzymes that convert starch into sugars. Those sugars can then be fermented by yeast into alcohol. It is one of the basic principles of modern brewing: malt the grain, convert starch into sugar and ferment it. There was, however, little resemblance between drinking li and knocking back a cold lager at Oktoberfest. Li was apparently sweet, thick and relatively light. It was also not necessarily filtered clear. Grain residue could remain in the drink, making it more like a slightly boozy, sweet porridge than a glass of Pilsner. It was sometimes filtered to make it go down smoother for formal occasions such as royal banquets. Li’s gentle character made it suitable for people who could not tolerate stronger alcohol. There is a record of a prince of the Han period (206BC-AD220) who would take great care to serve li to one of his trusted advisers because of the latter’s aversion to stronger drinks. But li eventually lost out to another Chinese brewing tradition. Instead of relying primarily on malted grain, brewers increasingly used qu, a fermented grain starter containing moulds, yeasts and other microorganisms. Qu helps break down starches and drive fermentation, producing stronger, more robust grain wines. As tastes changed, li came to be regarded as “thin in flavour”. Chinese scientist and encyclopedist Song Yingxing (1587-1666) later wrote that this change in taste ultimately caused both li and its brewing method to disappear. Beer eventually returned to China, but from a very different direction. Western-style brewing was introduced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with breweries established by foreigners in cities such as Harbin and Qingdao. Among the best known was the Anglo-German brewery founded in the coastal city of Qingdao in 1903. The beer it brewed, Tsingtao, would go on to become one of China’s most internationally recognised alcohol brands. Perhaps li would have suited me better: light, sweet and not too potent. But then again, historical records alone cannot shed light on whether I would like the taste or – crucially – if it would give me gas. For now, I will stick to the things I know I enjoy: good friends, delectable food and, when absolutely necessary, a very small beer.

title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino in Hong Kong with city team set for Cambodia Asean final
description: While city’s naturalised pool is drying up and ‘needs a few players’, Cambodia’s upturn has been boosted by raft of overseas-born talent.
content: A Hong Kong team “in transition” will battle upwardly mobile and ambitious Cambodia on Saturday for the unremarkable honour of being crowned Fifa Asean Challenge Cup champions. Although the city team copped some flak for their performance in a 2-0 victory over Brunei on Wednesday, having trounced the same opponents 10-0 three years ago, Roberto Losada and his players should be cut some slack after the head coach made nine changes from the 4-0 victory over Laos three days earlier. Equally, Hong Kong created a bundle of chances and on another night would have won by five or six. Still, Matt Orr, who marked his 50th international cap with a smart late strike, acknowledged that despite boasting a “strong core group”, Hong Kong needed “to find the next generation [of players] to come and support us, because we’re not getting any younger”. “It’s going to take everyone from the top to implement good youth training and systems, and to be aligned towards the same goals, to produce those players,” Orr said. “The team right now needs a few players to come in and support us.” While the city’s naturalised player pool is drying up, Cambodia’s recent upturn has been underpinned by the introduction of a raft of overseas-born performers. Originally from Colombia, Andres Nieto made his debut in December 2024, five years after arriving in the country to play for Phnom Penh Crown. The scorer of both of his team’s goals in their 2-2 draw with Timor-Leste on Wednesday, Nieto tormented Hong Kong in Cambodia’s landmark 2-0 victory over the city team back in June. He will be a danger in Saturday’s final, which is set to be attended by Gianni Infantino, the controversial Fifa president who is probably very grateful that Manchester City have elbowed him out of the media spotlight over the past week. Infantino is in Hong Kong and on Friday posted on Instagram pictures of himself alongside Pui Kwan-kay and Eric Fok Kai-shan, captioned with a message thanking the local football association president and chairman, as well as general secretary Charles Cheung Yim-yau, for their “warm and generous welcome”. Fok’s insistence that the Football Association of Hong Kong, China has not thrown its weight behind Infantino’s risible quest for a fourth term in office appears increasingly implausible. Candidates wishing to challenge the Swiss lawyer in next March’s election have until November 18 to show their hands. “People can see we’re improving, and we are coming,” Nieto said, adding that qualification for the 2030 World Cup was a genuine aspiration. “We’re making history, so why not dream? Cambodia had never reached a final before this week. We’d never beaten Hong Kong [in 11 attempts] before the last game against them.” Brazil-born attacker Iago Bento made his Cambodia debut in July, becoming the 10th naturalised player available to Koji Gyotoku, the Japanese head coach. Hong Kong, meanwhile, are still relying on the rump of the players who went to the Asian Cup finals in 2024, although against Brunei, Losada gave an international bow to late-blooming Tonio Chan Yun-tung, 24, who started alongside Ng Yu-hei, the expressive 20-year-old winger, and 22-year-old centre-back Jason Kam Chi-kin. Callum Beattie, 25, has earned his first two caps at left-back in the tournament. Told 24 hours ahead of time that he would start, right-back Chan “was happy at first, because I’d been really looking forward to that day for a long time; then I started to feel a little nervous and excited”. Like Orr, Chan spent time studying in the United States, in his case two years at Lake Placid’s Northwood School from 2018. “I saw how professional the players were, even though it wasn’t their job,” he said. “When they weren’t getting chances, they’d still do their best until it came. That inspired me to do better every day to fight for my chance.” Losada received an earful from travelling supporters following the recent defeat by Cambodia, which was only his second match in permanent charge. “In June, more players are thinking about their holidays than the window,” Losada said. “We’ll be more aggressive than in that game, and there are things we have to change to be competitive with Cambodia, but playing at home will make a huge difference.” Until he was benched for the meeting with Laos, Orr had started every Hong Kong match for which he was available since a friendly on Hong Kong’s infamous trip to Fiji two years ago. Although he “accepted whatever [Losada’s] plan was”, Orr said that being left out “lit a little fire in my belly to go out and prove a point [against Brunei]”. Acknowledging it had been “a big honour and privilege every time I’ve worn the Hong Kong jersey”, Orr celebrated his goal by pretending to tidy his lustrous head of hair. “A few people sent me an Instagram reel about how many times I fixed my hair when I came on [against Laos], so it was a joke in response,” he said. Nieto’s celebrations following his strikes against Timor-Leste were a nod to his wife being three months pregnant with the couple’s second child. A product of the same Academia Tolimense de Futbol that reared Colombian superstar James Rodriguez, Nieto acknowledged it had been “a risk” to quit South America for Cambodia. “But I liked everything,” he said. “I had some offers to leave but I wanted to stay to complete the five years to play for Cambodia. “It’s a respectful and safe country. Its football is growing up so fast, and it has a good infrastructure. The national team is also growing up.” The jury remains out on whether this inaugural Fifa Asean Cup has been a worthwhile exercise. Partway through, the global governing body quietly rebranded the second-tier event in Hong Kong as the Fifa Asean Challenge Cup, drawing a clear distinction from the glitzier eight-team top division being concurrently staged in Indonesia. Attendances for matches not involving the hosts have been desultory, while Hong Kong’s games have drawn 18,873 and 20,116 supporters to the 50,00-capacity Kai Tak Stadium. “I think 20,000 is a great turnout; the stadium is amazing and I think it’ll be close to full on Saturday,” Orr said, adding that the “big red wall” of home fans in the North Stand “reminded me of the Kop at Liverpool”. Nieto said he would welcome “playing under pressure in front of 50,000 people”. “Who doesn’t want to play in a full stadium?” he added. “It gives me more motivation.” Cambodia beat Myanmar with a very late strike in their opening game, before drawing against an enterprising Timor-Leste side that made a lot of friends during their short visit. Indeed, every game other than Hong Kong’s filleting of Laos has been closely contested. “It’s a tight tournament,” Nieto said. “We play every three days, and have little time to recover, but we have confidence.” Planning to play for “a good while longer”, the 29-year-old Orr could conceivably reach 100 caps, having got halfway in little more than five years. He said his goalscoring debut in a 3-1 defeat by Iran in June 2021 was the “most special” memory because “it was the beginning of the journey”. “Everything since then has flown by,” he added. In the period since Orr’s introduction, Chan had a spell of routinely losing with now-defunct HK23. “I had to keep my faith, but I was grateful the coach [Szeto Man-chun] kept playing me and kept me in football,” Chan said. He made “a step forward” during three years with Southern, before a career-changing move to local title challengers Lee Man this summer. Confounding expectations, Chan has started all five games and scored twice for his new club, having netted only five times in his previous 115 domestic appearances. In the final year of a social policy degree from Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Chan said: “As well as helping Lee Man win titles and qualify for Asian football, I want to keep going at international level and become a regular player. It takes time, so I’ll keep working every day.”

title: Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
description: Rail links and cycle routes make it easier for motorists to give up their cars as running costs and road charges rise.
content: When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years. Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades. High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society. Quarterly figures released by the government’s Land Transport Authority in July showed there were 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, the lowest number since 2019, even as the share of rental, ride-hailing and corporate cars had increased. Privately owned cars still accounted for 79 per cent of all those on the roads, however. When Tan bought his first car in May 2006, he said the COE cost S$10,000. A decade later it had climbed to S$50,000 and renewing again this summer would have cost more than double that amount. Other reasons to give up driving included rising road tax, fuel, maintenance and insurance costs, he said, as well as the city state’s congestion-charging system, known as electronic road pricing (ERP). An automated system that charges drivers a fee for using busy roads during peak hours, ERP dates back to 1998, though there were other paper-based systems in place beforehand. At the start of last month, ERP charges returned to the Orchard Road shopping district for the first time since the start of the pandemic in 2020. Singapore has been actively encouraging people to walk, cycle and use more public transport under the Land Transport Authority’s “Move Lite” campaign, first launched in 2022. In its early days, the campaign mostly focused on the positives of public transport and not owning a car, but the strategy has since moved towards spotlighting the downsides of driving such as being stuck in traffic and wasting time hunting for parking. Still, its main aim was to promote more sustainable ways of travelling, not deter people from driving, through its use of “relatable, everyday scenarios”, a spokesman for the authority said. “The campaign seeks to help commuters make informed travel choices while raising awareness of the increasingly convenient and accessible alternatives to driving,” he said, adding that planning and managing Singapore’s transport network meant balancing the needs of different road users while making the best use of limited land. To achieve this, the spokesman said Singapore was investing in public transport and “active mobility” infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to keep transport efficient and sustainable. “Our objective is not to prioritise one group of commuters over another, but to provide Singaporeans with more mobility options that are safe, reliable and sustainable for different journeys and needs.” Singapore only has 744.3 sq km (287.4 square miles) of land and roads take up about 12 per cent of it, which is why authorities have been working to make walking, cycling and public transport more accessible and convenient. The COE system, launched in May 1990, controls how many vehicles are allowed on the roads by requiring motorists to bid for a certificate in online open auctions. Each COE confers the right to own a vehicle for 10 years. Singapore has maintained a zero-growth policy for private cars and motorcycles since February 2018 and the Land Transport Authority aims to keep this cap in place until January 31, 2028, while allowing for a small expansion of commercial vehicle and bus fleets. With the cost of living on the rise, Tan said owning a car was a poor coping strategy for uncertain times, especially considering he had to “set aside contingency funds for young children and aged parents as well”. Rising costs have also prompted other car owners to think twice about renewing their COEs. Retired engineer Ricky Quek, 63, recently decided to stop driving after 28 years, citing high COE and petrol prices. Renewing his COE would have cost him S$130,000, he said. “Public transport is reasonably cheap and no hassle compared to owning a car,” Quek said. “Having a car is definitely convenient but drives up the expenses.” Small annoyances Mounting expenses are only part of the picture, however. Other factors discouraging driving include efforts to lower speed limits with stricter enforcement and penalties, and extensive road works linked to major construction projects. Work on a new multilayered expressway known as the North-South Corridor, the multimodal Changi Northern Corridor project near the airport and a new subway called the Cross Island Line is affecting a number of major arterial roads and highways. Tech entrepreneur Davidson Chua, 27, says he has noticed more of these roadworks recently, especially during the off-peak times when he likes to commute. “I do often feel a small annoyance when I am expecting less traffic but end up [encountering] lane closures because of road works or pruning,” said the self-proclaimed motoring enthusiast, adding that he typically preferred covered parking spaces though those could be harder to come by. Chua said he would only drive two or three days some weeks, “because I don’t see a point in driving down to areas like the CBD [central business district]. It costs more time and money.” His car is now on its second 10-year COE cycle, with the next renewal due in three years’ time. “I would love to renew,” he said. “But the COE price will definitely play a huge role in the decision-making process.” Gopinath Menon, a former chief transport engineer at the Land Transport Authority who led the ERP’s roll-out, told This Week in Asia that measures to limit car ownership had been a part of Singapore’s overall transport strategy since the mid-1970s. “Realising that the small island cannot keep building more roads to tackle traffic congestion, the strategy called for reasonable demand management for private vehicle travel and for public transport to be the main mode of travel,” said Menon, who is now an independent transport engineering consultant. Higher parking charges were first to be introduced, alongside an analogue predecessor to the ERP known as the Area Licensing Scheme in 1975. The COE bidding framework followed in 1990, with ERP being rolled out later that same decade. “Higher driving costs have pushed more people to switch from cars to vastly improved public transport and other public modes such as private-hire vehicles and active mobility,” Menon said, referring to walking and cycling. “This is called the push-pull strategy.” Speed bumps on the road to a “car-lite” concept included “ambition and attitudes towards car ownership”, he said. But infrastructure can help lead the way. Menon pointed to the increasing number of pedestrianised zones and bus lanes as ways to reclaim road space for non-car traffic. Some districts and towns are also car-lite by design, with amenities placed close together, public transport prioritised and access to cycle paths and footpaths improved. Given the high costs of car ownership, Singapore’s government needs to make the case that cars are a luxury, not a necessity, for the vast majority of citizens, according to public policy expert Terence Ho, an adjunct associate professor in practice at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. “There will naturally be some unhappiness about the high COE and ERP charges, particularly when certain roads are still congested at peak hours despite the charges,” Ho said. “But by and large, the vehicle control measures have been effective.” The number of private cars, excluding private-hire vehicles, had grown just 1 per cent over the past five years, he said, while the share of resident households owning a car had fallen from as high as 42 per cent in 2012/13 to 36 per cent in 2023. This was despite the fact that many households included young children or elderly family members, Ho said. For Derek Wong, 35, a car is a non-negotiable for ferrying around his two young children and ageing parents. He bought a second-hand Honda Freed in December, with a COE that expires in September 2035. “I just felt we had to bite the bullet and this will probably be our last car since we won’t need it when the children are older,” said Wong, a writer whose children are aged two and seven. “The benefits of the convenience still outweigh the drawbacks. It is a hefty investment but given the time it saves, we feel it is worth it.” Whether COE subsidies should be granted to large families or to those with elderly members, young children or people with disabilities has repeatedly been raised in parliament. In a reply on the government portal AskGov in November, the Transport Ministry said the difficulty lay in deciding which groups should receive preferential treatment. A COE subsidy for families would have to be substantial, it said, and lower-income families unable to own a car would be unlikely to benefit. “COE revenues go towards funding public transport,” the ministry said, adding that its approach was to provide high-quality public transport, complemented by taxis and private-hire cars. On the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), Singapore’s main underground and elevated railway system, reliability hit a record in August, the Land Transport Authority said in a report released last month. The network’s mean kilometres between failures, a measure of the average distance a train travels before a delay of more than five minutes, rose to 2.88 million km (1.79 million miles) from 2.37 million km in July. About seven in 10 resident households are already within a 10-minute walk from an MRT station and the government aims to raise that proportion to 80 per cent by the 2030s. Yet the overall decline in private car ownership had as much to do with the cap on total vehicle numbers as improving public transport links, said Walter Theseira, an associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences. This restriction tended to push car usage towards private-hire models whereby higher utilisation rates made the expensive COE premiums easier to justify, Theseira said. “The high willingness to pay for COEs suggests that the underlying private demand for cars continues to be strong,” he said. “The policy objective can’t be to help Singaporeans achieve car ownership ambitions, as it’s a zero-sum game, but … to help Singaporeans stop needing a car.” Alternative paths For those ready to ditch the car, Singapore’s expanding cycling network offers a ready alternative. The city state currently has more than 730km (454 miles) of cycling paths and dedicated traffic-free green corridors known as “park connectors”, with work under way to expand the network to about 1,300km by 2030. Bicycles have been allowed to share pavements with pedestrians since around 2010, according to Menon, with many walkways later widened to ease congestion and improve safety. Even so, he said cycling was still mainly used for recreation, running errands and so-called first- and last-mile trips to railway stations and bus interchanges. It was unlikely to become the No 1 choice for most commuters given the high quality of public transport, Menon said. Theseira agreed, pointing to Singapore’s hot climate and the relatively long distance of an average commute as limiting factors – though he saw potential in electric bikes and other motorised devices. “In many places, very quickly, when people get access to electrified modes of cycling, they usually take that up,” he said, while noting the city state’s current restrictions on such devices, imposed for pedestrian safety, and lack of suitable infrastructure. Jason Slaughter, an Amsterdam-based content creator who runs the YouTube channel Not Just Bikes, published a video late last month arguing that rules forcing riders to frequently slow down, give way to cars or dismount and push would limit the take-up of cycling in Singapore. He also critiqued the city state’s cycling infrastructure, highlighting what he called “questionable choices” such as 90-degree turns and lanes that end abruptly, adding he suspected it was “designed by people who never ride a bicycle”. His video, titled “Cycling Made Difficult (but it’s getting better!)”, had been watched almost half a million times as of Friday. For Tan, who now relies on public transport and bicycle paths to get around after giving up on car ownership, the trade-offs are worth it. “I grew up without a car, so I do not have much difficulty adjusting,” he said. “For my Japanese wife, my two young kids and business needs, the adjustments are not as easy. Yet for the amount saved, it’s worth the inconvenience.”

title: New fashion and homeware drops: Fendi, Hermès, Marimekko and more
description: From jumpers to a basketball hoop, and boots to ‘sneakerinas’, this eclectic mix includes new releases from Sacai, John Smedley, Simone Rocha, Lane Crawford, Pucci and Timberland x Telfar.
content: These latest launches offer something for every taste, from reimagined icons and richly textured wardrobe staples to playful collaborations and unexpected home accessories. Whether you are looking for an elegant pair of slingbacks, embellished sneakers, a statement basketball hoop or vibrant glass tableware, there is plenty to discover. Fendi For her first Fendi collection – fall/winter 2026 – chief creative officer Maria Grazia Chiuri revisited one of the label’s signature shoes, the Colibrì slingback, first introduced in 2018. Chiuri’s version, named Very Colibrì, features a thinner heel and a slimmer, more elongated silhouette. Wear it with a pair of slim-fit trousers or a pencil skirt for a more formal look. Hermès Whether you’re lucky enough to own a private basketball court or just want to decorate your man cave, this hoop from Hermès is one of those extravagant and unexpected pieces that the maison’s inventive designers and skilled ateliers delight in delivering. In true Hermès style, the birch and beech backboard is decorated with a horse motif while the hoop itself is made of calfskin. For those who actually want to shoot some hoops, the brand also dropped two basketballs in bull calf leather. John Smedley x Wales Bonner Designer Grace Wales Bonner of Wales Bonner, who next year will make her debut as Hermès’ men’s ready-to-wear creative director, is once again joining forces with knitwear specialist John Smedley for a range of separates made of merino wool and cotton. Pieces include a series of short- and long-sleeved polo shirts, and a crew neck sweater with tan, blue and red stripes. Lane Crawford This season Lane Crawford celebrates individuality and personal style with a selection of pieces from the fall/winter collections that highlight craftsmanship and textures. Tactile materials such as cashmere, cowhide and shearling appear in garments meant to age beautifully after each wear, such as this reversible rug-inspired coat from Lebanese label Bokja. Marimekko Add a touch of colour to your table setting with these plates from Finnish lifestyle brand Marimekko. Made of clear glass in colours such as green, pink and red, the plates are all in the shape of Marimekko’s Unikko flower motif. Pucci Come summer, Pucci’s colourful prints steal the show in glamorous spots such as Portofino, Capri and Saint Tropez. Creative director Camille Miceli, however, never fails to follow up that vibrant aesthetic with her fall/winter collections for the brand. This year’s – inspired by Il Palio, a horse race in Siena, a Tuscan city near founder Emilio Pucci’s home base of Florence – offers plenty of animal prints in rich colours and sexy silhouettes. Sacai Chitose Abe of Sacai is not the first designer to find inspiration in the work of photographer Robert Mapplethorpe but the Japanese designer chose to highlight his photographs of tulips and lilies – and a self-portrait of the photographer – in her collaboration with The Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation, rather than his more famous photos of the male body. The range includes T-shirts, hoodies and a leather jacket, some of them printed with Mapplethorpe’s quote: “I’m looking for the unexpected. I’m looking for things I’ve never seen before.” Simone Rocha Simone Rocha’s collaboration with Adidas Originals takes the “sneakerina” trend to the next level. Ribbon lacing, and pearl and crystal embellishments – both signatures of the Irish designer – adorn footwear, while a crystal hair clip comes in the shape of Adidas’ trefoil logo. Timberland x Telfar Back by popular demand, Telfar – the New York-based label known for its bestselling “shopping bags” – has teamed up once again with Timberland. Made of pebbled nubuck leather, the Timberland x Telfar Tall Pull-On Boot is an extra-long take on the American shoemaker’s signature waterproof boot. Soft and unstructured, the boot can be worn with a pair of jeans tucked in or with a mini skirt for a night out on the town. Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Editorial | China’s economic recovery calls for a bigger role for private firms
description: What households need most is a stable property market and rising income and employment. For that, the private sector is crucial.
content: In two months, Beijing’s reading of the economy has changed markedly. In July, the State Council brushed aside calls for stimulus, preferring to make “full and effective use of existing policies”. On Monday, a cabinet meeting chaired by Premier Li Qiang acknowledged emerging problems and pledged to “intensify countercyclical adjustment of macro policies”. The shift is welcome. But how the stimulus is delivered, and by whom, matters as much as its size. The case for urgency is plain. Growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, the weakest pace in almost four years, leaving Beijing staring at the floor of its 4.5 to 5 per cent target. Retail sales rose a mere 0.4 per cent in August. Property investment fell 19.9 per cent in the first eight months, eroding the principal store of middle-class wealth and, with it, the confidence to spend. Exports remain the bright spot, surging 25 per cent in August. Yet that strength is itself part of the reason Beijing is changing gears. The European Union’s goods deficit with China reached about €360 billion (US$405 billion) last year, and Brussels has set an October deadline for “tangible” results, with new trade defence instruments held in reserve. Other trading partners are raising barriers of their own. Building domestic demand is therefore not merely a cyclical fix but a buffer against a trade war that may come regardless of Beijing’s wishes. Here the politics becomes tricky. The Central Committee’s fifth plenum meets from October 26 to October 29, and the national party congress follows next autumn. Sustaining growth matters, but strengthening party discipline remains the overriding priority. Discipline in this sense extends beyond corruption to irresponsible and wasteful spending and investment. That concern is legitimate, but it carries consequences too. Local investment was long a principal engine of domestic demand, and officials who have grown cautious and risk-averse are in no hurry to revive it. Many localities remain focused on paring debt and lack both the capital and the political will to spend. Monday’s meeting was partly an effort to loosen the leash, with faster bond issuance and the tapping of unused local debt quotas. A fundamental shift in local behaviour is unlikely in the short run. Stimulus, which in recent years has become shorthand for government investment, will therefore rest largely on the central government. Beijing is expediting its “six networks” infrastructure programme – water networks, power grids, computing, next-generation communications, urban underground pipelines and logistics – to be funded mainly from the centre. But with so many railways, ports and airports already built, its short-term effect on household demand is uncertain. What households need most is a stable property market and rising income and employment, which notably featured in Monday’s statement but not in July’s. For that, the private sector is crucial. Private firms account for more than 80 per cent of urban jobs, and they are less bound by a political calendar that now appears to rank discipline above growth. Beijing should give them more room: further regulatory relaxation, fair access to credit and markets, prompt settlement of arrears owed by local governments, and firm legal protection for property and entrepreneurs. Meanwhile, the familiar call for China to build a social safety net is dated. Coverage has expanded at unprecedented speed: basic medical insurance reaches about 95 per cent of the population, and pension enrolment exceeds a billion people. The challenge is no longer breadth but sustainability as the population ages; 23 per cent of residents were aged 60 or above at the end of last year. Funding that promise will ultimately require thorough tax reform, a complicated and politically sensitive undertaking. There are signs that work is under way, but information is scarce. It is among the least understood aspects of China’s economy, and greater transparency would reassure markets and households alike. Beijing showed in September 2024 that it can act decisively when the moment demands. It should now ensure that discipline is met by initiative, and that the private sector is treated as a full partner in recovery.

title: How high is your risk of heart disease? A lipoprotein(a) blood test can help you find out
description: This test can reveal a lot about your risk of developing circulatory conditions. Experts advise what to do if your LP(a) level is high.
content: Ever heard of lipoprotein(a)? Don’t worry if you have not. That is the name of a cardiovascular risk factor that many people are genuinely unaware of. Two experts explain why it makes sense to have this value measured with a blood test at least once, and what to do if the result turns out to be too high. What exactly is lipoprotein(a)? Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a component of the blood. “It is structured like ‘bad’ LDL cholesterol,” says Anja Vogt, a specialist in internal medicine and deputy chair of a lipid disorders association in Germany. The difference is that an additional protein, apolipoprotein(a), is bound to it. According to the association, lipoproteins can be compared to “freight taxis” that transport fat and fatlike substances through the blood. How much Lp(a) circulates in the blood is genetically determined. Diet and exercise cannot influence the level. “Lp(a) probably once had a physiological role and may even have conferred an evolutionary advantage, but today it has no known benefit,” Vogt says. On the contrary: a high Lp(a) level is not good news, as it is a risk factor for various diseases. Why is Lp(a) considered a risk factor for heart attack and stroke? “If too much of it circulates in the blood, it is deposited in the arterial walls in the same way as LDL cholesterol. If additional risk factors are present, such as smoking, this effect is amplified,” Vogt says. The consequence of these deposits in the blood vessels is an increased risk of stroke, heart attack and also of peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD) – that is, circulatory disorders in the legs. “Ultimately, any artery can be affected – for example in the kidney or the aortic valve,” Vogt says. Lp(a) also promotes inflammation. “At higher levels, blood clots form more quickly and dissolve more slowly,” says Germany-based internal medicine specialist Norbert Smetak. The course of the disease varies considerably. Some people with elevated Lp(a) levels suffer cardiovascular disease at a comparatively young age. Others remain free of symptoms for a long time. From what Lp(a) level does it become critical? First, it is important to know that there are two different measurement methods that cannot be directly compared or converted into each other. Smetak gives an overview: The so-called normal value is below 30 milligrams per decilitre (mg/dl) or 75 nanomoles per litre (nmol/l). At 30-50 mg/dl or 75-105 nmol/l, the risk is moderate; above that, a person already falls into the at-risk group. Doctors speak of a very high risk from 180 mg/dl or 430 nmol/l upwards. “The higher the value, the higher the risk,” Smetak says. Other blood values and general health also play a role, however. “Especially in combination with a high LDL cholesterol level or high blood pressure, the likelihood of, for example, a heart attack increases,” Smetak says. A good risk assessment therefore requires looking at the whole picture, not just the Lp(a) level. How common are elevated Lp(a) levels? Do they change? “Around 20 to 30 per cent of all people have Lp(a) levels that are too high – so this problem is by no means rare,” Smetak says. Your level does not need to be measured at regular intervals and one test is generally sufficient. “Since the size of the lipoprotein particle is largely genetically determined, it normally only needs to be measured once in a lifetime. That is also what the guidelines recommend,” Vogt says. In Hong Kong, a stand-alone Lp(a) test could cost from HK$800 to HK$1,050 (US$100-US$134); a cardiometabolic risk panel including Lp(a) could cost from HK$1,040 to HK$1,880. My Lp(a) level is too high. What now? When Lp(a) levels are found to be high, your doctor is likely to tell you it is time for some lifestyle changes. Put more clearly: “A healthy diet, giving up tobacco and alcohol, [getting] plenty of exercise and strength training, and a healthy body weight enormously reduce the relevance of the value,” Vogt says. At present there are few options for significantly lowering Lp(a) levels, apart from lipoprotein apheresis – a kind of “blood washing” procedure that is used only in extreme cases because it is intensive, invasive and logistically demanding. If LDL cholesterol levels are also elevated, statins are used to lower them – and with it the overall risk of cardiovascular disease. There is also hope for new drug-based treatments, Smetak says. “Drugs that can specifically lower Lp(a) are in the final phase of clinical trials.” Until then, the clear priority is to minimise other risk factors such as smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes and lack of exercise as far as possible, and to ask a doctor regularly whether new treatment options have become available. Those with severely elevated levels or existing vascular deposits should be particularly vigilant – and take the opportunity to work on their own health.

title: Top 10: If you could bring one sport from the Asian Games to your school, which would it be?
description: Students propose introducing diverse sports to schools, highlighting benefits like teamwork, discipline and cultural enrichment.
content:
Our next question: If you taught a kindergarten class for a day, what creative steps would you take to help pupils with special educational needs feel valued? (This question has been sponsored by the Yew Chung College of Early Childhood Education.)
To take part, drop us a line via this form by 12pm on Tuesday, October 6 . Issac Cheung Chi-ping, 16, Fung Kai No 1 Secondary School: If I could introduce one sport from the Asian Games to my school, it would be sepak takraw. This sport is similar to volleyball, but players use their feet and heads to kick the ball over the net. It requires excellent flexibility and teamwork.
Wong Tsz-kiu, 15, Stewards MKMCF Ma Ko Pan Memorial College: I want to introduce esports to my school. Gaming has become increasingly popular, with games like PUBG and Brawl Stars even holding global competitions. Participating in esports can help students develop their communication skills and foster teamwork.
Tse Yuen-ting, 15, TWGHs Li Ka Shing College: If I could introduce one Asian Games sport to my school, I would choose track cycling because it is fast and thrilling. Riders race on an oval track using specialised bikes and pedal continuously. This sport builds our strength and teaches us courage.
Emma Lo Tsz-wai, 15, Chinese YMCA Secondary School: I want to introduce rugby to my school because we currently do not have a school rugby team. I am passionate about rugby, and I believe it would be a great experience for everyone to try it out and have fun.
Lauren Lee, 10, French International School: I would choose the Chinese martial art of wushu because it offers a unique blend of cultural and athletic elements that are distinct from the more common sports, like football, found in other countries. Wushu has been a competitive sport since the 1900s, making it an intriguing topic for both sports enthusiasts and historians alike.
Cheung Tsz-lam, 16, Fung Kai No 1 Secondary School: If I could bring one Asian Games sport to my school, I would choose shooting. It builds concentration, consistency and discipline, which help students develop resilience. For example, recovering from a missed shot teaches them to stay calm after a failed test and try again without frustration; blocking out noise and pressure during practice improves their ability to focus in noisy classrooms or during exams. I believe it trains students to manage time better and keep working steadily towards long-term goals, even when progress feels slow. Jonah Cheung Chun-ming, 14, Pui Kiu College: Archery is a sport that enhances focus, patience and accuracy, making it accessible to everyone, regardless of size or speed. It is truly an excellent choice for becoming a popular sport among students. After all, who wouldn’t want to carry a majestic bow at school? Chan Yik-ka, 13, St Mary’s Canossian College: Dragon boat racing would be an incredible addition to our school because it brings people together and fosters teamwork among students. It’s fast, loud, thrilling and intense, transforming a regular class into a cohesive crew where physical endurance meets pure collaboration on the water.
Lisa Lei Yuxin, 15, TWGHs Li Ka Shing College: Incorporating esports into school curricula can help students develop teamwork and leadership skills through engaging competitive gaming. Unlike traditional sports, esports do not require top fitness or involve intense physical activity, making it a less tiring option for students.
Caden Wong Chun-nok, 14, Stewards MKMCF Ma Ko Pan Memorial College: I would bring Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) to schools because it teaches valuable skills such as self-defence, discipline and excellent physical conditioning. By implementing modified, youth-safe rules that emphasise grappling and fitness over head strikes, MMA can help build students’ confidence and respect for themselves and others. Additionally, it offers an engaging and contemporary way for students to stay active.

title: Trump expected to name Jay Clayton as AI tsar
description: Clayton already oversees 18 US intelligence agencies as the nation’s top spy and is expected to keep that role.
content: US ⁠President Donald Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to be his top adviser on AI, a position the president has called “AI tsar” in ‌the past, according to a source familiar with the decision. Clayton already oversees 18 US intelligence agencies as the nation’s top spy and is expected to keep that role. “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the president,” a White ⁠House official said in a statement when asked about Clayton ‌being selected for the position. “Any reporting until then is baseless speculation.” Trump’s decision to name a new AI ‌tsar comes after AI researchers warned that people building the ⁠technology ⁠believe it could kill humans within a decade. Trump last month said he planned to ‌name a new “AI tsar” and create an “AI force”, though he gave no details about ‌either initiative ‌or how they would be implemented. This is the second time ‌Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the ⁠administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI tsar role at ⁠the beginning of Trump’s second term, before leaving the White House. Sacks still advises Trump on AI and attended a ‌meeting on Tuesday ‌with the president and industry executives. The news of an AI tsar was first reported by CBS.

title: US blast simulation targets China’s alleged secret nuclear testing
description: US Energy Department conducts underground explosive test in Nevada designed to detect low-yield nuclear explosions from China.
content: The US has conducted a non-nuclear underground experiment to enhance its ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions that it explicitly linked with a test that Washington suspects China carried out in 2020 – an accusation Beijing denies. The US Department of Energy announced on Wednesday that the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) conducted a “subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive” experiment at the Nevada National Security Site, which it said aimed to “increase the United States’ ability to detect low-yield nuclear explosions”. The experiment, which did not involve any nuclear explosions, collected data to validate scientific models and refine algorithms critical to US nuclear explosion detection capabilities. The Nevada test highlights the constraints of verifying suspected low-yield nuclear tests. Despite Washington’s allegation that Beijing has covertly conducted a nuclear test at the Lop Nur testing site in June 2020, Beijing denied the accusation, and the international nuclear-test monitoring body has said the available seismic data cannot establish the cause of the events with confidence. The US Energy Department’s press release said that the experiment would enhance understanding of the signature produced by underground detonation and strengthen the “unmatched” capability to detect any foreign nuclear testing. The department said that the experiment was especially focused on further enhancing the US capabilities to detect a “decoupled” explosion – a nuclear test where the warhead is detonated inside a large underground cavity instead of being in close contact with the surrounding rock, lowering the seismic signal that the nuclear detection sensors can detect. The Trump administration accused China of covertly carrying out a low-yield nuclear test in June 2020 at the Lop Nur nuclear test site in northwest China, alleging that China had breached the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). US President Donald Trump has also ordered the resumption of US nuclear testing for the first time since 1992 on what he said was an “equal basis” in October 2025. Beijing denies carrying out any covert nuclear testing Beijing denied the accusation and contended that it continues to abide by the terms of the CTBT. China’s last officially acknowledged nuclear test is known to have taken place at the Lop Nur site in July 1996, only two months before it signed the CTBT. Both the US and China signed the CTBT in 1996, but neither country has ratified the treaty, so it has not yet entered into force. The South China Morning Post has asked the Chinese embassy in Washington for comment. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said that the NNSA experiment can “certainly enhance” US capabilities to detect “illicit” nuclear explosions that violate the CTBT, but detecting and actually deterring nuclear tests requires international cooperation. He said that while the current Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation’s (CTBTO) International Monitoring System provides powerful nuclear test monitoring capabilities, very low-yield nuclear explosions may still escape detection. “Indeed, the US has accused China of conducting a low-yield nuclear test in June 2020, but the available data from the CTBTO’s monitoring system and other civilian seismic networks about the seismic event on that date are inconclusive,” said Kimball. “This is why it is so important for nuclear-armed states to engage in technical discussions to develop voluntary confidence-building measures to ensure ongoing and future activities at their former test sites are fully compliant with their obligations under the CTBT.” The CTBTO has stated that its International Monitoring System did not detect any event consistent with a nuclear test explosion on June 22, 2020 – the date that Washington suspects China of conducting the test – though it also said that there were “two very small seismic events” spaced 12 seconds apart on that day. Washington has ‘genuine concerns’ Russia, China conducted nuclear tests Tong Zhao, senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that Washington has “genuine concerns” that Russia and China have conducted nuclear tests in violation of their commitments as signatories of the CTBT. He said that the International Monitoring System established under the CTBT “may not reliably detect and distinguish very small nuclear tests”, where the NNSA experiment aims to enhance Washington’s own ability to “detect covert foreign nuclear tests”. “Such a capability could strengthen deterrence by increasing concern among rival countries that prohibited nuclear testing could be detected despite efforts to hide it. It could also enable Washington to develop a better understanding of foreign nuclear-warhead modernisation programmes,” said Zhao. “If China were indeed seeking to advance its nuclear-warhead designs through nuclear testing inconsistent with its CTBT commitment, improvements in US detection capabilities could complicate such efforts.” China has recently accelerated its nuclear stockpile. The Pentagon’s China military power report published in December last year estimated that the People’s Liberation Army remains on track to have over 1,000 warheads by 2030. According to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), China is estimated to have a nuclear stockpile of up to 620 warheads as of January 2026 and is expected to “keep growing over the coming decade”. Robert Kelley, a former official at the US Energy Department and the director of nuclear inspections at the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), said that the focus of the experiment seems to be to detect very small nuclear tests that could be used to collect data about “how a larger bomb may work” or to examine a new technology aimed at disruption of electronic systems. He said the experiment would help the US understand Chinese testing, and that the tests are part of a longer effort to detect “smaller and smaller underground tests since at least 1963”. “China might be doing very advanced nuclear experiments, even what are called ‘subcritical tests’ to polish very high-end complex physics knowledge,” said Kelley, who now serves as the Distinguished Associate Fellow at SIPRI. John Erath, senior policy director at the Centre for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, said that the test was part of “long-standing efforts” by the US to identify any nuclear explosion. “Such efforts are designed to detect nuclear tests, including those that would be contrary to the CTBT,” said Erath. “The Nevada experiment is specifically designed to improve detection of decoupled nuclear explosions, such as allegedly occurred at Lop Nur in 2020. This would likely be a reason for linking the current [US Energy Department] experiment to activity at Lop Nur.”

title: Exclusive | ‘No retreat’: key Trump ally urges continued US-China engagement on rare earths
description: Both sides need to keep working on their differences over critical minerals and other issues, Steve Daines tells the SCMP.
content: US Republican Senator Steve Daines, a close aide to President Donald Trump and a key interlocutor between Washington and Beijing, has called on the two capitals to stay engaged and “not retreat” over differences on issues including rare earth supply chains. Daines told the South China Morning Post that both sides still had issues that predated Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last week and that they would continue working on them after the summit. “So that’s again why it’s really important to keep the dialogue going on between two countries because both sides admit we’ve got some serious differences. But the answer is not to retreat. The answer is to stay engaged,” he said. The outgoing senator from Montana was responding to remarks by US ambassador to China David Perdue, who accused Beijing of “weaponising” its “single-source dominant position” on critical minerals against the rest of the world. The comments from Daines and Perdue underscore that rare earths remain a major source of contention between the two countries and will be a key agenda item for the leaders’ next meetings. Xi and Trump have agreed to meet again next month at the Apec gathering in Shenzhen, in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, followed by another meeting in December at the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida. A White House fact sheet on last week’s summit said both sides would continue to work on US concerns, including supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals, with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels. The Chinese statement on the visit was silent on the issue. Daines played a key backchannel role in the run-up to Xi’s visit, shuttling between Beijing and Washington and helping to narrow differences on key issues. He was the only US senator invited to the White House state dinner for the Chinese leader, which included some of America’s most prominent tycoons among the more than 130 guests. On Wednesday, Daines also attended Chinese National Day celebrations at the Chinese embassy in Washington, where he was pictured sitting next to Beijing’s envoy, Xie Feng. In the run-up to the summit, Washington repeatedly pressed Beijing to accelerate approvals for rare earth exports, citing concerns over insufficient supplies reaching the US. During Xi’s visit, rare earths access remained a top concern for Washington, with the two sides announcing a two-month extension of last year’s trade agreement reached in South Korea that included China’s commitment to increase critical metals supplies to the US. The October 2025 truce agreed in Busan helped to avert a broader crisis after Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April. China controls much of the world’s rare earth processing, with a chokehold over heavy rare earths used in high-performance magnets for defence systems, robotics and electric vehicles. China’s shipments of rare earth magnets to the US fell 13 per cent year on year to 512 tonnes in August. Under the Busan deal, the US cut tariffs on some Chinese goods, while additional US restrictions and certain Chinese controls on rare earth exports were paused. China also committed to buy US soybeans and curb shipments of fentanyl precursors. Asked about the uncertainty surrounding the issue of US arms sales to Taiwan, Daines said Trump was “probably one person that has that answer”, telling the SCMP that “it’s going to be an ongoing topic. It’s not going away.” The SCMP has reported that the US is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November and could extend the delay through to the end of the year. The White House paused a US$14 billion arms package of advanced air and missile defence systems – including PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System – for Taiwan shortly before Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, despite congressional approval. An earlier US$11 billion arms sale announced by Washington in December prompted a strong response from Beijing. In their meeting on September 24, Xi urged Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Daines also weighed in on the US ambassador’s remarks in an interview with Fox News, in which Perdue revealed that Trump had proposed selling weapons to China during his meeting with Xi. “I always said about President Trump, don’t always take him literally but do take him seriously,” Daines said, adding that “he’ll throw ideas out there to kind of mix it up. I wouldn’t necessarily take that literally.” Trump on Monday denied discussing US arms sales with Xi, though he noted that China would “probably like to buy” them. “I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am going to have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss.” As the next Xi-Trump meeting at the Apec summit in November approaches, Daines said that he remained in “close contact with a lot of folks who will be there”. “At this point, I don’t have another trip planned to China, but that could always change.”

title: US man arrested over alleged US$300 million scheme to smuggle Nvidia AI servers to China
description: Prosecutors say California tech firm owner routed restricted AI servers through Malaysia and Singapore to evade US export controls.
content: Amid intensifying competition in the AI technology race, US authorities have arrested a California technology company owner accused of using Malaysia and Singapore as transit points to circumvent US export controls and send more than US$300 million worth of restricted computer servers to China. Greg Lui, 38, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, of San Gabriel, was arrested on Thursday and charged with conspiracy to violate US export controls, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to the US Justice Department. John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said the indictment details alleged efforts to evade US export laws through false documents and complicated transshipment schemes designed to conceal China as the true destination for restricted artificial intelligence technology. “These chips are the product of American ingenuity,” Eisenberg said. “The National Security Division will continue to enforce our export-control laws to protect that advantage.” The Chinese purchaser is described in the indictment as an industrial company based in Hangzhou. The city is a major Chinese tech hub. The servers at the centre of the case contained US-manufactured Nvidia GPUs, including A100 and H100 chips, used in what the Justice Department calls “super intelligence” applications, technology that prosecutors said could contribute to the military capabilities of other countries. Lui, who owns City of Industry-based Earthmade Computer, allegedly bought hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of high-end servers from US manufacturers and arranged for them to be shipped to third countries before being re-exported to China without the required licences. Prosecutors said he and his co-conspirators used false documents to misrepresent the intended users and destinations, routing shipments through Malaysia and Singapore before they reached China. In one example, Lui allegedly ordered 27 Nvidia H100 servers worth about US$7.6 million in January 2024. The servers were shipped from Los Angeles County to Kuala Lumpur, and a Malaysian co-conspirator later told a government official that they had been transshipped to a Chinese buyer. In another shipment, 92 export-controlled servers were flown from San Francisco International Airport to Kuala Lumpur in June 2024, before being sent on to Hong Kong. Earthmade received more than US$176 million from two Malaysia-based transshipment companies between January and October 2024, prosecutors said. The indictment alleges that Lui helped broker almost US$300 million worth of export-controlled Nvidia server sales through the Malaysian companies. Nvidia confirmed the company was in cooperation with law enforcement. “This case shows yet again that smuggling is a losing proposition — legally, economically and technically,” an Nvidia spokesperson said. “We will continue to engage with law enforcement.” The arrest highlights a challenge for Washington as it tightens restrictions on advanced AI chips while Chinese companies access US-made computing power through infrastructure in third countries. Separate concerns have also emerged in Washington over Chinese AI companies obtaining remote access to restricted Nvidia chips installed in data centres in Southeast Asia. US export controls generally regulate the physical transfer of chips, potentially leaving a gap when the hardware remains overseas but Chinese companies can remotely access its computing power. US lawmakers are pursuing legislation that would require tracking technology for advanced chips and expand oversight of their exports as they seek to curb smuggling and the diversion of AI servers to China. The New York Post first reported that federal agents tracked Lui as he drove a Tesla Cybertruck from his San Gabriel home to Earthmade’s offices in a nearby industrial park, where agents arrested him at gunpoint shortly after he arrived. Lui did not speak as he was placed in a vehicle for processing, according to the outlet, which published exclusive video of the arrest. The outlet also reported that Lui’s “luxurious lifestyle” as he lived in a 4,300-square-foot, nine-bedroom mansion in San Gabriel. Federal agents searched the property after his arrest. Before entering the technology business, Lui was in the restaurant business. If convicted on all charges, Lui faces a statutory maximum penalty of 20 years in prison for conspiracy, 20 years for money laundering, and 10 years for outbound smuggling.

title: Being Chinese | I’m 80. It’s not too late to reconnect with my Chinese roots
description: I received a colonial education and went on to raise global citizens. Then came the reckoning that only age and a changing world could bring.
content: Every morning, I settle into my armchair in Kuala Lumpur, pen in hand, to tackle The Times cryptic crossword, freshly downloaded from the internet. It is a ritual I have observed since my university days in the United Kingdom. I have become rather adept at it; in fact, puzzle devotees might recognise Sayang, the pseudonym under which I set crosswords for the Financial Times. I can still recite the names of England’s 1966 World Cup squad in my sleep. My youth was scored to the sounds of Cliff Richard, The Beatles, The Hollies and The Rolling Stones. By almost any measure, I am an unrepentant Anglophile. Yet, at 80, I find myself watching my grandchildren and being overtaken by a profound swell of emotion. Suddenly, and with startling clarity, I feel incredibly proud to be Chinese. The road to this realisation has been long, winding and strewn with the cultural detritus of empire. My story begins in 1946, in Kluang, a small town in Johor in what was then Malaya. My father, an orphan from a village in Nanan, Fujian, had fled economic hardship in search of a new life across the South China Sea. When I was born, Malaya was still scarred by the Japanese occupation and the British colonial administration had only recently resumed its suzerainty. While my father dutifully sent most of my siblings to Chinese vernacular schools, fate or perhaps sheer happenstance steered me, the sixth child, to a kindergarten run by Roman Catholic nuns, where English was the sole medium of instruction. Thirteen years in government English schools followed before I found myself in Mother England, reading economics at the University of Newcastle upon Tyne. Along the way, I became a voracious reader, volunteering as a school librarian just to be closer to the world of Enid Blyton, P.G. Wodehouse, Thomas Hardy and Shakespeare. I could trace the Battle of Hastings and the lineage of British monarchs with ease. Of Chinese literature, I knew almost nothing – save for Dream of the Red Chamber and Journey to the West, and even then only in outline. Of Chinese sportsmen and women, I knew even less. I eventually married a wonderful woman, also wholly educated in English. While our own parents had spoken to us in Chinese dialects, our three children grew up speaking only the language of Shakespeare. They became “bananas” – yellow on the outside, white on the inside. Two went to Oxford; the third to the University of Western Australia. I had succeeded in raising global citizens, but the thread connecting us to our ancestral homeland had worn perilously thin. Then came the reckoning that only age and a changing world could bring. In recent years, the history books I once revered began to read very differently. The opium wars ceased to be mere footnotes; they became vivid, visceral acts of humiliation inflicted upon a people I realised, with a jolt, I belonged to. When I read the Western media, I began to notice a persistent, and often unfair, hostility towards China’s rise. Where I once nodded in passive agreement, I now felt a growing urge to defend China. The true turning point, however, was physical. I made trips to China, including two emotional pilgrimages back to my father’s birthplace in Fujian. Standing on the very soil he had left as a penniless teenager and witnessing the breathtaking transformation of the country, a profound pride swelled within me – a pride of kinship. At a beer festival in Qingdao, Shandong, where the Germans built a brewery in 1903, I learned that China had contributed to the first world war effort and requested the return of Shandong from a defeated Germany. I was stunned to discover that Western powers ignored China’s contribution and instead awarded administration of Shandong to Japan. Such a profound indignity inflicted on the ancestral homeland has never left me. It was around this time that I began, belatedly, to acquaint myself with Chinese athletes. I now know the names Quan Hongchan and Pan Zhanle, alongside Yao Ming and Li Na. It is a small education, but telling: proof that the gap in my knowledge was never about absence of achievement, only absence of attention. For years, I had felt a quiet inadequacy among my peers in Malaysia and Singapore. We shared the same colonial education, but many of us carried a silent grief for the rich heritage we had left behind. At my age, I assumed it was simply too late to change. But history has a beautiful way of righting itself. My second son married a remarkable woman who had received a traditional Chinese education before studying in Australia. She understands the importance of passing on our cultural heritage. Her two children are enrolled at Kuen Cheng, a reputable Chinese school in Kuala Lumpur. For years, I had felt a quiet inadequacy among my peers in Malaysia and Singapore. We shared the same colonial education, but many of us carried a silent grief for the rich heritage we had left behind My greatest joy now is sitting with my grandchildren, trading the complex cryptic clues of a Financial Times crossword for the tonal rhythms of Mandarin. I am learning from them, just as they are learning from me. I will still cheer for Malaysian athletes on international courts, and my Spotify library still holds 7,000 Western pop songs against a mere 10 Chinese tracks (mostly Teresa Teng and Frances Yip). But as I watch my grandchildren speak the language of my father, I know the circle is complete. I am an Anglophile by education, a Malaysian by loyalty, but in my heart and soul, I will forever be Chinese. China is the land of my father and today, I silently and proudly cheer it on.

title: Brazil’s Lula hails ‘bold’ Chinese investors as rival pitches rare earths to Trump
description: Brazilian president names China a possible partner in his critical minerals plans, as Flavio Bolsonaro courts Trump, with election looming.
content: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva named China as a possible partner in his critical minerals plans, three days before Sunday’s closely fought election. Lula told Flow, one of the country’s most-watched podcasts, on Thursday evening that Brazil should stop shipping out raw ore. “We want to transform them here in Brazil,” he said of the minerals. Asked whether China fit into his plans, Lula said it could be a partner “bringing technology to us”, as could the United States. “[Donald] Trump has to know that he takes care of the United States. I take care of Brazil,” he said. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves after China, and both Washington and Beijing are seeking supplies outside Chinese control. His main rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, has courted the Trump administration and pitched Brazil as “the only real alternative to China for the free world” in rare earths. The senator met Trump at the White House in May and promised a “long-term strategic partnership” on rare earths, with “shared re-industrialisation” between the two countries. Lula gave the podcast interview instead of attending TV Globo’s final televised debate, which the network cancelled less than an hour before airtime after a series of court rulings. One granted a request from Lula’s coalition to bar Globo from showing an empty lectern bearing his name. Bolsonaro then withdrew, citing “censorship”. A poll by Datafolha released on Thursday gave Lula 45 per cent of valid votes against 40 per cent for Bolsonaro, pointing to a run-off later in October. Companies from both countries are already mining in Goias state, where Chinese miner CMOC bought Anglo American’s niobium operations in 2016 and became the world’s second-largest niobium producer. In April, American company USA Rare Earth agreed to buy Serra Verde, which mines rare earths in the same state, for about US$2.8 billion. In September, Lula signed a law creating a council attached to the presidency to steer the sector. It will review foreign stakes in strategic projects and grant tax credits for processing until 2034. Asked about Chinese carmaker BYD, which builds electric vehicles in Bahia state, Lula placed Chinese capital alongside Western investment. “We have a lot of Chinese investment in Brazil. We have a lot of German investment; we have a lot of American investment,” he said. “What happens is that the Chinese are bold,” he added. In his account, Europe turned to former communist states after the fall of the Berlin Wall, while the US, which “always has an enemy”, stayed focused on war. “So the Chinese took the opportunity and came to invest in Latin America and Africa. And we are taking advantage of that,” he said. Lula’s ambitions went beyond minerals to goods that China now dominates. He asked whether Brazil would go on “depending on the Chinese to make electric batteries” and said it would start making them, along with chips and phones. Niobium leverage in talks with Washington Lula also invoked minerals in the trade dispute with the US, which imposed a 25 per cent tariff on a range of Brazilian goods in July. He said he had not yet used a reciprocity law allowing retaliation and pointed to US reliance on Brazilian niobium, a metal used in steel alloys and aerospace. “Sixty per cent of his niobium is from here in Brazil,” he said of Trump. Washington’s final tariff order, however, exempted niobium ores and ferroniobium, the alloy in which most niobium is traded along with rare earths. Rather than “crying about Trump”, Lula said, Brazil had gone looking for other buyers. Official data show exports to the US fell 9.7 per cent in the first eight months, while shipments to China rose 15 per cent. Lula also said he had spent an hour and a half on the phone with each of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Trump. He said he told them the permanent members of the UN Security Council were “not doing a damn thing to end wars”. Brazilian and Kremlin readouts date the calls to July and August. Brasilia said critical minerals came up in the call with Xi, alongside a China-Mercosur trade deal.

title: Panama auditor targets ex-port regulators, CK Hutchison’s subsidiary in canal probe
description: Anel Flores says additional material concerns ex-maritime authority board members, executives of Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison’s subsidiary.
content: Panama’s comptroller general said on Friday that his office would send prosecutors more audit material on former executives of CK Hutchison’s local subsidiary next week, as part of a criminal investigation into the Hong Kong conglomerate’s annulled Panama Canal ports concession. Speaking at the Atlantic Council in Washington, Anel Flores said prosecutors had requested documents concerning Panama Ports Company (PPC), the operator of the Balboa and Cristobal terminals at either end of the canal until February.
