In addition to some PPC executives, the material covers former board members of the Panama Maritime Authority, the regulator that oversaw the concession. Flores urged prosecutors to hold them accountable for changes to the concession terms that he said had disadvantaged the country, though he did not name anyone or announce charges. The request had become a point of friction between the two offices. In August, Flores told local broadcaster TVN that prosecutors had shown no movement on possible corruption at PPC for more than a year, prompting the Public Ministry to reply that its file already ran to more than 360 volumes and that it was still waiting for an expanded audit from his office. Prosecutors opened the inquiry in April last year, shortly after Flores presented an audit alleging that Panama had received US$483 million from the concession, against about US$1.34 billion owed under the original contract. He also accused PPC of using outsourced “satellite” companies from 2015 to drain profits from the operator, in which the state held 10 per cent; allegations the company denied. On Friday, Flores went further, arguing that strategic infrastructure such as ports should be state-owned and run by private firms under profit-sharing arrangements. “I think that most of these … highly important resources, like the ports, port system should be owned by the government,” he said, describing the idea as his opinion rather than the government’s position. The proposal runs against the course set by Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino, whose government plans to tender Balboa and Cristobal separately for private concessions of 25 to 30 years and expects to award them before mid-2027. Until then, the terminals remain with Maersk’s APM Terminals and MSC’s Terminal Investment Limited, which took over in February under interim contracts of up to 18 months. Court ruling and arbitration claims Flores launched the audit in January last year, as US President Donald Trump accused China of controlling the canal, and later used its findings to file two lawsuits with the Supreme Court. He has said the review was unrelated to US pressure. In January, the court declared unconstitutional the 1997 law approving the concession along with its 2021 extension. PPC answered with an International Chamber of Commerce arbitration claim that now exceeds US$2 billion. CK Hutchison opened a separate investment treaty case against Panama in August, seeking more than US$1.5 billion. Beijing also reacted to the ruling, which China’s Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office called “absurd”. The US Federal Maritime Commission said China detained nearly 70 Panama-flagged ships in March and linked the surge to the port dispute. Beijing denied retaliating, and the detentions fell after the two governments agreed in July to renew a bilateral maritime transport agreement, according to the Panama Maritime Chamber.

title: Taiwan coastguard uses water cannons to warn off mainland Chinese fishing vessel
description: Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration reveals incident occurred 27 nautical miles east of Dongsha Island in the South China Sea on Friday.
content: Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration (CGA) used water cannons to expel a mainland Chinese fishing vessel near Dongsha Island, authorities said on Friday. The incident occurred on October 1, 27 nautical miles east of the Taiwanese-controlled Dongsha Island, also called Pratas Island, in the South China Sea, the agency revealed. The CGA’s patrol vessel Yunlin directed its water cannon towards the fishing boat Jin Sha’s wheelhouse for about 90 seconds after initially spraying water into the air for about 30 seconds as a warning, the Administration said in a statement. The incident coincided with China’s National Day on Thursday. Moreover, the CGA detained two mainland fishing vessels on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, near the Penghu Islands in the Taiwan Strait, and arrested 14 crew members. On Tuesday, two China Coast Guard vessels reportedly patrolled waters east of Taiwan, as the CCG continues to conduct what it describes as regular patrols in the area amid rising tensions. The Jin Sha, along with another mainland Chinese fishing vessel, the Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066, was spotted anchored about eight nautical miles inside Taiwan’s designated “restricted waters” for mainland vessels, the statement said. The Jin Sha refused to leave despite three radio warnings, while the other boat departed before the Yunlin used its water cannon to drive the Jin Sha away. The CGA said the water stream was directed to avoid crew members on deck and the spraying stopped immediately after the Jin Sha started to exit the area. No official injury report was filed. However, the fishing boat suffered an engine failure and lost power following the intervention. The CGA said the Yunlin provided 35 meals at the fishermen’s request before the disabled vessel was towed outside Taiwan’s restricted waters later on Thursday. The Jin Sha was subsequently handed over to Chinese work vessel Haiyang Shiyou 681 Friday morning for return transport, it added. Taipei controls the Dongsha Islands in the northeastern South China Sea, but Beijing also claims them. In a report on September 23, the CGA said it had detained nine mainland Chinese small boats in eight cases in Dongsha waters in 2026. It also reported a series of encounters with Chinese coastguard vessels near Dongsha, including 12 instances in which Chinese coastguard ships were driven out of the “restricted waters” between January and early September 2026. Under its regulations regarding relations with mainland China, Taipei designates two types of controlled waters. The “prohibited waters” extend 12 nautical miles from the sea baseline and beyond that, the “restricted waters” extend to 24 nautical miles. Mainland vessels entering these zones without permission may face enforcement measures by Taiwanese authorities. Beijing does not recognise such restrictions. It sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: King Charles to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of colonial rule on Caribbean tour
description: The UK monarch will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana alone, followed by a trip to Antigua and Barbuda with Queen Camilla.
content: King Charles will acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery while touring Caribbean countries on a visit beginning this month, a Buckingham Palace spokesman said on Friday. The king will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana alone, followed by a trip to Antigua and Barbuda with Queen Camilla, where Charles will give a speech at a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government, the palace said. Charles, 77, who is still receiving treatment for cancer, will visit former colonies that are now independent from Britain and are members of the British Commonwealth. He remains head of state in the archipelago nations of the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, a role that is largely ceremonial. The palace spokesman told reporters the king’s visit, from October 27 to November 4, would not “shy away from the ‘darkest days of our past’ as His Majesty has described them”. Charles used the phrase in a speech in Barbados when he attended the ceremony in which it became a republic in 2021, removing his mother, Queen Elizabeth, as head of state. He also said then that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” stains Britain’s history. The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge “the wrongs of the past” and “right inequalities that endure”, and on this trip would “renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process”. The UK government reiterated last month its rejection of calls for the payment of slavery reparations after a Jamaican delegation filed a petition addressed to Charles on the issue. It called on the monarch to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London. Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade that enriched their ancestors, but like the UK government have not issued an official apology for the slave trade. The palace said discussions about the colonial legacy and the slave trade were “important” but “primarily matters for governments to address”. On a 2022 Caribbean tour, Charles’ son William and his wife Kate were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for slavery reparations. Charles’ younger brother, Prince Edward, later that year cancelled a visit to Grenada after pro-republican protests there. In Antigua and Barbuda, a state named after its two main tropical islands, the royals will attend a parade to mark 45 years of independence. Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, is a republic and so Charles will be making a state visit on the 60th anniversary of its independence from Britain. The trip will feature plenty of meetings with local people and will focus on “the vibrant present and promising future of each country”, the palace said. The programme includes meetings with cricketing legends in Antigua and Barbuda, where the West Indies team is based, and with conservationists responsible for Guyana’s rainforest.

title: New York governor attacks handling of Cornell gang rape case, appoints special prosecutor
description: Hochul is seeking to change a state law that makes it harder to prosecute sex assault cases where the victim voluntarily became intoxicated.
content: New York Governor Kathy Hochul on Friday faulted police and prosecutors for failing to fully investigate an alleged gang rape in 2024 at Cornell University, saying she was “deeply disturbed” by how the incident was handled. Hochul was speaking at a press conference alongside state Attorney General Letitia James, ‌whom she appointed on Thursday night as a special prosecutor to investigate the allegations. The case has drawn fresh scrutiny after the alleged victim filed a lawsuit accusing fraternity members of raping her while she was intoxicated, prompting widespread outrage over how the matter was handled in 2024. On Monday, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said he was reopening an investigation, which will now be overseen by James’ office. Van Houten has defended his office’s decision in 2024 not to pursue ⁠charges, saying that the woman’s sworn statement to police did not contain allegations that rose to the level of a crime under ‌state law. New York law makes it more difficult to prosecute sexual assault cases in which the victim voluntarily became intoxicated, according to experts and advocates. Some news outlets have reported in recent days that the woman ‌told police unequivocally that she was raped, but that investigators did not include that claim in the ⁠sworn statement that was provided to ⁠prosecutors. Hochul criticised Cornell police for that omission, while also questioning why Van Houten’s office did not interview the woman directly or review the full transcript of her ‌police interview. “This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect ‌her,” Hochul said. In ‌a statement after the press conference, Van Houten said he supported James’ appointment and would cooperate with her investigation. “It has become ‌clear that we were not provided the full picture by the university,” he added. “The focus has been and should continue to be ⁠on the victims.” A Cornell spokesman said the school supports James’ appointment and is “committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how ⁠Cornell has handled this case” but did not address Hochul’s specific criticisms. In an interview with CNN, the woman’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, endorsed Hochul’s decision to appoint James, saying he had little faith in local prosecutors’ handling of the ‌case. Hochul also said she would work ‌with the state legislature to update the state’s sexual assault laws and eliminate the current distinction between victims who voluntarily consumed intoxicants and those given substances without their consent. Several lawmakers have already renewed calls to pass legislation addressing what they described as a loophole in the law. “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol,” Hochul said.

title: Gianni Infantino brings global goodwill tour to Hong Kong ahead of Fifa Asean final
description: Under-fire president of world governing body has been trying to shore up support among the smaller associations ahead of next year’s election.
content: Hong Kong has become the latest stop on Gianni Infantino’s global tour to shore up support ahead of next year’s Fifa presidential election. The under-fire boss, who is still recovering from the fallout of his ill-fated plan to sell off the World Cup, arrived in the city on Friday and is expected to stay for the inaugural Fifa Asean Challenge Cup final between Hong Kong and Cambodia at Kai Tak Stadium on Saturday. While Eric Fok Kai-shan, chairman of the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) has done everything he can to avoid confirming his support for Infantino, when asked about his stance ahead of the fledgling tournament, Fok said that “whoever supports Hong Kong football development, we will support, and we are working closely with Fifa on delivering this landmark event”. Infantino’s expected presence in Hong Kong this week has been a poorly kept secret, although both Fifa and the HKFA have greeted any suggestion that the Fifa boss meet the media in the city with long bouts of silence. Instead, Infantino announced his arrival with a series of pictures on his official Instagram account of him alongside the likes of HKFA president Pui Kwan-kay, Fok and CEO Charles Cheung. “What a delight to be in Hong Kong, China, as the Football Association of Hong Kong, China, are successfully hosting the Fifa Asean Challenge Cup, with an historic final taking place tomorrow,” Infantino wrote. “A big thank you to the @hkfa_official delegation, led by President Pui Kwan Kay, Chairman Eric Fok and General Secretary Charles Cheung, for your warm and generous welcome!” He finished the post with #FootballUnitesTheWorld.

title: Off-duty senior ambulanceman dies after abseiling fall on Kowloon Peak
description: Unconscious man airlifted to hospital but later pronounced dead.
content: An off-duty senior ambulanceman has died after falling from a cliff while abseiling in Hong Kong. The Fire Services Department said on Friday that it had received a report at 2.33pm that a man had fallen from Kowloon Peak in Wong Tai Sin while abseiling. Rescuers and a government helicopter searched the area and found an unconscious man at a nearby cliff. Another man with minor injuries was found on a nearby trail. The department mobilised its mountain and high-angle rescue teams during the search and a drone was also deployed. Both men were airlifted to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan for treatment. The unconscious man was later pronounced dead. The department confirmed the two men were both off-duty senior ambulancemen. “The department expressed its utmost sadness over the death of its member and extended condolences to his family members,” a spokesman said, adding that it would provide all possible help.

title: 2 Hongkongers held in Philippines for months after prison terms end
description: Chinese embassy in Manila expresses concern over the cases of two men who had completed sentences for drug cases in 2000 and 2001.
content: The Chinese embassy in Manila has expressed concern over the cases of two Hongkongers who have remained in custody in the Philippines for months despite being discharged from prison, according to the Immigration Department. The department confirmed on Friday night that it was handling the two cases following an appeal from a former lawmaker and a Hong Kong man who returned to the city on Tuesday after serving 26 years in a Philippine prison for drug offences. The returned Hongkonger, Tang Lung-wai, met the two residents, surnamed Cheung and Ng, in prison. He said he had also been held for weeks at the same immigration facility in the country as the pair while he waited to be deported. Tang said Cheung and Ng were both arrested over drug-related offences in 2000 and 2001 and had completed their jail terms. The Philippines Bureau of Immigration issued deportation orders, seen by the South China Morning Post, to Cheung and Ng in March and June, respectively. Tang said the pair were still waiting to complete their identity confirmation process. Tang said Cheung had his fingerprints taken for the first time after waiting for six months. Ng had his fingerprints taken six or seven times, but they had not been accepted. Ng and Cheung both received 40-year jail sentences. Ng was supposed to have been discharged in January 2025 and Cheung in January this year. However, their transfers to immigration facilities were also delayed. Former lawmaker Paul Tse Wai-chun, who had been helping Tang for years, also appealed on Facebook for an early return of both of them. “I hope that the [Hong Kong] government and other lawmakers will continue to pay attention and help them return as soon as possible,” he said. The Immigration Department was actively following up on two cases involving residents who had completed their sentences in the Philippines and required repatriation to Hong Kong, a spokesman said. He said the department would provide feasible help and had been liaising on the cases with the Office of the Commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Chinese embassy in the Philippines, including verifying the identities of the individuals and issuing entry permit documents for their return. “The [Chinese] embassy in the Philippines has also expressed concern over the relevant cases and will continue to liaise with the Philippine authorities to coordinate the relevant repatriation arrangements,” he said. The department said the Hong Kong government had always attached great importance to cases involving residents detained or imprisoned outside the city, paying close attention to their legitimate rights and interests and striving to provide them with help. Tang was convicted of drug possession in 2011 and handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines amounts to a maximum of 40 years in prison. A Manila court ruled in July that Tang’s sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct and he was ordered to be released and deported immediately. Tang waited three weeks in the immigration facilities before he was deported on Tuesday after his family appealed to the Hong Kong government for help.

title: Hong Kong could overtake London as top arbitration hub in decade: Bar Association head
description: Jose-Antonio Maurellet says Hong Kong’s status as global fundraising capital fuelling rise as city increasingly chosen to resolve high-value disputes.
content: Hong Kong could dethrone London as the top choice for arbitration within the next decade given the Asian city’s status as a global fundraising capital for businesses in mainland China and beyond, the head of the Bar Association has said. Jose-Antonio Maurellet, chairman of the Hong Kong Bar Association, told the South China Morning Post on Friday that the city had enjoyed rapid growth in arbitration work, with high-stakes cases attracting elite international legal talent. Hong Kong tied with Singapore as the second-most preferred arbitration seat globally last year in a survey by Queen Mary University of London, trailing only the British capital. The total amount in dispute in arbitration cases administered by the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, the city’s oldest arbitration body, last year was HK$117.7 billion (US$15 billion). Maurellet said Hong Kong could overtake London’s arbitration crown in less than 10 years as the city was increasingly chosen to resolve high-value disputes linked to its role as an international capital-raising hub. “What we see in Hong Kong actually is more and more big players from the United States or even London acting for clients in Hong Kong,” Maurellet said. “It means we get to cross swords with the best from elsewhere.” The association chief made the remarks after attending a ceremony in London to mark the opening of the legal year in England and Wales. More than 100 senior figures from legal organisations from over 40 jurisdictions worldwide attended the event at Westminster Abbey on Thursday. Maurellet explained that a key factor driving overseas interest in Hong Kong’s arbitration services was the international composition of the city’s arbitrators. The senior counsel said one-third of arbitrators at the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre hailed from other common law jurisdictions such as England, Australia and New Zealand. However, Maurellet acknowledged that some foreign practitioners still viewed Hong Kong primarily as a forum for China-related disputes. “They’re quite interested in basically asking, well, is it all about China?” he said. Maurellet stressed that the broader international scope of the city’s arbitration caseload should be highlighted to build global confidence. “Although a big part of the business is China-related, and we all know the advantages of being bilingual, there’s also, as the pie grows bigger, a part of that pie is available for international lawyers,” he said. He added: “We also have interesting new markets like Brazil, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates, and I think that really raises quite a lot of interest.” Maurellet said he had received more inquiries than anticipated regarding the Hong Kong-headquartered International Organisation for Mediation, with lawyers showing keen interest in its mandate to resolve interstate conflicts and asking how to join as mediators. “I think for certain jurisdictions, which for whatever cultural or geographical reasons in the past would not have gone to the more traditional historical places where this sort of work was done, I think Hong Kong opens up one more option, so I think it’s seen extremely positively,” he said.

title: G7 nations agree to release diesel and oil stocks after Trump pressure
description: The decision came after a warning from Washington that failure to act could lead to a US ban on diesel exports.
content: Group ⁠of Seven countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from energy export restrictions after pressure from US President Donald Trump. The US led a pressure campaign on the European Union to draw down emergency diesel inventories, with the Trump administration warning that failure to act could lead to a US ban on diesel exports. Such a ban could sharply reduce supplies to Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on US diesel, and potentially inflict high economic costs on ‌the bloc. Trump is seeking to cool surging fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for Alabama that the US would not impose a diesel export ban. He said the plan was never really on the table, even though in the past two weeks he had said several times that such a ban was under consideration, and that he supported the idea. “Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we. And we’re not going to be doing the export ban. We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do,” Trump said. The Iran war sparked the biggest emergency stock release ever of 400 million barrels in March, coordinated by the International Energy Agency. “Taking into ⁠account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels,” the G7 said in a joint statement. It was uncertain how much of the ‌petroleum in the new agreement would come from what remains from the March pact. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said this week that members had released about two-thirds of the 400-million-barrel agreement. The release will begin immediately and last four months, with a substantial amount of diesel to be released within 20 days by G7 members and ‌partners, the statement said. It did not provide a breakdown of the volumes of crude, diesel and other products to be released or say which countries would take part. “We will convene ⁠in the context of the IEA in ⁠the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the statement added. “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately,” Trump wrote in a social media post. Trump is ‌seeking to bring down fuel prices as he faces a career-low 32 per cent approval rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll, with voters particularly concerned about the cost of living. The poll, conducted September 17-20, found that just 17 per cent of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of the cost of living. The ‌administration has ‌made lowering energy prices a central focus as it seeks to ease the impact of the Iran war and high fuel costs on consumers and diesel-dependent industries such as trucking and farming. The White House is ‌preparing an executive order to tackle record US diesel prices that could be unveiled as early as next week, two people familiar with the process said. The order is expected to include measures to expand the use of ⁠tax-exempt red-dyed diesel and other tax changes to lower fuel costs, the people said. Details are still being worked out and could change. The G7 statement said member countries would refrain from imposing ⁠export restrictions on energy products among themselves, a move that could ease pressure on the Trump administration to impose a US diesel export ban. “This is a political statement rather than a specific and binding commitment with the large headline number intended to persuade President Trump not to impose a diesel export ban,” analysts at Energy Aspects said in a note. Europe has boosted its ‌imports of US diesel this year as the Iran war ‌disrupted supply from Gulf producers. EU governments had discussed on Friday a proposal by France for European countries to release 50 million barrels of diesel, and for IEA members to release 50 million barrels of crude oil, three sources familiar with the discussions said. A 50 million barrel release of diesel would equate to around 17 per cent of the EU’s total emergency stocks of diesel and gasoil, Eurostat data showed, or about 3 per cent of the bloc’s annual consumption. US diesel futures fell after reports of the stock-release discussions by 3.25 per cent to US$4.49 a gallon. Benchmark European diesel futures fell by roughly US$83 per tonne, down 5.75 per cent, LSEG data showed.

title: Exclusive | Donald Trump is planning trip to the Philippines for Asean summit
description: Trump may also be accompanied by his wife, Melania, who has not travelled to Asia with her husband since 2020, sources say.
content: US President Donald Trump is planning to attend the Asean summit next month, the South China Morning Post understands, as Washington vies with Beijing for influence in the region. If the trip happens, Trump’s appearance at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations meeting, expected to run from November 16-18 in Manila, will be his second consecutive appearance at the gathering during this term. Trump was in Kuala Lumpur for Asean last year and in Manila for the meeting in 2017. Sources told the South China Morning Post that the White House was discussing plans for Trump to first go to Manila for the summit and then hold bilateral talks with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr the next day. He is also expected in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit next month, when he is set to hold his third face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a year. Xi is not expected to attend the Asean summit. Discussions are also under way for Melania Trump to join the US president on the Asia tour, according to a source familiar with the talks. She skipped his state visit to Beijing in May and last travelled to Asia with him in February 2020, on a state visit to India. The last time the couple were in China together was in November 2017. One source said Southeast Asian nations, including the Philippines which chairs the regional bloc this year, have lobbied the US leader to attend, hoping his presence would signal Washington’s continued support for and engagement with the region. Another added that the Manila leg of Trump’s trip would mark the 80th anniversary of US-Philippine diplomatic ties and be an effort to reassure Indo-Pacific allies. The Asean summit comes as tensions between Beijing and Manila continue to run high, following repeated confrontations between their vessels in the South China Sea. China’s claims over most of the strategic waterway and its features are disputed by several Asean members, most notably the Philippines, a US treaty ally. A third source said Washington was considering a stop in Manila in addition to Shenzhen so the trip looked like a visit to Asia rather than a visit to China. That would send Beijing a message without Trump having to say anything explicitly anti-China, while reaffirming America’s political, economic and security engagement with Southeast Asia, the source said. A fourth person familiar with the discussions said a Manila stop was “very likely”, noting that Marcos had invited Trump to the Philippines for the Asean meetings while he was in Washington last year. Washington has repeatedly condemned what it calls Chinese aggression in the South China Sea, while Beijing has insisted that the United States is not a party to the dispute and should not get involved. Asean is also working to conclude its negotiations with Beijing over a South China Sea code of conduct, which aims to establish rules to prevent clashes and manage competing claims in the disputed waterway. Trump’s attendance at the summit this year would offer some assurance to Southeast Asian countries, after the US leader’s tariffs and transactional approach towards long-time allies left many in the region questioning Washington’s reliability. The US has long sought closer ties with Southeast Asia, where China, its geopolitical rival, remains the largest trading partner. But the region has been uneasy about inconsistent US engagement, including the repeated absence of US leaders from the annual summit. At the Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur last year, Trump signed deals with several Southeast Asian economies, including an agreement on critical minerals with Thailand. He also co-signed a declaration aimed at ending tensions between Thailand and Cambodia, a resolution he took credit for. He told the region’s leaders at the summit that he was proud to settle the conflict and “forge a future for the region where proud independent nations can prosper and thrive”.

title: What’s in a name? Why Trump wants to rebrand AI as ‘super intelligence’
description: The US president’s insistence on using the term ‘super intelligence’ reflects a wider debate over the technology’s future, analysts say.
content: US President Donald Trump wants to retire one of the technology sector’s most recognisable acronyms, arguing that the term “artificial intelligence”, or AI, is no longer fit for purpose. On Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order directing US federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” in official communications and non-statutory documents. He also instructed the White House science adviser to draft a new federal definition. The move formalises a rebrand Trump launched at the United Nations General Assembly last week, where he claimed calling the technology “artificial” made it sound “fake”. The change has sparked debate and put US tech leaders in an awkward position. SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself using the old term during a recent appearance with Trump, before correcting himself: “SI, pardon me.” Meanwhile, California Governor Gavin Newsom pushed back on Wednesday, ordering state agencies to stick with “AI”. Does this semantic tussle signal a deeper shift in how Washington views a technology central to the US-China rivalry? Why the name change? The White House argued frontier systems had moved beyond merely imitating or automating aspects of human intelligence, making “super intelligence” a better reflection of their growing capabilities and potential. The shift aligns with Trump’s broader push to accelerate American tech development. At the UN, he rejected calls to slow progress, arguing he would not “stifle growth” in an industry that could eclipse the Industrial Revolution in terms of its impact. This contrasts with recent calls from AI industry leaders – including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Musk – to pace model development over safety concerns. Instead, Trump cast technological leadership as a global race the US could not afford to lose to China. The rebrand follows Trump’s summit in Washington with Chinese President Xi Jinping, where both nations agreed to establish a dialogue and communication channel for AI-related incidents. Trump said he discussed his preferred “super intelligence” phrasing with Xi. Analysts view the shift as an attempt to control the narrative. Su Lian Jye, chief analyst at Omdia, said the rebrand could be seen as a way to “introduce a new phase in AI development” to project American dominance. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, noted that “branding and optics matter a lot” to Trump, who likely wanted to hype the technology and tie it to his legacy. Does the terminology matter? Industry observers expect limited practical impact – and warn the move could create confusion. Chan said the shift was unlikely to change public attitudes towards AI, warning it might actually “heighten some people’s perception of risk and fear”. Su noted that while consumer adoption was unlikely to shift, it could “create more confusion around standardisation and governance”. Complicating matters, “superintelligence” already has an established technical definition, generally referring to systems surpassing human capabilities across all domain tasks. For instance, Meta Platforms rebranded its division to Meta Superintelligence Labs last year. Reactions among tech and political leaders have been mixed. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang backed the move, writing on X that “super intelligence offers an extraordinary opportunity to advance discovery, productivity, security, health and prosperity”. California Governor Newsom warned the rebrand could distract from safety risks and signed an order stating that the move could not hide an “impotent and craven failure to address well-documented emerging security and safety risks”. How has China reacted? Beijing has approached the rebrand with caution. China’s foreign ministry said it “respects” Washington’s choice while continuing to use the term “artificial intelligence”. Su noted that adopting terms like “super” would be “very out of character” for China, which has favoured a pragmatic tech approach. Wang Zichen, deputy secretary general at the Beijing-based Centre for China and Globalisation, said many in China were likely to view the rebrand as an “idiosyncratic preference” of Trump that added no value to the US-China debate. However, Wang noted that “Beijing naturally has reason to take [Trump’s] preferred wording seriously and accommodate it diplomatically”.

title: Manchester City lodge ‘comprehensive’ appeal against verdict in financial-rules scandal
description: The club were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches over nine seasons but have always maintained their innocence.
content: Manchester City have filed an appeal against an independent ⁠commission ruling that found the club ⁠guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s ⁠financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid potentially severe sanctions. The league said on Tuesday that City had used “sham” commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million (US$1.19 billion) over nearly a decade. City were found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league’s ‌financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation. The 10-time English champions have denied wrongdoing throughout the process. “Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026, the Club lodged its comprehensive appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter,” the club said in a statement. “The Club’s firm position is that, on multiple ⁠grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. “The Club is innocent of the accusations made ‌by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.” The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member Appeal Board ‌appointed by the chair of the league’s judicial panel. “The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the ⁠Judicial Panel,” the league said ⁠in a statement. “The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted.” The Premier League’s rules state that an appeal hearing ‌should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding. The appeal will take place in private, ‌as ‌did the original hearings. The board will review the commission’s decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case. The ‌board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or ⁠compensation order imposed. A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit ⁠a subsequent arbitration process. With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league. City can also ‌separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains ‌unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard and whether they would take effect immediately. A league representative said they could not discuss the process for confidentiality reasons. While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11. Meanwhile, the English Football Association broke its silence on the case on Friday, saying that the commission’s decision “has significant implications for the integrity of the game”. “We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate,” the national governing body said in a statement. “As proceedings between the Premier League and Manchester City Football Club remain ongoing, we do not intend to comment further at this stage. We will, however, continue to monitor developments closely.”

title: If young US people accept Xi’s invitation to China, what will Beijing show them?
description: The itineraries of previous trips reveal the image the country wants to project – eco-friendly, multicultural and hi-tech.
content: China is ramping up its efforts to bring young Americans to China, and ready to be seen as a country concerned with environmental protection, lifting people out of poverty, protecting minority cultures and building the technology of the future. During his trip to the United States last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping said his country aimed to welcome 100,000 young Americans on exchange or study trips over the next five years. That builds on an earlier target announced in 2023 that set the goal of bringing 50,000 US youth people to China by 2028, which the authorities said they had reached ahead of schedule. The Young Envoys Scholarship (YES) initiative was launched to support this target. It is run by the China Education Association for International Exchange, a non-profit organisation under the Ministry of Education. The YES initiative coordinates with Chinese institutions, mostly universities, which create itineraries and curricula, and manage the visitors on the ground. Universities set varying admissions criteria for their programmes, but in general, the YES initiative is open to non-Chinese citizens between the ages of 18 and 45. Marine conservation For one group of students, their China trip began at sea. Starting in March, a group of 20 Chinese and US students spent 10 days travelling up the Chinese coast from Hong Kong to the eastern cities of Ningbo and Shanghai. The three stops are all coastal cities with links to marine research and the ocean economy. The trip was organised by two Chinese state-linked non-profit organisations and the Ray Dalio-backed OceanX, with support from China’s Second Institute of Oceanography, the Ministry of Education and the Chinese University of Hong Kong. The programme included marine exploration, visits to research facilities and laboratories and discussions about international cooperation in ocean science, according to the organisers. In one activity, the students collected marine biological samples and identified species including the Calanus sinicus crustacean, which has been studied by Chinese scientists for decades. “I am delighted to know that the students from both countries have embarked on an unforgettable friendship voyage aboard the China-US Youth Friendship vessel,” Xi said in a letter to the programme in May, state news agency Xinhua reported. China has emphasised marine science in recent years, with its latest five-year plan – which runs from this year through to 2030 – calling for more research, expanded deep-sea exploration and deepened international cooperation. The US and China are the two biggest contributors to oceanographic research in the Pacific, with the US first in terms of the share of publications and China second between 1992 and 2021, according to a study published in the Ocean Sustainability journal. The two countries have also cooperated on marine research under the broader US-China Science and Technology Agreement, first signed in 1979 and extended for another five years in 2024. Under the agreement, a protocol on cooperation in marine and fishery science and technology provides a framework for collaboration between China and the US. Minority culture A programme organised by Shanghai’s Donghua University took US students into ethnic minority communities in southwestern China’s Guizhou province, with field studies focused on the intangible cultural heritage of the Bouyei, Miao, Shui and Dong peoples. The initiative aimed to “promote the global dissemination of outstanding traditional Chinese culture and enhance the international influence of intangible cultural heritage”, according to the university. In the city of Kaili, students attended a workshop on batik dyeing techniques and later wore traditional costumes to take part in a “village runway” event with residents. Guizhou has used its ethnic minority culture to drive tourism as part of its poverty alleviation and rural development efforts, with tourism projects helping nearly 900,000 people increase their incomes between 2017 and 2019, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. China’s rural revitalisation plan for 2024 to 2027 calls for stronger protection and use of traditional villages and intangible cultural heritage. China’s latest five-year plan for intangible cultural heritage also seeks to promote Chinese intangible cultural heritage overseas as part of efforts to strengthen the global influence of Chinese culture and promote cultural exchanges. Poverty alleviation Peking University said it organised a trip through Ningxia, Sichuan and Chongqing focused on “poverty alleviation, regional development and urban renewal”. In Ningxia, students visited Minning, a town established over two decades ago that is touted as an example of China’s east-west cooperation in poverty alleviation. The town has developed industries including wine, goji berry cultivation and photovoltaic agriculture supported by investment and technical aid from the wealthier coastal province of Fujian. Minning’s per capita disposable monthly income rose from about 500 yuan (US$74.50) in 1997 to 20,292 yuan last year, according to the local authorities. The five-year plan calls for an institutionalised system of support for underdeveloped areas, including measures to consolidate poverty alleviation gains and strengthen industrial and employment support. It also calls for improving east-west cooperation and other forms of regional assistance. In Sichuan and Chongqing, the trip’s focus shifted towards agricultural modernisation and urban development. Cutting-edge technology The Suzhou-Hangzhou-Shanghai itinerary, also organised by Peking University, offered a very different picture from the previous two: an image of how China is seemingly building the future. The trip took students through three cities in the prosperous Yangtze River Delta and focused on advanced manufacturing, robotics and the digital economy. The group visited Unitree Robotics and carmaker Geely, two companies working in sectors that have become increasingly important to China’s push up the value chain. This has intensified competition between China and the US, with advanced chips, artificial intelligence and other strategic technologies at the centre of the rivalry. The five-year plan calls for the faster development of strategic, emerging and future industries while encouraging technological innovation and the upgrading of traditional manufacturing. Lasting impression “You cannot truly understand another country from books. You have to experience it first-hand,” said Anoushka Soni, a University of California, Berkeley student who visited China this year, according to a Peking University social media account. The university quoted her as saying that the stories she encountered “cannot be found in textbooks and cannot be presented simply by searching the word ‘China’ online”. Saanvi Bhatia, a Stanford University fourth-year student from Pennsylvania who took part in Tsinghua University’s summer fellowship last year, said she also made unexpected discoveries. “I did not know how involved China was in climate stuff and how much they cared about making it non-toxic to us,” Bhatia said. During her visit to Guizhou, Bhatia and other students were shown how waste was incinerated and treated so that only water vapour was released into the environment. “I feel like a lot of the perspective of China and the US is seen [through] rivalry. We’re both kind of competing, and so then to be on the other person’s land and knowing what they are interested in was very cool,” Bhatia said. Additional reporting by Tim Yuen Lingk

title: Shark remains stranded in South Korean canal after second rescue attempt
description: They now hope that the shark will eventually swim out to the open sea on its own.
content: A second attempt to guide a shark stranded in a canal in the South Korean port city of Busan back to the open sea ended without success on Friday, with the animal staying in the waterway into its third week. Rescuers, who had been using a net to try to coax it out, had to end the operation after a two-hour chase due to ‌the risk of their huge net getting caught on rocks. They now hope that the shark will eventually swim out to the open sea on its own, after leaving the net in place to limit how far back up the canal it can swim. The 3.5-metre (11.48-ft) shark was first spotted in a narrow waterway at North Port on September 18. Nicknamed “Bukangi”, which is derived from “Buk Hang”, the Korean name for North Port, and the Korean suffix “-i”, about 600,000 people have flocked to the area to see the shark. Experts say it could be a bronze whaler, a species typically found in warm ⁠temperate waters and which has been seen off South Korea’s coasts. The shark’s prolonged stay drew particular attention because of the unusual location. The narrow canal ‌is situated in North Port, close to high-rise buildings and a major high-speed rail station in the heart of Busan. Authorities first attempted to guide the shark towards the sea on Tuesday using vessels equipped with water jets, but the shark swam away ‌from jets and remained in the canal. For the second attempt, authorities used a 50-metre-long and 6.8-metre-high net to prevent the shark from ⁠turning back towards the canal. A vessel pulled ⁠the centre of the net while five people on each side moved along the waterfront, coordinating their speed to guide the shark towards the sea. But the shark remained in the canal. The ‌net now limits the shark to swimming in a 100m stretch that leads to the sea. “As the water level changes and the current shifts, we expect the shark may eventually be able to make ‌its ‌own way out,” said Kim Hyun-woo, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Fisheries Science who has been leading the operation. “Once we confirm that it has ‌completely left the canal and made its way out into the open sea, we can consider the operation a success.” Noise, lights and electrical ⁠signals could have been making it difficult for the shark to find its way out, he said. “For the shark, there are just too many external physical stimuli coming ⁠from different directions.” Hundreds of people gathered along the waterway to watch the rescue on Friday. Some visitors said they would be sad to see it leave, while others said the shark should be returned to the sea and its natural habitat as soon as possible. “I do ‌hope it eventually heads back out to ‌the open sea. But I guess it likes Busan, too, since it’s still here,” Busan resident Jo Won-ho said. Bukangi’s appearance has also drawn attention to changes in the waters around South Korea. Experts have pointed to warming sea temperatures as one possible factor behind the growing number of large shark sightings. An analysis by the National Institute of Fisheries Science found 46 sightings of large sharks along the country’s east coast during the first half of this year, compared with 12 over the same period last year.

title: K-drama Dive into You: Kim Ji-yeon, aka Bona, leads superficial time-travel body-swap romcom
description: K-pop star Bona plays an emotionally numb actress who uses a camcorder to travel back in time with her twin brother, played by Jang Se-hyuk.
content: Lead cast: Kim Ji-yeon (aka Bona), Park Seo-ham, Jang Se-hyuk Latest Nielsen rating: 0.5 per cent In the new fantasy romance Dive into You, a mysterious camcorder allows a pair of superstar siblings to travel back in time and swap bodies in a desperate bid to save a loved one. Kim Ji-yeon (Twenty-Five Twenty-One) – also known as Bona from the K-pop girl group WJSN – appears as screen siren Yoon Ha-na, who has reached the top of her field but is experiencing an emotional numbness that affects her acting. Jang Se-hyuk (Our Unwritten Seoul) plays Ha-na’s twin brother Ha-ru, who is a star judo athlete and happens to be dating Seo Ye-rang (Moon Seung-you, Would You Marry Me?), the boss of Ha-na’s talent agency. Ha-ru is also best friends with Ha-na’s dashing bodyguard Jung Woo-jae (Park Seo-ham, Our Universe). Ha-na, Ha-ru and Woo-jae have been close since their school days, when Woo-jae was also a judo athlete. Woo-jae was actually poised for greatness on the mat before an accident dashed his aspirations. Although Ha-na and Woo-jae have been friends for years, it is easy to see that their friendship has long threatened to turn into something else. Woo-jae is intensely protective of Ha-na but he is also the picture of professionalism: he would never dare cross the line he so clearly wishes to. Tragedy strikes one evening at an awards show when Ha-na is attacked by a deranged stalker. Woo-jae steers his charge clear of harm’s way but in doing so pays the ultimate price, dying by Ha-na’s side as the stalker escapes. After Woo-jae’s funeral, Ha-na and Ha-ru are forced off a bridge by an oncoming truck. As they sink into the water below, Ha-na notices a strange light coming from her old camcorder. Selecting the thumbnail of an old recording transports the siblings back to their school days, albeit in each other’s bodies. Because they arrive during a judo match between Woo-jae and Ha-ru, the timing is less than ideal. Comedic high jinks ensue, but the twins are also overwhelmed to see Woo-jae alive again. Before they can really process what is happening, they find themselves back in the present and in their original bodies, recuperating in a hospital after the crash. Desperate to prevent Woo-jae’s untimely demise, Ha-na and Ha-ru fiddle with the old camcorder until they find a way to return. Dive into You actually begins back in the trio’s school days, on the morning Ha-na was walking to school and bumped into a mysterious busker who sold her the camcorder for a mere 1,000 won (less than US$1). Already dreaming of the bright lights, Ha-na immediately uses the camera to record the trio’s experiences. In the present, the camera is initially broken, but Woo-jae secretly goes to repair it and winds up bumping into the same ageless busker, who fixes it – once again for just 1,000 won. The repaired camera becomes the gateway to their shared memories, and the siblings learn to use it to revisit those specific times, albeit only by swapping bodies. Dive into You offers a marginally different spin on the Korean fantasy romcom, combining time-travel and body-swap tropes. Despite its sweet characters and a mix of the glitzy entertainment world and hazily nostalgic school backdrops, the show struggles to stand out in what is already a very crowded field. No one in the cast puts a foot wrong, but they are also unable to elevate the admittedly thin material they have been given to work with. Romance is clearly in the offing for Ha-na and Woo-jae, but it will take a little time for them to reach that new point in their relationship – particularly since Ha-na is trapped in the wrong body. This offers ample fodder for comedy, although sadly too much of the gender-swap comedy in the early episodes defaults to lame and arguably homophobic gags of men hugging too enthusiastically. The humour is likely to settle in the coming episodes, but what Dive into You really needs is a bit of character to anchor its emotional aspirations. So far, this ho-hum fantasy romcom mash-up has given us little reason to expect that it will suddenly turn into appointment viewing. Dive into You is streaming on Viu.

title: US job growth slows sharply in September, unemployment rises
description: Economists noted that payrolls tend to underperform when the Labour Day holiday falls late ‌in the month, as was the case this year.
content: US job growth slowed more than expected in September, but that likely does not signal a material shift in the labour market, with the weakness likely related to a calendar quirk. Nonfarm payrolls increased by 29,000 jobs last month after ‌a downwardly revised 133,000 rise in August, the Labor Department’s closely watched employment report showed on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 90,000 after a previously reported 162,000 surge in August. Estimates ranged from as low as 35,000 to as high as 180,000. Volatility linked to seasonal adjustment factors, the model the government uses to strip out seasonal fluctuations from the data, probably accounted for both the meagre payroll gains last month ⁠and the downward revision to August’s count. Payrolls have a tendency to underperform when the Labour Day holiday falls late ‌in the month, as was the case this year, economists noted. There have been no signs of a broad increase in lay-offs. First-time applications for unemployment benefits have been hovering at ‌57-year lows amid robust corporate profit growth and resilient domestic demand. Economists, however, expected that growing headwinds ⁠from the US-Israel war with ⁠Iran, including high energy prices and strained supply chains, would start disrupting the labour market by the end of this year and into 2027. Diesel ‌prices are at record highs and could start to exert pressure beyond the transport and agricultural sectors. Ongoing tariffs also are a source of concern, ‌with an ‌Institute for Supply Management survey on Thursday showing rising anxiety among manufacturers over the trade war with Canada. The unemployment ‌rate increased to a still-low 4.2 per cent last month from 4.1 per cent in August. The unemployment rate is being kept low as ⁠retirements and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown reduce labour supply. The economy needs to create between 50,000 and 80,000 jobs ⁠per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population, economists estimated. The Federal Reserve last month raised its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75 per cent-4 per cent range, the first hike in ‌three years, and flagged further increases ‌in borrowing costs ahead. The odds of another rate hike this month were diminished by cooler-than-expected inflation readings for August and July. Ahead of the employment report, financial markets are pricing in a roughly 22 per cent chance of further monetary policy tightening at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting, down from about 69 per cent a week ago, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed.

title: China’s C919 jet faces further delivery delays amid US export chill: analysts
description: Washington has reportedly restricted exports of aircraft parts to China to gain leverage over Beijing, adding to Comac’s supply pressures.
content: A reported move by the United States to restrict exports of aircraft parts to China would place another speed bump on production of the C919 – a Chinese passenger jet designed to compete with Airbus and Boeing – as alternative sources of critical components for the plane are not readily available, according to analysts. The US Commerce Department has slowed export licensing for civilian aeroplane parts to China in recent weeks to strengthen Washington’s position in trade talks with Beijing, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing unnamed sources. The move was designed to prevent the state-owned Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) – the maker of the C919 – from stockpiling parts, Reuters said. US officials have also reportedly expressed interest in regulations that would make it easier to restrict shipments of aviation hydraulic fluid. Analysts said the restrictions would create further supply issues for Comac, which was already falling behind on production of the C919. “This supply slowdown has only been an issue for the last few weeks,” said Richard Aboulafia, managing director at the US-based aerospace consulting firm AeroDynamic Advisory, referring to the Reuters report. “That means the past six months of practically non-existent deliveries are due to other internal problems at Comac,” he said. He suggested the manufacturer was “not building planes for other reasons”. Comac has received more than 1,000 orders from Chinese airlines for the C919, but the company has struggled to ramp up production. Last year, it delivered 15 of the jets, well below its target of 75. In the first quarter of 2026, it made just three deliveries. Analysts have cited several reasons for the low output, including earlier US restrictions on component exports and Comac’s focus on quality over speed. Last year, Washington placed temporary restrictions on exports of aircraft parts to China and slowed licence approvals. The US firm GE Aerospace is now “reluctant” to export aircraft engines to China because it can sell to Airbus and Boeing at higher prices and with less effort, according to independent aviation analyst Li Hanming. That was the reason CFM International – a joint venture between GE Aerospace and France’s Safran Aircraft Engines – failed to reach a deal with China during US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, Li said. CFM has supplied Leap-1C engines for the C919 in the past. “After last year’s embargo, China was angry and insisted that these parts should be prerequisites for Boeing orders,” Li said. China agreed to place a huge order for 200 Boeing aircraft during Trump’s visit in May, but the deal has yet to materialise. Prospects for a wider agreement appear to have faded, with no new deals mentioned during or after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington in late September. Neither Comac nor GE Aerospace immediately responded to requests for comment on Friday. Comac relies on imports of several critical components – including the engine and avionic and hydraulic systems – to produce the C919, experts believe. China was developing replacements for US parts, but they would be “a long time coming”, Aboulafia said. Aero Engine Corporation of China is developing its CJ-1000A turbofan aircraft engine for the C919. China is also working on sealants, paints and bolts to replace Western-made aircraft parts, according to an aircraft engineer. US export controls would spur China to perfect those components and Comac was unlikely to face long-term setbacks, said Victor Gao, vice-president of the Centre for China and Globalisation think tank in Beijing. “The only purpose (export controls) will serve is to make China completely self-reliant,” Gao said.

title: Cutting New World ties over 11 Skies averts ‘lose-lose’ deal: Airport Authority
description: Development to be renamed and given new identity before management seeks investors and tenants, authority says.
content: The Airport Authority has averted a “lose-lose situation” by terminating a nearly 50-year contract with Hong Kong developer New World Development for the 11 Skies commercial project, with most facilities now set to open in 2028, the statutory body’s directors have said. Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, said on Friday that it could no longer work with a debt-ridden partner on the ambitious development and that the project needed to be brought forward. He said the authority could adopt a “technical solution” of taking New World to court for failing to deliver the project, but it would come with pitfalls. “We could have sought a settlement in court, but it sacrifices time, and we need to bring forward the development,” he said. “If we went for a technical solution, it risks a lose-lose situation.” New World, which is owned by the Cheng family through the private holding company Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, announced on Wednesday that it would return the project to the authority by surrendering the infrastructure. As part of the move, the developer will pay a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee, spending HK$1.05 billion to complete the remaining works and provide agreed services, and offering a HK$1 option to buy company shares. “The whole package represents the biggest efforts of the major shareholder [of New World],” Lee said. “We have tried to maximise what we get. The option is a bonus.” The option for the authority to buy 750 million New World shares from Chow Tai Fook Enterprises also came with a string of conditions that have raised questions about its feasibility. Under the conditions, the authority can only exercise the option within three years and must buy the shares in one go. When it buys the shares, it cannot breach any bank covenants and cannot exceed the controlling shareholder’s interest. The authority would also be required to hold onto its stake in the company until September 2032. The 750 million shares already represent 29.8 per cent of New World’s total issued share capital of 2.52 billion shares. Chow Tai Fook Enterprises holds about 45 per cent of New World and has indicated it intends to maintain its control of the developer. The exercise price of the option will be HK$2.25 billion, or HK$3 per share – a nearly 50 per cent discount on Friday’s closing price of HK$5.82. “New World will have a series of movements to follow,” Lee said without elaborating. The developer has been offloading assets and refinancing capital to cut debt after a liquidity crisis emerged in 2023. As of June 30 this year, its total debt stood at HK$143.3 billion and its net debt was HK$126.3 billion. The contract was signed by New World in 2018 and was originally scheduled to run until 2066. The termination has attracted controversy as the move means the authority will give up its entitlement to receive guaranteed rent or revenue rent representing 20 per cent of the gross revenue from 11 Skies from 2027 to 2066, depending on which was higher. The handover is due to be completed by April next year. The 11 Skies project was intended to complement the authority’s goal of developing Skytopia, a HK$100 billion landmark surrounding Hong Kong International Airport, featuring commerce, culture, leisure and entertainment elements. Cissy Chan Ching-sze, the authority’s executive director for commercial, said 11 Skies would soon be renamed and given a new identity before management hunted for investors and tenants. “It will no longer be a mall,” she said. “It will be an entertainment hub.” Originally, the HK$20 billion 11 Skies development was expected to include three grade A office towers totalling 52,955 square metres (570,000 square feet), and about 247,000 square metres of retail and dining space, representing 70 per cent of the entire project. In May, the South China Morning Post reported that signs had emerged of the authority having regained control of the project. In the financial year ended June 30, the company wrote off HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions on 11 Skies, following HK$2.7 billion in the same period in 2025. Chan said some spaces in one of the office towers had been leased, while the other two were pending tenant recruitment. “We aim to attract companies that organise exhibitions to move from Wan Chai to leverage more exhibitions to be held at AsiaWorld-Expo,” she said, adding that other potential tenants included private wealth and insurance companies. The retail and dining spaces were repurposed as a destination for entertainment, wellness and experiences. She cited restaurants offering jet-fresh seafood, go-karting, pet-friendly areas and spaces dedicated to visitors’ experiences as examples. Chan said key components of Skytopia would be completed in 2028. These include most parts of 11 Skies, an autonomous transport system that connects the Hong Kong checkpoint of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge with the Tung Chung MTR station, a 12,000-square metre waterfront piazza, a water recreation area and the expansion of nearby facilities at AsiaWorld-Expo. AsiaWorld-Expo will add 100,000 square metres of exhibition space and a 20,000 seat arena for concerts and other events. Chan added that a section of the yacht berthing facilities was also expected to be ready for use in 2028.

title: Ukraine war: Japan’s new sanctions on Russia target oil exports
description: The 35 sanctioned vessels are believed to transport Russian crude oil to countries, providing a major source of revenue for Moscow.
content: The Japanese government on Friday announced additional sanctions against Russia amid the ongoing invasion of Ukraine, targeting a so-called shadow fleet of vessels engaged in transporting sanctioned oil from Russia. Joining international efforts to crack down on sanctions evasion by the fleet, Japan has decided to impose restrictions on the provision of services to 35 vessels, according to the Foreign Ministry. The measures restrict the provision of services including insurance, maritime transport, crew employment and dispatch, and repairs to the vessels, which include cargo ships and tankers. The sanctioned vessels are believed to transport Russian crude oil to countries including China and India, with those exports providing a major source of revenue for Moscow. Japan also announced restrictions on payments and transactions involving 33 entities and nine individuals associated with Russia. An additional 102 goods have been made subject to restrictions on exports to Russia. Four entities based in the United Arab Emirates and Turkey have also been made subject to export prohibitions, the ministry said. The move is aimed at reducing the revenue available to Russia to fund its war in Ukraine, as it continues the full-scale invasion of its neighbour that it launched in February 2022. Japan, in lockstep with the other Group of Seven members, has imposed economic sanctions on Russia, including freezing the assets of Russian President Vladimir Putin and other individuals. The latest sanctions come a day after Putin expressed interest at an event in Moscow in pursuing “mutually beneficial” relations between Japan and Russia once current difficulties between the sides are overcome. Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, the top government spokesman, said on Friday morning that Tokyo had taken note of the remarks and added that it is “important” for the countries to maintain communication. Japan and Russia are also engaged in a dispute over Russian-held, Japanese-claimed islands off Hokkaido called the Northern Territories by Tokyo and the Southern Kurils by Moscow. In August, Putin visited one of the islands for the first time as president, dealing a fresh blow to ties.

title: As I see it | How a Chinese film exposes Hollywood’s dehumanising Mideast propaganda
description: The novelty here is that a blockbuster from an outside power declines to exoticise the locals as nameless props, villains or victims.
content: For more than a century, the Middle East has reached Western cinema audiences through a narrow and familiar lens: the amber filter, the call to prayer laid over a crowded bazaar, and bearded men shouting lines no one bothers to subtitle. As the YouTube channel Wave Media observes in a recent video essay, such figures “are not characters, they’re weather” – the hostile terrain in which a protagonist, usually a heroic but conflicted American soldier or spy, must fight to survive. A blockbuster Chinese film now asks a subversive question: what happens when the camera treats those locals as people rather than foreign objects in their own land? Once Upon a Time in the Middle East (or Welcome to Dragon Restaurant in Chinese) is directed by Wen Muye, of Dying to Survive fame, and stars Shen Teng as Xu Fu, a debt-laden chef whose restaurant in a fictional Middle Eastern city becomes a sanctuary for civilians and orphans. The war is, in all but name, the 2003 US invasion of Iraq. Wen drew on the experiences of Chinese restaurateurs in Baghdad such as Chen Xianzhong. Middle Eastern filmmakers – from Iranian cinema to Nadine Labaki’s Capernaum and Hany Abu-Assad’s Paradise Now – have long depicted their own region with complexity and sensitivity. The novelty here is that a commercial blockbuster from an outside power declines to exoticise the locals as nameless props, villains or victims. That has been the default mode of American cinema. According to Jack Shaheen, the late scholar and author of the essay, the book and the documentary, Reel Bad Arabs: How Hollywood Vilifies a People, the vast majority of more than 900 Hollywood films produced between 1896 and 2000 reduced Arabs to sheikhs, terrorists and belly dancers. By his count, only 5 per cent of Arab roles depicted normal human beings. He wrote that moviemakers “falsely project all Arabs as Muslims and all Muslims as Arabs”. Their distorted lenses have shown Arabs as “brutal, heartless, uncivilised religious fanatics and money-mad cultural ‘others’ bent on terrorising civilised Westerners, especially Christians and Jews”, or as “abusers of women”. He compared the stereotype of the hook-nosed Arab with a similar depiction of Jews in Nazi propaganda materials. This critique extends to post-9/11 cinema. Self-questioning American films such as The Hurt Locker, American Sniper and Zero Dark Thirty, Wave Media essayist Jiwon Kim argues, still treat the region as the stage on which Americans endure their moral crises. “Even the films that question the war, that say it’s more complicated than you think, do so by demanding empathy for the perpetrators,” she says. “And so, we, the audience, are asked to feel the trauma of the soldier who kicked down the door. The people behind the door are still part of the furniture.” Admittedly, there is a moral problem of conflicting perspectives even for genuine artists from an imperialist power. Even the great Albert Camus was criticised for his alleged colonial sympathy against Algerian independence. Unlike Hollywood, Wen’s film depicts violence not as spectacle but with dread – the chaos of a panicked crowd, the uncertainty of a night in a shelter. Its refrain, hao hao chi fan – eat well – echoes the words of an Iraqi journalist quoted in the video: for those who lived through the war, “sitting down to eat one peaceful meal is in and of itself a luxury”. The video essay argues that war films generally mirror their nation’s foreign policy grammar. It contrasts Washington’s shifting justifications for the Iraq war with President Xi Jinping’s 2016 speech at the Arab League, in which he declared that “instead of looking for a proxy in the Middle East, we promote peace talks”. Kim admits discomfort with how a Chinese protagonist ultimately rescues Arab children, raising the charge of China casting itself as “the white saviour in beige”. In the end, though, Xu’s only reward is to go home to dinner, and the final image belongs to an orphan, grown up and running his own restaurant. The South China Morning Post’s film reviewer James Marsh found the film “bombastic”; mainland state media have openly framed it as an expression of Chinese diplomatic values. Beijing’s professed policy of non-interference contrasts with America’s long history of war and destruction in the name of spreading democracy and freedom. Unicef estimates that more than 473 million children – over one in six worldwide – live in conflict or war zones. Whether a story comes from Hollywood, China or anywhere else, the moral test should be: are the people on screen granted interiority and agency? That a Chinese film feels refreshing says much about the diet Western audiences have been fed.

title: India and Pakistan cricketers set for firecracker clash in ‘inspiring’ Hong Kong Sixes
description: Cricket’s biggest rivalry coming to city this month, along with Ashes battle and pair of mouthwatering matches for city team.
content: India will clash with Pakistan in a blockbuster opening-day clash when the “unique and inspiring” Hong Kong Cricket Sixes gets under way later this month. The city team, meanwhile, currently nursing the deep frustration over being eliminated from the Asian Games after their quarter-final with Pakistan on Monday was washed out, will slug it out with Australia and England in an intriguing group. This 2026 edition will be the third iteration since the Sixes was removed from cold storage in 2024. “It was a brilliant initiative from Cricket Hong Kong, China [CHKC] to bring it back, because it’s part of our cricketing culture,” Anshy Rath, Hong Kong’s gun opening batsman, said. “You won’t find a player who’s had a bad experience at the Sixes. It’s a fantastic benchmark for Hong Kong players, and allows the city to be broadcast to the world”. Rath grew up watching the tournament at its old Kowloon Cricket Club home, and was coached by a who’s who of greats from visiting All Stars teams: Stephen Fleming, the new England Test head coach, Brian Lara, Shane Warne, Glenn McGrath and Anil Kumble, among them. “It’s inspired a lot of players here, and long may it continue,” Rath said. “I’m deeply proud and honoured to represent Hong Kong in the Sixes.” Awarded ‘M’ Mark funding by the government's Major Sports Events Committee (MSEC), the three-day Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground jamboree will reach its climax on November 1. Defending champions Pakistan, targeting a record-extending seventh title, are pooled with the United Arab Emirates as well as arch-foes India, while 2024 winners Sri Lanka are in a group with Bangladesh and debutants Scotland. South Africa, Afghanistan and Oman will contest the fourth pool. “The Sixes is unique; it’s not just about cricket, it’s about globally showcasing the vibrant city of Hong Kong … and it’s an opportunity for our players to compete with some of the world’s best,” Burji Shroff, CHKC chairman, said. “We’re profoundly grateful for the government’s unwavering support. Their decision to award the Sixes ‘M’ Mark status for a third consecutive year is both an honour and a strong vote of confidence.” Hong Kong have a series of critical 2028 T20 World Cup qualifiers in Malaysia this month, but Kaushal Silva, the head coach, said the Sixes was “a huge date in our international calendar”. Recalling the theatre of Aizaz Khan clattering 30 off the final over to win last year’s plate final for Hong Kong against Bangladesh, Silva said: “I was in the dugout listening to the crowd chanting, ‘Go Hong Kong’, and it was so inspiring to hear. “If we can build on that, improve our game, and show our talent to this community, they'll start to feel some love for us.” Silva acknowledged the Sixes atmosphere was “completely different” from that for any other cricketing occasion in the city. An accomplished former wicketkeeper-batsman for Sri Lanka who took a Test century off an Australian attack featuring Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, Silva added: “The appetite among kids today is for a short format. I grew up loving cricket and always wanting to play more. This is a great platform for creating a culture where the Hong Kong community falls in love with the sport.” Rath, who clubbed six sixes in a quick-fire unbeaten 45 during last year’s plate semi-final victory over Afghanistan, said playing in the tournament had initially been “daunting because all those past memories of the Sixes came flooding back”. “Some players try to swing from the hip every ball, but that can be counterproductive,” he said. “You work it out as you go along.” Rath said Kuwait’s charge to the final 12 months ago had established a blueprint for the associate members. “It’s a great way for the world to see what Hong Kong cricket can do,” the former captain added. “Anyone can win, which is what sport lovers thrive on. The brilliance of the format is that it bridges the gap between regular international cricket, and international cricket in the Sixes.” With Sony Sports Network signed up to beam the tournament around the globe, Wilfred Ng Sau-kei, chairman of the MSEC, said: “There are more and more expectations on ‘M’ Mark events. [The Sixes] brings many overseas guests, and has more than 100 million [television] viewers. “It’s a good platform to showcase Hong Kong to our overseas friends, and we’re really happy to support this event.”
