title: MTR Corp pays out HK$2.25 billion for high-speed rail construction delays
description: Rail firm and Hong Kong government also reach consensus on avoiding payout over delays to completion of Sha Tin to Central Link.
content: The MTR Corporation will hand over HK$2.25 billion (US$287 million) to the Hong Kong government as a one-off settlement for the delayed completion of the high-speed rail line, while reaching a consensus to avoid a payout over hurdles affecting the Sha Tin to Central Link. While the transport firm oversaw the design, construction, testing and operation of the two projects, both are owned by the government and involved public funds. Under the arrangements announced on Friday, the MTR Corp will pay the government, its majority shareholder, HK$2.25 billion for the delay to the commencement of the 26km (16.1-mile) local section of the cross-border high-speed rail, which was completed in 2018. But the MTR Corp and authorities also agreed not to pursue further claims over the Sha Tin to Central Link, as the rail firm had shouldered HK$2.8 billion in extra costs to address quality issues and delays. The project, which connects Admiralty MTR station to stops at the Hong Kong-mainland Chinese border, was completed in 2022 after repeated delays and a scandal over the substandard construction of Hung Hom station. “The government has been following up in a serious, rigorous and professional manner with [the MTR Corp] on its responsibilities as the project manager in respect of programme delays in the construction of the [high-speed rail and Sha Tin to Central Link] projects, in order to safeguard the legitimate interests of the government and the public,” the Transport and Logistics Bureau said. A government spokesman said both parties had learned lessons from the delays and implemented a series of mechanisms to strengthen railway project governance, supervision and cost control. Jeny Yeung Mei-chun, CEO of the MTR Corp, said the firm had encountered significant difficulties during the course of construction. “The corporation has drawn lessons from the two projects and conducted reviews and rigorous follow-up in light of their specific circumstances,” she said. “Drawing on our extensive experience in railway construction and operations, we will continue to provide the railway infrastructure critical to Hong Kong’s future development and support the city’s long-term sustainable growth.” Smart Transport Alliance director Gary Zhang Xinyu, who is a former lawmaker and MTR Corp engineer, said the roles of the government and the company in the high-speed rail project had been complicated due to the adoption of a concession model, leading to many legal and commercial disputes during delays of work. In this model, the government paid for the construction of the high-speed rail line and owns it, while the MTR Corp was responsible for operating it and paying a concession fee to the government. “The incidents surrounding the high-speed rail and the Sha Tin to Central Link served as a deeply profound lesson for all railway engineers and practitioners in Hong Kong,” said Zhang, who chaired the Legislative Council’s subcommittee on matters relating to railways and handled the issue. “The commercial settlement has now been finalised. More importantly, the government has followed the mainstream advice from the industry, including me, by promising not to take forward new railway projects with the model.” He also said that the government had now turned to the “ownership model” – in which the MTR Corp builds and owns the railroads, while being ultimately responsible for any additional financial burdens – in all ongoing projects.

title: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls Flydubai cockpit attack
description: Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously injured in the attack and is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital.
content: The Indian airline captain who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a Flydubai flight described on Friday how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent. Captain Smit Machchhar, recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a televised video call that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save his passengers. “I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives,” he told Modi. Machchhar, who is from Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero, with world leaders saying he helped avert a disaster. The flight, carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing. Flydubai said on Wednesday that the jet was secured by on-duty crew members “who diverted and landed the aircraft safely”. A regional official said the crew members were pilots in training. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. The motive for the attack was not immediately clear. Modi told Machchhar his “courage, patience, and presence of mind” saved many lives. Machchhar said his flying experience allowed him to sense the plane’s steep descent even after he was knocked down by the attacker. “I have been flying planes for 17 years and serving as a captain for the last 11 years. I can sense exactly what is happening with the aircraft even with my eyes closed. When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting,” he said. Machchhar said that during those difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a Hindu devotional hymn dedicated to Lord Hanuman, the monkey god, and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage. “Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi. Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for Flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet. Philip Kean, CEO of Mainland Air, the New Zealand flight school where Machchhar trained, said pilots are taught how to take over if a fellow crew member becomes incapacitated. But the training does not typically prepare them for a stabbing attack by a colleague, he told Associated Press on Friday. “I don’t think there’s much in the handbook for being stabbed,” Kean said. “You’re friends and you’re flying together,” he said. “Nobody would expect … a person to have a go at you like that.” Meanwhile, Israel was set to begin repatriation flights to bring back passengers stranded in the United Arab Emirates after commercial travel between the two countries was suspended following the attack. Israel and the UAE agreed on the repatriation flights, beginning on Friday, according to an Israeli official who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity. Earlier, the national carrier El Al had said the UAE was holding up the necessary landing permits to allow it to fly into Dubai. The Ben Gurion International Airport in Tel Aviv listed carriers Arkia and Israir with flights scheduled to arrive from Dubai late Friday and early Saturday. El Al was expected to fly passengers from Dubai to Israel on Sunday.

title: McDonald’s sells Hong Kong shop for US$15.3 million as ‘old money’ returns to retail
description: May Cheong toymaker family linked to buyer of first McDonald’s outlet in New Territories; fast-food chain has sold 13 shops for HK$1.2 billion since last year.
content: As “long-dormant old money” steps back into Hong Kong’s retail property market, McDonald’s has sold the property housing its first New Territories restaurant for HK$120 million (US$15.3 million), extending its year-long sell-down of self-owned shops. The property at 10-22 Tsuen Wan Market Street, spanning the ground floor to the second floor, was sold to Keen Charm Holdings (HK) Limited, with the agreement for sale signed on August 31, according to the Land Registry. Company Registry listed Ngan Chi-hung, Ngan Chi-wai and Ngan Tuet-ching as directors of the purchasing vehicle. They are reportedly identified as family members behind a Hong Kong toy manufacturer, May Cheong Group. The family-owned company was founded in 1967 in a small factory in Hong Kong by P.Y. Ngan and Y.C. Ngan, according to its website. The group did not respond to a request for comment. Land Registry records show McDonald’s Restaurants (Hong Kong) Limited bought the property for HK$8 million in 1987, giving the company a HK$112 million gain, or a 14-fold return, on the sale. Shop values in Hong Kong have come under pressure in recent years as the pandemic and shifts in consumer spending have weighed on retail demand, particularly in traditional shopping areas. Eunice Tang, executive director of capital markets at JLL, which is marketing some of the McDonald’s shops, said the sales had attracted interest from “long-dormant old money” and “high-net-worth buyers” seeking prime retail properties backed by blue-chip tenants. “[The interest] is driven largely by the shops’ reputable tenants and extended lease commitments,” Tang said. The restaurant opened in 1978 as the first McDonald’s outlet in the New Territories and the chain’s 11th in Hong Kong. McDonald’s now operates 11 outlets in Tsuen Wan. It will continue operating from the property under a 20-year lease that runs through December 2036, according to the Land Registry. The sale comes as McDonald’s continues to monetise properties accumulated over decades of expansion. The company initially planned to sell all 23 of its self-owned shops in Hong Kong, with the portfolio valued at about HK$3 billion. Since launching the disposal programme in July last year, it has sold at least 13 properties for about HK$1.2 billion, including the latest Tsuen Wan transaction, according to South China Morning Post calculations and Land Registry records. The sales come as transactions for retail properties valued above HK$50 million have remained sluggish in Hong Kong. Industry representatives have estimated that shop mortgage lending has fallen to about 20 per cent of its peak. Landlords have said banks are increasingly reluctant to lend against retail properties, leaving potential buyers unable to secure financing.

title: China’s PLA sets up new military academy colleges for AI, drones and discipline
description: Restructured academies aim to build a technical workforce and strengthen the anti-corruption push across China’s military.
content: China has set up several new institutions at military academies to train specialists in hi-tech and discipline inspection as the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) works towards its centennial modernisation goals. The College of Unmanned and Intelligent Engineering, the College of Combat Support NCOs (Non-Commissioned Officers) and the College of Equipment Support NCOs were established within the PLA Army Engineering University on Wednesday. On the same day, the National Defence University (NDU), the PLA’s highest academy, formally inaugurated the College of Discipline Inspection, Law and Politics at its Xian campus in Shaanxi province. Also on Wednesday, the PLA Joint Logistics Support Force Engineering University, which was launched last year, announced the addition of four colleges and one institute under its umbrella. The PLA AEU, formed in 2017 during President Xi Jinping’s massive military reform, is tasked with training engineering and technical personnel as well as command officers for the PLA Ground Force. The establishment of the College of Unmanned and Intelligent Engineering at the PLA Army Engineering University highlights the military’s growing emphasis on uncrewed systems and artificial intelligence. It coincided with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement on the same day of plans to establish a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command to accelerate the development and deployment of drones, AI and robotic systems across the US military. The creation of the two new NCO colleges – focused on training career soldiers with specialised technical and operational skills at the grass-roots level – underscores the PLA’s efforts to build and retain a more professional military workforce. NDU’s College of Discipline Inspection, Law and Politics was restructured based on the university’s Political College at the Xian campus. The university said missions for the new college included professional training for military discipline inspectors, rule-of-law literacy training for commanders, postgraduate education and military vocational education in relevant specialities, as well as courses on Yanan revolutionary history. The college has been established against the backdrop of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign within the PLA. Numerous senior military officials have been removed in recent years, including five of the seven serving CMC members, with further investigations ongoing. “[The college] will firmly shoulder the significant responsibility of cultivating personnel in discipline and law, vigorously foster a clean and upright environment, and comprehensively pioneer a new phase of development,” NDU political commissar Xia Zhihe said at the inauguration ceremony on Wednesday. The joint logistics university did not give further details about the new colleges and institute in its announcement. After the Joint Logistics Support Force became a service branch of the PLA in 2016, the university was formed in 2025 through the merger of PLA Ground Force’s Logistics Academy and the Military Transport University, including the latter’s affiliated Automobile Cadet College. In its initial undergraduate admission last autumn, the university offered 21 majors – including traditional specialisations such as financial management, auditing, logistics management and military energy engineering – as well as more hi-tech programmes, such as national defence engineering and its intelligentisation, uncrewed equipment engineering and intelligent transport engineering.

title: China stockpiles ASML lithography tools, spurring US calls for complete export ban
description: DUV tools, though not as advanced as EUV, can be adapted to manufacture 7-nm logic chips and advanced memory for AI processors, report says.
content: Chinese semiconductor plants amassed hundreds of immersion lithography machines worth billions of dollars in recent years, according to former US officials, who urged Washington and its allies to shut down further exports. Chinese-owned fabs had acquired an estimated 343 immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems by early 2026, said a report published in late September by the Centre for Technology & Statecraft (CTS), a Washington research group established in August. Co-authored by former US export control official Nicholas Brown and Saif Khan, a former White House and commerce department technology policy adviser, the study adds fresh data to the debate in Washington over whether Western allies should impose a total blockade on immersion DUV tools bound for China. Blocked from buying Dutch toolmaker ASML’s most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools, Chinese chipmakers have leaned heavily on immersion DUV systems – some models of which remain exempt from Western export bans – to produce sophisticated semiconductors. The report estimated that about 270 of the machines acquired by Chinese-owned plants were ASML’s Twinscan NXT:1980i immersion DUV systems. Though technically behind EUV, these tools can be adapted to manufacture 7-nanometre-class logic chips and advanced memory for artificial intelligence processors, including Huawei Technologies’ Ascend series, the authors said. Chinese fabs spent over US$13 billion acquiring about 90 NXT:1980i machines in 2024 and another 89 in 2025, according to the report. The purported buying spree is reflected in ASML’s financial disclosures. China accounted for 41 per cent of the Dutch firm’s net system sales by shipment destination in 2024 and 33 per cent in 2025. Sales to China have since moderated, dropping to 19 per cent of ASML’s total in the first quarter of 2026 and 14 per cent in the second. ASML previously said that its high level of 2024 shipments was partly driven by fulfilling backlogged orders delayed by earlier supply chain constraints. The Netherlands began requiring export licences for ASML’s NXT:2000i and more advanced immersion DUV systems in September 2023. Those models have since been effectively barred from China. It extended the licence requirement to the NXT:1980i a year later, but shipments of that model can still be approved case by case. The report argued that this approach left a major loophole, warning that even tools sold for mature chipmaking nodes can be repurposed or relocated to advanced production lines. To close the loophole, the authors recommended a complete China-wide ban on all immersion DUV equipment, alongside restrictions on replacement parts and servicing at advanced facilities. They suggested Washington coordinate with the Netherlands or unilaterally extend American export rules to foreign-made systems using US tech. The push aligns with growing pressure in US Congress. The bipartisan Match Act, introduced in April, seeks China-wide restrictions on sales and servicing for chipmaking equipment that China cannot easily manufacture at home – explicitly targeting immersion DUV tools. Senators renewed calls for its passage in September, and Khan publicly endorsed the bill earlier this year. While cut-offs would have little immediate impact because Chinese fabs have already built up an inventory of imported tools, the authors argued that the long-term difference would be substantial. Under the study’s most expansive theoretical projection, if China overcame other chipmaking bottlenecks and continued importing about 90 NXT:1980i systems a year, its DUV fleet could support an annual output of up to 434 million AI chips equivalent to Nvidia’s H100 by 2035. Halting new imports in 2027 would cap that ceiling at 153 million units, it said.

title: Hotstone Yoga director arrested over unfair trade practices after abrupt closure
description: Closure also prompted lawmakers to urge authorities to widen scope of proposed statutory cooling-off law to cover wider wellness market.
content: A director of Hotstone Yoga has been arrested on suspicion of contravening the Trade Descriptions Ordinance by accepting prepayments for services before the wellness chain’s abrupt closure, as the amount of financial losses claimed by customers surpassed HK$4 million (US$510,000). The company’s closure on Wednesday has also prompted lawmakers to urge the government to widen the scope of a proposed statutory cooling-off law to cover more sections of the wellness market. Chong Kai-shing, a divisional commander at the Customs and Excise Department who specialises in investigating unfair trade practices, revealed on Friday that the suspect, a 61-year-old male director of the chain, had been apprehended. “We have found the merchant in question was still selling services and courses before its closure, accepting prepayment from customers,” Chong said. “It was suspected to contravene the Trade Descriptions Ordinance by wrongly accepting payment. Namely, when accepting payments, there was no reasonable ground that it could deliver the relevant service within the prescribed time or a reasonable period.” The chain’s closure triggered a backlash from customers who were caught off-guard after pre-purchasing services. Chong said that by 5pm on Friday, the department had received 381 reports in connection with Hotstone’s closure, with the complaints involving losses of HK$4.07 million. The largest reported individual loss stood at HK$46,000, he added. He added that further arrests would not be ruled out. Earlier on Friday, lawmakers urged the government to revise its previous proposals to establish a statutory cooling-off period for prepaid fitness and beauty contracts. Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah previously said authorities hoped to introduce the amendment bill to the Legislative Council in the first half of 2027, although timing remained subject to other agenda priorities. The administration has proposed rolling out a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts. It has also suggested exempting lower-value contracts to minimise disruption, with the threshold ranging from HK$3,000 to HK$15,000 or above. But legislators said the current proposals were too narrowly focused on fitness centres and beauty parlours, leaving consumers unprotected against evolving wellness trends. Lawmaker Jeff Yiu Ming said the legislation needed to keep pace with shifting market trends, pointing out that fitness offerings now included kickboxing, Pilates and yoga. “The government might need to define statutory terms with precision to ensure all emerging wellness concepts fall within the law’s purview,” he said. Lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu also urged the government to expand the scope of the legal framework to protect the rights of the public. “We need a clear overarching legal framework covering all business-to-customer prepaid contracts for future services across all sectors,” he said. Tang added that while government officials assured him that centres offering both yoga and general fitness classes would fall within the scope of the statutory cooling-off period, real-world market operations presented numerous grey areas. Without explicit statutory coverage, “everyday consumers without a legal background are easily left in the dark,” he warned, acknowledging that broader restrictions would likely face pushback from the business sector. A customer who identified herself only as Chan earlier told the South China Morning Post that she understood at least 500 customers had suffered financial losses due to the abrupt closure of Hotstone. A closure notice, issued by law firm Cheung & Co and posted outside the studios, stated the chain was shutting down after careful consideration due to “business operations and other actual circumstances.” It stated the company would cease operations at the end of regular business hours on Wednesday and included an email address for parties holding “rights, debts or other claims against Hotstone” to submit documents. The notice added that affected staff could inquire with the relevant government departments about their rights and file related applications, and Hotstone would provide the necessary documents and information “where reasonably practicable” to facilitate procedures. The company said it would pay outstanding wages for September and refund class fees from that month by October 5. Most of Hotstone’s social media pages were disabled by Thursday afternoon. According to its Threads account, the business operated for 10 years and had studios in Central, Causeway Bay, Aberdeen, Jordan, Tsuen Wan, Sha Tin and Kwun Tong. It also claimed to be the first studio in Hong Kong to provide hot stone yoga sessions, stating it employed more than 100 veteran instructors to teach yoga, stretching, dance and gym classes. The Consumer Council said that as of Friday 5pm, it had received 286 complaints related to the chain’s closure involving claimed losses of HK$3,909,444. Police said they had received multiple reports since October 1 from individuals who claimed to have bought class packages at a local yoga centre that abruptly closed. The case will be referred to relevant departments for follow-up.

title: Chinese language teachers leave the Philippines over safety fears
description: Educational exchanges are in the firing line as tensions between the two countries spill over into the classroom.
content: Around 150 Chinese language teachers in the Philippines are returning home following mounting criticism from Philippine security officials that educational exchanges involving China could pose national security threats. The withdrawal affects teachers stationed at schools including the Immaculate Conception Academy in Greenhills and Jubilee Christian Academy in Quezon City, both in Metro Manila, according to local media. The Manila-based Chinese Commercial News reported on Friday that the inviting organisations – the Philippine Chinese Education Research Centre and the Federation of Filipino-Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry – made the decision after families of Chinese instructors expressed safety concerns amid growing scrutiny of Chinese educational programmes. The report said that Chinese teachers left the Philippines on Thursday. Schools notified parents on Thursday that their Chinese instructors would be returning home, leaving administrators scrambling to maintain language classes using substitute teachers and online classes. The sudden withdrawal underscores how educational exchanges are caught in the crossfire of deteriorating ties between Manila and Beijing, already strained by repeated confrontations in the South China Sea. Chinese-language education has deep roots in the Philippines, where there are an estimated 1.5 million ethnic Chinese Filipinos. Many schools in the community offer Chinese-language instruction but have long struggled to attract the qualified teachers they need. In 1991, the Philippine Chinese Education Research Centre sought to address this shortage by launching a programme to bring instructors from China to teach at Chinese-Filipino schools. In 2004, it also introduced another initiative to send graduates to Chinese universities for language education degrees. The centre partners with several universities to train these professionals, including Jinan University and South China Normal University, both in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou. Yet it is precisely these institutional ties that have drawn attention. The withdrawal comes two months after Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr warned that academic exchange programmes with China risked being exploited as channels for “grey-zone” influence operations. Teodoro also called for tighter supervision by academic bodies to guard against possible national security threats. He renewed such concerns last weekend, telling the media that China could use educational collaborations and academic links as tools for information collection. “We have seen, too, information regarding the use of these educational exchanges to gain a foothold into the Philippines in order for them to scope for information,” Teodoro said, while cautioning against discrimination against Chinese people due to security concerns. His comments followed a report in July by SeaLight, a maritime transparency initiative, which identified Jinan University in Guangzhou as the “single largest training site” for Chinese teachers entering Philippine schools. The report alleged that the university maintained strong links to Beijing’s political influence network and played a key role in shaping Chinese-language education in the Philippines through teacher training, curriculum design and career placement. Beijing has singled out Teodoro for particularly harsh criticism, imposing sanctions against the defence secretary. It said Teodoro had repeatedly made erroneous remarks against China, undermined its legitimate interests and damaged bilateral relations. Last week, the Chinese embassy in Manila lashed out at him again, branding him “extremely anti-China”. “Teodoro aims to interfere with and undermine China-Philippines relations, sever the friendship between the Chinese and Filipino people, and create antagonism between the two countries and their people,” the embassy said in a statement on Sunday.

title: Chinese designers make a bold statement at London Fashion Week 2026
description: London Fashion Week featured the most Chinese designers in years. Here are looks from the likes of Yuhan Wang and less-established talents.
content: London Fashion Week drew the clothing crowd from New York to the British capital to see the highly anticipated return of Alexander McQueen and the debut of Christopher Kane at Mulberry. The event, which ran from September 17 to 21, showcased memorable collections from Erdem, Roksanda, Simone Rocha and Pauline Dujancourt. The week was rounded off by Burberry designer Daniel Lee’s collaboration with textile designer Celia Birtwell. London Fashion Week has since also become a platform for the Chinese fashion diaspora, many of whom studied at Central Saint Martins or the London College of Fashion. The spring/summer 2027 showcase saw one of London Fashion Week’s longest lists of Chinese creatives since before the Covid-19 pandemic, with eight designers on the official roster including Susan Fang and Yuhan Wang alongside young talents Oscar Ouyang and Yuhan Ao. Mithridate was also there. Founded in 2018 by Tina Jiang and headquartered in Guangzhou, in China’s Guangdong province, the label hired British designer Daniel Fletcher – formerly creative director of the Italian jeans and street style label Fiorucci – in 2025. Collegiate looks, military detailing, tartan, pencil skirts and Sex and the City-esque pink tutus made the latest collection feel rooted in the New Romantic movement that took off in London in the 1970s. Romanticism and femininity are the cornerstones of Susan Fang and Yuhan Wang’s aesthetics. Wang, from Weihai in China’s Shandong province, launched her eponymous label in 2018. Fang, from Ningbo in China’s Zhejiang province, established her label in 2017. She has shown at Shanghai Fashion Week and, in 2025, was selected to present in Milan, where she was supported by Dolce & Gabbana. Fang now splits her year between London and Shanghai: “China is home and family while London is where I found my direction,” she says. “London is a great support for creativity, and I feel so much creative energy here, but I think Shanghai is also growing its own fashion direction.” Handicraft and technology underpin Fang’s collections, from floral appliqués to 3D-printed sandals. Fang’s new collection, called Air-Illusion, featured the Chinese qipao silhouette in a nod to the 1993 film M. Butterfly, which is loosely based on Puccini’s opera Madama Butterfly. The film and opera are interpretations of the true story of a French diplomat who fell in love with a Chinese opera singer, who was, in fact, a male spy. Fang will design the costumes for the 2027 rendition of the opera at Belgium’s federal opera house La Monnaie / De Munt and this collaboration fuelled her latest collection. Air-Illusion’s qipao silhouettes were embellished with organza and plastic butterfly-like petal appliqués, and blue-and-white digital prints were inspired by Chinese porcelain. Secret letters and numbers were hidden in the prints. Broken pieces of porcelain adorned models’ hair, while earrings made in collaboration with a Beijing-based jade master carver adorned their ears. Fang credits the handcrafted element in her designs to her mother, who knitted her clothes as a child. Fang herself loves to crochet. “We always have handicraft; even though we use technology [3D and digital printing], we always hope the two harmonise and that you can always see the craft element,” she says. Wang dialled up her signature femininity in her latest collection, called Sweet Nightmare, with dreamy garments that blurred the lines between lingerie and daywear. Loungewear has always been part of her design vocabulary since her graduation collection of men’s pyjamas, “but now it is more feminine”, she says, adding that her collections these days are inspired by traditional Chinese ideas of femininity and their connections with Western culture. Sweet Nightmare is about that strange wandering state of mind just before sleep. “It is about exploring the inner world of a woman and using her bedroom to present her personal, private space separate from how she is expected to be or exist,” Wang says. “It’s about her desires, emotions and memories.” Wang’s designs combined sensuous silky camisoles and French underwear with tiny cardigans, satin bras pinned to T-shirts, and babydolls and nightdresses worn with half-unravelled stockings and leather court shoes. To this, Wang added hairbrushes and combs tucked into waistbands and a floral cup and saucer for that late-night cuppa. The collection portrayed innocence but also desire. Ouyang and Ao combined menswear and womenswear in a neo-romantic way. Beijing-born knitwear specialist Ouyang graduated in 2023, and describes his third fashion week outing as akin to a house party where kids have been let loose in the attic with heirloom clothes to chop up and concoct new looks. “It’s about reinventing the classics,” he says. This ethos resulted in tailoring, flounced shirts, reconfigured waistcoats, chopped-up dresses and embroidered men’s shorts seemingly cut from an evening gown. Ao made his second fashion week appearance with a menswear show inspired by the 19th century French poet and libertine Arthur Rimbaud. Ao, who graduated with an MA in menswear in 2024, is obsessed with the cut of trousers and fabrics. “I grew up in a linen textile company in Jiangxi [in southeastern China], where I watched my grandfather and grandmother spinning linen fibres by hand,” he says. “It taught me that I needed to respect the process, as did my internship in Savile Row.” He wants to honour those craft processes and wants his audience to “love and respect them, too”. Ao referenced his heritage with flax fibres woven into his models’ hair and fabrics woven from Chinese-grown ramie with mohair he developed with his mother. His jackets were loose cut and featured white topstitching details from the tailoring process, while his women’s jackets were nipped in and slipped over voluminous miniskirts. It is early days for Ao and Ouyang, but London Fashion Week showed its relevance as a launch pad for talented new designers.

title: India’s Modi faces dual pressure from ‘cockroach’ movement, opposition parties
description: The two groups’ objection to the revised voter rolls has fuelled speculation that they could become a new potent political force.
content: India’s opposition parties and the youth-led “cockroach” movement took to the streets on Friday, demanding action over alleged irregularities in voter rolls and calling for the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, as the combined pressure from the two groups poses a new challenge for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government. The protests have brought the opposition closer to the youth movement that it has sought to engage with, according to analysts. While their convergence could boost India’s fragmented opposition, turning it into a lever to yield concessions from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would be harder, they added. Leaders of around 20 parties in the opposition India National Developmental Inclusive Alliance, or INDIA, rallied against the Election Commission’s revised voter rolls, which critics say have potentially removed millions of eligible voters from the electoral register. Chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has come under scrutiny after The Indian Express reported last month that he bypassed two other election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, before the revision. The two commissioners had repeatedly raised objections to aspects of the process, including deletion and addition of voters, according to the report. The Election Commission has rejected suggestions of an internal crisis, saying all three commissioners approved the changes and that their different views are normal during its deliberations. In addition to calling for Kumar’s exit, the main opposition Congress Party has demanded Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah resign, saying they have no “moral right” to remain in office. Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator, said the success of the student-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had given the opposition momentum in seeking more public support. The movement emerged in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to people with fake or bogus degrees as “cockroaches”, remarks that were widely interpreted as a swipe at young Indians facing problems with education and employment. Kant later clarified that he was not referring to Indian youth, but by then the “cockroach” label had taken on a life of its own, with young protesters adopting it to mobilise and air their grievances over jobs and the country’s educational institutions Thousands of students and young supporters joined CJP demonstrations across New Delhi and other cities in June and July, protesting a medical entrance exam paper leak and other alleged irregularities in the examination system and demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. After weeks of protests, Pradhan resigned on July 25, handing the movement a significant victory. The opposition has sought to ride on the movement’s momentum. Several INDIA parties have backed CJP’s protests and demands, although the movement has maintained that it is not part of the opposition alliance. Snigdha Sony, who works as a senior researcher on labour and migration issues after completing her master’s degree in development studies from Delhi University, said she supported the demand for Kumar’s resignation and the cockroach movement’s protests, hoping they could lead to changes in the entrance examination system. Ramaswamy said: “The opposition’s calls are making sense among citizens, and that is echoing through the non-political organisations like the cockroach movement.” The examination issue is unlikely to pose a serious threat to the government, according to Ramaswamy. New Delhi would not agree to demands for the chief election officer’s resignation weeks after the education minister’s resignation, as doing so would signal its weakness, he added. However, he warned: “If the government resists the cockroach movement or tries to suppress it, it could burst into a larger issue.” Who leads the opposition? The INDIA opposition alliance lacked the wherewithal to leverage the issue compared with the BJP’s well-oiled machinery and strong backing from its ideological mentor, the Hindu group Rashtriya Swayamsewak Sangh, Ramaswamy said. “There is consensus among them [the opposition parties] on national issues, but they don’t have continuity. When it comes to elections in states, they fight among themselves,” he added. “They don’t have one central key figure.” Several Indian states are due to hold elections next year, including Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat, Manipur and Goa. Rahul Gandhi, the main opposition Congress Party’s de facto leader, may have gained in stature in recent months as a political leader, but he is not a top contender to replace Modi as the country’s leader, according to Ramaswamy. Kingshuk Nag, an author and independent political commentator, said: “Gandhi is gaining support, but not enough. Not many people see him as a guy who can take over from Modi. Modi is seen as far smarter than him.” The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance is currently serving a historic third consecutive term in office. Modi is the second leader in Indian history – and the first outside the Indian National Congress – to have won three straight general elections in 2024. After the BJP lost its outright majority in the last parliamentary election and had to rely on its allies to remain in power, it went on to secure victories in important state elections including West Bengal, Bihar and Delhi. Nag said there was uncertainty over how 76-year-old Modi could handle the responsibilities of the top job at his age. Nilanjan Mukhopadhay, an independent political commentator, said that given the BJP coalition’s slim parliamentary majority, it would have to be more accommodating to the demands of Indian voters. Calling the parallel protests by the opposition and the student-led cockroach movement a positive development, Mukhopadhyay added: “In terms of democracy, this is a good sign. It paves the way for the government and ruling party to be more consensual in nature.”

title: National Day travel surge drives China’s highway EV charging volume up 60% to new high
description: Average daily EV travel volume during the holiday could be 1.6 times the usual level as road travel will be more than 90 per cent of all trips.
content: China’s EV charging volume on its highways hit a new high on the first day of the seven-day National Day holiday, as the country’s rapidly expanding electric vehicle fleet drives up demand for charging infrastructure. Single-day charging volume reached 28 million kWh, a 60.4 per cent increase compared with the first day of last year’s National Day holiday, marking the highest one day level during a national holiday period, according to a statement issued by the National Energy Administration on Friday. China kicked off its “golden week” holiday on Thursday, one of the busiest periods for transport, as the long break – along with toll-free highway travel for passenger cars – sees millions of people head off around the country. The average daily EV travel volume during this year’s National Day holiday could reach 1.6 times the usual level – around 9.8 million trips on a normal day – as road travel was expected to account for more than 90 per cent of all trips during the holiday, transport officials said at a press conference last week. There were around 49 million EVs on roads in China as of the end of June, accounting for 13.19 per cent of all vehicles, up 2.92 percentage points year on year, according to official data. As China’s EV fleet has expanded rapidly in recent years, a shortage of charging facilities has remained a challenge, especially during national holidays when peak travel adds additional pressure on the charging infrastructure. Beijing has been working to ease the shortage. In the first eight months of this year, China added 11,000 high-power charging guns for EVs on highways, a figure equivalent to the total added in all previous years combined, according to transport officials at last week’s press conference. The country also aimed to double the number of charging stations to more than 40 million by 2030, up from 20 million at the end of 2025, according to a five-year plan for China’s power system released in July. That would be able to meet the charging needs of 110 million electric vehicles.

title: Clara Chan retains helm at HKIC as HK$62b state fund aligns with city’s 5-year plan
description: As of August, 11 firms from HKIC’s portfolio had gone public locally, with 30 more having applied or planning to apply for a listing.
content: Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC) has extended the tenure of its current CEO, Clara Chan Ka-chai, for another three years as the city vows to boost emerging industries in its first five-year plan. The wholly government-owned investment vehicle, which manages HK$62 billion (US$7.9 billion) in funds, announced that Chan would stay on as head through October 2029, according to a statement on Friday. “I look forward to Clara’s continued leadership of the HKIC over the next three years, contributing to the growth of Hong Kong’s financial sector, innovation and technology sector and emerging industries, while supporting the development of the Northern Metropolis and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area,” said Financial Secretary and HKIC board chairman Paul Chan Mo-po in a statement. The reappointed CEO said she would remain committed to “harnessing the power of patient capital to support Hong Kong’s long-term development”. “I firmly believe that amidst this pivotal window of strategic development of Hong Kong, the HKIC could play our part in leveraging Hong Kong’s strengths to serve the national needs, contributing to the high-quality development of Hong Kong and our country,” Clara Chan said in a separate statement. The strengthening of emerging industries and the planning for future industries were included in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan unveiled by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in mid-September. Under the plan, Hong Kong would guide “patient capital investment” and other financial resources into frontier industries and technology development, together with government funding schemes. As of September, HKIC had invested in over 200 projects since its inception, including Beijing-based humanoid robot start-up Galbot, artificial intelligence-driven drug developer Insilico Medicine and sustainable aviation fuel maker EcoCeres. Chan was appointed HKIC’s first CEO in 2023, after the government-backed vehicle was established in 2022 to channel medium- to long-term funds to support the development of the city’s innovation, technology and strategic industries. The initial funding of HK$62 billion is being allocated to four sub-funds, including the “Hong Kong Growth Portfolio”, “Greater Bay Area Investment Fund”, “Strategic Tech Fund”, and “Co-Investment Fund”, with themes covering hard technology, biotech and new energy. As of August, 11 firms from HKIC’s portfolio had gone public on the local bourse, with 30 more having applied or planning to apply for a listing in the city this year, Chan said at an earlier event. Dubbed Hong Kong’s version of Singapore’s Temasek Holdings, HKIC said that for every Hong Kong dollar it invested it had attracted more than HK$8 from global institutional investors including sovereign funds, pension funds, family offices and university funds. Last year, HKIC’s operating profit surged 181 per cent year on year to HK$6.3 billion, while total assets expanded 9 per cent to HK$69.7 billion over the same period. The net internal rate of return, which was disclosed for the first time, stood at 14 per cent, according to the investment vehicle’s second annual report released in July.

title: Taiwan hails F-16V delivery as sign US support holds after Xi-Trump summit
description: While the ruling party welcomed the arrival of two jets, the opposition KMT criticised delays to the fighter programme.
content: Taiwan has hailed the much-delayed arrival of two F-16V fighter jets as a demonstration of continuing American military support, despite a US presidential hold put on a separate multibilllion-dollar arms package. The two single-seat aircraft, which reached Chihhang Air Base in the eastern county of Taitung on Friday, are the first new F-16s received by the island since deliveries of its original F-16A/B fleet began in 1997. Compared with the earlier versions, the F-16V configuration incorporates the Northrop Grumman APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, updated avionics and improved target detection and tracking capabilities. The pair are part of a NT$247.2 billion (US$7.76 billion) sale of 66 F-16Vs approved by Washington in August 2019, during US President Donald Trump’s first term. The two jets had been expected to arrive in Taiwan in late August, about a month before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States last week. Neither Taipei nor Washington has given a public explanation for the delay. A separate weapons package for Taipei worth about US$14 billion, which has cleared informal congressional review, remains on hold pending presidential approval. Friday’s delivery was hailed by Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) after Trump’s warm welcome for Xi caused some uncertainty on the island. Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te thanked Washington for its “long-term support” for Taiwan’s self-defence and for continuing to deepen security cooperation between the two sides. He also linked the delivery to regional stability, saying it showed the US commitment to “working with Indo-Pacific partners, including Taiwan, to advance security”. Chen Kuan-ting, a DPP legislator, also said the delivery showed that there had been “no structural change” in US arms sales since the summit. By contrast, opposition Kuomintang legislator Ma Wen-chun said the planes’ arrival should not distract from the delays to the programme, urging the defence ministry to provide a clear schedule for the remaining aircraft. “Two have arrived; the remaining 64 must arrive on time,” she said. Taiwan’s defence ministry had originally hoped to take delivery of all 66 fighters by the end of the year, but the programme has fallen far behind schedule. Taiwanese officials have cited production-line relocation and supply chain disruptions among the main factors affecting the timetable. Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung said on Friday that further F-16Vs would be handed over by the end of the year, without offering a specific number. The journey of the first two fighters was itself unexpectedly drawn out. They left the United States mainland on August 17 and reached Joint Base Pearl Harbour-Hickam in Hawaii on August 21, using aerial refuelling for the trans-Pacific journey. They had been expected to continue towards Taiwan within days but instead remained at the base for almost six weeks. Taiwanese media and military observers raised several possible explanations, including technical problems, adverse weather and the unavailability of tanker aircraft. The unexplained delay also prompted speculation in Taiwan that Washington may have wanted to avoid a politically sensitive delivery shortly before Xi’s state visit to the United States. Taiwan’s United Daily News, citing an unnamed source, reported this week that after an equipment problem delayed the aircraft in Hawaii, Washington did not want the delivery to create further complications around Xi’s visit. Neither US nor Taiwanese authorities have linked the delivery timing to Xi’s Washington visit. The South China Morning Post reported before Xi’s Washington visit that the administration was considering postponing major new Taiwan arms sales, with sources saying Beijing had privately pressed Washington to refrain from approving new deals around Xi’s trip. The US$14 billion weapons package had already been put on hold earlier this year, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressing that Washington must also take account of its own military requirements, production capacity and the need to replenish weapons stocks when considering arms sales. During the summit with Trump last week, Xi reiterated hopes that the US would oppose “Taiwan independence”, and handle the Taiwan question with caution. The US State Department sought to stress that broader US policy towards Taiwan remained unchanged after the summit. Taiwan has placed considerable importance on the F-16V programme as it seeks to strengthen its air force amid increasing People’s Liberation Army activity around the island and growing demands on its existing fighter fleet. Taiwan has already upgraded its older F-16A/B fleet to the F-16V configuration, including installing the APG-83 radar, so the new aircraft do not introduce those capabilities to the air force for the first time. But the purchase adds 66 newly built fighters rather than relying solely on upgraded aircraft whose airframes date from the 1990s. The new jets also incorporate airframes designed for a longer service life and have conformal fuel tanks that increase fuel capacity without occupying underwing weapon stations.

title: Who is Chad Lowe’s wife, Kim Painter? What to know as the couple mourns their daughter, Fiona
description: Fiona Lowe, who tragically died at age 13, was the second daughter of Lowe and Painter – the couple met through their connection to Star Wars actress Carrie Fisher.
content: On September 29, actor Chad Lowe and his family, which includes his wife Kim Painter, 52, announced the passing of their 13-year-old daughter Fiona Hepler Lowe. A medical examiner determined the cause of death to be suicide, People magazine reported on October 1. In a statement shared with People, Fiona’s heartbroken family described her as “a loving young girl who was smart, creative, and loved to dance”. She had an older sister, Mabel, 17, and a younger sister, Nixie Barbara, 10. “She was adored by her sisters, and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives,” read the family’s statement, which also included contact information for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the US. Another source told People that Fiona had a “very artistic soul” and that her friends are mourning her loss. Meanwhile, journalist Rob Shuter has exclusively revealed on his Substack that Chad Lowe’s older brother, Rob Lowe, 62, “dropped everything” to support his 58-year-old sibling during this difficult time. Early last year, the Lowe family also lost their home in the Pacific Palisades Fire. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chad Lowe (@ichadlowe) So, what do we know about Fiona’s mother and Chad Lowe’s wife, Kimberly Painter? What is Kim Painter’s background? Painter grew up in Maryland, according to her bio on the Geffen Playhouse website. She attended Severna Park High School and later studied writing and photography at Salisbury State University, per her LinkedIn. She eventually moved to Los Angeles to pursue freelance photography before venturing into the entertainment industry. What does Kim Painter do? Painter began her Hollywood career in 1997, working as an assistant at Jerry Bruckheimer Films, per her LinkedIn. She was an assistant producer on Conversations from the Edge with Carrie Fisher and worked with the Star Wars actress on her 2004 novel The Best Awful There Is. In 2006, she co-produced Fisher’s one-woman show Wishful Drinking, followed by the 2010 documentary of the same name. She was the actress’ executive assistant. Additionally, Painter worked as a still photographer for the 2002 film Ted Bundy and a casting director for 2005’s Instant Dads. How did Chad Lowe and Kim Painter meet? Lowe crossed paths with Painter while reaching out to Carrie Fisher for a function he was organising, he told TV Guide in 2007. His divorce from Hilary Swank was finalised that year. “We clearly had a fancy for one another and decided that maybe we should go and have coffee,” Lowe recalled. The couple welcomed their first daughter, Mabel, in May 2009 and tied the knot in August the following year. Fiona was born in November 2012, and Nixie followed in March 2016. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Chinese woman, 60, becomes gaming streamer after playing to understand son’s addiction
description: Zhong and her son’s roles have reversed; she dedicates significant time to gaming, and he prevents her from playing too late into the night.
content: A 60-year-old woman in southern China has defied public stereotypes surrounding senior citizens by becoming a popular e-game live-streamer. Zhong Juanjuan, affectionately known as Auntie Juan by internet users, has amassed 527,000 followers on social media. She hosts two daily live-streaming sessions, each typically attracting around 10,000 viewers, as reported by Beijing News. Zhong, who lives in a suburban area of Meizhou in Guangdong province, only began playing computer games six years ago. Before that, she held various part-time jobs, including sales and childcare, due to her limited educational background, having only completed primary school. She retired about 10 years ago, according to the report. Once, Zhong viewed e-games as a foe to her family. Two decades ago, when her younger son was a secondary school student, he became addicted to gaming, which resulted in a significant drop in his grades. She recollects the many times she visited local internet cafes in search of her son, often dragging him out by force. This led to a prolonged feud between them regarding his gaming hobby. In 2020, Zhong developed an interest in e-games when she observed her son, known as Suode, spending long hours gaming at home after leaving his job. Curious about what fascinated him so much, she decided to explore this world herself. Suode was surprised by his mother’s new-found enthusiasm but patiently taught her how to play. Unsurprisingly, Zhong struggled, grappling with her declining vision and slower reaction time. Suode noted that in the initial days, his mother had difficulty moving in a straight line within the game world, turning around upon hitting walls, or climbing stairs. However, Zhong, who refused to give up, dedicated herself to relentless practice. Feeling confident in her gaming abilities, Zhong began live-streaming in 2022. Viewers were delighted to discover that she, looking like an ordinary rural grandmother using basic live-streaming equipment, played remarkably well, often employing gaming terminology specific to younger players. To date, Zhong has amassed over 8,000 hours of gameplay, specialising in shooting games. Her rise to fame came in December 2024 when she was invited to participate in an online exhibition match for the game Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO). Her competition included a 17-year-old Russian prodigy known by his alias “donk”, a world champion just before their match. In a surprising twist, Zhong managed to eliminate him in the game. Over the years, Zhong has faced scepticism. Some internet users questioned whether a younger individual was secretly playing on her behalf. To dispel these doubts, Suode set up multiple cameras to film his mother from different angles while she engaged in gameplay. While some criticised her passion at her age, Zhong responded, stating: “As a mother, should I only be relegated to household chores?” Now, Zhong’s son serves as her full-time agent, and their roles have reversed from two decades ago: the mother dedicates significant time to gaming, while the son ensures the internet is turned off at midnight each day to prevent her from playing too late into the night. Zhong expressed pride in having been recognised at a wet market by a middle-aged man who told her: “Auntie Juan, I saw you playing games on social media.” “Many say that women of a certain age should take care of their grandchildren or join square dancing. But gaming sharpens the brain and enhances hand-eye coordination. Isn’t that better than idling around?” Zhong argued. “It is never too late to start learning something new.”

title: AirAsia chief mocks Singapore Airlines’ food – and social media hits back
description: Tony Fernandes claimed AirAsia’s in-flight meals beat Singapore Airlines’, but travellers tell him to concentrate on fixing flight delays.
content: AirAsia co-founder Tony Fernandes has caused a stir online after taking aim at Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) in-flight meals, claiming the food served by the carrier lagged behind his own airline’s offerings. “Just flew with Singapore Airlines, couldn’t get AirAsia, service was great, internet amazing, food was poor, Santan is far far better and crew admitted. Great flight but we are not far off,” Fernandes wrote in a social media post on Thursday, referring to AirAsia’s in-flight dining brand. The post included a photo of his meal, which looked like noodles served with beef and vegetables, and a photo of himself on board a Singapore Airlines flight. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tony Fernandes (@tonyfernandes) Social media users were quick to flood the comments section. While some agreed that Santan offered a good selection, most said that passengers did not choose an airline just for its meals. “Santan food is good, but the delay? Still far from SQ,” read one comment, referencing Singapore Airlines by its airline code. “While food on AirAsia is great, nothing else is, I’m afraid,” another user wrote. “Considering all things, especially delays, service, cancellations and accountability, give me Singapore Airlines anytime.” Complaints about unpunctuality were a common theme in the comments. “We’re taking a flight, not going to a restaurant to compare how delicious the food is. What passengers care about is getting to the destination on time and having a reliable flight schedule,” one said. “Constant rescheduling, long delays, and even cancellations are what frustrate passengers the most. AirAsia, please wake up and focus on the basics – respecting passengers’ time.” According to data from the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia, around 87 per cent of AirAsia’s domestic flights departed on time in August, compared with Malaysia Airlines’ 97 per cent. However, when looking at reliability, only about 67 per cent of domestic AirAsia flights and 65 per cent of international AirAsia X flights operated as scheduled. One user poked fun at the chief executive directly: “Couldn’t get your own flight cos it was delayed? Or cancelled? Yah ... I feel you bro, been there too.” Fernandes is well known for his unconventional antics. In AirAsia’s early days, he was often seen passing out food and drinks to passengers on board. In 2013, he famously won a bet with Virgin Atlantic founder Richard Branson, resulting in the British billionaire donning a female flight attendant uniform in AirAsia’s signature colours and serving passengers. In 2024, videos of Fernandes dancing solo – captioned “when a billionaire hires you as his private DJ” – went viral. He also had the internet buzzing in 2023 after posting a photo of himself shirtless and being massaged during an online call. Fernandes’ latest post comes just days after Singapore Airlines – which was named the world’s best airline of 2026 last month by Skytrax – released its new SIA Chef’s Selection menu, featuring more than 100 dishes across all cabin classes. Economy class passengers can now choose dishes such as oriental-style fish with yellow bean sauce and roasted chicken breast, while those in business and first class have options that include Indonesian jackfruit opor (a coconut-based gravy) with blue pea rice and beef short rib in sambal percik (spicy chilli sauce), The Straits Times reported. Some of the new dishes are already being served on board, with the other dining upgrades such as new drinks and tableware being introduced from November. The new menu was developed based on “customer feedback, evolving preferences and emerging dining trends”, the airline told the Asia One news website. “The result is a combination of thoughtfully crafted dishes, carefully curated beverages, elegant serviceware and thoughtful touches that make dining on board more memorable for our customers,” said Yeoh Phee Teik, Singapore Airlines’ senior vice-president of customer experience.

title: Hundreds of French high schools shut as new violence erupts
description: Students have been protesting excessively long school hours, inadequate conditions, and excessive staff absences.
content: French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating. The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police. The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions are inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences. The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast – with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said “the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups”, adding that nearly 400 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country were expected to be closed on Friday. Many high schools have also planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille. At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV. Some 170 students have been wounded while over 100 high schools have suffered “severe damage”. “Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go” to the protests, he added. “What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger.” Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and “pay for repairs”. Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody” – 90 per cent of whom were minors”, Darmanin said. In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence. “As far as we’re concerned, we’ve won – our school is closed this morning,” said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name. She condemned what she said was police violence. “It makes us even angrier – the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us.” Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said. The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) – whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency – of being behind the movement. But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of “descending into conspiracy theories”. In a bid to ease tensions, Geffray said he was on Friday meeting with education unions and high school student associations to find common ground for dialogue.

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Antonelli aims to bounce back from ‘worst weekend’, faces rain test
description: After a qualifying crash in Azerbaijan last week, Italian competition leader now faces an abrasive asphalt track, potentially heavy rain.
content: Kimi Antonelli will have to deal with an unfamiliar track and potentially heavy rain as he aims to recover from the “worst weekend” of his 2026 Formula 1 title challenge. The unusually named Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia takes Antonelli and his rivals to a track Formula 1 last visited in 2017 – when he was 11 – in a race hurriedly added to the calendar because of the disruption caused by the Iran war. It will take place at the Sepang International Circuit, about 60 kilometres (35 miles) south of central Kuala Lumpur. With rain possible on all three days of on-track action, it could be the first real wet race since Formula 1 shook up its regulations for the 2026 season, and the abrasive asphalt tends to chew up tires, too. Antonelli still has a dominant 66-point lead over teammate George Russell, but that was trimmed from 81 last week after his crash in qualifying made for damage limitation in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Antonelli scrambled from 16th on the grid to finish fifth, helped by plenty of incidents ahead of him, while Russell held off Max Verstappen for his first win in almost three months. “Last weekend was probably the worst weekend from me, from my side of the season,” Antonelli said. “ After the race, I wasn’t happy with the result and everything, but I learned many things and the most important is that I need to always be 100 per cent. “I need to really do my best to achieve the best result because if I don’t do everything right, or I don’t try to do everything right in my power, then nothing is going to come my way.” Russell has made no secret of his struggles in getting used to the 2026 cars as he has had to watch his younger teammate dominate week in, week out. After using the midseason break to change his approach, a process he has likened to a golfer getting used to a new swing, Russell finally seemed comfortable in Azerbaijan. He went fastest by almost a second in qualifying, and his narrow margin of victory over Verstappen in the race owed more to an unusual yellow-flag decision on track than anything else. Mercedes have brought a package of upgrades to their car for this week, something Russell said could help him. “I’m enjoying it more than I have done recently because I just feel more at one with the car and hopefully this new upgrade with a few characteristic changes that will also play into my favour a bit more,” he said on Thursday. “Bring it on.” Lewis Hamilton, meanwhile, said Ferrari remained united as he criticised attempts to “break our spirit” after the Italian brand confirmed they retained confidence in Fred Vasseur as team principal. “Outside sources seem to be so negative towards us as a team and trying to break our spirit, but they’re not succeeding,” Hamilton said. The latest speculation over Vasseur’s future came after former Red Bull boss Christian Horner told the Times of London last week that Ferrari were the only team in F1 he would consider joining without an ownership stake, calling it “the dream” and a “sleeping giant”. On the track, Ferrari are struggling, with no podium finishes in the past five races for Hamilton or Charles Leclerc. Verstappen, meanwhile, was fastest on Friday in the first practice session in a time of one minute, 37.520 seconds on a dry track and under often blue skies. Russell was in second, 0.0383 seconds behind, with Antonelli in fifth, just over a second behind Verstappen. A second practice session will be held later on Friday ahead of a third practice session and qualifying on Saturday for Sunday’s race. The forecast is for thunderstorms on Saturday but mostly dry on race day.

title: Why Sabah has Malaysia watching South China Sea tensions more closely
description: The proximity of US-backed Philippine bases on Balabac Island has raised concerns in Malaysia of a possible spillover in a regional conflict.
content: Malaysia’s long-standing strategy of non-alignment amid US-China rivalry in the South China Sea could soon be tested, with the eastern state of Sabah sitting near a potential flashpoint involving Philippine territory. Observers pointed to comments by Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin, who last week voiced concern that a conflict or “unexpected incident” in the maritime region could spill over into Malaysia. Khaled, who singled out Sabah, added that Malaysia was looking to strengthen its national defence as a precautionary measure. “We know the challenges in the South China Sea and the rivalry between major powers. If something happens in that geographically small area, it could also affect our country,” local media quoted Khaled as saying on Saturday. The Philippines and the US have deepened defence cooperation since 2014, including by expanding American military access to Philippine facilities under the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) as tensions with China have mounted. Two of the nine EDCA sites accessible to US forces are in Palawan, an island province north of Sabah. They include Antonio Bautista Air Base in Puerto Princesa and Naval Station Narciso Del Rosario on Balabac Island. The sites remain under Philippine control and while they do not function as permanent US bases, the agreement allows American forces rotational access. Balabac, the southernmost EDCA site and closest to Sabah, is being developed to include a 3km (1.86 mile) military runway. About 50km (31 miles) away lies Banggi Island, the northernmost part of Sabah state that sits at the southern end of the so-called first island chain – a Cold War-era American defence concept describing an arc of islands extending from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines and Malaysia that act as a strategic bottleneck for China’s navy. Hoo Chiew-Ping, a senior fellow at the East Asian International Relations Caucus, said this proximity meant Malaysia could no longer ignore the possibility of a conflict spreading southwards even as it sought to remain non-aligned. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim raised concerns over Balabac in August, pledging to strengthen Malaysia’s defences in response to the growing US-backed Philippine military presence on the nearby island. “As a neighbouring country closely affected by claims over Sabah, we are somewhat concerned with the tension, even though our bilateral relations with the Philippines remain very good,” Anwar said on August 18. Malaysia could not match the scale of military facilities being developed on Balabac, he said, noting a need to strengthen basic defensive capabilities as the regional security environment became increasingly shaped by US-China competition. Hoo said Malaysian defence and security strategists had yet to fully recognise this reality despite long-term defence cooperation with the US, including extensive joint military exercises in these areas. “The assumption that a US-China military confrontation could occur near Borneo stems from concerns over a Taiwan Strait contingency, where the Philippines would become the immediate frontline,” Hoo said. “If the conflict is about Taiwan, strategic space will become extremely narrow.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. While a major conflict would inevitably add pressure on countries to choose sides, Hoo said Malaysia would make every effort to stay out of it, prioritising protecting and evacuating its citizens instead. She argued that Malaysia’s existing defence relationship with Washington gave both countries established channels to discuss concerns over US deployments and regional escalation, rather than addressing them through public political statements that could reflect “limited substantive bilateral dialogue”. Over the years, Malaysia has maintained close defence ties with both Washington and Beijing. Malaysia has taken part in joint drills with the US for more than three decades, including maritime exercises such as Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training. This July, nearly 2,850 Malaysian, US and Australian personnel took part in Exercise Keris Strike in Kota Belud, Sabah, involving tactical and live-fire drills aimed at strengthening interoperability. In October 2025, Malaysian and Chinese forces held the Aman Youyi exercise in the Strait of Malacca, including maritime interdictions, search-and-rescue and surveillance drills between the Malaysian and Chinese navies. Innocent passage? Distancing itself from any conflict would require Malaysia to enforce its neutrality consistently against both sides, said Mohd Hazmi Mohd Rusli, a maritime law expert at the Islamic Science University of Malaysia. Hazmi said Malaysia should also make its position clear in advance so both Washington and Beijing understood the limits of what it would allow. “If a US-China conflict spills over near Sabah, Malaysia … should not allow its territory, territorial sea or airspace to be used by either side to conduct hostile military operations,” he said. But Malaysia’s exclusive economic zone would present a different challenge, Hazmi said, as other states retained freedom of navigation and overflight under international law. Foreign warships could still pass through Malaysia’s territorial waters during an armed conflict provided that their passage remained “innocent”, he added, referring to Article 19 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia, said the conundrum for Southeast Asian states would revolve around requests by rival powers for logistical support or access to facilities in the event of a conflict. “Their acquiescence or refusal will be seen by either big power as alternately friendly or hostile,” Oh said. Andrea Passeri, a programme director for international relations at Taylor’s University in Malaysia, said there was a “breaking point” where maintaining non-alignment would become difficult if the rivalry escalated into open conflict. “Non-alignment would not vanish as a principle, but it would become much harder for Malaysia and many Southeast Asian states to sustain in practice,” Passeri said, adding that even states seeking autonomy could find their waters and airspace increasingly important for military access and surveillance. The pressure could also expose internal fault lines within Asean, he said, with the Philippines pulled directly towards Washington while other members faced pressure to clarify positions they had deliberately kept ambiguous. “Consensus becomes harder precisely when collective diplomacy is most needed,” Passeri added. Such pressures could also deepen existing divisions within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, whose 11 member states maintain vastly different relationships with Washington and Beijing. “There are already Asean member states which are viewed as either very pro-US or very pro-China,” Oh said. “Their vastly different positions are likely to deepen should a conflict break out between the two big powers.” This Week in Asia has contacted Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin for comment.

title: Developers vie to land plum HK$2 billion residential site in Ho Man Tin
description: The government received 10 tenders for the site on Fat Kwong Street ahead of a deadline on Friday.
content: The sole residential site included in the Hong Kong government’s latest land sale programme has attracted interest from a host of major developers, with 10 tenders being submitted before a noon deadline on Friday. Chinachem Group, Wheelock Properties, Kerry Properties and Sun Hung Kai Properties all confirmed to the South China Morning Post that they had submitted individual bids for the site on Fat Kwong Street in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon, while Sino Land issued a joint tender with Great Eagle Group. Representatives from other developers including CK Asset Holdings, K Wah International, China Overseas Land & Investment and Poly Property were also seen submitting bids at a government office, according to media reports. The Land Department said it had received 10 tenders in total. The site has a maximum gross floor area of 19,300 square metres (207,750 square feet) and is expected to accommodate about 250 flats. It was originally included in the government’s 2026-2027 land sale programme. The successful bidder will be required to build an elderly care centre and a community centre at the site, as well as level the access road connecting the development to Fat Kwong Street.
