Midland Surveyors director Alvin Lam said the site’s location in an established luxury residential neighbourhood, proximity to Ho Man Tin MTR station and moderate development scale could attract a range of developers, including smaller players. The firm estimated the site’s value at about HK$2.39 billion (US$305 million), based on an expected land premium of HK$11,500 per square foot of gross floor area. Lam said the site could accommodate a mid-to-high-end residential project, with upper-floor homes potentially enjoying open views and partial sea views. Its proximity to the Hong Kong Polytechnic University could also support rental demand, he added. The heated competition for the Fat Kwong Street site comes as developers weigh limited opportunities to secure well-located urban land against still-cautious expectations for the property market. Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said in July that the government would release just one residential site in the July-to-September quarter, arguing that other sources of housing supply would help keep the city on track to meet its targets. The government has lowered its land premium revenue target for the 2026-2027 financial year to about HK$18 billion, while CBRE estimates actual revenue could reach HK$14 billion to HK$16 billion. Developers have nevertheless continued to replenish their land banks as Hong Kong’s residential market shows signs of recovery after a prolonged downturn. Kerry Properties and Sino Land have been among the developers actively pursuing new development opportunities. Earlier in September, a Sun Hung Kai Properties subsidiary won the tender for MTR Corporation’s Tuen Mun A16 Station Phase Two Property Development, with total investment costs projected to exceed HK$20 billion. The second phase’s residential portion spans 249,979 square metres and is expected to yield around 5,510 homes. The broader bidder pool echoes a trend in recent land sales. In May, construction company Able Engineering secured rights to a Tung Chung residential site for HK$1.63 billion, beating five major developer groups with a bid that exceeded analysts’ estimates. Market watchers cited localised optimism and growing confidence among alternative investors for the higher-than-expected bid.

title: Hong Kong raises helpers’ monthly minimum wage to HK$5,220
description: Government says current minimum wage of HK$5,100 to be increased by 2.35 per cent, but food allowance will be unchanged.
content: Hong Kong authorities have raised the minimum wage for domestic helpers by 2.35 per cent to HK$5,220 (US$665) per month, while keeping their food allowance unchanged, citing “more favourable” socioeconomic factors. The government announced on Friday that the minimum wage for domestic workers would rise from HK$5,100, with the new rate applying to all contracts signed on or after Saturday. Authorities added that while most employers provided free food to their helpers, those choosing to pay an allowance in lieu will continue paying at least HK$1,236 per month. “In this year’s review, we comprehensively considered a basket of socio-economic factors in accordance with the established mechanism, including Hong Kong’s general economic performance and labour market conditions over the past year, near-term economic outlook, affordability of … [domestic helper] employers and basic living needs of [helpers],” a government spokesman said. “Having carefully assessed and balanced the views of all parties, and comprehensively considered that this year’s socio-economic factors are more favourable than those at the time of last year’s review, the government has decided to suitably increase the [minimum allowable wage] to HK$5,220 per month.” The government added that the Immigration Department would continue to process employment contracts signed on or before Friday using the previous minimum, provided they were submitted by the end of the month. The increase fell short of what worker groups had sought. The Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions earlier proposed raising the wage level to HK$6,670 and the food allowance to HK$2,770. Employers, meanwhile, had called for a pay freeze. Last year, the government raised the minimum wage for helpers by 2.2 per cent from HK$4,990, while keeping the food allowance unchanged. The pay adjustment drew criticism from both sides. Chrystie Lam Hau-yiu, president of employers’ group the Coalition of Global Home Service Sustainable Development, said the move could put more pressure on employers while potentially curbing employment opportunities for helpers. “Many families are facing inflation, rents or mortgage payments, as well as costs for raising children and keeping domestic workers,” she said. “I believe the government has not considered the real costs faced by employers.” Lam, citing an earlier survey of 6,000 employers, warned that up to 70 per cent of respondents said they might consider forgoing hiring helpers following a pay rise. She called on the government to introduce tax allowances for expenses related to helpers and toughen its enforcement against job-hopping. Phobsuk Gasing, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions, said helpers were disappointed by the “very tiny increase”, arguing it offered no real gain after inflation. “We are especially frustrated by no increase in the food allowance. It has been HK$1,236 since the year of 2023,” she said, adding that those who received the money had to spend about HK$1,000 a month to feed themselves. “The Hong Kong government should inform the public what the indicators are for their decision on … the [minimum allowable wage] and food allowance.”

title: Crop outputs grew up to 100% in China’s big agricultural experiment: scientists
description: Peking University scientist says solar-activated mineral water improves photosynthetic efficiency across major crops.
content: Large-scale field trials across China show that irrigation water treated with natural minerals radiated by sunlight could dramatically increase the yields of several crops, according to Chinese scientists behind the experiments. The team said the trials, including on rice, wheat, soybeans, peanuts, sweet potatoes, sugar cane and vegetables, improved photosynthetic efficiency. Their study, conducted from Heilongjiang province in northeastern China to Hainan province in the south, recorded yield increases of up to 40.6 per cent for rice, 24.7 per cent for wheat and 45.7 per cent for sugar cane, according to the scientists who said one sweet potato trial recorded an increase of 109.5 per cent. Lu Anhuai, the lead scientist of the team and a professor at the School of Earth and Space Sciences at Peking University, said the approach could offer alternative ways of increasing agricultural production, such as improved crop varieties and fertilisers, by using irrigation water to improve how efficiently plants use sunlight. “This is a new track,” Lu said in an interview on September 22. “In the past, agricultural yield increases relied first on seeds and second on fertilisers,” he said, adding, “We rely on water [and] on improving photosynthetic efficiency”. The results are part of a research programme led by Lu that has evolved over more than two decades. He said the technology could have broad applications because it was not limited to a particular crop. “It can be used for all crops that need irrigation water,” he said, referring to rice, wheat and other major agricultural crops. He said the approach could eventually be expanded across a wider range of agricultural regions around the world and asserted that Western countries did not have such research. The trials covered rice in Sichuan, wheat in Henan, soybeans in Heilongjiang and Inner Mongolia, sweet potatoes and peanuts in Shandong, sugar cane in Guangxi, cherries in Gansu and vegetables in several provinces. The researchers said the field data included a Sichuan trial in which the rice variety Chuanyou 617 produced 849.2kg per mu – a Chinese unit of measurement that corresponds to 0.16 acres or 0.07 hectares – an increase of 33.0 per cent. Another variety, Shuxiang You 668, recorded a 40.6 per cent increase, a wheat trial in Henan recorded a 24.7 per cent increase for Xiyuan 151, while sugar cane trials in Guangxi reported increases of up to 45.7 per cent, according to the team. In Shandong, a trial using the sweet potato variety Yanshu 25 recorded a yield of 5,229.0kg per mu, 109.5 per cent higher than the comparison figure, the researchers said, while adding that trials with cherries and peanuts also had improved yields. They said some of their most striking results came from the rice experiments, including a 4.4-mu field in Sichuan’s Tianfu Granary National Modern Agricultural Industrial Park, they said. The team said the crop was irrigated five times during the grain-filling stage – the rapid growth stage after the flowering and pollination of cereal crops – and strong winds caused severe breaking in three of the four varieties in the control plots, while none of the four varieties treated with the mineral functional water did. Lu has worked on environmental mineralogy since the 1990s and has led two major projects under China’s National Key Basic Research Development Programme, commonly known as the 973 Programme, serving as chief scientist for projects that ran from 2007 to 2011 and from 2014 to 2018. He was also president of the International Mineralogical Association. The state-funded projects helped lay the groundwork for his team’s later research into the interactions between minerals, sunlight, microorganisms and biological energy conversion. In 2019, Lu and colleagues reported in PNAS (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) that iron and manganese-bearing mineral coatings on rocks and soils could convert sunlight into electrical energy via semiconductor photoelectric effects. They then asked whether similar mineral-driven solar conversion could affect biological systems. They focused on a manganese oxide material called birnessite. Deep inside plant cells, the manganese cluster (Mn₄CaO₅) drives photosystem II – the catalytic centre in chloroplasts that splits water to generate plant energy – leading to their “mineral functional water” in which minerals modify irrigation water instead of being applied directly to crops. A paper by the team published online on August 27 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Acta Mineralogica Sinica which detailed the yield results described this as part of a programme from mineral photoelectric effects to mineral-assisted microbial metabolism and plant “semi-artificial photosynthesis”. The proposed mechanism: minerals absorb broader wavelengths of sunlight and convert them into energy that alters water’s physical properties, including hydrogen-bond structure, making water easier to split during photosynthesis. “Our technology works outside the chloroplast, using water as the medium,” Lu said. “The materials convert solar energy into the internal energy of the water. “When this water is used for irrigation, it is easier to split at the manganese cluster in the chloroplast.” Water splitting produces protons and electrons that feed into the photosynthetic electron-transfer system, enabling plants to convert carbon dioxide into organic matter. In the field method described by the team, mineral powder was added to ordinary irrigation water at about 0.5 per cent, stirred under sunlight for one hour and then allowed to settle, with the clear water above the settled materials then used for irrigation. Because the minerals did not dissolve in the water, the materials at the bottom could be reused, they said. “The materials are cheap. They are natural minerals and it is easy to make,” Lu said, adding that the core formulation was proprietary and protected by patents. “It’s a mixture of ingredients. But the core formula is our secret.” Lu said this technology for increasing crop yields had no harmful effects: the materials did not dissolve into the irrigation water and were neither a fertiliser nor a pesticide. He said they contained no heavy metals and did not introduce the dissolved mineral load associated with conventional fertiliser use. The technology was moving towards commercialisation, according to Lu.

title: China seen doing ‘just enough’ with targeted fiscal support to defend GDP growth
description: Finance Minister Lan Foan vows reasonably faster public spending and broader subsidies as Beijing battles prolonged property slump and weak domestic demand.
content: China’s finance minister has pledged to roll out incremental and targeted fiscal policies to help achieve leadership’s full-year growth target for the country, following a freshly announced package of supportive measures. However, analysts expect Beijing to stop short of a major stimulus, providing only “just enough” support to meet the target. Lan Foan made the pledge in an article published on Thursday in the Communist Party’s leading theoretical journal, Qiushi, calling for the broadened coverage of an interest subsidy policy, the onboarding of more implementing agencies, and moderately raised funding limits to unlock consumption potential and catalyse private investment. Furthermore, he vowed to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending “in a reasonable manner” and strengthen oversight and guidance for regions where spending progress has been slower than expected. The article came two days after Beijing released a fresh package of measures to boost the real economy, including an interest-rate cut for policy banks and the introduction of the country’s first interest subsidy for first-time homebuyers. While the package signals that Beijing is now willing to use the central fiscal budget to support housing demand, Robin Xing, chief China economist at Morgan Stanley, said in a report on Tuesday that it was a “modest package to defend the growth floor”, with its impact likely to be more about signalling than providing substantial support. Meanwhile, a report led by Larry Hu, chief China economist at Macquarie, noted that Beijing would do “just enough” to achieve this year’s growth target, describing it as a pattern that Beijing has followed since 2024. “We don’t expect major policy stimulus as long as exports remain strong,” the report said. China set this year’s growth target at “4.5 to 5 per cent” – a slight shift from the “around 5 per cent” goal that had been the recent norm – as the economy has been grappling with numerous headwinds, including weak domestic demand, a prolonged downturn in the property market and rising external risks. Meeting this year’s target could prove challenging after gross domestic product growth came in at 4.3 per cent in the second quarter – the weakest reading since the end of 2022. According to Lan, as the year enters its final quarter, the coming months will be “critical” for authorities to operate effectively and ensure the annual growth target is achieved, securing a solid start to the nation’s five-year planning period covering 2026 to 2030. “[We should] accelerate the implementation of existing measures, formulate more targeted policy support, and make greater efforts to improve the effectiveness of the more proactive fiscal policy, helping achieve this year’s economic and social development goals,” he said. On the prolonged issue of financial pressure facing local governments across the country, Lan said China would advance tax reforms to strengthen local revenue sources and orderly transform local government financing vehicles – off-balance-sheet corporate debt structures facing severe pressure due to the enduring property slump. Lan also called on government departments to improve the efficiency of public spending and help local governments better utilise idle assets and resources. He stressed that party and government institutions should maintain spending discipline, cutting costs wherever possible and reducing administrative expenses. Top authorities have also stepped up their commitment to further policy support. Earlier this week, Premier Li Qiang chaired a State Council executive meeting that called for a series of policies to strengthen support for the economy, including encouraging local governments, where conditions allow, to pilot measures to boost consumption.

title: Consumer spending picks up in Hong Kong, with retail sales rising 5.6% in August
description: Sales in the first eight months of 2026 rise by 8.5 per cent compared with the same period last year.
content: Hong Kong’s retail sales rose by 5.6 per cent year on year in August, with the latest figures showing consumer spending picking up after growth eased for two consecutive months. Retail sales value reached HK$32 billion (US$4.1 billion), according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Friday. Sales in the first eight months of the year rose by 8.5 per cent compared with the same period in 2025. “Growth was seen across many types of retail outlets, while online retail sales value grew notably, reflecting a continued shift in consumer spending towards digital channels,” a government spokesman said. The latest figures followed a 4.5 per cent increase in July, when sales reached HK$31 billion, the lowest monthly value recorded in the first seven months of the year. Growth had slowed from 7.9 per cent in May to 4.6 per cent in June. Sales of electrical goods and other consumer durables recorded the strongest increase in August, rising by 29.1 per cent year on year, followed by jewellery, watches and clocks, and valuable gifts, at 11.9 per cent. Motor vehicles and parts recorded the steepest decline, falling by 22 per cent. The Hong Kong Retail Management Association had previously warned that August sales fell short of expectations. Its survey, which covered about 3,100 shops and 75,000 employees, found that about 40 per cent of respondents reported weaker-than-expected performance. Annie Tse Yau On-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Retail Management Association, said August sales had fallen short of retailers’ expectations as weak visitor spending limited the benefit of increased arrivals. She said improved weather had helped, but residents’ summer travel continued to put pressure on retailers serving the local market, while stronger visitor numbers had not translated into equally strong spending. “Against a low comparison base, I would describe growth of 5.6 per cent as relatively steady, rather than particularly outstanding,” she said. Tse attributed the sharp rise in sales of electrical goods to new product launches by certain brands and clearance promotions ahead of the release of other models. Discounts at major bookstores also helped lift sales in the books, stationery and gifts category, which rose 11.2 per cent compared with last year. She said the decline in motor vehicle sales continued to reflect purchases brought forward to March to take advantage of tax concessions. The association’s latest survey, covering about 4,400 outlets and 89,000 employees, found that three-quarters of respondents recorded year-on-year sales growth in September. Tse said better weather supported retailers serving local customers, with optical shops, furniture sellers, clothing retailers, department stores and convenience stores reporting single-digit increases. Cosmetics retailers reported mid-teen growth, while personal care and jewellery businesses recorded low-teen increases. Supermarkets and health supplement retailers reported mixed results, while car sales continued to decline. About 70 per cent of respondents reported sales growth on the first day of the National Day “golden week” holiday on Thursday, although Tse said it was too early to assess the overall performance. The association’s executive director, Bond Law, cautioned that the uneven performance across retail categories meant the sector had yet to fully recover. “We can only say it has returned to a relatively stable state,” he added. The association maintained its forecast for single-digit retail sales growth this year.

title: Can Indonesia’s new police chief repair the force’s image, commit to reforms?
description: A commission has called for reforms including transforming the police’s work culture and limiting officers holding other public positions.
content: Indonesia’s new police chief faces a difficult task to balance growing public demands for accountability and independence as the force seeks to repair its image following a series of scandals in recent years. Even as Suyudi Ario Seto, 53, replaced Listyo Sigit Prabowo on Thursday, the government is weighing recommendations to reform the powerful institution, including changes to its work culture and limits on police officers holding public positions outside the force. In addition to appointing Suyudi, President Prabowo Subianto also reshuffled his cabinet, announcing sweeping changes to key ministerial and senior government posts, with Listyo heading the Executive Office of the President (KSP). Parliament approved the appointment of Suyudi, who was sworn in within hours of his parliamentary hearing. “Suyudi was the middle-ground candidate as he was seen to be able to accommodate all the interests of different factions within the government,” said Muradi, a former adviser to two Indonesian police chiefs from 2015 to 2025. Basing his assessment on insider information, Muradi said Listyo had wanted current Jakarta police chief Asep Adi Suheri to succeed him, while Defence Minister Syafrie Syamsuddin had championed East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko. “In the end, Dasco ended the tug of war by vouching for Suyudi,” said Muradi, referring to Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, a senior politician from Prabowo’s Gerindra Party who serves as deputy chairman of Indonesia’s House of Representatives. Suyudi assumed several top police positions over his career, including Jakarta director of criminal investigation in 2019, deputy director of the National Cyber Crime Unit in 2020 and police chief of Banten from 2024 to 2025. Last year, Prabowo appointed Suyudi to head the National Narcotics Agency. As the outgoing police chief, Listyo still has considerable clout in the force, according to Muradi. Rendy Pahrun Wadipalapa, a political scientist at the National Research and Innovation Agency, also noted that Listyo had not been removed from the centre of power. “Moving him from Polri [Indonesian National Police] to KSP looks more like a redistribution of roles and not political exile.” Highlighting some of Listyo’s achievements during his tenure, Rendy said: “He oversaw the expansion of digital public services by the police and tried to make the institution more accountable and transparent to the public.” However, Jacqui Baker, a lecturer and researcher on Indonesian security issues at Perth’s Murdoch University, argued that Listyo had left a tainted legacy concerning police reform. “In the last [presidential] election we saw him wield his powers to pursue political rivals and strong-arm political parties to consolidate power under the winning ticket,” Baker said. The police also tried to erode civil society and break the coalition of forces supporting democratic reform, she added. Several major police scandals happened during Listyo’s tenure. In 2023, Ferdy Sambo, a high-ranking police general, was convicted of orchestrating the 2022 murder of his subordinate, Nofriansyah Yosua Hutabarat. Ferdy is serving a life sentence after his initial death penalty was commuted. In the same year, 135 people died in a stampede at Kanjuruhan Stadium in Malang, East Java, after police fired tear gas into crowds following a football match. Earlier this year, two police officers in Jambi were dismissed after being accused of promising aspiring police cadets admission to the force in exchange for money. Muradi described incoming Suyudi as “significantly more open-minded and objective” than Listyo. “By the virtue of the police force directly answering to the president, a police chief is never absolutely neutral within Indonesia’s system of government, but he or she can retain objectivity by not being blatantly in servitude to the president,” Muradi said. Rendy pointed out that Suyudi was Prabowo’s first-ever police chief pick. “Prabowo now exerts greater ownership and control over Polri’s leadership,” he added. During his hearing with Indonesia’s parliamentarians on Thursday, Suyudi pledged to make the police institution more responsive to public needs and sensibilities. “The public shouldn’t have to assume that if a case doesn’t go viral, then the police are slow to act. I wish to change this,” he said. Suyudi also vowed to prioritise several issues, including equality before the law, eliminating illegal extortion by officers and curbing the use of excessive force. “My ambition is simple: When a child sees a police officer, he or she will feel safe rather than afraid,” Suyudi told parliamentarians before his appointment. In May, a government-sanctioned reform commission, chaired by former Constitutional Court Chief Justice Jimly Asshiddiqie, published its report recommending reforms, including the need to “demilitarise the police’s work culture” and formulate rules restricting police officers holding other public roles outside the force. Despite the long list of grievances about the police, two polls released this year by Litbang Kompas and FIXPOLL Indonesia ranked public satisfaction with the police at over 80 per cent. Baker, however, is not hopeful about the force’s transformation even with Suyudi at the helm. “Police reform is dead. Every time there is a scandal, and there have been many, the police promise reform, but it’s never fully clear what is being reformed and to what end?” she said. Since 1999, Indonesia’s police reform has amplified the power and impunity of the force, according to Baker. Lukas Luwarso, a political commentator, said that to prove the police chief was serious about reforming the force, he had to fulfil a key litmus test. “If one of his first acts is to make drastic top personnel changes, then perhaps he’ll be able to make good on those pledges. If not, then he is just more of the same paper tiger,” Luwarso said. However, Supriadi, a 26-year-old Surabaya resident, said he was confident about the new police chief’s capability to make changes that benefit the public. “He has a trustworthy face. I hope he will achieve positive things for our police.”

title: Opinion | How the US went from ‘a position of strength’ to ‘gung-ho’ on China
description: Years of decoupling showed that independence was an economically ruinous illusion while pragmatic bargaining yields vastly superior returns.
content: Not so long ago, Washington’s approach to relations with Beijing was anchored by a single assertive phrase: dealing “from a position of strength”. It was rooted in a unipolar mindset: a belief that the United States could dictate terms, manage competition unilaterally and demand compliance from a distance. Yet, at their recent summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump formally established a new strategic framework: a “constructive strategic stability relationship based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”. The shift in the American mindset was visible in the reception of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, from the moment their plane landed in Washington. Trump and first lady Melania Trump took the extraordinary step of welcoming the couple on the tarmac. Accompanied by a 21-gun salute, full military honours from every service branch and a dramatic fighter jet flyover above the White House, Washington sent an unmistakable signal that it acknowledged China as an equal on the global stage. As Xi noted, achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can run in parallel. America’s mindset shift was forged in hard realism. Years of attempting to decouple and sever supply chains showed independence to be an economically ruinous illusion. When the diplomatic and economic teams sat down, they delivered tangible results. The formalisation of trade and investment councils, extension of the Kuala Lumpur trade outcomes and the US$30 billion “reciprocal tariff” reduction showed that pragmatic bargaining yields vastly superior returns to endless tariff wars. Even in the fiercely contested arena of artificial intelligence (AI), both nations chose maturity over recklessness. By establishing formal communication channels for AI incidents and locking in a dedicated dialogue by November, Washington and Beijing acknowledged a shared truth: unmanaged technology poses a systemic threat to all mankind. From restoring direct military crisis communication to executing joint law enforcement operations against illicit drug precursor networks, both nations proved that treating each other as equals is the only viable way to manage friction. Alongside the evolution in Washington’s approach, a quiet realignment is taking place in American domestic opinion. Recent US public polling reveals a striking demographic divide. While older political elites in Washington remain trapped in zero-sum cold war orthodoxies, America’s Gen Z and millennials recognise that global challenges cannot be solved through coercion. They are increasingly exhausted by foreign policy brinkmanship. They do not view China as an existential bogeyman to be conquered but as a formidable civilisational power with which coexistence is mandatory. Great statecraft also demands emotional resonance and shared memory. One of the summit’s most memorable moments occurred during Trump’s welcome address, when he invoked the expression “gung-ho”. Originally coined for the Chinese industrial cooperatives in the 1930s, the term was brought to the US Marine Corps by officer Evans Carlson, who had observed Chinese workers and soldiers rallying together during wartime. It became the legendary battle cry of the US Marine Raiders, symbolising teamwork and boundless enthusiasm. In referring to the gung-ho spirit and honouring the memory of Chinese civilians who risked everything to rescue downed American Flying Tigers pilots during World War II, both leaders reminded a global audience that beneath today’s intense competition lies a proven legacy of standing shoulder to shoulder. This spirit of mutual respect permeated every cultural detail of the visit. The White House hosted a grand state dinner in the East Room, tastefully decorated in red and attended by leaders from the US Cabinet, Congress and American civil society. Trump guided Xi on a private tour of the National Archives – thoughtfully mirroring Xi’s invitation to the historic Temple of Heaven during Trump’s visit to Beijing. Coupled with the arrival of giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang at Atlanta Zoo, these human touches provided a vivid reminder that soft power and civilisational respect remain potent remedies for political tension. Ultimately, a healthy and stable China-US relationship is good for both nations and essential for the entire world. When the world’s two largest economies choose dialogue over confrontation, global financial markets find certainty, international trade routes remain secure and existential risks, from rogue AI to nuclear proliferation, are kept safely under human control. Yet, the true foundation of China-US relations has always resided in the hearts of their people, and its future rests squarely on the shoulders of the youth. China’s visionary announcement to invite 100,000 young Americans to study, travel and build connections across the country over the next five years represents perhaps the most strategic investment made during the summit. When young Americans and Chinese study in the same classrooms, collaborate on AI algorithms and build international businesses together, they dismantle propaganda and cultivate genuine empathy. The posture of dealing “from a position of strength” was the outdated relic of a unipolar past. The future belongs to the spirit of gung-ho – to working together, as equals, for a peaceful global order that neither nation can afford to break.

title: How Hong Kong New Wave directors hijacked martial arts and crime films to make art
description: Directors like Ann Hui, Tsui Hark and Patrick Tam were united by a desire to experiment and an ambition to modernise the local film industry.
content: It is easy to misremember the Hong Kong New Wave of the late 1970s and 80s. Nearly five decades after its inception, that iconic chapter in the city’s cinema history is generally thought of as a socially inclined art-house movement that addressed everyday issues – a stark contrast to the martial arts films that dominated the local box office at the time. While partially true, viewing New Wave films merely as local iterations of 1960s and 70s rarefied European art-house cinema misses the mark. The movement maintained a push-pull relationship with Hong Kong’s entrenched commercial cinema scene, producing firmly genre-based works. Moreover, despite viewing martial arts films as outmoded because they said nothing about modern Hong Kong, some New Wave directors even made wuxia movies. Their goal was to inject contemporary sensibilities – concerns that reflected the issues of the day – into established genres, making them palatable to conservative investors reluctant to risk money on experiments. The public, too, preferred entertaining narratives over being preached to. “Most early works of the New Wave are genre works,” noted critic and historian Sam Ho in his introduction to the restored Blu-ray edition of Ann Hui On-wah’s 1979 film debut The Secret. “These works are, each in their own way, challenges to their respective genres, with experiments in form and content while labouring to stay within generic confines.” While Allen Fong Yuk-ping’s social-realist dramas Father and Son (1981) and Ah Ying (1983) closely align with the European art-house model, others boasted massive scale and scope, such as Hui’s Vietnam-set Boat People (1982), an almost epic tale. Martial arts also played a part. Hui directed the ambitious wuxia The Romance of Book and Sword (1987), while Patrick Tam Ka-ming – who became the New Wave’s most experimental filmmaker with Love Massacre (1981) and Nomad (1982) – debuted with the sword-fighting film The Sword in 1980. Interestingly, although Tsui Hark debuted with the idiosyncratic wuxia The Butterfly Murders in 1979, he then made two politically provocative films – the eccentric We Are Going to Eat You and the nihilistic Dangerous Encounters of the First Kind (both 1980) – before adapting his unique brand of wildly imaginative filmmaking to commercial requirements. Foreign influences and a modernised language The New Wave was united by a desire to experiment with style, form and content, and an ambition to modernise the local film industry through technical and creative innovation. While most 1970s filmmakers still learned on the job, many New Wavers studied abroad – Ann Hui in the UK, Tsui Hark in the US – gaining exposure to foreign films and up-to-date techniques. Tam, for instance, studied for nine months at a San Francisco film workshop, recalling being particularly impressed by the “complexity” of Francis Ford Coppola. Eager to implement their ideas, the filmmakers found a willing industry, albeit an inherently conservative one. By the late 1970s, producers seeking a younger, urbanised audience gambled on these new directors, provided their work remained commercially acceptable. The gamble paid off. Film historian Law Kar noted they used “a modernised cinematic language” to update an industry “increasingly mired in archaic ways.” The television training ground Before entering cinema, New Wave directors honed their skills at local television stations. Driven by a high demand for home-grown programming, returning graduates found immediate employment. TVB’s head of production, Selina Chow Liang Shuk-yee, proved vital, offering untested filmmakers like Tsui, Tam and Hui both jobs and creative freedom. Television deeply influenced their cinematic style. TV stations relied on cheaper location shooting, injecting unprecedented realism into the directors’ work. Additionally, television fostered a quasi-documentary approach to research. Directors often based TV episodes on real-life incidents, interviewing participants and reading newspaper reports – methods that subsequently shaped the films of Hui and Allen Fong. Early New Wave crime stories stemmed directly from programmes like TVB’s popular C.I.D. series, which featured fictionalised real-life cases. Alex Cheung Kwok-ming’s police stories Cops and Robbers (1979) and Man on the Brink (1981) brought realistic characters and locations – like crowded alleyways and public housing estates – to depict working-class struggles. Similarly, Hui’s debut, The Secret, loosely based on the real-life 1970 Pok Fu Lam murders, subverted the traditional crime structure to deliver an unnerving psychological drama. Subverting tropes with Hong Kong pragmatism The New Wavers’ martial arts films came as a surprise to some, as some of the directors had claimed their works were a response to the genre. They felt it was stylistically out of date – the penchant for zoom shots certainly made it look old-fashioned – and expressed Confucian values that did not reflect modern Hong Kong life. Foreign critics, who expected the New Wave to progress along the model of European neo-realism, were confused. Unaware of the deep cultural resonance that martial arts films – and the practice of martial arts itself – had in Hong Kong life, they formed the impression that the filmmakers were selling out. Yet the New Wavers were simply exhibiting the very Hong Kong quality of pragmatism: since martial arts films were still relatively popular, producers offered the directors work making them. They took the jobs hoping to adapt the format to say what they wanted, and that generally worked out. Hui’s adaptation of a Louis Cha Leung-yung novel, The Romance of Book and Sword, is a grounded affair that focuses heavily on political strategy, while Tam, who accepted a Golden Harvest commission for The Sword, stripped away the normal Confucian tropes of the genre to serve up a bleak, thoroughly modern existentialist view of life. Eddie Fong Ling-ching’s An Amorous Woman of Tang Dynasty (1984) is a particularly fascinating work. Although it is not exactly a martial arts film – it is more of a period piece – Fong uses the genre to explore female sexuality, female repression and sex as a tool for political power. As the 1980s progressed, however, the movement struggled. The filmmakers had been accustomed to making whatever they wanted for TV, but their freedom in the film industry evaporated when producers began to demand wholly commercial fare. Some directors, like Kirk Wong Chi-keung, carved out successful careers as commercial directors, while others, like Allen Fong, simply dropped out of filmmaking. Others still returned to TV and advertising work. Nevertheless, the New Wave’s impact endured. Mainstream cinema began depicting contemporary life in hits like Police Story (1985), and directors realised they could inject social or political messages into commercial projects. As critic Sam Ho noted, the New Wave films were “the harbingers of what Hong Kong cinema would become”. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: David vs Goliaths: Singapore builds most accurate clock ever, leaves US and China in dust
description: The decade-long project could help to pave the way for a redefinition of the second, researchers claim in a new paper.
content: A small Singaporean research team has beaten scientists in China and the United States to build the world’s most accurate atomic clock. The clock, built with a single ion of a rare earth metal element known as lutetium, is so precise that it would lose one second every 260 billion years – nearly 20 times the age of our universe. It is about four times as accurate as the previous record holder, a calcium-ion clock developed by a Chinese Academy of Sciences team in Wuhan, and also surpasses an aluminium-ion clock unveiled last year by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. The decade-long work could improve timekeeping and help pave the way for a redefinition of the second, according to the team at the National University of Singapore’s Centre for Quantum Technologies. It could also provide a powerful tool to test fundamental physics, from Einstein’s theory of general relativity to the search for dark matter, the researchers wrote in a paper published last week in the journal Nature. Murray Barrett, the research team leader, said he did not see how their clock “can be beat” in the future, pointing to lutetium’s unusual resistance to changes in temperature and magnetic fields. The clock would remain stable “from the hottest place recorded on Earth in Death Valley to the coldest place in the Antarctic plateau”, a university statement quoted Barrett as saying. In an email to the South China Morning Post, Barrett said that developing an atomic clock did not require a large team, but getting such a project off the ground could be difficult. He credited the Centre for Quantum Technologies for backing the research early on, when it might have seemed risky, and Singapore’s funding agencies for their continued support. “I think that this effort is an example of Singapore’s ability to internationally compete through backing good ideas, strategic investment in core technologies, and development of technical competencies,” Barrett said. For most of human history, time was measured by watching the heavens – from the movement of the sun across the sky to the Earth’s rotation and the motion of the moon. When mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the 13th century, gears moving at a steady rate made it possible to keep time without watching the sky. Atomic clocks took precision much further, using microwaves or lasers to measure atoms whose electrons jump back and forth between energy states, like tiny pendulums swinging in sync. Their precise timing is essential for modern technologies such as GPS, telecommunications and navigation systems. Laboratories around the world are racing to improve the technology. Leading optical clocks in the United States, China, Europe and Japan have used elements such as strontium and ytterbium, whose atoms have extremely stable transitions that can be precisely measured with lasers. The Singapore team said it was probably the only group in the world using lutetium for atomic clocks. Lutetium has another unusual advantage: it can remain in an excited state for about a week, compared with just a few minutes for strontium. This gives scientists more time to measure its frequency precisely, according to the paper. To verify the clock’s accuracy, the researchers built two independent lutetium clocks and compared them directly. After 200 hours of measurements, the two agreed to within 5.7 parts in 10¹⁹ – the most precise comparison between two atomic clocks ever reported, they wrote. The researchers said their next step is to miniaturise the clock into a transportable system so that it can be taken out of the laboratory without sacrificing accuracy. Passionate about science?
