title: Abby Choi struck with hammer during car trip ruse to fetch daughter, court hears
description: Prosecution also details how three of Choi’s former relatives rented remote village house and bought meat mincer days before attack.
content: Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung died of head injuries after being hit with a hammer during a car journey she believed was to pick up her daughter from school, a court has heard. Prosecutors on Friday detailed how three of Choi’s former relatives rented a remote village house and went shopping to acquire items they needed before allegedly killing the 28-year-old and disposing of her body on February 21, 2023. Choi’s ex-husband Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, are standing trial in the High Court after pleading not guilty to a joint count of murder. Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial. The killing allegedly arose from a family feud over the sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat at the upscale Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin. The elder Kwong, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the flat and enlisted his two sons to help kill the influencer so he could keep it for himself. Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC said the defendants showed significant pre-planning when they bought a wide variety of items between February 4 and 17 in preparation for the murder. Those items included a 1lb (450-gram) ball-peen hammer – the alleged murder weapon – a commercial meat mincer, a 14-by-14-inch (36-by-36cm) soup pot, an electric saw, three knives, a second-hand refrigerator and multiple containers. Draycott said Kwong Kau rented a 600 sq ft flat at Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village, where Choi’s body was dismembered, and asked a friend to rent a high-rise flat at The Arch in West Kowloon, which would be used as Alex Kwong’s hideout. On the day of the alleged murder, Choi boarded a white Toyota Alphard driven by Anthony Kwong, who was working as her chauffeur at the time, under the impression that he would take her to a school in Pak Shek Kok where her eight-year-old daughter was studying. The prosecution alleged that during that trip, Alex Kwong, who was sitting on the left side of the back seat beside Choi, used the hammer to hit her on the head, either killing her or rendering her unconscious. Surveillance camera footage retrieved from the Moko shopping centre in Mong Kok showed Anthony Kwong meeting Alex Kwong at a coffee shop shortly before the trip, during which the elder brother appeared to demonstrate to his younger sibling how to drag Choi by her hair and strike her in the head. Draycott suggested that Choi could have been attacked shortly after 2.44pm on February 21, 2023, as her text conversation with her mother-in-law had come to an abrupt stop at that time. The two brothers met up with their father outside the village house in Tai Po and discreetly carried a box believed to contain Choi’s body inside the flat after 3pm. Draycott noted that Choi, who was 152cm (five feet) tall and weighed about 90lbs (41kg), was small enough for the accused to hide her body inside one of the plastic containers they had bought in advance. She also highlighted the trio’s unusually calm demeanour outside the village house, saying none of the accused appeared shocked or frightened by what must have been a violent attack inside the car. “They were not worried. They were not upset. It was exactly what they expected to happen,” the prosecutor said. Later that afternoon, Alex Kwong changed his clothes and left the village house on foot, “leaving his father Kwong Kau and his brother to clear up the mess”, according to the prosecution. When the crime came to light on February 24, Choi’s head was found inside the soup pot and her legs inside the refrigerator. Flesh was also discovered inside a smaller pot and on a wooden chopping board, while multiple electric saws were seized from the premises. Draycott said there was no evidence that any of the accused intended to cannibalise Choi’s body. “They cooked her to make her flesh unrecognisable,” she added. Police held Kwong Kau and his elder son for questioning on the evening of February 23 before arresting them in the early hours of the following day. Under caution, Kwong Kau said he had “no idea” about the murder and that he had nothing to explain. Anthony Kwong said: “I was only responsible for driving, driving Abby to Tai Po at that time. I just knew that Abby was talking on the phone at the back.” Police arrested Alex Kwong at the Tung Chung Development Pier just as he was about to flee Hong Kong on February 25. Among his belongings were more than HK$680,000 in cash, five luxury watches, five credit cards – including one belonging to Choi – and identification documents belonging to his elder brother. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

title: Hong Kong ranks 7th globally in drawing next wealthy class – trailing Singapore: study
description: Younger wealth holders increasingly global, prioritising lifestyle, wellness and values when choosing where to live and invest, Savills says.
content: Hong Kong ranked seventh globally as a destination for attracting and retaining the next generation of high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), trailing traditional rival Singapore in sixth place, according to a Savills study. The two top finance hubs in the Asia-Pacific region have been stepping up efforts to strengthen their positions as regional wealth-management hubs amid an unprecedented global transfer of wealth between generations. “Hong Kong offers many incentives similar to Singapore,” according to the global real estate adviser’s Next-Generation Wealth Hubs Index released on Thursday. “It provides low taxation, financial sophistication, safety and connectivity, reinforcing its position as a leading hub for wealth preservation and family offices in Asia.” The study focused on individuals under the age of 40 who have inherited significant fortunes, are expected to benefit from wealth transfers, or have built their own wealth through entrepreneurship. New York topped the global rankings, followed by Miami and London, respectively, according to the report. In the Asia-Pacific region, Tokyo ranked third, followed by Shanghai and Bangkok. Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future Kelcie Sellers, Savills World Research Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future Hong Kong was also home to 71 HNWIs under the age of 40 with net assets of at least US$5 million, making it the 12th-largest concentration in the world and the largest in Asia-Pacific, according to the study. It also defined HNWIs as those with partially valuated dossiers with total assets of at least US$2 million. Singapore ranked 13th with 70 individuals in the same category. “Recent trends suggest a shift in HNWI demographics, with a growing proportion of wealthy individuals from mainland China who are drawn to the high quality of life and ease of access,” the study said. Hong Kong “acts as a key gateway to wider international markets, with one of the most active [initial public offering] markets in the world and has the highest proportion of millionaires relative to the population across [Asia-Pacific]”, Savills said. Additionally, Hong Kong’s wealth-hub status was being strengthened by the city government’s continuing investment in “top-end medical facilities and yachting infrastructure”. The report also cited Hong Kong’s lifestyle appeal, noting that it was home to 287 Michelin-listed restaurants and hosted prestigious sporting events annually. The city is set to host the Hong Kong Open later this month at the Hong Kong Golf Club in Fanling, carrying a prize purse of US$2 million. The Bank of China Hong Kong Tennis Open, which has regularly attracted some of the world’s top men’s tennis players since its return in 2024, is scheduled for January. Alongside the growth, a significant transfer of capital is under way. An estimated US$84 trillion was expected to transfer between generations over the next two decades, according to consulting company Capgemini, with US$72 trillion likely to pass directly to heirs, and a further US$12 trillion to philanthropic causes. Younger wealth holders were becoming increasingly global in outlook and placed greater emphasis on factors including lifestyle, education, wellness and personal values when deciding where to live, invest and establish businesses, Savills said in a separate statement. Kelcie Sellers, associate director at Savills World Research, said capital was likely to become increasingly selective as wealth moved across borders and generations. “Scarce, turnkey and highly serviced assets in markets that combine legal stability, lifestyle quality, privacy and long-term liquidity are likely to remain most resilient,” Sellers said. “Residential real estate must now deliver more than capital preservation alone. It must support how wealth holders and their families want to live, work, travel, connect and plan for the future.” To identify locations best positioned to attract the next generation of global wealth, Savills assessed more than 100 wealth hubs across four key pillars – business, governance and connectivity; wealth clusters and local environment; wealth management and taxation; and lifestyle.

title: Missing Malaysian found safe in flood-ravaged Nepal after 37 days
description: The solo traveller’s return home sparks hope for 54 other Malaysians still missing in the disaster-stricken nation.
content: One of the Malaysians unaccounted for following the devastating floods in Nepal has been confirmed safe and has returned to Malaysia, according to the group representing Malaysians missing in Nepal. Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (Masfih) spokesman Manivannan Rethinam said the person had reported themselves to the Malaysian embassy in Kathmandu. “For Masfih and the other families, the finding of a safe Malaysian 37 days later is an extremely relieving and meaningful development,” Manivannan said in a statement on Friday. “We are thankful because one of the Malaysians, who was previously unaccounted for, has returned to his family.” Manivannan added that the individual was a Chinese Malaysian and among the solo travellers who went missing. Manivannan added that he had also personally contacted the individual’s next of kin and confirmed the person’s safe return. “We were informed that the person was at Nagthali viewpoint at 3.26pm on August 25, which was one day prior to the devastating floods,” he said. “Based on the information given by the person’s next of kin, the person was stranded temporarily due to the destruction of the roads and bridges in the area, alongside the absence of electricity and water supplies. “There was also no internet access, which further limited the person’s movement and communications.” He also said the development was not just about reducing the number of missing Malaysians from 55 to 54. “It is about a family who is able to reunite with their loved one after 37 days of uncertainty,” he said. Masfih, he said, was also eagerly waiting for an engagement with the Attorney General’s Chambers and Bank Negara Malaysia. “We are also still awaiting the opportunity to meet the prime minister physically. “These requests are not just to express our concerns but for us to get a better understanding about steps moving forward for the next of kin, developments for the past 38 days and also aspects that require further attention and action at the highest levels of the government,” he said. On August 26, devastating flash floods struck the Nepal-China border, killing more than 1,400 people to date, while thousands more remain missing. According to an analysis by the United States Geological Survey, a Himalayan glacial collapse was believed to have triggered the incident, generating energy equivalent to a 5.2 magnitude earthquake. This story was first published by The Star

title: Mainland tourists pack Hong Kong stores, but retailers report modest spending
description: Visitors hunt for gold, outdoor gear and rare books, citing favourable exchange rate, while others keep tight grip on purse strings.
content: Mainland Chinese tourists have poured into Hong Kong during the first two days of the National Day “golden week” holiday, but retailers have warned that the surge in visitor numbers is not translating into an equally strong boost in spending. The Hong Kong Retail Management Association said on Friday that visitor spending remained relatively restrained even as shopping districts were busy. “The increase in visitor numbers may be bigger than the increase in retail sales,” association chairwoman Annie Yau Tse Yau On-yee said, adding that tourist spending had improved but was “not particularly outstanding”. Hong Kong recorded more than 277,300 mainland arrivals on Thursday – the first day of the week-long break – representing about 47 per cent of all inbound arrivals for the day, according to immigration figures. Overall, the city expects about 1.29 million mainlanders between October 1 and 7. On Friday, Mong Kok’s shopping streets were crowded with visitors. Beauty shops and tea shops were filled by noon, while a long queue formed at the entrance of Sim City, a shopping centre known for camera equipment. David Liu Haibo, a university student from Hunan province, said he came to Hong Kong with two friends to go hiking and planned to visit Grass Island, or Tap Mun, in Sai Kung. Liu said they were looking to buy outdoor gear at Grand Plaza in Mong Kok, having learned from mainland social media platform RedNote that it offered a wide selection. “We’re each planning to spend around HK$2,000 [US$255] on windbreakers and outdoor backpacks,” Liu said. “The Osprey outdoor backpacks especially, as they may cost about HK$500 to HK$600 more back on the mainland, and the Hong Kong dollar to yuan exchange rate is very favourable right now, saving us a lot of money.” A 23-year-old Sichuan tourist surnamed Sheng said he was on a two-day trip with friends. Instead of visiting shopping centres, he made bookstores his main stops, including Commercial Press and Joint Publishing. His biggest purchase was a collector’s edition of the classic Chinese novel Jin Ping Mei, which cost HK$1,580 and was not available on the mainland. “I really enjoy historical folklore and popular fiction,” Sheng said, adding that the different volumes included commentaries by Huang Lin, a distinguished professor at Fudan University and president of the Chinese Jin Ping Mei Research Association. “I really enjoy reading his commentaries, and I also have a version of Dream of the Red Chamber with his review.” A woman from Zhejiang province who gave her surname as Wang said she was part of a group of two families, including four children. They were visiting for two days and had spent about HK$2,000 on bags, medicine and cosmetics on the first day, she said. Her two sons also wanted to buy sportswear, including football jerseys of teams such as Real Madrid. Shoppers also packed malls in Tsim Sha Tsui, with some tourists hauling suitcases for a final round of purchases before leaving. Jewellery stores such as Chow Tai Fook, Chow Sang Sang and Laopu Gold saw steady foot traffic, with customers filling the shops as uniformed staff presented items on velvet trays. Some shoppers tried on rings and bangles, while others inspected necklaces or earrings. Inside a Chow Tai Fook store in Harbour City, two women browsed the counters while their boyfriends, carrying suitcases and bags, waited outside the door. One of the women, surnamed Zhang, 30, said they had come from Jiangsu province for a two-day shopping holiday, focusing on gold. “We plan to get one we really like before we leave West Kowloon high-speed rail station nearby, without any budget,” she said. “The low exchange rate is the most important reason to come to Hong Kong to buy gold, and the designs here are also more stylish and fresh compared with those back home.” Amy Li, in her thirties, who works at an American company in Shenzhen, said she was on a one-day “gold-seeking” trip with three friends. “I’m planning to buy a new gold bracelet with a budget of around HK$30,000 to HK$40,000,” Li said, noting the favourable exchange rate could save her “up to 200 yuan per gram”. Elsewhere, the wet weather dampened sightseeing at some attractions, leading to short queues at The Peak Tram terminus in Central and visitors staying inside the shopping and dining complexes at the top. Jasper Huang, a mechanical engineer in his twenties from Xiamen in Fujian province, said he and his friends had budgeted about HK$5,000 each for sightseeing and food during their four-day trip. At the West Kowloon Cultural District, visitors gathered at the Hong Kong Palace Museum, where Sue Zheng, a tourist in her thirties from Nanjing, was visiting with her daughter. Zheng said the family had also visited an exhibition at the M+ contemporary art museum. But she said they had resisted spending at the museum shop. “We only looked at the souvenirs and books, but didn’t buy anything, even coffee,” she said. “It’s all quite expensive.” Additional reporting by Edith Lin

title: Rain dampens visitor numbers at Hong Kong attractions on day 2 of ‘golden week’
description: Wet weather keeps Peak Tram queues short and drives visitors indoors, but mainland Chinese tourists still plan to spend three to four days in city.
content: Wet weather dampened visitor numbers at some of Hong Kong’s popular attractions on Friday morning, the second day of mainland China’s National Day “golden week” holiday. Queues at the Peak Tram terminus in Central remained short, with passengers waiting less than an hour to board. Among them was Jasper Huang, a mechanical engineer in his twenties from Xiamen, Fujian province, who was visiting Hong Kong with friends for four days. “We plan to visit some famous spots like Victoria Harbour and the streets of Central, and spend around HK$5,000 [US$637] each person for sightseeing and food,” he said. The group was staying at a hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui, with most of its itinerary focused on Hong Kong Island and Kowloon. At the Peak Galleria, showers drove visitors indoors from the rooftop terrace. A 35-year-old visitor from Yunnan who gave only his surname, Liang, said the weather had disrupted his sightseeing. “It is a shame about the view. I’ll go to some indoor cultural spots instead, like Tai Kwun and the museums in West Kowloon,” he said. Liang and his wife were staying at a hotel in Mong Kok. He said they would spend three days in Hong Kong, with a budget of up to HK$10,000, before returning to Yunnan to spend the rest of the holiday with family. Another visitor, Li Ling-ling, an 18-year-old university student from Guangdong province, was staying with relatives during her four-day trip. “I will visit the Avenue of Stars later, and on other days I will spend a few hundred on cosmetics and check out Kowloon attractions like Temple Street,” she said. In the West Kowloon Cultural District, tourists gathered outside the Hong Kong Palace Museum to take selfies in front of its red gates, which mirror those of Beijing’s Forbidden City. Most were seen snapping pictures before heading inside Sue Zheng, a visitor in her thirties from Nanjing, said she had brought her daughter to see the museum’s exhibitions. The family are staying in a hotel in Wan Chai for their five-day Hong Kong trip. “We have come this far, so we will definitely go in to see the exhibition. Before that, we visited the design exhibition at M+,” she said. “We only looked at the souvenirs and books, but didn’t buy anything, even coffee. It’s all quite expensive.” Hong Kong’s Immigration Department recorded more than 277,300 mainland arrivals on the first day of the holiday, which runs from Thursday to next Wednesday. They accounted for about 47 per cent of total inbound passengers. The city also welcomed more than 68,800 arrivals from the mainland by 10am on Friday.

title: Lula and Bolsonaro clash in final scramble for Brazil presidency
description: Incumbent leftist and far-right rival locked in a dead heat as mudslinging and a religious row dominate the campaign finale.
content: Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his election rival Flavio Bolsonaro are leaving no controversy unturned in their last-ditch efforts to discredit each other and win over voters ahead of Sunday’s nail-biter election. A campaign dominated by scandals and insults has done little to ease the deep political polarisation in Latin America’s biggest economy, one of the last major leftist bastions in the region. The tight race pits Lula, 80, against the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of Donald Trump who has backed a wave of victorious right-wing candidates in Latin America. Trump said Thursday he was watching Brazil’s election “very closely”. Opinion polls predict the vote will go to a run-off on October 25, with Lula and Flavio in a dead heat. “The race is tied but not at a standstill: the final week will determine where the voters who can still be swayed will go,” Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute, said. Many of the nation’s 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options and were deprived of a debate between the leading candidates when both declined to attend a televised show on Thursday evening. Marcelo Vilanova, 32, a fish market manager in the southeastern city of Juiz de Fora, said he was voting for Lula as the “lesser of two evils”. “He did good things for me, for my family,” he said, referring to Lula’s social welfare programmes. “I have criticisms of him too.” Lucas Sales, 38, a mobile phone shop owner in the city, is voting for Flavio Bolsonaro even if “he himself isn’t the best option,” citing his promise to be tough on crime, a key concern for many Brazilians in this election. The race for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage. In recent days, Brazil’s beloved patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, depicted as a Black Madonna, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her post if elected. Flavio issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the saint, declaring that “messing” with her was “unacceptable”. The electoral court ordered Thursday that posts with the “untrue” claims be taken down. Lula tends to have more support among Catholics while Bolsonaro has the backing of a booming Evangelical population. Next, Flavio Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were “cowards” when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while “women learn to receive a touch from a young age”, referring to gynaecological exams. Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse, and Flavio Bolsonaro accused Lula of being “sexist”. “It’s really turned into a circus … my vote won’t go to any of them,” said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee. In another jab during a podcast Thursday, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified “to serve as a building manager”. Veteran leftist Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age. The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest. Nevertheless, voters complain about a high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime. Lula unveiled a flurry of measures in the run-up to the election to win over voters, increasing social welfare payments and banning sports betting that has ensnared many in gambling addiction. “Only Lula has the political clout and credibility to carry out reforms,” Edinho Silva, president of Lula’s Workers’ Party, said Lula made Brazilian sovereignty a central plank of his campaign, warning Trump not to “meddle” in his country’s elections. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has remained a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic Dark Horse about his father. He was forced during the campaign to admit he had asked jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, at the heart of one of Brazil’s largest financial fraud cases, to bankroll the film. Bolsonaro was also confident of a first-round win, vowing that Lula would be “ousted from the presidency” on Sunday.

title: Indonesian cabinet reshuffle: how Prabowo is looking to restore credibility amid criticism
description: The new line-up suggests that the president, halfway through his term, wants a cabinet that is closely aligned with his agenda, analysts say.
content: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s reshuffling of his cabinet signals an urgent need to address criticism and dipping ratings by banking on experienced technocrats and trusted figures in key positions. But while the appointment of a new foreign minister has raised hopes of some restraint on Prabowo’s more impulsive foreign policy decisions, analysts say the president’s self-imposed role as “chief diplomat” is unlikely to change. In his second senior cabinet change in under three weeks, Prabowo on Thursday named his country’s former permanent representative to the UN, Arrmanatha Nasir, as the new foreign minister, with the outgoing Sugiono appointed coordinating minister for human development. Golkar party politician Muhammad Sarmuji was named minister of industry, replacing Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita. Presidential Chief of Staff Dudung Abdurachman will now serve as the coordinating minister for political and security affairs while Bahlil Lahadalia has been appointed coordinating minister for downstreaming and energy transition, a new position in the cabinet. The changes involve 10 ministerial and deputy ministerial appointments, as well as eight other senior leaders of agencies and the police force. All 18 were sworn in at the presidential palace in Jakarta on Thursday afternoon. On September 14, Prabowo replaced finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa with his deputy, Suahasil Nazara. Dedi Dinarto, associate director at strategic advisory firm FGS Global, said the reshuffle showed Prabowo balancing political consolidation with the need to maintain technocratic credibility. “He is placing trusted figures in key positions, while also promoting experienced technocrats such as Suahasil and Arrmanatha,” he said. “This suggests Prabowo wants a cabinet that is closely aligned with his agenda, while ensuring that key portfolios are still run by people with strong professional and institutional experience.” ‘Stem the tide’ Since Sarmuji hailed primarily from a political rather than a technocratic background, Dedi said businesses and investors would be watching how the new industry minister handled a highly technical portfolio. The reshuffle also reinforced Golkar’s standing as a key political ally of Prabowo, Dedi said. Golkar is the second largest party in Indonesia’s parliament and a core member of the ruling coalition. Julia Lau, principal fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute and coordinator of its Indonesia studies programme, said Prabowo was approaching the halfway mark of his first term as president and needed to “stem the tide of negative sentiment and criticism, as well as dents in his personal popularity ratings, fast”. The new foreign and finance ministers would hopefully restore some balance and order to their respective ministries and stem perceptions of disarray or conflict in the country’s policies, Lau said. “If Prabowo has struck the balance correctly in his cabinet, we should not see a similarly large reshuffle again soon,” she said. “However, if more adjustments come within the next six months, it can also reflect a dissatisfaction with particular individuals or a more uncertain political balance as we approach 2029, a critical election year.” Criticism of Prabowo stems from concerns over his authoritarian governance style, democratic backsliding, economic strain from costly state-led programmes and hostile stance towards critics. His signature free meals programme has come in for particular criticism due to mass food poisoning outbreaks, multimillion-dollar corruption scandals and severe budget reallocation away from other vital sectors. The recent cabinet reshuffle points to an effort to sideline senior figures associated with former president Joko Widodo, according to Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. These figures include former coordinating minister Pratikno and former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who has been moved to the comparatively less powerful role of head of the Executive Office of the President. “That does not necessarily mean Jokowi’s broader political influence has significantly weakened, as many of his allies and networks remain embedded across government,” Gatra said, referring to Widodo by his popular nickname. “But it does suggest that Prabowo is increasingly seeking to put his own stamp on the administration.” Foreign reins Arrmanatha’s appointment was particularly significant, Gatra said, as he was an experienced diplomat who rose quickly through the ranks under former foreign minister Retno Marsudi and was likely to hold views that were more closely aligned with the ministry’s. “There will be significant expectations within the foreign policy establishment that he can provide a degree of restraint on some of Prabowo’s more impulsive foreign policy decisions, particularly where these diverge from its [the ministry]’s preferred positions,” he said. However, whether Arrmanatha could do so effectively was uncertain as Prabowo might place a premium on “loyalty and perhaps even compliance” over substantive bureaucratic advice, Gatra added. A major change in direction was not expected, Dedi said, as Prabowo would remain Indonesia’s “chief diplomat and continue to drive foreign policy personally”. “Arrmanatha’s role is expected to bring more substance and follow-through to the president’s active diplomacy,” he said. Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has taken control of Indonesia’s foreign policy, visiting nearly 30 countries to position Jakarta as an active mediator and independent middle power. Lau said the president’s “personalised style” of meeting leaders of large countries and conducting diplomacy in person was not expected to change. However, she said Prabowo should let his diplomats and new foreign minister restore confidence in Indonesia’s “free and active” foreign policy and demonstrate leadership in Asean. “One priority would be the nomination of the Asean Secretary General and working well with the next Asean chair, Singapore, on key regional and transnational challenges,” Lau said. Pressing issues now facing Arrmanatha include the transboundary haze that has bothered Indonesia’s Southeast Asian neighbours in recent months, the country’s accession to the OECD and maintaining the delicate diplomatic balance with the US and China, according to Lau. Internally, given the “inconsistent” moves made during the previous foreign minister’s tenure, Arrmanatha might also have to improve morale among his career bureaucrats and diplomats and provide them with clear direction, she added.

title: Hong Kong users caught off guard as Anthropic tightens VPN access to Claude
description: Some tech-savvy users are bypassing the blocks by routing connections through Singapore via VPNs and registering with foreign payment details.
content: US artificial intelligence company Anthropic appears to have stepped up enforcement of geographical restrictions on its Claude models in Hong Kong, with local users reporting abrupt account suspensions after accessing the service through virtual private networks (VPNs). A wave of complaints surfaced on social media platforms X and Reddit on Thursday, as users who had operated accounts for months using VPNs found them suddenly disabled. One Hong Kong-based user posted on the “r/claude” subreddit that they received an email from Anthropic’s safeguards team citing “suspicious signals” associated with their account, which would be revoked for usage policy violations. “I used it with NordVPN from Hong Kong for six months and today this happened,” the user wrote, adding that they were trying to retrieve their conversation history and data. While Anthropic has not publicly announced a new policy regarding VPNs, the sudden surge in suspensions suggests a deliberate tightening of long-standing regional restrictions. Hong Kong is excluded from Anthropic’s list of supported locations, alongside mainland China and Macau. Despite these limits, tech-savvy users in the city had bypassed blocks by routing connections through supported markets like Singapore via VPNs and sometimes registering with foreign payment details. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday outside normal US business hours. The apparent enforcement push comes amid growing friction between the San Francisco-based firm and Chinese developers. In a report published last month, Anthropic accused seven Chinese AI labs of conducting “industrial-scale” model distillation – harvesting outputs from Claude to train competing models. Anthropic alleged that companies including Beijing-based Moonshot AI and Hangzhou-based DeepSeek circumvented geographic blocks using thousands of fraudulent accounts and third-party proxy networks. Moonshot alone allegedly routed more than 23 million exchanges to Claude between May and July, disguised through accounts appearing to originate from Singapore and Japan. Beijing has rejected US allegations of AI distillation as groundless. Geopolitical tensions have been growing around AI development. In an essay last month calling on frontier labs to pace the release of advanced systems, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that a Chinese lead in AI would pose a “grave danger” to the world, urging Washington to maintain export controls on advanced semiconductors to China.

title: Hardly any buyers for Singapore luxury condos seized in money-laundering case
description: The unsold properties point to a softening of Singapore’s luxury housing market, where policies have thinned the pool of foreign buyers.
content: The first apartment came up for auction and nobody moved. More than 60 people crowded into a room in Singapore to watch seven properties seized in one of the world’s biggest money-laundering cases go under the hammer. Their opening prices totalled more than S$43 million (US$33.6 million). But when bidding began for a luxury unit at Gramercy Park, an upscale condominium near the city state’s Orchard Road shopping district, not a single hand went up. Next came a 2,658 sq ft (247 square metres) marble-clad unit with a private lift for S$7.55 million. Seven minutes of awkward silence passed before someone offered S$4 million. The room erupted in laughter and the bid was quickly rejected. An hour later and all seven properties remained unsold. Three years after a S$3 billion money-laundering case stunned Singapore, the government is selling more than 80 properties and over 1,000 designer purses and jewellery forfeited from 10 convicted China-born launderers and other foreign nationals linked to the gang. The auctions have drawn interest from a public keen for a glimpse into the criminals’ lavish lifestyles. Yet the unsold properties point to a softening of Singapore’s luxury housing market, where government policies have thinned the pool of wealthy foreign buyers while local bidders prove reluctant to meet the sellers’ asking prices. Of the over two dozen properties offered at auction in recent weeks, only four luxury flats have sold via that format. Two units at Martin Modern, near the Singapore River, fetched S$2.12 million and S$2.08 million, close to their previous transaction prices. Two units at Wallich Residence, which occupies the upper floors of Singapore’s tallest skyscraper in the downtown business district, sold below their opening prices for S$6.6 million and S$5.48 million. “People often go to auctions with the mindset of ‘I’m looking for a bargain’,” said Nicholas Mak, chief research officer of Mogul.sg, a local property portal. With reduced transaction volumes in the luxury property sector, bidders are more likely to hold out for a good deal, he said. “It’s becoming a buyer’s market.” Part of the problem is that the pool of possible buyers is limited. Most foreigners in Singapore face a 60 per cent additional buyer’s stamp duty on residential purchases, one of the most extreme examples of a slate of government efforts to calm soaring housing demand in recent years. Meanwhile, fewer local buyers can afford homes priced in the eight figures, Mak said. Auctioneers are betting on the fact that Singapore’s private property market continues to attract a fair bit of interest despite the curbs, with a price index for private property prices accelerating at the fastest quarterly pace since 2024. Sales during the quarter declined by about 30 per cent from the preceding three months. That is also coming up against pockets of weakness in some major luxury districts the gang bought heavily into. On the resort island of Sentosa, for example, unit prices of villas in the enclave have fallen by around 11 per cent in the last decade through 2025. That has reflected in some properties already advertised at lower prices. Lin Baoying, one of the people convicted in the case, paid nearly S$29 million for two detached houses in Sentosa in 2021. A property broker is offering them at a combined guide price that is more than S$6 million cheaper, according to marketing materials seen by Bloomberg News. Deloitte’s Singapore unit, which is overseeing the liquidation, is releasing assets in phases through mid-2027. Repeated failures to sell may encourage buyers to wait for further cuts, Mak said. But lowering prices too quickly presents its own difficulty. “The sellers may have to be a bit more dynamic, but they cannot be seen to be desperate to sell,” he said. More than 200 properties, many situated in prime locations like Orchard Road and Sentosa, were seized by authorities after over 400 police officers conducted raids across the island in 2023. The launderers became known as the “Fujian Gang”, as all of the convicted individuals hail from that southern province in China. The scandal also embroiled some of the biggest financial institutions in Singapore. Nine firms, including Credit Suisse, United Overseas Bank and Citibank, were ordered to pay a combined S$27.45 million in penalties for breaches of anti-money-laundering requirements linked to the saga. The case’s notoriety has proved part of the attraction for buyers chasing the smaller spoils. At a sale run by auction house Hotlotz, every luxury goods lot found a buyer. A limited-edition Louis Vuitton bag shaped like a pumpkin, designed in collaboration with the late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, had been estimated at S$12,000 to S$16,000. It drew 81 bids and sold for S$87,000. Sue Jean Tay, 38, had placed an online bid of S$3,600 for a butterfly-shaped Graff ring set with diamonds and emeralds. By the time she inspected it in person days later, 15 other bidders had joined in and the price had reached S$8,000. A jewellery enthusiast who is professionally trained in grading diamonds, Tay said part of what makes jewellery interesting is the story behind each piece. She had already pictured herself explaining the ring’s provenance: “Oh, you know, just from the biggest money laundering case in Singapore.” A rare luxury product can prompt buyers to act in an auction because they do not know when another will appear, said Olivier Gergele, EY-Parthenon’s Asean and Singapore consumer products and retail leader. By contrast, property markets tend to be more anchored to valuation, he added. “Even if there is significant buyer interest, they typically stop bidding once the price exceeds their assessment of fair value.” So far, about S$1.4 billion in cash and proceeds from assets already sold has gone into the government’s consolidated fund – the equivalent of its bank account – according to police figures through the end of March. That is more than the roughly S$1.07 billion the government allocated for cost-of-living vouchers for citizens in the last financial year. Maintaining and managing the seized assets cost police S$5.26 million over the three financial years through March 2026. Another 14 Hotlotz auctions are planned, with the next one scheduled for November. Coming rounds will feature Hermes handbags and watches from Patek Philippe, Richard Mille and Rolex. Dozens of properties also remain. The question for their sellers is whether the buyers will meet the prices. “There has been a lot of hype generated,” Tan Tee Khoon, Knight Frank Singapore’s head of auction and sales, said after the first seven properties failed to find buyers. “Some of them literally tell me, ‘I just want to come and see.’”

title: From stock losses to bond bets: 5 figures investors are watching in China
description: Fresh policy support, falling stocks and rising demand for Chinese bonds shape the week’s market narrative.
content: A sell-off in technology stocks pushed mainland Chinese equities to their lowest level in more than a year, even as Beijing stepped up support for the economy with a key interest rate cut. At the same time, Chinese government bonds attracted fresh interest as US Treasury yields climbed to a new high. Here are some figures that have captured market attention this week. China’s CSI 300 Index hits 13-month low Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 2.2 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since August 21 last year, while the technology-focused Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent. A 31 per cent plunge in the Star Market 50 during the third quarter contributed to a 12 per cent decline in the CSI 300. Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks could face a bumpy road in the fourth quarter amid underwhelming stimulus measures, concerns over further interest rate increases and changing sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related investments, analysts said. Key lending rate cut by 0.25 percentage points China’s central bank cut the one-year pledged supplementary lending rate to 1.5 per cent from 1.75 per cent on Tuesday, aiming to encourage policy banks to provide funding for projects aligned with national priorities. The move came alongside a mortgage interest subsidy programme for first-time homebuyers, offering an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for up to five years for loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000). China’s 30-year bonds gain favour as US yields climb Citi Research analysts on Monday recommended going long on China’s 30-year sovereign bonds, forecasting yields to fall towards 1.8 per cent, while the 10-year yield could decline to 1.6 per cent. On Tuesday, yields on China’s 30-year special treasury bonds fell to an intra-day low of 2.11 per cent, while 10-year yields dropped to a one-year low of 1.68 per cent. Meanwhile, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury rose to 5.25 per cent on Tuesday, while the 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.56 per cent, its highest level since 2004. Chinese vehicle exports projected to top 12 million units The China Passenger Car Association, a government-backed industry group, forecast overseas sales of Chinese-made vehicles – including passenger cars, buses and lorries – to top 12 million units in 2026, up 44 per cent from last year’s 8.3 million. The projected figure is 20 per cent higher than the previous estimate of 10 million vehicles made by the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. China’s R&D spending reaches 2.8 per cent of GDP China’s spending on research and development exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of gross domestic product. For the first time, the country’s R&D expenditure surpassed the average among members of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

title: Return of 11 Skies project to Airport Authority will spur hub development: experts
description: Airport Authority board member and hospitality expert suggest ways to boost visitor numbers and develop attractions to draw tourists to Hong Kong.
content: The move by the Airport Authority to take over the 11 Skies project will catalyse the development of its aviation hub, a government adviser and a hospitality sector expert have said, calling for better access and immersive entertainment to attract visitors. Their remarks came on Friday, two days after developer New World Development (NWD) announced it would return the project to the authority next year – including an entertainment complex and three office towers – and provide cash or equivalents of more than HK$3 billion (US$382.3 million), on the back of major losses. Lawmaker Perry Yiu Pak-leung, a board member of the authority, supported the move and said the statutory body was bringing together other projects under the Skytopia blueprint, which envisions the development of a shopping, dining, hospitality, business and entertainment experiences hub. He highlighted the AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 development, which includes an indoor arena with a seating capacity of more than 20,000, as well as future yacht berths and other infrastructure and business activities covered by the blueprint. “I believe that resolving the issue and reaching an agreement can enable us to achieve synergy and advance it faster,” Yiu told a radio show. “The agreement can allow the project to kick off in 2028 … We are not required to raise extra funds for the initial capital. Under such circumstances, it has laid a solid foundation for the authority to advance the project.” On Wednesday, the authority said it was taking forward the project “full steam ahead” and aimed to create a unique entertainment hub that would open in the 2028-29 financial year. Yiu, who is also chairman of China Travel Service (Hong Kong), said 11 Skies would focus on offering innovative entertainment experiences that were currently lacking in the city, instead of retail and catering services. He cited the example of a collaboration between a go-karting facility and car brands, as well as leveraging the airport’s cold chain logistics to build a fresh food market offering different products and cuisines. “The public is looking for experience and immersive entertainment, rather than simple product sales and promotion,” he said. Yiu also suggested improving the complex’s accessibility, noting that the airport should ensure quick and smooth transport for tourists. He also highlighted the potential footfall brought by the Southbound Travel for Guangdong Vehicles scheme. Private cars under the scheme can park at the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge, allowing visitors to travel around the city or transfer flights. “It can integrate with the fishing village culture and green tourism resources on Lantau Island, building it into an international tourism island,” he said. Appearing on the same radio show, Dennis Wong Ka-wing, head of the Hong Kong Institute of Vocational Education’s hospitality department, said the deal would boost tourism under the aviation hub blueprint. But Wong pointed out that 11 Skies had little footfall, as surrounding sites were under construction and visitors had few incentives to go to the shopping centre. “In the future, the authority can consider opening more walkways to divert footfall … It has a walkway connecting AsiaWorld-Expo, but it does not have an obvious visitor route to the airport,” he said. He also suggested that the authority provide parking at cheaper rates to entice locals to the area. “It can drive a huge amount of footfall and stimulate consumption. Whether they spend much or not, at least it can drive footfall and create a talking point among the community,” Wong said. Apart from attracting tourists through the cross-border driving scheme, Wong said the authority should also focus on drawing crowds attending large-scale concerts and performances at the future AsiaWorld-Expo Phase 2 development. He also saw the project’s potential as a draw for high-end travellers, as its office buildings could provide premium medical services close to the airport. He added that hotels and future berthing facilities in Skytopia could attract high-spending tourists. The announcement from NWD came as it entered its third year of deleveraging after liquidity concerns surfaced in 2023. The company has since stepped up asset disposals and capital recycling to improve liquidity and reduce leverage.

title: A Hong Kong flat gets a stylish, Scandinavian-inspired makeover – and a sewing room
description: This 1,300 sq ft Mid-Levels flat was gutted, and a bedroom and corridor were removed to free up space and allow for a room for the owner’s hobbies.
content: It is almost impossible not to remark on the view from Rebecca Chan’s one-bedroom, one-study, two-bathroom flat in Hong Kong’s Mid-Levels. Directly opposite the entrance to her 1,300 sq ft (120 square metre) home are French doors that lead onto a balcony and frame a lush vista of what feels like at least 50 shades of green. Architect Liz Lau Win-wa was so captivated by the nature on Chan’s doorstep that she used it as the starting point for the design concept after being commissioned to revamp the flat. “It is quite rare to find such a concentrated pocket of trees in a central location,” says Lau, founder of interior design studio Laud. “It both feels like Hong Kong and like somewhere else entirely. It was a great backdrop to work with and set the design tone for the apartment, driving a lot of the materials we picked.” The original three-bedroom, two-bathroom flat had been owned and occupied by Chan’s parents for years, and by the time Lau saw it, it was crying out for a full renovation. With dark wood finishes and heavy furnishings reminiscent of the 1990s, the apartment felt cramped and dated. Lau responded by gutting the property and removing a poky bedroom and corridor to open up the living area and maximise the natural light. To connect the various sections of the main space and give the apartment a more cohesive identity, she installed a full-height shelving cabinet along the length of the living and dining room and encased the flat’s central walls in oak – the kitchen, guest bathroom and a sewing room are behind them – playing with the direction of the wood grain to add interest. “I now love having a larger living room, with a multipurpose space behind the sofa for reading, work and music,” says Chan, who moved from the UK to Hong Kong in 2019 to care for her ageing parents. Lau’s designs are influenced by a love of Scandinavian style, characterised by clean lines, good-looking yet functional furniture and the liberal use of wood. Chan shares this sensibility, which made design decisions refreshingly straightforward. The pair deliberately chose an understated palette, reasoning that Chan’s books, plants and other possessions would supply an additional layer of colour and personality. Lau experimented with different paint shades and textures, observing how the colours shifted throughout the day as the light changed. “Don’t confuse simple with easy,” she says. “The paint was applied very softly, using special fibre rollers to give that European matt eggshell texture. Our contractor was old school, a real craftsman, who took his time to get everything right.” Light was treated almost as another material. Lau collaborated with a specialist lighting designer, Christopher Mok from Spectrum Design & Associates, and incorporated multiple layers of illumination rather than relying on overhead sources alone. This ensures a gentle, even diffusion that accentuates specific features, materials and textures while allowing different areas of the flat to glow at night. The dining area pendant, for example, highlights the furniture around it without casting a shadow. Given Chan’s love of dressmaking and textile arts, Lau proposed dedicating an entire room to her hobbies – a rare luxury in space-tight Hong Kong flats. How often do you get to design a sewing room in Hong Kong? Liz Lau Win-wa, architect Using materials consistent with the rest of the home, Lau designed a continuous worktop that reads as part of the overall interior and added a large pegboard above it for easy access to scissors, yarn and other tools. “How often do you get to design a sewing room in Hong Kong?” Lau says. “It was a fun project for us, too.” Customisation runs throughout the home. Lau and her team designed and made most of the furniture, which allowed them to tailor pieces closely to Chan’s taste and habits. Since Chan is a fan of hotpot, for example, the dining table discreetly incorporates a cut-out for the electricity cable, which runs unseen down the table’s central support and plugs into a floor socket, keeping the table clear and clutter-free during meals. Though the dust has long settled, the renovation having been completed at the end of 2025, Chan is still relishing her renewed surroundings, brought firmly into the present. “I didn’t know what to expect because I was so used to the flat in its run-down state and then seeing it as a building site,” she says. “It has turned out so much better than I could have imagined.” Entrance Among Thousands of Mountains by Hong Kong-based American artist Jesse McLin. Side table designed by Laud, with recycled Formella Fern tiles from Claybrook Studio. Living area Shelving and audiovisual units designed by Laud. Offset sofa by Audo Copenhagen from Wool Studio. Curved Bench coffee table with Curved Boxes by Kristina Dam Studio. Fiji sculpture by Volta Mobiles. Rug by Pinton 1867. Kitchen Kitchen, designed by Laud and made in collaboration with Kitench. Living Ceramics splashback tiles from Anta; counter in Caesarstone. Study Shelving, desk and window seat, designed and made by Laud. Lamp from Zara Home. Vehicle of Peace: Girl & Cat (2023), sculpture by Ichizo Ino, from The Gallery by Soil. Drawn chair by &Tradition from Wool Studio. Tavole Oak Giulietta flooring by STP from Equal. Sewing room Workstation, shelves and peg board, all designed and made by Laud. Lamp from Archetypal. Bedroom Bed and bedside tables designed and made by Laud. Comodin wall lamp by Santa & Cole from Wool Studio. Dining area Dining table designed and made by Laud. Drawn HM3 chairs by &Tradition from Wool Studio. Dot 600 Dali pendant lamp by Lumina from Forth Furniture.

title: Finland on alert after ‘significant’ number of intrusions at MPs’ homes
description: Prime Minister Petteri Orpo says foreign power involvement ‘very possible’ after suspected break-ins leave nothing stolen.
content: Finland is investigating a slew of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, which the prime minister said could be linked to a foreign power. Following media reports, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho on Thursday said parliament had been made aware of a “significant” number of apparent intrusions at the homes of several politicians. Finland, which shares a 1,340km (830-mile) border with Russia, has been on high alert since the Kremlin sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022. “I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant,” Halla-aho told a press conference. He said the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago. Nothing was stolen or damaged, but signs of intrusion were left inside the homes, Halla-aho said, adding that while some indicators may not have been immediately spotted, “it is possible that these signs were deliberately left where the occupants would notice them”. “At this stage, there is no information about the motive or who was responsible,” he stressed. The speaker also said there were no common denominators among those who have been targeted regarding party affiliation or gender. Asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be involved, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said it was “very possible. Quite possible in these times”. “If someone tries to destabilise Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity,” he said. Orpo said investigations were vital as Finland was preparing for a general election in April 2027. “We can see in several European countries that Russia has tried to influence elections,” Orpo said. Deputy speaker Paula Risikko, who leads the parliamentary security group, said she had been informed last week and added that Helsinki police had been tasked with the “initial stage of the investigation”. “The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time,” Helsinki police said. All members of parliament had been told to keep an eye out, report observations and file police complaints if necessary. Newspaper Ilta-Sanomat earlier reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins last week, and that the daily was aware of at least two home intrusions. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said “an attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy”. “It should not be allowed or accepted in any form,” he told reporters. Russia’s war on Ukraine prompted Finland to abandon its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and it joined Nato in April 2023. The Nordic country has in the past accused Moscow of “hybrid warfare” and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023 – a charge the Kremlin denied. Additional reporting by Reuters
