title: Who is Jim Carrey’s actress-artist wife, Min Ah?
description: Carrey – who has been married twice before, and dated Renée Zellweger and Jenny McCarthy – has reportedly tied the knot in a private ceremony in Los Angeles.
content: Actor and comedian Jim Carrey is a married man – again. Carrey has just tied the knot with Min Ah, whom he’s been linked to since 2022, in a small private ceremony in Los Angeles, his representative confirmed to E! News on Wednesday. TMZ was first to report the news, which comes just seven months after Carrey and his now-wife made their highly publicised debut as a couple at the 51st César Awards in Paris on February 26. Carrey, who has been previously married to actresses Melissa Womer and Lauren Holly, was last linked to his Kidding co-star Ginger Gonzaga, an actress over 20 years his junior, after they walked the red carpet together at the 2019 Golden Globes. Their split was reported just nine months later. So who is Min Ah, the woman Carrey first gave a passionate shoutout to at the César Awards, and is now married to? What does Min Ah do? Not much information is publicly available about Min Ah. However, she is said to be an actress and an artist from Los Angeles and is also known as Minzi, per People. Her low profile online comes as no surprise, given that her beau is also notoriously private. The César Awards were his first public appearance since inducting Soundgarden into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November last year. When did she and Jim Carrey start dating? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jim Carrey Fans (@jimcarreythebest) According to reports, the 51st César Awards earlier this year marked the first time Carrey and his partner, Min Ah, stepped out in public. While it is not clear when their relationship started, the pair were reportedly linked in 2022. They were seen exiting Los Angeles’ Largo at the Coronet after a comedy charity event fronted by Judd Apatow, per People. Carrey was previously married to Melissa Womer – with whom he shares daughter Jane – and Dumb and Dumber actress Lauren Holly. His past girlfriends include his Me, Myself and Irene co-star Renée Zellweger, The View alum Jenny McCarthy, make-up artist Cathriona White, and Kidding actress Ginger Gonzaga. What has Jim Carrey said about Min Ah? When Carrey took to the podium after winning the honorary César, he gave a loving shout-out to Min Ah during his acceptance speech. It was seemingly the first time he spoke of her publicly. “I love you, Min Ah,” he declared, calling her his “sublime companion”. Additional reporting by Gloria Tso

title: Seoul ups the ante in Ukraine feud over North Korean POW transfer disclosure
description: President Lee warned of ‘additional measures’ against Kyiv unless it offered a public apology over the episode.
content: South ‌Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Friday threatened unspecified measures against Ukraine unless Kyiv acknowledged what Seoul says was a confidentiality agreement covering the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers and apologised. “If the refusal to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology continues, we will take additional measures,” Lee said in a social media post. Lee also expressed “grave regret” over what he described as Ukrainian remarks about an imminent ⁠military clash between North and South Korea, saying they amounted to encouraging war on the Korean peninsula. Seoul and Kyiv ‌have been locked in a diplomatic dispute since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced at the United Nations General Assembly last month that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners ‌of war captured while fighting for Russia to South Korea. Seoul subsequently accused Kyiv of violating an ⁠agreement to keep the ⁠transfer confidential to protect the soldiers, while Ukrainian officials said no such agreement existed. Ukraine was seeking to mend ties with ‌South Korea, Ukrainian media reported on Thursday, quoting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. “I would not like to call this an incident. Let’s say, it’s a diplomatic ‌misunderstanding,” Sybiha ‌told journalists at an event, according to a report on news website nv.ua and other media. A senior South ‌Korean foreign ministry official told reporters on Friday that the countries’ foreign ministers had been discussing how Kyiv could address Seoul’s concerns, including a possible apology, according to South Korean media reports. Foreign ‌Minister Cho ‌Hyun and Sybiha had been in direct contact and were discussing what level of response Seoul was seeking and what Ukraine could ‌accept, while taking into account Ukraine’s wartime circumstances and the need to avoid causing either side a loss of face, according to the reports. The dispute comes ‌at a sensitive time for Lee’s administration, which has sought to reduce tensions with North Korea and is also ⁠dealing with political fallout from a recent landmine incident in the demilitarised zone. Cho Han-bum, a senior fellow at ⁠the Korea Institute for National Unification in Seoul, said any additional measures would most likely involve support South Korea already provides to Ukraine, including humanitarian, financial and reconstruction help. “Ukraine has more to lose than ‌South Korea because it is receiving ‌support from Seoul,” Cho said. South Korea has provided humanitarian and financial aid to Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 invasion and in July pledged an additional US$100 million in non-lethal support on the sidelines of the Nato summit. “However, neither side benefits from a prolonged confrontation,” Cho said, noting that South Korea relies on Ukraine for information related to North Korea’s military activities.

title: Why sapphires are useful for modern technology
description: This gemstone is made up of strong ionic bonds that make it extremely hard and stable – perfect for making many important devices.
content:
Most people imagine jewellery when they think about sapphire. But did you know this gem is also in many devices we use?
Sapphire is useful in modern technology and engineering.
It is a mineral called corundum. It is known chemically as aluminium oxide (Al2O3). Over millions of years, natural sapphires form under extreme heat and pressure deep in the Earth’s crust. There, minerals rich in aluminium are changed into solid corundum.
Pure sapphire has no colour and is transparent. But if the corundum has trace elements, it can come in different colours (see chart). In fact, when corundum has more chromium, its colour is red, and it is called a ruby.
In sapphire, aluminium ions (Al3+) and oxide ions (O2-) are bound together. These ions are packed in a direction-dependent pattern. This means its properties can change depending on the direction of measurement.
The strong bonds between the aluminium ions and oxide ions give sapphire its special properties.
Extreme hardness: Sapphire resists scratches to its surface. On the Mohs hardness scale (see graphic), it ranks nine out of 10. It is second only to diamond.
High thermal stability: Sapphire melts at about 2,030 degrees Celsius, so it can withstand high heat without changing.
Electrical insulation: The electrons on the outer shells of sapphire atoms are tightly held by ionic bonds, so there are no free electrons to conduct electricity. This makes sapphire a great electrical insulator.
Chemical inertness: Sapphire’s tight ionic structure is very stable. This allows it to resist attack from most strong acids and alkalis at room temperature.
Broad optical transparency: Pure sapphire can transmit a wide range of wavelengths – from ultraviolet (UV) and visible light all the way to infrared (IR).
Natural sapphires are too rare, small and flawed to be used in technology. Instead, engineers grow large, flawless sapphires in hot furnaces. They are then sliced into thin discs called sapphire wafers. These can be used in modern technology.
Protective covers: Sapphire’s ability to resist scratches makes it a perfect protective material. It is used to cover luxury watches, smartphone camera lenses and screen protectors.
LED lighting and displays: Sapphire is often used as a base layer for gallium nitride (GaN) films. These are used to make blue and white LEDs, power electronics and high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs). HEMTs are key for satellite systems and electric vehicles.
Silicon-on-sapphire (SOS) technology: Thin layers of silicon and sapphire help reduce electronic interference. This is key for satellite communications and mobile signal transmissions.
Optoelectronics: Sapphire’s broad optical transparency allows UV, visible and IR light to pass through. This makes it a key material for laser diodes, optical sensors and light-transmitting lenses.
Young Post has partnered with Hong Kong Science Museum and Hong Kong Space Museum to encourage your pursuit of science. Every month, the museums answer questions about the world around us, the cosmos and beyond.

title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever diplomatic ties as northern fighting escalates
description: Tensions between the two African neighbours reach crisis point amid fears of renewed full-scale war in the Tigray region.
content: Ethiopia and Eritrea broke diplomatic ties on Thursday, accusing each other of stoking internal conflicts as fighting continued in northern Ethiopia. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing a rebel group, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched a major assault against government forces last week, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020–2022 civil war that killed an estimated 600,000 people. Addis Ababa said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who “pose a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security” and would shut its embassy in Asmara. Eritrea’s foreign ministry responded shortly after that it “has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”. Hundreds have been killed and wounded since heavy fighting resumed in northern Ethiopia last week. The TPLF, which dominates the state of Tigray, launched attacks into neighbouring Afar and Amhara states, fighting alongside local militias. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who has yet to comment on the crisis, was due to be sworn in for a new term on Monday after winning elections in June. But he faces conflict on multiple fronts as several armed groups have formed an alliance against him. Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, without giving a reason. The two countries have also been at odds – particularly over a mega dam being built by Ethiopia on the River Nile – and Egypt has built closer ties with Eritrea in recent months. Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and they fought a brutal border war from 1998 to 2000. Ties improved when Abiy came to power in 2018, and the two countries even fought together against the Tigrayans during the last civil war. But relations then deteriorated sharply, with Eritrea voicing fears that landlocked Ethiopia intended to invade and seize access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia “has been pursuing an agenda of incessant hostility … against Eritrea for three years in pursuit of ‘the imperative of acquiring sovereign access to the sea’ through the invasion of sovereign Eritrean ports and coastal areas,” the Eritrean foreign ministry said on Thursday. Meanwhile, an overnight explosion at the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) headquarters in Addis Ababa raised fears that the army’s conflict with rebel groups had reached the capital for the first time. Diplomatic and security sources confirmed the blast but could not say its cause or who was responsible, nor give any casualty figures. “The explosion took place at the HQ and was powerful. It shook the surrounding area and triggered significant panic among people in the vicinity,” a worker at a nearby bar told Agence France-Presse, relaying what he said was information from colleagues there working at the time. On Wednesday, the National Intelligence and Security Services ordered a ban on all drone flights around the capital. Conflict monitor ACLED said drones suspected to be linked to the anti-government alliance targeted army and civilian airports in Oromia and Amhara states on Sunday. On the front lines of the internal fighting in northern Ethiopia, there were signs that the Tigrayan rebels were being pushed back on Thursday. A humanitarian source said the TPLF had been dislodged from the town of Erebti in Afar, which it seized earlier this week, and was now fighting near the mountainous border between Afar and Tigray. A pro-government militia said on X it had retaken Erebti, as well as Maychew town in southern Tigray. Locals earlier this week said Maychew had endured heavy shelling. Verification is difficult as media are prevented from travelling to affected areas and there are significant communications disruptions. Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said it had registered more than 420 wounded at Korem and Alamata hospitals in Tigray by September 25, and more than 300 at Shire in western Tigray. The humanitarian source estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar.

title: What does Philippines seek with new Thitu map in South China Sea?
description: By publishing coordinates, charts and the legitimate basis of its position, the Philippines is aiming to reduce legal ambiguity, experts say.
content: Thitu Island and its residents have come under the spotlight after the Philippines, in a bid to reinforce its claims in the South China Sea, announced plans to file an updated maritime chart with the United Nations. Observers say the filing would not establish Philippine sovereignty but could help Manila identify and challenge competing claims in more precise legal terms. More than just a technical document, the updated map is a means for the government to formally document its presence and claim sovereignty over Thitu, known locally as Pagasa, according to Presidential Assistant for Maritime Concerns Andres Centino. The former military officer said the map charted water depths, island contours and features around Thitu, Lawak and other parts of the Kalayaan island group, including those that remained above water at high tide. “It is not just a dot on the map,” Centino said last Friday at a ceremonial unveiling of the map on the island, which lies about 480km (300 miles) west of the Philippine province of Palawan. Beijing claims the island, which it calls Zhongye Dao, as part of its Nansha island group, known internationally as the Spratlys. It rejects a 2016 arbitral ruling that found no legal basis for its claims to historic rights within the nine-dash line. Chinese coastguard ships, maritime militia vessels and research ships have been sighted near Thitu. China has insisted that its actions are lawful and has accused Manila of intruding on its territory. Manila, meanwhile, is strengthening its physical presence on the island, home to about 100 families. Construction observed during a visit by This Week in Asia included work to extend a runway at Rancudo Airfield by 200 metres (660 feet) to about 1,500 metres. Alongside a newly built hangar, the Philippine Air Force is constructing an observation tower to monitor activity around the island. Evelyn Grenanda, 35, a mother of four who owns a small grocery store, said the uncertainty could spur some residents to seek opportunities elsewhere. “The island is so isolated that they still need to go to the mainland.” Another resident, Gemelyn Amlang, 26, preferred to remain on the island as long as the Philippine government provided work and livelihood support. But the 26-year-old, who said she had grown accustomed to seeing Chinese ships daily, saw few prospects for herself and her four-year-old daughter. They moved to the island from Palawan three years earlier. “We are on an island called Hope but it seems there’s no hope. We’re just here, going around in circles. There’s nothing else to do,” she said. That feeling is shared by fishermen such as Joseph Warina, 32, whose fishing grounds in the contested waters are sometimes “blocked” by Chinese vessels. “I hope what we always fear will not happen,” he said, referring to the prospect of armed clashes. Such fears persist despite earlier diplomatic assurances. In April 2019, then Philippine ambassador to China Jose Santiago Santa Romana said Beijing had assured Manila it had no intention of occupying or using force against Thitu. Against this backdrop, Manila is considering diplomatic steps. Centino said the proposed filing to the UN was separate from the Philippines’ recent submission of its official nautical chart of Scarborough Shoal, another contested marine feature. On record Experts said depositing the updated map with the UN Secretary General would be primarily an act of legal clarification and international notification under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), which sets out countries’ rights and responsibilities in the world’s oceans. “Manila [is placing] on international record a precise description of the maritime entitlements it considers to flow from the features it claims,” said Arnaud Leveau, a geopolitics professor at Paris Dauphine University. “This carries strategic weight, because ambiguity tends to favour the strongest actor at sea. By publishing coordinates, charts and the legal basis of its position, the Philippines narrows that ambiguity,” he added. Sylwia Monika Gorska, a political analyst at the University of Central Lancashire, said the updated chart gave Manila a more precise record of Thitu and nearby features. “If Manila deposits baselines or maritime limits under Unclos, those coordinates would enter the formal international record,” she said, adding that they would give Manila a fixed reference point for future diplomatic protests, negotiations and responses to activity at sea. Beyond legal filings, Leveau said maintaining a civilian presence was important because it distinguished the island from being a purely military outpost. “A functioning civilian community strengthens Manila’s position without reducing Pagasa to a purely military confrontation.” Legal efforts were also more effective when backed by a sustained physical presence, he added. On Thitu, the runway, civilian settlement, public facilities and government administration amounted to a second layer of Manila’s strategy. Beijing has already challenged the updated chart, with Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun calling it “illegal, null and void” and a violation of China’s sovereignty. But the proposed filing would also sit within a wider Southeast Asian pattern of using UN mechanisms to place maritime positions on the international record – a process that can expose differences among other claimants. In June 2024, for example, the Philippines submitted scientific information to a UN commission to establish the continental shelf’s outer limits beyond 200 nautical miles in the West Palawan region. China, Vietnam and Malaysia challenged the submission on different legal grounds. The case, Gorska said, showed that opposition to Philippine claims could come from different directions. “The more important lesson is that a Philippine legal move directed largely at strengthening its position against China can still trigger objections from states that otherwise share some of Manila’s concerns about Chinese claims,” she said.

title: Asian Games, day 13: Hong Kong sailors lead medal haul; Wong, rugby teams face gold chances
description: Squash women win silver while tennis duo get key bronze; fellow bronze winner Ceci Lee says she ‘always can’t win gold in the omnium’.
content: Hong Kong’s sailors had themselves a golden day at the Asian Games on Friday, while tennis star Coleman Wong Chak-lam has a shot at one of his own, although there is more at stake than just gold in his men’s singles final on Saturday. Victory over China’s Wu Yibing, whom he beat in the third round at the Games in Hangzhou, would earn Wong a place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Wu also has that target in mind. Saturday could prove to be a historic one for Hong Kong’s athletes. The gold medals secured on Friday in the boys’ skiff, by Louis Polson and Ethan Kiu, and in the girls’ skiff by Chloe Kong and McCarley Wong, were the sixth and seventh of the Games, one shy of the record eight the city has managed on three occasions: 2010, 2018 and 2023. “We are very excited,” McCarley Wong said. “We are very happy that we have achieved this medal. It’s still quite surreal.” With sailor Nicholas Halliday and the women’s squash team adding silver, and two bronze coming from women’s doubles tennis and track cycling, Hong Kong’s total medal count has now reached 46, with 17 silver and 22 bronze to go alongside the gold. Wong is likely to be the first to increase that figure on Saturday, and after crashing out in the quarter-finals in Hangzhou, it will be his first Asian Games medal, whatever happens. There was a moment on Friday when he almost had to settle for bronze, with Khumoyun Sultanov breaking early to take the first set 6-3 before Wong took control to win the next two 6-3, 6-2. “I think I am just doing what I am supposed to do,” Wong said. “So, here I am at the final now, so let’s just keep going because you won’t know the outcome until after you give it a go with your full strength.” Gold or silver aside, the bronze won by his teammates Eudice Chong and Wong Hong-yi secured tennis’ Tier A status in the Hong Kong Sports Institute for another four years. The city’s rugby players, meanwhile, are still on course to match their performances in Hangzhou, and for the men that would mean a third consecutive gold. Another dominant day involved a 22-0 win over China in Pool A, followed by a 50-0 thrashing of Malaysia in the quarter-finals. Jevon Groves’ side head into Saturday’s semi-final against South Korea without conceding a point. “It just shows our determination and ruthlessness and our grit of sticking to our structure, our plan and being assertive when we go on the pitch,” said Juan Esono Mba Oyana, who scored a hat-trick against Malaysia. Hong Kong’s women, who won bronze in Hangzhou, could afford to lose 24-10 to China and still make it into the semi-finals as the third-best finishers in the pool stage. Their reward for doing so is a meeting with Japan. The positivity of many was not reflected in Ceci Lee Sze-wing’s attitude after her bronze in the women’s omnium. The 25-year-old called it “not the result I expected” and acknowledged she believed gold was a realistic goal at the Izu Velodrome. Lee probably should have walked away with silver, as she did in Hangzhou, but made mistakes in the points race that ultimately left her behind Kazakhstan’s Rinata Sultanova. Gold went to Japan’s Yumi Kajihara. “I am always second – sometimes behind Japan, sometimes behind China – I always can’t win gold in the omnium,” she said. “I always want to change the colour [of the medal], but I didn’t expect to change it to bronze.” The medal-filled Friday started on the water, with Halliday finishing second in the men’s dinghy. South Korea’s Ha Jee-min finished a considerable distance ahead of the fleet to take gold, with Malaysia’s Khairulnizam Mohd Afendy claiming bronze. Next came Halliday’s younger teammates, with 15-year-olds Polson and Kiu winning all 12 of their races. Kong and Wong won nine of the dozen they took part in. “Over the moon about winning every race and thankful to everyone that helped us,” Kiu said. “I wouldn’t say that we’re better than everyone else by that much, but we backed ourselves with confidence on the start line and then held our speed throughout the races.” There was also a silver medal for the city’s women’s squash team after they were beaten 2-1 by Malaysia in the final. In a repeat of the final in Hangzhou, Simmi Chan Sin-yuk edged past women’s singles champion Sivasangari Subramaniam 3-2 to draw level for Hong Kong, after Tomato Ho Tze-lok lost 3-0 in the first match against Aifa Azman. Lee Ka-yi then lost 3-0 to Aifa’s sister Aira Azman and Hong Kong had to settle for a silver medal. While there was obvious disappointment, Chan thought that eventually the team would be “very pleased, looking back at it, because everybody played their best and made their full effort and that is what really matters”.

title: Letters | Outcome of Trump-Xi summit was quieter than a grand bargain
description: Readers discuss the meeting between the presidents of the US and China, pollution from marine vessels in Hong Kong, and a scheme for carers for the elderly.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. What did we actually learn from US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s two days of diplomacy in Washington? Perhaps less than the ceremony suggested – but more than what first appeared to be the case. There were grand words, handshakes, a state dinner and all the choreography expected of a visit at this level. Trump played the role of host with unusual restraint, while Xi arrived with his own priorities, from Taiwan to artificial intelligence. Yet despite the public statements, remarkably little is known about what the two leaders said behind closed doors. That may be the most revealing part of the visit. There was no dramatic breakthrough capable of transforming US-China relations, and neither side appeared ready to show its full hand. Instead, the clearest message was simpler: Washington and Beijing want to keep talking. That matters. The differences between the world’s two largest economies are too deep to disappear over dinner and a 90-minute meeting. Trade, Taiwan, technology, Iran, Ukraine and the Korean peninsula cannot be resolved through diplomatic choreography alone. But the talks did not end in Washington. Trump and Xi intend to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 summits hosted by China and the United States respectively later this year, creating further opportunities for face-to-face diplomacy. So Washington did not give us a grand bargain. It gave us something quieter: a willingness on both sides to maintain dialogue despite profound disagreements. In today’s US-China relationship, that is not insignificant. The real test will come at the next meetings. By then, we may know whether the smiles, handshakes and carefully chosen words in Washington had substance behind them – or whether they amounted to one very well organised dinner. Christos Kazantzoglou, Changsha, China More of Hong Kong’s ferries should go electric Hong Kong’s first five-year plan contains many laudable objectives, particularly the target of PM2.5 concentration of the air we breathe not exceeding 14 µg per m³. With quite diverse air quality in different parts of Hong Kong, I’m curious to know how and where such measurements are made. Living very close to the harbour, I would hazard a guess that one of the most challenging spots to achieve this target would be pretty much anywhere along the harbourfront, due to the frequent passage of marine vessels. While electric cars whisper through the streets of other metropolises and China’s conversion to renewable energy leads the world, our coastal city continues to face the obdurate problem of emissions from marine transport. Vast international freighters passing in and out of their berths at Hong Kong’s cargo terminals may release a large part of the noxious compounds one gets from burning long-chain hydrocarbons, but PM2.5 pollutants are experienced most tangibly by many residents in the breezy wake of ferries, coastal freighters plying local waters and other seaborne craft. As a ferry or a barque of anglers passes, some hold their breath while others light a funereal cigarette, reckoning that their throats can’t register a difference. Surprisingly (or not), there is actually a solution available: electric ferries. The one I spotted recently looked dangerously top-heavy, pitching and rolling in its berth in Kwun Tong. Something could be learned by studying mature infrastructure with comparable aims in other countries more closely. One thing I hope will be done is the electrification of the Star Ferry fleet but in such a way as to preserve that iconic silhouette, the patina and the genius of those reversible wooden seats. May modern bottoms brush history under benevolently inhalable skies. Julian Lees, Yau Tong Scheme for carers for the elderly opens can of worms The government has proposed a scheme to bring in foreign domestic carers specifically to look after the elderly. These carers are expected to have experience and training in addressing the needs of older adults. Does this mean that a family with elderly members as well as children needs to employ a helper responsible for caring for the elderly in addition to a regular foreign domestic worker for help around the house? Will foreign domestic workers not be allowed to assist the elderly? This policy opens a can of worms. Dr Wing K. Tsang, Discovery Bay

title: Paris Fashion Week: The best SS27 looks from Balenciaga, Chloé, Schiaparelli and Rick Owens
description: From Balenciaga’s elevated basics to Gwyneth Paltrow’s daughter Apple Martin making her debut on Chloé’s runway, here are the highlights from day four of PFW.
content: Day four of Paris Fashion Week was filled with back-to-back shows and presentations. The longest day of the week began with Chloé at 10am and ended 12 hours later with a glamorous show by jewellery house Messika. Here’s what you need to know about the four biggest shows of the day. When Schiaparelli’s creative director Daniel Roseberry started designing ready-to-wear for the haute couture house in 2023, he set out to build the foundations and codes of today’s Schiaparelli, a historic brand that had been dormant for decades before Tod’s owner Diego Della Valle acquired it in 2007. How do you make a maison steeped in surrealism and fantasy relevant to modern-day luxury consumers? For Roseberry, this collection was a chance to distil the essence of Schiaparelli’s ready-to-wear and go back to basics, so to speak. Many of the looks in the spring/summer 2027 collection – shown in a salon filled with gilded chandeliers inside the Carrousel du Louvre to a soundtrack of 90s hip-hop and R&B hits like Mariah Carey’s “Honey” and Faith Evans’ “Love Like This” – will look familiar to those who have followed Roseberry’s tenure at the brand. From long-sleeved draped gowns with gold hardware to moulded bodices paired with pleated skirts and embroidered velvet jackets, Roseberry has shown variations of all those looks before but that was the purpose of the show: to showcase the power of consistency and clarity in a world filled with too many mixed messages. The designer, who hails from Texas, has never shied away from injecting a bit of his background into Schiaparelli; this season he wanted to celebrate the ease and freedom of American sportswear, not necessarily with the outfits themselves, but with this idea of “choose-your-own-adventure dressing” that he sees as inextricably linked to his native culture, as he explained in the show notes. The mainly monochrome line-up – filled with exquisite takes on wardrobe staples like the black cocktail dress and the tuxedo shirt – stood out for its clarity of vision. The only patterns came in black-and-white stripes and eye-catching swirling motifs, while the lavishly embroidered jackets that closed the show added playfulness to the subdued line-up. A key part of Schiaparelli’s revival has been its success with accessories, especially gold-embellished shoes and handbags, and much-copied costume jewellery instantly recognisable for its anatomical motifs. This season, animal-inspired jewels, handbags with mouth-shaped handles and heels with a ball on the toe were among the new offerings. Rick Owens has never officially designed a haute couture collection, but his spring/summer 2027 range certainly comes close to that most rarefied form of dressmaking. While the American designer is often associated with a gothic aesthetic and dystopian undercurrents, he is a true dressmaker at heart and loves nothing more than experimenting with techniques and fabrications. The polished line-up he showed this season had an “elegant stoicism”, as the collection notes aptly said. Structured silk duchesse gowns vied for attention with sheer, diaphanous dresses that billowed as the models walked down a sloping runway erected above the reflecting pool of the Palais de Tokyo amid powerful water jets. The designer also introduced innovative materials like a rigid, duchesse-like fabric made from a nylon webbing strap used to transport shipping crates. A couple of millefeuille jackets made of thousands of circles of nylon tulle were simply terrific, but just as outstanding were the more accessible denim separates that will please Owens’ loyal fans, as well as the select retailers that do brisk business with his products. Accessories ranged from wraparound sunglasses to heeled thong sandals in PVC and crystal-embellished wedges that rose to the knee and almost looked like braces. This was another strong, powerful show from one of fashion’s most original and singular voices. Les Coraux de la Liberté (The Corals of Freedom in English) is an art installation by French artist Aude Franjou that was placed inside the column on the Place de la Bastille in Paris last year. Comprising hundreds of coral tentacles made of raw linen, the artwork reflects the fragility of life as well as its resilience, using coral as an emblem of both mortality and strength. A version of the artwork appeared mid-runway at Balenciaga’s spring/summer 2027 show to symbolise a couture house as a “living, breathing, alive ecosystem”, according to the show notes. “No one shines alone. Much like coral […] we, and the ideas we carry, require two fundamental elements to flourish: protection and reciprocal exchange,” said creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli in the notes. He also wore a coral necklace when he walked out to take his bow. Balenciaga is the quintessential couture house, an aspect of the maison that Piccioli wanted to highlight this season. The designer reworked everyday wardrobe staples such as the T-shirt, the bomber and the jeans, giving them couture touches through simple gestures like draping and cutting. A leather jacket, for instance, featured a peplum detail, while a simple white T-shirt with its hems rolled up just so was rendered in what appeared to be stiff satin. Cargo pants in billowing shapes were open at the sides while bomber jackets featured balloon sleeves. Balenciaga signatures like the sack dress, the cocoon silhouette and the swing back were reinterpreted for today’s customers. The outfits were accessorised with chunky gold jewellery and long chain earrings. Gold hardware also appeared in some garments, such as a black jacket with scrunched sleeves and gold rings at the elbows. Piccioli is a fan of flip-flops and has been showing them since his debut at Balenciaga one year ago. For this collection, he introduced heeled versions with gold chain straps or PVC uppers, as well as more casual flat models with fuzzy fabric straps. One of today’s most talented designers, Piccioli delivered a beautiful show that was very “him” and also captured key elements of Balenciaga’s DNA. He just needs to shake things up a little and show that there is more to Balenciaga than couture techniques and grand gestures. Chloé’s Chemena Kamali has been doing a perfectly fine job injecting a much-needed dose of energy into a beloved brand that has come to embody the beautiful cliché of the boho chic Parisienne. One has to wonder, however, whether she’s getting all the attention she needs from parent company Richemont, which has an amazing track record of managing watch and jewellery houses such as Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels but has had less success with its fashion division. Named the “Obsession”, the spring/summer 2027 show was a modern take on Chloé’s archetypes – “not stereotypes”, as the show notes emphasised – and Kamali’s own Chloé obsessions, from white dresses in broderie anglaise to oversized outerwear. As always at Chloé, there were plenty of textures: fringes, tassels, scalloped edges and floral appliqués adorned most of the looks. A couple of bodysuits added a hint of sexiness to the demure line-up. Shoes ranged from towering wedge sandals with PVC inserts to fabulous knee-high boots in perforated PVC and strappy sandals with bow motifs. The casting was a who’s who of top models, including noughties favourites Natasha Poly and Caroline Trentini, 90s icon Eva Herzigová, and even the ultimate nepo baby, Apple Martin, Gwyneth Paltrow’s daughter.

title: Golden Horse Awards 2026 nominations in full: Arrested Memory and Girl lead the race
description: Arrested Memory has 11 nominations, Girl has 10. We Are Born Good leads Hong Kong films with nine nods, the same as Taiwan’s Double Happiness.
content: Japanese director Sabu’s Arrested Memory leads the race for the 63rd Golden Horse Awards in Taiwan with 11 nominations, including best picture, best director and acting nods for Ethan Juan Ching-tien and Akira Huang Guan-zhi. The crime thriller, which recently premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, is closely followed by Girl. A coming-of-age drama marking the feature directorial debut of Taiwanese actress Shu Qi, the film secured 10 nominations, including best picture and best new director. Rounding out the nominations for best narrative feature are Double Happiness, a wedding comedy by Taiwan’s Joseph Hsu Chen-chieh; We Are Born Good, a comedy drama by first-time Hong Kong filmmaker Yeung Leung-chuen; and We Are All Strangers, the Singaporean drama by Anthony Chen. The last of those, which competed at this year’s Berlin International Film Festival and concludes Chen’s “Growing Up” trilogy, also earned a best director nomination alongside acting nods for Yeo Yann Yann and Andi Lim. We Are Born Good leads a notable contingent of Hong Kong productions with nine nominations, including best new director for Yeung, as well as acting nods for Yeung Wai-lun, Chung Suet-ying – the 2024 best leading actress winner for The Way We Talk – and Kearen Pang Sau-wai. Other prominent Hong Kong contenders include veteran filmmaker Herman Yau Lai-to, who is nominated for best director for his grim social drama We’re Nothing at All. The film also earned a best supporting actor nod for Mirror member Anson Kong Ip-sang. The acting categories will also see Hong Kong’s Angela Yuen Lai-lam (Afterpiece) and Jennifer Yu Heung-ying (Double Happiness) vying for best leading actress, while industry veteran and spokesman Tenky Tin Kai-man is nominated for best supporting actor for Double Happiness. In addition, two Hong Kong films, The Whisper of Sunlight and Scenes from Departure, are in the running for best documentary feature. The winners of the 2026 Golden Horse Awards will be announced at a ceremony in Taipei on November 22. title: Christa Pike in ‘life-saving care’ after botched Tennessee execution
description: Lawyers for death-row inmate demand clemency after two doses of lethal drug fail to kill her.
content: A condemned female murderer who survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee was in critical condition and receiving “life-saving care”, her lawyer said on Thursday. In an extraordinary chain of events, Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital. “What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care,” Randy Spivey said in a virtual news conference Thursday afternoon, declining to provide further details. He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike’s death sentence. “After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now.” Experts on the US death penalty said the case was unprecedented. “This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” said Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre. The centre counts seven inmates whose executions could not be carried out because medical staff were unable to establish IV lines, but “Pike is the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs”. Late Thursday, US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike’s could fail, telling reporters that it “shouldn’t be very difficult”. The case had already attracted scrutiny as Pike would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Kim Chandler, a media witness with Associated Press, told CBS News that “Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began” at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. “A couple of times she looked around the room. At one point she looked towards prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way,” Chandler said. Pike later began snoring and witnesses listened from the viewing area for about an hour before being ushered out. The condemned woman was “loudly snoring, clearly very alive” as journalists left, Chandler told CBS. Pike’s legal team had previously objected to the execution IV protocol, saying it would have caused needless suffering due to her small veins and a blood condition. “I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt” to start an IV line, Spivey said. Lawyer Stephen Ferrell said medical experts had warned of needles becoming dislodged or piercing through the vein, causing lethal drugs to flow into Pike’s arm instead of the bloodstream. “It sounds like that is likely to have occurred,” he said. Media witnesses said Pike told execution staff her arm felt like it would “burst open”, and Spivey said he saw her right arm turn purple, especially after the second lethal injection. Pike had not been scared to die, Ferrell said. “It was a fear of a prolonged, painful, traumatic death, and that’s what happened, minus the death.” The Tennessee Department of Correction said it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol,” adding that Pike was subsequently taken to an “off-site medical facility”. Governor Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” of the failed execution. The state’s remaining scheduled execution – convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton is scheduled to die on December 3 – would not be carried out this year, Lee added. Pike’s case had sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals. She was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp. The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, told NBC News the botched execution was “a mess”. Pike’s lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer’s killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder. Following a flurry of legal filings that delayed the execution by several hours, the US Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the punishment to go ahead. In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike. “The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished,” his office said on X.

title: ‘Surrounded by love’: China director, 75, criticised over plans for fifth child with wife
description: Critics question the age of Zhang’s wife, Du, and accuse the couple of using childbirth as a publicity stunt.
content: China’s veteran filmmaker Zhang Jizhong, 75, and his 44-year-old wife, Du Xinglin, ignited online debate after announcing they are contemplating having a fifth child. The Beijing-born director and producer is renowned for his adaptations of celebrated television versions of classic Chinese novels, including Water Margin and Demi-Gods and Semi-Devils. Du, who studied in France, holds a doctorate in intellectual property law. The couple married in 2017 and have since welcomed a son and two daughters, including their youngest daughter, affectionately nicknamed “Little Dragon Pearl,” who was born in October 2024. Zhang also co-parents a Eurasian son named Martin, whom Du conceived through IVF before their marriage. During a recent live-stream, Du revealed her interest in having another child and jokingly referred to the hoped-for son as “Prince Dragon.” The comments quickly went viral, attracting mixed reactions. Supporters argued the couple should be free to make their own family choices if they can adequately provide for their children, while critics expressed concerns about Du’s age and questioned whether the couple were leveraging childbirth for publicity. “They seem a little too focused on themselves. By the time the child reaches adulthood, the father may already be gone. Is that truly happiness?” read one comment. This discussion occurs against the backdrop of China’s ongoing demographic decline, with births plummeting to 7.92 million last year, a decrease of about 17 per cent from the previous year. On September 8, Du addressed the controversy, stating she would not deliberately plan for a fifth pregnancy but would “let nature take its course.” She expressed that each child represents a different stage of life for both her and Zhang. “Children become more lovable and smarter the more you have. Our family has already entered a positive cycle,” she remarked, adding that they hope “there will always be a little child in the family.” Du also emphasised that the joys of motherhood outweigh the challenges of pregnancy: “I have the ability to ensure that every child grows up surrounded by total love.” She later clarified that her desire for a boy was meant as a joke, stressing that “boys and girls are equally precious.” The couple share their parenting experiences and perspectives on Chinese culture on mainland social media, where they have more than 5.6 million followers. Zhang’s wealth has never been publicly disclosed; however, he has denied rumours claiming he is worth 30 billion yuan (US$4.5 billion), describing himself to Jiupai News as “an ordinary film director.” After the birth of Little Dragon Pearl, Zhang vowed to provide his daughter with all the love and support he could offer. The couple have since faced online criticism, with some users ridiculing Zhang’s age and others jokingly referring to him as their “father-in-law,” teasing that they wanted to marry Little Dragon Pearl. In response, Du later took legal action, gathering evidence of what was deemed online harassment and filed lawsuits against some internet users.

title: DeepSeek effect? How China’s quant funds thrive amid tight regulatory scrutiny
description: Strong returns are attracting investors to quant funds, with DeepSeek highlighting the sector’s potential role in China’s tech ambitions.
content: China’s quantitative investing sector has added 18 new members to the ranks of funds managing more than 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in assets this year, underlining the industry’s ability to generate competitive returns despite a tight regulatory environment. The firms were among 159 Chinese hedge funds overseeing more than 10 billion yuan each, according to financial news agency Cailian Press. Their growth has been fuelled by technology-driven momentum in the world’s second-largest stock market. Among the latest entrants to the club were AXQ Capital, Hopeseek Fund and Huanian Fund, according to financial data provider Wind. “Many quant funds are now doing exceptionally well,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at economic research firm Gavekal Dragonomics. “China’s onshore equity market is less sophisticated than major global markets,” Beddor said. “[That means] quant funds can often generate solid returns by deploying systematic trading strategies that were first developed abroad.” Amid China’s push towards fiscal self-reliance, quant funds helped improve the efficiency of the onshore equity market, according to Beddor. More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance Gary Ng, Natixis Gary Ng, economist at investment bank Natixis, said Chinese investors increasingly viewed hedge funds favourably. “More Chinese investors are moving into financial assets due to low deposit rates and weak real estate performance,” he said. Quant funds are also becoming more accessible. Chinese brokerages, such as Sinolink Securities and Shenwan Hongyuan Securities, have started promoting quant trading services through their mobile apps, allowing eligible investors to apply for access to China’s quant trading platforms. Despite their competitive returns, China’s quant funds operated in “a very tricky regulatory environment”, Beddor said. Even though “China’s financial regulators are much more invested in market outcomes than regulators in other major markets,” they “can and do crack down on quant funds if they feel those firms may be contributing to market volatility”, said Beddor. While the rise of the 18 quant funds highlighted the sector’s success, the “tighter regulatory regime” introduced in late 2024 had “clearly crimped some funds at the margin”, Beddor said. He pointed to DeepSeek, backed by Chinese quant fund High-Flyer, as a possible turning point in how policymakers viewed quant funds. “DeepSeek was created by a fund, not a traditional tech company,” he said. “Its breakthrough was the first time that policymakers seemed to have realised the fund industry could play a serious role in technological development.” The 18 quant funds took an average of 8.4 years to surpass the 10 billion yuan assets-under-management mark, although five reached the milestone in less than five years. China’s discretionary-fund sector has also expanded, with 18 funds crossing the 10 billion yuan asset threshold this year as of late September, according to Cailian Press. Chinese private securities investment funds, including but not limited to quant funds and discretionary funds, managed more than 9 trillion yuan in assets as of the end of August, according to the Asset Management Association of China.

title: Sapphire is not just a pretty gem – here’s how it is used in modern technology
description: Thanks to the ionic bonds making up its structure, this mineral’s valuable properties include extreme hardness and high thermal stability.
content:
Most people imagine expensive jewellery when they think about sapphire. But did you know this gemstone is also inside many gadgets we use every day?
Far from being just a luxury gem, sapphire is also useful in modern technology and engineering.
Sapphire is a type of mineral called corundum, a compound known chemically as aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃). Over millions of years, natural sapphires form under extreme heat and pressure deep within the Earth’s crust, where aluminium-rich minerals recrystallise into solid corundum.
Pure sapphire is colourless and transparent, but the presence of trace elements can create a spectrum of vibrant colours, including yellow, green and pink (see chart). In fact, rubies are closely related to sapphires as they share the same chemical formula (Al2O3). When corundum contains a higher concentration of chromium, it exhibits a red hue and is classified as a ruby.
In a sapphire crystal, aluminium ions (Al³⁺) and oxide ions (O²⁻) are bound together in a highly ordered, repeating 3D lattice. These ions are packed in a specific direction-dependent pattern, making sapphire an anisotropic crystal. This means its properties, like light refraction, vary depending on the direction of measurement.
The exceptionally strong bonds between the aluminium ions (Al³⁺) and oxide ions (O²⁻) give sapphire its remarkable physical characteristics.
Extreme hardness: Ranking nine out of 10 on the Mohs hardness scale (see graphic) – second only to diamond – sapphire resists surface scratches and abrasive wear.
High thermal stability: With a melting point of about 2,030 degrees Celsius, sapphire easily tolerates intense heat without expanding or warping.
Electrical insulation: The electrons located on the outermost shells of sapphire atoms are tightly held by ionic bonds, so there are no free electrons to conduct electricity. This makes sapphire an excellent electrical insulator.
Chemical inertness: Sapphire’s tightly packed ionic structure is extremely stable, allowing it to resist attack from most strong acids and alkalis at room temperature.
Broad optical transparency: Pure sapphire transmits a wide range of wavelengths – from ultraviolet (UV) and visible light to infrared (IR).
Natural sapphires are too rare, small and flawed for industrial use. To solve this, engineers grow large, flawless synthetic sapphire crystals in high-temperature furnaces. They are then sliced into ultra-thin discs called sapphire wafers, which are essential for modern technology.
Scratch-resistant protective covers: Synthetic sapphire’s extreme scratch resistance makes it a perfect protective material to cover luxury wristwatches, smartphone camera lenses and screen protectors.
LED lighting and displays: Sapphire is often used as a base layer for gallium nitride (GaN) films, which are used to make blue and white LEDs, power electronics and high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs). HEMTs are key for high-power and high-frequency applications such as satellite systems and electric vehicles.
Silicon-on-sapphire (SOS) technology: Thin layers of silicon deposited onto sapphire substrates help reduce electronic interference. This technology is crucial for high-performance radio frequency (RF) chips, which are used in satellite communications and mobile signal transmissions.
Optoelectronics: Sapphire’s high transmittance allows UV, visible and IR light to pass through, making it a crucial material for laser diodes, optical sensors and light-transmitting lenses.
Young Post has partnered with Hong Kong Science Museum and Hong Kong Space Museum to encourage your pursuit of science. Every month, the museums answer questions about the world around us, the cosmos and beyond.

title: Style Edit: Anteprima finds curiosity in everyday dressing with its SS27 collection
description: Creative director Izumi Ogino takes inspiration from Alice in Wonderland, blending romance and practicality with playful, versatile fashion.
content: Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland is an escapist classic that has inspired generations of designers. But for spring/summer 2027, Anteprima looks to this enduring muse not for surreal ensembles, but for the book’s wit, shifting perspectives and invitation to question the familiar. Under the title “Curiouser and Curiouser”, creative director Izumi Ogino has unveiled Anteprima Giardino: an imaginary garden where romance, practicality and playful sensibility meet. The collection centres on self-discovery, expressed through contrasts that reflect how women dress today. Softness meets structure; vintage-inflected craft meets contemporary lightness; and a tension between the visible and the concealed emerges. The result is a flexible wardrobe that prizes individual interpretation over any single prescribed look. Lace, ruffles, rose-petal embroidery, pointelle knitting and sheer embroidery bring tactility and movement to the season. Floral motifs appear alongside embroidered logo and rabbit details that run delicately along garment hems, while layers of translucent fabric create depth without heaviness. These are romantic ingredients, to be sure, but the collection avoids tipping into saccharine sweetness by setting them against cleaner, more purposeful shapes. Here, lightweight fabrics are paired with oversized trousers and tailored skirts, while pinafore-inspired tops and skirts are edged with fine lace. Such combinations give the collection its distinctive cadence: precise but not rigid, decorative yet easy to wear. This approach mirrors Ogino’s view of the Anteprima woman as both rational and imaginative, practical and romantic in equal measure. The garden world extends to the season’s accessories. The Wire Ruffle series brings cascading ruffles to the Boxxie Wirebag, while hand-crocheted roses lend sculptural texture to the Standard Miniatura Wirebag in the Floreale series. Elsewhere, watering-can-shaped bags and floral charms introduce a deliberately offbeat note through the Giardino line. Meanwhile, the Lucchetto II Wirebag is reimagined in soft colour-block combinations, refreshing the established silhouette with a more dreamlike palette. For Ogino, the Alice reference is ultimately a way of seeing differently rather than a childhood fantasy – it’s about noticing colours, perspectives or other facets of oneself. That sensibility gives Anteprima’s spring/summer 2027 offering its appeal: a wardrobe that doesn’t define a woman, but one that accompanies her as she keeps discovering who she might be.

title: Putin’s hopes for ‘productive’ Apec fuel talk of summit with Xi and Trump
description: Observers say a meeting between the three leaders in Shenzhen is possible but would rest on some groundwork.
content: A meeting next month between the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers is possible but hinges on the three sides finding common ground and setting realistic expectations about outcomes, according to analysts. National Day congratulations from Moscow to Beijing on Thursday fanned speculation that the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could meet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen next month. In a letter to Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said his meeting with Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum would be “productive” and help strengthen the two countries’ comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation. US President Donald Trump is also expected to attend the forum, which will be Putin’s first since 2017. The possibility of a meeting between the three men was raised publicly by Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek on September 1. Asked about the possibility of such a meeting, Ushakov said “this issue was discussed”. Liu Xu, a research fellow at the National Academy of Development and Strategy at Renmin University of China, said the possibility of a trilateral meeting “remained high”. “Because China and the US are expected to have four meetings this year, different occasions will naturally create different expectations for outcomes,” Liu said. He said that for Putin, a meeting with Trump and Xi would have symbolic weight by showing that despite its continued confrontation with much of the West over the Ukraine war “Russia remained a major player in international affairs”. With the war well into its fifth year, Western sanctions have eroded Russia’s economy and Putin’s authority at home. But Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said that while the three leaders might be attending the same summit, that did not mean they would have a formal trilateral meeting. “There is a realistic possibility, but there is still a distance between attending the same summit and agreeing to hold a formal trilateral meeting,” Sun said, adding that they might have informal talks instead. China, as host, could facilitate communication among the three leaders, but the key question would be whether they could identify a common agenda and develop reasonable expectations about the outcome, he said. “A brief exchange or informal meeting has a relatively lower threshold, while a trilateral summit with a clearly defined agenda would require more preparation,” Sun said. For Beijing, a trilateral meeting could open another channel for managing relations with both Washington and Moscow, according to analysts. Liu said China had not sought to publicly lead mediation between Russia and Ukraine, instead calling for a political settlement. “But a meeting of the three leaders could demonstrate China’s willingness to play a greater role while allowing Beijing to balance its relationships with Russia and the West,” he said. Sun said the larger significance of a trilateral meeting for China would be turning its ability to maintain communication with both Washington and Moscow into a practical mechanism for reducing confrontation among major powers. “It would demonstrate China’s constructive role in promoting dialogue and maintaining stability,” he said. Trump also invited Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December but according to a Bloomberg report last week, Kremlin sources said the chances of Putin going were slim.

title: 2 new islands appear near Indonesia’s Anak Krakatoa volcano after eruption
description: The island-like mounds are likely the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s 1883 eruption.
content: Two new islands have appeared off Anak Krakatoa, potentially the first in nearly a century to emerge within the caldera left by Krakatoa’s catastrophic 1883 eruption. The formations, discovered following a 25-hour eruption in early September, sit hundreds of metres off opposite sides of Anak Krakatoa – one to the northwest and the other to the southeast – almost on a straight line through the volcano’s crater, according to Indonesia’s Geological Agency. The agency places one about 760 metres (0.5 miles) off Anak Krakatoa’s northwest coast and the other some 495 metres to the southeast. It has not verified their dimensions or elevation above sea level. The agency’s preliminary interpretation is that relatively fluid magma released during the continuous eruption reached the surface via an elongated northwest-southeast opening, with erupted material forming two island-like mounds offshore. For 96 years, the caldera’s story has been the making and remaking of Anak Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra. No other separate island is known to have emerged in the caldera since Anak Krakatoa became permanently established above sea level in 1930. The most striking public glimpse of either feature came by accident nearly two weeks after the eruption, as volunteers searched for a group of journalists and others missing at sea. Yodistara Nugraha, a tourism activist from Kalianda, South Lampung, spent the day flying a drone over shorelines and shallow water around the caldera looking for any signs of them or their speedboat, which had disappeared on a reporting trip to Anak Krakatoa. In footage from his final flight of the day, the drone crossed the channel between Sertung island and Anak Krakatoa, where it captured waves breaking over a low, dark mass. The footage appears to show the new northwestern island. The search found no trace of the missing group and it was only afterwards that Yodistara realised he might have documented a geological event. “I didn’t realise at first that I might have captured something new,” he said in an interview. “It was only later I understood how interesting and potentially significant the footage could be.” Anak Krakatoa – or “Child of Krakatoa” – had been quiet for more than two years until activity resumed in July. That culminated in 25 hours of continuous eruption beginning late on September 4, with lava flows and pyroclastic material adding nearly 33 hectares (81 acres) to the island’s area, according to the Geological Agency. Weeks later, the agency received reports of new island-like formations from mariners and volunteers who had sailed through and photographed the area, it said. The formations are also visible in Sentinel satellite imagery since the eruption. The agency has released annotated Sentinel imagery marking the two sites with red triangles, but no clear close-up images of the formations themselves. Heruningtyas Desi Purnamasari, who heads a volcano team within the agency, said key questions about the land masses remain unresolved. “At this stage, we cannot confirm the origin or composition of the two features based on satellite imagery alone,” she said. “In particular, we cannot yet confirm whether volcanic material was directly erupted at these locations or whether they represent new eruptive vents.” One of the main questions is what the formations are made of, said Asri Oktavioni Indraswari, an assistant professor in the geosciences department at the University of Indonesia. “There are two possibilities: new vents or eruption materials just piling up in the shallow part of the old caldera,” she said. “If they’re new vents where magma is erupting, that would mean activity is no longer confined to Anak Krakatoa’s central conduit.” Anak Krakatoa emerged decades after the massive 1883 eruption of Krakatoa that destroyed most of the original island, killed more than 36,000 people and affected climate and skies worldwide for years. The explosions were heard almost 5,000km (3,106 miles) away, while pressure waves circled the globe multiple times. Telegraph links turned the disaster into one of the first global news events. Whatever the origin of the new land masses, their survival as islands will depend on whether they remain above water at high tide and withstand erosion. Anak Krakatoa itself took multiple attempts to become an island. The first clearly observed submarine eruptions at the site began in late 1927. Erupted material initially broke the surface in 1928, then disappeared beneath the waves. The sequence repeated until the island was finally established in 1930. “Landforms around volcanoes close to sea level can be very dynamic environments, with erosion and transport of material – particularly loose material deposited from explosive volcanism – competing with deposition and growth during eruptive activity,” said Sebastian Watt, a professor of vulcanology at the University of Birmingham. “The form of the island changed a lot in those early years,” he said. “It was composed of loose material produced by explosive eruptions, which deposited material on the sea floor and then gradually built up the land mass around the vent, eventually emerging above sea level. This material was then eroded outside eruptive periods, so the land mass appeared and then disappeared.” The island’s appearance can change in a flash. In December 2018, a major flank collapse and eruption cut its peak from more than 330 metres to roughly 110 metres. A July Geological Agency report put its peak at about 157 metres. “We still see this pattern around Anak Krakatoa today,” Watt said.

title: Singapore’s crackdown exposes market for fake 5-star reviews
description: Experts warn that review ecosystems are constantly evolving and consumers should be more discerning about what they read online.
content: Singapore’s biggest crackdown so far on fake online reviews has exposed how businesses exploit the appeal of five-star ratings to game the system, with experts warning generative AI will make fake reviews more rampant and consumers need to be more discerning about what they read online. The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) has taken action against 45 companies – including a funeral parlour, a law firm and an aesthetics clinic – after finding they bought reviews from a provider whose services included AI-generated testimonials resembling real customer experiences. The companies had to take down the reviews and publish a public apology for six months as part of the first phase of investigations. About 100 companies were involved. Alton Chua, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University’s Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, said online review ecosystems were constantly evolving. “Some companies will always try to game the system while users learn to adapt their trust in what they read,” Chua said. “Companies are using AI to generate fraudulent reviews while smart shoppers are using it to spot them.” With the advent of generative artificial intelligence, “we can expect fake reviews to be more rampant”, he added. “For one, it is virtually free for unscrupulous merchants to create realistic and humanlike text that is indistinguishable from authentic customer feedback.” Elmie Nekmat, an associate professor of communications and new media at the National University of Singapore, said reviews were powerful because they provided “social proof”. “A five-star rating, for example, can influence consumers to pay attention to a particular company before they even get a chance to examine the business in detail or the choices that they have,” he said. “In Singapore, under the consumer-protection framework, to deliberately mislead consumers through fabricated reviews also constitutes unfair trade practices.” The CCS’ two-phase investigation into the issue is its largest fake review inquiry to date, with the second stage already under way. There were 47 businesses investigated in the first phase, with two declining to provide undertakings on the commission’s required terms. The CCS said it would continue its investigations and take firmer enforcement action if necessary. An individual named Julian Tung Yan Kai was found to have provided fake review services to about 100 businesses. Tung was the sole director of Reputifly and owned and operated websites BuyReviewSG and GetReviewSG, which the CSS said provided fake review services. Businesses would buy packages of fake reviews from Tung to be periodically posted, investigators found, and could use a rating calculator to work out how many five-star reviews they needed to reach their desired Google rating. The provider used generative AI to create reviews designed to resemble genuine customer experiences by varying writing styles and sentence structures, incorporating details such as the Singapore context and introducing natural imperfections. Clients were able to edit the generated reviews before publication. The CCS told This Week in Asia that Tung had promised to stop providing fake review services and voluntarily committed to donating proceeds to charity, without claiming any tax deduction from the donation. Criminal red lines Posting or procuring fake reviews can be considered an unfair practice under Singapore’s Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act 2003 (CPFTA), the CCS has said, as it risks misleading consumers into believing a business is more popular or of higher quality than it really is. “Unlike some criminal statutes, the CPFTA does not ordinarily make the act of posting fake reviews a stand-alone criminal offence,” said Joyce Khoo, a criminal lawyer at Quahe Woo & Palmer. Instead, she said the commission could investigate the business, seek court injunctions, demand the removal of fake reviews and mandate corrective measures such as public apologies. According to Khoo, criminal liability generally arises if a business obstructs the investigation or disobeys a court order, meaning the company and any individuals held responsible could face contempt of court proceedings. The CCS similarly noted that under the CPFTA, engaging in an unfair practice was not a criminal offence and did not attract fines or financial penalties. However, if the business failed to comply with a court injunction, the commission might commence contempt of court proceedings, which could result in a fine or imprisonment. It cited a case involving a managing director of Nail Palace Entities who was jailed for three months last year for persistently failing to comply with a court order related to the CPFTA. What about influencers? On whether social media influencers paid to rate services were also a form of fake reviews, Elmie said paying them to promote a product “is not inherently deceptive if the person clearly discloses the commercial relationship and genuinely communicates their experiences”. By contrast, a fake review created the impression that an independent consumer had a genuine experience, he said, when in fact that person might not even be real. Chua said that while fake reviews tended to be associated with bots, anonymous users or those whose identities were obscured, the use of influencers usually involved reviewing products or services on a complimentary basis. “Because these endorsers are well known, the reviews they write command greater perceived credibility,” he said.

title: Exclusive | ‘Money is money’: US, UK firms still coming to Hong Kong, commerce chief says
description: 2026 has been a challenging year because of the geopolitical situation, but Hong Kong’s stability continues to draw investors, Algernon Yau says.
content: Companies from the United States, Britain and Singapore have been among the leading sources of inbound foreign capital in Hong Kong so far this year, the city’s commerce minister has said, insisting that “money is money” despite geopolitical instability. In an exclusive, wide-ranging interview with the South China Morning Post, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah described 2026 as a very challenging year because of the geopolitical situation. Nevertheless, the government’s investment promotion arm, InvestHK, had helped 516 overseas and mainland Chinese companies set up or expand businesses in the city in the first eight months of the year. The US and the United Kingdom accounted for 27 and 21 companies, respectively, behind the mainland with 307 and Singapore with 29. Yau said the figures showed people had “a lot of confidence” in doing business in Hong Kong. “Money is money. Businesspeople are very practical. Despite the geopolitical situation, seeing is believing; they come over here seeing that Hong Kong is very stable, safe, free, and they will come over to invest,” he said. He added that Hong Kong was the world’s top destination for initial public offerings last year. “The geopolitical situation is changing every day, overnight … But business is business. When they see there are business opportunities in Hong Kong, especially across the border, going into the Greater Bay Area, they come,” Yau said. The Greater Bay Area is a central government scheme to link Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province into an integrated economic hub. As of last year, the number of companies in Hong Kong with mainland or overseas parents jumped by 11 per cent to 11,070. About 28 per cent, or 3,090, of them were from the mainland. Another 14 per cent, or 1,550 companies, were each from the US and Japan, followed by the UK, which accounted for 770, or about 7 per cent of the total, and Singapore with 590, representing about 5 per cent. They were mainly from the finance, education and trading sectors, as well as start-ups, Yau said. Some settled in Hong Kong before setting foot on the mainland, he said. “So you can see, despite this geopolitical instability, United States companies are coming to Hong Kong to make good money because there’s been a very huge trade surplus between Hong Kong and the United States for the past 10 years,” Yau said. “The trade surplus is on their side; it’s not on our side.” Asked about competition for foreign investment with economies such as Singapore and Dubai, Yau said Hong Kong competed and collaborated with Singapore. “We have the support of the Greater Bay Area with a population of 88 million and a GDP of about US$2 trillion. But in Singapore, they do not have any backup. Surrounding them [are] Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, all competitors. We are much stronger in our support,” he said. “The size of our financial market is about 10 times that of Singapore. So you can tell whether we are in very keen competition or we are in competition as well as collaborating and cooperating with Singapore in all different areas.” He added: “[For Dubai], Hong Kong is about 20 times their size in terms of the financial centre. They are growing, but it will take a bit of time for them to become competitive with us.” Yau noted that InvestHK had been given a key performance indicator of helping at least 1,200 enterprises set up or expand operations in Hong Kong across 2026 and 2027, with an aim of creating 12,000 jobs and bringing in HK$120 billion in capital. He said the agency was on track to meet the 2026 target. Since the government established the GoGlobal Task Force in October last year, it has supported more than 340 mainland enterprises in setting up or expanding their businesses in Hong Kong, with firms operating in the logistics, industrial, fintech, finance and construction sectors. They were expected to bring in about HK$57.4 billion in direct investment and create around 7,800 jobs in Hong Kong. Asean countries, the Middle East, Central Asia and parts of Europe, such as France and Turkey, were identified as key GoGlobal destinations. Yau, who steers the task force, said helping media groups expand overseas was also very important in telling successful stories about Hong Kong and establishing cultural links. He said local media outlets establishing cooperation with other countries could facilitate the sharing of information and data, and help the other side understand more about different areas of Hong Kong. He cited Hong Kong media outlets signing memorandums of understanding in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, as an example. The Post signed three agreements there. Yau said he planned to visit Egypt and Turkey in January next year to explore business opportunities and markets in both countries. He said Turkey was a fast-growing economy linking Asia, Europe and the Arabian Peninsula, while Egypt was the gateway to Africa with the Suez Canal Economic Zone. Yau said his priorities for the coming year were the GoGlobal scheme and helping Hong Kong develop from an international trading centre into a high-value-added trading centre and a high-value supply chain centre serving China’s economic development. Asked if he had plans after the government’s term ended in June next year, Yau, 68, said the decision was not his alone and that he would focus on his current duties. “It depends on whether there’s a need for me to stay or there’s a need for me to enjoy life. So I’m very flexible and I take it easy,” he said. “My intention is to serve, of course, because I’m still too young to retire. So if there’s a chance, I would like to serve the city and the country more.”

title: Opinion | Investing in Hong Kong’s mental health makes good economic sense
description: Mental well-being is more than a public health concern. Evidence shows investing in mental health generates robust economic returns.
content: Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s recent policy address set out an ambitious reform agenda designed to sharpen Hong Kong’s competitive edge while enhancing people’s livelihoods. As we enter Mental Health Awareness Month, we should reflect on the role mental well-being can play in the city’s fortunes. Lee’s address mentioned an integrated approach featuring 11 measures as part of efforts to promote mental health.
