These include extending the Three-Tier School-based Emergency Mechanism, expanding the Healthy Mind Pilot Project to all District Health Centres and broadening participation in the Mental Health Workplace Charter. These measures are welcome, but one important argument remains underdeveloped in the discourse around mental health. Mental well-being should be seen as a basic component of economic infrastructure. An economy based on high-value human capital, professional services and innovation while also being able to handle psychological distress is not a luxury but a strategic long-term investment in prosperity. The World Health Organization estimates that depression and anxiety cost the global economy 12 billion working days and US$1 trillion a year in lost productivity, making untreated psychological distress a substantial economic burden. Japan’s long history of karoshi, or death from overwork, is just one example of the harm that heavy workloads and long hours can inflict on workers’ physical and mental health, as well as the wider organisational and social costs. In Hong Kong, University of Hong Kong researchers have used statistical modelling to estimate that depression will cost around HK$2.4 billion (US$305.9 million) in all-cause healthcare spending by 2032 if current trends continue. However, direct medical spending is only the visible part of the fiscal picture. Larger losses accumulate quietly inside workplaces through absenteeism and, more significantly, presenteeism, where employees go to work while unwell and can function with reduced focus, cognitive stamina and productivity. A 2024 research report by Deloitte estimated that poor mental health among the workforce cost UK employers around £51 billion (US$67.5 billion) a year. Presenteeism accounted for about £23.8 billion annually, surpassing £19.5 billion from staff turnover and £7.3 billion from sickness absence. In addition, working parents’ concern over their children’s mental health issues incurred an estimated £8 billion a year in costs. Firms in high-pressure industries in Hong Kong face similar structural risks. When chronic workplace stress goes unmanaged, output can deteriorate, operational errors can multiply and valued staff can leave prematurely, resulting in a talent drain. Some in the business community might worry that comprehensive mental health programmes place an extra financial burden on employers, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises already operating on tight margins. There could also be concern that expanding workplace charters and counselling services amounts to unfunded overheads that raise operating costs without a compelling return. In an uncertain business climate, it is natural to question the short-term justification for wellness spending. The evidence tells a more optimistic story. Deloitte’s cost-benefit analysis found that, on average, employers can yield a £4.7 return for every £1 spent on workforce mental health and well-being, with organisation-wide and proactive approaches among the top performers. We also have compelling local evidence from Hong Kong’s digital intervention ecosystem. A health economics evaluation by the Hong Kong Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention on Open Up, the city’s 24/7 text-based emotional support platform for young people that launched in 2018, estimated that an investment of HK$47.7 million generated HK$226.1 million in total social value, equivalent to a return on investment of HK$4.74 per dollar spent. Productivity gains associated with reduced suicide risk accounted for 75.4 per cent of the estimated social value. The estimates should be interpreted cautiously as the analysis relied on modelling and proxy valuation, but they nevertheless show the potential economic significance of digital support. Early prevention and wellness promotion can generate substantial societal dividends over time. Well-timed mental health intervention can be an economic multiplier, protecting today’s labour productivity and preserving tomorrow’s long-term fiscal capacity. To translate the policy address blueprint into solid economic gains, the government and businesses should consider shifting from crisis management to proactive institutional investment. Also, policymakers should improve access to evidence-based early-intervention digital platforms such as Open Up, incorporating them into schools, tertiary institutions and entry-level employment services to alleviate barriers to access and stigma among young workers. The administration should implement the endorsed stepped-care model with specific competency benchmarks and tailored subsidies to small firms adopting accredited workplace wellness schemes. Finally, corporate leaders need to move beyond one-off awareness days and gestures. Workforce psychological safety should be treated as a genuine board-level operational metric, tracking burnout risk and presenteeism alongside financial performance each quarter. Hong Kong’s prosperity has always depended on the drive and ingenuity of its people. If we treat mental health as foundational economic capital rather than a peripheral concern, we stand a much better chance of building a healthier, more productive and sustainably competitive workforce for generations to come.

title: Online claims revive mercury mystery around tomb of first Chinese emperor
description: A Weibo hashtag about ancient cinnabar sites has reignited debate over the ‘rivers and seas’ in Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum.
content: Online claims that archaeologists have identified the source of mercury in the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang – China’s first emperor, who unified the country more than 2,000 years ago – have revived interest in ancient cinnabar sites in northwestern China’s Shaanxi province. The claims, which sent related hashtags trending on social media late last month, centred on three sites in Xunyang where archaeologists last year found evidence of cinnabar mining, processing and transport during the pre-Qin and Qin-Han periods. The underground burial complex, at the northern foot of Lishan Mountain, has never been opened, but one of the most enduring accounts of what lies beneath comes from Sima Qian, the early Han dynasty (206BC-AD220) historian who described a vast subterranean realm, elaborate in its design and ambition, that mirrored the heavens above and the Earth below. In his masterwork, the Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, Sima Qian wrote that mercury was used to recreate the “rivers and seas” inside the tomb, with a mechanism designed to keep the metal flowing. Cinnabar, a naturally occurring mercury sulphide mineral, was the main ore used to produce mercury in ancient times. The identification of ancient cinnabar sites in Xunyang has therefore raised the possibility that the region could have supplied some of the mercury described by Sima Qian. For decades, archaeologists and historians have used non-invasive surveys and historical records to assess how far the surviving evidence supports Sima Qian’s account of the tomb. There has also been renewed debate over whether the tomb should ever be opened. In a 2024 interview with state broadcaster CCTV, Wu Yongqi, honorary director of Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum, which oversees the first emperor’s burial complex, said fragile underground relics should not be disturbed unless excavation was necessary for their protection. “Underground cultural relics are indeed very fragile,” he told the state broadcaster at the time. “We should have a sense of awe and respect for heaven and Earth, nature and our ancestors. “If we have advanced technology that allows us to understand what is inside the tomb without opening it from above, and without disturbing this old man who has been sleeping for 2,000 years, then from the bottom of my heart, I would say: don’t touch it in the future.” The mausoleum is one of China’s most significant archaeological sites, built for Qin Shi Huang after he unified the warring states in 221BC. Tens of thousands of square metres of burial pits and the imperial tomb itself remain underground, with thousands of statues still to be unearthed. The sprawling complex includes the terracotta warriors, discovered in 1974, as well as numerous burial pits containing figures, weapons and other objects intended to accompany the emperor in the afterlife. There is consensus among archaeologists that imperial tombs should not be proactively excavated in China. This principle was reaffirmed by the State Council, China’s cabinet, in 1997, when it said in a notice on cultural heritage conservation that large imperial tombs should not be excavated until the necessary scientific and technical conditions for protecting relics were in place. Between 2002 and 2003, Chinese researchers used remote sensing and geophysical techniques to conduct a large-scale, non-invasive survey of the mausoleum, producing the first outline of the underground palace’s structure and layout without opening or disturbing the tomb. Wu said previous surveys had indicated the presence of mercury in the mausoleum, with mercury concentrations in the soil above the tomb more than 70 times those of the surrounding ground. Although the contents of the underground complex remain unknown, Wu said the tomb should be left undisturbed unless a rescue excavation was needed to protect the relics. In particular, artefacts made from plant and animal fibres could deteriorate immediately if the tomb were opened without adequate preparation, he warned. Huang Songtao, a Chinese history blogger and cultural relic restorer, told Chengdu-based Fengmian News that the discovery of the three cinnabar sites was an important lead, but did not conclusively establish that Xunyang supplied mercury for Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum. The report, published on September 21, said current surveys could show only that mercury levels in the soil above the tomb were abnormally high. They could not determine the total amount of mercury underground nor link it directly to any particular mining site. Xunyang alone may not have been able to meet demand if the mausoleum contained hundreds of tonnes of mercury, raising the possibility that the metal came from multiple sources, the report continued. Qin Shi Huang was a controversial and often brutal ruler, but his measures to achieve da yitong, or “great unity”, are considered to have established China’s first unified, centralised, multi-ethnic state. The concept of “great unity” has featured prominently in China’s ethnic governance narrative, with the Qin unification often cited by President Xi Jinping and Chinese scholars as a historical foundation for national cohesion.

title: Philippines’ jeepney drivers ‘stuck between a rock and a hard place’ despite fare increase
description: Drivers say the overdue fare increase of 1 peso ‘barely makes a dent’ as the sector battles the massive loss of livelihoods.
content: Reggie Manlapig, 46, has been driving jeepneys for nearly 25 years and has weathered rising fuel prices – but with costs spiking amid the global energy crunch, he is now wrestling bigger demons. “The impact has been huge. Before, in a 16-hour shift of driving, I could take home 400 to 500 pesos [US$6.30 to US$8] – now there’s a big cut to that income,” said Manlapig, who plies a two-hour daily round route from Malolos in Bulacan, north of Manila, to San Fernando, Pampanga. “Doing the full route five times straight in a day really pushes you. Before, three round trips alone would already give you decent earnings – especially on days with no classes, holidays, or student holiday periods; those are especially hard.” His sentiments reflect the broader grievances of jeepney drivers and other public transport operators in the Philippines, who continue to bear the brunt of soaring fuel prices from the gridlocked Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war. On Monday, increased prices finally implemented by the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr took effect, raising jeepney fares by 1 peso – a long-overdue move that was first suspended in March. “We’re grateful for it, but it’s a very small help – very small for us. What good is a one-peso fare increase if fuel prices keep rising one after another – 10 pesos, 8 pesos at a time? How is that one peso supposed to keep up? It barely makes a dent,” Manlapig said. The high costs had forced drivers off the road, leading to longer wait times for commuters and crowded vehicles, Julius Dalay, founder of the concern group Commuters of the Philippines, told This Week in Asia. Diesel prices rolled back by 7.57 pesos this week after reaching nearly 100 pesos per litre in some areas in the Philippines. Yet for the country’s transport sector, the latest adjustments are insufficient to make up for the massive loss of livelihoods as prices continue to rise. Transport group Piston held a two-day strike on Tuesday, demanding the removal of excise and value-added taxes on petroleum. It also urged authorities to restore diesel costs to 55 pesos per litre – its last price the week before the Iran war began – and repeal a 28-year-old oil deregulation law that leaves the discretion of price caps to private companies. “With every price increase, income shrinks, and the cost of basic goods rises faster than workers’ small incomes and wages can keep up,” Mody Floranda, leader of Piston, told This Week in Asia. Floranda said the group first petitioned for fare increases in February when diesel prices rose following the Gulf conflict. “It took six months for the [government] to finally grant it, timed right as we announced the strike. So we consider the increase a win from people’s mobilisation – but small as it is, it’s no longer enough for our drivers’ needs,” Floranda said. The extra 1 peso was “nowhere near the scale of what our drivers are losing”, he lamented. He noted that many drivers, unable to keep up with the rising transport costs due to mounting debts and repair expenses, had moved to other jobs such as construction work or farming in the provinces. Nanoy Rafael, convenor of the PARA-Commuters Network, told This Week in Asia his group had estimated a 10 to 20 per cent reduction in public transport vehicles before August. Data from the transport ministry in August reflected the group’s predictions, Rafael said. The figures showed 18,000 traditional jeepneys had stopped plying the roads year on year, down from 128,000 units in August last year, he said, while only 8,000 electric jeepneys remained operational. “So that was really the first effect: we have nothing to ride,” Rafael said, adding that in March and April, cities such as Baguio in northern Philippines nearly ground to a halt. His group supported the fare increase despite the cost of goods outpacing wages “because there’s nothing else. We’re stuck between a rock and a hard place”. The persistent price shocks in the Philippines highlight the country’s differences in preparation and supply compared with Southeast Asian neighbours that may be better equipped to cushion the blow, according to Jaideep Singh, an analyst at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia. “For Southeast Asia, the conflict in West Asia, including periodic closures of the Strait of Hormuz, manifests primarily as a supply chain and energy shock. However, the first-order economic effects of the crisis depend on the trade and energy profiles of Asean countries, particularly their exposure to fuel imports from the Gulf region,” Singh said. Among the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Philippines remained the most vulnerable as over 97 per cent of its crude petroleum imports were sourced from the Gulf, mainly Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Singh said. These pipelines were prone to supply-side disruptions beyond Hormuz, such as Houthi attacks, he noted. “What exacerbates the situation for the Philippines is its negligible domestic production and structural challenges in diversifying imports.” By contrast, other major oil importers in Asean such as Thailand and Singapore have sufficient stockpiles of crude petroleum and considerable refining capabilities that help cushion the direct impact on fuel prices. Malaysia has diversified its oil imports and continues to have sizeable oil reserves, remaining a net exporter of liquefied natural gas, a critical commodity for electricity production. Malaysia and Indonesia also expanded their use of palm-based biodiesel to reduce reliance on conventional diesel. “While the Philippines has mandated a 10 per cent bioethanol blend into all petrol sold nationwide, there is inadequate domestic supply of ethanol to satisfy rising demand,” Singh warned. He also pointed to differing fiscal policy responses on how authorities passed the buck to consumers through pump prices. Malaysia has a fuel subsidy scheme for citizens that keeps petrol prices stable, subject to an adjustable quota, though fiscal resources are increasingly under strain. Vietnam manages domestic fuel prices through a hybrid mechanism that encompasses a maximum retail price, alongside a petroleum price stabilisation fund. “In the Philippines meanwhile, given its very high exposure and limited manoeuvrability, pump prices are largely market-driven, with efforts geared towards providing cash assistance to the most price-sensitive consumers,” Singh said. The Philippines offers few, if any, subsidies for consumers to manage pump prices, while public transport drivers and operators have lamented the uneven and inconsistent implementation of these subsidies. “When it comes to the government subsidy, there’s favouritism involved – not all drivers and operators actually receive it,” Manlapig said, noting that only certain petrol stations allowed the subsidy to be claimed. Floranda urged the government to remove the excise and value-added taxes on petrol to ease citizens’ burden.

title: Hangzhou launch for Project B league in January just part of busy Chinese sports year
description: Newly founded basketball league will be preceded next week by return of NBA China Games in Macau, many other sports events till end of 2027.
content: The newly founded basketball league Project B earlier this week announced the first stop of its inaugural global basketball grand prix: in Hangzhou in January next year. While the debut of the global basketball tour has seen a slight delay – from its intended start this November – and the announcement of the Chinese host city came months later than anticipated, Project B is one of many major sporting events to be held in mainland China between now and the end of next year. “China has always had incredible energy around basketball, and I’ve experienced that personally throughout my career,” said Russell Westbrook, who retired from the NBA in August before joining Project B as co-founder and chief strategy officer last month. “Project B is connecting basketball with culture in each place we play. I have deep respect for the history and tradition here, and also the constant drive to create what comes next. This combination is powerful.” Li Meng, a Chinese women’s basketball player, said that Hangzhou has a “unique mix of history, nature, culture and innovation”, and the project’s senior executives also believe that Hangzhou, home to the highly praised 2023 Asian Games, will “set the standard” for the remaining stops, which include Tokyo and Valencia. “We’re bringing the best players in the world together to compete at the highest level, and we’re also creating an environment where they can experience new cultures and build real connections with fans,” said co-founder and chief basketball officer Alana Beard. “Starting in Hangzhou gives us an incredible stage for both.” While the first competitive stop of Project B may still be almost four months away, sports fans, particularly basketball fanatics, do not have to wait that long for their sporting fix. The NBA China Games in Macau are entering the second year of their five-year deal and are taking place next week. With China seemingly beginning to reopen to events again, it is only natural to wonder whether the NBA will play there again soon. Last October, Commissioner Adam Silver said that “games can take place in other parts of China, concurrent with our Macau arrangement”, despite the fact the Macau deal was understood to be exclusive and all current matches were expected to remain on the peninsula. Whether Macau was the stepping stone as the NBA sought to re-enter China for the first time since 2019, the real question, said a source with knowledge of the situation, was not whether four games could be held over two stops within the same country in almost the same time frame, but whether it was feasible or worthwhile to create rivalries boasting very similar audience bases. “That’s a five-year deal right there, and Macau did it to ensure their exclusivity,” said the insider with NBA knowledge. “Of course, there had been Chinese cities knocking on the door, and they were not only the traditional cities like Bei-Shang-Guang-Shen [Beijing-Shanghai-Guangzhou-Shenzhen]. “The likes of Chengdu, Chongqing, Hangzhou, or what we call China’s new first-tier cities, those which have staged major events or even multi-sport games, are anxiously awaiting too, but nothing is likely to happen until after Macau’s deal.” Judging by the live broadcast of the NBA in China and the conclusion of other events, including the NBA 3X China in Shenzhen last month and the NBA Shanghai Basketball Festival the month before, the source added that there were no indications that the NBA had encountered problems entering the country, which boasts roughly 150 million passionate basketball fans. “Chinese cities are competing among themselves, so another consideration would be whether a new city is sustainable,” the source added. “Macau has done such a good job in its first year. The proximity of the venue and hotels, for example, and the facilities Macau now has, are not comparable to when they held the previous China Game in 2007. “The NBA House last year was almost like a benchmark, too: ‘Can the rest of you do it to this same level?’” After the two games between the Dallas Mavericks and the Houston Rockets at the Venetian Arena in Macau next week, hosted in partnership with Sands China Ltd, there will be three more editions of the NBA China Games. Sources told the South China Morning Post that the Boston Celtics were “the most talked about team” that might come to the Far East next. Mario Ho Yau-kwan, the youngest son of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun, was a part of the consortium that acquired the 18-time champions, who last triumphed in 2024, in August 2025. But it was not only that. “The Celtics were mentioned in almost every conversation I am aware of, but most outsiders only see the direct rivalry between two different casino brands and are puzzled. You’re going to see some of the events happening outside of the Sands next week,” the source said. “The NBA China Games are not only a Sands thing; the government and the tourism board are heavily involved, too.” But it is only basketball: China has long been the home to many other sports tournaments in different events, including table tennis, tennis, Formula 1, badminton, athletics, fencing and snooker, to name just a few. The UCI Track Cycling World Championships are being held in Shanghai later this month, and the World Table Tennis Cup Finals are taking place in Chengdu at the end of November, almost concurrently with the World Aquatics (25m) Swimming Championships in Beijing. The World Athletics Championships will also be held in the capital next September. All of this could be seen as local governments carrying out national policy, as China is promoting the integration of sports, culture and tourism, and stimulating consumption by hosting various events. On Wednesday, the State Council of China proposed exploring the potential integration of sports events and cultural tourism, as well as promoting the branding, integration and commercialisation of sports events. The hope is that by 2030 a modern sports event system with Chinese characteristics will have been established and sports events with global influence will have been cultivated. “The government spends money on sports and culture every year. It’s just a matter of what specific projects that money is spent on,” said another source connected to the World Snooker Tour Shenzhen Open, which is taking place across the border until Sunday. “One characteristic of snooker tournaments is that they are international competitions. “One of the performance evaluation criteria for local government leaders is whether they have introduced international sporting events. Some local governments do not want to fail to meet these evaluation standards, so the demand for international sporting events has always existed. “Here, we’re not talking about purely commercial invitational or exhibition events. The government hopes to attract formal, influential tournaments, and they assess each year who should receive this funding.”

title: Asking for a Friend: Help! How can I improve my communication with others?
description: Each week, we respond to a question from our readers and give advice and resources they can turn to.
content:
Do you have a personal question you’ve been too afraid to ask? Whether it is about school, family or your social life, you can share it with us through this form . Don’t worry, you’ll remain anonymous.
I feel lonely because I don’t have many friends. People tell me I’m too direct, and I think that’s keeping me from making friends. At night, my mind won’t stop replaying past conversations, and I think about how I could have said things differently. Please tell me how to better connect with others.
Feeling alone and overthinking social interactions can be emotionally draining, and wanting meaningful connections with people is natural.
Replaying conversations in your head means you care about making friends and want to do better, but ruminating on them may negatively affect your mental well-being. When these thoughts arise at night, take a few deep breaths, gently acknowledge them and remind yourself that everyone meets difficulties in social settings.
When you replay the past conversations, what did you say that might have been too direct? It is helpful to try to understand the emotions you caused the other person to feel.
Was it a criticism of someone’s appearance or performance? If someone hasn’t directly asked for feedback on their appearance or performance, they might find it rude if you are very direct about something negative.
If the situation does not call for your direct criticism, it might be better to keep those thoughts to yourself. But if you’re working on a group project, then your feedback is needed, and you can find a gentler way to communicate your thoughts.
Were you sharing your opinion about a topic? Someone might feel like you interrupted them or that you didn’t try to understand what they were trying to say.
In most cases, there are more delicate ways to share your thoughts and feedback.
Being too direct in communication may hurt others’ feelings, even when your intentions are good. Here are some tips for expressing your thoughts.
Use “I” as a buffer : Start with phrases like “I think” or “From my view” to frame thoughts as personal opinions, which may sound softer than making a blunt statement.
Practise active listening : Show genuine interest in what others are sharing and let them speak fully before offering your feedback.
Focus on feelings : Try to acknowledge how the other person might feel and give them time to digest. There is no rush to provide a solution; if you want to share an honest opinion, try to understand their feelings first.
Use the “sandwich” method: Sandwich any criticism with positive feedback. Start by complimenting something that was done well. Then, transition to your constructive criticism and focus on how this aspect could be improved. At the end, share an overall comment that highlights the positive aspects of their work.
Being open and respectful allows space for different personalities and perspectives to connect. You do not have to agree with everything someone says, but respect provides an environment for understanding to grow over time.
Making new friends takes time and the right environment. Joining clubs, interest groups, sports teams or volunteer activities can put you in environments where people share your passions and common hobbies. Shared activities naturally ease the pressure of conversation, making it easier to create connections over time.
Building confidence and forming lasting friendships take time. If you feel overwhelmed or lonely, talk to a family member, teacher or counsellor. They might be able to share some advice on how to make friends.
If you need someone neutral to talk to, you can consider these resources.
Mental Health Support Hotline: 24-hour hotline and WhatsApp at 18111 or visit shallwetalk.hk
Open Up: 24/7 online text emotional support platform on openup.hk
This question was answered by clinical psychologists from Shall We Talk, a mental health initiative under the Department of Health launched in collaboration with the Advisory Committee on Mental Health.

title: Could Northern Metropolis draw educational leasing from Hong Kong’s Grade A office sector?
description: Education groups leased 49,050 square metres of commercial space in the city from January 2025 to August this year, according to CBRE.
content: As education sector demand supports Hong Kong’s Grade A office leasing activity, analysts said infrastructure that will serve the Northern Metropolis could decide whether schools and universities move their administrative and other services to this potential new centre of the city. “Over the medium to long term, the Northern Metropolis could be a viable option for institutions seeking to expand their teaching, research and administrative facilities,” said Kelvin Lee, director at property agency Midland Commercial. “It may be particularly suitable for uses that require substantial space or close collaboration with technology companies and research organisations. Whether universities locate general office functions there will depend on the availability of suitable premises, transport links, costs and operational needs.” The Hong Kong government laid down plans for the Northern Metropolis under the city’s first five-year blueprint, which expanded the three university towns and opened applications for interested institutions to submit their proposals for the first one, in Hung Shui Kiu, by the end of this year, with the results to be announced in early 2027. The announcement for the planned new university towns comes amid rising demand from the education sector for commercial space in Hong Kong. Between January 2025 and August this year, education groups leased a total area of about 49,050 square metres (528,000 square feet) of commercial space in the city, covering both retail and office property, according to data tracked by CBRE. They also acquired properties worth HK$845 million (US$107.72 million). The property consultancy believes the city’s international schools and universities are likely to require more real estate to accommodate an additional 200,000 non-local students, comprising foreigners and mainland Chinese, by 2035. For international schools, another 40 to 50 new school campuses are likely to be required, which could mean up to 1.11 million square metres of gross floor area. At the tertiary level, universities are likely to expand their academic space by 1.39 million to 2.14 million square metres. Additionally, CBRE has tracked a record high of 46,451 square metres of demand for commercial space from existing schools and new groups currently trying to set up a campus in Hong Kong. This demand is providing some relief to Hong Kong’s office property market, where vacancy rates for overall prime office space remained at double digits – 12.5 per cent in August, down from 12.8 per cent in July – according to commercial real estate firm Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL). While Northern Metropolis could provide ample space for the property needs of schools and universities looking to expand their space, not all their functions could be relocated in the district. Research and campus-support teams could be more suited there, while postgraduate and executive programmes were likely to favour in-town locations for the convenience of working professionals, said Jack Tong, director of research and consultancy at Savills Hong Kong. “Research, technology transfer and industry partnerships benefit from being close to the new campuses and innovation clusters,” he said. “But universities will still need city-centre offices for functions that depend on regular contact with businesses, donors and professional advisers. “Central and Admiralty should therefore retain a role in university leasing, even as a new education cluster takes shape in the north,” Tong added. For now, plans for the Northern Metropolis are yet to be realised, transport and connectivity would have to be established first, said Chris Hui, executive director and head of landlord representation for office services at Colliers. “For example – transport – will it be as convenient and as well connected as what we may envision now?” he said. “These are long-term infrastructure requirements that need to be built in place before other activities commence.” Additionally, with the planned university towns intended to develop integrated ecosystems for emerging industries, these initiatives will need to mature, said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL. “The spillover benefits to surrounding commercial real estate assets are unlikely to materialise immediately,” she said. “Consequently, it is unlikely that the Northern Metropolis will materially divert office demand associated with traditional academic programmes from established CBDs (central business districts) in the near term.”

title: Family of Renee Good, US woman killed by ICE agent, sues Trump administration
description: The lawsuit says there has been ‘no accountability’ for her death, which took place amid a crackdown on migrants in Minneapolis.
content: ⁠The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by ⁠federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, sued the Trump administration on Thursday, saying there had been “no accountability” for her killing during deportation sweeps. Good, 37, was shot dead in her car by a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on January 7 when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily protests against masked and armed federal agents deployed to Minnesota to arrest migrants for deportation. The two lawsuits accuse Jonathan Ross, the ICE agent who shot Good, and senior Trump administration officials of unconstitutional negligence and excessive force that violated the ‌civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis, demanding a jury trial and damages. They are among the first major civil actions taken against US President Donald Trump for his unprecedented deportation sweeps in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge. “What happened to Renee was completely senseless and the fact that there’s been no accountability, no investigation, no expression of condolence, no change in policy is completely mind-blowing,” Brent Ganger, Good’s brother, said at a press conference in Minneapolis. “What happened to America? Something must change now.” Ross could not be reached for comment on Thursday, while a White House spokeswoman called the lawsuits baseless. Good’s killing intensified the backlash in Minnesota and beyond against the sweeps, involving thousands of immigration agents deployed to street patrols in Minnesota. Trump ended the Minnesota surge in February, but says his anti-immigration policies are ⁠needed for the safety of native-born Americans. Days after Good’s death, an ICE agent shot and wounded Julio Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan delivery driver, in the leg, and two weeks later immigration agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, an American ‌nurse working for the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Senior Trump administration officials initially branded Good a “domestic terrorist” and the Department of Justice stopped its federal prosecutors in Minneapolis from investigating the agents involved in her killing, prompting at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest. None of the agents involved has yet faced any ‌charges. The lawsuits describe Good as a poet and mother of three children, and that she and her wife, Becca Good, dropped their six-year-old son off at school before stopping ⁠her car in the middle of Portland Avenue after ⁠seeing patrolling ICE agents. “Renee honked her horn to warn her neighbours,” according to the lawsuits. “Her partner got out and began to film. Renee stayed behind the wheel. She was not the target of any investigation, and she was breaking no law that any federal officer had ‌authority to enforce.” Becca Good, in her first public remarks, said of her wife: “She was pure love. She was funny. She was smart. She was gorgeous.” “Renee believed in something simple: that being good can change the world,” she said. “She believed everyone deserves love and compassion, care and ‌dignity, no ‌matter who they were or where they came from.” Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said the administration would “vigorously defend” itself against the lawsuits. “The Trump administration views the deaths of countless innocent Americans at the hands of criminal ‌illegal aliens as a tragedy that should warrant equal coverage from the mainstream media who choose to ignore these victims of illegal alien crime,” she said in a statement. Good’s killing was captured on ⁠widely viewed videos that showed Ross approaching Good in her car partly blocking the road moments after he had driven past her. Ross circled her car on foot, recording on his cellphone. In her last words, Good ⁠can be seen on video saying to Ross: “That’s fine, dude, I’m not mad at you.” Moments later, another ICE agent approached the car and told Good to get out. She can be seen reversing briefly, then putting the car into forward gear and turning the steering wheel to her right, apparently trying to drive away. As the car moves forward, Ross, who at that ‌point had returned to the front left of her car, ‌shouts “Whoa!” and shoots into the car, hitting Good three times: in her head, arm and torso. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, the chief elected prosecutor in Minneapolis, is investigating the agents who killed Good and Pretti for possible violations of Minnesota law. The investigations have been slowed because the Justice Department withdrew its usual cooperation and evidence-sharing with local law enforcement agencies. Minnesota has sued the Trump administration to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes. Ross has not publicly discussed Good’s death or his actions that day. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE and related agencies, has defended the conduct of Ross and other immigration officers as justified uses of force in dangerous situations.

title: In Focus | The myth of brotherhood: Hong Kong’s triads evolve amid new criminal landscape
description: Former gang member and experts say today’s triads eschew traditional rites and crimes, and now recruit youths online in an age of digital fraud.
content: Not long after he entered secondary school, Hong Kong youth Jason* was bullied by an older student with triad links. He was relieved when another senior stepped in to protect him. He helped Jason take revenge on the bully, then recruited him into a syndicate. Without undergoing any initiation ritual, Jason paid his protector a red packet to become an informal triad member. Later on, he discovered that the two seniors belonged to the same gang but took orders from different bosses. At first, Jason was just a street-corner kid, pushing people around at a housing estate. But as he drew closer to the triad’s core group, Jason began to realise that brotherhood was a myth and that business was the order of the day. In the underworld, everything was built on money. ‘Once I got closer to the boss, I started realising how it worked. He was using the triad to make money. I felt I could actually make a living off this, so I joined the inner circle to give it a shot,’ he said. Soon Jason was taking job orders from his boss, which were sometimes conveyed through messaging apps. His tasks ranged from property damage to procuring bank accounts for laundering fraudulent funds. Through these assignments, his illusions about brotherhood evaporated. He saw peers chicken out during vandalism runs and scramble for excuses when the boss ordered them to engage in street fights. To protect himself, Jason avoided direct involvement in high-risk operations by outsourcing most of his tasks to his peers, taking a cut of several hundred to several thousand dollars each time they completed a job. “I stayed away as much as I could to avoid getting arrested,” the 26-year-old said. Shifting focus in illicit activities The triad Jason joined 14 years ago was Shui Fong, one of four major syndicates still operating in Hong Kong. The others are Wo Shing Wo, Sun Yee On and 14K. According to experts in the field – including police, a retired anti-triad investigator and a youth organisation – the four triad groups have evolved over the past decade, with rituals simplified and street violence transforming into white-collar crime and cybercrime. Triad groups also often see one another less as rivals than as partners in making money. “The violent clashes and bloody scenes are gone. Instead, there are less conspicuous crimes, involving underground banking networks, cross-border money laundering and cybercrime. They do not require a physical presence and are much more low-profile,” said Superintendent Joe Au Yeung Tak of police’s organised crime and triad bureau. According to police, triad-related crimes rose to 2,554 cases in 2022, up 35 per cent from the previous year. Au Yeung said the spike was driven primarily by a sixfold jump in fraud, with 591 such cases accounting for nearly a quarter of all triad crime that year. Before the surge, the city’s triad-related crimes between 2016 and 2021 hovered at around 1,700 to 1,900 cases annually. The number of triad-related cases dipped to 1,353 in 2019 amid a wave of social unrest in the city, with police diverting resources to manage widespread violent protests, according to Au Yeung. As triads shifted into the digital sphere, law enforcement was adapting to keep pace. “As they transformed, we evolved,” he said. Historically, police relied on high-profile sweeps and mass arrests to deter gangs. Now their strategy has shifted towards intelligence-led operations targeting deception and financial investigations to cut off the triads’ sources of income. “Our focus has shifted to tracing the illicit funds, specifically the channels they use to launder the money, and figuring out how we can freeze those assets and confiscate them. Hitting them where it hurts financially is the only way to make them truly feel the pain,” Au Yeung said. Police also cooperated with other jurisdictions and organisations such as banks and telecommunications service providers to combat triad-related deception. This multipronged approach has yielded positive results. The number of triad-related deception cases decreased steadily to 323, 162 and 129 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. The total number of triad-related crimes was below 2,000 last year. Besides deception, triads also engaged in money laundering, which often involved the use of cryptocurrency, Au Yeung said. In such cases, his team relied on the expertise of colleagues from the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau. While low-level triad members still relied on traditional crimes such as vice, gambling, drugs, extortion, illicit cigarettes and illicit fuel for survival, other businesses – selling pirated video discs, controlling red minibus routes and managing nightclubs, for instance – had grown obsolete as society evolved. Au Yeung said different triads and factions had started cooperating in recent years, creating a “win-win situation” for themselves. “If the pie is big enough and transnational, it’s really not surprising at all for several triad factions to team up and work on it together,” he said. In the past, each of the 18 districts in Hong Kong was dominated by a single triad faction, a situation Au Yeung described as “strictly demarcated territoriality”. However, over the past decade or so, territorial boundaries have become increasingly blurred. “When everyone shares a common interest, focusing on making money rather than fighting, even different factions can collaborate. Nowadays, having multiple factions coexisting peacefully within the same region is actually not uncommon,” he said. Tougher laws lay bare the myth of brotherhood Gregory Lau Tat-keung, a former superintendent who retired from the police force in 2013, is another close observer of the gangs and has written a book about them. He has testified more than 40 times against gangsters in court as a triad expert. “A lot of people have been misled into thinking that the triads are all about loyalty and brotherhood,” he said. Despite hailing from a supposedly long tradition of ritualistic oaths, Lau recalled that many of the gangsters he had arrested had lined up to be prosecution witnesses. “Let me be a tainted witness. I’m ratting out my boss. Otherwise, how can I get my sentence reduced?” he said, describing the detainees’ thinking. “We shouldn’t believe in loyalty. Actual substantial interests are what matter most, including [having] fewer sentences and getting more money for informants.” The Prisons Ordinance was amended last year to tighten restrictions on inmate visits, including prohibiting them from receiving outside food. The changes were made after the enactment of the national security law in 2020. Lau said he believed the amendment was effective in deterring minor offenders from taking the fall for syndicate bosses because they were subject to stricter prison rules while on remand. “Before, it was relatively easy to convince them to break the law for the mastermind, because they mistakenly believed that as long as they could receive outside food [while on remand], their boss still controlled everything,” he said. “It wasn’t until they were convicted in court that they realised they were in trouble. They suddenly realised they were subject to strict prison regulations, no outside food, no special perks and fewer visitation rights.” The stricter rules also made it more difficult for visitors to bring inmates cigarettes, which served as a kind of “underground currency” in prisons, Lau said. History of political resistance According to Lau, the triads could be traced back to around 1644 with the formation of the Hung League, a Han underground organisation dedicated to overthrowing the Manchu-led Qing dynasty. Sun Yat-sen, leader of China’s 1911 revolution, was a member of the league. Over time, some exploited the name of the Hung League, with several developing into secret society factions, known as “huidang”, that turned to illegal activities after the fall of the Qing. Lau said the history of local triad societies could also be traced back to Cheung Po-tsai, a notorious pirate who was granted an amnesty after giving himself up to authorities in 1810. Some of his followers who refused to do the same turned to banditry, establishing what was considered the earliest prototype of triad societies in the city. The four main triad groups still active in Hong Kong have different origins. The 14K triad has historical roots tied to the Kuomintang. According to Lau, its original headquarters was located at 14 Baohua Road in Guangzhou, with the “K” in its name allegedly standing for Kuomintang. Similarly, Sun Yee On was founded by Kuomintang general Heung Chin. Originating from Chaozhou, “Yee On” was the historical name of the region. The organisation was originally registered with the Hong Kong government as the Yee On Commercial and Industrial Guild. After this registration was revoked, the members formed a new group, prefixing the name with “Sun”, meaning new in Chinese. Many triad groups in Hong Kong traditionally carried the suffix “Wo”, meaning harmony, including Wo Shing Wo. According to Lau, the naming originated from Chung Wo Tong, a secret society formed by Yau Lit, a close ally of Sun Yat-sen, to support the revolution. Another prominent group with the Wo suffix was Wo On Lok, commonly known as Shui Fong. It was originally established by workers of the Connaught Aerated Water Co Ltd, with “On Lok” being a Chinese transliteration of the company’s name and “Shui Fong”, meaning “water factory”, used as a shorthand for the aerated water plant. Traditional rituals succumb to modernity Lau’s book, From Hung League and Huidang to Modern Triads, published earlier this year, offers a rare glimpse into the triads’ traditional initiation ceremonies. The rituals – gruelling affairs that could last for hours – centred around a sacred altar draped with command banners and ancestral tablets honouring fallen members. New recruits were required to recite secret verses before lighting joss sticks and being covered with a sandpaper quilt. They shredded paper lotuses and chopped a chicken’s head to seal a blood oath. They had to pledge allegiance by reciting 36 oaths and swear to abide by 21 regulations, 10 prohibitions and 10 punishments. Finally, new recruits would present their “protectors” with a red packet containing HK$3.60, a symbolic figure invoking the phrase “three times three never ends, six times six is infinite”. According to Lau, the knowledge of traditional initiation rites has waned over time, with triads either forgoing rituals to avoid arrest or struggling to maintain them in the face of modern limitations. “Take chopping off a chicken’s head [as an example]. Where do you even get a chicken’s head nowadays? Ever since the avian flu outbreaks, there are no chicken heads any more. So it turned into chopping an egg,” Lau said. “And taking a blood oath? What about cross-contamination? We might as well just drink red wine.” He added that he had seen triad members using a red plastic hosepipe or a red mop handle to symbolise the rank of “red pole” – a senior member responsible for organising fights and enforcing gang rules. To avoid attention from law enforcement, some triads held ceremonies in the mountains, on barges or in mainland China. More commonly, initiations were reduced to a mere verbal agreement, a practice known as “hanging the blue lantern”, Lau said. More like rogue ‘employment agencies’ Michael Leung Siu-kei, a supervisor at the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups’ youth crime prevention centre, said triads in the past would recruit youths loitering in public spaces such as football fields, but that practice had faded into history. Triads nowadays were more like “employment agencies”, with syndicates using Telegram, Signal or even in-game chat rooms to advertise various “well-paying part-time jobs” to lure teenagers to work for them, he said. “They list how much [they pay] for splashing red paint, how much for distributing illicit cigarettes, how much for criminal damage.” He added that syndicates paid around HK$500 (US$64) for young people to distribute illicit cigarette leaflets at an entire housing estate overnight and HK$6,000 for a group to commit criminal damage against an office. They offered HK$1,000 to anyone willing to lend a physical bank card and HK$2,000 for an online bank account to launder money. Once a person accepted a job, it effectively meant they had pledged loyalty to a specific triad boss, although these allegiances were often loose, Leung said. “In fact, when we ask some youths about their gang ties, they’ll say: ‘I’ve never even met my boss.’ Sometimes they claim to belong to one triad faction, but after a while, we find them working on another job under a different faction.” Leung said he had to constantly warn youths of the risks and serious consequences of accepting these jobs. Au Yeung agreed that triads’ tactics for recruiting young people were no longer as blatant as in the past, as police deployed undercover officers to catch recruiters. “The triads use a much softer entry point these days. ‘Want to make some quick cash?’ ‘Come out and meet some new friends.’ ‘There’s free beer’,” he said. Police also worked closely with schools to prevent triads from infiltrating campuses and conducted cyber patrols to combat online recruitment, Au Yeung added. For Jason, earning quick money came at a cost as he became wracked with anxiety about being followed and developed a drug habit. “You get paranoid. You worry people or enemies might have followed you home and know where you live. Whenever I slept, even the slightest noise woke me up,” he said. Jason was once arrested by an undercover police officer after divulging that he was a triad member, but was acquitted by the court due to lack of evidence. At the age of 15, he began taking Ice and got involved in drug trafficking. But as his addiction grew more severe over a year, he started consuming his own supply and ended up owing the triad HK$40,000 for the drugs. Raised primarily by his grandparents, Jason was surprised when his estranged father stepped in to help clear his debt. “It felt like he had not given up on me,” he said. Around that time, the death of his beloved grandfather proved a final wake-up call for Jason, prompting him to quit drugs, cut ties with the triad and return to school. He now runs his own small delivery team. Looking back, he said he regretted joining the triad and could see more clearly how the organisation had exploited him. “At the end of the day, the triads are driven purely by self-interest,” he said. “Your family is always your strongest backing. No matter what happens, they will always support you.” *Name changed at the interviewee’s request.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong can capitalise on its unique role to benefit the nation
description: National Day came at a critical juncture for Hong Kong and the nation, just after President Xi’s state visit to the US and the launch of the city’s five-year plan.
content: National Day is a celebration of this country’s achievements. China has much to be proud of since becoming a republic in 1949. The sentiment resonated in Hong Kong as it too celebrated National Day amid increased integration with the mainland’s development goals. What sets the 77th anniversary apart is the timing – at a critical juncture in the affairs of the nation and Hong Kong. President Xi Jinping has just returned from a state visit to the United States that included a summit with US President Donald Trump, the second of an unprecedented four face-to-face meetings in one year. In Hong Kong, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has just launched the city’s first five-year plan to align development with the nation’s 15th five-year plan, which is central to China’s high-quality development and technology self-reliance amid the global tech race. Xi’s National Day address was his first to the nation after his state visit to the US and came weeks before the Communist Party’s fifth plenum later this month, a critical meeting ahead of the party’s five-yearly national congress next autumn. Xi projected pride and confidence in the nation’s ability to overcome the challenges posed by a complex geopolitical environment. “We are extremely proud of the world-renowned achievements of New China and full of confidence in the bright future of Chinese-style modernisation,” he said. Xi called for steady approaches to reform and opening up while striking a balance between growth and national security. He also pledged to “unswervingly” implement the “one country, two systems” principle and better support Hong Kong and Macau in integrating into China’s overall national development and long-term stability and prosperity. In his address to a National Day reception in Hong Kong, Chief Executive John Lee said that, over the past 77 years, the Chinese nation had achieved a historic transformation – from standing up and growing prosperous to becoming strong. “Today, China has become the world’s largest manufacturer and merchandise trader, its leading contributor to scientific research output and much more, exerting significant influence on international affairs,” he said. Lee said Hong Kong’s five-year plan allowed its people to apply unique advantages under “one country, two systems”, embrace modern trends and seize the opportunities brought by national development. The warming of China-US ties evidenced by the recent summits, and the potential opportunities it creates, has not gone unnoticed by Hong Kong officials, with Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po saying in late September that increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers would provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns. Hong Kong is positioned to play a unique role, connecting China with the rest of the world and attracting capital, he said. At the National Day reception, the chief executive said Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan highlighted its DNA as an international city while emphasising the market economy. He said the city needed a blueprint with strategic vision amid the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape and accelerated growth of artificial intelligence. He stressed that the plan “adheres to the ‘one country, two systems’ principle”. “This means that the five-year plan must be developed under the Basic Law framework,” he said, adding that the city will keep the practice of capitalism and the common law system as well as the free flow of people, capital and information. To underline the importance of concerted efforts, he quoted a line from Huainanzi – The Ruler’s Techniques: “Victory is ensured when people pool their strength; success is secured when people put their heads together.” The line is from a work by Liu An, a grandson of the founding emperor of the Western Han dynasty. Implementing Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint calls for concentrated collective wisdom and the joint efforts of the whole community. National Day kicks off the “golden week” holiday. It is a celebration that should be shared by all. Hong Kong enjoyed a spectacular fireworks display over Victoria Harbour on Thursday night while restaurants and retailers hope an array of concessions will be good for business. The city is expecting 1.29 million mainland tourists, which will hopefully help boost consumption. We should make them welcome.

title: How China’s Wudang Mountains draw droves of visitors in search of spiritual cleansing
description: The sacred mountain range dotted with ancient Taoist temples attracts pilgrims and visitors praying for everything from peace to good weather.
content: A banknote clasped between her hands, Liu Haiyan prays to the protector of the Wudang Mountains. The range in central China’s Hubei province has long been considered sacred in Taoism. “I asked him to bless our motherland with favourable weather and to make it even more prosperous,” Liu says while sitting outside the Golden Hall, a Taoist temple at the summit of Tianzhu Peak. “This place watches over our country,” she adds. “We’re Chinese, and this is part of our faith.” Tourists and pilgrims in a steady stream make their way through Wudang every day. Its scenic peaks, ancient palaces and religious sites drew 14 million visits in 2025, according to government figures. Wudang’s Taoist buildings date as far back as the 7th century. The complex expanded over centuries through China’s Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties. Liu travelled several hundred kilometres from Hebei province with her daughter, Ji Jiaxin. She also prayed to Wudang’s protector, known as Zhenwu. “He can guide people towards goodness,” Ji says. “He also watches over all the living things that grow across the land.” Both women see Wudang as a place of scenic beauty and spiritual significance. Perched at about 1,610 metres (5,280 feet) above sea level, the Golden Hall is a place where they experience a sense of spiritual purification. “Everyone comes here with a sincere heart,” Liu says. “With sincerity, the divine will respond.” Nurturing heaven and Earth The Wudang Mountains comprise 72 peaks, all thought to converge towards Tianzhu. Its lower slopes are associated with fire, while the deity enshrined at its summit is linked to water. “Water at the top can moisten the earth, while fire below provides warmth and enables all living things to grow,” says Shu Chenghai, director of social education at Wudang Museum. The Golden Hall’s construction also reflects this symbolism. In the traditional Chinese concept of the five elements, metal is believed to generate water. And since natural sources can run dry over time, the bronze hall serves to nourish heaven and Earth. “It embodies prayers for favourable weather, abundant harvests and peace and prosperity throughout the country,” Shu says. Taoist priests and monks look after the religious sites throughout Wudang. With their hair tied in high buns and dressed in distinctive blue robes, they glide through the temples, talking to visitors and scanning tickets at the entrances. Their role also connects Wudang’s spiritual life with the communities that call the mountain home. Cai Hongping was born in the area. Her family settled beside Zixiao Palace, a major Taoist temple complex. “Some of the elderly Taoist priests there were exceptionally kind and compassionate,” Cai says. “Sometimes they gave us dates, peanuts or fruit.” Life in the mountains was difficult when Cai was a child. Food and other material goods were scarce, but she remembers the temples as places of happiness and joy. “I often went with the Taoist priests to identify Chinese medicinal herbs, practised martial arts with them, and sometimes stole fruit that had been left as offerings,” Cai says. Her connection to the mountain extended beyond its temples. Cai’s grandfather was a heritage conservation worker in Wudang, focused on preserving and cataloguing cultural relics. Her father also made walking sticks for visitors. Cai and other relatives sometimes joined him in gathering medicinal herbs to sell. “The entire mountain was my childhood,” Cai says. “It has also given me a reverence for life.” Connections with the Forbidden City Wudang’s palaces and temples flourished during the Ming dynasty, when the Yongle Emperor, Zhu Di, undertook a major building campaign to align his imperial regime with Taoism. At its height, the complex included dozens of temples, palaces and monasteries. More than 60 sites survive today. Wudang’s development coincided with another major project commissioned by Zhu Di: the Forbidden City in Beijing. “When we say, ‘The Forbidden City was built in the north, and Wudang was developed in the south,’ we mean that these two World Cultural Heritage sites are like twins,” Shu says. “The two places conveyed a message to the world: one represented heaven, while the other represented the human realm.” Wudang’s special connection with Ming dynasty emperors remains visible today. Along the route taken by tourists and pilgrims are several steles that mark ritual proclamations made on behalf of emperors during the first year of each reign. “An emperor needed to make a ritual proclamation to Zhenwu,” Shu says. “He would declare that he had succeeded to the imperial throne and express his hope for heaven’s support.” Long ago, the mountain drew people seeking solitude and spiritual cultivation. Shu says its distinctive landscape embodies the traditional Chinese concept of dong tian fu di, or “grotto-heavens and blessed lands” – places traditionally regarded as sacred retreats. “The idea is that a profound harmony between humanity and nature is not merely something human beings can create,” Shu says. Beyond the Golden Hall, visitors encounter other temples and figures associated with different needs, from health and inner balance to martial arts. Wang Xia recently travelled from Inner Mongolia and visited Taizipo, or Prince Slope, a Taoist temple complex linked to Zhenwu’s legendary early life as a prince. “The fact that the crown prince once studied here makes it particularly appealing,” Wang says. “I wanted to pray for my child, to wish her academic success and a bright future.” Her first encounter with Wudang came in books. She read about the Ming dynasty and began to dream about visiting the site herself one day. “I imagined that coming here would give me the feeling of entering the world of Taoist immortals,” Wang says. “That is what this place feels like: a mountain of immortals.”

title: Our cheat sheet for the best things to do in Hong Kong, October 2-10
description: Have a Sunday dim sum blowout at Ho Lee Fook, take a cultural deep dive at ‘Arts in the City: Revisit Tai Hang’, try a California-inspired cocktail at Swim Club and soak up Korean artist Kang Myonghi’s time-honoured show at Villepin.
content: EAT THIS Ho Lee Fook Spice up your weekend dim sum sesh at Ho Lee Fook’s reimagined Good Fortune Club. On the first Sunday of each month, the neo-Cantonese restaurant hosts an unlimited feast, where chef ArChan Chan Kit-ying’s creations – such as the kurobuta pork char siu puff, mala pork xiaolongbao, crispy coffee and salted egg yolk lava buns and the amusingly named Har Har har gow – just keep on coming. Ho Lee Fook’s collection of Chinese wines is part of the experience, too; each guest can select one bottle from a range of Shanxi, Ningxia, Yunnan and Xinjiang labels. 1-5 Elgin Street, Central; to book, go to holeefook.com.hk DO THIS Arts in the City: Revisit Tai Hang From now until October 31, “Arts in the City: Revisit Tai Hang” presents a diverse programme of workshops, installations, guided tours and other experiences to encourage residents and tourists alike to explore the charming neighbourhood beyond its well-known fire dragon dance. Join a papier-mâché class to craft a guardian creature from Chinese folklore, embark on an architectural and heritage walk to understand Tai Hang’s transformation from village houses to traditional tenement buildings, or marvel at woven “kites” recalling classic Hakka patterns. Various locations; click here for details DRINK THIS Swim Club From Hong Kong to the Hollywood Hills – that’s the “liquid travelogue” Swim Club is taking its guests on as summer draws to a close, evoking a mood board of slow sunsets, coastal drives, rooftop pools and California dreamin’. Beverage director Benjamin Boyce’s new drinks menu, Vertical Echo, introduces 13 libations with West Coast inspirations. Vine & Vine marries basil-infused tomato water, caviar and champagne vinegar with gin or vodka for a tangy, umami blend; Opuntia honours its namesake desert cactus with a prickly-pear cordial and gin; and San Rosarito builds on the classic daiquiri with coconut, white chocolate and lime. 50/F, Kimpton Tsim Sha Tsui Hong Kong, 11 Middle Road, Tsim Sha Tsui SEE THIS What Remains to Be Seen Celebrated South Korean artist Kang Myonghi returns to Hong Kong for a dedicated gallery exhibition to showcase recent works. Running from September 29 to November 15, at Villepin, “What Remains to Be Seen” reflects more than six decades of observation, experimentation, contemplation and expression on canvas and paper, capturing landscapes, nature and motifs that Kang revisits over the course of months or even years as part of her devotion to the art of “looking”, so much so that time itself becomes a crucial element, shaping her abstract pieces. Villepin, 53-55 Hollywood Road, Central

title: Greer says no specific timeline set for enforcing US-China Board of Trade
description: United States Trade Representative confirms recommendations must go through a legal process before implementation of new economic initiative.
content: United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Thursday that there is no timeline yet for implementing the US-China Board of Trade, one of the key economic outcomes of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last week. Speaking on the sidelines of the Group of 20 Trade Ministers’ meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, Greer said the tariff reductions under the mechanism were “a policy outcome” and that the recommendations would have to go through a legal process before implementation. The US government could put the Board of Trade recommendations out to the public, Greer said, adding that there would then be a “common process” in which the government could go “back and forth” before making a legal determination on whether to adopt them in a tariff action. “We have to stick to our legal processes,” he said. At last week’s summit, Beijing and Washington launched the Board of Trade mechanism and on Sunday unveiled lists of non-sensitive products worth up to US$30 billion each that would be eligible for tariff reductions. The White House released tariff-reduction lists covering 77 categories of Chinese imports into the US and 1,619 US products headed for China. The US import list included a range of consumer goods, from microwave ovens and electric irons to Christmas ornaments and toys. China’s list was dominated by agricultural products such as beef and vegetables, along with coal, timber and medical devices including hearing aids and pacemakers. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Monday that more than 90 per cent of the products covered by the agreement would receive most-favoured nation tariff rates, with reciprocal tariffs fully waived. The two sides also agreed to keep their Busan trade truce in place until January 10, 2027, extending it by two months beyond its original November 10 expiry. The agreement, reached in South Korea in October 2025, reduced US tariffs on some Chinese goods, put additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies on hold, and suspended certain Chinese rare earth export controls. No G20 consensus on forced labour, excess capacity The two-day G20 Trade Ministers’ meeting in Milwaukee ended without consensus on forced labour and excess capacity, two of Washington’s major priorities for its 2026 presidency of the forum. As it maintains a fragile trade truce with China, Washington has used its G20 presidency to highlight Beijing’s global trade surplus and press members to address what it calls “excessive imbalances” and forced labour practices. China has denied the allegations. “It is unfortunate that we could not reach consensus on the forced labour statement,” Greer said at a press conference on Thursday. “Believe it or not, we have countries in the G20 that do not want to commit to having a prohibition on the import of goods made with forced labour,” he noted, indicating that opposition to the proposal extended beyond China. In July, the US imposed tariffs against 60 economies, including China, Japan, South Korea, India and European Union member states, ranging from 10 to 12.5 per cent after a trade investigation into forced labour allegations. Experts say the forced labour allegations are a pretext for imposing tariffs as part of US President Donald Trump’s broader “America-first” trade agenda. Similarly, Washington failed to secure a consensus on excess capacity, another issue where it sought broader G20 backing. Without naming China, Greer said excess capacity “plagues” a range of sectors, including steel, automotive production, batteries and solar panels – industries where Beijing has a dominant global position. “Nearly all countries agreed that this is an issue that requires action,” he said. “Again, it’s unfortunate we couldn’t reach consensus on a statement on this issue to address structural excess capacity and production.” US proposes new global framework to address steel production capacity Washington proposed a new global framework on Wednesday to address excess steel production capacity, which Greer said could prompt other countries to follow the US lead. “The United States has taken robust measures, and it probably makes sense for other countries to do that too,” Greer said after a meeting of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity (GFSEC). The forum adopted the framework, which calls for countries to reduce or eliminate “market-distorting subsidies” and share “information on non-market policies and practices” in countries outside the group. The GFSEC has 28 members, including Canada, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, France and Germany, and works to address excess steel capacity globally. China is not part of the grouping. China’s dominance of the global steel industry has drawn growing scrutiny over the past two decades, with multiple countries imposing tariffs, anti-dumping duties and other measures on its steel imports. It produced around 960.8 million tonnes of crude steel in 2025, accounting for nearly 52 per cent of global output. According to Greer, the G20 trade ministers reached consensus on denouncing the weaponisation of food through coercive trade actions.

title: EU to hold emergency talks on soaring diesel prices as US ramps up pressure
description: Washington demands allies tap reserves as high energy costs threaten Republicans in the coming midterms.
content: EU nations will meet Friday, aiming to develop a unified response to soaring diesel prices, a day after the US called on its European allies to release strategic reserves “immediately” to stem the crisis. The emergency meeting between EU member states and the European Commission is scheduled for early in the day, a Commission spokesperson said late Thursday. Washington is piling on pressure to get European help with fuel costs, with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday floating the possibility of banning diesel exports. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters Thursday on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers gathering in Milwaukee that any move by the US to ban diesel exports would be “unexpected for Europeans.” “It would have very dramatic consequences for our economic performance,” Sefcovic said of any potential diesel export ban. Sefcovic told reporters that he did not go into details with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on energy exports at the meeting, but the transatlantic partners “decided to stay in close touch to avoid any surprises here”. Reports said the Trump administration wants France and Germany in particular to tap their stockpiles of diesel to try to curb prices sent soaring by the US war on Iran. “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a post on social media. High energy costs loom as a threat to Trump’s Republican Party in next month’s midterm elections. “It is in Europe’s best interest to work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers,” a US official said. At G20 trade talks in Milwaukee, Greer struck a conciliatory tone, saying there was an “eagerness on both sides to work together” on the diesel issue. And Trump told reporters in Texas on Thursday that he “may” ask European countries to release diesel reserves. France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier, said in Milwaukee: “I can’t imagine that there will be a ban”. He stressed the importance of diesel to the United States and European countries, adding both sides will “try to find solutions”. “In France, we’ll try to find balanced solutions all over the world,” Forissier added. “If not with the Americans, it will be with other countries.” Trump on Wednesday said he was still considering a possible ban on US diesel exports, while adding that he thought it could ultimately cause petrol prices to rise. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. Speaking alongside Trump, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Wednesday that the world would “hear announcements from our friends in Europe” to push diesel prices down. Asked about a release from strategic reserves, the French presidency said no such demand had been made when Emmanuel Macron and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last week. Macron would also soon convene a video meeting of G7 leaders “to make progress on the various levers that can be used to address the rising fuel prices … including coordination on releasing reserves”. Macron announced on September 18 a plan for such a meeting. The G7 gathering is expected in mid-October, according to Macron’s press office. Average US diesel prices have surged more than 70 per cent to US$6.39 a gallon (3.78 litres) since the start of the Iran war, according to AAA motor club data. Fuel prices have caused living costs to soar, leaving Trump’s Republican Party fearing it could lose control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

title: Panda diplomacy: all the countries currently hosting China’s beloved ambassadors
description: The arrival of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang in the US following the Xi-Trump summit in Washington continues a Chinese diplomatic tradition.
content: Two giant pandas arrived in the US following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, continuing a decades-old tradition in which the beloved fuzzy ambassadors have become symbols of China’s ties with countries around the world. Zoo Atlanta announced the arrival of giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang on Sunday, saying it was “overjoyed” to welcome the pair after the zoo’s previous 25-year partnership with China ended in 2024. Xi said during his US visit that the pandas would be sent as an “envoy of friendship” between the Chinese and American people. What is panda diplomacy, how does it reflect bilateral ties? For decades, China has used its unique giant pandas as symbols of friendship and goodwill in its relations with other countries, in a practice known as panda diplomacy. The exchanges have often been linked to diplomatic initiatives and major trade deals. It gained international attention in the 1970s when China sent pandas to countries including the US and Japan following major diplomatic developments, including the establishment of diplomatic relations with Japan in 1972. Cooperation has also sometimes been suspended, or loan deals left unrenewed, with no new pandas for countries when relations have soured. Japan is currently without any giant pandas. Twins Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei returned to China in January against a backdrop of strained Beijing-Tokyo ties following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks about Taiwan. In November, Takaichi told the Japanese parliament that a Taiwan contingency could trigger the deployment of her country’s defence forces. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Where are China’s pandas? Following the arrival of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang in the US, China has 40 giant pandas living overseas in 15 countries, according to Chinese official figures. South Korea has hosted giant pandas since 2016, when Ai Bao and Le Bao arrived under a joint conservation programme following Xi’s 2014 visit to Seoul that helped deepen bilateral ties.
