Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have also hosted giant pandas under conservation partnerships, while Adelaide Zoo in Australia remains the only panda facility in Oceania. Qatar became the first country in the Middle East to receive giant pandas when Si Hai and Jing Jing arrived in 2022, shortly before the Fifa World Cup, as China-Qatar ties expanded in areas including trade and cultural exchanges. In Europe, pandas have been part of long-running conservation partnerships with countries including France, Germany, Austria, Spain, the Netherlands and Belgium. France received pandas in 2012, while Belgium’s pair arrived in 2014 during Xi’s state visit, when he and King Philippe opened their enclosure. Russia received its first giant pandas in 2019, when Ru Yi and Ding Ding arrived for a joint conservation programme marking the 70th anniversary of China-Russia diplomatic relations. Xi and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin attended the opening of the panda enclosure during the Chinese leader’s visit to Moscow. In the US, pandas became a symbol of China-US engagement in 1972, when Beijing sent Ling Ling and Hsing Hsing following then-president Richard Nixon’s historic visit to China and the two countries moved towards formal diplomatic relations. The pair later died in the US, with China ending its practice of gifting pandas and shifting to loans to better protect the endangered species. Since then, successive generations of pandas have lived in US zoos under such agreements. Several US zoos returned pandas to China in 2023 and 2024 as agreements expired during a period of strained bilateral ties over trade, technology and geopolitical disputes. The US currently has six giant pandas across three zoos – more than any other country outside China. Xin Xin, born at Mexico City’s Chapultepec Zoo in 1990, is the world’s only giant panda that is not owned by China. She is descended from a pair gifted to Mexico in 1975, before Beijing changed its global ownership rules and turned them into loans.

title: Opinion | Tung Chee-hwa’s task as Hong Kong’s chief executive was without precedent
description: Hong Kong can pay tribute to Tung by bringing the same seriousness, patience and sense of common purpose to its next chapter of development.
content: The farewell to former chief executive Tung Chee-hwa was moving because it marked the passing of a figure who stood at the beginning of a wholly new chapter for Hong Kong, a city to which he devoted so much of himself. For many, Tung will always be associated with the formidable demands of the early years after the return to the motherland – the Asian financial crisis, the bursting of the property bubble, severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) and sharp social divisions. The institutions of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region were new; the expectations placed upon them were immense. The official eulogy, delivered on behalf of the central government by Shi Taifeng, vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), deserves to be read in that context. It did more than honour a public servant. It offered an authoritative assessment of Tung’s place in Hong Kong and China’s history. In describing him as an outstanding contributor to “one country, two systems”, a renowned patriot, an exceptional social activist and a close friend of the Communist Party, the eulogy recognised the breadth of his contribution. It also made clear that his role cannot be understood only through the events and controversies of a particular political moment. Tung belonged to the generation entrusted with translating a historic national policy into the everyday work of governing a complex international city. That was a task without precedent. No handbook existed for how Hong Kong’s new constitutional order should meet the pressures of global markets, public expectations and an evolving relationship with the Chinese mainland. Tung accepted that responsibility. My late parents were long-time friends of Tung and his wife, Betty. Long before I worked with him in public life, I knew the warmth of the Tung family’s friendship. My public journey began after I entered the Legislative Council in 1998. Six years later, he appointed me to the Executive Council and, in 2017, invited me to join the board of governors of Our Hong Kong Foundation. I saw a side of him that formal accounts do not always capture. He worked extraordinarily hard. His mind was invariably on the next challenge: how to strengthen Hong Kong’s economy, widen opportunities for young people, tackle housing and social inequality, and better understand the motherland. He also attempted difficult institutional reform, notably the Principal Officials Accountability System, introduced in 2002, which sought to strengthen political accountability but exposed tensions between politically appointed officials and the career civil service. What impressed me most was his magnanimity. Tung did not harbour anger towards his critics. In public life, that can be rare. His instinct was to listen, persuade and, where possible, find common ground. The eulogy resonated because it recognised the historic weight of the responsibility Tung was asked to carry. One country, two systems is clear as a principle, but in 1997 it had never been tested. It required Hong Kong to preserve its capitalist system, common law tradition and way of life, while finding its place within a country whose institutions, economy and social development had followed a very different path. Before 1997, Hong Kong’s ties with the mainland were mainly commercial, centred largely on trade and manufacturing investment. Those ties deepened as the economy advanced and regional cooperation grew. Two systems remained the foundation, but closer economic links, greater social contact and changing expectations brought new pressures. Tung was the first leader required to navigate that terrain. He had to uphold Hong Kong’s distinct system while responding to a rapidly changing country and an increasingly connected region. He also had to do so amid the Asian financial crisis, the bursting of the property bubble, Sars, public anxiety and intense scrutiny. Many criticised him, and some still judge him through the difficulties of those years. But any fair assessment must recognise the scale of the task he accepted. In that sense, the central government’s tribute was not simply ceremonial. It acknowledged that Tung had undertaken one of the most difficult responsibilities in Hong Kong’s modern history. After leaving office, Tung continued to serve Hong Kong, the country and the wider region. He served as a CPPCC vice-chairman from 2005 to 2023. In 2008, he founded the China-United States Exchange Foundation; in 2014, he established Our Hong Kong Foundation to bring long-term thinking to public policy. The finest tribute to Tung will not be found in ceremonial language alone. It must lie in Hong Kong bringing the same seriousness, patience and sense of common purpose to the next chapter of development that he brought to its first.

title: Putin warns Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in arsenal if any of its territory is attacked
description: Moscow has told Nato it won’t hesitate to use nuclear arms to defend Kaliningrad against attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave.
content: Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal. In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels. His remarks followed Moscow’s warning to Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”. They accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by saying Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilising attacks with drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd. “There should be no mistake – Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if Nato countries try to isolate [the] Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday. Asked at the Valdai Club forum Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with Nato or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.” Putin said that “everything is written correctly” in the earlier warning to Nato. “If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories – of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” he said. Putin didn’t specify whether Moscow would use nuclear weapons but said it has arms that “no one else has” and would determine which to use in case of an attack. Nato spokeswoman Allison Hart confirmed on Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the US-led military alliance. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said in a statement. Hart insisted Nato was not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply noting that “Nato is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia”. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said Wednesday the bloc’s response to the message was “short and concise”. “Basically what we said is, ‘Hey, listen, we are a defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful,’” Rutte told Euronews. Nato’s response also urged Russia to stop its “unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine”, now in its fifth year. The Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad sits between Nato members Poland and Lithuania. It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets, and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there. Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever attack any Nato ally. Nato allies have conducted military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months. More are planned in October. It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines. On August 18, Nato held an exercise over northern Poland and the Baltic region involving several aircraft, including an EA-37B Compass Call – a sophisticated American plane that can jam communications and radar, the US Air Forces in Europe said. Defence analysts believe the unannounced large-scale exercise would not have been welcomed by the Kremlin. European leaders and intelligence services have warned that Russia could be ready to strike at another country within a few years, especially if it wins its war on Ukraine. Rutte told Euronews that Russia is trying “to divide us and lose the focus” on defending Ukraine. “We will not,” he said, adding that the best way to respond is to provide Kyiv with more support. “That’s the message. Calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going. That’s how we deal with it,” Rutte said.

title: Trump vows to hit Iran ‘very hard’ if linked to Flydubai cockpit attack
description: US president warns of retaliation as Israeli PM claims co-pilot who attempted to crash jet underwent radicalisation.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Tehran was likely to be involved in an attack by a pilot on a Flydubai flight to Israel and that Iran would be “hit very hard” if it was. The co-pilot allegedly assaulted the captain before passengers managed to save the plane from crashing. Israel’s prime minister said the man had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”. “I would say the answer, based on what I’m hearing, is yes but we’re working on it right now,” Trump said when asked by reporters at the White House whether Iran was involved in the incident on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. On whether the US would retaliate against Iran if it was responsible for the attack, Trump replied: “Oh, they’ll be hit very hard, don’t worry”. In the first comment by the Saudi government on the incident, the Interior Ministry said in a statement that the initial investigation indicated the co-pilot assaulted the captain, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in Tabuk. The ministry said the captain and co-pilot, who were both treated in hospital for injuries, left for Abu Dhabi on Thursday morning after receiving medical clearance, adding that Saudi Arabia conducted the preliminary investigation alongside security teams from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE has started investigations seeking to establish the circumstances and motives and determine “whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction”, the UAE state news agency reported on Thursday. Netanyahu identified the attacker as an Omani national. Omani authorities have not commented. “We have constraints that say you can’t have pilots from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. So obviously he was able to go through that,” Netanyahu told Fox News. With the co-pilot now in the UAE, Israeli investigators “can now join the UAE’s investigation team and get precise knowledge of what his motives were, who was behind him, what his plans were”, Netanyahu’s spokesperson David Mencer told Fox News. Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi have hailed the captain of flight FZ1073, Indian national Smit Machchhar, as a hero. The pilot was recovering well, the Indian embassy in the UAE said on social media platform X. Israel has also lauded the passengers who intervened to subdue the attacker. The US leader’s threat of retaliation came as he took a harsher tone on the stalled Iran war overall. Trump was quoted as saying in a Time magazine interview published on Thursday that it was “possible” he may resume bombing Iran after US midterm elections next month. Republicans fear they could lose control of Congress in the November 3 election, with Trump’s approval ratings at near-record lows over the Iran war and a surge in the cost of living fuelled by high oil prices. He also reiterated the threat to “annihilate” Iran that he made in his speech to the UN General Assembly last week, despite having previously cast himself as the “president of peace”. “Yeah, I would do that. It’s possible,” Trump told Time. “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world. With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.” Iran continues to exert control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz more than seven months after the initial US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic. Trump says the war is about preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. The United States was meanwhile set to send a third US aircraft carrier and up to 10,000 extra service members to the Middle East by the end of November, The Wall Street Journal reported. It was not immediately clear if the new carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, would replace one of the two carriers already in the region. Trump had told aides he expected to resume bombing by late November, the Journal quoted him as saying. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Xi has left Washington, but remains in Trump’s photos on White House walls
description: Different photographs show China’s president with Trump, while an embassy display highlights their meetings and calls for cooperation.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping has left Washington, but he still has a place at the White House. At least two, in fact. Two different photographs of Xi with US President Donald Trump feature on its walls: a handshake image that Trump showed his guest during last week’s state visit, and another beside a Palm Room doorway showing the presidents standing side by side. Journalist Jacqueline Alemany shared an image of the Palm Room display on social media, noting that photographs of Trump with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin lined the doorway area. The Xi photograph sits in an ornate gold frame against a white lattice-patterned wall, beside an arched doorway and beneath a crystal chandelier. The two presidents face the camera, with Chinese and American flags behind them. It differs from the photograph Trump showed Xi during his visit, which shows the leaders facing each other and shaking hands. White House's Palm Room doors now lined with photos of Trump standing alongside Putin & Xi: pic.twitter.com/VgIuyxAgZY — Jacqueline Alemany (@JaxAlemany) October 1, 2026 In the separate handshake photograph, the leaders face each other. Pointing to it during Xi’s visit, Trump asked: “Who is that? I don’t recognise him.” Xi turned towards members of his delegation and appeared to give a brief laugh. The Palm Room’s photographic collection predates last week’s summit. CNN Newsource reported in January that the renovated room featured gold-framed images of Trump with Xi, Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, alongside photographs of the US president alone and with football star Cristiano Ronaldo. It remains unclear whether the Trump–Xi image currently beside the doorway is the same one reported in January, or whether it has been moved. The SCMP has asked the White House when it was installed, which meeting it depicts and who selected the photographs. Across town, the presidents’ encounters also featured prominently at the Chinese embassy’s reception to mark China’s National Day on Wednesday evening. Large photographic panels on easels highlighted their meetings in Beijing in May and Washington in September. Three were labelled “Beijing, May 14, 2026”, including one showing Trump and Xi at the Temple of Heaven. Beneath that image was a message urging the countries to “lengthen the list of cooperation and shorten the list of issues”. Another panel, dated September 24 in Washington, showed the presidents seated with their wives, Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan. Its caption called for friendship, expanded cooperation and improvements to the well-being of both countries’ people. Xi’s September 23-25 state visit included an airport welcome from Trump, talks at the White House and a state dinner. The visit is over. The photographs remain.

title: Canada fast-tracking oil pipeline designed to diversify economy away from US
description: The ‌new pipeline could make Canada a major global energy supplier, as Asia looks outside the ‌Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict.
content: Canada will fast track the approval process for a new proposed crude oil export pipeline to its west coast that could generate over C$20 billion (US$14 billion) a year in GDP, Prime Minister ‌Mark Carney said on Thursday. The pipeline, which was announced in July, is a crucial part of Carney’s bid to diversify the economy away from the United States and help lessen the effect of US President Donald Trump’s tariffs. Carney said Ottawa would officially list the Pacific Link pipeline as a project of national interest, which enables it to proceed through a single federal regulatory review process. He said Ottawa aimed to complete the process by September 1, ⁠2027. “A pipeline to the west coast is part of our mission to transform our economy, to double our non-US exports ‌over the next decade … [and] to unlock our full potential as a global energy superpower,” he told reporters in Fort McMurray, hub of Alberta’s oil sands industry. Ottawa says the 1 million barrel a ‌day project would create 140,000 jobs and generate over C$20 billion in GDP per year and C$100 billion ⁠in government revenue by ⁠2060. Canada currently has just one east-west oil export pipeline in Canada, the 890,000-barrel-per-day Trans Mountain pipeline. An expansion of that pipeline was completed in 2024, ‌but it is already running at capacity. For years, Canada has sent more than 90 per cent of its crude oil exports to the US via pipeline. A ‌new oil ‌export pipeline could make Canada a major global energy supplier, as Asia’s top importers seek oil from outside the ‌Middle East in the wake of the Iran conflict. Filling the pipeline, however, would require new oil sands expansions of the type ⁠no company has undertaken in more than a decade. The pipeline will be built by government-owned Trans Mountain Corp in coordination with ⁠Pembina Pipeline Corp. Alberta estimates it could cost between C$35.2 billion and C$43.7 billion. The majority owners will be the federal government and the government of Alberta. Indigenous communities will be offered a minimum of 10 per cent ‌ownership interest. Chief Raymond Powder ‌of the Fort McKay First Nation told reporters his community is interested in potentially pursuing an equity stake in the pipeline. Previous oil pipeline projects in Canada have faced strong opposition from environmentalists and indigenous groups, resulting in the cancellation of some projects and leading to cost overruns and construction delays with others. Carney said there will be “extensive” consultations with indigenous groups on the proposal.

title: UK-Iranian man arrested over suspected Fairford airbase plot
description: The dual national, 27, has been held on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts at the facility used by the US to target Iran.
content: British counterterrorism police investigating ⁠a suspected plot involving ⁠an airbase used by the US ⁠to target Iran said on Thursday they had arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. In an incident which triggered a huge police response, raised alarm among Western allies, and remains largely unexplained, five British men in their 20s ‌were arrested on Sunday on suspected terrorism and explosive offences near RAF Fairford in western England. The men were later released without charge on police bail. But counterterrorism police said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved in the incident and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday it might have had an Iranian link. Iran has said accusations it was involved were ⁠baseless and on Thursday summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue. In the latest development, police ‌said they had arrested the 27-year-old dual national in London while a second British man, 26, had also been questioned under caution and searches carried out at ‌two properties. “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our ⁠specialist teams are interrogating multiple ⁠lines of enquiry,” Britain’s Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said in a statement. “As we’ve made clear, we’re ‌looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.” Police launched a massive operation in the early hours of Sunday “due to a ‌range of ‌information” including an alert from a local farmer who became suspicious of the men who ‌she had seen near the base in three vans. However, the Times newspaper reported that one of ⁠the men had also called emergency services shortly before being arrested. Detectives have confirmed that although petrol was found ⁠in the vans used by the men, no improvised explosive device was present. Burnham said Britain was working closely with the US, whose bombers have in recent months used Fairford to ‌launch missions against Iran, although US ‌President Donald Trump said he would not have released the men, who police said were only freed under stringent conditions. Trump previously said those involved had planned “big damage” while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the “hands of a foreign actor” in the incident.

title: French school protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest
description: Students have been protesting over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms.
content: A protest by French secondary school students over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and crumbling facilities deepened on Thursday, with fires set outside schools and blockades in several cities. More than 160 schools were shut down on Thursday, while university students joined the protests in Paris and Marseille. The movement in the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France, has seen hundreds detained. The government said the protests had become “urban violence”, and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Thursday urged all ministers to postpone any travel nationwide, according to a source close to the minister. Since last week, pupils have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes, and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year’s heatwaves. The protests have spread across the country from the Paris suburbs, and the government has accused hard-left politicians of encouraging the unrest. Riot police have been deployed to confront the students, and the force has launched internal probes after accusations of brutality against three pupils, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. Some 340 protests were under way in front of high schools midmorning, with more than 160 establishments shut down as a result, police said. University students joined on Thursday, blocking access to around 30 campuses, including in Paris and the southern city of Marseille, a student union said. In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting fire to dustbins would instead protest “with words”. “We’re showing against overcrowded classes, against this government that spends millions on anti-phone pouches but doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or our teachers’ salaries,” she said, after the government at the start of the school year banned smartphones in schools. In the northwestern city of Nantes, firefighters had to intervene to put out a fire in the entrance of a high school “following a gathering marked by violence towards staff”, the regional education board said. Authorities reported violence near high schools, mainly in Nantes, blaming “violent individuals” who “join the students to carry out acts of vandalism”. In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, trams were ordered to grind to a halt to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said. Raphael, a 17-year-old who did not give his surname for fear of reprisals, was among the protesters outside a school in Strasbourg, where some used barriers to obstruct the nearby tramway tracks. “There are 35 of us per classroom. With 35 degrees Celsius in summer, it’s unbearable. There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms,” Raphael said. “The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors,” he said. Nearby, students took photos of themselves in front of burning rubbish bins, holding up the sign with their school’s name ripped off the tram stop. Most pupils did not take part in any vandalism, instead breaking out into a sprint down an avenue when the police fired tear gas. In the southern city of Toulouse, hundreds of young people flooded the tram tracks, some toppling trash cans and starting fires, hurling projectiles or smashing bus shelters, AFP journalists said. In the northern city of Lille, AFP reporters saw young people wearing black hoodies destroy the glass of a bus stop. Firefighters intervened to put out the flames on upturned dustbins set on fire. The government has accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the protests. But LFI’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Melenchon, said on Wednesday that his party “called for non-violent methods of struggle”. Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the French capital’s largest suburb Saint-Denis, said it was his responsibility to check in on students. “It is the place of an elected official,” he said, defending himself when questioned about going to see protesters outside a high school in Saint-Denis this week. The mayor of Saint-Denis notably visited the Paul Eluard high school in his city on Monday and Tuesday, where part of the main gate was knocked down during the blockade. In neighbouring Belgium, there were protests and damage at a handful of schools in the eastern city of Liege, police said.

title: US jobless claims fall to lowest since mid-July
description: The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices.
content: The number of people applying for US unemployment benefits dipped last week to the lowest level since mid-July as lay-offs remain low and most American workers enjoy job security. The Labor Department said on Thursday that initial jobless claims ticked down to 197,000 from a revised 198,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped by 2,500 to 200,000. Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for lay-offs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have mostly stayed below 220,000 – historically low. The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began February 28. The US on Tuesday reported that US employers posted fewer job openings in August. The Labor Department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that lay-offs fell and the number of people quitting their jobs – a sign of confidence in their prospects – retreated slightly in August. The JOLTS report’s measure of gross hiring – before subtracting people who quit or lost their jobs – ticked up modestly in August but remains at low levels. “Jobless claims continue to defy expectations and remain exceedingly low, dovetailing with the JOLTS reports’ lay-off rate, which shows that while businesses aren’t hiring at a rapid pace, they are reticent to let their current crop of workers go,” wrote Matthew Martin, senior US economist at Oxford Economics. Lay-offs are low. Businesses, remembering the labour shortages that followed the end of pandemic lockdowns, are reluctant to let go of staff. They’re hiring – but modestly by the standards of recent years. So far this year, employers – companies, government agencies and non-profit – have been adding an average of 80,000 jobs a month, including a surprising 162,000 in August. That is an improvement on a lacklustre 2025 when monthly job creation averaged 9,700 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring. The Labour Department will release the jobs report for September next week. It is expected to show that employers added 90,000 jobs and that the unemployment rate remained low at 4.1 per cent, according to a survey of forecasters by the data firm FactSet. Hiring remains well below the 166,000 monthly jobs created, on average, in 2023 and 2024, and the 491,000 per month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed Covid-19 lockdowns.

title: Why US Himars missile shortfalls raise stakes for a potential Taiwan Strait conflict
description: Ammunition could prove to be the defining issue as mainland China’s defence industry appears to be operating at an elevated tempo.
content: A potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait could see crossfire exchanged between two mobile rocket systems: the US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), and its mainland Chinese counterpart, the PHL-16, also known as the PCL-191. Taiwan is set to receive all 29 Himars systems from its initial orders by the end of this year, with another 82 systems approved for purchase in a follow-on deal, bringing the planned total to 111. This does not include the US military’s Himars systems already deployed in the region. Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is estimated to have deployed more than 200 PHL-16 systems. The real question, however, is ammunition. Two long-range missiles fired from the Himars platform – the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) and the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) – are among the US munitions most heavily depleted during the war with Iran. The US Army has used “virtually all” of its global stockpile of these two missile types, according to a Reuters report in August, citing people familiar with the data. The draining of US stocks raises questions about Taiwan’s plans to expand its ATACMS inventory. The island’s military has received 64 of the systems and is expecting 20 more this year as part of its initial order. Washington approved the sale of an additional 420 in December last year, which would bring the total number ordered to 504. At the same time, Lockheed Martin, which makes the ATACMS, is in the process of phasing out its production. How fast the stocks can be replenished and delivered to Taiwan remains highly uncertain. Meanwhile, although exact ammunition stockpiles remain classified, the PLA has recently released footage of live-fire training exercises involving the PHL-16 system, showcasing two distinct munition types. These were an airburst “steel rain” guided rocket designed to disperse large quantities of high-velocity fragments over a wide area and a 750mm tactical ballistic missile with a 500km (311-mile) strike range, making the modular PHL-16 the world’s longest-range rocket artillery platform. More broadly, mainland China’s defence industry appears to be operating at an elevated tempo. The Pentagon estimates that, as of 2024, China had at least 3,150 ballistic missiles and 300 ground-launched cruise missiles. From 2015, those represented 147 per cent and 50 per cent increases respectively. A Bloomberg analysis in May identified 81 companies in China’s missile supply chain – more than double the 32 firms identified in 2013, when President Xi Jinping first took office. Moreover, it found that nearly 40 per cent of these companies reported record sales in 2025, also the highest proportion since 2013. “The build-up indicates that China is flush with missiles just as US stockpiles have been depleted,” it said. The United States’ growing munitions shortfalls were explicitly acknowledged by the Pentagon’s inspector general in a recent report on the war in Iran. Of the estimated US$33.4 billion spent on Operation Epic Fury between February 28 and June 30, some US$22.3 billion – 67 per cent of the total – went towards munitions, according to the inspector general’s first-of-its-kind report to the US Congress released on Monday. “The munitions expenditure on [Operation Epic Fury] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report said, referring to the joint US-Israeli military campaign targeting Iran. This marked a rare official acknowledgement by the US Defence Department regarding its depleted munitions supplies and pressure on the industrial base. Until recently, US President Donald Trump and top Pentagon officials had repeatedly denied reports concerning US munitions shortages. In recent months, media outlets and think tanks have repeatedly warned of the rapid depletion of America’s critical munitions during the conflict with Iran, such as long-range precision-strike missiles and air-defence interceptors, noting that this exposed a vulnerability in the event of a western Pacific confrontation with Beijing. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Besides the “virtually all” used up ATACMS and PrSM, nearly 80 per cent of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) missile inventory and about half of the Patriot interceptors had also been depleted compared to pre-war stockpile levels by August, CNN reported. The Washington Post detailed some consumption figures for key munitions during the first month of the conflict, which included more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors, and more than 1,300 army tactical ballistic missiles. Although Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has been urging the US defence industry to increase weapons manufacturing, it may take over three years for the inventories of Tomahawk, THAAD and Patriot systems to be restored to their pre-conflict levels, according to estimates by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). Beyond these advanced munitions, the US has faced difficulties expanding production of lower-technology conventional ammunition because of a diminished industrial base, despite efforts to rebuild capacity in response to rising demand since the Ukraine war. An example is a newly built artillery-shell plant in Mesquite, Texas. As part of the US Army’s effort to increase 155mm production, the US$469 million facility was intended to produce 30,000 projectiles a month by October last year, but as of March, nearly two years after coming online, it had yet to produce a single one. According to Chinese military researcher Liu Yi, the origins of the problem can be traced back to a 1993 dinner hosted by then-US defence secretary Les Aspin, when the Bill Clinton administration outlined plans for post-Cold War defence budget cuts. This led to a wave of consolidation in the US defence industry in the following years. Soon after the so-called last supper, the number of major US defence contractors fell from 51 in the 1980s to just five by 2000, Liu said in an article in Chinese military magazine Modern Ships in September. The continued dominance of the “Big Five” – Lockheed Martin, Raytheon (now RTX), Boeing, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman – has since left the industry highly concentrated. Since the early 21st century, demand for these high-performance munitions had remained weak for an extended period, Liu said, as the US military shifted its focus towards counterterrorism operations. “The profit margin on munitions is relatively low, and the procurement orders were limited for much of the time, with roughly half of them coming from overseas,” he added. “This has driven the ‘Big Five’ to scale down their ammunition-production capacity,” Liu added, noting that the broader decline in America’s manufacturing base had left smaller contractors either unable or unwilling to fill the gap. Military commentator Song Zhongping argued that the concentrated structure of the industry was keeping prices artificially high, weakening the US military’s bargaining power and making it difficult to bring down the cost of weapons, which had ultimately contributed to the lack of inventory. “Excessively high costs per unit limit the quantities the US military can afford to procure, even as the defence budget continues to rise,” said Song, a retired PLA officer. He also cited the large share of munitions production for overseas buyers, saying that foreign customers generally paid higher prices, giving contractors an incentive to prioritise exports. Although China’s defence industry was similarly concentrated within a few mega contractors, its state-owned nature ensured strategic alignment with the PLA’s demands rather than pure pursuit of profit as happened within the US military-industrial complex, Song added. One example highlights the difference. The US Navy effectively abandoned plans to field the 155mm main guns on its Zumwalt-class destroyers, largely because the custom Long-Range Land Attack Projectiles, developed jointly by BAE Systems and Lockheed Martin, reached an estimated cost of about US$800,000 per round. Meanwhile, Chinese defence reports have suggested that a 155mm naval gun under development could leverage the PLA’s existing 155mm artillery ammunition and technology base. If so, it could reduce duplicate research and development and supply-chain costs while accelerating development and deployment. “There is still internal competition among state institutes and private companies are increasingly participating to improve drive efficiency,” Song said of the Chinese defence industry. “By achieving full domestic sourcing across the supply chain and complete indigenisation of its defence production, China has ensured full control over production capacity, unit costs and delivery timelines. “This means China’s war potential is immense.” During the 1993 dinner that reshaped the US defence industry, China “wasn’t even on the cards”, according to attendee Norman Augustine, who at the time was chief executive of defence contractor Martin Marietta and later served as Lockheed Martin’s CEO from 1996 to 1997. But 30 years later, Augustine warned in a 2023 interview that the US no longer had “as many companies as we need in the defence world … particularly with the evolution of China and aggression from Russia”. “We may have to restructure the industry,” he added.

title: ‘No beardos, no weirdos’: Hegseth deepens Pentagon purge as China channels reopen
description: Pentagon chief reshapes US military’s top ranks as his own job comes under question and Beijing and Washington work to avoid crisis.
content: As Beijing and Washington take tentative steps to keep a military crisis from erupting, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is reshaping the top ranks of the American military while facing questions about his own future at the Pentagon. Hegseth told junior officers and sergeants on Wednesday that the military had already cut its generals and admirals by 10 per cent and planned to cut another 10 per cent. He called the 20 per cent reduction the bare minimum, dismissing critics who called the shake-up a “purge”. “The number crunchers say we fired 10 per cent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said in a “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia. “And I know, because I directed it, that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 per cent. So yes, a 20 per cent reduction across the board.” “The media calls that a purge,” he said. “I call it accountability, and long overdue.” Hegseth also used the speech to spell out the kind of force he wants. He used a string of derogatory terms for people he said should not serve in the military: “No fatties, no t******s, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” The larger cut is due to be completed by January 1 next year. It doubles an order from May last year calling for at least a 10 per cent reduction in general and flag officers. The cuts were only one part of Hegseth’s plan. He also announced a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command with service-like authorities to accelerate the development and deployment of drones and robotic systems across the military. “The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” he said. An interim programme, Project Agincourt, will run for the next year under Defence Innovation Unit head Owen West and US Navy Seal senior chief Max Strasiser. It will bring operators, engineers and private companies together in shorter development cycles, with decisions and funding pushed closer to combatant commands. A four-star commander has yet to be named. The command is expected to be fully established by October 1 next year. Hegseth also announced a 120-day study of future warfare, Project Meridian, to be led by Elon Musk, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey and former US House speaker Newt Gingrich. Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael will oversee the project. Hegseth said the study was not intended to produce a new strategy, but to “identify the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master”, from below the ground to beyond the moon. None of the three co-leaders has served in the US military. Musk and Luckey already hold multibillion-dollar defence contracts. Hegseth’s speech came just four days after China’s foreign ministry said Beijing and Washington had agreed to conclude a memorandum on “crisis communication and prevention” as soon as possible. The agreement was reached at the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart Donald Trump in Washington from September 23 to 25. Ahead of the summit, the South China Morning Post first reported that the two sides planned to unveil measures to activate more military communication channels and strengthen those already in place. People familiar with the matter said communication had improved at multiple levels – not just between the two defence ministers – since Trump returned to power in January last year. On July 29, US deputy assistant defence secretary Alvaro Smith told a reception at the Chinese embassy that the channel was “stronger than it has been in years” and that a repair was proceeding under Hegseth. But Hegseth’s own position has grown precarious. The SCMP reported in August that Trump was privately losing patience with the stalled Iran war and that Hegseth was close to losing his job. The White House has since said the president has complete confidence in the Pentagon chief. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Hegseth’s relationship with Republican lawmakers had deteriorated. A Democratic takeover of the US House of Representatives on November 3 could bring renewed calls for his impeachment. Republican congressman Thomas Massie filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth last month. The New York Times reported last month that Hegseth had fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 generals and admirals. The Trump administration has overseen a rapid shake-up of top military brass, replacing five of the eight members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff – the senior military officers who advise the president. The departures have included Joint Chiefs chairman General Charles Q. Brown Jnr and Admiral Lisa Franchetti, both of whom were dismissed early last year. The turnover has also extended to the Pentagon’s civilian leadership, with US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigning on September 1. The Iran war hangs over the shake-up. A CNN/SSRS poll conducted in mid-September found that just 26 per cent of US adults approved of Trump’s handling of Iran. Among Republicans, approval had fallen from 73 per cent in March to 60 per cent. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on September 21 put Trump’s approval at 32 per cent, a career low, and found registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans for the midterm elections by 43 per cent to 35 per cent. At Quantico on Wednesday, Hegseth defended the war as an operation “every red-blooded American is proud of” and said reporting he disliked was “treason, actually”.

title: EU retools Trump trade war tripwire into China shipments surge alarm
description: Bloc’s trade enforcement chief says the system is already picking up what may be worrying trends in a range of product categories.
content: In April last year, Brussels launched an obscure “import surveillance task force” to track the impact of US President Donald Trump’s trade war with China on the EU economy. The bloc was concerned that Chinese shipments bound for the United States would be diverted to Europe at lower prices, imperilling local manufacturers. Eighteen months on, the European Union is on the cusp of its own trade war with China and is repurposing the task force as an early warning system for what it sees as dangerous surges in Chinese imports. The intelligence it gathers could help Brussels decide where to strike when it comes to restricting Chinese goods, Denis Redonnet, the EU’s top trade enforcer, said on Thursday. The scale of the warning is striking. Redonnet, who is also the point person for trade policy on China, told lawmakers that the system was detecting “potentially worrying trends for almost a quarter of all imports into the EU”, with China the main driver. Results of the so-called import barometer published last week flagged 902 individual product categories in which imports were rising unusually quickly while prices were falling. Machinery was the biggest segment, with 141 product lines flagged, followed by textiles with 116, basic metals with 110 and chemicals with 107. The analysis covered the year to June. These are also among the sectors in which the EU has or is considering opening safeguard investigations, which would allow it to quickly impose tariffs and quotas in instances of harmful import surges, with Redonnet confirming that the tool could help identify cases for such action. “There are sectors now, important sectors of our economy, facing sustained and abnormal import increases,” he told the European Parliament’s trade committee. “There might be cases where we might envisage an ex officio trigger of safeguard investigation,” Redonnet said, meaning Brussels could launch a case without waiting for industry or a member state to request one. “I cannot exclude it, nor am I announcing it either.” The comments come as Brussels considers new weapons to deal with the surges in imports identified by the barometer. Several sources confirmed that the commission was considering an instrument that would permit it to raise tariffs on goods when imports from China or another dominant trading partner hit a certain level in key sectors. This “overcapacity instrument” comes on top of a new diversification tool, set to be proposed in December, which would compel firms to broaden their pools of suppliers beyond a single country. On Wednesday, the commission called for evidence for this mechanism, confirming that it would “present a diversification package aimed at supporting faster supply chain diversification and reducing dependencies in critical sectors”. Beijing has threatened to retaliate against any such measures, particularly any tool that would mirror the US’ Section 301 tariff platform. “If the EU engages in dialogue and consultation with China on the one hand while ratcheting up a show of strength against China on the other, this will seriously damage mutual trust, disrupt the overall consultation process and affect the broader picture of China-EU economic and trade cooperation,” the Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday. EU leaders, meanwhile, are gearing up for a crucial debate on China at the European Council summit this month – just a week after EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing for meetings with his counterpart, Wang Wentao. On Wednesday, the political leaders of France and Spain discussed China policy in Madrid. Paris has been a strong advocate of forceful trade action while Spain has grown closer to Beijing in recent years. Nonetheless, the sides downplayed their differences on the matter. “We must protect European industry much better, much faster … from October, we are going to put this into practice,” French President Emmanuel Macron said at a press conference, alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez. The French leader accused Beijing of “massively dumping just to kill the players in a sector and take over the whole sector” and of “massacring our industrial base”. Sanchez said the two countries were “not so far apart” on China policy. “On the contrary, it has to be common across Europe as a whole because our objective is the same,” he said. Sanchez described China’s trade surplus as “not acceptable and cannot be borne by any economy”, but cautioned that the EU must pursue “cooperation wherever possible, competition whenever necessary, and the constructive management of disagreements”.

title: Hong Kong autumn 2026 art auctions top HK$2 billion as Kusama works get a cool reception
description: Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips drive sales proving the appetite for art is still strong as collectors pursue top Western and Asian art.
content: The autumn 2026 marquee auctions by Hong Kong’s three international auction houses – Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips – from September 28 to 30 generated more than HK$2 billion (US$255.78 million) in combined totals. This marks a fair increase from the HK$1.3 billion achieved during the spring season, signalling a disciplined market anchored by competitive depth for fresh-to-market works with strong provenance. Christie’s led the series with HK$956.5 million, up 17 per cent year on year, driven by broad international participation and a 30 per cent influx of new young buyers. Sotheby’s posted a near-identical HK$956 million – a 35 per cent jump over its March series – achieving a 91 per cent sell-through rate and five artist records. Phillips rounded out the season with a HK$94.5 million sales total for modern and contemporary art, delivering a 96 per cent sell-through rate by value in its Evening Sale. More than 200 lots were offered at the three auctions over three days, with nine lots withdrawn. Across all three houses, the results confirm that buyers around the world are still interested in top-tier Western masterworks, Asian modernism and blue-chip contemporary art. Beyond these headline figures, the season revealed evolving auction business models and provided a crucial test of market performance following the death of prominent artist Yayoi Kusama in August. The back-to-back series commenced with Sotheby’s first single-artist sale in Asia, “The Foujita Lexicon: Works from the Lewis Collection”, on September 28. Marking the 140th birth anniversary of Japanese-French painter Leonard Tsuguharu Foujita, the collection attracted significant attention, with several sold works requested by the Clark Art Institute, in Massachusetts, in the US, for inclusion in its upcoming Foujita exhibition slated for the summer of 2028. The auction achieved a white-glove result, with 80 per cent of lots selling above their high estimates. The top lot was the 1949 Foujita painting Le Rêve (Hommage à La Fontaine), one of only four known anthropomorphic works created during the artist’s influential visit to the US between 1949 and 1950. The painting was hammered down at HK$21 million before selling for HK$26.52 million with fees, more than 500 per cent above its low estimate. “Foujita’s appeal stems from his cross-cultural identity and distinctive visual language,” Kwai Fung Hin Art Gallery founder Catherine Kwai says. Nonetheless, she describes the result as measured, noting it remains below Foujita’s auction record established in 2018, when La Fête d’Anniversaire (1949) – an animal-themed canvas measuring 76.5cm by 101.7cm (30 inches by 40 inches) – sold at Bonhams London for £7.1 million (US$9.4 million). “The price difference demonstrates that the market continues to make careful distinctions between individual works, evaluating scale, subject matter, rarity, quality and historical importance within Foujita’s oeuvre,” she says. Meanwhile, Sotheby’s noted that the Foujita series surpassed the performance of any single-owner collection presented since “A Long Journey: A Selection from the Liu Yiqian and Wang Wei Collection” in late 2023. However, Foujita’s Le Déjeuner de Bébé (1918), offered at Phillips’ day sale on September 30, performed below expectations, fetching a hammer price of HK$500,000 against a pre-sale estimate of HK$600,000 to HK$800,000. Another focal point of the season was the first Kusama works auctioned since her death . The tension in the room was palpable whenever a signature pumpkin canvas hit the podium, as collectors waited to see whether the artist’s death would trigger a speculative surge. A total of 14 works by Kusama were offered across the evening sales, yielding moderate results. Both lots at Sotheby’s sold within estimate. At Christie’s, A-Pumpkin (YHP) (2011) achieved HK$47 million, 2 per cent below its low estimate. Phillips offered the largest selection of Kusama canvases, though only three of 10 lots surpassed their high estimates. Among them, the top performer was the 1990 canvas Pumpkin, which fetched a hammer price of HK$2.9 million at Phillips on September 30 – above its HK$2 million low estimate. Conversely, Day Will Break in Time (1975) achieved a hammer price of HK$400,000, falling nearly 30 per cent below its low estimate. “Kusama’s market remains active, but collectors have become far more selective and rational,” Kwai says. “Results falling within or below estimates do not necessarily indicate weakening demand. Instead, established buyers are exercising greater discipline, demanding verified provenance and data to justify valuations. Meanwhile, newer collectors are seeking fresh works that demonstrate undeniable quality and artistic vision rather than buying solely for brand appeal.” The autumn season also introduced several major market debuts, including Zao Wou-Ki’s Sans Titre (Untitled) (1957), which sold for a hammer price of HK$17 million; Chu Teh-chun’s Automne (1985), which achieved a hammer price of HK$30 million; and Lalan’s Untitled (1959-1960), which fetched HK$3 million. All three were offered by Christie’s on September 29. Christie’s benchmark records were claimed by Western masterworks – including Paul Cézanne, Henri Matisse, Sir Peter Paul Rubens and Salvador Dalí – while Sotheby’s record results were led by Asian modernists Tran Luu Hau and Park Seo-bo. “Seasoned collectors remain the principal buyers for high-value works that carry complex art-historical significance or require deeper scholarly understanding,” Kwai says. Regarding younger buyers, she notes a preference for artists showing strong technical execution at accessible price points. “Auction houses are incorporating emerging names previously unfamiliar to the secondary market,” she says. “A notable cohort of new collectors has emerged from technology, AI and blockchain sectors – including founders, senior executives and finance professionals. They bring distinct purchasing habits and evolving tastes to the market.”

title: Investigators probe why co-pilot stabbed captain of Flydubai flight to Israel
description: The suspect, an Omani citizen, is under arrest and Saudi authorities are working with countries, including Israel, to determine a motive.
content: Investigators worked on Thursday to determine why an Omani pilot stabbed the captain of a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously before others on board landed it in Saudi Arabia. Passengers on the Flydubai plane – which was carrying 174 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv – have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the co-pilot and stabilised a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away. “We felt helpless, suspended in mid-air, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” Asaf Rajuan, who was among those who intervened, said in a statement shared by Israel’s presidency. A regional official briefed on the investigation said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest and confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. He said the UAE, the United States and Oman also were involved. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss an ongoing probe. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, without giving details, claimed the attacker underwent Islamist indoctrination. Asked who helped radicalise him, the prime minister said on Fox News that he did not know. The co-pilot has not been publicly identified. Video shot inside the plane by Shota Musayev, a dentist who treated the captain, shows the co-pilot on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back. The co-pilot’s name has not been released, and his condition was not known. Captain Smit Machchhar, widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was reportedly in stable condition, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said overnight. Israeli intelligence and security officials were in Saudi Arabia to help investigate the co-pilot, according to another regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity. Israel has requested that the co-pilot be sent to Israel for the investigation, though it is unclear if that request will be granted, the official said. Saudi Arabia does not have formal diplomatic ties with Israel, but the countries have long cooperated on security and intelligence matters through alternative channels. The UAE government said its own investigation team had begun looking into the attack and “whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose”, noting its authorities have jurisdiction because the plane is registered there and UAE law applies to crimes committed on board. Asked if there is any indication of Iranian involvement, Netanyahu told Fox News “it’s too early to say”. Netanyahu said he also spoke with the UAE’s president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect. US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” by phone and it seemed as though the co-pilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”. Oman’s government has not commented. Netanyahu had warned in recent days of heightened security threats, though he told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning. The country is a week away from the anniversary of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which has triggered the war in Gaza – and weeks away from an election. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said most of the people on board were from Israel, along with others from India and the UAE. The US State Department said four passengers had American citizenship. Flydubai has said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended. Netanyahu told CBS that Israel plans to fly home anyone stranded in Dubai as a result. In the chaos that began about 2½ hours after take-off, the flight descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet (around 10,000 metres to 5,100 metres) in about a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk, according to Flightradar24. The site identified the aircraft as a Boeing 737 Max 8. Flydubai said crew members on board helped secure the plane but released no details about them. The head of the New Zealand flight school where the Indian captain trained, Philip Kean, called it “miraculous in the way that the aeroplane was never, ever kind of designed for that sort of dive and survive that, the aeroplane actually didn’t break up completely”. Trump praised the US-based Boeing for producing a plane “that was able to withstand G forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed”. During the frantic search for a place to land, a person who heard the flight’s communications with air traffic control described the plane being turned away by Saudi Arabia and Jordan before eventually landing in Tabuk in Saudi Arabia while passengers screamed in the background. The pilot’s voice was trembling as he called “mayday” and said a hijacking was taking place. The air traffic controllers gave no reason for the refusals. The person who heard the communications spoke on condition of anonymity.

title: Extended Victoria Park lantern show attracts thousands for National Day
description: Many people arrive early to avoid huge crowds after social posts warned of past overcrowding at the International Lantern Spectacular.
content: Thousands of Hongkongers, domestic helpers and tourists have taken advantage of the extended lantern show in Victoria Park as the National Day “golden week” holiday began in mainland China. Many people arrived early at sunset on Thursday to avoid the huge crowds that had previously gathered for the International Lantern Spectacular, organised by the Hong Kong Tourism Board, which has attracted more than 500,000 visitors since its debut in September. Before many of the lanterns were turned on in the evening, the South China Morning Post observed hundreds of visitors snapping selfies and walking around, including domestic helpers, tourists and locals. Among the early birds was Anant Raj, a 36-year-old banking employee visiting the lantern show with his wife and their two young sons. Raj, an Indian national who has lived in Hong Kong for a year, said the family was keen to take part in the National Day celebrations and would head to the harbourfront to watch the fireworks later in the evening. “Even though we are in essence foreigners, you can see all segments of society, all people, enjoying the atmosphere,” he said. Initially scheduled to run until September 27 to coincide with the Mid-Autumn Festival, the Tourism Board on Wednesday announced a second extension, with the show now set to wrap up at the end of the golden week on October 7. The event has attracted enormous public interest, with entry times on certain days being cut short to prevent overcrowding. The Tourism Board said the event recorded about 580,000 visits over the first 13 days after it opened on September 17, with peak daily attendance exceeding 200,000. Zhou Sipeng, a 25-year-old visiting from Shenzhen with her boyfriend, James Chau Chun Yeung, said the lanterns were part of the reason they chose to visit Hong Kong for the holiday. “It’s very popular on [mainland] Chinese social media,” she said. “The [World Lantern Boulevard] is the one I’m looking forward to the most.” Zhou was referring to an installation that features a path showcasing 3,000 lantern designs from different countries and regions. The Tourism Board announced that during the golden week holiday, it would adjust the queuing area of the installation to “provide the public with a better experience”. The new queuing system appeared to be more efficient, with shorter waiting times overall and a steady flow of traffic – in contrast to the sometimes hours-long backlogs seen in previous days. Other highlights of the show include the Giant Masterpiece Lantern – an eight-metre (26-foot) banyan tree installation that greets visitors as they come through the entrance. “It’s really beautiful,” exclaimed 31-year-old Victoria Ling Ouyang, who was visiting from Shenzhen with her family. Ling said the family were visiting the city for three days and was staying at a hotel in Central. They also planned to catch the fireworks after seeing the lanterns. While Hongkongers have left the city in droves for National Day, the SCMP had observed that many had nonetheless chosen to stay and check out the displays. Among the locals visiting the event was Polytechnic University student Carly Cheung, who was visiting with her boyfriend Isaac Tsang. Cheung said the couple had been too busy earlier in the week to visit and had seen lots of posts on social media warning about the huge crowds. “We saw on social media that it took nearly an hour to line up and get in,” the 20-year-old said. “It was the right choice to come early. She said she was interested in seeing the World Lantern Boulevard installation the most, but would skip the fireworks afterwards to avoid the large crowds.

title: Red Bull’s Max Verstappen eager for first win of season at Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
description: Dutch ace has earned only seven podium finishes this season, coming close with second-place finishes in his past two outings in Madrid, Baku.
content: Max Verstappen said he wants to win “at least one race this year” as ⁠the four-time Formula 1 champion sits ⁠in an unfamiliar sixth place in the championship ⁠standings after 15 rounds. Having dominated Formula 1 in recent years, Verstappen has managed only seven podium finishes this season and is still searching for that elusive first win, coming close with second-place finishes in his past two outings in Madrid and Baku. Verstappen’s desperate charge against George Russell on the final straight in Baku on Saturday ended in his fourth runner-up finish in the past eight races. He’s sixth in the standings with barely half of leader Kimi Antonelli’s points tally. Exactly how many races are left in 2026 for Verstappen to chase an elusive win remains unclear given the uncertainty over the final two scheduled races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Eight are left on the schedule including those races, but if they cannot go ahead, Formula 1 could opt for one replacement event in Italy. Verstappen is one of a few drivers who have driven at Sepang, which is ‌hosting a Formula 1 race for the first time in nine years after the Bahrain Grand Prix was moved because of the conflict in the Middle East. While Red Bull have outscored both Ferrari and McLaren over the past three races, Verstappen conceded that the gains counted for little with Mercedes holding a commanding lead in both the drivers’ and constructors’ championships. “Unfortunately, we’re not outscoring Mercedes. They’re actually the fast ones, or at least they were for most of this season,” he said. “I’m ⁠trying everything I can. We are scoring quite a few podiums now, but I want to win. That’s what I’m here for ‌and I’m getting close. I want to at least win one race this year. So I hope we can do it at some point.” The 29-year-old was the last driver to triumph at Sepang in ‌what was his second career victory but admitted he felt disoriented when he returned to the circuit after almost ⁠a decade. “I walked into the ⁠paddock and I had no idea where I had to go. So it’s been a long time,” Verstappen told reporters on Thursday. “I always enjoyed racing here because ‌I think I really liked the track layout. It was not very straightforward because there was always high [tyre] degradation, hot in general. So quite uncomfortable in a way to drive ‌physically.” ‘Big learning curve’ Verstappen said that the car upgrades introduced in Baku showed promise, though he cautioned that the street circuit has historically suited ‌Red Bull’s characteristics. “So we have to wait a little bit now in the coming races to see how the car is going ⁠to perform, which is also quite good for us probably to see all these different kinds of tracks. “For next year we’ll learn ⁠a lot now, in these coming races, of what we need, what we want to do with the car. We’re anyway not fighting for the championship, so for us, it’s a big learning curve.” With no decision yet on whether ‌the final two rounds will go ‌ahead in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, Verstappen said he trusted Formula One and the governing FIA to make the right call. “I love going there, but of course it has to be on the right terms,” Verstappen said. “I trust that F1 and the FIA will make the right decision because they have more information than we do. That’s what we rely on. I trust that they’ll make the right call.”

title: US says F-47 will be first sixth-gen jet. China’s J-36 and J-50 are already flying
description: As competition intensifies with the PLA over future air power, American officer says the aircraft will fly during Trump’s term.
content: Washington is “not too far away” from a production line for its F-47 sixth-generation fighter, a senior US Air Force official has said, as China presses ahead with flight-testing two different next-generation combat aircraft of its own. During a virtual event hosted by the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies on Monday, Brigadier General Timothy Helfrich, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the F-47 would be “the world’s first sixth-generation fighter”. He said the aircraft was on track to fly before US President Donald Trump’s term ended in January 2029. Its first flight is targeted for 2028. Meanwhile, China’s two tailless next-generation fighters, commonly known as the J-36 and J-50, have been observed on test flights since December 2024. The secrecy surrounding the programmes makes direct comparisons difficult. US officials have said the F-47 builds on years of classified demonstrator testing, while Beijing has offered few details about either Chinese aircraft beyond brief footage released by Chinese state media in June. A day after Helfrich’s comments, the US Navy selected Boeing – already developing the F-47 – for its F/A-XX carrier-based fighter under a development contract worth more than US$20 billion, putting both US sixth-generation fighter programmes under the same roof. The award adds weight to Helfrich’s description of fighter production capacity as a “strategic asset”. He noted that the US had only three active fighter lines – for the F-35, F-15EX and F-16. Andreas Rupprecht, an aviation analyst and expert on the Chinese air force, cautioned that Helfrich’s comments might not mean “serial production” was imminent, noting that the first F-47 development aircraft was still some way from completion. The US Air Force plans to acquire at least 185 F-47s, which are expected to have a combat radius of more than 1,000 nautical miles (1,850km). Helfrich said the fighter would be “much more survivable” than existing fifth-generation aircraft. Rupprecht said the J-36 – built by Chengdu Aircraft Industry Corporation (CAIC) – currently had “no true US Air Force counterpart”, while the smaller Shenyang aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50 was the closer comparison with the F-47 in size and configuration. Brendan Mulvaney, director of the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute, broadly agreed that the J-50 looked closer to the F-47 in size and appearance, but cautioned against “mirror imaging”. Similar shapes could partly reflect the requirements of low-observable aircraft, he noted, while their technologies, weapons and roles could still differ. The J-36 is a large, three-engined tailless aircraft with a side-by-side cockpit. The South China Morning Post reported earlier on what appeared to be a possible fifth prototype, suggesting CAIC was continuing to refine the design through successive prototypes as flight-testing progressed. More recent footage has complicated efforts to determine how many are flying. Rupprecht said the number 36011 had appeared on three apparently different aircraft. He said it was unlikely that they represented a single aircraft repeatedly modified, given changes to the intakes, engines, exhausts and, most significantly, the landing gear. Clues about the J-50 have also surfaced. Research published in August by the Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute pointed to future fighters using greater autonomy, satellite-independent navigation and reconfigurable formations of uncrewed aircraft. The paper did not name the J-50 or confirm that it would have those features, but the emphasis on autonomy and networking has parallels with the US approach: the F-47 is intended to operate alongside collaborative combat aircraft. “Especially in these highly contested environments, no one’s going to be fighting alone,” Helfrich said. Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum, said the two militaries appeared to be exploring similar ideas but were still experimenting with how best to combine crewed and uncrewed systems. “It may take some time before we have clarity on their exact visions,” he added. Rupprecht described the visible changes to the J-36 and J-50 as “technical and aerodynamic refinements”, saying the programmes appeared to be progressing from a “rather rudimentarily equipped prototype” towards later aircraft showing “signs of integrated systems”. The latest prototypes appeared to be moving towards aircraft equipped with radar, “more comprehensive avionics” and potentially newer engines, he said. Mulvaney was more cautious, describing the changes as “evolution” rather than maturity. “If it were ‘mature’ then they would stop the changes and move to testing and production,” he said. “We haven’t seen that yet, so they aren’t ‘ready for prime time’ yet.” Rupprecht said the next indication of progress would be the appearance of further aircraft, which could suggest a design had been “finalised”. The war in Ukraine has shown the importance of large drone inventories, integration with regular forces and ample stocks of missiles and other weapons, according to Heath. He added that both the US and Chinese militaries were likely drawing lessons from the conflict on how to use and defend against drones in a high-end war. Yet which aircraft flew first may be a poor measure of who is further ahead. Rupprecht cautioned against drawing conclusions from public flight dates, saying “we simply know far too little” about the respective programmes to determine which side was further ahead. He said it was safe to assume that aircraft developed under the US Next Generation Air Dominance programme had flown before the Chinese designs, but it was unclear how representative those demonstrators were of the eventual F-47. He added that there could also have been classified precursors to China’s aircraft and that it was unclear whether US and Chinese requirements were comparable enough to conclude that either side had an edge. “I would simply wait and see on this one.”

title: Opinion | Whatever Trump claims, weaponisation of space makes losers of us all
description: It takes little imagination to realise a space war would inevitably escalate into all-out conflict, almost surely involving nuclear weapons.
content: When the US Space Force announced on September 14 that “the US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action”, I thought of Isaac Newton’s well-known declaration that he could not calculate the madness of people. This is the first time a country has admitted to deploying weapons in space. Today, the orbits are congested and contested with many nations conducting military activities, such as surveillance and reconnaissance, early missile warning, satellite communications and navigation. While the United States stands alone with an independent Space Force as a full separate service, many other states such as China, Russia, Britain, France and Japan have built dedicated space combat organisations. However, none of them has publicly acknowledged deploying on-orbit space weapons, unwilling to face the global backlash against turning outer space into a battlefield. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty already bans nuclear weapons in space. Deploying any other weapon will also draw widespread international criticism. Another reason people have refrained from talking about the weaponisation of space is because there is no clear definition of what constitutes a space weapon. That is probably why the Pentagon vaguely refers to “kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities”, without spelling out specific details. In simple terms, counter-space technology falls into four categories: co-orbital weapons match the target satellite’s orbit, track it closely, and disable it through impact or explosion; direct-ascent weapons strike passing satellites without entering their orbits; directed-energy tools, such as lasers and high-power microwaves, cripple satellite functions in an instant; electronic and cyber tools jam signals or hack both satellite and ground systems. And a major grey zone still exists – systems that have a civilian purpose can be used for military purposes.
