For example, an ordinary satellite can instantly turn into an offensive weapon if it extends a robotic arm to seize other spacecraft. Two opposing views now dominate global space security debates: no weaponisation vs responsible behaviour. For nearly two decades, China, Russia and many Global South countries have called for a legally binding treaty to ban space weaponisation entirely. The US-led Western bloc, however, argues that space militarisation is inevitable, so the world should instead focus on establishing non-binding “responsible behaviours”. In other words, it is impossible to empty a busy road of all traffic, but rules can still be set to prevent crashes. China is not against the idea of “responsible behaviours”. In 2021, two SpaceX Starlink satellites – Starlink-1095 in July and Starlink-2305 in October – made dangerously close approaches to China’s space station while Chinese astronauts were on board. Unexpected orbital shifts forced the station to execute emergency collision-avoidance manoeuvres. If ordinary commercial satellites can create such severe risks, dedicated space weapons would only amplify these dangers exponentially. The United States, Russia, China and India have all tested anti-satellite weapons in low-Earth orbit – and these tests need to stop. Even attacking a small number of satellites produces massive, long-lasting space debris. This fuels growing concerns over the Kessler Syndrome, a catastrophic chain reaction where continuous orbital collisions could render low-Earth orbit unusable for every country on Earth. The US stands to lose the most in a space war as the largest spacefaring nation. It operates over 10,600 active satellites and SpaceX aims to eventually have up to 42,000 satellites. Space weaponisation is a core part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome project for missile defence. Its design hinges on space-based interceptors because ground-based defences cannot reliably hit missiles during their brief boost phase. Only orbital platforms can deliver persistent global coverage to destroy rockets soon after launch. Yet, Trump’s claim that “we must have American dominance in space” is nothing more than a fantasy. Leaving aside its astronomical costs and extreme technical difficulties, no defensive system can fully counter the full spectrum of attacks by ballistic missiles, manoeuvrable hypersonic vehicles, fractional orbital bombardment systems and dual-use satellites at the same time. It takes little imagination to realise a space war would inevitably escalate into a large-scale, all-out conflict. Strikes targeting satellites would not remain confined to space; they would immediately cripple critical national infrastructure on the ground, triggering cross-domain retaliation and dragging adversaries into a full-spectrum war. And no conflict in space can remain confined to conventional warfare. It is almost surely part of a nuclear war or a prelude to it. Any major-power strike against rival space assets is impossible to conceal and will invite overwhelming retaliation. “A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” This hard-learned consensus emerged from the Cold War nuclear arms race, and all five nuclear-armed states still officially uphold this principle, at least on paper. It is interesting to note that during the Cold War, despite decades of bitter geopolitical rivalry, the two superpowers still managed to cooperate in peaceful space exploration, most notably the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project – humanity’s first international crewed space mission. It is a bitter irony, then, that the weaponisation of space – which even the Cold War rivals had the wisdom to avoid – is unfolding before our eyes. Three centuries after Newton admitted he could not calculate the madness of men, that madness has reached the stars. To march down this self-destructive path is not merely a strategic error; it is a doomsday scenario of our own making.

title: Anti-South Asian online hate surges in US under Trump 2.0, study finds
description: Trump’s immigration crackdown and economic anxiety have led to a spike in racist posts targeting South Asians, especially on X.
content: Anti-South Asian hate in the United States has spiked since Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, with racist, dehumanising and xenophobic slurs and narratives proliferating across both mainstream and fringe social media platforms, a US-based report has revealed. The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Washington-based Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH), found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the United States on the social media platform X rose 240 per cent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843. The hate speech is largely aimed at Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis, according to the report, which traces the surge to Trump’s immigration crackdown, economic anxiety and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in American life. Similarly, South Asian political figures from both major US political parties have faced racist and xenophobic attacks, the report found, including Kamala Harris, former vice-president and Democratic presidential nominee; Usha Vance, current second lady of the US; Kash Patel, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation; Zohran Mamdani, the first Muslim mayor of New York City; and Democratic representative Raja Krishnamoorthi. CSOH executive director Raqib Naik said the research, which focused on online sentiment towards South Asian Americans since December 2024, showed a clear and significant rise in targeting of the demographic, particularly Indians, since Trump’s second term. “The administration is part of the problem. Our report has outlined how incendiary rhetoric from top offices in the country is contributing to anti-South Asian hate, especially the federal government helping to fuel harmful and hateful narratives,” Naik said. He added that though some states were putting in place measures to mitigate the hate, most members of the South Asian community felt vulnerable as online hate manifested in real life. The report warned that the enormous scale of online hate showed the wide reach of social media platforms and algorithms that amplified hateful content. “It also reflects the growing alignment of powerful technology executives and owners like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg with the Maga movement and the rollback of hate speech policies, fact-checking programmes, and other trust and safety measures by platforms,” it said, adding that the transformation of X – formerly Twitter – after its acquisition by Musk led to the “normalisation of a violent and racist discourse” that was previously largely restricted to fringe online spaces. Naik urged the US government to take the lead, especially in controlling social media platforms, which he said had been weaponised to fuel hate. Citing the CSOH study, Indian-American congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi accused the Trump administration and the Maga movement of contributing to the rise in hate speech and what he described as systemic racism. “The 240 per cent surge in monthly anti-South Asian hate on X did not come out of nowhere. We have watched politicians demonise South Asians over something as ordinary as attending a college-football game and the Trump administration traffic in racist stereotypes targeting people named Singh,” said Krishnamoorthi on X in reference to tirades by Texas Republicans against brown people and a racist poster used by the administration. “Americans of every background, and leaders of both parties, need to speak out against racism and xenophobia wherever they appear. South Asian Americans are as much a part of the fabric of America as anyone else, and no amount of hate can erase the contributions we have made to this country,” Krishnamoorthi said. According to the report, more than half a million anti-South Asian posts appeared on X between January 2025 and June this year. The volume rose 75 per cent over this period and 240 per cent from January 2024 to June this year. Five of the six highest-volume months occurred between November 2025 and June 2026, showing that anti-South Asian hate continues to intensify. The report identified 397,522 hateful and dehumanising mentions targeting South Asians across the 4chan, 8chan, and Gab bulletin boards in 2025, with monthly volume remaining at a persistently high baseline for much of the year. Last month, Indian travel YouTuber Paramvir Singh Beniwal said he was subjected to racist remarks during a recent visit to Las Vegas. Beniwal, known online as Passenger Paramvir, shared a 57-minute YouTube vlog in which three men approached him and his friend, with one claiming to own 73 7-Eleven stores across the US before offering Beniwal a job as a cashier. Beniwal said he believed the offer was intended as a racist joke rather than a genuine job offer. He said the exchange was a reference to a stereotype that Indians often worked as cashiers at 7-Eleven stores. The video has garnered 6.8 million views in eight days, with viewers praising Beniwal for confronting the men over the remarks. According to the report, six key factors collectively drove the surge in anti-South Asian hate, including posts portraying South Asians as “invaders, job thieves, and a demographic threat” on X. The report identifies the H-1B visa programme, the American Tech Workforce Act of 2025, and the Visa Cap Enforcement Act as major triggers for anti-South Asian hate, especially against Indians, who in 2024 constituted 71 per cent of H-1B visa workers. An H-1B visa is a temporary US work permit that allows companies to hire foreign professionals in specialised fields. Indians are the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme, accounting for 71 per cent of approved H-1B petitions in the 2024 financial year, according to data from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Trump administration has curbed new H-1B visas by raising the fee for workers in this category by US$100,000. Of those subject to the higher H-1B fee, 82 per cent were Indian nationals, according to an analysis from the Penn Wharton Budget Model at the University of Pennsylvania. About 30 per cent of all posts on X and 45 per cent of mentions on fringe platforms with references to South Asians contained the word pajeet and its variants, according to the CSOH report. Pajeet is a slur mocking the sanitation habits of South Asians. David Kalal, Communications Director of Hindus for Human Rights, a US-based nonprofit advocacy organisation, said that he and others in the community were consistently getting hate messages on social media. “We have just launched a very civil and polite new platform called The Speaking Tree [on Instagram]. The first post that we put out asked the question, ‘What kind of Hindu future do you hope to see? Read a thought. Add your own’... and we received a lot of abuse,” Kalal said. The community was getting messages such as calls to deport US-based Indians and “end cow worship”, and slurs referring to“public sanitation” and “poopjeet”. Harsh V. Pant, vice-president for studies and foreign policy at the Observer Research Foundation, said that anti-South Asia hate in the US had also taken a toll on the relationship between New Delhi and Washington. He referred to comments on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly summit last month by Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who referred to hiccups in the bilateral ties, including immigration, trade negotiations and terrorism. “Indians have been seen as taking jobs away from Americans, which has vitiated the atmosphere, creating problems, particularly for the Indian government to invest in this relationship, and it is a big problem,” Pant said.

title: China leads drone patent volume but US matches quality as start-ups drive innovation: study
description: The market for civil unmanned aerial systems is expected to add up to a total of US$150 billion in the period from 2023 to 2032.
content: Chinese and US firms are “neck-and-neck” in the quality battle for the next generation of drone patents, despite China having a lead in volume, a study published on Thursday shows. Chinese companies accounted for 44 per cent of the world’s drone patent filings in 2024, against 17 per cent for American firms, according to a report published by LexisNexis. Measured by value, however, US drone patents were on a par with China’s, leaving the two countries roughly even in total global patent asset value for the technology, as calculated by LexisNexis. DJI, the Shenzhen-based global industry leader, has also been losing its dominance in patent filings, holding only 4 per cent of the industry’s total patent assets, barely ahead of US firms such as Boeing and Amazon, according to the report. This compares with roughly 24 per cent of the industry’s total patents held by DJI at the end of 2018, which was more than all the other companies in the top 10 combined. “The company seems to have allowed the bulk of its patents to lapse since that peak,” the report said, adding that this could be caused by factors including tighter US restrictions on drone imports, DJI’s own patent pruning to focus on its strongest defensive patents, or the company’s strategic shift towards protecting selected technologies as trade secrets instead of via patents. “As DJI retreats from the patent field, the space is wide open for the next generation of drone start-ups to drive patent innovation and market leadership,” said Marco Richter, managing director and chief commercial officer for LexisNexis Intellectual Property Solutions. “While China is clearly winning on the volume of patents filed, it’s the quality battle that best predicts future leaders in emerging technologies, and that race is neck-and-neck,” Richter said. “The companies – and countries – that win this innovation race will build new industries that control the skies over the coming decades.” The stakes were high as the market for civil unmanned aerial systems was expected to add up to a total of US$150 billion in the period from 2023 to 2032, while the military market could be worth US$187 billion during the same time frame, the report said, citing market data from Teal Group. The contest for technology supremacy between China and the US has shown little sign of slowing down. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr said earlier last month that the FCC was considering whether to prohibit the continued marketing and import of certain previously authorised drone models, extending a previously announced import ban on new models. Among the world’s top 10 innovative drone start-ups ranked by LexisNexis, China has two – Shenzhen-based Autel Robotics at No 1 and Beijing-based Zero Zero Robotics in fifth spot – while the US has four, with Skydio, Valqari, Anduril and Zipline taking the second, third, sixth and ninth spots, respectively. Japan, Israel, Switzerland and Sweden completed the top 10 with one firm each.

title: Chinese start-up behind laser mosquito killer plans to start shipping orders this month
description: Photon Matrix Lab says it expects to produce up to 5,000 devices a month initially, and then increase production capacity next year.
content: People have been trying to fend off mosquitoes for thousands of years – using methods ranging from physical barriers to chemical insecticides – but a Chinese start-up is now taking pre-orders on a hi-tech solution that uses lidar detection and lasers to zap them out of the air. Photon Matrix Lab, based in Changzhou, in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, said it expected initial monthly production of the device – which became a breakout hit in overseas crowdfunding – to be between 3,000 and 5,000 units. Lawrence Leng, the firm’s sales director, said the first batch was expected to ship later this month. The device comes in two versions, one with an infrared laser and the other with a blue laser, priced at US$988 and US$1,088 respectively, according to the company’s website, which said they would ship within 120 days of the receipt of a pre-order. It said both offered the same mosquito-killing performance, but the infrared version, with an invisible laser, was designed for indoor settings, while the blue laser version, with a visible beam, was better suited to gardens and outdoor use. Leng said Photon Matrix Lab had received more than 5,000 orders since the crowdfunding stage, mainly from Europe and North America, followed by the Middle East. “This distribution aligns with the product’s core value: in markets where pesticide use is restricted or chemical control is less accepted, purely physical mosquito-killing solutions are clearly more accepted,” he said. Photon Matrix Lab said the device, which looks like a power bank, used high-precision lidar to scan its surroundings, detect small, slow-moving flying objects, and trigger its attack mechanism. It could also identify people and large animals and shut down before they entered the strike zone. Leng said he expected demand would grow steadily and production capacity would increase by three to five times over the next year. The start-up set a goal of raising US$20,000 on Indiegogo, a US-based crowdfunding platform, last summer, but has since raised more than US$2.8 million after going viral on social media. But delays in mass production and concerns over safety followed its crowdfunding success. The company previously said on its Douyin social media account that it would begin mass production in July. The principle behind using lasers to kill mosquitoes has been demonstrated in laboratories for years, but for a long time it remained confined to papers and prototypes. Photon Matrix Lab founder Wang Chuan said it took longer than expected to move the device into commercial production. “We originally expected to build the product in three months, but it actually took three years,” he told state broadcaster China Central Television in August. Leng said the hard part was not whether a laser could kill a mosquito, but detection accuracy, strike precision and energy balance, as well as cost and ease of manufacture. “To truly reach the consumer market, you have to get the supply chain and manufacturing process in place while ensuring performance and safety – that’s where many concepts stall,” he said. In a previous interview, he attributed the firm’s success to China’s mature local supply chains, which made it possible for grass-roots Chinese innovators to repurpose military or industrial technology, such as low-cost lidar and edge computing, for everyday consumer products.

title: Manchester City scandal risks damaging Premier League’s booming global brand
description: The club’s rule-breaking could see English top flight lose one of its marquee players in Erling Haaland and also leave fans feeling cheated.
content: The Premier League has won a lengthy legal battle with Manchester City over financial impropriety, but the consequences could leave lasting damage for a league that has long been the envy of world football. City face severe sanctions after being found guilty of more than 100 charges between 2009 and 2018, with an independent commission exposing “sham” contracts to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million (US$1.2 billion). A hefty points deduction resulting in relegation, stripped titles and even expulsion from the English top flight have been mooted as potential sanctions. But the damage may not be limited to City alone, with an entire era of the Premier League now under a cloud. A takeover in 2008 by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, transformed City’s fortunes but also the face of the Premier League. The club’s first top-flight league title for 44 years was one of the most iconic moments in Premier League history when Sergio Aguero netted the winner against QPR in the 94th minute to deny Manchester United the title. Some of City’s rivals have been quick to revel in their downfall. “Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet,” posted former Manchester United defender Rio Ferdinand, who was part of the United team that finished second to City in the 2011/12 season. Yet there could be more lingering collective consequences for a league that has become accustomed to flexing its financial muscle to hoover up the best talent from around the globe. The question now is whether fans will be turned away from the Premier League after feeling cheated over what they have witnessed over the past 18 years. In total, City have won eight titles in the last 15 seasons. They rewrote the record books, becoming the first side to ever achieve 100 points and win the English top flight for four consecutive years. All of those achievements are now labelled with an asterisk. “If I were a player, I’d be 100 per cent sticking those medals in the bin. Of course you would, it’s cheating,” former Manchester United captain Roy Keane said. Despite the Premier League’s spending power, English clubs have still struggled to keep the world’s biggest superstars away from Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain. City’s demise could also see the Premier League lose one of its marquee players in Erling Haaland. “The Premier League is Britain’s greatest soft power cultural asset,” Simon Chadwick, professor of Afro-Eurasian sport, said. “What happens when people start to question, ‘what have I been watching all these years?’” By contrast, the Premier League has argued the City case is proof of strong governance. The league pursued and persisted with an investigation that began in 2018 despite City’s best attempts to frustrate the process. “This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history,” the league’s chief executive, Richard Masters, said. “It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. “It is paramount that the league remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.”

title: South Korea hits back at Trump’s investment claims in ‘tit-for-tat move’
description: President Lee Jae Myung says further talks are needed and ‘commercial viability’ must be a prerequisite for South Korean investment in the US.
content: US President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement of a “colossal” South Korean investment package has prompted Seoul to clarify that the deal is far from finalised, laying bare stark differences between the allies over the terms of their trade agreement, observers have said. On Wednesday, Trump announced that South Korea would invest in the construction of a natural gas-fired power plant in Texas, eight large-scale nuclear power plants across the United States and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska. Hours later, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung issued a clarification that effectively pushed back against Washington’s portrayal of the investment package as a done deal, making clear that further negotiations were still necessary. Trump’s announcement comes just weeks before the highly competitive November midterm elections, apparently aiming to bolster the Republican Party’s economic record and support vulnerable candidates, including Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan. It followed protracted negotiations over the implementation of Seoul’s commitment to invest US$350 billion in the US – US$150 billion in the shipbuilding sector and US$200 billion in strategic industries – in return for Washington lowering tariffs on South Korean goods. Trump touted the three projects as a “colossal package” that marked a “major step towards securing our critical energy supply chain, ensuring American energy dominance and making our partnership with South Korea and the entire Pacific region stronger than ever before”. He said Seoul would invest up to US$200 billion in US energy infrastructure, including US$22.3 billion for a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas and US$120 billion for the eight nuclear power plants. “And at long last, the Alaska liquefied natural gas pipeline. That’s a big one,” he added. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also said the investment in the Alaska LNG project would exceed US$50 billion, and the eight nuclear reactors would be built in Ohio, Tennessee, South Carolina and Kentucky. Seoul’s position is that only the Texas project has been finalised, while the commercially contentious Alaska LNG project and the eight nuclear power plants remain subject to further discussions. On Thursday, Lee reiterated that “commercial viability” must be a prerequisite for South Korean investment in the US. “Among the investment projects in the United States announced by the US, we have agreed to begin ‘working’ on the Alaska LNG project on the condition that its commercial viability is confirmed and that it complies with South Korea’s legal procedures,” he said on social media. Lee’s emphasis on “working” appeared intended to underscore that both sides had yet to bridge their differences over the project’s commercial feasibility and the conditions for Seoul’s participation. A joint statement issued by the two governments appeared to support Lee’s interpretation concerning where Seoul’s investment would be made. The statement said both sides had “agreed to commence working” on the Alaska LNG project, subject to “meeting commercial reasonableness and all applicable domestic legal requirements”. South Korea’s Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said last week that the Alaska project remained under review. “We will review the Alaska LNG project under the clear principle that we will proceed only if its commercial viability is established,” Kim said. The joint statement also said both sides “have agreed to a comprehensive cooperation framework” for constructing eight large-scale nuclear power plants. Lee has stressed that the commercial viability of each nuclear power plant must be assessed individually, apparently contrasting with Washington’s position that the investment should be evaluated as an overall package. His clarification comes despite reports that both countries agreed on the operating arrangements for a US$200 billion umbrella investment vehicle to govern the investment component of Seoul’s commitment. Under the reported mechanism, revenues from individual projects would be consolidated, allowing profits from commercially successful ventures to offset losses incurred by others. Both sides would initially share profits equally, with a 50-50 split maintained until South Korea recovered its principal investment and interest from each project. Only then would the profit-sharing ratio shift to 10 per cent for Seoul and 90 per cent for Washington. Even after the recovery of principal and interest, however, the 50-50 arrangement would continue across the entire portfolio, including projects whose individual investments had already been recouped, Lee said. He added that the arrangement was designed to minimise investment losses and ensure South Korea recovered its overall investment. Observers say the arrangement suggests that both countries still need to resolve important details concerning the investment mechanism, including how commercial risks and returns will be assessed and distributed across the portfolio. “This is a tit-for-tat move by President Lee in response to Washington’s unilateral action,” Hur Jung, a professor in the economics department at Sogang University, told This Week in Asia. Trump’s announcement was designed to appeal to voters ahead of the midterm elections, while Lee, facing declining approval ratings and domestic criticism over his handling of negotiations with Washington, also needed to send a strong message to South Korean audiences, Hur said. “President Lee’s remarks, however, are throwing up new obstacles in negotiations with Washington. He is doubling down on his stance as part of his negotiation tactics, but there is little possibility of the talks breaking down,” Hur said, citing the strategic importance of the two allies to each other. Kim Jae-chun, a political-science professor at Sogang University, said Lee was “staking out his firm position” to secure South Korean interests in the negotiations, but warned that “it would be very difficult for Seoul to withstand Washington’s pressure” given that Trump’s term runs until January 2029. The conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), meanwhile, accused the government of deceiving the public, arguing that it had already agreed on specific investment amounts with Washington but concealed the details from the National Assembly. It described Trump’s announcement as a “serious diplomatic disaster” for South Korea. The PPP urged the government to disclose whether it had agreed to invest in the Alaska LNG project, release detailed plans and the criteria for determining commercial viability and seek parliamentary approval for the investment. Lee and Trump reached the trade deal last year, under which Washington agreed to lower its so-called reciprocal tariffs on South Korean goods to 15 per cent from 25 per cent in return for Seoul’s US$350 billion investment commitment. Both sides have since engaged in difficult negotiations over the selection and implementation of investment projects, with Seoul seeking to ensure its commitments are commercially viable and do not expose South Korean taxpayers and public finances to excessive risks.

title: How Westernised Cantonese opera Sleepless Moon marries Turandot and The Flower Princess
description: Hong Kong composer and soprano Lora Chow adapts The Flower Princess into a Western-infused production to make the genre more accessible.
content: What happens when two operatic heavyweights – Warren Mok Wah-lun in Western opera and Alis Lin Yingshi in Cantonese opera – meet at an ad hoc music jamming session? “A crossover opera that combines Turandot and The Flower Princess,” says Lora Chow Hiu-ching, a Hong Kong composer and soprano. What began as an informal artistic exchange session quickly evolved into a serious artistic endeavour. Four years later, Chow is fine-tuning acoustics at the East Kowloon Cultural Centre, where cross-cultural production Sleepless Moon will premiere on October 1. Chow is one of the lead creators of Sleepless Moon, alongside producers Ivy Tse Yan-wah and Eddie Tam Sun-keung, a Cantonese opera performer. Although Chow was not present when Mok proposed a crossover opera, Tam, a guest at the private jam session, put her name forward. Both Chow and Tam are alumni of Yale University, in the US state of Connecticut. This is not the first time the Cantonese opera classic The Flower Princess, which depicts the tragic romance between Princess Changping and her husband during the fall of the Ming dynasty, has been reinterpreted. By playwright Tong Dik-sang, The Flower Princess premiered in 1957 and has since inspired various adaptations. However, a full reinterpretation in a Western operatic format – like Giacomo Puccini’s Turandot – remains rare. “Eddie was thrilled about Warren’s idea,” Chow says. “He felt that Westernising Cantonese opera could make the genre more accessible and expand its audience reach.” Modernising Cantonese opera For decades, Cantonese opera has struggled to shed an outdated image among younger generations. In a city where British colonial heritage historically favoured Western classical arts, education rarely prioritised Cantonese opera. Chow, in her thirties, grew up playing the violin in school orchestras and spending family holidays attending the opera in Vienna, Austria. The early exposure to Western classical music led her to specialise in opera during postgraduate studies. Although she had heard of The Flower Princess from a young age, she had never attended a live Cantonese opera production until a 2024 performance at the Xiqu Centre in Hong Kong – and even then, it was an excerpted showcase. “My first impression was that it’s very poetic. It felt like a piece of valuable Chinese heritage that we ought to preserve,” she recalls, noting that the climactic scene where the lovers sacrifice themselves moved her deeply. “When you are so intensely in love, you would rather die together. It reminds me of Romeo and Juliet.” “I used to assume Cantonese opera instrumentation, particularly the percussion, was overly loud and piercing,” she continues. “But that experience changed my perception. I grew to appreciate how rich and harmonious it can be, and it became something I wanted to recreate in my own composition.” With Sleepless Moon, Chow’s musical score leans towards a Western operatic structure. Nevertheless, she remains eager to experiment with traditional Chinese instrumentation, weaving musical motifs from The Flower Princess alongside traditional instruments into her orchestration. Expanding her creative horizons Although Chow lacks formal Cantonese opera training, she credits her technical understanding to her sister, Bona Chow Hiu-yan, an amateur pipa player, and to her previous role as associate music director at Shanghai Disneyland, where she was commissioned to compose symphonic and musical scores incorporating Chinese instruments. She also benefited from the guidance of Cantonese opera masters including Tang Mi-ling, Loong Koon-tin and Hing-Cheung Chu, as well as Chinese music composers Alfred Wong and Ng Cheuk-yin. “The musical style of Sleepless Moon is an amalgamation of cinematic, Disney and classical opera influences,” she says. “These familiar elements make Cantonese opera far more accessible.” She clarifies that while her work is not strictly a traditional Cantonese opera, she hopes it will inspire audiences to explore original Cantonese opera productions. The production, which runs until October 4, has since received a pending invitation to perform at a music festival in Shenzhen in November. For Chow, the experience has expanded her creative horizons. She plans to compose more theatrical works, ballets, film scores and multidisciplinary works – a process she considers fundamentally aligned with opera creation. “Opera is the highest art form because it integrates so many disciplines: vocal performance, drama and orchestration. In Cantonese opera, performers undergo rigorous training across singing, recitation, acting and martial arts,” she says, adding that she aims to push creative boundaries further through cross-cultural collaboration. “Hong Kong is the ideal launch pad for this kind of fusion opera because of its cultural diversity,” she says. “We have an abundance of young talent across Cantonese opera, Western opera, musical theatre and set design. “Bringing these disciplines together unlocks endless creative possibilities.” “Sleepless Moon”, East Kowloon Cultural Centre, 60 Ngau Tau Kok Road, Kowloon. October 1-4, 2026. For tickets, visit Urbtix.

title: Hong Kong celebrates National Day with dazzling fireworks extravaganza
description: Multimillion-dollar display themed ‘Eternal Radiance’ draws massive harbourfront crowds to celebrate 77th anniversary of country’s founding.
content: Revellers packed promenades along Victoria Harbour to watch a 23-minute National Day fireworks display that illuminated Hong Kong’s skyline on Thursday night with cascading ribbons of light, red hearts and smiley faces. At the Wan Chai Ferry Pier, crowds clapped and cheered in awe, raising their arms to capture the spectacle on their phones. Fanny Yao, 34, travelled with her family from Fujian province to Hong Kong for a third consecutive year to watch the celebrations. Yao, who is a fan of Cantonese TV dramas, said she enjoyed Hong Kong culture and wanted her 10-year-old daughter Mia to develop a sense of patriotism. “I feel that the patriotic atmosphere is alive and well in Guangdong province, and in Hong Kong and Macau, and wanted her to experience that,” she said. “Coming to Hong Kong for the National Day fireworks show has become a ritual at this point.” The family had been waiting for the show since 6pm, which led to Mia, holding a national flag in her hand, sulking a little in the heat. “But it was worth it, especially the finale, which was riveting,” Yao said. Prola Gao, a tourist in her twenties from Guangdong, said she was amazed by the display, which she described as “stunning”. Gao said the 30-minute wait and braving the sweaty, jostling crowd were worth it. “My favourite part was the red heart-shaped fireworks and the finale,” she said. Gao said she and her family were spending two days and one night in Hong Kong and that they enjoyed the lively atmosphere along the promenade. Fireworks in the shape of hearts, stars and smiley faces drew the loudest “oohs” and “ahs” from the spectators. The HK$18 million (US$2.3 million) display was sponsored by insurance provider Sun Life Hong Kong. The show, coordinated by the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau, involved 31,888 pyrotechnic shells launched from nine firing points on three barges and six floating pontoons. Authorities earlier said they expected the event to draw 260,000 people. By mid-afternoon, photography enthusiasts, tourists and residents had already claimed prime spots along the harbourfront, settling in for the hours-long wait with umbrellas, folding chairs and picnic mats Among them was Vina Ke, who arrived at Wan Chai Harbour Promenade at 4.30pm, as temperatures in urban areas topped 33 degrees Celsius (91 Fahrenheit). Ke, a Taiwanese tourist, and her two friends sat on picnic mats with plenty of snacks and drinks, sheltering under an umbrella. “We came early because we were afraid it would get crowded,” the 24-year-old graduate said. “We learned that there would be a fireworks display during our trip so we thought we should come and see it.” Their week-long trip to Hong Kong and Macau coincided with mainland China’s National Day “golden week” holiday, and Ke said they had felt the brunt of high hotel prices. Mainlanders Victoria Yao and Betty Xu, both graduate students who had just arrived in the city, were also waiting near Wan Chai pier. Yao, 22, and Xu, 25, who came from Xian and Anhui province, respectively, said they had arrived early to snag front-row spots for the fireworks. Equipped with only a portable fan and sunglasses, the two students said they were ready to stand for at least three hours on the harbourfront before the display. “It is so hot,” said Yao, who was sweating and fanning herself. Despite the heat, the pair were eager to see what the display would bring. “But we are very excited. I don’t know what special fireworks designs will be shown so it will be like opening a blind box,” Xu said. The display, themed “Eternal Radiance”, marked the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Hong Kong police began closing parts of Tsim Sha Tsui, Central and Wan Chai from 5pm in anticipation of large crowds heading towards the harbour. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department reminded spectators to keep the areas clean and take their rubbish with them, while the Marine Department urged those watching from the sea to pay attention to marine safety.

title: Elon Musk returns to US government for Pentagon war study
description: He will co-lead Project Meridian with Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defence tech firm Anduril Industries, and former House speaker Newt Gingrich.
content: Tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump’s government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war. Musk served as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency before departing in May last year, having publicly fallen out with Trump. In a speech at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said “Project Meridian” will be “an effort led by America’s best minds to study the future of warfare”. “We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists,” Hegseth said. Musk will be a co-leader of Project Meridian alongside Palmer Luckey, the 34-year-old co-founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries, and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year-old Republican former House speaker. Musk threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, but the men later had a high-profile blow-up over the president’s spending legislation. He later resumed giving to Republican causes, including multimillion-dollar donations to individual candidates and conservative political groups. Hegseth said the project’s purpose is to “creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master”. Project members will include hand-picked private sector leaders and subject matter experts from across the innovation, academic and policy ecosystems. Hegseth said he has directed Project Meridian’s findings to be completed and submitted within 120 days.

title: Days after Xi-Trump summit, the US marks China’s National Day with pared-down note
description: Washington’s brief message omits the word ‘prosperity’ and makes no mention of Xi’s visit, offering a snapshot of shifting US-China ties.
content: Five days after Chinese President Xi Jinping left Washington, the US State Department marked the 77th anniversary of the People’s Republic of China with a greeting short enough to fit on a calling card. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s congratulatory statement landed on Wednesday, a few hours before dawn on National Day in Beijing. It made no mention of Xi’s visit, the trade understandings reached during the trip or the meetings the two leaders have scheduled for later this year. Washington continued its tradition of marking China’s National Day before October 1 arrived in the United States. But it pared down the message. “On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of China on the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China on October 1,” it said. “The United States wishes the people of China goodwill, along with peace, health and happiness in the coming year.” Unlike Rubio’s greeting last year, this year’s version dropped the word “prosperity”. The previous statement wished the Chinese people “health, happiness, prosperity and peace in the year ahead”. That wording change sits against the backdrop of a week of high-level contact. Xi just completed a state visit to Washington, while US and Chinese officials announced outcomes on trade and other topics. Hours before Xi’s arrival in the US, Rubio himself described the US-China relationship as one that would “define the 21st century”. Atul Kumar, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, said Rubio’s note introduced “goodwill” while dropping “prosperity” and made no reference to the summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump or their planned meetings later this year. “As Xi seeks strategic persuasion and a constructive, stable relationship with Trump and the US administration, the inclusion of goodwill seems noteworthy,” he said. “However, the omission of ‘prosperity’ underscores deeper bilateral economic rivalry.” He added that the framing kept the State Department’s “formal, ceremonial language of diplomatic courtesy without explicitly endorsing or institutionalising Trump’s leader-level summit diplomacy”. Speaking at the Chinese embassy’s National Day reception in Washington on Wednesday, Chinese ambassador Xie Feng called the Xi-Trump rapport the “most valuable strategic asset” in the bilateral relationship, adding that head-of-state diplomacy anchored ties. The personal connection between the two leaders had “helped keep China-US relations on course at critical moments”, he added. Manoj Kewalramani, chair of the Geostrategy Programme at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru, said the latest statement still pointed to engagement. “The signal essentially remains that the US is looking to build some sort of a working relationship with China rather than simply manage difficult issues or compete intensely,” he said. From cooperation to competition The National Day greeting has been more than a holiday courtesy. Its wording has offered a small annual snapshot of how Washington describes its relationship with Beijing, with the length and tone broadly tracking the state of ties. During Barack Obama’s presidency, the messages contained references to cooperation. In a September 29, 2011 statement, then US secretary of state Hillary Clinton said the two countries were “developing the positive, cooperative and comprehensive relationship envisioned by our presidents”. She cited the state visit by then Chinese leader Hu Jintao in January of that year as well as the Strategic and Economic Dialogue that May. “A thriving China is good for America and a thriving America is good for China,” she added. John Kerry, who succeeded Clinton as secretary of state, took a similar tone. In 2013, the year of the Sunnylands summit between Xi and Obama, Kerry said the relationship had “grown by historic measures since President Nixon’s visit to China 41 years ago”. He added that “a prosperous China is good for the United States, and a prosperous United States is good for China”. In 2014, marking the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations, Kerry called cooperation on climate change, Ebola fever and nuclear proliferation “indispensable”. And in 2015, just a week after Xi’s previous state visit to Washington, Kerry wrote that the two sides had “shown how much we can accomplish through cooperation”. He closed with a wish for “peace and prosperity over the coming year”. The messages became shorter as tensions deepened during Donald Trump’s first term as US president. On September 30, 2017, the US State Department issued a statement while then secretary of state Rex Tillerson was in Beijing, ahead of Trump’s November state visit. It said that “a strong, constructive relationship between the United States and China is important for the prosperity and stability of our two countries as well as the world”. Tillerson also wished the Chinese people “peace and prosperity”. By 2019, in the middle of the US-China tariff war, references to the bilateral relationship largely disappeared from the holiday greeting. Former secretary of state Mike Pompeo’s message wished the Chinese people “happiness, health, peace and prosperity in the year to come”. His 2020 message came a few months after Washington closed China’s consulate in Houston and Beijing closed the US consulate in Chengdu. It wished the Chinese people “health, prosperity, happiness and peace in the coming year”. Blinken returns to ties Antony Blinken, secretary of state under former US president Joe Biden, brought the relationship back into focus. After a frosty meeting with top Chinese diplomats in Alaska in 2021, Blinken said Washington sought to “work cooperatively to solve the challenges we all face” and wished the Chinese people “peace, happiness and prosperity”. A year later, just weeks after then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan, he pointed to areas where the two sides could work together, including “health, climate change, counternarcotics and other areas where our interests intersect”. That language continued in 2023, following controversy over an alleged Chinese surveillance balloon and a summer of high-level US visits to Beijing. Blinken highlighted cooperation on “the climate crisis, public health, counternarcotics, food security and global macroeconomic stability”. Then, in 2024, the message arrived after October 1. It said the US was “committed to responsibly managing our bilateral relationship with the [People’s Republic of China] and will maintain open lines of communication”.

title: Chinese hair embroidery uses human hair instead of silk thread to create ultra-fine portraits
description: Some artists split the hair into finer strands or blend it with silk and gold threads for expressionistic effects.
content: While China’s iconic silk embroidery is world-renowned for its exquisite detail and painterly effects, an even more meticulous traditional technique surpasses it. Originating in Dongtai, located in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, during the Tang dynasty (618–907), hair embroidery relies on the incredibly fragile medium of human hair. With a rich history spanning over 1,000 years, a single intricate piece can take skilled artisans anywhere from several months to multiple years to complete. It is said that young women in Dongtai first used their own hair to weave images of Buddha as a demonstration of their piety. In China, there is a traditional saying: “Our bodies – to every hair and bit of skin – are received from our parents, and we must not presume to injure or wound them.” Thus, embroidering with hair is also a profound expression of dedication. The skill declined during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1368–1912). In the 1960s and 70s, some Su embroidery professionals and artists were sent to Dongtai during the Cultural Revolution, which led to the rediscovery and revival of this ancient hair embroidery technique. Hair embroidery requires the hair of young, healthy women no shorter than 30 centimetres. The hair undergoes a series of treatments, including degreasing, softening, colour-fixing, and preserving, to maintain its best quality over time. While silk embroidery can utilise machines, hair embroidery must be executed by hand due to the ultra-fine quality of the material and the intricate details required. A hair embroidery artist employs multiple stitching techniques, such as stemming, swirling, and wrapping, to achieve a vivid and natural combination of shades and densities. One piece of hair embroidery art, especially larger works, is often a collaborative effort and could take months to years to complete. One of the most famous examples, Prosperous Suzhou, is an over 12.4-metre-long and 36-centimetre-wide piece crafted based on a 1759 painting, featuring 12,000 figures, 400 boats, and 500 shop signs. It took artist Zhou Yinghua and more than 10 embroidery artists three years to accomplish in 2009. The hair material is particularly effective in depicting human and animal features in a work. Traditionally, only black hair was used in hair embroidery, leading to its alternative name, moxiu, or ink embroidery. Due to the limited shades of hair available, the themes of hair embroidery tended to focus on portraits with minimalist backgrounds. As dyeing techniques advanced in modern times, hair can now be dyed in various colours, allowing for the representation of themes such as flowers and birds, as well as natural and urban landscapes. Some artists also split the hair further into finer strands or combine hair with silk and gold threads to achieve expressionistic effects. In 2021, Dongtai hair embroidery was recognised as a national intangible cultural heritage.

title: National Day: Hongkongers visit Shenzhen for shopping and 60cm egg tarts
description: Residents head north to enjoy trending treats, cheap wellness services and warehouse grocery runs over public holiday.
content: Hongkongers flocked across the border on National Day for grocery shopping, massages and trendy 60cm-long egg tarts, citing lower prices and a wider variety of leisure activities. Immigration Department figures showed that 238,112 residents had left Hong Kong by 9pm on Thursday, while the city had welcomed 269,567 mainland Chinese visitors. At the Lok Ma Chau spur line control point, crowds of Hongkongers gathered in the morning to head north, while mainland visitors travelled in the opposite direction to celebrate the first day of their National Day “golden week” break. Among those heading to Shenzhen was Lina Li, a 58-year-old retiree who visits the mainland city twice a month. Li said she and several friends were making a one-day trip, adding that she planned to spend more than HK$1,000 (US$127) on food, a massage and a head spa session, all booked. “I really enjoy the services here,” she said. “A massage in Hong Kong can cost over HK$700, but in Shenzhen I can get a really good one for about HK$300. A head spa can be as cheap as around HK$100, which you do not often find in Hong Kong.” Li also brought a small trolley with her and said she would pick up things that took her fancy, from baked goods to groceries. Also travelling to Shenzhen was Hong Kong resident Rose Crut, along with her husband and their two sons. She said they were only doing a day trip to Futian, as the boys had school the next day. The family arrived in Shenzhen at around 11am and planned to have lunch at a shopping centre near the checkpoint. Crut said the mainland city was a great place for a family day out. “There’s so much to see and do, and the shopping is really convenient,” she said. Her husband had brought along a large suitcase, as the couple hoped to stop by the grocery warehouse store Costco in Longhua district and had set a budget of about HK$2,000. “We come here quite often, on average four times a year, but sometimes once a month – it really depends,” said Crut, who is originally from Mexico and has lived in Hong Kong with her family for 10 years. Some Hongkongers also travelled to Shenzhen to catch special events during the public holiday. “I came to Shenzhen last night and plan to eat and shop around the malls, take pictures with my friends to celebrate the holiday together,” said a woman surnamed Chiu. Chiu said she and her friends had already spent a night at the Hilton Hotel in Futian and had picked the district because one of them wanted to buy a new car at the Shenzhen International Auto Show, which runs from Thursday to Monday at the nearby Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Centre. “I don’t have a specific amount to spend in Shenzhen. I’ll just buy everything I like,” she said. Over at a shopping centre connected to Futian’s Exhibition Centre railway station, large crowds could be seen flooding into the mall. Shoppers wheeled suitcases of all sizes through the crowds, squeezing past vendors and promoters who called out in Cantonese to draw them in. Trolleys rattled across the floors, shopping bags rustled and queues formed outside popular restaurants, shops and massage parlours. Some even queued outside bakeries selling 60cm-long (24-inch) egg tarts, which have become a recent trend on the mainland. A bakery worker surnamed Chen said that, judging by conversations with customers, most of those buying the long egg tarts were from Hong Kong and were attracted by the novelty of the product. “Some will even take photos with our poster after they have bought them,” Chen added. Another shop said it had been baking the special egg tarts all day without stopping, selling at least “hundreds of boxes by the afternoon”. A Hong Kong bank employee, who gave her surname as Choi, said she was taking her mother and son to Shenzhen for an extended weekend and had taken an extra day off on Friday. “The weather is really hot in Hong Kong. And even though there are also events and promotions back home, we just do not want to stay as we’ve already been to those scenic spots like Disney and Ocean Park many times,” she said. The family said they would spend one night in the city before heading to Zhongshan for the weekend. “We want to use this holiday as a staycation, to just be chill,” Choi said. “Just like a lot of Hongkongers do, even more Hong Kong stars have now moved to Zhongshan.” Additional reporting by Jess Ma

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo appoints new foreign minister
description: Arrmanatha Nasir is a career diplomat who was Indonesia’s former permanent representative to the United Nations in New York.
content: Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto replaced ⁠his foreign minister with a career diplomat on Thursday, in his second change to a top post in his cabinet in less than three weeks. Prabowo ‌in a cabinet reshuffle named as foreign minister, the ministry’s former permanent representative to the United Nations in New York, with the outgoing Sugiono appointed Human Development minister. The appointment of Nasir, who was Sugiono’s deputy, is expected ⁠to mark a shake-up at the ministry. It comes after Prabowo ‌sacked his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, on September 14, replacing him with his deputy, Suahasil Nazara, ‌which investors welcomed as a move that could help restore ⁠confidence ⁠in the US$1.5 trillion G20 economy after months of uncertain policymaking. Nasir said after the inauguration that his priorities included maintaining stability in the region and promoting multilateralism. Analysts have said Sugiono’s ‌foreign ministry had been sidelined as Prabowo played a more dominant role in foreign policy. Dewi Fortuna Anwar, a foreign policy analyst at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency, said long-time diplomat Nasir was expected to play a more ‌assertive role. “He can be a foil to Prabowo,” she said, adding that the foreign ministry ⁠under the “even-keeled” Nasir will ⁠now be under pressure to scrutinise every diplomatic deal more carefully. Dewi cited the furore caused by a joint statement signed with China in 2024, ‌which pledged to develop projects “in the overlapping waters claimed by the two countries”. The statement was widely interpreted as a recognition of China’s sweeping territorial claims in ‌the South ‌China Sea. Dewi also said she hoped Nasir could help “get Indonesia back on the map” within Asean by ‌shaping the Southeast Asian bloc’s response to Myanmar, which has been engulfed in a nationwide civil war since the military ⁠seized power in a 2021 coup. Keeping ‌a ‌low profile and hardly appearing in media, Sugiono was not ‌a diplomat and came from Prabowo’s Gerindra party. State news ⁠agency Antara had described Sugiono as Prabowo’s “ideological child” and one of ⁠his most trusted aides. Sugiono oversaw some notable foreign policy initiatives, including Indonesia’s entry into Brics, the grouping ‌of major emerging economies, ‌and Jakarta’s decision to join US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace initiative for Gaza. Indonesia also pledged troops to a proposed international stabilisation force for Gaza.

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo appoints new police chief following scandals at the force
description: Listyo Sigit Prabowo’s dismissal comes amid allegations of police impunity, abuse of power and brutality.
content: Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto is replacing Listyo Sigit Prabowo as the country’s police chief with the head of the National Narcotics Agency, Suyudi Ario Seto, amid reports of police transgressions under Listyo’s watch in recent years. Chairman of the House Commission on Legal Affairs Habiburokhman confirmed on Thursday morning that the house had received a presidential letter dismissing Listyo and nominating Suyudi to the post, according to Tempo news magazine. “This morning, we received a letter from President Prabowo … concerning the proposal to dismiss the current national police chief and appoint a new one,” he said during a meeting at the house complex in Senayan, Jakarta. “Commission III of the house has been tasked with conducting the fit-and-proper test for General Suyudi, the nominee for national police chief.” Prabowo’s move ends weeks of speculation that the president was planning to appoint a new police chief following allegations of impunity, abuse of power and police brutality in the force when Listyo was in charge, according to The Jakarta Post. Listyo, who took office during former president Joko Widodo’s administration, has been in the post for over five years, making him the second longest-serving national police chief. During his tenure, the force faced major scandals, including the case of Ferdy Sambo, the head of internal affairs, who was convicted of killing his bodyguard in 2022. The country’s police also came under scrutiny during last year’s nationwide protests, when an armoured vehicle belonging to the force’s Mobile Brigade hit and killed delivery rider Affan Kurniawan. Since last year, Listyo has been embroiled in tensions with the Attorney General’s Office related to overlapping corruption and money-laundering investigations involving high-level officials at both institutions. When asked why Listyo had to go, speaker of the House of Representatives Puan Maharani told Antara news agency: “It was his time.” At his fit-and-proper test on Thursday, Suyudi presented his strategic vision titled Polri Bersama Masyarakat (Police with the Community), promising closer cooperation between law enforcement and local communities to maintain public safety and order. The commission has endorsed Suyudi’s appointment and approved Listyo’s honourable discharge. Suyudi, 53, has a long track record in the police force, Kompas newspaper reported. Since graduating from the police academy in 1994, he has held senior posts in the force, including head of the Criminal Investigation Unit at several stations and regional police chief. He has been carrying out his duties as the head of the National Narcotics Agency since August 25 last year. The number of high-profile drug raids under him counted towards his nomination as police chief, said Sugeng Teguh Santoso, chairman of the Indonesia Police Watch. “As a member of the National Police, he has previously led the National Narcotics Agency and has also served as chief of the Banten regional police, as well as the deputy chief of the Metro Jaya regional police. I believe this is a significant note that he understands the management of a large unit, including the National Police,” Sugeng told Kompas. Suyudi faced significant challenges, Bambang Rukminto, a police observer from the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies, told the newspaper. He would need to restructure the organisation, implement unfinished cultural reforms, and adapt to technological advancements, particularly artificial intelligence. Another big challenge would be to transform the force into an independent institution. “The independence of the police chief does not mean being opposed to or disobedient to the president, but rather how to lead the police to always adhere to the constitution,” Bambang said.

title: Asian Games: China’s Wang Xiyu ousts Philippines top seed Alexandra Eala in semi-finals
description: World No 85 Wang will face compatriot Zhang Shuai after beating world No 18, who was aiming to become first woman from her nation to win gold.
content: Philippines tennis star Alexandra Eala saw her bid for Asian Games gold, and ⁠qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles ⁠Olympics, end in Thursday’s semi-finals after a stunning 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 loss to China’s world No 85 Wang Xiyu. Top seed and world No 18 Eala was looking to become the first woman from the Philippines to win the title. The 21-year-old will instead go home with only a bronze medal, which she had also won at the last Games in Hangzhou, where she also won bronze in the mixed doubles. She had given up a chance for ranking points and prize money at the concurrent China Open to compete in Nagoya and may get a fine and ranking penalty from the WTA for skipping the mandatory event ⁠in Beijing. Eala said she had no regrets. “I’m really happy to have experienced this, to experience the ‌support ... and to be with the team and, yeah, to compete for the country,” she told reporters. Eala played two matches the previous evening but showed no sign of fatigue as she raced into a 5-0 first-set lead. Wang then began showing signs of life and went on to level the match in the second set before breaking Eala’s serve early in the third. Eala could find no way back as Wang closed out the match to set up an all-Chinese final against world No 57 Zhang Shuai. “[Wang] was more consistent. I had a couple of ups and downs during the match, ‌which is ‌something I have to talk to my team about and process,” Eala said. Eala was eliminated from the women’s doubles competition after she and partner Shaira Rivera lost in the second round. Eala last month became the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA Tour title. She has become wildly popular in the Philippines, her every match followed by large numbers of cheering fans. Wang may have her hands full against former Wimbledon and ⁠Australian Open quarter-finalist Zhang, who rolled back the years to beat Kazakh Yulia Putintseva 6-4, 6-2. Zhang has ⁠won medals at three previous Asian Games, taking silver in the 2018 singles in Jakarta and a team gold at her home Games at Guangzhou 2010. She will be in ‌her 40s when the next ‌Games launch in Doha in 2030 but was not ruling out playing. “I always feel like this may be my last Games. But look, aren’t I here again?” she said. “As long as you don’t give up on yourself, no one else in this world can give you that death sentence.”

title: Why Japan is looking to Ukraine’s front lines to overhaul its defences
description: A senior Japanese politician is in Kyiv to study battlefield drone tech as Tokyo seeks low-cost ways to counter rising regional threats.
content: Japan is increasingly tapping into Ukraine’s war experience against Russia as a valuable source of intelligence on military technologies that could strengthen its defensive and offensive capabilities. A visit to Kyiv this week by senior ruling Liberal Democratic Party lawmaker and former Japanese defence minister Itsunori Onodera demonstrates this interest, analysts say, against the backdrop of Tokyo’s mounting regional security concerns. Onodera arrived in the Ukrainian capital on Wednesday to meet local officials, including Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement. “Ukraine is ready to develop mutually beneficial cooperation with Japan, drawing on our experience and capabilities, and to identify areas in which our countries can strengthen each other’s security,” Sybiha said. Beyond bilateral security cooperation, both sides agreed on the need to step up pressure on Moscow, including cracking down on sanctions evasion. The trip by Onodera and a delegation of Japanese lawmakers was aimed at examining rapidly evolving drone technologies on the battlefield and assessing the extent of military cooperation between Russia and North Korea, according to a report by the Yomiuri newspaper on Sunday. The delegation’s findings will feed into Tokyo’s efforts to strengthen Japan’s defence capabilities ahead of planned revisions to the country’s three key security documents – the National Security Strategy, the National Defence Strategy, and the Defence Buildup Programme – with formal updates expected by the end of the year. Grant Newsham, a senior research fellow at the Japan Forum for Strategic Studies, said Ukraine’s experience was “very relevant” to Japan, particularly in terms of drones and unmanned aerial vehicles. “Onodera’s visit is just an indication of how seriously Japan takes Ukraine,” Newsham said, adding that Tokyo was particularly interested in Kyiv’s combat-tested missile defences. Although its current focus was mainly on surveillance and defence, Japan had also shown an interest in attack drones, Newsham said. “Drones and other unmanned vehicles are going to be an important part of Japan’s defence,” he said, further noting that Ukraine had the most extensive real-world battlefield experience among Western nations. Newsham said that Tokyo was also wary of a Taiwan contingency, especially if Japan itself “comes under attack”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but oppose any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force. In addition to learning from afar, Japan was also cooperating with Ukrainian drone developers, Newsham said. In March, Japanese drone maker Terra Drone acquired majority stakes in two Ukrainian drone start-ups, Amazing Drones and WinnyLab, to co-develop combat interceptor drones. Military ties between Russia and North Korea have grown in recent years, driven by Pyongyang exchanging munitions and troops for Russian military technology and economic aid under a formal mutual defence treaty signed in June 2024. Newsham said that North Korea’s military capabilities had improved considerably over the last five years, particularly in naval, missile, cyber and electronic warfare. “That alone is an increased threat to Japan,” he said, warning that the prospect of coordinated military operations between Moscow and Pyongyang posed real concerns for Japanese and US defence planners. This would require Tokyo and Washington to amass more combat power and stockpiles, including long-range precision strike weapons, missile systems and improved surveillance networks, Newsham added. “The ability to operate with a cooperative South Korea would be a major force-multiplier for Japanese and US forces,” he added. The economics of modern warfare Michito Tsuruoka, deputy director of Keio University’s Keio Centre for Strategy, said seeing how Ukraine countered drone and missile attacks was vital as Japan looked to establish new doctrines of warfare. “One of the most significant elements of the new way of warfare is the need to decrease the cost of addressing attack drones,” Tsuruoka said. “It is too costly and therefore not sustainable for us to intercept cheap drones with expensive air defence missiles.” Using costly surface-to-air missile systems like the US-made Patriot to counter cheap kamikaze drones is economically unsustainable, Ukrainian officials and military experts have said, as doing so rapidly drains vital strategic reserves. To correct this imbalance, Kyiv has turned to localised, low-cost solutions, including mass-producing interceptor drones at a fraction of the cost of traditional missiles and testing high-speed interceptor variants. “Ukraine is leading the process of making air defence more affordable and thereby more sustainable,” Tsuruoka noted. Masahiro Matsumura, a professor of international politics and national security at St. Andrew’s University in Osaka, said that as a two-time former minister of defence, Onodera was well-versed in the details of weapons procurement policy. “He strongly endorses drone procurement,” Matsumura said, referring to Onodera’s push to integrate advanced drone technology into national defence policy. In June, Onodera welcomed efforts by Ukrainian drone manufacturers to partner with Japanese defence firms, saying Tokyo urgently needed equipment “that is actually demonstrating effective power”. He also led a parliamentary delegation to Israel in January to inspect its drone and missile defence networks, noting at the time that such technology would be critical for formulating Japan’s future security strategy. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Japan has become one of Kyiv’s most important financial and humanitarian supporters in Asia, providing aid commitments exceeding US$20 billion.

title: Helena Law Lan’s horror film legacy; Hong Kong’s Gen Z jeweller: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From Peng Liyuan’s influence on China’s soft power to the future of heart health, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. How Helena Law Lan, 91, became Hong Kong cinema’s grand dame of horror Few figures are as synonymous with Hong Kong horror films as Helena Law Lan, who has been a household name for over half a century. 2. How Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan is a symbol of China’s fashion soft power Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan has long been a symbol of China’s fashion soft power at high-profile global summits as she accompanies President Xi Jinping. 3. The hidden risks of using Chinese medicine with Western prescriptions An elderly woman with a mechanical heart valve was taking warfarin, a blood thinner to prevent and treat blood clots, when she began using the Chinese herb danshen, often marketed for “blood circulation”. Her blood lost its ability to clot normally, resulting in severe bleeding complications. 4. Who was Wang Zhenyi? Chinese female scientist who defied gender expectations As moon-gazers look skyward during the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend, they should spare a thought for Wang Zhenyi, one of China’s most notable astronomers and mathematicians – and a woman. 5. Gen Z jewellery maker quit her finance job. Then she built a million-dollar brand Alarm at 6am. J.P. Morgan trading desk by 7.45am. Clock out at 6.30pm. Design custom jewellery until 1am. For months, Koyo Song ran her jewellery business, Benalor, while holding down a full-time corporate finance job in Hong Kong – surviving on five hours of sleep and her ambition to build her own brand. 6. Can potassium lower your blood pressure without cutting back on salt or flavour? For millions across Asia, high blood pressure is more than just a clinical metric – it is baked directly into the region’s rich culinary spread. From soy sauce and fish sauce to dim sum broths and salted egg patties, high-sodium condiments and preserved ingredients are at the core of daily flavour. 7. What’s the future of heart health? Cardiologists on advances, life-saving habits Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally, accounting for a third of all deaths. The tragedy? It is largely preventable.

title: Macroscope | Another Chinese bear market? Don’t rely on Wall Street forecasts
description: Investors should look to sectors that benefit from policy support while remaining sceptical about US banks’ predictions.
content: Last November, Morgan Stanley released its year-ahead outlook for Chinese equities. It said it expected “2026 to be a year for the market to strive for stabilisation and sustainability, before potentially clearing a path for a further major breakthrough, while dealing with several domestic and external moving factors”. Given that the MSCI China Index, which tracks Chinese firms listed at home and abroad, had already risen nearly 40 per cent in the first 10 months of 2025, the bank’s cautious optimism seemed sensible. Even so, the fact that many investors questioned why it was not more bullish attested to Wall Street’s unequivocally upbeat view of Chinese equities at the end of last year. Goldman Sachs, which had an overweight position in Chinese stocks, anticipated gains of 20 per cent this year, underpinned in part by stronger growth in corporate earnings and advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Bank of America, which also had an overweight position, said “authorities had successfully cut off tail risks, restoring confidence in market stability.” Fast forward to today, and it is clear Morgan Stanley was not cautious enough. Since the beginning of this year, the MSCI China Index has lost almost 14 per cent, putting it on the cusp of a bear market. Onshore stocks have also suffered. Since June 22, the CSI 300 index of Shanghai- and Shenzhen-listed shares has lost 15 per cent. Having been one of the top-performing major equity markets in 2025, China is the worst-performing one this year along with India. The deterioration is amplified by the surge in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, which is up about 20 per cent this year. Mainland China’s weighting in the gauge has fallen to 20 per cent, while semiconductor-heavy South Korea and Taiwan account for nearly half the index. At Bank of America’s Asia-Pacific conference in Hong Kong last week, “investor sentiment was strongest towards Taiwan and [South] Korea” while “China sentiment was mixed”, with strong interest in AI offset by concerns about the weakness of private consumption. The underperformance of Chinese stocks stems from a confluence of factors. The most important one is worse-than-expected economic data. Fixed-asset investment fell by a sharper-than-anticipated 7.2 per cent in the first eight months of this year while monthly growth in retail sales has not exceeded 1 per cent for five straight months, a figure Barclays called “an unprecedented stretch outside the pandemic years”. Citigroup’s economic surprise index – which measures how often data comes in above or below expectations – for China dropped into negative territory in May, just two months after reaching its highest level since May 2023. The unexpectedly poor performance of Chinese stocks has led analysts to downplay their bullish predictions or try to explain them away by pointing to divergences between offshore and onshore stocks. In a report on June 3, Goldman Sachs said “the [year-to-date] performance of different China indices shows the stark differences between different parts of the China equity universe”. However, the reality is that when it comes to Chinese equities, the forecasting record of Wall Street banks is poor. False dawns and persistent volatility have spooked investors and analysts. An overly bullish view of Chinese stocks last year has given way to an excessively cautious outlook. In Bank of America’s latest Asia Fund Manager Survey on September 15, China was the least favoured major equity market in the region along with India. That the weak domestic economy appears to be the main reason for the deterioration in sentiment casts doubt on the rationale for being bearish on Chinese stocks given that a deceleration in growth increases the probability of more stimulus. In a report on September 3, Morgan Stanley said one of the triggers for a recovery in Chinese equities was more forceful policy support: “Any meaningful easing would likely be a positive catalyst for both Hong Kong and A-share markets.” While measures announced earlier this week to lower financing costs and boost bank lending are unlikely to materially lift credit demand, much less fix the acute problems in the housing market, they send a signal that more support is forthcoming if domestic demand weakens further. Furthermore, it is important not to throw the baby out with the bathwater. Like China’s economy, the stock market is K-shaped. The Star Market 50 Index, the onshore gauge that offers the highest exposure to technology hardware, is up almost 14 per cent this year, outpacing the S&P 500 index. Earnings growth for the Star Market was a staggering 187 per cent in the first half of 2026, underpinned by policy “tailwinds from tech self-sufficiency progress”, HSBC said. Moreover, it is not all about AI. A gauge of Chinese bank stocks hit a record high last month amid stabilising net interest margins and higher dividend payouts. Passive investing no longer works in China. Investors need to focus on themes and sectors that benefit from policy support. The forecasts of Wall Street banks, moreover, should be treated with caution.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, October 2-4
description: An ice cream festival, yoga by the pool and a photo exhibition on Hong Kong’s neon lights are among the picks this weekend.
content: The National Day “golden week” break is upon us, and with it comes the familiar dread: packed MTR carriages, huge crowds and a slow-moving tide of visitors. But as always, there are several ways to escape the hordes, whether that is trying experimental gelato, practising poolside yoga or checking out an exhibition of Hong Kong’s beloved neon lights. 1. Ciao!
