Gelato Fest 2026 The city’s first large-scale Italian gelato festival is back at PMQ for another edition, bringing together 20 brands from Hong Kong, Macau, Italy and Portugal, with more than 30 flavours created specifically for the event. Skip the safer flavours and try less conventional options such as garlic, porcini, foie gras from brands like Edenly Gelato, I Scream Gelato and Kai’s Gourmet. For something less challenging, The Frozen Club is collaborating with Kwan Hong Bakery to offer Italian mochi ice cream in three distinctly local flavours – Hong Kong-style French toast, triple Ovaltine and mango pomelo sago – while Mamegumo is offering a tofu pudding brûlée canelé. The event runs from October 1 to 4 and October 9 to 11. PMQ, 35 Aberdeen Street, Central 2. Poolside yoga at Eaton HK Eaton HK is hosting a series of poolside yoga sessions curated by instructor Karen Chiang, running this Saturday morning on the hotel’s Wellness floor. The line-up features three classes for different energy levels and intentions, from a gentle Hatha session to a more vigorous flow and a yoga-Pilates hybrid. The first class, Morning Flow, runs 8.30am-9.30am and offers a nurturing Hatha practice suited to beginners, focusing on guided poses and breath awareness. Invigorating Flow follows at 10am for an hour, a mixed-level class built around a monthly theme that blends mindful movement, alignment work and skill-building. The final session, Yogalates Flow, runs from 11.30am to 12.30pm and fuses yoga with Pilates to strengthen the core, glutes and spine mobility. To reserve a spot, click here. 21/F, Yoga and Fitness Room, Wellness, Eaton HK, 380 Nathan Road, Kowloon 3. City of Lights Those hoping to reminisce about old Hong Kong have one last weekend to see “City of Lights”, a free exhibition at Blue Lotus Gallery in Sheung Wan. It brings together hundreds of previously unseen photographs by Keith Macgregor, who moved to Hong Kong in 1970 and in 2002 became the first photographer to dedicate a book to the subject, Neon City Hong Kong, documenting Hong Kong’s neon heyday. The show draws on Macgregor’s archive of images from the 1990s and 2000s. More than 100,000 signs lit the city’s streets during the 1980s; now, a few hundred remain. A companion volume published by Blue Lotus Editions expands the archive with essays and interviews; its cover is a collage of roughly 200 layered signs that took about 200 hours to assemble. Blue Lotus Gallery, 28 Pound Lane, Tai Ping Shan 4. Kalos Blocks x Coca-Cola pop-up The Kalos Blocks collection with Coca-Cola, styled as a retro American convenience store pop-up, ends this weekend. Highlights include a Coca-Cola vending machine that dispenses real drink cans, two blind box series, Coca-Cola crates, beaded phone charms, magnets, keychains, stickers and display cases. The collection reimagines familiar Coca-Cola imagery and everyday scenes through playful Kalos building blocks, with the pop-up also featuring photo spots inspired by the convenience store concept. LG2, Festival Walk, 80 Tat Chee Avenue, Kowloon Tong 5. Cyclone Philip Yung Tsz-kwong’s Cyclone is an alternately transgressive and lyrical drama charting the sexual escapades of a transgender woman fleeing her traumatic past. The film takes its name from the protagonist’s chosen alias – a literary allusion that may enlighten and confuse audiences in equal measure. It references Cyclone Mei, a fabled villainess from Louis Cha Leung-yung’s wuxia epic The Legend of the Condor Heroes. Forged by a tragic childhood into a ruthless killer, she is the rebellious idol whom our protagonist has aspired to become since she was a young, feminine boy. The titular sex worker of Cyclone – played with great courage in a layered turn by Chinese actress Liu Yuqiao – is a mainland Chinese immigrant awaiting gender-affirming surgery in Hong Kong. Facing thinly veiled prejudices over both her origins and her trans identity, she finds sanctuary only within the confines of a run-down brothel. Read the full review here. Cyclone opens in cinemas on Friday.

title: Hong Kong authorities probe Hotstone Yoga closure as customers turn to watchdog
description: Consumer Council says it has received 27 complaints involving HK$429,326 in losses related to sports chain’s closure so far.
content: Hong Kong authorities are investigating the abrupt shutdown of the Hotstone Yoga chain on Thursday, with customer losses of roughly HK$430,000 (US$54,800) already reported to the consumer watchdog. The Consumer Council said that by 5pm on Thursday, it had received 27 complaints involving losses of HK$429,326 related to the closure of Hotstone Yoga. The Customs and Excise Department also posted a notice outside the company’s studio in Kwun Tong to inform the public that it was investigating the matter. A customer who only identified herself as Chan told the South China Morning Post on Thursday that she understood at least 500 customers had suffered financial losses due to the abrupt closure. “Some [customers] said the company asked them to purchase extra classes on Sunday and Monday … There are some new members as well, with the most expensive package reaching HK$29,700 for 180 classes,” she said. Chan said she only received the closure notice from Hotstone via WhatsApp just an hour before her scheduled class at the Kwun Tong studio the night before. The notice, issued by law firm Cheung & Co and also posted outside the studio, said that the sports chain was shutting down after careful consideration due to “business operations and other actual circumstances”. It said the company would cease operations at the end of regular business hours on Wednesday, and included an email address for parties who had “rights, debts or other claims against Hotstone” to submit documents. The notice added that affected staff could inquire with the relevant government department about their rights and file related applications, and that Hotstone would provide the necessary documents and information “where reasonably practicable” to facilitate procedures. The company said it would pay wages for September and refund class fees from that month by October 5. Most of Hotstone’s social media pages were disabled by Thursday afternoon. According to its Threads account, the business operated for 10 years and had studios in Central, Causeway Bay, Aberdeen, Jordan, Tsuen Wan, Sha Tin and Kwun Tong. It also claimed to be the first studio to provide hot stone yoga sessions, stating it employed more than 100 veteran instructors to teach yoga, stretching, dancing and gym classes. Despite Hotstone’s assurances, Chan – who purchased an HK$11,880 package for 63 classes in July and had only used 19 sessions – expressed scepticism about receiving a refund. She said some customers had contacted police, customs and the Consumer Council, and had tried to request refunds through credit card call centres. Chan added that two instructors she met at the Kwun Tong studio on Wednesday said they had been unaware of the closure. She also spoke to only the staff member on duty, a cleaner, who told her that the company had instructed employees not to tell members about the situation. Chan added that the cleaner also said that Hotstone’s management had instructed staff to remove payment machines and customer information from the computer. Customs said on Thursday that the department had received reports regarding the matter and would take enforcement action if it found any breaches of the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. The SCMP has reached out to Hotstone and police for comment.

title: Hong Kong needs new funding model to draw investment from global drug makers: AstraZeneca
description: The pharmaceutical giant has conducted more than 60 clinical trials worth US$25.5 million in the city over the last three years.
content: Hong Kong can attract more global biotech investments if the city builds up a new healthcare financial model, according to AstraZeneca, a Cambridge-based multinational pharmaceutical giant. While global drug makers have been doubling down on investments in mainland China in recent years, AstraZeneca brought over 60 clinical trials to the city and invested over HK$200 million (US$25.5 million) over the past three years. Hong Kong was still a key research and development hub for the firm, David Fredrickson, executive vice-president of oncology business, said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Hong Kong has great science and a modern regulatory system,” he said. “[It] now needs to make sure there’s modern funding to go along with that, then I think that is a very compelling opportunity to continue to attract research and development investment.” The “modern funding”, which could come from public dollars, is supposed to be able to help cancer patients access personalised medicine and cutting-edge treatments out of pocket, according to Fredrickson. It comes as the world’s seventh-largest pharmaceutical company by market capitalisation is promoting the inclusion of lung cancer in the government-backed screening programmes in Hong Kong, a scheme that currently covers cervical cancer, colorectal and breast screenings since the launch in 2004. Fredrickson highlighted the effect of early-stage detection for lung cancer treatment. If a patient is diagnosed early, like at stage 1, the five-year survival rate could be as high as 80 per cent, versus around 15 per cent for those who are diagnosed late at stage 4. Early screening is estimated to help patients save spending to enjoy quality life. After low-dose computed tomography, a smoker needs US$14,122 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY), while a high-risk non-smoker would spend US$9,610 per QALY, far lower than the pre-screening threshold of US$24,302 to US$40,202, according to Herbert Loong, associate professor in the department of clinical oncology of The Chinese University of Hong Kong. In 2023, lung cancer was the most common and fatal cancer in Hong Kong, with 6,111 new cases and 3,880 deaths recorded in the year, data from the Hospital Authority showed. “The Chief Executive of Hong Kong has made lung cancer screening a priority,” said the AstraZeneca executive, while calling for a concrete implementation plan with a strict deadline to deliver real outcomes for residents. In a June briefing, the Cancer Coordinating Committee chaired by Lo Chung-mau, the Secretary for Health, mentioned that a local university had been commissioned to conduct a study for developing local lung cancer screening strategies. Meanwhile, lung-focused screening schemes are available in about 11 regions globally, spanning from the UK to Canada to Taiwan. “There is growing global momentum to put resources behind lung cancer screening,” said Fredrickson. Besides early detection, Hong Kong also needed personalised medicine and funding for new drugs, the AstraZeneca executive noted. “If they can come together, I am confident that Hong Kong will have an opportunity to make progress against lung cancer,” said Fredrickson. The oncology business is a major driver for AstraZeneca, contributing 46 per cent of total revenue by earning US$14.1 billion in the first half of the year. The cancer-related candidates also accounted for 111 out of 183 projects in the pharmaceutical giant’s pipeline as of July 27.

title: Hong Kong’s National Day perks draw locals, surprise tourists
description: Diners at Tai Hing Restaurant praise discount drive, with one saying: ‘The bill went from HK$89 to HK$62. It’s a bargain’.
content: Hongkongers have come out in droves to take advantage of restaurant discounts and transport promotions on National Day, while visitors have said the offers are a happy surprise. Businesses rolled out bargains and freebies to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China, which falls on October 1, ranging from restaurant discounts to free MTR rides. Residents were seen taking the train and visiting restaurants covered under the promotion push to capitalise on the slashed prices on Thursday, though visitors were generally unaware of the deals. At 10am, Tai Hing’s Tsim Sha Tsui branch was almost full of customers taking advantage of a 30 per cent discount on all dine-in bills throughout the day. The deal extended to restaurant chains Men Wah Bing Teng and Asam Chicken Rice, which are also part of Tai Hing Group. “I don’t usually come here, so, of course, I ordered the most expensive set, at around HK$60,” a Tsim Sha Tsui resident surnamed Wong said. “I also came on National Day last year for the discount. Having these discounts is great for Hong Kong’s economy.” A semi-retired resident, surnamed Chan, also visited the restaurant for breakfast because of the 30 per cent discount. “The bill went from HK$89 to HK$62. It’s a bargain,” the 60-year-old said. Chan said the restaurant was busier than usual and that he had queued for 10 minutes for a seat at 9am. More than half the people in the queue were tourists, he added. He also said he had no plans to visit Shenzhen during the holiday, as he was worried it would be crowded over the border. “It might be packed, and I’ll be in queues for a long time. I’m not sure if service quality might be affected too, making the trip an overall loss,” Chan said. More than 3,800 restaurants are taking part in the drive, with most offering discounts of up to 30 per cent or special deals on selected menu items on National Day. Hong Kong’s Immigration Department earlier forecast that the city would welcome about 1.29 million travellers from across the border during the mainland’s National Day “golden week” holiday, which runs from Thursday this week to next Wednesday. Some tourists dining at Tai Hing said they were unaware of the discounts. Jennifer Dong, who travelled to Hong Kong from Shanghai with her family, said she was pleasantly surprised to get 30 per cent off her bill. The IT professional said she had already spent several thousand yuan in Hong Kong over the past three days. The MTR Corporation also joined the promotion campaign, giving away 77,000 electronic single-journey rides in a lucky draw on its MTR Mobile app between 9am and 6pm. The rides can be used for Airport Express, cross-boundary and intercity trips. The Tsuen Wan line was busy by 9.30am, with families, tourists and domestic workers among the crowds. Sally Cheung, a beautician in her forties, was among those who won a free ride in the draw and took the chance to visit a friend in Mong Kok. “I saw the discount on Facebook last night and got up early to join the draw, so I thought, why not head out to Mong Kok? I live in Yuen Long, and the Tuen Ma line fare is quite costly,” she said. Cheung said the draw was better than nothing, but felt that the MTR Corp should have offered free rides to everyone. The public also enjoyed free travel on all passenger tram routes and on several ferry routes operated by Star Ferry and Fortune Ferry. At the Star Ferry pier in Tsim Sha Tsui, many of the passengers were tourists who welcomed the free rides. A Shanghai tourist surnamed Pei, who is in her twenties, said she had not known about the free ticket in advance. “We arrived, and the staff told us we could just get on board. They were really friendly, and the weather is great for enjoying the sea views,” said Pei, who planned to stay in the city for four days. Passengers were also seen lining up in Central to board the trams, which were all packed. Lew Liu, from Guangdong, also said he was unaware of the free rides until he arrived. “It is good to ride for free,” he said. “The ‘ding-ding’ is a special part of Hong Kong and I was hoping to take a ride.” Liu added that he would return to Shenzhen the same day, as he had other holiday plans.

title: Fully booked but half-empty: more than 1,200 no-shows at Po Pin Chau on National Day
description: Majority of people who registered to visit volcanic rock attraction fail to show as real-name booking system put to test.
content: Half of the visitors who registered to visit the volcanic rock columns in Hong Kong’s Sai Kung failed to show up on the first day of the National Day break. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said on Thursday night it had received bookings for 2,420 people, exceeding the official maximum capacity of 2,000, yet only 1,160 people showed up, a tally that included walk-in registrations. The booking system, which requires visitors to register via Klook using their real names, was introduced in August to better manage crowds at Po Pin Chau. Trial runs also suffered large numbers of no-shows. Earlier in the day, department Director Mickey Lai Kin-ming said about 440 visitors had entered the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung between 9am and 11am. He was at the site to observe the situation alongside lawmakers Perry Yiu Pak-leung, Vivian Kong Man-wai, Christine Fong Kwok-shan and Steven Ho Chun-yin. Describing the situation at Po Pin Chau as “generally smooth”, Yiu said the Legislative Council subcommittee on ecology and tourism would discuss the booking system with relevant government departments after the “golden week” break, review the data and explore ways to improve it. “We hope to give visitors a good experience, while at the same time balancing conservation, education and tourism,” he said. Yiu added that he hoped the government could improve facilities at Pak Tam Chung as a transport and tourism hub so visitors would know what to expect and how to prepare before entering Sai Kung Country Park. Fong said she had observed that local transport operators had adjusted their capacity based on booking-system data to cater for more visitors at certain times, describing it as an “initial success”. She said the next step was to collect data and consider whether visitors who failed to turn up should face penalties, such as forfeiting a deposit or paying a fee. Fong added that 94 per cent of those who had made reservations were from mainland China. Ho said facilities at Pak Tam Chung were very old and could meet only about 10 per cent of visitors’ needs. “You could see there were few people [in the tourism centre], many displays were outdated and even the windows had turned yellow,” he said. Ho added that a long-term plan was needed to manage visitor flows, including transport arrangements. Officers from the AFCD and police were stationed along the route and at the entrance, helping to guide visitors. Shenzhen tourist Yu Jun, 30, arrived with three friends at about 9.30am despite booking a 3pm slot. “I booked the slot about four days in advance,” he said. “We will be there for a while to wait for the remaining slots [in the morning], but if we can’t make it, we will go to Long Ke Wan instead.” Yu said they learned about the reservation system on RedNote and booked the 3pm slots through Klook’s app, adding the process was smooth. They were eventually allowed in at about 10am. Hong Youyong, 42, is visiting from Changsha with a 12-person tour group for three days. He said it was his first time visiting Po Pin Chau and that booking a morning slot had been easy. “I initially thought there would be many people during the National Day holiday, but it was smooth when I took the taxi here and not very crowded,” he said. He added that the guidance provided along the way was effective. Hong Kong is expected to welcome 1.29 million mainland visitors over the break, with Po Pin Chau emerging as a hotspot for hikers from across the border. The AFCD said on Wednesday that it would use drones equipped with broadcasting functions to conduct regular surveillance above the Po Pin Chau viewing platform and remind visitors not to cross the railings. The department’s “Enjoy Hiking” platform, which shows real-time crowd levels, reported moderate visitor numbers at 10am, with between 200 and 499 people at the site. The real-name reservation system applies from 9am to 5pm on selected weekends and holiday periods, including the mainland’s National Day break, which runs from October 1 to 7. A South China Morning Post reporter checked on Thursday morning and found that the first six days of the holiday were fully booked, with slots available only for the final day. Under the arrangement, a maximum of 2,000 people can enter the Po Pin Chau section each day, divided into four two-hour slots, each with a limit of 500 visitors. Sai Kung town centre was also less crowded than during last year’s golden week. At about 4.50pm, some visitors were returning by boat from nearby islands, but there were no large crowds at the Sai Kung New Public Pier. About 80 people were queuing at the minibus station for rides back to urban areas, in stark contrast to last year, when crowds filled the bus and minibus terminals.

title: Nearly a third of Singaporeans open to nuclear energy’s potential, highest in Asean: study
description: Singaporeans’ wider support for nuclear power was due to a lack of green energy sources aside from solar in the city state, an analyst says.
content: Just under a third of Singaporeans, or 31.4 per cent, believe that nuclear energy promises a clean power source with the greatest potential in the city state, representing the highest acceptance rate in Southeast Asia, a new study has found. The approval rate represented an 11.1 per cent increase from 2024, the Southeast Asia Climate Outlook 2026 Survey found, even as solar energy continued to be the most popular choice. Singapore is studying advanced nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors, as part of its long-term planning for a net-zero power system, but the government has not decided whether to deploy nuclear energy. The latest study, released on Thursday by the Climate Change in Southeast Asia Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and the Lee Kuan Yew Centre for Innovative Cities at the Singapore University of Technology and Design, showed that public acceptance of civilian nuclear energy is growing. In the region, solar came out on top with 65 per cent of respondents selecting it as a top two clean energy source, followed by hydropower with 33 per cent and biofuels with 27.4 per cent selecting it. Singapore showed a disproportionately higher acceptance of nuclear energy compared with the rest of the region, with experts and researchers noting that clean energy options were limited in the city state and opinions might change once the realities of nuclear energy, like facility location and safety, were brought into question. Tan-Soo Jie Sheng, assistant professor and Director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore, said Singaporeans’ relatively wider acceptance of nuclear power was down to a lack of alternatives aside from solar. “Singapore will continue to depend heavily on imported energy, but we have relatively few non-fossil fuel options for large-scale electricity generation domestically beyond solar. Nuclear therefore presents a different proposition: it could potentially diversify our energy system while providing a significant source of low-carbon electricity generated within Singapore. That may partly explain why Singaporeans appear more open to nuclear power than people elsewhere in the region.” Tan-Soo said on Thursday. The study, conducted from June 8 to July 13, garnered responses from 3,706 participants across all 11 Asean members, representing an increase of more than 25 per cent from the previous edition. The survey was available in English, Bahasa Indonesia, Burmese, Khmer, Tetum, Thai, and Vietnamese. Tan-Soo noted that the findings in the survey were consistent with his study on online perceptions of nuclear energy published in June, which found that acceptance of nuclear energy was the strongest in Singapore followed by Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Yet he noted that nuclear energy also had a regional dimension, since having a plant in one country would likely draw responses from neighbouring countries. “Whatever happens in Singapore will have implications beyond our borders. Nuclear is a long-term issue with a strong regional dimension, so I think it is something that countries in the region will need to discuss and work through together,” he added. In the Southeast Asia Climate Outlook 2026 Survey, unemployment and economic recession (55.3 per cent) came out ahead of climate change and extreme weather events (53.6 per cent) and domestic political instability (46 per cent) when respondents were asked about the top three challenges facing the region. On whether AI was good or bad for the environment, responses leaned positive, with 47.9 per cent seeing it as somewhat good or clearly good and 20.2 per cent seeing it as somewhat bad or clearly bad. Over a fifth, or 21.9 per cent, said they did not know enough about artificial intelligence’s environmental costs or benefits to judge, indicating a gap in public understanding of the technology’s footprint. Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said at the launch of the report in Singapore on Thursday that the energy crisis provided a good reason for the region to transition to renewable energy to deepen regional resilience, such as by advancing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ power grid. The Asean power grid, meant to function as a unified electricity grid, has been in the planning stages for decades. Fu noted that the Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project, which enables multilateral cross-border trade of up to 100MW to 200MW of renewable hydropower from Laos to Singapore via Thailand and Malaysia, had shown that multilateral electricity trade was feasible. “The next phase requires clearer rules for cross-border trade and practical norms for submarine power cables,” Fu said. As Singapore takes on the role of Asean chair next year, Fu stressed that regional cooperation was not just “good to have” but necessary and as some countries would have excess clean energy while others like Singapore would always be in a deficit, therefore, there was a need to find an alternative trading system for renewable energy. On how climate change could be balanced with economic needs, since a potential recession ranked as a bigger concern to Asean respondents than environmental ones, Fu said the ideal situation was to balance economic, social, and environmental issues. “Lacking any one of the three is not sustainable,” said Fu, noting how innovation in technology had to be done with considerations of its social and economic impact on people as well as on the environment. “If we can square the triangle, so to speak, it’s really the ideal and optimal outcome. And we are trying to do that, to find the right landing zone,” Fu said.

title: Tourists, locals brave the heat to enjoy National Day festivities at Sha Tin Racecourse
description: Spectators fanned themselves while watching special performances from acrobats, China’s Three Tenors and an action-packed race meeting.
content: Sha Tin Racecourse was filled with music, acrobatic displays and cheering on Thursday as some 10,000 tourists and local residents gathered to celebrate National Day. Despite Hong Kong sweltering in 33-degree Celsius (91.4 Fahrenheit) heat on October 1, spectators fanned themselves under clear morning skies, eagerly awaiting special performances for the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China and the marquee Group 3 National Day Cup. Jockey Club boss Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges said it had been a “good day”, with turnover at HK$1.6 billion (US$203.90 million). While turnover was up marginally today, it had been down for most of the start of the season, and Engelbrecht-Bresges had previously said he was trying to discover why. “We have the same number of people betting, but they are betting a little bit less per race and on fewer races,” he said. “So, we talked to around 500 customers and we explained certain things. The other aspect was I think we had too many races in a short period of time. I was really concerned because I’ve never seen anything like this, but let’s see.” The 11-race card drew almost 30,000 attendees, including Chief Secretary for Administration Eric Chan Kwok-ki and Hua You, deputy commissioner of the foreign ministry’s office in Hong Kong, who both attended the opening ceremony at the parade ring. The festivities were kicked off by the Cangzhou Acrobatic Troupe of Hebei Province, who showcased cultural heritage through their Dragon Leaping Over China – Flagpole Acrobatics performance. Spectators gasped as acrobats balanced heavy traditional flags on their foreheads, palms and shoulders. The troupe was followed by China’s Three Tenors – Dai Yuqiang, Warren Mok and Wei Song – who returned to Sha Tin Racecourse together for the first time since performing at the venue for the 70th National Day celebrations seven years ago. The trio captivated the crowd with renditions of “O Sole Mio”, “I Love You, China” and “My People, My Country”, instilling national pride alongside horse racing. Finally, the tenors led the crowd in singing the national anthem, accompanied by the Hong Kong Police Band, signalling the official start of the race meeting. Among the spectators were local racegoers Mr and Mrs Chow, who applauded the performance enthusiastically before taking photos with National Day posters. “The performance was part of it, but the main reason [we came to Sha Tin] was National Day. We really came for the nation’s day of celebration, and I’m very happy,” Mr Chow said. “Hong Kong actually lacks that kind of patriotic atmosphere, so when there are holidays like this, we should participate.” Attending the races for the fourth time, the couple said that, as Jockey Club members, they usually attend major race meetings only to “watch and take part”. While they did not believe the holiday necessarily brought extra luck, they still placed small wagers to “enjoy the atmosphere”. The event also attracted first-time visitors, including Russian tourist Gleb Kudriavtsev, who said attending the National Day meeting was a highlight of his 10-day trip across Hong Kong, Macau and Shenzhen. “We like this atmosphere. So many people, it’s very nice,” Kudriavtsev said. “We chose National Day [to visit] the racecourse.” Experiencing a horse race for the first time, Kudriavtsev admitted that working out the wagering options was daunting. “It’s crazy, so many positions, so many ratings – I don’t know,” he said. However, Kudriavtsev was optimistic about his debut on the track, planning to place a HK$50 bet with hopes of winning a HK$5,000 payout. “I want to win money, yes. I want to take a bet and win,” he said. “This is a great day for China and Hong Kong, and wish me luck.” Mike McCarron from the United Kingdom came to the track after his trip to see a friend in Hong Kong coincided with National Day. Having placed a “tiny bit” of a bet, he said his interest in horse racing stemmed from his family. “My dad used to [bet] back in England, so I thought I’d come for the races today,” Mike explained. To select his picks, he weighed various factors, including distance, race time, heat, weight, odds and jockey experience. “We check if [the horse] looks excited in the parade ring, then head out to watch on the barrier for the final stretch; it’s good fun,” he said. “It’s a bit of a risk, isn’t it? It’s a bit of a gamble, hence the name, but we’ll see.” For mainland students Tina Wang, Holly Huang and Cameron Xia, all first-year students at Hong Kong Baptist University, it was a special event during their break. “What attracted me most was the unique racing culture, which doesn’t exist on the mainland,” Wang said, noting they were also drawn by online promotions for the special National Day activities. On betting, Xia admitted the process was intimidating: “My mum told me I could place a bet after I arrived, but I saw the betting slip looked like an exam answer sheet, so I needed to learn it first.” The students also picked up commemorative horse items, enjoying the 30 per cent discount for the country’s 77th anniversary. “It looks really cute and nice, and it’s on discount,” she said. “So we will definitely buy one even if we actually know less about these horses now.” Also among the crowd were mainland professionals working in Hong Kong, Zhang Shuwei and Chen Yue, who brought a visiting friend staying for two to three days to experience the racecourse atmosphere. After watching the opening performances, all three members of the group placed wagers and tensely followed each race on the card before betting on the marquee National Day Cup. “I feel everyone’s spirits are quite high today,” Zhang said, explaining that horse racing provided a unique experience absent on the mainland. “It’s very novel, and there is a strong sense of participation. You can join in with just HK$20.” Having placed a minimum stake of HK$20 on the feature race and recovered her principal, Chen noted that betting made watching the action far “more exciting”, adding that celebrating National Day at the track seemed to bring some good holiday luck. “We plan to place one last bet before leaving because it’s too hot, and we want our friend to win a bit and leave happy,” Chen added.

title: Ukraine scrambles as Russia’s jet drones breach Kyiv’s defences
description: Daily strikes turn the Ukrainian capital into frontline city as Moscow deploys high-speed drones.
content: Russia’s new class of jet-powered drones rip across the night sky in Kyiv at hundreds of kilometres per hour, leaving Ukrainian air-defence units only moments to intercept them. It’s rarely enough time. With many of the drones getting through to the capital, defence manufacturers are scrambling to develop a new generation of interceptors to counter the deadly threat. They are building their own jet propulsion systems and training artificial intelligence to help guide the chase. They need to move fast because the Russian drones are driving a new tactic, ramped up in recent weeks, to hit the infrastructure keeping Ukraine’s war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centres, telecom networks, petrol stations and grain exports. Russia also has an advantage with its ballistic missile arsenal, which poses another challenge as Ukraine runs low on interceptor missiles. The effects of the barrage are being felt in Kyiv, which increasingly resembles a frontline city, without the relative safety that had long set it apart from the fighting. Food supplies have been disrupted, explosions echo day and night, and residents scramble for cover from strikes that reach closer to the city centre. Ukrainian officials say they are testing new interceptors that have successfully hit jet-powered Russian drones, which fly much higher and faster than propeller-driven drones and are much harder to stop. “They’re moving so fast that we can’t get a proper lock on them,” said Volodymyr Serdiuk, commander of an air defence unit. Building the prototype interceptors in sufficient numbers, and training pilots to fly them, could take up to six months, manufacturers say. President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for faster production. Air-defence crews have no time to wait. Facing constant waves of drones, they improvise, but lives are lost almost daily. Serdiuk’s air defence crew begins their night shift at 8pm. He studies a tablet connected to a centralised radar system to track the sky above his sector. A circle marks the stretch of airspace his unit is responsible for protecting. “It’s like chasing a pig in the forest,” he said of the new drones, which are based on Iranian-designed Shahed models. His son is serving on the front line in eastern Ukraine and now calls him in Kyiv just to check that he is safe, a measure of just how much life in the capital has deteriorated. To the west, the lights of Kyiv twinkle on the horizon. To the east, the green countryside and suburbs stretch into the darkness, with a power plant visible in the distance. Then a red marker appears on the screen, moving rapidly across the map. It’s a jet-powered Shahed drone. “Exit!” someone cries. Serdiuk looks up. Moments later, the Shahed streaks across the night sky. It is already beyond his unit’s reach. His team relies on heavy machine guns, but their rounds cannot match the drone’s speed or altitude. Then, a flash. Seconds later, the sound of an explosion reaches them from several kilometres away. In that particular attack, it was not clear if the blast was from the Russian drone that flew past them, as official channels reported, or from a Ukrainian air defence rocket, as witnesses at the site told Associated Press. The same sequence happened again and again throughout the night. Even if the drones pass directly overhead, “the problem is they’re flying too high” to fire at them accurately, said Sean Almeida, a former US Marine and volunteer for the unit. Ukraine’s air defences use electronic warfare and AI to steer incoming Russian drones into narrow corridors in the sky, giving interceptors a better chance of catching them. But the latest jet-powered Shahed drones are testing that strategy. The fastest Ukrainian interceptors typically reach 300 to 400km/h (186 to 248mph), not fast enough to meet the new threat. Crews have started training on a new interceptor that includes a cooling system to keep its batteries from overheating as the drone is pushed to higher speeds to match the jet-powered enemy. For now, salvation can appear on a radar screen as a blue blip representing one of Ukraine’s few F-16 fighter jets, scrambled to hunt down the fastest drones. They are capable of stopping the drones, but they need a lot of maintenance. Many are currently out of service and awaiting repairs. Casualty reports soon began appearing on news channels. A mother and her child were killed in Kyiv’s Fastiv district, one said. The deaths were from the explosion Serdiuk watched from several kilometres away. As air defence crews hunt drones, Ukrainian engineers are racing to set up industrial production. Ukraine had been warned that faster, jet-powered drones were coming, but manufacturers did not have a ready solution when the new variants appeared, said Oleksii Babenko, CEO of Vyriy Drones. Defence companies are now pursuing faster interceptors, new propulsion systems and autonomous guidance capabilities. The biggest challenge is scale. Acquiring components, testing designs and training crews take time. Miniature turbojet engines are one of the bottlenecks, with much of the supply coming from European manufacturers whose production capacity is far below Ukraine’s potential needs. At least one Ukrainian defence company has successfully tested an interceptor against the new threat. Babenko estimates it could take three to four months to scale up and close the gap. Military analyst Taras Chmut puts the timeline at six months or more. “Right now, we’re in a race for speed,” Babenko said, “trying to build faster interceptors and new solutions”. The improved interceptors cannot come soon enough for Ukrainians such as Daria Kuchynska. The 31-year-old had just stepped into the road Friday outside her Kyiv flower shop when an explosion from a jet-powered drone went off without warning. The blast threw her to the ground and filled the street with dust and smoke. Beside her lay an unconscious woman. Kuchynska checked for a pulse, but the woman was already dead. “So many people are constantly dying around us. I don’t know how we survive. It’s simply a matter of luck,” she said. “It’s unreal.”

title: India’s erratic monsoon plays havoc with harvests, raising fears of spending slowdown
description: Consumption typically takes a hit when rainfall is deficient, as weaker harvests mean less cash in farmers’ pockets.
content: For Ajay Kumar Chutani, whose family has run a sari shop in the north Indian market town of Karnal since the 1970s, the months after the monsoon are always his busiest. During these cool weeks, he sells enough lengths of silk and embroidered cotton to tide him over the leaner seasons, as farming families prepare for weddings and the frenetic festival season. This year, after erratic rains through the wet season and the country’s weakest rainfall since 2015, Chutani is keeping a close eye on the till. “The next three months decide our annual profit,” he said, adding he was hopeful for a sales increase. Across India’s northern grain belt, including in the breadbasket state of Haryana, farmers are bringing their harvest to market – a time of frenzied activity when seasonal windfalls dictate spending on special items from tractors to wedding gold. But this year, rice yields are down and costs are rising. Farmers say more chemicals and fertilisers are required to limit production losses. The monsoon is one of the world’s most important weather events, delivering about 75 per cent of India’s annual rainfall and determining livelihoods in a country where only about half of farmland is irrigated. Meagre harvests are not just bad news for hundreds of millions of rural dwellers – they also augur poorly for the rest of the nation, as the knock-on effects of weak rural consumption and rising prices spread, a headache for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) when it meets next week. India is also among the world’s biggest producers and consumers of wheat, rice and sugar, meaning shortfalls come with global implications at a time when large importing markets are also battling other inflationary pressures, including higher fuel prices. Knock-on effect “The monsoon shock is now less about rainfall and more about its income effects,” said Madhavi Arora, economist with Emkay Global Financial Services. “The risk is that weaker crop outcomes translate into softer farm incomes and hence slower rural consumption.” Cumulative precipitation during the June to September monsoon period was 12.6 per cent below the long-term average, the India Meteorological Department said on Wednesday. It comes as the current El Nino weather phenomenon, linked to weak rains across swathes of Asia, is expected to be one of the most powerful on record. Rice is one of the first monsoon crops to be harvested, and the grain market in Gharaunda – a 20-minute drive from Karnal along the historic Grand Trunk Road that cuts across northern India – was bustling last week with farmers bringing in their initial hauls. Jitender Sandhu waited for more than an hour for his grain to be unloaded, returning later to watch it be bagged and sold. It had been a weak harvest, he said, with yields on the 50 hectares (125 acres) he farms in Haryana running about a fifth below last year. Crop diseases also thrived in the dry weather, forcing him to buy more pesticides – on top of extra fuel to keep irrigation systems running. The pumps at his farm typically run off the grid, but overnight outages forced him to hire a diesel alternative. A weak monsoon typically means hotter weather and stronger demand for cooling, but also crimps hydropower generation. India’s electricity deficit surged to the highest for September in nearly a decade. Even as rice prices rise, it will not fully cover Sandhu’s production loss. “We’ve had to spend extra on repairing and maintaining water pumps and other farm equipment,” he said. “Diesel costs have also increased because we’ve had to run the pumps more often.” The erratic nature of the rainfall has also wrong-footed farmers. Mumbai recorded its wettest start to July in decades, but Maharashtra – the state where the city is located and a sugar production hub – has since declared a drought. In the north, heavy rain during the crucial grain-filling stage in Uttar Pradesh sharply cut rice yields. “When my crops needed water, it didn’t rain, but during flowering, it rained continuously,” said Jaipal Singh, a farmer in nearby Haryana, as fertiliser was loaded on to his tractor at the Gharaunda market after selling his rice. His yields were about 10 per cent below last year’s. Light rain, light pockets Weaker harvests mean less cash in farmers’ pockets, much of which must go towards seeds and inputs for the next crop. It also leaves less money for big-ticket purchases typically made at this time of year – and fewer customers for shop owners like Satpal Rana, who sells refrigerators, televisions, washing machines and other household appliances near the market. In the first three weeks of September, he sold five to six fridges and TVs. In the festival period, that typically rises to five or six a day. Many customers have recently made inquiries, but he is now waiting to see whether the purchases will come through when harvests are concluded. While the link between rural wage growth and agricultural growth had weakened over the past decade, consumption typically took a hit when rainfall was deficient, said Aurodeep Nandi, Nomura Holdings’ India economist. Big purchases such as motorbikes or tractors are often seen by economists as an indicator of sentiment, prompting them to watch brands like Hero MotorCorp, whose motorcycle sales dipped in August. According to the RBI, year-on-year growth in tractor sales slowed to 0.8 per cent in August from 28.1 per cent in July, while two-wheeler sales growth eased to about 20 per cent from 28 per cent the previous month. Even in the north, reservoir storage in most major wheat-producing states was at three-year lows, Goldman Sachs economist Santanu Sengupta said in a recent note. “El Nino-related weather conditions remain a key source of uncertainty,” he said. The full economic impact of the shortfall over the monsoon months will become clear only later this year, when winter crops are growing and more produce has reached the market. But it is unlikely to improve the outlook for already rising prices. Food accounts for more than a third of the retail inflation basket, and higher prices later in the year could spill over into other goods and services. Even before the full effect of the monsoon was felt, inflation rose to 4.82 per cent in August, its third straight month above the central bank’s 4 per cent medium-term target, driven by food prices. For farmers like Sandhu, near-term concerns dominate. He remains focused on finishing the second half of his rice harvest and will turn to wheat sowing next. His neighbours, he says, were similarly focused on battling through falling yields and rising costs. “Farming is our livelihood,” he said. “Almost every farmer in my village is facing the same situation.”

title: Maxwell smart: new Chinese embodied model tops global AI ranking on physical tasks
description: Developed by the CAS Institute of Artificial Intelligence for Industries, it scored 91.9 on the Meta-World benchmark – the highest recorded.
content: A new embodied AI model known as Maxwell – developed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Artificial Intelligence for Industries – has shot to first place on the Meta-World benchmark for robot physical tasks. Maxwell scored 91.9 – the highest ever recorded on the simulation benchmark. Meta-World was set up by researchers from Stanford University, UC Berkeley and other institutions to evaluate how well robots perform 50 everyday physical tasks. They range from grasping and carrying to opening doors and using drawers. The list draws submissions from leading teams worldwide, including Physical Intelligence, Google DeepMind, Alibaba, Meituan, Carnegie Mellon University, MIT, the University of Cambridge and the Toyota Research Institute. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Of the latest submissions, from July, second-placed FabriVLA – developed by Shenzhen-based Youibot – scored 90. SUREFlow, developed by researchers at Kyungpook National University in South Korea, was third with a score of 88.3. This means the Chinese large models are surpassing their American rivals on learning to act – beyond thinking and talking, they are entering the real physical world. Robots can already perform precise operations on assembly lines. But even the most precise work is often limited to fixed settings and preset commands. For robots to truly enter daily life, complete tasks on their own and adapt to new behaviours, the key is for them to understand the physical world by themselves. To complete a task in Meta-World, a model must understand the spatial relationship between objects and targets, carry out a sequence of actions such as approaching, grasping and moving, and adjust its actions based on contact. Beyond the score, according to a release on the institute’s website, Maxwell was able to perform more than 200 tasks without additional fine-tuning. Those included moving objects, adjusting positions, and operating switches and containers. In demonstrations, Maxwell could move a nut onto a target post, use a handle to open cabinet doors and drawers, and grasp objects and carry them across containers. The team also tested the model in LIBERO – a simulation environment that puts more emphasis on continuous operations. There, it showed the ability to connect multiple steps in different scenarios: turning on a stove and putting a kettle on it; placing a cup in a microwave; putting a book into a storage box; and putting chocolate into a drawer. Its success rate was 99.1 per cent. Maxwell is also designed for edge deployment – where the data is processed close to the user or data source, rather than through centralised cloud deployment. It has 1 billion parameters and supports single-card inference, meaning it also has relatively low hardware requirements. The achievement of the CAS institute is not isolated – many Chinese companies have recently made progress in this field. They include Beijing-based DeepCybo, which built physical foundation model PhysBrain. Earlier this month, the robot was assessed against 28 benchmarks and achieved an overall score of 72.5. Against other open-source entries, PhysBrain topped 14 of the evaluations and came second in 10 of them. It was just edged out by the best-performing closed-source model – OpenAI’s latest GPT-6 Astra – which had a score of 73.3. Chinese company Unitree Robotics also open-sourced a foundation model on September 10. It has 6 billion parameters and can drive robots to complete more than 60 whole-body mobile and tabletop tasks. They include organising shoe racks, cleaning a kitchen, arranging tableware, doing laundry, making beds and taking food out of a microwave – with the idea that robots could be trained as butlers. Once focused on making joints and motors, Unitree Robotics was previously seen as a hardware company. But public information shows that after going public, the company plans to invest nearly half of its IPO proceeds in research and development for intelligent robot models.

title: Health chief warns overstated claims of job shortages could lead to fewer new nurses
description: Lo Chung-mau says exaggerated claims of graduate unemployment could discourage new blood from entering nursing sector at city’s expense.
content: Hong Kong’s health minister has warned that the city will need to “bear the consequences” of exaggerating concerns over the employment prospects of nurses, as such remarks could deter new blood from joining the profession. “I do not want recent comments, such as claims that ‘[nursing] graduation equals unemployment’, to dampen the interest of our younger generation in joining the nursing profession,” Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said on Thursday. “Training nurses takes time, and [the number of nurses] cannot be increased overnight … if certain inaccurate statements affect our recruitment next year or in the period ahead, we will have to bear the negative consequences.” Lo’s remarks followed a heated debate over the employment prospects of nurses in the city. The Association of Hong Kong Nursing Staff on Wednesday renewed warnings over employment prospects for newly graduated nurses. The group had previously called for a suspension of the admission of non-local nurses through special or limited registration routes. The health chief stressed that the Hospital Authority had recruited 20 per cent more nurses over the past year and urged the public not to exaggerate individual cases. “In the discussion, especially by certain professional organisations, I believe any accusations they raise should be based on actual data, rather than isolated cases,” Lo said. “For example, some people claim they cannot find a job when [in fact] they were offered a position by the Hospital Authority after graduation but chose to take a gap year instead … using these cases to suggest that all nurses struggle to find jobs is irresponsible.” Lo said the authority primarily served poor, acute, serious and critical patients and might not always be able to offer nurses their preferred positions or hours. But he urged nurses to recognise their obligation to care for all patients. The health chief had previously dismissed reports of insufficient public-sector nurse vacancies as a “rumour”, saying that there were positions available but that some graduates chose not to apply for public hospital roles. The controversy was sparked by a complaint from a psychiatric nurse to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu during a radio phone-in programme a day after the release of the annual policy address last month. The caller claimed that nurses in the city were struggling to find work and attributed the problem to an “unwritten rule” under which the authority reserved a proportion of its recruitment quotas for mainland nurses. The row escalated when Tommy Cheung Yu-yan, a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, said earlier this week that Hong Kong faced a nurse shortage and supported importing overseas nurses, while suggesting that the caller was a labour union member. The caller later refuted this claim. The government later said that the authority had hired 95 per cent of local applicants for nursing positions in 2025. It added that only about 60 per cent of nursing graduates in 2025 applied for jobs in public hospitals, showing that not all graduates chose to join the public healthcare system. The authority received 3,000 job applications from newly graduated nurses this year and issued around 2,200 offer letters in the first phase.

title: China’s carmakers eye record 12 million overseas sales in 2026 as ‘go global’ plan pays off
description: Buoyant overseas sales could also cushion against a weak domestic market, which slumped 20 per cent in the first eight months of the year.
content: Chinese automotive groups have cause to celebrate their go-global strategy amid breakneck export growth in recent years, with deliveries in 2026 expected to beat expectations already buoyed by an international energy shock caused by conflict in the Middle East. Leading carmakers from BYD to Chery Automobile have doubled down on overseas expansion, with some evolving into powerful contenders in markets such as Europe and Africa, which were once dominated by the likes of Volkswagen. “A sluggish domestic market has been fuelling carmakers’ efforts to spur exports,” said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). “The export boom from January to August exceeded our expectations and we saw a hefty sales jump in the European Union and Africa.” The government-backed industry body recently forecast that overseas Chinese vehicle sales – which comprise passenger cars, buses and lorries – could top 12 million units in 2026, up 44 per cent from last year’s 8.3 million. The projected figure represents a 20 per cent rise from an earlier estimate of 10 million vehicles by the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. In the first eight months of 2026, China’s vehicle deliveries outside the mainland climbed 51 per cent year on year to 7.45 million units, CPCA data showed. Overseas sales include exports of Chinese-made vehicles and deliveries of Chinese-branded cars made in plants outside the mainland. “Chinese carmakers have reasons to pop champagne corks as some of them have already evolved into international automotive giants, several years ahead of their schedule,” said Phate Zhang, founder of Shanghai-based industry data ­provider CnEVPost. “Top players have stunned the global auto sector with their electric vehicles (EVs) as the Middle East conflict [that hiked fuel prices] piqued the interest of consumers in battery-powered cars.” Chinese-made EV exports shot up 70 per cent from a year ago to 3.46 million units during this year’s first eight months, CPCA said. BYD, the world’s largest EV builder, posted an 85.7 per cent year-on-year sales surge in the January-to-August period, topping 1.16 million units. At the start of the year the company targeted a 24 per cent growth rate for its international businesses in 2026. State-owned Chery said its exports between January and August soared 68.2 per cent to 1.34 million vehicles. The numbers stand in stark contrast to the carmaker’s earlier forecasts, which anticipated selling 1.5 million vehicles abroad in 2026, up 12 per cent year on year. If Chinese car makers achieved annual overseas sales of 12 million vehicles, it would translate into a nearly 12-fold jump from the 1.08 million units recorded in 2020, according to the CPCA. China has been the world’s largest vehicle exporter since 2023 when it overtook Japan in terms of overseas auto sales. Buoyant overseas sales could also cushion against a weak domestic market, which slumped 20 per cent in the first eight months of this year to 11.7 million units. Chinese carmakers, whose vehicles often sell at higher prices abroad, could enjoy a net margin of 20,000 yuan (US$2,975) per car in overseas markets – four times higher than at home, according to Nick Lai, head of auto research for Asia-Pacific at JPMorgan. On September 1, Beijing for the first time published guidelines governing Chinese carmakers’ operations abroad, requiring them to refrain from offering steep discounts in overseas markets. Analysts said a high base this year and a potential reduction in the tax rebate rate – a government incentive to encourage car exports – could slow the growth momentum in 2027. However, CPCA’s Cui sees it differently. “Chinese carmakers are [entering] various markets where demand for EVs is growing,” he said. “The growth trajectory can be maintained over a long period.”

title: Malaysian medical body raises alarm over high doctor ‘no-show’ rate in Sabah, Sarawak
description: The Malaysian Medical Association is calling for allowances and incentives to attract and retain healthcare workers in the Bornean states.
content: The Malaysian Medical Association (MMA) has expressed concern over reports of high “no-show” rates among medical officers assigned to permanent postings in Sabah and Sarawak. The medical body urged the government to take action by reverting to a percentage-based allowance and introducing incentives to attract and retain healthcare workers in East Malaysia. MMA president Sivanaesan Letchumanan pointed to reports which said that a number of medical officers failed to report for their permanent postings on Monday. “Some facilities reportedly received no new medical officers, while others recorded no-show rates of between 70 per cent and 76 per cent,” Sivanaesan said in a statement on Thursday. He called on authorities to verify and make the official figures public. Some facilities received no new medical officers, while others recorded no-show rates of between 70 per cent and 76 per cent MMA president Sivanaesan Letchumanan He said that the recent trend of contract medical officers declining these offers served as a warning that conditions in East Malaysia were deterring healthcare professionals. “This is not simply about permanent versus contract employment,” Sivanaesan explained. “Doctors may be required to relocate far from their families, bear substantial moving costs, and serve in severely understaffed facilities with demanding workloads and, in some areas, inadequate accommodation and support.” Sivanaesan said that workforce shortages and retention strategies were recently discussed during a meeting with Sarawak Deputy Premier Sim Kui Hian. “We must stop blaming doctors and start asking why the system is failing to attract and retain them,” he said. “An empty post does not treat a patient. A permanent appointment without a credible retention strategy is merely a number on paper.” To tackle the issue, the MMA lists several recommendations for government action, starting with financial and compensation reforms. The association called for a return to the previous percentage-based regional incentive payment. Additionally, it recommended establishing a dedicated East Malaysia service allowance for medical officers, accompanied by supplementary incentives. Beyond direct allowances, the MMA urged the government to overhaul relocation aid and clarify posting terms. Moving allowances should be reviewed to reflect actual costs and disbursed before relocation. For doctors whose long-term goal is to serve in Peninsular Malaysia, the association proposed setting clear, fixed time frames for East Malaysia postings, supported by a transparent transfer pathway upon completion. Finally, the recommendations addressed living standards and long-term career growth. The MMA said that rural living quarters must be upgraded to ensure they were safe, well maintained, and equipped with reliable water, electricity, internet connectivity and transport options. To further motivate medical professionals, the association said that rural service should count towards career progression, directly supporting postgraduate training, specialist pathways, promotions and preferred future placements. With Budget 2027 on the horizon, the association hoped that the government would allocate resources to strengthen healthcare incentives, upgrade living conditions and improve workforce retention. The MMA reiterated its call for Malaysia’s public healthcare budget to be increased to 5 per cent of the gross domestic product. This article was first published by The Star

title: Indian pride swells as Flydubai pilot who saved 174 lives hailed as ‘absolute hero’
description: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised Smit Machchhar for unlocking the cockpit door to avert a crash after his co-pilot’s attack.
content: An Indian pilot’s extraordinary bravery during an apparent mid-air hijack attempt has ignited a wave of national pride, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailing the pilot as a hero for saving 174 lives on a Flydubai plane – adding a dramatic chapter to a career that began almost by chance. Captain Smit Machchhar was critically injured after taking the brunt of a knife attack on Wednesday, but managed to open the cockpit door so crew and passengers could overpower the attacker. “Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO. In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi wrote on social media on Thursday morning. “India is proud of Captain Machchhar. Praying for his speedy recovery, renewed strength and good health.” Modi joined Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in praising the pilot. The Israeli leader singled out Machchhar for acting with “extraordinary bravery”. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” Netanyahu said. Social media users across India rushed to embrace their countryman as a hero. “This dude is an absolute hero. Saved everyone on that plane,” one wrote. Another, referencing India’s thriving Bollywood film industry, posted: “Indians will make a movie on this now, starring Akshay Kumar as the hero.” Machchhar was also praised in New Zealand, where he trained for 18 months. Philip Kean, an instructor at Mainland Air, told the RNZ radio station he was “really pleased” with how his former pupil “handled the situation, the best way he could with a knife in his side”. Flight FZ1073 was about two and a half hours into a routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when Machchhar’s Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked him with a knife and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max 8, according to news agency reports. Flight tracking data recorded the aircraft dropped 14,000 feet (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds during the struggle for control. Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia told state-run broadcaster Al-Ekhbariya that it received a distress call at 8.44am local time requesting an emergency landing. The plane touched down about an hour later, landed safely by two crew members who were travelling as passengers. Machchhar was taken to hospital in Tabuk city where he underwent surgery, according to the Hindustan Times. He is currently in a stable condition. “We are in touch with his family and assure them that we will continue to follow up on his health with Saudi authorities and extend all possible assistance for his well-being,” the Indian embassy in Riyadh said in a statement. Machchhar, who comes from Ghatkopar East in Mumbai, was living in Dubai for work, according to the Hindustan Times. His parents have left Mumbai to look after him. His LinkedIn profile shows he has been with Flydubai for four years, following a decade with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier. He has logged over 9,750 flying hours and has over 13 years of experience piloting the Boeing 737 fleet. His brother was also a pilot with the Emirati budget airline, Indian network NDTV reported. Machchhar originally studied management to run his family’s textile business before a chance seminar redirected his career into aviation. In a YouTube interview with host Zalak Mehta last October, Machchhar reflected on his unexpected transition into flying as a 19-year-old. “I attended an aviation seminar, where I first thought about becoming a pilot,” he said, recalling that his mother was initially scared of his career choice. His first commercial flight, he remembered, “was from Bengaluru to Delhi”. He is careful, though, to keep flying separate from his personal life. “When I get out of the cockpit or the aircraft, I don’t want the other guy to know that I’m a pilot. I don’t want to discuss aviation,” he said. “When I wear the uniform, then no nonsense and just do your job, finish the job. When you walk out of the cockpit, that’s it. Stop thinking about that. Someone else needs you now. The kids are there. They want to play with you.” The underlying motives behind the attack remain unclear. Flydubai issued a statement warning against “premature speculation”, Reuters reported. The airline said all flights between its hub in the United Arab Emirates and Israel had been suspended “while the investigation continues”. Before the incident, the airline operated 10 daily flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

title: Opinion | Disgusting Food Museum’s Hong Kong show has bull testicles and more. Is it in good taste?
description: The Swedish museum’s pop-up in Kai Tak features everything from bovine genitalia to insects. Is it educational or a ‘freak show’?
content: As someone who enjoys savoury, pickled and highly pungent foods, my interest was piqued when I saw that the Disgusting Food Museum had come to Hong Kong. If I loved even the strongest of blue cheeses and stinky tofu, surely I would have a good time at the exhibition. Founded in Sweden in 2018, the museum went viral through a mixture of grotesque fascination and cultural pushback, as critics questioned the fairness of labelling traditional foods – such as the Chinese century egg – as “disgusting”. The museum established its current permanent location in Malmo, Sweden, in 2021. Now, it has landed in Hong Kong as a pop-up exhibition – running until November 26 – at Kai Tak’s Airside mall. This iteration features more than 80 polarising delicacies from around the globe, showcasing them through real displays, replica models, scent installations, video archives and, of course, the infamous tasting bar. But is the travelling museum truly as educational as it claims to be, or is it simply relying on the shock factor for internet clicks? From bull penis to Pop-Tarts Upon entering, I am relieved to find the scents of all the real foods safely contained under bell jars – which staff will heavily encourage visitors to lift up. The artificially recreated scents custom-crafted by local perfumers are kept in spray pumps, providing an interactive opportunity for visitors to guess each one. I am then greeted by raw bull penis, cooked and eaten in various parts of mainland China for its supposed health benefits. Also on display are bull testicles, eaten in North America, where they are affectionately known as “Rocky Mountain oysters”. “Our goal is never to make it shocking or for it to become a freak show,” museum co-founder Andreas Ahrens says, adding the main goal is to educate the public about cultural foods, and that the perception of what is “disgusting” is simply a social construct. “We’re all equally disgusting,” he says. The exhibition highlights this by contrasting items such as Cambodian fried tarantula, Caribbean stinky toe fruit and Scottish haggis with mass-market foods including Pop-Tarts and KitKats. And then there is pork. Displayed as a piglet model pierced with needles, the museum argues that commercially available pork can also be considered disgusting due to questionable production methods including the use of antibiotics and poor farming conditions. One section of the exhibition also prompts visitors to consider foods we may be willing to eat in an age of food insecurity and climate change. “Looking back, many foods we now take for granted were once unfamiliar, rejected, or even difficult to swallow,” an exhibition plaque reads. While the labels provide a few sentences about where the food is from and how it is typically eaten, there is a lack of information about how communities have come to rely on certain survival foods or why they believe in certain health benefits. I also notice not all items are treated equally. Shirako (fish milt) is displayed as a sushi topping, and Pop-Tarts are presented with toasters. Meanwhile, Cambodian fried tarantula is presented in plain cadaver form in a display more befitting of a science museum. It makes sense that the exhibition needs Instagrammable items to draw people in, but how might the entire atmosphere change if all items were displayed in their full cultural and culinary context? Other than that, the bright overhead lights, holographic curtains and a wall collage of brightly coloured fruit are jarring and seemingly made for the sole purpose of selfies – in contrast to the serious and inquisitive ambience of the flagship museum in Sweden. Braving the tasting bar While I mull these thoughts over, I finally arrive at the tasting bar, which resembles huge purple lips with glowing LED lights. I start with a plain cricket; its body is woody and crisp, but its head has an unpleasantly bitter, pasty texture that leaves me wanting seasoning. Next up, Vegemite and Swedish cod roe paste (also known by its brand name Kalles Kaviar) are delicious and would be especially so on toast. And then comes the hakarl, Icelandic fermented shark, which Anthony Bourdain once described as “the single worst, most disgusting and terrible tasting thing” he had ever eaten. The bite-sized cube has an intriguing, surprisingly chewy texture but smells intensely of ammonia due to the high urea levels in its tissue. I manage to swallow it, though it would have probably tasted much better if I were eating it during Iceland’s midwinter festival – basically the only time it is eaten in the country today – chased by a shot of traditional spirit. I am just glad I did not need to use one of the exhibition’s provided vomit bags and become another statistic on the museum’s infamous “vomit counter”. Despite the slight gagging, I was enjoying the opportunity to learn about new foods. Throughout the tasting experience, Ahrens comes across as a down-to-earth person who genuinely encourages people to keep an open mind. He acknowledges that some visitors view the exhibitions as a novelty or a “freak show”. He cannot fully control how others will represent the exhibit on social media; the best his team can do is focus on educating people. While I found some of the foods foul-tasting, I do wonder whether branding the museum’s food as “disgusting” is the most proactive path to education. The marketing strategy seems to be “rage-bait first, educate second” – which makes sense in today’s attention economy. But I worry the museum’s branding may hinder its professed mission of breaking down psychological barriers. The pop-up is a fun excuse to go to Kai Tak, but I suspect there will be far more influencers miming exaggerated gasps for the camera than people who visit sincerely informed about international food cultures. The Disgusting Food Museum Hong Kong, GATE33 Gallery, Airside, Kai Tak, Kowloon, until November 26, 2026. For tickets, visit airside.com.hk.

title: Shows, tours and film as China marks 90 years since the end of the Long March
description: Communist Party has rolled out a series of commemorative activities to promote the historic trek and revive its ‘spirit’.
content: China’s ruling Communist Party is marking 90 years since the end of the Long March with exhibitions, tours, film and television productions as it tries to mobilise the nation to contribute to its vision for the future. Ahead of the October 22 anniversary, commemorative activities are under way to promote the history of the Long March and revive its “spirit”. The Long March was an epic retreat between 1934 and 1936 by the party’s Red Army to evade Kuomintang, or Nationalist, forces during the civil war. Red Army troops left from Ruijin and Gucheng, in the central province of Jiangxi, covering a distance of around 10,000km (6,200 miles) before they arrived in Yanan, a remote part of Shaanxi province in the northwest where they set up a new headquarters. The historic trek – embodying resilience and sacrifice – was a key part of the Communist revolution and its legacy is frequently drawn upon by Chinese leaders and state media to unite the party and the nation. President Xi Jinping called for a “new Long March” when he marked the 80th anniversary of the military retreat in 2016. “Today, the Long March of our generation is to achieve the two centenary goals and to realise the Chinese dream of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese people,” Xi said in the speech. The first goal is seen as having already been achieved – to build a moderately prosperous society by the party’s centenary in 2021. The second is to transform China into a modern, prosperous, democratic, culturally advanced socialist nation when the People’s Republic turns 100 in 2049. In line with Beijing’s emphasis on the Long March, local authorities and cultural bodies have launched a series of celebrations, particularly at key locations along the route. Exhibitions have opened in museums and memorial halls across Beijing featuring historical photographs and relics such as the wooden walking sticks and torches used by the Red Army during the trek. One of those exhibitions – “Promoting the Great Long March Spirit, Embarking on the Long March of the New Era” – has drawn large crowds since it opened at the Military Museum of the Chinese People’s Revolution on Friday. Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi attended the exhibition opening along with some 600 representatives of the military and the party and members of the public. Cai called on Chinese to embrace the Long March spirit and to unite around the party leadership under Xi to drive national rejuvenation. Interactive highlights of the exhibition include the “Frozen Memories” installation, which allows visitors to physically feel the biting cold experienced by Red Army soldiers as they crossed the snow-capped mountains, according to official newspaper Beijing Daily. Meanwhile, a five-episode documentary series titled Three Days in Zunyi – produced under the joint guidance of National Radio and Television Administration and Guizhou authorities – was released on Monday to mark the anniversary. The southwestern province of Guizhou was a crucial battleground during the Long March and it played host to the Zunyi Conference in January 1935, which is seen as a turning point in the party’s history. Facing setbacks against the Kuomintang forces, Communist leaders convened in Zunyi to review their strategy. The meeting ended with a leadership change that saw Mao Zedong, who later founded the People’s Republic of China, take the helm of the party and military – a move widely credited with saving the Communist revolution. The documentary series looks at the historical significance and contemporary value of the meeting and it will be broadcast across television channels nationwide. During the Long March, the Red Army spent the most time – and endured the harshest conditions – traversing southwestern Sichuan province. To mark the trek, the Red Army Long March Library opened in the Sichuan city of Luzhou on Wednesday. It houses historical materials related to the Long March and its opening was marked by the release of six new publications on the Red Army’s expedition through the province, according to state-run Sichuan Daily. It said the publications were based on archival records, field surveys and oral histories and aimed to fill research gaps on the Long March through Sichuan. In the northwestern province of Gansu – where three main Red Army forces converged to mark the end of the Long March – a tour retracing some of their steps has been launched, aimed at young Chinese. Visitors can follow some of the Red Army trails through the province, visit revolutionary memorials and sites, and see how the region has developed along the route. Meanwhile in Shanghai – the birthplace of China’s Communist Party – the Shanghai Symphony Orchestra hosted a special concert to mark the Long March. Featured pieces included the classic “Ode to the Red Flag”, the world premiere of “The Path of Faith: Spark and Journey”, which was commissioned to mark the anniversary, and the “Long March Symphony”, which debuted in 1962. Hong Kong and Macau also launched a series of activities, including a tour aimed at young people where they can visit the mainland and retrace the Long March, visit revolutionary heritage sites, watch stage plays and weave the type of straw sandals worn by Red Army soldiers at the time. Several new Long March-themed films are also set to dominate the big screen during the seven-day National Day holiday that starts on Thursday. Among the most anticipated releases are The Woven Promise, which follows a Red Army soldier’s decades-long quest to reunite with his fiancée after carrying her handmade sandals during the march, and Light Chaser, which is set in the aftermath of the Battle of Xiangjiang River in 1934 and centres on soldiers stranded in the mountains.

title: Australian man arrested in Hong Kong for allegedly carrying imitation gun
description: Suspect, 36, apprehended at Yau Ma Tei bar on Wednesday night, later rearrested after he allegedly smashed wall while in custody at police station.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a foreign man at a bar in Yau Ma Tei on suspicion of possessing an imitation firearm.
