The 36-year-old Australian was arrested a second time on Wednesday night for criminal damage after he allegedly vandalised the detention facility while in police custody. Police were first alerted at 10.14pm on Wednesday when a passer-by reported a person behaving suspiciously near an alley at 213 Shanghai Street while carrying a gun-like object. The suspect subsequently entered a bar at 192 Temple Street with the weapon, prompting another police report. Officers arrived at the scene and seized an air gun from the suspect. They arrested him for alleged possession of an imitation firearm. A source said the man smelled of alcohol at the time of his arrest. While in custody, the suspect grew agitated and smashed a wall beside a smoke detector inside Yau Ma Tei police station. He was arrested again for alleged criminal damage. The Yau Tsim district crime investigation team is investigating the case. In Hong Kong, possession of an imitation firearm carries a maximum two-year jail sentence, while criminal damage is punishable by up to 10 years’ imprisonment.

title: 14 new Hong Kong restaurants and bars in October, from all-you-can-eat Wagyu to froyo
description: From pizza and exotic cheeses to Korean pot rice and a modern British gastropub, Hong Kong foodies have a lot of new choices this October.
content: This month’s round-up spans the city’s most exciting openings, from a South Korean pot rice chain with more than 70 stores back home to a froyo counter tucked inside a Sai Wan launderette. There’s a relocated Michelin-recognised French-Japanese tasting menu in Causeway Bay, a neo-retro rooftop revival in Central and a Cantonese concept that curiously shares its name with a famous Michelin three-star institution. British pub classics land in SoHo, American soft-serve arrives soon and Wagyu takes centre stage in Mong Kok. Here are the places to check out this October. 1. Raf by Roucou Wan Chai’s Star Street precinct welcomes Raf by Roucou, a contemporary pinza bar from the team behind Michelin-listed cheese-focused restaurant Roucou. Named after the acronym for rape a fromage (French for cheese grater), the restaurant features pinza, a smaller, flatbread-based pizza that is popular in Rome, Italy. At Raf, it is made with a 72-hour fermented dough with a crisp, cloudlike crumb; flavours range from classic margherita to Umami Bleu. With the name Roucou behind this concept, diners can also expect a selection of fantastic cheeses. 8 Star Street, Wan Chai (entrance on Wing Fung Street) 2. Bar 41 Opening on October 1, Nina Hotel Tsuen Wan West’s new cocktail lounge on the 41st floor boasts panoramic views that have made this level a stand-out feature for guests. The drinks programme takes centre stage with signature cocktails, reimagined classics like the whisky sour, old fashioned, mojito and margarita, and bar snacks such as Wagyu burger with foie gras and chilli con carne quesadillas. 41/F, Nina Hotel Tsuen Wan West, 8 Yeung Uk Road, Tsuen Wan 3. The Grill Room The Grill Room has opened its third Hong Kong location at Grand Plaza, in Mong Kok, bringing Western-style all-you-can-eat Wagyu to one of the city’s busiest districts. The 6,500 sq ft (604 square metre), 144-seat restaurant has an open kitchen and bar, plus a private dining room, with exposed brickwork and warm timber finishes. Lunch starts at HK$268 per person, while dinner has three choices: Classic Cuts (HK$298), Signature Cuts (HK$368) featuring Australian Bell Valley Wagyu, and Prime Cuts (HK$468) with unlimited Japanese A4 Satsuma Wagyu from Kagoshima. A dessert trolley and free-flow drink packages complete the experience. Shop 208, 2/F, Grand Plaza, 625 & 639 Nathan Road, Mong Kok 4. Moon Lok Chao Shan Moon Lok Chao Shan has opened at Hong Kong International Airport’s Departures hall near Gate 28, bringing contemporary Chiu Chow fare to travellers. The fast-casual concept is anchored by an almost 60-year-old master stock, used in soy-braised goose meat, pork belly, cuttlefish and tofu with egg. The new mala master stock options add numbing heat. Airport-exclusive shaved ice desserts and playful canned drinks such as preserved vegetable soda and sparkling kung fu tea add extra interest to the menu. Unit 6Z514, Level 6, Terminal 1, Hong Kong International Airport 5. Amber Amber has opened its doors in Quarry Bay, but it has nothing to do with the three-Michelin-star French institution inside the Mandarin Oriental The Landmark. The new Amber is a refined concept offering creative Cantonese cuisine across 200 seats at Berkshire House in Taikoo Place. The ambience is one of understated luxury, with light blue-green tones, marble textures and modern pendant lighting. Signature dishes include the Spanish Iberico pork char siu, coffee bean-smoked pigeon that has been aged for 20 days, passion fruit prawn balls and black truffle abalone slices. 2/F, Berkshire House, Taikoo Place, 25 Westlands Road, Quarry Bay 6. Solsot Solsot, the popular Korean pot rice chain with more than 70 outlets in South Korea, has opened its second branch in Hong Kong. The new branch – on Kimberley Street, Tsim Sha Tsui – offers signature dishes like steak pot rice, abalone pot rice and cheese dakgalbi (spicy chicken) pot rice. Each set follows a two-step ritual: mix the rice and toppings bibimbap-style, then pour broth into the hotpot to create scorched rice soup. Sets include banchan, seaweed and a yogurt drink. 14 Kimberley Street, Tsim Sha Tsui 7. Chill Hill Chill Hill, a new frozen yogurt shop, has opened inside a self-service laundromat on Hill Road in Sai Wan. The chef crafts dense Australian yogurt bricks mixed with French cream, whole fruits and nuts, which are then blended to order. There is no refined white sugar or soft-serve fillers. Cups include Medi Delight, Very Berries and Banoffee from HK$50, while build-your-own options start at HK$40. The compact counter shares seating with the adjacent laundry, so you can enjoy a treat while waiting for your next load of laundry. Open daily except Mondays. Shop A, 31-37 Hill Road, Sai Wan 8. Commune Maison Commune Maison, a mainland Chinese chain with more than 100 branches, has brought its all-day dining-and-bar concept to Lee Garden Three in Causeway Bay. A relaxed, versatile addition to the neighbourhood’s dining scene, the venue shifts from casual lunches to afternoon tea and buzzy evening hang-outs, with warm, open interiors spilling onto the street. The menu covers Neapolitan-style pizzas, pasta, juicy burgers and all-day brunch plates. Drinks include global craft beers, barrel-aged cocktails, wines and speciality cocktails. Shop G11-G15, Lee Garden Three, 1 Sunning Road, Causeway Bay 9. The Boar The Boar is a modern British gastropub from the team behind Twist Pasta Bar, Terracotta Lamma and Honky Tonks Tavern. Expect elevated pub classics such as Scotch eggs with black pudding, prawn cocktail toast, loaded jacket potatoes and fish and chips, finishing with sticky toffee pudding. The venue has more than 20 rotating beers and craft cocktails, and there is an upstairs dining room. 55 Elgin Street, Central 10. Cardinal Point Cardinal Point has reopened atop Landmark’s Gloucester Tower in Central following a full neo-retro refurbishment. The redesign has tones of dusky amber, peach and rose tones, burgundy velvet, walnut and terracotta. There is also an upgraded sound system and a new lit outdoor DJ booth. The menu has also been refreshed with elevated Italian-American sharing plates, which include Reuben sliders, squid ink linguine, wood-fired pizzas and Wagyu sliders, and new signature drinks such as Larry Bird and West Face Killa. 43/F-45/F, Gloucester Tower, Landmark, 15 Queen’s Road Central, Central 11. Ankoma Ankoma has relocated from Tsim Sha Tsui to Causeway Bay, marking an ambitious new chapter for chef Frankie Wong’s Michelin-recognised French-Japanese restaurant. The larger 28-seat venue – a more personal, technically ambitious version of the original – features a private dining room, dedicated ageing facilities and its first pastry chef, Tina Lam. The 10-course tasting menu (HK$1,580) has doubled down on the Hong Kong influence, reimagining curry fish balls, lion’s head meatball and lo hei through French-Japanese techniques. Optional wine (HK$880) and non-alcoholic (HK$650) pairings are available. 16/F, Cubus, 1 Hoi Ping Road, Causeway Bay 12. Messina Wan Chai Gelato Messina has opened its third Hong Kong location, this time in Wan Chai’s Star Street Precinct, taking over half of Greek restaurant Artemis & Apollo’s space on Moon Street. To celebrate the occasion, the gelateria has launched three Wan Chai-exclusive flavours: the honey and yogurt My Neighbour Yia Yia; the butterfly pea and guava Fly Me to the Moon; and the lemon and olive oil, Scents of Santorini. Messina’s signature 40-flavour cabinet will be open for business between noon and 10pm daily. 9-11 Moon Street, Wan Chai 13. Teemtonefai To celebrate its 10th anniversary, ice cream specialist Teemtonefai has opened a permanent flagship store in Sheung Wan. Known for creative, quirky frozen treats previously only found at pop-ups, this beloved Hong Kong brand by Thomas Fung offers all-natural ice creams that are free from artificial additives. Teemtonefai offers Hong Kong flavours made with local ingredients, such as the tea-forward lychee bi luo chun (green tea) and caramel apple da hong pao (oolong). 19 Upper Lascar Row, Sheung Wan 14. Tienmo Tienmo brings Korean bunsik – street comfort food – paired with champagne, to SoHo’s Staunton Street. The menu elevates everyday classics with premium ingredients such as the yookhwe caviar gimbap, which pairs Hanwoo beef tartare with Oscietra caviar, or Wagyu truffle jjapagetti featuring Miyazaki A5 Wagyu. The table-side Korean fried chicken service features crispy chicken served with Kaviari caviar. 9-11 Staunton Street, Central

title: Vietnam charms Denmark’s Pandora into opening world’s largest jewellery factory
description: Vietnam stands out because of its skilled workforce, jewellery-making tradition and supportive business environment, Pandora’s CEO says.
content: Danish jewellery maker Pandora opened a US$150 million factory in Ho Chi Minh City on Thursday, its largest manufacturing facility and its first production site outside Thailand as it bids to diversify its manufacturing footprint and bolster supply-chain resilience. The Vietnam factory, Pandora’s fourth worldwide, will increase the company’s overall manufacturing capacity by around 50 per cent and is expected to employ 7,000 workers once it is fully operational. The company sold 112 million pieces of jewellery in 2025 and has until now manufactured all its products in Thailand, where it operates three factories. The plant, which Pandora described as the world’s largest fine jewellery crafting facility, will be capable of producing up to 60 million pieces of jewellery annually. “To start with, Vietnam will be around 15 per cent of our global capacity, but when we are at full capacity by 2030, it will be a third of our total capacity,” said Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier. “We’re building this facility for the next decade, not the next quarter … When volatility happens, we ‌focus on operational efficiencies and integration across the business,” she said when asked about trade-related uncertainties, including the possibility of higher US tariffs on goods made in Vietnam. Pandora, the world’s biggest jewellery brand by items sold, sells silver charm bracelets from US$80 and counts the United States as its biggest market. The factory, built on a 7.5-hectare (18.5-acre) site in business and manufacturing hub Ho Chi Minh City, will support demand across Pandora’s global business rather than serve specific export markets. De Pablos-Barbier, who took charge on January 1, said Vietnam stood out among potential locations because of its skilled workforce, long jewellery-making tradition, strong infrastructure and supportive business environment. The factory will also play a key role in the company’s plans to expand its production of platinum-plated jewellery as it diversifies beyond its traditional focus on silver and reduces its exposure to wild swings in the silver market. The facility has achieved LEED ‌Gold certification and will operate solely on renewable electricity. All silver and gold used at the site will be recycled, and the company is exploring additional renewable energy options, including on-site solar generation and a potential solar farm partnership.

title: Hong Kong power outages hit Ho Man Tin, disrupting 1,000 households and hotel
description: First of two outages lasted more than four hours overnight into Thursday after equipment near Waterloo Road malfunctioned.
content: Two power outages hit Hong Kong’s Ho Man Tin, the first lasting more than four hours overnight into Thursday, disrupting hotel operations and about 1,000 households. CLP Power, which supplies electricity to Kowloon and the New Territories, said equipment near Waterloo Road in Kowloon first malfunctioned at 11.18pm on Wednesday, affecting about 1,000 customers. “After CLP Power’s engineering personnel conducted an emergency repair and deployed some mobile electricity generators at the scene, the power supply was resumed at 3.47am on Thursday,” a spokesman said. “As residents consumed power on Thursday morning, the temporary power supply experienced instability due to heavy load, temporarily affecting power supply for about 650 customers. Following emergency repairs, electricity was progressively restored to the affected customers by 8am.” CLP said its community support team and customer service managers stayed in contact and coordinated with the Home Affairs Department’s district office, district councillors and property management companies. It added that it had provided batteries and emergency lighting systems to affected buildings and properties. Police received four reports of power outages between 11.36pm on Wednesday and 1am on Thursday from residents on Waterloo Road and Argyle Street. The Fire Services Department also received three reports at around 11.30pm on Wednesday of people trapped in lifts in buildings on Argyle Street and Waterloo Road. An elderly man wearing an oxygen tube in his nose was seen being taken away by ambulance from Richland House on Waterloo Road. The outage also affected operations at Metropark Hotel Kowloon, where staff used flashlights and visitors sat in the lobby. A tourist told the media that his hotel room had no air conditioning, so he had to cool off on the street. He added that the hotel’s lights and one of its lifts were still working. Some residents also took to social media with one user saying she could not get home and had to stay on the street.

title: Asian Games, day 12: Hong Kong cyclists add track silvers to sailing, squash medals
description: Ceci Lee and Chloe Leung leave it late in women’s Madison, Chu Tsun-wai second in men’s omnium. Rugby sevens stars up and running.
content: Hong Kong’s athletes edged the city ever closer to another historic medal haul at the Asian Games on Thursday, with the cyclists, sailors and men’s squash team all adding to the tally. The women’s squash team have guaranteed themselves at least a silver on Friday, while tennis star Coleman Wong Chak-lam eased into the semi-finals of the men’s singles, and in rugby sevens, the men began the defence of their title with two dominant performances in Nagoya. Ever since the schedule came out, there has been a certain anticipation surrounding Ceci Lee Sze-wing’s arrival on the track at the Izu Velodrome, and the triple National Games gold medallist did not disappoint. She and partner Chloe Leung Wing-yee grabbed a breathtaking silver in the women’s Madison, denying China at the very last in a race Japan won at a canter. Lee and Leung waited until the final moments to grab the sprint points they needed, finishing on 31, with China taking bronze on 30. The hosts, who led from start to finish, claimed gold with 53. Leung said the medal was “like medicine” after she was injured in the build-up to the Games, and then finished with bronze in the women’s road race. “I’ve been on a roller coaster,” she said. “It’s been a long 10 days. In the road race I didn’t perform well. My mood was down, way at the bottom. After that, I had to give everything I have.” Soon after, teammate Chu Tsun-wai added another silver in the men’s omnium, taking the city’s medal haul to five for the day, and making it 40 overall. Earlier, the city’s sailors had claimed a silver and bronze in the men’s and women’s skiff events. After a frustrating few days on the water, Russell Aylsworth and partner Akira Luke Sakai got some racing done and claimed bronze in the men’s skiff. China took gold and India silver. While Aylsworth admitted to being disappointed the pair had not managed to grab silver, he acknowledged some relief that they were able to get on the podium at all. “We’re quite happy and proud to come home with a medal, because there was one point in the race where it was looking like we would be empty-handed,” Aylsworth said. “I’m just proud that we can get another medal for home.” Soon after, women’s pair Emily Poulson and Tiffany Mak Hui-tung won silver, finishing just behind hosts Japan. China claimed bronze. The 17-year-old Poulson said that when it had first been suggested two years ago that the pair could win a medal in Japan, the immediate response was “that seems nearly impossible”. “And to be standing here today with the silver medal, I am happy about it,” she added. “We’re fairly new, I think we’re the youngest here. I mean, you put it into perspective; it’s a good result for us. So we’re very happy with it.” There will be at least a silver in women’s team squash, after Hong Kong battled past India in their semi-final. Tomato Ho Tze-lok’s victory over Joshna Chinappa secured Hong Kong a place in Friday’s final, after a back-and-forth tussle at Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena. Ho’s 3-0 win in the final match gave Hong Kong a 2-1 triumph after Chan Sin-yuk had fought her way past individual silver medallist Anahat Singh, only for Tanvi Khanna to even things up by beating Lee Ka-yi. “I haven’t played the deciding match for many years, so I had almost forgotten how nervous it can be,” Ho said. “I was a bit tense, but I didn’t want to show it. I just wanted to look very calm to the others. “Luckily, I could feel their power and support, so I wanted to fight back.” Malaysia await Ho and her teammates in the final. The men, however, had to settle for bronze after losing 2-1 to Pakistan in their semi-final. Elsewhere, the city’s men began the defence of their rugby sevens gold medal with comfortable wins over Uzbekistan and Malaysia in Pool A. Hong Kong outscored their opponents 93-0, and captain James Christie said the most pleasing part of the day had been shutting out the opposition. “We always talk about how defence wins tournaments, and that’s obviously shown today,” he said. The women, meanwhile, swept past India 33-7 in their opening encounter in Pool E, and then saw off Malaysia 36-12. Tennis top seed Coleman Wong Chak-lam had little trouble in his men’s singles quarter-final, cruising past Thailand’s Kasidit Samrej 6-3, 6-0. “At the previous Asian Games, I actually played in three events, but this time I’m really focused solely on the singles,” Wong said. “This means I can focus very intently on taking it one match at a time, match by match. I’m really happy to get through this round today.”

title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives 2 doses of lethal drug
description: Governor orders independent review after state fails to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike.
content: Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Pike to death on Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug. A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee’s governor halted the remaining execution for the rest of the year. Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her lawyers said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they had not been told about her condition. She had been scheduled for execution at 10am on Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the US Supreme Court overturned that stay. Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers said in court filings late Wednesday. Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the remaining scheduled execution would not take place this year. “Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said. The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office”. The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set. Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre, said what Pike experienced was “singular and unparalleled”. Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said. Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7.27pm, showing Pike strapped to a gurney. “I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words. She described herself as at peace. But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing. By 8.26pm, execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered. Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8.53pm. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area. Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and a district court. It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution. In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital. Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case garnered widespread attention in part because of a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s. Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit US Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing. Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1 per cent of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the US this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday. Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.

title: Hong Kong marks National Day with fireworks, discounts as Lee hails city’s global role
description: City leader John Lee highlights Hong Kong’s international role and strategic goals as a market economy under ‘one country, two systems’.
content: Hong Kong marked National Day on Thursday with discounts, free rides and a fireworks display that drew huge crowds to Victoria Harbour, while the chief executive emphasised the city’s international role and its first five-year plan. About 380,000 spectators packed both sides of the harbour for the 23-minute fireworks show in the evening, as businesses dished out dining discounts and shopping deals, while some transport operators provided free rides. More than 3,800 restaurants offered up to 30 per cent discounts or special deals on selected menu items. Addressing a National Day reception earlier in the day, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said Hong Kong needed a blueprint with strategic vision amid a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape and rapid advances in artificial intelligence. He highlighted three features of the five-year plan unveiled last month. “[It] adheres to the ‘one country, two systems’ principle. This means that the five-year plan must be developed under the Basic Law framework,” Lee said, referring to the city’s mini-constitution. “The Basic Law expressly provides for the practice of capitalism and the common law system, as well as the free flow of capital, people, goods and information in Hong Kong, while the first five-year plan stresses a market economy and upholds the two-pronged approach of ‘effective market’ and ‘capable government’.” Lee said another feature was to clearly define Hong Kong’s strategic place in the world, with both the five-year plan and his latest policy address attaching importance to the city’s global role. “The two documents reiterate the importance and establishment of Hong Kong’s global positioning, which powerfully illustrates that it is part of our city’s DNA,” he said. “One of the initiatives for implementing the first five-year plan is to fully leverage Hong Kong’s unique advantage as a connector between the country and the rest of the world. “The ultimate focus of the plan is, in fact, to capitalise on this aggregate advantage: drawing on the momentum of the country’s development to gain stable support, while leveraging an international platform to access global resources and achieve two-way interaction.” Lee said the five-year plan leveraged Hong Kong’s unique strengths and would guide the formulation of policies and major projects grounded in the city’s actual conditions and characteristics. He said the aim of the blueprint was not merely to list a series of measures, but to lay out a strategic plan that exploited the advantages of one country, two systems to help Hong Kong seize opportunities that aligned with national development. “Time and tide wait for no man. We must act decisively and respond to changing circumstances by formulating the five-year plan to ride the wave of opportunities, keep pace with the times, and integrate into and serve the overall national development,” he said. “This can only boost Hong Kong’s progress and allow the people of Hong Kong to enjoy more development dividends.” Concluding his speech, Lee described the blueprint as the fruit of collective wisdom gathered through extensive public consultation. He said it would drive reform, unlock opportunities and improve people’s livelihoods. To underline the importance of concerted efforts, he quoted a line from Huainanzi - The Ruler’s Techniques: “Victory is ensured when people pool their strength; success is secured when people put their heads together.” The line, from a work by Liu An, a grandson of the founding emperor of the Western Han dynasty, was also cited by Chinese President Xi Jinping in his keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the World Economic Forum in 2017. “I am confident that as long as we, each dedicated to our respective roles, join hands and work in synergy with one another, Hong Kong will certainly be able to set out on a path to a brighter and more prosperous future,” Lee said. Hong Kong’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, also addressed the reception from aboard the Tiangong space station to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Lai said she was proud to celebrate from the Tiangong, adding that being part of a national space mission filled her with confidence about the country’s strength. “Our country’s full support is always the strongest backdrop and the greatest source of confidence for Hong Kong and Macau,” she said. Crowds began gathering on both sides of the harbour hours before the 8pm fireworks display, despite temperatures topping 33 degrees Celsius. The show, themed “Eternal Radiance”, elicited cheers as red hearts, smiley faces and cascading ribbons of light burst across the skyline. Fujian visitor Fanny Yao, 34, who had waited with her family since 6pm, said watching the National Day fireworks in Hong Kong had become “a ritual”. Across the city, visitors filled shopping districts and tourist attractions on the first day of the mainland’s National Day “golden week” break, while Hongkongers headed north for shopping, dining and leisure activities. Students Ni Xinyi and Wang Han, both 23, travelled by high-speed rail from Zhejiang for a two-day Ho visit but chose to stay in Shenzhen, saying they could save as much as 3,000 yuan (US$420) on accommodation. Others headed for the outdoors, with hundreds of hikers visiting Po Pin Chau in Sai Kung. The scenic attraction is operating under the city’s first countryside real-name reservation system during the holiday, with authorities saying 1,160 people showed up between 9am and 5pm – fewer than half of the 2,420 who registered. Shenzhen tourist Yu Jun, 30, arrived with three friends at about 9.30am despite holding 3pm reservations, hoping to enter early. They were eventually admitted at about 10am. Hongkongers, meanwhile, streamed across the border to Shenzhen for shopping, meals and services. Retiree Lina Li, 58, said she planned to spend more than HK$1,000 on food, a massage and a head spa. “A massage in Hong Kong can cost over HK$700, but in Shenzhen I can get a really good one for about HK$300,” she said. At Victoria Park in Causeway Bay, thousands visited the International Lantern Spectacular, which has recorded about 580,000 visits since opening on September 17, with peak daily attendance exceeding 200,000. At Sha Tin Racecourse, crowds gathered for the National Day race day, with performances by acrobats, a tenor trio and the police band ahead of the meeting. Additional reporting by Lo Hoi-ying, Jess Ma and Lexi Tian

title: 439,532 mainland Chinese trips made to Hong Kong over Mid-Autumn break
description: Visitors from the mainland made nearly 440,000 trips to Hong Kong over the extended Mid-Autumn Festival weekend.
content:
Visitors from mainland China made nearly 440,000 trips to Hong Kong over the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend. According to figures released on Monday, Hong Kong’s Immigration Department recorded 439,532 inbound trips by mainland visitors from September 25 to 27.
The figure accounted for about a quarter of the 1.73 million inbound trips, including those made by Hong Kong residents, during the three-day period.
The Immigration Department also said it expected about 1.29 million mainland visitors to arrive in the city during China’s seven-day National Day golden week holiday, which began today.
It also forecast that the average daily number of visitor arrivals from across the border would surpass last year’s figure by more than 5 per cent.
If mainland residents combine this golden week with the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival break at the end of September, taking an additional three days of leave from Monday to Wednesday, they would be able to enjoy a continuous 13-day holiday.
Travel Industry Council chairman Tommy Tam said the sector’s own National Day holiday estimate was in line with the government’s forecast.
“Of course, in traditional popular districts, such as Tsim Sha Tsui, Causeway Bay and Central, [hotel occupancy rates] will exceed 90 per cent,” he told a radio programme. “And I heard from the industry that room rates this year have increased by nearly double digits.”
Hotel prices in Causeway Bay, for example, were significantly higher for October 1 to 3 – during the National Day holiday – than for September 29 and 30, according to searches by the South China Morning Post on booking platform Trip.com.
Average nightly prices rose by between 36 per cent and more than 230 per cent across budget, mid-range and luxury hotels. For example, a room at the Regal Hongkong Hotel in Causeway Bay, for example, rose by 65 per cent from HK$828 to HK$1,367, including taxes and fees, according to prices on Trip.com.
Tam said visitors were opting for staggered travel arrangements and multi-destination itineraries, arriving in Hong Kong a few days early or late before continuing to Macau or other cities in the Greater Bay Area.
He also said the industry was optimistic about spending on catering and high-end retail businesses.
Geoparks in rural areas are among the destinations that have gained popularity with mainland visitors.
But official data showed that about half of those who reserved places for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail failed to show up.
During the initial trial weekend, only about 1,560 people arrived despite more than 3,200 bookings. During the Mid-Autumn Festival period, an average of about 1,170 visitors showed up each day, compared with 2,360 reservations.
Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan, who represents the New Territories South East constituency, suggested introducing an admission fee or deposit to reduce the number of no-shows.
“I referenced, for example, mainland geological parks in Shenzhen and other places. They actually charge about 80 to 100 yuan [HK$93 to HK$117], so I think the deposit could be similar to these fees,” she said.
Authorities have said they will conduct a comprehensive review of the reservation system after the National Day holiday period is over. The “golden week” ends next Thursday.

title: Beijing slams ‘harassment’ after Manila challenges research ship near Batanes
description: The Philippines claims the Jia Hai Ke 7 has been ‘loitering’ near islands that have become a flashpoint amid boundary talks.
content: China and the Philippines have launched a war of words after their coastguards challenged each other in the waters off the Batanes Islands, an area that has become the latest maritime flashpoint as Beijing ramps up pressure against Manila-Tokyo delimitation efforts. The Philippine coastguard said on Thursday it had sent one of its biggest vessels and an aircraft to “disrupt and drive away” a Chinese research ship – the Jia Hai Ke 7 – which has been operating in the waters off the islands over the past several days. “At 7.55am, BRP Teresa Magbanua closed in on Jia Hai Ke 7 to less than 100 yards (91 metres) and launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to disrupt the research vessel’s illegal marine scientific research and compel it to leave the area,” coastguard spokesman Jay Tarriela said in a post on social media. The Jia Hai Ke 7 has spent more than a week conducting operations near the Philippines’ Batanes archipelago, located between the country’s Luzon island and Taiwan. Footage posted by Tarriela showed the Philippine coastguard issuing radio warnings and one of its inflatable boats circling the Chinese vessel. He added that the coastguard aircraft, the PCG Islander 251, circled the area several times at low altitude to support the operation, vowing to continue to “challenge, disrupt and drive away the survey vessel until it leaves Philippine waters”. During the operation, a Chinese coastguard vessel “abruptly” arrived in the area to shield the survey ship and moved towards the Philippine ship while repeatedly issuing radio challenges, Tarriela said. The Philippine ship then “shadowed” the Chinese coastguard vessel from about 1,000 yards away while remaining close to the research ship, he added. He said the presence of the Chinese coastguard “raises serious questions about who Jia Hai Ke 7 is really working for” and “what data the vessel has collected over the country’s undersea cable corridors”. In response, Beijing denounced Manila’s “harassment” and insisted its research vessel was conducting “normal operations in waters under Chinese jurisdiction” in accordance with international law. “China has taken, and will continue to take, resolute measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests,” Guo Wei, deputy spokesman of the Chinese embassy in Manila, said in a social media post on Thursday. Guo also urged the Philippines to cease its “provocative interference with China’s normal scientific research activities”. Tarriela fired back on social media, telling Guo to stop “meddling” and saying that the Philippine coastguard “will continue to oppose and drive away Chinese research vessels that have no right to study our own seas without permission!” Data recorded via the vessel’s Automatic Identification System (AIS) for September, tracked by MarineTraffic, revealed that the Jia Hai Ke 7 research ship departed from Xiamen on China’s southeastern coast on September 19, arrived near Itbayat in the province of Batanes on September 22. The Philippine coastguard confirmed the survey ship’s presence on Monday. Tarriela said the vessel was around 38 nautical miles (70km) northwest of Itbayat and displaying behaviour inconsistent with innocent passage. “Rather than steaming on a steady course and speed, Jia Hai Ke 7 has been loitering and holding position in the same area – the movement pattern of a vessel conducting marine scientific research, not transit,” Tarriela previously said on social media. The vessel’s presence has stirred concerns in Manila over critical subsea telecommunications cables traversing the seabed of the Luzon Strait, which connect Southeast Asia to North America and northeast Asia. Philippine aerial patrols issued three radio challenges demanding that the ship declare its mission and cease unauthorised surveys, but received no response. The deployment comes amid heightened friction over the Batanes Islands. Some Chinese researchers argued in June that the islands were a natural geographical extension of Taiwan and therefore fell under Chinese sovereignty. The assertion is not officially endorsed by Beijing. The ship’s deployment has also raised concerns over China’s use of research vessels to assert claims, map seabed terrain for potential military applications, and gather intelligence on undersea infrastructure in disputed waters. Beijing’s concerns about the area have risen following Manila and Tokyo’s decision in May to launch formal negotiations on delimiting their overlapping exclusive economic zones and continental shelves. Beijing said the bilateral initiative was unlawful and void, arguing that the waters formed part of Chinese maritime zones projected from Taiwan. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, Japan and the Philippines, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. The state-run Global Times said the Jia Hai Ke 7 was conducting “legitimate and lawful” offshore marine geological surveys and scientific investigations in waters under Chinese jurisdiction. “By forcibly overstretching the concept of security and militarising civilian research, the Philippines not only interferes with China’s normal navigation and scientific operations, but also deliberately stokes regional tension,” the newspaper said. According to the China Classification Society, the 70-metre (230-foot) vessel is China’s first privately owned research ship equipped with a Dynamic Positioning Class 2 system, tailored for precision station-keeping and offshore marine geological surveys. It was built for Zhuhai Jiahai Marine Technology Co and entered service in April last year. The incident marks the latest in a pattern of Chinese research vessel deployments to sensitive maritime areas that have generated controversy across the region. These operations typically involve research activities inside the exclusive economic zones and contested waters near Taiwan, the Philippines and Japan. Since May, mainland Chinese research vessels have appeared in waters east of Taiwan on multiple occasions, raising alarms in Taipei. Last month, the Philippine Coast Guard accused another Chinese survey vessel, the Haiyang Dizhi 10, of conducting “illegal” operations for 25 days within the Philippine exclusive economic zone, including the territorial sea of Scarborough Shoal. The disputed shoal, known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines, has become a frequent maritime flashpoint in South China Sea disputes between Beijing and Manila. Manila also said the Haiyang Dizhi 10 occasionally switched off its AIS transponder in what it described as an attempt to evade detection. Meanwhile, the Chinese coastguard patrolled the disputed Scarborough Shoal, Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal on Thursday, marking the country’s National Day holiday with a display of its claim to the South China Sea regions.

title: Review | The Mark Hotel in New York, where Upper East Side elegance meets Met Gala glamour
description: The independent luxury hotel in one of The Big Apple’s poshest neighbourhoods counts Middle Eastern royalty and A-list celebrities among its clientele.
content: Located just off Fifth Avenue – a stone’s throw away from Central Park and some of New York’s most prestigious cultural institutions, including The Metropolitan Museum of Art – The Mark Hotel is the de facto town square of the Upper East Side, Manhattan’s poshest neighbourhood. One of the few, if not the only, independent five-star hotels in New York, The Mark attracts an eclectic international clientele, ranging from Middle Eastern royalty to European jet-setters. Most of them are repeat visitors drawn to the quiet of the Upper East Side, New York regulars who want to take a break from the buzz of downtown Manhattan. What makes the place truly special, however, is the local clientele. If you want to get a real-life snapshot of the colourful characters who call the Upper East Side home, there’s no better place than the hotel’s lobby and its dining venues. Ladies who lunch with their chihuahuas and Birkins in tow vie for attention with tanned gentlemen in navy blazers and Loro Piana-clad European aristocrats who split their time between the Old Continent and New York. People-watching aside, The Mark is a hidden gem in a city with plenty of five-star offerings. Pretty much every single global chain – from Peninsula to Aman, Mandarin Oriental, Park Hyatt and Rosewood – has a presence in New York. The Mark is the rare exception: an independent hotel that has become a beloved institution even without the bells and whistles of its competitors. In recent years, The Mark has attracted a lot of attention as the home base for celebrities and high fliers during the Met Gala, when guests of the glamorous event decamp to the hotel with their retinues to get ready for the big night. The property, however, has a very long history and was a destination for those in the know long before it became a favourite of the fashion set. Housed in a 1927 building just off Madison Avenue, The Mark Hotel began its life as the Hyde Park Hotel before becoming the Madison Avenue Hotel in the 1980s. Its current incarnation began in 2009, when French designer Jacques Grange unveiled his redesign of the space, known for its black-and-white colour palette and elegant interiors that have since become a benchmark for luxury hotels worldwide. Now owned by New York-based developer Alexico Group, The Mark eschews unnecessary technology and the cookie-cutter approach of most luxury properties, offering a real New York experience. While most hotels rely on famous skincare brands for their toiletries, for instance, The Mark created its own. Even the dinnerware and the velvet slippers available for use in each room bear the hotel’s signature branding, a little touch that makes a difference. All the suites and rooms are cosy and comfortable, luxurious retreats, but to truly experience Upper East Side living at its best, you should book one of the hotel’s penthouses. With terraces overlooking Central Park and the quaint Upper East Side skyline, they’re the definition of the high life, New York style. You could say that the pet-friendly hotel is slightly old-fashioned in the way it does things, but that’s what makes it stand out amid a sea of sameness in luxury hospitality these days. Where else could you get a shoe-shine courtesy of John Lobb, the celebrated British shoemaker? Or a lovely pedicab ride around the neighbourhood? Caviar Kaspia at The Mark, a branch of the famous Parisian eatery, comes alive in the summer and spring, when its outdoor seating area attracts a stylish crowd of locals and travellers enjoying alfresco dining. For something a little bit more formal, The Mark Restaurant by Jean-Georges offers the celebrated cuisine of chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten in one of New York’s favourite spots for power lunches and glamorous dinners. The varied menu offers Western classics such as prime beef tenderloin as well as Asian favourites such as chicken and coconut milk soup, which is the definition of comfort food and is also available on the in-room dining menu. While some might feel that the property could do with a little bit of sprucing up and that the service is a bit on the relaxed side, so to speak, especially if you’re used to the efficiency of Asian hospitality, a stay at The Mark is one of those bucket-list experiences that you will cherish for a lifetime. The author stayed as a guest of The Mark Hotel.

title: Letters | Hong Kong need not build its ‘AI City Brain’ from scratch
description: Readers discuss the government’s plan to use artificial intelligence, and the death of a boarding school student from Hong Kong in the UK.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The chief executive’s latest policy address proposes to set up an “AI City Brain”, an integrated management system that links and consolidates relevant big data collected by departments with city governance matters. I strongly welcome this. With extreme weather becoming more frequent, the risk of major incidents rising and public expectations for efficient services increasing, Hong Kong needs a central hub that can connect departmental information in real time and use artificial intelligence (AI) to support decision-making, breaking down long-standing data and administrative silos. At present, different government departments run separate systems. Even when each system works well on its own, their interfaces are often incompatible, and their data cannot be shared smoothly between departments. This prevents true coordination when it matters most. Fully connecting all departmental systems into an “AI City Brain” will require significant effort – reallocating resources, unifying technical standards, and changing interdepartmental collaboration culture. It cannot be achieved overnight. The most practical near-term approach is therefore to build on an existing platform with a proven foundation and cross-department involvement, then upgrade and expand it step by step rather than starting from scratch. A strong starting point is the Civil Engineering and Development Department’s Common Operational Picture (COP), developed over 10 years ago and formally operational in 2020. The COP is a geographic information system-based electronic information platform that enables departments to share incident information in real time, and it already involves over 20 government departments. However, the COP is currently limited mainly to natural disaster scenarios such as landslides and flooding. Its potential is not fully realised. Upgrading the COP – while introducing advanced technologies such as geospatial AI, digital twins, satellites, drones and sensors – could create a single platform for stronger collaboration and better data interoperability. To deliver an AI City Brain quickly, the priority should be to integrate the Common Spatial Data Infrastructure, Underground Utility Information System and COP – using a geographic information system (GIS) as the coordinating backbone. These three platforms each unlock critical layers of urban data: above ground, underground and real-time incident intelligence. With a single GIS spatial framework, their information can be overlaid, aligned and acted upon together. This is the fastest, most reliable route to achieving data interoperability, strengthening cross-department operational coordination and ensuring AI analytics can translate information into better decisions. If Hong Kong is serious about making smart governance real, it’s the time to commit to this integration and scale it decisively. Dr Winnie Tang, adjunct professor, School of Computing and Data Science, University of Hong Kong, and founder and honorary president, Smart City Consortium Scrutiny of ‘education guardians’ in the UK required An investigation published in the Guardian tells the story of Luna Wong, a 16-year-old from Hong Kong who died alone during a summer school placement in London in 2023 and was not found for two days. Her parents had cashed in a pension to send her to a British boarding school. As a psychologist practising in London, I want Hong Kong parents to understand one thing the article makes clear. The “education guardian” every boarding school in the United Kingdom requires you to appoint is subject to no legal standards at all. No training in safeguarding or mental health. No criminal record check. Accreditation exists but is voluntary, and many international pupils’ guardians are not accredited. Luna’s guardian had no mental health training, earned undisclosed commissions on services she arranged and did not tell her parents how unwell their daughter was. None of it was against the law. A British safeguarding review recommended regulation in 2024. The UK government has not acted. Until it does, the only protection is the questions parents ask before they sign: Is the guardian accredited by the Association for the Education and Guardianship of International Students (Aegis) or the Boarding Schools’ Association? What training do they have? What commissions do they earn? How and how often will they report to you? Hong Kong is the second largest source of overseas pupils at British independent schools, after mainland China. Schools and agents will listen to you long before they listen to me. Dr Louise Legg, London

title: Huawei steps up Tau chip roll-out, with Mate XT 2 on track for 1 million sales
description: The Chinese tech giant plans to use its self-developed advanced chips across the new Mate 90 series as it overcomes stringent US tech curbs.
content: Huawei Technologies is making rapid progress in rolling out a new breed of advanced chip based on its self-developed Tau Scaling Law, with the Chinese company set to adopt the processors across the newly released Mate 90 smartphone series. The roll-out marks another step forward in the Chinese tech giant’s push to overcome stringent US export curbs, which has seen Huawei rewire its smartphone business to run on home-grown technology. Speaking at a press briefing on Tuesday, Huawei consumer business chief Richard Yu Chengdong said the company had already shipped about 100,000 Mate XT 2 trifold phones since the model’s release on September 12. The new handset – the first to integrate mobile processors adopting the LogicFolding architecture based on Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law chip design principle – is on track to surpass 1 million in total sales, and Huawei plans to launch the phone in markets across Asia-Pacific, the Middle East and potentially Europe, according to Yu. The Mate 90 series, which Huawei unveiled on Thursday, will also deploy Kirin chips based on the Tau chip design, which the company developed to bypass US tech sanctions and overcome China’s lack of cutting-edge chip manufacturing facilities. “Technologies like extreme ultraviolet lithography certainly are valuable to deliver advanced semiconductors … but China does not have that,” said Yu. “That’s why Huawei develops LogicFolding and the Tau Scaling Law to try to mitigate the gap.” The Mate 90 series starts at 5,999 yuan (US$895), a 1,300 yuan markup compared to the Mate 80 series launched last November. The Kirin 9050 Pro chipset – Huawei’s most advanced processor, which is also used in the Mate XT 2 – will power the series’ top-of-the-line models: the Mate 90 RS Ultimate Design and Pro Max Premium Edition. A slightly less powerful system, the Kirin 9050, will be deployed on the Mate 90 Pro Max. Both chipsets adopt Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture. The Tau Scaling Law and its LogicFolding chip architecture allow Huawei to build more powerful processors without needing to access advanced lithography machines. The approach focuses on shortening signal paths and ultimately packing more transistors into a smaller space. The architecture boosts computing power and data transfer by reducing critical path latency by 30 per cent, according to Huawei. The Mate 90 Pro Max Premium Edition boasts a 31 per cent performance improvement over last year’s Mate 80 Pro Max, according to the company, largely thanks to the new model’s use of the Kirin 9050 Pro. The Kirin 9050 Pro outperforms Apple’s 3-nanometre A17 Pro chip, despite being produced using technology equivalent to a 7-nanometre process node, according to a recent report by Bernstein. The new chip meant that Huawei was now just three years behind Apple in terms of chip technology, down from roughly four years during the previous generation, the report said. The Mate 90 Pro is equipped with the Kirin 9035, while the base model Mate 90 is powered by the Kirin 9030. The two chips are both based on the Tau Scaling Law but they adopt an older architecture rather than LogicFolding. Despite being tight, Huawei’s semiconductor capacity was currently sufficient to meet the company’s shipping needs, Yu said. But surging memory costs have weighed on the company and overall market demand. Huawei’s production costs have risen by more than US$200 per phone due to skyrocketing memory prices, according to Yu, adding that the crisis had hit the company harder than its rivals as it adopted higher configurations that were subject to steeper price increases. The cost surge has dealt “a severe blow” to the company’s profitability, even after it raised retail prices, according to Yu. “Our profitability is dropping very sharply, to be honest,” Yu said. Huawei would “inevitably” have to introduce further price rises in the future, he added, though they were unlikely to be large. “A company cannot operate at a loss,” he said. “We have to survive and face the challenge together.” Beyond the memory crisis, Huawei is also facing increasingly intense competition in the phone industry. Apple recently unveiled its first foldable handset – the iPhone Duo – entering a segment that Huawei currently dominates in China. “We’re actually very pleased to see the launch of iPhone Duo from our American peer,” Yu said. Huawei’s Pura X Max, featuring a similar passport-style design to the iPhone Duo, saw a 76 per cent surge in sales after Apple introduced its foldable handset, according to Yu. The model has now surpassed 1.4 million in sales since its launch in April. Apple’s iPhone Duo will not hit store shelves until October 23. “Healthy competition can motivate more users to opt for the foldable products,” Yu said.

title: Australia’s card surcharge ban forces cafes, shops into price increases
description: The change, one of the biggest shake-ups in decades, comes at a difficult time for businesses already grappling with rising costs.
content: Ross Surace is preparing to raise the price of a coffee by 50 Australian cents and a panini by A$1 (US$0.70) when the country bans credit card surcharge fees starting on Thursday. The co-owner of Lennox Street Deli in Melbourne’s Moonee Ponds neighbourhood said bank-imposed card fees already cost his business more than A$1,000 (US$690) a week, even after the cafe recoups some of the expense by adding a 1.9 per cent surcharge to customers’ card payments. Once that option disappears, Surace estimates the cafe could pay an additional A$1,200 to A$1,500 a week to process transactions. The coffee and panini price increase “just covers the surcharge that we’re losing”, he said. Thousands of smaller Australian businesses face a similar choice: absorb the cost of customers tapping their cards, squeezing already thin margins, or build it into prices and risk driving away cash-strapped consumers. The change is one of the biggest shake-ups of the country’s payments system by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) in decades, but comes at a difficult time for retailers and restaurants already grappling with higher wages, inflation and weak discretionary spending. “Supply chain cost increases and other operating costs have risen, while customers are carefully watching what they spend,” said Glenn Fahey, chief economist at the Australian Retail Council. “Businesses have to weigh up those costs against the risk of raising prices in a highly competitive market.” Merchants will no longer be able to impose surcharges on payments made with Visa, Mastercard and eftpos debit and credit cards. American Express and China’s UnionPay are also removing surcharges, while PayPal follows from October 5. About 16 per cent of Australian businesses currently surcharge, according to the central bank, with consumers paying about A$1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion) annually in the fees. The ban does not stop banks, card networks or payment providers from charging businesses to process transactions. Instead, merchants can no longer pass those costs directly to customers as a separate fee – meaning some of that A$1.6 billion could ultimately resurface in higher prices. Australia’s new policy brings it in line with the UK and European Economic Area (EEA), where surcharges on most consumer debit and credit cards are banned. The changes unwind a system introduced more than two decades ago to steer shoppers towards cheaper payment methods. But with cash now accounting for only about 15 per cent of Australian transactions, that rationale has largely disappeared. The central bank says the change should deliver greater transparency for consumers. “The price that the consumer sees when they’re shopping for the good ends up being the price they pay when they tap their card,” Ellis Connolly, the RBA’s head of payments policy, said in an interview. The impact will be particularly visible in Australia’s ubiquitous cafes and restaurants, where margins are thin. The average restaurant made a net profit of just 2.6 per cent last year, according to John Hart, national president of Restaurant & Catering Australia, which represents 57,000 eateries and caterers. “What they’re concerned about is that in resetting menu prices, they’re going to push menu prices to a point where it will affect demand,” Hart said. Large listed chains are relatively insulated because surcharging is already rare among them, while smaller businesses are more exposed. Retailers typically had profit margins of about 5 per cent to 10 per cent, said Craig Woolford, senior consumer discretionary and retail analyst at MST Financial. “If you’re sitting at a 5 per cent margin and you’ve got to absorb an extra percentage point, then you have a 20 per cent hit to earnings,” he said. “We will see smaller businesses attempt to pass it on where they can.” The RBA is trying to soften the blow by simultaneously lowering interchange fees, which merchants’ banks pay to cardholders’ banks on transactions. From Thursday, the maximum rate on domestic consumer credit card transactions will fall to 0.3 per cent, bringing Australia further in line with UK and EEA policy. How much that offsets the surcharge ban would depend on how much payment providers pass through, the Retail Council’s Fahey said. “It’s critical that the fee savings reach retailers, especially smaller operators.” The surcharge ban has already been factored into ticket prices at Arthurs Seat Eagle, a scenic gondola attraction on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula that draws about 270,000 visitors a year. Chief executive officer Matthew Mulkearns said the changes were expected to cost the operator hundreds of thousands of dollars annually. “We’re going to have a really good hard look at what the net cost to us is,” Mulkearns said. “Then we might, like all businesses, consider whether we need to introduce a service fee or an admin charge for our ticketing.”

title: Expert gives grim warning after Swiss glaciers shrink 20% in 5 years
description: Glaciologist says ice could vanish within 15 years as record summer triggers second-biggest melt on record.
content: Switzerland’s glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20 per cent of their mass in five years, experts said on Thursday, with 2026 registering the second biggest melt on record. Swiss glaciers saw 5.5 per cent of their volume melt away this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study, published after a record hot summer preceded by a winter with little snowfall. “The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice,” said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, describing 2026 as “a catastrophic year”. “There will be probably no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years,” he added. Between 2022 and 2026, the melt rate at Switzerland’s glaciers was “more than twice as high as in any previously monitored five-year period”, the GLAMOS report said, noting an ice volume loss of almost 20 per cent since 2021. While Switzerland’s glaciers have long been shrinking, the melt has recently sped up dramatically. While 10 per cent of Swiss ice volume disappeared between 1990 and 2000, 27 per cent was lost in the past 10 years, the report showed. GLAMOS based its findings on extensive measurements at 23 reference glaciers in September, which it extrapolated to the nearly 1,300 glacial formations still found in Switzerland. The report comes after a summer where the months of June, July and August were each the hottest ever recorded in Switzerland since measurements began in 1864, according to the Swiss Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology. This year, the protective snow cover on the glaciers had already partially disappeared during the June heatwaves, and had completely disappeared by September, even at high altitudes, GLAMOS said. “Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions,” GLAMOS said in a statement. Due to significant melting this year, the researchers even had to reposition measurement stakes – including on the highest-altitude glaciers – further up after the ice melted away in the original locations. The average ice thickness of some glaciers decreased by 2.5 to 4.0 metres, while the more exposed glacier tongues saw losses of up to 10 metres of thickness over the summer. Although temperatures were higher this year, the ice loss did not surpass the record set in 2022, since many glaciers saw more snow before the summer melt than they had four years ago. Less dust from the Sahara Desert also settled on the glaciers this year, allowing more sunlight to be reflected back into the atmosphere rather than being absorbed by the snow. There were exceptions, however. Four major glaciers experienced record melting this year, including the iconic Rhone Glacier and the Aletsch – the biggest glacier in the Alps. As the glaciers retreat, concern was meanwhile growing over the future availability of water resources. Between July and September this year, the glaciers lost a total of around 2.2 trillion litres of water. Huss said that quantity was “difficult to imagine”. “It’s more than four times the annual freshwater consumption of Swiss households,” he pointed out.

title: SOTY 25/26: Healthcare advocate and mentor’s impactful journey
description: Dy Valerie Moreno empowers students aiming for careers in healthcare through support and first aid training initiatives, fostering connections and growth.
content:
Dy Valerie Moreno is a people connector who creates initiatives to support and connect students passionate about healthcare.
In 2023, she was excited to volunteer with the Hong Kong NGO Crossroads Foundation, where knowledge of Cantonese was not a prerequisite for participating in their community service activities.
“They assigned us to different parts of the warehouse so we could help with specific tasks, mainly inventory duties,” recalled the 17-year-old, who is now in Grade 12 at the Australian International School Hong Kong.
“Meeting people I wouldn’t normally talk to made the sessions enjoyable. It’s the idea of connection that motivates me.”
Valerie said that volunteer opportunities for students who only speak English are limited in Hong Kong.
As a student aspiring to a career in healthcare, she searched for a first aid course but struggled to find one accessible to her.
“First aid courses in Hong Kong were often taught in Cantonese, held far from school or scheduled at times that clashed with students’ timetables. Several friends faced the same barriers,” she explained.
To address the issue, Valerie collaborated with her school’s nurse, who also teaches first aid to staff, to bring certified English training to her school campus.
She made the programme affordable and scheduled it immediately after classes to enhance accessibility for students.
“I first consulted the school nurse to learn about the provider’s certification, lesson structure and costs, then coordinated with teachers and extracurricular staff to set up student registration, parent communication and payment, and scheduling,” she said.
Implementing the programme was a challenge: the provider set a minimum quota for the number of students that needed to sign up, and although Valerie actively promoted the initiative through assemblies and personal conversations, students’ schedules complicated recruitment efforts.
“At first, only about 10 students from Years 9 to 12 signed up, but interest grew. By the following year more than 100 students from Years 8 to 12 had earned their certificates,” she noted.
Through these programmes, Valerie helped create a space where students could connect, learn and grow.
“The practical sessions were serious – we had to learn techniques like CPR – but they became more comfortable and even fun because of the people around me whom I had become familiar with,” Valerie said.
In addition to the first aid classes at her school, Valerie also launched a peer mentorship programme focused on careers in healthcare after noticing the lack of accessible information for students about pathways into this field.
“I first heard about the UCAT [University Clinical Aptitude Test] for medicine programmes in an assembly. It made me realise I needed clearer information to consider healthcare seriously,” she said.
Researching options across different regions felt overwhelming, and discussions with other students showed that many shared similar questions.
A career adviser connected her with a senior student, and together they established a mentorship group to share practical information and make the field feel less intimidating.
“My senior friend and I prepared presentations on different careers and pathways, including many options beyond becoming a doctor,” Valerie explained.
As the group matured, it invited students studying medicine at local universities to join. “Having speakers who had just gone through the application and study process made their advice especially practical and relevant,” she said.
Valerie also invited healthcare professionals to share their experiences.
“They shared insights into what it’s actually like to work in the field, interact with patients, and what day-to-day life looks like,” she recalled.
Leading the group demanded significant effort.
“I didn’t know exactly what I was getting into at first; it began as an idea to make healthcare knowledge more accessible to students. Leading the group proved demanding, but my passion and the number of students involved kept me going,” Valerie said.
She noted that leading the group has also boosted her confidence, making it easier to organise events and secure speakers.
Valerie evaluates success by the number of students who have flourished through the programme.
“One younger student who arrived unsure about healthcare grew into a confident leader after attending our sessions and talking with me. She’s pursued healthcare and service, and she’s helped us start new projects at school,” she said.
In Valerie’s view, healthcare is a way to help others: “I view healthcare as a vehicle through which I can help people reach their potential and live authentically,” she said.
Valerie’s efforts to share knowledge with her peers earned her an award in the Best Devotion to School category at the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards. The event was organised by the South China Morning Post and sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.

title: Philippines’ uranium find a ‘vital’ boost for nuclear energy ambitions
description: The discovery of uranium-bearing minerals in Luzon comes as the country explores integrating nuclear power into its future energy mix.
content: Researchers have identified a potential source of uranium in a long-explored mining district in the southern Philippines, as Manila moves to establish nuclear power and expand its critical minerals industry. The discovery, which could provide uranium for the nuclear fuel cycle if further exploration confirms its viability, was made in the Larap-Paracale mining district in Camarines Norte province, where exploration began in the 1950s. Researchers from the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (PNRI), the University of the Philippines Diliman and Akita University in Japan confirmed that surface deposits collected from the area contained uraninite as the main uranium-bearing mineral, and that the material could be processed into a product with higher uranium content. “The findings are vital as uranium may become important in the country’s foray into nuclear energy,” PNRI said in a statement on Friday. The researchers said the material could potentially be processed into uranium concentrate, commonly known as “yellowcake”, an intermediate product in the nuclear fuel cycle. Although the Larap-Paracale district has been explored for decades, the latest samples came from the Bessemer area, a newly identified zone of uranium mineralisation. About 180kg (397lbs) of material was collected and tested in the laboratory, where uraninite grains were found among other minerals. PNRI said more work was needed to determine the site’s economic significance, which would include “detailed geological, radiometric and geophysical surveys followed by systematic drilling and analysis of drill cores”. The study comes as the Philippines is taking steps to integrate nuclear power into its future energy mix, targeting at least 1,200 megawatts of nuclear capacity by 2032 according to the country’s long-term energy road map. It also coincides with a pivotal moment as the nation explores moving up the critical-minerals value chain and building its manufacturing sector. “The finding is very significant if further exploration proves that the uranium in Camarines Norte is large enough and economically viable to develop,” said Djoan Kate Tungpalan, a professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s department of mining, metallurgical and materials engineering who led the uranium extraction and recovery work. She told This Week in Asia that having a domestic option “could significantly strengthen our long-term energy security and resilience and make us less dependent on fluctuations in international markets and supply chains”. However, Tungpalan said the “sensible first step” for the Philippines as a newcomer to nuclear power was to import nuclear fuel from established suppliers, such as Kazakhstan. The Philippines “is essentially rebuilding a nuclear fuel cycle capability” that was first developed over four decades ago when the country was preparing for nuclear power under then president Ferdinand Marcos Snr, said Angel Bautista VII, a scientist and head of nuclear materials research at PNRI. He said much of the initial work had slowed after the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant was mothballed amid corruption allegations in 1986, following that year’s Chernobyl disaster. Bautista, who leads a government-funded nuclear fuel cycle research programme launched in 2024, said the initiative was still in its first phase, developing capabilities such as uranium recovery and radioactive waste management. Other aspects of the programme included establishing a nuclear power plant simulator, he said. However, the Philippines is still a long way from developing a commercial nuclear-fuel industry, according to Bautista. Progress was still “at an early stage”, he said, meaning continuous support would be needed to help the country meet its 2032 target. Tungpalan countered that the Philippines need not “build every step of the nuclear fuel cycle on its own”, as it could strategically develop capabilities in certain areas while relying on international partners for others. Powering higher ambitions The discovery of uranium in the Philippines coincides with discussions regarding not only nuclear power generation, but also the establishment of an industrial base capable of consuming vast amounts of electricity. Carlo Arcilla, a former PNRI director and a professorial lecturer at the University of the Philippines’ National Institute of Geological Sciences, said nuclear energy would form a cornerstone of the Philippines’ industrial ambitions, particularly as the proposed Pax Silica hub would require far more power than the country could currently supply. Spanning 1,620 hectares (4,000 acres) of Luzon island, the Pax Silica “AI-native, hi-tech hub” is envisaged as feeding into semiconductor, artificial intelligence and critical mineral supply chains. Yet it would require an estimated 3 gigawatts of embedded generation capacity – equivalent to 16 per cent of the Luzon grid, which itself is responsible for 74 per cent of the Philippines’ total power demand. “Only nuclear can power Pax Silica,” Arcilla said, adding that the hub would “need power, which we don’t have”. Meanwhile, observers say alternative energy sources such as solar power would require enormous amounts of land to supply the needed capacity. Reviving the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant would be a sound option, Arcilla said, though he suggested that the country focus on building new sites instead to steer clear of the political controversies associated with the old plant. In August, the Department of Energy identified seven new potential sites in the provinces of Bataan, Palawan, Masbate, Pangasinan and Camarines Norte. Tungpalan said the Philippines could start small by developing local capabilities in uranium mining and processing, before turning to international partners for more sensitive phases such as enrichment. “The value of [this finding], therefore, is not that it must supply our first nuclear power plant, but that it could give our country an important strategic option as our nuclear energy programme grows.”

title: Chinese women spend top dollar on male model shoots, turning staged romance into viral trend
description: These commercial models and online influencers command fees based on their appearance, height, follower count, and acting ability.
content: A growing number of young Chinese women are paying for romantic photo shoots with male models, seeking a brief taste of love through a novel form of emotional companionship. This trend has gained significant traction on mainland social media, with customers spending up to 8,000 yuan (US$1,200) for an hour-long session featuring couple-style poses, including hand-holding, embraces, staged kisses, and even touching the models’ abdominal muscles. In July, lifestyle blogger Xue Dinge spent 4,520 yuan on a 30-minute romantic photo shoot with two male models. In a cosy studio setting, the photographer guided her and the models through intimate poses, including face-holding and forehead-to-forehead shots. A second model appeared shirtless, showcasing his toned physique as he embraced her in a bathtub and struck affectionate poses. Sharing the experience online, Xue remarked: “Congratulations on entering the era of female-oriented services.” Another customer, Wenji from Chengdu in southwestern China, paid 3,000 yuan for a couple-style photo shoot. She crafted a storyline in which she had a quarrel with her “boyfriend” and later found him waiting outside her door, tearful and heartbroken. “The model is simply a tool for me to create beautiful images. Taking photos is like crafting a dream. I am paying for a scene that makes my heart flutter,” Wenji shared. Many customers describe the experience as an opportunity to briefly indulge in romance. One online observer noted: “This is what true enjoyment looks like. These photos fulfil all the fantasies of individuals who do not have boyfriends.” However, another questioned the appeal, stating: “Why would I spend money on photos that include a stranger? They are neither my friends nor celebrities.” A third user commented: “This service should not simply be labelled as female-oriented. Women pay to dress up and take intimate photos with men, yet it feels like the male models are the ones benefiting.” Based in Nanjing, eastern China, Mu Zhao Studio claims to be the country’s first photography studio offering couple-style shoots with male models. Its packages range from 7,200 yuan for nine edited photos to 28,000 yuan for a full-day “couple experience” featuring multiple outfits and 120 images. The models are typically commercial models or online influencers, with fees determined by factors including appearance, height, follower count, and performance skills, according to mainland reports. Founder Mu Zhao observed that some customers come primarily for attractive couple portraits, while others seek to experience the feelings associated with dating a handsome man or use the photos to alleviate family pressure regarding marriage. Mu Zhao emphasised that intimate poses are designed within appropriate social boundaries, with the studio avoiding any exchange of contact details between customers and models, despite some clients developing feelings for them.
