She believes that more women are becoming confident in expressing their needs, whether related to appearance, intimate desires, or emotional fulfilment. “Women should be brave enough to articulate their own needs. Spending money to make themselves happy is enough,” she added. This trend reflects a broader shift towards paid companionship services in China, where women can hire male companions for activities ranging from outdoor pursuits to immersive role-playing games.

title: Xi-Trump rapport is ‘most valuable strategic asset’ in US-China ties, envoy Xie says
description: Beijing’s ambassador remarks on head-of-state diplomacy in a speech marking National Day celebrations at the Chinese embassy in Washington.
content: The Chinese ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, has described the personal rapport and “mutual respect” between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump as the “most valuable strategic asset in our bilateral relations”. “Their personal connection and in-depth dialogue have helped keep China-US relations on course at critical moments,” Xie said during a speech on Wednesday marking National Day celebrations at the Chinese embassy in Washington. “Head-of-state diplomacy anchors the bilateral relationship.” The ambassador’s comments come days after Xi’s state visit to the US, during which Trump pulled out all the stops to make the trip a grand affair. It included an airport welcome, a formal White House reception, a state dinner attended by leading American business executives, a meeting over tea and a visit to the National Archives. During the meetings, both sides agreed to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”. Xie also highlighted expected meetings between the two leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) gathering in Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December. He said their “support for each other” gave “fresh momentum to Asia-Pacific cooperation and global governance”. The relationship Xie described dates to April 2017, when Trump first hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, saying they had “developed a friendship”. That personal channel survived a trade war, the pandemic and a four-year interruption under president Joe Biden, before being revived last October on the sidelines of the Apec meeting in Busan. Repeated phone calls kept the contact alive until Trump travelled to Beijing in May, the first visit by a sitting US president to China in nearly a decade. At the White House arrival ceremony last week, Trump said: “From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people.” Xi returned the favour, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” He said he had come to Washington “to carry on our friendship”. This year’s National Day celebration at the Chinese embassy had more invited speakers and more emphasis on people-to-people connection between the two countries than last year. In keeping with tradition, the US State Department issued a congratulatory note on its website: “The United States wishes the people of China goodwill, along with peace, health and happiness in the coming year.” During his speech on Wednesday, the Chinese ambassador highlighted China’s advances in technology, pointing to developments by tech giant Huawei and AI start-up Kimi as evidence of the country’s progress despite US restrictions on access to advanced technology. “The Tau Scaling Law gives a new approach to improving chip performances,” Xie said. In May, Huawei unveiled the Tau Scaling Law and chip architecture that it said could deliver 1.4 nanometre-level performance in coming years without relying on advances in chipmaking equipment tools. As part of a US-led campaign to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductor technology, Chinese companies are barred from acquiring the most advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, traditionally required to produce powerful chips at the 3nm and lower process nodes. While last week’s summit produced no breakthrough on easing US chip controls, the two leaders covered a wide range of issues. In their meeting on September 24, Xi urged Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence, saying he hoped the US side would “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, according to a statement from Beijing’s foreign ministry. The White House did not mention Taiwan in its statement. On Monday, Trump denied discussing US arms sales with his Chinese counterpart, disputing US ambassador to China David Perdue’s account in a Fox News interview a day earlier that the US president had proposed selling weapons to China. “I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am gonna have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss.” Speaking to Fox News after Xi’s visit, Perdue said: “[Trump] actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.” Perdue did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how Xi responded. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. According to the Chinese embassy, the two militaries also agreed to conclude a memorandum of understanding on “crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible”. The US side made no mention of military cooperation. The South China Morning Post reported earlier this month that the two sides were expected to announce measures to improve military-to-military communication. Among the economic deliverables, both sides extended the Busan trade agreement for two more months, until January 10, 2027. The deal signed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025 lowered US tariffs on some Chinese goods, suspended additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, paused certain Chinese rare earth export controls, and secured new Chinese commitments to buy American soybeans. The arrangement was due to expire on November 10. At the summit last week, Beijing and Washington also launched the Board of Trade mechanism and on Sunday announced a range of products in non-sensitive sectors, capped at US$30 billion each, for tariff reduction. The White House released tariff-reduction lists that included 77 categories of Chinese imports into the US and 1,619 US imports into China. The US import list covered a range of consumer goods, including microwave ovens, electric irons, Christmas ornaments and toys. China’s list was dominated by agricultural products, including beef and vegetables, but also included coal, timber and medical devices such as hearing aids and pacemakers. On artificial intelligence, the two sides announced an AI dialogue to exchange views on the technology’s “risks and benefits”, with the next meeting scheduled for November. They also agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” to discuss AI-related incidents.

title: Trump touts US$200 billion South Korean energy deal ahead of US midterms
description: South Korea agreed to invest US$350 billion in the US and boost its purchases of US energy as part of a July 2025 trade deal with Trump.
content: US President Donald Trump has announced US$200 billion in energy investments from South Korea, including US$54 billion towards a long-discussed liquefied natural gas project in Alaska and more than US$100 billion in planned longer-term nuclear power investments. Besides the Alaska LNG project and pipeline and the nuclear plants, the Trump administration announced a US$22.3 billion natural gas-fired power project in Texas that would be supported by Seoul. “The colossal package of investments we are announcing today is a major step towards securing our critical energy supply chain, ensuring American energy dominance and making our partnership with South Korea and the entire Pacific region stronger than ever before,” Trump said during a White House event on Wednesday, joined by energy industry executives. South Korea had agreed to invest US$350 billion in the United States and boost its purchases of US energy as part of a July 2025 trade deal with Trump that set 15 per cent tariffs on South Korean goods imported into the United States. The announcements come amid deep voter dissatisfaction with the cost of living and Trump’s stewardship of the US economy, putting his fellow Republicans in danger of losing control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Trump in recent days has sought to tout investments in states with vulnerable Republicans, seeking to bolster his party’s election hopes. The president was joined by Senator Dan Sullivan, an Alaska Republican locked in a tight re-election contest with former Democratic representative Mary Peltola. Trump hailed Sullivan as an ardent champion of Alaska LNG, saying the venture would be “one of the largest energy projects in American history and a gigantic win for the people of Alaska”. “You know, I won Alaska by a lot, many, many points,” Trump said. “So we shouldn’t have a problem. But one of the reasons I won is we’ve done more for Alaska than anybody in history times 10.” Asian interest The Alaska project, championed by industrial project developer Glenfarne Group, envisions the construction of a 1,300km (800-mile) pipeline to transport natural gas from the Alaska North Slope to a liquefaction facility near Anchorage to prepare for export to Asia. Alaska officials have considered such a project in the past, but have not moved ahead due to questions about project costs and consumer demand for the LNG. While Alaska has decades of history as a petroleum producer, environmental concerns have historically constrained some developments. But the Trump administration has largely brushed aside environmental concerns, cancelling regulations to reduce emissions that cause global warming while pursuing an “energy dominance” agenda that favours fossil fuel development. Trump has repeatedly touted the planned venture, and his administration has sought to lure foreign capital – and contracts – to back it. It is also benefiting from renewed interest from Asian buyers looking to further diversify their energy supplies as conflict in the Middle East curbs roughly a fifth of the world’s LNG production and flows. The US is already the world’s largest LNG exporter, and it is set to double its capacity through the next decade with massive projects under construction and slated to expand. While Alaska LNG is closer to potential Asian markets than US Gulf coast rivals, it would join “an already saturated field of new LNG projects”, said Ira Joseph, senior research associate at the Centre on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University. The natural gas power facility in Texas will provide 6,472MW of energy to data centres located at the same site in the town of Encinal, a US Commerce Department statement said. The facility is expected to come fully online by 2032. The investment deal’s nuclear power component sets aside US$120 billion under “a broad agreement to reach a finalisation for investment projects in the US nuclear power sector”, according to the Commerce Department. That figure includes US$100 billion for construction costs and US$20 billion in contingency reserves. The department said that US$10 billion would be made available by the end of the year for the projects. Trump’s industrial ramp-up envisioned for his widespread energy projects faces a potential labour shortfall, according to experts. The United States needs to fill an estimated 1.7 million skilled trade openings through 2035, according to a report released on Wednesday by the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, an organisation made up of Ford, Blackstone, Nvidia and other large companies. The report found the current training programme produced just 55 workers for every 100 needed. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: As China’s birth rate falls, vacant schools are transformed into aged care facilities
description: Data shows primary and preschool enrolments each fell by 10 per cent last year, leaving classrooms empty while the elderly population grows.
content: Primary schools and kindergartens in China are being converted into elderly care facilities, as falling birth rates and a shrinking youth population leave classrooms empty. According to data from the Ministry of Education, primary school admissions and preschool enrolments each fell around 10 per cent in 2025. The total number of educational institutions nationwide declined by over 6 per cent to 440,700 from the year before. Some of these vacant campuses are being repurposed to serve a demographic that is rapidly expanding as young populations shrink – the elderly. Across the country, local communities are converting classrooms into elderly care centres, nursing homes and community dining halls. Xiji county in the northwestern Ningxia Hui autonomous region, for instance, plans to transform 65 idle school buildings into rural elderly care service facilities in five years, state media People’s Daily reported in August. There are some 191 idle school buildings across the county’s 19 townships and more are expected over the next few years as schools merge. “It’s exactly what you would expect as populations change,” said Stuart Gietel-Basten, the associate director of Hong Kong University of Science and Technology’s Centre for Aging Science. Gietel-Basten predicted that secondary schools and in some regions even universities might be closed and repurposed as China’s population continues to age. China recorded just 7.92 million births in 2025, down 17 per cent from 2024, as its overall population shrank for a fourth consecutive year. The national birth rate fell to a record low of 5.63 per 1,000 people, well below a death rate of 8.04 per 1,000 people. While China can adapt to a shifting age structure at the national level, smaller and sparsely populated areas face a harder adjustment, Gietel-Basten said. In rural villages and industrial rust-belt towns, the departure of young workers for employment elsewhere has left behind a particularly pronounced demographic decline. “These places have been hollowed out, not only because of demographic changes, but also because of the lack of economic opportunities,” Gietel-Basten said. This could lead to a “negative spiral”, with falling local tax revenues making it more difficult to provide public services and economic opportunities, which in turn could drive further migration out of these areas, Gietel-Basten added. In one video shared on Chinese social media, a former resident revisits his old primary school in rural Jiangxi province, to find that it has been converted into a senior activity centre offering classes and subsidised meals for the elderly. The village saw only six births last year, the resident said, a stark contrast to the cohort of roughly 80 children when he attended the school. This left an overwhelmingly older population behind as younger generations move away from the village. While the road ahead is challenging, Gietel-Basten noted that some rural regions in other rapidly ageing societies, such as Japan and Italy, have attempted to reinvent themselves through tourism and relocation incentives. Similar strategies are emerging in China too. Beyond elderly care, some local communities are converting abandoned schools into rural guest houses in a bid to revitalise the local economy. For instance, a primary school in Sichuan province’s mountainous Pingwu county, left vacant since 2020, recently reopened in late June as a luxury boutique inn. The renovations cost 10 million yuan (US$1.49 million), and the inn is set to welcome 10,000 guests a year, according to a local government notice. The guest house is also expected to provide employment for more than 10 residents in the village, while purchasing around 500,000 yuan of agricultural produce from local farmers each year.

title: Opinion | How China became the world’s gold superpower
description: Beijing built its dominance through innovation and meticulous planning, not superior natural reserves.
content: Beijing’s push to build a gold-backed monetary architecture serves a larger goal: yuan internationalisation. While this article traces China’s path to becoming a gold superpower, Part 2 and Part 3 focus on Hong Kong’s vital role in safeguarding the nation’s financial security. Perhaps no story illustrates the secret of China’s industrial success better than its rise as the world’s gold superpower. China has revered the metal for millennia, yet it has never had a gold-based economy. Its own deposits were simply too scarce. In 1975, as China began its economic modernisation, it desperately needed gold to fund reform and build up foreign reserves. Despite its best efforts, it produced a meagre 13.8 metric tons a year. South Africa, then the undisputed king of gold, produced many times that. Canada, the United States and Australia each comfortably outproduced China as well. Then, slowly but surely, everything changed. In 2007, China overtook South Africa to become the world’s largest gold producer, and it has held that position ever since. Today it churns out 380 metric tons a year, more than South Africa, Indonesia and Mexico combined. This was no miraculous bonanza. Beijing did set up a “gold troop” in 1979, sending the military across the country to hunt for deposits. Yet high-grade finds remained elusive until the past two years, when China announced two world-class mines: Dadonggou and Wangu. By then, the country had long since secured its crown. Its journey from a gold-poor economy with low-grade ore to the top of the league table is among the most remarkable industrial turnarounds in modern history. It came from technological innovation, state-led industrial policy and meticulous planning. From the 1990s, Chinese state research institutes began to master pressure oxidation (POX) for treating refractory ore. In layman’s terms, it lets miners profitably process ore with vanishingly low gold content, sometimes as little as one gram per metric ton of rock. Overnight, China’s vast, previously ignored low-grade fields became viable, and the country effectively gained a wealth of new reserves. Today, about a third of China’s output, or 130 metric tons, comes from low-grade fields. POX has helped China become a leading gold producer, ahead of second-placed Russia and more than double the output of the seventh-placed United States. Curiously, China neither invented the technology nor built the biggest plants. Nor are its operating costs the lowest. The US and Canada pioneered commercial POX in the late 20th century, and some of the world’s largest and most advanced facilities are still in Nevada. Russia took it to scale: its Amursk hub has the world’s biggest POX autoclave vessel, and abundant cheap gas and hydropower must give Russian plants the lowest running costs anywhere. So China wins in no single category in the POX race. It is often runner-up. Yet it dominates the game because it is the most efficient player, thanks to careful planning and coordination. Rather than build behemoths, China runs hundreds of medium-sized mining clusters across the country. In the United States, about 75 per cent of gold comes from a single region, Nevada’s Carlin Trend. China’s operations are widely dispersed, so one accident or glitch will not gridlock the whole system. And unlike South Africa’s mines, China’s are tightly organised by the state. Production, financing, transport and security are integrated in a closed loop. China did not build one or two mega facilities; it built an ecosystem. The real source of wealth is human labour combined with technology, thoughtful planning and organisation, not natural resources The cost advantage is real, if nuanced. China’s operating costs are higher than Russia’s, but notably lower than those in North America or South Africa. Russian plants may be slightly cheaper to run, but their set-up and logistics costs are far higher. Chinese POX facilities typically need 30 to 50 per cent less upfront capital than their Western rivals, according to an industry insider. The boom had a dark side. China hit its all-time high in 2016, mining 453.5 metric tons, but local governments prized output over the environment, and pollution became serious. From 2017, Beijing enforced strict environmental and safety standards and shut down thousands of small, illegal or heavily polluting mines. Output fell by more than 25 per cent at one point before stabilising at around 380 metric tons a year. The industry that emerged is cleaner, more efficient and more competitive. Its leading operators are now expanding aggressively overseas, building plants across Africa, Central Asia, South America and even Papua New Guinea. POX is only one pathway. China is also developing a wide range of other processing technologies. As the world’s largest refiner of base metals such as copper, lead and zinc, it recovers tonnes of gold every year as a by-product of its smelters, without running a single dedicated gold mine. That amounts to 80 metric tons a year, roughly Kazakhstan’s entire annual output. It also echoes China’s dominance in rare earths. A common misconception is that this rests on rich deposits. In truth, the real strength lies in its industrial ecosystem. In the end, China leads because it has planned and organised better than anyone else. The real source of wealth is human labour combined with technology, thoughtful planning and organisation, not natural resources. Here is the twist. Although China has been the top producer since 2007, it has also been importing gold aggressively, about 1,000 metric tons a year. Add domestic output, and China takes in some 1,400 metric tons annually. About 80 per cent is believed to go to domestic consumption, while the People’s Bank of China steadily builds up its reserves. That accumulation is just one piece of a much larger puzzle. Beijing is hoarding gold not for the metal’s lustre but to support the internationalisation of the yuan. It is best understood as a dual strategy: insulating China from Western sanctions while gradually building trust in its currency as a global one.

title: Asian Games: Eala takes on Wang with gold in her sights, Olympics in her dreams
description: Alexandra Eala says decision to head to Japan was a tough one, but representing her country ‘very close to my heart’.
content: Alexandra Eala faces her toughest test of the Asian Games so far on Thursday when she takes on China’s Wang Xinyu in the semi-finals of the women’s singles. Victory will take the 21-year-old a step closer to gold, but after battling past Chinese Taipei’s Joanna Garland in the last eight, she said it had not been an easy decision to come to Japan in the first place. While Eala and the rest are in Nagoya, the China Open is taking place in Beijing, and as a WTA 1000 event, it is mandatory for tour players. Officials could opt to fine her US$10,000 for skipping, although the WTA has not responded to South Morning Post questions as to whether they intend to do so. “It was a difficult decision,” Eala said after beating Garland 7-5, 6-0. “But representing the country and playing these types of games – SEA Games, Asian Games, and hopefully the Olympics one day – they’re very close to my heart and a big part of my dreams. “And I get to be with my teammates. These events are really fun, really competitive, and a great experience for me both in terms of learning and just experiencing. “The Asian Games is a different life to what other tournaments normally have, and what each country brings to their delegation is amazing.” Wang needed three sets before she finally saw off Japan’s Moyuka Uchijima, winning 6-4, 3-6, 6-1 at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre. The Chinese player will go into the game as the underdog, a position Eala knows all too well. She won’t be taking her opponent for granted. “Being a professional tennis player and a competitive tennis player, you have to understand that losing is part of the job and losing is always a possibility. “I’ve been on both sides – on the underdog side and more recently more on the seeded side. Each come with their own set of adversity. Not to say that one is more difficult than the other, it’s just different types of difficulties, but it’s always better to be on top. “At the end of the day, there’s always going to be someone better than you, in tennis and in life. So with that philosophy you just have to take everything step by step.”

title: Retailers expect ‘golden week’ sales growth, but trade groups warn of modest gains
description: About 1.29 million mainland Chinese visitors are expected over holiday, but trade groups say cautious spending could limit gains across wider sector.
content: Some Hong Kong retailers are forecasting double-digit sales growth over the National Day “golden week” holiday, but industry leaders have warned that the expected influx of mainland Chinese visitors may deliver far smaller gains across the sector as tourists remain cautious about spending. The cautious outlook came after authorities estimated that about 1.29 million mainland visitors were expected between October 1 and 7, with average daily arrivals projected to exceed last year’s figure by more than 5 per cent. Businesses are offering discounts, shopping rewards and events to persuade visitors to spend more, while some hotels are counting on late bookings to fill their remaining rooms. “The net effect is that total retail receipts may still increase, but the growth will be disproportionate to visitor arrivals,” said Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank. He added that a stronger yuan could make shopping in Hong Kong more affordable, but cautious consumer sentiment was likely to limit spending per person unless businesses offered particularly attractive discounts. Cosmetics retailer Sasa was more optimistic after its Hong Kong sales during the May Day golden week exceeded expectations. “The group expects sales performance to continue improving over the National Day golden week in October, with both footfall and average transaction value anticipated to record high double-digit growth,” a spokesperson said. Sasa said more mainland visitors were seeking out its products after reading positive reviews on mainland social media. It is running a shopping festival promotion from late September to mid-October and plans to expand in tourist districts. Retail sector lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai said many shops hoped to grow their business by close to 10 per cent, particularly sellers of gold and jewellery, dried seafood and cosmetics. Andrew Kwok Chi-wah, president of the Hong Kong Small and Medium Enterprises Association, said many of his retail members expected a similar increase. Kwok cited promotions on mainland social media and the crowds drawn to Victoria Park’s Mid-Autumn Festival lantern displays as reasons for their optimism. But the restaurant he runs in Wan Chai had a quiet festival break, he said, underscoring the uneven benefits to businesses. Michael Leung Chun-wah, chairman of the Association for Hong Kong Catering Services Management, expected restaurants to do about 20 per cent more business over the National Day break than during a normal week, similar to last year’s holiday. He said nearly 4,000 food outlets were joining this year’s discount campaign, up from about 3,000 last year. “Wherever diners go, they are bound to come across [an outlet] offering discounts. That will be hard to resist,” he said. Hotels, meanwhile, are seeing different booking patterns. Peter Tam, deputy general manager of Metropark Hotel Mong Kok, said reservations had reached about 95 per cent for the first four days of the golden week and 80 per cent for October 5 to 7. The average room rate was around HK$1,200 (US$153), slightly above that of a typical October weekend. “To be conservative, I’d say business will be on a par with last year,” he said. Some guests had arrived as early as September 27 to secure lower rates before the holiday, while others planned to continue to Shenzhen or Macau after a short stay in Hong Kong. Lawmaker Alan Chan Chung-yee, who is also chief operating officer of Miramar Group, said bookings at its hotels were still below 60 per cent, slightly behind the same point last year. He nevertheless expected last-minute reservations to lift final occupancy above 90 per cent at its Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay properties. With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day falling in separate holiday periods this year, hotels could spread out demand rather than fill up early during one long break, Chan explained. “If you gave me two bowls of rice in one meal or spread them across two meals, of course I’d rather eat them separately,” he said. Both hotel executives said guests tended to dine and explore outside their properties. Tam said most visitors at his hotel ate no more than one meal there before heading into Mong Kok, while Chan said tourists increasingly sought out local shops and diners. Chan also saw a chance to attract younger visitors later in October through Halloween. “National Day tends to feel a bit more traditional and older. Halloween is younger; young people like dressing up and cosplaying,” he said. He suggested offering hotel guests costume rentals and discounts to encourage them to join celebrations around Tsim Sha Tsui. An earlier Hong Kong Retail Management Association survey found that nearly six in 10 retailers expected golden week sales to rise, while more than two in 10 expected them to remain flat and nearly two in 10 foresaw a decline. Association chairwoman Annie Tse Yau On-yee had pointed out that mainland visitors had spent less per person over the summer despite rising arrivals. Across the city, more than 3,800 restaurants and food outlets are offering National Day deals, including discounts of up to 30 per cent, while cinemas will sell half-price tickets on October 1. Shopping centres are pairing promotions with events. Langham Place in Mong Kok is offering a HK$250 voucher package to shoppers who spend HK$1,500, while New Town Plaza in Sha Tin has lined up nearly 200 limited-time offers and themed exhibitions. New Town Plaza and MOSTown in Ma On Shan each expect double-digit growth in footfall and sales during golden week.

title: Loro Piana CEO Frédéric Arnault on navigating the Italian luxury brand’s complexities
description: The LVMH heir talks about the maison’s commitment to fabric development, sustainability goals, non-celebrity campaigns, and resistance to fleeting trends.
content: Frédéric Arnault grew up surrounded by luxury executives and creative directors, and has been exposed to the inner workings of the world’s top luxury brands from a very young age. He is the son of Bernard Arnault, chairman and CEO of LVMH, the world’s largest luxury group and the company behind brands such as Louis Vuitton, Dior, Bulgari and Fendi. The young Arnault spent most of his adult life working at LVMH’s watchmaking division, first as CEO of Tag Heuer and later as CEO of LVMH Watches. All that experience, however, didn’t fully prepare the 31-year-old for the complexity of a brand like Loro Piana – one of the most unique luxury companies – as he himself explained in an interview during Milan Fashion Week. Last year, Arnault joined Loro Piana as CEO, a role that comes with significant scrutiny. One of the crown jewels in the LVMH portfolio, Loro Piana has been one of the group’s most successful acquisitions, with consistent growth thanks to its relentless focus on quality and its ability to court very wealthy customers uninterested in trends or logos. Arnault not only had to move to a different country, learn a new language and become familiar with a new category, but he also had to fully immerse himself in the internal operations of a brand that doesn’t operate like any other in the fashion industry. Founded in the Piedmont region of northern Italy in 1924 as a wool mill and acquired by LVMH in 2013, Loro Piana is the purveyor of the finest fibres in the world – from baby cashmere to merino wool and vicuña. While Loro Piana has successfully expanded into categories such as footwear and handbags, it is first and foremost a fabric manufacturer. For most of its history, the brand supplied luxury brands and tailors with the finest fabrics; it began producing garments under the Loro Piana label only in the 1980s. “It sits between soft and hard luxury,” says Arnault. “We make clothes, leather goods and shoes but don’t operate like other fashion brands. [We] are closer to watches and jewellery brands in the lead times of development, the way we make products and develop icons, our relationship with our customers and the lifetime of our products.” As one of the few fully vertically integrated brands, Loro Piana sources its raw materials from places such as Mongolia, Australia, New Zealand and Peru, and then produces textiles at its factories in Northern Italy. In September, the brand inaugurated a knitwear plant in Ghemme, also in the Piedmont region; it is the largest factory investment in the company’s history. “It’s a very impressive process,” says Arnault, describing all the steps involved in manufacturing a piece of knitwear. “Every time I go, I discover new things; it’s all different techniques and know-how, and it requires years of skill, from dyeing to ironing.” Arnault shares that Loro Piana recently acquired a small firm that specialises in ironing precious knits, a specific and rare skill that the brand has now brought in-house. It’s just an example of the complexity involved in creating something as seemingly simple as a cashmere sweater and an element of the company that clearly fascinates Arnault. “One aspect that’s unique to Loro Piana is that fabric development is super important,” he says. “We have our own spinning mills and weaving department and teams who focus on research and development to source the best fibres in the world. We always think of what kind of fibres we’re going to use.” He brings up as an example CashDenim, a delicate blend of cashmere and cotton yarns woven in Japan. While another luxury label would be happy to rely on what’s available in the market to make jeans, Loro Piana went the extra mile and actually developed its own signature denim. Given its global supply chain, Loro Piana pays close attention to sourcing its raw materials. To support Mongolia’s herding communities and cashmere cooperatives, for instance, the house launched Resilient Threads last year, a multi-year programme to protect the biodiversity of Mongolia’s Eastern Steppe and safeguard the well-being of its inhabitants. This is just one example of the brand’s commitment to sustainability, which also comes into play when considering the durability of its products. “We make sure we produce what we sell and sell what we produce,” says Arnault. “Of course we launch new products and collections, but we keep them in stores for longer periods of time compared to other brands. Nevertheless, we still have seasons because that’s inherent to the fashion industry. People buy a linen shirt in July, and a vicuňa coat in December, and we have new collections that have a vision, and we have unique campaigns.” Don’t expect those campaigns, however, to star celebrity ambassadors or known figures. Unlike other top brands, Loro Piana doesn’t work with celebrities, letting instead the products speak for themselves. In the rare instance a celebrity is seen wearing Loro Piana, the relationship is completely organic and begins with the celebrities themselves. Take actor Jeremy Strong, who helped make Loro Piana part of the pop culture conversation with his role as Kendall Roy in the blockbuster HBO television series Succession. While preparing for the role, Strong was travelling in the Italian region of Umbria and chanced upon an extremely well-dressed gentleman, who happened to be clad head to toe in Loro Piana. It didn’t take long for Strong to ask the show’s costume designer to source pieces from the label for his character, including a cashmere baseball cap that went viral when it debuted on the series. That baseball cap has joined the Summer Walk shoes and the Extra Pocket bag as one of the label’s most coveted items, something that would have been unthinkable as early as 10 years ago, when Loro Piana wasn’t a real player in the accessories category. Loro Piana never set out to aggressively build or develop its footwear and leather goods segments, but they grew organically, as Arnault explains when asked about the runaway success of those widely copied white-soled shoes and rectangular bags. He points out that the Summer Walk has been among the brand’s offerings for years, long before the LVMH acquisition. Sergio Loro Piana, an avid sailor, invented the shoe as a chic alternative to the boat shoe and initially made it available only to his inner circle. The same was true of the Extra Pocket, which the brand never promoted and which took off organically. “We have a unique communication strategy and don’t hold fashion shows,” says Arnault. “We don’t use celebrities in ads, which are about the spirit of the brand and the products first.” That product-centric approach is evident in everything Loro Piana does. Arnault talks about the importance of what he calls “the art of touch”. “When customers visit our stores, feel the product and try it on ... they discover the durability. They see that the cashmere sweaters they’ve been wearing for many years are still impeccable,” says Arnault. “This creates a sensation of quality, [which] is not something you can claim. If the quality is not there, the customers can feel it, even if the company says otherwise.” Arnault observes that younger generations are “very knowledgeable” and increasingly focused on quality, scrutinising how products are made and whether they retain their value. Over the past few years, Loro Piana has struck a chord with this demographic, fueled by the “quiet luxury” trend that swept the fashion world post-Covid. Arnault, however, is deeply aware that short-lived trends are not what the Italian maison is about. “We stay true to who we are and care about our core customers,” he says. “Maybe right now there is a trend in the market about the positioning we represent, and maybe eventually this will end, but we strongly believe in what we do. Our core customers will always be here, [and they’re who] we care about in everything we do. Our approach of quality and craftsmanship won’t change.” Next on the horizon is the opening of a leather goods factory in Tuscany, which Arnault says will allow the brand to treat leather the same way it does precious fabrics. This is part of Loro Piana’s aim to control every single aspect of its production process without having to rely on third-party suppliers, something that has become even more important for luxury brands in Italy in their efforts to take full control of their supply chain to avoid issues such as hidden subcontractors and dubious labour practices. Loro Piana has a long history in Asia, both as a source of its fibres and as a market for its creations, but Arnault says that the region has a lot of untapped potential for the maison. This month, it will open a flagship store in Tokyo, following a recent expansion of its Hong Kong boutique in the Landmark mall. “Asia is super important for us, but because our first Loro Piana products began in the 80s and 90s, we don’t have the same presence and history as other brands,” says Arnault. “Many luxury brands have been present in Japan for many decades, for instance, but we are smaller there and are opening a new boutique in Tokyo’s Omotesando with a magnificent facade. Our Landmark boutique in Hong Kong is a big improvement from before, but we will increase it further in the future.” While it has been a steep learning curve for Arnault, he is clearly in his element at Loro Piana – a brand that may have started as a traditional wool mill in the Italian countryside but is now a global force to be reckoned with. Describing Loro Piana as a “historic company”, Arnault says the founding family was very present and hands-on, while long-serving employees have passed down its heritage. However, the CEO adds that it is also good to welcome people joining from other industries and brands. “The company is more global, so we have to be relevant to different markets. We work with local teams who know exactly what is going to resonate with Chinese customers, for instance, because that can’t come from Italy,” he adds. Arnault is also happy in his new home, Milan, a city that has undergone major changes in recent years, transforming from Italy’s financial capital into a vibrant metropolis with a global outlook. Milan’s trajectory mirrors the rise of Loro Piana, in a way, and reflects a newfound sense of optimism in the country Arnault now calls home. “I have always loved Italy and have been coming for a very long time. I used to go to other places more than Milan,” says Arnault. “Milan is having a great moment after the Winter Olympics, and fashion is thriving here, and it’s very stable and economically it’s doing well, and it’s very welcoming,” he says, adding with a wry smile, “And the restaurants are also great.”

title: ‘China’s Warren Buffett’ adds Moutai shares for 3rd time as baijiu sector seeks bottom
description: Duan Yongping takes bullish long-term view on ‘irreplaceable’ brand, while analysts see sector becoming ‘zero-sum’ amid falling consumption.
content: Chinese-American billionaire investor Duan Yongping, often called China’s Warren Buffett, has added 30,000 shares of Shanghai-listed baijiu maker Kweichou Moutai to his portfolio in his third public stake increase this year amid a deep sector-wide adjustment. Moutai’s premium valuation has long relied heavily on corporate and social gifting demand. Yet stricter supervision, more prudent corporate spending and ongoing anti-corruption efforts in recent years have dented demand, according to industry observers. “We believe demand remains sluggish for the sector as a whole, but conditions vary by category,” said Jennifer Song, senior equity analyst at Morningstar. “Premium baijiu – especially Moutai – and leading mass-market baijiu brands are showing early signs of stabilisation.” Most other players, particularly sub-premium names, were still struggling with channel destocking and had yet to confirm a bottom, she added. Once the most expensive mainland-listed stock, shares of Moutai edged up 1.86 per cent to 1258.62 yuan on Wednesday. So far this year, the stock has declined about 8.6 per cent. Chinese baijiu sales have deteriorated since the second half of 2024, and the sector has lagged the broader market owing to an ageing population and lower per capita drinking rates, according to Morningstar. On Monday, Duan posted on Xueqiu, a Beijing-based social and trading platform, that he had bought some Moutai shares. He showed a screenshot indicating he bought 30,000 shares at 1,230.85 yuan per share, for a total investment of 36.93 million yuan (US$5.5 million). Earlier this year, Duan said investing in Moutai required little macroeconomic analysis, as its unique value was “irreplaceable”. The brand’s official app had curbed counterfeiting and price speculation, unlocking consumer demand, he said. “Duan’s rationale has consistently been long-term,” Song said. “Consumers may drink less but better, and a short-term sales slowdown does not change Moutai’s long-term value. This is largely in line with our view.” The distiller’s second-half financial results would improve compared with the first half, helped by a low base, she added. Over the medium to long term, the sector was expected to become zero-sum, such that only companies with durable competitive advantages would emerge as long-term winners by taking market share, she added. In the first six months, Moutai posted sales of 92.28 billion yuan, up 1.3 per cent year on year, while its net profit fell 1.95 per cent from a year earlier to 44.52 billion yuan. “The baijiu sector may gradually bottom out, with listed liquor firms expected to see earnings improvement on a low base,” Shengang Securities said in a report last week.

title: Border mine blasts show why both Koreas urgently need to restore communication
description: With North Korea stepping up fortification works along the border, constant contact is needed to avoid accidental clashes, experts say.
content: The two Koreas urgently need to restore military communication to prevent a landmine dispute in the demilitarised zone (DMZ) from escalating into an armed clash, according to observers. The danger is growing as North Korea presses ahead with leader Kim Jong-un’s order to fortify its side of the 4km (2.5 mile) wide buffer zone separating it from the South. South Korea views the works, including the laying of mines near the sparsely marked Military Demarcation Line (MDL) running through the centre of the DMZ, as a violation of the 1953 Korean war armistice agreement. Last Monday, two South Korean soldiers clearing routes south of the MDL to monitor North Korean activities were wounded when two anti personnel mines exploded. “With the risk of an accidental clash growing, Seoul should strongly urge Pyongyang to reactivate emergency military communication channels to prevent further escalation,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. “Seoul should actively make the proposal and maintain pressure regardless of whether North Korea accepts it.” South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday urged North Korea to apologise and halt its border fortification work, warning that Pyongyang would otherwise be held responsible for all the consequences. A team from South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command (UNC) concluded its investigations on Tuesday. It found three North Korean mines south of the MDL, including the two that injured the soldiers last week. “Based on the findings of the investigation, UNC determined that an armistice agreement violation occurred,” it said in a statement. North Korea flatly denied responsibility, accusing Seoul of fabricating the findings and warning of “immediate and merciless” retaliation if its troops came under fire. Kim Yo-jong, the North Korean leader’s powerful sister, said in a statement on Wednesday that “the armed gangsters” of South Korea were shifting the blame to the North to justify future provocative actions. She insisted that North Korean soldiers had “never crossed the border”, while accusing the South’s military of threatening them with warning broadcasts and gunfire. Pyongyang is building what it describes as an impregnable “permanent” southern border, including erecting barriers, laying mines and blocking roads along the DMZ. North Korean troops involved in the project have repeatedly crossed the MDL, said Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification. “This fuels concerns that even a simple exchange of warning shots in the border area could escalate into a conflict involving tactical weapons, albeit a localised one,” Lim said. Building justification North Korea’s actions suggest it intends to build a justification for retaliatory strikes, according to experts. “It needs to portray South Korean warning shots or the findings of the mine investigation as interference with the construction project and an infringement of its sovereignty, while laying the groundwork for retaliation in the event of an exchange of fire,” Lim said. Last week’s explosions recalled a similar incident in August 2015, when two South Korean soldiers on a routine patrol inside the DMZ were severely wounded by landmines. In response, Seoul resumed anti-Pyongyang propaganda broadcasts through loudspeakers along the border for the first time in years. High-level talks eventually led to North Korea expressing regret over the incident, defusing the crisis. This time, however, the chances of Pyongyang accepting responsibility were slim, Oh said, noting that in 2015 South Korea had presented compelling evidence – including footage showing North Korean soldiers laying mines south of the MDL. “North Korea’s statement is intended to deter the South from taking military countermeasures as it continues with the border fortification work,” he said. “To prevent further escalation and an exchange of fire, the two sides should reopen communication channels for talks.” Inter-Korean military communication channels were effectively severed in 2023, when North Korea began ignoring routine daily hotline calls. Pyongyang has since defined inter-Korean relations as those between two hostile states, rather than between two halves of a divided nation awaiting reunification. Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Kim’s swift statement, issued before the South Korean and UNC investigation had reached its final conclusion, appeared intended to “contain the fallout” from the incident. It was also intended to pre-empt any resumption of psychological warfare operations by South Korea, including loudspeaker broadcasts along the border, Yang said. Such broadcasts pose a challenge to Pyongyang’s efforts to prevent outside information from reaching its troops and undermining frontline morale. South Korea’s opposition People Power Party has urged President Lee Jae Myung’s government to resume the broadcasts, even as Lee pursues dialogue and exchanges with the North despite Pyongyang’s refusal to engage. North Korea appeared to view what it called a “staged incident” as Seoul’s attempt to “build a justification for military action against the North”, Yang said. Pyongyang has cited South Korean warning broadcasts and shots since August as evidence of harassment of North Korean troops and alleged incursions across the border. “By defining the incident as a deliberately planned ‘staged operation’, North Korea is rejecting a 2015-style approach to resolving the issue,” Yang said. “This suggests a rejection of subsequent procedures such as fact-finding, determining responsibility and demanding an apology.” Heightened tensions along the DMZ and other border areas could also be intended to put pressure on Washington ahead of possible North Korea-US talks, he said. Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said North Korea appeared concerned about the possibility of personnel involved in the project being fired on, potentially forcing work to be suspended. Kim’s intervention at such a high level, rather than a rebuttal issued through military channels, reflected Pyongyang’s confidence amid strengthened ties with Russia and China, as well as advances in its nuclear arsenal and modernisation of its conventional forces, Hong said. “However, Pyongyang remains wary of a rapid escalation before the border fortification project is completed and ahead of possible talks with Washington.”

title: Woman told Cornell police 2 years ago she was 100% sure she was raped, transcript shows
description: The account raises new questions in the high-profile case about the district attorney’s decision not to prosecute anyone at the time.
content: A woman who filed a lawsuit saying she was sexually assaulted by seven men at a Cornell University fraternity house told police weeks after the incident that she could “say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped”, according to a report by CBS New York, which said it obtained a transcript of her interview with investigators. The transcript, which has not been publicly released, raises new questions surrounding the local district attorney’s decision not to prosecute anyone at the time. In recent days, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has maintained the woman’s first account to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex. Yet, he also said he had reopened the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which was filed this month. Cornell has agreed to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how the university handled the woman’s allegations, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced on Wednesday. The woman initially went to Cornell’s campus police about three weeks after the alleged attack that began on October 19, 2024, then went back on November 14 and 15, 2024, to be interviewed. “Yes. It was coercion, yes,” she told a campus police officer, according to the transcript obtained by CBS. According to CBS News, she said she was “completely and totally incapacitated” before some of the sexual abuse. The woman acknowledged she had been drinking alcohol and used drugs the night she visited the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, and that she had gaps in her memory. She also told police she was comfortable with an initial sexual encounter with two of the men, but not with what happened later in the night, when other men began to enter the room. “And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard,” she told police, according to the transcript. “I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped,” it said she told investigators. The woman, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in the lawsuit, filed a complaint on September 16 saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. She became completely incapacitated while fraternity members were sexually assaulting her, she said. The district attorney, Van Houten, did not immediately respond to emails and phone messages from Associated Press on Wednesday, but he told CBS News he never saw the transcript of the woman’s interview when his office declined to bring charges and relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer but signed by the accuser. Van Houten has released a summary of that statement, with some of her direct quotes included. He has defended his office’s decision not to do additional investigation after the woman first came forward in 2024. “There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” Van Houten told CNN earlier this week. Cornell University first publicly disclosed that it was investigating the woman’s allegations on November 8, 2024, the same day she first went to the police. The school sent students an email alert warning them that a person had reported they had been sexually assaulted at a fraternity house and coerced into consuming drugs. Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity the same day. In another public statement to students in late November 2024, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said campus police were investigating “deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence” at the fraternity house. Later, Cornell appointed a task force designed to address sexual assault on campus. But with the district attorney’s decision not to pursue charges and the university’s internal disciplinary investigation being shielded from the public, attention on the matter waned. Cornell said in a statement this week that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus, but the university has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.

title: ‘Red tourism’: retracing China’s revolutionary roads in real time
description: High-speed rail has made the pivotal locations of China’s modern history easier to reach and transformed remembrance into real-life journeys.
content: The first thing you notice about “red tourism” is the scale of Yanan, in Shaanxi province, where Mao Zedong solidified his leadership, developed his core ideology and built the foundations for victory in the Chinese civil war. Tour groups in matching caps, lines of coaches, queues for photographs beside Mao statues – what was once a school trip has become one of the most visible forms of domestic travel in China, and younger people are now driving much of it. Red tourism is no longer about remembrance. It has become a way of retracing a story that feels unfinished. SHANGHAI TO TIANANMEN In July 1921, 13 delegates representing 57 party members gathered in Shanghai for the Communist Party’s first congress. First, they met under cover of a summer study group; then, they moved to a shikumen town house on Zingye Road, but had to flee when a French Concession police informant was spotted at the door. Eventually, the congress was completed on a boat on South Lake, in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province. Of the 13 men at that table, only two would stand overlooking Tiananmen Square in 1949, when the People’s Republic was proclaimed. Shanghai to Zunyi to Yanan to Tiananmen is a 28-year arc. Red tourism is the attempt to walk it. THE PULL FOR THE YOUNG Officially, red tourism relates to sites linked to Communist Party history from 1921 to 1949. In practice, it is patriotic education, pilgrimage, school trip and family outing. The numbers are large enough to sound unreal. Red-tourism sites receive about 800 million visits a year. During the 2024 Ching Ming Festival, hotel occupancy in Yanan was nearly at capacity before the holiday had even begun. This is not simply an older generation revisiting its own past; it is also a younger one working out a history it did not live through but still inherits. That shift matters, because red tourism is not only about loyalty; it is about origin stories and a hunger to visit the places where a modern identity was forged. These sites are where the national recovery began, and a confident China keeps returning to them to see where it started. High-speed rail has changed the emotional geography of all this by making the interest easy to act on. Once the distances shrink, the communist revolution stops being a set of disconnected monuments and becomes a route. ZUNYI AND THE PIVOT If Shanghai is the beginning and Yanan the destination, then Zunyi, in Guizhou province, is when the story turns. The Zunyi Conference took place in January 1935, in a merchant’s house. The Red Army was exhausted, retreating and close to collapse. The old strategy had failed. In three days of meetings, the Communist Party changed direction and Mao emerged with control of the army. What makes Zunyi worth visiting is the atmosphere – this was a moment of doubt, not triumph. Victory is easy to memorialise; confusion and fear are much harder. Zunyi preserves a moment when the communist revolution might have gone differently. YANAN, FINALLY Yanan feels different. It sits in the loess hills of Shaanxi, a landscape of yellow earth, steep gullies and cave dwellings. It was the Communist base from 1935 to 1948, the place where the party members regrouped after the Long March and turned survival into statecraft. At Yangjialing and Zaoyuan, the cave homes are bleakly austere. A table, a bed, a desk and earthen walls – the plainness is unsettling because the scale of what was decided in these rooms does not match their modesty. This is where Mao’s thought was formalised, where the Red Army rebuilt its discipline and where the Yanan Rectification Movement began in 1942. Yanan is origin and warning all at once – the place where a campaign found its voice and where it learned the habits of ideological control that would define its future. The landscape stands out as much as the politics. These sites absorb history rather than decorate it. Nothing here feels embalmed – that is why Yanan lands in a way the other sites do not. It is not grand, and it does not try to be. It feels inhabited. A REVOLUTION AS PERFORMANCE Red tourism does not only preserve history; it stages it. Zai Hui Yanan is an immersive production on the edge of the city in which the audience moves through multiple settings, living through key moments of Yanan’s revolutionary years rather than watching them from a seat. It tells the story through young people rather than the leadership, closer to a memory than a pageant. Part of red tourism’s appeal is that it doesn’t run on solemnity alone. It makes history feel current rather than archived. If a memorial hall is where the facts are stored, a production like this is where the facts are made to move. STANDING TO ATTENTION Matching caps, group selfies, choreographed reverence: all of that is real, and easy enough to dismiss from the outside. Harder to dismiss is the seriousness with which people arrive. What I noticed in Yanan was attention, not performance: people who had travelled a long way to stand in a small room, a cave dwelling or a merchant’s house, and think about what happened there. Then, the silence breaks. Someone starts singing a national song in Chinese, unprompted, and within seconds, the room is singing with them, the sound thickening in the cave’s acoustics until it fills the space. China’s high-speed railway did not invent the impulse to travel here. It only made it easier to act on. In the end, that is what red tourism offers: not history as remembrance alone, but history as a route – something with distance and direction that can be travelled through and felt underfoot. From a shikumen in Shanghai to Tiananmen Square in Beijing, the distance is no longer only political. It is physical, navigable and, for millions of people, worth covering.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong must balance boosting public housing supply with other goals
description: The plan to build public housing on part of the Fanling golf course pitted conservation against development and social privilege against community needs.
content: The government has finally decided not to appeal a court ruling revoking environmental approval of a controversial proposed housing development at the Hong Kong Golf Club. This casts serious doubt on plans to build 12,000 public flats on 9.5 hectares out of 32 hectares of land resumed from the Old Course at the club in Fanling. The future use of the land is now uncertain. It remains to be seen what course the government will adopt, including how it will remedy a flawed consultation process. Some concern groups have urged the government to clarify the future of the housing plan and the site as soon as possible. Hong Kong needs a continuing supply of land to meet residents’ demand for public housing, and it also needs to provide space for mega-events that attract people to the city. It should not be necessary to meet the needs of one at the expense of the other. The government’s decision not to appeal is therefore welcome if another site can be found for the public housing project. A significant addition to the public housing stock has been delayed long enough. The decision was reached after officials considered legal advice “holistically” – or, rightly, by looking at the wider picture. That would take into account Hong Kong’s need for more public housing for the underprivileged and for venues that raise its profile as a host of international sporting events as well as the environmental implications of any proposal. A plan to house tens of thousands of people in a public housing development on a luxury championship course run by a 137-year-old golf club was always going to be controversial. It is testament to unmet demand for decent, affordable housing, demand that needs to be addressed one way or another. But it pits conservation against development and social privilege against community needs. It also raises conservation issues, such as the fate of a 0.39 hectare patch of woodland with 186 native trees, including 20 incense trees considered vulnerable internationally and of significant conservation value. Testament to the international attraction of world-class venues such as the Fanling course for sporting and entertainment was the star-studded, Saudi-backed LIV Golf Hong Kong tournament at Fanling last March. It attracted galleries of thousands including high-end overseas visitors. Sadly, its future is now under a cloud after LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States. But the tournament helped Hong Kong bounce back from the pandemic. Since then the calendar of mega-events has gathered momentum, especially with the opening of the Kai Tak Sports Park. In a judgment delivered ahead of the government’s decision not to appeal, the Court of Appeal found that the government’s endorsement of the project’s environmental impact assessment report was marred by an unfair public consultation process, the imposition of improper conditions and a failure to meet wildlife conservation objectives. A government spokesman said the judgment had clarified some important legal principles under Hong Kong’s environmental impact assessment process. The clarifications included that authorities had to consider the nature of a case before deciding whether new information that updated the report should be mentioned in a follow-up consultation. In 2024, the Court of First Instance ruled that the government had failed to consult the public again when civil engineering authorities provided additional information regarding the development’s ecological impact, which formed part of the report. The judgment also said that, based on the principle of fairness, it was necessary to conduct a further but limited public consultation on the additional information. Authorities said the Environmental Protection Department would follow these guidelines to ensure future approvals were fair, legal and transparent. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department currently manages the 32 hectares of land from the golf course that was returned to the government in September 2023. The government has made the resumed land available for the hosting of major international events. We trust it will continue to do so. It is to be hoped the Northern Metropolis mega-project can help provide enough land for future development of affordable housing.

title: 5 new Hong Kong cafes and coffee shops to try in October 2026, plus must-visit events
description: International Coffee Day on October 1 kicks off a month of new openings and fun events for coffee obsessives and casual drinkers alike.
content: Every month in Hong Kong brings a fresh line-up of cafes and coffee shops, but this October will see brew nerds even more caffeinated than ever. International Coffee Day kicks things off on October 1, a day that also sees two new coffee festivals begin: one held across multiple districts over three consecutive weekends, and one focusing on Japan-based roasters and cafes. The weeks after are filled with opportunities to try new beans and blends from new coffee shops, while drinkers can also look forward to the return of PMQ’s annual Coffee Agenda festival. Read on for our pick of the newest cafes plus details of three must-visit coffee events in October. 1. Lowkey While this cafe has no relation to the popular South Korean cafe of the same name, there are similarities: both have a trendy, industrial aesthetic and an impressive array of house-made salt breads on display. Coffee-wise, the new Lowkey roasts its own beans and offers that mainstay of Korean-style cafes: the creamy, sweet Vienna coffee topped with rich cream. 21 Old Bailey St, Central 2. Kusp Featuring a serious line-up of beans roasted by Offshoot Coffee, Kusp is wooing local drip coffee fans with its elegant brews. Among the recent roster have been selections from Colombia, Peru and Ethiopia, and a Honduran Cup of Excellence competition winner: the Honduras La Salvaje Geisha. There is also a small selection of treats baked in-house, such as warm madeleines and banana bread. Shop 7, Wah Lok Building, 7 Yim Po Fong St, Mong Kok 3. Koen If you’re a Central office worker, a coffee place that opens early is vital. Koen, conveniently located inside Chater House when you come off the pedestrian walkway connecting to Exchange Square, is perfectly placed for an on-the-go brew, opening at 7.30am on weekdays. Promising to serve “warm bread [and] serious coffee”, this cafe bakes its own offerings with a Japanese twist, such as pork floss and Comté cheese mochi buns, bergamot hojicha melon pan (bread), and ham and Emmental cheese shio (salt) pan. To handle the crowds, batch brew coffee is on hand as well as the usual line-up of filter and espresso options. Shop 101, 1/F, Chater House, 11 Chater Rd, Central 4. Woofy Doofy This pet-friendly cafe will be the perfect hang-out when the cooler weather arrives, with outdoor benches wrapping around a curved facade, and an appealing selection of brunch-style dishes and coffee options. It also has a pet grooming centre for “pawrents” who want to tick off a styling session for their furry friend as well as get their coffee and cake fix. Shop B3, 15 Fa Po Street, Kowloon Tong 5. Islet Coffee Lab This Central favourite has a new location, but fans of the original need not look far – it has moved from one side of On Lan Street to the other. The new Islet Coffee Lab feels more grown-up, rendered in deep emerald green with cosy nooks all facing the bar for enjoying a coffee and conversation. 8-10 On Lan St, Central Coffee events in October 1. Tokyo Indies Coffee Fes The inaugural Tokyo Indies Coffee Fes will be held at Sndo Reads, an independent bookshop and lifestyle store in The Twins shopping centre in Kai Tak, from October 1 to 4, 12pm-8pm. Although Tokyo is in the name, the festival actually brings together eight up-and-coming roasters from across Japan, from Akita to Hokkaido, allowing visitors to meet and mingle with like-minded coffee fans. Among the line-up are Matenrou Coffee, Hikage Coffee, Blank Coffee and Osmo Coffee Roaster. Sndo Reads, 7/F, Tower II, The Twins, 12 Muk Chui St, Kai Tak 2. Coffee Voyage Swire Properties is hosting a cross-district celebration of coffee over three consecutive weekends. It starts with the Starstreet Precinct (outside Three Pacific Place on Star Street in Wan Chai) from October 1 to 4, which will feature a diverse range of coffee roasters and award-winning baristas from Hong Kong and Japan. The following week, head to Cityplaza and Taikoo Place from October 8 to 11, where coffee fans can sample coffee from Philocoffea’s head barista Rikuto Tanaka, who will be debuting his new brand Rikuto at the festival. There will also be a coffee run hosted by the East Hong Kong hotel in Quarry Bay on the morning of October 11. The coffee events come to a close at Citygate Outlets in Tung Chung from October 22 to 25. 3. PMQ Coffee Agenda Back for its 11th edition between October 16 and 19, PMQ Coffee Agenda is themed “Adventure” this year. It features an expanded layout, four themed experiences, and plenty of hands-on workshops and coffees to taste. The event is co-presented by Coffeeder and brings together more than 50 local and international coffee brands from London, Seoul, Bangkok and Taipei. Some new elements this year include a Coffee x Movie segment curated by Islet Coffee Lab, which has created four coffee drinks inspired by four art house films in celebration of Broadway Cinematheque’s 30th anniversary. There will also be a “roast your own beans” experience, and a workshop on how to taste coffee like a professional. The festival takes place on October 16 from 3pm-7pm, and October 17 to 19 from 11am-7pm. Entry is HK$45 for a standard day ticket. PMQ, Courtyard & Marketplace and Qube (2/F), 35 Aberdeen St, Central

title: Trump claims he discussed release of political prisoners in China with Xi at summit
description: US president says he had ‘some very, very important discussions’ with his Chinese counterpart, but did not identify specific cases.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that he discussed the release of “political prisoners” in China with his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Washington last week. “We talked, and I think we had some very, very important discussions. Hopefully fruitful discussions,” Trump told reporters in the White House. Families had stepped up pressure on the Trump administration to push Beijing to release their loved ones ahead of Xi’s three-day state visit. Trump was asked whether he had raised the cases of “political prisoners”, such as American scholar Min Zin and former Hong Kong media tycoon Jimmy Lai Chee-ying, with Xi, to which he replied: “I did.” The president did not identify specific cases, and it was not immediately clear which prisoners Trump and Xi discussed. Min and Lai’s family and supporters were among those who wanted Trump to raise the cases with Xi. Trump had raised Pastor Ezra Jin, who was later freed, and Lai when he met Xi in Beijing in May. Zin was detained in China in June and accused by authorities of espionage and endangering China’s national security. US officials believe Min’s background as a former student activist in Myanmar and US-funded academic work may have attracted the attention of the Chinese security services, the Wall Street Journal reported. The family of Chinese-American scientist Chen Youlin, whose case was not mentioned on Wednesday, also ramped up pressure over the last few weeks. Chen has been accused of espionage by Chinese authorities, likely linked to previous work analysing seismic data that included North Korean nuclear tests. Chen travelled to China in November 2024 for a month-long holiday and as he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing. “Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” his wife Rong Yufang told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.” Chen and Zin have both been formally designated as “wrongfully detained” by the US government, but Beijing has rejected those designations. In the lead-up to the summit, the White House said Trump expected to bring up cases of people “wrongfully detained” with the Chinese leader. He has made releasing Americans detained overseas a priority during his presidency. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The families of Dawn Michelle Hunt and Nelson Wells Jnr, who have spent over a decade in Chinese prisons following drug convictions, also pressed for their freedom on humanitarian grounds ahead of the summit. Peter Humphrey, a former SCMP China correspondent and fraud investigator who was imprisoned in China with his wife from 2013 to 2015, is working with the Hunt and Wells families. “We have been constantly hearing from our lobbying contacts in Beijing that the Chinese side is very ready to consider a humanitarian release, so long as there is a request from the American president,” Humphrey said.

title: US criticises China’s WTO compliance as industry groups mount complaints
description: Senior US trade official says Beijing targeting entire industrial sectors for global dominance, while retaining a non-market economic system.
content: At a hearing reviewing China’s compliance with its World Trade Organization (WTO) commitments, a senior US trade official said Beijing was targeting entire industrial sectors for global dominance while retaining a non-market economic system. Terry McCartin, Assistant US Trade Representative (USTR) for China, Mongolia and Taiwan Affairs, said China’s anticompetitive behaviour posed a major challenge to the global trading system. “More critically, after 25 years of WTO membership, China still embraces a non-market economic system,” McCartin said in his opening remarks at the hearing. He said China’s approach had evolved, with Beijing now focused on targeting entire industrial sectors for global dominance. This came as US steelmakers urged Washington to consider additional tariffs and coordinate with other countries to counter China’s steel overcapacity, as industry groups outlined complaints about Beijing’s trade practices ahead of the Wednesday hearing. By law, US Congress requires the USTR to submit an annual report monitoring China’s compliance with its WTO commitments, utilising public comments and hearings. Washington accuses Beijing of not meeting WTO commitments The US has long accused China of failing to meet its WTO commitments. In its latest report, released in March 2026, USTR said China’s state-led economic model had deepened rather than softened after nearly 25 years of WTO membership. The report argued that China’s industrial policies, state support and efforts to promote domestic industries continued to create challenges that existing WTO rules were not designed to address. It said the US therefore needed to use tools outside the WTO to respond to what it described as China’s non-market practices. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Beijing has historically rejected US allegations regarding its trade practices, previously accusing the USTR’s compliance reviews of exposing a pattern of unilateral thinking and “consistent bullying” by the US. Chinese officials have consistently rebuffed Washington’s claims over industrial excess capacity, arguing that the issue is being politicised and used as a pretext for protectionism and restrictive trade measures. In its past policy papers, Beijing maintained that its industrial expansion is driven by innovation and global demand, calling for capacity disputes to be resolved through multilateral cooperation. In written public comments submitted ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, 17 groups from sectors including agriculture and food, technology and digital industries, healthcare and consumer products outlined their concerns. Four representatives testified in person on Wednesday morning. In its comment, the American Iron and Steel Institute (AISI) accused China of maintaining massive steel overcapacity through government subsidies and industrial policies, saying Chinese steel production far exceeded domestic demand and was exported worldwide, hurting US producers and workers. AISI called for additional tariffs and stronger international coordination. “For American steelmakers, the Chinese government’s flouting of market principles reiterates the need for clear, concerted action to address steel overcapacity,” Kevin Dempsey, president and CEO of AISI, wrote in its statement. The comments came as USTR Jamieson Greer announced on Wednesday that countries taking part in the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity had agreed to a new framework for joint action on global steel overcapacity. US eager to work with ‘like-minded partners’: Greer Greer said the US would work with “like-minded partners” to address the market distortions caused by excess capacity and highlighted tariffs and other Trump administration policies as having helped revive the US steel industry.
