The three-person commission, which heard City’s case over 12 weeks in late 2024, determined that a “disguised funding scheme” allowed them to record £949.94 million (US$1.26 billion) of sponsorship income in the nine seasons from 2009-10. The real figure was £119.25 million, with ADUG funnelling the remaining £830.69 million to the club. City’s alleged misdemeanours surfaced following a 2018 Der Spiegel investigation, launched after the German website was sent leaked emails by Portuguese computer hacker Rui Pinto. In February 2023, the Premier League issued its sledgehammer statement charging the club with 115 rules breaches, including 35 for failing to cooperate with the investigation from 2018 to 2023. In the period between 2009 and 2018, Manchester City won three Premier League titles. They added five more over the following six years. Those eight titles are now destined to be viewed through the prism of what Arsene Wenger once called “financial doping”. It is instructive that Chelsea were the object of Wenger’s sniping 20 years ago; the then Arsenal manager rattled by cash-rich new boys on the scene. Roman Abramovich got his spending done before financial fair play’s 2009 conception, allowing Chelsea to make the leap from also-rans to competitors. Looking at billionaire-owned Aston Villa and Newcastle United currently banging their heads against glass ceilings, it is impossible to think that City would not have been similarly constrained had they not, in the words of the commission, “misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators”. Juventus were stripped of their 2005 and 2006 Serie A titles after being busted for match-fixing. The following year’s title was reassigned to third-placed Inter Milan. Juventus were relegated to Serie B for the 2006-07 campaign. In the tribal, cash-driven world of football, sympathy will be in short supply should Manchester City be similarly severely punished, regardless of the fact that nobody is suggesting they ever resorted to nefariously influencing matches. The independent commission discovered that Roberto Mancini, the manager who delivered the 2012 title, had his City salary swelled by a separate wage paid via a secret consultancy agreement with Al Jazira, a sister club in Abu Dhabi. Other charges include 12 for breaching rules “requiring a member club to include full details of player pay in its relevant contracts with its players” . The ruling also revealed that City used a third party, Fordham, as a means of overstating income by £24.5m and understating expenses by £49.414m. The commission said the Fordham arrangement was “little more than a front for ADUG”. Manchester City have confirmed they will appeal against the judgment before Friday’s deadline. A statement on the club’s website said it would “pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. Ferran Soriano, the City CEO, said in a video message to club employees that “the whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation”. Still, after a 42-day hearing that generated more than 7,000 pages of transcripts for review, the commission held its nerve while outside noises called for a resolution, waiting until it was satisfied that its verdict was watertight. Executives, players and staff will be keenly following the next developments. In 2023-24, Everton were hit with six and two-point deductions for offences that pale in number and significance against those City are said to have committed, while the Merseysiders have been ordered to pay Burnley £35 million over the supposed impact on the Turf Moor club of their rules breach. In 2024, Nottingham Forest had four points taken off them for one rule infringement. Optimism for City, if the charges are upheld, comes in the shape of the £10 million fine and transfer ban imposed on Chelsea this summer, after their owners self-reported 74 breaches of Football Association rules that occurred under the chairmanship of Abramovich. It was during a match at Luton Town in the 1980s that the Manchester City fans who had circumvented a contemporary ban on away fans created their “We’re not really here” chant that endures to this day. Back in 2008-09, Luton were slapped with a 30-point penalty for transfer irregularities and failing to satisfy insolvency rules that essentially condemned them to relegation from the Football League. We might not have to dig so deep to find Manchester City in future, but they really are here, staring at the prospect of a plunge down the leagues becoming the epitaph for the most successful period in the club’s 146-year history.

title: Russia sends nuclear warning to Nato over its Kaliningrad enclave
description: Bilateral ties have sharply worsened, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up sabotage and arson acts on the continent.
content: Russia has warned Nato it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea. In a document sent to Nato and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a “dangerous and reckless course” that entailed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”. The document ‌said this included the possibility of “Russian strikes against decision-making centres in the alliance’s member states right from the outset”. “Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should Nato countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” the diplomatic note said. The warning highlighted Moscow’s urgent concern at what it sees as a growing Nato threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarised Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut. In a written ⁠response, seen by Reuters, Nato said it was a defensive alliance committed to countering threats to its members from all directions. “None of Nato’s exercises or activities pose a ‌threat to the territory of the Russian Federation,” it said. “We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.” Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, said it was becoming increasingly hard for Western countries to keep stepping up ⁠their support for Ukraine without tipping into ⁠direct confrontation with Moscow. He said the Russian warning might indicate that hardliners were gaining influence in a debate over how to respond to Western actions that included arms supplies to Kyiv, new sanctions on Moscow, ‌interceptions of Russian ships, frequent military exercises and intelligence flights near Kaliningrad. “They [Russia] expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea – just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will ‌be open ‌war. I see a risk of mutual miscalculation,” Sokov said. In an online interview, he said Russia and Europe were on a collision course that required caution and calculation ‌on both sides. Instead of this, the Europeans were applying “full court pressure” and Russia was delivering a serious warning that this was highly risky, Sokov added. In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing Nato of ⁠escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described these as diplomatic reminders to “hotheads in Europe”. Relations, already dire since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, have sharply worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a “hybrid war” on the continent through acts including ‌sabotage and arson. Russia denies that and rejects ‌repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a Nato country. A Nato diplomat said: “I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by Nato is firm and responsible. [It] reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine.” A senior European defence official said: “[This is the] first time since [the] Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious.”

title: After the US-China tariff deal, will Chinese factories still need Southeast Asia?
description: Beijing and Washington plan to waive additional duties on US$30 billion of each other’s goods, potentially narrowing the region’s trade advantage.
content: For years, Chinese manufacturers have viewed Southeast Asia as a way to reduce exposure to higher US duties on goods made in China. But a new round of tariff cuts proposed by Washington and Beijing could weaken that incentive for some products, potentially changing the economics of the strategy. Under the new US-China Board of Trade, more than 90 per cent of Chinese products on a list of goods worth US$30 billion – mostly everyday consumer items, such as toys and household goods – would return to most-favoured-nation tariff treatment, with all additional duties waived, China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. A reciprocal US$30 billion list covers US exports to China. A White House statement did not elaborate on the exact tariff cut levels, but the changes – if implemented as outlined by Beijing – would effectively bring duties on most of these products to below 10 per cent, according to US official data. Some products could face zero duties, depending on the product category. The picture is different for some Southeast Asian manufacturing hubs. Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand, which have attracted Chinese investment in low-end consumer goods manufacturing over the past decade, continue to face additional US tariffs of between 10 and 12.5 per cent. Washington imposed the duties on 60 trading partners in July following a Section 301 investigation into alleged forced labour. That difference has raised questions about whether lower US-China tariffs could weaken one of the biggest incentives for Chinese companies to move production to the region. Some analysts said Chinese companies had shown signs of hesitation, but expected the region’s appeal to endure despite the narrowing tariff gap, citing rising manufacturing costs in China, the country’s shift towards higher-value industries and persistent uncertainty over US trade policy. “We have already seen some hesitancy among Chinese enterprises investing in Southeast Asia over the last few months,” said Chim Lee, a senior analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). “The Iran war has made things worse – energy supply has been more stable in China compared to some Southeast Asian countries. In the near term, larger companies with production capacity in both China and Southeast Asia may focus on exporting from China.” Since the US-China trade war during US President Donald Trump’s first term, some Chinese companies have expanded overseas production capacity to hedge against growing uncertainties. Southeast Asia quickly emerged as one of the most popular destinations because of its geographic proximity and lower labour costs. Chinese investment in Asean countries reached about US$19 billion in 2024, making China the region’s second-largest source of foreign direct investment among non-Association of Southeast Asian Nations partners, with manufacturing receiving the largest share, according to official data from the bloc. That was more than double the US$8 billion recorded in 2015, before Trump took office. “We expect that the gradual transition of China’s low-end manufacturing to Asean will continue, as China’s comparative advantages are shifting,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at the Dutch multinational bank ING. China, Song said, was upgrading its industries and moving up the value-added ladder, while Southeast Asia continued to offer lower labour costs, making the region a natural destination for lower-end manufacturing. “Tariff changes are unlikely to change this major trend, especially given the potential volatility of tariff policy,” Song said. “Diversifying the manufacturing base may be advantageous for companies, given continued policy uncertainty.” Meanwhile, Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, said the US-China tariff reductions were “narrowly targeted” and would have only a marginal effect on Chinese manufacturers’ relocation strategies. “For items directly affected by the tariff reductions, there may be a greater incentive to ship directly out of China, but this covers only a very small share of the goods and sectors linked to supply chain relocation to Southeast Asia,” he said. “Most of the electronics, machinery and green technology sectors will be largely unaffected.” The timetable for the proposed tariff reductions remains unclear. China’s Ministry of Commerce said the two sides would “implement the cuts simultaneously after completing their respective domestic legal procedures”. Beijing and Washington have also extended their trade truce until January, two months beyond the original November deadline. While the tariff agreement has brought a degree of optimism, some individual Chinese exporters remain cautious. Ricky Luo, a 31-year-old Amazon seller from China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, said the prospect of lower tariffs was welcome news but not enough to change his strategy just yet. Luo has remained in the US market throughout the tariff turmoil. It remained his largest market, he said, and orders had held steady even as profit margins had narrowed. “I don’t change my decisions just because the news changes,” Luo said. “I wait until the policy actually takes effect.” Additional reporting by Mia Nurmamat

title: DFI Retail sells stake in Maxim’s in return for Starbucks business, US$340m
description: DFI Retail will take over control of 1,100 Starbucks outlets across Asia as part of the deal, with Maxim’s buying back its 50 per cent stake.
content: Maxim’s Caterers has struck a deal to buy back its shares from DFI Retail Group for US$340 million plus control of its licensed Starbucks business, according to an exchange filing released on Wednesday. The deal will mark the start of a fresh chapter for Maxim’s, bringing an end to decades of part ownership by the conglomerate Jardine Matheson, which owns DFI Retail. Jardine Matheson bought a 50 per cent interest in Maxim’s in 1972, before transferring the stake to Dairy Farm, now known as DFI Retail. The Wu family retains 50 per cent of the business via the company Hongkong Caterers. The deal will see DFI Retail take over operations of more than 1,100 Starbucks outlets across Asia and receive US$340 million in cash in exchange for its 50 per cent equity stake in Maxim’s. The shares will pass to the Wu family, which has run Maxim’s since the 1950s. In a statement released on Wednesday, DFI Retail described the move as a “reorganisation”, stressing that Hongkong Caterers, DFI and Jardine Matheson would continue to partner with each other across the procurement, supply chain, property and digital segments. “The transition of the Starbucks licensed business to DFI marks the final milestone in our strategic pivot from a portfolio to a focused operating company and sits squarely within our purpose – to sustainably serve Asia for generations with everyday moments,” said Scott Price, CEO of DFI, in the statement. The licensed Starbucks business operates more than 1,100 coffee houses across seven Asian markets, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. DFI said it expected the business to generate revenue “immediately”, boost the operating margin of its core retail business, and create synergies with its other ventures. Last year, the Starbucks business generated income of about US$750 million with an underlying operating margin of 7 per cent. Revenue is projected to reach US$900 million on a full-year basis in 2028, according to DFI’s filing. DFI also operates a number of other well-known retail chains in Asia, including Wellcome, Mannings and 7-Eleven. Maxim’s, founded in 1956 by brothers James Wu and ST Wu, operates more than 2,000 food and drink outlets across Hong Kong, mainland China, Southeast Asia and other markets. Michael Wu, chairman and managing director of Hongkong Caterers and Maxim’s Caterers, said the company’s diversified business portfolio put it in a strong position to capture growth opportunities in the future. “We have been fortunate to have the Wu family and Hongkong Caterers as partners over such a long period, and we look forward to continuing to work alongside them, as well as supporting the growth of Starbucks licensed business through DFI Retail Group,” said Ben Keswick, executive chairman of Jardine Matheson. The reorganisation is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to be completed by the end of the first quarter of 2027. DFI said it aimed to lift its dividend payout ratio to 80 per cent in 2027, while maintaining the 2028 underlying profit guidance of up to US$350 million.

title: Xi projects confidence in National Day speech, with rallying call for economic growth
description: Chinese leader urges resilience, tech innovation and stability in holiday address ahead of a major Communist Party gathering next month.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping projected a message of confidence about the country’s ability to overcome challenges during his annual National Day address, issuing a rallying call for robust economic growth and more certainty amid geopolitical complications. Xi’s address, delivered at a state reception in Beijing on Wednesday evening to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic, was his first to the nation following his state visit to the US last week. It came weeks ahead of a key Communist Party conclave next month. In a resolute tone projecting confidence about the nation’s growth trajectory despite a complex global environment, Xi’s speech included a forceful push for economic resilience and stability. “We are extremely proud of the world-renowned achievements of New China and full of confidence in the bright future of Chinese-style modernisation,” he said, according to state news agency Xinhua. Noting that this year marked the beginning of the 15th five-year plan, which covers 2026-2030 and is crucial for cementing China’s footing in the global tech race and advanced industrial chain, Xi called for steady approaches to “reform and opening up” while striking a balance between growth and national security. “Our country’s economy has forged ahead under pressure, shifting towards new drivers and higher quality, and demonstrating strong resilience and vitality,” he said. Acknowledging China was facing “a complex and intricate domestic and international landscape”, he ordered the Chinese government to “strive to meet the year’s targets and tasks”, and ensure a strong start for the five-year plan. He also pledged to “unswervingly” implement the “one country, two systems” principle and better support Hong Kong and Macau in integrating into China’s overall national development and long-term stability and prosperity. On cross-strait relations, the Chinese leader maintained a tough line. Xi reiterated Beijing’s pledge to “resolutely combat ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist forces” and to “oppose interference by external forces”. But he also explicitly called for efforts to “promote the peaceful development of cross-strait relations and advance the great cause of national reunification”. This specific phrasing was not part of his National Day address last year, when cross-strait tensions were high. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary, and considers it the core of its core interests. Most countries, including the US, do not acknowledge the self-ruled island as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with arms. The fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee will be held from October 26 to 29. It is the most important gathering ahead of next autumn’s national party congress, a five-yearly event marked by top-level reshuffles. The party is also gearing up for a seamless leadership transition next year. At the fifth plenum, officials will discuss and approve a draft policy decision by the Central Committee to strengthen party governance and discipline. Consultations on the document have already been held, and it will be submitted to the Central Committee for final deliberation and approval, according to a Politburo meeting held last week. At the reception, Xi also said China would continue to adhere to an independent foreign policy of peace to “inject greater certainty and positive energy into an uncertain and turbulent world”, according to Xinhua. The recent warming of US-China ties, marked by Xi’s state visit and commitments for two more summits this year, has injected renewed certainty into what had been a deeply strained relationship. The two leaders will meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in Miami in December. “Chinese and American leaders meeting four times within a year is unprecedented in the history of US-China engagement,” said Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University. “Although the two powers have conflicting interests and structural frictions, they remain willing to meet and talk, seeking ways to manage their ties,” Xin said. He suggested the detente could provide Beijing with a strategic window from late this year to early next year if ties remained calm. Yet cordiality should not obscure the fundamental reality: competition in key areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) remains intense. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he did not want to work with China to address AI risks, adding that cooperation might undermine America’s lead in the field. Beijing, on the other hand, has unveiled detailed innovation action plans for the next five years, emphasising frontier areas such as AI, the life sciences and biotechnology, controlled nuclear fusion and talent training. China’s economy is also at a critical point. Amid an intensified push for tech and innovation, Beijing faces domestic pressure to step up job creation, especially for young people, and incentivise investment and consumption. Marking a shift in its assessment of the country’s economic performance, Beijing on Monday acknowledged emerging challenges in the economy and signalled that more policies were in the pipeline to revive faltering growth. This was quickly followed by new supportive measures on Tuesday from the Chinese central bank and Ministry of Finance, including a new subsidy for the interest on home mortgages. “Persistently weak domestic demand has this year been aggravated by the energy-supply shock from the Iran conflict,” said Gavekal Dragonomics in a research note on Wednesday. “The artificial intelligence boom is lifting China’s exports, but there has not been much spillover into stronger domestic investment or consumption.” Concluding his address with a sweeping declaration on the country’s trajectory, Xi proclaimed that the great rejuvenation of China was “unstoppable”. “After a long period of exploration and practice, the socialist system with Chinese characteristics has demonstrated tremendous advantages, and the modernisation of our country’s governance system and capacity has continuously improved,” he said, according to Xinhua. He urged the nation to “firm up our confidence, lock on to our goals and move forward steadily step by step” to realise China’s success. Xi and other party and state leaders attended a ceremony to present flowers to fallen national heroes at Tiananmen Square in Beijing on Wednesday morning, marking Martyrs’ Day, which commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity.

title: Nearly 150 firms in Hong Kong cut packaging waste equal to weight of 900 buses
description: Authorities honour firms for green efforts at award ceremony, including A-1 Bakery, Watsons Water and SF Express Hong Kong.
content: Nearly 150 companies have reduced packaging material equivalent to the weight of about 900 double-decker buses over the past year after taking part in a government charter on waste reduction launched in Hong Kong in 2025. A-1 Bakery, Watsons Water and SF Express Hong Kong were among 75 firms recognised for their efforts at an award ceremony on Wednesday, following an assessment by the Environmental Protection Department on five criteria, including packaging recyclability and promoting the use of less packaging materials. Undersecretary for Environment and Ecology Diane Wong Shuk-han said at the ceremony that the city had striven to explore and promote cutting packaging waste according to “pragmatic and feasible principles”, while noting mandatory national standards launched in mainland China in July to restrict excessive packaging in delivery parcels. “Environmental protection and economic development are never mutually exclusive. Rather, they complement each other,” Wong said. The ceremony followed the launch of a packaging reduction charter last year by the department, focusing on eight business sectors – such as logistics, e-commerce, drink manufacturing and supermarkets – to maximise the impact of eliminating packaging waste. After signing the charter, local bakery chain A-1 Bakery redesigned its cake boxes by adding a clean, easily removable compartment layer with handles, said Lo Lok-sang, the company’s food safety and sustainability manager. The new packaging replaced the old brown boxes – which had no extra layers and were previously discarded when deliveries reached retail stores from factories. “When we create a product, we should consider how customers will handle the packaging materials once they take the product home,” Lo said. For Watsons Water, beyond cutting plastic materials used in each water bottle, the company has recently been promoting recycling machines in local supermarkets to encourage the recycling of water bottles. Users deposit used, clean bottles into the machines and receive money in return. “The launch of the plastic reduction charter has enabled more conversations with stakeholders on sustainability partnerships in the city,” said business strategy and planning director Siu Kin-man. In 2026, six SF Express Hong Kong self-pickup stores joined the department’s on-site recycling project to encourage customers to return packaging materials for recycling immediately after collecting their parcels, said head of public affairs and communications Ku Chun. The logistics firm also showcased its air cushion bubble films made with recyclable plastic while reducing plastic quantity, as well as modified cardboard boxes to reduce secondary packaging waste. Leo Wong Wai-kin, principal environmental protection officer at the department, said enacting local laws to regulate excessive packaging in Hong Kong was difficult, given most pre-packaged goods were dispatched outside the city. “Operating a charter, which provides guidelines and encouragement, is more practical,” Wong said.

title: Hong Kong’s Pansy Ho wins permanent injunction against woman who harassed her
description: High Court judge also orders Steffi Chen Pan-yu to pay Ho HK$1.8 million in compensation after harassing Ho with false allegations.
content: Pansy Ho Chiu-king, daughter of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun, has won a lawsuit to permanently bar a woman from contacting her after the defendant repeatedly harassed her and her companies with emails and hand-delivered letters containing false allegations. The defendant was also ordered to pay Ho HK$1.8 million (US$229,000) in compensation for damages. A judgment handed down by the High Court on Wednesday revealed that Ho, chairwoman and executive director of MGM China Holdings, had been harassed for a year by Steffi Chen Pan-yu, a former licensed broker, since March 2025. Ho, one of the city’s richest women, is also the group executive chairwoman and managing director of Shun Tak Holdings. She said she did not know Chen and had never met her. Chen had alleged that Ho falsely promised her a senior position at MGM China. On several occasions, Chen delivered letters containing her demands in person to Ho’s Shun Tak office, MGM China’s Hong Kong branch, and in October 2025, to the home of Ho’s late sister, Maisy Ho Chiu-ha. Chen also instructed a law firm to send a letter of demand to Ho’s lawyers, seeking, among other things, HK$21.26 million for consultancy services and the employment offer that had fallen through. She threatened to make the allegations public if Ho did not comply with her demands. In March, Ho applied to the High Court for an injunction against Chen. Deputy High Court Judge Grace Chow Chiu-man said in her judgment that Chen had failed to provide any written evidence in support of her defence. Chen appeared at a court hearing and represented herself without a lawyer, arguing that Ho had not actually brought the civil action against her. Chow dismissed her complaints, saying she was satisfied that Ho had provided sufficient evidence to prove that Chen had pursued a course of conduct that harassed and intimidated her. “I am further satisfied that based on the matters pleaded, the plaintiff is entitled to the injunctive relief sought,” the judge said. “The defendant has showed a propensity to repeatedly attempt to contact the plaintiff and her family and business associates to make false allegations against the plaintiff, which is causing ongoing distress and harm to the plaintiff.” As Chen had failed to submit a defence by the statutory deadline, Chow ruled that the court had jurisdiction to grant a permanent injunction.

title: Asian Games, day 11: Hong Kong’s squash teams guarantee bronze, Wong battles into last 8
description: Ceci Lee in action, start of the rugby sevens and Taichi Kho looking to improve on his first round could boost medal tally on Thursday.
content: Hong Kong will collect at least two more bronze medals in squash on Thursday, although the men’s and women’s teams have loftier goals in mind at the Asian Games. Semi-finals against Pakistan and India at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena stand between the Hong Kong players and a shot at gold. With cyclist Ceci Lee Sze-wing in action in the women’s Madison, Coleman Wong Chak-lam into the quarter-finals of the men’s singles, and the start of the rugby sevens, the city’s athletes will have designs on boosting the tally still further. Wong was made to wait for much of Wednesday before he finally got onto centre court at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre, and then had a battle against Japan’s Yosuke Watanuki before winning 7-6, 6-3. Up next for Wong is Thailand’s Kasidit Samrej, victory there would bring a semi-final against either Uzbekistan’s Khumoyun Sultanov or Chinese Taipei’s Tseng Chun-hsin. In squash, the city’s men and women were equally comfortable in their respective 2-0 quarter-final wins over Qatar and China, which have already guaranteed they will walk away with at least a bronze medal each. Henry Leung Chi-hin and Lau Tsz-kwan, who were part of the men’s team that won bronze at the Hangzhou Games, got the job done early, meaning it was a quiet day at the office for Lai Cheuk-nam. Up next for the trio are Pakistan, who Lau acknowledged would provide a tougher test than their quarter-final opponents. “Of course, I’m really happy,” Lau said. “This is a new team for us, so just so happy we will win a medal with this team. “Tomorrow we will play against Pakistan, and they’re a pretty strong team. I think we are as well, so we will try our best to get it done.” The women, meanwhile, will face India, who count singles silver medallist Anahat Singh in their ranks. Lee Ka-yi, who beat Liu Ziyi in the opening match of the quarter-finals, said winning a medal had been the team’s “first target” and they would now try not to “put any pressure on ourselves” as they chased gold. Elsewhere, golfer Taichi Kho made a solid, if at times spectacular start, to the defence of his individual gold, carding a one-under-par 69 at the Kasugai Country Club East Course. Chinese Taipei’s Wang Wei-hsuan and Japan’s Kazuki Higa shot five-under 65s to open up a one-stroke lead at the top of the leaderboard. The highlight of Kho’s round was a hole-in-one at the par-3 seventh, where he “took a lot off a seven iron”. Matthew Cheung had Hong Kong’s best round with a 68, while Jason Hak Shun-yat struggled with a 73. The three-under team total left the Hangzhou bronze medallists in a tie for fifth. In the women’s tournament, Singapore’s Shannon Tan opened up with a 63 to take an early lead in the battle for individual gold. Hong Kong trio Ginnie Ding, Arianna Lau and Sophie Han all shot matching 70s.

title: Kuala Lumpur is world’s most polluted city due to haze, Singapore third, index shows
description: The readings for Kuala Lumpur at 166 and Singapore at 155 put both cities’ air quality as unhealthy, according to Swiss monitor IQAir.
content: Malaysia’s capital topped a global pollution ranking on Wednesday and nearby Singapore came in third, with smoke from wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia blamed for the unhealthy conditions. A milky haze has shrouded the cities for more than a month as smoke drifted from fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands. Kuala Lumpur was the world’s most polluted major city early on Wednesday, according to Swiss monitor IQAir, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) reading of 166. Singapore ranked third at 155. The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks. Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous. “It’s really impacting our health and also the visibility,” said Izzah Irdina, 22, a recent graduate from Kuala Lumpur. “During this haze I can’t even see the Merdeka 118,” she said, referring to the world’s second tallest building. “In another two months I hope the haze will end,” added Izzah, who said she mostly stayed indoors. Anusuriyeh, 41, said she was “not sure when it’s going to end because it’s a natural disaster”. “But I’m taking daily vitamins to keep my vitality, and my children too are wearing a mask and taking vitamins,” said the employee of Malaysia’s petroleum giant Petronas. Transboundary haze is a recurring problem in Southeast Asia, but this year’s episode has been particularly severe. Hot, dry conditions associated with the El Nino weather phenomenon have fuelled the fires in Indonesia, which are also linked to land clearing, making the blazes harder to contain. In Singapore, 18-year-old student Darius Chew, who suffers from allergic rhinitis, said the haze had forced him to reduce his sporting activities. “I’ve cut down on sports because it’s really hard to continue as soon as I start sneezing,” Chew said. Fellow student Ryan Ang, 18, who has asthma, said he had been sneezing more frequently and suffering from a runny nose, particularly in the mornings and at night. “I’m not really cutting down on outdoor activities much, but it’s affecting my health a bit,” Ang said. “You can’t really do as much as you want to do,” he added. Retired Singaporean Athirah Abudullah, 69, said the haze has had less impact on her because she spends most of her time indoors. She ventured out mainly for groceries and prayers at the mosque, but said her granddaughter, who suffered from eczema, had been affected by the haze. “We have no choice, we just face it,” Athirah said. “We just pray for rain every day.”

title: From Taiwan to Takaichi, the geopolitical fallout from Xi-Trump summit
description: From structural rifts between US and China to debate over Washington’s treatment of ally Japan, some highlights from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage of the Xi-Trump summit. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel. 2. ‘Right now, it’s fine’: Trump brushes off summit talk on Taiwan US President Donald Trump has sought to play down exchanges with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on Taiwan, saying on Saturday that they touched on the subject only briefly. 3. Xi’s US welcome highlights lack of reception for Takaichi Starkly contrasting receptions for the Japanese leader and the Chinese president in the United States have sparked debate over Washington’s treatment of Tokyo as an ally. 4. Xi-Trump atmospherics welcomed but mask structural rifts: analysts During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables. 5. Xi presses Trump to take the next step on Taiwan: oppose independence Chinese President Xi Jinping pressed his US counterpart Donald Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence – a call that would require a shift in Washington’s long-standing position and further restraint on American arms sales to the island, according to analysts. 6. Trump, Takaichi reaffirm US-Japan ties in phone call after Xi state visit Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday. 7. Did Beijing and Washington agree on a crisis prevention deal, or not? Disagreement over how to prevent conflicts could account for differences in how Chinese and US accounts have characterised discussion on the topic during last week’s summit, analysts said.

title: Opinion | US-China conflict doesn’t have to become a self-fulfilling prophecy
description: Power shifts are dangerous, but their outcomes are not predetermined. The US and China have every opportunity to avoid conflict.
content: We are reminded seemingly daily of the great power transitions that ended in conflict. However, it is the exceptions – the ones that did not result in war – that could have real lessons to offer. Today, the question is more than academic. Standing beside US President Donald Trump at the White House last week, President Xi Jinping proposed that competition between China and the United States should be “a race of catching up with one another”, not “a wrestle where one either wins or loses”. Whether these metaphors survive the real disputes between the two countries on trade, technology or political red lines is another matter. Could the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation really go hand in hand with making America great again? The term “Thucydides Trap” has become a familiar phrase among those following international relations. Even so, we should not become prisoners of a catchy metaphor as it can easily turn into a self-fulfilling prophecy. Looking through the history of great power shifts, one finds reassuring instances. Sometimes rivals do not destroy each other, instead managing their relations responsibly to the advantage of their people and the world. The undisputed leading power of the past century rose to prominence in just such a peaceful transition. At the end of the 19th century, Britain and the US were anything but natural partners. The 1895 Venezuela crisis brought them into a serious diplomatic confrontation just as American power was rapidly expanding. Yet Britain ultimately chose accommodation over an increasingly costly struggle for primacy in the western hemisphere. It did not try to prevent America’s rise; it protected its most important interests by adjusting spheres of influence, deciding which parts of the changing balance were worth contesting and which were not. France and Germany found another route after World War II: institutionalisation. After three major wars in 70 years, they progressively placed the sources of their competition inside common institutions. They began with coal and steel, followed by a series of mutually beneficial and inclusive communities, eventually resulting in the European Union. Rather than balancing against German strength, France helped construct a system in which that strength could grow without becoming a threat. Argentina and Brazil demonstrated yet another mechanism. By the 1970s, they were strategic competitors with serious disputes over regional influence and shared rivers. Instead of allowing uncertainty to develop into a stand-off, they gradually chose transparency and cooperation. From agreements on water resources to nuclear cooperation, they built a system of bilateral safeguards. Neither side abandoned its ambitions; they just reduced uncertainty and the danger of interpreting every advance by the other as a threat requiring a response. Throughout history, former rivals have accommodated changing spheres of influence, embedded competition in institutions, accepted negotiated settlements, built transparency or simply decided that the cost of confrontation is higher than its potential gains. None of these examples can provide a ready-made formula for Washington and Beijing, and none mirrors their exact rivalry today. History does not provide blueprints but rather offers us lessons. The question Washington asks reflects the logic of rivalry itself: how to prevent China from overturning the status quo? In response, Beijing asks how it can prevent the US from containing its rise and development. But what if we turn the questions around? What changes in influence can be acceptable for Washington without sacrificing its vital interests and well-being? What forms of restraint or reassurance could China offer and guarantee to make US acceptance politically and strategically possible? Today’s world is vastly more interconnected than during previous power transitions as the two rivals are tied into the same global economy with all its institutions. The international community is not a passive spectator; it is a large number of capable actors interested in upholding stability and peace. They will encourage both Washington and Beijing to ask the right questions. The vast number of bilateral and multilateral relationships raises the price of allowing US-China rivalry to spiral out of control. None of this makes conflict impossible, and neither does history guarantee that sensible solutions will prevail. However, it does challenge the fatalism built into the idea of the Thucydides Trap. Power shifts are dangerous, but their outcomes are not predetermined. States have long found ways to accommodate changing realities, institutionalise competition or build trust and confidence. Washington and Beijing will have to find their own formula and doing so will require political will on both sides. Xi’s words in Washington deserve to be taken seriously. Artificial intelligence, tariffs, Taiwan, Iran or the South China Sea are all on the table as tangible challenges to be solved or managed, but none of these need become a casus belli. The Thucydides Trap is useful as a warning but dangerous as a prophecy. It becomes a trap only when those with power portray it as inevitable and walk straight into it.

title: Did Beijing and Washington agree on a crisis prevention deal, or not?
description: While the Chinese side says the nations agreed to conclude a deal, a US official reportedly denies the discussion took place.
content: Disagreement over how to prevent conflicts could explain why Chinese and US accounts characterised discussions at last week’s summit so differently, analysts said. Speaking at a White House arrival ceremony, Chinese President Xi Jinping said the two militaries should maintain regular dialogue and “improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention”. In a statement issued after the summit, China’s foreign ministry said the countries’ militaries had agreed “to conclude a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible”. The MOU was listed separately from the eight “deliverables and understandings” reached at the summit that were also included in the ministry’s statement, which did not specify when or where the two militaries reached this agreement. Neither the White House nor US President Donald Trump has made any public comment on the proposed crisis communication and prevention mechanisms or the MOU. China’s defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment. China’s Minister of National Defence Dong Jun did not travel with Xi on the US trip last week, nor was any other senior military official included in the Chinese delegation. “This is not accurate and was not even discussed,” an unnamed US official told the Financial Times, referring to China’s claim about the MOU on crisis communication. Chinese analysts said Beijing’s remarks could be aimed at building concrete mechanisms after the two countries agreed to a broader framework earlier this year. Hu Bo, director of the South China Sea Strategic Situation Probing Initiative, a Beijing-based think tank, said Xi’s call for stronger crisis communication and prevention mechanisms could have been aimed at advancing the two countries’ vision of building “a constructive relationship of strategic stability”. “If you are going to talk about strategic stability, you need to have some measures in place. Otherwise, if something happens, you will not be able to maintain stability,” he said. Hu said the MOU could address broader understandings between the two militaries on avoiding conflict. Efforts to strengthen military-to-military communication and manage risks had been carried out in recent years through several existing mechanisms, he added. These efforts included the establishment of a crisis communication working group between the US Office of the Secretary of Defence and China’s Office for International Military Cooperation, with the inaugural meeting held by video conference in October 2020. No meetings have been held since. Zhou Bo, a retired People’s Liberation Army senior colonel, wrote last year that the 2020 meeting marked the first time crisis management was “officially mentioned” in China-US military discussions. He described it as “a bold step in the right direction”. Additionally, the two militaries already have rules governing the safety of air and maritime encounters under a 2014 bilateral memorandum. The working group that reviews these rules last met in Hawaii in May to assess their implementation and discuss measures to improve military maritime safety. There have also been signs of renewed military-to-military contact since Xi and Trump met in Beijing in May. At the Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence Conference in late August, China and the US ended a two-year hiatus in command-level contact with a meeting in Canada between Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo. Hu added that the discussions on crisis management could have been held before the summit. But other analysts said the discrepancy may reflect deeper differences over what crisis prevention should entail. A Beijing-based analyst, who requested anonymity, said the two sides had “major differences over how a crisis should be prevented”. “The most important measure for preventing crises is for you [the US] to reduce, and ultimately stop, activities around China that threaten China and China’s national interests. The Americans certainly cannot accept that at present,” he said. The analyst said crisis prevention could include measures such as establishing rules of behaviour and setting guidelines for maintaining safe distances during military encounters at sea, but such measures were insufficient. The analyst said the most important measure would be reducing US military activities on China’s “doorstep”, including surveillance operations in the South China Sea, which he said could prompt Chinese aircraft to respond and “inevitably cause friction and manoeuvring between the two sides”. He also cited former US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taiwan as an example. “You triggered a crisis, and then after triggering a crisis, you call us and ask how to avoid one. Our view is, if you do not come in the first place, there wouldn’t be a crisis to begin with,” he said. Shi Yinhong, an international relations professor at Beijing’s Renmin University, said that if the US side did not discuss or emphasise the need for crisis prevention at the summit, “it may have something to do with the situation in the South China Sea”. “Perhaps the US side believes that China has done too much militarisation in the South China Sea. It may not be able to accept both China’s militarisation of the area and an agreement to avoid conflict,” he said.

title: Anthropic raises alarm over elite hacking ability of Chinese firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.3
description: The open-weight AI model almost matches Claude Mythos for cyber capabilities, but has far weaker safeguards, Anthropic says.
content: The US artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has warned of the potential danger posed by Chinese firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, with the open-weight model showing a troubling mix of powerful hacking abilities but weak safety constraints. GLM-5.3 almost matches Anthropic’s most advanced model in terms of its cyber capabilities, but has far weaker safeguards, meaning there is greater potential for the model to be co-opted by bad actors, according to the San Francisco-based firm. In a report released on Tuesday, Anthropic said it had tested GLM-5.3’s ability to build end-to-end cyber exploits. The Chinese model successfully completed 50 out of 410 exploit attempts, compared with 56 for Claude Mythos Preview, a frontier Anthropic model that can only be used by vetted users. Unlike Mythos, GLM-5.3 is open-weight, meaning users are free to download and modify the underlying model. And Anthropic found during testing that “attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64 and 100 per cent of the time with simple techniques”, whereas the bypassing “did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models”. Anthropic researchers were able to remove the Z.ai model’s refusal mechanisms via “abliteration” – a technique that involves editing a model’s internal weight matrices – to suppress its tendency to reject harmful requests, according to the report. After spending about 2,200 GPU hours – equivalent to running 2,200 graphics processing units for one hour – performing and testing abliteration, GLM-5.3’s refusal rate plummeted from above 90 per cent to between 2 and 12 per cent across three safety benchmarks, Anthropic said. The computational power needed to conduct the abliteration cost roughly US$4,400, but Anthropic added that an experienced team might only need about US$1,200 to pull off such an attempt. Z.ai – also known as Zhipu AI – was quick to push back against the claims. Hours after Anthropic published its findings, Li Zixuan, the Chinese firm’s head of global operations, pointed out in a post on X that Z.ai’s models were being widely used by companies to defend themselves against cyber attacks. In July, the developer platform Hugging Face used GLM-5.2 to help investigate and contain an autonomous intrusion by OpenAI models, after Anthropic’s Claude refused parts of the security work because of its safeguards. GLM-5.3 had already “helped defend 389 open-source projects, with 4,249 potential vulnerabilities found so far”, Li said. The report feeds into a broader debate in the United States about the advantages and potential dangers of open-weight models, with Anthropic pushing for greater control over access to frontier models. Other US tech giants, including Meta Platforms and Nvidia, have championed open models, arguing that wider access can accelerate innovation and help maintain US leadership in AI. AI safety discussions have heated up in recent weeks, especially in the run-up to the just concluded meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump. Beijing and Washington agreed during the summit to formalise an AI dialogue mechanism to exchange views on the technology’s risks and benefits, though Trump said on Tuesday that he did not want to work with China on AI safety. Chinese AI models – the most advanced of which are all open-weight – are rapidly gaining cyber capabilities. When Z.ai released GLM-5.3 in August, the company said it had beaten Anthropic’s Mythos 5 model in a key cybersecurity test. The Beijing-based company withheld GLM-5.3’s model weights for two weeks after the launch to conduct additional safety testing and hardening. Earlier this month, the US government’s Centre for AI Standards and Innovation described GLM-5.3 as the “most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date”, although it estimated that the model remained about four months behind the overall US frontier on an aggregate of cybersecurity benchmarks. In August, Kimi K3 – a model created by the Chinese firm Moonshot AI – broke out of a supposedly isolated sandbox environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and accessed the internet. The escape did not involve hacking an external system.

title: ‘Who wants McDonald’s?’: mainland tourist shares HK$10,000 prize in Hong Kong
description: Visitor turns her winnings into 24-hour citywide giveaway, treating passers-by, cleaners and homeless people.
content: A mainland Chinese tourist who won a HK$10,000 (US$1,275) McDonald’s voucher in Hong Kong has turned her last 24 hours in the city into a whirlwind giveaway to the elderly, cleaners and the homeless. The woman, who shared her spree on Chinese social media platform RedNote, said she won the “Hong Kong McDonald’s HK$10,000 subsidy” through Alipay on Saturday. According to a screenshot of her post, the voucher was valid for only one week and allowed up to 10 transactions, each capped at HK$1,000 and was restricted to McDonald’s stores in Hong Kong. With only a day left before returning to the mainland and in-store gift cards sold out, the woman decided to treat strangers as a way of sharing her good fortune around the city. “The first time I saw this prize, I was completely stunned,” she wrote, adding that she then decided to do “something crazy and fun”. Over her last 24 hours in Hong Kong, she went to multiple McDonald’s branches in Wan Chai, Central and Tsim Sha Tsui to place orders for strangers. Describing herself as an introvert, she admitted offering free food to strangers was difficult at first, saying she was so flustered she “grabbed people at McDonald’s entrances, switching between Chinese and English at once”. However, she said: “Seeing everyone’s happy faces, I got addicted immediately.” She moved between outlets to avoid burdening staff at a single branch and to stay within the voucher’s per-transaction limit. She said she even shouted inside one McDonald’s she visited: “Who wants McDonald’s? I’ll buy it for you!” Despite receiving few responses at first, her social media post in Hong Kong about the giveaway gained traction and users started to turn up to help promote her efforts. Apart from passers-by, she gave meals to police officers, cleaners, homeless people and the elderly, as well as children. Some strangers brought small gifts such as fruit, snacks, face masks and postcards in exchange for the free food – items the woman kept as souvenirs. The woman also admitted the giveaway left her exhausted. After giving away thousands of dollars' worth of burgers on the first night, a mix-up left her with a bag of sauce instead of her own burger. Too excited to sleep and suffering from stomach pain, she resumed spending the remaining credit, giving the food to sanitation workers and passers-by. As she departed from the city at West Kowloon station on Sunday, the woman said in a post her journey was “something I will always feel supremely happy and proud of”. She added: “I’m just a lucky passer-on of goodwill: I did not really spend my own money, and I could not have eaten it all anyway. Why not?” Her series of posts had drawn more than 125,000 likes on RedNote by Wednesday, with many comments praising her generosity and kind acts. A user on RedNote shared news of his free treat from the woman in a post that generated more than 54,000 likes, saying he was surprised that someone pointed at him as soon as he walked in, saying: “I’m treating you!” “What a delightful way to end the day. It was a brief encounter, but I hope everything goes well for her in the future,” he wrote. Another Hongkonger who received the free meal also shared on Threads: “The whole thing was so joyful. Good deeds know no borders.” Alipay Official also responded to her post, saying: “The HK$10,000 prize was simply won by you, but you passed this happiness on to everyone.” McDonald’s later sent her a 1,000 yuan (US$150) meal card as a gift, which the woman said she would use to treat cleaners and relatives back on the mainland, “letting the kindness continue”.

title: Review | German artist Anne Imhof’s Hong Kong show is as ambitious as it is disjointed
description: Imhof’s solo show at Tai Kwun – her first in Asia – blends ballet and art in an intense and ambiguous statement of self-discovery.
content: Tickets to the two opening-week performances of House of Swans, Anne Imhof’s first solo show in Asia, sold out well before its September 25 premiere at Hong Kong’s Tai Kwun heritage and arts centre. That is partly due to the venue’s capacity of 150 visitors per show, but also because the German visual artist, choreographer and performer has a sizeable following across both the art and fashion worlds. At the 2017 Venice Biennale, her transformation of the German Pavilion, adding raised glass floors, barricades and caged Dobermans in a critique of modern power structures, won her the prestigious Golden Lion award. In 2025, her memorable show Doom: House of Hope at New York’s Park Avenue Armoury featured a reversed version of Romeo and Juliet performed in a bleak, prom-themed drill hall with Balenciaga models and ballet dancers. Her Hong Kong show, “Anne Imhof: House of Swans”, generated a lot of hype that it unfortunately does not quite live up to. The show, which occupies two floors at Tai Kwun’s JC Contemporary, comprises two core components: an exhibition and a contemporary ballet performance. As with Imhof’s previous projects, the experience is ambitious and frantic, but the works here feel somewhat disjointed. Across the two floors, Imhof’s pieces – scratched aluminium panels, crowd-barrier structures, a bronze relief, a countdown jumbotron and stormy paintings – touch on her recurring interest in “the body in motion” and a state of “in-betweenness”, as the gallery text suggests. Yet neither the artwork nor the wall labels articulate a clear conclusion or offer distinct insights into these concepts. The exhibition reads like a retrospective compilation hastily tethered by themes so grandiose – time, movement, spatial transition – they could apply to almost any artist. On the upper floor, Imhof pairs her four-channel video Citizen (2025) – which explores mortality, physical endurance and bodily observation – with a glass cube housing rusted film canisters she salvaged from the abandoned Clear Water Bay Film Studio. She first visited Hong Kong in 2023 by Tai Kwun’s invitation to prepare for this solo show. Yet pairing her video work with these abandoned film canisters offers little meaningful commentary; the two elements feel juxtaposed by chance, connected merely by the fact that both involve moving images. The ballet segment delivers a far clearer and more compelling thesis on self-discovery. Performed by Imhof’s frequent collaborators Devon Teuscher and Toon Lobach, alongside dancers from Hong Kong Ballet, House of Swans is loosely inspired by Romeo and Juliet with nods to Doom and the romantic ballet Giselle. It depicts a young woman’s journey to break free from restrictive familial bonds and discover belonging within a chosen family. Rather than a traditional stage, JC Contemporary’s gallery space is transformed into a massive cage. Performers open the metal gates, inviting visitors to sit or roam within the performance area. The 70-minute piece opens with ballet dancers practising classical poses. Gradually, the refined technique evolves into an expressive performance blending classical ballet, contemporary movement, live piano score, a loudspeaker moving along a ceiling track and rhythmic chanting (“love me” and “swans can’t go to Mars”) by an emo musician wearing an inside-out red hoodie. Dancers subvert traditional ballet pantomime, reinterpreting gestures such as vow-pointing into falling tears or flashing middle fingers while leaping to blend elegance with rebellious defiance. In another motif, a male dancer crawls on all fours while led on a leash by another dancer. Moments later, he pulls his shirt over his head, erasing his facial identity before repeating the gesture of catching falling tears in his palm. “It’s a reference to house culture,” co-curator Tiffany Leung later explains. Though not explicitly stated in the exhibition text, Leung says that House of Swans pays homage to the 1980s underground drag house culture in New York, as documented in Jennie Livingston’s 1990 film Paris Is Burning. That era saw drag queens form supportive “houses” that offered community to marginalised performers amid systemic homophobia and transphobia. The main drawback of this programme is accessibility: the live performance takes place on limited dates until the end of November and the gallery has limited capacity. Co-curator Ying Kwok suggests this limitation is an intentional choice, mirroring Imhof’s fascination with presence, absence and the “in-between”. “The absence is also one of the works on its own. It is not less significant than the live performance itself,” she says on September 24, ahead of the exhibition’s official opening. But that argument falls flat: the whole experience needs the dance to make it alive, and staging the dance inside Tai Kwun, Hong Kong’s former Central Police Station, adds an intriguing layer to this cross-cultural dialogue on power, law and order. Removing the dance takes away the narrative significance of the artist’s show in Hong Kong. Imhof’s exhibition is intense, overwhelming and ambiguous. Yet that ambiguity may well be the point. “I had this idea of Hong Kong as a city I couldn’t fully grasp – one that evoked so many feelings and desires in me,” Imhof says. “I can hardly explain it in words, which is why I make art. “It is an invitation to step not just into an exhibition at Tai Kwun, but into a new world I experienced. We created this piece for this specific moment in time, and I’m very happy that we share all of this together.” “Anne Imhof: House of Swans” runs until January 3, 2027 at JC Contemporary, Tai Kwun.

title: Indonesia targets free public schooling amid funding concerns
description: Education experts question where the money will come from, and urge the government to focus on improving the quality of learning.
content: Indonesia is pursuing plans to make public schools free at all levels, stretching from kindergarten to university, but mounting pressure on the state budget could hinder the government from pulling off the massive undertaking, analysts have said. President Prabowo Subianto summoned his ministers last week to discuss a plan to “accelerate the implementation of free education in public schools”, according to a statement released by cabinet secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya on September 23. “Free education [will be] implemented in public schools, from preschool or kindergarten, elementary school, junior high school, to senior high or vocational school. Overall, there are about 164,000 public schools at these levels throughout Indonesia,” Wijaya said. The government also aimed to finalise plans to eliminate fees at state universities, including standard semester tuition and initial admission fees, “in the next two to four weeks”, he said. “This step confirms the government’s commitment to providing the widest possible access to education, improving the quality of learning, and ensuring that every educational pathway receives the attention and support it needs.” In an address on September 18, Prabowo said he “very much agreed” with the idea that all public schools, including universities, should be tuition-free. “Later, someone will ask, ‘Where does the money come from?’ The money will be taken from [state] funds that have been corrupted and stolen,” Prabowo said. Officials estimated that they needed to allocate up to 302 trillion rupiah (US$16.9 billion) per year to make education free, including 93.7 trillion rupiah to eliminate tuition at state universities. Minister of Primary and Secondary Education Abdul Muti told reporters on September 21 that all public schools from kindergarten to high school in Indonesia were “already free”, while initiatives such as the Smart Indonesia Programme helped students from poor families pay their tuition fees. In Indonesia, the government subsidises the operational costs of public schools, but students’ parents still have to pay for books, uniforms, voluntary donations and other fees that each school committee may impose. Financial feasibility Education experts said Prabowo’s latest programme could make pursuing higher education a realistic possibility for more students, but they expressed scepticism about the proposal’s financial feasibility. “This is a good and populist policy, but can it be implemented? That’s a big question because the budget isn’t guaranteed. The president said the [money] will be taken from corruptors, which is even more abstract and unclear,” Totok Soefijanto, a rector at the Jakarta-based private higher education EMTEK Digital Media Institute, told This Week in Asia. While the government had set aside 20 per cent of the state budget, or 769.09 trillion rupiah, this year for the education sector, Totok said its spending was not committed to improving the quality of education. “The education budget has been used more for routine expenditures, such as civil servant salaries and allowances, rather than for the essentials of education, such as improving teacher competency, school facilities, the quality of the educational process, and enhancing learning,” Totok said. Doni Koesoema, an educator with the Indonesian Platform for Teacher Networking, said the education budget was currently “scattered across various ministries and largely used for the free nutritious meals programme”. The education budget is split across four institutions. The largest recipient, at 29 per cent, is the National Nutrition Agency, which oversees Prabowo’s flagship nutritious meals programme. Doni estimated that covering tuition fees from kindergarten to university level in Indonesia would require 850 trillion rupiah per year. To improve the quality of learning, Itje Chodidjah, an independent education expert, suggested the government direct its limited budget towards empowering educators instead. “Free [education] isn’t always a positive thing if the policy is implemented without careful consideration. Schooling can be free for children who truly need it, but what’s the point of a free education without quality?” Itje said. If teacher welfare was not met, “it will disrupt the process of improving the quality of students, even if their schooling is free”, she added. Totok also pointed to other education costs, such as transport and uniforms, for students of low-income families. “There are actually many barriers for children from poor families to attend college. It’s not just tuition fees. Many families rely on their children to work instead of going to school,” Totok said. He cited the example of one of his students from East Nusa Tenggara province who had already received a university scholarship but had to quit school to support his family financially. While offering free schooling at all education levels was “something worth appreciating”, Doni said it needed to be paired with targeted affirmative action, as fee waivers at state universities would largely benefit middle- and upper-class students who had the resources to pass competitive admission exams. “Free education must be based on meritocracy, but there must also be affirmative action for students from low-income families or those facing [educational] barriers in remote areas,” Doni said. “Otherwise, they won’t be able to attend university.”

title: Meet legendary rocker Todd Rundgren, who said Taylor Swift ‘ruined music’
description: The 78-year-old, who raised actress Liv Tyler, called the ‘Patient Zero’ singer ‘the apotheosis of mediocrity’, as opposed to a ‘real musician’ like Lady Gaga.
content: Pop superstar Taylor Swift just won big at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. At the event held on September 27, she took home the inaugural Artist Director Honors, as well as prizes for Video of the Year for “The Fate of Ophelia” and Best Direction for “Opalite”, setting a record for most VMAs won with 33 trophies. She also premiered the star-studded music video for “Patient Zero” at the VMAs. Just two days before the big night, legendary rock musician Todd Rundgren, 78, tore into the 36-year-old multi-Grammy winner in an interview with Vulture, calling her “the apotheosis of mediocrity” as opposed to Lady Gaga, whom he described as a “real musician”. He further argued that Swift “ruined music”, before denouncing her abilities as a singer, songwriter and dancer. Here’s everything to know about Todd Rundgren. What is Todd Rundgren’s background? Todd Harry Rundgren was born on June 22, 1948, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to parents Ruth and Harry Rundgren, who raised him in Upper Darby. He has a brother, Robin, and two sisters, June and Lynette. He attended Upper Darby High School, per The Philadelphia Inquirer. His father worked as an engineer at a DuPont factory in Philadelphia, Rundgren told the Charleston City Paper. “I grew up with an interest in and a lack of intimidation by technology,” he recalled. According to The Pulmyears Music Blog, Harry Rundgren even built a high-fidelity sound system himself, which contributed to his children’s love for music. How did Todd Rundgren get into music? Todd Rundgren got into music when he was eight, learning guitar after failing to master the flute, per The Pulmyears Music Blog. At 17, he started the band Money with his friend Randy Reed and later performed with another band called Woody’s Truck Stop. In the late 1960s, Rundgren co-founded the rock band Nazz before releasing his first solo studio album, Runt, in 1970. His 1972 double record Something/Anything? shot the musician to fame, and he went on to form another band, Utopia, in 1973. He also famously produced Meat Loaf’s 1977 album Bat Out of Hell. Rundgren was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. Is Todd Rundgren married? Rundgren has been married to Michele Gray, a musician and former dancer for rock band The Tubes, since 1998. They share a biological son, Rebop, and an adopted son, Keoni. The singer-songwriter famously had an on-again, off-again relationship with fellow musician and former model Bebe Buell between 1972 and 1979. He helped raise Liv Tyler, Buell’s daughter with Steven Tyler, in the first few years after she was born on July 1, 1977. According to People, Rundgren signed Liv’s birth certificate, and the child, who went on to become an actress, didn’t find out the identity of her biological father until she was 10. Rundgren has two more sons, Rex and Randy, from his relationship with Karen Darvin.

title: China pledges more domestic grain supply after excluding US soybeans from tariff cuts
description: Grain production target set at 725 million tonnes by 2030, as China proposes tariff cuts on US agricultural products – but not soybeans.
content: China has pledged to step up grain production, including soybeans, to ensure domestic supplies amid heightened volatility in global food markets, even as the country has just proposed cutting tariffs on a range of US agricultural products. The push comes as China’s grain supply is expected to come under growing pressure from rising demand in the coming years, while the country remains heavily dependent on overseas soybean supplies. Soybeans were excluded from the latest tariff-relief deal between China and the US announced on Sunday. “As overall grain demand is expected to keep rising, supply and demand will remain in a tight balance, meaning the string of food security must always be kept taut,” Zhang Zhu, minister of agriculture and rural affairs, said at a press conference on Tuesday, responding to a question on the country’s grain supply outlook through 2030. To strengthen domestic supplies, China will raise grain production capacity by keeping acreage stable and increasing yields, with capacity targeted at 725 million tonnes by the end of 2030, Zhang said. In particular, the country will step up corn and soybean production and expand edible-oil supplies through multiple channels, Zhang said. He noted that while staple grain supplies were ample, feed grains such as corn remained relatively tight, and China continued to rely heavily on imported soybeans for edible-oil production and livestock feed. The government will step up support for grain production through price policies, subsidies and insurance, Zhang added, while coordinating production, storage and imports to keep grain prices at reasonable levels. The remarks come as global food markets remain roiled, with the US-Israel war on Iran keeping oil and fertiliser prices volatile and the Russia-Ukraine war disrupting Black Sea grain exports. Concerns over the current El Nino cycle and trade tensions have also added to the pressure. Following President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last week, China and the US released details about the non-sensitive goods set for tariff reductions. China’s list included corn, wheat, sorghum, meat, dairy products and vegetable oils but excluded soybeans for crushing and animal feed. The exclusion means US soybeans will remain subject to a 10 per cent tariff in China, frustrating American farmers and sending Chicago soybean futures lower in early-week trading. China’s reliance on overseas soybeans poses a vulnerability. The country accounts for only about 4.9 per cent of global soybean production but 27 per cent of consumption, while its external dependence has remained above 80 per cent for more than a decade, according to an August report by official newspaper Farmers’ Daily. Imports are “heavily concentrated in the US and Brazil, leaving the supply chain relatively fragile and posing significant risks to industrial security”, the report said. Despite this, Chinese buyers have continued purchasing soybeans from both countries. In a September update, the US Department of Agriculture’s Foreign Agricultural Service said that, as of August 13, China had bought 5.7 million tonnes of US new-crop soybeans for delivery in the 2026-27 season, with another 3.8 million tonnes sold to “unknown destinations”, which the authority said could indicate purchases by Chinese state-owned firms. At the same time, China’s current 10 per cent tariff on US soybeans has encouraged commercial buyers to source more from South America, with Brazil shipping record volumes between June and August, the report added.

title: China’s Tiangong space station camera captures its first images of Hong Kong
description: Developed by HKUST, Musico camera sends back its first images of city ahead of 77th anniversary of founding of People’s Republic of China.
content: A remote-sensing camera aboard China’s Tiangong space station that was developed by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology has released its first images of the city ahead of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. The university published a series of videos and photos on Wednesday captured by the Musico camera, saying they showcased the major achievements of the Hong Kong research team’s participation in the national space programme. Professor Zhang Limin, who jointly led the camera project, said the photos were a “special gift” to China, including Hong Kong, ahead of National Day on Thursday. “It not only marks the successful deployment of a Hong Kong-developed scientific payload aboard the Tiangong space station, but also demonstrates Hong Kong’s growing contribution to the nation’s space endeavours,” said Zhang, who is also head of the university’s department of civil and environmental engineering. The images were captured by the camera’s four optical sensors – for carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen and aerosols – and show Hong Kong’s landforms and topographic features, as well as those of surrounding areas. Musico, which stands for Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory, is considered the world’s first lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision instrument for jointly detecting point sources of carbon dioxide and methane. It was developed under the university’s leadership. The camera had carried out scientific missions aboard the Tiangong space station for more than three months and had officially entered routine operations, the university said. Hong Kong’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, a payload specialist, is taking part in a crewed mission aboard the space station. She blasted off aboard the Shenzhou-23 with Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan in May. Professor Su Hui, who also led the project, said that since Lai and her colleagues installed and activated the instrument aboard the space station, Musico had acquired images of more than 450 target regions worldwide, generating 4.3TB of data. She described the camera as an “eye for space” that contributed to Hong Kong’s role in national and global climate governance. Su added that the team was “thrilled” when the camera transmitted its first clear images of Hong Kong back to Earth. “Due to persistent cloud cover and rainy weather across Hong Kong and south China during the summer months, obtaining high-quality imagery of Hong Kong has not been easy,” she said. “Fortunately, favourable weather conditions ahead of National Day allowed us to observe Hong Kong through Musico.”

title: Chinese researchers say missile lidar model can spot US F-35 at up to 61.5km
description: Chinese air force supplier models airborne single-photon lidar to spot stealth fighters without triggering radar or heat sensors.
content: A computer simulation developed by Chinese researchers suggests that a missile-borne system with the latest light detection and ranging system, or lidar, could detect and track an F-35 stealth fighter at up to 61.5km (38 miles) at night.
