The theoretical model developed by a leading Chinese air force missile supplier says that under ideal conditions, the claimed range could have implications for the F-35’s ability to survive while facing China’s stealth fighters. But one analyst is sceptical that the development would allow the user to find a stealth target in a vast sky with a narrow laser beam. In air-to-air combat, the F-35 can carry short-range missiles, such as the AIM-9X Sidewinder, which has a reported range of about 16km to 32km and uses an imaging infrared seeker. It can also carry medium-range missiles, such as the AIM-120D-3 AMRAAM, although conventional missile-borne radars struggle to detect next-generation stealth fighters. While a 60km detection range would expand a missile’s tracking window, it is within the engagement distance of the F-35’s main long-range air-to-air missiles, which can strike targets past 160km. The research was led by Li Zhiyuan of the China Airborne Missile Academy, which specialises in air-to-air missiles and serves as a research and development centre as well as a base for mass production. The paper was published in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Aero Weaponry on September 18. The study examined whether a missile-borne single-photon lidar could detect and track stealth fighters. Unlike radar, which detects targets using radio waves, single-photon lidar uses reflected laser light and is designed to detect extremely small numbers of photons returning from a target. The technology could provide another means of detecting aircraft designed to reduce their radar signatures. The lidar system described in the Chinese study would, at least in simulation, extend the potential engagement distance into the beyond-visual-range domain. The study examined whether a missile-borne single-photon lidar operating at a wavelength of 1,064 nanometres could detect an F-35C under different light and atmospheric conditions. The researchers developed a mathematical model for a single-photon array lidar mounted on a missile. It incorporated detector dead-time corrections – accounting for sensor recovery time between detections – atmospheric transmission over a distance of 15km, and background noise from the sky, atmospheric backscatter and detector dark counts. Designed around the size and power constraints of a missile-borne system, the simulation used low-power 1.0 millijoule laser pulses and a compact 100mm lens. Even with these constraints, the researchers calculated that the lidar required a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.8 decibels – corresponding to at least 9.4 detected echo photons – to cut through the atmospheric noise and lock onto the F-35C. The maximum simulated detection range was 27.7km during the day and 61.5km at night. At 27.7km, the system could achieve sharp target detail accurate within 20cm in depth and transverse resolution within 50cm. The authors said the 1,064-nanometre wavelength was chosen because stealth aircraft had fewer dedicated countermeasures against active laser detection than against conventional radar and infrared sensing. Recent Chinese military equipment displays have highlighted other work on airborne laser systems. At an exhibition in Beijing, the China Precision Engineering Institute for Aircraft Industry, also known as the 303 Research Institute, unveiled an airborne suspended laser weapon pod, indicating efforts to reduce the size of airborne laser equipment. Shenyang Aircraft Corporation has also mentioned laser weapons in its complete design drawings for China’s next-generation J-50 and J-36 stealth fighters. The study does not establish that the system has been built, flight-tested or integrated into an operational missile. A military analyst who requested anonymity questioned whether the laser beam could function as an early-warning search system. “The laser beam is so narrow, it probably couldn’t serve as an early-warning radar; in the early stages, it’s just a rangefinder,” the analyst said. Another expert familiar with military equipment said: “I don’t understand it, technically.” Li said further work would focus on optimising photon-related parameters and developing more accurate methods for detecting stealth targets using missile-borne single-photon lidar.

title: Zheng Qinwen in confident mood ahead of China Open, but admits to pressure of playing at home
description: The 23-year-old has been placed in the same quarter as world No 1 Elena Rybakina, who beat her in the quarter-finals at the US Open.
content: Zheng Qinwen begins her China Open campaign on Friday confident she can recapture the form that made her among the best women’s players in the world, despite the pressures that come from trying to win at home. The former world No 4 and Olympic gold medallist said she was fully prepared for what lay ahead, even though she dropped outside the top 100 at one stage this season. But an impressive run to the quarter-finals of the US Open has helped her bounce back to near the top 50, and good performances during the WTA Tour’s Asian swing will lift her even further. “The biggest challenge [during the Chinese swing] is finding a balance between training, sponsor obligations and matches,” she said. “Many fans want me to perform well at home, and so do I. That brings extra pressure. “I don’t want to put pressure on myself, but whenever I compete during the Chinese swing, that pressure is always there.” For Zheng, the swing carries the weight of a “fifth grand slam”, with winning a title in front of home fans remaining one of her biggest dreams. However, she conceded she has yet to fully return to her expected level. “My ranking is still around No 50, and there are many matches ahead,” the 23-year-old said. “The injury and surgery forced me to start from scratch. I know my capabilities, and my current results don’t reflect my true level. I believe I still have the chance to achieve higher goals and do better in the future.” After undergoing elbow surgery last summer, Zheng made a brief comeback at last year’s China Open, winning just one match before suffering a setback that sidelined her until the Doha Open in February. Having dropped outside the top 100, Zheng fought through qualifying at the US Open and reeled off seven straight wins to reach the quarter-finals, signalling her return to form. Returning to the China Open singles draw, Zheng has been placed in the same quarter as world No 1 Elena Rybakina, who beat her in New York. She will face qualifier Shi Han in the opening round, with a potential second-round match-up against 15th seed Anna Kalinskaya. “I know why I am ranked where I am right now. Without the surgery, I might have kept moving up,” Zheng said. “But the surgery set me back, and I just had to start from zero.” Zheng is convinced her ranking does not reflect her true level, rather is a result of how she has performed over the past eight months. “Of course, I believe I can rank higher. My career-high was world No 4, and I still believe I can do better than that,” she said. “I really want to see how far I can go because deep down I know myself – I just need to prove it to everyone.” While acknowledging her strong performances at the US Open, Zheng believes this week represents a “fresh start”. Zheng goes into the tournament on the back of the Billie Jean King Cup in Shenzhen, where she lost in straight sets to Italy’s Jasmine Paolini as China missed out on a semi-final spot. After that match, she revealed she was not at 100 per cent physically and had taken painkillers to play. Following a few days of rest, Zheng said her health was improving. “I still have an occasional cough that hasn’t fully cleared, but I don’t think it’s a big issue. Overall, I’m feeling quite good,” she said.

title: All you need to know about OG Superman Christopher Reeve’s son Will, who battled cancer
description: The ABC News correspondent and Good Morning America host, who was diagnosed with testicular cancer this year, continues his parents’ impactful work.
content: Hollywood may have a new Superman in David Corenswet, who plays the Man of Steel in James Gunn’s 2025 film, but fans of the superhero can never forget the OG Superman, played by the late Christopher Reeve. Reeve played the Last Son of Krypton in four Superman films before a spinal cord injury left him paralysed from the neck down. He passed away in 2004. His lookalike son, Will Reeve, whom he shared with Dana Reeve, makes a cameo in Gunn’s Superman as a TV reporter, continuing his father’s legacy. In real life, Will Reeve works as an ABC News correspondent and Good Morning America host. He has interviewed Prince Harry, and calls himself a “tortured English major”. Now, two decades after losing his mother to lung cancer, Reeve is opening up about his own cancer journey. In a recent interview with People, he spoke about being diagnosed with testicular cancer, with 95 per cent of the cancer identified as an aggressive type called embryonal carcinoma. He was treated at Memorial Sloan Kettering, where his mother passed away. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Good Morning America (@goodmorningamerica) Reeve underwent an orchiectomy in May and a six-hour operation in June to remove multiple abdominal lymph nodes, with testicular cancer detected in three of them. He also received chemotherapy. “I was experiencing life as each of my parents at the same time,” he recalled, relating to his mother’s life with cancer and his father’s final years, when he needed care from his family. Reeve is cancer-free as of September 8. So, what else do we know about Will Reeve? Will Reeve’s family Will was born to Christopher and Dana Reeve on June 7, 1992. He was three when his father was met with the tragic equestrian accident that changed his life, and 11 when he passed away. A year and a half later, his mother, who had been a non-smoker, succumbed to lung cancer. According to Bedford & New Canaan Magazine (B&NC Mag), Reeve was taken in by his neighbours at his mother’s behest so he could finish his education where he started. He went on to graduate from his mother’s alma mater, Middlebury College, where he studied English and American literature. Reeve has two half-siblings from his father’s relationship with Gae Exton, Matthew and Alexandra Reeve, who appear together in the 2024 documentary Super/Man: The Christopher Reeve Story. He admits to being a nepo baby with a ‘normal childhood’ When asked about being Superman’s son, Reeve clarified to B&NC Mag, “I’m not, I’m Christopher and Dana’s son,” adding, “They taught me not to use our name to get something and never to expect special treatment.” However, the 34-year-old admits there was “nepotism at work” when he got to be on Sesame Street. Reeve had previously told People that he had a “totally normal childhood” despite his parents’ celebrity status or his father’s medical condition. He has a love of sports Reeve also revealed to B&NC Mag that he wanted to become a professional athlete before pursuing his dream job at ESPN. Sports played a crucial part in family bonding for the Reeves. Per People, the day before his unfortunate passing, Christopher watched his youngest son play hockey and they spent the rest of the day watching baseball together at home. Besides his career in sports journalism, Reeve has kept his love for sports alive through marathons, combining them with fundraising for the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation. He’s an ambassador of the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation Will is a board member and ambassador for the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation, which operates with the mission of “Today’s Care. Tomorrow’s Cure”. Reeve explained to People that his dad was “obsessed with finding a cure for paralysis”. On the other hand, his mother was focused on caregiving and “making sure that people living with paralysis and their families can enjoy as close to a normal life as possible”. The foundation works on expanding research towards this end. While covering a Good Morning America story about a man who had been paralysed for 10 years, walking again with the help of AI, Reeve said, “If I can be a proud son for a moment, you can draw a straight line from [my father’s] advocacy to developments like today.” He accidentally appeared on TV without pants When WFH goes wrong (or, your self-framed live shot goes too wide). Hope everyone got a much needed laugh 😂 pic.twitter.com/GbyLBhL7Be — Will Reeve (@ReeveWill) April 28, 2020 Reeve’s “underwear-gate” went viral during the Covid-19 pandemic when he appeared on a GMA segment wearing a suit and … shorts? Or at least that’s what he promised they were. “Trying to be efficient I got ready for a post-GMA workout a little too soon this morning,” he explained in a post on X (formerly Twitter). Will Reeve is married Reeve tied the knot with event planner, designer and producer Amanda Dubin, 30, in Miami this January, per People. It was Dubin who encouraged Reeve to get an ultrasound, which led to his cancer diagnosis. “We talk about ‘in sickness and in health.’ We got an early test of our vows, just a few months in,” he told People. The missus, for her part, added, “The silver lining was that we had validation early in the marriage that we are well equipped to tackle anything.”

title: Norway’s ministers questioned in parliament over Epstein ties
description: A total of 11 officials, including current Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, will speak before a committee.
content: Norway’s parliament began hearings on Wednesday of current and former ministers to examine practices in the diplomatic service, following revelations about ties between late US convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and senior Norwegian officials. The hearings come against the background of the foreign ministry’s payment of more than 130 million kroner to the International Peace Institute (IPI) between 1997 and 2018, a think tank headed by Norwegian diplomat Terje Rod-Larsen from 2005 to 2020. The Epstein files have shed light on ties between the US financier and Rod-Larsen and his diplomat wife Mona Juul, the architects of the 1993 Oslo Accords who are now under investigation in Norway – she for “aggravated corruption” and he for “complicity in aggravated corruption”. The couple denies any wrongdoing. In total, 11 officials who have held the positions of foreign minister or development aid minister since 2005, including current Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, will speak before the Storting’s standing committee on scrutiny and constitutional affairs. In addition to Rod-Larsen and Juul, the Epstein documents have highlighted ties between the sex offender, who died in prison in 2019, and Thorbjorn Jagland, a former prime minister, foreign minister, secretary general of the Council of Europe and chair of the Nobel Peace Prize Committee. Epstein also had ties with former foreign minister Borge Brende. Jagland is also under investigation on suspicion of “aggravated corruption”, but is not among the officials summoned by parliament, in part because he was foreign minister before 2005. Brende, who resigned in February as president of the World Economic Forum, is due to be heard on Wednesday. “The Epstein documents raise serious questions about abuse of office, a culture of accountability failures and poor management of development aid funds,” said Jonas Andersen Sayed, a member of the oversight committee. “The issue concerns public trust in the entire system. It is essential that all the facts are brought to light, that accountability is established, and that the necessary reforms are implemented,” he said. The hearings themselves will not result in any sanctions. Parliament has also set up an independent inquiry tasked with a much broader examination of the case, which is due to submit its final report by January 31, 2028.

title: 12 of the best new K-dramas to watch in October 2026, including 100 Days of Deception
description: October must-sees include historical spy drama 100 Days of Deception, romcom Make Me Tingle, and medical drama Doctor X: Mafia in White.
content: October brings with it cooler weather and 12 new shows sure to keep K-drama fans very busy, from romantic comedies to mystery thrillers. Read on to find out what to watch over the next month. 1. Your Personal Taxi Lead cast: Cha Tae-hyun My Sassy Girl’s Cha Tae-hyun is back on screens in the heartwarming limited series Your Personal Taxi, based on a webtoon of the same name by Mose Lee. Cha plays a kind taxi driver who chauffeurs passengers and listens to their special stories. He helps his fares – played by guest stars such as Lim Se-mi and Joo Jong-hyuk – through their woes and comforts them with a song they request. (Fuji TV, October 1) 2. Between Steps Lead cast: Choo Young-woo, Kim So-hyun Choo Young-woo (The Tale of Lady Ok) and Kim So-hyun (Good Boy) team up in the romantic drama Between Steps. Choo stars as Park Min-jae, a young man whose promising swimming career is waylaid after losing his left leg to bone cancer. After hitting rock bottom, he finds a new lease on life as he pursues a mechanical engineering degree and a career in robotics. Meanwhile, Im Yu-jin (Kim) transfers to the same school following an incident in her own life. (ENA/Disney+, October 5) 3. Merry Berry Love Lead cast: Ji Chang-wook, Mio Imada Ji Chang-wook and Mio Imada share the screen in the latest Korea-Japan co-production, Merry Berry Love. Recently seen in Netflix’s The Scandal, Ji plays Lee Yoo-bin, who travels to a remote Japanese island to start over following a devastating failure back in Korea. There, he meets Karin Shirahama, a strawberry farmer suffering from a secret illness played by Imada, who is known for the live-action series and film adaptations of the manga Trillion Game. (Disney+, October 7) 4. Doctor X: Mafia in White Lead cast: Kim Ji-won, Lee Jung-eun, Son Hyun-joo Queen of Tears actress Kim Ji-won leads the medical drama Doctor X: Mafia in White, an adaptation of the long-running Japanese drama Doctor-X: Surgeon Michiko Daimon. Kim plays the brilliant but cold surgeon Gye Soo-jung, who fills a surgical vacancy at the Guseo University Hospital, where she quickly proves her worth. Her resolve to expose corruption in the medical field leads to clashes with hospital director Bu Seung-kwon (Son Hyun-joo, Your Honor). (SBS/Netflix, October 9) 5. Take Charge of My Heart Lead cast: Kim Young-kwang, Chae Soo-bin Chae Soo-bin (When the Phone Rings) and Kim Young-kwang (Somebody) form an unusual bond in the romcom Take Charge of My Heart. Chae is Na Bo-bae, a screenwriter who suffers from an unusual condition. After being struck by lightning as a child, she developed the ability to administer electric shocks through physical contact, forcing her into isolation. Her life changes when she meets corporate heir Baek Ho-rang (Kim), who is completely immune to her touch. Meanwhile, Ho-rang finds that his ailing artificial heart battery can only be recharged by Bo-bae. (Netflix, October 9) 6. 100 Days of Deception Lead cast: Kim Yoo-jung, Park Jin-young Set during the Japanese occupation of Korea (1910-45), the lush 100 Days of Deception stars Kim Yoo-jung (Dear X) as Ga Gyeong, the most gifted pickpocket in Gyeongseong (the colonial-era name of Seoul). She enters into a deal with the independence army, agreeing to pose as a fake spy at the Japanese Government-General of Korea for 100 days. As her assignment slowly turns into a real one, she becomes entangled with Kim Tae-woong (Park Jin-young, Our Unwritten Seoul), a Korean interpreter working in the building. (tvN/Netflix, October 10) 7. Make Me Tingle Lead cast: Nam Ji-hyun, Kim Jae-young In this romcom series, Nam Ji-hyun (Little Women) plays Yeon-su, who was raised in a very conservative family and now works at a marketing company while holding strict views on romance. Her ideals are challenged when she meets new client Dokgo Dal (Kim Jae-young, The Judge from Hell), the head of a company that sells adult sex toys. As their worlds collide, the two begin to challenge each other in unexpected ways. (Tving, October 15) 8. Love in Disguise Lead cast: Im Si-wan, Seol In-ah, Kim Jung-hyun The year’s latest workplace romcom stars Im Si-wan (Squid Game season 2) as Yun I-jun, an eccentric corporate heir who is a suspect in the murder of his secretary. Seol In-ah (Business Proposal) plays Kang Jae-hui, a tenacious police officer who disguises herself as a man and goes undercover as I-jun’s new personal secretary and bodyguard. (tvN/Prime Video, October 19) 9. Final Table Lead cast: Ahn Hyo-seop, Hong Hwa-yeon In the culinary drama Final Table, Ahn Hyo-seop (Business Proposal) stars as Kang Han, a star chef who, after being swept up in an unfortunate incident, takes part in a competition to select Korea’s best chef. Also competing is Choi Song-yi (Hong Hwa-yeon, The Price of Confession), a restaurant manager who enters the competition to save her family’s business. (JTBC, October 24) 10. Oh! My Guard Lead cast: Jung Yong-hwa, Hong Seung-hee Jung Yong-hwa (Sell Your Haunted House) and Hong Seung-hee (Move to Heaven) join hands in the romantic comedy Oh! My Guard. Jung plays Um Tae-bong, a soap opera star harbouring a secret, while Hong features as a woman who, after an accident, comes to believe she is the heroine in Tae-bong’s show. (Lifetime, October 24) 11. Summer Vacation Lead cast: Cho Yi-hyun, Jin Young Ahead of All of Us Are Dead season 2 later this year, Cho Yi-hyun headlines the drama Summer Vacation, in which she plays Kim Ha-yeon, an 18-year-old girl who experiences a mysterious summer break before returning to reality. Jin Young (Police University) co-stars as Jo Yu-gyeom, a boy the same age as Ha-yeon. Summer Vacation completed production in 2023 and is finally finding its way to screens. (Wavve, October 26) 12. The Perfect Lie Lead cast: Seo Hyun-jin, Yoo Yeon-seok The mystery thriller series The Perfect Lie stars Yoo Yeon-seok (Hospital Playlist) and Seo Hyun-jin (The Trunk) as a man and woman who experience a surprising aftermath to a perfect date. Yoo is cardiac surgeon Min Joon-ho – a widower raising his middle-school-aged son – who goes on a date with his son’s teacher, Ji-seon (Seo). The day after their date, Joon-ho and Ji-seon have different recollections of their time together and begin clashing over the truth. (MBC, October 30)

title: Review | Cyclone review: Philip Yung’s transgender drama is bold, lyrical and utterly divisive
description: Yung’s tale about a transgender mainland Chinese immigrant woman who finds sanctuary in a Hong Kong brothel is spellbinding if flawed.
content: 3.5/5 stars Philip Yung Tsz-kwong’s Cyclone is an alternately transgressive and lyrical drama charting the sexual escapades of a transgender woman fleeing her traumatic past. The film takes its name from the protagonist’s chosen alias – a literary allusion that may enlighten and confuse audiences in equal measure. It references Cyclone Mei, a fabled villainess from Louis Cha Leung-yung’s wuxia epic The Legend of the Condor Heroes. Forged by a tragic childhood into a ruthless killer, she is the rebellious idol whom our protagonist has aspired to become since she was a young, feminine boy. The titular sex worker of Cyclone – played with great courage in a layered turn by Chinese actress Liu Yuqiao – is introduced via a nasty nocturnal transaction in a phone booth before the opening title card. The encounter swiftly devolves into a humiliating flurry of urination, profanity and furious kicks. A mainland Chinese immigrant awaiting gender-affirming surgery in Hong Kong, Cyclone struggles to find conventional employment. Facing thinly veiled prejudices over both her origins and her trans identity, she finds sanctuary only within the confines of a run-down brothel. The film’s emotional anchors lie in Cyclone’s entanglements. Her volatile relationship with Bian (stage actor Edwynn Li Yu-hin), a slimy food courier who moonlights as a drug dealer, is fraught from the outset. By contrast, she finds unexpected solace with Xiaomei (erotic model Jenny Suen Wo-yee), a seductive new arrival. The lively scenes within the establishment deliver a jarring blend of gritty realism and dark, Fruit Chan-esque humour. Functioning almost like a twisted sitcom ensemble, this cosy community even includes a sex worker who lives with her photographer husband and deeply disapproving son. As Cyclone navigates highly specific kinks in scenes that verge on exploitation, her deepest fears arise from a past that refuses to stay buried. Reality intrudes through distant memories of a boy yearning to play Cyclone and the pleading calls from her sister (a fleeting Fish Liew Chi-yu) about their dying father. Despite its fragmented narrative, much of the film remains a spellbinding watch. Yung and his co-writers deserve credit for granting their characters the grace of complex humanity, allowing them the freedom to feel and behave in ways that defy conventional expectations. Sadly, this unpredictability evaporates in a 15-minute coda detailing the harrowing conversion therapy Cyclone was once tricked into enduring. Abandoning the preceding acts’ moral ambiguity, it inspires one single reaction – suffocating pity – reducing a magnificently defiant protagonist to a mere victim. Then again, perhaps that is the entire point. As Cyclone’s doctor suggests in one scene, the power of imagination – the liberty of the mind – may well be all there is for those trapped in a perpetual state of flux. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Chinese-Malaysian woman proud to find grandad honoured in China for secret WWII sacrifice
description: Kuang’s family only learned of his wartime service a decade ago when historical volunteers visited their home.
content: While travelling in Kunming, southwestern China’s Yunnan province, a Chinese-Malaysian woman unexpectedly came across photos of her late grandfather showcased in a public exhibit. The display celebrated the historical contributions of overseas Chinese machinists who played a vital role in supporting the nation during World War II. The woman’s Chinese name is Zhang Huiqing, although she uses the handle @Huiching on social media. In mid-September, she released a video revealing that during her travels in Kunming, she discovered two photos of her grandfather on Xinwen South Road. The clip garnered one million views within just two days, attracting 10,000 comments, as reported by state media Xinhua. “I was walking down the street while holding a cup of coffee. Suddenly, I felt someone watching me. I crossed the road and found my grandfather’s photos on the wall,” Zhang shared excitedly on social media. “This is my grandpa,” she said tearfully while pointing to a picture. “This is his name, and these are his words.” Zhang’s grandfather, Kuang Jinyuan, is among the overseas Chinese machinists honoured on the wall, commemorating their efforts to help China resist the Japanese invasion during WWII. Kuang was born in 1914 in Alor Setar, northern Malaysia. As the Sino-Japanese War erupted in the 1930s, all of China’s coastal ports came under Japanese control, and a major road in the northwestern region, along with a railway between Yunnan province and Vietnam, was destroyed. In 1938, Chinese workers constructed a road connecting Yunnan and Myanmar, which became the sole route for transporting materials into China. However, China lacked experienced drivers and mechanics. In February 1939, the Overseas Chinese Relief Fund issued a call for young people skilled in driving and vehicle repair to come to China and offer their support. At the age of 25, Kuang answered the call, travelling to China while keeping his mother unaware. According to his diary, his work in China included repairing trucks on the road, rescuing vehicles that had fallen from cliffs, and collecting military supplies scattered along the route. In 1942, Kuang endured an 18-hour siege by Japanese soldiers. Ultimately, he broke free from the encirclement and trekked for 24 days to reach Baoshan, Yunnan, during which he lost two comrades-in-arms. A total of 3,200 overseas Chinese workers dedicated themselves to fighting against Japanese forces in China, with over 1,000 losing their lives. Kuang returned to Malaysia in 1946 and passed away in 1993 at the age of 76. “I never expected to encounter my grandfather in this way. I am proud of him. I will cherish this moment forever,” Zhang expressed in her video. Kuang had never shared these experiences with his family. Zhang noted that they only became aware of this history a decade ago when volunteers from the Overseas Chinese Relief Fund visited her home to collect historical materials. They uncovered Kuang’s photos, diaries, and work certificates in a trunk containing his relics. Zhang’s video has elicited a wave of emotions across mainland China. “Highest salute to those overseas Chinese workers! We will always be grateful to those who helped China,” one internet user remarked. “Thank you for your grandfather’s selfless devotion. This is your home. Welcome back!” another commented. Zhang expressed her relief that China still remembers and honours her grandfather. According to Zhang, Kuang’s parents hailed from Lingbei Village in Taishan, Guangdong province in southern China. A local media outlet, Jiangmen Daily, quickly traced other family members from his clan in the village. Zhang mentioned that she plans to visit the village soon.

title: Meet actor Jack Martin, who is dating Lili Reinhart of The Love Hypothesis
description: The La Brea actor connected with the Riverdale actress when he made a TikTok video joking about the show ... after which she slid into his DMs.
content: Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman’s irresistible chemistry in The Love Hypothesis (2026) has fans swooning worldwide. The film, which premiered on Amazon Prime Video on September 23, is based on Ali Hazelwood’s bestselling novel of the same name. It follows PhD student Olive Smith (Reinhart), who begins a fake relationship with brooding professor Dr Adam Carlsen (Bateman), only for their feelings to start turning real. The Love Hypothesis is currently the most watched film on the streaming platform, according to FlixPatrol. In real life, Reinhart’s heart belongs to her boyfriend Jack Martin, who’s also an actor. Speaking to Cosmopolitan in July, she called their relationship “really beautiful” and “the best relationship [she has] ever been in”. So, what do we know about Jack Martin? What is Jack Martin’s background? Jack Martin was born on August 3, 1998, in Columbia, Maryland and grew up in McLean, Virginia, per his website. While his parents have remained out of the public eye, he has often spoken about how close he is with them. In an interview with the arts and culture magazine A Book Of, the 28-year-old actor recalled that the hardest part about filming the series La Brea in Australia during the Covid-19 pandemic was not being able to see his parents for nine months. How did Jack Martin get into acting? According to Martin’s bio on his website, he was in his final year of primary school when he came close to being cast in a major feature film. Although he lost the opportunity, he realised he had caught the acting bug. His initial career aspiration was to go into politics after studying political science, he told Bello Mag, but after spending a semester at Georgetown University, he changed his mind. Halfway through university, with support from his mother and a friend, Martin decided to pursue acting. He graduated from Georgetown in 2019 and trained in acting at the University of Southern California’s School of Cinematic Arts and New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts. The actor rose to popularity by making TikTok videos, got signed, and broke through with La Brea. He has since appeared in shows like The Rookie and Not Suitable for Work. How did Jack Martin meet Lili Reinhart? Martin met the Riverdale actress after he made a TikTok video joking about the show, and she slid into his DMs, per Marie Claire. In July 2023, they became Instagram-official, and that September, they attended the Venice Film Festival together. Martin gushed over Reinhart in an interview with Entertainment Tonight this May, telling the outlet, “I love her more than anything. I am grateful for her literally every day.”

title: Hong Kong route linking Yau Ma Tei and Tseung Kwan O to fully open in December
description: Route 6’s completion to be marked by opening of key section of long-awaited Central Kowloon Route.
content: The final section of Route 6 will open in December, cutting travel times from Yau Ma Tei to Tseung Kwan O from about 65 minutes to roughly 12 minutes, Hong Kong’s transport chief has said. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Wednesday at a Legislative Council meeting that the Kowloon Bay section of the Central Kowloon Route would open to traffic on December 6. The Central Kowloon Route is a key part of Route 6, with construction beginning in 2017. “Together with the Yau Ma Tei section that opened at the end of last year, this marks the full commissioning of Route 6, which encompasses the Central Kowloon Route and the Tseung Kwan O-Lam Tin Tunnel,” she said. “Once fully open, Route 6 will seamlessly connect traffic between Kowloon West, Kowloon East and Tseung Kwan O. Travel time for the entire route is expected to drop substantially from around 65 minutes to about 12 minutes.” Chan said authorities had been conducting tests on fire safety equipment and other facilities in recent months, with the project now in its final preparation stage. “Relevant departments have reported that everything is currently progressing smoothly, and they hope to perfect the route’s systems, public transport arrangements and roadwork before the official opening,” she added. The Central Kowloon Bypass (Kowloon Bay Section), formerly known as Trunk Road T2 and Cha Kwo Ling Tunnel, is a key component of Route 6. It connects the Central Kowloon Bypass (Yau Ma Tei Section) to the west and the Tseung Kwan O–Lam Tin Tunnel to the east. When it opens, the project will help divert traffic between East and West Kowloon, enhance the capacity of the major road network, and relieve traffic pressure on existing roads in Tseung Kwan O and Kwun Tong. The Central Kowloon Bypass (Yau Ma Tei Section) is a 4.7km-long (2.9 miles) dual three-lane trunk road connecting Yau Ma Tei Interchange in West Kowloon to the Kai Tak Development Area and Kowloon Bay in East Kowloon, including a tunnel spanning about 3.9km. The Yau Ma Tei section is estimated to cost HK$42.36 billion (US$5.4 billion), while the whole bypass carries a price tag of HK$58 billion. Ringo Lee Yiu-pui, governor and honorary life president of the Hong Kong, China Automobile Association, said the route would provide a more convenient alternative for motorists travelling from Tseung Kwan O to urban areas. It would also help ease congestion on the Kwun Tong Bypass, which links Lam Tin and Kowloon Bay. “There will be another convenient alternative and less congestion in East Kowloon,” he said.

title: Blake Lively has parted ways with her long-time publicist, Leslie Sloane – who is she?
description: The It Ends with Us star’s legal drama with Justin Baldoni has ended but her publicist, who has past ties to Harvey Weinstein, is now in the spotlight.
content: It Ends with Us actors Justin Baldoni and Blake Lively’s 18-month legal feud reached an anticlimactic end in May when both parties settled. Baldoni and Lively’s lawyers released a statement, focusing on the film being a “source of pride” for those involved. “Raising awareness, and making a meaningful impact in the lives of domestic violence survivors – and all survivors – is a goal that we stand behind,” they added. The lawsuit was set to go to court in New York just two weeks later. The long-running saga started in December 2024, when Lively sued the Man Enough Podcast host for sexual harassment, per TMZ, citing “severe emotional distress”. A day later, The New York Times revealed that a smear campaign devised by Baldoni and his PR team may have been behind the recent social media takedown of the Gossip Girl star. Not long after, Baldoni’s lawyer, Bryan Freedman, shared plans of counter-suing, guaranteeing revelations that will “shock everyone”, including claims that it was Lively’s publicist, Leslie Sloane, who was feeding negative narratives to the press about his client, reports the Daily Mail. However, Sloane was not one to back down either. “It’s clear that Mr Baldoni and his Wayfarer Associates are suggesting that I originated press stories about HR complaints on set, which is false,” she asserted to People. In February 2025, Sloane moved to have herself and her company Vision PR dismissed from Baldoni’s US$400 million defamation and extortion lawsuit. On September 29, Page Six reported that Sloane has reportedly been let go by Lively after the actress faced criticism for her multimillion-dollar legal battle with Baldoni. So who is Leslie Sloane? She’s a renowned publicist View this post on Instagram A post shared by Vision PR (@vision.pr) Sloane has decades of experience in public relations under her belt. She worked at Baker Winokur Ryder for 17 years, where she served as co-president, per The Wrap. In 2007, she was named one of New York’s 50 Most Powerful Women by the New York Post. In 2014, she was fired by BWR, per The Hollywood Reporter, following which she founded her own PR company, Vision PR. Sloane has ties to Harvey Weinstein In 2014, The Hollywood Reporter revealed that Sloane’s new firm, Vision PR, would be funded by now-disgraced producer and convicted sex offender Harvey Weinstein through The Weinstein Live, a branch of The Weinstein Company. Sloane previously served as Weinstein’s publicist, per Page Six. Regarding this investment, the 72-year-old once said, “Leslie’s next move is going to rock the industry,” reported the outlet. Vision PR also received backing from Madison Square Garden executive James Dolan. Who are some of her clients? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Vision PR (@vision.pr) Sloane has famously represented A-listers including Katie Holmes, Megan Fox, Zoe Saldana, Melissa McCarthy, Britney Spears, Chris Rock, Sienna Miller and Lively. She also worked with Lindsay Lohan but in 2010, made headlines for removing her from her roster of clients, per HuffPost. However, the two women seem to be working together again, as evidenced by Vision PR’s Instagram. Sloane also served as Beverly Hills, 90210 star Shannen Doherty’s publicist until her untimely death in July from cancer.

title: US ends troop mission in Iraq, Baghdad to celebrate Sovereignty Day on October 1
description: Some fear pro-Iran armed groups could expand in Iraq with the withdrawal of a US-led coalition originally deployed to fight Islamic State.
content: A US-led coalition deployed in Iraq more than a decade ago to fight jihadists concluded its mission on Wednesday, a move celebrated by the country’s leaders, but which some fear will embolden pro-Iran armed factions. Coalition troops deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight Islamic State, which had seized large swathes of territory, committing massacres and forcing thousands of women and children into slavery. The group was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group’s remnants. The United States and Iraq agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition’s mission, and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region. On Wednesday, the US announced the mission’s formal conclusion. “Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests,” the Pentagon said in a statement. The US Department of Defence, however, added that it would “continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners”. The US-led coalition did not defeat IS alone. Kurdish Peshmerga fighters played an important role in crushing IS, as did powerful Iraqi factions, including pro-Iran groups that have yet to disarm. The Iraqi government, which celebrated the withdrawal, believes it will deprive Iran-backed factions of the excuse they have used to retain their arsenal. But many Iraqis fear the pull-out might embolden the pro-Iran factions further and draw the country deeper into the Middle East war. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi hailed the end of the mission as the start of a new chapter. “A new phase has begun, defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, unity of decision-making and balanced partnerships with its friends,” Zaidi said at a ceremony on Wednesday. He had also declared that October 1 would be celebrated as Sovereignty Day. It is “a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq’s path towards sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions”, the heads of Iraq’s executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday. They added that “the presence of weapons outside state authority must be addressed … in line with timelines set by the government, in a manner that strengthens state sovereignty”. Zaidi, who came to power this year with the US’ blessing, has vowed to reinforce the state’s monopoly on arms and ensure that armed factions hand over their weapons to the state. His government initially set September 30 as the deadline for factions to disarm, but later withdrew the time limit as talks continued to “regulate” weapons – an issue that has fuelled division and is expected to take much longer to resolve. With several powerful groups refusing to disarm, senior politicians have intervened and are now hoping to work out a compromise deal. Factions have put forward conditions that include not only the withdrawal of foreign troops but also an end to American political and economic interference. The powerful Kataeb Hezbollah group said the withdrawal of “the occupation forces … is a start towards achieving full sovereignty”. But the group also threatened Zaidi’s government. “A government that doesn’t work for the good of its people will be brought down by all possible means,” it said. Pro-Iran groups have long demanded the withdrawal of US troops and have begun targeting them with drones and missiles, triggering US retaliatory strikes that killed several faction commanders over the years. During the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran and allied factions intensified their attacks in Iraq, targeting US-led troops in the Kurdistan region.

title: Asian Games crowds ‘disappointing’ as 998 fans watch football in 50,000-seat stadium
description: Organisers in Aichi-Nagoya claim that more than one million tickets had been sold for the continent’s biggest sporting spectacular.
content: Under 1,000 spectators watched Asian Games hosts Japan beat South Korea in the semi-finals of the women’s football at a 50,000-capacity stadium, with a top official admitting Wednesday that attendances at some events were “disappointing”. Japanese organisers have been on the defensive over ticket sales since the opening ceremony on September 19 took place in front of thousands of empty seats in Nagoya. Officials said on that occasion that the threat of a typhoon put people off, and heavy rain fell from Sunday until Tuesday this week. While some competitions have played out to healthy crowds, others have struggled to attract fans. Tuesday’s first women’s football semi-final at the stadium in Shizuoka, a venue for the 2002 Fifa World Cup, saw North Korea beat China 2-0 in front of an official attendance of 564. With rain falling steadily, 998 people then watched the hosts defeat South Korea by the same scoreline. Japan and North Korea will meet for gold on Friday at the same stadium. Takashi Yamazaki, head of ticketing, told reporters on Wednesday: “Sports that are selling well are ... at 80 per cent or 90 per cent or more.” But he added: “On the other hand, the large venues for baseball and football, as well as athletics, have struggled from the start because of their size. “Tickets usually surge in the final stretch before an event. But as you know, there was a long spell of cold rain, and sales stalled. “We were already struggling more than expected, and then sales stalled further. “That is a little disappointing.” Organisers in Aichi-Nagoya said Tuesday that more than one million tickets had been sold for the continent’s biggest sporting spectacular. But they also admitted they were “not satisfied” after the men’s and women’s 100m, the blue-riband athletics events, took place in front of thousands of empty seats on Friday.

title: Former in-laws’ anger over HK$72 million flat sale drove murder of Abby Choi, court hears
description: Rift between Choi and ex-husband’s family began to grow after she tried to sell luxury flat at Kadooria residential estate, prosecution says.
content: Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s former father-in-law enlisted his two sons to help him murder the 28-year-old and dispose of her dismembered body after he became “extremely resentful and angry” over her insistence on selling a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat where he was living, a court has heard. The prosecution on Wednesday began delivering its opening statement in what is expected to be an eight-week High Court trial over the influencer’s murder and the illegal disposal of her body in a Tai Po village house in February 2023. Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body between February 21 and 23. Their father, retired police sergeant Kwong Kau, 68, pleaded not guilty to the same offence. All three defendants deny murdering Choi. Prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC said a rift between Choi and her former in-laws’ family began to grow after she tried to sell a luxury flat at the Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin in 2022. According to the prosecution, Choi bought the flat in 2019 for HK$60 million, which was about 17 per cent off the sales price, so the two children she had with Alex Kwong could be looked after by her former in-laws at a place close to her residence in Kowloon Tong. Choi decided to register Kwong Kau as its legal owner so that she could avoid significant stamp duty charged on those with more than one property under their name. “The prosecution says it was her decision to do so that set off the chain of events that led to her death,” Draycott said. The court heard that Kwong Kau had initially refused to sign a power of attorney to allow Choi to negotiate with property agents. On one occasion, the accused reportedly lost his temper and “lunged at” the socialite, hoping to hit her before he was restrained by others present. In private audio messages she sent to her mother, Choi spoke of her former in-laws in “very unpleasant” terms, calling Kwong Kau a “crook” and his wife a “ghost”, while expressing regret for her generosity. In one message, the influencer said: “A huge amount of money was spent on that flat, and it was spent for them. To be honest, for the sake of my children, for the sake of my two children and my good heart, that’s why she can lead such a good life, right?” She added: “I divorced his son so many years ago, and I am still helping her son and providing for his children. Yet this kind of person is ungrateful. If she is not a ghost, what is she?” Draycott said the senior Kwong acceded to Choi’s request in November 2022 fearing her mother would take legal action. Choi also evicted Kwong from the flat and accused him of driving a wedge between her and her children, forcing the retired police officer to share a one-bedroom flat with his elder son at Sheung Man Court, a subsidised residential complex in Kwai Chung. Draycott alleged that the family feud reached a critical point in 2023 when Kwong Kau decided to kill Choi so that he could keep the Kadooria flat for himself. The prosecutor argued all three defendants had their respective roles to play in the murder scheme, from renting a flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Tsuen and driving Choi to the obscure location to dealing her the fatal blow. “If you find out that were the case, it does not matter which one actually killed her because they were all operating together,” Draycott told the nine-member jury. In her one-hour opening statement, Draycott also described how 18-year-old Choi married Alex Kwong in 2013 before divorcing him and starting a relationship with Chris Tam Fong-chun, who was “extremely wealthy” and with whom she had two children. “I mentioned the money because it was the root of what happened,” the lawyer added. The Kwong family, compared with the Chois and Tams, was far from affluent. Alex Kwong and his mother were jobless, whereas Kwong Kau relied on an annual pension of HK$145,000. Draycott said Choi had remained on good terms with her former husband despite their divorce and had continued to provide for his relatives. The prosecutor highlighted that Alex Kwong previously stole a total of HK$6.29 million from six people so he could appear to be rich and successful. He also reportedly frequented mainland China despite the fact that he had been wanted by police over the theft case since 2015. The prosecution’s opening statement continues on Friday.

title: Southeast Asia faces ‘sleeper’ food crisis from Hormuz fertiliser bottleneck
description: The Middle East shipping gridlock risks a regional hunger crisis unless Asean resists export controls and pushes a US-Iran deal, experts say.
content: A hunger crisis could creep up on Southeast Asia if the region does not guard against export restrictions amid a fertiliser shortfall, International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Secretary General John Denton has warned. On the sidelines of the Future of Trade Forum in Singapore on Wednesday, Denton urged the city state, as the next Asean chair, to prioritise the “sleeper issue” for the region. He argued that the real story centred on food, despite the Strait of Hormuz gridlock being widely seen as an energy crunch. He noted that the UN was able to carve out the Black Sea Grain Initiative during the Russia-Ukraine war by getting both sides to sign off on an agreement that allowed for the safe export of grain from certain ports, alleviating a global food emergency. Under a UN-led task force on Hormuz, the ICC is involved in trying to implement a similar initiative through the troubled strait. However, the United States and Iran have yet to sign off on the plan. “The context of Hormuz is different, but the actual elements of it are similar, in that you’ve got a trade route which has been effectively frozen, militarised,” Denton told This Week in Asia. The ICC is a global business organisation representing companies and associations across more than 170 countries. Many member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations – including Thailand, the Philippines, Cambodia and Myanmar – rely heavily on imported phosphate, potash and nitrogen fertilisers from outside the region. Asean producers currently focus on managing domestic price caps and subsidies rather than restricting regional exports. Indonesia, for instance, uses domestic market obligations and fertiliser subsidies to protect its local agricultural sector. However, about one-third of the global seaborne fertiliser trade passes through the Strait of Hormuz. The ongoing conflict in the Gulf has severely disrupted shipping routes, causing major supply bottlenecks and price surges. The consequences of restricted access to fertiliser were not immediate, Denton noted, as it took 12 months to see the effects on crops and would be compounded by El Nino. “Politicians focus on the problems of today, but this is what you call a sleeper issue,” he warned, pointing to a solution that hinged on an agreement between Washington and Tehran, overseen by the UN’s secretary general office. On the role Asean could play to help itself, Denton stressed it was very important for member states not to introduce export controls. “A number of economies around this region have actually inhibited access to fertiliser movement to try and protect their own suppliers. That distorts market conditions, and that actually adds to price increases,” he said. This issue should be a key focus of Singapore’s tenure as Asean chair in 2027, Denton added. “Asean maintaining its focus and action against any export controls is very important. To actually ensure that there’s focus on this at the United Nations – and that they’re vocal in their support of getting something done to avert a food crisis – would be very important,” he said. While the US and Iran have engaged with the proposal and understand the mechanism, Denton noted that they had yet to agree. “The issue is: do they want to be responsible for the political consequences of hunger in developing emerging economies? It’ll come from a failure to deploy this.” In a keynote address at the forum, Singapore Minister-in-charge of Trade Relations Grace Fu said that as chair, the city state aimed to deepen integration, strengthen Asean’s capacity to respond to change and expand the regional bloc’s partnerships with existing and new allies. Fu, who is also Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, said: “Taken together, these efforts are about giving businesses more pathways to grow and more options to navigate disruption – by opening new markets, strengthening connectivity and keeping trade flowing even in times of uncertainty.” During a fireside chat, Fu stressed that Singapore saw itself as a trusted anchor in a “very unpredictable, uncertain world”. She said that Singapore’s port had been very busy since the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz as it had served as a hub for countries forced to divert goods and restructure their logistics. “If you have a disruption in trade rules and therefore you need to rearrange your supply chain, Singapore would be the place for you to do that because we have the fundamental infrastructure, fundamental processes that probably reach the most number of countries, the shipping connectivity and so on,” Fu said.

title: Singapore beefs up rivalry with Hong Kong by picking 5 firms to boost equity market
description: Five global asset managers appointed to spearhead the plan aimed at lifting liquidity and expanding trading activity beyond blue-chip stocks.
content: Singapore’s central bank has selected five international asset managers to handle S$1.45 billion (US$1.3 billion) in locally focused equity strategies, making its latest effort to revive the city state’s stock market amid sharpening rivalry with regional financial hub Hong Kong. Amundi, Franklin Templeton, HSBC Asset Management, M&G Investments and Natixis Investment Managers were named on Tuesday as part of the third batch of mandates awarded under the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) Equity Market Development Programme. The programme, launched with S$5 billion in February 2025 and enlarged to S$6.5 billion this February, aims to crowd in private capital alongside public funds to boost liquidity and broaden trading activity beyond Singapore’s largest blue-chip stocks, authorities said. Alongside the manager appointments, MAS committed an additional S$20 million to a grant scheme designed to support market-making activities for roughly 80 small and mid-cap companies through the end of 2028. Pang Qi Lim, CEO of HSBC Asset Management Singapore, said the firm was “excited to contribute to the continued development and internationalisation of Singapore’s equity market”. “We look forward to leveraging these strengths to attract capital, broaden investor participation to further support the growth of a more vibrant and internationally connected equity market,” Lim said. The central bank’s initiative comes as Singapore faces increasingly fierce competition from Hong Kong. In the latest Global Financial Centres Index released earlier this month, Hong Kong ranked third globally and first in Asia – holding a narrow one-point lead over fourth-placed Singapore. Hong Kong also captured top spots in the index’s fintech, investment management, insurance and finance sector rankings, while Singapore led in professional services. As Singapore pours billions into invigorating its capital markets, local trading activity has started showing signs of traction. Daily average securities turnover on the local exchange reached S$1.8 billion in the year to June – its highest level in 18 years. However, Hong Kong continues to hold a massive lead. The city’s initial public offering market raised HK$210 billion (US$26.77 billion) in the first half of 2026, ranking second globally behind Nasdaq. Its cash market’s daily turnover averaged a record HK$283 billion in that period, official data shows. The duel between the two Asian financial powerhouses has extended heavily into wealth and asset management. In August, Singapore announced tax exemptions on selected profits earned from strong fund performance, following Hong Kong’s move to cut taxes on carried interest – the share of profits paid to fund managers. Singapore’s assets under management grew 10 per cent year-on-year to S$6.7 trillion in 2025, according to the annual survey. By comparison, Hong Kong’s total asset and wealth management industry – which incorporates private banking – handled a record HK$42.2 trillion in 2025, according to data from the Securities and Futures Commission. Hong Kong also overtook Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth centre in 2025, managing US$2.9 trillion in cross-border wealth.

title: On This Day | Tai O rope-ferry in Hong Kong ends service after 100 years – SCMP archive
description: The rope-guided ferry was the only way to cross a 15-metre creek in Tai O before the construction of a pedestrian bridge.
content: This article was first published on September 30, 1996. New footbridge ends 100 years of rope-ferry service by Shirley Kwok The century-old rope-ferry between Lantau and Tai O saw its years of service come to an end yesterday (September 29, 1996) with the opening of a new $15 million pedestrian bridge between the islands. Until yesterday, the ferry was the only means of crossing the 15-metre Tai O creek, and passengers had to pay 50 cents for each trip. Director of Territory Development Lee Shing-see said at the opening ceremony that the bridge represented “a major step forward in the overall development programme for Tai O”. Mr Lee said the rope-ferry service had already become unable to cope with the traffic demands generated by a rapid growth in tourism and commercial activities. “The completion of the bridge today will not only improve local traffic, but will bring another rural characteristic to Tai O,” he said. The 56 metre-long bridge has a central span which can be lifted by one person to allow large fishing junks to pass.

title: 4-winged fossil found in Liaoning challenges single origin of dinosaur flight
description: While both birds and some winged dinosaurs could fly, they built their ‘flying kit’ in a different order.
content: Scientists have unveiled an exceptionally well-preserved 100-million-year-old fossil of a small, feathered dinosaur in northeastern China that could reshape our understanding of how dinosaurs took to the skies. The newly discovered species, named Norellraptor barsboldi, is a four-winged predatory dinosaur measuring 57cm (22 inches) long. Belonging to the microraptorines – small dinosaurs with feathers and wings closely related to birds – the creature offers fresh evidence that flight evolved independently in different dinosaur lineages rather than from a single common origin. “These results dismiss a shared developmental pattern driving the evolution of the flying dinosaurs and support multiple and independent selective regimes at the origin of the winged taxa in Paraves,” the researchers wrote, referring to the group that includes birds and microraptorines. The team of scientists from institutions in China, Italy and Slovakia published their findings in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications on Tuesday. For decades, palaeontologists have been looking into whether the aerial abilities of birds and microraptorines shared a single evolutionary origin or arose separately. While fossils have previously shown that some microraptorines had long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting flight adaptations, it was not clear whether these features marked the origins of flight in Paraves or evolved independently. In the latest study, the “exquisitely preserved” fossil with a complete skeleton and parts of its plumage was unearthed in the Lower Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation in the northeastern coastal province of Liaoning. The geological formation, estimated to be between 145 million and 100 million years old, is home to similarly well-preserved fossils from the late phase of the Jehol Biota, a key Early Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystem. The new Norellraptor barsboldi species was named after American palaeontologist Mark Allen Norell and Mongolian palaeontologist Rinchen Barsbold to honour their work in studying birdlike dinosaurs. They both died in 2025. Analysis of the dinosaur, which was at least three years old when it died, revealed a collection of features associated with flight. The scientists compared these results across an evolutionary tree and found that about 30 per cent of anatomical changes in microraptorine evolution also evolved in the bird lineage. However, the two groups acquired these shared features in a different order. While birds first fused their wrist bones and elongated their breastbones before shortening their hand digits, microraptorines shortened their manual phalanges – finger bones – much earlier to reduce their grasping ability. “The sequences of flight-related novelties reconstructed along the two lineages differ consistently,” the researchers wrote. This finding challenges the idea that birds and microraptorines inherited a shared flight apparatus or that a common developmental process drove its evolution. Rather, distinct selective pressures are likely to have influenced the development of their flight-adapted traits. Future research will require sampling more fossils across birdlike dinosaurs to determine how widespread this unique growth pattern was and to further untangle the forces that launched dinosaurs into the air.

title: Apple leads China smartphone sales after launch of iPhone 18 Pro. Can the momentum last?
description: Sales in the first three days were 12 per cent higher than the previous generation’s entire first week.
content: Apple has claimed the top spot in China’s smartphone market following the release of its iPhone 18 Pro series, giving a potential boost to a sluggish handset market weighed down by weak consumer demand and soaring component costs. Sales of the new Pro models in their first three days after launching on September 18 were 12 per cent higher than sales of the iPhone 17 Pro line-up during its entire first week last year, according to a report published on Wednesday by Counterpoint Research. That strong start catapulted Apple to the No 1 position by smartphone sales for the week of September 14 to 20, with the company capturing 33 per cent of the market. “The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have driven some consumers to trade up to the Pro series,” said Ivan Lam, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research. “Price hikes of over US$200 on many Chinese flagship models may have raised the price anchor, strengthening the iPhone’s relative value proposition.” Counterpoint expected China’s smartphone market to gain momentum as domestic brands roll out their flagship devices ahead of the National Day holiday starting on Thursday. Huawei Technologies recently launched the widescreen Pura X View, while Xiaomi added the 18 Fold to its line-up. Apple could receive a further boost from its first foldable handset, the iPhone Duo, which will go on sale on October 23. UBS said in a research note last week that Chinese consumers continued to show greater interest in foldable devices compared with other international markets. UBS maintained its forecast for Apple’s global iPhone sales for the current financial year, projecting shipments to reach 261 million units, up 15.4 per cent year on year. These gains come against a backdrop of challenges facing the wider industry. The global smartphone market is grappling with a shortage of memory chips, as surging demand for AI infrastructure puts pressure on supplies for consumer electronics. China’s weekly handset sales have declined by double digits year on year since July, according to Counterpoint, which attributed the weakness to soft consumer spending and elevated chip costs. The memory shortage is expected to drag global smartphone shipments down this year. IDC forecast in August that shipments could contract 16.7 per cent, the steepest annual drop on record, while Counterpoint projected a 14 per cent market decline for 2026.

title: Seoul residents up in arms over school for North Korean defectors
description: Opposition from residents in Gangseo district has led the principal of Yeomyung School to kneel and beg for acceptance.
content: Residents of a district in the South Korean capital of Seoul are up in arms over plans to build a permanent school for North Korean defectors in their neighbourhood. The dispute escalated to the point where the school’s principal dropped to her knees to beg protesters to “embrace the children”, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Yeomyung School, which educates middle and high school students who fled North Korea or are children of North Korean defectors, has been unable to afford its own facility since its establishment in 2004, according to NK News, an American website covering North Korea. It has been renting buildings and has relocated three times in those 22 years. A proposal to establish a permanent presence in Eunpyeong, another district in Seoul, in 2019 fell through after residents opposed. Since 2023, the school has operated out of the Yeomgang building in Gangseo. The lease was due to expire next February but in July, the Ministry of Unification, the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and Hyundai Motor Group signed an agreement to construct a new building at the location. Principal Cho Myung-sook said then that the permanent arrangement would allow the school “to focus solely on education” without worrying about moving for at least 20 years. The new facility “will become a place of hope where students can dream bigger and build their futures”, Hyundai president Sung Kim said in a press release. The company pledged about 6 billion won (US$4.4 million) for the project. Yeomyung has 100 students – 93 of whom were born to North Korean defectors and seven born in the North. Alternative schools for North Koreans were necessary because many of them struggled to keep up with curriculums at local schools, defector Kim Chol-song told NK News. “Many people who came from rural areas near the northern border had limited access to education,” he said. “They are likely to have weak foundational knowledge in subjects such as maths.” However, fierce opposition from residents threatens the plans from going ahead. They maintain that Yeomyung’s occupation was always meant to be temporary and that the plot had been earmarked for an early childhood facility. Tensions boiled over at a community briefing on September 17, during which principal Cho knelt and tearfully pleaded with residents to accept the students, the Chosun Biz reported. “They have nowhere to go. Please let the kids study,” Cho said. “I will donate all the assets I have saved over the past 20 years to improve the educational environment.” Residents responded by kneeling as well. “Please save us, too,” they said. Some criticised the meeting, with one saying: “They gave us just one day’s notice, and now they are appealing to emotion. Doesn’t that just make us out to be the villains?” At the heart of the issue is not the school itself but the perception that the government has been steamrollering residents’ protests for decades. The residents are also opposing plans for about 1,000 public housing units around Yeomchang Park, an 800-metre (2,600-foot) walk from Yeomyung School. “We believed the government when it promised to turn the site into green space for residents,” a protester, surnamed Lee, told the Korea JoongAng Daily. “How could they pull the rug out from under us like this?” Another resident called on the rest to keep up the pressure. “Gangseo district already has a disproportionate share of facilities that often meet local resistance, including public rental housing and special education schools, so they seem to think the district is an easy target,” said Yang, a resident of 20 years. “More residents are starting to feel that if we sit back and say nothing, we will be steamrollered.”

title: Can India curb childhood obesity by banning junk food near schools?
description: The proposal will not be effective on its own, parents and experts say, calling for more comprehensive measures.
content: Shivanjali Singh has worked hard to raise two healthy, athletic children in India, but worries about their ability to resist the lure of junk food constantly surrounding them. Her children, aged 14 and 10, are national-level skaters and have grown up on home-cooked food and drinks such as coconut water rather than fizzy drinks and crisps. Yet Singh, who lives in Noida in the National Capital Region, sees sugary drinks and unhealthy snacks everywhere from school surroundings to sports events. “When my children started going to school, we would see really obese children around and it would really scare us,” she said. She welcomed the Indian government’s proposal to restrict sales of food high in fat, salt and sugar, known as HFSS, within 50 metres (160 feet) of schools. “But I doubt its efficacy,” she added, pointing to the ubiquity of unhealthy foods aimed at children in the country. India is moving closer to introducing the proposed restrictions as authorities step up efforts to curb unhealthy food consumption and rising childhood obesity. The rules are likely to affect family-run shops, restaurants and food stalls selling HFSS products near the country’s roughly 1.5 million schools. Authorities in India are also considering warning labels for products high in fat, salt and sugar, potentially bringing its regulations closer to those adopted by countries such as Chile and Mexico, according to Reuters. The World Obesity Federation estimates that the number of overweight or obese Indians aged five to 19 increased from 28 million in 2015 to 41 million in 2025. The figure is projected to reach 56 million by 2040. Holistic policy The challenge is that children encounter unhealthy food far beyond the school gates, according to Singh. “We need a holistic policy,” she said, suggesting a comprehensive awareness campaign, alongside measures to tackle the issue at its roots. Health experts agreed that restricting sales of junk food near school premises alone was unlikely to curb childhood obesity. Bobby John, a public health policy expert, said there was “good thinking” behind the proposed policy measure, but far more would be required to make it effective. “A child coming into school is likely to carry a lunchbox. What is the content of that? The box itself may contain something you are trying to prevent from buying,” John said, adding that every unhealthy food item was likely to be available near their homes. Policy initiatives must include promoting healthy and nutritious food consumption in schools, along with physical activity such as cycling or walking from home, he said. Affordability was another part of the problem, said Amir Ullah Khan, adjunct professor of Public Policy at Tata Institute of Social Sciences. Rising urbanisation was contributing to the popularity of cheap and convenient unhealthy foods such as pizzas, burgers and sugar-laden packaged juices, he said. He suggested increasing taxes on such food items to bring down consumption. “You have to ensure that the demand comes down and that happens when prices increase.” Prices of vegetables, fruits and milk had been persistently increasing in India, Khan said, adding that this reduced the incentive to buy simple and healthy food. School-going children must also be encouraged to run about and play outdoors, with greater access to spaces for physical activity. “A sedentary lifestyle will result in obesity. We are missing the elephant,” he said. Sugar tax Other countries have tried to tackle unhealthy diets through measures that go beyond restricting where children can buy food. In 2018, the UK introduced the soft drinks industry levy, a two-tier tax applied directly to manufacturers and importers of sugary drinks. The fee, based on sugar content per litre, is designed to encourage companies to tweak their formulas. Saleema Razvi, a Hyderabad-based health economist with research think tank Copenhagen Consensus, said a similar tax could prove effective in Asian countries struggling with childhood obesity. She questioned whether a ban on sales by vendors near schools would be easy to implement. “How will you enforce it? The costs will be too high,” she said. Authorities would need to consider how much money enforcement would require and whether it would be better spent in different ways to promote hygiene. “It has to be about developing healthy behaviour. Children will eat what they want without really thinking about the implications,” she said. “If you look at the obesity levels, it is really alarming. It has to be dealt with at a very different level.” Debasree Basu, an adviser at G.M. International School in Mumbai, agreed that developing a healthy environment was crucial. This could be done by promoting healthy habits through initiatives in schools, such as teaching botany in a garden instead of a classroom. Parents also had to play their part, she said. “Parents can, for example, take their children to watch a sports event live on weekends rather than sit glued to a television or mobile screen on weekends.”

title: Opinion | Saudi Arabia’s mBridge exit shows the limits of financial de-dollarisation
description: Riyadh’s choice is practical, not ideological. Countries seeking payment diversification aren’t abandoning the dollar – they want efficient, cost-effective alternatives.
content: Saudi Arabia’s decision to end its participation in mBridge, the cross-border digital currency platform involving mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, is significant for reasons that go beyond central bank digital currencies. The Financial Times reported that the Saudi Central Bank, or SAMA, completed its mBridge proof of concept in May 2025 and ceased participating thereafter. The disclosure is significant because Saudi Arabia occupied a strategically important position in an initiative increasingly associated with efforts to diversify away from dollar-centred financial infrastructure. mBridge was created to address genuine weaknesses in cross-border payments. The platform uses central bank digital currencies and distributed ledger technology to allow participating banks to conduct cross-border payments and foreign exchange transactions more directly. It reached minimum viable product stage in 2024, when Saudi Arabia became a full participant. For China, mBridge offers an opportunity to develop financial infrastructure in which the renminbi can play a greater role in international transactions, while for other participating economies it offers a potential means of improving payment efficiency and flexibility. That does not necessarily mean replacing the US dollar. This distinction is becoming increasingly important as discussions about de-dollarisation often blur together several different developments. A country can diversify its payment infrastructure without abandoning the dollar. It can expand local-currency settlement while continuing to hold dollar reserves, or deepen financial ties with China while remaining deeply integrated with US capital markets and Western financial institutions. Saudi Arabia illustrates this dilemma precisely. Riyadh has been strengthening ties with China through trade, investment and cooperation in emerging financial technologies. At the same time, it remains deeply embedded in the dollar-based international financial system. Its currency, the Saudi riyal, remains pegged to the US dollar, while its energy exports and international financial relationships continue to operate within an overwhelmingly dollar-centred environment. For countries in this position, the attraction of alternative payment infrastructure is therefore practical rather than necessarily ideological. The ability to settle transactions directly in digital versions of national currencies could reduce costs and improve speed while providing additional options at a time when geopolitical tensions have made access to financial infrastructure an increasingly strategic consideration. But the existence of an alternative does not automatically create a reason to use it. Payment systems derive much of their value from network effects. Banks and companies prefer infrastructure that connects them to the largest number of counterparties, currencies and financial institutions. The dollar benefits not only from the size of the US economy but also from decades of accumulated liquidity, market depth, legal infrastructure and institutional familiarity. This may be the most important lesson from Saudi Arabia’s mBridge experience. SAMA’s departure should not be interpreted as the collapse of mBridge. The project has continued to develop after the Saudi proof of concept ended. The Monetary Authority of Macau joined and activated the platform for participating banks in June, with three banks completing 23 cross-border transactions involving mainland China, Hong Kong and the UAE on the first day. Nor was Saudi Arabia the first major institutional change for the project. The Bank for International Settlements ended its direct involvement in October 2024, arguing that mBridge had reached a stage where its central bank partners could carry the project forward independently. The BIS has also stressed that mBridge was not created as a Brics mechanism for circumventing sanctions. The remaining challenge is therefore not simply technological. It is geopolitical and commercial. For mainland China and Hong Kong, the future value of mBridge will depend on whether the platform can attract enough participants and real-world transactions to generate meaningful network effects. For countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE, participation in alternative financial infrastructure will have to be weighed against their broader relationships with the United States and the existing international financial system. This creates a more fragmented future for global payments in which countries may increasingly participate in several overlapping networks rather than move from one system to another. That is a more complicated form of financial de-dollarisation than the dramatic headlines sometimes suggest. The real transformation may be less about the end of dollar dominance than about the gradual expansion of choice around it.
