Saudi Arabia’s mBridge experience therefore demonstrates the limits of assuming that technological diversification automatically produces monetary realignment. Building an alternative payment rail is possible. Convincing major economies to make it part of their permanent financial architecture is considerably harder. For China, this makes the next stage more demanding, requiring the project to demonstrate that faster, cheaper and more direct cross-border settlement can deliver sufficient economic value to overcome the network advantages of the existing system. The future of international payments may ultimately not be a contest between the dollar and its alternatives. It may be a world in which countries increasingly use both, choosing between different financial networks according to the transaction, the counterparty and the geopolitical circumstances. That would represent a significant change in global finance, even if the dollar remains at its centre.

title: Noodles, dim sum, Chiu Chow: a wine and spirits writer’s Hong Kong restaurant picks
description: Cecilia Wong takes her food seriously and loves Shanghainese, Vietnamese, Cantonese and Chiu Chow flavours, as well as classic Italian.
content: Wine and spirits commentator Cecilia Wong regularly contributes to various publications including Ming Pao Daily and Headline Daily and is president of the Hong Kong Wine & Spirits Writers Association. She spoke to Andrew Sun. Growing up in a family of passionate epicures – especially my father – food was never just sustenance. It was an education in seasonal nuances. As a wine and spirits critic, my approach to dining is all about curation. I dine for precision, texture and flavour harmony. Among my favourites are, for lunch, Hao Tang Hao Mian (Shop B, Fashion Walk, 9-11 Cleveland Street, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2374 1128). The noodles are the ultimate Cantonese comfort in a bowl. Their broth has incredible depth and umami without feeling heavy, paired perfectly with al dente noodles. It’s my go-to soul food for a midday reset. Nha Trang Vietnamese Cuisine (various locations including Shop 1303, Times Square, 1 Matheson Street, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2506 2220) is reliable, vibrant and refreshingly consistent. From pho to banh mi, I love the light, uplifting flavours. More creative fine-dining Vietnamese is Le Le (3/F, 8 Lyndhurst Terrace, Central. Tel: 2798 0668). Their lunch menu reimagines classic Vietnamese flavours with French techniques. It’s inventive, balanced and surprisingly affordable for high-end dining. Shanghai Lane (Shop A, 63-81 Electric Road, Tin Hau. Tel: 2510 0393) is authentic Shanghainese soul food. Their Shanghainese wonton, drunken chicken and jellyfish with radish are must-tries and perfectly seasoned. For modern dim sum with dramatic harbour views, Nanhai No. 2 (12/F, World Trade Centre, 280 Gloucester Road, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2435 3088) is ideal. For dinner, Ye Shanghai (Shop 332, Pacific Place, 88 Queensway, Admiralty. Tel: 2918 9833) offers a masterclass in refined Shanghainese heritage. The yan du xian (salted pork, fresh pork and bamboo shoot soup) has incredible richness, while the scrambled egg whites imitate crabmeat with a remarkably delicate texture. I love Dieci (Basement, 29-31 Gough Street, Central. Tel: 9077 2629) for pure, authentic Italian comfort. Their handmade pasta is consistently al dente, and the beef tartare is expertly seasoned and tasty. Pak Loh Chiu Chow Restaurant (23-25 Hysan Avenue, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2576 8886) has served heritage Chiu Chow cuisine since 1967. It is famous for its master-braised lo shui goose and fried prawn/crab rolls. The winter melon stuffed with Jinhua ham showcases ancient Cantonese steaming techniques and delicate broth clarity. My midnight Canto-seafood sanctuary is Tai Woo Seafood Restaurant (9/F, Causeway Bay Plaza 2, 463-483 Lockhart Road, Causeway Bay. Tel: 2893 0822). It has an old-school vibrancy. Picking live seafood from tanks and enjoying perfectly steamed fish is my ultimate late-night ritual. I also love Rakuen (12/F, Circle Tower, 28 Tang Lung Street, Causeway Bay. Tel: 3580 8858) for lively Okinawan izakaya. I enjoy the briny sea grapes, rich peanut tofu and deep-fried pork knuckles paired with a refreshing Awamori highball for pure late-night happiness. When I have visitors who love trends and culture, I like Dionysus and Loong (3 Tsing Fung Street, Tin Hau. Tel: 6587 5174). This neo-Cantonese izakaya, with street-art flair by LMF’s MC Yan, encapsulates Hong Kong’s modern, rebellious energy. Order the smoked pigeon, spicy watermelon and fried chicken skin with ginger spring onion sauce for bold flavours that pair wonderfully with natural wines or craft beer. Nothing beats the authentic local experience of Sing Kee Seafood Restaurant (33-39 Sai Kung Tai Street, Sai Kung. Tel: 2791 9887). Stroll the Sai Kung promenade, then choose from the fish tanks and have it cooked immediately. The interactive experience is fresh and theatrical.

title: Hong Kong’s IPO haul in first 9 months smashes record despite Nasdaq’s fundraising lead
description: A growing pipeline and potential megadeals bolster hopes of a record IPO year for the Hong Kong stock exchange, industry players say.
content: Funds raised through Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs) doubled in the first nine months of 2026, reaching the highest level for the period since records began in 1980. A total of 112 companies raised US$48.4 billion on Hong Kong’s main board during the first nine months, according to data released by LSEG Data & Analytics on Wednesday. A further two companies listed on the city’s Growth Enterprise Market (GEM). By deal count, the combined total of 114 new listings on the main board and GEM rose 72 per cent year on year, marking the busiest nine-month period since 2018. The city, however, still trails Nasdaq, where companies raised US$144 billion during the period. The US exchange widened its lead after Elon Musk’s SpaceX completed the largest IPO in history in June, raising US$86.2 billion, LSEG data showed. Hong Kong remained well ahead of the New York Stock Exchange, which ranked third with US$17.8 billion in IPO proceeds. Mainland China’s Nasdaq-style SSE Star Market and the Shenzhen exchange ranked fourth and seventh with US$12.2 billion and US$5 billion, respectively. Despite the gap with Nasdaq, the outlook remains positive for the Hong Kong stock exchange. More than 500 companies were currently in the listing pipeline, a figure expected to exceed 600 when confidential applications are included, while three to four candidates could each raise more than HK$10 billion (US$1.3 billion) in the fourth quarter, accounting firm Deloitte said last week. “The overall Hong Kong IPO sentiment remains strong, with good investor interest in artificial intelligence and tech-related companies, metals and mining, and healthcare,” said John Lee Chen-kwok, vice-chairman and co-head of Asia coverage at UBS in Hong Kong. Technology dominated IPO and secondary-listing activity in the city, accounting for 46.9 per cent of total proceeds, or US$22.7 billion, up 11 times from the first nine months of 2025, LSEG said. Semiconductor, telecommunications equipment and electronics issuers were the primary drivers of activity. We expect Hong Kong to remain among the top three in terms of IPO fundraising, but it could claim the top spot by number of listings this year John Lee Chen-kwok, UBS To capitalise on the aerospace boom, bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) planned to launch a consultation in the first half of next year on revising listing rules aimed at attracting space-related IPOs, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his latest policy address. Still, Hong Kong may struggle to retain the global IPO crown it held last year and in the first quarter of 2026. Nasdaq was expected to pull ahead, boosted by Anthropic’s planned listing in November, which could raise up to US$100 billion, according to media reports. UBS’s Lee said the investment bank expected full-year IPO fundraising in Hong Kong to reach between HK$400 billion and HK$450 billion, with the upper end surpassing the nearly HK$450 billion raised in 2010 and setting a record. Nine mega-listings have raised over US$1 billion each in Hong Kong so far this year, led by three secondary offerings from mainland Chinese companies. Optical transceiver manufacturer Zhongji InnoLight tops the list with a US$7.8 billion share sale in July – Hong Kong’s largest listing since Alibaba Group Holding’s US$12.9 billion debut in 2019. It was followed by Apple supplier Luxshare Precision Industry and printed circuit board maker Victory Giant Technology. “We expect Hong Kong to remain among the top three in terms of IPO fundraising, but [it could claim the top spot] by number of listings this year,” Lee said. Kenneth Ho Shiu-pong, co-head of equity capital markets at Haitong International, said: “Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, deal velocity is expected to remain strong as issuers rush to tap the market, particularly over the next two months.” He added that Hong Kong was uniquely positioned to capture primary mainland Chinese issuances while continuing to attract top-tier global institutional investors. To boost market agility, HKEX launched the second phase of its listing framework review in September, focusing on streamlining spin-off and compliance requirements, according to a recent consultation paper. Under the proposal, HKEX planned to shorten the post-listing waiting period for spin-offs from three years to one year and reduce the number of transactions requiring shareholder approval – moves widely seen as enhancing the city’s appeal as an IPO destination. The proposals build on the bourse operator’s broader efforts to modernise its listing regime and IPO process. Recent measures include introducing the fast interface for new issuance – or Fini – settlement platform to shorten the settlement times, lowering listing thresholds for specialist technology and biotech companies, and enabling confidential listing filings.

title: EU weighs sweeping new trade powers against China before make-or-break October
description: The mood in Brussels is hardening and Europe’s actions in coming weeks could set the course of EU-China relations for years to come.
content: Brussels and Berlin are steeling themselves for a make-or-break October with China, as the mood towards Beijing hardens in both capitals. The month ahead could help set the course of the increasingly thorny EU-China relationship for years to come, as Europe gears up to present a slew of new tools for countering Beijing’s trade practices, likely to come in December. Before then, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing on October 8 and 9 for crucial meetings with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. These will assess how much progress has been made in rebalancing trade ties since the last showdown in June. The European Commission is pushing China to set voluntary export limits on products such as plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, sales of which have soared in tandem with a downturn in Europe’s own automotive fortunes. The bloc wants to put the brakes on a surge of Chinese imports that, combined with sluggish EU exports to China, have extended a gaping trade deficit. Officials said talks had been progressing surprisingly well, and there might well be some deliverables from next week’s meetings. Nonetheless, Beijing has publicly rebuked any suggestion that it would curb its shipments. These meetings will inform the agenda of an EU national leaders’ summit in Brussels the following week. The European Commission will present the outcome of its China negotiations and expects to receive the green light to propose new weapons in early-December. Official and diplomatic sources say China is not expected to be named in the customary written conclusions of the European Council summit, as the bloc hopes to maintain diplomatic decorum with Beijing and draw less retribution. However, multiple sources said that firm action was now expected this year, regardless of the outcome of next week’s meeting in Beijing. “Nothing is going to happen in the meeting next week that prevents this train from leaving the station,” one official source said. In her state of the EU speech this month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen asserted that while “some say the second China shock is looming … it’s already here”. Fears abound that unfair Chinese trading practices are contributing to a deindustrialisation of Europe’s manufacturing heartland, including in Germany but also spreading through central and eastern Europe. In recent weeks, Berlin has come closer to the long-standing view in Brussels and Paris that the trading situation is unsustainable and that something has to change. “There is a sense of emergency … Germany has changed dramatically. There is this total destruction of employment, of factories. There is a lot of stress,” a diplomatic source said. Among the planned tools are a diversification instrument that would oblige firms in critical sectors to have at least three suppliers spread across several countries, and a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by retaliation from China or any other trading partner. Speculation has been mounting in recent days that a third weapon is also in the works, one which could give broad tariffing powers to the European Commission, akin to those used by the US government through its Section 301 tool. Various reports have described a commission-controlled emergency trade power that could rapidly restrict Chinese imports when dependency or overcapacity crosses a systemic threshold, without waiting for traditional product-by-product investigations or a positive vote from member states. Two newsletters, Dossier Bruselas and Watching China in Europe, reported that a joint paper on China from France and Germany would propose achieving this through reworking the dormant anti-coercion instrument, which would provide broad retaliatory powers but have a high bar to be activated. Diplomatic sources confirmed that the paper will be presented to the European Commission before the European Council summit. “It is basically finalised … the instrument that we are calling for would allow us to cut China off from the European market within 24 hours,” one official was quoted as saying in the Watching China in Europe newsletter, written by analyst Noah Barkin. A new 301-like tool would “risk weaponising trade policy”, the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU said in a statement on Wednesday. “European industry has also experienced the negative impact of similar unilateral trade measures. International trade instruments should not become subject to a ‘race to the bottom’, nor should unilateral measures replace multilateral rules,” the chamber said, urging the EU to avoid “beggar thy neighbour approaches”. In recent weeks, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz under huge pressure from the electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany, Berlin appears to have shifted decisively on China. Previously the main proponent of engagement, it is now signalling support for protectionist measures. On Tuesday, the German government notified the European Commission of tighter telecoms security and certification rules aimed at further restricting certain vendors’ access to German networks. Huawei Technologies is not named, but the Chinese company is widely understood to be the main target. Some of the country’s major business lobby groups have come out in favour of a more protectionist trade stance towards Beijing, including those that have previously warned against action. In a policy paper last week, the Federation of German Industries (BDI) – which has previously backed harsher policies on China – warned that the cost of doing nothing would outweigh that of any Chinese retaliation. “Even if de-risking entails costs, including in the form of counter-reactions, passivity would in the long term be economically considerably more costly and irresponsible from a security policy perspective,” the BDI wrote. While the group said it favoured WTO-compatible solutions, it also signalled that some flexibility might be required. “Given the critical situation, particularly China’s state-induced massive overcapacities … WTO-compatible temporary defensive measures sometimes take effect too late or are insufficient,” it wrote. “The advantages and disadvantages of possible instruments such as local-content requirements, tariff-rate quotas, sector-wide or even general tariffs must be carefully examined and weighed against each other.” In contrast to the BDI, the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) has been a strong opponent of defensive trade action against China, with its views proving influential across the German government. Now, however, it appears to have had a change of heart. According to German business daily Handelsblatt, an internal VDA note said “imbalances have arisen in trade with China in recent years” and that “trade defence instruments” could be used “from a certain point of distortion of competition”, for example in cases of “proven unfair practices”. “Germany, which has long been known for its opposition to a hardening of trade policy towards China, is beginning to shift its stance,” wrote Pascal Canfin, the European Parliament trade committee’s lead rapporteur on China, in an article for Le Grand Continent, a French magazine. “The Germany that blocked tariffs on electric vehicles in 2024 is different from the Germany that is today open to discussions, alongside France, on how to respond to China’s aggressive industrial policy.”

title: Passengers foil bid to crash Israel-bound flight after co-pilot stabs captain
description: Heroic struggle halts mid-air plunge on Flydubai jet before emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
content: Passengers on a ⁠Flydubai flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after customers and crew foiled a co-pilot’s attempt to ⁠crash the aircraft, Israeli officials said, in a struggle that began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. Passengers and crew entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and enabled a second pair of Flydubai pilots who were aboard the flight to land the jet safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, Israeli officials said. More than 10 hours later, the passengers arrived at Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport aboard a Flydubai replacement aircraft, with several describing the episode as a miracle and recounting a frantic struggle to prevent a catastrophe. Israeli officials said the attacker’s motive aboard flight FZ1073 from Dubai to ‌Tel Aviv remained under investigation. Israel and the United Arab Emirates, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalising relations in 2020. The incident sharpened concerns about global aviation security in a region scarred by years of conflict, prompting Israel to tighten checks on pilots flying into the country. “I just can say that it was a miracle. It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it, we didn’t think we will make it but thank God we are in Israel. We are back home. And we are happy to see everyone here,” passenger Lital Shachaf said. Israel’s ambulance service said a 51-year-old man was taken to an Israeli hospital to be treated for injuries to his upper body. The man was in a “mild condition,” it said. Describing the event as “a serious security incident,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saudi authorities would interrogate the co-pilot. Flydubai said in a statement that the underlying reasons for the event remained unknown and warned ⁠against “premature speculation”. An Israeli official identified the co-pilot as an Omani national. There was no immediate comment from Oman. Israeli officials applauded the passengers, who they credited with avoiding a much more serious disaster. Netanyahu said there were 174 people on board the flight ‌from Dubai, most of them Israeli nationals. US President Donald Trump said he spoke “at length” with Netanyahu on Wednesday about the incident. He proceeded to give reporters in the Oval Office a detailed account of what happened, adding: “This is the story that I heard – I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story that I got from Bibi (Netanyahu).” A Netanyahu spokesperson told Reuters that ‌the wounded captain, identified by the Israeli leader’s office as Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was covered with blood on the floor when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door. Passengers who ⁠entered found the co-pilot bashing at the plane’s control panel, the ⁠spokesperson said. “This is something you do without thinking, just running to save your daughter’s life, your family’s life,” said Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who helped restrain the attacker. He spoke with a forehead still bloodied from the struggle. Netanyahu’s office released a video showing the prime minister at Ben Gurion Airport giving ‌a hug to another passenger, Yaniv Hayun, who his office said “broke into” the cockpit. “I see you and I see a lion – a big hero,” Netanyahu told the man, who was still wearing the bloodstained shirt he had on during the flight. Flydubai operates daily return flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv, a route that is popular among Israeli ‌nationals. The flight ‌path normally uses airspace over Saudi Arabia and Jordan. It is not the first time a flight between Israel and the UAE has landed in Saudi Arabia. A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Riyadh ‌in September 2025 due to a medical incident, Israeli media reported at the time. Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, said both pilots had been hospitalised after sustaining injuries. The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote in the first election ⁠since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks, with Israel’s security figuring prominently in the campaigning. Responding to the incident on X, far-right security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir wrote: “Terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached”. Israeli media published conflicting reports on the incident, with some outlets reporting that a pilot had tried to crash the passenger plane in an alleged suicide attempt. Some Israeli media outlets initially identified the pilots as Omani and Emirati nationals, while others said they were Russian and Ukrainian. “Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron ‌Spielman, a Netanyahu spokesperson, told Reuters. Netanyahu met on Sunday with UAE ‌President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan during a rare visit to the Gulf country. Israel and the UAE have forged close security, military and economic ties since establishing diplomatic ties. Israel provided the UAE earlier this year with Iron Dome air-defence systems and Israeli personnel to operate them, helping defend against Iranian attacks launched after Israel and the US began strikes on Iran. The UAE government had yet to comment on the Flydubai incident, while the Dubai state-owned airline said an “altercation” occurred in the cockpit and the flight subsequently diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely. The UAE’s aviation regulator, the GCAA, said the flight “experienced a security incident that was brought under control”.

title: Behind closed doors, a fatal beating exposes Malaysia’s parallel boarding school rules
description: The fatal beating of a 14-year-old student reveals how informal disciplinary rules continue to operate behind closed boarding school doors.
content: The death of a 14-year-old student at a Malaysian boarding school has renewed scrutiny over student safety, raising questions over whether reforms introduced after the high-profile death of Zara Qairina Mahathir last year have changed what happens behind dormitory doors. Police in Kuala Pilah, Negeri Sembilan, have detained two 16-year-old students as they investigate the death of Muhammad Idlan Fareeq Shahril. They said Idlan was caught vaping by a hostel warden on September 23. Two days later, a 16-year-old student instructed a peer to bring Idlan to his dormitory, where he was allegedly struck on the soles of his feet with a rubber hosepipe, forced to remove his shirt and hit on the chest and back until he collapsed. Idlan was later taken to Hospital Ampuan Najihah, where he was pronounced dead. As of Tuesday, police had detained the two students, recorded statements from 68 witnesses and were investigating claims of bullying involving several students, including that one of the suspects had previously bullied them. The case has revived painful memories of the death of 13-year-old Zara Qairina Mahathir, who was pronounced dead on July 17 last year, a day after being found unconscious outside her dormitory at an Islamic boarding school in Sabah. Her death triggered nationwide protests and intense scrutiny of boarding school safety after police initially closed the case without a postmortem. The Attorney General later ordered her body exhumed for further examination and launched a fresh investigation. Five teenagers were subsequently charged with making threatening or insulting communications towards Zara, while an inquest into her death is ongoing. Child rights advocates are now calling for deeper scrutiny into informal senior-junior hierarchies, adult supervision and whether students are still being allowed to exercise disciplinary authority over their peers. Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, chairman of the Parent Action Group for Education Malaysia, told This Week in Asia that the latest case raised questions over whether recent reforms had actually reached boarding school hostels, arguing that safety could not be measured by circulars issued, audits conducted or complaints logged. “It must be measured by whether a child is actually safe when no parent is there,” Noor Azimah said. She said deterrence on paper and prevention on the ground were two separate things, particularly in boarding schools where power hierarchies can develop and younger students may be reluctant to report older students who control their daily environment. “Students cannot be allowed to assume that being older or more senior gives them authority to punish younger students,” Noor Azimah said, adding that responsibility must rest with the school and the Education Ministry. “A hostel is not simply accommodation. Once parents entrust their children to a boarding school, the institution assumes a significant duty of care, including during evenings and prep periods,” she said. While students could serve as prefects or peer mentors, Noor Azimah said authorised adults must retain disciplinary authority. Asked whether students should ever be allowed to discipline peers, she said: “They should not be. Full stop.” James Nayagam, a child rights advocate and consultant with the Suriana Welfare Society, told This Week in Asia that the Kuala Pilah case highlights alarming gaps in boarding school supervision, though he warned against assuming the problem was universal. “The Kuala Pilah case should trigger an audit of whether informal senior-junior punishment exists elsewhere, not an assumption that it does,” Nayagam said. He said informal punishments by senior students could create a parallel disciplinary system within hostels where student leaders determined guilt and administered punishment. Nayagam said that while Malaysia already had a substantial framework to protect students – including warden guidelines, safety audits and reporting channels – implementation on the ground remained the unresolved issue. “Can the ministry demonstrate, school-by-school, that the standard operating procedure is being followed?” he asked, calling for scrutiny of night-duty rosters, dormitory inspections and complaint response times, as well as an explicit ban on student-administered punishment. “Students may report misconduct, but they must not become a parallel disciplinary authority,” Nayagam added. On Saturday, Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said in a statement that the ministry and school would cooperate fully with the police investigation. She said that she had ordered the Inspectorate of Schools to immediately audit school safety and procedural compliance to identify any breaches. “At the ministry level, school safety and compliance with established procedures will be thoroughly reviewed,” Fadhlina said. “No party will be protected if misconduct or breaches of the law are found to have occurred. Appropriate action will be taken based on the findings.”

title: In Malaysia and Singapore, Palestine is a breaking point on concerts’ legal limits
description: Ed Sheeran and Macklemore tour split is the latest in Gaza activism and global music acts in Asia.
content:
When American rapper Macklemore said “Free Palestine” at a New Jersey stop of British pop star Ed Sheeran’s United States tour, he lost his job as opener. But in Malaysia, it was Sheeran’s music that was pulled from airwaves.
In contrast, in neighbouring Singapore, a “Free Palestine” chant and display of a Palestinian flag had resulted in a ban for British band Massive Attack.
The opposing cases highlight the competing pressures on foreign artists in Southeast Asia, where political expression can cross different red lines set by governments, promoters, venues and audiences, analysts and industry figures say.
In Malaysia, where public support for Palestinian liberation runs deep, promoters must still weigh an artist’s politics against commercial considerations and concert rules. Singapore, meanwhile, draws a sharper line between humanitarian expression and what it considers political advocacy.
The disputes come amid demands for musicians to speak out against Israel’s actions in Gaza. A United Nations commission of inquiry concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide, a finding Israel rejected.
Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s tour earlier this month prompted other supporting acts to quit. Promoter Messina Touring Group said stadium owners would not accept him on the bill, while stadium owner Robert Kraft cited allegations of antisemitic rhetoric, which the rapper rejected.
On September 15, Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was the promoter’s, after venues on the tour threatened to pull their shows if the rapper remained.
Three days later, Malaysian radio station Fly FM pulled Sheeran’s songs, declaring that “some things matter more than music”.
Sheeran apologised for his handling of the dispute at a Philadelphia concert the following day, calling the situation in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable”.
In Malaysia, pressures on foreign artists extend beyond the airwaves. Foreign acts must also comply with concert rules, leaving promoters to balance an artist’s political stance with commercial considerations and authorities’ requirements.
Rohit Rampal, founder and CEO of Malaysian concert organiser Hitman Group, said an artist’s political stance would not automatically rule out a booking, but ticket demand was only part of the decision.
“Their public perception, suitability for the Malaysian market, and brand all come into play,” he said. “A decision that’s considered acceptable or necessary in another market may be perceived very differently in Malaysia.”
Asked how he would respond if an overseas partner wanted a pro-Palestinian performer dropped, Rampal said he would raise the prospect of a Malaysian backlash and explore alternatives.
In Singapore, two members of Massive Attack received stern police warnings after displaying the Palestinian flag at their July 29 concert, with one shouting “Free Palestine”. Both were banned from re-entering the country, and authorities said future applications for the band to perform would not be accepted.
Abraham Vergis, managing director of Providence Law Asia, said Macklemore’s actions could be considered political advocacy in Singapore and invite a similar reaction from authorities.
“At the very least, I would expect a police investigation and some difficulty getting approval to perform here again,” he said.
The purpose of an artist’s intervention mattered, Vergis said. “Expressing sorrow for those caught in a war, or calling for peace, is unlikely to trouble anyone. Leading a crowd in political slogans or waving a flag on stage is different, because that is asking the audience to take a side in a foreign conflict.”
Singapore does not allow the open display of foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit.
In Malaysia, foreign performances require approval through the Unit for Application for Foreign Filming and Performance by Foreign Artiste, known as Puspal. Organisers must also be able to halt shows that breach conditions.
The “kill switch” measure followed British band The 1975’s performance at the Good Vibes Festival in 2023, when frontman Matty Healy criticised Malaysia’s anti-gay laws and kissed a male bandmate, prompting authorities to cancel the rest of the festival.
Later that year, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim defended Coldplay against calls to cancel its Kuala Lumpur concert, citing the band’s support for Palestinians, while organisers agreed to a kill switch.
Korean-American singer Eric Nam cancelled a planned Kuala Lumpur show in 2023, citing threats after liking a post about the Israel and Gaza. Bruno Mars performed there in 2024 despite Muslim student activists’ objections over his previous concerts in Israel.
A Pew Research Centre survey published in June found that 89 per cent of Malaysians and 86 per cent of Indonesians viewed Israel unfavourably.
Musicians from both countries have used their work to raise money for Palestinians. Cholil Mahmud, vocalist of Indonesian band Efek Rumah Kaca, and Malaysian artists Noh Salleh and Kayda collaborated on Our Power , released in July, with royalties pledged to Palestinian aid.
“We hope this song encourages people in Indonesia and Malaysia, and their governments, to care more about this issue,” Cholil told Indonesian outlet Medcom.
Malaysian singer-songwriter Azmyl Yunor, who also lectures at Sunway University, said treating Palestinian solidarity as an unwelcome intrusion of politics missed the depth of support for the cause at home.
“It’s beyond politics – it’s about being human,” he said. “The Malaysian public, from what I’ve observed, has a clearer and broader understanding of the issue, albeit with some confirmation bias based on your own personal beliefs and faiths.”

title: Hong Kong to expand IP financing sandbox after 7 firms secure cheaper loans
description: Scheme helps businesses secure larger loans at lower interest rates, as banks take companies’ IP valuations into account, HKMA says.
content: The Hong Kong government has pledged to expand its intellectual property (IP) financing sandbox scheme by adding more banks and enterprises, after seven corporate users found that a nine-month trial helped lower their borrowing costs. “This will help refine the IP ecosystem, including valuation practices, professional service costs, supporting measures and market awareness,” Carmen Chu Lap-kiu, executive director of banking supervision at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), said on Wednesday. “These initiatives can also better support the development of the Northern Metropolis and key industries, while helping small and medium-sized enterprises go global and explore new markets.” She said the scheme was expected to support key industries in the megadevelopment, such as hi-tech, logistics and education, with their future financing needs. Chu’s remarks came as the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau, the Intellectual Property Department and the monetary authority – the city’s de facto central bank – announced the first batch of successful pilot cases. The seven cases span the electronics, construction, toy manufacturing and medical device sectors, with loan amounts ranging from HK$1 million to HK$39 million (US$127,460 to US$4.97 million). Proposed in last year’s policy address, the initiative provides a “pioneer and pilot” approach and a collaborative, risk-controlled environment for banks, enterprises and relevant professional services organisations to test the full life cycle of financing arrangements based on IP assets, aiming to build practical experience. The city’s three note-issuing banks – Bank of China (Hong Kong), HSBC and Standard Chartered Hong Kong – took part in the scheme. Chu noted that the project had enabled businesses to secure larger loans at lower interest rates, as banks took enterprises’ IP valuations into account when assessing future business development and repayment capacity, and accepted the valuations as collateral to mitigate credit risk. “Banks incorporate IP valuation reports into their credit assessments. Based on these valuations, banks can award additional points in the credit evaluation, enabling enterprises to obtain larger and cheaper loans,” she said. “From the successful cases, we can see that after taking IP valuations into account, the loan amounts secured by enterprises have increased by 25 to 50 per cent, and the interest rates on the loans can also be reduced by 25 to 150 basis points.” Chu said banks were already processing additional cases and expected the number of successful applications to keep rising. While authorities planned to expand the trial by inviting more banks, enterprises and professional institutions to take part, Chu said a rigid timeline or specific target for the number of participating banks and businesses had not been set. Helen Chung Chi-ching, deputy secretary for commerce and economic development, said the scheme addressed lending challenges faced by companies with high-quality IP that lacked physical collateral, describing the trial as a solid start. “We aim to accumulate more diverse cases across different industries so that we can observe market responses, learn from the experience and consider how to expand in the next phase,” Chung added. “[We hope] that the participating enterprises will be more diversified. As we see, there are currently four industries involved; all comers are welcome in the future.” Among the pilot cases was Man Yue Technology Holdings. Its executive director and managing director, Eugene Chan Yu-ching, said the company held more than 100 patents that had generated a virtuous cycle of capital using the sandbox scheme. “IP financing allows us to develop products and optimise production lines with greater flexibility,” he said. “The patents and technologies generated then form a virtuous cycle and become new assets for our company.” Chan added that the funds raised supported the company’s power supply projects for AI data centres, new energy projects and the customisation of electronic products. He also stressed that recognition from banks and financial institutions of the value of the company’s IP constituted an important reputational asset that helped promote the business. Another participant, AluHouse International Trading Company, is a building technology firm specialising in modular integrated construction. Its chairman, Eric Kwong Hoi-fung, said the company held more than 300 patents worldwide. Kwong added that he once saw patents as mere pieces of paper to protect business rights, but now realised they could be converted into capital. He noted that the company’s research and development efforts and global expansion were long-term initiatives that required continuous capital investment, and that the scheme had provided more diversified financing options beyond traditional lending. The government also announced the launch of the two-year Pilot Patent Valuation Support Scheme through the Hong Kong Technology and Innovation Support Centre on Wednesday. It provides one-off funding capped at HK$80,000 through a matching grant model to support small and medium-sized enterprises in commissioning a qualified service provider to value their patents and other IP assets.

title: Singapore jails man for slapping preschooler at bus stop over rude gesture
description: Muhammad Firdhaus was also ordered to pay US$133 in compensation to the mother of the boy, who suffered lasting trauma from the incident.
content: A man became angry after a four-year-old boy pointed his middle finger at him while he was picking up his son from preschool in Singapore. He pursued the boy to a nearby bus stop that was crowded with other young kids, grabbed the boy by the arm and slapped him hard on both cheeks. The boy, who was his son’s schoolmate, suffered bruises on his face and ringing in his ear, on top of emotional trauma that lingered for months and required his parents to change his preschool. The aggressor, Muhammad Firdhaus Mokhtar, was sentenced to 14 weeks’ jail on Wednesday. He was also ordered to pay S$170 (US$133) in compensation to the mother of the victim, who was in court to watch his sentencing. Firdhaus pleaded guilty to one count each of voluntarily causing hurt and using criminal force on a minor, with a third charge taken into consideration. At about noon on March 6 this year, Firdhaus went to his son’s preschool to pick the boy up. The name of the preschool was redacted in accordance with the gag order, which prevents the publishing of anything that can identify the victim. Firdhaus’ son was playing with the victim when the victim pointed his middle finger at Firdhaus. Firdhaus was angered and called the boy to come over but the boy ignored him and skipped towards his domestic helper. The helper was at a bus stop outside the school where other preschool children, including the victim’s friends, were waiting. Firdhaus followed the boy to the bus stop and grabbed him by the arm. When the boy tried to break free, Firdhaus told the helper to tell his parents not to let him point his middle finger at others and threatened to slap him. The boy tried to hide behind a pillar, but Firdhaus pulled him out by his collar and slapped him on the right cheek with the back of his hand. He then slapped the boy’s left cheek and ear with such force that the child fell to the ground. When the helper tried to help the boy up and pull him away, Firdhaus kept his grip on the boy’s arm. He shoved a finger in the boy’s face, threatening to break his finger and shouting that he would return for him on Monday. Firdhaus then swung the boy backwards, causing him to stumble backwards before leaving. The assault was witnessed by members of the public at the bus stop, including several preschool children and captured on police camera footage. The helper brought the crying boy home, where his mother noticed redness around his ears, cheeks and jaw. At the hospital, he was found to have bruises on both cheeks and was discharged with a five-day course of paracetamol for pain relief. The hospital lodged a police report. Shaken by the assault, the boy wept twice in his sleep that night and did not dare to attend school for the next few days. In the months after the assault, he asked his mother anxiously whether the next day was Monday and whether he had to go to school. He feared going to school because “I am scared the uncle will slap me hard again”. His parents eventually transferred him to another school. But he continued to have flashbacks of the assault and cried for prolonged periods. He also continues to have nightmares of the assault to this day. Deputy public prosecutor Etsuko Lim sought four to six months’ jail, listing multiple aggravating factors including the sustained aggression and the viciousness of the slaps. She said Firdhaus was brazen, slapping the child in broad daylight at a crowded bus stop, alarming and shocking bystanders. The assault was also “deeply scarring” on the young victim, who would have taken the threat to break his finger seriously since he had also made good on the threat to slap him. Firdhaus was represented by Daryl Lim from the Public Defender’s Office, who said there was no version of events that day that was “acceptable by any means”. “A young child was hurt both physically and emotionally, and my client does own that fully,” he said. The mother of the victim was in court with family members. She told the court that although her son was recovering, he was not “recovering fully” as he still has nightmares. His confidence level has also gone down, she said. “I must say that I’m very perturbed with this incident,” said the woman while Firdhaus stood stiffly in the dock. “We had to engage in a lot of activities to keep him occupied to gain his confidence back again, to assure him that things are as normal,” she said. “It also perturbs me to the fact that, now, it puts the puzzle into the picture on why my son has been asking [about] Monday,” the boy’s mother said. “Because I’ve never known from him that he actually was being threatened to [have his finger broken] or [that the accused would] see him on the following Monday.” She said she did not want to prolong her son’s distress, especially since the other child involved was his classmate and had been in the same class as her son since play group. “As [his] mother, I felt that we want to have a closure for him,” the woman said. “And we also hope that the accused will acknowledge the harm that he caused and apologise to [my son].” She said that while an apology cannot undo what happened or restore her son’s sense of safety, it is important to the family. Firdhaus then apologised to the victim’s family in court. “To the victim’s family and everybody in the court, I wish to sincerely apologise for the actions that I did, and I hope you really forgive me and also give me a chance to be a better man in the future,” he said. The victim’s mother also asked to see the footage of the assault, but was told to ask the investigating officer. District Judge Koo Zhi Xuan said inflicting such raw violence on a young victim was “a vile and intolerable act”. “Such violence would not have been morally justified, had the accused committed the same acts against his own children at home, let alone a child he was not even acquainted with in a public and crowded setting where other children were present,” he said. He agreed with the prosecution on several of the aggravating factors, saying the emotional turmoil suffered by the victim and his family was “particularly weighty”. Firdhaus asked to defer his jail term until November 13, as his wife, who was also in court, is 23 weeks’ pregnant. His lawyer said the couple have a hospital appointment on November 12, as the fetus remains in a breech position. They will obtain advice on whether that will necessitate an earlier delivery. The judge noted that granting the request may lead to further applications for deferment, such as if Firdhaus’ wife requires surgery. However, he granted the application when Firdhaus gave his word that he would surrender on November 13, and not seek further deferments. The judge allowed the victim’s family to leave the courtroom first before allowing Firdhaus and his wife to leave. For voluntarily causing hurt to a minor, he could have been jailed for up to six years, fined up to S$10,000, or both. For using criminal force on a minor, he could have been jailed for up to six months, fined up to S$3,000, or both. This story was first published by CNA

title: China’s 2030 solid-state battery goal, Chinese carmakers see boost in Europe: 7 EV reads
description: From VW and Gotion deepening ties to CATL’s trial production in Hungary, here are seven EV stories you may have missed.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on electric and new energy vehicles from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. As Chinese carmakers diversify beyond CATL, Beijing warns of market overreaction A publication under China’s industry ministry has pushed back against market chatter of “de-CATLisation” as a growing number of the battery giant’s automotive partners diversify their suppliers, with the company’s shares falling recently. 2. Tesla auditing Chinese suppliers ahead of Optimus roll-out: sources Tesla officials and engineers have begun auditing part of the firm’s Chinese supply chain, as Elon Musk’s company aims to quickly ramp up production of its Optimus humanoid robot after it hits the global market later this year, according to sources with knowledge of the matter. 3. Chinese EV battery giant CATL starts trial production in Hungary Contemporary Amperex Technol­ogy Ltd (CATL) has cleared all regulatory hurdles for its mega factory in Hungary, a development that analysts expect will help the world’s largest producer of electric vehicle (EV) batteries extend its reach to international marques like BMW and Volkswagen. 4. China’s EV and battery makers tussle over lithium-ion tax: sources China’s electric vehicle (EV) makers and battery manufacturers are locked in negotiations over which party should pay a resumed consumption tax, according to industry sources, a conflict that underlines carmakers’ struggles amid weak home market demand. 5. VW, Gotion deepen ties with US$3.7b commitment to EV battery production Volkswagen Group and its Chinese partner Gotion High-tech have stepped up a gear in tapping global demand for electric vehicle (EV) batteries with plans to invest a combined €3.22 billion (US$3.66 billion) to set up three production lines in Europe and North Africa. 6. Chinese carmakers gain as high petrol prices boost European EV sales Chinese carmakers have gained ground in Europe’s shift to electric cars, emerging as the biggest winners in plug-in hybrids despite moves by Brussels to curb their expansion. 7. China outlines 2030 solid-state battery road map to extend global EV dominance China has set a goal to achieve initial volume production of solid-state batteries by 2030 – a next-generation technology still in the early stages of commercialisation – as the country seeks to extend its global advantage in the battery industry from conventional lithium-ion batteries into emerging technologies.

title: China diving star Chen Yuxi, 21, becomes oldest winner at Asian Games for 52 years
description: The 10m platform victory sparks comparisons online with compatriot Quan Hongchan, who is two years younger and missed event through injury.
content: China’s 21-year-old Chen Yuxi became the oldest gold medal winner in women’s 10m platform diving at the Asian Games for 52 years on Tuesday. The victory marked Chen’s first individual Asian Games gold medal, finishing ahead of teammate Lu Wei, 20, who claimed silver. The pair had previously topped the podium together in the synchronised event. Chen’s win also rekindled interest in her compatriot Quan Hongchan, who is two years younger and missed the Asian Games through injury. China have claimed an unprecedented 14 consecutive titles in the women’s 10m platform at the Asian Games since 1974, routinely securing both gold and silver. Yet within China’s national diving team, where internal competition eclipses international opposition, securing an Asian Games spot in one’s early twenties was previously almost unthinkable. Chen is the oldest platform champion since Zhong Shaozhen won springboard and platform gold at 26 years old when China made its Asian Games debut in Tehran in 1974. An emotional Chen broke down in tears during her post-competition interview, admitting she had considered giving up but persevered thanks to the support around her and her own refusal to quit. “Diving is a very important part of my life,” Chen said. “Without the help of my coaches and team leaders, as well as my own refusal to give up, I couldn’t have made it to Tokyo again [after the 2020 Olympics].” “I feel every stage has its own difficulties, but I also feel very fortunate that these difficulties were never overwhelming. There were always a few challenges, and those challenges pushed me to keep moving forward,” she said. Looking ahead to the Los Angeles Olympic cycle, her goal was to remain grounded: “Next, I will take it step by step, staying grounded, taking every step firmly and solidly.” Chen made history last year as the oldest Chinese world champion in the event. Should she claim gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Games, she would become the first Chinese diver past 20 to win Olympic gold in the individual 10m platform, eclipsing Chen Ruolin, who won when she was 19 years old. Historically, China’s women’s diving team have featured younger athletes, with many forced to transition to the springboard once they hit puberty. Lighter bodies were believed to offer advantages in height, rotation and entry splash control. Prominent divers like Fu Mingxia and Guo Jingjing both moved to the 3m springboard when they grew older rather than staying on the platform, reinforcing the perception that China’s platform scene belonged almost exclusively to teenage athletes. Chen’s victory led to social media users comparing her to Quan, who missed the Asian Games. In her Olympic debut in Tokyo, Quan won gold in the women’s 10m platform with a record-breaking 466.20 points at just 14 years old. Chen claimed silver. In recent years, physical growth, weight gain and injuries have led to fewer competitions and inconsistent results for Quan, shifting public expectation into disappointment and online criticism. Following her victory, netizens suggested Chen benefited from an opportunity created by Quan’s absence, while others credited her discipline in managing her weight over the years. “[Chen Yuxi] holds herself to extremely high standards, is very disciplined and smoothly navigated the growth phase,” one netizen wrote. “Individual weight variations are significant. You can see it with Quan Hongchan, gaining weight after puberty isn’t something you can easily control even if you want to,” another noted. In the final, Chen executed one of the most difficult dives nearly flawlessly on her fourth attempt, drawing perfect 10s from four judges for 97.35 points. She sealed the title with a total of 432.65 points, finishing 47.25 points ahead of Lu, while North Korea’s Jo Jin-mi took bronze.

title: Mainland China’s PCB giant wins Hong Kong approval for planned US$3b listing: sources
description: Shenzhen-listed Dongshan Precision’s share sale could rank among the city’s largest IPOs in the fourth quarter, sources say.
content: Mainland China-based printed circuit board (PCB) maker Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing has cleared its final listing hurdle in Hong Kong and is moving towards a share sale that may rank among the city’s largest initial public offerings (IPOs) in the fourth quarter, according to people familiar with the matter. The company passed its listing hearing with bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) recently, the people said, requesting anonymity because the information was private. The Shenzhen-listed company said in a Tuesday announcement that it had received approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission for its planned Hong Kong listing, allowing it to issue up to 234 million shares. Dongshan Precision, which makes PCBs, optical transceivers, precision components, touch panels and liquid crystal modules used in smartphones, PCs, automotive systems, industrial equipment and Internet of Things devices, initially aimed to open its order books as early as October to raise up to US$3 billion, according to the sources. The timetable, however, could be pushed back slightly, although the listing would still take place this year, they added. As the listing process was under way, details including the size and timetable remained subject to change, the sources said, adding that the IPO would be among Hong Kong’s largest in the fourth quarter. Despite falling 40 per cent from its peak, Dongshan Precision’s Shenzhen-listed shares have jumped more than eightfold since 2024, touching a historical high of 208.08 yuan in July and giving the company a market capitalisation of about 308 billion yuan (US$46 billion). IPOs in Hong Kong raised more than HK$380 billion (US$48.4 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, already surpassing last year’s total, accounting firm Deloitte said last week. Most of this year’s large listings have involved mainland China-listed companies. Optical transceiver maker Zhongji InnoLight raised HK$53.4 billion in July, making it Hong Kong’s largest share sale since Alibaba Group Holding’s US$12.9 billion offering in 2019. Deloitte said it expected three to four additional IPOs to raise more than HK$10 billion each in the fourth quarter. Dongshan Precision reported revenue of 40.1 billion yuan for 2025, up 9 per cent from a year earlier, with overseas clients contributing 81.4 per cent, according to its filing. Net profit rose 28 per cent to 1.39 billion yuan. UBS Group, Guotai Haitong, GF Securities and Citic Securities are joint sponsors of Dongshan Precision’s listing.

title: China’s DeepSeek open-sources tools to help Huawei chips supplant Nvidia in AI
description: With introduction of suite of six tools, AI model developer aims to create ‘independent’ software ecosystem for AI processors.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek on Wednesday open-sourced a suite of core tools tailored for Huawei Technologies’ Ascend AI chips, marking a step forward in the country’s push to end dependence on processors from US giant Nvidia amid US export curbs. Hangzhou-based DeepSeek released six software modules that mirror its prior open-source tools for Nvidia’s AI chips, aiming to build a new “independent and controllable” software ecosystem for graphics processing units (GPUs), according to a post on its official WeChat account. Among the releases is an Ascend-compatible version of TileLang, a custom programming language designed to streamline the development of high-performance kernels – essential computation programs – to run on GPUs and central processing units. While TileLang lists Nvidia as its primary back end, it now officially supports Huawei’s Ascend 950 accelerators, offering “native code generation, automatic scheduling, and synchronisation”, according to an update on the project’s GitHub page. “As an open-source project, the TileLang Ascend version aims to serve as an example for building a highly available software ecosystem for more AI chips,” DeepSeek said. Alongside TileLang, DeepSeek released a set of underlying libraries tailored for high-throughput training and inference on Ascend chips, including DeepGEMM Ascend, a matrix multiplication kernel library, and DeepEP Ascend, which enables efficient, large-scale cross-device communication. Others were designed to improve the efficiency of long-context processing and data filtering on Huawei chips. DeepSeek said the new tools delivered computational and communication performance that approached “the hardware limits” in several tests. The development of the Ascend-facing infrastructure was made possible through “close collaboration” with Huawei, DeepSeek said, as the two sides worked together on the optimisation of a supernode architecture powered by 128 Ascend 950 processors. The two firms have worked closely to answer Beijing’s call for tech self-reliance. When DeepSeek’s V4 model was launched in April, Huawei soon announced “full support” with its chips to serve in inference – the act of using a trained AI model to make predictions on new data. Other Chinese chip giants have followed suit, including Cambricon Technologies, Moore Threads and Alibaba Group Holding’s T-Head, all of which have confirmed compatibility with the DeepSeek model. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Huawei, meanwhile, has accelerated its pace of rolling out new AI processors. It announced earlier this month that the Ascend 960DT chip, designed for AI model training, would be “ready in the first quarter of 2027”, three quarters ahead of schedule.

title: Philippines urged to adopt Malaysia’s lasting tourism strategy
description: Senators say changing national taglines with every election wastes resources and dilutes global recognition.
content: Philippine senators have urged the Department of Tourism to stick with a single marketing campaign to build long-term international recognition, pointing to long-running successes such as Malaysia’s “Truly Asia” tagline. Newly appointed Tourism Secretary Dita Angara-Mathay was asked about her plans for the current slogan, “Love the Philippines”, during a departmental budget hearing on Monday, the Philippine Star reported. Senate finance subcommittee chairman Erwin Tulfo suggested keeping the current slogan rather than starting afresh. “It’s like we’re the only country that changes its tourism slogan with each administration. There’s ‘Love’, ‘More Love’, ‘Love-Love’, ‘It’s More Fun’, and ‘Wow Philippines’. Why?” Tulfo said, adding that he would not be surprised if another rebrand occurred under the next government following the 2028 presidential election. “Why do we change? I don’t see anything wrong with ‘Wow Philippines.’ What is going on here?” Tulfo cited Southeast Asian neighbour Malaysia, whose “Malaysia, Truly Asia” campaign has stayed the same since its launch in 1999. A recent ranking by digital travel platform Asia Guide placed “Malaysia, Truly Asia” at number 1 globally. “Love the Philippines” ranked ninth, behind “Incredible India”, “Amazing Thailand” and “Wonderful Indonesia”. To prevent constant rebranding, Tulfo filed a bill during the hearing that would require the Philippines to retain an official tourism slogan for at least 15 years, according to the Manila Bulletin. “While changes in tourism campaigns may be intended to reflect evolving priorities, frequent replacements result in discontinuity, dilute public familiarity and require substantial resources for rebranding and implementation,” he said. Senate finance committee Chairman J.V. Ejercito backed the proposal, saying: “I agree to stick with one branding.” In response, Angara-Mathay agreed that a permanent slogan would be preferable. She was in favour of keeping “Love the Philippines” because it reflected the warmth, care and hospitality of the Filipino people. The department and its subsidiaries have proposed a 4 billion peso (US$63.8 million) budget for next year, according to the National Expenditure Programme. Angara-Mathay told the Daily Tribune on Sunday that the department would shift its focus from visitor arrival numbers to driving higher visitor spending, attracting capital and creating jobs. Ahead of the Asean Leaders’ Summit in November, which the Philippines is hosting as this year’s chair of the 11-member bloc, the department is prioritising improving infrastructure, gateways and air connectivity. “We want to be defined as an agency that’s proactively taking the lead in tourism readiness,” Angara-Mathay said. According to Philippine Statistics Authority data, tourism contributed 8.1 per cent to the economy in 2025, generating 2.27 trillion pesos in revenue and supporting 7.7 million jobs nationwide.

title: China’s R&D spending hits record 2.8% of GDP, beating OECD average for the first time
description: Beijing plans to double down on basic research, cutting-edge technologies and scientific talent as it strives to achieve tech self-sufficiency.
content: For the first time, China’s spending on research and development as a share of gross domestic product has surpassed the average for Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members – a trend one analyst expects to continue as Beijing seeks to strengthen technological self-reliance amid intensifying global competition. R&D expenditure exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (US$584.8 billion) in 2025, accounting for 2.8 per cent of GDP, Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun said at a press conference on Tuesday. The OECD average stood at 2.7 per cent for the year, the National Bureau of Statistics reported. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the achievement showed how China’s investment in innovation had reached a level comparable to that of developed economies. He expected the share of GDP devoted to R&D to keep rising, with a greater focus on optimising funding allocation and improving research efficiency. “We must continuously increase the proportion of investment in basic research to build a solid foundation for ‘zero-to-one’ original breakthroughs,” Wang said, while ensuring that “large-scale R&D investments translate more efficiently into industrial competitiveness”. “Zero-to-one” innovation describes an original, high-risk discovery that leads to technological breakthroughs or reshapes industries. The milestone comes as Beijing ramps up efforts to achieve technological self-sufficiency under its latest five-year plan amid intensifying competition with the United States in fields such as advanced chips and artificial intelligence. China is also facing growing global scrutiny of strategic industries such as clean energy, electric vehicles and critical minerals. Minister Yin outlined government plans to strengthen basic scientific research, calling it essential to achieving technological breakthroughs and addressing national security and other strategic priorities. Beijing would also ramp up efforts to address bottlenecks in critical sectors such as semiconductors, industrial machinery and high-end instruments, Yin added. Research into frontier technologies including AI, quantum technology, biotechnology and brain-computer interfaces would also receive greater support as China seeks an edge in emerging fields. “The 15th five-year plan period is a critical period for building China into a leading science and technology power,” Yin said. “We will ... seize the historic opportunities presented by the latest wave of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, with accelerating high-level technological self-reliance and self-strengthening while fostering new drivers of growth as our main priorities.” Technological progress would also depend on talent cultivated through education, Yin noted, pledging greater support for young researchers and a stronger focus on emerging and interdisciplinary fields. In a letter released on Tuesday, President Xi Jinping urged Sichuan University to draw on its interdisciplinary strengths in the humanities, sciences, engineering and medicine to support China’s national strategy. The Ministry of Education, meanwhile, announced plans last week to add 76,000 undergraduate places at top-tier Chinese universities between 2027 and 2030, targeting in-demand fields such as AI, semiconductors, biomedicine and new energy.

title: Mainland Chinese, Hong Kong stocks face bumpy fourth quarter as risks mount: analysts
description: Weak stimulus, Fed tightening and shifting AI sentiment may keep mainland and Hong Kong equities under pressure, analysts say.
content: Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks may face a challenging fourth quarter as investors contend with underwhelming stimulus measures from Beijing, tighter financial conditions in the US and a shift in the narrative around the artificial intelligence trade, according to analysts. The two markets were likely to consolidate through the rest of the year as investors digest the negatives before settling on a clearer direction, according to brokerages including Zheshang Securities and CCB International. CCB International, the investment banking unit of China Construction Bank, predicted that the Hang Seng Index would trade in a range between 22,500 and 26,000 over the next three months, with risks skewed to the downside. The benchmark closed the third quarter at 24,613.27. Sentiment on stocks has been deteriorating heading into the fourth quarter. Rates traders are now pricing a 47 per cent probability of a quarter-percentage-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve in October, leaving US Treasury yields at multi-year highs. At the same time, China’s growth risks undershooting the lower end of its annual target. Economists said Beijing’s latest support measures, including mortgage subsidies for homebuyers and a cut in the interest rate on a relending facility, were unlikely to bolster domestic demand. “The markets have entered a period of consolidation amid uncertainty of expectations about global rate increases, geopolitics and the shift in the AI narrative,” said Liao Jingchi, an analyst at Zheshang Securities. “They are still finding where the bottom is.” China’s CSI 300 Index fell 12 per cent in the third quarter, weighed down by a 31 per cent slump in the tech-heavy Star Market 50 gauge, its worst quarterly performance on record. The Hang Seng Index fared better, gaining 7.6 per cent, thanks to its limited exposure to AI plays. By comparison, the S&P 500 rose 2.3 per cent during the period, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 4.7 per cent and South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 19 per cent. For the equity market, the absence of a policy surprise may extend the weak market sentiment, and a year-end rally is much less likely to happen Richard Tang, Julius Baer On top of monetary tightening and inflation pressures, fiscal strains in the US and Japan, along with simmering trade tensions between China and the European Union, could also pose risks to equities in the fourth quarter, according to Cliff Zhao, strategist at CCB International. There are optimists. China Asset Management, which oversees 1.36 trillion yuan (US$202.8 billion) in assets, said the pullback in the third quarter had created room for an upside in stocks, with technology and commodity companies likely to post strong results in the coming reporting season. The firm said the CSI 300’s decline to a one-year low this week was largely a result of investors hedging risks before the National Day “golden week” holiday starting on Thursday. Low trading volumes indicated selling pressure was easing and that there could be limited scope for further declines, it added. China’s official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index returned to expansion territory in September after two months of contraction, rising to 50.1 from 49.8 a month earlier, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday. A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below that level signals shrinkage. Beijing’s move on Tuesday to offer mortgage subsidies and lower the interest rate on pledged supplementary lending – a low-cost financing tool used by policy banks to fund investment projects – failed to impress investors. The measures would have a limited impact on the economy because the subsidy programme was mainly applicable to buyers of low-priced homes in non-top-tier cities, where many residents still expected property prices to fall further, according to Lu Ting, chief China economist at Nomura Holdings. Swiss private bank Julius Baer said the mortgage subsidy programme would cover only up to 25 per cent of home transactions, offering modest relief to household cash flows but having no material impact on consumption. “For the equity market, the absence of a policy surprise may extend the weak market sentiment, and a year-end rally is much less likely to happen,” said Richard Tang, an analyst at the bank. “Within the market, we favour AI hardware and dividend stocks.”

title: Hong Kong urged to boost private housing supply as student demand jumps 45%
description: Government forecasts annual demand for non-local student housing at 2,310 flats over next decade, 45 per cent higher than last year’s estimate.
content: Hong Kong authorities are facing calls to increase the proportion of private housing in selected districts and work more closely with developers to expand accommodation for non-local students. The government forecasts annual demand for non-local student housing at 2,310 flats over the next decade, 45 per cent higher than last year’s estimate, according to the latest Long Term Housing Strategy progress report released on Monday. The Housing Bureau based the figure on an average annual increase of about 7,100 student visas between 2016-17 and 2025-26, noting that roughly 65 per cent of those students did not live in university-provided halls or hostels. The latest projection comes as five public universities in Hong Kong ranked among the top 100 in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings. Lawmaker Scott Leung Man-kwong, also a member of the Housing Authority, said on Wednesday that the number of non-local students would inevitably rise as Hong Kong positioned itself as a premier destination for tertiary education. “When universities cannot provide sufficient accommodation, demand will shift to the private market – the government must devise a careful plan,” he told a radio programme. Leung noted that districts such as Western, Sha Tin, Tai Po, Yuen Long and Tuen Mun – all near universities – were already under pressure from rising rents. Other transport hubs with strong connectivity to those campuses, such as Olympic Station, are also popular among those students. “As students enter the rental market in traditional residential districts, limited supply may lead to competition with local residents and drive up rents – a trend that is already under way,” Leung warned. To avoid overwhelming certain neighbourhoods, he suggested universities partner with property agents to recommend suitable, reasonably priced flats in alternative locations with convenient transport links, thereby spreading demand across different areas. Under the current Long Term Housing Strategy, the overall public-to-private housing supply ratio stands at 7:3. Leung proposed raising the private proportion in selected districts. “Some communities have relatively less public housing, such as Pak Shek Kok … I believe the government could run a pilot to increase private housing supply there, while maintaining the overall ratio for the rest of Hong Kong,” Leung said. He said he believed that this approach could balance prioritising lower-income housing needs with responding to private-market demand, without triggering rapid price increases. Professor Joshua Mok Ka-ho, president of the Hang Seng University of Hong Kong, said land shortage remained the biggest challenge as the city developed into an education hub, whether for accommodation or teaching facilities. “Universities do not have the resources to build so many hostels on our own and must rely heavily on the market,” he said. “The government could further relax policies to incentivise developers to participate in developing a university town, including student accommodation.” Mok added that his institution was working with a hotel group and a developer to provide extra beds at a hotel in Sha Tin and a stand-alone building in Ngau Tau Kok. He said such accommodation also played an important role in helping non-local students adapt to life in Hong Kong. “The overall strategic direction of ‘Study in Hong Kong’ is very beneficial for the city. However, we must proceed with caution,” he said. “If we recruit students without adequate supporting infrastructure, including hostels, campus facilities and teaching staff, that will undermine the student experience and ultimately do more harm than good.” Last year, the city’s leader announced a plan to raise the cap on non-local students at public universities to 50 per cent from the 2026-27 academic year, followed by measures to relax rules for converting commercial buildings and hotels into student hostels under the “Hostel in the City” scheme. As of June, authorities had received 40 eligible applications, with the projects expected to provide 9,100 student beds.

title: Former CSRC chairman Yi Huiman formally prosecuted for taking ‘especially large’ bribes
description: Prosecution comes as Beijing intensifies an anti-corruption campaign in the financial sector.
content: Yi Huiman, the former chairman of China’s securities regulator, has been formally prosecuted for allegedly accepting “especially large” bribes, as Beijing presses ahead with a sweeping anti-corruption campaign in the financial sector. Prosecutors in the eastern city of Qingdao recently filed a case against Yi with the Qingdao Intermediate People’s Court after an investigation by the National Commission of Supervision, state-owned Xinhua News Agency said on Wednesday. Yi allegedly used his positions at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), as well as influence derived from those roles, to seek benefits for others and illegally accepted an “especially large amount of property”, prosecutors said. The statement did not disclose the value of the alleged bribes, or provide details about the beneficiaries. Yi, 61, spent most of his career at ICBC, China’s largest commercial lender by assets, rising through the ranks to become its president in 2013 and chairman in 2016. He was appointed chairman of the CSRC in January 2019 and headed the watchdog until February 2024, overseeing a period of capital-market reforms including the introduction and expansion of a registration-based system for initial public offerings. China’s top anti-corruption watchdog placed Yi under investigation in September last year for suspected “serious violations of discipline and law”. He was expelled from the Communist Party and removed from public office in April. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection said at the time that he had abandoned his regulatory responsibilities and failed to properly perform his duties in regulatory enforcement. It also accused him of abusing his positions to help others secure promotions, stock-listing approvals and bank loans in return for bribes, as well as accepting gifts and money in violation of party rules. His prosecution comes as Beijing’s years-long anti-corruption campaign increasingly turns its attention to the financial sector, with policymakers seeking to strengthen oversight of banks, brokerages and capital markets. Yi is not the only former senior CSRC official who played a prominent role in China’s capital-market reforms to come under scrutiny. In July, former CSRC vice-chairman Fang Xinghai, seen as a reform-minded official who served as a key liaison between regulators and foreign investors, was also placed under investigation for suspected serious violations of discipline and law. The broader crackdown has coincided with tighter scrutiny of Chinese wealth held overseas. Beijing introduced tax rules in July requiring mainland residents to report and pay individual income tax on certain assets and income held through offshore trusts, while authorities have also stepped up enforcement involving returns from offshore insurance policies. Chinese lawmakers last month also began reviewing a cross-border anti-corruption bill aimed at strengthening authorities’ ability to track and recover illicit assets held overseas.

title: US social media users urge Koreans to unmask Cornell sexual assault suspect Winston Lee
description: The online hunt for information about Lee’s education and military service intensifies across borders.
content: The sprawling online hunt for information about Winston Lee, a Korean student who is among seven defendants in a Cornell University sexual assault lawsuit, is increasingly crossing borders, with English-speaking social media users calling on their Korean counterparts to help uncover more information about him. As the “Cornell 7” case continues to draw intense attention across the United States, Lee has become the subject of a parallel search focused on his Korean identity and background.
