Publicly available information about him remains limited compared with the volume of material circulating about some of the other defendants. Some English-language users have begun openly looking to Koreans to take the search further. “OK Korean people, we’re counting on you to track one of your own people down,” one user said. “Leaving it up to the knetz,” wrote another, using shorthand for Korean netizens. Other comments described Korean internet users as “ruthless hunters” and said they “know how to punish their own”. The search has also spread to Korean and Korean-American online communities, where users are attempting to identify Lee’s Korean name and piece together information about his education, military service and whereabouts. A social media user celebrated after another posted what was purported to be Lee’s Korean name, writing, “Hey, you got his Korean name!” The name has not been independently verified. Online users have linked Lee to Seoul Foreign School and UWC Atlantic in Wales, while a LinkedIn profile attributed to him has listed service in the Republic of Korea Army. Cornell’s directory currently lists Lee as a student, while social media users have claimed he has returned to campus and is attending classes. The search comes amid a broader crowdsourced effort to uncover information about all seven defendants, whose names, photographs, workplaces and personal histories have spread widely across social media. A dedicated website has also emerged publicising information about the group. Lee’s ties to South Korea, however, have given the online hunt an unusual international dimension, with users reaching across languages and borders for information that has proved difficult to uncover in the US. The expanding search has also led to the rapid circulation of unverified claims about Lee’s family and identity. This story was first published by The Korea Times

title: Chinese firms trail global peers on profits, but AI power boom offers bright spot: Natixis
description: China’s corporate health continues to lag global rivals, but power surplus has become a key advantage in AI race, bank says.
content: China’s corporate sector remains considerably weaker than it was before the Covid-19 pandemic, but the country is emerging as a key beneficiary of the global artificial intelligence boom thanks to its ample power capacity, according to a Natixis survey of thousands of firms and a separate research report. Profit margins at Chinese firms had stabilised at about 4.5 per cent for the first half of 2026, but remained well below the nearly 9 per cent recorded by their global peers, according to the French bank’s latest China corporate monitor presented on Tuesday. Returns on capital at Chinese firms hovered at around 6 per cent in the same period, compared with more than 11 per cent globally, the report said. The findings were based on a comparison of about 2,300 Chinese firms and 9,000 overseas counterparts. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at Natixis, highlighted what she described as the “duality of the Chinese economy”, arguing that it extended well beyond macroeconomic data. “The duality is more complex than just exporting and not consuming,” Garcia Herrero said. “It’s really entrenched in China’s corporate governance.” The divide was evident in the differing fortunes of central state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and private firms, economists said. The interest burden for central SOEs was falling faster than for private firms, reaching 2.2 per cent and 3.2 per cent, respectively, giving state firms a borrowing advantage. Yet private firms remained more profitable. “It’s a tale of two cities: stagnant SOEs are benefiting from the system, while private companies are trying to survive in this system and exporting their way out,” Garcia-Herrero said. Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis, said Chinese firms continued to face challenges in revenue generation and capital returns. However, “the debt burden of Chinese firms has reduced a lot, which is a positive sign”, he added. Despite these comparative weaknesses, Natixis identified energy capacity as a major area of strength for China in the AI era. “China can easily power AI data centres,” said Natixis economist Haoxin Mu. Natixis estimated that AI data centres would account for only about 5 per cent of China’s annual increment in power consumption, compared with 48 per cent in the United States, 28 per cent in Europe, and 66 per cent in Japan. That meant nearly half of the additional energy needed to meet future demand growth in the US could be absorbed by AI data centres. “This would crowd out other sectors that need energy,” Mu said. By contrast, China had the “power capability to continue to build data centres”, Garcia-Herrero said. China’s exports of power equipment used in AI data centres had soared in recent years, Mu said, adding that the segment had become a “key engine for China’s export growth”. Barring international pushback, Garcia-Herrero said any Chinese company doing electrical equipment for data centres would do well.

title: There’s been buzz around Carney for a prize long coveted by Trump
description: Canadian prime minister’s rising global profile fuels speculation for two annual awards.
content: Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to US President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine’s Person of the Year. Carney briefly became the favourite Monday for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Kalshi, a US-based prediction market, when traders on the exchange put his chances at 14 per cent. His odds later fell, illustrating the highly speculative nature of the wagering. There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee’s secret shortlist for the prize that will be announced October 9 in Oslo, Norway. But the buzz about the Canadian leader possibly winning the esteemed peace prize reflects the message that has raised his profile: Middle powers should band together to defend sovereignty as great powers increasingly use economic and military leverage. Whether that position resonates with the Nobel Committee is impossible to know. One thing is certain, though: the Nobel and Time’s annual award happen to be two honours Trump covets. Carney and Trump are locked in an escalating trade war, with 50 per cent US tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods and Canadian retaliation. Trump also has told Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs. Trump, who has twice been Time’s Person of the Year, has repeatedly complained about not receiving the Nobel, saying in July that he “should have won that award more than anybody”. “President Trump would be furious, of course,” said Daniel Beland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. “If this ever happens, I would love to be a fly on the wall of the Oval Office to see the president’s face when he learns about it.” Trump already possesses a Nobel medal, just not one awarded to him. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel laureate, presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Trump accepted it, while the Nobel Committee stressed the prize itself remains hers. “Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel,” said Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. “If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are.” Time already named Carney one of its 100 most influential people of 2026 and specifically noted his popularity increased as he stood up to Trump. On Tuesday, Carney was the second choice on major prediction markets for Time’s Person of the Year, behind New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The winner will be announced December 10. Time has described Trump’s cumulative impact as helping create a “new global order” increasingly shaped “not by systems or institutions, but by the will of a single man”. Carney’s answer has been to urge middle powers to band together rather than bend one by one. New York University professor Scott Galloway said Carney has it in the bag and called him “the leader that Europe’s been looking for for the last 20 years”. “I believe, hands down, Time’s Person of the Year has already been decided and it’s going to be Mark Carney,” Galloway said. On Galloway’s podcast, journalist Fareed Zakaria said Carney is winning admiration abroad and has given countries facing a less predictable United States “a kind of language and a path” to build new alliances rather than simply bend to Washington. Carney’s standing abroad took off in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where he declared the old international order was not coming back and urged middle powers to work together rather than wait for its restoration. His speech came as European leaders were confronting Trump’s push to acquire Greenland and tariff threats. “We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition,” Carney said in his speech, which received a standing ovation. Carney has since tried to put the argument for a new global order into practice, pushing Canada closer to Europe and seeking new partners in Asia as Trump’s tariffs fractured the old Canada-US relationship. European lawmakers gave Carney another standing ovation this month as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member. “Carney’s international profile has been driven by his standing up to Trump, unlike the Europeans and Asians who rushed to make deals with him,” Wiseman said. “Trump’s pressure on Canada has helped elevate Carney in the eyes of the world.”

title: How Japanese beef specialist Tsutomu Ito brings the finest Wagyu to Hong Kong
description: The owner of Gyu+Bar by Miyoshi in Causeway Bay, chef Tsutomu Ito talks about his dedication to serving the best Wagyu in the city.
content: Tucked away in an alley in Kyoto’s Gion district, Niku no Takumi Miyoshi – popularly called Nikushi no Miyoshi – is easy to miss. This small, unassuming establishment, opened by Tsutomu Ito is widely celebrated as a premier Wagyu destination, earning Michelin acclaim and legendary status among international gourmands. After establishing Miyoshi as a premier culinary location in Japan, Ito also opened q+M, a members-only French space in Kyoto specialising in Wagyu, and Kanegura, a more casual hotpot restaurant. The chef recently made his international debut by bringing Gyu+Bar by Miyoshi to Hong Kong. Located in Lee Garden One, in the city’s Causeway Bay neighbourhood, the new venue merges his Kyoto Wagyu techniques with Japanese-French wood-fired brasserie dining, serving Wagyu across sashimi, consommé, sushi, shabu-shabu and wood-fired preparations. What may surprise guests is that Ito is entirely self-taught. The Kyoto-born chef has never attended culinary school. In fact, he majored in business administration and his journey to the pinnacle of Japanese beef cuisine began not in a kitchen, but behind a bar. During university, he spent most of his days working part time as a bartender at an izakaya in Kyoto. His mother also ran a bar and lounge in Gion, known for its geisha culture. “I got so hooked that I thought about making [bartending] my career,” says Ito, 50. “I just loved creating things and building flavours.” Behind that bar, Ito crossed paths with an old friend who would alter the course of his life. “He started working at a meat-processing plant, and he let me taste freshly slaughtered beef for the first time,” Ito says. “Until then, my concept of beef was that you had to age it, taking time to draw out the umami. But when I tried this incredibly fresh meat, I was so shocked. The texture was different. The aroma was different. The sweetness was different. I had to figure out what it was.” In 2004, Ito took over his mother’s bar, making light renovations to turn it into a casual dining spot. The same restaurant that would later be celebrated by food critics as one of Japan’s best restaurants for Wagyu. The setting could not have been more personal – the building was his childhood home, where he was born and raised – and the craft he was about to pursue could not have been more foreign. Ito knew nothing about butchery. He launched the business with a partner: Ito handled the cooking, while the partner took charge of sourcing, going to the slaughterhouse each morning and returning with freshly slaughtered meat. “Every day, I would eat it and research, eat it and try a different technique, eat and try again, eat and try again,” Ito says. “How can I remove the smell? How can I make it easier to eat?” He bought books and studied them, but they only showed standard cuts that bore little resemblance to the whole carcasses arriving at his door. Ito admits that most of his knowledge was gleaned from trial and error – and a lot of failures. He also learned from the veteran butchers and producers he befriended along the way. In Japan, offal rights and high-grade meat rights are usually separated, meaning premium beef typically goes to auction through brokers. Bypassing the auction to buy directly from farmers is rare – and something Ito has only been able to do in the past five or six years. “Bypassing the auction allows me to give direct feedback to the farmer,” he says. “‘I want you to raise this one a little longer,’ or ‘I don’t need this much marbling.’ Being able to have those conversations and achieve my exact ideal meat is a recent development.” Today, he has established relationships with farmers across Japan, including in Kyoto and Kobe; his primary supplier, however, is Okazaki Farm in Shiga prefecture, known for its Omi Wagyu. What sets the farm apart is its approach to raising cattle. Wagyu are famously high-maintenance, and a stress-free environment is not a matter of indulgence but biological necessity – one that directly determines the quality of the final cut. When a cow experiences stress, it releases cortisol, which can lead to tough, dry meat and inhibit the web of marbling that Wagyu is famed for. Normally, farmers put three cows in one pen. But since Ito only uses virgin female cows for their flavour and lean cut structure, grouping them can lead to bullying. At Okazaki Farm, they keep only one cow per pen. In addition, they don’t hand over pre-mixed dry feed, instead boiling millet and barnyard grass, mixing it with straw, and feeding the cows this “cooked food”, which Ito says is much easier on the stomach and organs. Instead of rushing to fatten them up in 30 months, they raise them slowly for 40 to 50 months. Ito can detect flavour changes immediately. “One time, I noticed that the taste of the meat changed, and the farmer told me they changed the feed,” he says with a laugh. “If something is different, I always tell them, and we figure out together exactly what changed.” The butchers who supplied Ito’s meat also taught him their rustic traditions. They had their own traditional ways of cooking offal – for lunch, they would layer hard-to-cook vegetables at the bottom of a pot without adding water, relying on the meat’s moisture, and pile quick-cooking offal on top. It was the butcher’s equivalent of a fisherman’s stew. “Put this offal in boiled tofu, it’s delicious,” they would tell him. Ito took these traditional techniques and spent years refining them into the dishes that now appear on his menu, particularly integrating their specific ways of preparing the internal organs and entrails, a food Ito previously disliked with a passion. “Japanese people love liver sashimi, but I actually hated it,” he says. “It smelled so bad. I couldn’t understand how everyone else ate it. The standard way was to dip it heavily in sesame oil to mask the smell.” But when he looked at the incredibly fresh Wagyu liver delivered one morning, he decided to study it. People used to soak liver in milk to remove the smell, but Ito found that gently washing it with running water and pressing it in a certain way drained the blood perfectly. He even tried flushing water directly through the veins and taught himself to cut, too, endlessly experimenting with different angles. “Figuring out: if I cut it this way, the texture improves; if I cut it that way, the sweetness stands out,” he says. “That was the biggest shock. A food I absolutely despised became delicious to me.” Ito’s restless curiosity soon found a new outlet: applying traditional washoku – preserving and fermenting – techniques directly to beef. One of his signature dishes utilises kombujime, an Edo-period technique where delicate white fish is cured by sandwiching fillets between sheets of rehydrated kombu (kelp). Ito applies this to ultra-fresh black Wagyu ox tongue by removing blood vessels before curing the slices in kelp. The kelp absorbs surface moisture, firming the protein and transforming the tongue into a velvety, sashimi-like texture while removing gamey notes, negating the need for heavy sauces. Another innovation is dashi-pulled tenderloin: rather than searing or grilling lean cuts like fillet, he briefly immerses the beef in a gently simmering dashi made from top-grade kombu and katsuobushi (dried bonito shavings). The gentle heat raises the fat to its ideal melting temperature without burning or charring, while the savoury, marine-rich broth seasons the exterior and wraps the fat in a clean, light layer. Beyond these techniques, Ito applies washoku principles throughout his kitchen. Custom knives are engineered to slice through individual muscle groups for maximum tenderness. Beef bones and lean cuts are simmered into clear consommés instead of relying on fish or kelp broths. Most importantly, Wagyu is treated as a seasonal component, paired with distinctly Japanese markers – matsutake in autumn, bamboo shoots in spring, fresh wasabi and ponzu – ensuring his meat courses carry the same harmony as the finest kaiseki. “What I value most is to always ‘doubt’,” Ito says. “Even when I’ve decided this is the right and most delicious way, I always question: ‘Is this really it? Isn’t there a way to make it even better?’” Gyu+Bar by Miyoshi, Shop 401 & 404, 4/F, Lee Garden One, 33 Hysan Avenue, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong.

title: 6 table tennis phrases to help you keep your eye on the ball
description: These idioms and nouns will help you learn more about the sport and tap into its exciting, fast-paced atmosphere.
content:
With the World Table Tennis (WTT) Grand Smash China in full swing, we are sure to see a lot of fiery action on the tables.
Grand Smashes are the biggest WTT events, and the previous three this year were held in Singapore, the United States and Sweden. Winners of both singles and doubles earn 2,000 ranking points – a massive boost for any player’s standing.
Take a break from your screens and textbooks and experience the electric atmosphere of table tennis! These English idioms and nouns can help you out.
Meaning: to stay focused on the task or goal at hand Example: In a fast rally, you have to keep your eye on the ball, literally and mentally.
Meaning: to remain alert, ready to move quickly in any direction Example: Our coach told the team to stay on our toes during the final minutes of the match.
Meaning: to reach your best level of performance Example: After losing the first game, he finally hit his stride in the second.
Meaning: to make a decision or go for a winning shot Example: The player waited too long to pull the trigger on the play, missing his chance.
Meaning: a defensive, soft return shot with backspin, usually used to keep the ball low and short over the net Example: She used a deep push to force her opponent into a misstep.
Meaning: a powerful topspin shot where the player brushes the ball upwards and forwards to create heavy spin Example: Wang Chuqin’s forehand loop is almost impossible to block.

title: HSBC unveils RedCoin as name of Hong Kong stablecoin for 3.3 million PayMe users
description: A survey by the lender shows that 74 per cent of customers know at least one use case, but there are also misunderstandings.
content: HSBC on Wednesday named its stablecoin offering HSBC RedCoin, paving the way for Hong Kong’s biggest lender to make the coin available to the more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe app for money transfers, shopping and dining. When launched before the end of the year, the stablecoin would be offered only through PayMe and HSBC’s Hong Kong mobile banking app, HSBC said. The bank said it was optimistic about retail usage of HSBC RedCoin, as 74 per cent of respondents to a survey of more than 1,000 customers recognised at least one use case for stablecoins. The most recognised case, chosen by 57 per cent of respondents, was stablecoins being used for digital asset trading and tokenised investments, the survey showed. Person-to-person money transfers ranked second at 53 per cent, while cross-border remittances and merchant payments each stood at 52 per cent. The survey also showed that 60 per cent of customers could correctly define a stablecoin – a digital asset backed by a stable reference asset, often a fiat currency. However, there were also misunderstandings, as 26 per cent assumed stablecoins were government-issued. In fact, they are issued by entities authorised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, which in April issued licences to a Standard Chartered-led consortium and HSBC. About 10 per cent of consumers said stablecoins would pay interest, but that is not allowed in Hong Kong’s regulatory framework, HSBC said. “This survey confirms the strong interest among Hongkongers in embracing digital assets,” said Maggie Ng, CEO of HSBC Hong Kong. “HSBC RedCoin isn’t a leap into the unknown, but is a natural next step.” She added that incorporating the bank’s corporate colour into the name reflected its heritage. HSBC, which has operated in Hong Kong since 1865, has 7 million customers in the city and is the largest of the three note-issuing banks. “Launching our coin is just the beginning,” Ng said. “Our goal is to support Hong Kong’s financial innovation, underpinned by the security, trust and simplicity that define HSBC.” HSBC will roll out the stablecoin in phases, starting with everyday use cases such as person-to-person and person-to-merchant payments. The bank earlier said the stablecoin would be accessible through its mobile payment app, PayMe. In the second stage, the bank will expand the stablecoin’s use into wholesale and corporate banking applications. The lender did not give a timeline for these phases but said it would launch a comprehensive education series, with a focus on scam prevention and how to redeem the stablecoin.

title: Slow is beautiful: China launches war against AI drama, goes beyond algorithms
description: Rapid expansion in production has intensified concerns over copyright and the mounting pressure on human creators.
content: China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI. Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration. “Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content. AI has rapidly expanded the scale and efficiency of microdrama production in China while intensifying concerns over copyright and the mounting pressure on human creators. Wang’s remarks, made at a press conference on September 17, follow a proliferation of formulaic and derivative content as producers race to churn out more dramas in pursuit of hits and profits. The scale of the shift is striking. Around 430,000 microdramas were released in China in the first eight months of 2026 – as much as 13 times the figure for the whole of last year – with AI dramas accounting for more than 90 per cent of new releases, Wang said. According to Wang, the regulator will step up its initiative to promote and distribute high-quality microdramas, guiding platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas while providing financial support so that quality productions can find audiences and generate returns. Microdramas or duanju, meaning short or mini dramas, have exploded in popularity in China in recent years. Built for mobile screens and short attention spans, the fast-paced, scripted and often melodramatic shows are divided into dozens of episodes, usually in a vertical format, with each lasting just a few minutes. AI is moving beyond a supporting tool and into almost every stage of production – from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, and onwards to post-production – upending an industry that supports more than 2 million jobs nationwide. The change has spawned a new format known as AI microdramas – AI-generated animation and live action-style dramas featuring lifelike digital characters that reduce the need for conventional filming. Companies can now churn out AI-generated content at a pace that was previously impossible, lowering production costs and technical barriers while allowing producers to test more titles in the hope of finding hits. Johnny Chan, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, said microdrama platforms created a self-reinforcing cycle: the more you watch, the better the algorithm learns what keeps you hooked. Creators keep refining the cliffhangers and paywalls that work, while the platforms invest more money to make the experience even stickier, he wrote in a paper published in August by the journal Systems Research and Behavioural Science. Chan wrote that while people would usually get bored eventually by the formula, the ability of AI to rapidly generate endless fresh stories and variations meant the natural “boredom brake” might never fully kick in, causing viewers to keep scrolling for longer. According to data from the China Netcasting Services Association, more than 275,000 AI microdramas were released online in the first half of 2026, an average of about 1,500 each day. The explosion in numbers has created a broader regulatory challenge for Chinese authorities: how to encourage this form of cultural production while preventing speed, scale and platform-driven consumption from coming at the expense of quality, originality and rights. The expanded use of the technology has given rise to various types of regulatory abuse, including content plagiarism and repackaging, as well as AI face-swapping and voice cloning, along with copyright infringement involving online literature. Many high-profile actors and the general public alike have accused AI microdrama producers of using their likenesses without consent. The speed at which AI is reshaping the industry has also exposed a growing gap between production capacity and the quality and originality of what gets made. In the first half of 2026, only 0.48 per cent of new AI microdramas released on the social media platform Douyin surpassed 100 million views, according to industry data provider DataEye. Lydia Chen, a 30-year-old AI microdrama writer and director producing live action-style dramas for overseas audiences, said the industry’s rush for hits had made copying almost routine. Platforms and production companies often copied each other’s hits and were used to taking dramas that had already gone viral in China, tweaking the plot and transplanting the story to a foreign setting, she said. For example, a Chinese tale of a ba zong – internet slang for a bossy president or a powerful, domineering businessman – and a female lead from the countryside can be repackaged as a New York billionaire falling for a woman from rural America. “You can see the productions becoming increasingly like internet products,” said Chen, who worries that as real-world filming declines, the craft itself will stagnate while AI models will have fewer new examples of real filmmaking to learn from. “If everyone keeps copying past hits, where will the new ideas of the future come from?” Chen also noted that some storylines adapted for overseas audiences reproduced traditional and conservative Chinese cultural attitudes towards gender, relationships and family – as they catered to the tastes of the mass-market microdrama audience. She pointed to the plotline of a “bossy president” falling for a rural woman whose virginity is portrayed as part of her appeal, along with plots idealising women as stay-at-home mothers with multiple children. “Sometimes I wonder whether this is really the kind of culture we should be exporting,” she said. “To me, some of these ideas feel quite outdated.” Beijing has responded to the challenges by tightening oversight of both the content and the systems through which it reaches audiences. The National Radio and Television Administration launched a two-month campaign in June targeting “harmful, lowbrow and pirated” microdrama content. The campaign focused on material harmful to children as well as sexually suggestive scenes, wealth-flaunting, “distorted” views on marriage and relationships, along with superstitions, violent revenge, sensationalist titles and copyright violations. Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to … make money. Shiliu, microdrama director Wang told the press conference that since the beginning of the year, regulators had removed 68,000 microdramas that violated the rules and guided platforms to punish more than 1,200 accounts. More than 90 per cent of the problematic content involved AI dramas, he said. The government has also introduced rules specifically addressing the use of AI in production. The microdrama development and management measures, which took effect on September 1, require clear labelling for every episode of AI-generated microdramas, along with “respect for original works, copyright protection, fair competition and more orderly industry development”. Platforms must also regularly review and assess their recommendation algorithms, models and data, give priority to high-quality microdramas and prohibit suggestions that are designed to encourage user indulgence or excessive consumption. The pressure is also being felt by people working inside the industry, with microdrama actors facing a harsh reality. Since the beginning of the year, many have said they are struggling to find roles, with some actors taking on part-time work as AI-generated dramas increasingly replace live-action productions. For those still working in AI microdrama production, greater efficiency has not necessarily meant an easier workload. Shiliu, a 28-year-old AI microdrama director who joined the industry 2 ½ years ago, said his team was expected to complete five dramas a month, each running for 50 to 70 episodes. As the team shrank, he found himself taking on multiple roles and working 14 to 16 hours a day, said Shiliu, who asked not to be identified by his real name. “Because AI is so convenient, bosses only focus on efficiency,” he added. “Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to [fulfil demand] and make money.” The workload eventually took its toll, prompting him to quit the industry. The state-run Economic Daily urged the industry last month to move away from scale-driven growth in favour of higher quality, more original and professionally produced content. Familiar formulas were being repeatedly recycled while a flood of lookalike content competed for limited attention, the paper said in an article published on August 13. “Promotion and computing costs rise, leaving producers caught in a cycle of producing more without earning more,” it noted. “Audiences’ willingness to pay is further eroded while the industry’s reputation is bound to suffer.” DataEye estimates that the overseas market for Chinese microdramas will exceed US$6 billion in 2026, with AI-generated animated and live-action style dramas accounting for more than US$4 billion. The netcasting services association said that China’s AI microdrama industry was reaching a turning point, shifting from rapid, loosely regulated expansion towards more disciplined and quality-driven growth. In Chen’s view, as AI lowers the technical barriers to content creation and more people without a professional background are able to turn their ideas into original works, individually created non-formulaic projects will have a better chance of standing out. “We must strike a balance between encouraging innovation and upholding safeguards,” Wang said. “Ultimately, AI is a tool, while people remain the creators. The faster AI dramas develop, the more important it is to ensure content quality.”

title: Pentagon picks Boeing to build new carrier fighter jet to replace F/A-18
description: Next-generation aircraft will replace Super Hornets and fly alongside F-35s starting in 2030s.
content: The Pentagon has chosen Boeing to build the US Navy’s next-generation fighter jets in a contract valued at US$20 billion, officials announced Tuesday. The contract is to produce F/A-XX aircraft or “strike fighters” under the “Next Generation Air Dominance Program,” a Pentagon statement said, adding that the new jets would replace the legacy Super Hornets fleet beginning in the 2030s. The announcement marks the second time Boeing has been selected by the Pentagon during the second Trump administration for a sixth-generation weapons system. In March 2025, Trump announced the US Air Force chose the storied aerospace giant to build a new stealth fighter. “Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly. We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programmes,” said Steve Parker, head of Boeing Defence, Space & Security. “The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities,” said Pentagon undersecretary Michael Duffey. “We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities.” Boeing said construction was continuing at its “secure manufacturing” facility in St Louis, which the company said is the largest of its kind in the United States. “The technical and programmatic details of F/A-XX remain classified under US national security and export laws,” it said. Boeing was competing for the contract with Northrop Grumman. “For F/A-XX, Northrop Grumman offered a highly survivable, digitally advanced sixth-generation fighter to the US Navy,” Northrop said Tuesday. “We look forward to receiving additional information about their selection.” At a May 2026 hearing, Admiral Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, told a US Senate panel that the next-generation system needed to “extend the reach, survivability and lethality” expected to work with unmanned systems. “Failure to field next-generation carrier aviation capability on schedule will introduce risk to air superiority, strike reach and the long-term viability of carrier-based operations in contested environments,” Caudle said. Winning the massive contract marks a boost for Boeing, which has struggled to rebuild its reputation following two deadly crashes in 2018 and 2019 involving its 737 Max commercial jets, and a near-catastrophic 2024 Alaska Airlines flight in which a fuselage panel blew out mid-air. Several subsequent problems combined to help send the company into a multi-year slump. Boeing has staked its recovery in large part on Max production growth, and it has been heading towards certification of the new 737 Max 10, the largest version of the jet. But US air safety regulators recently delayed certification until they could determine that a new glitch in the plane’s automated navigation software poses no safety risk. The US Navy contract follows a Monday announcement by Nasa that the US space agency was planning new missions using Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, the first since the vessel’s botched test flight left two astronauts stranded for months at the International Space Station.

title: Letters | Why Lebanon is crucial to Iran’s negotiations with the US
description: Readers discuss a development in the conflict in the Middle East, Hong Kong golfers’ success, and the death of Chinese musician.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Recently, Iran announced seven conditions for restarting negotiations with the United States. As it did in the failed memorandum of understanding signed earlier, Iran has made ending the conflict in Lebanon the first condition. Iran is no longer treating Lebanon only as a battlefield against Israel. By making Lebanon central to its negotiations, Tehran has transformed it into diplomatic leverage. Both Iran and Israel strategically converge in viewing Lebanon through the lens of a “forward-defence strategy”, intercepting threats away from the borders. Southern Lebanon should be seen in this context, with the Iran-backed non-state actor Hezbollah acting as a key part of Tehran’s broader deterrence strategy by providing strategic depth against Israel. Israel has severely weakened Hezbollah, with the assassination of secretary general Hassan Nasrallah and senior leaders being neutralised. But Israel’s primary objective is to completely disband the group from Lebanon’s soil. US President Trump seemed aligned with Israel on this but in June warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cease strikes on Beirut. He backed an agreement with the Lebanese government to take responsibility for disarming Hezbollah. The first reason Iran has linked Lebanon to the peace process is apparently to directly advance its interests by providing Tehran with diplomatic leverage in the negotiations. Iran indicates that any attack on Lebanon targeting Hezbollah could trigger escalation in the conflict. Prolonged conflict would raise the military and economic costs for Washington and its allies, thereby strengthening Iran’s bargaining position. The second reason is that it provides an opportunity for Hezbollah to recover from its setbacks. Raz Zimmt, director of the Iran research programme at the Institute of National Security Studies, has noted that Iran has been directly involved in managing Hezbollah’s affairs through the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and that Tehran has sought to renew weapons and funding supply routes through Syria. Lebanon is crucial to Tehran advancing its diplomatic interests and also reinstating Hezbollah as a stronger organisation that serves as Iran’s principal instrument of deterrence. M.P. Yuvaraj, Chennai, India Hong Kong’s golfers have come a long way I was delighted to learn that the Hong Kong amateur golf team won the Putra Cup earlier this month. My congratulations to the team’s members: Jeffrey Shen, Kim Joon-ho, William Tang and Timothy Chan. A wonderful achievement. Sixty-five years ago in 1961, my late father Bill Leighton, together with his team members Hugh Staunton, Alan Sutcliffe and Jock Mackie, won the inaugural Southeast Asian Amateur Team Golf Championship in Malaysia. They were all great amateur golfers and were members of what was then called the Royal Hong Kong Golf Club. With the exception of Jock Mackie, they all became club captains over the following 20 or so years. All of them were passionate about golf as a sport. They were equally passionate about their love for Hong Kong. I remember the day the team flew to Malaysia for the tournament well. I was nine years old at the time and at Kai Tak airport watching the team board their plane. It was an unforgettable day and so exciting. The Hong Kong team of 1961 would, if alive today, be so proud to see the progress golf has made as a sport in the region. I’m sure they would welcome the opportunity I’ve been given to congratulate the Hong Kong team on their magnificent win at Fanling. Iain Leighton, Hampshire, United Kingdom Liu Huan’s journey can inspire young people Liu Huan’s passing at the age of 63 silences a voice that charted modern China’s cultural trajectory. From the 1990 Beijing Asian Games to the 2008 Olympics, his music formed the soundtrack of a nation stepping onto the world stage. Like China’s own reform journey – crossing the river by feeling the stones, without an advance script – this untrained French major pioneered an original path for Chinese pop through television landmarks and films like The Wandering Earth 2. For young people navigating an era of profound uncertainty, his life is a quiet reassurance: enduring cultural confidence is built through trial, resilience and unwritten possibilities. Lucia Luo and Simon Wang, Kowloon Tong

title: Malaysia’s Mahathir in hospital for observation a day after wife’s death
description: The former prime minister’s office says it is waiting for the diagnosis from his doctors.
content: Malaysia’s two-time prime minister Mahathir Mohamad has been admitted to hospital for observation, his office confirmed on Wednesday, in the latest health scare involving the 101-year-old. Mahathir was admitted to the National Heart Institute (IJN) on Tuesday night, barely a day after his wife of 70 years, Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, died at the same hospital. It is unclear why the former leader was admitted. Sufi Yusoff, Mahathir’s long-time aide, told reporters that they were awaiting diagnosis by his doctors. “He was admitted to IJN for observation. The past two days have been quite stressful for Tun M, but for now, he is OK and there is no cause for concern,” Mahathir’s son Mokhzani told state news agency Bernama on Wednesday. Mahathir has had a series of hospitalisations in recent years, triggering public concern over his deteriorating health. In January, he was warded for three weeks after fracturing his right hip in a fall at his home, effectively consigning him to a wheelchair after his doctors ruled out surgery due to his age. Just a few months prior, he was admitted to the heart institute for fatigue after attending a picnic to celebrate his 100th birthday in July. In October 2024, he was warded for two weeks after contracting a lung infection. Mahathir has had a history of heart problems. He underwent two bypass surgeries in 1989 and 2007. The former leader came back into the spotlight this week, as condolences poured in from Malaysians and regional leaders over the sudden loss of his wife. In a short video posted on his social media accounts, Mahathir was seen sharing his disbelief over her death when speaking with Pahang ruler Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah. “I did not expect to lose her today,” he said. A lifelong Malay nationalist, Mahathir is Southeast Asia’s last surviving strongman of his era. In his first term as prime minister from 1981 to 2003, he reshaped Malaysia’s agrarian economy into one of the region’s industrial juggernauts with sprawling highway networks and a burgeoning manufacturing sector feeding the country’s all-important exports. Mahathir was also credited with saving the country from falling into deep debt when he refused to take a loan from the International Monetary Fund at the height of the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s, opting instead to peg the ringgit currency to the US dollar to stabilise the economy. But he was also famously intolerant of dissent. In his early years as prime minister, over 100 opposition politicians, activists and journalists were detained under Ops Lalang that targeted voices critical of his administration. Malaysia made international headlines towards the end of his first term, when he saw to the jailing of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim – then his deputy – on charges of corruption and sodomy after the pair had fallen out.

title: US Supreme Court lets Trump resume deportations to third countries
description: Trump administration granted emergency request to overturn a lower court ban on rapid expulsions.
content: The US Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump’s administration continue swiftly deporting people to countries other than their own for now, while the justices consider whether the policy is legal. The apparent 6-3 order temporarily lifts lower court requirements for migrants to get a chance to object before being sent to countries to which they have no ties. The Supreme Court will hear arguments in December. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson would have kept the lower court order in place. The Trump administration said last week the lower court order forced the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying about 70 people bound for three countries. The conservative majority has sided with the administration before on the core Trump administration policy, allowing deportation flights to temporarily continue last year. The court said it would consider several questions: whether the policy was lawful, whether lower courts had the authority to consider the case and issue a sweeping block, as well as other questions the government deems appropriate. The order “has now allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they may face persecution, torture, imprisonment, or other grave danger,” said Trina Realmuto, executive director of the National Immigration Litigation Alliance and one of the lawyers representing immigrants in the case. “But today’s order does not decide that the government’s policy is lawful,” she said in a statement. “The Court will hear that question on an expedited schedule.” Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported some 25,000 people to more than two dozen countries, from Liberia to Guyana. The vast majority have been sent to Mexico. The bilateral deals extend to 31 countries willing to accept non-citizens, according to The Washington Post. Many of those nations have notorious human rights records, with a recent New York Times report describing deported migrants being hooded and beaten at a remote hotel in Equatorial Guinea. Trump’s Republican administration has said that it sends people with final deportation orders to third countries when they cannot be returned to their homelands or their native countries would not accept them, including those who have criminal convictions. Those governments provide assurances that people would not be persecuted or tortured, federal lawyers said. US Attorney General Todd Blanche called the policy “an entirely lawful and critical tool for immigration enforcement” in a social media post. Some migrants, though, have found themselves imprisoned in countries they had never heard of before their arrivals. Others also face serious safety risks and are left with little choice except to return to the home countries they were fleeing. Many have no criminal convictions and have been found to be at risk of torture or persecution, lawyers for the immigrants said. The case comes amid a sweeping immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which has pledged to deport millions of people who are living in the United States illegally. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Paris Fashion Week: Best of Matières Fécales, Saint Laurent, Dior and Maison Margiela for SS27
description: Anthony Vaccarello’s golden affair at Saint Laurent and Jonathan Anderson’s contemplative mood at Dior were among the standout moments in Paris.
content: Paris Fashion Week is under way in the French capital, where powerhouses ranging from Chanel to Louis Vuitton and Dior are showcasing their spring/summer 2027 collections. The blockbuster show of day one was undoubtedly Matières Fécales, the label that went viral earlier this year for designing one of Zendaya’s most talked-about red carpet looks. Held in the Place de la République and named The Ninety-Nine Percent (a follow-up to last season’s The One Percent), the label’s spring/summer 2027 show was a celebration of marginalised groups around the world, from India’s pariahs (co-founder Steven Raj Bhaskaran has Indian heritage) to underground queer communities. The highly varied line-up – also diverse in terms of casting – ranged from punk-inspired get-ups to takes on the Indian sari and exquisite feather gowns. As statements go, it was a moving and poignant moment – notwithstanding a major delay due to front-row guest Rihanna’s tardiness. Bhaskaran and co-founder Hannah Rose Dalton clearly have talent in spades; now they need to focus on building a signature fashion identity for a brand that, in only a couple of seasons, has become one of the hottest names in the business. Over more than a decade at the helm of Saint Laurent, designer Anthony Vaccarello has set a very high bar for fashion show production. Always held opposite a gleaming Eiffel Tower at night, the brand’s Paris shows are riveting and enrapturing spectacles. Without relying on gimmicks, and instead on great ideas and often very simple sets, the designer never fails to wow, season after season. For spring/summer 2027, which rumours suggest could be Vaccarello’s swan song, models walked down a jet-black runway with rows of baroque chandeliers suspended above. They were clad in all-gold looks. Saint Laurent classics such as the safari shirt, the blouse and the pencil skirt, and Vaccarello’s signatures like broad-shouldered coats all came in matt, shiny and pale shades of gold. Against the night sky and those gilded chandeliers, the show felt more like a theatre performance than a runway presentation. The fabrics were just as rich as the deep shades of gold on display. From brocade to organza and lamé, they shimmered and glinted, transforming models into walking jewels. Cropped tops and jackets with fur cuffs, paired with matching gold brocade trousers, looked fabulous. Tone them down with jeans, and you have the perfect outfit for a night on the town. A smattering of black looks at the end – including gowns made of layers of chiffon and velvet blouses paired with matching skirts – felt almost like a palate cleanser after the radiance of the golden parade. As the models returned for the finale, Charlotte Gainsbourg walked on stage to perform a song, later joined by Vaccarello himself and the entire cast of models. If this is really the designer’s last show, he is going out with a bang. Few designers have stayed as consistent and clear-eyed over a decade. His laser-sharp focus and unmatched vision – which touched every aspect of the label, from its boutiques to its campaigns and celebrity endorsements – will be hard to replicate. Vaccarello’s Midas’ touch, indeed. Dior’s Jonathan Anderson was in a contemplative mood for spring/summer 2027. After discovering the Chinese tradition of wénwán walnuts, he felt it was time to truly get to the core of the brand – to its kernel, so to speak. Often used as a meditation tool, wénwán walnuts have a porcelain-like finish achieved through months, even years, of hand rubbing (the show invitation came with two wénwán walnuts, which also appeared on the runway as a minaudière). Thinking about the origin of things – and garments – inspired the designer to reimagine pieces that are pillars of the Dior lexicon. Take the Bar jacket, the quintessential tailoring item at Dior. In this collection, it lost its structure and became as soft as a silk blouse. Deconstructed tailoring, tweed coats that looked as cosy as robes, and airy chiffon confections conveyed lightness and ease. Even the accessories were “let loose”, from scarf bags decorated with fringes to mismatched chandelier earrings (one ear adorned with cascading petals and the other with strings of pearls) and sandals with undone zippers as straps. “What looks symmetrical in nature is often not quite,” said Anderson in the show notes. It was nice to see the designer relinquish some control and show a bit of vulnerability in a thoughtful collection that captured the fragile beauty of imperfection. After unveiling his final collection for Diesel in Milan last week, Maison Margiela’s Glenn Martens, who until this season was working on both brands, returned to Paris for the house’s latest collection (Maison Margiela’s last show took place in Shanghai earlier this year). Upholstery fabrics, flower-printed synthetic materials reminiscent of shower curtains, nude undergarments worn under tailored jackets, and reinterpretations of wardrobe staples such as the trench coat were among the key looks in a collection that distilled the codes of the brand known for its four-stitch label. Held on a runway made of walls plastered with bouquets of wilted flowers (a homage to fellow Belgian designer Raf Simons’ haute couture debut at Dior), the collection was “a study into the concepts of hard and soft”. Tailored jackets, for instance, were folded and draped at the sides, while stiff panels were inserted into flowy dresses to add structure. It was a simple yet clever idea that showcased Martens’ skills as a dressmaker and tailor. The pantsuits, including one in a houndstooth pattern and a double-breasted tuxedo jacket paired with matching pants, stood out in the line-up.

title: At 52, how Hong Kong skateboarder Julius Brian Siswojo is redefining ageing and longevity
description: Skateboarding pioneer Julius Brian Siswojo talks about how the sport and diet changes have helped him stay fit into his fifties.
content: Julius Brian Siswojo is as well known for co-founding Hong Kong’s pioneering hip-hop group 24Herbs as he is for championing skateboarding in the city. Having been “on the deck” – skateboarding, for the uninitiated – since 1988, the 52-year-old is acutely aware of the negative stereotypes associated with the culture: rebellious youths causing trouble in the streets late at night. But Siswojo, who says he does not drink, smoke or touch drugs, stays focused on a healthy lifestyle – not just for himself but also for his loved ones. From Jakarta to Hong Kong, a skate nerd’s journey Born in Jakarta, Indonesia, Siswojo moved to Hong Kong in 1985 at age 11 because his mother insisted on providing him and his elder sister with a better education. “It was already very hard for my parents to pay for [our] living expenses,” he says, “so since I was little, I felt I had to make sure they were proud of their decision.” He discovered skateboarding at 14, and with it, refuge from growing pains and freedom from the constraints of his small Hong Kong home. He says skating “erased all of my negative thoughts”, and that he would “just concentrate on skating and learning new tricks”. “No money can buy the feeling of riding on a board,” he says. “I was basically never home. I was always outside with my board. But growing up on the streets, I saw a lot of … gang fights or whatever. Everyone around me started smoking [cigarettes] and then weed, and then slowly [taking] drugs.” He did not join them, he says, because he did not want to disappoint his parents: “I can’t be flying to Hong Kong to study and start drinking and smoking and doing drugs.” While maintaining a strong sense of discipline, Siswojo became a self-proclaimed “skate nerd”. In 1999, at age 25, he founded his own skateboard and streetwear shop and label, 8Five2, as well as the All Hong Kong Skateboards Association to promote the sport in the city. It organises four to six events a year, from contests to demonstrations. “To me, skateboarding is the most fun, and it’s a very creative outlet,” he says. “That’s why I want people to experience it and have been preaching skateboarding for [38 years].” Losing weight and regaining freedom Siswojo entered Hong Kong’s entertainment scene in the mid-2000s, co-founding six-piece hip-hop group 24Herbs in 2006, under the pseudonym Sir JBS. Four years later, he branched into acting with a role in Felix Chong Man-keung’s Once a Gangster (2010). While Siswojo mostly played on-screen toughs, his real-life habits were remarkably disciplined. But there was one vice that affected his health: food. “I was insane,” he says. “Ice cream at midnight, instant noodles … I ate everything – all the fat, all the sugar, all the candy, all the ice cream … everything. That was my vice.” He weighed 95kg (210lb) in 2000, when he reached a turning point. “I hurt my back and couldn’t even get up from the sofa,” he says. “I had to get an injection – I think it was like a painkiller for relief – at the hospital.” That incident motivated him to lose weight by cutting down his sugar and carb intake, intermittent fasting and doing some light exercises. He shed 11kg to reach 84kg, “which was not bad”, he says. “Skating felt pretty good again.” But this did not last. His weight fluctuated, and he did not work out regularly. Outside his regular skate sessions, he did “a few push-ups here and there” and only a little exercise. A few years later, family inspired a return to self-discipline. When his wife, Annie Lee, became pregnant with their daughter in 2009, Siswojo went vegetarian for the entire nine months, even though Lee was not vegetarian. Siswojo holds a quiet belief in the power of restraint and sacrifice. “My mum was telling me, ‘Brian, if you can give up something – if you can be a vegetarian – it’ll be good for your wife and kid.’” He changed his diet immediately. It was a spiritual exercise more than a physical one. However, when his daughter Tayla was born in 2010, Siswojo did not return to “eating heavy, gnarly” foods. In fact, having a daughter made him want to live more consciously so he could “hang out with her for as long as I can”. For the first 15 years of her life, he was pescatarian. “We love her so much, it was easy for me to be … more disciplined in terms of my health,” he says. Dining mix-up widens options and sparks a podcast On a visit to Tokyo early in 2025, Siswojo mistakenly ate pork thinking it was a plant-based alternative – and liked it. After that, with his family’s encouragement, he decided to add meat back into his diet. He still limits his sugar and carb consumption, and occasionally practises intermittent fasting. Earlier this year, Siswojo started his online restaurant talk show, Let’s Go Eat with Brian. It covers the full spectrum of Hong Kong gastronomy through interviews with industry friends he made during 24Herbs’ peak years in the late 2000s and 2010s, including Daniel Wu Yin-cho, Stephen Fung Tak-lun and Janice Vidal. “Pretty much all the restaurants we feature are in Hong Kong because I want to introduce good food and restaurants here,” Siswojo says. “It’s getting really tough [for the local F&B industry right now], so if we can kind of push it from our end, it’d be really good.” Rolling back the years View this post on Instagram A post shared by J Brian Siswojo 李凱賢 (@jbs8five2) While Siswojo’s diet has evolved, his commitment to physical longevity has only intensified. In 2018 – when he was 44 – he met his current personal trainer and began training daily: cardio and weights on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays; swimming on Saturdays; running on Sundays; and skating on Tuesdays and Thursdays. “Since 2018, I’ve never missed a day basically, unless I was under the weather,” he says. “I’m doing all that … every day, to help with the longevity of my skating [life].” Siswojo now uses his own journey to mentor young people on healthy living. “I’ve been trying to share with a lot of the younger skaters that they can do some workouts on the side and eat healthier so they can skate more, skate better and don’t get hurt as easily,” he says. “Because that’s what I’ve been doing, I want to keep on skating.” This dedication to longevity mirrors his optimism for skateboarding’s future on the global stage. The sport was added to the Olympic programme in 2020 and debuted at the Summer Olympics in Tokyo in 2021 with park and street disciplines for men and women. It returned at Paris 2024 and has been confirmed as one of the mandatory sports at the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, alongside surfing and sport climbing. The skateboarding community has mixed feelings about the inclusion. Many traditionalists and underground players have concerns about commercialisation and trend exploitation, as well as losing the sport’s raw, creative nature and the subculture’s anti-establishment roots. Siswojo, however, belongs to the more optimistic camp that welcomes mainstream growth, believing it could lead to increased global recognition, better funding and skate parks and career stability for professional skaters. “I was like, ‘Yeah, why not?’” he says. “A lot of the public perception was very positive. They looked at the skateboarding event at the Olympics and went, ‘That’s so cool. They’re all different; they can listen to their own music while they’re doing their tricks, and they have no uniform and can dress in their own style.’” For Siswojo, staying active at 52 is ultimately about preserving the craft that saved him as a teenager in Hong Kong. “You have to fall 10,000 times in order to land a trick,” he says. “The core skaters might be hating [the Olympics inclusion], but me, I love it all. I just want people to experience and try skateboarding because it really helped a lot in my life, my career, my everything.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Beijing criticises push for EU to develop Section 301-style trade tool to counter China
description: Ministry of Commerce says such a move would ‘seriously damage mutual trust’, affect broader economic and trade cooperation.
content: The Ministry of Commerce has criticised a reported Franco-German push for the EU to develop a trade tool similar to the US’ Section 301 to counter China, calling it “protectionist and unilateralist” and warning that Beijing would “resolutely respond” to any discriminatory measures against Chinese companies or products. “The EU has itself been a victim of such tools in the past: do not do unto others what you would not have done unto yourself,” it said in a statement issued on Tuesday. The timing of the reported push, which comes as Beijing and Brussels prepare for a second round of trade talks this month, also drew the ministry’s ire. “If the EU engages in dialogue and consultation with China on the one hand while ratcheting up a show of strength against China on the other, this will seriously damage mutual trust, disrupt the overall consultation process and affect the broader picture of China-EU economic and trade cooperation,” it said. The ministry urged the European Union to stick to dialogue and said China would watch Brussels’ next moves closely, vowing to “resolutely respond and defend the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industry” if the EU introduced “discriminatory” restrictions on Chinese firms or products. The worst outcome would be to set up a power struggle and then back down at the first sign of difficulty Pascal Canfin, European Parliament member Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with Rhodium Group’s China practice, wrote in his monthly newsletter on Sunday that Paris and Berlin were finalising a policy paper urging Brussels to create a tool that could mirror America’s Section 301 tariff authorities. The tool would enable the bloc to cut China off from the European market “within 24 hours,” according to an unnamed official cited in the newsletter. Washington used tariffs applied under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to target unfair trade practices by specific countries, with duties imposed after an investigation. Spanish media outlet Dossier Bruselas reported on Monday that Paris and Berlin were finalising a plan to reform the EU’s Anti-Coercion Instrument and make it easier for the European Commission to activate it. Commerce Minister Wang Wentao held a video call with German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche on Monday. The German side said Wang and Reiche used the call to “take stock of the state and perspectives of bilateral trade”, while Beijing said both sides “exchanged opinions” on China-EU and China-Germany trade and economic ties. Calls have been growing within the EU for the bloc to weaponise its market for Chinese imports as the second round of trade talks approaches. Pascal Canfin, a French member of the European Parliament who sits on its Committee on International Trade, urged Europe to turn its market into “an instrument of power” against China in an article published in Le Grand Continent, a French online journal focused on geopolitics, last week. “European decision-makers, in both the public and private sectors, will need to show great steadfastness, because the worst outcome would be to set up a power struggle and then back down at the first sign of difficulty,” he said.

title: Boom News founder Tang Ho-wing, 1 other arrested by Hong Kong national security police
description: Journalist whose online news outlet has 60,000 Instagram followers arrested on suspicion of ‘incitement by spreading disinformation’.
content: Hong Kong national security police have arrested two people, including the founder of online media outlet Boom News, on suspicion of “incitement by spreading disinformation”, the South China Morning Post has learned. A source familiar with the matter said journalist Tang Ho-wing, the 37-year-old founder of Boom News, was apprehended at around 7am on Wednesday, along with activist Lee Ying-chi, a dentist. “The National Security Department has arrested two people on suspicion of incitement by spreading disinformation,” the source said, adding that the alleged crimes had taken place outside Prince Edward MTR station on August 31. The arrests were linked to the apprehension of three others – two men and a woman – earlier this month for allegedly shouting seditious slogans and holding white flowers outside the station on the same date, the source said. The force said on Wednesday night that the trio, aged between 33 and 79, had been released on bail following their arrest for acting with seditious intent on September 3. Following further investigation, police said its National Security Department conducted additional enforcement operations on Sunday and Monday, arresting another local man and two local women – aged between 46 and 65 – on the same charge. All three have been released on bail pending further investigation. The pair arrested on Wednesday were remanded in custody for further investigation. Tang, known to internet users as “Boom head” or Bobby, was previously a journalist with the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s student newspaper, Chinese University Student Press, and the news arm of the local online forum HK Golden. In 2020, he started Boom News, which mainly operates on social media platforms. As of Wednesday morning, the outlet had about 66,000 followers on Instagram. The bio section of its page states: “Please join Patreon to support independent journalists and uphold what remains of our struggling press freedom.” The outlet also accepts donations from readers via PayPal, the Faster Payment System (FPS) and other payment platforms. Prince Edward MTR station became a flashpoint during the anti-government protests, after police chased demonstrators into the facility and pursued them onto trains, resulting in injuries during an operation on August 31, 2019. Protesters have accused police of indiscriminately beating commuters, while the force said its officers were targeting those who had changed out of their trademark black outfits to blend in with passengers. A police spokesman said on Wednesday night that the so-called August 31 incident was not based on facts, with individuals trying to undermine social stability by exploiting it to spread lies, attack the government and smear police. The force said such acts could constitute the offence of doing acts with seditious intention.

title: In Japan, free BitTorrent porn downloads bring legal trouble and fines
description: Adult content users face summonses and hefty penalties for downloading clips as copyright holders widen IP-based enforcement.
content: Japanese BitTorrent users who thought they were simply downloading adult videos for free are increasingly receiving court notices and demands for hundreds of thousands of yen, as copyright holders step up efforts to identify users through their IP addresses. One self-employed man in his 40s living in Tokyo began using the file-sharing software after reading about it online. He would start downloading adult videos before going to bed and switch the software off the next morning, giving him access to large numbers of videos without paying. Then in May, a letter arrived at his home. It appeared to have come from a court, although the man initially had no idea what it concerned. The notice said a court had approved the disclosure of information identifying him, including his name, address and telephone number. About 20 days later, another letter arrived, this time from a lawyer acting for a video production company. It demanded 500,000 yen (US$3,200) and said civil or criminal action could follow if he did not pay. “My first thought was that it had to be some kind of scam,” the man said. But after looking into the documents, he came to believe they were genuine. The notice referred to rights covering the online transmission of copyrighted material, and he realised his use of file-sharing software was probably behind it. “I decided I had better treat it as genuine and get proper advice,” he said. “Going to a lawyer seemed like the safest option.” Cases involving settlement demands over alleged copyright infringement linked to adult videos have been rising sharply in Japan. According to the Tokyo District Court, applications for orders to disclose identifying information filed with its intellectual property division rose from 814 in 2023 to 2,454 in 2024 and 5,320 in 2025. A communications ministry survey found that 95.6 per cent of disclosure requests received by major internet service providers and others in 2024 concerned alleged copyright infringement involving adult videos. Video production companies have in recent years introduced systems that can identify the IP addresses of people suspected of sharing copyrighted material through file-sharing software, according to records from similar lawsuits. They can then seek court orders requiring internet providers to reveal information identifying the user before pursuing settlements or damages. The communications ministry has warned people against casually using file-sharing software as disputes over such payment demands continue. BitTorrent and similar services commonly use peer-to-peer technology, allowing users’ computers to exchange files directly rather than through a central server. The system can also upload parts of a file while it is being downloaded, meaning users who think they are only receiving material can at the same time be distributing copyrighted content to others. The Tokyo man contacted a law office he found through online reviews. His lawyer told him there was no reason to panic or immediately pay the 500,000 yen being demanded. Because the case involved adult videos, the man said he had been unable to tell his family what was happening. “Even when I was at work, it would suddenly pop into my mind,” he said. The anxiety began affecting his everyday life, he said, but things improved after the lawyer took over dealings with the other side. Negotiations are now under way to reduce the amount sought. “I’m glad I didn’t just ignore it and instead went to someone for advice,” he said. The man admitted he had known there was something questionable about what he was doing. “I really wish I had never started,” he said. “I won’t be using it again.” Izumi Toda, a lawyer who represents video production companies and other copyright holders, warned against online advice suggesting that recipients can simply ignore settlement demands and wait for the statute of limitations to expire. “That is not something people should assume they can get away with,” he said. “If someone refuses to respond, there may be no other way forward, and rights holders can decide to pursue a criminal complaint. I have handled a number of cases like that.” Toda said BitTorrent requires users to install and configure software and argued that this can make the conduct appear deliberate rather than accidental. “Using it requires a certain amount of knowledge and preparation,” he said. “That can lead rights holders to view the infringement as more serious.” But he said copyright holders did not automatically want to take cases to court or seek criminal penalties. “From their point of view, these people could also have been paying customers,” he said. “If someone responds sincerely and there are circumstances worth taking into account, there may be room to reduce the settlement.” Yasufumi Sasanami, a lawyer who has advised more than 1,000 people facing similar claims, including the Tokyo man, said production companies had developed systems allowing them to pursue cases on a large scale. “They now have an established process for making these claims in volume and it has become a substantial source of income,” he said. Sasanami also warned that settling one claim may not necessarily bring the matter to an end. Many users download numerous titles from different companies, meaning further demands can follow over other videos. “The sums being sought for individual titles are high and I don’t think the level of liability matches the conduct involved,” he said. “The courts need to provide clearer standards on what constitutes an appropriate amount of compensation.”

title: Somali pirates kill 5 crew on hijacked tanker before rescue by security forces
description: Deaths aboard the Palau-flagged MT Honour 25 appear to be the first involving Somali pirates in over a decade.
content: Somali ⁠pirates killed five crew members of ⁠the hijacked MT Honour 25 petroleum products tanker before it was rescued by security forces, Somalia’s semi-autonomous state of Puntland said on Tuesday. Puntland’s authorities said they also rescued a second vessel on Tuesday that had been hijacked in May. The deaths ‌aboard the Palau-flagged ship appear to be the first at the hands of Somali pirates in over a decade. The ship with 17 crew members was seized by pirates in April during a resurgence of Somali piracy that experts have attributed, in part, to impacts of the Iran war, including elevated oil prices that make tankers more attractive targets. The MT Honour 25 reportedly had 18,500 barrels of oil on board when it was hijacked. Puntland’s information ⁠ministry said in a statement that a rescue mission had successfully freed the ship and captured 16 pirates. “Before ‌the operation begun, the pirates on board the ship killed five of the crew. Among those killed were three from Pakistan, one from Myanmar and ‌one from India,” it said. Four crew members – three Pakistanis and one Indian – ⁠were also injured, the statement ⁠said. The rescue follows another rescue mission last week, when Puntland’s maritime police force freed the US-sanctioned tanker Sibu 1, which ‌Somali pirates had hijacked in August. One pirate was killed, four wounded and 15 captured in the operation, while the 20-strong crew was safely rescued. However, 28 of 41 pirates arrested in that operation later escaped while being transferred to jail, with several Puntland security officials accusing local police of complicity. Puntland’s Maritime Police Force (PMPF) said in a statement late on Tuesday that it had also rescued ‌an ‌oil tanker called MT Eureka which had been hijacked in May after its hijackers fled when ‌police approached the vessel. “As PMPF forces approached the area, the pirates fled towards the shore and ⁠moved inland,” it said. “PMPF forces continue to pursue the individuals involved and are conducting further operations ⁠to apprehend those who escaped.” The rescues bring the total to five out of the six ships held by pirates off the Somali coast as of late August ‌that have now been freed. A ‌previous wave of piracy from 2008 to 2014 disrupted one of the world’s busiest shipping routes, cost the global economy billions of dollars and resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in ransom payments. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Looming interest rate rises will not hit Hong Kong as hard as 2022: analysts
description: The spectre of looming interest rate rises has revived memories of the 2022 downturn, but the damage will be less severe this time, analysts say.
content: Hong Kong looks set to be hit by a wave of interest rate rises in the coming months, but the city’s property market is unlikely to suffer the same level of damage seen during the last rate cycle in 2022 and 2023, according to analysts. Though major Hong Kong banks have so far held rates steady despite the US Federal Reserve raising its benchmark rate earlier this month, they are widely expected to increase them if the Fed follows through with further tightening later this year. The combination of renewed Fed tightening and weaker demand on the Chinese mainland had “revived uncomfortable memories” of 2022 and 2023, when property prices in Hong Kong plunged by double-digit levels, Morgan Stanley said in a report on Monday. But analysts stressed that the city’s property market was in a better position to deal with the fallout of higher interest rates than in 2022, with banks carrying more deposits and steady talent inflows boosting local demand. Concern over the looming rate increases was visible on Tuesday, when Yuexiu Property offered nearly 30 per cent discounts on the flats at its The Atlas project in Yau Tong. The discounted prices – which averaged HK$13,988 (US$1,783) per square foot – were the lowest seen for a project in urban Kowloon in a decade, according to Centaline Property. They were even lower than CK Asset’s Coast Line II launch in the same district in 2023, which sparked a price war among developers at the time. Nevertheless, analysts said the outlook for Hong Kong property was different from the earlier period in several ways, with Morgan Stanley saying it expected the rate shock to be “a hiccup, not a stall” for the city’s property upcycle. For one thing, Morgan Stanley expects the coming rate increase cycle to be “short” and “shallow” compared with the previous cycle. The Fed is likely to raise rates by 0.75 percentage points over the next six months, whereas in 2022 and 2023 rates soared by more than 5 percentage points over 17 months, according to the bank. The pass-through to local borrowing costs is also likely to be more limited than in the past, as Hong Kong’s loan-to-deposit ratio has fallen to a 19-year low, reducing banks’ need for wholesale funding, according to Morgan Stanley. 2026-2027 is not a deja vu of 2022-2023 Morgan Stanley The investment bank expects the one-month Hibor – an interbank lending rate in Hong Kong, which serves as the basis for most mortgages – to rise about 0.5 percentage points to 3.5 per cent by March, with prime rates increasing by just 0.125 percentage points. “2026-2027 is not a deja vu of 2022-2023,” the report said.
