Angus Luk, senior director at CBRE, made a similar distinction, pointing out that the damage caused to Hong Kong property in 2022 and 2023 “reflected cumulative tightening pressure”, with buyers facing the impact of a prolonged and rapid rate-increase cycle. The property market is also starting from a stronger base. Primary-market transactions in 2026 were 38.2 per cent above 2023 levels before the latest Fed rate increase, while secondary transactions were up 13.4 per cent, CBRE data shows. Rents, meanwhile, have risen 10.6 per cent since 2023, while the median monthly income for two-person households has increased 10 per cent to HK$33,000, according to CBRE. However, Luk still expects price consolidation, slower transactions and wider negotiation margins in the secondary market. Developers were likely to use discounts and financing incentives rather than broad headline price cuts, he said. Morgan Stanley expects property prices to stay broadly flat in the fourth quarter before rising 5 per cent in 2027. Steady talent inflows were helping to sustain demand for property in Hong Kong, it noted. In a bull case, prices could gain 10 per cent next year and return to their 2018 peak if Middle East tensions ease, oil prices normalise and mainland economic rebalancing accelerates, it added. UBS struck a more cautious note, saying interest from mainland investors in Hong Kong property assets remained limited in a research report published on Monday. The European bank expects home prices to correct moderately in the fourth quarter, putting full-year 2026 growth at 5 per cent to 10 per cent, below the 12 per cent gain so far this year.

title: Manchester City guilty of using ‘sham’ deals to distort finances, Premier League says
description: Commission says club’s schemes distorted finances by more than £900 million, but City deny wrongdoing and will appeal.
content: Manchester City used “sham” commercial contracts as part of schemes ⁠to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million over nearly a decade, ⁠the Premier League said on Tuesday after an independent commission ruled the club guilty of serious breaches of financial rules. The commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league’s financial rules over nine seasons, between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 campaigns, as well as three of four charges concerning their failure to cooperate with the investigation. The club, which denies wrongdoing, said in a statement it would appeal “on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. No sanction has yet been imposed, leaving unresolved the potential consequences for ‌a club that has dominated English football over the past decade. A significant punishment could affect past and future title races, European qualification and the distribution of tens of millions of pounds in prize money. The case has also raised wider questions about financial governance, competitive integrity and the Premier League’s ability to hold its most powerful clubs to account. An independent commission found that City arranged “sham” contracts that misrepresented the true agreements with several commercial partners and relied on similar agreements with others to inflate their revenue and reduce costs artificially, the league said. It found that several sponsors were required to pay only part of the fees recorded in the relevant agreements, with the balance supplied by the club’s owner Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG). The commission also identified arrangements funded by ADUG that allowed City to record lower operating expenses. The schemes inflated City’s revenue ⁠and reduced their costs, creating the appearance that the club complied with financial regulations, the league said. The report also found that a number of the club’s witnesses presented false evidence at the hearing, which ran for 42 days, and ‌some knowingly misled the commission. The commission concluded that City would have breached both the Premier League’s and Uefa’s spending limits “by a very substantial amount” had the agreements been reported accurately. “The core decision … details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade,” Richard Masters, the Premier League’s CEO, said. Masters described the case and decision as “the ‌most significant in Premier League history” but said key elements remained unresolved, most notably the sanction to be imposed. “Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the ⁠remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the ⁠League, our clubs and fans,” he said. City said they were disappointed and surprised by the commission’s opinion. “The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case,” ‌it said. “Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.” The club has until Friday to lodge an appeal. When asked by Reuters whether an appeal by City would automatically ‌suspend any ‌sanction, a league representative said they could not “get into the process” because of confidentiality. City chief executive Ferran Soriano addressed staff in a video in which he rejected the allegations and accused the commission of supporting the ‌league’s “conspiracy theory”. “The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation, that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi,” Soriano said. “This is just not true. ⁠Irrefutable evidence has been provided to the Premier League commission that shows it could not happen and that it did not happen.” The announcement came near the end of the European Football Clubs general assembly in Copenhagen, leaving representatives of ⁠English clubs checking their phones during the closing minutes. Representatives of Arsenal and Nottingham Forest declined to comment when approached. A Manchester United representative also declined to comment when contacted by Reuters. EFC Chairman Nasser Al-Khelaifi reserved judgment on the case and praised Soriano’s work as an EFC board member. “His knowledge, you know, throughout his career is fantastic. That’s why I think they did a lot of positive things also,” Al-Khelaifi ‌said. British sports minister Lisa Nandy said the ‌league’s report was “incredibly stark” and called for a swift and fair conclusion to the case. “This is not only causing a lot of concern for Manchester City fans. It’s also obviously causing a lot of concern for all fans of Premier League football,” she told the BBC. “Premier League is one of our crown jewels. We need to see the investigation concluded swiftly and fairly, but swiftly particularly because we need to uphold the integrity of the game.” Yasin Patel, a barrister specialising in sports law at London’s Church Court Chambers, said he expected City to fight “with all their legal might.” “Round one was to the Premier League, let round two begin,” he added.

title: Taiwan plans US$850 million ammunition spend to prepare for potential PLA blockade
description: Taiwan should boost conventional ammunition stocks through local production while asking US to speed up weapons deliveries, analyst says.
content: Taiwan’s military plans to spend more than NT$27 billion (US$850 million) to quadruple critical ammunition stocks to 120 days’ supply, strengthening its ability to sustain combat operations during a wartime blockade. The proposed six-year “urgent ammunition replenishment” programme, running from this year until 2031, comes as Taipei seeks to strengthen its ability to keep fighting if a cross-strait conflict cuts external supply lines. The spending proposal was revealed on September 26 and still requires legislative approval. The programme is expected to cost NT$27.59 billion, with NT$7.3 billion allocated this year through a supplementary budget. A further NT$7.3 billion is proposed for 2027 to accelerate procurement of various types of critical ammunition. Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi, the strategic planning director of Taiwan’s defence ministry, said this month that the military aimed to gradually increase its combat-ready ammunition stocks from the current 30 days to 120 days. He said more frequent combat-readiness drills and exercises in recent years had also increased ammunition consumption, requiring stocks to be replenished more quickly. The programme covers critically needed munitions, including 120mm and 105mm tank rounds, 30mm cannon ammunition, propellant charges for 155mm artillery shells and high-powered explosives. The military is also separately replenishing missile stocks, including thousands of additional Stinger missiles, while seeking to expand local ammunition production, according to the spending proposal. The push reflects concern in Taipei that the People’s Liberation Army could seek to blockade the island during a conflict, disrupting overseas supplies and forcing Taiwan to rely on existing stockpiles and locally produced ammunition. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In a report to the legislature earlier this year, Taiwan’s defence ministry said the island’s geography made it particularly vulnerable to a PLA blockade intended to cut supply lines and prevent outside forces from intervening. It originally proposed using a special defence budget to make large one-off ammunition purchases and build 14 additional munitions production lines, arguing that gradually replenishing stocks through annual budgets would not meet wartime requirements. Officials said the additional lines would double production capacity. But the legislature in May reduced the ceiling of the government’s proposed NT$1.25 trillion special defence programme to NT$780 billion and limited it largely to US arms purchases, excluding general-purpose ammunition and the expansion of local production lines. Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, the defence minister of Taiwan, told lawmakers that plans to build the 14 production lines and raise ammunition stocks to 120 days had been removed from the special legislation. The ministry has since sought to fund some of the requirements through supplementary and annual budgets. Lawmakers have questioned whether Taiwan has sufficient ammunition to sustain a prolonged conflict. Lin Pei-hsiang, a legislator from the main opposition Kuomintang, said lessons from the Ukraine war showed that even sophisticated weapons could be systematically destroyed without adequate survivability, camouflage, mobility and dispersed deployment. “What really determines combat capability is ammunition stockpiles, resupply capacity and the ability to sustain production during wartime,” Lin said, questioning how much precision-guided ammunition Taiwan would have if fighting lasted more than two weeks. Chen Kuan-ting, from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party, said security investment should extend beyond weapons to broader resilience, including energy reserves, backup power, critical supplies, communications, ports and other infrastructure. “We need to look at what our opponent is preparing and ask ourselves whether we are sufficiently prepared,” he said. Taipei is also expanding storage capacity to accommodate the larger ammunition stockpile. From next year, the army plans to spend about NT$4.18 billion on six blast-resistant ammunition depot projects with a combined capacity of 10,250 tonnes. Together with depots already under construction, the projects are expected to add 18,250 tonnes of storage capacity by 2033. Analysts said larger reserves were important because Taiwan could face high ammunition consumption while waiting for outside assistance. Chieh Chung, a researcher with the Taipei-based Association of Strategic Foresight, said that even if US forces were to assemble in Hawaii, they could take another two to three weeks to reach the first island chain and would have to contend with a PLA maritime blockade and other threats. “If it becomes a protracted war, and the PLA lands and we enter the territorial defence phase, we will inevitably consume huge quantities of conventional ammunition,” Chieh said. He said Taiwan should increase conventional ammunition stocks through local production while asking Washington to accelerate deliveries of precision-guided weapons that the island could not produce itself. Wang Hung-jen, executive director of the Taipei-based Institute for National Policy Research, has also said Taiwan must recognise how much ammunition is consumed in modern warfare and move beyond a defence strategy focused mainly on deterrence. Speaking at a Taipei seminar in April on the global impact of the US-Iran conflict, Wang said long-term planning should also cover ammunition and other supplies, as well as the protection of critical infrastructure. “Taiwan’s security does not come only from external support,” Wang said. “Taiwan itself must have sufficient preparedness and manage risks in advance.”

title: China bans online promos for loans, insurance by private brokers to prevent loan misuse
description: The new regulations start today and will only allow financial institutions and third-party internet platforms to carry out online marketing.
content: Starting on Wednesday, new regulations governing the online marketing of financial products – including loans, insurance and deposits – by loan-assisting service providers take effect in China. According to analysts, one of the driving considerations behind the measure is to curb the improper use of bank loans. The regulations were jointly released by eight ministries, headed by the People’s Bank of China in April. They explicitly stipulate that only financial institutions and third-party internet platforms may carry out online marketing for financial products. All other entities and individuals are barred from such activities, “including in any disguised form”. The move has been welcomed by many mainland consumers. Over the past several years, advertisements from loan-assisting providers have proliferated, with promotions for bank loans topping consumer complaint lists. “As soon as you search for something like ‘loan’ on WeChat or any other social media platform, these ads will pop up as you scroll. They typically appear to come from a specific bank. Once I clicked, I landed on a registration page run by some company,” said Yu Qing, a Shanghai resident. As of Tuesday, promotions persisted on WeChat Moments shared by staff working for several Shanghai‑based loan‑assisting providers. The posts either highlighted fast bank loan approval speeds, or publicised the loan amounts their clients had secured through them. It is precisely these advertisements that fall under the new regulatory scope. According to the new rules, the scope of financial products covers nearly all offerings available on the market. “After the new rules take effect, advertisements – both text-based and video-formatted – will generally drop significantly in the short term,” said Huang Xianwen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing DHH Law Firm. “It is worth noting that the eight ministries issuing the new regulations include the Cyberspace Administration of China, which is tasked with cleaning up the online space,” Huang added. According to the National Internet Finance Association of China, there were at least 500 loan-assisting service providers across the country as of last October. A cleaner online environment is only one dimension – curbing the irregularities conducted by some loan‑assisting firms is considered equally urgent. “Regulators also aim to contain financial risks while shielding consumers from misleading marketing, personal‑data leaks and over‑indebtedness,” said Huang. He explained that the root causes behind the flood of financial service ads partially lay with the financial institutions themselves. For example, banks set aggressive internal new-loan targets in a bid to preserve their business volumes and market standings. “This pressure frequently gets passed down to their partnered loan-support institutions. The intermediaries thus cast a wide net in search of potential borrowers, fuelling a surge in non-compliant lending ads,” Huang added. This incentive has given rise to inappropriate conduct following the disbursement of bank loans. An employee at a Shanghai-based loan-assisting institution, who requested anonymity given the sensitive nature of the matter, said the firm would at times help clients deploy lower-rate business loans to pay off residential mortgages. And they would also casually suggest that borrowers could channel such proceeds into the stock market – all of which constitute improper practices. Such misuse of loan proceeds is “an open secret” across the industry, “among both lenders and loan-assisting organisations”, he added.

title: China warns officials, fires kindergarten principal over ‘mops in cooking pots’ scandal
description: Whistle-blower expresses relief upon seeing the announcement, saying, ‘The children there can eat clean food now’.
content: Local Chinese authorities have issued warnings and demerits to 11 officials and dismissed the entire kitchen staff at a kindergarten following a teacher’s revelation about unsanitary practices, including washing dirty mops in cooking pots. On June 30, several children at the Affiliated Kindergarten of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology in Jiangsu province exhibited symptoms such as nausea and vomiting during and after lunch. Parents had been inquiring about the kindergarten’s hygiene throughout the summer break, but they received no official response until September. The situation came to light when a health teacher and canteen safety supervisor, referred to as Wang, disclosed the issues on her social media account. She detailed various unhygienic practices in the kindergarten kitchen, including washing mops and drain covers in cooking pots and disinfecting mosquito nets in food preparation sinks. Allegations also surfaced regarding staff members stealing food ingredients. Wang shared photographs she had taken of staff members involved in these unsanitary practices with the Xinmin Evening News. Despite her repeated reports to the kindergarten principal, the issues remained unresolved. Initially, the kindergarten and the local neighbourhood office refuted Wang’s claims, accusing her of spreading rumours. However, after reviewing surveillance footage that corroborated her allegations, the kindergarten principal attempted to deflect blame, claiming Wang had directed the staff to engage in these unhygienic behaviours. Seeking justice, Wang blew the whistle on the kindergarten after resigning. She admitted to hesitating for two days before taking this significant step, fearing it would jeopardise her chances of employment in the industry. Nevertheless, she firmly asserted the importance of not failing the children and maintaining a sense of conscience. On September 22, the district government formed an investigative team, which confirmed the “serious problems” present in the kindergarten kitchen. Following the investigation, they fired the principal, the deputy principal responsible for logistics, and all kitchen staff. Additionally, 11 officials from the neighbourhood office, district administration for market regulation, and district education bureau received warnings and demerits for their failure to fulfil supervisory duties. Wang expressed relief upon seeing the announcement. “The children there can eat clean food now,” she said. Some people raised concerns regarding the lack of criminal liability pursued against the kindergarten principal. Under China’s Criminal Law, personnel responsible for food and drug safety supervision who neglect their duties leading to severe consequences may face imprisonment of up to five years. However, this provision specifies that it applies to “a functionary of a state organ.” In May, the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Ministry of Education jointly issued new guidelines regarding food safety in kindergartens, effective from June. These guidelines clarify that the principal bears primary responsibility for food safety but do not specify the potential criminal repercussions for those in charge. In a notable case from 2021, a restaurant owner was sentenced to seven years in prison for selling pork ribs containing nitrite to a primary school, resulting in food poisoning for 56 students. In 2025, a Gansu kindergarten principal, investor, and kitchen staff faced criminal custody after 247 children and 28 staff members suffered severe lead poisoning due to the deliberate addition of toxic decorative paint to school meals. An online observer questioned: “If the responsible parties are not subjected to severe penalties, how can we prevent similar food safety issues from recurring?”

title: Can pay-as-you-earn funding fix Southeast Asia’s higher education debt problem?
description: A Singapore scheme linking tuition to graduate income is testing if private finance can fill the ‘missing middle’ in regional student loans.
content: A Singapore-based education financing programme is testing whether income-linked funding can widen access to higher education without an unmanageable debt burden, a model analysts say could help ease repayment pressure faced by graduates across Southeast Asia. Global Financing for Education’s (GFE) Pay It Forward scheme, publicly launched in September, provides students with funding for their education in return for 3 to 10 per cent of their subsequent income for one to 10 years. The income-linked repayments graduates make to GFE are typically capped at twice the original funding amount. The arrangement shifts the risk of weak employment or low earnings from students to the financing pool. But economists say its private-sector structure raises questions about selection criteria and whether students pursuing lower-earning careers could ultimately be excluded. GFE founder Mario Ferro said the programme had already disbursed about US$25,000 among 11 students since May, while the total amount requested by students was more than US$3 million. Eight of the initial recipients are studying abroad, five of them in Thailand. Ferro cited the case of one student who received US$5,000 for graduate studies in Singapore and agreed to contribute 10 per cent of income for three years, totalling US$3,600 by the end of the period. “If the agreed term expires before contributions total US$5,000, the graduate does not owe the difference,” Ferro said, noting that the funding pool absorbed any shortfall while higher earners might contribute more up to the capped amount. Selecting for outcomes Ferro said GFE considered financial need alongside the field of study, institution and likely employment outcomes, as the objective was to fund “a credible path into work”. Despite traditionally modest earnings in nursing, GFE was running an outreach drive for nursing training, Ferro said. This aimed “to support the growth of a profession that is in high demand given the current demographics and [offers] a solid career outcome”, he explained. Bruce Chapman, the Australian economist who designed his country’s income-contingent student loan system, said public and private providers handled earnings risk differently. “The government pools the risk. [The] private sector wants a return on every person.” Governments could verify earnings through national tax and payroll systems, but student loan providers from the private sector face an incentive to select applicants who are most likely to generate financial returns, according to Chapman. While private income-linked contracts could help cash-strapped students, they could not finance higher education universally, as applicants pursuing lower-earning professions might be excluded, Chapman said. “It can never be a general solution to finance the system,” he added. Ferro said GFE required graduates to document earnings using payslips, employment records or bank statements. While there was no fixed income threshold that automatically suspended contributions, graduates experiencing hardship could receive a temporary pause, extension or restructuring for repayments. Chapman expressed reservations about case-by-case verification, saying hardship provisions depended on reliable income checks. “They’ve got to set up an administrative system which verifies whether people are really in financial trouble,” Chapman said. Filling the ‘missing middle’ Such trade-offs play out differently in countries where public help targets the poorest students but leaves middle-income households struggling to cover the full cost of higher education. In Indonesia, economist Elza Elmira said income-linked finance could reach households that were too affluent for the government’s KIP Kuliah help programme but were unable to afford tuition and living expenses. “An income-contingent model could reach the ‘missing middle’ that KIP Kuliah does not cover,” Elmira said. “Because repayments rise and fall with earnings, it lowers the risk of default.” Indonesia’s KIP Kuliah provides tuition and living allowances for students with academic potential but limited financial means, with priority given in 2026 to those from the bottom 40 per cent of household incomes. Elmira said an income-linked model could help incentivise both students and institutions amid ongoing debate over Indonesia’s large number of higher education institutions and their variable quality. Under such a system, students would evaluate course choices based on expected future earnings, while institutions would be forced to compete to attract more students. However, Elmira warned that this could inadvertently favour stronger applicants, high-earning fields such as medicine and engineering and top public universities in Java. “That has the risk of reinforcing regional and institutional inequalities in Indonesia,” Elmira said. To prevent financing from concentrating in top-tier programmes, Elmira suggested that the government should take part as a lender or guarantor, restrict eligibility to accredited programmes and subsidise priority fields with lower expected financial returns. “Fair terms should also include an earnings threshold, payments below 15 per cent of income, automatic suspension during unemployment, debt cancellation after a fixed period, death or permanent disability and regulatory oversight,” she said. Public alternatives In Malaysia, economist Geoffrey Williams said GFE resembled a privately administered graduate tax but was too small to replace a national student financing system. “It is a nice scheme but is limited to a handful of people,” Williams said. “A private scheme would be difficult to scale up to hundreds of thousands of people burdened with PTPTN in Malaysia,” Williams said, referring to the country’s National Higher Education Fund Corporation. PTPTN receives about 3 billion ringgit (US$735 million) annually through borrower repayments and government-backed bonds to support around 600,000 continuing and new students – equivalent to roughly 0.9 per cent of Malaysia’s 2026 operating expenditure. Williams said GFE could serve as a model for reforming PTPTN by replacing traditional loans with government funding recovered through taxation. Under this proposal, graduates earning more than 5,000 ringgit monthly could pay an additional 1 to 2 per cent in tax, while workers in socially necessary, lower-paid fields could be exempt. “Those in higher-paid jobs pay more, even under a fixed-rate tax, because they are benefiting more,” Williams said. He argued the best way would be to end PTPTN’s loan disbursement model entirely and transition to direct state funding. He added that private education loans in Malaysia had limited take-up because students could draw on PTPTN or their Employees Provident Fund savings, making private financing more relevant for professional courses and overseas studies. In the Philippines, students rely mainly on direct public support. Its Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education programme covers tuition and fees at state universities, complemented by the Tertiary Education Subsidy for priority students. A supplementary government student loan programme offers short-term financing, but generally requires repayment within 12 months alongside a co-signer, who is equally and immediately liable for the debt. Unlike GFE, it does not link payments to subsequent earnings, leaving borrowers to absorb the financial risk if employment or income falls short. According to Chapman, these models differ in who bears the financial burden when graduates earn too little: the borrower, the provider or the state. “It’s the ones who don’t get it [financing] that the issues are about,” Chapman said.

title: US-China trade truce remains ‘fragile’ after Xi-Trump summit, analysts say
description: Asia Society experts say modest economic gains leave deeper disputes unresolved, as Washington tests Beijing with a short extension.
content: The two-month extension of the US-China trade truce remains fragile despite last week’s summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, with modest economic concessions leaving deeper disputes unresolved, Asia Society Policy Institute analysts said on Tuesday. “In my view, this truce is very fragile,” said Wendy Cutler, an Asia Society Policy Institute vice-president and former acting deputy US trade representative. “I think they’re testing each other.” Xi’s three-day state visit to Washington produced a further extension of the tariff ceasefire and plans for targeted tariff reductions, but Cutler said the economic results reflected little urgency. “My takeaway would be the economic deliverables, while important, were pretty modest, and frankly, there wasn’t a whole lot of urgency to them either,” she said. Cutler was speaking on a panel examining the summit’s outcomes alongside Asia Society president Kevin Rudd and technology specialist Paul Triolo. The trade truce was extended from November 10, 2026 to January 10, 2027 following an unscheduled meeting between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent shortly before Xi landed in Washington. Cutler said the short extension reflected Washington’s calculation “that smaller or shorter extensions could provide some leverage” to ensure China fulfils its agricultural commitments and resumes full shipments of critical minerals and magnets. Details of the summit’s outcomes emerged after Xi departed the US. The White House on Sunday released lists of non-sensitive goods worth US$30 billion recommended for tariff reductions on each side, amounting to US$60 billion in total. The lists were coordinated under the US-China Board of Trade, a bilateral body established during Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May. More than 90 per cent of the products covered by the agreement would receive most-favoured-nation tariff rates and all reciprocal tariffs would be waived, China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. “The levels are so low compared to our overall trade, and frankly, more and more of our trade is falling into the sensitive basket,” Cutler said. Rudd said Beijing wanted diplomacy led by the two presidents to ensure a “minimal number of surprises coming out of the United States between now and the end of next year” as the ruling Communist Party’s 21st congress approaches. “The Chinese, when they want stability, what they mean by that is no more new tariffs, and can we get existing tariffs down? That’s stability mode,” he added, linking Beijing’s push for predictability to China’s sluggish domestic economy. Another notable outcome of the summit was the establishment of a government-to-government dialogue on artificial intelligence, with Beijing stating the two countries should “maintain dialogue and strengthen cooperation” on the technology. But the scope for cooperation remained uncertain. Trump on Tuesday said the US would not collaborate with Beijing to govern artificial intelligence as it would make it more difficult for American companies to get ahead as the two countries race for global AI supremacy. “Both governments have never really dealt with this issue of how to govern AI models domestically. It’s a new issue, so having a dialogue on this at the government-to-government level is really complicated,” Triolo said. The two leaders also pledged to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and at the Group of 20 in Miami in December, which would mark an unprecedented four face-to-face meetings between the presidents in a single year. “Strategic competition is the operational strategy of both sides,” Rudd said. “The question is whether it’s managed strategic competition or unmanaged strategic competition on the way through.”

title: Opinion | Raising Hong Kong’s birth rate is an economic imperative
description: Economies competing in an AI-driven future will need more highly skilled workers, not fewer. Low fertility is not only a social challenge – it’s an economic threat.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and latest policy address have put demographic sustainability on the public agenda. Among the measures announced are an extension of the newborn bonus scheme and increased financial support for the second and subsequent children. These are welcome steps. But the fertility debate should not be reduced to whether a bonus is large enough to change family decisions. The bigger challenge is whether Hong Kong can remain dynamic and competitive while its younger generation continues to shrink. Demographic trends are often discussed in terms of ageing, labour shortages and pressure on public finances. Yet low fertility has a less discussed consequence: its impact on innovation. Innovation ultimately depends on people: scientists making discoveries, entrepreneurs building companies and skilled professionals turning ideas into products and services. The stronger the talent pipeline, the greater the likelihood of breakthroughs. This matters even more in the age of artificial intelligence. AI may offset some labour shortages, but it still depends on capable people to develop, deploy and improve it. Economies competing in an AI-driven future will need more highly skilled workers, not fewer. That is why low fertility should be viewed not only as a social challenge but also as a competitiveness challenge. A key reason fertility has fallen across advanced economies is that society and families experience its costs and benefits very differently. The benefits of raising children are widely shared. Children grow into workers, taxpayers, consumers, researchers, entrepreneurs and carers, sustaining growth and supporting ageing populations. Yet the costs fall largely on individual families, from housing, childcare and education to career interruptions and lost earnings. That does not mean having children should be treated as a public obligation rather than a personal choice. But governments, employers and institutions shape the conditions under which the decision is made. For that reason, it is encouraging that Hong Kong is treating demographic sustainability as a long-term policy issue. But one-off financial incentives are unlikely to be enough. Parents are also concerned about housing affordability, access to childcare, education costs and the impact of family responsibilities on career progression. These concerns cannot be addressed through a single payment at birth. Experience across Asia suggests a broader approach is required. Governments are increasingly moving beyond one-off incentives towards policies that provide sustained support throughout childhood. From next April, Singapore will provide support from birth until the age of 17, including a S$10,000 (US$7,822) baby gift, annual “child credits” cash payouts, Child Development Account grants and a top-up to an education account. The package provides the same level of support regardless of birth order. Japan also expanded its child allowance system in October 2024. Coverage now extends through to high school-age children, income restrictions have been removed and the monthly allowance for third and subsequent children has increased to ¥30,000 (US$190). The underlying principle is straightforward: if raising a family is a long-term commitment, support for families should also be long-term and predictable. Still, financial support represents only one part of a larger ecosystem. Affordable childcare, parental leave, family-friendly housing policies and a supportive labour market all influence fertility outcomes. Perhaps most importantly, societies must address the perceived conflict between professional success and family formation. For many, the years in which they are expected to establish themselves professionally are also when it is biologically easiest to start a family. In expensive and highly competitive cities, this creates a difficult trade-off. Women continue to bear a disproportionate share of caregiving and often face greater career disruption after becoming parents. Young professionals worry that family commitments may limit opportunities for advancement. High housing costs add more uncertainty. If parenthood is viewed as incompatible with ambition, persistently low fertility should not come as a surprise. This is why employers must be part of the conversation. Family-friendly workplace policies should not be seen merely as employee benefits. They are increasingly a talent strategy. Flexible working arrangements, meaningful parental leave and clear pathways back to career progression can help talented employees remain engaged without forcing them to choose between work and family. In ageing societies, employers that successfully support families will be better positioned to attract and retain skilled workers. Creating a more family-friendly Hong Kong will require sustained government leadership, enabling policies, and support from employers and the wider community. Demographic policy is economic policy: a long-term investment in human capital. Hong Kong will continue to benefit from global talent. But it also needs a stronger domestic pipeline of innovators, entrepreneurs and professionals. That starts with making it easier to pursue family life and professional ambition together. Asia’s low-fertility challenge took decades to emerge and will not be reversed by a single policy announcement. But the direction should be clear: supporting families is an investment in talent, innovation and resilience. For Hong Kong, the fertility debate is ultimately about competitiveness.

title: Family of 4 in hospital after fire at Sha Tin public housing estate
description: After trying and failing to put out fire on their TV stand, family escapes building with about 140 other residents.
content: A family of four was sent to hospital on Wednesday morning after a fire broke out at a public housing estate in Sha Tin, prompting the evacuation of about 140 residents. Police received a report at 6.48am as thick smoke poured from a mid-rise flat in Yan Chuen House at Shui Chuen O Estate. The family tried to put out the fire, which started on their TV stand, but failed to do so, and fled, police said. Firefighters arrived and extinguished the fire at around 7.10am. All four members of the household were taken to Prince of Wales Hospital in Sha Tin to be treated for smoke inhalation, while about 140 residents were safely evacuated. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

title: ‘Hold the status quo’? US Congress reviews Xi-Trump summit outcomes
description: Talks between the two leaders in Washington produced a string of joint announcements, but some say it was more about managing tensions.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit to Washington is over, but China watchers in Congress and the US-China policy community are still parsing a wide range of outcomes, with two more leadership summits expected before the end of the year. The talks between Xi and US President Donald Trump produced a series of joint announcements, including an extension of the US-China trade truce, investment commitments, an agreement to continue an AI dialogue and high-level engagement, as well as measures involving visas for Americans, fentanyl precursors and giant pandas. But some American China watchers said the results fell short of a major breakthrough and were more about managing tensions than resolving the fundamental differences between the two countries. Mike Kuiken, vice-chair of the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told the South China Morning Post that the summit was largely about “how do we hold the status quo in place”. “I just don’t expect breakthroughs,” Kuiken said. “I think every breakthrough – which I would argue is probably most likely to be incremental – is going to be through hard-fought diplomatic discussions and negotiation.” The commission, an independent advisory body established in 2000, provides Congress with annual reports and recommendations on the national security and trade implications of the US-China relationship. The two sides agreed to cut tariffs on non-sensitive goods worth about US$30 billion each way and establish an agricultural trade working group, while Kuiken said farm and related purchases were the summit’s biggest deliverable. On sensitive political issues, the two sides continued to articulate their respective positions. Xi urged Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence, while US ambassador to China David Perdue said after the summit that Washington’s policy on the island had not changed. “We don’t support independence, and we don’t support coercion,” Perdue told Fox News. Ami Bera, the Democratic ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific, has urged Trump to stand firm on Taiwan and maintain long-standing US commitments in the Indo-Pacific while using direct diplomacy with Beijing. “I would hope President Trump upholds our decades-long commitments to the ‘one China’ policy,” Bera told South Korean news agency Aju Press. “Our goal is to maintain the status quo. Our goal is to avoid confrontation.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Trump’s warm welcome for Xi also drew criticism from some members of Congress. Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the state visit a “WTF moment” in an interview with CBS News, questioning Trump’s decision to give Xi a lavish reception while, in Tillis’ view, spending less time with democratic allies. Tillis also criticised the administration’s delay in approving a proposed US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan. John Moolenaar, the Republican chairman of the House Select Committee on China, offered a more favourable assessment of Trump’s negotiating posture while arguing that Xi left Washington without securing major concessions. Some Republicans in Congress who have taken a tougher line on China also attended the state dinner for Xi. According to the White House guest list, they included House Speaker Mike Johnson, Representatives Richard McCormick and Jason Smith, and Senator Steve Daines. “A truly incredible evening at the White House,” Daines posted on social media about the state dinner. In another post, he said he hoped the summit would result in increased “strategic stability and mutual benefits for both of our economies”. The two leaders are due to meet again twice before the end of the year – first at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and then at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December. For Kuiken, however, the additional meetings do not necessarily signal that the underlying differences are disappearing. “It’s a very complicated relationship,” Kuiken said. “I just don’t see a lot of alignment between the two sides right now.”

title: Cheap and illegal: mainland Chinese post social media adverts for services in Hong Kong
description: Despite recent crackdown, mainland operators use RedNote to offer tour guide or photography services in city ahead of ‘golden week’ break.
content: Hong Kong’s crackdown on visitors abusing visas to illegally offer tour guide, photography and other services has failed to deter adverts for such unlicensed work on mainland Chinese social media ahead of the National Day “golden week” break, the South China Morning Post has found. A search of RedNote by the SCMP turned up accounts listing themselves as Shenzhen-based photographers offering their services in Hong Kong. Many of them also asked clients to reimburse their travel expenses between the two cities. One of them offered photography services at Hong Kong Disneyland at 220 yuan (US$33) per hour, with a minimum booking of two hours in addition to travel costs of about 120 yuan. Asked by an SCMP reporter posing as a potential client whether she held a visa allowing her to work in Hong Kong, the RedNote user said she did not. “If you are afraid [of legal consequences], you should find a Hong Kong photographer,” she said. Mainland residents will enjoy a seven-day holiday from October 1 to 7 to celebrate National Day, and Hong Kong authorities expect to welcome 1.29 million visitors from across the border during the period. Other RedNote posts selling photography services at Disneyland during the holiday charged similar rates, with most of them claiming that they held local residency to work legally. Independent photography and tour guide services are banned at Disneyland, regardless of the providers’ immigration status, according to park rules. But the advertisements have persisted despite recent high-profile law enforcement action involving officers posing as potential customers, booking services and arresting mainland service providers operating in Hong Kong. On Sunday and Monday, the Immigration Department arrested four female mainland visitors, aged 20 to 31, on suspicion of working illegally in the city. The suspects had allegedly advertised make-up, photography and tour guide services in Hong Kong on social media platforms and were subsequently apprehended by immigration officers when allegedly providing the services in the city. One arrestee was a make-up artist who allegedly charged HK$700 (US$89) per day for her services. The other three were photographers who also acted as tour guides, charging HK$400 to HK$600 per package. They allegedly said they could plan tours for clients in popular venues such as the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront, the West Kowloon Cultural District and local theme parks. They also offered to take photos for clients and provide advice on styling. Two local women were also arrested in the same operation on suspicion of helping visitors breach their conditions of stay. Earlier in September, the department and the Travel Industry Authority, the sector’s watchdog, also launched a joint-operation, arresting two mainland visitors who allegedly provided tourist guide and photo-taking services in the city. The department said it had distributed leaflets to the public and visitors at tourist hotspots, urging them not to hire illegal workers. In September last year, the department arrested eight mainland visitors – four photographers and four make-up artists – for working illegally in Hong Kong. On Tuesday, a person claiming to be a Shenzhen-based photographer on RedNote offered a full-day photography package in Hong Kong to the SCMP reporter for 1,500 yuan, which included 10 “meticulously Photoshopped” pictures. “It is fine. I go there [for photo-taking] every month,” the user said, addressing concerns about possible arrest for hiring illegal workers. Another RedNote post charged 89 yuan per hour for taking photos at the West Kowloon Cultural District promenade and requested reimbursement for the 15-yuan single-entry travel authorisation. Make-up artist Erika Lau, 32, said local small businesses such as hers had been affected after customers increasingly turned to mainland service providers in recent years. “Cheap prices are a huge draw for [the customers]. I think people care less about the quality these days,” she said. The artist pointed out that in the context of wedding make-up services, service providers from across the border could charge as little as HK$4,000 (US$510) for a one-day job, about a third of the local price. On RedNote, make-up artists promoted various packages for special occasions, such as visiting Disneyland or concerts. Some charged just HK$250 to HK$380 per session. Lau said Hong Kong artists had to catch up with mainland trends and understand what was popular across the border to keep their businesses competitive. Her fellow artists had closed down their studios one after the other, she said, adding she was also receiving fewer jobs now. Under Hong Kong laws, illegal employment carried a maximum penalty of a HK$50,000 fine and two years in jail, while anyone caught hiring illegal workers risks a fine of HK$350,000 and three years’ imprisonment. Authorities stepped up enforcement actions ahead of the National Day “golden week” break, including revoking the licences of two travel agencies and a guide after finding they had failed to protect members of mainland Chinese tour groups from “coerced shopping”. The actions against Go Go Ming Travel Services, Grandee Travel Company and guide Sun Kwun-ying involved two cases of mainland tour groups handled by the agencies in February and April.

title: Gaza on stage: concert activism meets Malaysia, Singapore red lines
description: With global acts also touring Asia, UK star Ed Sheeran’s concert fallout in the US raises the question of how the saga would play out regionally.
content: American rapper Macklemore lost his spot on British pop star Ed Sheeran’s US tour after speaking up for Palestinians, but in Malaysia it was Sheeran’s music which ended up being pulled from the airwaves. In neighbouring Singapore, British band Massive Attack faced a different kind of fallout, barred from returning after members displayed a Palestinian flag during a July concert. The contrasting cases highlight the competing pressures on foreign artists in Southeast Asia, where political expression can cross different red lines set by governments, promoters, venues and audiences, analysts and industry figures say. In Malaysia, where public support for the Palestinian cause runs deep, promoters must still weigh an artist’s politics against commercial considerations and concert rules. Singapore, meanwhile, draws a sharper line between humanitarian expression and what it considers political advocacy. The disputes come amid demands for musicians to speak out against Israel’s actions in Gaza. A UN commission of inquiry concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide, a finding Israel rejected. Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s tour after declaring “Free Palestine” at a New Jersey concert this month prompted other supporting acts to quit. Promoter Messina Touring Group said stadium owners would not accept him on the bill, while stadium owner Robert Kraft cited allegations of antisemitic rhetoric, which the rapper rejected. On September 15, Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was the promoter’s, after venues on the tour threatened to pull their shows if the rapper remained. Three days later, Malaysian radio station Fly FM pulled Sheeran’s songs, declaring that “some things matter more than music”. Sheeran apologised for his handling of the dispute at a Philadelphia concert the following day, calling the situation in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable”. The pressures on foreign artists in Malaysia extend beyond the airwaves. Foreign acts must also comply with concert rules, leaving promoters to balance an artist’s political stance with commercial considerations and authorities’ requirements. Rohit Rampal, founder and CEO of Malaysian concert organiser Hitman Group, said an artist’s political stance would not automatically rule out a booking, but ticket demand was only part of the decision. “Their public perception, suitability for the Malaysian market, and brand all come into play,” he told This Week in Asia. “A decision that’s considered acceptable or necessary in another market may be perceived very differently in Malaysia.” Asked how he would respond if an overseas partner wanted a pro-Palestinian performer dropped, Rampal said he would raise the prospect of a Malaysian backlash and explore alternatives. “International tours involve many stakeholders, and not every decision is ultimately within the control of the local promoter,” he said. Stage directions In Singapore, two members of Massive Attack received stern police warnings after displaying the Palestinian flag at their July 29 concert, with one shouting “Free Palestine”. Both were banned from re-entering the country, and authorities said future applications for the band to perform would not be accepted. Abraham Vergis, managing director of Providence Law Asia, said Macklemore’s actions could be considered political advocacy in Singapore and invite a similar reaction from authorities. “At the very least, I would expect a police investigation and some difficulty getting approval to perform here again,” he said. The purpose of an artist’s intervention mattered, Vergis said. “Expressing sorrow for those caught in a war, or calling for peace, is unlikely to trouble anyone. Leading a crowd in political slogans or waving a flag on stage is different, because that is asking the audience to take a side in a foreign conflict.” Singapore does not allow the open display of foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit. Tan Kiat How, senior minister of state for digital development and information, said earlier this month that while Singapore did not prohibit artists from “expressing concern” for those affected by global conflicts, the city state “should not be used by foreigners as a platform to further political causes, including those relating to conflicts or political issues overseas”. Sociologist Tan Ern Ser said most Singaporeans probably opposed mixing politics and entertainment, although some welcomed artists speaking about causes they supported. “While I don’t think there is any serious polarisation in Singapore, there would be some who are fine with, even encouraging of, having an entertainer with a message on Palestine and Gaza,” he said. Concert conditions In Malaysia, American gospel singer Israel Houghton’s proposed October appearances in Sabah state have drawn objections over his support for Israel. Sabah Police Commissioner Jauteh Dikun said on Monday that police would advise postponement if a formal application were submitted, state news agency Bernama reported. None had reached the state government despite publicity advertising the shows. Houghton had expressed support for Israel in a social media post on October 8, 2023, according to Bernama. Checks by This Week in Asia found the post was no longer available. Foreign performances require approval through the Unit for Application for Foreign Filming and Performance by Foreign Artiste, known as Puspal. Organisers must also be able to halt shows that breach conditions. The “kill switch” measure followed British band The 1975’s performance at the Good Vibes Festival in 2023, when frontman Matty Healy criticised Malaysia’s anti-gay laws and kissed a male bandmate, prompting authorities to cancel the rest of the festival. Later that year, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim defended Coldplay against calls to cancel its Kuala Lumpur concert, citing the band’s support for Palestinians, while organisers agreed to a kill switch. Korean-American singer Eric Nam cancelled a planned Kuala Lumpur show in 2023, citing threats after liking a post about the Israel-Gaza war. Bruno Mars performed there in 2024 despite Muslim student activists’ objections over his previous concerts in Israel. Benjamin Loh, a communication and media studies lecturer at Monash University Malaysia, said authorities would be mindful of protecting the country’s standing as a concert destination even when public pressure mounted. “Musicians are bound by their popularity, and any hit to their reputation will directly impact their income,” he said. A Pew Research Centre survey published in June found that 89 per cent of Malaysians and 86 per cent of Indonesians viewed Israel unfavourably. Musicians from both countries have used their work to raise money for Palestinians. Cholil Mahmud, vocalist of Indonesian band Efek Rumah Kaca, and Malaysian artists Noh Salleh and Kayda collaborated on Our Power, released in July with royalties pledged to Palestinian aid. “We hope this song encourages people in Indonesia and Malaysia, and their governments, to care more about this issue,” Cholil told Indonesian outlet Medcom. Malaysian singer-songwriter Azmyl Yunor, who also lectures at Sunway University, said treating Palestinian solidarity as an unwelcome intrusion of politics missed the depth of support for the cause at home. “It’s beyond politics – it’s about being human,” he told This Week in Asia. “The Malaysian public, from what I’ve observed, has a clearer and broader understanding of the issue, albeit with some confirmation bias based on your own personal beliefs and faiths.” While commercial pressure still discouraged mainstream musicians from speaking out, “pop artists who have a broader potential to influence their audiences can do more”, Azmyl said.

title: Man City might be biggest cheats sporting world has ever seen. What comes next?
description: Ben Johnson’s Olympic gold and Lance Armstrong’s 7 Tour de France titles were wiped out, will City’s Premier League crowns go the same way?
content: “Don’t get me started on financial fair play,” Vincent Kompany said, immediately after his Bayern Munich team had beaten Aston Villa in a pre-season friendly at Kai Tak Stadium last month. The same billionaire-owned Aston Villa that in May won the Europa League; that is competing in this season’s Champions League, yet was forced to sell a host of A-list stars over the summer to comply with financial regulations. As Bayern head coach, Kompany hugely benefits from the spending restrictions that are ostensibly designed to protect a privileged few historically successful clubs, capping the ambitions of newly-moneyed prospective challengers. Witness Newcastle United’s unimaginably wealthy Saudi Arabian owners having to play poor when what they really wanted after their 2021 takeover was to embark on a Roman Abramovich-style raid of domestic and European rivals. As a player, Kompany joined Manchester City in August 2008, one month before the club was bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group. His 11-year stay included the period between 2009 and 2018 that is now viewed through the lens of City having been hit with 80 charges relating to financial wrongdoing over those nine years. Another 35 charges over failing to cooperate with a Premier League investigation from 2018 to 2023 were added to the club’s charge sheet. Last week, it emerged that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges. Ferran Soriano, the City chief executive, vowed that it would “take a lot more time” before a conclusive outcome is reached, with the club planning to vigorously appeal against the landslide verdicts. Juventus were stripped of their 2005 and 2006 Serie A titles after being busted for match-fixing. So endemic was the corruption in Italy’s top flight during the former campaign that the Italian Football Federation decided against crowning a champion. The following year’s title was reassigned to third-placed Inter Milan. Juventus were relegated to Serie B for the 2006-07 campaign. Away from football, Ben Johnson was stripped of his 1988 100m Olympic gold after testing positive for an anabolic steroid. The Canadian’s title was awarded to Carl Lewis, who would later be revealed as one of six men in the Seoul final to have committed doping transgressions during their careers. For seven straight years from 1999, the Tour de France is listed as having no winner following the exposure of “champion” Lance Armstrong as an incorrigible drugs cheat. Should the Premier League’s judgment on City’s guilt survive the appeals process, and they go down the route of redistributing the three titles that went to the Etihad Stadium in the nine years from 2009, the beneficiaries would be Manchester United, twice, and Liverpool. The runners-up to Pep Guardiola’s team in their five title-winning campaigns between 2018 and 2024, in order, were Liverpool, Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Arsenal. Three self-sustaining clubs, with their global fanbases and rich revenue streams, who perhaps stood to gain most in England when the introduction of an FFP framework was agreed in 2009. In 2013, Liverpool agreed a £1 million [around US$1.3 million] settlement fee with Manchester City after employees of the Merseyside club, apparently, repeatedly accessed their rivals’ scouting database. City’s alleged crimes came to light in 2018 following a Der Spiegel investigation, launched after the German website was sent leaked emails by Portuguese computer hacker Rui Pinto. Now living under police witness protection, Pinto tweeted the City verdict “was a historic decision for English football, and one that comes to crown the work I carried out through [his website] Football Leaks”. “Today, we all know that, through structural manipulation and financial manoeuvring, Manchester City did not merely circumvent the rules, they turned them into a mere formality, challenging any attempt to preserve the integrity of the competition,” Pinto wrote. Pinto uncovered evidence of Manchester City employing various underhand methods to misrepresent their financial situation. Among other offences, they were said to have inflated the value of sponsorship deals, and paid Roberto Mancini, the head coach who led City to the 2012 title, via two contracts to obscure the reality of his salary figure. In February 2023, the Premier League issued a sledgehammer statement outlining the 115 alleged rules breaches committed by City. Fifty-four related to their failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information between 2009 and 2018, while they faced 14 charges over failing to provide accurate reports for player and management compensation over the same period. Between 2015 and 2018, City were said to have breached the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules. Five charges centred on the club’s failure to comply with Uefa rules, including financial fair play regulations. The 35 charges over failing to cooperate with Premier League investigations were added to the rap sheet. It is believed that the number of charges against City has since climbed from 115 to 130. In charge of Burnley at the time of the Premier League’s offensive, Kompany, 3½ years ago, said: “I kind of look at it and sometimes roll my eyes a little bit. “No doubt there’s a lot of righteousness in the world to come and tell you what you’ve done wrong. “And then if everybody looks at themselves, I think the football industry, in general, is not one that can afford to point the finger too many times.” City’s case was heard by a three-person independent commission, from September 16 to December 6, 2024. That more than 21 months elapsed after the 12-week hearing before a verdict surfaced, via leaks to the media, would support Khaldoon Al Mubarak’s assertion that “the Premier League process still has a long way to run”. In an open letter to supporters on the club website, the Manchester City chairman added: “Our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.” Al Mubarak also stated that “there remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity”. Joe Hart, the goalkeeper in City’s 2012 and 2014 title-winning sides, said he had “no reason not to trust Khaldoon”. “I’m very proud of what I’ve achieved and what I did with Manchester City, and what we achieved as a team, and that doesn’t change,” Hart added. Back in 2020, City successfully appealed in the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) against a two-year Champions League ban imposed by Uefa, the European governing body. They were fined €10 million [around US$11.3 million] for not cooperating with Uefa’s investigation. In this instance, they will have no recourse to CAS, instead having their plea heard by a new independent three-person panel. Theoretically, that appeal verdict will draw a line under the process, but should City be unhappy with the result, they could potentially argue in the High Court that the initial verdict seeping out through unofficial channels compromised their case. They cited media leaks in their action against Uefa six years ago. Regardless of how it plays out, this episode has infiltrated every corner of the Premier League, driving a bus through the English top flight’s pompous claim to be the world’s best domestic competition. A penny for the thoughts of executives at Sky Sports, currently paying around £1.3 billion a year to screen a league where nobody knows whether what they have watched over the past 17 years was for real, in legal terms, at least. With their wish to tighten the belts of fat cats who would have gladly poured their own cash into clubs, and, by extension, invested in the English game, the Premier League has tied itself in knots. Railroaded into straitened circumstances, clubs are increasingly selling major assets overseas, leading to a steady talent drain. Still, if Manchester City are found to have ridden roughshod over rules they agreed to be bound to, all bets are off regarding their punishment. Everton have been hit with six and two-point deductions for offences that pale in number and significance against those City are said to have committed, while the Merseysiders have been ordered to pay Burnley £35 million over the supposed impact on the Turf Moor club of their rules breach. In 2024, Nottingham Forest had four points taken off them for one rule infringement. Leicester City, architects of the most uplifting story of the 34-year Premier League era, were last year hit with three charges over financial misdemeanours. Their six-point penalty cost them their Championship status. Optimism for City, in the event that the charges are upheld, comes in the shape of the £10 million fine and transfer ban imposed on Chelsea this summer, after their owners self-reported 74 breaches of Football Association rules that occurred under the chairmanship of Abramovich. The nuclear option for the Premier League would be to relegate Manchester City. Italian football’s slide from relevance accelerated after Juventus’ enforced demotion. In the 20 years since, two of the country’s clubs have been European champions, against 10 in the previous 50 years. Champions League winners in 1993, Marseille were relegated 12 months later after being found guilty of match-fixing offences. Writing in The Times newspaper this week, former striker Tony Cascarino, who joined the French club for their first season in Ligue 2, said that despite them regaining their top-tier status after two seasons, “Marseille have still not recovered from their demotion, and it happened 32 years ago”. In the tribal, cash-driven world of football, sympathy will be in short supply should Manchester City suffer a similarly sorry fate, regardless that nobody is suggesting they ever resorted to nefariously influencing matches. No, they stand charged with distorting their balance sheet, the document that increasingly determines modern football’s winners and losers.

title: Hong Kong’s executives are ‘ill prepared’ for AI era, report finds
description: The city’s firms have a severe lack of AI and cybersecurity expertise at the board level, leaving them ‘ill prepared’ for the coming era, report finds.
content: Executives at Hong Kong’s largest listed companies have a severe lack of technological expertise, with fewer than 1 per cent of directors possessing dedicated artificial intelligence or cybersecurity skills, according to a new report by Grant Thornton Hong Kong. The firm’s 15th annual Corporate Governance Review – which surveyed 100 major listed firms on Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Composite Index – found that 59 per cent of companies view cybersecurity or AI as principal business risks. Yet only 11 per cent had established specialised board committees to oversee digital threats and technology integration. These gaps have persisted despite the introduction of updated Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) Corporate Governance Code standards last year, which introduced mandatory director training, board skills matrices and stricter overboarding limits. “While overall disclosure quality on HKEX has improved, there remains a disconnect between acknowledged risks and technical expertise at the top,” said Barry Tong, head of advisory at Grant Thornton Hong Kong. Only 0.56 per cent of directors possessed cybersecurity expertise and just 0.26 per cent had specialist AI skills, while progress on gender diversity remained gradual, Tong added. “Hong Kong boards remain largely designed for an era focused on capital allocation and traditional risk,” said Ivan So, advisory director at Grant Thornton Hong Kong. “While that approach supported stability for decades, it leaves boards ill prepared for autonomous AI systems and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.” As many as 37 per cent of board seats are still filled by executives with traditional backgrounds in finance, accounting, business and economics, leaving nearly two-thirds of large-cap companies without a single director with technical information technology or cyber expertise, according to the report. However, boards are being refreshed at an accelerating pace ahead of HKEX’s introduction of a hard nine-year cap on independent non-executive director (INED) tenures. The average INED tenure in the city dropped from 6.8 years in 2025 to 5.8 years in 2026, the report found. Female representation among directors edged up slightly to 22 per cent, though it continues to lag behind European benchmarks of 34 to 40 per cent. Tong urged companies to leverage coming director turnover to recruit digital talent, warning that lagging capability in emerging risk areas was leaving firms vulnerable to operational disruptions and investor scrutiny.

title: From Hong Kong to Guangdong, exploring the rich tapestry of Cantonese culinary traditions
description: The region’s diverse food culture spans Cantonese, Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines, each with unique traditions yet interconnected flavours.
content: The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine? Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer. Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms. From Guangdong’s northern coast, the traditional Chiu Chow or Chaoshan dish of poached saltwater chicken sees the meat steeped in a heavily seasoned salt brine or master stock, cooled and served at room temperature with a pounded garlic vinegar dip. Hakka culinary heritage, founded in the hills of the province’s interior, takes an entirely different approach, wrapping the chicken tightly in paper and burying it completely in a pot of blazing hot, coarse sea salt. Four distinct takes, four very different culinary approaches. Yet all of these dishes developed in the historic Guangdong province, an area roughly a third the size of France or Spain. Despite their common origin, should these different culinary traditions all be considered Cantonese? Yes and no, says Silas Li, chef at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983. “I look at this almost like a family tree,” he says. “Technically, they represent distinct cultural traditions, but practically – and especially here in Hong Kong – they live under the same big roof.” Historically, geography is a key determinant of a cuisine’s evolution. Li calls it the “true mother of recipe development”. Shunde, sitting within the fertile Pearl River Delta surrounded by streams and fish ponds, supported a cuisine based on freshwater fish, mud carp, milk-yielding water buffalo, and tender river vegetables. For Li, this is the “cradle of classical Cantonese cooking”, the place where the region’s core standards for knife skills, slow-braising, seafood precision, and controlling the wok were established. Elsewhere, along Guangdong’s Chaoshan coast, Chiu Chow communities had direct access to the ocean, inspiring a cuisine centred on deep-sea catches, saltwater poaching, and marine preserves, such as home-made fish sauces. Hakka communities, however, were historically migratory and lived up in landlocked, rugged hills that offered no easy access to the coast or rivers. Consequently, they relied on calorie-dense pork, preserved salted vegetables and heavy salt-baking. In Hong Kong, however, the different traditions have lived together for so long that the lines have naturally blurred. “For me, Shun Tak is Cantonese core, while Chiu Chow and Hakka are sibling traditions that make our local food scene so much richer,” says Li, who draws inspiration for modern and classic dishes from all three culinary traditions at his restaurant in Happy Valley. Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing from Puning in Chaoshan is behind Shanghai’s two-Michelin-starred Amazing Chinese Cuisine and Selection by Du. Du says he prefers not to view the question of whether Chiu Chow is part of Cantonese cuisine as a “battle over belonging”. Instead, he casts a wider, more inclusive net, thinking of both traditions as integral parts of the cuisine of Lingnan, a geographical area below the Nanling mountains that encompasses Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Hong Kong, Macau and northern Vietnam, once occupied by the ancient Baiyue people. “From the perspective of Chinese culinary culture, Lingnan cuisine has always been a rich and open system. Cantonese (Guangfu), Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines together form the essential components of Lingnan culinary culture,” he says. Cantonese and Chiu Chow cooking both place great emphasis on seasonality, ingredient quality, natural flavours and a high level of craftsmanship. But for Du, the main defining feature of Chiu Chow cuisine is not a specific classic dish or set of dishes, but an obsessive pursuit of xian, or freshness/umami. “This freshness is not just about flavour, but an overall respect for seasonality, origin, firepower, knife skills, and the state of the ingredients. People in Chaoshan often talk about ‘eating fresh’ (shi xian), which means savouring the best possible state of today, this season and this exact moment,” he says. If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience Silas Li, Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 Chef Huang Jinghui, better known as Chef Fei, was born and raised in Chaoshan. He runs a small empire of celebrated restaurants, all of which specialise in Cantonese and Chiu Chow dishes. Chef Fei also highlights how porous boundaries between culinary traditions can be. “I see Chiu Chow cuisine and Cantonese cuisine as deeply interconnected culinary traditions, rather than two that need to be clearly separated,” he says. He points to the considerable overlap in ingredients, techniques and culinary traditions – from delicacies such as abalone, sea cucumber and fish maw to Chiu Chow-style braised dishes, Cantonese barbecue and traditional slow-cooked soups, each with its own expression across the two cuisines. However, he says that at the same time, Chiu Chow cuisine has its own distinctive regional character and culinary traditions. “For me, rather than focusing too much on how Chiu Chow cuisine should be categorised, what matters more is the flavour, craftsmanship and traditions it represents, and the richness and diversity it brings to the dining experience,” he says. While Du and Chef Fei are less fussy about a fluid, inclusive view of Cantonese cooking, Li at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 argues that maintaining distinct categories remains essential for the dining experience itself. “If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience,” he says. “If we just call it generic Chinese food, it dilutes the respect these ancient subcultures deserve.” While he finds diners from the communities whose cuisine he cooks to be his toughest critics, Li notes that the average local guest has become far more sophisticated. “The modern Hong Kong diner – and even international guests – is way more educated now,” Li says. “They aren’t just looking for a vague ‘Chinese meal’; they want provenance, they ask about techniques, and they appreciate the subtle regional nuances.” At Yan Garden in Beijing – a restaurant conceptualised by Chef Fei and led day-to-day by executive Chinese chef Peter Chen at the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen – Chen sees this curiosity playing out among broader audiences. He notes that around 10 to 15 per cent of guests are international, while the remainder are local Chinese consumers, with the dining experience itself serving as an educational bridge. “Dishes such as our traditional marinated specialities, seafood preparations and seasonal Chiu Chow delicacies often spark conversations about the cuisine’s heritage and techniques,” Chen says. Du observes a similar dynamic at Selection by Du in Shanghai. “Guests from Europe and the Americas tend to view us as ‘Chinese cuisine’, hoping to discover Chinese food through this meal,” he says. “Guests from Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau – owing to the deep Chiu Chow or Nanyang cultural roots in their home regions – more easily recognise the delicate nature and emphasis on original flavours in Chiu Chow cuisine.” This evolving awareness reflects a broader transformation across Chinese gastronomy. Over the last 10 years, Du notes that diners’ knowledge has expanded rapidly, moving regional cooking into a dynamic new phase. “More regional cuisines are establishing their own brand identities – Yunnan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Taizhou, Shunde and Zhejiang cuisines are all receiving increasing attention,” he says. “This does not mean Cantonese cuisine’s influence is waning, but rather that Chinese dining as a whole is becoming richer and more specialised.”

title: 7 must-visit exhibitions in October 2026, from BTS star RM’s collection to Jackson Pollock
