description: Explore the K-pop icon’s personal collection at SFMOMA, the legacy of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner, Issy Wood’s self-portraits, Rafael Pavarotti’s photography and more.
content: September may be one of the busiest months on the global art calendar, but October’s offerings are no less compelling. From BTS’ RM, who is opening his collection to the public in San Francisco, to exhibitions paying homage to the likes of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner, there is something for everyone whether you’re an art aficionado or a novice looking to discover the scene. Brâncuși: The Artist and His Studio Romanian artist Constantin Brâncuși, who rose to prominence in the first half of the 20th century thanks to his sculptures depicting the human shape in abstract form, is the subject of an exhibition at MOMA (Museum of Modern Art) in New York. Occupying the entire sixth floor of the museum, “Brâncuși: The Artist and His Studio” features pieces that include his artworks, tools and furniture, all lent from Paris’ Centre Pompidou, currently closed for an extensive renovation. From October 25 until February 27, 2027 Cézanne to Modigliani: Gifts of Modern Art from the Pearlman Collection Lovers of modern European paintings and sculptures should check out “Cézanne to Modigliani: Gifts of Modern Art from the Pearlman Collection” at the Brooklyn Museum in New York this autumn. A Brooklyn-born businessman who died in 1974, Henry Pearlman amassed a collection of works by the likes of Degas, Gauguin, Manet, Pissarro, Toulouse-Lautrec and Van Gogh. The show features more than 50 works from his important collection. From October 2 until April 18, 2027 Issy Wood: Self-Portraits London’s National Portrait Gallery inaugurates its new contemporary programme, named Artist Focus, with an exhibition dedicated to Issy Wood. Twelve portraits by the American-British artist will be on display at the exhibition, which is free to the public. Titled “Issy Wood: Self-Portraits”, the show includes the artist’s depiction of herself as a baby to close-ups of her face covered with a sheet mask. From October 9 until February 28, 2027 Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous Jackson Pollock, the leading pioneer of abstract expressionism, met fellow artist Lee Krasner in 1942. They married three years later and stayed together until Pollock’s death in 1956. An exhibition at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York – “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous” – traces their parallel lives and careers with more than 120 pieces from more than 80 US and international lenders. The show’s subtitle comes from a 1976 painting by Krasner, who passed away in 1984. From October 4 until January 31, 2027 Rafael Pavarotti The Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris celebrates the work of Brazilian photographer Rafael Pavarotti with an exhibition bringing together more than 130 photographs, including portraits of celebrities such as Rihanna, Beyonce and Harry Styles. Pavarotti’s fashion photography, which often pays homage to his roots, is also on display at the show, presented in partnership with Brazilian shopping mall operator Iguatemi. From October 2 until May 2, 2027 RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me In an unexpected move, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is teaming up with RM of BTS, the K-pop group, for an exhibition. An avid art collector, RM co-curated the show in collaboration with América Castillo and Hyoeun Kim of SFMOMA. “RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me” features almost 200 works from his personal collection and that of the museum. Artists ranging from Chang Ucchin and Kim Yun-shin to Georgia O’Keeffe and Henri Matisse are represented. From October 3 until February 7, 2027 The 90s: Art and Fashion Former British Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful is the curator of an exhibition at Tate Britain in London that pays homage to one of the UK’s most exciting times in fashion and pop culture. “The 90s: Art and Fashion” explores the creative energy of a decade when fashion designers like the late Alexander McQueen, multimedia artists like Tracey Emin and photographers like Wolfgang Tillmans first rose to prominence. From October 8 until February 14, 2027 Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Ex-American Idol singer Caleb Flynn convicted of murdering wife, staging home invasion
description: Former Ohio pastor faces life in prison after shooting spouse while having affair with an intern.
content: A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on American Idol was convicted of murder on Tuesday in the killing of his wife while he was having an affair. Prosecutors said Caleb Flynn, 40, staged a home invasion in February after shooting his wife, Ashley Flynn, a 37-year-old teacher and volleyball coach. Flynn, who claimed his wife was killed by a burglar, could get up to life in prison without the chance of parole when he’s sentenced on Monday. Flynn closed his eyes, shook his head to the side and fought to maintain his composure as the judge read the guilty verdicts on charges of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence. He began sobbing while the judge dismissed the jury. His lawyer called the verdicts “disappointing” and said he expects to file an appeal. He wanted to keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself Matthew Joseph, prosecutor Flynn appeared on American Idol in 2013, telling television viewers about how his wife had encouraged him to chase his dreams on the singing competition. He sang before judges Mariah Carey, Randy Jackson and Nicki Minaj but did not advance to the main competition in Hollywood. Prosecutors told jurors during closing arguments on Tuesday that Flynn wanted out of his marriage when he shot his wife at their home in Tipp City, a suburb north of Dayton. Flynn and the couple’s two daughters were home when police arrived. The night before the fatal shooting, he sent a text to his lover saying: “I choose you. I’m free. Actions will come tomorrow,” said Matthew Joseph, an assistant Miami County prosecutor. Flynn did not want to lose his daughters, his high-paying job at his wife’s family business or his position in the church, prosecutors said. “He wanted to keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself,” Joseph said. Prosecutors did not find the gun used to kill Ashley Flynn, but they said his fingerprints and DNA were all over the scene. They also said his devices showed that he was moving about the house even though he told investigators he was sleeping when his wife was shot. During the trial, the woman who said she was having an affair with Flynn testified that he said he hated his wife and had thoughts of killing her. Flynn’s lawyer told the jury on Tuesday that investigators never found evidence that Flynn had fired a gun that day. “His being unfaithful doesn’t equal murder,” Patrick Mulligan said. “The issue here isn’t, ‘Was he a good husband?’” Text messages Flynn sent to his lover complaining about his wife were meant to make her feel good, Mulligan said. Alleigha Botner testified she met Flynn in 2022 while she was a 20-year-old intern at his church and had an affair with him for more than a year. Botner read some of her text messages with Flynn. About six months before the killing, Flynn wrote: “I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail.”

title: 5 universities in Hong Kong rank in top 100 in ‘historic’ shift from West to East
description: University of Hong Kong retains position as city’s highest-ranked institution, at 33rd, in Times Higher Education World University Rankings.
content: Five public universities in Hong Kong have ranked in the top 100 of a renowned British publication’s latest global league table, as part of a trend described as a “historic realignment” of academic prowess from West to East. The University of Hong Kong remained the city’s highest-ranked tertiary institution, holding onto 33rd place from the previous year, in the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings, released on Wednesday. The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) ranked 42nd, down from 41st a year ago, while the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology maintained its position at 58. CUHK said it achieved full marks across five core performance metrics – research excellence; patents; research and institutional income; research productivity; and the proportion of international staff – while making notable gains in teaching reputation, student-staff ratio and the proportion of international students. “These results reflect the university’s sustained strength in teaching quality, research capability and global outlook,” it said. Meanwhile, City University climbed three spots to 70, its highest position yet, while Polytechnic University advanced one position to 79. Baptist University ranked 205th, compared with last year’s spot in the 201–250 band. Lingnan University, which made its debut in the previous rankings, reached 257th in the latest showing, up from its past place in the 301–350 band. An Education Bureau spokesman said on Wednesday that the rankings reflected the strength of Hong Kong’s higher education system and its world-class levels in teaching, research and international outlook. “Even in the face of intense global competition, the performance of Hong Kong’s universities continues to remain stable and excellent,” he said. “Looking ahead, with the comprehensive implementation of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, the promotion of the integrated development of education, technology, and talent, and the development of the Northern Metropolis University Town, Hong Kong’s higher education is ushering in a golden period of development full of promising potential.” The spokesman added that the government would spare no effort to promote the integration of Hong Kong’s higher education sector into the country’s overall national development, helping to make China a world leader in education. The latest rankings cover a record 2,297 universities across 118 countries and territories, an increase of 106 institutions, compared with the previous year. According to THE, the rankings were built on an analysis of about 20 million research papers, around 1 million votes from an academic reputation survey and “detailed institutional data” from more than 3,000 universities worldwide. The 17 performance metrics were grouped into five categories: teaching; research environment; research quality; industry; and international outlook. THE noted that the latest rankings reflected a particularly strong showing for Asian institutions. A record number of universities took part this time, while many top-ranked institutions improved their position, it said. Asian universities also ranked in the global top 15 for the first time ever. The continent’s top-performing institution was Beijing’s Tsinghua University, at 11th and up one spot from last year, followed by Peking University at 13th and the National University of Singapore at 15th. THE described mainland China overall as Asia’s “leading light,” boasting more than 100 universities in the ranking, eight of which were in the top 100. Phil Baty, THE’s chief global affairs officer, said the latest rankings featured many instances of what he called “symbolic landmarks”, including the first time a mainland university had ranked ahead of any institution in continental Europe. He also said the latest rankings had the lowest number of American institutions in the top 200. “It is now clear that the tectonic plates of global higher education are shifting permanently,” Baty said. “The latest World University Rankings suggest that we are witnessing a historic realignment of academic power from West to East.” Despite the broader shift, universities from the United States and the United Kingdom continue to dominate the top 10. The UK’s Oxford University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the US held onto first and second place, respectively, from last year. Princeton University and Stanford University tied for third place. Rounding out the top 10 were the University of Cambridge, Harvard University, the California Institute of Technology, Imperial College London, the University of California, Berkeley and Yale University.

title: Editorial | Both China and Asean must capitalise on Pinglu Canal’s potential
description: The canal offers a new gateway for trade between China and Southeast Asia, cutting travel time and logistics costs.
content: For centuries, geography has been a burden for China’s southwest. Cargo had to travel a long way east to reach the sea through the ports of Guangdong. The Pinglu Canal, which opened to navigation in Guangxi in September, changes all that. It is the first river-to-sea canal built since the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949. A feat of engineering, it is a new gateway for trade between China and Southeast Asia. Whether it becomes a two-way gateway will depend on the choices made by Beijing and by members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). The canal will reduce both distance and cost. A 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway, it links the Xijiang River with the northwestern arm of the Gulf of Tonkin stretching between southern China and northern Vietnam. It gives large swathes of southwest China, including provinces such as Yunnan and Guizhou, a shorter route to the sea and to markets in Asia. For goods leaving the southwest, it cuts more than 560km off the journey to the sea compared with the traditional routes through Guangdong. It can take vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes. Three lock complexes or “water elevators” – at Madao, Qishi and Qingnian – lower ships through a 65-metre drop. Guangxi officials estimate that logistics costs will fall by 18 to 30 per cent, saving more than 5 billion yuan (US$745 million) a year. The project cost 72.7 billion yuan, a large sum but proportionate to the trade it serves. China-Asean trade reached 5.95 trillion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 20.6 per cent year on year. Asean has been China’s largest trading partner for six years in a row. Beibu Gulf Port, at the canal’s southern end, grew its container capacity from 2.28 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) – standard units which measure cargo capacity – in 2017 to 10.06 million last year. On a September 16 maiden journey, a container ship left Nanning, sailed through the canal and docked at Can Tho Port in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta. On the return trip, it carried 40 containers of Vietnamese rice bran bound for inland Guangxi. Exporters in the delta, whose rice, fruit and seafood spoil quickly, have long had to tranship goods at several coastal ports. They now have a more direct route into the Chinese interior. The Vietnamese coffee chain Trung Nguyen Legend says seagoing barges carrying its coffee beans could sail straight to Nanning without transferring to smaller vessels. Asean imported US$546 billion worth of goods from China in the first eight months of this year, up 25.8 per cent year on year, while the bloc’s exports to China stood at US$316.7 billion. At the China-Asean Expo in Nanning, a Thai trade official warned that a faster, cheaper route for Chinese parts and machinery could widen that trade gap further. Her concern is reasonable. Infrastructure does not choose which direction goods flow. Prices, market access and regulation decide that. It behoves all sides to work together for free trade. The canal gives it a practical way to do just that. Customs clearance for Asean agricultural products should be quicker, sanitary approvals should be simplified and the upgraded China-Asean Free Trade Area 3.0 protocol should be implemented fully without delay. Asean governments and their private sectors need to proactively work together to take advantage of the new opportunities rather than wait for the Chinese side. The canal has had a human cost. According to official figures, 11,228 people in 2,764 households had to be resettled. But custom-designed homes, financial compensation and job training served to mitigate the drastic disruption to their lives. The Pinglu Canal will also be a strategic asset. The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has shown how fragile trade becomes when it depends on a few chokepoints. Diversified routes like the one offered by the canal make the whole region more resilient. The canal is the new gateway for trade and commerce. Beijing and its neighbours must now make sure trade flows freely in both directions.

title: Hong Kong-born, London-based designer Katie Ko wanted to be a ballet dancer. What changed?
description: Sculpture or fashion? Katie Ko talks about embellishing her garments with unusual materials and how ballet remains a big part of her work.
content: London-based fashion designer Katie Ko blurs the line between fashion and fine art, turning unconventional materials such as bamboo strips and preserved flowers into wearable narratives that seemingly defy gravity. Taffeta ruffles and feather-adorned layers explode from Ko’s silk bodices while other pieces evoke the elegance of porcelain. The 26-year-old also pays homage to her hometown, Hong Kong, which she left at 18. She says her 2025 spring/summer collection, “Chrysanthemum Dew”, was inspired by Hong Kong brand Vitasoy’s chrysanthemum tea drink. “I loved that growing up,” she says, “and I was really missing Hong Kong food.” But Ko, who founded her eponymous label in 2024, was not always into fashion; in fact, she did not pick up a needle until she was 17. She dedicated her formative years to dance and fine arts and dreamed of becoming a professional ballet dancer. Ko’s art teacher at school, Andrea Dryland, introduced her to Hong Kong-based artist Leanne Claxton, who specialised in screen printing. Ko worked for her as a high school student and even into university, learning how to create print designs on fabric. “It wasn’t a path that my parents really wanted for me – you know, Asian parents,” Ko says of her choice to pursue fashion. “But my art teacher at the time, she was the most supportive teacher I could ever ask for.” Ko eventually moved to the UK to enrol at the London College of Fashion, then studied for a bachelor’s degree at Ravensbourne University London and got her master’s degree in fashion from London’s Royal College of Art. From art student to brand founder Following apprenticeships at small independent brands after graduation, Ko felt a pull to start something of her own. “I don’t really like listening to other people about what to do – I’m not very good at that,” Ko laughs. She had a bit of money saved up from working part-time jobs and bought fabrics and materials. But, ultimately, Ko thanks her parents for financially supporting her through her schooling. “It’s not one of those sob stories, like, ‘Oh my god, I couldn’t afford anything,’” she says. “My parents did support me. It is really tough in fashion when you don’t have that. But when I graduated and I started my own brand, I was still working all these other jobs because I didn’t want to fully rely on my parents.” Ko is the only full-time employee in her company, but she hires freelancers and fashion students to help her with projects. She recalls how grateful she was when she landed internships and wants to provide the same for others now that she is in the position to. Bamboo, flowers and fashion as sculpture Despite having a background in fine art, Ko says painting alone did not make her feel complete, and that she wanted “to push that idea even further”. This is how textiles eventually made their way into her craft. Today, many of Ko’s pieces are made out of fabric she has hand-painted. Ko’s fashion philosophy lingers in the liminal space between sculpture and garment. She begins her creative process by playing around with shape and texture. “Because of my fine art background, I kind of approach my work sculpturally as an art piece more than a wearable piece in the beginning,” she says. She then fine-tunes the piece as sculpture or garment. This is how she was inspired to use bamboo strips in her 2026 autumn/winter collection, “Beneath the Lotus”, which introduced a new architectural challenge. “It’s really fragile … we had to soak the bamboo in water for a bit so that it then softened a bit before we moulded it and twisted it into shape,” Ko says. The process was so laborious that her mother even helped her out. The garment’s upper body is decorated with thin bamboo strips twisted into shapes akin to Chinese knots. Ko also sews real, preserved flowers into her pieces. Working with Hong Kong florist Anita Li, Ko learned how to stitch flowers onto her fabrics, which “fall and break”. “I kind of love that because it’s so natural,” she says. “And when it falls during a shoot, as well, it’s actually so beautiful because that’s just the nature of things. You can’t expect something to stay perfectly like that forever.” Ko recently began creating bridal gowns, which she says is quite a different process requiring thinking about the entire wedding aesthetic and not just the dress in isolation. To safeguard her design standards and protect her artistic vision, Ko turns down requests from brides when their ideas diverge too far from her own aesthetic. Flowers and organic forms remain Ko’s ultimate muse, from which she thinks she will continue to draw endless inspiration. A full circle ballet moment Although Ko’s interest in fashion overtook ballet, it remains a big part of her work. For Ko’s debut solo show for her 2025 autumn/winter collection, “Étude”, she collaborated with Royal Ballet soloist Valentino Zucchetti, who choreographed a performance for the models wearing her garments. “I’m still looking at ballet-like movements and the way fabric moves when a dancer is wearing it,” Ko says. “It’s part of my creative process that it just didn’t make sense to then have a static model wear my clothes at the end.” Ko emphasises that any aspiring artist should just trust their gut. When she was in university, she was told “not to do this and that, and to change my style and everything” and says she “ended up hating my work”. Ko had to learn to listen to herself and focus on what she wants. Perhaps it is not bad advice – after all, Ko has found a way to merge her two biggest loves. She is also working on a custom gala piece for Royal Ballet principal dancer Melissa Hamilton. “It really feels like a full circle moment,” Ko says. “Being a dancer and then a designer and then still being connected to ballet now.”

title: AI uptake sees wealth management headcounts in Hong Kong trail growth in assets
description: Capco research finds that private wealth assets rose 24 per cent last year, but number of people employed by industry rose just 2 per cent.
content: Hong Kong has seen strong growth in private wealth assets, but the industry has not yet seen the same scale of hiring, as private banks and wealth management companies have adopted technology including AI to serve customers, according to consulting firm Capco. “When assets under management by private banks are growing rapidly, the relationship managers are not increasing at the same rate as the use of technology and AI are enhancing the productivity of the team,” Simon Smallcombe, Capco’s insurance and wealth leader in the Asia-Pacific region, said in an interview on Monday. Financial firms in Hong Kong managed HK$42.2 trillion (US$5.38 trillion) worth of assets last year, up 20 per cent year on year, according to the Securities and Futures Commission, with a 24 per cent increase in private bank and family office assets – to HK$12.9 trillion – driving the growth. However, Smallcombe said that Capco research based on commission data had found that headcount in the private bank industry had risen just 2.2 per cent – from 9,920 in 2024 to 10,140 last year. A report detailing the firm’s findings will be released on Wednesday. Many private banks and wealth management companies had adopted artificial intelligence and other technology tools in recent years, allowing bankers to spend less time on administrative work, Smallcombe said. When they need to have succession planning or sophisticated investment decisions, they would talk to someone they can trust Simon Smallcombe, Capco He said the trend would continue, allowing private banks and wealth management companies to support rising assets without the need to increase the size of their workforces. However, Smallcombe added, AI would not replace humans in the industry. “The clients may search simple information via AI, but when they need to have succession planning or sophisticated investment decisions, they would talk to someone they can trust,” he said. Bankers employed at private banks did not need to worry about competition with AI, but should embrace AI to do their jobs, Smallcombe said. “The role of the relationship managers at private banks will change as technology will allow them to have greater capacity,” he said. “When AI and technology help to remove the burden of administration from the relationship managers, they can have more time to spend with the customers.” He also said clients wanted to see their relationship managers use AI to quickly provide them with more information. “Customers’ expectations are elevated because they can order something online and the goods could be delivered the next day,” Smallcombe said. “They can order food, and that can be delivered instantly. Their expectation of speed has escalated.” That meant bankers also needed to use technology to provide high-quality services that helped clients make quick investment decisions, and to deliver unimpeded processing. “The combination of technology and humans would be a powerful blend to enable relationship managers not only to sell products, but also to offer comprehensive financial advisory services to customers,” he said. “The role of relationship managers in the era of technology could actually be expanded to other areas such as succession planning.” Smallcombe noted that HSBC had announced a plan to hire more relationship managers in Singapore while at the same time investing more in AI.

title: WestK Picnic Fest brings Hong Kong’s favourite pastime to the heart of the city
description: WestK launches its first large-scale urban picnic festival this autumn at the Art Park, featuring gourmet food, live music, cultural workshops and slow-living experiences.
content: Hong Kong has enjoyed a rich history of picnic gatherings at scenic locations since the 1970s, when dedicated facilities and infrastructure were first introduced through the establishment of country parks to encourage outdoor recreation. While getting together at beaches and in the countryside remains a beloved pastime, the West Kowloon Cultural District is redefining this tradition with an urban picnic concept in the heart of the city. Set against the sweeping views of Victoria Harbour and iconic Hong Kong Island skyline, the sprawling green spaces of the Art Park’s Harbourside East Lawn offer all the charm of an outdoor escape without compromising on convenience. As the refreshing autumn air sets in, WestK Picnic Fest will run on weekends and public holidays until October 11, making for an enticing alfresco outing for families, friends and four-legged companions. Central to the WestK Picnic Fest is a mouth-watering array of gastronomic offerings. Sixteen food and beverage venues in the West Kowloon Cultural District, including restaurants and cafes such as Pano, Haru, Cupping Room, Lau Bak Livehouse, Lau Kee Boat Noodles, Play With Years, Baby Sonny’s, Sawadee Car and more, are partnering with the event to present exclusive picnic sets. Limited-time food stalls are in the mix as well, offering an eclectic range of flavours, from elevated Hong Kong street snacks and Korean bites to artisanal doughnuts, craft beers and cocktails. Best of all, with rental options available for picnic essentials – tables, mats, foldable chairs, portable fans and lanterns – visitors don’t have to lug their entire living room to the Art Park, provided they snag the items early, as all are provided on a first-come, first-served basis, with refundable deposits required. Aside from food, views and, hopefully, excellent weather, the WestK Picnic Fest also brings the fun with a programme of activities. Community-wellness group The Picnic Club will be at the event to promote the art of slow living under the theme “Localisation”. Join workshops inspired by Hong Kong’s natural landscapes and cultural heritage, such as harp therapy, making botanical ceramics and crafting natural fragrances, or enjoy curated farm-to-table encounters featuring seasonal ingredients, in collaboration with Hong Kong coffee brand Nutmad. If you want to do it all, WestK’s Bike & Picnic Pass bundles rentals for bicycles, picnic mats and lanterns into one, and includes access to themed experience sessions, as well as special merchant offers. No outdoor festival is complete without a lively atmosphere and entertainment. Local musicians will perform acoustic sets, jazz numbers and more, while the family-friendly “DJ x Bubble Party”, on October 4, promises upbeat music with bubbles, creating a memorable afternoon for children and adults alike. Harbour breezes, shared meals on the grass and lingering sunsets – the WestK Picnic Fest serves as an open call to the city, inviting residents and tourists to slow down in style. WestK Picnic Fest. Every Friday, Saturday, Sunday and public holiday until October 11. Harbourside East Lawn, Art Park, West Kowloon Cultural District, Tsim Sha Tsui. Free entry

title: Morocco’s king appoints El Mansouri as first woman prime minister
description: Her Authenticity and Modernity Party, which pushes for social modernisation and secular-leaning views, won the recent election.
content: King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri on Tuesday as Morocco’s first woman prime minister after her liberal-centrist party came out on top in a September 23 parliamentary election, the royal palace said. The king asked El Mansouri to form a new government, the palace said in a ‌statement. El Mansouri’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) was created in 2008 by an adviser to the king and has since positioned itself as a counterweight to the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) by advocating social modernisation and secular-leaning views. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy where the king retains sweeping powers over foreign policy, defence and other key portfolios. Under Morocco’s constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that wins the largest number of seats in the House of ⁠Representatives. PAM, which was the second-largest member in the outgoing coalition, moved up to the top spot, bolstered by the recruitment of Fouzi ‌Lekjaa, Morocco’s football federation chief and two-time government budget manager, who joined weeks before the vote. El Mansouri, a lawyer who was housing minister in the outgoing government and Marrakech mayor, will lead talks to ‌form a coalition government and submit a list of cabinet members for the king’s approval. The incoming ⁠government will oversee the ⁠last stages of a US$20 billion push to get ready for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Portugal and Spain. It will also implement economic policies ‌aimed at addressing widespread youth discontent, an issue highlighted by a mass border rush on the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July and deadly Gen-Z-led protests last year. PAM ‌won 97 ‌seats, followed by its partners in the outgoing government, the liberal-centrist National Rally of Independents (RNI) with 66 seats, and the ‌conservative nationalist Istiqlal with 65. During the campaign, PAM had ruled out staying in a coalition with the RNI – the two had ⁠traded blame over policy shortcomings including a failure to halt rises in food prices. But El Mansouri said on Thursday she would ⁠have no “red lines” when it came to negotiations. “We have turned the page,” she said. Abdelilah Benkirane, former prime minister and leader of the PJD, which won 54 seats, said the party would stay in opposition. Three leftist parties took smaller shares ‌of the seats. Turnout, closely watched as ‌an indicator of trust in elected institutions, fell to about 38 per cent from around 50 per cent in the previous elections five years ago, when the moderate Islamist PJD was dealt a crushing defeat after a decade in power. In recent years, King Mohammed VI had appointed a female adviser, and Morocco has had women in senior institutional roles. The outgoing government had four women ministers.

title: Exclusive | Xi-Trump summit drew Chinese CEOs. So why couldn’t they get a seat at the table?
description: Of the 134 guests at White House state dinner, only 19 were part of the Chinese delegation.
content: As American billionaires gathered at the White House to honour Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan last Thursday, a group of Chinese business leaders spent the evening on the sidelines. They had travelled to the US capital to join the state dinner. But their invitations never arrived. For weeks, their participation was the subject of intense discussion between Washington and Beijing. While it was under consideration until the summit’s final hours, they were ultimately excluded due to poor communication between the two governments, the two sides’ differing views on reciprocity and the White House’s unclear attitude towards Chinese investments in the United States, according to multiple sources. More than 130 high-profile guests attended the dinner, including some of America’s most prominent tycoons. Several were seated at the main table alongside the leaders and first ladies, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Apple executive chairman Tim Cook. Of the 134 guests, only 19 were part of the Chinese delegation. This was in sharp contrast to Trump’s May state visit to Beijing, where the US delegation featured Musk, Cook, Huang, and David Solomon from Goldman Sachs. They attended several events and meetings, including the banquet at the Great Hall of the People. The South China Morning Post first reported in August that Chinese and US officials were discussing the possibility of business leaders joining Xi’s delegation. Figures from some of China’s most prominent firms – including electric vehicle maker BYD, battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited and smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi – were expected to be part of the Chinese business delegation. Two sources said that Washington first proposed the idea of inviting Chinese business leaders during the preparations for the summit as a matter of reciprocity – the guiding principle of Xi’s visit – following Trump’s May trip. The sources added that China accepted the proposal in principle and requested further details from the US regarding planned meetings and official engagements. However, the White House side was slow to address these inquiries. While frustrated by the delay, the Chinese side told several companies that their executives should be ready to travel to Washington at short notice, the sources said. Two sources noted that Beijing viewed the lack of communication as evidence of Washington’s reluctance to invite Chinese businesses to the White House. One source familiar with the matter said the two sides differed over what reciprocity meant in practice. For Beijing, the American business leaders who accompanied Trump on his May trip were part of the delegation, which set a precedent for Xi’s visit. Washington, however, only wanted to extend this reciprocity to senior government officials, the source said. The SCMP earlier reported that divergence between Washington and Beijing over potential Chinese investment announcements also created roadblocks for the business delegation’s participation. A source said that Washington and Beijing remained divided over the Board of Investment, particularly on the terms for potential Chinese investments in the US, further casting a cloud over the delegation’s participation. The investment forum was one of the outcomes from Xi and Trump’s last summit in Beijing. Another source said the two sides had discussed potential deals that could be announced during Xi’s visit, including one involving Chinese batteries, but the negotiations failed to make headway. The official accounts released after the summit confirmed the lack of progress. While the US fact sheet repeated its May reference to the investment board, the Chinese read-out made no mention of it. Washington’s position on Chinese investments in the US – especially in the auto sector – remained unsettled ahead of the summit, with American carmakers and lawmakers increasingly pushing back against the prospect. Trump, however, said earlier this month that Chinese carmakers could establish manufacturing plants in the US. “If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” he told Fox News. Despite Trump’s openness to the idea, his administration was seeking to address concerns at home as its political base remained divided over Chinese investment in the US, a source said. “In this instance, even Trump could not bend his administration, let alone his party, to his will,” another source added. Just three days before the visit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng at JPMorgan’s headquarters in New York to finalise the summit’s deliverables. Two sources said the issue of the Chinese business delegation came up, but the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. By that time, the SCMP had already reported that a small group of Chinese CEOs had independently travelled to Washington ahead of Xi’s arrival. A source familiar with the issue said the group was expected to include representatives of Chinese electric-vehicle companies, which had shown particularly strong interest in investing in the US. Bessent and He discussed the matter again during a second meeting last Wednesday at the World Bank’s offices in Washington, but made no progress, the sources said. The business leaders’ presence at that stage became a matter of optics rather than substance, according to another source. While the optics mattered to Beijing, which was unhappy with Washington’s stance, it chose not to press the issue further and risk overshadowing a state visit otherwise marked by pomp and pageantry. The Chinese business leaders “should’ve come in numbers and attended the state dinner regardless of what they could achieve or not achieve”, a source said. “It would’ve been a huge soft power coup.” Additional reporting by Khushboo Razdan and William Zheng

title: Man dragged to death by New York subway train after bag gets caught in door
description: Passenger was killed in Brooklyn during evening rush hour as he attempted to exit a train.
content: A man was dragged to death by a New York subway train when a bag he was carrying got stuck in the door during the Monday evening rush hour commute, police said. Yaw Boahene, 57, was exiting the train at a Brooklyn subway station at around 6pm when his bag, which police described as a shopping bag, snagged in the closing train doors. The Brooklyn resident was pulled onto the tracks and run over by the train as it left the station, police said in a statement. Officers arrived to find Boahene “unconscious and unresponsive” on the train tracks, police said. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The medical examiner’s office will determine the cause of death. The police investigation is ongoing. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which runs the subway system, said both the train operator and conductor have been removed from service, as is routine while the investigation continues. The agency said the train was one of the fleet’s newest models. It was inspected after the man’s death and also previously in July, and no mechanical issues were found. Dragging deaths happen from time to time on the nation’s largest subway system. In 2022, a 20-year-old commuter was killed after his backpack or a piece of his clothing got stuck in the door as he was trying to get onto a train at the Columbus Circle station in upper Manhattan.

title: Opinion | America’s foreign policy of coercion must end
description: Trump’s routine use of threats and ultimatums in place of diplomacy may yield immediate gains, but it inflicts lasting damage to America’s global standing.
content: If you want to understand how Washington exercises power in the world, watch what it does when its closest allies try to deepen ties with each other. When EU chief Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union’s first-ever “associate member”, US President Donald Trump’s response was swift and blunt: “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.” He called the idea “laughable” and Canada – America’s neighbour and closest ally – a “terrible trade partner”. In place of diplomacy, the US uses threats and ultimatums as an instrument of statecraft. Trump has threatened to seize Greenland by force, never mind that Denmark is a Nato ally. He has threatened tariffs on Brics nations if they try to create an alternative currency to the US dollar. More recently, the US State Department reportedly drafted a letter warning its partners against joining a China-led AI framework. The examples are too many to list. Coercion has become a go-to tool of US foreign policy. Washington now routinely uses market access, technological control, financial infrastructure, security guarantees and diplomatic isolation as tools to force compliance – targeting not only strategic rivals, but also non-confrontational developing countries and even allies. Why has Washington embraced coercion with such abandon? Part of the answer is Trump’s mercantile mindset: maximum pressure yields maximum concessions. But the deeper answer lies at the intersection of US hegemonic habit and declining soft power. Coercion is not new to US foreign policy. After the end of the Cold War, coercion became a hallmark of US diplomacy. As the world’s sole superpower, possessed of unrivalled economic and military might, the US leaned on coercive pressure when it suited its interests. Many in China remember former secretary of state Antony Blinken’s warning, ahead of the 2021 high-level Alaska talks, that the US would speak “from a position of strength”. At the same time, Washington’s use of coercion also reflects America’s declining soft appeal: the ability to attract and persuade, not merely to coerce. The shift from what some scholars call US systemic legitimacy to coercive dominance began after the events of September 11 and accelerated through the 2010s as the US increasingly weaponised financial surveillance, secondary sanctions and executive action. A decline in soft power means Washington has to dominate by fear. What once depended on persuasion, institution-building and collaboration with foreign elites now relies on unilateral legal action, naked threats and unapologetic coercion. Consequently, a Morning Consult survey across 41 countries last year found China’s net favourability rating at 8.8, against negative 1.5 for the US. Since he returned to the White House, Trump’s coerced gains have been nothing short of impressive: over US$4 trillion (over US$5 trillion, according to the Peterson Institute for International Economics) in investment commitments from key economies, priority access to critical minerals from Ukraine and African countries, and energy from Saudi Arabia, a tighter hold over the Latin American “backyard”, increased Nato members’ spending, “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland – Trump’s words – and “America first” clauses embedded in bilateral deals. The harm to the rest of the world, however, is far-reaching. When Washington forces them to choose sides, for instance, it does not just constrain their foreign policy – it undermines the premise of sovereign equality on which small and mid-sized states rely. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has repeatedly rejected forced alignment, seeing the notion that Asean, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must choose sides as untenable. Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan struck a similar note – in 2021, he said Singapore would “be useful but … not be made use of”. Being useful means cooperating on one’s terms; being used translates to someone else setting the terms. Coercion can win short-term victories for Washington. But Trump’s threat over Canada’s EU associate-member status exposes its fundamental flaws. Threatening trade retaliation against a decades-long ally over a purely regional integration project sends a clear signal to every capital worldwide: no nation, friend or foe, is safe from American punitive pressure. The international community wants diplomacy built on sovereign equality and mutual benefit in this multipolar age. If Washington does not rein in its reflex of coercion, its global influence will keep slipping.

title: Burnham vows big shake-up for UK in high-risk political speech
description: Prime minister promises national care service, electoral reform and EU reset while warning of pension funding trade-offs.
content: New British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out a sweeping political vision on Tuesday, pledging to give Britain “a new social contract for the 21st century”, reform the country’s electoral system and reset its relationship with its European neighbours. But he acknowledged that economic constraints make delivering his sweeping plans a big political risk. “Small things will not get us through what are difficult times,” Burnham said in a tough-love speech to the centre-left Labour Party’s annual conference. Two months after becoming leader of the UK’s governing party, Burnham set out a crowd-pleasing vision of more social housing, better education and more affordable care for the elderly. But he warned that money would have to come from welfare and pension spending to deliver the changes. Anticipating opposition to his plans, Burnham said: “I have given you what you often say is missing from politics: honesty, ideas and a clear direction for the country we all love”. Some of Burnham’s announcements in the hour-long speech will spark big political fights. Burnham said he would stake his political legacy on establishing a “national care service” to fix what he called a “ broken” social care system. He said that like the much-loved but overstretched National Health Service it would be free to use and would be paid for through taxation. Burnham held back tears as he spoke about his experiences of the care system with his father, Roy, who died earlier this month. To help fund the care service, which will be introduced if Labour wins the next election, Burnham said he would water down the long-unassailable pensions triple lock, an expensive policy that guarantees pensions rise each year by the annual increase in consumer price inflation, average wage growth, or 2.5 per cent, whichever is highest. “I accept I may pay a political price,” he said. “But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.” Burnham argued that Britain took a wrong turn in the 1980s with the free-market reforms and privatisation of key industries under Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. “Deindustrialisation. Deregulation. Privatisation. Austerity. Brexit. And what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest,” he said. Burnham vowed to “move beyond a decade of drift and division” and end the economic and political turmoil that have made him the UK’s seventh prime minister since the country voted in 2016 to leave the European Union. In a major move on that front, he said Labour would contest the next election on changing Britain’s winner-takes-all electoral system to a form of proportional representation. He also promised a rethink of Britain’s relationship with the EU, saying “Brexit has done more harm than good” and the UK needs “clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in”. Also on Burnham’s ambitious agenda: ending street homelessness, cutting youth unemployment and exerting more public control over Britain’s privatised utilities. Labour’s conference slogan this year was “Hope Again”, and Burnham’s relaxed, social-media friendly confidence has been a tonic to his party. As the sun glinted on the River Mersey beside the conference centre in Liverpool, the mood was a world away from last year’s downbeat gathering, when delegates despaired about then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s dire approval ratings and the seemingly unstoppable rise of the anti-immigration opposition party Reform UK. Events came to a head months later when a panicky party forced Starmer’s resignation and his replacement by Burnham as party leader and prime minister in July. But as delegates gathered, terror arrests near a US-run airbase in England brought home the daunting global situation and unexpected challenges facing the neophyte prime minister. Five men were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offences outside the RAF Fairford base in western England. They have been released on bail while police probe lines of inquiry including a link to a hostile state. That meant Burnham and his cabinet were peppered during the conference with questions about security lapses and potential threats from Iran or Russia. Burnham also acknowledged the gloomy economic backdrop against which Treasury chief John Healey will deliver the government’s budget on October 28. The US-Iran war continues to choke shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices soaring and pushing up inflation and the cost of government borrowing. Burnham said his government would “stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down”. “I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford,” Burnham said. The next general election does not have to be called until 2029, but Labour’s “Burnham bounce” has sparked talk of a snap election. Burnham insists he will not go to voters early, and John Curtice, professor of politics at the University of Strathclyde, said that it was a wise decision. Curtice said Burnham had given Labour “a halo effect from a popular leader”. “But the challenge for this party now is to change that halo effect from the leader to the party,” Curtice said. “This party needs to make much more progress before it can contemplate the prospect of an election.”

title: Trump rejects calls to work with China on AI safety despite Xi summit progress
description: US president also announces voluntary accord signed by leaders of six major US tech companies to address concerns surrounding AI technology.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday he does not want to work with China on addressing artificial intelligence (AI) risks, arguing that cooperation could undermine America’s lead in the fast-moving technology, as he announced a voluntary accord signed by the leaders of six major US tech companies to address growing concerns surrounding the technology. “Whoever wins superintelligence wins. You’re gonna have a winner and a loser, and you’re probably not gonna have a second place,” Trump said on Tuesday morning. “We’re leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way … The only way you can keep it that way is to do exactly what we’re doing right now.” In recent weeks, there have been growing calls for the US and China to collaborate on mounting concerns that frontier AI systems could be misused for cyberattacks and bioweapon development, following a string of high-profile incidents involving US companies OpenAI and Anthropic. However, Trump claimed that any suggestion of a “joint venture” with China on AI would risk the US giving up “secrets” to China. Instead, he told reporters after a lunch meeting with 17 US tech industry leaders at the White House that “self-policing” would be enough to address AI risks. Trump released a two-page document, including the signature page, outlining the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence” in a Truth Social post after meeting with tech leaders, which he said will be “morally binding”. The document outlined four layers of controls and audits that the companies “should” implement. These include internal controls to ensure their respective AI systems do not conduct “unintended” hacking and working with external auditors to independently evaluate whether the internal controls are working. The six participating companies – Google, Nvidia, Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta Platforms and SpaceXAI – will also “meet regularly” to establish best safety practices, though the document did not say how regularly. The voluntary accord came days after a high-profile summit between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, where the two countries agreed to launch an AI incident notification hotline and an ongoing dialogue on AI risks, with the next round slated for November in Shenzhen. Details about what the two sides will discuss have yet to be announced. However, an early point of contention is what the technology will be called. Trump also signed an executive order on Tuesday directing all agencies of the US executive branch to use the term “superintelligence” (SI) in place of AI in all official communications, as the term “more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies”. Earlier in the day, Trump repeated claims that President Xi also “loves” the term, though Beijing has so far continued to use the term AI. Another uncertainty is what the new risk management mechanisms between the two countries will achieve. On Tuesday, Trump presented US AI leadership as his administration’s top priority, in line with previous statements dismissing the most extreme warnings about AI risks as a “hoax”. “President Xi knows that we’re leading by a lot and we don’t want to mix it up too much either,” he said, noting that the US already had guardrails in place to ensure that AI companies stay “honest”, such as the US Department of Justice and the FBI. Trump made his remarks part of a day-long event on Tuesday in Washington that touted the importance of AI and featured members of his Cabinet. The lunch meeting drew most of the US’ top tech leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Tesla’s Elon Musk, and Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, along with US House Speaker Mike Johnson. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and OpenAI president Greg Brockman were also present, representing start-ups whose recent AI hacking incidents have sparked calls for tighter scrutiny of the AI industry. The administration’s AI push comes as the technology and its accompanying infrastructure, most notably data centres, grow increasingly unpopular among the US public. A poll from The New York Times and Siena University, published earlier this month, found that 61 per cent of likely voters opposed building data centres to power AI. Trump on Tuesday also signed an EO directing every federal government agency to integrate their public-facing services with America.gov, a one-stop-shop website that lets US residents access federal government information and services more easily. “This is a day all Americans will be extremely proud of your country,” he said. “[It’s] gonna save you a lot of accuracy.”

title: China takes strategic military step overseas with new Laos air force centre
description: Beijing says jointly operated facilities at Ban Keun Airport will support pilot training and deepen cooperation between the two militaries.
content: China has launched an air force support and training centre in Laos, its third overseas military outpost, which observers say could help the PLA expand its footprint and interests in the region. The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Centre and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy are now in operation at the Ban Keun Airport, aiming to help the Laotian Air Force train its pilots, China’s defence ministry said in a statement. The two institutions would be jointly maintained and operated by both sides, the statement said, without providing details on the personnel or equipment based at the airport. This move marks a strategic expansion of China’s limited overseas military presence, adding another foothold in Southeast Asia following a similar joint naval facility in Cambodia. Brian Hart, deputy director of the CSIS China Power Project, noted that Ban Keun was China’s first acknowledged overseas military facility centred on air power, unlike its naval-oriented facilities in Djibouti and Cambodia. The ministry said the construction and operation of the facilities were the result of mutual respect and equal consultation. “They comply with domestic laws of both sides as well as relevant international law and international practice, and do not target any third party,” it said. “They will help further strengthen practical cooperation between the two militaries and safeguard regional peace and stability.” The wording is almost identical to its statement last year for the official inauguration of the China-Cambodia Joint Training and Support Centre at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. Hart said the repeated use of the “joint training centre” model suggested the People’s Liberation Army was taking an incremental approach to expanding its overseas footprint. “This facility could start as a joint facility with Laos and grow into China steadily building a deeper presence over time,” he said. “What is visible now may just be a starting point.” He noted that China expanded the pier at its Djibouti base years after it opened and has continued adding capabilities there, including for communications and potentially intelligence collection. Ban Keun Airport is in the northwestern Vientiane province, about 45km (28 miles) north of the Laotian capital Vientiane. Situated at the heart of the Indochina peninsula, the airfield formerly functioned as a tactical support site in the US network of airstrips in Laos during the Laotian Civil War and Vietnam war era and ceased active operations after the conflicts. According to reports based on commercial satellite imagery, construction at the Ban Keun site began around October last year and had reached a substantial scale by September this year. The longest runway is about 2,000 metres (6,562 feet). Hart said the speed at which the facility appeared to have developed suggested the People’s Liberation Army’s footprint elsewhere could also grow quickly “if the conditions are right”. Previous Chinese overseas defence projects have drawn concern from Washington and its allies. The PLA set up its first overseas military outpost – a naval logistics base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa – in 2017 to support its anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden and other operations in East Africa and the Middle East. Last year, Beijing opened the China-Cambodia Joint Training and Support Centre at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand. The Cambodian government has denied the permanent stationing of PLA forces, stressing that the base remains open to visits from all nations. Days later two vessels from Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force became the first foreign naval ships to make a port call at the naval base. Timothy Heath, head of defence research firm Perceptum, noted that the Laos base was in a strategic location. “Southeast Asia will likely play a leading role in the future of Asia’s economy, so the base is a way for China to involve itself more deeply and possibly position military forces in an area of strategic value,” Heath said. The new base and the Ream base in Cambodia could be key to China’s regional interests, he said. “Both bases are near the South China Sea, which is the route for the Maritime Silk Road, a major seaway for China’s economy,” he said. But he cautioned against comparing the three overseas China-linked bases to US bases overseas. “None of these bases are similar to the US-style military bases with full military defensive capabilities,” Heath said. “China has no alliance with any of those countries and thus there is no justification for the PLA to conduct combat operations against countries like the USA from any of these bases.” Hart said signs of a more substantial PLA presence would include how long Chinese aircraft or personnel stayed at Ban Keun, whether Beijing obtained exclusive access to parts of the facility, and the balance between Chinese and Laotian forces there. The Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force operates a small fleet of fewer than 40 aircraft, mainly transport helicopters and light jet trainers, with no modern fighter jets in service. Laotian pilot training has long depended heavily on foreign partners, particularly China and Russia. Laos and China have maintained close ties for decades, with increased cooperation in recent years. The China-Laos Railway, a key Belt and Road Initiative project, opened in 2021 and has significantly improved connectivity between the two countries and helped deepen economic integration.

title: Mystery deepens over UK airbase incident as police find petrol, not explosives
description: Surprise decision to release five suspects on bail fuels uncertainty over RAF Fairford security scare.
content: A UK probe into a suspected bomb plot at an airbase used by the United States was mired in confusion Tuesday, as police said no explosives but a “quantity of petrol” was found in vehicles seized nearby. Police were called to the Royal Air Force Fairford base in southwest England on Sunday after a resident saw several vans “acting suspiciously”, triggering an evacuation of the nearby village and the declaration of a “major incident”. “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination … and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered,” National Counter Terrorism Policing head Laurence Taylor said. The development came as British media reported that a member of the group called police around an hour before a local farmer alerted officers after spotting the men and vans. There have been huge questions around the incident after five London-based Britons were released on bail Monday after being arrested early Sunday on explosives and terror offences, with Washington criticising their release. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision,” Taylor added, after US President Donald Trump said he was “surprised” by the decision. “I wouldn’t have done that,” Trump told reporters, as his Secretary of State Marco Rubio alleged a “foreign actor” was involved. Speculation was rife about the incident near the Fairford airbase, which is used by the US military to launch strikes on Iran. Iran’s embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved. The latest update lends credibility to some theories that the men could be fuel thieves, as energy prices rise in the UK. But the scare forced 85 homes in a nearby village to be evacuated, with many residents having to stay elsewhere for at least one night. Police said they had searched homes in London and were hoping to stand down investigative operations on Wednesday. A resident in the neighbouring village of Kempsford, Patricia, 60, said it was “very embarrassing that people around the world thought it was a terrorist attack. But in the end, no – it’s a lot of noise for nothing”. The security scare became public after a farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase rang police after seeing the three vans blocking a road and a group of masked men fleeing the scene. British media later reported that officers had already been alerted by one of the suspects before the farmer’s call, although police have not publicly commented on the reports. Armed officers arrested the five men – all London residents in their mid-20s – on suspicion of explosives offences and, later, “suspicion of preparing a terrorist act” under anti-terror laws. Police said the men “remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work”. Security at the base had reportedly been heightened recently. Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran” to destroy Iranian missiles at source. US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base – the only one on Britain’s mainland used for this purpose. Aerial footage of the vans showed they appeared to contain barrels, and at least one was marked with a fake logo and phone number, giving the false impression that it was owned by a legitimate diesel delivery firm. The legitimate firm said in a statement on its website that “neither the vehicle nor any of the individuals involved has any connection whatsoever with Fuel2U”, adding it was cooperating with the police. “It’s a bit odd they were here in the middle of the night,” one local said as she did some gardening in the nearby village of Kempsford. “If they were true terrorists, they wouldn’t have released them,” she added, asking not to give her name. A British military camp was the victim of a “security breach” last year after intruders cut through a fence to steal fuel from a tanker.

title: Spain aims to ban evictions after pensioner’s removal from home sparks protests
description: Coalition government proposes sweeping housing reforms as 87-year-old accepts deal to return to Madrid flat.
content: Spain’s coalition government said it had agreed on proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country’s housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests accepted an offer to return home. Hundreds of ‌people remained camped in one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes. Health Minister Monica Garcia said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement with junior partner Sumar on Tuesday for a set of new measures, including rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market. However, the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented ⁠parliament. The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that ‌buys housing for speculation, Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez told a news conference, naming Urbagestion, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category. Urbagestion did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ‌measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted in parliament on Friday, with the majority in a first decree. ⁠The “final sticking point” of automatic ⁠contract rollover is in a second decree, Social Affairs Minister Pablo Bustinduy told a news conference. “It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance ‌between ordinary citizens and vulture funds,” Garcia wrote on social media. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday that it was still far from ‌agreeing on ‌all measures and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain. “We all agreed that evictions – where ‌the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros – obviously need to be stopped,” Junts parliamentary spokeswoman Miriam Nogueras ⁠said on RTVE. “Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property – putting them all in ⁠the same basket – is a mistake,” she added. Madrid’s tenants’ union criticised the government’s decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned. The lawyer ‌for pensioner Abascal said on Tuesday that Urbagestion, ‌the fund that owns her flat, had offered a preliminary agreement that will allow her return to her home, paying 30 per cent of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 (US$569) a month. This would see her paying a similar level as before the eviction. “She should never have been forced to leave,” Beatriz Duro told reporters. “I hope this case serves to provide a collective response to the housing crisis.”

title: Eiffel Tower chief to step down over removal of women staff for Hindu group visit
description: Decision to accommodate religious group’s request regarding female employees sparked walkout and closure of landmark.
content: The operating company that runs the Eiffel Tower said on Tuesday its chief would step down at the end of this year in the wake of a controversy over the removal of women staff during a visit by a Hindu religious group. Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, would leave his job at the end of the year after an internal probe revealed that “operational flaws and shortcomings” in organising the visit led to the “unacceptable” removal of women staff, the company SETE said in a statement. The removal of women staff during a visit by the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement on September 5 prompted a staff walkout and the closure of the monument for a day, as well as an outcry across the political spectrum in France which prizes secularism and gender equality. At the time, SETE acknowledged the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit “interactions with women” and said that “these conditions should not have been accepted”. “The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions,” said Ariel Weil, SETE’s board chairman. He said he was demanding the creation of a “dedicated protocol department” and the implementation of a new set of measures and training programmes to promote gender equality. The Eiffel Tower, which is owned by the city of Paris, says it receives nearly 7 million people a year. The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, had lambasted the move to remove women staff as an “absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision” and ordered two separate probes. The mayor on Tuesday “acknowledged Patrick Branco Ruivo’s responsible decision” and commended “his commitment to the Eiffel Tower and SETE” since his appointment in late 2018, a person close to him told Agence France-Presse, asking not to be named. “It is now imperative to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions and to fully learn from the situation so that such unacceptable incidents cannot happen again,” the person added. The BAPS spiritual movement, close to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling conservative Hindu nationalist party, has apologised for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by the incident. BAPS had opened its first major temple near Paris the same weekend. Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement they were given instructions that led to “female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation. “Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present.”

title: Cyclist likely bitten by several dogs and died from throat injuries, source says
description: But government forensic pathologists fear it may ultimately be impossible to determine which exact animals were involved, SCMP told.
content: A young cyclist who died after a suspected canine attack in Hong Kong earlier this month was likely bitten on the neck by several dogs, but government forensic pathologists fear it may ultimately be impossible to determine which exact animals were involved, the South China Morning Post has learned. The SCMP has learned that the victim was Fairview Park resident Eva Chu, who was found on Pok Wai South Road near Nam Sang Wai at 12.42am on September 20. CCTV footage showed that three dogs chased the 27-year-old woman along the road while she was riding a shared bicycle about 30 metres (98 feet) from where she was discovered near a Drainage Services Department sewage pumping station. Chu, who worked as a background music operator, was taken to Pok Oi Hospital in Yuen Long and pronounced dead. Police said she suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal. A source told the SCMP on Tuesday that government forensic pathologists had initially determined that the victim was highly likely to have died after being bitten on the neck by several dogs, with injuries to her windpipe believed to be among the fatal wounds. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department and police conducted operations to capture stray dogs in the area following the incident. Eight dogs were caught, three of which were microchipped. Investigators were examining whether any of the eight mongrels, as well as nearly 20 warehouse guard dogs found in the vicinity, carried the victim’s DNA, the source said. Authorities had been trying to identify the animals involved by comparing bite marks on the woman’s body with the teeth of the captured dogs, the SCMP learned. The results will be submitted to the Coroner’s Court, which will decide whether an inquest should be held. However, the SCMP learned that drawing definitive conclusions from the test results would be challenging. “It may ultimately be impossible to determine which dog, or dogs, were responsible,” an insider said. “Similar situations have occurred in other countries. Nonetheless, experts from various fields are determined to try their best and will exhaust all possible means.” One of the three microchipped dogs captured was registered in the name of an animal welfare activist, who was later charged with failing to keep one of them under proper control and keeping a dog with an expired licence. But the activist, Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of the animal rescue group Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, who has microchipped many stray dogs to prevent them from being euthanised, told the SCMP that the 13-year-old mongrel in question was not responsible because it was exceptionally gentle and could only walk very slowly. April Yip, founder of Home for Homeless Dogs, also said that many volunteers chose to register as keepers of stray dogs so they could get the animals neutered. She urged authorities to exempt these volunteers from prosecution. “We are simply trying to help solve a community issue, so why can’t an exemption be granted?” she said. However, Luk explained that granting such exemptions would be difficult, saying: “It will be extremely chaotic because anyone can claim to be a volunteer, yet there is no official recognition.”

title: US consumer confidence sinks to 12-year low over inflation, stagnant wages
description: The consumer confidence index fell to 81.9 in September, the lowest reading in the Conference Board’s survey since April 2014.
content: Americans’ confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this month as prices remain elevated and wages stagnate amid the ongoing Iran war. The Conference Board said Tuesday that its consumer confidence index tumbled 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, down from 88.6 in August. That is the lowest reading in the board’s survey since April 2014 and below the lowest level reached during the pandemic. Respondents’ views of their present situation fell by 7.9 points to 109.3. Their short-term outlook also slid, falling 5.9 points to 63.6. Americans remain flustered by the economy after five years of elevated inflation, potentially posing a risk to President Donald Trump and Republicans in the midterm elections, which are a little more than a month away. Write-in responses to the board’s survey, collected from September 1-23, were mostly pessimistic this month, with frequent references to the high cost of gas, goods and services. “The Consumer Confidence Index deteriorated notably in September, following two prior months of softening,” said Dana Peterson, the Conference Board’s chief economist, adding that consumers’ views of current business conditions became negative for the first time since September 2024. Trump has continued to blame high prices on his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, yet inflation has risen since Trump’s inauguration last year. Earlier this month, the government reported that consumer inflation accelerated last month and gas prices spiked as fighting in the Middle East dragged on. The consumer price index rose 3.4 per cent last month compared with a year ago, the Labour Department said on Friday, just like July. But inflation quickened month to month as costs jumped 0.4 per cent from July, quadrupling the 0.1 per cent registered in the previous month. The Federal Reserve two weeks ago raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation, and the central bank signalled another rate hike could occur later this year. The quarter-point increase lifted the Fed’s key rate to about 3.9 per cent and over time could result in higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. Petrol prices – which currently average US$4.46 for a gallon of regular – are not all that is rising. Prices for appliances, car repairs and wireless phone services also jumped in August. The most recent measure of the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge – the personal consumption expenditures price index – was up 3.7 per cent in June from a year earlier. That was down from May’s 4.1 per cent year-over-year increase but up from 2.8 per cent before the Iran war began on February 28. It was 2.5 per cent when Trump was inaugurated in January 2025. The government issues its August PCE data on Wednesday. Consumers’ views of the current labour market also worsened in September, but remained in positive territory, the board said. Respondents broadly said they expected their household incomes to rise, but not as much as in previous months. The US labour market bounced back in August as employers added a surprising 162,000 jobs, ending a summer of lacklustre hiring. The unemployment rate remained at a low 4.1 per cent, but some of that can be attributed to significant numbers of people giving up on their search for employment in previous months. Inflation has dominated conversations this year in business and households, and meagre pay rises have made rising prices more painful for many. Average hourly wages rose 3.1 per cent last month from a year earlier, the weakest year-over-year increase since May 2021. The government issues its September jobs report on Friday.

title: Israel’s Gaza air strike kills Hamas commander behind October 7, 2023 attack
