description: The Israeli military says it has killed at least ‌20 Hamas figures this month, while Hamas accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal.
content: An Israeli air strike killed the head of Hamas’ armed wing in north Gaza on Tuesday, officials on both sides said, with the militant group describing him as a leader of the October 7, 2023 attack that precipitated war in the Palestinian enclave. Israel’s government said its military had targeted and killed Izz al-Din Al-Beik, ‌who they said was involved in planning attacks and recruiting. Hamas confirmed his death. Medics said the Israeli strike hit a building in Gaza City’s Nasr neighbourhood around dawn. A second person died from wounds after the attack, health officials said. Later on Tuesday, an Israeli air strike near a medical clinic in Jabalia refugee camp killed one person, taking the day’s death toll to at least three, doctors said. The military said it had targeted a militant in the area. Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in ⁠violation of an October ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. The Israeli military says it has killed at least ‌20 Hamas figures this month, including some it identified as senior commanders, people who took part in the October 7, 2023, attacks or those who held Israeli hostages. Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal ‌and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Also on Tuesday, Palestinians in the Nuseirat refugee camp in ⁠central Gaza buried the remains ⁠of 41 people killed by Israeli fire nearly three years ago. Their bodies were recently recovered from ruins. Hundreds of relatives and friends gathered in an open space to pay respect as ‌the remains were placed in white shrouds decorated with Palestinian flags. “There are mixed feelings between relief, sadness, and pain. But thank God, the fire in my heart has eased a little, ‌because my husband ‌now has a grave that my orphaned children and I can visit,” said Areej Farajallah, who lost her husband in the October 31, ‌2023 strike. Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 bodies remain buried in wreckage. A Palestinian recovery team that combed wreckage in Gaza City last month said ⁠it found the remains of 112 people from the same clan. “With minimal equipment, their remains were recovered after hours of work, retrieving what was ⁠left of bones, some skulls, and hair with which it is extremely difficult for us to identify them,” said Rami Al-Ayedi of Gaza’s Civil Defence Service. Last year’s US-brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made as ‌negotiators have failed to agree on terms ‌for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops. Israeli air strikes have continued. At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while Israel says four soldiers have been killed. Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

title: The Vertex developer hit with HK$770,000 fine over disclosure failures
description: Twin City failed to properly record transaction details for the residential project in Cheung Sha Wan, according to the government.
content: The developer of The Vertex – a residential project in Cheung Sha Wan once owned by failed property giant China Evergrande Group – has been fined HK$770,000 (US$98,100) for failing to properly record transactions related to the complex. Twin City Holdings Limited was found to have violated a residential properties ordinance by failing to disclose details of payment terms – such as price discounts and other financial incentives – on sales at the development, according to a government statement released on Tuesday. The infractions related to deals for 11 residential properties across the east and west wings of the complex, with Twin City failing to enter the required payment details into the project’s register of transactions within 24 hours of executing the preliminary agreements. The irregularities had led to the developer facing 11 charges and a total penalty of HK$770,000, according to the Sales of First-hand Residential Properties Authority (SRPA). A spokesman for the SRPA stressed that vendors involved in arranging or facilitating commission rebates for buyers during first-hand property sales must treat these rebates as financial incentives or benefits linked to the purchase. Consequently, all such figures must be transparently disclosed in the transaction register. “The SRPA will take action seriously and carry out investigations on any suspected cases of contravention of the ordinance to further enhance the transparency and fairness of the sales of first-hand residential properties, protect the interests of purchasers, as well as provide a level playing field for vendors,” the spokesman said in a statement. The fine is the latest issue to affect The Vertex. The 414-flat project was transferred to the VMS Group in late 2021 after its original owner, Evergrande, fell into a liquidity crisis that eventually led the giant property firm to collapse. In August, a court in Shenzhen sentenced Evergrande founder Hui Ka-yan to life in prison for “multiple combined crimes”. Hui’s personal property was all confiscated.

title: Economist formally apologises for ‘sexist’ campus talk as students urge suspension
description: Terence Chong says he failed to consider choice of words and setting, as Chinese University of Hong Kong students and alumni demand action.
content: An economist at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has issued a formal apology for a campus talk criticised as “sexist”, as an online petition calling for his suspension from college duties drew nearly 100 signatures. Terence Chong Tai-leung, an associate head of New Asia College and an associate professor in CUHK’s Department of Economics, posted the apology on his personal Facebook page on Tuesday, a week after making the remarks during an assembly presentation. Chong also offered an apology last week when asked by the South China Morning Post about his remarks. “I sincerely apologise for the public discontent and offence caused to some individuals by my remarks at the recent New Asia College assembly,” Chong, who is also an alumnus of the college, wrote on Tuesday. “I apologise for any misunderstandings the remarks had caused and for any discomfort felt by members of the public.” Chong said he had failed to consider carefully whether his choice of words and the setting were appropriate when expressing his views. “I deeply respected women, firmly believe men and women were equally important and capable in society, and supported equal opportunities for both sexes to receive education and realise their potential,” he said. The controversy erupted after Chong gave a talk titled “How to invest in your life?” at a New Asia College biweekly assembly on September 22. One of the slides was titled “Economics of Partner Choice” and carried the heading “The Cost-Benefit Analysis of Women Marrying for Money”. Chong was reported to have told students that “it’s pointless for women to get high GPAs; they need to marry rich in the end anyway” and that “women had better not pursue a PhD because their youth is precious”. The comments sparked outrage among students, who accused him of reducing women’s choice of partners to financial considerations. Critics described the remarks as gender-biased, objectifying and unfair. On Tuesday evening, an online petition initiated by New Asia College students and alumni had attracted 98 signatures. It called for Chong to be suspended from his college duties and for disciplinary action to be considered. The petition also urged the college to issue a public apology and strengthen its vetting of guest speakers’ positions on activities organised by the college, in order to uphold the core values of university and college general education, and the foundations of a diverse society. Two New Asia College students told the SCMP last Friday that they were disappointed with Chong and the handling of the incident. A second-year female student who attended the assembly and wished to remain anonymous said she felt uncomfortable and patronised while listening to Chong’s presentation. “He gave the impression that the destiny of women was just to get married when they are still young,” she said. “He raised no academic evidence when discussing these personal perspectives either.” She recalled that the talk initially felt boring, but the atmosphere turned tense when Chong raised gender-related topics. Many students began whispering to one another and taking photos of the presentation slides. During the question and answer session, two female students challenged his views on women. The audience applauded them before the host abruptly ended the session. The second-year student said the issue underscored the urgent need for college management to listen to students and involve them in decision-making to prevent similar problems from recurring. According to the college website, students are required to attend at least one biweekly assembly each semester. The Committee on Biweekly Assembly, the organiser of the assemblies, has 14 staff members, including Chong, and two student seats, which are vacant. Previously, one seat was reserved for a student union member, while the other was filled through an open recruitment process run by the union. The union folded last December, and the college began recruiting for both positions this month. A third-year student, who also wished to remain anonymous, questioned whether the college management had failed in its oversight. Staff, the student said, should have received the presentation slides in advance and offered guidance to ensure the talk aligned with students’ interests and met its learning objectives. Wong said the college should also improve communication with students, who could complain only through an online assembly feedback form or by emailing the college. “New Asia College was built on the foundation of humanism and teaching by example, not purely on imparting knowledge. Whether our teachers have the capacity to communicate and listen to our feedback – that, to me, is the true essence of the founding values,” he said. “Professor Chong’s views, while utilitarian, offer an opportunity for open debate. Could the college provide a platform for such a meaningful and critical dialogue? That is a way we could improve the general education.” CUHK previously said New Asia College had reminded the speaker to be mindful of his comments and to consider the feelings of members of the university community and the wider public. The university added that the college would continue to foster an inclusive campus environment based on mutual respect and diversity.

title: Legal aid chief denies stricter vetting as aid for policy challenges hits decade low
description: Legal Aid Department approved funds for just two challenges against government policies and decisions last year, down by 90 per cent from 2016.
content: Hong Kong authorities approved only two legal aid applications for judicial review challenges against government policies and decisions last year, the fewest in the past decade, although its director has dismissed claims of tightened scrutiny or diminished access to justice. The Legal Aid Department received 110 applications concerning judicial reviews of government policies and related organisations’ decisions last year, an almost 60 per cent drop from 2016, its annual reports show. The department last year approved two legal aid certificates for such applications, down by almost 90 per cent from 2016. In an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday, Director of Legal Aid Chan Chak-ming denied that the department had adopted a more stringent approach in vetting applications, following past criticisms of overly lenient approvals. “I would not use the word tightened or stringent; I am not using those words,” Chan said. “Because my powers and duties are always specified under the law. So we are simply discharging our duties in accordance with the Legal Aid Ordinance.” Individuals whose financial resources do not exceed HK$452,320 (US$57,660) are eligible to apply for legal aid. The department examines the facts and evidence of the case, as well as the relevant legal principles, to determine whether there are reasonable grounds to grant the request. Chan stressed that each application was assessed on its own merits. “I don’t have a target number. We are a government department,” he said. “The mission is simple: to provide legal aid to eligible applicants who will not be denied access to justice simply because of lack of means.” The department assessed not only the prospects of success but also the reasonableness of the case and the public interest involved, he said, adding it would not fund a purely academic debate. The director also attributed part of the decline to shifting public sentiment and lower overall application numbers. “It is simple mathematics … The lower number of applications, then there are fewer cases [for] legal aid certificates to be granted,” Chan said, although he stopped short of explaining why the number of approvals fell by a larger margin than applications over the past decade. He assured the public that Hong Kong’s legal aid system remained robust and fair, noting that applicants retained the right to appeal. He also highlighted that funding judicial reviews against government authorities was far more accessible in Hong Kong than in jurisdictions such as Singapore and Australia. But critics argued that the process has become increasingly difficult. One of the refused cases involved a 2024 judicial review of the approval of the San Tin Technopole project’s environmental study, in which applicant Eddie Tse Sai-kit, a retired social worker, failed both the means test and the case merits test. Tse argued that the department had become more stringent in recent years, noting that it sought external legal advice on his case even after the court had granted leave to apply for a judicial review and recognised the public interest involved. He recalled that similar earlier cases with comparable reasonableness, including a 2015 challenge to the environmental impact assessment of the airport’s third runway and a 2016 challenge over the government’s decision not to incorporate six enclaves into country parks, had been granted legal aid in a smooth process. He eventually abandoned his case involving the San Tin Technopole. Ronny Tong Ka-wah, a senior counsel and member of the government’s key decision-making Executive Council, defended the department’s handling of applications. “If the [department] previously used an incorrect standard in granting applications, leading to more legal-aided judicial reviews, I do not think that means it should continue,” Tong said. “[Another] explanation may simply be that the government’s current administration is more lawful, more procedurally proper and involves fewer unsubstantiated or baseless policies. With fewer of these, there are naturally fewer legal challenges.”

title: US Navy launches drone command that could reshape Taiwan war planning
description: The centre aims to integrate air, surface and underwater unmanned platforms into a unified combat-ready force.
content: The US Navy has set up a dedicated command to turn its growing array of aerial, surface and underwater drones into an integrated fighting force – a capability US commanders have linked to disrupting a PLA attack on Taiwan. The Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Centre, formally established on September 24 in Virginia, will develop doctrine and tactics for unmanned systems, train sailors to use them, and test whether they can keep operating under realistic conditions. In a message marking the centre’s launch, Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle said the navy had spent years developing and testing robotic systems, but much of that work had taken place separately across different warfighting domains. “The next step is integration,” he said, adding that proving an individual system worked was not enough. “A prototype is not combat power.” The gap between successful prototypes and a force able to use them at scale was also showing up in how the navy managed the programmes. In June, the US Government Accountability Office found that robotic and autonomous systems remained divided by platform and operating environment, with unclear responsibilities and inconsistent leadership slowing progress. It recommended organising them as a “portfolio” to meet the navy’s objectives “across warfighting domains”. The new centre is intended to address the operational side of that problem: how different unmanned systems should work together and be commanded, as well as how they should operate alongside conventional warships, submarines and aircraft. Michael Bosack, head of the Parley Policy Institute, said the significance of the centre lay in its “centralisation and institutionalisation”, providing a hub to bring different efforts together and commit resources to a longer-term mission. Peter Jones, a retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral and adjunct professor with the Naval Studies Group at UNSW Canberra, said the move partly followed Ukraine’s decision to create a separate branch of the armed forces dedicated specifically to unmanned systems. He noted that bringing unmanned systems under one command could help transfer technology and lessons, simplify component supply chains, and give the navy a flag officer who could act as a “champion” for uncrewed system development and applications. Despite these potential advantages, Bosack said the practical hurdles facing the new centre ranged from managing the frequency spectrum to adapting personnel to new systems and incorporating the capabilities into operational planning, decision-making and execution. The organisation’s first commander, Rear Admiral Melvin Smith, said the centre would bring together the navy’s work on unmanned systems and develop combined tactics. “This is just day one,” he said. The navy has not announced when the centre will become fully operational. One potential application of such an integrated force is a Taiwan contingency. US naval leaders have pointed to the “hellscape” concept as one possible model. The idea is to coordinate large numbers of unmanned systems to disrupt or slow a People’s Liberation Army amphibious assault across the Taiwan Strait. Admiral Samuel Paparo, now commander of the US Pacific Command, publicly outlined the concept in 2024. This is part of a wider US push that includes the Pentagon’s Replicator initiative. Launched in 2023, it aims to field thousands of relatively low-cost autonomous systems across multiple domains to counter Beijing’s military build-up. Jones said an inherent advantage of uncrewed systems was that they could be fielded in large numbers, which could make them a major source of casualties among invading forces. But Caudle acknowledged in February that the navy had not yet worked out how such an unmanned force should be organised and commanded. He said commanders might ultimately need “packages” of unmanned capabilities to achieve specific mission outcomes. Another challenge is keeping such a force operating when an adversary jams or disrupts its communications. That is why the new centre will also test unmanned systems against realistic threats and in conditions where communications are degraded or denied. This issue is not unique to the US Navy. Chinese military planners are also focusing on integrating unmanned forces with the wider force under heavy electromagnetic interference. Beijing’s five-year plan covering 2026-2030 calls for faster development of “unmanned intelligent combat forces” and counter-drone capabilities, closer integration of combat systems and more realistic military training. PLA Daily, the Chinese military’s official newspaper, reported in June that unmanned warfare required changes in technology, doctrine, organisation and command, with greater emphasis on manned-unmanned teaming and testing under electronic interference and cyberattack. The Chinese navy is already testing elements of that approach. In a report published on September 21, PLA Daily said a special mission aircraft and several drones had linked up over the sea and exchanged information in real time. When simulated electronic interference disrupted the network, the force adjusted its communications and continued the exercise. Bosack said the exercises were useful for stress testing systems and collecting data while reducing the risk of losing or damaging equipment. He warned, however, that this was ultimately “different from having to learn and adapt under dynamic, real-world circumstances”.

title: In Focus | How years of thin investment have stalled Germany’s rail network as China’s speeds ahead
description: Germany sold high-speed trains to China 21 years ago, but now its network is slowing to a crawl as China’s continues to improve.
content: Wang Xixi still remembers her first experience with Germany’s trains 21 years ago. It left her with a question: how could a railway be so empty, clean and punctual, and still make money? The carriages were bright, the toilets almost spotless and the fittings modern. During four years as a student in Bavaria, travelling on a regional rail pass, she barely remembers a delay. At the time, China’s high-speed railway network was just getting started, while Germany was a major exporter of the technology. Siemens sold China 60 trains capable of 300km/h (186mph) in 2005. Wang never expected that, years later, delays would become routine on Germany’s railways – sometimes minutes, sometimes hours. The reasons run the gamut: a train ahead blocking the track, faulty points, signal failures, speed restrictions imposed where tracks have worn out. Most point back to an ageing and overloaded network. Wang began travelling regularly between Berlin and Frankfurt for work in 2022. “Now I don’t remember a single trip that wasn’t delayed,” she said. To make sure she arrived in time for a meeting, she had to take a 5am train and leave two or three hours of extra time. Sometimes she flew instead. “It’s such a short distance, and flying is terrible for emissions,” she said. “But there was really no other way.” Her experience with China’s railways has been the complete opposite. In 2001, Wang travelled with her father from Xian to Beijing on an overnight train, a roughly 1,200km (746 miles) journey that took more than 12 hours in a crowded carriage. Today, the fastest train covers the same route in just four hours and 11 minutes. “Convenient, clean, quick,” she said of travelling by train in China today. The numbers bear her out. Over the same two decades, China has built the world’s largest high-speed railway network, with more than 95 per cent of trains on time, according to the World Bank. Germany’s long-distance punctuality, by contrast, has hovered around 60 per cent for three years and fell to 52.6 per cent this summer. Rail investment in China has stayed high year after year Li Hongchang, Beijing Jiaotong University The contrast points to a deeper gap between China and Germany: Beijing can commit to long-term investment in key infrastructure such as high-speed railway lines and see it through, while Berlin struggles both to sustain the investment and to deliver the projects needed to maintain and upgrade its railway system, with growing consequences for competitiveness. China laid nearly 50,000km of high-speed track in less than two decades, at about two-thirds the cost per kilometre of other countries, according to the World Bank, which credited a 15-year railway plan backed by successive five-year plans. Such a model, it noted, depended on a government that was able to commit to a decades-long programme. “Rail investment in China has stayed high year after year,” said Li Hongchang, a professor of transport economics at the Sustainable Transportation Innovation Centre at Beijing Jiaotong University. It has topped 700 billion yuan (US$104.3 billion) a year for the past decade, and reached 901.5 billion yuan last year, according to state-owned operator China State Railway Group. To sustain investment on that scale, public financing and government backing were essential, Li said. Alongside central and local budgets, a state-approved railway construction fund levied on freight since 1991 raises about 60 billion yuan a year. He described it as a steady and critical source of funding that also guaranteed the operator’s construction bonds. The railway system borrows heavily on top of that, backed by its state ownership and passenger revenue. China Railway had 6.2 trillion yuan in liabilities at the end of 2024, with a debt-to-asset ratio of 63.5 per cent, according to its annual report. Li estimated that the cost of public service obligations – covering loss-making services required by the state, from thinly used lines and discounted fares for students and disabled veterans to disaster relief transport – amounted to about a quarter of annual railway spending. Debt on that scale brings its own problems. Analysts have long questioned its sustainability and how long it will take to pay down. Lu Dadao, an economic geographer at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, wrote last year that only a few lines on China’s east coast were breaking even. “But we also need to look at the wider benefits it brings,” Li said. His study of 200 Chinese cities found that the boost to economic output provided by high-speed railways substantially outweighed their large fixed costs, depreciation and subsidies. Still, bringing down the debt would require deeper market reforms and new sources of revenue, he added. China’s approach stands in contrast to Germany’s, where a constitutional provision has tightly limited government borrowing since 2011. Deutsche Bahn (DB), the main rail operator, is wholly state-owned but operates like a private company, with each of its subsidiaries under pressure to limit losses. Before the pandemic, it was largely profitable. But years of thin investment are now catching up with Germany in the most visible form: an ageing rail network causing greater economic knock-on effects. Unlike China, Germany struggled for years to invest enough money to maintain and modernise its railway system, despite efforts in recent years. Labour shortages and bureaucracy had added to the problem, analysts said. “Too full, too old and too prone to faults” is how DB board member for infrastructure Berthold Huber described the network in an interview with the Suddeutsche Zeitung newspaper in 2023. Since the mid-1990s, passenger traffic has risen more than 45 per cent and freight by about 90 per cent, according to DB, while the network has shrunk from 40,800km to about 33,500km. Fast and slow trains share the same tracks, causing delays to ripple across the network. The cause is years of underinvestment, even though DB’s annual infrastructure assessments long insisted the network was in good shape. “They all said everything is fine,” said Christian Boettger, a rail economist at HTW Berlin University of Applied Sciences. It was only in June 2022 that the government and DB admitted the network had been “pushed to its limit”, announcing an overhaul of its busiest corridors. Revamping those lines comes with a considerable bill. The cost of replacing worn-out tracks, signals and bridges stood at about €106 billion (US$120.6 billion) last year, up from €92 billion in 2023, according to DB InfraGO, the group’s rail infrastructure company. We now have a punctuality of 25 per cent … It’s absolutely horrible Markus Hecht, Technical University of Berlin To reverse decades of underinvestment, Berlin set up a €500 billion special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality last year, exempt from the constitutional debt brake. The railway network is a major beneficiary, with €18.8 billion earmarked for the sector this year. But several estimates suggested that part of the fund’s infrastructure spending was not additional at all, Boettger said. The German Economic Institute said in September last year that €13.7 billion had been cut from the core rail budget compared with 2024, meaning much of the €18.8 billion from the fund replaced existing spending rather than adding to it, contrary to the government’s pledge that the money would be strictly additional. And more money did not solve a shortage of workers, Boettger said. The network could handle about 9,000 construction sites at a time, he said, but it ran 26,000 last year. “The entire system is overwhelmed,” he said. Meanwhile, the timetable for fixing the network keeps slipping. Germany began overhauling its 40 busiest and most delay-prone corridors two years ago, with completion initially due in 2030 before being pushed back to 2036. Even completed projects have fallen short. The Berlin-Hamburg line reopened in June after nearly a year of closure. “Punctuality afterwards was not better than before. We now have a punctuality of 25 per cent,” said Markus Hecht, a professor of rail vehicles and former institute director at the Technical University of Berlin. “It’s absolutely horrible.” All of this comes as Germany loses ground to China in key industries. Berlin has hardened its trade stance, blaming subsidies, overcapacity and an undervalued yuan for imbalances squeezing German business. But economists and industry groups argue that tariffs alone will not restore competitiveness. Lagging infrastructure, high energy prices and bureaucracy were leaving Europe behind, Germany’s car industry association said this month. The group has long argued that politicians must do their own “homework” first. “The problem is not only the railway, but public infrastructure as a whole,” said Shi Shiwei, a professor at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing who recently completed a stint as a guest lecturer in Berlin. At a conference on Germany’s infrastructure crisis this month, which the country’s transport minister attended, Shi recalled an executive asking: “Half the trains are late, the roads are falling apart, and hundreds of bridges need rebuilding. Why has none of this been dealt with?” The strain is showing up in business. A record 84 per cent of firms surveyed by the German Economic Institute in October last year said poor transport infrastructure regularly hampered their business. Among those affected, 71 per cent pointed to the railways – the first time more than half of all respondents had cited the network as an obstacle. In a speech on September 15, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz cited the €500 billion fund and a new law to speed up infrastructure approvals. “All of this will become tangible and visible in the coming months,” he said. But analysts and industry figures are less convinced, particularly when it comes to the railways. The harder question, they said, was whether Germany could sustain investment whose benefits might take years to materialise, well beyond the country’s four-year election cycle. In August, official figures still put long-distance punctuality below 55 per cent. The delays have become a cultural punchline – when someone arrives late to an event, people sometimes quip that “Deutsche Bahn is coming.” Wang, the rail traveller, had a joke of her own about the situation. “Maybe they need a Chinese-style five- or 10-year plan.”

title: Nvidia and AMD chiefs join Tsinghua advisory board as US-China chip tensions persist
description: Huang and Su were among three new members appointed to the advisory board of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management.
content: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang and AMD chief Lisa Su have joined an influential advisory board at a prestigious Chinese university, placing the two US artificial intelligence chip leaders in a high-level forum known for connecting global executives with senior Chinese officials. Huang and Su were among three new members appointed to the advisory board of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management (SEM), alongside Marc Pictet, senior managing partner of Swiss wealth and assets manager Pictet Group, according to a post published on the school’s official social media channel on Tuesday. Huang was introduced as founder at Nvidia, a company that “invented graphic processing units” and “ushered in the modern AI era”, while Su’s leadership successfully “transformed AMD into a leading high-performance and adaptive computing firm,” the Tsinghua school said in the post. The appointment of Huang and Su comes after both were among US business executives who attended a White House state dinner during President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last week. While semiconductor export controls did not feature prominently in public readouts from the Xi-Trump summit, most restrictions remain in place. Huang’s appointment had been expected after the Nvidia chief reportedly accepted an invitation to join the Tsinghua board earlier this year. Su’s joining means the leaders of the world’s two biggest suppliers of advanced AI chips will serve on the influential body at a time when semiconductors remain a major flashpoint in US-China tech tensions. Both Nvidia and AMD have sought to maintain access to China, one of the world’s largest semiconductor markets, while navigating increasingly complicated restrictions imposed by both countries. The appointments also underscore the continuing role of Tsinghua SEM’s advisory board as a channel connecting some of the world’s most powerful corporate executives with China, even as geopolitical tensions have complicated technology and investment ties between Beijing and Washington. Established in 2000 with the backing of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, who was also the founding dean of Tsinghua SEM, the board includes some of the world’s most prominent business executives, academics and economists. Tsinghua describes the board as a platform for strengthening the school’s ties with the wider business and academic communities, while helping improve its research and teaching and supporting its ambition to become a world-class business school. Last year, Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met representatives of the board at Beijing’s Diaoyutai State Guesthouse, telling them he hoped they would continue to play a “bridging role” in supporting China’s economic development and exchanges with other countries, Tsinghua University said in a statement last year. Apple chief executive Tim Cook has chaired the body since 2019, while former Chinese vice-president Wang Qishan serves as its honorary chairman. Five executives will also join the board as successors to previous members from their respective companies. They include BMW chairman Milan Nedeljkovic, Walmart president and CEO John Furner, Coca-Cola CEO Henrique Braun, General Atlantic co-president Martin Escobari and BP CEO Meg O’Neill, according to the school. The board will hold its 27th annual meeting in Beijing on October 13 and 14.

title: China’s generative AI user base crosses 700 million, covering over half the population
description: Nearly half of users employ AI tools to process images or videos, while 38 per cent use it for text processing and 33 per cent for work notes.
content: China’s generative artificial intelligence user base surpassed 700 million at the end of June, accounting for more than half of the population as wide AI adoption pushes the technology’s penetration rate to a record high in the country. The user base data, released Tuesday by the China Internet Network Information Centre, represents an increase of 16 per cent from the end of 2025, when China had 602 million generative AI users with a penetration rate of 42.8 per cent. Question-and-answer services remain the most common use of generative AI in China. In a survey of users, 76 per cent said they used the technology to seek answers. Nearly half, or 48 per cent, employed AI tools to process images or videos, while 38 per cent used it for text processing and 33 per cent for work summaries, meeting notes or presentations. The report said AI adoption had also expanded beyond software. Some 39 per cent of users had bought smart hardware online during the past six months. As well as gaining traction in the consumer market, Chinese AI labs – which develop models to power the consumer applications and hardware – have advanced their technologies, according to the report, citing trillion-parameter open-weight models launched this year from domestic giants including DeepSeek and Moonshot AI. The digital infrastructure that lays the foundation for AI computation also grew rapidly. As of the end of June, intelligent computing capacity in the country surged by 177 per cent to 2,185 eflops from a year earlier, the report said. Eflops, short for exa floating-point operations per second, is a unit for measuring the speed of a computer system. The rapid expansion echoed an earlier Morgan Stanley survey that found AI adoption in China has surpassed that of the United States. Some 80 per cent of Chinese respondents used AI for personal purposes at least once a week, compared with 54 per cent in the US, the bank said in a report earlier this month. It attributed China’s advantage largely to the integration of AI into widely used shopping, messaging, search and entertainment platforms rather than superior model performance.

title: Hong Kong police record 1,503 suspicious iPhone charges so far worth HK$30m
description: Police say all unauthorised iPhone 18 Pro transactions have been cancelled and Apple has been asked to review its payment security measures.
content: Hong Kong police have received more than 1,500 reports of suspicious credit card transactions involving Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro series, totalling more than HK$30 million (US$3.82 million). In an update on the case, which has drawn public attention, the force said the number of reports had risen to 1,503 as of Tuesday, from about 1,200 two weeks earlier. It added that all the transactions had been cancelled. Speaking at a Kowloon City district council meeting, Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming noted that in the cases involved, Apple’s online commerce security measures were not in effect and the transactions did not require verification. “This meant that one-time passwords or mobile app verification were not required, allowing fraudsters to place large orders using illegally obtained credit card information,” he said. Chow added that police found the IP addresses involved had used VPN technology, while recipient information was either false or incomplete. The force has requested the cancellation of all related transactions to ensure that cardholders, banks and Apple have not suffered any losses. Earlier this month, many social media users reported unauthorised credit card transactions involving Apple’s new iPhone models, which were available for pre-order on September 11. The cards had been issued by different banks. Ahead of the presale of another new iPhone model next month, Chow said police were continuing to investigate the fraud and had asked Apple to review its transaction processes to prevent similar incidents from happening again. The police chief also noted that the overall crime rate in the city rose slightly, by 0.2 per cent, to 59,213 cases from January to August compared with the same period a year ago, but most major serious crimes fell. He said the police campaign against investment scams had proved effective: online investment scams fell by one-third, while losses decreased by 30 per cent in the first eight months of this year. Chow also said the level of terrorist threat facing Hong Kong remained “moderate”, but undercurrents still existed. The force will also begin testing a central drone management system on Hong Kong Island in the third quarter of this year to monitor drone patrol missions and coordinate resources for joint high-altitude patrols. Chow added that drone hangars would be installed on the rooftops of police stations and some government buildings to enhance patrol coverage and mobility.

title: Sell family jewels for latest iPhone? In India, craze dials up debate
description: The new iPhones might not make sense financially in India, but the desire for one is not always rational, analysts say.
content: Tens of thousands of people thronged Apple stores in India this month to snap up the newest iPhone models – the 18 Pro and Pro Max – but the frenzy has kicked off public debate in the country about affordability and consumer debt. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at 164,900 rupees (US$1,700) and goes up to 179,000 rupees, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at 179,900 rupees and maxes out at 329,900 rupees. Apple also unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first-ever folding smartphone, essentially setting a new price benchmark with the top-end variant at 449,000 rupees (US$4,700), breaching the psychological threshold of 400,000 rupees for the first time in the Indian market. The excitement among consumers – with some standing in line for hours – underscored how India, the world’s second largest smartphone market by volume, has emerged as one of the fastest growing sales sources for Apple. There are no official sales figures for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max yet, said Navkender Singh, an India-based analyst for IDC. Pre-orders for the Duo will start on October 16 and Singh forecast that it would sell well in India despite its price tag. “It is a huge signal of wealth and affluence,” he said, pointing to what he called the “brand halo” of the tech giant. The model was priced high because it was not being locally produced and was a luxury or aspirational product, he said. “It will tell the world that you have arrived – that you are rich enough to buy such an iPhone.” Interest in the luxury devices has prompted scrutiny on social media over how young Indians with moderate incomes are increasingly relying on long-term, zero-cost monthly instalments to normalise spending beyond their means. A man from New Delhi went viral on Monday after saying he had sold jewellery he inherited from his great-grandmother and grandmother to buy his wife an iPhone 18 Pro. In the interview outside an Apple Store in Noida, where he was queuing, he said he did it because he believed in enjoying life. Social media users have also circulated memes juxtaposing the cost of an iPhone Duo against major financial milestones such as buying a car. “An iPhone Duo top variant in India is priced around [450,000 rupees]. Just to put this into perspective, for this much amount, you can: fund a foreign family trip; front-load your Systematic Investment Plans which will give you 11-12 per cent returns; a couple of years of kids school fees; 30 grams (1oz) of gold; upgrade your house with four to five good quality white goods; house rental for a year in Tier 2 cities,” Kapil Vats Prince posted. Another user, Aakash Yadav, pointed out that unless an individual earned at least an annual salary of 13 million rupees (US$135,400), buying the created a “substantially larger labour burden than it does for the average US worker”. Price difference Some questioned what the price disparity between the phones sold in India and those in the United States. An iPhone 18 Pro sells for between US$1,199 and US$2,399 in the US. IDC’s Singh said part of the reason was India’s 18 per cent goods and services tax. Prices in the US do not show taxes, which vary from state to state in the country. Also, a Duo is likely to cost about 70,000-80,000 rupees more in India than in the US because it is imported as a fully built unit, according to Singh. Apple’s average selling price for phones had stayed above US$800, while India's overall smartphone average price sat between US$150 and US$250, Singh said. “That gap is the clearest evidence of Apple’s pull in India.” And yet, despite the gripes about price, sales of iPhones keep growing, reflecting their utility. “This is one of the most important things we use every day,” Singh said. “We may forget our hankies or sunglasses when leaving our house but we can never forget our phones. It is part of our personality now.” The price difference was part of the criticism against the phone’s affordability, said Samit Sinha, founder of Delhi-based Alchemist Brand Consulting. “It is causing more heartaches than the absolute price.” India is Apple’s second-largest production base for iPhones globally, ranked only after China, but that does not automatically mean more competitive pricing in the Indian market, according to Sinha. Given the size of the Indian market – estimated at 1.5 billion consumers – widely divergent reactions are likely. Buyers were those who had been iPhone users or had aspired to one for a long time, while critics were likely to be those who had not been users, he said. The top 5 per cent who could afford the luxury gadget still amounted to around 75 million people. “That is a pretty large market and that is where luxury brands operate,” he said. ‘Emotional aspect’ The desire for the latest iPhone did not have to make sense, Sinha said. “Frankly, I don’t think an iPhone or any Apple product is bought strictly for rational reasons. There is certainly an emotional aspect to it. You sort of resonate with your own self-image.” The affordability debate came into stark focus last month after a teenager who reportedly bought an expensive iPhone but was unable to afford the repayments jumped off a cliff. Both his parents, who had refused to give him the money for his repayments, followed him down the hilltop. Apple always managed to create a sense of excitement about its products, said Lloyd Mathias, a Delhi-based angel investor and business strategist. That was why people were willing to go to great lengths to buy an iPhone. They want the bragging rights and they tend to go to crazy extremes Lloyd Mathias, a business strategist “People who may be even conservative about their mode of transport are willing to strengthen their chequebook for an iPhone. They want the bragging rights and they tend to go to crazy extremes.” India also has a large and growing market for used and refurbished iPhones – which adds longevity to the products more than in other markets, according to Mathias. “There is always a consumer who says they want the joy of holding an Apple iPhone. India has a long track record of trading in second-hand phones. There is somebody who finds value in this.” Some, though, said they did not get the hype. Rajender Nager, a Delhi-based real estate consultant, said he felt there was no need for anything more than an Android phone that costs under 40,000 rupees. “That also lasts two to three years, so why should I spend so much? There is no limit to your spending if all you want is a status symbol,” he said. Radhakrishnan Swaminathan, a recent college graduate who works as an intern at a motor and switchgear trading firm, said many of his friends were interested in getting the latest iPhone, but he was content with his iPhone 15 and a MacBook. “I can get an iPad for 50,000 rupees and an Apple Pencil. People want to upgrade to the latest technology. What I feel is that if you are rational and you know what you want to achieve in life, you will not be blinded by luxury appeal,” he said. “For 300,000 rupees, you can buy a car or bike.”

title: Retired Hong Kong woman loses HK$2.9 million in online romance, fake app scam
description: Case among at least 18 online romance scams reported in past week, with total losses nearing HK$7.8 million, according to police.
content: A retired woman in Hong Kong lost nearly HK$2.9 million (US$369,670) in a romance scam after a fraudster posing as a power company employee won her trust and lured her into a bogus investment scheme. Police said the case was among at least 18 online romance scams reported in the past week, with total losses nearing HK$7.8 million, according to the force’s CyberDefender social media page. The 71-year-old retiree met a man on Facebook who claimed to work for a power company. The pair gradually developed an online romantic relationship, despite never meeting in person. After gaining the woman’s trust, the man introduced what he described as a sure-profit waste recycling investment project in Singapore and persuaded her to download a fake investment platform app. She was then instructed by purported customer service staff to open an account and deposit money. Although the platform showed her investments generating increasing returns, the woman was unable to withdraw any funds when she tried to cash out, with customer service staff repeatedly citing various reasons for the delays. The scammer also claimed he had been arrested in Singapore on money-laundering allegations and pleaded with the victim to transfer money for bail and legal fees. He further instructed her to visit cryptocurrency exchange shops and deposit cash into designated digital wallets. Police said the woman exhausted her savings and borrowed money from friends and finance companies, transferring nearly HK$2.9 million in 17 transactions. The victim only discovered the scam after a finance company pursued her for debt repayment. She turned to her daughter for financial help and learned she had been cheated.

title: Vietnam charges 3 men with terrorism as abduction claim emerges
description: Viet Tan says the pair, who hold Norwegian and Australian citizenship, entered Cambodia legally and planned to leave four days later.
content: A Vietnamese pro-democracy organisation has alleged that two of its members, who hold Norwegian and Australian citizenship, were abducted in Cambodia and taken to the border with Vietnam, where Hanoi authorities later accused them of illegally entering the country. Vietnam has charged the two men, along with a third alleged member of the organisation, with terrorism and document forgery, saying they were caught crossing the border from Cambodia with forged identity documents. The organisation, Viet Tan, said the two men, Nguyen Duc Thuan and Ho Pham Hiep Huy, were reported missing in Cambodia hours before Vietnamese authorities said they were caught. A representative told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that Thuan and Huy had entered Cambodia legally on September 15 and were due to leave on September 19. “This was an abduction,” the representative said. The allegation has not been independently established and Vietnamese authorities have not publicly addressed the claim that the two men disappeared inside Cambodia. Viet Tan said the two men had not travelled to Vietnam and had used legal travel documents, pointing to their itinerary as evidence that they had planned to leave Cambodia on September 19. The comments came a day after Vietnam’s Ministry of Public Security said its Security Investigation Agency had launched criminal proceedings against Thuan, Hiep and Thai Cong Truong Son on charges of terrorism under Article 299 of the Penal Code and forging seals and documents of agencies and organisations under Article 341. Vietnamese authorities said border guards at the My Quy Tay border station in Tay Ninh province caught the three men at about 9.50pm on September 18 while they were illegally entering Vietnam from Cambodia. According to the ministry, Thuan, 52, was carrying two fake Vietnamese identity cards – both bearing his photograph – under the name Phan Duc Trung, and a Norwegian passport in his own name. Huy, 51, was carrying an Australian passport in the name of Tran Hiep. Son, 46, is from Dong Thap province. The ministry said the three men told investigators they were members of Viet Tan, which Hanoi designates as a terrorist organisation, and had carried forged documents to enter Vietnam illegally to conduct terrorist and sabotage activities. Viet Tan describes itself as a pro-democracy political organisation advocating peaceful political change in Vietnam. The Supreme People’s Procuracy approved the prosecution and detention orders on Monday, according to the ministry. The investigation is continuing and no court has yet ruled on the charges against the three men. Viet Tan first raised the alarm on September 24, saying Thuan and Hiep had travelled from Bangkok to Phnom Penh on September 15 and were due to return to Bangkok on September 19. The organisation said their last known communication was on the morning of September 18 and that they did not board their scheduled flight. It said the two had gone to Cambodia to meet Vietnamese human rights activists. Viet Tan has identified Thuan and Hiep as long-time members of the organisation. It says Thuan lives in Oslo with his wife and two children, while Hiep lives in Melbourne with his wife. The organisation has urged the Norwegian and Australian governments to seek direct access to the two men and ensure their safety. It has also said Thuan requires daily insulin for diabetes and should have continued access to medication and medical care. The case has prompted criticism from Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates. In a statement on Tuesday, Robertson described the arrests as an example of what he called Vietnam’s use of transnational repression. He called on Norway and Australia to seek the men’s release. The reported timeline is central to the competing accounts. Viet Tan says Thuan and Hiep were last in contact on the morning of September 18, while Vietnamese authorities maintain that the three men were intercepted at the border more than 12 hours later. The organisation said the families of the two men had been in contact with Norwegian and Australian foreign ministries and embassies in Bangkok and Phnom Penh. They also appealed to the United Nations Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, according to Viet Tan. The third man, Son, has received less attention in Viet Tan’s public statements. Vietnamese authorities, however, have included him in the same investigation and said all three men admitted being Viet Tan members. Viet Tan has publicly identified Thuan and Hiep as its members but has provided fewer details about Son.

title: Opinion | What trap? US-China relations show conflict is far from inevitable
description: The Thucydides Trap that has dominated debate for a decade is a poor fit for reality. Beijing and Washington are both showing they can share the stage without drifting into war.
content: For a decade, foreign policy circles have treated war between the United States and China as something close to destiny. The theory has a fancy, fashionable name borrowed from ancient Greece: the “Thucydides Trap” – the idea that a rising power and an established one are fated to collide, the way two articulated lorries merging into a single lane rarely ends well. The term is widely used in commentaries on US-China relations. Frictions get written off as “inevitable” regardless of what actually happened. But a closer look at how the two governments behave, not just how pundits describe them, tells a different story. Both sides are, for now, choosing the diplomatic equivalent of indicating before they change lanes. Any analysis about power transition has to start with power itself, so here is where the two superpowers stand at the moment. By market exchange rates, the US economy was worth about US$30.6 trillion in 2025 against China’s US$19.4 trillion, putting China’s economy at roughly 63 per cent of the size of the US. China has led the world in manufacturing value added for 16 straight years, hitting 34.7 trillion yuan (US$5.2 trillion) in 2025, an industrial base that the US would struggle to replicate even if it wanted to. China’s research and development spending passed 3.9 trillion yuan in 2025, with strengths in renewable energy, artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and robotics. For its part, the US still holds the cards in several areas that China cannot easily match: the US dollar’s reserve currency status, deep basic science, a global network of allies and the ability to project military power anywhere on Earth. This is not a story of one power overtaking the other. This is two heavyweights circling each other, neither able to land a knockout blow. There are three reasons the US-China rivalry might not end in war and tragedy. First, the guard rails still hold. Nuclear deterrence, tangled global supply chains and shared problems such as climate change and public health form a kind of ballast keeping both ships upright. Regular summits between the two countries’ leaders are not mere photo ops. They are how great powers check their assumptions before a small miscalculation turns into a large one. Second, Washington’s bark might be worse than its bite. US policy on China often looks less like grand strategy and more like a barroom argument that resets every election cycle. Extreme partisanship, congressional gridlock and the tussle between state and federal power all make it hard for the US to sustain one consistent approach to China for longer than one electoral term. Taking a hard line on China might play well on the campaign trail. However, a slogan is not a strategy, and slogans rarely survive contact with a change of administration. Third, the US-China relationship is far from the only source of global friction. Under US President Donald Trump, Washington has often been at loggerheads with its own allies. Some of these disagreements have been every bit as bitter as anything between the US and China. As it turns out, friction is simply what happens when large economies with different interests share a planet. It does not herald a war on its own. Perhaps the more significant shift is that China has stopped merely responding to the moves the US makes and started trying to shape the global agenda itself. That shift rests on three foundations. The first is economic gravity. China runs the world’s most complete industrial supply chain. More than US$600 billion in annual bilateral goods trade gives both sides real reasons to avoid a clean break, however tempting decoupling might sound in a campaign speech. China remains the largest trading partner the US has outside North America. The second is a consistent playbook: no compromise on sovereignty, open competition on technology and industry, and practical cooperation on shared problems such as climate change and food security. That tiered approach stops the relationship collapsing into a zero-sum fight every time a new dispute appears. The third is a wider stage. With the Brics bloc of developing economies expanding, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation deepening and Global South ties growing, the US-China relationship is no longer just a two-player game. Much of the rest of the world would rather not be forced to choose a side, and that reluctance is itself a brake on both Beijing and Washington. None of this means the danger has passed. The hard edge of US-China policy shows no sign of softening soon. A single incident in the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea could still upend the relationship overnight. Escaping the Thucydides Trap was never going to mean the end of competition. It means building rules sturdy enough to keep that competition within a peaceful lane and keeping military conflict off the table altogether. Sparta and Athens never had to worry about nuclear weapons, global supply chains or a shared climate crisis. Borrowing their story to predict the 21st century is like using a horse-drawn buggy manual to help fix a Tesla. It might contain a grain of wisdom, but it will not get you very far. Whether China and the US can build a genuine peaceful coexistence is not a private matter between two capitals. It will help decide the shape of global stability for decades. Power does not have to change hands at the point of a sword. In an interdependent world, two great powers can still work out how to share the stage.

title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on company supplying vehicles to Ukraine
description: Moscow has been accused by Western officials of carrying out sabotage acts to undermine support for Ukraine and destabilise European nations.
content: Estonian authorities said on Tuesday they had concluded that an arson attack in mid-August on a defence company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that “such actions are absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s charge d’affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry. A fire broke out overnight on August 15 at a building in Estonia’s capital used by Milrem Robotics, but was quickly brought under control, the BNS news agency reported. On August 17, two Latvian suspects were detained in neighbouring Latvia, and a third followed the next day. The suspects were handed over to Estonia. Milrem has supplied THEMIS unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine. The Estonian Internal Security Service said that it had concluded that the arson attack “was a deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services”. It said in a statement that “the modus operandi of the Milrem attack is consistent with other acts of sabotage carried out in Europe on behalf of Russia”, adding that it “assesses that the attack is directly attributable to the Russian Federation”. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that “such statements are unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever.” Peskov added: “We cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t.” Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations. The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. That includes organising plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defence technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. In a recent case that pointed to an escalation of such activity, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August using a drone laden with explosives. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michael wrote on social media that “we will not be intimidated”.

title: Analysis | Hong Kong’s Asian Games mix of good, bad and ugly, but record medal haul still possible
description: Success will be judged on whether the 580-strong delegation surpasses the 53 medals won in Hangzhou three years ago.
content: Hong Kong’s athletes were sent to the Asian Games in Japan this month with the demand they “achieve even greater success, bringing more glory to the country and Hong Kong” and the weight of a city’s considerable expectations on their shoulders. In this instance, greater success is surpassing the record 53 medals won in Hangzhou three years ago, although the message might also have been “look at how much money we give you, don’t disappoint us”. Whether the 580 sportsmen and women tasked with amassing more than the eight gold, 16 silver and 29 bronze bagged last time succeed, depends entirely on the events of the next five days. So far, the tally stands at 35; five gold, 12 silver, 18 bronze. A quiet Tuesday for Hong Kong, when athletics came to its predictably fruitless conclusion, was enlivened by the cyclists winning bronze in the men’s team sprint. If the medal count is to be beaten, never mind the number of golds, then there is a lot riding on the likes of cyclist Ceci Lee Sze-wing, the city’s golfers, the men’s rugby sevens team, the men’s and women’s squash teams, sailor Nicholas Halliday and tennis star Coleman Wong Chak-lam. Of those, Wong would appear to be under considerably more pressure than most, simply because a failure to secure any podium spot is expected to put future funding for the city’s tennis association in doubt. With rain once again causing chaos in Nagoya, Wong finally began his men’s singles tournament with a routine 6-4, 6-1 victory over Jordan’s Zaid Al-Mashni. Far greater challenges lie ahead; on Wednesday he must overcome Japan’s Yosuke Watanuki, who won silver three years ago while Wong was losing in the quarter-finals. Rugby sevens, where Hong Kong’s men are looking for a third straight gold, and Lee’s time at the Izu Velodrome both begin on Thursday, while golfer Taichi Kho begins the defence of his individual title a day earlier. All involved know what it means to compete and win under pressure, something Siobhan Haughey, who won two golds and two silvers at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre last week, called “a privilege”. Table tennis player Doo Hoi-kem had a rather different take after she and partner Pedrey Ng Wing-lam won women’s doubles bronze on Monday. It was debutant Ng’s first medal at the Games, and it was Doo’s first since a women’s team bronze in 2018. “Of course, we could have done better, but in the end, winning a bronze medal in the women’s doubles still makes us very happy,” Doo said. “I hope people will not always judge or write us off solely based on results.” Gymnastics might consider itself lucky not to have been judged on results over the past decade, but Ng Ka-ki’s unexpected bronze in the men’s vault will ensure its continued existence as a Tier A sport at the Hong Kong Sports Institute (HKSI). Before Ng’s performance, Stone Shek Wai-hung’s gold at the 2018 Games in Jakarta was the only medal the city’s gymnasts managed in the previous eight years. Maybe the key in this instance is in taking responsibility away from the HKSI and local coaches, and handing it over to those running the China national team, who spent two months in Beijing before the Games knocking Ng into shape. “Their trials created a very good environment and helped me prepare better for this competition,” Ng said. It could be the answer for the city’s track and field team too. The problems developing athletes in Hong Kong stretch back years, and were perfectly highlighted in Japan by the disqualification of the women’s and mixed teams in their respective 4x100m relays and Tiffany Yue Nga-yan’s performance in the long jump. Yue’s bronze in Hangzhou must feel like a lead weight at times, setting what may have been unreasonable expectations on her shoulders. Still, as a paid athlete, going from hitting 6.50 metres in 2023, to not clearing 6.00m this season until your third jump in the final, is as concerning as two relay teams being DQ’d because they could not get the baton change right. As you might expect, there were moments of individual achievement. Vincent Lam and Lo Ying-chiu both ran season-best times in the men’s and women’s marathon, while racewalker Chin Man-kit finished fifth in his half-marathon. But Hong Kong sent 38 track and field athletes to Nagoya, and of the 11 that took part in medal events, only three had qualifying rounds: Lin Mingfu in the men’s long jump, Yip King-wai in the men’s 200m and Shing Cho-yan in the women’s 100m hurdles. Needless to say, none came close to making the podium, and the loss of Tier A status, which could be triggered after four years of collective failure, should come with a complete overhaul of those running the sport in the city. Others have nervous waits too, and not just in seeing if the medal count can be matched or even bettered. The city’s equestrians also technically need a medal, while even those sports that did get one might be looking over their shoulders. Before the Games, triathlon head coach Andrew Wright complained about governing bodies not setting the bar high enough. In his case, it’s not the bar that is the problem, a second team bronze cannot mask the fact individual success appears as far away as ever. But expectations ebb and flow depending on the sport, and it will need some athletes to defy those if the greater success Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu had called for is to be achieved by the closing ceremony on Sunday.

title: Hong Kong firms lag mainland China on AI adoption amid legacy-system burden: Accenture
description: Only one in 10 firms has deployed generative AI across multiple functions, compared with about one in five on the mainland, consultancy says.
content: Hong Kong businesses are lagging behind their mainland Chinese peers in adopting artificial intelligence, as entrenched legacy systems and a risk-averse corporate mindset slow the city’s digital transition, according to a senior executive at consultancy Accenture. Only 10 per cent of Hong Kong firms surveyed by Accenture had integrated generative AI across multiple business functions, compared with about 21 per cent of mainland enterprises, said Robert Hah, Hong Kong office lead at Accenture Greater China, in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. Mainland China’s rapid adoption of enterprise AI has been fuelled by falling model costs and a flourishing domestic developer ecosystem led by firms such as DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post. Tech giants including Ant Group, Tencent Holdings, Alibaba and Baidu rushed to roll out enterprise-focused AI agents at this year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai – the country’s top AI event – signalling a shift in the industry battleground from building foundation models to embedding AI directly into corporate workflows. While mainland firms benefited from access to this expanding ecosystem, Hah said a “mindset shift” remained the key differentiator between the two markets. There are legacy infrastructures in place that may make it less meaningful or worthwhile to make a quick change right away Robert Hah, Accenture Greater China Mainland companies were moving faster because of their willingness to “lean in and reinvent”, whereas Hong Kong’s entrenched IT infrastructure made local businesses hesitant to overhaul established operating models, Hah said. “There are legacy infrastructures in place that may make it less meaningful or worthwhile to make a quick change right away,” Hah said, comparing the current gap to Hong Kong’s historically slower embrace of e-commerce relative to the mainland. The divide underscores a growing challenge for Hong Kong as the local government pushes to position the city as a tech hub. Under its first five-year plan, Hong Kong has placed AI at the centre of efforts to upgrade its economy. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu recently pledged to pursue dual strategies of “AI for industries” and “industries for AI” to modernise traditional sectors while cultivating home-grown tech players. Planned initiatives include an “AI city brain” system to manage extreme weather events, major incidents and public order. “Our industries will be more diversified, education enhanced, [the city] more international, and we will be a highly technologically empowered Hong Kong,” Lee said earlier this month. Despite the policy push, the biggest barriers to AI deployment remained organisational rather than technological, Hah said. He cited a disconnect between companies’ broader business strategies and their AI plans, as well as persistent shortages of digital talent. While 84 per cent of Hong Kong organisations surveyed said they intended to create entry-level jobs for “AI-fluent” talent, more than half reported they were struggling to find talent that could work with the technology. To bridge this gap, companies needed to rethink jobs and workflows rather than just adding AI tools to existing processes, Hah said. However, labour shortages and other economic pressures were expected to push Hong Kong firms to accelerate automation efforts, led by early adopters in financial services, banking and insurance, while retail, consumer goods and hospitality trailed behind, according to Hah.

title: US and China need shared risk vocabulary to manage AI threats: Beijing-linked think tank
description: State security ministry-linked think tank urges dynamic system of ‘risk changes and response levels’ rather than seeking abstract ‘red line’.
content: Beijing and Washington should first develop a common language around AI risks rather than seek to resolve their broader technology rivalry, a leading Chinese think tank has advised. The call from the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations (CICIR), affiliated with the Ministry of State Security, comes days after Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to formalise a new AI dialogue mechanism during their summit in Washington, their second such meeting this year. Under the agreement, both sides will exchange views on the risks and benefits of AI, as well as establish a bilateral communication channel for AI-related incidents, with the next dialogue due to be held in November. Liu Chong, director of CICIR’s Centre for Sci-Tech and Strategic Studies, said the dialogue should begin by building a shared understanding of emerging AI risks and gradually establishing trust between the two sides. In an article published on Monday, Liu wrote that the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) meant there was unlikely to be a single point at which technology could be clearly divided into safe and unsafe categories. Instead, he proposed developing a dynamic system of “risk changes and response levels” compared with searching for an abstract “red line”. Given the fluid nature of “superintelligence risks”, effective international governance must prioritise fostering mutual knowledge over pushing for comprehensive rule books, Liu argued, using the preferred Trump administration term for AI. “This is where China and the US first need to get on the same page,” he wrote. A White House statement following last week’s summit said the leaders had agreed to use the term “superintelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence” for the emerging technology under discussion. Beijing has said it respects the US’ choice of terminology and that further communication will be needed as the technology evolves. Liu also suggested an approach to governance that respected sovereignty over technology while maintaining dialogue. “China and the US do not need to adopt the same AI industrial policies, nor do they need to share model parameters and core technologies,” he wrote. Lin suggested that they should rather develop a set of risk terms that could be understood by governments, companies and researchers on both sides. This would include common understandings of what constituted dangerous autonomy, such as when model behaviour should be treated as a security incident and when training should be slowed or halted. CICIR’s call for a shared understanding comes as the two countries continue to compete over advanced technology, with Washington tightening restrictions on Beijing’s access to advanced chips and AI capabilities. It also called for stronger oversight of frontier AI companies, arguing that a small group of leading firms “should not determine” the direction of AI governance. Liu said US frontier models were largely closed-source and that the lack of transparency had increased concerns outside the companies. “US companies should take the lead in disclosing information about AI risks,” he wrote. This month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that the US should maintain its technological lead over China and continue restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment to Beijing. Chinese officials have rejected such an approach and called for international cooperation on AI instead. Liu acknowledged the tension, writing that the central challenge for AI governance was whether Beijing and Washington could preserve enough “trust space” to cooperate while their technological competition continued or intensified. “The goal of dialogue should be to establish a minimum framework for managing risks that could survive even as the US-China technological competition continues or intensifies,” he wrote. Beyond managing risks between Beijing and Washington, broader international access to AI safety tools and capabilities as part of global AI governance was needed, he said. As AI advances, mature and widely applicable capabilities should be converted into accessible public goods, Liu added. “The governance of superintelligence must look beyond merely curbing the spread of offensive risks,” he wrote. “It must also actively promote the adoption of defensive safeguards.”

title: Hong Kong turns Halloween into month-long event with street parties, free rides
description: Street celebrations to run across three consecutive Saturdays in Central, Lan Kwai Fong and other areas under new Tourism Board drive.
content: A new month-long campaign to transform Hong Kong into Asia’s premier Halloween destination will feature street parties across five neighbourhoods along with free rides on decorated buses and trams. The Tourism Board’s inaugural “Hong Kong Halloween Month” will bring street celebrations to Central, Kai Tak, Lan Kwai Fong, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays from October 17, culminating on Halloween night. The events will run alongside promotional events at Disneyland and Ocean Park. “We want to turn up the festive energy across all corners of the city,” Tourism Board executive director Anthony Lau Chun-hon said, adding that he hoped Hong Kong would become the first destination people thought of for Halloween celebrations in Asia. The campaign follows a tourism strategy outlined in February’s budget to put greater emphasis on festivals that are less prominent in mainland China, including Halloween, to draw more visitors to the city. The five selected areas will have different attractions. In Central, Statue Square Gardens will host illuminated Halloween installations, and a large costume party will be held on Chater Road on October 31. Kai Tak Sports Park will combine cosplay with Cantopop DJ sets and a pet photo area. A haunted red minibus installation will be displayed in Mong Kok, while Tsim Sha Tsui East will hold DJ parties and a Halloween market. In Lan Kwai Fong, organisers are planning three themed street celebrations with performers, music and photo spots. Allan Zeman, chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Group, said about 80,000 people visited the nightlife area during last year’s Halloween celebrations. He expected the expanded festivities to bring additional business to restaurants, bars and shops. The Tourism Board has also arranged a Halloween-themed open-top Citybus route linking major celebration sites on October 17, 24 and 31. Two decorated trams will run between Causeway Bay and Sheung Wan on the same evenings. Visitors in costumes can use both services free of charge. Lau said the board was extending a celebration previously concentrated on Halloween night and individual venues into a month-long promotion, with the aim of spreading visitor spending across different parts of the city. Halloween displays and activities elsewhere, including at the West Kowloon Cultural District and Tai Kwun, will also be promoted as part of the campaign.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong man returns to city after 26 years in Philippine prison for drug offences
description: After two-month delay in wake of court ruling commuting his life sentence, Tang Lung-wai, 55, returns home still protesting his innocence.
