content: A Hong Kong man imprisoned in the Philippines for 26 years while fighting against convictions for drug possession has been released and returned home on Tuesday evening. Tang Lung-wai, 55, was seen hugging his elder brother, Billy Tang Lung-piu, as he arrived from Manila at the Hong Kong International Airport. Asked how he felt after arriving in his home city, he said: “After spending 26 years in hell, I am unflappable.” “The moment I got out of the car [in Manila], uncuffed, I felt finally free,” he said earlier in the day. “I am really lucky to be able to walk out physically sound.” Tang Lung-wai was arrested in Manila in July 2000 for possession of methamphetamine, also known as Ice, and placed on remand. He was convicted more than a decade later, in 2011, and was handed a life sentence, which in the Philippines amounts to a maximum of 40 years in prison. A Manila court ruled this past July that Tang’s sentence would be commuted in view of his good conduct, and he was ordered to be released and deported immediately. His family appealed to Hong Kong authorities for help after Tang was further detained after the ruling, with severe weather and administrative issues delaying his release by two months. First, storms shut down the Philippine Bureau of Immigration’s office in late August, and he was only sent to the bureau’s detention centre on the night of September 7. Then he had to wait a further three weeks for the paperwork for his deportation to be completed. Tang recalled the moment he was admitted to the immigration facility and allowed to change out of his orange prison uniform into his own clothes. “That feeling [from the civilian clothes] was completely different. I did smile, a knowing smile,” he recalled. “I was finally not an inmate. I was relaxed and happy at that moment.” He left the bureau’s facility located near the maximum-security New Bilibid Prison compound on Tuesday afternoon and was taken to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport, where he was greeted by a Chinese embassy representative before boarding a flight home. He was accompanied by three Hong Kong immigration officers who had flown to Manila to assist him. As Tang looked out the window of his departing flight, he recalled having to answer roll-calls in prison four times a day. “I would kneel on the football pitch and look up at the sky. Whenever a flight flew by, I always asked myself: ‘when would it be my turn to board a flight?’ Now I am finally on that flight,” he said. Tang, who fought for years to prove his innocence on the grounds that he was not in the Philippines when surveillance for the crime took place and wrote two books about his experience, said other deportees at the immigration facility had asked him how he had survived the 26 years in prison. “A lot of people thought they would die in prison, and so did I. I never thought I would survive. So how did I make it? I keep an ‘Ah Q mentality’,” he said, referring to the famous protagonist created by novelist Lu Xun, who sustains himself by insisting he is a moral or spiritual victor. “I keep telling myself I still have a chance, I still have hope … Nothing is all good or all bad; every dark cloud has a silver lining.” Tang said he had been anxious and did not sleep well in the months ahead of the decisive hearing. Having returned to Hong Kong, he would rest first before sweeping the tombs of his parents and grandparents and having a reunion meal with his family the following day. Despite having mild diabetes and losing a few teeth due to gum disease, Tang said he had kept exercising behind bars and lost some weight. He aimed to obtain a driving licence in Hong Kong so he could work as a driver or delivery worker. He said he would be staying in his brothers’ homes for some time, but wished to be allocated a public housing flat for a single person. Tang thanked the Chinese embassy in the Philippines, Hong Kong’s Immigration Department, former lawmaker Paul Tse Wai-chun, former chief executive Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor, the Hong Kong media, the Tang Lung-wai Incident Concern Group and all the people who had offered help over the past two decades. Tang, who held a British National (Overseas) passport when he entered the Philippines in 2000, also thanked the British embassy in Manila for its help. On Tuesday, the Hong Kong government expressed its gratitude to the Office for the Commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the city and the Chinese embassy in Manila for their support and assistance in facilitating the swift return of Tang, whom it had been helping since 2003, following his release. A government spokesman said the Immigration Department and the embassy had actively liaised with relevant authorities in the Philippines to follow up the case and immediately issued Tang with a document for returning to Hong Kong, helping expedite the overall repatriation procedure. Former legislator Tse, a lawyer who helped Tang for years, said he was happy and excited for him, although he expressed some regret that Tang could not make it back before the Mid-Autumn Festival, a time for reunions, which fell on September 25. “It has been a wrongful detention of over 20 years,” Tse said. “Of course, I hope he can come back and start afresh. Things have changed a lot in Hong Kong as he has been away for so many years.” He recalled that he started helping Tang in 2010, when he was also pushing for the release of Tang’s co-defendant Cheung Tai-on. Cheung had also been sentenced to life imprisonment and died behind bars in 2016. Tse said he had sought help from Hong Kong’s director of immigration, Benson Kwok Joon-fung, who contacted the Chinese embassy in the Philippines to expedite the paperwork on both the Chinese and the Philippine sides while Tang was awaiting deportation. The former lawmaker said it was one of the longest cases he had worked on providing pro bono legal aid, and he would continue to help Tang reintegrate into society. Tang has insisted on his innocence over the past two decades, with his case drawing high-level diplomatic attention. In 2018, then-city leader Lam wrote to Rodrigo Duterte, the country’s president at the time, urging his government to hasten its search for immigration records that would allegedly prove Tang’s innocence. Although those records indicated that Tang was not in the Philippines during the period local police said he was under surveillance, the country’s Supreme Court dismissed his final appeal in 2020.

title: How Asian Film Awards Academy’s filmmaking camp is grooming a new generation of directors
description: Asian Film Awards Academy’s 2026 International Film Camp brought together 16 of Asia’s emerging filmmakers in Macau. We spoke to four of them.
content: Far removed from the sweeping historical epics and sleek commercial blockbusters that have long defined the region’s cinematic exports, a quieter evolution is unfolding across Asian cinema. An emerging cohort of storytellers is eschewing grand spectacles to navigate the intimate, the unspoken and the marginalised. In doing so, these young directors are carving out a new path – one they view as more grounded and representative of contemporary life. Nadia Chui and Law Yik-man from Hong Kong, Bo Hanxiong from mainland China and Jonathan Chan Chon-sin from Macau – all in their twenties or early thirties – are four filmmakers who took part in this year’s International Film Camp, organised by the Asian Film Awards Academy from September 18 to 22, 2026, at The Londoner Macao. Supported by Hong Kong’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau, Macau’s Cultural Affairs Bureau and Sands China, the annual camp was set up in 2024 to provide mentorship, masterclasses and networking opportunities to help young directors launch and advance their careers. In 2026, 16 filmmakers were selected from more than 450 applicants across Asia to participate in the five-day programme themed “When Strangers Meet”. Acclaimed Singaporean filmmaker Anthony Chen, who has served as a mentor since the camp’s inauguration, views the initiative as a vital platform for new voices. He noted that many participants chose to shine a light on overlooked experiences or subjects traditionally considered taboo in mainstream Asian cinema. “Some of our participants attended film school overseas and bring a very international, Western technical training to their craft,” Chen says. “Yet their sensibility and storytelling DNA remain deeply rooted in the unspoken – what we refer to in Chinese as liubai, or leaving white space. “For instance, rather than spelling out your love for your family, the emotion is held in reserve,” he says. “That combination of poetry and artistry is wonderful in modern Asian filmmaking.” Genuine connections and invisible borders Chan’s short film, Tower, follows a young woman from mainland China who travels to Macau to meet her online boyfriend for the first time. As they wander through a landscape filled with replica European architecture, the couple attempts to connect through artificial role-playing and superficial banter. “My idea is about how two people try to find genuine love in a fake city,” Chan says. “There is a sense of absurdity in Macau’s artificial landscape. When I walk through The Venetian, I see hundreds of people taking photos of a fake sky,” he adds, referring to the ceiling of the Venice-themed shopping centre. In Tower, Chan parallels this artificiality with his characters’ flawed relationship. “Beyond examining human connection, I wanted to address social dynamics in my city, specifically the complex relationship between mainland Chinese visitors and Macanese locals,” he says. Similarly, Law’s film Unproven – which is inspired by Law’s real-life observations of LGBTQ asylum seekers – depicts a chance encounter between a Pakistani student and a Hong Kong immigrant in a Vancouver laundromat. The former is applying for LGBTQ asylum as his visa nears expiry, while the latter is struggling to assimilate. During their conversation, they adopt rehearsed, constructed identities. “As their conversation deepens, the audience begins to question whether this is a genuine confession or a performance,” Law says. “I am drawn to the invisible borders people carry within themselves. The memories they guard, the identities they struggle to articulate and the stories they reshape to be understood. “The film asks a fundamental question: if something cannot be proven, does that make it any less real?” Law, who was one of the more experienced filmmakers at the camp, has worked on major Hollywood blockbusters, including Avatar: Fire and Ash and Tron: Ares, but considers independent small-budget shorts equally compelling. “Unproven inherits a tradition in Hong Kong cinema that I deeply admire, which is the quiet tension between characters and the suspense that arises from not knowing whether to trust someone,” Law says, citing classics such as In the Mood for Love (2000) and Infernal Affairs as key creative influences. “With Unproven, which features no gunfights or chase scenes, I wanted to translate that cinematic tension into an everyday, intimate setting.” Capturing a generation adrift Bo explores authenticity through a different lens. He was the only filmmaker in the cohort to employ a documentary-style approach for a fictional narrative, casting non-professional actors. His short film, Under a Burning Sun, follows a group of young drifters travelling across China in a battered van. While the road offers freedom and camaraderie, their journey is sustained by a morally ambiguous hustle involving intimate encounters with strangers. I wanted to capture this generation’s sense of drift, desire and loneliness Bo Hanxiong “The inspiration stems from my love of road trips and road movies,” Bo says. “I love the visual rhythm of being on the move.” During Bo’s research at highway service areas across China, he observed a growing trend of young people pursuing transactional relationships for financial survival. “What intrigues me is not merely this precarious lifestyle, but the underlying uncertainty: when the future feels unclear, some choose to burn through the present rather than wait for tomorrow,” he says. “I wanted to capture this generation’s sense of drift, desire and loneliness.” Fostering a supportive network Beyond technical skills, featured speaker Fala Chen says the camp’s greatest asset is the supportive global network it fosters. “As we enter the era of AI, nothing can replace genuine human interaction,” says the Hong Kong actress and singer, referring to the camp’s collaborative workshops and pitching sessions. “I hope this community continues to exchange ideas, support one another and even collaborate on future projects.” She also expressed hope for more female directors to share authentic perspectives in a space defined by “less hierarchy, clear communication and positive energy”. Around half of this year’s shortlisted participants were female. Among them was Chui, director of Where the Sorrow Overflows, which explores the tense relationship between two neighbours – a Nepali single mother and an elderly man caring for his ailing wife – whose shared efforts to repair a persistent water leak gradually mend their emotional divide. “Female filmmakers bring a distinct, nuanced perspective,” Chui says. Inspired by her grandmother, the primary carer for her ill grandfather, and a widowed Nepali neighbour struggling to earn a living, Chui made the film about quiet resilience and subtle human behaviour rather than dramatic confrontation. On the final day of the camp, eight of the 16 participants, including Bo and Chan, were awarded production grants to realise their short films over the coming months. In previous editions, alumni projects have gone on to screen at prestigious international film festivals, including the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland, the Far East Film Festival in Udine, Italy, and the Toronto International Film Festival in Canada. “By the end of this year, we will have produced 24 short films in three years, which is quite a significant achievement,” says Roger Garcia, former executive director of both the Hong Kong International Film Festival and Asian Film Awards Academy, and a founding jury member of the camp. Garcia plans to curate an official film library, allowing international festival programmers to select short film packages that showcase the potential of Asian storytellers. “Asian cinema is exceptionally vibrant right now,” Garcia says, noting there are also exciting developments in emerging regions across Central Asia and Africa. “It’s so important now to expand the [global film community’s] horizon by connecting Asian storytellers with the rest of the world.” Want more articles like this?
