title: AI, robotic arms power Hong Kong public hospital laundry and meal centre
description: ‘Automation has greatly improved our occupational safety and health, reducing the repetitive strain and heavy lifting that workers previously endured,’ official says.
content: Hong Kong’s Hospital Authority has adopted artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic automation at its new support services centre to handle laundry and meal production for public hospitals, aiming to boost efficiency and worker safety. The six-storey, 62,000-square-metre centre, which houses the central laundry and food production unit, opened its doors to the press for the first time on Tuesday since beginning operations in March last year. Located in Tung Chung on Lantau Island, the facility meets about half of public hospitals’ laundry and meal requirements, using X-ray sorting, robotic arms and “cook-chill” kitchen technology. The complex’s central laundry, which occupies three floors, features Hong Kong’s first automatic X-ray sorting system to detect foreign objects in clothing and linens collected from 13 public hospitals. Robotic arms pick up dirty laundry from a conveyor belt, where items are scanned by an X-ray machine before washing, eliminating the need for manual checks. “The laundry can be extremely hot and humid in a traditional workplace,” said Dr Law Chun-bon, chief executive of the Kowloon West cluster. “Automation has greatly improved our occupational safety and health, reducing the repetitive strain and heavy lifting that workers previously endured.” A one-way workflow links every stage of the laundry process – from washing, drying, folding and ironing to final packaging and delivery – via a hanging-bag system and conveyor belts. Heavy linen bundles are handled by a robotic transport and stacking system – the first of its kind in Hong Kong – before being transferred to a fully automated storage rack, where automated guided vehicles transport sorted cages directly to delivery bays. Law said the system could reduce the risk of musculoskeletal injuries among workers. The facility’s central food production unit currently prepares patient meals for 15 public hospitals, using automated cooking, packaging and freezing lines. Meals are prepared using cook-chill technology, which cools food from 75 Celsius to below 4 degrees (167 Fahrenheit to 39.2) within two hours to lock in freshness and ensure consistent quality, while X-ray machines check the food for safety. “We hope that after trying it, the concept that hospital meals are unappetising can be changed,” Law added. The Tung Chung centre currently meets about 50 per cent of the authority’s overall support service demand, handling 33.2 million kg of laundry and 14.7 million meal sets annually, with the remainder covered by individual hospitals or outsourced providers. The authority expects the new centre to expand to cover nearly 70 per cent of demand by the end of 2026. The centre also houses an information technology (IT) corporate data centre with 500 server racks and Central Emergency Stores holding about 25 per cent of the authority’s required personal protective equipment. “The space freed up in hospitals is extremely precious,” said Antony Lui, chief manager for business support services at the authority’s head office. “The space each hospital puts forward will reflect its own development needs and service requirements, and it will definitely be used for clinical or patient services.” The centre is a key project under the city’s First Hospital Development Plan, which aims to expand and improve public hospitals to meet rising demand.

title: India-Europe trade corridor gets Trump’s backing, but can IMEC survive war?
description: Pitched as a rival to China’s Belt and Road, IMEC must bypass vulnerable Gulf chokepoints if it is ever to become operational, analysts say.
content: US President Donald Trump’s recent endorsement of a trade corridor connecting India to Europe via the Middle East has renewed focus on the three-year-old project, but analysts warn it must expand to withstand ongoing geopolitical conflicts. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) was first unveiled at the G20 summit in 2023 as an alternative to existing routes and China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Backed by India, the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel and the European Union, the project envisages combining shipping lanes, railways, energy pipelines and data cables into one corridor that is still largely a work in progress. Though some existing infrastructure can handle parts of the proposed route, key rail links, ports and other connections are still being developed. Trump tied his support for IMEC to efforts to move Middle Eastern energy infrastructure away from vulnerable maritime routes amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. “Iran’s terrorist attacks on commercial shipping in neighbouring countries have shown the need to shift Middle East energy infrastructure away from the Iranian checkpoints,” Trump said on September 22 at a meeting with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. “That’s why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and other places of getting oil out, whether it’s pipelines or anything else,” he said, adding that “together we are on the verge of overcoming challenges that have plagued this region for a decade”. The corridor represents a rare area of continuity between the second Trump administration and Joe Biden’s presidency, despite Trump’s backing having been erratic until recently, according to Alberto Rizzi, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. Trump’s recent endorsement helped build political momentum for the project, Rizzi said, even if “it is currently difficult to imagine that this political approval will translate any time soon into financial support from the US”. He said conflict in the region had also exposed a fundamental weakness in IMEC: how resilient can a trade corridor be if its key gateways rely on the very chokepoints it was meant to bypass? The near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war was already changing the scope of the project, Rizzi said, creating an “IMEC on wheels” in which trucks crossed the Arabian deserts to transport goods to the Mediterranean. Reliance on Omani and Emirati ports outside the strait had also grown, though this remapping had largely been spontaneous and not necessarily coordinated or interoperable, he said. Rizzi said the crisis had added weight to the argument for turning IMEC into a network with built-in redundancies. “A single route can be disrupted easily; a network of lanes instead can deal with disruptions much better,” he said. This weakness is clearest on IMEC’s eastern maritime leg, which connects Indian ports to UAE ports such as Jebel Ali and Khalifa before cargo travels overland through the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan towards Israel and Europe. Because UAE ports sit inside the Persian Gulf, ships arriving from India must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. At the other end, the corridor’s western gateway to the Mediterranean at Haifa in Israel is directly exposed to regional conflict. Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, founder and president of the Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies in Goa, said the Iran conflict had laid these weaknesses bare. “The corridor’s design depends on ships carrying goods from India across the Arabian Sea to the UAE, and that route runs through waters where the Strait of Hormuz and the approaches to it are hostage to any escalation involving Iran,” D’Souza said. “IMEC was conceived as a reliable alternative to the Suez route. But under the present circumstances, it can only become a corridor that swaps one chokepoint risk for another.” The Gaza war, which erupted just weeks after IMEC’s launch, had already delayed the project amid regional tensions and logistical challenges. The Iran conflict has only added to the uncertainty. Afaq Hussain, a non-resident senior fellow with the Project for Middle East Integration at the Atlantic Council, agreed with Rizzi that the IMEC’s geographic footprint needed to be diversified. “It shouldn’t be a single-line corridor,” Hussain said. “Making it a network of corridors [will] be more secure and diversify risk.” That could mean integrating ports such as Salalah in Oman, as well as routes through Egypt or Syria via Jordan, while addressing vulnerabilities at other regional chokepoints such as the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea, he said. Samriddhi Vij, an associate fellow in the Middle East programme at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, called the problem IMEC’s “paradox of resilience”, adding that the crisis had validated the case for diversification while making the corridor harder to operationalise. “Its eastern maritime architecture relies on Gulf ports inside or adjacent to Hormuz, while its western gateway around Haifa remains exposed to regional conflict,” Vij said. “Higher war-risk insurance and geopolitical uncertainty raise the corridor’s cost of capital. The crisis has therefore made IMEC simultaneously more strategically necessary and commercially harder to implement.” One response would be to build alternative gateways. Fujairah, on the UAE’s eastern coast outside the Strait of Hormuz, is one option. On September 20 – two days before Trump’s remarks – Etihad Rail and AD Ports launched a direct freight service connecting the Port of Fujairah with the Industrial City of Abu Dhabi. Cargo arriving at Fujairah could now travel inland via the UAE’s national rail network, turning an outside-Hormuz gateway into an increasingly practical logistics route, said foreign affairs analyst Robinder Sachdev. “Oman provides a second, potentially more structural option,” Sachdev said, noting that a 238km (148-mile) rail project was being built to connect the Omani city of Sohar to the UAE. But moving the IMEC’s gateways “cannot by itself solve the geography of modern warfare”, he said. “I would call it less a redrawing of IMEC than a redesign of IMEC.” The different components of IMEC need not follow the same geography, Sachdev said: freight could follow one alignment, while energy pipelines, electricity grids and digital cables follow others. “The crisis has not weakened the logic of IMEC – it has weakened the logic of a single-gateway IMEC,” he added. “The next stage should transform IMEC from a corridor into a network, because a line can be broken at one point; a network can reroute.”

title: Meet Matthew Stafford, the NFL star featured in Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ music video
description: The Los Angeles Rams quarterback, who has four daughters with his ex-cheerleader wife Kelly, won Super Bowl LVI in 2022 and was named the MVP in 2025.
content: A Taylor Swift music video is never complete without Easter eggs. When the pop superstar debuted the “Patient Zero” music video at the MTV Video Music Awards on September 27, fans were treated to a treasure trove of references and celebrity cameos. One of the familiar faces that popped up was Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, who was joined by his wife, Kelly Stafford. The two weren’t at the VMAs – the Rams were playing the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, and the NFL star’s wife and four daughters were there to support him – but their surprise appearance in the music video was a delight for American football fans. The couple are close with Swift and her husband, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, and were invited to their July wedding, per the New York Post. Their daughters, aged nine to six now, even attended the singer’s Eras Tour concert in 2024. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kelly Stafford (@kbstafford89) Here’s everything to know about the 38-year-old NFL player. What is Matthew Stafford’s background? Matthew Stafford was born on February 7, 1988, in Tampa, Florida, to parents John and Margaret Stafford, who are now separated. He grew up in Dunwoody, Georgia, per The Sun, before the family moved to Dallas, Texas. He attended Highland Park High School with former MLB star Clayton Kershaw. Both showed athletic prowess in school, playing football, American football, basketball and baseball together, according to MLB’s website. Stafford went on to attend the University of Georgia, where he met Kelly, who was a cheerleader. They married in April 2015. His father was a swim coach View this post on Instagram A post shared by U.S. Masters Swimming 🏊🏼🏊‍♀️🏊🏿‍♀️🏊🏾‍♂️🏊🏻🏊🏼‍♀️ (@mastersswimming) Stafford’s father was a swimmer throughout secondary school and his time at Florida State University, according to SwimSwam. He worked as a graduate assistant coach at the University of Georgia and later became the head coach of the men’s team at his alma mater. After quitting coaching in 1982, he entered the insurance industry. However, he eventually returned to competitive swimming and won a US Masters national title in 2023 in the 1,000-yard freestyle event – equivalent to around 914 metres. When did Matthew Stafford get into the NFL? Stafford’s profile in American football started rising while he was in secondary school. Under coach Randy Allen, he was considered the best quarterback of his class. His success continued with the Bulldogs at the University of Georgia, making him the first pick in the 2009 NFL Draft, after which he joined the Detroit Lions. In 2021, he joined the Rams and won Super Bowl LVI the following year. He was named the 2025 NFL Most Valuable Player by the Associated Press this February.

title: Xi urges universities to help drive China’s tech and innovation ambitions
description: The central government is pushing academic institutions to break down traditional silos, embrace interdisciplinarity and support national development.
content: President Xi Jinping has urged a major university to harness its interdisciplinary strengths in the humanities, sciences, engineering and medicine to support China’s national strategy, as Beijing looks to higher education institutions to help advance hi-tech development. Xi made the remarks in a letter released on Tuesday congratulating Sichuan University on its 130th anniversary and responding to faculty members and students at the prominent public university in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province. “I hope you will strive to play a pioneering role in supporting national strategies in the new era and contribute to China’s efforts to build itself into a strong country in education, science and technology, and talent,” Xi said in the letter, according to state-owned Xinhua News Agency. His message comes as Beijing steps up efforts to position universities as central pillars of innovation. In guidelines issued earlier this month on reforming China’s vast higher education system, Beijing urged institutions to develop distinct roles aligned with different national priorities. The central government said research universities should serve as a “key force” supporting major national strategies and that industry-specific institutions should strengthen their ability to serve the real economy. A five-year education development plan released by the State Council, China’s cabinet, in June also highlighted the need for universities to adapt to a new wave of technological and industrial transformation by strengthening their innovation capabilities and cultivating home-grown talent. The plan called for greater interdisciplinary collaboration, encouraging universities to move beyond the traditional discipline-driven model and contribute more directly to national innovation priorities. Higher education access in China has spiked over the past decade and a half. Nationwide enrolment reached 48.7 million in 2025, with a gross enrolment rate of 61.3 per cent – more than double the 30 per cent recorded in 2012 – according to the Ministry of Education. Some Chinese universities traditionally known for specialised academic profiles are broadening their offerings as Beijing pushes for greater interdisciplinarity. On Tuesday, the Beijing-based University of International Business and Economics, known for its strengths in business and economics, said it had introduced micro-majors in fields such as artificial intelligence, data science and digital humanities. The short, specialised programmes are designed to complement students’ main areas of study, with classes held on weekends, during summer breaks or in the evenings.

title: Philippine coastguard battles funding cuts amid bigger South China Sea role
description: Ronnie Gil Gavan says his agency is functioning at almost ‘90 per cent operational tempo’, leaving a very short time between overhauls.
content: The Philippines is preparing to give its coastguard more responsibilities in the contested South China Sea even as the agency faces a more basic problem: whether it has enough ships, aircraft and personnel to carry them out. The proposed overhaul comes as the coastguard is being stretched by increasingly demanding operations around Philippine-claimed waters, while funding constraints threaten to limit its ability to keep its existing assets at sea. That tension is evident in the 2027 budget. The coastguard has sought funding for more vessels, unmanned systems, stations and personnel, while key allocations for patrols, intelligence and ship maintenance face cuts. The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) currently has a fleet of about 40 vessels, according to Coast Guard chief Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan, who said in June that the agency planned to add more than 40 vessels over the following five years. But the number of vessels on the books does not necessarily reflect the number available for operations. Gavan told Senate finance committee chairman Joseph Victor Ejercito on September 18 that “it’s just a matter of time that we will run out of ships, with the cuts in the repair and maintenance budget”. Gavan said the coastguard was “operating at almost 80 per cent to 90 per cent operational tempo”, leaving a short turnaround time between operations and overhauls. “The repair and maintenance requirement of our ships is already [at] dangerous [levels], you know. We might not be able to sustain [operations].” The percentage Gavan cited “refers to the amount of time spent at sea”, according to Australian geopolitical analyst Dr Hunter Marston. “In that case, the vessels and service members would be at sea 80 or 90 per cent of the time and only ashore for resupplies, repairs or rest 10 to 20 per cent of the time, which is pretty high.” In comparison, “I think the US navy aims for about 33 per cent”, Marston told This Week in Asia. Gavan said the coastguard might also run out of planes since only one was operational while the second was under repair. The cuts came on top of 3.3 billion pesos (US$52.7 million) in reductions for acquiring air and floating assets, which Gavan said were needed to address the shortage. Its sea-based patrol funding under the Maritime Security Law Enforcement Programme was trimmed by 812 million pesos. Political risk analyst Ronald Llamas told This Week in Asia the cuts were the result of “tight fiscal space” due to higher debt service and other priorities. Independent budget specialist Zyza Suzara also said on television that “there is very little fiscal space” due to increased debt servicing, higher operational costs and the mandatory tax allotment to local governments. Gavan warned that if the cuts took place, “we will be constrained [in our] daily operational response” and “obviously, it will have a very significant impact on our activities”. The request for “unmanned tactical capability” consisting of surface and undersea drones was also cut by 600 million pesos, Gavan disclosed, while the agency’s intelligence funds were reduced by 150 million pesos for next year. The PCG had also requested funds for fresh recruitment, 360 million pesos for hospital insurance for its personnel’s families and eight new coastguard stations worth 25 million pesos each, including on Palawan island and the Kalayaan Island Group in the Spratlys. The pressure on the service could be seen in its recent encounters with Chinese vessels in the South China Sea. On Thursday, Chinese coastguard and naval vessels intervened during a Philippine resupply mission to the grounded Philippine warship at Second Thomas Shoal, according to Manila. Beijing said its personnel were conducting lawful enforcement in response to a Philippine provocation. On Sunday, the PCG challenged a Chinese coastguard vessel near Occidental Mindoro, while the following day a PCG aircraft tracked a Chinese research vessel near Batanes. Manila said the ships were operating within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. The two sides continue to dispute the legal status of the waters. China claims sovereignty over much of the South China Sea, including Second Thomas Shoal, and rejects a 2016 international arbitral ruling that found no legal basis for its claim to historic rights over resources within the sea areas covered by its nine-dash line. Beijing considers the ruling illegal and non-binding, while Manila relies on it in asserting its maritime rights. Expanding mandate The encounters illustrate why the coastguard’s capacity has become a strategic question for Manila. The agency is a civilian service, but it has increasingly been at the centre of the Philippines’ efforts to assert its maritime rights and maintain a presence in contested waters. The proposed revised Coast Guard Law, which has already cleared the Senate and is moving through Congress, would formalise some of those responsibilities. The measure seeks to address perceived gaps in the existing Republic Act 9993 by giving the agency a clearer mandate to enforce and maintain maritime security, as well as “prevent or suppress terrorism at sea”. It would also empower the coastguard to directly “recommend” to the president regulations that would direct when and to what extent the Philippine military should extend support and assistance. The proposed law would require a “minimum manning level” to ensure it could adequately patrol more than 36,000km of the country’s coastline. It therefore envisages a coastguard with a broader set of responsibilities and a more clearly defined role in maritime security. But the budget debate suggests that the more immediate question is whether the agency can maintain the capability it already has. House deputy minority floor leader Antonio Tinio told This Week in Asia on Monday that he was unsure if any of the cuts would be restored. As for the Senate, Ejercito promised on Sunday in an interview with radio station DZBB that he would restore some of the cuts by “realigning” funds from agencies with historically low utilisation rates of their annual budgets. “Be reassured that we have been very consistent in supporting the coastguard,” he said. “We will find ways to ensure that we have the capability to respond. We may not be able to trade shots with China, but at least we should have a minimum credible defence posture.”

title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile at Singapore reservoir that led to search
description: Water and park authorities went to Pandan Reservoir to search for the crocodile while water activities were suspended.
content: A 30-year-old man was charged on Tuesday over an AI-generated image of a crocodile at Pandan Reservoir in Singapore that prompted authorities to search for the reptile and suspend water activities there. Ye Lin, a Myanmar national, was handed two charges – one count of communicating a false message and one count of obstructing the course of justice. Speaking through an interpreter, he told the court that he intended to plead guilty, and would not be engaging a lawyer. On August 20, Ye Lin allegedly sent an artificial intelligence-generated image depicting a crocodile at the reservoir to a person named in court documents as Min Min Oo. The documents did not state their relationship, but the police said in a news release on Monday that Ye Lin had sent the image to his colleague. The next day, Ye Lin allegedly deleted the AI-generated images and the log history on the Gemini AI app from his mobile phone. This is the basis of the obstructing the course of justice charge. National water agency PUB had received information on August 20 that a crocodile had been sighted at Pandan Reservoir. PUB informed the National Parks Board and both agencies conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were also told to suspend all water activities in the reservoir. On August 21, PUB said that the photo of the crocodile had been found to be fake and that a police report was lodged. Water activities at the reservoir were subsequently resumed. The police warned on Monday that they will not hesitate to take action against anyone who communicates falsehoods. “Apart from causing fear and inconvenience to members of the public, such falsehoods also result in public resources being unnecessarily deployed to deal with these incidents,” they said. Ye Lin will return to court on November 10. This story was first published by CNA

title: Singapore or bust: how Indonesian student’s crowdfunding plea shows degree of desirability
description: A woman’s appeal for sponsors to fund her US$78,000 programme has drawn criticism but not dimmed her dream of studying in Singapore.
content: For 28-year-old Indonesian professional Evelyn Clarissa Siregar, asking strangers to help fund her MBA in Singapore was a gamble: she knew the request was unconventional but hoped putting her dream out in public might open a door. Instead, her appeal for more than S$100,000 (US$78,000) to fund her business programme at Singapore Management University (SMU) drew fierce online criticism, with some labelling her entitled and questioning her plans. “I never expected the backlash to become this big,” Siregar told This Week in Asia, saying she felt “overwhelmed” by the response. “Once I finally had the capacity to face everything again, I went back and read all [their] comments and responses. One by one. I cringed, feeling uncomfortable.” But Siregar said the experience had not changed her desire to study in Singapore. The city state continues to attract Indonesians with its high-ranking universities, proximity and reputation – even though the cost can put a degree there beyond many students’ reach. “Singapore is a small country, but it’s packed with experts in finance, business and science,” said Siregar, who works as a sales manager at an internet services provider in Jakarta. “Everything feels within reach. That’s what really attracts me to Singapore.” On September 16, Siregar was accepted into SMU’s MBA programme, which will start in January and require S$82,480 in tuition. She secured a S$3,000 Asean student discount but that was “far from enough”, she said. The price tag is particularly stark for an Indonesian student. SMU’s S$82,480 tuition works out to about 1.15 billion rupiah. By comparison, the School of Business and Management at Indonesia’s well-regarded Institut Teknologi Bandung lists total tuition of 99.15 million rupiah for its General Management MBA. Siregar said she had applied for three scholarships but secured only one. She also tried to apply for a job in Singapore, but nothing panned out. “In my [MBA] application, I’ve stated that I wouldn’t rely on my parents financially and that I would rely heavily on scholarships and internships or part-time work,” she said. Three days after receiving her acceptance, she published a pitch on Instagram asking internet users to fund her study and living expenses, which she estimated would cost “S$2,000-S$2,500 per month, for 10-15 months”. Siregar wrote that she would pay back her investors with her “skills and experiences”. “I’ve always believed in negotiation. If someone says no, I don’t necessarily take it as the end,” she said. Her pitch ultimately brought no sponsors, but it did bring a barrage of criticism, as commenters questioned her credentials and the feasibility of her plan. “As someone who invests in a lot of business, you are all talk. There is no fixed guarantee if you can replace the capital I spent … you are just a kid with entitled behaviour. No numbers, no return on investment. We all have dreams; know the boundaries if you can’t afford it,” one social media user said. “Why not come to Singapore, work for a few years, and earn enough to go for a master’s? Isn’t that probably a better approach? That’s what most locals here do instead of asking for a donation based on a pitch with zero return,” another said. Sought-after destination Singapore’s appeal to Siregar lies not just in its universities but in the access she believes studying there could provide. That aspiration is shared by other Indonesian students, although their routes can look very different. Tri Maira Pangestuti, who graduated in August from a master’s programme in environmental management at the National University of Singapore (NUS), received an Indonesian government scholarship in 2022 as her mother is a farmer raising three children on her own in a village in Central Java. She was also accepted into a master’s programme in Sydney, but chose NUS because “it was ranked the eighth best university in the world at that time”, she said. Studying at NUS yielded professional benefits, from acquiring practical skills closely tied to industrial needs, such as conducting environmental risk assessments for international supply chains, to receiving strong backing from her academic advisers for her PhD applications, the 28-year-old said. “I really want to be a professor at NUS. I’m currently applying for a PhD at Stanford University and the University of Helsinki in Finland. I don’t know which university will accept me, but I plan to return to Singapore as an assistant professor after receiving my PhD,” Tri said. Tri, who uses a prosthetic as her left eye is blind, said she also appreciated how NUS accommodated her disability – for example, by giving her an additional 25 minutes during exams. “In Indonesia, I attended public schools from kindergarten to undergraduate, never a school specifically for children with disabilities. In ninth grade, my gym teacher held back my report card because I couldn’t swim. The gym teacher didn’t provide any learning adjustments,” Tri said. NUS ranks third as the foreign university destination for Indonesian students, Kompass newspaper reported in May 2024. As of 2022, there are 2,282 NUS alumni from Indonesia, 769 of whom graduated from the business studies programme. Sulfikar Amir, associate professor at the School of Social Sciences at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, said many Indonesian students were drawn to the city state because of its reputation as an elite educational hub and the availability of scholarships from the government, universities and corporations. “Singaporean universities offer world-class infrastructure and educational facilities, which are on a par with, and sometimes even better than, universities in the US, Britain and elsewhere in Europe,” Sulfikar said. “There’s also added value … because Singapore’s culture is relatively similar to Indonesia. Students can still experience warmth, unlike in cold and individualistic Europe.” For Siregar, the path towards a Singaporean degree remains uncertain. Though she has yet to receive any sponsors from her pitch, that had not stopped her from pursuing “other passions and stories”. “I’ve put my dream out there, and if anyone wants to follow along, that’s great,” she said. “But I’m more than my MBA journey.”

title: Early birds for Wang Fuk Court buy-back get first pick of subsidised houses
description: Some residents pleased with new homes offered under schemes, with others calling for stamp duty waivers to help ease financial burden.
content: Residents who lost their homes in Hong Kong’s deadly Tai Po fire started choosing their replacement flats on Tuesday, with some calling on authorities to introduce stamp duty waivers to help ease their financial burden. After last November’s blaze at Wang Fuk Court, authorities rolled out a HK$7.8 billion (US$994 million) plan to buy back flats at the eight-block subsidised housing estate. Under the scheme, participants can use the cash compensation to buy a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to purchase new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement. A special arrangement also gives priority selection to the first 35 households that signed their letters of acceptance by June 30, giving them the pick of 4,400 flats at 10 subsidised housing estates. The estates, developed by the Housing Authority and Housing Society, are located in areas such as Kowloon Bay, Kai Tak, Tseung Kwan O, Kwun Tong and Fanling. Among them are Sierra Terrace in Fanling, which was completed earlier this year, and Shing Chi Court in Kowloon Bay, which is due to be ready by the end of this year. The remaining developments are expected to be available in 2027 and 2028. A resident surnamed Lee, who lived in Wang Shing House at Wang Fuk Court, was the first to select a replacement flat when he visited the Green Form Subsidised Home Ownership Scheme Sales Office in Kwun Tong’s Pioneer Place. But Lee, who is in his seventies, said he had not yet received the flat-for-flat voucher and had only signed a document to secure his new home at Kai Yeung Court in Kai Tak. “I chose a Kai Tak flat because the transport there is more convenient and the facilities are well developed,” he said. “It is also in the urban area, so I am glad to have made this choice.” Lee said the flat he planned to buy with his life savings was 420 square feet (39 square metres), 40 square feet smaller than his previous home, adding that he needed to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars more to cover the price difference. He added that he would welcome a stamp duty waiver, potentially saving him hundreds of thousands of Hong Kong dollars, but felt estate residents should not be treated as a special case. For flats valued at between about HK$5 million and HK$6.6 million, stamp duty ranges from just more than HK$100,000 to about HK$200,000. Another resident, surnamed Cheung, picked a flat in Hemma Sapphire in Kwun Tong because of its view and larger size, with the home measuring 515 square feet compared with his previous home of 447 square feet. Cheung, who is in his seventies and used to live in Wang Fuk Court’s Wang Yan House with his family of three, said he was unenthusiastic about the homes on offer. “I am not particularly happy with the selection, as we are being forced to buy a flat,” he said. “I did not consider New Territories projects such as Sierra Terrace in Fanling because I do not want to have to pass Wang Fuk Court again.” Cheung estimated that he would need to pay at least HK$1 million more to secure the new flat. “Together with stamp duty, this has created an economic burden. I hope the government can waive the duty, which costs more than HK$100,000,” he said. “I did not choose a high floor at Hemma Sapphire because I am concerned about the quality of the Modular Integrated Construction and possible water leakage problems.” He was referring to the technique that employs free-standing, integrated modules manufactured in factories to build new flats in Hong Kong. A fellow Wang Fuk Court resident surnamed Tam, 79, was the last of the group to choose a flat and said she was relieved to have secured a home at Sierra Terrace, as her current tenancy was set to end soon, forcing her to live outside the New Territories. “I live with my 87-year-old husband in a rented house in Tai Po, but the landlord does not want to rent to elderly tenants, so our contract will end in February,” she said. “I am so happy to have secured a place in the New Territories, as I have lived in the area for over 40 years.” Tam said she and her husband expected that they would need to rely on their savings to pay about HK$2,500 a month to cover the additional HK$400,000 needed to secure the new flat. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin said on Monday that other applicants would be invited to take part in a random house selection over the next two months. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Housing Bureau said Wang Fuk Court owners who had signed the sale agreement could select flats even before transfers of ownership were completed and flat-for-flat vouchers were issued. The chosen flat would then be reserved with no deposit required, with the government completing the purchase once a transfer of ownership was finalised and the voucher could be used for payment. It said most flat-for-flat cases were expected to be completed in October and November, aside from exceptional cases. Lee, Cheung and Tam were among nearly 5,000 people displaced by Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades, which tore through seven of Wang Fuk Court’s eight blocks and killed 168 people.

title: China cuts key interest rate, offers mortgage subsidy to boost economy
description: Beijing has cut the interest rate on its pledged supplemental lending facility to 1.5 per cent, while offering homebuyers a mortgage interest subsidy.
content: China’s central bank has announced a fresh package of measures to boost the real economy, cutting an interest rate for policy banks and introducing the country’s first interest subsidy for commercial mortgages. The People’s Bank of China cut the interest rate on its pledged supplemental lending (PSL) facility by 0.25 percentage points, lowering the one-year PSL rate from 1.75 per cent to 1.5 per cent. The move aims to better incentivise policy banks to support the real economy and align with national strategic priorities, according to an announcement made by the central bank on Tuesday. On the same day, the bank – along with the Ministry of Finance and the National Financial Regulatory Administration – announced that a mortgage interest subsidy policy for first-time homebuyers would come into effect from October 1. The policy is tentatively set to run for one year, according to the notice. It will mark the first time China’s central fiscal authorities have provided subsidies on the interest from commercial individual housing loans. Huang Yiping, dean of the National School of Development at Peking University, said the new measures were part of a broader effort to boost the property market and support homebuyers. “This package of policies centres on a coordinated toolkit to underpin the real estate sector and lower housing costs for residents. The aim is to stimulate first-time purchases and upgrade demand while mitigating risks across the property chain,” Huang said. “Unlike previous single-rate cuts, the current approach combines interest subsidies, rate reductions and central bank liquidity support to work in tandem, directly easing monthly repayment burdens for numerous homebuyers.” Loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000) will be eligible for the mortgage subsidy, with fiscal authorities providing an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for a maximum duration of five years. The policy will only be available to first-time homebuyers. The property in question must have a floor space of 120 square metres (1,290 square feet) or below and be priced at 1.5 million yuan or less. Yan Yuejin, deputy director at the E-house China R&D Institute, said the extra support for first-time homebuyers “sends a very positive policy signal”. Borrowers with a 1 million yuan mortgage would save roughly 50,000 yuan thanks to the policy, which “represents meaningful relief”, according to the analyst. “If pent-up demand fails to be unlocked, it will weigh on subsequent trade-up and improvement housing demand,” Yan said. Meanwhile, the central bank said the PSL would be expanded to cover lending to projects related to the “six networks” – Beijing’s massive infrastructure investment initiative spanning water, power, computing, next-generation communications, underground pipelines and logistics networks. The People’s Bank of China also said its relending quota targeting tech innovation, the private sector and small businesses would be expanded by 700 billion yuan. The announcements came a day after Chinese Premier Li Qiang chaired a State Council executive meeting that called for stronger macro policies to support the economy and boost domestic demand. China’s economy remains under pressure amid sluggish investment and consumption. Overall fixed-asset investment – covering infrastructure, manufacturing, property and other major areas – fell by 7.2 per cent year on year during the first eight months of 2026, according to official data. Economic growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, down from 5 per cent in the first quarter, marking the weakest quarterly expansion since late 2022. Huang said a sustained recovery in the property market would be crucial to rebalancing the Chinese economy and boosting growth. “External imbalances and internal growth pressures have both intensified recently, with the real estate sector representing a significant contributing factor to the drag on growth,” he said. “The new policy package is therefore of particular importance at this juncture.” Additional reporting by Emma Ma

title: China mourns death of music legend Liu Huan, voice of 2008 Beijing Olympic theme song
description: Widely recognised as China’s contemporary vocal king and a pioneer of Chinese popular music, Liu’s artistic impact was profound.
content: Renowned Chinese singer and songwriter Liu Huan passed away in Shanghai on September 25 at the age of 63 due to illness, prompting widespread mourning among the mainland public. The University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, where Liu taught the History of Western Music for three decades, issued an obituary but did not disclose details about the illness. His death saddened many, as Liu was a beloved figure across China. As one of the country’s most famous and respected male singers, Liu performed the anthem for the Beijing Olympics, You and Me, alongside British soprano Sarah Brightman in 2008. Brightman paid tribute to Liu on her social media account, describing him as an “amazing talent and a true gentleman.” According to a member of the Beijing Olympic Games Organising Committee, Liu was chosen to perform the Olympic song because “he has China’s best male voice, with an effortless deep, resonant baritone and striking high notes,” and he seamlessly fused Chinese and Western singing styles while maintaining a positive public image. Widely recognised as China’s contemporary vocal king and a pioneer of Chinese popular music, Liu’s artistic impact was profound. Born in 1963 into a teaching family in northern China’s Tianjin municipality, Liu once performed crosstalk with his schoolmate Dai Zhicheng, who later became a celebrated crosstalk comedian. Although Liu’s mother discouraged a career in comedy, he chose a different path as he matured. Upon enrolling in the French literature programme at the University of International Relations, he developed a passion for classical music. This enthusiasm later led him to explore popular music and begin composing his own songs. As a university student, Liu made a name for himself in various singing competitions. After graduating, he dedicated a year to volunteering as a music teacher in the countryside. Liu first showcased his talent on a China Central Television show in 1986 and recorded his first theme song for a television drama in 1987. Subsequently, he enjoyed an illustrious music career, delivering numerous classic theme songs for television dramas from the 1980s through the 2010s, including Youthful Aspirations are Unburdened by Sorrow, Cannot Live Like This, Asking Ten Thousand Times, and Heroes’ Song. Liu also composed music for several renowned TV series, including the 1993 drama A Native of Beijing in New York and the 2011 series Empresses in the Palace. He was celebrated as one of the few artists whose singing consistently resonated deeply, whether with ballads or robust, dramatic pieces. In addition to his musical endeavours, Liu was a dedicated teacher, committing a significant portion of his life to educating young students about Western music history, regardless of his fame. In 2019, he co-established a programme to fund one million yuan (US$150,000) annually for an original singer-songwriter. Liu last performed at a New Year’s Eve gala this year, singing Asking Ten Thousand Times and I Want to Become an Immortal. Following his passing, his wife, Lu Lu, shared a heartfelt message on her private social media, referring to Liu as her “forever love and forever pain.” Liu and Lu tied the knot after meeting for just nine days, yet they remained devoted to each other for 38 years. His love for Lu was immediate when he first saw her as a host, director, and producer at Hunan Television. On their wedding day, it rained, and Liu insisted on registering the marriage himself to shield Lu from the rain, only to discover later that both parties needed to be present for registration. The couple welcomed a daughter in 1991. When she attended secondary school in the US, Liu declined numerous job offers to accompany her. She got married last year with her parents’ blessing. On Chinese social media, many remembered Liu with touching messages. “Liu Huan is a rare celebrity who is cherished by people of all ages. No one else will achieve the same level of popularity as he did,” remarked one online observer. “One of his students recalled: “Professor Liu is a celebrity, but to us, he was an approachable teacher. I can still vividly remember his class.” “His devotion to his wife and daughter demonstrated what a remarkable person he was. Rest in peace,” commented another.

title: Does Jelly Roll’s ex-wife Bunnie Xo have a new man? Meet reality TV star Dylan Wolf
description: The self-styled ‘Malibu’s Cowboy’ and Calabasas Confidential star has been linked to his co-stars Emma Medrano, Suede Brooks and Jemma Durrant.
content: Bunnie Xo may have a new beau, and she’s not hiding it. The 46-year-old Dumb Blonde Podcast host, whose divorce from country music star Jelly Roll was finalised in July, sparked romance rumours with 24-year-old television personality Dylan Wolf that month. The two were spotted sharing a Fourth of July kiss at Jelly Roll’s Goodnight Nashville bar, per People. The podcaster, whose real name is Alisa DeFord, later said on her show that the kiss was “not an issue at all” and that she was “not dating anyone”. Wolf, who starred in Netflix’s reality series Calabasas Confidential, even told TMZ: “Sometimes a cowboy wants to hunt cougars.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bunnie Xo. (@xomgitsbunnie) Although the pair have not put a label on their romance yet, they have been frequently spotted looking loved-up on Bunnie’s social media, including a recent Instagram clip where Bunnie and Wolf danced and kissed in what appears to be an arcade. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bunnie Xo. (@xomgitsbunnie) In another video, Wolf feeds her waffles at Waffle House. In the comments, Bunnie wrote: “Hey guys, I’m having fun & he gave me my smile back. Ya girl is living her best life.” So, what do we know about Bunnie Xo’s new man, Dylan Wolf? What is Dylan Wolf’s background? Not much is known about Wolf’s background, except that he grew up in Southern California, per Hollywood Life. He attended Calabasas High School and, according to Netflix, is a self-proclaimed “mama’s boy”. He has a sister named Sabrina, who made a cameo appearance in Calabasas Confidential. What does Dylan Wolf do? View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dylan Wolf (@dylannwolf) Wolf’s social media presence seems to be built around a “Malibu Cowboy” persona. He works at a ranch in Malibu, per Grazia, and enjoys bull riding in local rodeos, per Netflix. Wolf is also a model and has been photographed for the Professional Bull Riders league. Who else has Dylan Wolf dated? Since starring on Calabasas Confidential, Wolf’s love life has been in the spotlight. In Season 1 of the show, he was linked to fellow Calabasas High alum Emma Medrano – with whom he had a fling during secondary school. He then got involved with influencer Suede Brooks, whom he met at the “Kiki-chella” house party, where their co-star Kimora Lewis – daughter of BET’s senior vice-president Kim Lewis – released a single. The third cast member Wolf was linked to was Jemma Durrant, whom he was intimate with in secondary school but never dated. “He didn’t just break my heart. He literally tore me apart,” she revealed, per TV Insider. Outside the reality series, which has yet to be renewed after its debut this May, Wolf was linked in November last year to Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin’s eldest daughter, Delilah Hamlin. In May this year, he told Decider that they were “no longer tied together”.

title: Eunis Chan, Angela Leong sell luxury Hong Kong properties as rate increases loom
description: Spike in high-end transactions may be short-lived as inventory clears and buyers adopt wait-and-see stance, agents say.
content: As the shadow of possible interest rate increases darkens Hong Kong’s property market outlook, well-known people including model-actress Eunis Chan Ka-yung and billionaire Angela Leong On-kei have recently decided the time was right to sell luxury properties, according to market sources. Chan sold a two-bedroom Mid-Levels flat for HK$32.25 million (US$4.1 million), making a profit of about 130 per cent, while Leong, a businesswoman and Macau legislator who was the fourth wife of the late casino tycoon Stanley Ho Hung-sun, sold a luxury house in Sai Kung for HK$70 million, netting less than 2 per cent, according to market sources. While some luxury owners had become more willing to negotiate recently owing to concerns of possible rate increases, buyers were exercising caution with their bids for the same reason, according to property agents. “Amid market expectations of interest rate increases and a lack of other positive news, buyers are adopting a strong ‘wait-and-see’ stance,” said Frankie Liu, sales director at Century 21 Goodwin Property. Chan originally listed her luxury flat on a lower floor of Tower 2 at Regent On The Park in Mid-Levels for HK$36 million in July 2024, market sources said. The 1,094-square-foot, two-bedroom property also included a parking space. After reducing the price by HK$3.75 million, or more than 10 per cent, the HK$32.25 million she got for the flat worked out to HK$29,479 per square foot, the sources said. Having held the property for almost 17 years, Chan realised a profit of HK$18.25 million, representing an appreciation of over 130 per cent, according to the sources. The Sai Kung property that Leong sold is a detached house at Royal Castle on Pik Sha Road, featuring a saleable area of 2,259 square feet and a four-bedroom layout. It includes a garden of more than 2,500 square feet, a swimming pool and a 1,018-square-foot rooftop terrace. The house was originally listed for sale several years ago at HK$168 million but following multiple adjustments, the asking price was lowered to HK$98 million in May of this year, sources said. The ultimate selling price of HK$70 million works out to HK$30,987 per square foot. Leong bought the house through a company in early 2012 for HK$68.8 million, so after holding the property for 14 years, she realised a profit of HK$1.2 million, sources said. Some owners of luxury homes in the Sai Kung district had recently been willing to increase their negotiating margin to 10 per cent, leading to a rise in high-value transactions, said Century 21’s Liu. “With the batch of discounted luxury homes now cleared, I expect luxury residential transaction activity in the area to slow down in the fourth quarter,” he added. In The Peak and Southern districts, recent transactions primarily involved established, traditional luxury estates, with local tycoons entering the market to upgrade their homes, said Joseph Yan, senior principal district sales director at Centaline Property. On September 17, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority lifted the city’s base interest rate to 4.25 per cent after the US Fed raised its target range. The city’s three note-issuing banks did not follow suit. But the Fed is set to meet again in late October, and another increase could trigger Hong Kong’s lenders to adjust their own rates, according to analysts. The city’s official property price index for large private residential flats of 100 square metres (1,079 square feet) or larger, released by the Rating and Valuation Department on Monday, rebounded to 288.4 points in August from 287.2 points in July. In contrast, the price index for small-to-medium-sized residential flats – those under 100 square metres – remained flat at 322.4 points.

title: Can China’s new satellite coordination standards boost PLA targeting and resilience?
description: Beijing panel of experts approves work on 10 proposals to support civilian and commercial low-Earth-orbit constellations.
content: Chinese researchers are drafting standards for autonomous satellite coordination and data sharing in a move analysts say could speed up military targeting and make People’s Liberation Army satellite networks more resilient. An expert panel convened by the Chinese Institute of Command and Control (CICC) in Beijing on September 21 approved work on 10 proposed voluntary standards, clearing the way for draft texts to be released for consultation. In an account of the meeting published last Thursday, the CICC said the standards were intended to support China’s civilian and commercial low Earth orbit satellites. The 10 proposed standards cover areas ranging from overall system design and the description of mission scenarios to distributed data services, satellite and mission data, coordination at constellation and smaller satellite-cluster levels, and the design of autonomous controllers. CICC said the standards sought to help different types of satellites work together more effectively in large, complex constellations. The institute’s announcement summarised the draft standards but did not include their full texts. In practice, common formats could allow satellites run by different organisations to describe tasks, report their status and capabilities, and exchange mission data consistently. If one satellite detected something of interest, for example, it could pass relevant task information to another with a different sensor or a better view of the area. According to Gregory Falco, an assistant professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at Cornell University, what was outlined in CICC’s announcement was significant. “Coordination of these types of satellites is not a trivial task,” Falco said. Blaine Curcio, founder of Orbital Gateway Consulting, contrasted China’s approach to building large satellite constellations with SpaceX’s Starlink. “Unlike Starlink, which is vertically integrated and manufactures all satellites in-house, China’s large constellations are much more dispersed,” he said. “That being the case, it would seem very important to create standards so that the satellites can eventually be interoperable.” Curcio cautioned that any benefits would take time because the standards would have to be incorporated into the designs before the satellites were built and launched. CICC’s standards effort also involved military and defence-linked institutions. The expert panel included PLA Unit 61646, which is active in satellite and remote-sensing information processing, while one of the institutions leading the drafting work was the China Academy of Space Technology’s 513 Institute, which works on electronics for space and defence applications. Timothy R. Heath, founder of Perceptum, a defence research and consultancy firm focused on China and security affairs, said the PLA’s involvement reflected China’s broader push towards dual-use capabilities. According to the Pentagon’s 2025 annual report on China’s military, many Chinese commercial companies were part of Beijing’s military-civil fusion strategy to develop dual-use technologies in the commercial sector for eventual integration into the military. For the PLA, such capabilities could shorten the chain between collecting information on a potential target and getting usable data to military operators, Heath said. “Satellite networks that operate with greater autonomy will do more tasks in space,” he added. “For example, satellites in a network could share data with each other, drawing from different types of sensors. Using AI, the satellites could quickly identify potential targets and then send that information to human operators.” In principle, a network able to share data and coordinate tasks in this way could also redistribute work. If one satellite were unavailable or poorly positioned, another could potentially take over part of the job. Falco said the architecture described by CICC also pointed to a shift towards processing data and making decisions where the information is collected, rather than routinely sending it back to the ground first. Heath likewise linked the technology to a broader shift in PLA warfare concepts. “The incorporation of AI and greater autonomy definitely reflects the PLA’s push towards a vision of building an ‘intelligentised’ force and networked warfare,” he said. The Pentagon report said Beijing believed the next revolution in military affairs would come with a transition to “intelligentised” warfare and the integration of artificial intelligence, big data, advanced computing and other technologies into the joint force. It also said the PLA was investing in and fielding automated detection and tracking from low-Earth-orbit satellites – capabilities it said had increased its ability to monitor, track and target US and allied forces. Falco said the technology could also improve resilience as satellites could continue operating when communications with ground stations were denied, reducing the risk that disruption of those links would jeopardise a mission. Namrata Goswami, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s school of advanced international studies, highlighted the potential for resilience at the constellation level. “Jamming or attacking one part of the network is not fatal if the remaining network can autonomously redistribute functions,” Goswami said. Despite those potential military applications, Heath cautioned against interpreting the standards primarily as a military project. “The main driver is civilian in nature,” he said. “The military aspect is just one consideration but not the main driver.” Meanwhile, the US military is pursuing related capabilities, although the programmes are not direct equivalents to the CICC standards. The US Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture uses common networking and optical-communications standards to allow satellites supplied by multiple vendors to operate as part of the same network. In addition, the US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency or Darpa is developing its Space-Based Adaptive Communications Node programme, or Space-BACN, to connect otherwise incompatible satellite constellations using different optical-link standards and coordinate communications between them.

title: China’s CXMT to favour domestic suppliers in US$5.2b memory-chip capacity push: source
description: As it begins massive output increase, China’s top memory supplier sets ‘aggressive’ target for local chipmaking equipment, source says.
content: Chinese memory chip giant ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) plans to invest 34.9 billion yuan (US$5.2 billion) in expansion, with a large portion of the capital going to domestic suppliers of chipmaking equipment, according to a source. The firm, listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s Star Market, would spend 24.1 billion yuan on a new technology research and development project and another 10.8 billion yuan on the second phase of a wafer testing base, according to a Monday stock filing. The spending plan underscores the capital-intensive nature of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) producer’s push into more advanced products. Nearly 22.4 billion yuan, or about 93 per cent of the R&D project’s budget, would go towards equipment purchases, the filing said. A large portion of CXMT’s latest equipment spending is expected to go to Chinese suppliers, according to a person close to the company’s supply chain who declined to be identified because the information is not public. “The localisation target is very aggressive,” the person told the South China Morning Post, without giving a specific target for the share of domestically made equipment. Now the most valuable company on mainland China’s stock market, CXMT plans to use 18 billion yuan of excess proceeds from its July initial public offering to fund the new projects. The plan is still pending shareholder approval. The company declined to comment on the localisation target or how much of the planned equipment spending would go to domestic suppliers. Chinese fabs are setting ambitious targets for sourcing equipment locally. One new fab in the city was aiming for 80 per cent localisation of its equipment, said Jie Chen, chairman of Britech Semiconductor Equipment (Shanghai), at an industry conference earlier this month in Wuxi, in the eastern province of Jiangsu. Such targets can be harder to achieve in advanced memory production, where some critical manufacturing tools from foreign suppliers remain difficult to replace. Morgan Stanley said in an August report that CXMT’s “equipment intensity” was likely to rise as it expanded capacity and moved towards more advanced DRAM technologies, which required increasingly complex etching, deposition, cleaning and inspection processes. The company’s investment plan also points to its effort to bring more of the production process in-house. The company said expanding its own testing capacity would reduce its reliance on external packaging and testing suppliers as wafer output and product variety increased. CXMT has been rapidly scaling up production as it seeks to narrow the gap with global memory leaders Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology. Founded in 2016, CXMT has become China’s biggest DRAM producer. Morgan Stanley estimated that CXMT’s monthly DRAM capacity would hit 500,000 wafers in 2028, up from 180,000 at the end of 2025. Amid Beijing’s push to reduce reliance on overseas semiconductor suppliers, the company’s product portfolio has expanded from DDR4 and LPDDR4X into the newer DDR5 and LPDDR5 products. Earlier this month, CXMT also announced mass production of LPDDR6 chips, which debuted in Xiaomi’s 18 Fold flagship smartphone. This month, CXMT said its fifth-generation DRAM manufacturing platform, dubbed G5, had entered mass production, marking another step in narrowing the gap with global leaders.

title: ‘Too low and dirty’: North Korea fires back at Seoul over DMZ mine blast blame
description: Seoul’s defence minister said the incident that injured two South Koreans was a violation of the Korean war armistice.
content: North Korea said on Wednesday that South Korea will pay a price for shifting the blame to Pyongyang for a mine blast ‌that seriously wounded two South Koreans at the demilitarised zone (DMZ) border and warned it will retaliate if the South opens fire on its troops. South Korea’s defence minister said on Tuesday that North Korean mines caused a blast last week and that it would take “corresponding” action. Kang Shin-chul also said North Korea likely planted mines as part of fortifying the border. South Korea, together with the UN Command that oversees the Korean war armistice, has been conducting an investigation over ⁠the blast that on September 21 wounded three South Korean personnel of a team on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide (2.49-mile) wide ‌DMZ. “The tribes of South Korea are trying to fabricate ‘material evidence’ for proving it after shifting the blame for the incident onto the other,” the North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo-jong, said in a ‌statement issued by the KCNA official news agency. Kim is considered an influential confidant of her brother and often ⁠speaks publicly on external matters. “Ringleaders ⁠of provocation should be prepared for paying a price for the farce of their own making,” she said. “It is too low and dirty as befitting ‌the tribes of South Korea,” she said. “Such a farce is by no means new.” She also said North Korean troops have never crossed the military demarcation line that runs ‌through the ‌centre of the DMZ. South Korea has said it believes there are signs North Korean soldiers breached the border line as ‌it conducted fortification work. Kim said the North had made no secret of its work to build barriers in the area to reinforce ⁠the border and “this is only a thorough exercise of sovereignty unrelated to any military purpose”. But the South was provoking tension by firing ⁠warning shots on the pretence North Korean troops were breaching the border. If live shots are fired at its soldiers, the North will take immediate retaliation, Kim said. “When a single bullet hits our land, they must be prepared ‌for a lot,” she said. The activities ‌at the border, which also include restoring guard posts, stem from a turn in its policy on the South, that it is a separate country and a “foe”, no longer a partner with which Pyongyang will work together for eventual unification. The mine incident could further complicate South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s efforts to reopen dialogue and improve ties with the North to ease military tensions.

title: Why Citi is betting on China’s 30-year bonds as US Treasury yields climb
description: Weak credit demand, policy support and easing supply pressures are expected to sustain demand for ultra-long Chinese debt, analysts say.
content: Citi Research has turned bullish on China’s 30-year government bonds, projecting that yields will fall further even as US Treasury yields climb. In a Monday research note, analysts at the Wall Street bank recommended that investors go long on China’s 30-year sovereign debt, saying they expected the yield to fall towards 1.8 per cent while the 10-year yield could edge towards 1.6 per cent. The analysts attributed the outlook to easing supply pressures and improved market dynamics for China’s ultra-long government bonds heading into the fourth quarter. “China’s recently announced 360-billion-yuan [US$53.7 billion] recapitalisation plan for some major financial institutions may boost duration demand, especially for the ultra-long end,” wrote Rohit Garg, Singapore-based head of EM Asia Rates and FX Strategy at Citi, in the report. On Tuesday, the yield on China’s 30-year special treasury bond reached a daily low of 2.11 per cent, while the 10-year government bond traded at 1.68 per cent, near a one-year low. In early September, Beijing rolled out a 360-billion-yuan capital injection into eight state-owned financial institutions, with 300 billion yuan from the Ministry of Finance and 60 billion yuan from the state tobacco monopoly. Citi analysts said there was room for China’s 10-year yield to slip towards 1.6 per cent, citing weak credit demand that limits upward pressure on yields. Continued bond purchases by the People’s Bank of China, the country’s central bank, are expected to provide an additional source of structural demand. According to the report, China had issued 90 per cent of its planned 1.3 trillion yuan in ultra-long special treasury bonds for the year by mid-September, with the remaining quota likely to be issued in October. But the analysts cautioned that risks remain, including tougher regulatory constraints that could limit a rally in ultra-long bonds and aggressive new policy support that could trigger large back-end selloffs. China’s credit data also pointed to subdued credit activity in August. New renminbi loans totalled just 60 billion yuan, while total social financing added 1.66 trillion yuan, both missing expectations, according to the report. “Weak domestic demand and subdued credit creation should continue to weigh on the growth outlook and keep duration demand well supported, in our view,” Garg said. Meanwhile, China reduced its holdings of US Treasuries to an 18-year low in July, falling to US$618 billion from US$633.4 billion in June, according to data from the US Treasury Department. Overall holdings by foreign countries also dropped for a second straight month amid growing concerns over the sustainability of American government debt. The US 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.25 per cent on Tuesday, while the 30-year government bond yield traded at 5.56 per cent, the highest level since 2004.

title: Review | Oh My Ghost! Oh My God! review: Naomi Watanabe gets lost in dismal Taiwanese horror comedy
description: Naomi Watanabe reunites with Soda Voyu, Esther Huang and Sakinu for this arduous folk horror story set in the mountains of Taiwan.
content: 1/5 stars Japanese comedian Naomi Watanabe plays a pop star who travels to the Taiwanese countryside in search of her ancestral home in the horror comedy Oh My Ghost! Oh My God! Marking the directorial debut of indigenous actor Soda Voyu, the film follows an eclectic group of oddball characters as they navigate all manner of supernatural obstacles in the hostile mountains, but fails spectacularly to be either scary or funny. A spiritual sequel to Hidden Treasures in the Mountain (2018), Oh My Ghost! Oh My God! reunites original stars Esther Huang Ching-i, Sakinu and Soda for a markedly different kind of adventure. While their first outing saw the trio encounter smugglers and wood thieves in the forests that surround their remote village, this second adventure pivots hard into the commercially lucrative genre of folk horror, which has produced a string of hits at the Taiwanese box office in the past decade, from The Tag-Along (2015) to Incantation (2022). Soda again plays Wan-de, although now it is revealed that he is the last in a long line of shaman priests – a calling he has struggled to fulfil. Huang plays Xin-lan, his girlfriend and an accomplished mountain guide. She is also the former classmate of Juliet (Watanabe), a half-Japanese woman who left their village years earlier and has since become a celebrity in the Japanese music industry. Following the death of her mother – a local – Juliet has returned to visit a remote lake high in the mountains to pay her respects. Her manager, Xiao Luo (Jasper Liu Yi-hao), is also along for the ride; his good looks immediately catch the eye of hairdresser Zumai (Sakinu), inspiring him to join the party. It does not take long, however, before the group gets lost, is split up and encounters a host of spooky characters and creepy phenomena that delve deep into each character’s troubled past while demanding Wan-de call his questionable shaman skills into action. Oh My Ghost! Oh My God! presents a fruitful set-up for both scares and chuckles, but Soda’s script fails to capitalise on these opportunities. Even the vivacious screen presence of Watanabe – an infectiously likeable performer on the cusp of global stardom – is largely squandered. Falling back too often on cheap, ineffective jump scares or repetitive lowbrow digs at the expense of Zumai’s sexuality, the film becomes an arduous slog, every bit as exhausting as being lost in the fog. title: Mahathir ‘lonely’ as family and Malaysia mourn Siti Hasmah
description: Daughter reveals family are taking turns to stay with former PM after burial of his wife of 70 years, as tributes pour in.
content: As Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, wife of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, was laid to rest on Monday, one poignant image stood out. Footage of her family members sobbing served as a reminder that before the 100-year-old was “Ibu Negara” (Mother of the Nation), she was first a mother of seven, grandmother to 18 and great-grandmother to four. Her latest great-grandchild, Eden Zakaria, was born just last month to granddaughter Meera Alyanna Mukhriz, better known as Ally. In a social media post on Monday, Ally paid tribute to her tok (grandparent), saying: “She was strong yet gentle, lenient but firm and always the glue that kept our large family close.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by alyanna 🪲 (@ally.mukhriz) “Bringing Eden into the world was tough but immensely worth it because he got to meet his wonderful nyang,” the new mother wrote, using the Malay word for great-grandmother. “Just two weeks ago, I was walking to the kitchen when I saw the front door open. Who else but tok herself, arriving unannounced just to see us and her cicit [great-grandchild], Eden. She would have held him all day if she could. She kept saying, ‘Ally, no pillows in his crib OK?’ She had endless tips for me. I only wish Eden had a bit more time with her, though we were so privileged to have her for 100 years.” She also thanked members of the public for their condolences and support. “She left such an indelible mark on me, and, judging by your messages, on so many of you too … I just wanted to say the deepest of thank-yous to everyone who has reached out to me or my family today.” Mahathir, 101, cut a lonely figure during the funeral, openly weeping as he watched his wife being laid to rest. “I didn’t expect her to die today,” he was overheard telling Sultan Abdullah of Pahang, adding that Siti Hasmah had seemed “quite well” the previous evening, the Borneo Post reported. Siti Hasmah died at about 9.25am on Monday at the National Heart Institute. Her son, Mokhzani Mahathir, said she had been in good spirits on Sunday night before her condition suddenly deteriorated. Another son, Mukhriz Mahathir, said Mahathir was by her side until her final moments. Siti Hasmah’s daughter, Marina Mahathir, told Malay-language newspaper Berita Harian on Tuesday that her father was in good health but was grieving the loss of his “lifelong companion”. “Of course he is sad. She was his partner for 70 years. He feels lonely,” Marina told reporters after putting flowers on her mother’s grave. In a previous interview, Marina had said her mother was Mahathir’s pillar of strength. “She always gave him her 100 per cent support. If she disagreed with him, she would do it privately,” she told The Star. When Mahathir retired in 2003 after serving as prime minister for 22 years, Siti Hasmah said she felt a sense of relief as the country and Malaysians “have returned my husband back to me and my family”. But she stepped back into the public eye without complaint after he became prime minister for a second time in 2018. It is hard to believe she is no longer with us Marina Mahathir, Siti Hasmah’s daughter According to Marina, family members have been taking turns to stay with Mahathir to ensure he is not left alone in his grief. She said the entire family was still trying to come to terms with the loss. “We all miss mother. We were so used to seeing her at home and now it is hard to believe she is no longer with us.” Marina also thanked members of the public who paid their respects at the mosque and later at the burial grounds. “Even today, many are still coming,” she said. The whole family was touched by the overwhelming show of affection and support, she added, with hundreds of messages of condolence pouring in on social media, making it impossible to respond to each one personally. “Some of them I know and some I don’t but they are paying their respects to mother because they see her as their own.”

title: AstraZeneca, Merck, Novo deals boost Chinese biotech as global interest grows
description: Deals involving novel cancer therapies and weight-loss drugs reinforce the growing global appeal of Chinese biotech innovation.
content: Shares of Akeso surged after British drug maker AstraZeneca moved to advance the Chinese biotech firm’s flagship cancer drug, while a new deal from US giant Merck further underscored the sector’s global momentum amid easing fears of US curbs. AstraZeneca on Tuesday announced a US$2 billion equity investment in Florida-headquartered Summit Therapeutics, which holds the exclusive rights to develop and commercialise Akeso’s immunotherapy drug ivonescimab outside China. Summit and AstraZeneca would “imminently” begin clinical trials to evaluate ivonescimab in combination with AstraZeneca’s antibody-drug conjugates, including gastrointestinal cancer drug sonesitatug vedotin, the companies said. Cui Cui, head of Asia healthcare research at Jefferies, said in a note on Tuesday that the partnership “further strengthened” the investment bank’s conviction that ivonescimab could become a foundational immunotherapy treatment when used alongside other medicines. Akeso’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed 15.5 per cent higher on Tuesday. New York-listed Summit Therapeutics soared more than 19 per cent in after-hours trading on Monday. China’s biotech industry also received a boost after Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo announced on Tuesday it would license drug maker Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals’ oral GLP-1 weight-loss drug HRS-1596 in a deal worth up to US$2.6 billion, including a US$300 million upfront payment. Hengrui’s shares closed 1.9 per cent higher on Tuesday in Hong Kong. On Monday, Merck agreed to pay up to US$2.13 billion for the rights to a cancer drug developed by Shanghai-based start-up SciBrunch Therapeutics. Merck would make an upfront payment of US$400 million for the exclusive worldwide rights to develop, manufacture and commercialise SciBrunch’s pre-clinical oral drug SPR2015, the companies said. The agreement was “very large for a pre-clinical asset”, said Tony Ren, head of Asia healthcare research at Macquarie Capital. Founded in 2024, SciBrunch focuses on small-molecule therapies to treat “mature targets” in oncology. The company announced a US$35 million pre-A financing round in January led by Shanghai-based Highlight Capital, after raising 200 million yuan (US$29.8 million) in an angel round in June 2025. SPR2015 targets KRAS G12D, a common mutation found in cancer. The drug works as a molecular glue, a type of protein degrader that forces a cell’s natural waste-disposal system to destroy proteins that cause disease. Merck’s deal with SciBrunch “is a testament to how good Chinese biotech has become in molecular glues and protein degraders”, Ren said. Chinese innovative drugs have continued to gain traction globally thanks to favourable domestic policies and easing geopolitical concerns. Out-licensing deals between Chinese and US companies are expected to “ride on a high tide” after the US Treasury Department reportedly leaned away from pursuing sweeping restrictions, and China unveiled an ambitious five-year development plan for the biomedicine sector.

title: Style Edit: Max Mara celebrates 1930s women explorers, as Sportmax lightens daily essentials for SS27
description: Max Mara welcomed stars like Kate Mara and Adria Arjona to its Milan Fashion Week front row, while Sportmax unveiled sheer tailoring designed for soaring heat.
content: Since their founding, Max Mara and sister brand Sportmax have been lauded for consistently delivering a covetable wardrobe of luxurious essentials that celebrate sophisticated, effortless Italian tailoring.
