Every collection’s unique blend of timeless elegance and everyday wearability has made it a mainstay in the wardrobes of style stars like Kate Mara, Leighton Meester, Yoona Lim and Adria Arjona – the latter received the 2026 Women in Film (WIF) Max Mara Face of the Future Award – all of whom attended the brand’s recent spring/summer 2027 show at Milan Fashion Week. The runway looks drew inspiration from the defiant, globe-trotting women of the 1930s, such as intrepid explorer Freya Stark and fearless aviator Amelia Earhart. Their pioneering spirits, which knew no boundaries, served as the backdrop for this empowering collection. Every style was re-envisioned for the multifaceted demands of a modern woman’s life, allowing her to pivot from outdoor adventures to the boardroom. Highlights include the safari jacket, which is reimagined in textured linen or lustrous gabardine, and worn draped and knotted to the side, or long and loose like a duster coat. Signature tailoring is toughened up with utilitarian pieces such as an upgraded cargo vest worn over a sartorial jacket cut, flight jackets featuring leather straps and D-rings, voluminous trenches and utilitarian overalls. Every piece has something to offer for the pioneering women of today who move seamlessly through the everyday realities of contemporary life. Lightness was the focus of Sportmax’s collection, which proposes a weightless yet functional wardrobe every woman will desire. Sheer tailoring is rendered in fabrics such as silk organza. The search for freshness runs through every silhouette, from feather-light denim and pinstripe voile tailoring to sleeveless buttery-soft leather jackets and coats featuring convertible panels that let the body breathe. Sleek cut-out swimwear is perfect for an after-work beach escape. The colour palette channels the pearlescent colours of water in glass, from greys to striking gem tones. Rounding off the collection are Lucite accessories and shoes that are as light as they are appealing, including slides with contrast details and icicle-bijou pumps.

title: As I see it | It’s the end of the world – and I don’t feel fine
description: Three authors warn that America’s techno-fascists are about to bring on the apocalypse for all of us.
content: Armageddon is what will happen when billionaires, or even trillionaires, are given free rein. Could this be the final outcome of late-stage American capitalism and democracy? Imagine a human-extinction event: a rogue artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, a new world war or runaway climate change. You likely already have a fair idea of where the safest places on earth and beyond are, if you have been following the ultra-wealthy individuals from Silicon Valley and Wall Street. They are building secretive, disaster-resistant shelters and bunker compounds in a few choice locations. Elon Musk, with his launch pads, has long hoped to take himself and his many children to another planet, colonise it and rebuild human civilisation. This is not fantasy, science fiction or satire. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is building a US$270 million compound on Hawaii’s Kauai island with a 5,000 sq ft underground shelter. Venture capitalist Peter Thiel purchased a 477-acre estate in New Zealand, planning a bunker. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has three properties on Miami’s ultra-exclusive Indian Creek island, colloquially known as the “Billionaire Bunker”. Strict non-disclosure agreements obscure exact numbers, but bunker manufacturers report surging demand from ultra-wealthy clients citing geopolitical and other concerns. But in a global catastrophe, you probably wouldn’t get anywhere near them as paramilitary units with shoot-to-kill orders would likely be stationed to protect them. All this has been happening for some time. The reason is that the interests of those Western billionaires, sometimes derisively called the “Epstein class”, do not simply differ from those of humanity. They actively run against them. Some of the world’s richest people have not been shy about profiting from the apocalypse, or even helping to bring it about, according to a new book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. And the political institution most blatant about serving those interests is also the world’s most powerful: the current White House. In End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, Klein and Taylor offer a stark thesis. They argue that some of the world’s most powerful people no longer believe in a shared future for humanity, or even with their own citizens. Instead, they are preparing to survive, and profit from, a collapse they are helping to speed up. In an interview with The New York Times, the authors contend half of American Christians believe we are living in the end times and describe an uneasy alliance of three groups. The first is religious end-timers, such as evangelical Christian Zionists, who want to hasten the return of the Messiah. The second is technologists who believe humanity is heading inevitably towards a digital superintelligence. The third is ethnonationalists who want to fortify the nation against immigration and cultural change. The Trump administration helps bind all three groups together. It draws heavy funding from Silicon Valley, and it appointed Mike Huckabee, a Christian Zionist, as ambassador to Israel. The authors also point to how the elite itself has changed. During Donald Trump’s first term, many tech billionaires criticised him for withdrawing from the Paris climate accord. By his second inauguration, they were lined up behind him. The shift is partly due to artificial intelligence and its enormous appetite for energy, which is being fed largely with liquefied natural gas and coal. Some of the world’s richest people have not been shy about profiting from the apocalypse, or even helping to bring it about … And the political institution most blatant about serving those interests is also the world’s most powerful: the current White House The authors also cite three examples: Peter Thiel’s 2009 essay arguing that democracy and freedom are incompatible; Musk’s remark that humanity increasingly looks like a “biological bootloader” for digital superintelligence; and the federal cuts Musk made at the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to programmes that millions of Americans rely on. Their arguments are not new or unique. Gil Duran has similarly argued in The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy that tech billionaires such as Musk and Thiel have aligned behind Trump to dismantle democracy. There are, according to Duran, deep connections between tech fascism and white supremacist ideology, including how billionaires have embraced hierarchical world views rooted in eugenics. He details how neo-reactionary ideas from figures like Curtis Yarvin of the so-called Dark Enlightenment movement – who advocated for purging the country of federal government bureaucracy – directly influenced Trump’s Doge initiative. He argues that confronting billionaire power constitutes the essential political struggle in America today. Meanwhile, Klein and Taylor tie up wide-ranging evidence and present a coherent case. Klein notes that far-right ideas once waved away as fringe have moved into government. And the evidence points to those who hold the levers of power planning only for the privileged few who can afford an exit. A society that has stopped believing in a common future for humanity or even their own citizens – the tech bros have admitted as much – is already lost, and is unfit to lead the world.

title: Hong Kong man jailed 3 years for hammer attack on associate who later died
description: Mo Tai-fung, 42, initially faced murder charge, but prosecutors amended it after autopsy found victim had died from effects of drugs.
content: Hong Kong’s High Court has sentenced a man with a triad background to three years and two months in prison after he attacked an associate with a hammer, leaving the victim bleeding on the street before he died of an overdose hours later. The court heard on Tuesday that Mo Tai-fung, 42, was initially charged with murdering the 33-year-old, having struck him on the head 11 times at about 2am on July 28, 2024, outside a building on Pilkem Street in Yau Ma Tei. Prosecutors amended the charge at an earlier hearing after an autopsy found that the victim, surnamed Pang, had died from the effects of drugs. The report said that although Pang had multiple deep lacerations to his scalp, his injuries were not fatal. Mo faced one count of wounding with intent and another of inhaling a dangerous drug. He confirmed his guilty pleas before Madam Justice Anna Lai Yuen-kee. The court heard that Mo met Pang at a Yau Ma Tei flat used as a “drug den” a few months before the attack. In the early hours of July 28, the pair were at a gathering in the flat. During a conversation, Mo was provoked by Pang, who was said to be arrogant and disrespectful. Mo told officers during the investigation that he only wanted to “teach Pang a lesson” and did not intend to kill him. Security camera footage from nearby showed Mo leaving a building and following Pang. Within seconds, he struck Pang on the head with a small hammer seven times. Mo hit Pang’s head four more times after he fell and was sitting on the ground. Shortly after Mo left, Pang got up and entered the building. Over the next few hours, Pang took drugs to relieve his pain. He eventually suffered a seizure and was found unconscious outside the building. He was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei, where he was pronounced dead at about 7am. In a mitigation letter, Mo wrote that he knew drugs had caused him great harm and led to this very serious incident. Judge Lai said Mo had an “appalling criminal record”, with 18 previous convictions, including multiple violent offences. He committed the current offence just a year after completing a three-year prison sentence for wounding. Lai said Mo was a person with a tendency to resort to violence. “I must say that in this case, the so-called provocation … does not warrant such a serious attack on the victim,” she said in sentencing. “Even if the defendant was provoked, the retaliation was wholly out of proportion.” Noting that wounding with intent was a serious crime, Lai cited precedents for similar offences that carried sentences of between three and 12 years’ imprisonment. She set a starting point of four years and six months for the wounding charge, then applied a one-third discount for Mo’s timely guilty plea. She imposed a further two-month sentence for the drug offence to be served consecutively.

title: Asian Games: double cycling gold for China, Hong Kong take bronze, Wong on move
description: Team sprint medal is Hong Kong’s first on track at Games, squash teams march on and Coleman Wong breezes into third round of men’s singles.
content: Hong Kong’s men got their track cycling campaign off to a strong start on Tuesday, winning bronze in the team sprint, while the city’s squash players continued to march through their respective team events. China, meanwhile, took gold in the sprint in a Games record time of 42.152 seconds at Izu Velodrome, consigning Japan to silver. The hosts finished in 42.511. There was victory too for China’s women, who set an Asian record of 45.370 in beating Malaysia to team sprint gold. Chinese Taipei took bronze. “For a long time, the Chinese women have a history of winning a gold medal, also at the Olympics,” China’s Lui Qi said. “In the men’s team, we have been dreaming about catching up with them. “So we are extremely fortunate to be able to win a gold medal on the women’s and men’s side.” After ranking fourth in qualifying, Hong Kong’s Mok Tsz-chun, To Cheuk-hei and Yung Tsun-ho then eliminated South Korea to advance to the medal play-off. The trio put in huge effort to finish in 43.507, beating Thailand to the podium, with their rivals finishing in 44.341. The men’s team sprint result marked a repeat of the Asian Track Cycling Championships in the Philippines in March, when Hong Kong also finished ahead of Malaysia for a historic bronze. It was the first Games medal for the men’s sprint team, and took the city’s overall total to 35, with five gold, 12 silver and 18 bronze. There should be more added to the tally on Wednesday, with the city’s women’s and men’s squash teams both one win away from securing a medal. The women’s team, featuring mixed doubles gold medallist Lee Ka-yi, individual bronze medallist Simmi Chan Sin-yuk, and Tomato Ho Tze-lok, breezed past their final Group B opponents Mongolia in straight games, with none of the encounters lasting more than 12 minutes each. Hong Kong’s men will face Qatar in the last eight at Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena, while the women are waiting for the outcome of the final group matches in their competition. The two sides won medals in Hangzhou three years ago, with the women claiming silver after losing to Malaysia in the final, while the men finished with bronze. Elsewhere, the rain continued to hamper efforts to get some of the outdoor events finished. The cricket quarter-finals were washed out for the second day running, with Sri Lanka and Bangladesh sent through at the expense of Nepal and Malaysia. The action at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre, meanwhile, was all indoors, not that it mattered much to Coleman Wong Chak-lam, who eased past Jordan’s Zaid Al-Mashni in straight sets, winning 6-4, 6-1. Teenager Kai Thompson, however, lost his second round encounter against Japan’s Hayato Matsuoka 7-6, 6-1. Wong, the men’s top seed this week, will face Japan’s Yosuke Watanuki in the third round on Wednesday. Watanuki won silver three years ago, while Wong lost in the quarter-finals to Hong Seong-chan, who went on to win bronze. The rain did not bring the wind needed to get the sailors offshore, and Nick Halliday and Stephanie Norton, plus windsurfers Cheng Ching-yin and Mui Ma Kwan-ching spent the day watching and waiting. Harris Tsolis, the sailing head coach, said the situation was more “boring than annoying, but that’s the sport sometimes”. “It’s just hard as we need to keep the sailors focused and active through the day to be able to jump in their boats and perform at a moment’s notice each day,” he added.

title: Indonesian prison chief suspended over secret VIP compound for inmates
description: Inspectors found a hidden compound at Cibinong Prison, complete with villas and a pool reportedly reserved for paying inmates.
content: The governor of an Indonesian prison has been suspended after authorities uncovered a suspected luxury compound for VIP inmates within the grounds, prompting a parliamentary inquiry. However, Director General of Corrections Mashudi denied the accusations during a House of Representatives commission hearing on Monday. Cibinong Prison in Bogor, West Java, came under investigation after inspectors from the Ombudsman’s office discovered a fenced-off compound behind the prison chief’s house during a surprise visit last Wednesday, according to the Jakarta Globe. Initially denied entry, the inspectors argued their way inside. “Of course, we started to wonder why we were being obstructed. When we arrived, it turned out there were many homes suspected to be occupied by inmates,” Ombudsman member Fikri Yasin told the Kompas newspaper. Inside the compound were several buildings that looked like villas, homestay flats and town houses. The Ombudsman’s office also noted a car park, a gym, a swimming pool and a golf simulator under construction. Several luxury cars were parked in the area. “They have special rooms, they have escorts, and so on. For example, if this is an inmate area, we noticed several luxury cars parked there, including a [Toyota] Alphard. Naturally, we have questions,” Fikri said. “The facilities appear to have different purposes,” another Ombudsman member, Syafrida Rachmawati Rasahan, told a news conference on Thursday. “But there also seems to be some standardisation, similar to accommodation with suite, deluxe and superior rooms.” Inspectors also found inmates inside the residences, Tempo news magazine reported. “When they realised this was the Ombudsman, they immediately ran into the bedrooms,” Syafrida said. “So, in our view, there are strong indications that there are special facilities for certain inmates at Cibinong Prison.” One inmate locked the door from the inside to prevent the inspection team from entering. Near the locked door, inspectors found a framed photo on a table showing Jimmy Masrin, who is serving a 10-year sentence in a corruption case linked to Indonesia Eximbank. Another inmate admitted to paying to stay at the compound. “Based on our interviews with those occupying the houses, they did pay a certain amount. It is clearly being commercialised, and this is something we will investigate further,” Syafrida said. The Ombudsman received a report alleging that prisoners were asked to pay 150,000 rupiah (US$8.33) a week, according to The Straits Times. At Monday’s hearing, Mashudi refuted accusations that the maximum security prison had created special living conditions for paying inmates. He said the compound housed official residences for prison staff and that one of the buildings was a cattle-fattening facility. All items inside – including bottles of whisky and beer – belonged to prison officers, Mashudi said. The area under construction was intended for storage lockers rather than leisure facilities, while the inmates seen there were taking part in assimilation and education activities, he added. Mashudi said the photo of Masrin had been confiscated during a security inspection and stored in the employee residence. His explanation failed to convince several lawmakers. “Don’t play games with the public. How could Jimmy Masrin’s framed photograph end up in an official residence?” said lawmaker Yanuar Arif Wibowo of the Prosperous Justice Party. “Don’t lie to cover up an earlier lie.” The Ombudsman has called for the special facilities to be dismantled before the next inspection. Cibinong Prison chief Wisnu Hani Putranto and four other prison officials have been suspended. The scandal echoes a case at West Java’s Sukamiskin Prison in 2018, when inmates were found to be paying between 200 million and 500 million rupiah to stay in upgraded cells with air conditioning, televisions and refrigerators. That prison’s governor was later arrested over alleged bribes linked to the special facilities. The non-governmental organisation Indonesia Corruption Watch has urged authorities to investigate possible corruption in the Cibinong case. “The Corruption Eradication Commission needs to trace whether there were transactions, flows of money or abuse of authority by prison officials or officers,” researcher Wana Alamsyah said in a statement on Thursday. “The experience of the Sukamiskin prison case shows that paying for special facilities and permission to leave prison is not merely a disciplinary violation, but can develop into bribery.”

title: China offers 15-year research grants to the world’s brightest young scientists
description: Agency offers scientists under 35 long-term financial backing with no short-term performance reviews but demands physical lab presence.
content: China is offering the world’s brightest young scientists generous 15-year research grants for free exploration, as the country accelerates its drive to become a global science powerhouse. Dou Xiankang, director of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the country’s top funder of basic research, told a recent academic forum that the agency was selecting a group of the brightest researchers under 35 for long-term financial backing. Once this group of exceptionally brilliant young people was identified, their sole performance metric over a 15-year period would be “whether they are in the laboratory”, Dou said on September 19. He said there would be no short-term performance reviews during this period. Those selected would be assessed on only one criterion: physical presence in the lab. “We do not mind if there is no short-term success; we just need you to settle down and stay in the laboratory,” Dou said. He revealed that 44 scientists had been chosen this year, nine of whom were from overseas, alongside more than 30 from within China. The 15-year backing would involve increasingly intensive support, Dou added. Funding will double after the first five years and double again after the next five. “This is a new initiative undertaken by the NSFC this year,” he noted. This new approach may prompt questions such as: where do scientific breakthroughs come from and where does the future of Chinese research lie? In the most innovative and passionate brains, according to the director. “It depends on whether we can more effectively inspire and mobilise the enthusiasm and creativity of the most innovative and dynamic individuals in China,” Dou remarked. “We want to encourage them by providing timely and effective support when they need the money the most, when they are at their most dynamic and at an age when they still have a passion for science, enabling them to stand out.” China’s academic sector has long been plagued by a system where resources are concentrated among a small number of influential, senior researchers, leaving younger academics to face fierce competition for grant funding. Since his appointment in April 2023, the NSFC director has focused on tilting resources towards younger researchers. In November 2023, the funding body announced that the brightest young scientists would receive a significant long-term boost, with the government offering up to 28 million yuan (US$4.17 million) over 15 years to support their work. In May this year, the NSFC announced a substantial expansion of its Young Scientists Fund, projecting an increase of 12,000 grants – a jump of more than 50 per cent – aimed at providing a steady stream of outstanding reserve talent for basic research. The scheme, now referred to as Category C projects, is primarily aimed at early-career researchers and is designed to help them independently select topics and conduct their research. Speaking at the conference, Dou explained that China was in a phase of accelerated technological development, producing an exceptionally high number of outstanding young minds. “Therefore, at this specific historical juncture, we must direct substantial funding towards this brilliant young talent,” he noted. He also revealed that nearly 90 per cent of the lead researchers on NSFC-funded projects were young people, with 75 per cent of the funding awarded to those under the age of 45. In addition, the NSFC is ramping up its campaign to lure top young scientists from abroad by extending a major funding programme for a second round – a move that could be aimed partly at US-based researchers facing budget constraints. In late July, the funder issued an additional call for applications for the Excellent Young Scientists Fund (Overseas), following its initial round earlier this year. Since its launch in 2021, the programme has awarded individual grants of between 1 million to 3 million yuan to thousands of scientists under 40, both born in China and overseas.

title: Exclusive | ‘180-degree flip’ sees global investors turn to China for diversification: Pimco president
description: Christian Stracke says US asset manager is pointing clients outside US towards Chinese offshore bonds.
content: Global investors are turning to China again in search of alternatives to crowded US asset markets, with Pimco seeing Chinese bonds as one of the safest ways to diversify portfolios after sentiment towards the world’s second-largest economy “flipped 180 degrees”. The US-based asset manager, which oversaw more than US$2 trillion in assets by the end of June, had been pointing its clients, particularly those outside the United States, towards Chinese offshore bonds, according to its president, Christian Stracke, because it was one way to reduce concentrations in US dollar and equity assets after years of strong gains in the American market. “We do get a lot of questions from our clients, particularly non-US clients, about what are some other ways to diversify away from US concentrations … and we talk about China – China offshore bonds in particular – as one of those ways,” Stracke said in an interview with the South China Morning Post in Hong Kong on Monday. “It’s not always that people are worried about the US. It’s just that their portfolios, because the US has done so well, have become very exposed to the US dollar, to the US equities market.” While Pimco viewed emerging markets, more broadly, as an option for investors seeking diversification from concentrated US exposures, the China bond market was “by far the least correlated [with the US] and the most stable among them”, Stracke said. Chinese bonds offered “true risk-off diversification”, he said, because China’s weak inflationary pressures left it less exposed to stagflation risks than other major economies. That meant Chinese bonds could outperform other assets in a global risk-off scenario, even though their yields remained relatively low. “You’re not buying them for the yield, you’re buying them for the diversification,” Stracke said. His comments come as investors reassess global asset allocations after this month’s interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve – the first in more than three years – sparked questions about how far the renewed tightening cycle could go and added to concerns about portfolios heavily concentrated in US assets. Pimco’s view of Chinese offshore bonds as a viable route for diversification coincides with Beijing’s efforts to capitalise on global investors’ growing demand for diversification by drawing more foreign capital into its financial markets. People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng told a conference in June that “China’s financial market depth and breadth provide important opportunities for overseas institutions seeking diversified allocations in a period of heightened global financial volatility.” Chinese bonds have been included in three major global bond indices, but overseas investors still account for only a small share of the market. Overseas institutions, including central banks, held 3.12 trillion yuan (US$464.7 billion) in China’s interbank bond market by the end of April, equivalent to 1.8 per cent of the total. Several years ago, foreign investors were pulling back from China amid concerns about slowing growth, geopolitical tensions and regulatory uncertainty. They’re now interested in finding ways of accessing China Christian Stracke, Pimco president Stracke said that two or three years ago, Pimco frequently heard investors around the world describe China as “uninvestible”. “You never hear that now,” he said. Instead, investors were asking how they could gain exposure to the market, encouraged by China’s export strength and advances in AI, robotics and automation. “Investor perceptions of China have flipped 180 degrees,” Stracke said. “They’re now interested in finding ways of accessing China.” China’s technological advances had played an important role in changing those perceptions, he said, adding that investors who once assumed artificial intelligence innovation would be concentrated in the US had been surprised by developments in China, including the release of DeepSeek’s open-weight models and advances in Chinese robotics and real-world applications of AI. “There really are two nodes of AI excellence, in the US and China, and they’re different,” Stracke said. The shift in investor sentiment comes amid signs of a stabilisation in relations between Washington and Beijing. The two sides agreed last week to extend their trade truce by two months, and US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping agreed in Washington to establish a trade council and hold further talks on AI. Stracke described the renewed engagement as “very constructive”, even if the chances of breakthroughs remained low. “What we need is no further intensification of global conflict,” he said. “To have them proactively, constructively working together is a very positive development.” Despite the improvement in sentiment, Pimco itself had not materially changed its China positioning, Stracke said, with the firm having maintained “meaningful positions” in Chinese offshore bonds over the past year while keeping light positions in China credit for years. In fixed-income investments, the firm favoured Chinese policy-bank bonds, which it viewed as a proxy for the central government, while it remained cautious about property debt. The property sector still had “a couple more years at least” of restructuring ahead after about five years of adjustment, Stracke said, with the adjustment taking longer than many investors had expected.

title: Philippines struggles to fill 20,000 teaching jobs: ‘we are facing a learning crisis’
description: Industry players call for transparency in the teacher hiring process and urge more concrete support for educators suffering from burnout.
content: The Philippines has 20,000 teaching vacancies to fill, a budget hearing has revealed, with sector insiders warning that the gap signals a mounting education crisis. Those in the industry are calling for transparency in the teacher hiring process, including clear figures on budget allocation and positions filled amid problems of mismatch and improper targeting of job applicants. At a House of Representatives plenary session last week, Antonio Tinio from the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) grilled officials over the lack of urgency, arguing that thousands of qualified applicants in the registry were still waiting for jobs. This Week in Asia has contacted the country’s Department of Education for comment. At the session, it said that some positions were “hard to fill” because they lacked qualified candidates for certain specialised roles. The department is tipped to receive some 976 billion pesos (US$15.6 billion) under the 2027 budget, with more than 31 billion pesos allocated for filling teaching vacancies and 12 billion pesos to promote 135,000 existing teachers. “The cost of delay falls on learners and on teachers already in service. We are facing a learning crisis; we cannot close learning gaps while leaving needed teaching positions vacant and asking existing teachers to carry additional classes and tasks,” said Ruby Bernardo, ACT chairwoman. Bernardo urged the government to provide teachers with concrete support rather than another promise of positions that went unfilled, citing a World Bank report that found 91 per cent of Filipinos aged 10 could not read or understand age-appropriate texts. “That makes timely hiring especially urgent,” she said. Hanibal Camua, executive director of Philippine Business for Education, a non-profit advocacy group, said the hiring gap reflected both a workforce alignment problem and a problem with teacher quality. “Some education graduates pursue opportunities abroad, where teaching can offer better compensation,” Camua said. “Others move to private schools or to sectors such as [outsourcing] and virtual assistance, which can offer competitive entry-level salaries and, in some cases, less administrative burden.” Figures from the Second Congressional Commission on Education, a national body created by the government to evaluate the country’s education system, show that the pass rate for teacher qualification exams between 2009 and 2023 was 33 per cent for junior school teachers and 40 per cent for secondary school teachers. “That tells us that we have to address both ends of the pipeline. We need to make teaching a career that can attract and retain good people, while also ensuring that the institutions preparing our teachers are producing graduates who meet the standards required in today’s classrooms,” Camua said. Teachers at state-funded schools in the Philippines begin with a monthly salary of 31,705 pesos (US$506), yet they are often saddled with non-academic tasks and overcrowded classrooms. But simply reducing the issue to quality “puts the burden of explanation on applicants without examining the system that recruits and retains them”, Bernardo said. “The education department should publish how many qualified applicants there are for each vacancy, where applicants withdraw, and which subjects and locations are hardest to staff. That would show whether the obstacle is a shortage of qualified applicants, a mismatch in deployment, slow hiring, or poor retention,” she said. Mismatched expectations The enduring shortfall raises questions about the broader state of education in the Philippines, especially after the department received a “historic” budget of 1.015 trillion pesos in 2026 – marking the first time the country has met the Unesco benchmark for education spending, which requires allocating 4-6 per cent of gross domestic product or 15-20 per cent of public spending to the sector. “We should acknowledge those allocations while asking a more important question: what has actually reached schools? How many teachers have been appointed and deployed? How many classrooms and materials are in use? Have class sizes, workloads and learning outcomes improved?” Bernardo said. The word “historic” did not match many teachers’ daily experiences due to a long history of chronic underfunding, she said, calling for “transparent reporting on actual spending and results” and measuring commitments against completed hiring and facilities. For Wilhelm Sheila A. Pineda, a top-tier educator known as a “master teacher” at the San Fernando South Central Integrated School in La Union province, Education Secretary Sonny Angara’s admission that budget cuts left his department unable to hire new teachers for next year is deeply concerning. “On one hand, we have qualified teachers waiting for opportunities, while on the other hand, our schools continue to experience shortages,” she said. “This is frustrating because teacher shortages are felt directly in schools. When there are not enough teachers, the workload does not simply disappear – it is absorbed by the teachers who are already there.” Salve V. Calderon, a fellow master teacher in Bataan province, said the teacher shortage was especially alarming, with educators facing heavy levels of burnout as student populations and the number of schools continued to grow. “Workload, burnout, compensation and too many non-teaching requirements are major factors. For me, teachers entered the profession to teach, but they are becoming exhausted by work that does not directly contribute to student learning,” Calderon said. Actual school experiences also showed teachers constantly having to adjust to new programmes, requirements and changes being introduced, Pineda pointed out. “Teachers are generally willing to contribute,” she said. “The concern is whether every new programme comes with adequate preparation, coordination, orientation, time and resources.” Calderon, who teaches English, said technology was creating another set of problems for teachers: “In many ways it has created more documentation, submissions, reports, programmes and sudden tasks.” The Philippines should not simply fill the 20,000 positions without addressing the underlying learning crisis, according to Camua of Philippine Business for Education, adding that it is equally important to provide teachers with the right support to help students learn effectively. Bernardo suggested that education officials set a public hiring timetable, identify bottlenecks in every division, speed up appointments and deployment, and regularly report on vacancies actually filled. “The goal is not merely to clear a vacancy count,” Bernardo said. “It is to ensure every learner has a teacher with the time, resources and support to teach well.”

title: Malaysia’s Forest City wants a rebirth. Scams, crime stand in the way
description: ‘I worry for the safety of my wife because she is alone at home when I’m at work,’ a resident says as the project tries to shed its ‘ghost town’ tag.
content: Behind the unmarked door of a shoplot along a quiet commercial stretch of Forest City in Malaysia’s Johor state, four customers sat tapping away, playing slot-style games on tablets. A stern-looking man stood guard at the entrance, his eyes darting around. The customers could place bets starting from around 20 ringgit (US$4.89). Instead of handing over cash, they paid for gambling credits using Malaysia’s Touch ’n Go e-wallet. They were then issued tablets from behind the counter with pre-installed slot games. “Most of our customers are foreigners. Many play for hours and usually top up their credits a few times,” said the woman manning the counter. Many of them are workers living in Forest City, she said. The apparent gambling operation observed on a recent visit is among several questionable or controversial activities that have emerged at the sprawling development as it tries to leave its “ghost town” reputation behind. A US$100 billion megaproject on the southwestern edge of Peninsular Malaysia, Forest City comprises high-rise flats, landed homes and villas interspersed with commercial shop lots. In July, Johor police arrested 335 people in raids on alleged online scam operations there. The police seized computers and mobile phones and said the syndicates were involved in schemes including fraudulent cryptocurrency investments and romance scams targeting victims overseas. That same month, the authorities ordered Network School, a community catering to technology entrepreneurs and digital nomads, to cease operations after finding breaches of licensing conditions and the approved use of its premises. Residents, property owners and experts said the episodes are a fresh setback for Forest City as it tries to rehabilitate its image and attract investment. The development has been trying to reinvent itself as an investment destination, anchored by its status as a special financial zone (SFZ). The SFZ is expected to surpass its 2 billion ringgit investment target this year after attracting more than 250 inquiries from prospective investors including financial institutions, family offices and business services firms. Criminologist P Sundramoorthy said the scam operations and episodes like Network School have “reputational consequences” for the development. “It can affect property values, business confidence, tourism, investment decisions and the willingness of people to live and work there,” added Sundramoorthy, who is with Universiti Sains Malaysia. For some residents, the recent police raids have raised concerns about crime. Muhammad Aidi Rashid, who rents a two-bedroom flat at Ataraxia Park on the southwestern part of the development, installed closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras outside his door and additional locks after hearing of alleged scam operations in neighbouring blocks. “I worry for the safety of my wife because she is alone at home when I’m at work,” said Aidi, 33, a technician at nearby Tanjung Pelepas port. Property agent Aqil Amran, who manages Forest City flats through local firm Ceiloz Realty, said his company has encountered suspected scam operations involving tenants even after the police crackdown. In one case, a flat owner became suspicious after a tenant’s electricity bill exceeded 1,000 ringgit a month. “When we went down to the unit to do checks, we saw many tech devices for [alleged] scam activity and we terminated the rental contract and chased the tenant out,” Aqil said, adding that the case was referred to the police. Sundramoorthy said Forest City’s sizeable number of vacant residential and commercial properties could make it vulnerable to such operations. Based on figures provided by Country Garden in 2023, 9,000 people were living in the development across 28,000 residential units. “It can provide opportunities for illicit operators to rent premises without immediately attracting attention,” Sundramoorthy said. Forest City’s location about 10km (6 miles) from the Tuas Second Link and proximity to Singapore could also be attractive to transnational criminal networks, he added, given that the city state is a global air hub. The July raids underscored the cross-border nature of such operations: police said 332 of the 335 people arrested were foreigners, most of them Chinese nationals, and their targets included people beyond Malaysia’s borders. Not all of Forest City’s recent controversies have involved alleged criminal activity. Network School was closed over licensing and premises-use breaches, but Johor-based property consultant Samuel Tan said the episode nevertheless “dealt a blow to Forest City’s public image”. “In the short term, [both Network School and the scam raids] have naturally heightened buyer and tenant circumspection,” said Tan, CEO of Olive Tree Property Consultants. “Retail investors and prospective occupiers are understandably cautious, leading to a temporary chilling effect on casual inquiries and rental momentum.” Before the controversies, Forest City was already seeing weakening prices and thin transaction volumes. According to property transaction service Datanah, Forest City’s median transaction price between June 2025 and June 2026 was 547 ringgit per sq ft, down 12 per cent from the preceding 12 months. It recorded only 13 sales between June 2025 and June 2026 in a development with at least 28,000 residential units. Its latest recorded transaction was on June 18, before the scam raids and Network School saga. However, experts cautioned that transaction data can lag and there is not enough evidence to attribute the subsequent absence of recorded sales to the controversies. Forest City’s property market has already struggled for years. According to Tan, its residential and commercial properties have historically traded at a discount to the wider Johor Bahru market. A three-bedroom Forest City flat is currently valued at around 550,000 ringgit, compared with upwards of 1 million ringgit in Johor Bahru, according to Aqil. “Because much of its organic residential demand was already subdued, the reputational hit has manifested more as headline noise than a catastrophic collapse in core asset values,” Tan said. But expectations had been growing that the SFZ and wider Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) could improve Forest City’s fortunes this year, he added. The development remains firmly a buyer’s market. “On sales especially, demand has been low because there are many owners looking to sell, but there are not many buyers,” Aqil said. Commercial property owners are feeling another consequence of the recent controversies: greater scrutiny. Singaporean Justin Ong, 59, who owns a Forest City shoplot for investment, said the management and local authorities have been asking businesses for permits, documentation and proper tenancy agreements following the Network School episode. Ong is currently renting his shoplot out to a food stall operator on an informal basis and now needs to draw up legal paperwork for submission. “It makes things cumbersome and businesses will be more wary [of moving operations to Forest City],” he said. “It also adds a layer of administrative work that was previously not required.” Tan, however, said tighter checks could ultimately benefit Forest City. “Legitimate financial institutions, family offices and corporate tenants require a well-regulated, clean jurisdiction,” he said. “Enforcing strict permit protocols signals to the market that the authorities are serious about governance.” CNA has asked master developer Country Garden about Forest City’s current occupancy rate and whether it has seen recent changes in residential or commercial demand. CNA has also asked Country Garden and the Johor police about measures to detect and deter illegal activity, and the latter for statistics on crimes reported in Forest City. Despite the recent bad press, some property owners remain optimistic. Singaporean investor Tan Kin Lian, who owns two Forest City flats, said the recent episodes have had little impact on residents’ everyday lives. “Even if these [operations] occupy some of the residential units, they don’t bother the other residents. Now that they are gone, I think life will continue as before,” he said. He acknowledged that his Forest City properties have declined in value over the years, but believes their relatively low prices and the opportunities created by the SFZ and the JS-SEZ leave room for growth. “The prices of property in Forest City as compared to that in Singapore are roughly eight times [less], so for Singaporeans, if you’re keen on purchasing a second home and don’t want to pay too much money … it’s an inexpensive option,” he said. Country Garden has publicly backed the police crackdown and called for a permanent police presence in Forest City. Munira Mustaffa, executive director of security consultancy Chasseur Group, said this could deter crime but would not address the underlying conditions that allow illicit operations to take root. Residential areas in Forest City can be accessed by registered owners and tenants using access cards and there are security guards at every entrance. However, Munira noted that this protocol has not been sufficient in deterring scam operations. The authorities and developers should also improve control of its access and surveillance, engage the community and find legitimate uses for vacant spaces, Munira said. Sundramoorthy suggested a broader framework involving the police, immigration and customs authorities, the local council and Forest City’s management. Property owners and agents could also flag warning signs such as unusually high electricity consumption, frequent short-term occupancy or excessive numbers of occupants, he said. Amid the negative publicity, there have been some promising signs. Besides the hundreds of investor inquiries about the SFZ through the Invest Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor, Malaysian entrepreneur Jeff Yew in August reportedly proposed reviving the former Network School site as a technology campus with a “Malaysia first” approach. “These are indeed substantive reasons for cautious optimism,” Tan said. Shedding the “ghost town” label will ultimately require legitimate businesses, jobs and people willing to live and work in Forest City for the long term, he added. For residents such as Aidi, a sense of security is the starting point. “Hopefully if people feel safe, the right businesses will open and the community will be more vibrant,” he said. This story was first published by CNA

title: Toxic online scrutiny affecting China table tennis star Wang Chuqin, former player says
description: World No 1 admits he is ‘gradually losing the feeling of enjoying and loving the court’ after defeat in Asian Games singles final.
content: Former China table tennis player Cheng Jingqi has warned that toxic online scrutiny is affecting Wang Chuqin and damaging the team, with the world No 1 admitting he is “losing the feeling of loving the court”. Wang lost 4-0 to 21-year-old compatriot Lin Shidong in the men’s singles table tennis final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday, with news of the defeat attracting over 6,000 comments and 18,000 likes on Chinese social media within two minutes. The comment section of the post announcing Wang’s silver medal was flooded with fans supporting the player alongside harsh criticism of his performance. Wang is currently the top ranked player in men’s singles, while Lin is ranked world No 8. In their four meetings before the final, Wang held a 3-1 advantage. Lin claimed a 11-5, 11-8, 13-11, 11-5 victory, securing his third gold medal of the Games. Serving as a guest commentator during the broadcast, Cheng said the public discourse was wearing Wang down. “An atmosphere has formed where he seems unable to lose, and if he wins, it is taken for granted. I think this public discourse is very unfriendly to him. Sometimes, even in matches he didn’t play in, he gets blamed if the team loses,” Cheng said. Cheng also said the public should treat athletes better, noting they had done nothing wrong by losing a match. “Such public pressure has already cost us an outstanding athlete [Fan Zhendong], which is why we are in such a passive position today,” he said. “If this constant drain continues and another capable player leaves, we don’t know what we will face in the future.” He urged fans to reflect on their behaviour and protect the sport together. Speaking to reporters after the match, Wang said Lin deserved the title. “He broke out of his slump. His breakthrough will be a huge help to the Chinese team going forward, and it marks a new starting point for him,” Wang said. Addressing his own form, Wang admitted he was struggling. “Playing table tennis now feels like a constant drain. I don’t know why I keep feeling exhausted. Since the world championships and the World Cup, I haven’t been able to find my rhythm, and I’m gradually losing the feeling of enjoying and loving the court,” Wang said. Lin was the only Chinese player to enter four events – men’s singles, men’s doubles, team and mixed doubles – reaching all four finals and collecting two gold medals and one silver before the singles final. The 26-year-old Wang, who competed in three events, hinted that this could be his last Asian Games. “I feel my table tennis career might just follow a spiral path like this,” he said. Wang’s long-time mixed doubles partner Sun Yingsha, born in the same year, also suggested the Nagoya Games could be her last, remarking that waiting five years for the next edition felt “a bit long”. The Asian Games will move to odd-numbered years after Japan, starting with the 2031 edition in Doha. Sun made the comment after losing 4-2 to Wang Manyu in the women’s singles final on Sunday.

title: Beijing and Berlin ‘exchanged opinions’ amid reported plan to shut China out of EU market
description: Days before crucial talks with Brussels, China’s Commerce Minister video calls his German counterpart to discuss trade relations.
content: Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao held a video call with German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche on Monday, just over a week before the next round of trade talks between Beijing and Brussels, amid reports that Germany and France are pushing for a new tool that would enable the EU to swiftly shut China out of the European market. Wang and Reiche “exchanged opinions on the Sino-German and Sino-European economic and trade relations”, according to a short statement published by the Chinese side on Monday. The German side has yet to release a statement, and did not reply to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment. The call came 10 days before Wang was expected to meet with his European counterpart Maros Sefcovic in Beijing on October 8 for the second round of China-EU trade talks. Sources from the Chinese side have described discussions as “difficult” and the team is likely to forfeit its national day holiday, which runs from October 1 to 7, in preparation for the talks, a source familiar with the matter told the SCMP. The call also came during reportedly intensifying preparation from the European side as well. Spanish media outlet Dossier Bruselas reported on Monday that Paris and Berlin were finishing a plan to reform the EU’s Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI). The ACI, also known as the “trade bazooka”, would enable Brussels to apply a wide range of retaliatory measures, including tariffs, quotas, export controls and market exclusions. The instrument needs a qualified majority of the bloc’s member states states to be triggered. The proposed reform will flip that requirement on its head: the European Commission would be able to activate the tool unless member states opposed to the measure could assemble a qualified majority to block it, according to Dossier Bruselas. The outlet also reported that Paris and Berlin planned to send it to EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the EU summit on October 15. The Elysee Palace and the German Federal Press and Information Office did not immediately reply to the SCMP’s request for confirmation. While their government was reportedly sharpening its tools for the talks, some German businesses have reportedly been preparing for the worst-case scenario. Politico reported last week that some German companies were “panicking” and “stockpiling” rare earths ahead of the second round of China-EU trade talks, citing a German industry official, in case the negotiation broke down and Brussels’ push to rebalance trade would trigger retaliation from Beijing. The German ministry of economic affairs declined to comment on the report.

title: Just 0.5% of nurses trained outside Hong Kong, authorities say amid hiring row
description: Dispute began after radio show caller said ‘unwritten rule’ reserved some Hospital Authority recruitment spots for mainland Chinese nurses.
content: Less than 0.5 per cent of registered Hong Kong nurses received their training outside the city, while 99.8 per cent of those working in public hospitals are locally trained, health authorities have said amid a growing row with a trade union over employment concerns. The latest figures were released on Tuesday after the city’s health minister repeatedly rejected claims that authorities had favoured mainland Chinese nurses over local candidates. On Saturday, the Association of Hong Kong Nursing Staff issued five demands, including a call to prioritise the hiring of local graduates. A government spokesman said the number of non-locally trained registered nurses admitted to Hong Kong through limited and special registration pathways was “very small” as of the end of last year, accounting for “less than 0.5 per cent” of all registered nurses. “About 99.8 per cent of registered nurses serving in the Hospital Authority are locally trained, reflecting that locally trained nurses remain the backbone of the public healthcare system,” he said. The spokesman added that about 50 non-locally trained registered nurses were serving in public hospitals, accounting for less than 0.2 per cent of the authority’s nursing workforce. Some private hospitals had also encountered difficulties recruiting nurses, the spokesman said, citing one facility that had 40 vacancies but received only 25 applications. The spokesman urged all sectors of the community to discuss healthcare manpower development “on the basis of facts and data”. On September 17, one day after the release of the policy address, two residents told Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu during a radio phone-in programme that they were struggling to find work. One caller, who described himself as a disciplined services psychiatric nurse on pre-retirement leave, referred to an “unwritten rule” under which the authority reserved a proportion of its recruitment quotas for mainland nurses. He added that his daughter, who had studied the same subject, had been unable to find a job after graduating. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau has sought to clarify the situation on several occasions. On Friday, he told a radio programme that the authority had hired 95 per cent of local applicants for nursing positions over the previous year. Lo said about 3,500 fresh graduates had registered as nurses, but only 2,500 had applied for authority vacancies. He attributed the gap to some graduates choosing not to apply for public hospital jobs, while acknowledging the difficulties associated with shift work and overnight duties. The following day, the Association of Hong Kong Nursing Staff issued five key stance points on social media, expressing concern about the employment prospects of newly graduated nurses. In addition to calling for a suspension of the admission of non-local nurses through special or limited registration routes, the association urged the government to improve nurse-to-patient ratios and advance primary healthcare reform. Appearing on another radio programme on Sunday, Lo reiterated his rejection of the claim that “nursing graduation equals unemployment”, dismissing reports of insufficient public-sector vacancies as a “rumour”. The psychiatric nurse who raised the difficulties faced in finding jobs with the city’s leader clarified on a radio show on Tuesday that he did not belong to any trade union and was not trying to criticise his mainland colleagues. He said he felt affronted by an earlier claim from non-official Executive Council member Tommy Cheung Yu-yan that the callers might be trade union members posing as ordinary residents during the phone-in session. On the same day, an authority representative disclosed the latest nurse recruitment figures, noting that about 3,000 job applications were received from newly graduated nurses this year, with around 2,200 offer letters issued in the first phase. Dr Danny Tong Wah-kun, the authority’s chief manager of nursing, said it had never absorbed all Hong Kong nursing graduates, citing “huge demand” from private hospitals and residential care homes.

title: Review | Violin virtuoso Kevin Zhu joins Hong Kong Sinfonietta for an evening full of Spanish flair
description: A seductive performance of Edouard Lalo’s Symphonie Espagnole was bookended by works by Beethoven and Adrian Wong.
content: Georges Bizet’s Carmen is not the only 19th century piece of music crammed with Spanish flair and flavour. A month before the March 1875 premiere of Bizet’s southern Spain-set opera came fellow French composer Edouard Lalo’s Symphonie Espagnole – a brilliant five-movement fiesta for violin and orchestra written for the legendary Spanish violinist, conductor and composer Pablo de Sarasate. Seduction was the word du jour for Hong Kong Sinfonietta’s concert centrepiece on September 26, when American violinist Kevin Zhu wowed as the veritable maestro del toreo, wielding his fearless technique, polished sound and natural musicality like a bullfighter’s cape. Zhu, 25, made sul G playing (high on the G string) – and the huge register leaps and flying up-bow staccatos along the way – look easy. But it was not just a show of pyrotechnical wizardry from the 2018 Paganini Competition first prize winner. Zhu’s musicianship, belying his years, was thoughtful and tasteful as he contrasted his brighter sound palette with a silky, subdued quality in Symphonie Espagnole’s more reflective passages, especially in the andante, the work’s only slow movement. Alert to Zhu’s whims and subtle usage of micro-rubato, the Sinfonietta and its musical director, Christoph Poppen (an accomplished violinist himself), were as attentive and agile in their accompanying roles as they were united in joyous tutti outbursts. To temper all that excitement, Zhu’s first encore was an intimate and insightful rendition of the A minor andante from Bach’s unaccompanied sonata, which worked as balm for the soul. But before Symphonie Espagnole, the concert opened with the Asian premiere of Space Jump!, Philadelphia-based Hong Kong composer Adrian Wong’s piece inspired by Austrian skydiver Felix Baumgartner’s 39km (24-mile) free fall from a helium balloon in 2012. Written for Philadelphia’s Curtis Symphony Orchestra, this revised double-wind version, commissioned by Hong Kong Sinfonietta, evokes the adrenaline rush leading up to the record-breaking free fall from the stratosphere. The orchestra captured the sense of exhilaration with tight, busy polyrhythms and syncopation. The brass and the trombones particularly impressed with their full-sounding chorales that developed into a soaring, almost cinematic theme, helping to make the piece engaging and dramatic in line with Wong’s musical credo. After the interval came Beethoven’s Symphony No 8 in F, Op 93. The “little symphony in F”, as Beethoven often affectionately called it, is possibly the German composer’s most experimental and one of the quirkiest and most compelling symphonies of the 19th century. Under Poppen’s direction, the Sinfonietta punctuated the symphony’s elements of surprise and relished all the loose ends that Beethoven deliberately left untied. The orchestra’s spirited opening, which begins with more of a closing gesture, boded well. Taut upper-string articulation was guided by long-serving Australian concertmaster James Cuddeford, helping to imbue the opening allegro vivace with an infectious sense of collective swing. The impish, unprecedented allegretto scherzando, which does away with the customary slow movement, saw the winds shine with crisp, metronomic semiquavers for Beethoven’s near-obsessive repetitions. In the tempo di minuetto, Poppen highlighted the movement’s quirky and unpredictable metre and pulse. Its trio saw guest principal cellist Daniel Chiou projecting spiky triplets with authority as first clarinettist Woo Hee-soo charmed with lots of lyrical expression. Poppen kept a tight rein, ensuring that the restless energy never sagged, although the final allegro vivace was too careful in both tempo and character. Though an increased sound presence in the lower strings was noticeable, even more primal rumblings and “ruder” interjections from the cellos and basses would have enhanced the drama of the false pauses and the finale’s barnstorming coda. Add oil, as the locals say. Given the eighth’s rhythmic imagination and harmonic invention, the public’s reaction to such music should, as it must have been in Beethoven’s day, be one of complete bewilderment.

title: US forces set to complete withdrawal from Iraq after 2 decades
description: Departure from Iraq bases seen as a boost to Iran and its allies, even as Washington wages war against Tehran.
content: US forces are set ⁠to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war. Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal – agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran – could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other US enemies to stage a comeback, including Islamic State. “Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition’s departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a ‌counterweight to Tehran’s influence in Iraq,” said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specialising in studying armed Shiite groups aligned with Iran. He predicted that the pro-Iranian militia groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also “seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making”. Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, described the US withdrawal as “a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and honourable Iraqis, and a crushing defeat for the American project”. “On September 30, we will celebrate the turning of a black page in Iraq’s history and the failure of the occupation to impose its will on our country,” he said. “Iraq has proven that its sovereignty cannot be secured by foreign forces, but by the resistance and the will of its people.” While the eventual departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, those who worry about ⁠the strength of the Iran-backed groups fear the withdrawal is premature. “We believe Iraq is still not fully ready to take over the security file at this time,” Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, once a bastion of anti-American resistance, said. “All Iraqis ‌aspire to full sovereignty, and no Iraqi would dispute that. But I believe that the (US-led coalition) leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear.” American forces invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Sunni Muslim dictator Saddam Hussein, and went on to occupy the country, install a Shiite-led government and fight a years-long counter-insurgency before withdrawing at the end of 2011. They returned less than ‌three years later to help Iraqi forces defeat the Sunni militant group Islamic State in a major war from 2014 to 2017. Around twice as many Americans died in “Operation Iraqi Freedom” as in the parallel war in ⁠Afghanistan, which ended with an abrupt US withdrawal in 2021. In ⁠recent years, Iraq has been the only country to maintain close political and military alliances with both the United States and Iran, which sometimes used Iraqi territory as a proxy battlefield. The United States killed a top Iranian commander, Qassem Soleimani, with a strike on Baghdad Airport in 2020. Iran’s allies repeatedly fired on US bases, ‌sometimes drawing reprisals. In this year’s war against Iran, 7 of the 18 US service members listed as killed were in Iraq, the last an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Arbil in July. Iran, which says its ultimate aim is to force American forces to leave ‌the entire ‌Middle East, casts the US withdrawal from Iraq as a victory for its “axis of resistance” of allied armed groups across the region. “Lasting security will prevail in Iraq” once the Americans leave the country and the region, the deputy chairman of the National Security ‌Commission of Iran’s Parliament, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said on Monday. Iran “welcomes the withdrawal of American troops from Iraq and will undoubtedly support it,” he told Iran’s parliamentary news service. “Resistance groups are currently taking action, sometimes targeting and confronting American troops”. Washington has accused Iran-backed militia groups in ⁠Iraq of playing a role in the wider Middle East conflict by launching attacks on neighbouring countries at the direction of Tehran, most recently hitting a major Saudi oil pipeline this month. The Baghdad government says it is trying to curb their influence. Some Iraqi security officials, both in the federal government and the semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, say the US pull-out also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network. At their height, the fighters occupied a third of Iraq and killed thousands of people, including hundreds they videotaped themselves gunning down inside a former US military base. A lack ‌of US intelligence, logistical support and drones would give Islamic State a ‌chance to regroup, said Kurdish commander Sirwan Barzani. “For more than two weeks, we have noticed movement by (Islamic State) sleeper cells, after it was announced in the general media that there will be an official withdrawal of the international coalition from Iraq by the end of September,” he said. “This has boosted, in my opinion, the morale” of the fighters. Iraqi security forces said a suspected Islamic State cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pull-out. The plot highlighted concerns that the militant group remains capable of exploiting security gaps despite years of military setbacks, said four Iraqi security and army officials. Islamic State “is seeking to send a message that the group is still powerful and capable of launching bloody attacks,” said Colonel Khalid al-Bayati, a senior security official in the strategic oil town of Kirkuk.

title: Japanese firms pull back from China amid geopolitical tensions, supply chain shifts
description: The research found 1,221 new Japanese entrants in China since the last survey in 2024, but that was still less than during Covid-19.
content: The number of Japanese companies operating in China has fallen nearly 30 per cent since its peak in 2012 and is down 22 per cent over the past two years, according to a survey conducted amid prolonged political tensions between Beijing and Tokyo. As of June, 10,118 Japanese enterprises were identified as having a presence in China, the lowest number since 2010, according to a survey and analysis released on Monday by the corporate credit research and business intelligence firm Teikoku Databank. The research also turned up 1,221 new Japanese entrants in China since the last survey in 2024, less than the total during the depressed Covid-19 pandemic years between 2020 and 2022. It identified 4,137 companies that had withdrawn from China or could not be accounted for since the last survey. The Tokyo-based firm drew its findings from a database of about 1.51 million companies, a credit investigation report file containing some 2 million companies and publicly available information. It tracked the activity of Chinese subsidiaries of Japanese firms, their affiliated companies and the establishment of representative offices. The highest recorded number of Japanese companies with a presence in China was 14,394 in 2012, Teikoku Databank said in its latest survey, the ninth in a series. China-Japan relations soured in November last year when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi upset Beijing by suggesting that Tokyo could deploy military forces in the event of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait. China will undoubtedly remain one of the world’s largest and most attractive markets Katsuya Yamamoto, Sasakawa Peace Foundation Since then, direct China-Japan flights, Chinese tourism to Japan and other commercial exchanges have declined after Beijing launched a series of retaliatory measures in response to Takaichi’s remarks. “China will undoubtedly remain one of the world’s largest and most attractive markets,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence programme. However, he added that unless Beijing improved the business environment for foreign enterprises and contributed to “stabilisation of bilateral relations”, Japanese companies were unlikely to expand as they did in previous decades. China has long been prized by Japanese corporations for its huge market and supply-chain integration. More than 40 per cent of Japanese companies operating in China this year were engaged in manufacturing, the largest share of the total, followed by wholesale trade, the survey firm said. Teikoku Databank said that in recent years Japanese investors had run up against a “real estate recession” in China, restrictions on rare earth exports from China, “overproduction issues” and price competition with government-backed Chinese companies. Those factors added to a “deterioration of Japan-China relations”, it said. Teikoku Databank said that some companies were sizing up the “unforeseeable risks of doing business in China”. “The trend of restructuring supply chains by relocating and diversifying bases to Southeast Asian countries such as Vietnam and within Japan is also noticeable, and the declining importance of China as a cheap production base is a factor influencing the reduction or withdrawal of Chinese businesses by small and medium-sized enterprises,” it said.

title: Hong Kong’s IPO revival faces test as 3 new stocks stumble on debut
description: The city’s busiest week for listings since July comes after a mixed third quarter when 14 of 30 new stocks debuted below their offer prices.
content: Hong Kong welcomed four companies to start trading on Tuesday after they raised a combined HK$14.4 billion (US$1.83 billion) – but three opened below their offer prices, adding pressure to an already sluggish month for initial public offerings (IPOs). Automated equipment manufacturer RoboTechnik Intelligent Technology was the largest company to make its debut, having raised HK$5.18 billion, but its shares closed 4.9 per cent lower at HK$414.4 (US$52.82) after dropping as much as 9.8 per cent. Shenzhen Kinwong Electronic, which priced its shares at the top of the marketed range at HK$69.88, plunged as much as 8.1 per cent on its Hong Kong debut after raising HK$5.1 billion, though the stock later recovered those losses and rose 10.2 per cent above its offer price, the best performance among the four. The volatile debuts followed a mixed third quarter for Hong Kong listings. As of September 29, 30 companies had listed in the city during the quarter, including blockbuster IPOs from Zhongji Innolight, Shein and Luxshare, according to the city’s bourse operator. Of those companies, 14 fell below their offer prices on their first trading day while 12 traded more than 20 per cent below their offer prices. The other two companies debuting on Tuesday were Shanghai-listed materials manufacturer Red Avenue New Materials and electric motor supplier Direct Drive Tech. Their shares closed 9.1 per cent lower and 7.4 per cent higher, respectively. Shenzhen Camsense Technologies, a producer of spatial sensors for robotic vacuum cleaners, is set to begin trading on Wednesday after raising HK$680 million. In grey market trading on Tuesday, the stock rose as much as 204 per cent to HK$152, according to Futu Holdings data. The Shenzhen-based firm attracted 158,000 subscription applications, making its public offering 3,551 times oversubscribed, according to people familiar with the matter. Together, the five debuts make this Hong Kong’s busiest week for listings since July when 15 companies started trading within a single week.

title: Malaysia begins sending thousands of Myanmar nationals back to war-torn homeland
description: Rights groups warn returnees face persecution and forced conscription under an opaque deal with Myanmar’s military-backed government.
content: Malaysia began an operation to send nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals back to their war-torn homeland on Tuesday, pressing ahead with a government-to-government repatriation deal despite warnings that returnees could face persecution and forced conscription. The first group of 1,476 is part of an agreement to return 5,000 people held in Malaysian immigration facilities under a programme Kuala Lumpur describes as voluntary, though human rights groups say it lacks adequate safeguards. Those being returned included 1,370 men, 79 women, 20 boys and seven girls, with ages ranging from eight to 60, state news agency Bernama reported, citing Home Ministry deputy secretary general Makhzan Mahyuddin. The detainees, drawn from 14 immigration depots, underwent final health checks and identity verification at a stadium before travelling in 46 buses to the Lumut naval base in Perak state, according to Bernama. This Week in Asia was told that only selected media could cover the operation when it sought access. In a statement on Tuesday, Malaysia’s Home Affairs Ministry confirmed that the first phase had begun, using a list submitted by Myanmar through an official diplomatic note, with three vessels, including a hospital ship, transporting the group. The ministry said the wider programme was based on “the Myanmar government’s agreement to accept them and the consent of the individuals concerned to return voluntarily”. It pledged “firm enforcement action without compromise” to address what it described as a long-standing refugee problem, while insisting that the operation remained humane. “The safety, welfare and interests of Malaysians remain the priority in every action undertaken,” it said. Further returns would depend on the completion of identification, documentation and verification procedures, as well as logistical readiness and coordination between the two countries, the ministry added. It remains unclear whether Rohingya Muslims are among those being returned, despite earlier references by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim regarding the repatriation of members of the persecuted minority. The deportations come amid growing hostility towards Rohingya in Malaysia, where an online petition calling for their removal gathered more than 424,000 signatures by June, prompting rights groups to warn that rising hate speech could spill into violence. Contested consent Mahi Ramakrishnan, founder of refugee advocacy group Beyond Borders Malaysia, said that authorities had excluded the UN refugee agency (UNHCR), the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia and civil society groups from the process. “We don’t really know who is on the list. There has been no verification because this entire exercise … is not transparent or accountable,” she said. Mahi added that her organisation had received reports that many detainees did not want to return, citing the absence of negotiated protections, including citizenship rights for any Rohingya involved. “This is a violation of customary international law, particularly the non-refoulement principle. We are sending them back to the conditions they fled,” she said. Debbie Stothard, founder of regional rights group the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, warned that returnees faced forced conscription, while those suspected of involvement in anti-coup activities risked detention and torture. “None of the countries that have forcibly returned or refouled refugees to Myanmar have been able to secure any access or any transparent monitoring of the safety of returnees,” she said. “We’ve already seen several cases where undocumented Burmese were handed over by Thailand to the military, and these people were forcibly conscripted.” The UNHCR said on September 1 that it was not involved in the programme and that the conflict in Myanmar prevented safe and sustainable returns. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision and take place in conditions of safety and dignity,” the agency told Reuters. Although Malaysia is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention, the UNHCR said customary international law banned all nations from returning people to places where their lives or freedoms were threatened. In a joint statement last week, 166 civil society organisations and over 140 individuals urged Malaysia to halt all deportations pending consultations and an assessment of conditions in Myanmar. “There must first be a halt to the atrocities that pushed refugees out of their country,” the statement read, warning of the threat of forced recruitment by the Myanmar military and rival armed groups. Prime Minister Anwar has defended inviting Myanmar’s military chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia to secure cooperation over returns. “We, following Asean, don’t want direct relations with Myanmar. So who are we supposed to negotiate with?” Anwar said during a recent podcast appearance. Min Aung Hlaing led the 2021 coup that plunged Myanmar into civil war and became president in April after an election dominated by a military-backed party, which the Association of Southeast Asian Nations has not recognised. Myanmar’s foreign ministry has described the operation as help for nationals detained for immigration offences, citing a similar naval transfer from Malaysia in 2021.

title: MTR technician, winner at global vocational competition, will apply insights to job
description: Technician Gordon Tang’s silver medal is among 15 prizes won by Hong Kong team across different fields at WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai.
content: A Hong Kong technician who won a global prize for train repair at an international competition for vocational skills has pledged to apply insights from the competition to his job, as he recalled three days of intense examination to fix railway system faults. Gordon Tang Kwong-tai, 22, an employee of the MTR Corporation for four years, said his participation in the WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai last week was a journey of determination that broadened his horizons as he challenged peers from around the world and went on to win a silver medal in his category. “This competition is quite niche, but I hope to contribute in this field, as well as show my skills in the international arena.
