I hope I can apply the knowledge learned from the competition to my job at the MTR,” Tang told a radio programme on Tuesday. Tang was part of a 41-member Hong Kong team that clinched 15 medals in this year’s competition, marking the city’s largest delegation to date and a record number of accolades at the tournament known as the Olympics for vocational skills. Hong Kong contestants won medals in a wide range of subjects, including concrete construction work, cybersecurity and patisserie and confectionery skills. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin attended the prize presentation ceremony in Shanghai on Sunday. She exchanged views with contestants, praised them for putting in their best efforts and boosting the recognition of vocational education in society. Tang competed in the rail vehicle technology trade category and was the top scorer for the Hong Kong team. He said the biggest challenge was identifying the cause of mechanical faults and maintaining stamina throughout the three days of competition. “What I learned from this competition was that … how I responded in the moment [really mattered] and time management was pivotal,” Tang said. His tasks included checks and repairs on train door systems, pantographs and bogies – both railway components – as well as malfunction checks. Tang said malfunction checks were the most difficult, with contestants having to identify the cause of a fault by considering numerous possibilities, then making the corresponding fix. “Some faults were sneakily elusive. Organisers would paste stickers showing cracks in the nooks and crannies for us to locate them,” he recalled. The technician said he relied mostly on observation and used a flashlight to identify faults at the bottom of train carriages and in welding joints – tasks that were similar to his daily duties. However, such tasks carried additional strain over the three days of competition, which required him to deal with a long list of situations and maintain concentration for a sustained period of time. “On the third day, the task was train door checks, which was my best area. However, after two days of intense competition, my mental state wasn’t ideal and I felt stressed,” Tang said. “By the final task, I told myself that I must persevere and focus on giving my all in [handling] every detail.” Lam Ka-ho, a manager for technical training at the MTR Corp who coached Tang for the competition, earlier said the event could foster young colleagues’ safety awareness and professional ethics. “The key to the competition isn’t only completing the tasks within a time limit, but demonstrating awareness of safety and occupational ethics,” he said. “Speed and accuracy both determine whether one succeeds or fails.” Tang, who graduated from the MTR Corp’s railway technical trainee scheme, had undergone additional training for 18 months to prepare for the competition. During the practice sessions, his employer arranged for Tang to practise checks and repairs on different kinds of train carriages and railway components. He was also sent on multiple training trips to mainland China to exchange knowledge with counterparts and familiarise himself with the tools and scenarios he would eventually face in the competition. Hong Kong’s rate of young people who are not in education, employment or training (NEET) was 6 per cent as of June, with a Legislative Council report in May putting the 2025 figure at 6.3 per cent – nearly double the overall unemployment rate. The city’s current rate is higher than what its regional competitors Singapore and Japan recorded in recent years. According to the Singapore government, the city state’s NEET rate stood at 4.1 per cent in 2024, while an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development report put Japan’s rate at 3.7 per cent in 2023. Observers earlier said that a shrinking demand for junior roles, job market mismatch and comfortable home environments had contributed to Hong Kong’s higher rate and urged authorities to boost training and apprenticeships for youngsters. Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, chairman of the Vocational Training Council since January, previously told the South China Morning Post that the institution’s curriculum was constantly adjusted based on technological developments.

title: One Bangkok flood battle after another as Thai Airways races to clear baggage backlog
description: The carrier has deployed air force personnel to support ground operations at Suvarnabhumi Airport, where about 5,000 bags remain stranded.
content: Standing water ⁠in Thailand’s capital is expected ⁠to clear within three days if there is no additional rainfall, the government has said, as flag carrier Thai Airways struggled to resume regular services following heavy rain and flooding. The ‌cabinet would discuss long-term plans to address flooding and recovery measures on Tuesday, government spokesman Ekkapob Pianpises told a news briefing on Tuesday. Bangkok was hit by around 320mm (12.6 inches) of rain over two to three days last week, nearly as much as the sprawling low-lying city ⁠usually gets in the whole of September. Although Bangkok’s main airports kept ‌running through the weekend rain and flooding, some baggage handling operations at Suvarnabhumi Airport were severely affected, with 69 Thai ‌Air Force personnel called in on Monday to support ground operations of ⁠flag carrier Thai ⁠Airways. Around 5,000 bags from Thai Airways ‌flights remained at Suvarnabhumi Airport and these would ⁠be ⁠cleared ‌within 72 hours, ‌the airline’s ‌CEO Chai ⁠Eamsiri told reporters ⁠on Tuesday. He said the airline planned to cut about ‌30 flights from Bangkok on Tuesday, adding that the reduction in services from the capital would last for at least three days. “Almost 100 per cent of flights over the past two days ⁠were delayed, with fewer than 3 per cent on schedule as operational capacity could not be ‌sustained,” he said. In a statement on social media early on Tuesday, Thai Airways said ‌34 of ‌its flights had been delayed on Monday and baggage from 52 ‌flights between Saturday and Sunday was being delivered to passengers. Tourism and Sports Minister Surasak Phancharoenworakul said Thai Airways’ handling of the disruption had hurt Thailand’s tourism image and called on the finance ministry, its largest shareholder, to convene an urgent board meeting. Some ‌1,267 businesses across ‌40 provinces have been affected by flooding, including 52 factories and 1,162 small and medium enterprises, according to Thailand’s Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa. At least 23 people had been ‌killed across Thailand, including four in Bangkok, due to heavy rains and ⁠floods in 42 provinces ⁠since September 16, the Thai interior ministry said in a statement. Nationwide, economic damage caused by the flooding was estimated at more than US$320 million.

title: China warns Japan over WWII history as business delegation visits Beijing
description: Top diplomat urges Tokyo to learn from historical lessons, in highest-ranking official reception since relations soured in November.
content: China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met Japan’s former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, marking the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year. Analysts, however, cautioned that the high-level reception should not be seen as an opening to a diplomatic thaw. Instead, they viewed the encounter as a calculated exercise by Beijing in selective engagement. Iwaya arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday at the head of a 50-member delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability to bilateral ties amid heightened friction. Meeting Iwaya on Monday, Wang warned that bilateral relations were facing a “severe situation” and had “yet to be normalised” ahead of next year’s 55th anniversary of diplomatic ties, according to a read-out from the Chinese foreign ministry. “A country that challenges its post-war ‘peace constitution’ or attempts to rewrite the history of wartime aggression … cannot face the world, let alone open up a future,” Wang cautioned. Wang also urged Tokyo to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leadership regarding Taiwan as soon as possible. Japan must learn from historical lessons on the 80th anniversary of the Tokyo Trials, established by the Allies to try Japanese war criminals after World War II, he added. Wang is a member of the ruling Communist Party’s elite 24-man Politburo and director of the Central Foreign Affairs Commission office. Iwaya previously travelled to Beijing in December 2024, during his tenure as foreign minister in Shigeru Ishiba’s government. On Tuesday, Iwaya also met Vice-Premier He at the Great Hall of the People, according to Kyodo News. The Japanese mission’s arrival in Beijing closely followed last week’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington, where the two leaders hailed the two countries’ wartime alliance against Japan during World War II. Tokyo has been watching the signs of a stabilising momentum between Beijing and Washington with unease, prompting a 20-minute telephone call on Saturday between Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Iwaya’s visit, as head of the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade, is part of an effort to help break a prolonged bilateral stalemate ignited by Takaichi’s remarks last year about Taiwan. In November, Takaichi told the Japanese parliament that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could permit Japan to respond as part of collective self-defence. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The political fallout from Takaichi’s remarks brought official ministerial exchanges between Beijing and Tokyo to an abrupt halt. On Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry issued a scathing rebuke, accusing Tokyo of “abandoning” bilateral diplomatic agreements. Asked about the “grave difficulties” in relations as the two sides mark 54 years of diplomatic engagement, ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that Takaichi’s Taiwan remarks “openly challenge China’s national sovereignty and renege on both the original spirit of normalising diplomatic ties and Japan’s political commitments to China”. Formal channels blocked The depth of the chill was on display in July when Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reported a brief interaction with Wang on the sidelines of Asean-related meetings in Manila. Beijing swiftly issued an outright denial, insisting no such contact took place. With formal channels blocked, Japanese commercial and parliamentary groups have stepped in to keep communications open. Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said Wang’s reception reflected an upgrade in diplomatic protocol, and that Beijing was beginning to selectively raise its level of engagement with Japan. China was drawing deliberate distinctions between the Takaichi administration’s security posture and the pragmatic interests of companies, friendship organisations, and moderate factions within the ruling party, he added. “For Beijing, the primary function of this meeting is not a thaw, but an occasion to reiterate Beijing’s conditions for normalising China-Japan relations.” Toru Horiuchi, a China-Japan relations expert at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, echoed this view, saying that Iwaya’s visit was a good opportunity for Wang to “reiterate the demand” that Takaichi retract her remarks on Taiwan “if she is serious about promoting better relations”. The ongoing trade association mission, originally scheduled for June, was delayed following the death of its long-time president, former foreign minister Yohei Kono, who met Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing during a similar trade delegation last year. During Monday’s talks, Iwaya acknowledged that current ties were “worrying”. He pledged that the association would honour Kono’s legacy and work to steer relations back to the principles of the four foundational China-Japan political documents. Zhang Yun, a professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Wang’s remarks reflected a hope that Iwaya could carry forward Kono’s legacy, continue contributing to China-Japan ties, and encourage other friendly Japanese figures and groups to contribute to the advancement of bilateral ties. He added that Japan’s current strategy – maintaining cordiality with the US while lacking communication with China – risked leaving it diplomatically compromised. “Out of fear of being bypassed, Takaichi rushes to meet the US beforehand to talk up the China threat, and afterwards hopes to be better informed about what was discussed. This model is unsustainable.” Rather than worrying about being bypassed, it would be better for Tokyo to contemplate how to actually improve relations with Beijing, Zhang said. The Wang-Iwaya meeting builds on a succession of Japanese business and legislative delegations to Beijing. Chinese foreign vice-minister Hua Chunying received an interim four-member mission of the Japanese trade association June, while Lu Kang, a deputy director of the ruling party’s international department, met a bipartisan group of young Japanese parliamentarians in late August. In mid-September, another delegation of young lawmakers from the Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union was received by assistant foreign minister Liu Bin. Meanwhile, with Takaichi showing no signs of retracting her remarks, Horiuchi expressed doubts that the encounter would pave the way for a bilateral leaders’ meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November. “Such a meeting without Japanese concession would be politically risky for Xi,” he observed. In a recent nationwide survey by Japanese media outlet Asahi Shimbun, 57 per cent of respondents were of the view that Takaichi should make efforts to improve ties with China. Among supporters of Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, 58 per cent said an improved relationship with China was necessary.

title: Exclusive | Why is JPMorgan expanding in China? CEO Dimon sees another decade of sharp growth
description: Jamie Dimon’s Hong Kong-to-Washington sprint captures the banking giant’s bet on both sides of the Pacific.
content: JPMorgan Chase, the world’s top bank by market capitalisation, plans to expand hiring and technology investment across mainland China and Hong Kong and is looking to take advantage of the city’s strengthening capital markets as well as its platform for serving companies operating in and out of the Chinese market, according to senior executives. CEO Jamie Dimon said the banking giant’s China-related business, measured by factors including client volume, has grown sharply over the past decade – and would likely continue to rise at a comparable rate. “We bank 300 or 400 companies – Chinese companies in China – and that number has probably doubled in the last 10 years,” the Wall Street veteran said on Wednesday in an exclusive interview during a visit to Hong Kong. “It’s probably gonna double again in the next 10 years.” Dimon first came to Hong Kong about 30 years ago, and he has also travelled to Shanghai several times to chair the bank’s annual China conference. “Every time I drive into Hong Kong, I look at this city and think it’s extraordinary. And most of what I see now wasn’t here when I first came,” the executive said. “They’ve done a really good job,” Dimon added. “This city is free enterprise at its best, driven by smart people who have the ability to act and react.” The New York-born financial leader specifically pointed to Hong Kong’s role in connecting global investors with companies seeking to raise capital. “Capital formation is what ultimately drives productivity,” he said. We educate the world about Chinese companies and the Chinese economy Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase Hong Kong ranked third among the world’s top financial hubs this month in the latest edition of the Global Financial Centres Index and retained its No 1 status in Asia for the fifth straight edition of the twice-yearly report. The city’s first five-year plan for economic and social development, also unveiled this month, included aspirations to “consolidate and enhance” its status as an international financial centre and close the gap with second-ranked London. The city’s capital markets have drawn particular attention in recent years. Amid intensified policy support from Beijing, Hong Kong led global IPO fundraising last year but ceded the top spot to New York this year following the blockbuster debut of SpaceX. In the first eight months of 2026, initial public offering fundraising on Hong Kong’s stock exchange rose 153 per cent from a year earlier to HK$342.4 billion (US$43.65 billion). After his Hong Kong visit on Wednesday, Dimon travelled to Washington on Thursday to attend a state dinner for President Xi Jinping at the White House – a globe-trotting itinerary that underscored the bank’s positioning in the realm of US-China commercial relations. He also noted that his bank was bridging business communities between the two countries. “We educate the world about Chinese companies and the Chinese economy,” he explained. “We bring 3,000 multinationals into China, Greater China, Hong Kong.” Dimon added that the bank’s role in China extends well beyond its local operations. When JPMorgan works with companies in the country, it also helps them expand into international markets – that work, he noted, often takes place outside the region. “A lot of what we do to help those clients doesn’t actually happen here. It happens in markets around the world where they are growing and investing,” he said. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s advantages have also been enhanced as JPMorgan, like many foreign peers, acknowledged the importance of the city’s Stock Connect and Bond Connect schemes in providing access to the mainland market and vice versa. “Hong Kong is a real entry point into the Chinese mainland market,” said Sjoerd Leenart, JPMorgan’s Asia-Pacific CEO. “And obviously, the connect system has allowed for easier access to the equity market and the bond markets. “We also see a lot of Chinese companies going around the world, and they like to do that from Hong Kong … We serve the region from here.” JPMorgan is among the US banks that have received the most business licences in mainland China, including approvals for a wholly owned securities firm, an asset-management company and a locally registered commercial bank. It was one of the 15 foreign financial institutions invited to a Beijing symposium with People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng on September 21 to discuss market access and operations. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that Washington and Beijing also discussed financial services at last week’s high-level trade talks, and that China will review and approve applications from foreign financial institutions, “including those with US capital”, to operate in China. Leenart said the bank’s China headcount had doubled over the past eight years, with business continually expanding. “We’re constantly adding bankers to cover more clients in the mid-cap sector, in the innovation-economy sector, and that is both in Hong Kong and in the Chinese mainland,” he said. “It’s a big part of our Asian business, and it has been growing [annually] at 20 per cent plus for the last few years.”

title: Safeguard the truth and strengthen global reach, John Lee urges Hong Kong media
description: City leader also calls on journalists to remain alert to ‘hidden dangers’ that could disrupt society.
content: Hong Kong’s media should eliminate falsehoods and expand their global reach, the chief executive has said, urging journalists to serve as “spokespeople” for good stories about mainland China and the city. City leader John Lee Ka-chiu on Tuesday outlined his two expectations for the industry in a speech at an event held by the media marking the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. His first expectation was for media workers to safeguard the truth, dispel falsehoods and promote the good, invoking a Chinese idiom that translates as “draining away filth and ushering in fresh water”. “The media is a transmitter of public opinion and a guiding light for people’s sentiments,” Lee said. “Professional news workers must adhere to professional ethics when reporting facts and uphold an objective, fair and impartial approach.” He also urged journalists to remain alert to “hidden dangers” that could disrupt society. “They must remain vigilant at all times against potential risks that could affect social stability, and push society forward through objective and fair reporting,” he said. The city leader’s second expectation was for the media to “serve as spokespeople” and “tell good stories” about the city and the wider nation. He pledged continued government support for local media as they sought to strengthen their international influence and competitiveness by “spreading authentic, good stories of mainland China and Hong Kong wider and further”. “This will allow overseas friends to better understand that today’s China is a source of strength and a stabiliser for global development,” he said. It would also help the world to better understand Hong Kong’s roles as a “superconnector” and “super value-adder”, as well as the opportunities the city offered, benefiting residents, businesses and international investors, Lee added. Lee and his administration have frequently promoted the idea of “telling good Hong Kong stories” since he first used the phrase in his inaugural policy address in 2022. The city leader added that certain external forces had been “deliberately smearing the country and distorting the situation”. He also said the city was a place where people could make their dreams come true, emphasising the need to “present the true picture of Hong Kong to the world”. In the city’s first five-year plan and his latest policy address, Lee expressed renewed support for the local media industry, including efforts to strengthen its global reach. He said on Tuesday that the government would continue to help Hong Kong’s mainstream media expand their networks overseas and tell good stories about the city. The measures for the media align with the latest national five-year plan, which calls for building China’s international discourse and improving communication effectiveness to present a “reliable, admirable and respectable” image of the country. The South China Morning Post previously reported that the initiative would assist local media organisations, including Chinese and English-language outlets, in reaching audiences beyond Hong Kong for a second consecutive year. The industry could provide media services in countries taking part in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, a source said at the time. Going global could create new sources of revenue for media companies and enhance their international profile, but they needed to strengthen their offerings locally and abroad, such as through marketing, public relations, event planning and social media, the source said.

title: Chinese brokerages get in line with Beijing’s crackdown on overseas stock trading
description: Decades-old loophole closes as Orient Securities and Guotai Junan notify customers with trading accounts in Hong Kong of bans on buying.
content: Some securities companies have begun to clean up non-compliant overseas stock trading by mainland Chinese investors following a regulatory crackdown that started months ago with fines on Tiger Brokers and Futu Securities International. Orient Securities’ mainland-based clients that have trading accounts in its Hong Kong unit will be banned from buying stocks and transferring in funds starting on Wednesday, according to a notice to customers seen by the South China Morning Post. Guotai Junan International Holdings, the overseas unit of Shanghai-based Guotai Haitong Securities, issued a similar notice earlier, saying that onshore investors could no longer add stock holdings through their overseas accounts starting this week. Chinese regulators issued informal “window guidance” over the weekend, instructing offshore units of domestic brokerages to enforce bans on buy orders and fund transfers for existing mainland clients, according to people familiar with the matter. Onshore investors seeking to execute buy orders were even required to confirm by phone that they were physically located outside mainland China, one source said. The actions highlight Beijing’s widening campaign to clamp down on trading of overseas stocks outside official channels, as top regulators tighten oversight of capital outflows that they see as adding to China’s financial vulnerability. The China Securities Regulatory Commission penalised Tiger, Futu and Long Bridge Securities for offering access to foreign securities without government licenses in May. The crackdown seeks to close a decades-old loophole that some investors took advantage of to bypass a regulatory hurdle on investing overseas. So far, China has not fully liberalised its capital account, meaning outbound investments by domestic investors are restricted. Onshore investors can get official access to overseas securities only through the Stock Connect programme with the Hong Kong stock exchange and the qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) scheme. But both of these are subject to quotas that fall short of rising demand for asset diversification by local investors. Some QDII funds targeting US stocks persistently trade at substantial premiums to net asset values because of the supply-demand imbalance. Orient Securities’ Hong Kong unit said in its notice that the move was intended to comply with the latest regulatory requirements and promote the development of relevant business in a standardised way. After the designated date, mainland-based clients would only be allowed to close out trading and transfer money out of their accounts, it said. Investors with overseas identities would be required to update related information in their trading accounts to keep normal operational functions in service, it added. Guotai Junan International sent out a preliminary notice on September 14 that it would adjust some services for existing accounts owned by mainland investors and would notify affected clients by email. In addition to the crackdown on overseas trading, Beijing took a slew of additional measures in recent months to scrutinise the pool of offshore assets owned by mainland residents, including a new tax on overseas trusts. These developments are seen as one of the hurdles holding back Hong Kong stocks this year, with the Hang Seng Index underperforming most of its global equity peers. Shares of hotpot chain restaurant operator Haidilao International Holding tumbled earlier this month on speculation that its founder was selling shares to raise funds to pay the new tax. Orient Securities is a Shanghai-based brokerage that started business in 1998, with total assets of 550 billion yuan (US$82 billion) and more than 8,000 staff. The company is listed in both Shanghai and Hong Kong. Guotai Junan International, which was established in 1993, was the first Chinese brokerage to list in Hong Kong. Last month, its controlling shareholder proposed to take the company private to end its 16-year listing status. Additional reporting by Yulu Ao

title: ‘Important and consequential’: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang on US-China AI race, risk management
description: Nvidia declares record US$150 billion buyback alongside announcement of Open Agent Safety Platform.
content: The US and China need to improve communication, work together more closely and more fully embrace technology to stem risks associated with artificial intelligence, the founder of Nvidia said on Monday. “We should recognise that we’re competitors, and competitors are still able to collaborate,” said Jensen Huang, head of the world’s most valuable company, with a market capitalisation of about US$5.5 trillion. “This is such an important and consequential technology. It has the incredible opportunity to do good. And we have to keep it from doing harm. And so we have to do that by collaborating, by talking.” This follows comments by US President Donald Trump before the United Nations General Assembly last week in which he rejected any attempts to subject US technology to international regulatory frameworks or global oversight and subsequent comments over the weekend rejecting any joint US-China AI safety framework. “The US is not going to be putting on brakes for AI,” he told reporters on Saturday. “We are way ahead of China with AI.” The 63-year-old entrepreneur met reporters hours after Nvidia announced authorisation to buy back US$150 billion of its own stock, a global record, and proposed a new software platform to address concerns that AI agents could “go rogue” and operate outside human control. The Taiwanese-American spoke at the Korea Society where he received this year’s Van Fleet Award for contribution to US-South Korea relations. Former recipients include US presidents George H.W. Bush, Jimmy Carter and George W. Bush as well as former South Korean president Kim Dae-jung. On Sunday, The Information reported that China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology was considering allowing China’s largest tech companies to buy Nvidia chips again after blocking them in a bid to bolster China’s tech self-sufficiency and make the country less vulnerable to US export controls. “On the one hand, I think the Chinese government has an interest in providing an opportunity for the Chinese companies to flourish without competition from Nvidia, and so that’s an understandable situation,” Huang said. “On the other hand, it is also important to realise that in the world of AI, compute is revenues … so, without compute capacity, the economy of the digital economy will be suppressed in China. “That’s where the tension is. I don’t know how it’s going to work out, but I think over time, the important thing for our industry is this: we would like to be able to compete globally, and the US administration, President Trump, would like us to be able to compete globally so that the American companies can go deserve its growth, and so we have to go compete for it.” Huang said the answer to AI concerns did not rest in constraining technology but rather in using technology to better control and shape its use, citing automobiles that were far more dangerous 100 years ago but now had airbags, sensors and anti-collision systems. “We need to embrace and we need to accelerate the development of AI technology for safety,” he said. “It’s not just when you think about AI. It’s not just capability, but it’s also AI technology for safety. They go hand in hand.” Earlier in the day, he announced on social media a proposed new industry safeguard. “Today, with over 100 industry partners, we introduced the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform,” Huang wrote on X, adding that the technology would let companies monitor every action undertaken by an AI agent as well as enforce policies. Political analysts say the US president, known for channelling and reacting quickly to public opinion, is out of step with the American public as control over AI becomes an increasingly heated issue leading up to the midterm election on November 3. A poll released last week by PBS News/NPR/Marist found 65 per cent of registered voters opposed the local construction of data centres. “If you want to be poor, have no jobs and watch other countries do great, or other states do great … if we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame,” Trump said earlier this month after calling those who opposed them “stupid people”. Huang conceded that the industry had fallen short in bringing the public along and gaining its support for the need for data centres amid rapid change. “With respect to all the communities and data centres that are cropping up all around it, we really could have done a better job being a guest, a new neighbour, to engage the communities,” he said, dressed in a suit instead of his trademark leather jacket. “Let them know what the plans are and invite them to be part of the success and the prosperity of our industry.” His company’s shares closed at US$228.86, up 1.68 per cent. “Nvidia is a strange company because Nvidia is already the largest company in the world. We’re also still one of the fastest-growing companies in the world, and so it’s unnatural for a company of our size to grow as fast as we are growing,” he told reporters. “As a shareholder, I would encourage you to hang on to your stock. Buy some more. Buy some more. Nvidia is quite inexpensive right now.”

title: Shoppers rejoice, farmers fume as Japan’s rice crisis turns into a surplus
description: ‘I’ve been hearing about quite a few people who plan to give up this year,’ a rice grower says amid excess supply and falling prices.
content: Last year, Japan was flooding its rice market with emergency stockpiles in a bid to mollify voters angered by the soaring price of its staple grain. Now, it has the opposite problem: a glut. That is welcome news for shoppers, but the whiplash is hurting people like Hiroshi Asano, 59, who farms a relatively large 38 hectares (93 acres) of rice fields in Chiba, close to Tokyo. He expects to make a loss this year, and he is worried smaller-scale farmers would not be able to survive. “I’ve been hearing about quite a few people who plan to give up this year,” Asano said, looking out across his windblown fields. The former trucker turned to farming later in life, first taking over his wife’s family fields and then expanding to land abandoned by relatives and neighbours. Extremes of weather, including record rainfall in the past few weeks, rising costs for machinery and lower prices for their products have all added up to insurmountable problems for many in an already shrinking sector. The number of farmers plunged by more than half from 2.4 million in 2000 to less than a million in 2026 as the population aged, according to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestries and Fisheries. About 70 per cent of people whose primary occupation is farming, not including for incorporated businesses, are over 65. Parents are increasingly reluctant to hand their farms down to children who have found other paths in life, Asano said. Japan’s rice producers operate under production guidelines and import restrictions meant to protect them from price slumps and help ensure food security. That means the local market often moves counter to international counterparts – as is the case this year. But the system cracked after an unusually hot summer in 2023 produced the lowest yield in more than 10 years. At the same time, rice demand surged as restaurants filled up after the pandemic and a government warning about a potential earthquake prompted hoarding. Shoppers sometimes struggled to find rice at local supermarkets. As consumer worries threatened to blow up into a crisis, the government for the first time tried to relieve shortages by gradually releasing reserves. But in selling 590,000 tonnes, or about a month’s supply, some think then agriculture minister Shinjiro Koizumi went too far. “Essentially Koizumi did not need to release that much stockpiled rice last year,” Asano said. “People were saying rice was expensive, so they released too much, and now there’s an excess.” On top of that, last year’s harvest exceeded demand after official forecasts failed to predict the extent of the drop in consumption prompted by rising prices, changing eating habits and an ageing population. Rice dropped to about 2,934 yen (US$18.70) for 5kg (11lbs) at supermarkets as of September 20, its lowest in more than two years, according to the agriculture ministry. It had hit a peak of more than 4,400 yen in January. In response, the ministry has announced that it will buy back about 210,000 tonnes of rice to replenish its stockpiles. Yet, even if the government replaces its reserves, prices are likely to keep declining, said Kimio Inagaki, a fellow at Mitsubishi Research Institute who researches farm policy. Asano said the Japan Agricultural Cooperatives, who act as middlemen for many farmers, are paying him less than 15,000 yen per 60 kg of unprocessed rice this year, down from 30,000 yen the previous year. He is trying to add value to his harvest by growing organic rice, processing it and packaging the final product himself. This has enabled him to diversify his buyer base beyond the cooperative to local rice shops and individual clients. Smaller farmers cannot afford to process and package rice themselves, so they are forced to accept the prices they are offered by the cooperative, he said. Of course, consumers are benefiting from cheaper rice and not only at the supermarket, with three convenience store chains announcing reductions to the prices of their popular rice balls. But the government is seeking to stabilise the market. The agriculture ministry has updated its rice forecasting model to incorporate real-time trends, such as population shifts, inbound tourism and milling yields, it said in an email. Under a newly revised food law, officials are also requiring food processors and food service businesses to report inventory and sales data to gain clearer visibility into market distribution. Still, Kunio Nishikawa, a professor at Nihon University who researches agricultural policy, agreed that rice prices will probably keep falling next year, given the extent of the oversupply. He added that the government should offer subsidies to help keep farmers in business, while warning this could be politically difficult. Farmer Asano advocated a government-set price floor for rice at what he calculated is a liveable level of around 20,000 yen for 60kg to help slow the outflow from the sector. He planned to stay in the business, having introduced technology such as drones and brought family members on board. “Now the farm has become this big, I think: If I quit, what are all these other people going to do?” he said. “But if it were just me, I might have given up already.”

title: Bangkok flood disaster, Indonesian victim of fake cash scam: 7 Asia highlights
description: From young Filipinos warming to China to Malaysians’ nettle bed joke, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Bangkok declares flood disaster across city as thousands flee from homes Entire Bangkok neighbourhoods were inundated on Saturday as the city government declared a flood disaster after the worst rains in years overwhelmed the Thai capital, submerging roads, cars and forcing thousands to leave their homes. 2. Siti Hasmah, wife of Malaysia’s Mahathir Mohamad, dies aged 100 Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, the wife of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, died on Monday aged 100. 3. Indonesian arrested in Singapore over fake banknotes was victim of fraud: lawyer The lawyer for an Indonesian businessman arrested in Singapore for allegedly using counterfeit S$10,000 (US$7,830) notes at a casino has said his client was a victim of fraud himself. 4. Why younger Filipinos are warming to China despite maritime tensions Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay. 5. Ukraine’s POW transfer reveal deals propaganda blow to North Korea Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. 6. Malaysians joke about nettle beds to end Negeri Sembilan royal row Malaysians on social media are offering increasingly outlandish solutions to a months-long royal tussle in Negeri Sembilan state, from making rival claimants sleep on a bed of nettles for a week to putting the entire state through Islamic spiritual healing. 7. Japan’s cut-price morgues cash in on legal loopholes as lonely deaths rise Unregulated companies are running a brisk trade across Japan storing and disposing unclaimed corpses, with a recent report revealing how such “cut-price morgues” are cashing in on legal loopholes to discard the nation’s dead.

title: 7 Pokemon experiences in Tokyo to celebrate 30 years of Pikachu and co
description: On top of Tokyo’s regular Pokemon attractions, the city is also holding special events to celebrate the franchise’s 30th anniversary.
content: Thirty years ago, Japanese video game designer Satoshi Tajiri combined round Gashapon capsules from coin-operated toy vending machines with his childhood bug-collecting hobby to create a virtual world where players could explore, catch and trade creatures with special abilities. When he released Pocket Monsters Red and Pocket Monsters Green for the Game Boy handheld game console in February 1996, a global phenomenon was born. Today, the franchise, which officially rebranded as Pokemon in 1998 for its North American and Western release, has expanded across generations of gaming hardware, spawning films, anime series, collectible merchandise and the mobile hit Pokemon Go, which sparked a massive second wave of worldwide fandom. With 2026 marking Pokemon’s 30th anniversary, Tokyo – Tajiri’s childhood home – is celebrating the milestone with an array of citywide events. As the ultimate pilgrimage destination for enthusiasts, the capital has themed cafes, flagship stores, high-concept lounges and dedicated neighbourhoods immersed in all things Pokemon. Here are seven stops around the Japanese capital that any diehard Pokemon collector or curious newcomer to the franchise needs to check out. 1. Legendary Pokemon encounter: Legend research in Nihonbashi and Yaesu While the mobile game Pokemon Go is still sending players outdoors to capture and battle rare Pokemon digitally, visitors can now pose with life-size monsters for Instagram until November 29. To mark the celebrations, the Nihonbashi and Yaesu neighbourhoods in Tokyo have been transformed into an expansive Pokemon hunt. Nineteen life-size Pokemon sculptures are hidden across six key architectural landmarks: Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, Coredo Muromachi 1, 2 and 3, Coredo Muromachi Terrace and Tokyo Midtown Yaesu. Admission is free. 2. Pokemon legend research: Awaken the legendary research report! For a more immersive experience, a ticketed mystery-solving adventure – “Awaken the legendary research report!” – also runs through November 29. Participants collect a mystery kit from Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower for 3,300 yen (US$21) before embarking on a puzzle-solving quest across Nihonbashi and Yaesu. The challenge revolves around decoding an ancient Pokedex file containing cipher codes connected to legendary Pokemon. 2-1-1 Nihonbashi-Muromachi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo 103-0022 3. Pokemon Card Lounge The sophisticated Pokemon Card Lounge opened in 2024. Beyond card sales, the venue hosts regular battle events welcoming seasoned players, beginners and solo visitors alike. Guests can bring their own decks or borrow from the lounge. Entrance starts at 1,650 yen per person for 60 minutes, which includes access to a selection of free drinks and snacks. QFront, 5/F, 21-6 Udagawacho, Shibuya City, Tokyo 4. Hareruya 2 Akihabara Tower Store Akihabara, Tokyo’s vibrant electronics district, remains the global capital for Pokemon Trading Card Game (TCG) collectors. Here, enthusiasts can hunt for rare single cards, Japanese-exclusive editions, sealed booster packs and cards with full-art illustrations. The stand-out is the Hareruya 2 Akihabara Tower Store, Japan’s largest speciality retail outlet dedicated entirely to Pokemon cards. Opened in February, the store occupies a building from the basement to the sixth floor, featuring extensive retail displays and a massive 152-seat arena designed for competitive card tournaments. The building is unmissable, featuring a striking exterior dressed in colourful window panels inspired by the game’s basic energy cards. Inside, an octagonal rotating display – a shape symbolic of harmony and prosperity in Japanese culture – anchors the main floor, while a dramatic golden chandelier displaying encased collectible cards serves as a luxurious visual centrepiece. Ishimaru No 3 Building, 1-2-13 Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo 5. Pokemon Centre Shibuya A premier shopping destination for collectors and gift hunters, Pokemon Centre Shibuya, an official retail flagship, houses an exhaustive selection of merchandise, ranging from plush toys and figurines to stationery, confectionery and trading cards. To prevent reselling, popular new trading card releases and limited-edition items often carry strict per-customer limits. The interior design is equally impressive, anchored by a life-size animatronic Mewtwo resting inside a glowing tank of liquid at the entrance, and sculptures of Pikachu and Fuecoco in the store. In honour of the 30th anniversary, visitors showing an active Pokemon Go account receive a souvenir sticker. 6/F Shibuya Parco, 15-1 Udagawa-cho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo 6. Pokemon Cafe Tokyo Conclude a day of retail exploration with a visit to the Pokemon Cafe for a themed culinary experience. The popular dining spot serves creative dishes and desserts including Pikachu-shaped curry rice, burger buns styled after Snorlax’s cream-coloured tummy, and milk tea topped with an Eevee cookie. Advance online reservations are encouraged, and booking at least a month ahead is strongly recommended due to high demand. Nihombashi Takashimaya S.C. East Building, 5/F, 2-11-2 Nihombashi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo 7. PokePark Kanto Nestled in the lush greenery of Yomiuriland in western Tokyo, PokePark Kanto serves as a crown jewel of Pokemon’s 30th-anniversary celebration. Spanning 2.6 hectares (6.4 acres), this permanent, open-air park that opened in February features two immersive areas: Pokemon Forest, a nature trail where more than 600 lifelike Pokemon hide in the wild, and Sedge Town, a lively hub with stage shows, custom merchandise and themed rides. The park is reached via the scenic Sky Shuttle gondola. Entry requires a reservation pass ranging from 4,700 yen to 7,900 yen. PokePark Kanto, 4015-1 Yanokuchi, Inagi City, Tokyo

title: AMD acquires ‘godmother of AI’ Li Fei-Fei’s start-up as battle with Nvidia intensifies
description: Acquisition gives US chipmaker greater exposure to world-model technology seen as crucial for robotics and physical AI.
content: US chip giant Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) has agreed to acquire World Labs, the artificial intelligence start-up founded by renowned Chinese-American computer scientist Li Fei-Fei, for US$8.2 billion in an all-stock deal, as the company steps up its rivalry with Nvidia. The acquisition, expected to close by the end of this year, would integrate World Labs’ research team and spatial-intelligence model expertise into AMD, according to an announcement on Monday. Li, a Stanford University professor widely known as the “godmother of AI” for creating the groundbreaking ImageNet database, would join AMD as executive vice-president and chief scientist, reporting directly to CEO Lisa Su, the announcement said. Founded in 2024, World Labs specialises in spatial intelligence, developing so-called world models that can perceive, generate and reconstruct 3D environments. The technology is considered increasingly important for robotics and physical AI, where models must interact with the real world rather than simply process text. Earlier this month, the start-up unveiled Atlas, its latest model capable of processing text, images, video and 3D data to generate new views of a scene based on spatial relationships. As our teams worked together, we realised what a natural fit it would be to bring together our AI ecosystem of software and hardware, foundation models and applications Li Fei-Fei, World Labs The US$8.2 billion deal exceeds the roughly US$5 billion valuation World Labs was seeking in a funding round earlier this year, according to a Bloomberg report in January. AMD was an investor in the start-up’s Series B round, and the two companies formed a partnership last year to optimise model training and inference on AMD graphics processing units. “Without having a focused hardware effort, AI is hobbled in efficiency. And scale,” Li wrote in a Substack post announcing the deal. “As our teams worked together, we realised what a natural fit it would be to bring together our AI ecosystem of software and hardware, foundation models and applications.” Su said on AMD’s website that the acquisition would help the company “develop the hardware, software and systems” that would “power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem”. The deal is widely viewed as a challenge to Nvidia, which has developed its Cosmos family of world models and this month agreed to acquire open-source AI platform Hugging Face for US$12.93 billion. Hugging Face serves as a hub for the open-source AI ecosystem, used by more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators, and hosting more than 3 million models. The acquisition gave Nvidia a direct foothold in the software and developer layer of the AI industry, potentially creating a pipeline of customers for its computing hardware as major clients including OpenAI, Meta Platforms and Microsoft develop their own chips. In a sign of the increasingly competitive nature of the sector, AMD was an investor in Hugging Face before Nvidia bought it, while Nvidia participated in World Labs’ US$1 billion funding round in February, according to the companies’ websites.

title: Man who allegedly hid 3 spy cameras in Hong Kong gym changing rooms out on bail
description: Fung Kwok-wang, 34, granted HK$2,000 bail pending further probe into alleged voyeurism at 24/7 Fitness branch in Sha Tin but cannot leave city.
content: A Hong Kong man who allegedly installed pinhole cameras in changing rooms at a branch of a popular gym chain has been released on bail pending further police investigation to identify potential victims. Construction site foreman Fung Kwok-wang, 34, was not required to answer a count of voyeurism during his first appearance at Sha Tin Court on Tuesday, as prosecutors sought an eight-week adjournment for further police inquiries. Acting Principal Magistrate Cheang Kei-hong granted the defendant HK$2,000 (US$255) bail on condition that he remain in Hong Kong, avoid contact with prosecution witnesses and stay away from the 24/7 Fitness branch on Lek Yuen Street in Sha Tin. The case will be heard again on November 25. The fitness centre reported the case to police on Friday after a customer spotted a small camera secured with black tape in the false ceiling of a changing room. Police combed through the premises and seized three pinhole cameras and three 12GB memory cards from three of the four individual unisex changing rooms. Officers subsequently recovered multiple video clips filmed between September 23 and 25. Fung was arrested shortly after 9pm on Sunday. The Sha Tin district investigation team is handling the case. Voyeurism is punishable by up to five years in prison, which is capped at two years when the case is heard by a magistrate.

title: Chinese deep-ocean drilling ship brings home ‘precious’ South China Sea samples
description: Maiden expedition reaches 5,000 metres below the ocean’s surface and more than 850 metres below the sea floor.
content: China’s ocean drilling ship Mengxiang has returned from its first expedition in the South China Sea, where it set a national depth record and obtained basalt core samples that could help to unravel the region’s tectonic history. The 30-day expedition organised by the China Geological Survey tested the operational capabilities of the world’s most powerful deep-ocean drilling ship, according to a report published on Monday by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily. During the voyage operated by the Guangzhou Marine Geological Survey, the ship conducted drilling and sampling at two sites and obtained “a large number of precious core samples and data”, it said. At one site, the ship’s maximum drill depth reached 4,929 metres (16,000 feet) below the ocean’s surface – penetrating 865 metres below the sea floor – setting a national record for scientific drilling, according to the report. The samples, which included a 4.27-metre core of basalt rock, will help researchers understand the formation and spread of the South China Sea, as well as the role that a spreading ridge jump and volcanic eruptions played in restructuring the seabed. The Mengxiang, which means “dream”, was commissioned in November 2024 as China’s first domestically designed deep-ocean drilling vessel. China is the third country, after Japan and the United States, to use a drilling ship to obtain hard rock samples from a deep ocean basin. The US research drilling vessel JOIDES Resolution was retired last year. The Mengxiang can drill to a depth of 11km (seven miles, or 36,000 feet) below the ocean’s surface and one kilometre more than the maximum capacity of the current world record holder for deepest scientific ocean drilling, the Japanese vessel Chikyu. For decades, scientists have been working to drill down into the sea floor to reach the Mohorovicic discontinuity – also known as the Moho – which marks the boundary between the Earth’s crust and mantle. While the Moho lies about 35km to 40km below dry land, it is only between 5km and 7km below the sea floor – after getting past a few kilometres of water – making oceanic drilling the most feasible path to reach it. Scientists hope that the samples recovered from this zone could yield critical insights into our planet, including crust formation, plate tectonics and its evolutionary history. The Mengxiang missions to drill to the Moho beneath the Indian or Pacific seafloors – where the crust is thinner – are expected to start by 2030, according to a letter from researchers at the China Geological Survey published last year in Nature Geoscience. According to the Science and Technology Daily report, preliminary studies on the samples from its first expedition suggest that large-scale volcanic eruptions occurred after a geological event called a spreading ridge jump in the South China Sea. In a ridge jump, an underwater spreading centre – a place on the ocean floor where tectonic plates pull apart and magma forms new crust – abandons its position to reopen at a new one. The findings provide crucial evidence that could resolve long-standing questions about how the ocean basin formed and evolved. Drilling at depths of around 800 metres below the seabed also uncovered rare structural features, such as alternating layers of red and green sediment, which could offer insight into ancient marine environments, the report said. The vessel’s coring system was tested and proved to meet the standards of the long-running International Ocean Discovery Programme of marine research that used deep-ocean vessels and platforms to study sediment and rocks. title: Hong Kong’s bruising WXV Challenger part of journey to becoming ‘force on world stage’
description: Women’s 15s team dealt salutary lessons in home tournament, but city coach and players identify gains before World Cup quest.
content: As the dust settles on their intense and increasingly fraught home WXV Challenger campaign, Hong Kong have begun absorbing the salutary lessons they received over what it will take to fulfil their goal of becoming “a force on the world stage”. After beginning with a gutsy, if slightly fortunate, win over Brazil, the city team were flattened by eventual champions Fiji in their second match. Favourites going into their closing fixture on Saturday against Samoa, they trailed from the second minute and lost 34-17. Tumua Ioane, the lead coach, said a rare opportunity for unbroken training and competition had made for a “fantastic on-and-off field experience”. Equally, after “having the eyes of the world on us” over three weeks when his squad “put in a lot of hard work and showed how good they can be”, Ioane acknowledged that Hong Kong needed to become more professional. “In terms of the programme, [we need to determine] how we can get more access to the players,” Ioane said. “Lots of them are giving time and effort to working or studying. Much of the improvement needed to come in understanding the game, Ioane said, pointing to the mental part as where he would “like to continue to work and see more growth”. World Cup qualification will be on the line in next year’s Asian Rugby Championship (ARC), although to qualify, Hong Kong will need a notable improvement on this year’s edition, where they were routed by Japan and drew with Kazakhstan. Should they reach the 2029 Australian tournament, they would have two years to mould a squad capable of avoiding the fate of their 2017 predecessors, whose 121-0 crushing by New Zealand, following a 98-0 loss to Canada, led The Guardian newspaper to conclude that the mismatch did “women’s rugby no favours”. Estimating that Hong Kong used “close to 60 players” across their Asian and Challenger campaigns, Ioane drew encouragement from a steadily deepening pool. He handed out four debuts over the three Challenger matches alone. “There’s some good young talent out there,” Ioane said. “It’s just being able to give them exposure to this level, where they learn from the senior players as well as the coaches.” Hong Kong’s rolling maul was almost exclusively responsible for their last-gasp victory over world No 25 team Brazil. They had some joy using the tactic against Fiji, and it was responsible for another pair of Tanya Dhar scores in the Samoa loss. Also a PE teacher and head coach of the girls’ section at her club, Valley, Dhar finished with five tries for the tournament. “[The challenger] exposed us to so much more than we’re used to … the experience was invaluable and it’s going to make us better,” the 26-year-old said, adding that a domestic league featuring growing numbers of foreigners and more highly qualified coaches had “made a huge difference”. “I think Hong Kong is doing really well,” Dhar said. “The Premiership is completely different from when I started at 16. You don’t just run through people any more, and you feel it the next day. We’re a little city, but we’re definitely on the right track.” Having imports breathing down her neck at club level has “pushed me to be way better than I was”, while Ioane said “international signings raise the level of the competition”. Nonetheless, he cautioned that “we need to find a sweet spot for the positions we’re bringing in”. “Our No 9s, 10s and front rowers are really important and we have to make sure we get exposure in the key positions,” Ioane added. The Kiwi bluntly said he was “out-coached” on Saturday by Bella Milo, the Samoa head coach who was in charge of the city women for their ARC matches in May. “Hong Kong have created a good mix of locals playing at home and players gaining experience overseas, then bringing that back, which is awesome for women’s rugby here,” Milo said. Milo’s team were unarguably the Challenger's greatest enigma. Abject in a 70-0 drubbing by the Netherlands, and not much better going down 61-21 to Spain, they finally found something of their powerful and purposeful selves against Hong Kong. Still, the tournament, staged at Kai Tak Youth Sports Ground, had a slightly unsatisfactory end when Spain’s meeting with Brazil was scrubbed after scorching temperatures caused earlier kick-off delays. Fiji beat the Netherlands 20-17 in their closing match to claim the title, with the Dutch in second and Spain third. Samoa’s belated victory was not enough to keep them off the foot of the table. Hong Kong were fourth and Brazil fifth. “The tournament showed how important it is for us to be on the world stage,” Milo said. “Having three weekends of footy and the improvement we’ve shown was massive.” Chow Mei-nam, the captain for Hong Kong’s 2017 World Cup campaign, and fellow 37-year-old Lee Ka-shun, the city team’s record cap holder and another veteran of the global competition nine years ago, both played their last international games at the weekend. Chow scored Hong Kong’s third and final try in the closing minutes. “It’s time to push through the next generation,” she said. “They have lots of potential … the world stage is waiting for us. Our physicality needs to improve. Other teams look bigger, but we can go for it with our speed. We’re small … but we can chop and stop them. We can also continue to gain more rugby knowledge, then we can play.” Also head coach of Premiership team Gai Wu, Ioane recently committed to three more years in Hong Kong, although he is unclear over his long-term position with the city women. “This time together has been brilliant, because they’ve begun to trust in the work,” Ioane said. “They’ve got to keep believing in that work and continue to move forward with future exposures and tournaments. “If they continue to put the time in and grow in that professionalism space, they’re going to be a force on the world stage.”

title: Shein drops 14% to record low after profit misses in first results since Hong Kong IPO
description: Revenue growth stalls and margins narrow as higher tariffs and freight costs weigh on online fashion retailer.
content: Shares of Shein Global Holdings fell as much as 14 per cent to a record low in Hong Kong on Tuesday after the online fashion retailer posted a 67 per cent drop in second-quarter profit in its first earnings report since listing, warning that tariff headwinds and logistics cost volatility would persist for the rest of the year. The stock sank to as low as HK$30.24 during the day and closed 10.7 per cent down at HK$31.50. Both the intraday and closing prices hit their lowest levels since the company’s debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange on September 1. Shein said in an unaudited filing on Monday that profit for the June quarter slumped to US$228 million, while revenue edged up 1 per cent to US$11 billion. Revenue from Europe and the United States, its largest markets, dropped 14 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively. The declines were partly driven by the removal of customs duty exemptions for low-value goods in both markets. In response, Shein “raised prices and lowered online advertising spending” in Europe, according to the filing. Chairman and CEO Xu Yangtian said in the filing that the first half of 2026 “presented a challenging global consumer environment, shaped by macroeconomic uncertainty, geopolitical complexity and shifting trade policies”. He added that the company expected “the external environment to remain uncertain in the second half of 2026, with tariff headwinds and logistics cost volatility likely to persist”. Despite those challenges, total orders in the first half of 2026 rose 6.4 per cent year on year to 549 million. The company also expected the fourth quarter, which includes Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the Christmas season, to “drive a meaningful uplift in orders”, Xu said in the filing. The quarterly performance came in “more than 10 per cent below the low end of the range” implied by the company’s initial public offering (IPO) prospectus in August, Jefferies analysts including John Chou said in a note on Tuesday. They cited margin pressures and a deteriorating regional revenue mix as challenges. Shein’s second-quarter margin narrowed to 2.1 per cent from 6.2 per cent a year earlier, “primarily driven by a sharp spike in oil prices and freight rates amid Middle East geopolitical tensions”, the company said. It added that it had chosen to absorb the cost increases rather than pass them on to consumers. Jefferies lowered its target price for Shein to HK$23 from HK$26, warning that net profit faced “significant downside risk”. The analysts projected a share price of HK$40 in an “upside scenario”, in which artificial intelligence helped lower the cost of refreshing product offerings while localising supplies outside China replicated the ecosystem in Guangdong, Shein’s biggest supply base. In a downside scenario, the share price could fall to HK$14. Four weeks after its listing, Shein’s shares have tumbled more than 30 per cent below their IPO price of HK$48.56. The company’s market capitalisation stood at about HK$133 billion (US$17 billion) on Tuesday, a fraction of its peak valuation of nearly US$100 billion in 2022, and well below the US$64 billion valuation achieved in its Series D+ funding round in 2023.

title: US prosecutors reopen case of alleged frat house gang rape at Cornell University
description: District attorney plans to file criminal charges against seven men in 2024 fraternity assault case.
content: US prosecutors reopened an investigation Monday into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University following claims the elite college failed to properly punish the men involved. The alleged victim said in a civil lawsuit this month she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students. Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students involved, several of whom were later expelled. The newly-released details of the alleged incident have fuelled allegations that the university was too lenient and reignited a debate over sexual assault on US campuses. Matthew Van Houten, district attorney for Tompkins County in New York, said that he planned to file criminal charges against the seven men. He said his office chose in 2024 not to prosecute because the victim’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent, but had now decided to do so in light of her latest allegations. “I recognise the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them,” Van Houten said in a statement. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence.” Kyle Kimball, vice-president of university relations at Cornell, said the Ivy League school supports the decision to reinvestigate the case. He also rejected a claim, made in the civil lawsuit, that the suspects were offered the opportunity to write essays to mitigate their conduct. “Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Kimball said. The 101-page civil lawsuit filed in New York gives graphic details on the alleged assault of the woman, whose identity is being protected. Notably, it provides a screenshot of a Snapchat group message advertising “free p****” during the incident, apparently an invitation for other fraternity members to take part. The suit seeks financial damages from Cornell and the seven suspects, adding that the woman has suffered “severe emotional and psychological distress”. British actor Florence Pugh has voiced her anger about the case, saying she felt “uneasy and sick and anxious” after hearing about it. “Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world,” she wrote on Instagram. “You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won’t be harmed in return,” Pugh said. Prominent Democratic lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned a “culture of rape” at elite institutions like Cornell. “Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can’t stay in school when something like that happens to you,” Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday. “She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again.” The case is the latest to put a spotlight on sexual-assault claims at universities. Baylor University acknowledged in 2016 that it had fundamentally failed to properly respond to reports of sexual violence. A decade earlier, allegations against members of Duke University’s lacrosse team became a national scandal before prosecutors dropped the charges and North Carolina’s attorney general declared the players innocent. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Letters | Core message of the Trump-Xi summit couldn’t be clearer
description: Readers discuss the Washington meeting between the presidents of the US and China, and the prospects for Hong Kong’s retail sector.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. A pat on the back, ties in matching purple, a three-course state dinner and an ocean of handshakes and smiles: the vibes between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at the White House last week couldn’t have been better. Beyond the widely covered 479-member military display, genuine chemistry played out in the quieter moments: Trump giving Xi a tour of his White House projects and light moments such as Trump calling Xi an “expert on stone”. “You make us feel truly at home,” Xi said when thanking the Trumps for the special arrangements made for the Chinese president’s first state visit to the US since 2015. The details do speak volumes, both in terms of optics and substance. On the policy front, Xi expressed conviction that China and the United States can find a path to avoid repeating the tragic historical cycle of great-power rivalry. “The Thucydides Trap can be overcome,” he declared, offering a firm answer to the question he had posed when hosting Trump in Beijing just four months ago. Xi has long maintained that Beijing and Washington should be partners, not rivals, framing this mindset as the foundational “first button” of China-US relations. Misaligning the first button on a shirt leaves every subsequent button out of place. Beijing uses the metaphor to argue that policy friction over security, trade and technology is merely a downstream symptom of a prior, more fundamental US decision: How does Washington choose to perceive Beijing? At their Beijing summit, both presidents agreed on a shared answer: a constructive relationship of strategic stability. In Washington, Xi went a step further, urging action on both sides to translate that shared vision into a reality where the world’s two largest economies steadily get along. The broader takeaway from Xi’s White House toast is that “making America great again” and making China great again can, and should, coexist. On this visit, Xi paired China’s national rejuvenation with Trump’s signature domestic agenda several times. He had invoked the concept in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025 and repeated it in Beijing in May. He reiterated it upon arriving at Joint Base Andrews for this three-day state visit and doubled down during the state dinner. “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” Xi noted at an arrival ceremony at the White House. These two ambitious goals, he reiterated a day later, can surely be mutually reinforcing. The core message of the Washington summit could not be clearer: China and the US can get along, and choosing cooperation ensures both sides win and win big. Tibby Chen, Beijing Hong Kong’s street-level retail won’t rebound easily Gone are the days when shop owners were wizards whose wands would change the fate of their tenants’ businesses. As documented in my letter, “Skyrocketing rents have driven businesses from Yuen Long” (May 2, 2011), their spells completely dictated whether tenants survived. With rents climbing by nearly 30 per cent – and street-level figures soaring even higher – landlords held absolute control over small businesses, much to my chagrin. The pendulum has dramatically swung. This drama is underpinned by the report, “Hong Kong landlords accuse banks of deepening shop slump with reluctance to lend” (September 7), which reports that shop prices have plummeted by more than 40 per cent since their 2018 peak, catapulting the retail vacancy rate to a 40-year high of 12.5 per cent by late 2025. The reasons for this shift are manifold, the focal one among them being the proliferation of modern shopping complexes, like YOHO Mall in Yuen Long. Before 2015, I routinely parked on the street to patronise local storefronts. Yet, following the progressive opening of YOHO Mall’s various phases, this habit halted; I became a regular visitor to the complex and forthwith ceased frequenting street-level shops altogether. Shop owners have united in the hope of boosting their shops’ value and rent. However, it is more than likely that the situation will not return to its heyday. On the contrary, it may be exacerbated by extreme weather, mercilessly rubbing salt in the wound. Ho Kam-tong, Yuen Long

title: Elderly in-laws arrested in California shooting death of New York Times employee
description: Jonathan McKinsey, slain in a car park, was embroiled in a divorce and custody dispute with the suspects’ daughter.
content: A couple in their late 70s gunned down their son-in-law in a California city park over the weekend, authorities said, and court documents showed the victim had been in a bitter custody dispute with their daughter. Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for The New York Times, was shot to death Saturday afternoon in the car park of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple, who were still near the scene, Dublin Police Services said in a news release. Authorities arrested Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 76 and from Dublin, on suspicion of murder and other charges. They were due to appear in court Wednesday morning. It was not immediately clear if either had obtained a lawyer, and phone numbers listed for their daughter, Candice Jang, were disconnected. The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since about 2012 and had three young children, court records show. Court records show that Jang reported McKinsey to police in 2023, accusing him of shoving one of their children and using rough physical discipline with them generally. Last October, she obtained a domestic violence protection order against McKinsey after he was arrested and charged with misdemeanour child abuse in another case. Police said he acknowledged having slapped one child and also charged him with endangering another. At the time of his killing, he was out on bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion programme, the San Jose Mercury News reported. McKinsey responded to his wife’s court filing by requesting a domestic violence protection order against her and filing for divorce. He since had sought more time with the three children, noting that he had been limited to two hours of supervised visits per week since last autumn, Alameda County court documents show. In his petition for a protection order, McKinsey, who was transgender, alleged that Chen had directed anti-LGBTQ+ slurs at him and at one of their children, the Mercury News reported. He also accused Jang of being abusive during medical procedures related to his transition. McKinsey joined The New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

title: China asks local governments to ‘intensify’ policy tweaks to boost consumption
description: Premier Li Qiang calls for more policy experimentation as retail sales remain weak, rising by just 0.4 per cent in August.
content: China’s Premier Li Qiang chaired a State Council executive meeting on Monday that called for a series of policies to strengthen support for the economy, including encouraging local governments, where conditions allow, to pilot measures to boost consumption. “In response to emerging challenges in the economy’s operation, efforts should be made to intensify countercyclical adjustment of macro policies and promote innovation-driven, high-quality and sound economic development,” according to a statement published after the meeting. The central government will continue to study and stockpile measures to boost demand, plan more levers with strong knock-on effects, improve supporting measures and encourage localities to pilot them first where possible, the statement said. Chinese domestic consumption remained weak despite previous efforts. Retail sales, a key gauge of consumer spending, rose just 0.4 per cent year on year in August, slowing from 0.6 per cent in July, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Economic growth slowed down to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, down from 5 per cent in the first quarter, marking the worst quarterly expansion performance since late 2022. Despite stronger easing rhetoric at the July Politburo meeting, local implementation of planned measures was slow in August, according to a report from Goldman Sachs on Monday. “ … fiscal policy remained a growth drag, and domestic growth momentum stayed subdued,” the report said. The investment bank expected the real GDP growth to be 4.4 per cent in the third quarter. Monday’s meeting discussed how to promote “efficient investment”. It vowed to step up implementation of interest-subsidy policies to expand investment and boost consumption, accelerate the pace of issuing and deploying all categories of bonds and push for major construction projects to start as quickly as possible. It also called for more policies to stabilise the real estate market, promote employment and increase income levels. The meeting pledged to announce a series of “grounded and useful” new policies, optimise fiscal spending and “make good use” of the unused local government debt quota. Incremental policy measures laid out by Li pointed to targeted and measured easing – primarily through fiscal and credit channels – rather than broad-based stimulus, according to the Goldman Sachs report. Meanwhile, significant pressure on local government finances should limit incremental easing to moderate measures, it added. The report also cautioned that tighter tax collection and weak incentives for local officials to launch projects amid intensified anti-corruption efforts and local government leadership reshuffles had been contractionary and may continue to weigh on policy transmission. Some prominent Chinese economists recently urged Beijing to expand central government borrowing and accelerate local debt restructuring, as China’s relatively low price levels offer a rare window for stronger fiscal support to bolster demand. The meeting also called for tighter source control of “new pollutants” such as persistent chemicals, with priority industries to be screened, a rolling list of substances under key control published and a registration system for new chemical substances enforced.
