It also approved draft regulations on public institutions, calling for their supervising bodies to be held accountable and for their public-interest services to be evaluated so that hospitals, schools and other such units stay true to their public mission.

title: 5 things to do over the National Day ‘golden week’ holiday in Hong Kong
description: From fireworks along Victoria Harbour to cycling through the New Territories, here are five suggestions on how to spend the holiday.
content: Hong Kong is set to welcome 1.29 million mainland Chinese visitors over the National Day “golden week” break, fuelling questions online about what locals and tourists can do during the celebrations. On popular mainland social media platform RedNote, many users have recommended a range of activities, such as visiting the countryside, exploring the Unesco Global Geopark in Sai Kung, cycling and watching fireworks. To help tourists and locals alike, the South China Morning Post shares some of the most talked-about itinerary items. 1. Fireworks at Victoria Harbour One of the most popular events being discussed is the National Day fireworks display along Victoria Harbour on October 1. The 23-minute extravaganza will run under the theme “Eternal Radian” and see 31,888 pyrotechnic shells launched from nine firing points on three barges and six floating pontoons from 8pm. All for the tidy sum of about HK$18 million. A RedNote user said he was particularly excited about the fourth and fifth sections of the display, referring to “Dreams in the Starry Galaxy,” set to the tune of Chinese singer Zhang Jie’s The Most Beautiful Sun, and “Love at Home” set to local Cantopop singer Joyce Cheng Yan-yee’s Embrace Love. “The [fourth scene’s] starlight fireworks over Victoria Harbour feels like a reminder: those chasing their dreams are never alone,” the user wrote. 2. Retreat into nature on Po Pin Chau Hong Kong also offers a chance to retreat into the country, with the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung becoming a hotspot for hikers across the border. “If you have one day for nature in Hong Kong, Po Pin Chau is a good place to go,” another RedNote user said, describing it as “a world-class geological wonder” with spectacular hexagonal rock columns. To manage the flow of hikers, the government launched a trial reservation system in August via Klook’s website, app and WeChat mini-programme. The system caps the number of daily visitors at 2,000 on select dates. According to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department’s website, the reservation system will be in place for the mainland’s seven-day National Day break. The department said on Sunday that an average of 2,360 people made reservations each day during the Mid-Autumn Festival extended weekend, while the average daily number of visitors actually stood at about 1,170. 3. National Day Race Day The Hong Kong Jockey Club will hold celebratory horse races at the Sha Tin racecourse on October 1, with free public enclosure entry to mark the occasion. Gates open at 11am, with the first race scheduled for 1pm. The highlight is the HK$4.2 million (US$535,400) G3 National Day Cup Handicap, which will feature some of Hong Kong racing’s best sprinters – Raging Blizzard, Tomodachi Kokoroe and Beauty Waves. The event’s opening ceremony will also feature “China’s three tenors” – Dai Yuqiang, Warren Mok and Wei Song – who will make their first-ever joint appearance to perform a selection of classic songs. 4. Extended Mid-Autumn lanterns show Visitors arriving for National Day will also catch the tail end of the Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival 2026 at Victoria Park, with the popular intangible cultural heritage event extended by a week to October 4. Themed “A Delightful Journey through the Lantern Garden”, this year's Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival features lanterns depicting local delicacies and a corridor of heart-shaped arches depicting scenes of daily life in Hong Kong. The event also features paper-crafted lantern displays showing rabbits embracing a giant moon, and other scenes. 5. Cycling from Sha Tin to Tai Mei Tuk The Sha Tin-to-Tai Mei Tuk cycling route is another golden week staple for outdoor enthusiasts. One RedNote user recommended a roughly 22km (13.7-mile) route that starts near the Shing Mun River in Sha Tin and follows the cycle lane along the Tolo Harbour coastline, Pak Shek Kok and Tai Po Waterfront Park before ending at Tai Mei Tuk. “The cycling path unfolds slowly, and when the weather is good, riding with the sea breeze is genuinely so relaxing,” the user said. “You can ride all the way to Tai Mei Tuk, and almost the whole way there is open scenery.”

title: China outlines 2030 solid-state battery road map to extend global EV dominance
description: The push comes after China’s battery industry has established an early global advantage but continues to face structural challenges.
content: China has set a goal to achieve initial volume production of solid-state batteries by 2030 – a next-generation technology still in the early stages of commercialisation – as the country seeks to extend its global advantage in the battery industry from conventional lithium-ion batteries into emerging technologies. According to a road map for the battery sector released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Monday, the country aims to accelerate the commercialisation of solid-state batteries by reducing costs, improving battery performance and stability, and developing key materials and manufacturing technologies. “Over the next five years, the new-type battery industry is at a critical window for technological upgrading and we must seize the strategic opportunities presented by technological and industrial innovation,” the ministry said. The push comes as China’s battery industry, after years of rapid expansion, has established an early global advantage, according to MIIT, but continues to face structural challenges, including limited original innovation capacity and supply-demand imbalances in the lithium ion battery sector. Solid-state batteries are widely viewed as a potential next frontier for electric vehicle power systems, offering advantages such as improved safety, higher energy density and better performance under extreme temperatures compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries that rely on liquid or gel electrolytes. The technology remains at an early stage, with such batteries yet to enter large-scale commercial production, partly due to high development and manufacturing costs. A limited number of vehicles, including some premium models from Shanghai-based Nio, currently use semi-solid-state batteries, which combine solid electrolytes with a small proportion of liquid components to improve performance. Industry executives have also said that large-scale adoption would take time. At the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of the New Champions, or “Summer Davos”, in June, Robin Zeng Yuqun, founder and chairman of CATL, said that an inflection point in the solid-state battery sector would not take place until 2030. Meanwhile, Chinese companies are continuing to explore the commercialisation of the technology. Earlier this month, Chery Automobile, China’s largest auto exporter by deliveries, said it would begin testing solid-state batteries next year. Also in early September, BYD said it would release one model with solid-state batteries next year, according to its executive vice-president Stella Li in an interview with Spanish media. Monday’s road map from MIIT also called for early strategic planning for the development of other next-generation batteries, including alkali metal-ion types, multivalent-ion units, and nuclear batteries. Further, the Chinese government aims to promote the application of new battery technologies in products such as smart devices and support the electrification of sectors including automobiles, shipping, aviation and intelligent robots while backing the development of next-generation power systems.

title: China reveals plan to map the entire surface of Mars by 2028 amid race with US
description: It will be the first AI-driven geological map of the planet and aims to be the global standard, chief scientist on Tianwen-3 mission says.
content: China plans to complete a geological map of Mars by the end of 2028, as its space rivalry with the United States intensifies. Hou Zengqian, chief scientist of China’s next Mars mission known as Tianwen-3, on Monday said the map would cover the entire surface of the red planet and it aimed to be the global standard for the Martian geological ages. State news agency Xinhua reported that the map would be the first AI-driven geological map of Mars and would be an important part of preparations for the Tianwen-3 mission. Hou said the map would incorporate findings from Zhu Rong, the first rover China sent to Mars. Those findings include evidence that Mars may have had an intercontinental-scale ancient ocean about 3.5 billion years ago and possible short-term flooding about 1.6 billion years ago. Zhu Rong touched down on the planet in May 2021 as part of the Tianwen-1 mission, making China the second country after the United States to land a rover on Mars. It operated on the Martian surface for nearly a year and travelled over 1.9km (1.18 miles). China’s map project will also produce a detailed 1:50,000 geological map of the Tianwen-3 landing zone and an atlas series, according to the Xinhua report. “It will provide a model for future geological mapping of the moon, Venus and asteroids too,” the report said. China plans to launch the Tianwen-3 mission in late 2028, aiming to collect and return at least 500 grams (1.1 pounds) of Martian samples to Earth by around 2031. If successful, that would make China the first country to complete a Mars sample-return mission. It will involve two launches, with one spacecraft carrying a lander and an ascent vehicle to collect Martian material and another carrying an orbiter and return module to transport the samples back to Earth. Meanwhile, a joint Nasa and European Space Agency Mars sample-return mission has been hit by soaring costs and repeated delays. The Perseverance rover – which has been operating on Mars since February 2021 – has collected and cached several dozen rock and soil samples. Under the original plan, these samples would be retrieved and ferried back to Earth in the 2030s. But Nasa estimated in 2024 that the programme could cost up to US$11 billion and return samples no earlier than 2040. In January, the US Congress effectively terminated the existing programme by cutting its funding due to its hefty price tag and repeated delays. That has resulted in some funds being diverted to a new Mars Future Missions initiative aimed at developing lower-cost technologies, while the architecture and timetable for any future Mars sample-return mission remain uncertain. The US completed its first Mars mission during the Cold War space race with the Soviet Union. Nasa’s Mariner 4 became the first spacecraft to conduct a fly-by of the planet and it sent back close-up images in 1965. That was followed by Nasa’s first Mars landing craft Viking 1 touching down on Mars in 1976. Since the first robotic rover, the Sojourner, reached Mars in 1997, five American rovers have explored the Martian surface, with Curiosity and Perseverance still operating today. China’s inaugural Mars mission, Tianwen-1, was launched in July 2020 and deployed the Zhu Rong rover. Zhu Rong completed its planned 90-Martian-day primary mission and continued operating through May 2022. It then went into a planned winter hibernation but failed to resume operations afterwards. Reports attributed the failure mainly to the heavy dust accumulation on its solar panels that prevented the vehicle from generating enough power.

title: How a Malaysian mother’s love gives her trans daughter refuge
description: Despite fear of religious crackdowns, one family in deeply conservative Kelantan has quietly accepted transgender Muslims.
content:
In Malaysia’s deeply conservative northeastern state of Kelantan, Rozi* has learned to ignore what people say about her daughter, Hana*.
They live in a village on the outskirts of Kota Bharu. Rozi had known for years that Hana was different. As a child, Hana preferred girls’ clothes and spent most of her time with girls. Later, after leaving Kelantan to study, she began transitioning and eventually returned home, living openly as a woman.
Her 58-year-old mother struggled to accept it at first, but what troubled her more was the thought that rejecting Hana might push her out of the family altogether.
“When you see your own child’s face, what mother does not love her child?” Rozi said. “No matter how bad people may think your child is, she is still your child. If I didn’t accept her, she would go further and further away from me. I don’t want her to be far away.”
That acceptance has turned home into a refuge for Hana, at a time when other transgender Muslims in Kelantan say they have had to become increasingly cautious in public.
In Kelantan, 95.5 per cent of the population is Muslim. The state has been governed by the Islamist Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party since 1990, becoming its political stronghold.
The state’s religious laws penalise gender transition and cross-dressing among Muslims. Recent prosecutions have heightened concerns within the local transgender community, who worry about intensifying state scrutiny.
Against that backdrop, Rozi said her initial resistance to her daughter’s transition had gradually given way to a quiet acceptance she once thought unlikely.
Hana, 27, now regularly returns home, joins family gatherings and brings transgender friends over for meals, while her mother happily fusses over the food.
“They are human, too. They want to eat like us, they want to feel loved,” said Rozi, a mother of three who works at a local mosque. “They don’t want to be thrown away by their families.”
Hana began taking hormones around 2019 while living away from Kelantan. By the time she returned, her hair was longer and her appearance had changed enough that her father, picking her up at the station, was taken aback.
“My mother said, ‘Whatever people want to say, let them. Just don’t stop coming home’,” Hana said.
The interior designer dresses more conservatively in Kelantan than she does in Kuala Lumpur, where she occasionally travels for work. She says her mother would object if a friend turned up at the family home in revealing clothing.
Still, Hana is free to be herself at home – a privilege she knows many of her peers do not share. “As long as my family accepts me, that’s enough,” she said. “What outsiders want to say, I don’t really care.”
Hana thinks carefully about what she wears before going out in Kelantan, favouring loose or unisex clothing and understated make-up to avoid drawing the attention of religious enforcement officers.
Most Kelantanese she encountered were not overtly hostile, Hana said. The uglier reactions tended to appear online, where videos circulated rapidly, and social media users tagged religious authorities to demand enforcement action.
Another member of Kelantan’s transgender community shared a similar account, saying that while transgender people could still run shops and deal with customers in daily life, public social spaces had noticeably shrunk.
“Before, [trans] people would still go out to eat, hang out and meet in public. Now it’s very different. People don’t really do that any more, and even when we gather, it’s usually in small groups, maybe four or five people,” the person said, asking not to be named.
“There is fear. Social media is where some of us make money, but at the same time it makes people know where we are and what we are doing.”
In February, local news outlet Malaysiakini reported that Kelantan had recorded its first prosecution under Section 18 of its 2019 sharia criminal code. The law criminalises changing one’s gender and was published in 2020. It was believed to be the first prosecution of its kind in Malaysia.
Then, last month, Kelantan lawmakers unanimously passed a revised sharia criminal offences bill, after Malaysia’s Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the earlier enactment in 2024 for intruding on federal jurisdiction.
The updated law retains strict penalties for Muslims who change their gender, help another person to do so or induce someone to transition without a reason permitted under Islamic law.
On September 8, a 25-year-old transgender person pleaded not guilty in a Kota Bharu sharia court to “posing as a woman” by wearing women’s clothing. The charge carries a maximum fine of 3,000 Malaysian ringgit (HK$5,760), up to two years in prison, or both.
Kelantan’s leaders have taken a hard line. Deputy chief minister Mohamed Fadzli Hassan said last year that the state “does not recognise deviant cultures that go against Islamic teachings”, describing LGBT practices as “a clear transgression of human nature”.
Thilaga Sulathireh, co-founder of the human rights group Justice for Sisters, said the recent cases reflected “a clear clampdown on the visibility of trans people” across the state.
“These laws completely disrupt all areas of a trans person’s life: [their ability] to work, move around freely, socialise and be who they are,” Thilaga said.
Back in their village, Rozi continues to pray for her daughter, viewing matters of faith as something Hana must ultimately answer for herself.
“That is between her and Allah,” she said. “It is not for humans to judge.”
What matters most for her is closer to home.
“As long as my child is safe,” Rozi said, with teary eyes. “She is still my child.”
*Names changed to protect interviewees’ identities

title: Style Edit: Richard Mille welcomes Turkish actress Serenay Sarıkaya to its family
description: Sarıkaya, who joins the Swiss watchmaker as its latest partner, previously won five Golden Butterfly Awards and was named GQ Turkey’s Woman of the Year in 2014.
content: There is a certain freedom in refusing to follow a predetermined path. It is a quality Serenay Sarıkaya has brought to a career that has moved effortlessly between television, film and theatre, and one that now connects her with Richard Mille as the brand’s newest partner. Having entered the industry at just 15, the Turkish actress has built her career by following curiosity rather than convention. Each new role has offered another opportunity to explore unfamiliar territory, from the stage to the screen and, increasingly, projects with an international reach. Her career has earned her five Golden Butterfly Awards, including two best actress honours, as well as recognition from GQ Turkey and the Afife Theatre Awards. More recently, her performance in Aile earned her a PRODU Award for Best Non-Spanish-Speaking Actress. Her association with Richard Mille feels less like a departure than a natural continuation of that mindset. A long-time watch enthusiast, Sarıkaya was already familiar with the maison before the partnership. What resonated with her was its willingness to challenge convention while maintaining a connection to heritage – an attitude she describes as having the courage to create your own rules. That philosophy is reflected in her choice of timepiece: the RM 037 Automatic in white gold with snow-set diamonds. Its technical character and jewellery-like detailing reflect the balance Sarıkaya sees in the brand – strength alongside elegance, sophistication alongside daring, and a sense of rootedness that leaves room for constant evolution. For Richard Mille, the connection is equally about character. “Serenay perfectly embodies the very contemporary spirit of the brand, but it is above all her personality and strong character that truly stood out. She is a woman with a long-term vision for her career, deeply grounded, and for whom family and human values hold a very important place,” says Amanda Mille, brand and partnerships director at Richard Mille. Her ambitions now extend beyond what she has already achieved. Sarıkaya hopes to work on more international films, spend time living abroad and travel the festival circuit, while also developing a film of her own. Through the characters she plays, she hopes to offer others the same encouragement she has drawn from the women who have influenced her: to be brave, take risks and trust what comes next.

title: China wife donates kidney to husband, defying sub 10% match rate for non-blood relatives
description: Abandoned by her parents post-divorce and raised by her grandmother, Liang says she found the love and family she desired with Chung.
content: A young Chinese wife selflessly donated her kidney to her husband suffering from uraemia because she “did not want to lose him,” despite the success rate being less than 10 per cent. In September, Liang, 25, donated her left kidney to her husband, Chung, at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University. Chung, 33, has congenital megaureter, a condition present from birth that involves an abnormally enlarged ureter. He underwent regular treatment for his condition, which progressed into uraemia four years ago. Despite Chung’s illness, Liang married him in January last year and gave birth to their son shortly afterwards. Chung had been on the waiting list for a kidney transplant from a deceased donor for three years; however, doctors indicated that suitable donors for his blood type, O negative, are scarce, and he faced another two to seven years of waiting. Unfortunately, Chung’s health did not permit further delays; he had even been hospitalised for acute heart failure once. It was during this time that Liang decided to donate one of her kidneys to him. “I felt I was losing him. He might not have time to wait for a kidney donation,” Liang said. Dr Zhao Jiqiang from the hospital’s organ transplant department stated that the couple were extremely fortunate to have matched successfully. Liang’s blood type is also O negative. Additionally, a complement-dependent cytotoxicity test showed a negative result, indicating no antibodies that would cause organ rejection in the recipient’s body. The doctor noted that the test could easily have shown a contrary result, especially since Liang had given birth to Chung’s child the previous year. Dr Zhao explained that the success rate of organ transplant between individuals who are not blood relatives is typically only five to 10 per cent. Fortunately, the transplant was a success, and Liang’s kidney is functioning well in Chung’s body. He made a successful recovery and was discharged from the hospital on September 23. Liang remarked afterwards that the surgical experience was “10 times more painful than delivering a baby.” However, she expressed no regret. “As long as my husband gets well, everything will be fine.” Liang shared that her parents favoured her brother and did not want to raise her after their divorce. Consequently, she was raised by her grandmother. She noted that Chung provided her with the love and family she had always desired. “I would have done the same if it were me,” commented one online observer on Liang’s video. “Such a wonderful wife. He should cherish her for life,” remarked another. Some critics disapproved of Liang’s decision, predicting that she would regret it, noting that the bond between husband and wife is not as strong as that between blood relatives. Some even suggested that Chung should not have accepted Liang’s donation if he truly loved her. To this, Liang responded: “We are not just lovers; we are family who will spend our lives together. True love means not rejecting your partner’s goodwill, but embracing it and valuing your body for the rest of your life.” Dr Zhao also observed that it is rare for someone so young to have such a strong will to donate an organ in order to save their partner. Chung stated that he would treat Liang better after his recovery. One of his biggest regrets was not being able to travel with her, and he hopes to take her around the world.

title: Japan enlists royal visit, subsidies to revive tourism in quake-hit Kyushu
description: Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako to visit Kumamoto as the government rolls out travel subsidies to win back visitors following July’s quake.
content: Travel companies in southern Japan are pinning their hopes on a business revival following a planned visit by Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako to the areas hardest hit by a major earthquake this summer. The imperial couple, who were scheduled to meet communities in Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, postponed the trip due to poor weather. On Wednesday, they will speak with families currently living in temporary accommodation after losing their homes and businesses. The prefecture was at the epicentre of the magnitude 7.1 quake that struck Kyushu island on July 28. Local tour operators say that the number of international and domestic visitors to Kyushu fell precipitously following the disaster. While there are signs that domestic tourism is picking up, operators are calling for a campaign to reassure tourists that the region is safe to visit again. Oliver Richardson, a British national working for the non-profit tourism hub Michi-no-Eki Aso, was inside a Costco outlet in Kumamoto city when the earthquake struck. He said the entire building shook violently, causing pallets of goods to fall and block the exits. It took several hours for emergency services to free Richardson and dozens of other shoppers. Nearby, a gas explosion at Aeon Mall Kumamoto caused by the quake killed seven people. Richardson, who is a long-term resident of Japan, went without tap water for three days after the disaster, like thousands of others in the area. Bullet train services were halted immediately after the quake, local rail lines were severely disrupted, bridges were damaged and nearly 7,000 people across the region had to be evacuated. At least 200 people were injured and 36 deaths were reported. Richardson said the disaster would likely affect tourism in Kumamoto and the wider Kyushu region for months to come. “Our region typically attracts a lot of tourists from Taiwan, but everybody just immediately cancelled flights and hotels,” he said. Areas of the city with older wooden buildings were particularly badly affected, he said. “The castle was also damaged again, which is really unfortunate because they have been working on rebuilding sections that were destroyed in the last big quake in 2016,” Richardson said, recalling how powerful aftershocks had followed that earlier earthquake. “People remember that. They were worried the same thing was going to happen again and they chose to stay away.” On September 2, the Mainichi newspaper reported that hotels across Kyushu’s seven prefectures lost 408,500 booked nights to cancellations. In neighbouring Kagoshima prefecture, tourists had cancelled visits despite the lack of damage, said Fuku Ito, assistant manager of the prefecture’s tourism promotion division. “The bullet train link to Kagoshima City was halted, which obviously made it harder for people to visit, but many people cancelled trips because they were worried about the possibility of strong aftershocks,” Ito said. “We issued statements saying there was very little damage and that Kagoshima was safe, but people were still concerned.” Kagoshima Airport typically receives 40 domestic flights a day, alongside international services from Hong Kong, Taiwan, mainland China and Seoul. All flights were initially suspended but have since resumed. Bullet trains were similarly reinstated on September 18. “Japanese [travellers] have been quite quick to come back, but foreign visitors have been slower,” Ito said. “We are hoping that around the New Year and Chinese New Year holidays, more people will come back.” Japan’s central government approved a support package for the region on August 28, allocating 15.1 billion yen (US$95.7 million) to subsidise travel across Kyushu. From Thursday, visitors to Kumamoto and Kagoshima prefectures can take advantage of 60 per cent discounts on accommodation under the scheme, and 50 per cent for the other five prefectures in Kyushu. Package tours with at least two nights in the affected region qualify for discounts of up to 35,000 yen (US$222). “We hope people will visit Kyushu and provide support to the affected areas, both materially and emotionally,” Tourism Minister Yasushi Kaneko said when announcing the subsidies, noting “a succession of cancellations” following the earthquake. Miyazaki prefecture, in southeastern Kyushu, escaped relatively unscathed, according to Satoshi Okumato of the prefectural tourism department. He said the government’s promotion campaign was already bearing fruit with domestic tourists. “Autumn is a good time to visit Kyushu because the tree leaves are changing colour and we see strong demand once again,” he said. “It has been more difficult in other parts of Kyushu, but nothing has changed in Miyazaki.” However, convincing international travellers to return was going to be more challenging, he added. “Places like Hong Kong do not have earthquakes, so people there do not understand what it means and they are frightened,” Okumato said. “We understand that and are trying to get the message across that it is safe to visit.”

title: Opinion | Hong Kong mustn’t miss the boat on the Pinglu Canal and Asean trade
description: The game-changing canal is a physical response to an economic reality: Asia’s growth is becoming more regional and more connected.
content: The official opening of the Pinglu Canal on September 16 is a milestone in modern Chinese history. More than an infrastructural feat, it signals a strategic recalibration of how China’s inland economies connect with the sea and Southeast Asia, and augurs the next phase of regional growth. Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway stretches from the Xijin reservoir in Hengzhou, an emerging city in Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin (known as the Beibu Gulf in China), providing southwestern inland provinces with a shorter and more cost-effective route to global markets. Strategically, it anchors the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a rapidly growing artery that was first conceptualised under the China-Singapore (Chongqing) Connectivity Initiative endorsed in 2015 by President Xi Jinping and Lee Hsien Loong, then prime minister of Singapore. The Belt and Road Initiative has entered a new phase of growth, with a stronger focus on deepening exchanges between specific Chinese provinces and countries with which they share substantial economic complementarities. Southwestern China has become a powerhouse for new energy vehicles, auto parts and the kind of products Southeast Asian economies need in the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. Chongqing’s new energy vehicle industry is gaining momentum, Guizhou is a major centre for lithium battery materials, while Yunnan draws on its hydropower resources to process silicon for photovoltaic panels; Sichuan, meanwhile, is home to one of China’s largest deposits of lithium ore, vital to long-range batteries. Traditionally, goods manufactured in these provincial economies would be routed to faraway eastern ports for export. The canal now provides a significantly faster alternative. Local authorities estimate savings of more than 5 billion yuan (US$744.80 million) annually in logistics expenses. The economic potential extends beyond immediate cost savings: the canal is conducive to expanding the hinterland of the Beibu Gulf and higher-value industrial clusters along the corridor, as well as strengthening the flow of manufactured goods, minerals, agricultural products and energy-related materials between southwestern China and Southeast Asia. The new waterway also connects with the China-Europe Railway Express, the China-Laos Railway and other key networks, offering enhanced transport and logistics connectivity. For manufacturers, the heightened efficiency and lower cost will be a boon. Equally significant are the employment opportunities; the canal created substantial employment during its four-year construction period and is expected to sustain jobs in port operations, warehousing, shipping and ancillary services. Yet the deeper significance lies in the timing. China’s trade with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time in 2025, and continued to gather pace in the first seven months of 2026, rising 24.7 per cent year-on-year to US$744.41 billion. China has remained Asean’s largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while the bloc has been China’s largest trading partner for six years running. The canal is a physical response to an economic reality: Asia’s growth is becoming more regional, more connected and more dependent on efficient corridors for goods, capital and opportunities. Asean’s economic rise is transformative for its population of 693 million and the rest of Asia. For Chinese businesses, Asean provides a sizeable middle-class consumer base; for Asean firms, China provides access to reliable financing, advanced technology, talent and sophisticated supply chains. The Pinglu Canal’s significance for Asean is both immediate and strategic. Speaking at the 23rd China-Asean Expo in Nanning, Asean secretary general Kao Kim Hourn stressed that the canal provides China’s landlocked southwest with a crucial direct gateway to maritime routes, opening up new opportunities for both sides. This complementarity can only deepen, following the signing of the China-Asean Free Trade Area 3.0 upgrade protocol in October 2025, which expands bilateral cooperation into the digital economy and the green economy. Here in Hong Kong, there are plenty of opportunities for us to contribute. Our city’s strengths in project finance, infrastructure bond issuance and green financing can support the ongoing development of canal-adjacent industrial zones and port facilities. Hong Kong’s marine insurance and reinsurance specialists can underwrite cargo moving through the canal, while our legal and arbitration services offer a trusted dispute resolution framework for cross-border commercial agreements. Logistics consultants and trade finance providers all have roles to play in optimising the flow of goods along this new corridor. Asean is one of the most important partners for Hong Kong and its importance will only continue to grow. This was underscored by the signing of the First Protocol to Amend the Investment Agreement between Hong Kong and Asean this month, which ensures non-discriminatory treatment for Hong Kong firms across the 11 Asean member states. The Pinglu Canal provides fresh impetus to the deepening of China-Asean ties through Hong Kong. The work of the relevant sectors would also reinforce the city’s standing as a global hub, superconnector and value-added partner for both China and Asean.

title: Australian firm drops US$842 million Sydney data centre plan after public fury
description: Goodman Group’s Project Mars development was 160 metres from a school, sparking anger from residents and activists.
content: Australian industrial property developer Goodman Group has withdrawn an application to develop a 24-hour data centre on Sydney’s north shore following public push back. Goodman said it would not proceed with its Project Mars development application after considering evolving federal and state policy and community feedback. Policy and regulation around large artificial intelligence data centres had “evolved significantly” since planning began in March 2025, the company said in a statement. The project was worth A$1.2 billion (US$842 million), according to the Australian Financial Review and other media outlets. Australia is undergoing a rapid data centre buildout, attracting investment due to its abundant land and renewable energy potential. The country’s data centre pipeline is worth about A$175 billion, with roughly A$110 billion of that investment likely to occur over the next three years, Westpac Banking senior analyst Pat Bustamante said in a research note this month. Project Mars was planned for the residential suburb of Lane Cove, roughly 20 metres (66 feet) from the nearest home and 160 metres from a public school, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. The proposal drew criticism from residents and activists amid broader concerns about locating data centres near homes. Victoria state recently also banned the construction of data centres in residential areas and said such facilities must “bring their own renewable energy supply”.

title: Alibaba deepens sports tech push with new Brooklyn Nets partnership
description: The Chinese tech titan becomes the NBA team’s official technology and cloud partner and jersey patch sponsor ahead of its 60th anniversary.
content: Alibaba Group Holding has become an official technology and cloud partner of NBA team Brooklyn Nets, as the tech giant pushes for a deeper presence in the sports industry. The collaboration was announced on Monday under a multi-year strategic partnership between Alibaba and Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, the parent company of the basketball team. It would also see Alibaba become Brooklyn Nets’ official jersey patch sponsor ahead of the basketball team’s 60th anniversary season, according to a joint statement by the two parties. Under the deal, Alibaba would leverage its cloud infrastructure to power a new real-time 360-degree replay system at the Barclays Centre in New York City, the home arena of the team, delivering faster and more innovative broadcast replays starting in the upcoming 2026-27 NBA season. The company would also introduce “Nets Figure Lab” – a digital activation allowing attendees to generate personalised collectible cards in the arena using Alibaba’s proprietary technology, the announcement said. “Alibaba has long partnered with leading sports organisations worldwide, giving us a deep understanding of how to deliver technology at the scale and speed live sports demand,” Toby Xu, Alibaba’s chief financial officer, said in a statement on Monday. Brooklyn Nets and its home arena are owned by Joe Tsai, who co-founded Alibaba in 1999 and has served as its chairman since 2023. Tsai completed his full acquisition of the Brooklyn Nets and Barclays Centre in 2019, marking a record transaction for a US sports franchise at the time. The Brooklyn Nets’ collaboration builds on Alibaba Cloud’s growing footprint in the global sports industry. The company became a worldwide partner of the International Olympic Committee in 2017, and most recently powered cloud-based broadcasting and AI-driven sustainability platforms for the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics. The announcement comes days after Alibaba Cloud introduced what it called China’s most powerful artificial intelligence chip at the company’s annual Apsara Conference, as the company doubles down on full-stack AI capabilities from models and cloud computing services to chips. It also teased plans to train an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters. “Alibaba is firmly investing in building full-stack AI ... to let AI move from a technological breakthrough to value creation,” Tsai said during his opening remarks at the event in Hangzhou. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

title: Chinese team sets world record with swarm of 116 underwater drones
description: Vehicles were deployed in sequence and carried out formation navigation with no human intervention during the test in a swimming pool.
content: A Chinese team has set a world record for the most autonomous underwater drones operating at the same time, deploying more than a hundred of the small robots in a swimming pool test. The Guinness World Record for “most autonomous underwater vehicles operating simultaneously” was set by a team from Northwestern Polytechnical University in collaboration with Xian Tianhe Maritime Technologies. The trial involved a swarm of 116 autonomous underwater vehicles – called TH-618s, the university said in a statement on September 24. It took place on August 29 in a pool measuring 50 metres (164 feet) long and 20 metres (65 feet) wide under the supervision of Guinness World Records officials, who have since certified and posted the record on their website. The vehicles were deployed in sequence and executed autonomous underwater formation navigation with no human intervention for 34 minutes over 500 metres, relying on real-time data to follow their preset route. “Enabling dozens or even hundreds of underwater vehicles to achieve fully autonomous, long-duration, and stable coordinated navigation in such an environment has always been a core challenge in the global field of underwater intelligent equipment,” the university said in the statement. “This time, the stable navigation of a cluster of hundreds of vehicles represents a breakthrough in the large-scale coordinated navigation of underwater unmanned systems.” China has been rapidly advancing its autonomous vehicle technologies, including trying to master drone swarms across land, air and sea as global combat shifts away from traditional manned platforms towards uncrewed systems. Ukraine in December said it had carried out the first underwater drone hit on a submarine, striking a Russian sub docked in Novorossiysk, a port city in the Black Sea. In July, researchers from Dalian Maritime University and the China Coast Guard Academy published a proposal which envisioned contested islands in the South China Sea being defended by coordinated machine swarms. Their paper, published in the Chinese-language journal Command Control & Simulation – supervised by the state-run China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation – included the use of underwater drones to help defend detection blind spots. Underwater drone swarms have also been tested elsewhere in the world, including the European Union-funded Collective Cognitive Robotics project with a swarm of 41 autonomous robots, according to the European Commission. Northwestern Polytechnical University said the TH-618 vehicles used in the trial were 61.5cm (24.2 inches) long and 20cm (7.8 inches) wide. It said the drones weighed 5.14kg (11.33 pounds), had a maximum range of 30km (18.6 miles) and could operate continuously for more than eight hours. The vehicles use a mobile phone vision camera system to navigate and can adapt to disturbances to their preset route to make corrections and adjustments. The university also pointed out the complexity of underwater navigation, including the difficulty of real-time communication as well as environmental challenges. It said the record was made possible through more than two decades of research in underwater target sensing, information sensing, acoustic communication and visual perception. The Chinese university’s partner, Xian Tianhe Maritime Technologies, is a marine equipment and vehicle supplier and a subsidiary of private defence contractor Xian Tianhe Defence Technology. The supplier said autonomous underwater vehicles were being used for more tasks as they developed, including research and infrastructure projects like detailed sea floor mapping and oil and gas pipeline inspection.

title: Can Hong Kong protect its eco-sensitive sites amid ‘golden week’ overtourism fears?
description: City bracing for 1.29 million mainland visitors, with places such as Po Pin Chau, Cheung Chau and Wong Mau Chau topping travel itineraries.
content: Hong Kong is bracing for a surge of mainland Chinese visitors to its eco-sensitive areas during the National Day “golden week” holiday, as strong interest in countryside attractions raises questions over whether the city can absorb crowds without overwhelming popular sites. A review of discussions on Chinese social media platform RedNote on Monday by the South China Morning Post found Po Pin Chau, famed for its dramatic volcanic rock columns, among the most talked-about sightseeing spots, alongside Cheung Chau, Sai Kung and emerging sites such as Wong Mau Chau – one of the city’s official coral zones. Also popular on travel itineraries are the National Day fireworks, cycling from Sha Tin towards Tai Mei Tuk and the National Day horse racing. Hong Kong is expecting about 1.29 million mainland arrivals over the October 1 to 7 holiday period, with the daily average forecast to rise by more than 5 per cent from last year. The Travel Industry Authority and the tourism sector forecast 1,180 inbound tour groups during the golden week break. Greenpeace Hong Kong campaigner Ha Shun-kuen said the government’s new reservation system for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail had helped regulate visitor numbers but warned that other Sai Kung hotspots remained vulnerable. “We are concerned that if the government only has a reservation system for Po Pin Chau but neglects management measures at other countryside hotspots, it will put considerable pressure on the country parks as a whole,” Ha said. Ha pointed to Ham Tin Wan, Sai Wan and Long Ke Wan, which had experienced overcrowding and environmental damage during previous holiday periods, and called for a broader ecotourism framework rather than relying on temporary patrols and clean-ups. Greenpeace visited Po Pin Chau on September 26 and found the viewing platform and narrow sections of the trail crowded even though only about 1,200 people entered that day, well below the daily cap of 2,000, Ha said. The group also observed littering and damage to the trail. The Po Pin Chau booking system, introduced earlier this month, limits entry to 2,000 people per day across four two-hour time slots on weekends and specific holidays. Ha urged authorities to lower the limit, repair damaged sections and consider temporary or seasonal closures where necessary. Authorities have said the Po Pin Chau reservation system will remain in place throughout the golden week. Additional staff, day and night patrols and CCTV cameras will also be deployed at Ham Tin Wan, Sai Wan and Long Ke Wan. Cleaning services and toilet facilities at Ham Tin will be enhanced. Sai Kung district councillor Christine Fong Kwok-shan said crowd management had improved over successive holiday periods, citing better traffic controls and promotion of the reservation scheme and “take your litter home” messages. She said Man Yee Road remained a traffic bottleneck, with sections beyond the West Dam narrowing to a single-lane two-way road and relying on passing places that taxi and minibus operators considered insufficient. Timothy Chui Ting-pong, executive director of the Hong Kong Tourism Association, dismissed concerns that the city faced the risk of overtourism during the holiday, saying the expected 1.29 million mainland arrivals represented only about 2.4 per cent of the projected 53 million visitors for the year. “There is no overtourism this time … there is no reason we cannot welcome this number across seven days,” Chui said, arguing that Hong Kong had handled close to 50 million visitors last year without reaching its overall tourism capacity. He said crowding was mainly concentrated in traditional tourist districts and individual attractions rather than reflecting a citywide problem. “Some places may be crowded, such as Tsim Sha Tsui, but it is normal for core tourist areas to have more people,” he said, adding that many districts were still hoping to attract visitors to support their local economies. Chui said he was also not concerned about pressure on popular countryside sites, pointing to crowd-control measures at the East Dam and Po Pin Chau that had already helped reduce visitor flow. Separately, the MTR Corporation will step up East Rail services for eight consecutive days from Wednesday, while additional high-speed rail services between West Kowloon terminus and Futian will operate from October 1 to 4. Police said on Monday that about 260,000 people were expected to gather on both sides of Victoria Harbour for the 23-minute National Day fireworks display at 8pm on October 1, with phased road closures in Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Central starting from 5pm. During last year’s National Day golden week break, Hong Kong received 1.4 million mainland visitors thanks to a longer holiday period of eight days that included the Mid-Autumn Festival. The High Island Reservoir East Dam drew 12,100 visitors during the eight-day period, which sparked public concerns over eco-sensitive areas, transport and hygiene issues.

title: Plan to turn Hong Kong office block into flats rejected amid high commercial vacancy rates
description: The Town Planning Board’s decision has cast a potential shadow over future applications while sellers struggle to fill commercial buildings.
content: Hong Kong’s Town Planning Board has rejected an application from a consortium of developers to rezone a commercial project in Kowloon for development as residential flats, leaving sellers struggling with high vacancy rates, according to analysts. A consortium formed by CSI Properties, Asia Standard International, and Chongqing-born property tycoon Cheung Chung-kiu applied to the Town Planning Board to redevelop “Harbourside HQ” – a grade A office building at 8 Lam Chak Street, Kowloon Bay, which they jointly own – into two residential towers providing 1,140 flats. The gross floor area of the proposed redevelopment project would have been about 45,787 square metres (492,800 square feet), representing a significant 36 per cent reduction compared with the existing commercial building’s total area of 71,664 square metres. The Planning Department previously indicated no objection to the application. However, the Town Planning Board rejected the development proposal after deliberating on it last Friday. The developers, who refused to comment on the decision, may apply for a review after receiving the refusal notice or can substantially revise the proposal and resubmit a completely new application based on the Town Planning Board’s reasons for refusal. Market observers had widely expected the application to be approved, so the eventual outcome was a complete surprise to many. Alex Leung, senior director at CHFT Advisory and Appraisal, anticipated that securing approval would be difficult even if the developers sought a review or resubmitted a modified proposal. Such a scenario is rare and may prompt developers to factor in additional risk regarding redevelopment projects Alex Leung, CHFT Advisory and Appraisal Since Harbourside HQ was only completed in 2010, some might view demolishing a 16-year-old grade A office building as a waste of resources that runs counter to sustainable development, potentially setting an undesirable precedent for future urban planning, he explained. Moreover, this year, market insiders felt the Town Planning Board had adopted an increasingly tough stance regarding developers’ proposals to rezone commercial land for residential use. In the past, applications that faced no objection from the Planning Department were rarely rejected by the Board. The Town Planning Board has reviewed three applications to convert commercial land to residential use so far this year. Only one of these – submitted by the Civil Engineering and Development Department and covering two sites in Sha Tin – was approved last Friday, according to the Board’s data. Another application was made by New World Development last October to the Town Planning Board to convert its K11 Artus hotel in Tsim Sha Tsui into serviced flats, but the application was rejected by the board in March. The developer has since submitted a request for a review, which is pending further deliberation. Leung pointed out that Harbourside HQ was the second application this year to rezone a commercial site for residential use that the Town Planning Board had rejected, despite the Planning Department raising no objections. “Such a scenario is rare and may prompt developers to factor in additional risk regarding redevelopment projects,” he said. Leung added he believed it would be difficult for the developer to convert Harbourside HQ for other uses. He pointed out that while the current market trend involved converting commercial buildings into student accommodation, the current buildings ordinance mandates that every habitable room in such facilities must feature operable windows. Furthermore, strict requirements regarding window area, natural lighting, views and room depth prohibit the creation of “windowless dark rooms”. “However, Harbourside HQ has large, deep floors and features a glass curtain wall,” Leung said. “I believe it would be quite difficult to convert it into student accommodation. The costs would be very high, and it might require sacrificing a significant amount of floor area.” Therefore, Leung predicted Harbourside HQ would simply remain on the rental market as is for the short term, leaving the developer with no choice but to wait for a recovery in the office market. However, according to the application documents, Harbourside HQ’s current vacancy rate is 25 per cent. The consortium also said there was already an oversupply of commercial area in Kwun Tong and expressed doubts over the need to retain commercial use at the site. A market report released by Centaline Commercial last week indicated that the overall vacancy rate for grade A office buildings in Kowloon stood at 15.7 per cent in August. Vacancy rates in the Kwun Tong and Kowloon Bay districts reached 17.13 per cent and 25.42 per cent respectively, representing year-on-year increases of 2.36 and 2.43 percentage points. As demand for commercial properties dwindles, six applications to rezone commercial land for residential use in Hong Kong have been lodged this year and are currently awaiting approval. These include a proposal by Paliburg Holdings and Regal Hotels to redevelop a five-storey shopping centre called We Go Mall in Ma On Shan that has been in operation for only eight years.

title: Hong Kong to celebrate 77th National Day with exciting activities and offers
description: Get ready to celebrate with dazzling displays, delicious deals, and lively activities this October 1.
content:
Hong Kong will celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China on October 1 with various activities and offerings for both locals and visitors.
The National Day “golden week” holiday in mainland China, which lasts from October 1 to 7, is expected to attract approximately 1.29 million visitors from across the border. However, residents of Hong Kong will have only one public holiday during this period, which falls on Thursday.
The South China Morning Post lists the discounts and perks available during the celebration.
First, a flag-raising ceremony will be held at 8am at Golden Bauhinia Square in Wan Chai, attended by officials and community leaders and followed by a fly-past and a sea parade by the disciplined services. No public viewing area will be set up.
The Hong Kong Jockey Club will then host a themed race at the Sha Tin Racecourse, with free admission for the public from 11.45am.
Hong Kong will stage a 23-minute fireworks display over Victoria Harbour at 8pm.
The HK$18 million (US$2.3 million) extravaganza will launch 31,888 pyrotechnic shells from nine firing points on three barges and six floating pontoons. Visitors can view the spectacle from several vantage points along the Tsim Sha Tsui and Wan Chai waterfronts.
The MTR Corporation will give away 77,000 electronic single-journey rides through a lucky draw on October 1. The public can also enjoy free rides on all passenger tram routes and several ferry routes of the Star Ferry and Fortune Ferry on that day.
Children using designated payment methods can ride most daytime franchised bus routes of KMB, Long Win Bus, Citybus and New Lantao Bus for free.
Greater Bay Airlines will offer a 23 per cent discount on original fares for all non-charter routes during the promotion period.
The Hong Kong Museum of Art and the Hong Kong Space Museum will also close early at 5pm on October 1 ahead of the fireworks display.
All commercial cinemas will sell tickets at half-price on October 1. Free admission will also be offered on the same day at several facilities and exhibitions in museums run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, and the Hong Kong Wetland Park.
The Police Souvenir Gallery, Hong Kong International Airport, Science Park, the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, the West Kowloon Cultural District, the HKTDC Design Gallery, and various shopping centres and department stores will also roll out offers on dining, consumption, parking and other perks.
MTR shopping centres will give away 77,000 gifts and e-coupons to celebrate National Day.
The Ngong Ping 360 cable car attraction and Ocean Park will offer ticket discounts, while The Peak Tram and Madame Tussauds Hong Kong will give out souvenirs to ticket holders.
More than 3,800 restaurants and catering businesses will provide dining promotions to celebrate the anniversary.
Offers include meal sets at 30 per cent off, fresh food items such as vegetable packs for HK$7 at food market stalls, crispy chicken for HK$10 a piece, buy-one-get-one-free bun deals and 30 per cent discounts at several hotels.
Multiple brands under the Tai Hing Group – including Tai Hing, Men Wah Bing Teng and Asam Chicken Rice – will offer a 30 per cent discount on all dine-in bills throughout the day.
Other fast food chains such as Cafe de Coral, Maxim’s restaurants and Spaghetti House have also offered different combinations of deals.
Several hotels – including Harbour Grand Hong Kong in North Point, the Ocean Park Fullerton hotel in Aberdeen, the Regal Hotel Group, Shangri-La Hotel Group and Nina hotels – are offering discounts for dine-in customers at their lounges, cafes and restaurants.

title: In Japan, anti-foreigner fake news drives far-right gains
description: Viral lies about foreign crime are fuelling political division in a country desperate for workers, analysts say.
content: Japan risks being pulled into a spiral of online disinformation about foreign crime that is stoking xenophobia and playing into the hands of the far-right, researchers warn. The trend is reportedly deepening divisions within Japanese society and creating a feedback loop that experts say will be difficult to break. In August, Constella Security Japan, a Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm commissioned by the government to counter online disinformation, hosted a webinar for officials and media on fake news targeting foreign residents. Among the cases highlighted were viral social media clips titled “metal theft by foreigners” and “stealing metal from railway tracks” claiming to show migrants cutting railway cables. The videos had racked up roughly 4.3 million views across various platforms by mid-September, Kyodo News reported. Constella has confirmed the clips were manipulated. The original footage first appeared on social media in Arabic in August last year. In March, the Arabic text was replaced with Japanese subtitles before the clip was recirculated locally, triggering a backlash online against foreign residents. “This sort of thing can be extremely damaging,” said Yo Nonaka, an associate professor at Keio University who studies Muslim communities in Japan. “Rumours and fake news on social media are deliberately designed to show foreigners doing wrong, and that … makes it much harder for Japanese people to accept them into society,” she said. Right-wing social media sites and political parties fed off each other, Nonaka said. “Influencers who want to spread fake news for clicks are helping to move Japanese society further to the right,” she said. “Far-right parties then spread the fake news to get more voters.” The tactic appears to be working. In August, online commenters responded to reports of foreign nationals allegedly stealing metal taps from farmers’ fields with posts calling it “a serious crime” that was almost unheard of “before there were this many foreigners”. “The country just lets in criminals and basically leaves them to their own devices,” wrote another. “That’s ridiculous.” Makoto Watanabe, a professor of communications and media at Hokkaido Bunkyo University, said false reports fuelled distrust at a time of rising tensions. “It is wrong that posts like these give a blanket negative image of all foreigners in Japan … that is then being used as a political tool by parties that campaign primarily on this issue,” he said. “These are criticisms based on lies and I wonder why more Japanese do not realise that.” Watanabe said the rising hostility echoed sentiments elsewhere, notably in the United States under President Donald Trump, in the rise of far-right political parties in the UK, France and Italy, and in recent electoral victories by the far-right AfD party in Germany. “The unfortunate thing is that Japan is desperate for more workers as the population continues to fall. The yen is weakening and there are more jobs in places like Vietnam than before, so treating all foreigners like criminals is only going to convince them to find work elsewhere,” he said. “Fake news is only going to hurt us by damaging our economy over the long term.” Chris Dunn, an Australian import-export business owner in Yokohama who has lived in Japan for 37 years, said that while crime by foreign nationals did occur and attracted intense media scrutiny, it needed to be put into perspective. He said he could “completely understand” that Japanese people did not want foreigners coming to the country to commit crimes. “But Japanese [people] break the law as well. What I hope is that a balance can be achieved that keeps both sides happy.” Whether such a balance can be reached remains to be seen. Official comments have only added to the hostility. In July, Kimi Onoda, minister in charge of policies on foreign nationals, claimed that one in four inmates in Japanese prisons was foreign. However, the figure only referred to Tokyo’s Fuchu Prison, which mainly holds male foreign inmates. Nationwide, foreign nationals account for just 6.6 per cent of the prison population. The minister’s remark nonetheless triggered a wave of online criticism. “To put it bluntly, if we didn’t allow foreigners to enter the country, crimes committed by foreigners could not occur,” read one online comment that blamed Japan’s “lax legal system” for the issue. “Personally, I think the total population of foreigners should be around 2 per cent – currently, it is around 3.5 per cent. I feel that’s a lot … and the goal should be almost zero.”

title: ‘Chill’ before the storm for rugby 7s captain as Hong Kong aim beyond Asian Games bronze
description: Chloe Chan is hoping to close gap with China and Japan, help grow the sport and spread positive messages to young girls.
content: The envy of other athletes, swimmers typically wrap up their major Games galas early and start letting their hair down while everyone else is still in monastic competition mode. Contrast their hedonistic lot with the rugby 7s players at this Asian Games: “on edge, practising and a bit nervous”, according to Chloe Chan, as they impatiently wait to join the party on Thursday. “But it’s good to be nervous going into a tournament; it means you care, right?” the Hong Kong captain said. Had the chips fallen differently, Chan could have been going to Japan swinging a racquet rather than leading Hong Kong’s pursuit of a second straight Games medal. She was in the team that beat Thailand 7-5 in Hangzhou three years ago for the city women’s historic bronze. “The feeling when the hooter went and everyone hugged each other will stay with me forever,” Chan said. “I keep thinking about that moment: that we’ve done it before and [a medal] is not out of reach.” Chan, 27, grew up as an aspiring tennis player. Her bedroom walls were plastered with posters of Novak Djokovic, while she treasures the memory of watching China’s Li Na win the 2011 French Open. “I was like, ‘Wow! A Chinese lady is winning one of the best tournaments in the world’,” Chan said. “She’s one of my role models.” Chan stumbled across rugby by accident, going to Discovery Bay Pirates’ training, aged around 14, “to hang out with my friends”. “At my first training session, I passed the ball forwards about three times,” she said. “Having my teammates there, it was fine. I knew if I made a mistake, we could just laugh about it afterwards. “The community and the friendship kept me going every Sunday. I loved playing with my friends, and I learned to love the game, too.” Still, with a daughter good enough to be playing tennis at Hong Kong Sports Institute, Chan’s parents each raised an eyebrow when their daughter started falling for a sport that would see her return home covered in bruises. “They were super hesitant, but as I played more, and they came and watched, they realised I was quite good at it,” Chan said. “Now they come to all my games.” Poised for a leading role in a series of youth women's rugby clinics, arranged by sports brand Under Armour, Chan believes she has a “responsibility to do more for local communities, and [attract] more local girls to rugby”. Along with coaching, and underlining the imperative of team work, confidence and self-belief, Chan wants to convey a message about body image. “Too many girls drop out of sports after high school,” Chan said. “Growing up, I thought having big muscles was a bad thing. That you’d look like a man. “Now, my narrative is so flipped. It’s sad to see young girls receiving those messages, especially through social media. It’s crucial that we spread a positive message about body image and good mental health. “Having muscles protects my body from injuries. [Being fit] is not just about looking nice, it helps you live a longer life.” Chan’s angular, sinewy frame, coupled with the hand-eye coordination she gained from tennis, opened up a world of possibilities. Unlike her elder brother, who went to boarding school in the UK at 14, Chan stuck around at ESF Discovery College, while making fast tracks with local Premiership club Valley, where she was a quick learner playing alongside her “idols”, the former Hong Kong internationals Samantha Scott and Colleen Tjosvold. “I was never the best in any team, but I liked that, I wanted to learn,” Chan said. With limited opportunities to study physiotherapy in Hong Kong, Chan secured a rugby scholarship at Northumbria University in Newcastle, England. “My mum’s been my biggest influence,” Chan said. “She instilled in me her ability to try different things. I’m not scared to try anything or to make mistakes. I also share her willingness to learn every day.” Chan needed a while to adapt to the freezing temperatures in England’s northeast. “For the first two months, I was thinking, ‘What have I got myself into?’,” she said. “The first training, it was so cold that I was, like, ‘This is not for me’. Everyone was in T-shirts, I had a puffer jacket. “But it turned into one of the best experiences I’ve had. I had to grow up by myself.” A classic high achiever, Chan gained first-class honours for her degree. Nonetheless, she abandoned her plan to stay in the UK for work after the then-Hong Kong 7s coach Iain Monaghan asked her to join the full-time programme. Chan returned home “a more confident player and having learned to mingle with different cultures”. She also had a new friend in fellow student Zoe Aldcroft, who would captain England’s women to their 2025 15s World Cup triumph. “As a captain now, I try to learn from the best and she’s one of them,” Chan said. “She’s an amazing person. I spoke to her recently, and you can always message her.” A Hong Kong debutant in September 2019, Chan found herself in a team with Natasha Olson-Thorne, 33, who recently surrendered her co-captaincy duties to focus on her own game, and Melody Li Nim-yan. “They were players I grew up watching, it was a dream come true,” Chan said. Over the past seven years, Chan has witnessed women’s rugby “grow tenfold”. “When I started, we had one or two tournaments a year, mostly in Asia, but now it’s global,” she said. A notable gap exists between Hong Kong and regional powerhouses China and Japan, the two teams that contested the past three Asian Games finals. We recently questioned on these pages why rugby sevens needs 72 players, across the men’s and women’s teams, contracted full-time at Hong Kong Kong Sports Institute. Another 28 are on junior grants. Pointing to the deep player pool in mainland provinces, Chan argued: “You improve by training with good players every day. “Hong Kong is such a small place, and people go away to university, then stay where they studied. We’re always trying to improve, to get players to stay in Hong Kong and train and grow with the squad for years. We get to a better place training and challenging each other.” Last year, Chan became the first Hong Kong woman to play club rugby in Japan, spending four months with Taiyo Seimei Women’s Sevens Series team Tokyo Sankyu Phoenix. “It was such a huge honour,” Chan said. “The level of rugby was incredible, and lots of Japan players were in my team. I went from being a senior player in Hong Kong to a beginner, and learning from everyone again. I really enjoyed that.” Playing overseas again is a big ambition, alongside achieving Olympic qualification after two failed attempts. Soon after her Japan stint, Chan suffered a disappointment that outstripped even not reaching Tokyo or Paris, when Hong Kong missed the National Games semi-finals by a points difference of one. “In sport, the lowest of the lows are so low,” Chan said, acknowledging that immediately after a tough defeat she “wants to be in my own space”. “I take time to remember that it’s not about the results, it’s about playing with a team and loving the sport,” Chan added. “I reflect and think about my journey, how I got to this moment, which makes me feel better and gives me the hunger to go again.” As captain, Chan “has a responsibility to bring people back up and put my personal feelings aside”. Despite “never actively seeking” the role, she was appointed two years ago this month. “I’m a quiet person, and looking at other captains around the world, I’ve seen they can be leaders, too,” she said. “In Japan, there wasn’t one massive voice in the team. Everyone plays their part and respects each other. “I lead by example, doing everything I can on the field, and being a good person off it.” Committed to a “brutal” and absorbing training regime, Chan will have to wait until rugby is done to indulge her ambition of completing a marathon. “I’m awful at long-distance running, but I like challenging myself and want to work hard,” she said. Chan occasionally shadows team physiotherapist Callum Chia, and studies her subject online to “keep my licence ticking over”. Relaxation comes in the form of hikes and watching true crime documentaries and HBO series Mobland. Now in the middle of the “chilled training week” that precedes a major tournament, Chan’s focus is narrowing on Hong Kong’s Games campaign. In a pool with India, Malaysia and China, it is very likely that they could end up with a bronze rematch against Thailand. The sides played each other twice in an Asian series leg last month, claiming one five-point victory apiece. “It would come down to grittiness, and whoever wants it more,” Chan said. “We’re so equal, always only five points apart. We have the skills and technique, so it’s just that mentality that makes the difference. “We want to do better than bronze, but we’ll really have to earn it.”

title: Photographer Irving Penn’s era-defining fashion imagery celebrated in Paris exhibition
description: Working for Vogue and others, he shot enduring images of Marisa Berenson and Lauren Hutton, and had a long-running collaboration with Issey Miyake.
content: One of the most celebrated photographers of the 20th century, Irving Penn is the subject of an exhibition at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) in Paris. Titled “Penn & Fashion”, the show, which also commemorates the 30th anniversary of the institution, was organised in collaboration with The Irving Penn Foundation and the Nicola Erni Collection. Known for his striking black-and-white photographs and meticulously staged images for fashion publications such as Vogue, Penn immortalised now-iconic and instantly recognisable haute couture looks from the likes of Balenciaga and Dior, as well as models including Marisa Berenson and Lauren Hutton. His portraits of Swedish model Lisa Fonssagrives have come to define an era. Remembered as the world’s first supermodel, Fonssagrives met Penn in 1947. They married in 1950 and stayed together until her death in 1992. Among the most beautiful pictures in the exhibition are two 1950 portraits of Fonssagrives – one showing her in a Balenciaga coat, the other in a harlequin dress. Spanning Penn’s career from 1947 to 2008, the show also dedicates a section to his long collaboration with Japanese designer Issey Miyake. From 1987 to 1999, Miyake sent samples of his sculptural garments for the American photographer to capture. Neither ever attended the other’s shows or shoots, giving Penn complete freedom to interpret the designs. The exhibition in Paris, which runs from September 30 until January 17, 2027, is a must-see for fashion and photography enthusiasts.

title: China expands high-speed rail network by 1,142km, linking in Xiongan
description: Network that now covers more than 50,000km also adds new sections in northeast, west and central regions ahead of the golden week holiday.
content: China officially opened 1,142km (710 miles) of high-speed railways in multiple parts of the country on Monday ahead of a golden week for travel, extending what is already the world’s largest network of its kind. The high-speed system would now link Xiongan New Area in northern China’s Hebei province to Shangqiu in the central province of Henan, and would eventually connect both cities with a Beijing-Hong Kong line, state broadcaster CCTV said. Xiongan, with a population of 1.4 million, was established nine years ago to take urban pressure off Beijing and was hailed as China’s ‘city of the future’ by President Xi Jinping. “You are looking finally at a [high-speed] rail link out of Xiongan, which hitherto has been a huge station with limited patronage but is now linked to the nationwide network,” said David Feng, an independent Chinese railway specialist. The 552km Xiongan line would lead to more long-distance trains coming from Beijing Daxing International Airport, he said. The airport, one of two international hubs serving Beijing, is 56km from Xiongan. Other additions to the high-speed network are a new line in northeast China’s Heilongjiang province connecting Harbin to the country’s northernmost high-speed station in Yichun, a section of a future railway connecting Xian in the northwestern province of Shaanxi with the southwestern metropolis of Chongqing, and a Xingshan-Yichang connector along the Yangtze River economic belt in the central province of Hubei. Top speeds on the added lines will range from 250km/h (155mph) to 350km/h, CCTV indicated. Monday’s additions extend a high-speed railway system that China has built to about 50,000km total since its inception just 20 years ago. On his WeChat channel, Feng described the four new railway lines as “one major addition” to the high-speed network, which he attributed to a “run-up” to the weeklong National Day break that begins on Thursday. China State Railway Group was expecting a record 284 million passenger trips during a 16-day span covering the just-ended Mid-Autumn Festival holiday and the National Day period, Xinhua reported. It was not clear whether 1,142km of new high-speed railway was a single-day record, but it was close, Feng said. On the Xiongan-Shangqiu segment, China’s railway operator would arrange as many as 64 high-speed trains per day for journeys as fast as two hours and 27 minutes, CCTV said. It said up to 20 high-speed trains a day would run initially on the new Xian-Chongqing section. And along the far northern route, as many as 38 high-speed trains would operate daily at first, CCTV said.

title: Judge blocks Trump from tying anti-terrorism grants to election changes
description: Washington district judge rules FEMA exceeded authority by requiring election changes to unlock US$1.1 billion in security grants.
content: A US judge blocked the Trump administration on Monday from conditioning counterterrorism funds to state and local ‌governments on changes to election administration. The decision by Washington-based US District Judge Amir Ali marks the latest defeat for US President Donald Trump in his bid to increase the federal government’s authority over elections ahead of the November 3 midterms, when his Republicans are fighting to retain majorities in both houses of Congress. Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced it would withhold 20 per cent of funding under ⁠grant programmes related to preparing for terrorist attacks and other threats until state or local governments adopted election administration measures favoured ‌by the administration. In his ruling on Monday, Ali sided with counties and cities in Texas, Ohio and Tennessee, which sued to block the changes on the basis that ‌the conditioning of such funds exceeded the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s authority. A coalition of mostly Democratic-governed ⁠states filed a ⁠separate legal challenge to the policy, which remains pending. The grant programmes, totalling about US$1.1 billion, have existed for years. None of them were designed ‌with election security specifically in mind. “Congress did not authorise the grant programme to be used for the sort of election administration reforms FEMA demands here - changes ‌that, ‌whether sound or not as a matter of policy, are not advanced to prepare for or respond to ‘acts ‌of terrorism’,” wrote Ali, an appointee of Democratic former president Joe Biden. Neither the DHS nor the Justice Department, which represents ⁠the federal government in court, immediately responded to requests for comment. In announcing the plan to condition the funds, DHS ⁠Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the new requirements would protect election systems from foreign interference and cyberattacks. The plan would have required grant recipients to use equipment that accepts hand-marked paper ballots rather than electronic voting ‌systems, manually audit at least ‌5 per cent of ballots cast, and compare their voter rolls to a DHS database to make sure no non-citizens were registered to vote. Trump has long made false claims about widespread voting fraud in US elections including the 2020 presidential election that he lost. Independent studies and audits have found voter fraud to be rare.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong moves in the right direction on minors’ social media use
description: The question is not whether governments should act to protect children online but how. The city has chosen careful study over slogans.
content: When Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu used his last policy address this month to announce an interdepartmental task force on minors’ use of social media and artificial intelligence platforms, he was placing Hong Kong within a widening international consensus. The digital lives of children can no longer be left to the goodwill of technology companies. Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok has since confirmed that legislation is among the options.
