This inquiry should proceed with an open mind. The case for scrutiny is strong. Heavy device use has been linked to poorer mental health, disrupted sleep and deteriorating eyesight among the young. Pornography, cyberbullying, content glorifying violence and, increasingly, AI-generated deepfakes now reach children with an ease no earlier generation has confronted. Guidelines and exhortations have struggled to keep pace. Local figures are sobering. The Hong Kong Institute of Family Education found that 34.7 per cent of kindergarten pupils spend at least an hour daily on social media, with over 80 per cent of parent-child disputes linked to screen time. Over half of children aged six to 10 own smartphones, according to parent-led group Look Up Hong Kong. There is also the need to combat AI-related crimes such as deepfake pornography to which children could easily be exposed. Hong Kong would not be acting alone. Australia became the first country to introduce a social media ban for minors under 16, covering platforms including Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok. Minors were barred from opening new accounts and existing ones were deactivated. Social media companies face fines for breaches, while parents and children are not penalised. Britain, New Zealand and Denmark have since proposed similar bans. Lam has pledged to study the effectiveness of Australia’s law and feedback on its implementation, while rightly noting that there is no uniform set of rules. Such examples suggest any legislative process needs to be carefully considered. A law that platforms can easily evade or ignore protects no one. Enforceable law proposals going beyond voluntary codes need to be carefully examined as they often carry unintended consequences. Hong Kong enjoys the advantage of not moving first. It can study which thresholds, verification methods and penalty structures have worked, and which have been less effective or not at all. Lam’s framing is sensible. Hard law, codes of conduct and education, he said, “are not mutually exclusive” and “may run in parallel”. No statute will substitute for parents who model healthy habits or schools that teach digital literacy. Nor should concerns about rights be brushed aside. Lam insists any law will comply with the Basic Law, and the purpose, protecting children from demonstrably harmful material, is one few would contest. But age verification inevitably touches personal data, and restrictions must be proportionate. The city’s privacy commissioner should be closely involved from the outset. The task force would strengthen public confidence by consulting openly, publishing its evidence and explaining the trade-offs. Urgency should extend to the wider AI agenda. Lam has acknowledged public concern over AI-related crimes and is liaising with the Law Reform Commission’s cybercrime subcommittee to prioritise its study. Existing laws can deal with offences such as scams, but more targeted legislation may be needed to keep pace with rapid technological advancement. A separate task force on legal liability for accidents caused by AI products is to hold its first meeting this year, consulting manufacturers, AI creators and consumers. That inclusive approach should serve as a model covering a range of related issues. The question is not whether governments should act to protect children online, but how to do so effectively. Hong Kong has chosen careful study over slogans and sensationalism. That is the right direction. The task force should now draw soberly on the experience of foreign countries, engage parents, educators and young people themselves, and deliver recommendations. These need to be robust enough to withstand legal scrutiny and the ingenuity of a tech-savvy generation. Our children deserve nothing less.

title: What’s the future of heart health? Cardiologists on advances, life-saving habits
description: On World Heart Day, three prominent cardiologists talk about their hopes for the future and simple things you can do to protect your heart.
content: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally, accounting for a third of all deaths. The tragedy? It is largely preventable. On World Heart Day on September 29, which continues its “Don’t Miss a Beat” theme, three prominent cardiologists share their hopes and fears for the future of heart health, the technologies that excite them, the simple daily choices that could save your life, and essential habits they practise to safeguard their own. 1. An early diagnosis advocate Among the most exciting trends in cardiology is that “we are moving from treating heart disease to finding it before it finds you”, says Dr Pinakin Parekh, a preventive, general and interventional cardiologist in Singapore. For some time, cardiology has been excellent at treating the consequences of heart disease – heart attacks, blocked arteries and heart failure. What excites Parekh now is the shift “upstream” – that is, picking up health hints in vulnerability early to protect the heart later. That includes better and more accurate imaging techniques, a more comprehensive understanding of inherited risks such as lipoprotein(a), and powerful new treatments for cholesterol, diabetes and obesity. Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a fatty particle that circulates in the bloodstream. It is similar to LDL cholesterol – low-density lipoprotein cholesterol known as “bad” because high levels lead to plaque build-up in your arteries, raising the risk of heart disease and stroke. But Lp(a) is more dangerous and can double or even triple a person’s risk of a heart attack. All adults should get an Lp(a) blood test at least once in their lifetime, according to new cholesterol guidelines from 11 major heart and medical organisations, published in March 2026 in the journal Circulation. The real battle against cardiovascular disease has to begin years – sometimes decades – before the first symptom Dr Pinakin Parekh, Singapore-based cardiologist Unlike other risk factors, Lp(a) is inherited and not typically affected by lifestyle. Learning your levels can help you take steps to protect your heart health. “The future of cardiology should not just be about saving someone during a heart attack,” Parekh says. “It should be about preventing that heart attack from ever happening.” What really worries him about heart disease is that it’s getting “younger, while prevention is still starting too late”. Obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, poor sleep, chronic stress, sedentary lifestyles, smoking and vaping are increasingly affecting people earlier in life, which means younger people are accumulating risk. “Many people still think of heart disease as something that happens when you are old. That disconnect worries me,” Parekh says. “We have remarkable medicines, stents and operations, but we cannot stent our way out of an unhealthy population. The real battle against cardiovascular disease has to begin years – sometimes decades – before the first symptom.” His top tip in protecting your heart is to “know your numbers before they become your symptoms.” Those numbers include your blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar levels. Know your family health history too, he says. His broader message: feeling well does not necessarily mean that your cardiovascular risk is low. Heart disease develops quietly over many years. The everyday things – moving more, eating better, not smoking or vaping, sleeping well, and controlling risk factors early – may not feel dramatic. But their effects can be. 2. A technology and equity advocate Like many in his field, Dr Hafiz Naderi is excited by the potential of artificial intelligence to identify disease – in this case, cardiovascular disease – earlier. “We are increasingly able to find subtle patterns in very simple tests, such as an ECG, that may tell us much more about a person’s heart than we could previously see,” says Naderi, who is a clinical lecturer in cardiology at Queen Mary University of London’s William Harvey Research Institute, alongside his clinical work at Barts Heart Centre in St Bartholomew’s Hospital in London. This is not about replacing doctors, Naderi says, but about “giving us another tool to identify people at risk earlier, when there is much more we can do to prevent disease”. His thoughts on cardiovascular disease echo the World Heart Federation’s message around this year’s World Heart Day: that it is a preventable killer. “High blood pressure is a perfect example: it is easy to measure and we have effective treatments, but globally huge numbers of people either do not know they have it or do not have it adequately controlled,” he says. As the World Heart Federation warns, high blood pressure often has no symptoms until you have a heart attack. High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so you can feel completely well while it is gradually damaging the heart, brain, kidneys and blood vessels Dr Hafiz Naderi, clinical lecturer in cardiology Naderi worries about uneven care – and as medical technology advances, we have to make sure that existing inequalities in global healthcare do not widen further, he says. A lot of those inequalities have nothing to do with tech, though, and are simpler to address than people may realise, he adds. “Some of the biggest improvements in global heart health will still come from getting the basics right, such as detecting and treating high blood pressure, reducing smoking, improving access to healthy food and making effective treatments affordable.” He stresses that “high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so you can feel completely well while it is gradually damaging the heart, brain, kidneys and blood vessels. Measuring it is simple, and finding it early gives you an opportunity to do something about it.” Thinking about heart health should be intrinsic to our lives – not just something we suddenly begin to think about as we get older, Naderi says. As a relatively young man himself, what is he doing to protect his heart health now? “I try to stay physically active, walk whenever I can and pay attention to my own cardiovascular risk factors. I also avoid smoking completely. None of us, including cardiologists, lives a perfectly healthy life, but the habits we repeat most days matter far more than occasional indulgences.” 3. A clinical strategist Medications to manage high cholesterol have done a tremendous amount to protect against developing heart disease, says Professor Yeo Khung Keong, CEO and a senior consultant with the Department of Cardiology at the National Heart Centre Singapore. He is excited by newer medications like GLP-1s because they have the potential to “dramatically change the health trajectory of millions of patients”. They not only help people manage weight, but they also help them avoid all the heart health risks that come with obesity. “The [GLP-1] medications are important because they help in patients with heart disease while also helping to prevent heart disease by improving risk factors. While some of these drugs remain costly and others are still being evaluated in clinical trials, I am excited about their promise.” Managing the costs of treating heart disease is a worry for him, though. “Heart disease can be sudden and it can be debilitating. Unnecessary testing consumes precious resources.” It is all about balance, he says. “How do we manage risk factors, treat disease, save lives and improve quality of life while managing precious resources?” He is unequivocal in his advice on how to improve and sustain heart health. “My number one tip is regular exercise. Exercise improves overall metabolic and heart health, among a multitude of other benefits. It is also usually inexpensive and an exercise like brisk walking requires no special equipment or resources.” He exercises six to seven times a week, getting in at least 30 minutes of cardio. “I usually exercise in the early mornings so that I can go to work on time. It has been … keeping me healthy and happy.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Hong Kong’s hottest new openings, from Abebe Bakery to Aoi by Kaiyo, Madé and Hokkien House
description: Korea’s Abebe Bakery brings a taste of Jeju with its doughnuts and buns, Hokkien House serves up modern Fujianese fare, Aoi by Kaiyo offers more than 100 Japanese dishes and it all off with a madeleine from Madé.
content: Abebe Bakery From a humble stall at a Jeju Island marketplace to growing international outposts, South Korea’s popular Abebe Bakery lands in Hong Kong with its bestselling cream doughnuts and buns. Regional Jeju ingredients such as green tea, black sesame, fresh milk, chocolate, apple mango and the hallabong citrus take centre stage in a range of tempting confections, with 16 creations available. For a distinctive textural experience, the cream bun combines soft dough with chewy rice cake and a smooth, airy filling. If stock sells out, the shop could close early on the day, so plan ahead. Shop W, 37 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui Hokkien House With chef-patron Levi You Zhenlong – the winner of the inaugural Michelin Guide Fujian’s Young Chef Award in 2025 – at the helm, Hokkien House draws on the Zhangzhou native’s deep understanding of Fujianese flavours to present a modern interpretation that honours craft, heritage and terroir. Signatures such as Buddha Jumps Over the Wall, steamed glutinous rice with mangrove mud crabs and stir-fried beef chuck flap with house-fermented radish are served on exquisite “mutton-fat” jade porcelain wares, custom-made by sculptors Jiang Sheng and Jiang Shenwei. Don’t miss the popiah, with a choice between traditional wrapping or deep-fried. 21/F, H Queen’s, 80 Queen’s Road Central, Central Aoi by Kaiyo Gaia Group’s modish izakaya Kaiyo inspired the opening of this laid-back offshoot. For the diner who appreciates diversity, the menu at Aoi by Kaiyo spans more than 100 dishes, from sashimi and sushi to tempura, sukiyaki, donburi, ramen and grilled items, including such options as the uni, caviar and toro sushi Napoleon, foie gras kamameshi, Japanese curry nabeyaki udon, lobster salad with nori, mentaiko tamagoyaki, Nagasaki Wagyu tartare roll, kabayaki-style eel with ochazuke – the list goes on. At the end of the meal, perhaps the salmon sushi cake for dessert? Shop 406, 4/F, K11 Musea, Tsim Sha Tsui Madé Madeleines, the scallop-shell-shaped sponge cakes, are the stars of the show at Madé, a boutique patisserie specialising in handcrafting the pillowy treats using premium French flour, almond powder, caramelised beurre noisette and a 12-hour dough-maturation process. From the Hong Kong-influenced egg tart to the comforting original, indulgent double chocolate, vibrant lemon and more, the selection of madeleines regularly rotates through six expressions and is packaged in portions of three, six, a dozen or 20 – if you want to share the joy. 54 Lyndhurst Terrace, Central

title: ‘Missed opportunity’: US soybean farmers question exclusion from China tariff cuts
description: Before the Xi-Trump summit last week, analysts and industry experts expected soybeans to be included in tariff-reduced arrangement.
content: US soybean farmers have described the exclusion of US soybeans from China’s import list under the newly announced Board of Trade mechanism as a “missed opportunity”, even as Beijing ramped up purchases of the crop ahead of last week’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. The trade forum, unveiled by both sides on Sunday, covered a range of US agricultural products for export to China, including meat, dairy, corn, wheat, sorghum and vegetable oils, but notably left soybeans off the list. “This was a missed opportunity for the American farmer,” said John Bartman, an Illinois-based fifth-generation soybean farmer. Before the summit last week, analysts and industry experts expected soybeans to be included in the tariff-reduced arrangement since US soybeans still face a 10 per cent tariff in China. The American Soybean Association, an industry group representing soybean farmers across 30 states and more than 500,000 growers, said it was “disappointed” by the crop’s exclusion from the tariff-reduced list. “China’s remaining 10 per cent retaliatory duty limits access for private Chinese importers,” it said in a statement. China-US to establish agricultural trade working group The United States and China have announced details of the non-sensitive goods covered by tariff reductions and agreed to establish an agricultural trade working group. The White House released tariff-reduction lists covering US$30 billion in goods from each side, including 77 categories of Chinese imports into the US and 1,619 US imports into China. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Monday that more than 90 per cent of the products covered by the agreement would receive most-favoured-nation tariff treatment, with all reciprocal tariffs on those goods waived. However, soybeans still appear to be kept under an earlier agreement between the two sides. The soybean deal was a key outcome of the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea, last year. It was expanded after another leaders’ meeting in Beijing in May, when China pledged to buy at least US$17 billion worth of US agricultural products annually for the next three years. Beijing also agreed to purchase 12 million metric tonnes of US soybeans in the 2025 season and 25 million metric tonnes in 2026. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said on Monday that Trump had continued to “deliver for America’s farmers and ranchers”. She highlighted that China had already bought 12 million metric tonnes in the 2025 season and said purchases of 25 million metric tonnes this year were “on track”, describing the two targets as “wins already on the books.” Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president at the Asia Society and a former senior US trade negotiator, said that the soybeans exclusion seemed like a “deliberate decision” given “the robust Chinese purchasing commitments already announced on soybeans as part of the trade truce”. Chinese state-run agricultural companies have already bought more than 12 million metric tonnes this year, more than half of the annual pledged amount. But Bartman said the existing 10 per cent tariffs make US soybeans “more uncompetitive” compared with exports from South American markets such as Brazil. He added that the existing agreement with China on soybeans is “less than the average of what they were purchasing before Trump was in office”. “This is not a good situation. This is not a winning situation for Donald Trump,” Bartman said. According to analysis by Purdue University’s Centre for Commercial Agriculture, even if China meets its soybean purchase commitments, shipments would still be 14 per cent below the five-year average of 29 million tonnes sent to China annually from 2020 to 2024. Overall, the agricultural trade pledges fall well short of the US$40 billion in agricultural exports to China recorded in 2022. US farmer welcomes inclusion of dairy products in China’s import list Jeff Winton, a dairy farmer in upstate New York, welcomed the inclusion of dairy products in China’s import list, saying he was “particularly relieved”, but added that he was “surprised and disappointed” that soybeans were not included. Drawing on conversations with farmers and farm groups across the US, he noted that some grain bins remained filled with soybeans from last season, while high diesel costs threatened to leave some fields unharvested this year, calling the situation “tragic”. Rising diesel and fertiliser costs have added pressure on US farmers, with fuel costs pushed higher by the US war in Iran. The loss of a significant share of the Chinese market and the impact of President Trump’s tariff policies have compounded those higher production costs, deepening financial strains across the US agricultural sector. Diesel prices reached a record US$6.53 a gallon on September 22 before edging down to US$6.45 on Monday, according to American Automobile Association data.

title: Israel files security complaint after TV station reports Netanyahu’s secret UAE visit
description: Prime minister’s office accuses broadcaster of endangering lives as Abu Dhabi later confirms high-level talks.
content: Israel’s domestic security service filed a complaint against a television channel that reported Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the UAE, his office said on Monday, the government’s first acknowledgement of the trip despite not naming the destination. “This evening the Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation,” read a statement from Netanyahu’s office, which oversees the security agency. On Sunday, Channel 12 and other Israeli media outlets reported that Netanyahu had visited the Gulf country to meet President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan. Abu Dhabi confirmed the visit and the meeting between the two leaders late on Monday. “The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them,” official news agency WAM said in a statement on Monday. The visit came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the Emirati president had warned Netanyahu ahead of Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which the Israeli premier did not pass on to the security services. Netanyahu has denied the story. According to Israeli media, Netanyahu flew to the UAE on Sunday to ask Mohamed to deny having given him that warning in 2023. The publication of his visit “endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad” spy agency and other top security officials, the prime minister’s office said in its statement. The visit was made public when the premier’s plane was still outside Israeli airspace, it noted. Mossad, which also operates under the prime minister’s office, issued a similar condemnation, according to the statement. Israel and the UAE formally established diplomatic relations in 2020 as part of the US-negotiated Abraham Accords.

title: Pope Leo says AI doom concerns not ‘fake news’ in apparent rebuke of Trump
description: Pontiff insists AI safety issues should be discussed and acted on following apocalyptic warnings from industry professionals.
content: Pope Leo on Monday ⁠said concerns that artificial intelligence ⁠could destroy the world are not “fake news” and should be taken seriously, in an apparent rebuke of US President Donald Trump. The first US pope, who has warned of the dangers of AI throughout his 16-month papacy, also directly criticised technology CEOs ‌who argued there should be no guardrails on the technology. “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously,” the pontiff said in a press conference on his flight back to Rome after a four-day trip to France. “I don’t think that that is fake news, as some have said.” Trump told ⁠the UN General Assembly last week that he believed fears about the dangers to humanity from AI ‌were a “hoax”. The pope said he had read on Monday that the head of chipmaker Nvidia had announced there could be a way to insert guardrails ‌into certain AI models. But Leo expressed scepticism, adding: “He’s the same one, however, ⁠that says there should ⁠be no limits placed and no government regulation”. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang told CBS News this month that he agreed ‌with Trump that safety concerns about AI were overblown. Trump is to meet tech CEOs on artificial intelligence on Tuesday at the ‌White ‌House. Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman are among those who ‌will meet Trump and House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson, according to sources familiar with the ⁠matter. Other possible attendees include Google CEO Sundar Pichai and SpaceXAI executive Elon Musk. Johnson said the talks ⁠would focus on finding a balance between innovation and oversight and warned that the US risks losing the AI race to China if it decides to “hyper-regulate this”. Leo urged the ‌world “to promote dialogue, study, investigation, ‌to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity”. “I think that there are enough people seriously interested in that … but we have to keep working,” said the pope. “We can’t just sit back and pretend nothing’s going to happen.”

title: Opinion | In the US-China AI race, the real fight is keeping humans in control
description: A crisis hotline is a start, but the deeper task is setting clear boundaries between human authority and machine autonomy – while we still hold the reins.
content: The US-China AI competition faces a dilemma. Both countries see artificial intelligence as a source of economic, scientific and strategic power, so neither has much incentive to slow down. Yet the more capable and autonomous AI becomes, the more important the question of human control. Last week’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping brought that tension into the open. Trump wants to leave AI “exactly where it is” rather than add new guardrails, while Xi believes China and the United States have a responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that it remains under human control. This is more than a disagreement over regulation. It reveals a deeper dilemma facing both powers. Competition rewards faster deployment and greater delegation to machines. Control requires limits, monitoring and the ability to intervene. The same systems that increase national power can therefore make human authority harder to preserve as AI becomes more autonomous. Conventional geopolitics treats AI mainly as an instrument: the US builds better systems, China builds better systems and each side uses them to advance human-defined objectives. But what happens when the instrument can act for sustained periods without continuous human direction? AI could then become an independent agent in international politics, not merely a tool used by states. The most consequential threshold is therefore not simply when AI becomes smarter, but when it becomes less dependent on us. A system with advanced reasoning, sustained autonomy, access to resources and the ability to plan and act in the world could develop meaningful operational agency. It would not need to be conscious, sovereign or legally recognised as a political actor. If it can pursue objectives, adapt to changing conditions and generate consequential effects across borders without continuous human authorisation, it can begin to shape the strategic environment on its own. That possibility changes the US-China AI race. The strategic problem isn’t just about which country has the stronger AI; it’s also about which can reliably direct, restrain and recover control of increasingly autonomous systems. A competition that assumes AI will always remain a controllable national asset could accelerate the very capabilities that make that assumption less secure. This tension is playing out in both countries. While Trump has repeatedly emphasised maintaining America’s AI lead, recently announcing plans for an “AI force” and a new AI adviser, leading AI executives have warned that capabilities are advancing faster than institutions and safeguards. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has called for coordinated measures to pace the frontier. The tension is structural: slowing can carry geopolitical costs, while accelerating can reduce the time available to make powerful systems governable. Once economies, infrastructure and security institutions become deeply dependent on autonomous systems, reclaiming human authority may be much harder than defining its boundaries today China faces a similar structural tension, even if its political language is different. Beijing has made broad AI deployment a national priority while also emphasising controllability. At the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Xi made it clear that AI should remain under human control. The conference chair’s statement went further, saying AI agents should operate within “clearly defined decision-making authority and behavioural boundaries”. At their Washington summit, both leaders supported continued US-China dialogue and cooperation on AI, according to the official Chinese readout. Xi specifically called for exchanges on AI risks and benefits, and joint efforts to prevent misuse and abuse. That is where bilateral cooperation can become practical. Before the summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed a US-China AI threat notification mechanism covering serious AI-related national security incidents. No major bilateral AI governance framework emerged from the summit, but a narrow incident channel may be more useful as a starting point. It could help the two governments distinguish an autonomous-system failure from deliberate hostile action, establish common categories of severe incidents, and create procedures for communication before an AI event escalates into a geopolitical crisis. But crisis communication addresses only the immediate problem. The deeper task is to define the relationship between human authority and machine autonomy while humans still design the systems, control the infrastructure and set the terms of deployment. A useful way to think about this is a global human-AI constitution. A constitution allocates authority. In the AI era, that means deciding which consequential decisions must remain under meaningful human authorisation, how much discretion an autonomous system may receive, how humans can interrupt or reverse its actions and where responsibility sits when it causes harm. This is why the window for action is shrinking. AI systems are taking on more complex tasks and operating for longer periods. Commercial incentives reward delegation because it lowers costs and expands capability. Geopolitical competition rewards it because autonomous systems can increase speed and strategic capacity. Each successful layer of delegation makes the next one easier. Once economies, infrastructure and security institutions become deeply dependent on autonomous systems, reclaiming human authority may be much harder than defining its boundaries today. The central US-China AI question is therefore larger than who wins the technology race. The two countries can help determine whether the next generation of AI remains an instrument of human power or begins to exercise power with increasing independence from human direction. They can remain technological competitors while still sharing a minimum interest in preserving the ability of people and governments to intervene. AI becoming more intelligent will transform international politics. AI becoming more independent could change who the actors in international politics are. The next steps taken by the US and China will be highly consequential. The window for defining the boundary between human authority and machine autonomy is open now, but the pace of the competition suggests it will not remain open for long.

title: China pledges to ‘firmly support’ Cuba as US escalates pressure on Havana
description: Spokesman Guo Jiakun marks 66 years of ties amid a US oil blockade and reports of military planning focused on the island.
content: China will stand by Cuba in defending its sovereignty and resisting outside interference, foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Monday as Washington stepped up its campaign to force political change in Havana. Guo made the remarks at a regular press briefing in Beijing on the 66th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries. “No matter how the international landscape evolves, China will firmly support Cuba in exploring the socialist development path suited to its national conditions and in safeguarding national sovereignty and opposing external interference,” he said. Cuba recognised the People’s Republic of China in September 1960, becoming the first Latin American country to do so. “In recent years, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, sustained and steady progress has been made in building a community with a shared future between China and Cuba,” Guo said. Guo did not announce new aid or name the United States, taking a softer line than Beijing did at the United Nations over the weekend. Addressing the UN General Assembly on Saturday, Vice-President Han Zheng urged “the relevant country” to stop threatening Cuba with force and lift the blockade and sanctions in full. Han spoke four days after US President Donald Trump told the same forum that his administration wanted “a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba”. Trump called the island a failed state that “will fall”, prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out. Pressure on Havana has built since January, when the United States cut the island off from Venezuelan oil after capturing Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro. Later that month, Trump signed an executive order describing Cuba as an “unusual and extraordinary threat”. Earlier this month, the US State Department sanctioned five state-run entities in the energy, mining and financial sectors and a grandson of former leader Raul Castro. The pressure has hit Cuba’s power grid hard, and a total collapse earlier this month left millions without electricity. Tourist arrivals fell 62 per cent year on year in the first seven months, according to official statistics. On Friday, CBS News reported that the US Army Reserve was assessing whether it could send military police, medical staff and other units to US Southern Command within four months. US officials told the broadcaster the planning was aimed at Cuba, though the internal Army message did not name the island. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is leading talks with Havana, also said last week that Cuba had a “golden opportunity” to change course. Trump told the General Assembly that Rubio was “deep into negotiations with Cuba” and vowed that Washington would not allow “a haven for foreign adversaries” on its doorstep. Havana has reported no progress in the talks, and Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio accused Washington of an “international crime” for blocking oil supplies. Beijing has paired its rhetoric with aid, and in January President Xi Jinping approved US$80 million in emergency financial help and a donation of 60,000 tonnes of rice. A Chinese vessel delivered 15,000 tonnes of that rice to Havana in May. After Trump signed an executive order expanding sanctions in May, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said the measures gravely infringed on Cubans’ right to subsistence and development. The spokesperson urged Washington to end the blockade and all coercion against the island.

title: US revokes visas of Latin American officials and others
description: Bolivian attorney general among those targeted in Trump administration crackdown across four allied nations.
content: The Trump administration is revoking the visas of 27 Latin American officials, former officials and their families, including Bolivia’s attorney general, over accusations of corruption. The officials and their families come from Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru – all nations with right-leaning leaders friendly with President Donald Trump. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru this month, pledging US support for their efforts to combat drug and human trafficking. Those leaders have complained that many of those targeted by the visa revocations were hindering their efforts to fight crime. The State Department announced the revocations Monday, saying they were being done “to fulfil the commitments to defend democratic governance across our hemisphere against corruption and narco-trafficking”. “Undermining a democratically-elected government is a threat to security and rule of law in the Americas and will not be tolerated,” it said in a statement. The Trump administration is billing the revocations as part of its broader efforts to clamp down on corruption, particularly related to the narcotics trade and illegal migration, by members of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” bloc in the western hemisphere that Trump created this year. The State Department has been denying permission to travel to the United States as a way to crack down on immigration or as a pressure tool against some governments, ranging from bans on South African officials accused of discrimination against white people to refusing to issue visas to the Palestinian delegation to attend an annual meeting of world leaders at the United Nations. The 27 targeted include Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca and more than 20 other Bolivian prosecutors and judges, 12 of whom were named as current visa holders and nine who will be denied visas should they apply. Two Colombians, a business mogul and a lawmaker, along with two Ecuadorians and one Peruvian judge are also affected. Mariaca is accused of abusing his public position by soliciting and accepting bribes to facilitate narcotrafficking and is also accused of helping violent criminals evade justice, according to the documents. “His actions endanger President Trump’s efforts to combat narcoterrorism while undermining the very democratic institutions Bolivia, as a Shield participant, is working to strengthen,” the statement said. Mariaca condemned the Trump administration’s visa restrictions against him, portraying them as political pressure on his office. He vowed to pursue investigations, including a sensitive case involving Fernando Cerimedo, an Argentine political strategist with ties to Trump’s circle who advised President Rodrigo Paz’s campaign. “The work we have been doing has not pleased certain political sectors, both inside and outside our country,” Mariaca said at a news conference in the Bolivian city of Sucre. “No political pressure, national or international, can stand in the way of establishing the facts, which must be investigated.” Mariaca, who was elected to a six-year term by lawmakers in 2024 under Bolivia’s previous left-wing government, has faced criticism over his office’s handling of drug trafficking cases. He led prosecutors in the eastern region of Santa Cruz when alleged Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastian Marset, now in US custody, escaped a police operation in 2023. He has since clashed with Paz, who has aligned Bolivia with Washington after nearly two decades of socialist rule.

title: Exclusive | JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon on how growth can untangle US-China strife, thorny global issues
description: In wide-ranging discussion, veteran bank chief flags ‘world peace’ as top concern, warns of Democrat vs Republican ideologies, and stresses economic growth.
content: Jamie Dimon’s recent whirlwind visit to Hong Kong followed a similar script: a schedule packed with meetings involving the entrepreneurs and business leaders connecting China with global markets. But it was his increasingly visible stance on global issues that appeared to extend his career beyond market strategy and financial industry leadership as CEO of JPMorgan Chase. His preoccupation with economic growth and world affairs drew particular attention in Hong Kong last week, shortly before boarding a private plane and jetting back to Washington for a state dinner at the White House to welcome President Xi Jinping. “My biggest concern is geopolitics – world peace,” Dimon, the longest-serving CEO of a major Wall Street bank, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday. His emphasis on global economic growth also echoed US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s views and the decades-old philosophy of China’s leaders, including Xi, that “development is of overriding importance”, laying the groundwork for China-US trade talks that were recently held at the bank’s New York headquarters. Markets: prepared, not scared Global markets have endured repeated panics this year, driven by surging oil prices, rising US Treasury yields, the Federal Reserve’s interest rate increase to fight inflation, and soaring debt – factors that have fuelled concerns about another major financial crisis. The world economy and global markets are also grappling with geopolitical conflicts – including the Ukraine war that began in February 2022 and the US-Israeli war on Iran that just crossed the seven-month mark – as well as persistent trade tensions between China and the United States, and increasingly louder warnings about artificial intelligence. You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase Dimon, whose signature financial strategy – a combination of low debt-to-equity ratios, high liquidity and large cash reserves known as the “fortress balance sheet” – often resurfaces in times of crisis, expressed concerns about “sticky inflation” in the US that has persistently hovered above 2 per cent for more than five years. “If you are in business, you should be thinking about whether you can handle higher rates, higher credit spreads,” Dimon said, speaking from the JPMorgan office in Central district, the bustling financial centre of Hong Kong. “Just as a normal course, how do you manage risk? “You always need to be prepared. Because if you look at economic history, the market isn’t always right.” However, Dimon noted that current conditions were “different” from the 2008 crisis, driven by excessive speculation on financial instruments backed by mortgage loans. Banks, the backbone of the financial system, are currently not overleveraged and have much more liquidity, while American corporations and consumers are not overleveraged either, he observed. “The highest debt is sovereign debt. So, governments need to be financially responsible. And hopefully, they will be before a crisis forces the issue.” Government data shows that US sovereign debt has doubled in a decade, topping US$40 trillion last month. The cost of capital is jumping as oil, grain and other shocks resonate, with the yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury bills at 5.234 per cent as of Monday afternoon, the highest in over 20 years. Although Dimon maintains that the US remains a permanent investment destination, and that its economy is still “hugely powerful”, talk of diversification and de-dollarisation has accelerated. This is accompanied by Beijing’s growing efforts to lure international investors and push for global use of the yuan. Many central banks and institutional investors also altered their strategies since March, reducing US bill holdings, purchasing gold, and diversifying away from the US dollar. Even Japan, an American ally, trimmed a total of US$135.4 billion in US Treasuries from March to July – a 10.9 per cent drop. While acknowledging that stock prices were quite high and credit spreads were quite low, Dimon said people should never be surprised about market fluctuations. “The markets aren’t always right,” he said. “Things are very good today, and there’s reason for some happiness.” China-US: growth is the antidote In the days preceding Dimon’s Hong Kong visit, JPMorgan Chase’s New York headquarters hosted a round of trade talks between Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US negotiators, including Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Underpinning these discussions was Dimon’s notion of government-business collaboration and a shared focus on growth, which he mentioned repeatedly in his interview, considering them vital to tackling many global problems. “Secretary Bessent mentioned the other day – which is dead right – growth is the best antidote,” Dimon said. “So, countries should be thinking about what policies will maximise growth. “You see a lot of politicians always speaking about raising taxes or cuts. Before you do that, why don’t we all fix the things that are inhibiting growth? Growth is good for all the citizens, not just good for business. When you have growth, you have more employment, more wages.” Such thoughts are strikingly similar to Beijing’s stance, which views economic growth as the foundation for well-being, social stability and debt resolution. “My view is: engagement is the best thing – at multiple levels and consistently,” Dimon said of bilateral relations, highlighting the importance of high-level meetings. “I’m glad that they are meeting and engaging. I think it’s important to hear each other out.” The latest talks yielded some results – Beijing and Washington agreed to extend a nearly year-long trade truce for two more months, until January 10. And for the first time, the two sides discussed AI, according to their official statements. Ahead of Thursday’s state dinner, in their speeches to officials and top American business executives – including Dimon – presidents Xi and Trump praised past friendships and downplayed current rivalries. While competition persists over AI, biotech and many other sectors, Dimon identified potential areas for cooperation between the two superpowers, such as working towards world peace, nuclear non-proliferation and counterterrorism. “We should keep reminding ourselves that China wants to lift up its people, America wants to lift up its people,” he noted. On AI: roll up your sleeves Despite market debate over the rapid deployment of AI, Dimon argued that the progression of the technology would move from machine learning to large language models and then, eventually, artificial general intelligence – thinking that matches or surpasses human cognitive ability. Dimon said the technology would transform lives and industries. “AI is real. We’ve been doing it for 13 years,” he said, citing its customer-oriented use to prevent fraud and to facilitate marketing, prospecting, design and call centres. “It’ll save lives, prevent car accidents and develop drugs and composite materials. If you have kids, they may live to 100. We may not have some of the diseases we were all afflicted with. So, yeah, you should applaud that.” As any technology carries potential downsides, he called for broad government actions to redeploy or retrain workers, but remained broadly positive on the technology’s future gains. “I think AI’s productivity benefits are still some way down the road. We don’t yet know exactly when they’ll be fully realised, but I believe it will be a huge plus.” It does create real vulnerabilities and drives the need for increased spending on cyber protection, Dimon said, mentioning possible threats through open-source code and internet access. “Again, my attitude is: roll up your sleeves, get to work,” he said. “It’s not like we’re ignoring it. “It may cause some disruption. But I don’t spend much time debating it. My job is to do a better job for my customers. We use computers, we use technology, and we’ll use AI the same way. The north star is serving customers better. AI is just another tool to help us do that.” If you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts Jamie Dimon, JPMorgan Chase The next chapter After spending more than two decades at the helm of one of the world’s most valuable banks, Dimon still maintains a sharp sense of global market risks and business deals. Increasingly, however, the 70-year-old multibillionaire has set his sights beyond bank profits and personal wealth towards some of the “big issues” facing the world. “You know, the war in Ukraine is terrible, and it’s causing a lot of issues in Europe now,” he said. “And it’s getting worse. Obviously, that affects oil and grain prices. And now you have the war in the Middle East – Iran – and that’s also affecting oil.” He is also keen on advising younger generations to develop critical-thinking skills and a strong work ethic. “You can’t have critical thinking without deep curiosity and an open mind and asking yourself, ‘Does this really work that way?’” he said, adding: “And learn, learn, learn, learn, learn.” When asked about any personal goals he may have, Dimon, who is already a business icon respected across Wall Street and Washington, started laughing. “It’s getting a little late for me to have personal-development goals,” he quipped, before quickly adding: “I want to be smarter and better and help people, and help lift up the world.” At a JPMorgan town hall meeting immediately before the interview, the CEO touched on global chaos. Later, with the SCMP, he expressed pride in the “vibrant, healthy, innovative” US economy while also flagging some of his home country’s shortcomings. “In America, there are things we have done really badly,” Dimon said. “And whether it’s Democrat or Republican policies, we’ve done a bad job for inner cities; our schools aren’t graduating enough kids. The only way you fix that is to acknowledge it, and then you can attack it. “But, if you make it ideological – Democrats against Republicans – and make moral statements about what works, then you lose sight of the facts. Sometimes our policies don’t work, and we have to be willing to say they don’t work.” Regarding questions about how he would help change the situation, Dimon shied away from personal pursuits, focusing instead on his company’s strategy. “I tell people that at JPMorgan, we hope we help cities, states, schools, hospitals, companies, governments,” he said. “We bank all the development banks, we bank the United States government. “And that’s what we’re there for.”

title: French far-right leader Bardella hits back at antisemitism allegations
description: National Rally leader threatens legal action over report on alleged 2013 private chat logs as Marine Le Pen decries ‘dirty tricks’.
content: A French investigative website on Monday alleged that far-right National Rally (RN) leader Jordan Bardella made antisemitic comments in writing in 2013, but the close ally of presidential front runner Marine Le Pen dismissed the claims as fake. According to the report by Mediapart, Bardella wrote, among other comments, in a chat: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. Bardella, 31, tipped to be prime minister if Le Pen becomes France’s president, wrote on X he “formally” rejected the allegations which he described as “crude forgeries”, saying he would take legal action against Mediapart. Mediapart’s investigation is built on comments in private chats allegedly written by Bardella in the summer of 2013 when he was 17 or 18 years old. Mediapart maintains it authenticated the comments. It did not specify where the messages had been written nor publish screenshots. The young activist, who had joined the far-right party then known as the National Front (FN) a year and a half earlier, allegedly also said: “And that is what they want: a New World Order dominated by Israel, with Jerusalem as the capital, of course”. He was also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”. Le Pen herself told reporters she believed the purported comments were “fake” and accused Mediapart, which has locked horns with the RN on multiple occasions, of “dirty tricks”. “I am, like everyone else, astonished by the violence of the antisemitic remarks attributed to Jordan Bardella, which obviously cannot be explained away even by youth,” Yonathan Arfi, president of the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions (CRIF), said. Slamming Bardella’s party as a “haven for identitarians and conspiracy theorists,” he said: “You cannot claim to be fighting antisemitism on the one hand while continuing to be a haven for identitarians of all kinds, especially those who propagate antisemitic rhetoric”. Bardella, a savvy user of social media who projects a clean-cut image, has been a key player in Le Pen’s project of “de-demonisation” to make the RN into an electable force. Both have moved to rid it of the legacy of her father Jean-Marie Le Pen who founded and led the FN and repeatedly made antisemitic remarks. Bardella in 2025 made an unprecedented visit to Israel, the first by a French far-right leader, in a bid to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. The allegations emerged as Le Pen’s prospects for the 2027 elections appear stronger than at any point in her previous campaigns. A new poll Monday showed that Le Pen lead the first round of voting to succeed President Emmanuel Macron, and suggested she could easily defeat potential rivals in the second-round run-off. She also hailed as “historic” the RN’s achievement in the elections for the upper house Senate – which is chosen by local officials – to win enough seats to form a faction in the chamber for the first time. Le Monde daily described it as a “breakthrough” for the movement and a “warning” for other parties. Bardella accused what he called an “activist media” of conducting a smear campaign “to destabilise the presidential campaign and attack my honour”. The Toluna-Harris survey for RTL and M6 published on Monday showed that Le Pen would win around 35-36 per cent in the first round of voting, scheduled for April 18, if the election were held now. In the second round, on May 2, the poll indicated she would emerge victorious against hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) leader Jean-Luc Melenchon or centrist front runner Edouard Philippe.

title: Putin orders 15,500 additional troops for Russian army
description: Expansion brings Russia’s armed forces to 2.44 million personnel, including 1.55 million active servicemen.
content: Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Monday boosting the size of the army by 15,500 troops in the fourth such order this year. Putin’s order comes as both Russia and Ukraine suffer mounting casualties in the more than 4½-year Ukraine war. The decree did not give a reason for the troop increase. “The authorised personnel strength of the Russian armed forces is to be set at 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 military personnel,” the decree said. Putin had previously signed documents boosting the size of the army in March, June and July. The combined increase since March amounts to 47,860 soldiers. The military expansion comes as Moscow dramatically ramps up its long-term war spending. Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion roubles (US$202.58 billion) on defence in 2027 – a 27 per cent increase over original projections that brings total three-year military spending to 50 trillion roubles, according to draft government budget documents seen by Reuters. To finance the ballooning cost of the conflict, the Kremlin doubled its 2026 budget deficit estimate to 3.2 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and outlined plans for new tax hikes, including a windfall tax on metals and mining companies expected to raise 200 billion roubles annually. Russia’s battlefield advances have slowed this year, as widespread drone use on the front has made swift, large-scale troop movements almost impossible. Ukraine has repeatedly accused Russia of preparing for another military call-up, a suggestion that Putin has called Ukrainian “disinformation”. Putin last ordered a mobilisation of reservists in 2022, following a string of military setbacks on the battlefield in Ukraine. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: US set to grant sanctions waiver for Iran-Iraq pilgrim flights
description: Trump administration to allow Iraqi Airways flights to and from the Shiite holy city of Najaf for one month to ease pressure on Baghdad.
content: US President Donald Trump’s administration was set to grant a limited waiver to its Iran sanctions programme on Monday to allow for flights carrying Shiite Muslim religious pilgrims between Iran and Iraq, a person with direct knowledge of the matter said. The source, who is involved ‌in the deliberations, said the US Treasury Department waiver would allow Iraqi Airways to fly back and forth between Iran and the Shiite holy city of Najaf in Iraq for one month, with a more permanent waiver potentially following. Iraq halted flights to and from Iran on Friday, in line with US sanctions. The source said the move aimed to ease pressure on the Iraqi government of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has sought to deepen ties with ⁠Washington while also balancing a strong relationship with Iraq’s influential neighbour, Iran. Trump’s effort to impose a crippling economic blockade on Iran ‌is forcing regional governments to scale back ties with Iran, creating potential backlash against those states, particularly those that balance their ties with both Washington and Tehran. Zaidi’s office over the weekend said Iraq was seeking an exemption for travel between Iran and Iraq for medical treatment, education and pilgrimage. An ⁠Iraqi official said the ⁠Iraqi government was in talks with the US about the Najaf exemption and expected flights between Iran and Najaf to resume within 48 hours. The US State ‌Department referred questions to the Treasury Department, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In recent days, countries including Turkey, the UAE and Iraq have ‌cancelled direct ‌flights with Iran as a result of US pressure. In response, Iranian officials have threatened to halt regional air travel ‌if Iran’s air links continued to be cut. With Shiite religious pilgrims travelling between Iran and Iraq each year to visit ⁠important shrine cities, Iraq is perhaps in the most sensitive position. Najaf, a centre for religious study, draws millions of pilgrims a ⁠year to the shrine of Imam Ali, the first Shiite leader, and the world’s largest and oldest active Islamic cemetery. The source said barring flights between the two countries could cause severe backlash against Iraq’s government by ‌uniting Shi’ites who follow Iran’s ‌supreme leader and those who follow Iraq’s Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, undermining US efforts to reduce Iranian influence in Iraq. Zaidi has offered to provide safeguards for the flights, including rigorous screening and information sharing as well as ensuring the flights are not used for transfer of weapons, sanctioned individuals or illicit money, the source said.

title: Trump announces US$15 billion Iowa steel plant, claiming it will be largest in US
description: Trump’s announcement appears aimed at giving Republicans a positive message ahead of November’s midterm elections.
content: US President Donald Trump on Monday announced a new US$15 billion steel plant being built in Iowa, highlighting an economic victory in a key battleground state where Republicans face competitive midterm races. Trump announced the new plant at an Oval Office event alongside steel executives and Iowa Republicans, including two running for office. The event highlighted Iowa’s elevated status for Republicans and for Trump, who on Monday pledged to campaign there in coming weeks. “We’re going to do a great rally. We’ll all be there together,” Trump said alongside Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the US Senate, and Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who is up for re-election. Also joining him were Governor Kim Reynolds and Senator Joni Ernst, who are not seeking new terms in office. The new steel plant is being built by Mesabi Metallics, a Minnesota company owned by India’s Essar Group, an industrial conglomerate. Trump said the project will become the largest steel plant in the United States. It is expected to produce 10 million tons of steel a year after it’s fully built out. The plant was projected to begin production in 2030, supplied by a new US$2.5 billion iron ore mine that Mesabi developed along Minnesota’s Mesabi iron range. The resulting steel will be produced from start to finish in the United States, the White House said. Trump said the American steel industry is “roaring back to life”, crediting it to the 50 per cent tariffs on steel imports that he imposed last year. “Everyone is building their plants here because they don’t want to pay tariffs,” Trump said. “It’s really not that complicated.” Trump in June also approved the takeover of iconic American steelmaker US Steel by Japan’s Nippon Steel, a move that had been blocked by Joe Biden, his Democratic predecessor, and initially opposed by Trump as a 2024 Republican presidential candidate. After returning to office, Trump later backed a deal that gave the federal government a say in some company decisions. Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance both have touched down in Iowa this year to shore up Republican enthusiasm and energise voters before the November 3 elections. Mesabi Metallics is based in Nashwauk, Minnesota. The Essar Group is an industrial conglomerate formed in India in 1969, with ventures in industries from energy and mining to technology and retail, according to its website. Joe Broking, CEO at Mesabi Metallics, called the announcement a “major moment for US-made steel”, saying the factory would be supplying a critical product that US national defence, cars and trucks, shipbuilding, household appliances, energy and infrastructure depend on.

title: FBI deputy chief announces resignation after just over a year in job
description: Trump ally Andrew Bailey, who oversaw election-related investigations, steps down weeks before US midterms.
content: Andrew Bailey, one of the FBI’s two deputy directors, said on Monday he is resigning his position, leaving the most prominent US law enforcement agency after a little more than a ‌year. Bailey, a Republican ally of US President Donald Trump who left his job as Missouri attorney general to join the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation), said he was leaving to return to his family. Bailey, serving under FBI Director Kash Patel, helped oversee election-related investigations and was present earlier this year when agents seized 2020 election ballots from Georgia. “I am confident Director Patel will ⁠continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organisational accountability, and restore ‌public trust in this institution of excellence,” Bailey wrote on social media. The deputy director’s post, which oversees day-to-day law enforcement operations, has traditionally been apolitical ‌and filled by career FBI officials. Trump has installed political allies in the role as ⁠he overhauls the ⁠agency to align with his agenda. Bailey initially served as co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a former US Secret Service agent ‌and conservative podcaster, who left the FBI in January. Christopher Raia, a veteran FBI official, has more recently served as part of a ‌three-person leadership ‌team with Bailey and Patel. Bailey joined the FBI following a series of high-profile stumbles by ‌Patel, including botched handling of investigative files on the late sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein that caused ⁠political headaches for the Trump administration and internal tension at the Justice Department. The latest high-profile departure ⁠at the FBI comes about five weeks before the US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has mobilised federal law enforcement agencies to investigate ‌voting in elections by non-US citizens. Bailey ‌during his tenure at the FBI has helped manage the Trump administration’s investigations into election issues. The FBI has scrutinised election records from several states but has not produced evidence to substantiate Trump’s false claims that widespread voter fraud led to his electoral defeat in 2020.

title: Mexico could see life-threatening floods due to Hurricane Polo
description: ‘Our people are concerned about this event. We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years’.
content: Residents of Mexico’s Baja California Sur state boarded up homes and workers hauled dirt and rubble to shore up embankments as Hurricane Polo bore down on the peninsula on Monday, threatening high winds, floods and mudslides. Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo could still bring torrential rain to parts of Hawaii even as the storm edged away from the state. In Mexico’s Puerto San Carlos, a fishing town of about 5,700 people, some feared high tides and pounding waves from Polo could breach barriers and send seawater into the community. Some families planned to head to shelters in Ciudad Constitucion, about 60 km (37 miles) away, while dozens of people elsewhere in the state were evacuated. “Civil Protection told those of us here in San Carlos to evacuate because this is a high-risk area. With the current tides, the expected waves and the wind, the earthen barriers they built (to prevent flooding) could give way,” said Rocío Sánchez, a fisherwoman. Polo was a Category 3 storm with top sustained winds of 115 mph (185kph) on Monday morning, the US National Hurricane Centre in Miami said. Forecasters said it would hit the Mexican mainland after lashing Baja California Sur with heavy rains, potentially causing life-threatening flooding and mudslides. It could bring heavy rain and flooding to parts of the US Southwest later in the week. “Polo is forecast to be near major hurricane strength when it reaches Baja California Sur later today, and is anticipated to be a hurricane when it makes landfall in mainland Mexico late tonight or early Tuesday morning,” the centre said. As swirling clouds and strong winds marked the region, Laura Velázquez, national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency, reported that Polo would make landfall later in the afternoon. At a Monday morning news briefing, she urged residents to stay off the streets and seek shelter if their homes are at risk. She said travel would be suspended in the area where the hurricane was expected to make landfall and that ports across the region would be closed. Nolo, meanwhile, was well southwest of Hawaii and moving away from the Big Island as the weekend drew to a close, but a wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Monday morning. Nolo’s maximum sustained winds had increased to near 155 mph (249kph). Storm activity in the Pacific has been above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec. He said that pattern is consistent with El Nino years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes. With Polo approaching Mexico, the Mexican navy said it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlán, on the Pacific Coast, and deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the storm. One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to medical facilities. “Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.” Robles Meza said on Sunday that soldiers arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and provide support for possible emergencies. Also on Sunday, Tropical Storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s southwest coast. The hurricane centre said Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (72kph) and was located about 402 km (250 miles) south of Acapulco. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect. Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20 inches (50cm) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands. More than 120 National Guard members were activated, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation. President Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorising the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate help and provide funding support. Hawaii residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala, which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

title: US police report raises more questions about Chinese researcher Wang Danhao’s death
description: Key details about semiconductor scientist’s visit from US federal agents the day before he took his own life mysteriously wiped from report.
content: A heavily redacted police report has deepened the mystery surrounding the death of a young Chinese semiconductor researcher at the University of Michigan, who took his own life soon after what US federal agents described as a routine and voluntary interview. On the cold morning of March 18, Wang Danhao, 31, spoke with two Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers for about 10 minutes outside his rented home in Ann Arbor. When one officer offered to end the interview because of the weather, Wang suggested they continue talking at a nearby coffee shop, where the conversation lasted another 30 minutes. Late the next night, Wang arrived at the university’s GG Brown Building with red eyes and appeared to have been crying. Moments after meeting a colleague who wanted to ask him about a research paper, Wang attempted to take his own life by falling and died from his injuries in hospital about two hours later. However, critical information – including the names of the federal officers, what prompted them to approach Wang and key details of their conversation – was withheld in the 39-page University of Michigan police report seen by the South China Morning Post. Mingwei Yan, an Ann Arbor-based lawyer handling Wang’s estate proceedings, said the extensive redactions had left the family with few answers. “It feels a little intentional,” she said, adding that she was considering objecting to the redactions in an effort to obtain more information. One of the most striking redactions appeared in the report’s final timeline. For March 18, the day Wang was questioned by the federal agents, two events are timestamped to the minute – 8.44am and 11.42am – but everything about what happened is blank. After Wang’s fall on March 19, police found his blood-soaked backpack containing a Homeland Security business card and a separate piece of paper bearing the words “Customs + Border Protection” and the name of an official. Neither official can be identified from the report. The report also omits the name of the lawyer Wang spoke to for 2½ hours on the morning of his death. But the lawyer, John Minock, had already spoken on the record to the SCMP in July, saying he had expected his name to appear in the police report. The redactions are only part of the mystery – nothing else in the report readily explains why Wang would have taken his own life so suddenly. Shortly before his death, Wang told the colleague that Minock had reassured him the federal questioning was “nothing serious”. Police found no suicide note and nothing in an initial check of his text messages suggested he was suicidal, depressed or in distress. Yet DHS remained involved even after Wang’s death. On March 20, university police contacted the agency and discussed working together on further interviews with witnesses and university staff. The agency later obtained a search-and-seizure warrant for Wang’s phone, laptop, USB drive and portable hard drive, according to the report. University police handed over the devices, along with a copy of data they had extracted from his phone. The SCMP also learned that the same two DHS officers took part in hours-long questioning of one of Wang’s colleagues at the airport months later as he was returning to China with his ashes. The SCMP reported previously that Wang had been preparing for a new chapter in his life before his sudden death. He had secured a faculty position at the University of Science and Technology of China in Hefei, his alma mater, and planned to return to China in May. He was also planning to marry his fiancée in the summer. His colleagues said his scientific work would leave a lasting mark. In an email sent days after Wang’s death, University of Michigan engineering dean Karen Thole described him as a “promising and brilliant young mind” whose semiconductor research published in Nature “stands as a landmark”. In the police report, Mingyan Liu, a chair professor of engineering at the university, told investigators that Wang’s research had been published “at the highest level”, calling it “a huge accomplishment for any researcher”. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: SpaceX’s Starship reaches orbit for first time but flight cut short
description: Spacecraft deploys 26 Starlink satellites before flight controllers bring it down early out of an ‘abundance of caution’.
content: SpaceX launched its enormous Starship into orbit for the first time on Monday and successfully delivered the most advanced Starlink satellites yet, but cut the flight short to ensure safety. The spacecraft re-entered over the Pacific and splashed down north of Hawaii three hours after blasting off from Texas. The company had been aiming for a 10-hour flight, spanning six full laps around Earth, to prove its readiness for Nasa’s Artemis moon programme. Starship tipped over and erupted in flames upon splashdown, a dramatic end to the mission. Founder Elon Musk’s Starship almost did not make it to orbit when one of its engines shut down prematurely. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided, after several tense minutes, to proceed as planned. “Starship is orbital,” Mission Control announced to cheers. Nasa Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on reaching orbit and “managing every step in a safe, responsible and especially inspirational way”. Musk’s showpiece rocket – the biggest and most powerful ever built – carried 26 of the latest Starlinks to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. They popped out of the spacecraft one by one, drawing more cheers from the SpaceX crowd at the Starbase launch site. The decision to end the flight early came soon afterwards. SpaceX said hours later in an online update that the decision was made “out of an abundance of caution” because of the early engine trouble. It was Starship’s 14th full-scale launch from Texas’ southern tip in three years. Earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space. This time, the intent was for SpaceX to circle the globe from an altitude of 275km (170 miles) – not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile. While Starship achieved the proper orbit, zipping along at 28,000km/h (17,500mph), flight controllers opted to play it safe and bring it back several hours sooner, after just a couple of laps. The first-stage booster was never meant to return to the Starbase launch site either, dropping instead into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning lift-off. SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase. If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, “our popularity would diminish very rapidly,” Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. “That’s why we’re being extremely cautious here.” Depending on the findings from Monday’s orbital debut, the next Starship could return to the launch pad, where giant mechanical arms would grab the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works – Musk gives it even or slightly better odds – then SpaceX will re-fly the spacecraft by year’s end or early next year. The 124-metre rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable, a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship’s heat shield based on hands-on inspections of the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase. SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step towards moon and Mars travel. Nasa’s Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Moon would blast off first, followed by Orion – which would close in for a link-up – and then Musk’s Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon is unleashed. The next mission, Artemis IV, is slated for no sooner than 2028 and would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires’ landers. Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet’s first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company’s frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida’s Kennedy Space Centre and a third is planned for Louisiana.

title: Hero’s burial for late Hong Kong constable paralysed for 21 years after attack
description: Source says Jacky Chu, who died earlier this month, to be buried in Gallant Garden on October 23 after police service funeral.
content: A former police constable who spent 21 years paralysed after an attack on duty will be buried in Hong Kong’s official cemetery for public servants lauded as heroes, the South China Morning Post has learned. A source said that Jacky Chu Chun-kwok, who died earlier this month, would be buried in Gallant Garden on October 23 after a police service funeral. Chu, a constable in the Police Tactical Unit, will receive the highest honours for the funeral service, which will also include a Taoist ceremony and Chinese-style marching drills. Chu was critically injured during a solo patrol when a man stabbed him in the neck with a six-inch knife on the morning of July 19, 2005. The attacker, Liu Chi-yung, was carrying the knife with the intention of robbing pedestrians when Chu stopped him for an identity check outside the Po On Road Municipal Services Building in Cheung Sha Wan. When the 30-year-old constable grew suspicious and confronted him, Liu pulled out the knife, stabbed him in the neck and fled. Chu took off in pursuit but eventually collapsed from excessive blood loss. His injuries resulted in brain oxygen deprivation and left him completely paralysed and in a vegetative state. The former constable was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) in 2006. In its commendation, the government noted the police officer had shown extraordinary courage despite his injuries in the attack, making every effort to arrest the armed assailant until he collapsed.

title: VW, Gotion ramp up battery production in Europe, Morocco amid rising EV demand
description: Gotion will invest about €1.6 billion to build three manufacturing facilities in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, with VW putting in a similar amount.
content: Volkswagen Group and its Chinese partner Gotion High-tech have stepped up a gear in tapping global demand for electric vehicle (EV) batteries with plans to invest a combined €3.22 billion (US$3.66 billion) to set up three production lines in Europe and North Africa.
