The factories, to be jointly owned by the German marque and China’s fourth-largest EV battery maker, would be capable of delivering 37.5 gigawatt hours (GWh) of lithium-ion battery capacity and 100,000 metric tons of cathode materials a year, Gotion said in an exchange filing on Monday. The signings were “in line with Gotion’s overseas expansion strategy to consolidate our footprint in the global EV battery market while further deepening our long-term strategic partnership with Volkswagen”, the company said. One GWh of EV battery power is enough to run about 20,000 pure electric cars with a range of 500 km (311 miles), according to industry officials. Gotion said it would invest about €1.6 billion to build the three manufacturing facilities in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, with VW putting in a similar amount. The biggest project, an EV plant in Valencia, Spain, operated by VW subsidiary PowerCo, requires a total investment of €2.26 billion to upgrade it to deliver an annual battery capacity of 29.1 GWh. “Chinese-developed EV batteries are in high demand outside mainland China,” said Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service consultancy. “Collaborative efforts with VW to build plants in Europe will give Gotion easy access to the market as it quickens its go-global pace.” Gotion, based in Hefei, the capital of eastern China’s Anhui province, is 24.3 per cent owned by VW. Battery cells from the European factories would be mainly supplied to VW, and Gotion would be involved in the development of key battery cell production zones on the continent, according to the exchange filing. In the first seven months of 2026, Gotion delivered 34 GWh of battery capacity to EV assemblers, up 44.2 per cent from a year ago, according to Seoul-based SNE Research. Its global market share between January and July stood at 4.7 per cent, compared to 3.9 per cent in the same period last year. Gotion, along with its three bigger domestic rivals – Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL), BYD and CALB – commanded a combined 64.4 per cent share of the global EV battery market in the first seven months of the year, SNE data showed. China’s manufacturing heft had given its battery makers a cost advantage, with average prices in the country falling 13 per cent year on year to US$84 per kilowatt hour (KWh) in 2025, an annual survey by BloombergNEF showed. Last week, CATL said it had cleared all regulatory hurdles for its €7.3 billion mega factory in Hungary, a development that analysts expected would help the world’s largest EV battery maker extend its reach to international marques like BMW and VW. The production base in Debrecen, the second-largest city in Hungary, has an intended production capacity of 100 GWh per year. Separately, VW planned to reduce its Gotion holdings to 19 per cent by selling 96 million shares of the company to an investment firm controlled by the Hefei government for 2.3 billion yuan (US$342.6 million), the battery maker said in another exchange filing on Monday.

title: Congo politician beaten to death after urging Ebola prevention on radio, his party says
description: The outbreak has left at least 3,901 dead. Sunday’s attack on Marie-Celestin Karondwa is the latest in a series of attacks on response teams.
content: A senior member of Congo’s ruling party was ⁠beaten to ⁠death after taking part ⁠in a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative said on Monday. The incident happened on Sunday in Butembo, North Kivu province, which has recently ‌become a hotspot in the ongoing Ebola outbreak. Marie-Celestin Karondwa, acting president of the UDPS party’s federal executive committee in Butembo and a party spokesperson, was attacked by residents of his neighbourhood after appearing on a radio show during which he promoted Ebola prevention measures, ⁠the UDPS federation in Butembo said in a statement. The party said ‌the attackers beat him, looted his belongings and set his house on fire. It was not immediately clear who ‌carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated ⁠it. But ⁠the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on ‌the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”. Karondwa later ‌died ‌from his injuries, the party said. The mayor of Butembo ‌did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The incident is ⁠the latest in a series of attacks on Ebola response teams, underscoring ⁠persistent mistrust among the population. On Saturday, armed men attacked a handwashing checkpoint in nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ‌person and wounding several others, ‌a local civil society group reported. The outbreak, declared on May 15, has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to government data released on Monday.

title: China targets AI and frontier tech in newly unveiled innovation blueprint
description: Top research body also names quantum technology, brain-computer interfaces and controlled nuclear fusion as priorities for five-year plan.
content: China’s top state research body has put artificial intelligence (AI) and other frontier technologies at the heart of its new five-year plan unveiled on Monday, as global competition in science and technology heats up. The Chinese Academy of Sciences, the country’s highest academic institution, laid out a detailed blueprint for research and technology development aligned with the national 15th five-year plan covering 2026 to 2030. The plan focuses on innovation in areas including AI and semiconductors while underscoring efforts to develop the next generation of scientific talent. It identified integrated circuits, AI, quantum technology, life sciences and biotechnology, brain-computer interfaces and controlled nuclear fusion as priority areas, alongside basic and interdisciplinary research. Under the blueprint, AI will also be used to reshape how scientific research is conducted, with the academy planning to apply the technology to basic science, strategic technologies and sustainable development. “The plan makes AI-driven transformation of scientific research a key focus in accelerating breakthroughs in scientific and technological innovation, with efforts to promote AI-enabled innovation in key fields,” said China Science Daily, the academy’s official newspaper. The plan also outlines measures to strengthen the country’s scientific talent pool, including training strategic scientists, top engineers, young researchers and innovation teams. It proposes attracting high-level talent – both domestic and overseas – and strengthening international scientific cooperation. The plan comes as Beijing continues to place greater emphasis on basic research. The central government’s science and technology budget has grown steadily since 2020, according to the Ministry of Finance. China’s 15th five-year plan has also set a target for total research and development (R&D) spending to grow by more than 7 per cent annually. “To become a global science and technology power, we must strengthen basic research,” President Xi Jinping said at a symposium in Shanghai on April 30, according to an article published earlier this month in Qiushi Journal, a flagship publication of the Communist Party Central Committee. Several of the technologies underscored by the academy have also become areas of strategic focus in the United States, including biotechnology, quantum information science and semiconductors, according to Washington’s Genesis Mission, an AI and science initiative launched last November. Washington and Beijing continue to compete over advanced technologies, with the US restricting China’s access to advanced semiconductors and related technologies, while China has imposed export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals. The competition has raised concerns about the wider impact on global technology supply chains and the decades of economic integration between the two world powers. AI and rare earth export controls were among the issues discussed during Xi’s recent summit with US President Donald Trump. But there appeared to be no new progress on semiconductor chip export controls, as there was no direct mention of them in Beijing and Washington’s accounts of the summit. With more than 73,000 employees across over 100 research institutes, the Chinese Academy of Sciences plays a crucial role in China’s efforts to advance science and technology as the country faces growing competition with the US over advanced technologies.

title: Child and 2 women ‘crushed to death’ during France to UK sea crossing
description: Asylum seekers pay smugglers thousands of dollars to board unstable and overcrowded dinghies to journey to Britain from France.
content: A 10-year-old child and two women died on Monday on the treacherous and illegal migration route across the English Channel from France, apparently trampled to death on a packed boat, French authorities said. The dinghy left the area of Sangatte in northern France at around 5.15am carrying 105 people, local prefect François Xavier Lauch said. The boat ran into difficulty with its passengers asking for help, authorities said. They called rescue services at around 8am when they were some six kilometres (nearly four miles) off the coast, Lauch added. Two women in their thirties and a 10-year-old boy who were believed to be Eritrean died, seemingly in a crush as the dinghy was carrying too many people, he said. Inflatable boats attempt the dangerous crossing after picking up people from the beaches of northern France, who wade into the sea to clamber aboard. A French maritime rescue boat took aboard 105 people, the maritime prefecture said in a statement. The child and the two women were declared dead by an intensive care team that was helicoptered aboard, it said. The women were believed to be in their 30s, the regional government said in a separate statement. “According to the initial findings of the investigation, it appears the deaths were caused by a stampede. The precise circumstances of the tragedy will, however, have to be established by the judicial investigation,” led by a prosecutor in the northern French port of Boulogne, the statement said. Nine other people required medical treatment, it said. France has long been a staging post for asylum seekers without visas hoping to cross the sea to Britain. They pay smugglers thousands of dollars to board unstable and often overcrowded rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Xi Jinping demands ‘safer’ China as Communist Party prepares for leadership reshuffle
description: The directive signals Xi is pivoting back to the domestic agenda following his summit with Donald Trump in Washington.
content: President Xi Jinping has ordered China’s security and legal apparatus to relentlessly eliminate risks and build a “safer” country a year ahead of the pivotal 21st Communist Party congress, which will usher in a major leadership reshuffle. The latest instruction, published by state news agency Xinhua on Monday night, is also the Chinese leader’s first major domestic directive since his state visit to Washington last week, signalling a pivot back to the domestic agenda – especially stability. In a written directive relayed at a high-level meeting, Xi said the security and law enforcement apparatus must advance the “Peaceful China Initiative to a higher level” to ensure “steady and sustained progress in China’s modernisation”. The initiative was first launched in 2013 with the goal of reducing security risks by mobilising all the country’s resources. These bodies must “prevent and defuse various risks” by addressing both symptoms and causes, Xi instructed. He urged officials to improve grass-roots governance, strengthen rule-of-law frameworks, and rely more on “technological empowerment” to maintain social order and mitigate potential unrest. The ultimate goal, according to Xi, is to achieve continuous visible progress in four key metrics: making the country more secure, society more orderly, governance more effective, and the people more satisfied. Xi hailed the security apparatus for its steadfast work since he took the helm at the 18th party congress in 2012, asserting that under his leadership, the nation had become “one of the safest countries in the world”. The instructions arrive at a critical domestic political juncture, as the Communist Party lays the groundwork for a seamless political transition at the national party congress, where a new leadership line-up will be unveiled. The ruling party is expected to convene its fifth plenary session at the end of next month, which will focus on strengthening party governance. China’s top security official Chen Wenqing, a Politburo member and head of the party’s powerful Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission, ordered his subordinates to “unswervingly implement” Xi’s instructions. He said the security system must “combine punishment with prevention, address both symptoms and causes, ensure coordinated efforts and synergy”, and strive to realise Xi’s security goals. Public Security Minister Wang Xiaohong also pledged to anchor the ministry’s work to the president’s new goals. Wang stressed the need to strengthen grass-roots policing and innovate law enforcement methods to maintain an iron grip on stability. Monday’s top-level gathering was attended by senior officials of the country’s law enforcement, judicial and security apparatus, including Zhang Jun, president of the Supreme People’s Court, and Supreme People’s Procuratorate head Ying Yong, according to Xinhua. Security has been one of Beijing’s top priorities in recent years as China continues to navigate complex domestic headwinds, including structural economic disruptions by AI, an ageing population and sluggish domestic consumption. In July, China officially launched a year-long intensive campaign to deepen a crackdown on organised crime and “evil forces”, specifically targeting new forms of crime that use online platforms.

title: Strong AI demand prompts Hong Kong trade body to raise export growth forecast
description: Trade Development Council expects Hong Kong’s merchandise exports to grow by as much as 47 per cent.
content: Stronger-than-expected global demand for artificial intelligence-related products has prompted the Trade Development Council to sharply raise its full-year forecast for Hong Kong export growth in 2026 to as much as 47 per cent. The latest revision follows the council in June raising its midyear forecast to 20 per cent growth, from an earlier estimate of 8 to 9 per cent. Its latest survey of the city’s major exporters also found that their business confidence and market expectations had remained strong and optimistic in the third quarter of 2026. Releasing its quarterly research report on Monday, the council said it had “substantially revised upwards” its forecast for Hong Kong’s merchandise export growth in 2026 to a range between 42 per cent and 47 per cent. “The AI-driven demand for related electronic products remains robust, leading to strong growth momentum for Hong Kong’s electronic exports, and it is expected to persist in the remainder of 2026,” the report said. The broad-based demand from the city’s key export markets, including mainland China and the Asean bloc, was also likely to continue, the research found. “The strong Hong Kong export growth recorded this year has been driven primarily by the rapid acceleration of global demand for AI-related products and infrastructure,” said Bruce Pang Ming, the council’s director of research. “Demand for semiconductors, memory chips, computer components, telecommunications equipment and other advanced electronics expanded much faster than expected, providing substantial support to Hong Kong’s exports.” The council also noted that this move reflected the city’s better-than-anticipated export performance, with 42.5 per cent year-on-year growth over the first eight months of 2026. Electronics accounted for about 80 per cent of Hong Kong’s total exports in the first eight months of 2026. Exports of electronics registered 52.8 per cent year‑on‑year growth, according to the council. “Major markets included the [mainland], Asean and the US, reflecting strong demand across global technology supply chains,” it said. “Particularly notable was the strong performance of items related to growing investments in AI infrastructure, cloud computing, data centres and next‑generation digital technologies worldwide. “AI‑related electronics now account for an increasingly significant share of Hong Kong’s exports.” The growth came despite the United States imposing an additional 12.5 per cent Section 301 tariff on imports from a number of trading partners, including the mainland and Hong Kong, according to the council. Such tariffs are additional duties imposed by Washington under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to address foreign trade practices that are deemed to burden or restrict US commerce. “While the latest Section 301 tariff measures have added a degree of uncertainty for businesses, the direct impact on Hong Kong exports is expected to be limited,” Pang said. “A substantial share of Hong Kong’s exports to the US consists of products covered by tariff exemption arrangements, particularly in the technology and electronics sectors.” He noted that Hong Kong’s exports to the US had remained resilient, rising by 63.4 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026. “Recent developments in China-US relations have also helped improve the trade environment,” Pang added. “The September Xi-Trump meeting and extension of the trade truce until January 2027, coupled with the US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement, provide a welcome period of stability, reducing the risk of further tariff escalation in the coming months. “The extended policy dialogue between the two sides has also led to further easing in bilateral trade tensions. “Together with the continued strength of global demand for technology products, these developments should help underpin Hong Kong’s export performance in the months ahead.” Pang’s deputy, Chu Wing-chor, also pointed to a “structural transformation” in Hong Kong’s trade profile, with exports increasingly concentrated in high-value, technology-intensive products such as integrated circuits, computer parts and advanced telecommunications equipment. “Hong Kong is increasingly handling products that are compact in size but exceptionally high in value, which are frequently transported via a combination of air cargo services serving overseas destinations and land transport links connecting Hong Kong with manufacturing centres in mainland China,” Chu said. “This transformation highlights Hong Kong’s evolution from a traditional trading gateway into a high-value-added international trade and supply chain management centre.” The council also released its Export Confidence Index for the third quarter, which also indicated “broadly positive” exporter sentiment. The index surveys more than 500 traders from six major industries on a quarterly basis to measure their near-term export performance. A score above 50 indicates expansion or optimism while a score below that threshold indicates a pessimistic or downward trend. The index is split into two key indicators, with one measuring current performance and the other measuring expectations. For the third quarter, the current performance index was 51.8, up from 51 in the previous three months. and above the two-year low of 46.5 reported in the first quarter. The expectation index was 51.3 for the third quarter. The council stressed that both figures stayed above the 50-point threshold. In his weekly blog on Sunday, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also noted that the rapid development of AI had added momentum to the economy. He also expressed confidence that Hong Kong would reach the government’s full-year economic growth target this year. This would also exceed the 10-year average before the Covid-19 pandemic. The forecast is for growth of between 3.5 per cent and 4.5 per cent, well above the 2.8 per cent average annual growth in the 10 years from 2010 to 2019. Hong Kong reported real gross domestic product growth of 3.6 per cent last year.

title: Hong Kong checkpoints to handle 7.44 million passenger trips for National Day break
description: Immigration Department says figure includes inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors using sea, land and air control points.
content: Hong Kong’s checkpoints are expected to handle about 7.44 million passenger trips over mainland China’s National Day “golden week” break, while people movements are anticipated to peak this weekend. The Immigration Department said on Monday that the figure would include inbound and outbound trips by Hongkongers and visitors travelling via the city’s sea, land and air control points between October 1 and 7. The department also said it anticipated that the most popular control points would be those at Lo Wu, the Lok Ma Chau Spur line and Shenzhen Bay, but added that none of the city’s checkpoints would have their service hours extended. Authorities earlier said they expected the city would welcome 1.29 million mainland visitors over the break. Last year’s figure reached 1.4 million thanks to a longer holiday period of eight days that included the Mid-Autumn Festival. To mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China on October 1, Hong Kong will host a 23-minute fireworks show along Victoria Harbour. Police anticipate the event will attract 260,000 revellers. The event is expected to cost about HK$18 million (US$2.3 million) and is being sponsored by insurance provider Sun Life Hong Kong. Chief Inspector Cheng Chun-kit of the force’s West Kowloon traffic enforcement and control division said road closures would be gradually implemented in parts of Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Central from 5pm on Thursday. Cheng said large crowds were expected near the Hong Kong Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui and suggested that revellers head further along the waterfront there or instead watch the show from the West Kowloon Cultural District or Hung Hom promenade. On Hong Kong Island, areas near Golden Bauhinia Square and the Convention and Exhibition Centre are expected to be the most popular. But new hotspots such as the East Coast Park Precinct in Fortress Hill and Victoria Park Road could also prove to be crowd favourites. “Based on past experience, about 260,000 people are expected to watch the display along both sides of Victoria Harbour, and we expect to handle a similar flow of people this year,” Cheng said. The Marine Department will enforce marine traffic control and step up the inspection of spectator vessels on Thursday to ensure safety requirements are met. Chief Inspector Lau Chun-ho of the force’s Hong Kong traffic enforcement and control division also reminded visitors to pay attention to public transport operating hours and prepare accordingly after the show had ended.

title: Hong Kong wage index rises 3.4% in June, with government expecting further gains
description: Adjusting for inflation, the overall real wage rate grew by 1.6 per cent year on year, keeping basic pay growth ahead of rising living costs.
content: Average wages including allowances in Hong Kong rose by 3.4 per cent year on year in June, with the government forecasting further pay rises ahead on the back of sustained economic expansion and labour demand. Figures released on Monday by the Census and Statistics Department showed that the 3.4 per cent nominal wage rate rise was broad based across all surveyed industries. After adjusting for inflation using the consumer price index (A), the overall real wage rate grew by 1.6 per cent in June year on year, keeping basic pay growth ahead of rising living costs. Wage rates include basic wages and other recurring and guaranteed allowances and bonuses. A government spokesman said that wages and labour earnings had continued to increase solidly in the second quarter of the year. “Looking ahead, wage growth is expected to remain positive, supported by the continued expansion of the local economy, which should sustain labour demand and contribute to further increases in wages and labour earnings,” the spokesman said. About 62 per cent of companies reported higher average wage rates in June than a year ago. Meanwhile, 33 per cent recorded decreases and 5 per cent saw virtually no change. Across major industry sectors, year-on-year increases in the nominal wage indices in June ranged between 2.4 per cent and 4.2 per cent, while real wage index growth ranged from 0.6 per cent to 2.4 per cent. The nominal wage indices of financial insurance activities recorded a 4.2 per cent increase in June compared with a year ago, the most among the selected industry sectors, followed by accommodation and food services’ 3.8 per cent and professional and business services’ 3.6 per cent. Total payroll per person engaged rose by 3.5 per cent in nominal terms and 1.6 per cent in real terms in the second quarter over a year earlier. The payroll measure is broader than the wage rate as it covers all elements of the wage rate plus irregular payments such as overtime allowances, non-guaranteed bonuses and back pay. It applies to employees up to supervisory level and does not include managers or professionals. Both wage indices and payroll indices are compiled quarterly. A wage index measures how the cost of labour changes over time. The payroll index of an industry is an indicator of the simple average payroll received per person engaged in the industry. Economist Simon Lee Siu-po said the 1.6 per cent real wage growth aligned with his expectations, though the overall figure obscured underlying sector disparities. He noted that weaker sectors such as retail and transport continued to struggle, while traditionally strong industries like finance and insurance maintained their momentum. However, Lee said that even the finance sector faced medium- to long-term headwinds as artificial intelligence adoption accelerated. Transport workers would also face mounting pressure as driverless technology from mainland China became increasingly prominent, he added. Whether the government’s optimistic wage forecast held true would be largely dependent on the sector, Lee said.

title: At least 21 Hong Kong-Bangkok flights delayed amid flooding in Thai capital
description: One Hong Kong-bound service departing Bangkok faces nearly 24-hour delay.
content: At least 21 flights connecting Hong Kong and Bangkok were disrupted on Sunday and Monday, with passengers on one service leaving the Thai capital facing a nearly 24-hour delay after the Southeast Asian city was hit by its worst flood in 15 years. Heavy rainfall lashed Bangkok – a top travel destination for Hongkongers – between Thursday and Monday, prompting Thai officials to declare the city a disaster zone. Despite the flight disruptions, Hongkongers in the Thai capital said the central tourist hub was less affected by the flood, with shopping centres remaining open even as some neighbourhoods were submerged. According to the Hong Kong airport’s website, 10 inbound flights and four outbound flights connecting with Bangkok on Sunday were delayed by at least one hour. Among them, flight TG 602D, operated by Thai Airways, was expected to arrive in Hong Kong on Sunday at 10pm initially. It was estimated to arrive in the city at around 9.30pm on Monday. A passenger who travelled with an infant took to social media on Monday to complain about the lack of support from the airline. “It is almost 6am. I have waited for 12 hours. There is no crew. No one has updated us. I suspect we have been abandoned,” the user, who posted from the airport, said. Three arriving flights and four departing flights on Monday were also delayed, with most delays reaching seven hours. The Immigration Department said that as of 5pm on Monday, it had received nine inquiries from Hong Kong residents currently in Thailand regarding matters such as flight arrangements. It said these Hongkongers had reported that they were in safe locations, and the department had provided advice and help. Hongkonger Winnie Yip, who lives in Phrom Phong, said the tourist area was less affected by the flood, with shopping centres such as CentralWorld remaining open despite the rain. “I still see many Cantonese-speaking travellers in the mall … I do not really see any signs of flooding in this area. However, other neighbourhoods, especially residential areas, have been inundated,” said Yip, who is in her thirties. She added that streets and pedestrian walkways near Phetchaburi MRT station, which connect tourists to the Airport Rail Link, were also flooded. She said she bought extra groceries in advance to prepare for the rain, noting that supermarkets and convenience stores near her home still had food supplies, despite packaged food such as instant noodles running low. According to another Thai-based Hongkonger Joey Ng, low-lying districts – including Huai Khwang where she lives – suffered from severe flooding. The district is close to Chatuchak Market, a popular weekend go-to destination. She added that the flood prevented her from accessing a nearby large-scale supermarket and shopping centre, but she could still buy daily necessities from grocery shops and convenience stores. She also noted on social media that some people had waited for their luggage for hours at the airport. Ng, who has been living in Bangkok for three years, observed that the public was caught unprepared for the heavy rainfall, with people rushing home and worsening traffic congestion. She added that the country lacked a rainstorm warning system like Hong Kong’s to facilitate residents in preparing in advance and leaving the workplace in an orderly manner. Steve Huen Kwok-chuen, executive director of EGL Tours, said that his company had tours departing for Bangkok on Monday and Wednesday, but the impact of the flood on their trips was “not too severe.” “The airline said that our luggage might not be delivered at the same time and would only arrive the next day, which would be delivered to our hotel,” he said. “We will adjust our itinerary and swap around the attractions as needed.”

title: Squash chief looks ahead to LA Olympics debut, is not taking Brisbane 2032 for granted
description: Speaking at Asian Games, World Squash chief excited about sport’s rapidly expanding footprint across populous nations India and China.
content: Squash may have secured its long-awaited Olympic debut at the 2028 Los ⁠Angeles Games, but the chief of ⁠the sport’s global governing body is acutely aware ⁠of budget and venue squeezes and is not taking a spot at the Brisbane 2032 Olympics in Australia for granted. While World Squash is leaving no stone unturned in its bid to retain its Olympic spot, banking on the game’s expanding global footprint and plug-and-play sustainability, its president Zena Wooldridge took a pragmatic view of things. “It’s been a ‌long journey, and we have to be patient. We don’t know whether we will be in there or not,” Wooldridge said at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, where squash finished the individual portion of its programme on Sunday. Hong Kong sit second on the sport’s medal tally behind Malaysia, after a gold for mixed doubles pair Lee Ka-yi and Tang Ming-hong, a silver for mixed doubles duo Toby Tse Yee-lam and Lai Cheuk-nam, and a bronze for women’s singles player Chan Sin-yuk. The city won a silver medal in the women’s team event at the last Asian Games in Hangzhou and started this campaign on Monday on a solid footing, beating South Korea and Pakistan with 3-0 scores. The men’s team also began well, beating Mongolia 3-0 and Japan 2-1. Wooldridge said that “because we’ve sat on the edge of being Olympic for so long, we really do appreciate the value of being included on the Olympic programme”. “The realities of organising a modern Olympics are very different these days, in terms of the economic constraints – big ambitions and big aspirations, but actually smaller budgets and in ⁠Brisbane’s case, fewer venues than LA has.” Rather than entering negotiations with rigid infrastructural demands, Wooldridge said, World Squash has adopted a lean, ‌collaborative model tailored to ease pressure on local organising committees. “Our approach is to work with the organising committees to say, ‘look, what’s your strategy? What are your challenges? And we’ll work with you to address those ‌challenges’. “We’re not coming in and saying, ‘look, these are our specifications, you must deliver this, this, this and this’.” Instead, the ⁠sport’s pitch rests on its portability, ⁠modularity and ability to drop into existing or multi-use spaces without leaving white elephants behind. “We are a bit like a snail – we bring our own home with us. ‌We’re small and compact. We can deliver a major event on a single court, and we can share the venue,” Wooldridge said. Asian giants Wooldridge singled out women’s squash as “a fantastic ‌product”, and ‌referred to the global spread across the top 15 in both the men’s and women’s world rankings to underline the sport’s universality. Also ‌pushing squash’s case for Olympic retention is its rapidly expanding footprint across the world’s two most populous nations, India and China. In India, government ⁠backing is accelerating elite success as shown by world junior champion Anahat Singh’s Asian Games silver on Sunday. China, meanwhile, is emerging as ⁠the structural engine of the game’s next phase of growth – both as a host and a manufacturing hub. Chengdu is set to host the World Junior Championships next year at a newly constructed facility housing 21 courts. China also stepped in ‌at short notice to stage the ‌Asian Junior Championships in May after the event was relocated from Iran. Crucially for squash’s Olympic sustainability pitch, Chinese manufacturers are driving down the price of glass courts historically sourced from Europe. “These are less than half the cost of a European court,” Wooldridge said of the structures that can be dismantled and repurposed. “It’s kind of changing and revolutionising the whole way that we look at our sport, and I love that.”

title: As the US weighs tighter restrictions on foreign drones, could Chinese makers lose ground?
description: Proposed measures could affect future imports and sales as Washington pushes to build alternatives to Chinese supply chains.
content: The United States is considering restrictions on some previously approved foreign-made drones, a move that could expand its push to build a domestic industry in a commercial market long dominated by Chinese manufacturers such as DJI. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is considering whether to prohibit the continued marketing and import of certain previously authorised models, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. Speaking in a discussion with Lisa Ellman, CEO of the Commercial Drone Alliance, Carr said the agency was gathering feedback on a proposed ban targeting certain models capable of operating in swarms. The review also covered potential restrictions on agricultural models, particularly larger drones capable of spraying aerosol products, he said. Carr clarified that the proposed measures would affect future imports and sales rather than drones already owned by customers. For now, the FCC’s “Covered List” – updated in December to include foreign-made drones – mainly restricts the authorisation of new models. “It’s good from a national security perspective, but we obviously still need these products in our supply chain. So it encourages onshoring and re-industrialisation,” Carr remarked. His comments came on Friday during President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US, when Beijing and Washington agreed to extend their trade truce for a further two months. They also agreed on recommendations under the newly established Board of Trade to grant more favourable tariff treatment covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods flowing in each direction. Drones, however, remain a source of friction. In August, US President Donald Trump signed a proclamation imposing a 100 per cent tariff on models weighing more than 25kg (55.1 pounds), as well as those equipped with thermal-imaging technology and containing certain critical components. In the same month, China’s commerce ministry said the tariffs unfairly targeted Chinese products and threatened global supply chains. “The fact that the FCC continued to push ahead during the two leaders’ meeting suggests the drone restrictions did not cross a red line in the broader US-China relationship,” said Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). Replacing Chinese suppliers would take time, Xu added. “Domestic manufacturers are expanding production relatively quickly in military, public-safety and industrial drones, but consumer drones and key components such as batteries, motors and electronic speed controllers still depend on overseas supplies,” he said. “What is more likely to emerge is a US-plus-allies supply chain that gradually replaces Chinese drones.” Addressing manufacturing hurdles during the discussion, FCC Chairman Carr acknowledged the challenge of replacing foreign-made parts. Companies shifting production to the US, he noted, could apply for exemptions or conditional approvals. This would apply when firms identified components that could not yet be replaced and provided a timetable for doing so, with decisions generally reached within about 30 days, he said. While Trump signed an executive order in June 2025 to secure US leadership in drone development, commercialisation and exports, Chinese manufacturers continue to hold a massive footprint in the global and US markets. The Washington-based Centre for European Policy Analysis estimated in May that China controlled 80 to 90 per cent of the global drone market, while a report published last November by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission put DJI’s share of the US commercial drone market at more than 90 per cent. Chinese-made aircraft also accounted for nearly 76 per cent of the 3,711 agricultural spray drones sold in the US in 2025, according to a January survey by the American Spray Drone Coalition. That was down from 93.52 per cent in 2024, while US-made drones accounted for 24.25 per cent of last year’s sales. Chinese drone exports to the US were already under pressure before Washington’s latest tariffs went into effect earlier this month. Customs data showed total drone shipments to the US falling 12.7 per cent year on year in August, with their value dropping 36.9 per cent. Shipments for heavier drones weighing between 25kg (55.1 pounds) and 150kg (331 pounds) fell by nearly 99 per cent.

title: Chinese commercial reactor achieves nuclear fusion with clean hydrogen-boron fuel
description: Feat hailed as ‘significant and valuable contribution’ to global research on magnetic confinement hydrogen-boron reactions.
content: In a first, a Chinese company has achieved high-parameter hydrogen-boron plasma control, marking a “significant and valuable” advance in research into neutron-free magnetic confinement fusion. ENN Group, based in Langfang, Hebei province, announced on Monday that its EXL-50U spherical device – a compact tokamak that uses a magnetic field to confine charged gas, or plasma, for nuclear fusion research – had successfully achieved hydrogen-boron fusion reactions. “This marks the first time a commercial fusion company has achieved a hydrogen-boron fusion reaction on its own device,” the company stated. Currently, mainstream-controlled nuclear fusion research, represented by the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) in France, predominantly uses deuterium-tritium (D-T) as fuel. While D-T fusion is relatively easier to achieve technologically, the availability of tritium is extremely limited. It exists only in trace amounts in nature, cannot be mined and is exorbitantly expensive. Furthermore, tritium is inherently radioactive, and the induced radioactivity potentially triggered by the high-energy neutrons released during the D-T fusion process cannot be ignored. In contrast, ENN Group, a leading Chinese clean energy provider, has opted for the hydrogen-boron route. This advanced fusion reaction combines a hydrogen proton with a boron-11 nucleus to produce harmless helium nuclei (alpha particles) and energy, without releasing high-energy neutrons. Several prominent private fusion energy companies – including TAE Technologies in the US and Marvel Fusion in Germany – are developing hydrogen-boron fusion, according to World Nuclear News. Yang Yuanming, the chief engineer who led the fusion project at ENN, previously told the South China Morning Post that the fuels for hydrogen-boron fusion were abundant and easily accessible. The reaction could generate electricity directly and the process did not release high-energy neutrons, Yang said. However, it is widely acknowledged that the most significant challenge facing this approach is the exceptionally demanding reaction conditions and the immense technical difficulty involved. Now, amid international commercial competitors, this Chinese experimental device has taken a significant step forward. The ENN team eschewed the conventional approach of universally raising the plasma temperature. Instead, through the synergistic effect of high-energy neutral beam injection and radio frequency waves, they precisely targeted and stimulated the energy region where the fuel is most prone to react, known as the “first resonance peak”. Under this mechanism, a large number of “fast protons” are rapidly generated within the system. Acting as a catalyst for the reaction, these high-energy particles triggered a chain reaction, pushing the overall fusion reaction rate beyond 100 million times per second. ENN Group said that more than 10 leading experts in the field, hailing from international research institutes and renowned universities, convened a special meeting to review the experimental results. The group reportedly “unanimously agreed” that the effective and repeatable measurement of alpha particles – the product of the fusion reaction in this experiment – substantiated the results. It added that the feat represented “a significant and valuable contribution” to global research on magnetic confinement hydrogen-boron reactions. ENN Group is among a number of private Chinese companies and state-backed enterprises racing to build a commercial fusion reactor by 2035 or sooner. Earlier this month, the company held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Helong-2 project at its fusion R&D centre. This third-generation fusion device built by ENN would serve as an important engineering platform in the drive towards a smart fusion power plant, the company said. Yang, the chief engineer, shared this latest milestone on social media on Monday morning, commenting: “[We will] strive to get the plasma to 100 million degrees Celsius (180 million degrees Fahrenheit) as soon as possible!”

title: Hong Kong launches 1-month consultation on arbitration law reforms
description: Stakeholder consultation part of efforts to enhance Hong Kong’s competitiveness as an international dispute resolution hub.
content: Hong Kong authorities have launched a one-month consultation on proposed reforms of arbitration laws, as part of efforts to enhance the city’s competitiveness as an international dispute resolution hub and advance an objective laid out in its first local five-year plan. The Department of Justice said on Monday that the one-month stakeholder consultation on amendments to the Arbitration Ordinance, which governs the use of the alternative dispute resolution mechanism, would cover four key areas to enhance the existing framework. “Ultimately, these enhancements will attract more businesses to choose Hong Kong as their seat of arbitration and enable them to benefit from our enhanced arbitration legislative framework that keeps pace with the times, and our internationally recognised arbitration services,” a department spokesman said. Under Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, announced earlier this month, one of the key themes is strengthening the city’s position as an international finance, maritime and aviation, trading, and innovation and technology centre and as a talent hub. One objective under this drive is bolstering Hong Kong’s status as an international dispute resolution centre, including reforming laws on arbitration and stepping up the promotion of its use for maritime, intellectual property and sports-related disputes. In last year’s Queen Mary University of London International Arbitration Survey, Hong Kong held joint second place with Singapore as the most preferred arbitration seat globally, as well as first in the Asia-Pacific region. The Department of Justice said the consultation would focus on four key areas concerning how arbitration was conducted: speed and convenience; confidentiality; scope; and fairness and justice. Proposals up for discussion include conferring statutory power on the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre to determine the number of arbitrators needed when parties fail to agree due to the absence of one or more parties but their mutual covenant requires an agreement to be reached. The centre was privately set up in 1985 with initial funding from the Hong Kong government. It is now an independent organisation that handles arbitration conducted in the city under its own set of rules. Another suggestion includes allowing arbitration parties to apply for a judicial review of negative jurisdictional rulings when a court decides that an arbitration tribunal lacked the authority to hear a dispute. The recommendations were compiled by a working group set up by the department in October last year and chaired by Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok. In a Facebook post on Monday, Lam said the proposed legislative changes would represent a significant step in cementing the city’s status as an international arbitration hub. “The proposed legislative amendments mark a significant step forward in ensuring that Hong Kong’s arbitration framework stays at the forefront of international development,” he wrote. Lam added that his department aimed to introduce the amendment bill to the Legislative Council early next year, in the hopes that legislative proceedings could be completed in 2027. Legal sector lawmaker Nick Chan Hiu-fung said that amending the ordinance would affect the rules of other private arbitration institutions in the city, as these organisations would examine their own rules to align with the official standard. “These changes are for all areas and not targeting particular disputes. It will make Hong Kong a more attractive place for arbitration,” Chan said. Currently, parties that do not specify which arbitration institution to use in case of a dispute will refer to the framework set out in the ordinance. Changes include allowing electronic signatures to be used on arbitral awards, which would make it faster for parties to be able to enforce results, as well as discussions on the confidentiality of arbitral rulings and whether parts of them could be published to improve ruling consistency on similar matters.

title: Opinion | China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
description: Manufacturing capacity is moving overseas but China, as a global hub for innovation and development, remains the ‘industrial brain’.
content: The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. For over two decades, China served as the dominant manufacturing centre, with an unmatched concentration of suppliers, skilled labour, infrastructure, logistics and engineering capabilities. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake. China is exporting parts of its manufacturing process while retaining the industrial capabilities that matter most. According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), since 2017, the share of electronics manufacturers from China – Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland – with overseas production has risen to 56 per cent from 12 per cent. BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable. From the early 2000s to the mid-2010s, companies concentrated production in China’s major industrial clusters to minimise costs. Low-cost labour played a significant role but the true advantage lay in the high density of the manufacturing ecosystem. This produced economies of scale and an operational efficiency few countries could match. Since 2017, rising tariffs, increasingly extensive export controls and stricter scrutiny of critical technologies have transformed the calculation. US President Donald Trump’s high tariffs on Chinese goods were intended to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing and force production back to America, but it has also increased the incentive for Chinese companies to establish production capacity in third countries. At the same time, Southeast Asia, India and Mexico began offering tax incentives, subsidies, industrial parks and other measures designed to attract manufacturers. Companies now see diversification as insurance against tariffs, export restrictions and sudden disruptions. But that does not necessarily mean abandoning China. In many cases, companies are relocating only the final assembly. Components, materials, tooling, machinery and engineering expertise continue to originate in China. This is producing a “hub-and-spoke” model: the hub remains China; the spokes extend into Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, India, Mexico and other countries. BCG estimates that about 76 per cent of Chinese manufacturers expanding in Southeast Asia are choosing Vietnam, Thailand or Malaysia. Vietnam is increasingly important for electronics assembly; Malaysia has strengths in semiconductor testing and packaging; India offers enormous domestic market potential; and Mexico benefits from its proximity to the United States. But all of these new centres remain deeply connected to Chinese supply chains. The most consequential development may lie beyond electronics. China’s industrial strategy is increasingly compatible with a division of labour in which advanced research, engineering, technological innovation and sophisticated manufacturing remain concentrated domestically. At the same time, it distributes selected production stages internationally. This could become a defining feature of China’s next stage of industrial globalisation. Rather than keep production concentrated in China, what matters more is control of the technologies, machinery, components, standards, engineering capabilities and supply-chain relationships underlying production. This is a fundamentally different conception of manufacturing power. The old model measured industrial strength largely by where factories were. The emerging model measures it by who controls the industrial ecosystem. This process carries an unmistakable irony. Washington seeks to reduce China’s role in global manufacturing by imposing tariffs and restricting access to technology. Instead, it has spurred Chinese companies to build production networks with greater geographic diversification and potentially higher resilience to political risks. Indeed, if Chinese companies can combine Chinese research and development, components, machinery and engineering with production facilities in Southeast Asia, India, Mexico and other markets, the result may be a manufacturing system less vulnerable to any single country’s trade policy. This does not mean China’s manufacturing dominance is guaranteed. Competitors will also develop their own supplier ecosystems, technologies and industrial capacities. Competition will only increase. But the main conclusion is already clear: globalisation is not ending; it is rapidly being reshaped. China is not abandoning its role as the “world’s factory”; rather, it is transforming what that concept means. It is becoming a global hub for innovation and development. While manufacturing capacity may continue to disperse across various countries, the “industrial brain” remains in China.

title: AIIB plans to double financing by 2030. Can it bridge Asia’s infrastructure gap?
description: The multilateral lender plans to channel more investment into projects spanning climate resilience, renewable energy and connectivity.
content: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) plans to double its annual financing to about US$20 billion by 2030 as the Beijing-headquartered multilateral lender enters its second decade, its president said on Monday. Announcing the target at the opening of the bank’s 11th annual meeting in Doha, Qatar, AIIB President Zou Jiayi said member economies had voiced a “remarkably consistent” need for greater project funding. “They need more infrastructure and more financing to build it,” Zou told reporters at a press conference, adding that she had visited about 30 member countries since taking office. Zou, a former vice-minister of finance in China, said member states increasingly viewed modern infrastructure as a “force of transformation” that could strengthen their economies over the long term rather than simply as physical assets. Under its policy road map, the AIIB said it would channel funding towards projects focused on climate resilience, renewable energy, digital transformation, regional connectivity, conservation and development aimed at improving people’s lives. To guide its next phase, Zou outlined a framework centred on what she called the “triple I’s”: impact, innovation and integrity. In practical terms, the focus would be on project quality and climate action, adapting the bank’s financial instruments and business models as well as maintaining high banking standards, she said. But she cautioned that addressing Asia’s vast infrastructure funding shortfall would require more resources than governments alone could provide. Infrastructure needs were “too large for any single institution or public balance sheet to meet alone”, Zou said, adding that the lender would need to attract more private investment and deepen partnerships with other multilateral and bilateral institutions to fund projects together. The AIIB began operations in 2016 and has sought to support sustainable development across Asia and beyond. It was initially seen as a potential rival to Western-dominated financial institutions like the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. During its first decade, the bank expanded its approved membership to 111 economies and approved more than US$79 billion in financing for 400 projects while maintaining AAA credit ratings from major global agencies. Turning to the future, Zou pointed out that traditional sectors such as roads, railways, ports and airports were becoming increasingly integrated with digital technology and artificial intelligence. She called for universal access to AI capabilities, saying the technology should “serve the benefit of all, not just a few”. Achieving that goal would require foundational investments in national data infrastructure, she added. Zou also highlighted the urgency of building climate adaptation measures into projects, citing the recent deadly floods in Nepal as a reminder that preparing for climate impacts was as critical as reducing carbon emissions. Despite differing geopolitical perspectives among its broad international membership, Zou reaffirmed the bank’s reliance on consensus building and dialogue. Multilateralism was “a form of infrastructure – the infrastructure for building trust”, she said, reiterating that international consensus had to prioritise economic development. “Development must return to the top of the global agenda,” Zou stated. “Development can only be achieved through cooperation.”

title: Hong Kong office expansion lags hiring push as tenants optimise current space: Colliers
description: Among industries, 31 per cent of respondents in the professional and business services sector are most likely to expand with new office space.
content: More than a third of Hong Kong’s office tenants are expecting to increase headcounts over the next 12 months, but only a fifth are likely to expand their real estate footprint, according to a survey by Colliers. The results of the fourth annual Hong Kong occupier survey by the property consultancy pointed to a “growing disconnect between hiring intentions and office expansion plans, as many occupiers continue to absorb growth within their existing premises through more efficient space utilisation and evolving workplace strategies”, Colliers said. Conducted between June and August, the survey sought the views of about 200 office tenants across various industries and company sizes. It asked about the short-term business outlook, office space strategies as well as emerging workplace trends. Companies are generally optimistic, with 41 per cent of respondents expecting business conditions to improve over the next 12 months. Only 16 per cent of respondents anticipated a deterioration. “Business confidence has strengthened considerably compared with previous years, supported by an improving economic backdrop,” said Chris Hui, head of landlord representation for office services at Colliers. “The survey suggests occupiers are becoming more selective rather than more expansive,” Hui said. “Most intend to remain in their current buildings, but they continue to evaluate opportunities to improve workplace quality and lease economics.” Among industries, 31 per cent of respondents in the professional and business services sector were most likely to expand office space, followed by 26 per cent in banking and financial services and 25 per cent for real estate and construction. The top reason given for expansion was anticipated business growth in the city, the survey found. On the other hand, 28 per cent of companies in technology, media and telecommunications were most likely to reduce their office size, the study showed. For those downsizing office space, cost reduction was the primary reason followed by shrinking business demand in Hong Kong and reduced headcount. Banking and financial services companies had the strongest hiring intentions, with 50 per cent of respondents expecting headcount growth in the coming year. Tenant retention would increasingly depend on delivering an “overall occupier experience”, as well as incentives and “effective rental strategies rather than headline rents alone”, Hui added. For tenants that were relocating, 71 per cent cited lower rents as the main reason, followed by an upgrade to a better-quality building and more favourable lease terms, including greater flexibility and rent-free periods. “While 43 per cent of respondents in Central/Admiralty are open to an increase in rents, 60 per cent from Kowloon East and 56 per cent from the Greater Tsim Sha Tsui [area] are demanding a reduction,” said Ivan Wong, Colliers’ head of office services for Kowloon. Among incentives, tenants favoured rent-free periods the most, Wong said. Colliers said a boom in initial public offerings and secondary listings, the expansion of financial firms and growing take-up of premium office buildings were contributing to a recovery in the Central business district ahead of the wider office market. Net take-up in the district reached about 56,857 square metres (612,000 square feet) in 2024 and 2025, and in the first eight months of 2026, more than 46,451 square metres (500,000 square feet) were absorbed, Colliers said. “While occupiers [in Central] still benefit from rents that remain below historical peaks, premium space is tightening and early planning will be increasingly important,” said Fiona Ngan, head of occupier services at Colliers. Given the rising demand for premium office space in Central, Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers, said future commercial land planning should support the district’s long-term evolution, with Admiralty and the New Central Harbourfront as an integrated business district.

title: Chinese chip foundry CanSemi’s IPO oversubscribed 2,360 times as investors chase AI boom
description: Momentum builds for CanSemi’s Shenzhen debut as investors back its silicon photonics push and role in domestic AI infrastructure.
content: Chinese chip foundry CanSemi Technology’s Shenzhen initial public offering (IPO) is emerging as one of mainland China’s most sought-after tech listings this year, as investors bet on its push into silicon photonics and its role in domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Guangzhou-based company’s retail tranche was oversubscribed by more than 2,300 times after clawback, according to a stock exchange filing late on Sunday, as investors scrambled for a piece of the domestic semiconductor pie. When trading begins, CanSemi is expected to set a milestone for the Shenzhen exchange as the first pure-play wafer fabrication company to list on its Shenzhen’s tech-heavy ChiNext board. Here is what you need to know about the company and the momentum behind its highly anticipated debut. What chips does CanSemi make? Established in 2017, CanSemi is widely celebrated as “Guangzhou’s top chip company”. As a contract chipmaker that manufactures wafers for fabless chip designers, it focuses on mature-node semiconductors, including analog and mixed-signal chips used in power management, automotive electronics and industrial sensors. What makes it stand out, however, is its bet on silicon photonics, a technology that uses light to transmit data and is increasingly seen as critical to next-generation AI infrastructure. The company launched a 90-nanometre silicon photonics technology platform in late 2024 and is now moving to 65nm process nodes. CanSemi did not rush to squeeze onto the single-plank bridge of advanced nodes, but instead built its business around mature 180nm to 55nm processes ICWise By April 2026, it had become the only enterprise in mainland China capable of large-scale mass production of 12-inch silicon photonic wafers, according to its prospectus, citing data from market research firm Frost & Sullivan. CanSemi “did not rush to squeeze onto the single-plank bridge of advanced nodes”, but instead built its business around mature 180nm to 55nm processes, according to a recent note by Chinese semiconductor industry consultancy ICWise. The company operates two 12-inch wafer fabs with planned capacity of 80,000 wafers a month. It had also started construction earlier this year on a third fab, which was expected to boost monthly capacity by 50 per cent, according to its prospectus. What drove the retail frenzy? CanSemi, which priced its shares at 12.01 yuan apiece and aimed to raise 7.5 billion yuan (US$1.12 billion), attracted bids from 14.4 million online accounts for a combined 423.4 billion shares, resulting in an initial online oversubscription of 3,303 times. That triggered a mechanism to claw back 20 per cent of the offline allotment to the online tranche, reducing the final multiple to about 2,360 times and leaving investors with a successful allotment rate of just 0.042 per cent. It ranked among the year’s most sought-after tech listings, alongside chipmakers Enflame Technology and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), which made their market debuts on Shanghai’s Star Market earlier this year. Enflame recorded a final online win rate of 0.025 per cent after 7.03 million accounts applied, while CXMT posted a 0.47 per cent win rate after 9.43 million accounts participated. Investor enthusiasm has been supported by CanSemi’s institutional backing. Its shareholders include state-backed investors such as the Guangdong Semiconductor and Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund and the Science City Investment Group, alongside several national-level industrial funds. Why does the listing matter for China’s chip sector? CanSemi’s push into photonics through mature-node manufacturing demonstrated that domestic foundries could secure competitive advantages through operational precision, ICWise said, rather than focusing solely on leading-edge nodes. The company said the bulk of the proceeds from the IPO – around 3.5 billion yuan – would directly fund the third phase of a 12-inch analog speciality-process production line, while 2.5 billion yuan was earmarked for advanced technology research and development, including silicon photonics. Beyond its optical interconnect ambitions, market observers expect the capital injection to strengthen CanSemi’s position across legacy downstream sectors. “Demand across the Internet of Things, automotive electronics, industrial controls and 5G communications remains robust,” said Guo Tao, an angel investor and committee member at the Chinese Association for Artificial Intelligence, pointing to rising electric vehicle adoption and smart-driving capabilities that continue to boost chip content per vehicle. CanSemi was “expected to capture market share on the strength of its local operating advantages”, Guo added.

title: Thai man’s jet ski stunt fuels anger in ‘unequal’ Bangkok as poor hit hardest by floods
description: The episode has been widely seen as an example of the insensitivity of some of the city’s wealthy to the suffering of its poor amid the floods.
content: A Thai man who zipped a jet ski across flooded Bangkok streets received a suspended jail sentence on Monday for causing a public nuisance after he used the capital – where tens of thousands of households remain submerged – as a backdrop for social media content. The stunt, widely shared on social media on Sunday evening, became a conduit for public anger over both the handling of the flood response and how climate calamities are experienced unevenly in the capital of one of Asia’s least equal countries. On Monday, a Bangkok court gave Sorn Keadsiri, the 27-year-old son of an actress, a suspended 15-day jail sentence and a small fine after he did doughnuts – spinning the jet ski in tight circles in the water – on a flooded Bangkok street while his friend filmed the antics. “The seized jet ski will also be confiscated,” Makkasan Metropolitan Police said in a statement revealing the court’s decision. Sorn said he had recently returned to Thailand and a foreign friend had cajoled him into the stunt to lighten the people’s suffering from the floods, local media reported. But the episode has been widely seen as an example of the insensitivity of some of the city’s wealthy to the suffering of its poor as they reel from the worst floods in 15 years. “People [who make viral content] could never truly understand or experience what it’s like to actually suffer from flooding. Instead of using their greater resources to help others, they use them to make content,” Thanayut Na Ayutthaya, a rapper better known as Elevenfinger, told This Week in Asia. The social activist said the unusually heavy rain was only one part of the problem, pointing to growing resentment over corruption, waste and centralised power that meant resources were given out by the government, limiting local solutions to chronic problems like poor drainage. “What we’ve seen is how the state spends our taxes. In the end, it’s always us, the people, who suffer most,” he said. “Same rain, unequal floods, unequal power, and the people are the ones who pay.” While the floods have been indiscriminate, hitting some wealthy Bangkok neighbourhoods, richer families often build higher in a notoriously flood-prone city, resulting in run-off from their properties pouring into the drains at road level where the homes of the less wealthy are located. A Bangkok contractor in one of the city’s more affluent areas said her clients built upwards ahead of each monsoon season. “Those without the means – who cannot afford to raise their foundations or renovate to keep the water out – are left in the lowest spots. When Bangkok floods, that water has to wait for the public drainage system to carry it away,” she told This Week in Asia, requesting anonymity due to her customer base. “And the houses in the lowest spots are, inevitably, the ones where the water sits longest.” The city’s working and middle classes have lost income as shops closed and even the gig economy came to a crawl, as the surging waters caught city authorities off guard. Meanwhile, those hit hardest have struggled without clean water and fresh food for a third day on Monday, including in two areas in eastern Bangkok where the floods have remained neck-high. “People feel angry when they hear ‘I’m so rich’,” said Elevenfinger, whose Klong Toei slum community was flooded. “Every car that’s submerged – some people spent years saving just to buy one. But there’s no compensation, no basic relief. By the time recovery comes, they will have already lost everything.” City Hall has declared Bangkok a disaster zone. Floodwaters still refuse to drain in the capital’s worst-hit eastern parts, exacerbated by continued rain. Parts of Bangkok and the surrounding provinces remained submerged on Monday as flood-stricken communities faced fresh perils from electrocution and encountering snakes flushed out by the drains. Late on Sunday, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was given a close-up view of the simmering resentment that the floods have caused. As he toured Khlong Chan flats, a residential block submerged since early Saturday in Bang Kapi district, some residents catcalled the prime minister, a scion of a construction empire who heads a conservative government stuffed with multimillionaires. Other trapped residents, who had no running water, electricity or fresh food, ironically chanted “I can’t wait to be rich”, a parody of Anutin’s election slogan where he declared that votes for him would ensure everybody became “so rich they wouldn’t know what to do with the money”.

title: 5 men released on bail in UK over suspected US-run airbase plot
description: Five British nationals freed under strict conditions as police track possible links to Iran, Russia or militant groups.
content: Five young British men arrested on explosives and terror charges near a US-operated air force base in England were released on bail Monday, and counterterror detectives said they were investigating “multiple lines of inquiry”, including whether there is a link to Iran. The men were detained early Sunday after three vans were spotted in the countryside near RAF Fairford, a UK-owned base that has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran. Investigators haven’t concluded whether the incident was state-backed. They are investigating a possible link to Iran, Russia or non-state militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners. The five suspects, who haven’t been named, were initially held over suspected explosives offences, and later also arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Police said the men are all British nationals from London and in their 20s. Britain’s national news agency, PA, reported without citing sources that police had not found viable explosives. Announcing that the suspects had been bailed, the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said that the suspects face stringent conditions and “absolutely remain under investigation”. Taylor said lines of inquiry include that the suspected offences were committed by “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”. Iran denied involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” about the incident. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an interview late Monday with Fox News host Sean Hannity that it “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” but did not name a specific country. Residents were evacuated from 85 homes in the village of Whelford near the base on Sunday, and army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine three white vans. The villagers were allowed to return home late Monday afternoon, though a cordon remained around the three vehicles, police said. Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of the government’s COBRA emergency committee on Monday “to make sure we have the full picture” of the incident, he said. It was unclear whether the arrested men had been on security services’ radar. Local residents described seeing heightened security around RAF Fairford in recent days, with heavy vehicles parked across entrance gates. US President Donald Trump said the suspects had been detained following cooperation between the US and Britain, and had been “under view” for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about “suspicious vehicles” near the base. A local farmer said she called police after seeing three oddly parked vans as she drove home late Saturday night, and that nearby she came across “a large group of men”, some with their faces covered. She said they scattered when they saw her vehicle. She declined to be identified to protect her identity because she was describing what she saw as potential security lapses. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the farmer “did exactly the right thing” by calling police but only had “a partial view” of the operation. The arrests came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British intelligence services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on UK soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50 per cent in the six months to December 2025. Britain didn’t join the US and Israel in the Iran war, which began on Febuary 28, and initially denied Trump’s request to use bases in the UK to strike Iran. But then Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the US use bases in Britain for what he called “defensive” operations against Iran’s missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on UK interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf. American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 160km (100 miles) west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict. Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the UK and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue. Several people also have been charged with plotting to commit arson in the UK on behalf of Russia-linked groups. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the incident is a “reminder of the threats our country faces”. Miliband met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations in New York last week and told him that “Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil”, according to a UK readout of the conversation. The US Air Force said that its personnel on the base “remain vigilant”, but “for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures”. Rubio thanked the British authorities for their cooperation and help in breaking up the alleged plot, which he called a “very serious situation”. He said the British had been “very cooperative” but declined to comment in more detail, particularly about the fact that the suspects had been released on bail. “I would argue that they’ve been very cooperative and very helpful on something that’s a very serious incident,” Rubio said in the Fox News interview, adding that the British response had been “appropriate”. The US embassy in London has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security. Trump said that authorities had the suspects “under view for a long time and we got them”. “It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday.

title: China deploys advanced WZ-7 drone for first time near Scarborough Shoal
description: The high-altitude reconnaissance platform took part in exercises around the disputed South China Sea flashpoint.
content: Beijing deployed its advanced WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone in the South China Sea for the first time during drills near the disputed Scarborough Shoal at the weekend. The People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command announced on Sunday that it had conducted joint air and naval exercises in the waters and airspace around the shoal earlier in the day. Scarborough Shoal – a coral atoll known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines – has emerged as a major flashpoint between the rival claimants in recent years. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Sunday that the WZ-7 long-range reconnaissance drone took part in the exercises and operated alongside various types of fighter aircraft taking off from multiple airfields. It marked the first official confirmation of the deployment of the WZ-7, which is also called the Xianglong or “Soaring Dragon”, in a real-time operation. “The WZ-7 provides imagery intelligence and can be used for both strategic and tactical reconnaissance. Its main missions include border reconnaissance, patrols over territorial waters and exclusive economic zones, and surveillance of key areas,” CCTV said. The WZ-7 made its first public appearance at the Zhuhai air show in 2021. Japan’s defence ministry said in January 2023 that a WZ-7 had flown through the Miyako Strait southwest of Okinawa. According to specifications released by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, the drone’s designer, the WZ-7 is 14 metres (46 feet) long, 3.9 metres high and has a wingspan of 22.8 metres. It has a cruising altitude of more than 18,000 metres, a mission range of more than 4,500km (2,796 miles) and can fly for more than 6.5 hours at a stretch. CCTV also described the WZ-7 as “the world’s second unmanned aircraft capable of freely crossing civilian air routes”. Civilian airliners typically cruise between 8,000 and 12,000 metres, a height at which most drones cannot operate, according to Fu Qianshao, a military analyst and former People’s Liberation Army Air Force officer. The first drone widely regarded as being able to conduct missions at this height is the United States’ RQ-4 Global Hawk, a high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned reconnaissance aircraft that was introduced in 2001. Fu said the WZ-7’s ability to loiter at high altitude for extended periods allowed it to provide real-time battlefield situational awareness over large stretches of sea. “The WZ-7 does not need to be deployed at bases in the South China Sea. It has long endurance and a high flight speed, so it can be deployed directly from land-based airfields along China’s coast and remain on station for extended periods,” Fu said. Footage released by CCTV on Sunday showed a WZ-7 taking off from a military base in southern China before heading towards the South China Sea. Beijing has repeatedly showcased its latest unmanned equipment in the area around Scarborough Shoal.
