Fu said he believed the waters around the shoal were well suited to be a testing ground for China’s latest gear. “The recovery of some shipborne fixed-wing drones is subject to certain limitations in the South China Sea, while high-altitude, long-endurance drones are well suited to operating there,” Fu said. “There are large areas of international waters in the South China Sea, and it is also a busy transport route. Beijing needs to monitor foreign ships and aircraft while also providing support for the safe navigation of its own vessels. Such complex mission conditions are suitable for new equipment to explore and test its capabilities.” Zhang Chi, a professor at the PLA National Defence University, told CCTV on Sunday that the exercises were primarily aimed at the Philippines. Scarborough Shoal has been under Chinese control since 2012. To reinforce its sovereignty claim, China in 2024 announced baselines for the territorial waters surrounding the shoal. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the baseline serves as the starting line along the coast from which a nation measures the extent of its territorial sea, exclusive economic zones and other maritime zones. The Philippines has periodically sent ships and aircraft into the area in moves intended to challenge China’s claim. In July, Manila submitted a chart of its baselines around the shoal to the United Nations.

title: Meet Kyle Clark, who plays Cam Dillinger in Netflix’s Crew Girl
description: Before starring in the teen drama opposite Miku Martineau, the Canadian actor appeared in shows like Riverdale and The Baby-Sitters Club.
content: After the success of teen romances like The Summer I Turned Pretty and My Life with the Walter Boys, viewers have a new love triangle to obsess over. Crew Girl is a Canadian coming-of-age series focusing on Teagan Tao (Miku Martineau), who joins an all-boys rowing team at Easton Prep after a family scandal forces her to move to the East Coast with her mother, Ella Tao (Jessica Paré). She’s the new coxswain, and vying for her heart are two rowers: the entitled yet charismatic Josh Regis (Sam Braun) and the talented underdog Cam Dillinger (Kyle Clark). As of Monday afternoon, the show is the second most-watched English television show on Netflix worldwide and has already been renewed for a second season. It has also brought major attention to the leading stars, especially Clark. So, what do we know about Kyle Clark? What is Kyle Clark’s background? Not much is known about Clark’s background, except that he was born in Canada and grew up in the Canadian Prairies, per TV Insider. In a July interview with Teen Vogue, he spoke about his father, who worked as a welder, and said his own upbringing helped him relate to his character, whose father is a mechanic. While his real age is unknown, his Crew Girl character is 16. Where have you seen him before? Although Crew Girl can be considered Clark’s breakthrough, he started acting professionally almost a decade ago. He made his screen debut with the 2017 television movie Switched for Christmas and went on to appear in shows like Riverdale – where he played a young Forsythe Jones – and Netflix’s The Baby-Sitters Club, where he took on the role of Scott. More recently, you may have seen Clark in the films Mommy Meanest (2024) and Girl in the Cellar (2025). How did he land the role of Cam Dillinger? Clark’s audition for Cam Dillinger seemingly had a great impact on the final version of the character. Speaking to What’s On Netflix, showrunner Vivian Lin revealed that Cam was initially supposed to be “very broody”. “[Clark] came in and read for that version, and then he brought this warmth and boyishness to Cam, which kind of translates, and then we realised that was the missing ingredient to Cam,” she gushed. Braun and Clark auditioned for Hulu’s The Hardy Boys adaptation in 2019 and stayed in touch despite not getting cast. “When I heard that Kyle got the part for Cam, I was like, ‘No way! This is finally happening,’” Braun told Teen Vogue. The actors learned rowing at the Vancouver Rowing Club together before Crew Girl’s filming began.

title: Hong Kong finds gold-trading leader in former exchange executive Bryan Chan
description: He will head Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing (HKPMCC), a wholly government-owned entity established in January.
content: The Hong Kong government has appointed Bryan Chan Ping-keung, a former executive at bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), as CEO to lead the development and operation of the city’s new central clearing and settlement system for gold. Chan will head Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing (HKPMCC), a wholly government-owned entity established in January to run the clearing system for precious metals. His appointment would take effect on October 2 for a three-year term, according to a statement released on Monday. Chan would be expected to deliver efficient and reliable clearing and settlement services for over-the-counter gold transactions, work closely with industry participants and collaborate with the government to build an international-standard gold trading ecosystem, the government said. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu, who is also chairman of HKPMCC, expressed confidence in Chan’s leadership. Hui said that Chan would enhance system operations, collaborate with stakeholders and facilitate global market participation, strengthening Hong Kong’s influence in Asian gold trading. The initiative aligns with goals highlighted in the city’s first five-year plan and the 2026 policy address to leverage gold for commodity market expansion. The central clearing system is scheduled for launch in the first quarter of next year. HKPMCC’s board includes representatives from the Shanghai Gold Exchange, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Securities and Futures Commission and 11 banks. Chan served as an administrative officer from 1988 to 2000, when he worked as the principal assistant secretary for financial services, responsible for securities and derivatives market policies, as well as the merger that created HKEX, and its listing. He joined HKEX in 2000 and was later promoted to managing director and co-head of equities and fixed income currency in the global markets division. Chan possessed deep knowledge and extensive experience in financial markets, market infrastructure and government operations, alongside outstanding management and leadership capabilities, Hui said.

title: Sweden’s Magdalena Andersson ends government-formation talks with no result
description: It means caretaker PM Ulf Kristersson may get another chance to form a coalition. He has promised to bring in the far-right.
content: Sweden’s election winner Magdalena Andersson said she is not currently able to form a government, underscoring the difficulty of building a coalition in the fragmented parliament after the election earlier this month. The Social Democrat leader returned her mandate to explore forming a government after the Left Party decided to support a centre-right candidate for parliament speaker in a vote later on Monday, she told reporters. The move does not necessarily mean Andersson will not be the next prime minister. She could still get another shot at forming a government if her rivals also fail. The latest development could give current caretaker Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson – in charge of the country since October 2022 – of the Moderates a chance to try to stitch together a coalition. He has promised to bring in the far-right Sweden Democrats. His bloc has 173 seats in parliament against 176 for the centre-left, meaning he would need to convince the Centre Party to switch sides for a majority. It has said it would prefer Andersson as prime minister, but also that it will not accept the Left Party in government. The Left Party, meanwhile, has said it will not back a government it is not part of. “The Left Party has chosen to work with the Moderate Party and now we’ll have to see how far that cooperation goes,” Andersson said. “We now need to see whether this new cooperation can lead to the formation of a government.” Under the Swedish system, a prime minister does not need backing from a majority of lawmakers but needs to ensure most members of parliament do not actively oppose them. There can be four parliamentary votes on a new prime minister before a new election must be called. Left Party leader Nooshi Dadgostar said Andersson’s view that her party had teamed up with the Moderates was incorrect. She told Swedish daily Expressen that the centre-right candidate for speaker, Andreas Norlén, deserved a third term in the role because he was experienced and had overseen previous government formation negotiations “with dignity”. Norlen belongs to Kristersson’s Moderate Party and has been Speaker since 2018.

title: Opinion | The worst Asian Games ever? Japan has failed to raise the bar in Nagoya
description: Three years on from a celebrated edition in Hangzhou, athletes have been left bemoaning a ‘sad and mediocre’ experience.
content: There have been times over the past week or so when you were left with the impression that Japan is holding the Asian Games only because everyone was too polite to say no several years ago. The rather haphazard nature of the organisation, and the tens of thousands of empty seats in venues around the Aichi-Nagoya region, is not indicative of a place that has wholeheartedly embraced its role as host to a sporting event that, in terms of competitor numbers at least, is bigger than the Olympics. Local media has expressed the fear that Japan could host “the worst Games ever”, while enthusiasm among residents for the whole event could be described as ambivalent at best. Organisers have conceded that not many tickets had been sold, and in some sports and for next weekend’s closing ceremony, fewer than 60 per cent of seats were taken. So, to suggest the Games have not been as good as in Hangzhou would be to understate the situation, and the issues go far deeper than just rows over athlete accommodation. Still, it’s hard not to compare the cruise ship and converted containers that are being used this year to the soaring blocks of flats for 12,000 people, dining halls, fitness centres and health clinics that stood as shiny new advertisements for China in 2023. In the days following the opening ceremony, there was little said about the mounting problems, although Satoshi Murate, the local organising committee’s secretary general, did eventually issue something approaching a mea culpa. “Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and ⁠make sure they don’t happen again,” he said on Saturday. “I think you can see that accommodation and transport have improved greatly compared ‌with the early days.” A little more than a day later, and India’s badminton star H.S. Prannoy was describing the whole experience as sad and dismissing the Games as “a very mediocre event”. “Straight from China, you expect things to be better three-four years later but in this event, [it went] downwards,” he said. “A lot of [athletes] ‌had ⁠difficult experiences in terms of accommodation and transport.” Those continuing failings aside, the event succeeds more because of the unfailing politeness and work of the volunteers, and a mend-and-make-do attitude among those in attendance, than anything else. Not all of the blame can be laid at the feet of the host nation; there is more than enough to go around for the Olympic Council of Asia and GL Events, the French company handed a 63 billion yen (US$401 million) contract that was apparently awarded because its bid was “overwhelmingly cheap”. The OCA, meanwhile, is the one who made the head-scratching decision to add sports that have no business being in the Games. Take padel, for example; popular enough as an amateur activity, but in reality, a game for people who aren’t good enough at tennis to compete at the highest level. Now the winners in both get gold medals. Meanwhile, the pasty-faced protagonists sweating their way through video games might be doing something, but it isn’t physically strenuous. That at least has been rectified, and esports will not be part of the Games going forward. The issue, of course, is that with just six days left, athletes are still being stranded without buses, spectators still aren’t packing out venues, interest locally appears lukewarm and while being labelled the worst Games ever would be a stretch, Japan certainly hasn’t done anything to raise the bar.

title: Review | Viral Korean dance group brings its high-energy show to Hong Kong
description: More Blackpink than Balanchine, Yunbyul Ballet Company’s Gat is a lively production that shines during its group numbers.
content: The Korean wave shows no sign of abating. From K-pop to kimchi, cosmetic brands to television dramas, Korean culture is everywhere. Among the country’s many international exports are outstanding ballet dancers, including St Petersburg-based Mariinsky Ballet’s biggest male star, Kim Kimin, while Seoul is home to three large-scale ballet companies. Yunbyul Ballet Company is a newcomer to the scene, founded in 2022 by artistic director Yun Byul who, like resident choreographer Park So-yun, returned to South Korea after an international dancing career. Gat is a breakthrough production created in 2024 that has propelled the company into the limelight. After going viral on social media and selling out a national tour of Korea earlier this year, Hong Kong is one of its first appearances overseas. It was easy to see why the lively, high-energy show with a strong Korean feel has been such a hit with audiences, and a packed house at the Kwai Tsing Theatre gave it a rapturous reception. The quirky concept offers nine scenes inspired by different types of classic Korean headgear and explores the connotations and stereotypes these hats represent in traditional culture. The most impressive sections were two versions of “Heunglip” – a traditional black hat with a wide brim and high crown that is also known as gat, hence the show’s title – which are instantly recognisable from numerous Korean films and TV shows. Though they are traditionally only worn by men, the production has one sequence for female dancers, highlighting sharp, precise pointework, followed later in the show by an all-male interpretation featuring powerful movements and big jumps. Another stand-out was the all-male “Jeongjagwan”, a witty trio led by Yun himself with some spectacular moves – and exceptionally elaborate hats. Park’s choreography is firmly based on ballet technique, incorporating a few traditional Korean elements and showing a nice contrast between strong, rhythmic footwork and soft, flowing arm movements. While the company’s stated aim is to “reinterpret classical ballet through a contemporary lens”, the lens is distinctly 21st century Korean in character – and it must be said that the overall effect is more Blackpink than Balanchine. There are two solo pieces but surprisingly little partnering apart from one brief duet, and the most artistically ambitious sequence, “Muninhwa”, was the least effective. Where Gat shone was in the group numbers, which were polished, professional and delivered with exemplary discipline, culminating in a rousing finale with the whole troupe on stage. Choi Young-jin’s chic, stylish costumes, Choi Min-ji’s well-constructed score and Choi Won-hyuk’s elegant lighting design completed an accomplished, entertaining production. Gat, Yunbyul Ballet Company, Kwai Tsing Theatre Auditorium. Reviewed: September 26.

title: US firms in China return focus to local rivals as bilateral tensions ebb
description: As relationship stabilises, bilateral ties drop to second place among concerns of US companies, according to business chambers.
content: Stabilising ties between the world’s two largest economies, fortified by US President Donald Trump’s hosting of his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington last week, have soothed the nerves of American businesses in China, which no longer see frayed bilateral ties as their primary challenge, according to prominent business chambers. “For enterprises, the stability of trade policies and export control measures will help reduce uncertainty,” said Eric Zheng, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai, adding that fallout from the Sino-US relationship had dropped from the “first challenge” faced by member companies to the “second major challenge”. Local competition was now the primary issue facing US enterprises in China, Zheng told Chinese state media over the weekend. After several months of engagement between Xi and Trump, the share of surveyed members citing US-China tensions as a top challenge fell 13 points to 53 per cent, according to the chamber’s latest China Business Report published earlier this month. The share of members expressing confidence in the five-year business environment rebounded 17 points to 58 per cent, the report said. This year’s survey underscored the impact of geopolitical stability on business sentiment, according to the chamber, which added that the outlook was now considerably more positive than it had been in several years. During Xi’s whirlwind 43-hour stay in Washington that began on Wednesday, the two countries further stabilised relations and made space for continued contact, including a new framework for dialogue on artificial intelligence. Other key deliverables included a two-month tariff truce extension to January 10, a finalised Board of Trade mechanism, two-way tariff reductions for US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods and a mutual affirmation to characterise ties as “constructive strategic stability”. The White House published a fact sheet on Friday, revealing that China would buy American coal and continue to work on US concerns over rare earth export controls and the flow of fentanyl precursors. Furthermore, it released more details about working procedures, frameworks and lists of imports under the Board of Trade. James Zimmerman, chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce in China, hailed these useful mechanisms for working through specific commercial issues, as well as the continued, regular leader-level engagement. “The fact sheet points to areas of continued economic cooperation, including the implementation of the Boards of Trade and Investment and work on tariff treatment and agricultural market access,” Zimmerman said. “For businesses, these are all useful mechanisms, although much will depend on how they are implemented.” Both presidents, meanwhile, confirmed more in-person interactions this year, with a pledge from Trump to attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November and Xi’s intended trip to Miami for the G20 summit in December. “Maintaining regular leader-level engagement and open channels of communication is important in itself, given the fact that companies need stability and predictability for long-term investment decisions,” Zimmerman said. The extension of the current tariff truce arrangements – albeit short-term – would still provide some continuity for companies, Zimmerman added, expressing hope that the stability would lead to progress on broader issues affecting the business environment. “These include market access, regulatory transparency and investment conditions,” he said. In a separate statement to the South China Morning Post, Zheng added that American companies were feeling more upbeat. “There is ample room for cooperation, and the differences that remain can be resolved through dialogue,” he said, adding that as relations steadied, sentiment among American companies had clearly improved. “We hope that trajectory holds, and that American companies in China can continue to serve this market and the wider world,” Zheng said. AmCham Shanghai also said that, with bilateral ties stabilising, it was working on practical cooperation, including in food and agriculture. “The complementarity is natural, and American producers are eager to sell,” the chamber said. “This industry is the focus of our pavilion at the upcoming China International Import Expo [in Shanghai in November], which we are organising for the fourth consecutive year with the US Department of Agriculture.” Earlier this month, a joint delegation from AmCham China and AmCham Shanghai also took a week-long “DC Doorknock” trip, taking on-the-ground perspectives of member companies in China to stakeholders in Washington, including US trade officials, Congress members and business leaders.

title: China professor sparks debate by claiming one-third of youth are ‘unsuitable for marriage’
description: While some agree marriage is not a mandatory milestone, others argue his view oversimplifies a complex issue.
content: A viral interview with Chinese professor-influencer Liang Yongan has reignited the debate over China’s evolving marriage norms after he argued that at least one-third of people in the country are ill-suited for marriage. Liang, 72, a professor of Chinese language and literature at Fudan University in Shanghai, has emerged as a significant voice on mainland social media, attracting nearly one million followers with his candid observations on youth culture, relationships, and social change. The remarks originated from a three-year-old interview that recently resurfaced online. “At least one-third of people are not suited for marriage because marriage requires the ability to care for and make sacrifices for another person,” Liang stated. His comments come as more young Chinese embrace independent lifestyles, with the “single economy” driving growth in solo dining, emotional companionship, and pet-related consumption. Liang argued that marriage necessitates commitment and compromise from both partners, urging young people to “grow first, then fall in love” by developing a stronger sense of self before entering relationships. The resurfaced remarks quickly sparked a lively debate online. Some users supported his view, asserting that marriage should not be treated as an obligatory life milestone. “Finally, an expert has articulated what many people are thinking,” one commenter wrote, adding: “Self-centred individuals should refrain from entering marriage, as they may harm their partners.” Others questioned whether his argument oversimplified a more complex issue. “Does stating that one-third of people are unsuitable for marriage grant those who choose not to marry a ‘free pass’, or does it simply elevate the criteria for marriage?” another user wondered. The discussion reflects broader shifts in China’s attitudes towards marriage. Official data revealed that marriage registrations fell by 7.5 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, while divorce registrations rose by 3.9 per cent to 1.38 million. Authorities have implemented measures to encourage marriage, including streamlined registration processes and incentives such as free health checks and consumption vouchers for newlyweds. Some local governments have relocated registration services into unconventional spaces, including banks, shopping centres, and underground stations to facilitate nuptials. However, critics argue that such measures do not address deeper structural issues, such as employment uncertainty, childcare costs, housing pressures, and work-life balance. Liang has long explored questions of love, youth, and personal development. He first gained widespread attention in 2017 after a speech regarding how young people approach romantic relationships. He has described contemporary society as entering a “golden age of being single,” suggesting that young people’s choices are influenced by various factors, including concerns over emotional hurt and lifestyle changes such as increased dependence on digital devices. Drawing on literature and film, including Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice, Liang suggests that meaningful relationships often arise not from deliberate pursuit but through personal growth, self-awareness, and maturity. He has even proposed that 40 may be a more suitable age to pursue love, as greater life experience can lead to a clearer understanding of oneself. Some critics, however, have pointed out the limitations of Liang’s views in addressing the complexities of real-life relationships. “The literary and film examples he references often reflect idealised relationship models that remain detached from the intricate realities of economic pressures, family responsibilities, and gender dynamics,” one observer noted.

title: The new Posh and Becks? Meet Sasha Attwood, partner of Manchester City’s Jack Grealish
description: Currently on loan at Everton, the footballer shares a baby girl with his childhood sweetheart, and they walked the red carpet at the Oasis film premiere in London earlier this month.
content: Manchester City footballer Jack Grealish, currently on loan at fellow Premier League club Everton, hit the red carpet earlier this month, when the UK film Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger premiered at Cineworld Leicester Square in London. Speaking to Manchester Evening News on the red carpet before the Oasis tour was officially announced, the self-described “massive Oasis fan” said he was eager for the reunion: “If it happens, I can’t wait. I’ll be at more than two shows.” Standing by Grealish’s side at the September 7 premiere was his long-time girlfriend Sasha Attwood, who was crowned the “Wag queen of holidays” by The Sun in 2025 after reportedly taking 10 luxury trips in a year. But who is Sasha Attwood and how long has she been with the 31-year-old football player? Read on to find out. What is Sasha Attwood’s background? Sasha Attwood has worked as a model since she was scouted at 13 while on a shopping trip with her mother in Birmingham, per The Sun. She later appeared in campaigns for various brands, including British department store chain House of Fraser. Currently, the 30-year-old, who goes by Sasha Rebecca on social media, has amassed over 306,000 followers on Instagram. She signed with Elite Model Management in 2021 and has worked with brands such as Boohoo and PrettyLittleThing, according to The Sun. How did Jack Grealish and Sasha Attwood meet? Grealish met Attwood when they were secondary school students at St Peter’s Catholic School in Solihull, a market town southeast of Birmingham in England. The couple have reportedly been together since they were 16. While Grealish and Attwood kept their relationship relatively private, the latter was spotted supporting the footballer during England’s Euro 2020 games and sadly became the subject of internet trolls, reportedly receiving death threats. “I was receiving 200 death threats a day. I’m not exaggerating when I say that,” Attwood said in a video on her YouTube channel. “I had so many messages every single day. I still get them now, all day every day.” They have a baby girl In September 2024, Attwood and Grealish welcomed their first child together, a girl they named Mila Rose Grealish. The baby mama shared a photo of her newborn holding her hand on Instagram in October 2024, with a caption saying “The most special moment of my life”. The childhood sweethearts, dubbed the “new Posh and Becks”, have yet to tie the knot. Attwood reportedly leads a luxurious lifestyle, having spent holidays in Paris, Portugal, Ibiza, Dubai and other destinations in a single year, The Sun reported.

title: India’s Supreme Court urges accountability over rapes
description: Over 80 rapes are reported across the nation each day. Last month, a teenager said she was gang-raped in a bus by the driver ‌and conductor.
content: India’s Supreme Court on ⁠Monday pushed for ⁠accountability over a recent spate of rape cases in the national capital and neighbouring districts, saying they reflected a “failure of law enforcement”, local media reported. Hundreds of students protested in Delhi last week demanding better safety for women after a teenager said she was gang-raped by three men at a city park. Protesters, most of them female, held placards and shouted slogans while marching near the crime scene. “Our body is our own,” some placards said. Others demanded freedom to go out at night without fear. Last month, a 17-year-old girl ⁠was allegedly gang-raped in a moving bus by the driver ‌and conductor, local media reported. The Supreme Court said public spaces, including parks and buses, ‌could not become “high-risk” zones because of poor lighting and surveillance and ⁠other basic facilities, legal news website Live Law reported. The court said ‌fixing accountability was necessary and directed its administration to file a public ‌interest petition on ‌the issue for the court to pursue, legal ‌news website Bar and Bench said. Sexual violence is ⁠a major problem across India, with more than 80 rapes reported ⁠to police every day, according to the National Crime Records Bureau. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta ‌told a TV ‌channel last week that there had been lapses and vowed to improve security, while Delhi Police said it had increased “visible policing” and intensified patrolling.

title: How Mary Jane Veloso’s case exposes gaps in Filipino migrant protection
description: Advocates say her case spotlights the dangers Philippine workers face overseas and Manila’s inability to sufficiently protect its citizens.
content: Migrant rights advocates have hailed the release of Filipino trafficking victim Mary Jane Veloso after 16 years in detention as a victorious milestone, but warn that her case exposes the dangers that still confront many vulnerable workers overseas. After coming harrowingly close to being executed years ago in Indonesia, Veloso walked free on Friday night from the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City, grateful for the absolute pardon granted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Marcos’ action removes the remaining criminal liability from Veloso’s drug conviction and restores her civil and political rights, closing a long chapter that began with her 2010 arrest in Yogyakarta after 2.6kg of heroin was found hidden in her luggage – drugs she insisted she did not knowingly carry. The single mother of two said she was deceived by recruiters who promised her a job abroad as a domestic helper – leading advocates to argue she was a victim of human trafficking. Veloso was set to be executed by a 13-member firing squad in 2015 but won a dramatic last-minute reprieve after then Philippine president Benigno Aquino III appealed to his Indonesian counterpart to spare her, allowing her to testify how a criminal syndicate duped her into being a drug mule. In 2024, officials in both countries signed a “practical arrangement” to repatriate Veloso to the Philippines, as part of the Indonesian government’s new policy for sending back foreign prisoners. The agreement allowed Veloso’s sentence to be governed by Philippine laws upon her return. Marcos said then that “everything is on the table” regarding granting Veloso clemency. In June, Veloso testified for the first time in person against her recruiters for human trafficking and illegal recruitment charges. Her lawyer, Edre Olalia of the National Union of People’s Lawyers, said Veloso was shaken but otherwise well during that time. “She was OK, but of course she was anxious and nervous … you have to marshal all your mental faculties to go back to the details of something you want to forget,” Olalia told This Week in Asia. Olalia said Veloso’s family was overjoyed at the news of the pardon. “Her mother was crying, her father was also beside himself, everybody was shouting, the kids were jumping for joy – you’d expect that kind of reaction after all these years.” For him and the National Union of People’s Lawyers, Veloso’s hard-earned freedom was a “miracle”. Labour groups and migrant welfare advocates welcomed Veloso’s freedom. “Mary Jane’s long-awaited freedom is a testament to the power of the people’s collective action,” overseas Filipino workers alliance Migrante International said in a statement on Friday. The Anti-Death Penalty Network (ADPAN) echoed the sentiment. “We commend Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jnr’s decision to grant absolute pardon to Mary Jane Veloso, just days before the World Day Against the Death Penalty,” it said on Friday. ‘One of many’ Advocates tell This Week in Asia that Veloso’s experience highlights the institutionalisation of labour export practices that have been in place for decades. Chat Dimaano, spokesman for Migrante International, said the case showed Manila’s inability to sufficiently protect overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), arguing there were “thousands” still abroad with “no outcry like there was for Mary Jane Veloso”. An estimated 8,000 to 10,000 Filipinos leave the Philippines every day to seek greener pastures abroad, according to Migrante statistics. Olalia agreed. “Mary Jane is just one of many, and there are other issues that should be addressed – why our countrymen are [working] away from their families and their children, and why our government didn’t help them in the first place.” “The fight is not yet over” for the OFWs still awaiting help, said Tom Temprosa, regional director of ADPAN. The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), an executive agency under the government, has promised to help Veloso and her family rebuild their lives with enterprise capital, skills training, livelihood starter kits and counselling. According to Dimaano, Veloso’s plight underscores how overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) are treated as second-class citizens in their host countries, often paid much less and afforded fewer protections than locals – a situation he claims is enabled by agreements between the Philippines and other countries. “If the government exports you like a commodity … the flip side is that the country you’re going to also sees you the same way,” Dimaano said. A July report by Amnesty International documented widespread abuses, including sexual violence, that Filipino domestic helpers faced in Saudi Arabia under its kafala system, which allows employers to control their entry, residence and ability to leave the country. DMW figures as of 2025 also show that about 3,000 Filipino workers abroad face various criminal, immigration, or labour-related charges globally, with 25 facing death row. The highest number of incarcerations is concentrated in the Middle East, where 1,215 OFWs across the region are reported to be behind bars. Most of the detentions concern immigration violations, local labour disputes, or strict local code infractions such as social media or cybercrime laws. “That number is quite staggering for a country that is sending its people to work abroad,” Temprosa said. In the United States, at least 200 Filipino migrant workers – both on land and at sea – have been unjustly targeted and detained, with some deported, according to Jom Dolor, deputy secretary general of Migrante USA. “Unless the Philippine government has the political will to strengthen the oversight of recruitment agencies and practices, and assert diplomatic leadership to ensure the rights and welfare of Filipinos overseas, we anticipate more Mary Jane Velosos waiting to happen,” Dolor said.

title: Hong Kong customs arrests 2, seizes HK$290,000 of ‘slimming injections’ from Japan
description: Man, 45, who collected parcel and woman, 41, who is named as consignee are released on bail, authorities say.
content: Hong Kong customs officers have seized 400 so-called slimming injections imported from Japan, with an estimated market value of about HK$290,000 (US$36,970), and arrested two local residents in an operation earlier this month. The case came to light on September 5, when officers intercepted a suspicious postal packet imported from Japan at the Air Mail Centre. “Upon inspection, customs officers found and seized 400 anti-obesity injection vials suspected to contain Part 1 poisons from the consignment,” customs said on Monday. The Pharmacy and Poisons Regulations contain the Poisons List, which sets out substances subject to regulation for their sale and possession. Items on the list can only be sold at authorised premises and those listed under Part 1 can only be sold by a registered pharmacist or in their presence and under their supervision. In a subsequent investigation, customs officers arrested two locals connected with the case – a man, 45, who collected the parcel and a woman, 41, who was the named consignee. “An investigation is ongoing. The two arrested persons have been released on bail,” the Customs and Excise Department said. In a similar case in June, customs seized 161 vials of weight-loss injections worth about HK$150,000 in postal packets from Japan and at the consignee’s address. The woman consignee, 31, was arrested. In Hong Kong, almost all anti-obesity drugs are prescription-only medication and should only be used under the close supervision of a doctor, according to the Department of Health. Under the Import and Export Ordinance, anyone importing pharmaceutical products and medication without a valid import licence commits an offence. The maximum penalty upon conviction is a fine of HK$500,000 and imprisonment for two years. And according to the Pharmacy and Poisons Ordinance, any person who possesses any poison included in Part 1 of the Poisons List other than in accordance with provisions commits an offence. The maximum penalty upon conviction is a fine of HK$100,000 and imprisonment for two years. Customs also urged the public to report any suspected smuggling activities to the customs’ hotline at 1828080 or its dedicated crime-reporting email account crimereport@customs.gov.hk, or the eform.cefs.gov.hk/form/ced002/ online form.

title: Hong Kong cracks down on tourists abusing visas to run one-stop shop services
description: Immigration Department says four women, aged 20 to 31, arrested for allegedly breaching conditions of stay to offer tourist services.
content: Hong Kong immigration authorities are cracking down on tourists abusing their visas to run unlicensed one-stop shops offering cosmetic, photography and tour guide services. Li Kwing-chiu, a task force commander with the Immigration Department, said on Monday that four women, aged 20 to 31, had been arrested for allegedly breaching their conditions of stay by running a one-stop shop that charged several hundred Hong Kong dollars a day for various services. The suspects entered the city on tourist visas on Sunday and Monday, he added. “We urge visitors and residents to be cautious when using social media to purchase services and avoid turning to unknown sources out of convenience, as this may risk breaking the law,” he said. Li added the department had noticed posts on several popular social media platforms offering a “one-stop shop” for make-up, photography and tour guide services in Hong Kong. The South China Morning Post found the adverts on mainland Chinese platform RedNote, with prices varying depending on whether the photoshoots were held inside or outdoors. Clients were asked to cover the service providers’ travel and visa fees. The adverts offered photoshoots in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, and said that clients would be given advice on how to pose for pictures. As part of their investigation, immigration officers posed as potential customers to contact the suspects and book the service packages. The four women were later arrested when they entered Hong Kong on tourist visas. “They were operating using their personal social media accounts and offered cheap rates to attract customers,” Li said. Among the arrested women, one was a make-up artist who allegedly charged HK$700 (US$89) per day for her services. The other three were photographers who also acted as tour guides, charging HK$400 to HK$600 per package. The women allegedly said they could plan a tour for their clients in tourist hotspots such as the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront, the West Kowloon Cultural District and local theme parks, as well as offer styling advice and take photos for them. Li warned that visitors to the city were prohibited from paid or unpaid labour without the express permission of the director of immigration. Anyone caught breaking the law could face a HK$50,000 fine and two years in prison, he added. In September last year, the Immigration Department arrested eight mainland visitors on suspicion of working illegally in Hong Kong as photographers and make-up artists at popular tourist destinations. Two local women were also arrested in the same operation on suspicion of partnering with these illegal workers and helping visitors breach their conditions of stay. In Hong Kong, employers caught hiring illegal workers risk a fine of HK$350,000 and three years’ imprisonment.

title: ByteDance grabs one-fifth of China’s data centre capacity as AI drives infrastructure boom
description: SemiAnalysis estimates that China has more than 24GW of delivered data centre capacity, with another 20GW in the pipeline.
content: ByteDance accounts for roughly one-fifth of China’s delivered data centre capacity, making the TikTok owner the country’s largest tenant and a main driver of its artificial intelligence buildout, according to new estimates by research firm SemiAnalysis. The estimate comes from the firm’s tracking of more than 1,000 facilities in China operated by over 60 companies. ByteDance rents nearly all of its data centre footprint, SemiAnalysis said. Its AI products include Doubao, an assistant that ByteDance says has hundreds of millions of users, and Seedance, a video generation model. While ByteDance’s financials remain undisclosed as a private company, capital spending by its listed peers has surged. Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and Baidu deployed a combined US$20 billion towards capital expenditure in the second quarter, more than double the figure from a year earlier, according to the report published on Friday. All three tech giants posted negative free cash flow in the same quarter for the first time on record. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. SemiAnalysis estimates that China has more than 24 gigawatts (GW) of delivered data centre capacity. Its model separately tracks about 20GW in the pipeline and another 30GW in announced projects. For comparison, the firm projects 56GW of capacity in the United States by the end of 2026, against about 15GW in the rest of Asia-Pacific and 14GW in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. That expansion is taking place alongside high vacancy rates at older facilities. The report traces the mismatch partly to the industry’s roots in telecoms: China’s three state-owned carriers still own about a third of national data centre capacity. Many were built to rent small numbers of low-power racks to individual customers and cannot easily accommodate the power demands of AI servers, the report said. Newer facilities leased in bulk to cloud and AI companies are filling more quickly. “The AI era is wholesale. The legacy retail stock is not participating,” SemiAnalysis said. The availability of chips presents a further constraint. Goldman Sachs said in a July research note that the pace at which Chinese customers occupied new data centre space had been slower than expected in the first half of 2026, probably because supplies of both domestic and imported chips were tight. China added 595 eflops of intelligent computing power during the first half, below the 802 eflops added in the second half of 2025, according to figures cited by the bank. The increase brought China’s total intelligent computing capacity to 2,185 eflops by the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. An eflop is one quintillion floating-point operations per second. Goldman estimated the first-half increase was equivalent to about 0.7GW of AI-related data centre capacity being occupied. It still expected China’s overall data centre demand to grow at a compound annual rate of 20 per cent from 2025 to 2028.

title: MTV VMAs: Madonna leads wins, Taylor Swift makes history and Dolly Parton honoured
description: MTV’s ⁠annual Video Music Awards on Sunday saw new records and old greats.
content:
The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday saw Taylor Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia” ⁠claim the most prestigious trophy, with the singer dedicating the honour to the late country music legend Dolly Parton.
Swift took home three awards at this year’s VMAs, bringing her career total to an unmatched 33. She had previously been tied with Beyonce at 30 awards apiece.
The music video for “Ophelia”, the first single off The Life of a Showgirl album, was named video of the year.
As she held her newest Moon Person trophy, ‌Swift praised Parton as “the ultimate showgirl” who told stories that were “so vivid and so rich”.
“I think that we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time,” Swift said.
Parton, an award-winning country singer, songwriter and businesswoman, died in August at the age of 80.
Earlier in the ceremony, Swift was awarded the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honours. The 36-year-old has written and directed 18 videos of her roughly 60 videos during her career. Her most recent single, “Patient Zero,” debuted during the ceremony. The video starred Dakota Johnson ⁠and Colin Farrell.
She also won best direction for her “Opalite” video.
The VMAs were broadcast live on CBS and MTV and streamed on Paramount+. The award ceremony was hosted by Snoop ‌Dogg. Winners in the top categories were selected by fan votes.
Pop music legend Madonna led this year’s field of winners with seven ⁠awards including artist of the year ⁠and best dance video for Confessions II - The Film . She recalled her 1984 performance of “Like a Virgin” at the first VMAs, which she said was considered too provocative for cable television at the ‌time.
“I think most of you were probably not yet born,” the 68-year-old told the crowd before explaining that she had to quickly recover during that performance from a shoe mishap.
“I dove onto the ‌stage to ‌try and make myself look cute and sexy ... My butt cheek was hanging out,” she said. “My manager told me my career was over.”
Speaking about the Confessions II album, Madonna said she spent the past 18 months “finding myself, believing in myself and really making ⁠the music I wanted to make”.
“To me, that really is the definition of being an artist,” she said.
Madonna kicked off the show with a high-energy ⁠performance of two of her recent collaborations. Sabrina Carpenter joined her for “Bring Your Love” – a song later named best collaboration – and Charli XCX took the stage for “Danceteria Afterhours” surrounded by dancers on a set that looked like a club restroom.
In a more quiet moment, Kacey Musgraves paid ‌tribute to Parton by singing the enduring ‌song “I Will Always Love You”.
Lisa, a member of the group Blackpink, won the VMA for best pop video for her solo effort “Dream”. She spoke through tears as she thanked her fans, known as Lillies.
“I wouldn’t be here without you guys,” she said. “Thank you so much for your love and support.”
English singer and songwriter Sienna Spiro, who combines pop, jazz and soul music, was named best new artist.

title: ‘Accomplices’ in espionage: Beijing’s stance on cryptocurrencies hardens
description: Ministry of State Security warns citizens not to be lured by ‘illusion’ of anonymous transactions.
content: China’s top intelligence and security agency on Monday issued a stark new warning on the risks of cryptocurrencies, highlighting their role in crime and stressing that transactions are not anonymous. Here are three things to know about the fresh warning from the Ministry of State Security (MSS) and China’s latest stance on virtual assets. What did the ministry say about cryptocurrencies? Virtual currencies facilitated money laundering activities and cyberattacks, and served as “accomplices” in espionage, the agency said in an article published on its social media account. Overseas intelligence agencies would try to dispel the concerns of people they were trying to recruit as spies by claiming that the circulation of virtual currencies was hard to verify, according to the Ministry. The MSS described the anonymity of crypto transactions as a “false proposition” and an “illusion”, saying that blockchains could fully retain transaction records and that exchanges between crypto and fiat currencies, as well as other payment interfaces, made real identities hard to hide. Crypto was often used by “overseas anti-China hostile forces” for activities that disrupted financial order and harmed national security, it said, adding that crypto businesses were illegal in China. How does the warning compare with other recent alerts from Chinese authorities? While the latest warning focused on cryptocurrency’s risks for national security and its use in espionage activities, China’s finance and market regulators have launched wider crackdowns on the sector. The People’s Bank of China, the country’s central bank, in February issued a joint notice with seven other government agencies that reiterated Beijing’s strict oversight of crypto activities and expanded its clampdown to tokenisation of real-world assets. The eight government bodies, also including the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Public Security, said that speculative activity involving virtual currencies disrupted “the economic and financial order” and endangered people’s property safety. How has China’s crypto policy evolved in recent years? After banning initial coin offerings and ordering the closure of exchanges in 2017, the Chinese government went further by banning bitcoin mining in 2021 and declaring all cryptocurrency-related businesses illegal. While some economists have questioned Beijing’s stringent crypto ban in recent years as US President Donald Trump vowed to make his country the “crypto capital of the world”, Beijing has not loosened its grip on domestic crypto activity despite giving Hong Kong the green light in 2022 to attract such businesses. The latest MSS warning would serve as “a timely reminder” that virtual currency trading remained banned in mainland China and would also be regarded by governments worldwide as carrying significant risks, said Andrew Fei, a partner at law firm King & Wood in Hong Kong. “The message being sent is clear: virtual currencies should not be mistaken for some kind of anonymous or untraceable safe haven for nefarious actors,” Fei said.

title: South Korea’s POW row with Ukraine puts ties and aid at risk
description: Analysts say Kyiv’s breach of secrecy over the North Korean prisoners of war may cause Seoul to halt non-lethal aid to Ukraine.
content: An escalating diplomatic row over Ukraine’s disclosure of a North Korean prisoner-of-war transfer is threatening to jeopardise South Korea’s future ties with and support for Kyiv, analysts say, even as it hands fresh ammunition to the political opposition in Seoul. South Korea’s presidential official issued a statement late on Sunday demanding an official explanation and apology for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s disclosure about the POWs at last week’s UN General Assembly. Seoul said it was reviewing additional measures in response to the “unilateral disclosure”, which analysts said could mean suspending some forms of support for Ukraine – though no such action had yet been confirmed. This Week in Asia has contacted the Ukrainian embassy in Seoul for comment. Jhee Byong-kuen, a political-science professor at Chosun University in South Korea, said the dispute had put President Lee Jae Myung “between a rock and a hard place”. “I don’t see any short-term solution to this row,” he said. “It will sour ties with Kyiv, raise tension with North Korea, further strain relations with Russia and raise some eyebrows in Washington.” In its statement on Sunday, Seoul accused Ukraine of breaching a non-disclosure agreement intended to safeguard the North Korean POWs and their families from potential danger. It was Ukraine that had initially requested confidentiality regarding the POWs’ transfer, said Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations. Zelensky’s UN speech was made in violation of that agreement “without sufficient prior explanation or specific consultation with our side”, Seong said in the statement. Kyiv has disputed Seoul’s characterisation of the issue, however. Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelensky’s official communications adviser, denied on Friday that Ukraine had breached a non-disclosure agreement with Seoul. He also argued that concealing where a POW was being sent would be wrong, according to a report by online media outlet Ukrainska Pravda. In an interview with Korean broadcaster MBC earlier this year, one of the POWs believed to be involved in the recent transfer expressed regret at having been taken alive. “If I’d had a grenade, I might have died rather than be captured,” he reportedly said. “But now, for the rest of my life, I feel the regret of not dying back then will return to me a hundredfold.” Fuel for the opposition Members of South Korea’s conservative opposition have accused Lee’s administration of attempting to conceal the POW transfer for fear of angering Pyongyang. There was no reason to keep the transfer confidential, People Power Party leader Jang Dong-hyeok said on Monday, adding that the soldiers’ identities and intentions had already been made public. “If there is any reason to hide it, it is only because of concern over Kim Jong-un’s mood,” he said, referring to North Korea’s supreme leader. Lee’s ruling Democratic Party of Korea, which has been attempting to reopen dialogue with Pyongyang, said in a statement on Friday that the government had no intention of taking credit for the soldiers’ arrival or exploiting the matter for political gain. “The People Power Party must not turn this issue into grist for political strife,” it said, urging the opposition to refrain from demanding disclosures about people under the state’s protection and to stop making “baseless allegations”. Jhee said the incident “was giving fuel to the opposition in rallying conservatives and bolstering its support base”. Yang Moo-jin, a political-science professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Seoul had been cautious about publicising defections in the past, especially when a liberal government was in power. “It’s one thing for the government to officially announce these defections but it’s quite another for them to become known to the public through news media leaks,” Yang said. “If officially announced, this would amount to sending a message of hostility to Pyongyang.” North Korea had in the past accused the South of luring defectors by “offering them handsome rewards”, he added. Jhee said Pyongyang was unlikely to publicly respond to reports of the defections, but said the revelation “throws up another obstacle to improving inter-Korean ties”. Aid to Ukraine at risk? In his statement on Sunday, Seong, the presidential spokesman, accused Kyiv of seriously undermining South Korea-Ukraine ties and trust with its “unilateral disclosure” and subsequent “false official statement denying the existence of the confidentiality agreement”. In addition to an explanation, Seong said Seoul was “reviewing additional measures that may be necessary” in response. These measures could include a suspension of non-lethal military aid to Ukraine, said Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. Non-lethal military and medical supplies South Korea has reportedly provided to Ukraine include helmets, bulletproof vests, tents, blankets and first aid kits, as well as financial and infrastructure assistance. South Korean law prohibits weapons exports to countries actively engaged in armed conflict. “Domestically, this disclosure could not have come at a worse time for President Lee,” Doo said, noting that the opposition had also accused the government of dragging its feet over an inquiry into a suspected landmine blast in the demilitarised zone earlier this month that injured three South Korean soldiers. Jeh Sung-hoon, a professor of Russian studies at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul, said the row could ultimately “make South Korea more reluctant to support Ukraine”. “Trust is important in diplomatic relations,” he said.

title: The View | Why Hong Kong and mainland China must not ignore property market transparency
description: As investors pile into alternative property sectors and seek more exposure to listed real estate, transparency becomes more important.
content: Every other year, JLL and LaSalle publish the results of their Global Real Estate Transparency Index. The index is a benchmark of market transparency that assesses the legal and regulatory environment, availability of data and operating conditions across 88 countries and 146 city markets. One of the key findings of the latest edition was that the most transparent markets – which include the United Kingdom, Australia and Japan – experienced the strongest growth in investment in commercial property. “Transparency drives investment growth,” the report noted. Another finding was that the Asia-Pacific led the improvement in transparency, with the region accounting for half of the top 10 improvers. India “led the upward trajectory through the expansion of its digital infrastructure, enhanced market data availability and expanding Reit [real estate investment trust] market”. However, a glance at the commercial real estate investment markets of Hong Kong and mainland China casts doubt on the role of transparency as a crucial driver of liquidity. In Hong Kong, which ranked 14th in the index and stood on the cusp of entering the 13-strong group of highly transparent markets, transaction volumes in the first half of this year reached US$4 billion. That was the lowest among the leading markets in the Asia-Pacific apart from India, according to data from MSCI. Even at the peak of the market in 2018, annual volumes were on a par with those in South Korea, which barely figured among the transparent markets and is currently ranked 24th. By contrast, a lack of transparency did not prevent mainland China – whose first-tier cities placed 31st in this year’s index – from being the most widely traded market in the Asia-Pacific in the first half of 2026, even surpassing Japan. In a CBRE survey of investor intentions from January, the level of market transparency did not even figure among the major challenges faced by investors in the region. High construction costs, geopolitical risks and tighter monetary policy were among the biggest headwinds. This does not necessarily mean transparency in Asian commercial property is overblown. Two crucial factors warrant more attention. First, transparency is more important for global investors and occupiers who need reliable and timely data to help them make informed decisions and manage risks in different markets. However, in mainland China, domestic investors account for the majority of commercial property transactions. Even when cross-border investment reached a record US$19.8 billion in 2019, domestic investors still constituted nearly two-thirds of transaction volumes, according to MSCI data. Moreover, the sheer size and scale of the market are a powerful driver of liquidity. “Given China’s size, it will always be one of the most widely traded markets in the region,” said Matthew McAuley, senior director of market intelligence and strategy in JLL’s research team. Local investors also dominate Hong Kong’s commercial real estate market, accounting for nearly three-quarters of investment activity in 2018. Moreover, concentrated ownership and limited availability of high-quality properties have acted as a constraint on liquidity. Trophy assets are tightly held by the city’s big and well-capitalised landlords, which tend to hold properties for a long period and are not under pressure to sell. The Asia-Pacific commercial property investment market as a whole is a largely domestic affair. The quarterly cross-border share of transaction volumes has hovered between 25 and 30 per cent during the past decade, according to MSCI data. In Europe, by contrast, the proportion of cross-border investment has often exceeded the domestic share since 2015. There is another factor that is just as important, even though it is less apparent. While there are many determinants of investment activity – including pricing, supply-demand dynamics, economic and geopolitical forces – market transparency is a potent structural force. “It matters over the longer term,” McAuley said. As institutional investors deploy more capital into alternative property sectors and retail investors seek more exposure to listed real estate, data availability becomes more important. “The expanding investible universe is creating an urgent demand from investors for higher-quality, comparable data to make informed decisions and manage risk,” JLL said. In Hong Kong, the prospects for student accommodation hinge on the institutionalisation of the emerging market. Detailed asset-level data on operational costs and capital expenditure are critical, particularly since many of the assets are conversions. In mainland China, the number of Reits has risen to nearly 80 with a market value of US$32 billion. This makes the listed Reit market, which was in its infancy five years ago, the Asia-Pacific’s third largest in terms of market value. As the democratisation of commercial property in mainland China gathers pace, the publicly traded Reit market is boosting transparency and liquidity. Transparency is just one of several drivers of investment in commercial property. Yet even in Hong Kong and mainland China, where other factors can be more influential, it plays an important but underappreciated role.

title: China’s Nio and Geely deepen commitment to EV battery swapping tech in stake sale
description: Deal that values Nio’s swapping subsidiary at US$2.4 billion clears way for the companies to develop unified standards.
content: Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Nio has deepened its partnership with Zhejiang Geely Holding Group after agreeing to sell a stake in its battery swap subsidiary to the automotive conglomerate in a deal that values the unit at 16 billion yuan (US$2.4 billion). Geely Holding, controlled by Chinese billionaire Li Shufu, would pay 640 million yuan in cash and contribute its wholly owned battery-swapping unit Yiyi Internet Technology in exchange for a 30 per cent share in Nio Power, Nio said in a filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange on Monday. The transaction would pave the way for the two companies to co-develop unified battery swapping standards and new models based on the technology, Nio added. The agreement reflected “industry recognition of Nio’s battery swapping technologies, network and operational capabilities”, the company said in the filing. “Nio expects to further promote the adoption of battery swapping, continuously enhance user experience, accelerate the growth of electric vehicle penetration and further unlock the long-term value of battery swapping.” Battery swap technology allows EV users to exchange a spent battery pack for a charged one in less than three minutes at a dedicated swapping station. It is designed to ease anxiety over range and slow charging. Shanghai-based Nio has been actively promoting the technology over the past three years, forming partnerships with leading Chinese automotive groups including Geely Holding and FAW. All Nio models feature the technology, which also allows users to charge their batteries in the conventional way. In November 2023, Nio and Geely signed a pact to collaborate on expanding swapping stations and improving operating capabilities. “An accelerated pace of electrification in China’s automotive industry has ushered in huge demand for fast-charging and swapping technologies,” said Eric Han, a senior manager at Shanghai consultancy Suolei. “Nio Power is one of the beneficiaries since it has already built a vast network of swapping stations.” As of early August, Nio owned and operated more than 4,000 such stations, most of which could ­navigate cars into position automatically. EVs hit a record market share of 65.2 per cent last month in mainland China as the US-Israel war with Iran drove a shift away from petrol cars, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association. Geely Holding, which owns Volvo Cars and a stake in Mercedes-Benz Group, is also developing fast charging technology, which could threaten swapping technology by easing drivers’ range anxiety. Early this month, Geely Auto, the Hong Kong-listed subsidiary of the group, unveiled its new technology, which charges the batteries in its Lynk and Zeekr models from 10 per cent to 70 per cent in less than five minutes.

title: Second Thomas Shoal stand-off sparks sharp exchange between US, China embassies
description: Beijing and Washington’s diplomatic representatives in Manila trade strongly worded accusations in public statements.
content: The Chinese and US embassies in the Philippines have exchanged sharp accusations following Washington’s defence of its treaty ally after a stand-off in the South China Sea last week. In a statement issued on Sunday, the US embassy in Manila backed the Philippines and said Beijing’s “dangerous blocking and irresponsible manoeuvres” had threatened a collision and prevented a lawful resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal, one of the flashpoints in the South China Sea disputes. The statement called on Beijing to “cease the use of escalatory tactics” and hailed Manila’s “professionalism and restraint”. The Chinese embassy in the Philippines hit back within hours, urging the United States “to stop fanning the flames” and refrain from actions that undermine regional peace and stability. Beijing said it strongly condemned Washington’s “disregard for right and wrong” and its continued support for Manila’s provocative and unlawful actions. The verbal sparring followed Manila’s complaints that Chinese coastguard and warships had “hindered” a routine mission on Thursday to deliver essential supplies and rotate personnel stationed on the BRP Sierra Madre. The World War II-era navy vessel was deliberately grounded in 1999 by the Philippines to assert its claim to Second Thomas Shoal, a submerged reef located in the disputed Spratly Islands chain of the South China Sea. The feature is known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines. Manila maintains a small contingent of troops aboard the vessel, which has been a persistent flashpoint in its maritime territorial disputes with Beijing. Sunday’s statement from Beijing’s embassy countered that Philippine vessels had disregarded Chinese warnings and proceeded with the resupply operation, deliberately hyping up the incident. Chinese coastguard measures, including on-site monitoring, tracking and verbal warnings, were “in accordance with the law”, according to the embassy statement. Thursday’s incident marked a rare publicly documented stand-off since a provisional agreement between Beijing and Manila took effect in July 2024. The agreement enables Manila to access the Second Thomas Shoal for resupply missions. The terms have never been made public. In early August, the Philippine foreign ministry said the provisional agreement resulted in 15 incident-free resupply missions to the Second Thomas Shoal. Thursday’s incident was part of a broader pattern of rising tensions in the disputed waters between the rival claimants. Since 2022, the two sides have engaged in increasingly escalatory stand-offs across several maritime features in the Spratlys. These have involved collisions, water cannon deployment, and allegations of military-grade lasers directed at Philippine vessels. Tensions peaked in June 2024, when Chinese coastguard personnel boarded Philippine boats and confiscated firearms near Second Thomas Shoal. It was after this clash that Beijing and Manila reached the provisional agreement. Manila has consistently rejected claims that the provisional arrangement requires Philippine forces to obtain Chinese approval for access to the Sierra Madre. It also rejected claims by Beijing’s embassy in Manila that the Philippines had promised to remove the vessel. Last week’s resupply mission unfolded against the backdrop of heightened regional naval activity. On Wednesday, the Philippines led a multinational maritime exercise near Scarborough Shoal – another flashpoint between Beijing and Manila – that brought together vessels from Asean member states and other countries, including the US, Australia, India and Japan. Beijing responded on Sunday, conducting air-sea exercises around Scarborough Shoal aimed at testing and boosting “combat capabilities in safeguarding China’s territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests”, according to the People’s Liberation Army Southern Theatre Command. The Chinese coastguard said separately that it carried out drills focused on boarding and inspection operations, intrusion interdiction and forced towing.

title: Hong Kong art space Para Site to leave its Quarry Bay home of 11 years and go nomadic
description: Para Site’s director James Taylor-Foster talks about an upcoming period of experimentation for the 30-year-old independent art organisation.
content: After months of speculation, the independent, non-profit art institution Para Site – which celebrates its 30th anniversary this year – has formally announced its departure from Quarry Bay on Hong Kong Island, where it has been based for more than a decade. It will be adopting a fully nomadic model as a response to the evolving arts ecosystem, says its executive director, James Taylor-Foster, who joined Para Site in May. “When Para Site moved into Quarry Bay in 2015, it was a completely different time in Hong Kong,” Taylor-Foster says. “There were fewer institutions, there were fewer galleries. White-cube exhibitions were really important because there were not so many of them happening. But jump over a decade later, Hong Kong’s cultural landscape is completely different.” Taylor-Foster previously teased the idea in an interview with the South China Morning Post soon after his appointment as the institution’s “wild card” director, when he was still new to Asia’s art scene. After spending the past six months getting to know Hong Kong, he believes the city and Para Site are ready for a big change. Founded by local artists in 1996, on the eve of Hong Kong’s handover from Britain to China, Para Site emerged against a backdrop of sociopolitical anxiety in a city widely perceived as a “cultural desert”. Against the odds, the art scene has since flourished. The 2010s brought the addition of international blue-chip galleries such as Gagosian, White Cube, David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth, while major institutions such as Tai Kwun and M+ have also been established. Combining the words “para” (beside) and “site” (place), the independent art space’s name reflects an experimental approach unlimited by its location, as well as “this idea of transience, of agility, of fluidity around what a place can be”, Taylor-Foster says. He adds that, for the past three decades, Para Site has served as “an incubator for many things” and that he wants it to continue to be one. He points out that Hong Kong’s cultural ecosystem appears to be “quite stable” with “amazing institutions”, adding that Para Site “can afford to be a little bit more daring again, and hold a space where care and risk can coexist, to make room for forms of experimentation – things that artists might not be able to do in other environments.” While most organisations expand as they grow and age, Para Site is instead turning inward, with experiments and reflection in its 30th year. On August 29, it invited Hong Kong’s arts and cultural community to “Para Site is Live”, a live public radio broadcast where anyone could drop in and share their views on the past and future of the independent art space and the local and international art world. It was an unofficial farewell to its Quarry Bay space, and somewhere between 150 and 200 visitors, from artists and art world professionals to non-artists, reportedly showed up throughout the afternoon. “I think that institutional health is about nurturing closer relationships and making space for [artistic practices] that have no obvious setting,” Taylor-Foster says. “It’s about asking an institution to pay attention and to make room, and sometimes that means you also have to redesign the room. “If you imagine a person at age 30 – you’ve played around, done some things, failed, succeeded … now we can be a little bit more confident in who we are,” he adds. The new nomadic model involves collaborating with art spaces, galleries and cultural institutions around Hong Kong and building an all-new 2027 programme that may extend beyond the typical – sometimes siloed – idea of contemporary art as it positions itself for a wider cultural audience. Para Site’s new vision is to become bigger than just one physical location or the typical white cube and, in the process, learn where it wants to go next. “How do we start working with artists and creatives in a more grounded way that maybe is not confined to a space or a format, like the ‘exhibition’?” Taylor-Foster asks. He adds that Para Site’s 31st year will be “one blip” in its history, when “everything we do is basically a test”. There will still be exhibitions and performances, but he wants to present them in unfamiliar, unconfined ways that portray artistic practices differently. In a full-circle moment, Para Site has moved to its interim office in an industrial building in Kennedy Town, where it was founded in 1996. The nomadic art space will announce its 2027 programme later this year. For now, it will continue its “Elsewhere in Me: Live Art in the City” programme, which began in June, foreshadowing its new move and exploration of space, or rather, lack thereof. There is a lot of uncertainty, just as the uncertainty in Hong Kong has not ceased since Para Site was founded a year before the handover. But it is precisely this fluid definition of the city that Para Site “has always understood and … needs to play with more”, Taylor-Foster says. “Hong Kong is a meeting point in the world, but it’s also very local,” he adds. “Para Site is extremely Hong Kong. We remain committed to Hong Kong and the paradox of being, on the one hand, very grounded and on the other hand, very internationally connected. “For one year, we’re going to test and experiment, nurture different kinds of collaborations and build different kinds of reciprocal relationships. We’re going to be closer to the streets, closer to the ground and try things out. All this will inform the kind of space that we end up moving into – a new anchor point for Para Site in Hong Kong.”

title: Japan denies ‘militarisation’ after Russia opposes permanent UN council seat
description: Japan’s top spokesman says Japan has ‘consistently defended freedom, democracy and the rule of law’ since the end of World War II.
content: Tokyo on Monday rebuked Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov after he voiced opposition over the weekend to Japan’s drive for permanent membership of the UN Security Council, claiming the country was on a “path of militarisation”. Lavrov’s comments came as the security council, tasked with safeguarding peace, is facing calls for reform amid accusations it failed to prevent recent conflicts such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, due largely to the veto power of its five permanent members: Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States. At the UN General Assembly in New York on Saturday, Lavrov said a reformed security council “cannot provide any extra seats” to Germany and Japan, which had taken “the path of militarisation”. Recalling last year’s 80th anniversary of the Allied victory “over German Nazism and Japanese militarism” in World War II, Lavrov blasted the notion of either country gaining a permanent seat on the powerful council. The US supports permanent seats for both countries and India while Russia is backing Brazil and India. Japan’s deputy UN ambassador Mikanagi Tomohiro responded to Lavrov at the end of the assembly, stressing that his country was “peace-loving” and that “freedom, democracy and fundamental human rights remain unshakeable foundations of Japan’s every decision and action”. Lavrov’s remarks drew pushback from Tokyo on Monday, with the Japanese government’s top spokesman, Minoru Kihara, telling a regular press conference that they were “contrary to the facts”. Kihara, who serves as chief cabinet secretary, said Japan had “consistently defended freedom, democracy and the rule of law since the end of the war, contributing to prosperity not only in Asia but around the world”. In addition to its five permanent members, the council has 10 non-permanent seats. Japan, which has served as a non-permanent member 12 times, most recently for two years through 2024, has long expressed its desire for a permanent seat on a reformed security council. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Mainland Chinese stocks hit 13-month low on tech sell-off as Hong Kong market holds up
description: Technology shares lead declines as investors weigh higher oil prices, elevated US yields and a looming holiday break.
content: Mainland Chinese stocks fell to their lowest level in 13 months on Monday as the sell-off in technology shares intensified amid concerns that elevated global capital costs and surging oil prices would curb risk appetite. Markets opened the week on a sombre note, with the CSI 300 Index dropping 2.2 per cent to close at a level not seen since August 21 last year. The chip-heavy Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent, capping its steepest single-day decline in five weeks and closing in on the low reached during July’s technology rout. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index bucked the trend, rising 0.5 per cent. Chinese technology stocks took a beating as crude oil traded above US$100 a barrel after the US rejected a proposal by Iran to restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The latest back-and-forth in negotiations kept inflation concerns alive and Treasury yields elevated. China’s economic recovery also remained uneven through August, with exports remaining resilient while domestic demand stayed sluggish. Market sentiment was further weighed down by speculation that Beijing could allow local companies to buy Nvidia’s chips, potentially increasing competition for Chinese chipmakers. Concerns that the nation’s biggest makers of optical transceivers such as Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology could face US sanctions also dented investor confidence. With no structural opportunities for technology stocks in sight, the market may be primed for consolidation for the rest of 2026 Fu Jingtao, Shenwan Hongyuan Group “The markets are pretty sensitive to oil prices, US Treasury yields and expectations about a [US Federal Reserve] rate increase in the short term,” said Fu Jingtao, an analyst at Shenwan Hongyuan Group. “With no structural opportunities for technology stocks in sight, the market may be primed for consolidation for the rest of 2026.” Investors also trimmed their bets on Chinese stocks in the shortened three-day trading week before the National Day “golden week” starting on Thursday, avoiding the risk of overseas developments during the trading break.
