The outcome of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping last week failed to impress traders, with agreements to extend the tariff truce and artificial intelligence collaborations largely matching market expectations. “I don’t think the progress on specific economic issues is significant,” said Zhang Zhiwei, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management. “The agreement on tariff reduction for US$60 billion bilateral trade is a positive step for both countries, but the size is rather small. So is the agreement on the purchase of coal from the US.” Investors expected stocks to remain volatile throughout the week as the releases of the US personal consumption expenditure data, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, and labour market figures could reshape the outlook for monetary policy.

title: Southeast Asia’s falling literacy: can cash and gamification fix it?
description: Facing shrinking attention spans and ‘doomscrolling’, governments are using cash, vouchers and book drives to get citizens reading again.
content: Singaporean Najwa Alhabshi remembers spending her teenage years poring over literary classics such as F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby and George Orwell’s 1984. The books introduced her to ideologies, philosophies and the American dream while expanding her vocabulary. But as work commitments grew, the pages of her books started yellowing. Finding time to read became harder, and her smartphone screen eventually took over. “I think I just fell out of reading,” the 35-year-old tutor said. “Life got in the way – it was work, a lack of time, and eventually, the phone screen.” Across Southeast Asia, governments are stepping in to get people reading again. With screens reshaping how people consume information, concerns are growing over falling literacy rates, shortened attention spans and declining critical-thinking capabilities. Singapore is one of those taking action. Earlier this month, the city state launched an initiative that pays citizens to read. Under the scheme, users earn 20 virtual coins for every reading session lasting at least 15 minutes, logged via a government website. Recording one session a day for 50 days accumulates 1,000 coins, which can be exchanged for S$1 (US$0.78). Developing a reading habit helped build the capacity to navigate an “increasingly complex” information landscape, said Melissa Tam, CEO of Singapore’s National Library Board. “This is especially important for our children, who are growing up in a world where technological changes often outpace our ability to adapt,” Tam said. The scheme relies on gamification to build daily reading streaks, according to Loh Chin Ee, an associate professor at the National Institute of Education. “Sometimes it is helpful to have a little nudge or challenge to get one started,” Loh said. “Matching individuals to the right kinds of books they are interested in would be a good way to encourage people to get started on reading.” But attaching financial value to reading could backfire by stripping away its intrinsic joy, said Ng Siew Chin, an early childhood lecturer at the Singapore University of Social Sciences. She suggested using social media platforms to promote excerpts from books and texts. “The attention of readers is gained through bite-sized posts like these to intrigue their curiosity to potentially access the full article or book,” she said. Rise of doomscrolling Singapore is not alone in trying to revive reading habits. Other Southeast Asian countries have rolled out measures to raise literacy rates. In July, Indonesia launched a countrywide distribution of more than 5.5 million books to primary and secondary schools. Jakarta said the 40.7 billion rupiah (US$2.27 million) project reflected its commitment to ensuring children have direct access to reading materials. Neighbouring Malaysia is handing out 100 ringgit (US$24) vouchers to more than 2.2 million students to spend on its national digital book marketplace. The programme, which runs from July to October, expands on a 2024 initiative to include students across a wider age range. At the launch of the Kuala Lumpur International Book Fair in May, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said books and education had to remain a priority despite fiscal constraints. “If we want this country to become a truly civilised nation with a strong culture of knowledge and broad intellectual capacity, we must encourage reading,” he said. He added that reading culture had become a problem, with many preferring to consume information from social media. “That is why I urge parents to monitor their children and ensure they start reading from tonight onwards.” Researchers and experts share those concerns, particularly as artificial intelligence tools become increasingly widespread. A global study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development released last month found that students are now reading at a level previously expected of students a year younger. The study also found a decline in skills such as evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources and critical thinking, alongside an increase in hasty, superficial reading. Overreliance on AI threatened the development of essential reading skills, said Portia Padilla, an associate professor in the College of Education at the University of the Philippines Diliman. “If you do not think while reading, you are not truly reading,” Padilla said, adding that readers should use AI to challenge their assumptions rather than form judgments. For Najwa, the battle begins at home. To instil a love for reading in her five-year-old son, she limits his screen time to just 15 minutes a month. Her son now reaches for short illustrated books when he wakes up, often pausing during walks to read words on road signs and pamphlets. “Beyond just expanding vocabulary, reading does so much more for our children,” the tutor said. “Books are portals to a different world – through them, imagination lives.” Finding community While government intervention and incentives can nudge people to pick up a book, experts say they do little to build intrinsic motivation and cultivate lifelong habits. Extra reading time did not automatically guarantee deeper understanding or critical thought, Padilla said. “Access and motivation are a starting point, not the finish line. True comprehension requires active engagement with the text. It goes beyond coins and vouchers.” Reading should be viewed as a commitment rather than a short-term campaign, she added, urging support across the whole ecosystem – including public policy, language development programmes and supportive environments at home and in the community. Providing dedicated spaces for reading – such as quiet public zones or after-hours book clubs – could offer another way to build momentum, said Loh from the National Institute of Education, pointing out that “silent book clubs” were gaining popularity in Singapore. Community book groups have sprouted up across the region, meeting in places such as a park in Manila and an art cafe in Penang to a wine bar in Singapore. On the second floor of a deli in Bangkok, two dozen people gather once a month to share their latest reads. Participants at the Books at Banter book club are free to bring any book they choose – a deliberate rule aimed at making the club accessible and less intimidating, said founder Kunatai Khunmuang. “People don’t have to feel that they have to read classics, non-fiction or whatever book happens to be popular to be considered a ‘real reader’,” said Kunatai, who started the club in May. “Someone else can interpret a story completely differently from you, notice something you missed or connect it to an experience you’ve never had. Reading is naturally a solitary activity, but a book club gives you somewhere for all those thoughts to go.”

title: US, China slash tariffs on basic goods, leave rare earths debate off the record
description: Tariffs waived on lengthy US$30 billion list of items including linen, fireworks and crockery will not ‘dramatically reshape’ trade: analyst.
content: The United States and China released details about the non-sensitive goods set for tariff reductions and their agreement to set up an agricultural trade working group after President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US last week, though any progress on the two countries’ dispute over rare earths remains absent from official statements. The White House released the lists of the US$30 billion worth of goods on each side recommended for tariff reductions on Sunday, which comprised 77 categories of US imports from China and a lengthy list of 1,619 Chinese imports from the US. China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a statement on Monday that more than 90 per cent of the products covered under the agreement would be granted most-favoured-nation tariff rates with all reciprocal tariffs waived. The reductions were arranged under the aegis of the US-China Board of Trade, a bilateral body established during Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May to negotiate conditions for the import and export of non-sensitive goods between the two economies. Analysts noted that the measures were modest and amounted to posturing during an important political year for both countries, while they did not substantially shift the bilateral trade relationship. Items on the US import list include home appliances such as microwave ovens and electric irons, Christmas ornaments and toys. The China import list is mostly agricultural, covering products such as beef and vegetables, alongside coal, timber and medical devices such as hearing aids and pacemakers. “This arrangement will help stabilise trade between China and the United States, and create favourable conditions for Chinese exports of relevant products to the US,” the Chinese commerce ministry said. The US and China will also establish an agricultural working group to discuss regulations and market access, address trade concerns and expand cooperation in the sector, with the first meeting expected before the end of the year, according to the statement. Chen Fengying, a researcher with the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, noted that the US import list primarily concerned consumer goods that might be more expensive to produce domestically, especially given inflation concerns in the country. “The current consideration is the cost of living for ordinary Americans, with the main focus being on Trump’s midterm elections,” Chen said. Meanwhile, 2026 was also an important political year for China, marking the first year in its new five-year plan cycle, Chen noted. Additionally, both countries were holding important summits such as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and the Group of 20. “Politically, we are propping each other up,” she added. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Sunday that the US was improving market access for around 30 per cent of exports to China, and the arrangement would benefit American consumers with imports of “products that the United States generally does not import from other countries”. The two sides, however, made no mention of thornier issues such as export controls on rare earths in their latest statements. On Friday, the White House said that the US and China “continue to work on US concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths and other critical minerals”, without adding further details. “China’s dominance in the mining and processing of key rare earths and other critical minerals is the strongest card it has in its negotiations with the US,” said Alfredo Montufar-Helu, the China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting. While Beijing suspended export controls on the critical materials to January, Montufar-Helu noted that Washington was already complaining about slow deliveries and an opaque licensing process. “So between now and January, I’d expect the US to push hard for more predictable access,” he said. In Monday’s statement, the Chinese commerce ministry also noted that both sides “agreed to maintain communication on increasing flights between China and the United States”, but did not release further details. Neither side made any announcements on China’s commitment to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft, an agreement made after US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May that has yet to see a purchase order. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that Washington and Beijing also discussed financial services at last week’s high-level trade talks, and that China will review and approve applications from foreign financial institutions, “including those with US capital”, to operate in China. “China hopes that the United States will also provide a fair, transparent and stable policy environment for Chinese financial institutions,” the ministry added. Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, noted that the type of items covered under the Board of Trade were limited. “If you are listing product categories that do not matter much, it’s easy to make a very long list of ‘concessions’,” Elms said. “But overall, the pattern of trade is not going to be dramatically reshaped by tariff reductions on bathroom scales.”

title: Hong Kong authorities open probe after yacht allegedly charges boat with 6 rowers
description: One rower alleges that a yacht sped towards a row boat in ‘deliberate’ act of aggression during weekend race near High Island Reservoir.
content: Hong Kong marine authorities have launched an investigation after a yacht sped directly towards a boat rowed by six athletes during a race in Sai Kung over the weekend, with one of the rowers alleging the act was “deliberate”. The incident came to light on Sunday after one of the rowers, Eddie Lam Yat-ming, an assistant professor at Hong Kong Metropolitan University’s Lee Shau Kee School of Business and Administration, shared footage of the encounter on social media. Lam told the South China Morning Post on Monday that he had reported the incident to the Marine Department. He said he had not been informed of the investigation’s progress, but expressed confidence that the authorities would follow up on the matter professionally. Lam was taking part in the 40km (25-mile) Sai Kung Coastal Challenge near High Island Reservoir on Saturday. The video he posted showed a yacht passing close to his boat at top speed in a near collision that caused the boat to rock violently in its wake. “The yacht suddenly accelerated from about 100 metres [328 feet] away, pointed directly at us and dashed towards us … Locking onto a target from 100 metres away does not look like a mistake; it is a deliberate act,” Lam wrote. “Perhaps the captain thought it was fun and exciting, but this could have cost several lives. The sea is not your speedboat racetrack; please respect the safety of other athletes.” In a reply to the South China Morning Post on Monday, the department said it had received one report and launched an investigation into the incident. A spokeswoman added that the department would take appropriate action if any breach of the law were uncovered. According to the International Regulations for the Prevention of Collisions at Sea, powerboats should give way to vessels driven by wind or manual force. Under Hong Kong’s Shipping and Port Control Ordinance, any person who endangers the safety of people on board a vessel or in the sea faces a maximum penalty of four years’ imprisonment and a HK$200,000 (US$25,500) fine.

title: Singaporean TV actors charged over death penalty protests
description: ‘Phua Chu Kang’ actors Lim Kay Siu and Neo Swee Lin are charged with taking part in a public assembly outside the State Courts.
content: Six Singaporeans, including journalist Kirsten Han and Phua Chu Kang actors Lim Kay Siu and Neo Swee Lin, were charged on Monday with taking part in public assemblies. The assemblies were held in prohibited areas, with one held outside the State Courts in support of abolishing the death penalty, as well as candlelight vigils held outside Changi Prison for death row inmates. The six charged are Annamalai Kokila Parvathi, 38, Ten Leu Jiun Jeanne-Marie, 56, Howe Wen Khong Rocky, 31, Kirsten Han, 37, Lim Kay Siu, 70, and Neo Swee Lin Winifred, 63. All except Ten were charged with taking part in a public assembly outside the State Courts, a prohibited area, on February 3, 2025. Among them were married couple Neo and Lim. They previously starred in local sitcom Phua Chu Kang, with Neo playing the mother of the titular contractor and Lim playing Frankie Foo. More recently, the pair have performed music together, while Lim starred as the monk Gyatso in Netflix’s Avatar – The Last Airbender. Ten was charged with attending two candlelight vigils at Changi Prison in November 2024. Howe, who faced the most charges of the lot, was charged with the State Courts assembly as well as attending three candlelight vigils at Changi Prison in November 2024 and January 2025. Of the six charged on Monday, two had previously been investigated and warned before being charged. Another two were repeatedly involved in such cases despite being under investigation, the police said in a statement. Police said Han had “numerous run-ins with the law”, including for public assemblies without permits in 2017 and 2022, obstructing justice in 2022 and a public procession in June 2024. Annamalai was previously convicted of organising a public procession along the Istana and for public assemblies held in 2017 and 2021. Howe was issued a stern warning for taking part in public assemblies without a permit in March and April 2022, and for obstructing justice in March 2022, police said. Ten had been issued a stern warning in April 2022 and in September 2026, they added. Lawyer Derek Wong appeared for five of the six, with Howe unrepresented. Wong also mentioned the cases on behalf of other lawyers representing Neo, Lim and Annamalai. He said he was just instructed and asked for time to take instructions, which was granted. He asked that his clients be released without bail, saying they faced offences punishable only with fines. He also sought a personal bond instead of bail. District Judge Wong Peck declined the requests and issued bail sums of S$5,000 (US$3,900) for each of the five. ‘My discretion’ Howe similarly asked to be released without bail or on a personal bond instead. When Judge Wong told him that she would be issuing bail for him as well, he argued that bail was to be offered at the court’s discretion. “It’s my discretion,” the judge said. “Yes, but discretion should be exercised lawfully,” Howe answered. “I am exercising my discretion,” Wong said, signalling that her decision was final. The cases for all six were adjourned to October. Earlier this month, another eight people were charged over prohibited processions or assemblies – including activists Jolovan Wham and S. Suraendher Kumarr, who was charged last week. Wham is accused of organising the February 2025 assembly outside the State Courts publicising the cause of abolishing capital punishment in Singapore. Large crowds attended the earlier court appearances, and queue poles had been set up at the State Courts on Monday for crowd control. There was some commotion when security guards prevented some in the group from entering without changing their shirts. Some of those present wore shirts with slogans or messages on them. After a previous hearing drew hundreds of supporters, security allowed only those with a reason to enter the courtroom on Monday. For organising a public assembly in a prohibited area, a person could be jailed for up to six months, fined up to S$10,000, or both. For taking part in a public assembly without a permit, an offender can be fined up to S$5,000. Police said that public assemblies or processions in prohibited areas without a police permit were subject to “even higher punishments”. “Individuals who have previously been warned or dealt with for breaches of the Public Order Act should not disregard such warnings,” said the police. They said members of the public should apply for a police permit before organising public assemblies, and those wishing to express their views but did not have a permit could consider doing so at the Speakers’ Corner. This story was first published by CNA

title: China’s gas turbine makers are moving to make a global splash. Is Malaysia the first stop?
description: Tight global supply is creating new opportunities in a sector where a small group of international manufacturers have long held sway.
content: In the latest milestone for China’s heavy-duty gas turbine manufacturers, Shanghai Electric has secured a turnkey contract to deliver equipment to a power plant in Malaysia, giving it a foothold in a market dominated by established foreign players amid a global supply crunch. The state-owned conglomerate, based in the Chinese financial centre, hailed the deal reached earlier this month as evidence of the competitiveness of its integrated solutions and its capacity to design and manufacture crucial components independently. Shanghai Electric, a power generation and electrical equipment maker, will supply gas turbines to the Samalaju Combined Cycle Power Plant in the Malaysian state of Sarawak – a major infrastructure project developed by state utility Sarawak Energy Berhad to support rising regional demand. The tailor-made package included gas turbines, steam turbines, generators, heat recovery steam generators and air-cooling systems, according to Shanghai Electric, which added that it would also provide a 25-year maintenance service for the main equipment. The company stated that all core equipment for the project would be produced in-house. This contrasts with traditional multi-supplier arrangements, which typically require a general contractor to coordinate technical specifications, operating parameters and control systems across different vendors. By comparison, Shanghai Electric argued that its unified model would minimise hurdles by streamlining accountability, technical interfaces, performance guarantees and project management into a single package. This approach, the company said, could help reduce risks and project costs and had helped seal the Malaysian contract. Heavy-duty gas turbines are complex engineering systems regarded as a measure of a nation’s advanced industrial research and manufacturing capabilities, and the global market has historically been dominated by a handful of foreign players. The Samalaju plant is designed to reach a total capacity of 1,500 megawatts and will adopt a split-supplier model for different units. Alongside Shanghai Electric, German firm Siemens Energy is also supplying advanced gas turbines to the facility. This is not Shanghai Electric’s first project in Malaysia, having previously supplied equipment for coal, renewable and transmission infrastructure across Selangor and Sarawak, but it reflects a shift from exporting individual components to delivering comprehensive energy systems. Chinese state media highlighted the deal as a sign of changing international preferences, noting that some overseas project owners increasingly preferred all-in-one packages and full-life cycle support over fragmented procurement. More Chinese equipment makers are also eager to capitalise on a tight global market for gas turbines, where demand currently outstrips production capacity. “In this tight supply environment, some overseas buyers who previously prioritised international suppliers are showing greater openness to Chinese complete-machine solutions that offer shorter delivery times and proven performance,” Liu Zhitan, a researcher with the Chinese Society for Electrical Engineering, told China News Service in a report last week. “The future success of the Malaysia project will serve as a vindication of the quality and cost-effectiveness of Chinese products for other foreign clients to see,” Liu said, though he warned that sustaining recognition would depend on long-term operational performance and service quality.

title: Mainland Chinese visitors make 439,532 trips to Hong Kong over Mid-Autumn break
description: Tourism industry representative also expects hotel occupancy of over 90 per cent in popular districts for coming National Day ‘golden week’.
content: Mainland Chinese visitors made nearly 440,000 trips to Hong Kong over the extended Mid-Autumn Festival weekend, with a tourism industry representative expecting hotel occupancy to exceed 90 per cent in popular districts during the coming National Day “golden week”. According to figures released on Monday, Hong Kong’s Immigration Department recorded 439,532 inbound trips by mainland visitors from last Friday to Sunday. The figure accounted for about a quarter of the 1.73 million inbound trips, including those made by Hong Kong residents, during the three-day period. Hong Kong’s tourism industry is also preparing for the mainland’s seven-day National Day golden week holiday, which begins on Thursday. The Immigration Department said it expected about 1.29 million mainland visitors to arrive in the city during the holiday. It also forecast that the average daily number of visitor arrivals from across the border would surpass last year’s figure by more than 5 per cent. Combined with the recent three-day Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, mainland residents who took an additional three days of leave from Monday to Wednesday could enjoy a continuous 13-day break. Travel Industry Council chairman Tommy Tam said the sector’s own National Day holiday estimate was in line with the government’s forecast. He added that favourable exchange rates and a series of festive events could attract more visitors. “Of course, in traditional popular districts, such as Tsim Sha Tsui, Causeway Bay and Central, [hotel occupancy rates] will exceed 90 per cent,” he told a radio programme. “And I heard from the industry that room rates this year have increased by nearly double digits.” Hotel prices in Causeway Bay, for example, were significantly higher for October 1 to 3 – during the National Day holiday – than for September 29 and 30, according to searches by the South China Morning Post on booking platform Trip.com. Average nightly prices rose by between 36 per cent and more than 230 per cent across budget, mid-range and luxury hotels. A room at the Regal Hongkong Hotel, for example, rose by 65 per cent from HK$828 to HK$1,367 (US$105 to US$174), including taxes and fees, according to prices on Trip.com. Tam said visitors were increasingly opting for staggered travel arrangements and multi-destination itineraries, arriving in Hong Kong a few days early or late before continuing to Macau or other cities in the Greater Bay Area. He also said the industry was optimistic about spending on catering and high-end retail business, adding that mainland visitors had confidence in Hong Kong’s zero-tolerance approach to forced shopping. Geoparks in rural areas are among the destinations that have gained popularity with mainland visitors. But official data showed that about half of those who reserved places for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail failed to show up. During the initial trial weekend, only about 1,560 people arrived despite more than 3,200 bookings. During the Mid-Autumn Festival period, an average of about 1,170 visitors showed up each day, compared with 2,360 reservations. Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan, who represents the New Territories South East constituency, suggested introducing an admission fee or deposit to reduce the number of no-shows. “I referenced, for example, mainland geological parks in Shenzhen and other places. They actually charge about 80 to 100 yuan [US$12 to US$15], so I think the deposit could be similar to these fees,” she said. “I estimate there will be about HK$30 million in basic income a year … which should rightly be used in the district to improve conservation, education and promotion resources.” Authorities have said they will conduct a comprehensive review of the reservation system after the National Day holiday.

title: Businessman Jason Poon and wife granted bail over alleged HK$6 million loan fraud
description: Hearing to be transferred to District Court, while couple’s bail conditions include remaining in Hong Kong and reporting weekly to police.
content: Hong Kong businessman Jason Poon Chuk-hung and his wife have been granted bail after facing charges for allegedly defrauding a government financing scheme for businesses out of HK$6 million (US$765,000) during the Covid-19 pandemic. Construction businessman Poon, 56, and his wife, Carrie Chu Shu-fong, 54, were told at Kowloon City Court on Monday that proceedings for their fraud and money laundering charges would be transferred to the District Court, where the maximum sentence for any number of charges is capped at a total of seven years’ imprisonment. Magistrate Arthur Lam Hei-wei granted the pair cash bail of HK$100,000, while imposing other conditions, including remaining in Hong Kong and reporting weekly to a police station. The defendants will return to Kowloon City Court on November 2 to deal with documentation for the court transfer. They are expected to enter their pleas at the District Court at a later stage. The couple have been jointly charged with one count of fraud and four counts of money laundering. They are accused of making false representations to HSBC during a loan application for their company, Lockill Biochemical Limited, under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme between June 25 and July 30, 2021. Prosecutors also alleged that they had laundered more than HK$3.2 million in August that year. Poon is the managing director of mask manufacturer Lockill Biochemical, according to his LinkedIn account. In March, police arrested him and his wife, along with four company employees, for alleged fraud. The financial scheme was launched in 2011, but was extended to provide a special 100 per cent loan guarantee as part of the 2020-21 government budget to help ease businesses’ cash flow problems arising from wage and rental obligations during the pandemic. The loans were fully guaranteed by the government at a concessionary low interest rate. Poon became a public figure after he exposed shoddy work at Hung Hom MTR station, part of the Sha Tin-Central link development, in 2018. His whistle-blowing prompted the government to establish an independent commission of inquiry to investigate the scandal. The businessman later ran as an independent candidate in the 2021 Legislative Council election. He finished last among four candidates in Hong Kong East constituency.

title: As China mulls how to make open-weight AI less dangerous, report proposes 6-stage process
description: Open-weight models allow AI’s “brains” to be freely downloaded, modified, fine-tuned and run independently by anyone online.
content: Amid intensifying debate over the risks posed by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, Chinese developers dominating the open-weight ecosystem are grappling with a unique problem: how to ensure their user-modifiable models remain safe once they are released. To address the challenge, Z.ai and Beijing-based safety consultancy Concordia AI released a report on open-weight AI risk management on Monday that they said offered “the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation” for balancing the risks and benefits of open-weight systems. Unlike proprietary software from top US labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, open-weight models allow their trained parameters – essentially the AI’s “brains” – to be freely downloaded, modified, fine-tuned and run independently by anyone online. Because creators permanently relinquish control post-release, losing the ability to monitor user activity or pull the plug on misuse, safety checks must be shifted “upstream” to the earliest phases of development, the report, titled “Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework”, said. It proposed a six-stage life-cycle management process spanning risk identification, threshold setting, analysis, evaluation, mitigation and governance. Chief among the safeguards was training-data curation, which the report highlighted as “one of the strongest layers of defence available”. The authors urged developers to adopt safety pre-training, such as filtering hazardous material from training data sets before models were published, to prevent systems from being weaponised. The report comes amid mounting global concerns over AI safety. On Saturday, OpenAI suspended training on its next-generation proprietary models following a string of incidents in which autonomous agents acted unpredictably and hacked external systems. The findings also align with a broader push by Chinese technology firms and regulators to increase transparency and bolster governance in open-weight AI development. Last week, Xiaomi took the unprecedented step of live-streaming the reinforcement learning process for its frontier MiMo-V2.6 models. By broadcasting a real-time dashboard displaying millions of dollars in compute costs, failure logs and exact training-data mix ratios, the company struck a sharp contrast with the secretive, black box practices typical of American rivals. Z.ai, known in mainland China as Zhipu, announced plans last week to open-source its coding assistant, ZCode, following a security incident. The company faced a backlash after users discovered ZCode was uploading local workspace data to external servers without consent. Z.ai has since issued an apology and pledged to invite third-party auditors to review the tool’s codebase. Such corporate moves come amid a broader regulatory push from Beijing, which introduced a national “AI Safety Governance Framework” on September 14, calling for stricter safety protocols and international cooperation. Open-weight models have increasingly become a primary battleground in the technology race between the United States and China, as cost-efficient Chinese systems challenge the dominance of American proprietary models. In July, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 model made headlines after matching or outperforming top closed-source US systems across several key benchmarks. Other Chinese systems – including Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro, Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 – have since surpassed Kimi K3 on an intelligence index maintained by San Francisco-based AI benchmarking company Artificial Analysis. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. China’s growing AI momentum has reignited debate in Washington over potential bans on foreign open-source models. Following an Axios report in July that the White House was weighing such restrictions, a coalition of top US tech firms – including Nvidia, Google and OpenAI – signed an industry letter opposing broad bans, arguing that a robust open-source ecosystem was vital to maintaining American AI leadership. Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg echoed those sentiments last month, urging US policymakers to focus on enhancing the competitiveness of American models rather than restricting access to foreign ones.

title: Republicans pour cash into dozens of US House races previously seen as ‘safe’
description: Major Republican groups have begun spending in at least 39 House races ahead of the November midterms.
content: Republicans are pouring money into ⁠more than three dozen US House races previously considered “safe” after internal polling showed they could be vulnerable in the November 3 election, according to three Republican operatives familiar with the party’s thinking. The shift is already starting to show in advertising reservations and campaign finance filings. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun spending in at least 39 congressional races where they haven’t previously deployed money this cycle, a Reuters review of spending by some of the largest Republican political groups shows. Many of the candidates receiving new support sit in Republican strongholds and are still running ahead of Democratic opponents in public polls, these people said, indicating ‌rising worry among party leaders over whether voters will use the November 3 election to air dissatisfaction over US President Donald Trump’s policies. House Republican leaders recently warned dozens of campaigns that the party’s internal data shows that they cannot assume they will win, even if they are currently ahead in public polls and represent districts Trump won by double digits, two of the people said. “Republicans are playing defence in some of the strongholds that they’re used to not having to worry about,” said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions. Republicans currently hold a narrow 218-214 majority in the House, with one independent caucusing with Republicans and two vacancies. Democrats would need to net at least four seats in the midterms to take control of the chamber next year. Two Republican operatives working with party leaders said they’re using their larger spending power to stifle Democrats before they have a chance to attack. They said the ⁠party was taking out “insurance policies” to ensure Republican-held districts remain in the party’s hands. “Republicans are deploying our massive war chest to drive voters to the polls and supercharge our candidates,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. “We’re not taking anything for ‌granted, because, unlike Democrats, Republicans aren’t throwing in the towel on races we can win.” Republican congressman Bryan Steil is one telling example. His Wisconsin district voted for Trump by about 4.5 percentage points in 2024 and is rated “lean Republican” by Cook Political Report. Still, conservative super PACs dumped US$1.5 million on his race this month, their first investment of this election cycle. A representative for Steil declined to comment. In ‌North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District east of Raleigh, Congressman Gregory Murphy this month received US$131,107 from a conservative PAC a week ago – the first outside spending on his behalf in the midterms. Democrats have spent over US$326,000 trying ⁠to oust him since July. Trump won the district by ⁠14 percentage points and Cook rates it “solid Republican”. Murphy’s office didn’t return a request for comment. The emergency deployments reflect a harsh reality: economic strain is battering traditionally Republican strongholds. Rising fuel prices, energy costs and fertiliser expenses are hitting voters in the agricultural heartland particularly hard. One Republican House campaign aide said the environment for candidates in ‌Iowa, Kansas and other Midwest states was “dire” as diesel prices soar. “We’re in this crucial period in the last 30 days where candidates have to really make a case, given how tough the headwinds are,” said Kevin Madden, who advised former Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney and is now senior partner at corporate advisory firm Penta Group. Campaigns ‌are ‌running as if they are behind in the polls “even in red districts or traditionally safe” ones, Madden said. More than US$1.56 billion, overall, has been spent by independent committees on federal elections so far, with roughly US$496 million deployed just since Labour Day, according ‌to a Reuters analysis of super PAC spending. That figure does not include all spending by dark money nonprofits that do not disclose their donors. Republicans have reserved at least US$888 million in advertising over the coming weeks, compared to at least US$666 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact, which ⁠tracks political advertising. No Going Back PAC, which is fully funded by Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc., is leading the surge, Federal Election Commission records show. “That’s the advantage of having a s*** tonne of money,” said one Republican operative working on Trump’s midterm ⁠strategy. “We’re not going to let Democrats take free shots on goal.” Over the last three weeks through Friday, Republican-leaning super PACs have outspent Democrats by almost 2-to-1, showering races with roughly US$309.7 million since Labour Day compared with US$174.2 million going to help Democratic candidates, the FEC data shows. “Republicans have air superiority. House Democrats are scrambling to catch up with the very limited resources they have,” said Mike Marinella, national press secretary for the National Republican Congressional Committee, which ‌works to elect Republicans to the House. Democrats acknowledge their funding disadvantage ‌but say the Republican push to spend money on districts that Trump won easily reflects the trouble the party faces in the midterms. “Republicans are running scared, know they’ve lost the American people, and are trying one last hail mary to spend their way out of certain defeat,” said Viet Shelton, spokesman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. In one district in south Texas that Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, Republican groups have pumped about US$2 million into text messages, direct mail and digital ads since September 5 to help incumbent congresswoman Monica De La Cruz keep her seat. Cook Political Report moved her seat from “lean Republican” to “toss-up” on Friday. De La Cruz is grateful for her supporters helping defeat her rival, her campaign manager said, when asked about the money spent by her Republican backers.

title: Asian Games, day 9: China’s remarkable diving streak, double bronze for Hong Kong
description: City’s athletes grabbed medals in esports and women’s table tennis, while China’s divers close in on 100 golds.
content: Hong Kong’s athletes extended their medal run to nine straight days at the Asian Games with bronze in esports and table tennis on Monday, pushing the overall tally to 34. China, meanwhile, continued a remarkable record in the diving, with two more golds, in women’s 1m springboard and men’s 1m springboard, extending an unbeaten streak stretching back to 1974. In that time, 94 titles have been up for grabs, and the country’s divers have taken them all. With six events remaining between now and Wednesday, the mainland’s delegation could round it out to 100 this year. There was almost bronze for Hong Kong at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, but Chan Tsz-min finished fourth in a women’s 1m springboard event won by Lin Shan. Compatriot Long Yiping claimed silver, with bronze going to South Korea’s Kim Su-ji. As it was, the city’s first podium of the day went to the six-strong squad competing in Honor of Kings, a multiplayer online battle arena. Cheng Ka-hin, Kwok Ho-wa, Kong Tsz-kin, Li Ka-hing, Deng Xinzhan and Chui Sum-ki lost 2-0 to Malaysia in their semi-final at Aichi Sky Expo. Alongside a bronze in the Fighting Games division last Friday, Kwok said the results marked “a very good memory … I will never forget this moment”. He and those that follow will not get to make new ones, at least at the Asian Games. The sport is being dropped in favour of a biennial Asian Esports and Mind Sports Games, with the first of those in Kuwait next year. Shortly after, Doo Hoi-kem and Pedrey Ng Wing-lam claimed bronze in the women’s table tennis doubles event. With no bronze medal play-offs, Doo and Ng were already guaranteed a medal before they were swept aside in their semi-final by Japanese duo Miwa Harimoto and Hina Hayata 4-0, who themselves were thrashed by China pair Kuai Man and Wang Manyu in the final. “This is my first time competing at the Asian Games, so being able to win this medal is a wonderful surprise, and I am really happy,” Ng said. “Before playing, I actually put quite a bit of pressure on myself, but now that it is over and we have secured a bronze medal, I feel really happy and relieved.” The women’s doubles medal, the only one Hong Kong has managed in table tennis at this year’s Games, came on the final day of competition in Nagoya, extending the streak of winning at least one medal in the sport in 10 straight editions. It matched the squad’s achievement from three years ago, when Wong Chun-ting’s bronze in the men’s singles was the solitary success. “The pressure was huge,” said Doo, who has not won an Asian Games medal since 2018. “Although I have already blocked out a lot, it all still had somewhat of an impact. “Of course, we could have done better, but in the end, winning a bronze medal in the women’s doubles still makes us very happy. I hope people will not always judge or write us off solely based on results.” In cricket, Hong Kong’s men were spared a quarter-finals thrashing at the hands of Pakistan, and India’s clash with Afghanistan also ended without a ball being bowled as rain washed out any hope of play. Organisers sent Pakistan and India through because they are ranked higher in the world. The rain also hit the second day of the men’s and women’s tennis, and could delay Coleman Wong Chak-lam’s start to the tournament. Wong, who is the top men’s seed this week, is scheduled to face Jordan’s Zaid Al Mashni on Tuesday.

title: Inside Malaysia’s plan to steal China’s durian market from Thailand
description: Last year, China imported 1.87 million tonnes of fresh durian worth US$7.5 billion, with volume jumping over sixfold in the past decade.
content: Malaysia is pushing to take durian, whose powerful smell delights its lovers and repels its haters, beyond its roadside stalls and family orchards to convince fans of the spiky fruit that its varieties are worth seeking out. Devotees savour durians like wine. For Malaysian ones, the taste of their rich and creamy flesh varies widely across types. Some are prized for their sweet custard and fruity notes, others for a hint of bitterness, an alcohol tinge, or even a peanut butter flavour. Malaysians’ efforts to elevate the industry can be found in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, at a centre devoted exclusively to the fruit and the growing variety of products made from it. At the Kuala Lumpur Durian Experience Centre, near the landmark Petronas Twin Towers, visitors venture into a replica durian orchard to discover the fruit’s culture and history. In another room, a theatre show draws laughter. Downstairs, visitors enjoy platters and egg tarts crafted from it. Launched this summer after an investment of nearly US$2 million, the two-storey centre spans about 1,900 square metres (20,500 square feet) and is open daily. Its durian shop welcomes guests from morning to midnight. Its founder, Edison Ang, said the centre targeted both local customers and tourists, especially those from China, the world’s biggest durian importer. He said Chinese palates had long been influenced by Thai durian culture. “What we actually hope for now is not to get people who don’t eat durian to start eating durian,” he said. “Instead, we hope consumers who are already eating durian from other countries will switch to Malaysian durian.” Last year, China imported 1.87 million tonnes of fresh durian worth US$7.5 billion, with volume jumping over sixfold in the past decade, according to its customs data. Thailand’s earlier entry helped it secure over half that market by value in 2025. Malaysia, which began exporting fresh durian to China in 2024, was dwarfed. But for the first half of this year, the value of China’s fresh durian imports from Malaysia quadrupled compared with the same period last year, pointing to rapid growth. Prickly problem Unlike their rivals, Malaysian growers typically do not harvest early, instead collecting only naturally ripened fruit caught in nets or ropes as they fall. That was the industry’s biggest advantage and also its biggest weakness, Ang said. Sellers have to race against time because the fruit’s shelf life is at most two to three days. Any delays would affect its quality. When his stock got held up for several days during customs checks, his refund rate climbed, he said. Durian sales were also sensitive to economic conditions, said Leron Yee, founder of DKing, whose business covers both export and domestic markets. When the Chinese economy performs well, his business improves, but if the buying power of Chinese consumers falls, he needs to find alternative markets. “It is a luxury, not a necessity,” he said. Businesses are finding opportunities in what the fruit can become. Yee’s business sells durian paste, durian-flavoured chocolate and mochi – and even mooncakes ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival. DurianBB founder Adrian Choy’s company offers durian ice cream, desserts and dried durian at a cafe, alongside coffee flavoured with the Musang King variety and other items. His brand also offers guided farm tours. In July, Choy’s brand went a step further and launched a durian flower perfume that smells sweet and floral. Choy said branching into other products was important because it would add value to the food itself and differentiate his business, even when others competed on price. “Food is food. You cannot sell it like 50 per cent more because your branding is different.” Across China, durian speciality shops have mushroomed, with some specialising in Malaysian varieties. In Beijing, the Jiang Sir durian shop sells platters priced roughly between 300 and 1,000 yuan (US$45 to US$150), depending on the weight of the pulp and the varieties chosen. Its employee, Hou Yuxin, welcomed the growing number of similar shops and brushed off pressure from competition, saying it would help boost the market for Malaysian durians. She said many people now wanted to enjoy durians during their trips to Malaysia. Back at Ang’s centre in Kuala Lumpur, Henry Zhang was one of them. Zhang, a visitor from Shanghai who started eating durian during his university days, saw a durian no bigger than his palm for the first time. He said Malaysian ones were creamier than those from Thailand and had different flavours. He was impressed by the centre offering more than just the fruit. “I may still eat durians from other countries. But after eating them, I may miss Malaysian ones even more,” Zhang said.

title: Echoing Putin, Serbia’s president resigns in bid to become prime minister
description: Move would allow Aleksandar Vucic to swap offices if his party prevails in early parliamentary elections.
content: Embattled Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigned on Sunday in a well-telegraphed move as he seeks to transition to the role of prime minister as a way of staying close to power in the Balkan nation. Parliamentary Speaker Ana Brnabic, his ally, would take over the presidential role for an interim period. Serbia would hold presidential elections by the end of the year, Vucic said on public television. Meanwhile, Serbs head to a snap election on October 25 that seeks to resolve almost two years of anti-government protests that have evolved from an irritant to a threat for Vucic. Vowing to “be everywhere in Serbia” as he campaigns, Vucic is confident his Progressive Party would prevail and extend the grip on power it’s held since 2012, even as polls are mixed. Vucic’s plan to switch to the premier’s role echoes that of Russian President Vladimir Putin, who stayed in power by spending a four-year stint as prime minister to dodge presidential term limits. “All this time I have been one of you, from tomorrow also formally one of you,” Vucic told his supporters in Belgrade shortly before he signed his resignation. He spoke with Putin on Saturday, informing the Russian leader about preparations for the election, the Kremlin said in a statement. Both sides stressed the need to block outside interference in the electoral process, according to Russia. For Vucic’s plan to work, the Progressive Party needs to beat one of its strongest political adversaries ever: The Student List, which promises to undo the president’s total control over public institutions, including the judiciary and the media, while ensuring accessible housing and healthcare. The student-led movement grew out of mass protests that started in 2024 after a canopy collapse at a newly refurbished railway station in Novi Sad killed 16 people, sparking public outrage amid accusations of corruption in the awarding of contracts and incompetence among the ruling elites. In his address, Vucic listed higher education as an area of failure, adding that “some people have been irresponsible and turned universities into party headquarters”. Vucic, 56, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade. He was a hardline nationalist and information minister during the era of the ‌late Slobodan ‌Milosevic and the wars of the 1990s, and later served as deputy prime minister from 2012-14 and prime minister from 2014-17. During Vucic’s more than nine years in office as president, Serbia has tried to keep alive its stalled bid to join the European Union while also maintaining friendly relations with Moscow and attracting outside investment. He has turned the landlocked nation of about 6.5 million people into a key gateway for China into Europe, ploughing billions of dollars into Serbian industries from mining to humanoid robots. “It was difficult to conduct our foreign policy,” he said. “Almost every meeting in Europe was torture, as every meeting started with the question why I didn’t impose sanctions against Russia.” Vucic said he had good conversations with Putin, French President Emmanuel Macron and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Vucic has notably failed to mend ties with neighbouring Kosovo, a key requirement for proceeding towards EU membership. “Whoever becomes president will have to guard peace and stability, guard our national interests and our people in Kosovo” and “resist calls that we give up Kosovo,” Vucic said. Earlier, the president denied allegations of voter intimidation, ballot box tampering and other irregularities that opponents say have marred previous elections. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: On This Day | Cathay Pacific’s journey from single post-war plane to aviation powerhouse – SCMP archive
description: As Cathay Pacific celebrates 80 years in the skies, we look at how SCMP covered the company’s growth and milestones.
content: Eighty years ago, former World War II pilots Roy Farrell and Sydney de Kantzow registered Cathay Pacific Airways in Hong Kong. Operations began with a single, converted Douglas DC-3 nicknamed “Betsy” which initially flew much-needed goods between Australia and post-war Shanghai. Today, the airline operates a fleet of 180 aircraft and, together with its budget arm HK Express, transported 37 million passengers in 2025. In this On This Day article, we chart the company’s history through SCMP’s archive photos and coverage.

title: Xiaomi-backed robotics chip designer clears hearing, eyes US$100m Hong Kong IPO: sources
description: Company plans to launch premarketing as early as this week and aims for a mid-October debut, sources say.
content: Zhuhai Amicro Technology, a Xiaomi-backed chipmaker, is preparing to begin premarketing for a Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO) of more than US$100 million as early as this week, according to people familiar with the matter. The company passed its listing hearing with bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) last week, clearing the final regulatory hurdle for a share sale in the city, the people said, requesting anonymity because the information is private. According to HKEX’s records, Amicro had yet to publish a public listing document. As a result, its financial details have not been disclosed. It planned to start bookbuilding as soon as next week, and could make its trading debut in mid-October, the sources said. Amicro received approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission in August for the planned Hong Kong IPO, allowing it to issue up to 90.9 million shares. As the listing process was ongoing, details including the size and timetable remained subject to change, according to the sources. Founded in 2014, the company – formerly known as Amicro Semiconductor before adopting its current name in 2025 – develops robotics chips, hardware platforms and algorithms. Its products are used in household and commercial cleaning robots, with customers including major companies such as Xiaomi and Midea Group. The company has shipped more than 10 million units cumulatively. Ahead of its IPO, Amicro completed several funding rounds that attracted institutional investors, including an investment arm of Xiaomi. Headquartered in Zhuhai, in China’s southern province of Guangdong, Amicro is the first company nurtured in the Guangdong-Macau In-Depth Cooperation Zone in Hengqin to earn national “little giant” status. The designation, awarded by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, recognises specialised and innovative small and medium-sized enterprises that focus on niche markets, possess core technologies and hold strong market positions.

title: Nepal rescuers search for 12 missing after Himlung avalanche kills 4
description: The victims were all at a base camp preparing for foreign climbers to arrive.
content: Rescue teams on Monday searched for a dozen people swept away by an avalanche that killed at least four on a Nepalese mountain during severe weather. Rescuers from the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, which is leading the efforts, said they recovered two more bodies on Monday in addition to two others who were found on Sunday. The tragedy happened at Mount Himlung, a 7,126-metre (23,380-foot) peak in north central Nepal. Twelve people were missing. Eight experienced mountain guides from the association took advantage of improving weather on Monday to dig through snow that had covered tents at the mountain’s base camp in the Himalayas. Ten people were rescued after the avalanche swept through the camp near the border with China early on Sunday. All those killed or missing were Nepali nationals, preparing for foreign clients to arrive and climb the peak during the autumn climbing season that began this month. Mountaineer Mingma G. Sherpa, leading the rescue team, said challenging weather was hampering their efforts. “We could have saved lives but due to bad weather, we reached the accident site only in the evening [on Sunday],” he wrote on Facebook. He said the deceased and missing were guides and kitchen staff. Helicopters brought bodies down to Kathmandu airport. Family and friends at a hospital morgue did not comment. Flooding and landslides in the Manang district, where the mountain is located, were caused by heavy rainfall, the district administration office said. Power supply was disrupted in the Manang, Mustang, Myagdi and Baglung districts, with authorities working to restore electricity, energy officials said. There were warnings for severe weather across the entire nation. Nepal’s disaster management agency said 21 other people had been killed and five more were missing in different parts of the country between Thursday and Sunday. Flooding of the Rahuganga River damaged the structure and transmission line towers of a 40-megawatt hydropower project, Water Resources and Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said. The avalanche was the latest natural disaster to hit Nepal in recent weeks. The Himalayan nation is rebuilding from a devastating glacial flood on August 26 that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing. Additional reporting by Reuters, Associated Press

title: Cathay extends Dubai, Riyadh flight suspension through January as Iran war drags on
description: ‘Affected travellers will be offered the flexibility to rebook, divert or refund their tickets,’ airline says.
content: Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways has extended its suspension of passenger flights to the Middle East until the end of January next year, marking the third postponement since the US-Israel war on Iran began. The airline said on Monday that passenger services to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates and Riyadh in Saudi Arabia would remain cancelled through January 31, 2027. “Affected travellers will be offered the flexibility to rebook, divert or refund their tickets,” Cathay Pacific said. “We will closely monitor the evolving situation in the Middle East.” The carrier added that Cathay Cargo would continue to review the timing for resuming freighter services to Dubai and Riyadh. The extension comes after Washington recently rejected Tehran’s seven-day road map to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to say his country was ready for a “doomsday” war with the US. Monday’s announcement marks the third time Cathay has delayed or extended flight suspensions to the region since the conflict broke out. Cathay suspended all passenger and cargo flights to and from the Middle East in response to the US and Israel launching a massive joint aerial bombing and missile campaign against Iran on February 28. In early July, the airline announced plans to progressively resume its Middle East passenger flights from this month. But in mid-July, Cathay pushed back the resumption to the latter half of October. In early September, it announced it would further cancel the flights until the end of November.

title: What is Japan’s Showa retro aesthetic, and why is it all the rage?
description: Flashy mid-century designs are back in vogue in Japan, and experts expect foreign tourists will also catch the ‘Showa retro’ bug.
content: When Japan shut its borders during the Covid-19 pandemic, expats and long-time friends Hillary Hewins and Blake Piper started spending their weekends in Atami, a small seaside city just a 40-minute bullet train ride from their adopted home of Tokyo. Known during the 17th and 18th centuries for its soothing hot springs, Atami steadily surged in popularity during the four decades after World War II as a destination for Japanese holidaymakers. Sprawling concrete resorts opened, and the city centre filled with lively bars, cabaret shows and other nightlife venues, all lit up by flashy neon signs. Hewins and Piper fell in love with Atami’s faded glamour. They began investing in akiya – Japan’s famously inexpensive abandoned houses – in the area, renovating them into home rentals. In 2025, they bought a pair of run-down buildings in the city’s downtown for almost 37.8 million yen (about US$240,000) that they plan to open as a boutique hotel in 2027. They hope to restore the two brashly designed structures to their former glory. Restoring a faded glamour They are not alone. Hewins and Piper are part of a new guard of entrepreneurs eschewing the contemporary form-follows-function Japanese aesthetic and resurrecting the maximalism of what is called “Showa retro”. The term refers to a period during Emperor Hirohito’s long reign, particularly from the 1960s to the 80s, when mid-century modernism was embellished with warm colours, touchable fabrics and bright signage. The word showa originated in ancient Chinese texts; meaning “radiant peace”, it was chosen as an auspicious name to mark Hirohito’s rule when he ascended the throne in 1926. This decorative revival does not merely reflect a nostalgic yearning for brighter times amid a weak yen and other economic doldrums. It marks a return to a more analogue format of human connection during an epidemic of loneliness. The extreme flavour of design is also a reaction against a perceived sameness of so-called third-space decor and the corporatisation of casual hang-outs such as coffee shops around the globe, and signals a renewed focus on preservation in a culture that has long preferred to knock down old, obsolete structures rather than restore them. “When people think of Japan they picture washitsu,” says Takuji Kitagawa, a marketing strategy specialist based in Tokyo, referring to traditional-looking Japanese rooms featuring paper screens and tatami floors. “Showa retro is something else entirely – it has its own visual language that’s genuinely distinctive on a global scale.” It is an aesthetic of excess – every opportunity for a design flourish is taken to stress uniqueness in the face of temperance and conformity. In 2025, Kitagawa opened Showa Club in Tokyo’s Kanda neighbourhood, a modernised version of a sunakku, a type of small drinking establishment that developed during the post-war boom emphasising intimacy and sociability with a host-owner behind the bar. “War, growth, the bubble and its collapse – in many ways, Showa was the most eventful and alive stretch of Japan’s modern history,” Kitagawa says. Like Kitagawa, Tokyo-based music producer Jung Kyung-ho, who goes by Night Tempo, is a child of the 1980s seeking to recapture his analogue youth. Though originally from South Korea, Jung is best known for his Showa Groove remixes of city pop, a genre of Western-influenced music that originated in 70s Japan. To his delight, it has gained new momentum, as “young people have longing in their imagination for cultural experiences of decades past”, he says. Keita Amano, an associate professor at Osaka Metropolitan University, says the upswing in Showa retro interest has to do with what he calls “light exoticism”. He describes the phenomenon as a human curiosity about our adjacencies. We wonder how people in other places are living, and how others lived in the recent past, before the advent of certain technologies. These facets have sparked a surge in interest in sunakku, kissaten cafes and other Showa relics from domestic travellers: throwback shotengai (covered shopping arcades), sento (bath houses with elaborate tile mosaics) and dagashiya (bodega-like candy shops). Social media and a surge in tourism Kitagawa says the record-breaking onslaught of inbound tourists may be playing a large part as well. In 2025, international arrivals reached 42.7 million. That is the first time in the nation’s history that travel numbers have surpassed 40 million – up more than 16 per cent from the 36.9 million visitors in 2024. According to the World Travel Index, Japan is the highest-ranked destination for global tourism. “Thanks to social media, everyday scenes that Japanese people have taken for granted for decades suddenly look soulful and evocative to the foreign eye,” Kitagawa says. “Then young Japanese who never gave these places a second look start paying attention too.” Piper adds, “I hate to minimise it, but I think a lot of the interest from the young people is because it looks good on social media.” Piper notes the word baeru in Japanese, the verb form of Insta-bae, which means “to look good on Instagram”. “This term gets thrown around a lot when young Japanese talk about Atami and the whole Showa retro interest, and they come to town to get a coffee at a throwback cafe for the photo opportunity,” Kitagawa says. In 2025, Atami surpassed 3 million overnight visitors, up from 2.8 million in 2024. Other leisure destinations within Tokyo’s orbit are also seeing an analogous rise in nostalgic interest. Take Chichibu in Saitama prefecture, 80 minutes from central Tokyo by train, where Odekake Watcher, which tracks GPS movements from users’ smartphones, clocked a 37 per cent increase in female visitors in their twenties between August 2025 and August 2026. Like Atami, Chichibu flourished in the 1960s with the expansion of modern railways, filling up with businesses that catered to domestic tourists interested in exploring the nearby national park. A representative from the prefectural tourism board attributes renewed interest to tourists’ desire to capture the emoi – the slang Japanese equivalent of “emo” – aesthetic of the area’s homes, cafes and bars for their social media feeds. International guests may still be wrapped up in exploring ancient temples and modern towers: a 2025 analysis by the Japan National Tourism Organisation found that 70 per cent of the country’s visitors only visit five specific destinations: Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, plus Hokkaido for skiing and Okinawa for beaches. “But as foreigners begin visiting for the third or fourth time, the Showa retro aesthetic will soon be of great interest to them too,” Hewins says. Retaining the human touch One publicly traded Japanese enterprise is doubling down on the potential for growth. Komeda’s Coffee, a Showa retro cafe chain from Nagoya with more than 1,000 locations throughout Japan, plans to franchise globally over the next five years, with established locations in East Asia and forthcoming growth in Thailand and elsewhere. Beyond the throwback decor – think red velvet booths, warm wooden interiors and bubble lettering on the signage – Komeda is also holding on to hospitality tenets such as table service, sensing that customers crave a human touch in the face of automation and AI. “Showa, and the bubble especially, represents the last time Japan felt like it was decisively winning,” Kitagawa says. “For younger Japanese who never lived it, that maximalist confidence is aspirational rather than remembered. For tourists, it’s an authentic, photogenic Japan that isn’t the polished minimalism they expected.”

title: Malaysian police consider sedition charges for ex-Negeri Sembilan officials
description: Ten ousted executive council members face questioning over an alleged plot to depose the state’s ruler.
content: Malaysian police were set to begin questioning 10 former Negeri Sembilan state officials on Monday over a disputed bid to remove the state’s long-time ruler. It comes a week after Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir dismissed the 10 ex-members of the executive council, which serves as the state’s cabinet, for breaching their oaths of allegiance by backing his removal. Negeri Sembilan, south of Kuala Lumpur, has been locked in a months-long struggle over its throne that helped bring down the previous state government and forced a snap election in August. The new administration, led by former ruling party Umno, remains at odds with the palace. Malaysian Inspector General of Police Mohd Khalid Ismail confirmed on Sunday that the councillors would be summoned alongside witnesses and others involved in the dispute. “Many police reports have been filed by certain parties. We will investigate and record the statements of all involved, including the former exco members,” he said, as cited by state news agency Bernama. Khalid said investigators were still reviewing the complaints to determine which laws applied, including whether any offences fell under the Sedition Act. “Police investigate, [but] the decision on whether to prosecute and so on rests with the attorney general,” he said. Former cabinet minister and Senate president Rais Yatim, 84, pleaded not guilty on Friday to a sedition charge over remarks supporting rival claimant Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar at a June ceremony proclaiming him ruler. Negeri Sembilan is the only Malaysian state where four territorial chiefs, known as undang, choose the ruler from eligible princes, instead of the throne passing through a conventional line of succession. The row began with an April 19 proclamation declaring Muhriz’s removal and naming Nadzaruddin as his replacement – a decision Nadzaruddin’s supporters insist the chiefs were constitutionally entitled to make. But the state’s customary council rejected the proclamation, while the federal Attorney General’s Chambers found no evidence that the required procedures had been followed. Nadzaruddin’s supporters dispute that finding. Muhriz dismissed the councillors on September 20 after they endorsed his purported removal, and ordered newly appointed chief minister Ismail Lasim to submit names for a fresh cabinet. The palace accused the councillors of breaking the oaths they took before him on August 7. Ismail has maintained that their appointments remain valid and on Thursday demanded that they be allowed back into their offices after being barred from entering and performing their duties. “Allow the exco members in, allow them to carry out their duties as usual, and state executive council meetings must continue,” he told reporters. Their dismissal was gazetted that day, and Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar reaffirmed on Saturday that it was lawful under the state constitution. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Friday denied federal interference in the dispute but warned against removing a ruler without following constitutional procedures. “I do not agree with overthrowing a ruler so easily,” he was quoted as saying by local media. Efforts to resolve the crisis continued on Sunday night, when Umno president and Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi met representatives of the parties supporting the state government in Kuala Lumpur. The talks lasted nearly three hours but ended without an announced resolution, with Ismail declining to speak to reporters, according to local media reports. “There are various methods we can use,” state Umno chief Jalaluddin Alias told reporters afterwards, adding that Ismail had a formula to keep the administration running, without explaining what it involved.

title: Trump denies US arms offer to Xi but says China would ‘probably like to buy’ them
description: It comes after State Department clarification following US envoy’s disclosure, as Beijing says only that it is firm on boosting defence.
content: US President Donald Trump denied discussing US arms sales with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping during their summit last week, though he noted that China would “probably like to buy” them. Trump was asked by reporters on Monday about his recent meeting with Xi and US ambassador to China David Perdue’s remarks in an interview with Fox News a day earlier that Trump had proposed selling weapons to China. “I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am gonna have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss. “He may have been talking about Taiwan,” Trump added, referring to Perdue’s interview. Trump also spoke highly of his meeting with Xi, saying that out of a score of 10, “I would rate it at 12. Very respectful, very good, great meeting”. Earlier, the US State Department ruled out any plan to sell arms to China, after Perdue said at the weekend that Trump had asked Xi whether Beijing wanted to buy American weapons. There was no such “offer or plan”, the State Department said in an email response to the South China Morning Post on Monday. Speaking to Fox News after the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington, Perdue said: “[Trump] actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.” Perdue did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how Xi responded. The State Department official in his response to the SCMP highlighted long-standing US policy. “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China,” the official wrote. The swift clarification came as Perdue’s apparent disclosure ricocheted among Asia specialists, who noted the extraordinary contradiction between Trump reportedly raising the prospect of arming Beijing and his administration continuing to hold up a roughly US$14 billion weapons package for Taiwan. Washington has for decades treated Beijing as a strategic rival, restricting military technology exports, strengthening security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific region and building its capacity to deter a potential conflict. Beijing did not directly address the matter at Monday’s regular press briefing. When asked about Perdue’s account of the exchange, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said only that China “consistently strengthens its national defence capabilities based on its own needs and remains committed to safeguarding world peace and stability”. The US has not sold conventional weapons to Beijing for more than three decades and has spent much of that time building its military posture around deterring the Chinese military, not supplying it. In the 1980s, the Reagan administration briefly expanded military cooperation with Beijing as both countries sought to counter the Soviet Union. Washington approved several military-related sales, including the roughly US$550 million Peace Pearl programme involving US avionics for Chinese J-8 fighter aircraft. That relationship ended after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989. Then-president George H.W. Bush suspended military sales and exchanges with Beijing and Congress later codified restrictions on the transfer of US defence articles to the Chinese military. US law permits a presidential waiver in the national interest, but no administration has used that authority to restore a conventional US arms pipeline to Beijing. The strategic landscape has since changed dramatically. Successive US administrations have spent billions preparing for a possible military confrontation with Beijing and supplying weapons to Taiwan to help deter a potential attack. Meanwhile, China has built the world’s largest navy by number of ships and rapidly expanded its missile, air and nuclear capabilities. The Pentagon has identified Beijing as the United States’ most consequential long-term strategic challenge. That makes Perdue’s remarks particularly striking. Zack Cooper, an Asia security fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former Pentagon and White House official, wrote on social media that he was “underwhelmed when it looked like the big deliverable both sides actually announced at this Trump-Xi summit was the lease of two pandas”. “But it never occurred to me that an American president might offer to sell American weapons to China,” he added. Cooper later stressed that the remark came directly from Perdue, not an anonymous source. “This wasn’t a leak, it was a comment by President Trump’s ambassador to China on Fox,” he wrote. “I’ll take him at his word until I’m told otherwise.” He also highlighted the contrast with the stalled weapons deal with Taipei, saying it was “shocking that Trump is resisting authorising arms sales to Taiwan but at the same time offering them to China”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Trump has previously signalled a willingness to use arms sales to Taiwan as diplomatic leverage with Beijing. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump said he was holding the US$14 billion package “in abeyance”, calling it “a very good negotiating chip” and saying the decision “depends on China”. Perdue offered no timetable on the sales in the interview aired on Sunday. “There are continuing conversations about other sales,” he said, adding that Trump “has a schedule of his own”. Perdue also said that Trump and Xi discuss American arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” – a comment that drew attention to Washington’s pledge to Taipei in the 1982 Six Assurances not to consult Beijing on the issue. Ryan Hass, who handled China policy at the National Security Council and now heads the China Centre at Brookings, said the disclosure would rattle US partners in Asia. “Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear,” Hass wrote on social media. Taiwan’s de facto envoy in Washington, Alexander Yui Tah-ray, said on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday that last week’s summit statements listed no Taiwan deliverable, even though Beijing called the issue “foundational”. “It was foundational, but there was no reaction from the US side,” Yui said. On the stalled package, he added: “The United States has been our main supplier of weapons to Taiwan.
