We hope that we can get that weapons package in as soon as possible.” Peace through strength, he argued, was “the best way to avoid any conflict”, adding that deterrence rested on the idea that Beijing would not attack if the island itself were strong. The episode has left a simpler question hanging over Washington’s China policy debate: was Trump seriously floating the idea, or was he joking with Xi? And if it was a joke, why did Perdue feel it was worth mentioning on national television? Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute said the key distinction was between Trump raising the idea and making a concrete arms offer. “There is no evidence that Trump made a concrete offer for China to purchase a specific US weapons package, nor that China accepted or seriously negotiated such a deal,” Simon said. “It appears to have been a rhetorical/negotiating manoeuvre rather than an actual arms-sales proposal.” But this did not make the remark insignificant, Simon said, particularly given its connection to Taiwan. “Trump’s logic appears to have been something like: ‘You object to our selling weapons to Taiwan. But America sells weapons to many countries. Why shouldn’t China be able to buy American weapons if it wants them?’,” he said. “That is an intentionally provocative way of reframing the Taiwan issue.” Simon said the episode pointed to a more transactional approach to Taiwan arms sales, in which the weapons package itself becomes leverage in the broader relationship between Washington and Beijing. In his formulation, Trump’s approach is closer to this: Taiwan needs weapons, Beijing objects, so let us see what Beijing is willing to give in return. He noted that Trump might also have been using the hypothetical sale to “tout the appeal of American military hardware”, suggesting that even Beijing might see US weapons as preferable to its own. Scott Kennedy of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies had a more immediate reaction. “Wow! Not sure why Amb Perdue decided it’d be wise to share that comment with the world,” he said on social media. Bonnie Glaser, who heads the Indo-Pacific programme at the German Marshall Fund, focused on another part of Perdue’s interview. The ambassador said Trump and Xi discussed US arms sales to Taiwan “every time they meet” and that Washington “doesn’t support Taiwan independence and doesn’t support coercion”. “Shouldn’t the US oppose coercion?” Glaser wrote. Bill Bishop, author of the Sinocism newsletter, offered a different interpretation, calling it “just more Trump joking” while adding that he was “not sure why Perdue mentioned it”.

title: China lights up ‘super microscope’ hopes with world-leading electron gun beam
description: By observing matter at the atomic scale, the Hefei Advanced Light Facility could drive breakthroughs in microchips.
content: China has produced an electron beam using a cutting-edge electron gun, taking a step towards building a “super microscope” that could help drive breakthroughs in everything from Alzheimer’s research to advanced microchips. The Hefei Advanced Light Facility (HALF) in central China’s Anhui province fired its first electron beam on September 20. Bunches of electrons generated by the gun were accelerated by a 192-metre (630-foot) linear accelerator until they reached 2.2 billion electron volts, marking a milestone for the fourth-generation light source project. “Producing a beam successfully means we’ve taken a key step towards our final goal,” He Zhigang, one of the scientists working on the project, told state news agency Xinhua. He said the beam’s quality, stability and reliability had a major impact on the experiments conducted with HALF. According to the University of Science and Technology of China, HALF’s designed brightness and stability were the highest in the world. Feng Donglai, the project’s chief and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said all the key equipment for the linear accelerator was built domestically. Like other light source projects, HALF is designed to use extremely bright X-rays, generated when high-speed electrons turn in magnetic fields, to observe the structure of matter at the atomic scale. Compared with earlier generations, fourth-generation light sources control electron beams more precisely. The beam is finer and more concentrated, producing brighter X-rays. The X-rays produced by HALF will be more than 100 times brighter and more coherent than those from third-generation sources. This is expected to lead to new experimental methods. The facility will feature up to 35 experimental stations to be shared by scientists worldwide and could help drive advances in high-temperature superconductivity, new energy batteries, advanced materials and life sciences, including Alzheimer’s research. The first batch of 10 stations will include a platform for extreme ultraviolet lithography – a key technology for manufacturing advanced semiconductors that is currently subject to strict US-led export controls. Other stations will focus on nano-devices. Construction of HALF started in 2023 and the project is expected to be completed in 2028. Together with the High Energy Photon Source in Beijing and the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility, it will form China’s advanced light source system covering high-, medium- and low-energy ranges. The kind of electron beam used by HALF was once just a by-product of high-energy physics experiments, and early light sources “piggybacked” on the Beijing Electron-Positron Collider, which began operation in the late 1980s. In 1989, China overcame huge technical challenges to build its first dedicated “super microscope”, the Hefei Light Source. Since then, third-generation light sources have produced many major results, including discovering the molecular mechanism by which arsenic treats leukaemia, revealing the three-dimensional structure of the Sars virus, and imaging a dinosaur fossil inside 99 million-year-old amber.

title: Asian Games: Hong Kong star Ceci Lee hunting nemesis in quest to make ‘biggest step’
description: Cyclist putting all her eggs in track basket in pursuit of omnium gold that would establish her as the continent’s best all-rounder.
content: A “more relaxed and less stressed” Ceci Lee Sze-wing will face the challenge of overcoming two-time reigning champion and hometown favourite Yumi Kajihara in her hunt for a potentially career-shaping Asian Games gold. Lee will link up with Chloe Leung Wing-yee in the Madison on Thursday, but it is in the following day’s omnium, which head coach Herve Dagorne labelled “the queen event”, that the 25-year-old could establish herself as the continent’s most complete track cyclist. She has sacrificed the road and thrown all her eggs in the track basket in Japan in a bid to upgrade the omnium silver she claimed behind Kajihara three years ago. “I was a little bit upset to miss the road, but I need to get over it and have the best result in the omnium, so that I regret nothing,” Lee said. Her emergence from the rubble of a desperately disappointing Paris Olympics into a headstrong, world-class competitor has been one of Hong Kong sport’s more uplifting stories of the past two years. She dominated last year’s National Games cycling, living up to expectations to claim Madison and omnium golds, after nervelessly executing a team plan that was months in the making to win a highly competitive road race. The sight of Lee timing her surge for the line, then demonstratively punching the air in victory, was illustrative of a renewed belief and spirit. Omnium and elimination race bronzes from this year’s opening UCI Track World Cup leg in March represented Lee’s first global honours. She took elimination silver when the competition moved to Hong Kong the following month. “I’ve gained a lot of big-race experience, and I feel more relaxed and not as stressed as before,” Lee said. “I’ve learned to enjoy the race and not focus only on the result. I’ve changed quite a bit this year. Previously, my sprinting ability was my strength, but I now have the ability to attack. I’m more of an all-rounder.” Kajihara pipped Lee to omnium gold from the 2023 and 2024 Asian Track Championships. Even with her nemesis missing, the Hongkonger again had to settle for silver in the following two editions, finishing behind Japan’s Mizuki Ikeda in 2025 and then Chen Ning of China 12 months later. Still, Lee won her first Asian gold in last year's scratch race, and added two more in the scratch and elimination this year. In the 2025 Hong Kong Track Cup, a National Games warm-up, she came within a whisker of toppling Japan’s Kajihara in the four-discipline omnium, summoning a performance that Dagorne called a career “turning point”. “It was physically the hardest race of her life, and all day she was technically and tactically involved in the race,” the Frenchman said. “She’s never suffered like that.” In the same Izu Velodrome that staged the 2020 Olympic track cycling programme, Lee will be up against not only Kajihara but a partisan crowd roaring on their local hero. “Physically ready” after a long altitude camp in mainland province Yunnan, Lee plans to “just try to imagine they’re supporting me”, while Dagorne said “the public won’t be hard for her”. “The main problem is the skill of Yumi,” added the coach. “She loves to compete, but she also loves to win. She’s not there for silver or bronze. That will be tough for Ceci, but she’s just focusing on her technique and delivering the performance she wants.” Another reason that Lee skipped the road in Japan was to keep something back for the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai next month. “If I had to stay in competition mode from the Asian Games road race to the world championships, it would have been too long, physically and mentally,” Lee said. “Two weeks is better for me. “The worlds are very important for us, because of the Olympic qualification points.” In the global event, she is likely to compete in the omnium and elimination race, as well as the Madison alongside National Games gold medal colleague Leung, who last week claimed Asian Games road race bronze. Underlining her increasing self-belief, Lee said she was “aiming for a medal” from the world championships. “I know it’ll be really hard, but I’m going to see how much I can go for it,” she added. She will link up with Leung in the Madison in Japan, 24 hours before gunning for Kajihara and the gold that would rank “super high” in her list of career achievements. “I’ve always been behind Yumi, and I really want something to change,” Lee said. “It would be good for me mentally and a big milestone.” Dagorne was even more emphatic over what dethroning Kajihara would do for his star rider. “When you target an event and want it so much, achieving it is a massive step,” he said. “I think it would solve a lot of problems and give her confidence. It’s like a trigger. Boom, you do it once and afterwards you realise, ‘OK, it wasn’t so hard’. “Of course, it is hard, but when you achieve it, it’s your biggest step. She hasn’t made that step yet, but I hope it will happen now.”

title: 17 injured as minibus hits truck on Hong Kong highway during morning rush
description: Accident temporarily blocked part of Fanling Highway, causing traffic to back up near Kwu Tung.
content: Seventeen people have been injured in Hong Kong after a minibus collided with a truck on Fanling Highway in the New Territories during the peak-hour commute. Emergency services were called to the scene at around 9am on Monday after the minibus, which was travelling in the direction of Tai Po, struck the truck near Choi Yuen Estate in Sheung Shui, police said. The truck had slowed down on the highway when the minibus failed to brake in time and crashed into it, the force said. The crash injured 16 passengers and the 78-year-old minibus driver. The driver was trapped in his seat and had to be rescued by firefighters before being taken to hospital after reporting chest pains. The injured passengers – 12 men and four women – sustained minor injuries and were taken to North District Hospital in Sheung Shui and Alice Ho Miu Ling Nethersole Hospital in Tai Po for treatment. The accident temporarily blocked part of the highway, causing traffic to back up near Kwu Tung. Photos from the scene show the green minibus had swerved into the road divider, leaving its bumper badly damaged. The windscreen was also left shattered, with broken glass strewn across the dashboard. Passengers could also be seen evacuating through the minibus’s rear door.

title: High Court discharges jury in Abby Choi murder trial over sick juror, causing delay
description: Judge says court cannot simply replace outgoing juror, according to legal precedent, and a new jury will be empanelled on Wednesday.
content: The High Court has discharged a recently empanelled jury from the murder trial of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s former relatives after one member asked to be excused for health reasons, leading to a delay in proceedings. Deputy Judge Brian Keith informed the seven men and two women on Monday that he had accepted the unidentified member’s request and decided that a new panel had to be formed to ensure the jury selection complied with legal precedent. A new jury will be empanelled on Wednesday. The prosecution was originally scheduled to present its opening statement on Monday, giving investigators’ account of the 28-year-old’s death and the disposal of her body in a Tai Po village house in February 2023. Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have been jointly charged with murder and preventing the lawful burial of the influencer’s body. Explaining his decision, Keith told the jury he could not simply replace an outgoing juror, as doing so would mean the panel was no longer lawfully constituted in accordance with legal precedent in Australia. He said all jurors must be picked from the same pool of candidates, but it would be impractical to recall them for another round of selection. While the trial could still go ahead with one fewer juror, Keith decided that it would be prudent to empanel a new jury since the trial had not yet begun. “So, members of the jury, unfortunately I have no option but to discharge you all from serving on the jury in this case,” he said. The latest turn of events may extend what was initially expected to be an eight-week trial into December. The court had previously spent a week resolving preliminary issues.

title: China’s fund managers warn of premium risks as fresh quotas fail to ease demand
description: Fund managers warn investors of losses as some US-focused products trade well above asset values.
content: Several Chinese mutual funds investing in US stocks have warned investors about risks associated with hefty premiums to their net asset values, highlighting persistent demand for US equities even after Beijing expanded quotas for outbound investment. At least six fund houses, including China Asset Management, Hua An Fund Management and China Universal Asset Management, issued warnings last week after the market prices of some of their funds rose substantially above their net asset values, cautioning that investors who chase the rally could incur losses if the premiums narrow. For instance, an exchange-traded fund (ETF) tracking the S&P 500 and managed by China Asset Management traded at a 5.8 per cent premium to its net asset value on Monday, while a biotech-focused ETF tracking Nasdaq-listed shares traded at a 4.3 per cent premium, according to data provider Shanghai DZH. Both funds have risen at least 10 per cent this year, outstripping a 6.3 per cent decline in China’s CSI 300 Index. Much like the price-to-book value for stocks of listed companies, a fund’s premium to net asset value measures how much fund prices outpace real values. A big aberration could imply a pullback ahead that would send prices down to reasonable levels. While the elevated premiums carry risks, they also highlight strong demand among Chinese investors for US equities as they seek to diversify portfolios amid low domestic interest rates and a prolonged downturn in the property market. China’s approval of US$6.84 billion in fresh quotas for overseas securities investment last month appears to have fallen short of easing the supply strain, analysts said, with many funds still imposing a daily cap on purchases by individual investors. China restricts direct investment in overseas securities by retail investors, with the qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) programme serving as the official channel for outbound investment. Under the scheme, licensed fund firms can issue products after receiving quotas from financial regulators. Since the programme’s inception in 2006, Beijing had approved 337 QDII products with a combined quota of US$183 billion for investment in overseas assets ranging from US stocks to commodities, according to data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange and financial data provider Wind. BlackRock, the world’s largest asset manager, was granted approval this month to sell QDII funds in China, pending approval of quotas. US stocks remain among the favourite overseas asset classes among Chinese investors because of their exposure to artificial intelligence plays and the market’s resilience. The Nasdaq 100 rose to a record high last week despite elevated oil prices and rising Treasury yields. China’s tech stocks continue to lag, with the chip-heavy Star Market 50 index still recovering from a brutal sell-off in July. The fervour of buying US stocks is not unique to Chinese investors, as global buyers have also poured money into the market at an accelerating pace. Net purchases totalled US$426 billion in the second quarter, the highest on record for any three-month period, according to data from the US Treasury Department. That added to net purchases of US$942 billion over the 12 months through July. Meanwhile, net buying of US Treasuries slowed to US$188 billion in the second quarter from US$314 billion in the preceding three-month period, the data showed.

title: Letters | As youth lose jobs to AI, Hong Kong must act
description: Readers discuss the impact of artificial intelligence on Hong Kong’s labour market, and preventing teen suicides.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong still lacks workers, yet many university graduates are finding it increasingly difficult to land their first job. The Labour and Welfare Bureau’s latest midterm manpower projection shows the city’s overall labour shortfall narrowing to about 130,000 by 2028, down from the estimate of 180,000 published two years ago. On the surface, this suggests talent policies and efficiency gains are working. But for fresh graduates, the picture is far less encouraging. The labour shortfall has shrunk for several reasons. Talent admission schemes have brought in workers to fill professional and technical roles. Artificial intelligence and automation are absorbing routine administrative tasks that once employed junior staff. Having moved past the post-pandemic scramble to refill vacancies, companies are now streamlining operations and prioritising immediate productivity over training new recruits. Hong Kong does not simply lack people; employers are actively looking for workers who can create value as soon as they are on board. Sectors such as healthcare, aviation and technology still face shortages, but many of these roles demand specialised skills or experience that fresh graduates cannot offer straight away. The problem is not just headcount, but skills mismatch. This creates a painful trap. Entry-level positions were traditionally where newcomers gained experience. Now, with employers less willing to bear training costs, graduates face a Catch-22: no experience, so no job; no job, so no experience. Even “entry-level” roles increasingly demand data skills, AI literacy and prior internship or practical work experience. AI is not eliminating all jobs. It is absorbing many of the routine tasks that once served as training grounds for junior employees. Graduates are squeezed from several sides: a growing supply of degree and postgraduate holders, competition from non-local graduates staying in Hong Kong under a special immigration scheme and returning emigrants with work experience, and employers’ preference for ready-made talent. The policy address’s 30,000 youth internship and employment places are therefore a step in the right direction. Internships are no longer a bonus; they are becoming a necessary bridge to full-time work. Yet quality matters as much as quantity. Placements must offer genuine, industry-relevant experience. Universities, too, must adapt. Internships, career planning and AI training should be embedded into curricula early, not left as last-minute fixes before graduation. As Hong Kong develops the Northern Metropolis, university towns and innovation industries, the priority should shift from simply importing more talent to matching talent more precisely with future industries while nurturing local youth. Hong Kong may reduce its labour shortfall. But without enough entry-level rungs, it risks failing to build the generation that will take over. Roy Ying, senior lecturer, School of Business, Hang Seng University of Hong Kong Kick-start economy to improve mental health There is no denying that the causes of youth suicide are complex, with problems at home and school acting as major intertwined contributors. However, the digital environment has become a significant amplifier of distress (“Social media must join the fight against teen suicides”, September 10). When tackling this vastly complicated issue, we tend to focus only on the discrete components of a complex machine. Instead, we need to adopt a holistic perspective. One underlying cause of youth suicide could be insufficient parental care. Teenagers today rarely see their parents because their parents are consumed by work. Furthermore, students retreat into video games and social media because school has become a form of torture. Trapped in classrooms from morning until late afternoon, struggling students absorb little while enduring constant reprimands from teachers for sleeping or drifting off. They refuse to learn or cooperate not out of malice; the curriculum is simply too difficult for them. If teenagers could spend more time with their parents and face fewer academic demands, would society be better off? Before 1990, when Hong Kong had only two universities, most people did not hold a university degree. Yet, many could easily secure employment and gradually build a healthy and prosperous life. Life was simpler yet more fulfilling, making quality family time a given. Facing less job insecurity, workers enjoyed more regular working hours and greater peace of mind. To restore Hong Kong to its heyday, the government should and must go further and kick-start the economy. As growth takes off, the entry-level job market will become less rigidly fixated on formal qualifications. Parents will face less workplace anxiety, and teachers will feel less pressure to drive their students relentlessly. In turn, the tight harness suffocating Hong Kong’s spirit will finally break. To realise this vision, unity across every sector of Hong Kong is the engine that will enforce collective accountability and help the city develop. Yu Mei-mei, Yuen Long

title: Fireworks, free rides and dining deals: how to celebrate National Day in Hong Kong
description: City rolls out array of deals from half-price movie tickets to discounts for attractions, as it welcomes 1.29 million mainland visitors.
content: Hong Kong will celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China on October 1 with a string of offerings for locals and visitors. The National Day “golden week” holiday in mainland China, which runs from October 1 to 7, is expected to bring in about 1.29 million visitors from across the border. But Hongkongers will only have one public holiday during the period, on Thursday. The South China Morning Post lists the discounts and perks available during the celebration. 1. What major activities are being held? First, a flag-raising ceremony will be held at 8am at Golden Bauhinia Square in Wan Chai, attended by officials and community leaders and followed by a fly-past and a sea parade by the disciplined services. No public viewing area will be set up. The Hong Kong Jockey Club will then host a themed race at the Sha Tin Racecourse, with free admission for the public from 11.45am. Hong Kong will stage a 23-minute fireworks display over Victoria Harbour at 8pm. The HK$18 million (US$2.3 million) extravaganza will launch 31,888 pyrotechnic shells from nine firing points on three barges and six floating pontoons. Visitors can view the spectacle from several vantage points along the Tsim Sha Tsui and Wan Chai waterfronts. 2. What transport offers are available? The MTR Corporation will give away 77,000 electronic single-journey rides through a lucky draw on October 1. The public can also enjoy free rides on all passenger tram routes and several ferry routes of the Star Ferry and Fortune Ferry on that day. Children using designated payment methods can ride most daytime franchised bus routes of KMB, Long Win Bus, Citybus and New Lantao Bus for free. Greater Bay Airlines will offer a 23 per cent discount on original fares for all non-charter routes during the promotion period. The Hong Kong Museum of Art and the Hong Kong Space Museum will also close early at 5pm on October 1 ahead of the fireworks display. 3. Are there deals for entertainment? All commercial cinemas will sell tickets at half-price on October 1. Free admission will also be offered on the same day at several facilities and exhibitions in museums run by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, and the Hong Kong Wetland Park. The Police Souvenir Gallery, Hong Kong International Airport, Science Park, the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, the West Kowloon Cultural District, the HKTDC Design Gallery, and various shopping centres and department stores will also roll out offers on dining, consumption, parking and other perks. MTR shopping centres will give away 77,000 gifts and e-coupons to celebrate National Day. The Ngong Ping 360 cable car attraction and Ocean Park will offer ticket discounts while The Peak Tram and Madame Tussauds Hong Kong will give out souvenirs to ticket holders. 4. What’s in store for foodies? More than 3,800 restaurants and catering businesses will provide dining promotions to celebrate the anniversary. Offers include meal sets at 30 per cent off, fresh food items such as vegetable packs for HK$7 at food market stalls, crispy chicken for HK$10 a piece, buy-one-get-one-free bun deals and 30 per cent discounts at several hotels. Multiple brands under the Tai Hing Group – including Tai Hing, Men Wah Bing Teng and Asam Chicken Rice – will offer a 30 per cent discount on all dine-in bills throughout the day. Other fast food chains such as Cafe de Coral, Maxim’s restaurants and Spaghetti House have also offered different combinations of deals. Several hotels – including Harbour Grand Hong Kong in North Point, the Ocean Park Fullerton hotel in Aberdeen, the Regal Hotel Group, Shangri-La Hotel Group and Nina hotels – are offering discounts for dine-in customers at their lounges, cafes and restaurants.

title: Milan Fashion Week: Bottega Veneta, Dolce & Gabbana, Ferragamo and Tod’s round out the best of SS27
description: The last few days highlighted the diversity of Italian fashion, from Ferragamo’s ‘40s revival to Tod’s elegant line-up of outerwear staples.
content: The last couple of days of a very happening Milan Fashion Week showcased the diversity of the Italian fashion industry, from the low-profile luxury embodied by Ferragamo and Tod’s – two labels known for their footwear and leather goods – to the Sicilian glamour of Dolce & Gabbana and Bottega Veneta’s celebration of textures. Louise Trotter’s third collection for Bottega Veneta felt like a breath of fresh air, which was probably how the designer envisioned the range from the start. In the show notes, she mentioned the passing of seasons in Milan, where she now lives, and how that made her think about shedding layers and “disrobing”, as she put it. The collection was as much about covering up as about revealing, with relaxed silhouettes, airy fabrications such as crochet, oversized tailoring and knitwear that fits loosely on the body. The show had a playful lightness, set in an all-white space built in collaboration with artist Illya Goldman Gubin, who made the cardboard stools guests sat on. The runway soundtrack, provided by Mark Leckey, gave the proceedings a kind of urgency that reflected the energy of the garments. Twisted, knotted and full of surface textures, the clothes were meant to give the wearer complete freedom of movement. Many looks were paired with quirky crochet hats, while the accessories were a sight to behold, from Intrecciato (Bottega Veneta’s signature woven pattern) bags in raffia to fringed fishnet flats and giant half-moon bags with Intrecciato handles. The Dolce & Gabbana spring/summer 2027 show was an ode to Sicilian extravagance. This was not the first time the designers looked to Sicily for inspiration (co-founder Domenico Dolce hails from the Southern Italian island). For this collection, the designers imagined opening the doors of a grand Sicilian palazzo and unearthing the contents of a bridal trousseau filled with clothes, jewels and beautiful objects. Lace, unsurprisingly, took centre stage, as did luscious fabrics like brocade silk, a nod to the lavish interiors of those palazzos. Animal prints were a veiled homage to The Leopard, the famous book by Sicilian writer Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa. Fringes, lace, leopard prints and gold accents often appeared in a single outfit, but the overall effect was never overwhelming. The brand’s loyal clients love nothing more than to make a statement. They will have plenty to buy come next season, from boyfriend jeans embellished with coral beads to jackets in gold brocade. Extravagance aside, this Dolce & Gabbana show also delivered closet staples like the perfect black dress that fitted like a glove and a polka dot chiffon blouse that looked chic and fabulous. Every season, Tod’s Matteo Tamburini brings something new to the table without rocking the boat, which makes sense for a brand steeped in craftsmanship and quality. Named Italian Attitude, the spring/summer 2027 collection was an elegant line-up of outerwear staples such as the trench coat and the biker jacket reworked in fabrications like perforated leather. Stand-out pieces included wraparound skirts with a leather apron attached to the front and a series of beautiful colour-blocked scarf dresses. A shoemaker at heart, Tod’s never fails to deliver on accessories. For spring/summer, the brand’s signature Gommino loafers come in PVC and perforated leather. On the runway, the iconic Gommino also appeared hanging from bags such as the T Signature and the Di Bag, further showcasing the label’s prowess with leather goods. Ferragamo’s Maximilian Davis loves mining a decade for inspiration. This season, the designer turned to the ’40s, when women entered the workforce, as he explained in the show notes. “It was a period where clothing, and its structure, created a certain posture and propriety, when the placement of a pocket would dictate how you would both stand and behave. I wanted to take elements of that silhouette and modernise it for today,” he said. That idea translated into broad-shouldered skirt suits styled with double belts, and utilitarian accents like army vests and cargo pockets. The designer experimented with materials such as “translucent rubber” for body-con dresses and trench coats. Transparency was a leitmotif, also achieved through chiffon in a series of diaphanous scarf dresses. Desert hues such as brown and taupe dominated a range that continued what Davis has been doing at the label. Accessories ranged from bejewelled stiletto slingbacks to new versions of the bestselling Hug bag in crinkled silk.

title: From laboratory tests to everyday choices: Annual ‘Digi-Science’ competition sparks student passion for food safety and scientific rigour
description: Students bridge the gap between classroom science and real-world testing, using creative storytelling to demystify complex chemical additives for the public.
content: Scientific accuracy plays a vital role in keeping our food safe. To help students grasp the real-world applications of testing and certification, the Hong Kong Council for Testing and Certification (HKCTC) and the Hong Kong Association for Science and Mathematics Education have jointly organised the annual “Digi-Science” Video Production Competition since 2016. Student innovators take centre stage Under this year’s theme, “Testing Science: Food Additives”, participating teams explored the chemistry of everyday meals by designing experiments with common ingredients. Students dedicated months to practical laboratory research, formulating original hypotheses and summarising their findings in two-minute video submissions. Through these projects, participants witnessed how testing and certification confirm scientific facts, maintain food quality, and safeguard public health. The judging panel, composed of HKCTC members Denise Hou, Dr Gray Ho, Dr Lesley Lam and Dr Zhao Wei, praised the consistently high quality of submissions. “The majority of students demonstrated strong communication skills and a solid command of testing principles, reflecting well on the HKCTC’s educational outreach,” noted the panel. Hou highlighted the students’ ability to distil complex theories into clear presentations. She pointed to the notable submission “The Fizzy Trap,” in which students broke down complex biochemical reactions into easily understandable concepts. By using soft drinks as illustrative examples, they conducted experiments to explore chemical additives, making intricate chemical processes accessible to the general public. Beyond the competition: building a safer and smarter future By blending rigorous scientific inquiry with creative video making, this competition empowers young innovators to move beyond rote learning. Throughout the process, students hone critical analytical skills, scientific perseverance, and dynamic communication capabilities that prepare them for future academic and professional pursuits. The rigorous thinking and spirit of truth-seeking nurtured through this experience will foster a new generation of young talent. HKCTC has long been a driving force in promoting testing and certification literacy across society. Beyond organising this annual competition, HKCTC actively develops teaching kits, hosts hands-on workshops and arranges laboratory visits that offer students an insider’s look into professional testing environments. After all, testing and certification are an invisible safeguard for public health, an engine for innovation and a guarantee of consumer trust. By nurturing our next generation, HKCTC ensures that science continues to serve as an empowering tool for smart, informed everyday choices and a safer society for all. Senior Secondary Division Championship: Kowloon True Light School Team members: Alice Chan Lok-yan, Angela Lee Ka-wan and Naomi Sze Hoi-nam Title of video: Effects of Acid Regulators in Soft Drinks on Type II Diabetes What began as a casual lunchtime chat led the team to challenge the assumption that sugar-free drinks are entirely safe for individuals with diabetes. Their research revealed that certain acid regulators containing phosphoric acid can rapidly hydrolyse sucrose into fructose and glucose, potentially impacting blood sugar levels of persons with Type II diabetes. Driven by this discovery, the students used their video to raise public awareness about hidden dietary health risks. Advanced concepts like acid hydrolysis and diabetes management are typically reserved for higher-level studies. “We had to conduct extensive literature reviews, analysing numerous scientific reports and academic papers,” the team explained. The project took four months of dedicated effort, with the team staying after school every day to run experiments in the chemistry laboratories and complete their final report. Beyond translating complex science for a general audience, the project aimed to promote more mindful consumption. The team said, “Our findings serve as an essential reminder for people to read nutrition labels carefully before eating or drinking, shedding light on the misconception that ‘zero sugar’ or ‘sugar-free’ claims guarantee a total absence of sugar derivatives.” Junior Secondary Division Championship: St Clare’s Girls’ School Team members: Dora Leung Kwan-lam, Hailey Tong Hei-yee and Hebe Cheung Yin-yin Title of video: Colouring Action Concerned by the link between excessive artificial food colouring and childhood hyperactivity, the team investigated the impact of Tartrazine (a commonly used yellow food colouring) using yeast as a model for human cells. Translating this concept into reliable data required navigating significant experimental hurdles. “Determining the precise quantity of yeast required for each test posed a major challenge,” the team explained. “Defining the exact micro-measurement demanded extensive calibration.” Starting with simple household bowls to observe fermentation before moving to school laboratories, repeated trial and error taught them that excessive heat denatures yeast. It also sharpened their problem-solving skills and perseverance along the way. “On top of the laboratory work, the true test lay in the creative execution, specifically scripting and structuring a compelling video that breaks down sophisticated chemistry topics into clear and accessible concepts for the general public,” the team said. Balancing the explanation of scientific theories with an engaging, visually appealing video presentation proved to be the most rewarding part of their journey.

title: Siti Hasmah, wife of Malaysia’s Mahathir Mohamad, dies aged 100
description: Her family confirmed on Monday that she died after being admitted to the National Heart Institute in Kuala Lumpur.
content: Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali, the wife of former Malaysian prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, died on Monday aged 100. Her family confirmed her death after she was admitted to the National Heart Institute in Kuala Lumpur. The cause of death was not immediately clear. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, whose decades-long feud with Mahathir defined modern Malaysia’s politics, said on Monday that Siti Hasmah would be granted a state funeral. “The nation will always remember her maternal presence and cherish her contributions,” Anwar said in a social media statement, adding that his thoughts and prayers were with Mahathir and Siti Hasmah’s family. Funeral prayers were held later on Monday at As-Syarif Mosque in Selangor state, where Anwar – accompanied by his wife Wan Azizah Wan Ismail – shook hands with Mahathir and the two briefly exchanged words. Other prominent figures in attendance included former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, Naimah Khalid – the widow of Mahathir’s long-time confidant Daim Zainuddin – cabinet ministers and foreign envoys. Pahang ruler Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah and his wife Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah paid their respects at the Mahathir family home earlier in the day, along with Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman and singer Siti Nurhaliza. The hearse arrived at the National Heroes’ Mausoleum in Putrajaya shortly before 6pm, where more than 300 people had gathered for the burial. Within 20 minutes, Siti Hasmah was laid to rest as a visibly grief-stricken Mahathir and their family stood at the graveside. Their son, Mukhriz Mahathir, said the family considered themselves fortunate to have had Siti Hasmah with them until the age of 100, describing her death as a profound loss after an exceptionally long life. “I consider myself one of the luckiest children because even at 62 [years old] until this morning, I still had a mother and I still have a father,” he told reporters. “That is a blessing that means a great deal to our family.” Celebrated as “Ibu Negara” (Mother of the Nation), Siti Hasmah built a legacy of care and compassion with her tireless work furthering the cause of women’s empowerment and the rights and protection of children both at home and abroad. She was among Malaysia’s first Malay women doctors, graduating in 1955 from the King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore, where she first met Mahathir. The pair married in 1956 and had seven children, including social activist Marina, business leaders Mirzan and Mokhzani, and former Kedah chief minister Mukhriz. She served as a medical officer across Malaysia, including in Mahathir’s home state of Kedah where she was appointed the country’s first female state medical officer in charge of maternal and child health in 1974. But she only really started to become a household name in 1981, cultivating a public persona seen as supportive, yet independent, of her ambitious husband. Siti Hasmah’s focus on empowering rural women and supporting the underprivileged, including the disabled, provided a balm for a nation split over Mahathir’s aggressive and often controversial policies. Her star power shone when she joined Malaysia’s national team to celebrate ending a quarter-century drought in the Thomas Cup – one of badminton’s biggest prizes – in 1992. Footage of her shedding tears of happiness won over many Malaysians and cemented her legacy as a force for good in the country. She was patron of the Badminton Association of Malaysia at the time. In a 2019 interview, Siti Hasmah said she knew her role was not to interfere with how the players and coaches went about their work, but rather to keep them together as a team. “I get emotional and start tearing [up] every time I revisit the year when we last won the Thomas Cup,” she was quoted as saying by the New Straits Times. “I will never forget that moment because these players were like my children and they saw me as their mother. And as a mother, it was my duty to keep them united.” Her relationship with her long-time husband also endeared her to many Malaysians, with their playful antics in public sometimes helping the populace forget Mahathir’s past authoritarian tendencies. In her 2016 memoir, Siti Hasmah described Mahathir as the “boy from the padi fields state” – referring to his home state of Kedah – and her hero for helping her push through and complete her studies. She almost never left his side, travelling with him on both official trips and holidays around the world. Malaysian singer-actress Bella Astillah visited Siti Hasmah and Mahathir last Thursday, accompanied by her fiancé MP Syed Saddiq. “Just imagine the joys and sorrows they have weathered together,” Bella wrote in a social media post about the visit, likely among the final ones the couple received. “Think of the patience, compromise, forgiveness and understanding required to reach a point where, after everything, the person by your side is still the very same person you chose all those years ago.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by B E L L A A S T I L L A H (@bellaastillah) Siti Hasmah touched upon some of those same themes herself in a 2015 interview. “You must support your husband, you must be knowledgeable, you must know what is happening around you and you must make sure to always be with your husband when meeting the people,” Siti Hasmah said. “You must always support but never ever compete with your husband.”

title: CDL’s Kwek clan looks to invest US$3.9b in Singapore, China, Japan to raise confidence
description: The company’s future has been a subject of intense discussion after a legal tussle between patriarch Kwek Leng Beng and eldest son Sherman.
content: City Developments (CDL), the Singapore property group controlled by one of the country’s wealthiest families, said it wants to invest S$5 billion (US$3.9 billion) in Singapore, China and Japan by 2029 as part of measures to regain investor confidence after a feud within the clan. The firm also aims to sell S$6 billion of assets within the same period either via outright divestments or seeding suitable assets into managed vehicles, according to an exchange filing on Monday. It wants to set up a dedicated fund management entity with an investment committee and leadership team to double assets under management to S$10 billion by 2029, via new real estate investment trusts, funds, partnerships and joint ventures. The company’s outlook and succession plans have been a subject of intense discussion among investors after a legal tussle between chairman and patriarch Kwek Leng Beng and his eldest son, Chief Executive Officer Sherman Kwek, early last year. The duo later agreed to settle their differences. Singapore’s largest listed developer by market value has been supported by the broad strength of the country’s residential market, which helped it to more than triple its profits in the first half of the year. Still, its shares have risen only 3 per cent this year versus a 23 per cent increase in the benchmark Straits Times Index. Sherman Kwek has said a key priority was to reduce CDL’s net debt-to-equity ratio, which includes the fair value of its investment properties and rose to 75 per cent in the first six months of the year. As part of the review, the firm now wants that to come down to about 55 per cent by 2029. He has also committed to selling assets in underperforming markets like China, as well as the UK. The release of the strategic review’s findings has been delayed since the middle of this year. Sherman had earlier said the developer’s board and management were not under review, and the 10-member board had signed off unanimously on its conclusions. The Kweks control about 49 per cent of the firm’s shares. The patriarch and his Malaysian cousin, Quek Leng Chan, dominate the family, which has a net worth of US$25 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, making them one of Asia’s richest clans.

title: Hong Kong to close deals with firms from strategic sectors in months: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief says cross-departmental committee in ‘close discussions’ with several firms over setting up operations in city.
content: A handful of leading firms from emerging industries are expected to receive preferential policy packages and set up operations in Hong Kong within the “next couple of months”, the city’s finance chief has said, as part of efforts to attract investment. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po provided an update on the city’s drive to draw international and national brands and strategic enterprises to set up business in Hong Kong through dedicated preferential arrangements. “We are in close discussions with a few. We hope to conclude this as soon as possible and make the announcement. The target is in the next couple of months,” Chan said. The policy address in mid-September revealed that a cross-departmental committee, led by Chan, was reviewing applications from “strategic emerging industries”, including aerospace and new materials, taking into account factors such as how much they were investing, potential growth and economic benefits in devising the packages. Chan said his committee would assess applications on a case-by-case basis and offer concessions through potential incentives such as land grants, tax reductions and co-investments with the government. He added that the administration would help firms secure approvals from authorities, including bringing in expertise unavailable in the local market. Chan said determining the package’s reduced tax rate depended on whether the firms were from priority industries the government sought to develop, and their business plans, the number of potential local hires and their estimated contribution to the economy and the broader community. Asked whether the firms would be subject to specific metrics, Chan said: “We have criteria, but they may not be quantitative. It is subject to negotiation.” The preferential policy package was proposed in last year’s policy address to facilitate negotiation between Hong Kong’s investment attraction agencies and target firms. The Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises and InvestHK can use the packages to finalise details with companies and report to the financial secretary for approval. This year’s policy address built on the government’s bid to attract enterprises, with the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau planning to roll out preferential tax rates of 5 per cent, or half‑rate, for selected enterprises operating in key sectors. The key industries include finance, advanced manufacturing, research and development in innovation and technology, headquarters activities and logistics and supply chain management. The bureau aims to table the bill amendment to the Legislative Council by the end of this year. Chan said authorities would be “very quick”, with hopes to get it “approved in the following few months”. While authorities push to develop new industries and diversify the economy, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports, a core pillar of gross domestic product, have seen runaway growth since March. Chan said he remained “cautiously optimistic” about export growth as Hong Kong engaged mainly in re-exports and mainland Chinese firms had been agile and flexible. He also observed that the recent increase in exports had been driven by artificial intelligence and electronic products, while export markets had been changing, with Asean and the Global South showing strong demand. “[They are] more than compensating [for] the slower increase in the United States and other established markets,” he said. “So I think for us, [we have] to remain agile and support the industry to adjust to and realign their positioning.” In the first eight months of 2026, total merchandise exports rose by 42.5 per cent from the same period last year, while total imports climbed by 43.2 per cent, resulting in a deficit of HK$371.2 billion.

title: ‘Everyone can attend university’: China unveils sweeping higher education reform
description: New guidelines urge universities to specialise as demographic change and a tougher job market reshape talent demand.
content: China has unveiled an overhaul of its university system, urging institutions to develop distinct roles as demographic change, a tighter job market and industrial upgrading alter the country’s skills needs. The general offices of the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee as well as the State Council, China’s cabinet, jointly issued guidelines for higher education reform, state news agency Xinhua reported on September 20. The document said universities must adapt to “changing trends in the school-age population”. It urged institutions to pursue differentiated development, build more integrated forms of higher education and explore new ways to train future innovators. In particular, Beijing called for universities to develop distinct roles. High-level research universities will be expected to support major national strategies, while industry-specific institutions must strengthen their capacity to serve the real economy. “With the total school-age population shrinking and higher education transitioning from an elite to a mass model, everyone will have the opportunity to attend university in the future,” said Fan Xiudi, director of the Education Evaluation Research Centre at Shanghai’s Tongji University. “This requires the education structure to adapt to changing demographic trends.” Fan said a major element of the overhaul would be encouraging universities to develop distinctive strengths while helping students make the most of their individual aptitudes. “In the past, all Chinese higher education institutions vied to become top-tier, comprehensive research universities with a full range of disciplines,” Fan said. “However, not all students excel academically, and everyone has different strengths.” The importance of cultivating a diverse talent pool has been repeatedly stressed in recent years. But Fan said it was unusual for the issue to be elevated to the central government level. “My understanding is that the central government also feels this issue is extremely urgent and must be resolved,” she said. “If China wants to become a leading educational nation, or to genuinely respond to individual development and societal needs, homogeneous development will be unsustainable.” Demographic data underscores this urgency. The population across all school-age stages in China is forecast to fall rapidly after reaching its peak, with numbers from preschool to junior secondary level already in decline. In 2022 researchers from Beijing Normal University and other institutions used national population census data to project a fall in China’s total school-age population from 328 million in 2021 to about 250 million in 2035. The university-age demographic is forecast to peak in 2032. Meanwhile, higher education access has expanded massively over the past decade and a half. Total nationwide enrolment reached 48.7 million in 2025, representing a gross enrolment rate of 61.3 per cent – more than double the 30 per cent recorded in 2012 – according to the Ministry of Education. “Such a massive higher education system cannot operate on a single track,” a ministry official was quoted as saying. “Policies must be applied to encourage universities to develop distinctive characteristics and better adapt to the diverse needs of the economy and society.” Under a 2024-35 education development outline jointly issued by the Central Committee and the State Council in January 2025, higher education institutions are to be differentiated by research-, applied- and skills-oriented missions, with management and funding tailored accordingly. In an interview with Science and Technology Daily, Liu Zhentian, a professor of education at Xiamen University, said research universities would be the main bastions for cultivating top innovators needed to advance China’s scientific and technological self-reliance. Applied universities would focus on regional development, helping to close the gap between talent supply and industry demand, Liu said. Skills-oriented universities, meanwhile, would focus on nurturing artisans as well as technical personnel for the country’s modern industrial system. Authorities will reportedly establish categorised incentive mechanisms, providing differentiated support based on each university’s functional positioning, actual contributions and distinctive advantages. Although such categorised development has been advocated for years, the difference now is that external conditions are “undergoing substantial changes”, according to an analysis by Zhang Duanhong, director of Tongji University’s Education Policy Research Centre, and Liu Hong, a researcher at Fudan University. The conditions that previously fuelled the homogeneous expansion of Chinese universities were beginning to unravel, the researchers wrote in a social media post on September 22. A shrinking population was altering the student base, a tight job market forcing a rethink of talent supply, and industrial upgrading redefining demand, they said. “Original innovation, technological development, engineering, industrialisation and on-site process improvements require the joint support of different types of innovation entities and talent,” they wrote in the post. Given these shifts, the authors said, the main role of the new guidelines was to grant universities the policy space to make proactive adjustments now, rather than waiting to be “forced to transition” when student numbers dwindled, funding tightened and graduate employment worsened.

title: Elderly resident sparks fury in China after cutting worker’s safety rope to hang laundry
description: Incident triggers fierce condemnation on mainland social media, with related posts amassing 61 million views; some brand act ‘attempted murder’.
content: An elderly resident in southern China sparked online outrage after cutting a high-altitude worker’s safety rope to use it as a washing line. The incident occurred when Liu, a worker from Foshan, Guangdong province, was repairing the exterior wall of a high-rise building on September 17. After descending from the 30th floor to a platform on the second floor, he discovered that one of his safety ropes had been cut, with part of the rope left on the platform. Fortunately, no workers were using the rope for high-altitude operations at the time it was cut. Liu reported that the rope was 120 metres long, and over 10 metres had been removed, leaving him unable to complete his descent to the first floor. He described the act as “thoughtless.” An investigation later revealed that the individual responsible was an elderly resident in their late 70s living on the second floor, though their gender has not been disclosed. The resident claimed they were unaware that the rope was safety equipment or being used for high-altitude work, stating that they cut it to serve as a washing line. Given the advanced age of the resident, Liu decided not to report the incident to the police. After discussions with the building’s property management company, he sought 400 yuan (US$60) in compensation for the damaged rope. The incident triggered a wave of condemnation on mainland social media, with related posts receiving over 61 million views. One online observer criticised the act as “attempted murder,” arguing that age and a lack of knowledge should not excuse the destruction of someone else’s property. Another commenter suggested that Liu should have reported the matter to the authorities, adding: “Being too lenient only diminishes the consequences for those who do wrong.” Wang Haogong, a lawyer at Shaanxi Haogong Law Firm, noted that the resident’s actions violated Liu’s property rights by cutting and appropriating the rope. If Liu experienced additional losses, such as lost income, he could pursue further compensation through legal channels. Wang also pointed out that the 400 yuan claim fell below the legal threshold for theft and would not typically be treated as such. Under Chinese law, individuals aged 75 and above may receive leniency in both civil and criminal cases, including reduced penalties or lighter legal consequences. They are generally exempt from the death penalty, except in cases involving exceptionally serious crimes. Similar incidents have been reported in China in recent years. In December 2017, a man surnamed Cao in Zhengzhou, central China, cut the safety rope of a high-altitude worker during a dispute over construction work. As a result, the worker fell from the fourth floor and sustained multiple fractures. Cao was subsequently convicted of intentional injury and given a nine-month prison sentence, suspended for one year.

title: Style Edit: Bvlgari’s Eclettica collection dazzles with the stars in Shanghai
description: The presentation at the Expo I-Pavilion saw celebrity ambassadors like Wu Lei, Jolin Tsai and Liu Yifei turning out for the Italian jeweller.
content: In high jewellery, the most interesting ideas often emerge from the meeting of different artistic disciplines. For Bvlgari, that has long been part of its creative vocabulary. With Eclettica, the Roman jeweller looks to sculpture, painting and architecture, translating their language of form, colour and proportion into a collection that places artistic expression alongside exceptional gemstones and craftsmanship. Following its debut in Milan in March, the collection arrived in Shanghai earlier this month, where the Shanghai Expo I-Pavilion provided the setting for an evening dedicated to Bvlgari’s creative vision. The event brought together the maison’s latest high jewellery and high-end watch creations, including nine exceptional Capolavori – masterpieces distinguished by their extraordinary stones and intricate craftsmanship. At the heart of Eclettica is a distinctly Roman sensibility. Since its founding in 1884, Bvlgari has drawn from the visual richness of its home city, where classical architecture, Renaissance art and contemporary life exist in constant conversation. This layered cultural landscape informs the collection, but Eclettica is not an exercise in historical reference. Instead, it reflects the maison’s continuing interest in reinvention, using contrasting influences to develop new forms of beauty. Sculpture, painting and architecture serve as three interconnected creative languages. Sculpture informs the three-dimensional volumes of the jewels, creating surfaces that interact with light and shadow. Painting finds expression in the colour and tonal relationships of gemstones, from saturated emeralds to vivid rubellites and turquoise. Architecture contributes a sense of structure, rhythm and proportion, giving the pieces their distinctive balance and presence. Together, these influences form a visual vocabulary that allows Bvlgari’s designers and artisans to work beyond conventional boundaries. Jewellery becomes a meeting point between artistic intuition and technical mastery, with each creation shaped by the dialogue between the person who imagines it and the craftspeople who bring it to life. Lucia Silvestri, Bvlgari’s jewellery creative director and gemstone sourcing director, describes eclecticism not as a passing aesthetic but as a method deeply embedded in the maison’s creative process. Her approach to Eclettica draws on the expressive power of painting, the challenges of sculptural volume and the measured geometry of architecture. The result is a collection in which contrast is not resolved through uniformity, but brought together in deliberate harmony. The Shanghai presentation extended this dialogue beyond the jewellery itself. Under layered architectural lighting, the Expo I-Pavilion became a setting where the collection’s artistic influences could be experienced through movement, colour and form. Models wearing the creations brought the sculptural qualities of the jewels into focus, while performances incorporating Chinese drum music, water-sleeve dance and contemporary dance introduced another dimension to the evening. Tradition and modernity, stillness and motion, became part of the same visual composition. The collection’s most striking expressions were seen on Bvlgari’s ambassadors and guests. Liu Yifei wore an Eclettica necklace centred on rich green jadeite, paired with translucent jadeite earrings and an emerald ring. The combination brought together Bvlgari’s Roman design language and the cultural significance of a gem long regarded in China as the “stone of heaven”. Carina Lau appeared in an Eclettica necklace featuring a 34.82-carat cushion-cut Colombian emerald. Matching earrings and a ring continued the emerald theme, with diamonds in varied cuts adding brilliance and contrast to the rich central stones. Jolin Tsai brought a more dynamic expression to the evening in a Serpenti high jewellery necklace. Rubellite, diamonds and turquoise traced the sinuous lines of Bvlgari’s iconic serpent, complemented by an Eclettica Color Treasures ring. Wu Lei, meanwhile, wore an Eclettica necklace featuring a remarkable 170.06-carat Colombian emerald, paired with a high jewellery ring and an Octo Roma watch. Across these creations, Eclettica presents high jewellery as wearable art – an evolving conversation between disciplines, cultures and craftsmanship. In Shanghai, Bvlgari offered a closer look at this philosophy, demonstrating how the meeting of diverse artistic influences can give precious materials an entirely new language.

title: In South Korea, plan to serve deportees airline meals splits officials
description: The US$5 meals are seen as a practical option for those awaiting deportation – instead of the current bread and drinks provided by officers.
content: A proposal to upgrade meals for foreigners awaiting deportation at Incheon International Airport has divided immigration officials, with frontline officers raising safety concerns and some questioning whether better food is appropriate for those ordered to leave South Korea for violating the law. According to immigration authorities on Sunday, the Incheon Airport Immigration Office under the Ministry of Justice is considering providing in-flight meal boxes to foreign nationals awaiting deportation through the airport. Foreign nationals ordered to leave the country are generally transferred to Incheon airport after local immigration offices confirm their illegal stay and complete the necessary procedures. After that, they remain in a designated departure waiting area until their flights. Those awaiting deportation are currently provided with bread and drinks supplied by local immigration offices. The Incheon Airport Immigration Office is now seeking to provide meals directly, replacing the basic food with airline-style meals, considering them the most practical option. The office views that those facing deportation should receive a decent meal before leaving the country, with the 6,910 won (US$5) airline-style meals seen as a reasonable option in terms of quality, airport security and delivery procedures, as well as accommodating different cultural and dietary needs. Airline-style meals are already provided in some cases to foreign nationals awaiting repatriation after being denied entry for failing to adequately explain the purpose of their visit. The office is now seeking customs approval to provide the same meals to deportees in the departure waiting area. The proposal, however, has divided immigration officials on whether foreign nationals ordered to leave South Korea for violating the law should receive the same meals as travellers who are simply denied entry. Frontline officers raised safety as the primary concern, warning that utensils provided with the meals could be used as weapons. Such concerns are heightened by the fact that the deportees include not only undocumented migrants but also foreign nationals with criminal records who are awaiting removal after serving prison sentences in South Korea. Concerns have also been raised about the risk of food spoiling in enclosed spaces such as the departure waiting area. Others argue that providing meals costing nearly 7,000 won each to undocumented migrants could send the wrong message and undermine the strict enforcement of immigration law. The Incheon Airport Immigration Office said the government remained responsible for the custody and welfare of deportees until they boarded their flights and therefore they needed to be fed adequately during that period. While reviewing the boxed meal plan, the office is also considering simpler alternatives such as sandwiches and hamburgers, given the limited facilities in the waiting area. With no tables or other furnishings available, deportees would have to eat boxed meals on the floor if the plan goes ahead. This article was first published by The Korea Times

title: Chickens in Malaysia are producing fewer eggs. Is haze a leading cause?
description: Small farmers in Malaysia and Indonesia who are also worried about rising heat are spending more to ventilate their sheds.
content: This year’s haze crisis has added to the heat woes squeezing livestock farmers in Malaysia and Indonesia as they struggle to keep their animals cool, fed and productive. While it is difficult to separately assess the effects of haze-related smoke from heat, water shortages, feed and disease, farmers and industry groups say the cumulative strain is severely affecting animal health, productivity and their finances. In Selama, Perak, poultry keeper Zaiful Zakaria, 42, had begun installing ventilation fans at his open-sided chicken sheds before the haze hit Malaysia in August. The fans were meant to draw out heat accumulating inside the sheds and protect the well-being of his mainly ornamental and heritage-breed chickens. Zaiful later also began installing a water-misting system. For a basic fan-and-mister arrangement, Zaiful estimated he had spent about 500 ringgit (US$120) per shed. Other refinements, such as solar panels and an automatic feeder, would cost more – up to 2,000 ringgit per shed, but these could save him money and effort in the long term. Another breeder, Mohd Hazarulhizam Mohd Shafie, shared a photo of his newly renovated shelter for his heritage chickens in Alor Setar, Kedah. He estimated the total cost to be 50,000 ringgit, including built-in exhaust fans, solar panels and auto-misters. “The figures are not final, but the haze and the weather were definitely reasons I rebuilt my reban [coops] to better protect my birds,” Mohd Hazarulhizam said. The haze followed weeks of hot, dry weather across parts of the region, with forest and agricultural fires in Indonesia sending smoke billowing into Malaysia. The poor air quality, heat and lack of water and feed have all stressed livestock. Against such a backdrop, it can be difficult for farmers and veterinarians to determine why an animal is ill, not putting on weight, or producing fewer eggs or less milk. Farmers and industry groups have reported significant changes in animal health and productivity during the hot and hazy period. Zaiful, who heads the newly established Malaysian Poultry Association, which focuses on heritage breeds and small-scale farms, said the association had received several reports of breeders losing large numbers of birds. “There were no veterinary reports to establish whether it was the smoke, weather or other reasons for those deaths. Many might keep silent out of embarrassment,” Zaiful said. Small-scale farmers with fewer than 500 birds, as well as backyard poultry keepers, were particularly exposed because their birds were often kept in basic, open-air sheds, he said, adding that these owners typically had less access to veterinary and animal husbandry advice than commercial producers, who had climate-controlled sheds, specialist consultants and tighter biosecurity. Small-scale breeders are not required to register with Malaysia’s Department of Veterinary Services. Livestock veterinarian Vijay Jayam said a similar divide existed among cattle, dairy and goat farms. Larger dairies were generally better equipped in terms of ventilation and biosecurity, while smallholders might only be able to douse their animals with water to help them cool down, he said. “Farmers should prioritise ventilation and clean drinking water,” Vijay said, adding that he would not attribute lower milk yields or slower growth to haze alone without considering other factors, such as feed, housing, disease and the animal’s stage of growth. Ari Ramash Supramaniam, a dairy and goat farmer, said milk production from the five milking cows out of his 23 Australian Friesian-Jersey crossbreeds had fallen by four litres to six litres (8½ US pints to 12½ US pints) per day. He estimated that the lost milk output had reduced his daily earnings by up to 60 ringgit. “For a small farmer, that is a lot,” said Ari, who started his farm about six years ago. He linked the decline to the cattle grazing less due to the daytime heat. Ari said he was giving his animals clean water mixed with molasses and ice to help them regain their energy and beat the heat, as well as increasing the amount of concentrate feed and mineral supplements in their fodder. Once the animals returned to the barn, they would finish their food and drink “within a few minutes”, he said. The extra supplements needed to ride out current conditions can prove costly, as Ari uses about 5kg (11lbs) of molasses a day, at 1.80 ringgit per kilogram. The price of a 50kg bag of feed had risen by between 3 ringgit and 5 ringgit during the El Nino period, he said. He also buys eight 30kg bags of fresh grass a day at 12 ringgit each to feed his animals at night, once temperatures have eased. Ari, who built his shed above ground level to allow natural airflow without having to use fans or turbines, said he was working harder and spending more just to maintain productivity. “Still, I have noticed saliva around the mouths of the goats and cows from the heat stress, and stressed animals will not contribute to expected results for farmers,” Ari said. Jeffrey Ng, an adviser to the Federation of Livestock Farmers’ Associations of Malaysia, said the organisation had begun recording weaker production up to two months ago. Some broiler chicken producers reported that birds were taking up to an additional week to reach their normal sale weight. The heat and haze were overlapping pressures, Ng said, adding that the federation had not received any reports of a rise in poultry mortality associated with the current haze. Malaysia’s Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living has received reports of hot weather increasing mortality rates among laying hens, causing egg production to drop, deputy minister Fuziah Salleh told local media. With demand unchanged, the tighter supply had contributed to higher egg prices, she said, adding that the increase remained under control. Across the border in Mempawah regency, West Kalimantan, Sakiman has been struggling to cope with the drought. He said he had spent two whole weeks in August trying to find enough grass and water for his six animals. The cattle farmer, who keeps six head of cattle and sells male calves and bulls for racing and meat, said much of the grass that was normally available had dried out, forcing him to look for fodder or buy it by the bundle early in the morning. “They are not eating as much as they used to, but it’s enough to keep them going,” Sakiman said of his animals. Water from the Mempawah River had also turned brackish and was no longer flowing strongly enough to reach the irrigation ditch he relied on, he said. “Now I buy about two drums [of water] at a time – one for household use and another for the cattle. They last about five days, and each drum can cost about 150,000 rupiah,” Sakiman said. Smoke particles may pose an additional risk, particularly in open-sided poultry sheds. A modelling study by researchers at Thailand’s Chiang Mai Rajabhat University projected that three days of exposure to PM2.5 – particulate matter 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter – at 150 micrograms per cubic metre could reduce a broiler chicken’s average daily weight gain by 5.2 per cent. But Kulisara Marupanthorn, a veterinarian and project supervisor for the research, stressed that these were “predictions, not observed farm losses”. study currently being prepared for publication, her team measured PM2.5 levels at bird-breathing height across three 35-day broiler cycles. Birds in the higher-pollution cycle had poorer respiratory health, weaker immunity and lower egg production. However, the researchers could not attribute these outcomes to PM2.5 alone, as there were also variations in temperature, humidity and rainfall. Marupanthorn advised small-scale farmers to keep their water clean and curb dust levels, but warned that closing curtains against smoke could backfire if it trapped heat and humidity. Zaiful, meanwhile, said he was worried about mounting financial losses because of lower production. “Sometimes some breeders only have 500 ringgit to start their breeding business with and if they lose their chickens to heat stress or illnesses, that is a lot of money to them,” he said.

title: Opinion | How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem
description: After decades of lucrative land sales, can the city finally build a system in which the land itself creates economic value?
content: When Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, announced his housing plan in 1997, the ambition was extraordinary. The government would produce at least 85,000 flats a year across the public and private sectors, and raise the home ownership rate to 70 per cent. The idea was simple. Build more homes, make housing more affordable and allow more families to own a piece of Hong Kong. Then history intervened. The Asian financial crisis struck. Property prices collapsed. The economy weakened. The 85,000-flat target quickly became politically toxic, and the government retreated. Nearly three decades later, Hong Kong is still wrestling with the same dilemma: how much land can the government release without destabilising the value of the land already in the system? That is the uncomfortable question behind the Northern Metropolis today. Rising land and property values can generate government revenue and household wealth, but they also make it harder for younger generations to enter the housing market. Hong Kong took this model to an extreme. Since the colonial era, restrictions on land supply and the sale of development rights have generated substantial government revenue. That helped Hong Kong maintain low taxation while funding infrastructure and public services. The model worked remarkably well for decades. But success creates its own problems. Once property becomes one of the largest stores of household wealth, a sharp fall in prices is no longer simply a housing market correction. It affects homeowners, banks, developers, consumption and government finances. The government therefore faces an awkward contradiction. It wants housing to become more affordable, but it also has powerful reasons not to let property values collapse. Tung was arguably looking at the right structural problem. Hong Kong needed more land and homes. But the policy arrived at the wrong moment. The combination of a huge supply increase, an economic downturn and the Asian financial crisis produced a property collapse of historic proportions. The lesson is not that Hong Kong should never increase land supply. It is that housing policy cannot be treated as a switch. Turn supply on too aggressively and the market can suffer a shock. Turn it off for too long and scarcity drives up prices, affordability deteriorates and intergenerational tensions deepen. People talk of a “high land price policy” but this is not official policy: successive administrations have rejected the idea that Hong Kong deliberately keeps land prices high. Perhaps the more useful question is whether the economic incentives created by Hong Kong’s land system still depend on valuable land. That is harder to dismiss. Consider the Northern Metropolis. Last month, the government awarded its first large-scale district development project in Hung Shui Kiu and Ha Tsuen to a six-company consortium including China Overseas Land & Investment, China Resources Land (Overseas), JD.com and Sino Land. The HK$1.03 billion (US$131 million) tender covers three residential sites, with the winning consortium also responsible for preparing other land and developing a smart logistics centre and public facilities. This is an important departure from a conventional land sale. Rather than simply selling a site and leaving the government to develop the surrounding area, the new model brings private-sector capital and expertise into the development process.
