There is a logic to this. The Northern Metropolis is an enormous undertaking, and asking the government to finance and build every component would place a considerable burden on public finances. The administration is therefore experimenting with different ways to share development costs and risks with the market. The policy address suggests this approach will continue, with a second large-scale land disposal pilot in Fanling North that could be launched by the end of the year. The government also aims to prepare about 2,500 hectares of “spade-ready” sites over the next decade, including about 1,000 hectares in the Northern Metropolis in the next five years. This is perhaps the most important change. Hong Kong is no longer simply asking how much a piece of land can fetch. It is increasingly asking what that land can help create. The Northern Metropolis is intended to combine housing with universities, technology, logistics, industry and new communities. The government’s latest plans put university towns and the integration of education, technology, industry and talent at the centre of the development strategy. If that works, the economic value of the Northern Metropolis will eventually come from the activity generated there, not just the price of the land beneath it. The lesson is not that Hong Kong should never increase land supply. It is that housing policy cannot be treated as a switch That would represent a meaningful evolution of Hong Kong’s land model. But the 85,000-flat episode offers a useful reminder. Big land policies need time, consistency and a willingness to absorb short-term uncertainty for long-term gain. The government’s approach of increasing supply while introducing more flexible development and financing mechanisms may offer a more measured route than the dramatic swings of the past. The more interesting question is whether the city can finally build a system in which land creates economic value, rather than economic value depending overwhelmingly on land value. The Northern Metropolis may be where we find out.

title: Asean firms hope Pinglu Canal will open China market, but fear flood of imports
description: The 134.2km Pinglu Canal, which opened earlier this month, helps connect China’s southwestern hinterland with international maritime corridors.
content: Vietnamese coffee chain Trung Nguyen Legend has been brewing up big business in China, serving its signature slow-dripped ground blends sourced fresh from Vietnam. As its network of stores expands across China, logistics has become a bottleneck. It focuses on buying coffee beans in season from plantations in Vietnam, but road-and-sea transport to China follows a circuitous route with occasional delays. It hopes China’s first river-to-sea canal, which opened earlier this month, will offer a short cut. Businesses across Southeast Asia also hope the Pinglu Canal, which fills a missing link between China’s southwestern hinterland and international maritime corridors, can be a conduit for the flow of goods into the world’s second-largest economy, not just another route for the tidal wave of Chinese exports hitting their shores. “Large seagoing barges carrying coffee beans from Vietnam will be able to sail along the new canal straight up to Nanning and other inland Chinese hubs,” said Trung Nguyen’s regional co-manager in Nanning, Huang Weiqiang. “No need to change to smaller vessels … potentially, this can bring more sales for us in China.” The 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations eagerly anticipated the launch of the 134.2km canal in southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. Many expect a positive spillover for trade and logistics, as it connects inland rivers and shipping arteries in southwestern China to the Gulf of Tonkin – known as Beibu Gulf in China. The canal is the first man-made waterway connecting a river to the sea to be built since the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, state-run Xinhua News Agency reported earlier. With a planned investment of 72.7 billion yuan (US$10.8 billion), the project, which began construction in August 2022, is designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes and save more than 5 billion yuan in overall transportation costs each year. But concerns have also been raised that the new infrastructure might make China-Asean trade even more lopsided. Exporters and trade officials from Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore at the annual China-Asean Expo in Nanning, Guangxi’s regional capital, which ended on September 21, said the canal should benefit foreign businesses to the same degree as Chinese exporters. “The canal should facilitate two-way trade, especially when Beijing has vowed umpteen times to expand imports,” an official from the Thailand Board of Investment’s Guangzhou office said. “It should not only be for China [exporting] to Thailand, but also Thailand to China. More Thai goods, be it durian, rice or electronic components, can [hopefully] flow via the canal deeper into China.” Hopes that the canal will spur more Chinese imports stem from the trade deficit that Asean has racked up with China, the bloc’s largest trading partner. Asean imported US$546 billion worth of goods from China in the first eight months of this year, up 25.8 per cent year on year, while the bloc’s exports to China stood at US$316.7 billion, China Customs data showed. As Pinglu Canal helps cargo skip transits through Guangzhou or Shanghai, slashing distances and costs and avoiding congestion, the Thai official said her country’s trade deficit might grow. “With the canal, Chinese companies operating in Thailand will get an easier, quicker way to import parts and machinery from China … there is a need for rebalancing the trade asymmetry,” she said. Analysts said the canal might bind Southeast Asia’s economic geography closer to inland China amid shifts in trade influence. “Pinglu is a double-edged sword; Asean as a whole must proactively study the implications and make the best use of it,” said Alice Chan, managing director at the Singapore-based APAC Innovation and Collaboration Centre. Chan added that trade accords like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership could ensure the canal’s benefits were evenly distributed and felt in China and Asean. Phar Kim Beng, professor of Asean Studies at the International Islamic University Malaysia, agreed that the canal should be a two-way trade street, not just another way for Beijing to project its industrial and trading dominance. “Once goods from Guangxi and China’s broader southwest enter the Beibu Gulf, they are already facing Asean … Pinglu is China’s new southern economic artery,” he wrote in a report published this month. “Asean must prevent the corridor from becoming a one-sided avenue … the greater opportunity lies in making Asean products penetrate deeper into western China’s markets.” He said the question was no longer simply how Malaysian products could reach Shanghai, Shenzhen or Guangzhou, and “Malaysia must examine how its companies can reach the enormous economic spaces beyond China’s traditional coastal centres.” While the Pinglu Canal evokes mixed reactions, direct freight routes that would not have been possible without it, like the one between Nanning and the Vietnamese port city of Can Tho in the Mekong Delta, hold the promise of two-way opportunities. Trung Nguyen, the Vietnamese coffee chain, was among the businesses that would consider using the new routes, its executives said at the expo in Nanning. The 14-year-old China–Malaysia Qinzhou Industrial Park, strategically located in the city where the canal empties into the sea, is also hoping to tap its potential and has stepped up industrial cooperation efforts to encourage more foreign manufacturers to set up shop there.

title: Why toothpaste and orange juice don’t mix
description: Brushing your teeth can temporarily change how orange juice tastes, leaving a bitter flavour instead of sweetness.
content:
What makes your clean, minty mouth taste so gross when it meets orange juice?
Before you decide you need to stop brushing your teeth to save your taste buds, know that this effect is temporary, lasting only a few minutes. Brushing with toothpaste is still important for your health.
But how does this change in taste happen? Let’s look at the science behind this phenomenon.
The orange juice many people drink with breakfast is naturally high in sugar. But it also contains citric acid. As a result, it’s a delicious combination of both sweet and a little sour.
But if you brush your teeth before breakfast, your orange juice tastes terrible. What’s changed?
Toothpaste contains the detergent sodium lauryl sulphate, which helps remove germs from your teeth.
If you ever do the dishes, you’ve probably seen what happens when you squirt detergent into a sink full of greasy water: the detergent breaks up the greasy fat, making it easy to wipe off the dishes and rinse them clean.
But there’s another type of fat in your mouth that the detergent in toothpaste disrupts – the lipids in the cell membranes of your taste receptors.
Brushing your teeth breaks up that layer of lipids, temporarily changing how you perceive taste.
Back in 1980, I conducted a study with a couple of my colleagues. We wanted to know how the tongue responds to sweet, bitter, salty and sour after being exposed to sodium lauryl sulphate, a detergent found in toothpaste.
We conducted an experiment with seven student volunteers. They tasted very high concentrations of sweet sucrose, sour citric acid, salt and bitter quinine, both before and after holding a solution of sodium lauryl sulphate in their mouths for one minute.
We found that a small amount reduced the intensity of the tastes of sucrose, salt and quinine, but the most important change was that a bitter taste was added to the sour taste of citric acid.
This is why, instead of tasting sweet with a bit of nice tang , your orange juice tastes bitter after you brush your teeth.
You could conduct your own version of this experiment with something sweet like sugar, a little table salt, orange juice and tonic water. Taste them before you brush your teeth and then after.
This article was first published in The Conversation . It was written by Linda Bartoshuk, a research professor of psychology at George Washington University.

title: Japanese fish farm loses 100,000 koi carp in Typhoon Dujuan flood
description: Typhoon damage to Chiba prefecture’s farming, forestry and fisheries sectors is expected to exceed US$550,000.
content: Around 100,000 ornamental koi carp ready for sale were swept away after heavy rain caused by a typhoon breached some levees at a lake in Chiba prefecture near Tokyo, it has been revealed as authorities assess the widespread damage to local farming and fisheries. Typhoon Dujuan, which approached the region about a week ago, inundated rice paddy fields and other farmland while flooding facilities where carp and eels were being cultivated near Lake Imbanuma in northern Chiba. Kenji Tani, who runs an aquafarm in Narita, realised the severity of the damage after returning home on Tuesday from an overseas trip to attend a nishikigoi (ornamental koi carp) exhibition. Ahead of the initially scheduled start of sales on Sunday, his farm had about 100,000 carp ready. All but 200 to 300 of them were swept away after the aquafarm facilities were flooded. “I want the levees to be restored even if it is a quick emergency fix. We cannot do anything if another typhoon approaches,” said Tani, 58. Japanese nishikigoi are popular overseas, including in China and Southeast Asian nations. Exports of the carp more than doubled in the five years to 2025 to around 10 billion yen (US$63 million), according to government data. In Chiba, damage to the farming, forestry and fisheries sectors is expected to swell from around 87 million yen (US$550,000) as of Thursday, in another blow to local residents who experienced similar disasters in the weeks before Dujuan. Torrential rain in August caused damage worth 8.22 billion yen in 33 municipalities and another downpour in early September left a bill of around 230 million yen in 17 municipalities. At a different location in Chiba, a strawberry farm was damaged by the overflowing of a nearby river. About 10 to 20 per cent of the strawberry seedlings at a farm in Kimitsu run by Nobuyuki Watanabe were affected. Watanabe, 48, said he had urged the local government to take measures against the river given its propensity to flood. “If they still don’t take action, I will be the last generation in my family to run the business.”

title: Discover the healing power of woodworking at a collective space in Hong Kong
description: The group uses resilience-building crafts and therapeutic ‘Crafts & Yaps’ sessions to foster connection, healing and joyful imperfection.
content:
Skilled artisans meticulously measured a wooden plank before deftly chiselling its surface with precision blades, carefully shaping the piece to perfection.
This is a type of woodworking found at A Collective Space, founded by Emmy Sandt and Sne Roy.
The design and wellness collective had its own intention: to be a place where mindfulness and healing met creativity and crafts.
For Sandt and Roy, woodworking is more than a homeware-making art; it is also a process that allows you to embrace your missteps and blunders .
“In woodworking, some mistakes are irreversible. You can only start again,” said Roy, the director of programmes.
“And that is the very definition of resilience, right? You keep going … It’s OK to start over from scratch. It doesn’t mean I wasted my effort; it means I perfected my skill.”
Roy, 35, and Sandt, 33, officially launched the collective in 2023.
Sandt, the head carpenter, was born and raised in Hong Kong to Finnish parents. She then moved to Australia at 18 and spent six years building wooden theatre sets, but the temporary nature of the work came to frustrate her.
“I felt quite disheartened by the way you would build something and then you would throw it away at the end of the show,” Sandt said.
“I wanted to have a bit more permanence in the stuff that we did.”
Sandt began to shift her focus to furniture. When she returned to Hong Kong, woodworking helped her through a tumultuous time between 2019 and 2021.
“I found woodworking deeply therapeutic,” Sandt said. “It was really my way to ground myself and to feel less dislocated from the world.”
Her partner Roy is originally from Kolkata in West Bengal, India, and moved to Hong Kong as a child before later working in education and counselling.
Sandt introduced Roy to woodworking shortly after the pair met in 2017. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Roy helped Sandt with different carpentry projects.
The women also realised woodworking’s potential to offer others a respite from the city’s stressful fast pace.
“In Hong Kong, we are not a very patient bunch. We are built for speed and efficiency,” Roy said.
“[But woodworking could be] a pleasant surprise … It can take you days and weeks, sometimes months and years, to fulfil a project from start to finish.”
Every month, A Collective Space, stylised in all lower case, organises two sessions of “Crafts & Yaps”, informal hour-long gatherings of about 10 people.
The group chit-chats while working on a “mystery craft”, which is only revealed upon arrival. They work with their hands while Roy guides the conversation with questions designed to help them open up.
Their goal was to eliminate the need to be perfect, and the pair envisioned a gathering where participants needed zero woodworking experience.
“You’re gonna fail. It’s gonna be ugly, and that’s OK,” Roy explained.

title: China-US dialogue will ease concerns, but competition will remain, Paul Chan says
description: Hong Kong’s finance chief gives a wide-ranging interview on geopolitics, the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting and more.
content: Competition between China and the US will persist, but increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers will provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns, with Hong Kong positioned to play a unique role, the city’s financial secretary has told the South China Morning Post. In a wide-ranging interview, Paul Chan Mo-po said more communication and dialogue between the two nations would be “good for everyone”, as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, wrapped up a historic summit in Washington last Friday, local time. Chan also shed light on his expectations for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, which takes place in Hong Kong on October 20 and 21, and will bring together hundreds of global leaders in the city. He anticipated that visiting political leaders would see Hong Kong and its vibrancy with their own eyes. The event will take place ahead of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which will be held in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Chan said Beijing supported Hong Kong’s hosting of the finance ministers’ meeting, as the central government wanted to elevate the city’s profile as a global financial centre. With the current Hong Kong administration having less than a year before the new term, Chan was also asked about his future plans. He said that officials had worked hard under the “capable leadership” of the chief executive. “At the moment, we are concentrating our energy and efforts on pushing forward the various policy agendas and initiatives. So this will remain our priority focus,” he said. Chan also touched on the three-day China-US summit last week, which saw tensions ease and a trade truce extended by two months until January. “We do believe more communication and dialogue are good for everyone,” he said. “And this is important, not just for the two countries or Hong Kong but for the global community, providing more certainty and removing some of the geopolitical concerns.” But Chan anticipated China-US competition would persist in areas such as financial services, adding that Hong Kong would strengthen its status as an international financial centre to further attract foreign capital and connect mainland China to the rest of the world. “So for us, under the ‘one country, two systems’ arrangement, we play the unique role of connecting the mainland with the rest of the world,” he said. Despite geopolitical tensions, Chan said Hong Kong had become a destination for investors to park their money over the past two years. Net inflows into Hong Kong-domiciled funds stood at HK$118 billion (US$15 billion) in the first five months of 2026 following a 118 per cent year-on-year surge to HK$357 billion in 2025. Total assets under management also grew by 20 per cent to HK$42.2 trillion in 2025 from a year earlier, with most coming from outside the mainland and Hong Kong. “Capital investors really vote for Hong Kong with their feet,” Chan said. He said China-US relations were bound to have “ups and downs,” and Hong Kong’s top priority was to ensure financial stability while taking advantage of development opportunities. At the core of Hong Kong’s financial development was the city’s stock market, which had recorded robust trading volumes and a larger number of new listings in recent years, Chan said. The stock market is also set to benefit from a series of measures floated in the policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, which were both released earlier this month. Proceeds raised in initial public offerings (IPOs) in the first eight months of 2026 were 153 per cent higher than in the same period last year, at HK$342.4 billion. The eight-month total has already surpassed last year’s IPO proceeds of HK$286.9 billion. The 2025 figure already represented growth of 226 per cent year on year. “So all these indicate that we remain focused on doing the right thing, enhancing our competitiveness, improving our listing regime, for example, expanding the possibility of attracting additional liquidity. Then, quality companies will come,” Chan said. “We are taking this window to further build, further strengthen our equities market. But at the same time, develop FIC [fixed income and currencies], develop commodities, trading and gold. This takes time, but we move on; we’ll invest in it.” Chan also highlighted plans to expand the global use of the yuan. While Hong Kong currently served as “a firewall” for the wider nation’s financial security, the city also planned to drum up yuan product offerings to raise liquidity and act as a testing bed for yuan products, the finance chief said. Hong Kong has the world’s biggest pool of yuan outside the mainland, sitting at about 1.1 trillion yuan (US$163 billion). “Our idea is that if we want to gather more liquidity, gather more investors coming to our market, then we need to enrich the product offering. We need to build the necessary infrastructure. We also need to provide the liquidity that is needed,” Chan said. He added that several central banks were planning to increase their yuan holdings in an effort to pursue diversification, which would generate more investment opportunities. Asked whether the push risked diminishing the role of the Hong Kong dollar – which is pegged to the US dollar – amid so-called de-dollarisation, Chan said “no”, and remained adamant that the linked exchange rate system, which debuted in 1983, had worked well and was an anchor for the city’s currency regime. “This is very core to us in terms of strength,” he said. “We have no intention at all to change this. This is very fundamental.” As the city is fast-tracking its push into gold trading and storage and a commodity ecosystem, Chan said the government planned to launch a “gold connect scheme” to facilitate more cross-border trade. Hong Kong and the mainland already operate various connect schemes that grant global financial institutions access to mainland stock and bond markets through the city. “The competition is keen,” Chan said, referring to competition between gold markets in Hong Kong, London and Singapore. “But our advantage is the strong hinterland. China is a major user of gold. The Shanghai gold exchange is very keen and has a strong market, but it needs to have an international connection. Hong Kong can play the role.”

title: Letters from readers about Disneyland rides, claw machines, pet birds and ‘Detective Conan’
description: This week, students share their favourite things to do in Hong Kong, why they love their pet bird Mango and how they became a fan of the ‘Case Closed’ anime.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
I am from New Zealand. I have been in Hong Kong for about a year and a half, and I love it! I like to eat bao, sushi and ramen. My favourite drink is hot chocolate because it tastes like Christmas.
My favourite thing to do in Hong Kong is go to Disneyland with my dad. We go on the teacups and the roller coaster in Grizzly Gulch. My favourite ride is the Star Wars one.
Sometimes, my mum and dad take me to the arcade. We play the coin toss because it’s the easiest game to win. I play the claw machines that have lots of Disney toys. My mum says I’m the Claw Machine Queen.
My favourite subjects are art and physical education (PE) because I like to draw people. I try my best to draw my friends. In PE, it is fun to play dodgeball together.
My hobby is chess and sometimes I win. It’s very fun to play with friends. I like birds because they can wiggle their tails and fly around. Also, their faces are so cute. I have a pet bird. Its name is Mango.
I have a father, a mother and a sister. Sometimes, my sister and I fight each other, but she is still my best friend. We play together, and when it’s bedtime, she tells me interesting stories.
During the summer holidays, I became obsessed with watching Detective Conan . It is a classic Japanese anime series, also known as Case Closed .
I was browsing online for something to watch because I was feeling bored. I stumbled upon Detective Conan and clicked on it. After watching just a few episodes, I found it unexpectedly entertaining.
Since then, I have become an enthusiastic fan of the series.

title: Feature of the Week: Liana Yang’s short story ‘The Bear Who Lives by the Sea’
description: The 10-year-old from Kowloon Junior School shares a thrilling adventure tale about a polar bear cub in the Arctic who wants to reunite with his family.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
In the frozen Arctic, hidden under layers and layers of snow, a little polar bear was born. Fuzzy the Polar Bear was no bigger than two medium-sized bananas, and he weighed as light as three apples.
It was so cold. Fuzzy huddled with his mother and siblings to stay warm. It was a big family, and he was the youngest. Fuzzy already had a lot of fur, and when he’d grow up, he’d have the furriest coat.
His family wanted him to be brave, but they worried humans would hurt him.
When Fuzzy got older, his family moved. But as the Arctic got warmer because of climate change, the ice began to melt. Fuzzy awoke one day and could not see his mother and siblings. He was all alone.
Fuzzy did not know how to take care of himself. He did not know how to hunt or swim.
How would Fuzzy cope? At night, he imagined himself cuddling with his family.
A few days later, a group of human volunteers found him.
“This cub has been starving and sick for days!” one exclaimed. “We need to bring him to the Arctic animal rescue centre.”
They took him to the rescue centre. They treated him with kindness and gave him some water, medicine, food and even treats! Now, Fuzzy knew not all humans were monsters.
Fuzzy was no longer hungry because the volunteers had fed him. He even knew how to hunt now. He had also learned to trust others, have faith and live after having lost hope. Fuzzy had healed.
The volunteers led Fuzzy to a new place where there were a lot of polar bears, snow, friends and food. As a volunteer released him, Fuzzy saw his family. Then, they lived happily together once again.

title: Advice: How can I show my mum that a ‘4’ on my sports jersey isn’t bad luck?
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
Your mother’s worry about the number four probably comes from a deep cultural belief. That means her not wanting you to use it on a sports jersey is her way of watching out for you.
People rarely change their deep cultural beliefs through logic. Try not to argue with her. Instead, show her you are listening. Tell her you understand why she is worried, even if you do not believe in the superstition yourself.
Then, you can help her look at the situation more calmly, which will lessen her worry.
You can point to other cultures that also think certain numbers bring bad luck. In this case, it is also important to remind her that the coach chooses your jersey number.
Finally, the best way to calm a parent down is to give them a clear plan for the future. Tell her directly that you will be careful and focus on staying safe during the game.
Parents usually worry much less when they know you listened to them and feel sure that you are prepared.
This question was answered by Tiffany Chiu, a child psychotherapist and play and behavioural therapist at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: Fifa Asean Cup: Hong Kong on brink of final as midfielder stars on return from exile
description: ‘Intense’ city team too powerful for callow Laos, but Kai Tak Stadium less than half full for convincing victory.
content: Vladica Grujic said Hong Kong played “a completely different level of football” from his Laos side, after the world No 186 ranked team were thumped 4-0 in the Fifa Asean Cup on Sunday. Sun Ming-him and Everton Camargo, brilliantly, netted in the opening half, before Dudu’s 55th-minute header defeated the flimsy defences of Souksamone Vethita, and Matt Orr emphatically converted a stoppage-time penalty. Unsurprisingly, Laos did not prove a hot ticket, although the 18,873 fans inside Kai Tak Stadium produced a characteristically partisan atmosphere. Most of them drifted away soon after full-time, leaving the 50,000-capacity venue nearly deserted for Cambodia’s 1-0 win over Myanmar that followed. Hong Kong need only one point from their game against Brunei on Wednesday to secure a final spot. “Thank you to the fans for coming to support ... I hope more people will come on Wednesday,” Roberto Losada, the Hong Kong head coach, said. Sun’s energy, and the relentless running of Wu Chun-ming, back in the team after being ignored for the past two years, epitomised a home performance that was too much for a team containing five teenagers in its line-up. “My players couldn’t cope with Hong Kong’s intensity,” Grujic said. “It’s a very big experience for them. In Laos, it’s an amateur league, you have more space. At this level, you don’t have time to think, or to take [extra] touches.” Losada’s name was booed by supporters when it appeared on the big screen before kick-off, but the best performance of his reign should take some heat off, for the time being at least. He sprang a couple of selection surprises, handing a debut to left-back Callum Beattie, and reintroducing Lee Man midfielder Wu, a mainstay of Hong Kong’s Asian Cup finals campaign 2½ years ago. Losada said the 28-year-old, who was one of the overage players in the city’s Asian Games squad in Japan, was “in very good shape, and we had to take advantage of that”. Wu said he had not spoken to Ashley Westwood, the former head coach, about his exclusion, other than “a few conversations about my physical condition” early in the Englishman’s tenure. A player whose industry Westwood’s predecessor, Jorn Andersen, considered indispensable, Wu said being back in the side was “really not such a big deal”. “I play every game with 100 per cent effort, and when the coach needs me to fit his tactics, I’m always here for him,” he added. “Sometimes, when your performance is not really good, and someone’s doing better than you, they take your position. That’s normal. Hong Kong’s results are the main priority.” After negotiating reams of Fifa red tape to become eligible for Hong Kong, Beattie, who was born in the city but had British citizenship, said it felt “amazing to put on the shirt” 12 months after obtaining his passport. “There were a few pre-match nerves, playing at Kai Tak and in my first international game, but I think I’ll just keep getting more comfortable,” Beattie said. Sun flicked a 13th-minute near-post header beyond 19-year-old goalkeeper Souksamone, providing Everton Camargo with the first of his two corner assists. Surprisingly for a player blessed with a fierce shot, it was only Sun’s third Hong Kong goal, and first since September 2022. Camargo delivered the game’s best strike 20 minutes later, collecting a firm pass from Sun, then striding past a sequence of challenges to hammer the ball high into Souksamone’s goal. Dudu’s header was too powerful for Souksamone, who looked like he had thwarted the wishes of the fans chanting “we want four” when he athletically saved from substitute Sohgo Ichikawa. Soon after, defender Seang Manilay, 18, panicked when confronted with the sight of Ichikawa on his wrong side and about to shoot, and swiped away the forward’s standing leg. Orr dispatched the penalty low to the left for his 14th Hong Kong goal. The striker is set to win his 50th cap this week. Acknowledging he would “definitely make changes” for the game against Brunei, Losada said the intensity of his side’s performance meant he was “mostly very happy”. “Maybe in the last 20 minutes, we slowed down a little bit,” he added. “In general it was good, but we could have scored more goals.” Beattie was one of those fleetingly guilty of switching off, hesitating and relinquishing possession in his own half, albeit the Laos attack, led late in the game by a player from Germany’s sixth tier in Roman Angot, ran out of steam. “Nando [Fernando Recio, assistant coach] made sure to kill me after that, which I respect,” Beattie said. “He said, ‘You had an amazing game, but there’s more to work on because you got tired’. “Mistakes happen, and there was definitely more good than bad in my performance.” For Wu, facing Laos brought back memories of his international debut in a 4-0 victory over the same opponents nine years ago. “It was a very special moment for me, and I’m really grateful that [then manager] Kim Pan-gon gave me my chance,” Wu said. “I’ve improved a lot since then. Physically I’m in good condition, and mentally, I’ve grown to become an experienced player in the team.” Grujic’s starting 11 boasted an average age of 20.8, exactly eight years less than Hong Kong’s equivalent figure. Wu saw the city’s next generation at close quarters in Japan, where Hong Kong began promisingly in a 2-0 defeat by the hosts, before collapsing to 5-1 and 4-0 defeats by Thailand and Kyrgyzstan, respectively. The goalscorer against Thailand, he said: “It was a very good lesson for our under-23 players to make sure that will not happen to them again. “It’s not just mentality, they need to learn about game management and gain experience.” In 196th ranked Brunei, Hong Kong will meet another side operating in damage-limitation mode. “We could have created more chances against a defensive team [in Laos], so in the final third I think we can still be more mature,” Wu said. Cambodia need only one point from their meeting with Timor-Leste on Wednesday to finish top of Group B, after Sin Kakada’s superb long-range strike secured a stoppage-time triumph against Myanmar.

title: Italy attracts wealthy Chinese property buyers with food, fashion – and flat tax
description: Hong Kong and mainland investors are increasingly eyeing property in Italy, drawn by its lifestyle and flat tax regime, agents say.
content: Italy is becoming a magnet for wealthy property investors thanks to its high quality of life and flat tax regime, and interest is also on the rise among mainland Chinese and Hong Kong buyers, according to property agents. Rome introduced a flat tax regime nine years ago to attract high-net-worth individuals, with foreign residents allowed to make a flat annual tax payment of €300,000 (US$342,000) on all their overseas income under the scheme’s latest rules. The tax incentive has become a draw for wealthy investors. The number of participants in the scheme has risen from about 3,000 in 2024 to roughly 5,000 currently, according to Knight Frank. The property consultancy has also seen a surge in the number of prime residential properties sold in Italy, with deals in the first eight months of the year up by about 140 per cent compared with the same period in 2025. The buyers are currently mainly from countries including the United Kingdom, United States, Switzerland, France, India and the Netherlands, according to Knight Frank. But “interest in Italy is growing” among Hong Kong and mainland Chinese buyers as well, said Anna Ward, the firm’s international residential research lead. For Hong Kong and mainland buyers, the tax considerations are a major attraction, though “lifestyle, diversification and long-term wealth preservation tend to be more important considerations”, according to Ward. About one-third of the prospective Italian property deals Knight Frank had in the pipeline for the autumn period were linked to tax-related relocations, the consultancy said in a separate report. Demand for Italian property was also coming from European second-home buyers, as well as international owners seeking to expand their existing Italian holdings across additional destinations, agents said. “Italy’s flat tax regime … continues to attract globally mobile wealth, with over 60 per cent of prime international inquiries through Knight Frank now driven primarily by tax considerations,” Knight Frank said. “This reflects a broader evolution in demand, from the introduction of the flat tax, through post-Covid lifestyle shifts, to the removal of favourable tax regimes elsewhere such as in the UK.” Many non-European Union residents relocating to Italy under the flat-tax regime also require visa arrangements, with relocation often going hand in hand with property acquisition and broader investment activity, according to Knight Frank. “For some of these buyers, Italy’s investor visa has emerged as a natural complement to the flat tax,” the company said. The visa is open to non-EU citizens investing in Italian businesses, innovative start-ups, government bonds or philanthropic initiatives. Entry thresholds start at €250,000. The Italian market is rising and luxury Italian lifestyle destinations are attracting Asia’s wealthy Kashif Ansari, Juwai IQI Other real estate brokers also expect more buyers from mainland China, Hong Kong and the wider Asia-Pacific region to snap up Italian property assets. Buyer inquiries for Italian real estate more than tripled in the second quarter of the year, compared with the preceding three months, according to property tech firm Juwai IQI, which has 7 million property listings across 111 countries. In the first half of 2026, Italy received the 14th highest number of inquiries from prospective Chinese buyers – ranking between Spain and Vietnam – said Kashif Ansari, Juwai IQI co-founder and group CEO. The top three were Thailand, Australia and the United Kingdom, he added. “We expect the number of Chinese living and buying residences in Italy to climb in 2027,” Ansari said. “At the top end, the flat tax and residency options are attractive. The Italian market is rising and luxury Italian lifestyle destinations are attracting Asia’s wealthy.” Chinese citizens were flocking to Italy owing to a variety of reasons, Ansari said. “Chinese workers find opportunities in Italy’s economy, and nearly one-third of new residency permits going to Chinese citizens are for the purpose of studying in Italy,” he added. “The Chinese are the largest non-EU group at Italian universities.” An estimated 290,000 Chinese citizens live in Italy, the fourth largest non-EU community in the country, he said. “Their numbers are climbing rapidly, by up to 8 per cent per year,” Ansari said. For Lisbon-headquartered Maia Properties, wealthy buyers are looking at Europe as a whole and picking the best base that suits their lifestyle and tax needs. The property agency helps clients purchase homes across major destinations in the region. “We are seeing wealthy international buyers becoming much more open to Italy, and I think Asian and Chinese buyers will increasingly be part of that,” said Luiz Felipe Maia, CEO and founder of the real estate broker. “What has changed is that clients are not necessarily coming to us saying ‘I want Portugal’ or ‘I want Italy’ any more,” Maia said. “They are looking for the right European base and comparing lifestyle, connectivity, schools, tax environment and long-term value across different markets.” Although Chinese demand for Italian property is still an “emerging trend”, Maia said “there is significant room for it to grow.”

title: Indonesia’s 3% deficit cap: guardrail or growth barrier?
description: As lawmakers weigh lifting the statutory deficit ceiling, economists warn of downgrades and higher borrowing costs.
content: Indonesia is considering lifting a statutory cap on government spending that has been in place for more than two decades, as President Prabowo Subianto pushes for faster economic growth. Supporters argue that greater room to borrow and spend would let Southeast Asia’s largest economy invest its way towards Prabowo’s target of 8 per cent annual growth by 2029. Economists counter that weakening the rule could push up borrowing costs and dent investor confidence. At issue is the mandatory ceiling that has long limited the budget deficit to 3 per cent of gross domestic product. The measure, introduced in the aftermath of the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, aimed to restore fiscal discipline and investor trust. Indonesia’s economy grew 5.11 per cent last year. Policymakers pushing to revisit the limit say greater fiscal flexibility is needed to fund infrastructure and priority projects and to help the country escape the middle-income trap. Debating the cap in parliament on September 17, lawmakers questioned whether the 3 per cent threshold remained appropriate for an economy seeking faster growth. “I asked which article stipulates it [the 3 per cent deficit cap], but no one could say,” Mukhamad Misbakhun, who chairs the parliamentary body overseeing financial affairs, told reporters afterwards. Such a cap “is not the norm”, he said, as cited by local media outlet Kompas. Misbakhun’s commission has been deliberating revisions to Indonesia’s state finance law of 2003, which mandates both the 3 per cent deficit ceiling and a debt ratio cap of 60 per cent of GDP. This debt ratio was also “not the norm”, he said, arguing that the rigid limit had held back Indonesia’s economic expansion. Misbakhun urged the government to capitalise on the country’s demographic dividend – the economic growth potential created by having a rising share of working-age people – and re-evaluate the deficit ceiling. On Friday, however, newly appointed Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara said he would hold the line. “We’re using 3 per cent as the maximum state budget deficit. And I’m committed to that,” he said. The ministry has said it is targeting a deficit of 2.4 per cent of GDP for next year’s budget. Double-edged sword The proposal has stirred debate over whether the cap constrains the nation’s economic potential or serves as proof of its financial discipline and credibility. Harry Su, managing director of Jakarta-based brokerage Samuel Sekuritas Indonesia, noted that the cap was adopted after a severe economic crisis marked by currency collapse and widespread banking failures. While it had strengthened fiscal credibility over time, he said it could also “limit government spending, borrowing and economic growth”. “On the other hand, this 3 per cent cap is the strongest anchor for Indonesia’s macroeconomic stability,” Su said. “Altering it without a watertight framework risks triggering negative market sentiment, credit rating downgrades from global agencies like Fitch or Moody’s and a sharp spike in government borrowing costs.” Both Fitch Ratings and Moody’s cut Indonesia’s credit outlook to negative from stable earlier this year, citing concerns over rising uncertainty and reduced policy credibility. Rizal Taufikurahman, head of the Institute for Development of Economics and Finance’s Centre of Macroeconomics and Finance in Jakarta, said that lifting the cap might temporarily allow the public to enjoy “additional social assistance, subsidies, infrastructure or public services”. “However, if such spending does not increase productivity and [state] revenue, the consequences will be greater interest burdens and increasingly limited space for productive spending in the future,” Rizal said. Dipo Satria Ramli, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia who attended this month’s parliamentary hearing, strongly opposed scrapping the threshold. “The government’s new debt next year will be around 870 trillion rupiah (US$48.7 billion), with interest costs reaching 650 trillion rupiah. This means that three-quarters of new debt will be used solely for debt interest payments,” he said. “We’re borrowing money to pay interest while our tax ratio remains unchanged. We strictly support the deficit ceiling at 3 per cent of GDP.” Taking on additional debt without optimising state expenditure or improving tax collection would yield little benefit, Dipo said. Indonesia’s tax revenue fell to 9.3 per cent of GDP last year, down from 10.08 per cent in 2024, according to the finance ministry – well below the Asia-Pacific regional average of 19.7 per cent listed by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development. and Development. “Many foreign investors are closely following this discourse. I met several large fund managers yesterday. They’re following it. I don’t think the market will take it lightly if this limit is removed,” Dipo said. Need for safeguards Any overhaul of Indonesia’s 3 per cent deficit cap must come with strict safeguards to ensure government interest payments do not swallow up too much tax revenue, Rizal said. Indonesia “relies too heavily” on the deficit and debt caps, he said, even though budgetary pressures were “also determined by the ability of state revenues to pay interest”. Debt could remain low relative to GDP but the country’s ability to spend would “shrink as interest absorbs more and more revenue”, Rizal said. Improving the quality and governance of state spending is equally critical, according to Su. “Extra fiscal flexibility does not automatically guarantee ample economic growth to justify the added debt,” he said. “The outcome depends entirely on the spending quality by the government and here lies the tricky part given continued rampant corruption in Indonesia’s economic growth programmes.”

title: From nodding statues in China to sports toys, bobbleheads are American classics
description: These figurines became a hit in the United States when baseball teams began giving them away to fans.
content:
The National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum is a museum devoted to bobblehead dolls. It is in the US city of Milwaukee and opened in 2019.
“I think they’re the ultimate Americana, sort of pop-culture icon,” Phil Sklar said. He is the founder of the museum.
The site offers visitors a chance to look at a vast array of figurines as well as learn more about their history. Sklar said there were head-nodding statues in China at least a few hundred years ago. In the 1960s, they became a hit in America when baseball teams gave away sports-themed dolls.
Soon after, companies began making bobbleheads of other celebrities.
Even though people’s interest in bobblehead dolls has risen and fallen over the decades, they have never truly gone away.

title: Venezuelans take to streets demanding free elections, opposition leader’s return
description: Supporters push for democratic transition after Maria Corina Machado is repeatedly blocked from re-entering the country.
content: Supporters of Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado took to the country’s streets on Sunday to demand her safe return and presidential elections that could lead to a democratic transition in Venezuela. The government has been widely accused of stealing elections, jailing dissidents and stifling freedom of speech. In Caracas, hundreds of activists in sky blue shirts – the colour of Machado’s Vente Venezuela party – rode motorcycles and drove through the city’s main avenues, honking their horns and waving Venezuelan flags. Similar demonstrations were held in state capitals including Valencia, Maracaibo and Merida. “This is not a matter of parties or politics,” said Flavio Valentini, a Vente Venezuela activist in Caracas who grabbed a megaphone and addressed the crowd. “This is a movement for the people and by the people.” Machado has been living in exile for the past nine months and has had her plans to return to Venezuela spoiled multiple times. Opposition activists have accused Venezuela’s government of blocking her return, a claim denied by Venezuelan authorities. Machado’s party said last week that on Monday night, the opposition leader made three unsuccessful attempts to return. “We hope this transition process leads us to presidential elections and consolidates a free, democratic country that will be the main ally of the United States,” said Anthony Romero, a leader for Vente Venezuela in the nation’s capital. Machado, one of Venezuela’s most popular political leaders, was barred from running in Venezuela’s last presidential election by courts under the control of former President Nicolas Maduro. But her stand-in candidate is widely believed to have won the election with almost two-thirds of the vote. Maduro claimed victory nevertheless and unleashed a violent crackdown against dissidents who protested the official results, forcing Machado and dozens of opposition leaders to go into hiding. Last year, Machado smuggled herself out of Venezuela after she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to restore democracy in the South American country. A US military operation removed Maduro in January. But Machado has been unable to return to Venezuela since then. The government is now led by Delcy Rodriguez, a Maduro ally who has opened Venezuela’s oil industry to foreign investment and is now working closely with the Trump administration. Machado’s team said on Monday that the opposition leader, who is now based in Panama, attempted to return to Venezuela by sea but the company that chartered her boat cancelled the trip hours before leaving, alleging its vessel was unfit for navigation. Machado later tried to fly to Curacao, her team said, from where she could take a speedboat to Venezuela but her plane was denied landing permits. In total, Machado has made seven unsuccessful attempts to return to Venezuela this year, her party says, with some critics questioning whether the Trump administration is also involved in the efforts to stop her from returning. Trump administration officials deny they are holding Machado back but have said that on some occasions they have advised that she should not return to the country due to safety concerns. Earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a news conference that Machado has “every right to enter her country whenever she wants to return”. On Wednesday, Rubio said he was unaware of Machado’s most recent efforts to go back to the South American country. Rubio said the United States would like to see thousands of Venezuelans return to their country and “open the businesses that they lost”. The secretary of state has long argued that before holding new elections, Venezuela must stabilise its economy and rebuild its institutions, such as its courts and its electoral council.

title: Brave Indonesian women battle fires and change their community
description: Irma leads Power of Mama, an all-female firefighting unit battling for health and safety.
content:
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.
She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives into the blaze.
“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother said.
Irma, who like many Indonesians only goes by one name, is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit.
They fight fires lit by poor farming communities who are burning to clear land the cheapest way they know how.
“We are the ones who feel its effects most,” Irma said. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it.”
The group was formed in 2022 by local NGO Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).

title: How Moon Tang spun unrequited love into a new album
description: The Hong Kong artist crafted her upcoming release over a single month and connected with fans and built community on the way.
content:
Listening to Moon Tang’s music feels like reading a close friend’s handwritten diary. It’s intimate and comforting when you feel lost.
But in her latest release, “Your Little Mozzie”, the Hong Kong singer-songwriter takes a step back from that familiarity . Now, she peers into something darker.
Tang’s new single is told from the point of view of a mosquito. She uses the tiny insect as a metaphor for an obsessive and fragile unrequited love.
The song captures the feelings of a creature that knows it is unwanted but remains helplessly drawn to the person it adores.
“Maybe it’s a little creepy, but parts of it are very relatable because everyone has their dark side – the side you don’t usually talk about,” the 26-year-old said.
Tang’s coming project is all about the uncomfortable parts of falling in love.
“This entire album revolves around the state of … someone who has an unrequited crush,” she shared.
Many young music artists in Hong Kong today absorb international sounds, from indie pop to contemporary R&B.
Still, they maintain a deep respect for those who came before them.
Tang honours that heritage by learning from the Cantopop divas who defined the genre : Cass Phang, Sandy Lam and Karen Mok.
“I was listening to their full albums … [that] had well-thought-out themes, song titles and content,” she said. “I think that’s amazing, and I realised Cantonese music can be so fun to play with.”
Tang’s previous album was essentially a collection of singles she had written over several years. In contrast, her coming release was crafted over a single month.
“[In] that month … I often said, ‘I’m lonely, but I’m content.’ Writing songs every day allowed me to explore this feeling from many different angles,” she said.
Her English releases this year – such as “Take Three”, which compares love to a film scene stuck on repeat – showcase this bolder outlook.
And while her past releases were often soft bedroom pop, her new music embraces an edgier sound.
“That’s something I don’t think the me from a few years ago would have felt capable of writing or pulling off,” she said. “Now, I feel more confident doing it, with more attitude and no self-doubt.”
Beyond writing music and performing, Tang’s creative universe spills over into everyday life through Tutufarm, a soft toy collection intended as comforting companions.
The singer paired each new song with a toy character.
“People nowadays love hanging plushies on their bags,” Tang said. “Everyone really needs emotional support.”
She has created five characters so far. Seeing them around the city has become a quiet way for the artist to feel connected to her listeners.
“Every time I see fans hanging the plushies on the street, it feels like we recognise each other through this little secret sign,” she said.
Whether she is designing or composing, Tang said her goal is to build community. To celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival, she organised an evening market on Saturday for 300 fans. It featured local brands, second-hand items and crafts made by her mother.
“It felt like bringing together everything I love – using music and my limited capacity to help people while interacting offline with my listeners,” she shared.
What advice would Tang give young people?
“Every success or failure happens for a reason,” she said. “So, everyone, don’t worry too much, OK?”

title: Singapore and China top 2025 global education rankings
description: OECD’s Pisa assessment has shown that pupils from the two countries excelled in maths, science and reading.
content:
Singaporean and Chinese students led the world in educational performance in 2025, according to a new assessment.
The survey was done by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
The OECD is made up of 38 member nations. It includes the United States, Britain, Australia and many European countries.
The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment surveyed 760,000 15-year-old students. They came from 91 countries and economies, including OECD members. This survey takes place every three years.
In the report, Singapore outscored China in reading. The city state also performed strongly in maths and science.
Students from mainland China led globally in maths with 612 points and in science with 597 points.
The students surveyed in mainland China came from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu province and Zhejiang province.

title: Editorial | Xi-Trump summit built muscle for US-China cooperation
description: The meeting was never going to clear every hurdle, but it set the tone for further relations on the basis of mutual respect and benefit.
content: If improved cooperation between China and the United States is any indication, the summit in Washington last week between presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump can be seen as a landmark in setting the tone for the future of the bilateral relationship on the basis of mutual respect and benefit. Xi’s state visit built on the foundations of better relations laid by the two leaders during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. It yielded eight cooperative outcomes, according to the Chinese statement released following the summit, from trade and tariffs to artificial intelligence (AI). For a sustained improvement in relations, the two countries affirmed in separate statements reciprocal support for each other’s hosting of major international conferences – the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen in November, and the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December. This means Xi and Trump will have three face-to-face meetings in three months, a boost to mutual understanding and cooperation. Analysts also noted the unusual mention in both statements of references to the US-China alliance during World War II, a partnership that Xi and Trump also highlighted last week. According to the Chinese statement, both sides agreed to open a communication channel on AI incidents. It is critical for China and the US to work together to ensure the safe and orderly development of this rapidly evolving technology. The two leaders also formally endorsed a US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement reached earlier by the Chinese and US trade teams, as well as an extension of their trade truce. The US statement also affirmed the establishment of a Board of Investment, which would discuss “potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments”. Some may want to see more concrete deliverables, but that discounts the importance of what has been achieved – improved cooperation on equal footing in preparing for the challenges ahead. The China-US relationship is very complicated, not least because of low trust on both sides. In this atmosphere, Xi and Trump could not be expected to settle the major differences between their countries in one summit. Instead, the summit can realistically set the stage for more collaborative efforts when the two leaders meet again during the Apec and G20 summits and beyond. There is significant room to close a gap in US knowledge about China by increasing the number of American students on the mainland. In that regard, Xi announced an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for study and exchange programmes over the next five years. People-to-people exchanges may be seen as less glamorous but play a unique and critical role in enhancing mutual understanding and friendship, which lays the foundation for bilateral relations. In terms of relationship-building, credit is due to the first ladies, Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump, for fostering a warm and positive atmosphere for the visit. Their friendly interactions went a long way towards softening the tone of the summit. In a further soft-power signal, China dispatched a pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta in the US state of Georgia. Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the exceptional reception given to Xi and Peng on arrival, including the personal welcome on the tarmac from Trump and his wife Melania, reflected respect for Xi and the importance of China-US relations to the US. The two sides also agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons and that no country or institution should impose tolls on international waterways. The US statement noted the arrest in August of 21 Chinese citizens for making and distributing precursor chemicals for illicit drug producers in North America, highlighting China-US cooperation on cracking down on the fentanyl trade. The issue of Taiwan, the major sticking point in China-US relations, was not mentioned in the post-summit statements of the two sides, although Xi had urged the US to maintain opposition to Taiwan independence and stop arms sales to the island. The US and Trump should not underestimate the sensitivity and significance of Taiwan in the bilateral relationship. Differences are inevitable in the relationship. Given that the ups and downs have global impact, it is imperative that the two leaders maintain good communication for the sake of world peace and geopolitical stability.

title: How potassium can lower your blood pressure without cutting back on salt or flavour
description: Many Asian dishes are high in sodium, and new research suggests that increasing potassium intake can offset salt’s effects on blood pressure.
content: For millions across Asia, high blood pressure is more than just a clinical metric – it is baked directly into the region’s rich culinary spread. From soy sauce and fish sauce to dim sum broths and salted egg patties, high-sodium condiments and preserved ingredients are at the core of daily flavour. While public health groups have long urged people to cut back on salt, fresh research suggests we have been missing half the equation: balancing sodium by significantly increasing dietary potassium at the same time. Salt – or sodium chloride – is essential to bodily functions in small amounts, but standard modern diets contain far too much of it. Excess sodium drives the global hypertension crisis, and contributed to an estimated 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). While WHO recommends keeping daily sodium intake under 2,000mg (0.07 oz) – less than a teaspoon of salt – most people in the region consume up to double that amount. Most of the excess does not come from the salt shaker, either – it is locked into processed foods, restaurant meals and cooking staples. Cutting back usually means changing what you buy and how you cook, as much as how much you sprinkle on at the table. It also means, usually, changing your tastes. The challenge is harder here in Asia because salt is “deeply embedded in the cuisine’s flavour architecture”, says Jim Lau, founder and head dietitian of Hong Kong-based holistic nutritional therapy clinic Nutrition Point. Common condiments are particularly concentrated sources of sodium. A single tablespoon of fish sauce contributes around 1,000mg – half a day’s allowance – in one spoonful, a tablespoon of chicken powder adds about 620mg, and oyster sauce around 390mg. Many traditional dishes add up fast, too: marinated jellyfish contains around 780mg of sodium per 100 grams, steamed chicken feet with black bean sauce about 620mg per 100 grams, and steamed minced pork patty with salted egg up to 730mg per 100 grams. Even something as simple as adding sauce to boiled vegetables can increase their sodium content by 300 to 540 per cent. Simply being told to “cut salt” rarely works, Lau says, “because umami and savoury flavours are central to our cuisine”. A fresh report from doctors and researchers at the University of Vermont’s Department of Medicine offers a realistic path forward. Rather than focusing solely on eliminating salt, it suggests that shifting the ratio of sodium to potassium across your total diet offers a more sustainable way to manage blood pressure without sacrificing flavour. “The evidence for this is robust,” Lau says. The WHO recommends adults get at least 3,510mg of potassium a day, based on strong evidence that potassium from food lowers blood pressure and cardiovascular risk. Sodium and potassium work as a team: sodium is the main mineral outside your cells, potassium the main one inside them. Together they regulate fluid balance, nerve signals and muscle contractions – including your heartbeat. Lau describes the report’s core finding: it is the ratio of sodium to potassium that seems to matter more than either mineral alone. Too much sodium raises blood pressure; too little potassium can make that effect worse. This has been proven in other studies. The Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS), which followed more than 20,000 Chinese adults with a history of stroke or with high blood pressure and aged 60-plus, found that replacing regular salt with a potassium-enriched salt cut stroke rates by 14 per cent, along with major cardiovascular events. If most people eat too much salt, at the same time they usually eat too little potassium, even though it is widely available. Bananas and avocados are well-known sources, but Lau points to plenty of local options that are just as good: spinach, sweet potato leaves, water spinach (ong choy), amaranth leaves (Chinese spinach) and broccoli are all high-potassium vegetables. Lotus root provides roughly 191mg to 230mg per serving, and mung beans and edamame are potassium-rich legumes. Not all greens are equal, though – potassium content depends heavily on serving size and cooking method. Gai lan (Chinese broccoli), for instance, is lower in potassium than most other leafy greens per standard serving. Lau uses this as a reminder not to assume all green vegetables are interchangeable – food-specific guidance matters more than broad rules of thumb. A caveat: more potassium is not automatically safe for everyone. If consumed from whole foods, it is beneficial for most people. It can be risky for people with chronic kidney disease, older adults and anyone on certain blood pressure medications, including ACE inhibitors and ARBs – that can cause potassium to build up in the blood – and potassium-sparing diuretics, “water pills” that already reduce how much potassium the body excretes. Anyone in the high-risk categories above should check with a doctor before boosting their potassium intake, even from whole foods, Lau says. A simpler approach is to swap in potassium-rich ingredients that preserve flavour while shifting the sodium-to-potassium balance – so reduce or replace salt-heavy marinades with tomatoes, mushrooms and leafy greens (which bring their own natural umami), and rely on fresh aromatics like ginger, spring onion, garlic and coriander to season instead of salt. A target that is consistent with the SSaSS study is to replace no more than 25 to 30 per cent of regular salt with potassium-enriched salt. That is enough to meaningfully raise potassium intake while staying palatable – potassium in larger amounts can make foods taste bitter or metallic. For sauces, reduce the quantity rather than cutting them out entirely. Serve sauces on the side rather than mixing them in, and pair high-sodium dishes with high-potassium sides – a soy-based braised dish alongside steamed leafy greens with minimal sauce, for example. Adopting this practice will help you develop a healthy habit sustainably rather than trying to cut foods out, hating the taste of something as a result and giving up. The takeaway is not to abandon the flavours you enjoy. It is to shift the overall balance of sodium to potassium across the meal, not eliminate salt from it. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Hong Kong’s first astronaut inspires students with live lesson
description: Lai Ka-ying and crewmates offer glimpse into their lives in space through live lecture.
content:
Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying led a live lesson from the Tiangong space station earlier this month. It was for pupils of her alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College.
The livecast was also streamed at other campuses across Hong Kong and Macau. Lai demonstrated how chicken wings are cooked in zero gravity and how she located the city’s lights from space.
It was a glimpse into her life in orbit and the experiments her team runs.
Lai encouraged students to build a solid foundation in maths and science. She told them to “keep pushing and never fear hardships”.
“I hope students can constantly equip themselves and be brave and proactive as opportunities come along,” she said.
Lai and her crewmates, mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, joined the “Tiangong class” at the school. It was jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency.
Lai also gave a tour of her sleeping area. It is decorated with her children’s drawings, family photos and models of Hong Kong street food.

title: Spark Deep Dive: Ulanqab emerges as a green tech powerhouse
description: The Inner Mongolian city leverages wind power and a cool climate for sustainable data centres, boosting green tech.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Ulanqab is leveraging its cool climate and abundant wind and solar energy to build massive green-powered AI data centres
Rapid AI expansion is straining energy grids worldwide
While an artificial intelligence (AI) query might take mere seconds for users to receive an answer, the process behind that response is complex. It involves a journey back to places like Ulanqab.
In this region, servers consume electricity, cooling systems manage heat and wind turbines harness the movement of air across the grasslands to generate power.
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing – was known for its windswept pastureland.
Strong breezes sweep through the Yinshan mountain range, powering giant wind turbines.
As AI’s rapid growth increases global demand for computing power and electricity, Ulanqab’s cool climate is transforming this pastoral city in Inner Mongolia into one of China’s most valuable industrial assets.
Envision, a green technology company, is developing its Galaxy Campus in Ulanqab. It is set to become one of the world’s largest AI computing hubs.
Envision selected this city to power its data centres with renewable energy sources, which provide 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s electricity. The region’s chilly temperature allows the facility to use outside air for cooling instead of energy-heavy air conditioning.
Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers.
Leading data-centre clusters in Ulanqab’s region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of nearly 1.5. This means in Ulanqab, a greater proportion of each watt of electricity is effectively reaching the server chips.
According to the National Energy Administration (NEA), China’s data centres consumed approximately 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025. This accounted for around 1.6 per cent of the country’s total electricity usage.
By 2030, the annual consumption by data centres is expected to increase to about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times the 2025 levels. It will represent roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use in 2030, as stated by Wang Hongzhi, the director of the NEA.
Greenpeace’s recent Clean Cloud report tracked the renewable energy use of 25 Chinese technology companies. By August, it found that eight reported achieving annual renewable energy ratios that exceeded 30 per cent.
In their 2024 report, only one company had achieved this ratio. Staff writers
