title: Moon Tang on crafting an album about unrequited, uncomfortable love
description: The singer-songwriter returns with an edgier sound as she reflects on solitude, learning from Cantopop legends and building community.
content:
Listening to Moon Tang is akin to reading a close friend’s handwritten diary – intimate music from a “girl next door”, comforting for anyone feeling lost. But in her latest release, “Your Little Mozzie”, the Hong Kong singer-songwriter has taken a step back from that breezy familiarity and peered into something darker.
Tang’s new single is told from the point of view of a mosquito, using the insect as a metaphor for obsessive and fragile feelings of unrequited love. The track captures the bittersweet sentiments of a creature that knows it is unwanted but is still helplessly drawn to the person it adores.
“Maybe it’s a little creepy, but parts of it are very relatable because everyone has their dark side – the side you don’t usually talk about,” the 26-year-old said.
In fact, Tang’s coming project is all about the uncomfortable parts of falling in love: “This entire album revolves around the state of ... someone who has an unrequited crush.”
Today’s young music artists in Hong Kong have struck a balance between absorbing international sounds – from indie pop to contemporary R&B – and maintaining a deep respect for the legends who came before them.
Drawing from global influences without losing their local roots, they redefine what it means to be a Hong Kong musician today.
For Tang, honouring that heritage means learning from the Cantopop divas who defined the genre. Tang shared that she had recently delved into classic Cantonese records by Cass Phang, Sandy Lam and Karen Mok, combing for inspiration for her coming projects.
“I wasn’t just listening to individual songs; I was listening to their full albums … [that] had well-thought-out themes, song titles and content,” she said.
“Nowadays, it feels like there’s very little space and time to create a thoroughly conceptualised album, but older albums were super coherent ... I think that’s amazing, and I realised Cantonese music can be so fun to play with.”
Tang is also incorporating this inspiration into the persona she embodies in her new music.
“I might want to go for a slightly more ‘diva’ vibe. While I’ll still keep that sense of vulnerability this time, I hope the next project will be more powerful and empowering,” she said.
While Tang’s previous album was a collection of singles written over several years, a little like a retrospective , her coming release was constructed in a single month.
“During that month, my deepest feeling was that I was on my own most of the time,” she said. “Back then, I often said, ‘I’m lonely, but I’m content.’ Writing songs every day allowed me to explore this feeling from many different angles.”
Her new music shifts from the soft bedroom pop of her past releases to one that embraces an edgier sound as she takes a deeper look at solitude.
“That’s something I don’t think the me from a few years ago would have felt capable of writing or pulling off,” she said. “Now, I feel more confident doing it, with more attitude and no self-doubt.”
Her English releases this year – such as “Take Three”, which compares love to a film scene stuck on repeat – showcase this bolder perspective.
Tang credits British singer-songwriter Olivia Dean as a key influence: “The English songs were heavily influenced by what I was listening to,” she explained. “At the time, I really loved listening to Olivia Dean.”
She said she also hopes to start collaborating more with other artists.
“I realised that previously, I hadn’t really released duets or actively sought out people around me to collaborate with – it was always just me and my producer. So I’ve reached out to different artists to write together,” she said.
Beyond writing music and performing, Tang has a side venture that intends to tap into her design roots and connect further with fans.
Her creative universe spills into everyday life through Tutufarm, an Instagram account and soft toy collection born from a conversation with her manager.
Many of Tang’s fans seem to enjoy her public presence and think of her as a comforting companion rather than an out-of-reach idol.
The singer decided to pair each new song with a dedicated plushie character. Each was designed with a university classmate from Tang’s time studying design.
“I saw a post earlier about how many people nowadays love hanging plushies on their bags,” Tang said. “Everyone really needs emotional support.”
Tang has created five characters so far and seeing them around the city has become a quiet way for the artist to feel connected to her listeners.
“Every time I see fans hanging the plushies on the street, it feels like we recognise each other through this little secret sign,” she said.
Whether she is designing or composing, Tang said her goal is to build community. “The most important thing is that you enjoy [what you create] because when you enjoy it, people can feel it,” she said.
To celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival, Tang organised an evening market on Saturday for about 300 fans, featuring local brands, second-hand items and crafts made by her mother.
“It felt like bringing together everything I love – using music and my limited capacity to help people, while interacting offline with my listeners,” she shared.
When asked what message she has for young people in Hong Kong navigating their own uncertainties, Tang pondered failure and possibility.
“If you miss an opportunity, there’s no need to be too sad because there will always be a next time – and maybe missing it opens the door for other possibilities,” she said.
“Every success or failure happens for a reason. I’m the type of person who will just open my hands, lie back and trust the process … So, everyone, don’t worry too much, OK?”

title: Activities to learn about primary and secondary colours
description: These colour-mixing crafts will help you understand how to make new colours using red, blue and yellow.
content:
Did you know? There are two groups of colours: primary colours and secondary colours. The primary colours are red, blue and yellow.
When you mix two primary colours together, you create a new colour. That colour is called a secondary colour. When you mix red and yellow, you make orange. When you mix red and blue, you get purple. And when you mix blue and yellow, you create green.
Here are two crafty activities to help you learn all about mixing colours.
4–5 tablespoons of contact lens solution with boric acid
food colouring in the three primary colours: red, yellow and blue
Pour the warm water into one of the large bowls. Mix the baking soda into the water. Stir until the powder has completely dissolved.
Put the glue into the other bowl. Once the water mixture is cool, add it to the glue.
Then, add drops of contact lens solution into the mixture. Add a drop at a time and stir after each drop. This will determine how sticky the slime is.
Pour your mixture into an airtight container and let it rest for one to two days.
Once the slime is fully translucent, split it into three equal parts. Use the food colouring to create red, yellow and blue slime.
Split each colour of slime into another two parts. Stretch and fold two differently coloured slimes together and watch secondary colours emerge.
fizzing tablets (such as Alka-Seltzer or a soluble vitamin)
food colouring in any two primary colours
Fill two-thirds of your bottle or jar with vegetable oil. Fill the remaining third with water. Leave a little space at the top.
Add 10 drops of each colour of food colouring. Try to predict what colour your lava lamp will be when the two primary colours mix together.
Break the fizzing tablet into three or four pieces. Once the drops of food colouring settle at the bottom of the bottle, drop all the pieces of the tablet in.
When the tablet begins to fizz, the two primary colours will mix to form a secondary colour. Check if your prediction was correct!
The tablet should swish the coloured blobs all around the bottle. This happens because the tablet creates gas bubbles of carbon dioxide that latch onto the food colouring, making the blobs look like swirling lava.

title: Far-right makes major gains in French Senate as Le Pen eyes power
description: National Rally and allies form first-ever upper chamber group months before Emmanuel Macron steps down.
content: France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies secured a record 14 seats in the right-wing dominated Senate in polls Sunday, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential election. RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen hailed a “historic victory” after the results were announced. Local elected officials vote for new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term. The far-right party entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023. Le Pen is eyeing her best chance yet at power in elections next year when centrist President Emmanuel Macron steps down. “This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate,” she said on X. Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, according to an Agence France-Presse tally of results, on top of the three who won seats in 2023. A further two were elected from RN ally Eric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party. RN president Jordan Bardella said the party’s senators would form a group with UDR allies. Ciotti quit the right-wing Republicans (LR) party in 2024 after calling for an alliance with the far-right. The upper chamber’s LR president of more than a decade, 77-year-old Gerard Larcher, is expected to be re-elected next week. The right, centre and left-wing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results. The hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party won its first-ever seat. Le Pen’s anti-immigration party emerged as the single largest party in the lower house National Assembly after Macron called snap polls in 2024, though it fell well short of a majority.

title: Deep Dive: Ulanqab’s cool climate powers China’s AI revolution with green energy
description: The Inner Mongolian city’s weather and abundant wind power are slashing AI energy costs and boost sustainable computing.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Ulanqab is leveraging its cool climate and abundant wind and solar energy to build massive green-powered AI data centres
Rapid AI expansion is straining energy grids worldwide
While an artificial intelligence (AI) query might take mere seconds for users to receive an answer, the process behind that response is complex. It involves a journey back to places like Ulanqab.
In this region, which plays a crucial role in driving the AI boom, servers consume electricity, cooling systems manage heat and wind turbines harness the movement of air across the grasslands to generate power.
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing – was known for its windswept pastureland. Strong breezes sweep through the Yinshan mountain range, powering giant wind turbines.
As AI’s rapid growth increases global demand for computing power and electricity, Ulanqab’s cool climate is transforming this pastoral city in Inner Mongolia into one of China’s most valuable industrial assets.
Envision, a green technology company, is developing its Galaxy Campus in Ulanqab. It is set to become one of the world’s largest AI computing hubs.
Envision selected this city to power its data centres with local renewable energy sources, which currently provide 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s electricity. The region’s chilly temperature allows the facility to use outside air for cooling instead of energy-heavy air conditioning.
Leading data-centre clusters in Ulanqab’s region have a power usage effectiveness (PUE) below 1.15, against a national average of nearly 1.5.
This means in Ulanqab, a greater proportion of each watt of electricity is effectively reaching the server chips.
According to the National Energy Administration (NEA), China’s data centres consumed approximately 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025. This accounted for around 1.6 per cent of the country’s total electricity usage.
By 2030, the annual consumption by data centres is expected to increase to about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times the 2025 levels. It will represent roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use in 2030, as stated by Wang Hongzhi, the director of the NEA.
Greenpeace’s recent Clean Cloud report tracked the renewable energy use of 25 Chinese technology companies. By August, it found that eight reported achieving annual renewable energy ratios that exceeded 30 per cent. In their 2024 report, there was only one company achieving that.
Technology giants are betting that Ulanqab’s wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a more sustainable foundation for AI infrastructure. Staff writers
1. How is an AI query related to Ulanqab in China? Choose two statements that apply. (1) Ulanqab’s wind turbines run the servers that might power an AI chatbot’s answers. (2) Ulanqab’s cold weather helps to cool down the data centres behind many AI companies. (3) Ulanqab’s economy relies heavily on importing electricity from Beijing to support its AI companies. (4) Ulanqab provides the human effort needed to manually calculate AI queries.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (3) only C. (2), (4) only D. (3), (4) only
2. Explain two factors that make Ulanqab a good location for hosting AI data centres.
3. Do you think Chinese tech companies are getting most of their power from sources like those found in Ulanqab? Explain your answer using information from News.
1. What is the difference between the electricity consumption of China’s AI data centres in 2025 and what is projected for 2030?
2. How does the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of data-centre clusters in the Ulanqab area compare with the national average? If more data centres had a PUE closer to what Ulanqab has, how might this affect the electricity consumption projection for 2030?
Ulanqab converts its vast wind potential and cold climate into major cost savings for AI companies
Soaring AI token consumption is driving Ulanqab’s push to reach over 200,000 petaflops of computing capacity
China’s appetite for AI tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025. It then exceeded 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data.
This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them, and every AI token comes with a cost.
“Every 1 million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data.
In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power.
Rates vary, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (HK$0.41) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can be 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant.
For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is a central part of the business model.
For Ulanqab, the next challenge is not simply building more servers but making sure those servers are connected to real demand.
Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates.
Meanwhile, much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based.
Beijing is pushing to connect its AI infrastructure with the country’s power system. In Ulanqab, wind farms could provide renewable electricity. Data centres could then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia.
The city is also seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens.
The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, with a focus on green computing for large AI model training and inference. It also aims to encourage investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent.
The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models. Staff writers
1. Why is low-cost electricity considered a central part of the business model for AI data centres?
2. What would be the benefit of connecting AI infrastructure with the wider power system in China?
3. What would it mean for Ulanqab to “move up the AI value chain”?
1. Using your own knowledge, what do you think has changed from 2024 to 2026 that has caused this increase in AI token usage?
2. What is the cost of generating these AI tokens? To what extent do you agree that companies and people should continue this trend of using increasingly more tokens?
Ulanqab : accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s wind resources, according to China’s Xinhua news agency. As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, based on local government data.
wind turbines: giant spinning towers with blades that convert wind movement into electrical power
power usage effectiveness : a measure of energy efficiency of a data centre. Perfect efficiency is represented by a PUE of 1.0, where every watt goes directly to computing, while higher numbers indicate energy wasted on supporting systems.
token : a measure for the units of text processed by AI models
petaflops : a unit measuring computing speed, equal to one quadrillion floating-point operations per second
1. A. (1), (2) only 2. Ulanqab’s cool climate allows for efficient cooling of data centres using outside air, reducing the need for energy-heavy air conditioning. Additionally, the region’s renewable energy sources ensure a sustainable power supply. 3. Only eight out of 25 Chinese tech companies mentioned in the Clean Cloud report achieved annual renewable energy ratios above 30 per cent. This indicates that the majority of these companies rely on non-renewable energy sources, which are harmful to the environment.

By 2030, this consumption is expected to rise to about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, indicating an increase of nearly five times the 2025 levels. 2. The PUE of data-centre clusters in Ulanqab is below 1.15, significantly better than the national average of nearly 1.5. If more data centres could achieve a similar PUE, they would be more efficient in electricity usage, potentially lowering the overall electricity consumption projections for 2030. This could help reduce the anticipated increase in demand from 800 billion kilowatt-hours. More efficient data centres would allow for greater sustainability in powering AI infrastructure.
1. Low-cost electricity is crucial for AI data centres as it constitutes 60 to 70 per cent of their operating costs. With the demand for AI tokens soaring, the electricity needed for generation significantly impacts overall expenses. Affordable power enables operators to reduce costs, making their business models more sustainable and competitive. 2. Connecting AI infrastructure with the wider power system in China would enable efficient delivery of computing capacity to users across the country, particularly in demand-rich eastern cities. It would also leverage renewable energy sources like wind farms, promoting sustainability. This integration can optimise the production of AI tokens and enhance the overall value captured from renewable power. 3. For Ulanqab to “move up the AI value chain,” it means transitioning from just being a data centre hub to a comprehensive AI services centre. This includes expanding computing capabilities, developing platforms for trading AI tokens and focusing on green computing. By enhancing these services, Ulanqab can create greater value from its renewable energy resources.

The increase in AI token usage from 2024 to 2026 likely stems from advancements in AI technology, growing demand from businesses for AI applications and improved infrastructure supporting larger-scale AI model training. Additionally, the availability of cheap electricity in regions like Ulanqab has made token generation more economically viable, fuelling further growth. 2. Generating 1 million AI tokens requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity, contributing to substantial operational costs for data centres. While the demand for tokens indicates innovation and growth, it is crucial to balance this with sustainability and the environmental impact of increased electricity consumption. Companies and individuals should pursue tokens thoughtfully, ensuring that the benefits align with ecological considerations and responsible energy use.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): JD.com unveils ambitious plan to revolutionise logistics
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
[1] The Chinese e-commerce company JD.com is speeding up its efforts to use robots and automation. They plan to make their logistics network, which is how they deliver products all over the country, more automated. At the same time, they are promising to help train their delivery workers to take on new technical jobs as machines begin to handle more of the frontline duties.
[2] Earlier this month, at an event in Beijing, the logistics arm of the company showed off its new series of industrial robots called the Wolf Robot series. Over the next five years, JD Logistics plans to buy 3 million robots, 1 million vehicles that do not need drivers and 100,000 delivery drones. This plan is to create a fully automated supply chain, according to Cao Peng, who is the chairman of the company’s technology committee.
[3] The Wolf Robot system is made to handle repetitive and hard jobs while working in tough conditions. It can pick up, sort, move and deliver items with very little help from people, according to Liu Lige, who leads the team that works on robots at JD Logistics. The collection of robots has special units that can work in very cold places, even when the temperature is as low as minus 20 degrees Celsius. This group also includes robots for delivering medicines and drones for making deliveries, Liu mentioned.
[4] The fast move towards automation is happening while JD and its partner companies still have around 700,000 delivery and logistics workers. To tackle worries about job loss, the founder Liu Qiangdong explained earlier this year a plan called the Nirvana Plan. This plan aims to retrain delivery workers and warehouse staff so they can learn new skills for technical jobs, like fixing and taking care of robots. This way, the company can keep its frontline workers even as automation becomes more common.
[5] JD is planning to use its many warehouses, retail stores and pharmacies to collect over 10 million hours of real-world data about how things work, according to Cao. The company also wants to set up more than 80 RoboBase hubs all over China. These are hubs that will focus on research in robotics, testing new production methods, labelling data, upgrading equipment and maintaining machines.
[6] To support the heavy computational demands of this ecosystem, JD recently signed a deal with Chinese chip designer Moore Threads to build a computing cluster powered by 100,000 domestic chips. The cluster would be used to train and run artificial intelligence (AI) models, as well as embodied AI applications. It will also help JD integrate domestic chips into an AI development pipeline that spans data collection, model training, simulation and deployment, according to the two companies. Source: South China Morning Post, September 9

title: Listen Up: Why scratching a bug bite is a bad idea
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the provided script for help.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Graeme Acres, a production editor on SCMP’s Hong Kong desk, and Young Post production editor Sakina Abidi.
Voice 1: You’ve probably heard this advice since you were a child: don’t scratch that bug bite or rash; it will only make it worse. But why can something that feels so satisfying be harmful?
Voice 2: Various factors can cause itchiness, including some serious medical conditions. Regardless of the cause, doctors have long cautioned that excessive scratching can injure the skin. Recent research has provided a better understanding of why even a mildly irritating itch can lead you into a cycle of itching and scratching if you give in.
Voice 1: How did the researchers uncover their findings? They used tiny protective cones, often referred to as “cones of shame”, on mice to study the cellular changes that occur when an itch is scratched versus when it is left alone. These cones are plastic medical devices typically used on pets to prevent them from licking, biting or scratching wounds. The study also provided insights into why scratching an itch, at least initially, brings a sigh of relief.
Voice 2: Interestingly, it is not only humans and other mammals that scratch their bodies; even fish do. This common behaviour suggests there may be an evolutionary reason behind it. The mouse experiment suggests itching provides limited protection against germs, but it does not justify scratching.
Voice 1: Dr Daniel Kaplan, a dermatologist at the University of Pittsburgh in the US state of Pennsylvania, studies immune reactions in the skin. He was investigating a run-of-the-mill itch known as allergic contact dermatitis, which is triggered by irritants such as poison ivy or nickel in jewellery.
Voice 2: Kaplan’s research team applied an irritant that causes rashes to the ears of mice. In normal mice, scratching triggered an influx of inflammatory immune cells into the area, leading to increased swelling. However, the rash was significantly milder in mice that had been bred with defective itch-sensing nerve cells.
Voice 1: So was the difference really the scratching? To find out, the normal mice were fitted with collars. Their rash still itched, but they could not scratch themselves. The result was that they had much less swelling and fewer inflammatory cells.
Voice 2: Kaplan said the evidence matches people’s everyday experiences: scratching really can make things worse. Ignore a mosquito bite, and the itch is gone in five or 10 minutes for most people, he said. But if you start scratching it, it’s your friend for a week, getting itchier and more inflamed.
Voice 1: To understand what was happening in the skin, Kaplan’s team took a deeper look at mast cells, which are among the immune system’s first responders. When called into action, they release compounds that can help fight germs or toxins. They also release a compound called histamine, which triggers itchy allergic reactions.
Voice 2: Scientists have long known that allergens can activate mast cells. But other signals can summon mast cells, too, including pain. And when we scratch, we tend to scratch until it starts to hurt, which releases a chemical messenger called substance P, Kaplan noted. In findings published last year, Kaplan’s team reported that substance P can activate mast cells through a different molecular pathway than allergens do. It is a double whammy that explains why scratching further inflames itchy rashes or bites.
Voice 1: Then why does a little scratching feel good? If we experience pain, like touching a hot stove, we learn not to do that again. But relief from a good scratch, in evolutionary terms, is positive feedback. One long-held theory is that it may help creatures slough off parasites like fleas or mites. But Kaplan was also intrigued by other labs’ findings that mast cells could fend off a common skin bacterium, Staphylococcus aureus.
Voice 2: So his team infected mice and then repeated the cone-of-shame itch experiment. Sure enough, those who scratched had lower levels of that germ on their ears, maybe because of the extra inflammation or some other mast cell-related compound. But that’s not enough of an upside to change the health advice. The best approach to an itchy bite or rash is still that you should avoid scratching.

title: Open Questions | Scott Kennedy on China’s ‘slow tech dragon’ and 2 more Xi-Trump meetings
description: American adviser on Chinese business and economics highlights different phases of US-China relations over the past 50 years.
content: Scott Kennedy is a senior adviser and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. His areas of focus include China’s hi-tech drive, US-China relations and global economic governance. Open Questions first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. How would you characterise the outcomes of the China-US summit compared to expectations going in? Is it largely a continuation of that track or do you see it moving the relationship a few steps forward? The summit continued the pathway set in May and, in terms of specific deliverables, met the low expectations that observers had going in. Most notably, they agreed to extend the economic ceasefire on tariffs and export controls, but only for two months, to January 10, 2027. That will provide a little reassurance to financial markets and to businesses that trade and invest between the US and China and elsewhere. But that’s still just four months away, and as we get closer to January, if nothing is resolved by November or December, people will get more worried. On the trade front, they agreed to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of products on each side and encourage trade of specific non-sensitive products, such as agricultural goods, fish and seafood, medical devices, and consumer goods. They also agreed, according to the US side, to refer to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” and create a notification system of serious incidents. [Chinese President] Xi [Jinping] emphasised the importance of keeping AI under human control in his opening remarks, views that were reaffirmed in subsequent Chinese statements. The other significant outcome mentioned by both sides is their common commitment that Iran should not be permitted to have a nuclear weapon and that no one should be able to charge tolls for international waterways. Another point of emphasis during the discussions, though not mentioned in the fact sheets, was Taiwan, with Beijing trying to further pocket what they saw as adjustments in US language and actions coming out of the summit in Beijing. But the summit’s deliverables were still quite modest. As with Beijing, there was much more pomp than substance. US officials have said Beijing proposed a “bigger deal”. What do you think China means by that? And what would Beijing want in return? We would need an explanation from either side, but one could hypothesise that the Chinese were looking to extend the commercial ceasefire to the end of the Trump administration, and in return would potentially offer larger and longer commitments to purchase American products, whether that would be commercial aircraft, agriculture, energy, or other goods. And they might have an offer to expand the amount of goods on each side that were tariffed at normal or below-normal levels. China could also have proposed an investment arrangement with specific deals identified, pilots, or a mechanism to evaluate new Chinese investment. All of that could have been part of a larger deal. US President [Donald] Trump said that coming out of one of the meetings [with Xi], the two sides had made “tremendous strides”, but based on the fact sheets, no such big deal was reached. You mentioned what China might want out of the summit. Are the two leaders just building momentum for when they meet again, say at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) or Group of 20 (G20) summits later this year to announce a bigger deal? China may be holding back on some things for Apec and the G20, and President Trump may also be. But I think China would have been totally satisfied if they had made a big deal in Washington. China’s goal is to keep the current relationship in this form, for as long as they can. The kinds of things they are likely offering to keep the trade peace are not giant sacrifices to China. None would require China to make any adjustments whatsoever in economic strategy or industrial policy. No attention is being paid to the thorny issue of imbalances. So, China would be happy to make this kind of deal any time, whether it had been in Washington or on the sidelines of the Apec leaders’ meeting or the G20 summit. So what limited the two sides from announcing a bigger deal in Washington? At a minimum, it was the US side and their concerns about obstacles obtaining rare earths. Over the past year, China’s rare earth exports globally have risen but they have fallen towards the US by about 25 per cent and dropped dramatically with regard to Japan. The US wants to ensure that the flow of rare earths returns to normal levels in line with China’s commitment. The US was also looking for support on Iran. Although we typically think of Iran as a security issue, a different bucket than on economics, we know that both sides in certain circumstances will connect different issues. It’s possible – although we don’t know – that the US made extending the ceasefire for a longer period conditional on greater Chinese support with regard to Iran, not just in word but in deed. Both leaders have played up their personal rapport while deliverables look thin. Can a relationship this consequential rest on the chemistry between two leaders? Is that enough and is it sustainable? People talk about a G2. The US and China do not have what is conventionally considered a G2, a group of two very powerful countries who collaborate in managing global affairs. That is not what they are doing. President Trump’s version of a G2, based on his language and behaviour, is probably more like “two guys”. In his mind, he and Xi have a very strong personal relationship that is the key source of stable ties. It’s reflected in his praise of Xi, why he went out to personally greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, had an extravagant welcoming ceremony and state dinner, and showed him the White House’s helipad and the East Wing construction site. We have not seen Xi explicitly frame their relationship in personal terms. In his various remarks, he is respectful of President Trump and expresses appreciation for his graciousness, but it is clear he is representing the Communist Party and China, not framing this as a personal friendship. Xi tried to be pleasant, and he looked comfortable with Trump, but it’s clear he is not returning the same kinds of personal compliments that he receives. And so for him the G2 is “two governments”, not a bromance. I don’t know whether Trump’s approach has something to do with a desire to be included among some of the world’s most powerful leaders or to develop friendships. He may be doing this strictly for utilitarian purposes or may be driven by something else. But he’s done this with several other political leaders. He may want to give Xi face, believing that will help keep the relationship stable and make Xi more amenable to making concessions aligned with US preferences. It’s clear that Xi and other senior officials avoid directly offending Trump, and they showed him a lot of deference when they hosted him in Beijing in May. So both sides are careful in how they handle the interpersonal relationship and questions of respect and face. You have been watching China for decades. Where does this moment in the US-China relationship rank against some past inflection points, including China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the 2018 trade war? For much of the past half-century, the US has been focused on trying to find ways to integrate China into the international system and have a stable relationship, and China has been interested in pursuing that path as well. That really describes much of the relationship through 2015, the last time Xi made a state visit to Washington. But the promise of that state visit and other meetings during the [Barack] Obama administration were not realised, and what we’ve seen is the US becoming more frustrated with China’s trajectory, and going back and forth between different kinds of approaches to deal with the China challenge. First, it tried under Trump’s first term to use unilateral pressure on China to push it to meet its bilateral and multilateral commitments. Then the [Joe] Biden administration concluded that China couldn’t be effectively integrated into the international order, and therefore its focus shifted to insulating the rest of the world from the problems that China’s economic system and foreign policy created for others. Under the second Trump administration, the US has decided to abandon that original international order and build a relationship with China on a very different foundation, rooted solely in power politics and a very different conception of the global order – in many ways, an order which China’s current leadership is much more comfortable with and more familiar with than what was critical to the original project the US was pursuing. And so we’re dealing with each other on very different terms than how the US and China interacted with each other for much of the last half-century. The US government is still grappling with finding the right framework. The label of “constructive strategic stability” – expanded with the modifier “on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity” in Washington – is more a slogan than a detailed concept and blueprint, but that’s where we are right now. What we’re seeing is an allocation of resources tilted heavily towards advanced technologies and away from other potential investments in human capital, in the social safety net and other areas Scott Kennedy You talked about this new approach towards China in Trump’s second administration. For now, the relationship has some semblance of stability, with Trump and Xi meeting up to four times this year. How do you view this new stability and engagement? Is it a genuine recalibration of ties or is it a kind of managed truce that still has sticking points? Those who are more optimistic about the potential endurance of stable ties believe that the US has essentially abandoned its mission to manage the world in line with the rules-based international order and instead be more pragmatic about how the world works and embrace realpolitik. As a result, that means being less concerned about the rules of the game and more about outcomes. So, it’s still a competition, but not a competition of competing orders. In fact, there may also be some areas of cooperation, since some of the issues that generate tensions in a competition of those two systems and their underlying values and ideologies are being put to the side. Those who think that the post-World War II, international rules-based order may have flaws but should be reformed and strengthened look at the current ceasefire as quite temporary and believe that there will eventually be a “snapback” and resumption of greater tensions. Once the US reduces its vulnerabilities, it will go back on the offence again. I honestly don’t know what the right expectations should be because the US is still trying to figure out what kind of world it wants to have and the same with many other countries. There appears to be a shifting balance of power between China and the West, but we don’t know how durable that is because we’ve got a lot of different variables that we’re trying to assess. Artificial intelligence has been repeatedly floated as an area where the US and China can cooperate. But the suggestion seems to be at odds with an escalating US campaign designed to slow China’s AI progress – and the two countries also view AI in fundamentally different terms. Is cooperation possible in a sector marked by deep differences and one in which the US is trying to contain China’s progress? Certainly, if AI is viewed strictly as a race to get to AGI [artificial general intelligence] because of the economic and potential military benefits that accrue to the country that gets there first, then that makes cooperation extremely difficult. But I don’t think that’s really what has been occurring. There’s growing evidence that we’re not strictly in a race. The US and China have different kinds of approaches to AI. There’s no certainty that there is some magical threshold that one crosses that differentiates yesterday from tomorrow. And there are significant risks from AI that are not a product of interstate competition, challenges that everyone faces from the technology and its potential consequences on the world – deepfakes, hallucinations, loss of control and military applications, and other kinds of risks. There’s also some amazing potential benefits that we could share that could help each other and the rest of the world. Given the complexities of the technology, the various different countries and stakeholders involved, we’re still at a very early stage. This is like the late 1940s at the very beginning of the nuclear era. We’re at the very beginning of the AI era. It’s really up to us – and “us” meaning everyone on the planet, not just powerful governments – to define what AI means and how we should address this challenge. This is a moment when the clay is still quite wet. In May, Xi and Trump struck a trade deal built on familiar terms: Chinese purchases of American soybeans and Boeing planes, similar to the phase one trade agreement reached in 2020. Given that history, can such trade deals really function as a stabiliser for the relationship? Or must real stability come from elsewhere? In an era in which we are involved in great power competition, trade and investment are not going to be an obvious ballast in the relationship. Since the two countries’ comparative advantages are increasingly overlapping, they are competing for the same section of the pie in the global economy. The US also is focused heavily on “new quality productive forces”, just as the Chinese are. And so, in an era when the two sides are inherently less competitive, interdependence is less problematic and serves as ballast. But in an era defined by rivalry, interdependence is viewed by both governments as a risk, and both have taken enormous steps to de-risk and hold the upper hand. The agreements on capping tariffs and continuing to provide rare earths, deals on individual products like aeroplanes and agricultural goods, those are very superficial arrangements which don’t suggest a high level of trust. If such transactions are the cornerstone of these summits, the two sides are just dealing with the most superficial elements of the relationship because the US and China are at fundamental loggerheads over the more serious challenges with no clear path to resolution. If you don’t think stability in the relationship can come from economics, then where can it come from? Can anything anchor the relationship? In this kind of world, with a shifting balance of power, competing visions of the global system and an unwillingness to anchor one’s actions on basic principles that should constrain the behaviour of everyone including themselves, instability is more likely to be the hallmark of the relationship. Without other stabilisers, avoiding conflict requires greater dependence on leadership diplomacy, and the leaders’ depth of involvement will depend on where the other country fits in the views of those two leaders and the dynamics of domestic politics. But the chances of a more fundamental stability seem out of reach. China’s hi-tech industries have become world-class, driving a narrative that it is overtaking the US. But China’s strengths in manufacturing, in exports and technology, coexist with weak consumption, high youth unemployment and a property slump. How should we understand this divergence, and does it complicate the story of Chinese strength? I think of China as a “slow tech dragon”, where it is simultaneously achieving amazing technology breakthroughs, manufacturing at scale, diffusing those technologies widely – not just within China but far beyond – while at the same time having a very slow macroeconomic environment. Those two things are the product of a common source, which is the emphasis by China’s policymakers on investment in technology as the primary source of China’s growth trajectory, replacing investment in infrastructure. As a result, what we’re seeing is an allocation of resources tilted heavily towards advanced technologies and away from other potential investments in human capital, the social safety net and other areas. In some ways, this is a misallocation of resources that is leading to a very imbalanced economy domestically, and therefore globally. China’s economy is at least one-fifth of the world’s economy, and any imbalances in China become global imbalances. China’s economy has both impressive strengths and significant weaknesses, and it likely will be a slow tech dragon for some time to come. It is that challenge that the world faces. We face a country that is technologically quite advanced but is choosing to focus on the supply side of technology as opposed to the consumption side. For China to continue with this growth model, by definition it needs the world to adjust and absorb the gap between what China produces and what it consumes. The rest of the world benefits in some ways, but on balance, it is going to be pushing back, aiming for China to rebalance domestically in order to address global imbalances. Of course, those global imbalances aren’t only created by China. The US overconsumes and has a massive amount of debt. In some ways these are mirrors of each other. But China’s approach is, on its own terms, creating challenges for others, and managing a relationship with a slow tech dragon is quite difficult. The US is still struggling to figure out a way to do so, and China is increasingly encountering pushback – in Europe and Latin America, not just the US – from the consequences of its economic growth strategy. How sustainable is this Chinese approach, especially when global pressure on China is building? There are three different kinds of ways in which the Chinese economic model will run into obstacles that it can’t overcome and which will force it to change. The first is debt, because China’s financial system is so inefficient and there has been a rapid build-up of debt to fuel investment. Even though China is a hi-tech power, many of its companies are not very profitable, and so China’s credit picture continues to worsen. The second potential obstacle is the effect of an economic transition on labour in China. In some ways, these great advancements are requiring a lot less labour, and in some sectors different kinds of labour, generating a mismatch between the type of human capital China has and what its economy needs. The Communist Party was created on the foundation of labour protests, and if this mismatch continues to worsen, labour instability is a potential challenge, not just for China but for others. The third obstacle is pushback from the rest of the world. Countries individually and collectively say they are not going to adjust any longer, and that instead they are going to make China adjust. Currently, because of the Trump administration’s approach, many countries in the world similarly view challenges emanating from China, but there’s no effective coordination among others. We saw a statement from the G20 gathering in Asheville [in North Carolina] recently about concerns over non-market practices, but there’s no significant coordinated action. If international unhappiness coalesces into joint or aligned steps, limiting China’s ability to have large trade surpluses, this could become a more effective constraint on China’s approach. Trade wars are no longer just a US-China story. The US is in an escalating one with Canada, and Beijing’s doing the same with the EU. If tariffs are becoming the default tool major economies use to settle disputes, what does this mean for the future of the global economy? The US still has tariffs on China of roughly 30 per cent in total. And if the investigation into manufacturing overcapacity yields a verdict soon, the US could impose an additional 7.5 per cent on China. Total US tariffs are much higher than the 3 per cent level average tariffs that the US had before. Although tariffs on China are still extremely high, they’re also high on just about everyone else. The US is still using tariffs to try to lower its bilateral trade deficits, encourage manufacturing at home, and raise additional revenue. It’s not been hugely successful in those goals, but the [Trump] administration is not giving up. US efforts are having a corrosive effect on the multilateral trading system because it’s clear that US actions violate its WTO commitments. But the US is not the lone bad actor. US protectionism is a reaction to changing terms of trade and a deep sense of unfairness by the US about its trading relationship with many countries, including China, and its view that industrial policy and non-tariff barriers have led to unfair changes in the commercial relationship, in market opportunities, bilaterally and globally. And so, US policy is born out of frustration. The Trump administration’s approach to that frustration further erodes the multilateral order, but it’s part of the back-and-forth tit-for-tat that’s been occurring for over two decades. Despite all of that, according to the WTO, 72 per cent of global trade still occurs on a most-favoured-nation basis. We see efforts by countries to push back on super high tariffs, and countries have cut bilateral and regional deals to expand their opportunities and sustain an open multilateral trading order. Having recently been in Geneva – in a Track 2 dialogue with Chinese counterparts – there is a lot of recognition at the WTO and by its members of these risks to the multilateral order in the context of growing great power competition. Brics has been pushing harder to settle trade outside the US dollar, and the Netherlands recently pulled roughly US$10 billion in gold out of American vaults. With US allies hedging against the US dollar, what does it say about how secure the dollar’s central role is? And will this be the start of something structural? Investors and governments are always making adjustments in their holdings of currency based on a variety of circumstances, including macroeconomic conditions across different economies and trends in exchange rates. We’ve seen significant adjustments in holdings of currencies, and we’ve also seen a shift towards shorter maturities recently. This could be normal, short-term adjustments. The American stock market is performing at record levels, with investment pouring in from around the world. This trend is built largely on optimism about AI and America’s own version of “new quality, productive forces”, the cutting of taxes in the US, and what looks in many respects like still a relatively strong economy. But there may be another story. Observers are concerned about growing geostrategic tensions, rising tariffs, and dangerous regional hotspots around the world. They’re worried about some of the foundations of the rule of law in the US, its democratic institutions, and the independence of the Federal Reserve. These worries may signal a transition that is more structural and not just a short-term blip. At the end of the day, a lot will depend on people’s confidence in the US government’s ability to be a wise steward of its economy and the international order. That said, even though there are worries about the US from a variety of quarters, there are not good alternatives to a dollar-based international monetary system. China is the world’s largest trader, but most of its trade still occurs in dollars, and most of its international financial transactions still occur in dollars. China still holds a lot of US Treasuries, and China’s capital account is still largely closed. China doesn’t have deep financial markets that are internationally open to serve as a significant alternative. Even with the variety of experiments and initiatives it has pursued, central authorities prioritise domestic financial stability above all. Limited investment opportunities in renminbi, insufficient policy transparency and concerns about the rule of law together are constraints on the renminbi playing a larger international role. Europe’s economy is growing very slowly. [There are] significant worries about Europe’s economy and European Union gridlock, concerns maybe even larger than those about the US. Hence, the euro is unlikely to be a clear, obvious alternative to the dollar. And so, in a world where money needs to take some form, and investments are relative, even with concerns about the US and the dollar, it looks like we will continue to live in a dollar-based global economy for quite some time. There are obvious risks, but I don’t see us shifting significantly in a different direction in the near term.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): Hong Kong flag day scam uncovered
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Hong Kong police have arrested a man related to a scam where at least 14 people were hired to “sell flags” for a group that helps animals. These people were seen carrying fake donation bags and mingling with registered volunteers to collect money from people walking by.
[2] The rare street scam came to light during the group’s flag day earlier this month. This initiative, approved by the Social Welfare Department, involved about 800 registered volunteers from the Hong Kong Saving Cat and Dog Association who were deployed across Kowloon from 7am to noon.
[3] Flag days are a traditional way to raise money in Hong Kong. During these days, approved charities ask volunteers to collect donations from people on the streets. The volunteers carry a special donation bag and a sheet of small stickers. These stickers have taken the place of the small paper flags that donors used to pin to their clothes many years ago.
[4] When passers-by drop coins into the bag or make a digital donation, the volunteer places a sticker on their clothing as a token of appreciation and recognition. The events are typically held on Saturdays, or occasionally on Wednesdays during school holidays. In Cantonese, flag days are called mai kei yat – or “flag-selling day”. Genuine volunteers reported on social media that a group of strangers had mixed into the crowd, displaying fake flag sheets and bags that were a different shade of blue.
[5] A police source said that the person who complained saw people acting like staff from an association near Langham Place in Mong Kok. Fourteen individuals who were carrying fake bags were stopped. Investigations found that they had answered a job ad on WhatsApp that offered HK$70 an hour for selling flags, and they thought they were just temporary workers.
[6] They were told to bring the bags back to a contact on Nelson Street, but the organiser never showed up. The fake bags were light blue instead of the dark blue bags that the real volunteers used, and they had a statement saying that the flag day had been approved by the department. The 14 recruits were taken to Mong Kok Police Station for questioning. After that, officers arrested a 22-year-old man for tricking people, a police spokesman said. Source: South China Morning Post, September 6

title: South Korea demands apology from Ukraine over disclosure of North Korean POW transfer
description: Seoul said Zelensky’s UN revelation has damaged trust between ⁠the two governments and that it is reviewing additional measures.
content: South Korea’s presidential office has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying ‌that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential. “The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement released on Sunday. He said the government was reviewing additional measures on the issue if necessary. Seong said Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the prisoners’ transfer with Seoul through various channels and had requested secrecy, arguing that public disclosure could trigger domestic criticism that ⁠Kyiv had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea agreed to keep the transfer confidential given security, diplomatic ‌and humanitarian concerns, including the safety of the prisoners and their families, he said. According to the statement, Ukraine later disclosed the transfer in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s address to the United Nations General Assembly without sufficient ‌prior consultation and subsequently denied the existence of any confidentiality agreement. Seong said the denial had seriously damaged trust between the two ⁠governments and could harm ⁠bilateral relations. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Zelensky told the United Nations General Assembly last week that Ukraine had transferred two ‌captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea. He said the men had recently been sent there after being captured while fighting for Russia in the war against Ukraine. South Korean President ‌Lee Jae Myung days earlier said Ukraine had disclosed the transfer in breach of a non-disclosure agreement. In a post on social media, Lee said “it was ‌appropriate in every aspect not to disclose” the transfer, given the potential consequences, and that the two sides had agreed to keep it ⁠confidential. “I do not know what circumstances led the Ukrainian side to disclose the matter despite the confidentiality agreement, but it is deeply regrettable,” ⁠he wrote. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since Pyongyang entered the war in 2024, helping Russia. South Korea had previously declined to ‌confirm the soldiers’ arrival, citing concerns for ‌their safety and that of family members still in North Korea. Seoul and Kyiv had been discussing a possible transfer after the two soldiers expressed a desire to go to South Korea, according to an opposition lawmaker in Seoul. The transfer comes as South Korea has backed efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, while US President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang.

title: Opinion | The US-China relationship has stabilised but on Beijing’s terms
description: Managed rivalry is not peace; it is a rules-based pause with China largely writing the rules. The test is whether the US can live with it.
content: For all the solemnity of the B-2 flyover with four F‑22 Raptors and a silent South Lawn drill, the real business of US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping last week was narrower than the choreography. The Chinese readout reiterated the concept that should frame the relationship’s next phase: constructive strategic stability – cooperation as the primary track, competition kept within bounds, differences managed, conflict avoided. Stripped of banquet rhetoric, the Washington leg of the 2026 Xi-Trump cycle cements a managed rivalry on Beijing’s terms: China sets the boundaries while Washington – constrained by rare earth dependence, market jitters and a crowded election calendar – accepts stabilisation over confrontation. Trump called it a “great meeting” and revived the “friendship” trope; Xi was more doctrinal. Having previously raised the Thucydides Trap and asked if their countries could transcend a rising power-vs-hegemon collision, he announced last Thursday: “The Thucydides Trap can be overcome.” Competition, he said, “should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses”; it should be “healthy”, “kept within bounds”. He also tied Trump’s “Make America Great Again” vision to China’s great national rejuvenation as complementary projects. The flattery is functional: it gives Trump a headline while embedding Chinese terms – strategic stability, bounded competition – into the public record. Trade shows the asymmetry. A “new joint arrangement” and a two-month truce extension paper over May’s blueprint: a Board of Trade framework with US$30 billion in reciprocal tariff cuts in principle, Chinese commitments to buy US soybeans and over US$17 billion of farm products annually, as well as at least 200 Boeing aircraft on commercial terms – none of it fresh. What has changed is leverage: China controls about 70 per cent of the world’s rare earth mining and 90 per cent of both the refining and separation as well as the magnet output. Last year’s export curbs and supply shocks explain why Trump made no new tariff threats. Trade stability is thus a Beijing-imposed limit on American coercion. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the weakest point. Xi insists on “human control” and a people‑centred approach; Trump pushes for “superintelligence” deregulation. An AI dialogue has been set up and a notification mechanism proposed by the US. The state dinner mirrored the gap: several CEOs from top US tech firms (Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft) attended but none from a Chinese AI company. Anthropic was conspicuously absent. China’s takeaway: talk to limit risk, but never let a divided US industry dictate AI governance. The Taiwan issue followed the same pattern: maximum Chinese red-line language, minimum US concession. Xi urged Trump to oppose independence and handle the issue prudently. Washington has not formally moved from “does not support independence” to “oppose”, and that gap is deliberate. An US$11.1 billion arms package to Taiwan was approved in December while a further record US$14 billion sale in the pipeline has been held off; Trump called it a “very good negotiating chip”. Beijing treats any major arms sale to Taiwan as a provocation; Taipei’s push to lift defence spending to 5 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030 does not alter the calculus. Xi’s call for regular military dialogue and crisis communication channels is the only concrete safeguard, and even that lacks a named working mechanism. On Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, the summit produced symbolism, not settlement. Trump wants China, as Tehran’s largest trading partner, to pressure Iran and help reopen the strait; Xi reportedly offered support for a return to the short-lived June US-Iran deal, with no breakthrough and no communique language on navigation. The Chinese readout briefly referred to “the situation in the Middle East”, reflecting Beijing’s preference to broker without joining a US-Israeli war that began in February and has kept energy markets tense since. It is a useful model for the rest of the Global South: China sells restraint and diplomatic cover without assuming military risk. None of this impressed Washington’s critics. Senator Jeanne Shaheen and 18 Democrats called it “pageantry over purpose”; former State Department official Danny Russel dismissed it as “diplotainment” and noted: “Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths.” Republicans, including Roger Wicker, objected to honouring the Communist Party leadership; Rand Paul countered that “talk more, war less” is the point. The sniping confirms why a staged, low-substance summit suits Beijing: it lowers the chance of abrupt escalation while US politics fights over whether anything was conceded. Soft power supplied the narrative glue. Beyond the red-decorated East Room and nod to the Nixon “Toast to Peace”, both sides traded historical props – mentions of the second world war, ping-pong diplomacy and pandas, a bald eagle sculpture – to manufacture a sense of inevitability about the relationship. Friday’s Red Room tea and National Archives tour added a historic touch. None of it commits either side, but it buys political cover: Trump gets a photo opportunity; Xi gets a civil farewell that masks the absence of a grand bargain. Read together, the visit shows a relationship stabilised on Chinese terms. Washington gets photographs, CEO access to Xi and a tariff truce that spares consumers before the midterm elections; Beijing gets recognition of bounded competition, a seat at the AI table and freedom to resist US demands on Taiwan, Iran and chip sovereignty. Managed rivalry is not peace; it is a rules-based pause with Beijing largely writing the rules. The real test will be whether Washington can live with a settlement it did not design.

title: Russian drones kill 5 across Ukraine, including market outside Kyiv
description: Zelensky accuses Moscow of terrorism after strikes hit Kyiv outskirts, Sumy and Kharkiv infrastructure.
content: Russian drones set ablaze a market outside the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Sunday, killing two people, while three others died in strikes by Moscow’s forces in different regions and Kyiv itself also came under attack, ‌local officials said. Ukrainian prosecutors said the drone attack hit a market in Sofiiska Borshchahivka on the western outskirts of Kyiv, killing two people and injuring about 10. Pictures posted online showed installations and vehicles on fire, with debris strewn on the ground. In the capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said nine people were injured, including a child. Six of the injured were being treated in hospital. Russian forces have long staged intensive attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, mostly at night. In recent weeks, they have ⁠launched strikes almost continuously throughout the day. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decried the latest attacks, saying the civilian targets made the acts unquestionably “terrorism”. “Russia has ‌no military objective whatsoever in doing this,” Zelensky wrote in a post on social media. “It is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society.” In the northern city of ‌Sumy, a frequent Russian target near the border, three glide bombs struck near a family support centre, killing two ⁠people, regional governor Oleh ⁠Hryhorov wrote on Telegram. Russia has long said it intends to turn areas of the Sumy region into a buffer zone. In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city in the northeast and another ‌frequent target, a drone struck a car, killing the driver, prosecutors said. Zelensky said Russia had deployed 277 attack drones of various types since Saturday, 155 of them of ‌the jet-powered variety ‌Moscow has recently used more readily as they fly higher and are difficult to intercept. He said the targets in Kyiv ‌had included a building used as a residence by the Saudi Arabian ambassador. Klitschko said on Telegram that a ⁠drone had struck a block of flats, triggering a fire in an eastern suburb and wounding one person. Emergency crews extinguished the blaze. He ⁠later said a drone had hit another block of flats in a central district, with emergency services investigating possible casualties at the site. Drones had earlier hit areas near a kindergarten and a playground in two districts, Klitschko said, and other areas ‌in the city also suffered damage. Ukraine’s largest ‌mobile service provider told the Interfax Ukraine news agency that Russian forces had hit its headquarters in continued strikes on Ukrainian data centres and communications infrastructure. There were no casualties. Russia’s defence ministry issued statements saying its forces had struck two data centres in Kyiv, a logistics hub in Odesa, as well as two cargo vessels headed for Odesa. Both sides in the war deny targeting civilians.

title: Netanyahu makes unannounced visit to UAE, meets Gulf state’s president
description: Reported visit comes with the Middle East still gripped by the Israel-US war launched against Iran in February.
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠visited Abu Dhabi and met with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan on Sunday, a senior Israeli official told Reuters. There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office and the UAE’s foreign ministry. Israeli TV channels 12 and KAN, as well as newspapers Haaretz and The Jerusalem Post, also reported that Netanyahu undertook a one-day visit to the UAE to meet Mohamed. The visit comes ‌after Haaretz this month reported that Mohamed had warned Netanyahu a week and a half before October 7, 2023 that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel. The warning was not passed to Israeli intelligence agencies or the military, Haaretz reported. Netanyahu, who has denied the report and ⁠threatened legal action against the newspaper, is facing a tough reelection campaign. Opposition leaders have accused ‌the prime minister of bearing responsibility for security failures that preceded Hamas’ October 7 attack. The UAE has declined to comment on the ‌Haaretz report but has said that UAE and Israel have maintained “open and ⁠direct lines of communication” ⁠since establishing diplomatic relations in 2020. A UAE source previously told Reuters that the UAE discusses security matters ‌with countries through the “relevant entities”, but not “at the level of national leaders”. Earlier this year, the UAE denied that ‌Mohamed ‌met with Netanyahu after the Israeli prime minister’s office said in May that ‌Netanyahu had “secretly visited” the Gulf country and met with the president. A source familiar with ⁠the meeting said at the time that Netanyahu and Mohamed met in Al-Ain, ⁠an oasis city in Abu Dhabi along the country’s border with Oman, on March 26. The outreach in the Gulf comes as Israel faces deepening diplomatic rifts with European allies over West Bank settlement policies. On Sunday, Israel revoked the diplomatic status of Dutch envoys to the Palestinian Authority following new Dutch settlement import bans, weeks after ordering the closure of Britain’s East Jerusalem consulate over similar trade restrictions. The Dutch ban followed coordinated action by 12 Western countries, including Britain and France, to sanction goods from Israeli settlements at the start of the month. Despite those Western headwinds and the ongoing regional war with Iran, the UAE has maintained its relationship with Israel under the 2020 Abraham Accords, viewing the partnership as a critical lever for regional influence and a direct line to Washington. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Trump says he expects new Iran talks after rejecting proposal
description: US president muses about resuming full-scale strikes, saying Iran ‘overplayed their hand’.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran. Iranian officials brought with them to the UN General Assembly in New York a plan for a seven-day truce followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel. Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume. “They want to make a deal but it is not the deal that I want to make,” Trump told Axios. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago.” “They overplayed their hand,” Trump said, in the interview published on Sunday. Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday. On Sunday, Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the Middle East war locked in a stalemate while fighting rages in Yemen. Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world’s energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the US and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran. Iran’s plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart. That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade. “Our conditions are clear and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said on Sunday, according to state broadcaster IRIB. “We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.” Washington’s ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table. “This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk,” he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday. “I think it’s kind of common sense that the president doesn’t have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago.” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, meanwhile, said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz. It said the underwater vehicle was being used “for espionage purposes”, adding that it was “now in the hands of the force’s specialists for data recovery”. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran’s nuclear programme. But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway. Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons. Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation. Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: “The choice now rests with the United States”. Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: “We will not cease punishing the US until Iran’s seven conditions are met”. Mohebi had told Agence France-Presse in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.

title: Shooting at Detroit after-hours strip club leaves 3 dead, 4 injured
description: Police chief says early morning fight led to gunfire at residential location known to law enforcement.
content: Three people were killed and four more were injured when an argument led to gunfire at an after-hours strip club Sunday morning in Detroit, officials said. Police responding to the 7.21am shooting on a largely residential street found three men who had been fatally shot, Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison told reporters at a news conference. Four more people – two men and two women – were taken in private cars to area hospitals. None are thought to have life-threatening injuries. All the victims are thought to be in their 20s and 30s, Bettison said. “A fight occurred, an altercation occurred, and as a result individuals decided to settle it with gun violence,” he said. “This address is not new to the Detroit Police Department,” he said, noting police had seven calls to the location this year. He said the department had leads but wouldn’t discuss them any further. “This was an after-hours location,” he said of the shooting scene. “Imagine a strip club … I’ll leave it at that.” Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield urged anyone with information to contact authorities. “We know that we need more people to speak up to bring justice to the situation,” she said at the news conference. “It’s heartbreaking and our community should not suffer from this type of violence.” Earlier Sunday, a shooting broke out at a birthday party at a park in Macon, Georgia, leaving 12 teens with gunshot wounds, Bibb County Sheriff David Davis said during a news conference. Two of the injured were in critical condition, while the others were stable. There were no immediate arrests, but Davis said investigators had several persons of interest.

title: Britain’s Labour Party launches annual conference buoyed by Burnham
description: New British leader faces pressure to deliver concrete plans as party enters Liverpool gathering ahead in opinion polls.
content: Britain’s ruling Labour Party on Sunday launched its first annual conference under Andy Burnham’s leadership, buoyed by his debut as prime minister as he pledged to take the tough decisions needed to tackle looming challenges. The former mayor of Manchester has injected new life into the centre-left party since MPs propelled him into Downing Street in July after ending Keir Starmer’s two-year premiership. In an interview from the conference in northwestern Liverpool, Burnham pledged to show in his speech on Tuesday that he will not shy away from taking hard actions. Burnham told the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) that people would “see that I am prepared to take those types of decisions because I won’t do what the previous Conservative government did and take risks with the economy that actually are still hurting us right now”. Burnham’s higher personal approval ratings, coupled with difficulties facing rival hard-right Reform UK, have helped Labour enter the conference ahead in some opinion polls. That is a sharp turnaround from the start of 2026. As the conference got underway, police arrested about 50 people among about 250 who staged a protest in support of a banned group Palestine Action. The prime minister was also being kept informed about an incident in southwestern England near an airbase used by the US Air Force. An army bomb disposal team was on the scene and several men had been arrested on suspicion of explosives offences, police said.
