Last year’s Labour conference was overshadowed by talk that Starmer’s days were numbered, while the 2024 edition followed criticism of several government policy decisions made soon after the party won that year’s election. Since becoming prime minister on July 20, just weeks after returning to parliament following a nine-year absence, Burnham has sought to give voters some “breathing space” from cost-of-living pressures exacerbated by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. He has cut electricity bills, capped bus fares and reduced business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues. Those measures, together with Burnham’s active social-media presence, have helped strengthen his public image. Burnham has also set up a “No. 10 North” office in Manchester as part of his plans to spur GDP by devolving more powers to cities and regions. Surveys suggest that almost half of Britons view him favourably. But he has so far said little about how he plans to fulfil pledges to end rough sleeping by homeless people, reform a ballooning welfare bill, fund a new social care service, reindustrialise the country and raise defence spending. Former minister Tony McNulty served alongside Burnham in Labour governments of the early 2000s. He told Agence France-Presse the prime minister had to start fleshing out a promised “10-year plan for Britain” during his keynote speech at the conference on Tuesday. “Much of it might still be broad brushstrokes but he needs to start the process of putting meat on the bone. “It needs to go beyond the TikTok and good vibes stuff,” he said. Labour MP Alex Sobel told Agence France-Presse he wanted to hear “what we’ll do to support” young people in terms of opportunities. Some 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 are not in employment, training or education, statistics show. Burnham has limited financial flexibility because of Labour’s election-winning manifesto commitments to not raise income tax, national insurance contributions or value-added tax. It makes finance minister John Healey’s first budget on October 28 a difficult one. Burnham has said he will use his speech to “say further about the direction I want to take the country”. “Let’s focus on where we are and let’s not get into a position where we’ve just got a narrative of doom about all of this,” he told the BBC. He said he was “very conscious” of the “febrile state of the global economy”. But the “fundamentals” of the British economy had been “moving in the right direction”, until the Middle East war broke out, he argued. A YouGov poll published on Thursday put support for Labour at 24 per cent and Reform on 22 per cent, a dramatic turnaround from last year when Nigel Farage’s anti-immigrant group enjoyed double-digit leads. If an election were held tomorrow, Labour would lose its majority but would probably be able to lead a progressive coalition, the survey suggested. “There’s still an underlying anxiety about how long … [Labour’s] bounce will last given the very tricky fiscal situation the government is in,” political scientist Tim Bale said.

title: Swiss reject push to toughen neutrality amid debate over Russia
description: Initiative dubbed ‘pro-Russian’ by critics fails as voters back government’s flexible diplomatic approach.
content: Swiss voters on Sunday roundly rejected a proposal to tighten their country’s neutrality, final results showed, dismissing an initiative championed by the hard-right and dubbed “pro-Russian” by opponents. While the Swiss widely embrace their neutrality, the initiative to enshrine a strict definition into the constitution exposed deep disagreement over what that neutrality entails. The proposal was rejected by 70.1 per cent of voters, according to the final results. “This result is not a vote against neutrality,” Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis told journalists in Bern as the figures were announced. “Switzerland was neutral yesterday, it will be neutral today and it will remain neutral,” he said. Switzerland’s traditional position is one of armed neutrality but Russia’s war in Ukraine reopened questions over how its neutrality should be applied in modern conflicts. Concerned over Bern’s decision to back the European Union’s economic pressure on Russia, the pro-sovereignty Pro Switzerland organisation collected enough signatures to trigger a referendum under the country’s direct democracy system on better anchoring neutrality in its constitution. The proposal was opposed by the government, parliament and most major political parties. Opinion polls had also suggested that most voters would also reject it. Moscow, which has slammed Switzerland for joining EU sanctions and accused Bern of abandoning its neutrality, praised the initiative - dubbed “pro-Russian” by some critics. The proposal called for the constitution to guarantee that Swiss neutrality is “armed and perpetual”. It would have prevented Switzerland, whose neutrality dates back to 1516, from pursuing closer ties with Nato, ruling out any military alliance except in the event of an attack on the country. It would have also prohibited the imposition of sanctions unless called for by the United Nations. All sides in the debate argued they wanted to maintain Switzerland’s neutrality. Both the Swiss government and parliament objected that the proposal was too rigid and would limit the country’s room for manoeuvre at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions. “Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility,” Cassis said during a recent televised debate. While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including to Ukraine, he stressed that “neutrality does not mean indifference”. The country, he said, would “not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace”. The only political party backing the initiative was the country’s largest, the hard-right Swiss People’s Party (SVP). “Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue,” SVP vice-president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. “To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality.”

title: Man charged over hidden cameras found in gym as police probe number of victims
description: Construction site foreman, 34, to appear at Sha Tin Court on Monday, after police identify suspect in recovered footage.
content: A 34-year-old man has been charged in connection with the installation of three suspected pinhole cameras found in changing rooms at a popular Hong Kong fitness chain, with investigators still reviewing the number of victims affected. The arrest on Sunday came a day after police launched an investigation into the suspected voyeurism case at the 24/7 Fitness branch on Lek Yuen Street. A police spokesman said on the same day that officers had arrested the suspect, a local man, in Sha Tin and he remained in custody as investigations continued. Police identified the suspect as a 34-year-old construction site foreman who was arrested at his home in Sha Tin on Sunday after officers analysed footage recovered from the devices. In an update on Monday, authorities said the man had been charged with a count of voyeurism and was due to appear at Sha Tin Court the next day. Chief Inspector Ng Yuk-pui of Sha Tin police district said investigators had recovered multiple video clips filmed between September 23 and 25. Officers also seized two desktop computers and a laptop computer, among other items, during a search of the suspect’s home. No voyeuristic footage had been found online so far, and there was no evidence to suggest the recordings were intended for sale, Ng said. She added that reviewing the footage would take time and that the number of victims was still under investigation, only saying there were “a certain number”. Ng did not disclose the number of videos recovered. In a statement on Sunday night, 24/7 Fitness said it had zero tolerance for any acts that infringed upon members’ privacy and had immediately suspended the membership of the individual involved. The company, which is the largest gym chain in the city, again apologised to affected members and all customers. It added that it had introduced new procedures and stepped up inspections across all branches, including using new technological devices, and targeted checks of concealed areas in bathrooms, changing rooms and toilets to ensure members could use its facilities in a safe and secure environment. The case was reported by a 38-year-old female employee of the fitness centre after a customer spotted a reflection near the ceiling of a changing room and alerted staff. Officers were alerted on Friday after a suspected pinhole camera was found attached with black tape to the false ceiling of a changing room in the fitness centre. Ng said the gym had one male and two female toilets and four individual changing rooms that could be used by men and women. Each room had a separate shower area and changing space, she added. The chief inspector said officers had conducted a thorough search of all toilets and changing rooms after receiving the report and found three pinhole cameras and three 12GB memory cards in three of the four individual changing rooms. Police have sent the devices for digital forensic examination and recovered video footage from the memory cards, enabling investigators to quickly identify the suspect. The force said the devices were bought from a major mainland Chinese online shopping platform. The cameras are small in size and consist of a lens connected to an electronic circuit board and battery. They are also equipped with a motion-activated function, allowing them to begin recording automatically when someone enters the room. Police said the cameras had been hidden inside the false ceiling above the changing areas. The case came to light after a male gym member posted a video online saying he had noticed an unusually wide seam in the false ceiling. According to the video, the man lifted a ceiling panel and found what appeared to be a pinhole camera secured with black tape. He said the discovery was immediately reported to police. The Sha Tin district investigation team is handling the case. Voyeurism carries a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment under Hong Kong law.

title: Pereira makes history with stunning 200m victory, Yan blows away field at Asian Games
description: Singaporean sprinter ‘brings fighting spirit’ to win gold, while China’s 18-year old javelin thrower only needs one attempt to set Games record.
content: Most of Sunday’s athletics events at the Asian Games were seen by many as background noise to the women’s javelin clash between China sensation Yan Ziyi and Japan’s Haruka Kitaguchi, although don’t dare suggest that to Singapore’s Shanti Pereira. While the much-anticipated throwing competition was ultimately as damp as the rain that blanketed Nagoya for much of the day, Pereira’s breathless victory in the women’s 200m was everything sprinting is supposed to be. The 30-year-old’s successful defence of the crown she won in Hangzhou also raced her into the history books, as the first woman to win the event twice at the continental Games. Pereira was pushed all the way to the line by Chinese rival Chen Yujie, who pipped her to gold in the 100m on Friday. Pereira won the longer race with a season-best 22.78 seconds, while Chen crossed the finish line in 22.93. India’s Harita Bhadra took bronze in 23.20. “On my God, I knew I could do it,” an emotional Pereira said. “I believe every muscle, every fibre in my body knew that I could come back. I channelled it as much as I could. I was like, ‘no – today is my day’. “I am so emotional because I wanted it so badly. For so many years, every time you see Singapore in a final, it’s me. Everyone else is different. I constantly show up. I constantly bring all my fighting spirit into every race I do. “It was a reflection of my journey and how far I have come to be where I am.” The sprint battle stood in stark contrast to the one between Yan and Kitaguchi, which had been given a little bit of added spice by the Paris Olympic champion’s victory at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship two weeks ago. As it was, Yan, who has been dominant this season, needed to throw just once to win gold at Paloma Mizuho Stadium. The 18-year-old’s opening attempt of 70.46 metres was not just a Games record, but the only thing she had to do all evening. “I didn’t expect that,” Yan said. “My plan was to make my first two throws count, but I didn’t expect to reach that distance on my very first throw.” A challenge never materialised, and Kitaguchi said she was “very upset about the result.” The 28-year-old fell woefully short with her first two attempts, hitting 56.48 and 57.61. It wasn’t until her sixth and final go of 62.70 that she broke clear of the chasing pack to secure silver. Bronze went to her compatriot Sae Takemoto, who put down a season’s best 62.15 with her final throw. Still, at least Yan represents growth in her sport. It is difficult to see one in the women’s long jump in Asia, which, like the organisation this year, has only got worse since the previous Games in Hangzhou in 2023. China’s Huang Yingying claimed gold with a leap of 6.55m, which three years ago would have secured bronze. The winning distance then of 6.73m from compatriot Xiong Shiqi was not good enough to qualify for the Paris Olympics, and the 6.53m that earned India’s Ancy Sojan silver, nor the 6.46m that gave Tan Mengyi bronze will be this time around. “My first jump was not good – just 6.14,” Huang said. “But at the same time, my opponents did not perform well.” Hong Kong had two athletes in the women’s long jump, Tiffany Yue Nga-yan and Jia Wai-yin. In Hangzhou, Yue claimed the city’s first Asian Games medal in a field event with a leap of 6.50, she had not touched that distance before and has not since. On Sunday, Yue managed just 6.05, the first time she has broken six metres this year. Jia’s 5.79 was some way short of her season best of 6.23.

title: Afghanistan says 28 dead fighters came from Pakistan as Islamabad denies ties
description: Pakistan’s information ministry rejected all allegations that its security forces or intelligence agencies are involved in Afghanistan at all.
content: Afghanistan’s defence ministry said on Sunday its forces had killed 28 fighters and wounded 32 in the eastern province of Nuristan after a group it said included Islamic State militants travelled from Pakistan. The ministry alleged Pakistani militias ‌had supported the fighters and that most of them were former Afghan government security personnel. Pakistan’s information ministry rejected the allegations, describing them as “frivolous, baseless and devoid of any truth” in a post on social media. The ministry denied that its security forces or intelligence agencies were involved in clashes in Nuristan, had recruited or trained former Afghan security personnel, or had facilitated Islamic State ⁠or other militant groups in Afghanistan. Kabul’s claim that Pakistani intelligence trained and sent former Afghan security personnel across ‌the border is a direct allegation of state involvement in an armed incursion. It comes less than a week after Pakistan launched air strikes inside Afghanistan, saying it ‌had targeted militants. Reuters could not independently verify the ministry’s account or its casualty figures. Pakistan has ⁠repeatedly accused Afghanistan ⁠of sheltering fighters who attack its territory, a charge Kabul denies. Afghanistan’s defence ministry said the group crossed into Kamdesh, a district of ‌Nuristan near the Pakistani border, on Saturday with the intention of carrying out attacks. Afghan forces launched an operation and the surviving ‌fighters fled back ‌across the border towards Pakistani militia positions, it said. It alleged that Pakistani armed personnel and militia members ‌had coordinated with the fighters but withdrew when fighting began. The ministry also accused Pakistani intelligence of ⁠taking former Afghan security personnel to Pakistan under the pretext of offering them assistance, training them and ⁠sending them towards Nuristan. Pakistan’s information ministry said Afghanistan had produced no evidence of Pakistani involvement. It disputed a video circulating on social media that it said was being used to support the ‌allegations, describing the footage ‌as staged. The video could not be independently verified. The incident follows Pakistani air strikes in Afghanistan on September 21 that Islamabad said killed 28 militants. Afghan officials said civilians were killed, and the UN mission in Afghanistan confirmed three civilian deaths.

title: UK arrests 5 on suspicion of terror plot near airbase used by US forces
description: Police investigate potential link to a foreign state after three suspicious vehicles prompt evacuations outside RAF Fairford.
content: UK police said that five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an airbase used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three vehicles. London’s Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12.45am related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be travelling towards RAF Fairford, a UK-owned base that is operated by the US under an agreement dating back to the Cold War. A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a “terror threat” alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking a road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas. She told the PA news agency she found it “astonishing” it had been effectively down to a “plucky amateur” spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm. The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the UK, with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50 per cent in the six months to December 2025. Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iranian missile sites under an agreement with former British prime minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the US and Israel on February 28. Authorities are investigating a link between the Fairford arrests and Iran as one possibility. Iran has previously indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target. US President Donald Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests. “It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great,” he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. “We had them under view for a long time and we got them.” The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act in the Whelford area, which backs onto RAF Fairford, which hosts the headquarters of the US Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron. Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot roaming between three white trucks. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around. The robot appeared to be working towards getting access to the third truck. Police gave no details as to the nationality of those arrested. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests, without an extension application. “We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” said Vicki Evans, the Met’s counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator. Evans said a 400-metre cordon has been put in place around the three vehicles that raised suspicion while the army conducts examinations. As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated while these examinations take place. Some have been taken to a nearby recreation centre. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he knew the incident would be “deeply concerning” for many. In a post on social media, Burnham thanked police and the armed forces for their response and said he was grateful to the residents who have been evacuated from their homes “while precautionary checks are carried out”. He urged people “not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts”. The defence secretaries of the US and the UK, Pete Hegseth and Wes Streeting, have also spoken about the incident. British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the UK and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Hong Kong police hunt for man who stole HK$10,000 from claw machines using key
description: Store owner files police report after seeing thief in CCTV footage, with officers investigating how man obtained key.
content: Hong Kong police are searching for a man who used a key to steal about HK$10,000 (US$1,275) from four claw machines’ deposit boxes at a store on Sunday. The force said that the store owner, a 46-year-old man surnamed Cheung, had filed a police report at around 11.10am after witnessing the theft via surveillance cameras in the shop at 159 Tai Kok Tsui Road. Cheung said he saw a man in his thirties use a key to open deposit boxes in four claw machines and make off with the money. Police are currently working to identify the man and determine how he came into possession of the key. CCTV footage circulating online shows a man wearing a black cap, T-shirt and white shorts and shoes entering the unstaffed claw machine shop at around 7.35am and scouting the area. The man, who appears to have a tattoo on his right arm, then pulls out a bunch of keys from his pocket and tries using one of them to open a claw machine’s deposit box. After the first key fails, he tries another and successfully opens the drawer, pulling out the deposit box and pouring all the money into a black bag. He repeats the process for three other claw machines using the same key, but fails to open a fifth one. He subsequently leaves the shop, spending less than 90 seconds inside. The case has been classified as theft and is being handled by Mong Kok police district’s duty investigation team. Last week, police arrested three men suspected of using crowbars to steal popular Jellycat dolls and other plush toys worth about HK$70,000 from a claw machine shop in Tai Wai to resell them.

title: China’s Wang Manyu beats Sun Yingsha in women’s singles table tennis final at Asian Games
description: Men’s doubles players Huang Youzheng and Lin Shidong also claim gold after beating Japan’s Harimoto Tomokazu and Shinozuka Hiroto.
content: China’s Wang Manyu beat compatriot and defending champion Sun Yingsha in the women’s singles final at the Asian Games on Sunday to cement her position as the sport’s new table tennis queen. Wang’s win came days after she displaced Sun at the top of the world rankings. China also enjoyed success in the men’s doubles final, with Huang Youzheng and Lin Shidong beating Japan’s Tomokazu Harimoto and Hiroto Shinozuka 4-2. Wang reclaimed the title she last won at the Jakarta Asian Games in 2018, overcoming Sun 4-2 at the Sky Hall Toyota arena. “This women’s singles final was a good match. Sun Yingsha and I both brought a high level of play to this final,” Wang said. “For us to meet in the gold medal match, I guess you can say that we’ve completed our mission in the women’s singles. “Today, I composed myself mentally pretty well and really went for it. Sun is a player I can learn a lot from, and someone I should challenge on court.” Sun was gracious in defeat and admitted that an earlier injury hampered her training for the Asian Games. “I congratulate Manyu on the result. We both performed well today. If I had taken the sixth game, maybe I could have had a chance to change the outcome,” Sun said. “Still, it’s a fact that I failed to take the initiative today or find a way to get the upper hand. In the first two games, if I had taken one of them and not been 1-3 down in the match … it did get quite hard to close the gap towards the end. “I was injured a while back and my training has not been structured. I was in the process of recovery before the Games. Frankly, before the Games, I wondered if I would be able to complete my mission of competing here.”

title: China’s Zhu Yuanling wins street skateboarding – just the latest teen winner at Asian Games
description: At 15, the women’s street skateboarding champion joins a growing list of medallists still in their teens in Nagoya – but there are concerns.
content: China’s 15-year-old Zhu Yuanling won gold in the women’s street skateboarding competition at the Asian Games on Sunday, the latest in a series of young winners at this edition of the continental multi-sport event. Zhu’s win came a day after Japanese primary school student Yuki Kurihara, 11, demolished opponents three times his age on the way to a historic gold in esports. Earlier in the Games, Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi, 13, became one of the faces of the event with three golds, all in record times. And in another skateboarding final on Friday, Chinese Taipei’s 12-year-old Ku Yong-yan took home silver in the men’s park final. The winner, Japan’s Izuru Nagahara, was a relative veteran at 15. Coming home third after Zhu on Sunday was defending champion Cui Chenxi, who is a year her senior. Held at the Aichi Sky Expo, the final saw the two young Chinese athletes claim medals with total scores of 166.57 and 156.60, respectively, as Japan’s Yumeka Oda took silver. The street final consisted of three run rounds and three best-trick rounds, with the total score calculated by combining the best run score and the best trick score. Zhu, who ranked fifth in the preliminaries, scored above 70 points in two of her runs and led the field with a 79.73 in her third run. As the contest moved to the best-trick section, Oda, who finished first in the preliminaries, executed an event-high 90.75 in the first round to briefly move into first, while Zhu scored 78.96 to fall to second overall. “The trick in my second best-trick round was something I’ve practised for a long time and can land whenever I want, so I didn’t need to be so nervous,” Zhu said after the event. In the second best-trick round, she scored 86.84 to take first place with 166.57 points, holding her lead to the finish. “I’m really amazing, so cool!” an emotional Zhu said after the competition. “Looking back at the whole contest now, I feel a bit stunned – I didn’t expect to win gold.” The victory marked Zhu’s first gold medal in international competition. Born in Guangning, Zhaoqing in 2011, Zhu entered the Guangning County Amateur Sports School at age seven as a trampolinist. In 2021, at age nine, she was selected for the national skateboarding squad through a cross-sport talent programme, becoming the second national skateboarder from Guangning after Zeng Wenhui. Also in the skateboarding was Mazel Paris of the Philippines, who was just nine when she competed at the previous Asian Games. Asked what has changed since Hangzhou in 2023, the 12-year-old replied: “I got taller for sure.” And this week will see another teenage phenomenon enter the fray, when India’s 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi competes in cricket. Abuse concerns But the presence of young children competing on the international stage against adults and under expectations to win for their country comes with a caveat. Kanae Doi, Japan director at Human Rights Watch, said before the Games that “moments of triumph do not come easily. They are built on years of disciplined training, often beginning in childhood”. “At its best, that journey should provide children with the joy of play and competition, along with opportunities for physical, mental and personal growth,” she wrote in the Japan Times. “Many young athletes instead encounter physical, verbal and even sexual abuse in the very environments meant to help them develop.” She said that in Games host Japan, children “frequently experience abuse in sports training within Japanese schools, federations and elite sports programmes”. In 2024, the International Olympic Committee released its consensus statement on youth athletes at the Olympic Games. It noted that 50 per cent of common mental health conditions first emerge before 18. Adolescent athletes are also more susceptible to certain injuries, it stated. Swimmer Yu became the youngest medallist in world championships history last year with bronze at age 12, and is now hotly tipped to make a splash at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. But when it came to reporters swarming around her after races, she looked very much like a teenager. “Interviews are way harder than the race,” she said.

title: As Chinese retirees boost nation’s economy, some hope for greater consumer freedom in society
description: Age bias is an obstacle to the growth of China’s silver economy, researchers say.
content: Even though he was an experienced swimmer and a medical check-up showed he had no condition that made exercise unsafe, 66-year-old Zhao Xin said he was stopped by staff at a local swimming pool from swimming with his grandson because of his age. “The pool’s staff said it wasn’t able to mitigate the risks of exercise for older people, and that if it admitted swimmers over 65, local authorities would penalise it,” Zhao said. “After I retired, I found that many times I want to spend money but am simply not allowed to,” said the former accountant from China’s eastern Zhejiang province. It is these energetic retirees like Zhao who are propping up China’s persistently lacklustre consumption in recent years. From rail travel to purchases of digital devices and cars, spending by China’s older cohort has seen rapid growth recently, research shows. Zhao was born in 1960, during China’s Great Famine, which was followed by a baby boom in the decade after. That cohort is now entering peak retirement age of 60 to 70, bringing enormous consumer momentum, while also putting pressure on pension funds. As a growing group of newly retired people are contributing an increasing share of consumer spending in the slowing Chinese economy, some researchers are calling for less of an age bias in society – as senior citizens deprived of access to social engagement and services because of their age. This is a major obstacle hindering the development of China’s silver economy, which is the “new engine” of future growth, they said. Zhou Hong, an expert at the Shanghai Association for Elderly Care Services and the Senior Care Industry, noted that over 20 million births took place per year during the baby boom, and that the generation was now entering a life stage with leisure time, energy and money to spend. These people represent huge potential to fill off-peak gaps at venues from shopping malls to theatres, he argued, to support China’s overall consumption. Zhou warned that there was a widespread stereotype of older people in society, equating them with “high risk” or “objects of care”. Age bias against senior citizens not only existed when it comes to gym memberships and air travel, he said, but also in employment. In a recruitment annoucement last year, the Shanghai Bar Association’s said it only would accept experts below 60. “This habitual age discrimination not only limits the scope of life for older adults, but also leads to a serious mismatch between supply and demand in the silver [economy],” Zhou said at a forum on the silver economy at NYU Shanghai last week. In the first quarter of this year, older consumers’ spending on digital devices and rail travel grew by more than 200 per cent and more than 500 per cent year-on-year, respectively, Zhou said, quoting data from UnionPay. Big-ticket car purchases by older people, increased by 37 per cent year on year, compared with a 17.4 per cent year-on-year decline in China’s total passenger car retail sales over the same period, he said. China has been grappling with weak domestic consumption in the past couple of years. Latest official data showed that last month, retail sales – a major gauge of consumer spending – grew by 0.4 per cent year on year. To take better advantage of older talent and ease pension pressure, authorities have been gradually raising the statutory retirement age as the population ages. Starting in 2025, the retirement age for men rose from 60 to 63, from 55 to 58 for women in white-collar jobs and from 50 to 55 for those in blue-collar work. Despite that, Chinese retirees remain some of the world’s youngest, with some scholars arguing that staying active and engaged in society was a beneficial way to age. A healthier older population could not only ease a country’s medical burden, but also free up family members from elder care tasks and improve the relatives’ labour market participation, said Yang Wei, director of the Institute of Gerontology at King’s College London. “Investing in services for older people doesn’t necessarily mean spending money or wasting it. To a large extent, it may save us money and even lead to a more rational allocation of resources,” she said at the NYU Shanghai event last week. Long-term improvement in the functional capacity of older individuals could lead to a 0.2 per cent growth in global GDP, her research found. Zhao, the Zhejiang retiree, said he and others his age could remain active consumers and contributors to society by buying new cars, renovating homes or engaging in travel. “Senior people’s demand is not just about being looked after – they also need a variety of products and services that can support a diverse lifestyle,” he said.

title: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang touch down in the US under new loan deal
description: Chinese vets and keepers are on hand in Atlanta to help the animals settle into their new home at the city’s zoo.
content: Two giant pandas have arrived in Atlanta to take up residency at the southern US city’s zoo. The pandas, male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang, left Chengdu in China’s southwest on Sunday, within days of Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapping up his three-day state visit to the United States. During the visit, Xi said the pandas would arrive “in a few days”. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, whose names mean peace and double blessings, arrived at Atlanta International Airport on a chartered flight, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Chinese zookeepers and veterinarians had already gone to the US to help the pandas undergo training and settle into their new home at Zoo Atlanta, according to the report. CCTV reported that Ping Ping had large dark eye patches and was good at climbing trees, and Fu Shuang had a tuft of white fur on her head and liked to search for food. The protected animals are on loan as part of a 10-year conservation agreement signed between the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association in April. The zoo previously had pandas from 1999 to 2024 and over that time the loaned panda pair Lun Lun and Yang Yang had seven cubs. The entire panda family has returned to China’s Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. China sends the animals to other countries as a token of goodwill, a strategy that is known as “panda diplomacy”. Any pandas on loan, as well as cubs born abroad, are eventually required to return to China. Through China’s extensive conservation efforts over the years, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s classification of the species was lowered from endangered to vulnerable. The new panda pair were both born at the Chengdu base in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. Ping Ping was born in March 2020, while Fu Shuang was born seven months later. Zoo Atlanta said the new agreement would allow them to “once again be able to have a meaningful impact on the conservation of giant pandas”. Pandas are also on loan to California’s San Diego Zoo and the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington.

title: My Take | How Beijing is neutralising Washington’s sanctions machine
description: As alternative networks like China’s CIPS gain traction, the multilateral pushback is steadily eroding US financial dominance.
content: Last week, the president of the United States stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly and asked aloud whether he should “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”. Donald Trump then turned to Venezuela’s oil and declared: “To the victor belong the spoils, you’ve all heard that …” He spoke as the Iran war neared its eighth month, a week after the UN Human Rights Council found “reasonable grounds to believe” that the US had committed war crimes. In the same speech, Trump said the United States would not join global regulation of AI and urged countries to abandon the International Criminal Court. Elsewhere this month, the picture looked very different. In Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, all 10 member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) gathered to mark its 25th anniversary. The bloc began in 2001 as a club of six. This year’s summit produced 27 documents alongside the Bishkek Declaration, which condemned the military strikes on Iranian territory by the US and Israel as violations of international law. The Bishkek summit stopped short of launching the proposed SCO Development Bank, even though the bloc had agreed to create it a year earlier. Days later in New Delhi, the 11 Brics members unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration. The consensus document called for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East and criticised unilateral sanctions not authorised by the UN Security Council. It also took aim at the global trade war without naming the US. The host, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, urged the Global South to become a “rule shaper” rather than simply accept rules set elsewhere. Brics’ emergence as a powerful non-Western bloc, said Allen Carlson, a political scientist and Chinese foreign policy expert at Cornell University, highlights how the balance of global power has changed over the past two decades. “Brics is no longer an incipient power bloc but the core of the emerging international order, with China at its centre … President Trump and his advisers clearly think the world still revolves around Washington, but this no longer holds true,” he said. “This is as much a result of American self-inflicted wounds as of Xi’s skill at home and abroad … But for better or worse, there appears to be a new sheriff in town.” China sits at the centre of this architecture, and its financial pillar is now substantial. The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), launched in 2016 over Washington’s objections, has grown to 111 approved members. In its first decade, it approved nearly US$70 billion for 361 projects across 40 member states. Its members include every AAA-rated sovereign except Liechtenstein, as well as 17 of the G20 countries. The Iran war has also tested China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which reported that its daily average transaction volume reached US$134 billion in March. Iran has charged ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz and accepted payment either in yuan, routed through the Bank of Kunlun via CIPS and outside Swift, or in cryptocurrency. Such channels undermine a pillar of dollar dominance: the power of financial sanctions. Other middle powers are hedging. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said his country would consider full SCO membership while keeping its Nato and Western ties. United Arab Emirates officials have reportedly said they may need to use the renminbi for oil payments. As the economist Paul Krugman has observed, the Gulf states’ actions show that even US allies are now considering the Chinese payment system. The dollar remains dominant, but the threat of US sanctions loses force once a workable alternative exists This is less a story of Beijing’s pull than of Washington’s push. The dollar remains dominant, but the threat of US sanctions loses force once a workable alternative exists. In a recent Substack column, Krugman argues that the rise of alternative payment systems, sharply accelerated by the Iran war, has seriously damaged the dollar’s supremacy as the foremost instrument of America’s global financial power. What has been lost is a non-military tool of coercion: the power to punish that the dollar’s dominance in international finance gave the United States. As Krugman explains, transactions in dollars normally pass through US banks, so US authorities can see them and block them. That is how Washington has been able to cut nations off from the world economy, most notably through years of sanctions on Iran. That power, he contends, is now diminished. Trump’s war has shown other nations that they can bypass the dollar-based payments system, largely thanks to China. In Krugman’s reading, the US has suffered a financial failure as well as a military one. Beijing has used the war to strengthen an alternative system that lets governments at odds with America evade both US surveillance and US sanctions. Settling in yuan lets those Washington calls rogue actors slip beneath its financial radar. The war has been an object lesson in the yuan’s value as an alternative currency. It has also boosted CIPS as a rival to Swift, the Belgium-based but effectively US-controlled network that still handles most international transactions. For Hong Kong, the stakes are practical. The city is home to the renminbi Clearing House Automated Transfer System (CHATS), the offshore yuan clearing system linked to CIPS, and has always thrived by connecting rival systems rather than choosing between them. Many commentators like to point out the authoritarian streak that Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping share. But as the two stood together at the White House last week, it was clear they represented opposing principles: multilateralism versus unilateralism, consensus versus domination. The country that insists on leading should not be the one that threatens loudest. We all know which country that is.

title: South African police probe mining feud shooting, 27 dead as elections near
description: Illegal miners live in the area, where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade.
content: South African police on Sunday were hunting the perpetrators of two separate shootings that killed 27 people within hours of each other, in stark reminders of the country’s problem with gun violence. Officials were still establishing the motives for the shootings near Johannesburg and Cape Town, but initial investigations suggested one could be a turf war between illegal miners and the other a business rivalry. Violent crime remains rife in South Africa, despite government efforts to curb one of the highest per capita murder rates in the world. In Wedela township, about 80 km (50 miles) from Johannesburg, 17 people were killed and 15 injured at a tavern when suspects armed with AK-47 rifles opened fire at around 9:30pm on Saturday, according to police. Shooting could be retaliation Many residents were reluctant to speak about the incident, but one said that illegal miners, known locally as Zama zamas from an isiZulu expression for “taking a chance,” live in the area, where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade. The province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters on the scene that one line of inquiry ‌was that the shooting was a “turf war in terms of illegal mining.” There was a shooting at the same tavern about a month ago and Saturday’s shooting could be retaliation for that, he added. No arrests yet Soldiers from the national army and police ‌pathologists had arrived in the township, where two burnt vehicles could be seen. The tavern where the shooting happened had a sign that ⁠read “No weapons allowed” below its trading hours. At ⁠the scene of the shooting in Lwandle, on the outskirts of Cape Town, onlookers had gathered behind police lines but did not want to speak to journalists, saying they feared for their safety. In that ‌incident, gunmen opened fire in a venue selling grilled meat around 2.00am on Sunday, killing 10 people and injuring 11 more. An eyewitness video from the venue shows people dancing and singing in a crowded outdoor ‌area when ‌a burst of shots rings out and screams are heard. A police official there said “a business jealousy might have been the issue,” as there were reports that ‌people had been buying alcohol in cheaper places and going to the venue to drink. No arrests have been made yet and detectives are working to find the gunmen, police ⁠said in statements. “South Africa has a serious illegal firearms problem, and firearms are frequently used by organised criminal groups as well as in gang-related and other violent ⁠crimes,” said crime expert Yusuf Abramjee. Threat to democracy “Every mass shooting should therefore trigger more than an investigation into the immediate perpetrators,” he said. “Authorities need to look at the wider networks behind the violence.” Crime is expected to be a major issue for voters in municipal elections in November, ‌as the ruling African National Congress faces further ‌erosion of voter support. President Cyril Ramaphosa said earlier this year that organised crime had become the biggest threat to South Africa’s democracy, and deployed the army to help police in some areas. A shooting at a house party near Durban on Tuesday night killed 11 people, while a series of women’s bodies found near Johannesburg since July has renewed fear and anger over high rates of femicide.

title: Keep out: why Greenland is the US military’s new eyes in the Arctic on China
description: Defence pact said to be aimed at Beijing and Moscow allows US to build two bases and calls for ‘stronger Nato engagement in the Arctic’.
content: Washington’s proposed military bases and expanded defence presence in Greenland will be akin to a “keep out” sign against potential Arctic military cooperation between Beijing and Moscow, according to analysts. The US, Denmark and Greenland signed a defence deal on Tuesday that allows Washington to build two new military bases on the world’s largest island, while reaffirming Denmark’s sovereignty over it. The deal – which updates and amends a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US – allows expansion and modernisation of the Pituffik US Space Force Base in northwestern Greenland and for additional military bases to be established in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, though they will still require approval from Greenland and Denmark. Narsarsuaq is a settlement located in southern Greenland with a former civilian airport and US airbase that was closed in 1958. Its population is only a few dozen people. A second base is planned for Mestersvig in the northeast of Greenland, which currently hosts the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit. The defence deal also calls for “stronger Nato engagement in the Arctic”, with non-Nato countries barred from establishing their own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland or from having a military presence there. They are also barred from making any investments in Greenland that could threaten US national security. Before the signing ceremony, President Donald Trump said the United States would “immediately begin” the process of developing a large military presence at the appropriate locations. Melting sea ice due to climate change is increasing the strategic importance of the Arctic, where an emerging northern sea route is set to become the shortest shipping lane connecting the Asia-Pacific and Europe. Situated between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean, Greenland has been strategically and geopolitically significant to the US and its Nato allies since the Cold War as a crucial defence against missile attacks and submarine operations. Not only is it located in the middle of the Arctic Ocean that separates North America from Russia, but it is also adjacent to the narrow strip of the northern Atlantic, with Iceland and the United Kingdom on the other side, known as the GIUK Gap – where the Russian navy could advance to the wider Atlantic Ocean. Marc Lanteigne, a professor at the Arctic University of Norway in Tromso, noted that not only does the new agreement allow for a larger US military presence in Greenland, but it also “calls for an expanded Nato presence”. “The stipulations that no non-Nato member country could establish any sort of military installations in Greenland, and … should be permitted to exercise control over investments seen as strategically sensitive, are very much directed at China and Russia,” Lanteigne said. While many of the elements of the deal were already enshrined in the 1951 Defence Agreement, a key concern in the Arctic is the need to monitor the strategic waterway off the Greenlandic coast, according to Lanteigne. “The two new bases would also likely have a political role, underscoring that Washington is quite serious about deterring outside threats or incursions,” he said. Troy Bouffard, an assistant professor of Arctic security at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said the deal focused on “closing the door” before either China or Russia could gain access to the Arctic. “Narsarsuaq restores a southern airfield and logistics node on the western end of the GIUK Gap, while Mestersvig gives the United States an eastern location for domain awareness, sustainment and undersea access towards the Fram Strait,” Bouffard said. “It’s more accurate to think of them as enablers for presence and surveillance.” Despite having no territory in the region, China framed itself as a “near-Arctic state” in a 2018 policy report, while strengthening its ties with Russia in scientific research, resources, shipping routes and infrastructure that could lead to an increased Chinese military presence in the region. In July 2024, Chinese and Russian bombers were spotted jointly operating in airspace off the coast of Alaska for the first time, prompting American F-16 and F-35 fighter jets and Canadian CF-18s to intercept the aircraft. Four Chinese navy ships were also spotted by the US coastguard in the Bering Sea near the Aleutian Islands that month. And in October 2024, China’s coastguard conducted its first joint patrol with its Russian counterpart in the Arctic. Lanteigne said while neither China nor Russia’s armed forces were operating near Greenlandic waters, the US had plans to incorporate Greenland within its proposed Golden Dome anti-missile shield and to deploy unmanned military installations. “At present, Sino-Russian Arctic activity has been far more focused on the Pacific Arctic region, including joint development of the Polar Silk Road between Northeast Asia and Northern Europe,” he said. “However, as the Central Arctic becomes more open to sea traffic due to ice erosion, the need to monitor the Arctic for military activities has been seen by Nato as more pressing,” he continued. “The end result is a ‘keep out’ sign directed at American adversaries.” Bouffard said the strategic benefit of a bigger US military presence in the region would be to “reduce opportunities” for China and Russia to “exploit surveillance gaps” and give the United States and its allies more warning and better options to respond. “That could make closer China-Russia cooperation harder to translate into military opportunity and advantage in this area,” Bouffard said.

title: GlobalFoundries sees ‘strong’ demand for Chinese optical modules amid data centre boom
description: US contract chipmaker is deepening its presence in the Chinese market, as it carves out a niche serving China’s optical module makers.
content: US contract chipmaker GlobalFoundries sees robust demand for Chinese optical modules amid the data centre construction boom, as the firm expands its presence in China to better serve its domestic clients. Shankaran Janardhanan, senior vice-president of the firm’s photonics and radio frequency division, told the South China Morning Post in an interview that demand in the optical networking module segment was “strong”. The surging appetite for Chinese optical modules – used to transmit data in high-performance data centres – had partly driven the company’s decision to bet heavily on photonics, Janardhanan said at the company’s recent annual tech summit in Shanghai. Chinese optical module makers were now shipping heavily to US hyperscalers as data standards transition rapidly from 100 to 200 gigabits per second per lane, he added. That is opening up new opportunities for GlobalFoundries, which makes speciality semiconductors for data centres, cars and other systems, to carve out a niche serving these Chinese optical module producers. US hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon and Meta Platforms, as well as Chinese tech giants like Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings, are all pushing forward optical connectivity to scale their AI data centres. AI chipmaker Nvidia is also working to develop the ecosystem, integrating silicon photonics into its architectures to overcome traditional electrical bandwidth limits. Alibaba owns the SCMP. While the industry debates whether pluggable modules, near-packaged optics (NPO) or co-packaged optics (CPO) will become the dominant data centre standard, Janardhanan said the major barrier to optical connectivity lay on the manufacturing side. “Whether it’s pluggables, NPO or CPO, being able to manufacture and test optics at scale is the key challenge,” he said. The company has launched solutions in silicon photonics and advanced packaging to address the bottleneck. One of the key products is its silicon photonics co-packaged advanced light engine – or “Scale” – which is designed to enable the mass production of the complex components and to support advanced optical connectivity roll out. China is moving very fast in real-world physical AI deployment Shankaran Janardhanan, GlobalFoundries The firm has operated in China for 12 years and already has deep ties in the country’s automotive industry. Now it is further expanding its Chinese manufacturing footprint as it looks to better serve its domestic clients. Earlier this month, it opened a new office in Guangzhou to deepen a manufacturing partnership with local foundry Zen Semi, focusing on 40-nanometre automotive chips. The deal aimed to transfer technological know-how and build manufacturing capability locally to serve the domestic auto market, Janardhanan said, adding the company would decide on a case-by-case basis whether to pursue further expansion plans. “The partnership provides proof that the model can work,” he said. “We selected a market and technology that China needed, and we will continue to assess opportunities as the market evolves.” He stressed that regionalisation must be balanced with global supply chain resilience. “In the semiconductor industry, I don’t think there is any single region that is able to independently cover the entire value chain,” he said, highlighting the company’s manufacturing facilities spread across the United States, Europe and Asia as a core competitive advantage. Victor Hu, GlobalFoundries’ China president, echoed this during a media briefing, noting that the new Guangzhou office aimed to “further pull manufacturing capabilities closer to clients”. Looking beyond the data centre boom, Janardhanan said that physical AI – a sector that includes humanoid robotics, autonomous vehicles and smart devices – could soon become a very large market. “China is moving very fast in real-world physical AI deployment,” Janardhanan said. “We are combining our semiconductor technologies with processor IP and software capabilities to evolve into a more holistic technology partner as this ecosystem rapidly unfolds.”

title: 3 hikers fall ill on Hong Kong trails as temperatures top 33 degrees
description: Two men in separate incidents were suspected of having heatstroke, while rescuers helped a third hiker who developed dizziness.
content: At least three hikers fell ill on countryside trails as temperatures in parts of Hong Kong climbed to a sweltering 33 degrees Celsius (91 Fahrenheit) on Sunday. A 25-year-old visitor was suspected of suffering from heatstroke while he hiked with friends on the popular High Island Reservoir East Dam-Po Pin Chau hiking route in Sai Kung at about noon. A government helicopter airlifted him to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai for treatment. The route is one of Hong Kong’s best-known hiking trails, attracting large numbers of visitors seeking views of the Unesco-listed volcanic rock formations and the dramatic sea stacks of Po Pin Chau. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department said that during the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival and weekend period, an average of 2,360 people per day booked visits to the Po Pin Chau route, while actual attendance averaged about 1,170 visitors daily, or around half of the reservations. The department said operations were generally smooth despite peak crowds between 10am and 2pm, with no serious congestion reported on the trail or the Po Pin Chau viewing platform. On the route at about 1.30pm on Sunday, a group comprising a 57-year-old foreign man and two women sought help after he developed dizziness. Rescuers helped him down the trail. He declined further medical treatment. Earlier, at 1.01pm, police received a report from a man hiking on the Plover Cove Reservoir Country Trail in Tai Po, saying he felt unwell and suspected that he was suffering from heatstroke. Rescue personnel later airlifted him to safety by helicopter. The Hong Kong Observatory issued a “very hot weather warning” at 6.45am on both Saturday, a public holiday following the Mid-Autumn Festival, and Sunday. By around midday on Sunday, temperatures in Sai Kung and Tai Po had risen to around 33 degrees.

title: The hidden risks of using traditional Chinese medicine with Western prescriptions
description: Some plants and procedures common in Chinese medicine can affect Western medicines such as blood thinners and depression drugs.
content: In the second instalment of a four-part Health Matters series on traditional Chinese medicine, Aidyn Fitzpatrick investigates the drug-interaction risks of combining Chinese remedies with Western medicine, and how Hongkongers can protect themselves from avoidable complications. An elderly woman with a mechanical heart valve was taking warfarin, a blood thinner to prevent and treat blood clots, when she began using the Chinese herb danshen, often marketed for “blood circulation”. Her blood lost its ability to clot normally, resulting in severe bleeding complications. The case, which Dr Raymond Wong Siu-ming encountered as a consultant at the Prince of Wales Hospital’s Poison Treatment Centre and a lead expert with the Integrated Chinese-Western Medicine Treatment Safety Centre, illustrates an increasingly common blind spot: Chinese medicine and Western prescription drugs are often used together, but patients may not always know the impact of the combination. For many Hongkongers, Chinese medicine is not an alternative so much as part of everyday life: a chrysanthemum tea, a bowl of tonic soup, a session of cupping, a proprietary pill bought from a pharmacy. The crucial distinction is not whether something is “natural”, but whether it is used as food, symptom relief or as a concentrated treatment alongside medicines that have their own powerful effects. “Just because a product can be bought over the counter does not mean it is automatically safer,” says Dr Phoebe Zhou, senior research fellow at the NICM Health Research Institute at Western Sydney University in Australia. “The level of risk depends on the product, its ingredients, how much is taken, how long it is used and the individual person.” This is important for people taking multiple medicines or those with liver or kidney problems. Zhou also flags medicines for diabetes and cancer, as well as antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs, as categories in which potential interactions have been reported. But she stresses that many reports come from laboratory or animal research; a possible interaction is not necessarily proven in people. The underlying mechanics are not unique to Chinese herbs. Popular Western supplements can alter how the body processes prescription drugs, either weakening their efficacy or amplifying side effects. St John’s wort (Hypericum perforatum) is one of the world’s most consumed medicinal plants and is used in both Chinese and Western medicine. In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) – where it is known as guan ye lian qiao in Mandarin and gwun yip lin kiu in Cantonese – it belongs to the group of plants that clarify heat. It is also used to treat infection and inflammation, and is recommended to help manage symptoms of depression and mood disorders. In Western countries, it is primarily used as an herbal remedy and dietary supplement, and is sometimes promoted for menopausal symptoms, anxiety and sleep disorders. This herb, however, speeds up how the liver breaks down medication, reducing the effectiveness of birth control pills, blood thinners, and drugs for depression or organ transplants. Similarly, supplements containing concentrated green-tea extracts, used primarily for weight management, fat loss and antioxidant support, can lower the absorption of certain blood pressure drugs, while goldenseal – a Western supplement for treating colds, respiratory infections, digestive issues, and skin or eye irritations – may reduce the effectiveness of metformin, a widely prescribed diabetes medication. To reiterate, many documented interactions stem from lab or animal studies and may not always manifest the same way in humans. However, for anyone managing diabetes, high blood pressure, depression or cancer, any concentrated herb or extract – whether Eastern or Western – should be treated as an active treatment requiring a professional check, rather than a harmless wellness add-on. When the stakes get higher Familiar remedies are generally less likely to create a serious herb-drug interaction than medicinal-strength products. A mild tea or tonic soup used occasionally is not the same as a raw herb decoction, a concentrated granule or an extract-containing proprietary Chinese medicine. That is not a licence to assume food therapy is risk-free, though. “Herbal medicines are often made up of many different ingredients,” Zhou says. “If a problem occurs, it can be difficult to know which ingredient caused it.” The picture becomes more complicated when a person is taking several medicines, herbs and supplements simultaneously, or uses a product for weeks or months without obvious symptoms. The most dangerous interactions involve drugs with a narrow therapeutic window, particularly anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs used to prevent clots, strokes and heart attacks. The blood thinner warfarin is especially sensitive: small changes can cause dangerous bleeding or leave a patient under-protected from clotting. In TCM, herbs intended to “promote blood circulation and eliminate stasis” are commonly used for symptoms or conditions associated with cardiovascular health. Some may also have antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity. When taken with a prescription blood thinner, their effects can add up. Danshen, or red sage, which is commonly used in Chinese medicine for cardiovascular conditions, is a clear example. A 2015 review of Chinese herbs and warfarin found case reports and clinical evidence suggesting that danshen can increase warfarin’s anticoagulant effect, while also noting that the evidence base is complex and sometimes conflicting. The Hong Kong Hospital Authority’s guidance classifies the danshen-warfarin pairing as moderate risk and recommends avoiding it where possible, Wong says. If concurrent use is unavoidable, the patient should have blood-clotting tests two to three times weekly. He also notes that ginseng may reduce warfarin’s effectiveness, meaning the hazard is not always excessive bleeding – in some combinations, the concern is inadequate anticoagulation and a higher clotting risk. Over-the-counter aspirin requires similar caution. Because it permanently disables platelets for their entire eight- to 10-day lifespan, the risk window for drug interactions is unusually long. Research reviewed by Singapore experts, including Dr Lau Tang Ching, a senior consultant in the Division of Rheumatology and Allergy at National University Hospital, suggests that pairing aspirin with danshen can double the blood-thinning effects and increase bleeding risks, even though much of the evidence remains experimental. Beyond pills and teas Caution should extend beyond what is ingested. External TCM therapies carry distinct physical considerations that require upfront disclosure. While acupuncture is generally low-risk, patients on blood thinners face higher risks of localised bleeding or heavy bruising. Pregnant women must also disclose their condition, as certain acupuncture points are traditionally avoided because they can trigger uterine contractions. Adding electrical stimulation (electroacupuncture) requires extra care: the microcurrents can interfere with cardiac pacemakers. Meanwhile, cupping creates strong suction that breaks capillaries – meaning it should not be treated as a risk-free spa treatment for anyone on anticoagulants or with fragile skin conditions. No matter if a remedy comes as a pill, a tea or a needle, the rule remains identical: disclose every health condition and prescription to your practitioner before starting. A useful safety rule Hong Kong’s Hospital Authority has developed an evidence-based process for Chinese medicines used in its integrated Chinese-Western medicine programme. As of April 2026, it had evaluated 336 Chinese medicines; around 9 per cent were identified as having interactions with certain Western medicines, Wong says. The authority’s guidance uses four risk ratings – high, moderate, low and no reported risk – rather than a simplistic list of “good” and “bad” herbs. It now includes recommendations for 90 herb-drug interaction pairs, ranging from avoiding a combination to monitoring clinical symptoms or laboratory results. That is a helpful model for consumers. A packaged product, a traditional remedy and a prescribed medicine are not inherently incompatible, but they need to be considered together. The most useful step is to tell every doctor what you take. Bring the packet, sachet, bottle or a photograph of loose herbs. Record the product name, ingredients, dose, frequency, when you started it and when any symptoms appeared. This helps a doctor, pharmacist or registered Chinese medicine practitioner assess what may be happening. If unusual symptoms begin after a new herbal product – such as bleeding, severe dizziness, a rash, palpitations, breathlessness or signs of low blood sugar – stop the new product and seek medical advice. Seek urgent care for significant bleeding, severe allergic symptoms or difficulty breathing. The key message is not that TCM and Western medicine must never be used together. It is that the combination should not be improvised. “Tell both of your doctors everything,” Lau says. “They cannot protect you from dangerous interactions if they only see half of the picture.” Safety tips before combining remedies or therapies with prescription medicines Document everything you use: Write down or photograph every product and treatment. That includes prescription medicines, Chinese herbs, Western dietary supplements, teas, granules, pills, topical oils and remedies bought online or overseas. Include the dose, frequency and start date. Treat concentrated extracts differently from food: A mild chrysanthemum tea or bowl of tonic soup is not the same as a raw herb decoction, commercial extract, concentrated granule, or high-dose supplement like St John’s wort or goldenseal. Concentrated remedies carry higher active doses and require a professional check. Flag high-risk medicines before starting anything new: Speak with your doctor, pharmacist, or registered Chinese medicine practitioner before adding an Eastern or Western remedy if you take anticoagulants (like warfarin or aspirin), cardiac drugs, diabetes medication, blood pressure pills, cancer treatments, immunosuppressants or anti-seizure medications. Disclose medical conditions before physical therapies: External treatments carry non-ingested risks. Always notify your practitioner if you are pregnant, wear a cardiac pacemaker or take blood thinners before undergoing acupuncture, electroacupuncture or cupping, as these can trigger contractions, interfere with devices or cause severe bleeding and bruising. Do not rely on “natural” claims: An over-the-counter proprietary medicine or herbal supplement may be natural and legally sold, but that does not guarantee it is safe for your specific condition or compatible with your prescription drugs. Act immediately on warning signs: Stop any newly started product and seek medical advice if you develop unexpected symptoms. Seek urgent care for unexplained bleeding, black stool, blood in urine, sudden severe headache, chest pain, difficulty breathing or severe dizziness. Never stop a prescribed medication without medical guidance. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Bangkok flood warnings ‘came too late’ Thais say, worst flood in 15 years
description: Nearly 4,900 people have been evacuated to shelters, with around 52,000 households affected by more than 13 inches of rain in some areas of the city.
content: Deep floodwaters in Bangkok drove thousands of residents into shelters as others scrambled to buy groceries or dry out their homes on Sunday after days of heavy rain inundated markets, roads, and residences. Pedestrians in plastic rain ponchos waded through murky knee-deep water in the Thai capital, some venturing into a supermarket while others floated their belongings in plastic tubs. “People cannot get out of their homes. We are running out of food, so I came out to purchase some,” Aduenan Surorot, a motorbike-taxi driver, said outside a grocery store. The shops near his house – where flooding was still at chest level – were low on stock, the 30-year-old said. He waited about two hours in the cashier’s queue, with customers crowded inside but few staff working. Some stores had empty shelves over the weekend as residents raced to buy essentials, while fresh produce at market stalls was kept dry in polystyrene foam boxes or hanging just above the water level. The prime minister’s office asked the public to avoid panic buying and warned that price gouging was a criminal offence. Thailand is used to wet weather and September is the peak of the rainy season, but several Bangkok residents said this year seemed worse than previous ones. Office worker Bandit Pankan was among those frustrated that official warnings came too late. “I didn’t prepare for it at all,” he said. “We got an SMS alert from [the disaster agency] yesterday, but the water flooded in the night before.” ‘Sleeping on the table’ More than 330 mm (13 inches) of rain fell in some areas of the city between Thursday and Sunday, the weather agency said. Nearly 4,900 people have been evacuated to shelters, with around 52,000 households affected by the floods, which prompted a disaster declaration across the capital, according to the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration. Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said on Sunday that several roads remained flooded and water levels in the city’s canals were still high but authorities were working to speed up drainage. Chadchart visited a temporary shelter on Saturday in a school in the Kheha Romklao area, where he said about 1,000 people were evacuated. Some rested on cots and benches with their dogs in hallways, while others lay with blankets on the floors of classrooms. Hundreds of schools will be closed on Monday according to city authorities. Kosin Nilset, who lives along the Premprachakorn canal on the outskirts of the capital, said his house was “underwater for about 30 hours.” “This time, the water level is higher than the 2011 flood,” the 44-year-old said, using a broom to sweep out water. Widespread deluges across the Southeast Asian country in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to heat up because of fossil fuel emissions. Flooding was also reported across 25 provinces in Thailand on Sunday according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation. More than 10,000 soldiers were deployed nationwide to aid in flood relief efforts, the defence ministry said. Rain was forecast throughout Sunday for Bangkok and its surrounding provinces and would begin to taper off on Monday, the metropolitan administration said. Thidarat Silsuwan, who lives alone in her partially submerged house along the Premprachakorn canal, said she did not want to go to a shelter as she worked to clean up and salvage her belongings. “I have been sleeping on the table for two days now,” the 56-year-old said.

title: Buyers snap up new Hong Kong flats ahead of likely interest rate rises
description: All of the nearly 300 new flats launched by Hong Kong developers over the weekend have already sold, as buyers look to buy before rates increase.
content: Hong Kong developers have already sold all of the more than 290 new flats they launched over the weekend, as buyers look to lock in mortgages ahead of an anticipated rise in interest rates later this year, according to property agents. The decision by the city’s major banks to hold rates steady despite the US Federal Reserve’s recent rate increase appeared to have given buyers a push, with many expecting local rates to rise in the coming months, said Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, head of research at Ricacorp Properties. “A notable number of home seekers are actively entering the market to secure properties ahead of anticipated local rate increases,” Chan said. On Saturday, Chow Tai Fook-owned Sky Ace Enterprises shifted all of the 140 apartments it made available on its State Residence project in North Point, agents said. The properties are a mix of one-bedroom to three-bedroom flats with between 28 square metres (301 square feet) and 56 square metres (603 square feet) of floor space. They were offered at discounted prices starting from HK$5.96 million (US$759,770). China Land Resources, meanwhile, found buyers for all 153 apartments at The Sterling II made available on Sunday via a price list, agents said. The flats – ranging from 28.5 square metres (307 square feet) to 67.8 square metres (730 square feet) – were also offered at discounted prices of HK$5.43 million to HK$15.01 million. The Southwest Kowloon project also offered 35 flats via tender starting Sunday. “Developers are likely to push out launches quicker to avoid interest hike uncertainty,” said Norry Lee, senior director of projects strategy and consultancy at JLL in Hong Kong. The latest sales performance is likely to provide some relief to the property market, after Hong Kong’s lived-in home prices fell 0.46 per cent in July, halting a 13-month upswing, according to the latest official data. Despite potential upside risks in US interest rates and the likelihood of Hong Kong following suit, prevailing market optimism continues to support transaction activity Derek Chan Hoi-chiu, Ricacorp Properties The index tracking second-hand home prices slipped to 321.5 in July from 323 in June, the first decline recorded in 16 months, Rating and Valuation Department data showed. The decline came weeks before the recent interest rate increase. On September 17, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority lifted the city’s base rate to 4.25 per cent after the US Fed raised its target range to between 3.75 per cent and 4 per cent following its latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting. The city’s three note-issuing banks did not follow suit. HSBC and Bank of China (Hong Kong) kept their prime lending rate at 5 per cent, while Standard Chartered maintained its prime rate at 5.25 per cent, according to separate statements from the lenders. The Fed is set to meet again in late October. If it raises its target rate again, that could finally trigger Hong Kong’s lenders to adjust their own rates, analysts said. “Despite potential upside risks in US interest rates and the likelihood of Hong Kong following suit, prevailing market optimism continues to support transaction activity,” Chan of Ricacorp said. The timing of the launches also had a positive impact on the sales, according to Lee of JLL. “Timing matters: with Mid-Autumn Festival this week and the National Day ‘golden week’ next week, developers are keen to catch this window for mainland buyers,” he said.

title: The other crop that built China: how millet became foundation for Chinese civilisation
description: While domestication of rice was crucial in southern China, it was millet that ruled the North, laying groundwork for birth of the country.
content: Rice may be the most universal ingredient in the world, serving as a cornerstone of the diet for billions in Asia. However, for much of Chinese history, rice faced a serious competitor, and entire cultures developed around a different cereal grain, one that has since diminished in significance: millet. Millet is a cereal grain that behaves and tastes similarly to rice but has a rounder form. It is often used in porridge, stir-fries, or even fritters. In certain regions of China, millet is favoured as a food for pregnant women, with millet porridge being particularly gentle on the stomach. Despite this, it cannot rival the cultural importance of rice. Yet, the domestication of millet, along with other cereals globally, stands as one of the most pivotal events in human history. Its domestication fundamentally altered natural landscapes and enabled humans to control the plants they consume, as opposed to surviving at the mercy of wild crops. In northern China, near the Yellow River, millet thrived in its dry, arid environment, while rice dominated the South, benefiting from the warm humidity and heavy rains. “[Millet] represents an early agricultural milestone in northern China, whereas rice signifies an early agricultural development in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River in southern China,” remarked Jiang Leping from the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Relics and Archaeology. “They emerged around 10,000 years ago, and there was no clear mutual substitution. The northern region later transitioned to wheat, while rice in the south later spread to Southeast Asia and numerous other parts of the world,” he told the SCMP. The emergence of millet is significant because the Yellow River is often regarded as the cradle of Chinese civilisation. However, recent research has illuminated a more nuanced understanding of China’s formation. If we adhere to the Yellow River narrative, one of the earliest cultures from that region, the Peiligang culture (7000 BC–5000 BC) , relied on millet as a vital component for their sustenance.
