Archaeological evidence indicates that the Peiligang culture engaged in agriculture while also processing wild seeds, marking a crucial transition in human history from hunter-gatherers to early-stage farmers. A 2020 study published in Vegetation History and Archaeobotany illustrated a domestication process spanning 2,000 to 3,000 years that was largely unconscious. Dr Robert N. Spengler III, director of the Paleoethnobotany Laboratories at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History in Germany and not involved in that study, noted: “What this looked like initially is still hotly debated. In my opinion, some of the first steps in the [domestication] process included keeping herbivores away from the fields (simply by hunting) and burning away competitive plants or cutting away bushes to open more area,” he said. “Much later in time, tilling, weeding, sowing, and most importantly, seed saving were adopted,” he said, adding that much of the domestication process remains unknown because of a lack of evidence. In a separate study published in Cell Genomics in October 2025, researchers depicted how communities of early millet-farming populations intertwined and how millet spread through population movements rather than cultural exchanges. “Evidence indicates that millet agriculture expanded significantly into neighbouring regions between 5,000 and 7,000 years ago,” the authors wrote. Ultimately, millet-based societies, such as the Yangshao culture (5000 BC–3000 BC), experienced major technological advancements, contributing to the rise of early Chinese civilisation. Millet thrived during the Shang dynasty (1600 BC–1046 BC), with foxtail millet (Setaria italica) appearing in 93.24 per cent of crop remains analysed in a study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in March 2025. The decline in millet’s popularity unfolded over centuries, but its status as a secondary crop is a relatively recent development. A straightforward explanation for this decline is technological advancements, such as the water mill, which facilitated the rise of wheat. In 1012, a new variety of rice known as “champa rice” was introduced to China, boasting a growing cycle of 100 days. Suddenly, rice could be harvested twice a year from the same plot of land, making it an appealing choice for farmers eager to boost production. However, millet remained a staple for many northern households for centuries, serving as an affordable ingredient in their diets. Eventually, the advent of industrialisation made it much easier to transport rice over long distances, and millet could no longer compete with the abundance of rice. During the post-industrial era, millet began to assume its modern status as a valuable ingredient, albeit not nearly as significant as its white-grained counterpart, which has become deeply embedded in the contemporary diet and shows no signs of waning popularity.

title: Meet DWTS star Rylee Arnold’s boyfriend, football player Walker Lyons
description: Connected by his Uber driver aunt, the dancer and BYU tight end share a common faith as they navigate a long-distance relationship.
content: Rylee Arnold joined the cast of Dancing With the Stars in 2023 as a professional dancer and has since become a regular on the show with four seasons under her belt. During her time at DWTS, Arnold has partnered up with online and TV personalities such as podcaster Harry Jowsey, as well as Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik. Now, Arnold is sharing the stage with comedian and podcaster Connor Wood for the popular TV show’s 35th season which premiered on September 15 – but who is Walker Lyons, Arnold’s partner in real life? Here’s everything you need to know about Rylee Arnold’s boyfriend. He is a college athlete Walker Lyons attended the University of Southern California where he played for the school football team until he transferred to Brigham Young University (BYU) in Provo, Utah in January this year. He plays as a tight end for BYU’s football team. They met through an Uber driver Arnold revealed during a December 2024 appearance in an episode of The Squeeze podcast that she met Lyons after her Uber driver, whom she described as a “really nice lady”, asked Arnold if she would be interested in her nephew. “I looked him up (on Instagram), and I was like, ‘OK, he’s cute’. So at that point, I was too scared to really do anything about it, and so I was just kind of like put it in my back pocket.” Later, after being prompted by her sisters, Arnold decided to reach out for a date and the pair have been together since. Both Arnold and Lyons are members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. In October 2024, Arnold hard-launched their relationship with an Instagram post of her hugging Lyons at one of his games. “Is this a hard launch??” she captioned the post. They are a long-distance couple With Arnold in Los Angeles for Dancing With the Stars and Lyons in Utah, the couple are doing long distance. “Honestly, we’re just going to hope for the best,” she told People about her relationship with Lyons. “It’s definitely going to be super hard because it’s my season and his, so we are both going to be very busy. We’re probably not going to see each other for the next three months.” She continued, “But it’s awesome that we both are so busy that we can support each other and be there for each other. It’s going to be a rollercoaster, but I know he’s so awesome and supportive, so it’s going to be great.”

title: Hong Kong men turn to plush ‘bag charms’ for self-expression, comfort
description: Men defying old stereotypes by joining trend of sporting plush toy keychains depicting characters from popular anime shows such as Chiikawa.
content: Whether he is commuting to work or meeting clients, 31-year-old Hong Kong architect Bryan Hui always has a plush toy keychain of Chiikabu – a beetle-like creature from the popular Japanese anime Chiikawa – hanging from his black backpack. Beyond its cute appearance, Hui is drawn to Chiikabu’s backstory as a conflicted character who practises self-restraint out of loyalty to his friends. “I carry it with me because it makes me feel comforted and healed,” he said, adding that he owns nearly 50 Chiikawa plushies at home. Hui is far from alone. Across Hong Kong, people of all ages and genders – from young women to adult men – are increasingly sporting “bag charms”, fluffy keychains and pop-culture accessories in public. What might have once been dismissed as a childish habit or restricted to specific demographics has evolved into a mainstream lifestyle trend, with men of all backgrounds proudly joining in. Clinical psychologist Dr Amos Cheung Chuen-yih said societal stereotypes surrounding plush toys had relaxed, with items once considered exclusively for women or children now being viewed differently. “The shift indicates a broader, more accepting trend in Hong Kong. Men hanging plush toys on their bags view it as a form of personal expression, rather than something carrying a negative label,” he said. Cheung noted that soft toys served as a source of comfort to people of all genders, helping to ease anxiety and lift daily moods. “It also reflects the psychological stress of living in this society, driving a need for emotional regulation and care,” he said. “Soft toys subconsciously bring comfort by evoking the reassuring feeling of being nurtured and protected during childhood.” Hui, a big Chiikawa fan, said he even saw no need to take the charm off his backpack for work meetings. “A person’s professional ability isn’t defined by whether they hang a toy on their bag,” he said, noting that even his phone case featured a character from the anime. When Hui first started attaching character charms in 2024, he admitted to feeling some hesitation about how others might judge him. “In the past, the public might have viewed it as childish, but as it became more widespread, people grew much more accepting,” he said. “As long as it doesn’t affect anyone, doing what makes you happy is what really matters.” Fellow fan Wayne Chiu Tsz-wai, a 39-year-old property manager, also started putting various charms on his bag two years ago after becoming drawn to the series. Sporting a charm depicting show character Hachiware, Chiu said he had mostly received positive reactions from people around him, although he had encountered some negative comments suggesting men should not have stuffed toys. “I usually don’t care or respond to those comments. The main point is that it makes me feel good about myself,” he said. “Wearing these charms is simply a way to express who you are.” William Yu Shing-wai, a 39-year-old building surveyor and long-time Pokemon fan, boasts a collection of more than 1,000 trading cards and dozens of plush toys, and now attaches smaller character charms to his work bag. “Everyone is hanging charms on their bags now, regardless of gender. I saw older men and retirees carrying them on the streets too, so I don’t feel embarrassed or childish,” he said. But psychologist Cheung said gender constraints could still exist when it came to choosing specific character charms. “I believe that as society becomes more open and inclusive, these limitations will gradually loosen,” he said. “I have also seen men with My Melody and Kuromi on their backpacks, and I guess this trend will become more common,” the psychologist added, referencing popular characters from the Sanrio franchise.

title: Remote section of China’s Great Wall damaged by 20 years of mine waste dumping
description: Whistle-blowers were repeatedly ignored as mining interests removed Ming dynasty stones to create a short cut to slag dump, CCTV reports.
content: While foreign leaders and their families walk the iconic restored sections of the Great Wall around Beijing, the ancient stones of a remote Ming-era stretch of the structure in northern central China have been sacrificed for cheaper dumping of coal-mining waste. For nearly 20 years, a section of the wall in Ningwu county, Shanxi province, was used as a short cut to dump slag, despite whistle-blowers repeatedly raising the alarm to officials, according to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. The damage to the Great Wall’s Guojiayao section began in 2007, when an unlicensed miner, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, dug a trench through the structure as a way to dispose of excavation waste, the report said. In 2013, Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry was established through the consolidation of multiple mining teams and continued using the breach to dump slag, bypassing the long mountain roads. CCTV said that local authorities did not respond to repeated reports by whistle-blowers that started in 2015, allowing the vandalism to persist for nearly two decades and leaving a six-metre (19-foot) gap in the wall. Ancient Chinese rulers built the Great Wall to safeguard their territories, with construction continuing through the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), when it became the world’s largest military structure, stretching more than 21,000km (13,000 miles) across northern China. As China’s most iconic World Cultural Heritage site and a symbol of Chinese civilisation, the wall is a globally renowned tourist destination. Its sections around Beijing, particularly Badaling and Mutianyu, are the most popular and also serve as key venues for diplomatic exchanges when world leaders visit the Chinese capital. The Great Wall has welcomed multiple world leaders and their families, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, former US president Barack Obama and his wife Michelle, as well as US first lady Melania Trump. In 2017, during President Donald Trump’s state visit, the US first lady toured Mutianyu while her husband departed for a summit in Vietnam. Trump’s son Eric and daughter-in-law Lara also visited the ancient landmark when they accompanied him in May. Far from the spotlight, the lesser-known Guojiayao section’s remote location left it vulnerable to neglect and vandalism, despite legislation enacted in 2006 to protect the wall. The Regulation on Protection of the Great Wall requires cultural relics authorities to take immediate control measures and notify higher-level authorities upon receiving reports of damage to the structure. The law also dictates the installation of physical protection markers. However, boundary posts were not erected along the Guojiayao section until 2025, the report said. Local officials told the state broadcaster that past damage to the wall went unnoticed because of weak conservation efforts and infrequent inspections. No penalties were issued nor higher authorities notified because the mining enterprise stopped excavation within the protected cultural relics zone after 2019 and officials had failed to prosecute past violations, they said. The provincial authorities did not step in until March this year when, driven by persistent public complaints and media exposure, Shanxi established a special task force to investigate the coal company’s alleged illegal mining and cultural heritage destruction. The company was later fined a total of 1 million yuan (US$149,000) for executing construction projects within a cultural relic control zone without approval, as well as severely damaging the historical site. Its former executive and actual controller were detained in May. According to the CCTV report, the problem extends beyond Guojiayao, with similar severe damage to multiple other sections of the Great Wall in Ningwu caused by earlier unmonitored mining. Dong Yaohui, former executive vice-president of the Great Wall Society of China, noted in the report that the destruction in Ningwu served as a stark warning of regulatory failure for local governments. “Heritage conservation cannot rely solely on public pressure. It demands daily oversight, detecting and resolving issues promptly, so as to nip destruction in the bud before it leads to grave consequences,” he was quoted as saying. On Tuesday, the Ningwu county government issued a formal notice promising a sweeping crackdown on heritage damage and illegal slag dumping. Local officials promised that emergency repairs and structural reinforcements would be carried out alongside ecological restoration in the surrounding areas. The county also confirmed that historical official negligence and duty breaches were now under active investigation, promising strict disciplinary and legal handling as it moved to strengthen long-term protection mechanisms.

title: 7 teens swept up in police crackdown on bicycle-related offences in Tseung Kwan O
description: Force reveals it recently issued summonses to seven boys, aged 14 to 17, as part of an enforcement operation.
content: Hong Kong police have clamped down on bicycle-related offences in Tseung Kwan O, with seven teenagers facing prosecution for allegedly failing to display bike lights at night and cycling on pavements. In a social media post on Saturday, police in Tseung Kwan O district said officers had recently issued summonses to seven boys, aged 14 to 17, as part of an enforcement operation. The force said the seven teens were facing prosecution for allegedly failing to display a front white light and a rear red light in the dark or in low visibility, as well as cycling on a pavement “without obvious need”. “Tseung Kwan O police district will continue enforcement actions to combat various types of illegal behaviour and ensure road safety,” the post said, urging residents to abide by traffic rules. The number of fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with a year earlier, with nine deaths recorded. Police have attributed the uptick to cyclists ignoring traffic signals and road signs. In early September, police in the New Territories North issued nine warnings and 159 summonses for cycling-related violations over two days of targeted operations. The clampdown followed a safety education campaign in August. Anyone convicted of failing to display front white and rear red lights faces a fine of up to HK$2,000 (US$255) under the Road Traffic (Traffic Control) Regulations. Under the Summary Offences Ordinance, anyone caught cycling on the pavement without an obvious need will be subject to a fine of HK$500 or up to three months in jail. Police also warned that using unregistered and unlicensed “electric mobility devices” on roads, pavements or cycle tracks was illegal and could lead to imprisonment. The term covers electric scooters, electric skateboards, electric unicycles, electric hoverboards and power-assisted pedal cycles.

title: ‘Right now, it’s fine’: Trump brushes off questions about summit talk on Taiwan
description: Comments follow Xi Jinping’s push for the US to take an explicit stand on the issue.
content: US President Donald Trump has sought to play down exchanges with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on Taiwan, saying on Saturday that they touched on the subject only briefly. “We didn’t talk about it too much. Right now, it’s fine. It’s just moving along,” Trump said. “We didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan. He understands very much how I feel.” During the summit in Washington last week, Xi pressed Trump to take an explicit position against Taiwan independence – a stand that would go beyond the US’ traditional formulation of “not supporting” independence. In an interview with American broadcaster CNBC on Friday, US ambassador to Beijing David Perdue reaffirmed that “there’s no change in the Taiwan policy”. Perdue said Trump remained fully committed to the US “one China” policy, anchored by the Taiwan Relations Act, the three joint communiques and the six assurances. “We’re not changing the language. We’re not changing our position there. We want peace across the [Taiwan] Strait,” Perdue said. “We don’t support independence, and we think that President Xi has gotten that message.” The island of Taiwan remains the most sensitive core issue in US-China relations. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Taipei moved quickly to welcome the post-summit signals from Washington. Wu Chih-chung, the island’s deputy foreign minister, said on Saturday that maintaining Taiwan Strait peace and stability was surely in the global interest. And ensuring that Taiwan’s semiconductor sector continued to serve the global market was a key interest for the US, he said. Wu also expressed confidence that the US would follow through on planned arms sales to the island, according to a report by the island’s Central News Agency. Zhu Songling, a specialist in Taiwan affairs at Beijing Union University, said other signs from the summit were positive signals for Beijing, including Trump’s references to the US-China alliance in World War II. He said those references hinted at Washington’s recognition of Beijing’s perspective on the post-war international order. The recovery of Taiwan to China from Japanese rule was itself a key outcome of the Allied victory in World War II, Zhu said, citing the Cairo Declaration’s clause that all territories stolen by Japan from China, including Taiwan – should be restored. Zhu also highlighted that both countries agreed to build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of “respect, fairness, and reciprocity”. He said these principles should be applied when handling the Taiwan issue. “If the US talks about strategic stability on one hand while providing political support for Taiwanese separatist activities on the other, it would be like building a bridge while simultaneously dismantling it.” Zhu added that as US midterm elections approached, the Trump administration’s posture on Taiwan could become erratic, as it saw the issue as a tactical bargaining chip rather than an ideological position that could not be compromised. Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Renmin University of China in Beijing, agreed with Zhu’s emphasis on the shared consensus regarding World War II and the recovery of Taiwan from Japanese colonial control. He also said that Washington’s restatement that nothing had changed was simply standard practice. “The US has a long-standing policy of ‘strategic ambiguity’ on the Taiwan issue, and Trump is just continuing that approach,” Wang said. Wang added that the Taiwan issue took a back seat because both nations had established a baseline understanding during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. During that trip, Trump cautioned Taipei against moves that could drag the US into a conflict. “We’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.

title: Pope Leo pledges action on child abuse by priests after meeting French survivors
description: The pope met privately with victims and heard proposals for how to improve the Church’s safeguarding measures, ‌said a Vatican statement.
content: Pope Leo reaffirmed his commitment to ending abuse of children by Catholic priests in a meeting with French abuse survivors on Sunday, the Vatican said, hours after the pontiff urged the Church to admit its own failings and heal its “deep wounds”. In a two-hour meeting with seven survivors in France, where Leo is on a three-city weekend visit, the pope met privately with each of the victims and heard proposals for how to improve the Church’s safeguarding measures, ‌said a Vatican statement. “He thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others,” it said. Leo is on a whirlwind four-day visit to France. Local Church leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church’s standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades. Earlier on Sunday, the pope told an estimated 150,000 people gathered for a mass in a field near the famed Catholic shrine in Lourdes that the Church must have the courage to face its past. “In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within [the Church], we must humbly place ourselves under the ⁠Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first American pope said. Leo also spoke about the abuse scandals in a closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sunday, according to a Vatican-provided text. The pope thanked the bishops for the “courageous ‌measures” he said they had taken to confront the scandals and urged them to buttress their safeguarding efforts and “continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance”. Leo has drawn large crowds on his visit to France. Around 800,000 people came for an outdoor mass on the Champs-Elysees with the pope in Paris on ‌Saturday. He has also again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence. Leo has previously apologised directly for abuse ⁠scandals that have damaged the Church’s credibility across ⁠the world. On a trip to Spain in June, he told bishops there that they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations. Ahead of the pope’s meeting with survivors on Sunday, some survivors said they were doubtful the encounter would result in quick ‌changes by the Church. “I am quite sceptical that the pope will solve the issue, at least not immediately,” Michèle Le Reun-Gaigné, co-president of an association for survivors in western France, told Reuters. “Things are moving very slowly,” she said. “It isn’t going to happen overnight.” Bishop Pierre-Antoine ‌Bozo, the ‌spokesman for the French bishops, said the pope’s desire to have the meeting “shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns”. The pope’s ‌itinerary in France included six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains that attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and ⁠purported healing spring waters. The site is also connected to a scandal that has dogged the Vatican in recent years. The shrine’s facade has a series of mosaics by Reverend Marko Rupnik, a prominent ⁠religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse. Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations. Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the pope on Thursday, sharply criticising a continuing Vatican trial of the cleric. The mosaics, storeys tall, have been covered for the ‌pope’s visit with large, muted yellow tarps. Arriving for ‌the mass on Sunday, Leo was driven in his open-top popemobile near the facade of the shrine and the covered mosaics. The pope, who on Friday sharply reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives two months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illnesses, again mentioned the Church’s pro-life stance in Lourdes. Meeting volunteers who help sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in the shrine’s waters, Leo urged them to remember the “profound meaning” of healthcare work. “That is to care for a suffering person, not to eliminate that person,” said the pope. “Medicine must never become the servant of programmed death!”

title: Opinion | A Hong Kong professor’s sexist views have been laid bare. That’s good
description: Students speaking up against an academic’s reductionist analysis of love and marriage is a welcome sight – better yet if it sparks a broader, needed debate.
content: Love is a many-splendoured thing – except when seen through the lens of economists, apparently. Prominent economist Terence Chong Tai-leung, a Chinese University of Hong Kong associate professor, confirmed this in an address last week to the university’s New Asia College. In a speech titled “How to invest in your life?”, he basically told the female students at the event that they were wasting their time on academic achievements, since women must aim to marry for money. Don’t pursue a PhD, he said, as a woman’s youth is precious. Invest in your looks instead, he urged. It’s no wonder backlash erupted. His speech was a slap in the face of the men and women who have been campaigning for gender equality and fighting the patriarchal stereotypes that hold women back. In fact, Chong didn’t just direct his unwanted advice to young women. In one of the slides of his presentation, posted on social media by outraged attendees, he said it was pointless for “boys” to show “girls their study ability, academic grades or future ambitions. In fact, these things hold zero attraction for girls who are mature in their thinking”. In response to the backlash, Chong offered a half-hearted apology of the “I’m sorry if you felt offended” variety. The Chinese University later sent Chong a reminder to mind his words. Remember Standard Chartered global CEO Bill Winters’ apology over his “choice of words” in May, after he said artificial intelligence adoption at the bank would replace some “lower-value human capital” – 15 per cent of back-office staff – by 2030? Winters said afterwards that he valued all of his colleagues. No surprise that “human capital” is an economic construct. If we can reduce people to their productive value, then reducing our life decisions to a cost-benefit analysis to maximise investment returns makes perfect sense. “Human capital” became widely used after economists like Nobel Prize winner Gary Becker popularised it. Interestingly, Becker’s views on love and marriage could be said to be a precursor to Chong’s jaw-dropping perspectives. In his 1981 book, A Treatise on the Family, Becker analysed marriage from the standpoints of market equilibrium and utility maximisation, not love. He was not the first to view dating as transactional and a process marred by imperfect information and high transaction costs. But his thesis was criticised for presenting biases as neutral gender norms. Chong appears to belong to that school of economics. Last week’s talk only touched on some of his thoughts. He, too, had written a book, first published in 2012, in which he elaborated at length on the cost-benefit analysis of women marrying for money. Some “gems” in the Chinese-language The Alchemy of Life, include his take on the “best strategy” for “high-quality wealthy men”, as reported by the Chinese press. Since these high-value men are aware that most women are in it for their money, their most economically rational strategy is to “simply enjoy a partner throwing herself at them without getting married”. They don’t even have to “grant” official status to these women, even if they have children together. So we should not take Chong’s apology seriously. He believes in what he said, obviously. Chong said he had no intention of offending or targeting women, and was willing to apologise and revise the presentation if some of the expressions he used made people feel uncomfortable. To that, we should say: no thanks. In fact, we should thank him instead for reminding us not to take dating advice from an economist. The episode also brought home again the importance of remaining vigilant and pushing back on bias and prejudice wherever they’re found. It was good to see university students raising their voices against Chong’s remarks. The human capacity for love should not be reduced to an analysis of diminishing returns. Such reductionist thinking may well convince people to open their hearts to love without all the theorising and calculations. Or it may spark curiosity in some to learn more. If you are curious, don’t just seek out Chong’s book. Study Becker’s work, in which many of these ideas originate. Take on those who still subscribe to such sexist thinking. This debate may be what we need to help our policymakers understand how to better encourage marriage and childbearing, for instance, instead of blaming high-achieving women for prioritising their careers and studies over marriage and family.

title: Hong Kong rocker Janice Laujan on her dark, disturbing but tender debut art show
description: David Boring lead vocalist Janice Laujan says her exhibition, ‘Memory & Punishment’, carries the same sentiment as her music.
content: The grimy basements of underground punk music and the pristine white walls of contemporary art galleries are usually opposing forces of the creative world, but to Janice Laujan – the screaming, growling frontwoman of Hong Kong cult band David Boring – they are simply different mediums through which she gets to “have a public breakdown”. “Performance is the only time I can be completely honest about something and project a very intense part of my personality,” says the Hong Kong artist. “It’s saying something very f***ed up publicly, and everyone will just have to watch. There’s something very cathartic about [expressing] this taboo, heavy s*** that no one wants to hear about.” Janice Laujan – who used to go by Janice Lau but is reincorporating her Chinese first name into her stage persona – has been David Boring’s lead vocalist and lyricist since 2014. In August 2026, Laujan opened her first art exhibition, “Memory & Punishment”. The exhibition – a sound installation featuring rotating hour-long performances – transforms Gold by Serakai Studio in Wong Chuk Hang into a quiet, dreamy, open-ended dimension. Artificial mist flows over lavender-coloured, furry “clouds” on which visitors can recline as they watch the dancers and performers – sometimes including Laujan but not always – contort their bodies and wrap themselves around one another. Catching the art world’s attention Formed in 2013, David Boring were angsty and nihilistic in the first few years, embodying a generational lostness, in reaction to the sociopolitical environment of Hong Kong and the modern world. As life went on, the members’ lives also evolved, and their message became more introspective and vulnerable while maintaining an experimental post-punk sound. Meanwhile, they blew up in the local indie music scene and had their Clockenflap debut in 2017. The festival gig caught the attention of Tobias Berger, then Tai Kwun’s head of art. “I remember being like, ‘What the f*** is that?’,” Berger says. “It was like a revelation. I was astonished. I’ve seen a lot of concerts in the last 10 years in Hong Kong. It’s always been clear that David Boring is quite up there.” After their 2018 appearance on the Hong Kong episode of Parts Unknown, the travel show hosted by the late chef and TV personality Anthony Bourdain, David Boring accepted Berger’s invitation to perform at Tai Kwun’s first Artists’ Night during Hong Kong art week in 2019. Then, in 2022, they played at Tai Kwun’s JC Cube as part of the Art After Hours: Loud programme. Laujan, now in her thirties, recalls an interesting shift, or perhaps a divide, in the crowd as David Boring caught the attention of the art world. “Our first-generation fans were mostly very introverted, shy and awkward young people who’d come and just implode, having this intense experience,” she says. “Then you started seeing more art people, who would go with a ‘checking out a new gallery’ or ‘watching performance art’ mindset.” Despite this new audience base, the band have not faltered in their expression. Yuen Chi-chung, a local music critic of more than 35 years, affirms they remain “absolutely a Hong Kong cult band”. “They’ve been quite persistent on a path that goes against the mainstream,” Yuen says. “Some indie bands want to take a more pop-oriented route, but David Boring definitely don’t. They hold a very distinguished standing within the Hong Kong indie scene. “Laujan’s performance style of immense, striking power is signature to David Boring.” During 2025 Hong Kong Art Week, Laujan teased the local art world by curating “Stare Out From Your Own Burning”, a one-off David Boring performance in which the band live-scored three of its music videos, directed by three different Hong Kong filmmakers. The performance took place at Current Plans, an independent art space in the city’s Wong Chuk Hang neighbourhood. Different vibe, same sentiment With “Memory & Punishment”, the soundscape is much more ethereal than Laujan’s aggressive, tightly structured band, but she insists that “in sentiment, it’s still very David Boring”. Laujan describes the exhibition as “dark, romantic, transgressive and disturbing – but in a tender way”, adding: “All of my [creative] work is equally personal, but with the band I’m mindful of representing everyone, and ‘Memory & Punishment’ is the result of having 100 per cent creative freedom.” Yuen, who attended the opening of “Memory & Punishment” in late August, feels it introduces a more fragile and restrained side of Laujan that contrasts with her dominant, hysterical persona in David Boring. “Even during the performance, she seemed to be on an isolated island, as if disconnected from the other performers,” Yuen says. “She was on her own; it felt very personal.” Laujan’s four bandmates have already performed at the exhibition, as have Hong Kong sound artists Gold Mountain, Nerve and Kelvin T. Why Laujan is a ‘total artist’ Berger, who is the curatorial director of Serakai Studio, admits both he and Laujan took “a big chance” creating the exhibition. However, as a David Boring fan for nearly 10 years and a personal friend of Laujan’s for a good few, he had a vision. “In Germany, there’s this wonderful word gesamtkunstwerk – an ‘all-in-one, all-encompassing artwork’ – and Janice is probably a gesamtkünstler [a ‘total artist’],” Berger says, adding that, as an accomplished architect who has worked with Hong Kong’s M+ museum, Laujan is “always concerned about space”. And giving her the entire Gold space – until the exhibition ends on October 3 – has worked out. Berger was looking for a local artist who pushes boundaries and brings different disciplines together – and he thinks Laujan has done just that. “It’s not so easy, but I think Janice is somebody who can do both [in art and music],” he says. “It’s amazing for a first exhibition.” Another gesamtkunstwerk aspect of Laujan’s work – whether in indie music or contemporary art – is that everything is an attempt at radical vulnerability. She says that she is increasingly seeing her work in both disciplines as “about finding myself again through very dark human experiences of grief, loss and heaviness”, which she uses “as a vehicle to talk about the human condition”. “It’s a very universal experience to have trauma, to have difficult, heavy, f***ed-up experiences,” she says. “‘Memory & Punishment’ comes from my own experiences, but it’s very important to me that people make the show about themselves. “Even when I’m not physically there as the ‘main character’, the entire piece acts as an incubator of potential for the visitor to project their own experience and interpret the work. The onus is on the visitor. If you don’t want to do the work, you can just come and it will mean nothing.” “Memory & Punishment” runs until October 3, 2026, at Gold by Serakai Studio, G/F, Remex Centre, 42 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Wong Chuk Hang. Open 2pm-7pm on Thursdays and Saturdays, and 2pm-8pm on Fridays. Free entry

title: Why Southeast Asia feels relief and caution after the Xi-Trump summit
description: Countries in the region could feel less pressure as the thaw in US-China ties continues but deeper disputes remain unresolved, analysts say.
content: Southeast Asia welcomes the continued thaw in US-China ties after the Xi-Trump summit, with analysts saying that less friction between the two powers over issues such as the South China Sea could lower the pressure on the region. Yet, caution persists as the summit left deeper disputes unresolved. “Stable great-power relations – competitive but with sturdy guardrails – will create more legroom for third countries to navigate an increasingly complex world,” according to Lucio Blanco Pitlo III, a research fellow at the Manila-based Asia Pacific Pathways to Progress Foundation. Such stability, he said, could ease pressure on countries of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to pick a side, slow supply-chain disintegration and reduce the intensity of great-power competition in long-standing flashpoints like the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea. Beijing described Xi’s visit, his second summit with Trump in five months, as a step towards a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, emphasising continued economic engagement, dialogue on artificial intelligence and the need for Washington to handle the issue of Taiwan cautiously. Trump’s lavish treatment of Xi suggested that both sought to avoid escalation, as “the language and tone coming out of the summit suggest a continuation of interest in stability on both sides”, said Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a non-resident scholar at Carnegie China. On the other hand, better US-China relations could revive concerns in the region about a “G2” dynamic in which major powers make decisions affecting the region without meaningful Southeast Asian input. “A sustained thaw would give Southeast Asia more breathing space, particularly economies such as Vietnam that connect Chinese supply chains with American consumers,” said Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the Vietnam studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute. “But no one in the region wants a ‘G2’ deciding everyone else’s interests over their heads. One Cold War was enough.” Chong expressed similar concerns, saying any US-China arrangement that made decisions about Southeast Asia without regional participation would curtail the agency of Asean states. Such new momentum across the Pacific may also draw their attention to how the two powers are handling issues over Taiwan and the South China Sea in the absence of a reference to the highly contested waters in the Chinese read-out. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Instead of mentioning the South China Sea in its read-out, the White House simply stated that the US military’s presence has “preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific” since World War II. According to Zhu Junwei, director of the Horizon Insights Centre consulting firm, while the disputed sea falls directly within the US definition of the “Indo-Pacific”, it was not a main agenda item and required no explicit mention. Its absence signalled an intent to avoid public friction given the two sides’ shared commitment to build towards the “constructive, strategically stable relationship”, Zhu noted. “Their differences on issues like the South China Sea should be managed and handled through consultation,” she added. “Unilaterally criticising the other party in the read-out does not help manage these differences. “Nevertheless, this will not stop the US State Department or the [American] military from continuing to speak out on the South China Sea in the future.” Such an approach might even be welcomed in some regional capitals, Giang said. “From that perspective, the absence of Southeast Asia and the South China Sea from the public read-outs may be welcome,” Giang added. “Southeast Asian capitals are not naive enough to mistake silence for indifference. But Beijing’s emphasis on Taiwan signals its priorities, at least in the short term.” Even as leaders spoke of regional stability in Washington, tensions flared again in the South China Sea. The Philippine Coast Guard accused China on Friday of obstructing a resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal, known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines. The China Coast Guard said it had lawfully monitored and warned a Philippine vessel delivering supplies to what Beijing described as an “illegally grounded” ship at the shoal. On Sunday, China carried out a joint air and naval exercise near Scarborough Shoal, calling the drill a “necessary action” to counter efforts by “individual countries undermining regional peace and stability”. The coral atoll, known as Huangyan Dao in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines, has been a persistent source of friction between Beijing and Manila. Having controlled the feature since 2012, China has stepped up scientific research and geological surveys on the shoal this year. As for Taiwan, it remains a significant concern for Southeast Asia because of the large number of its citizens living and working there and the broader security and economic implications of any conflict. “Over a million Asean nationals live and work in Taiwan, so a contingency there portends a serious human and economic tragedy for regional countries,” Pitlo said, referring to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “Constructive dialogue between China and the US may help avert a crisis over these hotspots. That said, US allies and partners hope that a modus vivendi will not come at their expense.” Meanwhile, the two-month trade truce extension between the US and China and their proposed economic arrangements could provide some immediate relief for businesses. But the longer-term impact on Southeast Asia will depend on how Washington and Beijing implement their commitments. Asean exporters have been concerned about transshipment risks and the spillover effects of a prolonged US-China trade war, particularly for those relying on Chinese inputs to manufacture goods for the US market. “Progress on the trade front is a welcome respite,” Pitlo said. Still, analysts cautioned that a more cooperative tone was unlikely to reverse continuing efforts by Washington and Beijing to secure supply chains and restrict sensitive technology transfers. Trump’s unpredictability also remains a risk factor. “Under the Trump administration, predictability still has a short shelf life,” Giang said. Southeast Asian countries therefore needed to compete on infrastructure, skills and local suppliers regardless of the direction of US-China relations, he said. That could make it increasingly difficult for Southeast Asian economies to continue benefiting from their traditional role as intermediaries between the US and Chinese markets, Giang added. On the proposed dialogue on artificial intelligence, Pitlo said a China-US understanding could help “assuage fears that great-power strife may lead to technology fragmentation” at a time when Washington and Beijing were advancing competing visions for future cutting-edge technologies. But Giang argued that an AI dialogue alone was unlikely to overcome deeper structural divides or resolve the region’s technology dilemma. “On AI and advanced technology, dialogue could help manage risks, but it does not automatically open access to advanced chips or bridge competing technological ecosystems,” he said.

title: Why Xi’s US trip leaves Europe relieved by the trade truce – but wary of what comes next
description: The summit in Washington eases near-term uncertainty over rare earths, but analysts fear the bloc could have less say over decisions shaping its economic interests.
content: As President Xi Jinping wrapped up his visit to the United States, observers in Europe welcomed the stabilisation of ties between the world’s two largest economies – particularly the two-month extension of their trade truce. But some also fear the continent risks being sidelined by bilateral negotiations in which it had no seat at the table, and opinion is split on whether this is good news for the next round of the European Union’s trade talks with China. “The stabilisation of relations between the United States and China benefits Europe, which fears both a new trade escalation and an unprecedented rapprochement at Europe’s expense,” said Marc Julienne, director of the Centre for Asian Studies at the French Institute of International Relations. Engin Eroglu, head of the European Parliament’s China delegation, said the absence of a breakthrough in China’s efforts to secure greater access to the US market could strengthen the EU’s negotiating position in its coming trade talks with Beijing, scheduled to kick off on October 8. Eroglu is scheduled to travel to China in October for the fourth time this year with the parliament’s Committee on International Trade. But the unusually warm welcome US President Donald Trump gave Xi – from the personal greeting on the tarmac to the red carpet – would not have gone unnoticed in Europe, according to analysts. “It is unnerving for the EU to watch Xi Jinping being feted in Washington at a time when the bloc is veering towards a trade conflict with China,” said Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with Rhodium Group’s China practice. The better Beijing’s relations with Washington became, Barkin cautioned, the less incentive China might have to compromise with Brussels. While acknowledging that some stability in relations between Beijing and Washington was good for Europe, Barkin argued the summit had gone beyond stabilisation. “By rolling out the red carpet for Xi without getting anything in return, Trump gave China a massive gift and undermined traditional US allies in Europe, Japan and elsewhere in the process,” he said. Europe had “to be feeling rather alone” following the visit, alongside Trump’s invitation to Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend December’s G20 summit in Miami, he said. The two-month extension of the trade truce failed to give Europe enough clarity over its rare earth supplies, he added. The continued flow of rare earths is among Europe’s main concerns. China’s export controls on critical minerals, which Beijing framed as a response to Washington’s trade measures, hit European industry just as hard, Julienne said. Ian Hernandez, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre, said that before the extension was agreed, one of Europe’s top priorities was for the US and China to extend the trade truce they reached in Busan, South Korea, given its implications for supply chains. There are also concerns over artificial intelligence, an area in which Europe has sought to lead global regulatory efforts. Hernandez said there were fears that Europe could be excluded while Beijing and Washington negotiated safety standards or agreements with significant consequences for the continent. “There’s always the saying that if you’re not at the table, then you’re on the menu,” he said. Hernandez said Europe’s bet on building a coalition of willing “middle powers” – countries sitting between the two superpowers and small nations – could succeed on some issues such as rare earths. On other matters, however, Europe would still need to work with the US, including through the Washington-led Pax Silica initiative, he added.

title: Hong Kong delays AI copyright law to focus on guidelines first
description: Government puts legal amendment on hold to draft guidelines balancing creative rights with tech development.
content: Hong Kong authorities will delay a proposed legal amendment to protect copyrighted works from being used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models and will issue operational guidelines first, the South China Morning Post has learned. The Copyright (Amendment) Bill 2025, which aimed to introduce an “opt-out” mechanism for text and data mining to support AI technology development, was originally scheduled to be submitted to the Legislative Council in the first half of last year. The item was removed from Legco’s legislative agenda last August. The legislative proposal, which was mentioned in last year’s policy address, did not appear in the 2026 blueprint or the city’s first five-year plan, delivered together earlier this month. The “opt-out” mechanism had raised concerns after it was proposed in 2024, with critics saying it would “involve a lot of effort” for copyright holders to approach AI companies to check whether their work had been used for AI-generated content. They counter-proposed an “opt-in” mechanism. Lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong, chairman of Legco’s panel on commerce, industry, innovation and technology, said that according to his understanding, the government had postponed the legal amendment and would first draft an operational guideline on its proposed “opt-out” mechanism. “If the copyright industry wants to pursue royalty recovery, you must present a complete operational solution showing how it can be executed,” he said. “If you lack such a solution, the industry will be sceptical.” He said the copyright industry wanted to understand the details of how the “opt-out” mechanism would be executed. “I think it is also fair to the IT sector,” he added. Ng said there was nothing wrong with the opt-out concept, but clarification would be needed on how to execute it, for example, whether a media outlet needed to exclude every article it published from being used for AI training. When contacted, the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau referred the SCMP to remarks made by its secretary on September 18. Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah responded to the SCMP’s questions during a policy address press conference and said the government had received “different views and ideas” after a two-month consultation in 2024. “So I believe we have to consider all the concerns and come up with a better solution at this moment to make some changes or recommendations or guidelines for this copyright [ordinance],” Yau said. Ng said he supported the government’s decision to be more prudent and monitor the developments in other jurisdictions after listening to public views. He added that the government told him there was no timetable for drafting the guidelines. The original amendment bill, which included a “text and data mining exception”, would allow for the “reasonable use” of copyrighted works for computational data and analysis processing used in training AI models. Among the five safeguards the government has proposed is an “opt-out” option, allowing copyright holders to expressly reserve their rights for content made public online from being used to train AI. Other protections include requiring AI users to have lawful access to copyrighted works and to maintain and disclose records of the sources of that content. Lawmaker Kenneth Fok Kai-kong, deputy chairman of the panel, said the legislative pause was a deliberate and prudent approach driven primarily by a lack of clear consensus both locally and internationally on how copyright law should intersect with AI. He said the creative industries had expressed deep concerns that decades of hard work could be freely ingested by AI training models without authorisation or compensation, potentially undermining the entire creative ecosystem. “It would be premature for Hong Kong to pioneer rigid statutory changes that might risk misaligning with global practices or imposing inflexible constraints on a rapidly evolving technology,” he said. Fok said a balanced, future-proof approach should focus on market-driven cooperation, supplemented by market-led licensing schemes, non-statutory guidelines and continuous benchmarking with global trends. Sharon Wong Yin-yue, executive director of the Hong Kong Reprographic Rights Licensing Society, said she attended a government briefing recently and was told the legislative amendment would not be tabled for discussion in Legco. Instead, the government would issue guidelines on using AI to different stakeholders, but she did not have the details. She said the industry was discussing how to safeguard creative rights amid the rapid development of AI, rather than focusing on the opt-out mechanism. She added that the society would introduce AI-related clauses to its licensing scheme and enhance public education on AI literacy. Joshua Chu, a lawyer and co-chair of the Hong Kong Web3 Association, said he believed the government needed to catch up with the fast-changing development of AI over the past year, especially with the recent incidents of agentic AI going rogue and launching cyberattacks without human intervention. He said, for example, the government needed to clarify the legal liability of AI agents if they had infringed on others’ copyright without being instructed by a human. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, said it would be difficult to resolve copyright issues related to AI as they would involve multiple jurisdictions and it was hard to trace the original copyright owner after content was processed by the technology. Fong suggested that copyright owners explore the possibilities of using encrypted watermarks that could be read by AI to protect their content. The government should also strike a balance between AI development and the protection of copyright owners, he said.

title: Global property investors see signs of recovery in China, but wary of oversupply: JLL
description: Firm’s Asia-Pacific capital markets CEO says balance is emerging between fresh supply of space and take-up.
content: International investors who have seen early signs of recovery in mainland China’s office and retail property markets are expected to start buying when oversupply concerns are eased, according to global real estate firm JLL. Stuart Crow, JLL’s CEO for capital markets in the Asia-Pacific region, said foreign institutions would fall back in love with mainland property assets when new supply was absorbed by fresh take-up. “International investors are waiting for the real economy to really absorb those commercial property spaces,” he said. “Probably we need to be a little bit more patient for the China value recovery.” Crow added that a balance between fresh supply of space and take-up was emerging in the world’s second-biggest economy, with oversupply concerns eased, but big institutions like real estate funds and insurers would not return unless commercial properties could generate sufficient income. Commercial property transactions shot up in major mainland cities including Shanghai and Beijing in the first half of this year as local buyers, including corporate investors and high-net-worth individuals, snapped up office buildings and hotels in prime locations on expectations that property prices would soon bottom out after a years-long downturn. In Shanghai, prices of office buildings had plunged 30 to 40 per cent from their peaks amid a national property crisis that started in 2021, prompting local investors to hunt for bargains, brokers said. Even though there may be an oversupply in the broader market, the best of the best office assets will recover first Stuart Crow, JLL The recent launch of the mainland’s first exchange-traded real estate investment trusts backed by commercial properties – a new financing source for property owners – had also helped spur buying, they added. Crow said the Chinese commercial property market had seen a ray of hope as global investors increased their asset allocations in the Asia-Pacific region to profit from its economic growth and liquidity. “Even though there may be an oversupply in the broader market, the best of the best office assets will recover first, and their rate of growth will be quicker,” he said. A report released by JLL last month that evaluated top office properties in Shanghai said some “elevated premium grade A” office buildings had exceptional resilience and were outperforming the market. “The elevated premium grade A offices have demonstrated consistent advantages in rental premiums and vacancy rates compared with regular grade A offices,” said Daniel Yao, head of research for JLL China. “Entering 2026, their office rents have stabilised and started to bottom out, driving the overall office market recovery.” The average rent for such offices stood at 8.5 yuan (US$1.27) per square metre per day in the second quarter of the year, with nearly 70 per cent recording positive or flat rental growth in the first half of the year, JLL data showed. The average rent for a regular grade A office in Shanghai was 6 yuan per square metre per day.

title: AI note-taking is easy, but here’s why you should stick to writing by hand
description: A psychologist explains that handwriting is key to how our brains learn new information and to our reading abilities.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Before artificial intelligence (AI) could summarise lectures, most students took notes by hand. But an expert says manual note-taking is an important way for the brain to learn new information.
According to Dr Kitty Yeung Kit-yu – a registered educational psychologist in Hong Kong – the act of writing helps our brains grow.
If you try to type out your teacher’s every spoken word, you won’t learn very much, Yeung said. Automated note-taking tools do even less for the brain.
Writing by hand is slow. So it forces the brain to digest and paraphrase ideas in real time. This process forces you to think more deeply and remember what you’re writing. As you do this, your brain is also being trained to solve problems and think critically.
“Handwriting forces students to stop, process and actively digest what a professor is saying,” said Yeung, who is also a specialist in child development and special educational needs (SEN) research.
“As you write, your mind actively processes the words, which in a way helps you recall them,” she said.
For young learners, this is important for their reading skills.
Yeung pointed to research that found that children who practise writing by hand had better reading skills compared with those who relied on keyboards. This shows that learning to read is connected to learning to write.
On a physical level, handwriting also trains the hands to make small, precise movements.
“Typing lacks this entirely ... You don’t practise flexing the wrist ... [changing] pressure – harder versus lighter – or executing delicate strokes,” Yeung said.
The role of handwriting is even deeper for character-based languages like Chinese.
A 2012 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences journal found that children in mainland China who relied on pinyin keyboard entry struggled more with reading.
This is because handwriting unites a Chinese character’s form, sound and meaning.
“Typing simply doesn’t evoke these features,” Yeung said.
Different parts of a Chinese character can represent its meaning and pronunciation. Take the character for pai (拍), meaning to pat, as an example. When writing it, the “hand” radical (扌) is a visual representation of the action, and it is paired with bai (白), which gives a hint as to how the word sounds.
“When typing – say, using the Quick ... Input Method – you might just press a key corresponding to a single horizontal stroke. That key stroke bears no relationship to the physical shape or the underlying ... meaning of ‘hand’,” she noted.
If children only learn Chinese through this typing method, they might struggle to fully learn a character’s form, sound and meaning.
Yeung said that schools should not ban AI tools from the classroom. Instead, she believes they should teach students how to use them without giving up their own critical thinking.
“Ultimately, a student’s writing must reflect their own critical thinking and reasoning – not let AI do the thinking for them,” Yeung said.
If you want to use AI tools to summarise a lesson, you can do that while also taking notes by hand. After class, you can check the accuracy of your notes against the AI summary and see if you missed anything.
Just as typing has its place when writing long essays or chatting with friends, AI tools also have their place.
But the core process of learning and thinking should remain in your hands.

title: Bangkok floods trap residents as PM Anutin cuts UK trip short to tackle crisis
description: ‘We’re all just left to fend for ourselves and take care of each other right now,’ a resident in the hard-hit eastern Bangkok says.
content: Bangkok residents stranded by neck-deep floodwaters on Sunday appealed for clean water and food, as Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a diplomatic trip to the United Kingdom to monitor the response amid growing criticism online. In the worst floods to hit the Thai capital in 15 years, life has ground to a standstill in parts of the city since Friday evening, prompting the town hall to declare a disaster in all 50 districts. Days of incessant rains that overwhelmed Bangkok’s creaking drainage system appeared to have let up on Sunday morning, leaving residents cautiously hopeful that the water may have stopped rising. But densely populated eastern Bangkok remains hard hit, with canals unable to drain the volume of water pouring out from inundated roads and homes. Residents of at least two large housing complexes in the east of the city took to social media to appeal for help as a deluge that has virtually submerged cars cut them off from fresh food and water supplies. In one block of flats in Bang Kapi district, residents said that with each passing hour without help they feared being exposed to mounting risks that come with floods in Southeast Asian megacities – including electrocution, disease and encounters with snakes flushed out from the drains. “The water [around the flats] is chest high. No one has come to help us at all,” Siraprapha Sangseeluem, 24, told This Week in Asia. “Someone in my neighbourhood was electrocuted. I’ve got 10 bottles of water and some mama (instant noodles) left but I’m not sure when the cooking gas will run out,” Siraprapha said. “I’m mostly concerned about running out of water to drink because the floodwater doesn’t seem to recede at all.” She also criticised the perceived sluggish response to the flooding by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) as “too little, too late”. “We’re all just left to fend for ourselves and take care of each other right now,” she said. City residents shared flood resilience tips online – including how to make “sandbags” without sand – by using plastic bags filled with floodwater to make barricades at the entrances to homes and businesses. Others found time for a lighthearted response to a crisis beyond their control, posting videos of swimming, fishing or lying on floaties in swimwear on inundated roads. Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt on Sunday said that if there was no more rain to add to the situation, authorities would accelerate the drainage-clearing work. “But the water cannot be drained quickly. As we pump the water out, water from higher-lying areas continues to flow in and replenish it. It will take several more days,” Chadchart said. He added that many stranded communities wanted to evacuate and taking care of such large groups, including 30,000 residents in the Rom Klao housing estate, was challenging. Earlier, Chadchart admitted that the BMA initially downplayed the risks of the rains, which had been raised by flood experts and city residents on social media in the days before the waters rose on Friday. The BMA has invested huge resources in cleaning and widening drainage, especially in deluge-prone areas ahead of the peak flood risk period which runs until late October. But its efforts appear to have been thwarted by the sheer volume of water dumped down on Bangkok since late Wednesday. An eerie calm descended over other parts of the Thai capital on Sunday, as drivers stayed off the traffic-clogged roads and residents in hard-hit areas waded through knee-high waters, pulling improvised rafts and basins to bring bottled water to stricken neighbours. Some began counting the cost of floodwaters that came without warning and attempted to start waterlogged cars and motorbikes, although it was too early to begin a clean-up with waters sitting at around 12 inches (one foot) high in many neighbourhoods. The disaster also prompted Prime Minister Anutin to end a trip to the United Nations in New York and then London early – conscious of the political stakes in a capital that largely did not vote him into office earlier this year yet retains outsize economic influence over the country. “During this time all of the ministers in my cabinet will not travel overseas, including myself,” he told reporters after a walk around northeastern Bangkok. “Our main goal is for the people to be able to return to work, for kids to go back to schools and for shops to reopen, for the public to be able to commute safely again.” Thailand is accustomed to the annual flooding season, but this year’s catastrophe has caught many by surprise. The rains were lighter but more persistent compared with the heavy storms that triggered the 2011 crisis, which killed 500 people across the country, including hundreds in Bangkok. Bangkok, which sits in a soft clay basin that experts say is slowly sinking, is highly exposed to climate extremes. But the climate crisis is challenging the resilience of its people and infrastructure like never before.

title: Hong Kong Stadium could host tennis events during Victoria Park court revamp: minister
description: Sports minister Rosanna Law says the stadium site is already well equipped, ensuring authorities can seek to host higher-level events.
content: Hong Kong Stadium could serve as an interim home for major tennis tournaments during the redevelopment of Victoria Park’s centre court, the city’s sports minister has said, adding that the government will seek to attract higher-level events even before the new facility is ready. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Sunday that authorities could reserve the stadium for tennis during certain periods each year and install temporary courts and other facilities. The plan remains under consideration. “Hong Kong Stadium is my answer,” Law told a television programme when asked where the city could stage large tennis tournaments during the Victoria Park redevelopment. Law said the stadium had extensive seating and enough space for a main court, secondary courts and warm-up areas, with the option of using adjoining facilities. Its availability would give the government a reason to pursue bigger tournaments while work at Victoria Park was under way, she added. The government announced in the recent policy address that it would study rebuilding the Victoria Park Centre Court and supporting facilities as an all-weather multipurpose venue. Authorities had previously said the aim was to accommodate at least an ATP 500 tournament, which requires about 7,000 seats, while a 10,000-seat venue capable of hosting an ATP 1000 event also remained a goal if space and resources allowed. The existing centre court can host ATP 250 events and has about 3,600 seats. The numbers 250, 500 and 1000 refer to the ranking points awarded to the singles champion. Higher-tier events generally offer more prize money and attract stronger fields. ATP 250 events are the lowest tier of the ATP Tour. Sports scholar Lobo Louie Hung-tak of the Education University of Hong Kong backed the idea of using the stadium as an interim venue, saying tennis tournaments could not simply stop for the years needed to plan and rebuild Victoria Park. “Using Hong Kong Stadium as a temporary venue during the Victoria Park redevelopment is the most ideal approach,” he said, adding that the transition could last seven or eight years once construction was included. He also said the stadium in Causeway Bay was underused, but its existing layout offered relatively little flexibility for other sports. He also expressed caution about the prospect of staging higher-tier tennis events there. Adapting it for an ATP 250 tournament “should not be too difficult”, he said, but whether a temporary set-up could accommodate ATP 500 or ATP 1000 events would require further study with the relevant sports bodies. Hot weather and rain would remain drawbacks for spectators at the outdoor stadium, he added. Law said a technical feasibility study was under way and she hoped design work could begin soon. Under Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, authorities aim to start construction sometime during the period covered by the blueprint, which runs to 2030. The minister did not specify when the work would begin. But Law said the rebuild could be finished in the early part of the next five-year development period. If the project went ahead, that timeline would require another major tournament venue to fill the gap for several years. On how much park space the expanded facility would occupy, Law said authorities would try to avoid disturbing the swimming complex and hard-surface football pitches. She noted that both were well used and that the swimming facilities had recently been rebuilt. But Law acknowledged that some smaller areas behind the existing tennis venue might be affected. An upgraded tournament venue would need practice courts and secondary courts as well as a main court, she said. Authorities have yet to settle on the size and design of the facility under the revamp. Law said the government was studying how to make it usable in different weather, while balancing the requirements of tennis with the ambition to host other sporting events and performances. She added that a larger venue in the city centre could also bring visitors and spending to Causeway Bay and the northern part of Hong Kong Island. The latest policy address also included a proposed one-stop Support Unit for Non-local Film Productions in the first quarter of 2027 to support mainland Chinese and overseas movie crews hoping to use Hong Kong as a location. Asked how the government would respond if a production portrayed the city negatively, Law said filmmakers receiving help would need to explain their film’s outline, story and intended message. The support team could then maintain contact with them from the location scouting stage and discuss any issues that arose during filming, she said. The government was also considering a relatively large, low-cost site where local productions could build sets and had some possible locations in mind, Law added, but declined to specify the sites.

title: Hong Kong tech chief sets June deadline for Hetao cross-border talent flow
description: ‘The flow of people must begin by June 30 next year at the latest,’ technology minister Sun Dong says.
content: Cross-boundary talent flows within the Hetao innovation hub will be launched by June next year at the latest, Hong Kong’s technology minister has said, after the city’s leader pledged to enable the free movement of data by the end of 2026. Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong revealed the deadline while also discussing how semiconductor production, which is due to begin at the Hong Kong Microelectronics Research and Development Institute (MRDI) this year, could commercialise scientific findings and pave the way for mass production in the Greater Bay Area. “We hope to launch a pilot scheme for data flows as soon as possible. The flow of people must begin by June 30 next year at the latest,” he told a radio programme on Sunday. Sun was referring to the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone, one of the city’s key innovation hubs. Building One of the park, the flagship launch pad for the Northern Metropolis University Town, had already reached an 80 per cent leasing rate, he said. The building would house the headquarters of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization’s centre of excellence on global advanced manufacturing in the second quarter of next year, as well as the headquarters of the Life and Health Technology Research Institute, Sun added. For the remaining about 20 land parcels in the park’s first phase, the government had received six bids from semiconductor, artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology companies, as well as developers, he said. The city’s first five-year plan sets out a “one river, two banks” and “one zone, two parks” vision for the cooperation zone, aiming to facilitate the secure and efficient flow of personnel, materials, capital and data between the Hong Kong and Shenzhen parks. Together with the San Tin Technopole, the Science Park and Cyberport, the zone will form a “north-central-south” development paradigm to build a world-class research and development platform, according to the blueprint. Separately, Sun said trial chip production at the microelectronics institute this year would help enterprises resolve technical pain points and test products in the city before launching large-scale manufacturing across the border, under a “Hong Kong trial production, bay area mass production” strategy. Established in 2024 and based at the Yuen Long InnoPark, the institute will lead the operation of Hong Kong’s first national manufacturing innovation centre, focusing on third-generation power semiconductors, according to the policy address supplement. The institute had already secured tens of millions of dollars in cooperation orders ahead of its official launch, Sun said. Once fully operational, its two pilot lines would be able to handle more than 50 cooperation cases a year, he added. To further support start-ups and industry growth, the government would establish a HK$10 billion (US$1.27 billion) innovation and technology industry-oriented fund by year-end, expecting the private sector to contribute HK$30 billion to create a total pool of HK$40 billion, Sun said. About 20 fund managers have been preliminarily selected and are currently raising capital for the initiative. The government had also earmarked an additional HK$1 billion to top up the Innovation and Technology Venture Fund to HK$2.5 billion, aiming for a HK$10 billion capital pool to support early-stage start-ups, he added. On the subject of AI infrastructure, Sun said phase one of the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster would begin partial operations before July next year, with an overall target of achieving 180,000 petaflops of computing power by around 2030.

title: From body language to ping-pong, decoding the symbolism during Xi and Trump’s meeting
description: Even small details and gestures during Xi and Trump’s summit in Washington were rife with meaning.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage of the Xi-Trump summit. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. From wine to ping-pong, Trump and Xi’s state dinner leans on historic symbolism When US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in the East Room, every detail of the state dinner was steeped in symbolism, with sparkling wine served as a nod to a pivotal moment in Sino-US relations and references to “ping-pong diplomacy”. 2. How China’s wartime cooperatives gave us ‘gung-ho’ Chinese viewers watching Trump welcome Xi to the White House on Thursday may have been puzzled by the US president’s reference to the “Chinese phrase” gung-ho. Turning to Baidu – or increasingly, Doubao, the country’s most popular AI chatbot – they may well have asked: what Chinese expression is he referring to? 3. Pat on the back? Xi and Trump’s body language speaks volumes Arm touches, laughs, and firm handshakes were on display as Xi and Trump began their high-stakes summit in Washington, which has so far featured a rare airport welcome, military pageantry and closed-door bilateral talks. 4. From ping-pong to pickleball: China’s unofficial approach to diplomatic messaging Before setting off for Washington on Wednesday, Xi had some correspondence to attend to. Dozens of students from 10 US universities, including Harvard, had written to him about their experiences on an exchange trip to China this year. According to the State Council, Xi responded with a call to the students to advance cooperation between the two countries. 5. Summits for all diplomatic seasons: how the US has set the stage for Xi Jinping Xi’s visit to the US was his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Trump. From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations. 6. What Trump and Xi revealed in the body language with their wives As Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump wrapped up their three-day state visit on Friday, a stark contrast in the two presidential couples’ hand-holding dynamics was on display, body language experts said. 7. How Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump opened a parallel track in US-China diplomacy First ladies Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump opened a new front in US-China exchanges last week, with their unusually frequent and spontaneous interactions putting a more personal face on ties during the presidential summit in Washington.

title: Psychologist explains why writing notes by hand beats an AI note-taker
description: Handwriting is key to learning – typing your teacher’s every spoken word offers little for your brain, and automated tools do even less.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Long before artificial intelligence (AI) began summarising lectures, jotting notes by hand used to be a universal learning practice. But an expert warns that the trend of automated note-taking risks abandoning one of our brain’s most powerful tools for comprehension.
