According to Dr Kitty Yeung Kit-yu – a registered educational psychologist in Hong Kong – the physical act of writing plays a vital role in cognitive development.
According to a 2025 study published in the science journal Life, researchers in Italy looked at brain scans to compare how adults’ brains reacted to writing with a pen versus typing on a keyboard.
The findings show that while typing encourages passive transcription, handwriting is more cognitively demanding. Because writing by hand is slower, it forces the brain to digest and synthesise concepts in real time, driving deeper thought, memory and problem-solving.
Typing every spoken word in a class offers little educational value, Yeung said. Automated note-taking tools do even less for the brain.
“Handwriting forces students to stop, process and actively digest what a professor is saying – engaging a deeper cognitive mechanism that directly fosters critical thinking,” said Yeung, who is also a specialist in child development, dyslexia and special educational needs (SEN) research.
“As you write, your mind actively processes the words, which in a way helps you recall them.”
For young learners, this lays the groundwork for literacy. Yeung pointed to research that had found that children who practise writing by hand had better reading fluency and letter-sound comprehension compared with those who relied on keyboards – proving that learning to read is rooted in learning to write.
On a physical level, handwriting also trains fine motor muscles.
“Typing lacks this entirely ... You don’t practise flexing the wrist, modulating pressure – harder versus lighter – or executing delicate strokes,” Yeung said. “Those refined motor skills only develop through physical writing practice.”
While this cognitive link is vital for alphabetic languages like English in which writing letters can connect sounds to spellings, handwriting’s role is even deeper for character-based languages like Chinese.
Yeung’s current research examines handwriting’s impact on child development; she stressed that physical writing remained a foundational pillar of Chinese literacy.
MRI scans reveal that when readers recognise Chinese characters, the regions of the brain responsible for writing light up simultaneously, meaning reading and writing characters are intertwined in the brain.
Handwriting unites a Chinese character’s three core dimensions: form, sound and meaning.
“Typing simply doesn’t evoke these features,” Yeung said.
Different parts of a Chinese character can represent its meaning and pronunciation. Take the character for pai (拍), meaning to pat, as an example. When writing it, the “hand” radical (扌) is a pictographic representation of the action; it is paired with bai (白), which gives a hint as to how the word sounds.
“When typing – say, using the Quick ... Input Method – you might just press a key corresponding to a single horizontal stroke. That key stroke bears no relationship to the physical shape or the underlying semantic meaning of ‘hand’,” Yeung noted.
If children only learn Chinese through this typing method, it could hinder their grasp of character form, sound and meaning.
A landmark 2012 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that children in mainland China who relied heavily on pinyin keyboard entry showed higher rates of reading impairment, as phonetic typing bypasses the motor memory necessary to master complex logographic scripts.
However, for dyslexic learners, who struggle to process a word’s visual form, Yeung noted that digital AI tools had many benefits for their learning. “If their underlying character recognition system is impaired, copying [by hand] won’t actually help them,” she said.
For these students, relying on audio tools and memorising Chinese characters by sound is more effective than relying on writing their notes by hand.
This is why SEN students can use speech-to-text tools during university entrance exams, Yeung said.
“By allowing dyslexic students to turn spoken language into text on a computer, they can bypass their output barriers in non-language subjects, ensuring their academic performance reflects their actual knowledge,” she said.
Yeung emphasised that schools should aim not to banish AI tools from the classroom, but to teach students how to use them without surrendering their own critical thinking.
“Ultimately, a student’s writing must reflect their own critical thinking and reasoning – not let AI do the thinking for them,” Yeung said.
For instance, if you want to use AI tools to transcribe a lesson, you can do that alongside taking notes by hand. After class, you can check your notes against the AI summary and refer to the transcription if you need to check the accuracy of something you wrote.
Just as typing has its place when writing long essays or chatting online, AI tools also have their place.
The core intellectual heavy lifting, however, remains in your hands.

title: Hong Kong can offer AI governance solutions for major economies: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief cites common law system, internationally connected standards and professional services as city’s strengths.
content: Hong Kong can offer trusted solutions in artificial intelligence (AI) governance for major economies by leveraging the city’s unique strengths, including its common law system, internationally connected standards and professional services, the city’s finance chief has said. “As major economies begin discussing AI governance, data, compliance and risk management, Hong Kong can leverage its unique strengths in providing ‘rules’ and ‘trust’,” Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday. “Hong Kong can offer trusted solutions in [AI] model training, cross-border data flows, privacy protection and dispute resolution.” He highlighted the city’s advantages in its common law system, biliterate and trilingual legal talent, internationally connected standards, professional services and strong financial support. Chan made the remarks as the government’s recent policy address highlighted seven key areas in AI risk governance, including combating AI-related crimes such as deepfake porn and online scams, introducing management guidelines for AI agents and promoting market assessment of AI ethical risks. The government published a report on manpower projections last week, predicting the city’s manpower shortfall would narrow to 130,000 in 2028, due to economic transformation, the adoption of AI and various talent and labour importation measures. But critical industries such as innovation, aviation, construction, city operations and healthcare will still face a manpower crunch. Chan said the city’s manpower gap would be concentrated in occupations that rely heavily on interpersonal interaction, on-site judgment and complex craftsmanship, underscoring the need for talent in areas that even the most advanced AI cannot replace. He added that Hong Kong would also need to nurture talent with an understanding of the AI industry, noting that the government had made efforts to promote AI training for all. “AI will bring new types of jobs and new pathways to Hong Kong,” Chan wrote. “Enhancing the labour force’s AI literacy and broader skills is about our future competitive advantage in the market, and also about Hong Kong’s need to adapt to AI development, as well as people’s work and lives.” Chan also set off for a two-day visit to Qatar’s capital, Doha, on Sunday to attend the annual meeting of the board of governors of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). He met Qatar’s minister of finance, Ali bin Ahmed Al-Kuwari, after he arrived. He is expected to meet other AIIB governors as well as local and international political and business leaders and will deliver a keynote speech at a thematic session on digital public infrastructure. He said he would share Hong Kong’s experience in promoting infrastructure development, enhancing regional connectivity and sustainable development and introducing the city’s new opportunities and advantages during the meeting.

title: Nearly 50, Jason Mraz is genre-shifting, living in the moment and done flirting
description: Ahead of his Hong Kong concert, the American singer spills all on love songs and ‘highlighting the goodness’.
content: “I’m not trying to be a flirt, like in my twenties,” American singer-songwriter Jason Mraz says, laughing. “I’m almost 50, and that’s not the vibe I’m putting out on stage any more.” It has been seven years since Mraz performed at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre as part of his “Good Vibes” Asia tour. Since that visit in 2019, Mraz has kept himself agile, releasing the full-length reggae record Look for the Good (2020), embracing disco-pop on the 2023 album Mystical Magical Rhythmical Radical Ride, and even taking runner-up honours on season 32 of Dancing with the Stars in 2023. On November 4, he will return to Hong Kong – this time at the AsiaWorld-Expo – as part of yet another Asia tour, with a redefined creative perspective. Don’t expect the same smooth-talking flirt with the fedora of the 2000s, he says. “As you get older, your attitudes and opinions or your agenda change.” His most recent album, Grandma’s Gospel Favourites (2026), finds the 49-year-old singer returning to the country and bluegrass influences of his childhood. Before he was playing stadiums and living in California, Mraz was a kid in Mechanicsville, Virginia, singing along to oldies and listening to his family’s piano music. Released in May, the latest album – a combination of traditional church song covers and original songs – was initially recorded in 2007 as a personal Christmas gift for his grandmother, Mary Helen Mraz-Fowler, affectionately known to him as “Nanny Razz”. Though she died in 2014, Mraz realised over the years that she would have wanted those songs shared far beyond their family. “For the style I got to revisit, which was this Americana bluegrass style, I feel the work for me was more in the musicianship and the fingering and the playing,” Mraz recalls of his creative process. Vocally, slipping into that country twang came easily to Mraz, who naturally reverts to a Southern accent whenever he visits home. In fact, he found the vocal sessions surprisingly liberating. “Just be relaxed and be at home and sing it to Grandma,” he remembers thinking, “because that’s the only person who’s listening.” Mraz on the evolution of his music In the late 1990s, long before his songs became multi-platinum global anthems, Mraz built his followers busking in New York and playing acoustic guitar at coffeehouses in San Diego, Southern California. Now, nearly 20 years since his biggest hits “I’m Yours” and “Lucky” were released, Mraz himself is aware of the evolution he has undergone. “I don’t write as many love songs any more, and I certainly don’t write gender-specific love songs,” says the singer who came out as bisexual in 2018. “I’m just not who I was in my twenties when I was trying to woo some girl and have all the swag on stage. That never really felt good to me.” Today’s pop songwriters tend to use confessional writing – publishing lyrics so specific that they could have been ripped out of their diaries. But, for years, Mraz has championed using an “inclusion pass” in his songs, meaning that he tries to ensure that everyone regardless of their sexuality or culture can relate to his lyrics. He still stands by this principle, even finding ways to perform old songs in a non-gender specific way. He still considers many of his songs to be deeply personal. “It’s not confessional, but it’s asking for guidance,” he clarifies. These days, Mraz often finds himself writing songs as a way to cheer himself on and to help him find comfort. Therefore, his goal in songwriting, both now and then, is to just be in touch with his humanity. “What we all have in common is that everyone’s doing the best they can and yet everyone suffers,” he says. “Everyone wants to know why we’re here and how we are going to get through the day or the year.” Country and folk music are certainly having their moment, Mraz says about the surge in mandolins and pedal steel incorporated into pop music. But it is a tricky topic, he admits, coming from the US where the collision of those genres with patriotism and nationalism is “already sort of staining the good vibes”. His return to Hong Kong will emphasise the celebration of song and “living in the moment, not worrying our lives away and being in the company of our best friends and our family – just highlighting the goodness”. The set list for his shows in Asia is not completely set yet, but Mraz promises to play songs from every record. He and his band will weave together medleys so they can pack more tracks into the set list while honouring fan requests gathered from social media. Nearly three decades into his career, Mraz has no intention of stagnating his creative growth. His foray into bluegrass is just his latest creative leap following his 2017 Broadway run in the hit musical Waitress and a dive into competitive dance – experiments he credits with making him a stronger, more versatile performer. “I think it’s important for musicians to be well-rounded and be able to cover lots of different musical styles,” he says. “I do want to explore genres for the rest of my career. I want to try all different sounds and styles, and that sometimes may call for a different accent or a different vocal approach.” Jason Mraz: Asia Tour 2026 in Hong Kong, AsiaWorld-Expo, November 4, 8pm. Tickets HK$880-HK$1,480 (US$112-US$189). For more information, visit asiaworld-expo.com

title: Asian Games, day 8: gold for squash, but ‘fencing Hong Kong’s No 1 sport,’ Fong says
description: City’s Lee Ka-yi, Tang Ming-hong take mixed doubles squash title, while Fong Hoi-sun adds men’s team épée bronze to individual medal.
content: The honour of winning Hong Kong’s fifth gold medal of the Asian Games fell to squash pair Lee Ka-yi and Tang Ming-hong on Sunday, and while it did not come with a place at the Los Angeles Olympics, it left the former feeling “amazing” and her partner “completely empty”. There was silver too, of course, with the final at Nagoya Kinjo-Futo Arena a clash against close friends and Hong Kong teammates Toby Tse Yee-lam and Lai Cheuk-nam. Another fencing bronze was added to the city’s growing tally, with Fong Hui-sun getting a men’s team épée medal to go alongside his individual one. The women’s sabre team did not fare as well, however, losing to South Korea in the quarter-finals. It took Lee and Tang just 21 minutes to win mixed doubles gold, which was a significant upgrade on the bronze Lee won with Wong Chi-him in Hangzhou three years ago. “It’s very amazing, I’m very excited at the moment,” Lee said. “It is my first gold medal in mixed doubles and I want to thank my partner for playing with me almost every day. It’s been two months since we have spent a lot of time together practising doubles. And I’m happy that the hard work paid off.” Tse, who was making her Games debut, said it had been harder playing against opponents they practised, trained and ate with almost every single day. The “big experience” left the 21-year-old hungry for more, although when that will be remains to be seen. Only men’s and women’s singles will be contested in 2028, with 16 players in each category. Gold medallists Ng Eain Yow and Sivasangari Subramaniam, who are both from Malaysia, also took the two Olympic qualifying spots up for grabs. A bronze medal in the men’s team épée, after a fairly convincing 45-34 loss at the hands of world team champions Kazakhstan in the semi-finals, prompted Fong to proclaim fencing “the most famous sport in Hong Kong”. “It’s No 1,” added Fong, who teamed up with Ng Ho-tin, Ho Wai-hang and Lau Ho-fung. “It’s not one of the best. It’s No 1. We have a lot of new, young, good fencers coming up to push us to go more forward, and I like the fight.” There had been an outside chance of a medal in women’s doubles badminton and in the men’s singles, but Yeung Nga-ting and Yeung Pui-lam lost 2-1 to Japan’s Kie Nakanishi and Rin Uesaka in their quarter-final, while Angus Ng Ka-long was dumped out in the last eight by Thailand’s Kunlavut Vitidsarn. Elsewhere, the tennis competition got under way with the first round of the men’s and women’s singles at Higashiyama Park Tennis Centre. Fans hoping to see Coleman Wong Chak-lam in action will need to wait until Tuesday at the earliest, but Alexandra Eala is expected to be in action on centre court on Monday, where the women’s top seed will take on Thailand’s Patcharin Cheapchandej. China’s Wang Xiyu is also among the favourites to win gold, and she started her week with a 6-0, 6-0 thrashing of young Indonesian Anjali Junarto. “From the score it looks like an easy match, but it wasn’t,” Wang said. “She has some special-hitting game, and you could see her serve is good. And she did well with first serves and I could feel pressure when returning. “Also, she had a good slice, good hands, so it was a good experience for me to play against her today.”

title: Forgotten no more: Filipino folklore finds footing on global stage
description: DreamWorks’ animated film, Forgotten Island, offers a rare point of recognition for Filipinos at home and abroad.
content: Stories of the manananggal, a creature said to split its body in two, and the tiyanak, which takes the form of an infant, are part of the folklore many children grow up hearing in the Philippines. Now, they are among the mythological creatures featured in DreamWorks’ animated film Forgotten Island, which opened in the Philippines on Wednesday and two days later in the United States. The film, described as the first major Hollywood production to showcase Filipino culture and mythology, offers a rare point of recognition for the diaspora while reflecting the US industry’s growing interest in Asian audiences. “We first saw the trailers in the cinema and I wasn’t expecting to see a movie with Filipino stories that I grew up with back in the 1990s,” Berlynn Tuazon-Bradshaw, 34, said. Bradshaw moved to the US after university in 2013 and now divides her time between California and the Philippines. Her daughter, five, is half-Filipino, half-American. “I think this will help her stay in touch with her Filipino roots as well,” she said. About 4.6 million people in the US identify as Filipino, according to the 2023 US Census Bureau. Filipino-Americans are the third-largest Asian-origin population living in the US, behind India and China. The film is co-directed by Filipino-American Januel Mercado and Joel Crawford and features a cast of Filipino entertainers including Grammy-winning artist H.E.R., Filipino actress Liza Soberano and Tony Award winner Lea Salonga. “There have always been Filipinos in Hollywood, kind of paving the way for all of us,” Soberano told Reuters. “But it’s only now that there’s really been a spotlight shown on Filipinos and Filipino culture.” Historically, Filipino or Filipino-American culture has rarely made it into the “mainstream”, according to James Zarsadiaz, an associate professor of history at the University of San Francisco who researches Asian-American history. “[They] have typically been relegated to independent or other digital spaces with niche audiences,” he said, adding that many of the films that were successful in the US “largely focused on Asian experiences in Asia” and featured East or South Asian stories. Cultural roots For Filipinos abroad, it is not just a question of Hollywood recognising their culture, but also whether it can help younger generations stay in touch with their heritage. Pia Lingasin was 16 when she and her family moved from Manila to Los Angeles. Now 38, the accountant wants her two children, who are full Filipinos, to understand what it means to be Filipino. “I want my kids to understand how rich our culture is even though we are far away from it geographically. I want them to appreciate their roots and learn to be proud to be Filipino,” she said. Seeing their culture reflected on screen carries particular weight for Filipinos, whose identities and experiences have been shaped by their country’s colonial history, according to media observers. American rule had formed institutions, language and world views in the Philippines but Filipino-American experiences were often poorly represented in the US, said Daphne-Tatiana Canlas, a broadcast communication associate professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s College of Media and Communication. The desire for representation “reads as a symptom of the longer histories of colonialism”, according to Leland Tabares, an assistant professor of race, ethnicity and migration studies at Colorado College. “Maybe the broader American base doesn’t really know how to make sense of them within the Asian-American cultural imaginary,” he said. Recognition was significant not only for Filipinos in the US but also for those in the Philippines, where migration and separation had shaped many families, Canlas said. “Almost every Filipino has a story about migration, separation, forgetting and the work of remembering,” she said. Watching their loved ones’ struggles appearing on screen assured them that “they are seen”. Asian audience Cultural recognition is only part of the explanation for Hollywood’s growing interest in Filipino stories. The potential size and purchasing power of Asian audiences are also factors, according to the observers. “As the third-largest cultural group of Asian heritage in the US, Filipinos and Filipino-Americans as an audience cannot be ignored any more,” Canlas said. Factors such as “the internet, outsourced labour, lowering of trade barriers and the pivot to Asian markets by transnational companies”, had made studios such as DreamWorks pay more attention to the region, said Cherish Aileen Brillon, an associate professor of broadcast communication at UP Diliman CMC. Asian audiences were also increasingly exposed to global popular culture, she said. Tabares compared the film to Netflix’s hugely successful KPop Demon Hunters, which put South Korean culture and a Korean-American story before a global audience. “KPop Demon Hunters and its popularity opened up space for other kinds of diasporic Asian ethnic communities to gain representational traction,” he said. “What drives it is consumer spending power. And there are issues around diversity and equity – it looks good for Hollywood to be diverse and equitable, especially in these highly politicised times.” But true representation should go beyond cultural symbols or isolated anecdotes, Canlas said. Filipino audiences wanted to understand “the complex web of events that led to current conditions” and how those histories had affected their communities. “The hope is that films and other media like Forgotten Island are similarly cognisant of the power they have to sustain these conversations, possibly inspiring other Southeast Asian creators to tell their own ‘forgotten’ stories.”

title: How Kenya’s sacred Mrima Hill became new front in US-China minerals rivalry
description: American and Chinese bidders are vying for rights to develop a sacred Kenyan forest rich in rare earths and niobium.
content: Mrima Hill, a sacred site about 65km (40 miles) southwest of Mombasa on Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast, is emerging as a new front in the US-China rivalry for critical minerals. US-led and Chinese bidders are competing for rights to develop the site, which is rich in rare earths and niobium, a metal used to make steel stronger and lighter. American officials have offered to support Kenya’s development of its domestic critical minerals processing industry as Washington seeks to challenge Beijing’s dominance of global rare earth refining. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Kenyan President William Ruto on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week. They discussed how Kenya’s critical minerals resources could “position the country as a key player in the sector while presenting opportunities for US firms to provide value addition”. A senior US delegation also made the case for such American participation at the AmCham Business Summit in Nairobi on September 9. It included Frank Garcia, assistant secretary of state for African affairs, and Chris Kulukundis, acting deputy assistant secretary of state for Southern Africa, foreign assistance and critical minerals. Washington is trying to reduce its reliance on China for processed rare earths. China accounted for about 85 per cent of global rare earth refining in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency. Aly-Khan Satchu, a geoeconomic analyst focused on sub-Saharan Africa, said the US-China contest went beyond simply securing mineral deposits. “Ultimately, the US-China competition around critical minerals is less about access to those minerals and more about the refining infrastructure,” he said. “China holds a decade’s worth of advantage,” Satchu added. Kenya, he said, should assess competing offers with that wider strategic context in mind. Garcia said Washington was prepared to support Kenya’s efforts to build its mining and processing industries. “Critical minerals are a top priority for President Donald Trump,” he said. “We are ready to work with Kenya as it becomes a regional leader in this space.” In remarks that appeared to take a thinly veiled swipe at China, Garcia said: “American companies are not here to extract and ship. That is not a partnership. That is extraction.” Garcia added that US involvement would include investment in communities, workforce development and technology transfer. He said Washington wanted more processing to take place in Kenya, creating local jobs and allowing the host country to capture more of the minerals’ value. At the same event, Kulukundis said two US-led consortiums were among the bidders seeking development rights at Mrima Hill, where historical studies indicate the presence of about 105 million tonnes of mineralised ore. Kenya launched an international tender in March to select a developer for the deposit, whose rare earth and niobium resources have been valued at US$62.4 billion. Mining principal secretary Harry Kimtai said six candidates remained in contention, down from 13 groups that initially showed interest. Two of the remaining bidders were Chinese, he said. “The deal has not been closed,” Kimtai said. The Mrima Earth Limited Consortium, led by New York-listed Critical Metals Corp, said in July that it had advanced in the tender. Australian companies RareX and Iluka Resources had formed a consortium and sought prospecting rights over Mrima Hill before the international competition began. The identities of the other bidders have not been publicly disclosed. Chris Berry, head of US-based commodities advisory firm House Mountain Partners, said the US government had proven to be aggressive when funding domestic rare earth projects such as MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. “The US presence in this bidding war indicates that Western interests are looking to diversify supply chains and bolster allied efforts to counter China’s grip on critical mineral supply chains both in Africa and globally,” Berry said. On whether US-backed processing in producing countries could compete with China, Berry said: “Absolutely, but the timing here is crucial. The US isn’t competitive today, but that can change with continued investment and offtake agreements.” He cautioned that reducing dependence on China would take years. “Japan has been working to minimise its dependence on Chinese materials for 15 years and is still perhaps 60 per cent dependent on Chinese imports, down from 90 per cent originally. Untangling supply chains is a long, hard slog.” US interest in Mrima Hill was apparent by June last year, when Marc Dillard, who was then serving as charge d’affaires at the US embassy in Kenya, visited the site. Agence France-Presse later reported, citing a community guard, that Chinese nationals had also tried to enter the area but were turned away. Local residents have resisted previous plans to mine Mrima Hill, which is a “Kaya”, a sacred forest and ancestral site for the Digo, a coastal people belonging to the nine-group Mijikenda community. The forest was designated a national monument in 1992. Residents fear mining would damage shrines and wildlife habitat, lead to evictions, and threaten farming and access to forest resources. Washington is also pursuing mineral agreements elsewhere in Africa. In December last year, the US signed an agreement giving qualifying American investors preferential access to selected mining projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Washington has since backed US-based Virtus Minerals’ acquisition of Chemaf, a local operator of copper and cobalt projects. The deal followed the collapse of a planned sale to a unit of Chinese state-owned Norinco after Kinshasa withheld approval, reportedly following US pressure. The outcome marked a direct US gain at China’s expense in the contest for Congolese minerals. The US is also seeking a larger role in Nigeria, where lithium, nickel, copper and rare earth prospects have been identified. Last month, solid minerals minister Dele Alake said he led a delegation to the White House to discuss American investment in Nigeria’s minerals sector. “We talked about moving beyond simple extraction and working together across the entire supply chain, from exploration and mining to local processing and refining,” Alake said after talks with National Security Council official David Copley. Washington is entering a sector where Chinese companies already have a sizeable presence. Chinese firms had invested more than US$1.3 billion in lithium processing since late 2023, including a US$250 million plant commissioned in Nasarawa state in July, according to the Nigerian government.

title: Australia just changed its visa rules. So what about its bespoke Hong Kong pathway?
description: New rules barring applicants from bringing along families have raised concerns among some Hongkongers on study-to-migrate pathway.
content: Hongkongers aiming to settle in Australia through a bespoke study-to-migrate pathway will not be exempt from new rules barring applicants from bringing along their families, the country’s home affairs authorities have said. The new rules, announced last month, have raised concerns among some Hongkongers, especially those who had hoped to bring their families while pursuing their studies in Australia before applying for temporary graduate visas to settle in the country. On September 17, Tony Burke, who serves as both Australia’s minister for home affairs and as its minister for immigration and citizenship, said authorities would no longer allow international students to attach family members to their student or graduate visas. But he added that the government would not break up “families onshore”. “We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over,” he said. The rules were revised as the Australian government faces mounting pressure from Pauline Hanson, leader of the far-right One Nation party, who has blamed the country’s housing crisis on migration. But exemptions have been granted to certain countries and students. “We have special visa conditions, which will still allow it for the Pacific and for the Asean nations, and for certain courses, for example, PhD courses, they’ll be able to bring family,” Burke said earlier. The South China Morning Post recently contacted the Australian Department of Home Affairs for comment on how the latest rules would affect the Hong Kong Stream launched in March 2022. The pathway allows Hong Kong and British National (Overseas) passport holders to graduate from Australian universities and then live in the country for three or four years on temporary graduate visas, after which they are eligible to apply for permanent residency. Australia, in the same vein as Britain and Canada, offered its bespoke immigration pathway for Hongkongers after Beijing imposed the national security law on the city in 2020. The scheme was described as a study-to-migrate immigration pathway under which student visa holders could bring their families. “There are no general exemptions for Hong Kong citizens and British National Overseas (BNO) passport holders for changes restricting the ability of student and temporary graduate visa applicants to include family members in their application,” a department spokesman said. “Family members will not be allowed to apply for a student or temporary graduate visa as a secondary applicant after the main applicant has been granted a visa. This will apply to all current and future student and temporary graduate visa holders onshore and offshore.” The spokesman added that applicants for permanent residency would continue to be able to include family members in their visa applications. Australia issued 11,594 student visas for higher education and 1,354 related dependant visas to Hongkongers between July 2022 and June 2026. The number of such student visas issued between July 2022 and June 2023, the first financial year of the pathway’s launch in Australia, reached 3,831, marking a 13-year high. The number of dependant visas during that period also shot up to an unprecedentedly high level of 608, compared with an average of 100 annually. Both numbers have come down significantly after the emigration wave subsided. Jane Poon, a leader of community group Australia-Hong Kong Link, said she hoped the country’s government could offer exemptions to temporary graduate visa applicants who had already brought their families over. “We are preparing to submit our views to the Home Affairs Department to reflect the concerns of Hong Kong students who now study in Australia and the ones who are ready to use the pathway to move to Australia,” she said. Willy Kwong, general manager at AAS Education Consultancy specialising in Australian overseas education and a registered migration agent in the country, said that while the details had yet to be worded in legislation, the new rules would generally affect two groups of people from Hong Kong. The first was those still planning to migrate with their whole families to Australia under the bespoke pathway, as they might be unable to use student visas to bring their dependants, while the second was those set to graduate and apply for dependant visas for their families, he said. But Kwong said he did not think banning student visa holders from applying for dependant visas would reduce the number of people going to Australia to study higher education. “The new policy would have minimal effect on the general high school and school leavers to [Australia’s] higher education market. Having dependant options is not a key consideration when choosing a study destination,” he said. “Factors like university rankings, subject rankings, career outlook, quality of teaching, cost of living remain the primary concerns.” He also noted that fewer than 200 dependant visas were issued to the families of student visa holders between July 2025 and June last year, which accounted for less than 8 per cent of the total number of student visa holders. Over the same period, Australia issued 2,446 student visas to Hongkongers who had pursued higher education in the country – a record low since such data became available from 2005-06.

title: Inside Blackpink star Lisa’s luxury watch collection: from Rolex and Hermès to Patek Philippe
description: From a ‘Tiffany Blue’ Rolex Oyster Perpetual to a customised Cartier Tank, the K-pop icon’s timepiece collection is far more eclectic than fans might expect.
content: Lalisa Manobal – better known to just about everyone on the planet as Lisa – has never been afraid to stand out. The Thai-born star smashed her way into the K-pop game as YG Entertainment’s first non-ethnically Korean star, broke records with girl group Blackpink and as a solo artist, and has since made the leap onto the small screen as an actress. Somewhere along the way, she’s also amassed a very cool watch collection. She has also become a fixture in the luxury fashion world, favouring chic French houses and a polished, often understated look over whatever trend is loudest. Her watches follow a similar pattern: elegant, feminine pieces from some of the biggest names in Swiss watchmaking, mixed with the occasional extravagant number that shows off her more playful side. And there’s no sign she’s slowing down. This November, Lisa will take to the stage in Las Vegas, becoming the first K-pop artist to headline her own residency in the city – another historic milestone in a career already full of them. From classic Rolexes to custom Bulgari creations, here are some of the stand-out luxury watches spotted on Blackpink’s Lisa. Rolex Datejust 31 Everose First up is a timeless classic that would look at home on just about anyone: the Rolex Oyster Perpetual Datejust. Lisa opted for an 18-carat Everose gold version with a 31mm case, complete with diamond hour markers and Rolex’s prestigious President bracelet – a fittingly boss choice for one of K-pop’s biggest stars. Rolex Lady-Datejust A rose-gold Rolex has a certain feminine aura, but sometimes it’s nice to wear an even daintier piece of horlogerie. Lisa is also reportedly a fan of Rolex’s Lady-Datejust collection, which takes the classic Datejust look and shrinks it down into a petite 28 mm case that won’t overwhelm a slender wrist. She’s been spotted in several references over the years, including two-tone and solid-gold models. Rolex “Tiffany Blue” Oyster Perpetual This one’s for the trend-lovers. Rolex’s turquoise-blue Oyster Perpetual became one of the hottest watches of the early 2020s, with its vivid dial helping turn an otherwise understated Rolex into a holy grail piece thanks to the informal association with the Tiffany brand. Lisa was among those spotted wearing one shortly after its debut, proving her keen eye for what’s happening in the watch world. The colour also landed at exactly the right moment. Turquoise – or Tiffany blue, as it quickly became known among collectors – became something of an industry obsession, with everyone from Patek Philippe, through its actual collaboration with Tiffany & Co., to far more accessible brands like Casio getting in on the action. Patek Philippe Complications World Time On the topic of Patek Philippe, Lisa has at least a couple in her arsenal. And for a jet-setter who’s constantly hopping between red carpets, performances and recording sessions around the world, a World Time feels particularly fitting (sure, you could check your phone for the time – but what kind of a flex is that?). This clever complication displays all 24 time zones at once, with cities from around the globe circling a hand-guilloché dial. Lisa’s Ref. 7130G-016 pairs an 18k white-gold case with a blue-grey dial featuring an old basket-weave motif and a blue alligator strap. It’s a practical choice for a star whose career and schedule are decidedly international. Patek Philippe Nautilus As a global megastar, it’s unsurprising that Lisa has managed to also get her hands on one of Patek Philippe’s most coveted models: the Nautilus. Hers, though, is a particularly feminine take on the icon. The quartz-powered 32mm Ref. 7010/1R-013 comes in rose gold with a rich purple lacquered dial and a bezel set with 46 diamonds. It’s still a serious watch-world status symbol, but one that still feels distinctly like her: playful yet polished, with a decent sprinkle of diamonds for good measure. Hublot Big Bang One Click King Gold Rainbow Next up is a banger of a watch: Hublot’s Big Bang One Click King Gold Rainbow. Despite the name, there’s no connection to Lisa’s fellow K-pop icons BigBang. Instead, the fireworks come courtesy of a riot of coloured gemstones, with sapphires, rubies, amethysts, topazes and tsavorites creating a full rainbow across the dial, bezel and case. Lisa’s version is the petite 33mm model, with a simple, complication-free dial that leaves plenty of room for what really matters here: more gems. Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Mini Big in name, tiny in size, Lisa’s Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Mini in Frosted Gold is almost as cute as she is. Measuring a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it 23mm, this six-figure piece sits at the tiniest end of the Royal Oak spectrum. Yet it still packs in the collection’s signatures – the octagonal bezel, exposed screwheads and integrated bracelet – rendered in shimmering Frosted Gold and shrunk down into a seriously dainty piece of wrist candy. And when she’s feeling something a little more heavyweight, Lisa also has a larger 37mm Royal Oak in rose gold that’s become a regular in her rotation. Hermès Faubourg Joaillière She’s not all about the Swiss watchmakers; Lisa has a fair few French jewellery watches in the mix, too. Among the most elegant is the Hermès Faubourg Joaillière, a super-dainty 15mm affair that is almost unbearably chic. This high jewellery version pairs the tiny white-gold case with a beautifully striated malachite dial, diamond hour markers and an emerald-set bezel, with even more diamonds and emeralds covering the slender white-gold bracelet. Something to pair with all her Hermès Birkin bags, which she’s also known to collect. Cartier Tank customised by LaCalifornienne She also has several Cartier watches to speak of, including a gorgeous vintage Tank customised by Los Angeles-based LaCalifornienne. The company takes classic vintage watches and gives them a California makeover with brightly repainted dials and colourful striped straps – Lisa’s pink-on-pink version being a particularly fun example. But she appreciates Cartier in its more traditional forms, too, with a sleek silver-toned Panthère de Cartier and the sculptural, now-discontinued La Doña also reportedly in her collection. Bulgari Serpenti Tubogas Of course, Lisa has been a Bulgari ambassador since 2020, so the Italian house is well represented in her watch box. The most luxurious might be the red-carpet-ready Serpenti Tubogas, an unmistakably Bulgari design with a flexible coiling bracelet that wraps around the wrist and a serpent’s head doubling as the watch case – all covered in demi-pavé diamonds. She’s also worn the sleeker Serpenti Seduttori, as well as the two limited-edition Bulgari watches created in her name. But while Bulgari may be the brand she officially represents, the rest of her collection makes one thing pretty clear: Lisa is genuinely into her watches. From Patek Philippe and Rolex to Audemars Piguet, Hublot, Hermès and Cartier, she has amassed some seriously special pieces over the years that she’ll likely hold on to.

title: Letters | Is Hong Kong efficient enough to deploy long-term mainland Chinese capital?
description: Readers discuss the role Hong Kong can play as the national pension fund diversifies its asset allocation, how ordinary Hongkongers can contribute to poverty alleviation, and flight costs.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to the report, “China’s pension fund doubles offshore exposure in quest for higher returns” (September 3). As China’s national pension reserve diversifies its sizeable asset allocation, Hong Kong stands to benefit. Hong Kong’s role as a gateway between mainland China and global markets is often taken for granted. Much of the discussion seems to revolve around one assumption: Hong Kong should not be left behind. But should we be asking instead whether Hong Kong is efficient enough to deploy such long-term capital? Investment cost should be a crucial consideration for a mega pension fund. According to the report, offshore investment assets held by the National Social Security Fund reached 580.02 billion yuan (US$86.4 billion) at the end of 2025. Even a seemingly modest investment cost of 0.1 per cent per year would amount to 580 million yuan per year, before taking investment returns into account. While the pension fund is sovereign wealth, it ultimately serves as a basic financial anchor for generations of ordinary Chinese as the population ages. Thus, if Hong Kong is to serve as a gateway for China’s pension fund to diversify globally, it must also be an efficient one, keeping investment costs low. Its financial markets should offer a sufficiently broad and cost-efficient shelf of investment products, spanning equities, bonds, commodities and alternative assets. Otherwise, Hong Kong risks serving merely as a financial transit hub, rather than adding unique value to the long-term capital that ultimately supports the retirement security of ordinary Chinese. In this sense, Hong Kong should focus more on how efficiently it can absorb and deploy long-term capital. Apart from expanding the financial product shelf, the real test of Hong Kong’s competitiveness is whether it can offer long-term investors efficient, scalable and cost-effective ways to diversify globally. After all, higher returns can be pursued but never guaranteed. Investment costs, by contrast, can be controlled. For a pension reserve of this huge scale and with such a long investment horizon, that difference matters. It should be central to how Hong Kong defines the value of its proposition as a financial hub. Jiannan Sun, Beijing Hong Kong’s wealth gap is a call to action The heat Hong Kong has experienced in recent weeks, particularly in August, has drawn attention to the suffering of residents of subdivided flats. The usual response to these appalling living conditions may centre around government subsidies and policies that alleviate poverty. While these measures can certainly effect large-scale change for low-income households in Hong Kong, we must not forget our power, as individuals, to make a difference. A problem like poverty could seem too vast for us to tackle, yet volunteering at The Borgen Project, an advocacy organisation focusing on global humanitarian issues, has taught me the many ways in which we can create a positive impact on the lives of the disempowered and impoverished, from donating to NGOs to posting a meaningful article on social media. When you think of Hong Kong, a city mired in poverty does not necessarily come to mind. However, behind the glittering skyscrapers are cramped cage homes and shabby streets. It may be tempting to detach ourselves from suffering, to reduce it to statistics and phone screens. However, if we look beyond the words of news reports to the real people and circumstances they describe, we may find the empathy and resolve needed to help the economically underprivileged in Hong Kong. The massive wealth gap in Hong Kong is not just a topic for intellectual discussion but a call to immediate, concrete actions that rely on no one but ourselves. Katy Wong, Taikoo Shing As flight prices soar, break journey “Soaring high” seems to apply more to Cathay Pacific’s prices than to aircraft altitude these days. As Hong Kong’s hub airline, it is unsurprising that direct flights to popular destinations demand a premium. Customers do, however, have a choice and bargains, regardless of class of travel, abound. Breaking your journey can be more rewarding than breaking the bank. Mark Peaker, The Peak

title: Japanese museums shun video artwork on wartime atrocities acclaimed abroad
description: ‘The work will only truly be complete when people can see it in Japan,’ Meiro Koizumi says of his award-winning creation.
content: A video installation built around the testimony of a former Japanese soldier on the killing of civilians and sexual assault in wartime China will go on display in London in October, even as its creator struggles to find a museum willing to exhibit the award-winning work in Japan. Created by contemporary artist Meiro Koizumi, “The Angels of Testimony”, has won acclaim overseas, but Japanese museums have been reluctant to exhibit the work, which confronts memories of violence committed by Japanese troops during the Sino-Japanese war. “The work will only truly be complete when people can see it in Japan,” said Koizumi, 50, who hopes it will eventually be exhibited in his home country. Three screens emerge from the darkness of the exhibition space. At the centre is the late Hajime Kondo, a former Imperial Japanese Army soldier who was 99 when the work was filmed. Kondo entered military service in 1940 and was sent to China, where he fought in areas including Shanxi province. A book published in 2005 compiling his testimony recounts an episode in which another soldier showed him the brain of a Chinese person, saying it could cure illness. “Do you remember?” Kondo is asked in the video. Apparently unable to recall the episode, he breaks down in tears. On the other two screens, young people recite Kondo’s testimony on the streets of Tokyo. They recount how Kondo, after being told it was part of his training as a soldier, bayoneted a Chinese person to death and how he joined other Japanese soldiers in sexually assaulting a woman they had captured. Koizumi believed such testimony needed to be passed on and chose to give it expression through his art. He began studying video art at a university in London in 1999 and later worked in the Netherlands before returning to Japan in 2007. Troubled by what he saw as the romanticisation in films and novels of Japanese soldiers fighting to the death and kamikaze attacks during second world war, Koizumi began confronting the realities of war through his work. “The Angels of Testimony”, centred on Kondo’s memories of violence he committed, received the Artes Mundi Prize, a major British contemporary art award, in 2021. The work has since been exhibited in countries including Britain, the United Arab Emirates and the Netherlands. In Japan, however, Koizumi said museums have asked him to substitute another work or exhibition plans have fallen through altogether. At the 2019 Aichi Triennale, an exhibition that included a statue symbolising “comfort women”, who were forced to work in the Japanese military’s wartime brothels, was temporarily closed after a series of protests and threats. Koizumi, who exhibited paintings at the festival, said the episode may have made museums more cautious. “Museum staff probably think, ‘What if something happens?’” he said. The London exhibition will run from October 1 to November 20 and is organised by the Daiwa Anglo-Japanese Foundation, a London-based organisation promoting exchanges between Japan and Britain. Nana Ota, 41, who is overseeing the exhibition, said she was moved by Koizumi’s determination to confront a history of violence that many would rather look away from and to pass those memories on to future generations. “Even if there are protests, we won’t call off the exhibition,” she said. “I hope people will see the work and think about how deeply wartime violence can become etched in the hearts of those who experienced it, while also reflecting on the wars taking place today.”

title: How Asia-Pacific property markets are drawing fresh capital despite US rate uncertainty
description: Hong Kong, Sydney and South Korea emerge as key targets as investors adjust strategies to a higher-rate environment, analysts say.
content: Property markets in the Asia-Pacific region are likely to remain attractive despite heightened uncertainty over monetary policy after the US Federal Reserve delivered its first interest rate increase in more than three years this month, analysts say, with several asset classes and sectors expected to draw investor interest. “We’ve seen volumes, specifically cross-border volumes in the region, increase by around 30 per cent to date,” said Emily Fell, senior director for living sectors in Asia-Pacific capital markets at Savills. “I think, as opposed to seeing a pullback generally, it’s more a change in strategy and a pivot in sector [focus].” Mainland China was the region’s most active real estate market, with investment surging 154 per cent year on year to US$13 billion in the second quarter of 2026, according to financial data provider MSCI. Japan ranked second with US$9.7 billion worth of deals, followed by Australia with US$8 billion. Hong Kong ranked fifth with US$2.5 billion, but recorded the strongest growth at 172 per cent. Across the region, commercial real estate transactions rose 20 per cent to US$46.1 billion in the same period, according to MSCI. By asset class, office properties attracted the most investment at US$15.7 billion, followed by retail at US$11.9 billion and industrial at US$9.7 billion. The market to focus on would be South Korea, where the ageing population will, over the next decade, provide very strong fundamentals for that sector’s growth Emily Fell, Savills Fell identified Sydney’s co-living segment and South Korea’s senior living assets as among the markets with the strongest growth potential amid continued uncertainty over monetary policy. “The Sydney co-living segment is focusing on the refurbishment of hotels or offices into co-living spaces,” she said. “Sydney’s central business district is particularly attractive because it has very clear planning pathways, favourable tax treatment and a wide demand pool, and remains structurally undersupplied. That’s a sector where we’re seeing a huge amount of capital interest.” At the same time, South Korea’s rapidly ageing population is creating opportunities for investors. “The market to focus on would be South Korea, where the ageing population will, over the next decade, provide very strong fundamentals for that sector’s growth,” Fell said. One deal highlighting investor confidence in the sector came in March, when Hyundai Haim Asset Management, backed by Hyundai Marine and Fire Insurance, signed a contract to acquire the Mokdong Artist Center in Seoul. The site would be redeveloped into a 400-room senior living complex in a project worth 500 billion won (US$368 million), according to Savills. Hong Kong – where monetary policy moves largely in lockstep with the US – was likely to continue attracting capital from investors in Singapore, Malaysia and elsewhere seeking property bargains, said Neil Brookes, head of Asia-Pacific capital markets at Savills. “Buyers here are not necessarily chasing yield, so they’re not coming in looking at the cost of debt at, say, 4.5 per cent,” Brookes said. “But what we have seen are discounts of 40 to 50 per cent to peak pricing.” Looking at the last 30 major deals in the first half of the year, most involved distressed assets, including receivership sales, he added. “So, I think a lot of groups are coming in because they see that there are really good discounts on previous pricing available,” Brookes said. As of early last week, Southeast Asian investors had emerged as the largest non-local buyers of Hong Kong commercial property this year, led by Singapore-based capital, according to Savills. Out of the HK$30.36 billion worth of commercial property deals, Southeast Asian investors contributed HK$3.37 billion, or more than 11 per cent of the total value, Savills said. When it comes to Asia, investors are driven by GDP growth and significant structural demographic trends which are not impacted by Fed rates Tim Graham, JLL Capital Markets Beyond defensive investment strategies, the overall fundamentals of Asian property markets remained strong and could cushion any impact from further monetary tightening, said Tim Graham, global lead of international and strategic capital at JLL Capital Markets. “The fundamentals of the market look strong heading into the fourth quarter and 2027,” Graham said. “On overall real estate sentiment, I maintain the view that when it comes to Asia, investors are driven by GDP [gross domestic product] growth and significant structural demographic trends which are not impacted by Fed rates, namely the rental market.” Graham said office markets with strong underlying fundamentals and limited development pipelines offered strong rental growth prospects and remained attractive to cross-border capital. “We are also seeing increased allocations to living sectors across the region, including purpose-built student accommodation, where demand is supported by structural drivers rather than cyclical factors,” he said. “These sectors offer investors resilient occupancy and income through periods of greater macroeconomic uncertainty.”

title: Should we ban children’s outdoor sports when the Observatory issues a heat warning?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
A University of Hong Kong study published last year found that heatwaves in the city over the past decade, 18 in total, may have contributed to 1,677 excess deaths.
Imagine: it’s climbing to 40 degrees Celsius and you have a physical education (PE) lesson coming up. I have experienced this: nonstop sweating and shortness of breath, as if I were moving through thick, heavy soup.
But aside from feeling unwell, there are dozens of other risks that come with sports in extreme weather. That is why I support banning outdoor exercise when the Hong Kong Observatory issues a heat warning.
Doing outdoor exercise in extremely hot conditions increases your risk of heatstroke. In June, an 11-year-old boy surnamed Tsang died from heatstroke after running at Tseung Kwan O Sports Ground, where both temperature and humidity were high.
This heartbreaking case illustrates how physical activity in hot weather can result in fatal heatstroke.
Research has found that our bodies’ natural cooling systems are easily overwhelmed by the combination of excessive environmental heat and internal heat generated by physical activity. Doing an activity outdoors in high temperatures also causes a sharp decline in endurance, as the heart works much harder to pump blood to the working muscles while trying to dissipate heat.
In my experience, running in hot weather is much more exhausting than in more suitable conditions. When we have to run under high temperatures, I end up walking for several of the laps.
In addition to reducing endurance, exercising outdoors in extreme heat also affects cognitive functions. We need more time to react and make decisions because hot weather forces your body to redirect blood flow to the skin to cool you.
This reduces oxygen delivery to the brain and impairs neural activity in regions responsible for memory and decision making.
Some may argue that cancelling outdoor sports means children would be unable to play any sports for the whole summer – during which the forecaster frequently issues hot weather warnings.
However, banning outdoor sports does not mean children cannot engage in physical activity. Instead, children can exercise safely in indoor areas, such as school halls and gyms.
Children should not be banned from outdoor sports when the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) issues a heat warning. A total ban disregards the established practice of risk management and our ability to adapt activities safely.
The primary goal should be to manage risk, not eliminate activity entirely. A more measured approach would be one focusing on modification, preparation and supervision. This would be more effective and beneficial for children.
The medical consensus is clear: with the right precautions, most healthy children can safely play an outdoor sport in hot weather.
In its policy statement on climatic heat stress and exercising children and adolescents, the American Academy of Paediatrics (AAP) emphasises that heat-related illness is “usually preventable” when known risk factors are properly managed. These factors, such as inadequate hydration, excessive exertion and insufficient rest, are all modifiable.
Blanket bans remove the opportunity to teach and practise these vital safety habits.
Hong Kong’s weather forecaster issues distinct heat-related warnings: “Very Hot” as it reaches 33 degrees Celsius and “Extremely Hot” for 35 degrees and above.
The guidelines state that when temperatures reach 35 degrees or above, “vigorous physical activities should be avoided”. The key word here is “vigorous”. The guideline permits lighter exercise, modified games or activities moved to shaded areas.
This is very different from a total ban on outdoor sports.
Other official guidelines from health and education authorities consistently recommend adapting activities, not cancelling them outright. They suggest measures such as rescheduling activities to cooler parts of the day, such as the morning or late afternoon, and ensuring they take place in shaded areas as much as possible.
You should also take frequent hydration breaks and rest periods in cool areas, and wear loose, light-coloured, breathable clothes.
Neither the HKO nor the Education Bureau mandates a total prohibition of outdoor activities. The bureau’s safety guidelines direct schools to “judge whether to proceed, adjust, postpone or cancel activities” based on the specific situation. This decision-making process is far more nuanced than a simple ban.

title: Chinese rubbish station worker scouted for striking looks refuses full-time modelling
description: Leng believes that while collecting rubbish puts food on the table, modelling is a dream, and the two paths do not conflict.
content: A 20-year-old woman who collects and sorts rubbish in eastern China gained online fame after her modelling talents were discovered by the renowned self-made “village supermodel” Lu Xianren, who shares a similar childhood background. Identified by her alias Chaoren Leng (translated as “Superman Leng” in English), the woman assists her boyfriend’s father in managing his rubbish collection business in Taizhou, Zhejiang province, as reported by Shenzhen TV. Born Leng Minghui in a village in Fuyang, eastern Anhui province, she caught significant attention in July last year through videos depicting her work at the refuse collection station. Internet users were captivated by her tall, slim figure and small, chiselled face – features often regarded as essential in the modelling industry – contrasting sharply with her dirt-tainted work clothes and the refuse surrounding her. Leng stands at 1.81 metres tall and weighs 50kg. “Her legs should grace the runway,” one internet user remarked. “She is the female version of Lu Xianren,” another noted, highlighting the striking resemblance between Leng and Lu. At 27, Lu is among China’s top male models. He hails from the rural Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region in southern China, where he was raised by his grandparents while his parents worked in Guangdong province. Lu is a self-taught model who gained attention by posting videos of his distinctive catwalks in the fields. In 2019, he rose to fame with his imaginative self-designed “couture” and fashion shows. To date, Lu has walked at prestigious domestic and international fashion venues, including China Fashion Week, Paris Fashion Week, and Milan Fashion Week. Last year, Lu expressed his desire to leverage his influence to support more children from rural areas with modelling aspirations. Lu also noticed Leng, complimenting her with: “You are a born supermodel.” Since then, Lu has not only shared catwalk tips with Leng but also introduced her to modelling job opportunities. Leng made her debut on the runway at the SS26 Fashion Source in Shenzhen last November. Dressed in an orange outfit inspired by the popular snack latiao (spicy strips), she received enthusiastic applause. Brands that have collaborated with her include car manufacturer CHERY and Chinese luxury art brand Zhu Bingren Copper. However, Leng has turned down offers from several modelling agencies, details of which remain undisclosed. Instead, she chose to stay with her boyfriend’s family and continue working at the refuse collection station as a way to repay their kindness. Leng’s parents divorced and left their hometown when she was just one year old. She was raised by her grandparents in the village. At 15, the death of her grandfather forced her to leave school. She worked as an assembly line worker, a cashier, and took various odd jobs until she met her boyfriend. His family welcomed her and provided financial support for her to complete her secondary school education. Last summer, she graduated from secondary school and took the national university entrance exam, known as the gaokao. Her scores were low, only allowing her to secure a spot at a junior college. Consequently, Leng chose to remain with her boyfriend’s family and assist in their rubbish handling business. Details regarding her boyfriend remain undisclosed in the report. Her videos depict a strong bond with his family; she often affectionately refers to her boyfriend’s 64-year-old father as “Dad.” On social media, she stated: “Collecting rubbish is a means to have a full meal, while modelling is a dream. These two paths do not conflict.” “I am fully aware that opportunities in modelling are rare for me. I must double my efforts,” she mentioned in her videos. Leng stressed: “I am focusing on perfecting details in my catwalk, head turns, poses, and more. Only by doing so can I truly shine on the runway.”

title: Indonesia eyes China for massive 2,772km railway project – with caution
description: As Jakarta explores foreign backing for the Trans-Kalimantan railway, analysts say costly past ventures could shape any coming negotiations.
content: Indonesia is considering Chinese investment to help build a massive 2,772km (1,722 mile) railway network through the vast, resource-rich region of Kalimantan, following the completion of Southeast Asia’s first high-speed line between Jakarta and Bandung, state media and analysts said. However, analysts noted that any future commercial agreements were likely to be negotiated cautiously, given the financial strains that dogged the high-speed line and the challenges that stalled a proposed underground metro project in the congested tourist province of Bali. The Indonesian government was “exploring” potential foreign investment to build the Trans-Kalimantan railway network, according to statements from Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi quoted by Indonesia’s official Antara news agency. The minister said China and Russia had expressed interest in the project. “I think China can offer Indonesia a complete railway ecosystem, including financing, engineering expertise, technology and experienced personnel,” said Siwage Dharma Negara, an Indonesian national and senior fellow with the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Siwage noted that the 142.8km (88.7 mile) “Whoosh” high-speed railway, built by Chinese state contractors on the densely populated island of Java, had already “proven China’s strong engineering capabilities”. The proposed Trans-Kalimantan network would seek to connect disparate areas across the region, which is Indonesia’s portion of the island of Borneo, as part of long-term expansion plans through 2045. The mineral-rich territory is home to Nusantara, the country’s planned new capital, but lacks an operational public railway network. David Feng, an independent railway specialist, said Chinese contractors could draw on extensive experience working across diverse domestic terrains, giving them an edge over competitors from smaller countries while probably costing less. “China has done it all over its own country, so geology-wise they’ve got it all,” Feng said. In Indonesia, he noted, “they might have far more humidity, unstable terrain, stuff like that.” Feng added that he expected China to export an integrated supply chain of railway contractors to Indonesia, from feasibility study researchers to railway builders. However, the legacy of Whoosh could give state planners pause. The line racked up billions of US dollars in debt amid cost overruns and delays, raising concerns about future infrastructure investments backed by China. Siwage called Whoosh’s construction a “cautionary story about project financing” that could prompt officials in Jakarta to negotiate more carefully over who bears commercial risks from future ventures. Paramitaningrum, an international relations lecturer at Bina Nusantara University in Jakarta, said the Kalimantan project also posed significant logistical hurdles, describing it as “high risk in terms of geographical position, technical and financial matters”. “If Chinese investors are involved, do they use the same methods as in developing Whoosh? Can they finish this project on time with good quality?” Beijing, meanwhile, has adjusted its broader international strategy. After years of heavy overseas lending to developing countries, China began tightening its approach to financing infrastructure projects under the Belt and Road Initiative around 2020, including a shift towards smaller projects, according to a report by the Green Finance and Development Centre at Fudan University. In another cause for concern, Bali abandoned plans for a US$20 billion underground metro system that broke ground in 2024, the online information platform Bali Discovery reported in August. The China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), which helped build the Whoosh line, partnered with local firms for the project. While cancelled and downgraded projects are not new to Chinese railway contractors, Feng observed that “obviously it does have an effect (on CRCC)”. A spokesman for Indonesia’s Directorate General of Railways, the national railway regulator and planner, told the South China Morning Post on Saturday that Bali was instead moving towards an electric autonomous rail rapid transit system, with the country’s main state-owned railway operator conducting an initial study with “relevant stakeholders”. The spokesman did not specify whether Chinese contractors could help build the transit system.

title: Hamas leader says Israel to use ‘blood’ of Palestinians as fuel for election
description: Khalil al-Hayya also said Hamas was ready to engage with Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas to ‘achieve genuine unity’.
content: The leader of Hamas brushed aside the possibility of change from Israel’s coming election in an interview, saying he expected Israelis to campaign off Gaza’s “blood”. “Whether this or that person comes to power, or this party or another – our people have suffered at the hands of all Israeli parties,” Khalil al-Hayya told the Qatari station Al-Araby on Saturday. “We absolutely refuse to allow the blood, suffering and cause of the Palestinian people to serve as fuel for Israeli elections. What matters to us is that our people achieve their goals, aspirations and legitimate rights.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight contest as he seeks to stay in power in the October 27 election. Netanyahu has vowed in the run-up to the vote not to withdraw troops from Gaza and rejected a US-led peace initiative in which Hamas said it would surrender weapons, a promise Israel views with scepticism. The vote is the first since Hamas led the deadliest ever attack against Israel on October 7, 2023, with militants storming into southern Israel and killing 1,221 people and dragging 251 others as hostages to Gaza. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has displaced virtually the entire population of Gaza, damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings and killed more than 73,900 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Polls show Netanyahu’s most formidable challenger to be Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who served in Netanyahu’s war cabinet but has accused him of failing strategically. The Palestinian Authority in turn has scheduled a legislative election for November 28, which would be the first in two decades, although there are widespread doubts about whether it will go ahead. Hamas won the last election, held in 2006, defeating Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas’ Fatah. Abbas, 90, has since been ruling by decree, with the legislature not allowed to convene and Hamas seizing control of Gaza. Abbas is based in the West Bank, where the Palestinian Authority wields limited autonomy. “We are ready to sit down with president Abbas to lay the foundations for a national programme and achieve genuine unity,” Hayya said. “If the Palestinian elections are postponed, that step must serve as an entry point for putting the Palestinian house in order.” Hamas has been working on an alliance with Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah figure born in Gaza who has been an interlocutor with the United States on its peace plan. “In the event of a postponement, the alliance will remain intact and open to all, aiming to forge a unified national front,” Hayya said. It remains uncertain if Hamas could even run in the election as Abbas has required all candidates to accept the platform of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, which has recognised Israel’s right to exist since 1993 at the start of the Oslo peace accords. On the regional front, Hayaa said that Hamas had offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, who have carried out escalating attacks against the kingdom since July. “I hope that this will be accepted,” he said of Hamas’ offer. “Hamas is loyal to these peoples, who are our base.” Both the Houthis and Hamas are backed by Iran.

title: In Malaysia, a mother’s love offers her trans daughter refuge
description: For transgender Muslims in Kelantan, quiet family acceptance at home contrasts with growing fear of sharia crackdowns.
content: In a village on the outskirts of Kota Bharu, in Malaysia’s deeply conservative northeastern state of Kelantan, Rozi* has learned to ignore what people say about her daughter. She had known for years that Hana* was different. As a child, Hana preferred girls’ clothes and spent most of her time with girls. Later, after leaving Kelantan to study, she began transitioning and eventually returned home, living openly as a woman. Rozi, 58, struggled to accept it at first, but what troubled her more was the thought that rejecting Hana might push her out of the family altogether. “When you see your own child’s face, what mother does not love her child?” Rozi told This Week in Asia. “No matter how bad people may think your child is, she is still your child. If I didn’t accept her, she would go further and further away from me. I don’t want her to be far away.” That acceptance has turned home into a refuge for Hana, at a time when other transgender Muslims in Kelantan say they have had to become increasingly cautious in public. Kelantan, where 95.5 per cent of the population is Muslim, is the political stronghold of the Islamist Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party, which has governed the state since 1990. The state’s sharia laws penalise gender transition and cross-dressing among Muslims, and recent prosecutions have heightened concerns within the local transgender community over intensifying state scrutiny. Against that backdrop, Rozi said her initial resistance to her daughter’s transition had gradually given way to a quiet acceptance she once thought unlikely. Hana, 27, now regularly returns home, joins family gatherings and brings transgender friends over for meals, while her mother happily fusses over the food. “They are human, too. They want to eat like us, they want to feel loved,” said Rozi, a mother of three who works at a local mosque. “They don’t want to be thrown away by their families.” Private sanctuary Hana began taking hormones around 2019 while living away from Kelantan. By the time she returned, her hair was longer and her appearance had changed enough that her father, picking her up at the station, was taken aback. “My mother said, ‘Whatever people want to say, let them. Just don’t stop coming home’,” Hana said. There are boundaries. The interior designer dresses more conservatively in Kelantan than she does in Kuala Lumpur, where she occasionally travels for work, and says her mother would object if a friend turned up at the family home in revealing clothing. Still, Hana is free to be herself at home – a privilege she knows many of her peers do not share. “As long as my family accepts me, that’s enough,” she said. “What outsiders want to say, I don’t really care.” Hana thinks carefully about what she wears before going out in Kelantan, favouring loose or unisex clothing and understated make-up to avoid drawing the attention of religious enforcement officers. “If you go out, go out for something important,” she said. “We try to avoid making the issue hot again. If there is nothing to do, it’s better to stay home.” Most Kelantanese she encountered were not overtly hostile, Hana said – the uglier reactions tended to appear online, where videos circulated rapidly and social media users tagged religious authorities to demand enforcement action. Another member of Kelantan’s transgender community shared a similar account, saying that while transgender people could still run shops and deal with customers in daily life, public social spaces had noticeably shrunk. “Before, [trans] people would still go out to eat, hang out and meet in public. Now it’s very different. People don’t really do that any more, and even when we gather, it’s usually in small groups, maybe four or five people,” the person said, asking not to be named. “There is fear. Social media is where some of us make money, but at the same time it makes people know where we are and what we are doing.” Shrinking public spaces The growing sense of unease has coincided with a series of recent legal actions. In February, local news outlet Malaysiakini reported that Kelantan had recorded its first prosecution under Section 18 of its 2019 sharia criminal code – which criminalises changing one’s gender – since the law was gazetted in 2020. It was believed to be the first prosecution of its kind in Malaysia. Then, last month, Kelantan lawmakers unanimously passed a revised sharia criminal offences bill, after Malaysia’s Federal Court struck down 16 provisions of the earlier enactment in 2024 for intruding on federal jurisdiction. The updated law retains strict penalties for Muslims who change their gender, help another person to do so or induce someone to transition without a reason permitted under Islamic law. On September 8, a 25-year-old transgender person pleaded not guilty in a Kota Bharu sharia court to “posing as a woman” by wearing women’s clothing. The charge carries a maximum fine of 3,000 ringgit (US$730), up to two years in prison, or both. Kelantan’s leaders have taken a hard line. Deputy chief minister Mohamed Fadzli Hassan said last year that the state “does not recognise deviant cultures that go against Islamic teachings”, describing LGBT practices as “a clear transgression of human nature”. Thilaga Sulathireh, co-founder of the human rights group Justice for Sisters, said the recent cases reflected “a clear clampdown on the visibility of trans people” across the state. Transgender entrepreneurs and social media personalities are particularly exposed, as the same platforms they rely on for income make them visible to religious authorities. “These laws completely disrupt all areas of a trans person’s life: [their ability] to work, move around freely, socialise and be who they are,” Thilaga said. “There is a lot of self-censorship. Movements are restricted.
