Many only go out at selected hours due to fear of arrest.” Justice for Sisters had documented instances of transgender women losing income after curtailing their online presence, Thilaga said, while others avoided shopping centres, beaches and other public spaces known for religious raids. The Kelantan Islamic Religious Affairs Department did not respond to a request for comment from This Week in Asia regarding its enforcement operations. Back in their village, Rozi continues to pray for her daughter, viewing matters of faith as something Hana must ultimately answer for herself. “That is between her and Allah,” she said. “It is not for humans to judge.” What matters most for her is closer to home. “As long as my child is safe,” Rozi said, with teary eyes. “She is still my child.” *Names changed to protect interviewees’ identities

title: Opinion | To understand where Hong Kong is going, start with Tung Chee-hwa
description: To understand Tung is to understand the historical moment in which he stood; Hong Kong’s post-1997 journey started there.
content: On September 8, Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, died. It prompted reflection, not only on a political figure who once stood at the centre of the city’s public life, but also on nearly three decades of change since its return to China. History is rarely shaped by a single person or isolated decisions. Individual choices, institutional adjustments, social expectations and external circumstances all interact to form the historical process. This is particularly true in Tung’s case. To understand the significance of Hong Kong’s first chief executive, one must return to the historical context. British colonial rule left Hong Kong with a highly developed administrative system built around efficiency, procedure and order. This administrative tradition became an important part of Hong Kong’s identity. However, colonial governance also operated under a distinct political structure, where questions of legitimacy, public participation and political accountability were addressed differently from those in modern constitutional systems. After 1997, Hong Kong entered a new stage. The transition was not merely a change of political authority or government institutions. It also involved a transformation in how society understood public power. Citizens increasingly cared not only about whether policies could achieve results, but also why decisions were made, how different views were considered, and who should bear responsibility for consequences. The challenges faced by Tung’s administration reflected a broader tension as Hong Kong moved from a long-established administrative model towards a more complex form of governance. Balancing administrative efficiency with social legitimacy, expert decision-making with public participation, and long-term planning with immediate expectations has become an issue that continues to shape Hong Kong’s public life. It is easy to overlook the uncertainty of that moment. Hong Kong was entering a new stage for which there was no ready-made blueprint. How to build a governance system under “one country, two systems” and the Basic Law; how to integrate institutions into a new constitutional arrangement; and how an international city should redefine its relationship with national development – these questions required answers to be discovered gradually through practice. The complex developments of the decades that followed cannot simply be reduced to one individual, a handful of policy choices or isolated events. Nor can difficulties encountered automatically be interpreted as evidence that Hong Kong’s governance has “failed” or that one country, two systems is fundamentally flawed. If a local housing failure could prove an entire political system flawed, or pandemic coordination problems could invalidate a constitutional framework, few modern systems would pass such a test. A mature understanding of history does not mean refusing to discuss achievements and shortcomings. Rather, it means resisting the temptation to compress history into a single label. A political leader may inevitably be shaped by the limitations of his era, and every administration will leave lessons that deserve reflection. But these realities do not prevent us from recognising the significance of a particular period within the broader historical trajectory. The Hong Kong of 1997 first confronted the challenge of identity and institutional transition. The 2003 Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement with the mainland marked a deeper integration. Subsequently, cross-border infrastructure projects and the development of the Greater Bay Area reshaped Hong Kong’s relationship with surrounding regions. Today, innovation and technology, the Northern Metropolis, new industrial strategies and housing improvement have become the central themes of governance. Each era brings its challenges, and each administration faces its own responsibilities. The significance of the Tung era lies first in its historical position as the starting point of Hong Kong’s post-1997 development. Some initiatives were expanded, some institutions continued to evolve, and some ideas were carried forward by subsequent governments. The story of Hong Kong over the past three decades has never been the record of a single leader. It has been a process shaped by governments, businesses, citizens and society. Looking back does not necessarily require another accounting of merits and faults, nor a reopening of long-standing controversies in a way that creates social division. Individuals eventually leave the historical stage but cities continue moving forward. Hong Kong has faced financial crises, economic restructuring, social challenges and public health emergencies. Its relationship with the mainland, regional connectivity and economic structure continue to change. Today, Hong Kong is still searching for new answers in housing, innovation, industrial transformation, regional integration and global competitiveness. Hong Kong’s journey can be understood as a continuous adjustment between constraints, opportunities and changing expectations. To understand Tung’s role is ultimately to understand the historical moment in which he stood. And to understand where Hong Kong is going, one must first understand where it has come from.

title: How Hong Kong’s old businesses are adapting to new times
description: Change does not follow a single formula and may involve creating new experiences, rebuilding unglamorous systems and adopting AI.
content: In the second of a two-part series on Hong Kong’s economic transformation, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong profile three established enterprises that have rejuvenated their brands and reinvented their businesses. Read part one here. Late into the night, Hong Kong football fans in their twenties, thirties and forties sat in Lin Heung Lau restaurant on Wellington Street watching World Cup matches over dim sum rather than pints at a sports bar. The historic restaurant, traditionally associated with elderly morning-tea regulars, extended its operating hours during the World Cup in the summer, drawing on the expertise of chairman Rocky Wong Hei-yan, a nightlife industry veteran behind once-bustling Lan Kwai Fong venues such as Club No 9, Club Beijing and Magnum. “On that occasion, we were not calculating money only,” he said. “We were looking at brand-building and opening another channel through which we could find customers.” The century-old Lin Heung Lau brand has been rejuvenated with new marketing and business strategies since 2024, when its management was revamped amid a decline in the tradition of people going out for dim sum. The restaurant has hosted a series of “dim sum raves”, taking social media by storm with its tea-infused cocktails and electronic music paired with steaming towers of pork buns and shrimp dumplings. Lin Heung Lau’s football and rave nights illustrate one solution to a question confronting established Hong Kong businesses: how can they follow changing customer habits and find new sources of revenue without discarding the identity that made them valuable? Interviews with family-business scholars and companies ranging from a traditional dried-seafood retailer to a long-established transport operator suggest that transformation does not follow a single formula. It can involve creating new experiences, rebuilding unglamorous back-end systems, adopting artificial intelligence (AI) or allowing a younger generation to experiment. Winnie Peng Qian, director of the Roger King Centre for Asian Family Business and Family Office at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, cautioned against assuming that every established company needed to pursue rapid or radical innovation. “People always think you need to innovate, need to react fast,” she said. “But you see a lot of century-old family businesses in Japan. They’re very small, fewer than 10 people, just a store doing the same thing.” Such companies could instead innovate gradually, she said, while adapting their traditions to remain relevant to the environment they faced. Nightlife meets yum cha Wong saw an opportunity in Lin Heung Lau when it closed during the Covid-19 pandemic, believing its brand had untapped potential despite the difficult environment facing Hong Kong’s catering industry. Wong, the restaurant’s chairman and primary investor, was granted the perpetual right to use the Lin Heung Lau brand in Hong Kong rather than ownership of the underlying intellectual property. He had known the restaurant for more than 25 years, having regularly visited for morning tea after finishing work at his clubs. “I was very familiar with the brand and knew its strengths and weaknesses,” he said. “It was not simply a matter of me taking over and benefiting from a powerful brand. It had already closed. I was setting out with it again and that was a major challenge.” Despite the obvious differences between running nightclubs and operating a traditional Chinese dim sum restaurant frequented in the morning, Wong said both businesses ultimately depended on the same thing: management. “If you manage people properly and they naturally follow the organisation’s instructions, you can succeed in even selling salted crispy peanuts,” he said. “But if management is poor and everything becomes too personalised, it will destroy the entire management system.” Since taking over the operation, Wong has sought to preserve Lin Heung Lau’s traditional yum cha atmosphere and handmade dim sum while reaching beyond the predominantly elderly clientele historically associated with such restaurants. “We are not taking a single direction and targeting only the silver-haired market,” he said. “We are adding new elements to attract different customers – middle-aged people, young people and even children.” Wong did not provide figures for the investment, sales or footfall generated by the football screenings but said they were profitable and attracted a largely younger crowd. He argued that their greater value was promotional, estimating that the equivalent publicity would have cost millions of dollars to reproduce through conventional advertising. Lin Heung Lau had opened or substantially redeveloped five outlets in just over two years, Wong said. Its latest restaurant occupies about 13,000 sq ft at the airport, while other locations include Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui. About 95 per cent of the menu is shared among its restaurants, but each has distinctive dishes or design features. Wong said operators could no longer simply open their doors and assume customers would arrive. “You have to catch the trend,” he said. “A business has to change. If it does not change, customers will not come.” More affordable ready-to-eat abalone At On Kee Dry Seafood, founded in the 1930s, transformation has been less visible to customers but no less extensive. The family business has made traditionally expensive dried gourmet seafood such as abalone more affordable by creating mouth-sized snacks that proved popular with younger shoppers at the city’s signature food fair. As preparing and cooking items like abalone, sea cucumber and duck’s feet can take a couple of days, the group has diversified into ready-to-eat offerings such as frozen and pre-cooked seafood, as well as ready-to-consume soups and desserts. “Our ready-to-eat products have proved to be very popular because they cater to the busy lives of Hongkongers who have a preference for convenience,” said Henry Poon, 27, the fourth generation of the family business. “About two years ago, we developed an individually wrapped abalone snack that could be consumed right away, designed for when people are feeling peckish.” The company was still relying heavily on handwritten notes and fax machines as recently as five years ago. Its six retail stores also handled about 1,000 online orders a day, forcing employees to pack e-commerce purchases on crowded shop floors while serving customers. “After all, we are a very traditional company,” Poon said. “Even five years ago, we weren’t a particularly digital company, relying heavily on handwritten notes and using fax.” Over the past two years, Poon has led a digital transformation, describing it as a “timely catch-up” with the market amid the growing popularity of e-commerce. An enterprise resource planning system consolidates orders placed through On Kee’s website and third-party platforms, streamlining stocking, packing and delivery. The company can process about 1,800 online orders a day, an 80 per cent increase from before. On Kee also introduced a point-of-sale system capable of handling more complex promotions, such as a 10 per cent discount on a second item and 20 per cent off a third. AI has reduced the time needed to calculate how much stock should be taken to exhibitions – important events for the business – from several days to minutes. “We’d typically look at the trend from the past three to four times we took part, as well as our previous orders,” Poon said. “The press of a button generates you a very good forecast table.” The transition remains unfinished. Poon estimated that it could take another three to four years for all the new systems to operate smoothly. ‘Standing still means falling behind’ At Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings, one of Hong Kong’s largest franchised and non-franchised bus operators, the changes in its business and strategies have been sweeping. Founded in 1948 as a car-cleaning service by the late entrepreneur Wong Kwoon-chung, the firm, which earned 82 per cent more year on year in net profit in 2025-26, at HK$268.4 million, is aiming high – literally. It made a breakthrough in the 1990s, taking over bus operations on Lantau Island and coach companies that catered to hotel and tour group operators. A landmark change took place in 2023, when third-generation family members Timothy and James Wong pushed through a new venture, KC Smart Mobility, by investing in electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOL), alongside autonomous vehicles, drones and ride-hailing services. In August, the company worked with mainland Chinese autonomous aerial vehicle manufacturer EHang and tech hub Cyberport to bring an eVTOL to Hong Kong, culminating in the city’s first successful demonstration flight of an unmanned heavy-duty aircraft. “These are medium- to long-term investments that will not be profitable soon,” said Newton Ng, business development director of KC Smart Mobility. “Standing still means falling behind. If we remain the same as we are today, there will not be expansion.” The company plans to buy 30 eVTOLs from EHang for more than HK$70 million, although the aircraft remain at the testing stage. Charging can take more than an hour for a flight lasting about 20 minutes, while Hong Kong does not yet have regulations for commercial operations. Ng said acting early could help the company capture market share. “If government policies are also directed towards newer modes of transport, the earlier we act, the sooner we can possibly capture a larger market share,” he added. Kwoon Chung has already encountered changing customer behaviour in its traditional passenger-transport operation. Its existing limousine customers previously had to telephone the company to reserve vehicles, but increasingly wanted to arrange their journeys online. The operator responded by partnering with ride-hailing company Uber to launch Uber Elite, a premium service combining Kwoon Chung’s vehicles, full-time chauffeurs and local operating experience with the US-based firm’s widely used booking platform and customer reach. The service, Uber’s first of its kind outside the United States, offers pre-booked rides in Mercedes-Benz vehicles for groups of up to six passengers, targeting C-suite executives and business travellers. Customers can book between two hours and 90 days in advance. Ng said demand during the first month was strong enough that the company could not always accommodate requests made at shorter notice. “It’s a changing consumption pattern,” he said. “If we do not develop a model that caters to the trend, some customers will of course drift away over time. “We’ll have to follow the habits of the younger generation and have a presence where they book their commutes.” Space for the next generation Kwoon Chung’s decision to place its experimental businesses in a subsidiary headed by third-generation members reflects one way family companies can pursue transformation without immediately disrupting their core operations. Jeremy Cheng Chi-yeung, an adjunct associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s business school, said such companies could initially be slower to adopt the latest trends but often committed substantial resources once they decided to proceed. One model, he said, was to allow the rising generation to establish a smaller agile unit, the kind created by Kwoon Chung. “The rising generation will build their own team, a small unit, which is meant to be agile, and they can lead faster changes,” Cheng said. “Once they are successful with that particular experiment, they tend to cross-fertilise that in different units in the business itself.” Victoria Wang, a professor at the same institution, said slower adoption did not necessarily mean a family business lacked the ability to survive. “They change slowly to go faster,” she said. “Tradition is legacy, purpose and identity. They very much want to make sure their identity continues.” Transformation, however, does not always require radical innovation. “If a tradition remains relevant, it is valuable,” Peng of Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said. “But if the family is static, very traditional and refuses to change, of course it cannot survive in the long term.” For Lin Heung Lau, this has meant continuing to serve handmade dim sum while challenging assumptions about who should eat it and when. At On Kee, the dried seafood remains, but the handwritten orders and fax machines are disappearing. For Kwoon Chung, the coaches continue operating while the next generation explores modes of transport extending from smartphones to the skies. Peng said the family businesses that endured tended to share two deeper characteristics – a long-term outlook and a sense of responsibility towards society. Their experience of surviving economic and political upheavals helped them look beyond immediate difficulties, while a broader purpose gave future generations a reason to continue beyond preserving their own wealth. “Sometimes you need to stick to who you are and your family values,” Peng said. “The first thing that stands out is a long-term perspective. The other is altruism. You need to care about society.”

title: Review | Godzilla Minus Zero review: visually stunning Japanese monster sequel is full of surprises
description: A new beast joins the chaos in Takashi Yamazaki’s film with Ryunosuke Kamiki and Minami Hamabe that looks good but falls flat towards the end.
content: 3.5/5 stars If the runaway success of 2023’s Godzilla Minus One proved anything, it is that there is plenty of life left in the old kaiju. This century’s revival of the fabled giant monster has been a sort of tit for tat between Hollywood – with Legendary Pictures’ Monsterverse films placing the creature alongside King Kong – and the Japanese originator, Toho, which has also rebooted the franchise. Godzilla Minus One – directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also wrote the script and oversaw the Oscar-winning visual effects – stylishly took audiences back to post-war Japan and the origins of the beast. Now comes the much-hyped sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero, set two years later in 1949. Again with Yamazaki at the helm, it brings us back into the orbit of Koichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a former kamikaze pilot who downed Godzilla in the previous film, and his wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe). “Will we ever live in peace?” Noriko asks early on, and the answer is a resounding “no”. A new giant winged beast named Ghidorah, capable of firing a golden beam akin to Godzilla’s heat ray, has arisen, destroying everything in its path. Those at the Disaster Response Bureau, led by Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), are tasked with defeating the creature, initially in collaboration with the United States military. A meteorologist even suggests a weather-related solution – bizarrely echoing the recent film Pressure, set on the eve of D-Day – until it goes disastrously wrong. Other equally barmy ideas include a “resonance wave amplifier” that lures crows to a building in an eerie take on Alfred Hitchcock’s The Birds. Yamazaki’s script is packed with surprises involving regeneration, revenge and, of course, the return of Godzilla. At its best, Godzilla Minus Zero is a stark reminder of the horrors of Hiroshima, complete with disturbing flashbacks to the aftermath of the atomic bomb. Shot in IMAX, the visuals are stunning, with Godzilla and Ghidorah roaring their way across a bleak post-war landscape. The dogfights and destruction are thrilling, and every bit as jaw-dropping as those in the recent Korean sci-fi blockbuster Hope. Far removed from Adam Wingard’s recent neon-drenched Godzilla films, Yamazaki’s artful endeavour is perfectly encapsulated by a single shot of a missile streaking across the sky, seen through the broken lens of a character’s spectacles. And yet the core relationship between Koichi, Noriko and their adopted child becomes tiresome, bogged down by an awful lot of crying and never delivering the emotional weight needed to complement the carnage. After an impressive first two-thirds, the final act of Godzilla Minus Zero lacks punch exactly when it needs it most. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Mired in match-fixing scandal, Hong Kong’s next opponents Laos hope reinvention holds key
description: Hong Kong open their Fifa Asean Cup against a Laos team where head coach Vladica Grujic is leading a youthful revolution.
content: Vladica Grujic skirted the question over why he wanted to remain Laos head coach after the dismal fallout from their recent Asean Championship campaign, but the inquiry was valid. The opponents for Hong Kong’s opening Fifa Asean Cup match at Kai Tak Stadium on Sunday, Laos made wholesale changes for the tournament after the country’s football federation called for an investigation into alleged match-fixing, bribery and illegal gambling among its own squad following a series of heavy Asean Championship defeats. In games against Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines and Myanmar, they were beaten 5-0, 4-0, 4-1 and 7-2, respectively. For context, in the same competition two years earlier, Laos drew twice, lost 3-2 to Myanmar, and went down 4-1 to eventual champions Vietnam. In the 2026 edition, Viengxay Sydavon scored two own goals, while there were two straight red cards for Phetdavanh Somsanith, and another for Sayfon Keohanam. Keo Souvannasangsgo, the goalkeeper, was the subject of social media scrutiny after he appeared to withdraw his hands from the line of a goalbound shot in the Malaysia loss. Without publicly pointing the finger at any individuals, the Lao Football Federation asked the country’s Ministry of Public Security to open an investigation into their team. They reportedly privately flagged four players. Appointed in February, Grujic named a 23-man Fifa Asean Cup squad featuring 12 uncapped players and 11 teenagers. At the grand old age of 26, forward Kydavone Souvanny is the senior player in the Laos party. In his team’s laboured 3-1 victory over Brunei on Thursday, Grujic fielded a back four whose ages were 16, 17, 18 and 25. Asked directly why he wanted to stay amid the prevailing chaos, Grujic said: “We want to make a new way with young players; they have to play international football. Everyone saw we had a problem when long balls were played behind our last line [against Brunei], but it’s time to learn something through playing senior football.” Although there has been no clear explanation over why this Fifa conception was needed hot on the heels of the Asean Championship finishing one month ago, Grujic echoed the thoughts of his Hong Kong and Myanmar counterparts, Roberto Losada and Jorn Andersen, who both welcomed the opportunity for more competitive football. In the Serb’s case, he was eager that Laos had a speedy opportunity following their Asean Championship debacle to “show our principles, and how we play football”. “We want fast transitions; to quickly win back the ball after we lose it,” Grujic, who spent time as Laos assistant boss 15 years ago, added. Grujic’s world No 186 team performed in keeping with that ranking against a Brunei side eight positions beneath them in the global standings. They were terribly vulnerable against balls struck from deep, and inefficient in front of goal, although in forward Bounphachan Boungkong they boasted the game’s best and most creative player. Nonetheless, Grujic, who has coached in Japan, Thailand and India, said he believed Laos could “beat Hong Kong with our style”. “[Hong Kong] play attacking football and want many touches, which they can do because they have quality players,” he added. The 63-year-old acknowledged, nonetheless, that his side would be at a physical disadvantage, having beaten Brunei in stifling humidity 72 hours before their clash with the city team. “My players won’t be fit like [against Brunei] but we’ll do everything we can to give a good performance and play our style,” he said. Andersen, meanwhile, warned his Myanmar team that they would have to “step up and be better” against Cambodia, also at the 50,000-seat Kai Tak Stadium on Sunday, or risk an early exit. Myanmar, the world No 158 team, had enterprising Timor-Leste’s wastefulness, as much as their own efforts, to thank for a 2-0 victory on Thursday. Although he partially attributed his side’s featureless display to the “very slippery” Mong Kok Stadium turf and the challenging weather conditions, Andersen said he had “never seen the team losing the ball so much”. “It’ll be very hard [against Cambodia],” he added, citing injuries sustained against Timor-Leste when he was already without four “very good” players. Andersen had an immediate impact following his July appointment, leading Myanmar to a landmark 4-1 win in the Philippines during a promising Asean Championship campaign. “Against Timor-Leste, we weren’t in the same shape as in the last tournament,” he said. “We weren’t the best team, but what is important in football is to win. I was proud that the team fought to the end. Winning while not playing well is an improvement for this side, but in the next game we have to take a step up and be better.”

title: After EU-Philippines trade breakthrough, is Asean-wide deal next?
description: A bloc-to-bloc free-trade agreement offers Asean real economic clout, but analysts warn there is still a ‘long way to go’.
content: After a decade of start-stop negotiations, the European Union and the Philippines have found their way to a “substantial agreement” on free trade – one that analysts say could pave the way for Brussels to lock in an Asean-wide pact. The breakthrough, announced on Tuesday, capped talks that began in 2016 and stalled a year later, only to resume again in 2024. “I am proud to say we have delivered a substantial agreement that reflects the ambition both sides brought to the table,” EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said following virtual talks with his Philippine counterpart Cristina Roque. Their call set the trade deal “on a clearer path towards its formal conclusion in the coming months”, the two said in a joint statement issued afterwards, in which they welcomed the promise of new opportunities for “businesses … farmers, manufacturers and consumers on both sides”. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is expected to travel to Manila next year for the deal’s signing once it has been finalised. “This is a major win for both European and Philippine businesses,” EU-Asean Business Council executive director Chris Humphrey said in a statement welcoming the agreement, adding that it paved the way for the Philippines to “strengthen its competitiveness … both as a destination for European investment and as a more important part of regional value chains”. “The challenge now,” Humphrey added, “is to translate the country’s strong fundamentals into a competitive operating environment, making it easier for companies to invest, produce and integrate the Philippines into regional supply chains”. The EU was the Philippines’ fourth-largest trading partner last year, accounting for 8.3 per cent of the country’s total goods trade, with bilateral trade in goods reaching €17.6 billion (US$20.7 billion), according to European Commission figures. In addition to Manila, Brussels has also been in prolonged trade talks with Bangkok and Putrajaya, the latter of which dates as far back as 2010. Negotiators are aiming for both EU trade deals with Thailand and Malaysia to be wrapped up by the end of 2027, the 50th anniversary of the European bloc establishing formal diplomatic relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “However, bilateral agreements should not be the end point,” Humphrey said, noting that European businesses had “consistently called” for a region-to-region free-trade deal. “We hope the EU and Asean will begin laying the groundwork for a broader economic architecture that reflects the scale and strategic importance of the relationship,” he added. Investor appetite Nearly four in five of the 150 European business leaders surveyed by the EU-Asean Business Council earlier this year said they expected to trade more with, and invest more in, Southeast Asia over the next five years. A little more than three in five also said Asean offered the best economic opportunities globally over the same time period. Humphrey said he was confident that the Southeast Asian bloc was “ready to embrace the idea” of a region-to-region deal, following consultations with Asean economic ministers, officials and others at a business summit held in Manila on Tuesday. “The question is the level of ambition on the EU side,” he added. Matthijs van den Broek, a geoeconomic analyst and business consultant based in Southeast Asia, said Asean could become a “central player and a stable economic force” as demand rose for diversified partnerships and supply chains amid growing global unpredictability. “This new reality has made individual Asean member states recognise the urgency not only to further increase intraregional trade and investment but also to complement and align country-specific priority and focus business sectors, consumer segments and products,” he said. Even the region’s “noodle bowl” of overlapping trade agreements need not be fatal to the project, he said, provided “access to the entire Asean region is guaranteed and facilitated by an aligned intraregional infrastructure and supply chain”. With such an alignment, “Asean will be in a better position to present itself as one region,” van den Broek said, adding that Thailand and Vietnam, for example, were already moving in that direction. ‘Long way to go’ Asean’s ongoing free-trade talks with Canada are evidence that the bloc can negotiate as a single entity, according to Humphrey. “There is no reason why they [Asean members] shouldn’t follow the same pattern with the EU,” he said, also pointing to 10 Asean members’ entry into the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2020 – though, crucially, these ascensions were signed and ratified individually, rather than en bloc. Other observers were less optimistic that a wider EU-Asean agreement would materialise any time soon. “Asean as a regional group works by consensus, but as individual sovereign countries, while the EU has a sophisticated majority voting system between its member states and its own EU parliament,” said Carsten Bermig, a policy adviser and director for governance and sustainable development at the Asia-Europe Foundation in Singapore. “That has an impact on the length of negotiations as well as the level of integration both regions can commit to.” Bermig said there was still a “long way to go” until a region-to-region deal was reached, noting that European free-trade agreements “tend to be deeper and more comprehensive than the ones Asean has entered into so far”, with question marks still hanging over the Southeast Asian bloc’s “level of regulatory integration and cooperation”. Then there is past precedent. Van den Broek recalled that initial EU-Asean free-trade talks, launched in 2007, were derailed that same year by a violent crackdown on protesters in Myanmar, where human rights concerns persist to this day. Rather than hold out hope for a fully fledged pact that might be a long time coming, Bermig said the two blocs should instead consider a lighter-touch arrangement, bridging the gap between existing bilateral deals and baseline World Trade Organization rules.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s fight against cancer must begin with early screening
description: The city’s achievements in cutting the rate of cancer-related deaths is impressive but more can be done to ensure timely diagnosis.
content: Cities that host major international medical conferences can expect their own healthcare sector to come under attention. As a popular venue for such “mega-events”, Hong Kong is no exception. These events are also an opportunity for the host to proclaim its achievements. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau did so at the World Cancer Congress, held in Hong Kong for the first time last week. Lo told delegates the city had cut its rate of cancer-related deaths by more than 40 per cent over the past three decades. He said that over the past 10 years, the annual decline in the age-standardised cancer mortality rate was 2.8 per cent for men and 1.7 per cent for women. “This is a remarkable achievement, showing that Hong Kong is really making significant life-saving progress against cancer,” he said. Hong Kong has, indeed, made great strides in the battle against cancer. But, as experts told the South China Morning Post’s Health Matters wellness series recently, there remains room for wider screening and early detection that could save or prolong even more lives. Since modern tracking began in 1983, the number of cancer cases has more than doubled to 38,000, but the risk of dying from the disease has nearly halved from an age-standardised death rate of 136.7 per 100,000 people in 1983 to 71.1 in 2023. This is among the lowest in developed economies. Experts attributed the success to Hong Kong’s access to world-class drugs and treatments but warned that the city must invest more in early prevention and screening to truly lead in cancer management. Hong Kong issued its first Cancer Strategy in 2019. Key areas include enhancing screening and reducing tobacco and alcohol use. The government has said it would evaluate the strategy’s effectiveness using data from the 2025-26 population health survey, to be conducted by the end of this year. Renowned oncologist Professor Tony Mok Shu-kam of the Chinese University of Hong Kong said advances in treating lung cancer – the most common and deadliest type in the city – such as targeted therapy and immunotherapy had improved global survival rates, including in Hong Kong. “The next frontier for Hong Kong is stage migration, finding cancer patients at an early stage and treating them with surgery,” Mok said. More than half of new lung cancer cases in 2023 were already at stage 4. “With the help of AI [artificial intelligence], we can cut costs by half because we no longer need to hire a radiology specialist,” Mok said. The government launched cervical cancer screening in 2004, colorectal cancer screening in 2016 and breast cancer screening in two phases in 2021 and 2025. The results appear promising: at least 50 per cent of cases identified through these programmes were detected at the first and second stages. However, overall statistics for 2023 reveal a persistent gap, with 50.5 per cent of colorectal cancer cases and 20.4 per cent of breast cancer cases only discovered at the third and fourth stage. Dicky Chow Ka-chun, assistant research director at think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, noted in the SCMP series that the city lagged in prevention, screening and primary care integration, despite its strengths in treatment and research. “Hongkongers tend to see health management as a specialised, professional matter rather than a personal responsibility,” he said. “They often go directly to specialists without seeing a general practitioner.” As a result, according to the 2020-22 population health survey, only 50 per cent of eligible women in Hong Kong had been screened for cervical cancer, compared with a World Health Organization target recommendation of 70 per cent by age 35 and again by 45. “We need to change the culture so people believe they are in control of their own health,” Chow said. He urged the government to leverage primary healthcare networks and private partnerships to ease screening and treatment caseloads while convincing the public that the quality of care is comparable. These arguments are a reminder that there is no substitute for early diagnosis, especially for an insidious disease such as cancer, and often no more effective means than community screening.

title: Hong Kong Gen Z jewellery maker quit her finance job, then built a million-dollar brand
description: Koyo Song left J.P. Morgan to start custom jewellery brand Benalor. She shares the creative process and how her corporate experience helps.
content: Alarm at 6am. J.P. Morgan trading desk by 7.45am. Clock out at 6.30pm. Design custom jewellery until 1am. For months, Koyo Song ran her jewellery business, Benalor, while holding down a full-time corporate finance job in Hong Kong – surviving on five hours of sleep and her ambition to build her own brand. In July 2026, Song, 28, walked away from her position as a sales associate – and a six-figure monthly salary – to run Benalor full time with her boyfriend and business partner, 28-year-old Avi Benita, who quit his job at a hedge fund this year, too. Founded in 2025, Benalor offers rings, bracelets, necklaces and more, with prices ranging from HK$3,000 to HK$20,000 (US$380 to US$2,550). All the jewellery can be customised for free, and original pieces can be made to order. A creative process with a conscience Benalor’s custom process is simple. Clients can send in their inspirations and rough designs. Then Song – along with her team of Thailand-based artisans – revises and approves the design through 3D models. The piece is then handcrafted in solid gold or platinum with diamonds and shipped to the client. Today, Song’s customers are based all over the world, from Hong Kong to Guatemala and Switzerland. Song always aims to ensure clients are happy with a piece, with back-and-forth conversations about each custom design taking up to two months. A lifetime warranty, free resizing and free shipping are all part of Benalor’s philosophy of honest craftsmanship – the company also champions “conflict-free diamonds” not traded or sourced in connection with war or violence. Most of Benalor’s pieces are made with lab-grown diamonds. “Chemically speaking, lab and natural [diamonds] are the same,” Song says. “So for a lot of [women], they’d rather get the four-carat lab diamond for a fraction of the price than a 0.2-carat natural diamond.” A family connection in Thailand Song was born and raised in Japan to Chinese parents and moved to the United States for high school and university. Immediately after graduating, she landed a full-time position at J.P. Morgan, where she worked for five years. While working, she shuffled through a few business ideas with her partner Benita, including convertible heels and a fashion styling service, before realising the answer was much closer to home. Song says Benita’s father has been in B2B (business-to-business) manufacturing for custom jewellery in Thailand for 30 years. “And we were like, ‘What if we turn that into B2C [business-to-customer]?’” Song adds. “Because we believe there’s another layer of B2B – mark-up – that we don’t like. If I just cut that part, I can pass on better pricing. “So we flew to Thailand, and we basically sat him down, and we were like, ‘Just teach us everything that we need to know 101’,” Song says. Song decided to start a custom jewellery business after spotting a gap in the market. She says that while Asia is much more tapped into the customisable jewellery market than the West, custom designs are offered mostly by older jewellery shops with “traditional taste”. With Benalor, Song hopes to make bespoke jewellery that young people can enjoy and express themselves with. Song also says Benalor has a relatively low-risk business model. It does not build up an inventory since all the pieces are made to order, and rent is not a budget consideration as it is an e-commerce brand. The initial start-up capital came from Song and Benita themselves, she says. Song says she learned many of the business skills she uses at Benalor from the corporate world. While working at J.P. Morgan, she would talk to investors to understand their desires and views on the market, then pitch various trades. “And custom jewellery is literally the same thing,” Song says. “You can come to me saying, ‘Oh, I want to create something sentimental that represents me and my mom.’ I basically understand you first, listen to you, come up with design ideas, then execute.” Balancing business and romance Co-running a start-up brand with a romantic partner is not easy. “We broke up once while running this business,” Song says. Without setting any clear-cut boundaries with each other, they quickly blurred the line between their personal and business lives. Since getting back together, Song and Benita are very intentional with how they run the business together. “We will say out loud when we’re at dinner, ‘I’m talking to you as my boyfriend. Or, let’s talk about business. Let’s not talk about business for the next three hours when we’re having dinner,’” Song says. Benita typically handles the logistical and financial side of things while Song manages all front-facing responsibilities and the brand’s social media marketing. Benalor generates US$1 million (HK$7.8 million) in revenue annually. Some of the company’s prominent clients include American actress Bella Thorne, who messaged on Instagram to request custom rings for her and her fiancé. Song’s goal used to be to set up a physical store in Hong Kong. But now, with Benalor’s international clientele increasing, she is no longer sure it would be the smartest business move. However, she hopes to create occasional pop-up stores or temporary stations where Benalor customers can have in-person customisable experiences. With her schedule now freed up from full-time work, Song is excited to finally work on the multiple projects that she had been putting off. She is now able to travel to Thailand every other week to better oversee the entire creative process. For Song, quitting her office job does not mean escaping the grind, but just switching to a new, much more creative one.

title: Why Xi Jinping skipped the UN after his Trump summit
description: China touts multilateralism and growing soft power even as Beijing gives greater weight to its relationship with Washington.
content: Han Zheng, China’s vice-president, called on “major countries” to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations and bring about a two-state solution for the “Palestinian question” on Saturday at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in an implicit dig at the US and Israel. This came as some analysts questioned why Chinese President Xi Jinping opted not to address the global body given his three-day summit in Washington with US President Donald Trump this week – despite the short distance between New York and Washington, Beijing’s long-standing assertions on the UN’s importance and active campaign to build soft power and promote its global initiatives. “Many months ago, Chinese officials said that Xi wouldn’t go to the UN unless it was to mark a major anniversary,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “Seems like a missed opportunity.” Since coming to power in 2012, Xi has addressed the annual General Assembly gathering once in person, in 2015 for the 70th anniversary. He appeared by video in 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic but missed the 80th anniversary last year when Premier Li Qiang spoke. In other years, China has generally been represented by other senior officials, including Han and Foreign Minister Wang Yi. China has also placed significantly more importance on Washington relations than on multilateral issues, analysts said. This week’s summit mirrored its counterpart hosted by China for Trump in May – limited to 48 hours with no side trips or multilateral events – to underscore the geopolitical parity Beijing sees as its due. “He’s not giving America any more honour than Trump gave to the Chinese,” said Jeffrey Moon, principal at China Moon Strategies, a former US consul general in Chengdu. “In the Chinese psyche, that was more important than attending UNGA. Somebody else can do the speech.” “Protocol-wise, [Xi’s appearance] would get slightly more benefit. But not appearing to be anything less than equal to the US would be probably more important.” Among the initiatives China has promoted at the UN in recent years, touted by Han on Saturday, are its vaguely worded global development, security, civilisation and governance initiatives aimed at promoting prosperity, stability, mutual trust and procedural justice. These dovetail with China’s growing global reputation. A Pew Research Centre survey released this month found that US favourability across 20 countries was 36 per cent in 2026, down from 58 per cent in 2023, while China’s rose to 46 from 32 during the same period. A Global Soft Power Index released in January saw the US maintain its No 1 ranking with a score of 74.9 out of 100 but it recorded the largest decline among the 193 countries ranked, while China strengthened its No 2 position modestly with a score of 73.5. “It is difficult not to make a connection between some of the ‘America first’ policies and the negative turn of the US perceptions internationally,” the survey said, adding that China’s “soft power gains are underpinned by a long-term policy-led programme”. Some wonder how much of the change is due to China’s actions, however, and how much to Trump’s deeply unpopular foreign policy, damaging tariffs, military adventurism and threats against long-standing allies. While it has strongly supported multilateralism and the UN Charter, China has not always walked the walk, some argue. “To fill the lane that America’s retreat has opened … China will need to put forward resources, not just rhetoric,” said Ryan Hass, a director at the Brookings Institution and former US National Security Council official. “Beijing clearly has ambition. I’m not clear that they’ll be able to realise it.” Analysts say China attributes the Soviet Union’s demise and what it sees as America’s inexorable decline to being overstretched, including the US actions in the Middle East. “Historically, global leaders have spent pretty generously to realise their vision of revising the international system. Beijing has not,” added Hass, a former US diplomat in Beijing, citing reduced Belt and Road Initiative largesse, perhaps given economic weakness and high youth unemployment at home. While nations welcome Chinese infrastructure projects and preferential lending, few appear keen to follow its governance model, Hass said. “They’ve been very tight-fisted,” he added. “It is striking how little progress Beijing is making in attracting followers to its vision. It reflects the limits in Beijing’s ability to attract support.” Others said it may be unrealistic to expect China to fill the US void. “The US has burned so many bridges and China has taken over so completely,” said Marc Limon, executive director of Universal Rights Group, a civic group based in Geneva. “They’re very good at coalition building with countries of the Global South. They have a huge number of friends. They really do try to help.” Han’s speech on Saturday comes as the Iran war started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nears its seventh month. Earlier in the week, in a fiery exchange, Netanyahu accused UN diplomats of “mind-blowing hypocrisy” over protests as he addressed the assembly on Thursday. Envoys booed loudly and many walked out during his speech, prompting him to accuse those leaving the cavernous hall of being “moral cowards”, claiming that many of their same nations had “privately thanked us for taking out Iran’s nukes”. Relations between Trump and Netanyahu have also grown notably cooler recently. Trump chose not to meet Netanyahu earlier this week when they overlapped in New York. The death toll now exceeds 73,600 Palestinians in Gaza since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel that killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as Netanyahu revs up campaigning for his late October re-election bid. Han on Saturday called on the international community to respect the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern nations. At a thinly attended Saturday morning session, Han called on the international community to “reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation”. “We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorisation.” He also called for efforts to safeguard peace, rebuild trust and reject unilateralism at the expense of multilateralism, echoing themes voiced this week by Wang. China’s vice-president did not join Xi during the Washington summit that saw Trump meet Xi on the tarmac when he arrived Wednesday evening. The Chinese president did not bestow the same honour on Trump when he landed in Beijing in May, a role he delegated to Han.

title: Write to Win: Where would you take aliens if they landed in Hong Kong? (Round 3)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form . The deadline for voting is 12pm on Tuesday, September 29.
Milky Way: I have many places in mind to take aliens during their visit. Our first stop will be The Peak, a popular tourist destination in Hong Kong, known for its stunning views of Victoria Harbour. Next, I will take them to the Avenue of Stars, where they can see the signatures of many famous film stars. After that, we will head to Ocean Park, an exciting theme park where they can enjoy thrilling roller coasters. Finally, I will take them to Stanley Market, a great place to buy souvenirs. Those are all the places I plan to show them.
Earth: I would take aliens to Kowloon City if they visited Hong Kong. Firstly, it offers them a first-hand look at human adaptation, starting with the site of the former Kowloon Walled City – a self-organised, lawless megastructure that was once the densest residential area on Earth. This experience would show them how humans transformed that chaotic space into a peaceful park while preserving the vibrant, sensory-rich environment of street markets and distinct cultural communities surrounding it.
Venus: I would take the aliens straight to a street stall in Mong Kok to try some stinky tofu. These extraterrestrial visitors likely travel the universe in search of new weapons or creatures, so introducing them to a crispy snack that smells terrible but tastes amazing would be a complete shock. If they can survive that olfactory challenge, I would then make them drink a bowl of bitter herbal tea to give them a taste of our local healing methods. If their alien stomachs can handle Hong Kong’s ultimate street food, they’ll be left craving more. They might even forget about invading Earth and realise that our food could easily conquer the universe!
Jupiter: If aliens were to land in Hong Kong, I would introduce them to the ultimate mix of human culture, local traditions, and the city’s vibrant diversity. Our journey would begin with a short but lively ride on the MTR to the Mong Kok Ladies’ Market, where they could explore the bustling stalls and pick out local outfits to blend in with the crowd. Next, we would ascend Victoria Peak aboard the historic Peak Tram, revealing the city’s iconic skyline. To conclude the experience, I would take them on the Big Bus panoramic night tour, showcasing humanity’s ability to illuminate the universe.
Mercury: Firstly, I would like to take them into the neon chaos of Tsim Sha Tsui, where they can see the dazzling signs. Next, we can enjoy a ferry ride across Victoria Harbour, taking in the iconic skyline and the spectacular views. I highly recommend trying some dim sum as well. We can conclude our afternoon by walking along Fa Yuen Street, which is lined with affordable clothing shops. I’m sure the visitors will fall in love with it. Lastly, we could take a sightseeing bus that offers an open-top experience, allowing us to fully enjoy the sights, sounds and street-level smells of Hong Kong’s bustling neighbourhoods without any glass windows obstructing our view.
Mars: I would take the aliens straight into a classroom at a secondary school in Hong Kong during exam season. Introducing them to our heavy backpacks, countless assessment books and strict teachers would undoubtedly blow their minds! Aliens might think their lasers are powerful, but witnessing how Hong Kong teenagers endure 10 gruelling hours of school each day, plus extra tutorials and studying for endless exams from sunrise to sunset, would absolutely terrify them. These exhausted creatures would quickly pack up, escape back to space and warn their alien king never to mess with the unbeatable students of this city.
Neptune: Hong Kong has a rich and ancient heritage, so I would take aliens to various museums, starting with the Hong Kong Museum of History. Since we haven’t always been this cosmopolitan metropolis, it would be fascinating to show them our evolution rather than just the skyline views they could likely see from their ship. From a humble fishing village to an international hub, I believe the aliens would find our history as captivating as I do.

title: Powerful storm pummels northeast US with rain and high winds
description: An unusually strong nor’easter is threatening to bring flooding and road closures to New York, Boston and Philadelphia.
content: Heavy rain and strong winds battered the northeastern US on Saturday as an unusually powerful autumn storm intensified, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and leaving tens of thousands of people without power. New York, Boston and Philadelphia were all in the firing line of the “nor'easter” – so labelled for its northeasterly winds – as authorities warned of potential major flooding and road closures. “This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the mid-Atlantic coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend,” the National Weather Service said in its latest forecast. “Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses.” More than 95,000 customers in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Pennsylvania were without power as of 3pm on Saturday, according to the monitoring tool poweroutage.com. New York state Governor Kathy Hochul said the storm was bearing down Saturday on coastal areas of New York City and Long Island. “Conditions are extremely dangerous. Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life,” Hochul said in a press briefing. Up to six inches (15cm) of rain expected on Long Island over the next few days. “We expect waves as tall as 20 feet (six metres) in some areas,” Hochul said. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned residents of the country’s most populated city about strong wind gusts and the possibility of downed power lines, saying: “Don’t travel if you don’t have to.” The storm forced the cancellation of hundreds of flights, with 253 at Boston’s Logan Airport alone, according to tracker Flight Aware. Major airlines including JetBlue, United and American issued travel alerts allowing passengers to change their flights without incurring fees. The United Nations, where world leaders are gathered for the organisation’s General Assembly, urged media outlets covering the event to clear broadcasting equipment from outside the New York headquarters due to strong winds. Major cultural events were also called off, including the Global Citizen and All Things Go festivals in New York, and Oceans Calling in Maryland. “Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we’ve had to cancel,” said organisers of the Global Citizen event in Central Park, which was meant to feature Lenny Kravitz, Lauryn Hill, Alicia Keys and country stars Lainey Wilson and Shaboozey. About five inches (12.7cm) of rain was forecast in areas of Massachusetts including Boston – the equivalent of more than a month’s worth of rainfall. After much uproar surrounding his tour, British pop singer Ed Sheeran’s weekend concerts near Boston were cancelled due to the storm, which had whipped up wind gusts of 113km/h (70 mph) along the New England coast. Some coastal areas of North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey have already seen flooding this week. Nor’easters can occur throughout the year but are more frequent between fall and early spring. They are almost always accompanied by heavy rain or snowfall, as well as strong wind gusts. Earlier this year, a Nor’easter that pummelled the northeast disrupted hundreds of flights and left thousands of homes and businesses without power. That storm came weeks after the region recovered from a devastating winter weather system that was linked to more than 100 deaths.

title: Amid many thorny issues with China, Trump pushes to rename AI as superintelligence
description: A foreign ministry spokesperson did not say if China would adopt Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence but respects the choice of the term.
content: US President Donald Trump is pushing for a rebrand of artificial intelligence (AI) — and looking to get the world’s other AI superpower, China, on board. All US government documents, and “hopefully the world’s”, will use the term “superintelligence”, or SI, to refer to the fast-evolving technology, Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. The same day, the US State Department ordered US diplomats to use SI instead of AI in all communications moving forward, the Associated Press reported on Wednesday. While President Trump has mooted a possible change to what the technology is called for months, the timing of his most forceful push this week coincided with his high-profile summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington. This meant that the linguistic change has already been elevated to the highest echelons of China-US relations, amid heightened attention on whether the two countries can collaborate on AI risks. The Trump administration highlighted the new term in its summary of the visit’s outcomes on Friday evening, saying that President Xi had agreed to use the term “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence”. “It’s actually much more elegant, much more accurate,” said Trump on Saturday. “[Xi] likes the idea of changing the name as I do because it’s much more accurate”. But China’s own eight-point summary of the summit’s achievements, released on Saturday, did not use the new terminology, calling a new “China-US AI dialogue” as such instead of what the US side called a “superintelligence dialogue”. On Saturday, a foreign ministry spokesperson did not confirm whether China would be adopting the new preferred term of the US president, only saying that Beijing “attaches importance to the position of the US side and respects their choice of the term”. AI has long been the term used to describe the branch of computer science that uses data and algorithms to build smart machines. SI, meanwhile, is a more recent term that typically refers to a hypothetical AI system that vastly exceeds human intelligence in every domain. The latter has more sci-fi connotations, with experts disagreeing about whether humans could develop such a system. But as AI continues to develop rapidly, some experts, including the “Godfathers” of AI, Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, have warned that SI could eventually be achieved, which would likely pose unprecedented risks for humanity. It remains unclear why Trump is pushing for the change to the well-established term of AI. He first grumbled publicly about the term in July 2025 when he unveiled his administration’s signature “AI Action Plan”, saying that he disliked what the technology is called. At his UN speech on Tuesday, he said that the word “artificial” makes AI “sound fake”. The rebranding comes as AI and its accompanying infrastructure, most notably data centres, are growing increasingly unpopular among the US public. A poll from The New York Times and Siena University published earlier this month found that 61 per cent of likely voters said they opposed the construction of data centres to power AI. There is also growing attention on the perils of SI in particular, with two progressive lawmakers, Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Greg Casar, unveiling a new bill on Wednesday that would outlaw the development of SI. Trump has dismissed these calls to regulate and slow down AI development as a “hoax”, with a senior White House official telling the UN Security Council on Wednesday that the US “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control of superintelligence”.

title: Famous godparent-godchild sets – from Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus to Elton John and the Beckham brothers
description: Taylor Swift is reportedly distancing herself from Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds, whose children she is godmother to – here are more celeb godparents to know.
content: Recently, it came out that Taylor Swift had reportedly distanced herself from Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds’ four children – James, Betty, Inez and Olin – and her role as their godmother. The decision came after Swift was dragged into Lively’s public legal feud with Justin Baldoni, which seemingly caused a rift between the two long-time BFFs. “It was one of the toughest decisions she’s ever had to make,” a source told the Daily Mail in July about Swift’s decision to sever ties with her godchildren. “It was very emotional because she loves the girls. It hurt her heart, but she had no choice given the circumstances.” While Swift and Lively’s friendship may not have stood the test of time, Hollywood isn’t lacking celebrity children with famous godparents. Here are a few of the most famous ones. Tyler Perry: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s daughter Lilibet Tyler Perry revealed in an episode of the Netflix docuseries Harry & Meghan that Meghan Markle and Prince Harry asked him in 2021 to be the godfather of their daughter, Princess Lilibet. “I’d absolutely be honoured,” the filmmaker said at the time. Perry and Markle became acquainted after he sent her a letter of support ahead of her wedding, when Markle became the centre of a media frenzy following controversy surrounding her relationship with her father. Eva Longoria: David and Victoria Beckham’s children, Cruz and Harper Beckham Eva Longoria and Victoria Beckham’s friendship spans two decades. The Desperate Housewives star has repeatedly praised Posh Spice in interviews and has said that they are “inseparable”. Longoria is godmother to two of the Beckham children, Cruz and Harper. Elton John: Brooklyn and Romeo Beckham Elton John has 10 godchildren, including David and Victoria Beckham’s sons, Brooklyn and Romeo. He is also a godfather to Elizabeth Hurley’s son Damian Hurley and John Lennon’s son Sean Ono Lennon. Macaulay Culkin: Michael Jackson’s daughter Paris Jackson The late Michael Jackson reportedly asked Macaulay Culkin to be godfather to his only daughter, Paris Jackson, when the actor was just 17. The Home Alone star and Paris share a close relationship and even got matching tattoos in 2017, per Hello! magazine. Dolly Parton: Miley Cyrus The late Dolly Parton was a close friend of the Cyrus family and had known Miley Cyrus since she was a baby. The “Jolene” singer, who sadly passed away on August 25 after battling cancer, even appeared in episodes of Miley’s Disney show Hannah Montana as her on-screen godmother. The two shared a close bond. When the country music legend passed, Cyrus penned an emotional tribute to her “Aunt Dolly” on Instagram, writing: “Our most sacred moments were private, and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts ... I will always love her and want to make her proud.” Joan Collins: Cara Delevingne Supermodel Cara Delevingne reportedly has 16 godparents, and Dame Joan Collins is one of them. Collins has been a close friend of Delevingne’s parents and reportedly even gave her the following advice about starting her acting career: “Don’t.” The Dynasty actress further explained in an interview with OK! that she discouraged her goddaughter from acting because it was an overcrowded industry. “Incredibly difficult, so she was clever, she began modelling and she has a wonderful look. I haven’t seen any of her work, but I hear she’s a wonderful actress. She’s an individual.” Marisa Tomei: Zoë Kravitz Actresses Marisa Tomei and Lisa Bonet share a close friendship, so when Bonet and her then-husband Lenny Kravitz welcomed Zoë in 1988, the Spider-Man: Homecoming actress was the obvious choice to be her godmother. Tomei is also godmother to Bonet’s two children, Lola and Nakoa-Wolf, with ex-husband Jason Momoa. Steven Spielberg: Drew Barrymore and Gwyneth Paltrow The Jaws director is godfather to not one, but two industry darlings: Drew Barrymore and Gwyneth Paltrow. Paltrow’s parents chose Spielberg to fill the role when she was born. The director later took up the role for Barrymore while they were filming E.T. (1982). Jamie Lee Curtis: Maggie and Jake Gyllenhaal Jamie Lee Curtis is a close friend of Maggie and Jake Gyllenhaal’s parents, screenwriter Naomi Foner Gyllenhaal and director Stephen Gyllenhaal. She is the siblings’ godmother and regularly supports their careers on Instagram; most recently, she supported Maggie’s film, The Bride!. “My goddaughter @mgyllenhaal has made @thebridemovie an audacious, bold, punk, feminist opera of a movie,” Lee Curtis wrote.

title: Why claims that China’s BeiDou satellite was refuelled in orbit could change space race
description: Research papers suggest the historic operation occurred in February last year, a manoeuvre that could have military implications.
content: Chinese researchers appear to have revealed a previously unknown satellite-to-satellite refuelling operation in high Earth orbit, putting the country at the forefront of a technology that could reshape the space race. In a paper undergoing peer review for the Journal of Deep Space Exploration, the team said China had “successfully provided room-temperature propellant refuelling for a high-orbit BeiDou satellite for the first time”. The researchers from the state-funded Deep Space Exploration Laboratory gave no details about the operation. They said it had given China valuable experience but emphasised the need to develop technologies for transferring extremely low-temperature propellants, which offered better performance for large spacecraft and deep-space missions. BeiDou is China’s answer to the US Global Positioning System or GPS, a globe-spanning satellite network that provides positioning, navigation and timing services. It underpins everything from smartphone maps and financial transactions to military drone swarms and hypersonic missile guidance. Launching a replacement when a satellite runs low on propellant is an expensive and time-consuming process, while in-orbit refuelling could extend a satellite’s life by years. For the BeiDou constellation, that would mean a more resilient, continuously available navigation service capable of outlasting and outmanoeuvring rival systems in a crisis. Scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) went further, naming the two spacecraft involved and even the amount of fuel supplied in a separate study published by the International Journal of Aerospace Engineering in April. According to the CAS researchers, the servicing satellite was Shijian-25, which was launched in January 2025 to refuel, repair and remove space debris from other spacecraft in orbit. “In February 2025, Shijian-25 successfully refuelled the BeiDou-2 G7 satellite with 142kg (313lbs) of propellant, extending its lifespan by eight years,” they wrote. After presenting the case as a real event, the team simulated a rendezvous between the same two satellites, starting on August 31, with Shijian-25 manoeuvring towards BeiDou-2 G7 over two days. If confirmed, this would be only the second known case of satellite refuelling in high orbit. The first took place in July 2025, when Shijian-25 docked with and reportedly supplied fuel to Shijian-21 in geostationary orbit. That operation was closely watched around the world, including by US spy satellites that flew in for a closer look. So far, China is the only country known to have carried out satellite-to-satellite refuelling in orbit. The technology’s military implications have raised concerns in Washington. In January, US Space Command chief General Stephen Whiting warned that China’s ability to refuel satellites could give it an advantage in a future conflict in orbit. “Dogfighting in space takes fuel. And if the Chinese are refuelling their effectors, what happens when we run out of manoeuvre in a fight?” he said at the Space Mobility Conference in Florida. The technology could also play a critical role in the new “moon race”, allowing spacecraft to make repeated journeys between Earth and the moon to build and supply lunar bases – or potentially fight in a future conflict in cislunar space. Neither paper cited a source for the claimed refuelling. Both Shijian-25 and BeiDou-2 G7 have been closely tracked by the US Space Force and their orbital records show they never came close enough to dock in February last year – or at any point in the first half of 2025. According to Jonathan McDowell, a former Harvard astrophysicist and expert in satellite tracking, BeiDou-2 G7 remained in geostationary orbit at around 110.5 degrees east from January to July 2025. Shijian-25 was tracked in a transfer orbit after its January 7 launch before disappearing from US tracking for six days. When it was picked up again on January 13, it was drifting near 120 degrees east and by the following day had settled there, where it remained until June before moving to 127 degrees east. “Could it have visited 110E during the six days it was out of sight? Not at the rate it was drifting on January 13,” McDowell said. “And I don’t think a rendezvous and refuelling is plausible on that timescale.” Unless the US Space Force had been tracking the wrong objects, “the rendezvous postulated in early 2025 could not have happened”, he added. The South China Morning Post has contacted the Chinese teams for comment. Passionate about science? title: Opinion | How China is seeking to transform the meaning of great power
description: By promoting a more just world order, Beijing hopes to exercise influence without making domination the organising principle of international relations.
content: As China has emerged as a peer competitor to the United States in many areas, an increasingly familiar question is whether it has become a superpower. The question, however, may rest on a definition of power that belongs to another era. China possesses many attributes traditionally associated with great powers: a large population, vast territory, a major economy, advanced technological capabilities and growing military strength. Yet Beijing describes China as a “major country” rather than a “great power” or “superpower”. Its white paper on global governance, for example, presents China as a major country advocating a more just and equitable international order. It reflects a different conception of what power is for, and perhaps what constitutes responsible power in the 21st century. The term “superpower” dates from the second world war. In his 1944 book The Super-Powers: The United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union – Their Responsibility for Peace, American political scientist William T.R. Fox identified the three as a new category of states whose military and geopolitical capabilities gave them an exceptional role in shaping the post-war order. The ability to move and sustain armed forces across major theatres of war, supported by overseas bases and extensive geopolitical reach, was a defining attribute of the new superpowers. Fox’s argument also carried an important implication: those possessing such exceptional capabilities would bear an exceptional responsibility for preserving peace. That concept remains relevant. Military power, strategic reach and the ability to deter or defeat adversaries continue to shape international politics. But they no longer exhaust the sources of national power. Over the past eight decades, economic interdependence, global supply chains, technology, finance and industrial capacity have become increasingly important instruments of geopolitical influence. Power can also arise from the ability to produce critical goods, control strategically important technologies, withstand economic pressure or impose costs on an adversary through disruption of commercial networks. This is one reason the experience of the past decade is difficult to fit neatly into a purely military definition of power. The US-China confrontation over trade and technology offers one illustration. During last year’s tariff escalation, China responded not simply with matching tariffs but with measures affecting critical minerals and other areas in which it possesses substantial leverage. The subsequent negotiations showed the degree of economic interdependence between the world’s two largest economies. Neither side could treat the other simply as an external adversary without incurring significant costs. The lesson is not that economic power has replaced military power. Rather, the two have become increasingly intertwined. A country with a formidable armed force may nevertheless be constrained by weaknesses in its industrial base, supply chains, finances or ability to sustain a prolonged confrontation. Conversely, a state without comparable military reach can acquire substantial bargaining power from its position in strategically important economic networks. The continuing strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, for example, illustrates how geography and asymmetric capabilities can give a regional power leverage over actors with vastly greater military resources. Military superiority does not automatically translate into unlimited political freedom of action. This raises a broader question: should a 21st-century great power be defined only by the ability to dominate other states, or also by its capacity to contribute to the stability and development of the international system? China’s answer is increasingly explicit. Its diplomatic language emphasises what it calls a “major country” role, with sovereignty, multilateralism, international law, development and a people-centred approach among the principles it associates with global governance. Its white paper presents the Global Governance Initiative as an effort to build a more just and equitable international system and stresses the importance of multilateral cooperation and the UN-centred international order. The concept of a “superpower” traditionally describes an exceptional concentration of capabilities. The concept of a “responsible major country”, by contrast, puts greater emphasis on how those capabilities are used. There is a historical logic to this distinction. China’s experience of statecraft has produced a political tradition in which stability, order and people’s welfare are important measures of performance. Contemporary leaders have adapted elements of that tradition to a modern conception of development and international governance. Its official discourse increasingly presents China’s international role in terms of development, cooperation and problem-solving, rather than formal domination. This does not mean China rejects power. On the contrary, its economic and technological rise, military modernisation and growing diplomatic reach have given Beijing considerably greater capacity to shape international outcomes. The more interesting question is how China chooses to conceptualise and deploy that capacity. The distinction between “superpower” and “responsible major country” points to a larger transformation in international politics. The ability to project military force remains a crucial component of power, but it is increasingly only one component. Industrial resilience, technological capacity, economic relationships, control of critical supply chains and the ability to provide international public goods can also shape the choices available to states. Fox’s 1944 insight was that extraordinary power carries extraordinary responsibility. Eighty years later, the nature of extraordinary power itself may be changing. The question for China may not be whether it can satisfy an old definition of superpower. It is whether it can show that a major power can exercise influence without making domination the organising principle of international relations. That would amount to more than a change in terminology. It would be a different answer to the question Fox posed in 1944: what should the world’s most powerful countries do with their power?

title: Thousands march in Spain over eviction of 87-year-old woman Maricarmen Abascal
description: Images of her being carried from her lifelong home after police broke down her door have put a spotlight on the country’s housing crisis.
