content: Thousands of people marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction earlier this week of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home, calling for greater protection for tenants. Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher on Wednesday after police broke down her door have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due in 2027. Protesters rattled keys, blew whistles, chanted slogans and held banners calling for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult as they marched through central Madrid. “You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner. Enrique Ortega de Miguel, a 38-year-old graphic designer who lives with his mother, said the housing market in Spain was “impossible”. “It is a struggle to find a place you can afford, then you live in fear of being forced out,” he said at the protest. Government authorities put the turnout at around 25,000, while organisers of the protest said 300,000 took part. “Maricarmen’s eviction has caused outrage and marks a turning point,” Alicia del Rio, spokesman for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told reporters at the start of the march which ended outside parliament. Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis, urged Spaniards to join the protest in a video message posted online just hours before it got under way. “I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction. “I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added in the video, posted by the tenants’ union. Abascal was forced to leave the apartment where she had lived for 70 years after a real estate firm acquired the property and raised the rent by 275 per cent to €2,650 (US$3,000), according to the union. Irene Lopez, a 33-year-old engineer, said the situation “has become unsustainable”. “There are people who can’t afford to live in cities, rents are out of step with salaries,” she said, describing the eviction of Maricarmen as “the last straw”. Another protester, Maricarmen Arnedo, a 76-year-old pensioner, said while older people were being forced out of their homes, “young people can’t move out of their parents’ homes”. “We want house prices and rents to come down, because I’m fed up with washing the underpants of my 53-year-old son,” she added. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who last year pledged to make housing a government priority, is under growing pressure to act. There have been regular protests across Spain since Abascal’s eviction. He has called Abascal’s eviction a “social tragedy that we cannot accept”. The government is expected to approve a package of measures dubbed the “Maricarmen decree” at its next cabinet meeting, including the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions. But it is unclear whether the package will be approved by parliament, where Sanchez’s government lacks a majority. While a similar bill was defeated earlier this year, Abascal’s case has increased pressure on political parties to act. The Bank of Spain estimates the country of around 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. Spain has little public housing, while rents have been driven up by increased demand, including from tourism and population growth linked to immigration, analysts say.

title: Beijing says US, China to pursue military crisis-communication pact
description: Chinese account says militaries will conclude a memorandum ‘as soon as possible’, but Washington has not publicly confirmed it.
content: China and the United States have agreed to pursue a new military crisis-communication pact following the summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, according to Beijing, potentially giving commanders another mechanism for managing dangerous encounters across the Indo-Pacific. China’s foreign ministry said on Saturday that the two militaries had agreed to conclude a memorandum of understanding on “crisis communication and prevention” as soon as possible. The South China Morning Post exclusively reported ahead of the summit that both sides would unveil measures to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones. The two militaries already have consultation arrangements and senior communication channels. The Chinese announcement did not explain whether the proposed memorandum would create a new hotline, establish procedures for using existing connections or define which incidents would trigger crisis consultations. That distinction could determine whether the agreement proves useful during an actual confrontation. Previous periods of improved military contact have been interrupted by political disputes, while formal communication mechanisms have not always produced timely exchanges during crises. The commitment was not included in the White House’s account of the summit, and neither the Pentagon nor US Indo-Pacific Command had publicly confirmed it as of Saturday. Beijing announced the proposed military agreement separately from eight summit deliverables covering trade, artificial intelligence, counternarcotics cooperation and international affairs. Its statement also said the two militaries would continue working together to locate the remains of missing US service members in China. The statement confirmed an exclusive South China Morning Post report earlier this month that the two sides could announce measures to improve military-to-military communication. The announcement offers a concrete, if still preliminary, answer to a question US military officials were considering before the Washington meeting: whether renewed senior-level engagement could produce communication channels capable of preventing an encounter at sea or in the air from escalating. “We pay very close attention to what comes out of it, who says what, and when and how,” a US Navy official told the SCMP before the summit. The official said the conversations leading up to the meeting mattered as well. Both governments appeared serious about holding a constructive discussion, he said, describing public dialogue between Washington and Beijing as a “confidence builder for everybody”. The remarks reflect the concerns of those managing the day-to-day military risks in the US-China relationship. Although trade and economic agreements dominated the public summit announcements, military forces from the two countries continue to operate in a region where an encounter at sea or in the air could quickly raise tensions. Another US military official, speaking on background, put the challenge this way: “I believe the US’ goal is to enable both strategic stability and deterrence by denial, and I believe respectful and professional communication with China does not preclude that.” Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun had also publicly emphasised communication before the summit, calling at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing for an approach to security based on dialogue rather than confrontation. The proposed memorandum would be the first indication that the two governments intend to translate that public emphasis into a new military mechanism. It would build on the recent resumption of senior-level contact between the armed forces. Admiral Samuel Paparo, the senior US commander in the Indo-Pacific, met General Yang Zhibin, commander of the People’s Liberation Army’s Eastern Theatre Command, during a defence conference in Victoria, British Columbia, in late August. It was their first meeting and ended a two-year interruption in theatre-level contact between the two countries. According to the US military, they discussed maintaining communication among senior leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and encourage safe, professional conduct by their forces. Yang’s participation was especially significant because the Eastern Theatre Command oversees PLA operations facing Taiwan, the East China Sea and Japan, placing him at the centre of several of the region’s most sensitive potential flashpoints. Even if concluded, the memorandum would not resolve the strategic disagreements driving military competition between the two countries. For Denny Roy, a senior fellow at the East-West Centre in Hawaii, expectations of a broader strategic breakthrough from the Washington summit should remain modest. Economic predictability appeared to be a priority for Beijing, while the Trump administration sought a bilateral economic agreement, he said. The underlying strategic rivalry continued. Military communication could nonetheless serve a practical purpose. Talks between commanders can help each side understand the thinking behind the other’s actions and, in some cases, prevent a manoeuvre from being mistaken for a hostile act, Roy said. The proposed memorandum focuses on crisis management rather than the strategic disagreements driving military competition. Its significance will depend on whether the two sides agree on specific procedures, identify officials empowered to communicate and ensure the channel remains available during the political disputes that make military contact most necessary. The test will not simply be how quickly the memorandum is concluded, but whether commanders are authorised to use it when an aircraft interception, naval encounter or operation around Taiwan leaves little time for consultation.

title: Why US chip controls took a back seat at the Xi-Trump summit
description: China’s growing semiconductor self-reliance may explain the relative calm, but looming US measures could put it to the test.
content: There is little question that Jensen Huang and Lisa Su, the heads of US semiconductor chip giants Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), had secured two of the best seats in the house at the White House state dinner on Thursday evening: at the head table alongside the two presidents and their wives. But what remains unclear is how much progress they were able to make on their primary goal of restoring access to the Chinese market, amid entrenched opposition to that happening in both China and the US. That is because US semiconductor chip export controls do not seem to have been a major sticking point during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s historic state visit to Washington this week, despite most of the restrictions still being in place. Early indications suggest that export controls were not a significant topic of debate during the talks, with no direct mention of them in the readouts so far from both Beijing and Washington summarising the achievements of the Xi–Trump summit. “This is especially strange considering that export controls were brought up regularly by Xi during his talks with [President Joe] Biden,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Washington think tank Brookings specialising in Chinese technology. On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that the US side had taken “off the table” all the export controls “that are national security issues” during trade talks this week. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Saturday did not mention export controls or Beijing’s usual references to US tech restrictions in its announcement of eight deliverables from the summit, including the launch of a China-US dialogue on AI risks. But if export controls have become less of a sticking point, it is not because they have gone away. The Trump administration has largely kept intact restrictions first introduced by the Biden administration in October 2022 on China’s ability to obtain advanced chips and chipmaking equipment. Some areas were even tightened at the start of Trump’s second term, including a ban on exporting Nvidia’s H20 chip to China, which the company had developed specifically to comply with US rules. According to Chan, Beijing has likely grown more comfortable with the export controls already in place as it looks to deepen its technological self-reliance campaign to reduce its reliance on US tech. “The biggest thing that’s changed is China’s growing confidence in its chip self-reliance efforts,” he said. “While the 2022 export controls may have surprised Beijing at the time, China has made real progress on building a domestic supply chain for advanced semiconductors in the years since”. A temporary stalemate When Washington first imposed sweeping export controls on China in 2022, Beijing treated them as a direct attack on China’s technological and economic rise and began regularly calling for their removal in talks with the US. The controls became a wedge issue in US-China relations. At China-US talks on AI safety in Geneva in May 2024, Chinese officials tied progress on AI safety to the US unwinding those controls, former Biden administration officials have said. This was not an issue this time around. Export controls were not brought up during the AI safety related talks between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last Sunday in New York, according to Greer, who also attended the meeting. The AI talks, which also resulted in the launch of a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents, were “candid, in-depth and constructive”, Beijing said. Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said Beijing is likely “pleased with progress that the domestic semiconductor industry has made despite the [US] controls”. Chinese chip manufacturers are taking a greater share of the domestic market. According to TrendForce, Chinese chip suppliers led by Huawei Technologies and Cambricon Technologies are set to capture nearly 80 per cent of the domestic AI server market this year. Nvidia, AMD and other foreign suppliers’ share is set to fall to 21 per cent in 2026 from 34 per cent last year, according to the Taipei-based research firm. Domestic chip substitution is expected to further ramp up in the coming years as tech self-reliance remains a central pillar of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan. Earlier this year, Beijing resisted efforts by both President Donald Trump and Nvidia’s Huang to push for the US chip giant’s less powerful H200 chips to be allowed back into the Chinese market. Beijing has since allowed a small number of Chinese tech companies to purchase the chip with the quantities capped, as it continues to promote domestic chip adoption instead. Meanwhile, the delayed approval caused Nvidia to take a US$400 million charge due to excess H200 inventory in the first half of the year. Spanner in the works Still, talk of an export control impasse might still be premature. That is because Beijing is likely to push back forcefully against any new restrictions the US introduces, with some already on the horizon, according to Triolo. A major area of concern is US congressional efforts to bolster its export controls regime. One of these is the Match Act, which would require US allies such as Japan and the Netherlands to more closely align with US restrictions on selling advanced semiconductor equipment to China, such as Dutch firm ASML’s deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography machines. The bill has been folded into the National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA) in the US Senate, improving its chances of becoming law. “Chinese officials view any new controls as a violation of the Busan agreement, and [would] retaliate strongly via expanded controls on rare earths and related production equipment,” said Triolo, referring to the economic detente reached in October 2025 between the two countries that paused escalating tit-for-tat tariffs and export controls, which the two leaders agreed to extend to January. “Beijing likely sought assurances on this [this week],” he said. Even as the official readouts of the two presidents’ meeting have largely focused on trade and investment, senior Chinese officials have referenced US technological restrictions on China in statements elsewhere. On Saturday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a post-meeting statement that China and the US should not “adopt a defensive posture towards each other” in the emerging field of AI. The relative quiet on export controls this week might therefore reflect strong domestic pressure on both sides not to concede ground, Triolo said, with powerful contingents in the US pushing for tighter controls and those in China for greater self-reliance. “Neither side will acknowledge progress on any of these issues, given domestic sensitivities around anything that could be perceived as a concession,” he said.

title: Iran says only diplomacy can end Hormuz crisis after Trump rejects deal
description: Tehran said the proposed pact would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
content: Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel after US President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting. “Our conditions are clear and any move towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of ‌this deadlock.” Iran announced a peace proposal earlier this week at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators. Trump on Saturday said he rejected the plan and argued that desperation drives the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the vital waterway. “They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters at the White House. Despite Trump’s public statements, mediators easing US-Iran talks with the US have not officially relayed a US rejection of the plan, according to Araghchi. “We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us and ⁠we will make a decision based on them,” Araghchi said. The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to stop Iranian attacks on vessels ‌in the Strait of Hormuz, which have drastically reduced shipping through the area even as Trump repeatedly asserts that the US controls the waterway. The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials. It said Trump was privately sceptical that ‌Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm election. A US ⁠official had said earlier that discussions ⁠with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”. The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows ‌through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy. Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting. “If ‌there ‌is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araghchi said. If the US were to agree, ‌the warring parties could start wider talks “on mutually agreed subjects”. That could potentially include discussions of Iran’s nuclear programme. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior ⁠Iranian official said that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the US accepted its peace deal. Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, ⁠including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but ‌will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” ‌Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks. Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging Iran’s already ailing economy. Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition said early on Saturday it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom. Meanwhile on Sunday, parents across Riyadh also received emails from schools in the Saudi capital on announcing a last-minute plan to shift to remote learning for a week, according to messages seen by Agence France-Presse.

title: Pope celebrates giant Paris mass in landmark visit
description: The first US pontiff was visiting France seven months before French voters went to the polls.
content: Pope Leo on Saturday celebrated an open-air mass in front of hundreds of thousands of faithful in Paris after riding in the Popemobile along the iconic Champs Elysees to the cheers of huge crowds clutching French and Vatican flags. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics is on a four-day trip to France, a secular country with deep Catholic roots, on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades. In the highlight of the visit’s second day, the 71-year-old pope led believers in a mass at Place de la Concorde, where a giant white canopy had been erected to serve as a makeshift altar. Dozens of screens were installed to allow worshippers to follow the hour-and-a-half long service. The trip stirred visible enthusiasm and spiritual fervour among the faithful. The pope’s prayers were accompanied by choir and organ music as the sun broke through the grey skies. “It is truly good and pleasant when brothers and sisters come together and glorify the greatness of God,” said Pope Leo, dressed in white liturgical vestments. Over a stretch of more than 2km (1.2 miles), some 700,000 people had gathered all the way beyond the Arc de Triomphe, the Vatican said. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops. Some people sitting on the pavement hugged their knees and dropped their heads in concentration as they listened to the pope’s voice echo across the Champs Elysees. Parents arrived with pushchairs and held children on their shoulders as crowds hoped to catch a glimpse of the pontiff. Jeanne de Montagnac, 29, came with her husband and two-year-old girl, who was perched on his shoulders with a telephone number scribbled in pen on her arm. “We’re happy that, even if she won’t remember it, we’re sharing this with her,” she said, a small golden cross dangling over her off-white jumper. “It’s an important moment for us to be surrounded by other people who also have faith.” The first US pontiff was visiting France seven months before voters choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the anti-immigration far-right eyeing its best opportunity yet to capture the presidency. A number of presidential hopefuls were present, including far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe. President Emmanuel Macron did not attend the mass and was represented by his wife Brigitte. “We’re incredibly lucky,” Suzanne Grange, 62, said ahead of the service. “We were already lucky enough to see Pope John Paul II in Paris back in 1980,” added her husband Pascal, 65. Earlier in the day, the pope met migrants as he visited Maison Bakhita, an association supporting refugees. Leo said it was “possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace”. He also stressed the “fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love”. The association said the pope’s visit sent a “message” ahead of the April-May election. On Friday, an estimated 300,000 people turned out to see the pontiff as he waved from his Popemobile on the way to the Notre Dame Cathedral. “There is a sense of fervour reminiscent of that experienced over 40 years ago with John Paul II,” Francois Mabille, director of the Geopolitical Observatory on Religion, told broadcaster RMC. On Friday, Pope Leo stressed the need for ethics to avoid an AI-driven “paradise of machines” and, as war rages in Ukraine for a fifth year, urged France to remain a “tireless champion of peace”. He also told young adults at a stadium outside Paris on Friday night that they were the “saints of France”. Later Saturday Pope Leo will head to Lourdes, a southwestern town where, according to Catholic tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared in a grotto in 1858 to a peasant girl. On Sunday, he will speak with seven victims of clerical sexual abuse. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as minors in France, over seven decades. For the last leg of his trip, in Metz on Monday, Leo is set to deliver a speech about peace in Europe.

title: 3 top reasons Trump will face a stronger Xi Jinping at November Apec forum in China
description: Vital host diplomacy leverage and upgraded US-China ties among reasons cited by experts forecasting an even more confident Chinese side.
content: When Donald Trump arrives in Shenzhen for the November Apec summit, he will face a Chinese leader even more confident than the one who left Washington this week after a state visit heavy on pageantry but light on concrete deliverables. Experts attributed this confidence to three key factors – a newly upgraded bilateral framework seeking a “constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”, the warmer tone during Xi’s three-day visit, and – crucially – the significant leverage of host diplomacy. In southern China’s Shenzhen – home to technological giants Huawei, BYD and Tencent – President Xi Jinping will have greater control over the agenda and showcase Beijing’s growing diplomatic clout in ways impossible during a bilateral summit. Meanwhile, the Washington spectacle will reverberate with US allies and middle powers, who experts said would need to reassess their China strategies. “As the Apec host, China will clearly possess far more autonomy in agenda-setting, topic selection, and preparatory work than it did during the Washington summit, where the US controlled the choreography while China held only participation and discussion rights,” said Chen Qi, director of the Centre for US-China Relations at Tsinghua University. The shift in leverage would be particularly evident in the multilateral setting, he added. “Beijing could also showcase its diplomatic influence and leadership far more effectively than in bilateral encounters.” Statements released by both countries on Saturday confirmed that Trump intended to travel to Shenzhen in November to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, setting up a third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year. Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, said the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting would help Xi highlight “China’s growing economic and diplomatic sway – including with several US allies and partners” shortly after midterm elections likely to be bruising for Trump’s Republican Party. “Xi appreciates how greatly Trump values opportunities to convey that the two leaders enjoy a strong rapport … Their Washington summit this week demonstrated his willingness to reverse or weaken US measures that might risk his meetings with Xi,” Wyne added. Zhang Chi, senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World (CCCW), called the upgraded relationship “a very successful strategic convergence” that placed Beijing and Washington on a fairer footing. “Equally important is that China has demonstrated that attempts by Washington to reshape the bilateral power balance through ‘maximum pressure’ are ineffective and create uncontrollable problems,” he said. Marking his second state visit to the US since 2015, Xi arrived to a rare tarmac greeting from President Donald Trump – a courtesy usually delegated to lower-level officials. The 42 hours of summitry that followed saw both leaders hold up China as an equal or near-equal power to the United States. Trump spoke warmly of an emerging “great friendship”, while Xi portrayed the bilateral bond as a “river that never stops flowing” as its leaders work to “steer the giant ship” of relations forward. Saturday’s statements by both countries further indicated a fourth Xi-Trump meeting this year, at the December Group of 20 summit in Miami. The pair last met in May, when Trump travelled to Beijing on a state visit. Just ahead of the Washington summit, the two sides agreed to extend the bilateral trade truce set to expire in November by two months. As part of the truce, Washington has pledged to pause new tariffs while Beijing will suspend some rare earth export controls. The unprecedented frequency of head-of-state interaction – four summits in eight months – signals a window of relative stability, according to Chinese experts. The high-frequency meetings this year make policy continuity “both a promise and an inertia”, said Zhang Zhizhou, from the school of international relations and diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University. This would potentially help to shield Beijing from disruptive unilateral actions by Washington in the interim, he said, while identifying several factors contributing to China’s increased confidence heading into the Apec summit. These include China’s rising technological strength, growing influence in the Global South and Belt and Road Initiative partner nations. All of this would make the Chinese side – which excels at host diplomacy – “more confident and bolster their negotiating position”, Zhang in Beijing said. Shortly after Trump and Xi wrapped up their Washington summit, the White House announced that both sides had recommended reciprocal tariff relief covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive trade moving in each direction. US exports slated for preferential treatment under the proposed framework include agricultural produce, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical equipment. The reciprocal Chinese list covers consumer goods such as small household appliances, toys, festive decorations and children’s car seats. But experts also urged caution on long-term predictability, noting that the present strategy remained tied to Trump personally and domestic pressures and geopolitics could test the diplomatic momentum. “Going forward, there are two key factors to watch: whether Trump can still honour his commitments once his hands are free, as upcoming midterm elections and the quagmire in Iran are currently draining his attention; and second, any provocative moves on Taiwan arms sales,” Zhang from CCCW said. Trump, who has described arms sales to Taiwan as a negotiating tool with Beijing, postponed a planned US$14 billion package following his May summit with Xi. The South China Morning Post reported this month that the US was considering postponing the announcement of arms sales to Taiwan until the end of the year, pointing to the potential Apec and G20 summits. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. But Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Ma Bo, associate professor at Nanjing University, said Washington was operating on two parallel tracks. While the White House projects cordiality at the top, the US security apparatus – aligning with its allies – continues to press ahead. “Detente at the leader level does not bind Congress, technological export controls, or the actions of America’s regional allies,” Ma warned. The current equilibrium is also seen as likely to prompt uneasy recalibration among middle powers and traditional US allies who watched Xi’s visit with a mix of relief and trepidation. Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for US Studies at Fudan University, noted that Washington’s regional partners – from Tokyo to Manila – were increasingly anxious about the potential erosion of US strategic support. “As [US-China] ties stabilise, the backing these countries can extract from Washington will inevitably erode,” Xin said. “If they attempt to use America to confront Beijing, they may find themselves without US endorsement, or even risk being left out in the cold.” According to Zhang from CCCW, Europe is in an “embarrassing” position, as the progress in US-China ties will make Europe’s own escalation of trade pressure on Beijing look increasingly discordant. Meanwhile, countries that recognise Beijing’s playbook in handling Washington – “those convinced that caving in to Trump brings no tangible benefit, will be the first to pivot towards Beijing with a more proactive and pragmatic posture”, he said.

title: Exclusive | China-based Brics bank set for lead role in hunger alliance this year, Brazil says
description: Brazilian minister Wellington Dias tells SCMP a fund to cut borrowing costs for the poor may launch by December as US marginalises the G20.
content: The Brics-founded New Development Bank could help launch a fund by the end of the year to guarantee cheap loans for poor families in Africa and Latin America, Brazil’s social development minister said. The scheme would be the Shanghai-based lender’s first financial commitment to Brazil’s global anti-hunger alliance, an initiative sidelined by Washington’s presidency of the G20 this year. Wellington Dias told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the chances of a first pilot programme, worth as little as US$200 million, getting off the ground by December were “very big”. The bank is designing the scheme with four other development lenders, he added, and each still has to run its compliance checks. The money would go to Brazil’s Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty, launched at the G20 summit Brazil hosted in Rio de Janeiro in November 2024 but dropped from the group’s agenda after the United States took over the rotating presidency in December last year. The Trump administration, which boycotted last year’s summit in Johannesburg, has narrowed the G20 agenda to deregulation, energy, technology and trade, leaving out priorities of Brazil’s 2024 presidency such as inequality and hunger. Dias, who co-chairs the alliance, said Washington had become “somewhat isolated” on hunger, but admitted that its reduction in aid was a “hard problem” for the group’s objective. This is because even though it has 215 members (including over 107 countries and 14 international financial institutions), the alliance has no money of its own and relies on members to fund the programmes it brokers. Much of the money so far has come from the Inter-American Development Bank, which pledged up to US$25 billion between 2025 and 2030. It approved US$4.1 billion in alliance-aligned operations last year and expects to approve US$5.8 billion this year. Dias acknowledged that neither the New Development Bank nor the Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank had financed any alliance programme so far, but added that the Brics’ bank contribution would come through the guarantee fund. That would be new territory for a lender set up in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa to finance mostly infrastructure. When it joined the alliance in October 2024, the bank offered help with water, sanitation, housing and irrigation projects, without naming a funding figure. In the model he described, local banks would lend to poor borrowers and the guarantee fund would absorb any defaults. “This will allow a poor person in the country being supported to walk into a bank and get financing,” Dias said. “The poorest are seen by banks as high risk, and the interest is very high. With the guarantee fund, that goes away. The rate collapses, and that matters for financing in both rural and urban areas.” The idea draws on Brazil’s Acredita programme, which offers microcredit to low-income families backed by a one billion reais (US$194 million) government guarantee fund. By October last year it had lent 1.7 billion reais, with a default rate of 0.36 per cent, according to the social development ministry. China steps up global anti-hunger alliance involvement The fund would also add a financial dimension to China’s involvement in the alliance, which it has lacked so far. When President Xi Jinping announced China would join the Rio summit in November 2024, Beijing’s statement of commitment covered domestic policy and knowledge sharing but left out the section on financial support that members can choose to sign. Its pledges were largely domestic, including a 50-million tonne increase in grain production capacity by 2030. Abroad, China offered advice on 13 types of policy, among them microcredit for poverty alleviation through the International Poverty Reduction Centre in China. That state-backed centre says it has trained nearly 15,000 officials from 140 countries and runs a poverty reduction forum with the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States. Its deputy director general, Li Xin, sits on the alliance’s Board of Champions as one of its vice-chairs. Asked what Beijing had contributed since joining the alliance, Dias began with China’s success in reducing poverty at home before turning to its investment in developing countries. “China is also one of the countries investing the most in Africa and South America, and with that it contributes, even if in a traditional way, to opening up opportunities for jobs and work,” he said. “It invests in infrastructure and so on.” On the alliance itself, Dias said Chinese financial support has been focused on family farming in African countries, alongside other donors. The minister also cited larger Chinese purchases from small producers’ cooperatives in Brazil, Africa and South America, including organic honey from Brazil’s north and northeast. Countries contribute “with knowledge, with money, but also with investment”, he said, and “in this field, China is a prominent partner”. Dias said Beijing could help fill the space left by US aid cuts, though as part of “a pact among several countries” rather than alone. But talks on that between the Brics bloc, the European Union and other forums were disrupted by the Iran war early this year, according to the minister. Cuba’s isolation and armed conflicts worldwide Alliance members have sent food to Cuba, mainly milk, and are backing better seeds, irrigation and fishing projects to help the island produce more of its own, Dias said. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts since Venezuelan oil shipments stopped after US forces captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, and Washington has since blocked tankers bound for the island. Dias described the positions of China, Brazil, Mexico and Spain on Cuba as “very firm”, and mentioned a Cuban target of 3.5 gigawatts of solar power. With 42 countries at war or in armed conflict by his count, Dias asked richer economies, China among them, to avoid further aid cuts or to compensate where they had happened. He framed it as self-interest. “When wars proliferate, when hunger and poverty are not dealt with, the richest also pay,” he said. “Look at disorderly migration. All countries pay, whether it is the United States, countries in Europe or Brazil.”

title: Suicide bombing at police checkpoint in Pakistan kills at least 11
description: About 30 others were wounded in the attack, for which the Pakistani Taliban has claimed responsibility.
content: A suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan on Saturday, killing at least 11 people and wounding about 30 others, officials said, in a sign of increasing violence in the region bordering Afghanistan. The attack occurred in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, said Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the provincial emergency service. Local police chief Safdar Baloch said most of those killed and wounded were security personnel and passers-by. The Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement. Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, a separatist group mainly active in neighbouring Balochistan province. The TTP is separate from but allied with the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021. Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Afghan authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks against other countries. The latest attack came two days after fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan along their southwestern border killed at least 13 Afghan Taliban, according to Pakistan’s government. It was the latest escalation between the neighbours following Pakistani strikes on alleged militant hideouts inside Afghanistan this week. The renewed hostilities threaten mediation efforts by China, Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia aimed at securing lasting peace between the two countries. Dera Ismail Khan is near South Waziristan, a former militant stronghold where the Pakistani military has carried out several operations in recent years. Militants also frequently target security forces in the region. In December 2023, a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, killing at least 23 security personnel in one of the deadliest attacks in the area. It was claimed by Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan, a small militant group believed to be an offshoot of the TTP.

title: China’s ‘invincible’ Zhang Ziyu helps women’s basketball team claim bronze at Asian Games
description: The 19-year-old is already taller than NBA legend Shaquille O’Neal and recently impressed WNBA star Caitlin Clark at the World Cup.
content: Zhang Ziyu played a starring role to drag China to women’s basketball bronze at the Asian Games on Saturday, with her coach predicting the teenager standing 2.2 metres (7-foot-3) will one day be “invincible”. The 19-year-old is already taller than NBA legend Shaquille O’Neal and she made full use of her advantage as China beat Chinese Taipei 77-64 in the third-place match in Nagoya. Zhang has made a name for herself in recent weeks, impressing American superstar Caitlin Clark at the Women’s World Cup in Germany. She has made her significant height advantage count at the Asian Games, with Philippines head coach Javier Alvarez Garcia calling her “amazing” and tipping her to become the world’s best player. Zhang said she had “a lot to work on” despite scoring 14 points against Chinese Taipei. “I just want to be able to do my part and contribute for the team,” she said. “I’m keen to work hard and learn more. I’ve put a lot of work into agility. “I’m thankful to all the effort put into helping me become a better player.” Zhang looked in a different league at times against Chinese Taipei, plucking the ball out of the air over her opponents’ heads and dropping it into the basket. She headed into the match with China’s highest points average per game. Mongolia’s Amari Robinson, who faced Zhang and China in the quarter-finals, said “her height alone is obviously another opponent”. “She has great hands, great footwork,” Robinson said. “I just tried to be as tall as I could with what I had.” Zhang drew praise from Clark during the World Cup, with the WNBA star saying she had “never played against a woman of that size”. Zhang could end up in the WNBA one day and Philippines coach Alvarez Garcia has no doubts that she can succeed there. “She’s great, she’s amazing,” he said. “She will probably be like top one, top two players in the world, for sure.” China coach Gong Luming said Zhang had “improved a lot in terms of her mobility”. He cautioned that she was far from the finished article but said the world is her oyster if she can keep developing. “Her height is one of her weapons, so we hope she can make the most of it,” he said. “If she can, she will be invincible.”

title: Trade truce extension aside, was AI the real Xi-Trump summit breakthrough?
description: New AI dialogue becomes latest formal channel to manage competition while coming leader-level meetings grant further room to stabilise ties, analysts say.
content: The Xi-Trump summit may prove more significant for stabilising relations and opening space for further negotiations between the world’s two largest economies than for its immediate trade outcomes, analysts said, pointing to the significance of a new dialogue on artificial intelligence. With the two leaders expected to meet again in the coming months, attention could shift from extending the latest tariff truce to building a more durable framework for managing economic and technological competition, they added. During President Xi Jinping’s three-day visit to Washington, which ended on Friday, the two sides agreed on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods in each direction under the newly established Board of Trade. They also agreed that China would buy American coal and established a “super intelligence” dialogue, according to a White House fact sheet released on Friday. The two countries would “continue to work on” US concerns over China’s rare earth export controls, while Washington urged Beijing to increase production of refined petroleum products to “stabilise global supply” and take further steps to curb the flow of fentanyl precursors, the fact sheet said. Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Renmin University of China in Beijing, said disagreements over tariffs and AI could become easier to manage after the two presidents reinforced what he described as a “triangle of stability” in bilateral ties. “Some common ground has been established by Trump and Xi. With this, specific issues from fentanyl to tariffs are left to working-level officials and relevant agencies from both sides to address,” he said. The developments on AI, Wang argued, were more significant than the specific trade measures announced following the summit. “The competition and consensus between China and the US over the next wave of the AI-driven Fourth Industrial Revolution will shape the future of globalisation and the international order,” he said. “This is a more decisive issue and will ultimately determine longer-term global standing for both countries.” AI has emerged as a high-stakes area of US-China competition. Washington has accused Chinese companies of using “distillation” – a machine-learning method in which a smaller model learns from the output of a larger, more powerful one. Some American tech leaders have also called for a voluntary slowdown in AI development to safeguard against potential risks, which Chinese state media and researchers have met with scepticism. The White House fact sheet said the two leaders had agreed to use the term “super intelligence” to describe the emerging technology and had established a US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue, whose next meeting will take place by November. China’s Ministry of Commerce confirmed on Thursday that the two sides had held their first AI dialogue, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent leading the talks for their respective sides. Wang said China had also hoped to establish what he called a “board of AI” or an equivalent framework to promote dialogue. “Thus there is hope that the consensus forged over AI, together with the existing Board of Investment and Board of Trade, will form a triangle of stability on the trade and tech fronts to buttress bilateral ties,” he added. According to the White House fact sheet, the two sides also backed China’s hosting of Apec and the US hosting of the G20, with Trump and Xi expected to attend each other’s summits. China’s state news agency Xinhua also released an eight-point summary of the summit’s outcomes. It highlighted several areas covered by the White House but did not mention coal purchases, rare earths or refined petroleum products. Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist of Pinpoint Asset Management, said progress on specific economic issues was limited, calling the tariff reduction and coal purchases a “positive step” but noting that their scale was relatively small. More significant, he said, were the planned appearances of the two leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and the G20, which would give them two more opportunities to meet in the next three months. “This means the bilateral relations will stay stable at least through the rest of this year, and there could be further progress on economic negotiations in those meetings,” Zhang said. Jack Lee, an analyst with the Zurich-based consultancy China Macro Group, expressed a similar view. “The talks in the White House mark a more routine, normalised in-person interaction between Trump and Xi, with more to follow for the remainder of the year,” he said. Ahead of the meeting between Xi and Trump, He and Bessent held an unscheduled meeting in Washington on Wednesday. The two sides agreed to extend the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea, in October, pushing the deadline from November to January, Bessent told Fox News. Wang of Renmin University said China had again showed its willingness to expand imports from the US, although the two-month extension of the current truce fell short of Beijing’s initial expectation that it would last for another year. In Lee’s view, China’s ambition “extends well beyond sustaining the immediate trade war truce.” “This is also a step towards further anchoring the bilateral relationship, including trade and economic ties, in more institutionalised mechanisms and diplomatic norms that aspirationally can outlast Trump’s presidency,” he said.

title: Why Xi’s flight from China to the US was hours faster than Trump’s in May
description: Russian airspace ban for American carriers gives some Chinese airlines an edge, prompting US aviation sector to oppose new flights.
content: Over private tea in the White House Red Room to mark the end of Xi Jinping’s state visit, US President Donald Trump struck a relaxed tone, marvelling across the table at how fast the Chinese leader had made the trip to America. “It’s a very fast plane … the fastest plane,” Trump said, in footage captured after the White House TV press pool resumed coverage following a court ruling that restored access to outlets previously banned by the US president. “[It was due to] its route,” Xi replied. “We go by Russia, Alaska, Canada, and then into the US.” “That’s fantastic,” Trump said. The tea session between the presidential couples and a tour of American founding documents at the National Archives marked the end of Xi’s three-day state visit to the United States, reciprocating Trump’s Beijing trip in May. According to data from the tracking platform Flightradar24, Xi’s aircraft touched down on American soil at around 5.40pm local time on Wednesday, after a 13½-hour flight from Beijing. When Trump flew back from Beijing, his flight time was considerably longer – at close to 16 hours. Mutual airspace bans triggered by the Russia-Ukraine war mean US aircraft must bypass Russian skies, adding hours to the journey. On Friday afternoon local time, Xi boarded his “special plane” – a modified Boeing 747 drawn from the Air China fleet – to fly the same route back. The journey took around 15 hours, the flight tracker showed. By contrast, Trump’s journey to Beijing aboard Air Force One in May took nearly 18 hours, excluding a refuelling stop of roughly 1½ hours in Alaska, according to US media. Russia barred US and many other foreign carriers from its airspace in 2022, in retaliation for Western flight bans imposed following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Meanwhile, Chinese carriers are allowed to use the shorter route through Russian airspace for eight weekly round-trip US flights. China has consistently positioned itself as neutral in the Ukraine war, calling for dialogue while refraining from condemning the Russian invasion and denying Western allegations that it was supplying Moscow with military support. At Thursday’s official White House welcome ceremony, Xi called for increasing direct US-China flights “to facilitate two-way travel and trade”. But with the Russian airspace ban still in place, the US civil aviation industry remains opposed to adding more flights, with one executive calling the situation “imbalanced” and “unfair”. That message came from Chris Sununu, head of the industry group Airlines for America, which represents carriers including American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines, Reuters reported on Thursday. “It’s not just a minor thing. It’s a huge cost to the airlines to have to go around Russia,” Sununu was quoted as saying. Russian airspace offers the shortest routes linking Asia with Europe and North America, reducing operational costs with shorter flight times and lower fuel consumption. Direct flights between the United States and China plummeted during the Covid-19 pandemic, and diplomatic friction has largely stalled efforts towards full restoration. Carriers from each side are allowed 50 weekly round-trip flights today – compared with more than 150 weekly round-trip passenger flights before restrictions were imposed in early 2020, according to Reuters. In October 2025, the Trump administration made a since-shelved proposal to ban Chinese airlines from overflying Russia on routes to and from the US, arguing that the reduced flight times gave them an unfair advantage over American carriers. Beijing had hit back at the proposal, warning that such restrictions would undermine people-to-people exchanges. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned earlier this month that Russian airspace was becoming increasingly unsafe for commercial airlines due to heightened military activity.

title: Why US deal on Greenland could narrow China’s Arctic engagement
description: New security accord could make western Arctic states warier of working with China and draw Beijing closer to Moscow, Chinese observers say.
content: The new US-Denmark-Greenland security agreement could narrow China’s room to engage in the Arctic – particularly in resource-rich Greenland – and potentially push Beijing closer to Russia, Chinese experts on the matter said. According to observers, the deal – signed on Tuesday – could have the broader effect of accelerating the securitisation of the Arctic and making Western Arctic states more cautious about cooperation with China. But it would be unlikely to significantly disrupt China’s existing Arctic cooperation with Russia, which is largely centred far from Greenland. The deal comes eight months after US President Donald Trump began pressuring Denmark and Greenland – an autonomous Danish territory – over the island’s future, including threats involving tariffs and military force. It expands the US military role on the island while leaving Greenland under Danish control. The agreement comes at a time when the US and its allies are seeking to build their own rare earth supply chains to counter China’s near-monopoly on the critical minerals, a prime source of leverage that continues to loom over talks between Trump and his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. Greenland sits atop some of the world’s largest undeveloped mineral deposits, including rare earth elements, as well as iron ore, graphite, tungsten, palladium, vanadium, zinc, gold, uranium and copper. Under the deal, non-Nato states cannot establish military installations or maintain a persistent military presence in Greenland without mutual agreement. Non-aligned foreign investment in resource extraction and critical infrastructure is also strictly limited. Zhang Yao, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Centre for RimPac Strategic and International Studies, said the agreement appeared to have China in mind because Beijing was neither a US ally nor a Nato partner. “The signing of this agreement will bring some negative factors for China’s future Arctic cooperation with Denmark and other Arctic states, particularly in and around Greenland,” Zhang said. Danish authorities might become more cautious about economic and infrastructure cooperation with China because they did not want to anger Washington, he added. But Zhao Long, director and a senior fellow of the Institute for International Strategic and Security Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said the agreement could not be described as a substantial setback to China’s Arctic interests. “China’s commercial presence in Greenland was already extremely limited,” Zhao said, adding that Chinese companies did not “view the island as a priority” due to commercial and operational constraints. The country’s 2018 Arctic policy white paper described China as a “near-Arctic state” and an “important stakeholder” in Arctic affairs, outlining interests in scientific research, environmental protection, shipping, resource development and Arctic governance. It also promoted the idea of a “Polar Silk Road”. Western scrutiny of China’s activities in the Arctic has since intensified. In 2019, then-US secretary of state Mike Pompeo challenged China’s description of itself as a “near-Arctic state”. In 2020, Ottawa blocked Shandong Gold Mining’s proposed acquisition of the Hope Bay gold mine in Nunavut, the remote territory in northern Canada that encompasses most of the Canadian Arctic. However, Zhang stressed that China’s Arctic interests were primarily focused on “low politics” areas such as trade, shipping, scientific research, environmental cooperation and exchanges with indigenous communities. “There are no military or geopolitical conflicts with Arctic states in these areas,” he said. Zhao argued that the more significant long-term effect could therefore be indirect: the agreement could further embed the Arctic in Nato’s security framework and make other Arctic states more cautious about working with China. Such a shift could affect Chinese participation in scientific research and Arctic governance, potentially adding to the fragmentation of Arctic cooperation, he added. That security shift also has implications for Russia, the dominant Arctic power and China’s most significant partner in the region. The atmosphere for international cooperation in the Arctic had deteriorated since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Zhang said. Finland and Sweden’s accession to Nato has left Russia as the sole non-Nato member among the eight Arctic Council states, while Western sanctions and corporate withdrawals have disrupted cooperation with Moscow in areas including energy. The Greenland agreement was unlikely to have a major immediate impact on China-Russia Arctic cooperation, experts said. “The impact on Beijing is relatively limited,” said Liu Xu, a research fellow at the National Academy of Development and Strategy at Renmin University of China. “Its main cooperation with Russia in shipping routes and energy is concentrated on the Russian and European side of the Arctic.” Liu argued that stronger US and Nato security involvement in the Arctic could, however, push China and Russia towards closer cooperation as competition over the region’s resources and shipping routes intensifies. Zhao, however, cautioned against drawing a direct link between the Greenland agreement and closer China-Russia cooperation. “Beijing’s Arctic drive with Moscow stems more from strategic and economic needs than from external pressure,” he said.

title: North Korea’s weightlifters target Olympic gold rush after world record haul at Asian Games
description: ‘World records not enough,’ says Oh Kwang-ok after three world-best lifts on the way to 57kg gold – and she is not alone.
content: North Korea’s weightlifters will flex their considerable collective muscle when they return to the Olympics for the first time in 12 years at Los Angeles in 2028 – and they could be in for an American gold rush if the Asian Games are any indication. The secretive nation has been the dominant force in global weightlifting since emerging from self-imposed Covid exile to smash six world records at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023. They also won six golds. At the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in Japan this week, North Korea’s strong women and men have taken five gold medals and two silvers from seven events so far. They had also set seven world records by Friday night, less than halfway through the seven-day weightlifting programme. Ri Song-gum started the avalanche on Wednesday with gold and three world records in the women’s 49kg class. Asked if she would consider moving up to 53kg, the lowest women’s category at the next Olympics, the pocket powerhouse replied “Yes” as the 28-year-old chases the only title missing from her collection. She will face competition from within as compatriot Kang Hyon-gong was also dominant in winning the women’s 53kg gold a few hours later. Oh Kwang-ok then set three more world records on her way to women’s 57kg gold on Friday. “The Olympic Games in 2028 are my target,” Oh said in response to a question. “I will try my best to win gold in Los Angeles. The world records are not enough.” First Olympics in 12 years North Korea did not send any athletes to the delayed Tokyo Olympics as it sealed its borders during the pandemic. After the Hangzhou Asian Games in September 2023, it was too late to qualify for Olympic weightlifting at Paris 2024. Since then North Korea have become an unstoppable force, especially in the sport’s lighter body weight classes. At the 2024 world championships in Manama, Bahrain, they were utterly dominant, winning 45 medals across all categories, 26 of them gold, with China next best on 14. A year ago in Norway, North Korea topped the standings by a distance again with 17 golds. It is a remarkable record for an impoverished country where food is in short supply. “The North Korean regime has long viewed sports as a powerful propaganda tool and makes use of sporting success to spread its narratives about the strength of socialist ideology,” Shreyas Reddy, a North Korea analyst at the website NK News, said. He added that the Pyongyang sporting authorities focus their meagre resources very scientifically. “Rather than chasing success in events where victory can come down to natural-born brilliance and flair, North Korea’s sporting authorities instead pour their limited resources into sports that rely on more controllable elements, like strength and technique,” Reddy added. Sports such as weightlifting send coaches to primary schools to hand-pick children with the right physical attributes and potential for intense training and support. “Coaches develop them into physically powerful and technically consistent competitors,” Reddy said. Where other Asian Games nations are wearing brand-new kit for Nagoya, North Korea seem to be making do with the same team vests and tracksuits used for a decade or more. ‘We are world leaders’ The latest fashion statement does not matter to North Korea, but nutrition does, so athletes receive the best available diet. “Despite North Korea’s well-documented food scarcity issues, the regime strategically allocates its limited resources to sports where it believes it has the best chance of success,” Reddy added. The success post-Covid has naturally raised questions about what North Korean weightlifters were doing while the borders were sealed to the outside world. But world doping authorities are back in the country. In January 2024, the World Anti-Doping Agency lifted non-compliant restrictions on North Korea after testing missions were resumed. The following month the International Testing Agency (ITA) conducted out-of-competition testing inside North Korea for the first time in four years. The country’s athletes are subject to international standard testing now like everyone else and, according to their officials, there is no secret to their success. “Our athletes put in so much hard work,” Jang Song-nam, manager of the North Korean weightlifting team, said. “Every gold medal is payback for our hardship over four years [of Covid isolation]. We are world leaders now.”

title: District councillor Peggy Wong resigns amid proxy-vote claims after Tai Po blaze
description: Wong, who has been criticised for her links to former owners’ committee of fire-hit Wang Fuk Court, cites health reasons for stepping down.
content: Hong Kong district councillor Peggy Wong Pik-kiu has resigned from office and several other community roles citing health reasons, following mounting controversy over her team’s alleged proxy-vote collection before last year’s fatal Wang Fuk Court inferno. Wong, a directly elected district councillor for the Tai Po South constituency, also stepped down from her duties as a member of the Tai Po South Area Committee and captain of the Tai Po Kwong Fuk and Plover Cove subdistrict care team. The Home Affairs Department announced the resignations on Saturday, issuing a statement in which Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen said she respected Wong’s decision. Wong, who is affiliated with the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment and Progress of Hong Kong, had served on Tai Po district council for more than 20 years. The resignation came after she skipped nine consecutive council meetings citing health reasons, following a media report last month alleging that Wong’s team had collected a proxy vote from a deceased flat owner. The department previously confirmed it had referred the matter to law enforcement agencies for investigation. Wang Fuk Court residents have said Wong collected proxy votes and tried to influence owners’ decisions on the estate’s renovation works before the fire. She admitted that she had collected votes for two meetings, but denied offering any benefits in return. She also wrote on social media in December last year, weeks after the fire, that she would file reports to police and the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) regarding the disaster, adding that she “would not tolerate any wrongdoing”. The 43-hour inferno that broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po in November last year killed 168 people, including a firefighter, and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. During hearings of an independent committee set up to investigate the fire’s cause, multiple residents mentioned that Wong, as well as individuals associated with her, collected proxy votes from residents at the estate owners’ assembly or had intimidated attendees who held opposing views. In a written statement submitted to the committee, Wong said she had collected proxy votes ahead of two meetings in 2021 and 2024, but had not offered any benefits in return for those votes. She also stressed that she had not collected proxy votes for the general meeting in 2024, at which owners selected the main renovation contractor Prestige Construction and Engineering. Directors of Prestige and senior members of project consultant Will Power Architects are among seven individuals and two firms charged in June by police and the ICAC with 25 offences in connection with the fire this year. The charges ranged from manslaughter to conspiracy to defraud, tax evasion and money laundering. Wong had also stepped down from another role as an adviser to the owners’ committee of Plover Cove Garden, another housing estate in Tai Po, in June this year. A spokesman for the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau said on Saturday evening that a by-election to fill Wong’s seat was a low priority, with a district council election scheduled for the end of next year. Home affairs chief Mak said on Sunday that whether to hold a by-election to fill Wong’s seat depended on the circumstances and had to be assessed for urgency. She added that the government was already scheduled to hold three major elections by the end of next year. Mak said law enforcement was following up on accusations that Wong’s team had collected a proxy vote from a deceased flat owner. She also declined to disclose Wong’s health condition, citing privacy concerns.

title: Meet LSU Tigers coach Lane Kiffin’s daughter Landry Kiffin, who’s studying at Ole Miss
description: Targeted by explicit banners in Oxford, Mississippi over her dad’s move to coach the LSU Tigers, the Ole Miss student has spoken out against the harassment.
content: Lane Kiffin’s decision to leave Ole Miss only days before their first college football playoffs to coach their long-time rivals, the LSU Tigers, has not been received well by his old team – and things got especially heated ahead of the LSU vs. Ole Miss match on September 20, with the latter claiming victory. Landry Kiffin, Kiffin’s oldest daughter, who is a student at Ole Miss, reportedly had several banners with inappropriate and explicit remarks directed at her. In response to the harassment, Landry took to TikTok ahead of the LSU vs Ole Miss face-off to call out the banners. “I opened my phone this morning to pictures of banners on houses around Oxford posted on different accounts saying really inappropriate things about me and with somebody that genuinely I have never met in my life which makes it even more frustrating to say the least,” Landry said. “I think that turning the girl into a punchline of a sexual joke because you’re upset at somebody she’s related to should not be OK,” Landry continued. “I understand emotions are high this week, and people are upset, but I’m my own person. I’ll never understand how someone can feel good about themselves putting such vulgar things about a girl on a giant banner hanging from their house,” she said. Here’s everything you need to know about Lane Kiffin’s daughter, Landry. Landry Kiffin is the oldest of Lane Kiffin’s three kids Landry Kiffin was born to Lane and Layla Kiffin in December 2004. The couple also share Landry’s younger sister, Presley, and brother, Monte Knox Kiffin. Lane and Layla originally split in 2016, but reportedly reconciled last year. Landry attended high school in Los Angeles for three years while her father coached the football team at the University of Southern California, per People magazine. She is currently a student at the University of Mississippi, where she is pursuing a degree in business administration. She is also a member of the sorority house Kappa Kappa Gamma, as per her LinkedIn. She is an entrepreneur View this post on Instagram A post shared by landry kiffin (@landrykiffin) While she chose not to pursue a career in American football like her father, 21-year-old Landry is an entrepreneur and kick-started her own clothing brand, Ju1ce, in 2023, as per her LinkedIn. In July, she launched another clothing brand named Fifth Year. The brand sells athleisure apparel. In addition to running her own clothing lines, Landry is a full-time Pilates instructor at Power Movement, a Pilates studio in Mississippi. Who is Landry Kiffin dating? Landry is reportedly in a relationship with Whit Weeks, a linebacker for Ole Miss’ rivals and her dad’s former team, the LSU Tigers. The couple hard-launched their relationship on Instagram in September 2025 – months before Kiffin made the decision to join LSU as their head coach. When asked if dating his coach’s daughter made things awkward between him and Kiffin, Weeks told SEC media: “It hasn’t affected my relationship with him at all. I know that when we go into that building, everyone in our building has the same mindset and same goals. When you’re in that building, you’re there for work. We like to have a lot of fun up there, too, but at the end of the day it is work.”

title: Woman arrested over child abuse in Hong Kong after dashcam video shows boy shoved
description: Wan Chai officers investigate child abuse case after dashcam footage shows a woman pushing a boy into a metal roadside railing.
content: A 44-year-old woman in Hong Kong has been arrested on suspicion of child abuse after dashcam footage appeared to show her shoving a boy into a roadside railing. A police force spokesman said on Saturday that the woman was arrested on Friday afternoon in Western district after a widely circulated dashcam video drew the force’s attention. In the video seen by the South China Morning Post, the woman gets out of a private car at a section of Wan Chai Road near Burrows Street, with a boy following suit. The woman then turns around to hold onto the boy by his waist, before the two walk towards the pavement next to the road. However, the woman in the video pushes the boy towards a metal railing on the roadside while on their way to the pavement. After the boy falls to the ground, the woman picks him up by his hand, before the two continue walking to the pavement. The force spokesman added that the woman had been released on bail and Wan Chai district’s criminal investigation team was following up on the case. Under Hong Kong law, the maximum punishment for child abuse or neglect is 10 years in prison.

title: Mid-Autumn light show in Yuen Long panned online over stench and execution
description: Drainage Services Department event at nullah draws strong turnout, but mixed reactions.
content: A government-hosted Mid-Autumn Festival light show at a nullah in Hong Kong has sparked widespread online criticism, with revellers complaining of foul smells and poor execution. Attendees posted their reviews on social media on Saturday after the opening night of the two-day “Yuen Long Flood Barrier and Nullah Improvement Scheme – Mid-Autumn Light Show” organised by the Drainage Services Department. The event was billed as an inaugural initiative to transform the Yuen Long nullah into a large-scale art exhibition space, but many visitors took to platforms such as Threads to express their disappointment. “A foul smell was coming out while I was watching the show,” an attendee posted on Threads, sharing videos showing light projections against a wide, open-air concrete storm drainage channel. Another said: “I wondered which ‘genius’ came up with the idea of just placing white boards to cover up the canal. The projected images only faced one direction and weren’t even clear. “It would have been much clearer if they had just suspended a huge white cloth across to cover the entire smelly section and projected it onto that instead.” A third user wrote: “The idea was good, but the execution was poor. It was projected downwards, but there are no elevated viewing platforms nearby, so you can’t see it clearly at all.” While some questioned how much the show had cost the taxpayer, others praised the display as beautiful when floral patterns of lanterns, rabbits and flowers were projected onto the drainage canal. The light show took place at the Yuen Long Nullah section between the MTR Long Ping station and On Ning Road, on both Friday and Saturday nights. Residents needed to register with the government before getting in the viewing area. Despite the backlash, the event drew large crowds to both sides of the canal on the opening night. According to the department, the show combined large-scale projection, animation and lighting effects, with reunion as the theme of the performance and site decoration. “Through captivating light-and-shadow stories, it guides the public to understand the project’s flood prevention functions, environmental enhancements, and the future vision of the revitalised nullah,” it said on the social media promotion page. The South China Morning Post has contacted the department for comment.

title: 6 dead after explosion destroys building in Athens
description: The blast on Friday destroyed a two-storey ‌building in Plaka, near some of Athens’ most visited sites.
content: Six people have died, the Greek fire brigade said on Saturday, after a two-storey residential building ‌in a tourist area of central Athens collapsed following an explosion which the capital’s mayor said was likely linked to gas infrastructure. Emergency crews in heavy gear and red helmets assisted by rescue dogs, cameras and sensors found the bodies of six people, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis ⁠said in a televised briefing. They were looking for an elderly couple who lived ‌in one apartment and four tourists who were staying in another as they removed debris from the building. The fire ‌brigade’s crime investigation unit was also on site to identify the ⁠cause of the ⁠blast after reports of a gas smell in an area which is home to hotels ‌and short-term rentals. The tourists, two American couples, had been expected to check in to catch a ‌flight from ‌Athens airport at 3pm local time on Friday but did not ‌show up, a police source said. Ambulances stood by on Saturday to ⁠take the bodies to the hospital for identification. Friday’s blast destroyed the building in ⁠Plaka, near some of Athens’ most visited sites including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus, damaging nearby houses, shops and cars ‌and sending rubble and broken ‌glass as far as three blocks away. The building was reduced to twisted metal, shattered tiles and concrete, strewn with household items and clothing.

title: Hong Kong-born cookie brand founder brings flavours of her youth to small-town France
description: Louise Lui founded Sucré in her French partner’s hometown to bridge cultures with East-meets-West treats. Not everyone got it immediately.
content: In 2024, French artisanal cookie company Sucré did a four-day pop-up in Hong Kong. The response was overwhelming, says Louise Lui, the brand’s Hong Kong-born co-founder. “There was already a queue forming outside 25 minutes before us selling,” she says. “And then I was just like, ‘Oh my God, how do you know about us?’” When developing recipes for the pop-up, Lui and her French partner in life and business, Victor Selle, wanted something that would bridge cultures. They landed on familiar Asian flavours such as milk tea, sesame and matcha, and the cookies struck a chord with customers. “No explanation is needed almost,” Lui says. “Everyone understood the cha chaan teng [traditional Hong Kong-style cafe] reference and went, ‘Absolutely, I’m going to try it.’ And they loved it.” But taking those flavours back to France yielded different results. Lost in translation “We got very extreme reviews,” Lui says. “Most people are like, ‘I don’t understand it. What is the middle? Is it caramel?’ But we like it because there’s so much you can push through and try to explain.” The boldest fusion in Sucré’s line-up turned out to be the white chocolate and miso cookie. “You can imagine trying to describe this to a bunch of older people in a small town,” Lui laughs. “Throwback to five years ago, miso was something that when you explained it – fermented soy paste – it could not sound any worse.” To many of their middle-aged French customers, the concept seemed deeply unappealing.
