But Lui says her perseverance built her brand’s identity. “It links to my stubbornness a little bit,” she says. “I’m not telling you that you have to buy it, but listen to my story.” Lui and Selle met in Hong Kong while working in the hospitality industry for the same restaurant group. The couple later moved to London, where they continued working in hospitality and found themselves inspired by the city’s food scene. When the Covid-19 pandemic hit, they found themselves separated – Lui was in London while Selle was stuck in his hometown of Reims, around 150km (90 miles) northeast of Paris. When Lui eventually joined Selle in Reims, she struggled with the language barrier. “No one speaks English. My French was horrible,” she says. “The only word I could spot at the bakery was ‘cookie’.” Except it was not exactly a cookie. “It was a very sad, dry biscuit,” Lui says, adding that before long, the couple decided to take matters into their own hands and build their own cookie business. Sucré’s most distinctive creations are where East meets West – and during the summer 2026 heatwave, Lui introduced a distinctly Hong Kong drink to the French shop: dong ling cha, or iced lemon tea. “Here, people are not very accustomed to having an iced drink, unlike us,” Lui says. “We grew up with iced lemon tea, iced milk tea and all of these amazing things. It pains me to see people drinking a hot Americano when it’s 43 degrees.” The first customer’s reaction was a nail-biting moment. “The first time a lady tried it, I was so nervous,” Lui says. “I was almost feeling like, ‘Is she going to reject my culture? Reject something that I grew up loving?’” The customer ended up loving it, and now, Lui says, the Asian flavours are what keep her regulars coming back for more. A deliberately small operation Sucré now has three permanent locations – one in Reims; one in the town of Senlis, around 50km north of Paris; and a new shop in the French capital that opened in June 2026. The brand continues to grow while staying true to its cross-cultural roots. It remains a deliberately small operation. Beyond Lui and Selle, the team includes a 22-year-old manager who has been with the brand for four years and runs the Reims shop with a part-timer, plus two staff members who help run the Paris store. Despite Sucré’s size, Lui and Selle are hands-on in every aspect of the business, from dough production and jam making to staff training and front-of-house service. That small-team ethos extends to the brand’s partnership model. In Paris, Sucré operates in a shared coffee shop space called All Good, owned by old friends they met in Hong Kong. Rather than a stand-alone Sucré shop, it’s a long-term collaboration. “We’re not after going viral or exponential growth,” Lui says. “We’re finding people that genuinely love what we do and building that loyal base of followership.” For Lui, the journey has been about more than just cookies – it has been about bridging two culinary worlds that she calls home. “The idea of Sucré is very simple: make something very simple, but good simple, with good ingredients,” she says. “We just want to share the love of good food, no matter which culture it’s coming from.”

title: Chinese doctor with PhD leaves medical career to deliver food, pursue music part-time
description: Liu knows a PhD means status and money, but she realises it is just not for her.
content: A Chinese doctoral graduate in medicine left her promising hospital job to embrace a “less meritocratic” lifestyle as a part-time freelancer. Liu Zihan, 31, delivers food, performs at a pub, sells breakfast, and explores a variety of part-time jobs that captivate her interests while providing for her living expenses. Before leaving her full-time employment in February, Liu served as a psychiatrist and postdoctoral researcher at a Grade 3A hospital in Zhuhai, in southern China’s Guangdong province. This hospital is in the highest, most prestigious tier of the national healthcare classification system. Liu characterised the first 30 years of her life as “meritocratic.” She grew up in one of the most competitive provinces, Hebei in northern China, and studied for a year at Hengshui High School, which is nationally renowned for its military-style discipline. She gained admission to the medical school at Sichuan University and further pursued her doctoral degree at the University of Macau’s Faculty of Health Sciences. By 2022, at the age of 27, Liu had earned her doctoral degree and already secured a position at a prestigious hospital in Zhuhai. Liu received positive feedback from her patients, some of whom even sent her thank-you letters and gratitude pennants. She noted that she enjoyed engaging with patients without distinguishing between their identities and social labels. “I prefer genuine communication between hearts,” she stated. Ultimately, she found it increasingly difficult to tolerate the conventional work environment, which necessitated adherence to a rigid daily schedule. It took her two years to finally decide to resign. Liu recognises that a PhD can lead to a respectable job and a good salary, but she realised that this was not the life she desired. After resigning, she first travelled, then sold breakfast and sang at a pub. During this time, she connected with a diverse group of friends who operate restaurants, pubs, and food stalls – jobs often deemed less glamorous. However, Liu found in them an “optimism, resilience, and chill” that were rare in her previous life. She learned from their experiences and embraced a free-spirited life as a part-time worker, without planning her next day or calculating monthly earnings. Liu continues to practise her profession part-time as a therapist. She expressed that the constraints she experienced at work, as well as her fears of exploring alternative lifestyles, are common among today’s youth. She is deeply moved by the kindness shown by gig workers towards one another. “Delivery riders share traffic updates, and pub singers and stall owners look out for each other. In comparison to grades and competition, there are far more significant values, like care and support.” Liu’s parents, while proud of her credentials as a PhD graduate and doctor, are puzzled by her choices. However, they are gradually coming to terms with her decision after she explained that countless new experiences await her. She dreams of hosting a concert, turning her journey into a film, and having a small yard where her cat can play freely one day.

title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia test limits of Mecca regional security pact
description: Turkey and Pakistan are unlikely to intervene despite the deal’s terms, which could hobble its deterrent effect, analysts say.
content: Just a month after Saudi Arabia signed a regional mutual defence deal with Pakistan and Turkey, attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against the kingdom’s energy infrastructure and military sites are testing the pact’s limits. At a hastily convened meeting of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh on Friday, military chiefs of the three parties reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence, according to the Saudi Press Agency. The agency said the talks focused on “intelligence cooperation, military coordination, and capability integration to strengthen deterrence and collective defence”. But there was no word on what military support Pakistan and Ankara would give Saudi Arabia. Chinese analysts said the attacks were an initial stress test for theagreement signed in August, but the outcome was unlikely to be direct Turkish and Pakistani intervention in the Saudi-Houthi conflict. As for China, observers noted that Beijing supported countries in the region taking greater ownership of their security and wanted to avoid a wider conflict. In recent weeks, Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and taken effective control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a maritime chokepoint connecting the sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Riyadh has responded with air strikes, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at targets on Saudi territory. Under the Mecca pact, an armed attack against any one of the three would be regarded as an attack against all, much like Nato’s Article 5. But the agreement does not specify what circumstances would require military intervention or what form such help would take. Zhang Chuchu, deputy director of the Centre for Middle Eastern Studies at Fudan University, said the Houthi attacks were the first test of the Mecca pact. Pakistan and Turkey did not want to directly intervene in Yemen or be drawn into the conflict, Zhang said, which could undermine the pact’s “actual deterrent effect”. “If others fail to step up during Saudi Arabia’s first major threat, Riyadh may respond in kind in the future,” she said, which would potentially make their military cooperation under the deal “very loose”. The meeting on Friday was aimed mainly at “turning the pact into a more concrete framework” and “preventing it from becoming a loosely structured initiative”, Zhang added. “The countries are likely to discuss establishing institutions such as a joint secretariat and working groups or committees to implement the agreement,” she said. They could also deepen intelligence sharing and military-technical cooperation, as well as cooperation on air defence and maritime security. “Such cooperation would not mean Turkey and Pakistan would directly intervene in the Saudi-Houthi conflict,” Zhang said. Li Weijian, a researcher at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said the agreement’s “symbolic significance is greater than its practical significance”, partly because its provisions were not clear on what constituted an “armed attack”. Turkey and Pakistan were unlikely to send troops, Li said, but could provide political support, intelligence or defensive help while pushing for negotiations between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. For Beijing, the Mecca pact reflected a broader push for regional countries to take greater responsibility for their own security, Li said. Li said Beijing viewed the Mecca agreement as “representing the right direction”. “In the past, the role played by external forces in the Middle East – often under the guise of providing security and protection – has actually not been a positive one,” he said, adding that China supported the pact’s open-ended nature and the possibility of other regional states joining. China did not want the Saudi-Houthi conflict to expand further and draw in more countries, he said. When they met in Beijing earlier this month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani that China supported countries in the region “holding their own future and destiny firmly in their hands”. He also called for “just and equitable new regional security architecture”. Reuters, citing Iranian sources, reported last week that China had privately asked Iran to help restrain the Houthis after Saudi Arabia appealed to Beijing. Disruption at the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb would hurt not only China’s energy and shipping interests but the global economy, Li said. “China, as a major global power, will certainly play a constructive role in this issue,” he said. Wang also met his Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in Beijing last week, and called for a political settlement to the country’s conflict with the United States. Regional tensions must not further spill over into Yemen, the Chinese foreign ministry quoted Wang as saying. Washington also appears reluctant to open another front in its war on Iran, even though Saudi Arabia is a close US ally. The New York Times reported that President Donald Trump had initially authorised preparations for strikes against the Houthis after Riyadh appealed for US intervention, but reversed course last weekend. Zhang said Washington was keen to “avoid direct involvement” and reluctant to repeat last year’s strikes against the Houthis ahead of the US’ midterm elections in November.

title: Billie Jean King says reforming tennis ‘a challenge’ as schedule sparks burnout concerns
description: Legend of the sport in Shenzhen for namesake tournament, joins former players Ilana Kloss and Conchita Martinez for panel discussion.
content: Tennis legend Billie Jean King and two former professionals acknowledged modern players are suffering from burnout, but believed any change would be affected by the differing needs of elite players and rest, and the commercial pressure of tournaments. At present, WTA rules say players ranked in the top 30 must compete in all grand slams and ten WTA 1000 tournaments, and skipping these events results in ranking penalties and heavy financial fines that directly damage world standings and core commercial interests. World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka labelled the WTA schedule “insane” earlier this year, revealing she plans to miss select mandatory events to protect her body despite the punishments that would bring. Similarly, six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek described the calendar as “madness”, confirming plans to reduce her 2026 commitments to rest and refine her game. The issue has drawn equal concern on the men’s ATP Tour after Carlos Alcaraz missed four months of the 2026 season with a wrist injury following a congested schedule, and then announced during the US Open that he was “going to take some breaks, some long breaks” because he felt it impossible to play all the tournaments. Eight-time major champion Andre Agassi recently urged administrators to implement a genuine off-season and adopt a “less is more” approach to safeguard player health amid rising injury rates. Speaking to the South China Morning Post during a recent panel discussion for the Billie Jean King Cup in Shenzhen, the three former players laid bare the harsh economic and logistical realities behind any potential schedule cutbacks. Former world No 1 women’s doubles player and ex-CEO of World TeamTennis Ilana Kloss admitted that while player fatigue is undeniable, the tour’s expansion has made scaling back far more complicated than simply adopting a “less is more” mindset. “I think we came from not very many tournaments, and now tennis is so popular that we keep adding tournaments,” Kloss said. “And the calendar is probably a little bit too crowded now.” Former women’s Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez, speaking from her perspective as coach to rising star Mirra Andreeva, pointed to shrinking off-seasons and stringent tour mandates as a primary driver of physical and mental exhaustion. “I remember back in the days when I was competing, we were fighting to have an off-season, like a real off-season of two months, because when you finish after so many tournaments, these competitions, so much pressure, I mean, it puts a lot into your body, so you need to rest physically, mentally,” Martinez said. She explained that a proper off-season allows players time to recover from injuries and undergo a thorough pre-season to prepare for the remaining eight to ten months of competition. The current season extends into mid-November for those competing in the WTA Finals, leaving players with little time to recover. “After that, what? You can take 10 days off, and then you have to prepare for the next year. What can you have? Maybe three weeks, and that’s not enough,” Martinez said. “And after year after year after year, we are already seeing a lot of injuries, so it’s not easy because the calendar is packed with tournaments.” Martinez emphasised that mandatory entry rules strip players of flexibility, highlighting the burden placed on her own player. “In the case of Mirra, the player that I’m coaching, she has to play mandatory six tournaments of 500, and all of the 1000 tournaments. If not, they penalise you,” Martinez said. “So it’s a lot. It’s a lot for the body, for the mental part. I mean, she’s young, but year after year, it gets to you.” Kloss mentioned that it’s very different for the top players who have to play from round one through the finals compared to those who exit a tournament early, while outlining the frustrating dilemma of trying to fix it. “For the players that lose in the first or second round, it’s different, they want more. So you’re trying to balance,” Kloss said. Furthermore, the former world No 1 women’s player and champion for social justice and gender equality, King agreed with Martinez, stressing that an athlete’s perspective on the schedule depends heavily on their standing in the game. “I think you said it all though. It depends where you are. If you’re ranked 200 in the world versus the top 10, and that’s the challenge,” King said. Having closely followed WTA 250-level tournaments, King highlighted how lesser-known players rely on a full calendar to build their careers and earn a living. “It’s the players who aren’t winning big tournaments, and so they need a lot,” King said. “If you’re losing first round every week, you’re playing one out of seven days. If you win, you played all seven days. So that’s a challenge, you know, where are they ranked, what do they need, because the needs are very different.” Addressing whether a two-tier tour structure could offer a solution, similar to the NBA’s G League and main league, Kloss acknowledged the idea of a “qualifying tour and then a main tour”, but underscored the immense political and commercial resistance to downsizing. “It is very difficult to cut things back. It’s much easier to grow,” Kloss said. “And tennis has been around a long time and it’s evolved, and you know, nobody wants to give up the tournaments.” Kloss also highlighted the importance of national team events like the Billie Jean King Cup, which serves as mandatory Olympic qualifiers while offering players a unique team dynamic. “When you play on a team, you get to have a much different experience. You’re all together and you learn from the other players, and I think possibly there could be an individual season and a team season,” Kloss said. “But you know, our sport, because it is so mature, it is a challenge.” Reflecting on the difficult nature of the debate, King concluded with a candid reaction: “Frustration is what that question brought up! I get frustrated.”

title: Thailand’s Bangkok declares flood disaster across city as thousands flee from homes
description: Rains have pounded the city since Wednesday, with no respite forecast until late Sunday as waters rise to at least two feet.
content: Entire Bangkok neighbourhoods were inundated on Saturday as the city government declared a flood disaster after the worst rains in years overwhelmed the Thai capital, submerging roads, cars and forcing thousands to leave their homes. Bangkok is flood-prone, especially during the monsoon season, but waters rarely linger for long. Nonetheless, the city’s drainage is notoriously ill-equipped to handle storm bursts as it struggles to cope with waters that have reached at least two feet (60cm) and are still rising. Over 48 hours of continuous rain have paralysed parts of Bangkok amid the intensifying, unpredictable extremes of the climate crisis. Rains have pounded the city since Wednesday, intensifying on Friday with no respite forecast until late Sunday. In the Pra Kanong district, a hodgepodge of markets, hotels, cafes and bars on the main Sukhumvit Road, floodwaters dumped garbage through narrow alleyways where expensive villas stand alongside working-class shophouses and blocks of flats. “In all the years I’ve lived here I’ve never seen flooding this bad,” said Bangkok resident Narin Wernthaisong, who was wading through thigh-high water. He said the exception was 2011 when floods left 500 dead and the central part of the country submerged – including much of the capital – for weeks. “This time, it feels very unusual. The rain hasn’t been particularly heavy, yet there’s been a huge amount of water accumulating. It’s just sitting there, and there doesn’t seem to be anywhere for it to drain.” Many flood-hit neighbourhoods were caught off guard after City Hall initially downplayed the potential for major floods, appearing to base its assessment on weather warnings that predicted continuous rain but not heavy storm downpours like those that caused widespread damage in 2011. The Bangkok Metropolitan Authority (BMA) has declared a disaster across all 50 districts. “Yesterday I didn’t think anything was going to happen. But around 3am, the water came into the house. Everything was floating. It really feels like something strange is happening this year,” Narin said. Despite the pains and inconvenience of living through the flooding – and the expensive, difficult days ahead to clear debris and cover damages – many Bangkok residents took the chaos in their stride with a sense of community and fun. A group of men played music, sang and drank beers under an umbrella, while neighbours helped each other with sandbags, moving belongings to higher floors and food to the elderly trapped in their homes. An online crowdsourcing campaign has begun to highlight flooded roads since Friday evening rush hour, when tens of thousands of commuters were stranded in traffic for hours. Thailand’s Meteorological Department has warned that the heavy rain would continue in most parts of the country through Sunday, citing a strong low-pressure system over the central region and strengthening southwest monsoon conditions. As of Saturday, more than 84,000 people in 21 provinces nationwide have been affected by flooding, especially in the central region. Authorities had sent emergency warning messages through the cell-broadcast system to people in affected areas, the government said. Bangkok’s flood woes are further compounded each year thanks to breakneck construction over soft clay soils while residents face more pressure due to a creaking drainage system, according to city planners. The BMA has been on a citywide push to widen and clean drains, but this weekend’s floods appear to have thwarted its efforts for now. Additional reporting by Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

title: How Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump opened a parallel track in US-China diplomacy
description: First ladies’ cultural outings and apparently warm conversations a ‘clear signal’ on willingness to advance understanding, analyst says.
content: First ladies Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump opened a new front in US-China exchanges this week, with their unusually frequent and spontaneous interactions putting a more personal face on ties during the presidential summit in Washington. The pair charted a parallel path of soft power diplomacy – sharing conversations, cultural outings and moments of apparent warmth during a visit otherwise shadowed by trade tensions, as well as artificial intelligence and other strategic issues. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Peng and Trump’s cultural exchanges had “brought the hearts of the two peoples closer”, according to a statement by the ministry on Saturday. “Warm and personable first-lady diplomacy has injected a softer force into the visit,” Wang was quoted as saying. According to US-China relations expert Sun Chenghao, direct interaction between the two first ladies presented “a more natural and personable side of bilateral relations” and sent out “a clear signal that both sides are willing to understand each other”. That dynamic was in full display at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday. After stepping off the plane with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Peng chatted briefly with the US first lady without an interpreter as they walked together on the red carpet. Later, Peng appeared to mouth the word “wonderful” after a military band played the US and Chinese national anthems, both incidents prompting viral online discussion about her English skills. Yet Peng’s role in cultural diplomacy long predates this week’s visit. A celebrated soprano who rose to fame as a military singer, Peng has accompanied Xi on overseas trips since he became president in 2013 and has used music, education and cultural activities as part of her public role. Her fluent English has also been part of that image – notably in 2015, when she delivered a powerful speech at the United Nations on education for girls and gender equality. What set the latest occasion apart was the setting. At the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art, the first ladies watched a youth choir perform Chinese songs. Peng smiled warmly as she sang along to “Jasmine Flower” – China’s most famous folk tune – calling out “bravo” as the performance ended. The scene offered something that formal summit diplomacy rarely does: an opportunity for the two countries to present themselves through culture rather than policy. “Cultural and people-to-people exchanges could complement formal summit diplomacy,” said Sun, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing. “They connect the two countries through experiences more familiar to ordinary people … [and could] lower the psychological barrier to understanding the other country,” he said. “They also allow the public to see areas of resonance between the two societies, helping to build broader social support for formal diplomacy.” The first ladies’ key role was reflected throughout their wider schedule. Melania Trump led preparations for Thursday’s state dinner, while the two women were seated together at the centre of a tea gathering at the White House’s Red Room on Friday, the final day of Xi’s visit. “For now, such interactions may be most effective at generating attention and curiosity,” Sun said, highlighting Peng’s English exchanges and interactions with the youth choir. “Whether they can be translated into sustained understanding depends on follow-up exchanges and the broader policy environment in both countries.”

title: Hikers urge live updates on free quota spots to fix Po Pin Chau booking confusion
description: Trial registration scheme for section of High Island Geo Trail should have real-time displays showing when time slots are available, visitors say.
content: Hikers flocking to a popular geological attraction in Hong Kong’s Sai Kung over the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend have called for real-time displays showing when time slots are available under a trial registration system. The High Island Geo Trail’s Po Pin Chau section continued to draw lines of visitors on Saturday morning – the second day of an extended weekend in mainland China. While hikers who booked a slot under a newly introduced trial registration system were seen queuing at the entrance in the hot sun, others hoped to try their luck on site for walk-in openings. Among them was Maria Chen, a mainland postgraduate student studying in Hong Kong, who said she had checked for reservations four days in advance, only to find the slots fully booked. “The staff asked us to wait 10 minutes or more to see if any on-site slots would open up, but we do not know how long we have to wait, so we are going to head to Long Ke to continue our hike,” she said. “It would be better if they could display in real time how many slots have been freed up by no-shows.” Within minutes of Chen calling it quits at around 9.40am, several slots opened up. Staff then called out for visitors without reservations to register online. During the first weekend of the trial system, September 5 and 6, more than half of the hikers who registered online failed to show up. The government later said it would review data from the trial run after the mainland’s National Day “golden week” break in October. Alex Lin, a 35-year-old visitor from Shenzhen, said she was unaware that on-site bookings were available. Although she had secured a 1pm time slot five days ago, she expressed concerns it would be too late in the day and had arrived at 8am instead, as no reservations are required before 9am. “I came from Shenzhen at 6am to make sure I could get onto the trail. The booking system itself is quite smooth, but I was not sure how the on-site quota release works,” she said. The city’s first countryside real-name reservation system, launched by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department earlier this month to manage surging visitor numbers at Po Pin Chau, caps daily entries at 2,000 during designated hours on selected weekends and public holidays. The 120-minute time slots, which allow for up to 500 people at a time, must be booked via travel platform Klook. Visitors must register using their real names and identity documents. The extended Mid-Autumn Festival weekend and the National Day golden week, running from October 1 to 7, are set to be the trial scheme’s first real test. Andre Yi, a 22-year-old university student from Hunan province, said he was spending the extended weekend in Hong Kong with friends and had set aside the second day to see the city’s natural scenery. “We visited Victoria Harbour and The Peak yesterday. We do not have a fixed budget for this trip – we’ll spend on whatever we like,” he said. “I saw this place on RedNote. It is very different from the landscapes and mountains back home in Hunan, so I wanted to come and see it for myself.”

title: Opinion | How Chinese firms can avoid a Europe-style backlash in Southeast Asia
description: If Beijing’s tech expansion ends up undercutting local economies, Asean partners will soon ask whose prosperity it actually serves.
content: China’s technology companies face a question that no pricing strategy can answer: what will their success do to their trading partners? In Europe, that question has become politically urgent. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warns of a “second China shock”, linking persistent trade imbalances to the erosion of Europe’s industrial base. Europe’s dispute carries a broader warning: affordable products can coexist with deep anxiety over the loss of productive capability. If industrial dumping is the charge China faces in Europe, Chinese companies must prevent “technological dumping” from becoming the charge they face in Southeast Asia. Such an accusation would gain traction if low-cost models, platforms and turnkey systems entered markets faster than local firms can learn, compete and develop products of their own. Low prices may win contracts, but they cannot secure lasting trust if host economies acquire advanced tools while losing the capacity to build and improve them. Eventually, those economies will ask whose prosperity the technology serves. The expansion of Chinese artificial intelligence in Southeast Asia must therefore answer four questions. Does it help host industries move towards higher-value production? Does it equip locals to design, adapt and improve technology, rather than simply operate imported systems? Does the Chinese provider put down roots through local hiring, procurement, research and reinvestment? And do citizens share the gains through better jobs, rising incomes and more accessible services? Every major deployment should make an industry more productive, a local company more capable and workers better equipped to earn a living. If AI increases profits while destroying livelihoods and concentrating the gains elsewhere, cooperation will breed resentment. The opportunity is considerable. The Asean-China Free Trade Area 3.0 upgrade protocol under ratification is designed to deepen cooperation in areas including the digital economy and supply-chain connectivity. Once in force, it could better match Chinese technology with demand across the economies of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, allowing a successful application in one country to be adapted and scaled across the region. The commercial momentum is visible. At the recently concluded China-Asean Expo in Guangxi, organisers established an “Asean demand zone” and reported 89 requests for cooperation spanning transport, smart logistics, urban management and industrial parks. They also reported more than 8,000 AI-assisted business matches before the event, while an AI marketplace featured about 500 products from 70 companies. These figures show the scale of the opportunity, but say little about where technological capability and commercial value will ultimately reside. Take Guangxi’s AI development strategy: it takes research and development in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, integrates the systems in Guangxi and offers the applications to Asean. The question is where capability accumulates after deployment. Every major China-Asean AI project should therefore pass three tests. The first is whether procurement builds independent capability. When projects are supported by public money or joint development funds, contracts should specify what local teams will be able to do after the foreign supplier steps back. This might include evaluating models, diagnosing failures, maintaining systems and adapting applications. The completion of a project should also leave behind engineers capable of operating, modifying and improving the technology independently. The second test is whether local firms gain genuine commercial agency. Chinese suppliers should retain ownership of the technology they bring. At the same time, Asean partners should secure clearly negotiated ownership, licensing or sales rights over the applications, data sets, interfaces and improvements they help create. If Asean contributes the languages, operating environments, industry knowledge and trial customers through which a product improves, it should capture a fair share of the resulting knowledge and commercial value. The third test is whether productivity gains reach workers, smaller businesses and consumers. AI will transform some jobs and eliminate others. The responsibility is to ensure workers do not bear the full cost of higher productivity. Chinese technology providers should bear their share of that responsibility. Where deployment may significantly displace workers, training, redeployment and transition measures should be included in project contracts and budgets. These costs should not be handed to the host government as an afterthought. Cooperation should help workers acquire more valuable skills, enable local businesses to expand and give consumers access to better, more affordable services. Measurable results offer the most convincing answer to any accusation of technological dumping. The clearest evidence of a stronger Asean technological base would be the emergence of local firms capable of becoming Chinese companies’ suppliers, long-term partners and, eventually, competitors. Europe’s disputes carry a plain warning for China: export success that undermines a partner’s confidence in its own industrial future will eventually provoke resistance. The strongest defence against a European-style backlash is visible local prosperity: Asean industries moving up the value chain, local companies gaining the capacity to innovate, and ordinary people finding Chinese AI has expanded their opportunities rather than threatened their livelihoods.

title: Hong Kong police investigate suspected pinhole cameras in gym changing rooms
description: Officers found three devices across three cubicles of 24/7 Fitness gym in Sha Tin, police say.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating a case of voyeurism after three suspected pinhole cameras were found in the changing rooms of a 24/7 Fitness branch in Sha Tin. The force said on Saturday that officers were alerted at 5.11pm on Friday to a suspected pinhole camera attached with black tape to the false ceiling of a changing room at the gym on Lek Yuen Street. Upon searching, officers discovered three suspected pinhole cameras across three of the gym’s changing rooms, according to police. The case had been classified as voyeurism, police said. The incident surfaced after a male gym member posted a video online saying that he had noticed an unusually wide seam along the false ceiling. When he lifted the ceiling panel, he discovered what appeared to be a pinhole camera secured in place with black tape. He added that the incident had been reported to police. The manager of the branch told the media on Saturday that staff had conducted a thorough inspection after discovering the suspicious tape. “Upon learning of this matter internally, we notified headquarters, and they have arranged for all branches to take the appropriate measures,” he said. Voyeurism in Hong Kong carries a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment.

title: How Hong Kong designer Kinyan Lam’s slow fashion label puts Chinese ethnic artisans first
description: Kinyan Lam’s eponymous brand champions natural materials, dyeing and embroidery from China’s Dong ethnic minority group.
content: Hong Kong designer Kinyan Lam’s autumn/winter 2026 collection, Grounded, is more than a seasonal drop. It sets a clear vision for the future of his eponymous brand: that slowing down is the only way forward. “I heard a saying that plants and trees have two ways of growing: they explode into the world, but their roots continue to dig deep into the soil,” says Lam, who is in his thirties. “Right now, I am just a small tree, and I want to grow my roots deeper so I can grow into a big tree. This is a moment for our brand to become really grounded.” After studying at the Hong Kong Design Institute (HKDI), Lam went on to earn a master’s degree at the London College of Fashion from 2019 to 2020. He later returned to Hong Kong to teach at his alma mater, where he developed a passion for textiles and natural dyeing. In 2021, he founded Genau Studio, which offers garment-dyeing services and workshops focused on natural dyes. Lam credits his love for nature to his childhood growing up in a small village in China’s Guangdong province, before he moved to Hong Kong aged 10. In 2023, he launched his fashion brand Kinyan Lam, focusing on natural materials, traditional dyeing techniques and embroidery produced in collaboration with artisans from the Dong ethnic minority group in China’s Guizhou province. Since 2024, Lam has showcased his work on international platforms, including Paris Fashion Week. This year, he was named one of Fashion Asia Hong Kong’s 10 Asian Designers to Watch. On September 3, he presented “Grounded” at the initiative’s inaugural fashion show, held at Rosewood Hong Kong. Lam was also named a semi-finalist for the prestigious 2026 LVMH Prize, bringing further international attention to his work. Despite the accolades, Lam is acutely aware of the fashion industry’s short attention span. “If you look at the life cycle of a brand, it’s really short,” he says. “Most brands start to fail after hitting the five-year mark, and that’s a concern for me.” For Lam, the threat of slowing sales is not only a question of his label’s longevity; it could also affect the livelihoods of the artisans he works with. He first learned of Guizhou’s rich craftsmanship during his studies. He travelled to the province, speaking with vendors who sold handmade pieces at flea markets, before venturing into nearby villages to seek out the artisans who would eventually collaborate with his label. Lam and his small team – his sister and a part-time assistant – travel regularly to Guizhou to work with more than 60 female artisans. “They’re all mothers who are taking care of their families,” says Hana Li, a former student of Lam’s at HKDI who now works part time as an artisan for Kinyan Lam. “We go to the villages to visit them and show them the designs we want them to produce. It usually takes them a few weeks to create the pieces, which they work on between taking care of their families.” Because of the nature of natural dyes and handmade embroidery, no two Kinyan Lam pieces are alike. Lam describes each one as a “fingerprint” of the artisan who worked on it. In an industry often criticised for extracting motifs and narratives from cultures without properly acknowledging their origins, Lam is deliberate about foregrounding the artisans and their craftsmanship rather than using their culture as a “marketing strategy”. “People always think our brand is sustainability-first. But we never use the word ‘sustainability’ to market our brand,” Lam says. “To us, it’s not a strategy – it’s our responsibility. And it’s the same for culture; it’s not our marketing strategy to get attention. “What you can do as a brand to get attention is use your own creativity. Creativity is not just about clothes – it can also be the structure of how a brand works with artisans.” Lam’s work also challenges the assumption that Western craftsmanship is inherently superior – a bias reflected in the fashion industry’s preference for labels that read “Made in Italy” over “Made in China”. “The craftsmanship in Guizhou is gorgeous,” Lam says. “They have the techniques, but maybe what they don’t have is the ability to adapt it into contemporary fashion. That’s why we’re important.” Since launching his brand, Lam has helped revive Guizhou’s dying craftsmanship, an aspect of his work that appears to give him the greatest sense of purpose. However, running a label rooted in slow, handmade production within a fast-moving industry presents its own challenges. Quality control can be difficult when every piece varies slightly, making it increasingly important to educate clients about the value of such differences. “The artisans we work with used to make clothes for their children, and now we ask them to make clothes for us, for our brand,” Lam says. “That’s why we want our customers and audience to really think about the person who worked on their clothes, so they treat the clothes well.” For now, Lam remains focused on staying grounded – pun intended. A recent trip to Nepal, where he explored local crafts and met a designer working with linen fibre and crochet, served as a reminder of why he started this journey in the first place. “Travelling to countries like Nepal and discovering new crafts is one of the ways I can relax,” he says. “It’s one of the methods that let me calm down.”

title: Hong Kong tycoon-backed start-up bets on new battery to challenge energy-storage giants
description: Co-founded by Peter Lee’s family office, EnerVenue has opened a facility in mainland China to scale its nickel-hydrogen batteries.
content: EnerVenue, a start-up co-founded by Full Vision Capital, the family office of Hong Kong tycoon Peter Lee Ka-kit, has begun manufacturing a new battery it expects to challenge existing energy-storage technologies dominated by mainland Chinese players, amid surging global demand for green energy. The California-based company can now produce 250 megawatt-hours (MWh) of nickel-hydrogen batteries annually at its factory in Changzhou, in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, and plans to raise capacity to one gigawatt-hour (GWh) in 2027. “In this [energy-storage] segment, we believe we are very competitive across the board on key metrics,” CEO Henning Rath told the South China Morning Post in an interview on Friday. “When it comes to safe, sustainable and long-duration energy storage, I think this is the market segment we want to play in.” The inauguration of EnerVenue’s plant in China comes five months after the company completed a US$300 million fundraising round backed by a clutch of investors including Full Vision Capital. “It’s the first battery of its kind that acts like infrastructure rather than a degrading asset,” Rath said. “It can operate in the world’s harshest environments and has no risk of fire from thermal runaway. What we prove here, we can build anywhere.” EnerVenue’s nickel-hydrogen technology, which has been used for decades in aerospace applications, relies on aqueous metal cells and is set to compete with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, one of the most widely used chemistries in mass-market electric vehicles (EVs) and energy-storage systems (ESS). The company’s nickel-hydrogen batteries could deliver 30,000 full charge-discharge cycles and had a design lifespan of 30 years, making them resilient in extreme weather conditions, Rath said. By comparison, an average LFP battery lasted 10 to 15 years and delivered about 6,000 charge-discharge cycles, according to analysts. EnerVenue’s batteries will also compete with other grid-scale storage technologies, including sodium-sulphur batteries, flow batteries and pumped hydro systems, which store energy by moving water between reservoirs at different elevations. The company said production would rise to multi-GWh scale in 2028 and that it had already secured multi-MWh orders from several clients. One project involving 26 energy prism containers, with a combined capacity of 11 MWh, would be deployed at an oilfield in northern China, it added. Named by Time magazine as one of the top 10 US green technology companies in 2025, EnerVenue has developed processes to commercialise nickel-hydrogen battery technology and reduce the total life-cycle cost of ESS technology. Its potential applications span solar photovoltaic projects, wind farms, EV-charging infrastructure and power grids. The Changzhou facility is EnerVenue’s first plant producing the water-based nickel-hydrogen battery. The company planned to deploy production lines in markets like the Middle East and the US, according to Rath. China dominates the global ESS battery industry, with mainland companies accounting for more than 80 per cent of the market, according to analysts. Global ESS battery demand rose 79 per cent year on year to 550GWh in 2025, according to Seoul-based SNE Research.

title: Asian Games, day 7: Hong Kong guaranteed gold medal in squash, China rule roost in diving
description: Two of city’s mixed doubles pairs win through to final, but women’s foil and men’s sabre fencers finish with bronze after semi-final losses.
content: The battle for mixed doubles gold in squash will be an all-Hong Kong affair at the Asian Games on Sunday, after the city’s duos both won their semi-finals on a day when the city’s athletes picked up another three bronze medals and some semblance of normality returned to table tennis. With swimming finally over at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, it was the turn of the divers to take centre stage, and to the surprise of absolutely no one, China won the two gold medals on offer on Saturday, the first of five days of competition. And with almost a week of the Games over, organisers finally acknowledged the scant crowds at some events and the continuing issues with transport and accommodation. For many, Sunday brings the highly anticipated women’s javelin contest between China’s teen sensation Yan Ziyi and Japan’s reigning Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi. Hong Kong’s eyes will mainly be focused on Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena, where four of its athletes will decide who takes home gold and who silver in the squash mixed doubles. Lee Ka-yi and Tang Ming-hong were the first to book their spots in Sunday’s final, beating India’s Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar 2-1 at Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena. Compatriots Toby Tse Yee-lam and Lai Cheuk-nam followed swiftly after, downing Malaysia’s Rachel Arnold and Ameeshenraj Chandaran 2-0 in just 21 minutes. Lai said he and his partner had been expecting a tough match and were “surprised with this result”. “We lost to them in June, so we didn’t think a lot before the match; we tried to perform our best,” Lai added. “We’ll give our best tomorrow and stick to our plans. It usually doesn’t happen [making a final], so we are nervous as well. And we are happy that the other mixed doubles team from Hong Kong [has made] it to the final.” There was one squash bronze handed to Hong Kong, with Chan Sin-yuk exiting the women’s singles with a 3-0 semi-final loss to Malaysia’s Sivasangari Subramaniam. “I knew my opponent was at a high level, and was recently in good shape,” Chan said. “I had to play better and more competitively today. I’m a little disappointed, but I’m not upset with how I played either.” Hong Kong’s fencers, meanwhile, put themselves in a position to reach two finals at the Asian Games on Saturday, with the women’s foil team and the men’s sabre side reaching the last four of their respective competitions. But the women lost 45-27 to Japan at Aichi Sky Expo and were forced to settle for bronze. The men also collected bronze after losing 45-24 to South Korea. The diving was over and done with quite quickly on Saturday, but there was still time for Chen Yuxi to successfully defend the women’s synchronised 10m platform gold medal she claimed in Hangzhou three years ago, although this time she won with a new partner, Lu Wei. Chen and Lu set the tone for the day, and for the four that follow, by scoring 347.82 in their opening gambit. North Korea’s Jo Jin-Mi and Kim Mi-Rae managed 317.64 in winning silver, while their neighbours to the south, Kim Na-hyun and Moon Na-yun, claimed bronze. In a short first day, Wang Zongyuan and Zheng Jiuyuan then won the men’s synchronised 3m springboard with 465.87 points. Japan’s Senri Ikuma and Haruki Suyama secured silver for the hosts with a score of 355.56. Malaysian pair Yong Rui Jie and Mohamad Nurqayyum took bronze with 345.81. Earlier, while Nagoya and the surrounding areas were stretching their collective legs, the marathon runners were already well into their stride. Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita won the men’s race while Bahrain’s Shitaye Habte took the women’s gold. Yamashita was cheered along for most of the 42 kilometres (26.2 miles) by fervent home support, something he called “an extraordinarily valuable experience and gave me energy”. “I felt bad that I couldn’t respond to the crowd directly because I lacked the mental strength, but it truly supported me,” he added. “Especially near the end, hearing the crowd shout out the time gap to the runner behind me helped me give that final push.” After the disappointing men’s team loss to Japan on Thursday, China finally had some table tennis news to celebrate, although the sight of world No 1s Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha being swept aside in the final of the mixed doubles will have raised some eyebrows. Lin Shidong and partner Kuai Man rocketed to a 4-0 win, which Lin said “wasn’t something we could’ve expected”. “We didn’t have the upper hand and were trailing at many points of the match,” Lin added. “But we never gave up and kept pushing. It was a close fight.” Sunday brings the semi-finals of the men’s doubles and the women’s singles, with China and Japan the only two delegations represented. How many fans turn out to watch remains to be seen. The men’s and women’s 100m in the athletics is one of the Games’ feature events, yet on Friday, the 30,000-capacity stadium appeared to be only a quarter full. Organisers said they were “not satisfied” with ticket sales, with fewer than 60 per cent selling for eight sports, including football. A seat at the closing ceremony is not a particularly sought-after item either. “We will keep aiming for full stadiums, keep selling tickets and work to make sure people who have secured seats actually come,” Satoshi Murate, secretary general of the Games organising committee, said.

title: How Alibaba is using AI to revamp its mapping app – and take on Meituan
description: Amap is harnessing AI to offer an array of new features, from 3D maps of indoor spaces to hyper-specific restaurant recommendations.
content: Late last year, Zhang Xuan’s small beef noodle joint in Shanghai suddenly began seeing a dramatic surge in orders. Sales over the past few months have been 50 to 60 per cent higher than normal, he estimates. The driver? The new Street Stars feature on Chinese tech giant Alibaba Group Holding’s Amap mapping app, which listed Zhang’s eatery as the fourth best restaurant in Shanghai’s Changning district. Prominently displayed on Amap’s main page, the system uses artificial intelligence to rate venues based on a huge volume of user data, including foot traffic, movement patterns and verified customer feedback, according to the company. The local recommendation guide is part of a broader revamp of Amap – China’s answer to Google Maps – as the service harnesses AI to provide its nearly 1 billion monthly users with an array of new features. The navigation app now offers everything from hyper-specific area guides – showing not only the most popular businesses in each neighbourhood, but also which venue is popular with certain types of people – to 3D maps of indoor spaces such as cinemas and shopping malls. In the process, Amap is shaking up China’s vast local services market, which has long been dominated by rival Chinese tech giant Meituan. Amap Street Stars now offers “local favourites” guides for 269 Chinese cities, and businesses featured in the guides are seeing dramatic upticks in sales: merchants that appeared in the 2025 list saw orders soar by an average of 424 per cent year on year, while those in the “top picks” category logged a 159 per cent rise, according to company data. “Amap has successfully built a consumer mindset around real offline visits by leveraging data on navigation routes and repeat visits,” said Bai Wenxi, chief economist at research platform China Enterprise Capital Union (CECU), adding that the strong order growth among small merchants suggested that Amap’s business model worked. A year on from the launch of Street Stars, Amap is now escalating its push with a sweeping technical upgrade – becoming a testing ground for Alibaba’s AI strategy. The centrepiece of the update, rolled out earlier this month to mark the feature’s first anniversary, is Flying Street View 2.0. Powered by ABot-Earth 0.7, which Amap describes as the world’s first native 3D urban world model, the system allows users to preview destinations – from theatre seats to shopping malls – in an interactive 3D environment, according to the company. “If large language models help us process text, I hope Amap’s spatial intelligence can help us better explore the world,” Amap CEO Guo Ning said at the launch event. The revamp highlights how the navigation unit, acquired by Alibaba in 2014, is transforming into an incubator for world models and embodied intelligence across the tech giant’s empire. That effort is backed by Amap’s world models, like FantasyWorld, which simulates real-world environments to train AI systems. The unit is also expanding into robotics. In July, Amap upgraded its ABot system, claiming it to be the first framework to integrate a robot’s “feet, hands, brain, central nervous system and motor nerves” into a single architecture. Amap’s AI pivot underscores how big tech firms view China’s local services sector as a launch pad for consumer AI applications. While Meituan has long dominated local transactions, deep-pocketed competitors like ByteDance’s Douyin and Amap are aggressively pushing into the market. To win market share, Amap is leveraging a massive user base of 996 million monthly active users (MAUs), as disclosed by the company in January. By comparison, Meituan had 512 million MAUs in early 2026, according to data from research firm QuestMobile released in May. The multi-platform rivalry is reshaping how small merchants acquire customers. “Previously, I only thought about how to boost ratings on Meituan,” noodle shop owner Zhang said. “Now Douyin and Amap have both become very important channels for getting new customers.” Some users are drawn to Amap’s algorithmic approach. “I like some of Amap’s niche rankings, like the best restaurants frequented by local taxi drivers, because that kind of data is harder to manipulate,” said Charlotte Li, an Amap user based in Shenzhen. She added, however, that she still cross-checked with Meituan due to its “more comprehensive dining ecosystem”. Meituan’s entrenched dominance stemmed in part from Amap’s incomplete transaction funnel, according to CECU’s Bai. “Even when users discover a great store on Amap, they are likely to jump over to Meituan to redeem group-buying deal vouchers because Amap does not treat completing transactions as its primary objective,” he said. While contending with domestic challenges, Amap is beginning to export its AI-driven discovery tools overseas. Last week, in partnership with the Singapore Tourism Board, the platform launched Singapore Street Stars – its first international edition developed with a foreign national tourism agency. The initiative introduces seven themed rankings spanning 104 attractions and lifestyle venues across the city state. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: How bobblehead dolls became an American classic
description: While there are head-nodding statues from at least a few centuries ago in China, these figurines got popular in the US in the 1960s.
content:
The National Bobblehead Hall of Fame and Museum is a museum devoted to bobblehead dolls. It is in the US city of Milwaukee and opened in 2019.
“I think they’re the ultimate Americana, sort of pop-culture icon,” Phil Sklar said. He is the founder of the museum.
The site offers visitors a chance to look at a vast array of figurines as well as learn more about their history. Sklar said there were head-nodding statues in China at least a few hundred years ago. In the 1960s, they became a hit in America when baseball teams gave away sports-themed dolls.
Soon after, companies began making bobbleheads of other celebrities.
Even though people’s interest in bobblehead dolls has risen and fallen over the decades, they have never truly gone away.

title: Japan esports whizz kid ‘feels a bit embarrassed’ after winning Asian Games gold
description: Yuki Kurihara, 11, did not even smile after beating South Korea’s 24-year-old Kang Dong-shin in the final of Puyo Puyo Champions.
content: Japan’s 11-year-old esports prodigy Yuki Kurihara said he was “embarrassed” after winning Asian Games gold on Saturday by thrashing a series of opponents up to three times his age. The bespectacled primary school student, believed to be the youngest competitor at the Games in Aichi-Nagoya, won the Puyo Puyo Champions final 10-2. He is the youngest athlete in host country Japan’s Asian Games history. Puyo Puyo Champions is a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of coloured blobs by lining them up and popping them. Looking unruffled throughout, Kurihara waltzed into the gold-medal match with a string of dazzling displays. He crushed Thailand’s Tanarak Wongkitkun – a relative veteran at 28 – 10-1 in the semi-finals to ensure at least a silver medal. He did not even smile after beating South Korea’s 24-year-old Kang Dong-shin in the final, having gone down 1-0 early on. “To be completely honest, I felt a bit embarrassed, so I couldn’t really show my expressions or change my face much,” he explained. Standing on the podium, he bowed slightly as he received his gold medal and gave a small wave to the arena. “I’m really happy. The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy,” he said. “Also, the plush toy is super cute, and it’s cool that it is gold-coloured too.” Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of primary school and soon started competing and winning in tournaments. He obtained his pro licence in April this year and regularly beats adults. “It’s hard having to balance it with school and cram school, but it’s really fun,” he said ahead of the Games. There are no publicly available records of the youngest medallists in the history of the Asian Games, which were first contested in 1951. But Indonesia’s Bunga Nyimas won bronze in women’s skateboarding aged 12 in Jakarta in 2018. Cui Chenxi, 13, won Games gold when she triumphed in the women’s street skateboarding event three years ago in Hangzhou.

title: Hong Kong minister vows to give public account of Queen Mary Hospital lift saga
description: Development chief Bernadette Linn stops short of saying whether new accountability system for department heads will be invoked.
content: Hong Kong’s development minister has promised a public account of her bureau’s oversight of the Queen Mary Hospital lift saga, while stopping short of saying whether a new accountability system for department heads would be invoked. Nearly two weeks after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu tasked the Development Bureau with submitting a report within a month, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said she would get to the bottom of the defective works at the hospital, which left 24 of the 28 lifts at its new 34-storey clinical block deemed unfit for use. “Why did those issues occur with the lifts? When were those problems identified, or why have they not been identified yet? All of this will be detailed in the coming report we will submit to the chief executive, which will subsequently be disclosed to the public as well,” she told a television programme on Saturday. But Linn stopped short of saying whether she would invoke the Heads of Departments Accountability System, unveiled in last year’s policy address, stressing the first phase of the follow-up investigation had already begun. “Right now, it is precisely that we have stepped in following the chief executive’s instructions,” she said. “Originally, at the bureau level, the Development Bureau was not involved in the Queen Mary Hospital project. We have now launched a review and investigation to examine whether the department directly under our oversight played its part properly across various stages of this project.” Sources previously told the South China Morning Post that Tuesday Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager for the Architectural Services Department, who oversaw the project at the new block at Hong Kong Island’s largest hospital, had been asked to resign and left her post over the scandal. The department denied that there had been any “forced resignation”, saying Li had quit for “personal reasons” after giving three months’ notice. Widespread installation defects, revealed last month, have delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, raising serious concerns over project oversight and civil service accountability. Linn also discussed the government’s decision not to appeal against a court ruling last month that overturned the environmental approval for a housing project on part of a golf course in Fanling. She said the government needed to evaluate the subsequent environmental impact assessment (EIA) procedures and other factors before determining the future use of the site. “As for how this former golf course site should be handled in the future and what will happen next with this public housing project, I believe we still need to review it,” she said. “In our current assessment, given that we no longer have that EIA report to support us, we need to carefully re-examine what further assessments we need to conduct, how the timeline for pushing this project forward will be affected and how its overall scale will be impacted.” Last month, the Court of Appeal upheld a lower court decision to overturn the project’s EIA approval, which would have allowed the government to use part of the 32 hectares (79 acres) of land taken back from the golf course to develop 12,000 public housing flats.

title: 20th Asian Games at Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in photos
description: The Games kicked off on September 19 and will run until October 4, 2026.
content:
The 20th Asian Games kicked off on September 19 with an opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan, and they will run until October 4. This is the third time Japan has hosted the multi-sport event, after hosting it in 1958 and 1994.
The 2026 edition features 43 sports, totalling 469 medal events. More than 11,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia are competing in the events. Padel, teqball and surfing are among the sports making their debut in the Games this year.

title: Aspiring Broadway star overcomes hearing loss to shine in musical theatre
description: Singaporean performer Sabrina Wong encourages others to boldly pursue their creative dreams.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Dressed in the vibrant colours of the Jackson High cheer squad, Sabrina Wong took her final bow as La Cienega in Bring It On: The Musical .
This performance not only marked the completion of her honours degree at Lasalle College of the Arts in Singapore but also represented a milestone in her journey as a musical theatre artist, who was born with severe hearing loss.
“It was such a memorable performance. Not only was Bring It On my graduation show, we also did cheerleading for the first time. It was a little chaotic, but it was really fun,” the 21-year-old said.
Born and raised in Shanghai, Wong started wearing hearing aids once a week when she was a few months old. But she stopped wearing them in kindergarten.
“In hindsight, I should have been made to do so right at the start,” she said. She added that not wearing hearing aids slowed her brain’s ability to process speech and sounds.
She did not want to wear the devices because of how uncomfortable they were. The older models were bulky and emitted a harsh static sound.
Wong added: “I became quite shy and introverted, and I fell behind in school because I couldn’t hear the teacher’s instructions. Most of the time, I just lived in my own world.”
But avoiding these devices affected her development; she still struggles to complete tasks at the same pace as her peers.
In primary school, she transitioned to smaller, more comfortable hearing aids, which she still wears today. Wong said that she was inspired by singers she saw on television and expressed that performing gave her a thrilling sense of empowerment .
The aspiring Broadway performer graduated with honours in musical theatre in August.
“I appreciate how the college gave everyone the same treatment because apparently for some programmes, if they find out that you have a disability, they might cut you from certain shows,” she said.
Wong believes that instead of having selective cutoffs for disabled and non-disabled applicants, theatre groups should give every child the opportunity to step into the spotlight.
Wong urged teenagers not to let fear stop them from pursuing their creative goals.
“It might take a lot of work in between, but go for it. You don’t want to be in a situation where you hate your life, so if you are able to do what you love, that’s absolutely the best,” she said.
She offered encouragement to students who worry that the performing arts take up too much study time.
“Doing musical theatre can actually help your grades,” she said.
Her heavy workload forced her to stay focused and stop procrastinating because she did not want to fall behind.
The artist is now preparing for graduate school – deciding between acting programmes in the United States and musical theatre in the United Kingdom.
As she looks towards her next chapter, Wong has an idea of how she would like her story to one day be shown on stage: a comedy-drama.
“After all, life is really not that serious. I’d want it to be fun and enjoyable,” she said.

title: China’s AI-led transformation is taking shape. Why are some economists urging caution?
description: As investors chase the next big AI opportunity, some are questioning lofty valuations and asking what the technology means for ordinary workers.
content: As AI becomes an increasingly important part of China’s economic transformation, economists and industry leaders are raising concerns about two potential risks: inflated valuations for humanoid robotics companies and the technology widening the wealth gap between rich and poor. Daniel Zhang, managing partner of FirstLight Capital and former chairman and CEO of Alibaba Group Holding, said the sharp fall in some Chinese humanoid robotics stocks reflected expectations that had become excessive. “Unitree [Robotics] is a great company with a visionary entrepreneur, but no company could withstand such high expectations,” Zhang said at the FutureChina Business Forum in Singapore on Friday. His remarks came as Unitree, a rapidly growing Chinese humanoid robot maker, saw its shares fall 55 per cent from their peak less than a month after its blockbuster listing on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-style Star Market. Chinese regulators had stepped up scrutiny of humanoid robot start-ups seeking to list on mainland China stock exchanges amid concerns about excessive market hype, according to The Information. The heightened attention is expected to affect companies such as Deep Robotics and Leju Robot, which remain unprofitable after filing for initial public offerings (IPOs). “Many robot makers are lining up for IPOs, but none of them could withstand seeing their valuation slashed by half after listing,” Zhang said during a panel discussion on China’s industrial transformation. “We need to respect the objective realities for the economy to move forward.” The annual two-day forum was organised by Business China, a non-profit organisation launched in 2007 by Singapore’s founding prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, to strengthen ties and promote dialogue across the region. Fan Gang, an economics professor at Peking University, warned the benefits of AI development were being concentrated among a relatively small group of people, while lower-income workers had yet to see comparable gains. “New growth dividends are benefiting the smaller group of people ... AI will make this problem even more serious,” Fan said, referring to the uneven distribution of economic gains. “If there is no salary increase for the general population, if there is no consumption expansion from the general public, the economy is faced with problems.” While investors have poured billions of US dollars into AI and robotics, Foo Jixun, senior managing partner of Singapore-based investment firm Granite Asia, highlighted new lifestyle innovations that were changing how young people spend their money. Foo cited the global popularity of Pop Mart’s Labubu toys and growing interest in fitness competitions such as Hyrox as examples of new consumer trends creating opportunities beyond technology. “When we think about making specific reforms in industrial upgrading or making breakthroughs in the economic transition, we need innovation,” Foo said. “However, that should not be limited to hi-tech and AI, but should also extend to the service sector and cultural industries.” Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Xi-Trump summit: Hong Kong’s Paul Chan predicts positive market response
description: Local business representatives expect that greater stability in bilateral ties may reinforce the city’s role as a connector between markets.
content: Hong Kong’s finance chief has predicted a positive market response to the Xi-Trump summit, saying that mitigating geopolitical uncertainties would bolster investor confidence, while local business representatives expect that greater stability in bilateral ties may reinforce the city’s role as a connector. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po made the prediction on a radio programme on Saturday after Chinese President Xi Jinping ended a three-day visit to Washington for talks with his US counterpart, Donald Trump. “I believe the market will have a positive interpretation … Previously, geopolitics caused concerns over economic prospects, leading to uncertainty and capital flow volatility,” Chan said. “If this factor can be mitigated, investors will feel more secure when positioning their portfolios.” Xi, accompanied by first lady Peng Liyuan, chief of staff Cai Qi, Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, left for Washington on Wednesday and returned to Beijing on Saturday afternoon. Despite the pomp and circumstance surrounding the visit, the leaders’ second meeting of the year was relatively short on new agreements. The two sides agreed to a reciprocal “more favourable tariff treatment” for US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods each, according to a White House fact sheet released following Xi’s departure. A two-month extension of the trade truce, until January 10, had been agreed ahead of the leaders’ meeting. A new “US-China super intelligence dialogue” – using Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence – was also unveiled. For Hong Kong, an open financial hub caught up in the wider geopolitical rivalry, the prospect of more stable bilateral relations was the most significant development. “The fact that the two sides are continuing to talk is encouraging, even if this meeting produced relatively few new announcements,” lawmaker Jonathan Lamport, who represents the business sector, said. “For Hong Kong, a steadier relationship can support sentiment around trade, investment and our role as a connector between markets … Of course, businesses will continue to watch how the dialogue develops and how outstanding trade and technology issues are handled.” Wingco Lam Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, said the tariff reduction could lower costs for local exporters and help them secure overseas orders. “However, trade and technology restrictions remain in place, so businesses should continue diversifying their markets and supply chains,” he said. Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said that Hong Kong, as a global trade and financial hub, had always been dependent on relations between major powers. “A stabilising Sino-US relationship under contained competition benefits Hong Kong by helping it attract and retain investment,” he said. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said the summit suggested that the two countries would seek to keep their relationship stable over the next couple of years, avoiding intense trade friction or conflict over Taiwan. “Under a stable US-China relationship, the US will be less inclined to take hostile actions against Hong Kong, such as trade sanctions or sanctions against Hong Kong entities or officials,” he said. “This will give Hong Kong a more peaceful and favourable international environment to pursue its development projects under its first five-year plan.” Political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said Hong Kong could indirectly benefit as a trading hub from greater stability, more direct flights between the two countries and China’s initiative to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit. However, it was not yet clear whether local airlines and universities would be included. “What happens after January 10? This extension may be a strategy to buy time for both parties to negotiate a trade agreement – particularly for sensitive sectors like chips and semiconductors, which require further deliberation,” he said. Chan, meanwhile, described Hong Kong’s hosting of the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on October 20 and 21 as another opportunity to promote the advantages of doing business in the city. “Beyond business delegates, the meeting will bring many political leaders to Hong Kong – this is important because having a deeper understanding of Hong Kong’s advantages, such as the uniqueness of ‘one country, two systems’ and the business environment, will ultimately help when they return home to consider policies and encourage their enterprises to do business here,” he told the radio show. Addressing a goal in the city’s first five-year plan to expand renminbi usage by settling government payments and commodity trading in the currency, Chan sought to reassure stakeholders that the move would not affect Hong Kong’s linked exchange rate system. “Our core strength lies in our unique advantages under one country, two systems … we have an independent, separate currency, and everyone knows very well that the exchange rate is anchored within that specific band,” he said. “This gives international investors peace of mind that whenever they transfer money in or out, the exchange rate stays strictly within that defined range. That certainty and confidence are vital to investors. For us as an international financial centre, it is equally indispensable. Therefore, this will absolutely never change.”

title: Why Pakistan’s endless war on militants fails to break the cycle
description: Tactical wins and retaliatory strikes have not delivered peace, even as two separate insurgencies appear to be converging.
content: For over two decades, Pakistan has waged countless counterterrorism campaigns against Taliban and Baloch insurgents in its western regions bordering Afghanistan and Iran, yet remains mired in a cycle of violence it cannot break. Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility. Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings. Pakistan’s military regularly hails the success of its counterterrorism operations, touting the eradication of hundreds of perpetrators each month. Its press releases often read like scoreboards, listing the number of insurgents “sent to hell” – with only a handful surviving to be interrogated. Yet these tactical victories have not translated into the strategic success Islamabad has long yearned for, analysts say. “Force alone won’t help in curbing security issues long term,” said Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “Force will continue to meet force, keeping the loop alive. There has to be some political solution and dialogue.” Such a solution would not appear overnight, she said, but without one – or at least a viable strategy to combat insurgency – Pakistan faced the prospect of continued instability deterring foreign investment, not least in its critical minerals sector. Border escalations Armed groups have long exploited the porous Pakistan-Afghanistan border to seek sanctuary, smuggle goods and provide logistical support. In recent years, months-long terrorist campaigns have driven up casualty numbers and prompted Pakistan to launch retaliatory air strikes against insurgents based in eastern Afghanistan. The latest came on Monday, when military jets struck Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) “terrorist camps and safe havens” in Afghanistan’s Paktika and Kunar provinces, killing 28 militants, Pakistan’s information ministry said, including what it said were suicide bombers in training. Monday’s air strikes followed an assault on a mosque on September 18 that left at least 31 people dead and more than 100 injured at a police compound in the northwestern town of Kohat, Pakistan. Zabihullah Mujahid, chief spokesman for Afghanistan’s Taliban regime, has repeatedly denied the existence of terrorist camps in his country and claimed in a statement that Pakistan’s air strikes killed three civilians. After he vowed revenge, border skirmishes intensified, culminating on Thursday in eight “rudimentary” drones being launched from Afghan territory into Pakistani airspace, security officials said. All were shot down, four of them near Kohat. Mujahid again denied responsibility for the drone incursions, though Pakistani officials view them as further evidence that Kabul is actively supporting the TTP, not merely tolerating its presence.
