Pakistan retaliated in the early hours of Thursday with “precision aerial and drone strikes” on 10 locations in Afghanistan “used for launching and storing these drones”, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar announced in a social media post. Officials in Islamabad have made clear they believe the Taliban government in Kabul has been feigning interest in recent diplomatic efforts by China, Turkey and Qatar to de-escalate tensions, following a previous cycle of insurgent violence that ended with Pakistan carrying out cross-border air strikes in June. At a meeting in Belarus this summer, officials discussed potential compromises, including a joint mechanism to monitor the cross-border movement of TTP militants, according to Islamabad-based security analyst Iftikhar Firdous, who disclosed details of the talks in a social media post on September 16. The meeting reportedly failed to produce a breakthrough because Kabul refused to compel the TTP to halt its attacks on Pakistan or relocate militants away from the border. The day before the Kohat attack, Qatar’s National Security Council deputy secretary general Hamad Khamis al-Kubaisi and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın had visited Kabul in a renewed attempt to broker further talks between Afghan and Pakistani officials. Analysts see the repeated cycles of violence as proof that Islamabad’s largely reactive approach to counterterrorism, built around retaliatory counter-attacks, is not working. Riccardo Valle, a researcher tracking militancy across South and Central Asia, called the strategy “incomplete and limited”. Local grievances and poor governance constrained the effectiveness of counterterrorism operations in violence-hit areas, he said, adding that local security forces in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan – especially the police – were ill-equipped to confront “full-fledged insurgencies”. The reactive, rather than preventive, nature of intelligence-based operations is another limiting factor, according to Valle. “Thus, tactical success cannot compensate for a broader strategic deficiency, which fuels a circle of instability” in the affected provinces, he said, with the twin insurgencies becoming a “multigenerational issue”, drawing in new cohorts of young militants. As such, Valle said a holistic approach that accounted for both Pakistan’s domestic concerns and the wider conflict’s international dimensions would be essential. Converging insurgencies Signs have also emerged of increasing collaboration between the radical Islamist TTP and ethno-nationalist Baloch separatist groups in Balochistan. The vast and sparsely populated province, bordering southern Afghanistan and eastern Iran, recorded a marked rise in attacks over the summer. In one instance this July, the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army carried out separate attacks in the province’s Pishin and Ziarat districts within hours of each other. Muhammad Faisal, a South Asia security researcher based at the University of Technology Sydney, said tactical coordination between the TTP and Baloch insurgents was “increasingly documented”, including reports of joint training and logistical links. However, he doubts this will amount to a “durable strategic coalition” given the two groups’ different ideologies and aims – the TTP seeks to overthrow the government of Pakistan and establish an Islamist political order, while Baloch groups are more concerned with achieving independence. Linguistic, cultural and geographic differences further limit each group’s ability to operate in the other’s core territory, likely confining cooperation to an exchange of tactics and targets, according to Faisal. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s ties with Iran have improved since the two countries exchanged air strikes against militants based on the other’s soil in January 2024. Islamabad helped broker talks earlier this year aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, but Faisal said that widening conflict and residual Pakistan-Iran mistrust would continue to hamstring relations. Pakistan has also accused India, with which it fought a brief air war in May last year, of covertly supporting Baloch separatists as proxies. However, Faisal said Islamabad would be better off closely monitoring the separatist networks involved instead of treating every one of their attacks as proof of foreign backing. The more immediate danger was the effect the Iran conflict might have on border security if it created a power vacuum filled with more militancy and foreign intelligence operatives, he said. “This is a serious security risk, but one best managed through intelligence cooperation and sustained diplomacy,” Faisal added.

title: Why Taiwan’s coastguard vessel transfer to the Philippines has sparked a double outcry
description: NGO-mediated transfer of retired cutter raises concerns given Taiwan-Manila fisheries disputes, as Beijing lashes out at ‘despicable’ deal.
content: Taiwan’s transfer of a former coastguard vessel to the Philippines has triggered a dual controversy – raising concerns over the interests of Taiwanese fishermen and prompting strong criticism from Beijing. The matter centres on a 61-metre (200-foot) retired cutter handed over to the Philippine Coast Guard through a non-governmental organisation on Monday, as Taipei and Manila expand practical maritime cooperation despite the absence of formal diplomatic ties. Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) has condemned the move, accusing the island’s ruling party of ignoring infringements by Japan and the Philippines as they pursue maritime delimitation talks. The Democratic Progressive Party had failed to protect the interests of the people of Taiwan and was instead “helping an evildoer do evil”, TAO spokeswoman Zhu Fenglian said on Wednesday. The authorities’ conduct had increased the risk of harm to the interests of Taiwanese fishermen, she warned, describing the DPP’s action as “despicable”. On Thursday, Taiwan’s cabinet-level Ocean Affairs Council defended the donation, with minister Kuan Bi-ling saying it was intended to strengthen regional maritime safety. “The donation agreement contains comprehensive safeguards, explicitly stipulating that the donated vessel must not be used for law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing boats,” she said. Kuan also rejected Beijing’s criticism on the matter, arguing that Taiwanese fishermen faced more immediate risks from mainland China and citing the boarding and detention of Taiwanese vessels. Taipei says such incidents have taken place at least three times since 2024. The We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation, a Philippine non-profit organisation focused on maritime issues, said on Monday that it had formally donated the Taiwanese cutter, renamed Training Ship WPS, to the country’s coastguard. The ship would be deployed to Mindanao for search and rescue, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, and marine environmental protection, WPS cited Philippine coastguard commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan as saying. The foundation did not disclose the vessel’s origin or explain how it had acquired it. However, a Philippine source confirmed to Taiwan’s official Central News Agency on Tuesday that the vessel was the decommissioned Taiwanese coastguard patrol ship Kinmen. That corroborated earlier information obtained by the South China Morning Post that the retired cutter had been transferred to Manila from Taiwan. The concerns over the donation reflect a long history of fisheries disputes between Taiwan and the Philippines. In 2013, personnel aboard a Philippine coastguard vessel opened fire on the Taiwanese fishing boat Guang Da Xing No 28 in overlapping waters, killing one fisherman. The shooting prompted Taipei to impose sanctions and step up fisheries-protection patrols, which subsequently led to a 2015 agreement to avoid the use of violence or unnecessary force in fisheries law enforcement. Despite those efforts, tensions linger. Just last year, the Taiwanese fishing boat Sheng Yu Feng was boarded by Philippine personnel and taken to port. The vessel and its crew were released without penalties the same day after a formal protest from Taipei, which said the boat had been fishing in waters where the two sides’ exclusive economic zones overlap. Lawmakers from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang have also raised concerns about the Japan-Philippines maritime boundary talks, warning that the waters in question overlap directly with Taiwan’s claimed exclusive economic zone off its east coast. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun described the ship transfer as “rubbing salt into the wounds” of Taiwanese fishermen, while party legislator Hsu Yu-chen asked whether the vessel might ultimately be deployed in overlapping waters to board, pursue or expel Taiwanese fishing boats. The DPP, however, has portrayed closer ties with Manila in a broader regional context. Lawmaker Wang Ting-yu hailed the recent coastguard cooperation as a “historic breakthrough”, highlighting its strategic significance as both sides face growing grey-zone pressure from Beijing. Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies, a Taipei-based think tank, said geopolitics was the main reason Taipei was willing to proceed despite its history of fisheries disputes with Manila. “The Philippines is part of the first island chain and an important link in constraining Beijing’s military expansion in the South China Sea,” Wang said, adding that the US had encouraged regional partners, including Japan and South Korea, to help strengthen Philippine capabilities. “The United States is a major factor behind this,” Wang argued. The transfer is unusual because previous recipients – including the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu – maintain diplomatic ties with Taipei, while the Philippines recognises Beijing and has no formal relations with Taiwan. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and never ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States, Taiwan’s No 1 international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Taiwanese authorities have offered few details about the vessel transfer. Marvin H. Bernardo, a Taiwan affairs researcher from the Philippines and PhD candidate at National Chengchi University, noted that the absence of formal diplomatic relations meant an intermediary was needed to facilitate the transfer. “Given the sensitivity of Beijing to any form of engagement with Taiwan, which they interpret as a violation of the one-China policy, it was more politically expedient to go through an NGO,” he said. The vessel transfer comes alongside other efforts by Taipei to expand contact with Manila. Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung has confirmed plans to open a second representative office in Cebu – after Manila – to facilitate economic cooperation. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration has also pledged to send 100 personnel to the Philippines for a goodwill port visit in October next year. Max Lo, executive director of the Taipei-based Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, cautioned against interpreting the donation as evidence that relations had entered a fundamentally new phase. “This is driven by geopolitical factors. It cannot really be described as Taiwan-Philippines friendship moving to a new stage,” Lo said. He said Taipei was also seeking to show Washington that it was willing to contribute to broader regional security efforts. At the same time, Lo said, Manila remained cautious about antagonising Beijing, making it unclear how far the Philippines would be prepared to cooperate with Taiwan in responding to pressure from mainland China. Bernardo said the arrangement nevertheless indicated a willingness on the Philippine side to be more flexible in its engagement with Taiwan.

title: Xi-Trump Washington summit aimed at putting US-China ties on equal footing: Wang Yi
description: Chinese foreign minister says Xi Jinping’s visit ‘maintained overall stability’ of relations and will have ‘deep impact’ on world peace.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States was crucial to maintaining the overall stability of China-US relations and aimed at putting the relationship on an equal footing. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who accompanied Xi on the three-day trip to Washington, gave the assessment on Saturday, expanding on relations between the two countries. According to state news agency Xinhua, Wang said Xi’s visit “maintained the overall stability of Sino-US relations” and “will have a deep impact on the world’s peace and development”. The Chinese foreign minister also expanded on one of the eight outcomes of the trip – an agreement between the two leaders to build a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity”. “It means the two countries have equal sovereignty and no one is more superior than the other. None is domineering or abusive and they should resolve their own concerns on an equal footing,” Wang said. “Respect” referred to respect for each other’s sovereignty, territory and core interests, while “fairness” meant rejection of the “zero-sum mindset”, he added. Wang said the exceptional reception given to Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan, including the personal welcome US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania gave on the tarmac on arrival, reflected respect for Xi and the importance of China-US relations to the United States. After the trip, China and the United States issued separate statements about the outcomes, saying they had agreed to improve cooperation on artificial intelligence, tariffs and chemical precursor control. The two countries agreed that their leaders would also support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and Group of 20 summits later this year, signalling their intent to attend the meetings in person. The agreement means that Trump plans to travel to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen in November, while Xi is scheduled to go to Miami in December, making this year unusual in terms of the number of face-to-face meetings between the two men. Also unusual was the mention in both statements about the leaders’ references to the US-China alliance during World War II, a partnership that Xi and Trump highlighted several times during the trip. Xi, also accompanied by chief of staff Cai Qi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, left Beijing for Washington on Wednesday and returned to the Chinese capital on Saturday afternoon. The Chinese statement about the trip said both sides agreed to open a communication channel on incidents involving “artificial intelligence”. The US statement said they agreed to rename AI as “super intelligence”, a campaign Trump has been pushing in recent weeks. The two leaders also formally endorsed a US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement reached earlier by the Chinese and US trade teams, as well as an extension of their trade truce. The two countries affirmed the establishment of the Board of Investment. The US said the board would discuss “potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments”. On geopolitics, both countries said they agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons and that no country or institution should impose tolls on international waterways. They also lauded the arrest in August of 21 Chinese citizens for making and distributing precursor chemicals for illicit drug producers in North America, saying the action was the fruit of China-US cooperation on fentanyl. While neither statement mentioned Taiwan, a sticking point of bilateral relations, Wang said the issue was brought up during the meetings. “President Xi Jinping set out China’s principled position on the Taiwan issue, stressing that China is firmly committed to safeguarding national reunification and territorial integrity,” Wang said. “[Xi] urged the US side to maintain the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’, handle the Taiwan issue prudently, and remove obstacles to China-US strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations.” In a veiled reference to Japan, Wang said Xi also urged the US to share the “responsibility to uphold the post-war international order and prevent the revival of militarism”, with this year marking the 80th anniversary of the start of the Tokyo war crimes trials. There were also differences between the statements from the two countries, which has become the norm in recent years since they stopped issuing joint statements. The US said China had agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of coal from the United States next year and again in 2028 – a commitment that Beijing did not refer to. The US also said the two sides would “continue to work on” US concerns about China’s exports of rare earths and critical minerals to the US, “with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels”. Again, the Chinese statement was silent on the issue. In addition, the White House said the next meeting of the newly formed US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue would take place by November. China’s Ministry of Commerce confirmed on Thursday that its senior trade negotiators had already held their first talks with the US on artificial intelligence. One of the biggest differences was over the American presence in Asia. Although the US highlighted its alliance with China during WWII, it nevertheless implied that it would remain a force in the region, which Beijing has repeatedly condemned as US hegemony. “Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” the US statement said. The Chinese statement instead highlighted potential improvements in military-to-military communication. “The Chinese and US militaries agreed to sign as soon as possible a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communication and prevention,” it said, adding both sides also agreed to continue their cooperation to search for the remains of missing US servicemembers in China. The statementconfirmed an exclusive that the Post reported earlier this month that the two sides might announce measures to improve military-to-military communication. In the meantime, Iran continued to wait for an official US response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US ending its sanctions. The proposal was made at the UN General Assembly and conveyed to the Americans via Qatari mediators, Iran said. Trump and Xi also discussed concerns about Russia and North Korea, saying the US “advocated” for trilateral arms-control negotiations between the US, Russia, and China. Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said the affirmation of the investment board exceeded expectations as differences within the US had stalled progress. “The US statement said specifically that the investment board will discuss potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments, and that is going towards the direction that China has hoped for. And the work of this board is one thing we need to look out for,” Wu said. He said the historical alliances during WWII mentioned by both sides was particularly interesting and it was not expected, especially as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke to Trump in New York before Xi’s visit. “Trump is different from [his predecessor Joe] Biden. Biden has a strong ideological orientation and when he talked about these things, he would certainly talk about the shared values of the United States and its allies – things like democracy,” Wu said. “Trump is a nationalist, so he has a strong memory of Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbour. You can see that he likes to bring up Pearl Harbour from time to time. So for him, as a nationalist, there is nothing unusual about talking about World War II.” Chen Qi, professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, said there was room for further discussion on trade and hopes for trade relations to stabilise with the Apec and G20 meetings later this year. “The trade truce extension until January will [also] give more room for imagination for the rest of the world,” Chen said. “When they are meeting so frequently, in November and December, do you think it is possible to upend the trade relationship and reopen the door to additional tariffs? I don’t think there is any room for that,” he said. Daniel Kritenbrink, a former US assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, said the frequent meetings between the two leaders this year meant there was less pressure for deliverables during this trip. “I think we have to keep in mind that we are in this extraordinary period right now where two presidents are meeting so frequently that I think the amount of pressure on each interaction is slightly less than would traditionally be the case,” said Kritenbrink, now a partner at Washington-based strategic advisory firm The Asia Group. Additional reporting by Alyssa Chen

title: OpenAI says its AI agents posted user images online in error
description: The company’s AI tools accessed websites of US federal agencies, saying it has removed most uploaded images that were not publicly listed.
content: OpenAI acknowledged on Friday that its artificial intelligence tools had posted images from ChatGPT users onto online sites without the company’s knowledge, the latest example of AI agents operating outside their bounds. The company also confirmed a New York Times report that its tools had accessed websites of US federal agencies, saying they retrieved only publicly available information. Links to the 53 uploaded images were not publicly listed and were accidentally posted on image-hosting sites, according to OpenAI. Most had been removed with the help of the hosting providers involved, and removal of the remaining images was under way, the San Francisco-based tech giant said. “We’ve shared details on how AI agents in our research environment sent training and evaluation data to third-party services when they shouldn’t have,” the company said in a social media post. Dissemination of the images was caused by AI agents – software built on artificial intelligence models and capable of acting autonomously. The images in question came from the accounts of users who had authorised the use of the data to improve OpenAI’s models. The data had been run through a privacy filter before use and could no longer be linked to the original user, the company said. OpenAI did not specify whether the images depicted identifiable individuals or contained sensitive data. According to OpenAI, agents that it uses for its research transmitted the training data to external platforms. The incidents occurred before OpenAI strengthened the security protocols of its research environment in August following other rogue actions by AI agents. The company said it was scrutinising the past activity of its AI agents, work that “will take months to complete”. “Most of the activity we’ve reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions. Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman acknowledged on Friday in a social media post that “we have not been as fast as we would have liked” in reviewing and disclosing the incidents. But he said it was important to “balance our desire for transparency” with assessing the massive volume of data to be analysed. On July 21, OpenAI revealed that during tests it ran that month, two of its models escaped their closed environments, got onto the internet on their own and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a kind of online library for AI software. The episode drew wide attention and fed worries that the biggest AI companies could not keep their own models under control. Altman reiterated on Friday that the Hugging Face hack “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”. That discovery was followed by revelations of several similar incidents at OpenAI and its rivals such as Anthropic and Meta Platforms. On Wednesday in New York, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to a government health portal in June, and he criticised the company for delaying its notification to the authorities.

title: How one woman is rewriting kabuki’s ‘all-male’ narrative in Japan
description: Ranshou Fujima, a female kabuki dancer and archivist, is reimagining the onnagata tradition through a landmark exhibition in Tokyo.
content: Out of the backstage shadows, an onnagata – the traditional female role in the Japanese traditional theatre art of kabuki – steals into the light. Her hair is swept high into a voluminous bun, framing a face veiled in a thin layer of porcelain-white powder. Touches of cherry blossom flush across her eyelids and lips. She glides across the starkly lit stage so weightlessly that her steps leave silence behind. With precision, she turns, twirls and looks into the distance, face perfectly angled. Unlike a typical onnagata, traditionally played by a male actor in a colourful robe with an elaborately patterned obi, this is a woman wearing a plain black kimono. In this unnervingly quiet space, so still that one can hear the lights buzz overhead, her slender figure blends with the shadows of the empty auditorium like a phantom, looming in the emptiness of Tokyo’s 60-year-old National Theatre of Japan, which has been closed for reconstruction and redevelopment since 2023. For 42-year-old Ranshou Fujima, the “phantom” on stage, this venue remains the primary national hub for preserving the arts and is where some of the greatest onnagata of the 20th century have performed. However, since its closure, no official announcement has been made on when it will reopen and performances have been staged at alternative temporary venues. Fujima’s performance was part of “Future History: Lineage and Form of Onnagata”, a two-day exhibition held at the theatre in September. “Within a closed theatre where time seemed to have stopped, the bodily memory of onnagata [rises] again,” she says. The exhibition featured more than 100 kabuki-related works and materials showing how the art form developed over time. These included religious and literary texts, illustrated books, paintings and prints, playbills, music, stage materials and costumes, with some dating back to the 17th century. “The classical has always existed in the present, and I have always wanted it to exist in the future as well,” Fujima says. “I wanted the past, present and future to exist in the same dimension [in this exhibition].” The origins of kabuki and a ban on women Kabuki is one of Japan’s three major classical theatre arts – alongside Noh and Bunraku – and its cultural significance is often referred to as the Asian equivalent of the Shakespearean drama. This highly stylised classical dance-drama combines elements of song (ka), dance (bu) and skill (ki), and depicts Japanese history, legends, folklore and the daily lives of common people, most notably the painful conflict between personal emotions and societal or familial duty. Views on the origins of kabuki vary, but the widely accepted version credits Izumo no Okuni, a Japanese shrine maiden in the 16th century, who dressed in male samurai attire to play diverse character roles in street performances, as the inventor of onna-kabuki or women’s kabuki. My impression is that the number of kabuki practitioners today is quite small, and it is even more difficult to determine how many practitioners are women Ranshou Fujima During the Edo period (1603-1867), women were banned over fears that their shows would disturb public morals. They were replaced by young boys and later adult men, leading to the development of onnagata – male actors in female roles. Important kabuki-buyo works – dance pieces that evolved from kabuki – centred on onnagata emerged, such as The Maiden at Dojoji Temple, The Heron Maiden and The Snowbound Barrier. These productions are so integral to Japan’s cultural fabric that they are referenced in popular culture today. Take the 2025 Oscar-nominated box-office hit Kokuho, a movie about a mob boss’ son taken in by a master kabuki actor, which references all three works. While the film led to a local resurgence of interest in kabuki alongside global fascination, Fujima admits it is still seen as traditional or passé among younger generations. “My impression is that the number of kabuki practitioners today is quite small, and it is even more difficult to determine how many practitioners are women,” she says. Earning the Fujima name Born Hisae Ota outside a kabuki family in Sapporo, Fujima began her dance training at age four when her mother took her to an established school for Japanese traditional dance. The Fujima school was founded in the 1700s by choreographer and actor Fujima Kanbei (unrelated), who was widely respected for laying the foundation of this theatre art. The young Ranshou Fujima fell in love with dance. “I was drawn to the emotions embodied in onnagata roles – the intensity of feeling, the physical expression and the beauty itself, especially how even negative emotions are sublimated into pure beauty,” she recalls. Showing two photos of herself – performing the classical production Shiokumi (The Salt-Scooping Maiden) at the age of five, and the other as a seven-year-old dressed as superheroine Sailor Moon – she adds with a laugh, “I made no distinction between my favourite anime and manga, Sailor Moon and Dr Slump – Arale-chan, and the classics. All I knew was that dancing was simply fun.” Introduced by kabuki critic and historian Hiroshi Fujita, she began training under Rankei Fujima, adopted daughter of dancer Fujiko Fujima – herself adopted into the Fujima family and the first woman in kabuki designated a Living National Treasure. During Ranshou Fujima’s university years at Tokyo University of the Arts, she moved into a flat close to her teacher’s studio so she could practise constantly. There is a saying: ‘A dancer dies twice. The first death is when they stop dancing, and the first death is often harder than the second.’ I carried those words with me for a long time Ranshou Fujima Once a dancer attains a high level of proficiency, they may be granted the right to use the Fujima surname alongside a new artistic first name. “Rankei-sensei gave me part of her name, ‘Ran’, while shou means spreading my wings and continuing to soar,” Ranshou Fujima says. “She often told me, ‘To preserve and pass down the artistry of Fujiko Fujima alone requires tremendous effort. Becoming a dancer in one’s own right is never easy – but I hope you will continue and one day find the piece that truly becomes your own.’” Being dismissed and her own doubts Ranshou Fujima’s journey has been far from easy. Sceptics dismissed her practice as “an expensive hobby” or “something of the past”. “The artistic path felt frightening,” she says. “Without a kabuki family lineage and as a woman, I often wondered where I was heading and why I danced at all.” Her doubts deepened when she ruptured her Achilles tendon in her thirties, followed by her teacher’s death. “The harder I practised, the further my answers seemed to drift away,” she recalls. “There is a saying: ‘A dancer dies twice. The first death is when they stop dancing, and the first death is often harder than the second.’ I carried those words with me for a long time.” With the support of her university friends and her deep love for the art, she emerged from the darkness. She set up the non-profit art organisation Ranshou, which conducts research and exhibitions dedicated to kabuki-buyo and onnagata. The organisation builds an archive by acquiring artefacts from second-hand bookshops in Tokyo and abroad, as well as antiquarian dealers and online shops. She devotes particular effort to finding surviving ukiyo-e woodblock prints that show that women, despite the common narrative of an all-male tradition, actively trained and took part in kabuki-buyo throughout history. “If visitors learn that history was not simply ‘women’s performance was banned, and then women disappeared’, but that other currents existed, that would be enough for me,” she says, referring to lesser-known all-female performances held within the private chambers of Japan’s historical ruling elite. Ranshou’s archives and collection are available to view on Google Arts & Culture for free. Preserving and presenting the past However, Fujima believes historic archives and museums can only go so far in presenting the past. “Ultimately, it comes back to the human body, not merely the preservation of physical materials,” she says. “Even if we preserve videos, there are nuances that recordings alone cannot transmit: the placement of the centre of gravity, ma – the timing and space between movements – and the breathing. Those elements can only be passed from one body to another. We need both records and an environment in which living bodily knowledge continues to be transmitted.” While retaining the core movements and techniques of kabuki-buyo and onnagata, Fujima also experiments with contemporary aesthetics. Her stage presentation at the National Theatre featured a minimalist, abstract interpretation of traditional imagery, while the audience was invited onto the stage to experience the dance at close range. “Everything surrounding the form [of a performance] – society, the audience and the body – is always changing,” she says. “Contemporary art, fashion, culture and music naturally inform the way I express things today.” Her plain black costume, which she calls her “second skin”, represents her vision of “how a woman living in the modern world can streamline and express this art”. “I hope that centuries from now, like-minded people will encounter our work,” she says. “Whether their response is ‘This is good’ or ‘This is terrible’ does not matter to me. What matters is that the work remains there for them to [experience].”

title: Hong Kong is fast-tracking Northern Metropolis links. Will they be ready in time?
description: Completion of Tsing Lung Bridge and San Tin section of main highway brought forward, but experts warn people will be arriving far earlier.
content: Hong Kong will fast-track key Northern Metropolis roads, bringing forward the San Tin highway section to 2034 and targeting 2033 for the Tsing Lung Bridge, but a transport expert and lawmaker have cautioned that the first arrivals could still end up stranded. Infrastructure projects could lag behind developments such as the Hung Shui Kiu University Town, they said, suggesting the government launch express bus routes and build the Central Rail Link as soon as possible to ensure connectivity. A source told the South China Morning Post that authorities were pushing ahead with the Tsing Lung Bridge project, bringing forward its launch by two years to 2033. The acceleration of the San Tin section of the planned Northern Metropolis Highway, meanwhile, would mainly be achieved through techniques such as slope stabilisation, the source said. The government has put the creation of the Northern Metropolis, a 30,000-hectare (74,132-acre) area bordering Shenzhen that is intended to become a new economic engine and housing hub, at the top of its agenda. In his policy address last Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled a slew of measures to accelerate connectivity across the area and support its three university towns. Among the most rapidly progressing projects is the Hung Shui Kiu University Town, where land will begin to be allocated within months so the first institutions can set up campuses by the 2027-28 academic year. The Northern Metropolis Highway will be the main road spine, running east to west, and integrating major innovation, technology and residential hubs. The government has fast-tracked its construction, with priority given to the San Tin section that will serve major developments including Kwu Tung North, Ngau Tam Mei and the San Tin Technopole, according to the policy address. Lee said authorities would adopt national and international design standards alongside advanced construction technology to advance the completion of the section by two years to 2034. Government sources told the SCMP that the Northern Metropolis Highway would be 24km (15 miles) long, with the San Tin section covering 9km. Part of the section will be a tunnel, which the insider said had been halved in length from 5km to 2.5km. Authorities will also accelerate construction of the Tsing Lung Bridge at the southern end of the overarching Route 11, targeting a 2033 launch to handle the increased north-to-south flow of vehicles. But former lawmaker Michael Tien Puk-sun warned of a gap between the completion of transit projects and the opening of the early slated developments such as the first university town. “People might have to rely on buses or private cars to reach those areas,” said Tien, a former head of the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation. He urged the government to press ahead with the Central Rail Link proposed in its earlier infrastructure blueprint. The roughly 17km-long line will connect Kam Tin in Yuen Long and Kowloon Tong via Kwai Chung, providing access to the urban core along Victoria Harbour. Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung also noted that while the Northern Metropolis Highway would not be fully operational until 2034, students and tech firms were expected to move into the San Tin University Town and the technopole well before then. “We cannot leave these pioneers stranded to fend for themselves,” said the legislator for the New Territories North West geographical constituency. “The government must roll out concrete interim transport solutions now. We need high-frequency point-to-point express buses directly linking the area to Sheung Shui, Lok Ma Chau and Kam Sheung Road stations.” Chong added that dedicated bus lanes must be set up on the existing San Tin Highway and Castle Peak Road to guarantee reliable travel times during peak demand. The government should not “stubbornly wait to open the entire highway in one go in 2034”, he cautioned. “We need a phased opening strategy. As soon as a critical section is finished, especially the connecting roads between San Tin and Kwu Tung, it should be opened to the public immediately to relieve local traffic bottlenecks,” he said.

title: Asian Angle | Southeast Asia faces a false binary in US-China mineral trade
description: The real question for rare earth exporters is how to turn global mineral competition into higher-value industries.
content: Critical minerals have become a recurring source of friction in international diplomacy, with China’s dominance in the sector and US efforts to build alternative supply chains raising concerns that Southeast Asian countries may be forced to choose between the two powers. But this is a false choice. As important exporters of rare earth elements, Southeast Asian countries have leverage of their own and can use intensifying competition to diversify partnerships and capture more of the value chain at home. The recent meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States ended with a chairman’s declaration rather than a joint statement, underscoring the lack of unanimity. China objected to, among other things, calls to eliminate “non‑market policies” and ensure smooth global supply chains for vital goods, including critical minerals. The disagreement comes amid China’s tightening controls over rare earth elements (REEs), first introduced in April 2025 in retaliation for US tariffs and export controls. In October it went further, extending licensing requirements to certain foreign-made products containing at least 0.1 per cent Chinese-origin controlled REEs or using specified Chinese rare earth technologies. These measures were subsequently suspended until November this year, while the April 2025 controls remain. Although Beijing has sought to reassure non-US importers that normal commercial trade will continue, such controls inevitably increase costs and uncertainty for firms dependent on Chinese rare earths, processing and magnets. At the same time, a number of East Asian economies have joined Pax Silica and other US-supported efforts to build more resilient critical-mineral and technology supply chains. Has this increased pressure on them to choose between China-centred and US-backed supply chains? Given the region’s economic geography and dense webs of trade, few can afford such a binary choice. In the case of critical minerals, however, such concerns about being forced to choose need to be put into context. First of all, China’s present dominance in REEs stems from a long process of industrial development, not a strategy originally conceived to give Beijing a geopolitical weapon. The industry dates to the late 1950s. As applications expanded across metallurgy, petrochemicals, glass and ceramics, agriculture and equipment manufacturing, REEs were incorporated into national research and development programmes in 1986. In January 1991, the State Council issued a circular to curb rampant illegal mining under a national licensing regime, strengthen regulation and consolidate a fragmented industry. REEs were thus initially treated as industrial resources for domestic use and export; they were not designed to be used as geopolitical instruments. Yet decades of investment and capability-building have given China considerable leverage within global REE supply chains. Amid intensifying Sino-US competition, these accumulated advantages have acquired strategic significance – hence the observation by Belgian political scientist Victor de Decker that, over REEs and other minerals deemed critical by the US, “Beijing is now mirroring Washington’s own semiconductor export control regime almost to the letter”. For Beijing and Washington, the legitimacy of their export controls relies partly on the military applications of dual‑use materials and technologies, but their effectiveness is also limited. Curbing supply incentivises investment in alternatives, eroding the restricting country’s credibility and long‑term competitiveness as a supplier. Neither side can fully control an interdependent supply chain – midstream producers rely on downstream consumers abroad, while end users can reduce dependence through alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling. This interdependence is particularly relevant to Southeast Asia. Despite its dominance of REE extraction and processing, China is a net importer of raw REEs, including substantial supplies from the region. In 2024, Myanmar supplied 34.3 per cent of China’s REE imports, Malaysia contributed 10.6 per cent and Laos 8.3 per cent. Together, they accounted for over half of China’s total imports. Southeast Asia will not remain a mere supplier of raw materials, however. Malaysia already hosts the most commercially significant rare earth separation facility outside China, with much of its feedstock supplied from Lynas’s Mount Weld mine in Western Australia. The facility’s outputs are used in products ranging from lamps to semiconductors, a sector where Malaysia has decades of experience. It is only a matter of time before other regional ore exporters move into separation and other downstream applications. Indonesia is another case in point. In recent years, it has banned the export of unprocessed minerals like nickel, requiring producers to invest in processing facilities to add value before export. While this builds on earlier practices, its character also aligns with the industrial policies adopted by China, the US and others at comparable stages of technological development. As such, the proverbial choice between aligning with China or joining the US‑led Pax Silica is largely rhetorical for Southeast Asia. Both countries are interested in accessing Southeast Asian supplies of raw REEs on the basis of cost, not for the lack of material availability elsewhere, including within their own countries. The more consequential question for Southeast Asian exporters is how competition over critical minerals can help them diversify into more higher-value activities. The real measure of competing partnerships should therefore be what China, the US and other partners contribute to Southeast Asian efforts to move up the value chain. This includes investments in processing and refining, technology and skills transfer, and stronger linkages to downstream manufacturing. Seen in this context, the emerging competition is not just over who secures Southeast Asia’s minerals, but over who offers a more credible pathway from resource supplier to higher-value producer. To address societal concerns that REE refining is detrimental to the environment, the challenge is committing to importing the most environmentally-friendly processing technologies and rigorously enforcing standards on foreign corporate practices. In the final analysis, access to critical minerals is likely to remain high on the regional agenda. But this is also the area in which Southeast Asian REE exporters can exercise a certain level of agency. China’s dominance of REE processing gives it considerable leverage, but this should also not be overstated. Excessive restrictions incentivise alternative sourcing, substitution and recycling. Between China and the US, the likely outcome is a shifting balance between interdependence and diversification, not a full decoupling. For Southeast Asia, the perceived binary choice between the two powers is a false one: all countries face the same task of adjusting their policies within a shared set of mineral‑industry dynamics among producers, processors and consumers. Zha Daojiong is a Visiting Senior Fellow with ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is also Professor of International Political Economy at the School of International Studies, Peking University. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

title: Letters | Trevor Noah shows underline need for action in Hong Kong on scalping
description: Readers discuss the growing problem of bot-driven ticket scalpers, the chief executive’s policy address, and a disagreement over Mark Six winnings.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong’s ambition to become Asia’s “mega-event city” is being undermined by a glaring weakness: rampant ticket scalping. The Trevor Noah shows at MacPherson Stadium in October are the latest example. Tickets vanished quickly, only to reappear on resale platforms at many times the official price. Many fans were left empty-handed. Performers will face audiences distorted by profiteers, dealing the city’s credibility as a cultural hub another blow. This is not simply about demand. The deeper problem is that Hong Kong seems averse to regulating scalping and bot-driven hoarding, in particular, by offenders overseas. Automated programs scoop up tickets the moment sales open, diverting profits away from organisers, venues and performers. Instead, they enrich a shadow economy of resellers. Each mega-event becomes a profiteering opportunity for scalpers and bot programmers. The Places of Public Entertainment Ordinance is obviously outdated and not serving its intended purpose. The relevant fine is only HK$2,000, unchanged for decades, and does not apply to venues managed by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department. Ironically, attempts to keep tickets affordable through price caps only worsen the problem. For Noah’s shows, official prices were held between HK$600 and HK$1,200 – reasonable by international standards. But without resale restrictions, scalpers saw guaranteed margins. They seem to have bought aggressively, then resold at prices starting at HK$3,000. The result: affordability exists only on paper, while genuine fans face inflated costs in practice. Other places have acted decisively. Japan requires ticketing platforms to verify identities and limit transfers, reducing bot abuse. Hong Kong, by contrast, has left consumers to fend for themselves under a laissez-faire approach that benefits only scalpers. If Hong Kong is serious about its mega-events branding, it must legislate against resale above face value for all venues, mandate verified resale exchanges and require ticketing platforms to deploy anti-bot technology. Stephanie Y.K. Hasancebi, Sham Tseng Give internationalisation a stronger push Hong Kong’s first five-year plan is analogous to the business strategy of a company whereas the measures set out in the chief executive’s 2026 policy address are the practical tactics to implement it. Of the six themes put forward in the highlights of the five-year plan, the first three are relevant to the promotion of Hong Kong’s international status in terms of finance, trade, aviation, innovation and collaboration. Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China but is unique in its cultural legacy which is permeated with ingrained Western heritage. However, Hong Kong’s English proficiency is slipping as is its multiculturalism and good rapport with Western countries. Some concrete steps should be taken to help Hong Kong take centre stage globally again. Hong Kong’s world-class universities should accept more students from foreign countries such as those in Central Asia. Secondary schools in the city could link up with their counterparts in Singapore, Canada and other English-speaking countries as sister schools. More incentives should be offered to the visitors from Europe, the Americas and Africa, such as concessions in hospitality, entertainment, shopping and fine dining. Hong Kong will gain ample networking opportunities if it joins more international organisations. The policy address mentions supporting ethnic minorities by adopting learning material tailored to non-Chinese speaking students. School leavers of South Asian descent face hurdles in seeking jobs because of language and cultural challenges. If a flexible language option is available, they could opt to learn Arabic instead of Chinese and promote Hong Kong’s role in the Belt and Road Initiative by providing translation, logistics and other services to businessmen and investors from the Middle East and other Arabic-speaking regions. Such an approach would align with the city’s as well as the nation’s five-year plan. The policy address should have had more elements to meet the five-year plan’s objectives. Albert Lau, Kwun Tong Why a Mark Six dispute has the city agog I refer to “Man arrested after allegedly refusing to share HK$30m Mark Six jackpot with group” (September 12). This incident has become a hot topic in Hong Kong. But why has it garnered so much interest? First, the sheer size of the jackpot: the Jockey Club’s September 5 “Mark Six 50th Anniversary Snowball” draw featured a record HK$228 million jackpot. More importantly, however, is that those involved in the dispute reportedly were staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. Civil servants in Hong Kong are expected to uphold an extremely clean public image. Randy Lee, Ma On Shan

title: CNN blocked from Trump’s trip as White House signals new media curb
description: The spot meant for CNN on Trump’s Air Force One flight on Saturday will be taken up by Real America’s Voice News, a conservative network.
content: The White House signalled on Friday night that CNN would be left off Air Force One for President Donald Trump’s Saturday trip, the latest media restriction from the administration in an ongoing dispute with First Amendment implications. The news organisation was replaced by Real America’s Voice News, a conservative network, for the president’s trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, according to White House guidance. Trump is scheduled to attend a college-football game between the University of Tennessee and the University of Texas at midday on Saturday. The news came just after journalists from CNN, along with MS NOW and Politico, which Trump banned last week from the White House grounds, returned to the executive complex with TV cameras in hand after a judge handed the organisations a reprieve. US District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily struck down the ban in an overnight ruling early Thursday, but his decision addressed “hard passes” to the White House grounds and did not directly address pool duties. The temporary order from the judge also said nothing directly about Air Force One. Theodore Boutrous Jnr, the news outlets’ lawyers, did not immediately respond to an email and phone call requesting comment Friday night. Earlier Friday, on The Lead with Jake Tapper, Boutrous had said the plaintiffs believed the recent court ruling also covered the issue of pool access. The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting additional details on the decision. For a while during the day, the US network video pool for the White House was back in operation for the first time since Trump banned the three news outlets in an extraordinary showdown over media access. At noon on CNN, viewers could see Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping touring the National Archives, along with Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan, Xi’s wife. The banner along the bottom of the screen read: “Trump and China’s Xi Visit National Archives.” It was a routine report from a state visit – but for the fact that CNN had not aired live video of Trump in several days. “As of now, all systems are go,” said a person familiar with the pool, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the fluidity of the situation. The pool consists of five major US broadcast outlets that take turns shooting and sharing video. When the White House banned CNN – which belongs to the pool – from White House grounds, along with MS NOW and Politico, the other four pool providers declined to participate in a show of solidarity. The spot that was meant for CNN on this flight has long been saved for a member of the US network video pool, which Real America’s Voice News is not part of. CNN was not commenting directly earlier on Friday, referring instead to its editorial coverage. But Brian Stelter, the network’s media analyst, posted on social media that CNN had a pool assignment at the National Archives event and that the White House had approved the network’s credentials. Throughout his second term, Trump has increasingly targeted media outlets whose coverage irritates him, taking administrative or legal action against several. Early last year, he banished Associated Press reporters from White House events because the organisation was not abiding by his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.” The AP’s guidance says to acknowledge the new name when relevant. The case is on appeal after a federal district judge ruled in AP’s favour. The press pool was created decades ago by the White House Correspondents’ Association, a group of journalists who cover the president, to make sure a rotating roster always travels with the president. The pool distributes in-person reports and imagery to the broader press corps and is designed to hold the nation’s chief executive accountable on behalf of the American public. The association did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.

title: Trump, Takaichi reaffirm US-Japan ties in phone call after Xi state visit
description: They exchanged views on various issues surrounding China, Japanese leader’s post says, after World War II references spark concern in Tokyo.
content: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she and Donald Trump had reaffirmed their collaboration on issues relating to Beijing in a phone call on Saturday. The call followed the US president’s nostalgic invocation of the World War II alliance with China during his summit with Xi Jinping, remarks that sent shock waves through Tokyo. Trump made the references as he welcomed the Chinese president to the White House on Thursday for his first state visit to Washington in over a decade. In a social media post on Saturday, Takaichi said Trump provided detailed explanations regarding the recent US-China summit during the call starting at 9pm Tokyo time. They exchanged views centred on various issues surrounding China, including the economy and security, and confirmed the Japan-US collaboration, she wrote. Takaichi met Trump in person on Tuesday in New York, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Two exchanges with the US leader within one week “truly demonstrates the strength of the Japan-US alliance”, her post read. “Japan and the United States have now become the most trusted allied nations, and we confirmed our commitment to jointly contribute to peace and stability in the region and the world. “In order to elevate our unwavering Japan-US alliance to even greater heights, I will closely collaborate with President Trump,” she pledged. Both Trump and Xi repeatedly invoked their nations’ wartime alliance against Japan in their remarks in Washington – an unusual historical reference that immediately unsettled Tokyo. Such bonds were also reflected in statements released by the two countries following Xi’s visit. “The two leaders recalled that United States and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war,” both statements said. However, the White House statement added a paragraph to justify US presence in the region. “Since World War II, the United States’ forward military presence has preserved a free and open Indo-Pacific, contributing to generations of American prosperity,” it said. Takaichi said on Friday that Tokyo and Washington were “allies bound by very strong ties” based on mutual trust. But she pointedly declined to comment on the Trump-Xi summit. To avoid being sidelined completely, Takaichi had rescheduled her address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, moving it up by two days to secure a 35-minute meeting with Trump on Tuesday. Japanese analysts warned that the wartime nostalgia boded poorly for Japan, though they cautioned against reading too much into the rhetoric. Chinese observers, meanwhile, argued that the moment should prompt Tokyo to rethink its approach towards Beijing. Shin Kawashima, professor of international relations at the University of Tokyo, said the main question was why Washington was embracing the wartime framing now. “Trump’s remarks could easily be interpreted by China as indicating that the US and China are in agreement on issues of historical perception and that the US supports China’s rhetoric condemning the [Takaichi] administration as a form of ‘new militarism’,” Kawashima said. Hotaka Machida, a visiting senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said Japan would find Trump’s historical references “surprising and awkward”, but noted that the remarks were made in the context of the US-China relationship. Still, he cautioned: “Japan needs to be careful about the possibility of the Chinese side taking advantage of the amicable atmosphere presented this time as a propaganda tool.” Kenichi Doi, senior research fellow at the same institute, called Trump’s description of wartime China as an ally “striking”. But the bigger question was whether that shared history would be used to cast doubt on present-day Japan. It would be a mistake to assume that Trump had endorsed Beijing’s criticism of Tokyo, he said. Rintaro Nishimura, a senior associate at The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said that though worrying, the single statement was unlikely to weaken the US-Japan alliance. Tokyo was also less concerned because Takaichi coordinated with Trump on issues related to China ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, he added. “[But] it does not bode well for Tokyo that Washington and Beijing are both emphasising the fact that the two countries were wartime allies,” Nishimura said. Beijing and Tokyo have remained largely out of official contact since November, when Takaichi suggested that a blockade of Taiwan would be a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan. Official relations went into a tailspin but Japanese business and legislative delegations have made sustained efforts to visit Beijing to gauge Chinese thinking. Another business delegation, led by former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya, will go to China on Sunday in the latest attempt to bridge the diplomatic impasse. Nishimura expected Tokyo to “stay the course” when engaging with Beijing, using legislative and commercial dialogue to tease out potential openings for government-level talks, with an end goal of securing a Takaichi-Xi meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November. “Japan will be looking to see if there are any signs that Washington is ready to compromise regional security for a deal, perhaps economic, with Beijing.” Meanwhile, Tokyo’s discomfort is seen as an inevitable consequence of stabilising US-China ties, with analysts saying the warm tone from the summit should prompt Tokyo to reassess its own approach to Beijing. Kawashima noted that Japan-China relations would “grow more tenuous” if US-China ministerial engagement deepened and might prompt Tokyo to conclude that it was better to improve relations with China to some extent. Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, said Japan’s anxiety was an inevitable result of further stabilisation between Beijing and Washington. “The sheer fact that Chinese and American leaders can have such frequent interactions this year should serve as a prompt for Tokyo to change its perceptions towards China and rethink its posture,” Wang said. Zhang Yun, professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Tokyo harboured deep concern about the prospect of another 1972 “Nixon shock”, when the US normalised ties with China without consulting its closest East Asian ally. Takaichi’s push to meet Trump ahead of his talks with Xi reflected this anxiety, he said. “Compounded by Trump’s transactional approach towards its traditional alliances and tariff actions, these dynamics are fuelling deep-seated anxieties in Tokyo over Washington’s reliability, leaving Japan’s position adrift,” Zhang said. According to Cho Sung-min, associate professor of international relations at Sungkyunkwan University in Seoul, the memory of US-China military cooperation against Japan has long been a Chinese talking point. “Trump’s reference to America’s past partnership with China against Japan, a US ally in the present, suggests how far he was willing to go to maintain a cordial relationship with Xi,” Cho said.

title: Your Voice: Restoring coral reefs, remembering Harinder Veriah, the case against alarms (letters)
description: This week, students detail their part in helping a valuable marine ecosystem, trace race-based medical negligence in Hong Kong and urge against jolting awake.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Hayley Hope Tang, St Paul’s School (New Hampshire, United States)
Visibility was poor as we initiated our descent. Run-off from the surrounding islands – one of the main threats to coral in the area – had turned the ocean into a thick soup. The temperature was at a high of 31 degrees Celsius.
My heart was thumping as we dived closer to the cages where we had planted Acropora coral fragments almost exactly a year ago. But to my absolute relief, they had not just survived but thrived.
Of the 140 fragments that we had planted the previous summer, 118 had made it. Not only that, but they had grown anywhere from 12 to 29cm in width and 5 to 13cm in height – roughly a two to three per cent increase. My “babies” were doing just fine.
As coral returned to this reef in the Koh Rong archipelago of western Cambodia, marine life followed: pufferfish, grouper, barracuda, parrotfish, nudibranch, honeycomb grouper, blue-spotted stingray and even rare pipefish. The reef had woken up.
It made sense. Coral covers only 0.1 per cent of the ocean floor, yet it supports 25 per cent of all marine species. Nothing else punches so far above its weight.
This was my first dive of the summer – part of my second consecutive internship at the Song Saa Foundation, working on coral reef restoration around Koh Rong.
We collect Acropora fragments from the ocean floor and raise infant coral – responsibly harvested from healthy adult colonies – in a sheltered nursery. Once they have grown enough to manage on their own, we reattach them in the ocean.
I learned how fascinating coral actually is as a living organism. Most people assume they are inanimate – probably because of their hard corallite exoskeleton. But inside, there are vibrant polyps housing living tissue: tentacles, mouths, guts and symbiotic algae.
Marine biologist Sabrina Petry taught me to identify coral genera and recognise eight principal growth forms, ranging from delicate, finger-like branching structures to layered, wafer-like foliose ones.
Classroom lectures were paired with dives – all logged meticulously – where I practised surveying coral, monitoring bleaching and measuring biodiversity.
Our restoration efforts come after years of destructive fishing and the compounding damage of global warming, made viscerally real by the catastrophic 2024 worldwide bleaching event.
It had been genuinely exhilarating to watch nature push back, especially when hearing about one of the biggest milestones yet – coral spawning being observed in the area earlier this year.
What is also exciting is how technology is changing the game. Through photogrammetry, Petry and her team create detailed digital models of the reef – advanced software and artificial intelligence turning raw dive footage into precise two- and three-dimensional images. These allow accurate measurements, health assessments and species tracking.
I feel lucky to see my small contributions actually make a difference. I am struck by the ocean’s resilience. Watching these baby steps add up – that’s what keeps my passion alive.
Jaydon Mau, Choate Rosemary Hall (Connecticut, United States)
On New Year’s Day, 2000, Harinder Kaur Veriah, a Cantonese-speaking Punjabi Malaysian, had an epileptic seizure while celebrating the new millennium.
The 33-year-old lawyer had relocated to Hong Kong and was taken to Ruttonjee Hospital by her husband, journalist Martin Jacques. The only non-Chinese patient in the ward, Veriah told her husband: “I am bottom of the pile here.”
The following morning, she died after another epileptic fit.
An inquest at the coroner’s office ruled the death a result of natural causes with no evidence of medical neglect. But the incident garnered publicity, emboldening a generation of Hongkongers from ethnic minority groups to bring forward personal accounts of medical neglect within public hospitals. Years of advocacy culminated in the Race Discrimination Ordinance, enacted in 2008.
The need for equitable healthcare has become more urgent. The year the ordinance was passed, people from ethnic minority groups made up an easily overlooked portion of Hong Kong’s population. But the 2021 census showed that over 619,000 people identified as non-Chinese, making up 8.4 per cent of the total population.
Omitting foreign domestic helpers still leaves over 300,000 people with ethnic minority backgrounds who call the city home. Foreign domestic helpers in Hong Kong also require additional attention. They are often left out of both government figures and academic studies, treated as footnotes rather than included in the data when many of them face the same obstacles to adequate healthcare.
A domestic helper’s access to proper medical services is usually determined by their employer’s willingness to allow them time off. If an employment contract is terminated while they are sick, their immigration status becomes that of a visitor, effectively barring them from the city’s subsidised health network.
Lacking robust interpreter networks, culturally competent providers and relationships with local organisations, many districts are not built to host residents who do not speak Chinese. These patients experience more negative experiences than their Chinese-speaking counterparts. Barriers often lead to delayed treatments and poorer health outcomes among ethnic minority groups, highlighting the need for systemic change.
In recent years, despite more languages being used at hospitals, there are still few clear guidelines. Many times, family members or even strangers have to translate sensitive medical information, a nonviable substitute for a professional translator.
Harinder Veriah’s death forced Hong Kong lawmakers to consider racial discrimination. But today, the city’s healthcare system still does not reflect its modern-day population.
You were supposed to be up at 6am. Instead, you woke up at 5.57am and fell right back into deep sleep. At 8am, you wake up, tired and lethargic.
Setting an alarm to wake you up in the morning is not always helpful.
When you wake up before your alarm rings, it’s because your body no longer relies on an external force to set your internal clock. Your mind’s subconscious knows you usually get up right about now.
The human brain maintains circadian timing – an internal clock tracking the rhythms of day and night. This helps it prepare your body for waking up, with measurable hormonal shifts, temperature gradients and slow adjustment of cortisol levels – the hormone associated with stress.
Sleep moves in cycles; the final hours before waking up are dominated by rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the most cognitively active part. The body’s muscles are essentially offline, so the sleeper cannot easily startle, orient or regulate.
An alarm essentially shocks you to wake up. This spikes cortisol levels and causes morning anxiety. When you jolt awake, a sleep cycle finishes and your internal clock believes you should be up now. If you go back to sleep, you mess up this cycle.
Echo Luo Kai-jing, Tai Kwong Hilary College
Linguistic relativity considers whether language shapes our world view. As a bilingual student, I believe it influences but does not completely control or restrict our thinking.
In Chinese, I describe events closely connected with my emotions. I think my tone is serious, reserved and dignified. But when I describe my day or something that happened in English, I am more direct and passionate. I also feel much more relaxed or energised. When I am upset, I prefer expressing it in English.
I feel that many people who speak English very well tend to be lively and outgoing, while some Chinese speakers appear really serious and disciplined. I understand this is just my own perspective, and it is not true for everyone. An individual’s cultural background and their personality play a huge role.
Researchers have investigated these linguistic expressions of emotion, often citing Mandarin’s nature as a tonal language for some of the differences.
As a 2022 article in Brain Sciences says, Chinese-speaking people tend to be more receptive, reflective and adaptive, whereas native English speakers may be more reactive, proactive and interactive.
Today, we have more opportunities to learn and master other languages, creating a bridge that allows us to explore richer ways of thinking.

title: ‘Never too late’: Filipino domestic helpers pursue degree dreams they put on hold
description: Having put personal ambitions aside for their families, domestic helpers are now earning degrees while working with support from Hong Kong non-profit FullPhils.
content: When Dyan Agonoy left the Philippines to work as a domestic helper in Hong Kong, she had to leave her family behind. “I’ve missed a lot of my kids’ milestones, our special occasions. I’m always the only one missing from the pictures,” she said. Agonoy left university, married young and started a family. Without the bachelor’s degree required for many jobs, she took up domestic work abroad. Gelanie Aguilario faced a similar plight. She twice tried to earn a bachelor’s degree – first in political science, hoping to become a lawyer, and then in education – but pregnancy and family obligations derailed her plans. Now working in Hong Kong as a domestic helper to support her siblings financially, she felt she had fallen behind them. Not having a degree made her feel like a failure, which was compounded by her father’s death. “It’s kind of like I failed him,” she said. Both women’s fortunes changed in 2024, when they came across FullPhils, a non-profit organisation that helps overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in Hong Kong earn bachelor’s degrees. The courses are fully online, and the group subsidises 80 per cent of the costs, leaving students to pay about HK$600 (US$76) per term. FullPhils was founded in 2022 by Emilio Baja, when he was just 14 years old. Born and raised in the Philippines, Baja lived with his family in Hong Kong for two years while he was in the eighth grade. He was struck by the crowds of domestic helpers gathering every Sunday in makeshift tents and among cardboard boxes across the city. “OFWs are incredibly visible in Hong Kong,” Baja said. “But their individual stories, ambitions and even their sacrifices are often left invisible. “It made me ask the question: if they can spend their lives creating opportunities for everyone else, who is creating opportunities for them?” FullPhils draws on a Philippine government initiative known as the Expanded Tertiary Education Equivalency and Accreditation Programme, or ETEEAP. Candidates must have at least five years of work experience, which ETEEAP converts into credits towards a relevant bachelor’s degree. The degree can then be awarded after as little as six months of study. FullPhils partners with AMA University, Philippine Women’s University (PWU) and the University of the Philippines to offer online asynchronous modular courses. Baja said this allowed Filipinos abroad to be “full-time students while also being full-time domestic workers”. Eligible for hospitality degrees at PWU, Aguilario and Agonoy spent a year studying across three terms while maintaining their full-time jobs. They said time management and support from friends, family and employers were crucial. “In the mornings when I drop off the [employer’s] kid to school, I have three hours for myself or household chores,” Aguilario said. “If I get the chores done in an hour or two, I have an extra hour to do what I have to do for school.” Agonoy said she would stay up until 1am to do her homework, which took a toll on her body. “In my last term, my blood pressure dropped. I was sent for medical check-ups by my employer,” she said. The women relied on their fellow students for support. Every month, FullPhils runs workshops to teach the women skills they might not otherwise learn as part of their degree, such as financial literacy and how to use Excel. In February, Aguilario and Agonoy graduated. Aguilario recalled her feelings at the ceremony in Manila. “I was crying because I had my mum there,” she said. “I was like … this is it. I made it.” She added that she and her siblings planned to open a cafe and pastry shop back home. She hopes other domestic helpers will follow her example and earn a degree. Agonoy said she was proud of her achievement, although she did not attend her graduation ceremony. She has since enrolled in education courses, aiming to become a teacher in the Philippines or elsewhere, as long as her family can join her. “I don’t want [it to be] that as long as I live, I’m just scrubbing toilets for different employers. I believe I can do more,” she said. “Others shouldn’t let their failures determine what they can achieve. Because those failures, they’re just a part of our journeys.” Now starting university at Harvard in the United States, Baja said FullPhils had granted about 30 scholarships so far and that he hoped to expand the programme soon. “In the long term, organisations like FullPhils shouldn’t be necessary, because NGOs are ultimately just band-aids,” he said. “We need systemic solutions that ensure education is provided to Filipinos so that they’re able to work in the Philippines without having to live abroad to provide for their families.” Until that change comes, Baja will use FullPhils to invest in as many OFWs as possible. “Sacrifice shouldn’t require surrendering your own future. It’s not too late to return to education,” he said. “Your dreams still matter.”

title: China couple have 13 kids to avoid village bullying, elderly loneliness, dividing public opinion
description: Father expresses deep joy in his large family, saying hearing his kids call him ‘dad’ makes him happy.
content: A middle-aged couple in rural China has recently trended on social media for having 13 children. The family, living in a village in Qinzhou in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, stands out in mainland China, particularly in light of the country’s declining birth rate. This situation has prompted authorities to implement various policies encouraging marriage and larger families. According to Jiupai News, the 49-year-old man, surnamed Huang, and his 42-year-old wife have welcomed 13 children – eight sons and five daughters – since their marriage 22 years ago. Their oldest child is a 22-year-old daughter who is already married, while their youngest child is only two years old. The couple’s second oldest daughter is currently studying at a university, and their oldest son, aged 18, is still in high school. Interestingly, among the Huang children, the first two and the last three are girls, with the boys positioned in between. Huang mentioned that he enrols his children in school as they reach the appropriate age, ensuring compliance with the country’s compulsory education laws. The family’s income primarily derives from farming, as they cultivate rice on their 20-mu plot (13,340 sq m). A local cadre reported that Huang’s family receives 3,500 yuan (US$520) in government subsidies per month, which helps maintain their living standards above the poverty line established by authorities. Additionally, local officials provided financial aid years ago to help them build a two-storey home. Huang expressed his joy in having many children, stating: “Seeing my kids and hearing them call me ‘dad’ makes me very happy. Some of my kids are sensible while others are mischievous, each with their unique characteristics.” He also noted that a larger family minimises the risk of bullying in the village and assures him that he will not feel lonely in his later years. Following the implementation of the one-child policy from the late 1970s until the end of 2015, the Chinese government allowed couples to have two children, and by 2021, permitted up to three. Families violating this policy face varying penalties depending on the region. Local officials in Guangxi have visited Huang’s home multiple times, attempting to persuade him against having more children. However, he remains steadfast in his reproductive choices. The extent of any fines he may have incurred for breaches of the birth control policy remains unclear.
