Huang has mentioned ongoing debts resulting from a construction site accident in 2016, which left him with serious injuries to his leg and waist, costing him 100,000 yuan (US$15,000) in medical expenses. “I have to work on the land all day and even into the evening to support my family. Sometimes I feel pain in my leg and waist from working too long, and I can no longer lift heavy objects,” Huang explained. His wife, he added, is in good health after giving birth to all 13 children. The Huang family has attracted mixed reactions on social media in China. One observer criticised them, saying: “He is so irresponsible for having too many children without the means to support them. Raising a child involves more than just providing food and clothing; it also requires education, guidance, and medical care, all of which necessitate money and energy.” Conversely, another commenter praised their efforts, stating: “Well done! The government should reward them for making such contributions to society.” A third observer expressed concern for Huang’s wife, saying: “I feel sorry for her. The man is crazy and doesn’t seem to care about her health.”

title: Offshore wind farm could create radar blind spots and ‘ghost’ targets, Chinese study warns
description: As China rapidly expands its wind projects near coastal areas, researchers find the turbines can complicate marine vessel detection at sea.
content: Offshore wind farms can reduce the coverage of shore-based radar systems and create areas where targets become harder to detect, according to a new study. The researchers found that at a range of 5km (3 miles), effective radar coverage fell by 6.9 per cent while blind spots increased by 14.9 per cent. The research, published online last month in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Radio Engineering, was conducted by Professor Liu Zunnian and his team from Qingdao Technological University and the Yantai Communication Centre of the Beihai Navigation Security Centre under the Ministry of Transport. The team found that large arrays of wind turbines could produce false “ghost” targets through reflected radar signals, potentially complicating the detection of vessels in coastal waters. “A wind turbine is itself a huge metal object, so it will inevitably interfere with radar signals,” said a military equipment expert who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the matter. The expert – who was not involved in the study – said the problem was not unique to China and had been studied in Britain for decades. “Foreign countries have faced the same problem,” the expert said, adding that because the issue had been identified relatively early, offshore wind projects in China - most of which were built after 2004 - should in principle have taken radar interference into account at the planning stage. China’s offshore wind projects would probably need to be assessed in relation to military radar coverage or kept away from areas designated as restricted zones, the expert argued. China has been rapidly expanding offshore wind power capacity near coastal areas and ports. It had 48.4 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity installed by the end of 2025, accounting for about 52 per cent of global capacity, according to the Global Wind Energy Council. China added 6.6GW of offshore wind capacity in 2025 alone, marking the eighth consecutive year it led the world in new offshore installations. The researchers ran their simulation in Shandong province, eastern China’s most vital port region. Here, the port of Qingdao acts as a key gateway for trade in northern China and the Yellow River region, while Yantai is a major hub for trade with Africa and a logistics link between northeast Asia and the Chinese interior. Ships operating from these ports could be affected by the presence of offshore wind farms. Similar effects have also been studied by US researchers. A 2022 report by the National Academies identified reflected clutter, radar shadows and ambiguous detections as the main problems that wind turbines could create for marine vessel radars. For their modelling, Liu and his team used an X-band shore-based surveillance radar operating at 9.46 gigahertz, and represented the wind turbines as 120 metre (394 feet) towers with blades about 100 metres long. This allowed them to assess changes in detectable, undetectable and ghost-target areas after a wind farm was introduced. The main mechanisms identified were obstruction, diffraction loss and multi-path reflections, with turbines weakening radar signals behind the array while reflected signals generated false returns. Distance alone was not a reliable measure of interference, as increasing the distance from 5km to 20km at a 90-degree angle did not steadily reduce ghost interference, which reached a peak of 4.5 per cent at 20km. At an existing radar site modelled in the study, located 5km from the wind farm at a 90-degree angle, radar coverage fell by 3.3 per cent while the undetectable area increased by 0.4 per cent. Liu said the main engineering measures included careful site selection, avoiding long rows of turbines along a radar’s main line of sight, improving radar algorithms to suppress clutter and false echoes, and deploying supplementary radars where coverage gaps could not be avoided. “There is no need to use distance as the only criterion for avoiding interference,” the expert said, adding that advances in radar technology could also reduce the practical impact of wind farms. “China’s radar technology is at an advanced level worldwide,” he added, citing the use of dual-band radars on Chinese naval vessels as well as improvements in electromagnetic compatibility and system integration. “Compatibility and integration are closely related to anti-interference capability to some extent. The better the compatibility and integration, the stronger the foundation for anti-interference.” He also said China had developed newer radar systems that used electromagnetic-wave propagation over the sea and could be less affected by turbine obstruction, although such systems were not assessed in the study. Liu and his team acknowledged that their model did not yet account for complex weather, dynamic sea conditions or different turbine designs.

title: How China’s mobile-payment overhaul helps foreigners spend money ahead of Apec meeting
description: Smartphone apps such as Alipay and WeChat Pay now link foreign cards and wallets, easing a cashless barrier that has long frustrated international visitors.
content: After three weeks of travelling across China, Bojan Tomic and his wife found that one of the biggest conveniences of the trip was being able to pay for daily expenses almost entirely via smartphone. The Croatian couple’s journey spanned the cities of Beijing, Xian, Chengdu and finally Shenzhen. Visiting China for the first time, they quickly adapted to the country’s dominant mobile payment ecosystem, using Alipay and WeChat Pay, two of China’s largest payment platforms, for most of their spending. Both apps can be set up with an email address and linked to a foreign bank card. “It’s super easy,” Tomic said. “At first, I didn’t know where to press [in the apps], but now I’ve got used to it. It’s so convenient because I don’t need to carry my wallet or any cash.” As China prepares to host the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November, connecting China’s payment ecosystem with overseas networks has become part of broader efforts to make the country more accessible to overseas visitors. For years, foreigners have complained about the difficulty of making simple, everyday payments in China’s largely cashless society. And economists have long argued that expanding links between domestic and overseas payment systems could boost visitor spending by reducing barriers to consumption. “Payment connectivity could not only improve the experience for overseas visitors, but also help transform China’s mobile-payment ecosystem into a consumer network that global users can access with fewer barriers,” according to an article posted to social media on Tuesday whose authors include Xu Qiyuan, deputy director of the Institute of American Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Survey findings released by the Payment and Clearing Association of China in August showed that 88.5 per cent of respondents used mobile payments daily in 2025, up 5.6 percentage points from a year earlier. Better links between domestic and overseas payment systems could encourage visitors to make more everyday purchases beyond essential spending, helping unlock more inbound tourism consumption, Xu’s article said. On Thursday, UnionPay said in a press release that foreign travellers using more than 200 overseas digital wallets across 37 countries and regions could directly scan UnionPay QR codes for payments in China, as part of its efforts to improve payment convenience for foreign visitors ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting. Users of more than 50 overseas e-wallets, including South Korea’s Kakao Pay and Thailand’s TrueMoney, can use Alipay+, Ant International’s wallet gateway, to make payments in China, the company told the South China Morning Post. Ant International is the overseas affiliate of Chinese fintech giant Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the SCMP. Meanwhile, Tencent Holdings launched TenPayGo on Thursday, a mobile-payment app designed for overseas visitors that allows them to pay in China by linking credit cards or digital wallets from their home countries. Tencent’s move follows its partnership with PayPal earlier this year, which enabled US users to pay WeChat Pay merchants in China directly through the PayPal app. Over the first seven months of the year, spending by overseas visitors in China reached 263.6 billion yuan (US$39.3 billion), up 27.8 per cent, year on year, official data showed. However, Xu said that partnerships between retail-payment apps alone cannot achieve broader payment connectivity. Moving beyond individual collaborations would require stronger underlying infrastructure, he wrote in the Tuesday article. “There should be continued improvements to systems such as the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to enhance the capacity, stability and coverage of cross-border yuan settlements, supporting broader uses including trade, services consumption and cross-border e-commerce,” he said.

title: TikTok settles lawsuit with Alabama for at least US$100m, to apply safety steps
description: Alabama has claimed TikTok’s algorithm pushes young users towards increasingly intense content about violence and self-harm.
content: Alabama said on Friday it had reached a settlement with TikTok and its Chinese parent company, ByteDance, that required the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhanced age-verification measures for users in the US state, resolving claims that the platform endangered children and misled consumers about its safety. The agreement, which came days before a scheduled trial, calls for TikTok to implement changes for teenagers in Alabama including a two-hour daily time limit, pauses after 15 ‌minutes of use and stricter age checks. TikTok will pay Alabama at least US$100 million under the settlement, but the state’s payout could grow to US$300 million if 40 other attorneys general sign on to similar agreements with the company within a specified time frame, according to the settlement. “This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations said in a statement. The deal marks TikTok’s first settlement with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s impact on teen well-being. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the company last year, and at least 27 other states and Washington, D.C., have brought similar lawsuits. “This is a great day for Alabama parents,” Marshall ⁠said in announcing the agreement. The trial, which was scheduled to kick off on Monday in Montgomery state court and expected to last two to three weeks, had been expected to provide a rare ‌look inside TikTok, which has settled prior cases selected for trial and sought to keep details of its operations from public view. Alabama had claimed TikTok’s endless stream of videos made it the most addictive social media platform and that its algorithm pushed young users towards increasingly intense content about violence and self-harm, ‌contributing to a teen mental health crisis and causing the number of accident and emergency visits for self-harm in the state to “skyrocket”. The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming ⁠it limited access to sexual and violent content ⁠for young users in order to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access to US users’ data. TikTok has said it designed its ‌platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability over user-generated content. In addition to the states’ cases, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school ‌districts ‌and municipalities over its alleged impact on young users’ mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap and Alphabet’s YouTube are also defendants in many of these cases. With the settlement in Alabama, TikTok has ‌settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district. Alabama’s lawsuit claimed TikTok asked users to self-report their ages, but it also allowed users to ⁠evade its questions about their age by viewing videos without creating an account, which still allowed the company to collect data on their viewing habits. The lack of an effective age restriction ⁠makes things like “Kids Mode,” which curates content for young users, entirely useless, according to the lawsuit. The state also claimed the platform trapped kids in so-called “filter bubbles”, feeding them increasingly intense content on subjects that captured their attention, including violent or harmful material. Last month, Meta reached a sweeping US$17.1 billion settlement with 47 states, Washington, D.C., and US territories. Meta, ‌which did not admit wrongdoing, agreed to make ‌changes to teens’ access to Instagram and Facebook as part of the deal and conditioned US$5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube’s adoption of those terms. TikTok has not said anything publicly about the deal. Like the Meta settlement, Alabama’s deal with TikTok would require the company to adopt additional restrictions if its rivals Snap, Google and Meta make similar changes. Those measures could further limit teens’ time on social media apps and restrict overnight access, according to the filing. Although the settlement applies only in Alabama, major platform changes could prove difficult to implement on a state-by-state basis.

title: Being Chinese | What’s so Chinese about US Open tennis players like Zheng Qinwen?
description: From afar, Chinese tennis stars can appear as a cohort, their names accompanied by the same flag. Up close, they’re nothing like one another.
content: “Woo-hoooo!” The cheers swirled as Wu Yibing ended the rally with a blistering forehand winner down the line. The first syllable was emphatically articulated, signalling that this was an intentional play on Wu’s last name, not a random shout after one too many honey deuces. It was Wu’s second-round match against Australian James Duckworth at the US Open earlier this month. Wu’s most vocal supporters turned out to be three white Americans sitting behind the baseline. Widely considered the most talented Chinese man on tour, Wu is the first Chinese player to have won an ATP Tour title. Although his career has been plagued by injury, he can deliver inspired tennis when healthy. Against Duckworth, he was proactive in redirecting balls. The seemingly straightforward shots were risky and required an exquisite touch. Wu is perpetually online when he is not on court and has endeared himself to his fans on RedNote (Xiaohongshu). When an earnest post asked whether any good-looking players were left in the draw after Briton Jack Draper withdrew, Wu resolutely answered in the comments: “Me.” Following his first-round win, he leaned into the gag by posting a spoof press release referring to himself as “Chinese hunk Wu Yibing”. Between points, a Chinese woman behind me filled in a cluster of curious fans on Wu’s humour, prompting guffaws and even more raucous cheers for him. Courtside, nationality seems both important and beside the point. Wu’s name gave the Americans in front of me an irresistible chant, while the woman behind me supplied the Xiaohongshu lore. But once the ball was in play, what mattered was the audacity of his shot-making. They weren’t cheering for China. They were cheering for Wu. Earlier in the day, another Chinese player, Bu Yunchaokete, who also goes by Bert, pulled off an upset against Spaniard Rafael Jodar. Before we found seats in the stadium, I had warned my friend that it could be a swift exit for Bu, given Jodar’s form. In the event, Bu closed it out decisively, before we could filter back in, after a rain delay, to witness the match point. The ethnic Mongolian’s dark complexion and rambunctious name draw equal parts fascination and confusion. “Is that dude Chinese?” someone murmured near me. Technically, Bu isn’t his surname. By Mongolian convention, the entire name functions as a given name. On maps of China, regions with large ethnic minority populations often adopt romanisations rooted in local languages rather than standard pinyin, producing city names like Urumqi and Hohhot. Regrettably, these considerations are not applied to people. Born in Xinjiang, Bu moved to Zhejiang at age five to train and was drafted into the provincial team. International audiences have long viewed Chinese athletes through the tired lens of this rigid state-sponsored system. Yet tennis has always been an awkward outlier in that framework because of the massive prize money, endorsements and global fame that come with it. In a hybrid model, Bu and Wu have roots in the state system but also the independence to hire international coaches, physiotherapists and managers. That freedom was hard-won. When Li Na, Asia’s first grand slam singles champion, pushed to leave the state system, it provoked debate over whether she owed something to the system that nurtured her. Eventually allowed to manage her own career following her success at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Li pioneered a model that subsequent generations of Chinese tennis players could emulate. Today’s youngsters relish the freedom to simply be themselves. It helps that tennis is an inherently personal game and offers athletes a platform to speak their minds on and off the court. Li’s more important legacy was perhaps showing Chinese athletes they could unapologetically be themselves. Her candour was something to behold, whether she was openly venting at her coach-cum-husband Jiang Shan in Wuhan dialect on court or joking about his snoring in English during a post-match interview. Growing up, I recognised in Li the directness and resilience often associated with the women of Hubei province, shaped as much by the relentless summer heat as by their decisive role in the household and the fierce competition inherent in an inland trading port. Her impatience took flight most easily in our local tongue. Her tone often triggered memories of being shouted at by my mother to stop procrastinating on summer homework. International audiences have long viewed Chinese athletes through the tired lens of this rigid state-sponsored system. Yet tennis has always been an awkward outlier in that framework Nowadays, Zheng Qinwen, the Olympic gold medallist also from Hubei, shows the same spirit. At this year’s US Open, she came back from a 0-5 deficit, twice, to defeat grand slam champions Madison Keys and Iga Swiatek before falling in a tight three-setter to the eventual winner, Elena Rybakina. Zheng speaks plainly too. Previously, she made headlines by admitting she wasn’t in the sport to make friends. And during her US Open run, she brushed off the criticism she had faced while recovering from injury. Wu, Bu and Zheng grew up in different circumstances and have developed entirely different relationships with competition and public life. From afar, they can appear as a cohort, their names accompanied by the same flag on the scoreboard. Up close, they are nothing like one another. One player inspires strangers to yell a pun on his name. Another leaves spectators wondering where in China he could possibly be from. A third reminds me of the women I grew up around. Then the point begins, and each must figure out alone what to do with the ball.

title: Manchester City ready to fight Premier League after reports club guilty of 100-plus charges
description: Report says City found guilty of 114 financial rule breaches spanning more than a decade; club have always denied ⁠any wrongdoing.
content: Manchester City plan to fight the Premier League for months if found guilty of alleged financial breaches in potentially the biggest scandal in English football history. Reports on Friday said an independent panel had upheld nearly all of the 100-plus financial charges against the club in a case that was initiated more than three years ago. City did not confirm the decision, saying their case with the Premier League was “ongoing”. City, however, would appeal against a guilty decision and the process would take several months, a person with knowledge of the situation said. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to respect confidentiality elements of the process. The Athletic first reported that City had been found guilty of all but one of more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League, which accused the club in February 2023 of providing misleading information about their finances over a nine-year period from 2009 to 2018. The report said the sanctions have not been decided and all possibilities remain open. The BBC also reported the story. In response, City said in a statement: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed and subject to strict confidentiality.” City added that their position “remains consistent” with previous comments about the case. The club have always denied the charges. “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years,” City said, “on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.” City’s punishment could be a huge points deduction, and as extreme as expulsion from the Premier League. When contacted on Friday, the Premier League said it could not comment on the reports. City have always protested their innocence after supposed leaked emails and documents, probably hacked, were published starting in 2018 by German magazine Der Spiegel. The documents allegedly showed City tried to mask the source of revenue from deals tied to Abu Dhabi, whose ruling family bought the club in 2008 and has overseen the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars on some of the world’s best players over the following two decades. City have been the most dominant team in England over the past 15 years, winning eight Premier League titles since 2012 as well as the Champions League in 2023. Over the period in question – 2009 to 2018 – City won the league three times, in 2012, 2014 and 2018. Friday’s news comes after Pep Guardiola stood down as City manager at the end of last season following an unprecedented period of success. Guardiola always maintained the club’s innocence. “What people accuse us of, we do not agree with what they say,” he said in 2023. And Spain midfielder Rodri, who played for City from 2019 until leaving this off season for Barcelona, said he still believed the club had done nothing wrong. “They always expressed the confidence that they never did something wrong, and we believe in that. That’s the thing,” Rodri said of City’s ownership. “Until the moment they are proved wrong, we believe in the club. I’ve been there, I know how they work and how they cooperate.” Speaking at Wembley Stadium on Friday night the day before Spain plays England in the Nations League, Rodri said nobody would be able to take away City’s recent titles. “It is something that is not paid by money; it is paid with effort, with partnership and with being shoulder to shoulder every day,” he said. “We had a lot of success over the years, and here in Wembley, so I can tell you everything was deserved and I’m glad I could live through one of the best eras of English football.” Former Manchester United and England player Rio Ferdinand suggested City’s titles should be expunged and awarded to the runner-up for each season in question. “Another premier league medal to be added to the cabinet,” he posted on X in reference to City’s 2012 title win over United. The Premier League competition has had financial fair play rules designed to ensure clubs essentially spend what they earn from deals that are assessed to determine if they are at legitimate market value. City had previously been accused by Uefa, European football’s governing body, of overstating sponsorship revenue to comply with Financial Fair Play (FFP) regulations. In 2020, Uefa ruled City had committed “serious breaches” of FFP regulations from 2012 to 2016. But a two-year ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport because allegations were either rejected or found to have happened too long ago to be investigated. The Premier League charges came subsequently, after a four-year investigation. City were accused of more than 100 breaches, including providing misleading information about their finances and failure to cooperate with the investigation.

title: How Hong Kong firms are future-proofing business in challenging times
description: Swire Coca-Cola is among firms leveraging AI and other cutting-edge technologies to drive growth and navigate economic headwinds.
content: Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises. Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy. The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”. Swire Coca-Cola’s mainland plants are also using AI-powered robots that can make decisions and adapt to changing operating conditions as they pick and sort heavy, shrink-wrapped loads of drinks from pallets at high speed – a breakthrough in the labour-intensive industry. These were some of the cutting-edge technologies Swire Coca-Cola had piloted on the mainland to transform its business, while looking to scale them to other provinces and even to Southeast Asia through and in Hong Kong, chief executive Karen So told the South China Morning Post. “Due to our geographic coverage, we’re exposed to many geopolitical risk factors which we have to manage,” So said, adding that one of the most obvious recent impacts had been rising raw material costs, including those of aluminium and sugar. “We have to stay very vigilant. Overall, we’ve had to make sure our brand and operations stay relevant in the past few decades to mitigate our external risks,” she said. The company, which started business in 1965, is now the fifth-largest Coca-Cola bottling partner in the world. As Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan sets out the blueprint for the city’s economic upgrade, businesses like Swire Coca-Cola are working to future-proof themselves against geopolitical headwinds and compete in an increasingly challenging environment. City leader John Lee Ka-chiu last week urged Hongkongers and businesses to adopt a long-term vision, saying enterprises had to stay competitive even as the government rolled out measures to cultivate new growth drivers for the city. “While the government works hard, business operators need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said. An uneven economic recovery Hong Kong’s economy has powered ahead in recent months, with merchandise exports hitting record highs on the back of overseas demand for AI-related products. The government has consequently upgraded its 2026 full-year economic forecast to 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent, from an earlier projection of 2.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent. Despite the stronger overall performance, streets are dotted with shuttered shops while retailers and restaurant operators continue to struggle. In a high-profile warning, real estate advocacy group Momentum 107 said the sharp decline in shop values in recent years had rapidly eroded the pool of available capital, undermining confidence in investment and consumption. It noted that shop prices had fallen by more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, while the overall vacancy rate had reached a 40-year high of 12.5 per cent in late 2025. The retail and food and catering sectors have also been hit by the continuing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border to spend their leisure time and money. Meanwhile, inflation has been on the rise. After war broke out in the Middle East on February 28 and triggered a global oil crisis, the city’s inflation rate jumped from 1.1 per cent year on year in January to 1.7 per cent in February and has hovered above 1.7 per cent as of August. ‘Companies are forced to change’ Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that looking solely at struggling high-street shops overlooked the bigger picture, as high-value sectors such as professional services and finance continued to drive the economy. However, consumer-facing sectors are undergoing structural shifts as mainland competitors catch up and local consumers spend more elsewhere. “Hong Kong’s local consumption market is relatively small, so retail and catering suffer from northbound spending and changing habits,” Yuen said. “Conversely, high-end services, technology and finance are holding up strong. But across the board, businesses rely heavily on international trade and foreign clients, leaving them exposed to global geopolitical frictions.” Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank and executive director of its Public Policy Institute, said companies faced three main challenges – high operating costs, disruption to global supply chains and geopolitical risks and barriers to technological transformation caused by shortages of funding and skilled workers. He said Hong Kong’s rents, wages and logistics costs were relatively high, placing pressure on companies’ cash flow, while AI was creating another divide. Large corporations often had money to invest but struggled to integrate new technology with legacy systems and secure cooperation across departments. While smaller businesses could be more agile, they frequently lacked capital and technical expertise. Shui cited a Productivity Council survey suggesting about 90 per cent of responding companies intended to increase their use of AI. The problem, he said, was not a lack of interest but uncertainty over how to turn that intention into practical transformation. “Many people think of technology or AI as something that can help companies reduce costs and save money,” he said. “But what is more important is how they can use AI to upgrade and transform themselves, innovate their business models or open up new markets.” Hong Kong appeared to be performing relatively well in adoption. Shui cited a survey by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology that found that about 72 to 73 per cent of respondents used AI at work daily or weekly, compared with a global average of around 30 per cent. Another study put AI adoption among Hong Kong firms at about 41 per cent compared with less than 30 per cent in Singapore, he said. But widespread use did not mean that companies were applying the technology effectively. Shui said the ideal outcome was “human-machine collaboration,” in which AI performed repetitive research, data processing and preliminary analysis, while employees devoted more time to decision-making and setting the company’s direction. “If your competitor is already doing this while you are making very limited use of AI, it will be very difficult to catch up,” he said. “This is something that many companies and employees will need to learn.” Yuen echoed this view, saying that true AI adoption required a complete overhaul of corporate workflows rather than superficial daily tasks. “The real productivity boost from AI isn’t just using it to write an email or draft a report – it comes when companies reshape their entire workflow from top to bottom,” Yuen said, comparing the current transition with earlier technological shifts such as the invention of the printing press, personal computers and the internet. “Legacy businesses face a dilemma because changing established processes while serving existing clients carries risk. It could take eight to 10 years for industries to truly integrate AI into their bottom line,” she added. Shui said Hong Kong needed a coherent AI development blueprint and stronger cooperation between the government, universities and industry. The planned Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute could provide a platform through which companies test applications, academics provide expertise and the government coordinates resources. Transform, transform and transform In Swire Coca-Cola’s case, So said transformation was robust across mindsets, strategies and business practices, pointing out that the 61-year-old business had in recent years embarked on a sweeping revolution. “The future of our business lies in moving from reactive, manual operations towards proactive, data-driven ecosystems that respond to modern consumer habits,” she said. The company’s “suggested order” system in Jiangsu province produced 20 per cent higher monthly sales volumes during a year-long pilot that ended earlier this year. She said it would be gradually rolled out to other markets, but conceded that it would take time for staff to get used to the AI tool. “Our employees need time to adapt to tools designed to change how they make decisions and approach customers,” So said. The project forms a key part of a transformation at Swire Coca-Cola, whose franchise bottling and distribution operations reach more than 940 million consumers across the western United States, 11 mainland Chinese provinces and Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taiwan and four Southeast Asian countries. The company’s transformation became more complicated as it expanded beyond its two main markets – Greater China and the US – into Southeast Asia. It acquired Coca-Cola bottling businesses in Cambodia in 2022, in Vietnam in 2023 and in Thailand and Laos the following year. “When we acquired businesses from local operators of Coca-Cola in Southeast Asia, they had their respective enterprise resource planning systems,” So said. “We faced a challenge but also an opportunity to form a consistent operating system.” Even basic data definitions varied among markets, including what constituted a home market sales channel and how revenue was calculated. The company had to clean up and standardise the information before it could perform reliable analysis to improve the decision-making process and help salespeople make more targeted calls. “The data alignment will take two to three years,” So said. Another tool transferred from the mainland to Southeast Asia was the smart cooler – a drinks refrigerator which customers unlock using an electronic payment code. Scales and cameras identify which drinks are removed and customers are charged accordingly. “The solution adapts technology and operating concepts proven in mainland China to the Hong Kong market, which combines digital payment and product-recognition capabilities to offer a seamless cashless purchasing experience,” So said. In Hong Kong, the group has deployed 120 coolers across a broad mix of locations including sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings. So said the company aimed to replace traditional vending machines with these smart coolers. Swire Coca-Cola’s regional expansion has also helped Chinese suppliers go global. Baosteel, China’s biggest listed steelmaker and a supplier of aluminium cans to Swire Coca-Cola on the mainland, established a factory in Ho Chi Minh City as the company expanded its presence there. “It is a win-win situation – we have a stable supply of aluminium cans while Baosteel expands out of China for the first time,” So said. “Hong Kong is where our ambition is set and our global system is run. A purpose-built solution developed in the Chinese mainland, and now ready to scale across the global markets we serve, shows the super value-added, superconnector role Hong Kong is positioned to play.” Shui said Hong Kong could also turn the technological rivalry between China and the West into an opportunity by developing a “dual-model” environment in which businesses could access systems from both sides. “Hong Kong has always been a bridge connecting mainland China with the rest of the world,” he said. “If both systems can be used here, companies coming to Hong Kong can choose the tools that best meet their needs or potentially use both.” To raise efficiency and reduce manpower, Swire Coca-Cola has teamed up with a Hangzhou-based tech company, Seth Robotics, to develop its own AI-powered solution for its bottling plant in Zhengzhou, Henan province. The plants boasts the world’s first AI-powered intelligent picking-and-sorting robot, according to So. Capable of picking 600 pallets of drinks an hour with 100 per cent accuracy in executing orders, and handling loads as heavy as 40kg, the robot works at twice the speed of manual labour. “Normally after the first hour of work, workers need to take a rest. The robotic deployment will enhance efficiency and minimise any work-related injuries of workers, too,” So said. She added that Swire Coca-Cola’s technology development also showed what a Hong Kong-headquartered company could contribute to embodied intelligence. Against the backdrop of these operational investments, the group reported solid financial results for the first half of the year – net profit rose 5.35 per cent to HK$846 million (US$107.9 million) while revenue increased 8.36 per cent to HK$23.3 billion, compared with the same period last year. Yet, as economist Vera Yuen noted, the rising cost of uncertainty left businesses with little choice but to adapt their models or risk falling behind. Ultimately, she said, the question was no longer simply whether companies adopted new technology, but whether they could restructure their core operations to deliver genuine value to consumers.

title: China’s biotech firms move up value chain as drug deals evolve beyond licensing: analysts
description: InnoCare’s pact with Eli Lilly, potentially worth up to US$3.35 billion, highlights a shift towards bigger partnerships, analysts say.
content: Chinese biotech deal making is moving beyond the licensing of individual drug candidates, as the country transforms from a follower to a global innovation leader, according to analysts. The latest transaction underscores that shift. Beijing-based cancer drug developer InnoCare Pharma said on Thursday that it had entered into a strategic research collaboration and licensing agreement with US pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly that could be worth up to US$3.35 billion. InnoCare said it would use its drug discovery platform to identify and advance compounds against up to five targets. The companies did not disclose the specific therapeutic areas covered by their partnership, saying only that the new drugs would seek to “address critical unmet medical needs”. China’s biotech sector had shifted from “speed-driven replication to differentiated innovation”, said Cui Cui, head of Asia healthcare research at Jefferies, in a research note on Thursday. The transition was fuelling expectations that more globally significant drug-development partnerships would originate from the country, Cui added, citing private discussions at the investment bank’s APAC Healthcare Conference in Shanghai earlier this week. Many Chinese biotech companies initially relied on out-licensing to fund their pipelines, a model in which a developer sells the rights to an early-stage drug candidate to another company, which then undertakes global development and commercialisation. However, as their resources and ambitions expanded, companies had increasingly moved towards co-development arrangements and broader platform partnerships, Cui said. The InnoCare deal would see Eli Lilly pay US$100 million up front, with the Chinese biotech firm eligible for up to US$3.25 billion in development and commercialisation milestone payments, InnoCare said in a statement on Thursday. It would also receive “single-digit tiered royalties” based on annual net product sales. The figures reflect the rising quantity and quality of China’s innovative drug research Jialin Zhang, Nomura Recent deals, including Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceutical’s collaboration and licensing agreement with US pharmaceutical giant Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) worth up to US$15.2 billion, also showed how quickly Chinese biotech companies were broadening their approach to global deal making, Cui said. BMS in May committed US$600 million in upfront payments to Hengrui – China’s largest drug maker by market capitalisation – to advance 13 early-stage programmes spanning oncology, haematology and immunology. Five of those assets would be jointly developed using Hengrui’s discovery platforms. Chinese research accounted for 29 of the 96 late-breaking abstracts scheduled for presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology (Esmo) Congress 2026, which will be held in Madrid in late October, said Jialin Zhang, head of China healthcare research at Nomura, in a report on Wednesday. They included five of the 12 studies selected for the prestigious presidential symposium. The figures reflected the “rising quantity and quality of China’s innovative drug research”, Zhang said.

title: Reflections | When centuries of Chinese knowledge were destroyed by a warlord who burned the capital
description: Xiang Yu’s razing of the Qin capital Xianyang, which left libraries full of vital texts in ruin, was echoed centuries later in Warsaw.
content: Before I went to Warsaw, I knew little of the city beyond the fact that it was Poland’s capital. I had not realised that much of present-day Warsaw, including its beautiful historic centre, was rebuilt after World War II. Warsaw’s wartime destruction was not merely the consequence of battle, but a deliberate campaign by its Nazi German occupiers to erase much of the city. In August 1944, the Warsaw Uprising – a Polish armed revolt by the city’s underground resistance against German occupation – began with the aim of liberating Warsaw. German forces fought to crush it, subjecting the city to sustained bombardment. When the uprising was finally suppressed after nine weeks, the surviving population was expelled, with tens of thousands of Poles sent to concentration camps. The emptied city was then systematically destroyed. German demolition units moved through Warsaw, wrecking or blowing up buildings that had survived the fighting. Churches, palaces, schools, theatres, libraries and historic monuments were reduced to rubble. By January 1945, almost 90 per cent of the city’s buildings had been destroyed. The cultural losses were particularly devastating. Libraries containing centuries of Polish manuscripts, books, maps and other collections were deliberately burned, while countless works of art and historical records vanished. Warsaw was left in ruins, its historic centre a smouldering pile of debris. The destruction was driven by a calculated ruthlessness that remains difficult to comprehend. Adolf Hitler and Heinrich Himmler’s Order for Warsaw, which stands among the war’s most chilling documents, reads: “Every citizen of Warsaw is to be killed including men, women and children. Warsaw has to be levelled to the ground in order to set a terrifying example to the rest of Europe.” Yet Warsaw was unbowed. In the decades after the German surrender and the end of the war, the city undertook an extraordinary reconstruction, drawing on photographs, plans, surviving records and even paintings to restore much of what had been lost. In the lean post-war years, the Poles could have cleared the rubble and built anew in steel and concrete, which would have been an easier, cheaper option. Instead, they chose the far more arduous task of reconstructing what had been destroyed. Today, Warsaw’s rebuilt historic centre is a Unesco World Heritage site, recognised as an exceptional achievement in the restoration of lost cultural heritage and a powerful symbol of national resilience. Warsaw was not the first great city whose destruction threatened to erase a people’s memory. More than 2,000 years earlier, a similar catastrophe unfolded at Xianyang, the capital of the Qin dynasty. When the warlord Xiang Yu vanquished the Qin in 206BC, he set Xianyang ablaze. The fire, which burned for three months, consumed far more than palaces and buildings; it also destroyed a vast store of knowledge from the centuries before China’s imperial unification. Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of the Qin, is remembered for his burning of books, yet important texts had survived. While the general population was prohibited from owning books, works on medicine, agriculture and philosophy were preserved in the libraries of the Qin palaces. These collections were more than books: they were a civilisation’s intellectual memory. When Xianyang burned, these works disappeared with it. The conflagration also consumed official records from the states conquered by Qin – chronicles, maps and administrative documents recording centuries of history. With these first-hand sources gone, later generations were left to reconstruct much of China’s ancient history from fragments and recollections. Whether it was the fire lit by Xiang Yu and his men more than 2,000 years ago or the Nazis’ methodical destruction of Warsaw in 1944, the human capacity for senseless destruction remains undiminished. This heart of darkness – to borrow the title of Polish-born writer Joseph Conrad’s novel – continues to cast its malignant shadow over the world.

title: Xi-Trump atmospherics welcomed but mask structural rifts: analysts
description: That two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability with caveats.
content: During their three-day summit that ended on Friday, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping worked overtime to underscore their increasingly close relationship even as the meeting produced few concrete deliverables. But the fact that the two economic and military giants are talking – and pledging to talk some more – suggests some period of relative stability ahead, certainly relative to last year’s all-out trade war, chest-thumping and market turmoil, said analysts, companies and former US officials. “Both countries are demonstrating some degree of restraint,” said Sara Schuman, managing director at consultancy Beacon Global Strategies and a former US diplomat in Beijing. “The optics that President Xi is travelling to Washington and he’s receiving a full state visit with a state dinner, this is in itself the core deliverable.” By that definition, the visit was chock full. Xi said the two leaders were “making history” with two summits in four months and two more meet-ups planned, one in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and another the following month at the G20 Trump is hosting in Miami. And Xi spent the Mid-Autumn Festival outside China, only the second time during his near 14-year administration he has done so. Trump, for his part, greeted Xi in person when he arrived at the airport, a role usually reserved for lower-level officials and a courtesy that the Chinese president did not extend to Trump when he landed in Beijing in May. Both leaders also spent the 42-hour visit implicitly or explicitly framing China as an equal or near-equal global power, outlining the “great promise” of the bilateral relationship built on “mutual trust”, foreshadowing “a truly great friendship” like a “river that never stops flowing” as they “steer the giant ship of China-US relations steadily forward towards the future”. No mention of rare earth minerals stand-off Unspoken was the hugely consequential cudgel China has unsheathed: its global grip on rare earth minerals, which has fundamentally shifted the power balance after Trump pushed Beijing to the wall, threatening tariffs in excess of 125 per cent during last year’s “Liberation Day”. Add China’s accelerated bid to diversify its trade dependence on US markets, its increasingly competitive artificial intelligence industry and its dominant position in electric vehicles, lithium batteries and renewable technologies, and it is not difficult to understand Beijing’s growing confidence. Since then, Beijing has negotiated a trade truce with the US, which was extended this week until January 10; seen the transactional US president reframe Taiwan and high-end semiconductors as negotiable; forestalled a planned US$14 billion arms package to Taipei; pushed away US threats to sanction Chinese banks and refineries for bypassing Washington’s Iran sanctions and watched as greater distance opened between Washington and such long-time allies as Japan and South Korea. “This is Xi Jinping’s world, and we’re all living in it,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). “The administration’s China strategy was poorly designed from the beginning. They thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, and that did not occur. In fact, the opposite did.” Time and relative stability afford China more time to develop its increasingly successful trade strategy, allow Beijing to focus on its domestic economy rather than respond to erratic tariff gyrations, and see Washington increasingly distracted by Trump’s war of choice in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and his record-low popularity leading into the November midterm election. Missing Chinese holidays, travelling repeatedly to the US by a president whose trips are carefully calibrated, displaying keen interest in Trump’s new helipad and supporting his bid to rebrand AI as “Super Intelligence”, expressing warmth hardly instinctual in China’s more austere political culture and making favourable references to Trump’s “make America great again” mantra may be a small price to pay. “China has flexed its muscle, established its ability to counterstrike and the credibility of its retaliation,” said Yun Sun, China director at the Simson Centre. “Xi Jinping will visit Washington any day to be the peer of his US counterpart.” In addition to the two-month trade truce extension, the week’s modest, more conventional deliverables included a likely Board of Trade deal involving reciprocal trade carve-outs subject to reduced tariffs that is likely to include some combination of “non-strategic” farm products, apparel, consumer electronics and other manufactured goods. Details are due out on Monday. But analysts also said the increasingly frequent meetings between Xi and Trump, who favours in-person negotiations unencumbered by extensive planning or expert input, make it difficult to expect the sort of big-dollar deals and structural reforms that often took years of intensive negotiation under past US administrations. Warm “friendship” at the very top also masks underlying seams, analysts said. Hawks on both sides quietly resist ostensibly closer ties. Important lower-level channels across the Pacific have winnowed as both presidents pared down officials in the military and broader bureaucracy. And growing competition and rivalry leave deep reservoirs of distrust. The lack of written agreements also lays the groundwork for misunderstanding. “There’s been so much miscommunication or differing perceptions from both sides coming out of these summits,” said Emily Kilcrease, senior fellow at the Centre for a New American Security and a former senior US Trade Representative negotiator. “Given how low the trust is between these two countries, it’s really important that people know who their counterparts are and can call them when there’s a crisis.” US visit helps Xi-Trump bromance to blossom Framing the budding Trump-Xi bromance are more than a few similarities, analysts said. Both believe they are battling “deep state” bureaucratic resistance. Both enjoy the pomp and pageantry of their power. Both believe their economic model is superior, that their AI and technology will win out. And both face domestic economic challenges. “When you see Xi Jinping and Donald Trump together, each of them believes that time is on their side,” said Edgard Kagen, a CSIS senior adviser and former political chief with the US Embassy in Beijing. “The US [believes it] will develop alternative sources of critical minerals and rare earths, and so time is on the US side. When Xi Jinping sits down with Donald Trump, he very much believes the US is in a hurtling decline and the time is on China’s side.” “Neither of them has an interest, at least at this point, in an escalation on trade issues.” Two more presidential meetings this year are likely to help maintain bilateral stability. They are also likely to push off any Taiwan arms package. But the prospect of Trump alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at both – Moscow’s representative attended the two-day G20 Finance Ministers meeting in North Carolina starting August 31, and Putin is expected in Shenzhen – could further weaken traditional US alliances, some said. “Trump continues to berate many of our closest allies, from Canada to Europe to Korea to Japan. At the same time, when he meets with US adversaries, usually he says relatively nice things,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and a former National Security Council official. “That message would be heard loud and clear, and it will just further accelerate the drive from a lot of US allies to decrease their reliance on the United States. And it may embolden Russia and China to test those alliances even more.” With so much at stake, experts say, the test will be whether this week’s atmospherics lead to longer-term equilibrium or a return to instability. “You can have a state visit, respectful rhetoric, a very good dinner, while both governments continue to build tools to compete with each other the next day,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Federation for the Defence of Democracies and a former US diplomat. “I don’t expect a reset in US-China relations. I do not expect a grand bargain on trade. I don’t expect Washington and Beijing to resolve their technology competition, economic security disputes, or any fundamental disagreement over Taiwan.” “It’s a summit about managing stalemate, not resolving it.”

title: Improved Zhang Zhanshuo, rising Yu Zidi headline China’s swimming hopes for 2028 Olympics
description: Five-gold winner Li Bingjie also strong contender as influx of young swimmers cuts workload for decorated swimmers Zhang Yufei, Qin Haiyang.
content: The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games may only be halfway through, but the swimmers checked out of the Tokyo Aquatics Centre on Friday. An extended rest was probably too much of a luxury for most of them with the Swimming World Cup just around the corner. A trio of three-day meets in Baku, Tashkent and Astana from the start of next month will also act as qualifiers for the short course World Aquatics Swimming Championships, which run in Beijing from December 1 to 6. Four swimmers, two each from Japan and China, swept the MVP accolades from the past three editions of the Asian Games in Incheon, Jakarta and Hangzhou, and it would be a major surprise if this trend were not to continue. China’s Zhang Zhanshuo and Li Bingjie – who won 12 gold medals between them in Tokyo – are the obvious favourites to take the awards this time. It is therefore an opportune moment to take a look at the Chinese contingent and get an idea of who is expected to head to Los Angeles in two years and to flourish there. While the world has already seen what Yu Yiting and, in particular, Yu Zidi are capable of, onlookers and rivals should prepare themselves for a completely different Zhang. Having put behind him a disappointing Olympic debut in Paris, where he failed to progress from the heats of all three individual events, teenager Zhang Zhanshuo appears to have reached a new level. Last November, he won five gold medals at the National Games, and he followed that up this week with a record-breaking haul at the regional Games. Having entered eight events and swum 4,000 metres over six days in the Japanese capital, Zhang walked away with seven gold medals, breaking the previous record of six at one edition jointly held by compatriot Zhang Yufei in 2023 and Rikako Ikee of Japan in 2018. Zhang’s ability to dominate distances from 200m to 1,500m has made him a new swimming icon, and he has also been a reliable teammate in the relays. Possessing a blend of explosive power and endurance, as well as speed and stability, the Shandong native has completely shattered the public’s preconceived notions about freestyle swimmers. The only title he missed out on was the 100m freestyle, a non-speciality event for him. Nevertheless, he achieved a personal best time of 48.23 seconds, finishing fourth behind compatriot Pan Zhanle and South Korean pair Kim Young-beom and Hwang Sun-woo. A particular highlight of the past week was the men’s 4x200m freestyle final, in which Pan and Zhang overcame a 3.47-second deficit in the final two legs to overtake Japan and set an Asian record of seven minutes and 0.17 seconds. Team China had trailed by 1.89 seconds when Zhang took the final leg, but won by almost a second in the end. Perhaps two-time Olympic champion Pan summed it up best when he said: “I found his abilities to be exceptional – powerful to a level that is truly beyond the ordinary. He told us before the race that we didn’t need to worry because he knows how to handle his own business. “He really is the wonder kid; there’s always a miracle in his final leg. Zhang is an individual event champion with the longest arm reach. It’s a combination of all favourable circumstances that placed him in the final position.” While the presence of Pan and Zhang has undoubtedly made China competitive in freestyle, the women’s squad seem to flourish in every swim style. Li Bingjie remains the undisputed queen of the long-distance freestyle events in the region, while also showing her value as a teammate in the shorter relays. The 24-year-old from Hebei won all five events she entered in Tokyo, including dominating the 400m, 800m and 1,500m events in back-to-back Asian Games. Then there were Wu Qingfeng and Tang Qianting, with the latter claiming gold in both the 50m and 100m breaststroke in game-record times. Wan Letian, 22, and Peng Xuwei, 23, also helped China win all three backstroke gold medals. The influx of young Chinese swimmers has naturally reduced the workload of a couple of the country’s most decorated swimmers. Hangzhou Games MVPs Zhang Yufei and Qin Haiyang, who won a combined total of 11 gold and one silver medal in 2023, halved the number of individual events they competed in compared with three years ago, with each swimmer competing in only two events, plus relays. Zhang, 28, delivered in the women’s 4x100m freestyle and medley relays, as well as the mixed 4x100m medley relay, while adding a 50m butterfly gold on the final day to go with a silver in the 100m butterfly, when she finished just 0.03 seconds behind her teammate Yu Yiting, who is seven years her junior. Qin, 27, had a similar mixed experience of team success and personal setback until he touched the wall first in the 50m breaststroke final in 26.68 seconds on the last day of the swimming competition. Nevertheless, Zhang Yufei and Qin are still expected to be the two leading figures in the Chinese swimming team when they head to Los Angeles in the summer of 2028. However, it is possible that, at 30 and 29 years old, respectively, they will focus less on individual events and more on the relays, just as Zhang did when she chose not to defend her 200m butterfly medal, which was won by Yu Zidi in a Games record on the first day. “I hope that, after switching to a new training regimen, I can achieve a time at the Asian Games that I’m satisfied with – one that makes me feel I’ve still got what it takes,” Zhang said before departing for the Asian Games.

title: Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
description: Viral misbehaviour, crimes and foreign-ownership scandals are exhausting the patience of a country famous for its hospitality.
content: At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles. Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand. The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared. Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya. The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists. Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance. Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since. “We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.” By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”. The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism. Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record. Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back. The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia. Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia. Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin. Misbehaving tourists Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners. But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them. Each post gets shared and reshared until the obvious disrespect for a proud local culture starts to sour public opinion on the costs of welcoming millions of strangers every year. “Thai people are pragmatic. We do like the money [tourism brings],” said Voranai Vanijaka, a prominent political and social commentator. “But at the same time, we are highly nationalistic and we don’t like tourists acting the fool.” This year alone, tourists have been caught performing sex acts in public, assaulting locals, trespassing on private property and vandalising local landmarks. Recent crackdowns have also revealed dozens of bars and restaurants run by foreigners but masquerading as Thai-owned enterprises. Other crimes are far more grave. In June, Australian national Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested on suspicion of murdering a teenage Thai girl, stuffing her body into a suitcase and disposing of it in the undergrowth near Pattaya. Authorities have separately uncovered Chinese and Korean cyberscam operators holed up in luxury villas, an Indian national flaunting firearms on social media and a steady stream of British cannabis mules. All the while, public attitudes against foreigners have been hardening – a sentiment Voranai said had also been fuelled by global nativist trends, nationalism stirred up by the recent border conflict with Cambodia and grievances over foreign nationals buying up land and businesses. “There is an anti-foreigner, anti-immigrant feeling sweeping the world; it’s not just in Thailand,” he said, describing a “mood and tone” within which every viral episode of misbehaviour now played out, and a “lower tolerance” for such actions. The steady drumbeat of bad news pushed Thailand to end its 60-day visa-free stays for tourists from September 15. Days later, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters he thought misbehaving foreigners had “gone too far”. Not for the first time, Thailand has said it will step back from playing the numbers game to focus on attracting fewer, higher-spending tourists instead. Officials describe 2027 as “the year of transformation”, aiming to attract wealthier travellers willing to stay a week or two at a time. A proposed flat fee of 450 baht (US$13.50) on all foreign visitors to fund tourism infrastructure upgrades is also being actively considered. But this soul-searching over who Thailand wants to welcome, and for how long, comes as hotel bookings during the current low season have disappointed and as travellers appear to be waiting until the last minute to book their stays in the crucial high season that begins in November. On the upside, Thai tourism authorities are anticipating 200,000 Chinese tourist arrivals during next month’s “golden week” holiday from October 1 to 7, just as a the baht’s recent retreat is offering travellers better value. Against this uncertain backdrop, Charoon’s crocodile farm has enjoyed something of social media-spurred revival. In its 1980s heyday, when his father welcomed dignitaries including Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, the business made headlines for encounters with reptiles that visitors elsewhere might only see behind glass. But as the novelty of live-animal shows began to wear off and tastes changed, the zoo’s weekday crowds thinned to a trickle. Then, in late August, a TikTok video showing a single visitor sitting alone in the stands at one of the zoo’s elephant shows found an audience all of its own, garnering more than 1 million likes and sending a flood of visitors streaming back through gates. “I was shocked. I didn’t expect that. I never thought one video could communicate to so many people,” Charoon said. “People are coming in their thousands. I just hope they keep coming.” Show respect, or go Thailand is far from alone in pausing to reconsider its relationship with visitors. In Indonesia’s Bali, a foreign-led running club accused of barring locals from taking part suspended operations this summer; in Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks held a violent protest outside a newly opened Jewish community centre known as a Chabad house last month, questioning its legality; and in Vietnam, authorities have vowed zero tolerance for foreign misconduct after recent drunken rampages and a deadly shooting linked to foreign nationals. Social media, as ever, amplifies both the insults delivered and how they are received. One Phuket business owner, who asked not to be named to protect his livelihood, told This Week in Asia that the types of tourists now visiting Thailand were more entitled, demanding unreasonable discounts and firing off insults at the slightest whiff of not getting their own way. “I don’t think Thais are xenophobic,” he said. “But my mindset has changed, like a lot of people on Phuket. Customers are customers, but if they’re not nice and don’t respect the culture and the people, we are happy to see them go.” This change in public sentiment appears to have influenced the government’s decision to halve the 60-day visa free-entry. It has also produced unusually blunt warnings from ministers who normally pull their punches when addressing foreign embassies. In August, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told the Chinese ambassador to “come out and explain” when sensitive issues arise “instead of speaking only to protect Chinese interests” – remarks that followed a viral confrontation between Chinese passengers and Thai officials at Bangkok’s main airport. His comments also came amid mounting evidence of Chinese nationals illegally owning land and companies in Thailand, in some cases via officials bribed with as little as 500 baht to issue fraudulent birth certificates conferring land-ownership rights. A small but vocal protest movement against official corruption and the influence of so-called grey money has since emerged, fronted by veteran conservative agitator Sondhi Limthongkul, who has rallied tens of thousands to take to the streets in the past. Prime Minister Anutin, who himself rode a wave of nationalist sentiment to victory in February’s election, has responded to the backlash by fast-tracking deportations of foreign criminals and opening a wider investigation into “nominee” arrangements that allow foreign business owners to hide behind Thais. Chinese, French, British, Indian and Russian nationals have all come under scrutiny, but it has been Israeli nationals – many of them military-aged and arriving in the wake of the war in Gaza – who have attracted the most intense attention, accused of building extensive “nominee”-business networks across southern Thai islands and of operating an illegal cemetery in Chachoengsao province. “This has gone too far,” Anutin told officials on September 17 in response to the outrage. “If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that. We have no objection whatsoever,” he said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here.” Anutin’s point man on the “nominee” scandal, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee, has since said he is investigating several Chabad houses across the country, warning that any found to have been built unlawfully could be torn down. Following a meeting with Thailand’s foreign minister earlier this month, Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm told local media that bad behaviour was not unique to citizens of her country, adding that Hebrew-language pre-departure awareness campaigns were being introduced outlining Thai laws and cultural norms. Nationalist commentators with large online followings have seized upon the anti-Israeli rhetoric, some veering into outright antisemitism. “There is a risk of this getting out of hand,” Voranai said, referring to growing anti-Israeli “paranoia” stoked by hardline conservatives chasing clicks and the political spotlight. Yet he doubts the swirling public anger will cost Anutin’s government much in the long run. “There is no risk to the government at all – except for bad press, which they don’t care about,” Voranai said. “Nor should they, they hold all the power and they can just ride it out.” Meet the neighbours Amid the blizzard of bad publicity, some are determined to build bridges between foreigners and their Thai hosts. John Ho, who was born and raised in Hong Kong but swapped a career in hospitality for a new life in Chiang Mai with his Thai wife a decade ago, this month launched CosmoLocal CNX – a government-backed “pop-up village” offering workshops, talks and communal meals to draw the Thai city’s digital-nomad population into closer contact with their Thai neighbours. “There’s a transitional period where you’re travelling as a tourist, when you may not care that much about the local culture and language,” Ho said. “But then, if you want to stay longer and set up a base, it naturally comes to a question of: ‘OK, let’s make friends’. It’s better to learn some Thai, and learn some of the laws around business and work.” His pop-up, which offers discounted tickets for Thai attendees to keep it accessible, trades on Chiang Mai’s slower pace of life, distinctive northern Lanna culture and small-town feel – qualities that have attracted legions of remote workers since the pandemic. It is a world away from the raucous party scene of Thailand’s southern islands, where many of the recent cultural clashes have occurred. “We see the tensions,” Ho said. “But the majority of nomads do care – maybe they need more facilitation to meet the locals. This is the first attempt to do that.” As for the seemingly endless churn of viral confrontations between Thais and foreigners? “News cycles are news cycles,” Ho said. “I think a lot of it is out of proportion. Everyone in Thailand welcomes foreigners.”

title: Q&A | From punk to Gothic: how Singapore’s Ask & Embla built a global jewellery brand
description: Ryan Gomes and Olivia Eleazar’s alternative aesthetics have found fans in celebrities from Teyana Taylor to Chappell Roan.
content: You’d likely never guess that a jewellery brand which leans into everything from punk rock aesthetics to Gothic art, and is worn by everyone from Teyana Taylor to Chappell Roan, is actually from Singapore. That brand is Ask & Embla, the brainchild of life and business partners Ryan Gomes and Olivia Eleazar, who started the brand in 2013 first by selling a curated edit of body jewellery products procured from other suppliers before Eleazar transitioned to creating her own designs. “I was 19 years old, listening to a lot of alternative music, and that shaped my world view,” says Eleazar, the brand’s creative director. “In 2018 or 2019 we started experimenting with our own styles – at that time [using] brass, now stainless steel and 925 silver – so we saw that anything Olivia designed would sell out almost immediately,” Gomes, the managing director, explains. Both Gomes and Eleazar worked full-time jobs outside of Ask & Embla until 2020, “when Covid hit and we decided to go all in designing everything.” Ask & Embla has skyrocketed ever since. Ahead, Gomes and Eleazar discuss how they built a global brand out of the little red dot that is Singapore. Ask & Embla’s look is totally different from mainstream brands in the Singapore market. What gave you confidence to lean into this alternative aesthetic in a place which can be quite conservative? Eleazar: Audacity [laughs]. I didn’t always have the confidence I have today. My mum started to see proof that I wasn’t just doing some lame project that was leading nowhere. Because we [initially] packed out of my house, our order volume got so big that I couldn’t just pack in my room any more. Envelopes spilled all over the floor, packing labels everywhere, and on one hand, she’s pissed that I made a mess, but on the other, she’s like, I’m proud of you guys. That first step was having audacity. Doing it scared. Tell me about the brand name. Eleazar: Ask & Embla means Adam and Eve in Norse mythology. The whole idea of Ask & Embla symbolises creation and duality. Duality can represent a balance between light and dark, masculine and feminine. All these forces that are not really opposites, but complementary, two sides to the same coin. The creative universe is influenced by, first, the world of all things Gothic. The second is mythology and the last is ethnology. We’re deeply inspired by things like beauty and darkness. That’s because I grew up Catholic and ironically the church is where I first encountered the idea of darkness. The church teaches you from a very early age the concept of heaven, angels and devils, coupled with all these beautiful visuals you see from either illustrations in the Bible or stained glass windows, that whole Gothic aesthetic. When I was a design intern in a branding company, I was tasked to brand a salad store and the owners really wanted something green, fresh, lush [laughs]. So I went down a Wikipedia rabbit hole and that’s how I got so nerdy about mythology, because I did this whole deep dive into the Garden of Eden as a concept [which] also exists by different names in other cultures. Could you speak more about the craftsmanship which goes into your pieces? Eleazar: I either sketch something or I explain what I’m seeing [to my team], and then we make 3D files, print it, send it to a supplier, sample and make moulds. It’s a very typical manufacturing process, but everything’s really tightly owned. We also pay attention to the material required for certain design details, stretch piercings, regular piercings. If it’s going to be a statement product larger than usual, is it still within the weight range that the ear can tolerate? Also, the price points. Those things are considered from the very start, when things aren’t even finalised and put in the box yet. Even from a sketch, we do think all the way to the end. What are the pros and cons of scaling a business from a tiny country like Singapore? Gomes: The biggest pro is that it’s super stable. During Covid, businesses around the world went through a difficult time figuring out how to navigate that. Singapore was one of the fastest [countries] to respond. All the support the government provided during that time was second to none. Even our positioning as a logistics hub is a huge deal as a small brand that’s trying to serve a global community. In recent years there are challenges with tariffs in the US and the EU, and oil prices going up. At the same time, going out of Singapore, it’s one of the best networks for flights.
