We work with small items, jewellery, so it’s quite easy versus if we were selling bags, for example, the shipping cost would be way more expensive. And being here allows us to be close to manufacturing hubs in Asia. Being Singaporean, we were brought up in a very disciplined environment and that naturally created our work ethic. We have no external funding, so it’s been bootstrapped from day one, and it required a tremendous amount of discipline to make that happen, and a great team. There is a decently-sized alternative community in Singapore, but most of them are individual creators doing their own thing. It’s not so easy to grow the team here working face to face, so we’ve been hiring from around the world. Where do most of your customers come from and do you rely on e-commerce? Gomes: Our orders have primarily come from the US – about 50-60 per cent of our revenue. The next best countries are the UK, Australia, Canada and the EU. We’re in the process of setting up a third-party warehouse in the EU so hopefully shipping will be much faster. We’ve been e-commerce all the way, just our own [site], up until this year. We launched our Tmall store to expand into Asia because most of our market has been [in] the West. Singapore is about 1 per cent of our business, actually, and the rest of Asia added up is about 3-5 per cent. We saw alternative [culture] is growing and it’s almost mainstream that people are expressing themselves with tattoos and jewellery. We saw that also in China. They have this whole subculture, yabi, and we were actually approached by Tmall to set up a store. We hope to launch our first physical store this year. The top candidate is London – time zone, language, community, all those boxes have been checked. What about the celebrities who wear your pieces? Which placement meant the most to you? Eleazar: Lisa from Blackpink. First, she’s huge, and second, she’s not part of the legacy audience you’d associate with Ask & Embla. That’s proof that the audience we’re acquiring is growing and appealing to people we call alt-curious. People who simply appreciate the attitude behind alternative style. It’s organic, not paid. What do you hope to see out of Singaporean brands in the future? Gomes: Many brands that come out of Singapore go into other categories like electronics. I’d love to see more creative fashion or lifestyle brands come out of Singapore. Many creatives end up going down the mainstream path. But if and when we become that kind of household name, people would believe they could do it, too.

title: Review | Anantara Siam Bangkok debuts a fresh look and Jim Thompson Suite
description: The 5-star urban sanctuary – on the site of the former Four Seasons, Peninsula and Regent – has unveiled an extensive redesign.
content: In 2015, Anantara Hotels & Resorts turned a building formerly occupied by the Four Seasons Bangkok into Anantara Siam Bangkok. Located in the city’s Ratchaprasong district, a stone’s throw from the famous Erawan Shrine, the structure – which dates back to 1983 and was designed by American architect George “Pete” Wimberly – has a long history housing luxury hotels, including the Peninsula in its first incarnation and later the Regent. More than 10 years after the most recent rebranding, Anantara completed a renovation of the rooms and common areas, turning the property into the de facto flagship of the Thai-based hospitality group. Established 25 years ago with the opening of Anantara Hua Hin, located a couple of hours away from Bangkok, Anantara Hotels & Resorts has become one of the world’s top luxury hotel chains. While it has an especially strong presence in Thailand and the rest of Asia, its properties span the globe, from the South of France to Rome. The much-overdue refurbishment of Anantara Siam Bangkok has stayed true to the building’s original design but modernised the space to meet the needs of modern-day luxury travellers. The common areas, for example, retain the same furniture, but every piece has been restored or reupholstered. The famous mural greeting guests at the entrance – painted on handwoven silk and depicting Thai cosmology – was touched up by the artist’s daughter. The meeting rooms and ballrooms – popular venues for weddings and other events – have been completely redone. Among the new additions is a podcast studio, available to rent for both digital nomads and local creators. The pool area – a green refuge in the middle of one of Asia’s busiest cities – received a major upgrade, as did the pool villas located on the same floor. If you want to experience the luxury hospitality Anantara resorts are known for but in an urban setting, book one of the newly added Garden Pool Villas and you’ll feel like you’re staying in one of the brand’s properties in Phuket or Koh Samui. With their outdoor gardens filled with lush vegetation, shaded patios with loungers and deckchairs, and private pools, the villas will make you forget you’re in the heart of Bangkok. There’s nothing like waking up to birdsong in the morning before heading out into the hustle and bustle of the city. Evoking a Thai summer residence, the Jim Thompson Suite marks a partnership between the hotel and the lifestyle company named after Thailand’s “silk king”, as the famous American was known back in the 1950s and 60s. Parichart Court, the open-air courtyard inside the hotel, still attracts a fashionable crowd of locals and tourists enjoying its popular venues – from Aqua Bar, where you can listen to jazz and have a drink amid koi ponds, to Madison Steak Avenue and Spice Market. Book the former if you fancy a feast of perfectly grilled meats in an atmosphere reminiscent of an old-school gentlemen’s club. Thai food reigns supreme at Spice Market, where chef Akkawin Pitrachart celebrates the best of the country’s cuisine with dishes such as Thai omelette with blue crab, spicy crab roe sauce and sriracha, and green curry slow-braised Angus beef cheek with baby eggplant. One of the most visited cities in the world, Bangkok has no shortage of out-of-this-world luxury properties, but if you’re looking for a city stay that also allows you to unwind and enjoy the utmost privacy, this grande dame of Thai luxury hospitality will definitely deliver and then some. The author stayed as a guest of Anantara Siam Bangkok.

title: Opinion | The porcupine dilemma: why US-China diplomacy is about distance, not deals
description: Xi and Trump’s latest summit shows the need for cooperation even as deep differences continue to shape ties between the two powers.
content: Arthur Schopenhauer’s classic parable of relationships may help us understand today’s China-US ties. The reclusive German philosopher famously described how wintering porcupines need to cluster together to survive the biting cold, but hurt one another with their quills if they get too close. In the end, the porcupines must learn to balance the need for shared warmth against the pain of pricking each other. Chinese President Xi Jinping received an unprecedentedly lavish reception from Donald Trump this week – one that would make America’s staunchest allies envious. On his second state visit to the US, a first for a Chinese president, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan schmoozed with the American first couple like old friends. Both presidents heaped praise on one another and pledged to do more to further the friendship of the two peoples. They will meet again in Shenzhen and Miami before the year is out: three presidential summits in four months set another record. Yet the warmth between the two leaders could not conceal the tensions sizzling beneath. The fact that the two sides only agreed to extend the truce in their costly trade war by two more months, after an unscheduled, eleventh-hour negotiation ahead of the summit, is telling. Expectations for any breakthrough on critical minerals or chip controls are low. Observers also doubt whether Washington is willing to fundamentally shift its policy on Taiwan, even though Trump did postpone an approved arms sale and was careful about public comments on the issue, mindful of Beijing’s sensitivities. To some, the three-day summit seemed heavy on pageantry but light on substance. One former US diplomat called it “theatrical pageantry” that “papered over real problems”. Yet often in diplomacy – and especially in this case – form is substance. Protocols and rituals function in human society as a way of setting the right distance. It is unrealistic to expect the two sides to reach any substantial breakthrough, given the sharp spikes these two “porcupines” carry on their backs. While Xi was given the highest honours by his host, the trip was overshadowed by domestic American political turmoil and Trump’s feud with the mainstream media. Most Americans saw little footage of the actual summit, as major television networks did not provide live coverage – a consequence of Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. When the visit was covered, the narrative was often coloured by the networks’ anger at the president. Trump was relentlessly criticised by liberal media for warming up to Communist China, and the tirades against Beijing often bordered on hysteria. We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other The underlying sentiment seems to be that Washington simply needs to “act tough” to strong-arm Beijing into submission. That script has been tried before, and it has never worked. Before this week’s meeting, the US and China had already settled into nine years of intense rivalry, fighting trade wars, tech wars, financial wars and narrative wars. We are where we are because neither side could land a knockout punch, and both hold enough leverage to make the winter hard for the other. It is fitting, if ironic, that it’s Marco Rubio – still on Beijing’s sanctions list – who offers the sharpest rebuttal to that view, now wearing his Secretary of State hat. “The United States and China are the two largest economies in the world. The United States and China are probably the two most powerful militaries in the world. The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Secretary Rubio said. “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to. That doesn’t mean we don’t have strong disagreements. Of course, we do.” The present entente between China and the US is hardly, as some commentators believe, the result of Trump’s tendency to cosy up to authoritarian strongmen. The two sides are being driven together by the need for “shared warmth” in the face of pressing internal and external urgencies. Unlike the Soviet Union and the US during the Cold War, there is no Iron Curtain separating the two sides in today’s globalised world. For all the efforts to decouple or de-risk, Chinese and American national interests remain deeply intertwined. A study released by the Peterson Institute for International Economics last month found that despite all the tariffs and trade restrictions imposed on Beijing by Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden, China’s share of total value added in American imports dropped by only 2 per cent. Chinese supply chains remain deeply embedded in the American economy. At the same time, the need for cooperation on issues like the regulation of artificial intelligence – or “superintelligence” in President Trump’s terminology – is real and pressing. The danger of artificial intelligence lies not so much in machines replacing humans, but in the disproportionate power it hands to those with access to advanced AI over those without. That imbalance opens the door to every kind of abuse and misuse. It also sharply raises the risk of miscalculated nuclear warfare. During the Cold War, a strategic missile launched from Soviet or American soil would take roughly an hour to hit its target. Today, hypersonic technology has cut that window to under 20 minutes, and sophisticated stealth technology makes early detection far harder. Cold War-era generals had time to assess intelligence and call each other for clarification in an extreme emergency. Today, no human being can do all of that in 8 to 20 minutes. Inevitably, this may mean ceding control of the nuclear button to AI – unless the two sides can reach some comprehensive agreement first. These are just some of the cold realities both sides must face. No matter how much you dislike the “spiky porcupine” across the room, you have to learn how to get close enough to survive the winter. This, in a roundabout way, is my explanation of what Xi means by “strategic stability” between the two sides. The term, first raised last October when the two leaders met in Busan, South Korea, describes how China and the US might find the “Goldilocks distance” – close enough to cooperate, far enough to compete, without risking bringing down the house. Seen this way, the success of this week’s summit should not be measured by the deals signed or missed, but by whether the two sides have established the right distance to contain their differences and allow controlled cooperation – one step at a time.

title: What Donald Trump and Xi Jinping revealed in the body language with their wives
description: Outing at National Archives Museum at end of three-day state visit showed stark contrast in hand-holding dynamics, experts say.
content: As Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump wrapped up their three-day state visit on Friday, a stark contrast in the two presidential couples’ hand-holding dynamics was on display, body language experts said. The exchanges between Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, and Trump and first lady Melania Trump, were closely followed on the trip, with the couples’ activities together on Friday culminating in an outing at the National Archives Museum in Washington. The couples’ divergent interactions offered a glimpse into their dynamics, according to body language expert Patti Wood. Upon their arrival, the couples walked up the building’s stairs together. Xi and Peng held hands as they walked, a gesture that appeared natural, said Wood, who added that the pair walked closely in sync. “That speaks well of their relationship and how natural it is,” she said. “It’s not always natural in that culture to hold hands, so it’s beautiful, especially beautiful.” Wood, who holds bachelor's and master's degrees in non-verbal communication from Florida State University and Auburn University respectively, juxtaposed Xi and Peng with the Trumps. The US president and first lady were at a further distance from each other as they moved, she said, calling them “not in sync with each other”. “They’re out of sync as they’re walking, and their postures seem stiff instead of fluid,” Wood added, saying she interpreted the disconnect as tension. And even though Xi and Peng stopped holding hands before entering the building, their bodies were still “in alignment”. “When a couple goes into a space side by side together, an intimate zone of space, in-sync walking, that also speaks well of the couple,” Wood said. “It’s just really interesting because we see that Trump and Melania are far apart in that same instance.” Once inside the museum, the US president showed Xi and Peng historical documents, including the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution. During the tour, there was a moment between Peng and Xi that Wood described as a “bid to play”. “She actually came behind her husband and touched him as he bent over to look,” said Wood of Peng, noting it would be difficult to plan or anticipate the moment. The movement was fluid and natural, she added. Wood interpreted it as a symbolic way of saying, “I want to be in this moment with you, together”. In response, Xi “just naturally lets her approach him from the back and get up close to him so that they can look together”. When the couples exited the building, the Trumps also began to hold hands, with Wood calling Trump’s reaching out to his wife an “abrupt grasp” and observing that her “body did not naturally relax and move in”. The US first lady then moved slightly ahead of Trump as they descended the stairs. Wood interpreted this gesture as supportive. “He just grabbed onto her, and she took care of it,” she said. After the couples bid farewell, the Trumps held hands while walking to their car, which Wood said appeared much more natural than when they arrived. “That’s a much more natural handhold,” she said. “But if you look at their body language as they’re holding hands, there’s tension in the handhold.” The farewell brought the state visit to a close after a programme that included bilateral talks accompanied by a state dinner, military review and rare airport greeting. Thursday’s state dinner also shed insight into the dynamics between the two world leaders, according to Lillian Glass, another body language expert. Glass, who has served as an expert witness in court on behavioural analysis, said Xi and Trump’s body language showed a connection. “Xi repeatedly inclined his head towards Trump, and his body oriented in Trump’s direction,” she said. “Trump reciprocated by turning directly towards Xi.” Trump’s head position when he greeted Xi and Peng was also significant, Glass added, saying the US leader cocked and tilted his head while interacting with them. “This softened his presentation and communicated warmth, attentiveness and respect during the greeting,” she said. “Melania was equally welcoming, smiling towards Xi and remaining visibly engaged throughout the encounter.”

title: Editorial | More work is needed to plug Hong Kong’s labour gap
description: Problems including workforce ageing and job mismatch demand a more precise, well-crafted government response.
content: Hong Kong’s latest manpower projection offers some short-term relief, but includes a big warning. The shortfall expected by 2028 has narrowed to 130,000, down from the 180,000 forecast two years ago. Yet the workforce itself is set to shrink from 3.47 million last year to 3.4 million in 2028. That is roughly 20,000 fewer workers each year, even after counting imported labour and talent. Without those import schemes, the labour force would fall to 3.21 million and the gap would widen to 300,000. The city is holding back a demographic tide, not turning it. The problems are threefold. The first is ageing. Workers aged 25 to 34 are projected to decline by 64,000 over three years. The median age of manual labourers has reached 54, and that of skilled technical workers is 50. Together, these two groups account for about 40 per cent of the projected shortage, with 48,000 to 53,000 technicians and 36,000 to 41,000 manual workers needed. Aviation, construction, healthcare, innovation and city operations – the sectors underpinning Hong Kong’s ambitions – remain the most exposed. The second is job mismatch. Unemployment has edged up to 3.8 per cent, with more than 150,000 people out of work, even as vacancies go unfilled. Roy Chan Kwok-fai, head of the Labour and Welfare Bureau’s research unit, estimates that 30,000 to 40,000 jobless people cannot find work without retraining. Long-term unemployment, lasting six months or more, has risen from a fifth of the jobless before the pandemic to nearly a third. Veteran chefs displaced by closures of Chinese restaurants illustrate how skills can become stranded in a changing economy. The third is artificial intelligence (AI), affecting clerical support staff who face a surplus of 25,000 to 30,000. Entry-level vacancies suitable for recent graduates have fallen by around 60 per cent compared with 2022, while approximately 70,000 clerical workers aged between 45 and 54 without post-secondary education are considered vulnerable. Fresh graduates and middle-aged clerical staff are expected to bear the brunt. These problems demand a more precise, well-crafted government response. Retraining must be targeted and driven by what employers need. The Employees Retraining Board and vocational institutions should design courses jointly with employers in shortage sectors and tie funding to job placement rather than enrolment. Training allowances generous enough to replace part of lost income would help middle-aged workers make the leap from clerical desks to technical trades. More underused groups willing and ready to work need to be brought back into the workforce. Women, older workers and retirees represent a significant reserve. More subsidised childcare, flexible working arrangements and incentives for employers to keep staff beyond age 60 would enlarge the labour pool without adding to housing pressure. Productivity must replace headcount as the engine of growth. Automation in construction, logistics and catering, alongside faster adoption of modular building methods, would help reduce dependence on scarce manual labour. Used well, AI can relieve shortages. And talent importation needs to be more targeted to be effective. More than 180,000 workers and professionals have arrived in recent years, above earlier projections. Yet the city’s main labour federation notes that niche fields such as green shipping and Islamic finance attracted almost no applicants. Officials have said they will update the Talent List, which covers 60 professions, by next year. That review should be data-driven and regular. Retention must be tracked; talent that departs within two years flatters the statistics. Furthermore, local workers must be seen to benefit. The new youth employment programme is a welcome step. Under the scheme, the authorities will subsidise part of the monthly pay for six months for 10,000 additional jobs for first-time entrants. Wage data suggests imports have not undercut locals, but transparent monitoring of hiring ratios and wages would sustain public confidence. Skills, participation, productivity and precise immigration policy must be made to work together. The narrowed labour gap is a reprieve; the government should use it wisely.

title: What I learned from 230km ultra-marathon race in Kenya over 5 exhausting days
description: The 2026 For Rangers Ultra brought animal encounters and tough lessons for Lily Canter, who discovered fitness only takes you so far.
content: Halfway up a long hill in the Kenyan wilderness, a photographer pointed towards the bush. Just 20 metres (66 feet) away, a hyena was running through the undergrowth, chasing its prey. It was exhilarating – and a little terrifying. I was taking part in Beyond the Ultimate’s For Rangers Ultra, a five-day, 230km (143-mile) race through five Kenyan wildlife conservancies, where encounters like this were all part of the unique experience. Armed rangers were stationed around 300 metres apart along the course, with additional lookouts on hilltops and a helicopter surveying the route. They monitored the animals and stopped runners when necessary, moving elephants away from the route with commands or vehicles. The helicopter also helped move big cats away from the runners. Headphones were prohibited – we needed to remain alert to the wildlife. There would be no escaping into podcasts or music when the going got tough. And tough it certainly became. Despite months of preparation, I came close to abandoning the race on day three. By the fourth morning, I was dehydrated, nauseous and struggling to eat. My fitness was excellent, but my body was falling apart along with my mind. Over five days, I learned some valuable lessons about looking after myself during an extreme endurance event. 1. Fitness alone isn’t enough I had gone into the race feeling well prepared. I had given up alcohol in a bid to maximise my recovery and earlier in 2026 I had completed a 100-mile ultra-marathon in the UK and spent a week running on Easter Island (Rapa Nui). I had also incorporated plenty of hiking with a heavy pack into my training. The Kenya route passed through the Lewa, Borana, Lolldaiga, Ol Jogi and Ol Pejeta conservancies, with around 3,500 metres of climbing and sections reaching just above 2,000 metres in altitude. On the first two days I was flying, finishing third in the women’s category on both occasions. My legs felt fantastic, particularly on the downhills, where I was overtaking runners who had passed me on the climbs. Remarkably, I experienced no muscle stiffness or delayed onset muscle soreness throughout the week. My legs only started feeling heavy on the final day, but I could still run. The training had clearly paid off. Unfortunately, I had made a fundamental mistake elsewhere in my preparation. For this self-sufficient race, the 75 runners had to carry their food, sleeping equipment, clothing and medical supplies. With water, my pack weighed around 10kg (22lb). I had spent hours weighing everything and selecting foods that provided the maximum calories for the minimum weight. This included five 800-calorie porridge packs, five dehydrated vegan meals including Thai curry, pasta and chilli (also about 800 calories each), 10 Styrkr rice energy bars with 50 grams of carbs each, and 30 FTP energy gel pastilles with about 15 grams of carbs each. Obsessed with reducing my pack weight, I had made the gamble that I could survive on 2,300 calories per day of carbohydrate-dense food. The mandatory requirement was 2,000 calories per day, so I was above that. It wasn’t enough. In hindsight, I needed at least 3,000 calories daily. As a result, by day three I completely bonked. I was hungry, nauseous and exhausted. My mood plummeted, and my running times fell off a cliff. I was not sleeping well either. I have never been a particularly good sleeper when camping, and going to bed hungry made things worse. By the fourth day, even eating was becoming difficult, and it took me 40 minutes to eat half a bowl of rehydrated porridge. Fortunately, several runners had brought more food than they needed and generously shared their supplies with me that evening. I gained an additional porridge meal, five energy chews and swapped my lower-calorie Thai curry for someone else’s high-calorie vegan chilli. Before bedding down, I had eaten about 800 additional calories, and the difference was remarkable. I slept better that night, woke up without feeling sick and found my mood had lifted considerably. On the final day, I was even running sections that other competitors were walking. 2. Do not wait until you are seriously dehydrated Hydration was another area where my strategy fell short. Before travelling to Kenya, I had a sweat test that suggested I needed around 1,000mg of electrolyte replacement per litre of water. I decided to take about half of that. In a previous race in Tanzania, I had managed with just 250mg per litre, so I thought I would be fine. But in Kenya, where I was drinking around four litres (1 gallon) of water daily, I was running faster and carrying a heavier pack. I also was not drinking enough after each race day: I did not want to go to the toilet in the middle of the night with the lions and hyenas prowling around the open campground. So by day four, I was breathing heavily, dehydrated and feeling sick as a dog. At the first checkpoint, the medical team made me sit down and drink a litre of rehydration solution. They also insisted I eat something substantial, such as a rice bar, rather than rely on energy chews. They would not let me leave until my urine was lighter in colour, so I spent about 25 minutes at the checkpoint before continuing. The experience taught me I could not simply assume that a hydration strategy that worked in one race would be appropriate for another. More importantly, I learned that when I felt seriously unwell, I needed to get a medical assessment rather than trying to push through. 3. Cooling down is worth slowing down for The heat was one of my biggest concerns before the race. Some sections were incredibly exposed, with little shade, and running with a heavy pack made it considerably harder. Having trained throughout the British summer heatwaves, I felt reasonably prepared, but I still had to make a conscious effort to keep cool. Rather than rushing through checkpoints, I stopped, soaked my hat in water and asked the medics to pour water over my head. These simple cooling strategies made a noticeable difference in how I felt. The heat undoubtedly wore me down and made my breathing more laboured, but it never completely overwhelmed me. I learned that taking a few extra minutes to cool down was far more useful than racing through a checkpoint only to struggle during the next section. 4. Mental resilience isn’t about ignoring warning signs My lowest moment came on day three, the longest day of 47km with a nasty steep climb near the end. After hours of struggling, I reached an elephant sanctuary beside our camp, where I was able to meet and touch an elephant and her calf. The overwhelming experience caused me to burst into tears. I was exhausted, felt incredibly sick, and had spent much of the day wanting to pull out. But that encounter was so moving that for a moment it made everything worthwhile. The following morning, however, I did not even want to start. So rather than thinking about the enormous distance remaining, I broke the race into manageable sections. My only goal was to reach the next checkpoint, and thankfully these were spaced at only 10km apart. Once there, I would sit down, eat, cool off, use the toilet and assess how I felt. If I improved, I could consider continuing. And every time I did. I also reminded myself why I had signed up for this race. Seeing breathtaking wildlife, including elephants, rhinos, giraffes, zebras and hyenas up close, and learning about the rangers’ conservation work was a unique opportunity. Focusing on my surroundings gave me something positive to hold on to. I might never have the privilege of such an experience again. I was elated for most of the final day, knowing that the finish was in sight along with a fully catered lunch and dinner. The rangers ran the final 500 metres with me, encouraging me with “so strong, so strong” as I sprinted into the final funnel. The sense of relief was overwhelming, and I raised my arms in the air and screamed. Would I do it again? Probably not. It was my toughest challenge to date but also one of the most extraordinary experiences of my life. I went to Kenya believing my fitness would get me through 230km. I came home understanding that looking after my body mattered just as much as having the strength to keep running. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Top 10: What would you have your bag magically, endlessly spawn?
description: From cats and spare change to classic cheeseburgers and restaurant coupons, readers share what they’d love to find inside their backpacks.
content:
Our next question : If you could bring one sport from the Asian Games to your school, which would it be? To take part, drop us a line via this form by 12pm on Tuesday, September 29 .
Aimee Cheng Sin-yu, 12, Carmel Alison Lam Foundation Secondary School: I would want to find a cat. This is because I do not see any cats at school, and cats are cute. I do not want to see homework every time I open my school bag. That is so bad.
Chung Pui-wai, 14, TWGHs Li Ka Shing College: I would choose Doraemon’s memory bread. It would help me memorise a tremendous amount of information quickly, allowing me to spend more time understanding difficult concepts, doing exercises and practising past papers. Although it would not replace genuine understanding, it could make revision more efficient. Better still, it could satisfy my hunger during long study sessions. What more could I ask for?
Linus Poon Long-yat, 15, Immaculate Heart of Mary College: A bag of currency would be great! Well, maybe I’m a bit greedy, but buying a house near my school is surely what I need. I could take a break at lunchtime at home and shower easily after exercising at school. Moreover, having an endless supply of money would definitely enable me to enjoy life more.
Williams Ekeji, 15, CCC Kung Lee College: I would pick classic cheeseburgers. Why? So I could start a food stall business with zero ingredient costs or give warm meals to people who need them. Let’s be honest, I would eventually get sick of eating cheeseburgers every single day. Turning an infinite supply of burgers into a business and sharing the rest just makes sense, so there you have it.
Kayton Chu Kai-yan, 15, Pui Kiu College: I would hope it would be box lunches. Although I’d rather buy from my school canteen, many of my classmates would prefer not to and either bring snacks themselves or skip lunch – just to save money. Many of them probably do not find school meals worth it, but as I am aware of the health concerns, I would really want them to have a better eating routine. Plus, maybe a box lunch would make their day.
Renee Lui Wing-yi, 13, St Mary’s Canossian College: Imagine: your teacher says, “Take out a piece of single-lined paper for a quiz”, and the stack of paper you swear you had this morning suddenly disappears. You’re forced to awkwardly borrow a sheet and receive judgmental side-eyes. If endless lined paper could spawn whenever I open my schoolbag, I would never have to worry about running out again. I would also gain prestige by lending paper to my classmates like a respected merchant.
Juniper Lai Hiu-yan, 13, St Paul’s Co-educational College: I would hope it could spawn a video of the best memories I had with my friends, which only I could see. I don’t usually have the motivation to go to school, so every night when I pack my bag, those memories can flow out and remind me that school is also a chance for me to be with my friends. And during break time at school, I could open my bag to see the video for motivation when I’m tired of learning.
Sin Cheuk-ying, 14, Ho Yu College and Primary School (Sponsored by Sik Sik Yuen): The classroom air conditioner remote control. Our room is eternally freezing, so controlling its climate would instantly make me the ruler of the classroom.
Lui Hiu-tung, 14, Madam Lau Kam Lung Secondary School of MFBM: I would want pens. I often run out of ink in class, and it troubles me a lot. If my bag could provide me with endless pens, I could write notes and finish homework easily. I would not need to bring spares.
Shirley Li Hiu-lui, 15, Kowloon True Light School: I think it would be random restaurant coupons, so I would not have to worry and think about what to eat for lunch. Every time I would want to go out for lunch, I could just open my bag and randomly grab a coupon – like a blind box every day. And I could also share it with my friends, so we all don’t have to worry about lunch any more.

title: This week in PostMag: a showcase of Hong Kong talent, from AIA Scholars to an award-winning fashion designer
description: Plus Kellett School’s marks its first half-century with a 10-year plan roll-out and how double-amputee snowboarder Neil Tsui came back from the brink.
content: Cramming for exams, lugging hardbound tomes from locker to class and back, scribbling essays on lined paper until your hand cramps – all that is long behind me. I dare not share too much in fear of showing my age, but back in my day – when does one arrive at “old enough” to use this phrase unironically? – cursive writing and fountain-pens were mandatory, breathing in chalk dust from the blackboard was a quotidian hazard and we were still wheeling cumbersome television-VCR combo sets through the halls. Now, of course, learning is digitised, computerised, technologised, with even more change on the horizon. How education is delivered has transformed, but one thing remains the same: it continues to open doors to a future that will be shaped by the next generation. AIA is investing in that future, and in the potential of young Hongkongers as the socially responsible, pioneering leaders of tomorrow, with the ongoing AIA Scholarships programme and a pledge to provide financial support to university undergraduates. In conversation with Nicole Hurip, five enterprising and go-getting AIA Scholars, from diverse backgrounds and academic disciplines as varied as clinical psychology and medicine to computer science and occupational therapy, talk about their hopes, dreams, purpose, achievements and plans for making a difference in the city they call home. Nurturing curiosity and preparing students for an ever-changing future are crucial considerations in how Paul Tough approaches teaching. With a comprehensive blueprint guiding the next decade and the path that lies ahead of Kellett School in Hong Kong – which just celebrated its 50th year and the opening of a new campus – the principal and CEO of the British international institution tells David Ho about building a learning experience that fosters individual and collective growth, and placing culture at the centre of it all. Encouraging budding talent extends far beyond the classroom. It happens in the workplace, in the community – and on a stage, in front of hundreds, if not thousands, of people, like at this month’s Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest, presented at the annual Centrestage showcase. Self-trained, uncompromising and with an unquenchable drive, competition winner Tsui Ao-lung’s unplanned foray into garment design – and to the grand prize – defies expectations. P.Ramakrishnan takes a peek inside the mind of the “accidental couturier” to decode his creative process and the source of his boundless energy. Resilience, adaptability and independence – these qualities, the ones that educators hope to instil, are things that Neil Tsui has in abundance. He was forced to face the ultimate test when he contracted necrotising fasciitis, a devastating bacterial infection, three years ago. A medically induced coma and a bilateral amputation below the knees saved his life, but left his future and his deep passion for snowboarding and active sports in doubt. Annemarie Evans speaks with the 2030 Paralympics hopeful about choosing positivity, overcoming challenges and how it took him losing his legs to feel limitless. Enjoy the read. We hope you find a spark of inspiration in this week’s stories.

title: As I see it | China and the US can make nice, if not peace
description: Outright enmity is too costly for both superpowers. Even without trust, shared interests leave room for pragmatic cooperation.
content: Washington and Beijing have spent nearly a decade trading tariffs, export controls and blacklists, with each round threatening rupture. Yet they keep recovering from the brink. Tensions soared before summits and plunged immediately after. For example, in 2019 at Osaka, Trump walked back threats to impose tariffs on US$300 billion of Chinese goods and eased curbs on Huawei after Beijing reportedly agreed to buy American farm goods. In Busan last October, he lowered tariffs and shelved export controls on thousands of Chinese companies after Xi Jinping suspended some rare earth restrictions and resumed soybean purchases. As the two presidents met at the White House this week, that pattern was repeating. Simply put, decoupling is proving ruinously expensive on both sides: two-way goods and services trade fell 25.1 per cent last year to an estimated US$494.6 billion, with American goods exports to China down 26 per cent. The effective tariff rate on many Chinese goods remains close to 30 per cent – the highest of any country – yet it comes at a mutual cost. Beijing’s leverage explains much of Washington’s current restraint. China controls roughly 70 per cent of global rare earth mining and about 90 per cent of processing capacity; that dependence cannot be engineered away quickly. The administration has notably refrained from threatening steep new tariffs or technology bans before this summit, in contrast to earlier meetings. The US is, after all, vulnerable to Chinese pressure and tacitly admits the need to maintain stable and secure access to critical minerals. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in April that the president seeks stability and is not looking for “massive confrontation” or “full-on conflict” with China. The administration’s November 2025 National Security Strategy declined to name China a competitor, speaking instead of “maintaining a genuinely mutually advantageous economic relationship with Beijing”. This is not friendship, and no one should pretend otherwise. Washington’s grievances – Chinese subsidies, forced technology transfer, opaque ownership, procurement rules that squeeze foreign firms – are here to stay. But don’t expect China to change. China has selectively opened market access but has not abandoned economic tools that so irk Washington. Both sides continue to calibrate entity (black) lists and export controls against each other. At least selective openness is not blanket exclusion. Reciprocal selectivity is an approach Beijing refined over three decades. Tesla’s entry into Shanghai without a local partner came with conditions on local data storage and, in time, deep local sourcing. The result was a profitable plant for the US company and a sharper domestic industry, with BYD emerging as a global rival. Trump’s first term pitted America against China, but tariffs in his second term targeted more than 100 countries, including allies in Europe and Asia. Washington has been dismantling the global trade order it built, rather than targeting only China. When Xi and Trump met in Beijing in May, they agreed their countries should pursue “constructive strategic stability”. This marks the first shared idea in years to keep relations from deteriorating further. A test came in June when the Pentagon added Alibaba, Baidu and BYD to its civil-military entity list. China placed 10 US entities on its dual-use export control list. Yet both kept countermeasures limited. The US should not complain about China. Washington has long had similar tools: national security agreements through the multi-agency Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), sectoral regulators, and the data and governance provisions tested in the forced sale of TikTok. Beijing has signalled further selective opening in advanced manufacturing, frontier research centres and medical technology. Many Chinese and US analysts agree there is a bargain to be struck, such that neither side surrenders security nor forfeits competitiveness. Sustained consultation and careful management of differences on both sides can still yield tangible results Taiwan remains the most sensitive flashpoint, with the People’s Liberation Army flying thousands of sorties into the island’s air defence identification zone and conducting large-scale naval exercises. They should be seen as replies to repeated naval exercises and provocative sail-throughs by the US and its allies in the Taiwan Strait and nearby waters. On a brighter note, Yang Zhibin and Samuel Paparo’s first command-level meeting in two years signals dialogue rebuilding at presidential, ministerial and frontline tiers, with suspended arms-control talks possibly resuming. Even without a diplomatic breakthrough at this week’s presidential summit, strategic stability and incremental progress on hot-button issues are not nothing. Bypassing fundamental divergences will not produce lasting stability, but sustained consultation and careful management of differences on both sides can still yield tangible results. The two superpowers may not be friends, nor enemies. As nuclear-armed giants with the world’s two largest economies, they cannot afford outright enmity.

title: Iran offers US plan to reopen Hormuz within 7 days
description: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the ball is now in Washington’s court, after setting out conditions for ending the war.
content: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed. Araghchi met with US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff for talks on Tuesday, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel. “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN on Friday. “The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. “I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.” Earlier media reports suggested the new plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon. It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least US$12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran. On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz. Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands. The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear programme. But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway. Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons. Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

title: Black woman Tasia Fortune’s hanging was ‘staged’ after her death, Mississippi police say
description: The killing – which recalled lynchings – appeared to be over a drug dispute, authorities say, and two black men have been arrested.
content: Investigators believe Tasia Fortune was already dead before the black woman’s body was hanged from a tree behind an abandoned home in the Mississippi capital this summer, a detective testified on Friday. The hanging of Tasia Fortune’s body, which was found on August 3, was “staged”, Jackson police detective Samuel Dukes testified, citing the medical examiner’s opinion. Authorities have not disclosed the exact cause of Fortune’s death, but they did rule it a homicide and have arrested two men, both of them black, on murder charges and issued a warrant for the arrest of a third person. Dukes also testified that the motive for the killing appears to have been a drug dispute. He said interviews with others revealed that Fortune fought hard before she was killed. The case has attracted widespread attention because the scene recalled lynchings in the Southern state, which has a long and troubled history of racial violence. Authorities have not said why they believe the defendants hanged Fortune’s body after she was already dead. Dukes testified at a hearing for Jarques Ratliff, 51, who was the first person arrested in the case earlier this month. Ratliff, who has pleaded not guilty, remains in custody in the Hinds County jail without bond. The purpose of the hearing, which will resume September 30, is to determine if there’s enough evidence to send the case to a grand jury for a possible indictment. Police arrested the second defendant, 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jnr, this week. During Friday’s hearing, Ratliff said that Fortune had been a friend of his. Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, has said her daughter, who had four children, struggled with homelessness in recent years, and that she was not sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death. She said Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.

title: Trade deliverables, Taiwan push and ‘strategic stability’: key Xi-Trump takeaways overall
description: Chinese leader’s whirlwind US state visit rich in pageantry sees American president pull out all the stops.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping has completed a whirlwind 43-hour trip to the United States, his first state visit to the country in more than a decade, with US President Donald Trump pulling out all the stops to make it a grand affair. The two leaders met several times during the visit, including at a ceremonial airport welcome, the White House reception and bilateral talks on a wide range of topics including trade, tariffs and Taiwan. They also attended a state dinner in Xi’s honour with top business leaders, held a tea meeting and visited the National Archives. Here are the key takeaways. Deliverables on trade As Xi and his wife, first lady Peng Liyuan, touched down in Washington on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent revealed on Fox News that the Busan trade agreement would be extended by two months from November 10 to January 10. Both sides also finalised the Board of Trade mechanism and are set to announce non-sensitive sectors and products capped at US$30 billion each for tariff reduction. US trade chief Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that Washington and Beijing had reached an agreement on a slice of “managed trade” and that more of it would be published on Monday. Xi stresses ‘strategic stability’ During the visit, Xi repeatedly stressed a vision of building a “constructive” Sino-US relationship of “strategic stability” – a concept adopted by the two sides after the last summit in Beijing in May. And during the tea meeting in the White House Red Room with Trump on Friday, Xi said the bilateral relationship would be “constructive” and based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”. Xi’s Taiwan push Xi pressed Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence during their bilateral meeting on Thursday. Xi said he hoped the US side would “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, according to a statement from Beijing’s foreign ministry. The White House did not release any details of the conversation. A banquet of big names A total of 134 guests attended the White House state banquet in honour of the Chinese leader. At the main table with the two presidents were prominent American business leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Apple executive chairman Tim Cook. World War II alliance invoked Both leaders invoked their countries’ alliance against Japanese aggression during the second world war as they emphasised a long history of US-China friendship and a need to seek common ground. While Trump called China a World War II ally without naming Japan, Xi explicitly named the island country and said the China–US friendship had been forged in “blood and fire”. Xi-Trump Apec, G20 meetings confirmed At Friday’s tea meeting, Xi confirmed two more engagements with Trump for the rest of this calendar year: at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting in Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 (G20) leaders’ summit in Miami in December. Trump said he and Xi would be “speaking a lot”. Military pageantry From the airport welcome and White House ceremonial reception to the final send-off, Washington put on a lavish military display for Xi’s visit. The Chinese leader’s arrival and departure at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland were both marked by a 21-gun salute. At the White House, Xi was welcomed with a military flyover featuring a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors, along with performances by military bands. On Friday, during their tea meeting, Xi thanked Trump for the visit, calling it “done to the highest order of perfection and various thoughts in every little detail”. Additional reporting by Holly Chik

title: Exclusive | China set to decide if Costa Rican or Guyanese diplomat becomes first woman UN chief
description: Rebeca Grynspan and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett lead a split Security Council as Beijing rules out Argentina's Rafael Grossi.
content: China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite. Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN. The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei. China has kept cordial but cooler relations with Milei since his 2023 presidential campaign, when he called the Chinese government “assassins” and promised to cut ties in favour of the “civilised side of life”. Under UN rules, the 193-member General Assembly appoints the secretary general on the recommendation of the 15-member Security Council. The winner will succeed current UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose second term ends on December 31. The assembly has never rejected a name put forward by the council. A candidate needs at least nine votes in the council and no veto from any of the five permanent members, which are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Before a formal vote, the council holds secret straw polls in which members mark each candidate “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion”. Colour-coded ballots, used in later rounds, show whether a discourage vote came from a permanent member, though not which one. Both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett travelled to Beijing this year to meet Foreign Minister Wang Yi, but China has not publicly endorsed either of them. Grynspan led the first straw poll in July with 10 encourage votes, and Rodrigues-Birkett came first in the second round in August. In the third poll a week ago, Grynspan received nine encourage votes, five discourage votes and one no opinion, according to diplomats with knowledge of the tally sheets. Rodrigues-Birkett received eight encourage votes, and her discourage votes rose from three to six. Grossi, Ugandan diplomat and former UN under-secretary-general Olara Otunnu and Senegal’s former president Macky Sall received five encourage votes each. Former Ecuadorian foreign minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa received three, and Ecuador’s Ivonne A-Baki received none. The results do not show whether any of Grynspan’s five discourage votes came from a permanent member. In the 2016 race, which took six straw polls, Guterres did not fall below 11 encourage votes. China has not said publicly which candidate it prefers, but the Brics summit in New Delhi earlier this month could serve as a hint of what Beijing thinks of the contest. During the summit, the Brics leaders adopted a joint declaration noting that “no woman has ever been elected for the role of Secretary-General” and that only one national from Latin America and the Caribbean had held the post. Also, China’s ambassador to the UN, Fu Cong, reportedly said in May that Beijing supported regional rotation for the organisation’s top job and would be “pleased to see a woman in the post”, according to Costa Rican news site El Observador. Grynspan thanked him for the remarks at the time. Bachelet’s withdrawal While the choice between the leading female candidates appears wide open, another contender has categorically failed to win China’s favour. While there is no confirmation on its position on Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett, three sources familiar with the matter told the SCMP that the Chinese delegation “decisively voted against” Michelle Bachelet, the former Chilean president. Bachelet withdrew from the race last Saturday, a day after she received one encourage vote and 11 discourage votes in the third poll. Her withdrawal left seven officially nominated candidates in the race. Chile’s government under President Jose Antonio Kast withdrew her nomination earlier in the year, and her candidacy continued with the backing of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Mexico. Conservative US lawmakers had also urged Washington to veto her over her support for abortion rights, Reuters reported. Bachelet’s relationship with Beijing deteriorated during her term as UN high commissioner for human rights. She visited Xinjiang in May 2022 and Western governments criticised the trip as too soft on China. Then, minutes before her UN term ended in August that year, her office published an assessment of Xinjiang. It said abuses against Uygurs and other mostly Muslim minorities in the region “may amount to crimes against humanity”. China’s mission in Geneva rejected the report as disinformation serving the US and other Western countries. Meetings with Wang Yi Grynspan met Wang in Beijing in June and, according to the Chinese foreign ministry, reaffirmed her commitment to the one-China principle. She also praised China’s support for multilateralism and the UN Charter. Wang told her that her remarks showed an understanding of the concerns of Global South countries. He said the next secretary general should uphold the UN Charter and be capable, fair and responsible, and that China would take part in the selection with a “constructive attitude”. Grynspan has led UN Trade and Development since 2021. In 2022 she helped broker the Istanbul agreements, which reopened Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea and eased Russian food and fertiliser shipments. Rodrigues-Birkett also met Wang in Beijing, although a month later. The ministry said she “expressed support for UN General Assembly Resolution 2758”, which Beijing cites as the basis of its claim to represent China at the UN, and “reaffirmed the one-China principle”. She also praised Chinese President Xi Jinping’s four global initiatives and China’s proposal for a World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. The Chinese-language readout quoted her as calling China “a leader on development issues”. After the meeting, Guyana’s Department of Public Information reported that China supported her candidacy. It later apologised and said the report had “mischaracterised Beijing’s position”. In February 2021, Guyana cancelled an agreement for a Taiwan office less than 24 hours after it was announced, following a public objection from the Chinese foreign ministry. Yet, two sources from countries represented at the Security Council told the SCMP that Grynspan had a slight advantage with Beijing. But they said the Chinese delegation was wary of her because of her ties to Israel and her perceived closeness to Washington. Chinese commentators have also pointed to Grynspan’s Jewish background and relatives in Israel. She would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general. Meanwhile, the New York Times reported this week that the US had indicated it would block Rodrigues-Birkett. The newspaper said the objection related to her statement to the Security Council in 2024 that “a veritable genocide” was taking place in Gaza. A State Department official told the newspaper that the US wanted a candidate who would pursue substantial reform and streamline the organisation. The Guyanese government has not commented publicly on the report. China’s mission to the UN and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. On Tuesday, Rodrigues-Birkett joined Guyanese President Irfaan Ali in New York as he signed the Shield of the Americas security communique with US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the sidelines of the General Assembly. Next steps The sources heard by SCMP said they expected the race to be discussed during Xi’s visit to Washington this week. They said it was not clear whether Xi would raise it with Trump or leave it to a meeting between Wang and Rubio. Xi met Trump at the White House on Thursday but did not travel to New York for the General Assembly’s high-level week. The race remains open, and diplomats said new compromise candidates who are acceptable to all five permanent members could still emerge if the deadlock persists. Some rumoured names could include Emirati diplomat and former UAE permanent representative to the UN Lana Nusseibeh , former Dutch minister Sigrid Kaag, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. None of them has said they would run. The split among the permanent members has no precedent in recent UN selections, and it risks disrupting the organisation’s leadership if no successor is chosen by the end of the year. Guterres has made clear he does not intend to stay on in an interim capacity while the council searches for a successor. He has already begun arranging his permanent return to Portugal, according to a UN source. A fourth straw poll could be held after the high-level week ends on Monday. In 2006 and 2016, the council held its final straw polls in early October.

title: US TV networks back at White House, as Trump praises ‘fair’ coverage of Xi visit
description: The US president had earlier barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the grounds, prompting other outlets to halt coverage in solidarity.
content: US television networks resumed coverage of President Donald Trump’s White House events on Friday, providing the first live pool access for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit, as a legal battle continues over restrictions on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Trump last week banned the three outlets from the White House, before a judge ordered the administration to restore their access. The White House television press pool aired video of Xi’s arrival at the White House for tea on the final day of the Chinese ‌leader’s visit, as well as the two leaders’ tour of the National Archives, which houses the US Constitution. CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC share the costs of covering the president and rotate coverage, providing pool footage to other outlets. The other networks’ refusal to set up cameras in solidarity meant there was no pool coverage of the first two days of Xi’s visit. Trump has long relied on the media to shape his public image and advance his agenda, even as he regularly casts news organisations as political adversaries. Since returning to office last year, his administration has taken an aggressive stance against major news outlets, including limiting access to the Oval Office and other restricted spaces. As pool coverage resumed for ⁠Xi’s arrival at the White House on Friday, Trump declined to answer questions from reporters on China and Iran, his media ban and a controversial new taxpayer-funded television ad that promotes his presidency. ‌ He later thanked reporters. “We appreciate the fair coverage. It’s been very fair. We appreciate it,” Trump later told reporters alongside Xi. The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the restored press access. Trump banned the three news outlets from the White House complex over coverage he asserted ‌was false or negative. Their access was reinstated on Thursday, after a federal judge deemed the ban as being likely to be unconstitutional and ordered their access to be immediately restored. CNN, MS ⁠Now and Politico sued Trump and other ⁠members of his administration, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations later ‌filed a legal brief supporting the action. Despite the temporary ruling restoring access, the court has not yet resolved the main challenge to the ban, based on the First Amendment of the US Constitution that protects the right to free speech and a free press. ‌ The news outlets now have until September 28 to ask the judge to keep their access in place while the case moves forward. Even if the outlets won a permanent injunction against the ban, Trump could still pursue his case in federal court. Trump has waged an unprecedented campaign against the media since returning to office last year, launching personal attacks on journalists, denying access to some ⁠outlets and suing news organisations, as well as calling on the Federal Communications Commission to strip broadcast stations of their licences. On Thursday, Trump made a joke to photographers in ⁠the Oval Office about China – which imposes strict censorship across its media – having the friendliest press corps, as he welcomed Xi to the White House. While the White House on Thursday told the court it had reinstated CNN, MS Now and Politico’s access, CNN and MS Now later said some of their journalists were denied access to cover Xi’s arrival ‌for the White House state dinner, according to ‌The Washington Post. A lawyer for the three outlets in court this week warned that the White House could again try to revoke the outlets’ White House access as the current litigation continues. David Ellison, CEO of Paramount Skydance, which is seeking to merge with CNN-parent Warner Bros. Discovery, attended the Trump-Xi state dinner on Thursday night. Critics have raised concerns about Paramount-owned CBS News tailoring coverage to favour Trump, although Ellison has promised to create an editorial independence board for both CBS and CNN as part of the deal.

title: Japan says Trump voiced concern over weak yen in summit with PM Takaichi
description: The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already high due to the Iran war, fuelling concerns about an inflation overshoot.
content: US President Donald Trump raised concerns about yen weakness at a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies. “At the recent Japan-US summit meeting, President Trump expressed concern about the yen’s weakness,” Katayama said at a regular news conference, adding that she was disclosing the exchange for the first time after consulting with the ‌Prime Minister’s Office. Katayama’s frank account of leaders’ talks, which governments typically keep confidential, points to shared concern in Tokyo and Washington over the yen’s continued slide despite their joint intervention in July. Takaichi, speaking to reporters later on Friday, confirmed Trump’s comments at their meeting, which took place in New York on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. “The US side said that the weak yen was creating difficulties for their trade, and I responded that, as a general principle, an undervalued yen is problematic,” she said. But she stressed that there was no discussion of monetary or fiscal policy at the summit, adding that the Takaichi administration’s economic policy stance remains unchanged. Previously, ⁠Takaichi told reporters that she and Trump had held a “timely” discussion about China ahead of the US president’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Katayama ‌said the leaders’ discussion on foreign exchange reaffirmed the shared US-Japan stance behind their July 31 coordinated intervention, including a commitment to counter excessive volatility and disorderly moves in the yen. “In light of this summit meeting, Treasury Secretary (Scott) Bessent and I will continue to communicate closely on ‌a range of matters, including foreign exchange,” she said. Katayama’s comments were swiftly reinforced hours later when she held a call with Bessent, according to a ⁠statement from Japan’s Finance Ministry. In a sign of ⁠Tokyo and Washington’s shared determination to address the weak yen, Katayama and Bessent reaffirmed that the currency’s undervaluation is a matter of concern and agreed to strengthen bilateral cooperation, the statement said. Bessent said in a post on ‌social media that Friday’s call built on Trump’s discussions with Takaichi earlier this week and included talks on the desirability of a strong yen reflecting Japan’s economic fundamentals. The dollar has been rallying against the yen and other major currencies, ‌driven by ‌strong US economic data, a hawkish Federal Reserve and surging US bond yields. The yen strengthened after Katayama’s remarks and gained further again after the ministry’s statement, rising from 158.60 per ‌dollar to trade around 157.20. The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already elevated due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, fuelling concerns about an inflation overshoot, ⁠a headache for Japanese policymakers and for the US, which is worried that a sell-off in Japanese bonds could spill over into the Treasury market. The benchmark 10-year ⁠Japanese government bond yield jumped to a 30-year high of 3.115 per cent on Friday following a steep sell-off in the US market. At a separate news conference, Minoru Kiuchi, the minister in charge of economic revitalisation and an ally of Takaichi’s reflationist camp, said the phase of Abenomics-style reflation policies, with monetary easing and agile fiscal ‌spending, was over. Kiuchi’s remarks appeared to respond to comments ‌from Bessent, who recently suggested that Japan’s priority should be fighting inflation rather than stimulating growth, signalling concern about what he sees as lingering elements of Abenomics in Takaichi’s policies and among her political allies. Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp, said remarks by both Katayama and Kiuchi reflected a heightened sense of concern over the yen’s weakness, particularly after Tokyo conducted rate checks on Friday, a move that is often viewed as a precursor to currency intervention.

title: Milan Fashion Week: Gucci’s Demna builds a massive store for star-studded show
description: From 1980s menswear to signature horsebit motifs, the new collection brought Tina Leung and Sabine Getty to an immersive retail runway.
content: Georgian designer Demna may have been at Gucci for only a couple of seasons but he’s clearly been enjoying his immersion into Italian culture. His tongue-in-cheek riffs on Italian stereotypes – from the tanned playboy to the Milanese sciura and the young bombshell – are spot on. The designer, formerly of Balenciaga, built a massive boutique that acted as a runway to unveil his latest collection for Gucci. Models and “real people” such as socialite Sabine Getty, stylist Amanda Harlech and influencer and stylist Tina Leung roamed the hallowed grounds of the luxury shop while checking themselves out in mirrors and winking at the audience. The first section of the show, aptly named The Store Show, was devoted to menswear. Oversized suits reminiscent of the 1980s, bomber jackets, chambray shirts, preppy polos and more closet staples – many of them adorned with the label’s signature horsebit metal hardware – dominated a line-up of flashy looks worn by a cast of very handsome young men. The women’s portion began with a couple of horse-riding-inspired outfits – a nod to the brand’s equestrian heritage – before a crescendo into all-out glamour. Chubby furs, including a fabulous one worn by Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, vied for attention with sparkly evening gowns with cutouts at the hips and tailored skirt suits. Among the best outfits were a series of bomber jackets paired with pleated checked skirts, and styled with layers of jewellery and plenty of accessories. Lady-like handbags, belts embellished with more of those horsebit buckles, tasselled slippers and oversized loafers with square toes were among the accessories on display – all cool takes on Gucci’s signature pieces. Some of the hoodies were adorned with zipper ends made of bamboo, another take on a key motif from the maison. After a polarising show last season that some felt was too much of a throwback to Tom Ford’s heyday at the brand, this collection distilled Demna’s vision for the Kering-owned house. As he explained in a letter sent to every guest before the event, “The Store Show will be the first collection in which I present my complete personal vision for the brand, based on everything I’ve learned about it since I arrived.” His joyous celebration of Italian archetypes and the dichotomy between good taste and bad taste (“whatever that means”, Demna said in the letter) at the heart of Gucci are the cornerstones of his vision for a brand that has been in need of a major reboot for quite some time. The powers that be at Kering – including group CEO Luca de Meo and Gucci CEO Francesca Bellettini – were beaming after the end of the show as they parted ways with celebrities including Shawn Mendes and Jannik Sinner. If the audience’s reaction is any indication, they can rest assured that the brand is finally on the right track.

title: Whistle-blower Jason Poon and wife charged over HK$6 million Covid-19 loan fraud
description: Construction businessman and spouse Chu Shui-fong accused of submitting fake sales and salary records to defraud HSBC under government scheme.
content: Hong Kong businessman Jason Poon Chuk-hung and his wife have been charged with defrauding a government financing scheme for businesses out of HK$6 million during the Covid-19 pandemic, the South China Morning Post has learned. A source said on Friday that construction businessman Poon, 56, and his 54-year-old wife, both out on bail, had been charged with conspiracy to defraud and money laundering and would appear at Kowloon Court on Monday. Poon, director of mask manufacturer Lockill Biochemical, his wife Chu Shui-fong and four company employees were arrested in March. The SCMP previously reported that police intelligence suggested a surgical mask manufacturer had allegedly defrauded HSBC out of HK$6 million via the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme during the pandemic. Poon, his wife and four employees have been accused of submitting fake sales records and “augmented” salary records between April and June 2021 to meet application requirements for the scheme. He allegedly transferred most of the loan into his and his wife’s personal bank accounts, using the money for personal expenses and repaying debts owed to finance companies, the source said. The scheme was launched in 2011, but was extended to provide a special 100 per cent loan guarantee as part of the 2020-21 government budget to help ease businesses’ cash-flow problems arising from wage and rental obligations during the pandemic. The loans were fully guaranteed by the government at a concessionary low interest rate. Poon rose to public prominence in 2018 for exposing the shoddy work at the Hung Hom MTR station, part of the Sha Tin-Central link project. His whistle-blowing account prompted the government to establish an independent commission of inquiry to investigate the scandal. The businessman later ran as an independent candidate in the 2021 Legislative Council election. He finished last among four candidates in the Hong Kong East constituency.

title: Chinese teen titan Zhang Zhanshuo counts out the golds after magnificent 7 at Asian Games
description: Zhang signs off with men’s 400m freestyle crown as China finish swimming programme with 30 golds from 41 medal events.
content: ⁠Teenage juggernaut Zhang Zhanshuo became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at an Asian Games on the final night at the Tokyo pool on Friday, when China cemented their superpower status. Sitting on a lane divider, the 19-year-old Zhang counted out the golds with his fingers to mark the moment after cruising to the 400 metres freestyle title in a Games record of three minutes, 41.28 seconds, ‌with Japan’s Kazushi Imafuku a distant runner-up. Having already won the 200m, 400m and 1,500m freestyle crowns and three relay titles to boot, Zhang eclipsed the six-gold hauls of China’s butterfly queen Zhang Yufei (Hangzhou 2022) and Japan’s Rikako Ikee (Jakarta 2018). Only North Korean shooter So Gin-man, who won seven golds and a silver in New Delhi in 1982, has a better total at a single Games. While calling it a good way to finish off the meet, Zhang said he was eyeing bigger prizes. “The Asian Games is not the goal. I’m still aiming for the ⁠Olympics and competing with the best,” he said. In Zhang, China may have found a successor to Sun Yang and his awkward legacy as both the ‌nation’s most decorated swimmer and an athlete banned twice for doping violations. The teenager’s haul helped China sign off from the swimming with 30 gold medals out of 41 medal events in the pool. Chief rival Japan was right there in many races, winning seven gold and 37 medals overall – also better than their totals from three years ago. The meet has been ground zero for an explosion of junior talent, with China's 13-year-old schoolgirl Yu Zidi ⁠winning three golds and Japan's 17-year-old ⁠Shin Ohashi claiming the only world record of the Games, taking the men’s 200m breaststroke on Thursday in 2:04.83. The previous record holder, Qin Haiyang, got one back for the grown-ups on Friday though, the 27-year-old retaining his ‌50m breaststroke crown in a showdown with bronze-winning Ohashi. China’s 13-year-old Yu was the most talked about swimmer heading into the Games and she did not disappoint, winning the 200m butterfly, and the 200m and 400m individual medleys. Her time in the 200 IM was 2:06.10, just off the world mark held by Canadian Summer McIntosh (2:05.70). Yu’s times are still a bit off McIntosh’s standard in all three events. But she is a legitimate threat at next year’s world championships and the 2028 Olympics where, of course, other swimming powers such as Australia and the United States will be present. China won gold medals in five of the seven races on Friday, just as dominant as they were all week. Zhang Yufei won the 50m butterfly, her fourth gold of the meet, shedding a tear on a nostalgic podium with old rival Ikee, who took ‌bronze. Zhang’s teammate Wu Qingfeng took silver. China’s Qin Haiyang took the men’s 50m breaststroke (26.68) with Ohashi – the record-setter on Thursday – settling for bronze. Other Chinese winners were Li Bingjie in the 800m free (8:24.02), Zhang in the 400m free (3:41.28), and the women’s 4x100m medley relay (3:54.55). Japan’s Kodai Nishiono won the men’s 200m backstroke (1:56.42), and Taiwan’s Wang Kuan-hung claimed the 200m fly (1:55.05).

title: US TV blackout and midterms turmoil overshadow Xi-Trump red-carpet treatment
description: Xi Jinping’s arrival was not covered by major American networks in protest over Donald Trump’s ban on three news groups.
content: Domestic US political turmoil and Donald Trump’s feud with the media overshadowed a summit that Beijing hoped would project an image of China on equal footing and help stabilise ties with the United States. Trump rolled out the full red-carpet treatment for Chinese President Xi Jinping as he paid his first state visit to the US in over a decade. In addition to Trump and his wife Melania greeting Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan on the tarmac on arrival, the “many special arrangements” included a lavish state dinner at the White House. But most Americans saw little footage of that hospitality as major US networks suspended live telecasts in an escalating feud with the US president, casting a shadow over diplomatic efforts to foster warm relations and stability between the two powers. On Saturday, Trump barred CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, accusing them of reporting “fake news”. The three outlets sued on Monday, arguing that the ban was unconstitutional. Other major television networks, including ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News, also withdrew from the pooled coverage of Trump in solidarity with their banned colleagues.
