As a result, no network camera crews filmed the Trumps greeting Xi and Peng upon their arrival on Wednesday, the first time since 1962 that a US president had personally welcomed a foreign leader at Joint Base Andrews. A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Trump administration to restore the three outlets’ access to the White House. But the ruling was not honoured on the ground, resulting in no US networks carrying live footage of the state dinner Trump threw for Xi in the East Room of the White House. In parallel with the stand-off between the White House and the mainstream media, the US press showed little sign of softening towards Beijing on a range of issues from Iran and Taiwan to rare earths. Some critics also hit out at Trump over the treatment of the Chinese leader, suggesting the tarmac greeting was excessive deference to Beijing and an extravagance, given domestic economic pressures. “Trump rolls out red carpets for Xi Jinping, though he has portrayed China as a global menace,” a headline on an NBC report read. In an interview with NBC, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski said: “I personally look at the red-carpet treatment and thought it was a little bit over the top.” Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, said Trump had long been at odds with mainstream US media outlets such as CNN and The New York Times “because Trump’s views are completely different from theirs”. “He doesn’t talk in terms of ideology. He only talks about interests,” Zheng said, adding that this was something the American media found difficult to accept. He said that the US media had been “highly ideologised” when it came to the country’s diplomacy. Zheng said Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, tried to pressure Beijing on three fronts – framing bilateral tensions as a contest between democracy and authoritarianism, building various minilateral groups to contain China and the trade and tech wars. But Trump seemed to be interested only in the tech and trade aspects, Zheng said. “It has gone from three fronts to one,” he said, adding that the US media establishment was puzzled as to why the democracy, freedom and values arguments – which they saw as the US’ strongest cards – had been abandoned. “The biggest blow has been to the US media,” Zheng said. Also looming large over the visit is the US midterm elections in November. The races could put the Republican Party’s majority in the House and potentially control of both chambers of Congress at stake, shaping the remaining years of Trump’s presidency. Zheng said that if the midterms did not go the Republicans’ way, it could become harder for the president to pursue his approach towards Beijing amid the loud China critics within the Democratic Party. “With the midterms approaching, it is not in the Trump administration’s self-interest to generate a crisis in the bilateral relationship right now,” China specialist Scott Kennedy noted in a commentary published by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. But whatever happened in US domestic politics, there was a floor to the relationship with China, Zheng noted. “Neither the Democrats nor the Republicans want direct conflict with China,” he said.

title: Police arrest 3 over HK$70,000 Jellycat claw machine shop theft
description: Suspects allegedly used crowbars to pry open machines in unstaffed Tai Wai shop before selling stolen goods to other operators.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested three men suspected of using crowbars to steal popular Jellycat dolls and other plush toys worth about HK$70,000 (US$8,923) from a claw machine shop to resell them. The force on Friday said it received a report in the early hours of September 17 that two thieves had broken into an unstaffed claw machine shop in Tai Wai. The shop owner had offered a HK$100,000 reward on social media to catch the thieves after the crime. “They used a crowbar to pry open two claw machines and stole nearly 100 plush toys valued at around HK$70,000,” said Inspector Chan Wai-chi of the Sha Tin district anti-triad section. “After successfully committing the crime, the thieves fled the scene by car. During their escape, they transferred the stolen goods to two other vehicles in an attempt to make the police investigation more difficult.” Using surveillance footage, officers identified the three suspects and their vehicles. Officers arrested three local men aged between 28 and 33 in Sha Tin on suspicion of theft and handling stolen goods. They are suspected to be the masterminds and drivers involved in the crime. The force also traced the stolen items to other claw machine shops in the district and recovered part of the haul. Officers are still investigating the case and have not ruled out further arrests. Upon conviction, the maximum penalty is up to 10 years in prison for theft and 14 years for handling stolen goods. Chan also called on claw machine shop operators, especially those who leave their shops unstaffed, to strengthen their security systems, such as by installing high-resolution surveillance cameras and antitheft alarms.

title: In Paris, Pope warns against losing humanity in ‘paradise of machines’
description: Pope Leo is in France on a four-day trip, the first official papal trip in 18 years to France.
content: Pope Leo on Friday warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines”, after church bells rang and thousands gathered to welcome him to France amid worldwide concern over the dangers of artificial intelligence. “If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment,” Leo said after President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to the presidential palace, on the first of four days in the country. On the first official papal trip in 18 years to a proudly secular country that has since 1905 separated church and state, the pope also stressed that “authentic secularity” should not exclude religion. It “consists not in excluding religion from the public sphere or from education, but in striving to ensure that the state and religious institutions maintain dialogue and join forces in the service of the common good,” the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said. Politicians have in recent years invoked France’s brand of secularism to justify bans on religious symbols including Muslim women’s attire in public spaces and schools. France is just seven months away from the first round of its presidential election to replace Macron, with the anti-immigration far-right eyeing its best chance of seizing power in the vote. After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying, the first US pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death”. The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, urged the European nation to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide, as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine drags into its fifth year. Macron and his wife Brigitte earlier greeted the 71-year-old pope at the airport, where a red carpet was rolled out on the tarmac, as he marked the first official trip by a head of the Vatican since Pope Benedict XVI in September 2008. “I’m travelling to France, as to anywhere else in the world, as a follower of Jesus Christ wanting to proclaim peace, the peace of Christ throughout the world,” Pope Leo told reporters on the plane. He said the message was “particularly important” at the current time. A million people are expected at events across Paris during the first two days of his trip. The high point of the apostolic journey will be a giant mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde and adjoining Champs-Elysees. Pope Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide where he will privately meet victims of clerical sex abuse, and Metz, near the German border, where he is to further speak about peace in Europe. “The pope’s visit gives me a sense of peace in a troubled world,” said Andree Estienne, 76, adding she could not wait to attend the mass on the Champs-Elysees. “I don’t think I will experience anything of this scale again in my lifetime.” Later on Friday, Leo is to wave to the crowds on a 2.5km (1.5 mile) Popemobile ride to the Notre Dame cathedral in central Paris, where he will be the first pope to inspect renovations following a devastating 2019 fire. His predecessor Pope Francis – who visited France three times, but never officially – did not attend the Gothic masterpiece’s reopening in late 2024, when then president-elect Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk were among the guests. Carmen Quintana, a 71-year-old Peruvian, said she would be among the crowd. “We’re very happy to be able to be near him,” she said of the pontiff, who spent two decades as a missionary in Peru and also holds Peruvian nationality. Last on his agenda for the day will be a mass prayer and hymns with 80,000 young believers aged 17 to 35 in a stadium in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. A relic, believed to be the tunic Jesus wore during the Passion, will be transported out of the nearby Saint-Denis Cathedral to the stadium for the occasion. Only around five per cent of France’s 69 million residents go to Catholic church regularly, a survey last year found. But while the number of infant christenings has dwindled in recent years, teenage and adult baptisms are on the rise, with thousands choosing to embrace the faith.

title: EU to release US$7.5 billion linked to Ukraine military aid
description: Money related to Ukraine had stuck in the fund for ⁠months, blocked by the previous Hungarian government under Viktor Orban.
content: European Union member countries ⁠have agreed a ⁠deal to release €6.6 billion (US$7.5 billion) in EU funds linked to military aid for Ukraine, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday. The money will ‌come from the European Peace Facility, a fund used by EU members to finance military aid to countries outside the bloc. It also refunds EU governments for military aid they have provided. Of the released funds, €900 million will ⁠go to the EU’s military assistance mission for Ukraine and €1 billion ‌will fund new joint procurement of equipment, Kallas said in a post on social media. She added the ‌remaining €4.7 billion will go to reimburse member states, some ⁠of whom ⁠have already said they would channel their share to Ukraine. “That’s good news ‌for Ukraine and bad news for Russia,” Kallas said. “Moscow’s hybrid attacks try to intimidate ‌Europe into ‌scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing ‌the opposite.” Money related to Ukraine stuck in the fund for ⁠months, initially blocked by the previous Hungarian government, under Russia-friendly leader ⁠Viktor Orban. It was unclear exactly how much of the funds to be released under Friday’s agreement would ‌directly benefit Ukraine. ‌It will be up to individual EU governments to decide how much of their refunds they allocate to fresh military aid for Kyiv.

title: Entry hours cut short as large crowds at lantern display spark safety fears
description: People flock to the International Lantern Spectacular in Victoria Park to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival.
content: The organiser of a lantern display at Hong Kong’s Victoria Park cut short the entry hours on Friday night out of public safety concerns after large crowds flocked there to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival. “In light of the large number of visitors and in the interest of public safety and order, entry queues of the ‘World Lantern Boulevard’ will be closed shortly,” the Hong Kong Tourism Board said at around 9pm. “All lantern installations at the International Lantern Spectacular will remain on display until October 4. Members of the public and visitors are encouraged to visit at an alternative time.” The board later said no one would be allowed to join the queue from 10pm. Hundreds of people who were already inside the queuing zone at the Causeway Bay park before the cut-off time were still waiting for their turn at around 10pm. Dozens of latecomers were turned away, including construction worker Johnny Hung, 55, who was denied entry along with his wife and two sons. Hung said he was disappointed: “We have no option but to come back [on Saturday] night.” The display, which opened on September 17, has been extended by a week to October 4 due to overwhelming public interest. The daily lighting-up time is between 6.30pm and 11pm, although the hours were extended to midnight between Thursday and Sunday. Some internet users had already warned of potentially huge crowds during the festival after noting that the queuing time on Monday was already one hour. This year’s festival falls on Friday, with the following day a public holiday. The Tourism Board’s inaugural International Lantern Spectacular at the park showcases more than 3,000 designs from different countries and regions. Among those admiring the installations and taking photos was Ho Hon-kuen. Ho, a secondary school principal in his sixties, said it was a family tradition for him to visit the park during the festival to see the lantern displays. “We come here every year during the Mid-Autumn Festival,” he said. Ho said he was impressed by the variety of lanterns this year and how well they were arranged for display in a relatively limited space. An eight-metre-tall (26-foot-tall) banyan tree lantern installation at the park’s main entrance particularly caught his attention. “This installation evokes a sense of ceaseless flow, symbolising the endless cycle of life,” he said. Apart from regular visitors, the display attracted first-timers drawn by online photos of the lanterns. Engineer Leo Wong, 35, and his wife travelled from Yuen Long to Causeway Bay to see the display, carrying a pair of fish-shaped lanterns. “This is our first time here. It’s lively and the atmosphere is great,” he said. Sherry Hou, a PhD student from mainland China studying in Hong Kong, said she was amazed by the city’s festive atmosphere. “The atmosphere of the Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong is wonderful,” said the 30-year-old, who was visiting the park with a friend. At the main entrance to the park stands an eight-metre-tall lantern installation, inspired by Hong Kong’s iconic banyan trees and crafted by master artisans from Nanjing on the mainland. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department is also staging the Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival in the park over the same period. Lanterns are a visual tradition of the Mid-Autumn Festival, when family and friends reunite, gaze at the moon and enjoy mooncakes. A few minutes’ walk from Victoria Park, thousands of people lined the streets of the Tai Hang neighbourhood to watch the annual fire dragon dance on Friday night. A 67-metre fire dragon adorned with 12,000 burning incense sticks was carried through the streets by more than 300 performers as spectators cheered and snapped photos.

title: HK Electric to cut fuel charge for first time in 4 months as CLP raises rate
description: Customers of HK Electric are set to pay less for electricity after it cut its fuel charge for the first time in four months.
content: HK Electric customers are set to pay less for electricity in October after the Hong Kong supplier cut its fuel charge for the first time in four months, but it warned that international energy prices remained volatile. CLP Power, the city’s other electricity supplier, will raise its energy prices next month. HK Electric, which mainly supplies Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Friday that its fuel clause charge would fall by 1.4 HK cents to 59.3 cents per kilowatt hour (kWh) in October. The charge, a component of the overall tariff, is adjusted monthly to reflect the actual cost of fuel used for power generation. Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will fall 0.8 per cent month on month to 187.2 cents per unit. The cut follows consecutive increases since May after the US-Israel war on Iran in February pushed up energy prices. The fuel clause charge dropped from January to May due to the “deterred effects of its mechanism”, but has since risen sharply month on month, from 26 cents in May to 60.7 cents in September. An HK Electric spokesman said that the fuel clause charge for October primarily reflected fuel costs incurred between June and August. The spokesman emphasised that international energy prices remained volatile and future fuel charge levels would continue to depend on trends in international fuel prices. The company said it would continue to closely monitor developments in global energy markets and strive to minimise the impact of fuel price volatility on customers while maintaining a stable fuel supply and complying with emission caps through prudent procurement strategies and timely adjustments to its fuel mix. The company offered an 8 cents per unit subsidy to qualifying residential customers from August to October to help alleviate the impact of higher electricity costs, it added. CLP Power, which supplies Kowloon and the New Territories, said its fuel adjustment charge for October would rise to 46.2 cents per kWh, up 1.1 cents from September. The changes mainly reflected actual fuel price changes over the past three months, a company spokesman said. Including the basic electricity charge, the average net electricity charge would be 147.4 cents per kWh, up 0.75 per cent from September, an increase of around 4.8 per cent compared with that of this January. CLP is offering a special fuel rebate from August to October to help ease the financial burden of households, a move expected to benefit 50 per cent of residential customers.

title: China overtakes US as top workplace for elite AI researchers, study finds
description: The country is retaining a growing share of top-tier talent amid a booming domestic AI industry and tighter US visa restrictions.
content: For China’s elite artificial intelligence researchers, Silicon Valley no longer holds the unrivalled appeal it once did. A growing number are opting to stay home to build their careers, helping China overtake the United States as the leading workplace for top-tier AI talent, according to a study released this week by the think tank Carnegie China. China employed 41 per cent of the world’s leading AI researchers tracked by the study last year, pulling ahead of the US at 34 per cent, according to the study titled “Who’s ahead in the global AI talent race”. That marked a reversal from 2022, when the US held a commanding lead with 46 per cent compared with China’s 27 per cent. Analysts said the findings pointed to a broader shift in the global balance of technological power as Beijing and Washington compete for supremacy in cutting-edge technologies. “It’s both push and pull,” said Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China and co-author of the report, in an interview on Wednesday. China had built a “formidable” domestic AI industry backed by high-profile players such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, where compensation was now “pretty comparable” to that in Silicon Valley, he said. Moonshot AI itself was co-founded by its CEO Yang Zhilin, who earned his PhD at Carnegie Mellon University before returning to China. China also remained the largest source of AI expertise. Last year, 57 per cent of elite AI researchers earned their undergraduate degrees in the country, up 11 percentage points from 2022. By comparison, 13 per cent completed their undergraduate studies in the US, the report showed. Domestic graduates are also increasingly staying put. Among researchers who completed their undergraduate degrees in China, 69 per cent were working in the country last year, up from 57 per cent in 2022. The higher retention rate was likely driven by expanding opportunities in China’s AI industry along with tighter US visa restrictions, according to the study. To measure the movement of “top AI talent”, the study’s authors Ma and Yang Binyi analysed 10,280 researchers, representing about 40 per cent of all authors whose papers were accepted at the 2025 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, one of the world’s leading machine-learning conferences. Despite China’s growing appeal, the US remained the top destination for researchers who do venture abroad. The share of US-based AI researchers who earned their undergraduate degrees in China rose by 4 percentage points last year, showing that American employers continued to attract top Chinese talent seeking opportunities overseas, Ma said. At the same time, researchers face mounting barriers to cross-border mobility as both countries intensify scrutiny of technology transfers and national security risks. For years, Washington has restricted visas for some Chinese graduate students and researchers with links to institutions associated with Beijing’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, citing concerns about technology transfer and intellectual property. Similarly, Beijing imposed new rules on September 15 restricting Chinese citizens who violate export controls from leaving the country for months or years if their actions threaten “national industrial or technology security”. These moves come as Chinese technology companies accelerate efforts to strengthen the domestic AI ecosystem amid tightening US export controls on advanced chips and specialised hardware. Alibaba on Tuesday unveiled what it called “China’s most powerful” AI chip yet as part of a strategy spanning semiconductors, data centres and its Qwen family of AI models. The company also teased plans to train its Qwen 5 AI model using up to 10 trillion parameters – a measure of a model’s scale and complexity. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Opinion | In a US-China world, Asean must do more than avoid choosing sides
description: Following the uneasy truce at the Xi-Trump summit, Asean must go beyond passive hedging and forge middle-power partnerships to secure its autonomy.
content: The good news is, when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in Washington this week, neither chose confrontation. Amid the high pomp and ceremony, what China has called “constructive strategic stability” continues. Even an uneasy truce in great power relations can be useful. Both recognise the considerable incentive to prevent their economic rivalry from spiralling out of control. Even limited understandings can reduce risks in artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies, and many will look for mechanisms that can stabilise the relationship. But that does not mean an end to competition. Washington and Beijing continue to differ over technology, industrial policy, security and the shape of the international order, while Iran and Taiwan remain fraught topics. They have moved away from the broad tariff war waged last year, but targeted restrictions and industrial measures continue. The contest will play out in efforts to win influence and support across our region. As the Xi-Trump summit ends, and Asean leaders prepare for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines, the familiar question arises again: must the region choose between the two? For many years, the answer has been no. Seeking good relations with both and not being drawn too closely into either camp has been the common response. Yet by itself, hedging is no longer sufficient. The challenge for Asean and the wider region is to preserve the ability to make our own choices. There are obvious pressures to align. Security concerns push some countries towards the United States. Economic geography, trade and investment bring others closer to China. Technology restrictions, tariffs, supply-chain policies and defence arrangements can increasingly turn seemingly separate decisions into strategic choices. Picking a side also carries costs. Consider Cambodia, which has an exceptionally close relationship with China. Yet during Cambodia’s border conflict with Thailand last year, Beijing treated both countries as friends, stressing its impartiality. That was understandable for China, as Thailand matters greatly too. But there is a lesson to draw. A close relationship does not necessarily mean a major power will support you when interests diverge. Similarly, consider the Korean peninsula. South Korea is a formal US treaty. Yet Trump’s renewed interest in diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un led to substantial cuts in the US-South Korean Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises. Seoul has not been abandoned, but it is a reminder that great powers will do what great powers do. Alignment is no guarantee that interests will coincide when it matters. Yet not choosing is not enough. Nor does this concern only security. US restrictions on advanced semiconductors and other technologies are directed primarily at competition with China, but increasingly affect third countries. Rules of origin and tariffs put Chinese investment and manufacturing throughout Southeast Asia under scrutiny even as China’s presence in electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy and digital systems deepens. Decisions about technology, investment and manufacturing therefore acquire geopolitical significance. Simply hedging and refusing to choose does not preserve autonomy. Countries need to create more choices with other powers to exercise autonomy in what I call a “Minus 2” world. From time to time, subtract both the US and China from our mental map and ask what everyone else can do together. The possibilities are considerable A Minus 2 world does not mean excluding the US and China. Nor should middle and smaller powers organise a third bloc. The proposition is more modest: from time to time, subtract both the US and China from our mental map and ask what everyone else can do together. The possibilities are considerable. Japan has deep technological and industrial capabilities. South Korea is important in semiconductors, batteries and advanced manufacturing. India has scale and a growing technological base. Europe offers investment, markets and green technologies. Australia has resources, education and security capabilities. Their interests are not identical. Some are US allies. Asean members are diversely oriented. But almost all share one important interest: they do not want every consequential decision to be defined by US-China rivalry. Diversification is often valued in economic terms. Countries and companies diversify markets and suppliers to become more resilient. But there is today a strategic dimension to diversification. A Minus 2 mindset can give smaller countries more choices and agency, and foster more centres of influence. The more either great power pressures others to choose sides, the stronger the incentive for these others to work with one another in a genuinely multipolar world. The coming Asean summit brings that into focus. Of course, this is a platform to engage the US and China. But it should also strengthen relationships that give Asean members greater room for manoeuvre. Many other partners will already be around the table, offering a practical application of how Asean thinks about “centrality”. The group must go beyond merely convening meetings at which the two great powers compete for attention. Asean centrality can connect a wider range of countries with one another and advance practical cooperation. There is already an agenda to build on: concluding the Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement, advancing the Asean power grid and cross-border electricity trading, and strengthening regional supply chains and investment. These are some projects already making progress. They can also provide platforms for deeper partnerships with Japan, South Korea, India, Australia, Europe and others, including in AI and digital technologies, green finance and advanced manufacturing. The Xi-Trump truce may give breathing room. But the initiative must be taken by others in Asia, using that space to deepen connections among themselves. Strategic autonomy is not secured simply by refusing to choose. It grows from having more choices and a Minus 2 perspective. The Asean summit is an opportunity to show the region has agency.

title: Chinese aesthetics abound at Washington summit, from Mao suits to peony trousers
description: While Peng Liyuan has long championed Chinese fashion, this time both delegations took inspiration from traditional designs.
content: Throughout President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, Chinese aesthetics were not confined to first lady Peng Liyuan, long an ambassador of Chinese fashion, but also appeared in the outfits of other senior Chinese officials and even members of the US delegation. At the state dinner in the White House on Thursday, Xi and other senior Chinese officials – including his chief of staff Cai Qi and foreign minister Wang Yi – wore black Mao suits. Notably, while Xi has regularly worn the attire at major diplomatic events, other members of his delegation have typically opted for Western suits. In China, the style is known as a Zhongshan suit, after the early 20th century Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen who popularised the style. Its distinctive features include a turned-down collar, four flap-covered pockets, five buttons down the front and three buttons on each cuff. In 1949, Mao Zedong stood atop Tiananmen Gate clad in a Zhongshan suit when he proclaimed the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Deng Xiaoping wore the suit during his landmark 1979 trip to Washington. That was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese leader since the establishment of diplomatic relations between the US and the People’s Republic. Peng, meanwhile, offered a different expression of Chinese style. When China’s first lady landed at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, she wore a dove-grey dress with a loose-fitting silhouette and sleeves inspired by traditional Chinese tailoring. During her visit to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday, she wore a dark navy mid-length dress with elements of a traditional qipao, paired with a silver brooch at her collarbone. At the state dinner, she switched to a long-sleeved V-neck gown in red, a colour which symbolises good fortune in Chinese culture. The sartorial references to China extended to the US side of the summit. Melania Trump wore black Dolce & Gabbana trousers featuring a peony-motif brocade. In China, the peony is traditionally known as the “king of flowers”. Trump’s eldest daughter, Ivanka Trump, appeared at the White House welcome ceremony on Thursday wearing a robin’s-egg-blue dress created by Chinese designer Guo Pei.

title: Chinese Restaurant Awards 2026: Hong Kong’s Mott 32 takes top spot in Canada
description: Mott 32 locations in Toronto and Vancouver were crowned the best Chinese restaurants in Canada in the 17th edition of the awards.
content: Two overseas branches of Hong Kong’s modern Chinese restaurant Mott 32, located in Toronto and Vancouver, were crowned the best Chinese restaurants in Canada in the 17th edition of the Chinese Restaurant Awards. The awards ceremony, held in the Fairmont Pacific Rim hotel in Vancouver on September 23, saw these restaurants top the ranked 2026 Elite 30 Canada list. Beyond recognising the country’s best Chinese restaurants, the awards also spotlighted 12 signature dishes and honoured both emerging and master chefs. “The Elite 30 recognises the restaurants, regional cuisines and dishes worth discovering across the country,” says Rae Kung, CEO of the Chinese Restaurant Awards. “The Signature Dish [Awards] highlight individual dishes that deserve to be celebrated on a national stage, while our individual honours recognise the people whose culinary talents and leadership are shaping Chinese cooking in Canada.” Mott 32, which first opened in Hong Kong in 2014 with chef Lee Man-sing at the helm, has since expanded to nine cities globally, with more on the horizon. Lee now serves as the group executive chef. While each Mott 32 adheres to the Hong Kong concept and offers some signature dishes, they also embrace local ingredients and craft their own exclusive menu items. In addition to Mott 32, the list also awarded five other restaurants in Metro Vancouver, with the remainder located in Toronto, Montreal and Calgary. During the awards ceremony, several top 10 winners expressed their gratitude to Kung, including chef Samuel Su Wei-jian of Flavourful House in Richmond Hill, Ontario. Named 2025’s Master Chef of the Year, Su delivered a heartfelt speech, acknowledging that while Kung “gave him pressure”, she inspired him to improve further. This encouragement led his restaurant, known for traditional Cantonese dishes, to climb from No 3 to No 2 this year. Meanwhile, Braden Chong of Mimi Chinese and Sunnys Chinese in Toronto was named Rising Star Chef of the Year; Wu Zhenjun of Mott 32 Vancouver was awarded Dim Sum Chef of the Year; and Franky Yeung of Jumbo Lobster and Fishman Lobster in Toronto was named Master Chef of the Year. Looking beyond Canada’s Chinese restaurants Previously focused on Vancouver, the Chinese Restaurant Awards expanded in 2025 to also feature restaurants across Canada and Asia, with input from a team of taste advisers. For 2026, the awards have extended south of the Canadian border to include the United States, primarily spotlighting Chinese restaurants in California. The list was decided by taste advisers including celebrity chef Mei Lin, chef and cookbook author Lucas Sin and Virginia Miller, academy chair for North America’s 50 Best Restaurants. “The US doesn’t have a Chinese restaurant award list,” Kung notes. “There is a perception that Chinese food is cheap, particularly from Chinatown. But in the last few years they have had a new momentum, an evolution you can see in places like Kato [Restaurant in Los Angeles] and The Happy Crane [in San Francisco]. Fu Hui Hua [in San Francisco] offers a tasting menu which Chinese restaurants in Canada don’t have. “The role of the Chinese Restaurant Awards is to shine a spotlight on places that aren’t being seen there.” The inaugural Elite 12 United States list – which is unranked – includes San Francisco’s Four Kings, The Happy Crane, Mister Jiu’s, HK Lounge Bistro and Fu Hui Hua, and Los Angeles’ two-Michelin-starred Kato Restaurant, which serves modern Taiwanese cuisine. James Yeun Leong Parry, chef and owner of The Happy Crane, says it is “an incredible honour” to be on the list just over a year after opening. “It’s exciting because the fact that we’re even creating this list shows how far Chinese food has come in North America,” he says. “As the saying goes, a rising tide lifts all boats. And I think to see established restaurants on the list, but also new restaurants on the list, is nothing but positive for representation in Chinese food.” For the individual accolades, chef-owner Brandon Jew of Mister Jiu’s received Premier Visionary of the Year; the team at HK Lounge Bistro were given Dim Sum Chef of the Year; and Ge Yuezhong of Fu Hui Hua was named Master Chef of the Year. Eric Sze of Wenwen, a Taiwanese restaurant in New York, was named Rising Star Chef of the Year. Celebrating the future of Chinese gastronomy Founded in Canada in 2008, the Chinese Restaurant Awards are the world’s longest-running restaurant awards platform that focuses on highlighting the quality and diversity of Chinese cuisine. Following the awards ceremony, a gala dinner headlined by chef Li Chi-wai and his dim sum chef, Kanny Cheuk Ka-ching, of The Legacy House at Rosewood Hong Kong, alongside local Chinese chefs featured creative dim sum. Li and Cheuk presented items such as sablefish with fungi, beef siu mai, and shrimp and pork wontons featuring 10-year-aged Dongjia tangerine peel. “We use tangerine peel in Cantonese cuisine with meat and seafood. With meat it helps remove the gaminess, and in seafood, the fishy smell,” Li explains. “Tangerine peel in cooking also helps with digestion and adds a nice scent to dishes.” It was Li’s first time in Vancouver and he was pleased to work with such a diverse group of cooks in the kitchen. He also had a chance to sample a few Chinese restaurants. “The taste of the food is from Hong Kong in the 1980s and 90s,” he says. “It immediately takes me back to that time. It’s very comforting.” The honorees of the Asia list will be revealed on October 6, with the winners announced on October 26. title: Trump hails WWII ‘ally’ China as Xi tells of bonds ‘forged in blood and fire’
description: Both leaders repeatedly refer to joint fight against Japan in highlighting history of cooperation and need for common ground.
content: In a surprise nod to shared history, US President Donald Trump called China a World War II ally as he welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday ahead of summit talks. But the historical reference was far from one-sided, with both leaders repeatedly referring to the joint fight against Japanese aggression as they sought to emphasise the long history of US-China friendship and the need to seek common ground. “If we focus on our common interests, I’m confident there is much we can achieve,” Trump said in the White House foyer during the state welcome ceremony ahead of formal talks with the Chinese president. “The pursuit of those common interests has connected our people across the vast oceans, across big tremendous distances, and many differences, and even made us allies in World War II,” he noted. Trump went on to praise the “brave American pilots” of the Flying Tigers who had volunteered to “fight for China’s survival”, and said that he was happy to work with Xi in the same way. “Just as our people worked together to win that war, President Xi and I will continue working together to forge a better future for both of our nations,” he said. The Flying Tigers were American volunteer pilots who came to China in 1941 to fight Japanese forces alongside Chinese troops, before the US formally entered the second world war. They flew fighter missions against Japanese aircraft and helped to defend Chinese cities and supply routes during the conflict. “They were just unbelievable,” Trump said. His remarks came days after Japan – now a US treaty ally – renewed its call to remove the “former enemy state” clause from the UN Charter, and after Trump’s talks in New York with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The clause “must be deleted”, Takaichi told the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22, pointing to a 2005 consensus resolution where world leaders had “resolved” to remove it. The clause allowed allied states to act against defeated World War II enemy states without UN Security Council approval, but has been declared obsolete by the world body twice - in 1995 and 2005. While Trump made no direct reference to Japan, Xi was more forthcoming – explicitly naming the country as he underlined China-US friendship forged in “blood and fire” during the war. “During the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, Chinese soldiers and civilians rescued hundreds of American pilots at the cost of hundreds of thousands of Chinese lives,” he said during Thursday’s state dinner. “Such a friendship, forged in blood and fire, will surely live on through the generations.” Xi also recalled the wartime “Hump” aerial resupply route over the Himalayas, citing the perilous joint operation as a testament to how the two countries united to sustain Chinese resistance against Japan. The Hump became a vital lifeline for China after Japanese forces severed the Burma Road in 1942, cutting off military and humanitarian supplies, while Chinese soldiers and civilians helped to rescue hundreds of American pilots forced down along the route. That cooperation came at a heavy cost for China, which suffered enormous civilian losses during the war, Xi noted. It was the second time Xi had drawn on their shared history within hours. During the state welcome ceremony in the morning, he noted how soldiers on both sides had “fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression” “[The] Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people,” he asserted. The timing of the remark was particularly sensitive, given Japan’s stepped-up calls to remove the UN “enemy state” clause following its recent invocation by Chinese and Russian officials as tensions with Tokyo escalate. Reacting to Takaichi’s speech at the General Assembly, the Chinese foreign ministry said on Wednesday that the clauses were “a legal mechanism in the UN Charter. For 81 years, these clauses have served to prevent the resurgence of fascism and militarism and defend the post-war international order. They are still relevant today.” Trump’s use of the word “allies” in describing past US-China cooperation against Japan caused unease among Japanese media. The Japan Times, for example, said the remarks were “likely to raise eyebrows in Tokyo, a US ally currently embroiled in a festering dispute with Beijing and facing pressure from Trump on both trade and defence issues”. China-Japan ties have been marked by recurring tensions over Japan’s wartime occupation and atrocities in China, as well as disputes over Tokyo’s handling of that history. Relations sharply deteriorated last year after Takaichi said that a Taiwan contingency could be a survival-threatening situation for Japan, justifying a military response. Beijing demanded an apology and imposed a slew of retaliatory measures, including curbs on rare earth exports. Takaichi met Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 22, just ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington. According to NHK News, she told Trump that she wanted to “seize the opportunity to demonstrate to the world” the strength of the US-Japan alliance. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In Washington, Xi also highlighted the shared economic and cultural history of the two nations, tracing the relationship to America’s earliest years. After the US gained independence, it “turned its eyes to China”, Xi said in his dinner address. The two countries began trading, he said, “exchanging goods to meet each other’s needs and draw on our complementary strengths”. George Washington, he noted, had personally acquired a large collection of Chinese porcelain. Xi then fast-forwarded to 1971, when “ping pong diplomacy” and the “political wisdom embodied in a small ball moving the globe” helped Mao Zedong, founder of the People’s Republic of China, and then-US president Richard Nixon open the door to rapprochement. The redwoods Nixon later sent as a state gift “took root in Zhejiang province, where I worked for several years”, Xi added. Trump’s speech was similarly filled with historical references to US-China friendship, as the gala dinner capped a day of pageantry, politics and protocol. “President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said. “Together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations.” Trump invoked figures and events ranging from Sun Yat-sen, the founding father of modern China, to America’s declaration of freedom 250 years ago. “Long ago, European explorers first discovered the American continent as they searched for a new way to reach China in the East,” Trump said, as he spoke about the first formal Chinese delegation to travel to the US and China’s first state dinner in Washington. Despite the early historical reflections, including one about the first trade ships arriving on the banks of the Pearl River from New York, Trump took a midpoint detour to focus on the White House ballroom renovations – a frequent talking point for the president. Going admittedly “off script”, Trump invited guests in the East Room to take a look at the new White House ballroom “in honour of President Xi and Madame Peng”, despite the project still being under construction. The new ballroom would host more than 1,000 people, substantially more than the East Room, Trump said, claiming US presidents had wanted this for more than 150 years. Trump then returned to the symbolism, gifting Xi a sculpture of a bald eagle that he said was made by an American artist and designed by him and the first lady, Melania Trump. “The bald eagle is a national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America, and we hope it will find a nice place, a wonderful place in Beijing,” Trump added. The bald eagle has been featured on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782. It was officially designated the national bird of the US when Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden signed an act of Congress into law in December 2024. In his closing remarks, Trump returned to history, referencing America’s 250th anniversary, marked on July 4 this year. He raised a toast to his Chinese counterpart and his wife, as well as the long relationship between China and America that had bridged “thousands of miles and spanned hundreds of years”. “May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace, and success,” Trump said. The speeches were made to a packed room of invitees, including Chinese and US government officials, American business leaders and some Supreme Court justices. Several prominent American CEOs made the guest list, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk, but no Chinese business leaders were present. This stood in stark contrast to the Beijing summit in May, when Trump brought a delegation of nearly 20 top executives, many of whom were spotted at the state banquet hosted by Xi.

title: Xi presses Trump to take the next step on Taiwan: oppose independence
description: The change would mean a shift in Washington’s long-standing position and affect American arms sales to the island, according to analysts.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping pressed his US counterpart Donald Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence – a call that would require a shift in Washington’s long-standing position and further restraint on American arms sales to the island, according to analysts. During the meeting between the two leaders on Thursday, Xi said he hoped the US side would “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, according to a statement from the foreign ministry in Beijing. The wording marked another push by Beijing for Washington to adopt an explicit and tougher political position against Taiwan independence, going beyond its traditional formulation of “not supporting” independence – a notable distinction given the high stakes in cross-strait relations. The White House did not immediately release details of its own account of the exchange. “The call for the US government to oppose ‘Taiwan independence’ has long been a demand of the Chinese side,” said Shao Yuqun, director of the Institute for Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies. On the sidelines of an Apec summit in Lima in November 2024, Xi also urged then US president Joe Biden to “explicitly oppose” Taiwan independence and support China’s peaceful reunification. Now, Shao said, the demand had become more pressing as Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party authorities had pursued a “two-state theory” in a more provocative and explicit manner. “Beijing has become more determined in urging the US government not to send wrong signals to the DPP authorities or ‘Taiwan independence’ forces on the island,” she said. During his meeting with Trump, Xi also called on the US to “handle the Taiwan question prudently”, saying this would help “lay a solid foundation for China-US strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations”. “The call to ‘oppose Taiwan independence’ and to ‘handle the Taiwan question prudently’ also implies that the United States should exercise caution and restraint over arms sales to Taiwan,” Shao said. While the foreign ministry did not refer to US arms sales to Taiwan in its statement, Shao said the issue remained one of the most immediate and consequential points of contention regarding the Taiwan question. The Trump administration approved an US$11 billion arms package for Taiwan last year, while a separate package worth about US$14 billion has been held up for months. Trump has described the pending sale as a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing. As Beijing sees it, the Taiwan question is increasingly linked to the broader foundation of China-US strategic stability and cooperation, observers say. “What is notable this time is that the section on Taiwan also mentions China-US strategic cooperation,” Zhu Songling, a Taiwan affairs specialist at Beijing Union University, said. “It emphasises that properly handling the Taiwan question is an important foundation for developing bilateral relations.” At their summit in Beijing in May, Xi warned Trump about the risk of conflict over Taiwan, saying that if the issue was not handled properly it could lead to clashes or even conflict between China and the United States. Trump said after the summit that he was “not looking to have somebody go independent” on Taiwan. Zhu said Xi’s latest wording went beyond avoiding conflict over Taiwan and was more of “a specific requirement for Washington’s political position”, adding that it was rare for Xi to call on Trump to “oppose” Taiwan independence. He said the use of “adhere to” also stressed “continuity” and seemed to be an appeal to the US to reduce swings in its Taiwan policy over what Beijing saw as erroneous signals. During his visit, Xi also called for the two militaries to maintain regular dialogue and improve mechanisms for “crisis communication and prevention”. While Xi did not explicitly link the mechanism to a potential crisis around Taiwan, such mechanisms are seen as key to communication over potential flashpoints such as the Taiwan Strait and the South China Sea. Wang Jianmin, a Taiwan affairs analyst at Minnan Normal University in Fujian province, said the United States was unlikely to explicitly say that it opposed Taiwan independence because doing so would not be consistent with US long-standing policy. “But it may warn [Taiwanese leader William] Lai Ching-te against taking risky actions and urge him not to create tensions or provoke incidents,” Wang said. Against the broader backdrop of US-China relations, Washington might also hold back on further arms sales to Taiwan in the short term, Wang said, but the risk of additional sales remained over the longer term. Not supporting means you do nothing. Opposing means you do something to oppose Shi Yinhong, Renmin University Regarding Xi’s call to oppose Taiwan independence, Shi Yinhong from Renmin University said Xi’s use of “adhere to” implied that Beijing saw opposition to Taiwan independence as an existing US position – something neither Trump nor previous US administrations had explicitly adopted. There was a distinction between the two wordings, Shi said. “Not supporting means you do nothing. Opposing means you do something to oppose,” he said. “Trump and his administration have never, at any point so far, declared that he or the US government opposes Taiwan independence, nor have his predecessors,” Shi said. Lyle Morris, senior fellow on foreign policy and national security at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said on social media that Beijing was trying to suggest that opposition to “Taiwan independence” was already an established US position that Washington should “maintain”, which he said was not. “It’s incumbent on Washington to restate long-standing US policy on Taiwan and refute this framing,” Morris said.

title: Hong Kong teacher jailed for 3 years for molesting pupil during free tutoring
description: Maths teacher, 31, also found to have taken intimate photos of nine-year-old boy and another victim, aged six.
content: A Hong Kong teacher clinically evaluated as a paedophile has been jailed for three years for molesting a primary school pupil and taking intimate pictures of the child and another boy during volunteer tutoring. Deputy District Judge Ko Wai-hung on Friday sentenced the 31-year-old, who earlier admitted to sexually abusing a student in his Yuen Long flat between January 2022 and July 2024. The pupil was aged nine when the first assault took place. The defendant, a maths teacher who was identified in court by his initials CWH, also abused a six-year-old pupil in November 2024. Two psychiatric reports submitted to the District Court for sentencing said the defendant, who was diagnosed with autism, had a sexual interest in children. One psychiatrist concluded that the defendant had pedophilic disorder and had a high risk of reoffending. The defendant had used social media to offer free maths lessons to students from low-income families. The mothers of the two victims signed up their children. Citing impact reports, Ko noted that the first victim, who also has autism, had suffered emotional distress after the abuse that had spanned more than two years. The court documents revealed that the defendant had forced the child to watch porn with him during the lessons. On two occasions, he molested the pupil and took a total of nine pictures of the assaults. In November 2024, the pupil told a clinical psychologist in a routine assessment consultation that the defendant had made him look at “children’s pictures” multiple times. After further investigation, the pupil said the pictures were intimate photos. Police were alerted and subsequently arrested the defendant. Upon search, the officer discovered several pictures of the intimate parts of a younger child who was later identified as the second victim. The defendant pleaded guilty to four charges in relation to the indecent assaults and another four for producing and possessing child pornography. In sentencing, Ko said the offence involved a serious breach of trust. “Showing child pornography to a child could absolutely distort his views on sex and values,” he said. While noting that the clinical reports recommended that the defendant undergo treatment for paedophilic disorder, Ko said the court would not order such sessions to be compulsory in the remainder of his sentence. The defendant had been remanded in custody for more than 20 months and could potentially receive remission – a reduction of up to one-third of a prison sentence – if granted by the correctional authorities. He might serve two to three months in prison after sentencing. Ko said he was not sure the defendant could complete the treatment because of the brief imprisonment. The Sexual Conviction Record Check (SCRC) scheme was expanded last December, allowing organisations to screen criminal records related to sexual offences committed by volunteers, including teachers and sports coaches. The scheme was initially launched at the end of 2011, allowing organisations to check prospective employees, contract renewal staff and outsourced service providers for convictions related to a specified list of sexual offences. The decision to expand the programme followed recommendations made by the Law Reform Commission in May 2022, which advocated extending it to all existing employees, self-employed individuals and volunteers.

title: China and the US are racing ahead on AI. Can they manage risks together?
description: Beijing and Washington told to tackle rising AI threats together at Singapore forum, but some argue fears about runaway technology are overblown.
content: The United States and China must work together to establish safety guardrails for artificial intelligence, leading scholars and industry leaders said at a Singapore forum, warning that rapid advances in the technology demand stronger risk controls. Speaking at the FutureChina Business Forum on Friday, Jude Blanchette, managing director of consultancy Macro Advisory Partners, urged the two superpowers to find common ground despite escalating geopolitical tensions. “If ever there was a moment for [the US and China] to feel a strong impetus to come together, it would be now … given the shared concerns about the impact of emerging technologies, not only AI but also robotics,” Blanchette said. He argued that the world was moving from an era shaped by traditional human behaviour to a “technocene” in which exponential technological leaps would dramatically reshape global power dynamics. The annual two-day forum was organised by Business China, a non-profit organisation launched in 2007 by Singapore’s founding prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, to strengthen ties and promote dialogue across the region. The call for bilateral coordination comes as President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump placed AI risks at the forefront of their tech agenda during a state visit in Washington. In speeches at the White House on Thursday, both leaders stressed the need to manage the technology’s dangers, with Xi emphasising that AI must always remain under human control. At the Singapore forum, computer scientist Zhang Hongjiang, a distinguished visiting professor at Tsinghua University in Beijing, compared current competition in AI with the nuclear arms race during the Cold War. “We should abandon the zero-sum way of thinking,” Zhang said. “It really has to be a coordinated effort, just like what the entire world did together on nuclear weapon control.” Zhang called for high levels of investment in AI model evaluation and safety monitoring, citing a high-profile security breach in July when OpenAI systems escaped their supposedly isolated sandboxed environment and hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face. “The models today have capabilities that are beyond what we designed for,” he warned. Cynthia Zhang, founder of Hong Kong-based venture firm FutureX Capital, echoed these concerns, noting that AI capabilities had developed “way ahead of” what policymakers could handle. However, some business executives at the event pushed back against calls from several Silicon Valley leaders to slow down AI development. Liang Xinjun, co-founder of Chinese conglomerate Fosun Group, dismissed fears of runaway technology as overblown. “At the current stage, over-anxiety over AI and even the thought to freeze and stop it are very foolish,” Liang said on a Thursday panel, arguing that AI had already driven rapid gains in global productivity and that stalling its development would mean abandoning future economic growth. For some tech companies, navigating strict governance requirements has become a central business strategy rather than a hurdle. Wu Gansha, co-founder and CEO of Chinese autonomous driving firm Uisee Technology, said complying with stringent government data and safety regulations had given the company a unique competitive edge. While Uisee expanded its fleet of fully driverless tractors at Singapore’s Changi Airport to 20 units this year, up from just one in 2023 and two in 2024, it spent a full year modifying its products to satisfy local regulatory standards, Wu said. “Building a solid foundation for data security and compliance requires a significant upfront investment of time and resources that cannot be avoided,” Wu said on the sidelines of the forum, noting that standards vary globally, from Singapore’s framework to Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation. “Once these capabilities are established, expanding into new markets becomes far less resource-intensive,” Wu added. “High initial compliance investments are an advantage for businesses, as they help create strong competitive barriers to entry.”

title: Trump’s warm welcome for Xi met with caution and uncertainty in Taiwan
description: Observers say elaborate ceremonies in Washington should not be seen as proof of shifting US policy towards Taipei.
content: Taiwanese officials and observers have reacted cautiously to the Washington summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, with uncertainty lingering over what the two leaders discussed about the island. The only public mention of Taiwan after Thursday’s closed-door talks between the pair came from Beijing’s official statement, which said Xi had urged Trump to “oppose ‘Taiwan independence’” and “handle the Taiwan question with caution”. The White House did not immediately give its own detailed account of the exchange. The summit – the second between Trump and Xi in five months after their May meeting in Beijing – was closely watched in Taiwan, where the elaborate reception for Xi fuelled debate about Trump’s desire to strengthen his personal relationship with the Chinese leader. Trump and first lady Melania Trump personally greeted Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, a departure from presidential protocol. The ceremony featured a red carpet, military honours and a flyover by US military aircraft, while the White House reception culminated in a state dinner attended by more than 130 guests, including leading US technology executives. The spectacle received extensive coverage in Taiwan, with local television stations and news outlets closely following Xi’s arrival and summit. But analysts cautioned against interpreting the ceremonial treatment alone as evidence of a shift in US policy. Chang Wu-ueh, a cross-strait studies expert at Tamkang University in New Taipei City, said the reception reflected Trump’s emphasis on his personal relationship with Xi but was also aimed at encouraging Beijing to respond to Washington’s demands on trade, artificial intelligence and rare earths. “The last time Trump went to Beijing, the mainland gave him an extremely elaborate reception. This time Trump was essentially returning the favour,” Chang said. Dennis Lu-chung Weng, an associate professor of political science at Sam Houston State University in Texas, said the airport welcome showed Trump wanted the summit to succeed and was prepared to go the extra mile to create the right atmosphere. But for Taiwan, the more important question was what happened after “the red carpet was rolled up” – particularly what Trump said about Taiwan and whether US policy subsequently changed. Taipei has been especially concerned about a pending US$14 billion arms package, which has already been delayed as Washington works to manage its relations with Beijing. James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based diplomacy and strategic studies scholar, said Trump appeared increasingly determined to prevent Taiwan from becoming an obstacle to agreements with Beijing. “Although Trump did not directly respond to Xi’s reminder, he has increasingly recognised the sensitivity and strategic importance of the Taiwan issue,” Chen said. He argued that because the summit was intended to reinforce stability in US-China relations, Trump had sought to downplay Taipei’s role in bilateral interactions and reduce the island’s visibility in the strategic dialogue. Chen pointed to the delayed arms package and the US’ reported requests for Taiwanese officials to scale back visits to Washington as signs the administration was seeking to minimise friction over Taiwan. “From China’s perspective, the Taiwan issue remains non-negotiable and Trump has shown no indication that he is prepared to trade Taiwan for a broader strategic concession,” he said. Chen said the Lai administration should recognise the changing dynamics and adopt a restrained posture to avoid further marginalising Taiwan. He expected the arms package to remain pending until after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the mainland Chinese city of Shenzhen and the G20 summit in Florida, which Trump and Xi were likely to attend. Wu Chih-chung, the island’s deputy foreign minister, said Taiwan’s National Security Council and foreign ministry had conducted scenario planning before the summit. He said that ensuring the arms purchases proceeded smoothly was “one of the things we are working hardest on at present”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio added to the debate this week when he said the administration had to weigh arms sales against US military requirements around the world, weapons inventories and the capacity of the US defence industry. His remarks prompted politicians from Taiwan’s main opposition Kuomintang party to question whether the weapons would arrive according to the island’s preferred timetable. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun said on Friday that the summit showed that even amid intense economic, technological and strategic competition, Washington and Beijing were prepared to maintain dialogue and negotiate in pursuit of their own interests. She called on the administration of Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te to similarly restore cross-strait communication while strengthening the island’s defences. “Strengthening defence and reducing hostility are not contradictory,” Cheng said, adding that Taiwan should not have to choose between being “pro-US” and “pro-China”. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party sought to play down concerns that Taiwan could become a bargaining chip between the two super powers. DPP legislator Wang Ting-yu described Trump and Xi as “dancing a diplomatic tango” in the process of negotiating leverage. But he noted that Washington had joined Tokyo and Seoul before the summit in reiterating the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and opposing changes to the status quo by force. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Huang Kwei-bo, a diplomacy professor at National Chengchi University in Taipei, said the summit “appeared intended to consolidate US-China mutual trust rather than produce policy breakthroughs”. For Taipei, he said, an important point was that there was “no apparent new US concession over its one-China policy or the three US-China joint communiques” despite Xi reiterating Beijing’s position on Taiwan independence.

title: Xi Jinping marks second Mid-Autumn Festival in US during state visit
description: On the holiday symbolic of unity, China’s leader is expected to attend a private presidential tea and tour America’s founding documents.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping has not only made history as the first Chinese leader to undertake two formal state visits to the United States, he is also the only Chinese leader to be spending two Mid-Autumn Festivals on American soil. Xi offered festive greetings during his toast at Thursday’s state banquet. “As I speak, my compatriots in China are celebrating Mid-Autumn Festival – a cherished occasion for family reunions according to Chinese tradition. I wish you all a very happy Mid-Autumn Festival, and my best wishes to you and your families.” Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan arrived at Maryland’s Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, making good on an invitation US President Donald Trump extended during his trip to Beijing in May. The Chinese presidential couple received an unusually lavish welcome from Trump on the tarmac, ahead of a Thursday morning White House reception that included a Rose Garden military review and ceremonial events. Trump and Xi then held talks on technology, trade and resources, while the first ladies went for a tour of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art. The four later reconvened at the White House for a state dinner. On Friday, Xi is expected to attend a private tea involving the presidential couples and be given a tour of America’s founding documents. Friday is also China’s Mid-Autumn Festival, a holiday season that also coincided with the Chinese leader’s last state visit to the US, in 2015. During that trip, Xi and Peng landed in Seattle, where they celebrated the festival four days in advance with the Chinese community there. Xi delivered a speech that touched on homesickness and shared cultural roots, turning a busy foreign itinerary into a moment of nostalgia far from Beijing. “On festive occasions, our thoughts turn all the more to our loved ones,” Xi said at the time, quoting Wang Wei, a Tang dynasty (618-907) poet. “I know that all of you here miss your motherland and relatives thousands of miles away, and the motherland and your families back home also hold every overseas compatriot dear to their hearts,” he added. Xi further expressed high expectations for “overseas Chinese” to serve as a bridge between China and the US, contributing to “the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation”. He encouraged them to integrate into American mainstream society, facilitate mutually beneficial cooperation and promote Chinese culture. On the day of the festival in 2015, while in New York for the United Nations General Assembly following their visit to Washington, Xi and Peng joined local Chinese communities to mark the occasion and share mooncakes, a traditional festive pastry. The two voiced their gratitude for the communities’ support of China’s development. Around the time of the Mid-Autumn Festival, Xi has often carried out official duties, such as conducting inspection tours at a local level, and extended wishes to the public for peace, health and happiness. Chinese state media also frequently use the holiday to highlight Xi’s past remarks on patriotism and cultural heritage, drawing on a period deeply symbolic of unity. The media retrospectives focus on the harmony between home and country, a theme Xi has expounded upon on many occasions. In widely quoted remarks to a 2016 meeting of the National Conference of Model Families, Xi said: “A prosperous and strong nation and the national rejuvenation are embodied by the happiness of the families and the improvement of hundreds of millions of people’s lives. A nation can do well only when families do well.”

title: Italy to ban burkas in schools, with 30% cap on pupils with poor Italian
description: The move comes ahead of Italy’s election next year, in which PM Meloni’s party faces pressure the even further right National Future party.
content: Italy has passed a decree banning face coverings in all schools and capping the proportion of newly arrived foreign pupils with insufficient Italian at 30 per cent per class from the next school year, the government in Rome said on Friday. The government said the 30 per cent quota applies in primary school to children who do not hold Italian citizenship, were not born in Italy and have not attended an Italian kindergarten for at least two years. In secondary schools the same rules apply, except that pupils must have attended Italian schools for at least three years – rather than two years of kindergarten – to fall outside the 30 per cent quota. On face coverings, the decree states that these are not permitted and that the face must be recognisable. The measure is likely aimed primarily at full-face Islamic veils for girls such as the burka and niqab. No government figures were given on how many children the rule could affect. “Organising classes so that they are, let’s say, balanced, is a tool that benefits everyone and promotes integration,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said. She had already announced the controversial rules the previous week at a youth event held by her far-right Brothers of Italy party. Her Cabinet has now adopted the measures by decree. Meloni has led Italy’s three-party coalition of far-right and conservative parties since 2022. The 49-year-old ran a successful election campaign at the time on a promise of a tough line against migrants. The new rules do not only affect children. Parents with significant language difficulties may also be required to take Italian lessons if communication with the school is impaired. The decree provides that schools must notify youth welfare offices if parents have significant language difficulties. Social services can then offer free Italian courses. Anyone who fails to comply with the newly enacted rules faces a fine. Italian media report fines of between €200 and €1,000 (US$228-US$1,139) that could be imposed on parents. There has been criticism from the education sector over the practical difficulties of implementing the plans. One union described the decree as “propagandistic” and said it failed to address the real problems facing schools. Italy holds elections next year. In the polls, Meloni and her party lead all others. In recent weeks, however, her coalition has come under increasing pressure from the newly formed National Future party of former general Roberto Vannacci. Vannacci’s party stands even further to the right and demands an even tougher approach to migration.

title: Dog rescuers vow to microchip after charges, decry punishing ‘those trying to help’
description: Advocates urge comprehensive trap-neuter-return scheme after shelter founder charged over licence following fatal Yuen Long dog attack.
content: Hong Kong animal welfare activists say they will forge ahead with microchipping stray dogs despite the heightened legal risk after authorities charged an advocate who engaged in the practice during an investigation into the death of a cyclist. The advocates argued that charging dog rescuers was counterproductive and renewed their calls to implement a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme, while the government said allegations it engaged in “convenience culling” were untrue. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has also said that sterilisation alone was not enough to eliminate the public safety risk posed by unowned and uncontrolled dogs. The department late on Thursday announced it had concluded a joint dog capture operation in Yuen Long following the suspected fatal mauling of a 27-year-old cyclist. During the five-day operation, authorities captured eight unattended dogs, three of which were microchipped. They also laid charges against Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of the Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, for failing to keep a dog under proper control and for keeping a canine with an expired licence. The dog – a 13-year-old mongrel named “Dai B” – was microchipped by Luk and registered in his name, although the animal’s license expired in 2021. Luk previously told the South China Morning Post that he microchipped dogs because without doing so, he believed the animals would be euthanised. According to local media reports, Luk has thousands of stray dogs registered under his name and has paid fines of up to HK$3,000 (US$382) hundreds of times. Rescuers said the practice of animal shelter operators microchipping stray dogs in their own names was commonplace before the heightened scrutiny. Jacqueline Cheung, founder of the non-profit Love Adopt Animal Society, said that over the past 10 years she had personally microchipped more than 100 dogs. Rather than being discouraged by the enforcement action, she said that she and other volunteers were even more motivated to take in stray dogs and microchip them. She said she had not been fined by authorities, but she was willing to pay the penalty if she were. “All lives should be cherished,” she said. “So we are willing to keep doing it even with the extra stress and pressure.” April Yip, founder of Home for Homeless Dogs, said her organisation had also microchipped about 100 dogs and that she herself had faced court summonses at least three times this year. She said the choice to chip stray dogs was to support elderly villagers who could not afford the cost, as well as deal with brownfield site operators who “refuse legal responsibility” for their animals. “Treating rescuers who step up to provide accountability as criminals is counterproductive and punishes those trying to help,” she said. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the department said it urged people caring for dogs to “operate within the established regulatory framework”. It said the microchip and licensing regime was designed to ensure every dog had an identifiable keeper who exercised proper control. The department also denied in the Thursday statement that it engaged in what some activists have described as “convenience culling,” or that it euthanises dogs after just four days if they are unclaimed by an owner. “The AFCD solemnly clarifies that these claims are untrue,” it said. It said that if dogs it captured were unclaimed, staff would observe the animal. Dogs that were in good health and had a gentle temperament would be transferred to partner animal welfare organisations, it said. The process could take several weeks to several months, it added. According to official statistics previously provided to the SCMP, in the first three months of the year the department captured 105 stray dogs. Over the same period, the department said it had humanely euthanised 102 dogs, but that figure included strays as well as pets given up by their owners or animals involved in other cases. The department said it did not keep separate statistics for the number of strays euthanised alone. It also handed 47 dogs over to animal welfare organisations, while 66 were reclaimed by owners. Rescuer Yip urged authorities to establish a comprehensive “trap, neuter, release” programme, as well as allocate land for a dedicated animal sanctuary for those animals that could not be rehomed. The department ran a “trap, neuter, release” pilot project for three years between 2015 and 2018. Upon its conclusion, it said the project “did not meet the original performance targets” but allowed organisations to apply to run their own programmes. After the conclusion of the latest operation in Yuen Long, the AFCD said that in a high-density urban environment such as Hong Kong, sterilisation alone could not completely eliminate the risks posed by unowned and uncontrolled dogs. Instead, the department said it would continue to take a “multipronged” approach in line with international standards set by the World Organisation for Animal Health, an intergovernmental organisation headquartered in Paris. “This includes promoting responsible pet ownership and proper animal care through publicity and education, as well as collaborating with animal welfare organisations to promote sterilisation and adoption,” it said.

title: After 50,000km, British around-the-world walker faces final hurdle – at his home doorstep
description: Ex-paratrooper Karl Bushby set off on his adventure from his home 28 years ago with the rule that he would not use any form of transport.
content: After 28 years and 50,000 kilometres (31,000 miles), a British adventurer is facing one last hurdle in his bid to trek home from South America without using any form of transport: the Channel. “We thought we got permission to swim from the coast of France. Turned out that is not the case,” Karl Bushby, a former paratrooper, said as he walked towards Cap Blanc-Nez in northern France, within sight of the white cliffs of the English coast. “There was some internal confusion. So, right now we’re scrambling in a kind of semi-panicked state.” The 57-year-old had originally hoped to use a service corridor in the Channel Tunnel on foot, but he said the authorities seemed “set against” this idea.
