So he resigned himself to swimming from Calais, even though he “hates” it. “I say I swim like a cat dropped in a bathtub. It’s not funny. It’s bad. But you just do what you’ve got to do,” he said. At an earlier stage of the journey he took 30 days to cross the Caspian Sea with a mixture of swimming and floating, resting – but not advancing – on a boat. He hoped to get permission to swim across the Channel, one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, before October 1, after which the winter weather would make the crossing too risky. When he set off in November 1998, Bushby set himself two rules: to not use any form of transport to advance, and to not return home – near Hull in northern England – except on foot. As he travels, he pushes a cart containing all his belongings that he nicknamed “the Beast”. Over three decades, he has paused his journey several times. Moscow refused him a visa for a long time, unhappy that he had crossed the Bering Strait separating Alaska from far eastern Russia on foot – something he said no one had ever done before. Between them, Bushby estimated, visa woes, the 2008 financial crisis, and then the Covid-19 pandemic have accounted for about 14 of his 28 years on the road. At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably in Mexico, then once the situation cleared, he would resume his journey at the exact spot where he had left off. As he nears England, Bushby looks back nostalgically on the very start of the adventure, on his trek up through the Andes and the difficult crossing of the Darien jungle between Colombia and Panama. “Then slowly but surely it becomes a job. You get older, it gets harder,” he said. Bushby is the subject of a documentary currently in preparation, and once the journey is complete he plans to devote himself to the film and to giving talks. “I’ve got to try and get established in the grown-up world again, because I’m going to arrive home with nothing,” he said. But first there is the Channel to cross, and despite the challenge, Bushby is optimistic. “I think we can work it out. If not, I’m living in France for the rest of my life!” he said.

title: Chinese RISC-V chipmaker Eswin seeks US$300m in Hong Kong IPO ahead of October debut
description: Revenue reached 2.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 20 per cent year on year, but net losses for the year stood at 1.5 billion yuan.
content: Beijing Eswin Computing Technology will start soliciting orders from institutional and public investors on Monday ahead of its Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), aiming to raise around US$300 million, according to people familiar with the matter. The Chinese chipmaker had already started gauging investor interest, with trading expected to start on October 8, said one of the people, who asked not to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue. The Beijing-headquartered company had earlier passed its listing hearing with bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, clearing the final regulatory hurdle for a listing in the city. Citic Securities (Hong Kong) and China Securities (International) Corporate Finance Company are the joint sponsors. With the listing process ongoing, details such as size and timing may change, the people said. Eswin Computing Technology’s parent company, Eswin Group, was founded by Wang Dongsheng, founder of flat panel display giant BOE Technology. Wang is widely recognised as the “father” of China’s LCD industry. The parent group has been spinning off and listing several businesses in recent years. Its 12-inch silicon wafer-producing subsidiary, Xi’an Eswin Material Technology, debuted on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-style Star Market in October 2025 and has a market capitalisation exceeding 120 billion yuan (US$17.9 billion). Eswin Computing Technology specialises in system-on-chip (SoC) products built on the open-source RISC-V architecture. Its customers are mainly in sectors such as artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) and consumer electronics, according to its IPO filings. The filing showed that the company remained loss-making. Revenue reached 2.4 billion yuan in 2025, up 20 per cent year on year, but net losses for the year stood at 1.5 billion yuan. Management expects further losses this year due to heavy spending on research and development. The company said it planned to use proceeds from the IPO to develop new chip products and iterate existing ones, as well as enhance the capabilities of its hardware-software integrated platform. It would also search for potential strategic mergers and acquisitions and further promote the RISC-V ecosystem.

title: Why did Xi and China’s first lady bring their own flasks to White House banquet?
description: While it may have been unexpected for some, vacuum flasks usually filled with hot water are an everyday sight in China.
content: Amid the polished silverware and fine crystal stemware on display at the state dinner in the White House on Thursday sat the vacuum flasks brought by Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan. The couple’s flasks, black for Xi and white for Peng, were spotted on their table during the formal dinner, signalling a subtle self-assurance as cultural authenticity met high diplomacy. Extending this everyday practice to the White House banquet was in tune with the host nation’s own eccentricity. US President Donald Trump’s fondness for Diet Coke – summoned via a dedicated red button on his Oval Office desk – is legendary. The sight was unexpected in a formal state setting, yet deeply familiar to those with experience of Chinese culture. In China, many people carry vacuum flasks filled with hot beverages once they pass a certain age, as warm liquids are thought to be better for digestion according to traditional Chinese medicine principles. Often, these flasks also contain herbs or berries believed to have medicinal value, such as goji berries. While it is unclear what Xi and Peng’s flasks contained, this is the most likely answer. The national devotion to warm drinks is built into China’s public infrastructure. Every domestic high-speed railway station, airport terminal and public rest stop across the country comes equipped with free, dedicated boiling-water taps, allowing commuters and travellers to refill their flasks on the go. Many Chinese tourists who travel to Western nations also carry their own vacuum flasks, allowing them to skip iced water or other chilled beverages. A preference for traditional hot beverages is also a feature of China’s domestic political routine. During major political gatherings in Beijing, such as the annual parliamentary meetings, the Chinese president is routinely flanked by two distinct teacups on his desk – a unique arrangement that sets him apart from other senior officials, who typically receive a single cup refilled periodically by attendants.

title: The Chinese roots of ‘gung-ho’ as Trump and Xi look to shared history
description: Trump’s mention of a ‘Chinese phrase’ may have puzzled some, but the US Marine Corps adopted gung-ho from the name of wartime cooperatives.
content: Chinese viewers watching Donald Trump welcome Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday may have been puzzled by the US president’s reference to the “Chinese phrase” gung-ho. Turning to Baidu – or increasingly, Doubao, the country’s most popular AI chatbot – they may well have asked: what Chinese expression is he referring to? It sounds Chinese, but gung-ho is neither part of everyday usage nor an idiom drawn from classical texts – making this moment almost as baffling as when US Secretary of State Marco Rubio used the phrase “unleash Chiang [Kai-shek]” while discussing an escalation of strikes on Iran. The word does have a genuine Chinese origin though. Gung-ho, or in pinyin, gong he (工合) is short for gongye hezuoshe (工业合作社) – literally, “industrial cooperatives”. These were grass-roots labour units set up in China in 1938 to produce small industrial supplies to support the war effort against the Japanese. The term was introduced into the English language by Evans Carlson, a US Marine Corps officer who served as a military observer of Chinese resistance forces in 1937-38. Impressed by the cooperative spirit of the workers, Carlson inaccurately interpreted the organisational acronym as a cooperative motto meaning “work together – work in harmony”. Later, as commander of the 2nd Marine Raider Battalion, Carlson employed the term to rally his troops. Their high morale prompted fellow marines to use the term to describe excessive enthusiasm. After the Raiders distinguished themselves in operations including the Makin Island raid and the Battle of Guadalcanal, Hollywood turned their story into the 1943 movie Gung Ho! The film helped introduce the term into American slang, where it came to mean someone enthusiastic, zealous or eager for action. Despite being far removed from its original 1938 meaning, the word is arguably a fitting symbol for the 2026 presidential meeting. With Washington and Beijing locked in a relationship defined by trade disputes, technology restrictions, military competition, geopolitical tension and mutual suspicion, diplomats from both sides were keen to find more positive themes for a friendly summit: namely, history, culture, old friendships and shared victories. The Flying Tigers, World War II, gifts of giant pandas, Xi’s 1985 Iowa trip … and maybe ping-pong diplomacy? The trouble is there is only so much material of that kind to draw on. World War II is particularly useful. Americans and Chinese did fight alongside one another as allies – a fact Xi said both countries had “never forgotten” – allowing the two leaders to invoke a shared history without immediately turning to tariffs, microchips or Taiwan. Look more closely, and the misunderstood marine slogan becomes an almost uncannily apt symbol for today’s event. America’s official World War II ally was Chiang Kai-shek and his Kuomintang. Yet Carlson on his China trip also visited the Red Army’s base in Yanan, where he met Mao Zedong and Zhu De, and was impressed by the Eighth Route Army’s guerrilla warfare. Carlson’s unconventional combat tactics, leadership philosophy and approach to organising his battalion were heavily influenced by what he learned from the Communists. “I was trying to build up the same sort of working spirit I had seen in China, where all the soldiers [of the Eighth Route Army] dedicated themselves to one idea and worked together to put that idea over,” Carlson told Life magazine in 1943, explaining why he adopted “gung-ho” as the rallying cry for the 2nd Marine Raider Battalion. The original gong he organisation – the industrial cooperatives – closed in 1952 after the Communists won the civil war in 1949. Re-established in 1983 as the Chinese Industrial Cooperative Association, it remains active to this day, promoting cooperative enterprises and operating within the Communist Party’s united-front system. Xi Jinping’s father, Xi Zhongxun, was also involved in activities associated with the organisation. Yet, beyond the historical detail, the simple idea of “working together” captures the main message of the summit: that Washington and Beijing are still prepared to look for common ground before settling down to tackle more difficult business. Even, that is, if they have to reach back more than 80 years to find it.

title: Young Chinese women sew own underwear, clothes, amid frustration with fast fashion
description: For many, learning to sew exposed long-standing flaws in fast fashion – poor fits, inferior fabrics, and monotonous designs.
content: Frustrated by low-quality materials, careless craftsmanship, and escalating prices, some young women in China are taking matters into their own hands by learning to sew their own underwear, accessories, and handbags. This summer, a surge of sewing enthusiasts flocked to RedNote to showcase their handmade creations. Many beginners embarked on their journey with underwear, assuming it would be a straightforward first project due to its minimal fabric requirements. However, they quickly encountered the complexities of working with stretchy materials that are challenging to cut and tend to curl at the edges. One user had been sewing for only three days when she decided to tackle a pair of underwear. After breaking needles and running out of fabric, she crafted an imperfect yet heartfelt piece she humorously dubbed “affair-proof underwear,” joking that its awkward appearance might prevent anyone from wanting to take it off for someone else. Her creation resonated with many users, prompting others to share their own sewing blunders, like sewing sleeves backwards. For many, the journey of learning to sew also revealed the problems long accepted in fast fashion – poor fits, inferior fabrics, and monotonous designs. Some people added linings to uncomfortable pyjamas, while others replaced bra materials with fabrics offering enhanced breathability and coverage. After teaching herself to sew for three months, folk singer Xie Chunhua fashioned a pair of cargo pants with pockets spacious enough to accommodate a tablet, an umbrella, and even packets of instant noodles. Her post garnered over 100,000 likes, with numerous commenters voicing their frustrations about the state of women’s fashion in China. One shopper noted that after buying a dress, she checked the label only to discover it contained minimal high-quality fabric. The stitching details were also lacking, despite the dress’s price tag of more than 1,000 yuan (US$150). Another consumer received an empire dress ordered online, only to find the fabric was thinner than her household bedsheets upon delivery. Other widespread complaints include the removal of pockets for aesthetic purposes and the use of rough inner seams that irritate the skin. Industry reports indicate that online women’s clothing return rates in China can exceed 70 per cent on certain platforms. Meanwhile, the rapid rise of fast fashion has intensified clothing turnover, contributing to millions of tonnes of textile waste each year, with many garments discarded within a year of their purchase. Many female consumers express nostalgia for the durable garments of earlier times. Today, manufacturers often eliminate essential features like dress linings and pockets to reduce costs, prompting some women to buy additional safety shorts or turn to men’s clothing for practicality. Others are taking up sewing to gain greater control over their wardrobe choices. One online observer remarked: “After a full day of work, all I want is to go home and sew. Those moments of focus restore the part of me that work has drained.” “In a world dominated by mass production, handmade items hold greater significance. The true value lies in taking responsibility for what I wear,” another user commented.

title: India’s ‘cockroach’ movement targets election chief in political pivot
description: The Gen Z group that forced out an education minister is demanding the election chief’s resignation over alleged voter roll irregularities.
content: India’s “cockroach” youth movement is testing whether it can turn anger over education and jobs into a broader challenge to the country’s political establishment, two months after its protests helped force an education minister to resign over alleged entrance exam leaks. Its latest target is another powerful institution: the country’s election watchdog. The shift marks a transition for the movement from high-profile demonstrations in New Delhi to a more diffuse campaign of school audits, meetings with authorities and demands for electoral reform. Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on Thursday demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after a local newspaper reported allegations that his handling of voter-list revisions could disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine confidence in India’s electoral process. The Indian Express reported on Wednesday that two election commissioners had raised questions or expressed concern to Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, mostly over the process of updating voter lists that began last year. The report alleged that Kumar repeatedly bypassed the two other election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi – who had formally raised objections – making critical decisions regarding voter lists, registration and deletions without their knowledge or consent. The dispute has heightened scrutiny of a large-scale exercise to revise electoral rolls, with critics questioning whether voters excluded from draft lists will have adequate safeguards and opportunities to challenge their removal. “When millions of names can disappear from draft rolls, the burden is on the commission to establish that every exclusion is lawful, transparent and subject to meaningful reviews,” said CJP National Convenor Abhijeet Dipke. If Kumar did not resign by Saturday, the CJP would launch a nationwide protest, Dipke said. Anjali, a national executive member of the All India Students Association, said 300 to 400 young people representing different backgrounds had already launched protests demanding Kumar’s resignation. “We believe this [the chief election commissioner’s actions] weakens democracy to the core. So along with civil society and concerned citizens, we have staged a protest at Jantar Mantar,” she said, referring to the venue in the capital that was the focal point for earlier demonstrations. She added that they had been detained by the police. The CJP began in May as a satirical online campaign after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant referred to unemployed young people as “cockroaches”. It then turned its attention to alleged irregularities in the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) – a nationwide medical examination – and other grievances with the education system. Its protests at Jantar Mantar in Delhi helped force the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July. But the movement has since shifted from high-decibel demonstrations in the capital to less prominent school audits and meetings with authorities across at least six states. The non-political movement, which has given voice to middle-class anxieties over opportunities for young people, highlights a growing challenge for political leaders trying to respond to one of the largest sections of India’s electorate. “There is a definite Generation Z factor coming up. That Generation Z factor is largely anti-establishment,” said Yashwant Deshmukh, an independent political commentator and founder of C-Voter, a public opinion research firm. The younger generation’s grievances had exposed a cross-party challenge that all political parties were struggling with, Deshmukh said: connecting with young people’s hearts and minds. India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is now in its third successive term – this time at the head of a multiparty coalition – has gradually recovered ground in state elections after losing its outright majority in 2024. The BJP’s dominance has only grown amid a fragmented opposition led by the Congress party, which held sway for decades following India’s independence in 1947. Analysts say it is too early to predict whether the cockroach movement could trigger broader political changes ahead of a string of elections next year in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur, Himachal Pradesh and Gujarat. “It is going to create problems for anybody in power in those states. It is not one-way traffic,” Deshmukh said, referring to the BJP’s political fortunes. On Friday, Congress was set to stage protest marches at state election offices across India to demand Kumar’s arrest. “No matter what narrative is created by the opposition and Congress, eventually it will come down to what kind of party infrastructure they have to turn that traction from Gen Z into votes against the BJP,” Deshmukh added. Young voters’ challenge The cockroach movement’s expansion beyond education has coincided with what independent political commentator Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay described as a change in India’s “political drift”. Demanding the removal of the chief election commissioner was likely to catalyse that change further, Mukhopadhyay said. “What has happened is that the movement has triggered the erasure of fear from the minds of youngsters,” he said, pointing to a protest against the gang-rape of a 17-year-old girl on Thursday by students from Lady Shri Ram College for Women in Delhi as an example. But Mukhopadhyay warned that the protests did not mean the BJP was facing an electoral rout, saying next year’s state elections would provide a clearer test of its popularity. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of Congress has also been seeking to connect with Gen Z voters through a nationwide student outreach programme called Chhatron Ki Goonj (Echo of Students), aimed at amplifying grievances over the education and examination systems. The initiative had given Gandhi greater credibility among young people, Mukhopadhyay said. Meanwhile, a high-powered panel led by technology entrepreneur Nandan Nilekani is examining structural reforms to the NEET. The panel was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi after weeks of protests against alleged irregularities in the exam, which culminated in Pradhan’s resignation and the government agreeing to several of the movement’s demands. Its report is due by the end of this month. Suhruda Dasyam, who graduated from the London School of Economics in December and currently works in London, said she took part in solidarity protests in the city in July to express her support for the movement. “I think there is a larger issue that needs to be addressed. People are unemployed and struggling to get by. I sought education in a country that is not mine because I feel that I don’t have the same opportunities in India,” she said. “I feel so many people share the same sentiment. I just hope that we can get there some day.” Dasyam said the movement had not lost momentum, although its focus had shifted since Pradhan’s resignation. The cockroach movement had also been trying to build a presence beyond the capital, with its leaders personally inspecting facilities in government schools across different states, said Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator. “Their network is growing well. What they have not been able to do is attract more people to do the job in a decentralised way,” he said, pointing out that visiting India’s roughly 1 million state schools would be physically impossible without support from other groups. The audits had struggled to capture national attention, partly because the CJP’s founders had refused to align with any political party, reducing local media interest, Ramaswamy said. Pradhan’s resignation also appeared to reduce the movement’s momentum, he added, as many young supporters felt the job was done.

title: China and EU deadlocked on medical devices, still talking on PHEV curbs: source
description: Sources on the Chinese side recently described the talks as difficult and expressed frustration over the EU’s inflexibility.
content: Beijing and Brussels remain “deadlocked” on trade in medical devices following discussions in Beijing this week, a source said, adding that “intensive consultations” were under way about Brussels’ plan to launch import safeguards against made-in-China plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). Vice-Minister of Commerce Ling Ji – China’s deputy international trade representative – held discussions with Ditte Juul Jorgensen, the European Commission’s director general for trade and economic security, on Wednesday and Thursday in preparation for a second round of trade talks, the Ministry of Commerce said in a statement issued on Thursday. The European Commission declined to comment, while China’s commerce ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The public procurement of medical devices and imports of Chinese PHEVs have been points of tension between Beijing and Brussels. The European Union barred Chinese medical device companies from bidding for public tenders worth more than €5 million (US$5.7 million) for five years in June last year after it said an investigation found “clear evidence” of Chinese discrimination against European firms in limiting EU medical device producers’ access to government contracts in China. The following month, China excluded EU companies without operations in China from government medical device contracts valued at more than 45 million yuan (US$6.7 million). German business daily Handelsblatt reported in June that the European Commission was preparing to impose anti-subsidy duties on PHEVs imported from China. And this month, the Financial Times reported that Brussels was seeking a commitment from Beijing to restrict sales of made-in-China hybrid vehicles to about 15 per cent of the EU market. The Ministry of Commerce said such a measure would “seriously violate” World Trade Organization rules. Europe must stand firm and be able to use trade defence instruments … but this must not become a vicious circle Nicolas Forissier, French Trade Minister Two Chinese sources recently described talks with Brussels as “difficult” and expressed their frustration at what they said was the EU’s inflexibility and unwillingness to make compromises. Meanwhile, France – one of the most outspoken champions of protectionist measures aimed at reining in Europe’s rising trade deficit with China – expressed its willingness to reach a deal with Beijing, while reiterating its stance that the EU had a legitimate right to safeguard its market in a changing geopolitical context. “Europe must stand firm and be able to use trade defence instruments when justified, anti-dumping in particular, as it has done in the past, but this must not become a vicious circle,” French Trade Minister Nicolas Forissier told journalists on Thursday. He described France’s position as a “partnership proposal” and stressed the need to return to a “more cooperative partnership-based” approach to trade to avoid a situation that would be destructive for everyone. With China, as with the EU’s other trade partners, France was open to building partnerships that were win-win for both sides and which would involve concessions, Forissier said, adding that he believed China was also open to reaching long-term compromises. “We do not want to wage a trade war,” he said.

title: Why Hong Kong banks have shut down 40% of branches in recent years
description: With the ability to transfer funds at 2am and AI to help plan investments, branches on every corner no longer make sense, local bankers say.
content: New York may be known as the city that never sleeps, but many Hongkongers like to take care of banking transactions at 2am – a truth that helps explain why 40 per cent of physical branches have disappeared in recent years, according to local bank executives. While the number of Hong Kong licensed banks had remained stable around 150 for many years, the number of bank branches had dropped 40 per cent to about 900 from 1,500 in recent years, said Sunny Cheung, CEO of Shanghai Commercial Bank. “[In that,] you can see the change in the model of how we do banking,” Cheung said on Friday during a panel discussion at the annual conference of the Hong Kong Institute of Bankers, a professional body providing training and certification for banking qualifications. The shift was permanent, said Simon Chung, CEO and managing director of Fubon Bank (Hong Kong), who spoke on the same panel. “The number of branches has dropped very significantly in the last few years, and I believe that this number will not increase because our customers have changed their habit of interacting with banks altogether,” Chung said. Chung said his bank’s IT department found that a lot of customers use the Faster Payment System (FPS) to transfer funds in the wee hours of the morning. Developed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, FPS is an interbank electronic payment network that allows registered users to transfer using simple identifiers, such as phone numbers. “[I am] not talking about just 10 or 20 customers, but hundreds of them remain awake in the morning to transfer funds,” he said. “This is something we need to understand, and we need to make sure the bank is still available to these customers to satisfy their banking needs.” Even setting aside the night owls, there were other reasons banks were pouring resources into digital banking and artificial intelligence-driven customer service, according to HSBC Hong Kong CEO Maggie Ng. “At HSBC [Hong Kong], we have 7 million retail customers,” she said. “Even if I hire all the relationship managers in Hong Kong, it will still not adequately serve all our customers. And I would not do that because it would be super expensive.” As such, HSBC had been adopting AI to serve its large number of clients, not only with banking transactions but also with investments, Ng said. “AI will come to support our client services even better,” she said, hastening to add that HSBC would not use AI to replace the human touch. HSBC also employed many AI tools that helped its bankers to serve customers, as well as to prevent fraud, she added. Each month, the bank used AI to screen over 1.2 billion transactions for signs of financial crime, which had significantly reduced fraud, Ng said. Ng and other bankers on the panel said tokenisation of assets would be part of the way forward for banking, as customers liked to invest in tokenised bonds, deposits, gold and other assets. Tokenisation refers to representing and trading real-world assets in digital form using blockchain, or distributed ledger, technology. Market capitalisation of tokenised assets could reach US$2 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey.

title: Chinese marques in driving seat as high petrol prices accelerate EU shift to electric cars
description: Chinese brands’ share of plug-in hybrid registrations across Europe climbed from about 20 per cent in January to 35.3 per cent in August.
content: Chinese carmakers have gained ground in Europe’s shift to electric cars, emerging as the biggest winners in plug-in hybrids despite moves by Brussels to curb their expansion. As petrol prices climbed across the EU, hitting a record high of more than €2.30 a litre (US$9.91 a US gallon) in Germany this month, the move to battery power gathered pace. Battery-electric registrations jumped 62.7 per cent year on year in August and accounted for 21.7 per cent of new registrations in the first eight months of the year – equal with petrol-powered cars – according to data published by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) on Thursday. Chinese carmakers took almost all of the new volume. The European Union market grew by 30,720 vehicles in August, a year-on-year increase of 4.5 per cent, with BYD, Chery, Leapmotor and SAIC accounting for about 92 per cent of the net increase, based on ACEA figures. BYD’s registrations more than doubled to 20,845, while Chery’s tripled to about 14,000. Much of that growth came from plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). “Every third PHEV is Chinese now,” said Julian Litzinger, an analyst at data provider Dataforce. Its latest figures showed Chinese brands’ share of PHEV registrations climbing from about 20 per cent in January to 35.3 per cent in August across Europe, more than double their share of the battery-electric market. Since October 2024, the EU has imposed anti-subsidy duties of up to 35.3 per cent on Chinese-built battery-electric cars, while PHEVs face only the standard 10 per cent tariff. Litzinger said Chinese carmakers had continued to “double down” on the segment, “securing a record market share in Europe”. PHEV demand is booming in some of Europe’s biggest markets, with registrations in the first eight months of the year up 77.6 per cent in Italy, 33.9 per cent in Spain and 15.6 per cent in Germany, according to ACEA. BYD said its Seal U was Germany’s bestselling PHEV in June and July. Multiple media reports have said Brussels has pushed Beijing to rein in hybrid exports ahead of a new round of trade talks, asking China to voluntarily cap Chinese-built hybrids at about 15 per cent of the EU market. The Ministry of Commerce said in Beijing on September 18 that it was firmly opposed to “voluntary” export restraints. Meanwhile, Europe’s established manufacturers are losing ground. Based on ACEA figures, the five largest European manufacturers – Volkswagen, Stellantis, Renault, BMW and Mercedes-Benz – saw their combined EU market share slip to 64.6 per cent in the first eight months of the year, down from 66.8 per cent in the same period last year, while the five largest Chinese groups – BYD, SAIC, Chery, Leapmotor and Geely, whose figures include Volvo – lifted theirs to 9.6 per cent from 6.2 per cent. Volkswagen Group remained the EU’s largest carmaker, but its August registrations fell 3.2 per cent and its market share dropped to 25.9 per cent from 28 per cent a year earlier. This month, VW’s supervisory board approved 50,000 more job cuts, on top of 50,000 already planned, as it grapples with US tariffs, weaker sales in China and intensifying competition from Chinese rivals. Sales by premium marques Mercedes-Benz and BMW were relatively stable in the EU, with registrations up 7.2 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively. But both have admitted to losing ground in mainland China, with Mercedes’ car sales down 28 per cent year on year in the first half of the year, and BMW’s down 20.4 per cent. The pressure is reshaping the German automotive industry’s stance on trade. On Thursday, German business daily Handelsblatt reported that the Association of the Automotive Industry, long seen as a brake on tougher measures against China, now considered trade defence instruments justified “from a certain point of competitive distortion”. But some analysts doubt tariffs can slow China’s advance. EU tariffs and other protectionist measures had instead accelerated China’s integration into Europe’s car industry, Philipp Seidel, from the consultancy Arthur D. Little, said, as Chinese carmakers increasingly localised production. He said China’s strength came from an integrated ecosystem that spanned everything from batteries to supply chains and featured fast development cycles. “Trade measures can change the route through which that competitiveness reaches Europe, but they do not make the competitiveness itself disappear,” Seidel said.

title: Philippines’ short-lived Discord ban exposes cracks in online safety strategy
description: The abrupt ban following recent school shootings has drawn backlash over ‘performative governance’ and free speech risks.
content: The Philippines’ decision to block messaging platform Discord for less than a day following a series of school shootings has raised questions about the government’s response to child safety online, with analysts describing the move as a show of regulatory muscle that did little to address underlying problems. The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) announced on Thursday that it had lifted the ban after what officials described as successful negotiations with Discord over compliance with child safety measures. The government’s action came days after a shooting on September 18 at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, where a student opened fire on classmates, killing two students and himself, and injuring eight others. Authorities said they were investigating whether the student had been influenced by online conversations, while the government also raised concerns about online communities being used to groom or radicalise minors and potentially encourage real-world violence. On Wednesday, the government gave Discord and Reddit 24 hours to establish a physical office or assign a resident agent, alongside detailed explanations of their safety protocols, rapid-response mechanisms and age-assurance systems. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre (CICC) said Discord had servers associated with nihilistic violent extremism and grooming, but stopped short of blaming either Discord or Reddit for the recent shootings. Reddit was given an extension to comply, while Discord was blocked after failing to meet the government’s deadline. ‘Performative’ governance? The move drew widespread public criticism, as it disrupted communications for enterprises, workers and students who use the platform. “People use Discord for work meetings, school and running small businesses. Block it and they all get hit, while bad actors just move to another app,” Filipino actor Paulo Avelino wrote on social media. “Child safety matters. So fix the actual problem, not just the easiest target.” “We now live in a world of super powerful AI swarms,” said Carl Javier, executive director of ethics organisation Data and AI Ethics PH, describing their ability to “hack into government systems and cause catastrophic harm to key digital infrastructure”. “And the department that wants to be at the head of dealing with these threats … does not know how Discord works?” The CICC apologised for the inconvenience caused by the hours-long ban. “Please don’t worry, as we are already working to resolve everything,” Renato Paraiso, undersecretary and executive director of the CICC, said at a press conference. The CICC was also responsible for banning the video game GoreBox, which was part of officials’ investigation into a school shooting in Tacloban City in June. Beyond the immediate disruption, digital rights and child safety advocates said the incident highlighted a lack of foresight in creating coherent and feasible regulatory systems. “When access to a platform can disappear abruptly, the consequences reach far beyond a single app,” volunteer-led civic technology initiative BetterGov said in a petition to protect digital democracy. “Work can be interrupted, learning disrupted and communities cut off. People deserve to know who made the decision, what evidence supports it, how long it will last and how it can be challenged.” The government likely banned Discord to flex its regulatory muscle and look like it was tackling online harm, but the decision ultimately proved to be “careless”, said Jason Torres, a tech consultant and founder of BetterGov. “I don’t think they properly consulted the people affected. We use Discord to organise volunteers and get work done. Others depend on it for school and income. You can’t ignore that impact just because you want a platform’s attention,” Torres said. Javier shared similar views regarding the government’s approach. “Performative governance allows them to seem like they are taking steps to ‘protect us’, threatening bans on platforms when these don’t actually fix the root causes of the problems,” Javier said. Torres added that the incident showed the Philippines’ lack of capacity to address online harm properly, despite rising cases. Ysrael Diloy, a child protection specialist at the Manila-based non-profit organisation Stairway Foundation, said the “more useful way of looking at this is not whether a 24-hour directive by itself inspires trust, but whether we are developing a coherent, realistic and sustainable system for holding platforms accountable”. The CICC’s requirement for platforms to designate local representation was legitimate, Diloy said. “When there is an immediate threat to a child – sexual exploitation, grooming, a credible threat of violence or digital evidence that needs to be preserved – authorities should not have to spend critical time figuring out whom to contact in another jurisdiction,” he said. “However, regulatory demands also have to be realistic and feasible.” Setting up in a new physical office within a 24-hour time frame was unrealistic, Diloy said, even with the alternative of appointing a local representative. “That naturally raises an important question: why 24 hours, and what exactly is expected to be realistically accomplished within that period?” Constitutional questions Digital creators and advocates said targeting platforms such as Discord and Reddit also raised concerns over free and protected speech. “Blanket blocking raises constitutional questions, especially when the legal basis and due process are unclear,” Torres said. “When I was undersecretary of the DICT … pressures were coming in from Congress for us to block websites, apps, and even to take down critics’ posts,” former DICT Undersecretary Jeffrey Ian Dy told ABS-CBN News on Friday. “But we didn’t do it because, number one, it is unconstitutional. There was already a ruling by the Supreme Court that there shouldn’t be unilateral blocking of any websites except those that are clearly defined to be blockable under the law,” Dy added. “Last time I checked, we’re still a democracy so they should work within the boundaries of the law.” Speaking on a podcast hosted by tech founder Ann Cuisia on Thursday, Dy accused Congress of holding the DICT’s budget hostage in exchange for action against posts critical of public officials. He said he suspected the issue of child safety was being “used” by congressmen as a smokescreen to get negative posts about themselves taken down. “If you look at the transcripts of Congress hearings regarding DICT’s budget. Congressmen were asking why DICT was unable to take down posts negative to them … They’re talking about child safety and ‘fake news,’” Dy said. “The real reason why our politicians want to regulate social media is that they can’t take the heat,” Carlo Ople, founder of Creators Against Corruption, posted on social media. “They want the people who are talking about their alleged corruption and alleged illegal activities to be silenced. This is a question about free speech, more than anything else.” While the intention of the Discord ban might not have been to stifle free expression, Javier said it ran counter to previous court rulings. “It runs over due process, and whether they intended it or not, if allowed to stand it would’ve set a dangerous precedent,” Javier said. “At present, the DICT and CICC continue to invoke ‘protecting children’ as their motivation. But they need to balance that with defending our rights as well.” Diloy said authorities could earn the public’s trust by carrying out reforms, not by how quickly they acted after an incident. “It is whether we see a sustained, technically informed and evidence-based approach – one that invests in prevention, investigation, child protection services, regulatory capacity and meaningful engagement with technology companies,” he said.

title: 6 missing after explosion fells building in heart of touristic Athens
description: The ‘unbelievable disaster’ that happened near the Acropolis is believed to have been caused by a huge gas leak.
content: Six people, including four tourists, were missing after a building collapsed following an explosion early Friday in Athens’ historic Plaka district that was probably due to a huge gas leak. The city’s mayor Haris Doukas called the blast an “unbelievable disaster” and spoke of the likelihood of an “explosion triggered by … a very significant gas leak” that led to the collapse of the two-storey building at around 7.30am on Friday morning. The building is just below the Acropolis. According to the police, the number of missing rose from five to six in the evening. “Operations are continuing, all the machinery is here, the search will go on throughout the night,” said Doukas, who went to the scene. “These are difficult hours. We stop whenever necessary to keep silent, so we can see if we can hear any sound” made by possible survivors, he added. According to the public television channel ERT, the missing are a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor. On the first floor, four American tourists were staying in short-term rental accommodation. The blast on a small street shook the area, which is normally busy with hundreds of foreign visitors. The fire service had earlier said they included two elderly people who lived in the building’s top floor, and three tourists believed to have rented the apartment below. Thirty firefighters were deployed with six vehicles as well as three search and rescue dogs, according to the Greek news agency ANA. Excavators are clearing the rubble and thermal cameras have been deployed at the scene by rescuers. “The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building,” the mayor said. “We are talking about an incredible disaster,” he said, adding that two adjoining buildings are in very poor condition. “Inspections have begun to determine whether they can remain standing or whether they too must be demolished.” Earlier, two women were rescued from an adjacent building and taken to hospital. Another person was slightly injured by debris. Neighbouring buildings and vehicles parked nearby were damaged. The owner of the ground floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini news outlet he had tried to contact “the elderly couple, around 70 years old” without success. The Plaka district is one of the most touristy areas of Athens. It is near Hadrian’s Arch, one of the main monuments from the Roman period in the Greek capital, where the tourist season continues to be in full swing.

title: Why is the National Archives the last stop on Xi and Trump’s summit itinerary?
description: The presidents and their wives will get a personal view of the National Archives and the documents that define the American system.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s trip to the US will conclude not at the diplomatic negotiating table, but in front of America’s founding documents. After morning tea in the White House Red Room, US President Donald Trump and his wife Melania will take Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan on a tour of the National Archives, the home of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and other texts that established the basis of the US government. According to the Office of the First Lady, the two couples will also “view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history”. For Trump, standing with the Chinese leader in front of these materials is a chance to project an image of enduring American strength as the two powers are locked in a bitter rivalry over trade, technology and global influence. For Xi, a stop at the temple of US history could also carry the weight of how China and the US have navigated two centuries of competition, cooperation and coexistence. “As this year marks the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States and the facility remains open to the public, the US side likely arranged this visit against the broader backdrop of these 250th anniversary celebrations,” said Yuanchong Wang, an assistant professor in the University of Delaware’s history department and the author of The Meeting of China and the United States: Power Diplomacy and the Rise and Fall of Late Qing, 1784-1911. The neoclassical National Archives Building is halfway between the US Capitol and the White House, part of the civic core of Washington. In addition to housing the original Declaration of Independence, Constitution and Bill of Rights, its dim, marble-lined grand rotunda also displays the Emancipation Proclamation, issued by Abraham Lincoln in 1863, which declared that enslaved people in Confederate states “henceforward shall be free”. It is also the headquarters for the US National Archives and Records Administration, a nationwide system of 40 facilities, including 15 regional records centres, and 15 presidential libraries. Among the collections are millions of pages documenting the complex, shared history of both powers. For example, records of the US Army Forces in the China-Burma-India Theatre during World War II, which document a rare chapter of close military alliance between China and the US, are preserved at the National Archives at College Park, Maryland. The College Park venue, a larger complex that is known as Archives II, also stores the key official US government files, diplomatic correspondence, and intelligence briefings, including those regarding “ping-pong diplomacy”, the table tennis exchanges in 1971 that helped to pave the way for then president Richard Nixon’s trip to Beijing the following year. Some records of important diplomatic events, including the so-called Three Communiques that Beijing has long said form the bedrock of bilateral relations, are kept elsewhere. The Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum in Yorba Linda, California, preserves the official records of the 1972 Shanghai Communique, which was released on the last day of his trip to China and marked the start of reengagement between Beijing and Washington. The Jimmy Carter Presidential Library and Museum in Atlanta, Georgia, keeps archives for the 1979 Joint Communique on Normalisation, the formal agreement in which the People’s Republic and the United States established diplomatic relations, as well as the official transcripts of meetings between Carter and the paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in the White House in January that year. Meanwhile, the 1982 August 17 Communique, which stated that the US took no position on Taiwan’s sovereignty and that this was an issue the two sides of the strait should resolve, is stored in the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum in Simi Valley, California. Some records document the hardships and resilience of the early Chinese diaspora, which laid the foundation of today’s Chinese-American community. For example, the National Archives holds thousands of detailed immigration case files documenting the exclusion era, including interrogation transcripts and family photographs of early Chinese immigrants to the US. Some documents date back to the beginning of diplomatic relations between the US and Imperial China, such as the 1844 Treaty of Wanghia, the first of the unequal treaties imposed by Washington on the Qing dynasty (1644-1911).

title: Opinion | How Chinese firms can optimise their ‘going out’ strategy in Southeast Asia
description: While local partners gain valuable technical and marketing skills, Chinese companies must navigate vastly different regulatory and cultural landscapes to succeed.
content: In an era of profound geopolitical and economic shifts, two concurrent trends define the global landscape. First, while the United States sees capital flowing into its equity markets amid the AI boom, central banks and asset managers are diversifying away from US bonds and US dollars to hedge against historically high fiscal deficits and debt levels. As the US pushes for onshoring manufacturing and Europe defends its industries, East Asia – particularly Asean+3 – is deepening supply chain integration. Today, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and its partners China, Japan and South Korea together boast the world’s largest market. Second, alongside China’s record export performance, Chinese state-owned and private enterprises are exporting capital, investments and talent to Brics nations, with Asean emerging as a primary destination. This shift carries enormous implications for business models, host-country trade and employment, and brings intense competition to domestic businesses. As I mentioned in a speech to the CGS China-Asean Business Leaders’ Summit this week, in today’s big-power contest, Asean has emerged as a region of immense potential and strategic significance. With a population approaching 700 million and a combined gross domestic product of around US$4 trillion, it ranks among the world’s fastest-growing regions, with sustained growth rates of over 4 per cent. North and Southeast Asia are highly complementary. The North has ageing populations and resource scarcity, particularly in oil, gas and critical minerals, while Asean possesses abundant energy and agricultural output. Furthermore, through the Strait of Malacca, Asean links North Asia with South Asia, the Middle East and Europe via long-standing cultural, religious and linguistic ties. Bolstered by the implementation of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and successive enhancements to the China-Asean free trade agreement, Asean is China’s largest trading partner. Bilateral trade exceeded US$1 trillion in 2025 and maintains robust growth trajectories. Investment flows mirror this deepening trade integration. Asean is a leading destination for Chinese investments, mainly in manufacturing, with expanding footprints in wholesale and retail trade as well as mineral and resource development. Several factors drive Chinese enterprises’ accelerated “going out” strategy towards Asean and Brics. First, geopolitical tensions and US tariff escalation have forced Chinese manufacturers to relocate their facilities to Southeast Asia. Second, geographic proximity, existing free-trade architecture, improved maritime and rail connectivity, and extensive Chinese diaspora networks reduce transaction and cultural friction. Chinese firms are attracted by lower labour costs and purpose-built industrial zones, such as those in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. Third, Asean’s abundant energy, raw materials and growing consumer markets create integrated supply-chain and new-market opportunities. Fourth, anecdotally, Chinese private enterprises are inclined to put family offices in Singapore, while deals and initial public offerings remain in Hong Kong. There is also a growing presence of Chinese banks and securities houses in both financial centres to serve their mainland Chinese clients. This trend of Chinese firms “going out” is not without speed bumps. Host nations are increasingly formulating regulatory and legal frameworks to safeguard domestic industries, employment and comparative advantages. Examples include Indonesia’s policies mandating domestic value-added processing in nickel production, rather than raw material export, and Thailand’s tiered foreign equity ownership restrictions. Host countries are worried that Chinese companies are importing Chinese “involution” (intense internal competition) into their countries. Chinese firms have to learn to adapt to local cultural, work and regulatory practices. What works in one country may not work in another. In many cases, Chinese management is only just beginning to realise that a going-out strategy requires a much better understanding of diverse local conditions, even as host governments and businesses need to learn from Chinese businesses that operate with engineering skills and increasingly skilful marketing, especially in social media and digital channels. To compete, Asean businesses must raise their game in AI, robotics, engineering skills and branding, because they can no longer rely on cheap labour and low-end products that permit easy market entry. For a win-win situation to occur, all sides will have to learn how to work together to build a more efficient and resilient ecosystem. Competitive and cooperative partnerships will foster regional integration; they can be the pathfinder for Chinese enterprises going global.

title: How to relax and detox through ikebana, the ancient Japanese art of flower arranging
description: Mindfulness and creativity meet in ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arranging, whose benefits are similar to those of yoga and meditation.
content: Ikebana, the Japanese art of arranging flowers, is a form of expression that dates back more than 500 years. It continues to blossom quietly – not only with traditionalists, but also with newcomers who find its blend of creativity and mindfulness to be restorative. Ikebana can be a bit like solving a puzzle, except there is no fixed answer. Because each flower and human individual is different, there are multiple solutions. “There’s a ‘detox’ purifying factor and a healing,” says Hiroyuki Okada, 40, who began taking lessons in ikebana about seven years ago. He now teaches ikenobo, the oldest of three major ikebana schools. Okada, who also teaches backflips to anyone who wants to learn, usually wears silver chains and jeans, although he wears a nice kimono when he formally demonstrates his arrangements. He considers himself typical of those drawn to ikebana today, people looking for joy, purpose or solace from the daily grind or pain of modern life. “In arranging [flowers], you are dealing with the life that is there, the beauty, of course, but you find what’s in your heart,” Okada says. “You come face to face with yourself.” The Kyoto-based Ikenobo school, which is rooted in Buddhism, now has chapters around the world. Okada’s previous job at a non-profit involved talking to people from around the world, and he realised how different – and alike – people were. When he switched to his current job at a flower shop, he decided to take up a pursuit that was Japanese, so he could explore that aspect of himself, and one that could be done for a long time alone. Ikebana involves interacting with nature, although on a small scale – usually in a little vase. “It is about the relationship of the creator with the flowers,” says Senko Ikenobo, headmaster-designate of the Ikenobo school. Her family dates back generations to the originators of the art. Her father is the current headmaster. Jeannette Haviland-Jones, professor of social psychology at Rutgers University, in the US, says studies have shown “that flowers and even flower scents promote happiness in people. We suggested a coevolutionary theory for this in which flowers became the ‘pets’ of the plant world.” Besides a flower’s beauty and fragrance, the feel of its petals and leaves to the touch is crucial, like petting a kitten or a puppy, according to Okada. There are toddlers who do Ikenobo, copying their mothers, and there are devoted centenarians. The headmaster-designate has seen ikebana help women who are juggling work and motherhood, or taking care of ageing parents. Ikebana has a healing effect similar to that of yoga, meditation or play, says Mayu Shimizu, who works for an online educational service and has been taking lessons from Okada for about three years. “I like this moment of nothingness when you are concentrating on the flowers before you,” she says. “My mind feels clearer. I feel more at peace and gentle.” One traditional Ikenobo arrangement is shoka shofutai, which attempts to arrange the flowers, leaves and branches as they might look in nature, reaching towards sunlight or bending in the wind. The vase, sometimes crafted from wood or pottery, also becomes part of the arrangement’s vision. Yet the overall look is pure and simple, expressing the life cycle of flowers – from blossoming through withering – through three main elements. Shin, the tallest element, is arranged first, representing one’s core, reaching up towards the sky. Soe, which is trimmed to about two-thirds the height of the shin and is placed at the side, expresses the flower’s individuality. The leaves might be slightly faded, representing the later stages of life. Tai, the third element, is the future. Choose a blossom or fresh small leaves – things that are being born. There are also freer, spin-off styles that look more like casual, Western-style bouquets than the stoic, textbook-oriented shoka shofutai. That may feel easier and more fun for beginners. Just as ikebana connects a person with flowers, those who practise the art say it is also about the passing of the art over generations, connecting people.

title: Trump gives Xi a tour of his pet White House building projects, including the ballroom
description: Viral video shows Donald Trump praising Chinese president as an ‘expert on stone’ during South Lawn walkthrough.
content: Property developer-turned-president Donald Trump appeared to relish showing off the White House’s latest building works to Xi Jinping on Thursday, eager to give his Chinese counterpart a glimpse of his construction ambitions since they last met in China. In May, Trump was hosted at Beijing’s Great Hall of the People, a sprawling complex that the US president compares with his planned White House ballroom. After their talks in the Oval Office, Trump led Xi out to the South Lawn, where his helicopter, Marine One, was waiting on the newly completed granite helipad. Videos showing the two presidents talking near the olive-green helicopter marked “United States of America” and accompanied by just two interpreters went viral, drawing comments on platforms such as X, Threads and Facebook. Trump appeared to explain the features of the US$5 million helipad as Xi occasionally asked questions and listened. Trump then invited Xi inside Marine One, giving the Chinese president a closer look at the aircraft used to transport the US president. As the US president walked through a series of construction projects, granite, in particular, appeared to catch Xi’s attention. After the tour, Trump told reporters that Xi “has great interest in granite” and “likes granite”, adding that he was “an expert on stone, aside from many other things”. Xi responded with a smile. “It’s INCREDIBLE to see how much better Xi’s relationship is with Trump than it was with Obama,” one post on social media read. Some comments mentioned Trump’s reactions and described him as “overjoyed”. At the state dinner, he invited Xi to take a look at another signature White House project: the vast construction site where the new ballroom is being built. Trump has increasingly made the physical transformation of the White House a feature of his second term. The East Wing was demolished last year to make way for an 8,360 square metre (90,000-square-foot) ballroom, which he has repeatedly promoted as a “gift” to the American people and a project that would improve White House security and allow for larger events. Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May appears to have provided a recurring point of comparison for the project. After his trip to China, Trump posted a photograph of himself and Xi in the Great Hall of the People, writing: “See, they have a Ballroom ... It’s very large and beautiful. Why do people fight me for having something even better?” Earlier this month, Trump again compared the planned ballroom with the Great Hall, claiming the new White House facility would “top it”. Born into a New York real estate dynasty, Trump joined his father Fred Trump’s firm after graduating from the University of Pennsylvania. He expanded the business from Queens and Brooklyn into prime Manhattan, erecting landmarks such as Trump Tower. He is the first US president with no prior government or military background.

title: More US-China flights? Passengers ready to pack, but US airlines balk at Xi Jinping’s call
description: Analysts say demand exists for more direct flights, but US carriers will resist while their Chinese peers have an advantage.
content: Travellers in China and the US would welcome more direct flights, as suggested by Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week, but the American civil aviation industry has less interest in adding such routes as long as their planes cannot fly over Russian airspace. At a White House arrival ceremony on Thursday, Xi said that “our two sides may also increase direct flights to facilitate two-way travel and trade”. Analysts said passenger demand existed for more than the 50 weekly round-trip flights that carriers from each side are allowed today – down from a combined 320 or more before the Covid-19 pandemic. “Demand isn’t like it was pre-Covid, but you have to look at the supply, which is a tiny fraction, so demand is obviously sufficient for more nonstops,” said Brendan Sobie, founder of the Sobie Aviation consultancy in Singapore. Efforts by China to draw international travellers by improving the quality of tourist destinations and the accessibility of Chinese payment systems may add to air passenger demand “moving forward”, said Lynn Song, chief ­economist for Greater China at the Dutch multinational bank ING. “A modest increase above the current cap is possible, as it appears that the current cap is more or less being utilised.” But the head of Airlines for America, an 11-member trade association including major carriers such as Delta and United, told Reuters this week that he opposed adding more direct US-China flights. US airlines are disadvantaged because their Chinese counterparts are allowed to overfly Russia on eight flights, Chris Sununu, President and CEO of the association, told the news agency. Russia has banned a list of European and North American airlines from its airspace in retaliation for their home countries’ sanctions against Moscow relating to the war in Ukraine. China-bound planes from the US on certain routes must take costly detours. The association head said he had been advocating that Trump administration officials not give in, Reuters reported. “Currently Chinese [carriers] are more active than in the US,” said independent civil aviation analyst Li Hanming. “US carriers are worrying over the competition. US carriers are not willing to cross the line of 50 [weekly flights].” Direct China-US flights dwindled during the pandemic amid a sharp global decline in long-haul travel and struggled to take off again afterwards because of diplomatic friction – giving a lift to air routes with transit stops. To add more direct flights, the US Department of Transportation would negotiate route rights and frequencies with the Civil Aviation Administration of China. “It’s possible that regulators may request Chinese airlines to avoid Russian airspace for the relevant flights,” Song said. US visas for Chinese nationals could be another flashpoint in any effort to add two-way flights, Li said. He noted that 10-year visas issued to Chinese nationals under US ex-president Barack Obama were expiring, with no guarantees of new ones. Current visa holders would need to file new forms, pay an application fee and in some cases schedule interviews with US authorities.

title: Indonesian coal deal fuels doubts over production quota approvals
description: The sale of a stake in Bayan came as the coal miner was facing a delay in getting approval for three subsidiaries’ production quotas.
content: A major coal deal in Indonesia is set to secure a powerful new partner for one of the country’s biggest miners, even as the industry worries a delay in the government’s approval of production quotas could have a severe impact on the business outlook. Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, the biggest shareholders of Bayan Resources, agreed on September 16 to sell a 30 per cent stake in Indonesia’s third-largest coal producer to fellow tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad, better known as Haji Isam. The deal comes at a sensitive moment for Bayan after the government delayed approval of additional coal quotas for three of its subsidiaries. The uncertainty sent Bayan’s shares sharply lower in the days before the deal announcement. It rose by about 20 per cent as soon as news broke about the stake deal, hitting the upper auto-reject limit. The timing has fuelled speculation that the quota hurdle might be linked to the deal, a suggestion that the government has rejected. Under the conditional agreement, the Lows would sell 10 billion Bayan shares to Jhonlin Baratama, a subsidiary of Haji Isam’s Jhonlin Group, a commodities and logistics conglomerate. The deal would give Jhonlin a substantial stake in a major Indonesian coal producer. Bayan produced 68 million tonnes of coal last year, compared with Jhonlin’s output of 24 million tonnes. “Acquiring a major stake in a top-three coal producer like Bayan fundamentally rewires our energy landscape. The state must ensure this consolidation doesn’t birth a mega-cartel,” said Dipo Satria Ramli, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics. Indonesian media have described Haji Isam as an ally of the president. In 2025, Prabowo awarded him the Bintang Mahaputera Utama, one of Indonesia’s highest state honours. Haji Isam has set his sights on expanding Jhonlin’s coal output after having applied for a 60-million-tonne production quota, known as Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB) in Indonesia, for the rest of this year. Ahmad Zuhdi Dwi Kusuma, principal at Energy Shift Institute, an independent energy finance think tank, said Jhonlin’s 30 per cent stake in Bayan would strengthen its market position. “Haji Isam can connect the existing ecosystem he has under his group to Bayan,” he said. Assuming Jhonlin was successful in acquiring its new 60-million-tonne quota, which was separate from the Bayan quota, its output combined with Bayan’s could account for about one-eighth of Indonesia’s coal market, Zuhdi said. Details about the deal remain scant, pending further announcements from Bayan. The Lows currently hold 62 per cent of Bayan’s shares. If the 30 per cent stake sold to Jhonlin comes entirely from their holdings, they would be left with about 32 per cent, potentially leaving control of the company uncertain. But Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based Four Capital, a family office investment firm, said control of Bayan would likely remain with the Lows after the sale. “Like most Indonesian conglomerate families, they have a lot of nominees in the rest of the 38 per cent stock.” Under Indonesia’s RKAB system, mining companies must obtain government approval for their production volume. Without an approved quota, miners cannot legally produce beyond an amount authorised by the government. On September 11, the three Bayan subsidiaries notified customers and invoked force majeure, citing the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources’ failure to issue additional production quota permits for the rest of 2026. “The approval has not been issued to the company’s subsidiaries, although applications for approval to amend the RKAB have been submitted in accordance with applicable laws and regulations,” Bayan director Low Yi Ngo wrote in a statement. Without the permits, Bayan’s production in 2026 is expected to total 39 million tonnes, 43 per cent lower than last year. When Bayan announced the force majeure status to the Indonesian Stock Exchange on September 14, its shares fell by as much as 9.2 per cent that day. The company eventually received approval for the subsidiaries’ quotas on Wednesday, a week after the deal was announced. The episode highlighted how coal mining operations could be severely curtailed because of delays in government approval of production volumes, according to analysts. Without the RKAB, Bayan would face difficulties in planning its production and budget, Zuhdi said. With its quota cut by almost half, it had no choice but to declare force majeure on its existing obligations to clients, he added. “This serves as a reminder that the regulatory side of the industry in Indonesia is increasingly the be-all and end-all factor for a miner.” According to a report by The Jakarta Post, the government has faced questions over whether Bayan’s permit delays were linked to Haji Isam’s acquisition. Other Indonesian media outlets highlighted that the quotas were approved shortly after the deal was signed. This Week in Asia has reached out to Bayan and Jhonlin for comment. Ho urged caution over drawing a link between the two developments. When questioned by reporters in Jakarta on September 16 on why Bayan’s permits were not issued on the same day as the deal announcement on September 16, the director general of minerals and coal at the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, Tri Winarno, said: “It’s still being evaluated and examined in terms of technical aspects, so it will take time.” He also pointed out that not all of Bayan’s permits were held up. “From all Bayan’s coal subsidiaries, only three are having their permits re-evaluated. So there’s no deliberate targeting here.” Bayan Resources has 16 subsidiaries – all of which have separate permits to mine coal – covering 126,000 hectares in East and South Kalimantan. Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia on Wednesday rejected any connection between Bayan’s quota crisis and its stake sale. “The two were separate processes with no link whatsoever,” he told reporters. Nonetheless, the developments have left market participants worrying about uncertainty over regulatory decisions and their impact on the value of Indonesian mining assets. Calling it an “unpalatable aftertaste” for investors, Ho said: “The optics remain remarkable because a regulatory approval becomes critical to production, the company declares force majeure, a major ownership transaction is signed, and the regulatory uncertainty clears almost immediately.” Dipo said the developments would affect investors’ perceptions of official transparency. “Investors will be even more cautious about potential government intervention in the future,” he added. Katherine Hasan, a researcher at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, said that beyond the deal, Bayan and others in the coal industry would have to balance between staying competitive even as the Indonesian government sought to increase the proportion of energy production from green sources. The Prabowo administration is seeking to phase out all coal and fossil fuel power plants by 2040 and increase solar energy production to 100 GW by 2029. While Bayan and its peers were aiming to bolster their cash flows by increasing domestic coal production, they faced the “political reality” of Jakarta seeking to curb its fuel subsidies and enhance the country’s long-term energy security.

title: Asia-Pacific hotels a ‘most compelling’ investment amid travel growth, flat supply: CBRE
description: Rising air travel bodes well for growth after regional investment rises 21 per cent to US$8 billion in first six months, property firm says.
content: Investor appetite for hotel assets increased in Hong Kong and the wider Asia-Pacific region in the first half of the year as consumers showed growing eagerness to travel and constrained supply supported property values, according to CBRE. The region netted US$8 billion of investment in the period, up 21 per cent from a year earlier, with Japan, mainland China and South Korea attracting the most activity, the property consultancy said in a report on Thursday. “Hotels have become one of the most compelling real estate investment sectors in Asia-Pacific,” said Steve Carroll, head of hotels and hospitality for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “Strong travel demand and limited new supply are supporting both operating performance and asset values.” Higher borrowing costs could moderate investment activity in some markets during the second half of the year, Carroll said, adding that investor interest remained concentrated in markets with strong growth and positive supply-demand fundamentals. Passenger traffic in the region is forecast to grow 5.1 per cent this year, according to the International Air Transport Association, slower than a 7.3 per cent estimate before the onset of the US-Israel war on Iran in February. Still, Asia-Pacific would be the second-best performing region behind Africa’s 10 per cent increase, data in the CBRE report showed. Markets such as Vietnam and Japan defied the travel disruption brought about by the conflict. Hanoi extended its visa exemption policy to 12 additional European countries, and Japan received more visitors from the Americas and Europe, offsetting a decline in arrivals from mainland China. Supply of new hotels in Asia-Pacific would remain largely flat, with an estimated compounded annual growth rate of 2.3 per cent from 2025 to 2029 falling below the historical average of 5.1 per cent, the report said. Mainland China would account for 49 per cent of the new hotel supply, it added. In Hong Kong, hotel occupancy still lagged pre-pandemic levels, but increased by 3 per cent year-on-year as of July as “the conversion of some upper-midscale hotels to student accommodation helped ease pressure”, the report said. The city recorded HK$8.2 billion (US$1.04 billion) worth of hotel property deals involving about 2,550 rooms so far this year, according to Colliers. Most of these transactions were for student accommodation conversions, it added. “New hotel development remains challenging across much of Asia-Pacific due to elevated construction and financing costs,” said Ada Choi, head of research for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “As a result, investors are looking to unlock value through repositioning and conversion strategies rather than ground-up development. With new supply expected to remain limited in many markets, existing hotel assets are well positioned to benefit from sustained demand growth and improving operating performance.”

title: Malaysia’s Najib ‘has no money’ to pay fine for house arrest, lawyer says
description: The ex-prime minister’s legal team also dismisses a ‘stupid question’ about ‘the billions’ donated by the Saudi royal family.
content: Former Malaysian leader Najib Razak has no money to pay the fine to secure his transfer to house arrest, his lawyers have said, as they question the delay in releasing the full details of the conditional pardon granted by Malaysia’s king last week. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar last Friday decreed that Najib would be allowed to serve out the remainder of his sentence at home, on condition that he pay his 50 million ringgit (US$10.3 million) fine. The decision triggered widespread outrage among Malaysians over the purported preferential treatment for the corruption-tainted former prime minister and a fundraiser launched by his former ruling Umno party to settle the fine. Najib’s release into house arrest, however, was far from certain as he currently had no means to raise the funds on his own after the authorities froze access to all of his bank accounts, his lawyers said outside the Kuala Lumpur court complex on Friday. “Datuk Seri Najib on his own cannot afford to pay [the fine] … he has no money,” Najib’s lead lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah told a news conference, using the former leader’s honorifics. Last week’s house arrest decree is the second pardon granted to Najib, who was jailed in 2022 after failing to overturn a conviction for stealing 42 million ringgit (US$10.3 million) from a former unit of the troubled state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). In 2024, then-king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah halved his 12-year sentence and reduced his fine from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit. But Najib faces the prospect of serving an additional 15-year jail sentence – on top of an 11.4 billion ringgit fine – after he was found guilty by a high court last December on multiple counts of abuse of power and money laundering involving 2.2 billion ringgit in funds siphoned out from 1MDB. Shafee said it was clear throughout Najib’s 1MDB trial that he did not keep any of the funds allegedly donated by the Saudi royal family, having returned the balance after spending about 300 million ringgit on election campaigns, corporate social responsibility and welfare work. “If you ask where are the billions, that is a stupid question. Because the testimony has clearly shown, he does not have the money,” said Shafee, adding that Najib did not ask for public contributions. The lawyer said Najib’s legal team was also unclear on the exact conditions of the latest pardon, as neither Najib nor the prisons department had received any official letter outlining the details of the king’s decree. The lack of clarity could impair their ability to take the necessary steps to fulfil the conditions laid out by the king, Shafee said. “We don’t know why that letter is taking so long … it is not normal for it to be delayed like this,” he said.
