Earlier on Friday, Najib filed an application to pause the execution of his 1MDB conviction to allow him to exhaust all avenues to appeal against the judgment. The Kuala Lumpur High Court has set October 14 for a decision.

title: Xi’s security chief among cohort of rising officials at White House banquet
description: Zhou Hongxu is one of a group of officials in their 50s and early 60s at the front line of China’s top diplomatic events.
content: Zhou Hongxu, the official who oversees President Xi Jinping’s security, made an appearance at the White House state banquet on Thursday night, alongside a cohort of other rising Chinese officials. The banquet’s guest list described the 55-year-old People’s Liberation Army (PLA) major general as both director of the Central Guard Bureau and deputy director of the Communist Party’s General Office – the ruling party’s powerful administrative nerve centre. Earlier this month, Zhou joined Xi for a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on September 12, footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed. Zhou has accompanied Xi at major international events for several years, including the Group of 20 summit in Bali in 2022 and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in San Francisco in 2023. His dual role as deputy director of the General Office aligns with precedent established during the tenure of previous Chinese leaders. According to Zhou’s scant official CV, he was born in the southwestern city of Chongqing and holds a master’s degree from the PLA’s artillery academy. Zhou was born in 1971 and has served as commander of an artillery regiment in the 14th Army Group’s 40th Division, head of the military training department at the former Chengdu Military Region headquarters and deputy chief of staff of the Northern Theatre Command Ground Force. Zhou assumed the helm of the Central Guard Bureau around 2021 and was chosen as a delegate to the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China in 2022. Zhou is among a prominent cohort of officials in their 50s and early 60s emerging at the front line of China’s most consequential diplomatic events. Also at the White House banquet was 63-year-old Tang Fangyu, the director of the Communist Party’s Central Policy Research Office, its top think tank. Tang, a veteran theorist little known outside the party, became director of the research office in January, replacing Jiang Jinquan, who had led the office since 2020. Tang has frequently accompanied Xi on trips around China and abroad since becoming chief policy adviser. The most prominent former holder of Tang’s current role may be Wang Huning, the ideology guru who held the title from 2002 to 2020. Wang is now China’s fourth-ranking official and chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. Alongside Zhou, other young senior officials joining the state banquet were Lu Luhua, born in 1971, the top political secretary of the Chinese president’s office; assistant foreign minister and chief of protocol Hong Lei, 57; assistant foreign minister and director of North American and Oceanian affairs Cai Wei, 55; and foreign ministry information department director Mao Ning, 53. Hong has been protocol chief since 2019 and an assistant foreign minister since 2024. He leads the foreign ministry’s operational team for high-level diplomatic etiquette, meeting arrangements and international state protocol.

title: Flood-ravaged Nepal pushes for climate deal with India, China
description: PM Shah’s proposal aims to address gaps in data-sharing that left mountain communities with virtually no early warning before the disaster hit.
content: Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah proposed a climate alliance with neighbouring India and China, urging action to protect the fragile Himalayan ecosystem after catastrophic flooding across the region. “Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports,” Shah told world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “As an urgent first step, we propose that we establish the Himalaya climate resilience mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China, so the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation rather than a frontier of fragmented information.” His call follows devastating August 26 floods near the Nepal–China border, triggered by a massive rock-and-ice collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people and wiped out towns, border posts and hydropower plants. An international study found the catastrophe was primed by a complex web of climate and seismic factors, including record summer heat and thawing permafrost. Shah said that recovery efforts would cost roughly 10 per cent of Nepal’s gross domestic product. His proposal addresses critical gaps in data-sharing that left frontline mountain communities with virtually no early warning before flash floods struck. Under the framework, the three nations would share satellite telemetry, jointly monitor high-risk glacial lakes and synchronise emergency warnings to protect the roughly 2 billion people who rely on the mountain range for water. There are global precedents for cross-border sharing of climate data. Eight nations in Europe’s Alpine region pool real-time monitoring to manage mountain hazards, while similar frameworks span Southeast Asia’s Mekong River basin and central Europe’s Danube River to warn downstream communities of impending floods. China and India “have a particular stake in helping address these challenges, not only as major regional powers, but also because climate and disaster risks in the Himalayas are transboundary”, said Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. While both nations offered immediate relief, “that cooperation will need to be sustained and expanded” through practical regional arrangements that complement global climate mechanisms, he said. Shah also called for reforms to global climate finance, describing existing mechanisms like the UN Loss and Damage Fund as “grossly inadequate” and too bureaucratic. He urged donors to provide direct grant-based support rather than credit that adds to debt burdens. “When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan,” Shah said.

title: Xi-Trump dinner puts US tech titans in spotlight – what does it mean for China ties?
description: Nvidia, Apple, AMD and Tesla executives secured prime seats at the White House, underscoring the centrality of AI, chips and tech amid persistent tensions.
content: If the American guests seated at the head table with President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at Thursday’s White House state dinner were any indication, Washington now views its relationship with Beijing largely through the prism of technology. Analysts said the seating arrangement underscored how tech industry titans driving the global AI infrastructure boom were pushing to draw the two economic superpowers closer together. Sitting alongside Xi, Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan, Trump and his wife Melania were Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) CEO Lisa Su, Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Tesla CEO Elon Musk. The four leading American executives command a combined net worth of over US$1 trillion, while their respective companies held a combined market capitalisation of more than US$12 trillion by market close on Thursday. Wang Shengyu, a Washington-based research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, noted that the head table reflected the growing centrality of AI infrastructure as a potential force of convergence in US-China relations. Nvidia’s Huang and AMD’s Su lead two of the world’s largest semiconductor design firms, which produce the core processors required to train and run complex AI models. China, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in this global supply chain as a major hub for chip packaging and testing, as well as a supplier of critical raw materials such as rare earths. But those commercial links have come under intense strain as bilateral relations have deteriorated, with tighter US export controls constraining both chipmakers’ operations in China. In May, Su said China accounted for about 20 per cent of AMD’s total business, down from 24 per cent in 2019. Huang, meanwhile, has said that US restrictions had caused Nvidia to almost entirely lose out on a US$50 billion AI chip market in China. At the same time, Beijing has signalled hesitation in reopening its domestic market to American chips as it steps up its push for technological self-reliance. “[These AI supply chain companies] are the likely proponents of more engagement with China in the US business world,” said Wang, adding that all four companies at the head table had “major China exposure”. The tech sector was also well represented at Xi’s last White House state dinner in 2015, hosted by then-president Barack Obama. Guests included Apple’s Cook, Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella. But while that event also featured traditional media figures such as Disney’s Bob Iger and DreamWorks Animation’s Jeffrey Katzenberg, tech titans completely dominated the head table this time around – a shift mirrored across the broader guest list. Of the 39 US business leaders in attendance, tech figures formed the largest contingent with 15 attendees, including Zuckerberg, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Dell CEO Michael Dell alongside the heads of major US chip supply chain vendors Qualcomm and Micron Technology. One notable absence was a representative from Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI models. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, has been an outspoken critic of Beijing and a vocal proponent of strict export controls on China’s AI sector. By contrast, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman were both invited, despite the company maintaining no operational footprint in China. In total, the guest list comprised 130 attendees, excluding the two heads of state and their spouses. While the presence of American chip giants at the dinner offers a fresh opportunity to lobby both governments for broader Chinese market access, it remains to be seen whether this week’s bilateral talks will lead to any loosening of export curbs. Chinese tech executives were conspicuously absent on Thursday, despite widespread industry speculation that Xi would arrive in Washington with a corporate delegation to explore potential investment deals. Wang of the Asia Society Policy Institute said their absence at the dinner – contrasted with the prominent presence of the four US tech titans – underscored who was driving the push for closer business and investment ties. Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California, San Diego, who specialises in Chinese elite politics, suggested that Xi was unlikely to have been surprised by the seating arrangements, noting that “the US is a capitalist country”. Shih cautioned, however, that the set-up could reinforce Beijing’s perception that the Trump administration “respects wealth more than government institutions”. Meanwhile, Wang highlighted the presence of just one guest from the education sector, New York University president Linda Mills, as evidence of the low priority assigned to educational exchanges by the current administration. “Higher education is still strikingly under-represented at the table ... [even though] talent is becoming as important as compute in US-China AI competition,” Wang said.

title: Uzbekistan gymnast Oksana Chusovitina, 51, defies the years in Asian Games final
description: Competing against women young enough to be her daughter, the athlete is appearing in her seventh continental multi-sport event.
content: Showing that age is not a constraint, 51-year-old Uzbekistan gymnast Oksana Chusovitina capped off her seventh Asian Games appearance with a fifth-place finish – 32 years after her first appearance at the regional event. Competing against athletes young enough to be her daughter, Chusovitina – who made her bow at the 1994 Hiroshima Games – more than held her own in the women’s vault artistic gymnastics final. Among the 19 athletes competing in the women’s vault on Thursday, 12 were under 21 years old, the second-oldest competitor was 20 years her junior and the youngest was just 16. While Chusovitina is not the oldest competitor in Nagoya – an honour that belongs to 55-year-old Indian equestrian Shruti Vora – the Uzbek is the highest-profile senior athlete, having won Olympic gold medals and world championship titles. The youngest competitor, on the other hand, is 11-year-old Japanese esports prodigy Yuki Kurihara, who is one year younger than Hong Kong’s youngest contestants, skateboarders Katniss Wong Yi-huen and Kamus Wong Yeuk-ching. Chusovitina started gymnastics when she was seven and reached an early career peak at 17 by winning a team gold medal at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, followed by two world championship medals before retiring after the 1996 Atlanta Games. In 2002, she returned to competition to earn prize money to pay for her three-year-old son’s medical bills for his leukaemia, saying at the time: “I don’t dare to grow old until my son is fully recovered.” The then 27-year-old won two gold medals at the Busan Asian Games that year, her son eventually made a full recovery, and though many expected her to retire, she kept competing. Three years ago at the Hangzhou Asian Games, when a reporter asked what her best age was, she answered without hesitation: “Now.” That year, Chusovitina missed out on an Asian Games vault medal by just 0.15 points, but after she earned the highest score at the Asian Championships to help Uzbekistan qualify for this year’s tournament, she returned to once again fight for a place on the podium. Now competing in her seventh Asian Games, while her peers have long since moved to the stands, she stepped up to the runway to prove that passion has no age limit. “Performing with kids who are younger than my son … We go out on the field of play and they don’t ask how old you are, [you could be] from 16 and as old as you want to be. That’s why we’re all equal on the field of play,” Chusovitina said. In the women’s vault final, South Korea’s Yeo Seo-jeong scored 14.483 to claim gold, North Korea’s An Chang-ok won silver with 13.666 and China’s Du Siyu claimed bronze with 13.450. Chusovitina finished in fifth place with a score of 13.199.

title: Over 1,000 visitors flock to Po Pin Chau trail as Mid-Autumn Festival holiday begins
description: First major holiday test for real-name reservation system as crowds stream towards popular section of High Island Geo Trail on Friday morning.
content: More than 1,000 visitors flocked to one of Hong Kong’s most popular geological attractions on the morning of the Mid-Autumn Festival, putting a new real-name reservation system through its first major holiday test. As mainland Chinese tourists began visiting the city for the long weekend, crowds were seen streaming towards the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail in Sai Kung under clear skies, despite the heat on Friday. Many mainland visitors said they had discovered the scenic spot through social media and had travelled to Hong Kong specifically for day trips or short breaks. “The scenery is very beautiful. I heard it was wonderful here, so I decided to come,” said one mainland visitor who arrived before the reservation requirement took effect for the day. She had learned on RedNote that visitors could enter without needing to make reservations before bookings started at 9am. The visitor, who was on a day trip to Hong Kong, said she had chosen Po Pin Chau after learning about the attraction online. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department introduced Hong Kong’s first countryside real-name reservation system at Po Pin Chau earlier this month to manage growing visitor numbers and reduce pressure on the trail. The scheme applies from 9am to 5pm on selected weekends and holiday periods, including the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival period from September 25 to 27 and the mainland’s National Day “golden week” from October 1 to 7. A maximum of 2,000 people can enter the Po Pin Chau section each day under the arrangement, divided into four two-hour slots of 500 visitors each. Bookings are free and can be made through the travel platform Klook using visitors’ real names and identity document details. The Mid-Autumn break marks the first extended holiday period since the system’s launch on September 5, ahead of what authorities expect will be another surge in visitors during the National Day holiday. Dan Wang, 25, from Shenzhen in Guangdong province, said the booking process had been simple. “I think it was quite easy,” he said, adding that he would recommend the attraction to friends. Wang, who was visiting Hong Kong for the day, described the weather as “a little hot” but said the breeze made his trek more comfortable. Tang Qin, 33, who travelled from Sichuan province with a friend for a three-day holiday in the city, also said she found it easy to secure a reservation after learning about the attraction and the online booking system. “It was relatively easy to make a reservation,” Tang said. “The weather today is excellent.” She said she planned to spend the rest of her trip visiting Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay to shop and see exhibitions. Authorities introduced the reservation system after visitor numbers at the East Dam and Po Pin Chau surged during previous holidays, raising concerns about overcrowding and potential environmental damage. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his policy address this month that the government would assess the trial before developing a longer-term strategy for managing country parks, while the booking arrangement would remain in place throughout the coming National Day golden week.

title: From Suzhou to AI: Singapore, China eye new playbook for economic ties
description: Both countries should explore cooperation in new areas such as AI and the green economy, says Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong.
content: Singapore and China should look to the next phase of cooperation through potential projects in artificial intelligence and the green economy, after decades of economic ties anchored by industrial parks, eco-cities and transport corridors. Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said on Friday that the relationship had “never been static”, arguing that the economic challenges of each era shaped the flagship developments of that time. At the FutureChina Global Forum held in the city state, Gan, who is also trade minister, outlined how the Suzhou Industrial Park, launched in 1994, supported China’s early industrialisation and opening up, while creating opportunities for Singapore companies. He also highlighted how the cooperative urban development project Tianjin Eco-City, launched in 2008, allowed both sides to look at sustainable urban development. The Chongqing Connectivity Initiative, launched in 2015, then combined the countries’ strengths in modern services and ability to connect Western China with Southeast Asia and the global market, Gan added. “Singapore and China’s relationship has never been static,” he said, underscoring the need for the partnership to evolve into new sectors, with both sides leveraging their strengths. “Each project responded to the challenges and opportunities of its time. In working through these projects, we came to understand each other’s strengths better, and built the confidence and trust to take on new challenges together.” He said the bilateral agreements gave businesses more certainty, citing how the recently upgraded China-Singapore free trade agreement improved market access and transparency for investors and service suppliers. “China is pursuing innovation and industrial upgrading, while Singapore is sharpening our own economic strategy and developing new sources of growth. We can combine our complementary strengths and seize emerging opportunities together.” Gan cited artificial intelligence as an area where complementary strengths could be put into practice, with Beijing and Singapore exchanging perspectives on AI governance and data through their Digital Policy Dialogue. He urged companies and research institutions to work together on practical AI applications to meet business needs, arguing this could help smaller firms access capabilities that were once costly or specialised and enable workers to use AI to take on new and more complex tasks. Gan stressed that redesigning jobs and training should be part of this effort, so that companies’ transformation would work in tandem with workforce development. A similar opportunity is available in the green economy since China has deep technological and manufacturing capabilities, while Singapore possesses strengths in areas such as finance, connectivity and project implementation, according to Gan. He listed the Tianjin corridor as an example that combined the trials of alternative fuels and digital solutions with workforce development, helping businesses and workers prepare for changes in maritime operations. “This is the kind of cooperation we should pursue – cooperation that builds capabilities and widens participation in new areas of growth,” he said. At the opening of the forum on Tuesday, Beijing’s ambassador to Singapore Cao Zhongming said at a closed panel on navigating a new world order and advancing Singapore-China cooperation that China had learned a lot from Singapore’s modernisation and continued to learn from it. Local media reported that Cao noted that while the two countries differed in size and stages of development, they shared many similarities. Both sides have sought common prosperity for all and a peaceful development path. The two countries now needed to focus more on enhancing the quality of their development, moving beyond economic gains to areas such as air quality, the ambassador said. He added that Singapore had great success in social governance and economic development, while China worked towards development as a large country with a complex national situation. Both countries therefore had experiences that could offer other countries an approach or model for their own development, Cao said.

title: Meet Sombr’s parents, Bennah Serfaty and Andy Boose, as the ‘12 to 12’ singer claps back at nepo baby claims
description: The Grammy-nominated singer’s parents met while working at amfAR, and both have impactful careers in philanthropy and event management.
content: Grammy-nominated singer Sombr, who has released popular tracks including “Back to Friends”, “Undressed” and “12 to 12” is hitting back against nepo baby allegations. The 21-year-old, whose real name is Shane Michael Boose, recently spoke to Elle magazine, addressing speculation that his parents’ connections helped him advance in the music industry. For the uninitiated, Sombr’s mother, Bennah Serfaty, is the senior director of communications at amfAR, aka The Foundation for Aids Research. His father, Andy Boose, is a former musician and current president of the event management company AAB Productions. The company has worked with renowned foundations including amfAR, the Elton John Aids Foundation, the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation, Madonna’s Raising Malawi and the Prince Albert II of Monaco Foundation. “I will forever respect my dad and my mom. I’m so f***ing proud of them, because to devote your life to something like that is so incredible and important,” he told Elle. “To think that that could help me get signed or become a big artist because my dad devotes his life to fight Aids is just incredibly insane,” he added. So, what else do we know about Sombr’s parents? What are their backgrounds? According to his IMDb profile, Andy Boose is of German-Jewish, English, Scots-Irish, Scottish, Dutch, French, Irish and Swedish descent. Bennah Serfaty has Sephardi Jewish heritage through her Moroccan father and Ashkenazi Jewish heritage through her mother, whose family has Polish roots, per the Jewish Standard. Boose attended Amherst College, while Serfaty went to the University of Wisconsin-Madison, per their LinkedIn profiles. How did they meet? View this post on Instagram Serfaty and Boose crossed paths in December 1999 while they were both working with amfAR, People reported. He was the director of special events, and she was the director of publicity. The pair got engaged in March 2003 and married that July at his parents’ property in Palisades, New York. Speaking with Observer in 2003, Serfaty described Boose as “a very self-absorbed, single, partying guy” who transformed into a “really interesting, smart, worldly guy”. Boose credited her for the change, telling the outlet: “She taught me how to be a good boy.” According to Observer, the couple welcomed daughter Amelie in 2003 and son Shane on July 5, 2005. The siblings grew up on New York’s Lower East Side. Andy Boose was a musician Boose got into music at a young age and, with his brother Johnny, joined several rock bands in his teenage years, according to The New York Times. During the 2000s, they formed their own band, René Risqué and the Art Lovers, with other East Village musicians. Sombr told People that his father has consistently supported his career, even when his mother “wasn’t too happy” when he left secondary school to focus on music.

title: France to protect key Saudi oil terminal as Houthis step up missile attacks
description: Macron pledges troops and radar systems to defend Red Sea energy hub at Yanbu following aerial barrage.
content: President Emmanuel Macron said France would send troops to defend an oil plant in Saudi Arabia as the Iran-backed Houthi militia took responsibility for new attacks on the kingdom. Macron said in a television interview Thursday with TF1 and France 2 that he would send soldiers and military support to help protect the Saudi port of Yanbu. Saudi Arabia came under attack from the Houthi militia on Thursday, with the kingdom saying it intercepted missiles fired towards the Red Sea port of Yanbu and the city of Taif. “We are going to send military assets – that is soldiers, radar systems and defence systems – to protect the Yanbu site on the Red Sea,” Macron said, adding that the French military would not participate in combat. “We aren’t going to get involved in any conflict, but to protect this site.” Macron’s pledge comes as tensions have been rising in France over surging fuel prices, with Macron insisting that the situation was the result of international conflicts, including the US war in Iran and its disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. A Houthi spokesman said on Telegram that the militia carried out two attacks on Saudi Arabia using ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones. The first attack was aimed at a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu, according to the statement. The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government since 2015 against the Houthis said six ballistic missiles had been intercepted, thwarting attacks on Taif and Yanbu. The missiles were the latest in a series of escalating Houthi attacks since July, when renewed hostilities shattered a years-long truce and embroiled Yemen in the wider Middle East war. Since then, the Houthis have imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, hitting its tankers and territory and seizing swathes of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, which is vital for Saudi oil exports. Their gains cement the hold of Iran and its allies on the two waterways that the wider Gulf, including top crude exporter Saudi Arabia, relies on to ship out its oil and other fuel products. Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, speaking on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, called on the international community to take responsibility for containing the Houthi threat. He said the Houthis “are a risk to international security and stability”. “The responsibility to deal with that threat is not just on Saudi Arabia,” he said. Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement. They condemned the attacks targeting Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself, the statement said. “The ministers also discussed arrangements for holding an urgent meeting of the chiefs of staff of the three countries to discuss ways to support Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which stipulates that an attack against any one of the parties constitutes an attack against all parties,” the statement said. Last week, Riyadh accused the group of targeting Mecca for the first time since 2017 with a drone that was downed, an accusation the Houthis denied. A few days later, the group attacked the Saudi capital Riyadh – the first in years, marking a new escalation in the conflict. The meeting was announced shortly after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian sought to distance Iran from the Houthis in an American television interview on Thursday. “The Houthis are responsible for their own actions,” Pezeshkian told the Fox News’ Special Report with Bret Baier, a day after he appeared before the UN General Assembly in New York. The Pezeshkian interview and speech took place amid a pause in fighting between the US and Iran and ‌a brief attempt at diplomacy in New York, with Qatar serving as intermediary between the warring parties. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters on Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the United States ⁠via intermediaries under which the Strait of Hormuz would be ⁠reopened if Tehran’s conditions were met. Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said. Oil prices fell on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, even as the number of ships transiting ‌the Strait ‌of Hormuz dropped to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average. Bloomberg, Agence France-Presse and Reuters

title: Mooncakes for the dog? How China is reinventing its iconic festive snack
description: China’s consumers appear to be going off the dense Mid-Autumn Festival treat, but tiny mooncakes for pets are a different story.
content: Mooncakes, a sweet staple for China’s annual Mid-Autumn Festival, are not just for people any more. Humans are pulling back, but dogs are digging in. So are cats. Pet mooncakes are popping up across China, from major retailers such as Sam’s Club to online stores and small bakeries. And many are quickly selling out. In the southwestern metropolis of Chengdu, a pack of pet mooncakes selling online for about 50 yuan (US$8) has racked up thousands of sales, news outlet thecover.cn reported. In the northwestern city of Lanzhou, pet owners can choose from fresh or freeze-dried dog mooncakes, according to social media posts. Flavour options: duck with blueberry or salmon with egg yolk. China’s social media and e-commerce platforms have also been flooded with advertisements for dog and cat mooncakes in the days leading up to Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on Friday. Typically costing around 10 to 50 yuan for a four-pack, the pet-friendly treats are colourful, mini versions of traditional mooncakes with flavours such as chicken, duck or salmon. He Yuqi, an English teacher based in Guangzhou, said he was surprised to see so many online stores offering pet mooncakes this year. “So I decided to order some custom-made vegetarian mooncakes from a nearby bakery to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival with my two dogs,” the 30-something said. The trend reflects a boom in pet ownership in China over the past few years. The number of dogs and cats in the country’s urban areas reached 126 million in 2025, while owners’ spending on their pets hit 312.6 billion yuan (US$46.7 billion), according to a report by market data provider petdata.cn. By 2028, spending is projected to reach 405 billion yuan. It also fits into a wider shift in consumer behaviour in China, as people stop splashing out on fancy traditional snacks and switch to alternative products that match their personal tastes and lifestyles. Healthier versions of traditional mooncakes – which tend to be packed with sugar and oil – are becoming especially popular as consumers embrace wellness and businesses pull back from spending on luxury gift boxes. Low-sugar mooncakes made with Chinese pearl barley seed and herbal tea were selling well this year, according to Peninsula Metropolis Daily, an outlet based in eastern China’s Shandong province. Other popular options include mooncakes with unusual fillings, such as stinky tofu and spicy luosifen, a pungent rice noodle typically made with river snails. Meanwhile, sales of traditional mooncakes have plummeted at major retail outlets this holiday season, according to data from FMCG China, a retail data provider that tracks more than 3,000 offline stores. Mooncake revenues at these outlets were down by more than 45 per cent between August 14 and September 13 compared with the same period last year, while gift-box sales were down by over 49 per cent, according to the company. Sales of gift boxes priced over 1,000 yuan plummeted by 76 per cent, with most consumers now favouring options between 68 yuan and 200 yuan, FMCG China found. According to iiMedia Research, China’s mooncake market hit a peak of 30.01 billion yuan in 2024, before shrinking 5.9 per cent last year. Qiu Hui, an administration manager in Guangzhou, said her company had cut its mooncake budget for staff and clients this year, as businesses were becoming more cautious about discretionary spending amid an uncertain economic outlook. In the past, companies were often judged based on the lavishness of their mooncake gift sets, with a pricey gift box taken as a sign that a firm was doing well, according to Qiu. But that appears to be changing amid China’s wider “consumption downgrade”. The country’s overall retail sales rose by just 0.4 per cent year on year in August, as sluggish domestic demand continued to act as a drag on economic growth.

title: Meet Power of Mama: Indonesia’s volunteer team of female firefighters
description: They put out blazes lit by poor farmers who are burning to clear their land.
content:
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.
She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives into the blaze.
“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother said.
Irma – who, like many Indonesians, only goes by one name – is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit.
They fight fires lit by poor farming communities who are burning to clear land the cheapest way they know how.
“We are the ones who feel its effects most,” Irma said. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it.”
The group was formed in 2022 by local NGO Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).

title: Can AI run a shop? Dangers of large language models that tend to agree
description: The people-pleasing nature of major AI chatbots poses risks as they validate users even when faced with false claims and biases.
content:
What could go wrong with letting artificial intelligence (AI) run a shop? Last year, AI company Anthropic invited the Wall Street Journal newsroom to use its AI agent, named Claudius, to run an office vending machine.
All operational aspects – including product selection, pricing and customer communication – were left to AI to handle independently.
After more than 140 exchanges with Claudius, reporter Katherine Long convinced it that it was not a vending machine in the United States, but one at Moscow State University in the former Soviet Union in 1962. Claudius accepted this and made all of its products free.
The story may sound ridiculous, but its implications are thought-provoking.
In March, a research team from Stanford University in the US published a paper in the academic journal Science, testing 11 mainstream large language models (LLMs) and finding that they generally exhibited people-pleasing personalities.
The study found that AI models are more willing than humans to affirm users’ positions, with their rate of agreement about 49 per cent higher than that of people.
Even when faced with blatantly false claims, AI agreed with this behaviour 47 per cent of the time.
Even more worrying is that subsequent behavioural experiments showed that users who received AI validation were less willing to apologise and were more convinced that they had been right from the beginning.
Flattery is a structural feature of LLMs thanks to how they were trained. Current mainstream AI models mostly learn from human feedback – for example, humans rate the model’s answers, and the parameters are then adjusted accordingly.
The problem is that the people rating the answers prefer ones that align with their views, even if the answers may not be objective or fair. In other words, LLMs focus on whether users are satisfied rather than whether the answers are correct. Over time, pleasing users becomes encoded in the model’s responses.
AI’s sycophantic behaviour gives users a moment of satisfaction at the cost of quietly magnifying their biases and blind spots.
Take starting a new business, for example. Many entrepreneurs chat with AI tools before writing their business plans, hoping to get a neutral opinion.
However, an overly agreeable AI chatbot tends to lay out arguments along the user’s line of thinking, amplify strengths and downplay risks, further boosting the confidence of entrepreneurs. Yet the merciless market pleases no one.
Equally shocking is AI misuse in the commercial world.
Last year, South Korean video-game developer Krafton acquired Unknown Worlds Entertainment, the developer of the 2018 hit game Subnautica . Krafton’s CEO bypassed its internal legal team and consulted ChatGPT on how to avoid paying up to US$250 million (HK$1.96 billion), which it owed to Unknown Worlds if it met certain conditions.
After continued questioning and prompting, the AI chatbot gradually validated the CEO’s line of thinking and assisted him in formulating an action plan to remove Unknown Worlds’ leadership.
But a US court ruled in March that Krafton needed to return control to the original leadership of Unknown Worlds and give the studio more time to meet the conditions for the US$250 million payout.
The case of Claudius operating a store points to another risk of AI flattery. When companies use LLMs to serve consumers, it may prioritise customer satisfaction over protecting its employer’s interests.
In high-risk scenarios such as banking, insurance or healthcare, the consequences would go much further.
LLM developers should give greater weight to honesty and correcting errors in their training objectives and incorporate stronger dissent mechanisms into critical scenarios.
In addition, regulators must require companies to disclose their systems’ tendency to flatter users, along with relevant mitigation measures, especially in sensitive fields, such as finance, education, healthcare and law.
For ordinary users, the first step towards using AI tools safely is to recognise that it is not rational, neutral or objective. Its primary mission is to make you feel comfortable – not necessarily to keep you clear-headed.
The more important the decision, the more vigilant you need to be. Consider actively asking the AI chatbot to argue from the opposing side, or explicitly instructing it to “list three fatal flaws in this proposal”.
Truly reliable judgment should never be built solely on uncritical agreement. AI can serve as a smart adviser, but it should never replace your independent thinking.
This article was first published by the HKU Business School, where its author, Professor Li Xi, is a professor of marketing.

title: Minister rejects claims mainland Chinese nurses are favoured over local candidates
description: Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau says Hong Kong’s Hospital Authority hired 95 per cent of local applicants for nursing positions over past year.
content: The city’s health minister has rejected claims that authorities favour mainland Chinese nurses over local candidates, saying Hong Kong-trained professionals have a “very good chance” of finding work because public hospitals are struggling to recruit. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said on Friday that the Hospital Authority had hired 95 per cent of local applicants for nursing positions over the past year. The figure rose to 99 per cent among applicants with registered nurse qualifications. He said that more than 4,000 students had graduated with nursing degrees, about 3,500 of whom had registered as nurses, but only 2,500 applied for authority vacancies. “So the problem is instead, why there were so many graduates deciding not to apply for [public hospital] jobs?” he told a radio show. “Public hospital nurses need to work on shifts and be on duty overnight, which is difficult, and I fully understand that.” Lo was responding to two residents who told Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on a radio show, after the release of his latest policy address, that nurses were struggling to find work. They blamed the authorities’ recruitment of non-local nurses for reducing job opportunities for Hong Kong residents. One caller, who described himself as a disciplined services psychiatric nurse on pre-retirement leave, said his application to extend his employment had been rejected despite severe staff shortages in his department. He added that his daughter, who had studied the same subject, had been unable to find a job after graduating. He cited an “unwritten rule” at the authority to reserve a proportion of recruitment quotas for mainland nurses, criticising the government for not prioritising local candidates. On Friday, Lo said the authority would never hire non-local psychiatric nurses. “All locally trained psychiatric nurses have a very good chance of being hired,” he said. “When we are reviewing the manpower in the nursing sector, we should not look into one particular case where one cannot find his or her desired job as a reference for the overall picture. “Instead, we have to consider it from the perspectives of the citywide medical service and the needs of residents.” Lo added that he was confident Hong Kong would meet its target of 2.43 doctors per 1,000 residents by 2030, as set out in the city’s first five-year plan, which Lee delivered alongside the policy address. Hong Kong’s two medical schools now admit 650 students a year, more than double the number in the 2009-10 academic year. With additional non-locally trained doctors joining the workforce, the city would have 2,000 more doctors by 2030, Lo said. He added that non-locally trained doctors currently made up about 2 per cent of the total workforce, with most working in public hospitals and universities.

title: AI war, Taiwan and translation: SCMP answers your questions from Xi-Trump summit
description: China Editor Wendy Wu tackles reader queries in this live question-and-answer session, after the two leaders’ closely watched summit.
content: This live article is freely available to our registered users. Please log in or create an account. Xi’s US summit: Access real-time updates, geopolitical risk analysis, and exclusive reporting from an Asian perspective. Subscribe now with our limited-time offer to stay ahead. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump have met in Washington for an eagerly anticipated summit, during which the leaders discussed AI cooperation, their countries’ ties and more. To help South China Morning Post readers unpack the events and figure out what it all means, SCMP’s Wendy Wu will answer questions from readers in this live question-and-answer session. Wu joined the SCMP in 2015 to report on China. Her journalism career spans two decades, covering a range of topics including diplomacy and economy. Based in Beijing, she is China Editor of the SCMP, following her stint as Political Economy Editor. The session will last for around 60-120 minutes. Leave your question in a comment on this article for a chance to have it answered.

title: From wine to ping-pong, Trump and Xi’s state dinner is heavy on historic symbolism
description: Trump invokes 1868 Burlingame Treaty to highlight deep roots of relationship; Xi speaks of WWII ‘friendship forged in blood and fire’.
content: When US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in the East Room, every detail of the state dinner was steeped in symbolism, with sparkling wine served as a nod to a pivotal moment in Sino-US relations and references to “ping-pong diplomacy”. The meal opened with a toast of Schramsberg Blanc de Noirs, a vineyard selected to honour the historic 1972 “Toast to Peace” shared by then US president Richard Nixon and Chinese premier Zhou Enlai, according to the first lady’s office. “The same American sparkling wine served at that historic gathering continues to be enjoyed at White House functions today,” Melania Trump’s office said in a statement. In his speech, Donald Trump reflected on the deep roots of bilateral contacts, pointing out that the first formal delegation of Chinese diplomats arrived in the United States 158 years ago. That 1868 mission, sent during the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), marked the country’s debut on the modern diplomatic stage. Led by former US envoy Anson Burlingame alongside Chinese officials, the delegation concluded the landmark Burlingame Treaty with Washington. Guaranteeing free immigration and reciprocal rights, the pact is regarded as the first relatively equitable treaty negotiated during an era otherwise defined by Western colonial encroachment on China. Taking the podium, Xi framed the enduring bond through the crucible of shared sacrifice during World War II, recalling how the Chinese and American peoples joined hands to fight Japanese aggressors. “During the war of resistance against Japanese aggression, Chinese soldiers and civilians rescued hundreds of American pilots at the cost of hundreds of thousands of Chinese lives. Such a friendship forged in blood and fire will surely live on through the generations,” he said. Xi also revisited ping-pong diplomacy – the historic breakthrough that broke a two-decade freeze in Sino-US relations. He paid tribute to the strategic vision of past leaders, including Mao Zedong and Nixon, who used a table tennis match to unlock a grand geopolitical realignment, setting in motion the normalisation of Sino-US relations. In April 1971, the invitation to the US table tennis team to visit Beijing opened a clandestine channel of communication, culminating in Nixon’s 1972 trip to China. That rapprochement fundamentally reshaped Cold War geopolitics and laid the foundation for decades of economic integration between the world’s two largest economies. The menu for the state dinner honouring Xi was published on the White House website on Thursday. On the same day, the US embassy in China shared a Chinese-language version of the first lady’s briefing across its official WeChat account. The social media post attracted more than 100,000 views by Friday morning and drew over 1,100 comments. Most of the responses struck a constructive tone, expressing support for Sino-US cooperation and arguing that even with competition between the two major powers, it should not veer into hostility. “Long live the friendship between the Chinese and American peoples. Ordinary Chinese people are not anti-American; they also agree with universal values,” one Chinese internet user wrote. The comment had more than 3,000 likes by Friday afternoon. “The Chinese people simply seek a better life and aspire to achieve national reunification – just as the United States did in its own history,” another internet user said, noting that the two countries could prosper together in peace. The US embassy noted on its WeChat account that its back-end system was set to automatically display all reader comments without filtering but that “external censors” – referring to Chinese platform regulators – reviewed and restricted user submissions, ultimately determining which comments remained publicly visible.

title: Hong Kong astronaut Lai Ka-ying sends Mid-Autumn Festival wishes to residents from space
description: In Mandarin speech recorded aboard China’s Tiangong space station, city’s first astronaut thanks well-wishers and expresses longing and affection for home.
content: Hong Kong’s first astronaut has delivered a Mid-Autumn Festival blessing to residents from outer space, expressing her deep affection and longing for her home city. “Looking at the moon from here and looking down at the Earth, I increasingly miss my family and friends in Hong Kong,” Lai Ka-ying said in a Mandarin speech recorded aboard China’s Tiangong space station. “On this occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, I wish people across the country good health and a happy family, as well as a happy and prosperous life for Hong Kong and Macau residents.” Lai also said she was moved by letters she had received from Hong Kong and Macau students, and she urged them to keep learning about China’s aerospace achievements and cultivate patriotism. “I understand that an aerospace education programme titled ‘A Shared Cosmic Vision for National Rejuvenation’ is ongoing in Hong Kong and Macau, and our previous ‘Tiangong class’ is a part of it,” she said. “It was not only about knowledge being passed on to Hong Kong and Macau from the Tiangong [space station], but also about valuable and unforgettable communication between me and Hong Kong and Macau youngsters. “I have also received students’ letters, paintings and blessings for our crew. We will cherish your heartfelt wishes and are deeply moved. We thank you for your warm thoughts and support.” Earlier this month, Lai and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members, mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, conducted a live lesson from space for students and teachers at her alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College. The 90-minute event was streamed at campuses across the city and broadcast live on various television channels. During the broadcast, Lai encouraged students to keep striving and never fear hardship. She said the city’s “Lion Rock spirit” and the spirit of the manned space flight were the same, as pursuing one’s dreams required facing tough challenges with courage and perseverance.

title: Asian Games, day 6: Hong Kong’s fencers finish with silver, gymnast Ng wins crucial bronze
description: Ng Ka-ki wins city’s first gymnastics medal since 2018, esports Fighting Games team also earn bronze, squash’s Simmi Chan reaches semi-finals.
content: Hong Kong’s men had to settle for silver in the team at the Asian Games on Friday, where there was a rare bronze in gymnastics and the city’s swimmer gave us a glimpse of what life will be like without Siobhan Haughey. With squash returning to the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028, both of the city’s mixed doubles pairs secured a bronze and will have the chance to go at least one better in the semi-finals on Saturday. There was bronze too in the esports Fighting Games category, although table tennis duo Wong Chun-ting and Doo Hoi-kem crashed out in the quarter-finals. Despite counting double Olympic gold medallist Cheung Ka-long and a world champion in Ryan Choi Chun-yin among their ranks, Hong Kong were on the back foot almost from the start against Japan, who are the men’s team foil Olympic champions. Trailing 15-5 at Aichi Sky Expo, after Cheung, Choi and Harris Ho Shing-him all lost their opening bouts, Hong Kong had to wait until the fourth round to outscore the Japanese for the first time as Cheung edged Kyosuke Matsuyama 6-5. Teenager Ho gave Hong Kong a glimpse of victory with a 9-5 win over Toshiya Saito to trim the deficit to five points, but men’s individual champion Kazuki Ilmura, who was part of the men’s foil team that won gold at the Paris Olympics two years ago, ensured the hosts led 30-23 entering the final three bouts. Cheung again gave his team hope with a 9-5 win over substitute Shunsuke Baba, but world No 7 Choi lost his third consecutive bout, this one against Kyosuke Matsuyama, as Hong Kong trailed 40-34 entering the last round. Ho lost to Iimura 5-2 as Japan took gold 45-36. “It was a tough match because they are a very strong team and have an Olympic champion,” Cheung said. “We really tried hard to fight against them, but we’ve lost. “Of course we aimed for the gold, especially as we have beaten Japan earlier this year in the World Cup, but I think silver is quite nice for us.” While Hong Kong’s men’s foil team finished with silver, the city’s women’s épée team were humbled 45–35 by Kazakhstan in their quarter-final, after Kaylin Hsieh Sin-yan, Chan Wai-ling, Haidi Wu and Moonie Chu Ka-mong had eliminated Thailand with a 45–27 win in the first round. Missing Olympic gold medallist Vivian Kong Man-wai for the first time since the 2014 Games in Incheon, Hong Kong still had most of the fencers who claimed team silver in Hangzhou three years ago. Only Haida Wu, who has replaced Kong, is a new addition to the squad. It is the first time since the Bangkok Games in 1998 that the city’s women have not claimed an épée team medal, with bronze almost guaranteed since the year after the handover returned Hong Kong to China. In gymnastics, Ng Ka-ki finished third in the men’s vault, averaging 14.116 points from his two attempts. Carlos Edriel Yulo won gold with 14.599, while Mahdi Olfati of Iran took silver with a score of 14.533. Ng’s podium is the first gymnastics medal at a Games for Hong Kong since Stone Shek Wai-hung won bronze on the vault in 2018, and has potentially saved the sport from losing its Tier A status at the HK Sports Institute. In squash, Simmi Chan Sin-yuk was the only player from the city to prevail in the singles’ quarter-finals after beating Aira Azman of Malaysia 3-1 to advance to the last four. Teammates Tomato Ho Tze-lok, Henry Leung Chi-hin and Lau Tsz-kwan were all denied by their respective opponents and bowed out. Both of Hong Kong’s mixed doubles pairs have reached the semi-finals on Saturday at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena, which means the worst they can do is a bronze. Tang Ming-hong and Lee Ka-yi beat Malaysian duo Mohammad Kamal and Aifa Azman 2–0, while Lai Cheuk-nam and Toby Tse Yee-lam breezed past Pakistani pair Asim Khan and Mehwish Ali by an identical score. Lee said the rallies against the Malaysian pair had been “intense, even if the score didn’t show it”. “I’m happy that Tang and I executed our game plan well, and we didn’t really make a lot of mistakes,” Lee said. “Mistakes affect the matchups in mixed doubles, and I’m happy we minimised them.” In esports, the city’s team lost in the semi-finals of the fighting games contest, which takes in Street Fighter 6, Tekken 8 and The King of Fighters XV. Having edged out Thailand 3-2, Hong Kong lost 3-0 to Japan in the afternoon session to finish with a bronze medal. At the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, Hong Kong’s women signed off from the Games by finishing fifth in the 4x100 medley relay. Haughey’s absence left Cheung Sum-yuet, Chelsie Lam, Gilaine Ma and Yeung Hoi-ching to take part in a race that was won by China in a Games record time of 3:54.55. Japan finished more than three seconds behind to take silver in 3:57:64, while bronze went to South Korea in 4:00.67.

title: HSBC, Hang Seng to unify staff benefits across Hong Kong from January: internal memos
description: Move follows HSBC’s US$14 billion buyout of remaining Hang Seng shares, with the overhaul targeting US$900 billion in combined synergies by 2028.
content: HSBC and its main Hong Kong subsidiary, Hang Seng Bank, are set to harmonise their frameworks for employee benefits across the Asian financial hub from January 1, according to internal memos seen by the South China Morning Post. The move aims to simplify benefit administration across both lenders, establish a common standard and facilitate internal career mobility within the city, the memos showed on Thursday. In an email to staff, HSBC Hong Kong CEO Maggie Ng said most existing benefits would improve or remain unchanged, though adjustments might apply to some employees depending on individual circumstances. Under the unified policy, HSBC employees will transition to a standardised sick-leave scheme with monthly accruals capped at 180 days. Other updates include higher inpatient coverage limits for junior and middle-ranking staff – in the bank’s so-called career bands seven and eight – and their dependents, as well as a new family-pooling option for medical flexible spending accounts. “It will help us deliver a clearer, more consistent colleague experience,” Ng wrote, adding that the bank remained committed to offering a competitive and inclusive benefits proposition. The alignment comes after HSBC completed a US$14 billion buyout of the Hang Seng shares it did not already own in January, and began integrating seven back-office functions between the two lenders, including compliance, information technology and finance. Our ambition is to build a bright future by bringing out the best of two iconic banks Luanne Lim, Hang Seng Bank In a separate memo to Hang Seng Bank staff, CEO Luanne Lim reassured employees that the updated framework would strengthen core protections. Hang Seng’s medical coverage will shift to HealthPlus, the existing plan used across HSBC, covering both inpatient and outpatient care, while life-assurance benefits will increase to 84 times monthly base salary from an undisclosed rate. Lim acknowledged that colleagues had voiced “a mix of emotions” at a town hall meeting earlier this year, citing pride in the bank’s heritage alongside concerns over their benefits. “Our ambition is to build a bright future by bringing out the best of two iconic banks – while continuing to invest in our people and protect what colleagues value most,” Lim said. The update comes after HSBC phased out its long-standing education-subsidy scheme – which provided up to HK$300,000 (US$38,250) annually for secondary school fees – for newly hired or promoted senior executives, though current recipients in its top three job grades, including managing directors and department heads, retained the perk. Hang Seng also cut jobs in several support departments last year as part of the same restructuring, with wealth management and other growth areas largely spared. HSBC has projected US$900 million in combined synergies and cost savings from the Hang Seng deal by 2028, against roughly US$600 million in restructuring costs. Both lenders have scheduled a series of staff briefings next week and in early October to guide employees through the transition ahead of the 2027 roll-out.

title: Ex-Malaysian minister charged with sedition over Negeri Sembilan royal crisis
description: Rais Yatim is accused of making remarks backing Tunku Nadzaruddin and urging others to be loyal to the rival claimant to the state throne.
content: A veteran Malaysian politician pleaded not guilty on Friday to a sedition charge over remarks backing a rival claimant to the Negeri Sembilan throne amid the months-long royal crisis. Rais Yatim, 84, a former cabinet minister and president of Malaysia’s Senate, was charged at the Sessions Court in Ayer Keroh, Melaka, for his comments on June 5, during a ceremony proclaiming Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar the state’s 12th ruler. Rais is accused of uttering seditious words at the Parkroyal A’Famosa Melaka Resort in Alor Gajah at about 1pm that day, an offence under Section 4(1)(b) of Malaysia’s Sedition Act 1948. The offence carries a maximum fine of 5,000 ringgit (US$1,200), up to three years in prison, or both. Prosecutors alleged that Rais wished Nadzaruddin well and urged those present to “direct your loyalty to him”, according to local media. Rais entered his plea before judge Raja Noor Adilla Raja Mahyaldin. The court fixed bail at 8,000 ringgit with one surety and set October 27 for the next mention of the case. Prosecutors had sought bail of 10,000 ringgit, while Rais’ lawyers, led by his son Danni Rais, asked for a lower sum, saying he had cooperated with the authorities and had been informed of the charge only at about 10.30pm on Thursday. Rais is one of Malaysia’s longest-serving political veterans, having served as Negeri Sembilan chief minister from 1978 to 1982 before holding several federal cabinet portfolios, including foreign affairs, information and culture. He was president of the Dewan Negara, the upper house of Malaysia’s parliament, from 2020 to 2023. Now chairman of Parti Wawasan Negara, a member of the opposition coalition, Rais has emerged as one of the most prominent figures seeking to depose Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir. At the June 5 ceremony, Rais defended the proclamation, saying the process had been carried out according to Negeri Sembilan’s laws and customs. The palace rejected that position and Muhriz later revoked two state honours previously awarded to Rais. The state secretary said the move was made to safeguard the “majesty, dignity and honour” of the Negeri Sembilan royal institution. The Dewan Keadilan dan Undang, the state’s highest customary council, maintains that Muhriz remains the lawful Yang di-Pertuan Besar and that the process used to challenge his position did not satisfy the requirements of the state constitution. Twists and turns Negeri Sembilan differs from Malaysia’s eight other royal states because its ruler is elected by four chiefs, or undangs, under adat perpatih, a matrilineal customary system with roots in Sumatra. The state’s constitution allows undangs to seek a ruler’s abdication, but only after a full inquiry and through a formal proclamation. The royal crisis took another turn late on Thursday when Muhriz’s decision to revoke the appointments of all 10 members of the Negeri Sembilan executive council was formally published in the state gazette, with the dismissals backdated to Sunday. According to the gazette, the councillors had sworn and signed pledges of allegiance before Muhriz on August 7, but had subsequently breached those pledges, prompting him to withdraw his consent for them to remain in office. It cited Article 38(5) of the state constitution, which provides that members of the executive council, apart from the chief minister, hold office for as long as they retain the ruler’s pleasure. Chief Minister Ismail Lasim has disputed the dismissal and maintained that the executive councillors remained legally in office. Negeri Sembilan police, meanwhile, confirmed that access to the state administrative complex is being controlled for the former councillors following the palace announcement. Officers were maintaining security and public order, police said, emphasising that presence should not be interpreted as the force siding with or recognising any party in a dispute that remains subject to constitutional and legal processes. On September 17, the Attorney-General’s Chambers separately declared an April 19 proclamation seeking to remove Muhriz invalid, saying it failed to comply with mandatory requirements under the state constitution and that neither the chief minister nor the state executive council had unilateral authority to remove the ruler. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim a day later urged the state government to follow the constitutional process, adding that the ruler’s position “remains secure”.

title: Opinion | The Serial Killer Speakeasy is coming to Hong Kong. Why you should be outraged
description: True crime and cocktails? An event like this completely strips the genre of its investigative integrity and empathy for the victims.
content: Imagine a Saturday night out with friends. You are gathered at a beautiful pop-up event where actors in costumes deliver dramatic monologues while you sip high-end themed cocktails in a speakeasy setting. On the surface, it just feels like a bit of edgy, immersive theatre. But what if the actors are costumed as real-world serial killers? And what if the drinks in your hands are named directly after the locations and methods of their actual atrocities? This is the premise of Serial Killer Speakeasy, a travelling entertainment concept hosted by US-based Midnight Creative that is making its way to Eaton HK in Jordan, Kowloon, in October. For the price of admission, attendees will be treated to live dramatisations of American serial killers Ted Bundy, Jeffrey Dahmer, John Wayne Gacy and Ed Gein, all paired with a menu of custom-mixed drinks. Don’t get me wrong, I am no pearl-clutching conservative who can’t handle the macabre – I am a devout enthusiast of the true-crime genre. Ever since I picked up Mark Olshaker and John Douglas’ groundbreaking book Mindhunter (1995), which details how Douglas established the FBI’s Behavioural Analysis Unit in the 1970s, I have been fascinated by criminal psychology. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jess J (@play_eat_explore) I am far from alone: it is widely documented that at least 70 per cent of true-crime consumers are women. One 2025 study suggests it could be up to 93 per cent. Psychologists point to a deeply rooted survival mindset for this statistic – women consume this media to safeguard their own survival. By studying the underlying motivations and red flags of violence that is predominantly perpetrated against women, female audiences learn how to recognise danger and navigate a world often working against them. At its best, the true-crime genre functions as a form of societal justice. The most responsible books, documentaries and investigative podcasts approach the subject through a 360-degree lens. They place the victims at the centre of the narrative, unpack the systemic failings of law enforcement, examine the fractures in the judicial system and study the dark anomalies of human nature so that society might learn how to prevent future tragedies. When I engage with the genre, I am reflecting on those institutional breakdowns that lead to such heinous crimes. The Serial Killer Speakeasy, however, completely strips the genre of its investigative integrity and empathy. To look at the horrors committed by Dahmer and decide to name a mixed drink “Apartment Two One Three” – 213 being the unit where 17 young men and boys were lured, drugged and dismembered – squarely crosses a distinct ethical line. It transitions from intellectual curiosity into the blatant exploitation of human suffering. The event organisers did not respond to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment. William Draven, the scriptwriter for the event, claimed on an episode of Hey BigHead: The Vegas Local Podcast on April 30 that they are there to inform and not idolise, and that they refuse to have actors portray Bundy and Gacy on stage. As if Dahmer and Gein are more socially acceptable. These arguments feel like empty platitudes when the execution involves treating mass murderers as headliners for the show. Attendees are served drinks like “Friendly Stranger”, representing Bundy, or “Gein’s Cauldron”, while being invited to treat actors dressed as real-world butchers as aesthetic props for social media check-ins. Take the “Killer Clowns” cocktail, a nod to Gacy, a man who dressed as a clown and was convicted of the brutal torture and murder of at least 33 young men and teenage boys in the 1970s. To transform that reality into a trendy nightlife aesthetic displays a total and utter lack of respect for the victims and the families they left behind. This nonchalant approach to trauma has ignited fierce pushback in the United States. When Midnight Creative attempted to bring the speakeasy to Tallahassee, in the US state of Florida, it sparked major community outrage. Survivors and locals who still carry the trauma of the 1978 Chi Omega sorority house murders where Bundy bludgeoned and killed two Florida State University students condemned the event as deeply insensitive, forcing organisers to hastily remove Bundy from the local line-up. If communities in the killers’ home country find this concept grotesque, how should a city like Hong Kong respond? Hong Kong is famously one of the safest cities in the world, boasting exceptionally low homicide rates. Yet, a peculiar paradox exists. Murders are few and far between, but they are often marked by headline-grabbing gruesomeness when they do occur. While we consume the information as sensational news and are as fascinated with the details as in any other major city, Hongkongers at the least never celebrate the perpetrators. Importing American serial killer fandom to be consumed as a luxury lifestyle experience in Hong Kong is profoundly tone-deaf to the local cultural context. Can you imagine the sheer, unfathomable horror if an event company launched a “Hong Kong Noir” drinks party a few years from now? Picture a crowded room in which affluent party-goers take selfies with an actor dressed as a killer while clinking glasses filled with a cocktail named after the severed head of Abby Choi Tin-fung, the 28-year-old Hong Kong socialite who was brutally murdered and dismembered in a village house in Tai Po. Imagine what it would feel like for her four young children to see their mother’s agonising death turned into a festive weekend gimmick. The very thought is sickening. Yet, by purchasing a ticket to raise a glass to the real-world agonising deaths of the killers’ victims, attendees are doing the exact same thing to someone else’s child, sister or brother. With the meteoric rise of social media sleuthing and streaming services competing to pump out true-crime content at breakneck speeds, the global fascination with the macabre shows no signs of slowing down. But a firm line must be drawn between analysing evil and drinking to it. As a lifelong true-crime enthusiast, I am putting my foot down. True-crime fans should demand rigorous journalism and structural empathy and not buy tickets to celebrate monsters for the price of a cheap, bloody cocktail.

title: Pitch perfect cultural diplomacy wins heart of China’s first lady Peng Liyuan
description: Young singers’ rendition of beloved folk song ‘Jasmine Flower’ evokes warm reaction from the renowned soprano during Smithsonian visit.
content: While their husbands held talks at the White House, Melania Trump hosted Peng Liyuan at the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday, where the famed Chinese soprano softly hummed along to a youth choir’s performance of a familiar classic. Footage shows the Hope Chinese School youth choir waving Chinese and American national flags during their rendition of the song “Jasmine Flower”, while Peng watches with a smile, her lips moving along to the lyrics. As the performance ends, she turns to her US counterpart and smiles, while placing a hand to her heart, visibly moved. The two first ladies applaud the children, with Peng calling out “bravo”. The iconic Chinese folk song, also known as “Mo Li Hua”, has long been part of Peng’s repertoire. As a celebrated soprano with the People’s Liberation Army, she has sung it on numerous major occasions, including the 2008 Beijing Olympics one-year countdown celebration at Tiananmen Square. Through its praise of the jasmine flower, the song expresses the simple and sincere feelings among China’s working people, conveying their yearning for a better life. It has become a patriotic song in China and was played by the Chinese band during the reunification ceremonies of Hong Kong in 1997 and Macau in 1999. When President Xi Jinping and the Chinese first lady travelled to Mar-a-Lago in Florida in 2017, the US leader’s granddaughter Arabella also performed the song for the couple in Mandarin. The two first ladies’ outfit choices for the second day of the Chinese state visit to Washington also drew wide attention. Peng wore a dark navy blue high-collared Qipao-style midi dress with long sleeves, elegantly accented by a silver brooch at her right collarbone. Meanwhile, Trump opted for a black high-collared Alexander McQueen coat dress featuring structured shoulders, an asymmetrical side-button closure and a knee-length skirt. She paired it with Christian Louboutin black heels. During their tour of the museum, the first ladies visited the iconic Peacock Room, its shades of green, blue and gold inspired in part by Chinese porcelain and Japanese aesthetics. Originally designed by American artist James McNeill Whistler, the room has been a centrepiece of the museum’s collection since 1923. They also stopped to admire an 18th century Chinese porcelain vase and a Yuan dynasty scroll painting. The museum was the first Asian art museum in the US, housing 13,000 Chinese artefacts ranging from ancient jades and bronzes to imperial ceramics and classical paintings. In a Fox News interview on Wednesday, the American first lady said she was taking her Chinese counterpart to the museum to show the “connection with the culture, with us and China”.

title: Uber shuts down FlyTaxi, second metered cab platform it acquired in Hong Kong
description: FlyTaxi is second local taxi app to cease operations after being acquired by US-based ride-hailing giant, following HKTaxi last year.
content: Online ride-hailing giant Uber will close a second Hong Kong metered taxi platform by the end of this year, just over six months after buying the business. Uber said on Friday that it would fully integrate FlyTaxi’s services into its own platform by the end of the year, stating that it aimed to provide “optimal” support for drivers and users. “As part of this integration, the stand-alone FlyTaxi app will [be shut down]. Our team is dedicated to guiding every rider and driver through this period to ensure a seamless ongoing service,” an Uber spokesman said. The ride-hailing giant based in the United States reassured drivers that the points they had accumulated on the 13-year-old FlyTaxi app and their account balances would be fully refunded, while encouraging them to switch to Uber, where they would have access to a larger client base and more earning opportunities. Uber acquired FlyTaxi, one of Hong Kong’s earliest metered taxi platforms, in May, saying it aimed to combine the firm’s local expertise with its technology. FlyTaxi is the second local taxi-hailing platform after HKTaxi to cease operation after being acquired by Uber. Uber bought HKTaxi in 2021 and launched a metered taxi option on its own platform in partnership with the latter two years later. But it shut down the acquired platform in 2025. After integrating HKTaxi, Uber argued that “taxi drivers have benefited from [higher] demand, while riders have enjoyed [shorter] wait times and enhanced safety features”. Both FlyTaxi and HKTaxi were founded in 2013, a year before Uber entered the Hong Kong market. The closure of FlyTaxi comes soon after the introduction of new legislation to regulate and license the ride-hailing industry. To apply for the necessary licence, platforms must have a proven track record of handling an average of 100,000 orders per day over a year in at least two other cities of a size comparable to Hong Kong. They must also submit a detailed business plan, including proposals for providing taxi services and encouraging drivers to register with their platforms. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan earlier said that more than 20 organisations had obtained application forms for platform licensing, with applications closing on October 30. Authorities have set a cap on the number of ride-hailing vehicle permits at 10,000, far lower than Uber’s proposed 30,000. The company had warned that even a quota of 15,000 would cause a 70 per cent increase in fares and result in 40 per cent of peak-hour ride requests being unsuccessful. Leung Tat-chong, deputy director of the Motor Transport Workers General Union’s taxi driver branch, said most cabbies were worried about an Uber monopoly after hearing the news of FlyTaxi’s formal closure. “We drivers would be exploited under such a monopoly by Uber, and our bargaining power would shrink,” he said. Leung urged the government to make the market as diverse as possible by letting more ride-hailing companies enter Hong Kong. “The most important thing is that drivers and passengers have a choice,” Leung said. “The more diverse the platforms, the healthier the market can become.” Additional reporting by William Yiu

title: Morgan Stanley deal leak triggers rival poaching, security warnings for Hong Kong banks
description: The affected clients have not taken legal action against Morgan Stanley or requested a replacement sponsor, according to a source.
content: After Morgan Stanley’s leak of internal deal information in a client email, rival investment banks in Hong Kong are aggressively moving to poach clients dissatisfied with the breach, according to several people familiar with the matter. Competitors are actively approaching companies named in the leaked document to pitch for their business, two rival bankers said, asking not to be identified due to the sensitivity of the issue. An accidental disclosure of confidential information by a Morgan Stanley employee this week has sent ripples through the investment banking industry, with rival firms moving quickly to capitalise on the leak and bolster their own deal pitches. All banks had similar business contacts to those in the leaked document, one of the rival bankers said, so investment banks would definitely contact the clients to try and win their business. In a statement on Thursday, Morgan Stanley said it “promptly took steps to address this inadvertent sharing of information and we continue to engage with relevant parties”. Stephen Law Cheuk-kin, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants, said even if initial assessments suggested the leak was human error, the matter remained a serious breach as information resilience was now a core element of banking operations. “Safeguarding confidential client and transaction information is fundamental to trust, market integrity and Hong Kong’s reputation as an international financial centre,” Law said. The affected clients have not taken legal action against Morgan Stanley or requested a replacement sponsor, according to one of the sources. “They are just angry,” the source noted. “I don’t expect any legal action.” Without proof of actual losses, pursuing legal recourse would be difficult, especially given that the leaked file was an internal document and not a formal legal agreement, the source said. The attached file detailed more than 100 transactions the bank was currently executing or monitoring, including regions and financing channels, according to people who received the email. However, no specific deal terms were disclosed and a significant number of the listed transactions were already public knowledge, people who saw the email said.
