Following the breach, rival firms began reminding staff to double-check email attachments to avoid similar missteps, according to a person familiar with internal bank communications. “The Morgan Stanley incident is a wake-up call for other banks and companies to review [whether] their email systems have any loopholes,” another source said. “Some big banks already use artificial intelligence to help prevent sending out documents with client information to external parties by mistake.” Steve Vickers, CEO of Steve Vickers & Associates, a specialist corporate risk consultancy based in Hong Kong, said Morgan Stanley probably needed an internal review of its classification system and oversight of access to confidential documents. “When investigating these things, you need to determine whether it’s a system problem, a people problem or a systemic error in how they protect data,” he said. “Normally, it’s not just one factor – it’s a combination of two or three factors.” “Replacing the Wall Street firm as a sponsor is not a practical option for companies preparing to list,” said the source who spoke about legal action. That is because changing an IPO sponsor triggers a mandatory two-month cooling-off period before a listing application can be resubmitted under Securities and Futures Commission rules. There was no real benefit for clients to swap sponsors, the source added.

title: Celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival magic in Hong Kong with lanterns and night tours
description: Lantern spectacles, fire dragon dances, moon-viewing tours and cultural picnics – this is your ultimate festive guide.
content:
Experience the magic of the Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong. From enchanting moongazing sessions and delightful picnics under the stars to bus rides that showcase the city’s vibrant energy, there is something for everyone to enjoy.
The South China Morning Post has curated a round-up of all the exciting offerings for this festive occasion.
At Victoria Park in Causeway Bay, the Hong Kong Tourism Board has organised the World Lantern Boulevard, which will showcase more than 3,000 distinctive lanterns from 20 countries and regions, such as South Korea and Brazil.
Since opening on September 17, the show has proved so popular – drawing crowds every night – that the board has decided to extend it by a week to October 4.
The show offers many photo-taking opportunities, including at the entrance, an eight-metre-tall lantern inspired by the city’s banyan trees and created by master artisans in Nanjing.
Just a few minutes’ walk from Victoria Park, locals and tourists can catch the Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance on the evenings of Friday and Saturday. A 67-metre-long fire dragon, a beast of legend, adorned with 12,000 burning incense sticks, will be carried through the neighbourhood.
In Wan Chai, Lee Tung Avenue will feature a 200-metre-long walkway lit up by a colourful canopy of lanterns.
Meanwhile, Citybus has partnered with the Wan Chai Blue House to launch the first-ever Mid-Autumn Festival-themed open-top bus route, H1M “Moon Viewing Tour of Hong Kong Island”.
The tour bus will pass Victoria Park and visit many locations on Hong Kong Island including Kennedy Town, the Hill Road Flyover and the Blue House, a four-storey pre-war building.
Across Victoria Harbour, at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre Piazza in Tsim Sha Tsui, the Leisure and Cultural Services Department will present a lighting installation until October 11.
At the West Kowloon Cultural District arts hub, the Harbourside East Lawn of the Art Park has been turned into a picnic ground until October 11, with food stalls, live music and themed workshops.
Visitors can also cycle along the Victoria Harbour waterfront and explore arts and cultural spaces.
According to the Hong Kong Observatory, the full moon will occur in the early hours of Sunday.
However, the forecaster said a bright, round moon should still be seen at night during the Mid-Autumn Festival period, weather permitting.
The best time for moongazing on Friday night is around 11.24pm, when the moon reaches its highest elevation in the sky.
On Friday, the weather is expected to be mainly fine and dry. On Saturday, there will be sunny periods with very hot weather during the day. But it will be cloudy in the morning and at night on both days.
On Friday, MTR lines – except the Airport Express, Disneyland Resort line and the section of the East Rail line to and from Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau stations – will run enhanced services from 3pm onwards.
Services on these lines will also be extended to the early hours on Saturday.
Eleven Light Rail routes and three MTR bus routes will also extend services to the early hours of Saturday, while tram and ferry services will be strengthened, subject to passenger demand.

title: Profile | How 91-year-old Helena Law Lan became Hong Kong cinema’s grand dame of horror
description: Law was a Hong Kong TV staple in the 1970s, but it wasn’t until later that she became a cultural icon playing mystical villains in films.
content: This is the 86th instalment in a biweekly series profiling major Hong Kong pop culture figures of recent decades. Few figures are as synonymous with Hong Kong horror films as Helena Law Lan, who has been a household name for over half a century. Unlike the typical “scream queens” who gain popularity playing damsels in distress, 91-year-old Law has been the city’s on-screen spirit medium for over three decades and for years served as Hong Kong theme park Ocean Park’s Halloween ambassador. Remarkably, it was not until her late fifties that Law became Hong Kong cinema’s go-to demoness; for the first few decades of her career, she primarily played minor supporting roles or villains in films and television series. Early struggles and a budding career Law, whose real name is Lo Yin-ying, was born in Hong Kong on November 13, 1934. She inherited non-Chinese ancestry from her mother’s side, though her exact heritage is uncertain. Law was reportedly raised in a fairly well-off family until her father, a lawyer and businessman, died during World War II when Law was nine. Her first of many acting experiences came earlier, at age four, as an extra in the 1939 film A Woman of Many Husbands (Part 2). Her career truly began, however, during a visit to a film set in Kowloon in 1950, when a crew member asked the then-15-year-old to play an unnamed factory worker in The Kid, with a nine-year-old Bruce Lee in his first leading role. Over the next decade, Law picked up a few more minor or uncredited roles – including a bit part in the social realist film In the Face of Demolition (1953). Her education had been severely hampered by the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong from 1941 to 1945, and she was ultimately forced to quit secondary school in the early 1950s. In the early 1960s, the film producer Wong Cheuk-hon discovered Law and offered her a three-year contract with Lan Kwong Film Company. With the city still facing post-war economic hardship, Law dived into a budding industry that paid considerably better than the office jobs she would have otherwise considered. From the start, her strong, well-defined facial features led her to be cast in villain roles. She was also given the stage name “Law Lan” to evoke a glamorous “bad woman” image. In a 2020 interview with Hong Kong news outlet HK01, she said: “I’d never thought I’d be the lead. Anyway, it’s acting.” A daily television fixture In 1971, when she was in her mid-thirties, Law signed with TVB after a brief stint with Rediffusion Television and was given a succession of roles playing mothers and eccentric women. She joined the cast of Enjoy Yourself Tonight, the longest-running Hong Kong variety show to date, primarily performing comedy. The 1970s saw Law become a daily fixture in local living rooms as she took on numerous supporting roles in television dramas. A bigger TV role came in 1983 when she played the facially deformed villain Kau Chin-chak in The Return of the Condor Heroes, starring Andy Lau Tak-wah and Idy Chan Yuk-lin as lovelorn martial artists – a role Law reprised in the 1995 remake. While many of Law’s contemporary female entertainers were concerned with maintaining a conventionally beautiful appearance, Law embraced her unconventional casting. “My look was quite terrifying, but many viewers remembered it,” she told HK01 in 2018. “As an actor, my job is to do justice to the script.” Late-career horror breakthrough In 1993, when she was 58, Law played her most iconic role to date: the supernatural medium Lung Po (or “Dragon Granny”) in Wellson Chin Sing-wai’s Thou Shalt Not Swear, a horror comedy about the Hungry Ghost Festival. Law’s performance bagged her a best supporting actress nomination at the 13th Hong Kong Film Awards. Her turn in the 1996 sequel July 13th – which focused more on her character – earned her another nod in the same category. Gradually, Law became a pop culture icon. She went on to play the same creepy, spiritual old lady with a piercing gaze and unnerving coldness in numerous films, such as the Troublesome Night series (1997-2003), Big Fortune Hotel (2015) and the musical comedy I Love You, You’re Perfect, Now Change! (2019). “I love watching horror films,” she told HK Magazine in a 2013 interview, noting that her first experience with the genre – a vampire movie she saw in her thirties – left her so terrified she had nightmares, prompting her mother to scold her for being a coward. Law’s reputation as a horror icon could be seen as ironic given her faith. In the same HK Magazine interview, the devout Roman Catholic credited her religion with saving her life. “When I was five, I had a severe fever and wouldn’t wake up. I was clinically dead. I miraculously awoke after a nun baptised me and prayed for me. It was God’s will.” When asked if starring in ghost films conflicted with her beliefs, Law said she was assured by a priest that it was fine as long as she viewed it purely as acting. “I don’t believe in ghosts just because I have played Lung Po,” she added. Law experienced a career high when she won best actress at the 19th Hong Kong Film Awards in 2000 for her role in Wilson Yip Wai-shun’s crime drama Bullets Over Summer. At 65, she became the oldest actress to receive that honour. The milestone victory was part of a critical sweep: her performance as a lonely elderly woman living with dementia also earned her a best actress win at the Hong Kong Film Critics Society Awards and best supporting actress at the Golden Bauhinia Awards. This success elevated her to a Hong Kong treasure known for her acting range. In 2002, she won a Life Achievement Award at the TVB Anniversary Awards, after which she continued to portray motherly characters on television for over a decade. An enduring cultural legacy From 2010 to 2019, Law served as Ocean Park Hong Kong’s official Halloween Fest ambassador, playing a series of eerie characters in the theme park’s annual promotional videos. She will resume this long-time collaboration in October 2026 for a special Halloween meet-and-greet event. Law has appeared in over 400 films. In recognition of her cultural impact, Lingnan University conferred an honorary fellowship on her in 2018. In recent years, she has continued to play a broad range of elderly characters while also taking on the occasional horror role, including as a supernatural medium in Tony Leung Hung-wah’s Synesthete (2021) and the maker of a haunted doll in Danny Pang Fat’s Reborn (2025). For all the success she has enjoyed in her career, Law is known for maintaining a down-to-earth lifestyle. She has spoken candidly in various interviews over the years about her past financial setbacks. Rather than chasing wealth, Law, who never married, has remained active in her charity and community efforts. The Hong Kong government awarded her a Medal of Honour in 2002 for her dedication to public service. Law suffered a fall in 2025 that led to an eight-day stay in hospital. Later that year, she parted ways with TVB after more than five decades with the broadcaster. She fell again in spring 2026, and it remains to be seen whether she will take up new roles. “Every time I watch TV, I ponder how I would interpret certain characters,” she told HK01 in 2020. “It’s clear that I have fallen in love with my work. I don’t know when my life will end, but for as long as I am able, I will keep doing it.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook.

title: Japan’s cut-price morgues cash in on legal loopholes as lonely deaths rise
description: One Tokyo-based company is offering to do everything from body collection up to ash internment for just US$1,040.
content: Unregulated companies are running a brisk trade across Japan storing and disposing unclaimed corpses, with a recent report revealing how such “cut-price morgues” are cashing in on legal loopholes to discard the nation’s dead. The business has shed light on the growing number of “lonely deaths” of elderly Japanese as the traditional nuclear family fades. Some industry insiders have expressed shock at the trend and are calling for regulation to block potential loopholes, while others point to public apathy as an enabling factor. The Asahi newspaper reported last week that nondescript industrial buildings in suburban districts were being used to store human remains in refrigerator units. Reporters visited a “makeshift morgue” operated by a private funeral company, which they called “the front line of a shadowy, unregulated industry now flourishing across Japan”. In Japan, when a “lonely death” happens and relatives cannot be traced, the funeral cost is passed on to local governments. Under growing financial pressure, they invariably seek the cheapest option to dispose of the dead. For as little as 165,000 yen (US$1,040), one Tokyo-based company will collect a body anywhere within a 150km (93-mile) radius to be transported to a storage site, then placed in a coffin with dry ice until the cremation can be carried out. Ashes are stored for up to five years before they are interred – all overseen by the company. That figure is around 20 per cent cheaper than the financial help given to welfare recipients to help cover the costs of a funeral. It also frees local governments from the additional cost of long-term care for the ashes and interment. Yuusuke Wada, a fifth-generation funeral director, suggests the cut-price morgues themselves are not a problem. In some ways, the operators of such services should be praised because they charged the bare minimum and were honest with their pricing, said Wada, founder of YEY Co, a consulting firm that promotes the introduction of advanced technologies, such as AI and blockchain, to modernise Japan’s funeral sector. “These firms use cheap locations and do everything else on the cheap before they pay low taxes.” “But 165,000 yen is not a funeral,” he said. “It’s a straight path to the crematorium, no blessing, no monk, no prayers – straight to the furnace.” According to a nationwide survey of 2,000 people released in May by Kamakura Shinsho, operator of the Ii Sogi Funeral Service, the average cost of a funeral is 967,300 yen, up 25,000 yen from a year earlier. No regulations Cut-price morgue operators were not doing anything wrong in terms of location either, Wada said. “These storage units may be in residential areas, but the one in the Asahi article does not seem to be in a densely populated place. There is no need to put up a sign and there is no law stopping anyone from being an undertaker. They can store the bodies in these places – and at least this place is using a refrigerator.” The laws that cover the industry do specify the amount of time that can pass before a cremation must be carried out, but make no mention of standards for bodies that are being stored before cremation, according to Wada. And as there are no qualifications or licences required to operate a funeral business, anyone can open a company without even needing a physical office. ( This lack of government oversight has consequences, however. In 2023, two decomposed bodies were discovered in coffins in a former funeral home in Aichi prefecture. And the bodies are piling up in ageing Japan. The Asahi reported that 56,447 people were granted financial help for funerals in 2024, a cost of 12 billion yen. The previous year, some 42,000 bodies were unclaimed across the country, while municipalities were storing 60,000 sets of unclaimed ashes in 2021. Another funeral director is not as sanguine as Wada. “There should be strict licensing and inspections,” said Robert Hoey, the Canadian president of Kanagawa-based Funeral Support Services. “If bodies are not being kept properly, there should be fines and licences taken away.” The problem is that the industry is unregulated, according to Hoey. “Anyone can set up a business offering extremely cheap services which lead to situations like this,” he said. “The government is offering these contracts to the lowest bidder rather than a reputable company. Providing extremely cheap options leads to problems.” He called for more regulation and government inspections “because businesses need to be held accountable” but is not optimistic that it is going to happen. “I don’t expect a backlash because the government will probably sweep it under the carpet rather than deal with it.” The Ministry of Justice declined to comment when contacted by This Week in Asia.

title: Letters | Make the Northern Metropolis Hong Kong’s zero-carbon test bed
description: Readers discuss a zero-carbon mandate for the Northern Metropolis, and the complex reasons Chinese students move and stay overseas.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan contains welcome targets for energy, carbon emissions, air pollution and water quality. Yet when it turns to the Northern Metropolis – the city’s main platform for innovation and new industrialisation – green development largely disappears as an organising principle. That separation could prove costly. The Northern Metropolis is a rare chance to design a new urban and industrial system from the ground up. Decisions now about its buildings, power supply, transport and landscape will shape Hong Kong’s economy for decades. The city should not build a 20th century industrial estate and market it as 21st century innovation. The national 15th five-year plan calls for about 100 national-level zero-carbon industrial parks. Shenzhen is also developing near-zero-carbon pilot zones. Hong Kong should not merely play catch-up. The government should designate the Northern Metropolis as its first zero-carbon, climate-resilient industrial and innovation district – and use the city’s financial and international strengths to improve on the mainland model. A credible zero-carbon district must count more than the electricity consumed within its gates. Much of its footprint will be created before its laboratories and data centres open, through construction materials, equipment and supply chains. Public contracts should reward low-carbon materials and whole-life performance. Energy, buildings, transport and data infrastructure should be planned as one system, rather than as separate projects with green labels attached. Resilience must also be designed in. Parts of the Northern Metropolis adjoin low-lying rivers, fish ponds, wetlands and Deep Bay. These natural systems store floodwater, moderate heat and sustain biodiversity. Treating them merely as land awaiting development would destroy protective infrastructure that taxpayers may later have to rebuild. Done properly, the Northern Metropolis could become more than a cleaner business park. Mainland companies could demonstrate green technologies there, while Hong Kong’s universities, engineers, lawyers and financiers help test, finance and adapt them for Asian markets. Regional experience could, in turn, feed back into Chinese innovation. This would make Hong Kong a two-way platform between China and Asia, not merely a showroom. The government should give the Northern Metropolis a zero-carbon mandate now, before yesterday’s infrastructure is poured into concrete. Lo Sze-ping, former CEO of WWF China, and special policy adviser to the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development Chinese move and stay overseas for complex reasons I read with interest the op-ed, “The unspoken reason my Chinese friends choose America” (September 19). The op-ed reduces modern socio-economic and familial pressures – intense career competition, urban pace and status anxiety – to a Confucian caricature. High expectations around success and personal choices are not unique to China or Confucian heritage societies. Romanticising the United States as a judgment-free zone overlooks its own realities: the widespread social isolation, economic precarity and hyper-individualistic pressure that shape urban American life. Presenting overseas movement purely as flight from cultural oppression also contradicts demographic evidence. Between 1978 and 2025, 9.46 million Chinese students went abroad; of the 8.01 million who completed their studies, 6.98 million returned – an impressive rate exceeding 87 per cent. Many of these returnees enter dynamic domestic tech and research sectors. Conflating discomfort with certain local social norms with a broad endorsement of American society misreads the calculus of global migrants. People move for career synergy, economic opportunity, research infrastructure and lifestyle preferences – not a simple binary between traditional expectations and American individualism. Youthful frustration with societal pressures often reflects personal navigation challenges rather than a systemic civilisational flaw; many choose to return, managing these environments successfully. Finally, framing personal space as a unique American gift ignores reality. Mainland Chinese migrants and students choose diverse destinations – Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, Canada, Europe and beyond. The United States does not have a monopoly on freedom, liberty or a good life. A more accurate account would recognise both the real pressures some experience and the data showing that the large majority of Chinese students ultimately build their futures at home. Nick Wang, North Point

title: Milan Fashion Week: Max Mara brings elevated safari style as Marni echoes utilitarian vibes for SS27
description: Inspired by 1930s female pioneers, Max Mara’s line-up featured linen as soft as silk, while Marni embraced colour and leaned into buckle and belt motifs.
content: The main shows of day three of Milan Fashion Week were Max Mara – the womenswear label that earlier this year celebrated its 75th anniversary with a show and exhibition in Shanghai – and Marni, where Belgian designer Meryll Rogge unveiled her second collection for the brand. Here’s what you need to know about the two shows. Fabrics always reign supreme at Max Mara, a brand that has a long history of developing high-quality textiles. The luxurious yarns the brand uses in its fall/winter collections – from wool to cashmere and alpaca – are second to none. The label’s spring/summer 2027 show, which kicked off day three of Milan Fashion Week, was built around a natural fibre that is synonymous with warm weather: linen. Safari jackets and shirts, practical vests, cropped cargo pants and other utilitarian staples such as suede backpacks – all in a rich palette of browns, khakis and taupes – dominated the elegant line-up. Linen is notoriously not an easy fabric to wear, but Max Mara made it look as luscious and smooth as silk. Named Far Horizon, the collection paid homage to intrepid female travellers from the 1930s, women like aviator Amelia Earhart and cross-continental driver Eva Dickson. As always at Max Mara, inspiration aside, the clothes looked desirable and modern and far from costumey. The show ended with a series of languid evening dresses – including an off-the-shoulder column gown and a couple of long-sleeved sheer dresses in black – that were the definition of polish and ease. After a well-received debut that was just respectful enough to the spirit of Marni without feeling too nostalgic, Meryll Rogge delivered yet another great collection for the Italian label. Held at the brand’s historic headquarters, where founder Consuelo Castiglioni previously presented her runway collections, the spring/summer 2027 presentation was a study in the act of revealing, according to the show notes. The show opened with a couple of shift dresses featuring a cut-out detail at the décolleté fastened by a buckle. That same silhouette returned at the end: the last three looks were similar versions of those shift dresses but made of leather and embellished with crystal-encrusted panels. What came in between was a parade of looks that stayed true to the brand’s DNA of whimsical design with an artsy bent. Exposed bras, synthetic fabrics, lingerie accents and strategically placed buttons were some of the elements that recalled the Marni of yore but looked fresh and modern. The utilitarian vibe that Rogge brought to Marni at her first show last season continued in this collection, with hardware details, drawstring fastenings and technical elements adorning many of the outfits. The designer paid homage to Marni’s fur heritage with a trio of terrific coats in Mongolian lamb, great examples of how to make fur look chic and modern. The styling was impeccable, showcasing a wide array of accessories – from knee-high socks worn with heeled sandals to leather drawstring bags, mirror-shaped pendant earrings, and new versions of the Trunkette bag.

title: Trump autopen joke at Biden’s expense draws rare laugh from China’s Xi
description: Trump autopen remark during White House tour prompts the Chinese leader to respond audibly to his host’s mockery of the former president.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping broke into rare laughter as his US counterpart Donald Trump showed him a framed “autopen” displayed in place of the former American leader Joe Biden’s portrait during a White House tour. The viral moment stood out against the Chinese leader’s otherwise restrained demeanour during his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade. A video released by the White House on social media showed Trump taking Xi along the White House colonnade on Thursday before stopping at the “Presidential Walk of Fame”, where portraits and plaques honour US presidents. “This is the autopen ... it’s Biden,” Trump said, pointing to the image. Xi laughed audibly, while several people accompanying the two leaders also appeared to join in. While parts of Trump’s remarks were difficult to make out in the video, he appeared to be referring sarcastically to Biden’s use of the autopen, a recurring target of the US president’s criticism of his predecessor. "This is the autopen... it's Biden." 🤣 President Trump shows off the legendary Presidential Walk of Fame to President Xi. https://t.co/qUQEM6XoLj — The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 24, 2026 The moment offered a striking contrast with Xi’s generally composed public demeanour during the state visit which is occurring against a backdrop of bilateral tensions over technology and rare earths. At Wednesday’s welcome ceremony, Xi showed little reaction when a jet taking part in a military flyover produced a thunderous roar as the US national anthem was being played. Trump, standing nearby, appeared startled by the noise and briefly grimaced. After Xi laughed at the autopen joke, Trump gave the Chinese president a friendly pat on the shoulder as they continued the tour. Trump is known for using expansive gestures and physical contact when meeting foreign leaders. During previous encounters between the two presidents, however, Xi has generally maintained a more formal posture. In Trump’s visit to China in May, Xi appeared to deny Trump his trademark tug of war-style handshake, holding firm as the US president tried to draw him closer. Thursday’s video quickly drew attention on social media. “I have never heard Xi laughing so genuinely with Trump about Biden’s autopen portrait,” one post said. “Quite a moment,” another commenter wrote. The image of an autopen has occupied the place of Biden’s portrait in Trump’s “Presidential Walk of Fame” since September 2025. Trump has routinely denigrated his predecessor, refusing to acknowledge his 2020 election loss to Biden and repeatedly peddling the claim that the result was rigged by voter fraud. He has also repeatedly accused Biden of relying on aides and the autopen to sign official documents by the end of his term in office, allegations that Biden’s administration has disputed. A separate video shared by White House staff also showed Trump stopping in front of a framed photograph from his meeting with Xi in Beijing in May. Trump pointed at the photograph and asked, “Who is that? I don’t recognise him.” Xi turned towards members of his delegation and appeared to give another brief laugh. US-China relations plummeted to new lows during Biden’s term as a sequence of events unravelled diplomatic ties. Sharp recriminations over the origins of Covid-19 were compounded by a major cross-strait crisis triggered by then-US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s Taiwan visit in 2022. Other tensions involved the 2023 “spy balloon” saga and an array of tech-containment measures targeting China’s semiconductor and investment landscapes. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. After Biden took office in January 2021, he held three formal in-person meetings with Xi, all on the sidelines of multilateral meetings, including the G20. No state visits were exchanged between Washington and Beijing during the former US president’s tenure. Xi’s last trip to the United States was in November 2023, when he travelled to San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and met then-president Biden. Before that, Xi’s last state visit to Washington was in September 2015, when then-US vice-president Biden and his wife Jill Biden welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at the airport.

title: Shanghai Gold Exchange pushes more Chinese banks to end retail leverage trading
description: Lenders in China are redirecting retail clients to fixed-price accumulation plans and physical purchases of precious metals, moving away from margin-based speculation.
content: At least a dozen Chinese banks intend to wind down retail leveraged precious-metals trading – a practice in which everyday investors post margin deposits to speculate on gold and silver contracts without owning the physical metal. The retreat comes amid sharp swings in international gold prices. Sources at two banks, including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China – the world’s largest lender by assets – said that this round of withdrawals was mandated by the Shanghai Gold Exchange, China’s main platform for physical precious-metals trading. The latest move came on Friday, when Beijing-based China Everbright Bank said it would phase out retail leveraged precious-metals trading for gold and silver on a to-be-determined date after October 19. Earlier this month, Shanghai Pudong Development Bank put out a comparable notice. In total, 12 major Chinese lenders have announced plans to exit the business, including ICBC, Bank of China (BOC) and China Construction Bank. “This represents an inevitable shift, and I anticipate that all the lenders will eventually exit the business,” said Xu Ying, an analyst at Shanghai-based Orient Futures. Mainland lenders have offered leveraged precious-metals trading for nearly two decades, typically aligning their margin requirement levels with those set by the Shanghai Gold Exchange, and allowing leverage of between five-fold and more than six-fold for retail investors. Xu said that leveraged trading placed high demands on investors, in terms of position-size management and market judgment. “That naturally makes it a poor fit for domestic retail clients, most of whom have limited trading know-how and tend to be risk-averse.” Since last year, as gold prices have climbed alongside greater volatility, banks have progressively raised retail-margin requirements. By the end of the first quarter of this year, state-owned banks had raised these requirements to 100 per cent, effectively eliminating leverage. And since then, banks have been moving towards a complete exit from the business. But retail-investor risk profiles are not the only factor driving the pullback. A source at BOC’s Shanghai branch, who had been involved in handling the fallout from the 2020 “fiasco” involving the lender’s retail crude-oil investment product, known as Yuanyoubao, said the shift was “expected”. The person declined to be named, having not been authorised to speak publicly. The incident occurred in April 2020, when a historic collapse in US crude oil prices resulted in many retail investors seeing their investments wiped out, leaving thousands owing money to the bank. “Following the high-profile Yuanyoubao incident, financial regulators began mulling a broader phase-out of retail commodity-linked trading products offered by domestic banks,” the source explained. “The fiasco itself was so disruptive that it prompted sweeping regulatory caution towards retail leverage instruments.” Later in 2020, China’s banking regulator fined BOC a total of 50.5 million yuan over widespread risk-management lapses, improper product design and a faulty position-rolling mechanism linked to the Yuanyoubao incident. “Back then, almost all the lenders suspended opening new accounts for retail leveraged precious-metals trading at regulators’ behest,” the source added. “Actually, from that point forward, the business ceased further expansion.” Going forward, that means mainland lenders are expected to offer only physical gold and non-leveraged gold-accumulation plans – products that let investors buy small, regular amounts of gold over time without borrowed funds – for retail investment purposes, according to the source. Spot gold swung above US$4,200 an ounce on Thursday, after surging to almost US$4,700 an ounce in late August. Xu at Orient Futures said that, “for the remainder of the second half, sticky-high inflation is expected to constrain the Federal Reserve’s policy room”. “Market expectations for interest-rate hikes will keep fluctuating, yet rate cuts appear unlikely, at the very least,” Xu added. “This leaves gold without sustained upwards momentum, and the metal is projected to trade mostly in a range.”

title: Ivanka Trump takes front-row seat to welcome Xi in dress by Chinese designer Guo Pei
description: US president’s eldest daughter had a prominent position at the ceremony and wore a striking blue outfit from Beijing-based couturier.
content: The US president’s eldest daughter Ivanka Trump had a front-row seat at a White House welcome ceremony for President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan on Thursday, wearing a dress by Chinese fashion designer Guo Pei. Trump, in a robin’s egg blue dress and matching jacket, and her 15-year-old daughter Arabella Kushner occupied a prominent position at the ceremony, alongside Vice-President J.D. Vance and his wife, Usha Vance. The arrangement drew attention since members of Donald Trump’s cabinet – including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth – were seated further back. US media reported that Ivanka Trump’s striking blue gown and jacket with silver embroidery were designed by Guo, while her daughter wore a white belted midi dress by London-based fashion brand Self-Portrait. The choice of a Beijing-based designer as well as the seating arrangement reflected the Trump family’s personal and commercial ties with China. During Donald Trump’s first term as president, his daughter Ivanka was an unpaid adviser and became an important conduit for Chinese officials in Washington. When Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan visited the United States in April 2017, Ivanka’s daughter Arabella performed the traditional Chinese ballad “Mo Li Hua” (Jasmine Flower) and recited Tang dynasty poetry in Chinese. Later that year in Beijing, President Trump showed Xi private video recordings of his granddaughter addressing the Chinese leader and his wife as “Grandpa Xi” and “Grandma Peng”. Meanwhile, Ivanka Trump secured multiple trademark approvals in China during her father’s presidency in 2018, sparking widespread discussion about potential conflicts of interest. Trademarks covered standard fashion and lifestyle goods and also services like voting machines and nursing homes. She shut down her business in mid-2018, saying that she would focus on her government work. In 2022, Ivanka Trump announced she was stepping away from politics and leaving the political arena. There was symbolism in wearing a dress for Thursday’s ceremony by Chinese designer Guo. The 59-year-old is best known for creating a spectacular trailing yellow embroidered cape with fur trim that pop star Rihanna wore to the 2015 Met Gala – a piece that took two years and more than 50,000 hours to complete. Ivanka Trump’s choice also echoed the Chinese first lady’s cultural diplomacy through fashion. Peng is known for championing home-grown Chinese designers and traditional culture through her fashion choices.

title: Singapore food watchdog investigates alleged illegal sales of dog meat
description: The move came after screengrabs shared on social media appeared to show an ad in Vietnamese offering various cuts of dog meat.
content: The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) is looking into a social media allegation that dog meat was being sold illegally in Singapore. The screengrabs shared on the Facebook group Dogs Singapore appeared to show an advertisement in Vietnamese offering various cuts of dog meat. A check on Friday morning found that the post containing the screengrab had been deleted. SFA has not approved any source of dog meat, the agency said early on Friday morning. “All food imports must meet SFA’s requirements. Illegally imported food products from unknown sources can pose a food safety risk,” the agency said. Meat and meat products can only be imported by licensed importers and must come from sources accredited by the SFA. It is an offence to sell meat and meat products that have been imported without a valid licence or import permit, SFA said. Those convicted of selling illegally imported meat and meat products can be fined up to S$50,000 (US$39,000), jailed for up to two years, or both. Repeat offenders can be fined up to S$100,000, jailed for up to three years, or both. SFA said food safety is a “joint responsibility”, adding that importers and retailers must ensure that food products they bring into Singapore for sale comply with its import requirements and are safe for consumption. Members of the public with concerns about food safety practices can report them to SFA through its online feedback form, it added. This story was first published by CNA

title: China seal touches hearts for swimming 200km back to island after missing humans
description: Experts believe that because Nana was cared for by humans for so long, she now associates people with safety.
content: A young seal gained widespread attention on social media in China after swimming 200km to return to an island where it had lived for months following its release into the wild. This two-year-old seal marks its second return to a human-inhabited area after being freed into open seas. Internet users were touched by videos showcasing the seal, affectionately named Nana, as it returned to the shores of Dachangshan Island in northeastern China’s Liaoning province. Nana was released into the ocean on September 7, but reappeared on the island on September 13 after covering the impressive distance of 200km, as reported by the Science Education Times, thanks to positioning equipment attached to its body. Local fishermen observed that the seal appeared significantly thinner after such an arduous journey. Nana had previously attracted considerable attention in June for its lack of fear towards humans, showing a preference for interaction with visitors at Dachangshan Island. Originally released into the sea near Sanshan Island, located about 110km away, in mid-April by marine animal specialists, Nana was the only one among five seals that chose not to integrate with a wild seal population, instead opting to remain at Dachangshan Island, which features human activities. Nana is classified as a sea calf, a wild species that enjoys the highest level of protection, designated as first-grade protected in China. It was first discovered on a beach in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region after a typhoon in September 2024. At that time, the young marine animal, just several months old, was found with numerous injuries. Authorities in Guangxi provided meticulous care for Nana, and local residents affectionately gave it the name, which is typically associated with girls. In November last year, Nana was transferred to a marine animal protection base run by the Liaoning Provincial Institute of Marine Fisheries Sciences, where it underwent rewilding training. Following its second release, tracking data indicated that Nana swam past several islands before arriving back at Dachangshan Island, where it had previously spent months during its training period. Wang Xin, a marine environmental researcher at Dalian Ocean University, told the media that Nana’s return was a decision driven by instinct, influenced by a sense of safety and memory. “It has been nurtured by humans for an extended period, thus it has developed an association between humans and safety. As a result, it has lowered its guard around human activities and formed an attachment to humans,” the scholar explained. According to Wang, Dachangshan Island provides a suitable habitat for Nana, featuring high water quality, abundant fish and shrimp, and sandy beaches. Local authorities currently maintain a “no intervention, no feeding” policy concerning Nana. In mid-September, the Changhai county government, which oversees Dachangshan Island, issued a statement urging the public to refrain from approaching Nana, feeding it, or disturbing it. “Nana is still adjusting to life in the wild. While it is not wary of humans, a stress response could be triggered if it is surrounded, fed, pursued, or disturbed. Relying on human feeding will complicate its return to wild populations,” the authority indicated in its statement. The county’s Marine Development Bureau established a social media account for Nana in late September to “protect it and promote its image.” “We will not control its behaviour, nor will we exploit it for publicity,” an official, identified only by the surname Dong, was quoted as saying. Many internet users have suggested allowing Nana to remain permanently. “Since it enjoys this location, I urge you not to relocate it again. We should respect its choice, right?” commented one user, receiving over 3,000 likes.

title: China tested a handheld submarine detector. It tracked a subway train underground
description: The tiny device is the size of a pencil and uses just 5 watts of power but can record a train braking into a station under a city street.
content: Chinese researchers have showed a handheld quantum magnetometer built for hunting submarines in a striking real-world test: it tracked a subway train rumbling beneath a city street. The device, developed by Peng Xinhua and colleagues at the University of Science and Technology of China, is described in a study published on September 14 in Acta Physica Sinica. Though it is scarcely larger than a pencil and draws only 5 watts of power, it can isolate the magnetic disturbance caused by a moving train in the Earth’s vast background field, clearly recording the train braking into a station, its stop and its departure under traction. The team said the same technology was intended for anti-submarine warfare (ASW), where detecting the magnetic anomaly of a submerged vessel is the main means of locating it. According to the paper, its other potential uses also include navigation and positioning, field mineral exploration, mine clearance and urban traffic flow monitoring. The magnetometer works by shining laser light through a small cell of rubidium vapour. When the magnetic field around it changes, the rubidium atoms respond differently, which changes how much laser light passes through. The system measures that change to calculate the magnetic field strength. The probe is only about 7 cubic cm (0.4 cubic inches). In the low-frequency window of 0.1 to 10 hertz, its sensitivity is about 10 picotesla per square root hertz. For comparison, devices such as superconducting quantum interference devices and spin-exchange relaxation-free atomic magnetometers are much more sensitive. They can detect fields below one femtotesla, the best performance now possible for weak magnetic fields. But they usually need very low temperatures or complete magnetic shielding, so they are hard to use when moving quickly or when magnetic interference is strong. This small magnetometer takes a different route: it is built to work reliably in real, complex and moving environments. When measuring, the magnetometer works like a radio locked onto one channel: the resonance frequency of the atoms. If the magnetic field changes too quickly, the probe tilts, or the field is uneven, it can drift off that channel. This is known as losing lock. The paper describes an algorithm that watches for this. It checks not only the signal strength but also whether the resonance peak still has the right shape. If the lock is lost, the system immediately scans the full frequency range to find the resonance centre again, regaining the lock in under a second. The algorithm plays a major role in the instrument’s robustness. The hardware provides the signal, while the algorithm keeps the lock stable. Without these algorithms, the magnetometer would easily lose lock in complex external fields. The paper notes that the Mz magnetometer made by the US company QuSpin has a slew rate of about 10,000 nanotesla per second. This magnetometer reaches 25,200 nanotesla per second, about 2½ times higher. That means it can track sudden magnetic field changes more effectively and is less likely to lose lock. The team tested the device in other real-world settings. In one test, it monitored Earth’s magnetic field over a long period and recorded a G4-level geomagnetic storm on June 1, last year. These are severe space weather events that can cause satellite drag and navigation system errors. The storm pushed the aurora to latitudes far lower than usual – such as California – and a rare pink aurora even appeared in Heilongjiang, China. Its data closely matched readings from an International Real-time Magnetic Observatory Network, or INTERMAGNET, station in Cheongyang, South Korea, including wave shapes, spike timing and overall trends. It kept running for a long time without stopping or losing its signal lock. The team also used it to locate a buried magnetic rod. In a blind test in a 40-metre (131 feet) by 25-metre area of farmland, with the rod buried about half a metre deep, they scanned in a serpentine pattern with the handheld device. It produced a 2D magnetic map and located the centre of the magnetic anomaly, which matched the rod’s actual position well. The paper also said this device could be used in urban traffic flow sensing, fault diagnosis of underground metal pipeline networks, resource exploration and the search for unexploded ordnance.

title: From ping-pong to pickleball: China’s unofficial approach to diplomatic messaging
description: Beijing has found various ways beyond direct government contact to send signals to Washington.
content: Before setting off for Washington on Wednesday, Chinese President Xi Jinping had some correspondence to attend to. Dozens of students from 10 US universities, including Harvard, had written to Xi about their experiences on an exchange trip to China this year. According to the State Council, Xi responded with a call to the students to advance cooperation between the two countries. The gesture extended a pattern. For decades, Beijing has often turned to unofficial channels, from prominent individuals to bridging organisations between the two powers, to get its diplomatic messages across to Washington. The tradition has been pronounced in recent years, as the fierce China-US strategic rivalry makes direct governmental contact challenging. For example, when the trade war sent shock waves through the trans-Pacific relationship in 2018, Beijing placed particular value on influential “old friend” and former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger, channelling its views on relations with Washington in multiple meetings with him. When Kissinger, the principal architect of the US’ rapprochement with China in the early 1970s, died in 2023, the baton for that intermediary role for Beijing appeared to pass to his student, Graham Allison. Allison, the former dean of Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government, visited China in March and June, meeting high-level Chinese officials on both occasions, including an encounter with Wang Huning, the country’s fourth-ranking official. Allison is the author of The Thucydides Trap, a book that popularised the theory that a rising power and an established hegemon are prone to conflict. Xi referred to the term in his talks with Trump on Thursday. With trade and investment such a large part of the relationship between the world’s two biggest economies, Beijing has also emphasised engagement with the American business community as a way to signal its intentions to Washington. Just days before Xi’s latest trip, Chinese Premier Li Qiang met a visiting delegation from the US-China Business Council in Beijing. The council was founded in 1973 with support from the White House and the State and Commerce departments, and has played a prominent role in the development of bilateral relations. Apple, Boeing and Nvidia are among its more notable member companies and their executives have made high-profile trips across the Pacific. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has made repeated trips to China and met several senior Chinese officials. He also accompanied Trump on his May visit to Beijing. And on Wednesday, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV released interviews in which Elon Musk, the US trillionaire and Trump ally, described Xi as “a great leader”. The National Development and Reform Commission, China’s top economic planning agency, also invited the American Chamber of Commerce in China for a roundtable on September 10. The influence of those potential messengers in the White House or on Capitol Hill has long been open to debate. Still, history shows that such players do not necessarily need to have official credentials to make a difference. In 1970, then Chinese leader Mao Zedong appeared with American writer Edgar Snow on the Tiananmen Rostrum to send a diplomatic signal to then US president Richard Nixon that Beijing was ready to reopen communications with Washington. The process was aided by “ping-pong diplomacy”, which helped to normalise China-US relations and remains a recurring reference in Beijing. The Chinese government has found contemporary successors to that legacy. In the past two years, for example, there have been multiple pickleball exchanges between Chinese and American teenagers. At a pickleball event in May, Beijing’s top envoy to Washington Xie Feng called on participants to “carry forward the spirit of ping-pong diplomacy” through the sport and to “write new stories of China-US friendship with the passion of youth”. It underlined Beijing’s broader emphasis on people-to-people exchanges as another channel that could help convey its views on the bilateral relationship. At the White House on Thursday, Xi announced that 100,000 young Americans would be invited to take part in exchanges and study in China over the next five years. The move followed his initiative in 2023 to invite 50,000 US youths over five years – a target Beijing said months earlier it had reached 2½ years ahead of schedule. Those initiatives came after years of escalating pressure from Washington led to the large-scale closure of Confucius Institutes in the US, stifling a key channel long regarded by Beijing for educational and cultural exchanges between the two nations. In recent years, Beijing has repeatedly used events commemorating the legacy of the Flying Tigers – the group of American volunteer pilots who fought Japanese forces in China and Burma during the Word War II – to invoke memories of close cooperation between the two countries. Trump also mentioned the US pilots in his remarks when hosting Xi on Thursday. In September 2023, when relations were beginning to return from a particularly low ebb, Xi replied to a letter from Jeffrey Greene, chairman of the Sino-American Aviation Heritage Foundation, and Flying Tigers veterans Harry Moyer and Mel McMullen, noting that China and the US “should, and must, respect each other, coexist in peace and pursue win-win cooperation”. During his visit to the US in November that year, Xi also referred to the Flying Tigers in a speech, as well as the friends he made in Iowa during his first visit to the United States in 1985. In February, he sent a reply letter and a Chinese New Year card to long-time friends in Iowa, underscoring continued China-US exchanges. Another similar people-to-people diplomatic channel is “Bond with Kuliang”, a cross-cultural initiative built around the historic ties between residents of a mountain resort in Fujian province and American families who lived, worked or vacationed there from the late 19th century.

title: Opinion | How Hong Kong is remapping the future of higher education
description: A planned university town offers a chance to re-examine the very logic and model of Hong Kong’s higher education development.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan marks an unprecedented milestone not only for its economic and social development, but also for how it governs itself. The plan, which drew on 16,000 public submissions – roughly 80 per cent from ordinary citizens – is a testament to the government’s commitment to long-term development, which shows an unusual convergence of public consensus and political will. For a city long accustomed to letting the market hold the reins, crafting a road map clear in aims, precise in methods and univocal in stance – and placing itself as the primary agent responsible for its execution – is an act of political self-reinvention. It betokens a willingness to embrace the role of direction setter and reform executor, to be held accountable for outcomes five years down the road rather than merely navigate short-term challenges at hand. Hong Kong’s reorientation away from a market-led approach indicates not only an upgrade of policy tools, but also a recalibration of governance philosophy. This road map attaches great importance to higher education. The integrated development of education, technology and talent is at the core of the strategy and seen as the pivotal powerhouse of Hong Kong’s long-term prosperity. This is especially evident in its vision for the Northern Metropolis – the 30,000-hectare redevelopment project that anchors the blueprint. Designed to develop another economic centre of the city closer to Shenzhen, the Northern Metropolis covers about one third of Hong Kong’s total area. It is, in effect, a second city being built from scratch – planned to house 2.5 million residents and create about 650,000 jobs, with land earmarked for advanced manufacturing, logistics, professional services and, most crucially, education. A university town spanning roughly 1,000 hectares incorporating industrial, residential and recreational space is expected to sit at the heart of the Northern Metropolis. By anchoring three separate campuses in San Tin, Hung Shui Kiu and Ta Kwu Ling, it will draw researchers, students, entrepreneurs and investors into the district to advance industry-academia-research integration and, ultimately, unleash the area’s economic potential. If the Northern Metropolis serves as the plan’s core engine, the university town is its powerhouse – ready to ignite the spark for economic rejuvenation, transforming Hong Kong’s higher education along the way. It starts by redrawing where universities sit and how they connect. The three university towns each include a campus area, a technology area, an industry area and a living community, developed under the “one town, five elements” framework. This is not just dividing land by function; it is designing institutions. It puts laboratories, start-up incubators, production lines and residential communities into one geographic unit. By forcing industry, academia and research into the same physical space, it uses geography to break institutional inertia. That works far better than simply telling institutions to collaborate more. It then removes the regulatory rigidities that have long stifled innovation. One of the plan’s most valuable contributions is that it confronts the lack of institutional flexibility that hampers technology transfer. For example, it proposes to accelerate the release and development of space using diverse means: adopting “large-scale land disposal” and “pay for what you build” schemes, allowing in-situ land exchange, introducing a dual-track system of direct land grant and tender to speed up land transfer, and establishing an industrial park company to enhance management efficiency. The innovative and bold approach adopted by the Hong Kong government showcases its commitment to pushing forward reform for high-quality development. Most crucially, it offers a chance to re-examine the very logic and model of Hong Kong’s higher education development. The plan calls for deepening industry-academia-research integration, which requires the higher education sector to re-evaluate whether its funding allocation, promotion criteria, curriculum design and talent cultivation have offered sufficient incentives and created a friendly environment for industry collaboration and start-up incubation. It is widely acknowledged that Hong Kong’s universities excel at training researchers and professionals for finance and services, but are far less effective in producing the engineers, designers and technological specialists who can move an idea from a laboratory bench to a production line. The university town, by embedding campuses within industrial clusters and requiring universities to align their academic strengths with the industries being built around them, tilts the balance. It gives institutions a reason to invest in basic research and applied sciences, not because rankings reward it, but because the ecosystem depends on it. It also changes what students are trained for – not merely to fill the best-paid jobs in finance and law, but to build the industries on which Hong Kong’s next chapter will rest. In this sense, the plan does more than offer a new direction; it adjusts how the city’s universities have understood their mission. With the launch of the plan, demanding tasks face these universities. It asks them to change habits built over decades and stand up to the resistance from those who benefit from the status quo. Yet Hong Kong’s universities have shown, time and again, that they are capable of reinvention. They have all the strengths needed – academic depth, international networks, institutional resilience and the commitment to act. If they are ready to rise to it, they will not merely serve the Northern Metropolis – they will define what Hong Kong becomes next.

title: Newcastle University under fire over Anant Ambani professorship amid Vantara scandal
description: The university awarded a sustainability role to tycoon Mukesh Ambani’s son, who is linked to the controversial wildlife centre in India.
content: Britain’s Newcastle University faced criticism on Thursday for awarding a sustainability professorship to Anant Ambani, the son of Asia’s richest man and owner of a scandal-hit giant wildlife centre in India. Vantara, which calls itself the world’s largest rescue centre, last month announced a major reset of its procedures following concerns about its rapid and vast acquisition of animals from around the world, including endangered species. Newcastle University said on September 14, it awarded the professorship of practice in sustainability to Ambani “in recognition of his significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”. “Work at Vantara closely aligns with the University’s world-leading research on global conservation and biodiversity targets,” the university in northern England said. It also noted his role as an executive director at Reliance Industries, a retail and oil conglomerate headed by his father and billionaire tycoon Mukesh Ambani. “Newcastle University is really stooping low here and making a mockery of sustainability,” Lyla Mehta, a researcher at the Institute of Development Studies affiliated with the University of Sussex, said on social media on Thursday. “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy,” Mehta earlier told The Guardian, which first reported the story. Wildlife conservationist Prerna Singh Bindra questioned the characterisation of Vantara, a sprawling 1,416-hectare (3,500-acre) facility, as a conservation site. “It’s a captive facility, a zoo. So how is this conservation? We need to protect wild animals in their natural habitats, not zoos,” Bindra said. “When we’re talking about a university, you’re nurturing, mentoring, skilling a generation of conservationists,” Bindra added. “But here you are changing the entire paradigm of conservation from protecting them in their natural habitat to one that says that accumulating animals in zoos is conservation.” Vantara has consistently denied any wrongdoing.

title: How was dinner? Takeaways from Xi and Trump’s evening at the White House
description: With culinary diplomacy on the menu and tech titans at the table, Xi spoke of ‘a new historical juncture’ for ties and Trump talked up trade.
content: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump addressed top American business executives and officials in the White House’s East Room on Thursday evening, ahead of a state dinner. The dinner capped a tightly scheduled day for the two leaders, who delivered speeches in the morning hailing close ties and urging deeper cooperation. During the day, Xi and Trump held their second face-to-face meeting this year – which Trump called a “great meeting” – touching on issues including Taiwan, the Middle East crisis and the Ukraine war. Trump then gave the Chinese leader a tour of the new White House helipad. Here’s what happened at the state dinner. For a round-up of their speeches in the morning, see here. Who’s at the main table? Sitting at the main table with the two presidents were all American tech titans whose business prospects are deeply tied to or dependent on the Chinese market. They include Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, and Apple board chairman Tim Cook. Musk, Huang and Cook also attended the state banquet at the Great Hall of the People during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. ‘New chapter’ in US-China ties Both leaders used their speeches to play up warm ties between the two countries, with Trump saying that even though the two countries have different systems “the ties between our people endure”. Xi said the “sincere and in-depth” exchanges with Trump earlier in the day provided “new strategic guidance” for ties. Describing relations as being at a “new historical juncture”, the Chinese leader said Trump’s “Make America Great Again” was complementary with Beijing’s commitment to realising the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. “Let us join hands and move forward side by side. Together, let us nurture the beautiful flowers of Sino-US friendship. Together, let us write a new chapter in our friendly relations,” Xi added. Long history of trade With the two countries having just agreed to extend their tariff truce by two months amid progress in trade negotiations, both leaders invoked the long history of bilateral trade, which dates back to the founding of the United States. “Americans and Chinese have always exchanged goods, knowledge, customs, and ideas,” Trump said. “This has been the foundation of commerce and mutual respect between our countries.” Xi, meanwhile, noted that George Washington, the first US president, personally acquired a large collection of Chinese porcelain as a symbol of that long commercial relationship. “Over 200 years ago, soon after its independence, the United States turned its eyes to China,” Xi said. “Our two countries started trading with each other, exchanging goods to meet each other’s needs and draw on our complementary strengths.” Heavyweight guests Apart from those at the table with Xi and Trump, other prominent US business leaders who attended the state dinner included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and the CEO of Micron Technology Sanjay Mehrotra. Also in attendance were JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, Lockheed Martin CEO James Taiclet, and Pfizer chairman Albert Bourla. No business executives from the Chinese side attended the dinner. American menu with Chinese touches Culinary diplomacy is on the menu for guests of the state dinner: American business leaders and government officials from both countries. Guests raised their glasses of blanc de noir from California in a toast. The sparkling wine is from the same vineyard that supplied wine for the historic 1972 “Toast to Peace” between then US president Richard Nixon and Chinese premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing. “The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together,” the office of American first lady Melania Trump said.

title: Hong Kong catching up with Dubai in ‘super-prime’ property sales amid Iran war
description: Dubai remains the world’s top market for luxury homes worth at least US$10 million, but Hong Kong has closed the gap fast, according to Knight Frank.
content: Hong Kong has significantly narrowed Dubai’s lead as the world’s top market for “super-prime” residential property in recent months, as rising conflict weighs on activity in the Middle East market, according to Knight Frank. Dubai retained first place for deals involving homes sold for US$10 million or more in the second quarter of the year, with 131 sales worth a combined US$2.17 billion, but the total value of those transactions fell 27 per cent compared with the previous quarter. Hong Kong, meanwhile, recorded 93 transactions worth US$1.67 billion, according to Knight Frank’s Global Super-Prime Intelligence report published on Thursday. Though the value of deals in Hong Kong declined 9 per cent, that still led Dubai’s lead over the city to shrink by more than half: from US$1.13 billion to US$498 million, the report showed. The volume of deals in Hong Kong also surged 75 per cent from a year earlier, while Dubai’s slipped 8 per cent, Knight Frank added. Mainland Chinese buyers have been central to a recent rebound in luxury home sales in Hong Kong, focusing on trophy assets in prestigious areas such as The Peak, according to a report by Centaline Property in July. “For now, Dubai remains the global leader, but Hong Kong’s recovery is increasingly well established,” said Liam Bailey, global head of research at Knight Frank. The broader super-prime market, however, remains under pressure. Globally, 572 transactions worth US$10 million or more were recorded in the April-to-June period, down 7 per cent from the first quarter and 6 per cent from a year earlier. The total value of those sales reached US$10.5 billion. Knight Frank said Dubai’s weaker quarterly performance did not materially change its position at the top of the global super-prime market. “Nevertheless, the second-quarter result provides confirmation of the impact of current regional geopolitical instability,” the report noted. Data from Centaline suggests that deals for properties priced at HK$100 million ($12.8 million) or above have accelerated in Hong Kong over recent months, as the luxury market rapidly recovers from a years-long slump. By the end of June, the number of deals for such luxury properties so far this year had already exceeded 85 per cent of the total recorded for the whole of 2025, according to Centaline. Trophy homes in sought-after developments can still command nine-figure prices, even as individual properties continue to sell at discounts. Hong Kong’s overall luxury property market has slowed in the second half amid external headwinds, including Chinese tax changes and tighter capital controls. With several developers claiming the policies have not had a major impact, firms are capitalising on the rebound by releasing inventory previously withheld during the downturn. High-profile deals recorded through August and September include K&K Property’s One Stanley, while CK Asset launched a new 10-unit tender at 21 Borrett Road on Thursday, having reaped over HK$2.5 billion from 14 prior sales since June. Yet broader macro headwinds persist. Although major banks in Hong Kong chose not to follow the US Federal Reserve in raising interest rates earlier this month, the upward trajectory of rates could potentially weigh on the broader market in the coming months. Property agents say owners in prime neighbourhoods are taking a wait-and-see approach, inviting private offers rather than setting formal asking prices.

title: Legislation among options to regulate minors’ social media use: justice minister
description: Paul Lam dismisses concerns that measures could infringe on individual rights, saying goal is to protect children in Hong Kong from online harms.
content: Introducing legislation to protect minors by regulating social media use is among the options on the table, Hong Kong’s justice minister has said, after the latest policy address unveiled plans to create a task force to review the situation. Speaking to the South China Morning Post and other media outlets on Wednesday, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok dismissed concerns that such measures could infringe on individual rights and freedoms, emphasising that the goal was to protect children from undesirable content such as pornography. His remarks followed Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address on September 16, when the city leader announced that the government would establish a dedicated task force to look at minors’ social media use. According to the policy address, the interdepartmental group, spearheaded by the Department of Justice, would review the associated risks of minors’ use of social media and artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, and assess whether legislative and administrative changes were needed. “Legislative intervention is one of the options, but it may not be the only option. In principle, I can imagine there are different ways to encourage minors to use [social media] in a more proper manner under proper supervision,” Lam said. “We have hard law on the one hand; we have soft law, guidelines and codes of conduct, those sorts of things. And then we have education, propaganda, public relations. There are many options, and they are not mutually exclusive. They may run in parallel.” Lam said there could be new guidelines for parents and teachers, as they had supervisory responsibilities. But he declined to specify measures or pre-empt the task force’s findings. Last November, Australia became the first country to introduce a social media ban for minors under 16, barring children from using a variety of platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok. Under the groundbreaking rule, minors were prohibited from opening new accounts and existing ones were deactivated. Social media companies would face fines for breaches, while parents and children would not be penalised. Countries including the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Denmark have since proposed similar bans for children. Lam said the government would draw on overseas examples, including studying the effectiveness of Australia’s law and feedback on its implementation. But he noted that there was no uniform set of rules. Asked whether the potential restrictions could curtail individual rights and freedoms, Lam said all legislation would comply with the entrenched rights set out in the Basic Law, Hong Kong’s mini-constitution. “I am not very concerned about any potential infringement because the purpose is not to restrict any sort of freedom,” he said. “We are only aiming at protecting our children to ensure that they will not be exposed to risks. In particular, the type of risk that I am sure everyone would agree contains undesirable elements, for example, pornographic materials, ideas that incite children to resort to violence.” City leader Lee previously highlighted seven key areas of AI risk governance, including combating AI-related crimes such as deepfake porn, in his annual policy blueprint. Lam acknowledged public concerns over AI-related crimes and said he was liaising with the Law Reform Commission’s cybercrime subcommittee to prioritise and accelerate its study of the relevant issues, seek public feedback, and provide recommendations. “Legal reform often covers a wide scope and really takes time. But we cannot wait, and we understand that it is better if it is done faster,” he said without offering a timeline for the review, noting that the commission worked independently. Lam also explained that existing laws were able to address AI-related crimes such as scams, but the goal of the review was to formulate more targeted legislation to keep pace with rapid technological advancement and handle cases more effectively. Another issue highlighted in the policy address was whether current laws adequately addressed legal liability arising from accidents caused by AI products. Lam said the government would establish another task force to look into the matter and hold its first meeting this year. But he declined to provide a timeline, citing the complexity of the issue and the need for a cautious and prudent review. He added that authorities would refer to other jurisdictions and ensure proper consultation with all local stakeholders, including manufacturers, AI creators and consumers. In the interview, the justice minister, who was among nine Hong Kong and mainland Chinese officials removed from an American sanctions list in July, was also asked whether he would consider visiting the United States. Lam did not respond directly to the question but said it was important to enhance foreign confidence in Hong Kong’s rule of law, adding that he would visit other countries if there were suitable opportunities based on “sincerity and mutual consent”. “Hong Kong is an international city. It is important to help others understand Hong Kong and to give them confidence in the city. If there is something I can do in my position, I will certainly do my utmost,” he said. “Even if we may have fundamental disagreements on many issues [with other countries], that should not be a reason to hinder communication.”

title: Culinary diplomacy on the menu for Xi and Trump at the White House
description: Evening features ‘American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence’, entertainment from military bands and plenty of red linen and flowers.
content: As Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met at the White House for a state dinner on Thursday, culinary diplomacy was on the menu for the guests who included business leaders and government officials. “The menu showcases American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence, bringing the culinary traditions of both nations together,” the office of American first lady Melania Trump said. Xi was dressed in a black Zhongshan suit – colloquially known as a “Mao suit” – while Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan wore a long red gown. Trump wore a black suit with a black bow tie, while his wife was dressed in a white blouse with a large bow paired with high-waisted dark trousers and heels. Guests began the evening by raising their glasses of blanc de noirs from California in a toast. The sparkling wine is from the same vineyard – Schramsberg – that supplied wine for the historic 1972 “Toast to Peace” between then US president Richard Nixon and Chinese premier Zhou Enlai in Beijing. The dinner menu featured a smooth yellow squash veloute, paired with a wild mushroom fricassee, crispy pancetta and a drizzle of scallion oil to start. For the main course, sesame-crusted sea bass was paired with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte of fresh herbs. And for dessert, a smooth vanilla cremeux with a sour cherry confit centre set on a walnut frangipane was accompanied by ice cream made with harvested White House honey. Entertainment for the evening featured classical tenor Christopher Macchio, who performed at Trump’s presidential inauguration last year, alongside elite military ensembles the Marine Band, the Marine Drum and Bugle Corps, the Army Chorus and Army Strings. The White House also leaned into the cultural significance of red in Chinese history, with plenty of red linen and red flowers including dahlias and ranunculus. On the tables were vermeil from the White House collection and china from the Reagan State Service with alternating gold and red bands. During Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, the state bouquet at the Great Hall of the People featured lotus flowers and miniature replicas of local landmarks, including the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. In Beijing, beneath glittering chandeliers, officials and business leaders mingled before Xi and Trump toasted a successful summit. The Chinese menu featured lobster in tomato soup, crispy beef ribs, Peking duck, stewed seasonal vegetables, slow-cooked salmon in mustard sauce and pan-fried pork buns. The dessert selection featured trumpet shell-shaped pastries, tiramisu, fruit and ice cream.

title: Ukraine’s POW transfer reveal deals North Korea a propaganda blow
description: Zelensky’s UN disclosure punctures Pyongyang’s soldier-loyalty narrative, but risks damaging ties with Seoul and endangering POW families.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has put North Korea in a propaganda bind, analysts say, by publicly revealing that Kyiv recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. The disclosure – made during Zelensky’s address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday – directly challenges Pyongyang’s narrative that its soldiers fighting alongside Russian forces would choose death over surrender. North Korea is unlikely to acknowledge the transfer publicly, but may strengthen ideological controls over its troops deployed to Russia to prevent further defections, observers say. “Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” Zelensky said during his UN address, using South Korea’s official name. “These guys are not easy to capture alive.
