One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself and he was shocked that fate didn’t let him die.” The two soldiers were reportedly captured by Ukrainian forces in January 2025 after being deployed to Russia’s Kursk region to support Moscow’s war effort. Zelensky said they subsequently expressed a desire to travel to South Korea, as indicated in interviews and handwritten letters sent to organisations representing North Korean defectors. South Korea’s Foreign Ministry declined to confirm any specific details regarding the POWs, citing concerns for the safety of the men and their families in the North. But it did say in a statement that the issue should be resolved in a manner that “respects the free will of the individuals concerned and is consistent with international law and humanitarian principles”. “In line with this position, the government has been engaged in necessary consultations with Ukraine and other relevant countries and organisations,” the ministry said, adding that this was “a sensitive matter” and it could not divulge details about bilateral consultations. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung expressed regret about the disclosure in a social media post on Thursday, calling it “a highly sensitive matter” that could have serious implications for diplomacy and security on the Korean peninsula. “Considering the various issues that could arise from making the matter public, keeping it confidential was the reasonable course of action in every respect, and that was what we agreed upon,” Lee wrote in Korean. “While I do not know the specific circumstances that led the Ukrainian side to break the agreement and go public, the situation is deeply regrettable.” South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said on Thursday that the two prisoners had left Ukraine last weekend, travelled via a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days earlier, likely under the protection of South Korean intelligence agencies. In July, Lee and Zelensky agreed on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara to handle the North Korean POW issue based on humanitarian principles while respecting the prisoners’ wishes. ‘Propaganda nightmare’ Zelensky raised the POW issue while accusing Russian President Vladimir Putin of recruiting foreign fighters to prosecute his war on Ukraine. “Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory … instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Zelensky said, adding that Moscow had recruited citizens from 47 countries, including Ghana, Nepal and India. Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said Pyongyang would likely remain silent to protect the narrative of absolute loyalty and self-sacrifice among its troops. “North Korea is likely to ignore the issue or show little interest, given the potential burden of allowing it to become a major political issue,” Yang said. “At the same time, Pyongyang is expected to strengthen ideological education and internal controls over North Korean troops in Russia to prevent similar defections.” Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, described the situation as a “propaganda nightmare” for Pyongyang, as it had consistently eulogised its soldiers as heroes who take their own lives rather than surrender. “For North Korean soldiers in Russia, this news opens a different option that is not death when they risk being captured,” Oh said, adding that Ukraine was likely to use the defection in psychological warfare targeting North Korean troops. Questions of trust Yang said that Zelensky’s decision to go public with the POW transfer could have broader geopolitical implications – potentially driving a wedge between Seoul and Kyiv. “Bringing such a sensitive humanitarian issue directly into the international spotlight at the United Nations could undermine trust in relations between South Korea and Ukraine,” Yang said. “The Ukrainian president could also face criticism that a sensitive humanitarian issue is being politicised.” Respecting prisoners’ free will should have included getting their consent before revealing their transfer, Yang added, given the risk of retaliation against their families remaining in North Korea. “Announcing their defection without first securing their consent would constitute an inhumane act,” he said. “Zelensky himself should make clear whether the prisoners’ consent to the public disclosure was explicitly obtained.” Yang dismissed speculation of a secret deal between Kyiv and Seoul, pointing to President Lee’s stated preference for diplomatic transparency. Oh said the disclosure could also serve Ukraine’s broader strategy of highlighting the deepening military relationship between Russia and North Korea as Kyiv sought continued international support for its war effort. While Seoul has provided humanitarian aid to Ukraine, it maintains a strict policy against supplying lethal weapons to any country at war. Asian Games defections? Zelensky’s disclosure coincided with an unconfirmed report that two members of North Korea’s delegation to this year’s Asian Games in Japan were seeking asylum. South Korea’s Monthly Chosun magazine reported on Tuesday that the pair – part of an estimated 180-member North Korean delegation – had approached Japanese authorities expressing a desire to seek asylum in Japan rather than South Korea. Citing a source linked to Japan’s Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office and the pro-Pyongyang General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, known as Chongryon, the magazine said the individuals’ identities and roles had not been disclosed. Japanese authorities have not publicly confirmed the report and it is unclear whether any defections have occurred at the Games.

title: Chinese teen swim sensation Yu Zidi set for Olympic stardom after golden Asian Games
description: Schoolgirl won all three individual events she swam this week in Tokyo in some of the year’s fastest times, will be only 15 in Los Angeles.
content: China’s 13-year-old swimming prodigy Yu Zidi has stamped her mark all over the Asian Games and she could cause a sensation at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years’ time. The schoolgirl won all three individual races she swam this week in Tokyo with Asian Games records – a series of performances that belied her tender age. Out of the pool, she has proved herself to be a typical teenager, joking around with teammates and freezing when asked about herself in interviews. She will be 15 when the LA Games come around in 2028 and likely to be a major medal threat with the world watching. “She hasn’t become that fast for no reason,” said teammate Ke Wenxi, whom Yu beat in the 400m individual medley final to complete her golden hat-trick. “I’ve seen how hard she works in training. During this national team training camp, I saw her working really hard every day.” Yu also won the 200m butterfly and 200m IM races this week in Tokyo. Her times were among the fastest in the world this year and her 200m medley swim was just 0.4 seconds off the world record. That mark is held by Canada’s Summer McIntosh, who is likely to be Yu’s biggest rival at the LA Games. Yu would not be drawn on her ambitions for the Olympics, saying only that she intended to “keep working hard”. It hinted at a mature attitude and a desire not to be shaken off in her pursuit of success. “I gained a lot from these Asian Games but there were also some regrets,” she said. “I’ll go back and keep reviewing what I didn’t do well, and I hope I can do better next time.” Room for two As might be expected of someone who does not turn 14 until next month, Yu was less comfortable out of the pool than in it. She complained that “interviews are way harder than the race”, openly admitting that she struggles in front of large numbers of reporters. “How do I answer this question? Can you teach me? You just want me to say what I feel?” she said after one question. When asked if competing this week had been easy, Yu stared in wide-eyed amazement for several seconds before replying: “Definitely not.” She has seemed most at ease in the company of her teammates, especially 15-year-old Ke. Yu and Ke, who shared a room in Tokyo, made heart signs and chatted happily together as they celebrated their one-two finish in the 400m medley. “There are three beds in our room – two are pushed together to make a big bed, and there is another smaller one,” Ke said. “I let her have the bigger bed because the smaller one was enough for me. “I wanted her to have somewhere more comfortable to sleep.” Yu has spoken in the past about struggling to deal with the heavy load placed on her. She was discovered by a swimming coach while at a water park aged six and since then has juggled schoolwork with training. “Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring,” she said in January. She called her Asian Games experience “challenging” and things are not likely to get any easier on the road to the Olympics. If she can maintain her focus, she could be one of the stars of the Games. “I don’t think about anything else,” she said when asked about what she thinks about before a race. “I just think about the little details and my movements.”

title: China’s EV and battery makers tussle over paying resumed lithium-ion tax: sources
description: Squeezed EV makers object to eating the cost, and negotiations on splitting the tax continue weeks after its official resumption, sources say.
content: China’s electric vehicle (EV) makers and battery manufacturers are locked in negotiations over which party should pay a resumed consumption tax, according to industry sources, a conflict that underlines carmakers’ struggles amid weak home market demand. Beijing is ending an 11-year exemption on a 4 per cent consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and related products. It returned to 2 per cent on September 1 and will be fully restored one year later. The country’s battery makers planned to pass the costs on to their clients in the downstream industry. For example, the fifth-largest battery maker by volume, EVE Energy, planned to add the 2 per cent consumption tax to domestic orders that shipped after September 1, according to a notice it issued to clients on July 24. But with their profitability squeezed amid reduced subsidies and weakening domestic demand in the world’s largest EV market, EV makers saw no choice but to push back, according to two people familiar with the matter. Now, despite the tax being officially back in place for weeks, battery firms and EV makers were currently still at the negotiating table trying to reach a consensus on sharing the levies, one source said. “The negotiation is a battle between the battery and EV makers in a weak market,” said Yale Zhang, managing director at the consultancy Automotive Foresight in Shanghai. “The results would be up to the bargaining power of companies in the market and even the ties between executives at the carmakers and the suppliers.” JP Morgan estimated in July that if EV makers bore the 4 per cent consumption tax, they would see a bite of up to 0.8 per cent from their selling prices, based on calculations using popular models including Geely’s Xingyuan and Li Auto’s i9. Despite robust exports, the industry-wide profit margin for China’s car manufacturers narrowed to 3.6 per cent in the first seven months of the year, far below the 6.5 per cent margin across all downstream enterprises in the country, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). In contrast, combined net profit for EV battery makers nearly doubled that of the major car manufacturers in the first half of the year. Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL), which dominates the market with a share of over 40 per cent, contributed more than 85 per cent of the combined net profits, earning 45.7 billion yuan (US$6.8 billion) in the January-June period. Some carmakers are racing to diversify their battery sources. Xiaomi and Li Auto turned to second-tier battery makers like CALB Group and Sunwoda Electronic, while Xpeng said it would make in-house battery packs starting this year. CATL’s Hong Kong-listed shares have lost more than 37 per cent from a peak in early June. Ming Lee, head of Greater China automotive and industrial research at BofA Securities, said the resumed consumption tax would have a limited impact on the battery makers, as they would negotiate with end-market clients to share the costs. Beijing will waive a tax on cutting-edge battery technologies like solid-state batteries until 2028 in a bid to upgrade the industry and guard against damaging cutthroat competition.

title: Actors, politicians among 100 arrested in New York anti-Netanyahu protest
description: Police detain Oscar winner and fellow activists blocking traffic near the UN ahead of diplomatic speech.
content: Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Emmy winner Hannah Einbinder were among a reported 100 people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they broke up a protest against the Israeli prime minister. NYPD officers handcuffed and led away Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demonstration as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was readying to address the United Nations General Assembly. The New York Post reported Einbinder, of the show Hacks, had also been frogmarched from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide”. A spokeswoman for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection. “Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokeswoman said. “They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested. Jewish Voice for Peace said on social media that more than 100 people had been arrested. “Over 400 people held a mass sit-in outside the UN demanding an end to the genocide and an end to US military funding to Israel,” the organisation said on social media. “We refuse to stand by while war criminals are given a platform to speak and while our government spends billions on war.” Democratic congressional ‌candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City council member Chi Osse were among those arrested. Before his arrest, Osse called Netanyahu a “demon” who should be “held accountable for his crimes”. Other prominent figures spotted among the demonstrators included actors Cynthia Nixon, Elliot Page and Indya Moore, comedians Mary Beth Barone, Caleb Hearon and Sarah Sherman, and musicians Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker, according to online reports. Inside the General Assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, in which he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine. “They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly. Sarandon, whose film hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza. She told journalists at the Venice Film Festival this month that she was losing work because of her outspoken views. “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said. “I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me. “But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she said. Additional reporting by Tribune News Service

title: ‘Fundamentally broken’: Amnesty urges US to abolish ICE
description: Report finds US government implementing system of mass detention fueled by racist, xenophobic rhetoric.
content: Amnesty International called for the abolition of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which is tasked with leading Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant crackdown, in a report released on Thursday. The report, titled “We Had Whistles, They Had Guns”, documents widespread human rights violations during ICE’s large-scale operations, the rights watchdog said. The release comes less than a week after a Venezuelan migrant, Wilber Garces Perez, was shot and wounded by an ICE agent in Austin, Texas, reigniting anger in the US over the immigration authorities’ methods. In January, the deaths of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37, who were shot by federal agents in Minneapolis, sparked outrage across the country. “Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn’t make our communities safer – it puts everyone in danger,” Nadia Daar, director of Amnesty International USA, warned in the report. The report is based on more than 150 testimonies gathered between March and June in four major cities where ICE concentrated its activities, Amnesty said. “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed,” Daar wrote. “For the US government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.” Amnesty said its research demonstrates that the Trump administration is “implementing a system of mass detention and deportation fuelled by racist, xenophobic and false rhetoric, with the aim of detaining and deporting as many migrants, asylum seekers and refugees as possible from the United States”. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Editorial | Universities must rise to the Northern Metropolis challenge
description: The significance of three university towns goes beyond enhancing higher education. They form part of a new engine for regional integration.
content: Hong Kong’s university town project is transforming from an ambitious vision into a concrete and deliverable action plan. With applications now open for campuses in Hung Shui Kiu, the government has set out the land, financing framework, timetable and strategic purpose of the first of three university towns. The challenge is to ensure that this flagship project becomes a showpiece of the Northern Metropolis mega development, paving the way for the mission to turn Hong Kong into a global education and talent hub under the city’s newly released five-year development plan. The government is inviting applications for the Hung Shui Kiu University Town until the end of the year, with results expected in early 2027. Three sites covering more than 26 hectares have been identified, with institutions allowed to propose new campuses, relocate existing facilities or develop teaching, research, hostel and other ancillary facilities. Taking into account the 100-hectare San Tin University Town and the 180-hectare Ta Kwu Ling University Town, the campus areas of the three towns will take up 300 hectares in the New Territories. It is encouraging that the project is no longer merely an idea attached to a long-term planning blueprint. It is gathering momentum with well-defined targets, parameters and timetables. The significance of the university towns goes beyond enhancing higher education. The Hung Shui Kiu, San Tin and Ta Kwu Ling sites form part of the Northern Metropolis, the new engine for Greater Bay Area integration under national development strategies. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, recently released by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, has reinforced the city’s development with a more structured framework, linking education, innovation, industry, talent cultivation and regional cooperation. With the economy becoming increasingly technology- and knowledge-based, while competition for skilled people is intensifying across the region and around the world, universities are no longer simply places where students obtain qualifications for better career development. They are also incubators of research, innovation, entrepreneurship, talent and international connections, which are crucial to the city’s next phase of development. The proposed role of Hung Shui Kiu reflects this direction. The site is to become a centre for applied post-secondary education in smart manufacturing and global talent cultivation. Institutions will be expected to work with local industries on curriculum design, internships, teaching and applied research. They will also be encouraged to collaborate with leading mainland and overseas institutions and enterprises, while sharing facilities. This is a pragmatic approach. It helps bring education closer to the needs of industry, equip students with the necessary skills and turn innovation into new economic forces. The government’s HK$10 billion loan scheme and land premium concession are positive steps forward. Understandably, favourable consideration will be given to the institutions that do not require a loan or are able to offer a financially competitive proposal. But officials also made clear that whether an institution applied for a loan was only one factor in vetting proposals, not the sole condition. Indeed, universities with less reserves may still possess exceptional academic and research strength. The vetting should therefore balance financial sustainability, educational quality, social benefit and strategic relevance. Individual universities must now rise to the challenge by making the most of their own resources and edges. Rather than taking the exercise as an opportunity to obtain inexpensive land or additional floor space, they are expected to demonstrate what new value it will bring. This could include distinctive programmes, high-quality research, promising industry partnerships, overseas collaboration and plans to attract students and scholars. The university towns will not transform the Northern Metropolis immediately, nor will they produce a new generation of talent overnight. Now that the momentum of the development is accelerating following the release of the five-year plan, it is imperative that education stakeholders make the most of the opportunity to scale new heights.

title: How Wang Zhenyi, Chinese female astronomer and mathematician, defied gender expectations
description: Wang shot for the stars with her work in astronomy and mathematics at a time when learned women did little more than write poetry.
content: As moon-gazers look skyward during the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend, they should spare a thought for Wang Zhenyi, one of China’s most notable astronomers and mathematicians – and a woman. Living during the Qing dynasty (1644-1912), when a learned woman was expected to do little more than ornament a household with poetry, Wang wanted something bolder: to explain eclipses. Her answer was physical, not mystical. It involved light, shadow and the movement of the moon. Using a round table for the Earth, a lamp for the sun and a mirror for the moon, she shifted them around until the shadows they cast made sense. The result was The Explanation of a Lunar Eclipse, written at a time when astronomy required imperial permission and women-led scientific research was virtually unheard of. Little of her work has survived to the present day. Wang was born in 1768 to a well-to-do scholarly family in Jiangning (now Nanjing). Her grandfather, Wang Zhefu, was a local official. More importantly, he had books – a vast home library described in one account as having 75 bookcases. Her grandfather opened his library to the unusually bookish girl and introduced her to astronomy. Her father, a doctor, encouraged her interest in mathematics and geography, while her grandmother taught her poetry. After her grandfather died when she was 11, she travelled north with her father and grandmother to Jilin, continuing her studies while learning how to ride and shoot an arrow. At 16, she travelled through China with her father. Wang was far from a secluded page-reading prodigy – she was a young woman of the world. Her travels exposed her to the reality of weather, motion and human hardship, subjects that later appeared in both her scientific prose and poetry. A scientist and a scholar While some women in Qing dynasty China did write and study, astronomy and mathematics remained strictly within the male domain, tied to official calendar-making, elite training and scholarly networks. The emperor’s direct permission was needed to study astronomy, and it was not accessible to the common scholar. Wang faced the same double barrier that female scientists such as astronomer Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner ran into in the West more than a century later: exclusion from the formal institutions that made scientific authority, and working in fields where being female was treated as a disqualification. In Barbara Bennett Peterson’s Notable Women of China: Shang Dynasty to the Early Twentieth Century, one surviving line attributed to Wang captures the friction: “There were times I had to put down my pen and sigh. But I love the subject, I do not give up.” In her own records, such as Glimpses of Astral Elements, Wang wrote that she was so absorbed in reading that meals and sleep could disappear from her attention. One of Wang’s greatest contributions to science was not in discovering new frontiers but in making difficult knowledge legible. She rewrote complicated mathematical material in plain language and produced beginner-friendly works including The Musts of Calculation, a guide to multiplication and division. Wang did not see education as an exclusive field for men, nor did she advocate for women alone. She believed learning should be practical and accessible to everyone, including beginners, everyday readers and women. Her mathematics was a form of public instruction, which is why her work on the Pythagorean theorem matters. It would be misleading to say that Wang “discovered” the theorem long known in both Chinese mathematics – where it was called the gougu rule – and the ancient Greek tradition. Her triumph lies elsewhere. As a largely self-taught mathematician, she wrote The Explanation of the Pythagorean Theorem and Trigonometry. Wang was able to handle an abstract, advanced subject and explain it, a scholar’s achievement made more remarkable by the social barriers that kept women from the usual routes into mathematical study. Her astronomical writing followed the same principle: observe, test and clarify. As well as eclipses, she wrote on the Earth’s roundness, the movement of celestial bodies, equinoxes and precession – the change in orientation of a planet’s rotation. Her eclipse demonstration took away supernatural explanation without stripping the heavens of wonder. A lamp, a mirror and a table were enough to show that the moon passes through the Earth’s shadow, and the cosmos could be understood without ceremony or privilege. A disappearing legacy None of Wang’s books on mathematics and astronomy survive today. We know of her and her works only through a posthumous compilation of her shorter papers in an archive titled Preliminary Collection of Defeng Pavilion and mentions of her work by other scholars. While sexism undoubtedly contributed to Wang’s near eradication from history, it was her own actions and her untimely death that proved decisive. Falling gravely ill at 29 with suspected malaria and believing that her work was unfit for publication, she destroyed 70 to 80 per cent of her manuscripts. She entrusted what little remained to a friend, who later passed them on to her own nephew, Qian Yiji. Qian in turn published a compilation of her papers as Simple Principles of Calculation. The rest of the manuscript was entrusted to a bookseller. Here, the female scholar’s writings disappear – likely neglected, lost or destroyed. Wang did not have time to recruit disciples and pass on her legacy to the next generation – she had no children – before she died. Qian, who knew Wang through her manuscripts and compiled her work posthumously, likened her to Ban Zhao, a prominent female scholar in the Eastern Han dynasty (25-220). A woman with limited access to books or formal education in the sciences figured out how to calculate equinoxes, eclipses, the Pythagorean theorem and more. One can only imagine what someone with Wang’s intellect could achieve today. One of her surviving poems reveals how heavily the limitations imposed on her sex weighed on her mind: “It is made to believe, women are the same as men; are you not convinced, daughters can also be heroic?”

title: UK foreign secretary warns Iran against hostile activity on British soil
description: Ed Miliband presses Tehran over domestic security and demands release of couple held in Evin prison.
content: UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in a face-to-face meeting that Britain will “not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil” from groups linked to his country. Miliband met his Iranian counterpart in the margins of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday. The Foreign Office said the pair discussed the war in the Middle East, the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz and the UK’s “unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil”. In a readout from the meeting, the department said: “The Foreign Secretary told Araghchi that Iran should choose de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war. “He underlined the importance of restoring freedom of navigation and the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, stressing the impact continued disruption has on global security and economic stability,” it added. “The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK’s unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community.” “The Foreign Secretary made clear that Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil and set out the measures the Government has taken in response.” Britain’s ‌National Cyber Security Centre said last ‌week Iranian state-linked cyber actors had used ⁠a spyware family known as “CHOSEN BRICK” to steal ⁠emails, messages and other sensitive information through “spear-phishing” campaigns on messaging platforms including WhatsApp ‌and Telegram. Miliband also brought up the detention of Craig and Lindsay Foreman from East Sussex, who were arrested by the Iranian authorities in January last year as they travelled through the country on a motorcycle trip. They are currently being held in Tehran’s Evin prison. The foreign secretary repeated the call for them to be immediately released, “stressing that their welfare remains a priority for the government”. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Blue Bottle bets that Chinese consumers will drink more premium coffee
description: US brand, recently sold by Nestlé to Chinese capital firm, will need to offer unique experiences and ‘new taste combinations’, analyst says.
content: US premium coffee brand Blue Bottle Coffee will open its first Beijing store in the capital’s central business district, as it seeks to tap into China’s still growing market for the drink. The California-based brand is taking a spacious unit at China World Mall. The location, currently enclosed by construction hoarding, was previously occupied by Japanese jeweller Tasaki. The brand has yet to reveal an official opening date, though industry sources said the shop was expected to open by the end of the year. “There should still be growth overall for the freshly brewed coffee sector in China, as the average annual cups consumed per capita still lags significantly behind that of other markets like Japan and South Korea,” said Cathy Chao, senior director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. Blue Bottle Coffee’s price point lies at the premium end in China’s coffee market. A cup of its Americano retails at 32 yuan (US$4.77), whereas lower-priced domestic chain Luckin Coffee charges 18 yuan before discounting, according to store menus. After debuting in mainland China in 2022 with a store in Shanghai, Blue Bottle now runs more than 10 outlets in Shanghai, in Shenzhen in the southern province of Guangdong, and in Hangzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. The brand also operates six stores in Hong Kong. Blue Bottle may face a challenge in the mainland market, where consumers have tightened their purse strings. Premium-priced American giant Starbucks lost market share to domestic rivals steadily in recent years, partly leading to the company’s sale of a 60 per cent stake in its Chinese operations to a private-equity firm last year. “[Blue Bottle] will need to justify the pricing with a differentiated in-store experience and high-quality coffee for the more discerning customers in first- and second-tier cities,” Chao said. It should also offer “a degree of product innovation” with “new taste combinations”, as Chinese consumers were more open to trying new flavours than those in other markets, she added. Earlier this year, Nestlé sold Blue Bottle Coffee to Centurium Capital – the controlling shareholder of Luckin Coffee – in a deal reportedly worth nearly US$400 million. It marked the first acquisition of a global premium coffee brand by Chinese capital. Nestlé announced the deal in its April earnings report, and the transaction was expected to close in the first half of the year. China’s per capita coffee consumption climbed to 28.6 cups in 2025, up from 16.7 in 2023, and the country has more than 550 million coffee drinkers, according to the research institute of Canyin88, a catering sector information platform. In South Korea, annual per capita consumption hit 405 cups last year – 2.7 times the global average of 152, according to data from consultancy Euromonitor.

title: Pat on the back? Xi and Trump’s body language speaks volumes
description: From firm handshakes and arm touches to bows and laughs, an expert decodes the gestures as the two leaders meet in Washington.
content: Arm touches, laughs, and firm handshakes were on display as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart Donald Trump began their high-stakes summit in Washington, which has so far featured a rare airport welcome, military pageantry and closed-door bilateral talks. While the outcomes of the pair’s discussions are being closely watched, so are the exchanges between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies. A body language expert who reviewed the interactions said Trump’s gestures appeared to assert dominance, while Xi remained formal but comfortable. Their interactions began when the US president and first lady Melania Trump met Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at the bottom of the aircraft steps at Joint Base Andrews, a gesture Patti Wood, a body language expert, said showed respect for the Chinese leader. “You know, the president doesn’t always come to the tarmac to do that. To me, again, that’s symbolic,” Wood said, noting that Xi looked very comfortable at the end of the airport greeting. Xi’s shoulder stance and the way he walked were normal for him, Wood said, adding, “I’m not seeing that he’s changing anything from the way he would normally be in these formal visits.” On Thursday morning, the couples kicked off another day of engagements. Xi and Peng joined the Trumps at the White House, just after 10am. As Trump walked out of the White House for Xi’s arrival, Wood noticed that his chin was tilted slightly downward. While he may have simply been looking down to see where he was walking, she said that, from a body language perspective, a downward-tilted chin non-verbally projects less authority than a chin-up or chin-forward stance. “Downward chin placement, no matter what the motivation is, typically shows less power,” she said. When the pair met at the White House, Xi executed a traditional head bow appropriate for Chinese culture, Wood said, while Trump immediately extended his hand straight out to shake hands without matching the bow or leaning back. She called their greeting “standard Trump” but noted that it did not take into consideration Chinese protocol, etiquette or cultural norms. Xi is “keeping decorum and is very formal. Trump is not affecting him in any of this”, Wood said. “Nothing would indicate that he is being affected by it, that this would ruffle him at all,” she added. During the handshake, Trump also patted Xi on the upper arm. His repeated arm and back patting, which is typical of the US president’s greetings, projects hierarchy, Wood added, symbolically saying “I am better” than you. Later, Xi was also recorded returning the gesture by patting Trump on the back. “That would be a little bit of a symbolic battle,” Wood said, interpreting Xi’s mirroring of the touch as a way of neutralising the perceived dominance. While a back pat can sometimes be perceived as warm and friendly in American culture, there is usually a close personal relationship involved, she said, explaining that even in the US, in formal or non-personal contexts, it functions as an “I am going above you in hierarchy”. Another closely watched moment saw Trump walk Xi along the White House colonnade and stop at the Presidential Walk of Fame, where they looked at the framed pictures. Trump pointed to his own portrait, then to former President Joe Biden’s place. There was a photo of an autopen signing his name, rather than of Biden himself. Trump has repeatedly claimed that an autopen, rather than Biden, was effectively running the presidency. Xi was seen laughing during this interaction. Outside the presidents’ interactions, the two first ladies’ exchanges were also observed. When they left their husbands to tour the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Asian Art, Wood said they relaxed away from the formalities of their husbands’ meeting. “They’re away from their husbands. They’re having a good time moment,” she said, noting that the pair had a “mutual gaze” and “a true smile, a true little moment”.

title: Inside Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan’s visit to the Smithsonian’s Peacock Room
description: The celebrated museum’s Chinese art collection and longstanding ties with China made it a fitting stop for first ladies’ 45-minute tour.
content: Melania Trump and China’s first lady Peng Liyuan toured Chinese artworks and a room shaped by Asian design at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art in Washington on Thursday, as their husbands held talks at the White House. The museum’s director, Chase Robinson, said the two women spent about 45 minutes there and were “full of questions”. Much of the visit centred on the Peacock Room, whose displays of Chinese porcelain made it a fitting setting for the occasion, he said. “What better place to introduce the two first ladies to our museum on the occasion of high-level conversations and discussions between our two countries?” Robinson told the South China Morning Post. The museum, more than a century old and sitting on the National Mall, is one of the country’s leading institutions for Asian art and holds tens of thousands of works spanning cultures across Asia. The two first ladies spent much of the tour focused on the iconic Peacock Room, Robinson said. Created by American artist James McNeill Whistler in 1876-77, the room combines blue, green and gold decoration inspired in part by Chinese porcelain and Japanese design. American collector Charles Lang Freer bought the room in 1904 and had it moved from London to the United States. It has been a centrepiece of the Washington museum since 1923. The tour also included an 18th-century Chinese porcelain vase decorated with colourful famille rose enamels, gold and iron red, as well as a Yuan dynasty scroll painting. Robinson said the museum has an exceptionally strong collection of Yuan and early Ming paintings, which were one reason for showing the work. He said both Peng and Trump enjoyed the visit. “I think they were both intrigued by the scale of 19th-century interaction between China and the United States,” Robinson said. The tour ended with a performance by students from Hope Chinese School, a Chinese immersion school. Why was this museum chosen for such an occasion? The office of the US first lady selected the venue, Robinson said, but the museum also has longstanding ties with China. Robinson recently returned from a trip to China, where he visited Xian, Dunhuang and Beijing. The museum has partnerships with the Palace Museum and other Chinese institutions and regularly sends staff to China. It also works closely with the Chinese embassy in Washington and the US State Department. “Given those kinds of relationships, given the opportunity to celebrate US-China relations, this was an appropriate place,” Robinson said. The museum also has an active programme of Chinese cultural events. Its Lunar New Year celebration, for example, draws as many as 15,000 to 16,000 people in a single afternoon. After Xi Jinping and former US President Joe Biden visited Filoli in California during Xi’s 2023 US trip, the historic estate drew renewed public attention. Robinson said he hoped the first ladies’ visit would have a similar effect. “We don’t doubt that there will be opportunities to celebrate their visit,” he said. “I hope [it will] inspire many more visits.”

title: Meet Courtney King, The Traitors star Dylan Efron’s long-time girlfriend
description: The reality star and younger brother of Zac Efron has kept his relationship low-profile, but admits he plans to propose.
content: Zac Efron’s younger brother Dylan Efron has made a name for himself as a reality television star and has appeared on previous seasons of shows such as The Traitors and Dancing with the Stars. Despite being a television personality and having a famous older brother, Dylan has kept his private life largely out of the limelight. More recently, however, the 34-year-old shared a rare insight into his relationship with long-time girlfriend Courtney King. “We’re doing really good,” Dylan said about his relationship during an episode of The Viall Files podcast on September 17. But what do we know about Courtney King? Read on to find out. When did Dylan Efron and Courtney King meet? Dylan has reportedly been dating King for over a decade. In March 2025, Dylan revealed on The Viall Files podcast that he and King hail from the same “town” and first crossed paths while attending Arroyo Grande High School in California. The couple began dating and have been together since. Dylan has described King as someone who is “not on social media” and “works a 40-hour-a-week job”. He previously tagged the account @coourtking in a 2019 Instagram post marking his girlfriend’s birthday. The account, which mostly shared photos taken in nature, last posted in October 2019. “It works out really well,” Dylan told the podcast. “It’s not like I’m hiding her from the world or anything. She understands the job, all that stuff. She doesn’t really like being on camera.” While her boyfriend may be in the entertainment business, King seems to prefer supporting Dylan quietly and out of the limelight. In November 2025, King was spotted at DWTS’ production studio to support Dylan for the show’s season finale. Are Dylan Efron and Courtney King engaged? Dylan has yet to pop the question, but he told The Viall Files hosts last year that he has plans to propose. “That’s something that’s definitely [on the horizon],” he said. “Well, she knows the answer. We’re working on it. Courtney’s so down-to-earth, she’d never [impose a deadline]. Look, we’re 33. She’s not going to put a deadline on it.” Dylan also shared a sweet detail of their relationship, saying that they like to fall asleep listening to audiobooks together. “We fight over whose audio we’re gonna listen to,” he said. “It’s like, ‘Are we gonna listen to Jeff Lewis?’ We both agree that we can listen to Viall Files, but otherwise, I have things I want to listen to that she doesn’t want to, so we fight over that quite a bit.”

title: In Focus | What Xi Jinping’s letter to old friends in Iowa means in an altered America
description: The personal thread may be intact, but the US agricultural partnership that once gave it weight is not.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Khushboo Razdan looks at how a presidential appeal to America’s heartland is playing out. Of the countless preparations being made for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s highly anticipated American trip, arguably the first came in the form of a personal letter. On February 16, seven months before his White House visit, Xi wrote to friends in the midwestern US state of Iowa, sending a Chinese New Year card across the Pacific. In it, the Chinese leader repeated a line Beijing uses when official relations are strained, saying the hope of the relationship “lies in the people”, its foundation “is grass-roots connections” and its future “depends on the youth”. Xi wrote to Luca Berrone and the circle that welcomed him in 1985 on his first-ever US visit – Sarah Lande, Gary Dvorchak, Rick Kimberley and Terry Branstad, a former Iowa governor and former US ambassador – as well as students from the youth exchange initiative the Chinese leader announced in 2023. No matter what direction politics took, Xi told them in the letter, the will of the two peoples “will not change”. China’s leader appears to have invoked his long-standing personal ties with Iowa to soften the atmosphere ahead of his White House visit, as American farmers remain deeply sceptical amid severe trade war losses battering the heartland. The personal thread may be intact, but the agricultural partnership that once gave it weight is not. And while those familiar faces still anchor the friendship narrative, they are also in the blast zone. Grant Kimberley lives in both realities. In February 2012, during Xi’s second visit to Iowa, his family hosted the then Chinese vice-president at the Maxwell farm. Kimberley, then 36, said ni hao in the yard. He is now senior director of market development at the Iowa Soybean Association. “The significance of the letter was as much about the relationship as the message itself,” said Kimberley, son of Rick Kimberley, calling it “a reminder that personal relationships built on mutual respect over decades still matter”. Yet, the letter did not change trade policy or market conditions. Farmers appreciate goodwill and friendship, Kimberley said, but ultimately look for “stable trade relationships and practical results”. He said he believed Xi “has a genuine appreciation for Iowa and its people”. And he still saw farm trade as “the ballast of the overall relationship”. Diplomacy mattered “because communication is always better than misunderstanding”, Kimberley continued, saying the real test was whether “markets remain open, customers remain engaged and trade relationships remain reliable”. The market that once seemed reliable now switches on for summits. US agricultural exports to China plummeted from US$24.5 billion in 2024 to US$8.4 billion in 2025, a two-thirds contraction that pushed China from a top-five farm customer to sixth. Soybeans took the biggest hit, tumbling from US$12.6 billion to about US$3 billion. From late May through late November 2025, official data showed no US soy shipments to China. Beijing instead bought from Brazil. North Dakota State University later estimated that Chinese retaliation cost US agriculture US$14.9 billion from March 2025 to February 2026. Iowa, California and Illinois each lost about US$1.2 billion. Soybeans alone accounted for US$6.8 billion – nearly half the total. Even after federal aid, the American Soybean Association put 2025 soybean losses at nearly US$75 an acre. This is the second major escalation in the US-China trade war since the original conflict began in 2018. The first taught Beijing it could live without Iowa beans. The second taught Iowa something else: China can walk away, while Washington’s relief arrives later and smaller. America’s new soybean marketing year began on September 1. The US Department of Agriculture said Chinese buyers took 136,000 tonnes that day, followed by flash sales of 202,000 tonnes and 192,000 tonnes in the next two sessions. After Xi and US President Donald Trump met in South Korea in October last year, China pledged 12 million tonnes in the short term, then 25 million tonnes a year through 2028, alongside about US$17 billion a year in wider US farm purchases. New crop sales to China resumed as the Washington date neared. The USDA said state buyers were buying against the Busan pledge. Commercial crushers continued to prefer Brazilian beans because of the 10 per cent tariff. American soy still pays that tariff. Brazilian soy does not. Brazil kept selling through 2025 without waiting for a presidential summit. Whether the new US cargoes keep coming after Xi leaves Washington is the test Kimberley’s members will watch for. According to Tao Wang, who teaches the history of US-China relations at Iowa State University, the February letter was more than a new year’s greeting. Xi sought “to reach not only his old friends but also, through them, a bigger American public”, Wang said. Iowa is useful because the tie is more than 40 years old and “looks personal, not only diplomatic”. “There is a farm calculation in that,” added Wang, who said keeping faith with a state that still wants to sell soybeans could “help strengthen the American groups who want stable, cooperative economic ties with China”. Wang refrained from suggesting that Xi asked anyone to lobby Washington. But he noted the letter’s timing came after a difficult period that included a surprise leaders’ call touching on Taiwan and “alongside signs that China will buy soybeans again”. A friendly letter, he said, was “a low-cost way to warm the atmosphere” before the White House visit. One would be hard pressed to call the 2026 and 2012 trips identical. In 2012, Xi was vice-president and looked the part of a future leader, Wang said. And the Iowa city of Muscatine had a job: to put a face on the rising statesman. In 2026, Xi was “the supreme leader with a full agenda of high-stakes negotiation”, the professor added. A stop on the Mississippi River “does not fit this kind of visit any more”, Wang said, adding that Xi’s letter offered a way to keep “that Iowa channel warm” without diverting precious time during the trip to Washington. Until now, the personal and student channels have proved fruitful. The “50,000 in 5 Years” programme Xi announced during his 2023 US visit still sends Iowa pupils to China, with the sister-state link through the non-profit Iowa Sister States and Hebei province moving delegations and farm exchanges. “More than a thousand young Iowans have already gone through this youth exchange initiative,” Wang estimated. What has fallen by the wayside is “open, unscrutinised institutional cooperation”, especially at universities, he said. Wang pointed to a letter in March from Iowa state congressman Taylor Collins, the Republican chairman of the Iowa House Higher Education Committee, to Drake University in Des Moines, the state capital, demanding files on its China partnerships. There was also an Iowa House-passed bill introduced in January that would stop Iowa universities hiring H-1B visa holders from China, he said, noting there were fewer Chinese scholars, researchers and students than a decade ago. The break with farmers is colder. After Iowa became a target of retaliation, growers “now see Beijing less as a stable partner and more as a transactional, unpredictable customer”, Wang added. Jonathan Hassid, who teaches China politics at Iowa State, is unsentimental about Xi’s letter. Hassid described it as a means “to bypass normal diplomacy and speak directly to ordinary citizens”, adding that it had received “little attention in the US or Iowa presses and is probably unfamiliar to most Iowans”. Nor could the circumstances be said to resemble 1985. “Candidates for political office regularly attack China” now, Hassid said, recalling that at this year’s Iowa State Fair, a low-flying aircraft towed a banner accusing a politician of having “sold out Iowa to China”. Beijing hoped that direct appeals might “slowly shift attitudes over time”, he added. “Whether the approach works is an open question.” Tourism both ways thinned after the coronavirus pandemic, Hassid said, and Chinese language enrolments “declined dramatically”. “The golden age of US-China people-to-people ties has passed.” And while Muscatine cherishes its Xi story, “most Iowans are simply unaware”. As Hassid sees it, “these visits matter more to the Chinese Communist Party than they do to most local Iowans”. Earlier this month, that disconnect was evident in the political chatter coursing through a riverfront hotel in Minnesota’s capital. Jeff Winton, a New York dairy farmer, spoke at the Midwestern Legislative Conference in St Paul attended by several hundred state senators, representatives and officials. The talk in the halls spanned beef imports, the fight with Canada, diesel and fertiliser after the war in Iran, drought, the November midterms and people feeling worn out. “Not once did China or President Xi come up during any of the conversations I had,” Winton said. “I truly believe that there are many more important things on farmers’ minds right now than China and President Xi.” At best, the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington was “political theatre” as the midterms approach, he added, “and nothing more than that”. The symbolism of the visit could be said to be mutually beneficial. Xi can invoke an Iowa relationship that predates the trade war. Trump can point to Chinese purchases returning. For farmers, neither means much if the market disappears again when the politics turn. John Bartman, an Illinois farmer, had not seen Xi’s letter until this week. He interpreted it as “another head of state that doesn’t want to deal with Donald Trump”. Bartman portrayed farmers as “stuck in the middle”, arguing that “food shouldn’t ever be used as a point of leverage”. China’s relationship with the American heartland changed under Trump, he said, with Beijing willing to “use any type of leverage” to get a better price. Of Xi’s Washington visit, Bartman said China “still hasn’t even bought half of what they promised”. As for Trump, the farmer said the US president “needs to have a good showing in rural America” ahead of the midterm elections. “If China buys one bushel … Donald Trump will make a big deal out of it … when he clearly doesn’t” support farmers.

title: Opinion | China’s industrial strengths must also benefit its trading partners
description: By shifting towards domestic consumption and exporting industrial know-how, Beijing can give global partners a genuine stake in its growth.
content: The European Commission is pressing China for progress by next month to address the widening EU-China trade imbalance, and raising the possibility of new protectionist trade policy. The deadline raises a question: how should China and its trading partners address perceived economic imbalances while sharing the benefits of Chinese industrial competitiveness? China’s merchandise trade surplus approached US$1.2 trillion last year even as other exporting economies press for controls. “Overcapacity” is accepted as the blanket explanation for China’s industrial success, with government support leading to a production glut. But this framing obscures more than it clarifies. China’s success is multifaceted, given the vast scale of its ecosystem, intense domestic competition and dense supplier networks. An effective response must distinguish between genuine imbalances and the productive advantages that offer opportunities for cooperation. China’s car industry showcases the strength of its competitive edge. The International Energy Agency found that while making an electric car costs 30 per cent less in China than in advanced economies, only about one-third of that difference is due to batteries. Furthermore, the gap for conventional vehicles is similar. China’s advantage is embedded in its manufacturing system rather than being the product of government subsidies. Research by Rhodium Group makes the point clearly. It estimates that Chinese carmaker BYD enjoys a cost advantage of about US$4,700 per vehicle over Tesla’s Chinese operations. Direct grants account for only around US$292; the bulk of the advantage is due to vertical integration and lower research, administrative and supplier costs. While industrial policy helped develop China’s industrial ecosystem, subsidies and government support do not explain the resulting cost structure. China’s experience in textile production offers a precedent. Even as wages rose and some production moved to Vietnam, Bangladesh and elsewhere, China retained a major presence – over 30 per cent of global textile exports – because of its supplier clusters, infrastructure, skills and capacity to upgrade production. That does not mean China should stay the course indefinitely. Chinese policymakers have been discussing consumption-led rebalancing for two decades, and policy commitment has become more explicit. The 2025 consumption action plan addressed wages, pensions, healthcare, childcare, paid leave and benefits for migrant and flexible workers. The government subsequently adopted China’s first five-year plan devoted specifically to consumption, targeting retail sales of about 60 trillion yuan (US$8.96 trillion) by 2030. We’ve seen incremental results. While household consumption still only accounts for around 40 per cent of the gross domestic product, Beijing is moving in the right direction. Last year, per capita, disposable income rose by 5 per cent and consumption expenditure by 4.4 per cent. Still, there is quite a bit of work to be done. China’s household savings rate reached an estimated 32.4 per cent in the first quarter of this year, compared with a pre-pandemic average of 29.6 per cent. The government is already directing more fiscal resources towards pensions, healthcare, unemployment insurance, childcare and portable benefits for migrant workers as part of the domestic transformation. Greater household security and wealth would reduce precautionary savings and support sustained consumption. Similarly, boosting an openness to foreign goods and services could translate into a stronger demand for imports. Addressing the sensitive topic of exchange-rate flexibility could support this adjustment; any resulting yuan appreciation would further increase Chinese households’ purchasing power abroad. But any adjustment must also occur internationally. I previously wrote about the trend of Chinese companies moving from producing “in China for the world” towards producing “in the world, for the world”. The competitive edge of Chinese enterprise can help support overseas industry through the same system of joint ventures, technology and local-supplier development programmes that took China into global markets. Chinese process knowledge combined with employment and industrial capacity in Europe and other markets would create meaningful local value, rather than the limited gains of merely assembling imported kits, which is what would happen if the doors to cooperation on win-win trade and investment were closed. China’s trading partners should reserve permanent protection for genuinely strategic vulnerabilities. Where import surges cause demonstrable injury, temporary and reviewable safeguards may provide time for industrial adjustment. Subsidy transparency, common environmental and safety standards, stronger competition rules and negotiated market-opening commitments would address distortions more precisely than an open-ended campaign against “overcapacity”. China is more than open to the idea – it has removed tariffs on imports from 53 African countries. Cooperation requires a rebuilding of trust. China should stick to strengthening domestic demand and encouraging overseas investment. Its trading partners should also widen the opportunities for cooperation. Restrictions on stopping China buying advanced chipmaking machines from Dutch tech giant ASML are looking like a positively archaic holdover. Governments should instead be working towards easing their technology and investment restrictions, using clearly defined security concerns and verifiable safeguards to guide those decisions. Such openings would create opportunities for businesses on both sides.

title: Costa Rica’s foreign minister fired for attending Trump meeting
description: President Laura Fernandez claims unapproved participation in anti-cartel session inflicted ‘great strategic damage’.
content: Costa Rica’s President Laura Fernandez on Thursday fired her foreign minister for attending a meeting on Latin America’s security led by US President Donald Trump without telling her. Fernandez said she should have been the one to attend the meeting of Trump’s anti-cartel “Shield of the Americas” alliance in New York, and that Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar’s failure to consult her caused “great strategic damage”. The meeting took place on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Tovar attended “without giving prior notice or informing” the president, a conservative Trump ally, of his participation, Costa Rica’s government said. The “Shield of the Americas” is a coalition of pro-US administrations convened by Trump to combat drug trafficking and organised crime across the region. At Tuesday’s meeting, 15 coalition members issued a joint statement declaring their intent to impose asset freezes and visa restrictions and seek criminal liability for members and supporters of 24 criminal organisations. Trump at the meeting referred to drug cartels as “the Isis of the western hemisphere”. Costa Rica, a tourist haven that has long been seen as a beacon of stability in Latin America, is grappling with a surge in drug-related violence. Tovar avoided commenting on his dismissal and simply thanked Fernandez, in power since last May, for including him in her cabinet. Indiana Trejos, Costa Rica’s minister of foreign trade, has been named acting foreign minister. She will assume the role upon returning from her mission at the UN General Assembly. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: US senators delay effort to permanently ban Chinese cars
description: Proposed ban is a move to ensure that hundreds of thousands of US automotive jobs are not at risk of ‘total domination’ by Chinese car firms.
content: The two US senators backing a permanent legislative ban on Chinese cars in the United States agreed on Thursday to delay their plan to use a fast track procedure to win Senate approval until next week, to seek the support of a lone holdout. Republican Senator Bernie Moreno and Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin had planned to seek ‌approval for the procedure – which requires unanimous Senate backing – on Thursday, the same day that US President Donald Trump met China’s President Xi Jinping in Washington. But instead they will delay things and hold talks with Republican Senator Rand Paul, who had raised some concerns, in an effort to convince him to allow passage, congressional aides said. Paul’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Paul told reporters that he would continue to discuss his concerns about the bill over the weekend and next week, according to Semafor. Moreno said he was hopeful the bill ⁠would be approved next week and the same legislation passed in November when the US House of Representatives returns to session. China is making nearly four ‌times as many cars as the United States, Moreno said, adding Congress needs to make certain that hundreds of thousands of US automotive jobs are not at risk of “total domination” by Chinese car companies. Earlier, Slotkin had said all ‌Democrats support moving ahead and only one Republican opposes the measure. “My understanding is it’s 99 to 1,” she said. Under the fast track ⁠procedure, a single opponent could block approval. The bill has significant momentum and a House version now tops 100 cosponsors, while car makers and legislative aides hope to win full passage this year. Trump’s meeting with Xi will address ‌a wide range of trade issues. China has strongly opposed the US vehicle ban and efforts to make it permanent. “I think if President Trump allows in these Chinese companies, it is [the] beginning of ‌the ‌end of the auto industry in the United States,” Slotkin, of Michigan, said. Earlier this month, Trump told Fox News he would accept Chinese car ‌companies building cars in the United States, sparking alarm among car makers. Last week, car makers, suppliers and dealers urged Trump “to maintain policies that keep the door firmly ⁠shut to Chinese automakers seeking to sell, import or manufacture vehicles inside the US”. A regulation imposed by former US president Joe Biden’s administration ⁠in early 2025 effectively banned all Chinese carmakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the US because they could send sensitive driver data to China. Washington also maintains more than 100 per cent tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Senator Ted Cruz said earlier that the bill ‌would ban companies with more than 15 per cent ‌ownership from Chinese entities from selling vehicles in the US. That could bar Mercedes-Benz because of Chinese investors’ nearly 20 per cent stake. Moreno said Mercedes-Benz would have until 2030 to comply and could still get waivers if needed. Slotkin said there were continuing conversations about how Mercedes could comply. The bill, which has 51 Senate supporters, would make the ban into law and prevent the White House from issuing waivers to Chinese manufacturers to sell vehicles in the United States. Argentina’s President Javier Milei, meanwhile, fantasises about barrelling through the streets of Buenos Aires in a Cybertruck, painted black and emblazoned with a golden lion. Or maybe an Italian car. “It would be marvellous!” the president of the South American nation told Bloomberg. But if the people of Argentina want to buy cars from China, Milei’s not going to stop them. “They can buy cars wherever they want. Who am I to say?” he said on Thursday in New York. “What Argentines buy is their problem.” Milei, once a harsh critic of China who called its government an “assassin” and said he would not negotiate with communists, has softened his tone since his election in 2023. Meanwhile, China is close to leapfrogging Brazil to become Argentina’s most important trading partner. That is partly because of the flow of commodities such as soybeans but it is also visible in the proliferation on Argentine roads of cars made by companies such as BYD, which is not permitted to sell in the US. Milei, who considers himself a libertarian, said he will not go down that route but he insisted he would not criticise Trump for his policy. “I can’t give recommendations to another governor or president in the world because I don’t know their situations or their restrictions,” he said. “If you want my opinion about Trump, he is a wonderful president.” Milei, who has also visited Elon Musk at Tesla Texas headquarters, may not have to wait long to buy a Cybertruck to bolster his “Batman image”, as he put it. The US car maker has been laying the groundwork to enter Argentina as soon as next year, according to the Buenos Aires Herald. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: US 30-year mortgage rates top 7%, highest in Trump presidency
description: It is the highest average level since January 2025, with affordability a concern for US voters weeks ahead of November’s midterm elections.
content: US mortgage rates have exceeded 7.0 per cent, data showed Thursday, reaching their highest level since Donald Trump returned to the presidency as voters grapple with high costs of living ahead of midterm elections. The popular 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.03 per cent as of Thursday, a stark uptick from 6.30 per cent the same period a year ago. This is the highest average level since January 16 last year, just days before Trump returned to the White House, according to data from mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac. Affordability is a major concern for US voters just weeks before key midterm elections in November. War in the Middle East, which unfolded after US-Israel strikes on Iran in late February, has caused fuel prices to surge as Tehran retaliated by blocking a vital waterway for energy transit. The costs of regular petrol, which US households rely on, and diesel needed by farmers and truckers have both rocketed - putting pressure on consumers and businesses alike. Higher diesel costs in turn threaten to filter through the world’s biggest economy more broadly. As inflation climbed, the US central bank this month raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 in an effort to fight price increases. Already, higher mortgage rates in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic have weighed on the US housing market. This week’s uptick is set to hit prospective homebuyers further. A separate report on Thursday by the Commerce Department showed that sales of new US homes rose by 6.4 per cent in August on a month-on-month basis. This took sales to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 684,000. Despite the month-on-month increase, the level is 2.0 per cent below that of August 2025.

title: US cybersecurity agency releases election infrastructure plan before midterms
description: Federal strategy details threats and safeguards for November vote following criticism over delayed assistance.
content: The US’ cybersecurity agency on Thursday released an election infrastructure security plan 40 days before November’s midterms, laying out potential threats to election systems and listing services it would offer to election officials to protect the vote. The plan, which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had originally promised to release by mid-August, comes after the Trump administration has been trying to kickstart efforts to help states protect voting systems. Election officials have argued that such efforts are too little, too late after the Trump administration gutted the agency’s election security work last year, forcing the officials to pay for private services to ensure they were prepared for the coming elections. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is housed under the Department of Homeland Security, has since its founding in 2018 helped warn state and local election officials about potential threats from foreign governments. But CISA, as it’s known, was largely absent from that role in last year’s elections after the Trump administration dismantled much of its role on election security. The administration cut some 1,000 employees from CISA and slashed US$10 million from two cybersecurity initiatives, including one dedicated to helping state and local election officials. CISA has also gone the entirety of Trump’s second term without a Senate-confirmed director, instead cycling through a series of acting leaders. The 13-page document released Thursday says DHS has “consistently supported CISA’s delivery of cybersecurity and physical security services to election officials”, and that such services are provided at no cost to state and local election officials at their request. Numerous state and local election officials around the country have told Associated Press otherwise, noting that services previously provided by CISA, like tabletop exercises and penetration tests to evaluate the security of their systems, were not available in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections.

title: Knife attack at Polish abbey leaves priest dead and 4 injured
description: Ukrainian suspect arrested after stabbing victims during assault at Benedictine monastery in Jaroslaw.
content: A man armed with a knife killed a priest and injured four other people during an attack on clergy and worshippers at a Benedictine abbey in southern Poland on Thursday, authorities ‌said. The man used a knife he took from a kitchen there to attack one woman and four men, including one priest who was in a confessional, a prosecutor said. The attack took place at a Benedictine Sisters monastery on the grounds of the abbey in Jaroslaw, local media reported. A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested, Bozena Harasz-Woloszyn ⁠from the District Prosecutor’s Office in Przemysl said. “Three of the victims are clergy members and ‌two are laypeople; one person has died ... Two people are in a critical, life-threatening condition,” she added. The motives behind the attack were not immediately ‌clear. Police said they were on the scene investigating the incident. “We are aware ⁠that Father Stanislaw ⁠has passed away and Father Marek is in serious condition. There are other casualties, but we do not have ‌further details,” Sister Barbara Dendor told state broadcaster TVP Info. “When I arrived, there was total panic,” she said. The mayor of ‌Jaroslaw, ‌Marcin Nazarewicz, told a press conference that a period of mourning was being declared until the ‌end of the week. Polish President Karol Nawrocki extended his condolences to the family of the ⁠priest who died, and wished the injured a quick recovery. “In the face of such acts, ⁠the state must be strong, act swiftly and relentlessly in enforcing the law,” Nawrocki wrote on social media. “The principles and values of our community must be respected by ‌all those residing in ‌our country.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the crime “horrific”. “We are shaken by this evil,” he wrote on social media. “We extend our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased. We wish all those injured a speedy recovery.”

title: Netanyahu blasts critics at UN, dismissing Gaza genocide accusations
description: Israeli prime minister denounces walkout delegates as ‘moral cowards’ during a fiery address defending the war against Iran.
content: Lashing out at his country’s critics, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu angrily dismissed allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza as “the biggest lie of the century” in a defiant speech to the UN General Assembly that asserted his nation’s right to wage war against Iran. Scores of delegates trooped out of the hall in protest. Netanyahu addressed the plenum after days of speeches by world leaders condemning Israel’s war in Gaza and accusing him of orchestrating a genocide against the Palestinian people. At times, the Israeli leader, facing a tough race for re-election next month, became emotional and indignant as he lectured his critics. Netanyahu, his voice rising in emphasis, said attacking Iran “was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make” and denounced as “moral cowards” a mass of delegates who walked out of the hall when he took the podium to speak. “In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall,” Netanyahu said. “In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran’s nukes.” When Netanyahu walked to the rostrum, a mix of cheers, boos and mass walkouts erupted. Scores of delegates marched out and a majority of visible seats sat empty afterwards. “If there are any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now,” Netanyahu said. Netanyahu’s remarks – which at times sounded like a stump speech – were aimed largely at the audience at home as the country prepares for elections on October 27. It was delivered during the evening prime time in Israel and filled with standard talking points used to defend policies in the occupied West Bank and treatment of the Palestinians. Netanyahu reminded the assembly of the scale of the October 7, 2023, attack in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people. “This is equal to 40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours,” he said, or 16 times the death count of the 9/11 attacks that left nearly 3,000 people dead in New York and more in Pennsylvania and at the Pentagon. Netanyahu said the attack left Israel with no choice but to hit Hamas hard. Many governments have accused Israel of committing war crimes, and Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court accusing him of crimes against humanity. He thanked US President Donald Trump for taking decisive action against Iran, and predicted Iran’s theocratic government would fall. Trump made a similar assertion at the outset of the war that began nearly seven months ago, but the Iranian government appears to remain firmly in charge. Netanyahu, known for using visual aids during his General Assembly speeches, at one point held up a pager while reminding the audience of the September 17, 2024, attack in which Israel remotely detonated thousands of pagers that had been distributed to the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon. The pager attack wounded more than 3,000 people and killed 12, including two children. Netanyahu dismissed incidents of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents” throwing stones, chopping down olive trees and lighting fires. “I can’t stand that. I won’t stand for vigilantism,” the prime minister said before accusing foreign leaders and the international press of distorting the scale of violence in the West Bank. Netanyahu’s government is dominated by settlers and their allies, and has made few arrests in the wave of settler violence. Israel captured the West Bank and east Jerusalem in the 1967 war, and the Palestinians want both as part of their future state. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs has reported more than 1,600 settler attacks this year. At least 104 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli settlers or soldiers this year, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry. Four Israelis have been killed by Palestinians over the same period. This week, a settler was killed and the son of Israel’s ambassador to the US was badly wounded in separate Palestinian attacks. Netanyahu also accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of spreading lies about Israel and endangering Jewish New Yorkers with his criticism of the country’s military actions in Gaza. Before the prime minister arrived in New York, Mamdani called him a “war criminal” and pushed for his arrest. The mayor has acknowledged that New York does not have the authority to execute an International Criminal Court warrant but urged federal authorities to do so. In past years, Netanyahu has used his General Assembly speech to both denounce the United Nations as biased and make Israel’s case to world leaders. The war in Gaza began on October 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked Israel, killing around 1,200 people and kidnapping 251. At least 73,922 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s subsequent offensive.
