Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas also addressed the UN General Assembly earlier Thursday, delivering pre-recorded remarks from his office in Ramallah after the United States denied him a visa to attend the gathering for the second year in a row. “How long will some countries continue to remain silent about Israel, or continue supplying it with weapons that it uses against our people?” Abbas said. “What, then, is the international community waiting for before it acts to protect the Palestinian people?”

title: Croatia clears extradition of Nord Stream blast suspect to Germany
description: German prosecutors have accused Ukrainian scuba diver of planting explosives on Baltic pipelines in 2022.
content: A Croatian court has approved the extradition of a Ukrainian man who is wanted in Germany in connection with the 2022 undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines, state media said on Thursday. The report from HRT Television quoted the suspect’s lawyer Ljubo Pavaskovic as saying that he will appeal the September 18 ruling. It was not immediately clear when the man could be handed over to Germany. He was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. German prosecutors have said that the suspect was a “trained scuba diver” who, along with others, “planted explosives” on the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm. The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the pipelines, which had been built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. The damage added to tensions over the Ukraine war as European countries moved to wean themselves off Russian energy sources after the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of its neighbour on February 24, 2022. The German prosecutor’s office identified the suspect only as Vladimir Z. A spokesperson confirmed to Associated Press that it was the same man who was arrested in Poland last year but was later released when a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany. Polish authorities identified him as Volodymyr Zhuravlov. In July, German federal prosecutors filed charges against a former Ukrainian army officer in connection with the same explosions. Serhii K. was detained in August 2025 in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow he was staying at with his family. He was extradited to Germany in November. The suspects allegedly used a yacht rented from a German company using forged IDs and intermediaries and set off from the German port of Rostock. The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process just before Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine.

title: B-2 Spirit, AI cooperation, no US-China conflict: key Xi-Trump takeaways so far
description: In morning remarks of state visit’s second day, US president and Chinese leader seek to project image of stability between the two sides.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping and his American counterpart Donald Trump delivered remarks at the White House on Thursday morning at the start of the second day of Xi’s closely watched state visit. Both leaders spoke warmly of their countries’ ties and pledged deeper cooperation in comments that sought to project an image of stability between the two sides. Trump said he and Xi would work together to build a “better future for both our countries” while Xi called for the two powers to “coexist in peace” and keep competition “healthy”. Shortly after the speech, Xi was welcomed with a military flyover consisting of a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors. The B-2 – rarely used in such flyovers – is a strategic bomber, one of the most powerful weapons in the American arsenal, built to carry nuclear and conventional loads across continents. Here are some key takeaways from their speeches. China’s door ‘always wide open’ Xi urged Washington to treat Chinese firms fairly, while vowing to keep China’s door “always wide open” to American companies. The two sides could lengthen the list of cooperation and shorten the list of problems, he added. “We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds,” Xi said. The Chinese leader also called for increased direct flights between the two countries to facilitate two-way travel and trade. Avoiding conflict Xi said the two countries’ militaries should maintain regular dialogue and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention. This, he said, could help the two countries overcome the Thucydides’ trap, a theory that a rising power and an established hegemon are destined for war. “China and the US must hold the bottom line of no conflict and no confrontation,” Xi said. He also called for strengthened communication in other government departments across foreign affairs, economic matters, financial cooperation and law enforcement. Artificial intelligence Both presidents emphasised the importance of their countries working together to manage the risks of artificial intelligence, though Trump referred to it as superintelligence (SI), his new preferred term for the technology. Xi said China and the US, as “leading nations in AI”, should ensure that AI always remains under human control. The two countries previously agreed in 2024 that humans, not AI, should have control over the use of nuclear weapons. Progress on bilateral issues Trump hailed “tremendous strides” on issues before the two countries, including the Board of Trade mechanism established during his May summit with Xi, calling it “unbelievably successful”. Discussions in Washington would focus on pressing issues concerning security, technology and artificial intelligence, the US president said. “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” he added. Strengthening people-to-people exchanges Xi also announced that two giant pandas, named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, would arrive at Zoo Atlanta in Georgia “in a few days”. Meanwhile, 100,000 young Americans would be invited for exchange and study in China in the coming five years. China said Xi’s invitation for 50,000 young Americans, extended in his previous visit in 2023, had already been fulfilled. Alliance during World War II Both leaders recalled the history of their countries fighting together during World War II against Japan, even though neither named the island country directly. Trump made reference to the Flying Tigers: American pilots who volunteered to fight in China. “Look at the greatness that we had together, fighting in World War II,” Trump said, adding that the “brave American pilots” fought for “the very survival of the legendary country”. Xi said Chinese people had never forgotten that part of history, nor had Americans.

title: Hong Kong’s IOMed poised to play key role in resolving Greater Bay Area disputes
description: International Organisation for Mediation can handle disputes among three Greater Bay Area jurisdictions, secretary general Teresa Cheng says.
content: An intergovernmental mediation body headquartered in Hong Kong is poised to play an important role in resolving cross-border disputes within the Greater Bay Area, as well as multinational disagreements tied to countries in the Belt and Road Initiative, former and incumbent justice ministers have said. The secretary general of the International Organisation for Mediation (IOMed), Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah, highlighted the organisation’s role in handling disputes within the bay area at a forum organised by the body on Thursday. The bay area is the central government’s scheme to link Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province into an integrated economic and business hub. “We cater for situations where it is within the same country, but with different legal jurisdictions and legal territorial jurisdictions,” said Cheng, a former Hong Kong secretary for justice. “When there are disputes among the three Greater Bay Area jurisdictions, they will be able to come to the International Organisation for Mediation.” The bay area contains three distinct jurisdictions with different legal systems – Hong Kong has common law, mainland China uses civil law, while Macau’s civil law is inherited from Portuguese legal traditions. The Wan Chai-headquartered IOMed was inaugurated in October last year. It counts 48 signatory and acceding states and 18 contracting states as of this month, and was set up to resolve interstate, investor-state and international commercial disputes via mediation. Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok told the forum, titled “Fireside chat – The journey to peace and prosperity through dialogue”, that the Greater Bay Area was a “good example” of the scope of IOMed’s work. “I think there can be a lot of synergy between the work on the [bay area] and the work of IOMed,” Lam said. He added that the Department of Justice had endeavoured to harmonise different sets of mediation rules and practice across the three jurisdictions by establishing a common accreditation standard and code of conduct for mediators, a set of model rules and a common list of Greater Bay Area mediators. Rimsky Yuen Kwok-keung, another former Hong Kong justice minister, told the forum that it was more appropriate for the city to have mediation clauses with the mainland under the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement (Cepa) free-trade agreement, rather than arbitration clauses using the top-down method governed by an arbitrator’s decision. “In the context of Cepa, which is unlike some other scenarios, such as cases dealt with by exit ... the background, the context are very different,” Yuen said. Cheng said that the use of mediation could allow disputing parties in projects under the Belt and Road Initiative – China’s plan to grow global trade – to maintain the spirit of joint development and benefits and prevent project standstills. “They can then continue and finish the job, rather than have an abandoned power plant or an abandoned highway structure,” Cheng said. She suggested that Hong Kong could consider whether to adopt the Singapore Convention on Mediation, which allows businesses to directly enforce mediated settlement agreements in signatory countries without starting new court proceedings. She also proposed exploring another possible avenue on the enforcement of mediated outcomes – a process called “judicial confirmation”, which is available in some civil law jurisdictions, including the mainland. This process would allow courts to recognise and enforce a mediation outcome like a judgment. “They are provisions in the domestic [Hong Kong] law to enforce mediated settlement agreements. If the Singapore Convention is not yet there, maybe [the city can] have a domestic regime to allow for [enforcement],” Cheng said.

title: Spain’s housing crisis in spotlight with eviction of pensioner, 87
description: Thousands have protested in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers.
content: The eviction of an 87-year-old from her Madrid home has highlighted a political paralysis that has thwarted efforts to resolve Spain’s chronic housing crisis, fuelling debate before next year’s election. Maricarmen Abascal’s 70-year stay at her home in upmarket central Madrid ended on Wednesday when she left escorted on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police on the other – a traumatic event broadcast live on TV. Unable to afford a 275-per cent increase to the monthly rent imposed by the real estate firm that owned her flat, she has become the cruellest symbol of a crisis that has stalked Spain for years. Thousands protested in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere on Wednesday night in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers – young and old alike. “The law was upheld and the market worked. But it is the law of the jungle in a broken market, and it is a failure,” left-leaning daily El Pais said in an editorial. In 10 years, the average price of a square metre for rent or purchase has increased by around 50 per cent, according to real estate portal Idealista and official figures. Spiralling prices have particularly affected Madrid, which has topped a world ranking for luxury properties by real estate firm Barnes for two years running. Residents in the world’s second-most visited country often blame short-term tourist rentals such as Airbnb for driving up prices and cutting supply, sparking large protests in hotspots including Barcelona. Popular anger is also directed at investment funds – called “vulture funds” by detractors – accused of acquiring properties with more concern for profit than for affordability. Part of the problem is a lack of public housing. Just 1.2 per cent of Spain’s housing stock is publicly owned, according to OECD figures, far below European peers such as Britain, France or the Netherlands. Spanish consumer group OCU said finding a flat in Madrid or Barcelona for less than €700 (US$796) a month was now “extremely difficult”, pleading for more “affordable” rental stock. The widespread outrage at the eviction has dominated the political debate as parties sharpen their pitches before next year’s general election. But any political fallout is hard to predict in Spain, where power is decentralised and local politicians often take the flak for perceived policy failures. The leftist government has spent years trying to reform the market, but powers over housing are primarily held by the regional authorities. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez blamed the conservative-run Madrid city and regional authorities for their role in Maricarmen’s eviction, slamming it as an unacceptable “social tragedy”. The Madrid region’s right-wing Popular Party (PP) leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso hit back on Thursday, accusing the government of “demagoguery” and “not doing anything” during Sanchez’s eight years in office. In a context of “inflation and loss of purchasing power”, “this situation helps none of the parties”, said Guillermo Fernandez Vazquez, a professor at Madrid’s Carlos III University. He said the eviction had “again laid bare the failure of all the housing policies of the government” and its “powerlessness”. Sanchez urged parliament to pass a law that would ban such evictions, but his coalition has no majority and is already showing signs of strain over the incident. Far-left junior coalition partner Sumar has demanded a rent freeze and the expropriation of Maricarmen’s former home. “There is no legal umbrella that enables the suspension of the eviction of vulnerable people,” Maricarmen’s lawyer Beatriz Duro told public broadcaster RTVE. But “these protections that have always existed through royal decrees end up being sticking plasters and insufficient”, she added. However, the PP would also “want to wrap up that matter as soon as possible” amid a row over a swanky Madrid penthouse that Ayuso allegedly acquired with public money, Vazquez said. Ayuso denies wrongdoing in the case.

title: Xi-Trump summit ends with modest deals, promises of more meetings
description: The two leaders extend their trade truce and signal progress on tariffs while striking a warmer tone on AI, security and bilateral ties.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping announced on Friday that he would meet his American counterpart Donald Trump again at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and at the G20 summit in Miami in December. This set a record, as no Chinese president before had travelled to the US twice in a year. Trump also said he invited to the G20 Russian President Vladimir Putin, who is expected to show up in Shenzhen as well. The announcement capped the final day of Xi’s whirlwind state visit to Washington, which featured tea and a visit to the US National Archives where the two leaders bid farewell after viewing foundational American documents. “We’ve had a tremendous visit,” Trump said. “We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.” Xi responded by thanking Trump for a visit “done to the highest order of perfection and various thought in every little detail”. The farewell and pledge to do it all again in two months followed the heart of the three-day summit on Thursday when the two leaders grappled over artificial intelligence safeguards, rare earth minerals, trade tariffs, Taiwan arms sales, the Iran war, Ukraine and bilateral military relations. Trump and Xi also agreed this week to extend a trade truce reached 11 months ago in South Korea by two months, seen largely as a way to buy time until January 10. And they teased an as-yet ill-defined “new joint arrangement”. That appeared to refer to a Board of Trade mechanism aimed at reducing tariffs on non-strategic products in equal measure. “Farmers are going to be happy, and America is very happy about this visit,” Trump said on Friday. “Great things for both countries, and it has been very productive.” Fox News reported on Friday that the Office of the US Trade Representative will announce additional tariff exemptions and new Chinese purchases in agriculture and low-tech goods on Monday. The Board of Trade “deliverable” has been deadlocked for weeks over the amounts involved, what products would be included and how to ensure compliance, sources said. At the National Archives, Trump acknowledged an age gap at the semiquincentennial anniversary of the United States, with a bit of his characteristic inflation regarding the duration of China’s civilisation, variously pegged at 3,500 to 5,000 years. “So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250,” Trump said. “But we are very proud of our 250.” Friday also saw an attempt by the US president to elicit Xi’s support for his latest branding exercise. This followed his push for Lake Ontario to be renamed “Lake America”, the Gulf of Mexico to be called the “Gulf of America” and a bid to append his name to Washington’s iconic cultural complex, the Kennedy Centre. “Like almost everyone else, he seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE,” the US president wrote on social media. “That would be ‘SUPER!’ Everyone last night agreed, also.” At Thursday’s state dinner, meanwhile, Trump gave Xi a large sculpture of a bald eagle, the US national symbol, adding that he and Xi represent different political systems but “the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better”. “Together we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations,” he said. Xi followed Trump in offering a parallel toast to the US president. “This has added new substance to the constructive China–US relationship of strategic stability and provided new strategic guidance for China–US relations.” The leaders started off Thursday morning with a formal arrival ceremony on the White House South Lawn. . Both presidents adopted a notably rosy tone throughout the day, highlighting areas of common ground, cultural touchstones and partnership efforts during World War II. “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” Trump said. Xi then invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China, offered a pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta and called for greater cooperation. “I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course e,” Xi said. “China and the United States are different in national conditions,” added Xi during his first summit on US soil since 2015, following their May summit in Beijing. “But through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better.” Xi gave a nod to Trump’s “America first” catchphrase twice on Thursday even as he emphasised the importance of recognising China as an equal. “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand,” he said. Xi and Trump’s time without their respective retinues lasted less than an hour. Xi stressed Beijing’s position on Taiwan, urging Trump to “carefully” consider the US’ stance and oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media. China’s first lady, Peng Liyuan, and US first lady Melania Trump also attended Thursday’s welcome ceremony, attracting robust attention before breaking off to tour the National Museum of Asian Art. Beneath the day’s florid language and repeated statements of friendship are a host of critical issues. “This is going to be a summit that’s relatively underwhelming with a small number of deliverables, but I think that works mainly to China’s advantage,” said Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, given the lack of movement on overcapacity or other structural issues. Relative to last year’s escalating tariffs and harsh rhetoric, however, many welcomed signs of a floor, however wobbly, under the fraught relationship. In far loftier and more substantive comments than his US counterpart, Xi touched on military communication, fentanyl, AI, investment and the need for more communication. The nations’ militaries could “maintain regular dialogue” as part of an overall relationship involving “healthy” competition that was “kept within bounds”, he said, noting the importance of ensuring that “AI is always under human control”. “We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States,” he added. Xi’s visit drew local supporters outside the White House, many singing the Chinese song “Bless the Motherland”, as well as pro-democracy protesters, including a parade of Tibetan protesters that marched from the Chinese embassy. The summit started with Trump’s unusual move of greeting Xi in person on his arrival at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday afternoon. But the world has come to expect the unexpected from Trump, an unabashed disrupter who relishes slamming through norms and flexing his power and US military might. Planners organised the week to mirror the Beijing summit four months ago with limited time on the ground, no side visits outside the capital and Thursday’s state dinner. The reciprocity – which did not see Xi greet Trump at Beijing’s airport or invite along a Chinese business delegation – was meant to underscore respect and the equality of the two wary competitors, an issue of particular importance to Beijing. While the White House has been juggling its Iran war of choice, a Canadian trade showdown, Trump’s record-low popularity and pending November elections, summit preparations were frustrated by the small number of US decision-makers and an impetuous president inclined to rip up plans on short notice, according to sources. Amid low expectations for deliverables this week, the world awaited some movement on artificial intelligence safeguards – a source of global concern – and on Iran. Trump badly wants Beijing’s help in forcing Tehran to the bargaining table to end a war he started over six months ago. In non-committal fashion, China said on Friday “the sovereignty and security of all countries should be respected”. Also closely watched by Washington and its allies has been the 90 per cent of global rare earth mineral processing that China controls. In recent months, Beijing has dispensed these critical resources sparingly to US and especially Japanese companies. “China-US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world,” Xi said on Thursday. “But without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems.”

title: Hong Kong hero back in town for Fifa Asean Cup, as current coach plays down key-man exit
description: Despite tournament’s shaky foundations, Hong Kong’s past and present coaches welcome opportunity for more football.
content: Scheduling the pre-tournament press conference less than five hours before the opening match did little to disabuse anyone of the impression that everybody involved in organising the inaugural Fifa Asean Cup is flying by the seat of their pants. It all got too much for Vladica Grujic, the fiery Laos head coach, as the clock ticked 15 minutes beyond the scheduled 12.15pm start time. “This is crazy, we’re playing this evening and my player [captain Bounphachan Bounkong] needs to have lunch,” Grujic said to nobody in particular. The Serb’s team went on to beat Brunei 3-1, the hopefully well-fed Bounphachan netting the opener from the spot, while Myanmar, now under the charge of former Hong Kong coach Jorn Andersen, overcame an easy-on-the-eye Timor-Leste side 2-0 in the second match at a quiet Mong Kok Stadium. When the talking finally started earlier in the day, after Fifa had agreed to the “commercial setting” for the media gathering at the Jockey Club HKFA Football Training Centre, it was Hong Kong coaches past and present, Andersen and Roberto Losada, who did most of the heavy lifting. Andersen tipped Losada, who is in the line of some supporters’ fire after only two matches in charge, to “take Hong Kong to a new level in the coming years”. Losada played down the exit of savvy technical director and close ally John Morling, who has left after 2½ years for a role with the ambitious United Arab Emirates FA, while “accepting the criticism” that has come his way. Back in Hong Kong in an official capacity for the first time since May 2024, when he quit as city team boss for an offer he “simply couldn’t refuse” from Chinese club Yunnan Yukun, Andersen’s fingerprints are already all over his hustling, high-pressing Myanmar team. Appointed in July after seven months out of the game, he masterminded a remarkable 4-1 away victory over world No 135 team the Philippines at the recent Asean Championship, where Myanmar, ranked No 158, also whacked Laos 7-2 but suffered narrow defeats by Malaysia and eventual runners-up Thailand. “The main difference under him is that in every match we’re playing to win,” Lwin Moe Aung, the Myanmar midfielder, said. “His instructions are very clear.” That month-long Asean competition finished only four weeks ago, which rather raises the question over the purpose of having this ill-thought-out version so soon afterwards. India and China were mooted as guest teams for Division One, the eight-team competition being staged concurrently in Indonesia, but both decided they had better things to do: for India, that meant home friendlies with Panama, Brazil and Uruguay. China are playing Maldives, New Zealand, Palestine and Tajikistan. Pakistan were hurriedly drafted into the top flight, despite boasting a world ranking of No 194 that is below all but 201st-ranked Timor-Leste of the six Division Two sides. Andersen, whose main gripe when in charge of Hong Kong was his minimal access to players he believed lost condition back with their clubs, and who adored coaching North Korea for two years because he could have his squad almost permanently in camp, embraced the opportunity for more football. “We have two big tournaments in a short time, so it’s almost like being a club coach,” he said. “It’s really good for me and my players, although we are missing some because of injuries.” Losada said: “We want more and more of this, and not only in the Fifa windows. You can test things and bring in players. Window to window is a long time; you don’t train often and it’s difficult.” The group-stage draw, which appeared something of a movable feast over the months since the Fifa Asean Cup was first conceived, has served up the delicious prospect of Andersen managing against Hong Kong in the final. Myanmar face world No 176 Cambodia in their second group match on Sunday. The coach who ended the city team’s 55-year wait to compete in a major tournament in 2023 when he led them to the Asian Cup finals, Andersen succinctly summed up the reign of his immediate predecessor, Ashley Westwood. “Westwood came here and tried to qualify for the Asian Cup, then he disappeared,” the Norwegian said. After Hong Kong fatally lost a home qualifier against Singapore last November, the baton passed to Losada, initially on interim terms, before his appointment was made permanent in June. “I’m very happy my friend Chino [Losada] has come in,” Andersen said, revealing that he had asked Losada to assist him in Yunnan. “He’s one of the best coaches who has ever worked in Hong Kong, and I think he can take the team to a new level in the coming years.” Losada returned: “[Andersen] is fantastic, and also a friend. We share thoughts, I learned a lot from him, and I’m still learning from him.” Implementing an in-your-face, fearless and energetic brand of football, Andersen quickly gained favour with Hong Kong supporters. Losada has endured a more complicated start. He was on a hiding to nothing in the Guangdong-Hong Kong Cup, FWD Insurance Chinese New Year Cup, and a meaningless Asian Cup qualifier in India, while the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) dawdled over naming their manager, rifling through more than 300 applications during a supposed worldwide hunt for a coach with “a global vision and professional competence”. Eventually given the gig, Losada began with a laboured 2-0 victory over Mongolia, then was the object of fans’ censure following a poor 2-0 defeat in Cambodia. “Because of the media, the internet, Facebook and so on, [the criticism] multiplies tenfold,” Losada said. “It’s very easy to criticise. But I accept it, it’s my responsibility, and I take it. But I’m not going to stop working. We’re fighting for one objective. I’m going to keep going with that and try our best to achieve this in the coming one or two years.” Currently down at world No 155, Hong Kong face Laos, ranked No 186, on Sunday, then meet No 194 side Brunei three days later, both at Kai Tak Stadium. The final is on October 3. Brunei defender Wafi Aminuddin, whose elder brother Afi played at the back when Andersen’s Hong Kong massacred Brunei 10-0 three years ago, said: “We’ve come with a lot of new faces, but some played in that match. They want to feel better and, hopefully, get revenge and win.” Philip Chan Siu-kwan, the Hong Kong midfielder who scored twice in that double-figure victory, said: “They’ve improved and the ranking is only a reference. “Our motivation is to give the fans what they want, which is to see Hong Kong play beautiful football and get to the final. We’ll try to show the best side of ourselves.” Losada, who will have his Asian Games contingent available after the city under-23s’ group-stage exit in Japan, said that losing Morling had “not affected us at all”. Still, he acknowledged that “it’s been a big loss because he knew how Hong Kong worked and had good links with everybody”. “We wish him all the best and we’ll stay in contact,” Losada added. The HKFA have not officially announced the Englishman’s departure, but they advertised on their website for a new technical director, closing applications on September 20. After they saw off admirably stubborn Brunei, Laos’s clash with Hong Kong is already looking like a straight shoot-out to reach the final. Xayasith Singsavang and Bounxai Xernvanglieng added to Bounphachan’s fourth-minute penalty, either side of a strike from Brunei midfielder Haziq Naqiuddin Syamra. A pair of powerful headers from Win Naing Tun and captain Than Paing were responsible for Myanmar’s winning start.

title: Singapore’s finance firms pledge to train 80,000 local staff in AI skills
description: The firms will also study how jobs are changing and test approaches to training and job redesign.
content: Singapore’s major financial institutions have pledged to train more than 80,000 local employees in AI skills as the country moves to cushion white-collar workers from potential job disruption. A pioneer batch of 23 banks, insurers and asset managers has committed to train all their Singapore staff by 2028, and more than half of them have already gone through programmes recognised by an industry association, according to Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong. The firms would also study how jobs were changing and test approaches to training and job redesign, starting with roles for leaders, wealth managers and operations staff, said Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). “We want AI to translate into better careers for Singaporeans and a more productive workforce,” Gan said in a speech at a banking and finance dinner on Thursday. The push in the Southeast Asian financial hub comes as banks increasingly deploy AI in areas ranging from compliance to wealth advisory. While this boosts efficiency, it has also raised concerns that the technology could replace jobs faster than workers can be retrained. The issue is all the more pertinent in finance, a key sector that accounts for about 14 per cent of Singapore’s economy and employs around 200,000 professionals. The current initiative expands on efforts announced a year ago, when Singapore’s three local banks pledged to train all 35,000 of their employees in the country to prepare for AI. “Equipping workers with new emerging skills is only part of the equation,” MAS managing director Chia Der Jiun said at the same event. “We also need to support workers as jobs and tasks evolve.” Their comments come days after Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong joined a group of world leaders in issuing a joint declaration calling for control and international oversight of frontier AI models. The statement warned that capable AI systems have circumvented testing safeguards, exploited vulnerabilities and gained unauthorised access to real-world systems. “We must continue to find practical ways to build common ground and bring more countries along,” Wong wrote in a Facebook post explaining Singapore’s support for the joint statement. “AI holds tremendous promise, but it must always remain under human control and oversight.”

title: China’s sulphur imports dive 65% as prices surge 3.5 times amid Middle East disruption
description: Country pays more for less of the key fertiliser ingredient, potentially pressuring the spring planting season, analyst says.
content: China paid more for far less sulphur in August, as Middle East supply disruptions pushed the element’s average import price nearly 3.5 times higher than a year earlier, putting pressure on the country’s planting season next year. August imports fell nearly 30 per cent from July and 65 per cent from a year earlier to around 277,300 tonnes, according to the latest Chinese customs data. But the value of those shipments rose by more than a fifth year on year. The divergence sent the average import price soaring by nearly 246 per cent from a year earlier – meaning China paid almost 3.5 times as much for each tonne. Across the first eight months of the year, the average price was 168 per cent higher than in the same period of 2025. Largely recovered as a by-product of oil and natural-gas processing, sulphur is used to produce sulphuric acid and phosphate fertilisers, making it an important raw material for both agriculture and the chemical industry. The Middle East accounted for about half of global sulphur exports before the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Argus Media, a London-based commodity price reporting agency. This left buyers exposed when shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was severely disrupted during the nearly seven-month war. The effect is now reaching China’s fertiliser factories. “Chinese import demand is expected to remain muted,” as buyers remain unwilling to accept offers above US$1,000 a tonne, said Deon Ngee, head of sulphur pricing at Argus. Purchases were likely to stay minimal in September and October, though lower prices could prompt buyers to rebuild inventories in November, Ngee added. High costs have already led some fertiliser producers to cut output. Ngee said average operating rates at phosphate fertiliser producers across several provinces dropped by 12 per cent recently from a year earlier. “China’s spring application season this year was less affected because of high port inventories carried over from late last year,” Ngee said. “If the sulphur shortage persists and inventories remain constrained, next year’s spring application season could face greater pressure.” As buyers sought domestic supplies, China’s sulphur price climbed from 4,050 yuan (US$603) a tonne before the war to a record 11,750 yuan in June. It had eased to 7,350 yuan by September 17, but remained well above its pre-war level, according to data provided by Argus. The shift is clear in China’s customs records. The United Arab Emirates, South Korea and Canada together accounted for 80 per cent of its sulphur imports in August, while no shipments were recorded from Qatar, Oman, Iran or India – all major suppliers a year earlier. The shortage extends well beyond a single month. In the first eight months of the year, China’s sulphur imports fell 60 per cent from the same period in 2025, yet its import bill still increased by 8.4 per cent. Shipments from Qatar, Iran and Kuwait fell by between 80 and 96 per cent, while imports from Oman, the UAE and Saudi Arabia more than halved. Meanwhile, China is softening the blow by increasing purchases from alternative suppliers including Singapore, Brunei and the UK. Beijing has also restricted exports of certain phosphate fertilisers and nitrogen-potassium blends, while sulphuric acid exports have reportedly been suspended.

title: Xi, Trump praise past friendship, downplay current rivalry at dinner – as it happened
description: Following an unprecedented reception upon landing, formal proceedings – including talks – between the two leaders took place today.
content: This live article is freely available to our registered users. Please log in or create an account. Xi’s US summit: Access real-time updates, geopolitical risk analysis, and exclusive reporting from an Asian perspective. Subscribe now with our limited-time offer to stay ahead. President Xi Jinping and China’s first lady Peng Liyuan arrived at the White House on Thursday, on Xi’s first trip to the US in nearly a decade, following US President Donald Trump’s trip to Beijing in May. Trump greeted Xi with a handshake, followed by a show of the US’ military might with a flyover by a B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22 Raptors, as well as a silent military drill. In speeches, both Xi and Trump said that their countries could achieve much by focusing on common interests, and Xi warned about the dangers of AI. The leaders then retired to the Oval Office, where Xi stressed Beijing’s position on Taiwan, urging Trump to “carefully” consider the US’ position and oppose Taiwan independence, according to Chinese state media. Xi later said that the two countries, which have been locked in a long-running trade war, had achieved a “new joint arrangement” on trade after a new round of negotiation. Meanwhile, US first lady Melania Trump accompanied Peng to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art, before both couples reunited for a state dinner. At the dinner, the two gave speeches to toast the bilateral relationship. Trump said that while he and Xi represent different systems, “the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” adding the two could “continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations”. Citing the two countries’ partnership in World War II – and explicitly naming Japan as their shared foe in that conflict – Xi said the China-US friendship was one “forged in blood and fire” that will “live on through the generations”. title: Exco declarations reveal new roles for ex-lawmakers as minister retains 22 flats
description: Executive Council’s annually updated declarations of interest shed light on positions taken by several former Legco veterans.
content: Updated declarations of interest by members of Hong Kong’s top decision-making body have revealed new business ventures and corporate board appointments for several former veteran lawmakers, while constitutional affairs chief Janice Tse Siu-wa remains the biggest landlord among ministers. The Executive Council’s annually updated declarations of interest were published on Thursday in accordance with regulations requiring all members, including senior politically appointed officials, to declare their investments, property ownership and membership of community groups. The documents shed light on the new roles taken on by several Exco members who stepped down as legislators last December. Former insurance sector lawmaker Chan Kin-por, who sits on the independent committee examining the cause of last November’s deadly Tai Po fire, declared that he had set up a new firm, KP Insurance Agency Company Limited, in which he holds a 60 per cent stake. He also took on the roles of chairman and independent non-executive director of Manulife Provident Funds Trust Company. Former catering sector lawmaker Tommy Cheung Yu-yan was appointed as a consultant to Uni-China (Business) Management Limited, a subsidiary of Uni-China Group, a major wholesale and retail company that also owns supermarkets and restaurants across the city. Earlier this year, Uni-China Group faced allegations that it had occupied government land near the Mai Po nature reserve and the Inner Deep Bay wetlands to operate fish ponds without permission. The company denied occupying any government land. Martin Liao Cheung-kong, chairman of the Hong Kong Jockey Club and formerly known as the “class monitor” of the pro-establishment camp, declared a new role as an independent non-executive director of Bank of China (Hong Kong). Government officials’ declarations of interest were also updated. Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse’s portfolio comprised 22 properties, down from 25 when she was appointed in March, but still more than those declared by any other principal official. Compared with her previous declaration, she had reduced her holdings by three flats in Central and Western district and one commercial property in Wan Chai, while declaring an additional commercial property in Central and Western district. She retained one commercial property in Foshan, Guangdong province, for her own use and a residential property in London for leasing. Tse also declared her shareholdings of more than 1 per cent in nine private companies, including newly listed Always Cheer Limited, whose business was not specified. According to a Companies Registry document, Tse held shares in Always Cheer through Veron and Company Limited last year but had not previously declared them.

title: Hong Kong model Abby Choi’s former relatives admit body disposal, deny murder
description: Guilty pleas revealed on Thursday, as nine-member jury empanelled for eight-week High Court trial.
content: Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s former husband and brother-in-law have pleaded guilty to illegally disposing of her dismembered body, but will still stand trial alongside their father on murder charges as prosecutors prepare to open their case on Monday. The pleas on the two charges were revealed on Thursday after the High Court empanelled a nine-member jury for the high-profile trial, which is expected to last about eight weeks. The seven men and two women will hear evidence and arguments on how the three former relatives of Choi allegedly conspired to murder the 28-year-old and dismember her body at a village house in Tai Po in February 2023. Choi’s ex-husband, 31-year-old Alex Kwong Kong-chi, and his elder brother, 35-year-old Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of the influencer’s body between February 21 and 23 that year. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, pleaded not guilty to the same offence. All three men also deny murdering Choi. Deputy Judge Brian Keith said the case had attracted enormous publicity locally and abroad, warning jurors against reading news reports or online commentary about the proceedings. Keith added that disturbing material, including photographs, would be withheld unless it was deemed absolutely necessary for the jury to view. The court spent about three hours empanelling the jury, with 59 of the 68 people randomly selected exempted from serving on grounds including limited English proficiency and pre-existing travel plans. One woman who was discharged said: “My English is not good, and personally I don’t like Mr Kwong, so I’m afraid I cannot make the correct decision.” Another was excused after revealing her husband was a government chemist who had handled evidence in the case. Fifteen of the 59 people, including 11 women, stepped down after defence lawyers objected to their participation. The court is expected to resolve outstanding preliminary issues on Friday before Charlotte Draycott SC delivers the prosecution’s opening speech on Monday.

title: Loved Heart of the Beast? 10 of the best dog movies where the canine takes the lead
description: From Hachiko to Good Boy, pooches not people deliver the biggest performances in these movies ranging from tear-jerkers to horror.
content: Few cinematic stories are as life-affirming or tug as effectively at our heartstrings as those exploring the bond between humans and dogs. The unwavering loyalty and adoration of a faithful pup can melt even the hardest of hearts, making it little wonder that filmmakers continually return to the subject. This week sees the release of David Ayer’s Heart of the Beast, starring Brad Pitt as a retired US Special Forces officer stranded in the Alaskan wilderness alongside his loyal dog, Odin – himself a decorated combat veteran. With Pitt practically blown off the screen by his canine counterpart, we take this opportunity to celebrate 10 other films where the dog rightly takes the lead. 1. Antarctica (1983) Based on real events, Koreyoshi Kurahara’s incredible film recounts how a 1958 Japanese surveying expedition to the South Pole was forced to evacuate prematurely due to adverse weather, abandoning a team of 15 Sakhalin huskies chained together outside the station. The story speculates on what happened next, with eight of the dogs breaking free and battling the elements to stay alive. Produced over three years and featuring an iconic score from Greek composer Vangelis, this emotional survival thriller reigned as the most successful Japanese release at the domestic box office for 14 years. 2. Cujo (1983) Lewis Teague’s stripped-down thriller is one of author Stephen King’s favourite adaptations of his work. Dee Wallace stars as the put-upon Donna, who spends most of her screen time trapped with her young son (Danny Pintauro) in a broken-down Ford Pinto as they are hounded by a giant, slobbering St Bernard, driven into a murderous frenzy after contracting rabies. Portrayed by a team of real dogs, mechanical puppets and even stuntmen in costumes, the titular beast ensures the name Cujo remains synonymous with ferocious mutts more than four decades later. 3. Hachiko (1987) The most famous tale of a dog’s loyalty to its owner this side of The Odyssey is undeniably the story of Hachiko the Akita, beautifully brought to life on screen in this box office smash hit. In 1920s Tokyo, Hachi would greet his master, Professor Hidesaburo Ueno (played by legendary actor Tatsuya Nakadai), outside Shibuya Station every day after work. Following Ueno’s untimely death, Hachi continued to wait for almost a decade. The dog became a national symbol of steadfast devotion, while the statue erected in his honour remains a popular meeting point outside the station’s “Hachiko Exit”. 4. Fluke (1995) Loosely based on the novel by British horror writer James Herbert, Fluke essentially reworks the hit romantic fantasy Ghost as a fluffy, family-friendly adventure. Told from the point of view of Fluke, a scrappy mongrel puppy voiced by Matthew Modine, the story follows the dog as he comes to realise he is the reincarnation of a human, Thomas, and attempts to reconnect with the wife (Nancy Travis) and child he left behind. The film’s stacked cast includes Samuel L. Jackson as the voice of Fluke’s street-smart friend, Rumbo, Eric Stoltz as Thomas’s best friend, and Ron Perlman as an evil dog catcher. 5. White God (2014) Winner of the Un Certain Regard prize at the Cannes Film Festival, Hungarian filmmaker Kornel Mundruczo’s extraordinary drama unfolds in a fictional near-future where mixed-breed dogs are subject to an expensive “mongrel fee” imposed by the government. This surcharge causes Hagen, an adopted stray, to be cast out onto the street by his young female owner’s cruel father. Forced to fend for himself, the discarded mutt gets into a number of scrapes as he evades the authorities, ultimately rising through the ranks to become the leader of a full-blown canine uprising against his human oppressors. 6. A Dog’s Purpose (2017) Josh Gad provides the inner monologue for our canine hero in Lasse Hallstrom’s unapologetically sentimental adaptation of W. Bruce Cameron’s novel. Across multiple lifetimes and reincarnations, we follow the consciousness of a single pooch as it experiences love and loss with various owners while searching for a greater purpose. The dog changes breeds and genders but retains the knowledge of its previous lives, especially its relationship with its first owner, Ethan. While life’s meaning remains somewhat elusive, the film’s purpose is to make its audience cry, which it achieves effortlessly time and again. 7. Little Q (2019) Simon Yam Tat-wah plays a pastry chef with declining eyesight who is assigned a seeing-eye dog, “Little Q”, in Law Wing-cheong’s remake of the 2004 Japanese hit Quill, itself adapted from Kengo Ishiguro and Ryohei Akimoto’s 2001 novel. Initially, Po-ting (Yam) is cruel to the mutt – and everyone else around him – but over time their bond grows strong. It is one of the veteran actor’s better performances in recent years, but even he is eclipsed by the lovable yellow Labrador with whom he shares the screen. Little Q is also elevated beyond schmaltz by its detailed portrayal of guide dog training programmes. 8. 777 Charlie (2022) A young Labrador retriever escapes from a cruel breeding facility and is begrudgingly adopted by a reclusive factory worker played by Rakshit Shetty in this hit Kannada-language road movie. Nicknamed Charlie – after silent film star Charlie Chaplin – the dog sets out for the snowy climes of the Himalayas with her new guardian, experiencing numerous exciting adventures on their journey. Taking a moralistic stance on animal cruelty and the importance of responsible pet ownership, 777 Charlie rises above trite sentimentality thanks to the impressive central performance of its four-legged heroine and stunning locations visited along the way. 9. Black Dog (2024) Guan Hu’s desolate drama documents China’s rapid economic overhaul in the run-up to the 2008 Summer Olympics, as seen through the eyes of Eddie Peng Yu-yan’s former stunt driver Lang, who returns to his hometown in the Gobi Desert following a stint in prison. Lang joins a team tasked with rounding up stray dogs and catches a notorious mutt believed to have rabies. Despite being bitten, he keeps the dog and the pair quarantine together, ultimately forging an inseparable bond. Apparently, Peng grew so close to Xin, his four-legged co-star, that he adopted her after production wrapped. 10. Good Boy (2025) First-time director Ben Leonberg cast his own pooch Indy as the lead in this spine-tingling low-fi horror flick that sees a dog and his owner, Todd (Shane Jensen), leave New York for the less welcoming environs of his late grandfather’s remote woodland home. Indy must fend for himself after Todd is bedridden by a worsening health problem and the house becomes overrun by an unnerving supernatural presence. Indy’s captivating performance earned the canine thespian an unprecedented “Best Performance in a Horror or Thriller” win at the Astra Film Awards, beating out the likes of Ethan Hawke and Alison Brie. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook.

title: Hong Kong have day to remember as Siobhan Haughey wins fourth medal at ‘final Asian Games’
description: Swimmer says her body had sent ’signals’ this should be her last Games as rowers bring in four medals, wushu wins first, fencing wins bronze.
content: Rower Chiu Hin-chun grabbed the gold he needed to complete his set of Asian Games medals, Siobhan Haughey won her fourth of the week, and there was a wushu first as Hong Kong’s athletes had a Thursday to remember in Japan. Chiu’s triumph in the lightweight men’s singles sculls was one of four medals the city’s rowers brought home in Nagoya and Tokyo. Winne Hung Wing-yan took silver in the women’s lightweight single sculls, while there was bronze for women’s pair Cheung Yuen-shan and Leung Wing-wun in the lightweight double, and for Lam Sun-tung and Chan Tik-lun in the men’s version. Away from the water, wushu athlete Leung Yu-hong won silver in men’s sanda, while fencer Fong Hoi-sun earned bronze in the men’s individual épée. The haul took Hong Kong’s overall tally to 23, made up of four gold, 10 silver and nine bronze. At the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course, Hongkonger Chiu was in contention and ranked second through the halfway point of his 2,000-metre race, trailing leader Firdavs Akhunov of Uzbekistan by just 0.63 seconds. But while World Cup silver medallist Akhunov could not maintain his pace and dropped out of the medal places completely, the 32-year-old Chiu held on and seized the lead with 500m to go, before crossing the line first in six minutes and 50.32 seconds. Iran’s Amirhossein Mahmoodpour Shahrestani claimed silver in 6:52.59, with South Korea’s Park Hyun-su sealing bronze in 6:53.35. It was Chiu’s third medal in as many regional Games after his silver in the lightweight category in Jakarta in 2018, and bronze in the men’s single sculls in Hangzhou three years ago. “I’ve been to three Asian Games since 2018,” Chiu said. “I got silver the first time, bronze the second time in Hangzhou, and I wanted this very badly because I had to collect all three colours of medals at the Asian Games. Now I have succeeded. “I’m very excited. I want to thank my family for coming over to Japan to support me. The weather wasn’t really nice; the typhoon made it complicated, but they still came. I really appreciate that.” The veteran was not the only podium maker for the city at the course as three women rowed themselves to two silver medals in the morning. Hung was first to get on the podium in the women’s lightweight single sculls, followed shortly by teammates Cheung and Leung in the women’s lightweight double sculls. Hung led halfway through before Fatemeh Mojallal Topraghghale, in the lane to her right, caught her. The Iranian, who also beat Hung to second in the heat, eventually claimed gold in seven minutes and 24.57 seconds. Hung managed a silver medal – her first at the regional games – in 7:28.54, while Thai rower Parisa Chaempudsa finished third in 7:40.61. Moments later, Cheung and Leung crossed the line in 6:59.24, just behind the Iranian duo of Kimia Zarei and Zeinab Norouzi Tazeh Kand, who took gold in 6:53.93. Japan’s Chika Yonezawa and Chiaki Tomita claimed bronze in 6:59.27. The medal hunt for the city’s rowers went on as Lam Sun-tung, who won the first gold medal for Hong Kong at the Hangzhou Games in 2023 with partner Wong Wai-chun, added a lightweight men’s double sculls bronze with his new partner Chan Tik-lun. It was also a third Asian Games medal for Lam, as the 28-year-old also claimed bronze in men’s lightweight eight in Jakarta eight years ago. In the capital city, Siobhan Haughey added a women’s 50m freestyle silver to her tally in 24.32 seconds as China’s Wu Qingfeng finished first in a Games record time of 23.98. The latest podium brought the Hongkonger’s medal count to four in what would be “my final Asian Games”. The decorated swimmer started off the week with a silver with her teammates in the 4x100m freestyle relay in a city record time. That was followed by two gold medals in her stronghold events of 100m and 200m freestyle. Haughey admitted she felt “complicated” at the conclusion of her last regional games, having just shrugged off an injury but competing throughout while carrying sickness. “It was really bad this morning [during the heat], but I knew I had to push through, so I am really happy and satisfied with my time, which is just 0.02 seconds off my personal best,” she said. “Overall speaking, this Games was better than I expected, by miles. “I injured my abductor a few weeks ago, so there were a lot of changes in my training. I can’t kick [in the water] or work on my lower body in the gym. I only recovered a few days before I boarded the plane, but then I was sick. I actually had no idea how I would perform here. “Obviously, I want to have the best preparation for the Asian Games, but you can’t expect everything to be perfect every time, so it was about learning how to handle things when you ain’t in the best state of preparation.” The four-time Olympic medallist added that “I was proud of myself”, having had to prepare for this event under the “most unideal situation” of her career. “I always thought I had to be perfect in every aspect to have good results, but the problem is, life is not perfect; there are lots of unexpected things,” she said. “So it’s about doing the best you can, and never just giving up. I feel like I’ve done the best I possibly can within my current scope. It wasn’t my 100 per cent at my peak, but I gave all I could. “I know it’s my last Asian Games, so of course I want to have a good, positive ending. Four years is a long time; I probably won’t keep swimming. Like this time, I’d get injured out of the blue during training, and then I’d get sick while training again … these must be signals my body is sending, so I always knew this was my last Asian Games.” There was a first, meanwhile, for two generations of athletes back in Nagoya. Leung Yu-hong’s sanda medal was Hong Kong’s maiden one, even if he came off second best to China’s Tang Sishui, losing their 60kg final on points at Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall. Tang scored five points in the opening round, and Leung managed only one point in the second. Leung said the silver medal made “all the hard work and all the sacrifice” worth it, not that he was getting carried away with the achievement. “I feel peace, I feel calm,” the 21-year-old said. “I don’t let my achievement define me. I am doing myself. I am who I am. I don’t care how other people judge me. I just focus on my goal.” At the Aichi Sky Expo, Fong, who was competing in his fourth Asian Games, made it into the semi-finals of the men’s individual épée, where he lost 15-13 to teenage Kazakhstan fencer Kirill Prokhodov, but it was good enough for a maiden bronze for the 33-year-old veteran.

title: UK far-right activist charged after migrant boat slashed in English Channel
description: Police said a 37-year-old man was detained and charged with one count of criminal damage and one of failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.
content: A British far-right activist who has led protests against migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats was charged on Thursday after allegedly slashing a dinghy in the water. The incident comes as agitators against immigration adopt a confrontational new tactic of trying to stop the boats landing on England’s shores, clashing with police and rescuers in the process. A video posted on Tuesday on social media appears to show Daniel Thomas, 37, taking a knife to an inflatable boat, which was empty of migrants but had a rescue services member aboard, while shouting “You’re in English territory”. Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a 37-year-old man was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life and endangering the safety of a vessel. The force said Thomas was charged on Thursday with one count of criminal damage and one of failing to disclose the PIN to his phone. He was ordered detained until a court appearance on Friday. Several hundred of Thomas’ supporters gathered outside a police station where they believed he was being held, chanting “Free DT”. Thomas, who goes by the nickname Danny Tommo, is a long-time associate of far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson. Patriot Platform, a group Thomas founded, is behind recent protests in which masked, black-clad men tried to stop migrants reaching the United Kingdom. Earlier this month, masked demonstrators blocked the port of Dover, in southeast England, and tried to stop migrants being taken ashore in Portsmouth on the country’s south coast. On Tuesday, hundreds of activists gathered at a marina in Gosport, near Portsmouth, as Thomas filmed himself going out to sea to try to intercept a dinghy carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel from France. Police said three people were charged with assaulting an emergency worker during the demonstration. Some anti-immigration activists have targeted the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), a 200-year-old volunteer force that rescues people in distress at sea, because it is often called out to meet the migrant boats. Some lifeboat crew members have been abused online and had their names and photos published and the RNLI’s Portsmouth station closed temporarily after the protest in the city earlier this month. Successive UK governments have struggled to stop people – more than 41,000 last year – making the dangerous journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians including Nigel Farage of the hard-right party Reform UK, and has been used as a rallying point by anti-immigration activists. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s centre-left government says stepped-up police cooperation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 per cent compared with 2025. Burnham’s government has condemned the “intimidating and thuggish behaviour” of recent anti-immigrant demonstrators. The UK has seen a wave of sometimes violent anti-immigrant demonstrations in the past two years. Protesters clashed with police last year outside hotels housing asylum seekers in London and several other cities. In June, masked men in Northern Ireland set fire to several homes in Belfast they believed to house immigrants after a Sudanese man was arrested over a stabbing.

title: China’s next carrier could be its longest – what are Beijing’s plans?
description: Analysts say the vessel’s hull and potential nuclear propulsion hint that China’s carrier fleet could be used further afield.
content: China’s next aircraft carrier could be longer than the US Navy’s largest warship, according to new satellite images that offer fresh clues about how far from home Beijing intends to operate its fleet – and the logistics it will need to do so. Captured on September 4, the images show that work has begun on the bulbous bow of the carrier under construction at Dalian Shipyard in northeastern China, defence intelligence company Janes reported last week. Measurements from the stern to the projected tip of the bow suggest an eventual overall length of 336 metres (1,100 feet) to 339 metres, according to Janes. That would put the ship on a par with the USS Gerald R. Ford, the US Navy’s newest carrier, which Janes puts at about 333 metres. It would also make the vessel roughly 20 metres longer than the Fujian, China’s most advanced carrier, which entered service last November. Beijing has not disclosed the designation, dimensions, propulsion mechanism or capabilities of the ship, which analysts commonly refer to as the Type 004. The size of the carrier matters because it largely determines how many aircraft it can carry, how much fuel and ammunition it can hold and how long it can keep fighting without resupply. Those factors shape how far a navy can project air power. Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia programme at Defence Priorities, said China was “definitely still in the experimental stage of wielding aircraft carriers” and that he was “not surprised that successive designs are larger and more capable”. He estimated that a ship of that size could operate perhaps 75 to 90 aircraft, compared with 50 to 60 on the Fujian, and could carry “more robust self-defence systems”. An analyst familiar with Chinese naval developments, who asked not to be named, said the roughly 20-metre increase in length over the Fujian should not be overstated. A larger hull would provide more hangar space and room for more aircraft, the analyst said, while nuclear propulsion could also free up space for more aviation fuel or munitions. Janes reported that the carrier’s size reinforced earlier indications that it could be China’s first nuclear-powered surface warship. Goldstein said that assessment “may well be correct”, saying that deploying such technology would be a major leap for China “in terms of power, speed and sustainment”. The anonymous analyst said the adoption of nuclear power in the Type 004 would be more significant than the modest increase in hull size in assessing how China intended to use the carrier, noting that the use of the technology would suggest the navy wanted to operate further afield. Yet even a nuclear-powered carrier would still depend on regular replenishment to keep its aircraft and destroyer escorts operational, Goldstein said. In July, satellite imagery offered insight into an enlarged fast combat support ship being built at the Comec Longxue shipyard near the southern city of Guangzhou. The vessel is thought to be about 271 metres long and 37 metres wide, placing it among the largest replenishment ships of its kind. Janes subsequently reported that satellite imagery indicated it had been launched between July 9 and 12. Satellite imagery captured on September 15 and posted by an open-source imagery analyst appears to show a second large replenishment vessel now being assembled at the same yard. Based on its dimensions and the shape of its hull, the open-source analyst assessed it as a second ship of the same design. The South China Morning Post could not independently verify this assessment. The anonymous analyst said the second hull could indicate serial production, noting that the vessel’s modular construction allowed large sections to be assembled ashore and joined relatively quickly once dry-dock space became available. The first vessel was previously assessed to be a larger variant of the Chinese navy’s existing Type 901 fast replenishment ship and likely tailored to supporting more advanced aircraft carriers such as the Type 004 and their battle groups. Goldstein said China appeared “quite focused on a steady expansion of its fleet of replenishment vessels”, a trend visible over many years, and that the navy practised replenishment at sea often, partly because it lacked an extensive network of overseas bases. He added that carrier and surface groups would need “continuous resupply of fuel and munitions for many key missions”, including in a hypothetical conflict around Taiwan. The expert also said one could “reasonably hypothesise”, given Chinese naval force structure patterns so far, that each of the navy’s three theatre command navies would eventually operate multiple carriers, deploying regularly across the Asia-Pacific and into the Indian Ocean. Both experts added that the larger hull would make little difference to an adversary’s ability to detect and track the carrier, since even a more modestly sized carrier would be highly exposed. However, Goldstein cautioned that “the overall trend for some years in naval strategy has been towards smaller, cheaper, more distributed unmanned assets”, adding that by “doubling down on ‘big decks’, China and the US both seem to be bucking this worldwide trend”.

title: Exclusive | Chinese CEOs fly to US on own, await invites to Trump’s state dinner for Xi Jinping
description: Sources say executives did not fly with Xi’s official party or aboard his aircraft, unlike Trump’s CEO-heavy entourage for May China visit.
content: A small group of Chinese CEOs holding US visas has arrived in Washington after travelling separately from President Xi Jinping’s official entourage, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. But with the clock ticking and the business optics of the Chinese leader’s White House visit hanging on the final twists of diplomatic negotiations, the executives are still waiting to find out whether they will secure a seat at Thursday’s state dinner for Xi. “Beijing’s security protocol is very different,” one of the sources said, noting that the executives did not fly with Xi’s official party or aboard his aircraft, unlike the American CEOs who arrived in Beijing alongside President Donald Trump in May. Two sources said it was unlikely any Chinese business leader applied for a new visa for the summit. They also said the final decision on whether the Chinese corporate chiefs would join state visit events was tied in part to talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, and the matter came up during their meeting on Wednesday. Bessent and He met that day at the World Bank in Washington, their second encounter in four days after talks on Sunday in New York to tackle what Bessent called “unfinished business” ahead of the leadership summit. After Wednesday’s meeting, Bessent announced that the two sides had agreed to extend the “Busan arrangement” on trade – reached after Xi-Trump talks in the South Korean city – by two months, until January 10. While US officials had played down the prospect of an extension being announced this week, the South China Morning Post had reported in August that an extension was “almost certain”. Two sources said the extension had left the door open for the executives to appear at the state dinner and at possible side events. However, their presence might ultimately yield more optics than substance, according to one source. They said the small delegation was unlikely to deliver the soft-power punch Beijing had hoped for, and some executives could even use the occasion to voice their dissatisfaction with US investment restrictions directly to officials. Indeed, the CEOs’ attendance was largely a formality, the source said. Another source familiar with the matter said Trump’s priority remained negotiating the new Board of Investment, rendering efforts to seat Chinese CEOs at the state dinner a “lower policy priority”. For Beijing, however, the optics matter. Having Chinese CEOs at the state dinner would help to balance the presence of US technology bosses and put China’s own corporate and technological muscle on display. The Chinese side viewed business leaders taking part in the banquet and other events as a message that the world’s two largest economies were intertwined, one of the sources noted. “I think given the current circumstances, some Chinese business representation at the state banquet is possible. Even if that didn’t take place, the American business leaders will arrange some gathering with them,” the source said. The same source said some of the names under discussion included executives from Alibaba, Xiaomi, CATL and BYD. Alibaba owns the SCMP. Another source said the backup group was likely to draw from Chinese electric-vehicle companies, which were the keenest to explore investment opportunities in the United States. According to one source, some American business leaders with substantial commercial interests in China were likely to entertain their Chinese counterparts privately if they did not make it to the banquet. Several top executives from Chinese artificial intelligence companies were foregoing the summit over security concerns, the source said. Another insider said the White House banquet venue could seat up to 100 guests, while the Chinese side had been allotted about 30 seats. In the event that the Chinese business leaders could not attend, the administration would invite a few more US guests, tapping into strong demand for the limited seats. On the US side, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook are among the business leaders confirmed to be attending Thursday’s dinner, after accompanying Trump to Beijing four months ago. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman – who was not part of Trump’s delegation in May – is also on the state dinner guest list. The May trip has become a heavily debated template for US-China diplomacy. Trump brought about 18 major chief executives with him, with Huang famously joining Air Force One at the last minute during a refuelling stop in Alaska. While their visit yielded no headline corporate deals, an informal gathering took place between Chinese and American counterparts in Beijing, and some US executives stayed on for a few days after Trump’s departure. Trump also had several CEOs come to the bilaterals simply to be introduced. Something similar was discussed for Xi’s reciprocal visit to Washington but was no longer on the table, sources said. The SCMP reported on Tuesday that differences over possible investment announcements had created roadblocks for a Chinese business delegation potentially accompanying Xi. A source familiar with the discussions said both sides had yet to reach common ground over the Board of Investment, particularly regarding potential Chinese ventures. Another source said a lack of communication and differing interpretations of the reciprocity principle had derailed the original plan. Beijing viewed the presence of Musk, Huang and Cook in Trump’s May delegation as a standard that should be mirrored in Washington. The US side, the source said, treated reciprocity as applying only to senior leadership. Poor logistics and a lack of formal engagement or arranged meetings for Chinese businesses coming to Washington added to the uncertainty. The last-minute uncertainty over the state dinner follows the same pattern the SCMP described in August. Sources said then that Chinese officials were rattled by disorganisation and poor coordination inside the Trump White House in the weeks before Xi’s trip, and that they had already watched the same chaos play out ahead of the US leader’s May state visit to China.

title: 3,800 Hong Kong food outlets offering up to 30% off to celebrate National Day
description: Food and catering businesses say they will offer an array of tasty deals across the city.
content: From restaurants and hotels to cafes and market stalls, Hong Kong’s catering industry has banded together to offer discounts of up to 30 per cent at more than 3,800 outlets to celebrate National Day on October 1. Food and catering businesses said on Thursday they would provide an array of tasty deals across the city to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Offers include meal sets at 30 per cent off, fresh food items such as vegetable packs for HK$7 (89 US cents) and seven fish balls for HK$7 at food market stalls, crispy chicken for HK$10 a piece, buy-one, get-one-free bun deals and 30 per cent discounts at several hotels. Catering sector lawmaker Jonathan Leung Chun said more than 3,800 outlets had joined the promotional event. The industry hoped to attract more residents to stay in Hong Kong to spend and dine on October 1, a public holiday. The National Day “golden week” holiday in mainland China, which runs from October 1 to 7, is expected to bring in about 1.29 million mainland travellers to Hong Kong, according to the Immigration Department. “Despite the complex business environment, the industry’s decision to offer discounts demonstrates its strong commitment to National Day,” Leung said. “This year, eateries taking part include many new elements, such as wet markets and food courts, alongside hotels, fast-food chains, cafes and convenience stores, providing residents and tourists with a wider variety of fresh choices. “We hope to make this event an annual mega-event to mark National Day.” Restaurants joining the promotion are mostly offering discounts of up to 30 per cent or special deals on selected menu items on National Day next week. Multiple brands under the Tai Hing Group – including Tai Hing, Men Wah Bing Teng and Asam Chicken Rice – will offer a 30 per cent discount on all dine-in bills throughout the day. Other chains are offering a 23 per cent discount on selected special dishes on the day or during the surrounding period. At Cafe de Coral, diners can enjoy the “Super Value Sizzling Plate Combo” for HK$49 until October 5. At Maxim’s restaurants, the chain’s boneless Hainanese chicken set will be offered at 23 per cent off its original price during lunch and dinner from October 1 to October 4. At Spaghetti House, patrons can enjoy a 23 per cent discount when ordering any pizza or spaghetti dish from September 28 to October 8. At Oliver’s Super Sandwiches, customers can enjoy a 23 per cent discount on spaghetti bolognese for purchases made after 11am from September 28 to October 8. At Fairwood, diners can enjoy selected dinner sets for two people at HK$99 from October 1 to October 5. On National Day, KFC’s crispy chicken will cost HK$10 a piece, while Bao Dim Sin Seng will offer a buy-one, get-one-free deal for a cold bun. At Fulum restaurant outlets, diners can enjoy a six-course National Day banquet for HK$488. At Hong Kong Market, a whole cornfed chicken will be priced at HK$77. At Chuk Yuen Market, patrons can buy seven fish balls for HK$7, and a pack of tomatoes will also cost HK$7. At hotels in the Regal chain, selected restaurants will offer 30 per cent off the bill from October 1 to 4, while the National Day banquet will be offered from HK$468 per person.

title: China’s overseas investment hits record US$214 billion. Why are US-bound flows plunging?
description: Chinese investment in the US has fallen to its lowest level since 2011 amid tighter scrutiny and trade tensions.
content: China’s outbound direct investment reached a record high of US$214 billion last year, even as investment in the United States plunged to its lowest level in more than a decade amid growing geopolitical and regulatory uncertainty, latest official data showed. Outbound direct investment was up 11.1 per cent in 2025 compared to the previous year, making China the world’s second-largest source of global capital, behind only the US and ranking ahead of Japan, according to an annual report jointly issued by the Ministry of Commerce and two other state economic bodies on Wednesday. This growth was partly driven by stronger investment in technology-related industries. Investment in information transmission, software and information technology services surged 88.3 per cent to reach US$13.1 billion as Chinese companies expanded their presence in such sectors abroad. Bucking that trend was direct investment to the US, which fell 71.3 per cent to US$1.91 billion – down sharply from about US$6.63 billion in 2024 and the lowest level since 2011.
