The US accounted for only 0.9 per cent of China’s total outbound direct investment in 2025, according to the report. “Political and regulatory risks in Western countries loom large for Chinese firms seeking to expand in those markets,” said David Zhang, a macroeconomics and policy analyst at advisory firm Trivium China. “The US in particular has become one of the hardest developed markets for Chinese firms to deploy capital into.” In early 2025, Washington issued an “America First Investment Policy” memorandum that ordered the use of “all necessary legal instruments” to curb Chinese-affiliated investment in strategic industries, including certain technologies, infrastructure and energy. Beijing, in response, described it as “discriminatory” and “very unreasonable”. Investment also declined across traditionally strong recipient sectors amid heightened geopolitical and trade frictions. Chinese investment in US manufacturing – the largest destination for its capital in the country last year – fell 55.4 per cent year on year, while wholesale and retail, another major area of investment, declined 18.9 per cent. Cross-border dealmaking felt a similar chill. Chinese outbound direct investment through mergers and acquisitions fell 40.3 per cent to US$15.3 billion. Officials in the report attributed the decline to “heightened geopolitical tensions and increased volatility in global capital markets”. Meanwhile, Zhang of Trivium China said stricter regulatory scrutiny at home and in major Western markets had made it more difficult to close large-scale overseas acquisitions, though he pointed to the overall resilience of outbound investment as companies increasingly turned to other channels to expand overseas. “Chinese companies are increasingly deploying capital overseas through channels other than acquisitions,” he said, noting a shift towards building or expanding new capacity. “The broader push to expand overseas remains strong, but Chinese firms will increasingly have to balance commercial opportunities against rising geopolitical risks.” Hong Kong retained its position as the top destination for mainland Chinese outbound investment in 2025, attracting US$137.5 billion, or 64.4 per cent of the total, up 18.4 per cent year on year. Investment in the European Union also saw strong growth, more than doubling to US$12.2 billion, a 106.9 per cent increase from a year earlier. By contrast, investment in Belt and Road countries fell 9.7 per cent to US$46 billion, accounting for 21.6 per cent of total outbound direct investment last year.

title: Opinion | Don’t let AI take over our human creative expression
description: The grand promise of AI has been inverted: while we continue doing the grunt work, AI is writing poetry and painting masterpieces.
content: More than three years ago, I articulated concerns regarding the existential threat of artificial intelligence in a piece entitled “How Hong Kong can play a role in preventing AI Armageddon”. There is an increasing number of articles about exactly this. Here I concentrate on a more insidious encroachment on our humanity – how AI is capturing our creative expression and replacing us in a way that is making it harder to discern what is creatively human. As a scientist, my inclination is to filter societal shifts through the prism of rigorous scientific methodology. What we are witnessing today, across the global cultural landscape, is a profound and deeply ironic AI technological inversion. It is as worrying as it is threatening to the essence of our humanity. For decades, the standard narrative on the emergence of AI was of the beneficent golden human age that would follow. An age that unburdens us from mundane chores by leaving machines and AI to perform those that are dull, repetitive, dangerous. By liberating us from these chores, AI was supposed to grant us an abundance of free time to pursue the arts, culture and (supposedly unique) human creative endeavour in general: from painting to poetry, prose to performance, from music to mime. We were envisioned as a society of liberated philosophers, artists, composers, poets and novelists, indulging our creative souls while silent algorithms kept the engines of civilisation humming ever so smoothly in the unobtrusive background. This is not how it is turning out! AI has taken a turn straight into the areas hitherto occupied by the human spirit. Today, generative AI platforms churn out thousands of canvases, sonnets, musical compositions and full-length novels in the blink of an eye. Indeed, at Aprim 2026, our major international astronomy conference in May, one member of my team got AI to generate new songs that heralded each major science theme. I was shocked at how good they were. So the grand promise of AI has been inverted. While humans still continue doing the grunt work, but increasingly guided by AI, AI itself is being used to write poetry, paint masterpieces and yes, even write scientific papers. You just feed the AI model the science data, get it to ingest past work in the field and then churn out a passable paper. AI is making scientific discoveries, spotting hidden but important data patterns and solving maths problems that remain beyond human capacity. All with breathtaking speed and efficiency. For the current crop of global scientists, it can be as demoralising as it is threatening. It also carries profound cultural and human significance for all creative industries. We now see AI capable of mimicking any classical master or style, devaluing the years of technical, human discipline required in any medium or the time needed to develop the innate talent a human may possess but which an AI algorithm can render obsolete or even second-rate in seconds. What is the cost to us of this automated, artistic and even philosophical appropriation of human experience by algorithms? When we look at a painting or read a novel, we are in an emotional connection that loops back to another human mind with a personal story. If we allow generative AI to monopolise our creative expression, where does it leave the human spirit and soul? If we cannot compete and our efforts pale against the magnificence of AI creations, what is the point? Does it matter if AI music makes us cry or an AI poem deeply affects us? Where does this leave the previous genuine human element and story? These are profound philosophical questions. This AI pivot made me consider the media landscape that shapes public opinion. It is clear that the text-generation capacities of AI have permeated journalism and commentary. I have watched this shift with a mixture of academic curiosity and increasing unease. Excessive AI use represents the artificial industrialisation of previously human opinion. We must actively decide whether to surrender the grandest expressions of our humanity to the cold efficiency of AI. Let machines calculate, optimise and manage our databases, but let humans, with our flaws, heartbreak and triumphs, continue to write the stories, compose the music, and paint the canvases that define what it is to be human. If we cede our creativity to AI, we may find that in freeing our hands, we have inadvertently imprisoned our souls.

title: Red carpet vs empty tarmac: Xi’s US welcome fuels debate over Takaichi’s no-show reception
description: Online comparisons of the two leaders’ arrivals in the US this week have raised questions over how Washington treats its Tokyo ally.
content: Starkly contrasting receptions for the Japanese leader and the Chinese president in the United States have sparked debate over Washington’s treatment of Tokyo as an ally. Sanae Takaichi arrived in New York at the start of the working week, beginning a trip where she addressed the United Nations General Assembly for the first time as the country’s prime minister. A photo taken on her arrival shows her waving across a relatively empty tarmac at John F. Kennedy International Airport. Footage released by the Japanese prime minister’s office on Tuesday showed Takaichi being greeted by several Japanese officials, with no senior US representatives present. The pictures quickly went viral on social media, where users contrasted the scene with the grand US welcome for Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland two days later. US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump were on the tarmac to greet the Chinese presidential couple, a courtesy not extended to Trump when he visited Beijing in May. Xi and Peng also received a 21-gun salute fired by artillery pieces, a 100-foot red carpet, a 21-person honour cordon and a flyover by two B-1 Lancer bombers. The welcome was widely viewed as an unprecedented gesture, unlike anything previously accorded to a Chinese president or even traditional US allies. While Takaichi’s trip is not a formal state visit like Xi’s, the disparity in the two leaders’ receptions has ignited intense online debate. Kazuhiro Haraguchi, Japan’s former minister of internal affairs and communications, said on social media that the contrast was “stark”. “Am I the only one who feels that as Japan’s national power has declined, its political presence in the US has plummeted?” Another influencer, posting under the handle @momotro018, took a swipe at the prime minister’s foreign policy. “Some defend this by saying the purpose was different, but the real question is: if the roles were reversed, would the reception still have been handled this way?” “Successive prime ministers up to the [Shigeru] Ishiba managed to build decent relations with China, but Takaichi blew it all up, dealing a massive blow to the Japanese economy,” the post read. Since taking office in October last year, Takaichi has sought a close personal relationship with Trump as part of Tokyo’s strategy to strengthen the US-Japan alliance and offset pressure from China. The two leaders met on the sidelines of the UN gathering – just one day ahead of Trump’s meeting with Xi – during which Takaichi said she and Trump held “frank” exchanges of views on issues including China and North Korea, while reaffirming their bilateral alliance and pledging to elevate ties to “even greater heights”. The US leader, meanwhile, praised his strong ties with Takaichi, saying she had done “a tremendous job”. In her debut UN address on the same day, the Japanese leader avoided directly naming Beijing or Taiwan, but her speech largely served as a counter to Beijing’s pressure following her controversial remarks on Taiwan. Ties between the two East Asian powers have sunk to historic lows, with no sign of improvement after Takaichi suggested in November that Tokyo could deploy military forces in the event of a Taiwan Strait conflict. Tokyo said on Thursday it would monitor the Trump-Xi summit “with strong interest”.

title: Hong Kong to only admit ‘few hundred’ foreign carers a year under pilot scheme
description: Welfare minister Chris Sun promises ‘rigorous’ approach for scheme to recruit skilled carers, following concerns of helper market disruption.
content: Hong Kong will admit “only a few hundred” skilled foreign domestic carers for the elderly annually under a new pilot scheme, the welfare minister has said, promising a “rigorous” approach in response to concerns about possible disruptions to the existing helper market. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han also said on Thursday that those recruited under the scheme would need skills equivalent to those of health workers at Hong Kong’s care homes for the elderly. He added that authorities would engage a recognised Hong Kong organisation to accredit training provided by institutions in carers’ home countries. “I want to emphasise that this is a pilot as I noticed that after we announced the scheme, some people thought it was good, while others had concerns,” he told lawmakers during a Legislative Council meeting. “We will be very rigorous in the initial phase.” “We expect to bring in only a few hundred foreign domestic carers each year after the pilot scheme is launched next year.” Sun also said that authorities would follow up on whether carers arriving in Hong Kong under the scheme had truly helped families, and assess the measure’s overall effectiveness. In his annual policy address last week, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced that the government would admit carers with more advanced training and experience in elderly care on a pilot basis, under a scheme modelled on the city’s existing foreign domestic helper regime, to help meet the home-care needs of older residents. A government source said those employed under the scheme must have experience in caring for the elderly and undergo relevant training in their home countries. Sun earlier said the minimum wage for such carers would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that for existing helpers, whose current minimum allowable wage is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month. But the plan has sparked concerns among some employers, who feared it could disrupt the city’s existing helper market, driving up wages and putting care beyond the reach of low-income older residents. Critics also questioned the need for a separate category of workers given that some of the city’s more than 378,000 foreign domestic helpers were already caring for elderly people. They warned that the new scheme could prompt existing helpers to demand higher pay or quit to take up the new employment opportunity, adding to families’ financial burden.

title: Private jet flap scare triggers ‘local standby’ at Hong Kong airport
description: Billionaire-favoured G650 jet reported flap problem as emergency crews were deployed to the runway before the aircraft landed safely.
content: A mechanical fault on a private jet triggered a precautionary “local standby” at Hong Kong’s airport on Thursday, with the aircraft later landing safely. The Gulfstream G650 reported a flap problem at around 5.21pm and estimated an arrival time of 5.53pm, prompting the Fire Services Department and other airport rescue units to deploy personnel to strategic positions along the runway in readiness to offer immediate assistance. An ambulance was also dispatched as part of the initial emergency response, authorities said. Emergency vehicles attended the scene primarily to monitor for overheated brakes. A flap issue on an aircraft of this class usually indicates that the wing’s high-lift surfaces did not move to their normal landing setting, potentially due to a sensor or system fault. Emergency vehicles are positioned on standby in case the aircraft needs immediate assistance after landing, including monitoring for potential brake overheating. The flight touched down safely at around 6pm without incident, and the standby alert was officially stood down at 6.04pm. Data from a flight-tracking application showed the aircraft being met and followed by two airport ground vehicles as it landed and taxied to the apron. The identities of the operator and passengers on board remain unconfirmed. The Gulfstream G650, or G650ER, is a top-tier ultra-long-range jet costing US$35 million to US$70 million, depending on the aircraft’s age and condition. The model is also widely favoured by billionaires and corporate leaders in China.

title: Xi-Trump summit day 1 highlights: red carpet for China’s leader, Rubio defends visit, and more
description: From first ladies Peng, Melania renewing acquaintance to helicopter that Xi likely won’t board, some highlights from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage of Xi and Trump’s meeting in the US so far. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Big picture or big deals? What the Xi-Trump summit holds for China and the US With the balance of power shifting between the US and China, the success of this week’s summit hinges not on headline-grabbing deals, but on practical, cautious consensus under a new strategic stability framework, according to Chinese researchers. 2. Video of US military adjusting red carpet for China’s Xi sparks online backlash A video clip showing uniformed US military personnel on their hands and knees making last-minute adjustments to a red carpet has gone viral online, with critics pointing to the lavish welcome President Donald Trump rolled out for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews. 3. Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump renew acquaintance as Xi arrives in US Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan shared a light moment with Melania Trump on Wednesday as the two women renewed an acquaintance dating back to the Trumps’ first term in the White House. 4. Rubio defends Xi’s US visit as essential despite deep disagreements US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the welcome planned for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, saying it would be “irresponsible” for the world’s two largest economies to avoid talks at the highest level despite their disagreements. 5. Trump grimaces, Xi unfazed during US military flyover for historic tarmac welcome At Joint Base Andrews where Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for the visiting Chinese president, Xi Jinping appeared unfazed during a ceremonial flyover by a screeching US bomber while the US president visibly winced at the noise. 6. US restricts visas for birth tourism ahead of Xi’s summit with Trump Hours before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in the US for a high-stakes summit, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved to restrict visas for those who “engage in or facilitate” birth tourism, a practice the Trump administration has increasingly accused China of. 7. Trump built a US$5 million White House helipad. Don’t expect Xi Jinping to use it US President Donald Trump has been very eager to show off to Chinese leader Xi Jinping his new US$5 million White House helipad, his latest bid to stamp his image on Washington. But do not count on Xi Jinping to actually use it.

title: Japan men stun China to claim Asian Games table tennis team gold, women even score
description: Sora Matsushima wins decisive match as men’s title fight goes down to the wire at Sky Hall Toyota, while later China’s women sweep to gold.
content: Japan’s men pulled off a stunning upset at the Asian Games on Thursday, beating China to claim table tennis team gold in front of a raucous home crowd. With the sides tied at 2-2 following a back and forth tussle, Sora Matsushima won the decisive match, downing Wen Ruibo 3-1 at Sky Hall Toyota. Matsushima recovered from just losing the opening encounter to Wang Chuqin, who laboured his way to a 3-2 victory, but was overpowered 3-0 by an inspired Tomokazu Harimoto, who set up the thrilling finale after the two sides had traded blows. It was Japan’s first win since Bangkok 1966, and ended China’s streak of eight straight Asian Games titles. Wang bemoaned his own performance in the loss to Harimoto, but also acknowledged how well the home side had played. “I could have done better in that fourth match. Psychologically, I ran into some problems. There were many shots that I didn’t handle well enough,” Wang said. “I always want to be the best, but clearly I still have something to work on. It’s more important now to come back from this. I still have a tough fight tomorrow. “We are familiar opponents. Sometimes we win, sometimes we lose. It was a close fight today. Our opponents were outstanding. We are better than this, but I guess we didn’t do enough today.” China’s women restored some measure of pride in their team final against Japan, cruising to a 3-0 victorty. Sung Yingsha, Wang Manyu and Kuai Man all won their respective matches at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. “I’m very happy to win this with my teammates,” Sun said. “We gave it our all in the final. When we met Japan in the world team championships recently, we had to really battle before winning eventually, so we knew this would not come easy.”

title: Students in Singapore and China top OECD’s Pisa global student assessment
description: The Programme for International Student Assessment surveys 15-year-old pupils every three years.
content:
Singaporean and Chinese students led the world in educational performance in 2025, according to a new assessment. The survey was done by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
The OECD is made up of 38 member nations. It includes the United States, Britain, Australia and many European countries.
The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment surveyed 760,000 15-year-old students. They came from 91 countries and economies, including OECD members. This survey takes place every three years.
In the report, Singapore outscored China in reading. The city state also performed strongly in maths and science.
Students from mainland China led globally in maths with 612 points and in science with 597 points.
The students surveyed in mainland China came from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu province and Zhejiang province.

title: Gulf nations keep oil flowing amid Iran war, but it’s getting costly
description: Despite the Strait of Hormuz blockade and other attacks, oil exporters and the US military have found workarounds, but they may not be sustainable.
content: When Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war, choking off sea passage for some 15 million barrels of oil a day, many feared that prices would skyrocket, cratering the world economy. Instead, nearly seven months on, oil is expensive but not exorbitant, and analysts say there is enough oil available to meet current global needs, even as the higher prices cause political problems for US President Donald Trump and others. That’s because Saudi Arabia and other Gulf producers quickly found alternative routes and reached for unused pipeline capacity. When Iran and its militant allies targeted those, the oil exporters and the US military found still other ways – workarounds for the workarounds – in an often clandestine game of whack-a-mole. With oil now at around US$100 a barrel – higher than before the war but not as bad as feared – Iran has diminished leverage, while a US naval blockade and tightened sanctions smother its own economy. But the workarounds are expensive and may not be sustainable. The drawing down of existing commercial oil stocks – especially by China – has also helped keep prices in check, but cannot continue indefinitely. And Iran could yet gain an edge with continued attacks on key oil facilities. Pipeline backups were ready Iran began attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz in response to the US-Israeli bombardment that started the war. In response, the Saudis turned to their East-West pipeline that carries oil to their Red Sea port of Yanbu. From there, tankers headed out through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Asia. Likewise, the United Arab Emirates used its pipeline cutting across neighbouring Oman to Fujairah – a route that skirts the strait. Both pipelines had spare capacity, and the UAE’s state oil company ADNOC and Saudi Aramco used it to keep exports from collapsing completely during the first weeks of the war. Meanwhile, some oil leaked out of the Strait of Hormuz. In May, ship operators willing to risk an Iranian attack started taking advantage of a US-supervised route near Oman, defying Iran’s demands to use its own vetted route. They shuttled back and forth at night with location systems and mobile phones turned off, and offloaded to tankers waiting outside the strait. Flows from Kuwait, Iraq, and the UAE started to rise again. But Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen disrupted the Yanbu workaround in July by declaring a blockade of Saudi oil shipments, threatening the Bab el-Mandeb – a repeat of the Hormuz disruption. In response, the Saudis redirected Asia shipments northwest to the Mediterranean, either through the Suez Canal or – for tankers too big to use it – a pipeline across Egypt to another tanker. The oil then made a huge detour as it was shipped around Africa and back to Asia. Then the East-West pipeline was attacked earlier this month and forced to shut down, potentially for weeks. With oil loading halted at Yanbu from September 11, the Saudis shifted again, joining other Gulf producers sending oil through the US-guided corridor in the Strait of Hormuz. On Monday, six supertankers loaded 12 million barrels at Saudi terminals on the Persian Gulf, according to shipping data company Kpler. US officials have touted the role of the southern corridor in keeping energy flowing while their blockade increases pressure on Iran. Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, said in a video on social media on Saturday that US forces had assisted 2,000 commercial ship transits and the transport of more than 1 billion barrels of oil from Gulf partner nations over “the past couple of months”. Analysts estimate some 6 million barrels of oil per day or more have been passing through the Strait of Hormuz on the dark shuttle route on average – some 40 per cent or more of pre-war flows. Workarounds keep the economy supplied, for now Rahul Choudhary, vice-president of upstream research at energy data firm Rystad Energy, did the maths as follows: with 6 million or 7 million barrels per day now flowing through the southern route, plus 2 million barrels through the pipeline to Fujairah, fully 8 million or so of the blocked 15 million barrels per day from before the war have been restored. That still leaves roughly 7 million barrels per day missing from pre-war flows. But wait: about 3.5 million barrels per day are being drawn down from the globe’s abundant oil inventories. Meanwhile, demand has fallen by perhaps another 5 million barrels per day, due to the higher price and sluggish economic growth in key markets. Add in 500,000 to 700,000 barrels per day from other suppliers such as the US, and that pretty much evens out the global oil market. “Our take is that the market is very tightly balanced,” Choudhary said. “That is why you are not seeing exceptionally high prices for crude; they are still in the US$100 range, and they have not touched US$140 to US$150 per barrel – which could have been the case if there was a deficit of 5 million to 6 million barrels.” In fact, Rystad foresees oil at US$85 to US$90 per barrel in the last three months of the year, and falling to US$80 to US$82 next year if Hormuz is reopened. The workarounds are time-consuming and expensive. Sending oil to Asia through the Suez Canal instead of the Red Sea can add as much as a month to the voyage. Meanwhile, the Hormuz shuttle trade involves expensive tankers waiting at least a day and a half in the Gulf of Oman for the ship-to-ship transfer. The demand for supertankers has sent charter rates – normally US$30,000 to US$50,000 per day – through the roof. Spot charter rates for Hormuz transits reached US$1 million per day on September 11, according to maritime data company Windward, equivalent to roughly US$26 per barrel. That means shipping is a quarter of the cost, instead of the usual 1 per cent to 3 per cent. And markets have braced themselves for further disruption. The attack on the East-West pipeline has shown pipelines can be vulnerable. Iran could try to disrupt the US route through the Strait of Hormuz or target areas near the Omani coast where the ship-to-ship transfers are taking place. If that happens, the workaround would be to do the transfers farther away – taking more time and running up even bigger bills.

title: China tech faces fresh scrutiny as US blacklist bill introduced, Lenovo case emerges
description: US lawmakers seek broader powers to restrict technology products as Lenovo faces a patent investigation.
content: China’s technology sector is facing fresh pressure in the United States as lawmakers seek to broaden the range of products that can be placed on a trade blacklist, while Lenovo Group has been drawn into a patent dispute involving memory devices. The Communications and Technology Transparency Act, unveiled by the US House Energy and Commerce Committee on Wednesday, would expand the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) Covered List from “communications equipment or service” to the much broader category of “information and communications technology or service” (ICTS). Products on the list cannot be legally imported, marketed or sold as new products in the US. The FCC has already restricted several Chinese-made items, including drones and robots, under the framework targeting designated “foreign adversaries”. Separately, the US International Trade Commission on Wednesday announced a Section 337 investigation into certain DDR5 memory modules and downstream products – including servers, computing systems and storage systems – following a patent-infringement complaint filed by California-based Netlist. As one of the US’ most potent legal weapons for policing intellectual property disputes, a Section 337 investigation can lead to the total exclusion of a product from the American market. Lenovo, Micron Technology, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Super Micro Computer were named as respondents. Netlist is seeking a limited exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders over the alleged infringement. Micron, Hewlett Packard, Lenovo and Super Micro did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday. The US bill, proposed by congressmen Frank Pallone and Brett Guthrie, also seeks to “streamline the process for barring” products and “clarify the method for determining what is considered malicious technology or equipment”. In addition, it would require the Covered List to be updated at least once every six months, replacing the current stipulation of “periodically update’’. Dai Menghao, a partner at the Shanghai and Beijing offices of law firm King & Wood who specialises in export controls and sanctions, said the proposed legislation was to make enforcement of the FCC Covered List more systematic and targeted. He said the timing of the bipartisan proposal carried symbolic significance, coming ahead of the US midterm elections in November. The bill also comes as US President Donald Trump hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping, with trade and technology tensions forming part of the broader backdrop to the meeting. The proposal came less than two weeks after the FCC finalised updates to its equipment authorisation rules, tightening restrictions on devices containing certain hardware components made by entities on the Covered List, but stopped short of targeting optical transceivers. The decision eased market concerns after Reuters reported in August that Washington was considering measures to block new Chinese optical-transceiver models. The bill, however, could potentially bring those products back into focus. Optical transceivers, which use photonic technology to convert electrical and optical signals, are widely used in data centres. Under US Commerce Department regulations referenced in the bill, ICTS covers products intended for the processing, storage, retrieval or communication of information or data through electronic means, including photonic technologies. A broader definition, however, would not automatically subject all Chinese-made ICTS products to restrictions. Equipment or services would still need to be supplied by an entity controlled by a US-designated “foreign adversary”, a category that includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. Huawei Technologies, ZTE, Hikvision, Dahua Technology and Hytera were among the first Chinese companies placed on the Covered List when it was launched in 2021.

title: How Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan is a symbol of China’s fashion soft power
description: Peng once again shows off exclusively Chinese designs as she accompanies President Xi Jinping on Washington visit.
content: Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan has long been a symbol of China’s fashion soft power at high-profile global summits as she accompanies President Xi Jinping. She has eschewed Western luxury labels and logos in favour of chic local brands and modern Chinese styles – a well-tailored qipao, say, or elegant scarves and coats in formal yet feminine colours. Case in point: the outfit she wore as she stepped off the plane for the much-anticipated Xi-Trump meeting in the US on September 23. Her grey dress, cinched at the waist, with a Chinese collar and small qipao-like slits on the long skirt, was paired with a pale pink scarf. A similar theme emerged on September 24 at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art; Peng’s diplomatic wardrobe spoke in a controlled tone, perhaps befitting of a famed soprano. Beside American first lady Melania Trump’s black tweed jacket and skirt from Alexander McQueen, Peng wore a navy qipao-inspired dress traced in crisp white piping at the high Mandarin collar and cuffs – an architectural contrast that sharpened the silhouette. A silver floral brooch sat near the collar; pearl earrings quietly echoed the white trim. There was an insistent precision to the look: covered buttons, a nearly imperceptible belt at the waist, black stilettos lending lift and formality. Peng’s clothes, even at their most ceremonial, tend to make their point through detail and proportion rather than great spectacle. The museum visit occurred while Xi Jinping and Donald Trump held private White House talks, a parallel programme intended to foreground cultural exchange amid the summit’s higher-stakes agenda. For the State Dinner, however, Peng allowed herself one unmistakable declaration: red. Her floor-length gown, in China red, in the fullest sense, was cut with an open Mandarin collar, long sleeves flared at the elbow and a skirt that broadened at the hip before falling cleanly to the floor. She paired this with pearls and a black clutch with a gold embroidered floral motif. In a picture otherwise dominated by black and white – Xi in a dark Chinese-style suit, Trump in a classic tuxedo, Melania in an exaggerated white bow Saint Laurent blouse and Dolce & Gabbana high-waisted black cigarette trousers – Peng’s dress had the force of punctuation and power. Red may signal luck, happiness and prosperity in Chinese culture, but it is also inevitably the colour most imbued with national meaning. Peng is known to prefer Chinese designers, with Ma Ke being the name most associated with China’s first lady. The Jilin province-born designer told the media in 2014 that when she designed for Peng, she did not go out of her way to highlight anything in particular, only to express the wearer’s inner confidence. “That is also my understanding of the quality and spirit of the Chinese people – there’s no need to please others, or to be ostentatious,” Ma said. “It is a kind of reserved elegance.” Most of Peng’s outfits and accessories remain logo-less. Even when she wears a specific designer, no Chinese brand would dare openly use her name for its own marketing purposes – a system very different from how American, British and French first ladies regularly endorse a variety of luxury brands, preferably from their own country’s fashion industry. Peng prefers a more understated approach to her fashion brand choices, but the effect is no less powerful for China’s home-grown brands. Her early embrace of structured silhouettes and modernised Chinese styles, such as the mandarin collar, was a precursor to the current Neo-Chinese Gen Z fashion trend that has swept over the mainland and beyond in the past three years. A former singer and military personnel, Peng is noted as being the first Chinese first lady in the Communist Party to project a glossy, well-dressed image on the global arena. Peng’s stylistic impact can be felt throughout China. The fact that it has even landed her on Vanity Fair’s Best Dressed List in 2013 is something that the Chinese are immensely proud of. Additional reporting by Kevin Kwong

title: Chinese retail chain faces rare backlash for limiting new hires to 4-year contracts
description: Critics brand policy ridiculous, calling it an excuse to exploit young talent and dump them as they grow experienced, harder to control.
content: Retail tycoon Yu Donglai, widely known as China’s “most conscientious” boss, recently triggered public controversy with a proposal to sign only a four-year “training initiative” contract with future new hires, without renewing it. Yu has been nationally acclaimed for the many unconventionally humanistic rules he set up for Pangdonglai, a supermarket chain he founded in central China’s Henan province in 1995. Yu, for example, once said his 8,000 employees’ after-tax monthly salaries average 9,000 yuan (US$1,350), higher than the province’s average. The company offers 30 days of paid leave plus 10 days of paid “unhappy leave” for those feeling emotionally unwell. Despite having branches in only two cities, Xinxiang and Xuchang in Henan, Pangdonglai has become a pilgrimage site for entrepreneurs and ordinary tourists alike. When Pangdonglai made 900 new jobs available last year, over 130,000 people signed up in the system and 83,000 applied within the first 45 minutes. The applicants’ enthusiasm even crashed the system. Applying for a job at Pangdonglai is even likened to sitting the civil service exam in China, which is largely considered a steady, benefit-rich job amid the economic downturn. Some even sold targeted training courses to Pangdonglai’s job applicants, priced at thousands of yuan (hundreds of US dollars). Thus, when Yu announced the four-year contract proposal for new hires on his personal social media account @shahuaidanyudonglai, or “silly badass Yu Donglai”, many expressed disappointment. “This is ridiculous. It sounds like an excuse to hire young people and kick them out when they are getting old, experienced, and hard to control,” an online observer commented. “People receive a diploma after studying four years at a college. What can they get from working four years at Pangdonglai?” questioned another. Some also pointed to the harsh job market, especially for applicants in their 30s and 40s. “Many would be in their 30s, childless or unmarried, which means it is even harder for them to find a new job,” another said. Yu explained that the proposal is meant to be a training programme that brings talents who have mastered working skills learned at Pangdonglai – and who understand a “scientific, civilised lifestyle” – to society. To this intention, one person replied: “Boss Yu, I understand your idea of making our society a better place with the staff you trained, but even the best seeds cannot blossom in bad soil. The only way to realise your ideal is to train millions of you.” Most comments debate Yu’s proposal peacefully, recognising his goodwill despite disagreeing with him. A staff member with Pangdonglai told the SCMP that the rule is not official, as it is not published on the company’s official account. Previously, Yu was also mired in controversy when he announced plans to prohibit bride prices and lavish weddings for his employees, and to punish those who failed to adhere by cancelling their company benefits. Yu later apologised and, instead of punishment, opted for a milder approach of awarding those who gave up bride prices and extravagant weddings. Some guessed that Yu uses his personal social media account as a testing ground for his ideas, which may not necessarily materialise.

title: US tenor Christopher Macchio booked for Xi-Trump state dinner performance
description: The vocalist has been a feature at a series of the president’s events, most recently at the Republican Midterm Convention.
content: American tenor Christopher Macchio will perform at the White House banquet for Chinese President Xi Jinping during his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade. “An honour to return to Washington DC to perform for the State Dinner with Donald Trump (originally @realDonaldTrump) and President Xi,” Macchio said on social media, tagging the official accounts of Trump, the White House, and the Trump campaign. Often referred to as “America’s Tenor”, Macchio is a classical-crossover vocalist who has sung at Trump rallies and events since filling in at the Mar-a-Lago New Year’s Eve gala in 2015. His announcement was posted shortly after Xi’s arrival at Joint Base Andrews for a three-day state visit, reciprocating Trump’s trip to Beijing in May. Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan were greeted on the tarmac by Trump and his wife Melania with a lavish welcome that featured a 21-gun salute, a red carpet, an honour cordon, and a flyover by two B-1 Lancer bombers. Xi and Peng will attend a state dinner hosted by the US presidential couple at the White House on Thursday, local time, alongside American guests that reportedly include tech executives Elon Musk, Jensen Huang and Jeff Bezos. Macchio, 48, was born and raised in New York. In addition to his performance at the Mar-a-Lago New Year’s Eve gala, Macchio was invited to sing at the funeral of Trump’s brother, Robert, who was also a fan of his music and died in 2020. He performed at the first-ever Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas two weeks ago and at the Freedom 250 rally in Washington in June. He also sang the US national anthem at Trump’s second inauguration in 2025. Trump has repeatedly praised Macchio publicly, calling him one of the greatest opera singers with an “unbelievable, magnificent” voice, and comparing him to late Italian tenor Luciano Pavarotti. Macchio also sang at rallies at Madison Square Garden and in Butler, Pennsylvania, in October 2024. He performed after Trump’s speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention. During Xi’s last official visit to Washington in 2015, Grammy Award-winning R&B artist Ne-Yo provided the musical entertainment for the state dinner.

title: Sri Lanka’s opposition protests against contentious judicial reforms
description: Opposition leader Sajith Premadasa says the legislation proposed will ‘annihilate’ judicial independence.
content: Sri Lanka’s main opposition took to the streets on Thursday to protest against judicial reforms, including raising the retirement age for judges, that the government says are needed to reduce legal delays. Opposition leader Sajith Premadasa told thousands of supporters outside parliament that the legislation proposed by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s left-wing administration would “annihilate” judicial independence. The government unveiled two bills last month to increase the number of courthouses, create new appellate courts outside the capital, raise the retirement age of all judges by two years and recruit additional magistrates and staff. Increasing the mandatory retirement age of superior court judges requires a constitutional amendment, which can be passed by a two-thirds parliamentary majority that Dissanayake’s government enjoys. A vote has been scheduled for Friday after two days of debate. “The 22nd Constitutional Amendment is being executed to destroy democracy in our country and completely annihilate the independence and freedom of the judiciary,” Premadasa said. He added that he was joining other opposition parties in seeking to defeat the constitutional amendment “in the minds of the people”, even if they did not have the votes in parliament to achieve it in practice. The government has argued that the reforms are necessary to clear a backlog of 1.1 million cases. Criminal proceedings usually take more than 17 years, while civil cases can take generations to conclude. Sri Lanka’s influential Bar Association has also opposed the constitutional amendment, calling it an attempt to prolong the tenure of Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena. Surasena, 64, is due to retire in November unless his term is extended under the 22nd Amendment. Dissanayake told the association last month that he planned to recruit 10,000 police constables, hundreds of forensic staff and court clerks in a bid to speed up the criminal justice system. “This is part of a much broader process,” Dissanayake said. “It forms part of an approach that looks at the entire process, beginning with investigations and continuing through the judicial process.” Several opposition parties have accused Surasena, who was elevated to chief justice last year, of being biased in favour of the government. Dissanayake’s administration denies the claim, as well as accusations that it seeks to influence the judiciary, saying that the changes are needed to improve efficiency and reduce delays. The judicial overhaul comes as authorities intensify corruption investigations involving former president Mahinda Rajapaksa and members of his family. They deny any wrongdoing.

title: First lady Peng Liyuan’s English takes the spotlight in exchange with Melania Trump
description: Video of Chinese and US first ladies goes viral as education experts debate the importance of English for students.
content: China’s first lady Peng Liyuan has sparked online buzz over her English-language exchanges with the US first lady without an interpreter during her visit to Washington with President Xi Jinping this week. On Wednesday, US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and Peng at Joint Base Andrews in a rare diplomatic move. After Xi and Peng stepped off the plane, the two couples spoke with the help of interpreters. But as they walked along the red carpet, Peng and Melania appeared to chat directly behind the two presidents. The pair smiled and spoke to each other until they reached the cameras for the start of the welcoming ceremony. Peng appeared to ask about Barron Trump, Donald Trump’s youngest son and Melania’s only child, according to professional lip-reader Nicola Hickling who was quoted in a US tabloid. Peng then raised a hand towards her forehead in an apparent gesture about his height. After their countries’ national anthems were played, Peng and Melania had another brief exchange. Peng appeared to mouth the word “wonderful” as the pair continued chatting without an interpreter for nearly a minute. The White House said the two would visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday after the state arrival ceremony. They are scheduled to attend a state dinner with their husbands that evening. Peng, a renowned soprano who performed with the People’s Liberation Army, travelled internationally to promote Chinese music and culture. Since Xi took office in 2013, she has accompanied him on numerous overseas visits and has taken part in public welfare campaigns. Unlike the wives of many previous Chinese leaders, Peng has maintained a relatively visible public profile. She is called “Mama Peng” by Chinese internet users. Her English-language experience stretches back years. In 2015, she delivered a speech in English at a United Nations event in New York, speaking about girls’ education and gender equality. “Education is about women and girls,” she said. “It is important for girls to go to school because they will become their children’s first teacher some day.” Videos of the speech resurfaced on social media after her exchange with Melania. “This is a video from 2015, and someone of Peng Liyuan’s level naturally has an English teacher, so her English must be even better now,” one post reads, pointing to her seemingly fluent conversation with Melania, who is also not a native English speaker. “Notice how attentive and polite Madam Peng Liyuan was, waiting for Melania, turning and smiling, saying something to break the ice,” reads another. While Peng’s latest exchange with Melania offered a public reminder that English remains a useful tool on the international stage, China is again debating the role of English in its education system. This month, an internet-famous maths teacher Tang Jiafeng called for English to be stripped of its status as a core school subject. He argued that Chinese children were being pushed to learn English before mastering their native language. Former Global Times editor-in-chief Hu Xijin, however, argued that foreign-language skills remained important in a globalised world. He said English could broaden people’s opportunities to take part in international exchanges. The debate is not new. Although English remains one of the major subjects in China’s school system alongside Chinese and maths, policymakers in recent years have explored ways to reduce its importance in some areas.

title: What a 2-month trade-truce extension between China and the US reveals as rifts persist
description: Analysts say that the relatively short window, while a positive sign, could also raise pressure on both Beijing and Washington.
content: An extension of the US-China trade truce, agreed upon at an unscheduled meeting between the two countries’ top economic officials, underscores a willingness to contain trade tensions, according to analysts who deemed it a positive signal for this week’s presidential summit. While the rollover extends the truce by only two months, the analysts said it provided businesses with a measure of short-term certainty while raising the stakes for the next round of talks to determine whether the truce can be sustained. Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held the unscheduled meeting in Washington on Wednesday ahead of a sit-down between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. Afterwards, the two sides agreed to extend the trade truce – reached in October in Busan, South Korea – pushing the deadline from November 2026 to January, Bessent told Fox News. Zhu Tian, an economics professor and vice-president at the China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, said the extension was still an encouraging sign for the numerous businesses with a stake in China-US trade. “The latest trade-war-truce extension, though just two months, is indicative of mutual hope to manage and solve differences through negotiation,” Zhu said. “The positive effect for China’s economy and exporters cannot be understated.” John Quelch, executive vice-chancellor at Duke Kunshan University in China, said the outcome was largely meant to “establish greater predictability” and reduce the risk of escalation. “It should be viewed primarily as a continuation of the economic-stabilisation process rather than as evidence that the underlying differences between the two countries have been resolved,” Quelch said. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis, also warned that the window for “constructive, strategic stability” was narrowing and the stakes were rising. “Instead of having a one-year renewal of the truce since [the Xi-Trump meeting in] Busan, now we only have two months, which means the November meeting at the Apec summit [of economic leaders in Shenzhen] is increasingly relevant to determine whether this strategic stability is going to continue further into 2027,” Garcia-Herrero said. The truce reached in Busan in October helped avert a crisis triggered by Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year. The two sides agreed in October to lower US tariffs on some Chinese goods; pause additional US restrictions and certain Chinese rare earth export controls; and secure Chinese commitments on US soybeans and fentanyl precursors. Bessent told Fox News that the Chinese side had proposed a “bigger deal” during Wednesday’s meeting, but that a shorter extension would give Washington time to assess whether Beijing was meeting its commitments. Zhu, meanwhile, noted differences in what Beijing and Washington were prioritising in managing their economic relationship. “China, of course, is more inclined to interpret it as a long-term, overarching framework, while the priority for the Trump administration is concrete, implementable business deals and tangible benefits for the US,” Zhu said. “These approaches need not be fundamentally contradictory.” He added that Washington may also have, to some extent, agreed to Beijing’s demand for a more strategically stable relationship, noting that White House communications following Trump’s China trip in May referred to a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”. China has the upper hand here, signalling to the market that the US is depending on China’s will Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis Attention now turns to Thursday’s meeting between the two leaders. Garcia-Herrero said China may be in a relatively “stronger position” when Xi sits down with Trump in the Oval Office, and she pointed to “inflationary pressures in the US” that could limit Washington’s appetite for further tariff increases. “China has the upper hand here, signalling to the market that the US is depending on China’s will,” she said. “And therefore, I think exporters firmly believe that the US cannot come up with new tariffs after January.” Research from the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE), published in early August, found that years of US tariffs had done more to shift the routes through which Chinese goods reach the US than to reduce underlying US dependence on Chinese production. China’s share of US imports fell from about 18 per cent in 2017 – before Trump’s first trade war with China began in early 2018 – to 11.2 per cent in 2024, PIIE’s findings showed. But the share of the value added embodied in those US imports – meaning the economic worth – declined by only 2.3 percentage points, from 17.7 per cent to 15.4 per cent, according to the research. Garcia-Herrero added that a US-China Board of Investment was at stake, more so than the Board of Trade. Following Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, both sides agreed to establish the Board of Trade to manage bilateral trade in non-sensitive goods, and a Board of Investment to discuss investment-related issues, though the latter has yet to get off the ground. “It’s quite clear that the US is not ready to open [its market for Chinese investments],” Garcia-Herrero said. “Otherwise, China would have sent its companies to [accompany Xi]. This means that the US was not willing to announce an opening of the US market.” Additional reporting by Sherry Wang

title: Hong Kong authorities won’t appeal court halt to 12,000-flat project on golf course
description: Court earlier revoked project’s environmental approval, with authorities opting not to appeal ‘holistically’ considering legal advice.
content: Plans to build 12,000 public flats on part of Hong Kong’s oldest golf course have been thrown into serious doubt after the government chose not to appeal a court’s decision to uphold a ruling revoking the project’s environmental approval. Authorities said on Thursday that they had decided against appealing after “holistically” considering legal advice following the Court of Appeal’s decision to uphold the overturning of conditional approval for the construction of 12,000 flats on part of the golf course in Fanling. The latest development has prompted some concern groups to suspect that the government will drop the housing plan, leading them to urge the government to clarify the site’s future use as soon as possible. In a judgment delivered earlier, the court found that the official endorsement of the project’s environmental impact assessment (EIA) report was marred by an unfair public consultation process, the imposition of improper conditions and a failure to meet wildlife conservation objectives. The ruling is likely to result in fresh public consultations over the development of the 9.5 hectares (23.5 acres) of land set aside for the project, which was initially slated for completion in 2029. The plot was among the 32 hectares that the government had taken back from the 172-hectare golf course three years ago. “Having holistically considered legal advice and conducted a cautious assessment, the government has decided not to appeal against the judgment,” a government spokesman said. He added that the judgment had clarified some important legal principles under Hong Kong’s EIA process. The clarifications included that authorities had to consider the nature of a case before deciding whether new information that updated the report should be mentioned in a follow-up consultation. In 2024, the Court of First Instance ruled that the government had failed to consult the public again when civil engineering authorities provided additional information regarding the development’s ecological impact, which formed part of the report. The judgment also said that, based on the principle of fairness, it was necessary to conduct a further but limited public consultation on the additional information. Authorities said on Thursday that the Environmental Protection Department would make sure to follow these guidelines to keep future approvals fair, legal and transparent. The Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance originally required a report for urban developments covering more than 20 hectares or involving a population exceeding 100,000. That definition was revised in June 2023 to cover projects of at least 50 hectares. The Leisure and Cultural Services Department currently manages the 32 hectares of land from the golf course that was returned to the government in September 2023. The government has continued to make the land available to the club during international tournaments. Authorities added that they would reassess the proposed public housing plan and announce their next steps at an appropriate time. The Hong Kong Golf Club, which manages the remaining 140-hectare course, won a judicial review in late 2024 to quash the director of environmental protection’s approval of the study conducted by the Civil Engineering and Development Department. The club said on Thursday that it respected the decision by authorities and would continue to align with government policy. It also expressed hopes of promoting Hong Kong as a centre for major international sports events. Chan Kim-ching, founder of the Liber Research Community, an NGO focused on land and development policy, said the government’s plan to build public housing on the golf course had effectively collapsed, ending an effort that began about eight years ago. He added that the housing plan was once backed by strong public consensus, but the development had been derailed after authorities decided not to appeal the ruling on the project’s EIA report. Chan stated that the government should continue its current approach of keeping the site for public use and making it available for major international sporting tournaments when needed. He also urged authorities to devise a backup plan to offset any shortfall arising from the potential scrapping of the plan to build 12,000 public flats. Former lawmaker Michael Tien Puk-sun called for the government to act swiftly and convert the whole site into a public golf course. Anthony Chiu Kwok-wai, executive director of the Federation of Public Housing Estates, said the economy could still benefit if the government dropped the project, as the land supply was less constrained than previously and the site could be used for hosting major international events on a flexible basis.

title: Traditional wind instruments from both East and West blow up a storm in Hong Kong concert
description: Wind instruments from China, Japan, Laos and beyond joined the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra to close the International Sheng and Reeds Festival 2026.
content: Comprising 100 performers, led by conductor Yan Huichang, “Thousand Reeds, One Universe” was both the beginning and the end. The concert on September 20 was the conclusion of the International Sheng and Reeds Festival 2026 and a successful commencement of the 2026/27 season of the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra (HKCO). Continuing the vision of the festival to forge a borderless world in harmony, the concert brought together a family of reed instruments from around China and the world, including the Chinese sheng – a mouth-blown wind instrument made of vertical bamboo pipes – the lusheng of the Miao minority group, the Japanese sho, the Lao khaen (also played in northeast Thailand) and the Western pipe organ, thus demonstrating a music heritage of humanity. A few soloists appeared in traditional attire, ranging from the Miao costume to the Japanese Heian garments, offering a rich visual feast that mirrored the sonic diversity on stage. The concert began with the premiere of Equilibrium and Legacy, an overture commissioned by the HKCO and written by Chew Hee Chiat. The piece attempts to resurrect the profundity and solemnity of Chinese court ritual music, in which the clanging bronze bells and stone chimes play a central part. Weaving these instruments together with a massive sheng ensemble and the Chinese orchestra, the overture’s prelude presented a grand texture, leading the audience through a dense, mysterious mist into the primordial past. This then gave way to the very different sound of a qin solo, which was heard coming through the loudspeakers with artificial reverb. The amplification of the soft and delicate seven-string zither – usually associated with the edified and contemplative mind – was an unexpectedly overt technological intervention. Following the grand conclusion of the overture was a piece written by Yang Zhengping and newly arranged by Ngai Kwun-wa. Titled Love Song from the Countryside, the piece is written for the lusheng and the Chinese orchestra. The lively and energetic rhythm delivered by the orchestra and soloist Yang gave an impression of a rapturous and frenetic dance, perhaps during a harvest festival. Providing a fitting shift in mood, the subsequent work, Silken Fragments of Plum Blossom, is a sheng concerto written by Liu Ruixin. The piece eloquently and poetically evoked the beauty, poignancy and evanescence of scattering plum petals through the diverse timbres and textures exquisitely executed by the orchestra and the sheng soloist Liu Chang. The first half of the concert concluded with another shift in mood. Showcasing different sheng techniques with a virtuosic solo passage, “Touei – Lake and Joy” is the third movement of the sheng concerto Yi Jing (2015), which was adapted from the Western orchestral piece Changes (2003), written by German composer Enjott Schneider. The second half of the concert opened with the world premiere of “One Breath. One World”, written by Chan Ming-chi. Commissioned by the HKCO, the piece puts the Siberian jaw harp, the sho and the khaen into a euphonious dialogue while preserving the idioms of the respective instruments, impeccably embodying the Chinese saying “harmony without uniformity”. Sounds as contrasting as the vocal mimicry of a horse neighing and the solemn tones of the Japanese court, evoked by the sho, are all put together in the same piece. The thoughtful arrangement unites these seemingly disparate sounds harmoniously. What truly transformed the concert hall into a harmonious universe was perhaps the engagement of the audience, which turned the performance from a one-way message into reciprocal communication. The ensuing piece, “Reeds”, written by Wang I-yu, extended the trans-Asian dialogue to Europe by incorporating the Western pipe organ. Finally, with Ng Cheuk-yin’s “Thousand Reeds in Harmony”, which showcased a wide variety of sheng accompanied by the players’ lively dance, the concert came to a spectacular conclusion. “Thousand Reeds, One Universe”, opening concert of the 50th Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra season, Hong Kong Cultural Centre Concert Hall. Reviewed: September 20.

title: 8 killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine, maternity clinic damaged
description: Moscow has stepped up its air ‌war in recent months, deploying more of its faster and harder-to-stop drones.
content: Russian drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv and its northeast killed eight people on Thursday in attacks that included a maternity hospital and a farm, officials said. Moscow has stepped up its air ‌war in recent months, deploying more of its faster and harder-to-stop drones while Ukraine is short of interceptors to down ballistic missiles. Two people died in the latest assault on Kyiv, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was in New York for the UN General Assembly. “As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky,” Zelensky said on Telegram. “Once again, the main targets of their strike were Kyiv and civilian infrastructure, residential buildings, a ⁠maternity hospital, energy infrastructure and logistics.” Police said nine homes, a post office, warehouses and dozens of cars were also damaged in ‌Kyiv. A separate Russian attack on a vegetable storage facility at a farm in a village of the northeastern Kharkiv region killed six people and injured a further 12, prosecutors said. The overnight ‌barrage around Ukraine included an unspecified number of hypersonic and ballistic missiles, 282 drones and other weapons, Ukraine’s ⁠air force said. In Kyiv, eight people were injured as well as the two fatalities, one of whom was in the car park of the maternity hospital, city ‌mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Part of the hospital’s facade, windows and doors were damaged, officials said, adding that no patients or doctors were injured. Authorities in the ‌northwestern region ‌of Rivne said infrastructure was damaged in overnight strikes that continued into Thursday morning, without providing further details. Volyn region bordering ‌Poland also came under attack. Insufficient pressure on Moscow was allowing it to launch repeated strikes, Zelensky said. “Right now, the ⁠United States has the opportunity to respond strongly,” he said. “We need ballistic interceptors to protect lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said its forces ⁠hit Ukrainian defence facilities, logistics and telecoms centres, as well as vessels used by the military. In the Black Sea port of Odesa, military administration head Serhiy Lysak said overnight Russian strikes damaged a medical facility and shattered ‌windows in nearby houses and ‌a school. Moldova’s President Maia Sandu said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace and at least one exploded, while Romania said a drone also crashed in its territory. Nato alliance member Poland said it deployed aviation twice on Thursday due to Russian attacks on Ukraine.

title: US regulators back multi-cancer blood test – but Hong Kong doctors remain cautious
description: Doctors say more data is needed despite growing interest in detecting multiple cancers from a single blood sample.
content: Efforts to detect multiple cancers through a single blood draw are gathering momentum after US regulators endorsed the technology for the first time, although experts say wider adoption in Hong Kong still faces challenges as doctors remain cautious about its clinical value. In a landmark decision for the emerging field of multi-cancer early detection (MCED) blood tests, a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) panel on Thursday voted in favour of US company Grail’s “Galleri test”, recommending it for premarket approval. MCED tests seek to identify signs of cancer in healthy, asymptomatic individuals by analysing abnormal molecules, including circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), in bodily fluids such as blood and urine. While the technology remains in its early stage, Hong Kong medical institutions are exploring ways to broaden its use. Lucence, a Singapore-based provider of MCED blood tests, has expanded its offerings at Hong Kong’s Gleneagles Hospital with a new programme that allows individuals to screen for cancers specific to their risk profiles, the company said at a joint briefing with the hospital on Wednesday, a day before the FDA move. Gleneagles introduced the original version of the test, known as LucenceInsight, six months ago. The test allows adults to screen for up to 50 types of cancer, including lung, breast and nasopharyngeal cancer. The technology offered advantages including minimal invasiveness and the potential for earlier detection, Gleneagles Hospital CEO Kenneth Tsang said at the briefing. MCED tests could become a “valuable addition to existing screening approaches” by helping improve patient outcomes through early treatment, according to an FDA report published on Wednesday before its official vote on the Galleri test. Wider adoption, however, continues to face challenges as many medical professionals remain sceptical of its efficacy. “Obviously, it’s very attractive, very appealing,” Anne Lee Wing-mui, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society, said on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong on Thursday. “But then we need more information, particularly on the cost-effectiveness side. Is it truly working?” Questions over effectiveness intensified earlier this year. Results from a trial involving 142,000 participants in Britain’s National Health Service showed that the Galleri test failed to meet its primary endpoint of achieving statistically significant reduction in late-stage cancer diagnoses among participants receiving both the test and standard care, compared with those receiving only standard care. The results, published in February, wiped out nearly half of Grail’s market value. Lucence said that its LucenceInsight test has a sensitivity rate of 81 per cent and a specificity rate of 99 per cent – respective measures of a test’s ability to correctly identify people with a disease and those without it. “The biggest problem is actually to convince the doctors. Doctors have been trained to believe in the gold standards,” Gleneagles’ Tsang said. “That’s why the one biggest barrier right now [that] we’re working together on [tackling] is to educate doctors [about] how this will change their practices.”

title: What can Asia, Global South learn from India’s new digital payment fee?
description: The roll-out is a good test of whether the system can generate enough revenue to pay for its own maintenance and expansion, experts say.
content: For millions of Indians, buying a cup of chai or groceries from roadside vendors has come to mean reaching for their phones rather than wallets – a habit made possible by a system that has so far charged consumers nothing for such everyday transactions. Now, a decade after the government launched the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), India is asking some merchants to pay for the hugely popular system – raising questions over whether it can preserve the low-cost model that drove its mass adoption while generating enough revenue to fund its own growth. Under a new framework, a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate – a processing fee merchants pay to banks and payment apps when they accept a digital payment from a customer – will apply to transactions above 2,000 rupees (US$21) starting from October 15. The charge has been capped at 300 rupees. Experts say the roll-out will be crucial in determining whether the system can generate enough revenue to pay for its own maintenance and expansion. Transactions will remain free for consumers, and 96 per cent of merchant transactions by volume will be unaffected, but some groups, including fuel dealers, oppose the move, fearing it could squeeze their margins. UPI has anchored a digital revolution in India, helping bring large sections of the population into a formal economy and becoming a backbone of a digital economy in which electronic payments are increasingly integral to everyday commerce. “The policy direction is economically defensible,” said Vishwanathan Iyer, a finance and accounting professor at Great Lakes Institute of Management in Chennai, highlighting that the payment system is estimated to cost about 200 billion rupees annually. According to government data, annual transaction volume grew 13,000-fold to 241.62 billion in the financial year that ended in March 2026 from 17.8 million in 2016-17, while transaction value skyrocketed 4,000-fold from 70 billion rupees to 3.14 trillion rupees over the same period. World’s largest UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, is the world’s largest retail fast-payment system by transaction volume, according to a 2025 IMF report. The government said in a statement on September 15 that the fee would apply only to “specific merchant transactions”, adding that the sum collected would be distributed among payment ecosystem participants, including banks and application providers, to support operations and continued expansion. Iyer said a predictable revenue stream would give banks and payment companies greater incentive to invest in cybersecurity, fraud detection and dispute resolution – as well as develop the next phase of the system, which would probably involve offering credit lines and expanding cross-border transfers. The weakness of the move is more in the design, he said. There is no fee for transactions below 2,000 rupees, while a 2,002 rupee transaction immediately attracts one – encouraging split payments. “A graduated fee on the amount above the threshold would create fewer distortions. The policy is sound, but its design should be reviewed using transaction-level data,” he said. Business sectors such as fuel dealers have a genuine concern, but the burden for them would effectively be only 0.1 per cent of the transaction, Iyer said. “Dealer resistance could result in a targeted exemption, compensation by oil marketing companies, or an adjustment to dealer commissions. It is unlikely to derail the entire framework because most UPI transactions remain unaffected,” he said. Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director at Delhi-based think tank Indic Researchers Forum, said the UPI system became a global success because “it felt like a public good, not a product”. “If India wants this rail to remain a digital public good rather than another fee-laden card network, the floor should be raised sharply towards 50,000 rupees or the levy should be paused,” he said. It would be counterproductive to years of digitisation if the levy made grocery vendors or petrol stations nudge people off UPI in favour of cash, he said. “Several Asian and Global South systems have studied UPI precisely because it proved you can scale without surrendering the switch to Visa, Mastercard or a foreign boardroom,” he added. Recouping costs Rohit Arora, co-founder and CEO of fintech firm Biz2Credit, highlighted that some cost recovery from merchants was inevitable after so many years of free use. “Capping it and protecting small-ticket, small-merchant transactions is a reasonable way to balance sustainability with UPI’s financial inclusion mandate,” Arora said. The UPI network is currently live in 11 countries, including Singapore, the UAE, France and Nepal, according to a Reuters report this month. Arora said that other countries were unlikely to do a “direct copy-paste” of India’s move. “What they will watch closely is whether India proves a modest merchant fee can coexist with mass adoption, since that’s the template every large real-time payments system eventually has to solve,” he said. Stuti Datanwala, Digital Payments Consultant and a former executive at Visa and National Payments Council of India, which owns and operates UPI, said the purpose of the move was to make the existing payment ecosystem financially sustainable. “Several Asian markets already have merchant charges in some form, so they would not necessarily be introducing them because India has done so,” she said. Indonesia already has a rate structure for its system, depending on merchant category and transaction size. Malaysia’s DuitNow merchant charges depend on the bank or payment provider, with waivers available in some cases. “Merchant discount rates are charged on person-to-merchant payments there, and in many cases they can be significantly higher than what India is proposing for eligible UPI transactions,” she said. The underlying issue for other countries was the same as India’s because building and running a secure payment network cost money, she said. “Countries looking at India’s experience will make their own decisions about how to balance affordability with those costs,” Datanwala said. “Keeping payments free for consumers, while asking eligible merchants to make a modest contribution, is a sensible approach, as long as small businesses are protected and the charges remain reasonable compared with other payment methods.”

title: Meet Woody Harrelson’s wife, Laura Louie, who joined him at the Brothers premiere
description: The couple, who first met during a taping of Harrelson’s hit sitcom Cheers, enjoyed a double date with Matthew McConaughey and his wife Camila Alves at the 2026 US Open.
content: The brand-new Apple TV comedy series Brothers, starring Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey, celebrated its Los Angeles premiere last week in a star-studded affair. The show, in which the two Hollywood stars play fictionalised versions of themselves, riffs on real-life speculation that they may share the same biological father. Harrelson walked the red carpet at the Hammer Museum with his wife, Laura Louie, who is known to be very private, while McConaughey was there with his mother Kay “MaMac” McConaughey, his wife Camila Alves McConaughey, and two of their children, Vida and Levi. Days later, Harrelson and Louie stepped out for the opening night of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles. So, what do we know about Laura Louie, the wife of the 65-year-old Now You See Me star? What is Laura Louie’s background? According to IMDb, Laura Louie was born on February 28, 1965. Little is known about her childhood, family background or education, but Harrelson described her as the “valedictorian of her class” in a 2006 interview with The Guardian. The actor previously told The Hollywood Reporter that they met in 1987, when Louie attended a taping of his hit sitcom Cheers as part of a media workshop organised by the University of California, Los Angeles. She later became his personal assistant. How long have Woody Harrelson and Laura Louie been together? Louie’s relationship with the Hunger Games star remained professional for three years until he confessed his feelings for her through a song, per People. In response, she revealed she had been in love with him for two and a half years already. They hard-launched their relationship in 1995, when Louie joined Harrelson for the premiere of his film Money Train. They wed in Maui in 2008. “I just was incapable of long-term relationships. I was with whoever would have me. Then I met my wife,” Harrelson gushed in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. The actor courted controversy in 2001 after being photographed in bed with three women, but he told the outlet that Louie forgave him. Louie and Harrelson share three daughters: Deni Montana, 32, Zoe Giordano, 30, and Makani Ravello, 20. The family once lived in an eco-village in Maui powered by solar energy, per SF Gate. “At the end of the night, when the lights go out, you just look out at the valley, and the only lights are stars,” Harrelson recalled. She’s an entrepreneur According to People, Louie is passionate about food and cooking, and she combined that passion with her love for the environment into a business. She is the co-founder of organic food delivery company Yoganics, which operated around Texas until 2015. She later launched another business, Yoganics Maui, focusing on wellness through yoga and health-conscious foods. Louie and her husband are also involved with the Voice Yourself web community, through which they support various environmental initiatives.

title: Summits for all diplomatic seasons: how the US has set the stage for Xi Jinping
description: From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Chinese leader’s past meetings reveal the roles of personal rapport and official diplomacy.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US is his first to the country since 2023 and his eighth face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump.
