From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Xi’s meetings across four American administrations show how personal rapport and official diplomacy reflect the growing complexity of US-China relations. Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America. According to then US president Barack Obama, “Our decision to meet so early [in Xi’s term] signifies the importance of the US-China relationship.” Instead of heading to the diplomatic protocol-heavy capital of Washington, Xi’s historic first meeting with Obama took place at the Annenberg Retreat at Sunnylands, a 200-acre (81-hectare) estate in Rancho Mirage, California. Originally built as a winter haven by publishers and philanthropists Walter and Leonore Annenberg – close friends of former US president Dwight Eisenhower – the estate holds a unique place in American history as a secluded sanctuary that has often hosted political heavyweights. Its rare blend of luxury and isolation made Sunnylands an ideal setting for the summit. Without the rigid and pre-scripted constraints of traditional diplomacy, its selection was considered unusual. But some suspicions remained. Xi and his delegation opted to stay at the nearby Hyatt Regency in Indian Wells rather than at Sunnylands, a move many in the American media attributed to concerns about possible US eavesdropping. Over June 7 and 8, Xi and Obama engaged in more than eight hours of dialogue spanning two formal sessions, a private dinner and a morning walk, during which they took a break in the shade on a custom California redwood bench that Obama presented to Xi. During the dinner, Xi reportedly toasted Obama with Moutai, China’s famed high-end liquor. China said the summit established the groundwork for a “new model of major-country relations”. White House officials later said the meetings built a stronger relationship between the two leaders, while yielding progress on important global challenges like cybersecurity, North Korea and greenhouse gas emissions. Xi’s first US state visit: a packed ‘unforgettable journey’ In September 2015, Xi embarked on his first formal state visit to the US. His cross-country itinerary began in Seattle, where he met with senior American officials and business leaders, continued to Washington for formal diplomatic engagements with Obama, and concluded in New York to attend the 70th anniversary summit of the United Nations. Upon their arrival in Washington on September 24, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan were greeted on the tarmac by then US vice-president Joe Biden and his wife Jill Biden. That evening, Obama hosted Xi for a private dinner at Blair House. Located across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, Blair House serves as the US president’s guest house for visiting diplomats and dignitaries. It is also where the US president-elect and first family live before taking the oath of office. The next morning, official protocol commenced on the White House South Lawn with a full military arrival ceremony, featuring a traditional 21-gun salute. Following a joint press conference, Xi attended a diplomatic lunch hosted in the US State Department’s Benjamin Franklin State Dining Room. The diplomatic high point came that evening with a lavish state dinner in the White House East Room. The guest list gathered about 200 prominent figures from Hollywood, Silicon Valley, international diplomacy and corporate leadership. The menu, created by Chinese-American Anita Lo, highlighted American cuisine accented with Chinese nuances. Guests were served wild mushroom soup, poached Maine lobster, grilled cannon of Colorado lamb and a poppy seed bread-and-butter pudding. During the toasts, Obama acknowledged lingering strategic differences while expressing hope that the two countries’ peoples would “work together like fingers on the same hand in friendship and in peace”. Xi described the visit as an “unforgettable journey”, noting the warmth he encountered from the west coast to the east. Following the state dinner, American R&B artist Ne-Yo delivered a performance of his hit “Because of You”, drawing applause across the room. Mar-a-Lago summit: ‘family-style’ diplomacy In April 2017, Xi met with Donald Trump, early in his first presidential term, at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, as both countries sought to steady a relationship frayed by months of friction. Trump had spent his presidential campaign repeatedly hammering Beijing over trade practices and had further unsettled mainland Chinese leadership by accepting a congratulatory phone call from then Taiwanese leader Tsai Ing-wen, marking a sharp departure from decades of diplomatic precedent set in 1979. The choice of Mar-a-Lago over a rigid White House visit was designed to create an informal backdrop for the two leaders to build personal rapport, echoing Xi’s 2013 Sunnylands summit with Obama. As with the 2013 visit, Xi and the Chinese delegation did not stay on the grounds of the meeting venue. Instead, they checked in at the nearby Eau Palm Beach Resort & Spa. The summit emphasised personal, family-centric diplomacy. Trump and his wife Melania Trump hosted Xi and Peng for a welcome dinner featuring pan-seared Dover sole, New York strip steak and Sonoma Chardonnay. A stand-out moment of soft diplomacy came when Trump’s granddaughter, Arabella Kushner, who learned Mandarin from a Chinese nanny, sang the traditional folk song “Jasmine Flower” and recited classical Chinese poetry for the visiting couple. However, the relaxed atmosphere was soon eclipsed by hard-power dynamics. Over chocolate cake for dessert, Trump informed Xi that the US had just launched missiles against a Syrian airbase in retaliation for a chemical weapons attack. Trump later claimed Xi understood the move, but analysts said that Beijing rarely welcomed such unscripted surprises. Filoli Estate summit: nostalgia to thaw a deep freeze? In November 2023, Xi travelled to San Francisco to attend the 30th Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) economic leaders’ meeting and hold a summit with then US president Joe Biden. While Xi stayed at the St Regis Hotel near downtown San Francisco, the retreat itself was staged 48km (30 miles) south at the historic Filoli Estate, a secluded country house. The summit came at a critical inflection point. Relations had plummeted to their lowest point in decades after Beijing severed high-level military contacts following then-US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in August 2022. Tensions spiralled further in February 2023 when the US shot down a suspected Chinese surveillance balloon off the US east coast. Against this backdrop, carefully choreographed personal optics were deployed to lower the temperature. As Xi arrived at Filoli, Biden greeted him. Later, Biden pulled out a phone to show the Chinese leader a photograph of a young Xi posing in front of the Golden Gate Bridge during a 1985 trip as a county-level official. “Do you know this young man?” Biden asked. “I know,” Xi replied with a smile. “It’s me 38 years ago.” “You haven’t changed a bit,” Biden quipped, drawing laughter from the crowd of staff and fellow officials. Following a four-hour working session and lunch, the two leaders took a short walk together through the garden grounds. Yet, tensions resurfaced shortly after the retreat concluded. At a solo press conference, Biden repeated his view that Xi was effectively a dictator in the sense that “he’s a guy who runs a country that is a communist country that’s based on a form of government totally different than ours”. The comment was captured alongside video of then-US secretary of state Antony Blinken visibly wincing in the audience, a moment that went viral worldwide.

title: Alibaba unveils ‘pragmatic’ AI road map to drive monetisation, infrastructure efficiency
description: Current investor sentiment has shifted from enthusiasm for AI catalysts to the need for tangible returns and infrastructure efficiency.
content: The artificial intelligence road map presented at its flagship Apsara Conference this week showcased a pragmatic pivot by Chinese tech giant Alibaba Group Holding, offering a clearer path to monetisation despite a sharp escalation in capital expenditure, analysts said. The conference, which ran from Tuesday to Thursday under the theme “Intelligence goes beyond”, highlighted “Alibaba’s disciplined execution across its full-stack AI ecosystem”, said Cathy Chan, an analyst at CCB International. She pointed out that current investor sentiment had shifted from last year’s enthusiasm for AI catalysts to the need for tangible returns and infrastructure efficiency. Alibaba’s pitch of treating AI tokens as a utility, using proprietary chips and cloud architecture to reduce inference costs, and releasing open-source model weights to retain developers in its ecosystem, was tailored directly to that more “pragmatic” mood, Chan noted. Speaking on Tuesday, Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu Yongming laid out three cornerstones of the firm’s push into what he called the “machine intelligence” era: AI models, chips and cloud infrastructure. Aligning with Wu’s vision, Alibaba introduced the Zhenwu V900, billed as “China’s most powerful AI processor”, alongside its coming Yitian 720 and 730 server central processing units due in 2027, as well as a matching Panjiu supernode server able to scale up to a 500,000-chip single cluster. The company also teased larger future AI systems with 5 trillion to 10 trillion parameters, alongside upgrades to its multimodal models, capable of processing and generating more than just text. To power internal and external AI models, Alibaba Cloud said it aimed to operate more than 20 gigawatts (GW) of global data centre capacity by 2032. “Alibaba continues to expand across both enterprise and consumer markets … potentially opening up further opportunities to monetise AI applications,” Citic Securities analyst Liao Yuan wrote in a note. At the application layer, Alibaba showcased Qwen Intelligence, an agentic solution for smartphone makers building agents that can act across apps, Model-as-a-Service platforms Bailian and Qwencloud, productivity tool QwenWork, and Accio Work for cross-border commerce. It also debuted a slew of new hardware, including the “agentic computer” QwenBook, AI glasses, earbuds and a note-taking device. Following the 20GW target announcement, Alicia Yap, head of Pan-Asia internet research at Citi, raised estimates for Alibaba’s capital expenditure in fiscal 2027, 2028 and 2029 to 258 billion yuan (US$38.5 billion), 283 billion yuan and 282 billion yuan, respectively, representing increases of 13 per cent, 41 per cent and 57 per cent above previous figures. Citic Securities estimates suggest the 20GW target could support roughly US$170 billion in annual external cloud revenue, aligning with Alibaba’s ambition to generate more than US$100 billion in combined external cloud and AI revenue by 2030. Citic’s Liao said the tighter coupling of Alibaba’s models, chips and cloud “strengthened the visibility of growth”. The buildout echoes a wider industry push. Morgan Stanley earlier this month forecast 8.5 trillion yuan of AI infrastructure spending in China between 2026 and 2030 – averaging 17 per cent of total spending by US peers – and expected China’s information technology power capacity to rise from 26GW last year to 81GW by 2030. Alibaba’s semiconductor road map showed the company’s bottleneck had moved beyond chip design, according to Parv Sharma, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research. “Leading-edge nodes, HBM [high-bandwidth memory] supply, and advanced packaging” were now the main constraints, Sharma said. He added that Alibaba was seeking to offset Nvidia’s single-chip advantage through cluster scale, interconnects and tighter integration with its Qwen model and software stack. “The key takeaway is not China overtaking the US, but two separate AI stacks,” Sharma said, adding that Nvidia was benefiting from global supply chains while Alibaba was increasingly dominant at home.

title: China, US hold first AI dialogue amid mounting tech tensions: commerce ministry
description: He Yadong, a spokesman for the commerce ministry, confirmed the completion of the AI dialogue while briefing reporters on Thursday.
content: China and the US held their first dialogue on artificial intelligence, with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent leading the talks for their respective sides, China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday. He Yadong, a spokesman for the commerce ministry, confirmed the completion of the AI dialogue while briefing reporters on the eighth round of US-China trade talks held in New York on Sunday. The dialogue comes as AI technology emerges as a high-stakes battleground between Beijing and Washington, with tensions escalating sharply in recent months. Despite Washington maintaining strict controls on Chinese access to advanced AI chips, US officials have accused the country’s developers of using “distillation” – a widely used technique where a smaller AI model learns from the output of a more advanced one – to replicate the capabilities of leading American systems. Beijing has dismissed the allegations as groundless, warning that it would retaliate if Washington weaponised the claim to stifle the country’s tech sector. In the US, prominent tech CEOs – including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and xAI founder Elon Musk – have publicly called for “pacing” the development of frontier AI, citing concerns that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them. But they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, the latter of whom dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week. China’s commerce ministry said during its regular press conference in Beijing on Thursday that the two sides had held “candid, in-depth and constructive” discussions on economic and trade issues of mutual concern, and had “reached a number of consensuses” during the talks in New York. The ministry’s statement came after He and Bessent held an unscheduled meeting at World Bank headquarters in Washington on Wednesday morning, where the two sides agreed to extend the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea last October. The Chinese side also proposed a “bigger deal” on trade, according to Bessent. Additional reporting by Xinyi Wu

title: Were smart glasses used in Singapore to film 2 female students?
description: The incident comes amid rising concerns about surreptitious filming using such glasses and modified spy cameras in Singapore.
content: Singapore police have launched an investigation after a video of a man allegedly filming female students using smart glasses went viral, sparking concerns about privacy and safety. In the social media video, a man wearing black-rimmed glasses and a face mask is seen walking behind two female students wearing what appear to be uniforms from Raffles Institution, a premier school in the city state. The girls seem unaware of his presence. The man clutches his phone to his chest and presses what looks to be a button. Noticing that he is being filmed, he abruptly makes a U-turn and walks off in the opposite direction. Although Reddit has since removed the original video, which went up on Monday, it has been reposted on other platforms. Those who have commented about the video say the man’s actions look suspicious. Some claim they have seen the man before near the school in Bishan. “He’s still at it?” a social media user said, according to the Asia One news portal. She said she had reported him “back when Meta glasses did not exist” and he was recording girls with his phone, but the police could not take any action as he had the right to be in a public area. A police spokesman told CNA on Wednesday that a report had been lodged and investigations were ongoing. Even before the advent of smart glasses, social media users in Singapore have been warning others about surreptitious filming using spy glasses and modified spy cameras. A woman posted a “public service announcement” in July 2022 about a suspicious man walking around the National University of Singapore campus with his phone held upright against his chest. She said he wore “thick black specs” with no lenses and a camera on the side. In September 2024, a cleaner was sentenced to seven months’ jail for using a modified camera disguised as spectacles to film his female colleagues changing, CNA reported. He was caught after one of the victims noticed a bright red light flashing from a pair of glasses on top of a cupboard. A closer examination revealed that the glass frame held a very small camera whose SD card contained footage of the woman. Smart glasses, such as those introduced by Meta Platforms in 2021, allow wearers to take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls or interact with an AI assistant. Early versions are typically hard to detect as their cameras are very small and do not always come with a recording light. China issued the world’s first industry code of conduct for AI-powered glasses in January. The voluntary code calls on smart eyewear manufacturers to adopt a “minimum data collection” approach, provide clear indicators when cameras or microphones are active and obtain explicit user consent before recording. In May, lawmaker Gerald Giam asked in Singapore’s parliament whether the Ministry for Digital Development and Information would introduce regulations mandating visual indicators for smart glasses and was taking any measures to prevent personal data from being recorded in public spaces. The ministry replied that there were laws in place and any recording “is subject to the same rules and principles regardless of the form factor of the device”. “Individuals should note that non-consensual recording, sharing or other misuse of intimate or private content may constitute criminal offences under existing laws, including the Penal Code and the Protection from Harassment Act,” it said. “Under the Online Safety [Relief and Accountability] Act, creators of online content may also be held accountable for harms caused to victims.” Companies such as Meta are adapting their products in response to concerns about privacy violations from tiny cameras on glasses and other wearables – dubbed “pervert” glasses by critics. On Wednesday, Meta launched an audio-only, camera-free version of its smart glasses. Its other models retain the camera functions but come with a more noticeable indicator light. Building in privacy features such as a recording indicator light was “really important”, Meta’s vice-president of AI product, Vishal Shah, told Agence France-Presse. “We wanted people to clearly understand that this was something that was recording, and we’ve only made that light more explicit over time.”

title: China’s humanoid robot IPO slowdown no threat to firms with ‘genuine strength’: Deloitte
description: The market is shifting from a ‘blind rush’ to ‘fine screening’, but funding is still there for firms with clear strategies, Deloitte China says.
content: Beijing’s recent tightening of approvals for humanoid robot makers seeking initial public offerings (IPOs) poses no threat to companies with clear commercialisation strategies, as funding channels remain wide open for qualified players, according to Deloitte China. “Market funds are shifting from the ‘blind rush’ of the past to ‘fine screening’,” said Dick Kay, Deloitte China’s capital market services group national leader, at a press conference on Thursday. Investors and regulators now placed more weight on whether companies had sustainable revenue growth, core technological barriers and real-world application scenarios, he added. Chinese regulators have heightened scrutiny of humanoid robot start-ups seeking IPOs on mainland stock exchanges amid concerns over excessive market hype, according to media reports. The shift came after robot maker Unitree Robotics saw its shares slump 55 per cent from their peak – wiping well over US$30 billion off the company’s value – less than a month after its blockbuster IPO on the tech-heavy Star Market in August. Six mega IPOs by artificial intelligence and robotics firms were launched on mainland Chinese markets during the first three quarters of 2026, and a wave of other hi-tech firms is reportedly pushing to go public. More than 500 companies have applied to list in Hong Kong, with the total estimated to exceed 600 once confidential listings are taken into account, according to Edward Au Chung-hing, Deloitte China’s southern region managing partner. But Kay stressed that for companies with “genuine strength and a clear commercialisation path, capital market financing channels remain open”. Au emphasised that Hong Kong’s growth momentum would stay robust, fuelled by a strong pipeline of mega listings, policy incentives for dual mainland and Hong Kong listings, and massive fundraising demand from mainland enterprises. Liquidity still exists, but volatility could arise if US rate hikes exceed expectations Edward Au Chung-hing, Deloitte China Deloitte has raised its full-year 2026 IPO fundraising forecast for Hong Kong to HK$480 billion – a record high and a 60 per cent jump from its June estimate of HK$300 billion. Au said that despite valuation swings in AI shares this year, valuations of AI companies – beyond chips and large-language models – had risen and come in higher than expected. With optimistic market views on AI valuations and a strong new listing pipeline in Hong Kong, Deloitte’s fundraising projection could even be exceeded, he added. Hong Kong might see three to four mega listings in the fourth quarter, each raising HK$10 billion or more, according to Au. Still, this would depend on the pace of large listings and market windows, and investors should watch out for US interest rate increases and potential black swan events, he cautioned. The US’ Nasdaq leads the world in terms of IPO fundraising so far this year, with the equivalent of HK$1.1 trillion (US$140 billion) raised as of the end of September, according to Deloitte estimates. Hong Kong ranks second with HK$387.9 billion raised, followed by the New York Stock Exchange on HK$163.2 billion. When asked about whether Hong Kong has sufficient liquidity, Au said Alibaba Group Holding and Z.ai recently raised large amounts of capital, showing Hong Kong could absorb the wave of AI financing. “Liquidity still exists, but volatility could arise if US rate hikes exceed expectations,” he noted. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Philippines pardons death row inmate repatriated from Indonesia
description: Mary Jane Veloso is expected to be freed after the clemency since there are no other active cases against her.
content: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said on Friday that he has pardoned Mary Jane Veloso, a former death row inmate detained since her 2010 conviction for drug trafficking in Indonesia. “I’ll give you a scoop: I signed her pardon yesterday,” Marcos told reporters during a visit to the northern town of Batac on Friday. Veloso is expected to be freed after the pardon since there are no other active cases against her, though Marcos did not specify when that will happen. Claire Castro, the president’s spokeswoman, earlier said that Marcos was seriously considering an absolute pardon for Veloso. Veloso’s lawyer relayed the news to her family, her mother Celia Veloso said by phone from their northern Philippine hometown. “They were so happy,” she said of Veloso’s two sons. “‘We will finally be able to be with mama,’ that’s what they told me.” Indonesia would not need to be informed, Castro added, as clemency was the prerogative of the Philippine government under the terms of Veloso’s repatriation. The overseas Filipino worker, then 25, was arrested at Yogyakarta’s Adisutjipto International Airport in 2010 after officials found 2.6kg (5.7lbs) of heroin hidden in her luggage. She was convicted and sentenced to death later that year. Veloso, a single mother of two, has maintained her innocence, saying she was deceived by recruiters who promised her a job abroad as a domestic helper. Advocates argue she was a victim of human trafficking. Scheduled for execution by firing squad in 2015, Veloso won a dramatic last-minute reprieve after then president Benigno Aquino III appealed to his Indonesian counterpart Joko Widodo. She remained at Yogyakarta Women’s Prison while the Philippines’ Department of Foreign Affairs negotiated her transfer with the Indonesian government. Reports that she was suffering from a possibly malignant ovarian cyst added urgency to the process. On December 18, 2024, Veloso flew back to Manila and was transferred to the custody of the Philippines’ Bureau of Corrections. The arrangement allowed her sentence to be governed by Philippine laws upon her return, including the executive authority to grant clemency or a presidential pardon. Activists have campaigned for the 41-year-old’s release since her return to the country. In February, Castro urged Veloso to write to the president personally to ask for clemency. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Hong Kong exports surge 53% to HK$667.9 billion, second highest on record
description: Consistent strong demand for AI-related electronic products fuels growth.
content: The recent strength in Hong Kong’s exports extended into August, with the value jumping by 53 per cent to HK$667.9 billion (US$85.6 billion) – the second-highest level on record after July’s peak – on strong demand for artificial intelligence-related products. Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Thursday showed that the total value of exports rose to HK$667.9 billion last month, following a 50.7 per cent surge in July. Imports, meanwhile, rose by 60 per cent to HK$739.1 billion, leading to a trade deficit of HK$71.2 billion, which is equivalent to 9.6 per cent of the value of imports of goods in August. August’s exports were the second highest on record, after an all-time high of HK$672.5 billion in July. A government spokesman said the surge in exports in August was driven by robust demand for AI-related electronic products, marking the 19th consecutive month of double-digit growth. “Looking ahead, sustained global demand for AI-related electronic products is expected to continue to support Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in the near term,” he said. “Nonetheless, given the geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and continued protectionist trade measures among major advanced economies, the external environment remains uncertain and warrants close monitoring.” In August, total exports to Asia leapt by 59.2 per cent year on year, with notable increases to most major destinations, particularly a 101.7 per cent rise to Malaysia, 83.3 per cent to Vietnam and 80.8 per cent to Singapore. South Korea led the growth in imports last month, with the value skyrocketing by 265.8 per cent from a year earlier, followed by increases of 111.6 per cent from the United Kingdom and 107.7 per cent from India. In the first eight months of 2026, total exports rose by 42.5 per cent from the same period last year, while total imports climbed by 43.2 per cent, resulting in a deficit of HK$371.2 billion. In terms of commodities, strong demand in tech sectors continued to contribute to exports, with the value of exports in electrical machinery and parts soaring by 62.6 per cent to HK$352.6 billion, while office machines and automatic data processing machines expanded by 131 per cent to HK$106.2 billion. Ryan Lam Chun-wang, head of research for Hong Kong at Shanghai Commercial Bank, estimated that the numbers in September would also be strong. “September is likely to post another solid figure after weather disruptions along the Chinese coast in August,” he said. “Front-loading shipments ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival can lend a hand.” Regarding AI products, Lam said they could face headwinds within months as the upgrade cycle was short.

title: Philippines impeachment: is path now clear to convict Sara Duterte?
description: Omitting absent senators cuts the votes needed to oust Sara Duterte-Carpio from 16 to 14, setting up a clash over the court’s legitimacy.
content: The Philippine Senate has made it mathematically easier to convict Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, but observers say the ruling could intensify a battle over an impeachment trial already viewed by the public as deeply divisive. The Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, ruled on Wednesday that only senator-judges who are able to take part in the trial should be counted in determining the threshold for conviction. Under the Philippine constitution, a two-thirds vote of the Senate is required to convict an impeached official. Four senator-judges have been unable to regularly take part in the trial: Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are detained over plunder cases; Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is at large, wanted on an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; and Loren Legarda is abroad on extended medical leave. The court has ruled that their absence should not count towards the denominator for the two-thirds requirement, reducing the number of votes needed for conviction from 16 to 14. Thirteen senators voted in favour of Wednesday’s ruling and one voted against, while six senators widely seen as allied with the Duterte clan did not take part in the proceedings. The ruling followed testimonies from four retired Supreme Court justices who appeared before the court, three of whom advised that the two-thirds rule must exclude senators unable to participate. Duterte-Carpio’s impeachment trial before the Senate addresses allegations that she made grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and his family, as well as charges she misappropriated more than US$10 million in confidential funds during her time as education secretary between 2022 and 2024. If convicted, she will be barred from running for public office, thwarting her intention to seek the presidency in the 2028 election. Not set in stone The lower threshold resulting from Wednesday’s ruling effectively increased the chances of conviction, said Paolo Tamase, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines College of Law. Tamase, who teaches constitutional law, said the decision to lower the threshold was sound, with the retired justices providing a “clear, learned justification” for interpreting the constitution in line with the realities of the Senate’s composition. “The constitution intends a conviction in impeachment to be difficult but not impossible. These are unusual times for the Senate, with many of its members facing corruption complaints and the more functional reading of the threshold allows impeachment to continue as a mechanism for accountability,” he said. However, Tamase said the ruling also “leaves the possibility for absent senators to appear before the verdict and affect the maths, which means nothing is set in stone”. Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and the founder of independent polling firm Momentum Research, said the ruling meant the prosecution now had to change focus from overcoming a narrow numerical threshold to winning over persuadable senators. “The prosecution is no longer confronting what initially appeared to be a very narrow path to conviction,” he said. “The battle now moves towards persuadable senators and, ultimately, whether the prosecution can consolidate a broad coalition around at least one article of impeachment.” Arguelles said securing 14 votes for a guilty verdict was “considerably more feasible” now, given that 13 senators had already voted in favour of the new threshold. “Of course … we should not treat yesterday’s 13 votes as 13 automatic votes for conviction. But the arithmetic tells us that conviction is no longer a remote scenario,” he added. Questioning legitimacy Senator-judges aligned with Duterte-Carpio could still move to undermine the credibility of the proceedings in the court of public opinion, political observers told This Week in Asia. “The minority may become even more emboldened to question the legitimacy of the proceedings at every opportunity,” said Jean Encinas-Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman. “Clearly, it means that it has now become easier to convict Sara,” she said, adding: “Politics has always been full of surprises in the Philippines.” Franco said the Duterte camp might ultimately challenge the decision before the Supreme Court “just to show that they still have options”. Tamase, however, said the testimony of the retired justices would make it harder for the vice-president’s camp to argue that the Senate had committed a “grave abuse of discretion”, reducing the likelihood of a Supreme Court reversal. Arguelles said the Duterte bloc had to make strategic use of its numbers. “If they believe they cannot prevail inside the impeachment court, one option is to contest the legitimacy of the process itself and take that argument outside the chamber,” he said. “Their non-participation has both an institutional and a public dimension.” Arjan Aguirre, an assistant professor of political science at Ateneo de Manila University, called the ruling a “risky yet inevitable move” that could undermine public faith in the outcome. “Public opinion adds another layer here. Several senators seen as acquittal-leaning are themselves facing separate corruption allegations tied to the flood-control scandal, which could make an acquittal vote look self-protective rather than a principled outcome,” he said. “Even if Duterte-Carpio manages to get convicted, the public will view the outcome with a low sense of legitimacy because people will know that it was adjusted.” According to Aguirre, unexcused absences function as de facto acquittal votes because senators cannot abstain during a final verdict. “They can just choose not to attend to further undermine the process,” he said. Defending her vote to lower the threshold, Senator Risa Hontiveros said the absence of certain senators during a trial should not paralyse the entire institution. “Beyond discussions about denominators, fractions and rounding, what we need to determine is: who among us is currently present in court and has the capability to fulfil our sworn duties?” she said. How the trial unfolded would have implications for the 2028 presidential election, Arguelles said. “All eyes will be on who, if anyone, crosses over. A defection would matter not only for the impeachment verdict, but for the broader configuration of political alliances going into 2028,” he said.

title: Actress Leila Tong sued over alleged contract breach and ‘manipulative conduct’
description: Hong Kong actress accused of breaching contract by dyeing her hair without consent and accepting outside engagements.
content: Former Hong Kong television actress Leila Tong Ning has been sued for allegedly breaching her management contract by abandoning her professional duties while suffering from depression and dyeing her hair without her agency’s consent. The High Court writ, filed by agency Tenjinmura Ongaku Limited, also accuses the 44-year-old former Television Broadcasts (TVB) artist of “coercive conduct” and accepting commercial engagements without the company’s approval after their relationship broke down in May 2024. Tong, whose real name is Leila Kong Lai-na, rose to fame as a child star with appearances in John Woo’s 1991 action comedy Once a Thief and TVB drama The Greed of Man, which aired the following year. After signing with TVB in 2000, Tong appeared in numerous series for the broadcaster and was nominated multiple times for the Most Improved Female Artiste Award at its annual ceremony. She has since stepped away from the spotlight and moved to New Zealand with her two children. The court filing, seen by the South China Morning Post on Thursday, alleged that Tong engaged in “a pattern of threatening, self-harming and manipulative conduct” to compel her agent to develop and expand her social media presence between 2021 and mid-2024. According to the writ, Tong, now based in Auckland, was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and would often resort to yelling and extreme acts of self-harm whenever her agent, Cheang Pui-ying, asked her to work. The filing stated that Tong went missing in November 2021 and was found unharmed the next morning inside a large tree hollow in a park, holding a rope. The following month, she reportedly stabbed herself twice with a fruit knife after Cheang asked her to fulfil her professional obligations. Tong spent three days in hospital. Tensions escalated further in early 2022 when Tong allegedly held Cheang at knifepoint, claiming she was trying to restrain herself from killing both of them. Tong also allegedly went missing for seven hours in April 2023, seven months after her depression diagnosis. The plaintiff’s lawyers said Cheang was forced to produce new content on Tong’s Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok pages – work that fell outside her ordinary duties – because the defendant refused to work. “If Ms Cheang did not perform the defendant’s work, no work would be produced. If the defendant was asked to complete even a simple task, she would frequently withdraw for hours and still fail to complete it,” the writ said. “Over time, the coercive conduct escalated whenever professional demands were made of the defendant, including whenever Ms Cheang, on behalf of the plaintiff, asked the defendant to fulfil her obligations under the management agreement.” The writ also accused Tong of failing to maintain good health, keep the agency informed of her whereabouts and remain in contact. After the relationship broke down in May 2024, Tong allegedly entered into commercial contracts with third parties without the plaintiff’s knowledge and changed the login credentials to her social media accounts to retain exclusive control of them. The defendant also allegedly engaged another management agency to act on her behalf while her contract with the plaintiff remained in effect. The plaintiff seeks an unspecified amount of damages, including restitution for the social media work Cheang performed for the former actress. The company is also seeking access to Tong’s social media accounts and a court declaration that her management contract remains active until September 2028.

title: American AI development ‘cannot separate itself from China’: Zheng Yongnian
description: Neither nation can manage AI risks alone, top Chinese policy adviser warns ahead of Xi-Trump summit where the tech is tipped to loom large.
content: China and the United States must prevent their AI competition from escalating into a cold war, a top Chinese policy adviser has warned, while asserting that a complete decoupling would be difficult. The remarks from Zheng Yongnian, a leading political scientist and dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, come ahead of the Xi-Trump summit in Washington, where artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to be among the top items on the agenda. Chinese leader Xi Jinping received a rare personal welcome from US President Donald Trump as he landed in Washington to begin his first state visit to the country since 2015. Their summit talks are expected to be steered by a desire to find common ground while managing risks as rivalry intensifies, with AI and its governance at the forefront. According to Zheng, existing rules on the emerging technology are shaped by “sheer strength” and China’s role in AI development by the US remains “indispensable”. He also rejected claims that the second face-to-face meeting between the two leaders this year was merely symbolic. “Many issues require consensus between the leaders first before the bureaucracies on both sides can push them forward … so many major decisions simply cannot be made at the bureaucratic level,” Zheng said in an interview. Xi’s trip is aimed at building on his May summit with Trump in Beijing, where both sides agreed to reframe their ties around “constructive strategic stability” to properly manage conflicts and keep relations between the world’s top two powers from derailing. But tensions continue to mount, especially around AI, as China quickly narrows the gap with the US, the early market leader. The heads-of-state talks at the White House come just days after the two sides finally agreed on an AI dialogue framework, a long overdue outcome from the May summit, following hours-long negotiations in New York led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng. According to Bessent, the US has proposed a new “notification mechanism” to address high-level AI incidents that could affect national security, while seeking “a shared vision of common goals and common threats”. Zheng said that neither the US nor China could manage AI risks alone – saying that the technology posed a far greater risk than nuclear weapons. While nuclear arms sat idle in silos under global oversight, AI was evolving rapidly in a regulatory vacuum, he cautioned. “Cooperation is essential to build an international framework … We can’t have two separate systems – a US one and a China one,” he said. “If that happens, it will devolve into a US-Soviet style [Cold War] dynamic which would be very, very terrible.” But differences already exist and the US-China AI rivalry is fracturing into two distinct camps. The US favours a high-cost AI model catering strictly to developed, wealthy economies, as underlined by the Trump administration’s Pax Silica initiative to secure semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains and cut reliance on China. Beijing, however, has championed an open-source, mass-market approach that aims to offer low-cost, accessible technology tailored to developing nations across the Global South. Nevertheless, Zheng said today’s dynamic differed fundamentally from a rigid bipolar divide. “Unlike the Cold War, where the US and Soviet Union were completely split into two isolated blocs, the US and China are still engaging with each other. That makes for a really interesting new dynamic.” However, translating high-level diplomatic intentions into concrete AI guardrails would not be easy, Zheng warned. Despite the vast potential for cooperation on AI, the “low level of political trust” remained the main barrier, a challenge Thursday’s summit could help address, he emphasised. Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, said Beijing might have the upper hand going into the talks, with the Trump administration under pressure from factors including the Iran war and the November midterm elections. “Of course, China also needs to maintain baseline stability in US-China relations,” Zhao said, pointing to the Communist Party Central Committee’s fifth plenary session coming up in October and the 21st national congress expected next autumn. “China equally requires a stable bilateral environment,” he said. The fifth plenum is the party’s most important political gathering ahead of the next five-yearly congress, usually the time for a massive top-level reshuffle. The summit comes at a time of rising US-China tensions over AI rivalry. Earlier this month, the Trump administration targeted Chinese firms, accusing them of stealing and copying American models through “industrial-scale distillation campaigns”. Beijing fired back, accusing Washington of seeking a “monopoly” on the new technology and warning of countermeasures. But a complete AI decoupling would not be easy, according to Zheng. American AI development “cannot separate itself from China”, he said, given US reliance on Chinese tech talent and Beijing’s ability to wield its pricing power as diplomatic leverage. Zheng further stressed that meaningful global AI rules required actual technological strength, otherwise they would not carry weight. “The world is realistic: rules must be backed by real power and capability. Without strength, who is going to listen to your rules?” “That is why real, effective rules must be forged by capable nations like China and the US,” he said, while calling for the framework to be open and inclusive, allowing other nations to take part. Beyond the US and China, international momentum is building to manage AI risks. On Monday, 20 countries and the European Union issued a joint statement urging international cooperation to keep AI under human control, proposing a new global body to set and enforce standards for advanced AI systems. Canada, Australia, Germany, South Africa, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates were among the signatories. China and the US – the world’s two leading AI powers – were not party to the declaration.

title: ‘Open, close, reopen’: return of choking haze traps Malaysian schools in limbo
description: All 108 schools in Serian close again as API readings break 200, highlighting the limits of cloud seeding while monsoon winds persist.
content: Malaysia’s haze crisis has flared again just weeks after emergency measures and cloud-seeding operations brought temporary relief, with experts warning that smoke from Indonesian fires could continue drifting across the country until monsoon winds change. All 108 schools in Serian, a district in the state of Sarawak on Malaysian Borneo, were ordered to close on Thursday after the air pollutant index (API) breached 200 on Wednesday night, forcing pupils back to home-based learning. By noon, Serian’s API reading was still at 211, making it the only location nationwide in the “very unhealthy” category, while nine other stations across Sarawak recorded unhealthy air. Malaysia classifies API readings above 300 as hazardous. Serian’s schools have been stuck in a stop-start cycle since mid-August, shutting when pollution worsens and reopening when air quality improves. The disruption peaked on September 4 when the API hit 518, causing the King to approve a state of emergency for the district. The emergency declaration was lifted three days later as conditions eased, although pollution remained very unhealthy and schools finally reopened on Monday last week. A 28-year-old teacher in Serian, who asked not to be named as they were not authorised to speak to the media, said the constant switching between classroom and online learning was taking a toll. “Some students were not able to join [online classes] as they did not have their own device and their parents are working, so they missed class,” the teacher said. The teacher added that older colleagues struggled to set up online lessons, while weak internet connectivity in rural villages made home learning difficult for both teachers and pupils. “This was the pattern: open, close, reopen, close,” the teacher said. “We thought everything was getting better.” Groundhog haze Malaysia has repeatedly turned to cloud seeding during the recent dry spell, with the latest operation in Sarawak running from September 3-7. It brought rain to several targeted areas, including Serian, though the Malaysian Meteorological Department reported that total rainfall fell below expectations. University of Malaya meteorologist Azizan Abu Samah said the relief could only go so far while southwesterly monsoon winds continued carrying smoke from fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra. Because the haze was mixed through the lower atmosphere – roughly 1km to 2km (0.6 miles to 1.24 miles) above the ground – rain could briefly wash pollutants out of the air, only for another polluted air mass to move in, he said. “Cloud seeding and local rainfall only help,” Azizan said, adding that until the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra were dampened by rain or the winds changed direction, “the haze will persist”. Relief could arrive in October as Malaysia enters into the inter-monsoon period and wind patterns shift, with the northeast monsoon later in the year expected to bring heavier rainfall. By late October and November, Azizan said conditions should finally improve enough for Malaysians to “see blue sky again”. Douglas Uggah Embas, deputy premier of Sarawak, made the same point when cloud seeding began earlier this month. “We hope the rainfall will help us reduce the haze,” he told reporters on September 3. “But we cannot promise the haze will disappear because we must not forget where the source of the haze comes from.” Smoke signals Transboundary haze has spread far beyond Malaysia this fire season, affecting Singapore, Brunei and parts of the Philippines as smoke moves across Southeast Asia. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ Specialised Meteorological Centre has kept its highest alert level – Level 3 – for southern Southeast Asia since August 26. In an update on Tuesday, the centre reported scattered to widespread hotspots across Kalimantan and Sumatra, with moderate to dense transboundary smoke over northern Borneo. Strong El Nino conditions and prolonged dry weather have raised the risk of severe haze, with the southwest monsoon expected to persist into early October. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto was briefed on Wednesday that active firefighting operations were ongoing across roughly 210 hectares (519 acres) in Sumatra and Kalimantan, according to state news agency Antara, while large-scale weather modification efforts would continue until seasonal rains returned. Last week, Prabowo accepted Malaysia’s offer of an aircraft, three helicopters and 52 firefighting personnel to help contain the fires in Kalimantan. Jakarta has also stepped up enforcement. Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni revoked the licences of five companies on Tuesday over fires on concessions across Kalimantan covering a combined 92,464 hectares. Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the Environmental Protection Society Malaysia, said Kuala Lumpur had little choice but to focus on measures reducing exposure while the fires continued elsewhere. “This is the best that the Malaysian government can do to try to reduce the effects of haze locally,” he said. “We have measures in place, such as health advisories by the Ministry of Health and the temporary closure of schools when API readings are high.” But repeated exposure carried risks that were harder to measure, Jeremiah warned. “There may be unseen risks related to periodic, prolonged exposure to haze over the long term, particularly for children, the elderly [and] individuals with cardiopulmonary diseases.”

title: Meet Tucker Wetmore, ‘Choosin’ Texas’ singer Ella Langley’s rumoured boyfriend
description: Wetmore, known for tracks like ‘Wind Up Missin’ You’ and ‘Brunette’, first sparked rumours after he was pictured with Langley in the British Virgin Islands last December.
content: Country music star Ella Langley is choosing love. The 27-year-old singer, whose hit song “Choosin’ Texas” has spent 23 weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100, breaking Mariah Carey’s record for “All I Want for Christmas Is You”, is reportedly dating fellow country musician Tucker Wetmore, per TMZ. According to the outlet, the pair have been together for a while now and were recently spotted spending some “You & Me Time” in Nashville after leaving the Nashville Songwriter Awards together. Langley took home the Song of the Year award for “Choosin’ Texas” at the event, which was held at the Ryman Auditorium. Langley and Wetmore first set off romance speculation in December 2025, when they were seen in the British Virgin Islands together, per People. The two met through mutual friends and music industry connections, TMZ reported. Earlier this year, the two performed an acoustic rendition of Wetmore’s “Sunburn” at the Heart Strings for Hope benefit concert. They have not addressed the dating rumours. So, who is Tucker Wetmore, Ella Langley’s rumoured new beau? What is Tucker Wetmore’s background? Tucker Payson Wetmore hails from the southern Washington town of Kalama, where he was born to parents Sia Gould and Robert Wetmore, who is of Samoan descent. His grandfather was a preacher at the Highway Tabernacle Church of God, per People. Sia and Robert worked in fugitive recovery and separated when Wetmore was 10. His mother raised him alongside his two sisters and two stepsisters, per Music Mayhem magazine. The 26-year-old has a “really tight” relationship with his mother, per Grammy, but not with his father. How did he get into music? Tucker Wetmore developed a knack for performance when he was only two, his mother revealed on the Got It From My Momma podcast. “I can say going back to probably two-ish years old, I just always knew he was built for something big,” Gould gushed. Young Wetmore enjoyed singing with his uncle and dancing at school. He also played a 32-key Casio keyboard before his school’s librarian gifted him a piano when he was 11, and Wetmore quickly took to the instrument. He almost went into sports Wetmore grew up playing baseball and running track, People reported. He played American football at Montana Technological University and planned to turn professional. By the end of his first year, he realised he “wasn’t on the right path”. Soon after, he broke his leg and took it as a sign to quit sports. After a few years of “soul-searching” and “getting right with God”, Wetmore ventured into music. He broke through with songs like “Wine Into Whiskey” and “Wind Up Missin’ You” and was named the Academy of Country Music Awards’ Male New Artist of the Year this May.

title: Macroscope | Who has the upper hand in financial markets, the US or China?
description: Against the rising resilience of Chinese markets, the sharp reappraisal of US debt and dollar risks makes the answer far from clear-cut.
content: As Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his much-anticipated summit with US President Donald Trump, it is clear which country emerged stronger from the tariff shock. Last month, China’s exports rose 25 per cent in annualised terms, causing the country’s trade surplus to swell to US$119 billion and putting it on track to exceed last year’s record of US$1.2 trillion. Moreover, China’s surplus with the US rose 44 per cent to US$29 billion, the widest gap since Trump returned to the White House. Not only has China’s export machine roared ahead, Beijing’s weaponisation of rare earths showed it has the power to severely disrupt the global economy. When it comes to the trade war, China “has the cards”, as Trump likes to say. In financial markets, however, things are less clear-cut. On the face of it, comparisons between the US and China are inapt. The US accounts for almost two-thirds of the market capitalisation of the MSCI All-Country World Index, a leading gauge of global stocks. It also constitutes 40 per cent of the global bond market. Furthermore, the dollar is the world’s pre-eminent reserve currency, while America boasts the deepest, most liquid and most transparent capital markets. Yet these are unprecedented times. Trump’s reckless and erratic decision-making has shaken confidence in US Treasury bonds and the dollar. As George Saravelos of Deutsche Bank noted, US debt and the greenback are “no longer the ‘safe’ but the risky asset[s] of choice”. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the world’s biggest, announced earlier this month that it was trimming its holdings of government bonds partly because it no longer expected sovereign debt to have “the same volatility-dampening effects in a government bond crisis”. Although it is increasing its exposure to other US bonds, its decision signified a “reappraisal of sovereign risk, especially in the US”, Saravelos said. The push to diversify investment portfolios has accentuated sources of resilience in China’s markets. First, the country’s government bonds have bucked the sharp sell-off in global sovereign debt markets. While the US 10-year yield breached 5 per cent last week – its highest level since 2007 – its Chinese equivalent has dropped to 1.6 per cent, slightly above its all-time low. Chinese government debt has returned almost 3 per cent this year, excluding currency swings, data from Bloomberg shows. Moreover, “China’s prolonged low inflation environment and accommodative monetary policy stance have created a persistent interest rate differential relative to the rest of the world, making renminbi funding increasingly attractive”, said JPMorgan. Issuance of offshore yuan-denominated debt, or dim sum bonds, by non-Chinese borrowers has risen sharply over the past year, contributing to the dramatic revival of Hong Kong’s capital markets. Second, the yuan has risen to its strongest level against the dollar since January 2023 despite China’s weak domestic economy and the recent rally in the greenback. China’s huge trade surplus, coupled with the country’s relative resilience to the energy shock, supports a stronger yuan. In a report in March, Gavekal said the scope for further appreciation was considerable given China’s massive trade surplus, pointing out that “China is now running a trade surplus roughly equivalent to Saudi Arabia’s 2025 GDP”. The research firm said the “value of the renminbi is the biggest anomaly in the global system”. Third, China’s competitive advantages in artificial intelligence (AI), which include cheaper and abundant electricity as well as the deployment of AI tools in the broader economy, provide investors with a hedge against threats to the buildout of AI infrastructure in the US. Bank of America notes that China’s AI ecosystem is “less correlated to the US AI capital expenditure cycle”, while JPMorgan believes China’s internet stocks benefit from demand for “AI monetisation and application-layer exposure”. The fierce backlash against the construction of new data centres in the US, amplified by mounting calls for much tougher AI regulation, strengthens the case for diversifying into Chinese tech stocks. However, it is important to contextualise the sources of China’s resilience in markets. The outperformance of the bond market stems from the persistent weakness of the domestic economy and expectations of further monetary easing. Monthly growth in retail sales has not exceeded 1 per cent for five straight months, “an unprecedented stretch outside the pandemic years”, said Barclays. The export-driven AI boom, moreover, underscores how unbalanced the economy has become. China’s resilience in markets goes hand in hand with the economy’s vulnerabilities. In the US, by contrast, the Fed is raising interest rates in part because growth remains buoyant. Services and manufacturing output expanded at the fastest pace in five years this month. Yet as the Trump administration becomes increasingly concerned about the dramatic sell-off in Treasury bonds, China can take comfort from the stability of its debt market. The last time Xi visited Washington for a state visit, in September 2015, China’s markets were in turmoil. This is not the case today.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this Mid-Autumn Festival weekend, September 25-27
description: Lantern carnivals, fire dragon dances, a Korean food extravaganza and more await Hongkongers this Mid-Autumn Festival weekend.
content: Few celebrations illuminate Hong Kong quite like the Mid-Autumn Festival, a time to light up the streets with glowing lanterns, gaze at the moon and share mooncakes with loved ones. This weekend features many Mid-Autumn-themed activities to make it a little more fun. Here are five things to do in Hong Kong to elevate your celebrations. 1. An Evening of Lunar Resonance Visual art and music collide in this Mid-Autumn chamber music event happening on Saturday. “Design × Chinese Orchestra: An Evening of Lunar Resonance” is an exclusive one-night concert hosted by the Hong Kong Design Centre and the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra. The 45-minute show fuses modern spatial design with classical chamber music, highlighting local heritage design exhibits alongside festive displays such as Italian designer Stefano Giovannoni’s glowing Qeeboo Rabbit Chairs. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong Chinese Orchestra will celebrate its 50th anniversary by performing a selection of classic and moon-inspired pieces. Tickets are HK$120 (US$15), though a 50 per cent discount is offered to full-time students and seniors. More information can be found here. The Steps, 2/F, DX Design Hub, 280 Tung Chau Street, Sham Shui Po 2. Mid-Autumn K-Festival Week The Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated widely across Asia, including South Korea, where it is known as Chuseok. Running until September 27, the “Mid-Autumn K-Festival Week” market is taking place at Central Market, organised by the Korean Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, the Korea Agro-Fisheries and Food Trade Corporation Hong Kong Branch, and Central Market, and held under the patronage of the Korean Consulate General. Having begun on September 21, this seven-day event is a showcase of Korean food. Though Friday’s cooking workshop hosted by monk chef Seonjae from the hit Netflix show Culinary Class Wars is already full, chefs Park Joon-woo and Lim Hee-won also host masterclasses on September 26 and 27, respectively, with no reservations needed to view. Visitors can also explore the Korean marketplace and K-beauty workshops at the festival. More information can be found here. Central Market, 93 Queen’s Road, Central 3. Full Moon Sound Bath and Tea Ritual Hosted by Sacred Space Therapy and Wellness, this sound bath and tea ritual is an intimate holistic gathering taking place on Saturday night. Designed to be a session of mindful resting, it is perfect for those who find it difficult to switch off even while on holiday and away from work. View this post on Instagram The 90-minute experience honours the harvest moon through a mindful tea ceremony and guided meditation. Every attendee will receive a mooncake made by a local artisan to celebrate the festival. Tickets range from HK$425 to HK$450. For more information or to sign up, click here. Room 2, 24/F, Wai Wah Commercial Centre, 6 Wilmer Street, Sai Ying Pun 4. Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival Those looking to shop over the weekend are in luck as an open-air artisan market will be embedded inside the flagship Lantern Carnival hosted annually at Victoria Park. Organised by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, the Mid-Autumn Lantern Carnival 2026 runs until October 4 and features spectacular lantern installations as well as a wide range of performances – including a fire dragon dance. Beyond the lanterns, a creative market offers festive trinkets, handmade accessories and local crafts straight from independent artisans. Visitors can also enjoy traditional knot-weaving activities, riddle games and live entertainment. Installations will be lit daily from 6.30pm to 11pm, with extended hours until midnight on Friday. Admission is free. Victoria Park, 1 Hing Fat Street, Causeway Bay 5. Lee Tung Avenue Those looking for even more shopping opportunities can also head to Lee Tung Avenue, where 800 Chinese red lanterns light up the street. Until Friday, visitors can explore the pop-up store by century-old Hong Kong pastry brand Hang Heung Cake Shop offering a treat in which the traditional “wife cake” meets the mooncake. Furthermore, from September 25 until October 7, Lee Tung Avenue is offering spending rewards. For every HK$1,000 spent there, customers can receive a HK$100 dining and shopping coupon – just make sure to use an approved electronic payment. Extra festivities, such as an LED fire dragon dance, are also scheduled for Friday night, starting at 8.30pm. Queen’s Road East, Wan Chai

title: Najib Razak’s fundraising in Malaysia draws 1 sen donations, mockery
description: Najib’s wife, Rosmah Mansor, claims that supporters from Singapore, Brunei, Italy and Canada are willing to contribute to the fund.
content: A fundraiser to help pay disgraced former leader Najib Razak’s 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine has become a lightning rod for insults and mockery, as Malaysians continue to pile criticism on a decision last week to allow him to spend the rest of his jail sentence under house arrest. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar last Friday granted Najib a “conditional pardon”, which will allow the jailed ex-prime minister to complete his term in the comfort of his home – provided he first pays off his fine. In response to the royal decree, Najib’s Umno has launched a donation drive urging its members and the public to voluntarily contribute to the party’s efforts to fulfil the condition of the pardon so he can be transferred as soon as possible from Kajang prison to his home in the upscale suburb of Langgak Duta in Kuala Lumpur. The party raised over 1 million ringgit as of the latest update on Saturday by Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki, barely a day after the fund’s launch. “Please continue donating even if it is 10 ringgit,” Asyraf said in a social media post. But Friday’s house arrest decision triggered outrage among Malaysians, who had voted out Najib and the former ruling Umno in a watershed 2018 national election over persistent allegations of widespread corruption, capped by the 1MDB multibillion-dollar scandal. Umno’s appeal has drawn a strong response, but not in the way that it had hoped. Some Malaysians projected their anger into meme-worthy posts on social media, where screenshots of 1 sen (0.01 ringgit) donations to Najib’s fundraiser have gone viral. One of the more popular posts showed a screenshot of an online banking receipt of a transfer of 1 sen with the description “Bapa Sakau Negara”, which roughly translates to Nation’s Father of Thievery – a not-so-subtle jab at allegations of grand corruption at 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), the state fund which Najib had founded. Screenshots of a separate 1 sen donation took a decidedly Gen Z approach, describing the donation as a contribution to “free my boi Najib”. Friday’s house arrest decision was the second pardon granted to Najib. In 2024, then-king sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah issued a decree that halved the former leader’s 12-year sentence and slashed his fine from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit, two years after he was jailed for siphoning 42 million ringgit from SRC International, a former 1MDB subsidiary. The stream of snarky “donations” poured in as Najib’s family thanked donors. Najib’s daughter, Nooryana Najwa, said her father was “deeply moved” by the support. “Daddy really did not expect so many people to be willing to contribute,” Nooryana said in a social media post on Sunday. In a separate post, Najib’s wife, Rosmah Mansor, said on Sunday that supporters from overseas, including Singapore, Brunei, Italy and Canada, had contacted her to express their support and willingness to contribute to the fund. “Today I realise who our friends are, those who have stood by us through good times and bad,” Rosmah said. Analysts have said that a successful transfer to house arrest for Najib could galvanise Umno, which is enjoying a resurgence following back-to-back victories over federal partners Pakatan Harapan (PH) in two recent state elections. The decisive wins in Johor and Negeri Sembilan over Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s PH coalition have emboldened Umno, as it demands snap polls in the hope that its current momentum can help it reclaim Putrajaya. Disillusioned supporters of Anwar and PH have pointed to Najib’s latest pardon as yet another sign of their failure to deliver on promised reforms. Experts, however, do not expect Anwar to buckle under Umno’s pressure to call for early elections, as he still has time to win back support before his term expires at the end of next year. “I believe PMX will fully utilise the mandate,” said Mazlan Ali, a political analyst at the University of Technology Malaysia, using a popular term referring to Anwar. “The available time will be used to carry out institutional reforms and strengthen the parties within the PH coalition.”

title: Investors pivot to selective China bets in technology as property growth fades: DBS Bank
description: DBS forecasts that China’s benchmark CSI 300 Index will reach 9,500 by 2040, more than double its current level.
content: The sentiment among investors that China is a “single bet” is giving way to picking individual winners, with technology displacing property as the engine of growth, according to DBS Bank (Hong Kong). “Instead of looking at China as one big thing, there are selective sectors that we think will benefit from this trend,” Dennis Lam, managing director and head of research at the bank, said during a media briefing on Thursday. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and innovative drugs would become key drivers for the Chinese economy by 2040, signalling “a clear shift away from traditional physical assets to technology,” he said. To identify potential winners by 2040, DBS evaluated listed Chinese companies in a newly released report and highlighted its top 10 picks. Contemporary Amperex Technology, or CATL, the world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) battery maker, topped the list, followed by drug developer BeOne Medicines, e-commerce giant Alibaba Group Holding, chip foundry Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp, and precision automation maker Inovance. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. However, no carmakers made the list. Lam said China’s EV sector was undergoing an intense shake-out following a massive influx of new entrants, meaning that “some companies will inevitably fail”. DBS expects mainland China’s equity market to “become deeper and more sophisticated” in the coming decades. The bank forecasts the benchmark CSI 300 Index would reach 9,500 by 2040 – more than double its current level. Whether the domestic equity market has kept pace with the broader economy remained a central question for global investors, said Moxy Ying, the bank’s Hong Kong and China equity market strategist. “Our answer is there’s still a long way to go.” China’s stock market capitalisation stood at 78 per cent of gross domestic product at the end of 2025, compared with 219 per cent in the US. DBS projects China’s ratio will climb to 96 per cent by 2040. The report comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping visits Washington for high-stakes bilateral talks with US President Donald Trump, with AI expected to be a primary focal point. Global investors are watching the summit closely for any signs of easing capital flows. Foreign holdings currently account for less than 4 per cent of total A-share market capitalisation in China, a stark contrast to roughly 30 per cent in Japan and South Korea and nearly 50 per cent in Taiwan. Stock markets in Hong Kong and the mainland have lagged regional peers such as Taiwan and South Korea largely because local indices are “not too exposed to the global AI supply chain”, Lam said. However, Lam noted that the sentiment of China being “uninvestable” had softened recently. He called on global funds to re-evaluate the market through the lens of sustainable advances in AI, robotics and advanced manufacturing. “Some investors have returned, but not in a big way,” he said. “I think the capital flow story is completely untapped yet.”

title: South Korean ex-skater tells fans he is alive and well, looking into false report of death
description: Supporters dismayed after obituary appears on Kim Gun-woo’s Instagram account, which he says had been hacked into.
content: South Korean former short-track speedskater Kim Gun-woo has moved quickly to reassure fans that he is alive and well, and that news of his death had been greatly exaggerated. An obituary had appeared on the 28-year-old’s Instagram account, spreading dismay and panic among supporters. However, it soon became apparent that the star’s account had been hacked and the fake news posted without his knowledge. In the early hours of Wednesday, a Korean-language obituary written from the perspective of his family appeared on the 28-year-old’s Instagram account, announcing his death. The post spread rapidly online, leaving the public shocked and mourning the young athlete, who had retired just three months earlier. The account was later updated to state that Kim was unable to access his social media profile when the problematic post was published earlier in the day, accompanied by an apology to “everyone who was surprised and concerned by this incident”. “At the time the post was published, I was personally unable to log into my Instagram account. Because I could not access it, I was completely unaware that the post had been made until I received messages from others,” he wrote. Kim stated that the post was neither written nor published by him, emphasising that it appeared on his account without his knowledge or authorisation. He added that he was investigating the cause of his account being locked and the circumstances surrounding the post. “I take full responsibility for the concern and confusion caused by the spread of the post before the facts were fully verified,” he wrote. However, he noted that as the details regarding account access and the posting remained under investigation, he felt it was best to tell the public of the accurate situation once the facts were fully established, rather than making conclusions based on unverified information. “Currently, I am taking necessary measures to investigate and address this situation,” he said, offering a sincere apology once again to those shocked or concerned by the incident. “I also kindly ask for your understanding, and request that everyone refrain from spreading unconfirmed information or speculating before the facts are confirmed. Thank you.” The Korean obituary posted earlier in the day was written in a formal tone. Although it did not state a cause of death, it expressed deep grief over the tragic news and asked family, friends and the public for condolences and prayers during his final journey, concluding with “may he rest in peace”. Kim was a key middle- and long-distance skater for the South Korean national short-track team, known for his strong outer-track overtaking ability. He announced his retirement from competitive sports in June 2026, marking the end of his athletic career with a thank-you letter. Kim won a gold medal in the mixed relay at the Harbin Asian Winter Games and a silver medal in the men’s 5,000-metre relay at the World Championships. He is reportedly a long-time friend of Lin Xiaojun, a former South Korean Olympic champion who now represents China in short-track speedskating.

title: SOTY 25/26: Scientist and Mathematician category finalist’s quantum leaps
description: Eason Xie Yichen champions foundational science, excelling in quantum computing and astrophysics, inspiring others through mentorship.
content:
Eason Xie Yichen spends his spare hours on foundational research in quantum computing, physics and astrophysics. The 16-year-old student at La Salle College believes that fundamental science quietly reshapes the world.
“I keep coming back to foundational research because it helps reshape how we live. It operates ... years ahead of any obvious use – yet those early insights become the invisible scaffolding of our future,” he said.
Eason highlighted pioneers like Nobel laureate Charles Kao, who demonstrated why light scatters in optical fibres long before there was a need for it.
That same physics now serves as the foundation of the internet.
“Marie Curie studied radiation without a plan to treat cancer, and her curiosity changed medicine forever. That’s why basic science matters: it creates the principles that let humanity build things we can’t yet imagine,” he said.
Eason’s passion for quantum computing began early.
“In primary school ... I devoured every single article I could find about it. I was captivated by the idea that it could be the future of computing – promising exponential speed-ups and a radically different way to solve problems,” he explained. “It felt futuristic and full of possibility, and that sense of wonder pulled me in and never let go.”
Today, Eason is particularly interested in Hamiltonian simulation, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum information science and computational physics. By secondary school, he was already balancing AI projects with an increasing emphasis on quantum research, actively looking for ways to combine the two fields.
Eason’s persistence opened doors. After his emails were ignored by top scientists, he discovered student competitions and used them to show his abilities.
“I dove in – learning the theory, experimenting with hybrid ideas and competing in challenges that let me collaborate with researchers from [around the world],” the teen noted.
“These competitions let me show what I could do ... I started approaching top researchers with concrete competition projects as proof of my skills, and that direct, evidence-based approach opened doors that ‘cold emails’ never did.”
He has worked with researchers at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge to model complex biological and chemical systems. This research has the potential to change the study of molecular dynamics and ground-state properties.
Eason also investigates photonic machine learning, attracted by its promise of energy-efficient artificial intelligence (AI).
“Because information is carried optically rather than electrically, there’s almost no resistive heating and far less energy dissipated when moving signals around a system,” he explained.
Some of these efforts resulted in published papers in globally recognised scientific journals, as well as practical applications such as financial modelling.
Competitions and hands-on projects have taught him to value mistakes as part of a learning process.
“Mistakes give me experience so that I know exactly what to avoid next time,” he said. “Research experience teaches you the details and the traps around a problem, so you don’t get caught off guard again.”
Those insights have also changed his priorities.
“I used to chase projects that looked good on a CV; now, I’ve become choosier and only take on problems that truly interest me,” he added.
“I stopped chasing prestige and started focusing on curiosity – the problems that keep me up at night are the ones I want to solve. The main goal for me is to step out of my comfort zone, interact with new people and experience different research environments.”
Eason also channels his enthusiasm into mentoring others: “I became captain of the school’s STEAM team because I want to teach others and make them understand the fields I work in,” he said.
He organises workshops on topics such as AI, quantum computing and astrophysics, teaching the mathematics behind the ideas and the challenges of research.
“I don’t just show polished results – I walk people through the long process of research, trial and error,” he shared.
“I show failed experiments and dead‑end calculations so students can see the messy reality of research – not the movie version where everything is fixed by pressing a few buttons.”
For Eason, the reward is seeing curiosity spread.
“Students with real passion come together; sharing knowledge and sparking interest has to evolve over time,” he said.
“Interacting with students and inspiring them to pursue their own questions is why I mentor – I want them to keep going after what excites them.”
Eason plans to study at a university abroad to immerse himself in a new academic environment. After his studies, he intends to return to Hong Kong and contribute to its development as a hub for quantum computing.
