His dedication to research was acknowledged when he became a finalist in the Scientist and Mathematician category of the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.

title: Indonesia commissions first aircraft carrier, bolstering sea defence
description: Indonesia’s navy renamed the former Italian warship KRI Sriwijaya-100 at a ceremony in North Jakarta.
content: Indonesia’s navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier on Thursday after acquiring the former Italian vessel to strengthen its maritime defences and disaster response. The Italian flag on the former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was replaced with the Indonesian flag on the carrier renamed the KRI Sriwijaya-100 as part of its official transfer at the ceremony held at Tanjung Priok seaport in North Jakarta. “The ship, which previously served in the Italian navy, now bears the name KRI Sriwijaya-100, flying the red-and-white flag as a symbol of sovereignty and service to Indonesia,” navy spokesperson Tunggul, who uses one name, said in a statement. The carrier, which Italy retired in 2024, arrived at the Indonesian seaport last week after a 25-day journey passing through the Suez Canal, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. It has the capacity for short take-off and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters. Unlike major naval powers, Indonesia will use the vessel as a mobile command and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across the archipelago. President Prabowo Subianto earlier said the ship would help fight forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of Southeast Asia with hazardous haze. Italy agreed in March to give the carrier to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the Southeast Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship. Indonesia is the second country in Southeast Asia with an aircraft carrier. Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain.

title: Trump grimaces, Xi unfazed during US military flyover for historic tarmac welcome
description: Viral reaction at Joint Base Andrews frames Chinese president’s visit as leaders prepare for crucial talks on trade and security.
content: At Joint Base Andrews where Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for the visiting Chinese president, Xi Jinping appeared unfazed during a ceremonial flyover by a screeching US bomber while the US president visibly winced at the noise. As Xi arrived at the military base just outside Washington, he was greeted with a ceremony that included the US Air Force band playing the American and Chinese national anthems, a 21-gun salute, a guard of honour, a display of six F-16 and six F-22 fighter jets, and a flyover by two B-1 Lancer bombers. Footage showed that near the end of the US national anthem, reacting to the roaring sound of the B-1 flyover, Trump, who was saluting, ducked, gritted his teeth, turned his head to look at the aircraft, and lowered his salute in front of reporters and cameramen. In contrast, Xi’s gaze followed the bomber to the right as it flew by, revealing minimal physical reaction. Afterwards, Trump could be seen in the video saying to Xi: “That was really loud.” Video of their different reactions circulated widely on both Chinese and US social media. It is a rarity for any world leader to be greeted by the US president at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. Trump’s reception for Xi was the first presidential welcome for a foreign leader, excluding popes, at Joint Base Andrews since 1962 when John F. Kennedy welcomed British prime minister Harold Macmillan, according to Fox News. The last time Trump greeted a world leader at an airport was when he met Russian President Vladimir Putin on the tarmac at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, for their summit in August last year. Then, as Trump and Putin walked on the red carpet next to each other, four F-35 fighters and one B-2 bomber flew overhead. Putin turned his head towards the sound of the warplanes three times while Trump barely reacted. Amid domestic criticism of Xi’s grand reception, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the welcome ceremony, saying “the relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century”. He also said “the United States and China are probably the two most powerful militaries in the world” and that China had “the second-largest economy in the world and a pretty substantial military that’s undergoing the most rapid military build-up, probably in history”. Reaction by China’s leadership to US military equipment is often viewed in China as a symbol of the military capacity gap between the two. A famous 1980 photo showing Admiral Liu Huaqing standing on tiptoe to observe weapons when shown around a US aircraft carrier for the first time is referred to as demonstrating the immense gap between the two militaries at the time. China has undergone what US defence chief Pete Hegseth has described as a “rapid, formidable and holistic” military build-up in recent years as the People’s Liberation Army modernises. In just a few years, China has narrowed the military technology gap with the US in a number of areas and in some technologies – such as satellite refuelling and hypersonic missiles – it has even taken the lead. Trump and Xi are expected to hold talks on trade, technology and geopolitical issues on Thursday, followed by a state dinner. The three-day visit will conclude on Friday with tea at the White House and a visit to the National Archives. Just days before Xi’s US visit, China’s sixth-generation fighter J-36 was seen conducting the latest round of flight tests, according to social media footage circulated online, which the South China Morning Post could not independently verify. Beijing released the first footage of its sixth-generation fighter prototype in action in June. While the US’ sixth-generation fighter programme faces challenges, some argue Beijing is ahead in the race.

title: Hong Kong reports more than 40% drop in cancer-related death rate over 30 years
description: Health minister Lo Chung-mau outlines Hong Kong’s ‘remarkable’ progress at the World Cancer Congress, being held in the city for the first time.
content: Hong Kong has cut its cancer-related death rate by more than 40 per cent over the past three decades, the health minister has said, as the chief executive renewed his pledge to make the city a hub for medical innovation. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau outlined the city’s progress in controlling the disease at the World Cancer Congress, which is being held in Hong Kong for the first time. Citing figures from 1993 to 2023, Lo said Hong Kong’s age-standardised cancer mortality rate had fallen by more than 40 per cent. Over the past 10 years, the annual decline was 2.8 per cent for men and 1.7 per cent for women. “This is a remarkable achievement, showing that Hong Kong is really making significant life-saving progress against cancer,” Lo said during a plenary session at the congress. He added that the progress had been made possible by government policy support, strategic planning, coordination and investment. Lo said measures including antenatal hepatitis B screening, vaccination for newborns and antiviral treatment had helped control liver cancer, the city’s third-leading cause of cancer-related deaths. He also said the number of new liver cancer cases had fallen by 8.2 per cent over the past decade, while deaths had declined by 7.6 per cent. “We will gear up to enhance cancer control in a sustained, evidence-based manner, powered by biotechnology as well as policy innovation from the government,” he said. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu echoed Lo’s remarks in a pre-recorded speech to the congress. He said the city’s approach to cancer was consistent with that of the rest of the world, and that it had made “sustained progress” in preventing and controlling non-communicable diseases. When Lee unveiled Hong Kong’s first five-year plan last Wednesday, he said the blueprint complemented the country’s “Healthy China” initiative. He said the city would continue to attract leading global pharmaceutical companies and world-class medical professionals, and strengthen international exchanges on public health and cancer control. “That is the Hong Kong we are building – an international hub for health and medical innovation,” he said. The three-day event, which began on Thursday, brought together nearly 2,000 healthcare delegates from more than 124 countries. Other prominent health officials attending the event included Dr He Jie, director of mainland China’s National Cancer Centre. World Health Organization director general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus also gave a pre-recorded speech. Dr He called for collaboration in tackling cancer. “Cancer remains one of the most severe public health challenges for all the countries. Facing this global health crisis, no country or institution can address it alone,” he said. Solidarity, collaboration and shared innovation were the “most powerful weapon in the global fight against cancer”, he added, noting that the mainland had always been an active participant in and contributor to global cancer prevention and control. According to statistics he presented, an estimated 5.15 million new cancer cases were diagnosed on the mainland in 2024, accounting for around a quarter of newly diagnosed cases worldwide. Lee announced last year in his policy address that Hong Kong would host the congress. The congress, held every two years, is organised by the Union for International Cancer Control, the world’s largest and oldest international cancer organisation. The Hong Kong Anti-Cancer Society is hosting it this year.

title: Skydiving, whale watching and a burst of bookings as holidays extend for millions in China
description: An alignment of Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays stretches time off for millions of Chinese, with breaks reaching up to 13 days.
content: A three-day public holiday used to be a big deal in China. Then came “golden weeks”, which would sometimes stretch to nine days, sending millions of people in search of new sights across the country and further afield. Now an alignment of the Mid-Autumn Festival and the National Day holiday will give many Chinese students and office workers up to a record 13-day break, potentially pushing tourist traffic to new heights. “The more interesting change this year is not simply higher volume, but the potential for longer and more complex trips,” said Subramania Bhatt, CEO of the marketing and technology firm China Trading Desk. The Mid-Autumn Festival break runs from September 25 to 27, followed by three working days before the National Day golden week from October 1. Because the Mid-Autumn Festival date shifts each year with the lunar calendar, its timing in 2026 places it just a few days before the National Day holiday schedule. Chinese media outlets reported that some 50 universities had combined the two holidays into a single break from September 25 to October 7, and that private companies in major cities had adopted similar arrangements. The longer break appears more likely to translate into longer stays and more complex itineraries than a sharp increase in spending per day Subramania Bhatt, China Trading Desk By the middle of this month, domestic flight bookings for the period from September 25 to October 7 had topped 8.58 million, more than 10 per cent higher than during the same time last year, a China Trading Desk survey found. It said bookings for longer air routes and hotel stays were also up. International and cross-border bookings have exceeded 2.18 million for the same period, up about 7 per cent year on year, while hotel bookings for trending cities were also ahead of last year’s levels, the firm found. Travel platform Trip.com said bookings for hotel stays of seven nights or longer had surged 123 per cent compared with the same travel season in 2025. Multi-destination itineraries increased by 84 per cent, particularly for trips to Europe and Southeast Asia. Seoul ranked as the top overseas holiday destination, with a 91 per cent increase in flight bookings, Trip.com said. Other hotspots were Australia and Thailand, travel platforms said. Chinese online travel platform Fliggy said in a September 15 statement that Madagascar, Romania and Slovenia were among the fastest growing “new” destinations overseas. Domestically, Chengdu, Urumqi, Kunming and Sanya topped its rankings. China State Railway Group was expecting a record 284 million passenger trips during a 16-day span covering the long break, Xinhua reported. To stimulate consumption during the coming holidays, local governments have distributed more than 60 million yuan (US$8.9 million) in travel vouchers through booking platforms, according to estimates from Tongcheng Travel. China Trading Desk’s third-quarter survey showed that 56 per cent of respondents expected their spending at destinations, excluding flights and hotels, to remain “broadly unchanged”, while 35 per cent expected to spend more. “The longer break appears more likely to translate into longer stays and more complex itineraries than a sharp increase in spending per day,” Bhatt said. Reflecting trends that have emerged over the past few years, travellers in China are increasingly prioritising experiences over sightseeing or shopping. Bookings for whale-watching expeditions and skydiving trips had risen markedly this year compared with the Mid-Autumn Festival-National Day period in 2025, Fliggy said. The platform said travellers also had shown stronger interest this year in concerts, self-driving tours and wildlife-watching activities. For Richard Wang, a fintech professor at Fudan University, the extended 2026 break would allow him to spend nine days with his mother in Taipei instead of the usual six. “Even if it wasn’t for the [extended] holiday, I’d go back, but it works out because China does have the holiday,” he said. Not everyone, however, will enjoy the full 13 days off – or make plans to unwind. A data management compliance specialist in Shanghai said he would spend two or three days showing his sons factories where some of his friends work. But he said the full 13-day break could be difficult for business, although it would help people achieve a better balance between work and “health and wellness”. China recorded 888 million domestic tourist trips during an eight-day National Day break in 2025, generated 809 billion yuan in domestic tourism spending, and registered 2.43 billion cross-regional passenger trips. Additional reporting by He Huifeng

title: Why did Trump wear gloves to greet China’s Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews?
description: Overcoat and gloves on mild autumn day prompt speculation, with Trump the only one of the two first couples dressed this way.
content: US President Donald Trump’s choice of attire at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday drew online attention as he made a rare personal appearance to welcome Xi Jinping. Trump was on the tarmac to greet Xi on Wednesday evening as the Chinese president arrived in Washington for his first US state visit in more than a decade. But while temperatures at the airbase were around 19 degrees Celsius (66 Fahrenheit), Trump was the only one wearing a dark overcoat and gloves as he and first lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan. Xi was in a dark suit paired with a purple tie, while Peng wore a dove grey dress with a pale scarf. Her US counterpart wore a dark two-piece suit. Trump removed his right glove to shake hands with Xi and Peng as they stepped off the plane, and later took it off again when greeting Chinese ambassador Xie Feng and other members of the Chinese delegation. He put the glove back on during the arrival ceremony and kept it on while saluting as the national anthems played. The seemingly unseasonal handwear quickly caught the attention of social media users. “It was a beautiful 66 degrees fall day in [Washington] DC when his video was taken, why is Trump wearing gloves?” one post read. “Trump is dressed like he’s going ice fishing, with a winter coat and gloves, and it’s in the mid-60s in DC,” read another. Others speculated the gloves were intended to conceal bruising on Trump’s hands, a detail pointed out by web users on several occasions. Last week, images of Trump from a campaign event for the November midterms again drew public attention to the hand bruising. This time, the marks were on his left hand and appeared different from bruises seen previously. US media reports noted that the discolouration differed from past sightings of larger areas of bruising across the back of his hand. The latest mark appeared more mottled, with clusters of irregular dark purple and blue patches. Trump has previously offered his own explanation for the bruising. In January, after a bruise was seen on his left hand, he told reporters aboard Air Force One that he had bumped it on a table, and that his aspirin use made him more prone to bruising. “I take the big aspirin,” Trump said, adding: “When you take the big aspirin, they tell you you bruise.” In an interview in the same month, he told The New York Times he had never been diagnosed with heart disease of any kind and had never had a heart attack. Last July, the White House cited a memo from Trump’s doctor saying that the visible bruising on the back of his hand was “consistent with minor soft tissue irritation from frequent handshaking and the use of aspirin, which is taken as part of a standard cardiovascular prevention regimen”. Trump, who turned 80 in June, became the oldest president in US history to take office when he was sworn in for a second term in January 2025.

title: Rohingya who fled Myanmar chaos now dread return from Malaysia
description: ‘I get a headache just thinking about where to go,’ a migrant says ahead of next week’s repatriation from detention centres.
content: As a Rohingya exile who abandoned his life in Malaysia to return to Myanmar, Ismail’s bleak prospects may portend what awaits others caught in Kuala Lumpur’s migrant crackdown. Weeks ago, the 25-year-old was eking out a living at a Malaysian fish market, one of legions of the Muslim minority group who left Myanmar to escape violence some monitors say amounted to genocide. But a wave of anti-Rohingya sentiment, migrant arrests and a government plan to repatriate Myanmar nationals drove Ismail back, even though the nation he fled still denies him full citizenship. “People without a country like us, we have nowhere to come back [to],” said Ismail, using a pseudonym for security reasons like other Rohingya in this story. He subsists jobless on the charity of family in Yangon, carrying ID labelling him a second-class citizen and cowering from the security forces who spearheaded the crackdown on his people. “We are the most discriminated people,” Ismail said, “the people from nowhere”. Nearly 1,500 Myanmar migrants are due to be sent home from Malaysia next week, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres. Malaysia’s foreign and home ministries have not responded to a query on what proportion will be Rohingya. But the group makes up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in the country, according to the United Nations. The Rohingya left Myanmar en masse starting in 2017 when a crackdown of mass killings, rape and arson began in western Rakhine state. Rights groups say it was a military-led campaign of ethnic cleansing, a claim the armed forces deny. Most Rohingya – 1.2 million – now live over the Bangladesh border in overcrowded camps, while Malaysia is the second-largest host nation. Despite Malaysia being a Muslim-majority country, the Rohingya there are facing pressure, including from an online campaign that rights advocates say is fuelling xenophobia and intimidation. For years, efforts to repatriate Rohingya to Myanmar have stalled over the ethics of returning them to a country where conditions have only worsened since a 2021 coup that triggered civil war. Some fear Malaysia’s return scheme will erode existing protections. “Whether or not Rohingya are among those returned, this could set a troubling precedent,” said one UN official in the region, speaking anonymously because they were not authorised to talk to the media. “Other countries in the region could follow suit despite ongoing risks in Myanmar.” With many Rohingya sequestered inside detention centres with reportedly dire living conditions, it is hard to judge how voluntary the repatriations are. “Given the choice, I don’t think anyone wants to stay there,” said Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with NGO Fortify Rights. “They would rather risk their lives and go back home.” The Myanmar government has pledged a “safe and dignified” welcome. But it is unclear where the Myanmar navy ships slated to carry them will dock and what their future holds. Myanmar-based activist Mohammad fears any fellow Rohingya may be sent to impoverished and besieged displacement camps in Rakhine. Four residents recently died there in a suspected cholera outbreak, while both sides of the civil war are accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. “I feel extremely helpless,” said 26-year-old Mohammad. “They don’t recognise us as human.” But he struck a note of resilience: “While they don’t count us as people, I still have my own life and hope – because I was born human.” Yap of Fortify Rights said the Rohingya are being treated as “bargaining chips”. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is “politically embattled” and “wants to be seen as powerful on immigration enforcement” ahead of the election due by early 2028, he said. Myanmar, meanwhile, is seeking favour from Malaysia as it tries to shake off its post-coup pariah status. Anwar has invited coup leader turned civilian president Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit in a bid to expedite the repatriation. It would be the first such welcome since the coup for Min Aung Hlaing, named as a chief architect of the Rohingya crackdown in numerous legal cases. The Myanmar military claims the campaign was targeting insurgents, but the International Court of Justice is weighing whether it constituted genocide. Caught between a hostile adoptive home and a motherland that denies their rights, Rohingya migrants in Malaysia, like 30-year-old Asif, face an agonising choice. “I get a headache just thinking about where to go,” he said.

title: ChinaAMC launches 3 Hong Kong ETFs as demand for targeted strategies grows
description: Funds eye potential mainland investor participation and could join ETF Connect within six months, asset manager says.
content: China Asset Management (Hong Kong), the offshore arm of one of mainland China’s largest asset managers, launched three exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in the city on Thursday, expanding its product line-up as investors seek more diversified strategies amid market volatility and a broader boom in the ETF market. The three products – a Hong Kong high-dividend ETF, a Hong Kong growth ETF and a Hong Kong-US “Halo” ETF – are scheduled to list on the Hong Kong stock exchange on September 30, with trading counters in Hong Kong dollars, yuan and US dollars. “Hong Kong’s ETF market is expanding beyond broad market access as investors seek products that serve more specific roles in their portfolios,” said Tian Gan, CEO of ChinaAMC (HK), at a media briefing on Thursday. “By offering both Hong Kong-focused and cross-market strategies, this launch can also reflect Hong Kong’s role in connecting local and international markets.” The high-dividend ETF tracks 50 Hong Kong-listed companies selected on factors including dividend consistency, profitability and volatility. Its underlying index recorded an annualised dividend yield of about 7 per cent in the 12 months through August, while the fund was designed to provide monthly distributions, according to the company. The growth ETF selects 50 Hong Kong-listed companies based on earnings growth, profitability and cash generation across sectors including industrials, healthcare, financials, energy and consumer businesses. The third product, touted as Asia’s first ETF built around the Halo theme – short for “heavy assets, low obsolescence” – invests in 60 Hong Kong- and US-listed companies with substantial physical assets and relatively low obsolescence risk across sectors such as resources, infrastructure and technology. The launch comes as Chinese regulators have taken steps to encourage mainland institutional investors to increase their exposure to Hong Kong-listed assets, potentially adding another source of demand for the city’s fast-growing ETF market. Last month, the National Financial Regulatory Administration (NFRA) said it would support mainland insurance funds investing in ETFs through schemes like Stock Connect, which allows cross-border trading between mainland Chinese and Hong Kong financial markets. ChinaAMC (HK) said the three funds were structured with potential mainland investor participation in mind and could become eligible for ETF Connect within about six months if they met relevant requirements. The products, however, were not developed “specifically for mainland insurers”. Recent regulatory moves had made the environment for cross-border investment “increasingly favourable”, Gan said. “I firmly believe that over the next five years, more mainland institutional and individual investors will participate in the Hong Kong market through compliant channels and cross-border schemes.” Mainland China’s ETF market is growing rapidly. The combined assets of the country’s 53 bond ETFs surpassed 1 trillion yuan (US$149 billion) for the first time as of Wednesday, up from 829 billion yuan at the end of last year, according to data compiled by China Fund News.

title: Asian Games, day 5: rowing gold completes medal collection for Hong Kong’s Chiu
description: Chiu Hin-chun chases down leaders to claim title in lightweight men’s single sculls, adding to medals won in Jakarta and Hangzhou.
content: Chiu Hin-chun completed his set of Asian Games medals on Thursday, winning gold for the first time in the lightweight men’s single sculls final. The Hongkonger was tracking second for the first half of the 2,000m race, trailing just 0.63 seconds behind leader Firdavs Akhunov of Uzbekistan. But the 32-year-old managed to hold on and took the lead with 500m to go, before crossing the line first in six minutes and 50.32 seconds. Akhunov could not maintain his pace and dropped out of the medal places completely. Iran’s Amirhossein Mahmoodpour Shahrestani claimed silver in 6:52.59, with South Korea’s Park Hyun-su sealing bronze in 6:53.35. Chiu won silver in the lightweight category at the Jakarta Games in 2018, and took bronze in the men’s single sculls in Hangzhou three years ago. “I’ve been to three Asian Games, since 2018,” Chiu said. “I got silver the first time, bronze the second time in Hangzhou, and I wanted this very badly because I had to collect all three colours of medals at the Asian Games. Now I have succeeded. “I’m very excited. I want to thank my family for coming over to Japan to support me. The weather wasn’t really nice, the typhoon made it complicated, but they still came. I really appreciate that.” Soon after, Lam San-tung and Chan Tik-lun won the bronze medal in the lightweight men’s double sculls, finishing in a time of 6:24.84. Gold went to the Uzbekistan pair Shakhzod Nurmatov and Sobirjon Safaroliyev in 6:19.94, with silver taken by Indonesia’s Rafiq Wijdan Yasir and Ali Mardiansyah in 6:23.41. “We tried our best and I think we did pretty well,” La said. “We prepared for the Asian Games with the ultimate goal of winning the gold medal, but it is what it is, so we won the bronze medal, and we are still pretty happy with that.”

title: Chinese drug loberamisal extends stroke treatment window from 6 hours to 2 days
description: Large-scale clinical trial with nearly 1,000 patients from 32 hospitals delivers 13 per cent leap in recovery over standard care alone.
content: Chinese medical scientists have shattered the brief window of time available to limit stroke damage, effectively shielding injured brain cells and dramatically improving the odds of a full recovery. Brain cells start dying within minutes of a clot blocking an artery, leading to facial droop, affected speech and in severe cases, paralysis or death. Emergency treatments, such as clot-busting drugs or surgery, must be given within a maximum of six hours. According to a study published by the top-tier Journal of the American Medical Association on September 10, clinical trials of the drug loberamisal found it was possible to expand the time available to 48 hours. The large-scale multicentre phase 3 trial found that 70 per cent of patients who received loberamisal intravenously within two days of a stroke regained complete functional independence – an increase of 13 percentage points over standard care alone. In just three months, they were able to resume their daily lives with no significant disability, according to the research team led by Wang Yongjun, one of China’s leading neurologists. Wang, a co-responding author of the paper, is vice-president of Beijing Tiantan Hospital, affiliated with Capital Medical University, and director of the neurology centre. “Among patients with acute ischaemic stroke treated within 48 hours of symptom onset, intravenous loberamisal, compared with placebo, resulted in a higher proportion of patients achieving complete functional recovery at 90 days,” the team wrote. Nearly 12 million new cases occur worldwide each year, meaning that on average there is someone suffering a stroke every three seconds or less – roughly the time it takes to read this sentence. Common treatments for stroke include intravenous thrombolytic therapy and endovascular thrombectomy. Yet, a considerable number of patients do not meet the indications for these therapies. At the same time, because the damage caused by cerebral ischaemia and hypoxia can be persistent, even if the blood clot is quickly removed, the recovery of the nervous system remains difficult. Loberamisal is a single-molecule multi-target neuroprotective drug that acts as a protective and reparative agent for brain cells, reducing their excitability and blocking neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. After a stroke, it reduces oxygen consumption and inflammation in the brain, saving as many brain cells as possible that have been injured by ischaemia but have not yet died, thus reducing the effects of hemiplegia, aphasia and other symptoms. Similar treatments have been developed in Canada, the United States and Japan but have failed in their trials. The Chinese study involved 998 patients from 32 hospitals. All had experienced a moderate to moderately severe stroke within the previous 48 hours. Typical symptoms included severe hemiplegia, aphasia, visual field defects, or decreased consciousness. Half of the participants were randomly assigned to receive 10 days of intravenous loberamisal therapy while the remainder received a placebo injection. Other treatments remained the same. Ischaemic stroke patients everywhere will benefit if confirmatory studies corroborate these first tantalising results Jeffrey Saver, neurologist At Day 90 of the treatment, 350 of the 502 patients in the loberamisal group had achieved complete functional recovery to the extent that they could fully resume daily work and life activities. Only 279 of the 495 people in the placebo group reached the same criterion, a difference of 13.4 per cent. According to the paper, the types and frequencies of adverse events experienced by the two groups of patients in the clinical trial were similar. The researchers concluded that this showed the safety data was reassuring and the overall results were encouraging. Neurologist Jeffrey Saver, associate editor of the journal, devoted his editorial to the Chinese findings in the same issue of the publication. “For more than 70 years, randomised clinical trials have tested neuroprotective and neuroreparative therapies. Hundreds of promising agents were tested. Tens of thousands of patients enrolled. The result: failure over and over again. Until, perhaps, now,” he wrote. “Ischaemic stroke patients everywhere will benefit if confirmatory studies corroborate these first tantalising results.” Passionate about science? title: Hong Kong vows safe Apec meeting with plans for terror and cyberattack threats
description: Security measures will cover hotels, venues and transport, with contingency plans to respond to terror threats and teams conducting cyber patrols.
content: Hong Kong will introduce security arrangements, including contingency plans for potential terrorist attacks, for the coming Apec meeting to ensure it is held safely and smoothly while minimising disruption to residents’ daily lives, the security chief has said. The Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting will be held in the city for the first time on October 20 and 21, at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from the 21 Apec member economies, as well as representatives of international organisations, are expected to attend. “Many ministerial-level officials will be attending, so we must safeguard hotel security, venue security and transport arrangements for their travel to and from meetings,” Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung told lawmakers at a Legislative Council security panel meeting on Thursday. “All of this must be achieved without inappropriately impacting the lives of local residents; we cannot simply shut everything down and disrupt people’s daily routines.” Tang was responding to lawmaker Erik Yim Kong, who asked what security measures would be put in place for the meeting and how authorities would prevent agitators from using it as an opportunity to endanger national security. Tang said contingency plans would be in place for potential terrorist attacks, while the government would defend against cyberattacks and safeguard national security. He added that the government would ensure the meeting was held safely, smoothly and solemnly. The Immigration Department and Customs and Excise Department would help protect visiting VIPs while making their stay convenient. Authorities would remain vigilant against terrorism, with a contingency plan in place to deal with the worst-case scenario, he said. The police’s cybersecurity and technology crime bureau, the office of the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-system Security) and the Digital Policy Office would also work closely to prevent cyberattacks, Tang said. He added that different intelligence teams would conduct cyber patrols to safeguard national security. Lawmaker Joe Chan Cho-kwong, a retired police officer who was part of anti-riot operations during the 2005 World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference in Hong Kong, told the South China Morning Post that authorities could not rule out the possibility of international groups staging protests at the coming Apec meeting. He recalled that Korean farmers’ groups had pledged in advance to stage protests in Hong Kong, prompting police to hold targeted training. During the WTO event in December 2005, violent clashes broke out in Wan Chai between more than 1,000 protesters, including Korean farmers, and police. “When we looked back at the Apec hosting venues over the past [few] years, we could see which protest groups were present and make targeted deployments in advance,” he said. For the coming Apec meeting, Chan said crowd control measures outside the venue, as well as security arrangements inside the exhibition centre, were expected to be handled by the police force, which would, for instance, run checks for explosives. Law enforcement officers would be in place at designated protest areas to prevent demonstrators from reaching VIPs, he added. Anti-Trump and anti-China protesters gathered in Gyeongju, South Korea, when the Apec summit was held there in 2025. The next major Apec gathering, the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, will be held in Shenzhen in November.

title: Hong Kong’s Gen Z revives herbal teas; experts on couple intimacy: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From a Hong Kong dancer’s creative journey to the rise of bespoke jewellery in Asia, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. All about Hong Kong’s herbal teas and how Gen Z is reviving the health tradition Long before modern chain pharmacies and over-the-counter painkillers were readily available in Hong Kong, there were leung cha: intensely bitter herbal “cooling teas” brewed in massive brass cauldrons in traditional open-front shops. 2. How much sex should a couple have? Focus on quality over quantity Satisfying sex boosts relationship happiness more than frequency, and intimacy thrives on connection, not a number, according to experts. 3. The inspiring story of Hong Kong dancer who started at 48 after leaving Apple Patsy Lo talks about making her latest dance film in Patagonia, being struck down by illness, and why she left Apple to pivot to dancing. 4. Why dementia is preventable – and the new tools that can reduce your risk On World Alzheimer’s Day, we take a look at the advances in dementia diagnosis and treatment, and why much of the risk may be within our own control. 5. Few still make Mid-Autumn Festival lanterns the classic way. This artisan does While mass-produced Mid-Autumn Festival lanterns of every size, shape and style can be bought with a single click these days, a dedicated few in Hong Kong are defying the fast consumerism trend by keeping the objects’ traditional craftsmanship alive. 6. Forget colour analysis – how colour pyramids can help you dress your best Don’t conform to a rigid palette with colour analysis, style experts say – instead focus on proportion, texture and your own preferences. 7. Why wear what everyone else is wearing? The rise of bespoke jewellery in Asia Jewellery with an “emotional connection” is redefining luxury for consumers in mainland China, Hong Kong and Singapore.

title: Authorities may appeal engineer’s non-custodial sentence in Queen Mary Hospital lift case
description: Government seeking legal advice after Law Wing-chai was sentenced to 160 hours of community service for improper submission of safety documents.
content: Hong Kong’s Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) is considering an appeal against the non-custodial sentence of an engineer held liable for faulty lift installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block. The department said on Thursday it was seeking legal advice on whether to apply for a review of lift engineer Law Wing-chai’s sentence after he was deemed responsible for issuing false safety certifications and failing to spot problems that led to malfunctions. Its statement came a day after Law, 54, was sentenced to 160 hours of community service on Wednesday. He was earlier convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates. The court’s decision came a month after authorities revealed 24 of the 28 lifts in the new block of Queen Mary Hospital, the largest hospital on Hong Kong Island, had serious defects. The faults at the new facility in Pok Fu Lam led to delayed services. In August, the Architectural Services Department said the defects had caused the lifts to start or stop abruptly, be misaligned with floor levels, or fail to open. The problems included damaged electronic components, faulty wiring connections and poor workmanship. According to court documents, the EMSD brought two summonses against Law last year. The EMSD said that following Law’s conviction on Wednesday, it notified him that his registration would be revoked, taking effect on October 8. “Following the findings of an earlier investigation, the EMSD suspended the registered lift engineer’s qualification for six months in March 2025,” the department said. “Since the temporary suspension, the engineer has not issued any test and examination reports or safety certificates.” Law was found guilty of producing documents on January 24, 2025, that he ought reasonably to have known were false or misleading in a material respect. He was also prosecuted for issuing a safety certificate for a lift when it or its equipment was not “of good design and construction or was not in a safe working condition”. Under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance, a new lift must be thoroughly examined and certified by a registered engineer as being in safe working order before it can be used. The department added that it would continue its investigation into cases related to the lift works at the new clinical block. “Should any illegal acts be identified, no leniency will be shown and prosecutions will be pursued in accordance with relevant laws,” it said.

title: High office vacancy rates spur bid to rezone Kowloon East site for residential development
description: Planning Department says it has no objection to application but suggests a number of approval conditions to Town Planning Board.
content: With office vacancy rates in Kowloon East remaining high, the Planning Department has indicated it has “no objection” to a request by some developers for a commercial project in the area to be rezoned for residential development. A consortium comprising CSI Properties, Asia Standard International and Chongqing-born property tycoon Cheung Chung-kiu has submitted an application to the Town Planning Board to rezone Harbourside HQ – a grade A office building at 8 Lam Chak Street, Kowloon Bay, which the three parties jointly own – for residential development. The consortium has applied to increase the plot ratio of the site from five to seven to redevelop it into two mixed-use commercial-residential towers – ranging from 30 to 38 storeys in height – that would provide about 1,140 residential units with an average size of around 400 square feet. It plans to complete the project in 2033. The Planning Department said the proposal, which would change the site to predominantly domestic use, was not entirely in line with the planning intention. Nonetheless, it did not consider the proposal would affect the integrity of the Kowloon Bay Business Area. It suggested a number of approval conditions and advisory clauses to the Town Planning Board, such as the submission of a refined building height profile – including rooftop structures – to ensure that the building height of the proposed development would not encroach on the 20 per cent building-free zone of the ridge line. The Town Planning Board will consider the redevelopment proposal on Friday. I believe the negative impact of redeveloping the property into residential use would be minimal, thus the chances of approval are high Alvin Lam, Midland Surveyors Harbourside HQ was formerly known as Octa Tower, a property owned by Nan Fung Group. A consortium led by CSI Properties acquired the building for about HK$8 billion (US$1.02 billion) in 2018 and subsequently carried out extensive renovations. The consortium said in its application that the vacancy rate at Harbourside HQ was 25 per cent. As at the end of 2024, the 22.1 per cent vacancy rate of commercial properties in Kwun Tong district exceeded Hong Kong’s overall vacancy rate of 16.36 per cent. Midland Surveyors director Alvin Lam said Kowloon East’s office vacancy rate was unlikely to improve in the short term. “Harbourside HQ is situated near the Kai Tak residential area and surrounded primarily by commercial buildings,” he said. “I believe the negative impact of redeveloping the property into residential use would be minimal, thus the chances of approval are high.” Alex Leung, senior director at CHFT Advisory and Appraisal, estimated that the land premium would be in the range of HK$640 million to HK$740 million if the redevelopment proposal was approved, which would be equivalent to HK$1,300 to HK$1,500 per square foot. “The premium seems to be relatively low for a plot of land so close to the waterfront,” he said. “This is because the developable gross floor area decreases when changing the use from office – which has a higher permitted plot ratio – to residential.” The consortium said the redevelopment would be in line with the government’s policy of increasing housing supply. A market report released by Centaline Commercial this week said the overall vacancy rate for grade A office buildings in Kowloon last month was 15.7 per cent. It said the vacancy rate in Kwun Tong was 17.13 per cent, a year-on-year increase of 2.36 percentage points, and the vacancy rate in Kowloon Bay was 25.42 per cent, up by 2.43 percentage points.

title: White House reinstates access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico following judge’s order
description: A federal judge had deemed Trump’s ban of the news outlets as likely to be unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored.
content: The White ⁠House said on Thursday it has reinstated journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after a federal judge deemed US President Donald Trump’s ban of the three news outlets likely to be unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored. The midday reinstatement came after a chaotic few hours earlier on Thursday when the journalists continued to be blocked from entering the White House grounds. That prompted the three news organisations to request an immediate hearing before US District Judge Tim Kelly, who issued his decision overnight. Kelly, acting in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Monday, ordered a halt to Trump’s ban for 14 days in a press freedom case that has played ‌out over the past week in the courtroom and White House grounds. Kelly found that the revocation of the White House credentials of the journalists “likely violated their constitutional due process rights”. The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice Department’s national security arguments for justifying the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage. Hours after Kelly issued his order, CNN, MS NOW and Politico told the judge they remained barred, and asked for the emergency hearing. Politico said its reporter’s credentials were confiscated. An MS NOW reporter said she was blocked from the White House. CNN said some of its staff members were denied entry to the grounds. In response, Micah Stopperich, the director of press operations at the White House, said in a court filing that the White House began the process of reinstating press badges for affected reporters at 7.25am and that the “White House ⁠press team dropped badges at the entry gate for members of the press to pick up around 9.55am”. After receiving Stopperich’s declaration, the judge denied the request by the news organisations for an emergency hearing but gave them an opportunity to tell him of any ‌factual developments later in the day. The sharpest conflict yet between Trump and the press played out during a key diplomatic moment for the US president: his appearance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and his hosting of Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday. It was unclear whether members of the White House television press pool would reinstate their coverage following CNN’s return to the White House. Earlier this ‌week, they had suspended pooled coverage in solidarity with CNN. There were no television pool cameras set up for Xi’s arrival on the White House’s South Lawn on Thursday morning, and FOX News, MS NOW and CNN did ⁠not broadcast the two leaders’ arrival ceremony live. During Trump’s welcome ⁠of Xi to the White House, the president made a joke to photographers in the Oval Office about the Chinese having the friendliest press corps. CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering ‌the president, take turns organising coverage and provide footage to other outlets. CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the General Assembly on Monday but was not able to provide a pool feed. Trump announced the ban on Friday on his social media platform, saying those news organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report ‌FICTION and ‌LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”. Trump framed their reporting as a threat to US national security. The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and ‌a free press, as well as their due process rights. A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations, including Reuters, later filed a legal brief supporting the three news outlets. Judge Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and stop ⁠enforcing the ban for two weeks. The judge rejected the administration’s stated national security concerns. “The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court ⁠orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” Kelly wrote. In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention. Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the three outlets, welcomed the judge’s decision in a statement, saying: “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate ‌the court’s swift action.” Although other presidential administrations have battled with ‌the press, Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. Upending decades of tradition, his White House had denied basic access to many major news organisations, launched personal attacks on journalists and filed multiple lawsuits against news organisations. Kelly’s ruling came a day after Trump experienced another legal setback. On Wednesday, an Iowa judge dismissed Trump’s 2024 lawsuit against the Des Moines Register newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer. Trump sued the Register, its parent company Gannett and Selzer over a poll published ahead of the November 2024 US election that showed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris leading him in Iowa. Trump accused the newspaper and its long-time pollster of fraudulently misleading readers. In his ruling on Wednesday, Iowa District Judge Scott Beattie said the poll was legally protected speech.

title: Tencent rolls out payment app for foreign travellers ahead of Apec summit
description: The app allows overseas visitors to make payments across WeChat Pay’s network using foreign cards and digital wallets.
content: Tencent Holdings on Thursday launched TenPayGo, a mobile payment app targeting foreign visitors, as the tech giant seeks to capture China’s growing inbound tourism market ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen. Developed by Tencent’s WeChat Pay team, TenPayGo allowed international travellers to make payments at tens of millions of shops, restaurants and attractions across the WeChat Pay network by linking their credit cards or their home-country digital wallets to the app, according to a company announcement on Thursday. The app supports seven international card networks, including Visa and Mastercard, as well as about 60 overseas digital wallets, with Starryblu from Singapore among the first batch of partners. Previously available in limited test versions on Apple’s App Store and Google Play, the app requires an email address to register, offering a simpler onboarding process for overseas travellers. Many apps in China require users to sign up with a local phone number. Beyond mobile payments, TenPayGo allows foreign visitors to access Shenzhen’s buses and metro systems using a QR code within the app, eliminating the need for a local phone number or a physical transport card. Leveraging Tencent’s artificial intelligence capabilities, the app also offers instant menu translation to help users order food and allows them to identify objects by scanning and circling items on the screen. Tencent was also working with local banks to add a tax-refund feature, according to the company. The launch of TenPayGo, Tencent’s first mobile payment app designed specifically for international visitors travelling to China, comes as the company’s home city prepares for an influx of foreign visitors during the Apec summit. Shenzhen, a tech hub in southern China’s Guangdong province, will host this year’s Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in November, becoming the third Chinese city to do so after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. The launch also underscores Tencent’s efforts to tap into a rise in international arrivals in recent years. Tencent has been expanding its support for international digital wallets, allowing travellers to use them to make payments in China through their domestic apps without downloading WeChat. Its partnership with PayPal earlier this year enabled US travellers to pay WeChat Pay merchants in China directly through the PayPal app. As inbound tourism gains momentum, transactions made through overseas accounts on WeChat Pay in China surged by more than 80 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, in both volume and value from a year earlier, according to Tencent.

title: Milei renews Argentina’s Falklands claim, rails against ‘useless’ UN
description: Firebrand Argentine leader calls world body a ‘useless organisation’ filled with ‘arrogant parasites’.
content: Argentine President Javier Milei reaffirmed Argentina’s claim to sovereignty over the islands known to Britain as the Falklands and to Argentines as the Malvinas, calling it a key issue for his nation and urging the parties to find a “peaceful solution” as tensions with London over the disputed archipelago grow. “The Malvinas for us is a national cause,” Milei, a strong ally of US President Donald Trump, said Wednesday while addressing the UN General Assembly in New York. Milei accused the United Nations of failing to enforce international resolutions that urge the parties to “refrain from introducing unilateral changes while the dispute remains unresolved”. He also called on Britain to resume negotiations to “find a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute”. “The Malvinas issue is not merely a matter between Argentina and the United Kingdom; it is also a question regarding this organisation’s ability to enforce its own resolutions,” he said. Milei has recently stepped up his efforts to draw attention back to the islands after facing some criticism of his strengthening ties with Britain and his professed admiration for Margaret Thatcher, who in 1982 led the British campaign to retake the archipelago during the Falklands War. Following Argentina’s invasion of the Falklands under the country’s then-military dictatorship, Thatcher sent a task force all the way down the Atlantic and retook the islands after just 73 days of Argentine control. The war killed 649 Argentine and 255 British troops. Earlier this month, Milei escalated the dispute with Britain, vowing new measures to halt an oil project near the British-controlled archipelago and praising Trump for saying Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. His government last week introduced a sweeping security bill that would toughen sanctions on companies exploiting resources around the islands without Argentine authorisation, create a national security council chaired by Milei and expand the military’s role in protecting critical Argentine infrastructure. Speaking to global leaders at the UN on Wednesday, Milei intensified his criticism. “Today I come to say that Argentina will not sit and wait for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. He also sharply criticised the United Nations and its role, accusing it of becoming “a useless organisation that serves only to feed a caste of fatally arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”. Against the backdrop of Milei’s recent remarks, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham also addressed the dispute during this high-profile diplomatic week, stating Tuesday that the UK’s position is “clear” and that it will “stand firm” in the face of any threats. “We will defend the right of the ⁠Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British,” Burnham told reporters following a meeting with Trump late Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN. In August, Trump said he was reviewing the United States’ neutral position over the remote South Atlantic archipelago as he criticised Britain for not doing enough to support the US war against Iran. The Falklands, which Argentines call the Malvinas, are a small archipelago of about 3,500 people located around 480km (300 miles) east of the southeast coast of Argentina. They have been a British overseas territory since 1833. In a 2013 referendum, the islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory, with 99.8 per cent voting in favour and just three votes against.

title: MMA makes its debut at Asian Games, but is it fighting a losing battle for recognition?
description: Athletes compete in open space across six weight classes in Japan, with different rules and enhanced safety features such as shin pads.
content: With minimal razzmatazz, an absence of semi-clad women carrying boards, or childish pre-fight hype, little evidence of claret on canvas and certainly no cages, this is not the MMA you know – and that is exactly the way officials want it. The sport made its debut at the Asian Games this week, an important step in a journey it hopes will lead to inclusion in other continental multi-sport events and eventually a place on the biggest stage of all, ideally at the Brisbane Olympics in 2032 if all goes well. Athletes competed in open space across six weight classes in Japan, and among those taking gold was Singapore’s Tiffany Teo, who beat Kazakhstan’s Khilola Sobirova, already a well-known professional fighter, in the women’s traditional 60kg category. For some, the unedifying spectacle of grown men and women beating each other senseless in cages, with flying elbows and kicks to all areas, as fans bay for blood belongs within the confines of the commercial boundaries already set. But the different rules and enhanced safety features – thicker gloves and shin pads among them – on display in Nagoya provide evidence that the competition taking place bears little resemblance to the corporate behemoth that packs out stadiums, and in the case of one, has visibly tied its colours to a very specific political ideology. That particular version would seem ill-suited to the ideals of the modern Olympics, and officials at the newly formed Federation of International Mixed Martial Arts (Fimma) would not necessarily disagree with you. “Number one is the removal of the cage or a ring ... we reduce the perception that the cage advocates violence,” Galastein Tan, the Fimma director general, told the South China Morning Post. “The focus here is, while you see the techniques between the modern and traditional athletes, we ensure and mitigate the risk of injuries to the athletes. “This is not a one night win-it-all and that is that. It’s important to note that we have a different pathway that we are taking to the youth. They can go pro in the end if they want, or they can stay amateur and be more Olympic.” According to Tan, when Fimma president Gordon Tang was in the process of launching the federation in 2022, he specifically looked at a rule set that was “more aligned to Olympic values and focused on the athletes’ safety and well-being”. The pathway is designed to allow those athletes with little desire to feed the public’s bloodlust to pursue their sport and achieve the recognition medal success brings. Teo believes Asian Games and Olympic status could ultimately encourage a new generation to take up the sport. “I think it will grow the talent pool a lot,” she said. “It will encourage more children and teenagers to take up the sport and take it seriously. “Because now there’s a clear pathway, right? You can join a national team, the next step you can go to the Olympics.” Although in a world becoming more acutely aware of the damage repeated blows to the head can cause later in life, there is also the debate over whether the kind of violence that is the sport’s lifeblood is something to be encouraged. That is one of the reasons that the rules governing MMA for the Olympics specifically say no head shots at youth level. When fighters become adults, as with everything, it is up to them to assess the risks. Alexander Engelhardt, who is Fimma’s executive vice-president, did not want to make comparisons with other sports, and said that while MMA had begun as an amalgamation of other disciplines, it now stood as a sport on its own, and there was more to it than just trying to knock someone out. “You have so many other techniques that you can learn and develop,” he said. “And even if you look at the fights and everything, in some sports you have a lot of focus only on the head, here you have a lot more techniques that you can do, which makes it also less focus on only punches or kicks to the head.” Then, of course, there is the debate over whether the Asian Games should have added to an already unwieldy list of events that has caused no end of headaches for organisers in Japan. Cruise ships and converted containers were supposed to only hold around 15,000 people, a number the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) blew past when it also invited the likes of padel, surfing, and for some reason virtual taekwondo – as if the real one wasn’t enough – to make their debuts. Fimma are obviously delighted to have been included, Tan called it “a big moment for us”, and hinted that inclusion in other continental Games was expected to follow. Whether those events, and certainly the Olympics, need another combat sport, when boxing, judo, wrestling and taekwondo all exist in that arena remains to be seen. If Tang, who is an OCA vice-president, has his way then it will be one of the others who ultimately lose out. “I think if you look at the IOC, with its recent Fit for Future agenda, the IOC is also trying to stay relevant with the modern fans and modern times,” Tang said speaking through a translator. “We believe that this sport is more relevant. “We are not here to compete with the other sports. There is always a review, there’s always the need to increase additional sports into the programme, there may be a need to reduce other sports, but that is something the IOC will have to decide upon.”

title: Could hit musical Hamilton be coming to Hong Kong in 2027?
description: Crossroads Live UK is recruiting for a tour of the Pulitzer Prize-winning musical, while social media posts point to Hong Kong as one stop.
content: Global theatre producer Crossroads Live UK has announced a worldwide recruitment drive for wigs, lighting and automation roles ahead of an upcoming multi-year world tour of the hit musical Hamilton. According to Crossroads Live’s website, the production “will visit a multitude of territories, starting in Asia in late 2026”, with salaries for the roles to be “discussed upon offer”. Meanwhile, recent social media posts appeared to show screenshots of a Hamilton website listing performance dates in Asia, including at the yet-to-open WestK Performing Arts Centre in Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District for November and December 2027. The venue, slated to open next to M+ in 2027, will serve as a performance space for dance, theatre and multidisciplinary productions. It will feature three theatres of varying sizes, a 148-seat hall and a nearly 5,000-square-metre (54,000 sq ft) dance house complete with rehearsal studios and a physiotherapy room. The West Kowloon Cultural District Authority announced on September 21 that the Hong Kong Ballet will be its first resident company. Other dates on the Hamilton tour as shown in the social media posts included Busan’s Dream Theatre from December 2026 to January 2027; the National Kaohsiung Centre for the Arts in October 2027; and Manila’s Solaire Theatre from December 2027 to February 2028. The details regarding the tour schedule could not be independently verified by the South China Morning Post, though the posts have already generated significant anticipation among theatre fans across Asia. The SCMP has reached out to the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority and Crossroads Live UK for comments but has yet to receive an official response. Meanwhile, a source at the National Kaohsiung Centre for the Arts said the performance at the venue remains under evaluation, with confirmation expected in October. Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Pulitzer Prize-winning musical tells the story of American Founding Father Alexander Hamilton, cleverly fusing hip-hop, jazz, R&B and traditional musical theatre to capture the narrative of “America then, told by America now”. Since officially opening in New York in 2015, Hamilton has enjoyed monumental success, winning seven Olivier Awards, including best new musical, and playing to sold-out, record-breaking crowds. Hamilton debuted in Asia during its 2023-24 international tour in Manila before travelling to Abu Dhabi and Singapore. Crossroads Live UK – led by Olivier Award-winning theatre producer David Ian – is also behind the international tours of other smash hit musical productions, including Cats, Chicago and Evita.

title: Italy greenlights return of nuclear power after decades-long ban
description: Parliament clears legal framework for next-generation reactors nearly 40 years after the Chernobyl disaster.
content: Italy’s Senate on Wednesday gave final approval to legislation paving the way for a return to nuclear power nearly four decades after the Chernobyl disaster prompted the country to abandon atomic energy. The measure cleared the upper house 81-51 with seven abstentions. It marks a major step in Premier Giorgia Meloni’s drive to bolster energy security and meet climate goals, even though the construction of possible new reactors is still years away. The bill, which earlier passed the lower Chamber of Deputies, establishes a legal framework for next-generation nuclear technologies. It authorises the government to draft implementing decrees over the next 12 months covering reactor licensing, safety standards, waste management and criteria for future sites. The vote puts Italy on a path towards reintroducing nuclear power after voters twice rejected it in national referendums, first in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster and again following Japan’s Fukushima accident in 2011. Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, minister for the environment and energy security, said the vote marked a historic step forward for Italy. “Nuclear isn’t a return to the past,” he said. “When integrated with renewables, it’s a winning technology, which can give extraordinary results for our energy security.” Meloni’s government argues that rising electricity demand, climate targets and energy security concerns exposed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine justify bringing nuclear energy back into the country’s power mix. Rather than reviving the large reactors of the past, the government is focusing on small modular reactors, or SMRs, and other advanced technologies that supporters say could be safer, more flexible and quicker to build. The legislation does not authorise the construction of any reactors. Instead, it creates the regulatory foundation needed before future projects can be proposed, assessed and approved. Italy was once among Europe’s nuclear pioneers, operating four reactors before a 1987 referendum effectively ended the programme. Since then, the country has relied heavily on imported energy and has become one of Europe’s largest consumers of electricity generated by nuclear plants in neighbouring countries. The government says electricity demand could rise substantially in coming years as homes, businesses and transportation become increasingly electrified and as data centres and other energy-intensive technologies expand. Italy’s move comes amid a broader European debate over nuclear power’s role in cutting carbon emissions and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. Countries including France and Poland are investing in new nuclear projects or planning major expansions.

title: Thailand’s Nene Royal wins America’s Got Talent, pocketing US$1 million
description: The teenage guitar sensation beat nine other finalists after emerging as the clear favourite before the finale.
content: Thailand’s teenage guitar sensation Nene Royal won the US$1 million top prize on America’s Got Talent, capping a viral run that made the 16-year-old a national celebrity and drew support from across her home country. Rattikarn Amloy, better known by her stage name Nene Royal, was crowned the winner during Wednesday’s live results show, beating nine other finalists after emerging as the clear favourite before the finale. During Tuesday’s final, she sang and played guitar on a rendition of “Seven Nation Army” by The White Stripes. “You should win. Give her the million, America,” judge Howie Mandel said after the performance. Fellow judge Melanie Brown praised Nene’s “mysterious, mystical stage presence” before adding, “You’re from the best place in the world, Phuket, Thailand. I love to go there.” “I’m very happy and you know I’m emotional right now,” said Nene, who beat a magician for the win. Her victory caps a rapid rise that began with a swaggering rendition of The Cranberries’ “Zombie”, in which she sang and tore through the song on guitar. The audition amassed more than 200 million views across AGT’s official online platforms, more than any other act this season. Nene’s run sparked an outpouring of support in Thailand, where her international profile drew backing from some of the country’s most powerful business and political figures. Among her most prominent corporate supporters was billionaire Dhanin Chearavanont, patriarch of one of Asia’s wealthiest families. His Charoen Pokphand Foods rented space on a giant screen in New York’s Times Square to feature Nene alongside messages of support from Thai fans ahead of the live rounds. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul also threw his support behind Nene, directing tourism officials to explore ways to promote the teenage guitarist. He also hosted her at Government House, where she played guitar while he sang a Thai rock song. Officials have discussed featuring her in campaigns promoting the country’s “Amazing Thailand” tourism brand. Anutin, who is in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, congratulated Nene and thanked her for showcasing Thai talent to a global audience and helping promote a positive image of the country through music and performance. “Nene’s success is proof that young Thais have the potential to compete with anyone in the world when they are given the opportunity, stay determined and continue to develop their talent,” he said in a statement. Her victory comes as Thailand increasingly looks to entertainment and popular culture to bolster its global profile and tourism appeal. HBO’s The White Lotus recently showcased the country’s luxury resorts and tropical scenery to an international audience, spurring interest in its Thai filming locations. For Nene, the US$1 million prize marks a remarkable ascent from the Phuket night market where she once played for donations. She started playing at seven on a 1,600 baht (US$48) guitar, a considerable expense for her family at a time when her father earned just over 10,000 baht a month. To help pay for lessons, he encouraged her to perform at the market. After her performance in Tuesday’s final, Nene reflected on how far she had come. “I was so young when I touched the guitar,” she said. “I was thinking, in my mind, I was like ‘I really want to become a rock star.’ My dream comes true.” Her school in Phuket held watch parties for students and teachers, and said in a social media post on Thursday: “You did it, congratulations, champion. We are so proud of you.” The Phuket night market where Nene cut her teeth also hailed her as an inspiration. It said: “This victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream.” Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Morgan Stanley ‘fat finger’ leak of confidential deal pipeline sets off alarm bells
description: Morgan Stanley says it ‘promptly took steps to address this inadvertent sharing of information’ and that it is engaged with relevant parties.
content: The inadvertent disclosure of confidential information by a Morgan Stanley employee this week alarmed Hong Kong’s banking industry, listed issuers and regulators, according to several sources familiar with the matter. An email sent by the Hong Kong-based employee on Tuesday afternoon included an attached file with details on more than 100 deals in the pipeline, including initial public offerings (IPOs), private equity arrangements, pension fund positions and other projects in Greater China, India, South Korea, Australia and South Asia, according to the sources, who requested anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The document gave the names of companies and institutional investors involved in the deals, which included pitches, ongoing discussions and those that had been put on hold, they said. Although Morgan Stanley later sent another email asking those who received the one sent in error not to open the attached file, the deal list had already been widely circulated in the financial sector, according to the sources. “Almost every banker in Central got hold of this list,” a source told the South China Morning Post. “Some even put it on social media. The companies on the list are of course extremely unhappy about the leak.” In a statement issued on Thursday, Morgan Stanley said it “takes client confidentiality extremely seriously”, adding that the bank “promptly took steps to address this inadvertent sharing of information and we continue to engage with relevant parties”. Hong Kong’s market regulator the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said all investment professionals needed to properly handle confidential information. “Whilst we do not comment on individual incidents, the SFC expects intermediaries to have robust internal controls in place to protect their clients’ confidential information and prevent data leakage which may harm the interests of their clients or impact the integrity of the market,” an SFC spokesman said in a statement provided to the SCMP. The US investment bank was the second largest bookrunner in IPOs and other equity fundraising in Hong Kong in the first half of this year, handling 19 deals worth US$4.7 billion, according to data from LSEG Data & Analytics. Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary ­president of the Institute of Securities Dealers, said investment banks needed to take measures to prevent such errors. “It is obviously a fat-finger error, but the result is disastrous as it sent out confidential information to the market,” Chan said. “All investment firms should have internal controls to protect clients’ confidential information and price-sensitive information. There should be measures in place to prevent these files from being easily sent out without approval by the company.”

title: Video of US military adjusting red carpet for China’s Xi sparks online backlash
description: 12-second clip goes viral, with US commenters drawing comparisons with Trump’s treatment of other world leaders.
content: A video clip showing uniformed US military personnel on their hands and knees making last-minute adjustments to a red carpet has gone viral online, with critics pointing to the lavish welcome President Donald Trump rolled out for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews. The 12-second clip, which circulated widely on US social media, captured several service members hurriedly smoothing and cleaning the 30-metre (98-foot) carpet moments before Xi emerged from his aircraft. Chinese officials – including Foreign Minister Wang Yi and the ministry’s protocol chief Hong Lei – can be seen watching the operation from the aircraft doorway. Trump delivered an unusually lavish welcome. It is rare for a US president to greet a foreign leader plane-side at Joint Base Andrews. In 1962, John F. Kennedy travelled to the base to meet the British prime minister Harold Macmillan as he landed. The ceremony this time included military flyovers by two B-1 Lancer bombers, six F-16 and six F-22 fighters, along with honour guards and a 21-gun salute. Trump and first lady Melania Trump were at the foot of the aircraft stairs to greet Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan as they descended. The brief clip drew immediate criticism from some US social media users, who described it as degrading to American military personnel given the geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing. One commenter said it was “freaking shameful” while others drew comparisons with Trump’s treatment of other world leaders. “[Russian President Vladimir] Putin and Xi get the red carpet treatment. Volodymyr Zelensky and Carney get the cold shoulder. Shows you who Trump views as his allies.” Amy McGrath, a former Marine fighter pilot and Democratic Party politician from Kentucky, commented that US service members did not “swear an oath to be props in some authoritarian ego-stroking spectacle”. The episode underscores the different approaches to diplomatic ceremony of the two superpowers. For Beijing, where protocol and the concept of “face” carry profound political weight, such welcoming ceremonies are painstakingly prepared to the finest detail. Washington’s more improvised approach reflects a different institutional culture, less focused on ceremonial perfection. While the viral footage provided critics with potent ammunition, analysts cautioned against reading too much into the ceremonial polish, emphasising that both countries retained formidable capabilities in their respective spheres of influence. An airport greeting is one aspect of China’s elaborate diplomatic choreography. When Trump visited Beijing in May, he was greeted by Vice-President Han Zheng, a senior state-level official who, despite not serving on the Politburo Standing Committee since 2022, holds a more elevated position in the national hierarchy. The lavish welcome for Xi comes as Trump’s US$400 million White House ballroom remains under construction, roughly 65 per cent complete and not expected to be finished until August 2028. Trump has long complained that the White House lacks a proper large-scale venue for hosting state dinners and major events, forcing the administration to rely on temporary facilities.
