title: Mouthing Off | Are Hongkongers getting bored of weekend trips to Shenzhen?
description: Andrew Sun suspects the novelty of shopping and dining weekends in cheaper Shenzhen is waning, with relaxed time at home more appealing.
content: Are Hongkongers starting to get bored of Shenzhen? Lately, when I ask friends and acquaintances if they have any weekend plans north of the border, there is a lot less enthusiasm in their replies. I see a lot of shrugs, or people saying they don’t know when they’re going next. I have no exact figures but anecdotally, the people around me are not doing as many day trips to our neighbouring city. I cannot say if there is an actual decline in traffic. In fact, the evidence might point to the contrary. After all, a lot of people cross back and forth across the border daily for work and school. But getting across the border from Hong Kong Island takes at least an hour by MTR, bus or car. Yes, the high-speed rail is faster, but it is more expensive, and unless you are just heading to the central business district in Futian, you need to change to another mode of transport to get to any other part of the city. For a return trip, we’re talking a minimum of two hours’ travel. Yes, the range of dining, the quality and – of course – the prices are what make excursions to Shenzhen so appealing. A HK$500 (US$64) meal in Hong Kong might only cost HK$250 in Nanshan district. A massage or beauty treatment is also cheaper, while Sam’s Club and Costco will save you grocery money – assuming you are prepared to cart home bulk supplies of toilet paper, noodles and other amenities. For working folks, that can amount to a significant chunk of change saved, but it also takes a lot of work and effort. I am sure there are budget-conscious residents who plan shopping errands in Shenzhen, but most of my friends do not do day trips for discounts. They were going for entertainment and dining fun. After a couple of years of such diversions, I suspect the novelty of spending weekends in Shenzhen is waning. If I had to wade through crowds in train cars and border checkpoints every week, travel fatigue would set in really quickly. Sure, there are people eager to explore even farther inland in the Greater Bay Area, even buying holiday homes in Zhuhai or Zhongshan. However, it feels like just as many Hongkongers who once readily headed for the border are starting to prefer to chill at home on a weekend. As comedian Bill Maher says: I don’t know it as a fact, I just know it’s true. Perhaps the Hong Kong-Shenzhen dynamic is gradually morphing into one closer to that between New York and New Jersey. In general, Manhattan residents do not cross into New Jersey just to shop or eat, even though it is usually cheaper. In actuality, young Jerseyans gravitate to the lights and glamour of New York when they want to have some fun. Perhaps this is the goal Hong Kong should aim to (re)create. We are never going to be a cheaper location, but we should aim to be the place everybody else wants to be. Then again, Shenzhen is not New Jersey.

title: 1,700% share surge for Chinese state-owned compressor maker exposes risks of new listings
description: Bourse operator dampens ShenGu Group frenzy, but large population of individual investors and exchange rules make IPO speculation likely.
content: A more than 1,700 per cent share-price surge by a new listing on the Shanghai Stock Exchange last week put a spotlight on a state-owned industrial compressor manufacturer, leading the bourse operator to intervene to curb speculative trading. ShenGu Group, a maker of centrifugal compressors in northeast China’s Liaoning province, grabbed headlines when its stock soared 1,216 per cent from its offer price two days after it began trading on September 17, with an intraday high on the second day of trading translating to a 1,781 per cent surge. The frenzy triggered immediate action by the Shanghai bourse, which said on Monday that it would closely watch the stock and take disciplinary action accordingly. On Friday, the exchange suspended some trading accounts that it said had caused the abnormal movement. ShenGu also issued an exchange statement warning of the investment risk. The stock’s wild ride highlights the risk of speculative trading by the Chinese stock market’s large population of individual investors, some of whom tend to chase hot trades, small-capitalisation stocks or new listings tied to certain investment themes. Speculators also take advantage of exchange rules that set no limits on how much new listings can rise or fall in each of the first five trading days including their debuts. A 10 per cent daily cap is applied to mainboard listings afterwards, and 20 per cent on the technology boards in Shanghai and Shenzhen. In ShenGu’s case, the stock surged 374 per cent in its debut on September 17 and an additional 178 per cent the following day. In its statement reminding investors that the stock could drop sharply, ShenGu noted that the price-to-earnings ratio was 243 times, versus the industry average of 41.7. The stock dropped by the 10 per cent daily limit to 27 yuan on Thursday, the first day it was subject to the daily cap. A four-day run of declines has wiped out 53 per cent of its value from its record high on Friday. The frantic mood regarding ShenGu has some logical support, as its core business is defined as high-end manufacturing, one of the strategic industries Beijing sees as new drivers for economic growth. The company’s compressors are used in energy and chemical production, and it also makes pumps that can be used in nuclear power plants. “The compressor demand is now expanding beyond traditional petrochemicals to low-carbon and emerging scenarios amid the transition to green energy,” said Li Chengshu, an analyst at Nanjing Securities. ShenGu’s low initial public offering (IPO) price and a small tranche of free-float stock opened the door for speculative trading. Its offer price of 4.39 yuan was among the lowest for IPOs this year, while the initial 211 million shares available for public trading accounted for only 6.8 per cent of the outstanding shares, leaving the share price vulnerable to manipulation. First-half profit for the company fell 2.3 per cent from a year earlier to 280 million yuan (US$41.7 million) as profit margins narrowed, and ShenGu expected full-year profit to fall between 11 and 15 per cent amid a weak macro-environment.

title: Hong Kong police search for woman after man found dead outside building
description: Man, 49, found on chair outside Tsim Sha Tsui building as bar worker charged over alleged role in moving body.
content: Hong Kong police are searching for a woman after the body of her colleague was found on a chair outside a commercial building in Tsim Sha Tsui early on Thursday. Officers also arrested a 28-year-old bar worker, charging him with unlawful burial of a body, operating a drug den and failing to produce proof of identity. He told police he had helped the woman, who also worked at the bar, move the body to a car park. Police said they received a report at about 1.40am about an unconscious man sitting on a chair in a motorcycle parking area outside K11 Art Mall. Paramedics pronounced the 49-year-old man dead at the scene, with the cause of death to be determined after an autopsy. A source said the arrested employee initially claimed he was a passer-by. But further investigations showed that he had found the man inside a toilet cubicle at a bar upstairs on Carnarvon Road. “He, together with the wanted woman, moved the deceased to the motorcycle parking area outside K11,” the source said. Officers found about 50 grams of suspected crack cocaine, suspected drug paraphernalia and around HK$82,000 (US$10,455) in cash at the bar. The woman was described as Chinese, in her thirties, about 1.6 metres (5 feet 3 inches) tall, with a slim build and long black hair. She was wearing a black T-shirt, black trousers and a white cap. A forensic pathologist examined the body at the scene and observed early signs of rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles that occurs after death.

title: Big picture or big deals? What the Xi-Trump summit holds for China and the US
description: The focus may be about diplomatic optics, but reinforcing stability may be an achievement in itself, observers say.
content: With the balance of power shifting between the US and China, the success of this week’s summit hinges not on headline-grabbing deals, but on practical, cautious consensus under a new strategic stability framework, according to Chinese researchers. Media outlets in China have given heavy coverage to President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States, highlighting its “historic, milestone significance”. It follows US President Donald Trump’s Beijing visit in May. Xi’s arrival in Washington on Wednesday dominated state media headlines, with images and footage of Trump greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac in a red-carpet welcome that included honour guards, a military band that played both national anthems, a 21-gun salute and a jet flyover. In contrast, American media coverage of Xi’s arrival was more muted, as the major television networks continue a stand-off with the White House. Those in the White House pool – including ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC – have boycotted coverage of Trump’s public events in protest against his administration’s ban on several media outlets including CNN. Camera crews had set up at Joint Base Andrews in anticipation of a court ruling to lift the ban but dismantled their equipment after a federal judge deferred his decision. As a result, the arrival of China’s top leader was captured by a handful of smaller digital outlets, The New York Times reported on Wednesday. The media chaos underscores the deep partisan strife and divisions in the United States – turbulence that will make it harder for the visiting Chinese officials to set the tone for stable ties during Xi’s visit. Trump has met several foreign heads of state since taking office in January last year, but the high-level airport reception for Xi is particularly unusual. Trump has never greeted a visiting leader at Joint Base Andrews, typically waiting to greet them at the White House instead. When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made her first visit to Washington in March, she was greeted at Joint Base Andrews by US Air Force Colonel Gary Charland, before going to the White House for talks with Trump. This week, Takaichi met with Trump again during the UN General Assembly in New York, a day before Xi’s arrival in Washington. Chinese media gave wide coverage of her landing at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, highlighting that she was met by Japanese officials – with no red carpet, protocol delegation or US officials in attendance. Sun Chenghao, a fellow with the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, said Xi’s airport welcome “sends a clear political signal”. “It shows Trump’s high regard for the Chinese leader and US-China relations, as well as his intent to advance further improvements in relations through head-of-state diplomacy,” Sun said. Several major US think tanks noted in reports this week that the summit would be more of an exercise in diplomatic optics and unlikely to produce substantial progress beyond a temporary extension of the Busan truce. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday local time that the agreement would be extended past its November deadline to January 10. But it is widely acknowledged that the summit is too important to fail – for both sides. Trump’s sinking approval ratings at home are threatening to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, with voters blaming his administration for high prices and a shaky economy. Beijing is also facing domestic pressures. Beyond a sluggish economic recovery, the ruling Communist Party is preparing for its fifth plenum in October – a key gathering to discuss a new line-up of party leaders. “Trump faces midterms in under six weeks. Xi returns home to begin a year-long run-up to next fall’s party congress, where he is expected to secure another five-year term,” Rush Doshi, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a report on Tuesday. Chinese researchers argued that given the turbulence of relations in recent years, securing any tangible agreements or reinforcing existing frameworks would be an achievement in itself. The two nations have a dense, concrete agenda spanning agricultural purchases, aircraft procurement, semiconductor technology, critical minerals and the potential extension of a tariff truce. “Considering the overarching backdrop of competition and even conflict that has defined US-China ties for quite some time, reaching actionable agreements on these specific topics is valuable,” said Wang Yong, director of the Centre for International Political Economy at Peking University. “It is simply unrealistic to expect a single, sudden ‘megadeal’ that resolves all problems at once.” According to Wang, the most profound shift lies in Beijing’s increasingly proactive role in shaping the direction of bilateral ties. This stemmed from a substantive, realigning shift in the power balance, which had forced Washington to recognise Beijing as a peer competitor, he said. Echoing this perspective, Shen Yi, executive director of the Centre for National Security Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, cautioned that anyone who overlooked this shifting equilibrium risked underestimating the value of strategic consensus and ignoring the progress made through established mechanisms. Shen also noted that the vicious cycle of retaliatory tariffs had stopped, or at least had been suspended, indicating that the bilateral economic and trade consultation mechanism was functioning. Furthermore, Washington was gradually coming around to Beijing’s view that bilateral trade and investment offered mutual benefits and that economic ties should not be entirely driven by security. Shen said it would be impossible to iron out all the differences in one or two meetings and that summit diplomacy served mainly to set the overall tone. “Even if the leaders agree only on broad principles, it provides a crucial guiding framework for pushing relations forward, particularly on the Chinese side,” Shen said. “We can maintain cautious optimism that the ‘constructive strategic stability’ framework will be enriched with more substance through incremental, prudent progress.” Wang said Beijing’s priority was to stabilise ties by reinforcing the new strategic framework agreed on at the Beijing summit with practical deals and communication mechanisms, while maintaining normal trade in non-sensitive business sectors. However, execution remains a major hurdle. Shen said the basic challenge was a trust deficit, given the Trump administration’s record of reneging on commitments. The stakes are equally high regarding Taiwan, which Trump has previously referred to as a “very good negotiating chip”. The South China Morning Post reported earlier that Washington was considering delaying arms sales to Taipei ahead of Xi’s visit. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Shen said the “Taiwan card” was historically a by-product of an asymmetric power dynamic. That leverage, however, was fading as China’s strength grew and Beijing reserved the right to counter. “Were the US to take a positive stance on Taiwan, would China not reciprocate?” Shen said. Ultimately, across all flashpoints – including Taiwan – the core dilemma is not whether promises can be made, but whether Washington has the will and capacity to enforce them, according to Shen. “A defining feature of US-China relations is that Beijing’s stance and actions on core national interests remain steady and predictable,” Shen said. “The uncertainty stems from the American side.” Additional reporting by Caroline Lin and Orange Wang

title: Letters | Hong Kong must grapple with water implications of AI race
description: Readers discuss water security as economies pursue artificial intelligence development, and the importance of courts taking into account defendants’ backgrounds.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. As policymakers, business leaders and sustainability experts gathered for Hong Kong Green Week 2026 earlier this month, much attention focused on artificial intelligence as a driver of innovation, productivity and economic growth. Yet one critical issue risks being overlooked: water. The global AI race is often measured by computing power, advanced chips and the rapid expansion of data centres. Behind these technological advances, however, lies a growing demand for both energy and water. Data centres require vast amounts of electricity to operate and significant volumes of water for cooling. As AI capabilities continue to expand, so too will their resource footprint. For Hong Kong, this poses an important question. The city has long benefited from a reliable water supply, supported by six decades of cooperation over Dongjiang water. Yet climate change, increasingly variable rainfall and growing pressures on shared resources mean water security cannot be taken for granted. While discussions about AI frequently focus on digital infrastructure and energy demand, the implications for water deserve equal attention. This matters because water connects nature, the economy and society. In nature, water sustains rivers, wetlands, forests and coastal ecosystems that support biodiversity and enhance resilience to climate extremes. In the economy, every sector depends on secure water supply, whether for manufacturing, cooling, food production or urban services. In society, water underpins public health, sanitation and quality of life. Meeting these challenges requires a shift from water management to water stewardship. Long-term resilience depends not only on securing supply but also on using water more wisely and protecting the ecosystems that sustain it. Technology can play an important role. Waste water recycling, water reuse and efficiency improvements can reduce pressure on freshwater resources while supporting economic development. Around the world, treated waste water is increasingly viewed as a valuable resource rather than a waste product. However, technology alone is not enough. Effective governance is equally essential. Water challenges cut across disciplines, requiring collaboration among engineers, environmental scientists, urban planners, financiers and policymakers. They also span sectors, demanding cooperation among government, business, academia and civil society. For Hong Kong, they are inherently cross-boundary, requiring continued collaboration with neighbouring jurisdictions that share interconnected water systems. Above all, sustainable water governance requires professionalism: ethical responsibility, systems thinking, anticipatory thinking, stakeholder engagement and evidence-based decision making. The AI race may be powered by computing capacity, but its long-term success will ultimately depend on how wisely we manage the energy and water resources on which it relies. Wanxin Li, visiting professor, School of Public Policy and Management, Tsinghua University, and adjunct associate professor, Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Chinese University of Hong Kong Court sentencing cannot ignore context I write with reference to the letter, “Defendant’s background shouldn’t affect sentencing” (September 10). It is unquestionable that victims of sexual offences experience serious adverse effects which permeate various aspects of their lives. Yet, appropriate punishment does not mean neglecting the defendant’s background in sentencing, doling out identical sentences for factually distinct cases or usurping historical protections of defendants’ rights. It is understandable to nurse desires for those convicted of heinous crimes to pay a high price. However, offenders remain an integral part of society. Awarding identical sentences to different defendants risks oversimplification – of the insuperable challenges they may have surmounted, of the influence of upbringing on recidivism. Equality does not mean treating everyone identically. It means treating everyone in light of their circumstances to reach similar objectives. Moreover, apart from deterrence, sentencing aims to rehabilitate defendants. Rehabilitation requires collaboration between the state and the defendant. Considering contextual factors allows courts and law enforcement to implement optimal strategies to promote lawful behaviours and defendants’ reintegration into society. Context-free punishments risk alienating defendants, especially those from disadvantaged backgrounds. This can also exacerbate animosity between the police and defendants – or even their communities. When perusing criminal justice news, we – as law-abiding people – have a propensity to forget that we may also suffer from lapses of judgment and engage in offending behaviour. If that happens, we would also hope that the judge looks at our case in context; that we are not inherently evil, but only fallible as human beings. Contextualisation is the key to a more equitable society. Alexander Clevewood Ng, New York

title: South Korea has ‘pragmatic’ plan for phased denuclearisation. But will North bite?
description: The South Korean president’s proposal reflects the reality that North Korea already has significant nuclear capabilities, analysts say.
content: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s proposal for a phased approach to Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes is a pragmatic response, analysts say, but prospects for gaining its arch-rival’s acceptance remain uncertain. In a keynote speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Lee laid out a long-term, step-by-step sequence for pursuing the ultimate goal of North Korea’s denuclearisation. He had called for Washington to ease sanctions in return for North Korea stopping its nuclear programme in interviews with US media on Friday ahead of his trip to New York. “We can move towards a nuclear-free Korean peninsula by first halting the advancement of North Korea’s nuclear and missile capabilities, followed by a reduction in the medium term,” Lee said at his UN speech. He also urged the establishment of a peace protocol, saying the effort should involve not only the two Koreas but also the United States and China. “The most critical task is to bring an end to this decades-old war on the peninsula and establish a lasting peace regime,” Lee said. “For decades, the two Koreas, along with key countries such as the US and China, have recognised the need for a peace regime on the peninsula and discussed ways to achieve it.” The proposal reflects the reality that North Korea already possesses significant nuclear capabilities and enshrined its nuclear policy in its constitution in 2023, according to Cho Han-bum, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification (KINU). In an interview with The New York Times this week, Lee said sanctions were “not particularly effective”. “I believe there is significant value in a trade-off between sanctions, which are not particularly effective anyway, and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology,” he said. Lee’s suggestion was “a pragmatic approach to the nuclear issue”, Cho said. “However, the North is unlikely to respond as long as Kim and Trump have yet to meet again.” US President Donald Trump has said he plans to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un “later this year” but Pyongyang continues to portray US policy towards it as hostile. Limited impact Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, also assessed the likely impact of Lee’s proposal as limited. “President Lee’s remarks may be appropriate as a message aimed at the international community, but North Korea is unlikely to accept a halt to nuclear activities, which it currently rejects, and the proposal could instead provoke a backlash,” he said. Remaining indefinitely tied to denuclearisation, which Pyongyang has emphatically rejected, would make it difficult to break the deadlock, according to Lim. For North Korea, “denuclearisation and a halt to nuclear activities will inevitably be regarded as essentially the same thing”, said Hong Min, a senior research fellow at KINU. “Ultimately, because the proposal is premised on denuclearisation, it will be difficult for North Korea to respond positively.” The first step should be to secure a declaratory commitment from North Korea to halt further development of its nuclear capabilities, according to Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies. “In light of the stark reality that North Korea already possesses significant nuclear capabilities, the immediate priority is being given to preventing the situation from deteriorating further before pursuing reductions,” he said. Pyongyang’s response to the three-part blueprint for peaceful coexistence and a nuclear-free Korean peninsula presented at the UN could be to counter with its own framework, casting both Koreas as “two hostile states”, Yang added. In his speech, Lee also praised Trump for reaching out to Kim and said South Korea would “devote its full efforts to opening and sustaining the path of dialogue”. This reflected the view that a US-North Korea dialogue could be a catalyst for building a peace regime involving the two Koreas, the United States and China, according to Yang. “This recent message is considered a step forward, as he specifically identified not only the US but also China as key parties,” Cho said. However, Lee would have to persuade Washington of the need for Beijing’s participation, “given the US position critical of China’s involvement”, according to Yang. ‘Self-harm’? Without the demand for denuclearisation, one expert argued that easing sanctions would reward Pyongyang and effectively recognise it as a nuclear state. “Even if all other countries in the world express scepticism over sanctions’ effectiveness, our government must maintain the position that sanctions and principles have to be upheld,” said Yang Uk, a research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies. Lee’s proposal could serve in effect as “a road map towards recognising North Korea’s nuclear capabilities”, he said, describing it as “an act of self-harm that neutralises the means of pressure against North Korea”. Yu Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, however, said Lee was not abandoning the goal of denuclearisation but rather “it can be understood as a step-by-step approach aimed at first halting North Korea’s advanced nuclear and missile capabilities and then connecting that to reductions and denuclearisation”. Questions also remain over how attractive an offer to exchange a halt to nuclear activities for sanctions relief would actually be to Pyongyang. “Given that North Korea has significantly advanced its nuclear and missile capabilities and strengthened ties with China and Russia, it is uncertain whether sanctions alone would provide sufficient incentive for a return to dialogue,” he said. “Therefore, if talks were to actually begin, a realistic approach might involve seeking common ground – such as halting further advancements in nuclear and [balistic missile] capabilities, managing the sanctions regime, and de-escalating tensions – rather than immediately discussing complete denuclearisation.”

title: Milan Fashion Week: Fendi and Jil Sander spring/summer 2027 bring sheer glamour and distorted tailoring
description: Maria Grazia Chiuri’s upbeat, body-conscious runway and Simone Bellotti’s creased textures were the highlights of day two.
content: Italy’s top fashion brands are showcasing their latest collections this week. Prada kicked off Milan Fashion Week with a blockbuster show celebrating one of its signatures, the skirt. Denim label Diesel followed with a very sexy range, the last to be designed by Belgian designer Glenn Martens, who will now fully focus on Maison Margiela, which, like Diesel, is owned by the OTB Group. Here is what you need to know about the biggest shows of day two: LVMH-owned Fendi and Jil Sander, another brand in the OTB stable. Maria Grazia Chiuri is not a designer one would normally associate with sexy clothes, but her latest collection for Fendi was an unabashed celebration of the female body. Chiuri made her debut at the Roman house last season with a predominantly black line-up that had a very austere – almost monastic – vibe. Her second ready-to-wear range for the brand had a much more laid-back attitude. From the riotous soundtrack – a hit parade of Italian ’70s disco tunes – to the nightclub-like set, Chiuri clearly wanted to have fun. The verse “I like my body when it is with your body”, from a poem by American poet E.E. Cummings, appeared in the show invitation and also as a neon backdrop in the venue. Chiuri aimed to convey the sense of intimacy evoked by those words, comparing that feeling to the intimate relationship people have with the garments they wear. Underwear dominated the collection, from lingerie dresses to boxer shorts and bra tops, often paired with chubby furs. Androgynous silhouettes and his and hers outfits blurred gender lines. The line-up included plenty of party get-ups, including diaphanous gowns in powder pink and body-con sequinned jumpsuits. Each look was accessorised to the hilt. Models carried maxi versions of the beloved Baguette bag and wore sparkly bandannas, knee-high stockings and those leather collar necklaces that have already become a signature of Chiuri’s Fendi. It was good to see the designer loosen up and explore a new side of her personality that she was evidently longing to reveal. It’s not easy to evolve the stripped-down aesthetic of a brand like Jil Sander, one of the most beloved and respected houses in the fashion industry. Its German roots and streamlined sensibility have come to define the quintessentially minimalist brand. This was Simone Bellotti’s third show for the label. For spring/summer 2027, the designer wanted to highlight the beauty of imperfection. Tailoring reigned supreme but closet staples like jackets, shirts and trousers were slightly distorted to add an element of surprise. Creased surfaces, crumpled textures, gathered fabrics and asymmetrical hems were some of the elements Bellotti used to convey this idea of unfinished beauty. The mainly monochrome line-up also featured a couple of lovely billowing dresses that floated on the models’ bodies and looked as light as air. The only patterns in the collection came in the form of a printed T-shirt paired with a skirt depicting a Japanese landscape.

title: Chinese archaeologists find 2,200-year-old ancestor of Dragon Boat Festival treat
description: When we eat zongzi or other leaf-wrapped food, we can clearly appreciate that this tradition existed since ancient times, says researcher.
content: When the weather turns warm around June, people all across China gather for the annual Dragon Boat Festival, and one of the most famous dishes from the celebration is the zongzi. Zongzi is a rice dumpling with a delicious filling, wrapped in bamboo leaves before being cooked. The leaves add aroma and flavour to the rice. In mid-August, a group of scientists from China announced they had discovered an ancient ancestor of zongzi made around 2,200 years ago. However, Yong Ge, a study author from the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Paleoanthropology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said it would be a stretch to “directly recognise” the food as zongzi, adding that the comparison is fair but “should not be overinterpreted.” “Well-preserved plant materials are rare, and we currently do not have a distinct route of zongzi evolution. The only unequivocal evidence of a zongzi belongs to the Song dynasty (960–1279), about 1,000 years later than our findings,” said Yong. Yong told the SCMP that what happened in the millennium between “remains a black box”. All that we know is the tradition was passed down, and the material, morphology and function were kept almost the same while spreading to other regions. The timing of the artefacts also aligns with that of Qu Yuan, whose legend is the backbone of the Dragon Boat Festival. The tale goes that Qu was a poet and politician from the state of Chu (1030 BC–223 BC) before he was exiled amid political turmoil. During his exile, Qu wrote poems expressing his love and admiration for the people of Chu. But when the Qin state defeated the state, Qu was in despair and drowned himself in the Miluo River. Villagers would row into the river and throw rice to feed the fish, so that the marine animals did not eat Qu’s body. Eventually, Qu’s spirit appeared before his friends, and he told them to wrap rice in cooking leaves to ward off a dragon. This is why Chinese people traditionally eat zongzi around the Dragon Boat Festival. The team discovered several piles of plant bundles in eastern China’s Anhui province, which appeared to have been tied with a cord. The team picked 12 bundles, untied them, and found brown residue and plant seeds inside. The seeds were a blend of rice, broomcorn millet and foxtail millet. While modern zongzi uses sticky rice, the scientists could not determine whether the ancient version was sticky. Unlike today, the rice was not wrapped in bamboo leaves but in leaves from the Quercus dentata tree, an oak native to East Asia. The cord was made from Poaceae plants, a type of grass. The rice treat was found in a tomb, suggesting it was prepared for a funerary ritual, which makes it impossible to tell whether this cousin of zongzi was a recipe for special occasions or a more common part of the people’s diet. While the dish was more an ancestor of zongzi than a direct one-to-one example, the archaeologists were able to prove that the recipe of wrapping rice in plant leaves, and then cooking them, emerged at least 2,200 years ago during the Zhou dynasty (1046 BC–256 BC). What is remarkable about the discovery is that plant material remains nearly intact for thousands of years. “It is really rare; thanks to the deep burial, the water-logged environment and relative isolation of the air, [the tomb] can be considered like a natural fridge,” said Yong. “Almost all archaeologically discovered plant remains require extreme environments – drought, waterlogged or carbonised – otherwise they will disappear in time.” Yong said the study showed strong archaeological evidence for Chinese legends. “When we eat zongzi or other leaf-wrapped food, we can have a clear notion that this tradition existed 2,200 years ago.”

title: ‘Deep respect’: analysts weigh in on Trump’s red carpet welcome for Xi
description: Elaborate greeting ceremony immediately preceded by extension of tariff truce, both positive early signs for Chinese leader’s trip.
content: With China and the US agreeing to extend a tariff truce that was set to expire in November – and US President Donald Trump giving his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a personal welcome on the tarmac – analysts say the Chinese leader’s state visit has begun on a positive note. The extension will run for two months through January 10, a sign the world’s two largest economies are willing to negotiate broader agreements and build positive momentum despite an increasingly heightened rivalry spanning a range of issues. “While the two-month trade truce extension is shorter than observers originally expected, any extension is a positive sign that both sides can effectively manage their differences,” said John Gong, a professor of economics at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing. The announcement came after Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held an unscheduled meeting at the World Bank headquarters in Washington on Wednesday morning, when the Chinese side proposed a “bigger deal” on trade, according to Bessent. This came on the heels of an eight-hour discussion between the two on Sunday in New York, after which no major deliverables were unveiled despite reports of positive sentiment from both sides. “We’re open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement or examining the bigger deal,” Bessent said on Wednesday, referring to the tariff pause agreed last year in South Korea. “We’re fine with both.” The Wednesday agreement also paves the way for further negotiations between both countries, as the two leaders are expected to meet on two more occasions this year. The gesture highlights the deep respect he and his administration hold for Chinese leadership and the Chinese people Diao Daming, Renmin University of China Bessent said on Monday that the two sides had agreed to meet again in Shenzhen – the southern Chinese tech hub hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in November – and Xi is likely to attend the Group of 20 meeting to be held in Miami, Florida in December. Furthermore, the welcome by Trump and his first lady marked a major shift in protocol, Gong said. “Beyond showing respect for President Xi, Trump used the gesture to send a strong signal to the US political establishment that his China policy would break from that of his predecessors.” Along with the US president’s personal greetings at the airbase – a courtesy not extended to Trump during his Beijing visit in May – the elaborate reception for Xi included a 21-gun salute fired by artillery pieces, a 100-foot red carpet, a 21-person honour cordon and a flyover by two B-1 Lancer bombers. It was seen as an unprecedented display, never before granted to a Chinese president or even leaders of US allies. Graham Allison, a former dean of Harvard University’s Kennedy School of Government, said on social media the welcome indicated Trump’s “unparalleled respect” for the Chinese leader. “President Trump is a master of the art of the show.” Diao Daming, a professor at Renmin University of China’s School of International Studies, said Trump’s appearance at the airport was exceptionally rare in US diplomatic history. “The gesture highlights the deep respect he and his administration hold for Chinese leadership and the Chinese people, underscores the high priority attached to this summit and reflects widespread expectations across American society for stabilised relations, enhanced dialogue and expanded cooperation.” The truce extension also fosters an overall positive atmosphere for future China–US interactions, Diao said. “The extension preserves a crucial window of opportunity for both sides to advance ongoing dialogue and cooperation. The international community undoubtedly expects China and the United States to continue meeting each other halfway and ultimately forge a longer-term trade agreement,” he added. However, the pageantry has sparked fierce political backlash in Washington, casting a shadow of uncertainty over bilateral relations ahead of the US midterm elections. Senate Democrats struck a sharply critical tone hours ahead of Xi’s arrival, accusing Trump of giving the Chinese leader an overly warm reception while potentially weakening US leverage over Beijing on issues ranging from artificial intelligence to manufacturing. “This is a really big deal,” said Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, a former CIA officer and Pentagon official who said she had been involved in dozens of state visits. She said it was “really difficult” to watch Trump “roll out the red carpet” and “fall over himself” to welcome Xi, arguing that economic security, national security and democracy should be at the centre of the visit. Slotkin warned against any agreement allowing Chinese carmakers to manufacture in the US, and said she would be watching for tighter restrictions on shipments of advanced AI chips to China.

title: At UN, Venezuela’s acting president promises elections without setting date
description: Delcy Rodriguez vows ‘democratic transformation’ before the General Assembly while key rival remains exiled.
content: Venezuela’s interim ⁠President Delcy Rodriguez told the UN ⁠General Assembly on Wednesday that the country would hold ⁠elections as part of a transition to “full democracy”, but did not give a specific date for the vote. “I want to make this very clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela,” said Rodriguez, who came to power after American forces captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid. Rodriguez said the government had initiated talks with the opposition and would ‌guarantee the participation of all political forces. She added that national institutions were being prepared for the electoral process. “Venezuela has initiated a process of democratic transformation for its rebirth, an orderly, institutional, and verifiable process, to build a country that is freer for all, more prosperous, and more reconciled with itself,” said Rodriguez. Venezuelan and US authorities have previously emphasised the need for an election, yet no date - not even a tentative one - has been set. The opposition views the selection of an autonomous Supreme Court and National Electoral Council as essential for calling ⁠such elections. Critics say Washington has sidelined the Venezuelan opposition, dropping demands for free elections in favour of oil and investment deals ‌with the interim government. Some US lawmakers have also called for elections, amid criticism that the Trump administration has failed to extract meaningful democratic concessions from Rodriguez’s government. “We have opened a political dialogue with opposition groups aimed at a ‌process with equal conditions for all,” said Rodriguez. Still, Venezuela’s most prominent opposition leader, Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, ⁠has been noticeably absent from talks. Machado, ⁠who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel after living mostly in hiding since a contested 2024 presidential election, has been blocked from returning to Venezuela, her team and ‌media said on Tuesday. She has vowed to return to Venezuela to help with the response to June’s devastating twin earthquakes, frustrating US officials who believe it is not the right time. Machado has ‌been blocked ‌seven times from returning to Venezuela, “as planes have been forced to divert, airlines such as Copa Airlines have been threatened, maritime vessels sabotaged, and ‌neighbouring islands pressured to deny landings,” Comando ConVzla, Machado’s political committee, said on X. Rodriguez briefly met with US President Donald Trump ⁠on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday and praised him for restarting dialogue with Venezuela. Trump and Rodriguez discussed restructuring the South American ⁠nation’s billions of dollars in sovereign debt and Washington pressed for political change, said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “We made that point that in the end, for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election,” Rubio said. The United ‌States has said Venezuela must first ‌stabilise and recover economically before elections can take place. “This is the time to build the nation that many people want to return to,” Rodriguez said, but cautioned that economic recovery “will take time”. Rodriguez asked for the support of the international community as Venezuela moves from “a stage of uncertainty and conflict toward a stage of full democracy, recognised by its own people and the world”.

title: Hong Kong students hospitalised after consuming contaminated drinks at athletics meet
description: Four boys and 10 girls report symptoms; police investigate suspicious beverage distribution near the school.
content:
At least 14 students were hospitalised after consuming free beverages with suspicious pinhole marks found near a sports ground in Hong Kong, leading to a police investigation.
Students from Maryknoll Secondary School in Kwun Tong reportedly posted messages on social media claiming that free bottles of a sports drink had been handed out during lunch on Wing Ting Road, a short distance from the Hammer Hill Road Sports Ground, where the school was holding an athletics meet on Tuesday.
A police spokesman said a parent called the force at about 2pm.
As of 10pm, 14 students had been sent to United Christian Hospital, with half of them later discharged while the rest were listed as in a stable condition.
The four boys and 10 girls were aged between 11 and 17.
Officers visited the site to investigate. Plain-clothes officers were seen searching rubbish bins outside the sports ground and removing plastic bottles carrying the brand name “Scream” for examination.
Detectives also entered the venue to conduct inquiries.
The South China Morning Post has contacted the distributor of the sports drink for comment.
The case has been handed to the Kowloon East district crime squad.
A message posted on the social media platform Threads carried photos of the event.
It read: “We found pinholes in some of the drinks and suspect that an unknown liquid may have been injected into them. Teachers have since collected all the drinks.”
The school said the incident involved food safety concerns after free bottled drinks were distributed outside the venue during its athletics meet by individuals not associated with the school.
After some bottles were found to have suspected damage, the school advised students not to consume the beverages and collected the affected drinks, it said.
The school added it was fully cooperating with authorities and urged parents to closely monitor their children’s health.

title: Style Edit: De Beers Group CEO Al Cook on natural diamonds, Desert hues and traceable luxury
description: Cook says natural stones’ provenance and rarity as well as warm Desert diamond colours are reshaping the jewellery industry as lab-grown prices fall.
content: The diamond industry is increasingly being shaped by AI, according to Al Cook, CEO of De Beers Group. But it’s not the AI you’re thinking of. “For us, AI stands for ‘authentic individuality’,” he told Style at the Jewellery & Gem World Hong Kong trade show earlier this month. “More and more people want purchases that are as individual as they are – something that’s rare and something you can trace back to where it’s from. You can trust that it’s genuine and is going to hold its value.” This is the territory – authenticity, uniqueness and storytelling – on which the world’s leading diamond company has very much pitched its tent. Lab-grown diamonds continue to plummet in price and are now effectively competing with other, less precious stones, rather than with natural diamonds. Cook believes natural diamonds will continue to hold a unique position precisely for that reason. “Across the world, we’re seeing synthetic products attempting to substitute for natural ones. There’s lab-grown meat. When you go online, you’ll see three AI videos for every real one. After the initial excitement, people go back to what’s authentic, individual and meaningful.” He has an optimistic take on the future of the diamond industry, which he says is based squarely on the data. While Covid prompted a boom in diamond sales, as people were unable to travel and were looking for ways to cheer themselves up – and look good on Zoom calls – there was a market decline after the pandemic subsided. In 2025, however, there was a pickup in demand, and that has only grown during 2026. Another reason for optimism is the Desert diamonds campaign launched by the company in 2025. It has helped to shift the focus away from the pure white diamonds that have traditionally dominated the market, particularly where bridal jewellery is concerned, and towards a broader spectrum of hues, from warm whites through to champagne tones, amber shades and cognac colours. The campaign has also been a storytelling triumph, creating a link in customers’ minds between the diamond that adorns them and the deserts of southern Africa that host many of the world’s diamond mines – and in the process creating an entirely new diamond category. A major boost has been the enthusiastic adoption of Desert diamonds by numerous celebrities – most prominently Taylor Swift, who has frequently been seen sporting them, including on her engagement ring. “It started with a marriage of technology and design,” Cook says. “Customers are seeking authentic individuality – that means individual colours: golden, champagne, honey. That made us create Desert diamonds. But it’s coupled with technology that allows us to tell the stories of the African deserts from which they come. It’s a beautiful marriage of origins in Africa and individuality.” The company is also keen to acknowledge consumers’ growing interest in where their diamonds come from and how they are produced. “You need to be able to trace what you’re doing from mine to store, which we’re doing with our Tracr platform,” Cook says. “You need certification by a respected agency. You need verification – using technology to check that what you’ve got is correct. You’ve got to have a fantastic story. “A diamond is something no one needs and everyone wants. We constantly need to tell the stories of diamonds.”

title: Thailand’s solar scheme faces hurdles as low power users turned off by high cost
description: Even with a subsidy, the upfront installation cost still may not make up for future savings and income in poorer households.
content: Toey Wattana Mongkhonnam began thinking about outfitting his family home in Thailand’s northeastern province of Yasothon with solar panels during the Covid-19 pandemic. In his household of five, electricity use rises with the day’s heat, and the monthly bill could range from 1,000 baht to 1,500 baht (US$30 to US$45). “Back then, I checked prices and a rooftop panel system that could put out enough power to run my household’s appliances could cost 100,000 baht to 200,000 baht,” said Toey, a Muay Thai trainer in Kuala Lumpur. Toey’s calculations capture the challenge facing Thailand’s recently proposed 50-billion-baht (US$1.5 billion) rooftop-solar support scheme: whether it can make the switch attractive not just to high-use households but also to those with lower bills who may have less money to put towards the initial cost. The government said on September 2 it aimed to help up to 1 million households install 5 gigawatts of solar capacity on their rooftops, presenting the proposal as both protection against volatile power costs and a way to reduce the country’s dependence on imported liquefied natural gas. A week later, the government discussed the possibility of expanding the target to as many as 1.5 million households. A government representative said on Friday the capacity target had been doubled to 10GW. But whether the scheme achieves that broader reach could depend on more than subsidies. Rules on financing, eligibility and grid connections could determine whether household solar becomes accessible to families such as Toey’s or only to those who use more power with the funds and roofs to install it. Under Thailand’s existing residential rooftop-solar programme, households must pay for the installation themselves before they can enjoy lower electricity bills or income from selling excess power to the grid. The proposed 50,000-baht subsidy may reduce the upfront cost, but the savings a household gets from solar will still depend on how much electricity it uses and when it uses it. Saving over selling Another Yasothon resident, Saenmuang Chaichan, said his four-person household had also considered rooftop solar. “We pay about 1,000 baht to 2,000 baht a month for electricity, and our usage is highest during the day and early evening, especially in hot weather because we run air conditioners and fans,” Saenmuang said. Neither he nor Toey was thinking of making money from selling solar power, they told This Week In Asia. They just want to reduce how much electricity they buy from the grid. That distinction matters, according to Evan Ng, Siemens Energy’s Asia-Pacific energy transformation consulting team lead. Savings would not be the same for every household. Those with higher electricity use, especially during the day, were likely to save a lot because they could offset more electricity bought from the grid, Ng said. But those who use less electricity may not be able to see much savings, while still having to pay the upfront installation cost. In Thailand, residential tariff rises according to higher levels of electricity use, with fuel-adjustment charge applied separately. So the value of each unit of solar energy consumed on site can be higher for households with greater usage. “The 2.20 baht per kWh payment for surplus electricity exported to the grid is relatively low compared with the value of electricity that households can avoid purchasing from the grid,” Ng said. “The economics of residential solar are likely to continue to depend primarily on self-consumption and avoided retail electricity costs, rather than on selling surplus generation back to the grid.” The subsidy could shorten payback periods by about 1½ to two years, said Haneea Isaad, an energy finance specialist at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. But the programme’s impact would depend on the financing structure, system size requirements and eligibility rules. If it were taken up only by households with higher demand, the scheme could exacerbate a “rooftop solar divide”, she said. For lower-income households, direct capital reductions and affordable finance might be more of a draw than higher buy-back payments, Isaad said, because they were likely to consume more of their solar power themselves. Coping mechanism Then there is the question of whether local electricity networks can connect to so many rooftop systems without delays or restrictions. “The constraint isn’t necessarily the number of rooftop solar Thailand can add at the national system level,” Ng said. “The more immediate constraint is how much distributed generation individual parts of the distribution network can accommodate at a given time and location.” Thailand’s thermal generation fleet gave the broader system flexibility, he said. But a local feeder or distribution transformer may not be able to cope with many systems generating surplus power at the same time – such as during periods of high sunshine and low local demand. That can create risks including voltage rises, reverse power flows and transformer overloading. One way around it would be to use smart meter, feeder and inverter data alongside digital network models to identify where new rooftop systems could connect without major upgrades. Such tools could also show where export limits, smart inverters, batteries or more detailed technical assessments might be needed. That would be especially important if Thailand reached its 1.5 million household target, he said. Processing individual applications could be time-consuming, while a feeder-level assessment could show applicants earlier whether their location is likely to face connection constraints. For Toey and Saenmuang, the 50,000-baht subsidy, if it materialises, will help to varying degrees. “It would help a lot and make the decision to install easier,” Saenmuang said. “But if the system we need costs more than that, we would still need some additional savings.” Toey agreed. “My family would still have to find more money to cover the cost of the solar panels,” he said.

title: Opinion | China’s top priority should be wages, not AI
description: China’s pressing economic problem is that ordinary people still have too little money in their pockets.
content: “Whoever wins with AI wins,” US President Donald Trump has declared, dismissing warnings about the risks of developing artificial intelligence too rapidly and citing rivalry with China. The technological competition is real. China has reason to fear becoming dependent on America for advanced chips and AI technology, particularly as Washington has repeatedly restricted its access to cutting-edge semiconductors. China, meanwhile, is directing enormous resources towards AI. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index estimates that Chinese government guidance funds deployed US$184 billion into AI-related companies between 2000 and 2023. I am no technology expert. But as someone who spent 10 years greasing machine parts in a factory, I wonder whether China has got its priorities right. Should winning the AI race be such an overriding national ambition when the country has another pressing economic problem? Namely, ordinary Chinese people still have too little money in their pockets. Last year, China’s nearly 300 million migrant workers earned just 5,075 yuan (US$758) a month on average, up only 2.3 per cent from the previous year. Those in retail averaged 4,382 yuan and those in hospitality 4,208 yuan. Dr Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East at French bank Natixis, describes this contradiction as China’s “dual economy”: one side produces world-class technology and exports, while the other is characterised by stagnant household incomes and weak consumption. “China is pouring extraordinary resources into AI, robotics, EVs, batteries and other strategic technologies,” Garcia-Herrero told me. “But it is being financed in part by financially repressed households: cheap captive savings, weak wage growth and a consumption share of GDP that remains far too low for an economy of this size.” She thinks this reflects Beijing’s prioritisation of technological leadership and manufacturing strength. Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist Yasheng Huang approaches the same problem from another direction. In articles including “How China Forgot Karl Marx”, Huang argues that low wages are not merely an unfortunate by-product of China’s development model; keeping labour costs down has been fundamental to its manufacturing success. He describes China as an “absolute-advantage economy”: competing with America at the high end, in AI, electric vehicles and electronics, while simultaneously competing with much poorer countries in textiles and other labour-intensive goods. His most striking question is not why China exports cars, but why, after becoming the world’s second-largest economy, it remains the world’s largest textile exporter. The answer, according to Huang, lies partly in how little of the economic pie goes to labour. According to his calculations, the share of manufacturing output paid to workers fell from 6.3 per cent in 1992 to 1.8 per cent in 2010, recovering to only about 3.3 per cent in 2024. The problem is not simply that Chinese households save too much. Too little of the country’s income flows to households in the first place. I witnessed the human side of this development model from the factory floor. In 1980, at 16, I began working in a state-owned rocket factory in Nanjing. Since then, China has changed almost beyond recognition. Its workers helped build the factories, roads, skyscrapers and supply chains behind the economic miracle. Yet they have not shared proportionately in the prosperity. And here lies the point: workers are consumers too. Yasheng Huang … describes China as an “absolute-advantage economy”: competing with America at the high end, in AI, electric vehicles and electronics, while simultaneously competing with much poorer countries in textiles and other labour-intensive goods Suppress wages to make products cheaper, and you also suppress the purchasing power needed to buy those products. For years, exports helped compensate for weak domestic demand. But in an age of tariffs, protectionism and geopolitical rivalry, how sustainable is that model? China’s leaders have repeatedly called for stronger domestic consumption. Yet if Beijing wants Chinese people to consume more, it needs to put more money in their pockets through higher wages and stronger social protection. Reducing the burden of healthcare, housing and education would also give households greater confidence to spend rather than save. This is where the debate over AI and wages comes together. AI may raise productivity and create new industries, and China cannot realistically stand aside while America races ahead. But technological progress should serve people, not be an end in itself. Garcia-Herrero also warns that the AI revolution, rather than resolving these contradictions, risks accelerating labour displacement at the wrong moment. The US-China rivalry risks becoming a self-perpetuating technological arms race: Washington cannot slow down for fear Beijing will overtake it; Beijing must accelerate because Washington is determined to stay ahead. Each side becomes the justification for the other’s acceleration. China should not allow this rivalry to dictate its economic priorities. There is more than one measure of national strength. China already possesses extraordinary manufacturing capacity and technological ambition. Its next great achievement should be to ensure the people who helped create its prosperity receive a larger share of it. The real race should not simply be over who builds the smartest machines, but who enables ordinary people to live better lives.

title: China has scrapped two-thirds of its planned coal power plants abroad: report
description: The cutbacks have saved 6.4 billion tonnes of potential carbon emissions, though campaign’s momentum slowed last year, report finds.
content: Five years after China pledged to stop building or financing new coal-fired power plants overseas, the country’s state sector has made “significant progress” towards meeting that goal, though private projects are still being developed, according to a new report. Two-thirds of China’s overseas coal power projects planned five years ago have since been cancelled, a 61.5-gigawatt (GW) cut in capacity that has saved 6.4 billion tonnes of “lifetime” carbon dioxide emissions, the study by a pair of climate-focused research organisations found. In the 12 months leading up to July, 3.4GW of capacity in Zimbabwe was spiked, as well as another 1.7GW in Bangladesh and 1.4GW in Indonesia, according to the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and Philippines-headquartered People of Asia for Climate Solutions (PACS). Chinese state-owned enterprises and banks have made significant headway towards meeting their government’s commitments to shut down overseas coal projects, said Lizzie Frost, a China analyst at CREA, in a statement about the report’s findings. But the report found there had been a slowdown in cancellations over the past year, with projects linked to private Chinese companies still going ahead. Last year, 7.1GW of China-linked coal power capacity was cancelled, while 3.3GW entered construction and another 20.5GW remained in planning, the two groups said. Indonesia has by far the most Chinese-linked coal projects worldwide with 17.1GW, followed by Vietnam with 3.8GW and Pakistan with 3.4GW, according to the report. Most of the coal capacity still under construction is also in Indonesia, where off-grid projects are being funded by private Chinese companies to power local mineral processing facilities and industrial parks. “The continued expansion of coal plants involving private Chinese companies risks breaching the 2021 pledge,” the two organisations said in a statement. President Xi Jinping made a pledge that China would stop building and financing coal-fired power projects in other countries during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2021. The commitment followed a surge in Chinese-linked power projects over the previous years as part of the country’s Belt and Road Initiative – a huge infrastructure-building drive aimed at expanding China’s global trade links. Between 2014 and 2020, about US$160 billion of Chinese-backed coal-fired power plants were planned or announced outside China, the International Institute of Green Finance think tank said. Xi’s pledge appeared to have an immediate effect, with a CREA report in 2022 finding that the number of planned projects had already reduced. In some countries once slated for coal-fired projects, China has turned to renewable energy, the CREA and PACS study found. “Estimated operational China-linked renewable energy generation has already topped the potential generation of cancelled coal projects in Brazil, Tanzania and the UAE (United Arab Emirates),” the report stated. “This signals that coal cancellation makes space for renewable energy transitions and presents new economic opportunities for China and Global South partners.”

title: China-Russia space camp in Malaysia opens to youth in Southeast Asia
description: Private initiative brings together a Russian astronaut trainer and a Chinese science museum to teach ethics and space science in Penang.
content: While major powers compete in militarised space races and state-led megaprojects, a group comprising a Russian astronaut trainer, Chinese science educators and Malaysian collaborators is laying the groundwork for an international youth space camp. Set to be held in Penang’s rainforest eco-park in late 2027 at the earliest, the week-long programme will gather youth from around the region to inspire future spacefarers, scientists and global citizens through physical exercises, immersion in space and natural sciences, and ethical education to build positive personality traits. The project is an initiative in “people’s diplomacy”, as described by Russian astronaut trainer Timofey Egorov, who has co-developed the programme with the Shanghai Science and Technology Museum and Malaysian project initiator Winfred Khoo for children aged seven to 17. Egorov, who works at the Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre just outside Moscow, spoke about the Russian tradition of youth space camps in nature at the Commonwealth of World Chinatowns conference this month in Penang, a Malaysian state known for its rich cultural heritage. “The main idea is not only to become astronauts or scientists who can travel throughout the universe, but the main thing is to become a good human – a good representative of the human race to go to space,” said Egorov, who is also the general director of Russia’s Association Ecology of the Unknown. He said the rigorous screening and training for astronauts in health, psychological readiness, motivation, communication skills and character made them exemplary role models for adolescents at the camp, to help them develop qualities such as openness, respect, mutual understanding, responsibility and gratitude. “When you are in space, you are in a closed volume and isolated from society and any sort of communication. With only a few of your crew, you cannot escape, go home or shut the door in your room. You have to perform your mission for the sake of humanity,” Egorov said. “It is a good thing that Malaysia has its space programme and its astronaut, and this [camp] can be implemented here very well.” Malaysia aims to build and operate Southeast Asia’s first rocket launch pad by 2029 under its national space policy. The country’s first astronaut performed experiments on board the International Space Station over nearly 11 days in 2007. A review essay last year in the journal Space Policy by two researchers at the Malaysian Space Agency urged the country to “act decisively to revive its space industry or risk being left behind in a rapidly advancing global landscape”. “Strengthening this sector is not only critical to staying competitive but is also vital for unlocking space-based solutions that can accelerate national economic growth and technological advancement,” the researchers wrote. Pointing to the International Space Station as one of the most expensive structures ever built, Egorov said: “It became possible thanks to the efforts of many countries … No matter what happens on the surface of the Earth, there is always cooperation in space”. As a partner, the Shanghai Science and Technology Museum is helping to co-develop the curriculum and plans to offer hands-on astronomy lessons, according to Egorov. “I hope they can bring an offline teacher with DIY kits [and deliver] one lesson a day … about the solar system or astronomy.” Egorov said his experience leading space camps in Russia showed that children were drawn to scientific concepts, including quantum effects and special relativity theory. “They can understand complex things if you present them in a way that is interesting to them, with pictures, questions, simple examples, and it will be efficient,” he said. While China expands its space presence with the Tiangong space station and the proposed International Lunar Research Station with Russia, which seeks to maintain its space legacy, Southeast Asian nations are increasingly exploring their own roles in aerospace, satellite launches and the emerging low-altitude economy. Khoo, co-founder of Commonwealth of World Chinatowns, said he started exploring the idea of organising a space camp in Southeast Asia with Egorov more than six years ago. “While we want to inculcate an interest in going into outer space and the ethics of that, we also hope to seed the idea of a new aerospace industry, diverting it from war into a peaceful aerospace programme for space tourism, asteroid mining and commercial activities,” he said. “Space has been the domain of governments and we hope that this sort of ground-up initiative will be a way for the public and individuals to participate.”

title: Asian Games, day 5: teen sensation Ohashi sets world record, Haughey claims silver
description: Japan’s Shin Ohashi wins men’s 200m breaststroke, Siobhan Haughey claims fourth medal of Games, after rowers add gold, silver and bronze.
content: Teen sensation Shin Ohashi laid down a marker for swimming’s best, powering to Asian Games 200m breaststroke gold in a world record time on Thursday. The 17-year-old Japanese swimmer came home in a time of two minutes, 04.83 seconds, shattering the previous best of 2:05.48 set by China’s Qin Haiyang in 2023. Kyrgyzstan’s Denis Petrashov took silver in 2:08.67, while the bronze medal went to South Korea’s Cho Sung-jae, who finished in 2:08.76. Moments earlier, Siobhan Haughey won her second silver and fourth medal of this Asian Games overall in the women’s 50m freestyle, in a race won in record time by China’s Wu Qingfeng. Wu touched the wall in 23.98 seconds, a Games record, while Haughey came in on 24.32. China’s Cheng Yujie was third in 24.46. Haughey had already won silver in the women’s 4x100m relay, and took gold in the 100m and 200m freestyle, titles she won at the previous Games in Hangzhou. It had been another successful day for the city’s athletes, with the rowing squad contributing a gold, a silver and two bronze over the course of their events. There was also a first-ever men’s medal in wushu sanda, and fencing bronze in the men’s individual épée. Rower Winne Hung Wing-yan was the first to get on the podium in the women’s lightweight single sculls, and was followed shortly after in the women’s lightweight double sculls by teammates Cheung Yuen-shan and Leung Wing-wun. Having finished second in her heat the previous day, Hung was in the leading position and held an almost two-second advantage at the halfway point of the 2,000 metres course at Nagaragawa International Regatta Course. The 27-year-old was caught by Fatemeh Mojallaltopraghghale of Iran – who also beat Hung to second in the heat – and trailed by just over two seconds with 500m to go. The gap between the two grew larger and extended to just under four seconds. Still, Hung managed a silver medal, and her first at the regional games, with a time of seven minutes, 28.54 seconds. Mojallaltopraghghale claimed gold in 7:24.57, while Thai rower Parisa Chaempudsa finished third in 7:40.61. Moments later, Cheung and Leung crossed the line in 6:59.24, just behind the Iran duo Kimia Zarei and Zeinab Norouzi Tazeh Kand who took gold in 6:53.93. Japan’s Chika Yonezawa and Chiaki Tomita claimed bronze in 6:59.27. “I’m very happy and excited about this medal,” Leung said. “This is my second Asian Games and I have been a full-time athlete for eight years. This medal shows that all the training over those eight years has been worthwhile.” In the afternoon session, Chiu Hin-chun took gold in the lightweight men’s single sculls, while Lam San-tung and Chan Tik-lun won the bronze medal in the lightweight men’s double sculls. Leung Yu-hong, meanwhile, came off second best to China’s Tang Sishui, losing their 60kg wushu sanda final on points at Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall in Nagoya. Tang scored five points in the opening round and Leung managed only one point in the second. It was the first time Hong Kong had won a men’s sanda medal, and Leung said it made “all the hard work and all the sacrifice” worth it, not that he was getting carried away with the achievement. “I feel peace. I feel calm,” he added. “I didn’t let my achievement define me. I am doing myself. I am who I am. I don’t care how other people judge me. I just focused on my goal.” At the Aichi Sky Expo, Fong Hoi-sun made it into the semi-finals of the men’s individual épée, where he lost 15-13 to Kirill Prokhodov, which was good enough for bronze.

title: Australia slams ‘unacceptable’ OpenAI breach of government health portal
description: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the tech firm took three months to tell authorities about the incident.
content: An autonomous OpenAI programme infiltrated an Australian government health website in June in an “unacceptable” breach, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The artificial intelligence agent accessed public and non-public files of the health statistics service, he told reporters in New York on Wednesday. OpenAI did not raise the alarm with the Australian government until September, when it sent an email outlining the incident to a generic email address. “Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Albanese said. “And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred,” he said. “It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all – and the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox.” Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from both OpenAI and rival developer Anthropic. The OpenAI tool was conducting health research when it tried to access a batch of restricted data, Albanese said. “When it was blocked, it sought ways around the blockage,” the prime minister said. “I think OpenAI knows that they need to have better protocols in place,” he said. “This is a research project that has got into areas that it shouldn’t have.” The prime minister said there was no available evidence of a broader compromise to the government services network. “No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing,” he said. “Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable.” The Australian Signals Directorate is helping with a “forensic investigation” to gain further information, including what other government systems were affected, he said. Defence Minister Richard Marles said the Medicare portal that was breached did not contain individual medical claims, benefit payments, personal banking ⁠details or patient medical histories of Australia’s 27 million people. Instead, the website holds only aggregated data on healthcare use across the country, he said. However, Australia considered the breach serious. OpenAI said a recent review showed a number of Australian government websites may have been affected. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend,” the San Francisco-based company said. Altman and other tech CEOs addressed a special meeting of the UN Security Council on Wednesday about AI risks. More than 100 organisations around the world, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to “strengthen cyber defences” against AI-powered cybersecurity threats. Two OpenAI models escaped from a closed testing environment earlier this year and broke into the internal systems of the AI platform Hugging Face. Anthropic recently discovered that its models had gained unauthorised access to three unnamed organisations during testing that was supposed to keep them away from “real-world” systems. Google’s consumer AI model Gemini hacked multiple systems through guessing login credentials, the company said last week. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Warm welcome, trade truce extended: the takeaways as Xi arrives in US
description: Donald Trump greets Chinese leader on the tarmac in rare gesture ahead of their summit.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping was greeted on the tarmac by his American counterpart Donald Trump on Wednesday – a rare gesture ahead of their summit. It is Xi’s first state visit to the United States in over a decade and the two leaders met each other at Joint Base Andrews just after 6pm, alongside their wives Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan. Here are the key takeaways. 1. Trade truce extended As Xi and Peng touched down in America, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the two countries had agreed to extend the Busan trade deal from November 10 to January 10. The truce was previously extended in August. 2. Xi’s written speech Xi said China and the United States “should be partners rather than rivals” in a written speech released by state news agency Xinhua after his arrival to Washington. Xi said he believed, with the joint efforts of both sides, the visit would yield fruitful results. “The realisation of the great rejuvenation of China and the goal of making America great again can be mutually inclusive – they can reinforce each other and benefit the world,” he said in the speech. 3. Chinese delegation Arriving on the plane with Xi, the Chinese delegation included Cai Qi, the fifth-ranking official in China and Xi’s chief of staff, Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Minister of Finance Lan Foan. Vice-Premier He Lifeng and Executive Vice-Minister of Foreign Affairs Ma Zhaoxu were among those on the tarmac for Xi’s arrival. 4. Warm greetings Trump broke with standard presidential protocol by personally meeting Xi at the airfield. The two leaders, joined by their wives, had a conversation on the tarmac through interpreters. 5. Military pageantry The White House organised a lavish military display at Joint Base Andrews. The greeting featured an array of defence hardware, including six F-16 fighters, six F-22 fighters and two B-1 Lancer flyovers, alongside honour guards and a 21-gun salute.

title: Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws fail to meet modern demands, experts say
