description: Legal experts call for authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms after spate of dog attacks in recent months.
content: Hong Kong’s existing animal welfare laws are no longer “fit for purpose” to deal with issues around pet abandonment and strays, legal experts have said, urging authorities to expedite long-delayed reforms to the city’s ordinances following a spate of dog attacks. The calls echo comments by Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan, who said on Wednesday that authorities would look at whether existing penalties for pet abandonment should be strengthened and bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of the year. Hong Kong’s animal welfare laws – namely the Protection of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance and Dangerous Dogs Regulations – have drawn intense public scrutiny following a string of recent incidents, including the suspected fatal mauling of a woman by stray dogs in Yuen Long last Saturday night. “Hong Kong’s Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance … remains fundamentally focused on prohibiting acts of cruelty,” said Kim McCoy, a practising barrister and founder of the Hong Kong Animal Law and Protection Organisation. “It is an outdated and fundamentally flawed framework, no longer fit for purpose and wholly incapable of meeting the demands of modern society.” Stray dogs have caused increasing concern as land clearance for the Northern Metropolis megaproject has led to a surge in abandoned animals. Preparatory land resumption for the megaproject in the New Territories has triggered a growing animal welfare crisis, as many residents and business operators abandon pets or guard dogs ahead of government clearance deadlines. Despite these concerns, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) previously told the South China Morning Post that no prosecutions had been brought against people for abandoning animals under the Rabies Ordinance – the law governing such matters – between 2023 and 2025. In his recent policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government would amend the city’s laws on animal care by the end of 2027 while also reviewing pet ownership and control regulations. Speaking to lawmakers on Wednesday, Tse said authorities would bring suggestions to the Legislative Council by the end of 2026. But animal law reform has been an ongoing discussion in the city for years, with the government submitting a paper to the Legislative Council in 2022 outlining proposed amendments to the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance. The proposals, which received support from 88 per cent of respondents during a public consultation exercise in 2019, included increasing the maximum penalties for animal cruelty offences and strengthening rules around animal abandonment. They also introduced a positive “duty of care” provision, long sought by animal welfare advocates and legal experts, requiring owners to ensure their pets’ safety and fulfil basic care obligations. Such requirements would include ensuring animals have a suitable diet and living environment, exhibit normal behaviour patterns, and are protected from pain, suffering and injury. While the 2022 paper suggested the bill amendments would be put before lawmakers that year, it was never formally introduced. In subsequent responses to lawmakers’ questions on the lack of progress, the government as recently as this February cited “divergent views” among stakeholders on the need for “duty of care” provisions and the extent of penalties. It is not yet clear whether the government’s new round of proposed amendments will match those introduced in 2022. Animal welfare advocates have argued that existing laws make it difficult to prosecute owners who fail to microchip or properly secure their pets, while allowing them to deny that an abandoned animal belongs to them. McCoy said introducing “duty of care” rules would define responsible ownership, and a person who acquired an animal would need to accept the responsibilities that came with their decision. “In the context of these recent incidents, a properly drafted ‘duty of care’ could help prevent neglect and abandonment, improve standards of supervision and enable earlier intervention where an animal’s welfare is being compromised,” he said. He also called for a comprehensive review of the city’s Rabies Ordinance. “While rabies prevention remains important, we should not be relying on disease-control legislation to address fundamental issues such as animal abandonment, irresponsible ownership and the humane management of stray animals,” he said. Amanda Whitfort, an associate professor at the University of Hong Kong specialising in animal law, said there was a need to introduce welfare standards for animals, prosecute abandonment, and introduce humane population control of strays in certain areas. Whitfort co-wrote a landmark animal law reform report in 2010 which, among a number of recommendations, called for the implementation of a new Animal Welfare Ordinance containing “duty of care” provisions. “Rather than take a holistic view of solving these problems, the [AFCD’s] policy has been to collect and pass on their responsibility for unwanted dogs to overburdened shelters. This policy has not been sustainable for some time,” she said. She noted that the department had not brought any prosecutions for animal abandonment in recent years, which she argued “sends the public the message that they may give up their responsibilities to their pets without significant repercussions”. Whitfort said it was too easy for people to keep dogs without obtaining licences under existing rules, and suggested that laws could be altered to reward those who spay or neuter their dogs with lower licence fees. She also called on authorities to follow Macau’s example, where failing to report the loss of a dog within a specific time period was an offence. In a reply to the SCMP, the AFCD said that pet owners had a responsibility not only to care for their pets but also to control them. “While ‘duty of care’ focuses primarily on the animal’s welfare needs, the concept of ‘pet owner responsibility’ encompasses welfare, safety, environmental considerations and public health,” it said. “We will encourage pet owners to understand and fulfil their responsibilities through reviewing regulations and conducting public education and publicity campaigns.” The department also reiterated that the government would consult the Legislative Council on proposals to step up efforts to combat cruelty to animals, and that it would work to complete the amendment exercise in 2027.

title: Yu Yiting overcomes form dip, and the rise of Yu Zidi, to defend her Asian Games title
description: Chinese swimmer wins 100m butterfly after losing 200m IM final to younger rival, with whom she hopes to take on all comers at next Olympics.
content: Three years is a long time in sport, and all athletes have to deal with ups and downs, but few have quite experienced the challenge that emerging Chinese swimmer Yu Yiting has had to face: the sudden, if not entirely unexpected, rise of her teenage compatriot Yu Zidi. But despite facing some serious challenges from the much younger swimmer, Yu Yiting rediscovered her form just before the Asian Games and took her medal tally in Japan to four on Wednesday, storming back from behind at the turn to win the women’s 100m butterfly gold in 56.41 seconds. Yu Yiting’s time put her just ahead of another compatriot, regional and Asian Games double-record holder Zhang Yufei, who finished 0.03 seconds behind in 56.44 seconds. The win ensured that Yu will leave Japan with an individual gold medal, a feat she first achieved on her Asian Games debut in 2023. In those delayed Games, Yu Yiting, who had just turned 18, was one of three women’s swimmers dominating multiple events, and won both the 200m and 400m individual medley (IM) races. Compatriots Zhang and Li Bingjie were the other two, winning multiple golds in their respective strongholds, butterfly and freestyle. In Hangzhou, Yu beat the then Asian record holder Ye Shiwen by 2.59 seconds to win the 200 IM but missed out on the 11-year-old Asian record by a mere 0.18 seconds. Yu made up for that regret almost three years later, at the China National Swimming Championships in June this year, but only after newcomer Yu Zidi had already seized the honour of breaking Ye’s time by 0.14 seconds at the National Games last November. Still, Yu Yiting did get her Asian record and said after the race: “I finally fulfilled a dream I had three years ago.” Fast forward to this week, when Yu Yiting and Yu Zidi went head-to-head in the 200m IM twice at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre in less than seven hours – in a heat and in the final. Entering the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games as the region’s fastest women, the senior Yu won the first battle, but it was the younger Yu who won when it mattered, and in style, chopping 0.72 seconds off Yu Yiting’s three-month-old record to win her second gold on her Games debut in as many events. Yu Zidi’s time of two minutes and 6.10 seconds was also the second-fastest time in the event’s history, behind only the 2:05.70 world record of Canadian star Summer McIntosh. After the Hangzhou Games, Yu Yiting witnessed separate improvement in each of her four medley disciplines, but overall progress in the 200m IM never came. There was even a period when she could not crack the 2:08 mark. “The more I practised, the more anxious I became; the more anxious I became, the more conflicted I felt, eventually turning into a state of ‘competing with myself’,” Yu Yiting recalled. “This event was like a nightmare for me last year; I was even a little afraid to swim in it.” The load on her shoulders proved so great that she opted for an extended break after the National Games last year. “That holiday was very important to me: I completely left the pool and didn’t do anything related to swimming; I just wanted to make myself a little more comfortable and relaxed,” she said. “When I returned to the training group under Michael Bohl, I felt like I was in a completely new state; not the way I had felt for two or three years, but more like I felt when I first joined the national team.” Yu said Bohl’s training model emphasised “high-intensity, short-distance stimulation, repeated pace control, turning practice and rhythm regulation”. She added that her training nowadays consists mostly of high-intensity 50-metre sprints and the repeated practice of turns – “completely different” from her previous training. After some hesitation and then adaptation, the results finally arrived in Hangzhou in June. Yu Yiting said that whereas she previously could not help but think about results, achievements, records, now she reminds herself to focus only on the process: how to swim every 50 metres, how to handle turns, whether the warm-up is done properly, and whether the pace is accurate. Yu’s path to enlightenment echoes what Hong Kong star Siobhan Haughey has been through in recent years, as the four-time Asian Games gold medallist explained to the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. Yu also recalled that after she broke the 200m IM Asian record in June, coach Bohl handed her a note – written at noon before the final – recording the time she should reach for every 50 metres, and those times perfectly matched her splits in the final. “After this competition, I have a lot of faith in my coach and in myself,” said Yu, for whom initial success and fame had come early. Zhejiang native Yu Yiting competed at her first Olympics in Tokyo when she was only 15 – the same age Yu Zidi, the teenage prodigy from Hebei, will be at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. With Yu Yiting turning just 21 earlier this month, and Yu Zidi becoming 14 only next month, it is almost certain that the two – who have combined to slice 1.47 seconds off the 200m IM regional record over the past 10 months – will continue to cross paths for years to come. “My older sister is a formidable opponent; she spurs me on to keep improving and working hard,” said Yu Zidi after she reclaimed the Asian 200 IM record on Monday. To which Yu Yiting responded: “I think this is a good thing. Only by consistently breaking Asian records can we dare to set our sights on world records and potentially challenge McIntosh or other elite competitors at the 2028 Olympics.” That challenge is not far-fetched – Yu Yiting, do not forget, did beat world record holder McIntosh at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August. The Yu swimmers’ battles with the best in the world have only just begun.

title: How China’s growing Reit sector is giving foreign property investors a route back in
description: Cross-border capital remains thin, but cheaper yuan financing and an expanding Reit market are opening pathways for global funds, analysts say.
content: Foreign investors are starting to look again at mainland China’s commercial property market after years of retreat, drawn by sharply lower asset prices, wider yields and cheaper yuan financing, even though cross-border capital remains a small fraction of the overall market, analysts said. The shift did not yet amount to a broad return of foreign money, they added. Instead, some international investors were finding ways to participate through China’s domestic capital markets, using onshore financing and real estate investment trust (Reit) structures to invest in selected assets and create an eventual route to recycle their capital, analysts said. “While cross-border capital mostly stays on the sidelines, the interest in re-engaging with mainland China’s commercial real estate market has been improving in the past 12 months, led by Asian investors,” said Glyn Nelson, head of capital markets research for the Asia-Pacific region at CBRE. The investors were targeting regional shopping malls, multifamily projects, logistics assets and offices in first-tier cities, Nelson added. The shift follows years of weak foreign participation. Cross-border commercial real estate investment in mainland China fell sharply after 2022 amid monetary divergence and geopolitical tensions, CBRE said. Foreign capital excluding Hong Kong accounted for less than 3 per cent of mainland Chinese transaction volume from 2023 through the second quarter of 2026, it added. One reason the market was becoming easier to re-enter was that exit options were evolving, analysts said. Reits allowed property owners to pool income-generating assets into investment vehicles and sell interests to investors, creating an alternative to a conventional property sale. For international investors, that could provide a way to recycle capital without having to sell an entire property, they added. The mainland Chinese Reit market is moving into a more sophisticated phase Andrew Chan, Cushman & Wakefield China’s Reit market is rapidly expanding beyond infrastructure into commercial property. The mainland accounted for 21 of Asia’s 27 new Reit listings between the end of 2024 and March 2026, far ahead of Japan and Thailand, according to Cushman & Wakefield. There is already evidence of international managers using the structures. CapitaLand, backed by Singapore state investment company Temasek, listed its China Commercial C-Reit in September last year, while Canadian global investment firm Brookfield listed the CICC Blinq Multifamily Private Reit in June. The two deals illustrated a model in which assets remained under international management while capital was recycled through domestic investment vehicles, Nelson said. The investment equation has also changed. China’s one-year loan prime rate remained at 3 per cent, while cap rates in first-tier cities were more than 4 percentage points above the 10-year government bond yield at the end of the second quarter, the widest spread in the Asia-Pacific region, according to CBRE. For international investors with onshore operations, cheaper yuan financing could support the acquisition, repositioning and leasing of assets that had been repriced after years of falling values, analysts said. The expanding Reit market provided another potential mechanism for recycling capital. China had 79 public infrastructure Reits with a combined market value of about US$32.1 billion as of March 31, according to Cushman & Wakefield. A commercial real estate Reit pilot launched in late 2025 has expanded the market to include offices, shopping malls, hotels, outlets and mixed-use properties. By June, China had 58 property rights-backed public Reits with a combined market capitalisation of 143 billion yuan (US$21.3 billion), while 60 private Reits had been filed, according to CBRE. Pilot land-tenure renewal policies in Guangzhou and Shanghai were also helping address uncertainty for commercial property investors, according to CBRE. “The mainland Chinese Reit market is moving into a more sophisticated phase,” said Andrew Chan, managing director and head of valuation and advisory services for Greater China at Cushman & Wakefield. For now, however, the opening remains selective. “Investors are very selective on the location quality and operational strength of assets,” Nelson said.

title: US turns to South Korea to ease ammunition bottlenecks amid global conflicts
description: Depleted stockpiles from the Middle East and Ukraine wars are spurring South Korean arms makers to build US production hubs.
content: Washington is increasingly turning to South Korea to ease ammunition supply bottlenecks triggered by wars in the Middle East and Europe, potentially accelerating Seoul’s integration into the US defence industrial base. Analysts say the United States may struggle to replenish stockpiles quickly enough if conflicts in Iran and Ukraine drag on, creating opportunities for South Korea’s defence industry to expand its presence in the US market. Jang Won-joon, a defence science professor at Jeonbuk National University, said the war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had made Washington acutely aware of shortfalls in its domestic defence production capacity. The US burned through US$22.3 billion worth of ammunition in just four months of the Iran war, according to the Pentagon, putting its defence industry under scrutiny and exposing what critics call a structural problem. Washington is now expected to build defence production networks with allies across the Indo-Pacific, including South Korea, Japan and Australia to help close the supply gap. “The US can’t do everything on its own and it is turning to allies in selected sectors such as munitions, missiles and battleships,” Jang said. “South Korea has emerged as a key partner for the US in such efforts.” Defence industry cooperation with South Korea could serve as a model for other US allies, Jang said, citing the US$150 billion “Make American Shipbuilding Great Again” initiative proposed by South Korea to revitalise the US maritime and shipbuilding sectors as part of a broader investment package aimed at securing lower tariffs. The initiative is anchored by South Korea’s largest shipbuilders – HD Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean – working alongside government ministries. “The US is likely to present defence industry cooperation with South Korea as a successful model to encourage other allies to follow suit,” Jang said. South Korea’s leading defence company, Hanwha Aerospace, has moved quickly to take advantage of the US ammunition bottleneck by expanding its integration with the American defence industry. On Tuesday, it announced a US$2.2 billion investment over seven years to build a production hub for 155mm (6.1-inch) artillery shells at a US Army site in Arkansas – potentially giving it an advantage in securing other American military contracts. Hanwha’s vertically integrated facility, covering the entire ammunition production process from raw materials to finished products, is set to manufacture components and propellant charges for 155mm shells. The US has been falling well short of its production targets for the shells because of manufacturing bottlenecks and contractor issues. Global supply is tight largely because the Ukraine war has consumed shells far faster than Western factories can replace them. Last month, Hanwha Defence USA, the company’s American subsidiary, signed a contract with the US Army to deliver six K9 Mobile Howitzer wheeled prototypes, in an initial deal worth roughly US$100 million that could reach US$263 million if an option for an additional 12 units is exercised. Hanwha is also building a facility in Opelika, Alabama for prototype assembly, integration and testing. “We will help take the capabilities of the US ammunition industry to the next level while actively contributing to the expansion of defence cooperation between the two countries,” said Michael Coulter, head of Hanwha Defence USA. Other South Korean manufacturers are also attracting global attention. LIG Defence & Aerospace, formerly LIG Nex1, is seeking to expand its market share in interceptor missiles, despite constraints on domestic manufacturing capacity. But industry officials warn that US shortages will not automatically translate into orders for South Korean firms. Foreign companies still face high barriers to entry, including “Buy American” procurement rules, strict tech-security regulations and demanding US military certification requirements. Kim Mi-jung, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade specialising in the defence industry, said deeper integration into the US industrial base was necessary for South Korea to clear these legal hurdles. “To advance into the US defence market, South Korea and others have little option but to set up and invest through US subsidiaries,” she said. Kim and other analysts say South Korea is well positioned to help replenish depleted US stockpiles, including 155mm shells, because the threat from North Korea has forced Seoul to maintain production capacity and substantial reserves even as other countries scaled back. “South Korea is almost the only option for the US to renovate its ageing ammunition production facilities on a short timeline,” Kim said, adding that the cooperation would strengthen Seoul’s leverage in trade and investment negotiations with Washington. Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said the Hanwha deal could pave the way for cooperation on other platforms, including maritime and aerial systems, missiles, drones and AI-based weapons. “South Korea is in effect the only arms supplier which the US could rely on to replenish its depleted arms depot quickly,” Doo said, adding that the two allies maintained interoperability across many weapons systems, including 155mm artillery. Washington could also turn to Hyundai Rotem’s K2 main battle tanks to address shortfalls, Doo said, and to LIG Defence & Aerospace’s Cheongung interceptor missiles to supplement Patriot systems that were also in short supply. “Defence cooperation with the US would benefit both countries, strengthen the bilateral alliance and give South Korea significant opportunities to expand its presence in the global market,” he said. Many countries no longer wanted to buy “finished weapons”, Jang added, but rather the “ability to sustain war” through local production, technology cooperation, maintenance, repair and overhaul, training and the capacity to rapidly scale up in a crisis. With this in mind, South Korea “must move beyond exports of finished weapons to ‘package exports’”, he said. “And ultimately to ‘ecosystem exports’ that support a country’s ability to sustain war.” Zack Cooper, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the South Korean defence industry’s ability to produce cheaply, quickly and at scale “makes cooperation attractive for the US”. “Allied co-production is one potentially attractive avenue to increase defence output, so is definitely attracting attention in Washington,” Cooper told This Week in Asia. “There are still many political hurdles that companies and countries will need to overcome, but I think there’s a lot of potential in deepening this type of cooperation.”

title: AI leaders to UN: for the sake of humanity, regulate tech we created
description: Tech bosses urge caution in AI development following growing warnings of uncontrollable systems and catastrophic risks.
content: The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people – by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing. “If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” said Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic. And from his competitor Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, came this assessment: “We could lose control of the future to AI”. Both said the countries of the world, through the UN Security Council, where they testified on Wednesday, have to set safeguards of some kind to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in. As the council met, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters in New York that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files. The AI leaders also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI is not concentrated in one company or country. They also touted the benefits of the technology for bettering humanity and what Altman called “giving people more power over their own lives”. Those tech leaders “are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the Security Council. “We cannot ignore them because they are right.’’ Miliband said when the UK leads the G20 next year, it will put controlling AI at the heart of discussions, looking for a single set of global standards “to ensure that AI development is safe”. But, the United States said: don’t do it. Worries about control of AI are “not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure”, said White House Science Adviser Michael Kratsios. “We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology.” His remarks echoed US President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday lauded AI as “super intelligence” and said the United States would reject efforts to control the technology as it tries to win the development race with China. Kratsios was one of the few speakers who used that term in the Security Council. Chinese UN ambassador Fu Cong emphasised that all countries should be able to choose AI technology as they see fit. He warned against “banding together into a petty us-vs-them clique in the tech sector and forcing other countries to take sides” and enabling unnamed major powers that he described as seeking “digital hegemony”. He called on countries instead to promote open-source models – China’s approach to the technology. For most of the world leaders, one key question about AI is this: who should control life-and-death decisions – human or machine? Amodei, Altman and Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue, who spoke via a glitchy remote connection, spoke with the UN’s most powerful council because they and world leaders are trying to figure out not just whether to control AI, but by whom, how it could possibly be done and when it might be just too late. The day before, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres warned of “killer robots”. Experts and European leaders said that’s not hyperbole but something that is either already a grim reality or perilously close. Amodei called on world leaders to agree on not letting AI build biological weapons, figure out how to verify what models have the capability to do and “establish common standards” for testing and for loss of control and misuse. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, whose country convened Wednesday’s meeting, compared the current state of AI to both the runaway computer HAL9000 in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey and the dawn of the atomic age. “Just as with the atom back then, the international community must now regulate AI in order to make the most of its potential and avoid the worst,” Barrot said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, speaking at the General Assembly, said some kind of human control over machines must be achieved soon. Otherwise, he said, for his country – at war for 4½ years – it may be just too late. “There is already a real possibility that AI, not only people, will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield. And we need peace before we reach that point,” Zelensky said. Last month, a Russian drone seemingly using AI “autonomously made a targeting decision that killed three Ukrainians. Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real. We should not be under any illusions otherwise,” Kentaro Toyama, an information technology professor at the University of Michigan, said in an email. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Editorial | Debate on dog ownership and control much needed in Hong Kong
description: The death of a woman after she was chased by dogs has revived discussion on the regulatory regime for canines and pet owners’ responsibilities.
content: People and dogs usually coexist peacefully in Hong Kong. The recent licensing of nearly 1,000 restaurants to admit dogs is evidence of that. The deaths of two young women after they had been mauled by dogs therefore comes as a shock. They have prompted reflection and soul-searching about the canine legal and regulatory regime and the responsibilities and accountability of pet owners. The government has pledged to review and strengthen its policy on stray dogs, which were apparently involved in one of the attacks. That has to be welcomed. What also has to be borne in mind is that dogs reflect an environment shaped and controlled by people; some canines have been abandoned and left to fend for themselves after being trained as guard dogs. Growing public safety concerns are understandable. Last month, a large, unleashed dog killed two small dogs near a shopping mall in Yuen Long. In the same week, a 33-year-old woman, who operated a pet-training and boarding centre in Ta Kwu Ling, was found dead after being attacked by a big mixed-breed dog awaiting adoption when she tried to return it to its cage after letting it out for feeding. She was alone at the time. Her injuries included head and neck wounds. In the case of this week’s victim, aged 27, security footage shows her leaving Yuen Long MTR on a cycle, then being chased by dogs along Pok Wai South Road. She was later found unconscious with wounds to her head and neck that are believed to have been fatal. The government’s promise of a policy review on stray dogs followed warnings from animal shelters of pets being abandoned in the New Territories amid land resumption for development projects. They note that many supposed “strays” involved in attacks are actually poorly secured warehouse guard dogs, sometimes without microchips, highlighting a significant loophole in current pet law enforcement. Many warehouses, open car parks and villages in the New Territories, including parts of Sheung Shui, Ping Shan, Fanling and Yuen Long have resorted to keeping guard dogs for decades. Following this week’s incident, the authorities have expanded their search radius to capture stray dogs and installed new surveillance cameras in the area where the suspected fatal attack took place. On Monday, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said it had worked with police to capture three stray mongrels near Pok Wai South Road, where the victim was found. The tragedies have sparked a debate Hong Kong needs to have on dog ownership, responsibilities and control. The AFCD had already stepped up inspections and seizures across the city following last month’s dog attacks. The incident at the pet training facility exposed loopholes in the city’s self-declaration microchip registration system, after the animal was found to carry genetic traits of the pit bull terrier, one of four fighting breeds banned from import and unauthorised breeding in Hong Kong. Mark Mak Chi-ho, founder and executive chairman of the non-profit Veterinary Services Society, has called for greater clarity and consultation before amending regulations. He said that while the crackdown had boosted demand for DNA tests to identify fighting genes, it could prompt anxious owners to abandon their pets out of fear of breaking the law. Many social media users have shared accounts of pets being injured or even killed by large dogs in Hong Kong. In one case, the owner of a large dog was fined HK$2,000 while the animal was classified as a known dangerous dog. The deterrent effect is an issue. Sally Andersen, founder of Hong Kong Dog Rescue, has said a loose licensing regime had created loopholes that allowed some dog owners to dodge responsibility. Some had abandoned or given away microchipped dogs without changing the registered owner. Some animal welfare advocates say a “duty of care” requirement for owners should be included in legislation. A public consultation begun in 2019 unearthed divergent views about this among stakeholders. While the response of the authorities to the tragedies might have made the city a safer place, the best way forward remains education on the duties of responsible ownership coupled with effective law enforcement and proactive control and neutering of potentially dangerous stray dogs.

title: A 1950s house in Singapore is reborn as a contemporary home open to the elements
description: Architect Chang Yong Ter blended old and new in reworking the 2,240 sq ft single-storey house that stays cool without air conditioning.
content: Singaporean architect Chang Yong Ter and his client go back to their army days in the late 1980s, when both attended officer cadet school. They lost touch afterwards, reconnecting only decades later when Chang’s work appeared in a magazine, and his old friend recognised the name. By then, the client had already set his sights on a plot: a corner site in Bukit Timah, one of the island’s toniest neighbourhoods. “I thought the plot had potential,” the client says. “It was squarish and elevated with an unblocked rear, and adjacent to a quiet cul-de-sac. We liked the location as it was a relatively quiet and small estate that was still close to amenities.” Living just down the road, he drove past it for years and, one day, the ageing 1950s house on the plot came up for sale. An elderly widow lived there at the time and it was barely habitable – the kitchen and bathrooms were stuck in another era, the roof tiles failing. But its footprint was worth keeping, the original walls were sound and the scale suited a family of three: the owner, his wife and their son, studying in Ireland and back only for summers. The brief he gave Chang, founder of Chang Architects, was just as compact: a single storey, three bedrooms, every room opening onto the garden, parking for two cars. “That’s really about it,” he says. That terse brief produced a house that, like a palimpsest, quietly carries its old self beneath the new. Chang kept the original roofline and rebuilt the pitched structure beneath it, extending the house at the rear and sides instead of starting over. He also levelled what was once a sloping driveway at the street entrance, so arriving now means climbing a few shallow steps before reaching the door – enough to keep the parked cars out of view from the street and to lend a low, unassuming house an unexpected quiet formality as you approach. Walk through the 208 square metre (2,240 sq ft) house today and the join between past and present is legible mostly in feeling, not in any visible seam. It is an intimate family home with the proportions of something built in a different age, but with none of its faded old rooms. That sense of continuity starts with orientation. The house stands almost directly on an east-west axis – a layout that, on paper, should mean punishing afternoon sun. Chang countered it with deep eaves and a screen of heliconia to keep direct rays off the walls, and a lawn to the west that absorbs the rest. Both ends open directly to the elements, letting air flow straight through. The result is that rare ability, in Singapore anyway, to live quite comfortably without the need for air conditioning. The materials underline the same instinct for shade, tactility and craftsmanship, giving the interiors a cabin-like warmth. The floors and walls are swathed in thin planks of sturdy balau, a tropical hardwood, while the ceilings are in marine ply. Outside, the decking and facade cladding are in Onewood, a Singapore-made reconstituted timber built to resist termites and fire without chemical treatment. Almost nothing about the construction is left raw or exposed – even storage has been folded away behind the timber panelling, so that no wall carries visible clutter. Chang’s bravura move was to insert a courtyard comprising a pond and a small porch anchored by a handsome Flore Pleno tree on the eastern end of the house. From every vantage point, the eye is drawn towards this bijou pocket of green and gently lapping water. The pond was originally meant for koi, until the owner’s son deemed them “a bit old-fashioned” in favour of goldfish, which have mostly settled into pond life undisturbed, save for the odd hungry bird. A sliding glass screen can close off the courtyard entirely, letting the adjoining lounge run on air conditioning when the weather calls for it. When not needed, the screen itself disappears into a pocket built into the stone wall. The interiors, meanwhile, are the owner’s own work, put together without a decorator and furnished with pieces acquired over years spent in Britain and Ireland. An antique breakfast table anchors the sitting area, a scatter of mid-century Danish furniture keeps a low-slung silhouette against the height of the pitched roof, and scattered on the walls are paintings by local artists such as Chen Wen Hsi and Lim Tze Peng. “I don’t think I have any particular style,” the owner says, though the mood throughout the house feels otherwise, with thoughtfully picked, unfussy pieces that never compete with the timber around them. Everything has been chosen with the same restraint Chang built into the walls – a fitting coda for a project that began, after all, with two old army buddies deciding to trust each other with something this personal. Living area Transit sofa and Nightfly chair from Time & Style (timeandstyle.com). Daybed from Handvark (handvark.com). Ten coffee table by CondeHouse (condehouse.com). Lucent side tables by Matthew Hilton for Case Furniture (casefurniture.com). Pukti table lamp from Iittala (iittala.com). TSSG108 sculpture stool between armchairs from Time & Style. Painting of Chinatown by Singaporean artist Tung Yue Nang, from Artsafe (artsafesg.com). Courtyard A pond and porch grace the eastern end of the house. Bathroom ME by Starck wall-hung toilet from Duravit (duravit.com). Shower hardware from Vola (vola.com). Main bedroom Eden h.28 bed from Bolzan (bolzan.com). Grace table lamp from Oligo (oligo.de). Main bedroom en suite A counterweighted vertical sliding window is integrated with a fixed mirror, allowing seamless adjustment of light, ventilation and views. HV1+30 1 handle mixer from Vola. Kitchen Chang Yong Ter designed the kitchen. Dekton countertop from Sirius (dektonsurfaces.co.uk). Cabinet door finishes are balau. Appliances from Miele (miele.com). Casual dining area Dining table from Air Division (airdivision.com). Antique dining chairs from owner’s private collection. Formal dining area Nineteenth century Regency-period mahogany breakfast table, William IV-period dining chairs, Regency-period rosewood side cabinet, all from owner’s private collection. Eames 670 lounge chair and 671 ottoman from Herman Miller (hermanmiller.com). Bedroom Slab desk from Tom Dixon (tomdixon.net). Aeron office chair from Herman Miller. Tried + Tested Clean lines and a houseful of stuff are not mutually exclusive. The trick is storage space deep enough to disappear. Build full-height shelving directly into the wall, then cover it behind timber panelling cut to match the grain and joinery running around it. There is no visible hardware, no seam giving the game away – just a press to release the catch. Those chasing genuinely calm, empty-looking walls do not need to own less. They just need a false wall with a few extra inches of depth behind it.

title: Peng Liyuan and Melania Trump renew acquaintance as Xi arrives in US
description: The first ladies shared a light moment beside the honour guard at Joint Base Andrews, where they had met during the Trumps’ first term.
content: Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan shared a light moment with Melania Trump on Wednesday as the two women renewed an acquaintance dating back to the Trumps’ first term in the White House. The first ladies smiled as they greeted each other at the foot of the aircraft stairs at Joint Base Andrews, where Peng arrived with President Xi Jinping for a visit to Washington. Walking behind their husbands along the red carpet, Peng gestured towards the honour guard, apparently remarking on the soldiers’ height. After the welcoming ceremony, Peng mouthed “wonderful” during another brief exchange with Melania. Their conversation was not audible. The two women had spent time together during Xi’s visit to Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida in April 2017. Later that year, during the Trumps’ visit to Beijing, they toured a primary school together, taking in classes and a student cultural performance. Melania subsequently called Xi and Peng “gracious hosts” and spoke of the personal conversations she had enjoyed during the trip. On Wednesday, Melania wore a dark two-piece suit with a white shirt, while Peng wore a pale grey-blue dress with a light scarf around her neck. Trump and Xi also held several conversations through interpreters during the ceremony, including before the Chinese couple departed in a Hongqi car. The first ladies are due to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art together on Thursday after the White House arrival ceremony. They are also scheduled to attend a state dinner with their husbands that evening.

title: Hong Kong rises in property market transparency rankings, but trails Singapore and Japan
description: Hong Kong jumped one place to 14th in list of world’s most transparent real estate markets as Asian destinations made progress.
content: Hong Kong has climbed one place in a list of the world’s most transparent real estate markets by property consultancy JLL and subsidiary LaSalle Investment Management, though it still trails regional peers Singapore and Japan in the rankings. The city secured 14th place in the latest edition of the Global Real Estate Transparency Index, a report released every two years. The new report covers 146 city markets in 88 countries and territories worldwide. The ranking was the highest of any market in Asia apart from Japan and Singapore, which placed 12th and 13th, respectively. Hong Kong’s score just fell below the threshold to be rated a “highly transparent” market, a label that Singapore and Japan managed to secure. “Hong Kong’s continued ranking among the world’s most transparent real estate markets underscores the strength and maturity of its market framework,” said Alex Barnes, JLL’s co-CEO in Greater China. “As global investors become increasingly discerning, access to reliable market information, regulatory certainty and technology-driven data will play an ever more important role in sustaining investor confidence and supporting capital flows,” Barnes added. “Further progress in emerging sectors, including alternative assets, credit markets and building performance, will strengthen Hong Kong’s competitiveness as a leading international real estate investment hub.” The rankings drew on both quantitative market data and a survey of JLL and LaSalle’s global business network to score each market across 260 factors, grouped into five transparency tiers. The index is intended for cross-border investors, lenders, developers and occupiers, as well as government and industry bodies benchmarking market conditions internationally. The United Kingdom took the crown as the world’s most transparent market, followed by France and Australia, respectively. The United States placed fourth. Meanwhile, the Asia-Pacific recorded the strongest regional improvement in this year’s survey, accounting for half of the world’s top 10 most improved markets. India led the gains, supported by the expansion of its digital infrastructure, greater availability of market data and a growing Reit (real estate investment trust) sector, the study said. Vietnam, South Korea and Thailand also made significant progress by strengthening corporate governance standards, enhancing legal enforcement and increasing disclosure across alternative property sectors. Australia, already among the world’s most transparent markets, also improved further, the study noted. The improvements have contributed to a sharp rebound in cross-border investment into Asia-Pacific, with direct transaction volumes in key markets – including India and Vietnam – reaching record highs, according to the report. Transaction volumes across the “highly transparent” markets had risen by 64 per cent over the past two years, outperforming the rest of the world by 20 percentage points, it added. As investors increasingly prioritise scale, timely price discovery and reliable data to manage risk, the 13 “highly transparent” markets now account for 56 per cent of the world’s income-producing real estate and more than 80 per cent of global direct investment, according to the study. “Over the past cycle, transparency gains have been concentrated in debt markets and niche and alternative sectors, which are steadily closing the gap with traditional sectors in terms of data availability,” said Dominic Silman, chief economist for LaSalle.

title: Turkey to hand over military base to Iraq
description: Ankara established the facility in Bashiqa in 2015 and deployed up to 600 soldiers there, sparking tensions with Baghdad.
content: Turkey will hand over control of its base in Bashiqa in northern Iraq to Baghdad, the Turkish presidency announced on Wednesday in a joint statement with its neighbour. “In light of progress achieved by these security measures implemented by Iraq, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan base to the Federal Government of Iraq in accordance with the agreed mechanism and timetable,” a joint statement said. The announcement followed a meeting Wednesday between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The handover’s timetable was not specified. The US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, hailed the agreement. “History rarely announces its turning points; it stitches them quietly. Ankara returning Zilkan to Baghdad by agreed mechanism and timeline is one such thread: Iraqi sovereignty and Turkish security, both served,” he posted on social media. With the agreement of the autonomous region of Iraqi Kurdistan, Turkey established a military base in Bashiqa in December 2015. According to the Turkish press, Ankara deployed up to 600 soldiers there. This sparked tensions with Baghdad, which accused Ankara of violating its sovereignty. Ankara and Baghdad also agreed on Wednesday to “fully restore state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of illegal foreign armed elements”. Turkey has in the past conducted military operations in the Sinjar region against fighters from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). As part of a peace process conducted with Ankara, the PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025, before holding a highly symbolic disarmament ceremony in July 2025 in northern Iraq, where only some fighters remain, according to Turkish authorities. Baghdad announced in early September that Sinjar would be placed under the full authority of the federal government and its security and administrative institutions, following an agreement reached with Yazidi armed groups for them to hand over their weapons to the state.

title: Can the US and China verify an AI deal? Start-ups are starting to build the tools
description: Researchers are developing technology to monitor AI development without relying on trust between Washington and Beijing.
content: There are growing calls for Washington and Beijing to agree to slow down development of artificial intelligence. But even if they wanted to do so, how could they verify that the other side would do the same? A group of researchers and start-ups is developing technology intended to make this a possibility, without relying on trust alone. Their proposed tools would allow third parties and governments to check some claims about how AI models are being trained or used – possibly without needing access to the AI models and infrastructure themselves. This work is drawing attention ahead of Thursday’s meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at which AI is expected to be a topic of discussion. Still, advocates of the technology, known as “AI verification”, acknowledge that much work still needs to be done before the technology could be relied upon to monitor the vast computing facilities used to develop advanced AI. Nonetheless, they argue that a recent surge in interest from both policymakers and industry is likely to rapidly accelerate progress in the field. “The level of interest has just kind of exploded in the last few weeks and months,” said Connor Dunlop, head of policy and strategy at San Francisco-based Lucid Computing, a leading AI verification start-up. On Monday, leaders and representatives from 20 countries including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong issued a public letter that called for greater controls on frontier AI systems. The letter cited recent incidents in which cutting-edge AI systems from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic circumvented safeguards and conducted cyberattacks. The call to action proposed the creation of an international governance institution that could perform AI verification, without specifying how this should be done. According to Tom Milton, co-founder of UK-based AI verification consultancy Amodo Design, there are two main claims that Washington and Beijing would likely want to be able to verify as part of any future international AI treaty: whether a data centre in the other country is training a new AI model or merely serving an existing one, and whether an AI model being served is the one it is purported to be. The reason is that data centres only serving existing AI models – a process called inference – rather than training new ones would mean that the country is not advancing AI capabilities. Meanwhile, the governments might also want to verify that a data centre in the other country is running a model known to be safe instead of an unsafe one. One proposed verification mechanism is called “recomputation”, in which an AI system’s outputs are checked by running the same calculation again on a different system, with the same inputs and settings, to see if the same result is achieved. According to a report from the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, equipping data centres with such verification technology could only cost a small percentage of the facility’s upfront costs, given that the recomputation process would rely on commodity hardware. Compute costs arising from the verification process could also be kept low by only testing a small random sample of all AI activity in the facility. Both Amodo and Lucid Computing have begun testing such solutions in real-world settings. Earlier this month, Lucid began 18 months of “adversarial” testing of its recomputation solution on a cluster of 16 Nvidia H100 semiconductor chips in Sweden, provided by the government-funded research institute RISE. Amodo is also in talks to scale up its testing to a cluster of 128 graphics processing units (GPUs), said Milton. He acknowledged, however, that the field is still in its infancy, with the need to validate such solutions at the scale of cutting-edge data centres, which have hundreds of thousands of GPUs installed. Political and commercial barriers also present a real challenge, with both China and the US pouring trillions of dollars into advancing their AI capabilities amid their fierce tech rivalry. Chinese state media in recent weeks have dismissed US industry giants’ calls to “pace” the development of AI as efforts to entrench their industry-leading positions and suppress China’s AI development. Bad blood between the two countries has affected proposed technical solutions to AI governance issues before. Beijing last year rebuffed suggestions that US chipmaking giant Nvidia could install technology in its chips to verify their location as part of efforts to comply with US export controls. Chinese officials feared the technology could be used by Washington to sabotage the country’s AI infrastructure. Still, the first step would be to let politicians know that technical solutions to verify AI development are there if they want them, rather than have them wrongly believe that verification is impossible on a technical level, said Milton. He pointed to US-Soviet nuclear arms control agreements in the 20th century, when the two countries overcame high levels of mutual distrust by using multiple verification mechanisms, including satellites and unique identifiers. “Obviously the technology is not perfect yet … but it doesn’t have to be to help build early confidence that an agreement is possible,” said Milton. Amid growing signals from industry and policymakers that such technology is needed, investors are also showing signs of interest. Last month, Israeli AI verification start-up Attestable raised US$20 million in seed funding with major investors including Silicon Valley hedge fund Altimeter Capital. The firm is applying a cryptographic technique called “zero-knowledge proof” (ZKP) to its proposed verification solution, using mathematics instead of recomputation to allow parties to verify that a response to a query was provided by the exact AI model specified. The technique, already used in blockchain technologies, is called “zero knowledge” because it does not reveal information about the underlying model or data. This could help allay the fears of governments and companies about leakage of sensitive information, said Miro Pluckebaum, founder of the Singapore AI Safety Hub (SASH). “The sentiment within the research community is that something workable can be built within six to 12 months,” he said. “The myth as we see it is that verification would be impossible.” SASH, a non-profit organisation based in the Asian city state, is trying to promote international collaboration on AI verification as early as possible to ensure that the field is not viewed as the exclusive tool of any country, said Pluckebaum. While Beijing’s stance on AI verification remains unclear, Pluckebaum said that the open-source nature of the field’s early results would allow Chinese researchers to also test the underlying cryptographic techniques and contribute to their hardening. Amodo, Lucid and SASH have all committed to open sourcing their research findings. Growing signals from politicians that this technology is needed will also help with one of the field’s main bottlenecks today, which is a lack of talent, said Lucid’s Dunlop. He estimates that there are only around 50 people working on AI verification technology globally. “I think there should probably be 100 times more people working on this, given what’s at stake,” he said. Government support could also spur greater participation among leading tech giants. To underpin a global AI treaty, AI verification would require compatibility with the wide range of chip and model configurations available in the market today, covering not just US but also Chinese chips and frontier AI models from the likes of Huawei Technologies and DeepSeek. “Ideally we would see many teams working on verification, both inside and outside frontier AI companies, trying out their solutions on as many different ‘stacks’ as possible,” said Dunlop. Dunlop, Milton and Pluckebaum are all in New York this week at the United Nations General Assembly to explain their work to politicians and experts. “There’s already been a lot of progress with an extremely small number of people working on this,” said Dunlop. “Let’s ramp that up and see how much more progress we can make.”

title: US restricts visas for birth tourism ahead of Xi Jinping’s summit with Trump
description: China has been a central focus of Washington’s efforts to crack down on the practice, with large-scale operations targeted.
content: Hours before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in the US for a high-stakes summit, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved to restrict visas for those who “engage in or facilitate” birth tourism, a practice the Trump administration has increasingly accused China of. “By restricting visa issuance of those who both engage in and profit from this fraud, we are sending a clear message: the United States will not allow foreigners to exploit our immigration system and violate the sanctity of US citizenship,” Rubio said in a statement on Wednesday. China has been a central focus of Washington’s efforts to crack down on birth tourism, with officials often targeting large-scale operations that cater to Chinese clients. “The demand for US citizenship for the children of Chinese nationals has led to unscrupulous companies assisting these individuals for profit,” said Republican congressman Chip Roy of Texas at a hearing earlier this month. Public discussion often casts birth tourism as particularly widespread among wealthy Asians, a Pennsylvania State University report said, adding that “the majority of birth tourists are Hispanic mothers”. While there is no federal dataset that measures the practice, available estimates indicate that birth tourism accounts for a small share of births in the US. In any year between 2014 and 2024, birth tourism accounted for fewer than 0.3 per cent of all US births, Penn State researchers estimated. “Annual birth tourism, measured as a foreign-born mother giving birth in the US to a child that does not remain a US resident, even at its height in 2015, represented fewer than 0.3 per cent of all US births,” according to the research brief. Despite such estimates, the administration has ramped up its attempts to curb the practice of birth tourism, following the Supreme Court’s decision on June 30 to block US President Donald Trump’s bid to restrict constitutional birthright citizenship. The new visa restrictions, which came just hours ahead of Xi’s state visit to Washington for a summit with Trump, target individuals who have knowingly engaged in or facilitated the practice in the US. This includes those who coach applicants to commit fraud, known as “visa fixers” and those “who support, abet and enable commercial birth tourism”. “These networks advertise and coach foreign nationals to lie on US visa applications and collect tens of thousands of dollars to arrange births on American soil for the sole purpose of obtaining US citizenship,” Rubio said. The State Department on Wednesday also launched an online tip portal, calling for members of the public to help identify and stop suspected US visa fraud and misuse. In August, the Trump administration announced the establishment of a task force to end birth tourism – one of a string of moves aimed at curtailing the practice after the Supreme Court decision. “I would like to congratulate President Xi, and the Great Country of China, on their massive Birthright Citizenship WIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP,” the US president wrote on social media after the verdict. Trump also signed two executive orders in early August seeking to curb birth tourism and respond to the Supreme Court ruling. One of the new orders directed officials to strengthen visa screening, investigate suspected birth-tourism operations and consider legal action against businesses facilitating the practice.

title: Xi lands in US for high-stakes summit with Trump amid deep tensions
description: Chinese leader begins 48-hour visit as Trump seeks progress on AI, Iran, rare earths and trade, with expectations for deals low.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping landed at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday afternoon after a 15-hour flight where he was met on the tarmac by US President Donald Trump in an unusual move for a top American leader as the two sides extended a trade truce. The closely watched visit – Xi’s first summit in the United States in 11 years – comes as the two nations grapple with a host of thorny issues beneath the flowery language and statements of friendship, including artificial intelligence, critical minerals, tariffs, Ukraine, the Iran war, Taiwan and military relations. Xi, accompanied by first lady Peng Liyuan, senior Chinese official Cai Qi, Foreign Minister Wang Yi and several other Chinese dignitaries, were greeted with a modest arrival ceremony. “China and the United States are great nations, and their peoples are great peoples.,” Xi told Trump, according to Xinhua News, in a written statement conveyed to the US president. “The two peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and their interests are deeply intertwined.” After an “unscheduled” second day of negotiations on Wednesday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, Bessent told Fox News that the two sides agreed that a trade truce set to expire on November 10 had been extended by two months. China’s embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. There was a several-minute delay after Xi’s plane landed as US personnel awkwardly steered a rolled-up 100-foot (30.4 metre) red carpet on a small trolley to a position beneath the Chinese aircraft. The trolley almost tipped over before staff righted it as, directed by a functionary seeking to get it properly aligned, unrolled the floor covering as military personnel on their knees removed creases and protocol chief Hong Lei and Wang watched from the aircraft doorway. Trump and first lady Melania then emerged from the “Beast” presidential limousine at 6pm and greeted Xi and his wife as they descended the jetway. The two couples chatted for a few minutes then watched a 21-person honour guard and listened as the Chinese and American national anthems played, cannons fired a salute and two B-1 bombers thundered overhead before the two sides parted in opposite directions after roughly 15 minutes. The concise ceremony also included a rendition of “Fanfare for the Common Man”, a short, loud, ceremonial piece featuring brass instruments and percussion traditionally played to announce someone important. Xi’s arrival has been framed as a mirror image of Trump’s summit in Beijing four months earlier. The time on the ground will be limited to 48 hours; there will be no side visits outside the capital; and the programme will include a state dinner and military viewing. The carefully choreographed visit is in part meant to underscore respect and the equality of the two wary competitors, an issue of particular importance to Beijing. A couple of big differences with the reciprocal May trip, however: there were no Chinese business executives accompanying Xi on his “special plane,” a modified Air China Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental, landing under grey skies on Wednesday, amid questions over whether they will appear at all. In contrast, Trump brought along two US chief executives aboard Air Force One in May, part of a 17 CEO contingent that reportedly arrived without giving Beijing much notice. Sources say the limited ongoing clarity over a Chinese CEO delegation is due in part to the lack of progress on a proposed Board of Investment and to bilateral communication problems. Xi urged the two sides to find common ground. “Both sides should move towards each other to foster a stable relationship characterized by cooperation as the mainstream, measured competition, manageable differences, and the prospect of peace,” Xi said, according to Xinhua. A second difference relative to China’s detailed hosting has been the shortfall in planning and logistics done by a distracted US administration in recent weeks compared with China’s near-compulsive approach. While the White House has been juggling its Iran war of choice, a Canadian trade showdown, Trump’s record-low popularity and a pending November election, summit preparation has also been frustrated by the small number of US decision-makers and an impetuous president inclined to rip up plans on short notice. This was seen in part by the addition of a second day of “unscheduled” negotiating by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng on Wednesday just hours before Xi landed. Traditionally, intense summit planning begins up to six months in advance with deals and deliverables are largely decided weeks ahead of the date. High on the agenda for a meeting with low deliverable expectations will be some movement on artificial intelligence, a key part of Bessent’s portfolio and a source of rising tensions in recent months as the two nations tout competing visions, promote rival companies and adhere to different regulatory environments. Another entrenched problem almost certainly on the agenda is Iran. Trump badly wants China’s help in forcing Tehran to the bargaining table to end a war he started nearly seven months ago. But China, which was buying over 80 per cent of Iran’s exported crude before the conflict, has balked at turning the screws on its Middle Eastern partner. Asked by reporters if Iran would be discussed, Trump said: “I’ll be talking about that and many other subjects but it’s all coming along, including that.” Another key issue involves the 90 per cent of global rare earth mineral processing that China controls. Beijing has meted out sparingly to US companies this essential component of most tech products since Liberation Day when Trump threatened tariffs of over 80 per cent on the Asian export behemoth. This has given China enormous leverage over the US and fundamentally changed the power dynamic between the world’s two largest economies, clout that China is in no hurry to give up. The two could also discuss further extending the one-year trade truce agreed to late last October in South Korea and now deferred until January. This could give the two leaders leeway to announce a longer truce at an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later in November or at a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December. Framing the tussle is a disagreement over how long an extension is acceptable. China would like to see it last through early 2029 when Trump’s tenure ends while Washington believes shorter, more frequent pacts give it greater leverage to ensure China follows through. Another dynamic in the background of this week’s talks is the divergence often seen between an increasingly pro-China Trump and China hawks in his administration and in Congress. Asked by reporters on Wednesday evening whether he agreed with Joseph Weirsky, his counterterrorism acting director, that fentanyl coming from China amounted to war by other means, Trump suggested the issue was largely settled. “That’s not good,” he said. “But they’ve been tariffed and really penalized very strongly.” Trump’s tarmac greeting on Wednesday marked the first time a US president welcomed a foreign leader at an airport in 11 ‌years, when President Barack Obama welcomed Pope Francis in 2015 at Joint Base Andrews. And before that, over a half century earlier, former US president John F. Kennedy met then British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan at Andrews Air Force Base, its former name.

title: Opinion | China is leveraging its diaspora to boost the economy, unlike India
description: While Beijing has turned its diaspora into an extension of its domestic economy, New Delhi has largely allowed its diaspora to strengthen other economies.
content: A country’s diaspora can be a symbol of its pride and power. A nation’s diaspora can help it build international value through success stories, promote its soft power through culture and contribute to its economic progress through remittances, investments and transfers of expertise. India and China have among the world’s largest diasporas. They also offer two very different models of how countries can leverage their diasporas. In India, before the 1991 reforms, people mostly saw those who left as a “brain drain”. But post-liberalisation, people started to see the Indian diaspora as an economic bridge to capital, technology and global markets. In 2004, India set up a ministry to oversee the affairs of Indians abroad, merging it with the Ministry of External Affairs in 2016. China’s case was different. It recognised much earlier that overseas education could serve national development. Among a group sent to France in 1920 as part of a work-study movement was Deng Xiaoping. Though the future leader’s studies were cut short due to a funds shortage, Deng would go on to make foreign education a national policy. In 1978, Deng announced that 3,000 would be sent overseas every year for further education to rebuild China’s scientific community. China did face a significant brain drain during the 1980s and early 1990s. But the strategy paid off after 2001, with World Trade Organization membership. Multinational corporations such as Microsoft, Intel and Oracle established research and technology centres in China, creating well-paid jobs that encourage Chinese expatriates to return. They became bridges between global companies and China’s new tech ecosystem, effectively shifting the cost of training new talent to Western institutions. China also developed programmes, such as the “Thousand Talents” initiative in 2008, to attract global talent. The government’s focus soon shifted to strategic fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, biotechnology and aerospace. Ambition and capital support changed the game as Chinese universities shot up global rankings. By 2018, China had surpassed the United States in the number of scientific papers published. It had broken the barrier from imitator to innovator. Still, the biggest achievement of China’s policy was the switch from brain drain to gain. Between 1978 and 2003, only 17.3 per cent of Chinese international students returned but between 2013 and 2018, the percentage had risen to 80 per cent – a reflection of the better opportunities and incentives at home. One prime example is Yang Zhilin, who obtained his PhD in America and returned in 2019, later co-founding Moonshot AI. Today, his Kimi K3 model is a serious challenger to Western frontier models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, using Silicon Valley-style engineering to offer affordable open-weight advanced AI models. China is becoming the place where the next AI founders believe they have a better chance to build a career. Beijing’s Zhongguancun is emerging as a serious rival to California’s Silicon Valley. This all traces back to Deng’s vision. Today, China produces more graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) than the US. As recently as a decade ago, someone like Yang was more likely to stay in the US and build his start-up there, following in the footsteps of immigrants such as Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. Today, China’s diaspora is keen to contribute to China’s intellectual and economic growth. Other countries may offer jobs, but China now offers a better ecosystem to build a company, a career, even a legacy. The focus is shifting from short-term economic gains to long-term impact – unlike with the Indian diaspora. For comparison, India received US$129 billion in remittances in 2024 while China received US$48 billion, according to World Bank estimates. India’s remittances also make up a bigger percentage of its gross domestic product, at over 3 per cent, compared with China’s 0.1-0.2 per cent. The difference is clear. The impact of India’s diaspora remains heavily tied to remittances and skilled labour, while China’s is increasingly reflected in investment, technology, intellectual property (IP) transfers and commercial networks. A 2023 study by the US National Bureau of Economic Research using 2018 data found that Chinese researchers who had come back from the US contributed to 38 per cent of research papers written from a Chinese address while China-born researchers in the US contributed to 27 per cent of US-addressed papers. Interestingly, papers involving Chinese diaspora and returnee researchers had a higher citation impact. China has emphasised bringing back its overseas talent to build long-term economic and technological strength through expertise, IP, businesses, institutions and capital, apart from remittances. On the contrary, India appears to have prioritised short-term economic gains through remittances over long-term capacity building. Neither the Indian government nor overseas Indians have shown the sort of intention that the Chinese have in building the ecosystem to create the next Google or Microsoft. So, when the US proposes to raise H-1B visa fees for skilled foreign workers or shorten the 60-day visa grace period for foreign graduates, India’s dependence on foreign ecosystems becomes painfully obvious. Of the H-1B visas granted in the 2024 financial year, 71 per cent went to Indian-born applicants. Today, many in the Indian diaspora face uncertainty, as returning to India can be difficult due to a lack of an ecosystem to absorb their skills. Their mass return would also affect India’s remittance inflows. While China has turned its diaspora into an extension of its domestic economy, India has largely allowed its diaspora to strengthen other economies. In leveraging global talent, China has clearly emerged as the winner in the diaspora power race.

title: Xi calls for cooperation with US after Trump’s airport welcome – as it happened
description: The Chinese president began a three-day visit to Washington, with a host of vital topics to be discussed.
content: This live article is freely available to our registered users. Please log in or create an account. Unrivalled Xi-Trump summit analysis: get real-time updates and exclusive boots-on-the-ground reporting from our US and China bureaus. Subscribe now with great savings to stay ahead. President Xi Jinping met US President Donald Trump at Maryland’s Joint Base Andrews airbase, in the first face-to-face talks between the Chinese and American leaders since Trump visited Beijing in May. On this first day of Xi’s three-day trip, he was met at the military airstrip by Trump himself, in an extraordinary break from protocol that Xi did not afford the American president on his trip to Beijing. In a written statement published after his arrival, Xi said the two countries “should be partners rather than adversaries” and foster a “stable relationship defined by cooperation as the mainstay”. And as he and first lady Peng Liyuan departed the base by motorcade for their Washington hotel, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that the US and China had agreed to extend their trade truce. Nevertheless, the trip – and Trump’s warm welcome – come amid a fluctuating US-China relationship. Both Washington and Beijing are jockeying for position in arenas as diverse as trade, artificial intelligence (AI), resources and global influence. title: Ukraine’s Zelensky warns of painful winter for Russia if energy truce talks fail
description: The leader described Russia’s Putin as the ‘patient zero’ from whom the idea of war keeps spreading further.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Moscow at the United Nations on Wednesday that his nation would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides cannot agree a truce on energy attacks before the cold sets in. Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating ‌facilities, while Moscow continues to show little interest in wider negotiations to end the war. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too,” Zelensky told the UN General Assembly during the annual gathering of world leaders in New York. Though Russia has a far bigger arsenal of missiles which it has used to pound its enemy throughout the war, Ukraine has developed and used thousands of long-range drones to strike back at Russian warehouses, port infrastructure and oil refineries. “That’s exactly why we say that de-escalation ⁠steps are needed before winter,” Zelensky said, calling for more robust diplomacy. Russian Foreign Minister ‌Sergey Lavrov held talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, after which Rubio said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced ⁠an interest in a limited ceasefire involving ⁠grain and energy-related targets. There was no immediate sign of any movement in the Russian position, however. A Russian foreign ministry statement said that at the meeting it had “reaffirmed its unconditional commitment to achieving the objectives of ‌its special military operation”, the phrase that Moscow uses to describe its war in Ukraine. Addressing the 15-member Security Council on the sidelines of the annual UN gathering of world leaders, Lavrov indicated that Moscow would not countenance ‌any temporary ‌cessation of hostilities. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons,” he told ‌a council session focused on the war in Ukraine. Britain, France and Denmark’s top diplomats used their speeches to deliver strong condemnations of Russia’s war, warning variously of dangerous escalation ⁠and the spike in civilian deaths this summer. Zelensky used his address to the General Assembly to single out Russian President Vladimir Putin’s role in driving ⁠the war, repeatedly describing him derisively as “patient zero” and “the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further”. “That is why ‘patient zero’ must be stopped. He must be denied the space to act – and the space to spread this evil further,” he said. Zelensky told leaders at a “Crimean Platform” summit ‌on the sidelines of the UN that Kyiv ‌was ready for a maritime truce in the Black Sea based on proposals such as those put forward by Egypt, India and Turkey. “We are waiting for Russia’s response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere,” he said. Top wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East and Africa that count on the Black Sea region for wheat have been finding it hard to secure supplies. Global wheat prices have soared.

title: Presley Gerber remembered, in the words of his exes Lexi Wood and Charlotte D’Alessio
description: Tributes have poured in for the late son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, and brother of Kaia Gerber, who died aged 27 at a rehab facility.
