content: Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, reportedly died of a suspected overdose at a rehabilitation facility on Sunday. He was 27. His family, including younger sister and model Kaia Gerber, have asked for “privacy during this very difficult and painful time”, TMZ reported. Lexi Wood, Gerber’s ex-girlfriend, took to Instagram two days after his passing to pay a heartfelt tribute, accompanied by a carousel of photos of her and Gerber. “It’s hard to put into words what it means to lose someone who was such a meaningful part of my life for so many years. Through every chapter and every version of our relationship, friendship was always at the core of it,” the Summer House star wrote. “Everyone who loved Presley and was loved by him knows he was one of the kindest, most open, loving and courageous people. He loved so deeply, so purely, was incredibly romantic and thoughtful. He was also incredibly resilient. He fought so hard for his life and he was brave enough to be open about that fight. More than anything, he wanted to use his story to help other people, and he did,” she added. Who is Presley Gerber’s ex-girlfriend Lexi Wood, and how have she and his other former partners paid tribute to him? Here is everything you need to know. Lexi Wood and Presley Gerber dated briefly Wood and Gerber hard-launched their relationship in November 2022 with a since-deleted Instagram post, captioned by Gerber: “Guys, I did it. I’ve found the person that makes me the happiest I’ve ever been.” The reality television star attended a Halloween party organised by Gerber’s parents that year, and even joined his family on the red carpet. The couple reportedly met through mutual friends several years prior, but things seemingly didn’t take a romantic turn until 2022. Gerber even professed his love for Wood during a Q&A session on his Instagram Stories in November 2022, saying “I have been in love with her since the day I laid eyes on her.” Unfortunately, their romance lasted only a month, with Wood reportedly ending things with him. While the relationship was brief, Wood wrote in her tribute to Gerber that she felt “lucky to have shared so many years of friendship, so many memories and so much love with him”. She added: “He will always hold such a special place in my heart, and we will all miss him forever.” Before her relationship with Gerber, Wood was known to have dated Brooklyn Beckham. Charlotte D’Alessio Gerber reportedly dated Canadian model Charlotte D’Alessio for two years from 2018 before he and Wood were romantically involved. D’Alessio took to Instagram on Monday to share photos of herself with Gerber. “Shared a pure love with you & for that I thank & honor your life. You deserved more time. You deserved more life. Very angry ab[out] this,” she wrote on her Instagram Stories, alongside an image of the late model embracing her. In a follow-up story, she shared further photos of the former couple, adding: “Love u Pres. always. Up there, down here. Don’t even doubt that. We all love you so much. I hope you can feel it.” Gerber was relatively private about his romantic life and revealed little to no information on his previous relationships. However, he was linked to models Sydney Brooke, Cameron Rorrison, Cayley King, Hana Cross and Isabella Jones, per TV Insider.

title: Donald Trump built a US$5 million White House helipad. Don’t expect Xi Jinping to use it
description: US president might aim to impress during Xi’s state visit, but Chinese protocol discourages its leaders from using helicopters.
content: US President Donald Trump has been very eager to show off to Chinese leader Xi Jinping his new US$5 million White House helipad, his latest bid to stamp his image on Washington. While Xi might act impressed and compliment the US president on his latest building project – part of Trump’s bid to match Xi’s splendour-filled hosting four months ago in Beijing and show the Chinese that Americans can build infrastructure too – do not count on Xi actually trying it out with a chopper ride this week during his first state visit to the US in 11 years. “I’m sure Xi will appear impressed, like, oh, this is really remarkable. I’m never getting on,” said Yun Sun, senior fellow with the Stimson Centre. “I don’t think the Chinese security protocol will allow for a helicopter take-off or landing or for Xi Jinping to take a ride.” “They know how dangerous that thing is. It’s a flying coffin.” True to form, Trump gave Xi an extensive tour of the helipad Thursday, pointing out its presidential seal and features, along with the interior of the presidential Marine One helicopter as the Chinese president mostly nodded politely. Xi has “a great interest in granite” and is an “expert on stone”, Trump said. There is no formal published statute or civil aviation law in China explicitly barring top leaders from flying in helicopters, experts said. But a de facto ban is enforced as part of strict internal protocol maintained by the Central Guard Bureau, which oversees security for the nation’s top leaders. Last month, Trump gushed for several minutes during a media show-and-tell about the helipad’s “flawless” black California granite, compressive strength and “million-year life”. From Trump’s perspective, the helipad is easy to show off. Its swift completion stands in sharp contrast to his other legally embroiled projects: the estimated US$800 million White House ballroom expansion, the US$100 million 250-foot (76.2-metre) “Arc de Trump” and the troubled US$15 million reflecting pool renovation. The US president appears to fully expect that his Chinese counterpart will be wowed. “We’re building a helipad, a beautiful helipad … It could be ready by the 21st [of September],” he told reporters last week, noting Xi’s coming visit. “The planned White House ballroom will not be completed in time, but the helipad will be.” Trump has expressed his belief that Xi – a leader the US president has variously described as his “friend for life,” “central casting, brilliant guy” and “tough, smart and a great leader” – would be particularly impressed by the 100-foot-diameter “Seal of the President of the United States” insignia affixed to the helipad surface. “It’s got the seal of the White House on it in granite, in carved granite. It’s really a beautiful thing,” he said. During his presidency, Xi has overseen some 25,000 miles (40,000km) of high-speed railway in China; about US$1 trillion in Belt and Road Initiative projects spanning 150 countries; building of the ongoing US$580 billion Xiongan New Area smart city; and the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, a new Beijing airport and the world’s longest bridge and tunnel sea crossing, to name a few. Some have suggested that an added benefit of the helipad from Trump’s perspective is that it would allow foreign dignitaries to avoid street demonstrations. “Trump had the heliport built over the Rose Garden for Xi, so he didn’t have to look at protesters en route in the motorcade from Andrews,” said Kevin Nealer, a principal with the Scowcroft Group consultancy and a former member of the President’s Intelligence Advisory Board. “Xi hates copters and avoids using them at home.” Nealer was referring to Washington’s Joint Base Andrews, where in a highly unusual, high-honour move, the president announced that he would greet Xi in person on the tarmac, a role usually reserved for lower-level officials. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has reportedly told overseas diplomats when arranging presidential trips that its top leaders travel almost exclusively by fixed-wing aircraft for long distances and in armoured motorcades for shorter distances. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Helicopters are statistically at greater risk of mechanical failure and rotor-related accidents. And China believes they are more difficult to defend against missiles or other attacks than vehicles or planes equipped with heavy armour, missile defences and secure jammer capability, according to a former US military official. During their 2019 summit in India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi travelled to the meeting site by helicopter, while Xi drove some 35 miles in his custom Hongqi limousine, adhering to Chinese rules disallowing leaders from using helicopters, Beijing’s foreign ministry said at the time. For the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea in 2018, other leaders travelled by helicopter or boat owing to local crime rates and infrastructure. In its lead-up, however, China funded and built a dedicated multi-lane highway called “Independence Boulevard” leading to the local parliament, allowing Xi to travel in a bulletproof Hongqi limousine along the pre-cleared roadway. At the 2015 Apec summit in Manila, Xi declined a helicopter lift availed by other heads of state from Ninoy Aquino International Airport directly to coastal hotels and the summit convention centre meant to circumvent the city’s infamous traffic. Lower-level officials and People’s Liberation Army officers use choppers. And senior officials have deployed them during inspections and disaster responses, including several flights by then-Chinese premier Wen Jiabao during the 2008 Sichuan earthquake. But by most accounts, the unofficial ban was cemented when Xi took power in 2012. Chinese helicopters have had a mixed record. In their infancy, they relied heavily on Soviet technology. In the 1950s, Moscow provided blueprints of its Mil Mi-4 “Hound” transport chopper that formed the basis of the Harbin Z-5, China’s first serial production model. Efforts to ramp up production coincided with the Great Leap Forward and the Sino-Soviet split, however, and early models saw severe manufacturing defects, including rotor-blade metal fatigue, structural vibrations and substandard metallurgical quality in engine and transmission parts. “China’s record of engine maintenance is not great,” said Dennis Wilder, a senior fellow at Georgetown University and former CIA officer. “I did once fly to the Great Wall on an old Soviet helicopter. Never again.” But quality has improved significantly, and its Z-20 multi-role platform, seen as resembling the Sikorsky Black Hawk, and Z-10 and Z-19 attack helicopters are credited with significantly upgrading the PLA Army’s air assault capabilities. Along with greater reliability, China has built an export market. Its selling points include a lower price tag and deals largely free of human rights or other political stipulations relative to Western suppliers, although some countries including Cameroon and Pakistan have reported operational and maintenance issues. In the nearly unimaginable eventuality that Xi did agree to fly on a US helicopter in Washington, he might well insist that another very special passenger tag along, analysts said. “If Xi Jinping really takes a ride, Trump will have to be on the plane with him. But I think the Chinese default answer is going to be no,” Sun said. “He’s only here for one day. It’s a very short trip.”

title: Grief and pain flow at hearing for Canadian suicide poison vendor Kenneth Law
description: Family members of those who killed themselves using chemicals he sold spoke about their loss before the judge deciding on Law’s sentence.
content: Relatives of people who committed suicide using poison sold by a Canadian man gave wrenching accounts of pain and loss on Wednesday in court before a judge tasked with deciding the former chef’s prison term. Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to aiding in the suicide of 14 people in Canada after prosecutors determined they lacked evidence to convict him of murder over his online forums where he advised people on how to end their lives. Law has admitted that he proactively looked for customers, appearing on a suicide discussion forum under a pseudonym, and made fatal substances available for purchase. “I cannot stop thinking that my little girl will never come back,” Maria Lopez, the mother of Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, who died in 2022 at the age of 18, said in a statement read out Wednesday by prosecutors. The girl’s father, Leonardo Bedoya, added: “The future we had imagined as a family disappeared.” Like these heartbroken parents, dozens of other people who lost loved ones to products sold by Law will make statements over the next few days in the courthouse in Newmarket, near Toronto. Law sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the UK, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defence and prosecution. There, 79 deaths are linked to him, according to Canadian prosecutors. Several affected families have voiced anger that Law would not face trial for murder, arguing he should be held directly responsible for prematurely ending the lives of mostly young, vulnerable people. “This man, Kenneth Law, should be treated for what he is: a serial killer. Because in there, in the courtroom, he doesn’t show any remorse at all,” Bedoya told reporters outside the courthouse. Despite dropping the murder charges, prosecutors are still expected to seek a stiff sentence for aiding suicides, possibly as long as 20 years, legal experts have said. “I’m no longer the same person I was before my brother died. Grief is now part of everything I do,” Adrienne Dalli, the sister of Maurizio Vadala, said in court as her voice choked with grief. I was just trying to serve a need that I thought was humane. Kenneth Law Judge Michelle Fuerst has allocated four days to hear victim impact statements and other evidence before determining sentencing. It is not immediately clear when Fuerst will decide on the sentence. Canada’s Globe and Mail newspaper published details earlier this month of Law’s interviews with a psychiatrist, which were conducted in prison after his guilty plea. “I was just trying to serve a need that I thought was humane,” Law said, according to court documents obtained by the paper. “I’m not a diabolical madman,” Law reportedly further said. In the court documents, Law recounted that he viewed himself as blameless following his arrest in 2023, insisting that he did not make the final decision to end anyone’s life and was just providing a product, the Globe reported. Law, who is in his 60s, worked as a chef at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto before launching his online suicide forums during the Covid-19 pandemic. He has admitted to shipping material containing lethal concentrations of the meat preservative sodium nitrite across Canada and abroad, often for about US$80. Leonardo Bedoya told reporters outside the court in May that he found his daughter dead in her bedroom. He called the decision by prosecutors to drop murder charges “a disgrace”. “She was my only daughter, my light, my life,” Bedoya said. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: All you need to know about a state visit, as White House rolls out red carpet for Xi
description: On these grand occasions, which aim to strengthen relationships between countries, it’s more than just pomp and pageantry involved.
content: A grand military welcome, a state dinner, tea at the White House and a tour of the National Archives: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington will see his American counterpart, Donald Trump, roll out the pomp and pageantry. The United States’ capital is bracing for high-level bilateral discussions served with a side of symbolic gestures, marking Xi’s first state visit to the country since 2015. But what exactly makes this a state visit, and how does it differ from other official visits? Does the distinction matter? The South China Morning Post breaks down what this means. Why is this a state visit? The White House Historical Association describes a state visit as a key part of presidential diplomacy that helps develop and maintain relationships with other countries. In this case, for the US, that relationship is with China. Traditionally, a state visit has been reserved for a foreign head of state, such as Xi, visiting at the invitation of the US president, rather than a head of government or lower-level official. Exceptions have occurred, including when the US has extended the designation to heads of government, such as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his 2023 state visit under Joe Biden’s administration. What makes it a state visit? State visits require a formal invitation from the American president, along with extensive planning and preparation. “A state visit is the highest level of diplomatic meeting between the US and the visiting country,” said Jeffrey Moon, founder of China Moon Strategies, who helped organise a state visit by Chinese president Jiang Zemin to Washington in 1997. “Strict protocols are observed to ensure the visiting leader is accorded the greatest honour and respect.” What happens at a state visit? These types of visits traditionally include an arrival ceremony, diplomatic talks, a state dinner, and ceremonial and cultural events, all of which are part of Xi’s itinerary. The visiting leader typically arrives a day before the main events. In this case, Trump will greet Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday. Moon said this rare gesture shows respect for the Chinese leader. During a state visit, foreign leaders typically stay at Blair House, directly across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, Moon added. On Thursday, the arrival ceremony, diplomatic talks, and state dinner will take place. “The ceremony, which will be held on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House, will feature 479 military personnel, representing all branches of the United States Armed Forces,” the first lady’s office said in a press release. Military pageantry is another key hallmark of a state visit, with the arrival ceremony set to feature a military review, performances by military bands and demonstration units, and a flyover by a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors. Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan will visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday as a cultural gesture. The state dinner in the evening is often one of the most closely watched events at a state visit, with menus combining the country’s own flavours with an American twist. Often three to five courses are served. “The leaders exchange toasts after the meal. There may be entertainment in the White House East Room after the meal,” Moon said. “There is also an exchange of state gifts during the visit.” Despite all of the pomp, the bilateral talks are an essential part of the plan, with trade, artificial intelligence and other issues expected to be on the agenda when Xi and Trump meet. To round out this visit, the American president will serve Xi tea in the Red Room on Friday, alongside the two first ladies. The couples will also tour the National Archives before Xi and Peng head back to China. What happened at Xi’s last state visit? It has been more than a decade since Xi’s last state visit to the US. In September 2015, then-President Barack Obama welcomed Xi with a formal ceremony on the South Lawn, full military honours and a 21-gun salute, followed by talks in the Oval Office. Why are not all leader visits state visits? Many leaders have visited the US, but not all of them are declared state visits. The US State Department’s historical records distinguish among state, official, working and other types of visits by foreign leaders. Xi last visited the US in 2023 for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Leaders’ Summit in California. He held a stand-alone meeting with then-President Joe Biden there, but the trip was not a state visit and did not include the ceremonial programme associated with one. Who else has been to the US for a state visit? Many state visits have taken place in the US over the years. During Trump’s first term, he hosted French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte Macron, for a state visit in 2018. This was the first state visit of Trump’s presidency. Then-President Biden hosted Modi for a state visit in 2023, even though India’s president, Droupadi Murmu, is the head of state and Modi is the head of government. His visit was an exception to the traditional head-of-state distinction. Meanwhile, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and British Prime Minister Theresa May both visited the White House to meet Trump during their time as leaders, but were not afforded state visits. As heads of government, they were not their countries’ heads of state. In both countries, Queen Elizabeth held that role at the time. In Canada and Britain, the monarch is the head of state. Today, King Charles is the head of state in both countries, while each country’s prime minister is the head of government. Trump hosted the king and Queen Camilla in April 2026 as part of a state visit.

title: Indian sailor killed in attack on vessel in Hormuz, India and Oman authorities say
description: A strike on the cargo ship Cape Dao led to a fire in the engine room, and 27 crew members had to be evacuated by the Omani navy.
content: An attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday killed an Indian sailor, Omani and Indian authorities said, with the latter condemning the ongoing attacks in the vital shipping lane. Since the start of the Middle East war, Iran has sought to impose its control over the maritime conduit for Gulf oil and gas, occasionally striking ships accused of failing to coordinate with its authorities or deviating from its preferred route. In retaliation, the US has been enforcing a counter-blockade of Iranian ports, carrying out strikes of its own on ships it says refuse to comply. Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said in a statement that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was attacked 2.5 nautical miles off the country’s coast “causing a fire in the engine room and leading to the death of one crew member”. Twenty-seven crew members were evacuated by the Omani navy, it added. In a statement, India’s foreign ministry condemned the attack on the Cape Dao, in which “one Indian national tragically lost his life”, urging the warring parties to return to negotiations. “The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways in the region must be restored at the earliest,” it added. India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide, and several of its mariners have been killed in Hormuz attacks since the Middle East war began. Oman sits across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, and ships seeking to skirt Tehran’s restrictions have recently been taking a route that hugs the Omani coast.

title: Paraguay’s president urges UN to let Taiwan in, calls island’s exclusion ‘a stain’
description: South American leader backs Taiwan’s UN participation and warns of global fallout from a strait conflict.
content: Paraguayan President Santiago Pena told the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday that his country “is not neutral” on the Taiwan Strait, pledging support for the self-ruled island and calling for its “full and meaningful participation” in the UN system. Casting a conflict in the strait as a potentially far greater threat than the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Pena warned of “ominous clouds gathering over the Indo-Pacific” and of a conflict that would hit Japan, the rest of East and Southeast Asia and global chip supplies. “Anyone pretending that this is far off or too distant to matter simply has not understood the 21st century,” Pena said, arguing that microchips had become to this century what oil was to the last. With stakes that “could scarcely be higher” and “the very future of humanity” on the line, neutrality was not an option for Asuncion. “Paraguay stands, and I say this loud and clear, with Taiwan.” Pena grounded that support in shared democratic values rather than “expediency”, described Taiwan’s exclusion from the UN as “a stain on the United Nations” and said Paraguay was ready to take a seat “on the front row” of any peace negotiation over the strait. Taiwan, officially the Republic of China, held China’s seat at the UN, including a permanent place on the Security Council, until October 1971. That month the General Assembly passed Resolution 2758, recognising the People’s Republic as China’s only lawful representative and expelling “the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek” as more governments switched recognition to Beijing. Taipei argues the resolution settled only who represents China and said nothing about the island’s sovereignty status. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise it as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons. The Chinese Mission to the UN could not immediately be reached for comment on Paraguay’s remarks. Pena’s alignment with Washington The Paraguayan leader did not mention mainland China at any point in the speech, in contrast to his visit to Taipei in May, when he condemned Beijing’s military and economic pressure on the island. The remarks came two days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of Japan and South Korea met on the sidelines of the assembly and stressed the importance of peace and stability across the strait, opposing any unilateral change to the status quo. Paraguay established relations with Taipei in 1957, during the US-backed dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner, and is the only South American nation that still recognises the island. It is one of 12 diplomatic allies Taiwan has left after Beijing systematically lured the others away. Pena, who studied in Taiwan, made his fourth trip to the island in May, his first as a state visit. The two sides signed a treaty on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and memorandums on cybersecurity and a jointly financed sovereign AI computing centre to be powered by Paraguay’s surplus hydroelectricity. The visit drew a sharp rebuke from Beijing, where foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun branded Paraguayan leaders willing “chess pieces” for independence forces on the island and urged Asuncion to recognise the one-China principle. Paraguay had already expelled Chinese envoy Xu Wei in December 2024 after he privately lobbied opposition lawmakers to switch recognition. Pena’s stance also tracks a deepening alignment with Washington, which signed a status of forces agreement with Asuncion last year granting visiting US military personnel and contractors immunity from local prosecution. Rubio praised Paraguay at the signing as one of the United States’ “strongest allies in the world”. At home, the relationship faces steady pressure from farm exporters, whose soy and beef cannot be sold directly to China and must be routed through Argentina and Brazil. Meanwhile, Taiwan remains a key buyer of Paraguayan meat, taking 12 per cent of beef exports and 86 per cent of pork exports in the first half of this year. In Pena’s account, Paraguay’s nearly seven decades of ties with Taipei amounted to more than “the product of a mere calculation” and stood as “a testament to the real friendship between our peoples”.

title: American views of China improve before Xi-Trump summit, Pew report finds
description: China’s average rating has risen from 28 to 37 since 2021, with younger Americans and Democrats expressing warmer views.
content: As Chinese President Xi Jinping makes his high-profile state visit to the US, Americans’ views of China remain negative but have improved in recent years, according to a new Pew Research Centre report. Using a “feeling thermometer” ranging from zero, the coldest rating, to 100, the warmest, Pew found that Americans gave China an average rating of 37, up from 28 in 2021. “The [Xi-Trump] meeting comes as Americans’ feelings about China have warmed in recent years, even though they remain cold overall,” Pew researchers Laura Silver and Laura Clancy wrote. The share of US adults giving China a warm rating, from 51 to 100, has risen from 11 per cent in 2021 to 19 per cent today. Meanwhile, the share with a neutral rating of exactly 50 has increased from 20 per cent to 27 per cent, while those with a cold rating of zero to 49 have fallen from 68 per cent to 54 per cent. Pew conducted the survey among 5,193 US adults from September 14 to 20, just before Xi’s three-day visit to Washington, which begins today. His schedule includes meetings at the White House, a state dinner and a visit to the National Archives. Views also differ by political affiliation and age. Democrats tend to rate China more warmly than Republicans, while younger Americans tend to express more welcoming views than older adults. The findings come as tensions persist between Washington and Beijing over issues including AI, rare earths and trade, with China hawks in Congress continuing to press for a tougher policy towards Beijing, even as Trump has repeatedly described Xi as a “great leader” and said the two have a good relationship. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Previously, in response to China’s rising global image, it said the country’s development and governance have gained wider recognition and called for closer ties and more exchanges between Chinese and American people. A recent Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey found a similar shift. Americans gave China an average feeling-thermometer rating of 39 this year, up from 26 in 2024, according to the Council. About 57 per cent said the US should pursue cooperation and engagement with China. The survey was conducted by Ipsos from July 10 to 21 among 2,156 Americans. Pew’s broader polling also found that views of China have improved on average in many countries. China is also more trusted than the US and EU to regulate AI in several countries surveyed, particularly middle-income countries.

title: Marco Rubio defends Xi Jinping’s US visit as essential despite deep disagreements
description: US secretary of state says Taiwan arms sales must be weighed against America’s military needs and voices hope Vladimir Putin will attend G20.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the welcome planned for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday, saying it would be “irresponsible” for the world’s two largest economies to avoid talks at the highest level despite their disagreements. Speaking to reporters at the United Nations hours before Xi’s expected arrival in Washington, Rubio was asked about criticism from Republican Senator Roger Wicker, who had argued against inviting the Chinese leader for a lavish visit. “The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Rubio said. “The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to.” Rubio, a former senator known for his criticism of Beijing, acknowledged friction over trade, supply chains and critical minerals. But he argued that direct communication was necessary between two powers with large economies and militaries, drawing a comparison with US-Soviet talks during the Cold War. The visit follows US President Donald Trump’s trip to China in May. Rubio said the leaders could meet again later this year at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China or the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Florida. Asked separately about arms sales to Taiwan, Rubio said proposed sales had to be weighed against the US military’s own requirements and its ability to replenish equipment. “If we sell you something, we don’t have it any more,” he said. The calculation applied to sales to any partner, he added, and took account of what American commanders said they would need in a potential conflict. “We rely on the input of the Department of War to determine what sales can happen now versus later,” Rubio said, referring to the Pentagon. America’s top diplomat pointed to what he described as the largest single US arms sale to Taiwan – valued at US$11 billion and completed in December – but did not announce a decision on any further sales. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Rubio also said he expected supply chains to come up in US-China discussions. Asked whether Trump would raise China’s commerce with Russia and Iran or alleged support for their military industries, he declined to set out a summit agenda, saying the leaders would discuss “everything that’s relevant”. Other global hotspots: Russia, Venezuela, Cuba and Iran On Russia, Rubio said Washington had invited President Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Florida in December and hoped he would attend. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president, but with other world leaders,” Rubio said of the Russian leader, adding that if Putin accepted, the gathering could give him and Trump a chance to talk. Rubio said the US was also willing to explore a limited agreement between Russia and Ukraine covering grain and energy infrastructure. Such a deal would not end the war but could ease some of its effects and possibly provide a basis for broader negotiations, he said. Turning to Venezuela, Rubio said Trump’s meeting with acting president Delcy Rodriguez on Tuesday had covered debt restructuring and the country’s political transition. Washington wanted to support economic recovery while helping establish the conditions for free and fair elections, he said. Asked about reports that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado had been prevented from returning to Venezuela, Rubio said he was unfamiliar with the specific accounts and would look into them. On Cuba, Rubio said its current governance model and US legal restrictions deterred investment. “No one is going to invest in Cuba under their current governance model,” he said. Rubio was sharply critical of Iran, saying its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had undermined previous understandings by attacking shipping. He said Washington would remain open to negotiations but argued that divisions within Iran’s leadership made an agreement difficult to secure.

title: Iran’s president accuses Trump of ‘bullying mentality’ in wartime speech to UN
description: Masoud Pezeshkian rejects US threats while signalling readiness for diplomatic talks to end conflict.
content: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused US President Donald Trump of a “bullying mentality” at the United Nations on Wednesday, saying Iran would not surrender in the war with the US but remained open to diplomacy to end the conflict. In a wartime address to the 193-member UN General Assembly, Pezeshkian said threats would only ‌harden Iran’s resolve, rejecting Trump’s warning that he could annihilate Iran if no deal were reached. “The remarks made by the US president yesterday … are a sign of a bullying mentality … The Iranian people will not bow to pressure … Those who are terrorists and train terrorists call us terrorists,” he said, referring to Trump’s description of Iran as the world’s leading sponsor of terrorism. Several times during his speech, Pezeshkian said Iran was ready to resolve tensions with the US through negotiations, but warned that ⁠Tehran would not accept the language of force. The US delegation walked out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech. The US mission to ‌the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Pezeshkian began his address by accusing the United States of killing civilians during the war, holding up photos that included an image of schoolgirls ‌in a classroom. A missile strike on a primary school in Minab on February 28 – hours after US ⁠and Israeli attacks on ⁠Iran launched the conflict – killed more than 175 children and teachers, according to Iranian officials. The Pentagon has not publicly released the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, ‌the deadliest civilian casualty incident involving the US military in decades. Reuters reported on March 5 that an initial internal US military investigation found US forces were likely responsible for the strike. Pezeshkian ‌said ‌Iran had no intention of seeking nuclear bombs, but would not give up its right to a peaceful nuclear programme. “Neither nuclear ‌weapons nor giving up nuclear knowledge,” he said. Seven months into a conflict that has rattled markets and pushed the Gulf to the brink ⁠of a wider war, Washington is unleashing an unprecedented economic offensive after military action failed to force Tehran to yield. Iranian leaders fear ⁠a worsening economy, marked by surging prices, weaker trade and pressure on household incomes, could reignite nationwide unrest that has repeatedly challenged the Islamic Republic. The Strait of Hormuz, conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas, has ‌become a focus of tensions between Iran ‌and the US. Tehran has conveyed its conditions to reopen the strategic waterway to the United States through mediators, Iranian sources said on Tuesday. “It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway,” Pezeshkian said. “The permanent deployment of hostile fleets and the expansion of the war will not lead to peace.”

title: Harvey Weinstein gets 15 years for sex assault after pleading for mercy
description: Disgraced Hollywood figure resentenced in New York for sexually assaulting a former production assistant.
content: Disgraced movie mogul Harvey Weinstein, who was at the centre of abuse allegations that spurred the #MeToo movement, was resentenced Wednesday to 15 years in prison for sexually assaulting a former production assistant. Weinstein, 74, forcibly performed oral sex in 2006 on Miriam Haley, one of dozens of women who have made accusations against the Pulp Fiction and Shakespeare in Love producer. Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in 2020 for the sexual assault, but it was overturned on appeal in 2024. A jury found him guilty again in 2025 after a retrial in New York. He made a last-ditch plea for leniency Wednesday as he addressed a packed Manhattan court, where Haley sat in the audience. “I am not a violent man, have some mercy,” said Weinstein, who wore a dark suit with a red tie and sat in a wheelchair due to health issues. “I sincerely apologise to anyone I have hurt,” he added, while continuing to maintain his innocence during remarks met by loud groans inside the court. After sentencing, his spokesman Juda Engelmayer said that Weinstein planned to appeal the latest sentence and conviction. “It is difficult to escape the conclusion that Harvey Weinstein is being sentenced not only for the crime of which he was convicted, but for who he is and what his name has come to represent,” he said, referencing the #MeToo movement. Judge Curtis Farber slammed Weinstein as a “sexual predator” who had failed to take responsibility for his actions. “You had it all. Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley,” Farber said. Prosecutors had sought 20 years in prison for Weinstein, while his lawyers warned that a longer sentence would likely see him die in prison. Haley said after the hearing that she believed the 15-year prison term “was fair, in my opinion. So I’m happy with it”. She earlier told the court that she had suffered a “life sentence” and suffered post-traumatic stress disorder after Weinstein assaulted her in New York. She said that Weinstein “abused his position of power” and that she “felt embarrassed that he thought I was so insignificant that he dared to do something like this”. Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg praised Haley for her “powerful, moving and eloquent” testimony in court. “I’m moved, as we should all be moved, by their courage and their steadfastness through what has obviously been a challenging process,” he told reporters. Weinstein once ruled Hollywood as a kingpin powerful enough to make or break projects and careers. But investigations by The New Yorker and The New York Times exposed a raft of abusive behaviour and prompted an avalanche of allegations from more than 80 people. Weinstein is also to be resentenced in California for the 2013 rape and assault of an actress in a Los Angeles hotel room, after an appeals court in June upheld the conviction but vacated his 16-year prison term. Meanwhile, a New York judge in May declared a mistrial in a separate case after jurors failed to reach a verdict on allegations he sexually assaulted actor Jessica Mann. It was the third time Mann had taken the stand against Weinstein after a 2020 guilty verdict was overturned due to mishandling of witnesses, and a 2025 case ended in mistrial after a jury-room feud. Prosecutors later said they would not pursue a fourth trial in Mann’s case. Still, she attended the court Wednesday in support of Haley along with Polish-born actor Kaja Sokola – Weinstein was acquitted of sexual assault against her in a 2025 retrial.

title: Bessent announces 2-month extension of US-China trade truce
description: Scott Bessent and He Lifeng held an unscheduled meeting in Washington on Wednesday following Sunday’s productive trade talks.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Wednesday that Washington and Beijing have agreed to extend the trade agreement reached in South Korea for just two months, as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit. “We have agreed ⁠today that we will extend what ⁠we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said in an interview with Fox News, adding ‌the agreement ‌will be extended for two months until January 10. Bessent made the remarks hours after an unscheduled meeting with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng at the World Bank headquarters in Washington, following their earlier engagement on Sunday at JPMorgan’s offices in New York. The South China Morning Post reported in August that the Busan trade agreement was likely to be extended, but the two sides differed on the truce’s duration. Beijing preferred an extension through the end of Trump’s presidency while Washington sought a shorter-term deal. The one-year agreement expires on November 10. Bessent added that a shorter extension would give the US time to assess whether China was meeting its commitments. “There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side,” he said. “So, we also want to see now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations to see if over the coming months they could be a bit more fulsome in enacting the agreement.” Washington has repeatedly raised concerns about inadequate flows of rare earths from China, saying Beijing needs to step up approvals for the strategic mineral exports. China’s shipments of rare earth magnets to the US fell 13 per cent year on year to 512 tonnes in August. Earlier in the day, Bessent said that Washington was also ready to sign on to China’s proposal of a more expansive agreement on trade. “The Chinese on Sunday came up with the idea of a bigger deal,” Bessent said. The comments stand in sharp contrast to US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer’s remarks on Monday, when he ruled out announcing an extension of the Busan agreement during the Trump-Xi summit. After eight hours of negotiations in New York, the two sides agreed to launch a dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI) and set in motion a bilateral trade body. Greer also attended Sunday’s meeting. Bessent’s remarks on Wednesday point to differing views within the US administration on the trade agreement with China. A source close to the discussion said the US side, especially the USTR, focused on the narrow trade mechanism of the US-China Board of Trade, where both sides select non-sensitive sectors and products capped at US$30 billion each for tariff reduction. Chinese delegation sought broader trade agreement Another source said that China’s “bigger deal” proposal seems like a “new idea” as the US side “wouldn’t have had the bandwidth to discuss it earlier”. The source suggested that Beijing had probably been working on the proposal and unveiled it only last weekend, with He remaining in Washington to work through the substantive details. The truce reached in Busan, South Korea, in October helped avert a full-blown crisis triggered by Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year. At the time, the two sides agreed to lower US tariffs on some Chinese goods; pause additional US restrictions and certain Chinese rare earth export controls; and secure Chinese commitments on US soybeans and fentanyl precursors. The second Bessent-He meeting comes as uncertainty remains over the presence of Chinese businesses in Xi’s delegation. The SCMP reported on Tuesday that differences between Washington and Beijing over potential investment announcements are creating roadblocks for a Chinese business delegation potentially accompanying Xi. A source familiar with the discussions said Washington and Beijing had yet to resolve their disagreements over the Board of Investment, particularly over possible Chinese investments in the US, adding to uncertainty over the delegation’s participation. The investment forum was an outcome of Xi and Trump’s last summit in Beijing in May. On AI dialogue, the Treasury secretary said that Beijing is “very eager” to engage with Washington on the technology. “We are working to define with them what we think the most important or the most perilous risk factors are, whether it’s uncontrolled AI agents, whether it is non-state actors using AI, either for cyber ops or for biologics,” he added. However, he noted that the reported “AI hotline” is still “yet to be determined.” Bessent reveals two sides will meet again at Apec summit in Shenzhen Bessent revealed on Monday that the two sides had agreed to meet again in Shenzhen, likely in two months, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. As the two sides move to formalise the AI dialogue, Senate Democrats on Wednesday urged the Trump administration to pair any cooperation with Beijing on AI safety with tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced US chips and chipmaking equipment. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer argued that the two goals were not contradictory, saying restrictions on advanced chips would preserve Washington’s technological advantage while giving it greater leverage to persuade Beijing to accept international AI safeguards. “If we stop them from buying these chips … we will have greater bargaining power over them,” Schumer said, adding that China would then be more likely to join efforts to impose AI guardrails worldwide. Senator Elizabeth Warren also took aim at the role of US technology executives in shaping China policy, singling out Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who is among the American business leaders expected to attend Thursday’s state dinner. “Mr Huang should be nowhere near the negotiating table during President Xi’s visit,” Warren said. The senators called for passage of three bipartisan measures – the AI Overwatch Act, MATCH Act and Chip Security Act – that would tighten controls on advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment and require tracking technology on some chips exported through third countries.

title: Led by China and US borrowing, the world now owes a record US$365 trillion debt: IIF
description: Debt climbs US$10 trillion in six months as fiscal strains deepen, exposing cracks in household and corporate balance sheets.
content: Global debt climbed to a record high of more than US$365 trillion in the first half of the year, with China and the United States accounting for the bulk of the increase, according to the latest findings by the Institute of International Finance (IIF) that come amid mounting concerns over global fiscal sustainability. The figure reflects total debt across all four major borrowing sectors – government, household, financial and non-financial corporate – in more than 100 mature and emerging market economies, and it marks the sixth consecutive quarterly increase, according to the banking trade group’s latest “Global Debt Monitor” report, published on Wednesday. Emre Tiftik, director of global markets and policy at the IIF, said the current debt wave differed from earlier ones, which were triggered by shocks such as the 2008 global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. “This time around, there is no specific crisis,” Tiftik said on Wednesday. “This is all driven by a super-cycle that is driven by healthcare, energy, AI, and IT and defence-related spending.” Because the spending is structural rather than cyclical, “debt is here to stay”, Tiftik added. Global debt rose by US$10 trillion in the first six months of 2026 – less than half of the expansion recorded in the same period last year, constrained by higher borrowing costs and volatility linked to the war in Iran, the IIF said, noting that the moderation was most evident among financial institutions and households. China alone accounted for more than US$4.8 trillion of the new borrowing, pushing its total outstanding debt to US$72.5 trillion, according to calculations based on IIF data. The rise highlights mounting fiscal pressures across China, where declining land-sale revenue and a prolonged real estate downturn have strained local government income. Corporate debt has also grown, with a number of companies grappling with thinner margins amid weak domestic demand and intense price competition. Meanwhile, in the US, total debt rose US$3.5 trillion to US$111.8 trillion over the six months, data from the IIF showed. This appeared largely driven by the financial sector and government, with federal debt reaching 122.3 per cent of gross domestic product in the second quarter. US federal debt surpassed US$40 trillion for the first time in August, according to the US Treasury Department, intensifying concerns over the country’s long-term fiscal sustainability. The key question is what could trigger an inflection point in dollar demand Institute of International Finance report Long-term US Treasury yields – the interest rate the government pays to borrow money over extended periods – have climbed in recent months to levels unseen since 2007. Total foreign government holdings of US Treasury debt fell for a second consecutive month in July, as Japan and China – two of the three largest creditors – trimmed their positions, according to the latest official data. However, despite ongoing debate over the US fiscal outlook and the safe-haven status of the dollar, the IIF noted that appetite for US debt has persisted, buoyed by expectations of high interest rates. “US securities remained well bid despite heightened volatility and speculation, partly because alternative markets lack comparable depth and liquidity,” the IIF’s report said. “The key question is what could trigger an inflection point in dollar demand,” the trade group added, warning that market reactions could sharpen as structural pressures, including the rising cost of servicing US debt, become more visible. A growing wave of corporate borrowing linked to artificial intelligence has not yet crowded out US Treasuries or diverted capital from emerging markets, with the share of global bond issuance from non-financial companies remaining stable, the IIF said. However, a sustained roll-out of long-dated AI-related corporate debt could eventually add pressure to long-term Treasury yields, the group warned.

title: In Focus | Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
description: Despite US AI leaders’ warnings over the risks of rapid development, they remain locked in a high-stakes race against each other – and China.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China. After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down. In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them. On Wednesday, Amodei pushed further for a slowdown when he addressed the UN Security Council by video link, warning that mismanaged AI posed an existential threat to humanity and urging nations to unite on global safety standards. These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety, among other issues. Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight. These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post. “Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.” It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability. This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development. “AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders. The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI What is driving calls to slow down? There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate. While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing. Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”. While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China. “Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”. Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader. Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls. China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week. Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power. “The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said. Existential risks, practical realities Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week. Huang dismissed such “doomerism” while on a New York Times podcast on Wednesday , arguing that fearmongering only slowed down industry adoption. There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies. As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely. Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety. Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards. Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down. According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers. China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels. Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week. “I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said. With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said. Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources. In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month. Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement. According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries. Genuine safety fears While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks. Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development. Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely. Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.” According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead. “At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.” Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”. Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development. Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration. “Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said. As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped. A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun. There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues. He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries. “Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

title: From moongazing to bus tours: how to celebrate Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong
description: Here’s a round-up of things to do and see for the Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on Friday this year.
content: From moongazing and picnics to bus rides and a lantern extravaganza, the Mid-Autumn Festival in Hong Kong has plenty of activities for everyone. This year the festival falls on September 25, a Friday, with the following day designated as a public holiday in Hong Kong. The South China Morning Post rounds up Mid-Autumn Festival offerings. 1. What are the highlights at night? At Victoria Park in Causeway Bay, the Hong Kong Tourism Board has organised the city’s first International Lantern Spectacular showcasing more than 3,000 distinctive lanterns from 20 countries, including South Korea and Brazil, and regions. Since opening on September 17, the show has proved so popular – drawing crowds every night – that the board has decided to extend it by a week to October 4. The show offers many photo-taking opportunities, including at the entrance, an eight-metre-tall lantern inspired by the city’s banyan trees and created by master artisans in Nanjing. Just a few minutes’ walk from Victoria Park, locals and tourists can catch the Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance on the evenings of Thursday, Friday and Saturday. A 67-metre-long fire dragon, a beast of legend, adorned with 12,000 burning incense sticks, will be carried through the neighbourhood. In Wan Chai, Lee Tung Avenue will feature a 200-metre-long walkway lit up by a colourful canopy of lanterns. Meanwhile, Citybus has partnered with the Wan Chai Blue House to launch the first-ever Mid-Autumn Festival-themed open-top bus route, H1M “Moon Viewing Tour of Hong Kong Island”. The tour bus will pass Victoria Park and visit many locations on Hong Kong Island including Kennedy Town, the Hill Road Flyover and the Blue House, a four-storey pre-war building. Across Victoria Harbour, at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre Piazza in Tsim Sha Tsui, the Leisure and Cultural Services Department will present a lighting installation until October 11. 2. What are the daytime highlights? At the West Kowloon Cultural District arts hub, the Harbourside East Lawn of the Art Park has been turned into a picnic ground until October 11, with food stalls, live music and themed workshops. Visitors can also cycle along the Victoria Harbour waterfront and explore arts and cultural spaces. 3. When is the best time to gaze at the moon? According to the Hong Kong Observatory, the full moon will occur in the early hours of Sunday. However, the forecaster said a bright, round moon should still be seen at night during the Mid-Autumn Festival period, weather permitting. The best time for moongazing on Friday night is around 11.24pm, when the moon reaches its highest elevation in the sky. On Friday, the weather is expected to be mainly fine and dry. On Saturday, there will be sunny periods with very hot weather during the day. But it will be cloudy in the morning and at night on both days. 4. Any special transport arrangements? On Friday, MTR lines – except the Airport Express, Disneyland Resort line and the section of the East Rail line to and from Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau stations – will run enhanced services from 3pm onwards. Services on these lines will also be extended to the early hours on Saturday. Eleven Light Rail routes and three MTR bus routes will also extend services to the early hours of Saturday, while tram and ferry services will be strengthened, subject to passenger demand.

title: Trump’s Board of Peace proposes US$2.45 billion Gaza reconstruction plan
description: Physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly US$35.2 billion in the medium term and another US$71.4 billion in the next 10 years.
content: The US-backed Board of Peace is proposing a six-month US$2.45 billion plan to begin reconstruction and governance in Gaza as President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan struggles to stay afloat. At a meeting of the group’s board, the governors unveiled a 66-project blueprint to get things started while acknowledging enormous hurdles that must still be overcome. The projects include ambitious infrastructure, education and health initiatives that are designed to support Trump’s 20-point plan to end the Israel-Gaza war. “The need is immense,” the board said, noting that full reconstruction from the physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly US$35.2 billion over the medium term and another US$71.4 billion in the next 10 years. The ceasefire, which took effect on October 10, was meant to clear the way for a broader process to rebuild Gaza under the guidance of the Board of Peace. The plan included additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas, the arrival of an international peacekeeping force and a new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory’s day-to-day affairs. It also envisioned an ambitious programme for rebuilding war-ravaged Gaza. But the US-backed plan has largely stalled. While the ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting and humanitarian conditions have improved, the Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza and now occupies some 60 per cent of the territory. Hamas has not given up its weapons. The international military force and new government still have not entered Gaza, and reconstruction has not begun. The vast majority of Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes. The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said progress hinges largely on Hamas disarming – a step the group has refused to take so far. But he also has pressed Israel to scale back its military operation. A key question the board faces today will be not only laying out plans for reconstruction, but a timeline for the deployment of the international force and new government, plans to disarm and bring badly needed building materials into the territory.

title: Japan finds child’s body on island, possibly missing boy
description: Police have been searching for Yuto Takahashi, a first grader, since he went missing on September 5.
content: The body of a child was found on Wednesday on the coast of an outlying island in northeastern Japan, with police investigating whether it could be a six-year-old boy who went missing in the area earlier this month. The body, which was found around 11.20am on Tobishima, Yamagata Prefecture, was dressed in what appeared to be a navy blue and red Spider Man-themed jumpsuit, similar to the clothing the boy was wearing when he disappeared, according to prefectural police. A man in his 70s alerted authorities after discovering the body. It was found face down on rocks about 5m from the waterline on the island, which is located around 40km (25 miles) northwest of the park on the mainland near the boy’s home, where he was last seen, police said. Police have been searching for Yuto Takahashi, a first grader at a special needs school in Sakata in the prefecture, since he went missing around 9.20am on September 5.

title: Activist charged after microchipped dog caught in probe into suspected attack
description: One of five strays caught in Yuen Long was registered to Kent Luk, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter.
content: Hong Kong authorities have charged an animal welfare activist after a stray dog captured during an investigation into a suspected fatal canine attack on a cyclist in Yuen Long was found to have a microchip registered in his name. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department and police have been conducting operations to capture stray dogs in the area following the suspected attack on Sunday. Police suspect a pack of dogs attacked a 27-year-old woman, who was found unconscious beside a bicycle on Pok Wai South Road and later died. She suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs. As of Wednesday night, eight stray dogs have been caught so far, including the latest batch of three on the same night. At least three of the eight were microchipped, according to the department. One of the microchipped dogs, a 13-year-old mongrel named “Dai B”, was registered to Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of the animal rescue group Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter. The dog was among three animals captured in the first round of operations late on Sunday. Authorities approached Luk the following day after finding that the dog’s microchip was registered in his name. Luk said he provided a statement to the department on Wednesday and was subsequently charged with failing to keep a dog under proper control and keeping a dog with an expired licence. Luk said the dog was found wandering alone on Pok Wai South Road and was later captured. He visited Dai B on Wednesday and confirmed that it was the same dog. “Definitely not him [in the suspected attack]. He is incredibly gentle, and at 13 years old, he walks very slowly.” He said he first took in Dai B in 2017 or 2018. “He originally belonged to an elderly woman who made a living collecting cardboard for recycling around Tai Sang Wai. The dog was always by her side,” Luk said, adding that she might have died as he failed to locate her home, now possibly demolished, during a recent visit. Luk said he would not contest the department’s summons and planned to pay the penalty and rehandling fees, amounting to less than HK$3,000 (US$385), as he had done on around 200 previous occasions. The dog licence expired in 2021. Luk said Dai B was once attacked by dogs kept at nearby storage yards and suffered injuries. As the elderly woman could not afford the treatment, she asked his group for help. “After he recovered, we arranged for him to be microchipped through the SPCA,” he said, referring to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. He earlier told the South China Morning Post that it was common practice among rescuers to microchip animals in their own names after treating their injuries or spaying them. Otherwise, unchipped dogs would have no registered keeper and could be euthanised if they bit someone and were captured. Authorities are conducting bite-mark analysis and DNA tests but have not announced whether any of the captured dogs were involved in Sunday’s incident. The case remains under investigation.

title: To increase China’s consumption, boost the nation’s social safety net, IMF director says
description: The global organisation found that savings of rural households decrease when social and healthcare spending is higher.
content: The Chinese government needs to increase its spending on social safety nets, including pensions and rural healthcare, and further relax urban household registration restrictions to give households greater confidence to spend rather than save, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) Asia-Pacific chief. In an interview with the South China Morning Post, Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, said the export- and investment-led model that powered China’s decades of economic reform “had run its course” amid several challenges, including limited social safety nets and an ongoing property slump. China needed to rebalance its economy towards more consumption-led growth, he said, but that shift would require Beijing to do more than it had done before. Srinivasan said Beijing’s policy announcements had so far delivered more promises than action, adding that it was important for China to meet its objective of significantly raising private consumption set out in Beijing’s latest five-year plan. More fiscal spending was needed, he said, particularly on healthcare, pensions and reform of hukou – China’s household registration system, which determined residents’ access to public services such as healthcare and education, as well as job opportunities and eligibility to buy homes, based on location. “China has to significantly boost fiscal spending towards improving social safety nets. This would lower households’ precautionary savings and boost consumption.” The comments echoed arguments made in a new IMF book, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, which Srinivasan co-edited. The book identified stronger social safety nets as a key part of the country’s shift away from an investment- and export-led model, towards one centred on household consumption, services and productivity gains. An IMF analysis found that higher social and healthcare spending significantly lowered saving among rural households by reducing their need to build precautionary reserves against future shocks, according to the book.
