An IMF calculation found that doubling social spending in more rural areas would result in an additional fiscal cost of 1.0 per cent of China’s gross domestic product (GDP) over five years, but increase consumption by 1.8 per cent of GDP and reduce the saving rate by 1.1 percentage points. “Social spending that targets rural households should be a priority, given the fiscal constraints facing local governments,” the book said. Further reform of China’s hukou system could also help. Many migrant workers with rural hukou who live in cities do not have the same access to benefits as residents with local hukou, which can encourage them to maintain higher savings. The IMF has called for further relaxation of hukou restrictions in larger cities and more equitable access to social benefits regardless of registration status. As the prolonged property downturn weakens household confidence, the need to strengthen the social safety net has become more pressing in China. “The biggest obstacle is the loss of confidence,” Srinivasan said. Housing was the biggest asset for many Chinese households, but the property crisis has eroded that source of wealth, he said. China therefore needed a “comprehensive resolution” to the property sector, including completing pre-sold homes, addressing unviable developers and providing support to affected households, he said. The IMF estimated that central government fiscal support, equivalent to about 5 per cent of GDP over three years, could help rehabilitate the housing sector. A stronger shift towards domestic demand would also help address China’s widening trade imbalances, Srinivasan said. Weak domestic demand and low inflation have helped make Chinese exports more competitive, contributing to a larger current-account surplus. “Reviving domestic demand is important, both for the good of China and for the world,” he said.

title: Hong Kong to welcome 1.29 million mainland Chinese visitors for National Day break
description: Immigration Department shares estimate as Hong Kong’s No 2 official says authorities to ‘make good preparations’ for ‘golden week’ break.
content: Hong Kong is expected to welcome about 1.29 million mainland Chinese travellers over the National Day “golden week” break, with city authorities planning to step up crowd management and tighten supervision of tour agencies and retail outlets. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Hong Kong’s No 2 official, chaired a meeting with various government departments on Wednesday to discuss preparations for the holiday on the mainland, which spans October 1 to 7. On top of the expected influx of about 1.29 million mainland travellers over the break, the Immigration Department said it expected the average daily number of visitor arrivals to surpass last year’s figure by more than 5 per cent. Last year, Hong Kong recorded more than 1.4 million mainland arrivals during the eight-day golden week break, with a daily average of about 175,360. “The government will make good preparations for receiving visitors and maintain close liaison with relevant organisations and the travel trade to prepare well for crowd management, information dissemination and arrangements of public transport and boundary control points, with a view to responding promptly to various kinds of emergencies and ensuring the smooth operation of various aspects in receiving visitors and offering them a high-quality experience,” Chan said. The Travel Industry Authority and sector leaders said they expected about 1,180 mainland tour groups to visit the city during the holiday. The industry watchdog pledged to coordinate with relevant parties to manage visitor flows at tourist spots and inspect districts with more registered shops for inbound tour groups as part of efforts to enhance travel experiences and protect visitors’ rights. Earlier this month, the authority revoked the licences of two travel agencies and a guide after finding they had failed to protect members of mainland tour groups from “coerced shopping”. The Customs and Excise Department also said on Wednesday that it would step up enforcement and inspection of shops serving visitors to combat unfair trade practices over the holiday. Authorities will activate the Interdepartmental Joint Command Centre over the holiday to monitor various border control points in real time, as well as maintain close contact with their mainland counterparts. The Security Bureau said it would activate the Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre during the break to coordinate public order at border-crossing facilities and help interdepartmental follow-up actions. The Transport Department said it approached public transport operators to increase capacity and reserve sufficient vehicles and manpower, in addition to speaking with companies offering transport services connecting different border checkpoints. Interdepartmental efforts will be stepped up at High Island Reservoir’s East Dam in Sai Kung and campsites, such as Ham Tin Wan, as authorities anticipated a “large number of visitors”. Police officers will also be deployed to control traffic during peak visiting hours, while the Transport Department will coordinate with the green minibus operator to increase service when necessary. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department said it would continue to adopt the real-name reservation system for the Po Pin Chau trail at East Dam. The department also pledged to deploy extra staff at campsites for patrols, enforcement action and ramped-up on-site publicity efforts. The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department will enhance cleaning services at the public toilet near the Ham Tin Wan campsite, with additional cubicles and washing facilities expected to be ready during the break.

title: US Air Force to shut down research centre focusing on Chinese military
description: The China Aerospace Studies Institute published open-source research on the PLA’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities.
content: The US Air Force is shutting down a major research centre dedicated to open-source analysis of the Chinese military’s air, space, cyber and missile capabilities. The China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) said in a statement on Tuesday that Air University, the US Air Force institution under which it operates, had decided to close the institute, with all of its roles becoming unfunded from October 1. CASI said its employees would continue to work and get paid for now and that it expected to honour its existing commitments “through at least March of 2027”. The institute will continue publishing articles and reports already in the pipeline and conducting courses on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) that it has already committed to provide to air force units. However, a 10th anniversary event scheduled for February will be cancelled. Unless the institute could “find a new home” within the air force for the whole CASI team, staff were expected to move to other jobs. “Once all of the civilians eventually depart, CASI will close,” it added. The issue emerged publicly on Monday, when a civilian CASI researcher wrote on LinkedIn that every civilian employee had been notified that their positions would become unfunded from October 1 and that they would become “surplus federal employees”. The institute’s announcement appears to contradict the position set out by the air force earlier on Tuesday. In a statement to US defence news website Breaking Defense, the air force said civilian staff would no longer be assigned to CASI as part of an “ongoing civilian restructure” within Air Education and Training Command, but that the institute’s mission would continue, with the organisation “leveraging assigned military service members to accomplish its objectives”. It also noted that affected civilian employees would remain in their present positions until further notice and would be evaluated for reassignment. The institute’s closure was announced after Breaking Defense published the air force’s comments. CASI’s mission statement describes it as the air force’s “premier centre” for studying China and its aerospace capabilities. Its mission includes primary-source research and translation covering air, space, cyber and missile-related fields, as well as analysis for senior air and space force leaders and policymakers across the US government. It has worked with other US military services and commands, allied militaries, defence think tanks and academic institutions. Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst in the Defence Strategy Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, described the closure as “a very bad move”, saying on social media that it sent a signal to Beijing that the United States was not serious about deterring China. CASI’s publications have included “PLA Rocket Force Organisation”, a 2022 open-source study that compiled dossiers on Chinese missile-force units and institutions, including their history, locations, leadership, equipment and force structure. In 2023, the institute published “PLA Naval Aviation Reorganisation”, which documented the transfer of most of the PLA Navy’s shore-based fighter, bomber, radar, air defence and airfield units to the PLA Air Force. CASI has also produced the regularly updated “PLA Aerospace Power” primer on trends in China’s military air, space and missile forces, whose fifth and latest edition was published in May. Alongside civilian researchers, CASI has hosted serving military officers through a fellowship programme that brings air force majors to the institute for a year-long course in place of attending Air Command and Staff College. CASI traces its roots to an earlier initiative at the Rand Corporation, a US policy research organisation, before coming under Air University in 2017. Rand said the original institute was created in 2014 at the initiative of US Air Force headquarters. A source familiar with the situation said the institute was modelled on the China Maritime Studies Institute (CMSI) at the US Naval War College and that the two institutes had routinely coordinated their work. The South China Morning Post understands that CMSI is unaffected by the air force’s decision.

title: Pakistani-made ‘micro film’ scoops top prize at Asian festival’s Hong Kong final
description: The event was the first Hong Kong finals of the Inspiring Asia Micro Film Festival, whose 2026 edition champions community empowerment.
content: A short film depicting an unexpected friendship between a Pakistani tailor and a Hong Kong florist has scooped the top Hong Kong prize at this year’s Inspiring Asia Micro Film Festival. Between the Unsaid, produced by Kaneeta Arshad and directed by Qasim Khan, champions integration and how different communities in the city should work and learn together. “We see this very commonly in Hong Kong with our parents or someone who comes from outside Hong Kong,” Khan says. “There’s a communication barrier, but they’re still able to bond with the locals without speaking the same language.” Arshad adds that a Pakistani-made film winning the award felt like “such a personal win” and a true testament to how this city is “a great home for diversity”. One of the five Hong Kong judges, Oscar-winning filmmaker Ruby Yang, who is also the director of the University of Hong Kong’s Journalism and Media Studies Centre, says: “Even when characters don’t speak the same language, they still make a connection, which is what film and media are about.” Between the Unsaid was initially 17 minutes long, say Khan and Arshad, who are both on the board of Visionary Bees, an NGO that uses the arts to encourage integration, inclusion, and social and economic mobility. They condensed it to six minutes during post-production, the maximum runtime allowed according to the festival’s “micro film” standards. This allowed them to centre solely on the characters’ emotions and wordless communication. In 2022, venture capitalist turned philanthropist Lionel Li Xiaobo launched the first Inspiring Asia Micro Film Festival to focus on social impact and innovation. Four years on, it has expanded to eight regional finals, from which winners advance to the pan-Asia main round. This year’s Hong Kong edition is the city’s inaugural event and is primarily supported by the Hong Kong Academy for Wealth Legacy, an organisation working with family businesses. Entries came from filmmakers, students, community leaders and NGOs, who competed in three categories: best micro film award, best AI film award and best project award. First-time filmmaker Chen Yimin won best AI film with The Story Hunter, which she wrote and directed. The film, based on the true story of an elderly person regaining her spark after a long period of emotional isolation, was co-created by about a dozen people, including students and elderly community members who provided voices and facial references. Chen is the founder of Ginger Innovation, a social enterprise dedicated to “ageing education”. Her team delivered the film in two weeks, balancing four days of AI image generation with 10 days of scriptwriting, editing and polishing. As attention spans shrink and generative AI grows, filmmakers must constantly find ways to engage an ever-changing audience. Yang says that, as an educator, she has seen first-hand how “attention spans are getting shorter”, but while there is “value in seeing a film in a cinema or projected on a big screen”, the film festival is also important in that it is “bringing different stakeholders – funders and filmmakers – into the same room to connect as a community”. She adds: “It’s important to showcase the work of Hong Kong AI filmmakers and NGOs, whose work is hardly highlighted. Because of consent and access, it’s hard to film in NGOs, so I’m pleased to see elderly people, people with Alzheimer’s and children born with disabilities [on screen].” Fen Jennifer Lin was also one of the five Hong Kong judges. The director of ArtX Hong Kong, a new arts and technology institute at City University of Hong Kong, says that “AI has become an inevitable topic”. “As each generation embraces its own technological innovation, AI is totally rewriting industry rules and norms on how to produce a film,” she says. “On one hand, we embrace this change because it’s inevitable, but we don’t embrace it blindly. We have to embrace it with responsibility … and nurture art intuition.” Lin explains that art intuition means focusing on “what story it tells, how it tells the story and what message is there”. “Without art intuition, you cannot produce something meaningful,” she says. “We must pay attention so technology doesn’t take away our judgment. “Lots of things have to be adjusted as technology advances, which is why lawmakers, policymakers, educators and creative professionals have to form an ecosystem to communicate and find solutions. We cannot just turn our backs on technology development.” The best project category is a slightly less technical award that prioritises the mission’s meaning rather than dissecting the mise-en-scène. Its winner, The Superpower of Little Hands, portrays children living with congenital limb differences in an optimistic way, unlike the doom and gloom some might expect when it comes to children’s disabilities. Edwina Lai, the founding president of the Hand in Hand Association, which produced the film, is a first-time filmmaker who prioritised “teamwork, clear communication and smooth execution”, she says. “We spent so much time talking heart-to-heart with our Hand in Hand families, making sure everyone felt safe, heard and aligned with the message. Because of that deep trust, all the families stepped up happily to share their own stories.” Despite working without generative AI, Lai and her team finished shooting the film in just one day. As the best project award winner, the Hand in Hand Association will receive resources from The Hong Kong Jockey Club Programme on Social Innovation to advance its community initiatives. The three winning Hong Kong films will advance to the pan-Asia main round and awards ceremony in Manila, the Philippines, on October 25.

title: ‘No broadcast, no problem’: Chinese media uses smartphones to stream Asian Games
description: CCTV devises unique solution to show table tennis match with star duo Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha after organisers limit cameras at venue.
content: Table tennis fans had a unique experience watching star duo Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha beat their Uzbekistan opponents in the Asian Games, after state media used three smartphones to stream the match live to viewers back in China. The reason for the extraordinary measure? Out of nine competition tables, organisers of the Asian Games equipped only Tables 1 and 2 with broadcast cameras, leaving the rest without live coverage. Wang and Sun played on Table 4 at Sky Hall Toyota arena on Wednesday. As the primary rights holder for the Asian Games, China Media Group (CMG) had been expected to broadcast the match on television. However, viewers tuning into its sports channel were met with scrolling text reading: “No broadcast signal for this match.” To accommodate fan demand, state broadcaster CCTV deployed reporters on-site to conduct a multi-angle “lightweight” live stream using three smartphones, broadcasting real-time footage on its sports app. Marking possibly the first time state media has broadcast a major match via mobile phones, the makeshift solution amused fans who watched the live stream. “Add this to the list of things I never thought I’d see in my lifetime, CCTV broadcasting a match on mobile phones. This Asian Games budget ... turning our heavyweight athletes into lightweight streams,” one fan wrote. “No broadcast signal, no problem – our CCTV will stream it on phones themselves,” another remarked. One commenter noted: “The ‘lightweight’ stream on the CCTV Sports app was actually good. The picture quality held up against the cameras on Tables 1 and 2. Audio and stabilisation were a bit worse, but the cameraman’s post-match tracking was fantastic! I didn’t even realise it was a person following them.” The fans who tuned in watched Wang and Sun beat Shokhrukh Iskandarov and Arujan Kamalova 11-4, 14-12, 11-2 in the mixed doubles round of 32. Normal broadcast service resumed for the men’s and women’s team semi-finals later that afternoon, as those matches were on Tables 1 and 2. China’s women’s team, comprising Sun, Wang Manyu and Kuai Man, defeated North Korea 3-0 to advance to the final. The women’s team final is scheduled for 6.30pm Hong Kong time on Thursday, where China will face either South Korea or Japan.

title: Xi-Trump summit: China’s state car has already proved a match for the US ‘Beast’
description: The custom-built Hongqi N701 caught the eye of then-president Biden when he met the Chinese leader in San Francisco in 2023.
content: US President Donald Trump has made no secret of how little he agrees with his predecessor, Joe Biden, on many things. So, as Chinese President Xi Jinping is about to arrive in Washington on Wednesday, local time, there is one object that may offer a small moment of entertaining comparison between the two American leaders: Xi’s car. Xi is expected to bring his own ride – a custom-built Hongqi N701, the Chinese state limousine that has accompanied him on overseas trips since 2022. In a brief exchange captured on camera during Xi’s visit to San Francisco in November 2023, then-president Biden and his guest stopped beside the Chinese limousine. “It’s a beautiful vehicle,” the American leader said. “It’s our Hongqi. Domestically made,” Xi responded with a smile, telling his staff to open the door so that Biden could take a look at the highly secure rear cabin. “It’s like that Cadillac we have over here,” Biden commented, drawing a comparison with the purpose-built state car that serves US presidents. Now the Hongqi is returning to the United States while “that Cadillac” – more commonly known as Cadillac One or the Beast – is now used by Trump, a president who has spent much time criticising Biden’s approach to China. So, what will Trump think of Xi’s car? The specifications of the Hongqi, which translates as Red Flag, have never been disclosed. Even “N701” is understood to be a convenient project code rather than an official model designation. What is known is that the vehicle is roughly 5.5 metres (18 feet) long. It is estimated to weigh more than three tonnes, reflecting the heavy-duty nature of its construction. The N701 is widely believed to be equipped with reinforced armour, bullet-resistant glass and run-flat tyres. Reports have also described advanced systems designed to protect the cabin from contaminated air, as well as highly secure communications equipment, placing it in the same category as the US president’s custom-made armoured limousine. But unlike Cadillac One, which shares some styling elements with the brand’s commercial models, the N701 is more exclusive to Chinese state missions, its unique design clearly differentiating it from the Hongqi line-up available to civilian buyers. While the N701 retains the brand’s iconic red flag bonnet ornament, it features a longer, cleaner and more contemporary look than the traditional Hongqi which served as China’s state limousine from the 1960s. The most distinctive design features of the modern state vehicle include a more square-shaped front fascia, along with a taller chrome-framed vertical grille and extended rear windows. Production is extremely limited. Reports citing the project plan indicate just 50 vehicles will be made over a 10-year period from 2020, averaging five units per year. The total investment for the entire project is reported to be 572 million yuan (US$85.4 million). The N701 made its first public appearance in July 2022, when Xi visited Hong Kong. Since then, it has carried him on state visits and summits around the world, from Asian neighbours such as Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia and South Korea to more distant destinations including Saudi Arabia, France, the US and Russia. The limousines are often deployed in pairs, a primary vehicle and a backup, and are typically transported to the destination by Chinese aircraft ahead of Xi’s arrival, as detailed in reports from some of his previous trips. The Hongqi brand was created in 1958 by China’s First Automobile Works when the country sought to build its own high-end state limousine. The first Hongqi luxury sedan was completed that August, and the CA770 – a classic model introduced in the 1960s – became famously associated with China’s top leadership and foreign dignitaries at major state occasions. However, the Hongqi production line came to an end in 1981 after China opened its economy and foreign luxury brands entered the Chinese market. For much of the next two decades, the brand struggled. That changed in the 2000s when Beijing began placing greater emphasis on developing a domestic motor vehicle industry and the Hongqi returned to the official car market, with the HQ3 model beginning to secure government contracts in the middle of the decade. In 2013, the L5 became the first Hongqi limousine to be restored to state diplomatic ceremonies, notably carrying the then French president Francois Hollande during his visit to China. The revival of the Hongqi as a top-tier diplomatic vehicle coincided with Xi’s rise to power and his efforts to promote the “Chinese dream” of national rejuvenation. In 2014, Xi brought two Hongqi L5s with him on a state visit to New Zealand – the first widely reported instance of a Chinese leader taking a home-built state limousine overseas. Xi’s L5 was eventually succeeded by the more modern N501 before it was replaced by the N701, the model that caught Biden’s eye. Chinese leaders traditionally used vehicles provided by their hosts, and showcasing a “domestically made” presidential limousine on foreign trips – like Xi presented to Biden – was a practice long associated with his US and Russian counterparts. Whatever Trump makes of the car, when Xi arrives at the White House and steps out of the N701, the limousine will already have done its job: as a symbol of modern China, carrying its leader onto the world stage.

title: Abused children at higher risk of long-term health problems, Hong Kong NGO warns
description: Against Child Abuse also calls for tiered prevention strategy, with primary focus on zero-tolerance approach and policy support.
content: Child abuse can impair victims’ development and increase their risk of long-term health problems such as obesity and heightened inflammatory responses, a Hong Kong NGO has said, calling for a tiered prevention strategy to strengthen protections. Against Child Abuse on Wednesday shared the results of an overview of local studies from recent years on the effects of abuse on children, while calling for more resources and enhanced measures to safeguard youngsters. One cited study, published in 2024, involved 661 children and found that adverse caregiving experiences in early childhood were associated with altered growth patterns. While more frequent neglect and psychological aggression contributed to greater subsequent reductions in body mass index, physical abuse was conversely linked to a higher likelihood of being overweight or obese, according to the study. Another study, which followed 63 abuse victims, showed that those who were maltreated reported poorer maternal care during childhood, lower family support and heightened inflammatory responses years later compared with those without a history of abuse. “Our children in Hong Kong are currently facing a very disadvantageous environment, including a continuously deteriorating family environment, which has consistently heightened the risk of child abuse, while family stress and family dysfunction are closely tied to the risk of children suffering abuse,” said Professor Patrick Ip Pak-keung of the University of Hong Kong, who was involved in both studies. A third cited study, involving 232 pairs of mothers and children, found that repeat pregnancy within two years was associated with higher maternal stress and an increased risk of physical child abuse, leading to recurrent mistreatment and more hospital emergency department visits for youngsters. Separate research also found that substance abuse among mothers was associated with an increased risk of physical child abuse. Ip, who is part of the university’s paediatrics and adolescent medicine department and an executive committee member of Against Child Abuse, called for greater effort by families and wider society to protect youngsters. “To effectively improve the health of children in high-risk families and reduce their risk of abuse, we must not only mobilise family strength, but more importantly, combine external support involving all sectors of society, schools and communities,” he said. NGO director Maple Lau Siu-kwan highlighted the importance of raising parental awareness about the harms of harsh parenting. She called for more support for vulnerable carers, alongside early identification and intervention. She suggested a three-tiered prevention strategy, with primary prevention focusing on a zero-tolerance approach to violence against children and supported by policies and measures such as promoting positive parenting skills and teaching youngsters how to protect themselves. Secondary prevention would focus on early identification of at-risk families and intervention, while the tertiary tier would cover prevention of repeated abuse through professional intervention, Lau said. The prevalence of child abuse in Hong Kong has worsened in recent years, with the NGO citing official data showing that recorded cases rose by 44 per cent from 940 in 2020 to 1,354 last year. The group attributed the rise to factors such as the Covid-19 pandemic, socioeconomic stressors, parenting styles and greater public awareness. In July 2024, lawmakers passed the Mandatory Reporting of Child Abuse Ordinance, which requires 25 categories of professionals in the social welfare, education and healthcare sectors to report suspected cases of serious child abuse to authorities. Under the ordinance, which took effect on January 20 this year, those who fail to make a report face up to three months in prison and a fine of HK$50,000 (US$6,400). In his annual policy address last week, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government was monitoring the implementation of the legislation to ensure adequate support measures were in place.

title: Trump offloads tens of millions in AI, tech shares, led by Microsoft, Amazon, Meta
description: US president made over 1,100 trades in July, selling up to US$31 million of Microsoft and US$26 million of Amazon, disclosures show.
content: US President Donald Trump has sold shares worth tens of millions of US dollars in major tech companies, including Microsoft, Amazon and Meta Platforms in July, a move that may reveal some of his views on the sector, especially as competition with China intensifies. Microsoft topped the list of sales transactions, with six trades totalling up to US$31 million, according to filings disclosed by the US Office of Government Ethics on Tuesday. The data detailed Trump’s trading activity in July, providing ranges rather than exact figures. He also offloaded up to US$26 million worth of Amazon shares, and up to US$630,000 and US$365,000 in Meta Platforms and Google’s parent company Alphabet, respectively. He sold some US$1 million worth of Nvidia shares during the month in two transactions, with another purchase of a similar value. He also continued to buy shares in other tech giants, despite the number of purchases being lower than sales for most of these companies. Across the month, sales outnumbered purchases by over 700 to nearly 400, according to the filing. The disclosures could reveal some of Trump’s views on artificial intelligence, one of the focuses of a highly anticipated meeting between Xi and Trump. High-level talks starting Sunday between top trade representatives from the world’s two largest economies were “very successful”, according to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, with Washington proposing a bilateral notification mechanism for national security incidents related to AI. The heads of nearly all of the tech giants mentioned above were expected to attend a high-profile dinner in Washington on Thursday, according to a CNBC report on Wednesday. That includes Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg. They would be joined by other industry heavyweights including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Apple’s Tim Cook, according to CNBC. The filings showed that Trump added positions in hardware and chip companies in the computing and telecommunications sectors, and in companies with domestic manufacturing footprints. On July 31, he bought up to US$500,000 in shares of US chipmaker Texas Instruments, as well as networking chip and software giant Broadcom. He also established new six-figure positions in legacy tech companies IBM and Cisco Systems. Trump is not alone in his apparent skepticism about the tech sector’s high-flying momentum. On Tuesday, prominent US hedge fund manager Michael Burry – known for being portrayed in the movie The Big Short – said he was doubling down on bearish bets on semiconductor and AI. Questioning the durability of the memory supercycle, Burry said shares in memory producers “really ran up to ridiculous prices for what they are” and would “sell down intensely”. He said he had added to his short positions “in some size” against Micron Technology, Nebius Group, Palantir Technologies and the broader iShares Semiconductor exchange-traded fund, according to a Substack post.

title: Opinion | Bad money decisions are coming home to roost for the US and Japan
description: For major economies that have relied on debt to maintain living standards since 2007, high inflation might be one way out.
content: The US Treasury market is in trouble, oil prices have been surging and the yen might slide again. Whatever Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent might have said, the United States government isn’t big enough to be “the house” that always wins when it comes to fixing global markets. Last week, the 10-year US Treasury yield briefly reached 5.04 per cent, the highest level since 2007, right before the global financial crisis. Bessent had tripled a Treasury buy-back operation on September 10 to US$6 billion, in an attempt to manipulate the market. He must have thought the market was a bunch of fools. How could this modest buy-back make a dent in the debt market, given that the United States government is on course to borrow US$2.1 trillion this year? Meanwhile, oil prices surged again, as Iran tightened its hold on the Strait of Hormuz. Yet prices have been relatively stable despite export flows out of the Gulf falling by more than 10 million barrels per day from pre-war levels. The release of US and other emergency oil reserves and lower Chinese demand have been cited as main factors. But it must be kept in mind that the gap between paper and physical oil prices has widened since the war, meaning that actual physical costs could turn out higher down the road. Last week, the yen fell, even after Tokyo and Washington jointly intervened – and Bessent dared currency traders to bet against the yen and himself, saying that “I am the house now”. So much for his attempt to manipulate the market. The US stock market has been a mystery for a long time. It keeps rising, never mind Covid-19, the Ukraine war, the Iran war and now, surging Treasury yields. The consolidation of the fund management industry could be a main factor here. A few persons could decide to hold up the market – until they can’t. Governments, it seems, don’t want to face the reality. Since 2008, the West has relied on debt to maintain living standards, while sweeping structural problems (such as declining competitiveness) under the carpet. Low inflation, driven by output expansion in China, allowed the US Federal Reserve and other Western central banks to keep interest rates low and support deficit spending. The stock of debts accumulated over the past 18 years cannot be serviced under normal interest rates without cutting spending and raising taxes. But no government wants to do either But now the West wants to decouple from China. This would translate into a secular inflationary force for the years or even decades ahead, making low interest rates unsustainable. While the 10-year Treasury yield seems high today, 5 per cent was a pretty normal level before 2007. What is happening in the interest rate market should be interpreted as normalisation. The challenge is that the stock of debts accumulated over the past 18 years cannot be serviced under normal interest rates without cutting spending and raising taxes. But no government wants to do either. The energy shock from the Iran war is coming to an inflation-prone environment. Governments are doing all they can to suppress the impact. But the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at a decades-low, and with the Houthis intent on blocking Saudi-flagged ships from the crucial Red Sea shipping lane, the Bab el-Mandeb, physical oil prices could soon soar. The Fed just raised interest rates last week. Could it stay ahead of inflation and quickly raise the rate to 6 per cent, even if it wanted to? It would be technically difficult. In 2007, the US’ publicly held debt was US$5 trillion or around a third of gross domestic product. It now stands at US$31 trillion, or 100 per cent of GDP. In 2025, US government revenue came to 17 per cent of GDP. If interest on national debt is more than a third of fiscal revenue, it leads to a vicious cycle. The market may not want to fund the debt, and the bond market could collapse. Considering such a fiscally impossible situation, a bout of high inflation might just inflate away the debt and offer a way out. Japan’s situation is even more dire. Even though it has cut its primary deficit to a manageable level, the public debt ratio is more than 200 per cent of GDP, and the stock is too high for debt servicing costs to be affordable at normal interest rates. Japan has about US$3.7 trillion in foreign assets. In theory, it could bring them home slowly to manage the yen’s decline, while maintaining a low policy rate and moderately high inflation; this way, the central bank could monetise the national debt gradually and inflation would lower the real value of the debt. But with the yen carry trade threatening to unravel and Japanese companies becoming quicker to repatriate assets, the gradual path out of debt might not be viable either. Japan may have to accept a sharp drop in the yen and a bout of high inflation for its debt level to be more sustainable. The die is cast, the deck is stacked. Major economies can expect to experience bouts of high inflation, maybe even hyperinflation, to reduce debt burdens. The savers of the world are about to be robbed.

title: Neurobiologist Ye Bing says his return to China is not spurred by Michigan campus tragedy
description: Prominent researcher takes over Nanjing University’s school of life sciences, rejecting claims US policy prompted his return.
content: Neurobiologist Ye Bing is returning to China after a long period in the United States, but he says his move is not linked to the suicide of another Chinese scholar at the same university or US policy under the Trump administration. Ye said his decision to join Nanjing University and leave the University of Michigan was not influenced by the death of Chinese scholar Wang Danhao on the same campus six months earlier – a day after Wang was interviewed by US Homeland Security officers. “This is a career choice and has no connection to the events mentioned in your email or the national policies [of the Trump administration],” Ye said in an email on Tuesday. “I have indeed joined my alma mater, Nanjing University, to participate in the development of its school of life sciences.” Ye, a neurobiologist and fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, had worked for 18 years at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. He now serves as dean and chair professor at Nanjing University’s school of life sciences. On March 19, UMich postdoctoral researcher Wang Danhao killed himself at the university’s George G. Brown Memorial Laboratory – a day after two Department of Homeland Security officers questioned him at his rented home. Around 8am on March 18, two Department of Homeland Security staff members arrived at Wang’s home for questioning, according to a police report published by local Detroit media on September 17. A source had identified them as an officer from Customs and Border Protection and an officer from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, also known as ICE. Wang, a semiconductor scientist who joined the university in 2022 to conduct postdoctoral research, had planned to return to China in May. Wang’s death came at a time of increased scrutiny by the Trump administration of foreign citizens on US college campuses and a crackdown on student visas. It is not known if Wang and Ye ever met, however Ye’s departure from the university prompted speculation that Wang’s death or the broader political climate spurred his decision. Ye said he decided to move for purely professional reasons. Ye has a long-standing connection with Nanjing University, where he completed his undergraduate studies and was awarded a bachelor’s degree in 1992. He obtained his master’s degree from the Shanghai Institute of Physiology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 1995, and his PhD in neuroscience from the school of medicine at Johns Hopkins University in 2001. He conducted postdoctoral research in neuroscience at the University of California, San Francisco from 2001 to 2008. From 2008, he served successively as an assistant professor and an associate professor with tenure at the medical school and Life Sciences Institute at the University of Michigan, a position he held until this month. Ye’s earlier work focused on the molecular mechanisms underlying the development and differentiation of neuronal dendrites and axons, as well as the relationship between defects in these processes and human diseases. He has focused on the role of genes associated with Down’s syndrome in neuronal development and brain disorders. In recent years, he has paid particular attention to the applications of artificial intelligence to neuroscience. In 2012, Ye was awarded a Kavli Fellowship by the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), a fellowship programme that began in 1989. Every year, the NAS selects scientists under the age of 45 to take part in a three-day forum on cutting-edge science. In 2021, he was elected an AAAS fellow, the largest scientific association in the world and the publisher of Science, one of the world’s leading academic journals. The webpage for Ye’s laboratory at UMich is no longer accessible, and his name does not appear on either the faculty directory or the emeritus professor list of the college. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Singapore’s entry-level job market shrinks despite salary growth, data shows
description: Aon data published last month shows a 3.2 per cent drop in entry-level headcount in the city state, amid a rise in AI use in the workplace.
content: While starting salaries for fresh graduates and entry-level workers in Singapore continue to creep upwards, the number of people in entry-level roles is shrinking, according to new data, indicating an increasingly tough job market for those at the start of their careers. Data published last month by global professional services firm Aon showed a 2.5 per cent year-on-year salary increase for entry-level employees, alongside a 3.2 per cent drop in entry-level headcount. The findings come as graduate employment in Singapore has also weakened. A joint survey by the country’s six autonomous universities released in March found that 83.4 per cent of recent graduates who sought jobs were working within six months of their final exams, declining from 87.1 per cent in 2024 and continuing a downward trend since 2022. Aon’s findings also point to a shift in employer expectations for new workforce entrants, as artificial intelligence takes on a growing role in the workplace. “AI is changing the first rung of the career ladder but it does not remove the need to build future talent,” said Rahul Chawla, partner and head of talent solutions for Southeast Asia at Aon. “Companies should redesign graduate roles around problem solving, judgment, human skills and the ability to work effectively with AI, rather than reduce entry opportunities and risk creating a capability gap in the future.” Aon on Wednesday also released its annual Salary Increase and Turnover Survey, which found that Singapore salaries increased overall by 4.1 per cent in 2026, down from 4.3 per cent in 2025 and the lowest growth among Southeast Asian countries. Vietnam saw the highest salary increases at 6.6 per cent in 2026, down from its 7.7 per cent mark in 2025. Aon conducted its 2026 study from July to September, analysing salary increase budgets and employee turnover rates among more than 1,200 businesses across Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. In Singapore, retail and hospitality saw the highest salary increase at 4.5 per cent, while life sciences and medical devices had a 4.3 per cent rise and technology a 4.2 per cent boost. In the study’s turnover data, financial services saw an 8.1 per cent involuntary turnover rate, followed by technology at 5.7 per cent and consulting, business and community services at 4.9 per cent. Several banks, including DBS and Standard Chartered, earlier announced that they would cut jobs amid advancements in AI. In response to a question on which skills were most in demand, 49 per cent of organisations chose leadership and people management skills, followed by data and analytical skills and AI and automation skills, which came in joint second with 48 per cent of firms choosing these options. “The organisations gaining a competitive edge are investing in continuous and targeted upskilling now, before a skills gap becomes a hiring crisis,” said Evon Lock, director of talent solutions in Southeast Asia at Aon. “They are building capabilities and infrastructure internally so employees can grow into the new roles AI is creating.” On Monday, the Ministry of Manpower said in a report that the number of workers laid off reached 4,620 in the second quarter of this year, the highest since the fourth quarter of 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. This was up from 3,830 retrenchments in the first quarter. While retrenchments rose, the number of job vacancies fell to 68,600 in June from 73,300 in March. This mainly reflected a drop in vacancies for professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) in sectors such as financial services and information and communications, the ministry report said. Still, entry-level PMET vacancies remained “broadly stable and sizeable”, accounting for 45.3 per cent of all job openings in June, it added. There were still more job vacancies than unemployed people despite the overall decline, with 1.48 vacancies per unemployed person as of June. The government has also introduced measures to help fresh graduates gain work experience and transition into full-time employment. The GRaduate Industry Traineeships programme, launched last year, provides industry-relevant training and work experience for graduates who have difficulty securing their first job. The ministry said in August that more than 550 of the programme’s 800 places had been filled as of the end of June, with the government extending the scheme to the 2026 graduating cohort. Nearly half of those who completed their traineeships had secured employment.

title: No toxic substance found in sports drinks linked to students’ illness: police
description: Force says reported ‘pinholes’ likely to be perforated lines in drink’s plastic wrapping.
content: Hong Kong police have found no foreign or toxic substances in a brand of sports drink linked to 16 secondary school students who fell ill, saying the reported “pinholes” on the bottles are likely to be perforated lines in the plastic wrapping. The update came a day after 16 students from Maryknoll Secondary School in Kwun Tong reported feeling unwell after drinking free bottles of “Scream” sports drink during lunch at an athletics meet on Tuesday at Hammer Hill Road Sports Ground in Wong Tai Sin. The students complained of symptoms including dizziness, vomiting and diarrhoea. A social media post had earlier claimed that pinholes were found on some of the bottles. Officers from the Kowloon East regional headquarters were seen collecting bottles from rubbish bins near the venue for testing after a parent alerted police. All 16 students, aged between 12 and 17, were discharged after treatment at United Christian Hospital in Kwun Tong, Senior Superintendent Bruce Hung Ngan of Kowloon East regional headquarters said on Wednesday. Hung said about 400 bottles were distributed by promotional staff as part of a brand marketing campaign on Tuesday. Government laboratory tests found no signs that the bottles had been intentionally tampered with, while toxicology examinations detected no poisonous, abnormal or foreign substances in the samples collected. Images circulated online earlier appeared to show liquid being squeezed out through small holes in the bottles. “Our investigation at the scene [on Tuesday] found that the sports drinks had been kept submerged in iced water before distribution. As a result, iced water had accumulated in the gaps between the plastic bottles and their plastic labels,” Hung said. “When the bottles were pressed or squeezed, the trapped water could seep out through the perforated tear lines, or even be sprayed out under pressure.” The bottles had been stored in iced water before being handed out by promotional staff. The perforations are a common package design to help with recycling and can be found on other bottled drinks. He added that investigators had yet to determine why so many students fell ill, suggesting that factors such as strenuous physical activity during the athletics meet or food hygiene issues could have played a role. The sports drink Scream is a product of Nongfu Spring, mainland China’s largest bottled water and drink company, founded in 1996 in Hangzhou. Tsim Sha Tsui-based Uni-China Group serves as its sole distributor in Hong Kong. Uni-China said it appreciated the swift investigation by police and the efficient and thorough manner in which officers handled and clarified the incident, helping to allay public concerns. The group added that the product was manufactured in a strictly controlled environment and had to pass internationally recognised quality and safety tests before leaving the factory. The school earlier said the incident involved food safety concerns after free bottled drinks were distributed outside the venue during its athletics meet by individuals not associated with the school. Hung also said investigators had no plans to check bottles of the same brand sold on the retail market.

title: Hong Kong sets yuan trading timeline, backing Beijing’s push to boost currency’s use
description: Move marks the latest step in Hong Kong’s efforts to advance internationalisation of the Chinese currency.
content: Hong Kong’s securities regulator aims to include a yuan trading counter in a cross-border channel linked with mainland Chinese investors by July 1, marking the latest step in the city’s efforts to advance the internationalisation of the Chinese currency. The measure, announced on Wednesday, is part of a strategic action plan unveiled by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) to support the implementation of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the 2026 policy address presented by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu last week. “We hope that Hong Kong will not only serve as a hub for yuan products but also become the platform of choice for yuan asset allocation and risk management,” SFC chairman Kelvin Wong Tin-yau said at a media briefing on Wednesday. He stressed that strengthening the ecosystem of yuan-settled products was one of the three priorities of the SFC. A yuan trading counter would allow mainland Chinese investors using the southbound Stock Connect scheme to buy and settle Hong Kong-listed shares directly in yuan, rather than converting their currency into Hong Kong dollars first. Our goal is to incorporate a yuan trading counter into the southbound Stock Connect scheme, and we aim to implement this by July 1 of next year Julia Leung, SFC The inclusion of a yuan counter via the southbound Stock Connect has been anticipated by Hong Kong’s financial community since the launch of the dual-counter model in June 2023. SFC CEO Julia Leung Fung-yee said the regulator would expand the range of yuan-denominated products. “Our goal is to incorporate a yuan trading counter into the southbound Stock Connect scheme, and we aim to implement this by July 1 of next year,” Leung said. Leung said in June last year that the SFC expected to realise the inclusion by the end of 2025. The revised timeline raises the prospect that the expansion could arrive as a symbolic policy gift from Beijing ahead of the 30th anniversary of Hong Kong’s return to Chinese rule, which took place on July 1, 1997. In Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, Lee pledged to further strengthen the city’s position as an international finance centre by enhancing its role as a global offshore yuan hub, alongside its status as an international asset and wealth management centre and an international risk management centre. As the world’s largest offshore yuan pool, Hong Kong registered a record 935 billion yuan (US$139 billion) in yuan-denominated loans last year and over 1 trillion yuan worth of new bond issuance. The SFC will also encourage more exchange-traded funds and other asset classes to be denominated, settled and traded in yuan. These could include gold, currency and commodity futures products, Leung said. Carlson Tong Ka-shing, chairman of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, said the SFC’s plan provides a clear framework for market development while reinforcing the city’s position as a leading international financial centre and enhancing its unique role in mainland China’s financial opening-up. Beyond expanding the yuan ecosystem, the SFC identified two other priorities: deepening capital links with mainland China and overseas markets, and improving the efficiency of Hong Kong’s capital markets, according to Wong. Leung said the regulator aimed to launch a new connect scheme for cross-border trading of real estate investment trusts in the first half of 2027. The strategic plan outlines 29 measures that could be implemented within a year and a further 22 longer-term initiatives.

title: China’s storage makers aim to climb value chain with advanced packaging bets
description: Biwin Storage Technology invests US$672 million in latest example of a storage firm looking to upgrade its business model.
content: Chinese storage makers, long known for packaging chips into modules, have been moving up the value chain into wafer-level operations, with the latest firm to make the jump investing 4.5 billion yuan (US$672 million) in an advanced packaging project. The sum, which Shanghai-listed Biwin Storage Technology will pour into the third phase of its advanced packaging and testing project in Dongguan, in southern China’s Guangdong province, will exceed the 3.09 billion yuan it put into the first two phases combined. The project, including the first two phases, had yet to generate mass production revenue, as it was still undergoing customer sampling, process verification and small-batch production, according to Biwin’s stock filing on Tuesday. The company estimated that the facility’s monthly capacity would more than triple to 10,000 wafers by the end of 2027, according to the filing and earlier investor meetings. The gamble marks a move into more sophisticated wafer-level technologies, as Biwin already operates a traditional memory and system-in-package, or SiP, packaging base in Huizhou, also in Guangdong, where it sources chips from external suppliers. The company is also trying to advance its packaging capabilities, including a “fan-out” technology for stacked memory and a separate package integrating 10 chiplets, allowing it to combine computing and memory. It is also working with customers on packaging for near-packaged optics. Other Chinese storage suppliers are also trying to step up their game. Shenzhen-listed Shenzhen Techwinsemi Technology, for example, has brought wafer die testing and testing of packaged chips in-house while continuing to outsource most actual chip packaging to contractors. Shenzhen Longsys Electronics, also listed in Shenzhen, said in June that its plant in Suzhou, in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, had established capacity to produce more than 1 million miniature solid-state drives a month. The product uses SiP technology to integrate the controller, flash memory, power management chip and other components into a single package, reducing the space required in devices such as AI PCs. Analysts see the investments as part of a broader effort by Chinese memory module suppliers to move beyond a business model centred on buying chips, assembling products and selling through downstream channels. Sinolink Securities said in an August report that although module makers traditionally occupied a weaker position between upstream wafer producers and device makers, their value increasingly lay in “product definition, supply-chain management and customer development capabilities”. The brokerage said packaging was shifting from a manufacturing step into a factor that directly affected product performance, integration and reliability, as AI devices demanded greater capacity and bandwidth, lower power consumption and smaller size. Advanced packaging is expanding rapidly worldwide. Global revenue from the sector is forecast to rise to US$79.4 billion in 2030 from US$46.1 billion in 2024, according to Yole Group estimates cited by industry association Semi, with AI and high-performance computing among the main growth drivers.

title: Hong Kong pledges lenient approach on 10-12 hours of civil service family leave
description: Civil service chief Ingrid Yeung says applications for new hourly leave scheme will be straightforward, with minimal proof needed.
content: Hong Kong authorities have pledged to take a lenient approach when approving applications for a new scheme granting civil servants 10 to 12 hours of family care leave annually from next year. The initiative, first announced in last week’s annual policy address, will allow staff to leave work temporarily to deal with personal matters, such as accompanying family members to hospital or attending parent-teacher meetings. Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan told a Legislative Council panel meeting on Wednesday she expected the application process to be “very straightforward”. Noting that civil servants might not have solid supporting documents in advance for special circumstances, she said “if the supervisor is satisfied, it should generally be approved”. “If proof is required afterwards, it will also be simple … we believe most colleagues will not abuse the system,” she added. Lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung raised concerns that supervisors might refuse to approve leave requests for cases not explicitly listed in the guidelines, and urged the government to ensure flexibility. Alex Chan Yuen-tak, deputy secretary for the civil service, said the bureau was finalising guidelines for departments to use as a reference and stressed that the policy was intended to allow staff to leave work temporarily in unexpected situations. The guidelines would list as many scenarios as possible, Chan said, including picking up children after a sudden class suspension or collecting elderly relatives from care homes in unforeseen circumstances. Fellow legislator Chau Siu-chung questioned whether the leave allowance would be sufficient, urging the bureau to consider raising the cap and allowing unused hours to be carried forward. In response, Yeung said 10 to 12 hours annually should be enough to deal with unexpected situations, adding that employees could also apply for personal or childcare leave if necessary. The new leave scheme is also part of the government’s broader efforts to boost the birth rate. However, business leaders have said the private sector has little incentive to adopt similar measures because of manpower and financial constraints, particularly among smaller firms. The government is Hong Kong’s largest employer, with more than 170,000 civil servants. In 2024, it introduced childcare leave for staff, entitling each civil servant to three days of leave annually for each child under the age of three.

title: Italy’s Colosseum closes after worker dies in accident
description: The incident comes less ‌than a year ‌after the death of a worker trapped under the rubble of a collapsed medieval tower near the Colosseum.
content: Italy’s Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli ordered the one-day closure of the Colosseum on Wednesday as a mark of respect after a worker was ‌killed overnight in an accident. Andrea Moretti, a 22-year-old technician, died after falling several metres while installing a new lighting system inside the ancient Roman arena. Built 2,000 years ago, the Colosseum was the biggest amphitheatre in the ⁠Roman Empire, used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts. ‌It is Italy’s most visited tourist attraction. “The news of the tragic death of Andrea Moretti, ‌a skilled worker who died overnight … has deeply shocked ⁠and ⁠saddened us,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said. Culture Minister Giuli also ordered the ‌suspension of all construction and maintenance work at the Colosseum until further notice. Initially, only ‌a partial ‌closure of the monument was announced, but this drew ‌protests from Italy’s biggest union, the CGIL. “Humanity comes before tourists,” ⁠said Natale di Cola, the CGIL’s Rome chief, adding that ⁠the union was calling on Giuli to explain all the circumstances surrounding Moretti’s accident. The incident comes less ‌than a year ‌after the death of a Romanian worker who was trapped for hours under the rubble of a partially collapsed medieval tower near the Colosseum last November.

title: Meet Bryan Seaver, the late Dolly Parton’s nephew accused of extorting her estate
description: The son of Cassie Parton spoke out against the ‘Jolene’ singer’s manager Danny Nozell, following his dismissal as head of security, and alleged intimidation.
content: Bryan Seaver, nephew of the late country icon Dolly Parton, has been fired from his role as her head of security after more than two decades. According to a termination letter obtained by TMZ, Seaver and his security companies were “immediately dismissed” from all of his aunt’s properties. The notice was reportedly issued the same day replacement guards took over at Parton’s properties. Seaver and his team have told TMZ that they were “dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions”. In remarks targeted at Parton’s manager Danny Nozell and Pinnacle Bank, which manage the DP Dean Trust that now looks after Dolly’s properties and businesses, they said: “We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dolly Parton (@dollyparton) According to the termination letter, while Seaver has been stripped of his role with Parton’s properties, his personal interest in the DP Dean Trust remains intact. Following Parton’s death on August 25, it was Seaver who confirmed the news to the public via an Instagram video. “This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality,” Seaver said at the time. “As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now.” Here’s everything you need to know about Bryan Seaver. He is the son of Cassie Parton Bryan Seaver was born to Parton’s younger sister, Cassie, and her husband, Larry Seaver. They also share a daughter, Rebecca Ann Seaver. Larry worked as head of security for the “Jolene” singer before his son took over the role. As a child, Seaver even joined his famous aunt on tour. He has been accused of extorting the Parton estate While little is known about Seaver’s private life, he has come under scrutiny following the country music legend’s death. In addition to being removed as head of security for the Parton estate, Seaver was served with a restraining order by the late singer’s management company on September 22. New court filings obtained by People magazine also allege that Seaver used his “self-proclaimed military contractor experience” to extort Parton’s estate for money. Seaver had reportedly boasted about his experience in arms dealing and warfare and told Nozell that he was seeking “vengeance for my people for the next 50 years. I have no debt. I only own swords and guns”. On September 1, days after Parton’s death, Seaver allegedly wrote to her trust and lawyer: “Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I’m going to f**k everyone.”

title: China hawks grumble over Trump’s lavish welcome planned for Xi state visit
description: Chorus of disapproval rises ahead of the Chinese leader’s arrival, even as others say the welcome is the show, not the deal.
content: Hours before President Xi Jinping’s aircraft lands at Joint Base Andrews, Washington is preparing for a scene that seemed unthinkable in recent years: his American counterpart waiting on the tarmac for the leader of a country that much of the US national security establishment regards as its foremost strategic adversary. While the Donald Trump administration is betting on warmth, deals and stability with Beijing, recent public surveys show that American anxiety over China has eased from its 2024 peak. But the China hawks who helped shape the debate have spent the week warning that the ceremony risks obscuring a more familiar reality: Beijing remains a rival, and the issues that have defined that rivalry have not gone away. They are making that case from outside the room. Since Trump returned to the White House, the chorus has lost resonance inside the building and with the public. The US president has disputed their arguments himself while calling Xi a “great gentleman”. Roger Wicker, a Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, told senators on Tuesday that “quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome”. Wicker reminded Trump that “his guest” sought to dominate his “neighbours and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America”. He also demanded the “America first” president raise reports during his meeting with Xi about Chinese satellite imagery allegedly used in Iranian strikes that killed American troops. Michigan Republican John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, wrote to Trump on September 18, saying that China remained “the United States’ foremost foreign adversary and greatest external threat”. Enabling Iran to use the images to hit US forces was “tantamount to an act of war” and should bring “the most severe consequences”, the letter continued. Beijing’s objections to Taiwan arms sales should be “rejected out of hand”. Democrats, too, have focused on what they see as the gap between the pageantry and the underlying tensions. Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chris Coons, Jack Reed, Mark Warner, Elizabeth Warren and Andy Kim said on Tuesday that China presented “a greater threat to American security and prosperity than ever before”. They also cited the Iran imagery and AI chips, accusing Trump of “rolling out the red carpet for President Xi and hosting closed-door dinners so his billionaire friends can strike deals”. The objections are not confined to Capitol Hill. Outside Congress, China hawks and former government officials have been making a parallel case, focusing less on the policy details than on what the lavish welcome says about the balance of power. Conservative commentator Gordon Chang, who regularly appears on Fox News, warned on social media that many would see the welcome “as the US acknowledging China as the world’s No 1 power”. “Xi, after all, did not greet Trump on his arrival in Beijing in May. This special treatment will make Xi even more arrogant,” he said. Trump has already waved him off, taking a shot during an interview with Fox in April. “You know, I listen to this Gordon Chang. He has no idea what he’s talking about. We have been very tough on China. Tough but fair.” But Rush Doshi, who ran China policy on former president Joe Biden’s National Security Council, reads the choreography of the visit as evidence of a deeper imbalance in the relationship. In a Substack post on Monday, Doshi noted that the honours planned for Xi exceeded those Trump received during his visit to Beijing. “Trump will be waiting for him … then comes a flyover by a B-2 and four F-22s and a meeting between Melania Trump and [China’s first lady] Peng Liyuan,” Doshi wrote, noting that nothing quite like that happened when the US leader went to Beijing in May. “Xi wasn’t waiting for him, there were no flyovers, and there was no meeting of the first ladies,” he observed, adding that “reciprocity” was the Trump administration’s “watchword”. “The asymmetry in pageantry reveals something about an overall asymmetry in the relationship.” For Doshi, the ceremony is a window into how the relationship itself may be changing. He argues that Beijing believes it has gained leverage through rare earth export controls, while the Trump administration has increasingly prioritised stability. He predicts that the meeting is unlikely to produce many major deliverables – perhaps an extension of the trade truce, some agricultural and energy purchases and an AI dialogue. On Taiwan, “Trump’s informal, unscripted remarks may be as consequential as any formal change”, he argues. China hawks have had less say over the tone and choreography of policy towards Beijing in the second Trump White House. Paul Heer, a former US national intelligence officer for East Asia, wrote this week that even the remaining China specialists inside the administration, including “hawks … probably frustrated with Trump’s more accommodative approach … have yet to forge a policy consensus”. The public mood has shifted too. A Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey released on Monday found Americans rating China at 39 on a 0-to-100 feeling thermometer, up from 26 in 2024. Fifty-seven per cent said they favoured “friendly cooperation and engagement” with China, while 40 per cent wanted to limit China’s power. The share describing Chinese territorial ambitions as a “critical threat” fell to 41 per cent from 52 per cent in 2022. “There’s not a bipartisan consensus among the public in favour of a competitive containment approach,” said Craig Kafura, the council’s director of public opinion and foreign policy. The hawks want a harder line. Other China specialists are asking a different question: whether the welcome is anything more than a show. Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute called the welcome “unusually conspicuous,” but said it did not “necessarily reflect the real substance of the relationship”. That Xi was making his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade “helps explain why former officials and China hawks are objecting to the optics. In their minds, China is the enemy,” he said. According to Simon, the test will be whether the administration’s negotiating positions are tougher than Trump’s rhetoric. “On AI, for example, the administration continues to confront China over advanced technology even as Trump has pursued a less restrictive approach to some chip exports,” he said. Simon also noted that Washington was still pressing Beijing on fentanyl precursors, even as China announced new export controls on related chemicals. In Simon’s view, the question that matters is less “why is Trump being so nice to Xi?” than whether the cordiality produces “concrete US gains, and what happens when the personal relationship collides with unresolved structural disputes”.

title: Asian Games: weightlifter Ri sets 3 world records to win North Korea’s first medal
description: Meanwhile, South Korea’s badminton world No 1 An beats Japan’s Yamaguchi in team event, but has stern words for her watching father.
content: North Korea’s Ri Song-gum set three world records to give her country their first gold in weightlifting at the Asian Games on Wednesday, while South Korea’s badminton world No 1 An Se-young had stern words for her watching father. Ri set the world records in the women’s 49kg class in Nagoya, joining an elite club of just four weightlifters who have won three Asian Games gold medals. The reigning two-time world champion added to her Asian Games golds in Jakarta in 2018 in the 48kg class and Hangzhou in 2023 at 49kg. The weightlifter hauled 94kg above her head in the opening snatch discipline, one kilogramme more than the previous world standard mark of 93kg. She then smashed the clean and jerk world record of 115kg twice by hoisting 116kg and then 121kg. Her total of 215kg obliterated the old world record by 7kg. “The reason I got this gold is for the feelings of my home country, the people had huge expectations for me,” Ri said. “I wanted to lift my country up on these two small shoulders.” Ri’s exceptional achievement was cheered to the rafters in a lively atmosphere at the Nagoya Trade and Industry Centre hall, made all the more raucous by a large number of Japanese North Korean fans waving flags. From August 1, the IWF, the governing body, introduced new weight classes leading up to the next Olympics and reset all its world records. If an athlete beats the newly introduced world standard mark they are deemed to have set a new world record. Ri has never competed at the Olympics. North Korea were absent from Tokyo in 2021 because of Covid and the country did not qualify in weightlifting for Paris in 2024. There will be no 49kg class at the next Olympics in Los Angeles because the competition has been slimmed down to six men’s and six women’s divisions. But when Ri was asked if she would consider moving up to 53kg, the lowest women’s category to chase Olympic gold, she replied “Yes”. India’s Mirabai Chanu, the silver medallist at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, finally won an Asian Games medal at the third time of asking. She had a total of 198kg after a snatch of 87kg and clean and jerk of 111kg to claim silver, while Indonesia’s Diana Tri Wijayana took bronze on 191kg, with 88kg and 103kg respectively. Ri became only the fourth lifter, and first woman, to win three Asian Games weightlifting golds. She joined Iran’s Mohammad Nassiri (1966-74), South Korea’s Kim Tae-hyun (1990-98) and Iran’s Behdad Salimi (2010-2018). No one has ever won four. Also in Nagoya, An, the reigning world and Olympic badminton champion, defeated home player Akane Yamaguchi in three tough games in the semi-finals of the women’s team event. But the 24-year-old was not always at her brilliant best against the world No 3, winning 21-9, 18-21, 21-11. “I think I expressed it too forcefully, to make myself notice that I was making mistakes,” she said of her visible frustrations. “I should not have done that. From now on I need to hold it in more.” An said the fact she could hear everything in the crowd, including the commentators, was proof of her poor concentration. Most of all, she said, she was aware of her parents watching in the arena. “Parents usually cannot bear to watch their own children compete, but my dad seems to watch perfectly happily, which is a bit much. “I am out there running myself into the ground and he is just cheering away in comfort.” Japan recovered to win the semi-final 3-1.

title: Ahead of Xi’s ‘historic milestone’ US visit, a fentanyl goodwill gesture from China
description: China’s top envoy to US hails safeguards from head-of-state diplomacy, as Beijing rolls out severe penalties for non-pharma fentanyl crimes.
content: China’s ambassador to the United States has hailed President Xi Jinping’s coming state visit as a “historic milestone” for bilateral and international relations. Xie Feng’s remarks came just as Beijing unveiled stringent new regulations on fentanyl, in a clear move to build diplomatic momentum ahead of the Xi-Trump summit in Washington. Under the strategic guidance of both leaders, the “giant ship” of China-US relations would continue to “break waves and sail ahead” along a trajectory of “mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, and win-win cooperation”, Xie told state news agency Xinhua. The interview was published on Wednesday, hours before Xi’s scheduled departure for the US. The two leaders had maintained “frequent, candid, and strategic communication on major global issues”, Xie said, noting that Xi’s trip would be the second such top-level exchange in just over four months, following Trump’s state visit in May. Head-of-state diplomacy provided “an important strategic safeguard for maintaining the overall dynamic stability of China-US relations amid turbulent winds and rough seas”, Xie said. “We look forward to both sides using this state visit as an opportunity to further align their direction, build consensus, overcome disruptions, and accelerate progress.” Reinforcing China’s commitment to this cooperative vision, Beijing’s top legal and law enforcement authorities on Wednesday issued a set of guidelines to severely punish fentanyl-related offences. Clearly timed as a goodwill gesture ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington, the move directly addresses a major domestic and foreign policy priority for US President Donald Trump. The new rules, jointly issued by the Supreme People’s Court, the Supreme People’s Procuratorate, and the Ministry of Public Security, establish strict quantity standards for prosecuting and sentencing fentanyl-related crimes. While not fully publicised – the 18-article directive legally divides fentanyl into pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical categories. It mandates that non-pharmaceutical fentanyl offences will now face the same severe penalties under Chinese criminal law as heroin cases. The judicial guidelines also mandate strict protocols for evidence collection, proving criminal intent, recovering illicit profits and managing cross-jurisdictional cases. Concurrently, separate rules for filing and prosecuting such cases advance Beijing’s commitment to strengthening drug control and protecting public health. Xie highlighted this momentum in his interview, pointing to breakthroughs in joint law enforcement and praising ongoing bilateral efforts targeting cross-border drug smuggling, overseas cyber fraud and the repatriation of key fugitives. As further evidence of progress, Xie cited advancing talks on a US$30 billion reciprocal tariff reduction package under the US-China Board of Trade, and the repatriation of 64 Chinese cultural artefacts and fossils from the US. He called on Washington to continue expanding the “cooperation checklist” while shrinking the “problem checklist” – through equitable dialogue in trade and benign competition in the technology sector. However, he also repeated Beijing’s unyielding stance on core national interests – the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, mainland China’s political system and path, and its legitimate right to development – often cited as the “four red lines”. “The Taiwan question is the core of China’s core interests and the very first insurmountable red line in China-US relations,” Xie said, urging the US to act with the utmost caution and adhere strictly to the one-China principle and the three joint communiques. Signed in the 1970s and 80s, the three China-US joint communiques form the political bedrock of relations between the two powers. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons. Xie also highlighted Xi’s initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China over five years, saying people-to-people friendship was the “deepest and most enduring force” driving US-China ties.

title: Why younger Filipinos are warming to China despite maritime tensions
description: A Pew survey shows 47 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 view China favourably, with some respondents also expressing confidence in its leadership.
