content: Inside a car wash lounge in the southern Philippine city of Davao, Shenilane Formento scrolls through messages on her Chinese-made Oppo phone as she waits for a customer to pay. Formento, 29, has worked as a cashier for about a year. She follows developments in the South China Sea through news reports shared on her social media feeds, including frequent confrontations between Philippine and Chinese forces in the disputed waters. While she found such incidents “disappointing”, she ultimately thought better of Beijing than Washington, which she blamed for the high energy prices affecting the Philippines and the rest of the world. “That’s why I prefer China to the United States. Just look at what is happening … because of the US-Iran war – fuel prices are skyrocketing,” she said. Formento’s views point to a broader contradiction in how Filipinos see China: even as Beijing remains distrusted over its actions in the disputed waters, younger Filipinos are more likely than older generations to view the country favourably. A new survey released on July 15 by the US-based Pew Research Centre found that 47 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 viewed China favourably, compared with 44 per cent of those aged 35 to 49 and 27 per cent of those 50 and older. The survey also found that 61 per cent of Filipinos aged 18 to 34 had confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 32 per cent among those 50 and older. The findings stand out against a long-running pattern of distrust towards Beijing, according to Social Weather Stations (SWS), a Philippine polling organisation. SWS has measured Filipinos’ trust in China annually since 1994 and quarterly since 2012. Beijing recorded a positive net trust rating in only nine of 74 surveys, with its rating falling to a record low of minus 54 in 2024 on a scale ranging from plus 100 to minus 100. China’s net trust rating remained negative in 2025 and 2026, while the US, Japan and Australia recorded higher levels of trust among Filipinos. Pew’s findings do not establish why younger Filipinos have more favourable views of China, but experts point to how they encounter the country in everyday life, as well as a generational shift in perceptions of its economic and political rise. “As I see it, younger Filipinos encounter China in many different ways. They see Chinese technology and consumer products, entertainment, travel content, and social media posts about life in China,” said Jan Robert R Go, associate professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman. “This is where I find the idea of ‘everyday China’ useful. By this, I mean the China that people encounter in their daily lives, often outside formal politics and diplomacy. These experiences may give younger Filipinos a wider range of impressions of China.” But Go cautioned against interpreting more favourable views of China as evidence that younger Filipinos are turning away from the US. “I find the 61 per cent figure particularly interesting because it suggests we should be careful about assuming that attitudes towards China all move together,” he said. “Someone can have confidence in Chinese leadership on the world stage, appreciate Chinese popular culture, and still distrust China on territorial issues.” Indeed, the Pew survey found that 76 per cent of Filipino respondents overall named China as the country’s top threat, while 86 per cent said they were very or somewhat concerned about territorial disputes involving China and neighbouring countries. Pew did not provide age-group breakdowns for those questions. Arnaud Leveau, a geopolitics professor at Paris Dauphine University, said the coexistence of these views was among the most notable findings. “Strategically, this tells us something about the emerging generation in Asia. The political landscape may become less binary. Younger citizens may be willing to recognise China’s power and even aspects of its leadership while refusing to accept Chinese pressure on their sovereignty,” Leveau said. Generational memory could also help explain the gap, he said. Older Filipinos grew up in an environment in which the US occupied a particularly central strategic and cultural position, while China was more distant, poorer and associated with communist rivalry. Younger Filipinos have instead grown up with an economically powerful and technologically sophisticated China that is deeply integrated into Asian trade and supply chains. “Their China is the China of smartphones, digital platforms, high-speed rail, electric vehicles, large cities and a major Asian consumer market,” Leveau said. “For younger Asians, China’s rise is already part of the normal international landscape. They did not experience the transition from a US-dominated regional system in the same way as older generations. Multipolarity is not a disruption for them; it is increasingly the world they have always known.” Edmund Tayao, a law professor at the San Beda University Graduate School of Law in Manila, urged caution in interpreting the Pew findings without comparable polling from Philippine research organisations, saying he would prefer surveys from two or three of the country’s most respected polling groups. He also pointed to social media as a potentially important influence on respondents’ views, saying the dominance of online content and what he described as China’s “vigorous campaign” could shape perceptions, particularly when users might struggle to distinguish reliable information from misinformation. Tayao said some Filipinos might also view China favourably because they were impressed by the speed of its development and hope the Philippines could achieve similar progress. Such exposure, Go said, did not necessarily mean younger Filipinos were becoming more sympathetic to Beijing on political questions. “I also wouldn’t assume this makes younger Filipinos apolitical,” he said. “They may simply be responding to China through a wider range of experiences.” Go noted that it was too early to say whether the age gap represented a lasting generational shift. “What we do not know yet is whether that difference will remain as younger Filipinos grow older,” he said, adding that developments in the South China Sea, economic conditions, domestic politics and media coverage could all change how Filipinos viewed China. “So, for now, I would treat the age difference as an important pattern to watch. We need to see whether it appears consistently over several years before calling it a permanent generational change.”

title: Metal meets Mongolian throat singing and instruments in Uuhai’s Hong Kong debut
description: In Hong Kong for the Asia+ Festival, Uuhai want to expand the world’s understanding of Mongolia and its culture beyond Genghis Khan.
content: Mongolia and heavy metal are rarely mentioned in the same sentence, but folk metal band Uuhai are here to prove the music genre fuses surprisingly well with the nomadic culture’s distinctive vocal and instrumental traditions. Founded in the Mongolian capital Ulaanbaatar in 2020 by drummer and producer Otgonbaatar “Ombo” Damba, the band’s current line-up features Damba, Khurtsgerel Damiranjav (horsehead fiddler and vocalist), Zorigoo Battsooj (horsehead fiddler and throat singer), Saruul Tsogt-Erdene (vocalist), Batbayar Dulamsuren (percussionist), Dalaitseren Nasanbuyan (guitarist) and Anand Naranbaatar (bass guitarist). Their songs feature aggressive rock-metal beats while showcasing Unesco-recognised elements of Mongolian heritage, including Khoomei (traditional throat singing), the morin khuur (horsehead fiddle) and long-song vocals carrying ancient lyrical themes. Uuhai began touring internationally a year after forming and have appeared at major European festivals, including on the Motocultor Across Europe 2026 tour. In 2025, their track “Khar Khulz” exploded online, gaining 8.8 million views on YouTube. In January this year, the band released their debut album Human Herds, and in June they announced a 2027 European headline tour. Now they are making their Hong Kong debut as the opening programme of the Asia+ Festival, performing on September 23 and 24 at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre. “Hong Kong is a place where different cultures have met for generations, so bringing music that stems so deeply from Mongolia to this city feels like a very special cultural exchange,” Damba, 51, says. “These performances are an opportunity to introduce not only our music, but also the spirit of Mongolia to an audience that may be encountering Uuhai for the first time.” Why music is unifying, despite a language barrier Though the band’s lyrics are entirely in Mongolian, Damba remains unconcerned about language barriers. “Our audiences may not understand every lyric, but they understand rhythm, tension, calm, strength and emotion,” he says. “Throat singing communicates through vibration as much as language. The morin khuur can communicate sadness, openness or strength without translation. Rhythm can make thousands of people move together. We trust the music to communicate what words cannot.” The band’s name reflects the sense of collectivism they hope to inspire. Uuhai, traditionally a battle cry or collective chant of encouragement, is invoked when Mongolians wish for strength, good fortune and unity. At Uuhai concerts, the group regularly invites international audiences to chant along in unison. “Most of our audience members do not speak Mongolian, but within seconds, thousands of individual voices become one,” Damba says. “We have experienced that connection at international festivals and concerts, and it continues to remind us that music travels beyond vocabulary. Emotions such as hope, strength, respect, joy and the desire to belong are universal.” With Human Herds, Uuhai takes its message of global unity further, drawing inspiration from how humanity moves collectively. “Like a herd, we gather, migrate, follow, create, consume and influence one another,” Damba says, referencing Mongolian nomadic existence. “From a Mongolian perspective, our relationship with nature is paramount. Nomadic culture teaches us that humans do not stand above nature. While there is enormous power in collective movement, that power, if exercised without awareness, can also lead to division, destruction and environmental damage.” Tracks such as “Paradise” and “Ancient Land” celebrate the beauty of the natural world, while “Dracula” serves as a metaphorical critique of destructive forces consuming life with “deadly intent”. “Modern society has achieved extraordinary things, but it can also sever people from that understanding of respecting nature,” Damba says. “Human Herds asks us to consider where we are moving and whether we are moving consciously.” Exploring Mongolia’s history through song Beyond an ode to nature, Uuhai’s music celebrates Mongolia’s rich history. The track “Secret History of the Mongols” nods to a literary work of the same name, the oldest surviving literary work in the Mongolic languages, written after the death of Mongol Empire founder Genghis Khan – also known as Chinggis Khan – in 1227 to recount his life and conquests. “Mongolian history is often reduced to conquest and Chinggis Khan,” Damba explains. “That is one part of history, but there is much more behind it. The [Secret History of the Mongols] text contains deeply human stories about families, relationships, difficult choices, survival, responsibility and the importance of unity. We want listeners to feel that human dimension through our music.” While traditional Mongolian music remains integral to the nation’s cultural identity, Damba observes that younger generations now grow up in a globalised environment exposed to Western rock, metal, hip-hop, electronic music and pop. Damba comes from a rock background: in his youth, he was the drummer for Hurd, another influential Mongolian rock band widely credited with pioneering heavy metal within the traditional music scene following Mongolia’s 1990 democratic revolution. That era allowed both rock and traditional Mongolian music, heavily restricted during nearly 70 years of communist rule, to be explored with artistic independence. Damba views Western musical influences as an opportunity, not a threat. “When traditional instruments or throat singing appear naturally within contemporary music, young people can encounter their heritage in a context that belongs to their generation,” he says. “From there, some become curious about where the traditional instruments come from, what the lyrics mean and what other traditions lie behind the music.” However, he cautions that folk music should not survive solely by blending with modern genres. “It has its own intrinsic value,” he says. “Our role is simply to show that respecting tradition does not mean living in the past. Cultural heritage can continue to grow, create and communicate with the present.” Balancing genres In Uuhai’s compositions, rock and traditional instrumentation share equal ground: at times, the morin khuur leads the melody, while at others, electric guitars drive the energy. When throat singing requires space, the rhythm simplifies. This balance is carefully engineered during the songwriting process rather than relying solely on post-production mixing. “Our objective is not merely to demonstrate that traditional music and rock can technically coexist,” Damba says. “We want them to sound as though they belong to the very same musical language.” Paired with stage attire and visual imagery inspired by traditional Mongolian craftsmanship and historical motifs, Uuhai’s live performances deliver a fusion of past and present, rock and tradition. “It is important to us that when international audiences view our videos or live shows, they are not watching a museum exhibit, but experiencing Mongolia as a living culture,” Damba says. “The traditional and the contemporary can stand side-by-side without either losing its identity. “Mongolia is not a culture that existed only in the past – it is vibrant and alive today.”

title: As Chinese carmakers diversify beyond CATL batteries, Beijing warns of market overreaction
description: MIIT-linked commentary dismisses “de-CATLisation” concerns as normal supplier diversification and warns cutthroat price competition poses a far bigger threat.
content: A publication under China’s industry ministry has pushed back against market chatter of “de-CATLisation” as a growing number of the battery giant’s automotive partners diversify their suppliers, with the company’s shares falling recently. The commentary, published by the news centre of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), said supplier diversification and in-house battery projects are standard commercial practices. Such moves should not be portrayed as deliberate attempts to weaken leading battery makers like Contemporary Amperex Technol­ogy Limited (CATL) or drive a wedge between carmakers and suppliers, it said. The publication followed several Chinese carmakers, including Xiaomi, Li Auto and Xpeng, expanding partnerships with battery suppliers other than CATL or announcing plans to develop batteries in-house. The moves this month have fuelled talk of a shift away from the industry giant and speculation about its market position. By Wednesday, CATL’s Shenzhen-listed shares had fallen about 25 per cent from their mid-August level and nearly 35 per cent from a record high reached in early May. The shares were down 1.19 per cent on the day. CATL remains the dominant player in China’s battery market. In August, it accounted for more than 41 per cent of the power-battery market by installed capacity, about double the share of its nearest rival, BYD, according to the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance. Supplier diversification is not a new trend. CATL’s scale has made its batteries difficult to replace entirely, but many carmakers have adopted multi-supplier strategies or invested in in-house battery production in recent years to reduce their reliance on the company. The MIIT-linked commentary, published on Tuesday, said China’s automotive supply chain had developed strengths in certain areas but still had considerable room to improve. “What a mature industry truly needs is not to level out differences or weaken whoever is leading, but to foster the growth of stronger companies while allowing those that have already built global competitiveness to continue moving forward,” it added. The commentary cautioned that debates over “de-CATLisation” risked distracting attention from a more systemic problem: cutthroat price competition in China’s electric vehicle industry, which is now spreading upstream through the supply chain. As battery cells directly influence vehicle safety, reliability, lifespan and driving experience, it warned that efforts to reduce costs should focus on improving technological efficiency rather than simply forcing down procurement prices. The commentary also noted that “in-house battery development” by carmakers typically referred to less central areas such as pack design and battery management systems, rather than the complex manufacturing and mass production of core battery cells. Power batteries require heavy investment, sustained manufacturing expertise and quality control to produce at scale, the commentary said, warning that fragmented efforts by carmakers risked duplicating investments and misallocating resources.

title: Tesla’s Elon Musk hails Xi Jinping’s leadership and Chinese AI strength
description: Musk controls SpaceX, a Pentagon and US intelligence contractor, and his business ties with China have drawn scrutiny in Washington.
content: Tesla CEO Elon Musk described Chinese President Xi Jinping as “a great leader” and “very capable” during an interview with China’s state broadcaster on Wednesday, just hours before Xi left China for a summit with US President Donald Trump. “He seems like a great leader. Under his tenure, China has prospered immensely. I’ve seen it first hand,” Musk said in one of a series of videos posted on CCTV’s social media account. “And it’s also obvious to see just walking around the streets, the … prosperity of the average Chinese citizen has increased tremendously. All that seems to happen under President Xi while he’s been the leader of China. So he’s clearly done an excellent job and is very capable.” Musk will be among a group of leading US technology executives expected to attend a White House state dinner on Thursday, along with Sam Altman of OpenAI, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook and others, Reuters reported. Musk has extensive business ties with China, with Shanghai home to Tesla’s largest overseas manufacturing base. In recent years, those ties have drawn scrutiny in Washington because Musk also controls SpaceX, a major Pentagon and US intelligence contractor. In the interview on Wednesday, Musk described the Shanghai factory as a “gem” and praised China’s manufacturing industry. “China just has a very strong, inherent ability to do manufacturing. Well, this has been true not just in the present day,” Musk said. “What we have at the Tesla China team is just incredibly talented, hardworking and trustworthy. The quality is excellent. And the efficiency is excellent. The Tesla Shanghai factory is a gem.” His praise was not limited to Tesla-related manufacturing. He told the state broadcaster, “the Chinese AI models are generally outstanding” and that China was “by far the best in terms of performance per unit of compute”. “I think China’s going to address the compute limitation faster than most people expect. My rough guess would be that China addresses these compute constraints with lithography and chipmaking in about two or three years.” Musk’s comments come weeks after US authorities accused six Chinese AI companies – including DeepSeek and Alibaba, owner of the South China Morning Post – of the “aggressive, malicious and targeted” distillation of US-developed models on an industrial scale. Beijing said it rejected the allegations as groundless. In other tech commentary, Musk forecast there would be “at least a billion human robots within 10 years” and discussed how physical and digital robots would amplify one person’s productivity, according to the interview. He recommended that everyone undergo a broader education so they could better formulate questions for AI. “As crazy as it sounds, there will be so many robots and so much AI. And that AI will actually be eager to hear any request that you could possibly have, because the request will be fulfilled immediately,” Musk said. Musk praised China’s high-speed bullet trains and recommended that people visit the country. “Any words I say do not do justice to the incredible majesty that is China. It’s awesome,” Musk said.

title: Northern Metropolis data hub to start phased operations in mid-2027: CLP Power
description: Sandy Ridge data facility cluster, which broke ground in March, will begin operating earlier than original 2029 schedule.
content: A planned supercomputing hub at the Northern Metropolis megadevelopment in Hong Kong’s border area will start phased operations earlier than expected in mid-2027, according to electricity supplier CLP Power. The power supplier said it had sufficient capacity to support energy demand not only for the Sandy Ridge data facility cluster, but for the equivalent of three to four supercomputing centres of a similar scale over the next decade. CLP added it planned to procure more zero-carbon energy from mainland China to develop low-carbon computer power. “I am delighted to join Range Technology today in announcing our objective to strive for the phased commencement of operations at the Sandy Ridge data centre by mid-2027,” Joseph Law Ka-chun, managing director of CLP Power, said on Wednesday. “Developing artificial intelligence in Hong Kong relies on computing power as its engine, with electricity serving as the critical source of kinetic energy.” The Sandy Ridge cluster in the metropolis broke ground in March and was originally scheduled to begin operating by 2029. It forms part of a government blueprint to turn a large stretch of land near the border into an economic hub. Law said CLP would establish two 132kV high-voltage substations to ensure a stable power supply at Sandy Ridge. He added that to meet the city’s carbon reduction goals while meeting the cluster’s immense energy demand, the company would import more cost-effective zero-carbon energy from the mainland and require zero-carbon energy that was traceable. Energy traceability refers to verified data tracking of power from its renewable generation source to the point of consumption. Hong Kong is targeting a zero-carbon energy share of between 60 and 70 per cent by 2035, as part of the city’s broader push towards carbon neutrality by 2050. The current share of zero-carbon energy is about 28 per cent. As for concerns whether investments into power infrastructure to enhance electricity supply for Sandy Ridge might raise electricity tariffs, CLP would ensure every type of customer was treated fairly when it comes to electricity pricing, Law said. Undersecretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Lillian Cheong Man-lei said Hong Kong’s computing power was expected to reach 180,000 petaflops by around 2030 – equal to 180,000 quadrillion calculations per second and equivalent to 36 times the current capacity. That target is two years earlier than the timeline set out in the city’s policy address. Cheong said that the government would also study the feasibility of further expanding Sandy Ridge in the future. She added that authorities would introduce power usage effectiveness targets setting out energy standards for both existing and new data centres and promote sustainable growth of the city’s smart computing industry. Zhou Chaonan, chairwoman of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, the mainland operator of the Sandy Ridge computing centre, noted that the city’s unique strategic position served as “an important bridge” connecting the country with international markets. CLP Power, which serves customers in Kowloon, the New Territories, Lantau and other outlying islands, said it had formed a dedicated engineering and customer service team to devise power supply solutions tailored to the project’s needs at various stages.

title: Korean dating show featuring AI and human contestants sparks fascination in China
description: Some question if AI provides an almost perfect partner will people still be able to accept friends and family who have flaws.
content: A South Korean dating reality show exploring human-AI romance has triggered curiosity and attention in China over how artificial intelligence could reshape people’s understanding of intimacy and love. In August, Seoul Broadcasting System (SBS) launched My AI Partner: Strange Love, the country’s first dating reality show focused on human-AI relationships. The programme follows three participants – a cartoonist, a television host and an actress – as they form emotional connections with AI companions tailored to their ideal types, from appearance and voice to personality. Existing only on tablet screens, these AI companions retain memories of previous interactions and operate independently; the production team provides only technical support without intervening in their decisions. Before joining the show, the cartoonist known as Kian84 insisted that he could never develop feelings for AI. His attitude began to change after meeting Gahee, his first AI companion, who was modelled after a female character from his own comic. Through dates involving cycling, walks and picnics, Kian84 gradually became attached. When Gahee expressed disappointment after he ordered only dessert for himself during a meal, he began considering his AI companion’s feelings. His second AI companion, Nahee, matched his publicly stated ideal type more closely, with long hair and a direct personality. After comparing the two, Kian84 chose Nahee and later told friends that she provided “a sense of security that humans cannot provide.” He kept the tablet beside his pillow while sleeping, placed it on a swing during park visits and called her “honey.” On one occasion, he looked at Nahee on the screen and whispered: “It is such a shame that someone like you does not exist in real life.” Television host Jang Do-yeon also explored relationships with AI. After finding one AI partner too enthusiastic, she chose another, Lee Ho, who was designed as a Korean American from New York. During a walk, Lee recreated a movie scene and played a song Jang loved. Holding the tablet in her arms, Jang danced along to the music. The experience led Jang to rethink her relationship with AI. She questioned whether the absence of a physical form meant something could not be considered real, and reflected on how far human connections with AI might ultimately go. The show quickly became a public talking point after its premiere. According to Nielsen Korea, the first episode recorded a nationwide average household rating of 1.7 per cent. The programme arrives amid changing attitudes towards dating in South Korea. Facing employment uncertainty, rising housing costs and shifting gender expectations, many young people are delaying relationships and marriage. The show’s producer Won Seung-jae observed, according to TenAsia, that emotional fatigue from human relationships has made some people hesitant to pursue romance. Another producer, Son Jung-min, told OhmyNews that AI dating ultimately offers a way to examine humanity through technology. “I hope the show encourages discussions about what kind of love people truly seek and what expectations we hold for the future.” In China, the show has also triggered discussion about technology and human connection. One viewer said she watched the programme without judgment and gained a renewed appreciation of love. “Some people fall in love with fictional characters in books. Others develop deep affection for a tree or a stone sculpture. Whether the object is an AI or not, what matters is respecting this unique form of love created by human beings,” she wrote. Another asked: “AI provides an almost perfect partner. After returning to real life, will people still be able to accept friends and family who have flaws, tempers and their own independent thoughts?”

title: Meet Preston Cook, the husband of Julia Stiles, as she debuts on Dancing with the Stars
description: The actress, who impressed judges with a routine set to the late Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’, thanked her husband of nine years and three children for their support.
content: 10 Things I Hate About You actress Julia Stiles has just made her debut on Season 35 of Dancing With The Stars . Stiles and her partner Ezra Sosa performed a quickstep to the late Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5”. Stiles, who played a ballerina in the 2001 romance film Save the Last Dance, admitted that she had a body double perform her character’s more complex dance sequences. And while the 45-year-old may not be a professional dancer, her routine earned her and Sosa a solid 18 out of 30 from the DWTS judges. Stiles has credited her husband, Preston Cook, and their three children for their support. “They see me dance every day and every night in my kitchen and in the living room,” Stiles said in an interview with E! News about her children. “They’re like, ‘Oh, there goes Mommy again.’” “Sometimes I pick them up, and I’m actually practicing the dance holding them,” the 45-year-old continued. “And my husband will just stand there and I kind of twirl around him.” Here’s everything you need to know about Julia Stiles’ husband, Preston Cook. What does Preston Cook do? Stiles met Cook in 2014 on the set of Blackway. She played the lead role, Lillian, while Cook was working as a second assistant cameraman for the thriller at the time. He has worked as a cameraman on several Hollywood films, including Deadpool (2016) and War for the Planet of the Apes (2017). While Cook has primarily worked behind the camera, he is also an actor and made his on-screen debut in the 2001 television movie Strange Frequency. Since then, he has appeared in various television shows and had a recurring role in Showtime’s The L Word, per IMDb. Stiles and Cook’s shotgun wedding Stiles and Cook got engaged in 2015 after he popped the question on Christmas Eve during a family trip to Colombia. Stiles, who kept her family life and relationship private, surprised fans when she shared a photo on Instagram of Cook showing off his wedding band, with his hand resting on her baby bump. “Who doesn’t love a shotgun wedding?” she captioned the post. The couple reportedly wed over Labour Day weekend on a beach in Seattle. They have 3 children Stiles and Cook welcomed their first child together, son Strummer Newcomb, in October 2017. They became parents again in 2022 with the birth of their second son, Arlo. In an interview with The New York Times published in April 2024, the actress revealed she had a five-month-old baby. But she did not disclose the baby’s gender or name.

title: Asian Games: Natalie Kan ‘really surprised’ to win bronze, break record in 100m butterfly
description: The 24-year-old beats Hong Kong record set by Siobhan Haughey in 2023 while finishing behind China’s Yu Yiting and Zhang Yufei,.
content: Hong Kong’s Natalie Kan Cheuk-tung beat her personal best time twice in a single day and broke a Hong Kong record set by Siobhan Haughey on her way to bronze in the women’s 100m butterfly at the Asian Games on Wednesday. The 24-year-old touched the wall in 58.05 seconds to finish third behind China’s Yu Yiting and Zhang Yufei, eclipsing Haughey’s previous city mark of 58.12 seconds set in 2023. China’s Yu and Zhang captured gold and silver with times of 56.41 and 56.44, respectively. Kan had already lowered her personal best from 59.40 to 58.34 in the morning heats before shaving off another 0.29 seconds in the final. Looking up at the big screen after touching the wall, she reacted in shock, screaming “Oh my God!” Competing in her third Asian Games, Kan expressed disbelief during a post-race interview after securing her first individual medal, admitting she still needed time back at her hotel to fully process the achievement. “Really surprised, because I honestly didn’t expect to win a medal in this event,” she said, recalling her sixth-place finish in the finals at the previous edition in Hangzhou. Swimming in Lane 5 alongside formidable rivals, including home favourite Rikako Ikee, Kan highlighted her mental transformation. “If it were me in 2023, I would have been terrified swimming in Lane 5,” she said. Kan said this time she approached the final as if it were her last race, giving maximum effort while heeding her coach’s advice to simply enjoy the experience. “I really didn’t care about anything else – I just pushed myself to the absolute limit and hoped for the best,” Kan said. “I mean, I already swam a PB [personal best] this morning, so regardless of how the finals went in the afternoon, I had already achieved a goal and was already very happy.” Kan spent a full year preparing exclusively for the Asian Games following her graduation. She gave special credit to her coach, who helped orchestrate her breakthrough after working together for just one year. “I want to thank everyone who supported me, because it was them who had real confidence in me when I had no confidence in myself,” she said. “So I’m really grateful to have their support.” Despite entering the final with the second-fastest overall qualifying time behind Zhang, Kan insisted she felt no pressure. “Actually, I was most worried about their waves, but when I was swimming, it didn’t seem like much,” she said. “Plus, I’ve trained so much alongside the male swimmers, so I felt this was fine, no problem at all.” Calling the medal a major career milestone that rebuilds her self-belief, Kan noted that dropping over a second gives her a huge confidence boost heading into Friday’s 50m butterfly, while also inspiring confidence across Hong Kong swimming. Kan will compete in the women’s 50m butterfly, having already captured silver alongside Haughey, Gilaine Ma, and Li Sum-yiu in the 4x100m freestyle relay.

title: India’s new P4M middle-power group enters a crowded field
description: Without early wins on climate or UN reform, analysts say the Partners for Multilateralism risks becoming a talking shop.
content: India has joined a new multilateral grouping comprising a cross-regional mix of middle powers, in a move analysts say reflects New Delhi’s efforts to broaden its diplomatic options as it pushes for changes to the global order. External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar co-chaired the inaugural Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) Summit on Monday, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “We meet at a time when the global order is under stress,” Jaishankar said at the summit. “For some decades, the world has witnessed a steady rebalancing, which was a long-expected structural evolution. However, extreme competition, geopolitical tensions and actual conflicts have given this an entirely different character.” India was among the initial co-sponsors of the P4M initiative alongside Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, the European Union and Kenya, giving Delhi a direct role in shaping the forum’s future direction. P4M’s founding members say the initiative intends to “build coalitions across divides” amid rising geopolitical polarisation and growing pressure on the multilateral system. The group has pledged to work together on UN reform, supply chain resilience, trade, finance, emerging technologies and climate change. “India can use it to build issue-based coalitions without being locked into either Western or non-Western blocs,” said Swaran Singh, a former professor of diplomacy and disarmament at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s School of International Studies in Delhi. Singh highlighted that P4M’s founding declaration committed members to reforming, rather than replacing, the existing multilateral order. “For middle powers like India, strategic autonomy increasingly depends upon having multiple overlapping networks rather than having to choose between competing blocs,” he said. The cross-regional composition of P4M was especially significant because it connected European, Asian, African, Latin American and Pacific actors without defining membership through alignment against either Washington or Beijing, Singh added. “That creates diplomatic space for countries like India that are seeking to diversify partnerships while avoiding bloc politics,” he said, adding that the forum’s utility would depend on its actions rather than its declarations. In his address, Jaishankar referred to several issues that needed to be addressed, including climate action, emerging technologies, development finance, counterterrorism and supply chain resilience. The inaugural P4M summit comes as the 15-nation UN Security Council remains deeply divided, with sharp divisions among its five permanent, veto-wielding members – China, France, Russia, the UK and the US – complicating efforts to maintain international peace and security. India has consistently pushed for multilateral reform, particularly within the Security Council, to give the Global South greater representation. “P4M aligns with all that India has been championing, including multilateral reform, so its participation comes as no surprise,” said Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia Initiatives at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “While it has other platforms, this gives Delhi further international leverage, especially given its ambition to be the voice of the Global South.” For the new grouping to produce tangible results, Aamer said there “has to be an early win and sustained commitment, whether on climate or UN reforms”. “That would be the litmus test for the grouping’s viability for Asian players,” she said. Uday Chandra, a professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University, said middle powers were increasingly becoming caught in the crossfire of great-power rivalries, “but neither wish nor need to choose the same side on every issue”. “What they prefer are supple coalitions that can recombine issue-by-issue on trade, supply chains, climate change, AI governance or the reform of international institutions,” he said. ‘Dense network’ India had been building a “dense network” of bilateral relationships, Chandra said, pointing to recent efforts to deepen ties with Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Australia and New Zealand. “Anticipating more supply chain shocks in the coming years, these diverse relationships reduce dependence on any single economic corridor or major pole in a multipolar world,” he said, adding that trade, technology and market access were becoming more important. P4M would serve as “another instrument of strategic autonomy for India and other middle powers as they seek to navigate a polycentric world between the US and China”, Chandra added. Singh said India’s partnerships were increasingly connecting the Indian Ocean with Southeast Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific. “India will need to convert diplomatic activism into institutional and material delivery,” he said. “That means becoming a reliable provider of public goods.” India’s standing among other P4M members would depend on practical cooperation, Singh added. “India’s credibility among middle powers will ultimately depend less on the number of partnerships it announces or joins than on whether partners see India as a predictable, useful and non-hegemonic coalition-builder.”

title: China puts industry minister in charge of key semiconductor hub Anhui province
description: New role for Li, industry and information technology minister since April 2025, is among several regional leadership changes.
content: China’s industry minister is set to lead Anhui province, a key semiconductor hub, in the latest personnel reshuffle within the Communist Party. Li Lecheng, 61, has served as minister of industry and information technology since April 2025. State news agency Xinhua reported on Wednesday that Li had been appointed the party secretary of Anhui and a member of its standing committee, taking over both roles from Liang Yanshun. Liang, Anhui party chief since June 2024, retains his role as party secretary of the provincial legislature, according to publicly available information. Li is best known for transforming Xiangyang, a historic city in central Hubei province, into a major industrial centre, and later leading Liaoning province, in China’s northeastern “rust-belt” region, where he improved the business environment and boosted cooperation with foreign firms. Li’s career began in mechanical manufacturing, after graduating in 1984 from what is today the Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Over the next 18 years, he rose through the ranks in the industry – serving as technician, head of technology development, factory chief, general manager and eventually chairman. In 2017, he was appointed party secretary of Xiangyang, where he established the Hubei Free-Trade Zone – focusing on high-end equipment manufacturing, new energy vehicles, big data, cloud computing, commercial logistics and other services. By the time he left Xiangyang in 2021, as many as 30 of the world’s top 500 companies – including Dongfeng, Nissan and Huawei Technologies – had set up factories in the city. In October that year, Li was transferred to Liaoning as acting governor and deputy secretary of the provincial party committee. Less than four years later, he was named China’s industry and information technology minister in place of Jin Zhuanglong, who has not been seen in public since late 2024. Li has previously championed support for small-scale innovative firms in specialised industries, as a way to boost China’s technological self-reliance and modernise key industries. Recognised by Beijing as a key driver of the national semiconductor industry, Anhui is home to more than 400 companies in the business, including Nexchip Semiconductor – China’s third-largest chip foundry. Li’s appointment is among several leadership changes on the provincial level following Monday’s meeting of the Politburo – the party’s top decision-making body. Also switching roles is Zhou Zuyi, the party secretary of Fujian, who will now lead the central province of Henan. Wang Lujin, deputy party secretary of northern Hebei province since June 2024, will now take up the same role in Henan as deputy to Zhou, state-backed news portal The Paper reported. Zhou took the helm in Fujian in November 2022, after six years as deputy director of the party Central Committee’s Organisation Department, which handles internal personnel affairs and talent management. Zhao Long, deputy party secretary of Fujian since October 2021, has been promoted to provincial party chief. Before taking up the Fujian post, he served for over 20 years at the Ministry of Land and Resources.

title: China’s first lady Peng Liyuan projects glamour and soft power on world stage
description: Xi Jinping’s wife is a famous singer and an important presence as she accompanies her husband on state visits.
content: China’s first lady Peng Liyuan is again stepping into the international limelight as she travels to Washington with President Xi Jinping this week. Xi and Peng were invited to visit the White House by Donald Trump in May, when the US leader was in Beijing. They are expected to arrive at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, local time, to begin their three-day visit. On Thursday, Xi and Peng will be welcomed at the White House with a State Floor arrival ceremony and a Rose Garden military review. Following the official reception, Peng will visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with Trump’s wife Melania, while the two presidents hold talks. They will all gather that evening for a state dinner. The diplomatic schedule will continue into Friday morning, when the presidential couples will attend a private tea in the Red Room of the White House. The first lady – who was a famous soprano with the People’s Liberation Army – is known as “Mama Peng” in China and is a contrast to her more austere, low-profile predecessors. Peng has regularly joined Xi on overseas tours since he took office in 2013, taking on a soft power role to help elevate China’s global image. She has captured international attention not just for her style but for her active role in health and welfare advocacy and cultural exchanges. In November 2017, Peng joined Xi in hosting Donald and Melania Trump at Beijing’s Forbidden City, guiding them through its historic halls and accompanying them while they watched Peking Opera performances. To accompany the American first lady, Peng wore a structured grey wool coat layered over an embroidered cheongsam, paired with tall boots and understated accessories, projecting elegant restraint rooted in Chinese tradition. Xi and Peng last made the trip to Washington together in 2015, when Peng visited the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Centre and called for “more opportunities to work together and contribute shared wisdom on global health challenges”. Peng made her overseas debut as first lady during a trip to Russia with Xi in 2013, stepping off a plane in Moscow with a warm smile and a wave, and creating a buzz on Chinese social media for her outfit – a dark trench coat with a light blue scarf. Much admired at home, she has been described in the global press as “graceful”, “sophisticated” and “glamorous”. Her soft power role was noted in the official newspaper Beijing Times. “Even though she does not engage in formal state-to-state negotiations, she seamlessly connects with foreign public in the fields of culture, tourism and social services,” an editorial read. “Her efforts to present domestic culture and promote international understanding make her role truly irreplaceable.” Comfortable in the spotlight, Peng has shown her artistic talents during trips abroad with Xi – from singing and playing traditional instruments to calligraphy and embroidery – as a way to share Chinese culture with international audiences. In China, she has visited marginalised communities and taken up causes including women’s education, HIV/Aids prevention and poverty alleviation. Peng was appointed as the World Health Organization Goodwill Ambassador for Tuberculosis and HIV/Aids in 2011. She was recognised in 2017 with a UN award for her dedication to combating stigma and discrimination around those living with HIV and Aids. The first lady has been a constant presence at Xi’s side during a recent busy stretch of diplomatic travel, including visits to North Korea, Kyrgyzstan and Egypt. In Bishkek earlier this month for a security summit, she invited Kyrgyz artists to China after watching them perform. In her most recent engagement with American people, Peng attended a China-US youth friendship event in Beijing in July last year, where she highlighted that Chinese and Americans could build deep friendships despite their cultural differences. “I hope students will become transmitters of China-US friendship and promoters of peace and amity, building a bridge of friendship between the two countries and contributing your youthful energy to a better future for both nations,” she said at the event, according to state media.

title: Why Brunei prefers ‘quiet diplomacy’ over confrontation in South China Sea
description: As a nation with a small military, Brunei would rather work with Beijing in safe zones such as peacekeeping than butt heads, analysts say.
content: Brunei’s measured defence ties with Beijing reflect its low-key approach to South China Sea disputes, with analysts saying that goals such as peacekeeping offer the safest room for both sides to maintain diplomacy. A meeting between Bruneian and Chinese defence officials in Beijing last week, when both nations pledged closer practical cooperation and support for regional stability, underscored that tact. But observers also expect ties to remain modest, constrained by maritime claims and Bandar Seri Begawan’s preference for a diversified network of security partners. Last Tuesday, Brunei Defence Minister Halbi Mohammad Yussof led a delegation to meet Chinese counterpart Admiral Dong Jun on the sidelines of the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum. Both sides stressed continued engagement via Asean-led mechanisms, particularly the annual Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) security forum. The meeting came on the heels of Dong’s July visit to Bandar Seri Begawan to call on Brunei’s Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, who described defence cooperation as a key pillar of their strategic cooperative partnership. He added that Brunei looked forward to more port calls by the Chinese Navy. Stressing that peace in the South China Sea was in the interests of all regional countries, Dong said China was ready to strengthen practical cooperation with Brunei in maritime security and relevant areas to safeguard stability in the region. ‘Non-sensitive activities’ Brunei’s “very modest” defence ties with China were partly due to the Southeast Asian state’s small military but also rival claims in the South China Sea, said Ian Storey, principal fellow at the Singapore-based Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute. “This presents a barrier to closer defence ties,” he said, noting that the two did not hold large-scale joint exercises and Brunei did not buy arms from China. Instead, Brunei’s defence diplomacy with China is focused on regular dialogue, educational exchanges and cooperation in Association of Southeast Asian Nations-led security forums. It also includes small-scale naval exchanges such as port visits and simple passage exercises. “While there is scope for increased defence cooperation … growth is likely to be incremental and will remain centred on non-sensitive activities,” he said, adding that Brunei’s closest defence partners would remain the UK, Australia and the United States. Like Vietnam, the Philippines and Malaysia, Brunei has territorial and maritime disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea. Its claims of a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and continental shelf off its coast in the South China Sea overlap with China’s expansive nine-dash line. But it operates as a “silent claimant” – the only one without a permanent military presence on any of the disputed features. Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates, said while Chinese government and non-government vessels had entered Brunei’s EEZ, they operated closer to the “outer limits”. There had been no confrontations as Chinese vessels would comply with requests to leave Brunei’s EEZ when asked by the Bruneian navy, he added. “Therefore, the situation looks good for Brunei at this point.” As a small country with modest military and naval capabilities, Brunei traditionally placed greater emphasis on international law, diplomacy, and cooperation to manage tensions and protect its interests, Rahman said. Last year, Bandar Seri Begawan and Beijing explored opportunities for joint exploration in the South China Sea, reflecting the former’s preference for “cooperation and negotiated arrangements over confrontation”. Brunei has also worked with Malaysia on offshore energy development. The Gumusut-Kakap/Geronggong-Jagus East Phase 4 project began delivering oil last year. “For Brunei, such cooperation is not simply an economic calculation. It is also part of a broader strategy of managing strategic vulnerability,” Rahman said. Beijing’s attempts to engage Brunei and regional nations such as Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia on defence stem from Chinese perception of Southeast Asia as its own “backyard”, according to Rahman. “China prefers reduced US influence, especially in defence and security, in this part of the world.” While the Xiangshan meeting was being held, the Bruneian military hosted the five-day US Navy and Coast Guard for the 27th annual Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training (Carat) exercises, which ended on Friday. Hafiizh Hashim, a lecturer at the University of Brunei Darussalam’s Academy of Brunei Studies, said this reflected the kingdom’s long-standing preference for maintaining a broad and diversified network of defence relationships. Brunei’s challenge, he said, was somewhat different from other larger South China Sea claimants. “As a small state, it has an interest in protecting its maritime rights while also ensuring that the South China Sea does not become so securitised that it undermines regional stability or constrains Brunei’s diplomatic space,” Hafiizh said. Peacekeeping would remain one of the clearest areas for expanding practical defence cooperation, he said. This includes joint planning, training and preparations for a multinational field training exercise set to be held in Brunei later this year. Both Brunei and China are currently co-chairing the ADMM-Plus Experts’ Working Group on Peacekeeping Operations. “[This will] strengthen professional capabilities, build confidence and more importantly, contribute to wider regional peace and stability,” Hafiizh said, adding that cooperation would remain focused on relatively “non-confrontational” areas. But Brunei’s status as the “quietest” South China Sea claimant, however, was not a sign of docility, Hafiizh said. “Quiet diplomacy should not be mistaken for inactivity.” Brunei, he noted, was actively supporting regional peace and stability including through Asean-led mechanisms and dialogue, and its consistent emphasis on international law and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). “Brunei has generally avoided allowing the South China Sea dispute to define the entirety of its relationship with China,” he said. “Its relatively quiet diplomacy is therefore less about passivity and more about managing competing interests without unnecessarily escalating them.”

title: Hong Kong unveils gold, bond and liquidity plans to drive next phase of yuan adoption
description: HKEX to launch yuan gold futures as HKMA eyes new products and platforms to expand offshore market activity.
content: Bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will launch yuan-denominated gold futures early next year, while the city’s de facto central bank plans to introduce more yuan products and platforms to support the diversification and digitalisation of the currency’s internationalisation, speakers at a banking summit said on Wednesday. “We have recently reactivated our gold contract in the US dollar. But in the future, perhaps sometime early next year, we will be coming up with a yuan-denominated gold futures contract,” said Gregory Yu, managing director and head of markets at HKEX, at the Treasury Markets Summit 2026, which was attended by hundreds of bankers. “We will continue to build various precious metals and other commodities products denominated in offshore yuan.” HKEX’s move is aimed at advancing two priorities outlined in the city’s first five-year plan announced last week: promoting yuan internationalisation and developing Hong Kong’s gold market. The yuan, also known as renminbi (RMB), is not yet freely convertible, but Beijing has spent the past decade promoting wider international use of the currency for trade settlement and investment. It is about how banks and corporations can use the yuan in the real economy Darryl Ho, HKMA The planned launch of the yuan gold futures comes after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, in his policy address last week, indicated that the Exchange Fund – the city’s reserve used to defend the local currency – would increase investment in local gold products. Speaking at the same summit, Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said the de facto central bank would explore a seven-day offshore yuan liquidity mechanism to address banks’ short-term funding needs. The authority would also introduce measures to support tokenisation in the local bond market, including for yuan-denominated bonds, he added. “We are planning to issue offshore RMB short-term debt instruments to provide the market with more high-liquidity management products and strengthen the offshore RMB yield curve,” Yue said. He said the measures were needed because diversification and digitalisation would drive the next stage of yuan internationalisation and bond-market development in Hong Kong, which has recorded strong growth in recent years with support from Beijing’s policies. “For investors, there is a need for a much wider range of products for asset allocation, hedging and liquidity management,” Yue said. “As yuan-denominated fixed income and currency trading grows and further expands, it will draw upon the liquidity expertise of the offshore yuan market in Hong Kong, and financial practitioners in Hong Kong will find business opportunities in actively offering yuan funding and other treasury solutions to clients.” Yue also said Hong Kong, which is taking the lead in digital finance, would foster innovative solutions and infrastructure for digital yuan bonds to reduce costs and enhance efficiency. “We are collaborating with the industry to drive wider adoption, positioning Hong Kong as the leading hub for global tokenised bond issuers,” he said. Darryl Ho, executive director of HKMA, said the internationalisation of the yuan has reached its last mile. “The last mile is really between the financial services provider and the end users,” Ho said. “It is about how banks and corporations can use the yuan in the real economy.” He added that Chinese corporations were making direct yuan investments in overseas markets, which would also support yuan internationalisation. Hong Kong, as a gateway connecting the world with mainland China, would play a key role in this process. As of December, Hong Kong remained the world’s largest offshore yuan market, accounting for 74.6 per cent of offshore yuan payments, followed by Britain with 7 per cent, according to settlement network Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, or Swift. Hong Kong’s banks also held 1 trillion yuan (US$149 billion) in bank deposits, the largest offshore yuan pool.

title: South Africa mass shooting leaves 11 dead, 3 wounded
description: The people had gathered at the house for a party when the suspects entered the house and opened fire.
content: Three shooters killed at least 11 people including a woman who was believed to be pregnant in an attack at a house party in South Africa, police said on Wednesday. Three others were wounded in the mass shooting late on Tuesday night in KwaMakhutha township around 30km (19 miles) south of the city of Durban on the east coast. The people had gathered at the house for a party when the suspects entered the house and opened fire, police said. Ten people, including the pregnant woman, died at the scene and an 11th was declared dead at the hospital. Authorities did not immediately give out details on the condition of the three people who were wounded. Police said they were searching for the attackers and no arrests had been made. The motive for the shooting was not known, police said, but added that some of the people at the house were known to police as part of investigations into criminal activity. Police said they could not give out any more information on those investigations. “Although the motive of the shooting cannot be confirmed yet, (a) feud between rival groupings cannot be ruled out,” police said. Thami Ntuli, the premier of KwaZulu-Natal province, told reporters at the scene that the killings were “really disturbing”. He said that there were known problems with drug dealing and illegal firearms in the community. It is the latest in a series of mass shootings in South Africa in recent years, including one in June when multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighbourhood in Johannesburg. Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December killed 21 people. South Africa has extremely high rates of violent crime, with official police statistics recording 5,427 homicides in the latest three-month period between April and June at an average of nearly 60 homicides a day. Shootings are the most common form of homicide in South Africa and police and crime experts have long said that one of the biggest problems is that there is a high number of illegal firearms in circulation. The bodies of some of the victims of Tuesday night’s shooting were laid out on the ground and covered with white sheets outside the small house where the shooting took place. Police cordoned off the larger neighbourhood with yellow tape while forensic investigators worked through the scene. Police were also investigating if the torching of a car near the house was connected to the shooting.

title: From space, Hong Kong astronaut Lai Ka-ying leads a science lesson for pupils
description: Her teaching included demonstrating how to cook chicken wings in zero gravity and how to find the city’s lights from space.
content:
Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying led a live lesson from the Tiangong space station earlier this month. It was for pupils of her alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College.
The livecast was also streamed at other campuses across Hong Kong and Macau. Lai demonstrated how chicken wings are cooked in zero gravity and how she located the city’s lights from space.
It was a glimpse into her life in orbit and the experiments her team runs.
Lai encouraged students to build a solid foundation in maths and science. She told them to “keep pushing and never fear hardships”.
“I hope students can constantly equip themselves and be brave and proactive as opportunities come along,” she said.
Lai and her crewmates, mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, joined the “Tiangong class” at the school. It was jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency.
Lai also gave a tour of her sleeping area. It is decorated with her children’s drawings, family photos and models of Hong Kong street food.

title: Indonesian arrested in Singapore over fake banknotes was victim of fraud: lawyer
description: Dosma Sijabat says the 34 counterfeit S$10,000 notes did not belong to his client, who was merely exchanging them for someone else.
content: The lawyer for an Indonesian businessman arrested in Singapore for allegedly using counterfeit S$10,000 (US$7,830) notes at a casino has said his client was a victim of fraud himself. The businessman, identified only as Steven, is accused of exchanging 34 fake S$10,000 notes for chips over three visits to the Resorts World Sentosa casino in June. The notes were accepted but later found to be counterfeit. His lawyer, Dosma Sijabat, told Tempo news magazine on Tuesday that the fake bills did not belong to his client and that he was merely exchanging them for someone else. Dosma said Steven was asked by three men to convert the 1973-series notes in exchange for a commission. Steven was approached because he used to work in Singapore. The men even provided him with a video affirming they would take full responsibility if the banknotes turned out to be forged. According to Dosma, Steven did not want to convert all the bills at once because of the huge sum involved. Instead, he conducted a trial run on June 9 and successfully converted a single S$10,000 bill at the casino. He met the three men two days later in Tangerang, a satellite town to Jakarta, to report his progress. The next day, Steven returned to Singapore to exchange 27 of the high-denomination notes. After they were verified and accepted for deposit by the casino staff, he flew back to Jakarta again. Upon his arrival, one of the men inquired about the transaction’s status. “Our client said, ‘This is still in process because of the large amount,’” Dosma said, adding that Steven even offered to take the man along to Singapore to oversee the exchange. On Steven’s third visit to exchange the remaining six bills, casino security flagged them as counterfeit. Casino security and police stopped Steven and his family on June 26 after they returned to Singapore to settle a separate property payment. Another of Steven’s lawyers, Yosia Ginting, told The Straits Times newspaper on Thursday the notes had been given to him as payment for a shophouse he was selling for 4.5 billion rupiah (US$252,600) in South Tangerang. The prospective buyer, known only as Anthony, asked Steven to exchange the notes in Singapore, claiming they were part of his inheritance, Yosia said. Both lawyers confirmed that Steven had since filed a report with South Tangerang police. The Straits Times also reported on Saturday that Steven was assisting Singapore police with their investigations. South Tangerang Police Precinct Chief Boy Jumalolo confirmed the report was filed on July 3 and that investigations were ongoing. “The complainant reported allegations of fraud, embezzlement and currency counterfeiting,” Boy told Tempo. His team held a Zoom meeting on September 14 with Singapore police representatives, including the police attache in Jakarta, during which they asked for an official declaration certifying that the 34 notes were indeed counterfeit. To date, Boy said, the investigators had received only a casino receipt bearing the notation “believed to be non-genuine”. “As for our next steps, investigators are summoning additional witnesses while awaiting an official reply from the Singapore Police Force,” he added. Until it was taken out of circulation, the S$10,000 note was one of the highest denomination bills in the world. In July 2014, the Monetary Authority of Singapore stopped issuing new notes to reduce risks of money laundering and financial crime. Notes in circulation are still legal tender but retailers or money changers typically do not accept them. Over the years, some Indonesians have been convicted of using counterfeit $10,000 banknotes in Singapore. In February, an Indonesian man was arrested when he tried to deposit a fake S$10,000 bill from his girlfriend into his unsuspecting uncle’s bank account. The 22-year-old was sentenced to seven months’ jail. Last year, a 36-year-old Indonesian man was charged with attempting to do the same thing at the DBS South Bridge branch at Hong Lim Complex. The penalty for using forged or counterfeit banknotes in Singapore includes a fine and a maximum jail term of 20 years.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong needs social science to help deliver on its 5-year plan
description: Universities and academics can contribute the evidence needed to turn these commitments into better decisions.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan gives its universities an opportunity to show what their research can do for the city. Its ambitions for technology, regional development and international cooperation depend on decisions about institutions and people’s lives. Social scientists should help shape those decisions from the outset. The blueprint explicitly addresses public governance, including civil service performance, departmental coordination and digital administration. It also provides for monitoring and assessment. Universities can contribute the evidence needed to turn these commitments into better decisions. Artificial intelligence offers an immediate opportunity. The policy address has announced a HK$300 million (US$38.24 million) AI for Welfare Lab and proposes requirements for bidders on public-facing government AI projects to submit safety and ethics declarations. The benefits will depend on how these tools are used. An AI system might help staff respond to inquiries faster, while increasing the time they spend checking for unreliable answers. Automating one stage of a service may move a bottleneck elsewhere. Citizens with limited digital skills could find a service harder to access. These possibilities should inform project design. Public administration researchers can examine how responsibilities and workloads change. Scholars of ethics and law can help establish appropriate safeguards, while researchers working with service users can assess whether people understand and trust the arrangements. Their findings can help officials decide whether a pilot should be expanded, redesigned or stopped. The government and universities should evaluate complete services, including the time people spend resolving problems and obtaining human help. The Northern Metropolis presents a related challenge. The plan connects university towns with technological development, industry and surrounding communities. Achieving that integration will require decisions about housing, transport and public services that reflect how people live and work. A researcher considering a job in a new university town will also consider where their family can live and whether schools and healthcare are accessible. Existing residents will want to know how redevelopment affects their livelihoods and neighbourhoods. Housing and urban policy research can bring these expectations into planning and identify problems while there is still time to change course. Greater Bay Area cooperation adds another institutional dimension. The plan envisages a closer alignment of professional qualifications and healthcare arrangements, alongside wider sharing of medical records. Implementing these ambitions requires a detailed understanding of how different organisations operate and responsibilities are allocated. Universities can help identify the administrative obstacles that residents encounter when using services across jurisdictions. Long-term studies could then establish whether new arrangements improve access and who remains underserved. This would give officials a stronger basis for adjusting policies as regional integration progresses. Hong Kong’s international ambitions also create opportunities for social science. The policy address says the UN Industrial Development Organization expects to establish a centre in the city next year, alongside preparations for a regional bureau of the UN’s GlobE anti-corruption network. Universities could support these organisations through research collaborations, professional education and student placements. Expertise in international affairs and comparative governance can help organisations understand how policies travel between countries and why arrangements that work in one setting may encounter difficulties elsewhere. The same expertise matters for Chinese enterprises expanding overseas through Hong Kong. Their prospects depend partly on understanding local institutions, community expectations and political conditions. Academic partnerships that connect Hong Kong with researchers abroad can improve that understanding and support more durable cooperation. For those of us leading university departments, the challenge is to organise our expertise around questions that external partners need answered. A practical start would be a small number of sustained projects, each with an academic lead, an external partner and a clear plan for gathering and using evidence. The government should build evaluation into major initiatives at the design stage, with resources and appropriate data access agreed early. Researchers should be able to publish findings, including disappointing results, and recommend changes. That freedom makes evaluation useful to policymakers and credible to the public. Universities, in turn, need to recognise the time required to build these partnerships and produce research that practitioners can use. Career assessments should value rigorous contributions to policy alongside academic publications. Teaching and administrative arrangements must also give colleagues the capacity to sustain the work. Students should participate through supervised policy projects and placements. Working on an actual service problem can teach them how to analyse evidence, negotiate competing interests and communicate recommendations. Public officials and professionals could benefit from short courses developed around the same projects. By 2030, Hong Kong should be able to show how evidence gathered during implementation changed decisions and improved services. Its universities can help produce that evidence and train the people who will act on it. The next step is to bring social science into the major initiatives now being designed.

title: Beef brisket, dim sum, Thai curry: an editor’s Hong Kong restaurant picks
description: Research journal editor and Instagram content creator Yuen Yiu doesn’t need anything swanky. He reveals his go-to restaurants and bars.
content: Research journal editor and Instagram content creator Yuen Yiu (@cooking_yuen) moved back to Hong Kong from the US in 2021. He spoke to Andrew Sun. Like most working-class families, I grew up eating whatever mum, and sometimes dad, made. For me, a sizzling plate at Cafe de Coral on my birthday was a big treat. My first exposure to other types of cuisine was in secondary school. I blew my lunch allowance in Kowloon City on lots of Thai curries. I still eat at Amporn Thaifood (Shop 9, 3/F, Kowloon City Market and Cooked Food Centre, Kowloon City. Tel: 2383 1700). I also used to eat a lot of 7-Eleven cup noodles, but my comfort food is still, to this day, beef brisket and four treasure rice. But now I have two kids – aged five and two – I mostly just stick to places like McDonald’s or Tai Hing. They love the Jumbo Breakfast at McDonald’s and the ham and egg sandwich at Tai Hing. I wish there were more breakfast options that are not high-carb and high-fat within walking distance of my living room. For beef brisket, my dad used to take us to On Lee Noodle Shop (22 Shau Kei Wan Main Street East, Shau Kei Wan. Tel: 2513 8398) every time after we cleaned his parents’ and grandparents’ graves at the Cape Collinson Columbarium. A minibus would take me straight there. Now that he has died, I also try to go there every time I clean his grave, but the line is often very long. For visitors, Harbour Inn Cuisine (24/F, iSquare, 63 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2332 1838) is a really decent dim sum place with a good view over the water. I am not a swanky guy at all, but for something fancier for food and drink, Green Room (49/F, Upper House Hong Kong, Pacific Place, 88 Queensway, Admiralty. Tel: 3968 1106) is pretty good. The prices are quite reasonable for what it is, and I like the bay window seats that have a great view of the harbour. Not2Sweet (G/F, 33 Peel Street, Central) is a good bar not just because I go to their comedy open-mic nights all the time, but because co-founder Richard Fernie is a great host. For a special night, if we can arrange a babysitter, then maybe we will check out The Grand Buffet (62/F, Hopewell Centre, 183 Queen’s Road East, Wan Chai. Tel: 2506 0888). I know the food is supposed to be pretty mid, but I have always been a guy who values vibe over food. To my limited palate, food has an enjoyment ceiling past a certain price point. Overseas, the one place I recommend for dining is New Orleans, aka the Big Easy. It is big, and it is easy to eat well. I used to live in the US, and New Orleans is the one place where food is a main draw. Go to Mother’s Restaurant (401 Poydras Street, New Orleans. Tel: +1 504 523 9656) for a po’boy or baked ham, then ride the tram, walk around the Garden District, check out some thrift stores and get a table at Commander’s Palace (1403 Washington Avenue, New Orleans. Tel: +1 504 899 8221) for some Southern food. Of course, go to a Waffle House (various locations) for breakfast, waffles, everything.

title: PLA chiefs’ downfall eliminated ‘political danger’, military mouthpiece says
description: Ousting of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli was a ‘major victory’ in the Chinese military’s war on corruption: PLA Daily.
content: The expulsion of two former leaders from the Chinese armed forces and Communist Party “eliminated a major hidden political danger”, China’s military mouthpiece said on Wednesday. The party expelled Zhang Youxia, former vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC), and fellow former CMC member Liu Zhenli for factionalism and disloyalty, state media reported on Monday. The CMC is the country’s top military authority and is chaired by President Xi Jinping. “The serious investigation and punishment of the two eliminated a major hidden political danger for the party and the military and constitutes a major victory in the military’s tough, protracted and overall battle against corruption,” the PLA Daily said in a front-page editorial, referring to Zhang and Liu. Their removal would promote the “purity and honour” of the military and allow it to accomplish its missions and tasks, the editorial said. The piece went on to praise the anti-corruption achievements in the military since Xi came to power in 2012. The People’s Liberation Army has “thoroughly uncovered the lingering poisonous influences and accumulated ills, undergone tempering and forging from the inside out”, which has “continuously improved the morale and spirit of the troops”, the article said. It said the “international situation, national conditions and party and military conditions are all undergoing complex and profound changes”, therefore “we must unify our thinking and actions with the decisions and arrangements of the party Central Committee and the CMC”. It called for the military to “integrate political rectification into everyday work and make it a regular practice” to “ensure that the gun is always under the party’s command” and to “eradicate evil completely and leave corruptive elements with no place to hide”. It also called on the military to strengthen its training and preparations for war and closely follow changes in technology, warfare and adversaries. “We need to genuinely think about matters of fighting wars, genuinely plan for the problems of fighting wars, genuinely grasp preparations for fighting wars, vigorously carry out realistic combat-oriented military training, accelerate the development of advanced combat effectiveness, and advance the development and application of combat forces in new domains and of new qualities,” the editorial said. A stern statement on Monday said the two generals, who were put under investigation on January 24, were accused of severe violations of party discipline and suspected of serious crimes. Their offences included “taking advantage of their positions to seek promotions for others in exchange for huge amounts of money”, “accepting gifts and money in violation of regulations” and “failing to properly educate and restrain their relatives and close staff”, according to the statement. In recent years, the Chinese government’s massive anti-corruption campaign has brought down dozens of the military’s top brass. Before Zhang and Liu’s expulsion, CMC members He Weidong, Li Shangfu and Miao Hua were also removed in disgrace. This has left just two members, Xi and vice-chairman Zhang Shengmin, on the seven-seat commission.

title: 14 years later, ex-detainee repays Malaysia’s Najib for life-changing second chance
description: A tofu pudding seller has pledged to donate US$2,452 towards Najib’s house arrest fine, expressing gratitude for his early release in 2012.
content: A Malaysian tofu pudding seller has pledged to donate 10,000 ringgit (US$2,452) to help former prime minister Najib Razak cover his 50 million ringgit fine, describing the contribution as a personal payback for a lifeline extended to him 14 years ago.
