In a social media post, Sunny Seow, founder of the Sunnycoco brand, shared that his motivation stemmed from a pivotal moment in 2012 when he was serving a sentence in Perak state’s Manjung for past mistakes. During a visit by Najib to the area that year, Seow sought the help of a local village chief to submit an appeal to the home ministry requesting an early release to care for his elderly parents. “Unexpectedly, I received a notification from the home ministry that I could end my detention early and return home,” Seow said. “For others, it might be just a letter or a bit of assistance, but for me at that time, it was an opportunity to start anew.” Following his early release, Seow rebuilt his life by starting a small business selling tofu pudding. “Seeing Datuk Seri Najib hoping to return home to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest reminds me of where I was 14 years ago,” Seow said, referring to the former leader’s honorary title. “Back then, when I needed help, he helped me. Today, within my ability, I want to do my part to repay that kindness.” Calculating that he earns roughly 1 ringgit in profit per bowl, Seow noted that his 10,000 ringgit contribution represents the profits of 10,000 bowls of tofu pudding. He clarified that his gesture was neither politically motivated nor a call for others to follow suit. “This is just a debt of gratitude I owe and want to repay in my own way,” Seow added. “You gave me a chance to come home back then. Today, I will do my best to help you.” Last Friday, Malaysia’s king granted Najib a “conditional pardon”, where the former leader is required to settle his fine before he can be sent to his home to complete his sentence, due to end on August 23, 2028. Najib has been serving a prison sentence at Kajang Prison in Selangor state since August 23, 2022, for misappropriating 42 million ringgit from a former unit of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. This story was first published by The Star

title: Hong Kong, Macau student trip to Beijing shows ‘fruitful results’ of patriotic push
description: Five-day visit by 1,200 students reflects ‘powerful’ synergy in patriotic education efforts, official commentary says.
content: A Hong Kong and Macau youth delegation trip to Beijing to pay tribute to the national flag has showcased the “fruitful results” of the two cities’ patriotic education efforts, according to the central government. A commentary published by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office on Tuesday also said that President Xi Jinping and the central government attached great importance to the five-day visit, during which the delegation received “vivid patriotic education” through immersive visits and experiences in the capital. “The event fully showed the fruitful results of the Hong Kong and Macau governments’ efforts to strengthen patriotic education for youth,” the office said in a commentary published under the pen name “Gang Ao Ping”. It added that both governments had thoroughly implemented the spirit of Xi’s speeches, institutionalising patriotic education for youth in recent years. The delegation, comprising nearly 1,200 students from primary and secondary schools and institutions of higher education in Hong Kong and Macau, visited Beijing from last Friday to Tuesday. They were received by Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang at the Great Hall of the People on Monday. Ding was said to have conveyed Xi’s greetings and expressed hope that all delegation members would understand, guard and bring honour to the national flag. The commentary said the delegation had also reflected the “powerful” synergy across all sectors of Hong Kong and Macau in promoting patriotic education among young people. That included efforts to allow them to participate first-hand in flag-raising ceremonies to enhance their sense of national identity, and study tours to help them learn more about the country’s modernisation. During their time in Beijing, students in the delegation watched the flag-raising ceremony at Tiananmen Square, visited several monuments and museums, and interacted with their local counterparts. According to the office, the students stood tall and sang the national anthem loudly during the flag-raising, continued to gaze at the flag and were reluctant to leave after the ceremony concluded. “Many expressed that watching the flag rise and singing the anthem in unison reinforced their pride and sense of belonging as Chinese citizens,” it said. Through a series of themed visits, students gained a deep understanding of China’s glorious history and culture, recognised the shared bond between Hong Kong, Macau and mainland China, and experienced first-hand the immense achievements of the country’s modernisation, further strengthening their national and Chinese identity, the office said. “The event fully showed the deep devotion and patriotic aspirations of the youth of Hong Kong and Macau,” it said. Since 2023, more than 180,000 secondary school students have visited the mainland on study trips to witness the country’s development and achievements first-hand, the office noted. The commentary also said Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan clearly stated the need to deepen patriotic education, national education and national security education, while systematically advancing the construction of youth patriotic education bases to nurture a new generation equipped with national pride and a sense of responsibility.

title: Hong Kong father admits repeatedly raping daughter over a 6-year period
description: The girl said her father began abusing her in 2015, when she was six, using threats and promises to ensure her cooperation.
content: A Hong Kong man has admitted repeatedly raping his daughter over six years, using threats and promises to ensure her cooperation. The defendant, identified in court only by his initials, FKY, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to 14 counts of rape for the persistent sexual abuse of his daughter between December 2015 and November 2021, when she was aged six to 11. But the High Court heard that the actual number of offences could be much higher. The girl said she was raped almost weekly after the defendant began taking her to various hotels to keep his wife in the dark. The court heard that the father used a carrot-and-stick approach to make his daughter accede to his sexual advances. Knowing she was addicted to online gaming, he would often promise to buy her game credits if she cooperated. On other occasions, the defendant threatened not to help her with her homework if she refused his requests. He committed the offences either when his wife was away from home or by lying to her that he was taking the girl to a theme park. The complainant, now 16, said she initially submitted to her father’s assault at their home in Tuen Mun when she was six without understanding what was happening. She said she had been raped almost 10 times in a public toilet in the district between the ages of six and seven. In early 2019, the defendant began taking his daughter to hotels across Hong Kong to rape her, as his wife was spending more time at home. The girl said her father had become so used to raping her that he would signal his intention to attack her with a hand gesture meaning “you need to give daddy”. On one occasion, the defendant complained that she had wasted his money on a hotel room because he had only managed to rape her twice. A police investigation found that the accused had made 49 reservations at four hotels in Tuen Mun, Tin Shui Wai, Kwai Chung and Tsim Sha Tsui between February 2021 and February 2022. The defendant was arrested in November 2022 after the girl complained to her school’s social worker. Mr Justice Tony Poon Siu-tung is expected to pass sentence on November 4. Prosecutors often face hurdles in bringing charges against sex offenders because victims may be unable to recall details of abuse spanning several years. Hong Kong authorities are considering a new dedicated law targeting long-term child sexual abuse as part of a broader legal overhaul. The government has also proposed expanding the offence of rape to cover sexual penetration without consent in areas other than the vagina.

title: China launches ‘mineral exploration offensive’ as global supply chain pressures mount
description: Beijing is scouring the nation for resources ranging from oil to rare earths, as it tries to shield its economy from rising geopolitical turbulence.
content: China has launched a huge new nationwide hunt for resources ranging from crude oil to rare earths, as it strives to shield its economy from a turbulent geopolitical environment in which raw materials are increasingly becoming instruments of leverage. The upgraded national campaign was designed to uncover and extract more of China’s own resources, as demand for key minerals was expected to keep rising in the coming years, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Tuesday. The high-profile drive, which deputy minister Zhou Xing dubbed a “mineral exploration offensive”, will focus on oil, iron, copper and aluminium – resources that China lacks – as well as rare earths, a sector that it already dominates. “We aim to discover as many mineral deposits as possible, especially large and high-grade ones … to significantly boost self-sufficiency in strategic mineral resources and strengthen confidence in safeguarding China’s energy and resource security,” Zhou said during a press conference. The plan, which covers China’s new five-year economic cycle from 2026 to 2030, would also include the construction of around 300 energy and resource bases, Zhou added. China’s renewed exploration drive comes at a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, as the US-Israel war on Iran intensifies worries over supply-chain security and countries compete for access to critical minerals amid rising economic, technology and military tensions. Between January and August, China uncovered nearly 70 million tonnes of recoverable oil and 610 billion cubic metres of natural gas reserves, according to the ministry. Major discoveries this year have included the super-large Maoniuping rare earth mine in the southwestern Sichuan province and the Chating copper-gold mine in the central Anhui province. The country will harness artificial intelligence to advance deep-earth and deep-sea exploration, as well as re-evaluate low-grade, hard-to-use mineral deposits that were once considered unusable, according to Zhou. China has been ramping up its mineral exploration efforts in recent years, investing a total of 500 billion yuan (US$75 billion) between 2021 and 2025, a 29 per cent increase compared with the previous five-year period, according to a ministry briefing in April. The extra activity appeared to pay off, with China logging a major uptick in newly proven oil and gas reserves over the period. The volume of new proven oil and natural gas reserves rose by 51.7 per cent and 44.2 per cent, respectively, compared with the previous five years, according to ministry data. As of the end of last year, China had the world’s largest reserves of 14 minerals, including rare earths and tungsten, and was ranked in the global top four for nine others, including coal, iron and lithium, the ministry said. China’s exports of rare earths – strategic minerals that have become a source of geopolitical leverage for Beijing – fell by 11.1 per cent year on year during the first eight months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.

title: Physical moves by online financial firms unlikely to pump up property market: analysts
description: Online brokerages and digital banks are opening branches across city after a sharp drop in shop rents in prime locations.
content: Digital financial service providers, including online brokerages and digital banks that used to trumpet their “zero-branch, fully online” models, have been opening physical stores across Hong Kong recently. Analysts described it as a strategic trend aimed at enhancing brand image and service quality to capture market share, but added that the impact on the city’s retail property market would be limited. Futu Securities International (Hong Kong) opened a new global headquarters at Pacific Place in Admiralty on Monday. It said in a news release that the new office, spanning about 42,000 square feet, would include a private wealth centre offering high-net-worth and institutional clients access to professional advisory services and tailored asset management solutions. It previously had 13 physical service locations in Hong Kong. Longbridge Securities, another online brokerage, opened its first Hong Kong flagship store in Tsim Sha Tsui a year ago and has opened three more this year. This month, market sources said Ele Bank – a joint venture between Futu and Xiaomi – had leased a ground-floor shop of about 1,640 square feet on Yee Wo Street in Causeway Bay for a monthly rent of HK$600,000 (US$76,494), with plans to open its first physical branch there. Earlier this month, ZA Bank announced that it had leased four floors of office space, totalling about 45,000 square feet, at Tower 3, Lee Garden Eight in Causeway Bay to serve as its new Hong Kong headquarters – expected to open next year. Bank management said it was exploring the use of part of the new headquarters to establish its first physical branch. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority revised its guidelines in late 2024 to allow digital banks to establish physical local branches. Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said Hong Kong people lacked confidence in digital financial service providers that did not have physical branches, and that had been a significant constraint on the firms’ services and growth. “Without physical branches, depositors lack confidence, so digital banks can’t attract large deposits or issue large loans,” he said. “Also, uploading documents for mortgages is a hassle.” Financial commentator and academic Simon Lee Siu-po said most users of digital financial service providers were young people with relatively few assets. With the luxury retail sector in a downturn in recent years and shop rents dropping sharply, brokerages have been able to snap up prime locations Stanley Poon Chi-ming, Centaline Commercial “Older individuals typically hold more assets, yet they tend to use traditional financial institutions,” he said. “Purely online institutions offer limited services, causing them to miss out on clients with substantial assets.” Lee said the online institutions were aligning with their client base by opening branches in a few select locations. “For instance, establishing a presence in areas like Central, Kwun Tong and Tsuen Wan would instil confidence in clients without causing operating costs to skyrocket,” Lee said. David Wu, Hong Kong financial services industry leader at Deloitte China, said digital players were pivoting towards the wealth management market, where affluent clients required face-to-face and personalised advisory services. Stanley Poon Chi-ming, managing director at Centaline Commercial, said the opening of physical outlets by online brokerages and digital banks did not constitute a mainstream trend in retail leasing. He said most brokerage firms had rented upper-floor premises in the past, when prime street locations were dominated by retailers of luxury goods, watches and jewellery. “With the luxury retail sector in a downturn in recent years and shop rents dropping sharply, brokerages have been able to snap up prime locations,” he said. “There are few industries left with strong rent-paying capacity.”

title: Engineer gets 160 hours’ community service over Queen Mary Hospital lift defects
description: Engineer convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates after 24 lifts at Hong Kong hospital were found defective.
content: A Hong Kong-registered lift engineer held liable for faulty installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block has been sentenced to 160 hours of community service after being convicted of submitting misleading documents and improperly issuing safety certificates. Eastern Court sentenced Law Wing-chai, 54, on Wednesday for two summary offences under the Lifts and Escalators Ordinance. The sentence came a month after authorities revealed that 24 of the 28 lifts in the new block of Hong Kong Island’s largest hospital had serious defects, delaying services. In August, the Architectural Services Department said the faults had caused lifts to start or stop abruptly, misalign with floor levels or fail to open. The problems included damaged electronic components, faulty wiring connections and poor workmanship. The defects raised questions about how the lifts had passed statutory safety examinations while remaining too unreliable to support clinical operations. Authorities did not name the workers involved at the time. According to court documents, the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department brought two summonses against Law last year. Law was accused of producing documents that he ought reasonably to have known were false or misleading in a material respect on January 24, 2025. He was also prosecuted for issuing a safety certificate for a lift when it or its equipment was not “of good design and construction or was not in safe working condition”. Under the ordinance, a new lift must be thoroughly examined and certified by a registered engineer as being in safe working order before it can be used. Law stood trial after pleading not guilty to both charges. Deputy Magistrate Ho Tsz-chun convicted him, finding that he had failed to exercise the due care and professional duty expected of an experienced engineer when inspecting the lift before signing the report. At Wednesday’s sentencing hearing, the magistrate said the case was serious because it concerned public safety at a hospital. He said Law had a statutory responsibility to ensure the lifts were safe to operate. The new block at the hospital in Pok Fu Lam was largely completed last year and staff have begun using the building. But the delay has prevented medical departments from moving in. Ho noted that Law, a veteran engineer with more than 20 years’ experience, had admitted in mitigation that he had “poorly communicated” with the contractor and underestimated the legal consequences and safety concerns. Taking into account his remorse, the magistrate accepted the probation officer’s recommendation and ordered 160 hours of community service. Last week, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu vowed that the government would pursue accountability, including among contractors, subcontractors, engineering personnel and other professionals.

title: China’s stealth fighters, critical minerals from lithium waste: 7 science highlights
description: From oil refining with reduced energy use to a self-powered neural device, here are some highlights from SCMP’s recent science reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on science from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. J-50 design team reveals leapfrog tech for China’s next-gen stealth fighters China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations. 2. Chinese scientists develop oil refining method that may cut energy use by 90% The new process, which works at a molecular level, may also produce higher value end-products, ranging from petrol to plastics. 3. Chinese team achieves fourfold leap in fuel-cell power Chinese scientists have developed a way to generate a fourfold increase in power output of hydrogen fuel cells, an advance that could broaden their use from road vehicles to space missions. 4. US, China trials suggest a single nanodrug shot might stop bad cholesterol forever Imagine swapping your daily cholesterol pill for a single injection that keeps “bad” cholesterol under control for a year, a decade – or even a lifetime. 5. World first: Chinese plant extracts critical rare metals from lithium waste A 500-tonne production line is up and running for rubidium and caesium, critical to advanced technology including aerospace and quantum computing. 6. I’ll write romance novels if AI solves all maths, Chinese Fields winner jokes Deng Yu, the 37-year-old Chinese mathematician who won the 2026 Fields Medal, has a backup plan if artificial intelligence puts him out of a job. 7. China’s self-powered neural device helps stroke survivors walk naturally Scientists have developed a lightweight, battery-free device that could help improve the mobility of people with difficulty walking, such as stroke survivors.

title: Marcos’ ‘existential battle’ with Sara Duterte intensifies in Philippines
description: The ⁠Senate lowers the vote threshold for conviction in Duterte’s impeachment trial as the president piles more pressure on his deputy.
content: The Philippine ⁠Senate, sitting as an impeachment ⁠court, on Wednesday lowered the number of votes needed to convict Vice-President Sara Duterte, reducing the threshold prosecutors must clear to secure a guilty verdict. The court ruled that only ‌senator-judges able to take part in the trial should be counted when determining the threshold for conviction. Four of the 24 senator-judges have been unable to take part in the proceedings and cannot vote. The decision means prosecutors now need 14 votes for a conviction, instead ⁠of the 16 votes required when all 24 are taking part. Some senators ‌had argued to keep the 16-vote threshold regardless of the four absences, which would have made it more challenging ‌to convict Duterte. The decision to lower the bar to convict Duterte is a pivotal moment in the trial, which has already been under way for 10 weeks and could stretch until December. She is accused of threatening to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr and his wife, misusing public funds and amassing unexplained wealth. She denies the allegations. “Marcos’ government is pushing the envelope with the cases against the minority senators to ensure that he wins this existential battle with Duterte,” said Ronald Llamas, who served as political affairs adviser during the presidency of Benigno Aquino. A loss for Duterte on this point increases the chances of her conviction, he said. Two Duterte-aligned senators, Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada, have both been arrested on corruption charges. Another staunch Senate ally, Ronald dela Rosa, is in hiding to avoid an international arrest warrant. And Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, is on extended medical leave while she faces an investigation over energy contracts. All have denied wrongdoing. Senate minority leader Alan Cayetano, who is also under scrutiny for past government projects, has called out the Marcos administration for pursuing “selective justice”. His office has responded that the cases against senators are based on evidence and they have the opportunity to challenge the charges in courts. The developments come amid a deepening power struggle ahead of the 2028 presidential election, where Duterte is an early favourite. While Marcos is ineligible for re-election because of term limits, the concern in his camp is that Duterte would turn the powers of the state against him and his allies if she wins. The rift has also complicated efforts to address the Southeast Asian nation’s slowing economic growth and elevated inflation. At least three more Duterte-aligned senators have legal troubles hanging over them. Senator Mark Villar and his sister Camille Villar are facing corruption charges related to their company’s water contracts. Senator Robin Padilla has been summoned to answer an obstruction of justice complaint for allegedly helping Dela Rosa escape in May. During the impeachment trial, prosecutors have repeatedly played a 2024 video of a furious Duterte saying that she feared for her life and had made arrangements for the killing of Marcos, his wife and cousin in the event she dies. Witnesses have also testified that Duterte’s aides have made unusually large cash withdrawals of about US$2 million each loaded into gym bags. They have also alleged the vice-president of using fictitious names to receive money intended for surveillance operations and then spent those funds on Christmas parties. Duterte’s lawyers have countered that she has been subjected to threats and harassment since her estrangement from Marcos, and that there was no irregularity in how the funds were spent. The vice-president has pledged to be “unbowed” by the impeachment trial, which she described as a “bloodbath and bludgeoning”. The defence team said it may appeal the Senate vote-eligibility issue. “If we see that our client’s rights are affected, we don’t deny that there’s a possibility that we will elevate this to the Supreme Court,” Duterte’s lawyer, Michael Poa, said last week.

title: Hong Kong’s Lydia Sham delivers on golden Asian Games promise to Exo member Kai
description: The 26-year-old attended a fan event where she met the K-pop star and says she became a professional athlete after seeing the band perform.
content: Hong Kong wushu athlete Lydia Sham Hui-yu said a gruelling training schedule allowed her to deliver on an Asian Games gold medal pledge she made to her idol, Exo boy band member Kai. On Tuesday, after winning the women’s changquan event to secure Hong Kong’s first gold of the Asian Games, the 26-year-old posted a video on social media sharing the medal ceremony and tagging the official accounts of South Korean boy band Exo and Kai. “I kept the promise I made to Kim Jong-in [Kai] at the fan sign [event] in July! I trained frantically just to make this happen,” she wrote in her caption. The video showed Sham meeting the K-pop star at a fan event, where Kai asked if performing the crown gesture from the band’s song “Crown” would help her win gold. Sham replied, “I’ll try my best” before Kai performed his signature crown dance move. The video then cut to Sham stepping on to the top of the podium, accompanied by English and Korean subtitles reading: “I kept my promise! I really got gold!” A day after posting the video, it had accumulated over 114,000 likes. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lydia🤍魚🐟🦈 (@lydia_sham) As a devoted fan of the band, Sham added that Exo had inspired her immensely, declaring she had reached the “pinnacle of fan success” by winning gold after meeting her idol. Sham said that a major reason she pursued a career as a professional athlete was seeing Exo perform on stage at a previous Asian Games. “It all started when they performed at the 2014 Asian Games opening ceremony – 12 years later, I stepped onto the podium!” she wrote. “Throughout my 13 years as a fan, I kept practising hard to get a chance to introduce myself to Exo in person and thank them for giving me the strength to grow stronger.” At the end of the video, Sham added that her competition outfit featured hexagonal patterns reminiscent of Exo’s logo. Following the popularity of her social media video, Sham revealed on Tuesday afternoon she had been interviewed by South Korean broadcaster SBS, writing it was surreal to appear on television in South Korea. “It’s so crazy, am I dreaming?” she wrote. “The SBS interview was insane. Recording a direct message to Exo was also crazy! Unlocked my first Korean interview, scared me to death. I’m going to faint; I have zero regrets in my fan journey!” Sham shared an update on Wednesday to let her followers know that SBS had informed her that Exo members were aware of her story. Following her victory, Sham also shared a photo holding her gold medal while displaying her Asian Games-themed nail art, captioned: “Showing off nail art this way beats 99.9 per cent of people! Thanks everyone for the support!” a post that was also widely popular. The wushu medal at this year’s event was the first for Sham across three editions of the Asian Games. Sham scored 9.713 points in the women’s changquan event at Aichi Prefectural Budokan on Monday, narrowly beating Macau’s Sou Cho-man, who scored 9.710. The Hongkonger won by just 0.003 points, with only 0.010 points separating the top four finishers. Indonesia’s Eugenia Diva Widodo placed third with 9.706, followed by Iran’s Zahra Kiani with 9.703. Sham was one of the city’s flag bearers for the opening ceremony of the Games, along with basketball player Ivan Yang, and she is eligible for a HK$1 million cash reward for her individual gold medal under the Jockey Club Athlete Incentive Awards Scheme.

title: Chinese banks, Ant International push instant cross-border digital yuan transfers
description: The Shanghai-to-Hong Kong settlements worth hundreds of millions of yuan bypassed traditional channels and could accelerate Beijing’s broader yuan strategy.
content: Two Chinese state-owned banks and Ant International have trialled cross-border digital yuan transfers worth hundreds of millions of yuan, marking the latest step in Beijing’s efforts to streamline settlements and promote wider international use of the digital yuan. The Shanghai branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) facilitated its first digital yuan transfer for Ant International to ICBC Asia, its Hong Kong subsidiary. The transaction from Shanghai to Hong Kong was completed within seconds, compared with the several days typically required for large cross-border transfers through traditional channels, domestic media outlet Financial News reported on Tuesday. Ant International is the Singapore-based arm of China’s Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post. Similarly, the Shanghai branch of China Construction Bank (CCB) also facilitated a digital yuan transfer worth hundreds of millions of yuan for Ant International to CCB Asia, the bank’s Hong Kong subsidiary, state-owned China Business Journal reported on Friday. “The cooperation focused on helping companies with overseas operations move funds more efficiently between their domestic and overseas accounts, while addressing challenges around speed and compliance in large-value cross-border transactions,” CCB’s Shanghai branch said, according to China Business Journal. “The initiative represents an exploration of how state-owned banks and fintech companies can work together to expand the use of the digital yuan in cross-border transactions, while offering a practical model for companies expanding overseas in areas such as fund transfers and cross-border settlement,” the bank added. The transfers come as Beijing continues to expand the digital yuan’s role in cross-border payments as part of its broader push to internationalise the currency, including through Project mBridge, a multilateral central bank digital currency platform led by China. In recent months, the platform has moved closer to broader commercial use among banks. One of the latest adopters is China’s Industrial Bank, which launched mBridge payment services for cross-border transactions with Macau, with the lender saying it also supports such settlements between the mainland and Hong Kong. Meanwhile, Bank of China said in July that its Shenzhen branch had used the platform to process a cross-border transfer of 11.3 billion yuan (US$1.68 billion), with the funds credited on the same day. As of June, mBridge’s cumulative transactions had exceeded 600 billion yuan, according to data from Bank of China. Separately, China has also developed the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), a Chinese alternative to Western-dominated settlement networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, commonly referred to as Swift. Both Project mBridge and CIPS are widely seen as part of Beijing’s broader effort to establish alternatives to traditional US dollar-centric payment networks, particularly amid persistent tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns about the potential weaponisation of the US dollar. On Monday, the People’s Bank of China pledged to steadily expand two-way access to financial markets, improve cross-border payment services and further ease the yuan’s international use to promote “high-level financial opening-up”. The pledge followed the central bank’s announcement earlier this month that it would expand bilateral currency swap agreements and local-currency settlements while improving CIPS.

title: Chinese EV battery giant CATL starts trial production at Hungarian factory
description: Analyst says development could see it secure massive orders from global marques such as BMW and Volkswagen.
content: Contemporary Amperex Technol­ogy Ltd (CATL) has cleared all regulatory hurdles for its mega factory in Hungary, a development that analysts expect will help the world’s largest producer of electric vehicle (EV) batteries extend its reach to international marques like BMW and Volkswagen. Production of battery cells at the €7.3 billion (US$8.35 billion) plant in Debrecen, the second-largest city in Hungary, began on Tuesday after it fulfilled all preconditions for a trial run, the company said. It added that mass production would start after production equipment and manufacturing processes were optimised and validated. The announcement came after months of delays as the plant faced protests due to local residents’ concerns about environmental and health risks. CATL said Hungarian government officials had confirmed after on-site inspections that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified earlier in the approval process. The Hungarian plant is of strategic importance to CATL’s internationalisation Gao Shen, independent analyst It had originally planned to begin production at the factory early this year. “The Hungarian plant is of strategic importance to CATL’s internationalisation, as it can secure massive orders from global carmakers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “It may also help offset CATL’s potential loss of market share in China.” The production base in Debrecen has a designed production capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours of batteries a year, enough to power 2 million electric cars, each with a driving range of 500km (311 miles). A year ago, CATL unveiled two specially designed battery packs for its European clients and said they would be manufactured in Hungary. The first pack was a long-life variant, usable for up to 12 years, that offers 758km (471 miles) of driving range, and the second was a fast-charging lithium-ion phosphate power pack that requires just 10 minutes of charging to drive up to 478km (297 miles). CATL’s sales outside mainland China climbed 54.8 per cent year on year to 87.1 billion yuan (US$13 billion) in the first half of this year, accounting for 31 per cent of its total revenue for the period. Hong Kong-listed shares of CATL slumped about 35 per cent from its year high in early June as mainland EV makers stepped up efforts to cut their reliance on the battery giant. In August, CATL delivered 32.5 GWh of EV batteries to its domestic clients, which represented a market share of 41.5 per cent, down from 42.3 per cent in July, according to data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance.

title: Youth arrests in Hong Kong rise 20%, driven by assault and criminal-damage cases
description: Hong Kong police chief says 1,580 young people aged 10 to 20 arrested between January and June, with many ‘exploited’ in debt collection crimes.
content: The number of young people arrested in Hong Kong in the first half of the year jumped by around 20 per cent, driven by cases of serious assault and criminal damage linked to debt collection activities. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming said on Wednesday that the force had arrested 1,580 young people aged between 10 and 20 from January to June, an increase of about 20 per cent year-on-year. Among them, 283 were arrested on suspicion of serious assault, representing a 47 per cent year-on-year increase, while 140 were apprehended for criminal damage, marking a rise of more than 50 per cent. In particular, 48 of them allegedly committed criminal damage as part of debt collection activities, compared with 18 in the same period last year. “We are aware that the majority of them had acted on impulse, instead of [making] premeditated attacks,” Chow said, noting that around 70 per cent of those arrested for alleged serious assault had acted without much deliberation. He added that many arrestees were “exploited” to commit criminal damage for quick money through debt collection, without realising the severe legal consequences. During the same period, 199 youths were arrested for scams and money laundering, a level similar to that of last year. Another 285 were arrested for drug-related offences, with 92 of them, or around 30 per cent, involving etomidate or “space oil”, a novel drug that was banned in Hong Kong last year. The figures were released alongside the launch of the force’s latest edition of a guide to fighting youth crimes for teachers and parents, which has been updated annually since it was first published in 2022. Chow said the booklet was renamed “Decoding Traps” to place more emphasis on preventive measures, encouraging teachers and parents to spot the signs of potential crimes by young people so they could intervene early. “Rather than having young people realise what they have done is wrong after committing a crime and being arrested, we would like to highlight pre-emptive moves as the first line of defence,” Chow said. The booklet features four topics: quick cash traps, online sexual grooming, teenage violence and novel drugs. It offers tips to teachers and parents to identify suspicious signs related to these illicit activities and advice on appropriate intervention. While it was important to prevent young people from committing crimes, Chow said it was also necessary to protect them from predators, as online sexual grooming had become a “global trend”. In online grooming, predators approach victims online and seek to win their trust by showing care, before persuading victims to share intimate pictures. The perpetrators then use the pictures to blackmail the victims for money or sexual acts. The government recently proposed legal changes that would criminalise the grooming of children and enable police officers to take early action before physical sexual offences are committed. “Criminalising this kind of activity would be very effective in terms of law enforcement,” Chow said, highlighting the importance of raising awareness among young people. He said police would adopt a “parallel” approach by investigating suspected grooming cases, while working with the social welfare and education sectors to step up publicity on protective measures.

title: Malaysians joke their way through Negeri Sembilan royal row
description: With two men claiming the throne and no legal exit in sight, commenters suggest nettle-bed endurance tests to end the fight.
content: Malaysians on social media are offering increasingly outlandish solutions to a months-long royal tussle in Negeri Sembilan state, from making rival claimants sleep on a bed of nettles for a week to putting the entire state through Islamic spiritual healing. The dispute has left Negeri Sembilan with two men claiming the throne, a state government at odds with the palace and no clear legal route to settle the fight. One social media user suggested reviving adat perpatih – the customary law of Negeri Sembilan – by subjecting ruler Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir and rival claimant Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar to the “stone mattress” test: seven days and seven nights on a stone covered with an intensely itchy variety of nettle, with whoever lasts the longest earning the throne. “Whoever can endure it becomes [the ruler],” the user wrote, adding that the idea “may look illogical, but it is a fact”. Another proposed dispensing with constitutional law altogether by carving up Negeri Sembilan, whose Malay name literally means “Nine States”, into “2x Negeri 4.5”. “Everyone wins,” the post read. Some went further, suggesting the “whole of Negeri Sembilan needs to be ruqyah”, referring to an Islamic practice of reciting Quranic verses and prayers for spiritual healing and protection. The jokes come amid a stand-off in Malaysia’s only state where the ruler is chosen by four traditional chiefs, known as the Undang Yang Empat, rather than inheriting the throne by birthright. The same royal feud already helped bring down the state’s previous Pakatan Harapan-Barisan Nasional government and force a snap election in August, after BN lawmakers withdrew support for then chief minister Aminuddin Harun over his handling of the dispute. Barisan Nasional then teamed up with former rival Perikatan Nasional for August’s election and the pair won 25 of the state’s 36 seats, while Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan won just 11. The latest confrontation began on Sunday, when Muhriz revoked the appointments of all 10 state executive councillors, accusing them of breaching their oaths after backing a disputed proclamation seeking to remove him. Chief Minister Ismail Lasim rejected the move the next day, maintaining that the councillors remained legally in office because he had neither been consulted nor advised the ruler to dismiss them. Anwar met Muhriz for about an hour on Monday evening, although no details of their discussion were released. The state government escalated the row on Tuesday by suspending its state secretary and legal adviser after the pair had resisted moves linked to recognising Nadzaruddin. Hours later, the Attorney General’s Chambers rejected the suspensions, arguing that the executive council had no legal power to discipline either official – a matter it said rested with the relevant service commissions. According to local media reports, a planned Wednesday morning meeting between Ismail, his executive councillors and Nadzaruddin was cancelled on security advice after neither side appeared at the scheduled venue.

title: AI trade outlook brightens on falling oil and Meta’s Muse agent ahead of Xi-Trump meeting
description: Nasdaq-100 hits record high while chip stocks in China and South Korea rebound, with investors betting that AI earnings can weather higher interest rates.
content: The global artificial intelligence trade is staging a comeback, as a confluence of falling oil prices, Meta Platforms’ launch of a new agentic tool and anticipation surrounding the China-US leadership summit reignite investor interest in technology stocks. The Nasdaq-100 Index – where tech firms make up nearly 70 per cent of the 100 companies featured – hit an all-time high on Tuesday, surpassing the previous record set in June. In Asia, China’s chip-heavy Star Market 50 Index and South Korea’s Kospi gauge, which is weighted considerably towards memory chipmakers, have been bouncing back since July sell-offs. The shift appears to mark a reversal in negative sentiment surrounding AI stocks, which had been battered by inflationary fears and calls from some US tech companies to slow the development of new models due to safety concerns. Market sentiment pivoted as oil’s retreat below US$100 a barrel eased inflationary pressure and as Meta’s Muse agent reinforced demand across AI supply chains. Meanwhile, positive rhetoric from a preparatory trade talk before this week’s sit-down between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump has fuelled optimism for a de-escalation of geopolitical tensions. “Lower oil and lower yields reopened the duration trade,” said Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “Meta’s agent story pushes AI beyond GPUs towards a wider compute trade built around inference, CPUs, cloud and digital labour.” The regaining of market leadership by tech stocks underscores investor belief that the AI sector will withstand last week’s interest-rate increase in the United States and continue to sustain resilient earnings growth. The US Federal Reserve’s first rate hike in three years prompted caution in sectors outside technology, amid mounting concerns about squeezed profit margins linked to higher financing costs. The retreat in oil prices amid diplomatic efforts to resolve the US-Israel war on Iran boosted risk appetite by alleviating investor jitters over further rate increases by the Fed. Crude fell for a sixth straight day on Wednesday after Trump said US officials had “very good” meetings with Iranian representatives. Meta’s 11 per cent surge in share price on Monday further validated the AI trade following the release of its Muse agent, which automates digital tasks on a user’s behalf. Muse downloads have soared, pushing it to the top of app charts. The Muse frenzy “suggests markets read Muse as confirming sustained inference and server demand, not just another GPU headline”, said Gary Dugan, CEO of financial services firm The Global CIO Office. Investors are now turning their attention to the gathering between Xi and Trump in hopes that the world’s two largest economies might extend a tariff truce and reach agreements on AI advancement or even the Middle East conflict. “Preparatory meetings between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng suggest that some progress has already been made on trade,” said Robert Gilhooly, an economist at Aberdeen Investments. “That could pave the way for lower tariffs on some non-sensitive goods, while China may offer to buy more US farm products, energy exports and Boeing aircraft.”

title: Chinese maker of robot-vacuum sensors launches Hong Kong IPO, undeterred by US ban
description: Camsense Technologies aims to raise about US$87 million in a Hong Kong listing backed by carmaker BYD.
content: Shenzhen Camsense Technologies, a maker of spatial sensors for robotic vacuum cleaners, launched a Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO) that aims to raise about HK$680 million (US$86.7 million), despite headwinds from Washington’s recent import ban on foreign-made vacuum robots. “The export and procurement for our existing client products remain normal, with potential disruption limited to new product development schedules,” Camsense co-founder Zhou Kun said about the ban’s impact. “We have maintained close communication with clients. Currently, our research and development progress and order intake remain unaffected.” In late July, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) added foreign-produced “advanced robotic devices”, including robotic vacuum cleaners, to its so-called Covered List, blocking new models from obtaining the equipment authorisation required for US import and sale. Camsense plans to sell 11.58 million shares at HK$58.85 each, according to a stock exchange filing on Tuesday. The shares are scheduled to start trading on September 30. Carmaker BYD and Shanghai-listed Jiaxing Zmax Optech, both Camsense suppliers, were the deal’s cornerstone investors, together taking up HK$110 million, or 16 per cent of the base share sale, with a six-month lock-up period, the prospectus showed. It plans to use proceeds from the IPO for research and development, to enhance its manufacturing capabilities and for working capital and general corporate purposes. China’s robotic vacuum cleaner industry has expanded rapidly, with leading brands such as Ecovacs Robotics, Dreame Technology and Beijing Roborock Technology selling products globally. As a maker of lidar (light detection and ranging) and line laser sensors – components machines use to sense their surroundings – Camsense has benefited from this momentum. The Shenzhen-based company had no direct sales to the US, but several clients sold vacuum cleaners and other devices containing its sensors there, according to its prospectus. To diversify its revenue, Camsense said it plans to expand into robots for yard work and pool cleaning, as well as humanoid robots. The company has delivered samples to multiple manufacturers and received intent orders from two pool robot makers and one yard robot manufacturer, Zhou said. China International Capital and Guosen Securities (HK) Capital are the joint sponsors.

title: Did North Korea’s missile launches target the Xi-Trump summit agenda?
description: Pyongyang typically holds such tests ahead of major global diplomatic and military events to maximise attention and leverage.
content: North Korea could be using missile tests to take its denuclearisation off the US-China summit agenda and drive home its demands for recognition as a nuclear power as a prerequisite for talks with Washington, according to analysts. On Sunday, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan, or East Sea, which, according to South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, were detected three hours apart, with the first flying about 450km (280 miles), while the second travelled more than 600km. The missile launches were confirmed by North Korean media on Tuesday as the test of a new type of its hypersonic missile and observed by North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Sunday’s tests came eight days after North Korea fired a mix of multiple short-range ballistic missiles, attack drones, tactical cruise missiles and large-calibre multiple rocket launchers on September 12 – a day after the Freedom Edge military drill between the US, South Korea and Japan ended. North Korea typically launches missile tests ahead of major global diplomatic and military events, seeking to send a political and military signal to maximise international attention and leverage. Sunday’s launch came a few days before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US for a summit with US President Donald Trump on Thursday. North Korea has made similar moves in the past. Days before the Xi-Trump summit in Busan, South Korea, in October last year, North Korea test-fired hypersonic short-range ballistic missiles and sea-to-surface cruise missiles. Trump has repeatedly said he wants to restart talks with Kim before the end of this year and has apparently made efforts towards the goal. In August, Trump ordered the joint US-South Korea military drill Ulchi Freedom Shield to end six days early, shortening the planned 11-day exercise to just five. He criticised the annual war games for their financial cost and called them “totally inappropriate and hostile” towards Pyongyang. Yet, Pyongyang has refused to back down in its drive to advance its military and nuclear build-up, maintaining that Washington’s recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state is a prerequisite for any bilateral talks. According to Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, the missile tests essentially sought to block cooperation between the US and China regarding North Korean denuclearisation. For Pyongyang, whether “even a single line” regarding the denuclearisation appeared in the statement after the Xi-Trump summit would be the focal point, Kang said. “[North Korea] is asserting its status as a nuclear-armed state, highlighting that they possess both nuclear and missile capabilities – specifically pointing to the recent short-range ballistic missile tests – to argue that denuclearisation is off the table,” he added. “They are steering the narrative to insist that any future negotiations between North Korea and the US must focus on arms control instead.” Lami Kim, Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security and defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said that through the missile tests, North Korea might have sought to grab attention before the Xi-Trump summit as well as a respond to recent US-led military exercises in the region. “If the United States and China refrain from condemning North Korea’s recent missile tests or from reaffirming their commitment to North Korea’s denuclearisation, that alone could constitute a diplomatic gain for Pyongyang by helping it further consolidate its status as a nuclear-armed state,” Kim added. While the fact sheet issued after the Xi-Trump summit in Beijing in May said the two leaders “confirmed their shared goal to denuclearise North Korea”, Beijing has recently strengthened diplomatic and defence ties with Pyongyang, seen by some as a quiet endorsement of North Korea’s nuclear position. During his visit to North Korea in June, Xi told Kim that both sides should improve exchanges in military affairs but did not mention denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula, marking a sharp contrast from his previous visit in 2019. China also omitted the phrase “support for the denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula” from its arms control white paper, released in November last year. According to Lim Eul-chul, professor of North Korean studies at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies, Kyungnam University, North Korea’s military moves are driven by sophisticated political and diplomatic calculations designed to “shake the major diplomatic landscape of East Asia” and intended to show their military and political standing and presence between the US and China. “The best-case scenario for North Korea would be the official removal of the existing ‘North Korean denuclearisation’ framework from the dialogue between the US and Chinese leaders,” Lim said. Patrick Cronin, the Asia-Pacific security chair at the Washington-based think tank Hudson Institute, said many issues were likely to be discussed at the White House summit, including North Korea. Officials might also discuss logistics for a potential Trump-Kim meeting, possibly on the sidelines of the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in November, he added. “The firing of ballistic missiles … is one way Kim shows even all major powers his intention to stand against compromises over his nuclear weapons,” Cronin said. “His determination to keep building nuclear weapons remains an obstacle to productive discussions with Trump, should another face-to-face meeting be possible.” Troy Stangarone, a visiting senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America, described North Korea as “playing hard to get”, with Pyongyang likely to believe it “holds the cards” and did not need to meet with Washington. Still, Stangarone said, “playing too hard to get means that Pyongyang may miss an opportunity to cut a deal that would give it options should the geopolitics in Moscow or Beijing turn disadvantageous for it”.

title: History of mooncake moulds and their designs, and those preserving the craft
description: Mooncake artistry flourished during the Ming and Qing dynasties, carved onto wooden moulds depicting flowers, birds and even deities.
content: As symbolic of the Mid-Autumn Festival as the legend of Chang’e and the Jade Rabbit, mooncakes have a history dating back centuries, with their first mention during the Song dynasty (960-1279) in author Wu Zimu’s Dreaming of Grain. Early mooncakes were a far cry from the creative and intricate designs we see today. The rudimentary cakes were flat and round, with a thin outer crust and fillings such as lotus seed paste or the auspicious five kernels. During the Yuan dynasty (1279-1368), emperor-to-be Zhu Yuanzhang and his adviser Liu Bowen came up with the idea of placing hidden messages inside mooncakes that called for a revolution to overthrow the ruling Mongol Empire. Mooncakes continued to rise in popularity. During the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) eras, mooncake artistry took shape, with intricate designs depicting flowers, birds and even deities commonly adorning the snacks. These auspicious symbols were carved into wooden mooncake moulds, some of which survive today as tangible links to the past. Designs that are not as common in modern times include depictions of the Eight Immortals and the Fu Lu Shou (also known as the three stellar gods, or Sanxing). Traditionally crafted from pear or jujube wood – which are dense and suitable for detailed carving – moulds are still made by a dwindling number of craftsmen today. There are more than a dozen steps before the designs are etched into the wood, including pattern drawing, crack removal, planing and hole chiselling. Completed moulds are air-dried for a minimum of two years before being used. The complex process of mould crafting – for both mooncakes and other traditional Chinese snacks such as almond cakes – was inscribed as part of the provincial-level intangible cultural heritage list for China’s Guangdong province in 2018. The value of mooncakes Today, mooncakes are ubiquitous in Hong Kong, with varieties available at many different price points. In the past, however, they were exclusively expensive and viewed as a high-value gift rather than a snack for personal consumption. Many people would put money into so-called mooncake clubs – essentially paying monthly instalments for Mid-Autumn Festival mooncake gift sets. In her essay “Kee Wah Bakery’s Mooncake Packaging Makeover in the 1990s”, published in the 2014 book Food & Material Culture, food writer Jennifer Wong wrote that the design and packaging of mooncakes had become “an increasingly important medium for expressing each bakery’s identity”. Many of Hong Kong’s high-end Chinese banquet restaurants used to be known for their mooncakes. One such restaurant was Tak Yu Restaurant in Yau Ma Tei, which opened in the 1920s and closed in 2012. Its original mooncake menus, gift boxes and moulds are on display at Artellex Galerie in Cheung Sha Wan until September 27 as part of the gallery’s month-long nostalgic food-themed exhibition, “After Taste”. The items were loaned from a private collector. “The collector acquired this set of moulds directly from Tak Yu Restaurant when it closed down, preserving pieces of Hong Kong’s culinary history,” says Artellex’s founder, Alex Chan. Alongside a few well-preserved wooden mooncake moulds bearing the restaurant’s name, the gallery also displays various intricate moulds used for shaping mooncake dough offcuts into whimsical “biscuits” resembling mythical beings and animals. “Piglet cakes and Buddha cakes were side products made from leftover mooncake dough and filling, given as free gifts to customers buying mooncake sets,” says Artellex’s Dorothy Wong. “That’s why side products didn’t have prices listed on the order forms. They were basically like a zero-waste baking tradition.” The moulds on display may well be some of the last of their kind, as companies increasingly turn to factory-made mooncakes rather than handmade versions. “Not many people make them any more,” Wong says. “Demand is low, and a traditional wooden mould lasts for decades.” Some of the vintage moulds on display have a soft shine, which Wong says has been imparted by mooncake dough oils over years of use. In others, a dull finish and telltale cracks in the wood speak volumes about the time that has passed since they were last used. The accumulation of oil makes it easier to release the pastries over time, Wong says. “It works like seasoning a cast-iron pan.” A modern chef holds on to tradition In the past, mooncake mould carvers had to spend hours chipping away at wood to create unique designs for their clients. Today, 3D printing and other technologies have made manufacturing quick and easy. However, mooncake purists see this as no replacement for tradition. “Wooden moulds are relatively blunter, meaning the mooncake’s pattern lines come out smoother and more rounded,” says Lo Kin-ming, the head dim sum chef at Lung King Heen at the Four Seasons Hong Kong. “If you use plastic moulds, the lines are sharper, and the mooncakes tend to crack along the edges.” He adds that traditional wooden moulds will always have two air vents. “If air isn’t released, when you press dough in, the air pressure traps it inside and you can’t knock the mooncake out,” he explains. “Sometimes when you knock a mooncake out and see a tiny bump on it, that’s actually caused by the air vent. But when we see that, we usually just pluck it off.” In terms of traditional designs, Lo says the simpler the better, and names the classic “full moon and blooming flowers” design as among his favourites. “If you ask me, mooncake moulds shouldn’t have overly bizarre patterns,” he says. “The more lines you add, as soon as a line gets pulled, the mooncake won’t look nice.” Lung King Heen’s handmade mooncakes feature intricate lines that form the restaurant’s name in traditional Chinese script. The mould was commissioned to Hong Kong’s Man Kee Chopping Board, a family-run business on Shanghai Street in Yau Ma Tei that sells all manner of mooncake moulds – some even featuring popular cartoon characters. Although he insists on using traditional moulds at Lung King Heen, Lo says home bakers can use plastic moulds. “If you knock a traditional mould on a home dining table a couple of times, it’ll be disastrous,” he laughs. “You’ll crack the table! Whereas with a hand-press mould, even if you press a bit harder, you can control it. With a traditional wooden mould, when you knock the wood, the surface area is fixed, and every mooncake has to be tapped out with force. “You learn after making a lot of them.”

title: Exiled opposition leader tries to enter Venezuela as Rodriguez meets Trump in US
description: Maria Corina Machado blocked from returning as New York talks mark first encounter since Nicolas Maduro’s capture.
content: Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado made three attempts over a 24-hour span to return home, but was unable to complete the journey. Machado sought to travel from Panama to Venezuela by different routes, according to a person with direct knowledge of her plans. The attempts came as acting President Delcy Rodriguez visited New York for the United Nations General Assembly, where she met with US President Donald Trump. The efforts included plans to travel by boat and to fly to the Caribbean islands of Aruba and Curaçao before continuing by sea, the person said. Colombia’s NTN24 first reported the attempts earlier Tuesday. The failed attempts by Venezuela’s most popular politician underscore the obstacles she faces as she seeks a role in the US-backed political transition following Nicolas Maduro’s capture in January. They also highlight the divergent paths of Machado and Rodriguez as Washington deepens its engagement with the acting president while keeping its distance from the opposition leader. The growing US ties with Rodriguez are also testing its stated commitment to a democratic transition in Venezuela. Rodriguez met with Trump on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN gathering, according to a White House official. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also attended. The encounter was the most visible sign yet of the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas. Trump has recognised Rodriguez’s authority, eased sanctions and deepened economic ties with her government, most recently through a major oil agreement. In his UN speech, Trump highlighted his administration’s cooperation with Rodriguez’s government and cast the oil deal as a reward for the US raid on Caracas that led to Maduro’s capture, declaring: “To the victor belong the spoils”. Machado’s daughter, Ana Corina Sosa, said Tuesday that her mother was actively trying to return but acknowledged that the process was complicated. “Right now she is trying to return, at this moment,” Sosa told NTN24 in New York, adding that there were “many forces” involved and that returning was not as simple as boarding a plane. Sosa spoke after accepting the 2026 Concordia Leadership Award on her mother’s behalf in New York. Machado has made several previous unsuccessful attempts to return, including in June when her plane was forced to divert. In an interview with the Wall Street Journal published last week, she said she was prepared to leave at a moment’s notice and could enter Venezuela by land, sea or air. It was not immediately clear whether the latest attempts were coordinated with Washington or whether Machado had received security guarantees. Trump has said he does not oppose her returning to Venezuela. Rodriguez’s meeting with Trump marks a remarkable reversal for Maduro’s former vice-president, who was removed from the US Treasury’s sanctions list on April 1. Maduro remains in federal custody in New York facing US narcoterrorism and drug-trafficking charges. Rodriguez arrived in New York on Monday, becoming the first Venezuelan leader to attend the UN General Assembly in person since Maduro in 2018. She met with UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres and representatives of the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and Inter-American Development Bank as her government seeks to rebuild ties with international financial institutions. Her visit and meeting with Trump have drawn opposition from some Venezuelans, with protests called in New York and Caracas. Machado’s return would add another complication to the political transition. She was barred from taking part in the 2024 presidential election, and her stand-in was later deprived of victory in a vote widely regarded as fraudulent. While Machado herself has been blocked, Rodriguez’s government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Machado’s closest allies. Machado went into hiding after the disputed election, saying she feared for her life as Maduro’s government targeted opposition leaders. She left Venezuela late last year in a clandestine operation to collect her Nobel Peace Prize and subsequently met Trump and other senior US officials in Washington. She has remained largely in Panama since her failed efforts to return in June.

title: Asian Games, day 4: Tsang adds silver, Kan bronze as city’s medal tally grows
description: Tsang Yee-ting finally earns karate medal at fourth Asian Games, and Natalie Kan recovers to claim bronze in women’s 100m butterfly.
content: Hong Kong karate veteran Tsang Yee-ting finally stepped onto an Asian Games podium on Wednesday, taking silver in the women’s 50kg kumite final, and adding another medal to the city’s growing tally. There was success in the swimming pool too, with Natalie Kan Cheuk-tung taking bronze in the women’s 100m butterfly, while earlier, the men had won bronze in the team kata. In wushu, Leung Yu-hong beat Bintang Reindra Nada Guitara of Indonesia 2-1 to reach the men’s 60kg final, where he will face off against Tang Sishuo of China for gold on Thursday. Chan Tsz-ching, however, lost 2-0 to Sogand Sinkaeichetan of Iran in the women’s 52kg semi-final and had to settle for a bronze. The day’s work took Hong Kong’s medal tally to 16 overall, with karate and swimming so far providing most of the hardware. The Games in Nagoya are Tsang’s fourth, and she stepped out at the Toyohashi City General Gymnasium with only the competition in mind. The 34-year-old quickly dispatched Chung Ya-chi of Chinese Taipei 6-0 before reaching the title fight after seeing off Filipino Marie June Adriano 5-4 in the semi-final. Neither Tsang nor her opponent, Shahmalarani Chandran, managed to score a point in the three-minute bout but the four judges – from Japan, Iran, Turkmenistan and Vietnam – awarded the victory to the Malaysian by decision. “I’m really happy,” Tsang said. “When I came here, I didn’t set myself a goal. I just wanted to enjoy the competition. I’ve achieved what I wanted to do.” Tsang’s teammates had earlier won the first medal of the session, beating Chinese Taipei 3-2 in the bronze-medal bout in the men’s team kata. After finishing fourth in Hangzhou three years ago, the bronze was Howard Hung Ho-wai’s second in a matter of days after his success in the individual tournament. “It’s like a dream,” he said. “You can’t imagine. Before, I never got one medal in an Asian Games. Never, never, ever. But now, I have got two in one of the hugest events in Asia.” Hung said he and his teammates, Tang Yu-hin and Li Chi-kong, had given a “high performance”. “Of course, we made little mistakes ourselves,” Hung added. “We know that, but we controlled it and kept our calm. It’s not perfect, but still excellent.” Elsewhere, the city’s squash players began their bid for success, and Tomato Ho Tze-lok, Lau Tsz-kwan and Henry Leung Chi-hin all reached the second round after convincing wins. In the mixed doubles of the table tennis, Wong Chun-ting and Doo Hoi-kem eased into the quarter-finals, where they will face India pair Manush Shah and Diya Chitale.

title: South Korea wants free, unlimited AI – but is society ready?
description: Seoul’s roll-out of free artificial intelligence for everyone is set to shake up classrooms, careers and crime – for better or worse.
content:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung is launching an “AI for All” initiative that will hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence (AI) – integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily life.
The government already has a 10 trillion South Korean won (HK$56.6 billion) AI budget for the current financial year and has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.
A beta version is set to launch soon this month.
It will give citizens free, unlimited access to general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by the country’s telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent by the government.
From next year, officials envision the temporary trial will become a permanent taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.
To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear marking of synthetic content.
Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked as a technical watchdog to evaluate pitfalls and ensure public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.
South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers alongside the United States and China.
But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting its consequences: automation eliminating jobs, a surge in deepfake crimes and a generation’s reading scores declining.
The number of working young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank. It estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation.
But South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem from criminal misuse. The Nth Room case of 2020 and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024. But police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.
Won Eun-ji, director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa. She has documented how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.
And in schools, educators protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll out AI-powered textbooks.
AI short-circuits the learning process, said Song Keun-sang, one of the educators who protested. “It simply gives you the answers,” the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

title: Beatings, electric shocks, sexual violence: women endure torture in Myanmar prisons
description: Human Rights Watch said detainees routinely experienced systemic abuse and life-threatening medical neglect.
content: Female prisoners in Myanmar are subjected to widespread torture, sexual violence and life-threatening medical neglect, Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday, underlining the chronic ill-treatment of thousands of detainees in the war-torn nation. Since the military seized power in a February 2021 coup, a protracted civil war ‌has gripped the impoverished Southeast Asian nation, devastating several regions and killing about 100,000 while displacing more than 3.5 million. In a report, the New York-based rights group said more than 6,600 women, including former leader Aung San Suu Kyi and 640 children, are among the more than 30,000 political prisoners detained since the coup. “Women who have been detained as political prisoners in Myanmar paint a deeply disturbing picture of a prison system in which suffering and neglect ⁠are both deliberate and routine,” said Bryony Lau, the group’s Asia deputy director. A spokesperson for Myanmar’s military-backed government, which took office ‌after a widely criticised election held between 2025 and early this year that allowed former junta leader Min Aung Hlaing to become president, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Prison ‌authorities beat some prisoners with sticks, chains, metal pipes and catapults, with some subjected to electric shocks, cigarette ⁠burns, prolonged stress positions ⁠and sexual violence, the group said. Its report drew on interviews with 17 former female detainees, comprising activists, journalists, aid and healthcare workers, members of their ‌families and lawyers, conducted in 2025 and 2026. The former detainees said they were prosecuted under multiple criminal code provisions, including a post-coup law to punish opposition and dissent ‌and a ‌sweeping counterterrorism law, according to the rights group. Reuters could not independently verify the accounts, but they echo a 2025 report ‌by United Nations investigators. The UN report documented torture in Myanmar detention facilities, enumerating “beatings, electric shocks, strangulation, gang rape, burning of sexual ⁠body parts and other forms of sexual violence”. At least 74 political prisoners aged between 18 and 35 have died in detention ⁠since the coup, some due to alleged inadequate medical treatment and harsh interrogation, Reuters reported in January. Prison authorities consistently block access to necessary medical care for serious chronic and acute conditions, former prisoners told the rights group, ‌with pregnant women also denied such access, ‌with some left to give birth inside their cells. “There was no ultrasound so there was no way to estimate the due date,” one former prisoner told Human Rights Watch, describing how her water broke at midnight but a letter to refer her to a hospital only arrived at 10am. “Chains were put back on my feet right after the delivery.”

title: Hong Kong rejects EU report’s claims on freedoms as ‘unfounded and biased’
description: Hong Kong government says the report misrepresents national security laws, ignores protections for rights and applies double standards.
content: The Hong Kong government has rejected an annual European Union report alleging that the administration is undermining the city’s fundamental freedoms, calling its claims “unfounded and biased”. The more than 4,500-word statement, issued early on Wednesday, followed the publication on Tuesday of the EU’s 2025 annual report on Hong Kong. The report was jointly issued by the European Commission and the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, Kaja Kallas. It highlighted national security trials involving opposition activists, including media tycoon Jimmy Lai Chee-ying and Joshua Wong Chi-fung, as well as the disbandment of the Democratic Party ahead of the second “patriots-only” Legislative Council election, among other issues. “The [Hong Kong] government strongly urges the EU to respect facts, abide by international law and basic norms governing international relations, and immediately stop its long-arm jurisdiction and interference in Hong Kong matters, which are purely China’s internal affairs,” a government spokesman said in the statement. The spokesman said the administration “strongly disapproved of and rejected the unfounded and biased content against various aspects of [Hong Kong] in the so-called annual report on Hong Kong”, adding that the city was an inalienable part of China and enjoyed a high degree of autonomy under the “one country, two systems” principle. He added that the implementation of the national security law and related legislation had effectively safeguarded national security, restored stability and social order, and provided a foundation for developments in Hong Kong’s economy, social life and other areas. The spokesman said the EU and its member states had also continuously enacted and amended laws in the name of national security or counterterrorism, with harsh provisions “ubiquitous”. “The EU disregards its own broad and stringent laws and regulations, repeatedly distorts and confounds right and wrong, unscrupulously smears the laws for safeguarding national security in [Hong Kong], which were strictly enacted according to its actual circumstances, continues to harbour biased comments against relevant laws, which is typical hypocrisy with double standards,” he said. The statement also asserted that constitutional rights, press freedom and academic independence remained protected, although they were subject to standard legal boundaries and the principles of “responsible journalism”. “Contrarily, 14 of the 27 countries in the EU were involved in the scandal for using the ‘Pegasus’ spyware to monitor media and citizens. They have absolutely no right to make absurd and fact-twisting comments on the issue of press freedom. The so-called report abuses press freedom as an excuse to break the law, again exposing the EU’s biased stance and double standards all along,” it said. The EU report said that Hong Kong’s national security proceedings placed the city’s rule of law under “severe strain”, pointing to considerable delays, prolonged pretrial detentions, the repeated use of solitary confinement, adjudication by hand-picked judges and the absence of juries in some high-profile national security trials. It also detailed the extraterritorial reach of the national security law, referring to arrest warrants with bounties issued for 34 overseas activists, including a European citizen. The report also cited the prosecution of Kwok Yin-sang, father of wanted activist Anna Kwok Fung-yee, under the Article 23 legislation. On the political front, the EU said the remaining space for political pluralism had continued to shrink as the remaining opposition groups – the Democratic Party and the League of Social Democrats – were disbanded under heavy political pressure. “The erosion of Hong Kong’s high degree of autonomy and of the fundamental freedoms and rights of the people of Hong Kong continued, despite China’s legal obligation to maintain them until at least 2047,” it said. The government spokesman defended the city’s independent judicial power and due process, saying high-profile national security trials were conducted strictly according to the evidence and law, without political interference. He also defended the revamp of the electoral system. “There is no single model of democracy in the world. The 27 member states of the EU each have different electoral systems and political traditions, which fully demonstrates that the forms in which democracy is implemented are inherently diverse,” he said.
