The Legislative Council also issued a statement expressing “strong dissatisfaction and opposition” to what it called false and biased content in the EU report, condemning it for distorting facts and smearing the city’s national security laws. A Legco spokesman rejected allegations of democratic backsliding, maintaining that the revamped “patriots-only” electoral overhaul ensured broad representation and balanced participation. He added that under the new electoral system, Legco had moved past its previous legislative paralysis and returned to “effective governance”.

title: Coach who slapped boy, 8, at Hong Kong training camp spared criminal charges
description: Court imposes three-year good behaviour bond on Zhao Yiqun, 51, after she was also accused of ordering boy to stand under hot sun at camp.
content: A coach accused of slapping an eight-year-old boy and ordering him to stand under the hot sun during a training camp in Hong Kong has been spared from criminal prosecution after she agreed to a three-year good behaviour bond. Chief Magistrate Victor So Wai-tak on Wednesday imposed the bond on Zhao Yiqun, 51, who faced two child abuse charges after she was alleged to have mistreated the boy during a training programme at the Jockey Club Ming Fai Camp, located on Cheung Chau island, on August 8, 2024. Zhao had originally been required to appear at Eastern Court to state her plea for the two charges – one for ill-treatment or neglect by those in charge of a child and another for assault by a person caring for a minor. But her lawyer told So that the parties had reached an agreement and that the Department of Justice would not continue the prosecution. According to court documents, Zhao, a sports coach, led a group of six children to a four-day training camp. On the second day, the boy hid behind a door in a room after being bullied by other participants. Zhao scolded him for hiding and causing trouble for those who had to look for him. The boy said that when Zhao found him, she slapped his right cheek once. Later, when the group was taking an archery class, the boy was not allowed to join, with Zhao telling him to stand in the playground for 15 to 25 minutes. He told his mother, who subsequently held a meeting with Zhao. During the meeting, Zhao admitted that she had hit the child’s back but denied slapping him. The mother reported the case to police. So told the defendant that a good behaviour bond meant she must not commit any criminal acts of a similar nature in the next three years, or she would have to pay HK$2,000 (US$255) and face a more severe penalty. The bind-over money, known as recognisance, is an amount a defendant promises to pay if he or she breaks the law again during the term of the order. Zhao accepted the bind-over order.

title: Malaysia’s local acts feel left out of live music boom: ‘missing middle’
description: Artists question efforts to develop local talent, highlighting ‘worrying trend’ of global stars with no Malaysian opening act.
content: Kuala Lumpur is making it easier and cheaper to bring international music stars to the city, hoping that a bigger concert calendar can help Malaysia capture more of Southeast Asia’s booming live-music economy. But as more global acts come to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysian musicians are asking whether the concert boom is creating more opportunities for local artists too. Fuad Alhabshi of Malaysian rock band Kyoto Protocol said local bands once routinely benefited when major international acts came through Kuala Lumpur, including opportunities to play support slots. His band has opened for Muse, Death Cab for Cutie and The Killers. “Of late, I feel there has been a worrying trend of foreign acts opting not to have a local opening act,” he said. Fuad said venues that could accommodate crowds of between 200 and 500 people were disappearing, creating what he described as a “missing middle” for Malaysian musicians trying to graduate to larger stages. Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh has argued that the city’s booming concert calendar shows a strong demand for live entertainment. According to Communications Ministry figures, Malaysia hosted more than 450 concerts nationwide last year, up from 408 in 2024, 335 in 2023 and 104 in 2022. The live-events industry contributed nearly US$422 million to the economy in 2025. “This shows that there’s a real appetite for concerts here,” Yeoh said in May. Live Nation Malaysia expects Kuala Lumpur to host 25 international music performances across six major venues throughout 2026, attracting more than 500,000 fans from Malaysia and across the region. But Fuad said the problem was bigger than a lack of suitable venues for smaller acts. He said stagnant wages and limited disposable income forced concertgoers to become increasingly selective, particularly as expensive international tours competed for their entertainment budgets. “In the end, I think it still falls back to the structurally low disposable income of the median Malaysian,” he said. For Indonesian punk band Dongker, Kuala Lumpur already has many of the ingredients needed to become a regional music hub, being affordable and easy to reach from neighbouring countries. “I think it is very possible,” the Bandung-based band said in a statement, pointing to Malaysia’s location at the heart of Southeast Asia and its proximity to Indonesia, the region’s largest music market. The band added that Kuala Lumpur’s cost of living was low enough for audiences to comfortably cover food, accommodation and transport on top of concert tickets. But what looks like an attractive destination at first glance becomes more complex on closer inspection. Dongker, currently in Malaysia for a mini tour, said cross-border movement between the Malaysian and Indonesian music scenes was already well established, especially among independent and underground musicians. The band pointed to acts such as Daighila, Piri Reis, Moneybag and Pasca Sini, all of whom have performed in Indonesia, with Indonesian bands making the reverse trip just as often. Dongker said Malaysian musicians including Noh Salleh, Masdo and Yuna had built audiences in Indonesia, adding that Singapore-born Malaysian rapper Alyph had also made inroads. “Malaysia is one of the most accessible countries for alternative and indie musicians from around the world,” the band said, adding “Malaysia’s music ecosystem will grow quickly.” Kuala Lumpur is trying to break into an increasingly competitive regional market. Singapore has already established itself as a leading Southeast Asian stop for global artists, with Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Ed Sheeran and Mayday drawing tens of thousands of visitors to the city state in 2024, proving the sector’s economic potential. Bangkok and Jakarta are also vying for a share of international bookings. Turning up the incentives Malaysia has responded with a package of federal incentives spearheaded by the Communications Ministry. Under its Concerts and Events in Malaysia Incentive (Cemi) programme, organisers of qualifying large-scale events attracting more than 15,000 attendees can claim back up to 30 per cent of eligible Malaysian expenditure, capped at US$368,000. The scheme, administered by MyCreative Ventures, is designed to stimulate the local economy and attract international acts. To qualify, productions must spend at least 20 per cent of eligible expenditure locally and ensure Malaysians make up at least 30 per cent of their crew. Organisers can claim an additional US$24,500 for featuring local artists if ticket sales exceed 60 per cent of capacity 30 days before the scheduled event. Alan Foo and Johnson Lowe, the chairman and deputy chairman of the Arts, Live Festivals and Events Association, have lauded Cemi as a sign of growing alignment between government and industry. “This grant gives our industry the momentum to do just that with structure, vision and urgency,” Foo said at the scheme’s launch in April 2025. The ministry has also overhauled regulations governing foreign performances under its Puspal Guidelines 6.0, revising blackout dates, speeding up approvals for smaller events and introducing pre-approval requirements for foreign artists’ promotions and ticket sales. Local councils have followed suit: Kuala Lumpur City Hall has halved the security deposit for foreign concerts to US$3,680 while keeping the cap at US$2,450 for local concerts. But Fuad questioned whether the growing investment and attention directed towards international performers was being matched by efforts to develop Malaysian artists, noting that major record labels were increasingly tilted towards promoting foreign acts. One way to redress that imbalance would be to harness the growing presence of Southeast Asian musicians in Malaysia to promote cross-border exchanges, he suggested. But this would only be a success “if the domestic industry is able to take that experience and put a considerable amount of effort into developing home-grown capabilities across the value chain”, Fuad said, pointing not only to performers but also event organisers, distributors, songwriters and producers. ‘Controlled’ experience Attracting more international acts to Kuala Lumpur is unlikely to stop Malaysians travelling abroad to see them, however. Aaron Matthew, a 45-year-old trader based in the city, said the restrictions governing live performances in Malaysia diminished their appeal. “Why pay so much for a ‘controlled’ performance or experience?” Matthew said. “If I can afford it, I’d pay for the full experience in a foreign country where the artist is allowed to perform their true self as much as possible.” Malaysia’s live-music scene has weathered a string of controversies over regulation and management in recent years. In 2014, the Future Music Festival Asia was abruptly cancelled on the final day of the electronic dance music festival after six attendees collapsed and died. Postmortem and toxicology results released two months later attributed the deaths to severe heatstroke. The most prominent controversy to date came in 2023, when the government cancelled the final two days of the Good Vibes Festival after Matty Healy, frontman of the British band The 1975, criticised Malaysia’s anti-LGBT laws on stage before kissing a male bandmate. The incident prompted authorities to require organisers of foreign concerts to have a “kill switch” that can shut off performances if necessary. Matthew questioned whether the current concert boom represented sustainable demand, suggesting social media had turned some shows into “must-go” events driven by fear of missing out rather than genuine fandom. Those who felt otherwise should embrace “Jomo”, or the “joy of missing out”, he joked. While Matthew said he preferred smaller, more intimate shows to large-scale spectacles, he conceded that one November performance could tempt him: “I might attend the MCR concert. There’s a ticket waiting, but I don’t know.”

title: Alibaba Cloud set to open new data centres in Europe next year as overseas push gains pace
description: The tech giant is set to add extra capacity to help international clients deploy real-world artificial intelligence.
content: Alibaba Cloud, Alibaba Group Holding’s cloud business unit, is set to launch data centres in Turkey, Finland and the Netherlands over the next 12 months, speeding up an overseas push as it seeks to win enterprise customers through its “full stack AI capabilities” spanning chips, cloud infrastructure and multimodal models. The first of these new data centres will open in the Netherlands in October. The cloud unit will also add to existing data centre capacity in Malaysia, Germany, the United Arab Emirates, France and Hong Kong, said Li Feifei, the CTO and president of international business at Alibaba Cloud, at the company’s Apsara Conference in Hangzhou, which runs through Thursday. “We are expanding our global cloud footprint to bring computing resources closer to customers and partners,” Li said, adding that companies were moving AI from experiments into real-world deployment. The company also announced partnerships with firms including Panasonic Digital, Unity China, Indonesian logistics group Lion Parcel, Malaysia’s Loomi Entertainment and business software provider Shake. Alibaba Cloud now operates 107 availability zones across 31 regions, according to the company. Gartner ranked it the world’s fourth-largest infrastructure-as-a-service provider by revenue in 2025, trailing US players Amazon, Microsoft and Google, and the largest in the Asia-Pacific region with 22.5 per cent market share. Alibaba Group Holding owns the South China Morning Post. Alibaba is putting together an impressive vertically integrated AI play, optimising its Qwen models with its own stack from chips to software Neil Shah, Counterpoint Research Revenue from AI and Cloud Computing Services, a key growth engine that combines Alibaba Cloud with chip-design arm T-Head, rose 45 per cent from a year earlier to 48.4 billion yuan (US$7.2 billion) in the three months ending June 30. Annual recurring revenue from model and application services, including model-as-a-service offerings, had now reached 20 billion yuan, up from 16 billion yuan in August, according to Li. The company also launched three AI products for overseas customers: Smart Studio allowed businesses to build and sell model-as-a-service platforms under their own brands; Smart Fusion combined models for a single task and could cut token spending by about half, Alibaba said on Wednesday; and Smart Video could generate videos up to an hour long in more than 20 languages. The international push followed a series of announcements on Tuesday covering Alibaba’s full AI stack. The group said its Qwen 4 model was in training and that future Qwen 5 models would be able to scale up to 10 trillion parameters. It also unveiled the Zhenwu V900 AI processor, due for commercial release in the first quarter of 2027, and set a target of operating more than 20 gigawatts of global data centre capacity by 2032. “Alibaba is putting together an impressive vertically integrated AI play, optimising its Qwen models with its own stack from chips to software,” said Neil Shah, a vice-president at Counterpoint Research. But full independence could slow the company in the near-to-medium term, while catching Western rivals in efficient “tokenomics” remained elusive, he added.

title: Inside Bangkok’s World Gourmet Festival, where top chefs share the kitchen
description: Acclaimed chefs including Álvaro Clavijo, Julien Royer and Josiah Citrin embrace the challenge of blending diverse culinary styles with niche Thai ingredients.
content: The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld. Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner. The pressures of collaboration Beyond now commonplace four-hands dinners and chef residencies, the World Gourmet Festival presents a unique set of challenges. Chefs must traverse language barriers, unfamiliar ingredients, and sky-high expectations from some of the industry’s most trained palates. For many, this tests more than culinary skill; it also challenges adaptability and creativity. Josiah Citrin, chef-owner of restaurants Mélisse and Citrin in Los Angeles, acknowledges the pressure this event brings. “The expectation is always high, but that’s what makes these events exciting,” he explains. “In the kitchen, food becomes its own language quickly. Once you start cooking together, you find a rhythm, and that’s part of the fun of doing these events around the world.” This balancing act – maintaining one’s gastronomic identity while embracing the unknown – is central to the festival’s spirit. Pastry chef Puyachart “Boy” Puttawong of Saneh Jaan in Bangkok frames the goal precisely. “A successful collaborative menu should allow guests to recognise each chef’s individual personality while still experiencing a clear and harmonious connection from the first course to the last.” Weaving a comprehensive throughline that connects each course, rather than jockeying for attention, helps diners understand the interplay between both cuisines and each chef’s culinary ethos. “Our intention is not to make every dish taste Thai, but to allow Thai culinary knowledge and ingredients to become part of the creative conversation,” Puttawong stresses. Creating a cohesive dining experience amid such diversity can be daunting. Chefs must develop a menu together that reflects their individual styles while maintaining culinary continuity across courses. “Menu development begins with understanding each chef’s strengths,” remarks chef Pilaipon “Toi” Kamnag of Saneh Jaan. “Compromise doesn’t mean weakening anyone’s culinary identity; it’s about making thoughtful adjustments.” Clavijo stresses the importance of listening rather than competing for space on the same plate: “I wouldn’t really call it ‘compromise’. If both chefs are trying to prove their identity in every single course, the guest feels that tension. A good partnership requires enough confidence to know when to speak and when to let the other person speak.” Communicating can be a challenge in itself, with chefs from so many different countries taking part. But for many involved, food serves as a universal tongue, reducing friction. Thanh Vuong Vo, executive chef of Coco Dining in Ho Chi Minh City, shares his perspective: “In a professional kitchen, communication goes beyond spoken language. You communicate through technique, timing, gestures, tasting and repetition,” he says. “If there is a difference in interpretation, we taste together and use the food itself as the common vernacular.” This fluidity allows chefs to communicate through actions and shared experiences rather than relying solely on verbal exchanges. Zee Zheng, chef-owner of Fabula in Shanghai, observes, “I believe a chef is simply a messenger of nature. My role is to act as a bridge – connecting dishes while weaving in subtle local touches that add a sense of discovery. “It’s all about both chefs working together to allow the ingredients to speak for themselves; that is what defines high-level cuisine.” This synergy cultivates an environment where innovation thrives despite the pressures of the event. Ingredient-led approaches Despite the challenges, one of the event’s most exciting aspects is the opportunity to experiment with niche Thai ingredients, from produce to proteins. For the chefs involved, these ingredients offer both inspiration and a challenge. Says Vo, “I want to understand the Thai ingredients and techniques first, then see how they can enter my own culinary language naturally.” His goal is to create something that feels like a genuine conversation between Vietnam and Thailand, rather than simply combining ingredients from both countries. “Understanding their role in Thai cooking allows me to incorporate them into my own cuisine in a meaningful way while keeping the Vietnamese perspective at the heart of my cooking.” This mindset of exploration is essential for chefs seeking to create dishes that resonate with both their own background and the local culture. Clavijo’s approach at his restaurant, El Chato, is deeply rooted in Colombia’s ecological variety, and he sees Thailand as a mirror rather than a contrast. “Even though Colombia and Thailand are far apart, there are many similarities in our ingredients as both countries share a tropical climate,” he says. “Rather than forcing Colombian and Thai cuisines together, I prefer to find natural connections and let the products guide us.” Julien Royer, chef-owner of Odette in Singapore, echoes this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding local flavours. “My culinary ideology revolves around the principle that ingredients are a reflection of terroir. My grandmother, Odette, was the one who taught me that respect for seasonality,” he says. For Royer, cooking with Thai ingredients is about respect and balance – finding a natural connection between two cuisines and letting them meet on equal terms. The costs and benefits of participation While the festival offers significant exposure and brand building, it also comes with sacrifices. Chefs must balance their responsibilities at home with the demands of such high-profile events. Citrin acknowledges this cost, stating, “Leaving your restaurant means leaving your team, your business, and your family. It has to have a meaningful purpose that extends beyond that one single event.” Clavijo agrees, explaining that collaboration must go further than mere visibility. “The real value is exchange,” he says. “The lasting benefits of meeting other chefs, discovering new products, and creating ongoing relationships are what make these experiences worthwhile for chefs and attendees alike.” A celebration of gastronomy The World Gourmet Festival mirrors the evolving culinary landscape in Bangkok and Asia. As local chefs collaborate with international talents, they bring new perspectives and techniques to the fore. “As Thai chefs, we are proud to be part of the hosting city,” says chef Toi. “Bangkok is no longer simply a destination where international cuisine is presented; it has become an active and influential participant in the global culinary conversation.”

title: In France, prosecutors probe secret filming of women with smart glasses
description: Investigation follows complaints of people secretly recording and publishing non-consensual footage online.
content: Paris prosecutors said Tuesday they had opened several probes after receiving complaints concerning women filmed on the street without their consent using smart glasses. Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant. Meta’s smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have become a commercial success. Meta sold 7 million pairs in 2025. Other companies, including Google and Snap, are also preparing to roll out AI-powered glasses. Calls have grown in Europe for action against what campaigners call “pervert” smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women has appeared online, with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale. In France, the e-Enfance association, which operates the national hotline for victims of online abuse, earlier this month sounded the alarm about videos recorded with camera-equipped glasses and shared online. The Paris public prosecutor’s office said on Tuesday it had received “complaints relating to violations of privacy linked to the use of smart glasses”. Prosecutors did not say which brands were involved. Prosecutors pointed to a “growing trend on social media involving women being filmed on the street with smart glasses without their consent and the videos being published online”. Under French law, such an offence is punishable by up to two years in prison and a €45,000 (US$51,000) fine. Prosecutors said that in some cases investigations had also been opened for sexual assault when “the acts are accompanied by non-consensual sexual contact”. The Paris prosecutor’s office said its cybercrime division “tested smart glasses in September in order to identify the commission of other cybercrime-related offences”. Such offences could include the theft of a cryptocurrency wallet’s recovery phrase, enabling criminals to steal the funds. The e-Enfance group said it had received around 20 reports from women as of September 8, most involving Meta glasses. “We need to strengthen oversight of these devices from the design stage,” said the association’s Veronique Bechu. “And when creators make a business model out of humiliating strangers, platforms must adopt a zero-tolerance approach and suspend repeat offenders,” she added. According to the association, the cases reported to its hotline tended to follow a recurring pattern: a content creator approaches a young woman or girl in a public place and discreetly films her using smart glasses. The aim is to “provoke a reaction, make her uncomfortable or place her in an embarrassing situation” before sharing the footage on social media, mainly TikTok. Those filmed often become the target of ridicule, misogynistic insults and even threats, the association said, citing the case of a teenage girl filmed in Paris during an annual French street music festival. After approaching her, a man wearing Meta smart glasses filmed her and posted the video on TikTok, Instagram and X, where it went viral. The teenager subsequently received “hateful comments and death threats”. Meta has said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with a blinking LED light on its glasses designed to indicate when recording is taking place.

title: China’s Premier Li Qiang calls for harnessing AI to propel manufacturing advances
description: Li calls for service platforms to help companies, particularly SMEs, with functions such as industrial design, pilot testing and maintenance.
content: Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for deeper integration of artificial intelligence and manufacturing during a visit to Shanghai, as Beijing seeks to expand advanced manufacturing and emerging industries amid intensifying global technology competition. “[We] should combine China’s strengths in manufacturing and digital technologies,” Li said during his visit to an AI application testing base in the city on Tuesday, Xinhua reported. He called for the creation of more manufacturing service platforms, covering areas such as industrial design, pilot testing and intelligent maintenance, to help companies – particularly small and medium-sized firms – upgrade operations more efficiently and at lower cost. Li’s comments followed President Xi Jinping’s call last week to make China’s supply chains more resilient and self-sufficient while accelerating the development of a modern industrial system underpinned by advanced manufacturing. While visiting an incubator for future industries in Shanghai, Li said future industries could become a “potential blue ocean” for advanced manufacturing, calling on the country to make breakthroughs in core technologies and strengthen the foundations of basic research. The country needed to expand venture capital investment, grow its pool of “patient capital” and establish mechanisms to increase investment in future industries while sharing risks, Li added, pointing to such sectors’ long development cycles and high market risks. He also highlighted talent as a “primary resource”, calling for more efforts to attract and develop talent through research institutions, innovation platforms, companies and technology programmes, while exploring new ways to nurture top innovators. Also on Tuesday, Li met executives of international charity organisation WorldSkills, who were in China to attend the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, according to Xinhua. Li said China would continue to improve its training, evaluation and incentive systems for skilled workers, while sharing its experience and public resources with other countries to help spread the benefits of skills development. “China will continue to support the WorldSkills organisation’s development and help expand its work in competitions, education and training, academic research, poverty reduction through skills and South-South cooperation,” he said.

title: Letters | Hong Kong’s mental health narrative must instil a sense of hope
description: Readers discuss how the chief executive positioned mental health in his policy address, and the suggestion that Hong Kong should import New York’s drug court model.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I read the chief executive’s policy address delivered last week from its first page to its last and one word never appears: hope. Its 11 mental health measures are all about coping. Two gaps stand out. First, the missing middle. Four of the 11 measures target students, teachers or parents. Working adults in general explicitly appear once, in a voluntary workplace charter. Yet those aged 25 to 40 are the ones who walk through our doors at TreeholeHK: too old for school counsellors, too young for elderly services, too busy for a psychiatry queue measured in years. This group is left almost entirely to the private market. Second, hope. A cohort study published in The Lancet in 2020, which followed Hong Kong adults for a decade, found that probable depression stood at 1.9 per cent in 2009-14, and rose to 6.5 per cent in 2017 and 11.2 per cent in 2019, with suspected post-traumatic stress disorder at 12.8 per cent in 2019. That 1.9 per cent is the point: remarkably low by any international standards. Our mental health machinery is far more sophisticated than it was two decades ago. But care alone cannot restore what the community has lost. Western Australia’s Act-Belong-Commit campaign, statewide since 2008, does not tell people to wait for a diagnosis; it asks them to act, belong to a club or cause, and commit to something larger than themselves. Around 80 per cent of adults recognise it, and one in six who do so acted on it. England’s National Health Service goes further: when a general practitioner sees loneliness, the “prescription” is a link worker who connects the patient to a gardening project or community kitchen, not a waiting list. Both treat the individual as owner of their mental health and the community as the medicine. Our policy address seems to treat Hongkongers as cases. Its vocabulary is telling: identify, assess, refer, follow up. Not one of the measures on mental health asks residents to build anything of their own. Hong Kong needs a community model alongside its care model, where working adults build something, belong to something and see a tomorrow they helped shape. A narrative that counts referrals tells people they are patients. One that builds community tells them they are citizens with a future. Every policy tells its people a story. This one says: you have symptoms; we will help manage it. Hong Kong deserves another: you are capable; the future is yours to build. Peter Chan, managing director and chief psychology specialist, TreeholeHK Limited City can’t simply adopt New York’s drug courts model As a defence lawyer in Hong Kong, I read the letter, “Why Hong Kong needs special courts for drug offenders” (August 26) with interest but I would be cautious about importing that model wholesale. The letter states that a criterion for eligibility for New York’s drug courts is the absence of a violent conviction. That appears to leave open the possibility that a low-level courier with no violent record could qualify for a treatment-and-supervision pathway. Hong Kong has long treated trafficking as distinct from personal use and warranting deterrence because it facilitates supply throughout the community. Any transplant of the New York model needs to close that gap before it can credibly apply here. The letter rightly notes that our drug addiction treatment model differs from that of New York, and that capacity is a constraint. But it is worth being precise about what already exists. Under section 4 of the Drug Addiction Treatment Centres Ordinance (Cap. 244), a court may order a suitable offender into a treatment centre in lieu of another sentence, subject to a commissioner’s report on suitability and place availability, with sections 5 and 6 providing a 12-month supervision order on release and recall on breach of orders. For personal users specifically, Section 54A of the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (Cap. 134) makes consideration of a commissioner’s cure-and-rehabilitation report compulsory before any custodial sentence for possession or apparatus offences. The genuine question, then, is not whether Hong Kong lacks a rehabilitative response, since it does not, but whether the existing statutory duty and supervision regime can be reformed and resourced to approximate the ongoing judicial monitoring and collaborative model the letter describes, without the sentencing leniency for trafficking that a wholesale transplant risks. Before concluding that Hong Kong needs an entirely new judicial institution, that narrower question deserves an answer first. Ahmed Ashfaq, Tsim Sha Tsui

title: How does Xi Jinping’s ‘special plane’ compare with Air Force One?
description: A look at the Chinese leader’s aircraft, which is bound to become part of the visual choreography of his state visit in Washington.
content: With Chinese President Xi Jinping expected in Washington this week, attention is turning to the aircraft that will carry him and how it stacks up against America’s presidential plane. The aircraft carrying China’s leader, often referred to in state media and official statements as a zhuan ji, or special plane, remains far less known to the world than Air Force One, despite both countries using Boeing 747s for presidential travel. For a head of state, a presidential aircraft is more than a means of transport. Its range, on-board facilities and security systems reflect the practical demands of presidential travel and diplomatic missions, and the aircraft itself becomes part of the visual choreography of a state visit. In one sense, it is one of the first symbols of a country to arrive in the host country, appearing in the sky before the president steps onto the tarmac. Air Force One is arguably the most recognisable symbol of the American presidency. It is also the technical call sign for any US Air Force aircraft carrying the president. But now the term is commonly used for the two highly customised Boeing 747-200Bs, designated VC-25A and bearing tail numbers 28000 and 29000, used to transport the US commander-in-chief. Across the Pacific Ocean, China does not operate a dedicated presidential aircraft. Aircraft used for Xi’s overseas trips have been drawn from Air China’s fleet and specially prepared for presidential travel. In 2013, when Xi had just taken office, his overseas trips were carried out on Air China Boeing 747-400s. The Boeing 747 is a large, long-haul, twin-aisle aircraft with a spacious cabin and a distinctive upper deck. In a 2013 state media report, Lu Peixin, a former acting director of the protocol department at China’s foreign ministry, gave two reasons China did not maintain a dedicated presidential aircraft. “One is to avoid waste and special treatment and increase aircraft utilisation,” Lu said. “The other is to ensure flight safety because an aircraft has millions of components and cannot simply sit idle for long periods.” The arrangement has evolved with the aircraft used for Xi’s long-haul travel. Just last weekend, Xi arrived in New Delhi aboard a Boeing 747-8 Intercontinental for the Brics summit, his first visit to India in seven years. The 747-8I is the passenger version of the 747-8 and the last passenger variant of the 747 ever built. Unlike the US, China has released relatively little public information about the aircraft used by its top leader. In official reports, Xi’s plane is generally referred to simply as a “special plane”, with few details of the aircraft itself. Whether for domestic or international missions, the dispatch and deployment of special aircraft are subject to strict procedures and a high level of confidentiality. By contrast, the White House maintains a dedicated web page on Air Force One that details its aircraft designation, tail numbers, on-board facilities and history. In China, for presidential flight missions, the Civil Aviation Administration receives the flight assignment and passes it to Air China through its office overseeing special flights, according to a rare media account in 2014. The crew would be determined and security checks and modifications to the aircraft carried out. According to Lu in the 2013 report, some seats on board would be removed and replaced with sofas and beds. Technicians from the PLA Air Force’s 34th Division would help with inspections and the necessary modifications. Lu said a refitted aircraft was generally divided into four sections. At the front was an executive section for the national leader, comprising a living room, office and bedroom. This was followed by a section for ministers and other senior accompanying officials, then seating for officials at the bureau and department level. The rear section was reserved for accompanying media and staff. By contrast, Air Force One is permanently configured for presidential travel. Air Force One has 4,000 square feet (372 square metres) of floor space across three levels, including a presidential suite with an office, lavatory and conference room, and separate accommodation for senior advisers, Secret Service personnel and travelling press, according to the White House. It includes a medical suite that can function as an operating room, and a doctor is permanently on board. In addition, there are two galleys that can be used to make up to 100 meals at a time. The aircraft is also equipped with secure communications systems, front and rear air stairs, a self-contained baggage loader and in-flight refuelling capability, according to the US Air Force. Beyond its on-board configuration, Air Force One carries a highly recognisable visual identity. The words “United States of America”, the American flag and the seal of the US president are emblazoned on its exterior, making the aircraft an immediately identifiable symbol of the American presidency wherever it flies. At present, US President Donald Trump is travelling on a newer member of the 747 family. The VC-25B Bridge, a customised Boeing 747-8I, entered presidential service earlier this year as an interim aircraft, bridging the gap between the two ageing VC-25A aircraft and Boeing’s forthcoming VC-25B jets, which have faced delays. Valued at an estimated US$400 million, the plane was given to the US government by the Qatari royal family and can fly faster and farther than the VC-25As. In recent years, questions have surfaced about why China’s top leader does not travel on the domestically produced C919, which has entered commercial service with Chinese airlines.

title: ‘I wasn’t scared’: young Hong Kong rare cancer survivor who stayed positive
description: Kevin Cureau describes how he stayed calm and confident of beating stage-three liposarcoma and the steps he took to protect his fertility.
content: When Kevin Cureau first spoke to his oncologist about the mass behind his knee, he was not stressed out. “It was more, ‘Oh, this is just something I have to get through.’ I wasn’t scared or anything,” says Cureau, 37, a French-Chinese cancer survivor born and living in Hong Kong who was diagnosed with stage-three liposarcoma in late 2025. Cureau took the news so calmly that even his doctor was a little surprised. But he admits that, at the time, he did not fully understand what liposarcoma was. Even when retelling his cancer experience to this reporter, he appeared nonchalant about his health scare. His doctor explained that, because of his relatively young age, his body was better equipped to handle the necessary treatments. “If she was confident, I had no reason to think otherwise,” Cureau says. Liposarcoma is a group of rare cancers that begin in the body’s fat cells, typically beginning in the belly, arms and legs. It usually affects adults over 50. But myxoid liposarcoma, also known as round cell liposarcoma, may affect people as young as 35. This variation developed behind Cureau’s left knee. Finding and diagnosing Cureau first noticed the small lump behind his knee a couple of years ago but did not pay it much attention. The unexplained mass grew much faster towards the end of last year, eventually making it difficult to bend his leg. By the time Cureau saw a doctor, an MRI showed the lump had grown into a fat-filled mass measuring 15cm (5.9 inches) by 10.5cm by 7cm – roughly the size of a grapefruit. He underwent surgery to remove it and perform a biopsy, which led to a diagnosis of stage-three liposarcoma. Doctors graded the tumour at a two, indicating a moderately fast proliferation rate and risk of recurrence. “I feel that I was lucky, and everything that happened was sort of the best-case scenario,” Cureau reflects. “The tumour itself, yes, it was large, but it was localised in one big pocket. It had not spread anywhere else. It was just attached a little bit to a nerve, but the doctor was able to remove everything in one go.” Cureau is among a growing number of cases of adults under 50 getting cancer diagnoses. One in eight new cancer cases in Hong Kong is among this age group. According to the latest figures from the Hong Kong Cancer Registry, Hong Kong recorded 37,953 new cancer cases in 2023, with early-onset cancers accounting for 12 per cent, about 4,500 cases. The silver lining is that younger patients generally handle intensive treatment better, and their cancers are often detected early enough to treat effectively. Treatment and side effects Cureau took a proactive approach by remaining optimistic, learning about his prognosis and safeguarding his fertility. Having private health insurance allowed him to start radiation therapy quickly in a private clinic, while he opted for the public hospital system for his chemotherapy to manage costs. He began radiotherapy treatment in January, five times a week for six weeks. The treatment was localised to the tumour. His skin there became dry and dark in colour – comparable to a “very intense sort of sunburn”. “My skin actually started cracking open. So it just sort of transformed into an open wound at the back of the knee,” he says. Quickly following radiotherapy, he had five rounds of chemotherapy, once every three weeks in a public hospital. Though scans showed that cancer cells had not spread from the original site, chemo was recommended as a precaution. The process was intense, each round requiring a two-night, three-day stay in hospital to receive a continuous 24-hour IV infusion of a standard drug regimen to eliminate any remaining cancer cells. “I don’t think you’re ever prepared for how tired and how nauseous you’ll be … you lose your appetite a little bit, and everything takes a bit more effort,” he says. Cureau’s family flew in from France to stay with him. Luckily, he could work remotely during treatment, and his employer was understanding about his health needs. While Cureau himself was not worried by his condition, his wife and mother were “definitely the most stressed-out people”. His four-year-old son did not understand what was happening either, and Cureau – being confident that he would soon recover – did not see the need to explain to him what cancer was. “I would tell him that I had to go to the hospital and his only comment was, ‘Again?’ That’s it. And then he just found it funny the day I came back and I had no hair. He started joking, saying, ‘Oh, can I get no hair, also?’” Staying positive Preserving his fertility was one of Cureau’s most critical decisions. He and his wife still hope to expand their family – a consideration rarely on the radar for the typical cancer patient in their fifties or sixties. Before starting targeted radiation or chemotherapy, both of which can permanently impair reproductive health, Cureau chose to freeze his sperm, keeping the door open for in vitro fertilisation (IVF). “You really never expect it to happen to you,” Cureau says of his diagnosis, despite having a family history of cancer and friends who have also battled the disease. His experience has made him an advocate for early detection, urging even young adults to seek immediate medical checks if they spot unusual symptoms. But he also encourages people to stay positive in the face of cancer, stressing that it is “not so much [of] a death sentence as it used to be” thanks to modern medicine. Today, about 14 weeks since his last round of chemotherapy, all of Cureau’s treatment is concluded and his hair has begun to grow back. The doctor’s orders still require him to have lots of rest, and it still “hurts a little bit” when he bends his leg, he says, “but it’s just something I’ll deal with slowly”. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Malaysia’s Anwar faces political reckoning in Melaka as state calls for poll
description: The Melaka state election is Malaysia’s third this year. Anwar’s coalition performed badly at previous polls in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
content: Melaka on Wednesday officially called for a state election – the latest test for Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government, which is already facing an internal feud and growing public frustration over failed reforms. The state assembly was dissolved effective from Wednesday following an official notification sent to the country’s Election Commission the previous day by Ibrahim Durum, the Melaka state assembly’s speaker. “A state election will be held within 60 days of the dissolution of the state assembly,” commission chairman Ramlan Harun said in a statement late on Tuesday, adding that the commission would convene a special meeting soon to decide on the date of the election. The Melaka contest is the country’s third this year. Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition has yet to recover from punishing back-to-back defeats in Melaka’s neighbours, Johor and Negeri Sembilan, at the hands of federal partner Umno. The United Malays National Organisation is the incumbent party in Melaka, after winning a landslide 21 of the 28 seats in 2021. It later formed a coalition government with PH – which won five seats – to reflect the partnership struck at the federal level when Anwar was appointed prime minister in November 2022. Caretaker Chief Minister Ab Rauf Yusoh had earlier indicated that the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition was talking to both PH and opposition front Perikatan Nasional (PN) about a potential electoral pact in Melaka. No decision has been made so far. Umno leaders have already launched a campaign to unify the country’s Malay-Muslim majority base, following their successful – albeit informal – tie-up with the Malay-nationalist PN led by the Pan-Malaysian Islamist Party (PAS) in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. That partnership helped Umno extend its supermajority in Johor to 48 out of 56 seats in July’s election, when PN actively urged supporters to vote for the incumbent party in seats that it did not contest. They later worked together to wrest control of Negeri Sembilan from Anwar’s PH in August. Umno and PN won a combined 25 out of the 36 seats to secure a comfortable majority. Analysts expect the Melaka state election to return another Umno majority, though PH may pick up votes from those wary of the ongoing constitutional crisis in Negeri Sembilan – where local Umno leaders endorsed a contested decision to replace the current ruler – and the recent royal pardon allowing house arrest for jailed former leader Najib Razak. “Current issues … could create better opportunities [for PH],” said Mazlan Ali, a political analyst at the University of Technology Malaysia. “Additionally, the lack of clear cooperation between PAS and Umno in Melaka could play a significant role.” Melaka could also provide a proving ground for new political realignments ahead of Malaysia’s next general election, due by February 2028, as PH and Umno’s federal partnership teeters on the edge of collapse. While Umno is allying with PN, Anwar’s coalition is widely believed to be negotiating a Melaka pact with Bersatu – a former PH partner that spearheaded the 2020 political coup which brought down a previous PH administration. “Umno continues to hedge, pledging federal cooperation while going against PH at a state level,” said Timothy Wong, a senior analyst with government affairs and public policy firm BowerGroupAsia. “This means that the political landscape is trending towards pacts made on a state-by-state basis, depending on state level dynamics between parties rather than federal level relationships.” Deepening dissent Still, Anwar has to contend with deepening dissent from PH’s predominantly urban and ethnic minority support base, which has accused his party of abandoning its reform pledges in favour of cooperating with Umno to remain in federal power. Najib’s house arrest proved a double-edged sword after PH became the target of a backlash over what critics had described as special treatment for the country’s elites. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar granted Najib a “conditional pardon” last week, allowing him to serve the remaining two years of his sentence at home, provided he first settles a 50 million ringgit (US$10.3 million) fine. The former prime minister already had his 12-year sentence halved and fine reduced from 210 million ringgit in 2024, two years after he was jailed for corruption linked to a former unit of the scandal-tainted state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. Friday’s house arrest decision caused immediate ruptures in PH. On Saturday, Anthony Loke – the leader of the Democratic Action Party, the largest party in government – announced he would resign from cabinet as a sign of protest. PH had its first taste of federal rule in 2018 in a watershed election that saw the end of Umno’s six decades of unbroken rule, as voters made clear their anger over alleged widespread corruption, particularly the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal that implicated then prime minister Najib. PH returned to power after a deeply split 2022 national election, when then king Sultan Abdullah appointed Anwar as prime minister on condition that he form a unity government of allies and rivals. Anwar had to lean heavily on Umno to provide legitimacy to rule among the country’s Malay majority. But his supporters were enraged after controversial court rulings freed senior Umno leaders of corruption charges – including 47 counts of corruption and money laundering against Umno president and Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi. Wong, the government affairs analyst, said PH “is in need of a confidence boost and must prove that it can still stand on its own merits rather than wait for its rivals to implode”. “The key issue is messaging and narrative control, which it [PH] continues to struggle with,” he added.

title: Most Singaporeans ready to let AI agents shop for them with more safeguards: study
description: The research also found 34 per cent of Singaporeans wanted a government-backed AI safety certification, the highest of the countries in the survey.
content: Singaporeans are among the most open to allowing an artificial intelligence agent to shop for them, but they also want the strictest guard rails, research shows. The latest agentic AI study from Global Payments released on Wednesday indicates the hoops agentic AI will need to jump through to be trusted to make purchases without human intervention. The study, which surveyed seven countries including the United States, China and the United Kingdom, found 59 per cent of Singaporeans are open to an agent shopping for them while 23 per cent have already used one. Only 15 per cent say they would let an agent shop, shortlist and pay entirely on its own. Payment companies and AI start-ups are working towards a digital future where people will authorise agents to make all sorts of purchases on their behalf. The survey results point to the gap between curiosity about agentic AI for personal commerce – everything from switching insurance policies to designing travel itineraries – and comfort in letting an agent do more than browse and recommend. “The same instinct that made Singapore an early adopter of fast, verified payments is exactly what’s holding the wallet back from agents,” said Phil Pomford, executive lead, Enterprise APAC at Global Payments. “Consumers want the confirmation step, the certification, the proof it’s secure, before they’ll delegate that final purchase click.” The study found 34 per cent of Singaporeans wanted a government-backed AI safety certification, the highest of the countries in the survey. Singaporeans also topped the list in terms of wanting a phone-push notification before an AI-driven purchase while 41 per cent would want a biometric sign-off versus 36 per cent globally. The biggest issues cited were security, including protection of payment details. That caution shows the challenges ahead globally for agentic AI in personal commerce, given Singapore is already at the forefront in many ways on digital payments adoption. Alongside questions around liability and fraud mitigation, there are more prosaic issues including what happens if someone simply dislikes what an agent ends up choosing and buying for them. An earlier study by consulting firm PwC and the Singapore FinTech Association showed digital payment adoption in Singapore stood at 92 per cent in 2025, with everyday use of mobile wallets and widespread QR code acceptance. It noted e-commerce sales in Singapore were projected to reach US$14 billion by 2027, nearly double the amount from the start of the decade. At the same time, losses to scams in the first half of 2025 showed schemes evolving in sophistication and business models. Singapore is seeking to become a global hub for AI, an industry now dominated by US and Chinese players. It is allowing companies to claim AI spending for tax deductions and allowances and is spending more than S$1 billion (US$783 million) to fund public AI research over the next five years. It has created an AI council chaired by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to provide strategic direction. At the same time, Wong said in February that AI “must serve our national interests and our people”. The Global Payments study found those surveyed in Singapore would trust an AI agent to spend fairly small amounts on average on their behalf for now: around S$49 for health and wellness and S$33 for a one-time digital purchase. Even then, they would want the same checks as they would demand for a wealth-management transaction. The survey also showed Singaporeans were comfortable with an agent enacting a modest S$400 money transfer or just under S$1,200 to execute a trade.

title: Rising US scrutiny on clinical trials could threaten China’s biotech advantage: analysts
description: China’s ability to conduct clinical trials quickly and cheaply has given it an edge in the biotech sector – and the US is growing concerned.
content: China’s edge in fast, cost-effective early clinical trials has propelled its emergence as a global biopharmaceutical powerhouse, but there is a risk that the United States could take steps to curb that advantage, according to analysts. US lawmakers and officials at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have raised the alarm about American pharmaceutical companies’ growing reliance on conducting early clinical trials in China, flagging the opaqueness of the process and the need to keep medical innovations on shore. While large multinational corporations’ compliance teams have been “on high alert for quite a while”, the recent ratcheting up of such rhetoric in Washington could prompt firms to “double click a lot more when evaluating China-origin target assets”, said Xianfeng Morgan Xu, a partner at US law firm Foley Hoag based in Washington. Last week, John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, called for greater due diligence and oversight of US firms conducting clinical trials in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region and at People’s Liberation Army-affiliated hospitals. Five major drug makers had been cooperating and sharing information with the US Congress regarding its probes into clinical trials at Chinese military hospitals, Moolenaar added. “We obviously have a relationship with China, we’re going to continue to have a relationship with China, but the way we’ve conducted business with China has been really on their terms,” Moolenaar said during an event organised by US biopharmaceutical publication Endpoints News. “And in the case of medicines here in the United States, I think we should have a much greater say in terms of how we conduct business with China.” Last month, Moolenaar and Congressman Ben Cline also sent a letter to the FDA, urging the agency to halt the use of Chinese drug trial data unless the FDA had audited the trial site within the past year. While greater scrutiny of Chinese clinical trials is “highly plausible”, it will not lead to any systematic exclusion of Chinese clinical data, according to Ruby Wang, director of the LINTRIS Health consultancy and author of the book China Cure. Wang said the lawmakers’ demands could bog down trial progress with “more bureaucratic ticking of boxes”, creating delays and inefficiencies that “may disincentivise some” companies. “Though the overall attraction and relevance and crucial global role of China as a clinical trial source can overcome any disincentivisation,” she added. Still, mitigating the risks would be “resource-intensive” for licensing deals already signed, according to Wang. The added time and cost to duplicate trial data outside China could potentially “erode some of the China advantages that made collaboration so attractive in the first place”, she said. China has risen to become a major global player in the biotechnology sector in recent years, as Western pharmaceutical giants turn to the country for innovative drug assets. It has also become “a major destination” for early-stage clinical development and proof-of-concept studies because of its “speed, scale and patient access”, Hogan Lovells Cadwalader lawyers wrote in a note last week. But that development model was now “facing increasing US geopolitical and regulatory scrutiny”, they said, pointing to an article published by the FDA this month that signalled intensifying “Good Clinical Practice” inspections at trial sites outside the US. Grace Graham, the FDA’s deputy commissioner for policy, legislation and international affairs, warned at last month’s Endpoints event of the risks associated with relying on China for generic medicines or cancer medicines, as the country could “stop shipping” to America – “as they’ve done with critical minerals and other things in the past”. The US drug regulator has also escalated its efforts to bring drug trials back to the country. Last week, it officially launched the Expedited Investigational New Drug (IND) Pilot programme, which aimed to fast track early-stage clinical trials to compete with China and Australia. Thanks to China’s advantages in scale, intense commercial competition as well as governance and regulatory reforms, the country can move an experimental drug from labs into patients “considerably faster” than in the US, according to Wang. “The FDA’s IND announcement acknowledges that growing gap in efficiency,” she said.

title: Why small quakes in Malaysia’s Sabah are sounding seismic alarms
description: Scientists say the mountainous regions of Keningau and Tambunan have been overlooked in the state’s monitoring for earthquake risks.
content: A series of small earthquakes beneath Keningau, an inland district of Sabah in Malaysian Borneo, is drawing attention to a part of the state where scientists say the fault lines are poorly understood and the consequences of a larger quake could be devastating. The latest, a magnitude 3.4 tremor on September 3, was felt in several parts of Keningau, prompting staff at the district office to suspend a meeting and move to a designated safe area. No serious damage was reported. The tremor was one of several weak earthquakes recorded around Keningau since 2023, raising questions about efforts to strengthen monitoring, development and disaster planning in the area. Experts say a stronger earthquake in the region could trigger landslides, cutting off roads and other vital infrastructure. Sabah has focused much of its earthquake monitoring and preparedness on Ranau, a district near Mount Kinabalu where an earthquake killed 18 people and caused widespread damage in 2015. But about 100km (60 miles) southwest of Ranau, the similarly mountainous Keningau and Tambunan valleys were identified as seismically active as far back as 2018 in federal planning guidance. Both lie within the Crocker fault zone, a network of geological faults in Sabah’s mountainous interior associated with earthquake activity. Yet neither Keningau nor Tambunan appear on the government’s published list of mapped active fault zones or areas where developers must check for earthquake risks before building. It is unclear how extensively the two districts have been mapped and monitored for seismic risks. The government’s Minerals and Geoscience Department did not respond to questions from This Week in Asia. “Sabah’s seismic hazard is broader than Ranau alone, our scientific understanding of Sabah’s earthquake sources has not yet caught up with the level of development and exposure that now exists,” said Felix Tongkul, a geologist at the University of Malaysia Sabah who has studied faults in the state for more than three decades. “What makes Keningau scientifically interesting is … the fact that several small earthquakes have occurred there over recent years,” Tongkul said. Keningau has experienced six weak earthquakes, ranging from magnitude 1.4 to 3.4, since April 2023, according to Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip, director general of the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia). Mohd Hisham told This Week In Asia on Friday that the sequence showed local seismic activity “associated with the release of tectonic energy”, with the “possibility of recurring earthquakes”. Of MetMalaysia’s 80 seismic monitoring stations, 28 are in Sabah – concentrated around the Mount Kinabalu area – while Keningau has only one. “For now, the current station network is sufficient for monitoring seismic activity on a regional scale,” Mohd Hisham said. The 13th Malaysia Plan, a national development blueprint covering 2026 to 2030 unveiled in July last year, does not list any new stations, though MetMalaysia intends to upgrade one station in Sandakan and four others across Sabah. Two new monitoring stations were announced in November after a series of tremors rattled Segamat in Johor – a state with no history of damaging earthquakes – along with four to be upgraded under the plan’s first implementation phase. Seismic records Johari Abdul Ghani, then the acting minister of natural resources and environmental sustainability, said in November that the Minerals and Geoscience Department had mapped 11 active fault zones nationwide between 2016 and 2020. Four were in Sabah: Lobou Lobou and Mensaban in Ranau, and Lahad Datu and Tabin in Lahad Datu. No faults in Keningau or Tambunan appeared on the list. This contrasted with a 2018 guideline from PlanMalaysia, the federal town planning department under the Ministry of Housing and Local Government, which named both Keningau and Tambunan as seismically active. “Ranau is relatively well studied, whereas places such as Keningau, Tambunan and parts of the interior are [not],” Tongkul said. Johari added that six fault-movement benchmark stations had been installed in Sabah. Arthur Joseph Kurup, who took over as natural resources minister in December, has announced 18 additional early-warning systems for Sabah. He said four of the nation’s 34 systems were in Sabah, with two in Kundasang. The ministry announced plans earlier this year to strengthen its 2017 hazard map underpinning Malaysia’s seismic building standard, including new active fault-mapping. In June, a community disaster-risk initiative in Kundasang included an earthquake simulation exercise, early-warning and evacuation procedures, and landslide-risk mapping. Sabah has held other disaster-preparedness exercises since the 2015 earthquake, largely centred on Kundasang and Ranau. In October 2024, the National Disaster Management Agency held landslide drills in Kundasang with the Sabah government involving more than 70 personnel from various agencies. This Week in Asia contacted the agency and the Sabah Fire and Rescue Department regarding earthquake contingency plans, preparedness and public education, but received no response. Hidden faults Rodeano Roslee, dean of science and technology at the University of Malaysia Sabah, said the geology of the interior left little doubt about the source of the quakes. Because Keningau and Tambunan lay within the Crocker fault zone, he said that normal faults – showing displacement of several metres – had been recorded cutting through young river gravels near Keningau. Some faults might also be hidden beneath valley sediments, Rodeano said. “We know enough to recognise Keningau and Tambunan as fault-controlled and potentially active areas, but not yet enough to quantify the hazard of individual faults with the confidence required for detailed risk-based planning,” he said. This uncertainty mattered for determining how far buildings were set back from active faults, as well as for predicting future earthquake intensity and designing critical infrastructure, Rodeano said. Rather than halting development altogether, he said “the level of geological investigation should be proportional to the consequences of failure”. The 2015 disaster in Ranau had shown what could happen when an earthquake destabilised slopes and rockfalls, Rodeano said, urging Sabah authorities to implement statewide fault mapping, better earthquake monitoring and stronger infrastructure planning. “The recent Keningau earthquakes are not grounds for alarm, but they are grounds for investigation,” Rodeano said.

title: Artworks reveal Chinese rulers and Cixi loved role-playing long before modern cosplay
description: What Emperor Qianlong did with his court painters is the 18th century equivalent of digital photo manipulation and Photoshop.
content: The Qing dynasty’s Empress Dowager Cixi is renowned as a cosplay enthusiast, leaving behind photographs and paintings of herself embodying the Buddhist Goddess of Mercy, Guanyin. However, she was not the first to engage in such role-playing while on the throne. Long before Cixi (1835–1908), the Qing dynasty’s emperors Yongzheng (1678–1735) and his son, Qianlong (1711–1799), indulged in role-playing, as evidenced in numerous paintings. Yongzheng, whose reign lasted 13 years, was known as a strict and relentless workaholic. Thus, the contrast of his playful side revealed in the role-playing paintings often surprised many. He left behind two albums titled The Album of the Yongzheng Emperor in Costumes, each featuring paintings of him portraying various characters, including a Taoist priest, a Buddhist lama, a Han intellectual, a peasant, and even a European figure. These paintings lack specific dates, with some scholars suggesting they were created before his ascension to the throne, intended to win his father Kangxi’s favour and secure the crown. One interpretation is that Yongzheng’s diverse portrayals demonstrate his openness and inclusiveness, suggesting his potential as a wise ruler. Conversely, by presenting himself as a peasant, he reveals an indifference to power, setting himself apart from his brothers. His son, Qianlong, took this cosplay hobby to new heights. Not only did Qianlong enjoy embodying characters in life, but he also commissioned painters to recreate ancient artworks he admired, placing himself in the role of the protagonist. For instance, favouring the Qing dynasty (1644–1912) painter Leng Mei’s Admiring the Moon, which is now part of the National Palace Museum’s collection in Taipei, Qianlong instructed court artists to replicate the piece with himself as the man admiring the moon – creating an early form of what could be likened to Photoshop. Often dubbed the famous narcissist emperor, Qianlong is recognised as the emperor with the most portraits in Chinese history. In fact, featuring him in a single painting was sometimes insufficient; he would appear in multiple roles within one artwork. A notable example is Qianlong Emperor Collecting Lingzhi, which depicts a composed Han man accompanied by a sika deer and a teenager carrying a basket and a hoe. It is believed that both men represent Qianlong himself. Moreover, Qianlong commissioned court painters to replicate an anonymous Song dynasty (960–1279) painting, again depicting himself as the primary character. In the unusual painting titled Emperor Qianlong Appreciating Antiques, he appears both as the appreciator of artefacts and as a figure within the artwork he admires. In this piece, he dresses as the original character – a Han person – though it is believed that Qianlong never donned Han attire in reality, as that contravened strict costume regulations. He also enjoyed displaying his costume portraits throughout the Forbidden City. Despite providing a wealth of visual evidence for their cosplay passions, these Qing dynasty rulers still fell short of Emperor Ling (156–189) of the Han dynasty (202 BC–220), who was documented as having cosplayed a street vendor in his palace’s harem. He also encouraged his concubines, maids, and eunuchs to participate in role-play alongside him.

title: Milan Fashion Week: Prada spring/summer 2027 spotlights the skirt, the brand’s ‘obsession’
description: From crystal-embellished hemlines to slashed satin and distressed leather, Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons put the humble skirt centre stage.
content: If there’s a garment that has come to define Prada – both the brand and the personal style of designer Miuccia Prada – it has to be the skirt. Back in 2005, the brand held a blockbuster exhibition at the Peace Hotel in Shanghai. Named “Waist Down”, the show was a celebration of the skirt, a closet staple that was also the centrepiece of the label’s spring/summer 2027 collection, unveiled on Tuesday at Milan Fashion Week. In the show notes, Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, who co-design Prada, referred to the skirt as “a Prada obsession”. Skirts came in all shapes and forms: pleated, embellished with crystals, slashed at the sides to reveal lingerie slips underneath, and made of materials ranging from distressed leather to satin and Prada’s signature Re-Nylon. A trope of femininity, the skirt is often seen as a symbol of female constraint – trousers were not considered acceptable attire for women in the Western world until the mid-20th century – but not in Prada’s world. “Engineered for freedom”, the Prada skirt is an emblem of autonomy, allowing women to move with ease and without constraints. A chameleon of the female wardrobe, the skirt can look sexy and provocative when paired with a bra top or prim and proper when worn with a wool sweater, as this collection cleverly demonstrated. Accessories – a very important category at Prada – included sunglasses with mismatched frames, tiny satin bags attached to bras, bejewelled kitten heels and ladylike leather bags. Once again, Prada struck a chord with a simple and sharp idea that stayed true to the label’s heritage but wasn’t just a sentimental exercise in nostalgia. This week the brand is also celebrating the opening of Prada Galleria, an eight-floor retail space in Milan’s historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II shopping arcade. The top floor of the immersive space is home to Pradasphere, a permanent exhibit exploring the history of the house since its founding in 1913. While this project may have put Miuccia Prada in a pensive and reflective mood, the spring/summer 2027 collection was yet another example of the designer’s unparalleled ability to constantly evolve while building on Prada’s rich visual vocabulary season after season.

title: Exclusive | Fissures over US investments stall plans for Chinese business leaders to join Xi visit
description: With the window for travel narrowing by the hour, uncertainty surrounds the inclusion of corporate leaders in China’s delegation.
content: Differences between Washington and Beijing over potential investment announcements have created roadblocks for a Chinese business delegation expected to accompany President Xi Jinping on his state visit to the US, according to sources. The window for travel is narrowing by the hour for these Chinese business leaders. Xi left China on Wednesday afternoon Beijing time for his first state visit to the US in more than a decade. He is accompanied by first lady Peng Liyuan, chief of staff Cai Qi, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, among others, state news agency Xinhua said in a brief report. Xi and Peng will be honoured with a military display at the White House on Thursday, with ceremonies taking place on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden. Xi will then hold a summit with US President Donald Trump at the White House, before attending a state banquet that evening. A source familiar with the discussions said Washington and Beijing had yet to resolve their disagreements over the Board of Investment, particularly over possible Chinese investments in the US, adding to uncertainty over the delegation’s participation. The investment forum was one of the deliverables from Xi and Trump’s last summit in Beijing in May. A second source added that poor logistics and a lack of formal engagement or arranged meetings for Chinese businesses coming to Washington were also adding to the uncertainty. The source noted that the Chinese side viewed it as a departure from the principle of reciprocity, under which the arrangements made for US businesses during the May summit in Beijing would be mirrored during Xi’s visit to Washington. Another source said that he still expected a Chinese delegation to show up, citing the presence of US business leaders at Thursday’s state dinner at the White House. On the US side, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Apple board chairman Tim Cook are attending the high-profile event. The South China Morning Post reported earlier that Chinese and US officials were discussing whether business leaders would join Xi’s delegation to Washington, with the idea framed around reciprocity after the US executives joined Trump in May. However, a final decision had yet to be reached. Figures from some of China’s most prominent firms – including electric vehicle maker BYD, battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL), and smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi – were expected to be part of the Chinese delegation. Another source said it was still possible that no Chinese business delegation would ultimately accompany Xi, although the plan had not yet been finalised last week. In Beijing, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declined to respond when asked whether Xi will be accompanied by a business delegation. “I don’t have the relevant information,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, hours before Xi’s departure. In the run-up to the summit, Washington has sent mixed signals on the prospect of Chinese carmakers investing in the US amid growing opposition from American motor vehicle manufacturers and legislators. Earlier this month, Trump said he would allow Chinese carmakers to set up manufacturing plants in the US. “If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” he told Fox News. The White House said last week that the “president’s comments speak for themselves” but that he was not “interested in compromising on our national security”. “Some of the rules and regulations that present hurdles would still have to be met for some of these types of investments to occur,” a senior White House official said. On Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Chinese carmakers already faced a “lot of natural obstacles” in the US market, indicating that a rollback of US measures was unlikely. “We also have rules about connected vehicles from China not being able to operate here. So, I think there are just a lot of natural obstacles that would make it challenging for the Chinese to invest here,” he said. The Commerce Department’s Connected Vehicle Rule, finalised in the final days of the Joe Biden administration, prohibits the import and sale of vehicles containing China-linked hardware or software and certain satellite communication technologies, citing national security concerns over data collection. Chinese cars also face tariffs of more than 120 per cent, effectively blocking them from the American market. Both sides continue to wrangle over extending the 2025 Busan trade agreement – even as they report progress on implementing a narrow tariff-reduced trade mechanism, the US-China Board of Trade. During Trump’s May visit to Beijing, the US business delegation roster also saw last-minute changes – most notably when Huang, the Nvidia boss, boarded Air Force One during a refuelling stop in Anchorage, Alaska. Alongside Huang, the delegation featured high-profile executives such as Tesla’s Elon Musk, Apple’s then-CEO Cook, and David Solomon from Goldman Sachs – most of whom walked away without concrete deals benefiting their companies. An exception was Boeing, represented by CEO Kelly Ortberg, which secured a commitment from Beijing for 200 jets, though the purchase has yet to materialise. During Xi’s 2017 US trip to meet Trump at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, no Chinese business executives accompanied him. However, during his 2015 state visit during the Barack Obama administration, 15 prominent Chinese corporate leaders – including Alibaba’s Jack Ma and Tencent Holdings’ Pony Ma – joined Xi for high-level business events in Seattle before he travelled to Washington. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Even if Chinese CEOs take part this time, political protocol could differ from that of the US. Unlike US executives boarding Air Force One, Chinese business leaders are more likely to travel separately, as in 2015, most had already landed in the US days before Xi’s arrival.

title: China launches its first commercial radio-tracking satellites in electronic warfare leap
description: The trio of satellites, named after an all-hearing mythical beast, can track enemy warships, hidden radars and electronic jammers.
content: China has just taken a quiet but critical step in space-based electronic warfare. A Lijian-1 Y18 rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northern China at noon on Sunday, carrying nine satellites. Among them were three Diting-01 satellites, which successfully entered their planned orbit. The trio is named after Diting, a beast from Chinese mythology that crouches beneath the desk of Ksitigarbha, the bodhisattva of the underworld, and can identify all things simply by listening. The name perfectly captures what these satellites are designed to do. The Diting satellites operate like sharp ears in space, constantly “listening” to radio signals rising from the Earth’s surface. They can pick up everything from warship radars and military communication networks to electronic jammers, and instantly locate where each signal is coming from.
