In a conflict, these satellites could track an enemy warship that has turned off its automatic identification system, pinpoint a hidden air-defence radar deep inside enemy territory, or map the entire electronic order of battle of an opposing force. The three satellites, developed by Chang Guang Satellite Technology and operated by StarRF, are the initial batch in China’s first commercial signals intelligence constellation. Space-based radio frequency sensing means placing radio receivers on satellites so they can monitor signals across large areas of land and sea from orbit. Compared with ground-based monitoring stations, satellites offer broader coverage. The company said in a press release that the constellation would be able to sense electromagnetic spectrum conditions over wide areas, rapidly and accurately locate radio emission sources, and provide “remote-sensing data” and data analysis services at the electromagnetic spectrum level. According to news portal Guancha, the satellites likely operate by simultaneously receiving the same radio signal from three distinct positions in orbit, using the time difference of arrival to pinpoint the emitter’s location with speed and precision. StarRF was founded in 2023. According to a job posting from the company, its founding team comes from Tsinghua University’s Department of Electronic Engineering and previously worked at companies including Nokia, Qualcomm and China Electronics Technology Group. The company aims to build a 60-satellite low-Earth-orbit electromagnetic spectrum monitoring constellation that is independently operated and capable of sensing signals emitted by various radio devices across wide areas. It plans to provide data and analysis services to customers in defence, public security, radio management, shipping, rail, transport, emergency rescue and other sectors. The launch puts China in the company of a handful of Western nations with commercial space-based radio monitoring. The American company HawkEye 360 launched its first three-satellite formation in 2018. Its customers include US defence and intelligence agencies, and it supports maritime surveillance and signals intelligence. France’s Unseenlabs is known for single-satellite geolocation. Its first generation of satellites focuses on maritime signals, while its second covers sea, land and space. Before ceasing operations in 2023, Luxembourg’s Kleos Space used satellite clusters to detect and locate radio transmissions, mainly for maritime intelligence and tracking illegal activities. These companies have maintained close commercial ties with militaries – a common feature of the space-based radio frequency monitoring industry, as such data is inherently dual-use. It remains unclear how extensive or accurate the Diting constellation’s monitoring will be. A Chang Guang Satellite representative said that no further information could be disclosed. As of publication, StarRF had not responded to an interview request.

title: As I see it | Taiwan might as well give up now
description: If Washington can’t or won’t defend the island, Taipei has no choice but to settle with Beijing.
content: The United States does not care much about democracy in general or Taiwan’s democracy in particular. Defending the island’s political system is a fairy tale it and its allies tell others; their real intention has always been to prevent China’s reunification and contain its rise. In reality, the island is a key node in the so-called first island chain for defence, or rather, offence against mainland China. It serves as a convenient pawn in disguising US dominance as defence of democracy. But secessionists in Taiwan such as those from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party have bought into the American propaganda, or rather, they happily propagate the fairy tale themselves. Taiwan’s routine purchase of outdated American weapons is not really for war, but more of a bribe constantly demanded by Washington. The weapons are not even being delivered on time. Taipei needs to maintain the pretence of deterrence, knowing Beijing has other options and would avoid a military operation as far as possible. It’s increasingly clear that the US not only won’t defend the island, but might not even help in a real crisis. Interestingly, an increasing number of mainstream US media outlets are admitting this reality. The Atlantic’s Simon Shuster has reported from Taiwan on what the island is willing to do to avoid war with mainland China. After speaking with officials in Taiwan and Washington, he concluded that the Taiwanese don’t trust US President Donald Trump, they don’t believe America will come to their defence, and that a deal with mainland China is starting to look inevitable. Shuster reports that the US war with Iran has helped Cheng Li-wun, leader of the opposition Kuomintang, make the case that resisting mainland China would be futile – with even Cheng’s opponents acknowledging that the Iran war has left the US less ready to defend Taiwan. Visiting Taiwan this past spring, Shuster saw how little faith remained in the US as a force for stability and protection. “This loss of confidence has forced many in Taiwan to rethink their attitude toward China,” he observed. Both Cheng and Chinese President Xi Jinping have expressed willingness to negotiate on the basis of shared identity, free trade, economic bonds and peaceful coexistence. But as Shuster notes, the US still has an economic incentive to exercise deterrence: more than 90 per cent of the world’s most advanced chips are made in Taiwan – including those driving the AI revolution, which has propped up the American economy – and the US is determined to deny mainland China access to that crucial resource. Otherwise, the game is almost up for the island. Shared principles of freedom and democracy no longer count for much in this debate. When the subject came up in my interviews in Taipei and Washington, people seemed embarrassed to talk about American values, as if the idea were quaint Simon Shuster “Taiwan and its defenders struggle to explain why Americans should care enough about their cause to risk war with China,” Shuster wrote. “Shared principles of freedom and democracy no longer count for much in this debate. When the subject came up in my interviews in Taipei and Washington, people seemed embarrassed to talk about American values, as if the idea were quaint.” Instead, the more forceful argument for defending Taiwan came from those looking to exploit the island “as a platform to secure American dominance over the Pacific”. But the unravelling of Pax Americana has become obvious. “China’s allies in Taipei need only point to Trump’s prevarications as proof that the Americans cannot be trusted,” Shuster wrote. “That may be all Xi needs to take Taiwan without firing a shot.” Writing for Foreign Policy, columnist James Crabtree argues that Trump has killed “strategic ambiguity” over Taiwan. The immediate fear is that Trump might trade away Taiwan’s security during his coming summit with Xi, he wrote, undermining America’s long-standing posture of “strategic ambiguity”. Developed in the late 1970s, the idea has been to avoid stating whether the US would defend Taiwan militarily, thereby deterring mainland Chinese aggression while restraining Taiwanese provocation. Trump’s instincts threaten this balance. He views Taiwan with suspicion, complains it “stole” America’s semiconductor industry, and questions the idea of travelling “9,500 miles to fight a war”. His administration’s “constructive strategic stability” framework with Beijing implies that support for Taiwan should be managed carefully to preserve broader relations. Some Trump advisers explicitly argue against defending Taiwan. While officials insist the policy remains unchanged, Trump’s rhetoric and actions – including holding up a US$14 billion arms package as negotiating leverage – suggest a drift towards non-intervention. The charade of American deterrence is increasingly obvious. Reports that Trump rejected Saudi pleas to help strike the Houthis in Yemen could only reinforce Taipei’s scepticism about Washington’s defence commitments. Taipei should reorient its stance, distance itself from the US, and approach Beijing with humility and goodwill with a view to reaching a final satisfactory settlement of its constitutional status within China.

title: Beat writer’s block with tricks to unlock creativity and get words flowing
description: Lower expectations, try free-writing, change fonts and talk it out to clear the way.
content:
We’ve all experienced it. You’re sitting at your desk, the air conditioner is humming, and your document is staring back at you with a judgmental, blinking cursor.
Whether you’re trying to tackle an English essay, draft a personal statement for university applications, or write a caption for your latest Instagram reel, your brain has completely shut down.
Welcome to writer’s block. It’s frustrating, stressful and can honestly make you want to close your laptop and scroll on your phone for three hours. But here’s the good news: your creativity isn’t gone; it’s stuck, much like a traffic jam during rush hour.
This is your ultimate guide to clearing the tracks and getting your words flowing again.
The biggest obstacle to writing isn’t a lack of ideas; it’s the pressure to create the perfect first draft. When you’re staring at that blinking cursor, you tend to edit while you write, which is like trying to drive a car with the handbrake engaged.
The rules: Give yourself permission to write the worst paragraph in history. Do not worry about grammar, structure or vocabulary.
Why it works: It is much easier to edit a poorly written page than a blank one. Once the words are on the screen, the pressure is lifted.
When the brain jams up, you need to trick it into moving again. Set a timer on your phone for exactly five minutes.
The rules: Put your fingers on the keyboard and start typing. You are not allowed to stop typing until the timer goes off.
Why it works: If you do not know what to write, just type: “I don’t know what to write.” Eventually, your brain will get bored with complaining and subconsciously drift back to the topic you actually need to work on.
If you’ve been staring at the same default Times New Roman font for an hour, your brain might associate that visual layout with failure. Break the cycle by switching up your font.
The rules: Change your font to something else – even Comic Sans. Writing in a “silly” font might even lower your subconscious expectations, making it easier to type without overthinking. You can always change it back to something else later.
Why it works: A change of font can make your work a bit more refreshing.
You don’t always need to stay in the same spot while you’re working.
The rules: If you are trapped in your bedroom, pack your bag and head to a public library or even another room in your house.
Why it works: Sometimes, a change of scenery and a little ambient noise are exactly what your brain needs to unlock.
Often, we get stuck because writing feels so formal. But if a friend sat down next to you and asked, “Hey, what is your personal statement actually about?” you wouldn’t freeze. You’d just tell them.
The rules: Open the voice recorder app on your phone and pretend you are explaining the topic to a friend. Speak naturally, use slang and do not overthink it. Once you’re done, play it back and type out what you just said. Boom – you’ve officially started writing.
Why it works: Not everyone learns best by writing. Some people’s brains work better when they are saying things out loud.

title: Shelters warn against poor treatment of warehouse guard dogs in New Territories
description: Veteran rescuer says free-roaming warehouse canines fall under definition of stray dogs, with issue in spotlight after suspected fatal attack.
content: Poor treatment of guard dogs at warehouses before ditching them in unfamiliar environments could make the animals easier to agitate, rescuers have said, calling for a “trap, neuter and release” approach, among other solutions. Concerns about the handling of stray dogs entered the media spotlight after a 27-year-old woman was discovered along a cycle path in Yuen Long after suffering lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs. She was later pronounced dead at Pok Oi Hospital. On Saturday night, three dogs were seen chasing the woman along Pok Wai South Road in an area with several warehouses. Jacqueline Cheung, founder of the non-profit Love Adopt Animal Society, said that free-roaming warehouse guard dogs fell under the broad definition of stray dogs, which also covered abandoned pets on the streets and wild canines that stayed in the mountains and away from urban areas. She warned that these dogs, which have strong territorial instincts, could turn aggressive if they felt someone was intruding on their territory. Much of a canine’s behaviour was shaped and conditioned by humans, the veteran rescuer added. “Some warehouse dogs are constantly chased away, beaten, splashed with water or have things thrown at them … while others may be chained up with heavy iron chains,” Cheung said. This factor, combined with the clearance of warehouses and car parks as part of land resumption works, could naturally leave dogs feeling anxious and insecure in an unfamiliar environment, putting them on high alert, she said. Cheung said many warehouses, open car parks and villages in the New Territories, including parts of Sheung Shui, Ping Shan, Fanling and Yuen Long – where the suspected attack took place – had resorted to guard dogs for decades. She estimated that about 80 per cent of dogs in those environments were kept as working animals and largely suffered neglect. Such dogs were often fed table scraps and leftovers, while warehouse operators would frequently leave them unfed over public holidays, she said. Cheung added that warehouse and car park operators typically did not neuter their dogs and raised them in a free-roaming manner. “It is very hard for us to tell whether they actually belong to someone or not. Some might have a collar, but most probably do not. It’s just that they constantly linger around those warehouses or car parks,” she said. When these free-roaming dogs were injured or infected, some owners would call volunteers to collect them after the animals ceased to be useful, she said. Cheung described the situation as a decade-long issue that needed to be solved at its roots. Temporarily trapping such canines, spaying them and then releasing them back into their original environment was the best solution for controlling the population while sparing their lives, she said. Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, said a possible long-term solution was creating a government animal shelter managed by charitable organisations that could neuter the dogs and help them find adopters, and an alternative to culling. Figures shared by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department on Tuesday revealed 338 dogs were euthanised in 2021, before dipping to 280 a year later. In 2023, the figure reached 372, before rising to 436 a year later and then dipping to 375 in 2025. Counting the 102 dogs euthanised in the first three months of this year, the tally since 2021 stood at 1,903. The figures included strays, animals surrendered by owners and dogs involved in court cases. The number of dogs transferred to animal welfare organisations for adoption arrangements dropped steadily from 348 in 2021, the same number the next year, before dipping to 319 in 2023, climbing slightly to 328 a year later and falling to 226 in 2025. But since 2004, complaints related to stray dogs had dropped from nearly 20,000 cases annually to about 1,300 in recent years, the department said. Luk said education and subsidies were needed to promote an adoption culture, adding that harsher fines and penalties should be imposed on pet smugglers to potentially help bring down the stray animal population. A San Tin resident also spoke to the South China Morning Post about his own experiences with dogs in the area. The resident, who only gave his name as Chan, recalled cycling home from Yuen Long in late February when his path was blocked by four or five dogs, about 1km (1,093 yards) from where the woman was found over the weekend. Chan said he tried to loop his bike back towards the vehicle road beside the cycle lane, but the dogs rushed onto the road and barred any way forward, forcing him to turn back and take a longer alternative route home. He said the problem had persisted for a long time, with many residents in Yuen Long and his village having been bitten or chased by dogs. The dogs behind the attacks included “free-range” animals kept at nearby container gardens, recycling depots and car workshops in the district’s big open-air working areas, he said. “The dogs are there to guard the entrance, but somehow they end up sitting further and further out, until they have basically left their original spot and wandered out onto the road,” Chan said. “I don’t have a problem with stray dogs existing as purely a road user, but it will be dangerous if they are blocking the road for passers-by.” A Thread user also shared in February that he, his father and a cousin were chased by about 10 more dogs near the Yuen Long Sewage Treatment Works in January. “I pedalled as hard as I could – I nearly lost my balance, and the bike nearly went out of control before I managed to shake them off,” he said.

title: Siobhan Haughey stakes claim as Hong Kong’s greatest athlete after fourth Asian Games title
description: Hongkonger says 100m freestyle title defence has ‘special meaning’ after injuries, need to change training regime in face of age, new rivals.
content: Siobhan Haughey may have cemented her place as Hong Kong’s best athlete ever after capturing yet another Asian Games gold medal on Tuesday. Touching the wall first in 52.45 seconds – ahead of a pack of swimmers at least three years younger – to defend her women’s 100m freestyle title successfully pushed Haughey’s gold medal count at the regional multi-sports bonanza to four, after she also retained the 200m freestyle crown she won in Hangzhou the previous day. From showcasing to the world her immense talent in the water at the World Junior Championships in Dubai in 2013, the Hongkonger has gone on to scoop medals, one after another, across every major event, for 13 years and counting. The five-time world champion is the city’s outright leader in Olympic medals with four – two silver and two bronze – from two Games in Tokyo and Paris. “I am very happy to win another gold medal, not to mention that my family was watching from the stands,” Haughey, who will turn 29 at the end of next month, said. “There was a special meaning for me to remain on top of the podium in back-to-back Games, especially after I’ve been through quite a lot over the past few years. “I have had an extended break, then there were injuries, and it’s not only that, because when you look at the current trends in the swimming world – where more and more very young teenagers are swimming incredibly fast and achieving impressive results – it’s truly not easy to get back to, and maintaining that level after a few years.” Whether Haughey could be considered the best athlete Hong Kong has ever had is a topic that would certainly spark endless debate. Elite fencer Cheung Ka-long would also be right up there with a pair of Olympic gold medals from Japan and France, as well as his podiums at the Asian and World Championships, and the junior world championships crown. And, of course, former windsurfer Lee Lai-shan would be the pioneer of them all. A maiden Olympic gold medal for Hong Kong in 1996, two Asian Games crowns and a trio of world championship titles speak volumes. Whichever way the debate goes, what is clear is that the difficulty in maintaining competitiveness at the highest level is something beyond most people’s comprehension. “The changes in me had to be the most difficult part, be it my mindset or my recovery ability,” Haughey said. “So the training methods I used in the past, I simply couldn’t go back to using them. “The issue is that, while those past methods were what got me to this peak level, my body really can’t keep up with that kind of training any more. “We have to keep changing and finding new ways – by reducing the training volume – to figure out how to maintain this high level of performance while swimming less.” While athletes usually leave the adjustments of training regimes to their coaches, the decorated swimmer from Hong Kong said there were also mental difficulties to deal with. “My recovery is not as fast now, plus the injuries, so every time I think of needing or wanting to make up for the training I missed, there were a lot of mental adjustments required too,” she said. “It’s really about how to wait patiently for my recovery, without feeling like ‘Oh no, I haven’t trained much over the past two weeks, how am I going to catch up?’ “So there were a lot of changes involved, both physically and mentally.” The man helping Haughey deliver world-class performances in the autumn of her career said his disciple was merely on the same path as any athlete as they age. “With any athlete, as they age, recovery becomes more important. They don’t bounce back from things; we all know this as we get older,” said coach Tom Rushton, who started working with Haughey after the Tokyo Games. “Life becomes a little bit harder, but at the same time, you become a little bit smarter and wiser about how to manage things. The younger athletes in my group do 10 sessions per week in the water, and that’s what Siobhan did between Tokyo and Paris. “Now, the older athletes are shifting down to nine sessions, and that was a change we made after the [last] Olympics. It’s about focusing on the volume of fast swimming, not the volume of total swimming.” Keeping herself motivated, after winning almost everything there was to win, was another thing to master, and Haughey said it was not about achieving “a specific time or winning a particular title” now. “The focus now is more on the race strategies and their execution, and making sure I still enjoy my daily training and competition to the fullest,” the 28-year-old said. “I will be giving myself so much pressure if it’s a time-sensitive target. “Say, if you plan to manage a 51-second swim, but you don’t have a plan of how you’re going to do it, you’d get stuck easily, so I’d rather focus on what changes I could make.” Haughey also said “I would have quit a long time ago” had she not felt motivated enough to want to go to the swimming pool after waking up. “I am motivated by the process, not the result. This is how I have always thought, only even more so in recent years,” said the veteran swimmer. “When you were younger, without many medals or records, you were always chasing a time standard and that worked back then. “But at this stage, I prefer not to put so much pressure on myself to maintain my training and competition schedule. So instead of focusing on results, it’s better to focus on what can be done each day. “As for Los Angeles, I do have some ideas in my mind, but right now the focus is still on the Asian Games.”

title: China’s AI self-reliance presents opportunities but valuations, geopolitics are risks: BofA
description: The nation’s tech firms are catching up with overseas rivals while a wave of high-profile listings has broadened investment opportunities.
content: China’s push for tech self-reliance is opening new investment opportunities in artificial intelligence stocks, but stretched valuations and geopolitical tensions make the sector an increasingly risky bet, according to Bank of America. The country’s tech firms are catching up with overseas rivals while a wave of high-profile listings has broadened investment opportunities, Winnie Wu, head of Asia-Pacific equity strategy research and co-head of China equity research at Bank of America, said in a media briefing in Hong Kong on Tuesday. “Localisation is no longer just a policy ambition,” Wu said. “The domestic players are closing the gaps in technology standards, gaining market share [and] making tangible progress.” The bank divided Chinese AI-related stocks into three broad groups, each offering a different risk-return profile. Semiconductor equipment makers, foundries, memory-chip companies and AI accelerator developers could benefit from both AI growth and Beijing’s drive for tech self-reliance and import substitution, Wu said. Their earnings were relatively insulated from a potential slowdown in US AI investment because they mainly served the domestic market, she added. Valuations, however, had become a concern, with some stocks trading at between 50 and 150 times earnings even after recent declines, while investor positioning had become relatively crowded, according to Wu. A second group was composed of Chinese suppliers benefiting from the global AI infrastructure buildout, including makers of optical components, printed circuit boards and other hardware, which trade at lower valuations of around 20 to 40 times earnings, according to the bank. However, they faced additional risks from their greater exposure to US AI capital expenditure and potential restrictions on Chinese technology, Bank of America added. Investors were more cautious towards a third category – AI applications from large-language models to humanoid robots and physical AI edge devices – due to the absence of a clear “killer app”, low switching costs and emerging price competition, Wu said. The assessment comes as investors await a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, with trade, AI and tech export restrictions on the agenda. Xi will visit the US from Wednesday to Friday and meet Trump on Thursday, their second face-to-face meeting this year. Wu said US restrictions on Chinese technology might have limited short-term impact on earnings since Chinese companies remained dominant suppliers for some US companies, but regulatory uncertainty could weigh on their valuations. “Market expectation is quite low, so there is not much room for disappointment,” Wu said. Separately, Bank of America forecast that China’s AI capital expenditure would rise from US$90 billion in 2025 to US$330 billion by 2030, as investments in computing infrastructure continue to drive demand in power equipment, energy storage and other parts of the supply chain.

title: Gulf tech firms turn to Hong Kong and Singapore as Iran war grinds on
description: Analysts point to growing adoption of a ‘dual-hub’ model, using secondary Asian bases to hedge against geopolitical risk.
content: Paul Bratby had already drawn up plans for expanding to Hong Kong when war broke out in the Middle East earlier this year. But the founder of xBratAI, a Dubai-based AI-powered trading signals platform, soon brought that timeline forward as the Iran conflict dragged on and widened in scope. “Our Hong Kong entity had been scheduled for a few years later, but we established it in early 2026,” he said. Bratby is not alone in looking east. As missiles continue to target Gulf capitals and shipping lanes, digital businesses and investors are increasingly setting up shop in Hong Kong and Singapore. “The war has influenced the pace of expansion into East Asian hubs more than it has redrawn the map. Firms that can relocate cheaply have done so,” Bratby said, adding: “Hong Kong and Singapore are now treated as primary growth markets.” For many, these new Asian bases supplement established operations in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, creating what Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based adviser to governments on blockchain and information technology, calls a “dual-hub” model. “We are not seeing an outright exodus from the Gulf, but we are witnessing an accelerated shift towards proactive geopolitical hedging,” he said. “Major digital and tech enterprises are no longer content with relying on a single operational anchor.” Ali Moosa, executive vice-chairman of Bahrain-headquartered Singapore Gulf Bank, said the conflict had accelerated Gulf businesses’ use of Asian financial hubs. “Business continues during uncertainty,” he said. “Companies still need to pay suppliers, buy equipment, meet payroll and complete projects.” In the long term, greater access to Asian capital and investment could support growth in the Gulf, Moosa said. The closer the Gulf becomes to Asia, the more capital Gulf businesses can access and the more opportunities they can pursue Ali Moosa, Singapore Gulf Bank “The closer the Gulf becomes to Asia, the more capital Gulf businesses can access and the more opportunities they can pursue,” he said, adding he expected “many of these relationships to continue after the immediate disruption ends”. The disruption could last for some time, however, as the conflict continues to widen. At the weekend, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis claimed missile and drone strikes on “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh and on an Aramco facility in the Red Sea oil export hub of Yanbu. Britain has agreed to help Saudi Arabia’s military counter the Houthis, whose attacks have increasingly threatened shipping near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Meanwhile, Singaporean financial institutions have been setting up cross-border digital networks and multicurrency settlement methods to carry Gulf capital into a region undergoing an unprecedented infrastructure boom, driven by the race for AI data centre capacity. Building AI infrastructure was enormously capital intensive, Lian said, pointing to the huge amounts of upfront investment required for high-voltage power grids, industrial cooling systems and the like. “Middle Eastern institutional capital is uniquely suited to this demand,” he said. “Gulf investors possess deep familiarity with massive, energy-intensive infrastructure projects, and they are deploying liquidity directly into Southeast Asia’s digital backbone.” The Asia-Pacific’s financial services industry is forecast to nearly double in value to US$4.8 trillion by 2035, according to a Deloitte report published last month – overtaking the United States, whose industry is projected to reach US$4.3 trillion over the same period. Gulf sovereign wealth funds were hungry for exposure to Asia’s consumer digital economy and industrial supply chains, and Asian fund managers and technology consortiums were more than happy to oblige, Lian said. Iranian attacks on data centres in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates led to service outages earlier in the conflict, fuelling a surge of interest in Southeast Asian alternatives, said Raj Kapoor, founder of the India Blockchain Alliance. This had “introduced something that technology companies historically treated as an unlikely tail risk”, he said. Even so, Kapoor said the Gulf would remain central to the global AI buildout as tech companies had already sunk billions of US dollars into the region, with government backing and it “therefore makes little sense” for them “simply to abandon those markets”. “So I see this mainly as diversification rather than relocation,” he said.

title: Manga mania: how Japanese comics conquered the world
description: From museum walls to blockbuster screens, Japan’s graphic storytelling is expanding its cultural reach, commercial power and international fan base.
content: “The Japanese are thrilled by the growing appreciation for manga around the world – that it’s now read from Saudi Arabia to France to the US – and all at the same time,” enthuses Nicole Rousmaniere, founder of the UK’s Sainsbury Institute for the Study of Japanese Arts and Cultures at the University of East Anglia. “Manga is becoming a universal language.” Certainly the distinctive imagery of the Japanese graphic novel tradition is increasingly finding its way from page to museum wall. Rousmaniere is also the curator behind the Brooklyn Museum’s forthcoming “Art of Manga” exhibition (running October 3 to January 31, 2027) – previously a hit at the de Young Fine Art Museum in San Francisco – while manga is a part of “Myths and Monsters: The Art of Fantasy in Asia” at Hong Kong’s M+ museum from October 17 to April 4, 2027. Indeed, move over, Marvel Cinematic Universe: manga – together with anime, the Japanese style of animation that often uses manga as its source material – has over recent years spawned global, multibillion-dollar entertainment properties, from Dragon Ball to Naruto, One Piece and Jujutsu Kaisen. And therein also lies a problem. Not only has manga, which translates roughly as “whimsical pictures”, traditionally been printed in black and white on recycled paper – “which has given people the impression that it’s ephemera and not worth much serious consideration”, says Rousmaniere, even as Japanese art has historically been ephemeral in nature. But also, the limited range of manga that has been translated, especially into English, and made available outside Japan, has long been aimed squarely at teenage boys, if only in the belief that that is what would sell. “They haven’t taken the risk to publish some of the truly exquisite work [around],” says Rousmaniere. And that is despite the fact that, just like written novels, there’s a manga for everyone, on any type of topic. Varieties of manga run the gamut from, yes, lots of boy-friendly battling robots, but also drama, romance, history, sport, politics and pornography. One recent hit has been on the mundane joys of solo camping. Today around half of manga’s readership is female, with the same going for its leading artists too. Relative to Western comic books, manga’s narratives are more mature as well: less stories of superheroic individuals and their inevitable victories, more a celebration of relatable characters who might not win, but at least stuck to the course. “It’s not about flashy shows of force,” says Rousmaniere. “Manga typically has more of an interior world for the reader to have a dialogue with.” Perceptions are changing though. Technology has played a huge part in manga’s spread over recent years, argues Helen McCarthy, author of new book The Manga Bible (Ilex Press), with digital editions making much more manga accessible worldwide. “So in most people’s eyes it’s suddenly leapt from being a very niche interest to seemingly being everywhere,” she says. Also of influence is the fact that manga now makes a lot of money: it is predicted that the manga/anime market will be half the size of the global movie market by 2033. Piracy has even become a major problem for manga publishers. “It wasn’t long ago that you’d hear about a kid maybe being the only fan of manga in their school – and being considered a weirdo for it. But now manga has been liberated, in its reach and its appeal,” enthuses McCarthy. “Manga first took off outside Japan in countries with their own established comic cultures – France, Spain and Italy, for example – not because theirs weren’t very good but because Japan’s offered something very different. And people today are seeing in manga different things about their own culture, seen through different eyes.” That is proving a template for other cultures too, with the rise of Indian and African manga. All the same, size doesn’t mean quality. Should manga really be considered an art form? Absolutely, argues Rousmaniere. Not only does manga “tell really fantastic stories through this distinctive visual language – and we’re all moving towards a more visual culture”, she stresses, but its imagery – typically drawn freehand, in black ink with nib pens, by a single artist, often over dozens and sometimes hundreds of volumes – is part of a much longer artistic tradition that, as Rousmaniere puts it, “is all in the line”. Manga, as a comic format, may be roughly a century old, but can trace its foundational roots back to the 12th century. The Japanese have been combining words and pictures in illustrated novels since the 1700s, and see the medium less as “Japanese cartoon strips” – as they’re often dismissed – as a means of cultural expression. Hokusai? Kyosai? These great names – as pertinent to the story of Japanese art as are Dürer or Monet to the Western tradition – practised a form of manga. “If people doubtful of manga being art went to see it, they’d come away thinking very differently,” says Rousmaniere. “Look at the quality and the storytelling and the impact [of some works] I don’t see how anyone could not call it art. There’s good reason why in Japan it’s considered a very developed art form.” Not for nothing has Weekly Shōnen Jump, Japan’s bestselling anthology – a phone book-sized weekly publication – sold some 7.5 billion copies since its launch in 1968. “That manga sometimes isn’t considered to be art [outside Japan] is just snobbery, and in the art world in particular,” says McCarthy, adding that comic books – privileging the visual image over the written word – have long been denigrated round the world as a working-class interest. It’s a viewpoint Rousmaniere echoes. When the subject was first proposed for the De Young exhibition, the museum was accused of “selling out”, she recalls. And when she devised a pioneering exhibition for the British Museum in London in 2019, “some people really thought manga should not have been in there too”. But, as Monkey D Luffy, the main protagonist in One Piece, puts it, “If you don’t take risks, you can’t create a future.” Manga may go back much further than many realise, but there’s little question that it’s also going to shape the visual world of tomorrow.

title: In pictures: the evolution of Hong Kong’s Mid-Autumn mooncake
description: From instalment plans to chilled ‘snow-skin’ innovations, Hong Kong’s mooncake traditions have continually evolved across decades of Mid-Autumn celebrations.
content: Mid-Autumn Festival preparations begin long before the autumn moon appears. Throughout the mid- to late-20th century, gifting mooncakes was an essential gesture of goodwill and familial respect in Hong Kong. However, they were a luxury that few could afford to buy outright, and so neighbourhood bakeries offered instalment plans – known as mooncake clubs – that allowed families to deposit small monthly sums to guarantee a cherished box of the stodgy treats come festival night. Although the classic lotus-seed-paste and salted-egg-yolk filling remains a staple, Hong Kong’s festive palate has evolved. Taipan Bread & Cakes, which closed its doors in 2025, revolutionised the market in 1989, with its delicate, chilled snow-skin mooncakes – instead of a baked, golden-brown pastry crust, the skin was made from cooked glutinous rice flour, and fillings included mung-bean paste, jam, matcha, chocolate, coffee, cheese and durian – which were a hit with younger generations. As preferences shifted, ice cream brought a cool modern spin to mooncakes, then “molten-lava” custard fillings sparked a trend. The emergence of mini mooncakes, meanwhile, made seasonal treats easier to enjoy and share. These modern innovations have offered a refreshing departure from traditional, heavy pastries without sacrificing the holiday spirit. Here’s a look back at how South China Morning Post photographers have captured the enduring Mid-Autumn tradition and the evolution of Hong Kong’s mooncakes.

title: Canada seeks to wrap up India trade talks soon, as US ties fray
description: PM Carney says his Indian counterpart Modi will visit Canada around the time of the G20 summit in Miami this December.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that trade negotiations with India are making “good progress” and that the two countries are aiming to conclude talks by the G20 summit in mid-December. Carney also said India had, to his understanding, confirmed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi would visit Canada around that time, though the precise date had not been finalised. “We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India,” Carney said at a news conference on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Carney said he and Modi had committed to try to conclude negotiations by the G20. The summit is scheduled for December 14-15 at Trump National Doral in Miami. Carney wants to double Canada’s non-US trade over the next decade and has made India part of a broader effort to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States as relations deteriorate under US President Donald Trump. Last week, Carney embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member, saying deeper ties with Europe would help ensure no country could control Canada’s markets or undermine its sovereignty. Carney also struck a deal with China earlier this year allowing a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at a sharply reduced tariff in exchange for China lowering tariffs on Canadian canola. Canada and India formally launched negotiations on a comprehensive trade agreement in March, with both governments committing to conclude talks by the end of 2026. The rapid economic rapprochement follows a deep diplomatic rupture over the 2023 killing of Canadian Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia. Former prime minister Justin Trudeau said there were credible allegations linking agents of the Indian government to Nijjar’s killing. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police later said it had evidence allegedly linking Indian government agents to homicides and other violent acts in Canada. Trudeau said Indian diplomats had collected information about Canadians that was passed to organised crime and resulted in violence. Canada expelled six Indian diplomats amid the allegations. India denied involvement and accused Canada of harbouring Sikh separatists. Carney has moved quickly to rebuild ties. His visit to India earlier this year was the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister since 2018.

title: Sunil Grover on bringing his hilarious Indian TV characters to Hong Kong
description: The Indian comedian and actor talks about celebrating what he’s done on TV and some of the Bollywood actors he’s going to impersonate.
content: Best known for his hilarious portrayals of characters such as Gutthi, Dr Mashoor Gulati and Rinku Devi on Indian television, comedian and actor Sunil Grover is bringing his trademark character comedy to Hong Kong for one night only at the Hopewell Hotel’s Grand Ballroom in Wan Chai on September 27. “This is all about celebrating what I’ve done on television so far,” Grover, 49, says. With a career spanning more than two decades, Grover rose to national fame for his iconic characters: Gutthi on Comedy Nights with Kapil, Dr Mashoor Gulati and Rinku Devi on The Kapil Sharma Show, and those in Bollywood films including Ghajini (2008), Gabbar Is Back (2015), Bharat (2019) and Jawan (2023). He confirms all will be part of the Hong Kong set. “Those characters which I have done … these are the popular characters people like watching, and I love performing these characters,” he says. “I’m bringing everything with me.” When asked about his favourite character, Grover is diplomatic – but honest. “All characters are my favourite. Characters which are liked by people are my favourite characters. But I like to perform as Dr Mashoor Gulati a lot, and of course I love dressing up in a sari for them.” He also promises to bring his infamous Bollywood mimicry to the stage. “Salman Khan, Aamir Khan, Shah Rukh Khan – actors who people love, I’m going to impersonate them,” he says. Emphasising that his television work is what allows him to tour, Grover explains that “both have different joys”. “Because we work behind the camera, people like watching us live also. It’s the outcome of performing in a studio that we get to perform live.” Having done tours for close to 13 years now, Grover says the thrill of being in front of an audience is like no other – an “energy that is altogether different”. For him, the biggest reward of live shows is the connection with the audience. “With live shows, you get to travel, you get to see the people who are on that other side of the screen. People see us – performers, actors, comedians – on the screen, but we get to see those people who are giving so much love from the other side. “That is the joy for me.” Sunil Grover Live, Grand Ballroom, Hopewell Hotel, 15 Kennedy Road, Wan Chai, September 27, 7pm. Tickets start from HK$450 and are available via Premier Tickets.

title: Editorial | Trump-Xi summit a key step towards managing conflict more wisely
description: The summit in Washington may not result in a grand bargain but discussions on AI, trade and the military offer hope of progress on managing disagreements.
content: After eight hours of talks in New York, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng managed to lay the groundwork for the two countries’ leaders to meet this week. Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump must be seen to make progress at their pivotal summit, even if few expect breakthroughs. Xi will arrive at the White House for the first time since 2015, as a trade war truce is set to expire on November 10, effectively a deadline that exerts intense pressure on both sides. Most people do not expect a grand bargain, but it will be a win-win if they succeed in stabilising the most consequential bilateral relationship of our era. US and Chinese officials hailed positive talks on artificial intelligence (AI), trade and investment ahead of the summit. The ceremonial weight is unmistakable. Washington will accord Xi an airport welcome of a kind not seen since a papal visit – a signal of how seriously the United States takes this relationship. Trump hinted he might attend November’s Apec meeting in Shenzhen. A pattern of high-level exchange is now consolidating, bringing with it a stabilising trend in a relationship that a fractured world can ill afford to see unravel. No one, on either side, is harbouring grand expectations. Both governments understand that their relationship is deeply complicated – freighted with tariff disputes, technology rivalry, Taiwan tensions, and accumulated distrust. Yet both also understand something more fundamental. Despite their many conflicts, they must learn to live with one another. The world, facing compounding crises, needs their cooperation, not merely their competitive coexistence. Nowhere is this more acutely true than in artificial intelligence (AI). The US has proposed a bilateral notification mechanism for national security AI incidents and backed a formal “US-China AI dialogue” around common goals and threats. This is a good beginning. Cooperation would benefit both sides, yet mutual suspicion may still prevent it. The critical question is whether AI safety discussions remain a ring-fenced technical channel between experts, or become absorbed into broader trade negotiations – another bargaining chip alongside tariffs and rare earths. Neither side would accept the unilateral imposition of rules on AI; common standards, developed and agreed on jointly, offer the only durable foundation. On trade, the agenda is dense and largely unresolved. The US-China Board of Trade, now in operation, opens a path to reduced tariffs on non-sensitive goods – consumer products, energy, agricultural exports and medical devices. They will need to chart a clear way forward before the trade-war truce expires in less than two months. One relatively easy deal would be to revive a US$6 billion-a-year trade in US liquefied natural gas of about 14 million tonnes. It has been suspended due to retaliatory tariffs. China is the world’s largest buyer of LNG and, because of the Iran war, faces pressing supply pressures following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. A long-term deal would serve both sides. China’s auto and battery executives – such as those from BYD and Xiaomi – will join Xi’s delegation, signalling possible US investments. Rare earths, fentanyl and the intriguing possibility of Chinese carmaker investment in the US crowd the agenda, reflecting how deeply the two economies remain intertwined. But any such Chinese investments will need US guarantees that they will be protected. The military dimension is somewhat encouraging. Commanders Yang Zhibin and Samuel Paparo met face to face in Canada, the first such command-level encounter in two years. Both sides are rebuilding dialogue at three levels: presidential, ministerial and frontline. Arms-control talks, suspended in 2024 over Taiwan arms sales, may well be revived. Progress remains slow but it can be sustained and deepened. This summit is a carefully managed encounter between two superpowers that approach each other with clear eyes and no illusions. It will not resolve what decades have entrenched. But the world does not need Washington and Beijing to agree on everything. It needs them to manage their disagreements and conflicts more wisely. This summit, carefully calibrated, will be a step forward in that direction.

title: As Buffett exits, can China win back Wall Street with own brand of his winning formula?
description: Chinese regulators push patient capital, reshape US$4.5 trillion mutual fund industry towards long-term holdings as foreign investors weigh risks against thin IPO pipelines.
content: China is betting that patient capital, rather than quick trades, will define its next phase of growth – a wager that has taken on new resonance since Warren Buffett stepped down last week after growing Berkshire Hathaway into a US$1 trillion empire over six decades. And as global investors watch this week’s US-China leadership summit for any sign of easing friction, one question is whether Beijing’s version of Buffett’s value-investing legacy can help Wall Street regain its appetite for Chinese assets. “The long-term return nature of Berkshire’s philosophy coincides with China’s economic philosophy,” said Tommy Ong, managing director of Hong Kong-based T.O. & Associates Consultancy. After Buffett, now 96, announced his retirement plans last year, Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, declared that the billionaire’s emphasis on “long-term value investing, rational investment, and striving to reward investors will never retire”. Regulators are also reshaping the country’s roughly US$4.5 trillion mutual fund industry, shifting incentive structures away from short-term speculation and towards longer holding periods. “China is treating long-term value investing not as a legacy strategy, but as a national financial objective,” said Bruno S. Sergi, an instructor at Harvard University with expertise in development economics and emerging markets. Policymakers, he explained, want investors to back priorities such as advanced manufacturing, electric vehicles and industrial upgrading over quick trades. Berkshire’s own exit from BYD last year put that philosophy to the test. The firm closed out a 17-year holding that turned an initial bet of roughly US$230 million into more than 20 times its value – one of the most profitable foreign investments in Chinese corporate history. Sergi also pointed to how Berkshire abruptly cut its holdings in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) just months after purchasing a multibillion-dollar stake in late 2022, and then started adding to Japanese trading houses. But Sergi characterised the move as broader caution about geopolitical exposure rather than a verdict on China alone. Buffett himself was widely quoted in April 2023 as saying that geopolitical tensions were “a consideration” in Berkshire’s decision to unload TSMC shares. Even so, that high-profile exit deepened doubts among foreign institutions that were already weighing political risks against a thinning pipeline of new listings. “They are more cautious now, due to the political-risk consideration,” said Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial in New York. He pointed to Chinese companies that listed in the US in numbers of roughly 50 to 60 in each of 2024 and 2025, against just two so far this year, leaving investors “very little to choose from”. Some big names are buying anyway. Appaloosa Management’s David Tepper nearly doubled his stake in Baidu to about US$148 million last quarter, according to regulatory filings, while billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller’s Duquesne Family Office returned to Chinese stocks for the first time in more than two years with a US$10 million position in the same company. Foreign holdings of yuan-denominated Chinese stocks tracked under the Qualified Foreign Institutional Investors (QFII) scheme jumped 87 per cent to about US$40.6 billion last quarter, according to data provider Wind. Attention now turns to President Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit that kicks off on Wednesday, with tariffs, rare earth supply chains and AI development controls likely on the agenda. Some analysts suspected that the summit was more likely to move sentiment than substance, at least in the near term. “A summit can improve sentiment for a quarter; only policy clarity can improve capital allocation for a decade,” Sergi said. Ong at T.O. & Associates further noted that a dearth of surprises in near-term economic performance and policy support – the type of developments that exceed market expectations – remained a barrier to US investors. Broader appetite, he said, would return only “if US investors see a large stimulus package from China”.

title: Zelensky meets Trump, says Ukraine ready for energy truce with Russia
description: The US president announced such a truce last week, but Russia ‌hit petrol stations in Kyiv the next day and Ukraine bombed an oil refinery.
content: Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday that he and US President Donald Trump had discussed efforts to end the four-year-old war with Russia, including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets. Speaking to the media after a 40-minute meeting with Trump at UN headquarters in New York, Zelensky said Kyiv was ready for any ‌format of an energy ceasefire with Moscow but there had been no discussion of Ukraine unilaterally halting its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump, whose approval ratings have slumped to a record low amid high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections in November, had expressed concern in recent days over the extensive damage done to Russia’s fuel-processing capacity, which he said was stoking diesel prices globally. Zelensky reiterated that he was ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a trilateral meeting with Trump, adding that he hoped the US would find a way to bring Moscow back to the ⁠negotiating table after talks unravelled earlier this year. Zelensky, however, said he had seen no indication that Putin was ready to talk. “I’m ready for a trilateral meeting. It ‌means that I’m agreed to end the war,” Zelensky said. Before their meeting, Trump told reporters that he and Zelensky would discuss Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries. “It is a serious hit on the Russians. It’s also a serious hit on the ‌price of diesel,” said Trump. He said he and Zelensky would also talk about solutions for ending the war, which began with Russia’s ⁠full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. “I ⁠think it’s going to happen,” Trump said. The US leader announced last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to strike energy targets, but any semblance of a truce disappeared when Russia ‌hit petrol stations in Kyiv the following day and Ukraine bombed a Russian oil refinery. Zelensky also met with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said he lobbied Trump to press for a Ukraine-Russia energy ceasefire ‌in his ‌meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart. Burnham also promised further financial support to Kyiv for infrastructure. Intensifying aerial attacks by both sides in the Ukraine war in ‌recent weeks have battered ports, warehouses, ships and energy infrastructure, as well as crippling Black Sea grain exports. Amid fears in Ukraine that Russia will once again pound ⁠its heating and power facilities as winter approaches, Zelensky said he had discussed preparations with Trump and asked the US for a package of Patriot air defence missiles – ⁠the only weapon in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of downing Russia’s ballistic missiles. The US war in Iran and the Ukraine war have depleted global supplies of Patriots, including US inventories. Zelensky said that, in return for Patriots from US stockpiles this winter, Ukraine would swap future supplies of interceptors ‌from its deal with Germany, which has ‌agreed to provide Ukraine with 600 Patriots in 2027 and 2028. He told reporters it was a “good step” that the idea was not rejected but acknowledged that Trump had not yet agreed to the proposal. Zelensky said that discussions for Ukraine to begin licensed production of Patriots itself were still ongoing, and a member of his team had held a positive meeting with Raytheon, a US producer of Patriots.

title: Hong Kong cyclist pays for brief Asian Games wobble but strikes back for redemptive medal
description: Chloe Leung content with bronze after troubled build-up, baton passes to city men on Wednesday as young duo prepare for Games debuts.
content: The briefest of wobbles cost Chloe Leung Wing-yee Asian Games road race gold on Tuesday, but 48 hours after a bitterly disappointing individual time trial, the Hongkonger and her coach were content with the bronze she captured in Japan. Herve Dagorne suspected his rider was destined for victory as the 90.4km tussle in secluded Shinshiro City entered its business end. Committing unflinchingly to her pre-race strategy of attacking on the downhills, however, Leung slipped to hand the initiative to Li Guo and Fariba Hashimi. Spying the chance for a two-way fight for gold, Li and Hashimi joined forces to isolate Leung, who mounted a courageous but forlorn chase. “I lost my [control of the] wheel in the downhill, as it’s quite slippery there,” Leung said. “Then I went fast, but I couldn’t really take the corner with them ... The two riders worked together, just going for it.” Li, the Chinese Asian Games debutant, won gold in two hours, 50 minutes and five seconds, pipping Hashimi of Afghanistan, who finished in the same time. Having closed the gap to the front pair to 17 seconds, Leung was stymied by a flat closing 5km that played into the hands of her pacesetting rivals, and she finished 41 seconds back. Teammates Kwan Tsz-kwan, 25, and Guardiola Cheung Li-tong, competing two days before her 22nd birthday, were 25th and 31st, respectively. “About 15 kilometres from the finish, I thought [Leung] was going all the way for gold,” Herve Dagorne, the Hong Kong head coach, said. “She was leading, but [Li and Hashimi] caught her on a downhill. She continued to push, then she slipped. She lost about 15 seconds, and a bit of confidence. “The two who were in front are not fast sprinters, so they worked together and she never got back.” As Leung battled on alone, Dagorne experienced a creeping fear that she might drop out of the medal positions altogether. That would have been one blow too many for a cyclist who placed fourth in Sunday’s individual time trial (ITT), an outcome that left her “upset and disappointed” three years after she had also finished best of the rest in Hangzhou. “I was expecting gold, but, in the circumstances, bronze is OK,” Dagorne said. “I began thinking about the group behind her, because I couldn’t imagine another fourth place. Finally, it was a good ending.” The Frenchman also praised Leung for quickly parking her ITT frustration. “It’s a big disappointment when you’ve worked so hard, then don’t deliver the performance,” Dagorne said. “But we went to the course the next morning and her smile was back, she was ready to fight.” Although Leung fastidiously prepared for her two road events, twice staging brief camps at the race venue, and practising her cornering on the winding streets of Spanish city Girona, her Games build-up was compromised by illness and injury. The 29-year-old broke the little finger on her right hand following a racing crash in Italy two months ago, while she has suffered with illness, along with a condition that intermittently causes inflammation of her jaw. “I didn’t have a really good few months before coming here … and I didn’t expect that I could get [the medal] today, because it was really uncertain,” Leung said. “I also felt that my legs weren’t great. I tried on the first lap [of four] to speed up a little bit, but I knew I would suffer from the beginning. On the last lap, I just thought, ‘Screw it, I’ll just go. If I try, no matter the result, at least I tried’.” It is over to the men on Wednesday, with Vincent Lau Wan-yau, ninth in the ITT, representing Hong Kong, alongside the budding young pair of Wu Chun-yin and Daniel Yip Hon-man. Dagorne said that Wu, 20, who was 12th in the under-23 road race at last year’s Asian Road Cycling Championships, had crashed while hurtling downhill on the first day of practice in Japan. “It’s affected his confidence, and the course has some super-fast downhills, so that’s not going to help,” Dagorne said. The 19-year-old Yip was junior champion at those Asian championships in 2025, prompting Dagorne to say that “he’s physically talented, hungry to win and knows what to do”. Nonetheless, the seven-lap, 161km Asian Games test promises to be a steep learning curve for the city’s inexperienced duo. In contrast, Lau, who will celebrate his 30th birthday on race day, has been around the block. An Asian Games ITT bronze medallist three years ago, he said: “They’re both very good, and we’re all of similar ability, but the advantage I have is my experience of riding elite races and managing all the technical stuff. “Before and during the race, I’ll try to give them good advice, so they maintain cool heads and can analyse what’s happening on the road.” Acknowledging that a podium finish for any of his riders would be “very difficult”, Dagorne said the formidable trio of Yevgeniy Fedorov, the defending champion, Nicolas Vinokurov, and the seasoned ITT gold medallist, Alexey Lutsenko, could complete a Kazakh clean sweep of the medals. “Fedorov is fresh from La Vuelta [the recent Tour of Spain] and flying,” Dagorne said. “But Vincent is technically good, and he’ll want to improve from the ITT.”

title: A look back at country star and The Voice coach Riley Green’s romantic history
description: Green has been linked to fellow country stars, including ‘Choosin’ Texas’ singer Ella Langley, and is believed to be the ex behind Megan Moroney’s break-up song ‘Who Hurt You?’.
content: Country musician Riley Green, who is known for hits like “I Wish Grandpas Never Died” and “Worst Way”, just made his debut as a coach on the latest season of The Voice. Alongside Green, Queen Latifah has also been announced as the show’s newest addition. The two newcomers join returning coaches Kelly Clarkson and Adam Levine for Season 30 of the NBC singing competition. Amid news of Green’s latest career move, it is his love life – specifically his speculated romance and feud with Megan Moroney – that is making headlines. The fellow country musicians sparked dating rumours in 2025 after posting photos from St. Barts at the same time. They both denied being romantically involved; however, in early 2026, Moroney released her track “Who Hurt You?”, which she confirmed is about Green in an interview with Cosmopolitan this July. The song hints at a relationship that ended badly. On September 18, Green released his latest album That’s Just Me, and fans can’t help but think one specific track titled “P.O.S.” is a dig at Moroney. In the song, Green accuses a person of dragging “every letter of my name on a chain through the Mississippi mud”. Green has reportedly denied that the song relates to Moroney, but this isn’t the first time the singer-songwriter has been involved in relationship drama. Who else has Riley Green been linked to? Here’s everything you need to know. Sophia Sansone Sophia Sansone is Riley Green’s only confirmed romance to date. The couple made their first public appearance together on the 2022 CMT Awards red carpet. Sansone is a managing partner at Make Wake Artists, a Nashville-based music management company. She has previously worked with artists like Luke Combs. While Sansone and Green kept their relationship largely private, she revealed during a December appearance on the ProbablyShannonFord podcast that they dated on and off for three years. During the episode, Sansone described the relationship as “a mess” and accused Green of breaking her phone and other electronic devices. Ella Langley Green was rumoured to have dated “Choosin’ Texas” singer Ella Langley after the two released their hit duet “You Look Like You Love Me” in 2024. However, Green and Langley have clarified that their relationship was purely professional. “Ella’s probably too smart to date me anyway,” Green said on the relationship podcast The Viall Files in December. “When we first started having success with that song, I kinda told Ella, ‘There’s gonna be a lot of things said, but I mean you don’t really gotta play into it or not play into it.’” Bryana Ferringer In December 2025, Green attended the CMA Awards with influencer Bryana Ferringer, who is known to have previously dated country musician Tucker Wetmore. Green and Ferringer were seen together at a basketball game in February this year.

title: In Focus | Can Xi and Trump use their leverage to actually make progress?
description: Analysts agree that keeping ties stable will be a priority when the leaders meet, and artificial intelligence could be an area for cooperation.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fifth part of a series, Fan Chen and Orange Wang look at the negotiating chips and areas where progress might be made. There will be some powerful bargaining chips on the table when Xi Jinping and Donald Trump meet in Washington this week. Both sides have economic and geopolitical leverage, and according to one analyst the negotiations will be as much about what they have chosen not to do to avoid retaliation. Others pointed to critical areas where the two powers are locked in fierce competition but could instead be working together – from artificial intelligence and military dialogue to trade and biosafety. But analysts agreed that keeping bilateral ties on a stable track would be a priority at the summit, and that was likely to be helped by a “tacit understanding” between Beijing and Washington on sensitive issues such as Iran and Taiwan. North Korea is also expected to be on the agenda. Since Trump visited China in May, both countries have seen that the leverage they hold actually “works”, according to Taiyi Sun, an associate professor of political science at Christopher Newport University (CNU) in Virginia. He said rare earths and critical minerals remained a key bargaining chip for China, while America still had leverage from its advanced semiconductors and related technologies. Sun noted that Washington still had options, including another tariff increase based on its Section 301 trade investigation and its delayed US$14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. Likewise, he noted that Beijing had room to adjust its commitments to buying American oil, planes and agricultural products. “What looks like goodwill today can become leverage tomorrow,” Sun said. But he said that while both capitals had powerful tools at their disposal, “neither can use them without expecting significant retaliation”. Expectations have been low for the presidential talks – the second face-to-face encounter between Xi and Trump this year. Still, Sun said artificial intelligence “could produce one of the summit’s least expected outcomes”, suggesting the US and China might share the strongest interest in preventing “catastrophic misuse or loss of control” of the emerging technology. AI governance has become a prominent part of the strategic rivalry between the world’s two largest economies. The issue has been in the spotlight in recent days, with warnings that the technology could create an extinction-level event for humanity and heated debate over slowing down development of advanced models. In marathon talks in New York on Sunday, US Trade Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng agreed to set up a dialogue on artificial intelligence with a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. The US said a bilateral Board of Trade was also operationalised during the talks. Strengthening communication on AI will be a key goal of the Xi-Trump talks, according to Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University. He said the two sides were likely to discuss domestic regulatory approaches and notification mechanisms for shared threats such as terrorism and transnational criminal groups using AI for malicious purposes. “They may also explore communication protocols for major AI risk events, including a US-China emergency hotline for critical AI incidents,” Zhao said, adding that these proposals were already under discussion through unofficial channels. Earlier this month, the Trump administration accused Chinese firms of stealing and copying American models through “industrial-scale distillation campaigns”. In response, Beijing said Washington was seeking a “monopoly” on the technology and warned of countermeasures. Huang Ping, assistant dean of the Chinese University of Hong Kong- Shenzhen’s School of Public Policy, said that given the timing, the US accusations would boost its leverage in the discussions on AI. He said a US-China dialogue mechanism on AI was of “very high” urgency, noting that they had clear differences over the definition of security and the purpose of regulation. But he remained “cautiously optimistic” about outcomes of the AI talks, saying he expected a statement on principles, a follow-up working mechanism and preliminary arrangements in some areas. According to Huang, Beijing and Washington were likely to discuss the rules, pace and boundaries of their AI rivalry. But he noted that their technological advantages, market interests and industrial growth remained the biggest issues – highlighting the clash between China’s low-cost, open-source ecosystem and an American commercial model that relies on closed-source, high-priced services. Ahead of the summit, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi on Thursday urged Washington to stick with its commitment to “constructive strategic stability” in the relationship during a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Zhao from Fudan said reinforcing and acting on that commitment would be Beijing’s “primary goal” for Xi’s US trip – his first state visit to the country since 2015. Both sides agreed to the concept in May, though the White House in its statement included US demands for “fairness and reciprocity”. Political scientist Zhu Zhiqun, from Bucknell University in Pennsylvania, said both the US and China “genuinely desire a stable and constructive relationship”. He also noted that Trump valued his personal relationship with Xi, seeing their rapport as key to stabilising bilateral ties. “When facing serious internal and external challenges such as rising gas prices and a prolonged war in Iran before the November midterm election, the last thing Trump wants is a rocky relationship with China,” he said. Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, expected Trump to “express further support” for constructive strategic stability when he met Xi. “With the Russia-Ukraine war grinding on and the Middle East morass expanding, Trump aims to preserve a tactical thaw between the two countries,” he said, adding that Xi was also likely to avoid a personal rupture with Trump. According to Sun from CNU, China has gained leverage since the Iran war began in February by avoiding using its “enormous purchasing power in the global energy market” and not adding more pressure on international oil prices. “I see that restraint partly as a favour to Trump – reciprocity for Trump’s restraint on issues that Beijing cares about,” he said, pointing to the US president putting the latest Taiwan arms sale on hold. “There is a tacit understanding between Trump and Xi on this front,” Sun added. “Neither side needs to publicly announce a quid pro quo for such an understanding to function.” Taiwan has long been “the first red line” for Beijing in managing its ties with Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that the US was considering postponing major arms sales to the island until after November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, citing Beijing’s strong opposition to the deal and US defence industry constraints. The SCMP also reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing possible announcements to strengthen military ties during Xi’s visit to the US. A potential trip by Trump to China to attend the Apec gathering could provide an opportunity for another face-to-face meeting with Xi, as well as a chance to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. The SCMP reported earlier this month that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue. Zhao from Fudan said it was possible that Trump and Xi had already discussed this in May, and that there had been further talks between Beijing and Pyongyang during Xi’s subsequent visit to North Korea in June. “As a result, I think Trump himself remains very interested in pushing for a new summit with North Korea’s top leader – and Shenzhen is a very likely location,” he said, adding that Pyongyang would be looking to improve its international standing with such a meeting. But he noted that China’s influence on its neighbour was limited and that friction between Washington and Seoul – following the recent cancellation of joint military drills – could stall diplomatic progress with Pyongyang. Wyne from the International Crisis Group noted that some of Trump’s advisers would likely be “wary of making China a diplomatic intermediary”. “Trump himself, though, would likely have little – if any – objection given his affinity for strongmen, his frustration that South Korea did not assist US efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and his hope that another tete-a-tete with Kim could burnish his peacemaking credentials by helping de-escalate tensions across the Korean peninsula,” Wyne said. According to Sun, North Korea is not a Chinese bargaining chip. “China can help open the door, but it cannot simply deliver Kim,” he said. There have been efforts to build positivity ahead of Xi’s trip to Washington, with the two governments signalling progress in discussions on reciprocal tariff cuts covering some US$30 billion in trade on each side and on counternarcotics cooperation. Zhao said extending the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea in October was likely to be the “most realistic deliverable” from this week’s talks. “This summit is vital for how China and the US coordinate their economic and trade relations and operationalise mechanisms such as the trade and investment councils,” he said. Meanwhile, growing warnings over AI-enabled biosecurity threats have fuelled calls for the two powers to work together in the health sector. Yanzhong Huang, a senior fellow for global health at the Council on Foreign Relations, said health issues were “unlikely” to be a summit focus, with fentanyl a possible exception. “That does not mean there are no urgent issues between the two sides. Pharmaceutical supply-chain resilience, China’s rise in biotech, dual-use research, and AI’s application to health are increasingly treated as health-security challenges,” Huang said. “US-China health cooperation is possible, but it will remain narrow and ad hoc,” he said, adding that given the lack of trust, formal cooperation in sensitive areas was unlikely and “joint R&D even more so”.

title: US ‘looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with raping 17-year-old
description: Social media creator Braden Peters was accused of giving the teen alcohol prior to the alleged 2025 assault.
content: The social media influencer “Clavicular”, who gained a following promoting the online “looksmaxxing” trend, has been charged in Massachusetts with raping a 17-year-old girl who told police she became heavily intoxicated after he gave her alcohol at his family’s Cape Cod home. Braden Peters, 20, is charged with rape, administering a substance for sexual intercourse and procuring alcohol for a person under 21 in the alleged May 23, 2025, assault in Chatham, according to court records. A clerk-magistrate found probable cause for the charges on September 4, and a criminal complaint was issued September 8. Peters’ spokesperson Mitchell Jackson said the accuser and her lawyer went to police after Peters moved to dismiss a civil lawsuit she filed against him and “refused to pay money”, Reuters reported. Peters, who lives in Florida and is not in custody, was scheduled to be arraigned in Massachusetts on October 14. “We are not commenting at this time since the proper authorities are handling this,” said Andrew Moss, one of the teen’s lawyers. The accuser told Chatham police that she and Peters began messaging on social media and that he later paid her to appear in “looksmaxxing” videos he streamed online. She said Peters knew she was 17 but that he told her to tell his viewers that she was 18 and that vodka he gave her was water, according to a police report. On May 23, 2025, the girl said she took a ride-share from her grandparents’ home to Peters’ family home on Morris Island, a gated community of multimillion-dollar homes overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. She told police she was greeted by Peters’ mother and grandmother before being escorted by Peters to his room, where he was live-streaming. She told police she drank what she believed amounted to two or three shots of vodka and became increasingly intoxicated. An officer who reviewed clips from Peters’ live stream said one showed the girl telling Peters: “Wait, I’m so drunk though”. Peters responded: “It’s OK”, before the two kissed, according to the police report. After the live stream ended, she said, they went to his bedroom, where she later fell asleep and awoke the next morning to Peters raping her. The alleged assault was previously described in a lawsuit filed against Peters in Florida in April. An amended complaint filed in June accused Peters of sexual battery over the Cape Cod encounter. The lawsuit also accuses Peters of later injecting the girl with a fat-dissolving substance during a live stream without consent. Peters’ lawyers have denied the lawsuit’s allegations, saying in a July court filing that the encounter was consensual and calling the lawsuit a “publicity grab”.
