Peters, the face of the “looksmaxxing” trend, is a well-known social media and internet personality whose pursuit of achieving traditional attractiveness by any means necessary became the subject of intense interest and discourse early this year. He live-streams his activities on close to a daily basis, often streaming his time at parties and clubs or talking with women. “Looksmaxxing” has origins that trace back to the “involuntary celibate” or “incel” community, an online subculture made up of people, primarily men, who believe society unjustly denies them sexual or romantic attention. Peters has denied being linked to the group in any way and said many times that looksmaxxing is about self-improvement. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Opinion | The question Hong Kong charities must answer
description: The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust’s impact report could help push the city’s NGOs towards a more serious culture of accountability.
content: Hong Kong does not lack institutions that speak the language of service and responsibility. What it lacks, too often, is a clear account of what difference they actually make. That is why the Hong Kong Jockey Club (HKJC) Charities Trust’s first impact report deserves attention. Publishing such a report may seem like routine institutional business. Up to a point, it is. But its publication opens up a bigger question, one Hong Kong has tended to skirt round: how should organisations with a public or social role be judged? Large charities, public bodies and companies have become very good at reporting what they have spent and launched, and how many people they have reached. Those figures can show scale, and sometimes efficiency. What they cannot show, on their own, is whether people’s lives have improved, a need was met or a problem eased in any lasting way. At its best, impact reporting asks a harder question: what changed because the work was done? For a funder with the HKJC Charities Trust’s reach, that is a fair question. As Asia’s leading philanthropic donor, its decision to publish a report of this kind may set a useful example for others in Hong Kong and beyond. Covering 2022-23 to 2024-25, the report reviews the trust’s major programmes and presents early evidence of the difference they have made. It also acknowledges that measurement should involve grantees and beneficiaries, and that its approach remains experimental. Yet impact is not a neutral category, however technical the language may sound. Someone must decide what success means and which evidence deserves weight. Those choices can privilege readily counted gains while undervaluing changes that are less visible but potentially more important. The same problem appears outside philanthropy. Hongkong Post is under review as the government considers how to reform a service under strain. Its financial losses cannot be ignored, but they do not answer a broader question of what the service exists to do. Reform should follow from that purpose, rather than treat cost reduction as the purpose itself. That applies just as strongly to philanthropy. It is easy enough to count grants, projects and participants. It is much harder to show whether a youth scheme helped someone stay in school or whether support for carers made life more manageable over time. Participant numbers reveal reach, not consequence. If a report can show only activity, the language of impact starts to look like decoration. Hong Kong is not starting from nowhere. Environmental, social and corporate governance (ESG) rules have widened corporate reporting, while the Audit Commission already asks whether public money is being well used. Both strengthen accountability, but neither tells the public, by itself, whether an institution has fulfilled its stated purpose. There is another difficulty. Impact is often defined from above, with those in charge deciding what success looks like before frontline organisations and service users are asked for evidence. Yet the people closest to the work do not always see it in the same way. Frontline groups know trust can take years to build. Service users may care less about attendance numbers than whether help was accessible and arrived in time – and ultimately whether it improved their lives. Excluding those views can produce a polished report that misses the experience it is supposed to assess. Measurement also creates its own incentives. Short funding cycles encourage quick returns, while dashboards make tidy numbers especially attractive. Effects that emerge slowly may be overlooked because they cannot be tied neatly to one intervention. Before long, institutions may find themselves managing for the report rather than for the work itself. A credible report therefore needs to explain not only what changed and for whom, but how confidently that change can be linked to the work. It should identify whose definition of success was used and acknowledge where the evidence is weak or the results disappointing. Candour about failure is not a flaw in impact reporting – it is part of what makes the exercise useful. This is why publication of the HKJC Charities Trust’s impact report is a welcome first step. Its longer-term significance will lie in whether it helps push Hong Kong towards a more serious culture of accountability among institutions that claim to serve the public good. Activity is easy to catalogue. The harder task is to show that the work produced worthwhile change.

title: US law enforcement tightens security for Xi summit as welcome and protest events planned
description: US Secret Service says it is committed to ensuring the safety and security of all foreign heads of state while they are on American soil.
content: Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, starting on Wednesday, US law enforcement agencies have increased security as Chinese diaspora groups organise welcoming events and protest groups plan demonstrations. The US Secret Service, which is leading security for the visit, said it is committed to ensuring the safety and security of all foreign heads of state while they are on US soil. “Secret Service personnel have been planning for the visit of the Chinese president for several weeks, in coordination with Chinese officials and our federal and local law enforcement partners,” the agency said in a statement. According to Washington’s Metropolitan Police Department (MPD), five groups have filed for rallies: the Falun Dafa Association of Washington, DC; Tibetan Youth Congress; the Wei Jingsheng Foundation; Protest the Chinese Government; and the Greater Washington Chinese-American Community. The Greater Washington Chinese-American Community (GWCAC) is a charity organisation that recently hosted a Chinese cultural festival and street fair near Capitol Hill. “The primary objective of [GWCAC] is to promote Chinese-American culture and heritage by organising, sponsoring, and coordinating appropriate social and cultural events in the Greater Washington area,” the group says on its website. On WeChat, Chinese diaspora groups mainly in the DC, Maryland and Virginia area, describing themselves as promoting better US-China friendship, have also been organising welcoming events for Xi, with different time slots available for sign-ups. The International Campaign for Tibet said several demonstrations have been planned, including protests outside the Chinese embassy and a candlelight vigil at Franklin Park at 5.30pm on September 24. Students for a Free Tibet posted on social media that “thousands of Tibetans, Uygurs, Hongkongers, and other peoples” will take to the streets. The MPD did not provide specifics on its operations, tactics, or staffing, but confirmed it is working with local, state and federal law enforcement partners during the visit. Areas around the White House and the US Capitol include federal land administered by the National Park Service (NPS). The NPS said demonstrations on NPS-managed land generally require permits when more than 25 people are expected to attend, but did not provide information on any planned demonstrations or permit applicants. In 2023, when Xi visited San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, clashes between protesters and supporters turned violent and made headlines. It remains unclear where protesters and welcoming groups will gather in Washington. The Secret Service said it respects the public’s First Amendment right to demonstrate and does not distinguish between groups by message or purpose. It said law enforcement partners are prepared to respond to unlawful activity. The agency also said DC residents and commuters should anticipate more visible security measures during the visit, particularly downtown. While every effort will be made to minimise disruptions, the public is encouraged to allow additional travel time. The agency said it will share information about road closures and parking restrictions shortly. Xi’s visit is scheduled to run from September 23 to 25, with events including a state arrival ceremony on Wednesday; meetings at the White House and a state dinner on Thursday; and a visit to the National Archives on Friday.

title: Trump praises Takaichi for doing ‘tremendous job’ ahead of Xi’s visit to US
description: Two leaders hail their good working relationship, with Sanae Takaichi saying the United States and Japan can look forward to deepening ties.
content: US President Donald Trump praised his strong relationship with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in New York on Tuesday, days before he is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The talks, held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, come as relations between Beijing and Tokyo show no signs of thawing. Both leaders hailed their good working relationship, with Takaichi saying the two countries looked forward to deepening ties. Trump lavished praise on the Japanese leader, saying she had “done a tremendous job” and was “going to go down in history”. “It’s an honour to be with her. She’s a friend of mine. We’ve gotten to know each other very well over the last period of time,” Trump said at the start of talks. He added that he kept a close eye on Takaichi’s approval ratings and was “pleased” with what he saw, describing her as “tough and smart”. Refraining from naming specific countries or crises, Takaichi said the meeting came as the security environment in Asia had become “so severe”, adding that her bilateral meeting with the US president “shows the world the strength of the Japan-US alliance”. Takaichi thanks Trump She also thanked Trump for his commitment to the alliance and told him that the cabinet reshuffle she carried out last week, which replaced 10 of her 18 ministers, had left his administration’s main interlocutors in Tokyo untouched. “All of your counterparts have stayed on,” she told him, naming Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa and Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi. This represented a continuity, Takaichi said, that would allow policymakers on both sides to deepen their personal ties and make the alliance “unshakeable”. She also told Trump that the two countries were making headway on economic security cooperation, pointing to artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals. “There are a lot of issues I’d like to discuss,” she said, without going into specifics. Taking aim at Beijing Takaichi did not mention Beijing or Taiwan in her first address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, but much of the speech appeared to answer the pressure Beijing has put on Tokyo since her remarks on Taiwan in November last year. When she turned to the rule of law, she repeated the language that Tokyo uses to describe Beijing’s activity in the East China Sea and around Taiwan. “Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world,” she said. The venue carried its own weight, since Beijing had already taken the dispute to the UN. Weeks after the row began, Chinese ambassador to the UN Fu Cong wrote to Secretary General Antonio Guterres accusing the prime minister of violating international law, and the letter was circulated to every member state as an official General Assembly document. That same month, the Chinese embassy in Tokyo posted on social media the charter’s so-called enemy state clauses, written to constrain the Axis powers after the second world war. The embassy said founding members such as China could take military action without Security Council approval against a former enemy state that renewed a policy of aggression. Beijing returned to the clauses in August, when foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian endorsed a remark by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Japan was still an “enemy state” under the charter. Takaichi used the podium in New York to demand their removal, citing a 2005 resolution in which member states had pledged to drop the references. “In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted,” she said, adding that she wanted to “strongly emphasise this position” because Japan took “pride and honour” in its 70 years of work at the UN. She also pushed back on Lin’s accusation, made at the same briefing, that her government was steering Japan away from pacifism and towards remilitarisation. Japan had contributed to peace for seven decades “as a peace-loving nation under its exclusively defence-oriented policy”, she said near the end of the speech, and “this policy will remain unchanged in the future”. In response, Beijing criticised Tokyo for “openly challenging the post-war international order” and “threatening regional peace and stability” by denying history and accelerating militarisation. “The international community pays far more attention to what Japan does than to what it says,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Wednesday. “We urge the Japanese side to take history as a mirror, reflect deeply on its past, and earn the trust of its Asian neighbours and the international community through concrete actions.” The economic side of the dispute also surfaced when the prime minister spoke on critical minerals. She told delegates that “concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community”, in a clear reference to China’s rare earths export controls. Beijing banned exports of dual-use items, a category that includes rare earths, to Japanese military users in January. A month later, it placed 20 Japanese entities under export controls, among them the aerospace units of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Kawasaki Heavy Industries. Souring ties Ties between China and Japan soured dramatically after Takaichi suggested in November that Tokyo could deploy its military forces in the event of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait. Beijing viewed her comments as a sign of Tokyo’s desire to return to its pre-war path of militarism. It has since urged its citizens to avoid travelling to Japan and has restricted exports of rare earths and related materials to the country. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not see Taiwan as an independent state but are opposed to any unilateral change in the status quo. As Beijing’s trade curbs continue to bite, Tokyo has sought to appeal to Washington – its long-time ally – to urge China to ease its rare earth restrictions against Japan. Trump reportedly discussed Japan with Xi during their sit-down in Beijing in May. Against that backdrop, the US, Japan and South Korea announced a new trilateral consultation on economic security on Monday aimed at strengthening supply chains and cooperation on critical technologies. Without naming China, the three governments pledged to oppose economic coercion, non-market practices that produce harmful overcapacity and arbitrary export restrictions. They also reaffirmed the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, sending a coordinated message ahead of Trump hosting Xi at the White House on Thursday. The Trump-Takaichi talks came a day ahead of Xi’s arrival in Washington, his first state visit to the US in more than a decade. Xi is expected to hold talks with Trump on Thursday. The South China Morning Post understands that Japanese officials have grown anxious about how forcefully Trump will discuss Japan with Xi and how hard he will press the Chinese leader on Beijing’s measures against Tokyo this time. Tokyo, viewing Trump as “flirtatious” with Xi, was worried he would “go soft” on Beijing, one source said. Crucial timing Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst at political risk consultancy Eurasia Group, said Trump’s meeting with Takaichi was particularly significant given its timing – on the eve of Xi’s arrival in the US – and the signal it sent about the continued strength of the US-Japan alliance. “Tokyo’s ties with Washington remain remarkably strong given how frayed the US’ ties have become with so many other erstwhile allies and partners,” he said. “For Takaichi, this meeting will allow her to be the last person to speak with Trump before he meets Xi and she will use it to underscore to Trump the centrality of Japan to his broader goals in Asia.” Chan suggested that while Takaichi would likely not directly ask for Trump’s support in persuading Xi to ease pressure against Japan, she would emphasise the damage Chinese rare earth export restrictions were doing to US companies that relied on Japanese suppliers for key inputs. “Takaichi will want to remind Trump of the value of the US-Japan alliance and everything that Japan has done to support his policy agenda,” Chan said.

title: Trump criticises UK’s Chagos deal, says new British PM Burnham will reconsider
description: The US president says ties with Britain are better, as he met the prime minister for the first time.
content: US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his country’s relations with Britain were better under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but he criticised a deal to hand over the Chagos Islands. Trump and Burnham shook hands as they met for the first time on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “No, I think they’re up – well, they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way,” Trump told reporters, referring to Keir Starmer. “Right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister Andy, I think that we’re doing very well.” Labour leader Burnham, 56, took over from Starmer in July. Starmer initially succeeded in charming Republican Trump, including by inviting him for a state visit hosted by King Charles a year ago, but they fell out after Britain refused to join the US-Israeli war on Iran. Trump, 80, added that he believed Burnham would be reconsidering a deal to return the Chagos Islands – which hosts the strategic Diego Garcia US-UK military base – to Mauritius. “I don’t support it, I think it’s terrible,” Trump said when asked about the Chagos deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” Trump said, as Burnham, sitting beside him, nodded and said: “yeah”.

title: Brazil’s Lula backs China peace push at UN, tells US his nation is ‘no one’s backyard’
description: Brazilian leader criticises tariffs and military pressure while demanding domestic benefits from foreign access to critical minerals.
content: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva renewed his backing on Tuesday for a peace initiative he launched with China to end the war in Ukraine, using his opening speech at the UN General Assembly to take thinly veiled aim at the United States over tariffs, military pressure and access to critical minerals. Speaking in New York just days before Brazilians vote in a tight presidential race, Lula described the war between Russia and Ukraine as a five-year humanitarian drama that “continues to claim lives”. There will be “no winners on the battlefield” and “diplomacy is the only option”, he told the assembly, pointing to “the Group of Friends for Peace, created by Brazil and China”, as proof that “there are forces in the international community willing to work for dialogue”. Beijing and Brasilia launched the group at the UN in September 2024, gathering representatives from 17 developing countries behind a call for a negotiated settlement. China received no criticism in the address. Lula framed the appeal within a wider indictment of the UN, telling delegates its credibility had “never been so low” and that members were “hostages to the immobility of a Security Council that does not fulfil its role”. “War is not the continuation of politics by other means. It is the total bankruptcy of politics,” he said. Criticism of US foreign policy The United States was not named during the speech but was the clear target of several passages. In one, Lula described the proximity of Latin America and the Caribbean to “the world’s greatest military power” as inescapable, “especially in a context of resurgent hegemonic temptations”. “Brazil does not fit in anyone’s backyard,” he said. He also rejected foreign military involvement in fighting organised crime, months after Washington designated Brazil’s two largest gangs, the Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho, as terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials had opposed the designation. Brazil “will not outsource the responsibility of defending our borders”, the president declared. “We do not need aircraft carriers watching over our waters.” Lula instead pointed to a proposal he had personally handed to US President Donald Trump for cooperation against arms trafficking and the laundering abroad of money by Brazilian criminal groups. He paired those warnings with a message to the foreign powers competing for Brazil’s rare earths, a contest in which Washington and Beijing are the main players. Brazil holds the critical minerals and rare earths “that the world needs to carry out the energy transition”, the president told delegates, and those resources will be exploited for the benefit of the Brazilian people. Foreign access to them, in his words, “will have as a mandatory counterpart the generation of value in our territory, the transfer of technology and the supply of strategic national sectors”. The remarks came six days after Lula signed a national critical minerals policy into law. It offers up to 7 billion reais (US$1.4 billion) in incentives for domestic processing and creates a council under the presidency with powers to vet changes of control at mining companies and international agreements involving strategic minerals. The issue has become a campaign flashpoint since April, when US-based USA Rare Earth agreed to buy Serra Verde, owner of Brazil’s only commercial rare earths mine, for about US$2.8 billion. Lula’s ruling Workers’ Party called the deal an attack on national sovereignty. Lula’s main challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, has taken the opposite line. The Trump ally argued that Brazil should position itself as an alternative supplier for a US still dependent on China, and a memo bearing his campaign’s branding, reported by the South China Morning Post this month, proposed a rare earths supply chain with Washington designed to isolate Beijing. The new rules apply equally to Chinese capital, which has been flowing into Brazilian mining at a record pace. Brazil was the top global destination for Chinese investment last year, receiving US$6.1 billion, and Chinese investment in mining more than tripled, according to the Brazil-China Business Council. The largest pending Chinese bet is MMG, controlled by state-owned China Minmetals, which agreed in February last year to buy Anglo American’s Brazilian nickel operations for up to US$500 million. That is the kind of change of control the new council is empowered to review. Brazil is also on course for a record in exports this year “despite the tariff barrage against our economy”, according to Lula. Exports reached US$250.9 billion between January and August, the highest on record for the period, while sales to China rose 15 per cent to US$77.1 billion and accounted for 30.7 per cent of the total, trade ministry data showed. A tradition that puts Brazil before the US Brazil has opened the General Debate every year since 1955, a custom that places its president at the rostrum immediately before the leader of the United States, the host country. Trump spoke after Lula on Tuesday. That running order produced an unexpected thaw last year, when Trump and Lula crossed paths backstage and embraced after months of trading barbs publicly over US tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Brazilian goods, which Trump tied to the trial of former president Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot. Trump told the assembly minutes later that they had shared “excellent chemistry”, opening a thaw that led Washington to roll back much of the tariff package. The combative tone of Lula’s speech this year, aimed squarely at US geopolitical decisions of recent months, was followed by a brief encounter on the floor. As the hall emptied after Trump’s address, as it usually does once the US president finishes speaking, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio quickened his pace to reach Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, the SCMP observed. Rubio was accompanied by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, first lady Melania Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. He pointed towards Lula as he spoke to Vieira. Their words were inaudible, but Vieira appeared to answer with a hand gesture suggesting the conversation would have to wait. Brazil’s foreign ministry and the US State Department had not responded to requests from the SCMP for comment on the exchange by the time of publication. Lula left UN headquarters at around the same time and went straight to John F. Kennedy International Airport for his flight back to Brazil. It was a break with his practice of holding a press conference after addressing the assembly. Tariff dispute No bilateral meeting between the two presidents is scheduled this year, according to Brazil’s foreign ministry. Relations have soured again since July, when the US Trade Representative imposed a 25 per cent tariff on some Brazilian goods. The action followed an investigation that targeted Brazilian policies on digital trade and electronic payments, among other areas. Lula addressed that directly in his speech, vowing that Brazil “will not give in to pressure from multinationals that want to privatise our PIX”, the free instant payment system run by the central bank. He also described the World Trade Organization as “on life support” and warned that “when governments capitulate before those who use tariffs as weapons of coercion and blackmail, the consequences are dire”. A source on the Brazilian side confirmed to the SCMP that negotiations with US officials are ongoing and that, to keep the talks going, Vieira is expected to remain in the country until the end of the month. Vieira is scheduled to attend the G20 trade ministers’ meeting, which is set for September 30 and October 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the source said.

title: Hayden Panettiere died from accidental overdose involving fentanyl, coroner says
description: The investigation into the 36-year-old US actress’ death is ongoing, police say.
content: US actress Hayden Panettiere died from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl, a coroner in South Carolina said on Tuesday. Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on August 16. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home. According to a statement from the Greenville County Coroner’s Office, a combination of fentanyl and its chemical by-product, as well as the anti-anxiety medication alprazolam, a muscle relaxant and a drug used to treat major depression and other serious mental health disorders, was found in Panettiere’s system. The office did not include further details from the autopsy report in its initial release. Asked for comment on the coroner’s report, Kasey Kitchen, a publicist for the family, said “the investigation is still ongoing and the case is complex”. Greenville Police confirmed on Tuesday that their investigation into Panettiere’s death is continuing. Paramedics responded to Panettiere’s apartment last month after an emergency call and performed CPR and other advanced resuscitation efforts for more than 40 minutes before she was declared dead. An autopsy found no signs of trauma that could have contributed to her death, Greenville County Coroner Mike Ellis said in a statement. The police report released after her death listed medications Panettiere had been taking, but the drug names were redacted. Panettiere soared to fame in the television shows Heroes and Nashville. In her memoir This Is Me, released in May, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame and acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014. She also endured family struggles and tragedy. Her parents’ marriage was strained and eventually ended. Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023 at age 28. Panettiere also talked about her long relationship with Brian Hickerson and allegations that the aspiring actor physically abused her. He was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse, and he pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner and served a short time in jail due to the case. He was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions. Hickerson completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours; that request was denied. Panettiere was one of two children born to Skip Panettiere, a former New York fire captain, and Lesley Vogel, a former soap opera star. She acted in commercials and soap operas, including as the ever-troubled Lizzie Spaulding on Guiding Light. In This Is Me, she wrote that the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother’s boyfriend, led her to associate “catastrophe with adoration”. She then played a cheerleader with supernatural powers in Heroes, which propelled her to fame in 2006. By 2015, Panettiere was playing a brash country upstart opposite Connie Britton on Nashville, which aired on ABC for four seasons before being cancelled and revived on CMT. She did her own singing in the show, which scored some hits on country charts, spawned US tours and earned Panettiere two supporting actress Golden Globe nominations. But she also said she was in a horrible cycle of using alcohol and drugs to battle depression and anxiety and had to find a way out of the darkness. She entered rehab while filming the show. “I was the one who put myself in the first treatment centre. I was drowning,” she said in a 2023 interview with Women’s Health magazine.

title: CUHK gives top economist warning over talk on women ‘marrying for money’
description: University’s New Asia College tells Terence Chong to be mindful of speech and others’ feelings after talk on women marrying for money.
content: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has told a top economist to be mindful of his words and other people’s feelings after he faced a backlash over his discussion of the costs and benefits of women marrying for money in a campus talk. The controversy erupted shortly after Terence Chong Tai-leung, an associate professor of economics, spoke about investing in one’s life at an assembly held every two weeks at New Asia College on Tuesday. Chong is also the executive director of the Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance at CUHK. He ranks 37th worldwide in theoretical econometrics and is among the top 1 per cent for the number of distinct works and journal pages, according to the university’s website. He is also considered to be among the top 5 per cent of economists globally. CUHK said on Wednesday that the college had asked the speaker to be mindful of his speech and to take into consideration the feelings of stakeholders at the university and in the wider community. It added that the college would continue to foster an inclusive campus environment based on mutual respect and diversity. According to posts on social media platform Threads, slides presented by Chong included one titled “Economics of partner choice”, which contained the heading, “The Cost-Benefit Analysis of Women Marrying for Money”. He also allegedly told the audience that “it’s pointless for women to get high GPAs; they need to marry rich in the end anyway” and that “women better not pursue a PhD because their youth is precious”. Chong reportedly said that women instead had “to invest in their looks, but for men, as long as they look OK, it’s fine”. Other remarks on the slides included: “I do not recommend finding a girl of the same age, nor a girl living far away from your home.” Another slide stated: “Boys try their best to show girls their study ability, academic grades or future ambitions. In fact, these things hold zero attraction for girls who are mature in their thinking.” The content sparked outrage among students, who accused Chong of reducing women’s criteria for choosing partners to material gain. Critics described the framing as gender-biased, objectifying and unfair. “I thought I was back in the Qing dynasty,” wrote one social media user who attended the assembly. “Listening to this is disturbing,” another wrote. Students also called on the university to launch a formal investigation into the talk, demanding a public apology from Chong alongside his removal or resignation as associate college head. Some online users, however, defended Chong’s remarks. “That’s how the real world works, and reality is always uncomfortable,” one wrote. When reached by the South China Morning Post on Tuesday night, Chong admitted that his presentation was poorly phrased and offered an apology. “I did not express it very well … It was definitely not what I meant. Men and women are equal. If anyone might feel uncomfortable, I am really sorry,” he said. When asked whether any university officials or attendees had raised concerns with him during or after the event, Chong said no one had done so as of Tuesday night. Chong holds various public service positions, including roles on the Commission on Targeted Poverty Alleviation, the Competition Commission and the Small and Medium Enterprises Committee, among other bodies. In 2022, he was awarded Hong Kong’s Medal of Honour in recognition of his contributions to the development of trade and industry. Sisi Liu Pui-shan, director of the Hong Kong Federation of Women’s Centres, said the comment that women should invest in their looks rather than their education created the impression of female objectification. “As we step into a knowledge-based society, we must remember that women fought long and hard across the globe for their right to education,” she said. “Suggesting that women don’t need a PhD and should instead focus on their appearance implies that depth and intellect don’t matter for women – a remark that is especially inappropriate coming from a professor in front of students.” Liu said she believed the incident had raised public awareness of women’s rights and social standing, while underscoring the need for greater efforts in equality education. “What we’ve been striving for all along is an equal society – one where people are defined by their capabilities rather than gender stereotypes, and where everyone has the freedom to choose,” she said. “While this started as an economics discussion, the world isn’t defined strictly by numbers and money – it also encompasses sociology, gender studies and diverse ideologies. Ultimately, it comes down to the kind of society we want to build.” Lawmaker Nixie Lam Lam said CUHK’s handling of the incident was appropriate, although she personally found the remarks out of touch. “The whole thing makes people uncomfortable because the ideas do not align with Hong Kong’s own values – whether for our younger generation or otherwise. When it comes to opportunities, women aren’t measured by this kind of thing,” she said. “Given that he has already apologised, I believe it’s appropriate to stop here.” Lam said she believed resignation from his leadership position was unnecessary as Chong was likely to have learned his lessons, adding, “after all, this isn’t something that deeply harmed society”.

title: Trump defends Iran war, touts ‘America is back’ agenda in UN speech
description: US president casts domestic policies as a global success while addressing conflicts, China and the prospect of renewed Iran talks.
content: US President Donald Trump addressed the global community on Tuesday morning with a speech that sought to justify his war with Iran, touted how he has “made peace” and argued that his “make America great again” policies benefit the world. His speech before the UN General Assembly came as the world grapples with years of conflict in Ukraine, Iran, Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and Lebanon, with no relief in sight. “I can report to you with pride that America is back, and our country is stronger today than ever before,” he said. “Our country is doing better than ever before, and our future is very, very bright.” In a speech that seemed at times more suited to a US campaign stop than the global community, he touted his record on cutting crime, encouraging US innovation, ending illegal immigration and enacting US tax cuts, selling them as wins for the global community. “While others have talked, I have acted. While others have spoken of peace, I have made it,” he added. “The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energised and a very powerful United States of America.” Trump largely kept to his prepared comments, other than a tirade against the “rogue” UN International Criminal Court and against critics of artificial intelligence. “This is the group that came up with the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax, climate change, open borders,” he said. “Whoever wins super intelligence, wins. That’s the group that wins. And we’re leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way.” The relatively on-message address – which even included a few kudos to the UN for passing favoured resolutions – was in sharp contrast to last year’s UNGA speech. Twelve months ago, he riffed on the UN escalators and teleprompters, its substandard building materials and environmental policies that “kill all the cows”. Trump spent a significant part of his remarks laying out his case for his war of choice in Iran. But even as Trump has called the Iranian leadership “vicious,” “violent” and “scum” on social media, his administration has teased a possible meeting this week with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is also attending the General Assembly. Both sides were being coy, however. Shortly before boarding his plane in Tehran, Pezeshkian said Iran was wary of more talks, having twice been attacked by the US and Israel during active negotiations. ‘To the victor belong the spoils’ Trump also highlighted on Tuesday his administration’s strategy for ending violence, instability and foreign interference in the western hemisphere, a region increasingly contested on the economic front with China, which has invested billions of US dollars. He revisited the US military operation in January that captured then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and said Washington was “working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future”. Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodriguez sat motionless and stern-faced as Trump referred to her government and did not applaud him at any point, a South China Morning Post correspondent in the hall observed. Trump praised an oil agreement signed with Rodriguez’s government last month, which he said covered 65 billion barrels. “It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” he said. “To the victor belong the spoils.” The deal gives the US 55 per cent of the effective output of 17 oilfields, including the right to buy oil at cost. Several of those fields had been operated or targeted by Chinese firms such as Sinopec, while Chinese lenders are still owed at least US$10 billion by Caracas, according to analysts. Trump said the operation proved “the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere”, adding that Washington would use its military might when necessary. Without naming a specific country, he accused previous administrations of letting the region be “infiltrated by hostile foreign adversaries” and mocked Venezuela’s imported hardware. “Venezuela had the finest equipment in the world from other countries, and guess what? It didn’t work [against US forces],” he said. Caracas relied on Russian missile systems and Chinese-made radars that Beijing had promoted as capable of detecting stealth aircraft. Trump also called drug cartels “the ISIS of the western hemisphere” and claimed US strikes on alleged drug boats had cut seaborne drug flows by 97 per cent. The campaign has killed at least 231 people since September last year, according to US Southern Command. He described Mexico as “the epicentre of the cartel violence” but praised ties with its government, which has repeatedly rejected US military action on its soil. The US president also predicted that Cuba’s communist government “will fall”, prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out of the hall. “Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba,” he said, “and safety and security will be coming to Mexico.” Greenland and the UN succession Trump’s speech came as his poll figures hit new lows at home and abroad. According to a Pew survey in June, a median of just 23 per cent of adults from 36 nations expressed confidence in his leadership of global affairs, citing tariffs, Gaza, Iran, Greenland and the Russia-Ukraine war. Even as Trump has repeatedly slammed the United Nations, questioning its purpose and inability to solve conflicts, he has relished the opportunity to address a large audience on a prominent stage. This year’s speech went ahead without the technical mishaps of last year, when an escalator halted as Trump and his wife, first lady Melania Trump, stepped onto it on their way to the hall. His teleprompter then failed for roughly the first 15 minutes of his 57-minute address, and he complained about the UN several times from the podium. UN officials later said a White House videographer had accidentally triggered the escalator’s emergency stop and that the teleprompter was operated by the White House. Trump nonetheless called the episodes “triple sabotage”, adding a claim that the sound in the hall had failed. In the days before this year’s general debate opened, the South China Morning Post saw UN staff working to rule out a repeat. On Monday, security officers were seen testing the escalator, the teleprompter and the earpieces that carry the audio feed from the podium microphone. In his address, the US president claimed the Pentagon had no shortage of munitions, called on Russia and Ukraine to “stop the killing” without mentioning that Moscow had invaded, and gave a shout-out to his wife. Trump also met with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after his speech and signed a deal allowing a larger US military presence on the world’s largest island, territory he has long coveted, that ‌could end a stand-off over the strategically located and mineral-rich territory. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday morning that the deal allows Washington “to put as many military bases as we need in order to defend everything”, adding that the US will screen potential investors in Greenland to block those linked to China or other adversaries that are not North Atlantic Treaty Organisation members. He also called for UN financial reform, slamming the UN’s human rights activities. “With all the genuine atrocities in the world, the UN’s top human rights officials spend their time criticising the United States for protecting our children from transgender mutilation and transgender insanity,” he said. “The craven hypocrites of [the] Human Rights Council have little to say about the persecution of Christians.” In his last major speech to the 193-member global body, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres opened the assembly with a plea for “a world built on interdependence”. “The fault lines in our world are widening,” he said, citing wars, climate change and artificial intelligence, among other crucial issues. The UN assembly comes as speculation heats up about who will replace Guterres when his second five-year term ends on December 31. No clear successor has emerged but the issue may well be on the agenda when Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping hold their summit on Wednesday in Washington. The US and China are the UN’s largest funders and most powerful Security Council members. Guterres on Tuesday also called for AI superpowers, widely viewed as the United States and China, to start a dialogue on the technology’s future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War. AI is expected to be a significant issue during the Trump-Xi sit-down following a pre-summit meeting on Monday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in New York. In an apparent dig at Trump, Guterres said superpowers must realise “that their power isn’t so super” and military power alone can’t secure peace.

title: Learning from Ukraine war, Chinese military doctors target injuries from drones
description: Head, face and neck injuries are becoming a big problem in armed conflicts dominated by uncrewed aerial vehicles.
content: China’s military medical experts are making progress in finding cures for common injuries seen in drone warfare, drawing on lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Chen Juxiang, a senior Chinese military doctor, told CCTV on Monday that cranio-maxillofacial injuries – damage to the hard and soft tissues of the head – had become a particularly big problem in conflicts dominated by drones. Chen, director of neurosurgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Naval Medical University, cited battlefield experience from Ukraine and the US-Iran conflict, saying that “in drone warfare, cranio-maxillofacial injuries account for more than 30 per cent of battlefield trauma”. Chen said his team had been preparing for the shift for years and had made progress in treatment protocols and haemostatic materials for these kinds of head injuries. “Our team began adjusting the direction of our military medical research as early as 2017 to make it more directly responsive to combat-readiness requirements,” said Chen, who has practised medicine for more than 30 years. Chen did not elaborate on the progress his team had made. The developments come as Beijing doubles down on building both offensive and defensive drone capabilities. President Xi Jinping has repeatedly stressed that China “must accelerate the development of uncrewed intelligent combat forces and countermeasure capabilities”. According to Fu Qianshao, a military analyst and former People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force officer, “China is continuously observing the use of drones on battlefields around the world and drawing lessons from them to build its own systems to adapt to drone warfare.” A 2024 study from the PLA General Hospital compared the proportions of different types of injuries among Ukrainian troops in conflicts before and after 2022, finding that traditional gunshot wounds were increasingly giving way to explosive injuries caused by kinetic weapons and drones. It often took more than six hours for casualties on the Russia-Ukraine battlefield to be moved from the site of injury to a casualty collection point, according to the PLA General Hospital study. Frontline medical units should therefore be able to carry out prolonged casualty care, damage-control resuscitation and repeated damage-control surgery, it argued. The researchers also proposed using drones to transport casualties, blood, oxygen and medicines, as well as to provide airway support. Another 2024 study from a PLA hospital said that injuries caused by drones were becoming more complex, including blast injuries, burns and chemical burns, with traumatic brain injuries and lung injuries among the most serious. This study proposed that, in preparation for future battlefields, China’s military medical system should consider using extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in the battlefield, or ECMO – an external system that provides respiratory and circulatory support – to treat critically wounded patients with severe lung injuries. The research comes as drones have become increasingly widespread in conflicts, with injuries different from those traditionally caused by bullets and artillery shells presenting new and serious challenges for military medical services around the world. The United States has reportedly also adjusted tactical casualty-care training for drone-dominated battlefield environments. US military news outlet The War Horse reported in April that an emergency medical course for 50 California National Guard soldiers had added a standard component on “modern warfare concepts, POV unmanned aircraft system explosives”. Its focus was the risk of aerial attack and the importance of high-quality burn care. In July, The War Horse cited Pentagon data covering about 400 wounded personnel in the US-Iran conflict between February and April, saying head injuries occurred more frequently than any other category amid extensive drone and missile attacks. Head injuries were recorded more than 170 times among the roughly 400 casualty incidents – a finding consistent with Chen’s assessment. The War Horse also reported that the large number of head injuries could result in traumatic brain injury (TBI) – damage to the brain that can affect thinking, movement and emotions – potentially making TBI a signature injury of the war. According to MedGlobal, an aid organisation providing medical support in Ukraine, drones detonating at close range can cause complex injuries to the upper body, neck and head. US media outlet Business Insider reported in January that medical workers in Ukraine were seeing relatively few gunshot wounds compared with blast and shrapnel injuries in what it described as a “war of remote destruction”.

title: China names new Tibet party chief as Communist Party reshuffles regional leadership
description: Hu Changsheng takes top Tibet post as regional transfers offer clues about broader political line-up ahead of national party congress.
content: Beijing has appointed a new party chief in Tibet as the Communist Party shuffles regional leaders ahead of its 21st national congress. Hu Changsheng, 62, will serve as the party secretary of Tibet autonomous region, leaving his post as party secretary of Gansu province to Wu Xiaojun, 60, currently the party chief of Qinghai province. Meanwhile, Luo Dongchuan, 60, Qinghai’s governor, will succeed Wu as party secretary of the province. The 21st party congress is expected to be held next year and will shape the leadership line-up for the next five years. Leadership changes at the provincial level ahead of the congress could offer clues about the party’s broader personnel arrangements and political line-up. Hu spent the early years of his career in Sichuan province before transferring to Qinghai in 2015. In 2017, he was reassigned to Fujian province, where he headed the provincial party organisation department. He was appointed party secretary of the city of Xiamen in 2019 and was promoted to deputy party secretary of Fujian in 2020 while continuing as Xiamen’s party secretary. President Xi Jinping spent more than a decade working in Fujian, where he served as party secretary of the provincial capital Fuzhou from 1990 to 1996, and as the province’s deputy party secretary from 1995 to 2002. Hu became governor of Heilongjiang province in 2021 and party chief of Gansu in 2022. Luo, who holds a doctorate in law, has extensive experience within the judicial system, having served in Beijing’s local courts and the Supreme People’s Court. In 2015, he was transferred to the Communist Party’s Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, where he assumed the role of director of the case trial office. After his tenure as head of the regional commission for discipline inspection in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region from 2017 to 2018, he returned to the Supreme People’s Court as vice-president, later assuming an additional role as president of its Intellectual Property Court. Luo also worked in Fujian as chief of the provincial political and legal affairs commission from 2020 to 2021, and as the provincial deputy party secretary from 2021 to 2024. Luo was transferred to Qinghai where he was appointed deputy party secretary in 2024 and as governor last year. Wu spent most of his career in Jiangxi province until being relocated to Qinghai in 2021. He was appointed governor of Qinghai in 2022 and party secretary in 2024.

title: Hong Kong workforce to shrink by 20,000 yearly as key sectors face shortages
description: Predicted 2028 shortfall will narrow to 130,000, but key sectors such as aviation, tech, healthcare and construction still face crunch.
content: Hong Kong’s workforce is forecast to shrink by around 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages remaining most acute among skilled technical workers. A government report on manpower projections on Tuesday found that although the labour shortfall would narrow to 130,000 by 2028, down by nearly a third from the original estimate of 180,000, the city would continue to face critical manpower challenges across key sectors. “Due to economic transformation, the adoption of AI [artificial intelligence] and various talent and labour importation measures, the predicted manpower shortfall in 2028 will narrow to 130,000, but most critical industries, especially innovation, aviation, construction, city operations and healthcare, still face a manpower crunch,” said Ho Kai-ming, the acting secretary for labour and welfare. “The adoption of AI is expected to accelerate and companies are likely to take a more cautious approach when hiring for entry-level positions. We believe demand for these roles will ease and some clerical jobs will undergo restructuring. Overall, fresh graduates and middle-aged clerical staff are expected to be most impacted.” The report projected that Hong Kong’s workforce would drop from 3.47 million in 2025 to 3.4 million in 2028 – a decline of roughly 20,000 a year – even after accounting for foreign labour and imported talent. The number of workers aged between 25 and 34 was expected to decline significantly by 64,000 over the three-year period. Without any labour and talent importation measures, the workforce would further shrink to 3.21 million as the population ages while the manpower shortfall would widen from 130,000 to 300,000. Roy Chan Kwok-fai, head of the research unit at the Labour and Welfare Bureau, said the government was aware of a mismatch between job requirements and jobseekers’ expectations, leaving vacancies unfilled even as unemployment remained elevated. Hong Kong’s latest unemployment rate rose slightly to 3.8 per cent, with more than 150,000 people out of work. “The mismatch has worsened compared with a few years ago, with 30,000 to 40,000 unemployed people in this situation,” Chan said. “They could hardly find a new job without undergoing retraining or changing their attitude.” He said the proportion of people who had been unemployed for six months or more had risen from 20 per cent before the Covid-19 pandemic to 30 per cent this year. Some of those affected were veteran chefs who had lost their jobs amid a wave of Chinese restaurant closures, Chan said. However, they could not easily switch to working in Japanese or Korean restaurants. However, he dismissed concerns that imported workers were taking local jobs, pointing to wage growth in the catering and retail sectors in recent years. “If there were direct competition driving out locals, salaries would be falling,” he argued. The report projected a shortage of 48,000 to 53,000 skilled technical workers and 36,000 to 41,000 manual labourers – together accounting for roughly 40 per cent of the total shortfall. Chan said the shortage was partly driven by the workforce’s rising education levels and the rapid ageing of workers in those sectors. The median age of manual labourers had risen to 54, while that of skilled technical workers had reached 50. The next largest gaps would be among managers, supervisors and professionals – such as in technology and finance – as well as service and sales workers, with a shortage of 33,000 to 38,000 for the former, and 28,000 to 33,000 for the latter. In contrast, clerical support workers would face a surplus of 25,000 to 30,000 due to the increasing adoption of AI. Chan said that administrative staff accounted for roughly 20 to 30 per cent of the workforce in import and export trade and finance. While these roles were expected to undergo restructuring rather than disappear overnight, he acknowledged it remained difficult to quantify how many jobs would ultimately be displaced by AI. Lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, who is also the chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, said that more than 180,000 labourers and talent came to work in Hong Kong over the past few years, well above the previous projection of 130,000, raising concerns that current policies had failed to fill the vacancies precisely while undercutting opportunities for local residents. He called on the authorities to review the talent list regularly to ensure that the city attracted workers with the skills it needed, pointing out that Hong Kong had attracted virtually no applicants in niche areas such as Islamic finance or green shipping. Lam also called for stronger safeguards for local workers, such as tightening the local-to-foreign hiring ratio to 3:1 and requiring businesses to prioritise local graduates over non-local candidates. The Hong Kong Institute of Human Resource Management attributed the narrowing manpower gap to talent admission schemes, workplace AI adoption and automation, and a more cautious hiring approach among employers. “While we have met the targets of the talent schemes, the government should continue to track the retention of those talents,” it said. “If those talents leave within one or two years, existing models will underestimate the future risk of a labour deficit.”

title: China’s Hygon moves beyond data centres with embedded processors for robotics, edge AI
description: Shanghai-listed firm says new chips will help bring AI from cloud servers to factory floors and industrial machines.
content: Chinese chipmaker Hygon Information Technology on Tuesday launched a suite of central processing units (CPUs) for robotics and industrial edge devices, expanding beyond cloud computing and into the fast-growing market for physical artificial intelligence. The firm unveiled its Hygon 1000 series processors, designed to be embedded into physical devices in industrial automation systems such as robotics and factory controllers, enabling computing and graphics processing to be handled locally. Built on Hygon’s x86-compatible C86 architecture, the four-core, eight-thread CPU supports both DDR4 and DDR5 memory. The company said the chips, priced between US$40 and US$80, were its first CPUs with integrated graphics capabilities. The Hygon 1000 series features the firm’s smallest chips to date, with a package size nearly half that of the 3450M processor introduced last year for laptops. AI will not only run in data centres, but will increasingly operate in the physical world, from factories and power stations to railway transport and medical devices Sha Chaoqun, Hygon The launch of Hygon’s first embedded edge-computing chips underscores its push beyond data centres and into machines that interact directly with their physical environments. “We are witnessing a clear trend of computing power moving from cloud-based systems to edge and device-based computing,” said Sha Chaoqun, CEO of Hygon, at the launch event in Shenzhen on Tuesday. “AI will not only run in data centres, but will increasingly operate in the physical world, from factories and power stations to railway transport and medical devices.” Unlike data centre processors that prioritise raw computing power, chips used in robotics and edge applications must meet strict requirements for real-time processing, low power consumption and security in unpredictable operating environments. “The edge AI market is in the midst of an explosive growth,” said Huang Wei, general manager of Hygon’s Innovative Product Department, at a media briefing on Tuesday. “The Hygon 1000 series targets the industrial-control market with embedded processors and addresses the growing integration of AI into industrial robotics and smart manufacturing.” The new chips expand Hygon’s current portfolio of CPUs and deep computing units, a type of accelerator card designed specifically for AI workloads. Hygon planned to release the next generation of the 1000 series in 2027, with computing performance doubling, according to Huang. The Shanghai-listed chipmaker is playing an increasingly critical role in Beijing’s broader drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency amid US restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips. Its current CPU product lines include the 7000 series for high-performance data centres, the 5000 series for mid-tier industry cloud and edge-computing customers, and the cost-focused 3000 series. Hygon is one of China’s leading developers of x86-compatible CPUs. Variations of the x86 architecture, originally developed by US semiconductor giant Intel, remain the foundation of most servers, desktop computers and laptops. The company’s first-half revenue rose 66.5 per cent to 9.1 billion yuan (US$1.4 billion) year on year, driven by strong demand for high-end domestic chips.

title: Is this the reel life? Sports events confront whole new world of social media, influencers
description: While some event organisers ban or limit the presence of mobile phones, many encourage their constructive use.
content: Madonna, Bob Dylan and Jack White have banned phones from their concerts. An exasperated Adele once asked an audience member: “Can you stop filming me? … You can enjoy it in real life rather than through your camera.” In the sporting sphere, however, those bastions of decorum at Augusta National Golf Club are alone in waging war on mobile devices, employing a strict cell phone ban for patrons attending the US Masters. Mark Calcavecchia, the 1989 Open Championship winner and veteran of 18 Masters, was hoofed off the premises this year after flouting the rule. Contrast that staunch technophobia with the routine sight of fans hungrily filming and photographing in football stadiums and rugby grounds, courtside, poolside and ringside, on fairways and in arenas. “People nowadays are constantly switching their attention,” Professor Chen Zhansheng, head of the department of psychology at the University of Hong Kong, said. “Also, because of social media, they constantly seek connections and approval. The need to belong is satisfied very differently from in the past: it comes from constantly uploading [content] to share. “It’s the difference between enjoying the moment and disassociating yourself from what’s happening. This creates problems, but it’s also part of the new way of living.” Rob James, senior vice-president of golf events for IMG, said this method of live sport consumption was “more noticeable now than 10 or 20 years ago”. Boasting nearly 30 years’ industry experience, including 4½ years as Manchester United’s Asia marketing head, he cautioned against event organisers following Augusta’s stringent lead. “Handheld devices are now so integral to a consumer’s everyday life that to do so would be seen as detrimental for the majority,” James said. After runners in the 2013 Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon caused pandemonium by stopping to capture images of themselves, race officials considered prohibiting phones on the course. They ultimately relented and with the genie now out of the bottle, promoters and administrators are increasingly keen to leverage punters’ attachments to their screens. James said that official event-week apps for both this year’s Open Championship and AIG Women’s British Open “showed double-digit growth”, alongside material increases in social media impressions, social engagements, social media followers and live-stream views. “Viewing short clips, checking the leaderboard or map on the event app, or listening to radio commentary have become big parts of the major-event experience,” he added. Marketers have long since had to get creative to cater for changing habits. The primary reason for the 2003 introduction of T20 cricket was to attract the time poor. It would become a juggernaut, as would social media, as Twitter, Instagram and TikTok infiltrated, then consumed people’s lives following their respective launches in 2006, 2010 and 2016. “As social psychologists, we feel the way people live their lives is rapidly changing,” Chen said. “But technology is changing so quickly, we’ve not kept up with what these changes mean for us. “We always say human beings are shaped by our environment and our language, but now, more than ever, with technology, smartphones and social media, there are new patterns. It’s more universal than sport and we probably need to observe our own decision patterns: the changes we do and don’t like.” The intrusive content capturing by so-called influencers irked both rank-and-file supporters and players at the recent US Open tennis tournament. One especially ignorant group staged a photo shoot during Naomi Osaka’s first-round victory over Anastasia Zakharova. “It’s common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette,” Osaka said. Among the stream of online comments about the roughly 100 influencers and content creators who were granted accreditation for the Flushing Meadows fortnight, one read: “I think the US Open is starting to fly too close to the sun with its anti-fan practices”. On a recent video call to discuss the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships, the Olympic 100m champion, Noah Lyles, said that “influencers are needed” but that “there’s a time and a place for them”. “It’s important to get the content and let people know an event is happening, and it can be fun and entertaining, but there can be a selected space for it,” he added. James said that a typical marketing blueprint today would “include the engagement of influencers to create additional content, promote an event and enhance the live experience for the public”. “With planning and care, this can be really effective, but if it’s not managed and there are no clear guidelines, the content might not be what the organisers were expecting,” James said, adding that the increasing presence of influencers “is a trend that will continue”. In the main, James welcomes paying fans posting their videos on social media because “viral clips and human-interest stories often reach a far wider and more diverse audience than that of a traditional broadcast”. “Partner activations and exhibition areas [on site] actively encourage it,” he said. Equally, James said that in his experience it was only “the novice eventgoers” who spent most of their day out watching through a screen. “It’s probably the unique factor of seeing a sportsperson so close in real life,” he said. “If it’s perceived as a once-in-a-lifetime experience for someone, they will try to film or catch a selfie. “Seasoned sports fans or event goers know when to view without a device, or when they can do both without ruining the experience.” Chen would advocate, where feasible, an approach similar to the one applied at the opera, where audiences are allowed short windows between acts to snap away. He said that in instances where people “are having a difficult time with others in their daily lives, then online networking, sharing and commenting can be beneficial”. “The validation can be quite reassuring,” Chen added. Nonetheless, those who unfailingly cannot resist shooting their team’s goal celebration, recording match point or filming the winning putt, rather than drinking in those moments, expose themselves to brain fog, according to Chen. “We have limited capacity,” he said. “Constantly seeking validation and not living in the moment can deplete your resources, then you tire easily and lose focus. Your moods swing because your resources are allocated among different focuses. “In the past, we encouraged multitasking, but I’m not sure it’s a good thing.” Before Galatasaray played Manchester United in a 2023 Champions League match, the Turkish club’s ultras told fellow supporters that phones and social media use were banned. “[Ninety] minutes of aggressive support. Go to war with the team,” read the missive. James, however, said that large numbers juggling watching what’s in front of them with using their phones “doesn’t negatively impact the atmosphere”. He said that audiences in smaller venues sitting close to courts or tables “are not viewing through screens”, while “larger events with bigger venues and crowds tend to have more distractions and things to watch and to film”. James cited the example of last month’s UTMB Mont-Blanc World Series Finals in Chamonix having “probably the best atmosphere in its 20-year history”. “The race start and the finish chute were packed with supporters, more people than ever filming the winners, but the noise was electric,” he said. “The action was also live streamed, so a spectator 30km away from the lead action could get updates on their handheld while waiting for other runners.” Like it or not, the Masters is destined to continue fighting a lone battle against mobile phones in sporting amphitheatres. “People constantly feel that if something exciting happens, they want to tell their friends right away,” Chen said. “It’s about the immediate satisfaction. You want to get instant feedback, and it’s hard to regulate.”

title: Committee to investigate Hong Kong district councillor’s sex crime conviction
description: Yuen Long councillor Sei Chun-hing faces sentencing after conviction for sex with 13-year-old girl as committee considers disciplinary sanctions.
content: Hong Kong authorities have appointed a five-member supervisory committee to investigate the conviction of a district councillor for having sex with a 13-year-old girl 15 years ago. Yuen Long district councillor Sei Chun-hing, 39, is the first elected officeholder to face possible imprisonment for a criminal offence since Beijing’s 2021 electoral overhaul, which restricted candidates to those vetted as “patriots”. The offence is punishable by up to five years in jail.. Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen said in a statement on Tuesday that the government placed strong emphasis on the conduct and integrity of district councillors. She said the performance monitoring guidelines for councillors expressly required them to conduct themselves at all times and in every respect in a manner in line with public expectations and commensurate with the reputation of the council and its members. Under the District Councils Ordinance, a member is disqualified if sentenced to more than three months’ imprisonment for an offence. Additionally, government-mandated performance monitoring guidelines stipulate that an officeholder can face sanctions for gross misconduct or a criminal offence carrying a custodial sentence, even if the term is not severe enough to warrant disqualification. The five-member supervisory committee comprises one non-district councillor and four council members from districts other than Yuen Long. “The supervisory committee will handle the investigation in a robust, fair, just, impartial, independent and objective manner in accordance with the established mechanism,” Mak said. The District Court accepted the complainant’s testimony earlier this month that Sei had committed sexual acts on her on March 14, 2011. The court heard that he told her he expected the then secondary school pupil to reciprocate a month after he gave her a handcrafted Valentine’s Day gift. Sei, a personal assistant to former cultural and sports lawmaker Ma Fung-kwok, was convicted of unlawful sex with a girl under 16. He was acquitted of a separate indecent assault charge relating to a 2008 incident on technical grounds. According to the government’s statement, the committee members are district councillors Lam Chui-ling, Deannie Yew Yat-wa, Lee Ching-har and Michael Liu Tsz-chung. The non-district councillor is Bunny Chan Chung-bun. “The supervisory committee will establish whether the facts on which the allegation was based are true; give its opinion on whether the established facts constitute grounds for imposing sanction under the ordinance; and, if there is ground for imposing sanction, give its opinion on the appropriate sanction to be imposed on the [district council] member concerned,” the government said. The committee will submit a report to the bureau for consideration. The Home Affairs Department said in a reply to the South China Morning Post that the Yuen Long district council chairman had noted that Sei’s office had ceased operating since Monday. Authorities stated that they had asked other district councillors from Yuen Long to assist in following up on the needs of residents. The court will hear mitigation arguments on October 27 before passing sentence.

title: Why China’s frontier AI pioneers are expected to miss this week’s Xi-Trump summit
description: Beijing has not officially announced details of the delegation, but the leaders of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI are absent from the reported list.
content: As President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to the United States to meet his American counterpart Donald Trump, attention is turning to the group of business leaders who could join him. The South China Morning Post previously reported that executives from electric vehicle maker BYD, smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi and battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited were likely to accompany Xi on the trip – though Beijing has yet to officially confirm the delegation. What has raised eyebrows, however, is the omission of leaders from China’s frontier AI companies – such as DeepSeek’s Liang Wenfeng and Moonshot AI’s Yang Zhilin – from all reported versions of the delegation. While it remains unclear who will ultimately accompany Xi, observers offered several possible explanations. These largely centre on protecting leading AI talent amid geopolitical tensions and the different levels of urgency with which Beijing and Washington approach talks on the technology. “It is to protect them, because their presence at this stage could put them in a difficult position,” said Chen Zhiwu, chair professor of finance at the University of Hong Kong. Another think tank analyst, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, echoed the sentiment that leading researchers and entrepreneurs in cutting-edge technologies like AI were particularly vulnerable in the current geopolitical climate. “Travelling overseas could expose them to unforeseen risks, so the absence could be a form of protection,” he said. By contrast, US AI leaders are expected to have a visible presence, with OpenAI President Greg Brockman and CEO Sam Altman reportedly planning to attend a White House state dinner for Xi. Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter, that DeepSeek would brief the United Nations Security Council on AI safety risks this week, though company founder Liang did not plan to attend. Other Chinese AI firms including Moonshot AI have also been invited to make statements, according to the report. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis, linked the potential absence of Chinese AI players to differences in their respective domestic environments. Washington, she noted, was facing growing domestic opposition and political pressure over the rapid development of the technology. “China knows the US needs a break – but not China, so Xi does not want to bring its AI team,” she said. “It is quite, quite clear to me.” In recent weeks, prominent Western tech leaders – including OpenAI’s Altman, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and xAI founder Elon Musk – have publicly called for “pacing” the development of frontier AI, citing concerns that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them. Beyond the domestic and geopolitical sensitivities surrounding artificial intelligence, the two delegations could also reflect the priorities agreed to by Beijing and Washington. Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting, explained that high-level delegations were subject to bilateral negotiations and mutual agreement. “Beijing puts forward the initial list, and I’d expect it to favour companies whose business matters to the bilateral agenda or that are directly affected by restrictions, much like the US executives who travelled with Trump to China in May,” he said. In May, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Tesla’s Elon Musk, Apple’s Tim Cook, BlackRock’s Larry Fink and Boeing’s Kelly Ortberg were among the business leaders joining Trump on his state visit. “But keep in mind that there is still no officially confirmed list of Chinese CEOs,” Montufar-Helu said.

title: Trump, Denmark and Greenland sign deal to resolve Arctic stand-off
description: Trilateral accord permits US ‘Golden Dome’ missile shield and new bases while backing island self-determination.
content: US President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed an agreement on Tuesday that permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a stand-off over the strategically located and mineral-rich island. The agreement, signed during Trump’s visit to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Trump’s demand that the US annex Greenland as a US territory to head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China. But the deal does codify a greater ‌US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover. A text of the deal released after the event said the US can establish a “Golden Dome” defence system in Greenland as a shield against ballistic missile threats. The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via the Arctic island, which is the location of the northernmost US military base.
